units.tr: To the illustrious and most powerful lords, the most excellent and most distinguished Orders of the United Provinces of Belgium, and likewise to the most noble, most eminent and most learned men, their most faithful councillors, lords whom I honour with the greatest respect: Paulus G.F.P.N. units.la: A quo tempore Studijs, quæ momenti majoris seriaque, tractandis animum adplicare coepi, VIRI MAGNI, præter Iurisprudentiam, quæ præcipue in oculis & mente semper fuit, incredibile, quantum mihi, liberum & effrenem amanti cursum, placuerit Πολυμάθεια quædam, & varia Rerum Divinarum Humanarumque, si non plena solidaque, certe aliqua, quæque Instituto primario juvando atque exornando satis effet, cognitio. Aevum namque hoc nostrum, quod sane doctum, delicatum, subactique judicij, pluris eos meritissimo censere animadvertebam; qui, quum primas inter Theologos, Iurisconsultos, Medicos obtinerent, latissimos reliquarum disciplinarum campos ingressi, nonnullam etiam rerum aliarum notitiam indefesso labore sibi comparant; de ijs, quae nunc haec, nunc illa in amplissimis Procerum Reip. litterariae Comitiis movebantur, disserere ausi. Sic animatus, Cosmographiae quoque, Mundique cum Aetherei, tum Elementarii Secreta rimari sum adgressus; eam praecipue ob causam, quod post abitum V. CL. Iusti Lipsii in celeberrimam hanc Academiam vocatus, conatum hunc meum magno mihi adjumento futurum aliquando viderem. Quum infinita collegissem, suetisque Adversariis, qui meus est mos, adscripsissem; visum quibusdam, nescio quo obcaecatis de mea industria errore, hortari me, ut quae potiora huius generis ducerem, publici facerem usus. Renitens aliquamdiu, conscriusque nihil ame grande praestari posse, tandem persuaderi me passus, quod petebar, sum auspicatus; iaetoque bono & artificioso, ut mihi quidem videbatur, fundamento ædificium, animo diu conceptum, exstruere cœpi. In eo dum sedulus essem, demandatam à Vobis suscepi Historiæ Bellicorum Tumultuum, quibus hodieque concutitur adfligiturque miserum in modum BELGICA, sermone Latino describendæ Provinciam. Quum totum fere Munus illud requireret hominem; segnius procedebant, quæ ab eo videbantur aliena; &, cum alijs, hoc Opus; quod nihilominus, ne quid paterentur, qui me ad scribendum suis precibus sæpius invitarant, ex abrupto filo detrimenti, erat absolvendum. Suffuratus igitur subinde nonnihil temporis, quod delato Historiographi titulo fuerat consecrandum, quodque cum publicæ Functioni, tum vestris peculiariter debebatur mandatis, hucusque tandē quidquid est, perduxi. Vlterius perrexissem, sequentiaque, quæ apud me jam adfecta, dedissem: sed quum ad meam postulationem ante pauculos dies decreveritis, ut Partes Historiæ Belgicæ, quibus ante biennium Coronidem impositi, typis vulgarentur, inq. manus emitterentur eorum, qui Res nostras, penitius fideliusque ex publicis Actis repræsentatas, avere cognoscere; consultum hic subsistere putavi. Agnoscent interim hic, scio, fumentque, spero, ex delineatis nobilissimis, quas ossero, Regionibus Exempla Methodosque alij, qui reliquas minus operosas & intricatas publicandi flagrabunt desiderio. Vobis, VIRI MAGNI, hoc mearum de Cosmographicis Commentationum Volume figo, dico, sacro; Vobis, quibus obstrictus jam illud in luminis auras produxi; Vobis, qui, ut vester Merula æterniora jam moliatur & promat, amotis, quæ remorabantur, obstaculis, volentes libentesque permittitis; Uobis, qui vestra fama Regiones, quas hic depingo, cum incredibili Mortalium omnium stupore impletis. DEVS OPTIMVS MAXIMVS Consilia vestra magis magis prosperet; suamq; ijs gratiam, quod, uti evidentissima docent indicia, hactenus fecit, adfundere pergat. Valete VIRI MAGNI. Lugduni Batavorum, 8. Eidus Iulij cioioc v.
units.tr: From the time I began to apply myself to studies of greater weight and seriousness, distinguished men, I have found it incredibly pleasing, besides jurisprudence, which has always been foremost in my eyes and mind, to pursue a certain polymathy: a varied knowledge of divine and human things. Since I love a free and unbridled course, I have sought this knowledge, if not full and solid, at least some, enough to help and adorn my main undertaking. For I observed that this age of ours, which is surely learned, refined and of discerning judgement, rightly values most those who, while holding the first place among theologians, jurists and physicians, have entered the wide fields of the other disciplines and by tireless labour have acquired some acquaintance with other subjects too, and have dared to speak on those matters which were now this, now that, being debated in the most distinguished assemblies of the Republic of Letters. Inspired thus, I also set about exploring the secrets of cosmography and of the world, both the heavenly and the elemental. I did so chiefly because, after the departure of the most distinguished Justus Lipsius, I had been called to this most famous academy, and I saw that this undertaking of mine would one day be of great help to me. When I had gathered an infinite store of material and noted it down in my commonplace books, as is my habit, some men, blinded by I know not what error about my diligence, thought fit to urge me to make public use of those things which I considered the more important of this kind. Resisting for some time and insisting that nothing great could be achieved by me, I at last allowed myself to be persuaded to what was asked, and, having laid what seemed to me a good and skilful foundation, I began to build the edifice I had long conceived in my mind. While I was diligently engaged in this, I took on the task you had entrusted to me: to describe in Latin the history of the warlike tumults by which Belgium is still shaken and miserably afflicted today. Since that whole office almost demanded a man, those things which seemed foreign to it progressed more slowly; and, together with others, this work had to be completed, lest those who had often invited me to write by their entreaties suffer any loss from the abrupt break in the thread. Therefore, stealing from time to time some of the time which had been set aside for the title of Historiographer conferred on me, and which was owed both to my public office and especially to your commands, I have so far brought to completion whatever it is. I would have gone further and published the sequel, which I had already prepared; but since, at my request, you decided a few days ago that the parts of the History of Belgium, which I had crowned two years ago, should be printed and put into the hands of those who long to know our affairs more fully and faithfully, as they are represented in the public records, I thought it wise to stop here. Meanwhile, I know, others here will recognise and take up, I hope, from the noble regions I offer, examples and methods, and those who burn with desire to publish the remaining, less laborious and intricate, subjects will do so. To you, illustrious men, I dedicate and consecrate this volume of my cosmographical commentaries: to you, to whom I am already bound, I have brought it forth into the light; to you, who, so that your Merula may now undertake and bring forth more lasting works, have willingly and gladly removed the obstacles that hindered him; to you, who by your fame fill the regions I here depict with the incredible wonder of all mortals. May the most good and greatest God prosper your counsels more and more, and continue to pour out his grace upon them, as the most evident signs show he has done hitherto. Farewell, illustrious men. Leiden, the eighth day before the Ides of July, 1634.

units.la: CTENNIVM jam est, amicissime Lector, quum qui Praxin meam anno XCII excuderat, suis me litteris interpellaret, rogaretque, ut Chartarum Thesaurum, quem Idiomate nostro concinnatum paullo post vulgarat, in Latinum verterem sermonē. Erat ille, cui non facile quid, quod in mea quidem erat potestate, denegandū putabam. Thesaurum mihi transmissum lego, scribendi modū examino, Chartas perlustro. Paucis dicā: Πολλὰ μὲν ἐῶ λἀ, πολλὰ δ' ἡ λυγρά. Non parum ego hic ibi desiderabam. Ne omnia: Chartis plerisque, praterquam quod essent nimis exigua, & non sat fide notationis, Gradus videbam deesse Longitudinis & Latitudinis; quibus deficientibus, ego haec talia nullius censere consueram momenti. Rescribens igitur, laboris potius, quod flagitabat, esse respondi, quam ingenij; & ab meis studijs esse prorsus alienum, foetus novorum hominum jure Latinitatis donare. Quum instaret, eo tandem me scriptus litteris deduxit, ut Chartas pro meo arbitrio emendatas, suisque Gradibus exornatas, petitus ex propria officina coloribus declararem. Quod non gravatim feci. Causas habuit suas (quum jam mecum esset conventum) V.CL. Petrus Bertius suscipienda, quam renueram, versionis: quam non infeliciter, quibusdam adjectis, perfectam in vulgus edidit. Opus igitur magnis viribus adgressus, quum in suas distribuissem partes, illud mihi, solita insistens Methodo; Fundamentum posui, quod in fine locatum Prima Partis. Singulas rursum in minora Segmenta vocavi; quemadmodum qua sequuntur, quaque tribus Prima, quam dixi, Partis libris, singulisque Secunda subscripta sunt Synopses, plene planeque docent. Quum aliquantum esset progressus, demandata mihi est ab Illustrissimis Foederatarum Regionum Ordinibus Provincia scribenda Latina Lingua Historia Belgica. Sic nonnihil morarum injectum est Orbis Delineationi. Ne vero Impressori, omisso Instituto, detrimenti quid crearetur; licet alio tractus, pergebam nihilo-minus: sed, quod ingenue fateor, tardo gradu. Excusis variorum scriniis, multa mihi Veterum Novorumque Monimenta erant legenda: multa in futurum usum hinc inde enotanda: cum multis difficultatibus depugnandum. Nam incredibile est, quantum mihi laboris obortum in committendis variorum, eorumque in hoc studio sadioque aetate nostra Principum, delineationibus. Unus hoc, alius illud de Loco, qui pro manibus erat discutiendus, tradebat: Alius unum eumdemque locum hic: alius, immenso abiens intervallo, illic ponebat: hunc quidam cis, nonnullus trans flumen statuebat; erant &, qui ne vastorum quidem Montium, latarumque Vallium habebant rationem. Stupebam, ut specialius quid dicam, ingens inter VV. CLL. Abrahamum Ortelium & Gerardum Mercatorem (alios minorum gentium insuperhabeo) in Bruttijs, Magna Gracia, Calabrisque designandis, dissidium. Consulebam identidem Strabonem, Plinium, Pomponium Melam, Stephanum, alios; sed in illis tantas sapenumero tenebras, tamque intricatas deprehendebam ambages; ut, perspectis ijs, incertior multo, quam fueram, plerumque discederem. Nam quis ignorat potiora diuturnitate temporis mutata; Regionesque, Urbes, Opida, Pagos, Flumina, Montes, Valles, & quidquid, praeter hac, talium, alias olim, quam quibus jamnunc nota, appellationes habuisse? Nihil certius, nihil exploratius. Ptolemaum frequenter adibam; sed fastidium movebant non pauca. Animadvertebam plurima Magno Auctori scripta esse ab auditu, & ex aliorum, qui sape fallunt, quorumque, quum qua visa narrant, verba nonnumquam non bene capiuntur, fide: eamque ob causam ipsius Geographica, ex alieno concinnata relatu, maleque & inemendate scripta, innumeris deformata esse erroribus; multa item, quae aliis nominatissima, negligenter in ijs omissa; multa sequiorem nacta stationem, & extra verum locata situm; multa dubiam adepta nomenclaturam; infinita non suis tributa Populis vel Regionibus; plurima denique cum ab aliys, tum ab seipso & alibi-dicta dissentientia. Probetur hoc, quis petit? Tadium Lectorem necaret. Vnam stalia (qua prater patriam vix alia ipsi, transmisso Magno Mari, vicinior) Regionem inspice Picenum: ibi duorum, qui nobilissimi, Fluviorum, Metauri & Isauri nullam facit mentionem: Idem in Gallia Cis-Padana Padi Fluminis Caput ad Larium describit Lacum: quod vere, sensu docente, meisque oculis id testantibus, in Vesulo Monte: Idem in Tabulis Ansanum, Samnitium Opidum, cis Sarum in Frentanis collocare videtur: in pictura vero trans eumdem Amnem in Pelignis. Tanto scilicet Ptolemaus certiora suis elucubrationibus expressit, nobisque reliquit, quanto cuiusque rei meliores habuit testes: tanto autem incertiora, quanto peiores: ideoque subinde vel ex alijs, cum antiquioribus, tum recentioribus: vel ex membranis castigandus, supplendus, transformandus: Nec suis carebat mendis Antonini, vel cuiuscumque censendum, Itinerarium: in quo emaculando suoque nitori restituendo egregiam posuerunt operam cum alij, tum vel maxime Abrahamus Ortelius, Vir monstris ex terrarum Orbe emoliendis planè natus, & Hieronymus Surita, Casar-Augustanus, quo in hoc argumento Hispania numquam habuit feliciorem. Hinc factum, quod majore cum fructu illud usurparim: commissum cum amplissima Tabula Itineraria, qua duētu Joannis Molleri, diligentissimi Typographi, auspiciys autem Viri Nobilíssimi, Marci Velseri, II-Viri Reip. Augustana, ex illustri Peutingerorum Bibliotheca in lucem prodijt. Plus habet illa in recessu, quam frons pallicetur. Licet infinita ibi sint depravata & turbationis ordinis, tamen comparata cum Antoninianis (quibus & hinc medicina non semel per me petita) nullo negocio possunt corrigi, & ad sua revocari castra: quod non infeliciter à me factum in Gallia Italiaque, res ipsa docebit. Procurrit hac Tabula ab Occidentali Oceano per Continentis totius longitudinem ad Orientalem usque: singula notans loca: nec non locorum, industria stupenda, distantias & intervalla. Totum complectitur, quantus quantus est, Antoninum; alterumque tantum, & amplius, adponit; si Civitates, Urbes, Opida, Pagi, Fluvij, aliaque talia diligenter examinentur: digna certe, quae sedulis Doctorum, non magis fellulorum, manibus terantur. Quo pacto autem in minores partes posset dividi, & libri instar edi; monstrabo fortean in singulari opere. Nam ad eius illustrationem animavit me aliquoties suis litteris optimus Velserus, & pervicisset jam, nisi ad graviora fuissem avocatus. Tantum igitur difficultatum, scopulorum, Syrtium, de quibus jam verba feci, tantopere meum animum consternavit; ut, quod initio proposueram, mutare fuerim coactus.
units.tr: It is now a decade, most friendly reader, since the man who had printed my Praxis in the year 1592 wrote to me and asked me to turn into Latin the Thesaurus of Maps, which he had recently published in our own language. I thought it hard to refuse someone who asked for something that was within my power. I read the copy sent to me, examined the style of writing, and went through the maps. To put it briefly: "Many things I pass over, and many are grievous" [Πολλὰ μὲν ἐῶ, πολλὰ δ' ἡ λυγρά]. I found much to miss here and there. Most of all, the maps were too small and not reliable enough in their lettering, and I saw that they lacked the degrees of longitude and latitude. Without these, I had always thought such things were of no value. In reply, I said that the task he asked for was a matter of labour rather than of talent, and that it was entirely foreign to my studies to give Latin citizenship to the offspring of new men. He kept pressing, and at last his letters brought me to the point where I agreed to revise the maps as I saw fit, to adorn them with their degrees, and to colour them in my own workshop at his request. I did this without reluctance. The most distinguished Petrus Bertius, who had already come to an agreement with me, had his own reasons for taking up the translation I had refused. He carried it out not unsuccessfully, with some additions, and published it for the public. Having then undertaken this great work, I divided it into its parts, and, following my usual method, I laid down a foundation, which is placed at the end of the First Part. I again divided each part into smaller sections. The three books of the First Part, which I mentioned, and the Synopses subscribed to each of them in the Second Part, as well as what follows, explain this fully and clearly. When I had made some progress, the Illustrious Orders of the United Provinces entrusted me with the task of writing the Belgian History in Latin. So some delay was thrown into the delineation of the globe. Lest the printer suffer any loss from the abandoned plan, I continued the work on the other project, though I went more slowly, as I frankly admit. After the archives of various men had been searched, I had to read many ancient and recent documents, and to note down much here and there for future use, and I had to struggle with many difficulties. For it is incredible how much labour arose for me in comparing the delineations of various men, in our age the princes of this study and of diligence. One gave this account of a place which I had before me to examine, another gave that. Another placed the same place here, another, at a vast distance, placed it there. Some located it on this side of the river, others on the far side. There were even some who took no account of huge mountains or broad valleys. I was astonished, to speak of one case more particularly, at the huge disagreement between the most distinguished men Abraham Ortelius and Gerard Mercator (I pass over others of lesser rank) in marking out the Bruttii, Magna Graecia and the Calabrians. Again and again I consulted Strabo, Pliny, Pomponius Mela, Stephanus and others. But in them I often found such great darkness and such tangled ambiguities that, once I had examined them, I usually left far more uncertain than I had been. For who does not know that the greater names have been changed over the course of time, and that regions, cities, towns, villages, rivers, mountains, valleys, and whatever else of this kind had other names in the past than those by which they are now known? Nothing is more certain, nothing more evident. I often went to Ptolemy, but many things caused me distaste. I noticed that most of what the great author wrote was taken from hearsay and from the report of others, who often make mistakes, and whose words, when they relate what they have seen, are sometimes not understood properly. For this reason his geography, put together from the accounts of others and written badly and carelessly, is disfigured by countless errors. Many famous places are negligently omitted from it, many are placed in a worse position and out of their true site, many have received a doubtful name, and countless things are assigned to peoples or regions that are not theirs. Finally, there are very many things in which he disagrees both with others and with himself elsewhere. Who would ask that this be proved? It would weary the reader to death. Take one example, Picenum, the region nearest to my own homeland (and, once one has crossed the great sea, almost the closest of all to me). There he makes no mention of the two most famous rivers, the Metaurus and the Isaurus. In Cisalpine Gaul he describes the source of the river Po as being at Lake Larius, whereas it is truly, as the evidence shows and as my own eyes testify, on Mount Vesulus. In the Tables he seems to place Ansanum, a town of the Samnites, on this side of the Sarus, among the Frentani, but in the picture he places it across the same river, among the Peligni. Ptolemy clearly expressed in his writings things more certain than others, and left them to us, in proportion as he had better witnesses for each matter. But he expressed things less certain in proportion as his witnesses were worse. Therefore he must be corrected, supplemented and reshaped from time to time, either from others, both older and more recent, or from manuscripts. Nor was the Itinerary of Antoninus, or whoever is thought to be its author, free from its faults. In correcting it and restoring its polish, many men labored with distinction, and above all Abraham Ortelius, a man born altogether to clear the monsters out of the globe, and Hieronymus Surita of Caesaraugusta, in whose work on this subject Spain never had a more fortunate champion. Hence I used the Itinerary with greater profit, comparing it with the very ample Table of Roads, which came to light through the work of Johannes Moller, a most diligent printer, and under the auspices of Marcus Welser, a most noble duumvir of the Augsburg republic, from the illustrious library of the Peutingers. That Table has more in it than appears at first sight. Although infinite errors and disorders are found there, nevertheless, when compared with the Antonine material (from which I have more than once sought remedy here as well), they can easily be corrected and restored to their proper places. What I have done with it in Gaul and Italy, not without success, the thing itself will show. This Table runs from the Western Ocean through the whole length of the continent to the Eastern. It notes each place singly, and also the distances and intervals between places, computed with astonishing care. It covers the whole of Antoninus, however large it is, and adds as much again, and more, if cities, towns, villages, hamlets, rivers and other such things are carefully examined. These are certainly worth being handled by the diligent hands of scholars, and not less by the hands of mere lovers of learning. In what way it could be divided into smaller parts and published as a book, I will perhaps show in a separate work. For the most excellent Welser has several times spurred me on with his letters to illustrate it, and he would already have persuaded me, had I not been called away to weightier matters. So great a number of difficulties, rocks and quicksands, which I have just mentioned, so greatly dismayed my mind that I was forced to change what I had at first proposed.

units.la: Decreveram totum Terrarum Orbem rimari, & qua, qua hic dantur, Methodo proponere: sed deterruerunt me partim (verum fatebor) negocium involutum laborque difficilis; Terra etiam, quod curiosius ipsam scrutarer, minante nonnumquam exterminium, cui facile succubuissem, perpetua confluctans cum invalitudine, gravissimoque Lienis adfectu: partim tanta Scriptorum omnium inter se discordia & serrarum reciprocatio; tanta quorumdam socordia; tam denique frequentes eorumdem navi & macula. Qua igitur universim ad Mundum, Spharamque Caelestem & Terrestrem pertinere visa, largitus; explicatis Europa Generalibus Provinciastres adposui; Universi huius extra controversiam Ocellos, quibus Latinus hodie in usu est, licet corruptus, Sermo; quaque omnium Antiquorum Novorumque monimentis maxime prae ceteris nobilitata; Hispaniam dico, Galliam, Italiam; mihi, quam reliqua, notiores.
units.tr: I had decided to search out the whole globe and to set it forth by the method that is available here. But I was deterred partly (I will confess the truth) by the tangled nature of the business and the difficulty of the labour. The earth itself, since I was examining it more closely, sometimes threatened destruction, and I would have easily succumbed to it, as I was constantly struggling with ill health and a very serious disorder of the spleen. Partly I was deterred by the great disagreement of all the writers among themselves and by their mutual contradictions, by the carelessness of some, and finally by the frequent slips and blemishes of the same men. Therefore I first treated those things that seemed to pertain to the world in general, the celestial and terrestrial sphere. Then, after setting out the general matters of Europe, I added its provinces one by one. I chose as the eyes of this universe, beyond dispute, Spain, Gaul and Italy, the regions where the Latin language, though corrupted, is still in use today, and which are more ennobled than any others by the monuments of all the ancients and moderns. They are better known to me than the rest.

units.la: Hispaniam ex probatissimis delineavi Scriptoribus: Galliam pleramque ipse quidem vidi, & ad Itineraria non infida peragravi; sed fidelibus solidisque danda symbolas suas liberaliter contulit Vir Nobilissimus Josephus Scaliger: Italiam ipse quoque adivi; & Leandro Alberto usus comite, majore cum fructu. Quod in tribus ego, conentur in reliquis alij: sic tandem plenam exactamque (absit arrogantia) habituri sumus Geographiam. Ne autem vos mei, quibus aliquando in Gallijs, Italia, lia, Germania, Anglia innotui, ignoretis, quis hodie, qualisque siem: Batavus, Dodracinatus, Lugduni Batavorum, XLVII. fere annorum: decem, si superstites, fuissem; quinque jam nunc sum; sex, si DEUS adspirat, futurus post semestre liberorum pater. DEO totus fido; quod videri volo, esse studeo; omnibus optime cupio, singulis decenter: prodesse nitor cunctis; proprium perpetuumque habens nocere neminem, bonos amare, malos tolerare, minoribus indulgere, cedere majoribus, pares ferre: morosam gravitatem nihil moror; effrenem levitatem detestor, hilarem in pectore, virtutem veneror: mei semper similis, si fortuna blanditur, non tollor; si mutat mutatue, non mutor: DEUM precatus, contingat mihi, quod expedit, non quod volo: meorum satagens sua suis relinquo: non credo, quidquid audio: non dico, quidquid scio: non facio, quidquid possum. Fallam vult necessitas, vel fallar? patior potius, quam faciam scelus: bono saepe malum vincens, ratusque seipsum vincere, summam esse Victoriam. Humilia sector: ne sit, unde gravi precipiter lapsu. Syrtes, saxa, vadaque forensia fugiens, turbasque & Honorum, qui saepe oblati, inania aversatus, Historiographum ago Illustrium Ordinum Foederatarum Provinciarum, & in celeberrima Batavorum Academia Ordinarium Historiarum Professorem; Praefectura quoque decoratus ab amplissimis ejusdem Academia Curatoribus Bibliotheca, post excessum nobilissimi Juvenis Jani Dusa. Meam, quod restat, legendo scribendoque vitam procudo: memor, eam sine Litteris mortem esse: hominemque nihil, aut certe perparum scire: immane enim quantum esse, quod nescit. Praeter Cosmographica haec, & quaedam quae minoris rei, dedi jam Praxin Provincialis apud Batavos Curia Civilem: Ennij, antiquissimi Poëta, fragmenta; Tragicam Historiam Angeli Merulae, Magni mei Patrui: daturus brevi, a quibus in praesentia calent prela, Κωνγετικά, Statumque cum Religionis, tum Politica Gubernationis: quibus inde succedent, si ab DEO vita mihi, Historia cum Belgica, tum Gel-
units.tr: I drew up Spain from the most approved writers. I had seen most of Gaul myself and travelled through it with itineraries that were not unreliable. But Josephus Scaliger, a most noble man, generously contributed his own contributions to those that were faithful and sound. I also visited Italy myself, using Leandro Alberti as my companion, with greater profit. What I have done for these three regions, let others attempt for the rest, so that at last we shall have a full and exact geography (let there be no arrogance in saying so). But in case you, my friends, to whom I became known in France, Italy, Germany and England, should not know who and what I am today: I am a Batavian, three-quarters of the way through the ordinary span of life, about forty-seven years old. I would have been ten if I had survived, and I am now five. I shall be six, God willing, and a father of children within half a year. I am wholly devoted to God, and I strive to be what I wish to appear. I desire the best for everyone and behave courteously to each individual. I strive to be useful to all, and I have the settled habit of harming no one: I love the good, tolerate the bad, indulge the young, yield to my elders, and bear with my equals. I pay no heed to morose seriousness; I detest unbridled levity; I cherish a cheerful heart and I revere virtue. I am always like myself: if fortune flatters me, I am not puffed up; if it changes, or changes again, I am not changed. Having prayed to God, may I obtain what is expedient for me, not what I wish. Attending to my own affairs, I leave to others what is theirs. I do not believe everything I hear; I do not say everything I know; I do not do everything I am able to do. Does necessity want me to deceive, or should I myself be deceived? I would rather suffer than commit a crime, conquering evil with good, and thinking that to conquer oneself is the greatest victory. I pursue humble things, lest there be a place from which I might fall headlong with a heavy crash. Avoiding rocks, shoals and the bustle of the forum, and turning away from the crowds and from the empty honours that were often offered to me, I act as Historiographer of the Illustrious Orders of the United Provinces, and as Ordinary Professor of History at the most famous Academy of the Batavians. I have also been honoured with the office of Librarian by the most distinguished Curators of the same Academy, after the death of the noble young man Janus Dousa. I forge the rest of my life by reading and writing, mindful that life without letters is a kind of death, and that a man knows nothing, or certainly very little, since the amount that he does not know is enormous. Besides these cosmographical works, and some minor things, I have already published the Practice of the Provincial Civil Court among the Batavians, the fragments of Ennius, the most ancient poet, and the Tragic History of Angelus Merula, my great uncle. Soon I shall give to the public, and from which the presses are at present hot, the Conjectures [Κωνγετικά], and the state both of religion and of political government. After these will follow, if God grants me life, the history of Belgium as well as of Gelderland

units.tr: We think that geography belongs to the philosophical discipline [φιλοσόφου πραγματείας], if any other does. For those who first ventured to take it up were of this sort: Anaximander of Miletus, and Hecataeus, a fellow citizen of Anaximander himself, as Eratosthenes also says; and Democritus, Eudoxus, Dicaearchus, Ephorus and very many others. After these came Eratosthenes, Polybius and Posidonius, philosophers.

units.la: NIVERSVM hoc, quod ob mentis humanæ sacraria magis, quam oculorum aciem obversatur, ab Elegantia persecta & absoluta Puritate Græcis KOΣMOΣ, quod illi nomen primus dedit Pythagoras, dicitur: Latinis MVNDVS. Is Plinio Naturalis historiæ lib. 11. cap. 1. cujus circumflexu tegantur cuncta. Apuleio, admirandam omnibus machinam depingenti, qui societate Cæli & Terra constat, & eorum Naturis, quæ utriusque sunt. Aristoteli ὡς κόσμος definitur ab Caussis quidem, ἡ τῶν ὅλων τάξις τε καὶ Διακόσμησις, ὡς δὲ τῆ καὶ ἀλλὰ ἱερὸν Φυλακὴ ἑαυτοῦ: à Partibus vero; σύστημα ἐξ ἀέρων καὶ γῆς, καὶ τῶν ἐν τύπῳ ψυχικῶν Φύσεων. Consonant Chrysippi illa: σύστημα ἐξ ἀέρων καὶ γῆς καὶ τῶν ἐν τύπῳ Φύσεων ἢ τὸ ἐκ θεῶν ἐν ἀνθρώπων σύστημα, καὶ ἐκ τῶν ἴσων τούτων γεγονότων: Aliis apud Suidam; σύστημα ἐκ στοιχείων καὶ ἀνθρώπων, &c. Operosior in eo describendo Apuleius: Mundus est, inquit, ornata ordinatio, Dei munere, Deorum recta custodia: cujus cardinem, sic enim dixerim Centrum, robustum & immobilem, genitrix atque altrix animantium omnium habet Tellus: supernis omnibus, ut videri potest, Aeris liquiditate ad modum tegminis, septis & opertis. Ultra Deorum Domus est, quod vocamus Cælum: quod quidem divinis corporibus onustum videmus, ignibus pulcherrimis & perlucidis Solis & Lunæ & reliquorum Siderum, cum quibus fertur per orbem, dierum noctiumque curriculis, agens Stellarum choros intermino lapsu, finem nulla aut defectione factura. His explicandis non immorabor, ad potiora properans. Singula patebunt ex sequentibus.
units.tr: This whole, which presents itself more to the sanctuaries of the human mind than to the gaze of the eyes, is called by the Greeks κόσμος [kosmos], from its elegant and absolute purity, a name first given to it by Pythagoras; by the Latins it is called MUNDUS. Pliny calls it, in Natural History book 11, chapter 1, that by whose circuit all things are covered. Apuleius, describing the marvellous machine, says it consists of the association of Heaven and Earth and of the natures that belong to each. Aristotle defines the world (ὡς κόσμος [hōs kosmos]) by its causes, as "the arrangement and orderly disposition of all things" [ἡ τῶν ὅλων τάξις τε καὶ διακόσμησις], and as a sacred guardianship of itself [ἱερὸν φυλακὴ ἑαυτοῦ]; but by its parts, as "a system of air and earth, and of the natures in it that are endowed with soul" [σύστημα ἐξ ἀέρων καὶ γῆς, καὶ τῶν ἐν τούτῳ ψυχικῶν φύσεων]. Chrysippus' words agree: "a system of air and earth and of the natures in it, or the system of gods and men, and of the things made from these equal parts" [σύστημα ἐξ ἀέρων καὶ γῆς καὶ τῶν ἐν τούτῳ φύσεων, ἢ τὸ ἐκ θεῶν καὶ ἀνθρώπων σύστημα, καὶ ἐκ τῶν ἴσων τούτων γεγονότων]. Others, in Suidas, say "a system of elements and men," etc. Apuleius is more elaborate in describing it: "The world," he says, "is an ornate ordering, by the gift of God, under the upright custody of the gods; whose hinge (for so I may call the centre) is robust and immovable, and the Earth, mother and nurse of all living things, holds it; above all the upper parts, as can be seen, it is closed in and covered, like a roof, by the clear fluidity of the air. Beyond that is the home of the gods, which we call Heaven; it is indeed seen laden with divine bodies, with the most beautiful and bright fires of the Sun and Moon and the other stars, with which it is carried round the world in the courses of days and nights, driving the choirs of the stars in an endless gliding motion, and never going to end or fail." I shall not linger over explaining these points, hastening on to weightier matters. Each thing will become clear from what follows.

units.la: DEr hoc opus confitemur Christiani cum Mosche, Geneseos cap. i. & ii. Davide Propheta, Psalmo viii. vers. 4. & xxxix, 12. Schelomone, Proverbiorum xvi, 4. Ieschahhia xl, 12. & seq. xlv, 7, 12, 18. Paullo, Epistola ad Romanos, xi, 36. & ad Colossenses, i, 16. Auctore denique Epistolæ ad Hebræos, i.10. Certe Mosche, eruditus quidem omni sapientia Ægyptiorum, ut de illo testatur Ambrosius lib. i. ἐξαμέρ. cap. ii. non persuasus tamen ab humana prudentia, sed à Spiritu Sancto & ipsa Veritate edoctus, tamquam testis divini operis, sic scribit: בראשית ברא אלהים את השמים ואת הארץ, In principio creavit DEVS Cælum & Terram. בראשית inquit, quum nihil adhuc esset, sed jam primum Creationem inchoare statuisset, quæ ab æterno fuerat, Divina Majestas. Ecclesiast. xviii, 1. Alij Principium hoc de Filio DEI, non de ipso Creationis momento capiunt; quorum curiosa pietas vix est ut careat periculo. Alij alio modo exaudiunt hanc vocem. Videndus omnino præter alios Basilius i. Homilia ἐξαμέρ. ברא אלהים Creavit DEVS; DEVS, qui menti humanæ, suis ratiocinationibus indulgenti, νοῦς καλῆς, Φεγοῦ δὲ ἀδυνατῶν, ut cum Mercurio Trismegisto loquar; DEVS, qui Sibyllæ apud Iustinum Philosophum & Martyrem, Ζεὺς ἐρμηνεύς, ἀθάνατος, Παντοκράτωρ, ἀόρατος, ἐρέμνῳ αὐτὸς ἀπάντα, Αὐτὸς δ' ἐν βλέπει Ἰησοῦς ὑπὸ σαρκὸς ἀπάντων.
units.tr: In this work we Christians confess, with Moses in Genesis 1 and 2; with David the prophet in Psalm 8:4 and 39:12; with Solomon in Proverbs 16:4; with Isaiah in chapters 40:12 ff., 45:7, 12, 18; with Paul in Romans 11:36 and Colossians 1:16; and finally with the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews 1:10. Moses, indeed, was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, as Ambrose testifies in book 1 of the Hexaemeron, chapter 2. Yet he was not persuaded by human prudence but taught by the Holy Spirit and by Truth itself, and as a witness of the divine work he writes: In principio creavit Deus caelum et terram [בראשית ברא אלהים את השמים ואת הארץ], "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." He says "In the beginning" because, when nothing yet existed, the divine Majesty had determined to begin the creation, which had been from eternity (Ecclesiasticus 18:1). Others take this "beginning" to refer to the Son of God, not to the very moment of creation; a curious piety of this kind can hardly avoid danger. Others understand this word in yet other ways. Basil in his first Homily on the Hexaemeron should certainly be consulted, along with others. Creavit Deus [ברא אלהים]: God created; God, who, as I would say with Mercurius Trismegistus, is the mind of the man who indulges his own reasonings, the beautiful mind, though he cannot be seen by the eye; God, who in the Sibyl quoted by Justin the Philosopher and Martyr is "Zeus the interpreter, immortal, almighty, invisible, who himself sees all things, but is seen by no one of all things" [Ζεὺς ἑρμηνεύς, ἀθάνατος, Παντοκράτωρ, ἀόρατος].

units.la: DEVS, unitrinus, Pater, Filius, Spiritus Sanctus, ut clare docent Propheta Psalmo xxxiii, 6. & Apostolus ad Colossenses i. 15. Unde, ut pie nonnulli volunt, usus Mosche vocabulo אלהים, indicans recte plures Personas creatrices, adposito tamen singulari ברא, ut unitas essentiæ significetur. Trinitatis notam sunt etiam qui latere volunt in primis tribus primæ vocis characteribus, & integra sequente בראשית & ברא. ב enim Filium designare ajunt, qui בן Hebræis, per quem venitur (nam litterarum ordinem in utraque voce etiam observant) ad agnitionem Patris; ר Spiritum Sanctum, qui רוח ipsidem, quique nexus mutui inter Patrem & Filium amoris; א denique Patrem, qui אב. Explicant planius Mosche verba David Psalmo, quem jam indicavi, Ioannes Evangelista i, 1. & seqq. & alij. Quod autem in Symbolo Apostolico Pater dicatur Creator Cæli & Terræ; fit aut ratione ordinis, aut ministerij, seu qualiscumq; differentiæ caussa. Patri enim primæ Personæ primum opus tribuitur, Creatio: ut Secundæ, Filio, Redemtio secundum; Spiritui Sancto, Personæ Tertiæ, tertium opus Sanctificatio: quum tamen tria hæc totius Trinitatis opera.
units.tr: God is triune: Father, Son and Holy Spirit, as Psalm 33:6 of the prophet and Colossians 1:15 of the Apostle clearly teach. Hence, as some devout writers hold, Moses used the word Elohim [אלהים], which rightly signifies several creating Persons, while joining it to the singular verb bara [ברא], so that the unity of essence is indicated. Some also wish to find the mark of the Trinity hidden in the first three letters of the first word, and in the whole of the following bereshith [בראשית] and bara [ברא]. They say that beth [ב] designates the Son, who among the Hebrews is ben [בן], through whom one comes (for they also observe the order of the letters in both words) to the knowledge of the Father; that resh [ר] designates the Holy Spirit, who is ruach [רוח] itself, and the bond of mutual love between the Father and the Son; and finally that aleph [א] designates the Father, who is ab [אב]. The words of Moses are explained more plainly by David in the Psalm already cited, by John the Evangelist 1:1 ff., and by others. As for the Apostles' Creed calling the Father the Creator of heaven and earth, this is done either by reason of order, or of ministry, or for some other difference of this kind. For the first work, creation, is attributed to the Father, the first Person; the second, redemption, to the Son, the second Person; and the third work, sanctification, to the Holy Spirit, the third Person. Yet these three are the works of the whole Trinity.

units.la: Veram hanc & sanam de Rerum omnium Creatore Confessionem, proxime sequuti, Orpheus, Archelaus, Sophocles, Plato, Antisthenes, Menander, Zeno, Cleanthes, Chrysippus, Archedemus, Posidonius; & apud Latinos Ovidius & Servius. Orpheus, quod de illo testatur Lactantius lib. i. de falsa religione cap. v. DEVM Verum, Magnum, μεγάλον appellavit; ante Ipsum nihil fuisse genitum, ab Ipso omnia esse generata fassus. DEVM Ἐνὸς titulo facit alibi insignem poëta doctissimus, ut paulo post audiemus.
units.tr: Orpheus, Archelaus, Sophocles, Plato, Antisthenes, Menander, Zeno, Cleanthes, Chrysippus and Posidonius most closely followed this true and sound confession concerning the Creator of all things; and among the Latins Ovid and Servius did so too. Orpheus, as Lactantius testifies of him in book 1, chapter 5 of De falsa religione, called the true God "Great" [μέγαν], and confessed that nothing had been begotten before Him and that all things had been generated by Him. The most learned poet, in another place, marks God with the title "the One" [Ἑνός], as we shall hear shortly.

Ipse Plato in Timæo; ἔτω δὲ πυρὸς τι καὶ Γῆς, inquit, Τ᾽ ὕδωρ Ἀέρα τι ὁ Θεὸς ἐν μέσῳ θεὶς, quæ sic interpretatur M. Tullius de Universo: Ita contigit ut inter Ignem & Terram Aquam D E V S Animamque (Aerem ita vocat Latine) ponéret, eaque inter se compararet & proportione conjungeret. Imo Timæus Platonis totus in eo est, ut D E V M probet hujus Universi parentem, pulcerrimique operis molitorem, fabricatorem, effectorem. Idem Plato apud Stobæum lib. i. ἐκλογ. Φυσ. cap. xiii. tria ponit Rerum principia; τὸν Θεὸν, τὸ Τ᾽ ὕλω, τὸ ἰδίαν, ὑφ᾽ ἕ, ἐξ ἕ, πρὸς ὅ. ὁ δὲ Θεὸς, inquit, νῶς ἐστὶ ἕ κόσμως; ἡ δὲ ὕλη τὸ ὑποκείμενον γενέσει ἢ φθορᾷ; ἰδέα δὲ ὕσια ἀσώματ� ἐν τῆς νοήμασιν, καὶ τῆς Φαντασίας ἕ Θεῷ. Exstat etiam Magni Philosophi locus in Epinomide: κόσμον, ait, ἐταξε λόγ�, ὁ πάντων θειότατ�; Verbum, ὁ λόγ� ille, qui est omnium Rerum divinißimus, mundum ordinavit: quæ de Filio D E I Platonem loquutum esse statuunt magni viri; præsertim quum idem Philosophus Hermiam, Erastum & Coriscum in Epistolis moneat, ut sanctè venerentur & omni studio atque pietate colant, τὸν τῶν πάντων Θεὸν, ἡγεμόνα τῶν τε ὄντων καὶ τῶν μελλόντων, τὴν ἡγεμόν� καὶ αἰτίᾳ πατέρα Κύριον: illum omnium D E V M, ducem & auctorem præsentium & futurorum: per quem Pater ἐξέπνευσεν τὰ πάντα καὶ τοῦ πάντ-ας; καὶ δι᾽ ἕ οἰκονομεῖ τι καὶ Βεβαίως. hausit hæc proculdubio divinus Philosophus ex historia Sacra. Profectus enim in Ægyptum, legit ibi, & plene, parum aberat, cognovit, ut scribunt Clemens Alexandrinus & alii, Mosche & aliquot Prophetarum scripta: quorum tamen doctrinam & veritatem, metu impeditus, &, quæ recens adhuc erat in omnium animis, Socratis calamitatem ob oculos habens, profiteri contra receptam publice πολυθεΐας opinionem, non fuit ausus. Videndus omnino Justinus in exhortat. ad Gentes.
units.tr: Plato, son of Ariston of Athens, according to Diogenes Laertius book 3, asserts that there are two principles of all things: God (whom, as Lactantius book 1 testifies, he calls the Maker of the World) and Matter [ὕλη]. He names God Mind [νοῦς] and Cause [αἴτιον]; he acknowledges matter as unformed and infinite [ἀχρημάτιστον ἢ ἄπειρον], and adds that things are composed of it; and he says that this matter, when it moved at some time rashly and without order, was gathered into one place by God. Matter of this kind, he says, was converted into the four elements, fire, water, air and earth, and from these the world and the things in it were born. A little later the same writer holds that God is the cause of the whole generation, and that the beginning of generation is the male cause, and that the world is given life from fire, water, air and earth: from fire, so that the world may be visible; from earth, so that it may be solid; from water and air, so that it may not lack proportion and balance; and finally from all of them, so that it may be perfect and nearly immortal. Plato himself, in the Timaeus, says: "Thus God set water and air between fire and earth," which Marcus Tullius, in his De Universo, thus translates into Latin: "So it came about that God placed water and the soul (which he calls air in Latin) between fire and earth, and joined them together in mutual proportion." Indeed the whole of Plato's Timaeus aims to prove that God is the parent of this universe, the builder, maker and author of this most beautiful work. The same Plato, in book 1 of the Physical Extracts of Stobaeus, chapter 13, posits three principles of things: God, matter, and form [τὸν Θεὸν, τὸ ὕλη, τὸ ἰδέα]; from which, by which and toward which things come. God, he says, is the mind of the world; matter is that which underlies generation and corruption; and the form is the incorporeal essence, grasped in thoughts and in the imagination of God. There is also a passage of the great philosopher in the Epinomis: "Word [λόγος] ordered the world, the most divine of all things," that is, the Word, that Reason which is most divine of all things, ordered the world. Great men hold that Plato was speaking here of the Son of God, especially since the same philosopher, in his letters, admonishes Hermias, Erastus and Coriscus to venerate reverently and to cherish with all zeal and piety "the God of all things, leader of things present and future, the leader and cause, the Father and Lord" [τὸν τῶν πάντων Θεὸν ... Κύριον]: that God of all, the guide and author of present and future things, through whom the Father "breathes into all things" and "through whom all things are ordered and secure." Undoubtedly this divine philosopher drew these teachings from Sacred History. For, having gone to Egypt, he read there, and, as Clement of Alexandria and others write, came very near to knowing fully the writings of Moses and of some of the prophets. Yet, hindered by fear, and keeping before his eyes the calamity of Socrates, which was still fresh in everyone's mind, he did not dare to profess publicly, against the received opinion of many gods, the doctrine and truth of these writings. Justin, in his Exhortation to the Greeks, should certainly be consulted.

units.la: Antisthenes Atheniensis, quamvis multos Deos populares agnosceret, unum tamen dixit naturalem, id est, summum totius Artificem. Legendus Lactantius.
units.tr: Antisthenes of Athens, although he acknowledged many gods of the people, nevertheless said that there was one natural God, that is, the supreme Artificer of the whole. Lactantius should be read.

units.la: Menander sane D E V M Universi Creatorem his versibus profitetur: τὸν ὄντα κύριον πάντων ἀεί Καὶ πατέρα, τῶν ἀλλὰ πίλης ἡμᾶν μόνον Ἀγαθῶν ποιητῶν Δεσπότη καὶ κτίστην.
units.tr: Menander, indeed, professes God as the Creator of the universe in these verses: "The one who is always the Lord of all, and Father, who alone made all good things, Master and Founder" [τὸν ὄντα κύριον πάντων ἀεί καὶ πατέρα, τῶν ἄλλα πάντων ἡμῖν μόνον ἀγαθῶν ποιητὴν δεσπότην καὶ κτίστην].

units.la: Iam Zenon Mnaseae F. Citticus περὶ ὕσιας libro, item περὶ ἕλης: Cleanthes περὶ ἀπο-μων; Chrysippus α. Φυσικῶν in fine: Archedemus περὶ στοιχείων, & Posidonius β. Φυσικῆς λόγ�, Diogene Laertio scribente lib. vii. duo volunt esse Rerum omnium Princi-pia, τὸ ποιοῦν καὶ τὸ πάσχον: hoc quidem esse τὴν ἄποιον ὕσιαν τὴν ὕλω; illud vero τὸν ἐν αὐτῇ λόγον τὸν Θεὸν (hoc omnino notandum, V E R B V M D E V M agnoscunt Universi Efficientem. quam prope absunt ab Rege Propheta, qui canit: Verbo Domini Cœli firmati sunt!) τῶν γὰρ ὄντα ἀίδιον Δι᾽ πάσης αὐτῆς δημιουργεῖν ἑκάστα (qui per quatuor in-fusus Elementa gignit Universa, inquiet mox Grammaticus Servius non Grammati-ce) Vnum D E V M esse, cum κατ᾽ ἀρχὰς καθ᾽ αὐτὸν ὄντα τῷ πάσῳ ὕσιαν δι᾽ Ἀέρ� εἰς Τ᾽ ὕδωρ convertisse; tum genuisse primum quatuor Elementa, Πῦρ, Τ᾽ ὕδωρ, Ἀέρα, Γῆν.
units.tr: Zeno of Citium, son of Mnaseas, in his book On Substance, and likewise On Matter; Cleanthes in his work On ...; Chrysippus at the end of the first book of his Physics; Archedemus in On the Elements; and Posidonius in the second book of his Physics. According to Diogenes Laertius, writing in book 7, they hold that there are two principles of all things: that which acts and that which is acted upon. The latter is the unqualified substance, matter; the former is the reason within it, God. (This must be carefully noted: these all acknowledge the Word of God as the efficient cause of the universe. How far they are from the royal prophet, who sings: By the word of the Lord the heavens were established!) They say that God, eternal, pervades the whole and creates each thing... (he who, infused through the four elements, begets all things, as the grammarian Servius will soon say, though not grammatically). That God, being at first alone, changed the whole substance through air into water; then he first generated the four elements: fire, water, air, earth.

units.la: Quin & Zenon, apud Theodoretum sermone iiii. ad Græcos Infideles, propius ad veritatem accedit: D E I, primi omnium Auctoris, nomen non celat: τ Θεὸν, ait de illo, quem laudavi, Ε᾽ τ᾽ Τ᾽ ὕλω ἀρχὰς ἐφησεν εἶναι. Et de eodem Stobæus lib. i. Φυσικ. ἐκλογ. ζῳων, inquit, Μπασαῖς, Κηπῶς, ἀρχὰς τ Θεὸν Ε᾽ τῷ Τ᾽ ὕλω, στοιχεῖα ἡ πασαρα ἐφησι.
units.tr: Indeed Zeno, in Theodoret's fourth discourse to the Greek unbelievers, comes closer to the truth. He does not conceal the name of the first author of all: "God," he says of the man I praised, "said that the principles are God and matter." And of the same man Stobaeus, in book 1 of his Physical Extracts, says: "Zeno, Cleanthes and Chrysippus say that the principles are God and matter, and the elements are..." (the rest is garbled in the text).

units.la: Ovidius, Lactantio teste, in principio præclari operis, sine ulla nominis dissimulatione, ab D E o, quem Fabricatorem Mundi, quem Rerum Opificem vocat, Mundum fatetur instructum. Sic enim canit i. Metamorph.
units.tr: Ovid, according to Lactantius, at the beginning of his splendid work, without any disguise of the name, acknowledges that the world was furnished by God, whom he calls the Fabricator of the World and the Maker of all things. For thus he sings in book 1 of the Metamorphoses.

units.la: Ante Mare & Terras, &, quod regit omnia, Cœlum, (obscure Plinius, Mundum diffiniens, proprietatem hanc, quæ parti tantum convenit, tribuit toti) Vnus erat toto Natura vultus in orbe, Quem dixere Chaos, rudis indigestaque moles: Nec quidquam, nisi pondus iners: congestaque eodem Non bene junctarum discordia semina rerum.
units.tr: Before sea and lands, and heaven, which covers all, (Pliny, defining the world, obscurely gives to the whole what belongs only to a part) Nature was one face over the whole orb, which they called Chaos, a rough and undigested mass, nothing but inert weight, and the seeds of things not well joined, heaped together in discord.

units.la: & paullo post: Hanc Deus, & melior litem Natura diremit.
units.tr: And a little later: This strife God, or a better Nature, settled.

units.la: (an recte Naturam in Rerum Creatione nominet cum Epidecto Ovidius, postea dicendum) Nam Cœlo Terræ, & Terræ abscidit Vndas, Et liquidum spisso secrevit ab Aere Cœlum.
units.tr: (Whether Ovid rightly names Nature in the creation of things, along with Epicurus, must be discussed later.) For he parted heaven from earth, and the waters from the land, and separated the clear sky from the dense air.

units.la: Deinde: Sic ubi dispositam Quisquis fuit ille Deorum,
units.tr: Then: So when he had arranged it, whoever that god was,

units.la: prudenter Ovidius, horrendis, ut plerique tum in Rep.Romana, immersus de Deo opinionibus: non solum veritus, ne in re tam insigni Hunc pro Illo Deum nominando, alia, quam quæ ab Senatu comprobata erat, religione lectorem illigaret, ut innuit Agellius lib. 11. Noct. Attic. cap. xxviii. sed & formidans ne Deum, cujus jam meminerat, parum grato nomine indicaret. Sic enim de Deo Ἀγνώστῳ, & de cujus certo nomine dubitabant, ne errore aliquo laberentur, veteres Romani cautim loquebantur. Quis quis es, ut videre est apud eundem Ovidium vi. Fastor. Plautum Rudente Act. 1. Sc. iv. Virgil.iv.Æn. Plin. 11. Nat. histor. cap.vii. & alios, Congeriem secuit, sectamque in membra redegit.
units.tr: Ovid wisely (being steeped, as many in the Roman Republic were at that time, in horrible opinions about God) did not only fear that, in so important a matter, by naming this one for that one he might bind the reader to a religion other than the one approved by the Senate, as Gellius hints in Attic Nights 11, ch. 28, but also feared he might indicate by an unwelcome name the God whom he had already mentioned. For the ancient Romans spoke cautiously in this way about the unknown God and about one whose certain name they doubted, lest they slip into some error. Whoever you are, as may be seen in Ovid, Fasti 6, Plautus, Rudens Act 1, sc. 4, Virgil, Aeneid 4, Pliny, Natural History 11, ch. 7, and others. He cut apart the mass and reduced the divided parts into limbs.

units.la: Et: Sic omnis inclusum numero distinxit eodem
units.tr: And: Thus he distinguished everything enclosed by the same number

units.la: Cura Dei.
units.tr: By the care of God.

units.la: Item: His quoque non passim Mundi Fabricator habendum
units.tr: Likewise: Nor was the Fabricator of the World to hold these things everywhere

units.la: Aera permisit.
units.tr: He allowed the air.

units.la: Denique: Sanctius his Animal, Mentisque capacius altæ
units.tr: Finally: A more holy animal, more capable of lofty mind,

units.la: Deerat adhuc, & quod dominari in cetera posset,
units.tr: was still lacking, one who could rule the rest,

units.la: Natus Homo est: sive hunc divino Numine fecit
units.tr: Man was born; whether the Maker of things made him by divine power,

units.la: Ille Opifex Rerum, Mundi melioris origo.
units.tr: That Maker of things, the origin of a better world.

units.la: & quæ multa ibi alia de admirando Dei opificio & pulcra Mundi structura. Non possum non adponere superiorum, & Servi sententiam; cujus de Deo Vniversorum Genitore, ad Virgilium, qui mox erit laudandus, hæc sunt verba: Quatuor sunt Elementa, Terra, Aqua, Aer, Aether; & Deus: præter hæc nihil est aliud: & hoc τὸ πᾶν Mundum non possumus dicere. Nam Mundus non est Totum. Ergo Deus, est quidam Divinus Spiritus, qui per quatuor infusus Elementa gignit Vniversa: & quæ multa ibi notatu digna.
units.tr: And many other things there about the admirable work of God and the beautiful structure of the world. I cannot help adding the opinion of Servius, quoted above, about God the Begetter of all things, from his commentary on Virgil, who will soon be praised. His words are these: There are four elements, earth, water, air, aether; and God. Besides these there is nothing else; and this whole we cannot call the world, for the world is not the whole. Therefore God is a certain divine spirit, which, infused through the four elements, begets all things. And many other things there are worth noting.

units.la: Apuleius etiam Mundum describit ornatam ordinationem, Dei munere.
units.tr: Apuleius also describes the world as an ordered adornment, by the gift of God.

units.la: Quam divine divini vates & Philosophi: quam non Christiani Christiane! Quod si, quæ Natura ducente senserunt, (ait Lactantius, quem dixi, loco) in perpetuum defendissent: eandem, quam Nos sequimur, Doctrinam, comprehensa Veritate, tenuissent. Alii Ethicientem non Dei nomine ostendunt; sed vel Μονάδα, vel Ἐνὸς, vel Αὐτὸς, vel Νοῦς, vel Spiritus & Mentis, vel Φύσεως, vel Ἀγαθὸν Δαίμονα, vel denique Ποιητὴν appellatione obvelant; qui sane non longe fuerunt à Veritate (ut de Virgilio testatur Lactantius) quam fere professi, quos nominavi, Vates & Philosophi; vere profitemur nos Christiani. Accedunt igitur, qui deinceps sequuntur, proxime. Clemens enim Alexandrinus στρωμ. λογ. τ. supremum illud Numen nomen non unum habere, sed varie ab variis appellari scribit: ἢ τοι Ἕν, ἢ Ἀγαθὸν, ἢ Ν̄ν, ἢ αὐτὸ τὸ Ὄν, ἢ Πατέρα, ἢ Δημιουργὸν, ἢ Κύριον. Quid si, ἢ Αὐτὸν, ἢ τὸ Ὄν?
units.tr: How divinely the divine seers and philosophers spoke; how little, Christians, you Christians have! But if what they perceived under the guidance of nature (says Lactantius, whom I quoted in that passage) they had held on to forever, they would have kept the same doctrine that we follow, the truth having been grasped. Others indicate the efficient cause not by the name of God but veil it under the names Monad, or One, or Self, or Mind, or Spirit and Intellect, or Nature, or Good Daemon, or finally Maker. These, certainly, were not far from the truth (as Lactantius testifies of Virgil), which the seers and philosophers I have named almost professed; we Christians truly profess it. Those who follow next come close. For Clement of Alexandria, in book 5 of the Stromata, writes that the supreme Divinity does not have one name but is called variously by various people: either the One, or the Good, or Mind, or Being itself, or Father, or Creator, or Lord. What if also Self, or Being?

units.la: Μονάς Rerum omnium Principium dicitur Mercurio Trismegisto apud Stobæum lib. 1. Φυσικ. ἐκλογ. cap. xrii. ἡ γὰρ Μονὰς, inquit, ἐκ πάντων ἀρχὴ καὶ ῥίζα, ἐν πᾶσιν ἐστιν; ἀνὰ δὲ ἀρχῆς ἰδίαν; ἀρχὴ δ' ἐξ ἰδίων, ἀλλ' ἐξ αὐτῆς.
units.tr: The Monad is called the principle of all things by Hermes Trismegistus, in Stobaeus, book 1 of the Physical Extracts, ch. 17: "For the Monad," he says, "is the beginning and root of all things; it is in all things; from the beginning it is its own; the beginning is from its own, but from itself." [ἡ γὰρ Μονὰς ἐκ πάντων ἀρχὴ καὶ ῥίζα, ἐν πᾶσιν ἐστιν.]

units.la: Τὸ Ἕν hic nominant Musæus & Orpheus. Ille quidem, docente Laertio in Proœmio, docet ἐξ Ἑνὸς τὰ πάντα γίνεσθαι, ἢ εἰς πάντων ἀναλύεσθαι.
units.tr: Musaeus and Orpheus name the One here. Musaeus, as Laertius teaches in the Proem, teaches that all things come into being from the One, or are resolved into the One. [ἐξ Ἑνὸς τὰ πάντα γίνεσθαι, ἢ εἰς πάντων ἀναλύεσθαι.]

units.la: Orpheus vero Musæi (ut notat Clemens Alexandrinus στρωμ. λογ. α.) discipulus, apud eundem Clementem σφραγισ. πρὸς Ἕν. sic non solum περὶ Ἑνὸς, verum etiam Αὐτὸς (quæ vox κατ' ἐξοχὴν Deo, majore jure, convenit, quam Pythagoræ, quam aliis) canens: Εἰς δ᾽ ἐς αὐτηφυΐς, Ἑνὸς ἐχοντα πάντα πίνυκ). Ἐν δ᾽ αὐτῆς Αὐτὸς πεῖνιοτε): ὧδέ πε Αὐτὸν Εἰσαγέα ὄνητῶν, Αὐτὸς δὲ γε πάντας ἐςᾶπη.
units.tr: Orpheus, the disciple of Musaeus (as Clement of Alexandria notes in Stromata book 1), in the same Clement's Exhortation to the Greeks, sings thus, not only of the One but also of Self (a word which applies to God par excellence, with greater right than to Pythagoras or to others): "Into the one who is self-produced, holding all things in the one..." (the rest of the verse is too garbled to render with certainty).

units.la: Τὸν Νοῦν, ut Efficientem edit Anaxagoras Clazomenius, Hegesibuli F. πάντα χρήματα γιγνέναι ἡμῖν: Νοῦν δ᾽ ἐλθόντα αὐτὰ Διακοσμήσαν, canit in operis sui principio; & de eo testatur Timon Phliasius in Sillis. Meminerunt Diogenes Laertius lib. ii. Plutarch. de Placitis Philosophorum, Aristoteles de Physica auscultat. Scribit etiam Cicero de Natura Deorum, Anaxagoram primum omnium rerum descriptionem & modum MENTIS infinita vi ac ratione designari & confici voluisse: in eo non vidisse, neque motum Sensui conjunctum & continentem in Infinito ullum esse posse, neque Sensum omnino: quo non ipsa Natura pulsa sentiret. Clemens Alexandrinus ... Quæ Clementis indicant Archelaum etiam hic sequutum præceptorem suum (notant Strabo lib. Geograph. xiii. Diogenes Laertius in Archelai vita, & Suidas, in voce Ἀναξαγόρας, emendatior à me in Commentario ad i. Annalium Ennii) Anaxagoram. Addam Platonis illud in Timæo Locro de Anima Mundi: Δύο αἰτίας ἡμῖν τῶν σωμάτων; Νοῦν μὲν, τὸ κατὰ λόγον γιγνομένων, ἀναγκαῖον δὲ, τῶν βίᾳ κατὰς δυναμεῖς τῶν σωμάτων. Quem autem Νοῦν vocant Anaxagoras, Archelaus, Plato; cum Ἐπινοίαν appellat hac in re Heraclitus, qui apud Stobæum i. Φυσικ. ἐκλογ. cap. xxv.
units.tr: Mind, as efficient cause, was put forward by Anaxagoras of Clazomenae, son of Hegesibulus: "All things were for us; Mind, coming, arranged them," he sings at the beginning of his work; and Timon of Phlius bears witness to this in his Silloi. Diogenes Laertius in book 2, Plutarch in On the Opinions of the Philosophers, and Aristotle in the Physics mention it. Cicero also writes, in On the Nature of the Gods, that Anaxagoras wished the first description and order of all things to be designed and brought about by Mind with infinite power and reason; in this he did not see that motion joined with sense and containing it could exist in the infinite, nor sense at all, by which Nature herself, having been pushed, would perceive. Clement of Alexandria... These things which Clement points out show that Archelaus also followed his teacher Anaxagoras (note Strabo, book 13, Diogenes Laertius in the life of Archelaus, and Suidas s.v. Anaxagoras, which I have emended more correctly in my commentary on Ennius's Annals book 1). I will add Plato's words in the Timaeus Locrus on the Soul of the World: "We have two causes of bodies: Mind, which is the cause of things that come about by reason, and necessity, which is the cause of things that come about by the force of the powers of bodies." Whom Anaxagoras, Archelaus and Plato call Mind, Heraclitus in this matter calls Thought (Epinoia), who in Stobaeus, book 1, ch. 25, says that the world arose not in time but by thought.

units.la: Mundum dicit ortum ἀ κατ᾽ χρόνον, ἀλλὰ κατ᾽ ἐπινοίαν.
units.tr: He says the world came into being not in time but by conception [οὐ κατὰ χρόνον, ἀλλὰ κατ᾽ ἐπίνοιαν].

units.la: Sequitur Virgilius, cujus de Summo DEO, omnium Rerum opifice, quem Spiritum ac Mentem (Νοῦν Anaxagoras & Archelaus, Ἐπινοίαν Heraclitus) nominat, hæc sunt verba: Principio Cælum ac Terras, Camposque liquentes, Lucentemque globum Lunæ, Titaniaque Astra SPIRITUS intus alit; totamque infusa per artus MENS agitat Molem & magno se corpore miscet.
units.tr: Virgil follows, and his words about the supreme God, the maker of all things, whom he calls Spirit and Mind (Anaxagoras and Archelaus call him Mind [Νοῦς], Heraclitus Thought [Ἐπίνοια]), are these: First, heaven and earth, the watery plains, the shining globe of the moon and the Titanian stars, a Spirit nourishes from within; and a Mind, infused through the limbs, moves the whole mass and mingles itself with the great body.

units.la: Spiritum eo loco Probus improbe interpretatur ad vi. Virgilii Eclogam non Efficientem Universi DEUM, sed ejus Materiam Aerem, & confirmando, quod sentit, advocat hoc Ennii: Quoi par Imber & Ignis Spiritus & gravi Terra.
units.tr: Probus wrongly interprets Spiritum at that place in the sixth Eclogue of Virgil as the matter of the universe, air, and not God the efficient cause of the universe; and to confirm what he thinks, he cites this line of Ennius: Whose equals are rain, fire, spirit and heavy earth.

units.la: quum Spiritus ibi non Aer: sed conjunctim Ignis Spiritus, qui Homero πυρὸς μένος, Vis ignis. Melius Servius ad locum Virgilii jam indicatum: Quatuor sunt Elementa, Terra, Aqua, Aer, Aether: & Deus: præter hac nihil est aliud. DEUS est quidam divinus Spiritus, qui per quatuor infusus Elementa ignis Universa. Et paullo post ubi Virgilius: Spiritus intus alit; Divinus, ait, & est unum, sive Mentem dicat, sive Animam, sive Spiritum. Intus alit, Vegetat & in aeternitate custodit, quia missus est, & nulla pars Elementi sine DEO est.
units.tr: But Spiritus there does not mean air; rather it means fire-spirit taken together, which Homer called the might of fire [πυρὸς μένος], the power of fire. Servius explains the passage of Virgil already cited better: There are four elements, earth, water, air and aether; and God: beyond these there is nothing else. God is a certain divine spirit, which, infused through the four elements, moves all things. And a little later, where Virgil says Spiritus intus alit: Divine, he says, and one, whether he calls it Mind or Soul or Spirit. Intus alit means that it vivifies and preserves in eternity, because it is sent, and no part of the element is without God.

units.la: Τὸ Φύσεως procreatum esse Mundum scribit apud Stobæum Epictetus, lib. i. Φυσικ. ἐκλογ. Ad cujus opinionem respexit fortasse an Ovidius, hoc versu: Hanc DEUS & melior Litem Natura diremit. Nam Cælo Terras & Terris abscidit Undas.
units.tr: Epictetus, in book one of his Physics as excerpted by Stobaeus, writes that the world was produced by Nature [Φύσεως]. Perhaps Ovid also had this opinion in mind in the line: This strife God and a better Nature settled; for he separated heaven from earth and sea from land.

units.la: Stultum est & impium, ut eleganter docet Ludovicus Vives lib. i. de Veritate Fidei Christianæ, de Mundi Creatione ex Legibus Naturæ statuere: quum Creatio Naturam antecesserit: tum enim Natura est condita, quando & Mundus: nec aliud est Natura, quam quod jussit DEUS, alioqui minister esset DEUS Naturæ, non Dominus. Φύσεως igitur appellatione DEUS, qui ejus, ut omnium, etiam est Conditor, exaudiendus.
units.tr: It is foolish and impious, as Ludovicus Vives teaches well in book one of On the Truth of the Christian Faith, to ground the creation of the world in the laws of nature, since creation precedes nature: for nature was founded at the same moment as the world. Nature is nothing other than what God commanded; otherwise God would be the servant of Nature, not its Lord. Therefore, by the name of Nature, God must be understood, who is the Creator of it as of all things.

units.la: Magi (Persis illi erant, qui Ægyptiis ...; Assyriis Χαλδαῖοι: Gallis Δρυΐδαι, καὶ Σαμαναῖοι; Bactris & Celtis Φιλοσόφοι; Indis Γυμνοσοφισταί; aliis Φιλόσοφοι Βάρβαροι, quemadmodum scite scribit Clemens Alexandrinus ... quique apud Persas Deorum vacabant cultui; preces illis, vota, sacrificia obserebant, de Deorum substantia & generatione differebant, qui denique quæcumque Deorum essent, tractabant) δύο εἶναι ἀρχὰς tradunt, Ἀγαθὸν Δαίμονα & κακὸν Δαίμονα; & quod illi quidem nomen sit Ζεύς & Ὠρομάσδης; huic vero Ἀδης & Ἀρειμάνιος; apud Aristotelem primo de Philosophia libro, Hermippum primo de Magis, Eudoxum ἐν τῇ πεδιάδι, Theopompum octavo τῶν Φιλιππικῶν. Εὐδαίμων Generans, qui procreat omnia & conservat; Κακοδαίμων Caussa est Corrumpens, quæ abolet eadem & labefactat.
units.tr: The Magi (they were Persians, called among the Egyptians ...; among the Assyrians Chaldeans; among the Gauls Druids and Samanaeans; among the Bactrians and Celts philosophers; among the Indians Gymnosophists; among others barbarian philosophers, as Clement of Alexandria neatly writes ..., and who among the Persians devoted themselves to the worship of the gods, offering prayers, vows and sacrifices, discussing the substance and generation of the gods, and treating in short whatever pertains to the gods) teach that there are two principles, a Good Daemon [Ἀγαθὸν Δαίμονα] and an Evil Daemon [κακὸν Δαίμονα]; and that the former is called Zeus and Oromasdes, the latter Hades and Arimanius. This is related by Aristotle in the first book of his work On Philosophy, Hermippus in the first book On the Magi, Eudoxus in the Plain [ἐν τῇ πεδιάδι], and Theopompus in the eighth book of the Philippica. The Good Daemon [Εὐδαίμων], the generator, produces and preserves all things; the Evil Daemon [Κακοδαίμων] is the cause that corrupts, which destroys and overthrows the same.

units.la: A Magos sequuti multo post Manichæi, qui anno Christi ccxxc. aut circiter, n-fixerunt, ab orthodoxa fide deviantes, duos esse Deos: alterum Bonum, Creatorem & Auctorem rerum bonarum, qui nominatus illis φῶς, à quo creata volunt pleraque, alterum vero Malum, pari potentia; à quo Conjugium, Imperia & omnia mala orta dicunt. σκότ© & ὕλη illis hic vocatus. Sed horum μανίαν refutat Epiphanius copiose lib. II. Tom. II.
units.tr: Long after the Magi, the Manichaeans followed them. About the year of Christ 230 they established, departing from the orthodox faith, that there are two Gods: one Good, the Creator and Author of good things, whom they name Light [φῶς], by whom they hold most things were created; and the other Evil, of equal power, from whom they say marriage, dominion and all evils arose. For them this one is called Darkness [σκότος] and Matter [ὕλη]. But Epiphanius refutes their madness at length in book two, volume two.

units.la: Ποιὼν denique hic agnoscitur Zenoni, Cleanthi, Chrysippo, Archedemo & Posidonio: quorum in re tam præclara paulo ante indicavi suffragia.
units.tr: Finally, this Maker [Ποιητής] is acknowledged by Zeno, Cleanthes, Chrysippus, Archedemus and Posidonius, whose support in so noble a matter I indicated a little earlier.

units.la: Bellissimæ igitur Fabricæ Parens & Auctor DEus: Mosche quidem, Prophetis, Apostolis, Christianis denique verus ille; Orpheo, Pythagoræ, Archelao, Sophocli, Platoni, Antisthenì, Menandro, Zenoni, Cleanthi, Chrysippo, Archedemo, Posidonio, Ovidio, Servio, quem ipsa Natura obscurius ob oculos ponebat; Trismegisto denique, Musæo, Orpheo iterum, Anaxagoræ, Archelao, Platoni, Heraclito, Virgilio, Epicteto, Magis, Zenoni, alisque, qui secretiore μονάδ©, Ἐνὸς, Αὐτὸς, Νοῦς, Spiritus & Mentis, Φυσις, Ἀγαθὸς Δαίμων & Ποιητής velo obductus. Nam quamvis varia ab varia virtute DEo nomina, res tamen una (crassius cogor loqui) DEvs, qui vere Μονὰς, vere τὸ Ἕν, vere Αὐτὸς; qui quum est à seipso, ut sit, accipit à nullo; à quo uno, quum omnibus vere sit Νοῦς, Spiritus, Naturæ Dominus, Ἀγαθὸς Δαίμων, quique solus quæcumque sunt fecit, Omnia; non à seipsis sunt & constant: qui solus mensus est pugillo Aquas, solus Cœlos palmo ponderavit, solus adpendit tribus digitis Molem Terræ. Οὐ δὲ γὰρ ἐστιν, ἃ μὴ τῷ αἰτίαν ἔ ἀναγ ὁ Θεὸς περιέχεται. Καὶ εἶνε ἰνεκεν τὰ πάντα; καὶ εἶνε αἴτιον ἁπάντων καλῶν.
units.tr: God, therefore, is the Parent and Author of this most beautiful fabric: indeed the true God for Moses, the Prophets, the Apostles and, finally, the Christians; for Orpheus, Pythagoras, Archelaus, Sophocles, Plato, Antisthenes, Menander, Zeno, Cleanthes, Chrysippus, Archedemus, Posidonius, Ovid, and Servius, whom Nature herself set before their eyes more obscurely; finally for Trismegistus, Musaeus, Orpheus again, Anaxagoras, Archelaus, Plato, Heraclitus, Virgil, Epictetus, the Magi, Zeno and others, who veiled under a more secret cloak the Monad [μονάδα], the One [Ἑνός], the Self [Αὐτός], Mind [Νοῦς], Spirit and Mind, Nature [Φύσις], the Good Daemon [Ἀγαθὸς Δαίμων] and the Maker [Ποιητής]. For although God has various names from his various powers, it is nevertheless one thing (I am forced to speak more crudely) : God, who truly is the Monad, truly the One, truly the Self, who, since he is from himself so that he is, receives his being from no one; from whom alone, since he truly is Mind, Spirit, Lord of Nature, Good Daemon for all, and who alone made all things that are, all things are not from themselves nor do they subsist by themselves. He alone measured the waters with his fist, he alone weighed the heavens with his palm, he alone balanced the mass of the earth with three fingers. [Οὐ γὰρ ἔστιν, ἃ μὴ τῷ αἰτίαν ... ὁ Θεὸς περιέχεται. Καὶ εἶνε ἰνεκεν τὰ πάντα; καὶ εἶνε αἴτιον ἁπάντων καλῶν.] For there is nothing which God does not contain as its cause; and all things are for his sake; and he is the cause of all good things.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: Varia variis Creandorum materia.
units.tr: The various matter from which created things were made.

units.la: CHristiani Spiritus Sancti doctrinam, ab Mosche scriptis mandatam, amplexi Mundum constanter adsirmamus factum ex Nihilo. בראשית ברא אלהים In principio creavit DEvs. בראׁ Creare, Interpretum omnium consensu, soli DEo convenit, qui vel ex Nihilo facit, id quod prius non erat; vel ex præjacente, ut sic loquar, materia novo modo, singulari consilio & stupenda potentia condit & exhibet, cui condendo & exhibendo nulla creatura par. Duplex illa vocis notio passim in Sacris literis. Turbat hoc Philosophos, qui Axioma illud suum, Nihil ex nihilo creari mordicus tenent, ingenitam adstruentes, hoc argumento usi: Si Materia prima facta, factam necesse est esse vel ex Se vel Aliunde. Nam ex Nihilo Nihil. Ex Se autem non fit, esset enim antequam fieret, & οὐκ ἐσὴ αὐτὸ τὸ ἑαυτὸ αἴτιον, inquit de illis Clemens Alexandrinus. Multo minus, Aliunde. Sic enim non esset Prima. Axioma satis validum, quod tamen exaudiendum de Potentia creata, non enim potest Nihil se creare ex Nihilo: non vero de Creatore, qui ex Nihilo potest creare, & vere creavit, Omnia. Legendus Augustinus lib. iii. de Trinitate. Quod Sensus non capit, credat hic Fides. πίστει νοοῦμεν, inquit Auctor Epistolæ ad Hebræos xi, 3. καταρτίζῃ τὰς αἰῶνας ῥήματι Θεοῦ, εἰς τὸ μὴ ἐκ φαινομένων τὸ βλεπόμενον γεγονέναι.
units.tr: We Christians, who have embraced the teaching of the Holy Spirit as handed down through Moses, firmly affirm that the world was made out of nothing. בראשית ברא אלהים [bereshit bara Elohim]: "In the beginning God created." By the agreement of all interpreters, to create belongs to God alone. He creates and brings forth either out of nothing, making what did not exist before, or out of pre-existing matter, so to speak, in a new manner, by a unique plan and a wonderful power; no creature is equal to him in creating and bringing forth. This double meaning of the word occurs throughout Holy Scripture. It troubles the philosophers, who stubbornly hold to their axiom that nothing is created out of nothing, and who assert that matter is unbegotten, arguing thus: if prime matter was made, then what was made must have been made either from itself or from something else. For out of nothing, nothing comes. But it did not come from itself, for it would have existed before it came to be, and "it is not its own cause" (οὐκ ἐστιν αὐτὸ τὸ ἑαυτοῦ αἴτιον), as Clement of Alexandria says of such men. Still less from something else, for then it would not be first. This is a strong axiom, but it must be understood of created power: a thing cannot create itself out of nothing. It is not to be applied to the Creator, who can create out of nothing, and truly did create all things. Augustine, book iii of On the Trinity, should be read. What the senses do not grasp, let faith believe here. "By faith we understand," says the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews (11:3), "that the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that things which are seen were not made of things which do appear" (καταρτίζῃ τὰς αἰῶνας ῥήματι Θεοῦ, εἰς τὸ μὴ ἐκ φαινομένων τὸ βλεπόμενον γεγονέναι).

units.la: Quæ creavit DEus ex Nihilo? שמים השמים ואת הארץ Cælum & Terram. Alij alio modo capiunt. Chrysostomus Cœli Terraque nomine significari scribit totum hunc Mundum corporeum; quasi Mosche consilio prudenti voluisset summatim ante oculos ponere universum hoc Mundi opificium; deinde per sex dies particulatim explicare; quidque singulis diebus ab DEo sit factum, enarrare. Notat illud hac de re suffragium Augustinus lib. ii. cap. iii. contra Manichæos, & lib. xi. de Civit. Dei cap. xxxiii. Notat, inquam, non probat. Nam lib. xii. Confession. cap. vii. Cœlum exponit Naturam Angelicam; Terram Materiam Informem, ut duo totius Entis creati extrema: illud quidem summum & prope Deum, qui Angelus; hoc vero infimum & prope nihil, quæ Materia prima. Idem Augustinus, parum sibi in re tam magna constans, volumine i. de Genesi contra Manichæos, tam Cœli, quam Terra appellatione putat indicari Materiam primam, ex qua omnia quidem constant Corpora; sed primo & principaliter, quæ primo nominantur, Cœlum & Terra.
units.tr: What did God create out of nothing? שמים השמים ואת הארץ [et hashamayim veet ha'aretz]: "heaven and earth." Others understand it in different ways. Chrysostom writes that by the name of heaven and earth the whole corporeal world is meant, as if Moses, with prudent purpose, had wished to set before our eyes in summary the whole work of the world, and then to explain it in detail over six days, recounting what God made on each day. Augustine supports this reading in book ii, chapter iii, against the Manichaeans, and in book xi, chapter xxxiii, of The City of God. I say he notes it; he does not prove it. For in book xii of the Confessions, chapter vii, he explains heaven as the angelic nature and earth as formless matter, as the two extremes of the whole created being: the former the highest and nearest to God, which is the angel; the latter the lowest and nearest to nothing, which is prime matter. The same Augustine, not very consistent with himself in so great a matter, in book i of his work On Genesis against the Manichaeans, thinks that by both the name of heaven and the name of earth prime matter is indicated, out of which indeed all bodies are composed; but primarily and principally, what are named first, heaven and earth.

units.la: Plerique nomine Cæli Cælum interpretantur, quod Empyreum indigetari vulgo solitum, addentes creatum illud mox Angelis fuisse repletum: Terra vero Materiam primam informem omnino, cui tamen inerat quædam ad formas futuras potentia, adumbratam Terra, Aqua & Abyssi quasi coloribus; quod quæ sua virtute & qualitate ad Omnium formas erat in Potentia, singulorum nominibus non incommode potuerit insigniri. Hujus mentis fuerunt Theodoretus quæst. x i. & x i v. super Genesin, Basilius homiliis 11. & 111. ad Genesin, Beda in suo Hexaëmero, Alcuinus, Rabanus, Magister Sententiarum; eosque sequuti, Scholastici Theologi, item Nicolaus de Lyra, Magister Historiæ Scholasticæ, & alij. Nonnulli quos lubens, ab validissimis motus argumentis, sequor, nomine Cæli intelligunt non unum duntaxat Cœlum Empyreum, sed universum Corpus cœleste, cunctos orbes complectens, perfectos quod ad substantiam, numerum, ordinem, magnitudinem, figuram, partium denique densitatem & raritatem; sine luce tamen, motu & distinctione Siderum, quæ mox addita. Vidend. Basilius homilia 11. super Genesin. Terram autem exaudiunt Ambrosius, Theodoretus, Chrisostomus, Beda aliique cum Græci tum Latini, quod nomen ipsum præ se fert verum Terra (quam initio, לפניים, id est, prius & ante alia fundatam canit Propheta Psalmo c i i. 26.) Elementum; intra quod quum plurimum reliqua tria Elementa contineantur, docente eleganter Basilio homilia 11. existimandum cum Terra simul Aquam, Aerem & Ignem facta, quod bene censent idem Basilius, Damascenus lib. 11. cap. v. & Beda loco sæpe indicato.
units.tr: Many interpret the name heaven as the Heaven of Heavens, commonly called the Empyrean, adding that this created heaven was soon filled with angels. Earth, however, they take as wholly formless prime matter, which nevertheless had a certain capacity for future forms, sketched as it were in colours by earth, water and the abyss; since it was, by its own power and quality, potentially all the forms, it could not unfittingly be marked by the names of each of them. Theodoret, in questions xi and xiv on Genesis, Basil in homilies ii and iii on Genesis, Bede in his Hexaemeron, Alcuin, Rabanus, the Master of the Sentences, and following them the Scholastic theologians, likewise Nicholas of Lyra, the Master of the Scholastic History, and others, held this view. Some, whom I gladly follow, moved by very strong arguments, understand by the name of heaven not only the Empyrean heaven but the whole heavenly body, embracing all the spheres, perfect as to substance, number, order, magnitude, figure, and finally the density and rarity of its parts; but without light, motion and the distinction of the stars, which were added afterwards. See Basil, homily ii on Genesis. Those who understand earth are Ambrose, Theodoret, Chrysostom, Bede and others, both Greek and Latin, since the name itself truly bears the sense of earth (which the Prophet, in Psalm 102:26, sings as founded first, לפניים, that is, before and in front of other things), as an element. Since the other three elements are largely contained within it, as Basil teaches elegantly in homily ii, we must think that earth was made together with water, air and fire. This view is rightly held by the same Basil, by Damascene in book ii, chapter v, and by Bede in the place often cited.

units.la: Terra autem, quam cum Cælo ante alia omnia creavit DEVS, qualis? Spiritui sancto, והארץ היתה תהו ובהו: Latino Interpreti Inanis & Vacua; alijs Solitudo & Inanitas; Inculta & vacua; Vanitas & Nihil; Otiosum & Indigestum; Desolata & Inanis; Septuaginta, Ἀόρατος καὶ ἀκατασκεύαστος, Invisibilis & Incomposita; Paraphrastæ Onkelo, דריא ודקניא deserta & vacua. תהו res bruta, stupens, attonita Hebræis, qui vocem hanc etiam referunt ad tenebricosam & deformem terræ faciem, eam ob causam, quod intendentes in illius cognitionem attonitos reddat. בהו ex vi vocis inchoatio & rudimentum Formæ.
