Si enim verbum verbo reddendum, sonat In eo est; adeo ut præter Subjecti potentiam, quæ jam erat inchoata, in eo Forma etiam esset intelligenda. Vult igitur his verbis Moyses Terram in principio fuisse sine Luce, sine ullo ornatu & decore, vacuam fuisse (ut Ionathæ habet paraphrasis) hominibus, animantibus, plantis; non distinctam in montes, valles, campos; non eminuisse supra Aquas, sed ijs omni ex parte opertam; talem denique, ut vere posset appellari materia invisibilis & informis. Sapient. xi, 18. utque merito חשך Tenebræ fuisse dicantur על־פני תהום super facies Abyssi חשך enim quasi Privatio (Peripateticis celebre rerum creandarum Principium) Formarum, quæ singulis propriæ & ad futurum ornatum necessariæ, mox erant addendæ. על־פני super facies, vel superficies; ut, indicante Cajetano, designetur utrumque hemisphærium obscurum fuisse, tenebrosum, altissimis aquis obrutum. תהום Abyssus, quam Basilius diffinit copiosam aquam, ad cujus fundum non facile penetrari potest deorsum versus: Augustinus vero ad Psalmum xlii. profunditatem impenetrabilem & incomprehensibilem, dici fere solitam in aquis; quibus altitudo, quæ penetrari usque ad fundum non potest.
units.tr: But what sort of earth was it that God created before all other things, together with heaven? The Holy Spirit says: והארץ היתה תהו ובהו [vehaaretz hayta tohu vavohu], "and the earth was without form and void." The Latin translator renders inanis et vacua (empty and void); others solitudo et inanitas (solitude and emptiness); inculta et vacua (waste and empty); vanitas et nihil (vanity and nothing); otiosum et indigestum (idle and undigested); desolata et inanis (desolate and empty). The Septuagint has Ἀόρατος καὶ ἀκατασκεύαστος (invisible and unformed), invisibilis et incomposita (invisible and unordered). The Chaldee paraphrast Onkelos has דריא ודקניא [dari va-dakinia], deserta et vacua (deserted and empty). תהו [tohu] is for the Hebrews a stupefying, bewildering thing, and they refer this word also to the dark and shapeless face of the earth, for the reason that it makes those who try to know it stunned. בהו [vohu], by the force of the word, denotes the beginning and rudiment of a form. For if the word is rendered word for word, it means in it is, so that, besides the power of the subject, which was already begun, a form too is to be understood in it. Moses therefore wishes by these words to say that the earth at the beginning was without light, without any ornament or beauty, empty (as Jonathan's paraphrase has it) of men, animals and plants; not divided into mountains, valleys and plains; not rising above the waters, but covered by them on every side; in short, such that it could truly be called invisible and formless matter (Wisdom 11:18). And it is rightly said that there was חשך [choshekh], darkness, upon the face of the deep, על־פני תהום [al-penei tehom]. For choshekh, like the privation celebrated among the Peripatetics as the principle of things created, is the lack of forms, each proper to its own adornment and necessary for the future, which were soon to be added. As for על־פני [al-penei], upon the face or surface, Cajetan's view indicates that each hemisphere was dark, shadowy and overwhelmed by the deepest waters. תהום [tehom], the deep, which Basil defines as a copious water whose bottom cannot easily be reached by going downwards; Augustine, on Psalm 42, says that it is usually called an impenetrable and incomprehensible depth in the waters, a height that cannot be penetrated down to the bottom.

units.la: ורוח אלהים Et Spiritus Domini, Sanctus, ut unanimi consensu tradunt Patres & Græci & Latini; non Ventus, ut vult adversus Hermogenem Tertullianus; non Aer, ut Theodoretus quæst. viii. super Genesin; non Vis, Impetus, & Efficacia quædam vitalis & fœcunditatis plena, Aquis impressa ab DEO; quæ mens Chrysostomo Homilia iii. in Genesin: nam nimis absurda Cajetani metaphora per Spiritum Domini, Angelos exaudientis.
units.tr: ורוח אלהים [veruach Elohim], and the Spirit of God, Holy, as the Fathers, both Greek and Latin, hand down with one voice; not wind, as Tertullian maintains against Hermogenes; not air, as Theodoret holds in question viii on Genesis; not some power, impulse and efficacy of life, full of fruitfulness, impressed on the waters by God, which is Chrysostom's understanding in homily iii on Genesis. For Cajetan's metaphor, which by the Spirit of God understands the angels who hear, is far too absurd.

units.la: מרחפת erat, ferebatur, volitabat, motabat se, flabat, ut Onkeli & Ionathæ paraphrases sonant; ad verbum incubabat, ut docent Hieronymus in Quæstionibus Hebraicis super Genesin, Diodorus Episcopus Tarsensis, & apud Basilium ad hunc locum Syrus quidam vir magnus: Elegante metaphora. Sicut enim Aves ovis incubant, ut calefaciendo & calore quasi animando pullos excludant: ita Spiritus DEI incubabat Aquis, ut ista Corpora, quæ animanda & formanda erant, vivificaret. Hoc enim Spiritus Sancti officium.
units.tr: מרחפת [merachefet] means was, was carried, hovered, moved itself, blew, as the paraphrases of Onkelos and Jonathan sound; literally it means brooded, as Jerome teaches in his Hebrew Questions on Genesis, Diodorus, bishop of Tarsus, and a certain great Syrian man cited by Basil on this passage. It is an elegant metaphor. For just as birds brood over eggs, so that by warming them and as it were quickening them with heat they hatch the chicks, so the Spirit of God brooded over the waters, to give life to those bodies which were to be quickened and formed. For this is the office of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: על־פני המים super facies Aquarum; Has ad Mundi generationem & originem pertinere, Stoicorum fuit sententia, quæ apud Senecam lib. iii. Natural. quæst. cap. XIII. Quanta vero fuerit tunc temporis Aquarum profunditas, quanta vis & copia, docent præter alios Beda & Cajetanus.
units.tr: על־פני המים [al-penei hamayim], upon the face of the waters. That these waters belonged to the generation and origin of the world was the opinion of the Stoics, as cited by Seneca in book iii of his Natural Questions, chapter xiii. How great the depth of the waters was at that time, and how great their force and abundance, is taught by Bede and Cajetan, among others, super facies Aquarum.

units.la: Talis igitur Christianorum de Rerum ex Nihilo primordiis, Spiritu Sancto docente, doctrina.
units.tr: Such, then, is the doctrine of the Christians concerning the primordial origin of things out of nothing, taught by the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Philosophi veteres Materiam Rebus omnibus advocant aliam alij: quorum veritatis fere assertores obtinent se, qui ὕλη & Chaos nominant. ὕλη definitur, Primum unicuique Subiectum, ex quo fit aliquid; & in quod, postquam quod factum corrumpitur, ultimum abit & resolvitur. Chaos autem, ab Græca voce χάω, nihil aliud illis, quam limus & fusilis materia, non diversarum naturarum, sed unius simplicis & indivisæ substantiæ & formæ, habens in se virtutem seminariam Rerum omnium, quas formaturus erat inde DEVS. Unde sequitur creata mox omnia matris suæ indolem, alia magis, minus alia, retulisse, ac pondus aliquod obtinuisse, quo ad medium inclinarent, suamque sympathiam tum ad Terram, tum inter se mutua quasi incubatione contactu & sensu veluti, hodieque, exercerent, ut latius hæc Gerardus Mercator in suo Atlante.
units.tr: The ancient philosophers each postulate a different matter as the basis of all things. Those who come closest to the truth, as they claim, are the ones who name it ὕλη [hyle] and Chaos. ὕλη is defined as the first subject of each thing, from which something is made, and into which, once the made thing is corrupted, it finally passes and is dissolved. Chaos, however, from the Greek word χάω [chaō], meant for them nothing other than a muddy, fluid matter, not of different natures but of one simple and undivided substance and form, containing within itself the seminal power of all the things that God was going to form from it. Hence it follows that all created things at once took on something of their mother's character, some more and some less, and acquired a certain weight by which they inclined towards the centre, and that they still exercise their sympathy both towards the Earth and among themselves, by a mutual contact and feeling, as it were a brooding, even today, as Gerardus Mercator discusses at greater length in his Atlas.

units.la: ὕλη Rerum omnium principium statuunt Ægyptij Philosophi, Zeno, & alij.
units.tr: The Egyptian philosophers, Zeno and others hold that ὕλη [hyle] is the principle of all things.

units.la: Ægypti apud Manethum in Naturalium Epitome, & Hecatæum I. de illorum Philosophia libro, volunt ἀρχὴν μὲν εἶναι τὴν ὕλην, ἐπὶ τὰ ποσαρα ἐπιχεῖα ἐξ αὐτῆς ἀγαπῆσιαι, καὶ Ζῶα τινα ἐκ τῆς ὕλης ... and living things from it.
units.tr: The Egyptians, according to Manetho in his Epitome of Natural Things and Hecataeus in the first book of his work on their philosophy, hold that the beginning is matter, from which [...] and some living things from matter [ἀρχὴν μὲν εἶναι τὴν ὕλην, ἐπὶ τὰ ποσαρα ἐπιχεῖα ἐξ αὐτῆς ἀγαπῆσιαι, καὶ Ζῶα τινα ἐκ τῆς ὕλης ...]

units.la: Zeno Citticus Mnasei F. Cratetis auditor, à quo Stoicorum secta initium sumsit, ὁ Θεὸς, ut Caussam Efficientem (quem paullo ante ὁ ποιῶν dixit) καὶ ὁ ὕλη, ut Materiam (quam supra τὸ πάσχον indigetavit) Rerum principia asserit: Theodoreto scribente sermone IV.
units.tr: Zeno of Citium, son of Mnaseas, a hearer of Crates, from whom the Stoic school took its beginning, asserts that God [ὁ Θεὸς], as efficient cause (whom he had just called "the agent" [ὁ ποιῶν]), and matter [ἡ ὕλη], as material cause (which he had earlier called "that which is acted upon" [τὸ πάσχον]), are the principles of things, as Theodoret writes in his fourth discourse.

units.la: Qualitatem ὕλη addunt, Plato, Xenocrates, Anaxagoras, Archelaus.
units.tr: Plato, Xenocrates, Anaxagoras and Archelaus add a quality to matter.

units.la: Plato, apud eundem Theodoretum, ὁ ὕλη σωματοειδὴς dixit esse, & ἀμερῆ αἰσθητὰ, καὶ αἰσθητικὰ, καὶ ἄπειρα ποιητικῶς. Qui potuisset felicius ἀλφηθεῖν Moisce illa תהו ובהו? Adscribit deinde divinus Philosophus ὕλη hanc omnia paullo post ἡ ὕλη τῆς ποιότητος accepisse. Ποιητικῶς ibi Platoni, qui eidem paullo ante Θεὸς. De hac autem Platonis opinione & M. Tullius Academic. quæst. I v. Plato, inquit, ex Materia omnia in se recipiente, (erat enim, ut dixi, בְּרֵאשִׁית, habens in se sua virtute quidquid producendum) Mundum esse factum censet à DEO sempiternum. Apud eundem tamen quatuor Elementa agnoscit, lib. I. de Nat. Deorum. Quibus enim oculis, ait, intueri potuit vestier Plato fabricam illam tanti operis, quam construxit à DEO atque ædificari mundum fecit quæ moles? quæ ferramenta? qui vectes? quæ machinæ? qui ministri tanti muneris fuerunt? quemadmodum autem obedire & parere voluntati Architecti Aer, Ignis, Aqua, Terra, potuerunt? Priore loco considerat Plato Materiam illam informem & indigestam ὕλης Molem; posteriore vero, quæ ex prima illa Materie sunt digesta; hic demum quasi hujus Universi, ibi vero causam principem.
units.tr: Plato, according to the same Theodoret, said that matter is bodily, indivisible, perceptible and capable of perception, and infinite in its capacity to be shaped. Who could have expressed Moses' tohu and bohu more happily? The divine philosopher then ascribes to this matter, a little later, that it received the quality of all things. The word "making" there refers to Plato, who had just before called him God. On this opinion of Plato, Marcus Tullius also writes in Academica, book I: "Plato," he says, "holds that the world was made by God, and is eternal, out of a matter receiving all things into itself (for it was, as I said, bereshit [בְּרֵאשִׁית], having in itself by its own power whatever is to be produced). Yet in the same work he acknowledges four elements, in the first book On the Nature of the Gods. With what eyes, he says, could Plato have looked upon that workshop of so great a work, which he built with God and caused the world to be constructed? What mass was it? What tools? What levers? What machines? Who were the ministers of so great a task? And how could Air, Fire, Water and Earth have been able to obey and serve the will of the Architect?" In the first passage Plato considers that formless and undigested mass of matter, the mass of ὕλη; in the second, the things arranged out of that first matter; here, finally, as it were of this universe, there as its chief cause.

units.la: Xenocrates Karthaginiensis, teste Theodoreto, Sermone quarto, ἄναρχον ὕλην, ex qua omnia sunt facta, dixit.
units.tr: Xenocrates of Carthage, according to Theodoret in his fourth discourse, spoke of matter without beginning [ἄναρχον ὕλην], out of which all things were made.

units.la: Anaxagoras quemadmodum de eo scribit M. Tullius lib. II. Academic. quæst.) Materiam infinitam dixit esse, ex qua omnia generentur: camque, particulas similes inter se minutas, eas primum confusas, postea in ordinem adductas à Mente divina. Augustinus lib. de Civitate Dei v I I I. cap. II. Anaxagoras, ait, ejus (Anaximenem designat) auditor, harum rerum omnium, quas videmus, effectorem divinum Animum sensit & dixit ex infinita Materia, qua constaret similibus inter se particulis, rerum omnium genera, pro modulis & speciebus propriis, singula fieri, sed Animo faciente divino. Eleganter autem memineunt & Cicero & Augustinus ex sententia magni Philosophi, Particularum inter se similium minutarum. Hinc enim apud alios Anaxagoræ ὁμοιομερεία, similium partium natura, vel partium similitudo. Lucretius lib. II. de Rer. Natura: Nunc & Anaxagoræ scrutemur ὁμοιομερείας, Quam Græci memorant. Et paullo post: Principium Rerum quam dicit ὁμοιομερείας: Offa videlicet è pauxilleis atque minuteis Ossibus; sic & de pauxilleis atque minuteis Visceribus viscus gigni; Sanguenque creari Sanguinis inter se multeis coeuntibus guttais; Ex aurique putat miceis consistere posse Aurum; & de terreis Terram concrescere parveis Sic ignem inter se parveis coëuntibus nasci Ignibus; exigueis Humorem humoribus esse. Cetera consimili fingit ratione putatque.
units.tr: Anaxagoras, as Marcus Tullius writes of him in Academica, book II: "He said that matter is infinite, from which all things are generated, and that it consists of tiny particles similar to one another, which at first were confused and afterwards were brought into order by a divine Mind." Augustine, in City of God, book VIII, chapter 2: "Anaxagoras, his hearer (he means Anaximenes), perceived and said that a divine Mind is the maker of all these things we see, and that from infinite matter, which consists of similar particles, each kind of thing is made according to its own measures and species, but by the making of the divine Mind." Cicero and Augustine rightly recall, in the words of the great philosopher, "tiny particles similar to one another." From this, in others, comes Anaxagoras's homoiomereia [ὁμοιομερεία], "the nature of similar parts," or "similarity of parts." Lucretius, in book II of On the Nature of Things: "Now let us also examine the homoiomereiai of Anaxagoras, which the Greeks mention." And a little after: "The principle of things which he calls homoiomereia: bones, that is, from tiny little bones; so too entrails are born from tiny little entrails; and blood is created by drops of blood coming together; and gold is thought to be able to consist of tiny grains of gold, and earth to grow from tiny earth particles. So fire is born from fires coming together, and moisture is made of tiny moistures. He imagines and thinks the rest by a similar reasoning."

units.la: Sic Justinus λογ. ΘΕΩΝΕΤ. ΠΡΟΣ ΕΛΛ. Αναξαγόρας, inquit, ὁ Κλαζομενίως δεχας τῶν πάντων τὰς ὁμοιομερείας εἶναι φησι. Servius item ad illud Virgilij iv. Aeneid. Exoriare aliquis nostris ex ossibus ultor.
units.tr: So Justin, in his Address to the Greeks [λόγος Θεωνέτ. πρὸς Ἕλληνας]: "Anaxagoras of Clazomenae, he says, held that the homoiomereiai are the principles of all things." Likewise Servius, on that line of Virgil in Aeneid IV: "Rise up, some avenger, from my bones."

units.la: Secundum Anaxagoram, inquit doctus Interpres, qui dicit ὁμοιομέρειαν, id est, membrorum similitudinem esse in rebus creandis, id est, ex ossibus, ex sanguine, ex medullis. Nam omnia pro parte sui transeunt in procreationem. Anaxagoras tamen ad vi. Virgilij Eclogam Rerum materiam ponit in Igne.
units.tr: "According to Anaxagoras," says the learned commentator, "who calls it homoiomereia, that is, the similarity of members, in the things to be created, that is, from bones, from blood, from marrow. For all things pass, each in its part, into generation." Anaxagoras nevertheless, on the sixth Eclogue of Virgil, places the matter of things in fire.

units.la: Auditorem habuit Anaxagoras Archelaum; qui non dubium quin ejusdem cum praeceptore fuerit sententiae de Materia Infinita: certe etiam ipse (scribit de eo Augustinus) de particulis inter se similibus (sic enim legendum) quibus singula quaeque fierent, ita Omnia constare putarit, ut inesse etiam Mentem diceret, quae corpora similia, id est, illas particulas conjungendo & dissipando, ageret omnia. Hic tamen apud Plutarch. & Diogenem Laertium lib. ii. praeter Αερα ἄπειρον, adfert duo εἶναι αἰτίας ἡρεστας, Θερμὸν καὶ Ψυχρὸν. Idem apud Justinum Martyrem, λογ. ΘΕΩΝΕΤ. Αερα ἄπειρον, & quae circa eum sunt, Πυκνότητα καὶ Μανωσιν, Omnium Rerum principia agnoscit. De Archelao, ut & Anaxagora, legendus etiam Joannes Stobaeus lib. i. φυσικ. cap. xiii.
units.tr: Anaxagoras had Archelaus as his hearer. There is no doubt that he shared his teacher's opinion about infinite matter. Certainly he too, as Augustine writes of him, "thought that all things consist of particles similar to one another (for so it must be read), from which each single thing is made, and said that Mind is also present, which, by joining and separating these similar bodies, that is the particles, drives all things." Here, however, according to Plutarch and Diogenes Laertius, book II, besides infinite Air he adduces two causes of generation, the hot and the cold. The same man, in Justin Martyr's Address to the Greeks, acknowledges infinite Air, and the things about it, rarity and density, as the principles of all things. On Archelaus, as also on Anaxagoras, one should also read Joannes Stobaeus, Physics, book I, chapter 13.

units.la: Chaos Rerum Materiam suggerunt Hesiodus & Ovidius.
units.tr: Hesiod and Ovid suggest Chaos as the matter of things.

units.la: Ille in Theog. Ἠ πι μὲν πεῶτα χαος ἡνετ', αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα Γαῖ' εὐρύστερνος πάντων ἕδος ἀσφαλὲς αἰεὶ Ἀθανάτων.
units.tr: Hesiod in the Theogony: "Verily, first of all Chaos came into being, then broad-breasted Earth, the ever-secure seat of all the immortals" [Ἠ μὲν πρῶτα χάος ἦν, αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα Γαῖ' εὐρύστερνος πάντων ἕδος ἀσφαλὲς αἰεὶ Ἀθανάτων].

units.la: Hic vero lib. i. Metamorphoseos: Ante Mare & Terras, &, quod tegit omnia, Caelum, Vnus erat toto Natura vultus in orbe, Quem dixere Chaos.
units.tr: Ovid, in book I of the Metamorphoses: "Before sea and lands, and heaven which covers all things, there was one face of nature throughout the whole orb, which they called Chaos."

units.la: quod quid sit, subjicit: ——— rudis indigestaque moles, Nec quidquam nisi pondus iners:
units.tr: What it was, he adds: "a rough and undigested mass, and nothing but inert weight."

units.la: תהו ובהו, ait Spiritus sanctus per Mosche; Τλη, inquit Plato σωματοειδὴς, ἄμορφος, ἀνειδὴς, αἰχημάτος, ἄπειρον παντῶς. Pergit Ovidius: ——— congestaque eodem Non bene junctarum discordia semina rerum.
units.tr: "Tohu and bohu" [תהו ובהו], says the Holy Spirit through Moses; hyle, says Plato, is "bodily, formless, shapeless, without figure, infinite in every way" [σωματοειδὴς, ἄμορφος, ἀνειδὴς, ἀσχημάτιστος, ἄπειρον παντῇ]. Ovid goes on: "and the seeds of ill-joined things, their discord heaped together in the same place."

units.la: Elementa primitus volunt Rebus omnibus initium dedisse multi Philosophi; eaque Unum vel Plura. Circa Unum versatos lego non paucos.
units.tr: Many philosophers hold that the elements first gave a beginning to all things, and that these are either one or several. I read of not a few who dwelt on the one.

units.la: Anaximenes Eurystrati F. Milesius, Anaximandri auditor, apud Plutarch. de Philosophorum Placitis, ἔρχεται τῶν ὄντων Αερα censet: ἐκ γὰρ τούτων τὰ πάντα γίνεσθαι, ἐξ εἰς αὐτὰ ἀναλύεσθαι. Testatur hoc de eodem Justinus Martyr λογ. ΘΕΩΝΕΤ. ΤΕΛΤΩΝ Αναξιμένης, inquit, κ... videndus & Stobaeus lib. i. Physic. Eclog. cap. xiii. Qualis autem hic Aer Philosopho? Notant alij. M. Tullius in Lucullo de Anaximene: Infinitum Aera esse dicit, ex quo omnia gignerentur. Et lib. i. de Nat. Deor. Anaximenes Aera Deum statuit, eumque gigni, esseque immensum & infinitum, & semper in motu. Augustinus lib. viii. de Civitate Dei, cap. ii. Ipse (Anaximander) Anaximenem discipulum & successorem reliquit, qui omnes Rerum causas Infinito Aeri dedit: nec Deos negavit, aut tacuit; non tamen ab ipsis Aerem factum, sed ipsos ex Aere ortos credidit. Diogenes Laertius lib. ii. ex mea emendatione: ἀπ, ait de Anaximene, δεχλῶ Αερα εἰπ τῶν ἀπείρων. Archelaum etiam apud Plutarchum, Diogenem Laertium, & Justinum ejusdem esse mentis, paullo ante docui.
units.tr: Anaximenes, son of Eurystratus, of Miletus, a hearer of Anaximander, according to Plutarch's On the Opinions of the Philosophers, holds that air is the principle of things, for from it all things come to be and into it they are resolved. Justin Martyr also attests this of the same man in his Address to the Greeks, and Stobaeus, Physics, book I, Eclogues chapter 13, should also be consulted. But what kind of air was this, to the philosopher? Others have noted it. Cicero, in Lucullus, says of Anaximenes: "He says that air is infinite, from which all things are generated." And in book I of On the Nature of the Gods: "Anaximenes made Air a god, and said that it is generated, and is immense and infinite, and always in motion." Augustine, in City of God, book VIII, chapter 2: "Anaximander himself left as his disciple and successor Anaximenes, who gave all the causes of things to infinite Air. Nor did he deny or pass over the gods, but did not believe that Air made them; rather, he believed they arose from Air." Diogenes Laertius, book II, on my emendation: "Anaximenes, he says, held that air is the infinite." I have shown above that Archelaus too, in Plutarch, Diogenes Laertius and Justin, was of the same mind.

units.la: Suffragatur Praeceptori suo Diogenes Apolloniates F. M. Tullius i. de Nat. Deor. Quid Aer, quo Diogenes Apolloniates utitur Deo, quem sensum habere potest, aut quam formam Dei? Sed qualis Aer? Theodoretus λογω δ. Θεῖ ὕλης καὶ κόσμω, hoc indicat, apud quem Philosophus scribit Σπιχεῖον esse τὸν Αερα, Κοσμος ἀπείρως, Κενὸν ἄπειρον· τὸν δὲ Αερα κυκνούμενον καὶ δεαυτούμενον γίνεσθαι ἀνειρηκέναι τῶν κόσμων· ἀρ ἐκ τοῦ μὴ ὄντος. μὴ ἐντῷ γίνεσθαι, ἐὰ εἰς τὸ μὴ ὂν φθείρεσθαι. Hunc Aerem compotem Rationis (ut Caussæ Efficientis) idem dicit apud Augustinum de Civitate Dei lib. viii. cap. ii. Diogenes quoque Anaximenis alter auditor, Aerem quidem dixit Rerum esse Materiam, de qua omnia fierent: sed cum esse compotem divinæ Rationis, sine qua nihil ex eo fieri posset. Apud Stobæum lib. i. Φυσικ. ἐκλογ. Ἀρχὰ ἀπείρον Principium rerum ponit.
units.tr: Diogenes of Apollonia supports his teacher, as Marcus Tullius says in book 1 of On the Nature of the Gods: "What is the air that Diogenes of Apollonia uses as a god? What sense can it have, or what form can a god have?" But what kind of air is meant? Theodoretus, in sermo 4 of the Graecarum affectionum curatio, makes this clear. There the philosopher writes that air is the element, that the cosmos and the void are infinite, and that air, by condensing and rarefying, produced the worlds, coming into being from what is not and passing away into what is not [ὅτι ἀὴρ στοιχεῖον, κόσμος ἄπειρος, κενὸν ἄπειρον; τὸν δὲ ἀέρα πυκνούμενον καὶ ἀραιούμενον γίνεσθαι; ἐκ τοῦ μὴ ὄντος, εἰς τὸ μὴ ὂν φθείρεσθαι]. Augustine, in book 8, chapter 2, of The City of God, says that this air is endowed with reason, as the efficient cause: "Diogenes too, another hearer of Anaximenes, said that air is the matter of things, from which all things are made; but that it is endowed with divine reason, without which nothing could be made from it." Stobaeus, in book 1 of the Physical Extracts, says he posits the infinite as the principle of things [ἀρχὴ ἄπειρον].

units.la: Heraclitus βλύσωνος F. Ephesius, apud Diogenem Laertium lib. ix. Plutarch. lib. i. περὶ τ' Ἀρσοχυτ. & Justinum arbitratur τὰ πάντα ἐκ πυρὸς σωτ-ζεναι, ἐ εἰς τὴν ἀναλύσεις. Idem apud Theodoretum λέγω δ. putat, Ἐν εἶναι τὸ Παν, ἀχιν-τον καὶ πεπερασμένον. Eandem huius Philosophi sententiam aperiunt M. Tullius lib. iv. Academicarum quæst. & iii. de Natura Deorum, ubi: Sed omnia vestri, Balbe, referre solent ad igneam vim, Heraclitum, ut opinor, sequentes, &c. Et Vitruvius lib. ii. cap. ii. Heraclitus Ephesius, inquit, qui propter obscuritatem Scriptorum à Græcis Σκοτεινὸς est appellatus, Ignem principium Rerum posuit. Gradus rerum notat ab Heracliti mente Plutarch. lib. i. Ignem crassissimis particulis præditum Terram fieri; deinde Terram, quum ab Igne laxatur, Aquam; hanc vero exhalantem & extenuatam, Aerem. Plutarchi verba sunt: ὅτι τὸ πυρὸς, εἰς αὐτὸ συστῆ-ναι, γίνεται γῆ. Heraclitì opinionem varie refutat Lucretius lib. i. de Rerum natura.
units.tr: Heraclitus of Ephesus, son of Blyson, according to Diogenes Laertius, book 9, and Plutarch, book 1, On the Opinions of the Philosophers, and Justin, holds that all things come from fire and are resolved back into it [τὰ πάντα ἐκ πυρὸς συνίστασθαι καὶ εἰς αὐτὸ ἀναλύεσθαι]. Theodoretus, in the same sermo, holds that the All is one, unborn and finite [ἕν εἶναι τὸ πᾶν, ἀγένητον καὶ πεπερασμένον]. Marcus Tullius, in book 4 of the Academic Questions and book 3 of On the Nature of the Gods, sets out the same opinion of this philosopher: "But all your school, Balbus, is accustomed to refer things to the fiery force, following Heraclitus, I think, etc." Vitruvius, book 2, chapter 2, says: "Heraclitus of Ephesus, who because of the obscurity of his writings was called the Dark One by the Greeks [Σκοτεινός], posited fire as the principle of things." Plutarch, book 1, notes the stages of things according to Heraclitus' view: fire, made of the thickest particles, becomes earth; then earth, when loosened by fire, becomes water; and this, when it evaporates and becomes thin, becomes air. Plutarch's words are: "because fire, when it condenses, becomes earth" [ὅτι τὸ πῦρ, εἰς αὐτὸ συστῆναι, γίνεται γῆ]. Lucretius, book 1 of On the Nature of Things, refutes Heraclitus' opinion in various ways.

units.la: Huius autem cum Heraclito sententiæ fuisse Hippasum Metapontinum notant Clemens Alexandrinus & Theodoretus sermone iv. Stobæus Physic. Eclog. i. c. xiii.
units.tr: Clement of Alexandria and Theodoretus, in sermo 4, note that Hippasus of Metapontum was of the same opinion as Heraclitus. Stobaeus, Physical Extracts, book 1, chapter 13, says the same.

units.la: Hos sequuti Stoici Ignem, apud August. lib. viii. de Civit. Dei cap. v. id est, corpus unum ex his quatuor Elementis, quibus visibilis hic Mundus constat, & viventem & sapientem & ipsius Mundi fabricatorem, atque omnium, quæ sunt in eo, eumq; omnino Ignem Deum esse putaverunt. De his multa M. Tullius lib. ii. de Nat. Deor. & iv. Academic. quæst.
units.tr: The Stoics followed these men in holding fire to be the principle. Augustine, in book 8, chapter 5, of The City of God, says that they thought fire, that is, the one body out of these four elements of which this visible world consists, is living, wise, the maker of the world itself and of all that is in it, and that this fire is altogether God. Marcus Tullius treats these matters at length in book 2 of On the Nature of the Gods and book 4 of the Academic Questions.

units.la: Thales Milesius, qui, teste cum aliis Lactantio lib. i. cap. v. de falsa religione, unus è septem Sapientum numero fuit, quique primus omnium quaesisse de rebus naturalibus tradidit: Aquam esse dixit, à qua nata sunt Omnia: Deum esse Mentem quæ ex Aqua cuncta formaverit (fere est ut putem ab Magno Philosopho lectum illud Spiritus Sancti: ורוח אלהים מרחפת על פני המים, Et Spiritus Dei incubabat super faciem Aquarum) Ita Materiam omnium posuit in Humore: principium caussamque nascendi posuit in Deo. Sic M. Tullius lib. i. de Nat. Deor. Thales Milesius, qui primus de naturalibus rebus quæsivit, Aquam dixit esse initium Rerum: Deum autem eam Mentem, quæ ex Aqua cuncta fingeret. Augustinus lib. viii. cap. ii. Ionici generis princeps Thales Milesius Aquam putavit Rerum esse principium, & hinc omnia Elementa Mundi, ipsumque Mundum & quæ in eo gignuntur, existere. Videndi idem, ejusdem lib. cap. v. Seneca lib. iii. Natur. quæst. cap. xiii. Vitruvius lib. ii. cap. ii. & in Proœmio lib. viii. Servius ad vi. Virgilij Eclogam, Justinus Martyr λογ. Ἑλλην. Stobæus lib. i. Ἐκλογ. Φυσικ. cap. xiii. Eundem designat Lucretius lib. i. —— aut Humorem quicunque putarunt Fingere Res ipsum per se.
units.tr: Thales of Miletus, who, as Lactantius attests with others in book 1, chapter 5, of On the False Religion, was one of the seven Wise Men and was the first to hand down that he had inquired into natural things, said that water is the origin from which all things are born, and that God is the Mind which formed all things from water. (I am almost inclined to think that the great philosopher read that saying of the Holy Spirit: "And the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters" [ורוח אלהים מרחפת על פני המים].) Thus he placed the matter of all things in moisture, and the principle and cause of their coming into being in God. So Marcus Tullius, book 1 of On the Nature of the Gods: "Thales of Miletus, who first inquired into natural things, said that water is the beginning of things, but God is the Mind which shapes all things from water." Augustine, book 8, chapter 2: "Thales of Miletus, the head of the Ionian school, thought that water is the principle of things, and that from it come all the elements of the world, the world itself and what is born in it." See also the same book, chapter 5. Seneca, book 3 of Natural Questions, chapter 13; Vitruvius, book 2, chapter 2, and in the Preface to book 8; Servius on the sixth Eclogue of Virgil; Justin Martyr, Hortatory Address to the Greeks; and Stobaeus, Physical Extracts, book 1, chapter 13, all agree. Lucretius, book 1, points to the same man: "or those who thought that moisture, whatever it is, forms things by itself."

units.la: Thaleti sex reliquos Sapientes consensisse primos, notat Tullius iv. Acad. quæst.
units.tr: Marcus Tullius, in book 4 of the Academic Questions, notes that Thales agreed first with the six other Wise Men.

units.la: Xenophanes apud Theodoretum λογ. δ. Terram opinatur omnium Rerum initium; Sic enim canit: Ἐκ γῆς γὰρ πάντα πάντα, ἐ εἰς γῆν πάντα πλάττα.
units.tr: Xenophanes, according to Theodoretus, sermo 4, holds that earth is the origin of all things. For he sings thus: "For all things are from earth, and all things are shaped back into earth" [Ἐκ γῆς γὰρ πάντα, καὶ εἰς γῆν πάντα πλάττεται].

units.la: Apud Stobæum lib. i. Φυσικ. ἐκλογ. cap. xiii. Τάλω ponit, Ἀφ' ἧς πάλιν. Fuit ejus fortean mentis & Hesiodus in Theogonia: Γαῖα δὲ τὶ πρῶτον μὲν ἐγείνατο ἴσον ἑαυτῆ Οὐρανὸν ἀστερόεντ' ἵνα μιν πὰρ πάντα καλύπτῃ.
units.tr: In Stobaeus, book 1, Physical Extracts, chapter 13, he posits earth, "from which again [all things are formed]" [ἀφ' ἧς πάλιν]. Perhaps Hesiod in the Theogony was of the same mind: "Earth first bore starry Heaven, equal to herself, to cover her on every side" [Γαῖα δέ, τὴ πρῶτον μὲν ἐγείνατο ἴσον ἑαυτῆ Οὐρανὸν ἀστερόεντα, ἵνα μιν πάντα καλύπτῃ].

units.la: & quæ sequuntur. Neminem tamen Physicorum τὸ γῆν Rerum principium pronunciasse testatur Aristoteles lib. i. τῶν μὴ τὰ Φυσ. Lucretius certe nonnullos fuisse innuit lib. i. ubi inter alia: —— Terramve creare Omnia, & in Rerum naturas vortier omnes.
units.tr: And so on. Yet Aristotle, in book 1 of the Metaphysics, testifies that none of the natural philosophers pronounced earth to be the principle of things. Lucretius certainly indicates that some did, in book 1, where among other things he says: "or to create all things from earth, and that all should change into the natures of things."

units.la: Succedunt, qui, ut Lucretij verbis utat lib. i. de Nat. Rerum: —— conduplicant primordia Rerum, Aera jungentes Igni, Terramque Liquori: Et qui quatuor ex Rebus posse omnia rentur, Ex Igni, Terra, atque Anima procrescere & Imbri. Terram & Aquam committit Homerus apud Probum ad v I. Virgilij Eclogam, hoc versu, Ἀλλ' ὑμεῖς μὲν πάντες Γ᾽ ὕδωρ καὶ γαῖα ἡψηόντε.
units.tr: Next come those who, to use Lucretius' words in book 1 of On the Nature of Things, "double the first beginnings, joining air to fire and earth to liquid; and those who think all things can arise from four things, from fire, earth, spirit and rain." Homer, in Probus on the sixth Eclogue of Virgil, joins earth and water in this line: "But all of you, water and earth, are..." [Ἀλλ' ὑμεῖς μὲν πάντες, γ' ὕδωρ καὶ γαῖα, ἡψηόντε].

units.la: Solam tamen Aquam videtur agnoscere apud Stobæum φυσικ. ἐκλογ. lib.1. cap.xiii. Ὡ κεαυὸς τ᾽ ἔσπερ ἥλιος πάντων πῦρ.
units.tr: Yet he seems to acknowledge water alone, in Stobaeus, Physical Extracts, book 1, chapter 13: "Just as the sun is ... fire of all things" [Ὡς ... πάντων πῦρ].

units.la: Aerem & Terram inducit apud eundem Probum Euripides.
units.tr: Euripides introduces Air and Earth, as Probus also reports.

units.la: Ignem & Terram ponit Parmenides Pyreris F. Eleates, Xenophanis auditor, qui apud Diogenem Laertium lib. ix. adfirmat δύο ἀρχαὶ στοιχεῖα, πῦρ καὶ γῆν; Ignem quidem δημιουργὸν τάξιν ἔχειν; Terram vero τ᾽ λης. De eodem legendus & Theodoretus
units.tr: Parmenides, son of Pyres, the Eleatic, a pupil of Xenophanes, holds that the two first principles are fire and earth. Diogenes Laertius, book ix, affirms this: "two principles, elements, fire and earth" [δύο ἀρχαὶ στοιχεῖα, πῦρ καὶ γῆν]. Fire has the role of craftsman [δημιουργὸν], but earth is matter [ὕλην]. Theodoretus should also be read on the same point.

units.la: 10 λογ. δ. Igni & Terræ tertium quid addit Pherecydes, Badyos F. Syrus, Pittaci auditor, χρόνον: quemadmodum de eo scribit Probus ad v I. Virg. Eclogam: Consentit & Pherecydes, inquit, sed diversa adfert Elementa: Ζεὺς μὲν, inquit, καὶ χθὼν λῶ καὶ χρόνῳ, Ignem, Terram, ac Tempus significans; ζλῶα εἶναι Æthera, qui regat Terram, qua regatur Tempus, in quo universa pars moderetur. Confirmat illa Diogenes Laertius lib. i. docens servari adhuc Pherecydis Syri libellum, quem scripsit de Rerum principiis, cujus initium erat, Ζεὺς μὲν ἐ χρόνῳ εἰς ἀεί, ἐ χθὼν λῶ. χθονὴ δ᾽ ὄνομα εἴρηται γῆ, ἀπασὴ αὐτῇ ζεὺς γίνεσθαι δίδοι.
units.tr: Pherecydes of Syros, son of Babys and a pupil of Pittacus, adds a third thing to fire and earth: time [χρόνον]. Probus, on Virgil's Eclogue vi, writes about him: "Pherecydes agrees," he says, "but offers different elements." Zeus, he says, and earth, and time: "Zeus indeed [Ζεὺς μὲν], and earth [χθὼν], and time [χρόνῳ]," signifying fire, earth and time. Aether is the one that rules the earth, and time is what rules the earth, and in time the whole world is governed. Diogenes Laertius, book i, confirms this, teaching that the little book of Pherecydes of Syros, which he wrote On the Principles of Things, survives to this day. Its opening was: "Zeus indeed and Time always, and Earth." The name Earth was given to the earth, which Zeus gave to Time as a gift.

units.la: Quatuor Elementa Rerum omnium primordia volunt πῦρ, Τ᾽ ὕδωρ, Ἀέρα, γῆν, Athimas apud Clementem Alexandrinum στρωμ. v i. Xenophanes Colophonius
units.tr: They hold that four elements are the first principles of all things: fire, water, air, earth. So Athimas, in Clement of Alexandria, Stromata v; Xenophanes of Colophon.

units.la: 20 apud Diogenem Laertium lib. ix. (hic tamen, teste Probo, Terram solum & Aquam prodit: scribente vero Theodoreto, ἐκ τῆς γῆς tantum φύσει ἀπαντᾶν εἰρηκεν) & Empedocles Agrigentinus apud Lucretium lib. i. Athenagoram in Apologia, M. Tullium lib. iv Academic. quæst. Servium ad vi. Virg. Eclogam, & alios: qui tamen, ut notant Clemens Alexandrinus στρωμ. ἐκ Ἀ. Justinus Martyr ἀπολογητικ. λογ. ἐκ Ἀ. & Diogenes Laertius lib. viii. Elementis addit duas primarias Potentias Amicitiam atque Dissidium, Φιλίαν καὶ Νεῖκος, quarum altera uniendis, altera distrahendis inserviat Elementis; ὧν ἡ μὲν ἰσι ἐνωτικὴ, τὴ δ᾽ διακριτικόν. Versus, quibus Philosophus suam de Compositione tam speciosa sententiam aperuit, quique sparsim apud varios & minus emendate leguntur; castigo & connecto in meo ad Annales
units.tr: Xenophanes of Colophon, in Diogenes Laertius, book ix (though here, according to Probus, he gives only earth and water, while Theodoretus says he held that everything arises by nature from earth alone); Empedocles of Agrigentum, in Lucretius, book i; Athenagoras in his Apology; Cicero, Academica, book iv; Servius on Virgil's Eclogue vi; and others. Yet, as Clement of Alexandria notes in the Stromata, Justin Martyr in his Apology, and Diogenes Laertius, book viii, Empedocles adds to the elements two primary powers, Friendship and Strife [Φιλίαν καὶ Νεῖκος], one of which serves to unite the elements and the other to separate them. Of these, the one is uniting [ἐνωτικὴ] and the other separating [διακριτικόν]. The verses in which the philosopher set out his view of composition, so striking, are read scattered among various authors and not well edited. I have corrected and connected them in my commentary on the Annals.

units.la: 30 Ennî Commentario: ubi etiam doceo, Poetam, quem dixi, & Lucilium in hac classe collocandos.
units.tr: 30 In my commentary on Ennius, where I also show that the poet I mentioned, and Lucilius, should be placed in this class.

units.la: Aristoteles Nicomachi F. Stagirites philosophatur, præter στοιχεῖα quatuor, quintum etiam esse, ex quo Αἰθέρα constituunt, ἀλλοίων ἢ αὐτῆ τ' κίνησιν εἶναι; κυκλοφορικὸν χῶρ, scribente Diogene Laertio lib. v. Quæ plautius notantur ab Theodoreto termone iv. Illustrio in ejus vita & Justino Martyre, qui in Appendice Confutationis quarundam Græcarum opinionum, sententiam magni Philosophi docte refellit.
units.tr: Aristotle, son of Nicomachus of Stagira, philosophizes that, besides the four elements (στοιχεῖα), there is also a fifth, out of which they constitute the aether, which is of a different kind and has a circular motion (κυκλοφορικὸν χῶρ). Diogenes Laertius records this in book v. It is noted more fully by Theodoret in the fourth discourse, by Justin Martyr in his Appendix to the Refutation of Certain Greek Opinions, and in the life of Aristotle by Illustrius, where Justin learnedly refutes the view of the great philosopher.

units.la: Sunt qui quatuor primas Qualitates, Calidum, Frigidum, Humidum, Siccum, statuunt Rerum omnium principia. Zeno Eleates Pyrrheti F. vult Naturam omnium Rerum γιγνόσθαι ἐκ Θερμῶν καὶ Ψυχρῶν, ἡ ξηρὸν ἡ γῆς, teste Diogene Laertio libro ix.
units.tr: Some hold that the four primary qualities, hot, cold, moist and dry, are the principles of all things. Zeno of Elea, son of Pyrrhetes, holds that the nature of all things comes into being out of the hot and the cold, or the dry and the moist (ἐκ Θερμῶν καὶ Ψυχρῶν, ἢ ξηρὸν ἢ ὑγρόν), according to Diogenes Laertius, book ix.

units.la: 40 Eo forte respicit Ovidius lib.1. Metamorph.
units.tr: 40 Ovid perhaps has this in mind in book 1 of the Metamorphoses:

units.la: Obstabatque aliis aliud: quia corpore in uno
units.tr: Each thing hindered the other, because in one body

units.la: (Intelligit Chaos & primam Rerum creandarum massam.)
units.tr: (He means chaos and the first mass of things yet to be created.)

units.la: Frigida pugnabant Calidis; Humentia Siccis;
units.tr: Cold things fought with hot, moist with dry,

units.la: Mollia cum Duris; sine Pondere habentia Pondus.
units.tr: soft with hard, and things without weight had weight.

units.la: Archelaus parum constans, nunc hoc, nunc illud sentiens, ut paulo ante dixi, apud Plut. περὶ τῶν Ἀρχῶν. & Diogenem Laertium lib. ii. adserit δύο εἶναι αἰτίας ψύχεσθαι Θερμὸν καὶ ψυχρὸν. De Calore & Frigore Universi caussis, multa Bernardinus Telesius lib. 1. de Rerum Natura, cap.i. & seqq.
units.tr: Archelaus, not very consistent, now holding one view and now another, as I said a little earlier, asserts in Plutarch's work On the Principles, and in Diogenes Laertius book ii, that there are two causes of cooling, the hot and the cold (δύο εἶναι αἰτίας ψύχεσθαι Θερμὸν καὶ ψυχρόν). Bernardinus Telesius, in book 1, chapter 1 and following, of On the Nature of Things, discusses at length the causes of heat and cold in the universe.

units.la: Strato, notante Stobæo lib. i. Φυσικ. ἐκλογ. Σπιχεῖα nominat & ψυχρὸν, Elementa & Frigidum. Idem apud alios nullum agnoscit Mundi Moliorem, sed cum suapte natura, vi ac potestate, qualis nunc est, talem ab omni æternitate fuisse censet.
units.tr: Strato, as Stobaeus notes in book i of the Physical Extracts, names as elements both the hot and the cold. Elsewhere he acknowledges no maker of the world, but thinks that it has been from all eternity such as it now is, by its own nature, power and force.

units.la: 50 Τὸ Ἄπειρον statuunt Anaximander & Melissus. Ille enim Milesius Praxiados F. vult omnium Rerum principium esse τὸ Ἄπειρον, non distinens Ἀέρα, ἢ Τ᾽ ὕδωρ, ἢ ἄλλο: ut scribunt M. Tullius iv. Academic. quæst. Augustin. lib. viii. de Civitate Dei, cap.ii. Justinus Martyr ἀπολογητ. λογ. ἐκ Ἀ. Diogenes Laertius lib. ii. Adeundi & Aristoteles lib. i. de Physic. Auscult. Plut. de Placit. Philosoph. M. Tullius de Natur. deor. Eusebius in Præpar. Evangelica.
units.tr: 50 Anaximander and Melissus hold the Infinite (τὸ Ἄπειρον) to be the principle. Anaximander of Miletus, son of Praxiades, holds that the principle of all things is the Infinite, without distinguishing air, or water, or anything else, as Cicero writes in Academica iv, Augustine in De Civitate Dei viii, chapter 2, and Justin Martyr in his Apology (ἀπολογητ. λογ. ἐκ Ἀ.). Diogenes Laertius book ii should also be consulted, as should Aristotle, Physics book i, Plutarch's On the Opinions of the Philosophers, Cicero's On the Nature of the Gods, and Eusebius in the Preparation for the Gospel.

units.la: Melisso vero Ithagenis F. Samio placet τὸ πᾶν ἄπειρον esse καὶ ἀναλλοίωτον καὶ ἀκίνητον, teste Diogene lib. ix. De eo M. Tullius in Lucullo, & Theodoretus sermone iv.
units.tr: Melissus of Samos, son of Ithagenes, holds that the All is infinite, unchanging and immovable (τὸ πᾶν ἄπειρον εἶναι καὶ ἀναλλοίωτον καὶ ἀκίνητον), according to Diogenes, book ix. Cicero discusses him in the Lucullus, and Theodoret in the fourth discourse.

units.la: Philolaus Pythagoreus, si Stobæo fides, lib. i. Eclog. Physicæ τὸ πέρας agnoscit, καὶ τὸ ἄπειρον; Finitum & Infinitum.
units.tr: Philolaus the Pythagorean, if Stobaeus can be trusted, in book i of the Physical Extracts, acknowledges the Limit (τὸ πέρας) and the Infinite (τὸ ἄπειρον): the finite and the infinite.

units.la: Occurrunt ultimo loco, qui Atomos Rerum principia imaginantur. Inter eos primi loci Leucippus Eleates, qui Zenonis fuit auditor. Hic enim censuit ἄτομα esse omnia, ἐξ ὧν ἀλλήλα μεταβάλλειν; & universum istud κενὸν esse ἐκ πλήρες σωμάτων: Mundos autem fieri, τῶν σωμάτων εἰς τὸ κενὸν ἐμπιπτόντων καὶ ἀλλήλοις εἰς δίνην ἐκλυομένων, &c. Quæ fusius explicantur apud Diogenem Laertium lib. ix. M. Tullium iv. Academic. quæst. Stobæum lib. i. Physic. Eclog. cap. xiii. & alios.
units.tr: Last come those who imagine atoms to be the principles of things. Among these, the first place belongs to Leucippus of Elea, a pupil of Zeno. He held that all things are atoms (ἄτομα), out of which the others are changed, and that the whole void is made up of full bodies. Worlds come into being when bodies fall into the void and are carried into a whirl against one another, and so on. These matters are explained at more length by Diogenes Laertius, book ix, by Cicero in Academica iv, by Stobaeus in Physical Extracts book i, chapter 13, and by others.

units.la: Ab Leucippo eruditus Democritus Milesius; qui, scribente eodem Diogene, lib. ix. Universi hujus semina affirmat ἄτομος ἐκ κενόν: Atomos autem & magnitudine & numero esse Infinitas, ferrique ἐν τῷ ὅλῳ διηρημένας, atque ita σχήματα τὰ συγκείμενα gignere, πῦρ, ὕδωρ, ἀέρα, γῆν. Videndi & Tullius in Lucullo & Theodoretus sermone iv.
units.tr: Democritus of Miletus, educated by Leucippus, according to the same Diogenes, book ix, asserts that the seeds of this universe are atoms and void (ἄτομος ἐκ κενόν). The atoms, he says, are infinite in size and number, and are carried about in the whole, divided, and thus form compounds, namely fire, water, air and earth. Cicero in the Lucullus and Theodoret in the fourth discourse should also be consulted.

units.la: Stultitiæ suæ hæreditatem, ut utar verbis Lactantii, Democritus reliquit Epicuro; de cujus opinione M. Tullius lib. i. de Finibus, Plutarchus περὶ τῶν ἀρχῶν. Theodoretus sermone iv. Diogenes Laertius lib. x. Augustinus de Civit. Dei, lib. viii. cap. v. Servius ad vi. Virg. Eclog. Justinus. Scripsit hæc ipse Epicurus lib. ii. περὶ φύσεως, & in μεγάλῃ ἐπιτομῇ.
units.tr: Democritus left his folly as an inheritance, to use Lactantius's words, to Epicurus. Cicero, book i of On Ends, Plutarch's On the Principles, Theodoret in the fourth discourse, Diogenes Laertius book x, Augustine in De Civitate Dei viii, chapter 5, Servius on Virgil's Eclogue vi, and Justin discuss his opinion. Epicurus himself wrote these things in book ii of On Nature and in his Great Epitome.

units.la: Eiusdem mentis Metrodorus Chius apud Theodoretum & Stobæum, quum Rerum initia facit ἄτομα (sic & vocat Atomos: quod ita sint exigua, ut nec sectionem nullam nec divisionem admittant) καὶ κενόν.
units.tr: Metrodorus of Chios shares the same view. Among others, Theodoret and Stobaeus report that he makes the beginnings of things atoms (which is also his name for them, because they are so small that they admit neither cutting nor division) and the void.

units.la: Horum de Principiis Rerum sententias sequutus Diophantus Syracosius, secta Pythagoreus, teste Theodoreto, sermone sæpe laudato.
units.tr: Following these views on the principles of things, Diophantus of Syracuse, a Pythagorean by school, according to Theodoret in the often-cited discourse, held similar opinions.

units.la: Epicureos esse se cum multis aliis sunt professi Lucretius & Virgilius. Ille quidem lib. i. ubi non paucis versibus canit totam hanc Rerum naturam duabus ab initio rebus constare Corporibus & Inani, in quo Corpora sita, & per quod huc illuc feruntur ac moventur: Virgilius vero Ecloga vi. qua Materiam Universi penit sub persona Sileni duplicem Inane & Corpora; ubi legenda omnino quæ scribit Interpres ejus Servius, docte satis & eleganter.
units.tr: Lucretius and Virgil professed that they were Epicureans, along with many others. Lucretius, in the first book, where he sings in not a few verses that this whole nature of things consists from the beginning of two things, bodies and void: the bodies are placed in the void, and through it they are carried and moved hither and thither. Virgil, in Eclogue vi, where under the persona of Silenus he portrays the matter of the universe as twofold, void and bodies. Here one should certainly read what his interpreter Servius writes, learnedly and elegantly enough.

units.la: Finem his faciam cum magno Philosopho lib. i. Physic. Ζητοῦντες οἱ ἐξ φιλοσοφίας περὶ τῶν Ἀληθείας, ἐκ τῶν φύσιν τῶν ὄντων, ἐξητεσάμενοι. In Rerum Principiis notandis plerique Philosophi magnas fecere ruinas, Et graviter magni magno cecidere ibi casu,
units.tr: I will end these points with the great philosopher in the first book of the Physics: "Those who, from philosophy, seek the truth about things, seek from the natures of beings" [Ζητοῦντες οἱ ἐξ φιλοσοφίας περὶ τῶν Ἀληθείας, ἐκ τῶν φύσιν τῶν ὄντων, ἐξητεσάμενοι]. In noting the principles of things, most philosophers have made great ruins, and the great have fallen there with a heavy fall, as Lucretius says.

units.la: ait Lucretius. Quanta autem inter omnes dissensio? Conciliari forte possent aliquo modo, sed cui bono? Veritatem hic nos docet ipsa Verbi Dei Veritas, cujus lucem in tantis tenebris si sequamur, nunquam aberrabimus. Ab Deo, qui Invisibilium maximus, omnium visibilium maximus est Mundus, inquit Augustinus libro de Civitate Dei xi. cap. iv. Sed Mundum esse conspicimus, Deum esse credimus. Quod autem Deus Mundum fecerit, nulli tutius credimus quam ipsi Deo. Ubi eum audivimus? nusquam melius, quam in Scripturis sanctis, ubi dixit Propheta ejus: In principio fecit Deus Cœlum & Terram. Numquid nam ibi fuit ipse Propheta, quando fecit Deus Cœlum & Terram? Non. Sed fuit ibi Sapientia Dei, per quam facta sunt omnia, quæ in Animas etiam sanctas se transfert, Amicos Dei & Prophetas constituit, eisque opera sua sine strepitu intus enarrat. Et paulo post: Ex his unus erat ipse Propheta, qui dixit & scripsit: In principio fecit Deus Cœlum & Terram: qui tam idoneus testis est, per quem Deo credendum sit, ut eodem Spiritu Dei, quo hæc sibi revelata cognovit, etiam ipsam Fidem nostram tanto ante prædixerit. Et quæ alia apud doctissimum Theologum. Deus igitur est, qui ex Nihilo cuncta creavit: ἐν ἐξ αὐτοῦ, καὶ δι' αὐτοῦ, ἐς οὗ αὐτὸν τὰ πάντα, inquit Paullus Apostolus epistola ad Romanos, cap. xii. in fine.
units.tr: But how great is the disagreement among them all! Perhaps they could be reconciled in some way, but to what good? Here the Truth of God's own Word teaches us, and if we follow its light amid such great darkness, we shall never go astray. Augustine, in the eleventh book of the City of God, chapter 4, says that of the invisible things of God, the greatest is the world, and of visible things the greatest is the world. "But we see that the world exists, and we believe that God exists. That God made the world, we believe no one more safely than God himself. Where have we heard him? Nowhere better than in the holy Scriptures, where his prophet said: In the beginning God made heaven and earth." Was the prophet himself present when God made heaven and earth? No. But there was present the Wisdom of God, through which all things were made, which also passes over into holy souls, makes them friends of God and prophets, and inwardly declares to them his works without noise. And a little after: Of these, one was the prophet himself, who said and wrote: "In the beginning God made heaven and earth"; he is such a fitting witness, through whom God is to be believed, that by the same Spirit of God by whom he came to know these things revealed to him, he also foretold our very faith so long before. And other things in that most learned theologian. God therefore is he who created all things out of nothing: "For of him, and through him, and to him are all things," says the Apostle Paul in the epistle to the Romans, chapter 12, near the end [ἐξ αὐτοῦ, καὶ δι' αὐτοῦ, καὶ εἰς αὐτὸν τὰ πάντα].

units.la: Ex nihilo: creatum esse quidquid in Rerum natura.
units.tr: Out of nothing: whatever exists in the nature of things has been created.

units.la: C A P. IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: CAP. IV. Ordo Rerum ab Deo Sex Dierum spatio creatarum.
units.tr: CAP. IV. The order of the things created by God in the space of six days.

units.la: QVVM Deus prima Mundi Corpora, eaque, ut dixi, indigesta & tenebrosa, ex Nihilo creasset, ab opere coepto non cessavit, sed Creatis jam ornatum conciliaturus primo die, sublatis Tenebris, Lucem addidit; secundo & tertio Confusionem ab Aquis removit & Terra; reliquis diebus, quae לפניים prius & ante omnia crearat, quibusque ornandis & digerendis triduum impenderat, Coelum porro Stellis, Aërem Avibus, Piscibus Aquam, Animantibus denique Terram complevit. Ordine de singulis hoc capite pauca dicam. Coepit Decor ille ab Creatorum jam Corporum, ut decebat, praestantiore, quod Coelum: huic duplex additum ab Deo ornamentum, Lumen & Motus; illud nominatur ut principem obtinens locum; hic subticetur, ut quod propter illud. Lumen per se sensibus omnium est notum; Motus non nisi doctis per Lumen. De Luce igitur primo die facta sic Spiritus Sanctus: Dixit Deus, יהי־אור, Fiat Lux; & facta est Lux: quo respiciunt Paulus epist. ii. ad Corinthios, iiii, 6. & Auctor Epist. ad Hebraeos xi, 3. Lux magnis Philosophis prima qualitas activa primi Corporis, id est, Coeli: non tamen intra illud contracta, sed ad omnes res corporeas effusa: quum ejus beneficio fit in Inferioribus, quidquid fit ab Coelo. Creanda sane erat, ut per eam, quemadmodum notant Basilius, Damascenus, Beda & alij, conspicua fierent & manifesta omnia Dei opera, eaque non modo humanis oculis cernerentur, sed cernerentur cum voluptate; quum ejus auxilio varietas & pulchritudo rerum omnium appareat: ut canit Auctor lib. iiii. Eldrae, cap. vi, 40. Certe auferatur Lux; omnia in tenebris ignota jacebunt, nec fieri poterit, ut proprium & indicum divinitus demonstrent decorem. Quid in rebus corporatis ad adspectum Luce jucundius? quid ad recreandum animos laetius? quid ad rerum usum commodius? Ad Mundi sane ornatum nihil esse pulchrius: ad percipiendam rerum omnium, cum primis coelestium, cognitionem nihil esse adcommodatius: ad repraesentandum denique res spirituales & divinas nihil aptius, quotidiana docet experientia. Quid dicam de adjiduo ejus & numquam cessante munere distinguendi tempora, dies & noctes. Quae pluribus prosequuntur cum alij, tum Dionysius de Divinis nominibus cap. iv. & de caelesti Hierarchia cap. xv. Fuit autem Lux illa primo die creata (quo Caeli loco, an in Oriente, Meridie vel Occasu; videndi Bonaventura ii. Sentent. dist. xiii. art. 1. quaest. 2. Hugo lib. 1. de Sacrament. part. 1. cap. 29. Magist. Sent. dist. xiii. lib. ii. Aegidius part. 1. cap. xvi. Cajetanus, & alij) non alia, quam quae postea Lux Solis, corporea & sensibilis (ut uno calculo volunt Patres, tam Graeci quam Latini, & omnes prope Theologi, ex quibus praecipue consulendus Bonaventura ii. Sent. distinct. xiii.) primo quidem triduo (primam enim distinxit & distinvit dierum nostrorum trinitatem, quod quo modo factum ostendunt, serram inter se reciprocantes, hinc Basilius ii. Homilia super Genesin, & Damascenus lib. ii. de fide Orthodoxa, cap. vii. inde Augustinus lib. 1. ad Genesin cap. xi. & xvi. Beda in ἐξαημέρ. Thomas 1. part. quaest. lxvii. art. 4.) informis & imperfecta, vel potius quod diffusior minoris claritatis, producta scilicet secundum communem lucis naturam: quarto vero die perfecta & in unum Solis corpus conglobata, datis illi non modo speciali & determinata ad particulares effectus, distinguendaque Dierum & Noctium tempora, virtute: verum etiam, quae jam habet, magnitudine, figura & pulchritudine. Legendi Dionysius loco, quem laudavi, eumque sequuti Thomas part. 1. quaest. lxvii. art. 4. & quaest. lxx. art. 1. Dionysius Carthusianus ad cap. 1. Genes. art. 9. & firmis, quae dixi, probans argumentis Benedictus Pererius in Genes. lib. 1. doctissime refutans alia sententes. Ambrosius enim Catharinus suo in Genesin Commentario Lucem, quae primo die creata, non aliam quidem fuisse notat, quam Solis, eamque perfectam aeque ac nunc est; S. Iem adfirmans & reliquos Planetas primo die factos: sed, quod quarto die Stellae inerrantes conditae, Moschen per ἀναφαλαίωσιν mentionem tunc simul fecisse insignium Astrorum, ostendendo numeris omnibus absoluto Caeli ornatui.
units.tr: When God had created the first bodies of the world from nothing, and these, as I have said, were unformed and dark, he did not stop his work there. Intending to give ornament to what he had made, on the first day he removed the darkness and added Light. On the second and third days he removed the confusion caused by the waters and the earth. In the remaining days he filled the heavens with stars, the air with birds, the waters with fish, and finally the earth with living creatures. These were the things he had created first and before all else [לפניים], and he had spent three days adorning and arranging them. I will say a few things about each of these in order. The ornamentation began with the most excellent of the bodies already created, as was fitting, namely the heavens. God added a twofold adornment to them, Light and Motion. Light is named first because it holds the principal place; motion is passed over in silence, because it exists for the sake of the other. Light is known to everyone through the senses; Motion is known only to the learned, through Light. The Holy Spirit describes the making of light on the first day in this way: "God said, יהי־אור, Fiat Lux, Let there be light; and there was light." To this passage Paul refers in 2 Corinthians 4:6, and the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews in 11:3. To the great philosophers, light is the primary active quality of the first body, that is, of the heavens. Yet it is not confined within that body but is poured out over all corporeal things, since by its agency whatever comes from the heavens takes effect in the lower world. It was certainly created so that, as Basil, Damascene, Bede and others point out, all of God's works might be made visible and manifest through it, and might be seen not only by human eyes but seen with delight; for by its help the variety and beauty of all things appear, as the author of the fourth book of Esdras sings (4 Esdras 6:40). Certainly, if light were taken away, all things would lie unknown in darkness, and they could not display their own proper and divinely appointed beauty. What is more pleasant than light for the sight of corporeal things? What is more cheerful for refreshing the spirits? What is more useful for the use of things? Everyday experience teaches that nothing is more beautiful for the adornment of the world, nothing more suitable for grasping the knowledge of all things, especially the heavenly ones, and finally nothing more apt for representing spiritual and divine things. What shall I say of its constant and never-ceasing office of distinguishing the times, days and nights? Others, and Dionysius in On the Divine Names, chapter 4, and On the Celestial Hierarchy, chapter 15, treat these matters at greater length. That light was created on the first day (as to its place in the heavens, whether in the East, the South or the West, see Bonaventure, Sentences 2, distinction 13, article 1, question 2; Hugh, De Sacramentis 1, part 1, chapter 29; the Master of the Sentences, distinction 13, book 2; Giles, part 1, chapter 16; Cajetan, and others) was none other than the light which afterwards became the light of the Sun, corporeal and sensible. So the Fathers, both Greek and Latin, and almost all the theologians hold in one voice (on this, Bonaventure, Sentences 2, distinction 13, is especially to be consulted). Yet it was at first unformed and imperfect for the first three days (for it was the first to mark and distinguish the threefold division of our days, and they show how this was done by the saws working against one another: Basil, Homily 2 on Genesis, and Damascene, On the Orthodox Faith 2, chapter 7; then Augustine, On Genesis 1, chapters 11 and 16; Bede, Hexaemeron; Thomas, part 1, question 67, article 4), or rather, being more diffused and of less brightness, it was produced in the common nature of light. But on the fourth day it became perfect and gathered into the one body of the Sun, endowed not only with a special and determined power for particular effects and for distinguishing the times of days and nights, but also with the magnitude, shape and beauty which it now has. Dionysius, in the passage I have cited, should be read, and after him Thomas, part 1, question 67, article 4, and question 70, article 1; Dionysius the Carthusian on Genesis 1, article 9; and Benedict Pererius, On Genesis book 1, who very learnedly refutes other opinions by firm arguments such as those I have given. For Ambrose Catharinus, in his Commentary on Genesis, holds that the light created on the first day was none other than that of the Sun, and as perfect then as it is now; he affirms that the other planets were also made on the first day. But he says that Moses, by a recapitulation [ἀναφαλαίωσιν], mentioned at that point the stars which were made on the fourth day, since the stars were then made at once, showing that the adornment of the heavens was complete in all its parts.

units.la: Beda in suo ἐξαημέρῳ. Hugo de S. Victore lib. i. de Sacrament. Mag. Sent. lib. ii. Nicolaus Liranus & Tostatus in Commentariis suis ad Genef. alijque arbitrantur, primam illam Lucem non fuisse Solem, sed corpus quoddam lucidum ad similitudinem densæ lucentisque nubis in superiore parte mundi; quod in orbem quarto die conversum, & recepto in se Sole, Dierum & Noctium cœpit efficere vicissitudines. Contra eos consulendus Thomas part.i. quæst. lxvii. art. ult.
units.tr: Bede, in his Hexaemeron; Hugh of St Victor, De Sacramentis book 1; the Master of the Sentences, book 2; Nicholas of Lyra; and Tostatus, in their commentaries on Genesis, and others, think that the first Light was not the Sun but a certain luminous body, like a dense and shining cloud, in the upper part of the world. On the fourth day this body was turned into a sphere, and having taken the Sun into itself, it began to produce the alternation of days and nights. Against them Thomas, part 1, question 67, article last, should be consulted.

units.la: Theodoretus ad Genef. quæst. xiiii. & xvi. docet, Lucem, quam primo die creavit Deus, fuisse splendidissimam, quamque simul confertam nec hominum nec animalium visus potuisset sustinere; eamque ob causam quarto die fuisse in Solem, Lunam, Sidera dispertitam.
units.tr: Theodoret, on Genesis, questions 14 and 16, teaches that the Light which God created on the first day was most splendid, and that, being so concentrated, neither human nor animal sight could have endured it. For this reason, on the fourth day it was divided among the Sun, the Moon and the stars.

units.la: Gregorius Nazianzenus in oratione de Novo die Dominico, & Basilius sexta in Genesin Homilia, memoriæ produnt, primo die productam esse naturam Lucis, purissimam, sinceram, immaterialem; (miraculum hoc, Lucem, quæ Accidens, ab omni separare materia) quarto autem die factum esse Solis corpus, futurum deinceps primogenitæ Luci instar vehiculi.
units.tr: Gregory Nazianzen, in his oration on the New Day of the Lord, and Basil, in his sixth Homily on Genesis, record that on the first day the nature of light was produced as something most pure, sincere and immaterial (a wonder: light, which is an accident, separated from all matter). But on the fourth day the body of the Sun was made, to serve thereafter as a kind of vehicle for the first-born Light.

units.la: Damascenus lib. ii. de Fide Orthod. cap. vii. & Hugo Annot. in Genesin cap. vi. mutuati suam sententiam ex Gregorio Nysseno in Homilia super ἐξαήμερ. existimant, Lucem illam fuisse Elementum Ignis, qui nihil aliud, quam Lux.
units.tr: Damascene, On the Orthodox Faith 2, chapter 7, and Hugh, in his Annotations on Genesis, chapter 6, borrowing their opinion from Gregory of Nyssa in his Homily on the Hexaemeron, think that the Light of that day was the element of Fire, which is nothing other than Light.

units.la: Mirum autem videri debet, Augustinum, virum alioquin acerrimi judicii, lib. xi. de Civitate Dei, cap. vii. ambigere, utrum Lux illa fuerit Corporalis an Spiritualis; paullo post autem cap. ix. ut & lib. i. ad Genesin cap. iii. & lib. xii. Confessionum cap. ix. & xvi. (suffragantibus illi Eucherio in Commentario ad Genesin, & Ruperto lib. i. de Trinitate eiusque operibus cap. x: refellente vero Bonaventura Sententiarum secundo, distinct. xiii.) membrum posterius amplexum, argumentando censere nomine Cœli, quod initio creatum, significari Naturam Angelicam; Lucis autem voce, primo die factæ, confirmationem insinuari & consummationem Angelorum in gratia; per divisionem autem Lucis & Tenebrarum indicari segregationem Angelorum, qui boni, ab malis.
units.tr: It must seem remarkable that Augustine, a man otherwise of most keen judgment, in City of God book 11, chapter 7, hesitates whether that Light was corporeal or spiritual. Shortly afterwards, in chapter 9, and also in On Genesis book 1, chapter 3, and in Confessions book 12, chapters 9 and 16, he embraces the latter view, supported by Eucherius in his Commentary on Genesis and by Rupert in On the Trinity and His Works book 1, chapter 10. He argues that by the name Heaven, created at the beginning, the angelic nature is signified; by the word Light, made on the first day, the confirmation and perfection of the angels in grace is suggested; and by the division of Light and Darkness the separation of the good angels from the bad is indicated. Bonaventure, in Sentences book 2, distinction 13, refutes this view.

units.la: Sed enarrandis horum suffragiis & enervandis laboratum ab aliis. Pergo ad opus secundi Dici, quod his verbis delineat Spiritus Sanctus: Dixit Deus. יהי רקיע Fiat Firmamentum in medio Aquarum & dividat Aquas ab Aquis. Firmamentum nunc κατ' ἐξοχὴν pars Corporis Cœlestis, Octavus orbis, in quo Moyses scribit Genes. i, 17. Stellas ab Deo positas, inerrantes; de eo dicam lib. ii: Aliquando Corpus ex octo Cœlis, octavo nimirum & septem Planetarum orbibus; appellatione æqualiter in omnes quadrantes; & hinc quod Moyses in opere quarti dici scribat Deum factos Solem & Lunam collocasse in Firmamento: Nonnunquam totum illud Spacium, quod pellis seu cortinæ instar circum Terram expansum & diffusum.
units.tr: But the labour of others has been spent in explaining and weakening these opinions. I proceed to the work of the second day, which the Holy Spirit describes in these words: "God said, יהי רקיע, Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters. Firmament, now, in the proper sense, is part of the heavenly body, the eighth sphere, in which Moses writes at Genesis 1:17 that the fixed stars were placed by God. I shall speak of this in book 2. Sometimes the body of the eight heavens is meant, that is, the eighth sphere and the orbits of the seven planets, taken together in all four quarters. And hence, because Moses writes that God placed the Sun and Moon in the firmament in the work of the fourth day. Sometimes the whole space which is spread and diffused around the Earth like a skin or curtain is meant.

units.la: Firmamenti vox, si prima notione capiamus, huic loco non congruit. Nam fuerint Aquæ supercœlestes (quod tamen secus esse parebit ex sequentibus) quæ constituant in Corpore cœlesti Nonum orbem; non video tamen, quo pacto Octavus orbis Aquas illas dividat ab Inferioribus, quæ inter Elementa secundum, interpositis cum septem Planetarum cœlis, tum Elementis Igne & Aere. Dividere enim quid proprie dicitur illud, quod, nihil interjecto, medius est dividendis terminus.
units.tr: If we take the word Firmament in its primary sense, it does not fit this place. Suppose there were waters above the heavens (which, however, will appear otherwise from what follows), making up a ninth sphere in the heavenly body. I still do not see how the eighth sphere could divide those waters from the lower ones, since the seven planetary heavens, and the elements of fire and air, lie between them. For that is properly called dividing where the middle term is the thing divided, with nothing interposed.

units.la: Neque magis Firmamenti vocabulum, si multorum Cœlorum complexionem illud esse dicamus, convenit. Nam omnes cœlos secundum ipsorum substantiam in principio, vel לפנים ante omnia alia, conditos antea probavi. Deinde inter omnes Cœlorum orbes nullus est, qui vere disterminet Aquas supra Octavum Cœlum imaginarias ab Inferioribus, quæ Terræ adhærent; nec quidem Lunæ, quum inter ejus orbem & Aquas terrestres Elementa sint constituta Ignis & Aer.
units.tr: Nor does the word Firmament fit better if we say it is the complex of many heavens. For I have already shown that all the heavens were created in the beginning, in their substance, or לפנים, before all other things. Moreover, among all the spheres of the heavens there is none that truly separates the waters imagined above the eighth heaven from the lower waters that cling to the earth. Nor is the Moon's sphere such a boundary, since fire and air are placed between its orbit and the earthly waters.

units.la: Restat igitur, ut Firmamentum secundo die factum, exaudiamus totum illud spacium circum Terram expansum, quod obsidet & implet Aer, nomen Firmamenti nactus, non quod Corpus sit firmissimum (videmus enim tenuem esse admodum Aerem, instabilem & perpetua agitatione) sed quia interstitium & terminus firmissimus atque immutabilis, qui Superiores Aquas in sublimiore sui parte generari solitas (eas enim intelligendas mox dicam) segregget ab Inferioribus, quæ sub se. Hujus sunt mentis Augustinus lib. ii. de Genesi ad litt. cap. iiii. & x. Thomas parte I. quæst. LXVIII. Durandus II. Sentent. distinct. XIV. Rupertus lib. I, de Trinitate ejusque operibus cap. XXII. Augustinus Eugubinus sublime in sua Cosmopœia, Cajetanus & Benedictus Pererius in Genesin.
units.tr: It remains, then, that we understand the Firmament made on the second day to be that whole space spread around the earth, which the air occupies and fills. It received the name Firmament not because the body is most solid (for we see that air is very thin, unstable and in perpetual motion), but because it is a most firm and unchanging interval and boundary. It separates the upper waters, which are usually generated in its higher part (for I shall say shortly that these are to be understood), from the lower waters beneath it. Augustine holds this view in On Genesis to the Letter, book 2, chapters 4 and 10; so does Thomas, part I, question 68; Durandus, Sentences II, distinction 14; Rupert, On the Trinity and His Works, book 1, chapter 22; Augustinus Eugubinus, nobly, in his Cosmopoeia; and Cajetan and Benedict Pererius on Genesis.

units.la: Acceptum ita Firmamentum eleganter Hebraica voce רקיע vocatur expansio vel extensio, ab רקע extendere. Aer enim extenditur circum Aquas Inferiores, tamquam cortina vel tabernaculum; scribentibus & utentibus רקיע voce Prophetis, Davide, רקיע. Psalmo CIV, 3. & Iefchahhia cap. XL, 22. Apud quos notandum obiter Cælum pro Aere positum: quemadmodum aliis etiam Sacræ Scripturæ locis Aer usurpatur non solum pro Cœlo Sidereo, sed & Aereo: inde Cataractæ Cæli, id est Aeris, dicuntur apertæ ad obruendas aquis terras, Genes. VII, 11. inde DEVS scribitur Cælum, id est Aerem operire nubibus, Psalmo CXLVII, 8. inde Cæli, id est Aer, dare rorem suum, apud Zachariam VIII, 12. Sed notius hoc, quam ut pluribus probetur.
units.tr: Thus the Firmament is elegantly called in Hebrew רקיע, an expansion or extension, from רקע, to extend. For the air is stretched around the lower waters like a curtain or tent. The Prophets, David and Isaiah, write and use the word רקיע: Psalm 104:3, and Isaiah 40:22. Here it should be noted in passing that heaven is put for air, just as in other places of Sacred Scripture air is used not only for the starry heaven but also for the aerial. Hence the floodgates of heaven, that is of the air, are said to be opened to overwhelm the earth with water, Genesis 7:11. Hence God is said to cover the heaven, that is the air, with clouds, Psalm 147:8. Hence the heavens, that is the air, give their dew, in Zechariah 8:12. But this is too well known to need proof by many examples.

units.la: Firmamentum hoc vocatur paullo post, Genes. I, 8. & alibi, ab DEO שמיים, quasi quis dicat, ibi Aquæ, שם enim ibi, מים aquæ: quod nulli in Universo rei magis conveniens, quam Aeri; in cuius regione superiore ingens est & perennis aquarum ad pluvias terris subministrandas generatio. Hieronymus Epistola XXXIII. ad Oceanum.
units.tr: This Firmament is called shortly afterwards, Genesis 1:8, and elsewhere, by God שמיים, as if one said there waters, since שם means there and מים means waters. This name suits nothing in the universe better than the air, in whose upper region there is a huge and perpetual generation of waters to supply the earth with rain. Jerome, Letter 33 to Oceanus.

units.la: In hoc Firmamento volare scribuntur Aves ab Moyse Genes. I, 20, ut in sequentibus notabo. Legendus Beda in expositione operis quinti dici.
units.tr: Moses writes that birds fly in this Firmament, Genesis 1:20, as I shall note in what follows. Bede should be read on the exposition of the work of the fifth day.

units.la: Quum igitur totum illud spacium, quod inter Terram & Lunæ Cœlum interfusum, aquea materia plenum & densis vaporibus crassisque nubibus obductum esset, Ecclesiast. XXIV, 6. Iob. XXXVIII, 9. pars materiæ nebulosæ tenuior & levior, secundo die, infinita Dei potestate, abiit in Aerem, qui secundum substantiam quidem suam cum reliquis cœlis jam antea creatus erat, sed secundo die vicem finitoris adeptus, qui Aquarum molem in duas partiretur partes: quarum levissima tum temporis supra Aerem in præparatum sibi locum migravit, gravior autem circum Terram subsedit; factus hoc die non simpliciter, sed ut esset Firmamentum & tamquam intergerius paries, munusque suscipéret Aquas dividendi ab Aquis.
units.tr: Since, then, the whole space interspersed between the earth and the heaven of the Moon was full of watery matter and covered with dense vapours and thick clouds (Ecclesiasticus 24:6; Job 38:9), a part of this cloudy matter, the thinner and lighter part, passed on the second day, by the infinite power of God, into air. This air had already been created in its substance along with the other heavens, but on the second day it took on the role of a divider, to separate the mass of waters into two parts. The lightest part then migrated above the air into the place prepared for it, while the heavier part settled around the earth. This was done on that day not merely in itself, but so that the air might be the Firmament, as it were an intervening wall, and might undertake the office of dividing the waters from the waters.

units.la: Ex iis, quæ dixi, perspicuum, quales hic Aquas intelligendum: alteras quidem, quæ Terræ proximæ adhærent: alteras vero quæ in superiori Aere (media Aeris regio Philosophis dicitur) Solis, vapores ex Terra & Aquis Inferioribus quasi exugentis & ad pluvias præparantis, potentia generantur. Augustin. lib. XI. de Genesi ad litt. cap. XI. Has notant cum Iob cap. XXVI, 8. tum Schelomo Proverb. VIII, 28. ubi Sapientia dicit se adfuisse DEO, שחקים, nubes (nam improprie vertit Latinus interpres Aethera) firmanti & fontes aquarum (cœlestium) libranti, inque excelso aere suspendenti.
units.tr: From what I have said it is clear which waters are meant here: on the one hand those that cling close to the earth, and on the other those in the upper air (which philosophers call the middle region of the air). These are generated by the power of the sun, which draws up vapours from the earth and the lower waters and prepares them for rains. Augustine, On Genesis to the Letter, book 11, chapter 11. These are noted both by Job 26:8 and by Solomon, Proverbs 8:28, where Wisdom says that she was present with God, שחקים, the clouds (for the Vulgate translator wrongly renders it aether), establishing them and balancing the fountains of (heavenly) waters, and suspending them in the high air.

units.la: Hæc Cæli non semel appellatione veniunt in sacris litteris, ut videre est apud Moschen Genes. VII, 11. Ieremiam II, 13. I, 16. Malachiam III, 10, & alibi.
units.tr: These heavens are called by that name more than once in Sacred Scripture, as may be seen in Moses, Genesis 7:11; Jeremiah 2:13 and 1:16; Malachi 3:10, and elsewhere.

units.la: Hæ nubibus illigatæ & stupendum in modum suspensæ adiduè prædicant DEI potentiam. Iob XII, 15. XXVI, 8. Plinius XXXI. Nat. hist. cap. I.
units.tr: Hung in the clouds and suspended in a marvellous manner, these constantly proclaim the power of God: Job 12:15; 26:8; Pliny, Natural History, book 31, chapter 1.

units.la: Has ad DEVM laudandum invitant David Psalmo CXLVIII, 4. & Triumviri hymno, quem inter ignes Babylonicos canebant, vers. 60. utrimque Cæli nominantur ex proprietate vocis ibi Hebraicæ, quæ caret Singulari; quod moneo ne quis Aquas imaginetur ibi potius supra Cœlos, septem, inquam, Planetarum orbes Cœlumque octavum: quam Aerem, quem etiam Cælum dici jam probavi. Videndus omnino Benedictus Pererius diligentissimus enarrator.
units.tr: David invites them to praise God, Psalm 148:4, as do the three men in the hymn they sang among the Babylonian fires, verse 60. In both places heavens is named from the nature of the Hebrew word there, which lacks a singular. I warn against anyone imagining that waters are meant there above the heavens, that is, above the seven spheres of the planets and the eighth heaven, rather than the air, which I have already shown is also called heaven. Benedict Pererius, the most diligent commentator, must certainly be consulted.

units.la: Origenis, Aquas Superiores Bonos, Inferiores autem Malos interpretantis Angelos, opinionem refutant Epiphanius in Epistola ad Ioannem Hierosolymitanum. Basilius, recte tamen, Homil. III super Genesin, Hieronymus epistola ad Pammachium, & Rupertus lib. I. de operib. Sanctis. Trinit. cap. 23.
units.tr: The opinion of Origen, who interprets the upper waters as good angels and the lower waters as bad angels, is refuted by Epiphanius in his letter to John of Jerusalem. Basil also rightly refutes it, in Homily 3 on Genesis, as do Jerome in his letter to Pammachius, and Rupert, On the Works of the Holy Trinity, book 1, chapter 23.

units.la: Augustinus lib. XIII. Confessionum cap. 32. Superiores Aquas intelligit Spirituales, Inferiores Corporales; recantans sequè corrigens lib. II. Retractationum, cap. 6. qui aliam suam sententiam, timidius indicat lib. priori de Genesi contra Manich. cap. 11.
units.tr: Augustine, Confessions, book 13, chapter 32, understands the upper waters to be spiritual and the lower ones corporeal. He retracts and corrects this in Retractations, book 2, chapter 6, where he more timidly indicates another opinion of his, in the earlier book On Genesis against the Manichaeans, chapter 11.

units.la: Iustino Martyri ad XCIII. quæstionem Orthodoxorum, Philoni, Iosepho, Basilio Homilia III. super Genes. Theodoreto quæst. XI. Gennadio & Severiano in Catena citatis, Ambrosio lib. II. ἐξαημέρ. Augustino lib. XI. de Civit. Dei cap. ult. lib. II. de Genesi & in Dialogo LXV. quæst. 27. Bedæ lib. de natura rerum, alisque statt veras & naturales aquæ esse supra Cœlum Sidercum, quod ordine Octavum.
units.tr: Justin Martyr, in his answer to the ninety-third question of the Orthodox; Philo; Josephus; Basil, Homily 3 on Genesis; Theodoret, question 11; Gennadius and Severian, cited in the Catena; Ambrose, book 2 of his Hexaemeron; Augustine, City of God, book 11, last chapter, and On Genesis, book 2, and in the Dialogue, question 65, question 27; Bede, in his book On the Nature of Things; and others, hold that the waters above the starry heaven, which is the eighth in order, are true and natural waters.

units.la: {Note}
units.tr: {Note}

units.la: Bonaventuræ denique 11. Sent. distinct. xiiii. Ægidio 11. parte operis, quod scribit in ἐξαημερ. cap. 14. & seqq. aliisque Scholasticis Theologis; item Nicolao Lyrano, Toftato, Cajetano sedet Aquas Superiores esse Nonum Cœlum, quod Crystallinum vulgo indigetatur; Firmamentum autem vel Octavum Cœlum tantum, vel ipsum & simul reliquos Planetarum orbes.
