units.tr: Finally, Bonaventure, Sent. 11, distinction 14; Giles, in the second part of his work on the Hexaemeron, chapter 14 and following; and other Scholastic theologians; likewise Nicholas of Lyra, Tostatus and Cajetan, hold that the upper waters are the ninth heaven, commonly called the Crystalline. They hold that the Firmament is either the eighth heaven alone, or that heaven together with the remaining spheres of the planets.

units.la: Sed duo posteriorum placita penfatius ponderanda sese offerent libro primæ partis secundo.
units.tr: But the two latter opinions will present themselves to be weighed more carefully in the second book of the first part.

units.la: Succedit opus dici Tertij. Ait Spiritus sanctus: Dixit DEVS, יקוּו המים מתחת השמים אל־מקום אחד ותראה היבשה, Congregentur Aquæ quæ sub Cœlo sunt in unum locum & appareat arida: Et paullo post: תדשא הארץ דשא עשב מזריע זרע עץ פרי, Germinet terra germen herbam feminificantem semen arborem fructus facientem fructum speciei suæ, cujus semen in ea super terram.
units.tr: Then follows the work of the third day. The Holy Spirit says: "God said, let the waters under the heaven be gathered together into one place, and let the dry land appear" [יקוּו המים מתחת השמים אל־מקום אחד ותראה היבשה]. And a little after: "Let the earth bring forth grass, the herb yielding seed, and the fruit tree yielding fruit after its kind, whose seed is in itself upon the earth" [תדשא הארץ דשא עשב מזריע זרע עץ פרי].

units.la: Tria fiunt die Tertio: Jubet DEVS Aquas in unum abire locum; Terram apparere; omnes Herbarum Arborumque species prodire.
units.tr: Three things happen on the third day. God commands the waters to gather into one place; the earth appears; and all kinds of herbs and trees come forth.

units.la: Primo præcepto naturalis ab eo die vis & propensio cœpit esse Aquis, jam ante omnia cum Cœlo & Terra creatis, ad declivIora defluendi, manendique in locis humilioribus. Iob. xxxviii, 10, 11. Basilius Homil. iiii. in ἐξαημερ. Ab eo die currere cœpit Aqua, Fontes labi in fluvios, Lacus derivari in Maria, ipsa Aqua se præcedere, urgere, sequi, Ambrosio scribente in ἐξαημερ. Terramque circumdare: unde Eam nonnulli volunt apud Hebræos passive dictam ab Currendo. ארץ enim vocata ab רוץ currere; quod in ea & circa eam currant Aquæ, quod in ea & per eam Aquæ fluant & refluant.
units.tr: By the first command, from that day a natural force and tendency began to be in the waters, which had already been created before all things along with heaven and earth: to flow down to lower places and to remain in the lower places. Job 38:10, 11; Basil, Homily 4 on the Hexaemeron. From that day the water began to run, springs to slide into rivers, lakes to drain into the seas, and the water itself to go before, press on and follow, as Ambrose writes in the Hexaemeron, and to surround the earth. Hence some want the earth to be named among the Hebrews passively from running, since the Hebrew ארץ is derived from רוץ, to run, because the waters run in it and around it, and flow and return in it and through it.

units.la: Secundo vero Terra, initio cum Cœlo creata, (nam hoc die factam sentiunt Augustinus lib. 1. de Genesi ad litt. cap. xiii. & lib. 1. de Genesi adversus Manichaeos, cap. xii, libro denique de Genesi imperfecto, cap. x, Magister Sent. Hugo de S. Victore, lib. 1. de Sacrament. Bonaventura, aliique; male: quum DEVS non dixerit יהי Fiat, sed תראה apparcat, ne amplius obruta lateret aquis: alia argumenta alio indicavi loco) suos ostendere cœpit Montes, suas Valles & Campos: ita ab sapientissimo Numine fundatos: ut neque illi, semel ascendere jussi, descendant terramque operiant; neque hi, semel depressi, consurgant. David Psalmo civ, 8 & 9. Quo modo autem Aqua prius universam obducens Terram tertio die in unum redacta fuerit locum, notant varie Augustinus lib. iii. de Genesi ad litteram cap. xii. Beda in ἐξαημερ. Basilius, Ambrosius, Catharinus, Pererius ad hunc locum, Thomas part. 1. quæst. 1 x1x & alij.
units.tr: Second, the earth, created at the beginning together with heaven (for they hold that it was made on this day: Augustine, On the literal meaning of Genesis, book 1, ch. 13, and On Genesis against the Manichaeans, book 1, ch. 12, and finally On the Unfinished Book on Genesis, ch. 10; the Master of the Sentences; Hugh of St Victor, On the Sacraments, book 1; Bonaventure and others. But they are wrong, since God did not say "Let it be" [יהי] but "Let it appear" [תראה], lest it lie hidden again, overwhelmed by the waters. I have given other arguments in another place), began to show its mountains, valleys and plains, which the most wise Deity had founded in such a way that the former, once bidden to rise, do not sink again and cover the earth, and the latter, once sunk, do not rise up again. See David, Psalm 104:8–9. How the water, which at first covered the whole earth, was gathered into one place on the third day, is explained variously by Augustine, On the literal meaning of Genesis, book 3, ch. 12; Bede, On the Hexaemeron; Basil; Ambrose; Catharinus; Pererius on this passage; Thomas, part 1, question 69, and others.

units.la: Tertio denique mandato omnes Herbarum & Arborum species non tam casualiter, ut vult Augustinus lib. v. de Genesi ad litteram cap. 4. quasi DEVS tunc terris indiderit naturalem vim & potestatem generandi efferendiquæ dixi; quam actu ipso ex terra, auxilio Dei supernaturali productæ; in perfecto statu, cum quod proxime ab Deo creatæ, tum propter incredibilem nascentis Terræ bonitatem (unde non absurde quidam censent ארץ Hebræis appellatam ab רצה quod est prompto esse animo ad benefaciendum) suavissimæ ad gustum, hominisque victum & usum adcommodatissimæ: ita etiam ut haberent semen, unde possent aliæ generari. Tunc enim unumquodque perfectum est, quum generare potest sibi simile, ut docet Aristoteles iiii. Meteororum.
units.tr: Third and finally, by the command, all the species of herbs and trees were produced, not so much by chance, as Augustine holds (On the literal meaning of Genesis, book 5, ch. 4), as if God had then implanted in the earth a natural power of generating and bringing forth, as I have said. Rather, they were produced by the earth itself, by God's supernatural help, in their perfect state, both because they were created immediately by God and on account of the incredible goodness of the newly born earth (whence some not unreasonably think that the earth was called by the Hebrews [ארץ] from [רצה], which means being ready in mind to do good), and they were most pleasant to taste and most suited to the sustenance and use of man. Moreover, they had seed by which others could be generated. For each thing is then perfect when it can generate what is like itself, as Aristotle teaches in the fourth book of the Meteorologica.

units.la: Ad quæ die Quarto creata venio: Dixit DEVS, ait, suggerente Spiritu sancto, Moische, יהי מאורת ברקיע השמים להבדיל בין היום ובין הלילה והיו לאתת ולמועדים ולימים ושנים & quæ sequuntur; Sint Luminaria in expansione Cœlorum; ad dividendum inter Diem & inter Noctem; & sint in signa & tempora & dies & annos.
units.tr: To the things created on the fourth day I now come. "God said," he says, the Holy Spirit suggesting it to Moses: "Let there be lights [יהי מאורת] in the firmament of heaven [ברקיע השמים], to divide between the day and between the night; and let them be for signs [לאתת] and for seasons [ולמועדים] and for days and years [ולימים ושנים]," and what follows: "Let there be lights in the expanse of the heavens, to divide between the day and the night; and let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days and years."

units.la: Hac DEI dictione Astris, quæ, partes Cœli densiores, lucem habentes & transmittentes, una cum Cœlis quo ad materiam, figuram, magnitudinem & densitatem suam, in principio בראשית, fuerant factæ, quarto denum die forma data est, quæ Lux; quum DEVS partes illas crassiores spissa luce compleret: datus item proprius (nam non idem est omnibus) Alotus; datæ denique peculiares singulis Vices. Videndi Philo de Mundi opificio, & Pererius Commentariorum ad Genesin lib. 1.
units.tr: By this word of God the stars, which were made at the beginning [בראשית], together with the heavens as to their matter, shape, magnitude and density, from the denser parts of heaven, having and transmitting light, were given their form on the fourth day as lights, since God filled those thicker parts with a dense light. Likewise each was given its own proper course (for it is not the same for all), and finally each was given its particular seasons. See Philo, On the Creation of the World, and Pererius, Commentaries on Genesis, book 1.

units.la: Sequitur opus dici Quinti; de quo sic Moische: Dixit etiam DEVS: ישרצו המים שרץ נפש חיה ועוף יעופף על־הארץ על־פני רקיע השמים Producant Aquæ reptile anima viventis, & volatile volet super terram super faciem extensionis cœli.
units.tr: There follows the work of the fifth day, of which Moses says: "God also said: [ישרצו המים שרץ נפש חיה ועוף יעופף על־הארץ על־פני רקיע השמים] 'Let the waters bring forth abundantly the living creature that has life, and let the fowl fly above the earth, across the face of the firmament of heaven.'"

units.la: Hoc jussu Aquæ produxerunt non caussaliter & potentialiter, ut ita loquar cum Augustino lib. iii. de Genesi ad litteram, cap. iv. sed actu & re ipsa: crassiores quidem, species infinitas Piscium (qui, omnium Animantium varias ob causas imperfectissimi, cur Reptilia vocentur, notat Bonaventura ii. Sentent. distinct. x v.) tenuiores autem & nebulosæ, quales sunt Vapores & Nubes, varia Avium genera: Rupertus lib. i. de oper. Trinit. cap. l. Augustinus loco paullo ante laudato, cap. iii. Thomas parte i. quæstione lxxi. art. i. Eugubinus in Cosmopœia; contra distinientibus Cajetano, Catharino, & Hieronymo Vuilelmio lect. xxii. in ἑξαήμερ. quibus cum alia, tum locus Geneseos cap. ii, 19. haud bene discussus persuaserunt, Aves non ex Aëre, Aquis, inquam, tenuioribus; sed Terra factas Priorem sane intentiam tuctur admirabilis illa inter Aves & Pisces cognatio: sive quis spectet locum, qui vel his vel illis naturalis & quasi Domicilium; utrumque enim & Aer & Aqua corpus est transparens, humidum, facile cedens: sive conformationem utriusque generis Animantium; utrique inest levitas & agilitas; quæ pinnæ Piscibus, Avibus sunt alæ; his pennæ, quæ illis squammæ; nec his nec illis aures (quarum vicem quidam subeunt meatus) vesica, mammæ, lac: Aristoteles ii. de part. animal. cap. xii. & lib. iii. cap. viii. libro denique iii. de histor. animal. cap. xx. Sunt item Pisces volantes in mari Atlantico; sunt passim Aves natantes: ut non immerito Aves pisces aerii, Pisces aves aquatiles dici possent, utrisque cauda cursum dirigentibus. Opus restat diei Sexti, qui ultimus. Illud suis coloribus sic delineat nobis Spiritus Sanctus: Dixit quoque Deus; תּוֹצֵא הָאָרֶץ נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה לְמִינָהּ בְּהֵמָה וָרֶמֶשׂ וְחַיְתוֹ־אֶרֶץ לְמִינָהּ Producat terra Animam viventem ad speciem suam & Iumentum & Reptile, & Feram terra secundum speciem suam. Deinde: אֶעֱשֶׂה אָדָם בְּצַלְמֵנוּ כִּדְמוּתֵנוּ וְיִרְדּוּ בִדְגַת הַיָּם וּבְעוֹף הַשָּׁמַיִם וּבַבְּהֵמָה וּבְכָל־הָאָרֶץ וּבְכָל־הָרֶמֶשׂ הָרֹמֵשׂ עַל הָאָרֶץ Faciamus Hominem in imagine nostra secundum similitudinem nostram, & dominetur in pisces maris & in volatile cœli & in jumentum & in omnem terram & in omne reptile reptans super terram.
units.tr: By this command the waters produced, not causally and potentially (as I would say with Augustine, On the literal meaning of Genesis, book 3, ch. 4), but actually and in fact: the denser waters produced countless species of fishes (which, being the most imperfect of all animals for various reasons, are called "reptiles," as Bonaventure notes, Sentences, book 2, distinction 15), and the thinner and misty waters, such as vapours and clouds, produced various kinds of birds. See Rupert, On the Works of the Trinity, book 1, ch. 50; Augustine, in the passage a little above cited, ch. 3; Thomas, part 1, question 71, art. 1; Eugubinus, Cosmopoeia. Those who disagree include Cajetan, Catharinus, and Hieronymus Vuilelmius, lecture 22, On the Hexaemeron. They are persuaded by other things, and also by the passage of Genesis 2:19, which has not been well examined, that the birds were not made from the air, that is, from the thinner waters, but from the earth. The former opinion is supported indeed by the wonderful kinship between birds and fishes, whether one looks at the place which is natural to each, almost their home (for both air and water are transparent, moist bodies that yield easily), or at the structure of each kind of animal: both have lightness and agility; fins are to fishes what wings are to birds, and feathers are to birds what scales are to fishes; neither has external ears (for some passages do duty in their place), nor a bladder, nor breasts, nor milk. See Aristotle, On the Parts of Animals, book 2, ch. 12, and book 3, ch. 8, and finally On the History of Animals, book 3, ch. 20. There are also flying fishes in the Atlantic Sea, and birds that swim everywhere. So not unfairly birds might be called aerial fishes and fishes aquatic birds, both steering their course with the tail. The work of the sixth day, the last, remains. The Holy Spirit paints it for us in its own colours: "God also said: [תּוֹצֵא הָאָרֶץ נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה לְמִינָהּ בְּהֵמָה וָרֶמֶשׂ וְחַיְתוֹ־אֶרֶץ לְמִינָהּ] 'Let the earth bring forth the living creature according to its kind, cattle and creeping thing and beast of the earth according to its kind.'" Then: [אֶעֱשֶׂה אָדָם בְּצַלְמֵנוּ כִּדְמוּתֵנוּ וְיִרְדּוּ בִדְגַת הַיָּם וּבְעוֹף הַשָּׁמַיִם וּבַבְּהֵמָה וּבְכָל־הָאָרֶץ וּבְכָל־הָרֶמֶשׂ הָרֹמֵשׂ עַל הָאָרֶץ] "Let us make man in our image, after our likeness, and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea and over the birds of the heavens and over the cattle and over all the earth and over every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth."

units.la: Duo igitur Sexto die Deus, Terram ornaturus & suos illi incolas tributurus, fecit opera; Animalia Terrestria & Hominem.
units.tr: So on the sixth day God, about to adorn the earth and give it its inhabitants, made two works: the land animals and man.

units.la: Terrestrium indicantur hic tria genera: בַּהֵמָה omnia domestica magis & familiaria homini, quales Equi, Boves & similia; רֶמֶשׂ quæ vox comprehendit tam quæ nullos habent pedes, ut Serpentes, quam quæ habent, breves tamen & exiguos, ut Formicæ & Lacertæ; חַיַּת אֶרֶץ denique animantes omnes non solum agrestes, quæ fere hominis imperium aversantur, ut sunt Leones, Pantheræ, Tigres; sed quorum flecti potest natura, ut Cervi, Lepores, & alij: de quibus plene Aristoteles lib. i. de historia Animal. & Plato in Politico.
units.tr: Three kinds of land animals are indicated here. [בַּהֵמָה] are all those more tame and familiar to man, such as horses, oxen and the like. [רֶמֶשׂ] is a word that comprises both those that have no feet at all, such as serpents, and those that have feet, though short and small, such as ants and lizards. Finally, [חַיַּת אֶרֶץ] are all the living creatures, not only the wild ones, which almost refuse man's rule, such as lions, panthers and tigers, but also those whose nature can be bent, such as deer, hares and others. On these Aristotle writes fully in the first book of On the History of Animals, and Plato in the Statesman.

units.la: Postremo loco fecit Hominem Deus ad Imaginem & Similitudinem Suam; non verbo imperiali, inquit Tertullianus ii. adversus Marcionem, ut cetera; sed familiari manu, nova quadam ratione & oratione singulari, præmissa cum blandiente tum plena consilii & deliberationis voce (de qua lectu digna Chrysostomus & Basilius in Genesin, Gregorius lib. ix Moralium cap. xxiii. Ambrosius lib. vi. ἑξαήμερ. cap. vii. Augustinus lib. xvi. de Civit. Dei cap. vi. Cyrillus i. adversus Julianum, Theodoretus quæst. xx. Rupertus lib. ii. de Trinit. eiusque operibus, in principio, & alij) נַעֲשֶׂה, Faciamus; ut tam multo ante sciret Sanctissimæ Trinitatis mysterium in Se primo patefactum: Se, quamvis post omnia factum, Omnium tamen esse Finem, qui Destinatis potior & præstantior; in omnia se potestatem ab Deo accepisse, (quam pulcre diffundunt David Psalmo viii, 7, 8, 9. Ecclesiast. xvii, 3. Basilius in Genesin, Ambros. lib. vi. ἑξαήμερ. cap. vi.) etiam post peccatum, infinita Dei bonitate (Geneseos vii, 2.) Ut item diceret Se esse μικρόκοσμον, partem ipsius Universi potissimam, & in Se ut conspici quidquid in Rerum natura admirandum, quidquid magnum, quidquid pulcrum: Habere Se quod Est cum Inanimis commune; vitam cum Stirpibus; Sensum Motumque cum Animantibus; Mentem & Intelligentiam cum Angelis; Imaginem cum suo Creatore, Animam scilicet Sanctitatis participem, Rationis compotem, Sapientiæ, Iustitiæ, Libertatis, Divinæ Gratiæ, Æternæ Beatitudinis, omniumque Dei Donorum capacem. Origenes lib. i. περὶ ἀρχῶν cap. vi. Victorinus disputation. adversus Arrium, Gregorius Nyssenus Homil. de Creatione Hominis, Basilius Homil. x. Eucherius lib. i. Commentariorum in Genes. Theodoretus quæstione xx. in Genes. Rupertus lib. ii. de Tri-
units.tr: Last of all God made man in his own image and likeness. He did not do so by an imperial word, says Tertullian (Against Marcion, book 2), as he did the rest, but with a familiar hand, by a new kind of reasoning and a singular speech, with a preface of a voice both coaxing and full of counsel and deliberation (on which passage read Chrysostom and Basil on Genesis, Gregory, Moralia, book 9, ch. 23; Ambrose, On the Hexaemeron, book 6, ch. 7; Augustine, City of God, book 16, ch. 6; Cyril, Against Julian, book 1; Theodoret, question 20; Rupert, On the Trinity and its works, book 2, at the beginning, and others): [נַעֲשֶׂה] "Let us make." So that he might know long beforehand that the mystery of the most holy Trinity was first revealed in himself; that though he was made after all things, he was nevertheless the end of all, and superior and more excellent than what was destined; that he had received from God power over all things (how beautifully David pours this out, Psalm 8:7–9; Ecclesiasticus 17:3; Basil on Genesis; Ambrose, On the Hexaemeron, book 6, ch. 6), even after sin, by the infinite goodness of God (Genesis 9:2). Likewise, so that he might say that he is a [μικρόκοσμον], the chief part of the universe itself, and that in himself may be seen whatever is wonderful in the nature of things, whatever is great, whatever is beautiful: that he has in common with inanimate things what he is; with plants, life; with animals, sense and motion; with angels, mind and understanding; with his Creator, the image, namely a soul sharing in holiness, endowed with reason, capable of wisdom, justice, liberty, divine grace, eternal blessedness, and all the gifts of God. See Origen, On First Principles, book 1, ch. 6; Victorinus, Disputation against Arius; Gregory of Nyssa, homily On the Creation of Man; Basil, homily 10; Eucherius, Commentaries on Genesis, book 1; Theodoret, question 20 on Genesis; Rupert, On the Trinity and its works, book 2, ch. 3.

units.la: Note fragments in margins: "Die denique Sexto Terra Animalibus & Homine."; "Homo factus Dei manu."; "Ad hibita quasi deliberatione."; "Omnium Finis, præditus ... ad cicatas potestate."; "μικρόκοσμον, gerens secum quidquid in rerum natura." de Trinitate & ejus operib. cap. iii. & v. Bernardus Sermone xiiii. in Psalmum xcı. Thomas part. 1. quæstione xciii. Magister Sententiarum. ii. distinct. xvi. Lippomanus in Cathena, Eugubinus, Oleaster, Pererius, & alij in Genesin. Vt denique cognosceret, Se, quum constet non ex solo Corpore, quasi Anima Φαντασμὸν quid esset & commentitium, ut volunt Dicæarchus Messenius apud Sex. Empiricum libro Hypotypos. & non alienus ab eo ipse Sextus cap. xxii. libri contra Mathematicos: non item ex sola Anima, quasi Corpus vehiculum esset Anima, vel vestis instar, ut Platoni placet 1. Alcibiad. & Dialogo de Morte, Auctori imperfecti operis in Mathæum, Homil. xxv. & Georgio Veneto in libris Problemat. Sacrae Scripturae; sed ex Anima & Corpore simul, ut qui sanioris doctrinæ sentiunt; Se, inquam, ita compositum, vinculum esse & nexum totius Universi, Se consociare res Incorporeas cum Corporeis, Immortales cum Mortalibus: Omnia quodammodo Se esse, quum omnia intelligat, Se quamvis nudum & inermem, Ratione tamen vestitum & Ingenio armatum Sibi munimentum non in Corpore, ut alijs Animantibus, sed in Animo positum esse: Se ut concludam, æstimata bene bonitatis divinæ indulgentia, in deliciis suo Creatori præ quod reliqua Creata, fuisse. Seneca lib. ii. de Beneficiis, cap. xxix. & Lactantius lib. ii. de Opificio Dei.
units.tr: Marginal notes: "Finally, on the sixth day, the earth for the animals and man."; "Man made by the hand of God."; "Applied as if after deliberation."; "Finis omnium (the end of all things), endowed with ... power over created things."; "a microcosm, carrying within himself whatever is in the nature of things." (See Augustine, On the Trinity and its works, ch. iii and v; Bernard, Sermon 14 on Psalm 91; Thomas, part 1, question 93; the Master of the Sentences, book 2, distinction 16; Lippomanus in the Catena, Eugubinus, Oleaster, Pererius, and others on Genesis.) Finally, so that he might know himself: since man does not consist of the body alone, as if the soul were a phantasm [φάντασμα] and a fiction, as Dicaearchus of Messene holds (cited by Sextus Empiricus in his Outlines of Pyrrhonism), and Sextus himself, who is not far from this view, in ch. xxii of his book Against the Mathematicians; nor again from the soul alone, as if the body were merely a vehicle for the soul, or a garment, as Plato holds in the First Alcibiades and the dialogue On Death, and as the author of the imperfect work on Matthew (Homily 25) and George of Venice in his Problems of Holy Scripture maintain; but from soul and body together, as those of sounder doctrine think. I say that man, so composed, is the bond and link of the whole universe, joining incorporeal things with corporeal, and immortal things with mortal. In a way he is all things, since he understands all things. Though he is naked and unarmed, he is clothed with reason and armed with wit, and his defence lies not in the body, as with the other animals, but in the mind. In short, having weighed the kindness of divine goodness, he was reckoned among the delights of his Creator above all other created things. Seneca, On Benefits, book 2, ch. xxix; and Lactantius, On the Workmanship of God, book 2.

units.la: Talis igitur creatus Homo quam fœde lapsus, quam horrendum suo lapsu degeneravit à primo illo, qui perfectissimus erat, statu! Obediens DEo, Sapiens, Innocens suo lapsu factus Insipiens, Inobediens, Nocens; Nocentior in Posteris; imo Lupus, non alijs tantum, in Liberos, Parentes, Fratres armatus sæpe sævius, quam in hostem; sed & Sibi, potiorem sui portionem & istam divinæ particulam auræ morti & interitui (quo quid crudelius?) statuens obnoxiam: quam insaniam insaniverunt Stoici, Epicurei, alijque Philosophi, quos recensent Aristoteles lib. i. de Anima, Plutarch. lib. iv. Placit. cap. vii. & Theodoret. lib. v. Græcan. Affect. eosque sequuti Lucretius lib. iii. de Rer. Nat. Seneca, ut patet ex epist. ad Lucilium & Consolatione ad Marciam, Plinius lib. vii. Natural. historiæ. O Saxa stolida!
units.tr: How shamefully, then, did man, created thus, fall, and how dreadfully by his fall did he degenerate from that first state, which was most perfect! Obedient to God, wise, innocent, by his fall he became foolish, disobedient, and guilty; more guilty in his posterity; indeed a wolf, armed not only against others, against children, parents, and brothers, often more savagely than against an enemy, but also against himself, making the better part of himself, that divine particle of the breath, liable to death and destruction (what could be more cruel?). This madness was raved by the Stoics, the Epicureans, and other philosophers whom Aristotle (On the Soul, book 1), Plutarch (Opinions of the Philosophers, book 4, ch. vii), and Theodoret (Cures of Greek Maladies, book 5) enumerate; and Lucretius (On the Nature of Things, book 3), Seneca (as is clear from his letter to Lucilius and his Consolation to Marcia), and Pliny (Natural History, book 7) followed them. O stupid stones!

units.la: O curves in Terram Homines! Cœlestium inanes!
units.tr: O souls bent down towards the earth! Empty of heavenly things!

units.la: Cogor clamare cum Antidamo vetere scriptore: Fabre compactum Animal, Hominem, quis ferat sic esse pecuatum? quis averruncasset tam arietinas (fatuas & insulsas) hominum mentes? Fulgentius de prisco sermone.
units.tr: I am compelled to cry out with the old writer Antidamus: Who could bear that an animal so skilfully put together, man, should be so sinful? Who could have driven away such ram-like (foolish and insipid) minds of men? Fulgentius, On the Ancient Speech.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAP. V.

units.la: Mundum Vnum esse & Finitum.
units.tr: That the World is One and Finite.

units.la: OMNIA, quæ hactenus commemoravi, ita ab Architecto sapientissimo collocata & dispositi; ut Vnum, idque Finitum & Rotundum constituerent Corpus; & Cuncta, quæ Ejus & in Illo, amico quodam consensu inter se consonarent.
units.tr: All the things I have so far described were so arranged and disposed by the most wise Architect that they make up one body, which is one, finite and round, and all the things that are in it and belong to it harmonise with one another in a kind of friendly agreement.

units.la: Vnum tantum esse Mundum, eumque omnia comprehendentem adserimus, qui sanioris judicii, cum Thalete, Pythagora, Empedocle, Ecphanto, Parmenide, Melisso, Heraclito, Anaxagora, Platone, Aristotele, Zenone, tota Stoicorum secta, bonaque Peripateticorum parte. Videndus, præter Diogenem Laertium, Plutarchum & alios, Stobæus 1. ἐκλογ. Φυσικ.
units.tr: We maintain that there is only one world, and that it comprehends all things, with the sounder judgement of Thales, Pythagoras, Empedocles, Ecphantus, Parmenides, Melissus, Heraclitus, Anaxagoras, Plato, Aristotle, Zeno, the whole school of the Stoics, and the better part of the Peripatetics. See, besides Diogenes Laertius, Plutarch and others, Stobaeus, Eclogae Physicae, book 1.

units.la: Rationes quis quæHrit? Dicam de DEo nostro, quod, in Vnitate Mundi stabiliendâ, de Vno illo absolutissimo Exemplari, divinus Philosophus in Timæo; quod de æterna & infinita rerum Natura Plinius lib. ii. Nat. hist. cap. i. Vnus DEvs Vnum tantum esse voluit Vniversum, in quo, tamquam in clarissimo speculo, Potentia, Sapientia, Bonitas ejus manifestissime conspicerentur.
units.tr: If anyone asks for reasons, I shall speak of our God. In establishing the unity of the world, the divine Philosopher (in the Timaeus) speaks of that one most perfect Exemplar. Pliny, in book 2 of the Natural History, chapter 1, speaks of the eternal and infinite nature of things: God, the one God, willed that the universe be one only, in which his power, wisdom and goodness might be seen most plainly, as in a very clear mirror.

units.la: Deinde, omne Corpus Simplex movetur certo, & quem totius Naturæ princeps determinavit, Motu: si plures essent Mundi; indubitatum omnino, Motum hunc confusum iri, quum Terra unius Mundi moveretur ad Terram & Centrum alterius; unde quam fœda commistio sequeretur Corporum Simplicium, nemo non videt.
units.tr: Next, every simple body moves with a fixed motion, which the prince of all nature has determined. If there were several worlds, it is quite certain that this motion would become confused, since the Earth of one world would be moving towards the Earth and centre of another. No one fails to see what a foul mixing of the simple bodies would follow.

units.la: Tertio, perfectæ & absolutæ elegantiæ (nam nomen hinc illi apud Græcos & Latinos) non potuissel videri, nisi omnia in admiranda ejus machina (quæ sua magnitudine & forma naturarum omnium & specierum satis est capax) fuissent quasi conclusa. Frustra enim fit per Plura, quod potest per Pauciora. Totus, inquit Plinius lib. II, cap. I, in Toto, imo vero Ipse Totum.
units.tr: Thirdly, the world could not have seemed perfect and absolute in its elegance (which is why the Greeks and Latins call it by its name) unless all things were, as it were, enclosed within its admirable machine, which by its size and form is quite capable of all natures and kinds. For what can be done through many is done in vain through fewer. The whole, says Pliny in book 2, chapter 1, is in the whole, or rather the whole is itself the whole.

units.la: Valeant igitur Anaximander, Anaximenes, Aristarchus, Xenophanes, Leucippus, Democritus, Epicurus, multique eos sequuti, de quibus Diogenes Laertius in Philosoph. vitis, Plutarch de Philosoph. Placitis, Clemens Alexandrinus, Iustinus Martyr, Stobæus I. ixλογ. Φυσικ. & alij) qui immanissimi totius Physicæ corruptores, suis plaudentes commentis, innumerabiles nobis Mundos conati sunt fingere.
units.tr: Farewell, then, to Anaximander, Anaximenes, Aristarchus, Xenophanes, Leucippus, Democritus, Epicurus, and the many who followed them, of whom Diogenes Laertius in the Lives of the Philosophers, Plutarch in the Opinions of the Philosophers, Clement of Alexandria, Justin Martyr, Stobaeus in the Eclogae Physicae, and others speak. These, the most monstrous corrupters of the whole of physics, applauding their own inventions, have tried to feign innumerable worlds for us.

units.la: Neque solum Unus ex Sanctorum mente Mundus, sed Unus ille etiam Finitus est & Certus: quæ sententia Meliorum hodie; olim etiam Homeri Iliados o, Ocelli Lucani, Platonis in Timæo, M. Tullij Ciceronis, Apulei, & aliorum: contra quos Infinitum, id est, Altitudinis & Longitudinis dimensionibus non constantem, ausi statuere Seleucus Erythræus, Heraclides Panticus, Peripatetici, & alij. Diogenes etiam & Melissus τὸ πᾶν quidem voluerunt Ἄπειρον, τὸ δὲ κόσμον πεπερασμένον.
units.tr: Not only is the world one in the mind of the Saints, but that one world is also finite and determinate. This opinion is held by the better sort today, and formerly by Homer in the Iliad, Ocellus Lucanus, Plato in the Timaeus, Marcus Tullius Cicero, Apuleius and others. Against them Seleucus of Erythrae, Heraclides of Pontus, the Peripatetics and others have dared to posit the infinite, that is, that which is not bounded by dimensions of height and length. Diogenes and Melissus indeed held that the whole [τὸ πᾶν μὲν ἄπειρον, τὸ δὲ κόσμον πεπερασμένον] is infinite, but the world finite.

units.la: Si Infinitum esset excellens illud Corpus, qui posset circumagi finito tempore? qui circulante rotari motu (quem scimus reditum ab eodem in idem punctum) si infinita esset punctorum distantia? si lineæ protractæ ab centro in infinitum abirent? Scite meo judicio Plinius Finitum dixit, sed Infinito simulem; Certum similem Incerto: quo modo? Finitus quidem habet enim in se certa spacia Motus ac Temporis: Infinito autem est similis, si tam vasta Mundi moles cum interioribus corporibus, quorum etiam difficilis enumeratio, vel intimo potius committatur, cum universa, inquam, Terra, quæ instar puncti ad reliqua. Iam vero Certum produnt certi Motus, qui finito temporis spacio revolvuntur; certi Ortus, Occasus, Limites; certæ deniq; surgentium cadentiumque siderum vices: Simulem Incerto docent Motuum, quos dixi, dissimilitudo & diversissimæ Apparitiones. Sufficit sane Unus ille, isque Finitus & Certus, qui omnes in Sui, suique Creatoris rapiat admirationem: absolutus adeo, ut absolutior meliorque (quamvis acerrimis telis pro maiore quantitate, plenitudine, duratione, & accidentali rerum naturalium perfectione pugnent Philosophi) fieri non potuerit. Nam è contraria parte quis validis evincet argumentis, substantialem hanc rerum perfectionem esse potuisse perfectiorem? quis partium cum ipsius Mundi, tum rerum, quæ in eo, meliorem ordinem, concinniorem dispositionem, decentiorem omnium inter se proportionem & cohærentiam? quis præstantiorem totius Universi gubernationem? Iam quæ reliqua obstrepuntur; Majorem quidem, Pleniorem, Æterniorem facere potuit potentissimus D e v s; sed sapientissimus noluit. Quur? Hoc me, hoc omnes latet: mihi pisque, scio, omnibus abunde est in Uno hoc, quod pulcerrimum certe, Opificio, quo divinum illud Numen ejusque gloriam laudibus gratiisque venerunt. Extera Mundi non indagemus: Non enim nostra interest, neque nostræ capit Mentis conjectura, ut cum Plinio loquar. Furor est profecto, furor egressum quasi Mundo velle quid amplius adfingere. Disputent cum Stoicis, Peripateticis, aliisque, extra Mundum Infinitum esse Vacuum, quibus ad stabiliendum illud Vacuum magis vacuæ Mentes. Scrutemur quæ ad pedes nobis. Nam quotusquisque nostrum est, qui vires Herbarum, qui naturas Animalium similiaque, qui denique se probe perfecteque novit? Hic Ingeniorum acumina & virtutes exerceamus. Mensuram alicujus rei numquam aget, qui sui nesciat: Mens hominis numquam videbit, quæ Mundus ipse non capit: Mundum ut superscandat Animi cogitatio nefas, prohibetur & per Naturam, & per Religionis Leges; Exodi xxxiii.
units.tr: If that excellent body were infinite, who could be carried round in a finite time? Who could be turned by a circling motion (which we know returns from the same point to the same point) if the distance between the points were infinite? If lines drawn from the centre ran off to infinity? Rightly, in my judgement, Pliny called it finite, yet likened it to the infinite, and the certain to the uncertain. How so? It is finite, for it has within it certain spaces of motion and time. It is likened to the infinite if so vast a mass of the world is compared with the inner bodies, whose enumeration is difficult, or rather with what is most inward, I mean the whole Earth, which is like a point compared with the rest. Now certain motions, which revolve in a finite space of time, reveal the certain: certain risings, settings and limits; and finally the fixed changes of rising and setting stars. The dissimilarity of the motions I have mentioned and their very diverse appearances teach that it is like the uncertain. That one world, finite and certain, is surely enough to carry all men off into admiration of itself and its Creator. It is so perfect that a more perfect and better one could not have been made, though philosophers fight with the sharpest weapons for greater quantity, fullness, duration and accidental perfection of natural things. For on the other side, who could prove by strong arguments that this substantial perfection could have been more perfect? Who could show a better order of the parts, both of the world itself and of the things in it, a more harmonious arrangement, a more fitting proportion and coherence of all things among themselves? Who could show a more excellent government of the whole Universe? As for the rest that is objected: the most powerful God could have made it larger, fuller and more lasting; but the most wise God did not will it. Why? This is hidden from me and from all men. For me, and I know for all the pious, it is abundantly enough in this one work, which is surely most beautiful, by which that divine power and its glory are honoured with praises and thanks. We do not investigate the outer parts of the World, for they are not our concern, nor does the conjecture of our mind reach them, to speak with Pliny. It is surely madness, madness, to wish to add something beyond the World, as if it were outside it. Let them dispute with the Stoics, Peripatetics and others whether an infinite Void lies outside the World; for establishing that Void, emptier minds are better suited. Let us examine what lies at our feet. For how few of us know the powers of herbs, the natures of animals and such things, or, in the end, know themselves well and thoroughly? Here let us exercise the sharpness and powers of our minds. He who does not know himself will never measure anything. The mind of man will never see what the World itself does not contain. For the mind to rise above the World is wrong, and is forbidden both by Nature and by the Laws of Religion: Exodi xxxiii.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAP. VI.

units.la: Mundum esse Rotundum.
units.tr: That the World Is Round.

units.la: Vnus igitur & Finitus: quin & Rotundus. Fecit enim Deus Universum hoc forma sphærali, & ut bene Plinius lib. II. natur. historiæ cap. I. in speciem orbis absoluti globata. Consentiunt hic cum Platone, Aristotele & tota Stoicorum schola plerique qui deinceps sequuti. Quid ni? Perfectissimo, & quod in se contineret omnia, Corpori forma debebatur prima, omniumque capacissima. Plutarchus de Placitis Philosophorum.
units.tr: The world is therefore one and finite, and indeed round. For God made this universe in a spherical form, and, as Pliny well says in Book II, chapter 1 of his Natural History, shaped into the likeness of a perfect globe. Plato, Aristotle and the whole school of the Stoics, and most of those who followed them afterwards, agree with this. Why not? The most perfect body, one that was to contain all things, was rightly given the first shape, the one that holds the most. Plutarch, On the Opinions of the Philosophers.

units.la: Docent Rotunditatem varia. Præter consonans apud Latinos ipsi Rei Nomen (Orbis enim dicitur hoc Vniversum; Orbes item omnes Vniversi portiones, Plinius lib. 11. cap. 11. & alij) Motus circularis; quo sic circumagitur, ut omnes partes pariter distent ab Centro. Deinde Horizontes seu Finitores, qui deprehenduntur ejusdem ubique magnitudinis. Consulendus omnino Plato in Timæo. Accedent, Formæ tali probandæ, in Partium, Cœli Terræque, cum quibus hic ejusdem naturæ Totum, explicatione alia.
units.tr: There are various proofs of roundness. Besides the name of the thing itself, which agrees with it among the Latins (for this universe is called orbis, and all its parts are likewise called orbes, as Pliny says in Book II, chapter 11, and others), there is the circular motion by which it turns, so that all its parts are equally distant from the centre. Then there are the horizons, or finitores, which are found to be of the same size everywhere. Plato in the Timaeus should certainly be consulted. Further explanation will follow, to prove this shape, of the parts of heaven and earth, with which the whole is of one nature.

units.la: Fuerunt qui Vniversum hoc Ovali figura, ᾠοειδῆ esse voluerunt; inter quos, ut notat Plutarchus de Placitis Philosophorum, primi loci Σαγχωνιάθων, Tyrius Philosophus, antiquissimus, quod memoriæ prodit Suidas, rerum Phœniciæ scriptor, qui vixit circa Troiana tempora, ab Philone Biblio in Græcam linguam translatus. Eo respicit M. Terentius Varro in Logistorico, qui inscribitur Tubero, sive de Origine humana, apud Probum Grammaticum: Cælum, inquit, est testa; item Vitellum, ut Terra: inter illa duo Humor, quasi Ilcinus clusus Aeri, in quo Calor. Innuit hoc & Proclus in Timæum; cui τὸ ὀρφικὸν ᾠὸν κατὰ τὸ Ζ Πλάτωνος ὄν, eadem. Hinc initiati Orgijs Liberi Patris Ovum in suis Sacris colebant, ut nimirum ex terete forma & pene sphærali undecunque clausa & intra se vitam includente. Mundi totius simulacrum cognoscceretur. Plutarch. in Symposiacis, Macrobius lib. vii. Satur. cap. xvi.
units.tr: Some have wished this universe to have an oval figure, [ᾠοειδῆ]. Among them, as Plutarch notes in On the Opinions of the Philosophers, first place goes to Sanchuniathon, the very ancient Tyrian philosopher, who, as Suidas records, wrote on the history of Phoenicia and lived around the time of the Trojan War, and was translated into Greek by Philo of Byblos. Marcus Terentius Varro alludes to this in his Logistoricus entitled Tubero, or On the Origin of Man, as quoted by the grammarian Probus: "The heaven," he says, "is a shell; likewise the yolk, like the earth; between those two is moisture, like the white enclosed in air, in which there is heat." Proclus also hints at this in his commentary on the Timaeus, where the Orphic egg, which is according to the Z of Plato [τὸ ὀρφικὸν ᾠὸν κατὰ τὸ Ζ Πλάτωνος ὄν], is the same thing. Hence those initiated into the rites of Liber Pater worshipped the egg in their sacred rites, evidently because its rounded and nearly spherical form, closed on every side and enclosing life within itself, was an image of the whole world. Plutarch, in the Symposiacs; Macrobius, Saturnalia, Book VII, chapter 16.

units.la: Certe si Mundus figuræ esset planæ, vel angularis, vel alius: partim sequerentur quæ fieri nequeunt; quum enim Mundi superiora sine ulla intermissione moveantur, necesse esset nonnulla Loca relinqui vacua, & Corpora nonnulla sine Locis: partim evenirent quæ Sensui nostro adversantur; Nam Planetæ reliquaque Sidera in hac Orbis parte nobis essent propinquiora, quam illa, &, quod æque absurdum, in parte propinquiore majora, in remotiore vero minora nobis apparerent.
units.tr: Certainly, if the world were flat, or angular, or of some other shape, then in part things would follow that cannot happen: since the upper parts of the world move without any pause, some places would have to be left empty and some bodies would be without places. In part, things would occur that contradict our senses: for the planets and the other stars would be nearer to us in that part of the sphere, and, what is equally absurd, they would appear larger to us in the nearer part and smaller in the more distant part.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: Creta omnia admirandis inter se concentibus consonare.
units.tr: That all things resonate with admirable harmonies among themselves.

units.la: LICET autem Mundus compactus fiet ex rebus quodammodo contrariis & inter se dissidentibus: omnia tamen sapientissimus Architectus ita temperavit; ut ea rerum repugnantia, vires suas vicissim frangendo & se aliquatenus corrumpendo, non solum exitio non esset Mundo, sed etiam saluti & ornamento. Quæ ingeniis discrepant & summis viribus inter se quasi dimicant, Opificis supremi moderatione ad bonum Vniversi ruendum mutuo & concordi fœdere conspirant. Alia non petam sufficiat si quod volo probatum fuerit & Elementorum & Hominis indole.
units.tr: Although the world is put together from things that are in some ways opposed and at odds with one another, the most wise Architect has so tempered all things that this conflict of natures, by breaking each other's forces and partly corrupting one another, is not a ruin to the world but even its safety and ornament. Things that disagree in their natures and, as it were, fight with their greatest strength are, under the moderation of the supreme Maker, brought together for the good of the whole universe, and they join in a mutual and harmonious league. I shall not seek other examples. It will be enough if what I want has been proved from the nature of the elements and of man.

units.la: Illa igitur & animo & oculis contemplatus quis non miretur eorum concordem discordiam, an discordem concordiam? Aqua humida est & frigida; prior qualitas propria illi, in posteriore participat cum Terra: hæc frigida est propriè, sicca natura Ignis refert: Igni in caliditate convenit cum Aere: qui in humido quid aliud quam Aqua? Addo ex Pythagoræorum doctrina, Ignem Aere duplo subtiliorem esse; triplo mobiliorem Aqua, duplo acutiorem: Aerem Aqua duplo acutiorem, triplo subtiliorem, quadruplo mobiliorem: Aquam vero duplo Terra acutiorem, triplo subtiliorem, quadruplo mobiliorem: quamvis autem Ignis in his sit subtilis, mobilis, acutus: Aer subtilis, mobilis, obtusus: Aqua mobilis, obtusa, corporea; Terra deniqué obtusa, corporea, immobilis: tamen (ô admirabilem collocationem!) inter Ignem & Terram ea lege Aerem & Aquam esse interjecta: ut, quemadmodum se habet Ignis ad Aerem, sic Aer ad Aquam, Aqua ad Terram; rursum sicut Terra ad Aquam, sic Aqua ad Aerem, Aer ad Ignem. Divine Boetius Pythagoreos imitatus: Tu numeris Elementa ligas, ut Frigora Flammis, Arida conveniant Liquidis, ut pugnor Igni Evolet, ut mersas deducant pondera Terras.
units.tr: Who, then, contemplating these things with both mind and eyes, would not marvel at their harmonious discord, or discordant harmony? Water is moist and cold: its proper quality is the former, and in the latter it shares with Earth. Earth is cold in its own right, and its dry nature resembles Fire. Fire agrees with Air in heat; and what is Air in moisture but Water? I add from the teaching of the Pythagoreans that Fire is twice as subtle as Air, three times more mobile than Water, and twice as sharp; Air is twice as sharp as Water, three times more subtle, and four times more mobile; and Water is indeed twice as sharp as Earth, three times more subtle, and four times more mobile. Although Fire among these is subtle, mobile and sharp; Air subtle, mobile and blunt; Water mobile, blunt and corporeal; and Earth, finally, blunt, corporeal and immobile: yet (O admirable arrangement!) Air and Water have been placed between Fire and Earth under this law: that as Fire is to Air, so Air is to Water, and Water to Earth; and again, as Earth is to Water, so Water is to Air, and Air to Fire. Boethius, imitating the Pythagoreans, sang divinely: "You bind the elements with numbers, so that cold things agree with flames, dry things with liquids, so that fire may fly upward in its battle, and weights may draw down the sunken lands."

units.la: Nec minus eleganter alio loco: Hæc Concordia temperat æquis Elementa modis: ut pugnantia Vicibus cedant Humida Siccis; Iungantque fidem Frigora Flammis; Pendulus Ignis surgat in altum; Terraque graves pondere fidant. Iisdem caussis Vere tepenti Spirat florifer annus odores; Aestas Cererem fervida siccat; Remeat pomis gravis Autumnus; Hiemem defluus irrigat Imber. Haec temperies alit & profert Quidquid vitam spirat in Orbe: Eadem rapiens condit & aufert Obitu mergens orta supremo.
units.tr: Nor less elegantly elsewhere: "This Concord tempers the elements by fair measures, so that moist things yield to dry in turn, and cold things join faith with flames; the hanging fire rises aloft, and the heavy earth trusts in its weight. By the same causes the flowery year breathes out its scents in the warm spring; the fervent summer dries the corn; heavy autumn returns with its fruit; the falling rain waters the winter. This temperance nurtures and brings forth whatever breathes life in the world; the same power, snatching away, buries and takes back what it has brought into being, sinking it at its last death."

units.la: Jam quid dicam, omnia Elementa, quod praestantissimorum Philosophorum scripta loquuntur, in Omnibus reperiri; in inferioribus quidem faeculenta & crassa; in Superioribus pura & nitida: supra Coelos vivida & omni ex parte benefica? Terra nobis stabile firmamentum omniumque seminum matrix; in Coelis densitudo, conspicua maxime, si Solem, si Lunam, si reliqua Sidera intueamur: in Angelis firma DEI subsellia, in Archetypo omnium firmissima & fecundissima natura. Aqua nobis, quae lavat & purificat omnia; in Coelis, quae defluvio suo Terram irrigat; in Angelis, quae docet & mundat; in Opifice, quae Peccata nostra abluit, quae nos regenerat, collustrat, pascit. Aer nobis quo respiramus, videmus, audimus, odoramur: in Coelis, inferioribus quidem, translucens natura; superiore vero, spacium ubi resonant suavissimi Beatorum concentus; in Angelis vitalis flatus & aura tenuis; in Opifice summa & perfectissima vita, spiritus ille, quo spirans in omnes dat omnibus ut sint, ut vivant; ille, inquam, quo Sanctis suis loquitur, & opera sua suaque mysteria intus sine murmure enarrat. Ignis, qui hic calefacit & urit, in Coelo Sol lucens, qui calore suo recreat inferiora; in Angelis fervidus est erga nos homines amor; in Archetypo Ignis ille idealis, ut sic loquar, & spirituale Lumen. Involuti essent negocij hic recenlere, quam amice conveniant Terra cum Luna: Aqua cum Mercurio & Saturno; Aeri cum Iove & Venere; Igni cum Sole & Marte. Quin quidquid Rerum Natura habet Compositorum, mira suavitate in Elementis conquiescit: Lapides indole sua Terram imitantur; Metalla quamvis, ut vult Hermes, ex omnibus constant, potiffimum tamen ex Aqua conflata naturam ejus sapiunt, testibus Timaeo Locro, Platone, Aristotele, Abubachere, Avicenna, Alberto Magno, & aliis; Aeris indolem Planetae mentiuntur, nam nisi sub dio non pullulant, non coalescunt, cognatum sibi Aerem semper petunt, putrescunt nisi subveniat Aquens humor; ex quo in Aerem, ex hoc rursus in Aquam amicissima vicissitudo & commutatio. Igni denique naturam repraesentant Animalia, quibus inde, DEO disponente, vita: ut non immerito Maro, quamvis specialius: Igneus est olli vigor, & caelestis origo.
units.tr: Now what shall I say, that all the elements, as the writings of the most distinguished philosophers tell us, are to be found in all things: in the lower regions indeed they are foul and gross, but in the higher they are pure and bright, and above the heavens they are lively and wholly beneficial? Earth is for us a stable foundation and the mother of all seeds; in the heavens it is density, most visible if we look at the Sun, the Moon and the other stars; among the Angels it is the firm seats of God, and in the Archetype it is the most firm and most fruitful nature of all. Water is for us what washes and purifies all things; in the heavens it is what waters the Earth with its outflow; among the Angels it teaches and cleanses; in the Maker it is what washes away our sins, regenerates us, enlightens and feeds us. Air is for us that by which we breathe, see, hear and smell; in the heavens, in the lower parts, it is a translucent nature, and in the higher it is the space where the sweetest harmonies of the Blessed resound; among the Angels it is the living breath and subtle breeze; in the Maker it is the supreme and most perfect life, that Spirit by whom he breathes life into all and gives to all that they may be and live; that Spirit, I say, by whom he speaks to his Saints and inwardly relates his works and his mysteries without a murmur. Fire, which here warms and burns, is in the heavens the shining Sun, which by its heat restores the lower things; among the Angels it is the fervent love they have for us men; in the Archetype it is that ideal Fire, so to speak, and spiritual Light. It would take too long to recount here how well Earth agrees with the Moon, Water with Mercury and Saturn, Air with Jupiter and Venus, and Fire with the Sun and Mars. Indeed, whatever compound things Nature has rest in the elements with a wonderful sweetness: stones imitate Earth in their character; metals, although, as Hermes holds, they consist of all the elements, nevertheless for the most part, having been formed from Water, savour of its nature, as Timaeus of Locri, Plato, Aristotle, Abubacer, Avicenna, Albertus Magnus and others bear witness; the planets feign the character of Air, for unless they are under the open sky they do not sprout or grow together, and they always seek the air akin to them, and they rot unless the watery moisture comes to their aid; from this comes the most friendly alternation and exchange, into Air and from it again into Water. Finally, animals represent the nature of Fire, and from it they have life, God so arranging it; so Maro, though more particularly, not undeservedly says: "Fiery is the vigour in them, and a heavenly origin." Igneus est olli vigor, et caelestis origo.

units.la: Quae dixi exaudiri velim de fortiore Elementorum interventu. Nam vix quid in hac mole, ad quod emoliendum non conveniant mirifico quodam consensu omnia Elementa; alia tamen aliis validius & operosius.
units.tr: I would have what I have said understood of the stronger working of the elements. For there is scarcely anything in this mass that the elements do not all help to build up with a wonderful agreement, though some do so more forcefully and laboriously than others.

units.la: Homo jam prodeat, nobilissima DEI creatura: In eo nihil non. Est, ut quidquid Inanimorum; Vivit, ut omne Stirpium genus; Sentit & Movetur, ut omnia animalia; Mente praeditus est & Intelligentia, ut Angeli; ad Imaginem denique creatus est fui Creatoris, Animam, ut paullo ante dixi, nactus, quae Sanctitatis particeps, quae Rationis compos, quae Sapientiae, Justitiae, Libertatis, divinae Gratiae, aeternae Beatitudinis, omnium DEI Bonorum capax. Quod in eo Rotunda Mundi figura; docet, praeter Caput, Orbis ab Umbilico per extremitates diductarum manuum pedumque circinatus. Numquid quatuor Mundi possidet Elementa? Paret hoc cum in quinque Sensibus; Visus enim respondet Igni, Aeri Auditus, Olfactus & Gustus Aquae, Terrae Tactus: tum in quatuor Humoribus, quos Galenus Medicorum princeps etiam Elementa vocat: Sanguis, qui calidus & humidus ex Corde oritur, Aeri suffragatur; Pituita, quae humida & frigida ex Cerebro manat, Aquae; Bilis atra, quae frigida & sicca ex Splene trahit ortum, Terrae; Flava denique; quae ex Iecore arida & calida, Igni. Legendus omnino Platonis Timæus; ubi speciosissimum ꝑ μιμροκόσμω ἀλάζω-ραφημα ad vivum depingitur per singulas partes & Animi & Corporis. Quam vero concors Homini cum Planetis reliquisque Sideribus consipiratio! Hæc enim, tamquam Ministri Opificis Summi, qui Rerum omnium origo, vi quadam occulta, quam D E V S indidit, in Inferiora, Hominem præcipue, qui Mundi typus, varia creduntur Platoni, Plotino, aliisque Academicis operari. Recipit, inquiunt, Anima in descensu ab Saturno vim Ratiocinandi, Intelligendi, Speculandi; ab Iove Agendi vires & in Praxin deducendi; ab Marte Animositatis ardorem; ab Sole Imaginandi, Sciendi, Opinandi potentiam; ab Venere Concupiscentiam & Desiderij motum; ab Mercurio Interpretandi, Pronunciandi, Penetrandi vigorem; ab Luna denique unde Generare, unde Augere queat: Deinde ab Saturno putant Philosophi influere Prudentiam; ab Iove Iustitiam: ab Marte Robur, & Fortitudinem; ab Sole Caritatem & Amorem; ab Venere Spem: ab Mercurio Fidem: ab Luna Temperantiam: Præterea Saturnum volunt iidem trahere homines ad sublimiora & quæ præstantiora; ad divinam scilicet & secretiorem Philosophiam, occulta Naturæ mysteria, facultatem omnia congregandi & æterna & quæ tempore pereunt; Iovem facere, ut homines condendis & servandis legibus, subministrandis quæ æqua, Subiectis alta pace & tranquillitate gubernandis invigilent; ab Marte vim instillari & desiderium cœpta ad finem moliendi; Solem dare fœtum & vitam; Venerem præstare leporem, festivitatem, amorem, quo agitati ardua cum delectatione perficiamus; Mercurium reddere promptos, acutos, solertes, cum ad omne opus, tum ad veritatem indagandam, adquirendam eloquentiam, gloriam conciliandam; Lunam denique, quæ Planetarum proxime nobis abest, varios concinnare motus. Non quod Planetæ sint fontes horum omnium aut domini; sed quia existimentur humana corpora & vires, virtute ab supremo Numine sibi insita, sic comparare, ut quæ dicta facile suspiciant. Iis enim qui male conciliati nocent omnia, & cedunt in malum. Nam mala proveniunt potius occulto DEI iudicio ex mala Recipientis dispositione, quam, ut nonnulli temere credunt, ex influentium malitia. DEVS omnia quæ fecerat, vidit esse valde bona: Cui igitur bono conviciis lacerabimus quæ bene ab illo creata? quur Saturni Sidus ut Malorum omnium columniabimur mare; concinnare illud clamantes Mortalibus sub se natis exilia, dolos, proditiones, carceres, damnationes, perfidiam, pertinaciam, iram, odium, metum, dolorem, funera, luctum, orbitates, furta, & id genus alia? facere vespillones, pollinctores, mogos? Quur Martis planetam adferemus in quacunque Cœli parte, mala majora hic, ibi minora semper minitari? Quur alios aliorum criminum faciemus reos? Exesto Albumasar Astrologus cum octo libris, quos scripsisti de magnis Conjunctionibus, Annorum revolutionibus & eorum profectionibus; exesto Alcabitius cum Isagoge ad iudicia astrorum vel ad scrutanda Stellarum magisteria, exeste denique cum Iulio Firmico Materno, alij Mathematici & Poetæ, quorum stulta de his commenta ab auribus omnium, ut monet Augustinus, procul sunt repellenda. Magnam toti cœlo facit injuriam, qui ibi, tamquam in amplissimo Senatu, Scelera facienda censet decerni. Non possum quin exclamem. Quam falso accusant Superos, stultique queruntur Mortales! etenim nostrorum causa malorum Ipsi Nos sumus; & sua quemque vecordia ledit.
units.tr: Let man now come forward, the most noble creature of God. In him there is nothing that is not found elsewhere: he exists, as all inanimate things do; he lives, as every kind of plant does; he feels and moves, as all animals do; he is endowed with mind and understanding, as the Angels are; and, finally, he was created in the image of his Creator, having received a soul, as I said a little before, which shares in holiness, which is master of reason, and which is capable of wisdom, justice, liberty, divine grace, eternal blessedness, and all the good things of God. That in him the round figure of the world is shown, the circle drawn from the navel through the extremities of his outstretched hands and feet apart from the head, teaches this. Does he possess the four elements of the world? This also appears in the five senses: for sight answers to Fire, hearing to Air, smell and taste to Water, and touch to Earth; and in the four humours, which Galen, the prince of physicians, also calls elements: blood, which rises warm and moist from the heart, favours Air; phlegm, which flows cold and moist from the brain, favours Water; black bile, which arises cold and dry from the spleen, favours Earth; and yellow bile, finally, which comes hot and dry from the liver, favours Fire. Plato's Timaeus must certainly be read, where the most splendid boastful piece about the microcosm is depicted to the life, part by part, of both soul and body. How harmonious, indeed, is the agreement of man with the planets and the other stars! For these, as ministers of the Supreme Maker, who is the origin of all things, are believed by Plato, Plotinus and other Academics to work upon the lower things, and man above all, who is the image of the world, by a certain hidden power that God has implanted in them. The soul, they say, on its descent receives from Saturn the power of reasoning, understanding and contemplation; from Jupiter the powers of acting and of putting things into practice; from Mars the ardour of spirit; from the Sun the power of imagining, knowing and forming opinions; from Venus concupiscence and the motion of desire; from Mercury the vigour of interpreting, pronouncing and penetrating; and from the Moon, finally, the capacity to generate and to increase. Then the philosophers think that Saturn pours in prudence, Jupiter justice, Mars strength and fortitude, the Sun charity and love, Venus hope, Mercury faith, and the Moon temperance. Moreover, the same men hold that Saturn draws human beings to higher and more excellent things, namely to divine and more secret philosophy, to the hidden mysteries of nature, to the faculty of gathering all things, both eternal things and those that perish in time; that Jupiter makes men watchful in enacting and preserving laws, in dispensing what is just, and in governing their subjects in high peace and tranquillity; that Mars instils strength and the desire to bring begun undertakings to an end; that the Sun gives offspring and life; that Venus bestows charm, festivity and love, by which, stirred, we accomplish difficult things with delight; that Mercury makes men ready, sharp and clever, both for every task and for searching out the truth, and for acquiring eloquence and winning glory; and that the Moon, which is nearest to us of the planets, arranges the various motions. Not that the planets are the sources or masters of all these things; but it is thought that they so fit human bodies and powers, by the virtue implanted in them by the Supreme Deity, that these bodies readily take up what has been said. For all things harm those who are badly disposed and turn to their hurt. Evils arise rather from the hidden judgment of God and from the bad disposition of the recipient than, as some rashly believe, from the malice of the influences. God saw that all the things he had made were very good. Why, then, shall we tear to pieces with insults what has been well created by him? Why shall we blame the star of Saturn as the sea of all evils, and cry out that it arranges exile, deceits, betrayals, prisons, condemnations, perfidy, obstinacy, anger, hatred, fear, grief, funerals, mourning, bereavements, thefts, and other things of that kind for mortals born under it; that it makes gravediggers, undertakers and hired mourners? Why shall we bring the planet of Mars, in whatever part of the heavens it stands, to threaten greater evils here and lesser ones there? Why shall we make some of them guilty of the crimes of others? Away with Albumasar the astrologer, with the eight books you wrote on the great conjunctions, the revolutions of the years and their profections; away with Alcabitius, with his Introduction to the judgments of the stars, or to the investigation of the mysteries of the stars; away, finally, with Julius Firmicus Maternus, and the other mathematicians and poets, whose foolish fictions about these matters, as Augustine warns, must be driven far from the ears of all. He does great injury to the whole heavens who thinks that wicked deeds are to be decreed there, as in the most august Senate. I cannot but exclaim: how falsely men accuse the gods above, and how foolishly mortals complain! For we ourselves are the cause of our evils, and each one is harmed by his own folly.

units.la: Iam in quibus cum Signis duodecim Homini conveniat, malim intelligat Lector Manilij Mathematici. quam meis verbis. Sic enim canit: Accipe diversus hominis per Sydera partes, Singulaque in propriis patentia signa figuris; In quis præcipuas toto de corpore vires Exercent. Aries Caput est ante omnia princeps; Sortitur censusque sui pulcerrima Colla Taurus; Et in Geminis æquali Brachia sorte Scribuntur connexa Humeris; Pectusque locatum Sub Cancro est; Laterum regnum Scapulaque Leoni; Virginis in propriam descindunt Ilia sortem; Libra regit Clunes; & Scorpius Inguine gaudet;
units.tr: Now, as to which of the twelve Signs correspond to the human body, I would rather the reader learn it from the Mathematician Manilius than from my own words. For he sings thus: "Take the parts of the human body as they are divided among the stars, and the signs spread out in their own figures, in which they exercise their chief powers over the whole body. Aries is first of all, the head; Taurus takes the neck, the fairest part of his own domain; in Gemini the arms are written as joined in equal lot to the shoulders; the chest is placed under Cancer; Leo rules the sides and shoulder-blades; the Virgin divides the loins to her own lot; Libra governs the buttocks, and Scorpio rejoices in the groin;

units.la: Centauro Femora accedunt; Capricornus utrisque In Genibus; Piscesque Pedum sibi jura poposcit.
units.tr: To Centaur the thighs fall; Capricorn holds both knees; and Pisces has claimed for itself the rule over the feet."

units.la: CAP. VIII. Mundum aliquando coepisse.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII. That the world began at some time.

units.la: EX ijs quae dixi, manifestum, Mundi conditionem, non, ut utar Augustini verbis, in tempore, sed cum tempore coepisse: quemadmodum cum sacro DEI verbo docent unanimi consensu, non solum Christiani (quorum omnium instar acutissimus hac in re, quem laudavi, Augustinus lib. xi. de Civit. Dei, cap. iv. & vi, item lib. xii. Confessionum) verum etiam vetustiores ante Aristotelem (quod ipse fatetur) Philosophi. Hi enim, ut & divinus ille Plato, ejusque discipuli, Probus, Posidonius, Plotinus, Seneca, Alexander Aphrodisiensis, Philo, omnesque fere Stoici, quum viderent solidas deesse Aeternitati confirmandae demonstrationes; maluerunt retinere traditam ab Majoribus suis sententiam, Mundum scilicet coepisse; quam sequius quid de eo statuere. Nam, ut ipse Plato perelegante, credibile est, Majores majorem & certiorem rerum divinarum cognitionem habuisse. Quum enim essent ab DEO orti; cognati quasi fuerunt illi; & propiores, quam nos, solidiora didicerunt. Scire certe & credere, Mundum ab aliquo temporis initio coepisse, facit ad DEI partim Bonitatem, ne ignoremus quem ad modum se voluerit nobis communicare; partim Magnitudinem, ut intelligamus, Quid & Quantum sit, quod potest. Potentiam enim quis unquam expendisset in Aeternitate? Abscondisset illa proculdubio & quasi obruisset Auctoris tanti vires; neque unquam quis, quantus Deus per se esset, quid, quantum, quatenus, quo modo singula fecisset, per obscuram illam Aeternitatem dextre & uti res flagitabat, judicare potuisset. Originem sane Mundi nobis ob oculos ponit ejus Progressus, quo non aliter quam hominem vel populum aliquem videmus eum adolescere. Docent, qui rudes quondam & imploriti, Mores hominum quotidie cultiores. Quam enim parum ab hinc tria annorum millia discriminis inter homines & feras? Habebant in Speluncis, solitarij fere, sine Rege, sine Lege; erecta paullatim Tentoria ex arborum ramis; hinc ventum ad Casas & Tabernacula; inde confieri coeperunt Pagi, & sensim Opida. Docent certi Ortus Auctusque, nobis Scriptorum beneficio notissimi, Nationum; quas, si aeternus Mundus, aeternas fuisse necessario dicendum. Docent denique, quae quotidie in Aedificiis, Victu, Vestitu, innumeris aliis, nova prodeunt Inventa; quasi Mundus, ut homo provectioris aetatis, pluribus indiges vitae instrumentis indigeat, qui olim, ut puer & pauciorum annorum, facile se quocunque modo tolerabat. Nam absurdum dicere, infinities eadem reperta infinities concidisse: nationibus, apud quas illa vigebant, sublatis, partim incendiorum injuria, vi partim eluvionum: postea vero rursum usu & ingenio reparata. Quasi vero immanissimis etiam calibus non superfuerint, qui secum Literas Artesque & Inventorum memoriam conservatam vel exercerent ipsi, vel posteris traderent. Iactura facile fit Aedificiorum & Divitiarum; non facile Inventorum humani Ingenij.
units.tr: From what I have said it is plain that the world's beginning was not, to use Augustine's words, in time, but with time. So the sacred Word of God teaches with one voice, and so do not only the Christians (of whom the most penetrating on this point, as I have praised him, is Augustine, in book 11 of The City of God, chapters 4 and 6, and likewise book 12 of the Confessions), but also the philosophers older than Aristotle (as he himself admits). For these, both the divine Plato and his disciples, Probus, Posidonius, Plotinus, Seneca, Alexander of Aphrodisias, Philo, and nearly all the Stoics, when they saw that there were no solid demonstrations to establish eternity, preferred to keep the opinion handed down by their ancestors, namely that the world had a beginning, rather than decide otherwise. For, as Plato himself says very elegantly, it is credible that the ancients had a greater and more certain knowledge of divine things. Since they were sprung from God, they were in a sense akin to him, and being closer to the source than we are, they learned the more solid truths. To know and to believe that the world began at some point in time serves, on the one hand, God's goodness, so that we may not be ignorant of how he chose to communicate himself to us; and on the other hand his greatness, so that we may understand what and how much he is able to do. For who could ever have weighed God's power in eternity? That eternity would undoubtedly have hidden and, as it were, buried the strength of so great a Maker. Nor could anyone, through that obscure eternity, have judged what God is in himself, how great he is, to what extent, and in what manner he made each thing, as the matter demanded. Certainly the progress of the world sets before our eyes its origin, since we see it grow up in the same way as a man or a people. We are taught this by the fact that men's manners, once rude and uncultivated, become more refined every day. How little difference there was, only three thousand years ago, between men and wild beasts! They lived in caves, mostly alone, without king or law. Little by little tents were raised from the branches of trees; from there they came to huts and tabernacles; then villages began to be built, and gradually towns. The certain rise and growth of nations, which we know well thanks to the writers, also teach this; if the world were eternal, these nations would necessarily have to be called eternal. Finally, the new inventions that appear every day in buildings, food, clothing and countless other things teach it. It is as if the world, like a man of more advanced age, now needs many more instruments of life, whereas once, like a boy of few years, it easily got along in whatever way it could. For it is absurd to say that the same discoveries were lost and made again countless times, the nations among whom they flourished having been destroyed, partly by the harm of fires and partly by the force of floods, and afterwards recovered again by practice and ingenuity. As if indeed even the most savage tribes had no survivors who preserved letters, arts and the memory of inventions, and either practised them themselves or handed them down to posterity. Buildings and riches are easily lost; the inventions of human genius are not easily lost.

units.la: Alijs Mundus est aeternus, alijs nimis antiquus. Aeternus Epicureis fere, male Magistrum sequutis, & Peripateticis omnibus; Aristoteli (qui videndus i. & viii. Physicorum) suffragantibus. De quibus consulat Lector Plutarchum ii. ἀεὶ τῶν ἀγενητῶν. τῆς φιλοσ. Diogenem Laertium in Democriti & Epicuri vitis; Diodorum Siculum lib. i. de antiq. gest. fabul. Lucretium lib. i. v. & vi. de natur. rerum: Galenum de Marasmo; M. Tullium lib. ii. de Divinat. & i. de Nat. Deor. Plinium lib. ii. natur. histor. cap. i. & alios. Rationes (si tamen tale nomen illis competat; Nam quid possunt, ut cum Origine loquar, adversus veritatem ipsam adducere, quod non ineptum, invalidum & falsum coarguatur?) quas illi ex ipsius Mundi Natura, Motu, Gubernatoribus, ipso denique Opifice, & aliunde, opinioni suae stabiliendae adferunt, prudens praetereo; refutas plene & docte ab Hannibale Rosselo Calabro (qui praecipuus Ocelli Lucani, Universum hoc & Interitus expers & Ortus adserentis, oppugnator) lib. v. in Poemandrum Mercurij Trismegisti, Comment. ii. cap. ii. Francisco Georgio Veneto Cantici de Harmonia Mundi 1. Tomo 1. cap. ix. & seqq. Iacobo Milichio in 11. Plinii natural. histor. librum; Nicolao Selneccero Enarratione in cap. 1. Genes. & aliis. Adeundus & Philo de Mundo.
units.tr: For some the world is eternal, for others too old. Eternal according to the Epicureans, who followed their master badly, and according to all the Peripatetics, with Aristotle supporting them (see his Physics, books 1 and 8). On these matters the reader may consult Plutarch, in the second book [ἀεὶ τῶν ἀγενητῶν. τῆς φιλοσ.], Diogenes Laertius in the lives of Democritus and Epicurus, Diodorus Siculus in book 1 of On Ancient Deeds and Fables, Lucretius in books 1, 5 and 6 of On the Nature of Things, Galen On Marasmus, Cicero in book 2 of On Divination and book 1 of On the Nature of the Gods, Pliny in book 2, chapter 1, of his Natural History, and others. I deliberately pass over the arguments (if indeed that name suits them; for what can they bring against truth itself, to use Origen's phrase, that is not shown to be silly, weak and false?) which they bring from the nature, motion and governors of the world, from its maker himself, and from elsewhere, to support their opinion. These have been fully and learnedly refuted by Hannibal Rossellus of Calabria (the chief opponent of Ocellus Lucanus, who maintained that this universe is free from destruction and has no beginning) in book 5 on the Poimandres of Mercurius Trismegistus, commentary 2, chapter 2; by Francesco Giorgio of Venice in the first volume of his Harmony of the World, chapter 9 and following; by Jacob Milich on book 11 of Pliny's Natural History; by Nicolaus Selnecker in his commentary on Genesis chapter 1; and by others. The reader should also consult Philo's On the World.

units.la: Aliis, ut dixi, nimis antiquus. Chaldæos adferere vulgo non puduit, habere se Siderum rerumque cœlestium scientiam, non minus quam quadringenties septuagies mille annorum observationibus comprobatam: quum interim non solum Callisthenes, expeditionum Alexandri Magni socius, excussis Babylone cum cura & diligentia secretissimis, quæcunque reperiri poterant, eorum monimentis, didicisse scribatur apud Porphyrium, observationes rerum cœlestium, quæ omnium erant vetustissimæ, non amplius fuisse quam mille nongentorum annorum; verum etiam Hipparchus & Ptolemæus Antiquitatem Astronomicæ sapientiæ non altius repetant, quam ab temporibus Nebucad-netzaris Chaldæorum regis, quem circa xxxix Olympiadem Iudæorum calamitates nobilitarunt.
units.tr: Others, as I have said, make it too old. The Chaldeans commonly were not ashamed to claim that they had knowledge of the stars and heavenly things, confirmed by observations of four hundred and seventy thousand years. Yet not only is it written in Porphyry that Callisthenes, a companion of Alexander the Great's expeditions, having carefully and diligently searched out in Babylon whatever could be found among their most secret records, learned that the observations of heavenly things, which were the oldest of all, amounted to no more than 1,900 years; but also Hipparchus and Ptolemy do not trace the antiquity of astronomical wisdom further back than the times of Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Chaldeans, whom the calamities of the Jews made famous around the thirty-ninth Olympiad.

units.la: Ægyptij, fingentes innumera Mundi sæcula, jactant apud Diodorum Siculum, Pomponium Melam, Diogenem Laertium & alios, exquo cœperunt innotescere, quater cursus suos vertisse Sidera; bis Solem occidisse, unde nunc oritur: Reges Ægyptiorum partim ex Dijs, partim ex hominibus ad novissimum regem Ptolemæum, Cleopatræ patrem, supra septuaginta annorum millia regnasse in Ægypto; postquam autem rationem Siderum comprehenderunt, amplius quam centum annorum millia numerari. Idem, apud Plinium lib. xxxv. nat. hist. cap. xiii. gloriantur 20 artem pingendi sex millibus annorum apud se floruisse, priusquam ea transfirer in Græciam. Narrat apud Cyprianum de Idololatria & Augustinum lib. xii. de Civit. Dei, cap. x. Sacerdos quidam Ægyptius Alexandro Magno, in sacris Ægyptiorum Litteris & Annalibus, omnium Regnorum tempora subtiliter adnotata contineri, in ijs tradi, regnum Assyriorum quinque annorum millia excessisse; Persarum autem & Macedonum Imperium plusquam octo annorum millibus diffiniri. Commemorat alius, apud Platonem in Timæo, Sacerdos Soloni, Athenas novem millibus annorum ante ejus ætatem fuisse conditas. Ut non fero portentosam gentis, quæ ad stuporem mendacia fingere & fabricare solita, nugandi de mutatis quater Siderum, bis Solis cursibus licentiam: sic quodam modo ferendam censeo, nominantem quamvis vix ferenda annorum millia. Antiquissimus enim Ægyptiorum annus bimestris fuisse legitur apud Censorinum; qui deinde ab rege Pisone quadrimestris factus; postremo ab alijs ad tredecim menses & dies quinque productus. Varro item, Diodorus Siculus, Plinius & alij nunc trimestres, nunc menstruos agnoscunt eorum annos.
units.tr: The Egyptians, inventing countless ages of the world, boast, in Diodorus Siculus, Pomponius Mela, Diogenes Laertius and others, that from the time when they began to be known the stars had four times changed their courses, and the sun had twice set where it now rises. They say that the kings of Egypt, partly gods and partly men, reigned in Egypt for more than 70,000 years, down to the last king, Ptolemy, father of Cleopatra; and that after they had grasped the reckoning of the stars, more than 100,000 years could be counted. In Pliny, book 35 of the Natural History, chapter 13, they likewise glory that the art of painting flourished among them for six thousand years before it passed into Greece. In Cyprian On Idolatry and Augustine in book 12 of The City of God, chapter 10, we read that a certain Egyptian priest told Alexander the Great that the sacred Egyptian writings and annals contained carefully noted times of all kingdoms, and in them it was taught that the kingdom of the Assyrians had lasted more than 5,000 years, while the empire of the Persians and Macedonians was reckoned at more than 8,000 years. Another priest, in Plato's Timaeus, told Solon that Athens had been founded nine thousand years before his time. I do not much mind the monstrous nation, accustomed to invent and fabricate lies to the point of astonishment, with its licence to babble about the four changes of the stars and the two courses of the sun; I think it can be tolerated in some measure, even though the numbers of years it names can hardly be tolerated. For the most ancient Egyptian year is said, in Censorinus, to have been two months long; afterwards King Piso made it four months; lastly others lengthened it to thirteen months and five days. Varro, Diodorus Siculus, Pliny and others likewise recognise their years at one time as three months long and at another as monthly.

units.la: Indorum apud Plinium lib. vi. natur. histor. monimenta, ab Libero Patre, qui primus iis arma intulit, ad Alexandrum Magnum Reges numerant centum quinquaginta tres; per annos sexies mille, quadringentos & duos; tresque, ne quid justo deesset calculo, menses; quum tamen Liberum Patrem, Ichoschuhha Hebræis imperante, floruisse accuratissimi notent Chronographi. 40
units.tr: The monuments of the Indians, in Pliny book 6 of the Natural History, count from Liber Pater, who was the first to bring arms among them, down to Alexander the Great, 153 kings, over 6,402 years and three months, so that nothing might be lacking in the exact reckoning. Yet the most accurate chronographers note that Liber Pater flourished in the time when Ichoschuhha ruled the Hebrews. 40

units.la: Prætereo Eudoxi & Aristotelis figmenta, confirmantium, Zoroastrem, qui Astronomiæ perhibetur parens, sex annorum millibus ante Platonis fuisse obitum. Certe æqualem fuisse Zoroastrem Nino regi; à quo ad Platonis mortem paullo plures mille septingentis annis, memoriæ produnt Diodorus Siculus; Iustinus, aliique scriptores.
units.tr: I pass over the fictions of Eudoxus and Aristotle, who affirmed that Zoroaster, who is said to be the father of astronomy, died six thousand years before Plato. Certainly Diodorus Siculus, Justin and other writers record that Zoroaster was a contemporary of King Ninus, and that from him to the death of Plato there were a little more than 1,700 years.

units.la: Tempus igitur illud creati ab Deo Mundi ex Nihilo certum per se; incertius autem, si momentum ejus ab hominibus quærendum. Nam Arenam Maris, Pluviæ guttas, Sæculi dies quis dinumeravit? inquit Ecclesiast. cap. 1. ubi Nicolaus Lyranus; Annos Mundi cognitos haberi notat, ratione quadam probabili, non tamen certitudine infallibili. Variant, ut videre est cum apud Sixtum Senensem lib. v. Bibliothecæ sanctæ, rum 50 apud Michaelem Erzingerum in Regnorum Mundi Pentaplo, mirum in modum Chronographi. Varietatis quatuor indicat caullas Benedict. Pererius in Genes. lib. 1. & vii. Collectiones auctoritas sacræ Scripturæ suffultas, & Meliorum, qui inter peccantes vel defectu vel excessu medij, calculos sequutus, censeo factam admirandam hanc Mundi machinam ante annos quinquies mille, quingentos, sexaginta, aut circiter: at quo anni tempore vix ausim dicere. Vernum, & in eo mensem Martium, communibus suffragiis edunt, post Virgilium 11. Geor.
