Theologi omnes & Ecclesiastici Scriptores; in ipso die notando variantes. xiix Martij nominant Strabus & Rabanus ad xii. caput Exodi, Glossa interlinearis ad cap. xxxv. Geneseos, Beda libro de ratione temporum cap. xxviii. x L. & alibi. xxiii. Martij diem edit apud Bedam initio libri de sex Mundi aetatibus, communis Patrum consensus in Synodo Palaestina, quam mandatu Victoris Papae congregavit Theophilus Episcopus Caesariensis. xxv. denique mensis eiusdem notant, Eusebius in omnimoda historia, Athanasius respondens ad quaestionem xvii. Antiochi, Cyrillus Hierosolymitanus Catechesi xiiii, Leo Papa sermone ix. de Passione Domini, Gregorius Nazianzenus oratione in Novam Dominicam, Isidorus lib. v. Etymolog. cap de Temporibus, Damascenus lib. ii. de Fide Orthodoxa, cap. vii. Qui omnes varia prebandis suis sententiis adscribunt argumenta, quae longum esset & taedio sum hic recensere. Autumni tempore conditum Mundum volunt Hebraeorum plurimi, & inter eos Josephus lib. i. Antiq. Iudaic. Adsentiunt illis Nicolaus Lyranus ad cap. vii. Genes. Tostatus ad cap. eiusdem libri i. quaestione xxi. & priore parte Defensorij cap. xiiii. Benedictus Pererius lib. i. in Genesin. validis suam mentem argumentis firmans, refutato ibidem docte Gerardo Mercatore; qui, sequutus fortean Aeculapium & Anubium, initio suae Chronologiae, unus Mundum mente Iulio conditum opinatur; scrutari conatus etiam in suo Atlante fere ipsius diei momentum, quum adserit in nocturnum tempus primam rerum creationem incidisse. Legendi omnino huc Caelius Rhodiginus Lect. Antiq. lib. i. cap. viii. Ioannes Lucidus lib. i, cap. ii. de Temporum emendatione, & alij.
units.tr: That time, then, of the world's creation out of nothing by God is certain in itself; but the moment of it is less certain if men try to seek it out. For, as Ecclesiastes chapter 1 says, Who has numbered the sand of the sea, the drops of rain, the days of the age? Nicholas of Lyra, on that passage, notes that the years of the world are known by a certain probable reckoning, yet not by infallible certainty. The chronographers vary wonderfully, as may be seen in Sixtus of Siena, book 5 of the Bibliotheca sancta, and in Michael Erzinger's Pentaplus of the Kingdoms of the World, where there are fifty. Benedict Pererius, in book 1 and book 7 of his commentary on Genesis, gives four causes of the variation. Gathering the authority of Scripture and the reckonings of the better writers, who followed the middle course between those who err by defect and those who err by excess, I judge that this wonderful machine of the world was made about 5,560 years ago, or thereabouts; but at what time of the year I would hardly dare to say. All theologians and ecclesiastical writers, by common consent, name spring, and in it the month of March, after Virgil in book 2 of the Georgics; but they vary in naming the day. Strabo and Rabanus name the 19th of March, in their notes on chapter 12 of Exodus; the Glossa Interlinearis on Genesis chapter 35; Bede in his book On the Reckoning of Time, chapter 28, and elsewhere. The 23rd of March is given by Bede at the beginning of his book On the Six Ages of the World, as the common consent of the Fathers in the Palestinian synod which Theophilus, bishop of Caesarea, convened by command of Pope Victor. Lastly, the 25th of the same month is named by Eusebius in his Universal History; by Athanasius, answering the seventeenth question of Antiochus; by Cyril of Jerusalem in his fourteenth Catechesis; by Pope Leo in his ninth sermon on the Passion of the Lord; by Gregory Nazianzen in his oration on the New Sunday; by Isidore, book 5 of the Etymologies, in the chapter on times; and by Damascene, book 2 of On the Orthodox Faith, chapter 7. All of these attach various arguments to support their opinions, which would be too long and tedious to list here. Many of the Hebrews hold that the world was created in autumn, and among them Josephus in book 1 of the Jewish Antiquities. Nicolaus Lyra agrees with them on Genesis chapter 7; Tostatus on the same chapter of the same book, question 21, and in the first part of his Defensorium, chapter 14; and Benedict Pererius in book 1 on Genesis, confirming his view with strong arguments and there learnedly refuting Gerard Mercator. Mercator, perhaps following Aesculapius and Anubis, at the beginning of his Chronology alone thinks that the world was made in July; and in his Atlas he tries to examine almost the very moment of the day, since he asserts that the first creation of things fell in the night-time. Caelius Rhodiginus, Lectiones antiquae, book 1, chapter 8; John Lucidus, book 1, chapter 2, On the Emendation of Time; and others are certainly to be read on this point.

units.la: Sed, inquiet Impius, si Mundo initium Ortus; DEVS, in quo motum aeternum esse praedicant Philosophi, quid mohebatur rerum ante novam Molis huius conditionem? quod habuit, quo reciperetur, domicilium? quur non antea multis saeculorum millibus Mundum protulit? quur non post? quibus Ministris vel cultoribus est visus? num Ocio torpebat? num loco carens nusquam erat? si nusquam, a quo, quo pacto, quo loco genitus? O homo; nefas mihi, tibi, omnibus, Caussas scrutari, quibus magni Numinis voluntas ad agendum velut adducta. Scrutator Majestatis, inquit Sapiens. opprimetur ab Gloria. AEterno DEO nihil prius; nihil posterius; omnia illi sunt praesentia, atque adeo τὸ ἐν vix illi congruit, ut Plato adfirmat in Timaeo. Agebat, ut cum magno viro propius accedam, DEVS ante Mundum, & sine Mundo, quod nunc cum Mundo; in sua felicitate seipso contentus, plenus bonorum omnium, ab aeterno constituerat Mundum procreare, atque ea condere quibus suam communicaret beatitudinem; sed tunc, non antea, nec post; quur? quia sic illi visum. Non hoc sufficit? Ante Mundum factum communicatio fuit Sapientiae inter DEVM Patrum, Filium & Spiritum Sanctum aeterna. Quid praeter ea respondeam, non habeo. Ingenij hic, cum Augustino, vela lubens contraho.
units.tr: But, the unbeliever will say, if the world had a beginning in time, while God, in whom the philosophers declare motion to be eternal, what moved him before the new construction of this mass of things? What dwelling-place did he have in which to be received? Why did he not produce the world many thousands of ages earlier? Why not later? To what ministers or worshippers did he appear? Was he sluggish from idleness? Was he nowhere, lacking a place? If nowhere, then from whom, in what manner, and in what place was the world begotten? O man, it is not right for me or for you or for anyone to search out the causes by which the will of the great Divinity was, as it were, led to act. "The searcher of majesty," says the wise man, "will be overwhelmed by glory." For the eternal God nothing is prior and nothing posterior; all things are present to him, and so the τὸ ἐν [the one] scarcely fits him, as Plato affirms in the Timaeus. Let me come a little closer to a great man: God was acting before the world and without the world, just as he now acts with the world. Content with himself in his own blessedness, full of all good things, he had determined from eternity to bring forth the world and to establish those things through which he would communicate his happiness; but then, and not earlier or later. Why? Because so it seemed good to him. Is this not enough? Before the world was made, there was an eternal communication of wisdom among the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Beyond these things I have no answer to give. Here, with Augustine, I gladly furl my sails of talent.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: Mundum Finem habiturum.
units.tr: The World Will Have an End.

units.la: SI igitur initium habuerit hoc, quod videmus: necessum est habiturum quoque sit Finem, qui Initio oppositus. Interiturum Opus hoc, est opus. Probant, ut illustrissima Sacrae Scripturae testimonia sileam, Mundum corruptioni obnoxium, eius Partes; quas, numquam & nusquam non, stupendum in modum videmus alterari, in peiorem plurimum conditionem. Veterascunt Omnia, Psalmo cii, 27. & in senilem quali vergunt aetatem, fiuntque minora & in pejus ruunt, Esdras lib. iiii. cap. v. vers. 52. & seq. Mundo senescente, Rerum atque Hominum passim iam decrementa, inquit Varro apud Agellium lib. iii. noct. Attic. cap. x. spectantibus eodem Virgilio lib. i. Georgic. & Plinio lib. vii. natur. histor. cap. xvi. ut Argumenta fere non defuerint nescio quibus, apud Aelianum lib. viii. Var. histor. cap. xi. Mundum sensim & sine sensu, suo quali senio periturum adsentiebus, utque non immerito nonnulli Universum hoc adsimilarint Homini; florentis illi & marcescentis aetatis nomina tribuentes D. Hieronymus Homilia i. super Euangelist. Sicut in Iuventute viget Corpus, forte & incolume manet Pectus, torosa Cervix,
units.tr: If, therefore, this world, which we see, has had a beginning, it must also have an end, since an end is the opposite of a beginning. This work will perish, because it is a work. To pass over the most illustrious testimonies of Holy Scripture, the corruptibility of the world and its parts proves this. We see them, always and everywhere, changing in a remarkable way, and for the most part for the worse. All things grow old (Psalm 102:27), and they approach something like old age, becoming smaller and declining for the worse (2 Esdras 4:52 ff.). As the world grows old, the decline of things and of men is already visible everywhere, as Varro says in Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights, book 3, chapter 10. Virgil, Georgics book 1, and Pliny, Natural History book 7, chapter 16, agree, so that there has been no lack of arguments for some, such as those in Aelian, Historical Miscellany book 8, chapter 11, who hold that the world will perish gradually and without feeling, by a kind of old age of its own. Not unreasonably, some have likened this whole universe to a man, giving it the names of flourishing and fading age. Saint Jerome, Homily 1 on the Gospels, says: As in youth the body is vigorous, the chest firm and the neck sturdy, and the arms full; but in the years of old age the stature is bent, the neck is shrivelled and lowered, the chest is pressed by frequent sighs, strength fails, and the breath of the speaker cuts short the words (for so the passage should be read); for even if sickness is absent, health itself is often troubled in the old. So the world in its earlier years, as in youth, was vigorous, sturdy for propagating the offspring of the human race, green in the health of bodies, rich in its abundance of goods. But now it is pressed down by its very old age, and, as if death were near, it is harassed ever more often by growing troubles.

units.la: C Cervix, plena sunt Brachia; in annis autem senilibus Statura curvatur, Cervix exsiccita deponitur, frequentibus suspiriis Pectus urgetur, Virtus deficit, loquentis Anhelitus verba intercipit (sic enim legendum) nam etsi languor deßit, plerumque senibus ipsa sua Salus agrit udo est: ita Mundus in annis prioribus, velut in juventute, vigut, ad propagandam humani generis prolem robustus fuit, salute corporum viridis, opulentia rerum pinguis: At nunc ipsa sua senectute deprimitur, & quasi ad vicinam mortem molestiis crebrescentibus, crebrius urgetur. Sic D. Ambrosius libro de bono mortis cap. x. Defecit multitudine generationis hoc seculum tanquam vulva generantis, & tamquam senescens creatura; robur juventutis suæ, velut jam marcescente virtum suarum vigore, deponit. Voluit idem D. Cyprianus tractatu 1. contra Demetr. Canos videmus in pueris, capilli deficiunt, antequam crescant, nec ætas in senectutem definit, sed incipit a senectute; & in ortu adhuc suo ad finem nativitas properat: sic quodcunque nunc nascitur, mundi ipsius senectute degenerat, ut nemo mirari debeat, singula in Mundo cœpisse deficere, quum totus ipse jam Mundus in senectute sit & infine. Idem: Illud primo in loco scire debes, senuisse jam Mundum; non illis slare viribus, quibus prius sicterat; nec vigore & robore eo valere, quo antea prævalebat. Et paullo post: Putasne tu tantam posse substantiam senescentis rei existere, quanta prius potuit, novella adhuc & vegeta juventute pollere? Suis etiam morbis & languoribus conflictari docentes. Origines tractatu xxiiix. in Matthæum: Sicut ægrotant corpora ante mortem eorum, qui vim non extrinsecus patiuntur; & quemadmodum in omnibus per infirmitatem fit via ad separandum animam a corpore suo: sic talis ac tanta creatura Mundi, quum corrumpi cœperit, quasi initium habens & finem, necesse est ante corruptionem, ut langueat. D. Ambrosius cap. xxi. in Lucam: Quia in occasu seculi sumus, præcedunt quædam ægritudines Mundi; ægritudo Mundi est fames, ægritudo Mundi est pestilentia, & quæ ibi alia. Quibus tamen, non recte, reclamant, Aristoteles lib. 11. Meteoror. qui ridiculum putat ob parvas levesque mutationes. Mundi totius permutationem adferre, indeque Universi cladem colligere; quum Terra magnitudo nihil profecto fit ad universum Cœlum, id est Mundum: & Columella, qui lib. 1. & 11. de re rustica, contra Veterum sententiam, senecla corripi Terram negat.
units.tr: So Saint Ambrose, On the Good of Death, chapter 10: This age has failed in the multitude of its generations, like a womb that no longer bears, and like a creature growing old; it lays down the strength of its youth, as the vigour of its powers already fades. Saint Cyprian, Treatise 1 against Demetrianus, held the same: We see grey hairs in children; hair falls out before it has grown; nor does life pass into old age, but it begins from old age; and at its very birth the nativity hastens toward its end. So whatever is now born degenerates in the old age of the world itself, so that no one should wonder that single things in the world have begun to fail, since the whole world is already in old age and its end. The same author: You must first of all know that the world has now grown old; it does not stand with the strength by which it stood before, nor is it strong in that vigour and power by which it once prevailed. And a little later: Do you think that a substance which is growing old can have as much power as it had before, when it was still strong in fresh and vigorous youth? Some also teach that it is afflicted by its own diseases and infirmities. Origen, Homily 23 on Matthew: As the bodies of those who do not suffer violence from outside fall sick before their death, and as in all cases sickness is the way by which the soul is separated from its body, so such and so great a creature as the world, when it has begun to corrupt, having as it were a beginning and an end, must necessarily languish before its corruption. Saint Ambrose, chapter 21 on Luke: Because we are at the close of the age, certain sicknesses of the world go before; the sickness of the world is famine, the sickness of the world is pestilence, and whatever else there is. Yet Aristotle, Meteorology book 2, who thinks it ridiculous to draw from small and light changes a change of the whole world and so to infer the destruction of the universe, since the magnitude of the earth is nothing at all compared with the whole heaven, that is, the world, does not rightly object to these views. Nor does Columella, in books 1 and 2 of On Agriculture, who denies, against the opinion of the ancients, that the earth is seized by old age.

units.la: Quod ad veterum Philosophorum hac de re sententias; eorum quibusdam Mundus, ut natus, sic periturus; quod censent Epicurus, Stoici, Anaximenes, Anaximander, Anaxagoras, Archelaus, Democritus, Leucippus, Empedocles, Lucretius: aliis natus quidem, sed permansurus, ut placuit Platoni ejusque discipulis: nonnullis, ut non natus, sic nec periturus, quæ mens Xenophanis, Parmenidis, Melissi, Philolai; Aristæi Ocelli: de quibus omnibus videndi Lucretius lib. v. & vi. Plutarchus περὶ τ᾽ Ἀρεσκόντ. τοῖς Φιλοσόφ. Iustinus Martyr, Clemens Alexandrinus, Ioannes Stobæus lib.
units.tr: The world, however, will perish by the eternal decree of God and his free will. Galeottus Marzio, in chapter 25 of his On Promiscuous Learning, is therefore wrong when he refers the cause of the burning to the eighth sphere, and says that the Crab and Capricorn will gradually change their places. In vain do the Chaldeans hold that the coming conflagration will be caused by the concurrence of the celestial signs and stars, which are by nature very hot; so too Berosus, as cited by Seneca, and Seneca himself in Natural Questions, book 3, chapter 29. Finally, Aristotle is also wrong, who in book 1 of the Meteorology hints at great alternations of the world under the names of flood (kataklysmos), its winter, and conflagration (ekpyrosis), its summer, holding that these happen in fixed cycles of years and through the passage of the stars, and inferring from this, with destruction denied, the everlasting duration of the world. Eusebius attributes this opinion also to Heraclides and Empedocles, and Athenagoras likewise to the Stoics. One should also consult Julius Firmicus, Astrology book 2, and Censorinus, On the Birthday.

units.la: 1. Eclog. cap. xxiv. Notat universim paucis verbis Arnobius lib. 11. adversus gentes: Mundum quidam ex sapientibus existimant, neque esse natum, neque ullo tempore periturum; immortalem nonnulli, quamvis eum conscribant esse natum & genitum: tertiis collibitum dicere est, & esse natum & genitum, & ordinaria necessitate periturum. Rabini etiam quidam Mundum volunt perpetuo duraturum, ex Genesis cap. 11x. versibus postremis: Nequaquam ultro maledicam Terra propter Homines. Sensus enim & cogitatio humani cordis mala ab adolescentia ejus, neque posthac percutiam ultra omnia viventia, quemadmodum feci. Deinceps quamdiu erit terra, sementis & messis, frigusque & æstus, æstasque & hyems, diesque & nox non cessabunt. Sed stulte hoc eos inde colligere notat Hieronymus ab Oleastro. Nam Pactum illud ad modum interitus referendum. Non enim amplius per diluvium Mundus est peritus. Eleganter Eucherius libro 1. in Genesin: Ipsum signum in Aqua & Igne ostenditur; quia ex parte est caruleus (loquitur de arcu cœlesti) & ex parte est rubicundus: quia utriusque judicij testis est, unius videlicet facti & alterius faciendi. Quod testamentum posuit DEVS inter se & homines & omem animam vivam; ne perdat eam diluvio, arcum qui apparet in nubibus. Et sane quid sibi vellent verba illa כל־ימי הארץ omnibus diebus terra? an non subindicant hos Terræ dies aliquando cessaturos, ut locum dent diebus Cœli; quibus futuri nos ut Angeli; propius DEVM agnituri, in ejus Sapientia nos oblectaturi, ejusque præsentia fruituri! Dion Prusiensis Sophista, cognomento Chrysostomus, ut Suidas testatur, librum conscripsit, ὁ Φιλόσοφος ὁ Κόσμος, quem temporis injuria nobis sustulit.
units.tr: 1. Eclog. chapter 24. Arnobius, book 2 Against the Gentiles, briefly notes the matter in general: Some of the wise think that the world was neither born nor will ever perish; some hold it immortal, although they write that it was born and begotten; to say a third thing is to say that it was born and begotten, and will perish by ordinary necessity. Some rabbis also hold that the world will last for ever, from the last verses of Genesis chapter 8: I will by no means again curse the earth for the sake of men, for the imagination of man's heart is evil from his youth; nor will I again strike every living thing as I have done. From now on, as long as the earth endures, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night, shall not cease. But Jerome, following Oleaster, notes that they draw this conclusion foolishly. For that covenant must be referred to the manner of ending, since the world was no longer to perish by the flood. Eucherius elegantly says in book 1 on Genesis: The sign itself is shown in water and fire; for in part it is blue (he speaks of the rainbow), and in part red, because it is a witness of both judgments, namely of one deed already done and of another yet to be done. God set this covenant between himself and men and every living soul, that he would not destroy it by the flood: the bow that appears in the clouds. And indeed, what do the words כל־ימי הארץ, all the days of the earth [kol-yemei ha-aretz], mean? Do they not hint that these days of the earth will one day cease, to make room for the days of heaven, in which we, like the angels, shall be closer to knowing God, delighting in his wisdom and enjoying his presence? Dion of Prusa, the sophist surnamed Chrysostom, as Suidas testifies, wrote a book, The Philosopher, or On the World [ὁ Φιλόσοφος ὁ Κόσμος], which the injury of time has taken from us.

units.la: Periturus autem Mundus æterno DEI decreto & libera ejus voluntate. Fustra enim est Galeotus Marcius cap. xxv de doctrina promiscua, Exustionis causam referens ad Octavam Sphæram, & Cancrum atque Capricornum loca sensim commutatumutaturos. Frustra Chaldæi, qui Exstionem futuram statuunt in Signorum Cœlestium Astrorumque, quæ natura calidissima, concursu; Berosus apud Senecam, & ipse Seneca lib. iii. cap. xxix. natural. quæst. Frustra denique Aristoteles, qui libro 1. Meteororum, magnas illas vicissitudines insinuat per καταχλυσμὸν scu Mundi hyemem & ἐκπύρωσιν, Mundi æstatem: statuens eas certis annorum curriculis & Siderum trajectionibus contingere: colligens inde, negato interitu, durationem Mundi sempiternam: quam sententiam Eusebius tribuit etiam Heraclidi & Empedocli; Stoicis item Athenagoras. Videndi & Iulius Firmicus lib. ii. Astrolog. & Censorinus de die Natali.
units.tr: The world will perish, however, by the eternal decree of God and his free will. Galeotus Marcius, chapter 25 of On Promiscuous Learning, is wrong when he refers the cause of the conflagration to the eighth sphere, and says that Cancer and Capricorn will gradually change places. The Chaldeans are wrong too, who hold that the future conflagration will come from the concourse of the celestial signs and stars, which are by nature very hot; so too Berosus, as cited by Seneca, and Seneca himself, Natural Questions book 3, chapter 29. Finally, Aristotle is wrong, who in book 1 of the Meteorology suggests those great alternations through a flood [kataklysmon], the winter of the world, and an ecpyrosis [ekpyrōsis], the summer of the world, holding that these happen in fixed cycles of years and by the passing of the stars, and inferring from this, with destruction denied, the everlasting duration of the world. Eusebius ascribes this opinion also to Heraclides and Empedocles; Athenagoras ascribes it to the Stoics. See also Julius Firmicus, Astrology book 2, and Censorinus, On the Birthday.

units.la: Quibus partibus? Non difficile solum sed & periculosum aliquid hic dissinire. De Inferioribus his certum: quid de Superioribus? כי שמיים inquit Isaiahias cap. li. בעשן נמלחו Nam Cœli, sicut fumus, sunt consumti. Hiob cap. xiv. vers. 12. Homo, quum dormierit, non resurget, עד בלי שמים usque ad non Cœlos; עד דלירו שמיא, donec non sint Cœli, ut habet Paraphrasis Chaldaica; &, ut lxx. Interpretes; ἕως ἂν ὁ οὐρανὸς ἡ μὴ συνῤῥαφῇ, quousque Cœlum non consutum fit: id est, donec atteratur Cœlum, non evigilabit, nec consurget de somno suo. De omnibus simul, ipsa in Euangelio Veritas, Christus apud Euangelistam Lucam cap. xxi, 33. ὁ οὐρανὸς καὶ ἡ γῆ παρελεύσονται, εἰ ἢ λόγοι μου οὐ μὴ παρέλθωσι. Sic Petrus Apostolus Epistola posteriore, cap. iii. vers. 7. εἰ δὲ τῷ αὐτῷ λόγῳ τεθησαυρισμένοι εἰσὶ, πυρὶ τηρούμενοι εἰς ἡμέραν κρίσεως καὶ ἀπωλείας τῶν ἀσεβῶν ἀνθρώπων. Deinde vers. 10: ἥξει ἡ ἡμέρα κυρίου ὡς κλέπτης ἐν νυκτὶ, ἐν ἡ οἱ οὐρανοὶ ῥοιζηδὸν παρελεύσονται, στοιχεῖα δὲ καυσούμενα λυθήσονται, καὶ γῆ καὶ τὰ ἐν αὐτῇ ἔργα κατακαήσονται, & quæ alia ibi sequuntur. Accedit probandæ Superiorum corruptioni, & aditerendo interitui, Cæli, Solis, Lunæ, quæ futura dicitur, innovatio, Isaiahiah. cap. xxx. lxv. & lxvi. Ioannes Apocalyps. cap. xxi. Petrus Epistola, quam laudavi, cap. iii. vers. 13. Stellarum casus de Cœlo, Isaiahiah. cap. xxxiv. Esdr. cap. iiii, 24. Ioann. Apocalyps. vi. & similia. Omnia Elementa exurenda & ipsos etiam Cœlos Superiores, opinantur, Theophylactus ad cap. viii. Epistol. ad Romanos, Augustinus & Ludolphus ad Psalmum cii. Alij duo Elementa consumenda putant, duo relinquenda, cujus mentis Beda. Sunt qui incendio corrumpendam Mundi machinam censent secundum partes, quæ diluvio fuerunt demersæ; ut (quemadmodum etiam videre est apud D. Petrum Epist. ii. cap. iii. §. 6. 7. & Augustinum xv. de Civit. Dei cap. xviii.) Illuvio atque Exustio sibi invicem quasi respondeant. Primasius Augustini discipulus ad cap. i. Epistolæ ad Hebræos, Anselmus Cantuariensis in cap. xii. ejusdem Epistolæ. Augustinus, parum sibi constans hac in re, non modicam partem Inferiorum Orbium una cum Superioribus expertem futuram exustionis, tradit lib. xx. cap. xiix. Epicterus denique Mundum conflagraturum, etiam ipsos Deos, ait apud AElianum lib. iii. cap. xiii. Variæ historiæ.
units.tr: Which parts? It is not only difficult but also somewhat dangerous to decide this here. Concerning the lower parts there is certainty; what of the upper? Isaiah, chapter 51, says: For the heavens, like smoke, shall vanish [ki shamayim kashan nimlechu]. Job chapter 14 verse 12: Man, when he has lain down, will not rise again [adh belî shamayim], until the heavens are no more, as the Chaldee paraphrase has it, until the heavens are not; and as the Seventy translate, until the heaven is no longer stitched together [heōs an ho ouranos mē syrraphē], that is, until the heaven is worn away, they will not awake nor rise from their sleep. Concerning all of them together, the truth itself in the Gospel, Christ, in Luke chapter 21 verse 33, says: Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away [ho ouranos kai hē gē parelevsontai, hoi de logoi mou ou mē parelthōsin]. So the apostle Peter, in his second epistle, chapter 3 verse 7: But by the same word they are stored up, kept for fire until the day of judgment and of destruction of ungodly men [tō autō logō tethēsaurismenoi eisi, pyri tēroumenoi eis hēmeran kriseōs kai apōleias tōn asebōn anthrōpōn]. Then verse 10: The day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night, in which the heavens will pass away with a rushing noise, and the elements will be destroyed by burning, and the earth and the works in it will be burned up [hēxei hē hēmera kyriou hōs klēptēs en nyktí, en hē hoi ouranoi rhoizēdon parelevsontai, stoicheia de kausoumena lythēsontai, kai gē kai ta en autē erga katakaēsontai]; and whatever else follows there. To prove the corruption of the upper parts, and their approach to destruction, there is added the renewal of heavens, sun and moon, said to be future, in Isaiah chapters 30, 65 and 66; John, Apocalypse chapter 21; Peter's epistle already cited, chapter 3 verse 13; the fall of the stars from heaven, in Isaiah chapter 34, 2 Esdras chapter 4 verse 24, John, Apocalypse chapter 6, and similar passages. Theophylact, on Romans chapter 8, thinks that all the elements, and even the higher heavens themselves, will be burned; so do Augustine and Ludolphus on Psalm 102. Others think that two elements are to be consumed and two left, as Bede thinks. Some hold that the machinery of the world will be corrupted by fire in the parts that were drowned by the flood, so that (as can be seen also in Saint Peter, 2 Peter chapter 3 verses 6 and 7, and in Augustine, City of God book 15, chapter 18) flood and burning may correspond to one another. Primasius, a disciple of Augustine, on Hebrews chapter 1, and Anselm of Canterbury on chapter 12 of the same epistle, say so. Augustine, not very consistent on this point, holds that no small part of the lower spheres, together with the upper, will escape the burning, in book 20, chapter 19. Finally, Epictetus says, as cited by Aelian, Historical Miscellany book 3, chapter 13, that the world will be consumed by fire, and the gods themselves with it.

units.la: Quo modo? Igne, ut ex multis jam Sacræ Scripturæ locis didicimus. Quali? Materiæ & corporis compote, qui nec fumo cariturus, ut putat Augustinus Anconitanus Commentar. in Matthæum. Unde venturo? Cœlitus pluviæ instar, ab ipso Deo, ut innuere volunt nonnulli regium Prophetam, Psalmo xi, 6, quemadmodum & alias ad puniendæ hominum scelera factum legimus. Geneseos cap. xix, 24. Iechezkel cap. xxxiix. 22. & alibi. Persuasum hoc de Igne & Veterum non paucis, ut Sibyllæ (mihi tamen suspectæ & supposititiæ) lib. iii. Oracul. apud D. Augustinum lib. xiix. de Civitate Dei, cap. xxiii. Hystaspi apud Iustinum Martyrem, Apolog. ii. Sophoeli apud eundem, libro de Monarch. Innominato Poetæ, apud Clementem Alexandrinum, τῶ πυρὶ τῶν σφιγμάτων. M. Tullio lib. ii. de Natura Deorum, Ovidio lib. i. Metamorph. Lucana lib. vii. belli Pharsal. Senecæ lib. de Consolat. ad Marciam, Plinio lib. vii. natural. histor. cap. xvi.
units.tr: How? By fire, as we have already learned from many passages of Holy Scripture. Of what kind? Fire that is possessed of matter and body, and which will not be free of smoke, as Augustinus Anconitanus thinks in his Commentary on Matthew. From where will it come? From heaven, like rain, from God himself, as some wish to infer from the royal Prophet in Psalm 11.6; and we read that such fire was also made for punishing the wickedness of men: Genesis 19.24, Ezekiel 38.22, and elsewhere. This belief about fire is held by not a few of the ancients: by the Sibyl (though she is suspect and spurious to me) in Book 3 of the Oracles, as cited by St Augustine in De Civitate Dei 18.23; by Hystaspes, as cited by Justin Martyr, Apology 2; by Sophocles, in the same author's book On Monarchy; by an unnamed poet, cited by Clement of Alexandria, [τῷ πυρὶ τῶν σφιγμάτων]; by Cicero, De Natura Deorum 2; by Ovid, Metamorphoses 1; by Lucan, Pharsalia 7; by Seneca, in his Consolation to Marcia; and by Pliny, Natural History 7, chapter 16.

units.la: Cui fini? Ut renovetur in meliorem faciem; Cœlo non amplius movendo, Elementisque mutabilitate, cui nunc subjacent, & qualitatibus corruptibilibus, quibus nunc sunt prædita, cariturus. Augustinus lib. xx. de Civit. Dei cap. xvi. Primasius in Apocalypsin, Hieronymus non uno loco, Thomas iiii. Dist. xlvii. quæst. 2. & opuscul. lx. cap. ult. Ludolphus Garthusianus ad Psalmum cii. Respicit huc Seneca in Octavia vers. 386: ——— uuu ——— nunc adest Mundo Dies Supremus ille, qui premat genus impium Cœli ruina, rursus ut stirpem novam Generet, renascens melior: ut quondam tulit Iuvenis tenente regna Saturno poli.
units.tr: To what end? That the world may be renewed into a better form, when it will no longer be moved by the heavens, and will be free of the mutability of the elements to which it is now subject, and of the corruptible qualities with which it is now endowed. See Augustine, De Civitate Dei 20.16; Primasius on the Apocalypse; Jerome in many places; Thomas, Sentences 4, distinction 47, question 2, and Opusculum 60, last chapter; Ludolphus the Carthusian on Psalm 102. Seneca also alludes to this in his Octavia, verse 386: "——— Now comes to the world that last day, which with the ruin of heaven will crush the impious race, so that, reborn and better, it may bring forth a new stock, as once the youth held the realms of heaven while Saturn reigned."

units.la: Quando denique ? incerto quidem nobis, certo tamen & determinato Divinæ Præaelstinationi tempore. Non est puræ Creaturæ, γνῶναι χρόνους ἢ καιρὸς, inquit Christus Actor. 1, 7. ὃς ὁ πατὴρ ἔθετο ἐν τῇ ἰδίᾳ ἐξουσίᾳ. Adeundi Augustinus lib. xiix, quem sæpe citavi, de Civit. Dei, & Epist. lxxxix. ad Hesych. item in Psalmum v i. Primasius in Apocalypsin. Hoc dicere licet, nostra hæc tempora Fini vicina. Sumus enim Nos, εἰς ἃς, ut ait Paulus Apostolus 1. Corinth. cap. x. 11. τὰ τέλη τῶν αἰώνων κατήντηκεν: & quibus, ut Ioannes 1. Epist. cap. 11. ἐσχάτη ὥρα ἐστί; illa quæ ab Christi adventu cœpit adesse, ut exponunt Ambrosius in dict. cap. x. & Augustinus lib. v 111. quæst. & Epist. lxxx. ad Hesych. Facit certe crebrior incertitudinis metusque Dei hujus iremissi commendatio hominibus excitandis, ut pie vivant, fugiant vitia, Virtutes amplectantur.
units.tr: Finally, when? Indeed, to us uncertain, yet certain and fixed by God's predestined time. "It is not for a pure creature to know the times or the seasons," says Christ in Acts 1.7, [γνῶναι χρόνους ἢ καιροὺς], "which the Father has put in his own authority" [ὃς ὁ πατὴρ ἔθετο ἐν τῇ ἰδίᾳ ἐξουσίᾳ]. Consult Augustine, Book 18 (which I have often cited), De Civitate Dei, and Letter 89 to Hesychius; also on Psalm 6; Primasius on the Apocalypse. We may say that our own times are near the end. For we are those "upon whom, as the Apostle Paul says in 1 Corinthians 10.11, the ends of the ages have come" [τὰ τέλη τῶν αἰώνων κατήντηκεν]; and for whom, as John says in 1 John 2, "it is the last hour" [ἐσχάτη ὥρα ἐστί], that hour which began to be present from the coming of Christ, as Ambrose explains in the passage cited on chapter 10, and Augustine in Book 8 of the Questions and in Letter 80 to Hesychius. Certainly the frequent recommendation of this uncertainty, and of the fear of God's hidden purpose, serves to rouse men to live piously, to flee vices and to embrace virtues.

units.la: Consulendi D. Chrysostomus Homilia xxi. super Matthæum, xxxiii. & xxxviii. in Ioannem, xxxiv. & xliix. operis Imperfecti, Basilius Homilia ii. in Psalmum vii. Cyrillus Hierosolymitanus Catechesi Mystag. xv. Nyssenus Oratione in v i. Psalm. Hilarius lib. ix. de Trinitate, & in Psalmum cxiix. & Canone xxv i. in Matth. Ambrosius lib. v. de Fide cap. viii. & ad Psalm. cxiix. Serm. iii. & x i i, Leo Serm. v. de Ieiunio, D. Gregorius in Homiliam Erunt Signa, & D. Bernardus Serm. iii. de Vigilia Nativitatis, & Epist. lxiv. Sancti horam Adventus Domini diligimus; & , ut prope sit, votis omnibus desideramus: detestati non solum eos, qui, certo & determinato tempore eam vel prope esse vel longe, putare non verentur; quales Abbas Ioachim, teste Thoma, Arnoldus de Villa nova apud Antoninum Archiepiscopum, Vbertinus a Casali de septem statibus Ecclesiæ, Telesphorus Eremita libr. de magnis Eccles. tribulationibus, Nicolaus Cusanus, Petrus Halyacensis in tractatu de Concordia Astron. veritatis, Ioannes Picus Mirandulanus, Franciscus Meletus, & alij; contra quos legendus Hieronymus Vielmius lect. vi. in cap. i. Geneseos: verum eos etiam, qui Dei certitudinem pronunciare scribuntur ausi ex Astrorum concursu; quæ mens cum Chaldæorum, Aegyptiorum, Pythagoreorum, Stoicorum & aliorum, quos refutat Aegidius Columnius Romanus de Prædestinat. cap. ii. cum eorum, qui hac in re confugere soliti ad Hebræorum, de sex millibus annorum, ex quodam Helia, non Thesbite deliria; quæ oppugnant Genebrardus in Chronic. & Hieronymus Magius lib. iii. de exustione Mundi, cap. xvi. Concludam cum D. August. lib. xviii. de Civit. Dei cap. lii. Deus omnium de hac re calculantium digitos resolvit, & quiescere jussit. Quod enim Apostolis quærentibus noluit indicare, nec aliis revelabit unde omnes illi, qui tempus hoc voluerunt numerare: hactenus falsiloqui sunt inventi.
units.tr: One should consult St Chrysostom, Homily 21 on Matthew, and Homilies 33 and 38 on John; Imperfect Work, Homilies 34 and 49; Basil, Homily 2 on Psalm 7; Cyril of Jerusalem, Mystagogical Catechesis 15; Gregory of Nyssa, On Psalm 6; Hilary, On the Trinity 9, and on Psalm 119, and Canon 25 on Matthew; Ambrose, On the Faith 5, chapter 8, and on Psalm 119, Sermons 3 and 12; Leo, Sermon 5 On Fasting; St Gregory, the homily "There Shall Be Signs"; and St Bernard, Sermon 3 On the Vigil of the Nativity, and Letter 64. "We love the hour of the Lord's coming, and with all our prayers we desire that it may be near." We detest not only those who dare to think that this time, fixed and certain, is either near or far away (such as Abbot Joachim, as Thomas reports; Arnold of Villanova, as cited by Antoninus, Archbishop; Ubertino of Casale, On the Seven States of the Church; Telesphorus the Hermit, On the Great Tribulations of the Church; Nicholas of Cusa; Peter of Ailly, in his treatise On the Concord of Astronomical Truth; Giovanni Pico della Mirandola; Francesco Melati; and others, against whom Girolamo Vielmi should be read, Lecture 6 on Genesis 1); but also those who are said to have presumed to pronounce God's certainty from the conjunction of the stars. This opinion is shared with the Chaldeans, Egyptians, Pythagoreans, Stoics and others whom Egidio Colonna of Rome refutes in On Predestination, chapter 2; and with those who, in this matter, are accustomed to take refuge in the ravings of a certain Elias (not the Tishbite) concerning the six thousand years of the Hebrews; these are opposed by Genebrardus in his Chronicle and by Girolamo Magi in Book 3, On the Burning of the World, chapter 16. I will conclude with St Augustine, De Civitate Dei 18.52: "God has loosed the fingers of all who calculate about this matter and has bidden them be still. For what he was unwilling to reveal to the Apostles when they asked, he will not reveal to anyone else; and so far all those who wished to count this time have been found to be liars."

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: Mundum ob varias causas esse factum.
units.tr: That the world was made for various reasons.

units.la: FECIT autem Deus Universum hoc, primaria quidem intentione (ut distincte notem causas δημιουργικὰς) propter Seipsum: secundario vero, Hominis causa. Propter Seipsum: Universa, inquit Schelomon Proverbiorum xvi, 4. propter Semetipsum (eo pertinent verba Aristotelis in Definitione Mundi, ᾧ ἤθον, apud me libri hujus cap. i.) c'ratus est Dominus; hoc est, quia ita placebat, utque in iis ejus gloria plene eluceret, Psalmo xix. 1. & ab falsorum Deorum turba notis evidentissimis discerneretur, Ieremias, cap. x. 11. non, quod Rabini volunt, cum alias ob causas motus, tum ut domum haberet inhabitandam. Mundo enim non indigebat (ut scribit Lactantius, verba faciens de ejus conditione) Deus, qui ab æterno fuerat sine Mundo: ideoque bene dicitur, Mundum etiam produxisse Hominis causa, qui tamen propter DEVM, ad quem omnia referenda. Paullus scribens ad Corinthios, priore Epistola, cap. iii, 22. πάντα ὑμῶν ἐστιν, inquit, εἴτε κόσμος, εἴτε ζωὴ, εἴτε θάνατος, εἴτε ἐνεστῶτα, εἴτε μέλλοντα, πάντα ὑμῶν ἐστιν: ὑμεῖς δὲ Χριστοῦ, Χριστὸς δὲ Θεοῦ. Ad quem locum distincte Augustinus Superiora nominat, Aequalia, inferiora; Superiora, ad per-
units.tr: God made this universe, indeed, chiefly for His own sake (to name the efficient causes distinctly), and secondarily for the sake of man. For His own sake: "The Lord has made all things for Himself," says Solomon in Proverbs 16:4. To this belong the words of Aristotle in his definition of the world, which I cite in chapter 1 of this book. The Lord made them because it pleased Him, so that His glory might shine forth fully in them (Psalm 19:1) and be distinguished from the crowd of false gods by the most evident marks (Jeremiah 10:11). It was not, as the rabbis hold, for other reasons and so that He might have a house to dwell in. For God, who had been without the world from eternity, had no need of it, as Lactantius writes when speaking of its origin. So it is rightly said that He also produced the world for the sake of man, though man too is to be referred to God, to whom all things must be referred. Paul, writing to the Corinthians in his first Epistle, chapter 3:22, says: "All things are yours, whether the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come; all are yours; and you are Christ's, and Christ is God's" [πάντα ὑμῶν ἐστιν, εἴτε κόσμος, εἴτε ζωὴ, εἴτε θάνατος, εἴτε ἐνεστῶτα, εἴτε μέλλοντα, πάντα ὑμῶν ἐστιν· ὑμεῖς δὲ Χριστοῦ, Χριστὸς δὲ Θεοῦ]. On this passage Augustine distinguishes the things above us, the equal, and the things below us. The things above are for enjoyment, as God Himself; the equal are for fellowship, as the angels, who already serve us and with whom we shall be equal in eternal life; the things below are for our use and service.

units.la: {§} secundario, Hominis causa. ad perfruendum, ut DEus ipse, inquit, Aequalia, ad convivendum, ut Angeli, qui & jam nobis serviunt & in vita aeterna nos eis aequales erimus; Inferiora, ad utendum eorum servitio. Necesse igitur hoc erat, ut, quum DEI praesentia conspectui non pateret humano, saltem ex rerum conditarum magnificentia & pulchritudine tantus artifex penitissime cognosceretur, nosque, tamquam gradibus quibusdam, in ejus evehueremur notitiam. Quamvis enim haec omnium mentibus naturaliter est insita (ut gravissimi Philosophi nusquam non docent) tamen, proh dolor, horrendum in modum obfuscata est & obruta. Egebamus adminiculis. Manifestant in admiranda haec rerum mole tanti Numinis Aeternitatem, Causarum inter se cohaerentium series, & ordinaria: Luminarium Coelestium revolutiones; Potentiam, Specierum conservatio & perpetua in generatione similitudo; Sapientiam, Dispositio sive τάξις, non Totius tantum, sed & omnium ejus Partium: Iustitiam, administratio singulorum prudentissima; Munificentiam, nobis concessus gratis omnium usus; alia alias divinae Majestatis docent proprietates. Τὰ ἀόρατα αὐτοῦ, ut Paulus ait Epist. ad Romanos cap. 1, 20. ἀπὸ κτίσεως κόσμου τοῖς ποιήμασι νοούμενα καθοράται, ἥ τε αἰδίος αὐτοῦ δύναμις καὶ θειότης, εἰς τὸ εἶναι αὐτοὺς ἀναπολογήτους. Diffundunt haec D. Pauli paullo fusius magni Primitivae Ecclesiae Patres & Antistites. Origenes in suo Commentario: Virtus DEI, inquit, sempiterna ex conjecturis cognoscitur Creaturarum: Virtus est, qua regit omnia: Divinitas, qua replet Universa. Ex hoc ergo inexcusabiles sunt: quia quum, manifestante DEO, cognoverunt DEUM; non, ut dignum est, coluerunt DEUM. Chrysostomus in eundem Pauli locum: Cognitionem Sui DEUS Hominibus ab initio indidit, Mundi creatione in medium propositá; ut possit Sapiens, Rudis, Scytha, Barbarus, ex ipso adspectu eorum quae oculis subjecta sunt, pulchritudinem edoctus ad DEUM considere. Ambrosius Commentario ad eandem Epistolam. Ex ipsa, ait, coeli fabrica iratus illi DEUS videtur. Idirco enim tam pulchra Astra condidit, ut ex iis, quantus & quam admirabilis Creator eorum est, possit agnosci & solus adorari: unde scriptum est in libro Sapientiae: A magnitudine Creaturae Creator earum poterat agnosci. Quod notum est DEI, ait Paulus, manifestum est illis: notitia DEI manifesta est ex Mundi fabrica. Ut enim DEUS, qui natura tam invisibilis est, etiam ex visibilibus possit sciri, Opus factum est ab Io, quod opificem visibilitate sua manifestaret, ut per certum incertum possit sciri: ut per hoc, quod ceteris impossibile est, ille esse DEUS omnium crederetur, qui hoc ipse fecit. Per Naturalem ergo Legem rerum facit genus humanum, potuerunt enim id per Legem Naturae adprehendere, fabrica Mundi testificante, auctorem DEUM solum diligendum. Augustinus Sermone LV. de Verbis Domini: Interroga, inquit, Mundi ornatum, Coeli fulgorem, dispositionemque Siderum, Solem Diei sufficientem, Lunam Noctis solatium; interroga Terram fructificantem Herbis & Lignis, Animalibus plenam, Hominibus exornatam; interroga Mare quantis & qualibus Natantibus plenum; interroga Aera, quantis Volatilibus vigeat; interroga omnia, & vide si non sensu tuo tamquam tibi respondent, DEUS Nos fecit. Haec & Philosophi nobiles quaesierunt, & ex Arte Artifícem cognoverunt. Itaque pulchritudo Creaturarum, confessio earum est: ipsa pulchra mutabilia fecit, qui est Incommutabilis Pulcher in Scripto. Habuit proculdubio magnus vir, quum illa scriberet, vel in oculis, vel in mente saltem, Hiobi verba cap. XII, 7. Nimirum interroga Jumenta, & docebunt te: & Volatilia coeli, & indicabunt tibi. Loquere terrae, & respondebit tibi & narrabunt Pisces maris. Quis ignorat, quod omnia haec manus Domini fecerit? & quae sequuntur. Cyrillus denique Dialogo de Trinitate, lib. IIII. A magnitudine, ait, & pulchritudine Creaturarum congruenter & ipsarum conditor spectatur. Mercurius etiam Trismegistus lib. v. Dialogo v. scribit, DEUM totius expertem invidiae per singulas Mundi particulas ubique splendere, atque adeo se notum praestare: ut non intelligere modo, sed manibus etiam ipsis liceat attrectare: undique nostris cum oculis obversari, se passim objicere, suamque inculcare imaginem. Plato item x. de L L. multis rationibus probat DEI praesentiam ubique in Creatis patere. Videndus idem in Epinomide & Plotinus Ennead. quintae lib. v. cap. IV. Galenus denique in histor. Philosoph. notat habere nos providentiam & agnitionem DEI ex pulchritudine & magnitudine Opificiorum ejus visibilium. Nihil enim ab eo factum frustra; sed omnia, quae pulcra sunt, monstrant sapientem Opificem. Hinc Euripides: Ἀ ςἰφες ἐν ἀέρα πολυμορφα πέλαγος πόντου. Ut non immerito Universum hoc nobis sit, tamquam Liber (quemadmodum non inelegantur aiebat Antonius Aegyptius Abbas, de quo lib. VIII. Tripart. hist. cap. I.)
units.tr: Thus, secondarily, for the sake of man. "The things above are for enjoyment, as God Himself; the equal are for fellowship, as the angels..." Augustine's words are as quoted above. It was therefore necessary that, since the presence of God is not open to human sight, so great an Artificer should at least be known most deeply from the greatness and beauty of created things, and that we should be raised, as by certain steps, to knowledge of Him. For although this knowledge is naturally implanted in the minds of all (as the most weighty philosophers teach everywhere), yet, alas, it has been dreadfully obscured and overwhelmed. We needed supports. In this wondrous mass of things, the eternity of so great a Deity is shown by the series and order of causes that hang together, and by the regular revolutions of the heavenly lights; His power by the preservation of species and their constant likeness in generation; His wisdom by the arrangement, or order, not only of the whole but of all its parts; His justice by the most prudent government of individual things; His bounty by the free enjoyment of all things granted to us. Other things teach other attributes of the divine majesty. "His invisible things," as Paul says in Romans 1:20, "from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even His eternal power and divinity, so that they are without excuse" [Τὰ ἀόρατα αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ κτίσεως κόσμου τοῖς ποιήμασι νοούμενα καθοράται, ἥ τε αἰδίος αὐτοῦ δύναμις καὶ θειότης, εἰς τὸ εἶναι αὐτοὺς ἀναπολογήτους]. The great Fathers and bishops of the early Church expound this passage of Paul somewhat more fully. Origen, in his commentary: "The eternal power of God, he says, is known from the conjectures of creatures: it is power, by which He governs all things; it is divinity, by which He fills the universe." From this they are therefore inexcusable: because, although God made Himself manifest, they knew God and did not honour God as is fitting. Chrysostom on the same passage of Paul: "God implanted in men from the beginning the knowledge of Himself, the creation of the world being set forth as a means, so that the wise man, the untutored, the Scythian, the barbarian, might from the very sight of the things that lie before their eyes, being taught the beauty, consider God." Ambrose in his commentary on the same Epistle: "From the very structure of heaven, he says, God appears angry to them. For He made the stars so beautiful so that from them one might recognise how great and how admirable their Creator is, and that He alone is to be worshipped; hence it is written in the Book of Wisdom: from the greatness of the creature the Creator of them could be known." What is known of God, says Paul, is manifest to them; the knowledge of God is manifest from the structure of the world. "For that God, who is by nature so invisible, might also be known from visible things, a work was made by Io which would reveal its maker by its visibility, so that the uncertain might be known through the certain: so that by this, which is impossible for others, he who made this should be believed to be God of all." Therefore through the natural law the human race was made such that, the structure of the world bearing witness, they could grasp by the law of nature that God alone, as author, is to be loved. Augustine, Sermon 55 on the Words of the Lord: "Ask, he says, the adornment of the world, the brightness of heaven, the arrangement of the stars, the sun sufficient for the day, the moon the comfort of the night; ask the earth fruitful with herbs and trees, full of animals, adorned with men; ask the sea, full of what great and what kinds of swimming creatures; ask the air, how many flying creatures it teems with; ask all things, and see whether they do not answer you, as it were, with their sense: God made us." Noble philosophers too have inquired into these things, and from the art they have recognised the artificer. Therefore the beauty of creatures is their confession: He who is the unchangeable Beautiful in Scripture made beautiful mutable things. Without doubt the great man, when writing those words, had in his eyes, or at least in his mind, the words of Job 12:7: "Surely ask the beasts, and they shall teach you; and the birds of heaven, and they shall tell you. Speak to the earth, and it shall answer you, and the fishes of the sea shall declare to you. Who does not know that the hand of the Lord has made all these things?" and what follows. Cyril, finally, in the fourth book of his Dialogue on the Trinity: "From the greatness and beauty of creatures, he says, their Creator is fittingly beheld." Mercurius Trismegistus too writes in the fifth book, dialogue 5, that God, free from all envy, shines everywhere through the individual parts of the world, and so makes Himself known: so that He may be not only understood but even handled with the hands; on all sides He presents Himself to our eyes, offers Himself everywhere, and impresses His image upon us. Plato likewise, in the tenth book of the Laws, proves by many arguments that the presence of God is manifest everywhere in created things. The same should be consulted in the Epinomis, and Plotinus, Ennead 5, book 5, chapter 4. Galen, finally, in his history of philosophy, observes that we have the providence and knowledge of God from the beauty and greatness of His visible works. For nothing is made by Him in vain; rather, all things that are beautiful show a wise Maker. Hence Euripides: "The ether... many-formed sea" [Ἀ ςἰφες ἐν ἀέρα πολυμορφα πέλαγος πόντου]. Thus this universe is rightly for us like a book (as Antony the Egyptian abbot, whom the Tripartite History mentions in book 8, chapter 1, not inelegantly said).

units.la: Deum esse fierct & credere: Ut ii non alio modo. cui, quot res creatæ, tot sunt folia; quæ quotidie volvenda revolvenda; ut DEI Sapientiam, Potentiam, Bonitatem, quantum homines adsequi possumus, cognoscamus, & discamus magnum ejus & admirabile nomen in universa Terra, Psalmo VIII, 9. Haudquaquam ergo, ut ait Damascenus lib. I. cap. I. nos deservit DEVS omnimoda Sui circumfusos ignorantia; quinimo cunctis cognitio (quod DEVS fit) ab ipso naturaliter insita est atque ingenita. Et cap. III. Cognitio, quod DEVS sit, nobis natura insita est atque ingenita. Merito hic reprehendantur illi Eidolorum cultores, & vani sint homines, οἷς πηρὰ ἀγνωσία, ... ταῦτα ὁ Δεσπότης ... quæ alia Sapientiæ cap. I.
units.tr: To know and believe that God exists, so that they do not do so in any other way. For to the one to whom every created thing is a leaf, and these leaves must be turned over and turned again every day, so that we may know, as far as men can attain, the wisdom, power and goodness of God, and learn his great and admirable name in all the earth, Psalm 8.9. Therefore, as Damascene says, Book I, chapter 1, God does not leave us surrounded by complete ignorance; rather, the knowledge that God exists is naturally implanted and innate in everyone. And in chapter 3: The knowledge that God exists is implanted and innate in us by nature. Rightly, here, are reproved those worshippers of idols, and they are vain men, in whom is ignorance of God [οἷς πηρὰ ἀγνωσία] ... these things the Lord [ταῦτα ὁ Δεσπότης] ... which is found in Wisdom, chapter 1.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI.

units.la: Mundum ab DEO gubernari.
units.tr: That the World Is Governed by God.

units.la: NEQVE solum DEVS quæ partim videmus, partim credimus, ex Nihilo fecit; condita Lucem, qua vteremur; discrimine inter hanc & Tenebras posito; constituta ad stuporem omnium Firmamento, terminatis, Aere interjecto, Aquis; indita Terræ vi, qua proferrent Fructus, unde quidquid Vita donatum alteretur; dato Herbis Arboribusque Semine; Aquis Piscium omnis generis copia repletis; ornata Terræ facie Volucribus, Bestiis, Iumentis, Reptilibus; formato denique ad imaginem suam Homine: verum etiam facta omnia ab se benigne conseruat, sapienterque gubernat. Testantur Viri DEI, David Psalmis XXIII, I. XLV, 7. LXXII, 8. CIV, 27, 28. CVII, 23, & seq. CXLV, 11, 13. CLXVII, 5. Schelomo Proverb. XXI, 1. & seq. Auctor libri Sapientiæ, cap. XI, 27. XIV, 3. Hiiob. cap. XXVIII, 24. XXXIV, 13. XXXVII, 5. & seqq. Isaiahias XLVIII, 17. & seqq. Auctor Epistolæ ad Hebræos cap. I, 3. Ipse Christus apud Mathæum Euangelistam VI, 26. & X, 29, apud Ioannem cap. V, 17. Sentiunt hoc nobiscum Socrates, Plato (qui tamen metu quodam variat) eorumque discipuli & alij majorum gentium Philosophi. Accedit Mercurius Trismegistus, qui Dialogo II, Actionem DEI nominat potestatem insuperabilem; scribens DEVM non esse otiosum, alioquin otiosa fore omnia; cuncta siquidem plena esse DEO. Canit magnus ille naturæ scrutator, Manilius, DEVM Infusum Cælo, Terræque, Fretoque, retro-poetas sequutus; quorum illa: Iovis omnia plena. Spiritus intus alit, totamque infusa per artus Mens agitat molem. Et: Iuppiter est, quodcumque vides, quocumque moveris. Planissime Boetius de Consolatione Philosophiæ: O qui perpetua Mundum ratione gubernas.
units.tr: God did not only create out of nothing the things we partly see and partly believe in. He also made light, which we use, and set a difference between it and darkness; He set up the firmament, to the amazement of all, with its boundaries; He interposed air and waters; He endowed the earth with the power to bring forth fruits, from which whatever is given life is nourished; He gave herbs and trees their seed; He filled the waters with every kind of fish; He adorned the face of the earth with birds, beasts, cattle and reptiles; and finally He formed man in His own image. He also constantly preserves and wisely governs all the things He has made. The men of God bear witness to this: David in Psalms 23.1; 45.7; 72.8; 104.27, 28; 107.23 and following; 145.11, 13; 167.5. Solomon in Proverbs 21.1 and following. The author of the book of Wisdom, 11.27; 14.3. Job 28.24; 34.13; 37.5 and following. Isaiah 48.17 and following. The author of the Epistle to the Hebrews 1.3. Christ Himself in Matthew 6.26 and 10.29, and in John 5.17. Socrates and Plato (who, however, wavers out of a certain fear) and their disciples, and other philosophers of the greater nations, agree with us in this. Mercurius Trismegistus agrees too: in his second Dialogue he calls the action of God an invincible power, writing that God is not idle, since otherwise all things would be idle; for everything is full of God. That great investigator of nature, Manilius, sings of God as infused into heaven, earth and sea, following the earlier poets, of whom one says: all things are full of Jove; a spirit nourishes them within, and a mind, infused through all the limbs, moves the whole mass. And: Jupiter is whatever you see, wherever you move. Boethius, in the Consolation of Philosophy, is quite plain: O you who govern the world by perpetual reason.

units.la: Quid ni? Est enim DEI optimi, optima producere, productaque adducere ad persectionem; Perfectio autem uniuscuiusque rei in Fine consistit: Vt igitur Divinæ Bonitatis interest, Res ad Esse producere, ita plane & ad ipsorum Finem adducere, quod est Gubernare. Iam vero quis Rebus, quæ conditæ, regendis moderandisque aptior, quam qui condidit; cui natura earum cognita & perspecta; à quo sunt illis Initia, Progressus, Finis? qui attribuit cuique Vires, quibus se tuerentur, actionesque exercerent sibi utiles & necessarias ad Vitam, Vigorem, Valentiam? cui ut Sapientissimo, non deest, regendi Scientia; non Voluntas, ut Optimo; non, ut Maximo, Vis & potestas, quæ illi immensa, & interminata? Verus ille Pan, quem diversis modis formabat, divina semper mysteria typis ænigmatum obvelans, Antiquitas. Cornua in Capite duplex Imperium (pro Regno enim Cornu accipi solitum, probat Hieronymus in Prophetiam Habacuc) denotabant in & Superna & Inferna; Barba prolixior infinitam significabat Virtutem, & in ima quæque protensam; Fistula septem Calamorum Harmoniam totidem Planetarum indicabat; Virga in manibus, Potestas erat, qua cuncta credebatur moderari; Ridens (sic enim fingebant) innuebat sempiternam suam Felicitatem; ἀστέρα stellatam in Pectore gerebat, quia bat, quia omnium Stellarum concursum atque vim unica pelle, unicoque nutu continere dicebatur; Deliciari faciebant in Echo, quæ vox resonans, Verbo enim DEVS Mundum fabricavit & fabricatum voce gubernat. Gubernat autem universim. Quemadmodum, enim nihil quod non ab DEO creatum; ita quod illius Gubernationi non obtemperet, nihil. Eousque porrigit se Gubernationis imperium, quousque extenditur ejus finis: Bonitas divina, quæ Gubernationis finis, omnia complectitur, ita etiam ejusdem Gubernatio. Ut nihil est, in quod non cadit DEI Bonitas; sic nihil in quod non ejusdem Gubernatio. Stulte dictum ab nonnullis apud Ezechielem Prophetam cap. 1x. vers. 9. Dereliquit Dominus terram, & Dominus non videt: quum Davide canente Psalmo XXIV, Domini est Terra & plenitudo ejus, Orbis terrarum & Universi qui habitant in eo. Intuetur & tuetur Omnia divinum illud Numen, etiam quæ nobis minimi & loci & precij. Falsus M. Tullius, quum II. de natura Deorum ait, Magna Deos curare, Parva negligere. Falsus Aristoteles, qui in libello περὶ κόσμου (si modo ejus est) DEVM facit similem magno Persarum Regi, Xerxi, Cambysi vel Dario, qui ipse per se maxima & plucerrima Regni obeat munia; minora & sordidiora mandet aliis; indignum arbitratus tantum Principem manus ollæ, aut scopis, aut strigili admovere. Falsus denique Plinius, DEI quasi miserrimus, quod tanta cum premat Regni moles, quod tanta molestia. Male sane agitur cum pietate Numinis, quoties humana infirmitas ad DEVM transfertur. Nam
units.tr: And why not? For it belongs to the best God to produce the best things and to bring what is produced to perfection; but the perfection of each thing consists in its end. Just as it is part of divine goodness to bring things into being, so it is likewise part of it to lead them to their end, and this is to govern. Now who is more fitted to rule and direct the things that have been created than the one who created them, who knows their nature thoroughly and perfectly, from whom they have their beginnings, progress and end? Who gave each thing its powers, by which it might defend itself and carry out actions useful and necessary to its life, vigour and strength? In the one who is most wise there is no lack of knowledge of how to rule; in the one who is best there is no lack of will; and in the one who is greatest there is power and might, which are immense and boundless. That true Pan, whom antiquity fashioned in various ways, always veiling divine mysteries under the forms of enigmas: his two horns on his head denoted a double rule (for it was customary to take a horn for a kingdom, as Jerome proves in his commentary on the prophecy of Habakkuk), over both the upper and the lower regions; his long beard signified infinite power, extended down to the lowest depths; the pipe of seven reeds indicated the harmony of the seven planets; the staff in his hands was the power by which all things were believed to be governed; his laughing (for so they pictured him) signified his everlasting happiness; he carried a star [ἀστέρα] on his breast, because he was said to hold together the concourse and force of all the stars by one skin and one nod; and they made him delight in Echo, the resounding voice, for God fashioned the world by the Word and governs what He has fashioned by His voice. He governs, moreover, universally. For just as nothing exists that was not created by God, so there is nothing that does not obey His government. The empire of government extends as far as its end extends. Divine goodness, which is the end of government, embraces all things; so government too embraces all things. As there is nothing on which God's goodness does not fall, so there is nothing on which His government does not fall. What some say foolishly, in the prophet Ezekiel 9.9, The Lord has forsaken the land, and the Lord does not see, is false, when David sings in Psalm 24.1, The earth is the Lord's and the fullness thereof, the world and those who dwell in it. That divine Power beholds and watches over all things, even those that seem to us of least place and worth. Marcus Tullius is wrong when, in the second book of On the Nature of the Gods, he says, The gods take care of great things and neglect small ones. Aristotle is wrong, who in the little book On the Cosmos (if it really is his) makes God like the great kings of the Persians, Xerxes, Cambyses or Darius, who himself performs the greatest and most important duties of the kingdom, and hands the smaller and baser ones to others, thinking it unworthy for so great a prince to put his hand to a pot, or to brooms or a scraper. Pliny too is wrong, who, as if God were most wretched, complains that the great mass of the kingdom weighs upon Him and causes Him such trouble. Certainly piety toward the Deity is badly handled whenever human weakness is transferred to God.

units.la: quid quæ adferuntur ad DEVM? DEO nihil majus, nihil minus: Omnia DEO curanti & gubernanti Magna; Omnia Mundi (quod appellatio clamat) apud DEVM munda. Magnus olim habitus Schelomo, quod disputarit ab Cedro Libani usque ad Hyssopum, quæ exit de pariete, quodque disserverit de Iumentis, Volucribus, Reptilibus & Piscibus: viluitne has ob res ejus Sapientia? Vilueruntne Aristoteles & Theophrastus; quorum ille de Animalium, hic de Plantarum natura disputavit? Hermes sapientissimus, Siderum, Lapidum & Herbarum singularem scripsit concordiam. Sapientes illi fuerunt, non quod singularia, sed quod Rerum species & universalem naturam speculati. Rerum gradus, ut aliæ aliis ad regimen sint digniores, ab Homine sunt, non ab DEO; qui vult, nihil despiciens, nihil vili pendens, nihil sua cura censens indignum; qui potest, solus omnibus sufficiens.
units.tr: For what is said about God? Nothing is greater for God and nothing smaller; for the God who cares for and governs all things, all things are great; all things of the world (as the very word "world" [mundus] proclaims) are clean [munda] before God. Solomon was once considered great because he discoursed from the cedar of Lebanon down to the hyssop that grows out of the wall, and because he discoursed about beasts, birds, reptiles and fishes. Was his wisdom cheapened for these things? Were Aristotle and Theophrastus cheapened, of whom the former disputed on the nature of animals and the latter on the nature of plants? Hermes, the most wise, wrote on the particular harmony of the stars, stones and herbs. Those men were wise not because they studied particulars, but because they contemplated the kinds of things and their universal nature. That things have different degrees, so that some are more worthy to be governed than others, comes from man, not from God; God, who wishes nothing to be despised, nothing held cheap, nothing judged unworthy of His care, who is able, alone and sufficient for all things.

units.la: Non absurdum tamen credere, DEVM mediate etiam, mutuatitia quasi opera, quæcunque sunt gubernare, & Cœlestia & Terrena; non Necessitate, sed Voluntate sua bona & libera. Carere enim posset iis, si vellet; quum solo suo nutu perfecerit, quod voluit. Quas per se absque Instrumentis res creavit; non advocata aliunde ope, regere potest & tueri. Movemus hodie post Archimedem Automata nostra sine Ministris Mitelli nos; non poterit DEVS? Ut tamen evidentior esset Naturæ concinnitas, Ministris quasi voluit uti magnus ille Rex: quum regiæ etiam humanitus conveniat dignitati, per ministros multa exsequi; ut Ministrorum ordine clarior reddatur dignitas. In Gubernatione duo consideranda; cum ejus Ratio, quæ nihil aliud quam Providentia; tum Rationis exsequutio, quæ proprie Gubernatio. Gubernationis Ratione DEVS omnia immediate gubernat; Rationis exsequutione quædam, aliis mediantibus, & (sic loqui liceat) coaccedentibus.
units.tr: Yet it is not absurd to believe that God also governs, mediately, as it were through borrowed works, whatever exists, both heavenly and earthly, not by necessity but by His good and free will. For He could do without them if He wished, since by His mere nod He accomplishes whatever He wills. He who has created things by Himself without instruments, without calling in help from elsewhere, can also rule and preserve them. Today, following Archimedes, we move our automata without any attendants; will God not be able to do so? Nevertheless, in order that the harmony of nature might be more evident, that great King wished to use ministers, as it were; for it also befits the royal dignity, in human terms, to carry out many things through ministers, so that the dignity may be seen more clearly through the order of the ministers. In government two things must be considered: its plan, which is nothing other than providence, and the carrying out of that plan, which properly is government. By the plan of government God governs all things immediately; by the carrying out of the plan He governs some things through other agents intervening and, if I may so speak, co-operating.

units.la: Cœlestia igitur contemplemur. Concors fuit Platonicorum, Peripateticorum, Stoicorum, aliorumque sententia, Orbes ibi, non sua vi, (quam hic agnoverunt nonnulli, Straton em Sampsacenum, Theophrasti discipulum, sequuti) sed divina ratione & potentia moveri ab Intelligente aliqua Natura. Innuit hoc etiam divinus Philosophus in Timæo; ubi, metu quodam DEVM Mundi gubernatorem facere non ausus, (Calamitatem enim, quæ Socratem, talia palam contra receptas de Dis opiniones fassum, adflixerat, horrebat) dicit Κόσμον εἶναι ζῷον ἔμψυχον ἔννουν, ὃν παρ' ἑαυτῷ ἔχει; τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν δὲ Κόσμῳ ἐν οὐρανῷ ponens. Qui vero se scire posset Cœlum, quod Corpus simplex & omnibus suis partibus secundum substantiam uniforme; in quo nihil distincte quis signabit, quod moveat, quod moveatur? Fdocti sanius solidiusque ministerium huc vocant Angelorum; qui (rationes enim addunt) nisi Cœlos moveant, quo modo cognoscentur? quo probabuntur; unde natura illorum deprehenderetur? quod illorum erit munus? quo pertinebunt illa Davidis Psalmo CIII, 4. qui facis Angelos tuos Spiritus, & Ministros tuos Ignem urentem: & Danielis cap. VII, 10. Millia millium ministrabant ei, & decies millies centena millia adsistebant ei? Quidquid sit: præcedit DEI Cura, DEI Providentia, cui ministrare Angelos, certum & indubitatum. Divina mihi illa Dionysij Areopagitæ libro de Cœlesti Hierarchia, Augustini non uno loco, aliorumque Patrum & Theologorum; ita Deum Providentia sua hunc Mundum administrare, scribentium; ut Infima regat per Media; hæc autem per Summa; hæc denique per Spiritus: quibus DEI jussu, completo tempore, non amplius moventibus, nullus post Iudicij diem futurus est Motus Cœli: quod, si sua vi, sua Natura moveretur, numquam suo Motu posset privari, nisi miraculo quodam & violentia, careretque perfectione quæ naturaliter illi convenit & debetur.
units.tr: Let us then contemplate the heavenly things. The opinion of the Platonists, Peripatetics, Stoics and others agreed that the spheres there are moved not by their own power (which some recognised here, following Straton of Lampsacus, the disciple of Theophrastus), but by divine reason and power, by some intelligent Nature. The divine philosopher [Plato] also hints at this in the Timaeus, where, not daring from a certain fear to make God the governor of the world (for he shuddered at the calamity which had struck Socrates, who had openly professed such opinions contrary to the accepted views about the gods), he says that the Cosmos is "a living being, animate and intelligent, which has it [the intelligence] within itself" [Κόσμον εἶναι ζῷον ἔμψυχον ἔννουν, ὃν παρ' ἑαυτῷ ἔχει], placing its ruling part in heaven [τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν δὲ Κόσμῳ ἐν οὐρανῷ]. But who could know that heaven, being a simple body and uniform in substance in all its parts, in which no one can distinguish anything that moves or is moved? Learned men more soundly and solidly summon here the ministry of the angels; who (for they add reasons) unless they moved the heavens, how would they be known? By what would they be proved? By what would their nature be perceived? What would be their office? How would those words of David in Psalm 103.4 apply, who makest Thy angels spirits, and Thy ministers a burning fire, and of Daniel 7.10, thousand thousands ministered to Him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before Him? Be that as it may, God's care and God's providence come first, and it is certain and indubitable that the angels minister to it. Those divine words of Dionysius the Areopagite in his book on the Celestial Hierarchy, of Augustine in many places, and of other Fathers and theologians, who write that God administers this world by His providence, so that He governs the lowest things through the middle ones, these through the highest, and these finally through the spirits; when, at God's command, once the appointed time is complete, these no longer move, there will be no motion of heaven after the day of judgment. And if heaven moved by its own power, by its own nature, it could never be deprived of its motion except by some miracle and violence, and it would lack the perfection which naturally belongs to it and is due to it.

units.la: Ad Terrena nunc descendamus. Docemur & in his locum esse Angelis. Nun ciant illi Nobis, faciuntque res omnino arduas & divinas. Daniel Propheta cap. XIIII, 15. Paull. 1, Epist. ad Thessalonicenses cap. IIII, 16. Excubant pro Salute nostra, vias nostras dirigentes, defendentes nos & custodientes, ne quid adversi accidat, Genes. XLVIII, 16. Exodi XIV, 19. Baruch VI, 6. Matthæus cap. II, 13. Consolantur afflictos & mœstos, Lucas XXII, 45. sumuntque supplicium de Sceleratis, Exod XII, 29. IIII Reg. XIX, 35. Psal. XXXV, 5.6. Iesaiah. XXXVII, 36. Actorum cap. XII,23. Infinita alia præterea.
units.tr: Let us now descend to earthly things. We are taught that the angels also have a place among these. They announce things to us and carry out matters that are altogether arduous and divine. Daniel the Prophet, ch. 14:15. 1 Thessalonians 4:16. They keep watch for our safety, directing our ways, defending and guarding us, lest anything adverse befall us: Genesis 48:16. Exodus 14:19. Baruch 6:6. Matthew 2:13. They comfort the afflicted and sorrowful: Luke 22:45. They also exact punishment from the wicked: Exodus 12:29. 4 Kings 19:35. Psalm 35:5-6. Isaiah 37:36. Acts 12:23. Countless others besides.

units.la: Sunt & suæ Hominibus ipsis in Universi centro partes. Regit enim Deus suo arbitrio Populos, Principum & Magistratus manu: pœnas sic exigit de Flagitiosis; sic Iudicia exercet; sic Pacem conservat publicam, fallos cultus prohibet, in mores nostros animadvertit. Et hinc videmus DEVM Principum rebus præsentius adesse; non, quasi splendore moveretur, propter eos, quum quivis illorum unus sit hominicio: sed quia in illis tam multa hominum millia continentur. Interea tamen Privatorum cura non minus tangitur, quam Principum. Examinet enim se suaque, qui in hominum numero vix homo; nusquam non deprehendet manifestissimam de se DEI curam. Non possum non detestari hic arrogantem C. Iulij Cæsaris apud Lucanum vocem. nunquam se cura Deorum Sic premit, ut vestra vita vestraque saluti Fata vacent; Procerum motus hæc cuncta sequuntur; Humanum paucis vivit genus.
units.tr: Men themselves also have their own parts in the centre of the universe. For God rules peoples by his own will, through the hand of princes and magistrates. In this way he exacts punishment from the wicked, in this way he executes judgments, in this way he preserves public peace, forbids false worship, and takes note of our morals. And from this we see that God is more present with the affairs of princes, not as if he were moved by their splendour, since each of them is only a man, but because so many thousands of men are contained in them. Meanwhile, however, the care of private persons is touched no less than that of princes. Let each one examine himself and his affairs; he who is scarcely a man among the number of men will nowhere fail to find God's most manifest care for him. I cannot but detest here the arrogant utterance of Gaius Julius Caesar in Lucan: the care of the gods never weighs so heavily that your life and your safety are left to fate; all the movements of the great follow these things; the human race lives for the few.

units.la: Speciatiorem vero curam rerum creatarum mandatam etiam nonnullis videmus. Sic enim genus humanum conjunctione Maris & Feminæ propagatur; sic Liberi Parentum opera educantur; sic Terra hominum labore culta fructificat.
units.tr: Yet we see that a more particular care of created things is also committed to some. For thus the human race is propagated by the union of male and female; thus children are brought up through the labour of their parents; thus the earth, cultivated by human toil, bears fruit.

units.la: Quid plura? Valeant, qui, cæcitate, quam in Ingeniis suis gestant, ad Naturæ gubernationem translata, nulla ex causa fieri opinati, quorum ipsi causam non inveniunt; regnum Mundi DEO abrogatum tribuunt, cum Epicuro aliisque minoris classis, temeritati Fortunæ, quos merito perstringit Iuvenalis: Nullum Numen habes, si sit Prudentia: sed te Nos facimus Fortuna Deam, Cœloque locamus.
units.tr: What more? Let those go hang who, transferring to the governance of nature the blindness they carry in their own minds, suppose that nothing happens without a cause, and, since they do not find the cause of things, ascribe the rule of the world to chance and deny it to God, along with Epicurus and others of the lesser sort, to the whim of Fortune, whom Juvenal rightly censures: You have no divinity, if there is prudence; it is we who make you a goddess, Fortune, and set you in heaven.

units.la: Qui sana illorum mens? Quid Casui & Fortunæ magis contrarium magisque inimicum, quam passim Ordinis invariabilis series? An non Universi nunc, quæ omni hominum memoria facies? Verissime Manilius: Non aliam videre Patres; aliamve Nepotes Adspicient.
units.tr: What a sound mind they must have! What is more contrary and more hostile to chance and fortune than the unchanging order of things seen everywhere? Do not the appearance of the universe now, and its appearance in all human memory, show this? Manilius speaks most truly: Fathers have not seen another order, nor will their descendants behold a different one.

units.la: Motus Cœlorum & Actiones sui semper similes; rerum Inferiorum species eodem semper modo procedunt. Nullus potest adfingi Naturæ Casus, nulla Temeritas; in qua tanta tamque perpetua constantia, tam certis omnia legibus descripta & constituta. Particulatim nonnumquam variat Natura, universim numquam. Nam una Causa Particularis ab alia impediri potest; Universalis vero nullis est capax impedimenti.
units.tr: The motions and actions of the heavens are always like themselves; the species of lower things always proceed in the same way. No chance or randomness can be attributed to nature, in which there is such great and such constant uniformity, and everything is described and fixed by such certain laws. Nature sometimes varies in particulars, never in the universal. For one particular cause can be impeded by another; but a universal cause is capable of no impediment.

units.la: Atqui objiciet quis illud Ecclesiast. cap. IX, 11. Vidi sub Sole, nec Velocium esse Cursum: aut Fortium Bellum; nec Sapientium Panem, nec Doctorum Divitias, nec Artificum Gratiam: sed Tempus Casumque in omnibus: & inferet hinc, non Omnia DEI gubernationi vel immediate vel mediate esse subjecta. Sed sub Sole ea proprie dicuntur esse; quæ, cujus motu, generationis corruptionisque vices recipiunt; in quibus omnibus Casus quodammodo invenitur. Tempus & Casus ab Sapiente posita, inquit Vir Magnus, ut nos moneret, secundum Temporis ordinem rebus naturalibus defectus caluacasuales accidere: Age vero, si ex tenebris in hanc Mundi, nunquam antea conspecti, nunquam verbis tibi delineati, lucem progressus, considerares Cursus & Actiones rerum, an non exclamares cura consilioque teneri haec omnia Principis, quo nihil sapientius, nihil melius, nihil potentius? Coelos, Elementa, Animantes, Herbas, Plantas, omnia denique ordine procedere, omnia suos habere Cursus destinatos & certos? Gubernat igitur omnia DEVS, non solum Illa; sed Haec etiam, quae nostra, quae nobiscum, quae ad pedes nobis. Nam si Terras adspernatur; quo tandem miserum Hominum genus confugiet? quanta in calamitatibus erit afflictio? quid? quanta desperatio, si Rex Naturae nos non exaudit, si est inexorabilis, si nulla gratia, nulla in nos caritate tangitur? Absit, absit, ut precibus nostris non moveatur, ut in Supremis sedeat otiosus, durus, indeprecabilis. Nihil enim Homini tristius accidere posset, vel acerbius.
units.tr: But someone will object that passage of Ecclesiastes 9:11: I saw under the sun that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong; nor bread to the wise, nor riches to the learned, nor favour to the skilful; but time and chance in all. And from this he will infer that not all things are subject to God's governance, either immediately or mediately. But those things are properly said to be under the sun which, by its motion, receive the alternations of generation and corruption; in all of these chance is found in some way. The great man says that time and chance were set by the Wise One so that he might warn us that defects and accidents befall natural things according to the order of time. Come now, if you were to advance out of darkness into this light of the world, never seen before and never described to you in words, and were to consider the courses and actions of things, would you not exclaim that all these things are held together by the care and counsel of a Prince, than whom nothing is wiser, nothing better, nothing more powerful? That the heavens, the elements, the living creatures, the herbs, the plants, all in short proceed in order, and that all have their courses appointed and certain? God therefore governs all things, not only those yonder but also these, which are ours, which are with us, which are at our feet. For if he were to scorn the earth, to what refuge would the wretched human race flee? How great would be the affliction in calamities? And what despair, if the King of nature did not hear us, if he were inexorable, if he were moved by no grace and no love for us? Far be it, far be it, that he should not be moved by our prayers, that he should sit idle, hard and implacable, in the heights. For nothing more sorrowful or bitter could befall a man.

units.la: PAVLLI G.F.P.N. MERVLÆ COSMOGRAPHIÆ PARTIS I. LIBER II.
units.tr: Of Paul G.F.P.N. Merula's Cosmography, Part I, Book II.

units.la: De potiore, quae constans æternaque, Mundi parte. CAP. I.
units.tr: On the more excellent part of the world, which is constant and eternal. CHAPTER I.
