units.la: Quidquid supra Elementa, æternum est & constans. Coelum quid; unde dictum; jucundissimum in ejus contemplatione versari; Coeli Forma.
units.tr: Whatever lies above the elements is eternal and constant. What heaven is, and whence it takes its name; that it is most delightful to dwell in its contemplation; the form of heaven.

units.la: UNIVERSI, quod hactenus Definitionis & Causarum coloribus delineavi, aliud est Constans & Æternum; aliud Inconstans & perpetuis obnoxium Mutationibus. Docet ex Platonicorum quorumdam mente Macrobius lib. i. in Somnium Scipionis cap. xi. Alii, inquit, Mundum in duo diviserunt, quorum alterum facit, alterum patitur. Et illud Facere dixerunt, quod quum sit Immutabile, alteri causam & necessitatem Permutationis imponit: Hoc Pati, quod per mutationes variatur. Et Immutabilem quidem Mundi Partem ab Sphaera, quae Ἀπλανὴς dicitur usque ad globi Lunaris exordium: Mutabilem vero ab Luna ad Terras usque dixerunt. Et vivere Animas dum Immutabili parte consistunt: Mori autem, quum ad Partem ceciderint Permutationis capacem. Et paullo post: Ab Luna enim deorsum natura incipit Caducorum.
units.tr: Of the whole universe that I have so far outlined in its definition and causes, one part is constant and eternal, and the other is inconstant and subject to perpetual change. Macrobius, following the opinion of certain Platonists, teaches this in Book I on the Dream of Scipio, chapter 11: Others, he says, have divided the world into two parts, one of which acts and the other is acted upon. They called that part acting which, being unchangeable, imposes on the other the cause and necessity of change; and that part acted upon which varies through changes. They held that the unchangeable part of the world extends from the sphere called the Fixed Stars down to the beginning of the lunar globe, and that the changeable part extends from the Moon down to the earth. They said that souls live while they remain in the unchangeable part, but die when they fall into the part capable of change. And a little later: For from the Moon downward begins the nature of things that perish.

units.la: Constantiam illam, Æternitatem, &, ut ita loquar, Insenescentiam adserunt ex Patribus, Dionysius Areopagita, Philo Iudaeus, Didymus Alexandrinus, Ioannes Chrysostomus Constantinopolitanus Patriarcha, Basilius Magnus, omnesque cum Thoma Aquinate 1. part. quæst. 66. Theologi, cum Aristotele plerique Peripatici, & in his Contarenus lib. v. Primæ Philosoph. Gab. Zerbus lib. viii. Metaphys. quæst. iii. Pernumia lib. ii. Philosoph. & Eugubinus lib. x. de perenni Philosophia. Videnda. & Iamblicus in lib. de myster. Ægyptiorum seg. v. cap. v. Aristoteles tamen, ut notat Alexander Aphrodisiensis in 1. de Coelo & Mundo librum & 1. Meteororum, Quidquid supra Elementa non absolute Passionum expers esse, dicere solitus. Vere: modo non exaudierit Passiones, quae per transmutationem fiunt secundum Formam; ab hac enim divina Corpora procul absunt. Nam inter Empyreum Coelum & Terram moventur omnia: Motus autem morae rei passionem conciliat, ut docent Physici. Sunt & quæ alienum recipiunt Lumen; quod pati esse extra omnem est controversiam. Alia item aliis ibi sunt puriora. Aristotele docente lib. i. Meteororum, quod tamen hic ratione non fæculentæ mistionis (ut observat cum Alexandro, loco quem dixi, Averroes Commentar. xv. in librum de Cœlo & Mundo) sed suarum partium collatione. Nam ab alienâ materia Cœlum esse segregatum canit etiam Virgilius lib. vi. Æneidos:
units.tr: Dionysius the Areopagite, Philo the Jew, Didymus of Alexandria, John Chrysostom, patriarch of Constantinople, Basil the Great, and all the theologians with Thomas Aquinas (Part 1, question 66) assert from the Fathers that constancy, eternity and, if I may so speak, freedom from ageing belong to this part. With Aristotle, most of the Peripatetics do so too, and among them Contarenus (Book V of First Philosophy), Gabriel Zerbus (Book VIII of Metaphysics, question iii), Pernumia (Book II of Philosophy) and Steuco of Gubbio (Book X, On the Perennial Philosophy). See them. Iamblichus also (in the book On the Mysteries of the Egyptians, section V, chapter v). Aristotle, however, as Alexander of Aphrodisias notes on Book I of On the Heavens and the World and Book I of the Meteorology, used to say that whatever lies above the elements is not altogether free of affections. This is true, provided that it does not undergo the affections that come about through change of form; for these divine bodies are far removed from such change. For everything moves between the heavenly empyrean and the earth, and motion, as the natural philosophers teach, brings a certain affection to a body. Some bodies also receive light from elsewhere, and that this is a passion no one disputes. Likewise some parts there are purer than others, as Aristotle teaches in Book I of the Meteorology; yet this is by reason not of a muddy mixture (as Averroes observes, along with Alexander, in the passage I mentioned, in his Commentary XV on the book On the Heavens and the World) but of the arrangement of its parts. For Virgil also sings that heaven was cleansed of foreign matter, in Book VI of the Aeneid:

units.la: purumque reliquit Æthereum sensum atque aurai simplicis ignem.
units.tr: and left it pure, the ethereal sense and the fire of simple air.

units.la: Sunt tamen qui Cœlum propter Hominis lapsum Corruptioni obnoxium, & prima illa excellenti natura destitutum, senioque quasi confectum colligant ex Pauli Apostoli verbis, cap. viii. epistolæ ad Romanos, vers. 20: Vanitati enim Creatura subjecta est, non volens, sed propter eum, qui subjecit eam in spe: quia & ipsa Creatura liberabitur à servitute Corruptionis in libertatem gloriæ filiorum Dei. Scimus enim quod omnis Creatura ingemiscit & parturit usque adhuc. Ad quem locum Theophylactus Bulgariæ Archiepiscopus: Vanitati, id est, Corruptioni subjecta est, inquit, Creatura, videlicet Corruptibilis reddita propter te, o homo: nam quum mortale & passibile corpus susceperis, ideo Terra & spentes & tribulos protulit: & Cœlum Vetustate confectum Mutatione indiget. At quare alterius gratia Corruptibilis facta est Creatura? quia propter hominem omnem profusus subiit servitutem. Liberabitur igitur hæc Mundi structura, nec ipsa solum Libertate potietur, quin etiam, quod te inferius est, hac perfruetur. Et quemadmodum ipse, quum corruptibilis permanente, servabit & ipsa Incorruptionem. Nam, ut adsolet Pater in Liberorum gratiam servos ornare, sic & Deus hanc Mundi machinam in vestram laudem decorabit. Ita & Petrus Longobardus Sententiarum libro iiii. distinct. xlvii. non obscure innuit, Cœlos post Adæ peccatum primæva fuisse destitutos perfectione; quod vero illis deest, pro Universi conflagrationem accessurum: quam ejus sententiam nonnulli etiam Theologi communi plausu excipere non dubitarunt. Quidquid sit, Elementorum respectu, recte dicuntur Superiora illa æterna & constantia.
units.tr: Some, however, gather from the words of the Apostle Paul in Romans 8:20 that heaven, because of man's fall, is subject to corruption and has been deprived of its first excellent nature, and that it is as it were worn out with age: For the creature was made subject to vanity, not willingly, but by reason of him who subjected the same in hope; because the creature itself also shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the glorious liberty of the children of God. For we know that every creature groaneth and travaileth in pain together until now. On this passage Theophylact, Archbishop of Bulgaria, says: The creature was made subject to vanity, that is, to corruption, made corruptible on your account, O man; for when you took on a mortal and passible body, the earth brought forth thorns and thistles, and heaven, worn out by age, needs renewal. But why was the creature made corruptible for the sake of another? Because it underwent servitude, overflowing, on account of man. This structure of the world, then, shall be set free, and it shall not only enjoy liberty but also share in what is lower than you, and just as you, though corruptible, will remain, so it too will keep incorruption. For as a father is wont to adorn his servants for the sake of his children, so God will also adorn this machine of the world for your praise. Peter Lombard too, in Book IV of the Sentences, distinction 47, clearly hints that after Adam's sin the heavens were deprived of their original perfection, and that what they lack will come at the conflagration of the universe. Some theologians have not hesitated to receive this opinion with general approval. Whatever the case, compared with the elements, those higher things are rightly called eternal and constant.

units.la: Æternæ igitur constantesque Mundi Partes sunt Cælum & Stella. Cælum vocatur, quidquid ab Luna sursum; totum illud expansum, quantum quantum est, quod elementarem regionem ambit & circum amplectitur.
units.tr: The eternal and constant parts of the world, therefore, are heaven and the stars. Heaven is the name given to whatever lies above the Moon: that whole expanse, however vast it is, which encloses and embraces the elementary region.

units.la: Sic appellatum ὀπὸ τῆς κοίλης: Cavum enim, & cujus complexu teguntur cuncta. M. Terentius Varro apud Plinium lib. ii. natural. histor. cap. iv. sic dictum vult, quod cælatum. Pictum enim veluti & inlustre, cum magnis istis Luminaribus Sole & Luna, tum splendentibus reliquorum Astrorum signis. Ejus mentis & apud Varronem lib. iv. de L. L. Ælius Gallus. antiquus Scriptor. Legendus & Isidorus lib. xiii. Erymolog. cap. iv.
units.tr: It is so called from the Greek [ἀπὸ τῆς κοίλης], that is, from being hollow, since it is a vault by whose embrace all things are covered. Marcus Terentius Varro, cited by Pliny in Book II of the Natural History, chapter 4, holds that it is so called because it is carved, for it is as it were painted and brightened, both by the great luminaries, the Sun and the Moon, and by the shining signs of the other stars. Aelius Gallus, an ancient writer, is of the same mind, as cited by Varro in Book IV of On the Latin Language. Isidore, Etymologies, Book XIII, chapter 4, should also be read.

units.la: Ut in Universi, sic versari jucundissimum in Cœli contemplatione. Huic adfixi quasi fuerunt Stoici. Mundus enim ijs opus erat, quod undique perfectum; quod omnia undique complexum; in quo, quidquid in hac rerum natura: & censebant Hominem, qui μικρόκοσμος, natum ad Mundum imitandum contemplandumque. Consulendus Lucilius Balbus apud M. Tullium ii. de natur. Deorum. Ardens hoc studium & sibi fuisse, clare loquitur Seneca in Octavia Act. ii. Sc. i:
units.tr: As in the whole universe, so it is most delightful to dwell in the contemplation of heaven. The Stoics were devoted to this. For they needed a world that was perfect on every side, that embraced all things on every side, and in which was whatever exists in this nature of things; and they held that man, who is a microcosm, was born to imitate and contemplate the world. Lucilius Balbus, cited by Cicero in Book II of On the Nature of the Gods, should be consulted. Seneca speaks plainly of how ardently he too was devoted to this study, in the Octavia, Act II, Scene 1:

units.la: O quam juvabat (quo nihil majus parens Natura genuit, Operis immensi artifex) Cœlum intueri, Solis & Cursus sacros, Mundique Motus, Solis alternas vices, Orbemque Phœbes, Astra quem cingunt vaga, Lateque fulgens Aetheris magni decus.
units.tr: Oh how it delighted me (than which nature, the great artificer of her immense work, has brought forth nothing greater) to gaze upon heaven, the sacred courses of the Sun, the motions of the world, the Sun's alternating changes, the orb of Phoebe, which the wandering stars surround, and the broad radiance that is the glory of the great aether.

units.la: Videndus idem Epistol. lxv. & Consolat. ad Elbiam cap. viii, ix. & ult. Veras illas Oculorum delicias notat & Lactantius lib. vi. Diuin. Institut. Aiunt multo esse praclarius, inquit, & Homine dignius, Cœlum potius quam Cælata intueri; & hoc pulcerrimum opus intermicantibus Astrorum Luminibus, tamquam Floribus, adornatum, quam Pictla & Fi-gura & Gemmis distincta mirari.
units.tr: Seneca's Epistle 65 and his Consolation to Helvia, chapters 8, 9 and the last, should also be seen. Lactantius too points out those true delights of the eyes, in Book VI of the Divine Institutes: They say it is far more splendid, and more worthy of a man, to gaze upon heaven than upon carved work; and to admire this most beautiful work, adorned with the twinkling lights of the stars as with flowers, rather than pictures, figures and jewels.

units.la: Rotundam ejus esse formam constat ex Universi natura & conditione, de qua superiore libro. Nam, ut specialius dicam de hac Universi parte: Corpori omnium primo, capacissimo, perfectissimo figura conveniebat globosa; qua inter figuras nulla prior, capacior, perfectior. Omnibus hæc suis partibus vergit in se, passim semetipsam concludit & continet.
units.tr: It is established that its form is round, from the nature and condition of the universe, of which I spoke in the earlier book. To speak more particularly of this part of the universe: the globular figure suited the first and most capacious and most perfect of all bodies; among figures none is earlier, more capacious or more perfect. Such a figure turns in upon itself on all its sides, and everywhere encloses and contains itself.

units.la: Addo Cœlum quaqua versum æqualiter a Terra distare; Stellis distantias suas ab hoc globo nusquam mutantibus; neque majoribus hic, minoribus ibi apparentibus. Quod enim circa cardines Orientis & Occidentis subinde videantur nobis majores; hit non ratione brevioris distantiæ, sed quod earum radij Vaporum, qui nonnumquam Stellis Oculisque nostris interfluunt, injuria frangantur. Consulendus Vitellio lib. ix. Opticæ.
units.tr: I add that heaven is equally distant from the earth in every direction, the stars never changing their distances from this globe, nor appearing larger here and smaller there. For if they sometimes seem larger to us near the eastern and western horizons, this is not because the distance is shorter, but because their rays are broken by the vapours that sometimes come between the stars and our eyes. See Witelo, Book IX of Optics.

units.la: Accedit Interiorum orbium (nam Supremus ἐκτὸς natura. Gyrant omnes; alij celeriore, tardiore Motu alij: Atque ad Motus hosce feliciter & sine impedimento peragundos, nulla forma aptior, quam Sphærica, cui nihil quod asperum, nihil quod offendat, nihil quod vel angulis vel amfractibus incisum.
units.tr: Add that the motion of the inner orbs (for the outermost is by nature apart) is such that all revolve, some with swifter and some with slower motion. And for these motions to be carried out happily and without hindrance, no form is more suitable than the spherical, in which there is nothing rough, nothing that offends, nothing cut by angles or bends.

units.la: Quid quod omne Corpus simplex & ὁμοιομερὲς, quale Cœlum, cujus omnes partes simplices & inter se similimæ, figura etiam simplici includatur & ὁμοιομερῆ?
units.tr: What of the fact that every simple body, such as heaven, whose parts are all simple and very like one another, is enclosed by a simple figure and one that is uniform in its parts?

units.la: Quin & formam hanc adstruunt etiam non pauca sacræ Scripturæ loca. Ait Psalmo civ. & versf. 2. David Propheta: Qui extendit Cœlum, veluti cortinam (כיריעה, ὡσεὶ δέρριν, sicut pellem.) Sic Sapientia apud Schelomon. Proverb. viii. verf. 27. Quando præparabat Cœlos illic eram, quando describebat Circulum, (חוג) in superficie abyssi. Ecclesiast. i. verf. 5. Et oritur Sol & occidit, & ad locum suum regreditur ubi oritur.
units.tr: Indeed, not a few passages of Holy Scripture also support this form. The prophet David says in Psalm 104, verse 2: Who stretcheth out the heavens like a curtain [כיריעה; Greek ὡσεὶ δέρριν, as a skin]. So Wisdom in Solomon's Proverbs 8, verse 27: When he prepared the heavens I was there; when he set a compass [חוג] upon the face of the depth. Ecclesiastes 1, verse 5: The sun also ariseth, and the sun goeth down, and hasteth to his place where he arose.

units.la: meridiem & circuit (סובב) ad Aquilonem subinde circumeundo (סובב סובב, ad verbum, circuitens, circuiens; κυκλεῖ κυκλῶν) pergit spiritus & ad circuitus suos (סביבותיו, ὅπι κύκλος) revertitur. Ecclesiastici cap. xxiv, 8: Τὸν γύρον οὐρανοῦ μόνη, Orbem Cœli circuivi sola. Sic denique Iesaiah. cap. xl. 22: Sedens super globum (חוג הארץ) Terra & habitatores ejus, ut locusta: extendens velut telam (כדק, ὡς καμάρας) Cœlos, & expandit eos tamquam Tabernaculum (לאהל, ὡς σκηνὴν) ad inhabitandum. Respicit eo Augustinus lib. ii. de Genes. ad litt. cap. ix: Non enim, inquit, Cœlum esse rotundum, pugnat cum eo quod est, habere ipsum similitudinem Tabernaculi, vel Camera. Cœlum enim secundum eam partem, qua supra nos, de qua proprie loquitur Scriptura, habet similitudinem Camera: superne continens & tegens hoc nostrum Hemisphærium: quare si Cœlum non est sphærica, ex ea parte Camera est, qua Terram tegit; sin autem totum est sphæricum, utraque ex parte Camera est. Nam sicut hæc pars Cœli, quæ nos tegit, est quasi Camera, respectu nostri Hemisphæry; ita Cœli altera medietas, quæ tegit Antipodas, respectu adversi nobis Hemisphærij, Camera est. Nec obstat, quod ait David, Cœlum extensum esse sicut pellem. Namque pellis potest distendi & in planum, & in orbem; uti cernimus, in utre, pila, vesica.
units.tr: ...to the south, and circling round to the north, the spirit goes on, turning again and again [סובב סובב, literally circuiting, circuiting; κυκλεῖ κυκλῶν], and returns to its circuits [סביבותיו, ὅπι κύκλος]. Ecclesiasticus 24:8: "I alone have compassed the vault of heaven" [Τὸν γύρον οὐρανοῦ μόνη], that is, I alone have encircled the orb of heaven. So too Isaiah 40:22: He sits above the circle [חוג הארץ] of the earth, and its inhabitants are like locusts; he stretches out the heavens like a thin veil [כדק, ὡς καμάρας], and spreads them out like a tent [לאהל, ὡς σκηνὴν] to dwell in. Augustine has this in view in book 2 of On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, chapter 9: For, he says, it does not conflict with the fact that the heaven is round that it has the likeness of a tent or vault. For the heaven, in that part by which it is above us, of which Scripture especially speaks, has the likeness of a vault, covering and enclosing this hemisphere of ours from above. So if the heaven is not spherical, it is a vault on that side which covers the earth; but if it is wholly spherical, it is a vault on both sides. For just as this part of heaven which covers us is like a vault with respect to our hemisphere, so the other half of heaven, which covers the Antipodes, is a vault with respect to the hemisphere opposite to us. Nor does it stand in the way that David says the heaven is stretched out like a skin. For a skin can be stretched both flat and into a round shape, as we see in a wineskin, a ball, or a bladder.

units.la: Absit igitur ut sequamur Iustinum, ubi respondet ad quæst. cxxx. Orthodoxorum, Lactantium lib. iii. Divinar. Institut. cap. xxiii. Chrysostomum Homil. xiv. & xxvii. in Epistol. ad Hebræos, Ambrosium lib. i in ἑξαήμερ. Basilium Homilia i. super Genesin, Procopium Gazæum ad Genesin, & alios; non modo Cœlum rotundum negantes; sed & auctos dicere, opinionem de Rotunditate Sacris adversari Litteris: quod quam verum, docent, quæ dixi.
units.tr: Let us therefore not follow Justin, who answers the 130th question of the Orthodox, nor Lactantius in book 3 of the Divine Institutes, chapter 23, nor Chrysostom in homilies 14 and 27 on the Epistle to the Hebrews, nor Ambrose in book 1 of the Hexaemeron, nor Basil in homily 1 on Genesis, nor Procopius of Gaza on Genesis, nor others, who not only deny that the heaven is round but also say that the opinion of its roundness is contrary to the Sacred Letters. How false that is, the things I have said show.

units.la: Certe si hac figura non esset præditum, si inquam esset ὀξύγραμμον, si vel ὀκτάεδρον, vel δωδεκάεδρον, vel εἰκοσάεδρον; si πυραμοειδὲς, si Φαρωνδις, si denique ὤσειδὴς: sequetur necessario vel angulosas exstantesque Cœli partes sine loco volutari; vel in loco quidem volutari, sed qui nunc expletus, nunc, quæ eminebant motu abreptis, esset vacuus. Ab Vacuo autem Natura abhorret. Nam licet sint, qui tantum Inanis extra Mundum esse volunt, quantum Cœlo (quod natura, ut volunt, igneum) ad respirandum sufficiat; Plato tamen, Aristoteles alijque, recte, nullum Inane admittunt.
units.tr: Certainly, if heaven were not endowed with this shape, if I say it were sharp-angled [ὀξύγραμμον], or eight-faced [ὀκτάεδρον], or twelve-faced [δωδεκάεδρον], or twenty-faced [εἰκοσάεδρον]; if it were pyramid-shaped [πυραμοειδὲς], lens-shaped [φακοειδές], or finally egg-shaped [ὠοειδής], then it would necessarily follow that either its angular and projecting parts would be rolled about without a place, or that it would indeed be rolled about in a place, but that place would now be filled and now, as the parts that stood out were carried away by the motion, would be empty. Yet Nature abhors a vacuum. For although there are some who want there to be outside the world only as much void as is enough for the heaven (which they say is by nature fiery) to breathe, Plato, Aristotle, and others rightly admit no void at all.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: De Cælo Empyreo.
units.tr: Of the Empyrean Heaven.

units.la: Cœlum autem vel est firmum & stabile; vel volubile circa Axem. Illud Empyreum solet indigetari; Mundi supremus terminus, Orbis summus (Psalmo xix, 7. Damascenus lib. ii. de Fide Orthodoxa, cap. vi.) & amplissimus; sublimior omni Cœlo Sydereo (Iesaiah. xliii, 13.) nullo Motui, nullique Passioni obnoxius;
units.tr: Heaven is either fixed and stable, or it turns about an axis. The former is commonly called the Empyrean: the highest boundary of the world and its uppermost and most spacious sphere (Psalm 19:7; Damascene, On the Orthodox Faith, bk. 2, ch. 6), higher than every starry heaven (Isaiah 43:13), and subject to no motion and no passion.

units.la: {y} nulla. noxius ; subtilitatis summæ; totus lucens, non luce densa, quæ radios fundat,& quæ mortalium oculis visibilis, sed inenarrabili, ut inquit Basilius 11. & 111. Homilia in Genesin, & qualis perhibetur in Elemento Ignis, quod supra Aerem orbi Lunæ subsidet. Sic dictum, quasi ardens & ignitum: non re ipsa, sed quod, ut volunt magni viri, lucè incomprehensibili perfusum, vel ab ipso unitrino D E o, qui in eo maxime conspicuus, inluminatum.
units.tr: It is of the highest subtlety and wholly luminous, not with a dense light that sends out rays and is visible to mortal eyes, but with an ineffable light, as Basil says in his Homilies 2 and 3 on Genesis, and of the kind said to exist in the element of fire, which settles above the air beneath the orb of the moon. It is so called as if burning and ignited, not in reality, but because, as great men hold, it is suffused with an incomprehensible light, or is illuminated by the triune God himself, who is most conspicuous in it.

units.la: Hoc Cœlum ab omni hujus Mundi volubili statu secretum, omnium mortalium inaccessible conspectibus, Essentiæ divinæ quasi sedes & ἀχαιμεα. Beda in ἐξαρτα. Nam quamvis DEVS nullo loco aut indiget aut circumscribitur, sed ubique est: Cœlum tamen hoc veluti præcipuam suæ Majestati delegit arcem: ut ab iis, quos in Terra producturus erat, tanti loci dignitate & excellentia sanctius, diligentius, commodius observaretur; utque in memoriam fidelius vocarent habitantis Cœlum illud Potentiam, Virtutem, Providentiam & Bonitatem. Psalmo cIII, 19. Huiob xxxv, 5. Inde Prospicere dicitur, & videre filios hominum, Psalm. xiv, 2. xxxiii,13. Hoc enim præparatum magno Numini ante omnia habitaculum, eodem Psalmo vers. 14. & cxiii, 5. cxxiii, 1. Iesaiah. lxvi,1. Paullus ad Coloss.iii,1. Isidorus lib. vii. Etymolog. cap. 1.
units.tr: This heaven, set apart from every changeable condition of this world and inaccessible to the sight of all mortals, is as it were the seat of the divine essence and [ἀχαιμεα]. Bede, in the Hexaemeron. For although God needs no place and is not confined to one, but is everywhere, still he has chosen this heaven as, so to speak, the chief citadel of his majesty, so that those whom he was about to bring forth on earth might observe it more reverently, diligently and conveniently, given the dignity and excellence of so great a place, and so that they might more faithfully recall that this heaven is the dwelling of his power, virtue, providence and goodness (Psalm 103:19; Job 35:5). Hence he is said to look down and to behold the sons of men (Psalm 14:2; 33:13). For this is the habitation prepared before all things for the great Deity (the same Psalm, v. 14; 113:5; 123:1; Isaiah 66:1; Paul to the Colossians 3:1; Isidore, Etymologies, bk. 7, ch. 1).

units.la: Hoc ornatum & distinctum novem Angelorum ordinibus, Basilius Homilia 11. & 111. in Genesin, Damascenus lib. 11. de Fide Orthodoxa, cap. vi.
units.tr: This heaven is adorned and divided into nine orders of angels (Basil, Homilies 2 and 3 on Genesis; Damascene, On the Orthodox Faith, bk. 2, ch. 6).

units.la: Hinc descendisse scribitur Christus, Iesaiah. xlv, 8. Ioannes Euangelist. 111, 3. Huc adsumptus Filius DEI cum nostri Corporis pignore. Marc.xvi,9. Luc. xxiv,51. Ioannis 111, 13. Actorum 1, 10. Hoc aperto gloriam vidit DEI, & Filium hominis ab ejus dextra stantem Stephanus. Actor, vii, 55.
units.tr: From here Christ is written of as having descended (Isaiah 45:8; John 3:13). Hither the Son of God was taken up with the pledge of our body (Mark 16:19; Luke 24:51; John 3:13; Acts 1:10). Having opened this heaven, Stephen saw the glory of God and the Son of man standing at his right hand (Acts 7:55).

units.la: Huc evolant Iustorum Animi Corpore soluti, nulla peccati labe contaminati. Basilius loco saepe indicato. Hoc Corporibus Beatorum, magno die, terreno pulvere potenter eductis, æternamq; gloriam & immortalitatem indutis, domicilium futurum in omnia saecula.
units.tr: Hither fly the souls of the righteous, freed from the body and untouched by any stain of sin (Basil, in the place often cited). Here, on the great day, the bodies of the blessed, powerfully raised from earthly dust and clothed with eternal glory and immortality, will have their dwelling for all ages.

units.la: Hoc in Sacris Litteris Cœlum Cœli, השמים שמים, Psalmo cxv, 16. Diodorus Episcopus Tarsensis, qui Chrysostomi fuit præceptor, in Catena Lippomani, Damascenus lib. 11. de Fide Orthodoxa, cap. vi. Isidorus lib. vii. Etymolog. cap. 1. Cæli Cælorum, שמי השמים, Psalm. cxlviii,4. Ecclesiast. xvi, 18. Cœlum illud Tertium, 30 in quod raptum arcana verba, quæ non licebat homini loqui, audivisse se scribit D. Paullus Epistola 11. ad Corinthios cap. xii. vers. 2. & seq. quemadmodum existimat Damascenus capite sæpe nominato; ut per primum intelligatur Aerum; per Secundum, Sydereum: per Tertium, Empyreum. Hoc Regio viventium, ארעית החיים, χώρα ζώντων, Psalm. cxvi, 9. Terra viventium, ארץ החיים, Psalm. cxlı, 6. Terram ἀσπλῶς vocat Christus apud Mathæum Evangel. cap. v. 4. cum quod sicut inter Elementa Terra sit immobilis; ita inter Cœlos Hoc: tum quod, quemadmodum Terra nunc est domicilium hominum mortalem vitam viventium; ita post resurrectionem Cœlum hoc futurum sedes justorum hominum, beatam vitam ævo perpetuo degentium. Hoc putatur adumbrare supra Firmamentum ממעל לרקיע Ezechiel Propheta cap. 1. vers. 26. & cap. x. vers. 1. per Sapphyrum (ספיר) in similitudinem Throni (כסא) ut color Sapphyri Lucis nitorem, Throni vero similitudo stabilitatem ejus & immobilitatem declaret.
units.tr: In Holy Scripture this heaven is called the heaven of heavens, [השמים שמים] (Psalm 115:16); Diodorus, bishop of Tarsus, who was the teacher of Chrysostom, in Lippomano's Catena; Damascene, On the Orthodox Faith, bk. 2, ch. 6; Isidore, Etymologies, bk. 7, ch. 1. It is the heavens of heavens, [שמי השמים] (Psalm 148:4; Ecclesiasticus 16:18). Into this third heaven, Paul writes, he was caught up and heard secret words that a man may not utter (2 Corinthians 12:2 ff.), as Damascene also thinks in the chapter often cited; so that the first is understood as the air, the second as the starry heaven, and the third as the Empyrean. It is the land of the living, [ארעית החיים], [χώρα ζώντων] (Psalm 116:9); the earth of the living, [ארץ החיים] (Psalm 142:6). Christ, in Matthew 5:4, calls the earth [ἀσπλῶς], since just as earth is immobile among the elements, so this heaven is immobile among the heavens; and since, just as the earth is now the dwelling of men living a mortal life, so after the resurrection this heaven will be the seat of righteous men living a blessed life in perpetual eternity. It is thought to be foreshadowed by the prophet Ezekiel (1:26; 10:1), who speaks of something above the firmament [ממעל לרקיע], in the likeness of a throne [כסא] of sapphire [ספיר]: the colour of the sapphire signifies the brightness of the light, and the likeness of a throne its stability and immobility.

units.la: Hoc illud, quod nonnulli, ut cap. iii. lib. 1. indicavi, creatum volunt בראשית, in principio, Genes. 1, 1. addentes creatum mox Angelis fuisse repletum. Beda in ἐξαρτμερ. & apud eum D. Hieronymus. Videndi & Theodoretus quæst. xi. & xiv. super Genesin, Alcuinus, Rabanus, Magister Sententiarum, Nicolaus Lyranus, Magister historiæ Scholasticæ, Toftatus, Catharinus & alij. Æternum quid & increatum esse somniat Augustinus Eugubinus in sua Cosmopœia, & tractatu quem scripsit de naturis incorporeis, hoc est, Lucem esse & Claritatem quandam ex DEI essentia manantem; in qua DEVS est, & ad cujus participationem atque fruitionem & boni Angeli & viri Justi admittuntur; addens hujus Lucis & Claritatis mentionem aliquoties facere Sacras Litteras. Sed Paradoxum hoc novam viri aliquin docti opinionem docte refutat Benedictus Pererius libro 1. Commentar. in Genesin, ad illa Cœlum & Terram.
units.tr: This is the heaven which some, as I indicated in chapter 3 of book 1, hold to have been created in the beginning [בראשית] (Genesis 1:1), adding that it was filled immediately with angels. Bede, in the Hexaemeron, and Jerome after him; see also Theodoret, Questions 11 and 14 on Genesis; Alcuin, Rabanus, the Master of the Sentences, Nicholas of Lyra, the Master of the Historia Scholastica, Tostatus, Catharinus and others. Augustinus Eugubinus, in his Cosmopoeia and in the treatise he wrote on incorporeal natures, dreams that this heaven is something eternal and uncreated, namely a light and a certain brightness flowing from the essence of God, in which God is, and into whose participation and enjoyment both good angels and righteous men are admitted; he adds that the sacred writings frequently mention this light and brightness. But Benedictus Pererius, in the first book of his Commentary on Genesis, on the words "heaven and earth," learnedly refutes this paradox, a novelty of an otherwise learned man.

units.la: Hoc Cœlum scribit Damascenus cognitum fuisse Sapientibus hujus Mundi memoriae prodītum: Vocari enim ab ipsis ἀνάσχον: quae Moschis propria sunt, sua fa-cientibus dogmata.
units.tr: Damascene writes that this heaven was known to the wise men of this world and handed down in memory; for they called it [ἀνάσχον], a term peculiar to the Moschians, who make their own doctrines.

units.la: Supra Empyreum sunt qui locant Cœlum Trinitatis; quod etiam magni viri dicunt esse nihil aliud, quam Virtutis Divinæ excellentiam, quæ continet & ambit omnia creata.
units.tr: Above the Empyrean some place the Heaven of the Trinity; great men also say that this is nothing other than the excellence of divine power, which contains and encompasses all created things.

units.la: CAP. III. Volvi Cœlos reliquos circa Axem, cuius extremitatis Poli.
units.tr: CHAP. III. That the remaining heavens revolve about the axis, whose extremities are the poles.

units.la: HÆC de Firmo & Stabili Cœlo: sequitur quod Volubile. Volvi vero (circu-latim, ut antea, ubi de Forma, dixi) creditur ita, ut admirabilis sit Harmonia & stupendus Corporum, quæ moventur, concentus; quemadmodum, præter alios, vult Plato, cujus hac de re sententiam Tullius in suo de Scipionis somnio recitat his verbis: Quis hic, inquam, quis est, qui complet aurēs meas, tantus & tam dulcis sonus? Hic est, inquit ille, qui intervallis conjunctus imparibus, sed tamen pro rata parte ratione distinctus, impulsu & motu ipsorum Orbium efficitur; & acuta cum gravibus temperans varios aquabiliter concentus efficit, & quæ deinceps. Hac de re multa Macrobius lib. II. in Somnium Scipionis cap. I. & seqq. ubi docet, non solum Concentum quemdam efficiri motu Corporum Cœlestium, sed etiam quibus adminiculis repertus ille fuerit à Pythagora; quibus indiciis & rationibus possit ostendi; qui fiat, ut inter sonos cœlestis illius Concentus alius sit acutior, alius gravior; quodnam ibi melodiæ sit genus: quæ denique tonus ille à nobis non audiatur. Sed quis non videt illa magni Philosophi figurate, non autem vere, accipienda: rebus cœlestibus ad suavissimam artem Musicam accommodatis? Absurdum ces (tamquam illi maxima cum Cœlo esset cognatio) accommodatis? Absurdum esse, Corporum Cœlestium collisione. Dubitat hic Plinius lib. II. natur. histor. cap. III. An sit immensus, & ideo sensum aurium facile excedens (Macrobius lib. II. in Somn. Scip. cap. IV.) tantæ molis rotantæ vertigine assidua sonitus, non equidem facile dixerim; non hercle magis, quam circumactorum simul tinnitus sidérum suavitate concentus, nobis qui intus agimus juxta diebus noctibusque tacitus labitur mundus. Quidquid sit de Concentu illo; volvitur sane Cœlum, ut etiam quibusdam huic judicium fuerit Αἰθὴρ: non, ut vult Anaxagoras, ἀπὸ τοῦ αἴθειν, quod ardeat; sed quod, juxta Platonem, aeri circumfusus semper currat. ἀεὶ θεῖ ἀεὶ ῥέων; vel, quæ mens Aristotelis, ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀεὶ θεῖν, quod perpetua volubilitate rotetur. Adeundus Auct. libr. de Mundo ad Alexandr. cap. I. Volvitur autem Cœlum circa Axem. Axis recta est Linea per centrum Sphærae extremitatem attingens: circa quam diurne motu ab ortu in occasum Cœlum universum rotatur. Geminus ἀπαγωγὴ εἰς τὰ φαινόμενα: τὰ ἢ κόσμου ἀεὶ ὧν φύεται ὁ κόσμος, ἀ ἕξει ἀεὶ ἀρχόμενος ἢ κόσμου ἐκ τῶν φαινομένων, Proclo, Gemino exscriptorem, Leontium & alios. Aratus Solensis ἐν Φαινομένοις. Αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ ἀὸ ἑλίγεον μεγαλείοτερον. ἀλλὰ μάλ' αὕτως Ἀξων αὐτὸν ἀέρμεν, ἀχὴ δ' ἀπάλαστον ἀπλήν Μεσσηνῆς γαῖας ἀεὶ δ' ἀέρα ἐς αὐτὴν ἀγινεῖ. Et interpres ejus Germanicus Cæsar; nam M. Tullius hic perijt: Axis at immotus semper vestigia servat, Librataque tenet terras, & cardine firmo Orbem agit extremum. Manilius denique: Aera per gelidum tenuis deducitur Axis, Librat umque regit diverso cardine Mundum: Sydereus circa medium quem volvitur Orbis, Æthereosque rotat cursus: immotus at ille In binas Arctos magni per inania Mundi Perque ipsum Terræ directus conspicit orbem. D
units.tr: So much for the fixed and stable heaven. Next comes the moving heaven. It is believed to revolve (in a circular motion, as I said earlier when speaking of its shape) in such a way that there is a wonderful harmony and a marvellous concert produced by the bodies that move. Plato, among others, holds this, and Tully recites his opinion on the matter in his Dream of Scipio in these words: "What is this," I said, "what is this sound that fills my ears, so great and so sweet?" "It is," he replied, "the sound produced by the impulse and motion of the spheres themselves, which are joined by unequal intervals, yet distinguished by a ratio exact in proportion. Tempering the high notes with the low, they produce varied harmonies in regular measure," and so on. Macrobius treats this matter at length in Book II of his commentary on the Dream of Scipio, chapter 1 and following. There he teaches not only that a certain concord is produced by the motion of the heavenly bodies, but also by what aids Pythagoras discovered it, by what signs and reasons it can be demonstrated, how it comes about that among the sounds of that heavenly concord some are higher and some lower, what kind of melody it is, and finally why that tone is not heard by us. But who does not see that these words of that great philosopher are to be taken figuratively and not literally, since they fit heavenly things to the most delightful art of music? It is absurd (as if music had the greatest affinity with the heaven) to say that the sound comes from the collision of the heavenly bodies. Pliny in Book II, chapter 3 of his Natural History doubts this: "Whether this sound, which, because the vast mass turns in constant whirling, easily exceeds the sense of hearing (Macrobius, Book II, on the Dream of Scipio, ch. 4), is indeed immense, I would not readily say; no more, by Hercules, than the concord of the stars, moving together, has a tinkling sweetness, while the world silently glides on, day and night, for us who live within it." Whatever may be the case with that concord, the heaven certainly does revolve. For this reason some have called it aether: not, as Anaxagoras would have it, from aithein, to burn, but because, according to Plato, it always runs around the air that surrounds it (aei theei, aei rheon, that is, it always runs and always flows). Or, as Aristotle thought, it is named from aei theein, to run forever, because it turns with perpetual motion. The author of the book On the World, addressed to Alexander, chapter 1, should be consulted. The heaven revolves about the axis. The axis is a straight line through the centre of the sphere touching its extremities, about which the whole heaven turns with a daily motion from east to west. Geminus, in his Introduction to the Phenomena, [says that the things which are always in the world, the world itself which is always moving, are learned from the phenomena]; Proclus copied from Geminus, as did Leontius and others. Aratus of Soli, in his Phaenomena: [Greek lines, garbled in the scan]. His interpreter Germanicus Caesar (for Cicero's translation of Aratus has perished) says: "The axis, unmoved, always keeps its place, and holds the earth balanced, and by its firm pivot turns the outermost sphere." Finally Manilius: "Through the icy air the slender axis runs, and holds the world poised, governing it with its opposite pivot. The starry sphere turns about it, and whirls the heavenly courses; but that axis stays still, and through the void of the great world it looks down, straight through the earth itself, on the two Bears."

units.la: Puncta Axem terminantia vocantur πόλοι Græcis ἀπὸ τοῦ πολεῖν: Latinis, M. Tullio, Virgilio, Germanico, aliis Vertices, ab vertendo, quod in illis vertatur Cœlum, Servius ad 1. AEneid. Geminus: τὰ δὲ πόλεα τὰ ἀξονος, Πόλοι λέγονται τὰ ἀρκτικά: quæ & apud Proclum, Leontium, aliosque.
units.tr: The points where the axis ends are called poles by the Greeks, from poleein, to turn. The Latins (Tully, Virgil, Germanicus and others) call them vertices, from vertere, to turn, because the heaven turns upon them. Servius on the first book of the Aeneid. Geminus: the extremities of the axis are called the poles, and those of the north are called the arctic poles. This is also found in Proclus, Leontius and others.

units.la: Verticum, qui & Cardines, unus Βόρειος & Ἀρκτικὸς Græcis; Latinis Septemtrionalis; qui ad Boream spectans nobis semper est in aperto: alter apud Græcos Νότιος & Ἀνταρκτικὸς; apud Latinos Meridionalis, & Australis; nobis perpetuo latens & sub Horizonte depressus. Geminus: τῶν δὲ πόλων ὁ μὲν λέγεται Βόρειος, ὁ δὲ Νότιος. Ut & Proclus ceterique Græci. Sic Aratus: Ναὶ μὴν πεφαίνονται δύω πόλοι ἀμφοτέρωθεν; Ἀλλ᾽ ὁ μὲν ὀφθαλμοῖς, ὁ δ᾽ αὖθις οὐ Βορέαο Τηλόθεν ὠκεανοῖο.
units.tr: Of the two poles, which are also called cardines (hinges), one is called Boreal and Arctic by the Greeks, and Septentrional by the Latins. It faces Boreas, the north wind, and is always open to our view. The other is called Notian and Antarctic by the Greeks, and Meridional and Austral by the Latins; it is always hidden from us and sunk below the horizon. Geminus: of the poles one is called Boreal, the other Notian. So also Proclus and the other Greeks. Thus Aratus: "Indeed two poles appear on either side, one visible to the eyes, the other, far off, beyond the Boreas and the ocean."

units.la: M. Tullius Arati interpres: Extremusque adeo duplici de cardine vertex, Dicitur esse Polus.
units.tr: Tully, translating Aratus: "And the furthest summit, at the double hinge, is called the pole."

units.la: Reliqua desiderantur. Germanicus Cæsar; alius ejus interpres: Geminus determinat Axem, Quem Graï dixere πόλον: pars mersa sub undas Oceani; pars celsa sub horrifero Aquilone.
units.tr: The rest is lost. Germanicus Caesar; another of his interpreters: "Geminus determines the axis, which the Greeks called the pole: one part sunk beneath the waves of the ocean, the other raised high beneath the bristling north wind."

units.la: Accedat his Virgilius lib. 1. Georgic. Hic Vertex nobis semper sublimis, at illum Sub pedibus Styx atra videt, manesque profundi.
units.tr: To these add Virgil, Georgics Book I: "Here the summit is always high above us, but beneath their feet the dark Styx and the depths of the underworld see the other."

units.la: Sub Æquinoctiali sitis ambo Poli, æquabili in Horizonte situ, conspicuntur, ut notant Geminus, Proclus & alij, idem testante nostrorum, qui loca illa navigarunt, fide.
units.tr: Under the equator both poles lie on the horizon at an even level and are seen, as Geminus, Proclus and others note, and as the faith of our own men who have sailed to those places attests.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CHAP. IV.

units.la: De Circulis.
units.tr: On the Circles.

units.la: COELVM, ita circa Axem volubile, solemus imaginari vel Circulis insignitum, vel ijsdem diremtum.
units.tr: The heavens, which turn about an axis, we are accustomed to imagine either marked with circles or divided by them.

units.la: Circulus Macrobio lib. 1. in Somnium Scipionis cap. xv. incorporalis linea, quæ ita mente concipitur, ut sola longitudine censeatur, latum habere non possit. Mathematicis est figura in planicie, quam una includit linea; in cujus medio punctum, a quo omnes lineæ rectæ ad περιφέρειαν ductæ sunt æquales.
units.tr: A circle, according to Macrobius, book 1, on the Dream of Scipio, chapter 15, is an incorporeal line which is conceived in the mind in such a way that it has length only and cannot have breadth. For mathematicians it is a figure in a plane, enclosed by one line; in its middle is a point from which all straight lines drawn to the circumference (περιφέρεια) are equal.

units.la: Circuli hic docendi gratia constituuntur decem, AEquator, Zodiacus, Coluri duo, Horizon, Meridianus, Tropici duo, totidem Polares. de quorum primi, quatuorque postremorum (qui nonnullis ἀπλανεῖς) Adfectibus, quales sunt Ἐπιφάνεια καὶ χρύψις, Μέγεθος, Τάξις, Δύναμις, καὶ Διάστασις, multa generatim apud Geminum, Proclum & alios non contemnenda.
units.tr: For the purposes of teaching, ten circles are set up here: the Equator, the Zodiac, the two Colures, the Horizon, the Meridian, the two Tropics, and as many Polar circles. Concerning the affections of the first and of the last four (which some call ἀπλανεῖς, the fixed circles), such as ἐπιφάνεια and κρύψις, magnitude, order, power and διάστασις (distance), there is much of general interest in Geminus, Proclus and others, not to be despised.

units.la: Decem autem Circulorum, alius est Major, alius Minor. Major qui Mundum in æqualia dispescit segmenta: estque vel Idem ubique, vel Alius alibi. Idem ubique intelligitur secundum Mundi vel Longitudinem, vel Latitudinem. Mundi Longitudo consideratur secundum ejus motum ab Ortu in Occasum, & inde in Ortum. Hic Circulus vel Rectus est vel Obliquus. Rectus is, qui æqualiter Polis interjacet; vocaturque AEquinoctialis,
units.tr: Of the ten circles, one is greater, another lesser. The greater circle is the one which divides the world into equal segments; and it is either the same everywhere or different in different places. The same everywhere is understood in relation either to the longitude or to the latitude of the world. The longitude of the world is considered according to its motion from east to west and back again from west to east. This circle is either straight or oblique. The straight one is that which lies equally between the poles, and it is called the Equinoctial.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAP. V.

units.la: De Æquinoctiali.
units.tr: On the Equinoctial

units.la: ÆQVINOCTIALIS est Circulus major, medio Sphæræ loco inter utrumque Mundi polum collocatus, & ab utroque æquali spacio disterminatus: Zodiacum in duobus punctis intersecans; in quibus quoties Sol concurrit, fit AEquinoctium omnibus terræ locis: unde & illi nomen; dies enim Noctibus adæquat. Græcis ἰσημερινὸς (Æquidialem nominant veteres Latini apud Glosso-graphum & Festum) dicitur, qui Gemino, ὁ μέγιστος τῶν πὰντῃ φαινομένων κύκλων, ὁ διὰ χορημένου τοῦ ὁρίζοντος, ὥστε ἡμικύκλιον μὲν ὑπὸ γῆν δολαμβάνειν; ἡμικύκλιον δὲ ὑπὸ τὸν ὁρίζοντα· ἐφ᾽ ᾧ ἡμέρᾳ ὁ ἥλιος τὰς ἰσημερίας ποιεῖ, τῶν τε ἡμερῶν καὶ τῶν νυκτῶν. Eadem apud Proclum, cujus & hæc: τῶν δὲ παραλλήλων ὁ κύκλος, μέγιστος μὲν ἐστιν ὁ ἰσημερινός. Item: ὁ δὲ ἰσημερινὸς κύκλος καθ᾽ ὅλου τοῦ οἰκουμένου διχοτομεῖται ὑπὸ τοῦ ὁρίζοντος, &c. De eo sic Aratus in Φαινομένοις: Μεσσίδη δ᾽ ἀμφιπίπτων, ἐως ὁ πόλιος γαλακτίης, Γαῖαν ὑποστρέφεται κύκλος, διχάζων ἰσχνῶς. Ἐν δὲ οἱ ἡμαῖς νυξὶν ἰσοίτην ἀμφιπίπτει, Φθινοπώρῳ ἕρει, τὸν δ᾽ ἄρα ἰσημέρια.
units.tr: The Equinoctial is the great circle placed midway between the two poles of the world, equally distant from each, which cuts the Zodiac at two points. Whenever the Sun meets these points, it makes the equinox for all places on earth, and so the circle takes its name, because the day equals the night. The Greeks call it ἰσημερινός [isēmerinos], which the ancient Latins also called Aequidialis, as found in the glossographer and in Festus. Gemino describes it as "the greatest of all the circles that appear, which, with the horizon revolving, cuts the sphere so that half of it is taken below the earth and half above the horizon; on this circle, on the day when the Sun makes the equinoxes, the days and the nights are equal" [ὁ μέγιστος τῶν πάντῃ φαινομένων κύκλων, ὁ διὰ χορημένου τοῦ ὁρίζοντος, ὥστε ἡμικύκλιον μὲν ὑπὸ γῆν δολαμβάνειν; ἡμικύκλιον δὲ ὑπὸ τὸν ὁρίζοντα· ἐφ᾽ ᾧ ἡμέρᾳ ὁ ἥλιος τὰς ἰσημερίας ποιεῖ, τῶν τε ἡμερῶν καὶ τῶν νυκτῶν]. The same is found in Proclus, whose words are also these: "Of the parallel circles, the equinoctial is the greatest" [τῶν δὲ παραλλήλων ὁ κύκλος, μέγιστος μὲν ἐστιν ὁ ἰσημερινός]. Likewise: "The equinoctial circle is bisected throughout the whole inhabited world by the horizon," etc. [ὁ δὲ ἰσημερινὸς κύκλος καθ᾽ ὅλου τοῦ οἰκουμένου διχοτομεῖται ὑπὸ τοῦ ὁρίζοντος, &c.]. Aratus speaks of it in the Phaenomena: "It falls around the middle of the sky, where the milky way turns, the circle that divides the earth, cutting it finely. And when the nights are equal to the days, it falls around the autumn season, and in spring, and there it makes the equinox" [Μεσσίδη δ᾽ ἀμφιπίπτων, ἐως ὁ πόλιος γαλακτίης, Γαῖαν ὑποστρέφεται κύκλος, διχάζων ἰσχνῶς. Ἐν δὲ οἱ ἡμαῖς νυξὶν ἰσοίτην ἀμφιπίπτει, Φθινοπώρῳ ἕρει, τὸν δ᾽ ἄρα ἰσημέρια].

units.la: Describit hunc Circulum Sol, quum occupat alterutrum Æquinoctij punctum, & diurno motu sub capitibus Arietis & Libræ revolvitur.
units.tr: The Sun describes this circle when it occupies one or other of the points of the equinox, and it is carried round by its daily motion beneath the heads of Aries and Libra.

units.la: Visus ab illo numerantur multigeneres; quorum principes:
units.tr: Several uses of this circle are counted; the principal ones are these:

units.la: I. Quod Æquinoctia distinguat: unum, quod verno, unde Vernum Latinis, Græcis ἰσημερία ἐαρινή: ut & Punctum, in quo fit, cœleste, Græcis τροπικὸν ἰσημερινὸν ἐαρινόν, Latinis Punctum Æquinoctij verni: alterum, quod autumnali fit tempore; Græci vocant ἰσημερία μετοπωρινή, Latini Æquinoctium Autumnale: Punctum autem ejus cœleste, hi ab Æquinoctio indigetant Autumnali, illi μετοπωρινὸν τροπικόν, appellant: illud quidem, Sole principium Arietis v. Eidus Martij; hoc autem Librae initium occupante, xvii. Kal. Sept. solet contingere, aut circiter: eodem enim movere paullatim singulis annis, doctum ab aliis.
units.tr: I. It distinguishes the equinoxes. One is the vernal equinox, so called by the Latins from ver (spring), and by the Greeks ἰσημερία ἐαρινή; and the point in the heavens where it occurs is called by the Greeks τροπικὸν ἰσημερινὸν ἐαρινόν, and by the Latins the point of the vernal equinox. The other occurs in autumn; the Greeks call it ἰσημερία μετοπωρινή, and the Latins the autumnal equinox. Its point in the heavens, some call the autumnal equinoctial point, others μετοπωρινὸν τροπικόν. The former usually falls when the Sun occupies the beginning of Aries, about the Ides of March; the latter when it occupies the beginning of Libra, about the seventeenth day before the Kalends of September. For these points gradually move backward each year, as others have taught.

units.la: II. Quod mensura sit Primi Mobilis. Nam quum cccix. sint illi partes; earum quindenæ singulis horis emergunt, occultantur autem totidem; totusque Æquator xxiv. horarum curriculo convertitur: quum autem æqualiter undiquaque disjunctus sit ab Mundi Polis; non dubium, quin & Primum Mobile eadem lege, eodem motu, eodem temporis spatio circumferatur.
units.tr: II. It is the measure of the Primum Mobile. For since the circle has 360 degrees, fifteen of these rise every hour and as many set; and the whole equator turns in the course of twenty-four hours. Since it is equally distant on every side from the poles of the world, there is no doubt that the Primum Mobile is also carried round by the same law, with the same motion, in the same space of time.

units.la: III. Quod regula sit Adscensionum rectarum & obliquarum; dirigens, velut Canon, ἀσυμμαλία Motus Zodiaci: cujus Signa nunc tardius nunc citius efferunt se propter obliquitatem Circuli; partibus Æquatoris una & eadem lege se vel evehentibus, vel occulentibus.
units.tr: III. It is the rule of right and oblique ascensions. Like a canon, it governs the irregularity of the motion of the Zodiac, whose signs rise now more slowly, now more quickly, on account of the obliquity of the circle, while the parts of the equator, by one and the same law, either rise or set.

units.la: IV. Quod Dierum tam Artificialium quam Naturalium diffiniat spacia. Licet enim Sol non solum quadripartitas Anni vicissitudines, sed etiam gratissimas Dierum Noctiumque vices efficiat: tamen, quum ingens sit in ejus motu ἀσυμμαλία, ut inde diurna nocturnaque spacia non facile quis colligat, partesque Zodiaci inæqualiter exsurgant, omnibus autem Æquatoris partibus idem sit motus, fit, ut Dies Horasque distinguat non Zodiacus, sed Æquator; cujus ab hac constanti lege Partes, χρόνοι Græcis vocantur, id est Tempora. Nam quindenæ Æquatoris partes, ut dixi, horam unam emersu suo; singulæ partes quatuor horæ scrupula; singulorum denique quadrantes unum horæ signant scrupulum.
units.tr: IV. It defines the spans of days, both artificial and natural. For although the Sun not only brings about the four changing seasons of the year but also the most welcome alternations of days and nights, nevertheless, since its motion is greatly irregular, so that one cannot easily work out from it the lengths of day and night, and since the parts of the Zodiac rise unequally while all the parts of the equator have the same motion, it follows that it is not the Zodiac but the equator that distinguishes days and hours. Its parts, which by this constant law are called χρόνοι (chronoi), that is, times, are measured accordingly. For fifteen parts of the equator, as I said, mark one hour by their rising; each part marks four minutes of an hour; and finally a quarter of each of these marks one second of an hour.

units.la: V. Quod ab hoc Circulo non solum declinatio partium Ecliptice (quæ λέξεως & ἐγκλίσεως Ptolemæo) sed & Stellarum declinationes (quæ nihil aliud quam illarum distantiæ ab Æquatore versus alterutrum Mundi Polorum) Locorumq; latitudine (id est intervalla ab Æquatore ad eorunde vertices in Meridiano collecta) numerantur.
units.tr: V. From this circle are counted not only the declination of the parts of the ecliptic (which Ptolemy calls lexis and enklisis) but also the declinations of the stars (which are nothing other than their distances from the equator towards either pole of the world) and the latitudes of places (that is, the intervals from the equator to their zeniths, gathered on the meridian).

units.la: VI. Quod consideret & metiatur longitudinem totius Terræ & locorum particularium in diversis Terræ partibus.
units.tr: VI. It considers and measures the longitude of the whole earth and of particular places in the different parts of the earth.

units.la: VII. Postremo, quod hic Circulus pervestigare doceat duodecim Cœli Domicilia, quum Themata ad prognostica Astrologica conformantur.
units.tr: VII. Lastly, this circle teaches how to investigate the twelve houses of the heavens, when the themes for astrological predictions are drawn up.

units.la: CAP. VI. De Zodiaco.
units.tr: CAP. VI. On the Zodiac.

units.la: ITA se habet Circulus Major, qui idem ubique secundum Mundi Longitudinem, Rectus: sequitur obliquus, quem Zodiacum vocant.
units.tr: Such is the Major Circle, which is everywhere the same according to the longitude of the world and straight. Following it is the oblique circle, which they call the Zodiac.

units.la: Zodiacus Circulus est major & obliquus, solus latitudine præditus, ubique idem, xii. ferens signa, sib quo Planetæ perpetuo decurrunt motu. Latini, M. Tullius, Ovidius, Lucianus, Plinius, Macrobius, Festus Avienus & alij Signiferum Orbem appellant. Dictus ζῳδίων, ab Signis; quæ hic ex Stellis in Animalium effigies efformata. Pollux lib. IV. ζῷα τὰ ἐν κύκλῳ, ἃ οἱ πλεῖ ζῳδία καλοῦσιν: ἀφ᾽ ὧν ὁ ζῳδιακὸς κύκλος. Aristoteles de Mundo, loquens de Zodiaco, ᾧ μέρος, inquit διηρημένος εἰς δώδεκα ζῳδίων χώρας. Alij ἀπὸ τῆς ζωῆς sic appellatum volunt, quod secundum Planetarum motum sub illo, rebus omnibus, DEO sic ordinante, vita: ut non immerito, quod ab eo Ortus Interitusque præcipuæ causæ defluant, Arx Mundi Manilio nominetur lib. I. Astronomic. E quibus & ratio fatorum ducitur omnis: Vt sit idem Mundi principium quod continet Arcem.
units.tr: The Zodiac is a major and oblique circle, alone endowed with latitude, everywhere the same, bearing twelve signs, along which the planets run with perpetual motion. The Latins, M. Tullius, Ovid, Lucian, Pliny, Macrobius, Festus Avienus and others call it the Signifer Orb. It is named zōdiōn [ζῳδίων] from the signs, which here are formed from the stars into the figures of animals. Pollux, book IV: "the animals in a circle, which most call zōdia; from these the zodiac circle" [ζῷα τὰ ἐν κύκλῳ, ἃ οἱ πλεῖστοι ζῳδία καλοῦσιν: ἀφ᾽ ὧν ὁ ζῳδιακὸς κύκλος]. Aristotle, in On the World, speaking of the Zodiac, says it is "divided into twelve regions of animals" [διηρημένος εἰς δώδεκα ζῳδίων χώρας]. Others want it so named from life [ζωῆς], because under it, according to the motion of the planets, life is given to all things, God so ordaining. Hence, not undeservedly, since the chief causes of birth and death flow from it, Manilius calls it the Citadel of the World in book I of his Astronomica: "From it too the whole reason of the fates is drawn, so that the same is the beginning of the world which holds the citadel."

units.la: Notus eidem ab appellatione Cæli Flammarum: Hinc vicina Polis, hinc Cæli proxima Flammis.
units.tr: It is also known by the name Sky of Flames: "Hence the neighbouring Pole, hence the sky nearest the flames."

units.la: Quid ni? quum sub ejus medio ζωὴ sit ἐκπυρωμένη; imo quum, ut simplicius loquar, per eum feratur Sol.
units.tr: Why not? Since under its middle lies the fiery life [ζωὴ ἐκπυρωμένη]; indeed, to speak more simply, the Sun is carried through it.

units.la: Zodiacus Arabibus Almantica seu Nitac. Auctor Alcabitzij: Mantica est circulus, qui latus est in medio & in ligatura strictus: & habet significare Circulum Zodiaci.
units.tr: The Arabs call the Zodiac Almantica or Nitac. The author of Alcabitius writes: "Mantica is a circle which is broad in the middle and narrow in the binding, and it has the meaning of the circle of the Zodiac."

units.la: Geminus sic definit: ζῳδιακὸς λοξὸς ἐπὶ κύκλῳ, ὁ τ ιβ. Ζῳδίων: ὥσπερ ἡ ἐκ ἡμέρων κύκλων συνίστηκεν; & quæ sequuntur. Similia apud Proclum, ejus ad litteram excriptorem. Aratus ζωδίων κύκλος vocat. Sic M. Tullius ejus interpres: Zodiacum hunc Græci vocitant, nostrique Latini Orbem signiferum perhibebunt nomine vero: Nam gerit hic volvens bis sex ardentia signa.
units.tr: Geminus defines it thus: the zodiac is an oblique circle on the circle of the twelve signs, just as it is composed of the [...] circles; and what follows. Similar things are found in Proclus, who copied him word for word. Aratus calls it the circle of the signs [ζωδίων κύκλος]. So M. Tullius, his translator: "The Greeks call this the Zodiac, and we Latins will name it the Signifer Orb: for it carries, turning, twice six burning signs."

units.la: Eleganter Seneca in Thyeste, Act. IIII. Choro: Hic qui Sacris pervius Astris, Secat obliquo tramite Zonas, Flectens longos Signifer annos, Lapsa videbit sidera labens.
units.tr: Seneca elegantly, in the Thyestes, Act IV, in the chorus: "He who, open to the sacred stars, cuts the zones by an oblique path, bending the long years as bearer of the signs, will see the sliding stars slipping away."

units.la: Dixi Obliquum, ab obliquo ejus situ. Quemadmodum enim Æquinoctialis æqualiter Mundi Polis interjacet; sic Zodiacus inæqualiter & oblique, cum Sphæræ Mundi, tum Æquatori obductus; hic a Polis disiunctior, ibi propior. Virgil. I. Georgic. —& via secta per ambas Obliquus qua se Signorum verteret ordo.
units.tr: I have called it oblique, from its oblique position. For as the Equinoctial lies equally between the poles of the world, so the Zodiac, unequally and obliquely, is laid across both the sphere of the world and the Equator: here it is farther from the poles, there nearer. Virgil, Georgics I: "...and the path cut through both, where the oblique order of the signs turns."

units.la: Ovidius lib. II. Metamorph. Secta in obliquum est lato curvamine limes.
units.tr: Ovid, Metamorphoses II: "The path is cut obliquely with a broad curve."

units.la: Manilius lib. I. Astronomic. Inflexum scribit Orbem: Sic per tres gyros inflexus ducitur Orbis.
units.tr: Manilius, Astronomica I, writes of the inflected orb: "Thus the orb is led, inflected through three turns."

units.la: Λοξὸς κύκλος cum Aristotele & Ptolemæo vocant Græci, διὰ τὸ λοξῶς πέμπειν τὰς ἀπολάμψεις, inquit Geminus, & ex eo Proclus apud quem tamen vox λοξῶς periit. Hanc Obliquitatem primus deprehendit Pythagoras, licet sibi laudem illam Chius Oenopides adscribere conetur, ut testatur Ioannes Stobæus. Φύσ.
units.tr: The Greeks, with Aristotle and Ptolemy, call it the oblique circle [λοξὸς κύκλος], "because it sends its reflections obliquely" [διὰ τὸ λοξῶς πέμπειν τὰς ἀπολάμψεις], says Geminus, and after him Proclus, in whom however the word λοξῶς has been lost. Pythagoras first detected this obliquity, although Oenopides of Chios tries to claim that praise for himself, as John Stobaeus testifies in his Physics.

units.la: Latitudinem autem solus habet hic Circulus, (quum reliqui simplici perimetro circumscribantur) ut latiore spatio Planetas oberrantes ultra citraq; complecteretur, ne limitibus præstitutis excederent. Nam secundum Ὣς τ πλανήτων παρόδους est definitus. Macrobius lib. I. Somnium Scipion. cap. XV. ubi de decem Circis, quorum unus est ipse Zodiacus, qui ex his decem solus potuit latitudinem hoc modo, quem referemus, adipisci. Et quæ ibi alia. Veteres ab Solis itinere, quod in medio collocabant, ut dicam, Zodiaco Latitudinem hujus Circuli æstimabant, datis illi utrimq; sex gradibus. τὸ δὲ πλάτος, ait Geminus, ὡς ἐκ ζῳδιακῆς κύκλου μοιρῶν ιβ. ut & Proclus, aliique. Recentiores binos utrinq; adjecerunt ob majores Martis & Veneris, quam aliorum, ab Sole digressiones: ut Zodiaci hodie Latitudo concludatur XVI. gradibus, id est, octo utrimque ab medio Solis Circulo Zodiaci polos versus exporrigatur. Nam quanta Vagantium maxima in utramque partem ἀπόκλισις vel Declinatio, tanta ejus Latitudo ponenda.
units.tr: This circle alone has latitude, whereas the others are bounded by a simple perimeter, so that by a wider space it might embrace the wandering planets on either side and they might not exceed their fixed limits. For it is defined by the passages of the planets [τὰς τῶν πλανήτων παρόδους]. Macrobius, Commentary on Scipio's Dream, book I, ch. 15, where he speaks of the ten circles: "of which one is the Zodiac itself, which alone of these ten could acquire latitude in the manner we shall relate." And there are other things there. The ancients, from the Sun's course, which they placed in the middle, as I shall say, reckoned the latitude of this circle, assigning it six degrees on each side. "The latitude," says Geminus, "is twelve degrees of the zodiac circle" [τὸ δὲ πλάτος ὡς ἐκ ζῳδιακοῦ κύκλου μοιρῶν ιβ'], as also Proclus and others. More recent writers added two on each side, on account of the greater departures of Mars and Venus from the Sun than of the others; so that today the latitude of the Zodiac is set at sixteen degrees, that is, it extends eight degrees on each side of the Sun's circle toward the poles. For as great as the greatest deviation or declination of the wanderers in either direction, so great must its latitude be set.

units.la: Longitudinis Zodiaci Principiū, quamvis in Circulo non videbatur posse, ut nec Finis designari; statui tamen solet a plerisq; in Puncto Æquinoctij Verni; a quo multis populis Anni quondam initium, sequutis Motus Solis, ejusque tunc temporis Effectiones. Totum Zodiacum secare solemus in xii. Signa, duce Luna, quæ quotannis Zodiaco tredecies peragrato, Soli tardius procedenti duodecies & in xii. Cœli locis conjungitur. De his Signis in Stellarum dicam historia.
units.tr: Although the beginning of the Zodiac's longitude could not seem to be marked in a circle, any more than its end, it is commonly fixed by most at the point of the Vernal Equinox; from which, long ago, many peoples began their year, following the motion of the Sun and its effects at that time. We are accustomed to divide the whole Zodiac into twelve signs, the Moon leading the way; for the Moon, traversing the Zodiac thirteen times a year, is conjoined with the Sun, which moves more slowly, twelve times, in the twelve places of the heavens. I shall speak of these signs in the history of the stars.

units.la: Medium Zodiacum dispescit orbita Solis, quæ Græcis inde ἡ διὰ μέσων κύκλος: Proclemæo, Gemino, Proclo, aliisque κύκλος διὰ μέσων τῶν ζῳδίων; Via Solis, Latinis, Macrobio & aliis Ecliptica; quod, quum in eo φωστῆρες conjungantur, Sol nobis obfuscetur; quum inter se opponantur, Luna deficiat. Dignus ille, qui ex Commentario in Somnium Scipionis, hæc de re verba faciens, audiatur: In Zodiaco Latitudinem signorum capacitas exigebat: quantum igitur spacij lata dimensio porrectis sideribus occupabat, duabus lineis limitatum est: & tertia ducta per Medium (διὰ μέσων τῶν ζῳδίων, inquiunt Græci) Ecliptica vocatur; quia quum Cursum suum in eadem Linea pariter Sol & Luna conficiunt, alterius eorum necesse est evenire defectum; Solis, si ei tunc Luna succedat: Lunæ, si tunc adversa sit Sol: ideo nec Sol umquam deficit, nisi, quum tricesimus Luna dies est; & nisi quintodecimo Cursus sui die, nec sit Luna defectum: sic enim evenit, ut aut Lunæ contra Solem posita ad mutuandum ab ec solitum lumen sub eadem inventur linea Terræ conus obsistat; aut Solis ipsa succedens objectu suo ab humano aspectu Lumen ejus repellat, &c. Est igitur Ecliptica Circulus major, in medio consistens Zodiaco, eumque secundum Latitudinem partiens in duos æquales ambitus, octo graduum spacio distinctos; quem motu suo, qui annuus, Sol, in uno tramite perpetuo incedens, efformat; in quatuor distinctum quadrantes ab quatuor Punctis Cardinalibus: quorum duo Æquinoctialia Latinis, ἰσημερινά Græcis, de quibus paullo ante dictum; totidem Solstitialia nobis, illis τροπικά dicuntur; quorum quod in ἡμικυκλίῳ Septemtrionali ἡλιοστάσιον, id est, Solstitij Æstivi punctum, quod ex opposito χειμερινόν, hoc est, Brumale, vocatur. Et hæc, ut illa, quemadmodum cap. v. dixi, suas mutasse sedes ostendunt magni viri. Ecliptica vero, ne usus ignoretur, docet exactissime Tempora, quibus Stellæ non solum Errantes, sed & Inerrantes, sint vel Septemtrionales, vel etiam Meridionales, oriantur & occidant.
units.tr: The orbit of the Sun divides the middle of the Zodiac. From this the Greeks call it he dia mesōn kyklos [ἡ διὰ μέσων κύκλος]; Ptolemy, Geminus, Proclus and others call it kyklos dia mesōn tōn zōdiōn [κύκλος διὰ μέσων τῶν ζῳδίων]; the Latins, Macrobius and others, call it the Via Solis or Ecliptic, because, when the luminaries [φωστῆρες] are conjoined in it, the Sun is obscured for us, and when they are opposed to each other, the Moon is eclipsed. Worth hearing is he who, in a commentary on the Dream of Scipio, speaks on this matter: "In the Zodiac the capacity demanded the latitude of the signs. So the space occupied by the stars when they are spread out in that broad extent has been bounded by two lines, and a third line drawn through the middle (dia mesōn tōn zōdiōn, the Greeks say) is called the Ecliptic; because, since the Sun and the Moon complete their course along that same line together, one of them must suffer an eclipse: the Sun's, if the Moon then comes in front of it; the Moon's, if the Sun is then opposite. Therefore the Sun never fails except on the thirtieth day of the Moon, nor does the Moon fail except on the fifteenth day of its course. For it happens that either the Moon, placed against the Sun, which it is accustomed to borrow light from, is found under the same line, and the cone of the Earth stands in the way; or the Sun, coming in front, by its interposition repels its light from human sight, etc." Therefore the Ecliptic is the great circle, lying in the middle of the Zodiac and dividing it by latitude into two equal circuits, distinguished by a space of eight degrees. The Sun, moving along it in one unbroken path in its yearly motion, traces it out; it is divided into four quadrants by four cardinal points. Two of these are called the Equinoctial points by the Latins [ἰσημερινά by the Greeks], of which we spoke a little earlier; as many are the Solstitial points for us, called tropika by them. Of these, the one in the northern hemisphere is the ēliostasion [ἡλιοστάσιον], that is, the point of the summer solstice; the one opposite is called cheimerinon [χειμερινόν], that is, the winter point. And these, as I said in chapter v, show that great men have changed their places. The Ecliptic, moreover, so that its use may not be unknown, teaches most exactly the times at which the stars, not only the wandering ones but also the fixed ones, whether northern or southern, rise and set.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CHAP. VII.

units.la: De Coluris.
units.tr: On the Colures.

units.la: HÆC de Circulis Majoribus, qui Idem ubique secundum Mundi Longitudinem: succedunt explicandi, qui ejusdem naturæ, sed secundum Mundi Latitudinem. Tales sunt Coluri, qui in Polis ad Angulos rectos se mutuo bisecant. Zodiacum autem, vel potius Ecipticam, quadripartiuntur in Æquinoctiorum Solstitiorumque Punctis, pro quadripartita Anni vicissitudine. Nomen ijs ab Imperfectione: quod revera sint mutili; nam eorum ἡμισφαίρια tantum κίκλοι, non κολοβοί; sed quia ea parte, qua nobis inutiles sunt, quasi mutili censeantur: alioquin & ἡμίσφαιρα illorum utilia sunt illis, qui ultra Capricornum habitant; ut quæ nobis utilia sunt, illis ea κάλυκα. Geminus: Κολούροι ἢ κύκλοι διὰ τὸ μέρη ἴσα αὐτῶν ἀφωρίσθαι γίνεσθαι. Eadem apud Proclum, qui tamen, agens de κολούροις, κολουρόπους est & corruptior, supplendus & emendandus ex eo, quem solitus exscribere. Sic Macrobius lib. i. in Som. Scrip. cap. xv. Præter hos, inquit, alij duo sunt (Circi) Coluri, quibus nomen dedit imperfecta Conversio. ambientes enim Septemtrionalem verticem; atque inde in diversa diffusi, & se in summo interse-cant, & quinque Parallelos in quaternas partes æqualiter dividunt: Zodiacum ita intersecantes; ut unus eorum per Arietem & Libram, alter per Cancrum atque Capricornum meando decurrat: sed ad Australem verticem non pervenire creduntur. Manilius lib. i. AstronomSunt duo quos recipit ductos a Vertice Vertex, Inter se adversi, qui cunctos ante-velatos, Seque secant, gemino coëuntes cardine Mundi; Transversoque polo rectum ducuntur in Axem; Tempora signantes anni, Cælumque per astra, Quatuor in partes divisum mensibus æquis.
units.tr: So much for the Greater Circles, which are the same everywhere according to the longitude of the world. Next I shall explain those of the same nature, but according to the latitude of the world. Such are the Colures, which meet at the Poles at right angles and bisect one another. The Zodiac, or rather the Ecliptic, they divide into four parts at the points of the Equinoxes and Solstices, in keeping with the four-part turning of the year. They are named from their imperfection, because they are in truth mutilated. Their hemispheres are only circles [ἡμισφαίρια, κίκλοι], not curtailed [κολοβοί]. They are called mutilated because, in the part where they are useless to us, they are regarded as incomplete. Otherwise their hemispheres are useful to those who live beyond the Tropic of Capricorn, just as what is useful to us they call [κάλυκα] for themselves. Geminus: "The Colures, or circles, are so called because equal parts of them are cut off" [Κολούροι ἢ κύκλοι διὰ τὸ μέρη ἴσα αὐτῶν ἀφωρίσθαι γίνεσθαι]. The same is found in Proclus, who however, treating of the colures, uses [κολουρόπους] and is more corrupt; he must be supplied and emended from the author he is accustomed to copy. Thus Macrobius, in book i of his commentary on the Dream of Scipio, chapter xv: "Besides these, he says, there are two other circles, the Colures, to which the imperfect revolution gave its name. For they encircle the northern pole, and, spreading out from there in different directions, they intersect at the summit and divide the five parallels equally into four parts each, cutting the Zodiac so that one of them runs through Aries and Libra, the other through Cancer and Capricorn. But they are not believed to reach the southern pole." Manilius, book i of the Astronomica: "There are two which the pole receives, drawn from the pole, opposite one another, which veil all the rest and cut across one another, meeting at the twin hinge of the world; and they are drawn at right angles to the axis through the transverse pole, marking the seasons of the year and the heaven through the stars, divided into four parts of equal months."

units.la: Reliqua ab docto poëta petenda.
units.tr: The rest is to be sought from the learned poet.

units.la: Sunt igitur Coluri duo: Æquinoctialis & Solstitialis. Ille, qui ductus per Mundi seu Æquatoris Polos & Puncta Æquinoctialia (principia scilicet Arietis & Libræ) cum Æquatore quidem angulos rectos (sphæricos) cum Zodiaco vero obliquos constituit: Hic, qui per Puncta Solstitialia (principia nimirum Cancri & Capricorni) & Polos Zodiaci atq. Æquatoris ductus, angulos format rectos sphæricos. Prior, ut usum aperiam, Æquinoctiorum, Verni & Autumnalis, puncta discernit: Solstitiorum vero, Æstivi & Brumalis, posterior; cujus & alia duo propria; prius quidem maximam Solis notare Declinationem, quæ est arcus hujus Circuli, principio Cancri & Æquatori inclusus; deinde fungi nonnunquam vice Meridiani. Succedit enim in qualibet diurna revolutione primi Cœli bis in locum Meridiani.
units.tr: There are therefore two Colures: the Equinoctial and the Solstitial. The former, drawn through the Poles of the world or of the Equator and through the Equinoctial points (namely the beginnings of Aries and Libra), forms right angles (spherical) with the Equator but oblique angles with the Zodiac. The latter, drawn through the Solstitial points (namely the beginnings of Cancer and Capricorn) and through the Poles of the Zodiac and of the Equator, forms right spherical angles. The former, to explain its use, distinguishes the points of the Equinoxes, spring and autumn; the latter distinguishes the points of the Solstices, summer and winter. The latter also has two other properties of its own: first, it marks the greatest declination of the Sun, which is the arc of this circle enclosed between the beginning of Cancer and the Equator; second, it sometimes serves in place of the meridian. For in each daily revolution of the first heaven it comes twice into the position of the meridian.

units.la: CAP. VIII. De Horizonte.
units.tr: CAP. VIII. De Horizonte.

units.la: DIXI de Circulis Majoribus, qui Idem ubique; postulor, ut exponam eos, qui Alij alibi. Sunt autem illi: Horizon & Meridianus. Græci: οἱ μεσημβρινοὶ καὶ οἱ ὁρίζοντες διαφοροί εἰσιν, ἡ ἀλλοι πρὸς ἄλλας· ἡ γὰρ καθ' αὑτὰς εἰσιν, ὥσπερ ἱστμένος· ἀλλὰ πρὸς τὰς εἰκήσεις. Circulos hos plerique conjunctim explicant, quû alter sine altero esse nequit. Omnis Horizon Meridianum suum recte secat; Poli omnis Horizontis sunt Puncta Orientis & Occidentis; Mundi sunt Poli omnium Meridianorum; ita omnis Horizon per Puncta Ortus & Occasus transit ut omnis Meridianus per Polos Mundi. Verba sunt Viri magni ad magnum Poëtam.
units.tr: I have spoken of the Great Circles, which are the same everywhere; now I am asked to explain those which differ from place to place. These are the Horizon and Meridian. The Greeks say that the meridians and the horizons differ, not in themselves, but in relation to one another; for they are not fixed in themselves, as one might suppose, but are relative to places [οἱ μεσημβρινοὶ καὶ οἱ ὁρίζοντες διαφοροί εἰσιν, ἡ ἀλλοι πρὸς ἄλλας· ἡ γὰρ καθ' αὑτὰς εἰσιν, ὥσπερ ἱστμένος· ἀλλὰ πρὸς τὰς εἰκήσεις]. Most writers explain these circles together, since neither can exist without the other. Every horizon cuts its own meridian at right angles; the poles of every horizon are the points of east and west; the poles of the world are the poles of all the meridians; and so every horizon passes through the points of rising and setting, just as every meridian passes through the poles of the world. These are the words of a great man, addressed to a great poet.

units.la: Horizon igitur Circulus est Major, non Idem ubique, sed cuilibet loco proprius, qui totam Mundi Sphæram in æqualia duo dispertit hemisphæria; quorum hoc Superum, illud Inferum. Geminus & ex eo Proclus: ὁ ὁρίζων, inquit, ἐστι κύκλος, ὁ διορίζων ἡμῖν τὸν φαινόμενον καὶ τὸ ἀφανὲς μέρος ἐκ κόσμου· καὶ διχοτομῶν τὸν ὅλον σφαῖραν ἐκ κόσμου, ὥστε ἡμισφαίριον μὲν ὑπὲρ τὴν γῆν δυσλαμψαλιπόν, ἡμισφαίριον δὲ ὑπὸ γῆ. Sic Leontius de Sphæra: ὁ ὁρίζων ὁ ἡμῶν τὴν ὑπὲρ γῆν ἡμισφαίριον, καὶ τὸ ὑπὸ γῆ.
units.tr: The horizon, then, is a Great Circle, not the same everywhere but proper to each place, which divides the whole sphere of the world into two equal hemispheres, the upper one and the lower one. Proclus, in agreement with Geminus, says: "The horizon is the circle which separates for us the visible part of the world from the invisible, and which cuts the whole sphere of the world in half, so that one hemisphere lies above the earth and the other beneath it" [ὁ ὁρίζων, inquit, ἐστι κύκλος, ὁ διορίζων ἡμῖν τὸν φαινόμενον καὶ τὸ ἀφανὲς μέρος ἐκ κόσμου· καὶ διχοτομῶν τὸν ὅλον σφαῖραν ἐκ κόσμου, ὥστε ἡμισφαίριον μὲν ὑπὲρ τὴν γῆν δυσλαμψαλιπόν, ἡμισφαίριον δὲ ὑπὸ γῆ]. Leontius likewise says in On the Sphere: "The horizon is that which divides for us the hemisphere above the earth from that below the earth" [ὁ ὁρίζων ὁ ἡμῶν τὴν ὑπὲρ γῆν ἡμισφαίριον, καὶ τὸ ὑπὸ γῆ].

units.la: Horizontis duplex est divisio: priorem Astronomorum Schola mutuavit ab varia Polorum elevatione; vel, ut cum Macrobio loquar, lib. 1. in Somn. Scipionis cap.xv. ab diversitate circumspicientis habitantisque. Estque hic vel Rectus vel Obliquus.
units.tr: The horizon is divided in two ways. The Schools of the Astronomers have taken the first division from the varying elevation of the poles; or, to use the words of Macrobius (Book 1 on the Dream of Scipio, ch. 15), from the difference of the place of the observer and the one looking around. It is either Right or Oblique.

units.la: Rectus, qui utrumque Mundi Polum suo plano attingit: Obliquus ab cujus plano Poli distant; alter elevatus, alter depressus. Ille unus tantum est, & cum Æquatore rectos constituit angulos, proprius Locorum, Asiæ, Africæ, Americæ: quæ Æquatori subjacent: Hic multifarie mutat, Terræ situ vertius Mundi Polos mutante, Locorum peculiaris AEquatori non subjacentium. Cuilibet enim suus est Horizon, qui, quanto Polorum alter altius elevatur, tanto est obliquior. De hac varietate M. Tullius lib. 11. de Divinatione: Quum illi orbes, inquit, qui Cœlum quasi medium dividunt, & adspectum nostrum diffiniunt, qui ab Græcis ὁρίζοντες nominantur, a nobis Finientes rectissime nominari possunt, varietatem maximam habeant, atque in aliis locis sint; necesse est ortus occasusque Siderum non fieri eodem tempore apud omnes. Obliquum autem vocant, quod cum Æquatore obliquos conformet angulos.
units.tr: The Right horizon is the one which touches both poles of the world in its plane. The Oblique horizon is the one from whose plane the poles are distant, one elevated and the other depressed. The right horizon is only one, and it makes right angles with the Equator. It belongs to places lying under the Equator, in Asia, Africa and America. The oblique horizon changes in many ways, since the position of the earth changes the poles of the world; it belongs to particular places not lying under the Equator. Every place has its own horizon, which is the more oblique the higher one pole is raised above the other. Marcus Tullius speaks of this variety in Book 2 of On Divination: "Since those circles which divide the heavens as it were in the middle, and define our view, and which are called horizons by the Greeks, may most correctly be called by us 'bounding circles', and since they have the greatest variety and differ in different places, it is necessary that the rising and setting of the stars do not happen at the same time for all. But they call it oblique, because it makes oblique angles with the Equator."

units.la: Alteram Horizontis distributionem petierunt Astronomi ab Hominis sensu & ratione; dixeruntque Sensibilem & Rationalem. Ille Terræ spacium est, rotundo diffinitum ambitu, quod cum plano & patenti campo oculorum acies, non læsa, non vitiata, non ab interjectu montium altiorumque locorum intercisa, circumscribit: proprie appellationem Horizontis sibi vindicans. ὁρίζων enim Græcis ὁρίζειν, quod visum finiat ac terminet. De eo Geminus, & exscriptor ejus Proclus: Hujus semidiametro Macrobius tribuit centum & octoginta stadia. Sic enim ait lib. 1. in Somnium Scipionis, cap. xv. Hinc Horizon, quem sibi uniuscujusque circumscribit adspectus, ultra trecentos & sexaginta stadios longitudinem in se continere non poterit. Centum enim & octoginta stadios non excedit acies contra-videntis: sed visus, quum ad hoc spacium venerit, necessu deficiens in rotunditatem recurrendo curvatur; &c.
