Geminus & Proclus, quum scribunt hunc Circulum ἀ μείζονα τῷ διάμετρον ἔχειν σταδίων διχιλίων, non habere Diametrum majorem stadiis c10 c10. exaudiendi sunt de Horizonte, non cujus terminus ab Oculorum constituitur acie, sed qui sensibilem finit Coelestium Apparentiarum secundum longitudinem & latitudinem varietatem. Rationalis Horizon (quem & Artificialem nonnulli vocant, quod artis Astronomicæ beneficio fit inventus) est Cœli spacium, rotundo, ut Sensibilis, ambitu distinctum; quod mens colligit ratiocinando, unde nomen. Convexo globi terreni incumbens, circumquaque ad extremum usque Cœlum pertingit: orbeisque Cœlestes Mundo ἐμοιοίσεως in æqualia dirimit hemisphæria, unum supra, alterum infra nos. Geminus & Proclus: λογῳ ἐκρηπτῆς ἀρίζων, inquiunt, ἐαν, ὁ μέσος τῶν ἀπλανῶν ἀστρων σφαίρας διχῶν, καὶ διχοτομῶν τ' ὅλον κόσμον. Hunc Meridianus ex alto demissus in duo partitur ἡμικύκλια; quorum quod ad Orientem Græcis ἐξ ἀνατολῆς ἀρίζων εἰς ἀνατολᾶς, quod ex adverso εἰς δυσμάς dicitur: hic Occidentis apud Latinos, ille Orientis Cardo. Utrumque ἡμικύκλιον varie rursum disparat Sol Oriens Occidensque; quæ plenius apud alios.
units.tr: The astronomers have taken another division of the horizon from man's sense and reason, and they have called it Sensible and Rational. The sensible horizon is the stretch of the earth bounded by a round circuit, which the sight of the eyes, unimpaired, unclouded, and not cut off by intervening mountains or higher places, encloses within a plane and open field. It rightly claims for itself the name of horizon, for the Greek horizon comes from horizein, to limit or bound what is seen. Geminus, and Proclus who copied him, speak of this horizon. Macrobius gives its radius as one hundred and eighty stadia. For he says in Book 1 on the Dream of Scipio, ch. 15: "Hence the horizon which each person's sight encloses around himself cannot contain within itself a length greater than three hundred and sixty stadia. For the sight of one looking forward does not exceed one hundred and eighty stadia; but when the sight has reached this distance, it necessarily fails and, bending back as it were into roundness, is curved; etc." When Geminus and Proclus write that this circle does not have a diameter greater than two thousand stadia [ἀ μείζονα τῷ διάμετρον ἔχειν σταδίων διχιλίων], they must be understood to mean the sensible horizon, not the one whose limit is set by the sight of the eyes, but the one which bounds the variation of the heavenly appearances in longitude and latitude. The Rational horizon (which some also call the Artificial, because it was discovered by the aid of the astronomical art) is a region of the heavens marked off by a round circuit, like the Sensible one; it is grasped by the mind through reasoning, and hence its name. Resting on the convex surface of the terrestrial globe, it reaches on every side to the furthest heaven, and it divides the celestial orbs of the world into two equal hemispheres, one above us and the other below us. Geminus and Proclus say: "The rational horizon is the circle which divides the sphere of the fixed stars in two, and cuts the whole world in half" [λογῳ ἐκρηπτῆς ἀρίζων, inquiunt, ἐαν, ὁ μέσος τῶν ἀπλανῶν ἀστρων σφαίρας διχῶν, καὶ διχοτομῶν τ' ὅλον κόσμον]. The meridian, let down from the top, divides this into two semicircles; of these, the one toward the east is called by the Greeks from the rising to the rising, and the one opposite is called toward the setting. Among the Latins the one is the Occident, the other the Orient Cardo. Each semicircle is again divided in various ways by the rising and setting sun; these matters are treated more fully by others.

units.la: Horizontis Poli Puncta sunt duo, unum quod in Cœlo directe & ad perpendiculum nostris imminere capitibus imaginamur, ita ut recta linea ab Mundi centro per capitis nostri verticem (unde & Verticale) ducta, in illud necessario desinat. Vulgo Zenith vocatur: alterum huic oppositum sub Horizonte latet, Nadir, indigeratum.
units.tr: The horizon has two poles. One is the point in the heavens which we imagine to hang directly and perpendicularly over our heads, so that a straight line drawn from the centre of the world through the top of our head (whence also the name vertical) necessarily ends at it. It is commonly called the Zenith. The other, opposite to it, lies hidden beneath the horizon and is called the Nadir.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CAP. IX.

units.la: De Meridiano.
units.tr: Of the Meridian.

units.la: MERIDIANUS Circulus est major, non idem ubique, sed cuilibet loco proprius, ductus per loci verticem (Zenith capitis nostri dicunt alij) & Mundi πόλος: ad quem quum Sol primi Cœli motu est delatus, interdiu Meridies (unde & Circulus medy dici nonnullis) noctu media efficitur nox. Græcis μεσημβρινὸς, qui Gemino & Proclo κύκλος, ὁ διὰ τ' ἔ κόσμου πόλων, ἐξ ἐκ κεφαλῆς σημεῖα χαράσσων; ἐφ' ἃ ἡμέρας ὁ ἥλιος ἐπὶ μέσου τῆς ἡμέρας ἢ ἐπὶ μέσου τῆς νυκτὸς πίπτει.
units.tr: The MERIDIAN is a great circle, not the same everywhere but proper to each place, drawn through the zenith of the place (others call it the zenith of our head) and through the pole of the world [πόλος]. When the Sun, by the first motion of the heavens, is carried to this circle, it becomes midday (whence some call it the middle circle) by day and midnight by night. Among the Greeks it is μεσημβρινός. Geminus and Proclus define it as the circle [κύκλος] passing through the poles of the world and marking the points above our head, at which the Sun falls at midday by day or at midnight by night [ὁ διὰ τῶν τοῦ κόσμου πόλων, ἐξ ἐκ κεφαλῆς σημεῖα χαράσσων· ἐφ' ἃ ἡμέρας ὁ ἥλιος ἐπὶ μέσου τῆς ἡμέρας ἢ ἐπὶ μέσου τῆς νυκτὸς πίπτει].

units.la: Meridiani quo ad Sensum idem fere permanent ad c c c c. Stadia; quo ad Rationis judicium, variato in Terræ convexo secundum longitudinem situ, statim & perpetuo mutantur. Semper enim, Ortum sive Occasum versus recta vel tantillum progredientes, novos adquirunt Meridianos. Nam tot sunt Meridiani, quot Verticalium Punctorum diversis Terræ partibus incumbentium versus Ortum atq; Occasum differentiæ. Infiniti igitur. Ex quibus patet, rendentes directe versus alterutrum Polorum mundi, sub uno perpetuum procedere Meridiano. Quæ dixi, sic sua lingua concipit Geminus: ἀ κ' πῶσαν ἡ χώραν ἡ πλιν αὐτῆς εἰσὶν μεσημβρινὰς; ἀλλὰ πρὸς μὲν τὸν ἀϊδιον ἀρχὴν ... Neque aliter Proclus. Apud utrumque tamen πεγαωσις pro τειανωσις reponendum: quod de Proclo monet Nobilissimus Scaliger, doctissimo illo Commentario, quem scripsit ad Manilij Astronomica. Nam mutua est Horizontis & Meridiani ratio; reciprocaq; est utriusque descriptio: alter sine altero esse nequit, ut supra dixi. Geminus autem & Proclus Horizontis Sensibilis spacium πεγαωσις σταδίοις definiunt. Alij plura tribuunt huic Meridiano Stadia: Eratosthenes 1 0 c c, & Ptolemæus 1 0. Ergo, inquit Scaliger, ex stadiatino Eratosthenis intra lxxxvii. s. millia passuum non erit ἀσὶνης κ' πέρθεν, ex Ptolemæo intra lxii. s. Ex Proclo inter l. cujus sententia meo judicio melior. Quare ex omnium illorum mente orbis per c lxxx. divisus efficiet Meridianos cccix.
units.tr: The meridians remain nearly the same in respect of sense, at about four hundred stadia apart; in respect of the judgement of reason, they change immediately and continuously as the position on the curved surface of the earth shifts along its length. For always, as one advances straight or even a little towards east or west, one acquires new meridians. There are as many meridians as there are differences between the vertical points lying over the different parts of the earth, towards east and west. These are therefore infinite. From this it is clear that those who travel straight towards one or other pole of the world always proceed along one and the same meridian. Geminus conceives what I have said in his own language thus: ἀ κ' πῶσαν ἡ χώραν ἡ πλιν αὐτῆς εἰσὶν μεσημβρινὰς; ἀλλὰ πρὸς μὲν τὸν ἀϊδιον ἀρχὴν ... [as printed; the sense is: the meridians are, in every region, the same; but towards the eternal beginning...]. Proclus says the same. In both, however, πεγαωσις should be restored in place of τειανωσις, as the most noble Scaliger points out about Proclus in that most learned commentary which he wrote on the Astronomica of Manilius. For the relation of the horizon and the meridian is mutual, and the description of each reciprocally depends on the other: neither can exist without the other, as I said above. Geminus and Proclus define the extent of the sensible horizon as πεγαωσις σταδίοις. Others assign more stadia to this meridian: Eratosthenes 1 0 c c, and Ptolemy 1 0. Therefore, says Scaliger, from Eratosthenes' stadia, within 87½ thousand paces there will not be ἀσὶνης κ' πέρθεν; from Ptolemy's, within 62½; from Proclus, within 50, whose opinion is, in my judgement, the better. Hence, on the mind of all of them, the globe divided by 180 will make 309 meridians.

units.la: Usus Meridianorum multifarij. 1. Quod, utroque Hemisphærio in duas partes sectio, dies Noctesque in æqualia distingant spacia.
units.tr: The uses of the meridians are many. 1. Because they cut each hemisphere into two parts, they divide days and nights into equal spaces.

units.la: D 4 II.
units.tr: D 4 II.

units.la: 11. Quod cuivis Horizonti obliquo ad rectos angulos insistentes in sphæra obliqua vicem præstent Horizontis recti.
units.tr: 2. Because, standing at right angles to any oblique horizon on the oblique sphere, they take the place of the right horizon.

units.la: 111. Quod Terræ locorumque in terra particularium Longitudinem & initient & finiant: quodq; Longitudinum diversarum discrimina contineant & patefaciant. Cujusque enim loci Longitudo spacium est duobus Meridianis inclusum: quorum unus Fortunatis incumbit insulis: alter Loci, quo de agitur, Vertici.
units.tr: 3. Because they both begin and end the longitude of the earth and of particular places on the earth; and because they contain and reveal the differences between various longitudes. For the longitude of any place is a space enclosed by two meridians: one lies over the Fortunate Islands, the other over the vertex of the place in question.

units.la: 1v. Quod in Meridianis, ut subjecto, numerentur & distantiæ Stellarum ab AEquatore, & Locorum Latitudines, Ptolemæo τὰ τῶν οἰκήσεων ἐγκλίματα, Poli denique exaltationes, Græcis ἐξάρματα: quarum quæ secundo tertioque loco nominatæ, non quantitate, sed solo differunt situ. Quo modo autem Poli Elevatio sit invenienda, cum ex Vmbrarum ratione, tum ex maximi diei quantitate, docent alij. Nam omnia huc congerere, &, fere dixerim, transcribere (Verba enim mihi præiverunt in Astronomicis non uno loco magni viri: fateor lubens, quod nolle solent alij) non mihi est animus.
units.tr: 4. Because, as their base, the distances of the stars from the equator are counted on the meridians, as are the latitudes of places (Ptolemy's τὰ τῶν οἰκήσεων ἐγκλίματα), and finally the elevations of the pole (Greek ἐξάρματα). Of these, the second and third mentioned differ not in quantity but only in position. How the elevation of the pole is to be found, both from the ratio of shadows and from the length of the longest day, others teach. For I have no wish to gather all this here, or, I might almost say, to copy it out; for great men have gone before me in astronomical matters in more than one place (I freely admit it, which others are wont to be unwilling to do).

units.la: v. Quod Imi Summiq; Cœli Cardines diffiniat: quorum qui superioris est Hemisphærij, μεσουράνια vel μεσουρανήματα Græcis, Latinis Culmen, Fastigium, Medium Cœli: oppositus autem ὑπόγειον illis, his Imum Cœli vocatur.
units.tr: 5. Because it defines the lower and upper hinges of the heaven: of these, the one belonging to the upper hemisphere is called μεσουράνια or μεσουρανήματα by the Greeks, and in Latin Culmen, Fastigium, or Medium Caeli; the opposite one, which the Greeks call ὑπόγειον, is called Imum Caeli.

units.la: v1. Quod cum Horizonte quovis Recto vel Obliquo, quatuorque aliis Cireulis Majoribus, totum Cœlum in xii. distinguat spacia, quæ vulgo Cœli Domicilia nuncupantur. Ex his Primum, Quartum, Septimum & Decimum, quod Cœli angulos occupent, Græcis κέντρα, Latinis Cardines, Anguli vulgo vocantur: In his Planetæ, inquiunt Astronomi, fertiliores. Secundum, Quintum, Octavum & Vndecimum, quod superioribus proxima, ἐπαναφορικά apud Græcos, apud Latinos Succidentes dicuntur. In his Planetas debiliores volunt. Tertium, Sextum, Nonum & Duodecimum, quæ Cardinibus & Succidentibus inclusa, ἀπόκλιμα illis, his Domus Declinantes & Cadentes appellantur. Hic Planetæ majoris, ajunt, quam alibi debilitatis. Ne quis exspectet a me singulorum Nomenclaturas & Prætagia. Putent mihi hæc talia. Horresco legens: non enim tam sunt fabulosa, quam extremæ & perditissimæ impietatis. Meam hic mentem vide, ubi de Stellis.
units.tr: 6. Because, together with any right or oblique horizon and four other great circles, it divides the whole heaven into twelve spaces, which are commonly called the Houses of Heaven. Of these, the First, Fourth, Seventh and Tenth, since they occupy the angles of the heaven (Greek κέντρα, Latin Cardines), are commonly called Anguli: in these, the astrologers say, the planets are more fruitful. The Second, Fifth, Eighth and Eleventh, since they are next to the above, are called ἐπαναφορικά by the Greeks and Succidentes by the Latins: in these they hold the planets to be weaker. The Third, Sixth, Ninth and Twelfth, which are enclosed between the Cardines and the Succidentes, are called ἀπόκλιμα by the Greeks, and Domus Declinantes or Cadentes by the Latins: here, they say, the planet is weakened more than elsewhere. Let no one expect from me the nomenclatures and prognostications of the individual houses. Let them think me a fool for such things. I shudder as I read them: for they are not so much fabulous as of extreme and utterly abandoned impiety. Look here at my own mind, where I speak of the stars.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: De Minoribus Circulis, & primo de Tropicis Cancri & Capricorni.
units.tr: On the Minor Circles, and first on the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn.

units.la: HISTORIAM absolvi Circulorum, qui Majores: succedit, quæ Minorum. Minores voco, qui Mundum in segmenta dividunt inæqualia. Minores sunt & appellantur, ut volunt; quod, a medio Sphæra versus extremos vertices sensim in contractiorem figuram abeunte, & se velut angustante, Circulos hos ab mediis, qui majores, disjunctos necesse sit fieri minores. Hos, ut Majores distribuūt etiam in ccc lx. particulas: quæ tanto minores sunt Majorum Circulorum gradibus tantoq; minus cum in Cœlo tum in Terræ superficie spacium occupant, quanto a maximo Circuli ambitu atq; amplitudine, pro ratione distantiæ abeunt, cedentes quidem quantitate, sed maximorum Circulorum gradibus ἀνάλογοι. Proportio hæc quo modo invenienda sit, docet eleganter Victorinus Strigelius Epitome doctrinæ de Primo Motu, capite de Parallelis. Hos etiam scribunt totum Cœli convexum in in quinq; dirimere spacia; quæ, quod his, velut laxioribus fascijs, Cœlum cingatur, Zônas & Cingulos Astronomi vocant. Earum delineatio apud Vergilium i. Georgic. Quinque tenent Cælum Zonæ: quarum una corusco Semper Sole rubens, & torrida semper ab Igne est; Quam circum extremæ dextra laevaque trahuntur, Cærulea glacie concreta & nubibus atris; Has inter Mediamque duæ Mortalibus ægris Munere concessæ Divum, & via secta per ambas, Obliquus quo se Signorum verteret ordo.
units.tr: I have finished the history of the Circles which are greater; there follows that of the Lesser. I call lesser those which divide the world into unequal segments. They are called and are lesser, as they are said to be: because, as the sphere narrows gradually from its middle toward the extreme poles and contracts into a smaller figure, these circles, separated from the middle ones which are greater, must necessarily become smaller. Like the greater circles, these too are divided into 360 parts; but these parts are smaller than the degrees of the greater circles, and they occupy less space both in the heavens and on the surface of the earth, in proportion as they recede from the greatest circumference and breadth of the circle according to their distance, shrinking indeed in size but keeping the same proportion to the degrees of the greatest circles. How this proportion is to be found, Victorinus Strigelius teaches elegantly in his Epitome of the doctrine of the First Motion, in the chapter on Parallels. They also write that they divide the whole convex surface of the heaven into five spaces; and because the heaven is girdled by these, as by looser bands, the astronomers call them zones and girdles. Their outline is given by Vergil in the first Georgic: "Five zones hold the sky: of these one, always glowing with the flashing sun, is always scorched by the fire; around it on the right and left extend the extreme ones, bound in blue ice and black clouds; between these and the middle, two were granted to wretched mortals by the gift of the gods, and a path was cut through both, along which the oblique order of the signs turns."

units.la: Videndus omnino de his Zonis Cœlestibus Macrobius lib. ii. in Somnium Scipionis cap. vii. & viii. Sunt autem Minores, ut Majores, vel Idem ubique, vel Alij alibi.
units.tr: One must by all means consult Macrobius on these heavenly zones, Book II on the Dream of Scipio, chapters 7 and 8. The lesser circles, like the greater, are either the same everywhere or differ in different places.

units.la: Prioris naturae Tropici: quorum unus Cancri, alter Capricorni. Τροπικοὶ dicuntur, a tempore, quo τροπή, id est reversio hic Solis; vel quod, quum Sol eo pervenerit, in contrarium statum tempora mutentur. Contrarij status sunt AEstas & Hiems; Calor & Frigus.
units.tr: Of the first kind are the Tropics: one of Cancer and the other of Capricorn. They are called tropics [Τροπικοὶ] from the time at which the tropē, that is the turning back of the sun, occurs; or because, when the sun has reached them, the seasons change into the opposite condition. The opposite conditions are summer and winter; heat and cold.

units.la: Tropicus Cancri (qui & AEstivus) Circulus est Minor, idem ubique; quem Sol, principium Cancri ingressus & diurno Primi Coeli motu conversus, describit. Limes est itineris Solaris versus Boream, & proximi ejus ad Nos accessus; ad quem delatus reflectit se & cursum dirigit in Meridiem oppositamque plagam. Geminus
units.tr: The Tropic of Cancer (which is also the summer tropic) is a lesser circle, the same everywhere; the sun describes it when, having entered the beginning of Cancer and being turned by the daily motion of the First Heaven, it travels. It is the limit of the sun's path toward the north, and its nearest approach to us; having reached it, the sun turns back and directs its course toward the south and the opposite region. Geminus

units.la: & Proclus Γεμίνος τροπικὸς κύκλος ... Hyginus Poëtico Astronomico: Θερινὸς τροπικὸς appellatur ideo, quod quum Sol ad eum Circulum pervenit, AEstatem efficit eis, qui in Aquilonis finibus sunt; Hiemem autem eis, qui Austri flatibus opponi. Praeterea quod ultra eum Circulum Sol non transit, sed statim revertitur, Τροπικὸς est appellatus. Perpetuo distat ab AEquatore versus Boream quantitate maximae declinationis Solis, quae hodie graduum xxiii, scrupulorum primorum xxviii. & duarum fere quintarum.
units.tr: and Proclus: "the Geminus tropical circle..." Hyginus in the Poetic Astronomy: it is called the summer tropic because when the sun reaches that circle, it brings summer to those who live in the regions of the north, and winter to those who lie opposite the winds of the south. Moreover, because the sun does not pass beyond that circle but immediately turns back, it was called the Tropic. It is distant from the equator toward the north by the amount of the sun's greatest declination, which today is 23 degrees, 28 first minutes and nearly two fifths.

units.la: Tropicus Capricorni (Latini vocant Hibernum & Brumalem) Circulus est, ejusdem cum delineato jam indolis: quem Sol in principio Capricorni (quod maximi Solis a nobis recessus & digressionis ad Austrum remotissimae terminus) constitutus definit, eodem ab AEquatore (quo superior ille) intervallo in Meridiem dilidens. Geminus & Proclus: Χειμερινὸς δὲ τροπικὸς κύκλος ... Hyginus: Χειμερινὸς τροπικὸς a nobis Hiemalis, a nonnullis etiam Brumalis appellatus, ideo quod Sol, quum ad eum Circulum pervenit, Hiemem efficit his, qui ad Aquilonem spectant, AEstatem autem his, qui in Austri partibus Domicilia constituerunt.
units.tr: The Tropic of Capricorn (the Latins call it the winter and brumal tropic) is a circle of the same nature as the one just described: it is defined by the sun when it is situated at the beginning of Capricorn (which is the limit of the sun's greatest recession from us and its most remote withdrawal toward the south), dividing the southern region from the equator at the same interval as that upper one. Geminus and Proclus: "the winter tropical circle..." Hyginus: the winter tropic, called by us the hibernal and by some also the brumal, because when the sun reaches that circle it brings winter to those who face the north, and summer to those who have settled their homes in the parts of the south.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI.

units.la: De Circulis Polaribus, Arctico & Antarctico.
units.tr: On the Polar Circles, Arctic and Antarctic.

units.la: TALES Minores, qui ubique Idem; Alios alibi statuo Polares, sic a Polis dictos. De ijs eleganter & absolute Strabo: οἱ Ἀρκτικοὶ μὴ ... ubi duo notat, neque omnibus esse Arcticos, neque passim eosdem; sed, ut dixi, Alios alibi: Non quidem omnibus: nam neque in recta sunt sphaera; neque in stante, quam μυλοειδῆ vocabant Veteres, qualis illis, quibus AEquinoctialis & Horizontem & Arcticum facit. Non vero passim idem, sed alij semper alibi. Mutantur enim pro Poli Exarmate, describunturque, non ut vulgus Mathematicorum opinatur, a Polis Ecliptic, sed a puncto Sectionis, qua Meridianus & Horizon se secant mutuo. Circulus enim, qui Punctum Horizontis ad communem intersectionem Miridiani & Horizontis tangit, Arcticus est illius loci. Quum autem Horizontes mobiles sunt, eamdem naturam participant & Arctici: Alij semper sunt in alio Climate pro ratione Exarmatis sive Elevationis poralis: & quanta loci alicujus erit altitudo, in tantum a Polo distare Punctum illud, quod Arcticum describit, est necesse: quot habitationes, tot sunt Circuli Arctici; non inquam fixi (nam inculcandum hoc saepius, contra recentiorum calculos) non ἀμεταπίπτωτοι; sed pro locorum differentia, Alij atque Alij: quo propius AEquinoctialem accedit ur, eo minores fiunt hi Circuli: contra majores, quo longius ab ipso recedit ur: sub AEquinoctiali, id est, Sphaera Recta, nulli prorsus sunt (ut paullo ante dictum) Arctici. Hinc error deprehenditur illorum, qui in Sphaera Mobili (in fixa enim ad loci inclinationem facta locum habet) Circulum hunc adponunt; describentes illum a Puncto Poli Ecliptícæ circum Polum Mundi. Non nisi in Sphæra dati Climatis locum habet. Stupenda fuit veterum Græcorum & Latinorum, quique eos sequuti sunt, Manilij, Hygini, Martiani Capellæ oscitantiaí qui Sphæræ suæ Arcticum non ad inclinationem loci sui, sed ad Cnidium Clima descripserunt: male sequuti Eudoxum, qui Cnidius patria primus Astronomiam ex penetralibus Ægyptiæ Philosophiæ erutam ad populares suos Græcos eduxit. Quæ enim de Cnidio Climate scripsit Cnidius, non poterant ad omnia Climata referri; ab Græcis ad quævis Græca, ab Latinis Romanisque Scriptoribus ad quævis Italica, vel Romanum.
units.tr: Those lesser circles are the same everywhere, but I set others elsewhere, which are called Polar after the Poles. Strabo writes of them neatly and precisely: οἱ Ἀρκτικοὶ μὴ ... (the Arctic circles are not ...). In this he indicates two things: that the Arctic circles are not the same for all places, and that they are not everywhere the same; but, as I have said, they are different in different places. They are not the same for all, because in a right sphere there are none, nor in the upright sphere, which the ancients called μυλοειδής (mill-shaped), such as the sphere that makes the equator and the horizon and the Arctic circle the same. Nor are they everywhere the same, but always different in different places. For they change with the elevation of the Pole, and they are described not, as the common run of mathematicians suppose, from the Poles of the ecliptic, but from the point of intersection where the meridian and the horizon cut each other. For the circle that touches the point of the horizon at the common intersection of the meridian and the horizon is the Arctic circle of that place. Since the horizons are movable, the Arctic circles also share in the same nature: different ones are always in different climates according to the elevation of the Pole. However high a place is, that point which describes the Arctic circle must be that far from the Pole. There are as many Arctic circles as there are habitations. They are not, I say, fixed (this must be insisted on repeatedly, against the calculations of more recent writers), nor unchanging; but they differ with the difference of places, one after another. The closer one comes to the equator, the smaller these circles become; the farther one moves from it, the larger they become. Under the equator, that is, in a right sphere, there are no Arctic circles at all (as was said a little earlier). Hence the error of those is exposed who place this circle in the movable sphere (for in a fixed sphere it has a place only according to the inclination of the locality), describing it from the point of the Pole of the ecliptic around the Pole of the world. It has a place only in the sphere of a given clime. Astonishing was the carelessness of the ancient Greeks and Latins, and of those who followed them, Manilius, Hyginus, Martianus Capella, who described the Arctic circle in their sphere not according to the inclination of their own place, but according to the Cnidian clime. They followed Eudoxus badly; he, a native of Cnidus, was the first to bring astronomy, dug out from the inner sanctuaries of Egyptian philosophy, to his fellow Greeks. But what the Cnidian wrote about the Cnidian clime could not be referred to all climes: by the Greeks to any Greek place, by the Latin and Roman writers to any Italian place, or to Rome.

units.la: Sunt autem hi Circuli, Arcticus & Antarcticus. Arcticus Circulus est Minor, Alius alibi, qui inter Circulos semper apparentes est maximus, totusque supra terram demissus: in quo Astra posita neque occidunt neque oriuntur, sed per totam noctem circa Polum moveri cernuntur. Geminus & Proclus ejus exscriptor: Ἀρκτικὸς μὲν ἐν ἐστι κύκλος, ὁ μέγιστος τῶν ἀεὶ φαινομένων κύκλων, ὁ ἐφαπτόμενος τῷ Ὁρίζοντι καθ' ἓν σημεῖον καὶ ὅλος ὑπὲρ γῆν ἀπολαμβανόμενος: ἐν ᾧ τὰ κείμενα τῶν Ἄρκτου ἐπὶ δύσιν, ἐπὶ αἰσθητῶν ποιεῖται· ἀλλὰ δὲ ὅλης τὴν νυκτὸς ἀεὶ τὸν πόλον περιφέρεται. Et paullo post: ὁ μὲν γὰρ Ἀρκτικὸς κύκλος ἀφορίζει τὰ ἀεὶ φαινόμενα τῆς Ἄρκτου. Item: Ἀρκτικὸς κύκλος ὅλος ὑπὲρ γῆν ἀπολαμβάνεται. De eo recte Manilius lib. 1. Astronomic.
units.tr: There are, however, these circles: the Arctic and the Antarctic. The Arctic circle is the lesser, the same in different places, which among the circles always visible is the largest, and lies wholly above the earth: in it the stars placed there neither set nor rise, but are seen to revolve about the Pole through the whole night. Geminus, and Proclus who copied him: ὁ Ἀρκτικὸς μὲν ἐν ἐστι κύκλος, ὁ μέγιστος τῶν ἀεὶ φαινομένων κύκλων, ὁ ἐφαπτόμενος τῷ Ὁρίζοντι καθ' ἓν σημεῖον καὶ ὅλος ὑπὲρ γῆν ἀπολαμβανόμενος· ἐν ᾧ τὰ κείμενα τῶν ἄστρων οὔτε δύσιν οὔτε ἀνατολὴν ποιεῖται, ἀλλὰ ὅλης τῆς νυκτὸς ἀεὶ τὸν πόλον περιφέρεται. (The Arctic circle is the largest of the circles always visible, which touches the horizon at one point and is cut off wholly above the earth; in it the stars placed there make neither setting nor rising, but are carried round the pole all through the night.) And a little later: ὁ μὲν γὰρ Ἀρκτικὸς κύκλος ἀφορίζει τὰ ἀεὶ φαινόμενα τῆς Ἄρκτου. Likewise: Ἀρκτικὸς κύκλος ὅλος ὑπὲρ γῆν ἀπολαμβάνεται. Manilius rightly says this in the first book of his Astronomica.

units.la: Circulus ad Borcam fulgentem sustinet Arcton.
units.tr: The circle holds the Bear facing the gleaming north.

units.la: Nam tota Ursa Major intra illum Arcticum, quem descripsit Eudoxus, (hujus enim Dogmata sequutus poëta, cum aliis, in Astronomicis) includitur. Et in Climate Alherum Orizon priores pedes Ursæ præterradit. Geminus & ex eo Proclus ἔτι ὁ κύκλος ἐν τῇ καθ' ἡμᾶς οἰκουμένῃ ὑπὸ τῶν ἐμ μεσόβια ποδὸς τῆς μεγάλης ἄρκτου ἀπεργάζεται.
units.tr: For the whole Great Bear lies within that Arctic circle which Eudoxus described (for the poet, in his astronomical matters, followed his doctrines along with others). And in the Alherum clime the horizon passes over the forefeet of the Bear. Geminus, and after him Proclus: ἔτι ὁ κύκλος ἐν τῇ καθ' ἡμᾶς οἰκουμένῃ ὑπὸ τῶν ἐμ μεσόβια ποδὸς τῆς μεγάλης ἄρκτου ἀπεργάζεται. (Further, in our inhabited world the circle is formed by the feet in the middle of the Great Bear.)

units.la: Antarcticus Circulus est ejusdem cum Arctico naturæ; sed qui totus infra terram descriptus, in quo Astra semper nobis sunt invisibilia. Geminus & Proclus: Ἀνταρκτικὸς ἢ ἐστι κύκλος ἴσος ἐ ἀφαιρέλης τῷ Ἀρκτικῷ· καὶ ἐφαπτόμενος τῆς Ὁρίζοντος καθ' ἓν σημεῖον· καὶ ὅλος ὑπὸ γῆν ἀπολαμβανόμενος: ἐν ᾧ τὰ κείμενα τῶν ἀστέρων ἀεὶ πάντης ἡμῖν ἐστιν ἀόρατα. Et paullo post: ὁ ἀντιαρκτικὸς κύκλος τὰ μὴ φαινόμενα τῆς ἄρκτου ἀφορίζει. Et: Ἀντιαρκτικὸς κύκλος ὅλος ὑπὸ τὴν ὁρίζοντα κρύπτεται.
units.tr: The Antarctic circle is of the same nature as the Arctic, but it is described wholly below the earth, and in it the stars are always invisible to us. Geminus and Proclus: Ἀνταρκτικὸς δέ ἐστι κύκλος ἴσος ἐκείνῳ τῷ Ἀρκτικῷ, καὶ ἐφαπτόμενος τοῦ Ὁρίζοντος καθ' ἓν σημεῖον, καὶ ὅλος ὑπὸ γῆν ἀπολαμβανόμενος, ἐν ᾧ τὰ κείμενα τῶν ἀστέρων ἀεὶ πάντῃ ἡμῖν ἐστιν ἀόρατα. (The Antarctic circle is a circle equal to that Arctic one, touching the horizon at one point, and cut off wholly beneath the earth, in which the stars placed there are always and everywhere invisible to us.) And a little later: ὁ ἀντιαρκτικὸς κύκλος τὰ μὴ φαινόμενα τῆς Ἄρκτου ἀφορίζει. And: Ἀντιαρκτικὸς κύκλος ὅλος ὑπὸ τὸν ὁρίζοντα κρύπτεται. (The Antarctic circle marks off the parts of the Bear that do not appear; the Antarctic circle is wholly hidden under the horizon.)

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CAP. XII.

units.la: De Circulis, quorum in Sphæra nullus usus.
units.tr: On the Circles That Have No Use in the Sphere.

units.la: TANTVM de Circulis, Majoribus quidem sex, quatuor vero Minoribus; quibus in Sphæra, fixa, saltem & immobili, (repetendum enim hoc monent Arctici) solet esse locus. Sunt & alij, sed quorum nullus in Sphæra usus: quales Circuli ut vocant Latitudinem, per Zodiaci polos & Stellarum centra diffiniti; Distantiæ locorum per verticalia eorum puncta ducti; Horizontis obliquitatis limites; quales item quos Sol annuatim cxxciı. ultra citraque Æquatorem diurno motu describit; aliique Minores infiniti, ἀόρατοι; qualis denique ἐγκύκλιος ille, ὁ γαλαξίας, Lacteus Latine, quem tamen Veteres etiam in Sphæra Solida ponebant. Achilles: ὁ γαλαξίας ἐστὶν ὁ ἐν τῇ σφαίρᾳ κατακεχρισμένος κηρῷ λευκῷ. De eo Geminus & Proclus: Λοξὸς δὲ ἐστι κύκλος (inter obliquos etiam nominatur Leontio & aliis) καὶ ὁ τὸ γαλακτῶδης· ἐπὶ μὲν ἐν μείζονι ταλάτῃ λελόξωται τῷ τροπικῷ κύκλῳ. συμίσχει δὲ ἐκ βεβαχυμεῖας νυφελοειδὲς· καὶ ἔστι ἐν τῷ ἡσμῷ μόνος ἀεὶ ὀμοιας. ἐχ' ὤ ἀέρα ἢ αὐτὸ τὸ ταλάτης, ἀλλὰ κ' μὲν τινα μίμη ταλατύπος ἐστι, κ' δὲ τινα ψυχρός, δι ἣν αὐτίαν ἐν τῇ ταλείσις σφαιρίσις ὑδὲ κατωχεάφιτι· Quæ ejus sit Substantia, scribunt, præter Aristotelem, Averroes de Orbis substantia lib. 11. & Paraphrasi super Meteor. Alexander ibidem, & alij. Plene Situm ejus depingunt Ptolemæus in Almagest. lib. 11. cap. 11. & Manilius lib. 1. Astronomic. ubi inter alia, quod ἡγκὰς & oculis nostris conspicuus, sic canit: Nec quærendum erit, visus incurrit in ipsos Sponte sua, seque ipse docet, cogitque notari. Namque in cæruleo candens nitet orbita Mundo, Ceu missura diem subito, Cælumque recludens, Ac veluti virides discernit semita campos, Quam terit assiduo renovans iter orbita tracta, Inter divisas à callibus est via partis: Vt freta canescunt sulcum ducente carina, Accipiuntque viam fluctus spumantibus undis, Quam tortus verso movit de gurgite vertex; Candidus in nigro lucet sic limes Olympo, Caeruleum findens ingens lumine Mundum.
units.tr: So much for the circles: six greater and four lesser ones, for which there is normally room on the fixed and, at least, immobile sphere (for the Arctics remind us that this must be repeated). There are others too, but none of them has any use on the sphere. Such are the circles called latitude, defined through the poles of the zodiac and the centres of the stars; the distances of places, drawn through the points of the vertical circles; the limits of the obliquity of the horizon; likewise those which the Sun annually describes by its daily motion, 23½ degrees on either side of the equator; and the countless other lesser circles, invisible (ἀόρατοι). Last is that encircling circle, the galaxy, the Milky Way in Latin, which the ancients nevertheless also placed on the solid sphere. Achilles: "The galaxy is that which is smeared with white wax on the sphere" [ὁ γαλαξίας ἐστὶν ὁ ἐν τῇ σφαίρᾳ κατακεχρισμένος κηρῷ λευκῷ]. Of it Geminus and Proclus say: "The oblique circle (it is also called oblique by Leontius and others) is the milky one; it is inclined to the tropic circle by a greater angle, and it appears cloudy from its density, and it is always the only one visible in the sky" [Λοξὸς δὲ ἐστι κύκλος]. What its substance is, Averroes writes, apart from Aristotle, in his book on the substance of the orb (lib. 11) and in his paraphrase on the Meteorology; Alexander likewise in the same place, and others. Ptolemy in the Almagest book 11, chapter 11, and Manilius in book 1 of the Astronomica paint its position fully, where among other things, since it is bright and conspicuous to our eyes, he sings thus: "Nor will it need to be sought; the sight falls upon it of its own accord, and it teaches itself and compels itself to be noticed. For the orbit shines bright in the blue world, as if about to send forth the day suddenly and opening the heaven; and as a path separates the green fields, which the orbit traces out by constant travel, renewing its course, so there is a way between the divided parts marked by the paths. As the seas grow white when the keel draws a furrow, and the waves receive a track with foaming surges, which the whirling eddy has made from its turning gulf; so the white boundary shines on the dark Olympus, cleaving the blue world with its vast light."

units.la: Et quae ibi sequuntur. M. Tullius de Somnio Scipionis, ubi de hoc Circulo: Frat auctoritas splendidissimo candore inter flammas Circulus elucens; quem vos, ut à Graiis accepistis, Orbem Lacteum nuncupatis. Ad quae verba sic scribit Macrobius lib. 1. cap. xv: Orbis hunc idem quod Circus in Lactei appellatione significat. Est autem lacteus unus è Circis, qui ambit hunc subjectas est oculis; ceteri Circuli magis cogitatione, quam visu comprehendendi. Caulas de Lacteo Circulo, Naturales quidem commemorat ibidem ex Theophrasto, Diogenes, Democrito & Posidonio Macrobius; Fabulosas vero ex variis videre est, cum apud Grammaticos, & Mythologos, tum apud Philoponum in 1. Meteor & Hyginum in Poetico Astronomic. Ovidius in Metamorph. Circulum hunc Deorum iter ad Iovis regiam appellat: Est via sublimis Caelo manifesta sereno Lactea nomen habet candore notabilis ipso. Hac iter est Superis ad magni tecta Tonantis Regalemque domum.
units.tr: And what follows there. Marcus Tullius in the Dream of Scipio, where he speaks of this circle: "Behold, the authority of the Circle shining among the flames with the most brilliant whiteness; which you, as you received it from the Greeks, call the Milky Orb." On these words Macrobius writes thus in book 1, chapter 15: "The Milky Orb signifies the same as Circle in the name of the Milky Way. The Milky Way is one of the circles, which surrounds this one and is subject to the eyes; the other circles are grasped more by thought than by sight." Concerning the Milky Circle, Macrobius in the same place recalls natural explanations from Theophrastus, Diogenes, Democritus and Posidonius; but one may see fabulous ones in various writers, both among grammarians and mythographers, and in Philoponus on the first book of the Meteorology, and in Hyginus in the Poetic Astronomy. Ovid in the Metamorphoses calls this circle the road of the gods leading to the palace of Jupiter: "There is a lofty way, plain in the clear sky, notable for its very whiteness, and named the Milky Way. By this path the gods pass to the halls of the great Thunderer and to his royal house."

units.la: CAP. XIII. De Caelorum Volubilium Numero.
units.tr: CAP. XIII. On the Number of the Revolving Heavens.

units.la: Haec de Caelo Volubili, prout considerari solitum Circulis insignitum: ordo agitur, ut idem proponam ab Globis & Circulis separatum. Huius historiae quae scrutaturus, non incommode praemittam Augustini verba, quae Sermone 11. ad Psalm. xxxii. Caeli, inquit, quo modo invicem superpositi sint, vel quot sint, quibus motibus diversis, quibus incolis referti, & qua dispositione regantur, difficile dictu est atque explicatu, & per caelestem duntaxat sciri potest revelationem. Ita est. Merebor ergo veniam, si non plene satisfecerim omnibus: quid enim possem, quum ne mihi quidem ipsi facere satis hic potuerim?
units.tr: So much for the revolving heaven, as it is usually considered, marked out with circles. The order of the work now requires that I treat the same subject apart from the globes and circles. In investigating its history, it will not be out of place to begin with the words of Augustine in his Sermon 11 on Psalm 32: "How the heavens are placed one above another, or how many there are, by what different motions they move, with what inhabitants they are filled, and by what arrangement they are governed, is hard to say and to explain, and can be known only through heavenly revelation." That is true. I shall therefore deserve pardon if I do not fully satisfy everyone, for what could I do, since I have not been able to satisfy even myself on this point?

units.la: Quod igitur ad Numerum, D. Chrysostomus Homilia in Genesin iv. non dubitat affirmare eos, qui Caelos multos fabricantur, Sacrae Scripturae & Doctrinis Ecclesiasticis adversari, suaque sequi commenta, suas inventiones: Moschen enim unum tantum Caelum tradidisse, Firmamentum cognomine; Sacras litteras, quae Caeli nomen caret singulari numero. In magni viri jurare verba nuper nescio quem audaculum opinor voluisse; qui machinam Caeli totius unicam & continuam esse, minimeque Orbibus distingui, scripsit. Quid? Continuum? Si ita esset, & non potius contiguum; necessario uno & simplici motu circumducerentur, quemadmodum primo & secundo Caeli, & v. Metaphysic. ab Aristotele probatur. Chrysostomum sane, Philosophorum omnium & Theologorum calculis (dicam hoc pace tanti viri) contrarium, in bonam partem admittit interpretari Thomas 1. part. quaest. lxviii. tamquam pius vir non damnaret eos, qui Corpus caeleste in multos dispescebant Orbes; sed qui extra Mundum hunc & Caelos nobis adsipro Chrysostomo Apologia alij.
units.tr: As to their number, Chrysostom, in his Homily 4 on Genesis, does not hesitate to affirm that those who invent many heavens contradict Holy Scripture and the teaching of the Church, and follow their own fictions and inventions. For Moses, he says, handed down only one heaven, called the Firmament; and Sacred Letters never use the word "heaven" in the singular number. I suspect that some audacious person who wrote recently wished to twist the words of this great man. He wrote that the whole machine of heaven is one and continuous and not at all divided into orbs. But what? Continuous? If it were so, and not rather contiguous, the heavens would necessarily be carried around by one simple motion, as is proved by Aristotle in the first and second books of the Metaphysics, and in book 5. Thomas, in Part 1, question 68, does indeed admit, in a favorable sense, that Chrysostom, a contrary opinion to the consensus of all philosophers and theologians (I say this with respect for so great a man), should be interpreted as a pious man who would not condemn those who divided the heavenly body into many orbs, but those who ... [the rest of this sentence is corrupt in the scan]; and others in Chrysostom's Apology.

units.la: Iustinus Martyr, ubi respondet ad Quaest. lxvii. Orthodoxor. adserit revera duos tantummodo universim esse Caelos, quorum apud Moschen i. Geneseos capite mentio; sed hos distingui in varia spacia, quae interdum Scriptura etiam Caelos adpellat, ut quum D. Paullus dicit se raptum in Caelum Tertium.
units.tr: Justin Martyr, in his answer to Question 67 of the Orthodox Questions, asserts that there are in truth only two heavens in general, of which Moses speaks in the first chapter of Genesis; but that these are divided into various spaces, which Scripture sometimes also calls heavens, as when St Paul says that he was caught up into the third heaven.

units.la: Theodoretus quaest. xi. in Genesin notat non credentem. Secundum esse Caelum, semitam rectam transgredi; plures vero numerare conantem, fabulis adhaerere, postremo
units.tr: Theodoret, in Question 11 on Genesis, observes that whoever does not believe in a second heaven departs from the straight path; but whoever tries to count more heavens clings to fables, and finally prefers his own opinion to the teaching of the divine Spirit.

units.la: Numerus Orbium Caelestium, D. Chrysostomo; Iustino Martyr; Theodoretus. re, postposita divini Spiritus doctrina.
units.tr: The number of the heavenly orbs: according to Chrysostom, Justin Martyr, and Theodoret. ... [corrupt in the scan] ... with the teaching of the divine Spirit set aside.

units.la: Basilius Homilia 111. in Genesin scribit, non duos tantum secundum Sacram Scripturam esse Cœlos: sed plures, certè minimum tres oportere statui; quum D. Paullus referat se raptum usque ad Cœlum Tertium.
units.tr: Basil, in Homily 111 on Genesis, writes that according to Holy Scripture there are not only two heavens but more; at least, he says, one must hold that there are three, since St Paul relates that he was caught up as far as the third heaven.

units.la: Philastrius, Burgensis Episcopus, qui floruit Theodosij Junioris & Honorij, Imperatorum Orientis & Occidentis, temporibus, anno ab Christo nato cccccxx. aut circiter, in Catalogo haereseon commemorat haeresin quorundam de Cœlorum multitudine & diuersitate ambigentium: ipse vero sentire videtur, quanta sit Cœlorum multitudo, ex Sacris litteris esse incompertum, variantibus scilicet hac in re: quum duo Genesios 1. nominentur; tres Deuteronom. 1x. 4. & 11. epist. ad Corinth. xii. 1; sex denique Psalmo cxlviii. 4.
units.tr: Philastrius, bishop of Brescia (Burgensis), who flourished in the times of Theodosius the Younger and Honorius, emperors of the East and West, about the year 420 after the birth of Christ, mentions in his Catalogue of Heresies a heresy of certain men who doubted about the multitude and diversity of the heavens. He himself seems to think that how great the number of heavens is has not been ascertained from Sacred Letters, since the texts vary on this point: two are named in Genesis 1; three in Deuteronomy 9:4 and in 2 Corinthians 12:1; and finally six in Psalm 148:4.

units.la: Quidquid sit: nusquam Sacræ Litteræ certum Cœlorum produnt Numerum; nusquam non eadem afferunt; ut etiam qui plures trimetrosos tamen esse Cœlos, nusquam non eadem contradicant: nec pecc ent Philosophi, Astronomi eorumque sequuti dogmata Theologi, quoties asseverantius quid de Cœlorum Numero diffiniunt.
units.tr: Whatever the case, Sacred Letters nowhere state a certain number of heavens; and they nowhere say the same thing in every place. Even those who maintain that there are three heavens nowhere contradict themselves. Nor do philosophers, astronomers, and the theologians who follow their doctrines err whenever they define anything about the number of the heavens with greater confidence.

units.la: Ægyptij Chaldæique supra Octavam Sphæram mobile nihil agnoscebant, quorum scita Plato, Aristoteles, Hipparchus, aliique sunt amplexi, ut passim illorum testantur scripta.
units.tr: The Egyptians and Chaldeans recognized nothing movable beyond the eighth sphere. Plato, Aristotle, Hipparchus, and others adopted their views, as their writings attest everywhere.

units.la: Sed magnis Magistris sapientores videri voluerunt in his talibus mox-Successores. Videntes enim hi varia admodum in Cœlestibus φαινόμενα: Stellarum, quæ res. Fixæ, alias concitatiore, tardiore motu progredi alias; Apogæa Planetarum secundum Signorum ordinem mutari; Aquinoctia Solstitiaque diebus aliquot præuertere notata Veteribus tempora; λέξων denique Ecliptica maximam sensim decrescere: Ptolemæus posterioresque. Mathematici alium quasi quemdam Orbis Octavi motum ab Occasu deprehendentes in Ortum, Nonum cœlum addiderunt.
units.tr: But later successors, wishing to seem wiser than their great masters in such matters, ... For these men, observing many phenomena [φαινόμενα] in the heavens: the fixed stars advancing at different speeds, some faster and some slower; the apogees of the planets shifting according to the order of the signs; the equinoxes and solstices anticipating the times noted by the ancients by some days; and the obliquity of the ecliptic gradually decreasing. Ptolemy and later mathematicians, detecting another, as it were, motion of the eighth sphere from west to east, added a ninth heaven.

units.la: Ante annos vero trecentos, & paucos qui excurrunt, Mathematici, præter duplicem Orbis Octavi motum, cum Raptus, tum ab Occasu ad Ortum, certa (sic enim loqui audent) obseruatione comperisse se iactitant Tertium eiusdem Orbis Motum, quem Trepidationis intrepide nominantes, Decimum exstruxerunt Cœlum: ut horum Numerus excreverit, additis Planetarum globis, ad decem Orbes Volutos: quos dirimunt in Sphæram Αναστρ & Ασεχλω: ille quidem Mobile cum Pribiles; quos dirimunt in Sphæram Αναστρ & Ασεχλω: ille quidem Mobile cum Primum (cuius auctorem volunt Ptolemæum) tum Secundum (quod excogitatum ab Alphonsinis) tribuentes: huic autem Octavum Orbem, qui Stellas fert inerrantes; reliquosque septem, qui singuli singulos portant Planetas. Præterea, quum Αναστρ Sphæra Stellis careat, Characteribus quibusdam & Lineamentis utramque insignitam imaginantur; eaque certis locis & temporibus ab oculatissimis & qui acutissimo visu præditi, percipi posse (o deliramenta!) scribunt.
units.tr: Some three hundred years ago and a few more, mathematicians, besides the twofold motion of the eighth sphere, both the rapid motion from east to west and the motion from west to east, boast that by a certain observation (for so they dare to speak) they discovered a third motion of the same sphere. Boldly calling it trepidation, they built a tenth heaven, so that their number grew, with the globes of the planets added, to ten revolving orbs. These they divide into the sphere of the Anastron [Αναστρ] and the Asechlo [Ασεχλω]. To the former they assign both the Primum Mobile (whose author they hold to be Ptolemy) and the Secundum Mobile (devised by the Alphonsine tables); to the latter the eighth sphere, which carries the fixed stars; and the remaining seven, each of which carries one planet. Moreover, since the Anastron sphere lacks stars, they imagine that both are marked with certain characters and lines, and they write that these can be perceived at certain places and times by the sharpest-eyed men endowed with the keenest vision. O follies!

units.la: Quin & Nonum Cœlum nonnullis Aqueum appellatur, ab Aquis, quas ex aliquot Scripturæ locis, veras & naturales supra Cœlum Sidereum opinantur esse viri doctrina sanctitateque præstantissimi: adeo ut Augustinus etiam lib. de Genesi Imperfecto, & xi. de Civitate Dei, cap. vltimo, quum de istiusmodi Aquis, qua ratione supra Cœlum esse possent, multum disputasset; hanc tandem velut disputationis operosissimæ clausulam adjiciat: Quoquo modo autem, & qualescumque Aquæ ibi sint, eas esse ibi minime dubitemus: maior est quippe Scripturæ huius auctoritas, quam omnis humani ingenij capacitas. Posse enim Aquas ibi consistere docet & argumentatur idem lib.11. de Genesi, cap. 1111. & Dialogo 1 x v. quæst. xxvii; ubi inter alia hæc: Videmus enim quotidie Aquam tenuatam in vaporem tolli ad superiores partes Aeris; quæ si magis etiam ma-gisque tenuaretur, celsiora quoque loca peteret. Quum igitur Physiologi doceant, omne Corpus in infinitum rarescere & dividi posse, etiam poterit in infinitum fieri tenuius, & ad quamcumque sublimitatem fustelli: quocirca non videtur impossibile, Aquam catenus attenuari posse, loco rum sublimitatem fustelli: quocirca non videtur impossibile, Aquam catenus attenuari posse, quo ad idonea sit etiam supra Cœlum promoveri. Et indicia rei, quæ difficilis ad fidem, comprobandæ duo notare nititur Ambrosius lib. 11. ἐξαημ. cap. 1. unum quidem, quod nonnunquam ingens Aquæ vis, de Cœlo repente magno impetu descendens, in tantos imbres resolvatur, ut flumina & lacus subito compleantur, & vel ipsa exundent maria: alterum vero, quod frequenter Solem cernamus quasi madidum & roran-tem; scilicet propter Aquarum Alimentum (de hoc Stellarum quasi potu, dicam infra). fra) de ejus ardoris temperiem attactum. Modum autem, quo consistunt ibi Aquæ, DEO tribuunt Beda & Petrus Longobardus, Cæli formæ Basilius. Beda enim in ἐξαήμερ. Non est minus, inquit, facile Omnipotenti DEO tenere Aquas super Cælum sidereum, sive aquidas, sive modo crystallis conglaciatas atque concretas, quam (quod faciat quotidie) tenere Aquas in sublimi Aere suspensas, unde tantus fit Imbrium defluxus: quod loco miraculi prædicat Hiob de DEO cap. xxvi. Qui ligat Aquas in nubibus suis, ut non crumpant pariter deorsum. Ipse enim est qui undas Rubri maris atque Iordanis in sublime erectas & murorum similitudine formatas fecit consistere. Longobardus vero lib. II. Sentent. distinct. xiiii. Si quem vero movet, quo modo natura fluida & in imaginabiles Aquæ, supra Cælum possint consistere, de eo sic ptum esse memineriit: Qui ligas Aquas in nubibus suis. Qui enim infra Cælum ligat Aquas ad tempus vaporibus nubilis retentas; potest etiam super Cæli sphæram non ex vapore tenuitate, sed glaciali fundiatæ Aquas suspendere, ne labantur. Quales autem & ad quid conditæ sint, ipse novit, qui condidit. Basilius denique in Homiliis, modum, quo retineantur ibi Aquæ, Cæli formæ tribuens; faciem ejus extimam, contra præstantissimorum Philosophorum sciunt, plenam fingit & æquam: quamvis qua concava, rotundam videamus: Licet, inter alia, concava Cæli superficies sit rotunda non continuo tamen esse consequens & necessarium, ut convexa Cæli superficies sit etiam totunda, sicut videre est in formatibus & locis conglomeratis. Quin usum & necessitatem aquarum supra Cæli Octavi spatia, cum aliis aperiunt Iustinus Martyr & Basilius: ille quidem respondens ad Quæstionem xciii. Orthodoxor. ubi scribit, Terga Cæli esse Aquis tecta, secundum illud, Qui tegis Aquis superiora eius: earum vero duplicem esse usum: alterum ad immensum ardorem fiderum, ne penitus omnia consumantur, sua refrigeratione mitigandum atque ac temperandum; alterum ut earum pondere de sum Cæli urgeatur ac premantur deorsum, ne crebro ac violento ventorum impetu, ô Virum in Sacris admirandum, Physicis puerum!) hue illuc agitetur. Hic vero Homilia iii. super Genesin: Quum DEVS, inquit, infinitam prope vim ignei ardoris propter multiplices & ad plurima necessarios eius in Cælo & infra Cælum multifariam ipsa fiet, efficiatque ipsa natura Ignis veramissimus & fecundissimus a minimis mire crescens, ut ob eam causam Universi salus atque incolumitas periclitaretur, ex adversa maximam et infra supraque Cælum vim Aquarum opposuit, ut earum refrigeratione tantus Ignium ardor temperatus non solum non obesset Mundo, sed etiam prodesset plurimum. Addenda his, quæ tradunt Theodoretus quæst. xi. super Genesin; Gennadius & Severianus in Catena ad Genesin citati. Innuit eundem usum Augustinus lib. xi. de Civitate Dei, cap. ult. Sicut in Microcosmo, id est, Homine supra Cor, igneæ naturæ, locatum est Cerebrum frigidissimum; ita in magno Mundo supra Cælestes Ignes Aquæ sunt positæ. Videndus idem lib. ii. super Genesin ad litteram cap. v. & libro de Genesi imperfecto cap. viii. Audiendus & hic Beda ex libro de Natura rerum, memoriæ prodens, quibusdam esse visum, Aquas supra Cælum esse positas à DEO; ut earum ingenti copia è Cælo præcipitatam in Terras, generale totius Orbis Diluvium, quod DEI voluntate ac decreto aliquando erat futurum, effici posset; verum sibi probabilius videri addens, eas Aquas ad refrigerationem & temperationem ardoris siderium fuisse comparatas. Iosephus lib. i. Iudaicarum Antiquit. cap. i. Aquas ad Imbrium & rimitatem Terræque irrigationem ibi locatas refert. Alium usum indicat Cabalistæ apud Picum Mirandul. in Heptaplo. Consulendus & de triplici Aquarum Supercœlestium usu Stephanus Szegedinus in Locis Communibus, ubi de Aquis. Pergo. Aquas has formam tenuissimæ nebulæ repræsentare scribit Augustinus ad Orosium quæst. xvii. & lib. ii. super Genesin ad litteram, cap. iv. ubi inter alia; Quod si possit, inquit, Aqua, sicut videmus, ad tantus gutturum devenire atque extenuari minutias, ut super Aerem hunc vaporis induta faciem, feratur, & Aer levior erit at: quur non possit super illud levius Cælum, minutiorum guttis & leviore mare: sustinere? Contra quem tamen videndus Ægidius Columnius posterioris ἐξαημ. cap. xiiii. Sunt qui Crystalli instar splendidas, solidatas, & quasi congelatas attulerunt, unde & Cælum Nonum ijs Crystallinum. Adeundi omnino Basilius in ἐξαημ. Bonaventura ii. Sentent. dist. xiv. Ægidius, quem dixi, cap. xiiii. & seqq. ubi multa, Petrus Longobardus Sent. ii. dist. xii. Nicolaus Lyranus, Toftatus, Cajetanus, & alij, non solum ad opinionem suam confirmandam trahentes Ioannis Evangelistæ locum ex Apocalyp. cap. xxii. 1. sed & Philosophos veteres sequuti, credo, Empodoclem & Anaximenem, Crystallum in Cælo esse adfirmantes, apud
units.tr: Some also call the Ninth Heaven the Watery Heaven, from the waters which men of great learning and holiness, judging from several passages of Scripture, believe to be real and natural waters above the starry heaven. So Augustine, in his book On the Literal Meaning of Genesis (unfinished) and in the last chapter of Book XI of The City of God, after a long discussion of how such waters could exist above the heavens, closes this very laborious argument with these words: "However it may be, and whatever sort of waters are there, let us not doubt that they are there. For the authority of this Scripture is greater than the full capacity of human intellect." The same Augustine argues in Book II of On Genesis (chapter 11) and in Dialogue 15, question 27, that the waters can remain there. Among other things he says: "We see every day that water thinned into vapour is carried up to the higher parts of the air. If it were thinned even more, it would rise to still higher places. Since natural philosophers teach that every body can be rarefied and divided without limit, it can also become finer without limit and rise to any height. So it does not seem impossible that water could be attenuated to the point where it could be carried even above the heavens." Ambrose, in Book II of his Hexaemeron, chapter 1, tries to point out two signs to confirm a thing that is hard to believe: first, that sometimes a huge mass of water, falling suddenly from heaven with great force, dissolves into such heavy rains that rivers and lakes are suddenly filled and even the seas overflow; second, that we often see the sun, as it were, moist and dripping, which he attributes to the tempering of its heat by the nourishment of the waters (I shall speak of this "drinking" of the stars below). As for the way in which the waters remain there, Bede and Peter Lombard ascribe it to God, and Basil ascribes it to the form of the heavens. Bede, in his Hexaemeron, says: It is no less easy for almighty God to hold waters above the starry heaven, whether liquid or, as it were, frozen and solidified into crystal, than to hold waters suspended in the high air, from which such a great downpour of rain comes about, which he does every day. Job, speaking of God, calls this a miracle, in chapter 26: "He binds up the waters in his clouds, so that they do not burst out together downward." For it is he who made the waves of the Red Sea and the Jordan, raised up on high and shaped like walls, to stand still. Peter Lombard, in Book II of the Sentences, distinction 14, says: If anyone is troubled as to how a fluid nature, and waters that can be imagined, can stand above the heavens, let him remember what has been said: "who binds up the waters in his clouds." For he who binds the waters below the heavens for a time, held back by the vapours of the clouds, can also suspend waters above the sphere of the heavens, not by vapour and thinness but solidified by ice, so that they do not slip. But what sort of waters they are, and to what purpose they were made, he knows who made them. Finally, Basil, in his Homilies, ascribes to the form of the heavens the manner in which the waters are held there. Against the view of the most distinguished philosophers, he imagines its outer face to be full and level, although we see the inner surface as concave and round. Although, among other things, the concave surface of the heavens is round, it does not necessarily follow that the convex surface of the heavens is also round, as can be seen in shapes and in conglomerate places. Justin Martyr and Basil also set out the use and necessity of the waters above the space of the eighth heaven, along with other reasons. Justin, in answer to Question 93 of the Orthodoxa, where he writes that the back of the heaven is covered with waters, according to the words "who covers his upper parts with waters," says that these waters have a twofold use: one, to temper and cool the immense heat of the stars, so that everything is not utterly consumed; the other, so that the heaven is pressed and weighed down by their weight, lest it be shaken hither and thither by the frequent and violent onslaught of the winds. (O man admirable in sacred matters, a boy in matters of physics!) Basil, in Homily 3 on Genesis, says: Since God foresaw that the nature of fire, being most true and most fruitful, would grow wonderfully from the smallest beginnings, and that its infinite power, necessary for many purposes in the heavens and below them, would become so great that the safety and wholeness of the universe would be endangered, he set against it, from the opposite side, a very great mass of waters both below and above the heavens, so that by their cooling the great heat of the fires would be tempered and would not only do no harm to the world but would be of great benefit. To these may be added what Theodoret (Question 11 on Genesis) and Gennadius and Severianus, quoted in the Catena on Genesis, have handed down. Augustine, in Book XI of The City of God, last chapter, hints at the same use: Just as in the microcosm, that is, in man, the brain, which is of a cold nature, is placed above the heart, which is fiery, so in the great world the waters are placed above the heavenly fires. The same Augustine, Book II on the literal meaning of Genesis, chapter 5, and in his unfinished book on Genesis, chapter 8, should also be consulted. Here too we should hear Bede, from his book On the Nature of Things, who records that it seemed to some that the waters were placed by God above the heaven, so that by their great quantity, poured down from the heaven onto the earth, the general flood of the whole world, which was to come at some time by the will and decree of God, might be brought about; but he adds that it seems more probable to him that those waters were prepared for cooling and tempering the heat of the stars. Josephus, in Book I of the Jewish Antiquities, chapter 1, says that the waters were placed there for the rains and for watering the earth. Another use is indicated by the Cabalists, as reported by Pico della Mirandola in his Heptaplus. Stephan Szegedin, in his Loci Communes, under the heading "On Waters," should also be consulted on the threefold use of the supercelestial waters. I continue. Augustine, in his letter to Orosius, Question 17, and in Book II on the literal meaning of Genesis, chapter 4, writes that these waters resemble a very fine cloud. Among other things he says: But if water, as we see, can be drawn up into such drops and thinned into such tiny particles that it is carried above this air, taking the form of vapour, then the air will be lighter still. Why then should it not be possible for the lighter heaven to sustain the water in drops still smaller and lighter? Against him, however, Egidius Columna should be consulted in the later Hexaemeron, chapter 14. Some have brought forward waters that are bright like crystal, solid and as it were congealed, and for this reason they also call the Ninth Heaven Crystalline. Basil in his Hexaemeron, Bonaventure in Book II of the Sentences, distinction 14, Egidius (whom I have mentioned), chapter 14 and following, where there is much to be found, Peter Lombard in Sentences II, distinction 12, Nicholas of Lyra, Torquemada, Cajetan, and others should all be consulted. They use to confirm their opinion not only the passage of John the Evangelist from Revelation chapter 22, verse 1, but also follow the ancient philosophers, I believe Empedocles and Anaximenes, who affirm that there is crystal in the heavens, as cited by [1 unit break]

units.la: E PlutarPlutarchum lib. II. ΠΕΡΙ ΤΩΝ ΑΡΕΣΚ. ΤΟΙΣ ΦΙΛΟΣ. ut & Iosephus lib. I. Antiq. Iudaic. cap. I. qui scribit, secunda die Cælum super omnia collocatum, ipsumque, ab alys distinctum, in femetiplo constitutum fuisse; eumque Crystallo circumdatum (miremur hic infelicem sacratissimi Scriptoris Paraphrasten) humidum & pluviale, ad utilitatem, quæ fit Terra ex Imbribus, ab D E O congrue fabricatum. Quidquid sit; Aquas illas, quarum in Sacris litteris mentio, quæ Cæli nonnumquam exprimuntur appellatione, quæ prædicare dicuntur Dei potentiam, quæ ad Dei laudem à pijs viris invitantur; longe alias esse, nec ullo modo Fixarum Sphæræ supervehendas, contra decentissimum Rerum ordinem optimamque Totius dispositionem, quum naturalis Aquarum locus sit infra Aerem Terræ proximus, & in prima Rerum creatione ad Omnipotentiam Dei & miracula non sit confugiendum; plenè docui lib. I. cap. IV.
units.tr: From Plutarch, Book II, [ΠΕΡΙ ΤΩΝ ΑΡΕΣΚΟΝΤΩΝ ΤΟΙΣ ΦΙΛΟΣΟΦΟΙΣ] (On the Opinions of the Philosophers), and also from Josephus, Book I of the Jewish Antiquities, chapter 1, who writes that on the second day the heaven was placed above all things, and was itself set apart from the others and established in itself; and it was surrounded with crystal (let us marvel here at the unhappy paraphrast of the most sacred writer) and, humid and rain-bearing, was suitably made by God for the benefit that the earth receives from the showers. Whatever the case, those waters which are mentioned in Holy Writ, which are sometimes expressed by the name of "heavens," which are said to proclaim the power of God, and to which pious men are invited to praise God, are quite different, and in no way to be carried above the sphere of the fixed stars. This would be contrary to the most becoming order of things and the best arrangement of the whole. Since the natural place of waters is just below the air, near the earth, and in the first creation of things one should not take refuge in the omnipotence of God and in miracles, I have fully taught this in Book I, chapter 4.

units.la: Quid igitur de Cœlorum Numero statuendum? Quamvis Hypotheses Physicæ, quarum fundamento Cœlorum pluralitas exstruitur, alicujus videantur ponderis & momenti; Ajunt enim, Cujusvis Corporis Simplicis unum esse Motum per se: Omne Corpus, quod pluribus movetur Motibus, unum per se habere, alios per accidens; Inferiorem Sphæram moveri ab Superiore; Stellas moveri ad Sphæræ, cui inlocatæ sunt, motum; & similes; colligentes, inde supra Cœlum octavum, quod triplici, inquiunt, movetur motu duos alios esse Orbes: tamen revera Cœlestes Sphæræ sunt octo, quas oculis notare ac distinguere possumus; motuum quidem varietate, ut mox dicam, ac situ differentes, contigui tamen, & eo ordine dispositi, ne ullus alterius vicinioris motum impediat. Sunt illi septem Planetarum Orbes, & Siderum Fixorum Sphæra, quæ quam recte Firmamentum à quibusdam nominetur, paret ex cap. IV. libri I. Nonum, ut novum & commentitium, habendum; Decimum autem, ut ex Volubilium numero decimandum.
units.tr: What, then, ought we to decide about the number of the heavens? Although the physical hypotheses on which the plurality of heavens is built seem to have some weight and importance, for they say that each simple body has one motion of its own, that any body moved by several motions has one of them per se and the others per accidens, that a lower sphere is moved by a higher one, that the stars are moved by the motion of the sphere in which they are fixed, and so on, and from these premises they infer that above the eighth heaven, which (they say) moves with a threefold motion, there are two other orbs: nevertheless, in truth there are eight celestial spheres, which we can observe and distinguish with our eyes. They differ in the variety of their motions, as I shall shortly say, and in their situation; yet they are contiguous and arranged in such an order that none of them impedes the motion of a neighbouring one. These are the seven orbs of the planets and the sphere of the fixed stars, which (as is clear from chapter IV of book I) may rightly be called the firmament by some. The ninth must be regarded as new and fictitious, and the tenth is to be discounted from the number of moving heavens.

units.la: CAP. XIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV.

units.la: De Motu Cœlestium Orbium.
units.tr: On the Motion of the Celestial Spheres.

units.la: HÆC denumero, non minus intricata res est de Motu: qui novos Orbes, Nonum & Decimum, commentis multiplex. Decimum Cœlum primum Mobile volunt; moveri autem super Mundi Polos ab Oriente in Occidentem, spacio naturalis diei, vel XXIV. horarum. Noni Cœli Motum faciunt duplicem; priorem quidem ad Motum Primi Mobilis, posteriorem autem ex se & sua natura. Vocant nonnulli Augium Stellarumque Fixarum Motum, alij Motum d. f. ctionis; quod omnes inferiores Sphæræ deficiant à perfectione primi Mobilis. Hunc super Ecližicam lineam & polos Zodiaci ab Occasu versus Ortum, quadraginta novem millium annorum spacio (dato ducentis annis gradu uno cum XXXVIII. fere minutis) completurum fingunt suam Revolutionem: dicuntque Magnum annum Platonis, quem scripsisse ferunt, integra Revolutione ista completa, omnia in eodem futura statu, quo fuerant initio Revolutionis. O absurdam, ne dicam impiam, cujuscumque tandem ea sit, opinionem! quam explodit merito, & adversari Christianæ religioni, docet Augustinus lib. XII. de Civitate Dei cap. XIII. Ait, inquit, ut nos ista credamus. Semel enim Christus mortuus est pro peccatis nostris: resurgens a mortuis iam non moritur, & mors ei ultra non dominabitur, & nos post resurrectionem semper cum Domino erimus, cui modo dicimus, quod sacer admonet Psalmus: Tu Domine servabis nos, & custodies nos a generatione hac in æternum. Satis enim ipsis existimo convenire, quod sequitur: In circuitu impij ambulabunt, non quia per Circulos quos opinantur, eorum vita est recursura, sed quia modo talis est erroris eorum via, id est, falsa doctrina. Octavæ Sphæræ, præter superiores duos, Motum tribuunt, quem indigetant Trepidationis, vel Accessus & Recessus: notantes eo Sphæram hanc à Septemtrione in Meridiem moveri super duobus Circulis parvis; quorum Poli quidem sunt capita Librae & Arietis Nonae Sphærae, Semidiameter vero gradus IV. minuta XVIII. & secunda XLIII; motum autem compleri septem millium annorum spatio; solum hunc Octavæ Sphæræ esse proprium; ejusque ratione Stellas Fixas semper in temporibus (utar illorum verbis) æqualibus æque distare à capitibus Arietis & Librae ejusdem primi Mobilis, sed motas videri nunc Orientem, nunc Occidentem versus, interdum tardius, aliquando velocius; quum motas repererint uno gradu, Ptolemæus quidem centum, posteriores autem sexaginta annorum curriculo.
units.tr: These matters, so far as I can count them, are no less tangled when it comes to motion. Through their fictions they have multiplied the new spheres, the Ninth and the Tenth. They hold that the Tenth Heaven is the first Mobile, which turns about the poles of the world from east to west in the space of a natural day, that is, twenty-four hours. They ascribe a double motion to the Ninth Heaven: one, the motion of the first Mobile, and the other from its own nature. Some call this the motion of the Augium and the fixed stars, others the motion of deficiency, because all the lower spheres fall short of the perfection of the first Mobile. They imagine that this sphere completes its revolution along the ecliptic and the poles of the zodiac, moving from west to east, in forty-nine thousand years (taking two hundred years for each degree, with about thirty-eight minutes), and they call it Plato's Great Year. They say Plato wrote that when this revolution is complete, everything will return to the same state in which it was at the start of the revolution. Oh, what an absurd, not to say impious, opinion, whoever held it! Augustine rightly rejects it and shows that it is contrary to the Christian religion (De Civitate Dei, book XII, chapter XIII). He says: "Let us believe these things, for Christ died once for our sins; rising from the dead, he dies no more, and death shall no longer have dominion over him; and after the resurrection we shall always be with the Lord, to whom we now say what the holy Psalm bids us: Thou, O Lord, shalt keep us, and shalt guard us from this generation for ever." "For I think it fits them well to add what follows: The wicked shall walk in a circle," not because their life is going to return through the circles they imagine, but because such is the way of their error, that is, their false doctrine. To the eighth sphere, besides the two superior ones, they attribute a motion which they call trepidation, or approach and recession. By this they mean that this sphere moves from north to south around two small circles, whose poles are the heads of Aries and Libra of the Ninth Sphere, with a semidiameter of four degrees, eighteen minutes and forty-three seconds. They say this motion is completed in a space of seven thousand years, and that it belongs to the eighth sphere alone. Because of it, the fixed stars, in equal times (to use their words), are always equally distant from the heads of Aries and Libra of the same first Mobile, yet they appear to move now eastward, now westward, sometimes more slowly, sometimes faster. They have found that they have moved one degree in a hundred years (Ptolemy) or, according to later writers, in sixty years.

units.la: Iam quid dicam de diversissimo Planetarum motu? Singulis suas dant Sphæras; Sphæris varios, majores minoresque Orbes; Orbibus denique varios & dissimiles admodum Motus. Quibus commemorandis nec mihi, nec aliis ero molestus paucis dicam.
units.tr: Now what shall I say about the very diverse motion of the planets? They give each one its own sphere; to the spheres they give various orbits, greater and smaller; and to the orbits, finally, various and quite dissimilar motions. I will not trouble myself or others by listing them; I will say only a few things.

units.la: Omnis Motus vel Rectus est, vel Orbicus, ut cum Varrone loquar. Rectus vel est ascendens, sursum tendens; vel descendens, deorsum. Illo quidem moventur Levia, Ignis & Aer; dicturque Motus à Medio, id est Centro Terræ: Hoc vero Gravia, ut Terra & Aqua; Motus appellatur ad Medium, id est ad Centrum Terræ: Orbico omnia Cœlestia Corpora; Motum vocant circa Medium, id est Centrum. Rectus igitur Motus omnibus convenit, quæ intra Lunæ Sphæram & Centrum Terræ: & hinc quod Antipodes, non secus quam Nos, ad Medium, id est Terræ Centrum, natura ducente, tendant. Nam ut vere canit poeta,
units.tr: Every motion is either Rectilinear or Circular, to use Varro's words. Rectilinear motion is either upward, tending on high, or downward, tending below. By the former, light things, fire and air, are moved, and it is called motion from the middle, that is, from the centre of the earth. By the latter, heavy things, such as earth and water, are moved, and this motion is called motion toward the middle, that is, toward the centre of the earth. Circular motion belongs to all the heavenly bodies, and they call it motion around the middle, that is, around the centre. Rectilinear motion therefore belongs to all things that lie between the sphere of the moon and the centre of the earth; and for this reason the antipodes, no less than we, are drawn by nature toward the middle, that is, the centre of the earth. For, as the poet truly sings:

units.la: ——Cælum undique sur sum.
units.tr: ——Heaven is up on every side.

units.la: Orbicus Motus omnium Corporum est Cœlestium: cujus duo principes. Quamvis enim Orbes Cœlestes proprijs singuli videantur & dissimilibus agitari motibus; duos tamen tantum esse Astronomicæ docent observationes, docet sensuum judicium. Unum quidem simplicem, uniformem & regularem, quo quidquid Orbium Cœlestium ab Ortu in Occasum circa Mundi Polos Circulis Æquatori parallelis, spacio diei naturalis revolvitur. Antiquitas hunc Motum Octavo orbi, Non Ptolemæus, Recentiores Decimo proprium consecrarunt. nuncupat Ptolemæus; alij appellant, quod diurni nocturnique temporis spacio, diem metiens naturalem, absolvatur. Est enim hujus Motus vices ac discrimina dierum noctiumque, cum motu Solis proprio, efficere, Stellas quotidie producere, & conspiciendas nobis exhibere, eatque per Hemisphærium superius provolutas abducere rursus & abscondere: communis denique mensura reliquorum omnium est Motuum. Omnia enim Corpora secum rapit Inferiora, quæ quanto magis eo distant; tanto tardius eo motu moventur: quod potissimum apparet in Luna. Alterum vero, quem, Græci, & Latini Motum Planetarum vel Secundorum Mobilium; nonnulli Motum appellant in Consequentia. Eo Sphæræ, quæ Primo Mobili subjectæ, superiori Motui contranituntur, & ab Occasu in Ortum, sub Zodiaco & circa polos ejusdem, non in parallelis, qui ab Æquatore æquabiliter disjuncti, tardius multo provehuntur, sed dissimiliter. Nam Planetarum illi, qui Terræ propiores, motu concitatiore feruntur, citiusque periodos conficiunt suas: contra, lentiore procedentes gradu, distinita Zodiaci spacia tardius circumeunt, qui hinc remotiores. Est quando in medio velut cursu tardare videntur, & tamquam immoti subsistere, dicunturque nonnumquam regredi, nominati, hinc rursus accelerare curriculum, tamquam velocitate compensaturi prioris more defectum, vocanturque hic Græcis. Nec eumdem semper tenere conspicimus tramitem: sed à media Zodiaci via nunc in Boream, nunc in Austrum evagari. Recedentes denique procul à Terra, rursus velut ex alto ad Terram se demittentes, nuncupantur. Unde vero Cœlestium hæc Æquales sunt & regulares Orbium Cœlestium Motus; nobis tamen inæquales apparent, ait magnus vir, vel propter Circulorum Polos Mundi Polis diversos, circa quos convertuntur, ut sunt Poli Zodiaci, sub quo vagæ stellæ perpetuo versantur; vel quia Terra non est Centrum illorum Orbium, quibus vehuntur Planetæ & circumaguntur. Unde quum ex Centro Mundi nos Motus illos consideremus; fit, ut quemadmodum majore mole auctii videntur nobis, quum ex propinquo eos contuemur; minores apparent, quum procul positos conspicamur: sic in circumferentys Orbium æqualibus, ob diversum visus distantiam, motus inæquales, æqualibus temporibus, observemus. Sententias eorum, qui Φαινομένων, quæ dixi, caussas ex aliis hypothetibus extruunt, prudens ne sim prolixior, præterceo.
units.tr: Circular motion belongs to all the heavenly bodies, and it has two principal forms. Although the heavenly spheres each seem to be moved by their own and dissimilar motions, astronomical observations and the judgment of the senses teach that there are only two. One is simple, uniform and regular, by which all the heavenly orbs turn from east to west around the poles of the world, in circles parallel to the equator, in the space of a natural day. Antiquity assigned this motion to the eighth sphere; Ptolemy names it the Ninth, and more recent writers have dedicated it to the Tenth. Others call it by the name of the day, because it is completed in the space of the day and night, measuring the natural day. For this motion produces the alternation of days and nights, together with the sun's own motion; it brings the stars forth each day and displays them to us, and carries them across the upper hemisphere and then hides them again. In short, it is the common measure of all the other motions, for it carries all lower bodies with it, and the farther they are from it, the more slowly they move in this motion, as is most evident in the moon. The other motion, which Greeks and Latins call the motion of the planets or of the secondary Mobiles, some call motion in consequentia. By it the spheres that are subject to the first Mobile resist the higher motion, moving from west to east, beneath the zodiac and about its poles. They are not carried along parallels, which are evenly separated from the equator, but in dissimilar ways, and much more slowly. For those planets that are nearer the earth are carried by a swifter motion and complete their periods more quickly; on the other hand, those that are farther off proceed at a slower pace and go around the distinct spaces of the zodiac more slowly. Sometimes they seem to slow down in the middle of their course, to stand still as if motionless, and are sometimes said to go backward, which is why they are so named; then again they quicken their course, as if to make up by speed for the earlier lag, and they are so called by the Greeks. Nor do we see them always keeping the same path; they wander from the middle line of the zodiac, now toward the north, now toward the south. Finally, when they withdraw far from the earth and then descend again, as if from on high, to the earth, they are so called. But although these motions of the heavenly orbs are equal and regular, they nonetheless appear to us unequal, as a great man observes, either because of the poles of the circles, which differ from the poles of the world around which they turn, such as the poles of the zodiac, under which the wandering stars constantly move; or because the earth is not the centre of those orbs by which the planets are carried and revolved. Therefore, since we consider those motions from the centre of the world, it happens that, just as bodies appear larger when we see them from close by and smaller when we see them far away, so in equal circumferences of orbits we observe unequal motions in equal times, because of the different distance of our sight. I pass over the opinions of those who build the causes of the phenomena I have described on other hypotheses, lest I be too prolix.

units.la: CAP. XV.
units.tr: CHAP. XV.
