units.la: Brevis Stellarum Descriptio, eaque tractata membratim & excussa
units.tr: A Brief Description of the Stars, Treated and Examined Part by Part

units.la: DE Cœlo, cui in Constante Perpetuaque Totius parte priorem dederam locum, quod habui dicere, pro instituta mihi methodo, absolvi: succedit, cui alteram adsignaram stationem, Stella; cujus tam Inerrantis, non solum in Zodiaco, sed & extra eum, quam Errantis historiam aggrediar, si quædam universim præmisero.
units.tr: Having finished, according to the method I have set myself, what I had to say about the heaven, which in the constant and perpetual part of the whole I placed first, I now come to the star, to which I assigned the second place. I shall take up its history, both of the fixed stars, not only in the zodiac but also beyond it, and of the wandering stars, if I first premise some general points.

units.la: Stellæ partes putantur suorum Orbium densiores; eæque lucidæ, simplices, rotundæ; ad Orbium, quibus inlocata earum corpora, motus moveri solitæ: ut, DEO, disponente, per spacia Cœli divina & admirabili ratione decurrentes, efficiant vices Temporum gratissimas, & in natura Elementari primas temperent Qualitates, aliosque effectus gignant. Adeundus Lactantius lib. ii. Divinar. Institutionum cap. v.
units.tr: The parts of the stars are thought to be the denser parts of their spheres. They are bright, simple and round, and are accustomed to be moved by the motion of the spheres in which their bodies are set. By God's arrangement they run through the spaces of heaven in a divine and admirable manner, bring about the most welcome changes of the seasons, temper the primary qualities in elemental nature, and produce other effects. Lactantius, Divine Institutes, book ii, chapter v, should be consulted.

units.la: Densiores suorum Orbium notavi Partes. Ideoq; quum ex mole constent coactæ quasi materiæ, & veluti lucis compactæ copia; Visui tamen, ut Orbes ipsi, non sunt perviæ.
units.tr: I have noted that the stars are the denser parts of their spheres. Therefore, since they consist of the bulk of a kind of compacted matter, and as it were a mass of condensed light, they are nevertheless not transparent to sight, as the spheres themselves are not.

units.la: Esse Lucidas addidi. Lucem mittam hic agnoscō. Stellæ enim cum proprio & congenito lumine (quod luce Solis imbecillius) lucent; tam alieno, quod illis ab Sole. Hic enim fons præcipuus (videntur infra quæ de Sole mihi scripta) & ἐχημα ἀπ' ὠπωγενὲς φωτὸς, lucis suæ splendore non solum Inferiores sc Planetas & Elementarem Orbem, verum etiam Superiores & Stellas omnes liberali suæ lucis demenso imbutas, radiorum reflexione collustrat & complet. Qualiscumque Lux Siderum statuenda; certa illam volunt esse magni Viri, qua, DEO hic ordinante, Astra calorem Inferioribus impertiunt: eam quum copiosiorem in se habet Sol, quam ceteræ Stellæ, potentiæ majoris esse sc let ad calefaciendum. Peripateticorum est sententia, Cœlum per Lumen facere tam Calorem, quam Frigus, diversa tamen ratione: illum quidem per se, hoc autem per accidens. Nam præsentia Luminis facit Calorem, absentia vero Frigus: quo enim Lumen Solis, aut nullo modo aut tenuiter pertingit, inibi Frigus vigere ac roborari comperimus. Nam quod Stellas naturæ censeant Igneas, dictasque, teste Fabio, quasi Ignis Stillas; & quum per se calidæ vaporibus ex aqua terraque sublatis & ad se tractis pasci, partim Stoici apud Ciceronem ii. de nat. Deor. & Theodoretum lib. iiii. Græcanic. Affect. eosque sequutus Plinius lib. ii. nat. histor. cap. ix, partim Augustinus, scribente Magistro Sentent. Dist. xiiii. lib. ii. Basilius Homilia iii. in Genesin, Ambrosius lib. ii. in ἐξαήμερ, & alii non pauci; validissimis eos Philosophi (inter quos principis mihi loci Benedictus Pererius in Genesin) confutant argumentis. Primo, Cœlum & Astra naturæ esse incorruptibilis: non igitur esse Igneæ. Ignem enim, quum & materiam habeat & contrarium, non posse non obnoxium esse Corruptioni. Deinde, naturalem Ignis Motum esse sursum ferri: eo autem Astra perpetuo carere. Tertio, Si Astra essent Igneæ; haud dubie futurum fuisse, ut jamdudum omnia deflagrassent, & ardore Siderum consumpta interijssent: quum tantus sit in Octavo Cœlo Stellarum numerus; quarum quælibet multis partibus Terra major: quibus si addantur Planetæ, esset sane Cœlestium Ignium supra Terram undique vis fidem superans, & quæ tolerari nullo pacto posset. Indignas, quæ refutentur, arbitror portentosas Philosophorum quorundam de natura Siderum opiniones, apud Plutarchum lib. ii ἀεὶ τῶν τῆς φιλοσ. ἀρεσκ. cap. xiii. ut Thaletis, glebosa quidem existimantis esse, sed ignita Sidera; Diogenis, pumicosa & Mundi spiracula: Xenophanis, ex Ignitis Nubibus concreta; Heraclitì & Pythagoræorum, unamquamque Stellam Mundum esse, Terram suam ambientem, putantium. Iam quod nonnulli addant, Sidera terrenis aquisque humoribus ad se tractis ali (ἐκ τῆς Ἡλιακῆς ἀναθυμιάσεως, inquit Plutarch.) eorumque splendorem hoc modo accendi; puerilem esse opinionem & indignam Philosopho dixit Philosophorum princeps, Aristoteles l. ii. Meteoror. Vapores enim ultra mediam Aeris regionem non subvehi: ibi coactos densatosque in pluvias resolvi, eosque, unde sublati fuerant, relabi. Et sane unde tot tantisque Sideribus perpetuo tantum pabuli & alimenti posset suppeditari? Quid! quantum mutationum singu-
units.tr: I have added that they are bright. Here I acknowledge that they give light. The stars shine with a light that is their own and innate, which is weaker than the light of the Sun, but they also shine with a light that is foreign to them, which comes to them from the Sun. For the Sun is the principal source (as is written about the Sun below), and by the splendour of its light it illumines and fills with its reflected rays not only the inferior planets and the elemental sphere but also the superior planets and all the stars, which are imbued with the generous measure of its light [ἐχημα ἀπ' ὠπωγενὲς φωτὸς]. Whatever the light of the stars is to be judged, a great man holds it to be certain that, God ordaining it here, the stars impart heat to the lower bodies. Since the Sun has more of this light in itself than the other stars, it is of greater power for warming. It is the opinion of the Peripatetics that the heavens produce both heat and cold through light, though in different ways: heat directly, cold indirectly. For the presence of light produces heat, and its absence produces cold; for where the light of the Sun reaches not at all or only faintly, we find that cold prevails and grows strong. As for the view that the stars are of a fiery nature, and are called, as Fabius says, as it were drops of fire, and that, being hot in themselves, they are fed by vapours drawn up from water and earth and drawn to themselves, this is held partly by the Stoics, as reported by Cicero in book ii of On the Nature of the Gods, and by Theodoret in book iv of Graecarum affectionum curatio, and by Plinius, who follows them, book ii of Natural History, chapter ix; partly by Augustine, as the Master of the Sentences writes in distinction xiv of book ii; and also by Basil in Homily iii on Genesis, by Ambrose in book ii of the Hexaemeron, and by not a few others. Philosophers (among whom Benedictus Pererius on Genesis holds the first place for me) refute them with very strong arguments. First, the heaven and the stars are of an incorruptible nature; therefore they are not fiery. For fire, since it has matter and a contrary, cannot but be subject to corruption. Second, the natural motion of fire is to be carried upward, and the stars are wholly without this motion. Third, if the stars were fiery, it would undoubtedly have followed that long since all things would have been set ablaze and destroyed by the burning of the stars; for the number of stars in the eighth heaven is so great, and each of them is many times larger than the earth; if the planets are added to them, there would surely be a force of heavenly fires above the earth on every side, beyond belief, and which could not in any way be endured. I think the monstrous opinions of certain philosophers about the nature of the stars, reported by Plutarch in book ii of On the Opinions of the Philosophers, chapter xiii, are unworthy of refutation: such as that of Thales, who thought the stars were earthy clods but fiery; that of Diogenes, who held them to be pumice-like and breathing-holes of the world; that of Xenophanes, who held them to be made of fiery clouds; and that of Heraclitus and the Pythagoreans, who thought each star was a world surrounding its own earth. As for what some add, that the stars are nourished by earthly and watery humours drawn to themselves (from the exhalation of the Sun, says Plutarch), and that their brightness is kindled in this way, the prince of philosophers, Aristotle, said this was a childish opinion and unworthy of a philosopher, in book ii of the Meteorology. For vapours are not carried up beyond the middle region of the air; there they are condensed and resolved into rain, and fall back to where they were lifted from. And indeed, from where could so many and so great stars be perpetually supplied with so much fuel and nourishment?

units.la: Absurda Philosophorum aliquot opiniones de Siderum natura. singulis momentis conciliarent Astris exfucti fœdissimis locis Humores? Absit; ut hæc sint vera. Valeant hæc talia sentientes Homerus Iliados x. Heraclitus, Empedocles, Plato, Stoici apud Plutarchum, Diogenem Laertium, Macrob. 11. in Somn. Scip. cap. x. & 1. Saturnal. cap. xxiii. & alios, Plinius lib. 11. nat. historr. Latinique poetæ, Virgilius lib. 1. Æneid. ubi Servius & Lucanus lib. 1. & vii. belli Pharsalici, Seneca in Hippolyto, Chœro Act. 11. Claudianus lib. 11. de rap. Proserp. Errant toto Cœlo. Nam Errorem vere nominat Marius Victorinus Commentario in Genesin.
units.tr: (Absurd opinions of some philosophers about the nature of the stars.) What? Would the stars draw to themselves at every moment such a quantity of changing humours from the most foul places? Far be it that these things are true. Let those who hold such views be disregarded: Homer in book x of the Iliad, Heraclitus, Empedocles, Plato, the Stoics as reported by Plutarch, Diogenes Laertius, Macrobius on the Dream of Scipio, book ii, chapter x, and Saturnalia, book i, chapter xxiii, and others; Pliny, book ii of the Natural History; and the Latin poets: Virgil in book i of the Aeneid, where Servius comments; Lucan in books i and vii of the Civil War (Pharsalia); Seneca in the Hippolytus, chorus, act ii; Claudian in book ii of On the Rape of Proserpina. They wander through the whole heaven. For Marius Victorinus, in his commentary on Genesis, rightly calls it an error.

units.la: Simplices dixi. Formatæ enim creduntur ex Orbium suorum simplicissima & purissima materia: quæ densata primum & contracta ad certam Cœli sui regionem, deinde Collectionis absolutæ beneficio in solidiorem orbem conglobata.
units.tr: I said simple. For they are believed to be formed from the most simple and purest matter of their spheres, which was first condensed and contracted into a certain region of their heaven, and then, by the benefit of complete collection, gathered into a more solid sphere.

units.la: Rotunda Stellarum Corpora docent cum Sphærica Solis Lunæque figura in Eclipsibus; tum φαινόμενα. Nam intuentibus, ex quacumque terreni globi parte, Globosæ apparent: quod non fieret, si vel essent planæ, vel εισκεδὲς, vel alius figuræ.
units.tr: The round bodies of the stars are shown both by the spherical shape of the Sun and Moon in eclipses, and by the appearances. For to observers, from whatever part of the terrestrial globe, they appear globular; this would not be so if they were flat, or of some other shape.

units.la: Ad Orbium, quibus inhærent, Motus moveri solitas adscripti. Non enim moventur Stellæ per spatium Cœleste proprijs per se Motibus; ut voluerunt, non solum Stoici, quod patet ex Aristotele lib. 11. de Cœlo, text. 43. & seqq. & M. Tullio lib. 11. de natura Deorum; sed etiam Scriptores Ecclesiastici, Iustinus Martyr respondens ad quæst. xviii. Orthodoxor. Origenes lib. v. contra Celsum, & lib. 1. περὶ ἀρχῶν vii. Chrysostomus Homilijs vi. xii. & xiii. Philastrius Brixiensis Episcopus Catalogo Hæref. Procopius Gazæus ad cap. 1. Genes. Legendus & Augustinus lib. 11. de Genes. ad litteram cap. x. verum accidentarijs ad Orbium, quibus infixæ, Motus: ut pars ad Totius, ut Clavus, dicis causa, ad Rotæ motum. Consulendus præter alios Macrobius lib. 1. ad Somnium Scipionis cap. xvii. Nam cuivis globoso Corpori duo tantum conveniunt Motus proprij: κύλισις quam volutationem dicere licet; & Δίνησις, quæ nihil aliud quam in gyrum conversio. Stellæ igitur, quæ Corpora globosa, si primarijs & proprijs agitarentur motibus, vel huc illuc volutarentur, vel in gyrum converterentur. Sed nec volutantur; nam loca quæ in Orbibus suis obtinent numquam mutant nec gyrantur; circumactas enim eam, quam semel nobis ostenderunt, faciem numquam variare, quod in Luna perspicuum, videmus. Accidit, quum Motus Diurnus fiat xxiv. horarum spacio, si Stellæ non æqualiter cum Orbibus suis moverentur, Orbes certe vel perrumpi & dissecari, vel rarefieri necesse esset. Stellæque namque velocius motæ finderent suos Orbes. Non est autem rationi consentaneum, inquit Philosophus 11. Cœli text. 45. ut Stellarum velocitates & magnitudines Orbium eandem habeant rationem. Nam una Stella ad aliam non habet eam in velocitate proportionem, quam unus Orbis habet ad alterum. Unde fit, ut ipsa pari velocitate cum suo Orbe nequaquam moveatur: Orbis enim, ut bene Hannibal Rolfelus ad Pymandrum Mercurij lib. iv. Comment. v. quæst. 1. ad Orbem in velocitate proportionem habet; non autem Stella ad Stellam. Sic enim Stella, utpote Mercurius, qui est in Orbe majori, velocior esset alia Stella, nimirum Luna, quæ est in Orbe minore. Quod si Orbes suos mutuo commutarent, utpote si Mercurius in Lunæ orbem migraret, & è diverso Luna in Mercurij; tunc Luna velocior esset Mercurio, idque propter Orbem Mercurij, in quo consisteret. Ex quo perspicuum est, Stellas ex se nullum Motum habere, nisi cum tantum, quem Orbis ipse.
units.tr: I added that they are moved by the motion of the spheres to which they are attached. For the stars do not move through the heavenly space by their own proper motions, as not only the Stoics held, as is clear from Aristotle, book ii On the Heavens, text 43 and following, and Cicero in book ii On the Nature of the Gods, but also ecclesiastical writers: Justin Martyr in answer to question xviii of the Orthodox, Origen in book v Against Celsus and book i On First Principles, chapter vii, Chrysostom in Homilies vi, xii and xiii, Philastrius, bishop of Brescia, in his Catalogue of Heresies, and Procopius of Gaza on Genesis, chapter i. Augustine, book ii On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, chapter x, should also be read. Rather, they have a motion that is incidental to the spheres in which they are fixed, as a part moves with the whole, as a nail, for example, moves with the motion of a wheel. Besides others, Macrobius, book i on the Dream of Scipio, chapter xvii, should be consulted. For only two proper motions belong to any round body: rolling, which we may call volutation (kylisis), and spinning (dinēsis), which is nothing other than turning in a circle. Therefore stars, being round bodies, if they were moved by primary and proper motions, would either be rolled hither and thither or would turn round. But they are not rolled, for they never change the places they hold in their spheres, nor do they turn round; for we see that the face they once showed us never varies, as is evident in the Moon. It happens that, since the diurnal motion takes place over a space of twenty-four hours, if the stars were not moved equally with their spheres, the spheres would certainly have to be broken and split or rarefied. For stars moved more swiftly would tear their spheres. Now, as the Philosopher says in book ii On the Heavens, text 45, it is not reasonable that the velocities of the stars and the magnitudes of their spheres should have the same ratio. For one star does not have to another the same proportion of velocity that one sphere has to another. Hence it follows that a star cannot move with the same velocity as its sphere. For the sphere, as Hannibal Rolfinck rightly says in his commentary on the Pymander of Mercury, book iv, comment v, question 1, has a proportion of velocity to the sphere, but a star does not have it to a star. For thus a star such as Mercury, which is in the larger sphere, would be faster than another star, namely the Moon, which is in the smaller sphere. But if they exchanged their spheres with one another, as if Mercury migrated into the sphere of the Moon and, conversely, the Moon into that of Mercury, then the Moon would be swifter than Mercury, and this on account of the sphere of Mercury in which it would then be. From this it is clear that the stars have no motion of their own, except only that which the sphere itself has.

units.la: Amplius dico. Si Stellæ Sphærarum suarum spacia proprijs motibus ferrentur; sequeretur, Cœlum esse Corpus fluidum, labile, solidioribus facile cedens, vel aquæ velaeri simile: quæ ab natura Cœlestis corporis & dignitate videntur alienæ; præsertim quum Hiobi cap. xxxvii. Scriptura Sacra doceat, Cælos esse solidissimos, & tamquam ex ære conflatos: quod innuit & Homerus lib. xxi. Iliados: Ἰσχὺν ἀλυμπιάδες διὸς πᾶς χαλκοβατὴς δῶ.
units.tr: I add this: if the stars were carried by their own motions through the spaces of their spheres, it would follow that the heaven is a fluid, slippery body, yielding easily to solid things, or like a sort of water or air. These seem alien to the nature and dignity of a heavenly body, especially since Holy Scripture teaches in Job chapter 37 that the heavens are most solid and as if cast of bronze; Homer too hints at this in Iliad book 21: "the brazen-floored house of Olympian Zeus" [Ἰσχὺν ἀλυμπιάδες διὸς πᾶς χαλκοβατὴς δῶ].

units.la: Quid plura? Multi quum ad Motus, qui Stellis esse possent proprij, stabiliendos rationes physicas animadverterent deesse; Vitam ijs & Animas easque intelligentes, cum ad alia peragunda, tum ad motus, quos dixi, conficiendos tribuere sunt ausi: multi nuquam, non solum Pphilosophi veteres, ut Pythagorei, Platonici, Aristotelici, Stoici; videndi omnino Plato in Epinomide, Aristoteles lib. 11. de Cœlo, text. 13. & 61. Philo lib. de Opificio Mundi, de Somnijs, de Gigantibus; Lucibus Stoicus apud
units.tr: Why say more? Many, when they noticed that there were no physical reasons to establish motions that could be proper to the stars, dared to attribute to them life and souls, and intelligent souls at that, to carry out other tasks as well as the motions I have mentioned. Many have done this, not only ancient philosophers such as the Pythagoreans, Platonists, Aristotelians and Stoics (one should consult Plato in the Epinomis, Aristotle On the Heavens book 2, text 13 and 61, and Philo in his books On the Creation of the World, On Dreams and On the Giants; the Stoic Lucius among others, in Cicero's On the Nature of the Gods, and Averroes in book 1 of On the Heavens and in his book On the Substance of the Sphere, and Avicenna in book 5 of the Natural Sciences, and others),

units.la: Non sunt animatæ.
units.tr: are not animated.

units.la: apud Ciceronem de Natur. Deor. Averroes lib. i. Cæli, & libro de substantia Orbis: Avicenna lib. v. Naturalium, & alij) verum etiam Ecclesiastici Scriptores: inter quos primum ducit agmen Origenes tomo i. Commment. in Ioannem, & lib. i. περὶ ἀρχῶν, cap. vii. & Homilia postrema in librum Numerorum. Ab Origenis opinione non omnino videntur abhorrere Aureolus apud Capreolum ii. Sentent. Scotus lib. ii. Sentent. Distinct. xiii. quæst. i. Thomas quæst. de Anima, art. viii. opusculo de Angelis, cap. ii. lib. ii. contra gentes, cap. lxx. & Cajetanus ad Psalm. cxxxv. vers. 5. D. Augustinum, quum prestius quæstionem hanc de Vita Sensuque Stellarum examinaret, in consilii quasi trivio fuisse, probant, quæ ab illo scripta lib. ii. de Genesi ad literam, cap. xviii. Enchiridij cap. xviii. libro de Immortalitate Animæ cap. xv. lib. vi. de Musica, cap. xiv. lib. xiii. de Civitate Dei, cap. xvi. libro denique i. Retractationum, cap. xv. Certe, opinionum hanc animus adversatus, contrariam sententiam amplectitur; utpote quæ probabilior, quæ sanior, quæ Doctrinæ Theologicæ convenientior. Nam Astra non esse Animata, non Vita, non Intellectu prædita, censent recte Basilius Homilia iii. in Genesin,& Comment. Psalm. xlix. Ambr. lib. ii. ἐξαημ. cap. iv. Hieronymus epist. lix. ad Avitum, & lib. xiii. Comment. in Iesaiah. Cyrillus Archiepisc. Hierosolymitanus lib. ii. contra Iulianum, Ioannes Damasc. lib. ii. cap. vi. Quorum omnium instar sit, Christianus ille Cicero L. Cœlius Lactantius, qui fallam Superiorum opinionem variis argumentis confutat lib. ii. Divinar. Instit. cap. v, cujus inter alia verba sunt hæc verissima: Inest Sideribus Ratio; sed Dei est illa Ratio, qui fecit & regit omnia, non ipsorum Siderum, quæ moventur. Ab Dei nutu pendet quidquid in Rerum natura: hic solus omnia gubernat & dirigit, mediate & immediate, ut primo libro plene dixi. Frustra sunt igitur, qui Stellas putant Animatas: magis autem, qui tamquam vita, Sensu, Ratione præditas colunt, ut Deos. Pythagoras apud Diogenem Laertium Solem, Lunam & reliqua Sidera Deos esse judicat, quum in illis superet calor, qui Vitæ auctor. Plato in Epinomide, jubet Astra in Deos cœlestes a nobis honorari & coli. Idem in Cratylo, docet Astra fuisse primos Deos a prisci s existimatos. Et sane cui non, ostensa Solis, Lunæ, Astrorum pulchritudine commemoratisque tot tantisque commoditatibus, quas ex illis perpetuo percipit genus humanum, facile persuaderetur Stellas tanquam Deos colendas? In errorem hunc prolapsi non modo Gentiles, sed etiam populus Dei, qui (quamvis præmonitus, & contra lapsus horrendos præmunitus ab Ductore Doctoreque suo Moyse; ne, quæ Deus in ministerium cunctis sub Cœlo gentibus creavit, coleret, Deuteronom. cap. iv, 19) quod Solem adoraret Orientem, quod Lunæ tamquam Cœli Reginæ sacrificaret, quod omnem Cœli militiam venerareturn, quam graviter à Prophetis objurgatus? Nimius essem si reprehensionum instituerem commemorationem. Divinæ Leo Romanus Præsul, Homilia ii. de Nativitate: Absit ab animis Christianis, inquit, impia superstitio prodigiosumque mendacium: ultra omnem modum distant à Sempiterno Temporalia, ab Incorporeo Corporea, à Dominatore Sub jectas; quæ etsi mirandam habent pulchritudinem, adorandam tamen non habent Deitatem. Illa ergo virtus, illa est Sapientia, illa est colenda Majestas, quæ Universitatem Mundi creavit ex nihilo, & in quas voluit formas atque mensuras terrenam cœlestemque substantiam omnipotenti ratione produxit. Sol & Luna & Sidera sint commoda utentibus, sint speciosa cernentibus: sed ita, ut de illis gratia referantur Auctori; & adoretur Deus, qui condidit; non Creatura, quæ servit. Et Homilia vii. Adduntur, ait, & illi, qui totam humanæ vitæ conditionem de Stellarum pendere effectibus mentiuntur; & quod est aut divinæ voluntatis aut nostra, indeclinabilium dicunt esse Deorum: quæ tamen ut cumulatius nocent, spondent posse mutari, si illis, quæ adversantur, Sideribus supplicetur. Unde commentum ipsum sua ratione destruitur: quia si prædicta non permanent, non sunt Fata metuenda; si permanent, non sunt Astra veneranda. De talibus institutis etiam illa generatur impietas, ut Sol inchoatione diurna lucis exsurgens, a quibusdam insipientioribus de locis eminentioribus adoretur, & quæ multa ibi sequuntur.
units.tr: but also the ecclesiastical writers, among whom Origen leads the way, in volume 1 of his Commentary on John, in book 1 of On First Principles chapter 7, and in his last homily on the book of Numbers. Aureolus, as cited by Capreolus in book 2 of the Sentences, Scotus in book 2 of the Sentences distinction 13 question 1, Thomas in the question On the Soul article 8, in the opuscule On Angels chapter 2, in book 2 of Against the Gentiles chapter 70, and Cajetan on Psalm 135 verse 5, seem not altogether to shrink from Origen's opinion. They also cite St Augustine, who, when he examined this question about the life and sense of the stars more carefully, was as it were at a crossroads of counsel; they appeal to what he wrote in book 2 of The Literal Meaning of Genesis chapter 18, in the Enchiridion chapter 18, in the book On the Immortality of the Soul chapter 15, in book 6 of On Music chapter 14, in book 13 of The City of God chapter 16, and finally in book 1 of the Retractations chapter 15. Certainly my own mind is opposed to that opinion and embraces the contrary view, as being the more probable, the more sound, and the more agreeable to theological doctrine. For Basil, in homily 3 on Genesis and in his commentary on Psalm 49, rightly holds that the stars are not animated, nor endowed with life or intellect; so too Ambrose in book 2 of the Hexaemeron chapter 4, Jerome in letter 59 to Avitus and in book 13 of his commentary on Isaiah, Cyril, archbishop of Jerusalem, in book 2 against Julian, and John of Damascus in book 2 chapter 6. The Christian Cicero, Lucius Caelius Lactantius, is worth more than all of them: he refutes the false opinion of the ancients with various arguments in book 2 of the Divine Institutes chapter 5, and among his words are these most true ones: "There is reason in the stars; but that reason is God's, who made and rules all things, not of the stars themselves, which are moved." Whatever is in the nature of things depends on the nod of God; he alone governs and directs all things, mediately and immediately, as I fully explained in the first book. They are therefore wrong who think the stars are animated, and still more those who worship them as endowed with life, sense and reason, as gods. Pythagoras, according to Diogenes Laertius, judges that the Sun, the Moon and the other stars are gods, since heat, which is the author of life, prevails in them. Plato in the Epinomis bids us honor and worship the heavenly stars as gods. The same man in the Cratylus teaches that the stars were regarded by the ancients as the first gods. And indeed, who would not easily be persuaded to worship the stars as gods, once the beauty of the Sun, Moon and stars is displayed and so many great benefits are recalled which the human race perpetually receives from them? Into this error have fallen not only the Gentiles but also the people of God, who, although forewarned and fortified against these dreadful lapses by their guide and teacher Moses, not to worship what God created as a service for all nations under heaven (Deuteronomy 4:19), nevertheless worshipped the rising Sun, sacrificed to the Moon as queen of heaven, and venerated the whole host of heaven, and were severely rebuked for it by the prophets. I would be too long if I set out a recital of the rebukes. The Roman bishop Leo, in homily 2 On the Nativity, says: "Let impious superstition and monstrous falsehood be far from Christian minds. Things temporal are at an infinite remove from the eternal, things corporeal from the incorporeal, things subject from their lord; and though these have a wonderful beauty, they do not have divinity to be worshipped. That power, that wisdom, that majesty is to be worshipped which created the universe out of nothing and brought forth the earthly and heavenly substance, in whatever forms and measures it willed, by almighty reason. Let the Sun, Moon and stars be useful to those who use them and lovely to those who behold them; but so that thanks for them are referred to their Author, and God is adored who made them, not the creature which serves." And in homily 7: "There are also those," he says, "who falsely claim that the whole condition of human life depends on the effects of the stars, and they call what belongs to the divine will or to ours the gods of unchangeable necessity; yet these, to do the more harm, promise that they can be changed if the stars opposed to them are supplicated. Thus the fiction is destroyed by its own reasoning: for if the predicted things do not come to pass, they are not fates to be feared; if they do come to pass, the stars are not to be venerated. From such institutions also arises that impiety by which the Sun, rising at the beginning of the daylight, is worshipped by some more foolish people from higher places, and much else follows there."

units.la: CAP. XVI.
units.tr: CHAP. XVI.

units.la: Astrologia quatenus licita.
units.tr: Astrology, so far as it is lawful.

units.la: FInes denique, Stellas praecedentis Capitis initio describens, indicavi: gratas ut Temporum vices efficiant; primarias temperent in Elementari natura Qualitates; aliosque effectus, Deo disponente, gignant. Genesis cap. 1. 14. Fiant Luminaria in Firmamento Caeli, & dividant Diem ac Noctem (להבדיל בין היום ובין הלילה) & sint in Signa, & Tempora, & Dies, & Annos (והיו לאתות ולמועדים ולימים ושנים) Sic Psalmo cvi. 19. Fecit Lunam in tempora (למועדים) Sol cognovit Occasum suum. Quorum illa, Sint in Signa, varias ab variis acceperunt interpretationes. Nonnulli referunt ad Signa Festorum; quae, ut Pascha, Succhoth, Novilunia & alia, ab Iudaeis annuatim celebrantur, quorumque observatio ex Lunae pendebat & computabatur cursu atque revolutione: Multi ad xlviii. Siderum Imagines, de quibus postea, Plerique ad Signa naturalium effectuum: utriusque, dico, notionis Tempestatum & Valitudinum, Annorum vel fertilium vel sterilium, & similium Prognostica. Sunt denique, qui sacratissimam magni Numinis vocem trahere non verentur ad Astrologicam Divinationem, qua ex Siderum observatione futura rerum Eventa praesciri praedicique posse volunt.
units.tr: Finally, in describing the stars at the beginning of the preceding chapter, I indicated their purposes: that they bring about the changes of the seasons, temper the primary qualities in elemental nature, and produce other effects, as God disposes. Genesis 1:14: Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven, and let them divide the day and the night [להבדיל בין היום ובין הלילה] and let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and years [והיו לאתות ולמועדים ולימים ושנים]. So Psalm cvi. 19: He made the moon for seasons [למועדים], the sun knows its going down. Of these, the words let them be for signs have received various interpretations from various writers. Some refer them to the signs of the festivals, which the Jews celebrate every year, such as Passover, Tabernacles, the new moons and others, and whose observance depended on the moon and was reckoned by its course and revolution. Many refer them to the forty-eight images of the stars, of which more later. Most refer them to the signs of natural effects: I mean, of both kinds, the prognostications of weather and health, and of years fruitful or barren, and the like. Lastly, there are those who do not hesitate to drag the most sacred voice of the great Divinity into astrological divination, by which they want future events to be foreknown and predicted from observation of the stars.

units.la: Duorum, quos nominavi primitus, interpretationi locus vix esse potest; ut quae artiore Coeli Terraeque spacio, quam par est, & divinae vocis mens flagitat, coerceatur: Horum quidem, quod Effectuum Naturalium praenotiones non tam sint in Stellis Fixis, quam Errantibus; quodque Signorum xlviii. formatura & nomenclatio (quarum hodie usus) ab hominum sint ingeniis; Illorum vero, quod unam solum In Mundi centro gentem respiciat. Nam ad quid in aeterna constantique illa Totius sede lex erat scribenda Festis, quae summam subitura essent Inconstantiam; quaeque, quum venisset τὸ πλήρωμα τῶν χρόνων (Galat. iv, 4.) non amplius essent futura; Festis, inquam, unius, cujusque populi, cujus ob ingratitudinem aliaque flagitia Status esset aliquando exterminandus? Reliquorum quos deinceps adscripsi opinio, Priorum quidem admittenda; Posteriorum vero, quod prava, pestifera, exsecrabilis, prorsus est proscribenda, odiisque premenda capitalibus.
units.tr: There can hardly be room for the interpretation of the first two, since they confine heaven and earth within a narrower space than is right, and than the mind of the divine word requires. Of the first, the claim is that the foreknowledge of natural effects lies not so much in the fixed stars as in the wandering ones, and that the shaping and naming of the forty-eight signs, which are in use today, come from human wit. Of the second, the claim is that it looks to one nation only, placed at the centre of the world. For why would a law for festivals be written in that eternal and unchanging seat of the whole world, when those festivals were destined to undergo the greatest inconstancy, and when, once the fullness of time [τὸ πλήρωμα τῶν χρόνων] had come (Gal. 4:4), they would no longer be in force? Festivals, I say, of one single people, whose state was at some time to be destroyed on account of its ingratitude and other crimes? The opinion of the rest that I listed afterwards is to be admitted in the case of the former; but the latter, because it is perverse, pestilent and detestable, is utterly to be proscribed and suppressed with deadly hatred.

units.la: Priorum, dixi admittendam; modo parce, salvoque, qui magno Numini debetur, Honore, & intemerata fiat illud ejus reverentia. Particularem enim rerum Coelestium notitiam DEVM sibi soli servasse, tam est certum, quam quod certissimum. Solus ille novit vires & operationes Stellarum: Ille multitudinem Siderum numerat, (יקרא לכלם שמות, τῶν ἀστέρων πλῆθος ἐν ὀνόμασι καλῶν) omnes impositis nominibus vocans, Psalmo cxlvii, 4. Ille educit in numero militiam eorum, & (בשם יקרא לכלם) omnibus ipsis indidit nomen prae amplitudine virium, prout fortis est robore, adeo ut quidquam non desit. Iesaiah xl, 26. Nomina Stellis audimus hic imposita; non dubium, quin a proprietatibus, quas solus perfecte sapienterque novit, qui potenter eas condidit: ut eadem Oda merito exclamet Propheta: Magnus Dominus noster, Magna Virtus ejus, & Sapientiae ejus non est numerus. Non enim solum Sol, Luna, Stellae Lucem toti Rerum naturae, quod oculi quotidie restantur, praebent; discrimina facientes Diei & Noctis; Laboris item Quietisque distinctes intervalla, Genes. 1, 19. 20, 21, 22, 23. Psalm. civ, 19. & cxxxvi, & 7, 8, 9: sed etiam adgenita quadam Influentia secundario variant & gubernant quodammodo Inferiora; excitantque certas Inclinationes virtute, qualem illorum Naturae Deus indidit, indicamque conservat. Prudenter Aristoteles 1. Meteoror. dixit, Mundum hunc Elementarem Superiorum motibus esse contiguum; ut ejus inde Virtus aliquo modo posset gubernari. A qua sententia non abhorret D. Augustinus lib. iii. de Trinitate, cap. iv. asserens Corpora crassiora locorumque inferiorum per subtiliora, ut quae potentiae penetrantioris, ordine quodam regi. Clarius autem lib. v. de Civitate Dei, cap. vi. ubi inter disceptandum cum Mathematicis haec inter alia profert, Non usquequaque absurde dici potest, ad solas Corporum differentias adflatus quosdam valere Sidereos, Sicut in Solaribus accessibus & decessibus videmus etiam ipsius anni tempora variari; & Lunaribus incrementis atque decrementis augeri & minui quædam genera rerum; sicut Echinos & Conchas & mirabiles (AEtus Oceani, non autem & Animi voluntates (notandum hoc) positionibus Siderum subdi. Placent mihi versus illi, qui in Palatio vetere Pragensi; Sidera Corporibus præsunt Cœlestia nostris, Influxuque regunt cuncta Elementa suo: Cogere sed nequeunt Animam Ratione frui tem; Namque sub Imperio solum illa DEI est.
units.tr: Of the former, I said it is to be admitted, provided it is done sparingly, the honour owed to the great Divinity is preserved, and reverence for him is kept inviolate. For that God has reserved to himself alone the particular knowledge of heavenly things is as certain as anything most certain. He alone knows the powers and operations of the stars: He counts the multitude of the stars [יקרא לכלם שמות, τῶν ἀστέρων πλῆθος ἐν ὀνόμασι καλῶν] calling them all by their names, Psalm cxlvii. 4. He brings out their host by number, and [בשם יקרא לכלם] gives a name to them all, by reason of the abundance of their powers, since he is strong in might, so that nothing is lacking, Isaiah 40:26. We hear here names given to the stars. There is no doubt they are taken from the properties which he alone knows perfectly and wisely, he who powerfully founded them; so the Prophet rightly exclaims in the same ode: Great is our Lord, great is his power, and of his wisdom there is no number. For the sun, moon and stars do not only give light to the whole of nature, which the eyes perceive every day, making the distinctions of day and night and likewise marking out the intervals of labour and rest (Genesis 1:19, 20, 21, 22, 23; Psalm civ. 19; and cxxxvi. 7, 8, 9). They also, by some added influence, secondarily vary and in some way govern lower things, and stir up certain inclinations by a power such as God has put into their nature and keeps as he designed it. Aristotle wisely said in the first book of the Meteorology that this elemental world is contiguous to the motions of the higher bodies, so that its power can be governed in some way from them. Augustine does not dissent from this view in De Trinitate III, ch. 4, asserting that grosser bodies and lower places are ruled in a certain order through finer ones, as being of more penetrating power. He is clearer in De Civitate Dei V, ch. 6, where, in disputing with the mathematicians, he advances among other things this: It cannot altogether absurdly be said that certain sidereal breezes avail only for the differences of bodies, just as we see that even the seasons of the year vary with the approaches and withdrawals of the sun, and by the increases and decreases of the moon certain kinds of things are increased and diminished, such as sea-urchins, shellfish and the wonderful tides of the ocean; but the wills of the soul (note this) are not subject to the positions of the stars. Those verses please me which stand in the old palace at Prague: The heavenly stars rule our bodies and govern all the elements by their influence; but they cannot force the soul to enjoy reason, for it is under the sole rule of God.

units.la: Suspiciamus veneremur mirificum Artificem, qui sursum & deorsum pulcre dispolui omnia, ut suavissimo concentu inter se respondeant. Non admittendum, quod Ratio naturalis admittit; non improbandum, quod probant Sacræ Litteræ; quæ testantur DEVM hæc nostra regere clementer per Superiora. Hoischehhæ cap. 11. vers. 21. Erit etiam die illo ut exaudiam (אֶעֱנֶה, ἐπακούσομαι) Iehovæ; exaudiam Cœlos, & ipsi exaudiant Terram, & Terra exaudiat frumentum & musnum & oleum, & ipsa exaudi ut Iezrahel. Audimus hic DEI voluntatem præcedere; ut intelligamus ab ea primario cuncta pendere; nihil in nos posse Astra, absque eius nutu. In eius enim conspectu omnes Viæ nostræ, Psalm. cxix, 168. Illæ vitæ nostræ vena, Psalm. xxxvi. 10. Omnes capilli nostri sunt ab eo numerati; nullus inde decidit absque DEI voluntate. Matth. x, 30. Lucæ xxi, 7. xxi. 18. Commendemus Nos, Viam, & Vitam nostram DEO; & ipse faciet, Psalm. xxxvii, 5. Clamemus cum regio Propheta, Psalm. xxxi, 16. In manu tua sunt tempora nostra; Vita & status Rerum nostrarum universus penes te est: à te dependet, non ab Astris, non aliunde. Nil timeamus nobis à Signis Cœli, Ieremiæ cap. x, 2. Sciamus Angelos vitæ nostræ comites & custodes: militemus bonam militiam, retinentes fidem & bonam Conscientiam, Paulus Apost. epist. 1. ad Timoth. 1, 19. & Auctor Epist. ad Heb. xiii, 18. Quin & Sol, Luna, Stellæ agitantes, adficientes, variantes, Elementa, Plantas, Animantia, Signa recte dicuntur, & revera deprehenduntur esse Tempestatum in regione Elementari, aliarumque Varietatum in Inferioribus Corporibus. Meminit ipse Christus apud Matthæum, cap. xvi, 2. Facto vespere dicitis, Serenum erit; rubicundum est enim Cœlum: Et mane, Hodie Tempestas: rutilat enim triste Cœlum: Faciem ergo Cœli dijudicare nostis: signa autem temporum non potestis. Huc igitur pertinent tot tantis viris, Arato, Virgilio, Plinio, Festo Avieno, aliisque observata, tam feliciter, non tamen tam vere, ut ipsi volunt, Prognostica ex φαινομένοις Solis, Lunæ, Stellarum; Nautis præcipue Agricolisque interventia: quæ Christianis etiam non inlicita, modo metæ serventur. Sunt enim Physicæ τερπνῆς, aliæ prorsus à Prædictionibus ἀστρολογικῆς & prohibitis. Temporum electio ad initiandum aliquod opus, aliis conceditur, in aliis improbatur. Conceditur seminaturis: plantaturis; ligna, ne tereditne perforentur, vel infestentur carie, in ædificia struenda cæsuris: venas pertusuris: ijs denique qui morbis medicinas facturi, aliaque auspicaturi. Volunt hoc illa, quæ paullo ante ex Augustini libro de Civitate Dei v. cap. vi. laudavi; Non usquequaque absurde dici potest, ad solus Corporum differentias adstatus quosdam valere Sidereos: ut &, quæ ejusdem, ad Ianuarium scribentis: Non autem, inquit, quisquam sapiens arbitretur, Observatores Temporum reprehendendos; qui dicunt; Non proficisci hodie, quia tempestas exorta est, &c. vel si qui forte alij naturales effectus circa motum aeris & humoris ad variandas Temporum qualitates ex Siderum ordinatissima conversione notati sunt; de quibus dictum est, quum conderentur; ut sint in Signa & Tempora, Dies & Annos. Improbatur autem observatio Temporum, si quis uxorem ducturus, quid vel emturus vel vendigurus, aliumve contractum celebraturus, & alia talia meditans. Irridet Augustinus, & merito, lib. v. de Civitate Dei cap. vii. O stultitiam, inquit, singularem: eligitur dies, ut ducatur uxor. Credo propterea quia potest in diem non bonum, nisi cagatur, incurri, & in felicitier duci. Superstitiosos hic fuisse Romanos legere est apud Festum, lib. xii. de verb. significat. cujus hæc: Nonarum, Fiduum, Kalendarum posteri dies nuptiis alieni habentur. Additur absurda ratio: Quoniam hi dies decreto Pontificum Atri iudicati sunt; quod quotiescunque Romani Duces belli gerendi gratia his diebus supplicaverunt, maiorem publicam gessere. Mensem etiam Maium nuptiis inauspicatum fuisse Romanis existimatum, scribit Plutarchus quæst. Romanar. xxxcvi. Hinc notum vulgo Proverbium, Mense Maio malas nubere Ovidius v, Fast. Nec Vidua tedis eadem, nec Virginis apta Tempora; qua nupsit; nec diuturna fuit. Hac quoque de causa, si te Proverbia tangunt,Mense malas Maio nubere, Vulgus ait.
units.tr: Let us look up to and revere the wondrous Artificer, who arranged all things above and below so beautifully that they answer one another in the sweetest harmony. What natural reason admits is not to be rejected, and what the Holy Scriptures approve is not to be condemned; they testify that God mercifully rules these our affairs through the higher things. Hosea 2:21: And it shall come to pass in that day that I will hear [אֶעֱנֶה, ἐπακούσομαι] Jehovah; I will hear the heavens, and they shall hear the earth, and the earth shall hear the corn, and the wine, and the oil, and they shall hear Jezreel. We hear here that God's will comes first, so that we understand that all things depend chiefly on it, and that the stars can do nothing to us without his nod. For all our ways are in his sight (Psalm cxix. 168); he is the vein of our life (Psalm xxxvi. 10). All the hairs of our head are numbered by him, and none falls without the will of God (Matthew 10:30; Luke 21:7, 18). Let us commit ourselves, our way and our life to God, and he will act (Psalm xxxvii. 5). Let us cry out with the royal Prophet (Psalm xxxi. 16): In your hand are our times. The life and the whole state of our affairs is in your power; it depends on you, not on the stars, not on anything else. Let us fear nothing from the signs of heaven (Jeremiah x. 2). Let us know that angels are the companions and guardians of our life, and let us wage the good warfare, holding faith and a good conscience (Paul, 1 Timothy 1:19, and the author of Hebrews 13:18). Indeed, the sun, moon and stars, by moving, affecting and varying the elements, plants, animals and seasons, are rightly said, and are in fact found, to be the signs of weather in the elemental region and of other changes in lower bodies. Christ himself mentions this in Matthew xvi. 2: When it is evening you say, It will be fair weather, for the sky is red. And in the morning, Today there will be a storm, for the sky is red and lowering. You know how to judge the face of the sky, but you cannot read the signs of the times. To this belong the observations made by so many great men, Aratus, Virgil, Pliny, Festus Avienus and others: prognostications, made from the appearances of the sun, moon and stars, happily though not as truly as they wished, and especially useful to sailors and farmers. These are not unlawful even for Christians, provided their limits are kept. For they are physical and pleasant, and quite different from astrological predictions, which are forbidden. The choice of times for beginning some work is allowed in some cases and disapproved in others. It is allowed for those sowing and planting; for those cutting timber, lest it be pierced or infested with rot, and for those building; for those about to open veins; and finally for those about to begin medical treatments or other undertakings. Augustine, quoted a little above from De Civitate Dei V, ch. 6, says the same: It cannot altogether absurdly be said that certain sidereal breezes avail only for the differences of bodies. So too in what he writes to Januarius: But let no wise man think, he says, that the observers of times are to be rebuked, who say, Do not set out today, because a storm has arisen, and so on; or if other natural effects concerning the motion of air and moisture, which vary the qualities of the seasons, have perhaps been noted from the most orderly turning of the stars, about which it was said when they were made that they should be for signs and for seasons, days and years. But the observation of times is disapproved if someone, about to take a wife, or about to buy or sell, or to make some other contract, is meditating such things. Augustine mocks this, and rightly, De Civitate Dei V, ch. 7: O singular folly, he says: a day is chosen for taking a wife. I suppose it is because one may fall into an unlucky day, unless one is careful, and be led into a happy one. That the Romans were superstitious in this may be read in Festus, book xii, On the meaning of words, whose words are: The days after the Nones, the Ides and the Kalends are regarded as unfit for weddings. He adds an absurd reason: Because these days were judged unlucky by a decree of the Pontiffs; whenever Roman generals made supplications on these days for the sake of waging war, they waged a greater public war. Plutarch, Roman Questions xxxcvi., writes that the Romans thought the month of May unlucky for weddings. Hence the common proverb, To marry in May is bad. Ovid, Fasti v: Nor is the same time fit for the widow's torches and the virgin's; she who married then did not last long. For this reason also, if proverbs touch you, the common people say: to marry badly in May.

units.la: Docet idem lib. Fastor. II. Conjugium etiam vitandum Parentalibus, quæ Februario mense celebrabantur; & lib. III. diebus Festis Saliorum. Contra tempus, quod Eidus Iunias sequitur, Conjugijs canit aptissimum idem poëta lib. Fastorum VI. Dies alij, qui nuptijs contrahendis vitabantur, recensentur ab Macrobio lib. I. Saturnal. cap. xv. Quid hic Nos? Potioris sint nobis momenti monita Augustini, quæ in Decreto Gratiani, 26. quæst. 7. Non observetis dies qui dicuntur Ægyptiaci, aut Kalendas Ianuarij, in quibus Cantilena quedam, & Comessationes, & ad invicem dono donantur; quasi in principio anni, boni fati augurio: aut aliquot Menses, aut Tempora, aut Dies, & Annos; aut Lunæ Solisque cursum: quia qui & has & quascumque Divinationes, aut Fata. aut Auguria observat aut attendit, aut consentit observantibus, inutiliter, sine causa, magis ad sui damnationem, quam ad salutem tendit; sive per quosdam numeros litterarum & Luna, per Pythagoricam Necromantiam Ægrotantium vitam vel mortem, vel prospera vel adversa futura inquirunt, sive qui attendunt somniatoria scripta & falsa, Danielis nomine intitulata; & Sortes, quæ dicuntur Sanctorum Apostolorum, & Auguria Avium, aut aliqua pro domo facienda, aut propter conjugia copulanda, &c. Quid ni? Adscribit in fine causam: Dicit enim Apostolus, inquit, Sive manducatis, sive bibitis, sive aliquid aliud facitis; in nomine Domini nostri Iesu Christi facite: in quo vivimus, movemur, & sumus. Et sermone LXIII: Omnium corda fidelium non dubitant nullis Mundi partibus, nullisque temporibus Providentiam abesse divinam; nec de Stellarum potestate, quæ nulla est, sacularium negociorum pendere præfectus, sed æquissimo & clementissimo summi Regis arbitrio cuncta disponi.
units.tr: The same author teaches in Fasti Book II that marriage must also be avoided during the Parentalia, which were celebrated in the month of February; and in Book III, on the festal days of the Salii. Against the period that follows the Ides of June, the same poet in Fasti Book VI sings that it is most suitable for weddings. Other days, which were avoided for contracting marriage, are listed by Macrobius, Saturnalia Book I, chapter 15. What shall we say to this? The admonitions of Augustine, which are in Gratian's Decree, 26 q. 7, carry more weight for us: Do not observe the days called Egyptian, or the Kalends of January, on which certain songs and revelries are performed and gifts exchanged among one another, as if they were an omen of good fortune at the beginning of the year; nor certain months, or times, or days, or years, or the course of the Moon and Sun; for whoever observes or heeds these and all such divinations, fates, or auguries, or consents to those who observe them, strives in vain and without cause, to his own damnation rather than his salvation; whether they inquire by certain numbers of letters and the Moon, by Pythagorean necromancy, whether the life or death of the sick, or their prosperity or adversity, will be; or whether they attend to dream-writings that are false and bear the name of Daniel, and to the lots that are called those of the holy Apostles, and to the augury of birds, or to anything for the building of a house, or for the joining of marriages, etc. Why not? He adds the reason at the end: For the Apostle says: Whether you eat, or drink, or do anything else, do it in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ; in whom we live, move, and have our being. And in Sermon 63: The hearts of all the faithful do not doubt that the divine Providence is absent from no regions of the world and from no times; nor do the affairs of men depend on the power of the stars, which is none, but all things are ordered by the most just and most merciful judgment of the highest King.

units.la: Quid amplius? Generales Influxuum Operationes, eorumque vires, quas in Inferiora hæc fieri per Cœlestium Corporum Lumen, Motum, Calorem comperimus, non est temere negandum adsequutos aliquo modo veteres Philosophos, & nos hodie adsequi posse; sed adspirante mentem & ingenium DEO. Particularis autem harum rerum notitia soli DEO est servata: Addo peccare largiter, & agere scelestè, qui eam rimantur; & omnes ingenij nervos explicant, ut hæc Divinæ Majestati prærogativa extorqueatur. Tales sunt mendacissimi Mortalium Astrologi, Chaldæi, Mathematici, Genethliaci, Iudiciarij, Planetarij vulgo vocati; quos non parum in opinione vanissima confirmat Origenis auctoritas, vocem DEI sacrosanctam (Genes. 1,14.) sic exaudiendam existimantis, ut refert Eusebius lib. VI. de præparat. Euangel. cap. IX. Ait enim, Astra ab DEO posita in Cœlo, ut per varios adspectus & conjunctiones præsignificarent, quæ consequentibus temporibus, tum universe tum sigillatim, euentura essent; non tamen ea efficerent. Itaque Cœlum esse dixit, velut quemdam Librum, in quo DEVS depinxit atque descripsit quæcumque in toto mundani ævi decursu suo quæque tempore futura. Id ut probet Origenes, citat librum, cui titulus erat Narratio Ioseph; qui apud multos olim magnæ & auctoritatis & fidei. In eo Iacob Patriarcha filios suos inducitur alloquens in hunc modum. Legi in Tabulis Cæli quæcumque contingent vobis & filijs vestris. Ejusdem mentis fuit Plotinus Origenis condiscipulus, ut patet ex Opere, cui titulus, Utrum Stellæ aliquid agant, & libro de Fato cap. vi. ubi notat, hunc etiam Stellarum esse usum, ut qui illas suspiciant & quasi litteras considerent, qui nimirum hujusmodi literaturam noverunt, futura legant; ex ipsis figuris comparatione quadam Analogica eorum significationem & intellectum solerter indagantes.
units.tr: What more? The general operations of influences, and their powers, which we find are exerted upon these lower things through the light, motion, and heat of the heavenly bodies, it is not rashly to be denied that the ancient philosophers attained to in some measure, and that we too can attain to today, provided God breathes on our mind and talent. But the particular knowledge of these things is reserved to God alone. I add that those who search it out sin grievously and act wickedly, and they strain every nerve of their intellect so that this prerogative of the divine Majesty may be wrested away. Such are the most lying of mortals, the Chaldeans, mathematicians, casters of nativities, judicial astrologers, and those commonly called planetary astrologers; and the authority of Origen, who thought the holy word of God (Gen. 1:14) should be understood in this way, confirms their most vain opinion not a little, as Eusebius reports in Book VI of the Praeparatio Evangelica, chapter IX. For he says that the stars were placed by God in heaven so that by their various aspects and conjunctions they might foreshadow what was to happen in the following times, both in general and in particular; yet they do not bring these things about. Therefore he said that the heaven is like a certain book, in which God has painted and described whatever is to happen in the whole course of the worldly age, each in its own time. To prove this, Origen cites a book entitled the Narrative of Joseph, which was once held by many to be of great authority and trustworthiness. In it the Patriarch Jacob is introduced addressing his sons in this manner: "I have read in the tablets of heaven whatever will befall you and your sons." Plotinus, a fellow student of Origen, held the same view, as is clear from his work entitled Whether the Stars Do Anything, and from the book On Fate, chapter 6, where he notes that this too is the use of the stars: that those who look up at them and, as it were, consider their letters, namely those who know this kind of literacy, may read the future, shrewdly investigating their meaning and sense from the figures themselves by a certain analogical comparison.

units.la: Sed infirmissimum esse quis non videt emendicatum illud ab Origine patrocinium? Damnat certe passim detestandum hoc & fanaticum hominum genus potentibus infidum, sperantibus fallax (sic enim Tacito dicitur lib. I. Historiar.) Sacra Scriptura: Exodi XXII, 18. Levit. XIX, 31. XX, 6, 27. Num. XXIII, 23. Deuter. XIIIX, 10. Samuel. XXIIX, III. Regum, XVII, 17. XXI, 6. Ieschah. II, 6. XLIV, 25. XLVII, 12. & seqq. Iirm. X, 2. ubi De Hieronymus, Michææ V, 11. Actor. Apost. XIX, 19.
units.tr: But who does not see that this patronage, begged from Origen, is very weak? Holy Scripture certainly condemns everywhere this detestable and frenzied kind of men, faithless to those who are powerful and deceptive to those who hope (for so Tacitus calls it, Histories Book I): Exod. 22:18; Lev. 19:31; 20:6, 27; Num. 23:23; Deut. 18:10; 1 Sam. 28:3; 1 Kings 17:17; 21:6; Isa. 2:6; 44:25; 47:12 and following; Jer. 10:2, where Jerome...; Mic. 5:11; Acts 19:19.

units.la: Damnant, cum Concilia, Toletanum I. in adsertione Fidei contra Priscillianistas, & Bracarense I. cap. IX. & X. tum Canones, 26. quæst. 2. c. Illos Planetarios, &c. sed & illud, &c. extuarum, de Sortilegijs.
units.tr: The Councils condemn them: the First Council of Toledo, in its affirmation of the faith against the Priscillianists, and the First Council of Braga, chapters IX and X; and the canons, 26 q. 2, c. Illos Planetarios, etc., but also that Illud, etc., of the Extravagantes, concerning sorceries.

units.la: Damnant non solum Iura & Imperatorum Constitutiones, I. artem. C. de malefic. & Mathematic. I. Mathematicos, 10. C. de Episcop. aud. Paull. v. Sent. tit. XXI. in Inscrip. & §. 3. & tit. XXIII. §. magicæ artis. Ruffin. tit. XV. Collat. legis Mosaicæ.
units.tr: They are condemned not only by the laws and constitutions of the emperors: Cod. I, "De artem," C. de malefic. et mathematic.; Cod. 10, C. de episcopali audientia; Paul, Sententiae Book V, title XXI, in the inscription and §3, and title XXIII, §"magicae artis"; Rufinus, title XV, Collatio legum Mosaicarum.

units.la: Genealis Coelestium Iuratorum nomia ab Hominibus latis fuerit particularis, DEO servata. Mosaic. 1. <bl>ἐκλογ.</bl> 39. <bl>τῶν μαθηματικῶν</bl>: sed & optimæ laudatissimæque Respublicæ. Roma certe quoties pulsi, cum cura notat CL. V. Iustus Lipsius ad 11. Annalium Taciti.
units.tr: The general knowledge of the heavenly motions has been granted to men, while the particular is reserved to God. Mosaic. Book I, [ἐκλογ.] 39, [τῶν μαθηματικῶν]: but also of the best and most praised commonwealths. Rome, certainly, how often she expelled them, is carefully noted by the most distinguished Justus Lipsius on Tacitus, Annals Book 11.

units.la: Avorsata semper Astrologiam, ut artem Magicam, veritam & damnatam primitiva legitur Ecclesia, scribente præter alios Epiphanio, libro de Mensuris & ponderibus: adeo ut qui deviarant ad illicitas has artes, non reciperet, nisi publice Confessio Reconciliatioque intervenirent. Orationem sæpe cum admiratione legi; quam, enarrato lxii. Psalmo, habuit D. Augustinus pro Mathematico, qui Erroris sui veniam ab Ecclesia publice petebat. Digna, quæ audiatur. Ille, inquit, ex Christiano & fideli pœnitens redit; & territus potestate Domini, convertitur ad misericordiam Domini: sed citius enim ab inimico, quum esset fidelis, diu Mathematicus fuit; seductus seducens; deceptus decipiens; illexit, fefellit, multa mendacia loquutus est contra DEVM, qui dedit hominibus potestatem faciendi quod bonum est, & non faciendi quod malum est. Ille dicebat, quod adulterium non faciebat voluntas propria, sed Venus; & homicidium non faciebat voluntas propria, sed Mars; & furtum non faciebat DEVS, sed Iupiter: & alia multa sacrilega non parva. Quam multis eum putatis Christianis nummos abstulisse? Quam multi ab illo emerunt mendacium? quibus dicebamus, Filii hominum usquequo gravi corde; ut quid diligitis vanitatem, & quæritis mendacium? Modo, sicut de illo credendum est, horruit mendacium, & multorum hominum interitum: se aliquando a Diabolo sensit illectum; convertitur ad DEVM pœnitens. Nostis in Actibus Apostolorum esse scriptum, cap. xix. quia multi perditi, id est, talium artium homines & doctrinarum nefariarum sectatores, omnes Codices suos ad Apostolos contulerunt: & incensi sunt libri tam multi, ut pertineret ad Scriptorem æstimationem eorum facere, & summam pretii conscribere. Hoc utique propter gloriam DEI; ne tales etiam perditi desperantur ab illo, qui novit quærere quod perierat. Perierat ergo ille; nunc quæsitus, inventus, adductus est, portat secum Codices incendendos, per quos fuerat incendendus: ut, illis in ignem missis, ipse in refrigerium transivet. Ante Pascha enim cœpit petere de Ecclesia Christi medicinam: sed quia talis est ars, in qua exercitatus erat, quæ suspecta esset de mendacio atque fallacia: dilatus est, ne tentaret, & aliquando tamen admissus est, ne periculosius tentaretur.
units.tr: Astrology, as a magic art, was always shunned, feared and condemned by the primitive Church, as is read, Epiphanius among others writing in his book On Measures and Weights; so much so that those who had strayed into these forbidden arts were not received unless a public confession and reconciliation took place. I have often read with admiration an oration which, in expounding Psalm 62, Augustine delivered concerning a mathematician who publicly sought pardon for his error from the Church. It deserves to be heard: He, he says, returns from a Christian and believer, penitent; and, terrified by the power of the Lord, he turns to the mercy of the Lord; but, for a long time, having been a believer, he had been a mathematician under the enemy: seduced, he seduced; deceived, he deceived; he enticed, he deceived, he spoke many lies against God, who gave men the power to do what is good and not to do what is evil. He used to say that adultery was not done by one's own will but by Venus, and murder not by one's own will but by Mars, and theft not by God but by Jupiter, and many other impious and not small things. How many Christians, do you think, did he take money from? How many bought lies from him? To them we used to say: Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek lies? Now, as we must believe of him, he has shuddered at the lie and at the ruin of many men; he has at some time felt himself enticed by the Devil; he turns penitent to God. You know it is written in Acts of the Apostles, chapter 19, that many of those who were lost, that is, men of such arts and followers of wicked doctrines, brought all their books to the Apostles; and so many books were burned that it was necessary for the writer to estimate their worth and set down the sum of the price. This was surely for the glory of God, so that even such lost men should not be despaired of by Him who knows how to seek what had perished. He had perished, therefore; now sought, found, and brought back, he carries with him the books to be burned, through which he had been destroyed, so that, when they had been cast into the fire, he himself might pass into refreshment. For before Easter he began to seek the remedy from the Church of Christ; but because such was the art in which he had been trained, which was suspect of lying and deceit, he was put off, lest he should be tested, and yet at last he was admitted, lest he should be tested more dangerously.

units.la: Detestati sunt Mathematicorum prædatorias prædictiones, ut meras nugas & quisquilias, non modo quorum doctissimos legimus ad Genesin Commentarios, in primis, Basilius Homilia vi. & Augustinus lib. ii. ad litteram, cap. ii: verum etiam alij, ut Eusebius de præpar. Euangel. vi. cap. 9. & xiv, 4. Chrysostomus & Gregorius in cap. ii. Matth. idem Augustinus de Doctrina Christiana, cap. xxi, & seqq: & lib. v. de Civit. Dei, Cyrillus lib. x. contra Iulianum; & alij, quos longum esset enumerare.
units.tr: They rejected the mathematicians' predictions as plunder and as mere trifles and fooling. Among those who wrote learned commentaries on Genesis, the most learned we read are above all Basil, in Homily 6, and Augustine, in the second book of his literal commentary on Genesis, chapter 2. Others did the same, such as Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel, books 6 (chapter 9) and 14 (chapter 4); Chrysostom and Gregory on Matthew, chapter 2; Augustine again in On Christian Doctrine, chapter 21 and following, and in City of God, book 5; and Cyril, Against Julian, book 10. There are others too many to list.

units.la: Riserunt ut futilem, ab omni fide vacuam, suos decipientem (Iesaiah. xl.vii, 10.) & in contemptissimis habuerunt gravissimi Philosophi, Socrates, Pythagoras, Plato, Democritus, Aristoteles, Eudoxus, Panætius Stoicus, Archelaus, Cailander, Scylax Halicarnassæus apud M. Tullium ii. de Divinatione; & non postremi habendus loci Phavorinus apud Agellium, lib. xiiii. cap. 1. Legendus & Persius Satyra vi, 15.
units.tr: Philosophers of the highest standing held them in contempt and laughed at them as empty, wholly without faith, and deceivers of their own clients (cf. Isaiah 47:10). These included Socrates, Pythagoras, Plato, Democritus, Aristotle, Eudoxus, the Stoic Panaetius, Archelaus, Cailander, and Scylax of Halicarnassus, as cited by Cicero in the second book of On Divination. Favorinus, cited by Gellius in book 14, chapter 1, should not be counted as least among them. Persius, Satire 6, line 15, is also worth reading.

units.la: Quid ni? Solus enim DEVS certam habet futurarum rerum præscientiam; Iesaiah. xli, 23. Xenophon in libro de Dictis Socratis (quod etiam notat Eusebius lib. xiv. de præparat. Euang. cap. iv.) scribit, Socratem dicere solitum, cognitionem futurarum rerum, quæ in potestate DEI sunt, non esse hominibus procurandam: neque enim posse homines eas res cognoscere; nec DEO gratum esse, si quæ ille occultavit, ea mortales velint nimis studiose curiosèque rimari. Ignorat homo quid sibi, quid aliis futurum, Schelom. Proverb. xxvii, 1. Ecclesiastis viii, 7. x, 14. Quam multa passim hujus classis apud Aristotelem: Futurorum contingentium non esse certam & definitam veritatem: Quæ per accidens quæque raro contingunt, non posse scientia comprehendi: Particularium & Corruptibilium Effectuum causas proximas & proprias esse particulares & corruptibiles; ob idque ad perfectam eorum cognitionem non satis esse cœlestes & universales Causas contemplari? Quis cogitabit quid velit DEVS? Sapient. ix, 13. Quis cognoscet sensum Domini? quis ejus Consiliarius? Iesaiah. xl, 13. Pauli. epist. ad Romanos, xi, 34. 1. ad Corinth. ii, 16. Quo modo enim certa prædicet Astrologus ex Astris, quorum non novit vires, res, defluxus & effectus? Cui quaeso plene cognita Caeli natura? cui Caelestium Orbium compertus ad amussim Numerus & Ordo? cui subtiliter explorata Motuum varietas, Astrorum lux, magnitudo, potestas? Fatetur hic ignorantiam suam ipse Philosophorum flos Aristoteles, de Caelo, text. 17, 60, 61. Quae in Terra & ad pedes, nemo digne potest aestimare; inveniuntur quae in prospectu cum labore: & quis absolute quae in Caelis sunt investigabit? Sapient. ix, 16. Quam autem multa, quae in Caelo, non videntur, vel videntur non clare, vel visa mutantur & controvertuntur? Quis certi quid sibi polliceatur ab Arte, quam tot Philosophorum digladiationes tanta certaminum rabie & atrocitate incertant? Acerrimis telis alter alterum oppugnant; non solum quidquid ejus artis (si ita dicenda) suspectum reddentes, sed quantum in se est evertentes; quorum vanitatem suis coloribus, ut aliorum, graphice delineat Cornelius Agrippa. Miror ego Astrologos (quid ni enim de his dicam, quod de Haruspice M. Porcius Cato, apud M. Tullium II. de Divinatione?) quum alter alterum videt, fallacis artis & imposturarum, quibus miseros homines deludunt, conscios, posse risum continere: quota enim quaeque res evenit ab his praedicta? aut si evenerit quidpiam: quid adferri potest, quur non casu id evenerit? βλακευτόμον apud Alexandrinos vetigal erat quod Astrologi persolvebant; sic nominatum ab stultitia: quaestus enim dicebatur fieri ex ingeniosa stultitia; & Astrologos consulere homines, non nisi stulti & temerarii. Praeposterum hominum genus, futura se praescire jactantium; quum praeteritorum oblivi praesentia insuper habent; alienarum satagunt, suarum rerum ignari! Et noverit Astrologus omnia: non posse tamen futura divinare, validissimis octo rationibus convincit doctissimus vir Benedictus Pererius lib. II. in Genesin, cap. III.
units.tr: Why would they not? God alone has certain foreknowledge of future things (Isaiah 41:23). Xenophon, in his book on the sayings of Socrates (which Eusebius also notes, Preparation for the Gospel, book 14, chapter 4), writes that Socrates used to say that knowledge of future things, which lie in God's power, is not to be sought by men, since men cannot know those things, and it is not pleasing to God if mortals eagerly and curiously pry into what he has hidden. Man does not know what will happen to himself or to others (Solomon, Proverbs 27:1; Ecclesiastes 8:7; 10:14). How many similar statements there are throughout Aristotle: that there is no certain and fixed truth about contingent future events; that things which happen by accident or rarely cannot be grasped by science; that the proximate and proper causes of particular and corruptible effects are themselves particular and corruptible, and so contemplating the heavenly and universal causes is not enough for their perfect knowledge. Who will think what God wills (Wisdom 9:13)? Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counsellor (Isaiah 40:13; Romans 11:34; 1 Corinthians 2:16)? For how can an astrologer foretell with certainty from the stars, whose powers he does not know, the events, flows and effects? For whom, I ask, is the nature of the heavens fully known? To whom has the number and order of the heavenly spheres been exactly ascertained? Who has carefully explored the variety of the motions, the light, the magnitude and the power of the stars? Aristotle himself, the flower of philosophers, confesses his ignorance on this point (On the Heavens, text 17, 60, 61). Nobody can properly judge what lies on the earth and at our feet, and what is found in view only with labour; so who will investigate fully what is in the heavens (Wisdom 9:16)? How many things in the heavens are not seen, or are seen not clearly, or, once seen, change and are disputed? Who can be sure of anything he is promised by an art which so many philosophers dispute with such fury and savagery of quarrels? They attack one another with the sharpest weapons, not only making that art (if it may be called that) suspect, but overthrowing it as far as they can. Cornelius Agrippa vividly portrays their vanity, as he does that of others. I am amazed that astrologers (and why should I not say of them what Marcus Porcius Cato said of the haruspices, cited by Cicero in the second book of On Divination?) can keep from laughing when they see one another, conscious of the deceitful art and the impostures by which they cheat wretched men. How few of the things they predict come to pass! And if anything does happen, what reason can be given why it did not happen by chance? The tax which astrologers paid among the Alexandrians was called blakeutikon [βλακευτικόν], named from stupidity, since the profit was said to be made from clever stupidity; and men who consult astrologers are none but fools and rash. What a perverse race of men, boasting that they foreknow the future, while they neglect the present, forgetting the past! They busy themselves with the affairs of others, ignorant of their own! Even if the astrologer knew everything, the learned man Benedict Pereira convinces us, in eight very strong arguments, that he still could not foretell the future (On Genesis, book 2, chapter 3).

units.la: De Genitura vero sit alicuius agendum: quis non intelligit difficillimum esse Temporis, quo quis natus, haberi momentum; & istius momenti constellationem Siderumque adspectum? Audiamus prosequentem haec fuse Basilium Homilia VI. super Genesin: Genethliacae artis inventores, quum in temporis amplo spacio complures figuras suam ipsorum scientiam fugere percepissent, in angustum admodum temporis contraxere mensuras, ut minutissimo quoque & subitaneo articulo, quale est quod Apostolus dixit, In momento temporis, in ictu oculi, plurimum differentia sit inter nativitatem & nativitatem. Ut is quidem, qui hoc in momento genitus est, futurus sit Rex Civitatum populorumque Princeps, locupletissimus, praepotens: is autem, qui natus est temporis sequentis momento pauper quidam sit futurus, aut mendicus circulator, vel praestigiator, ex oblys oblia permutans, quotidiani consequendi causa victus. Quamobrem eo orbe, qui Signifer appellatur, duodecim in partes divisor: quum in triginta dierum spacio partem Solis ejus obiti transfeat duodecimam, quem inerrantem appellant, triginta in portiones singulas illas duodecim partes secuerunt: tum singulis portionibus illis in se vaginta minuta divisis, minuta haec singula rursum in alia sexaginta modo simili dividere. Posito igitur enixu eorum, qui in lucem edunturvidecamus obsecro si hanc exactissimam temporis divisionem Auctores hi sibi valeant conservare. Nam simul ac editus pusio est, mas an femella sit, obstetrix exploras: tum vagitum exspectat infantis, nimirum indicium vitae ejus qui natus recens est. Quot hoc tempore vis sexagesima praeterisse minuta? Dicet Obstetrix deinde Chaldaeo partum, qui editus est: quot minutissima momenta vis, interea dum obstetrix loquitur, praetercurrisse, praesertim si forte fortuna fuerit non in conclavi mulierum Chaldaeus ille praesens, sed in aedium atrio aut vestibulo, tempus horamque repente. Et quum eum, qui diffinitus est diligenter tempus ac horam, exploratoria nimirum horarum percipere oporteat instrumenta, sive diurna sint sive nocturna: quot minutorum hoc quoque tempore, quaeso, praetervolat praeteritque examen? Compertam enim eam esse stellam, qua tempus horaque sit exploranda, non solum quanta in parte sit duodecima, sed etiam quam juxta duodecimae portionem partis, in quotequae minuto sexagesima eorum, in quae subdivisa sunt singula sexagesima illa prima, necesse est. Atque hanc tamen adeo tenuem subtilemque temporis inventionem quamquam attingere nequeunt singulis in stellis faciendam esse necessario ducunt, ut qualem ad caelo adfixas stellas ipsa dispositionem habitudinemve haberent, quandoque ipsarum esset inter sese figura, quum in lucem ederetur foetus, compertum sit tandem ac exploratum. Quae quum itaque sint: si fieri non potest, ut tempus illud exactissime quisquam attingat, variationeque vel brevissimi temporis fiat, ut tota via penitus aberrat; deridendi profecto non mediocriter esse videntur, tam ii qui studio hujus induserunt artis, quam in ratione rerum nusquam esse constat; quam illi qui hiantes ab illorum ore pendent intenti; perinde quasi omnia illi scire possint quae ipsis sunt eventura. Hominum enim istorum elegantes sententiae, sapientesque rationes per similes sunt aranearum telis, in quas si culex, culex, si musca, si quidpiam aliud inciderit invalidis hisce bestiolis simile, irretitum retinetur; sin validiusculum irruperit animal, inbelles illas perrumpit telas atque demolitur. Gregorius etiam Homilia Epiphaniae, captans occasione ab adparente, quam Magi viderant in Oriente, nato Christo, Stella, sic contra Mathematicos, adducto in medium Geminorum Iacob & Esau, qui nati simul erant, exemplo scribit: Certe quum Iacob de utero egrediens prioris fratris plantam manu teneret: prior perfecte nequaquam egredi potuit, nisi & subsequens inchoasset: & tamen quum uno tempore eodemque momento utrumque mater fuderit, non una utriusque vitae aequalitas fuit. Sed ad haec solent Mathematici respondere; quia virtus constellationis in ictu puncti est. Quibus ediverso nos dicimus; quia magna est mora nativitatis: si igitur in ictu puncti constellatio permutatur; necesse jam erit, ut tot duant fata, quot sunt membra nascentium. Sic Ambrosius, multis contra Mathematicos differens, lib. iv. Ἐξαημερ cap. iv. inter alia: Nonnulli, inquit, Nativitatum tentarunt exprimere qualitates; qualis sit unusquisque qui natus sit: quum hoc non solum vanum, sed & inutile sit quaerentibus, impossibile pollicentibus. Et non multo post: Redemti sunt Apostoli & congregati ex peccatoribus; non utique nativitatis suae hora, sed Christi eos sanctificavit adventus & ea a Dominicae passionis redemit a morte. Latro damnatus capite, ille cum Domino crucifixus, non beneficio nativitatis, sed fidei confessione ad Paradisi aeterna transivit: Jonam in mare non vis nativitatis, sed dissimulatio divinae praeceptionis praecipitavit & offensa. Petrum de carcere imminente morte periturum Angelus Christi, non stellarum series liberavit. Paullum caecitas converit ad gratiam; & percussum a vipera turbatumque naufragio, non remedia nativitatis, sed dei ordinis merita servaverunt. Quid de illis dicimus qui eorum precibus quum fuissent mortui resurrexerunt: utrum illos sua nativitas, an Apostolica gratia suscitavit? Avicenna lib. ultimo primae Philosophiae negat Astrologis esse credendum in divinatione futurorum, quod ipsi nec puncta caelestia teneant, neque naturas rerum inferiorum plane necessarias ad faciendum judicium de rebus futuris perspectas habeant; neque nituntur demonstrationibus, sed probationibus oratoriis & poeticis. Horrendum Natalitiis diebus Caelum in xii. domos dividere: in earum prima qualitates Animae rimari; in secunda Fortunam vel aequam vel iniquam; in tertia conscientiae arcana; in quarta Patris ejus qui in lucem editus, statum: horrendum augurari ex quinta domo, an & quales futuri Nato Filii; ex sexta quibus Morbis & quamdiu Natus sit conflictaturus, ex septima qui se habituros erga dissimilem sibi Sexum; ex octava quo Mortis genere periturus: horrendum denique nonam domum Nati Peregrinationibus consecrare: decimam Matris statui, Natique Honoribus, Potestati, Famae, undecimam Amicitiis & Vestimentis: duodecimam Inimicitiis, Carceribus & similibus. Non facta, non hominum vitae pendent ab Astris, ut vult cum aliis Manilius: non inde, sed a Deo coelitus omnia speranda & exspectanda. Ambrosius lib. iv. Ἐξαημ. cap. vii. Quum, inquit, ante dies paucos esset sermo de pluvia, quae fore utilis diceretur; ait quidem: Fece Neomenia dalit eam; & quamvis cupidi essemus imbrium, tamen hujusmodi adsertiones veras esse nolebam. Denique delectatus sum quod nullus imber effusus est; donec precibus Ecclesiae datus manifestaret, non de instis Lunae perandum esse, sed de providentia & misericordia Creatoris: quo exemplo, & vanitas istius Astrologiae confutata est, & efficacia Christianae pietatis visaque religiosarum precum re ipsa comprobata.
units.tr: Let me now say something about the genitura, the nativity itself. Who does not see how very hard it is to determine the exact moment at which someone was born, and the constellation and the aspect of the stars at that moment? Let us hear Basil, who discusses this at length in Homily VI on Genesis: The inventors of the genethliacal art, when they had perceived that over a wide span of time many figures escape their science, narrowed their measurements to a very small compass of time, so that with the tiniest and most sudden moment, such as the Apostle meant when he said, "In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye," there is a great difference between one birth and another. For he who is born in one moment is to be a king, a ruler of cities and peoples, very rich and very powerful; but he who is born a moment later is to be some poor man, or a beggar, or a street performer or conjuror, exchanging coppers for coppers to win his daily bread. Therefore they divided that circle which is called the Zodiac into twelve parts; and since the sun takes a twelfth part of it in the space of thirty days, which they call the wandering sign, they cut each of those twelve parts into thirty portions, and then divided each of those portions into sixty minutes, and each of these minutes again, in a similar way, into sixty others. Granting, then, the labour of those who bring children into the light, let us see, I beg you, whether these authors can keep up this most exact division of time. For as soon as the infant is born, the midwife examines whether it is a boy or a girl; then she waits for the baby's cry, of course the sign of life in the newborn. How many of the sixtieths of a minute have passed by this time? Then the midwife will tell the astrologer the birth that has taken place; how many most minute moments, I ask, will have run past while the midwife is speaking, especially if by chance that astrologer was not present in the women's chamber but in the courtyard or the vestibule of the house, when the time and hour suddenly ...
