And since, to fix the time and hour carefully, one must surely use the instruments for observing hours, whether daytime or night-time ones, how many minutes, I ask, slip away and pass by during this examination too? For it is necessary that the star by which the time and hour are to be observed be known, not only how far it is into the twelfth part, but also, in relation to the twelfth part's portion, in which minute of the sixtieth of those subdivisions, that first sixtieth is. Yet although they cannot reach even this thin and subtle discovery of time, they think it must necessarily be done for each individual star, so that what kind of arrangement and relation the fixed stars themselves had, and what their figure was with respect to one another, when the offspring was brought into the light, is at last ascertained and examined. Since these things are so: if it is impossible for anyone to hit that time with exact precision, and if a variation of even the briefest moment makes the whole course of the prediction go utterly astray, then surely those men who have devoted themselves to this art seem to deserve no small mockery, as does the matter itself, which is nowhere grounded in reason; and so too do those who gape and hang intently upon their lips, as though these men could know what is going to happen to themselves. For the elegant opinions and wise reasonings of these men are like spiders' webs: if a gnat, a fly, or anything else like these feeble little creatures falls into them, it is caught and held fast; but if a somewhat stronger animal bursts in, it tears through and wrecks those feeble webs. Gregory too, in his Homily on the Epiphany, taking occasion from the star which the Magi had seen in the East at the birth of Christ, writes against the mathematicians in this way, bringing forward the example of Jacob and Esau, the twins who were born together: Certainly, when Jacob came out of the womb holding his elder brother's heel with his hand, the elder could not come out fully unless the younger had also begun to come out. And yet, since the mother brought forth both at one time and in one and the same moment, their lives were not alike in every way. But the mathematicians are accustomed to answer this, that the power of the constellation lies in the instant of a point. To this we answer in turn that the birth takes a long time; so if the constellation changes in the instant of a point, then the fates must be as many as the limbs of those who are born. So Ambrose, arguing at length against the mathematicians in the fourth book of his Hexaemeron [Ἐξαήμερον], chapter 4, says among other things: Some have tried to set out the qualities of births, what sort of person each one born will be; but this is not only empty but useless to those who seek it, and impossible for those who promise it. And not long after: The apostles were redeemed and gathered from sinners; certainly not by the hour of their birth, but the coming of Christ sanctified them, and his passion redeemed them from death. The thief condemned to the cross, crucified with the Lord, passed into eternal Paradise not by the benefit of his birth but by the confession of faith. Jonah was thrown into the sea not by the force of his birth, but by his disobedience to the divine command and by his offence. The angel of Christ freed Peter from prison when death was about to take him, not a series of stars. Blindness turned Paul to grace; and when he was struck by a viper and tossed about by shipwreck, it was not the remedies of his birth but the merits of God's ordering that saved him. What shall we say about those whom, when they had died, their prayers raised up again? Did their nativity raise them, or the grace of the apostles? Avicenna, in the last book of his First Philosophy, denies that the astrologers are to be believed in foretelling future things, because they neither hold the celestial points nor have a full grasp of the natures of lower things, which are absolutely necessary for judging future events; and they rely not on demonstrations but on rhetorical and poetic proofs. It is monstrous to divide the heavens into twelve houses on birthdays: in the first to search out the qualities of the soul; in the second, whether fortune will be fair or unfair; in the third, the secrets of conscience; in the fourth, the condition of the father of the one born; monstrous to foretell from the fifth house whether and what sort of children the newborn will have; from the sixth what diseases and for how long the child will struggle with; from the seventh whom he will have as a partner of the opposite sex; from the eighth by what kind of death he will perish; monstrous finally to consecrate the ninth house to the journeys of the child, the tenth to the status of the mother and the honours, power and fame of the child, the eleventh to friendships and clothing, the twelfth to enmities, prisons and the like. Not the deeds and lives of men depend on the stars, as Manilius holds with others; all things are to be hoped and awaited not from there but from God in heaven. Ambrose, in the fourth book of the Hexaemeron [Ἐξαήμερον], chapter 7: When, he says, a few days earlier there was talk of rain, which was said to be going to be useful, he indeed said: "The new moon has given it"; and although we were eager for rains, I was unwilling to accept such assertions as true. At last I was glad that no rain poured down; until, granted to the prayers of the Church, it showed that rain must be sought not from the courses of the moon, but from the providence and mercy of the Creator. By this example both the vanity of that astrology was refuted and the efficacy of Christian piety, and of religious prayers, was in fact confirmed.

units.la: Non Nos Astris, non Astra Nobis, sed Verique dominatur Deus. Quid magis impium, quam quae mala eveniunt, Astris imputare, praestantissimis Dei Creaturis? Audi Augustinum lib. de Conf. iv. De Caelo tibi dicis, inquit, inevitabilem canssam peccandi accidere, & Venerem hoc fecisse, aut Saturnum, aut Martem: scilicet ut homo sine culpa sit, carro & sanguis & superba putredo: culpendum sit autem Coeli & Siderum Creator & ordinator? Et quid est ille, nisi Deus noster, suavitas & origo justitiae, qui reddit unicuique secundum opera sua? Quum ergo haec ita se habeant, satis perspicuum est puto, secundum Catholicos atque prisios illos philosophos, res humanas: casu & fortuna aut stellarum fato non gubernari. Videndus & Plotinus Ennead. ii. lib. iii. cap. ii. Deus quidquid creavit, vidit esse valde bonum: (כאר טוב) oculatiores illi viderunt Stellas noxias, flagitiosas, malorum influxuum; statuentes in sacratissimo caelestium Corporum genatu scelera facienda decerni. O Impios, qui quae solius Dei sunt, Astris tribuunt; qui nos liberos natos Siderum servos faciunt. Nos autem? Patiamur. Sed horresco referens, eo progressa est perniciosissima horum audacia, ut Christum etiam Astris adligarint; quem alii, extructa Genesi, docere non verentur Passionem suam & Mortis genus; alii Prophetam fuisse blaterant & tot inclaruisse miraculis, quod nascens habuerit adscendens Geminorum fidus (quis ferret detehoc àdiquc Saturno Mercurioque sub Aquario junctis in nona Cœli domo. Quid detestabilius & magis exsecrandum? Iam quod Astrologos vera praenunciare nonnumquam sciamus, & audiamus quotidie, fit hoc, ut plenius docet Pererius l. II. in Genesin cap. v. vel Daemonum, quibus futura saepe nota, instinctu, quo non raro homines agantur ad divinandum, Augustino scribente lib. v. de Civit. Dei cap. VII. & lib. II. de Genesi ad litteram, cap. XVII: vel ex occulta divinae Providentiae dispositione, ut videre est apud eundem Augustin. lib. IV. & VII. Confess. & de doctrina Christiana cap. XXII. & XXIII: vel ob stultam Consulentium credulitatem; vel denique per singularem quamdam sagacis ingenii solertiam, multiplicem rerum humanarum peritiam, & exquisitam negociorum quibus occupati, studiorum quibus dediti, ingeniorum quibus pollent, morum denique quibus consulentes praediti, notitiam & observationem. Quamvis lubrica (verbis utor Phavorini, laudante Agellio lib. XIV. noct. Attic. cap. I.) & ambagiosa coniectatione nitentes, inter falsa atque vera pedetentim quasi per tenebras ingredientes eant, & aut multa tentando incidant nonnumquam imprudentes in veritatem; aut ipsorum, qui eos consulant, multa credulitate ducente perveniant callide ad ea, quae vera sunt: tamen omnia, quae aut temere aut astute vera dicunt, prae ceteris quae mentiuntur, pars ea non sit millesima. Mendaciorum vendunt plerumque miseris hominibus plaustra. Bene M. Tullius lib. II. de Divinat: Quid plura? inquit, quotidie refert Chaldaei: quam multa ego Pompeio, quam multa Crasso, quam multa huic ipsi Caesari a Chaldaeis dicta memini, neminem eorum nisi senectute, nisi domi, nisi cum clarit ate esse moriturum; ut mihi permirum videatur quemquam exstare, qui etiam nunc credat ijs, quorum praedicta quotidie videat re & eventus refelli. Astrologi praedicunt vel bona vel mala: si bona, profecto Christianae pietati convenientius est exspectare illa a Deo, quam ab fallente plerumque lingua Astrologi; si mala, multis sane modis eorum ignoratio melior est, quam scientia, ut Cicero etiam disputat. Praestat semper in timore Dei esse & orare; quam diseruciari futurorum eventuum metu. Soli Numine divino adflati praedicunt futura particularia, inquit Ptolemaeus tractatu centum sententiarum, sent. I. a qua lux quintae ibidem sententiae: Potest is, qui scienst multos Stellarum, inquit, efficius avertere, quando naturam earum noverit, aut si ipsum ante illorum eventum rite praeparaverit: unde manavit illa multorum sermonibus trita sententia, Sapiens dominabitur Astris. Latinis etiam proverbium fuit, ut notat Donatus in Hecyram Terentii, Sapientem divinare; quod ex conjecturis prudenter collatis verum colligere nonnumquam solet non solum de praeteritis, verum etiam de futuris. Valeant igitur abutentis divinissimo Astrorum, quae Dei sunt organa, exercitu Mathematici: (nam de prudentioribus non mihi verba) valeant Planetarij, sordidos & illiberales per fas nefas quaestus facientes: valeant Genethliaci, elevantes se adversus Dei scientiam, & omne quod geritur in Seculo referentes ad ortus Stellarum & occubitus, ut inquit Hieronymus Comment. in cap. I. Sophoniae salutem alius, ut idem ad cap. XLVII. Ieschah. promittentes, sua ignorantes supplicia; satis aliorum pernoscendis operam dantes, sibi quid serus vesper sit adlaturus ignari; loquentes vani, quod insipientes opinantur; ait Augustinus sermone VI. de Epiphan. ubi Artem hanc (si nomen hoc mereatur) vocat non inscite stultitiam sacrilegam, & indoctam Doctrinam; ut & genus Fornicationis Animae, 26. q. 2. c. illud Sufficiat quod Varro gravissimus aevi superstitiosissimi & arti fallacissimae nimisquam deditus auctor, scribat, ex Astrologiae sinu superstitionum omnium profluxisse vanitates. Sufficiat quod Augustinus lib. II. quaest. Veter. & Novi Test. quaestione XVI, Astrologos dicat esse inimicos Veritatis: quod lib. III. quaest. XVIII. Astrologiam carpat, ut inimicam Legi divinae: monens inventam eam esse ab astutia & subtilitate Diaboli; nihil tam advertari Christianis, quam Mathematicis adhibere curam; hanc artem omnibus modis fugiendam; Curiosos ejus hostilibus in Deum esse animis; numquam esse sine solicitudine: semper suspensos exspectare, quod minime certum sciunt: quod idem ad Ianuarium scribens, Mathematicorum deliramenta cum detestatione deridenda clamet. Sufficiat denique, quod Picus Mirandulanus, non solum genere sed & doctrina nobilissimus, validissimis probet argumentis, ut & alij fecerunt, Artem hanc non Hominum sed malorum Daemonum esse inventum. Immortalem sane magnus vir meretur laudem; qui adversus Astrologos scripsit tanta copia, ut vix ullum praeteriret argumentum, tanta efficacia, ut ne acerrimi quidem Astrologiae propugnatores eam ab adductis Pici rationibus umquam sint saluaturi.
units.tr: Not we to the stars, nor the stars to us, but the one true God rules. What is more impious than to attribute the evils that happen to the stars, the most excellent creatures of God? Hear Augustine in Book 4 of the Confessions: You tell me that the inevitable cause of sinning comes from the heavens, and that Venus, or Saturn, or Mars has done this: so that man is without blame, flesh and blood and proud rottenness, while the Creator and ordainer of heaven and the stars is to be blamed? And who is he but our God, the sweetness and source of justice, who renders to each one according to his works? Since these things stand thus, it is clear enough, I think, that according to the Catholics and those ancient philosophers, human affairs are not governed by chance and fortune or by the fate of the stars. Plotinus, Ennead 2, book 3, chapter 2, is also worth consulting. God, having made whatever he created, saw that it was very good [טוב מאד]. Those more keen-sighted men saw stars that are harmful and wicked, sources of evil influences, and they decreed that crimes were to be committed under the most sacred births of the heavenly bodies. O impious men, who attribute to the stars what belongs to God alone; who make us, born free, slaves of the constellations. But what of us? Let us endure it. Yet I shudder to relate how far the most pernicious audacity of these people has gone: they have even bound Christ to the stars. Some, drawing up his horoscope, do not hesitate to teach that his Passion and manner of death were fixed by them; others babble that he was a prophet and became famous for so many miracles because at his birth the star of the Twins was rising (who could bear this?), with Saturn and Mercury joined under Aquarius in the ninth house of heaven. What could be more detestable and accursed? As for the fact that we know, and hear every day, that astrologers sometimes foretell true things, this happens, as Pererius teaches more fully in his commentary on Genesis, book 2, chapter 5, either through the demons, to whom future events are often known, and by whose prompting men are often driven to divine (as Augustine writes in City of God 5, chapter 7, and in The Literal Meaning of Genesis 2, chapter 17); or through the hidden disposition of divine Providence, as may be seen in the same Augustine, Confessions 4 and 7, and On Christian Doctrine chapters 22 and 23; or on account of the foolish credulity of those who consult them; or finally through a certain singular shrewdness of a keen mind, a manifold experience of human affairs, and an exact knowledge and observation of the businesses in which their clients are engaged, the studies to which they are devoted, the talents they possess, and finally the characters of those who consult them. Although they proceed by slippery and ambiguous conjecture (I use the words of Favorinus, praised by Gellius in Attic Nights 14, chapter 1), groping step by step among true and false as if through darkness, and although by trying many things they sometimes stumble upon the truth, or, led on by the credulity of those who consult them, arrive cunningly at what is true, nevertheless the part of all the things they say, whether rashly or cleverly, that are true, compared with the lies, is not one thousandth. They generally sell wagonloads of lies to wretched men. Marcus Tullius rightly says in Book 2 of On Divination: What more is there to say? The Chaldeans, he says, tell the same tale every day. How many things I remember being told by the Chaldeans to Pompey, how many to Crassus, how many to Caesar himself, and none of them would die except in old age, at home, and in glory. So it seems to me astonishing that anyone should still exist who believes in those whose predictions he sees refuted by fact and outcome every day. Astrologers predict either good or evil. If good, it is surely more fitting for Christian piety to expect those things from God than from the tongue of the astrologer, which mostly deceives. If evil, in many ways their ignorance is better than their knowledge, as Cicero also argues. It is always better to be in the fear of God and to pray than to be tormented by fear of future events. Only those inspired by the divine power, says Ptolemy in his Centiloquium, sentence 1, foretell particular future events; and the light of the following fifth sentence is this: He who knows the nature of the stars, he says, can avert many of their effects, or if he has rightly prepared himself before their occurrence; whence came that saying, worn smooth by the talk of many, that the wise man rules the stars. There was also a Latin proverb, as Donatus notes on Terence's Hecyra, the wise man divines; for by prudently gathering conjectures he can often draw out the truth, not only about the past but also about the future. Away, then, with the mathematicians who abuse that most divine instrument of God, the stars (for I am not speaking of the more prudent ones). Away with the planetary fortune-tellers, who make a sordid and illiberal profit by fair means or foul. Away with the casters of nativities, who raise themselves against the knowledge of God and refer everything that happens in the world to the risings and settings of the stars, as Jerome says in his commentary on Zephaniah 1, and again on Isaiah 47, promising salvation to others while ignoring their own punishments; busying themselves with knowing the fates of others, yet ignorant of what the late evening will bring upon themselves; speaking vain things, which fools suppose to be wise. Augustine says in Sermon 6 on the Epiphany, where he calls this art (if it deserves the name) not unwisely a sacrilegious folly and an unlearned teaching, and a kind of fornication of the soul (26, q. 2, c. Illud). It is enough that Varro, that most serious author of a most superstitious age, who was also too devoted to a most deceptive art, writes that all superstitions have flowed out of the bosom of astrology. It is enough that Augustine, in Questions on the Old and New Testament, book 2, question 16, calls astrologers enemies of the truth; that in book 3, question 18, he attacks astrology as hostile to the divine Law, warning that it was invented by the cunning and subtlety of the Devil; that nothing is to be more avoided by Christians than to give attention to mathematicians, that this art must be shunned in every way, that its curious followers have hostile minds towards God, that they are never without anxiety, always hanging in suspense and waiting for what they know to be most uncertain. He writes the same to Januarius, crying out that the mathematicians' ravings are to be mocked with detestation. Finally, it is enough that Pico della Mirandola, most noble not only by birth but also by learning, proves with the strongest arguments, as others have also done, that this art was invented not by men but by evil demons. Truly the great man deserves immortal praise, who wrote against the astrologers in such abundance that hardly any argument was left untouched, and with such force that not even the most fierce champions of astrology will ever be able to save it from the arguments Pico has brought forward.

units.la: HÆC de Stellis universim: ad singulariorem Siderum consideration em viam nobis pandet Distributio.
units.tr: So much for the stars in general. The distribution we are about to describe will open the way for us to a more detailed consideration of the heavenly bodies.

units.la: Stellarum alix Fixæ sunt, aliæ Errantes. Fixæ (quas & Inerrantes vocant doctí Scriptores) dici volunt Astronomi: non quod immobiles consistant, sed quod tardissimus, & qui fixam fere mentitur stationem, earum, immutabilibus semper à se invicem spacijs, sit in octava sphæra, cui omnes inhærent, motus. Ptolemæus certe ijs, quæ Aristillides, Timocharcs & Hipparchus observarant, cum quæ ipse perceperat, committis; Stellas centum annorum spatio gradum unum animadvertit conficere. Ævo nostro Copernicus examinatis, quæ considerarant Veteres, ijsque ad φαινόμενα quæ ipse notarat, comparatis; deprehendit Stellas annorum lxxii. curriculo gradum unum emetiri; quolibet anno, i. scrupula secunda; singulis diebus, viii. scrupula tertia & x. quarta; integram vero conversionem vicies quinquies annorum millibus, octingentis & sedecim absoluturas.
units.tr: Some of the stars are fixed, others wandering. Astronomers want the fixed stars (which learned writers also call Inerrantes, "non-wandering") to be so named, not because they stand motionless, but because they are all attached to the eighth sphere and share in its motion, which is very slow and keeps an almost fixed position, so that the distances between them never change. Ptolemy, comparing what Aristyllus, Timocharis and Hipparchus had observed with what he himself had perceived, noticed that the stars advance one degree in the space of a hundred years. In our own age Copernicus examined what the ancients had recorded, compared it with the appearances [φαινόμενα] he had himself noted, and found that the stars traverse one degree in a course of seventy-two years: each year 2 seconds, each day 8 thirds and 10 fourths; and that they will complete a full revolution in 25,816 years.

units.la: Numerum inire Fixarum nonnulli tentarunt. Periti apud Plinium lib. ii. Nat. histor. cap. xli. lxxii. (sunt qui liii. rectius proculdubio, ut minor sit eorum ab aliis dissensio, legunt, duabus denarij notis expunctis) Signa facientes cœlestia, notant mille sexcentas, effectu visuve insignes. Chrysippus his multo pauciores. sequentibus paullo plures: nimirum cIↄ. lviii. τὰ μὲν ἐν ἀπλανῶν, inquit, ἀστέρων ἀκαταλήπτων εἶναι τὸ πλῆθος, τὰ δὲ πλανώμενα ταπεινότερα τ' ἁπλανῶν. ... Ptolemæus, Hipparchus, cosque sequuti effigies xlviii. formantes, mille viginti duas numerare se profitentur, visu notabiles; non negantes interim alias esse non paucas, forma minimas, luce claritateque nostris oculis indiscrete conspicuas. Stellæ mihi non infinitæ, sed innumerabiles. Testatur non uno loco Sacra Scriptura eas ab homine numerari non posse. Genes. cap. xv; v. xxii, 17. xxvi, 4; Deuteron. 1,10. x, 22; Iirmias cap. xxxiii, 22; Nahum iii, 16; Paullus epist. ad Romanos cap. iv, 18. & alibi. Veteres etiam Philosophi negant Siderum Inerrantium numerum à mortalibus iniri posse; legendi Plato in Timæo: Aristoteles lib. de Mundo ad Alexandrum, & lib. ii. de Cœlo text. 61; Seneca lib. vi. Nat. Quæst. cap. xvi. Vnius enim Dei stellas putare, David Psalmo cxlvii, 4. Nam quis credat omnes videri posse? Quanto quisque acutius intuetur, tanto plures videt: oculis lynceis & acerrime cernentibus aliquas semper occuli omnino censendum: quæ mens est Augustini lib. xvi. de civit. Dei, cap. xxiii. Quot etiam alias cœli plagæ ἡμῖν ἀόρατα, & nostros fugientia visus Sidera: ut Manilio utar. Videndus Macrobius lib. i. in Somnium Scipionis cap. xvi. Qui loca australia sæculo nostro navigarunt, multas supra vulgo notas, & inter eas aliquot primæ magnitudinis & lucidissimas ibi se conspexisse adfirmant.
units.tr: Some have tried to count the fixed stars. The experts cited by Pliny (Natural History, book 2, chapter 41; some read 53 instead of 72, which is surely more correct, since it agrees more closely with the others, once two dots of the denarius mark are removed), in making their celestial figures, note 1,600 stars that are remarkable for their effect or appearance. Chrysippus counted far fewer, and those who followed him a few more, namely 1,058. "Of the fixed stars," he says, "the number is incomprehensible, while the wandering ones are lower than the fixed." ... Ptolemy, Hipparchus and those who followed them, forming 48 figures, profess to count 1,022 stars notable to the eye, without denying meanwhile that there are not a few others, minute in form, indistinctly visible to our eyes by their light and brightness. To me the stars are not infinite, but innumerable. Holy Scripture testifies in more than one place that they cannot be counted by man: Genesis 15; 22:17; 26:4; Deuteronomy 1:10; 10:22; Jeremiah 33:22; Nahum 3:16; Paul, Epistle to the Romans 4:18, and elsewhere. The ancient philosophers too deny that the number of the fixed stars can be ascertained by mortals; read Plato in the Timaeus, Aristotle in the book On the World to Alexander and in book 2 of On the Heavens, text 61; and Seneca, Natural Questions book 6, chapter 16. Only God, indeed, can be thought to number the stars, as David says (Psalm 147:4). For who would believe that all of them can be seen? The more sharply one looks, the more one sees; with lynx-like eyes, however keen, some stars must always be concealed. This is also the view of Augustine, City of God book 16, chapter 23. There are also other regions of the heavens, invisible to us, and stars escaping our sight, as I may say with Manilius. See Macrobius, Commentary on the Dream of Scipio, book 1, chapter 16. Those who in our century sailed to the southern regions affirm that they saw there many stars beyond those commonly known, and among them some of the first magnitude and most brilliant.

units.la: Qui porro certum Siderum numerum deprehendisse se volunt, eadem in sex secundum Magnitudinem Classes distribuerunt. Primæ Magnitudinis vocarunt quarum Diametros apparens est Scrupulorum octo: Secundæ, sex; Tertiæ, quatuor; Quartæ, trium; Quintæ, duorum; Sextæ denique, Scrupuli unius. Primæ Stellas recensent xv; quarum tantam tradunt molem, ut Terra sint vastiores centies septies cum undecim sexagesimis quartis. Secundæ, xlv; Terram superantes octogies fere septies. Tertiæ, ccviii; septuagies bis cum triente fere Terra immaniores, Quartæ, 50 cccci.xxiv; Terram excedentes quinquagies quater & ejusdem semisse, vel paullo amplius. Quintæ, ccxvi; Terram tricies semel vincentes. Sextæ denique i; Terra majores decies octies, & paullo amplius. His addunt Ἀμαύρως ix, Νεφελαιδῆς v. De Siderum Magnitudine plura Ptolemæus lib. v. Plinius lib. ii. nat. histor. cap. xi. Macrobius lib. i. in Somn. Scip. cap. xvi. Vitell. Optic. lib. x. propos. lix.
units.tr: Those who claim to have ascertained a fixed number of stars have also divided the same stars into six classes according to magnitude. They called those of the first magnitude the ones whose apparent diameter is eight scruples; second magnitude, six; third, four; fourth, three; fifth, two; and sixth, one scruple. They list 15 stars of the first magnitude, which they say are so vast in mass that they are seven hundred and eleven sixty-fourths times greater than the Earth. Of the second magnitude there are 45, exceeding the Earth about eighty-seven times. Of the third there are 208, some seventy-two and a third times larger than the Earth. Of the fourth there are 474, exceeding the Earth by fifty-four and a half times or a little more. Of the fifth there are 216, surpassing the Earth thirty-one times. Finally, of the sixth there is one, larger than the Earth eighteen times and a little more. To these they add 9 dim stars [Ἀμαύρως] and 5 nebulous stars [Νεφελαιδῆς]. More on the magnitude of the stars can be found in Ptolemy, book 5; Pliny, book 2 of the Natural History, chapter 11; Macrobius, book 1 on the Dream of Scipio, chapter 16; and Vitellio, Optics, book 10, proposition 59.

units.la: CAP. XVIII.
units.tr: CHAP. XVIII.

units.la: De Signis Cœlestibus universim.
units.tr: Of the Celestial Signs in general.

units.la: FIXORVM Siderum alia σωζόμενα, alia ἀσώστα: hæc quæ non eo collocata modo, ut Configurationem faciant: unde & Græcis ἀμεράφωα, quorum nulla ἀ-φοβία: illa vero, quæ ex pluribus sibi vicinis compolita certas constituunt Imagines. Græci vocant ἀστερισμούς; Ἀ̈στρον nonnullis nominantur, Ἀ̈στρον volentibus esse σύνημα τ̃ ἀστέρων, signum ex Stellis coactum, quod tamen non est perpetuum: Σχήματα Ptolemæus appellat; & Μορφώσεις idem lib. iv. Τετραβίβλος, cap. ωεὶ τ̃ μὴ ρεμίμων γαμων: Signa Lucretius, Virgilius, Horatius, Ovidius, Plinius, alij: Manilius & Hyginus Formæ & Corpora: Constellationes non inepta voce dicuntur vulgo.
units.tr: Of the fixed stars, some are σωζόμενα [sōzomena, "preserved"] and some are ἀσώστα [asōsta, "unsaved"]. The latter are those not placed in such a way as to make up a configuration; hence the Greeks also call them unshaped [ἀμόρφωτα], and there is no fixed name for them. The former are those which, made up of several neighbouring stars, form definite images. The Greeks call these ἀστερισμούς [asterismous, constellations]. Some name them "astra," while others, wishing them to be a συνημα τῶν ἀστέρων [synēma tōn asterōn, a combination of stars], a sign gathered from stars, which however is not permanent. Ptolemy calls them σχήματα [schēmata, figures], and in the fourth book of the Tetrabiblos, in the chapter on [those things] not spoken of, he uses the term μορφώσεις [morphōseis, forms]. Lucretius, Virgil, Horace, Ovid, Pliny and others call them "signa" (signs); Manilius and Hyginus call them "formae" and "corpora" (forms and bodies). In common speech they are not inappropriately called "constellations."

units.la: Nomina Signis his indita ex notarum rerum vel figurarum similitudine. Nam absit, ut credamus hæc talia purissimis locis immorari. Consilium hoc non nuperum, neque quod χῆς καὶ πρώτων natum, sed ex veterum Astronomorum doctrina desumtum. Πλειάδες, Ὑάδες, Ὠρίων, Ἀρκτοῦρος nominantur ab Homero & Hesiodo: & quæ non ab Arato, quem floruisse constat circa Olympiadem cxxiv; annis ante Christum natum fere ccc? Quin & in historia Sacra, quæ Monumentorum omnium antiquissima, Nominum Astris impositorum fit mentio. Hijobi cap. ix, 9. Faciens Arcturum (עש) Orionα (כסיל) & Hyadas (כימה) & plagas Australes (חדרי תמן) Græci; ὁ πιῶν Πλειάδα, καὶ Ἐσπέρον, καὶ Ἀρκτοῦρον, καὶ Ζαμιεῖα Νότα. Arcturum vertunt plerique; Aben-Hezra putat esse Ἀρκτον & Ἀμαξαν: videtur esse generalius quid, Stellarum congregatio, ab עש Congregare, nulli Formæ convenientius, quam Vrsarum Majoris Minorisque cum implexione Draconis; quæ juxta Polum Arcticum. Sic ejusdem Hijobi cap. iv, 9. Conterent eos, donec fuerit Arcturus (לפני עש) Rabbi David in libro Radicum vertit, Omni tempore, quo Arcturus movet, id est semper. Hieronymus: consumentur, velut à tinea. Ibidem cap. xxxviii, 32. Numquid producis Luciferum in tempore suo, & Arcturum (עיש) cum filiis ejus (id est minoribus Stellis) duces eos? Hieronymus: Et Vesperum supervilios terræ confungere facies. כסיל secundum Hieronymum Orion, ab inconstantia; juxta quosdam, quod ejus ortus tempestatibus Orbem varie turbet. Sic Ieschah. xiii, 10. Quia Stellæ Cælorum & Oriones eorum (וכסיליהם, Hieronymus, & Splendor eorum) non expandent lumen suum. Sunt qui Ὑάδας seu Suculas, voce non abludente, censent esse; quod fortean voluit & Rabi-Ionah, quum Arabice סוחיל scribit appellari, כימרה apud Hijobum vertit Hieronymus Hyadas; Rabi-Ionah σύνημα vult esse Stellarum, quod Arabice אלתודין, Græcis Ἀρκτος, quemadmodum & vocem hanc interpretatur Hieronymus Hamos cap. v, 8. Aben-Hezra in Hijobi cap. xxxviii, 31. memoriæ prodit כימה antiquis esse septem Stellas in fine Arietis (non in Ariete, sed in Tauri tunt dorso) ex quibus sex conspicuæ, à Latinis Septemtriones dici solitas, sibi vero videri Stellam esse magnam (primæ est magnitudinis) quæ Oculus Tauri sinister חדי תמן interiora penetralia: Ζαμιεῖα Austri, id est, Astra Meridionalia: .sic dicta, quod occultentur & non videantur ab his, qui nostrum habitant hemisphærium. Celebrat Vir Sanctus Deum conditorem Astrorum: tam quæ Meridionalia, nostros fugientia vultus, quam Septemtrionalia, nostris obversantia perpetuum oculis. Quæ omnia probant novum nequaquam esse commentum, Stellas in certas effigies partiri. Plinius lib. ii. natur. histor, cap. viii. scribit, Signis primum nomina potuisse Cleostratum; quod an verum, alijs investigandum relinquo.
units.tr: These signs have been given names from the resemblance of well-known things or figures. For we must not believe that such things were invented in the purest times. This practice is not recent, nor did it arise from the ignorance of the first ages; it was taken over from the teaching of the ancient astronomers. The Pleiades, Hyades, Orion and Arcturus are named by Homer and Hesiod, and not only by Aratus, who is known to have flourished about the 124th Olympiad, nearly 300 years before the birth of Christ. Indeed, in Sacred History, which is the oldest of all records, mention is made of names given to the stars. Job 9:9: "Who makes Arcturus [עש, ʿAsh] and Orion [כסיל, kesil] and the Hyades [כימה, kimah] and the chambers of the South [חדרי תמן, chadrei teman]." The Greeks [render it]: "who makes the Pleiades, and Hesperus, and Arcturus, and the chambers of the South" [ὁ ποιῶν Πλειάδα, καὶ Ἕσπερον, καὶ Ἀρκτοῦρον, καὶ ταμιεῖα νότου]. Most render "Arcturus," but Ibn Ezra thinks it is the Bear and the Wain [Ἄρκτος and Ἅμαξα]. It seems to be something more general, a gathering of stars, from the root עש, "to gather," and fits no figure better than the Greater and Lesser Bears together with the coiling of the Dragon, which lie near the Arctic Pole. So also in the same Job 9:9 [recte 38:32?], "Until Arcturus [לפני עש] ..."; Rabbi David in his book of roots renders it "at every time when Arcturus moves, that is, always." Jerome: "They will be consumed, as by a moth." In the same chapter, 38:32: "Can you bring out the Morning Star in its season, or guide Arcturus [עיש] with its sons (that is, the lesser stars)?" Jerome: "And make the Evening Star fall upon the brows of the earth." According to Jerome, כסיל [kesil] is Orion, from its inconstancy; according to some, because its rising disturbs the globe with varying storms. So Isaiah 13:10: "For the stars of heaven and their Orions [וכסיליהם] will not give forth their light," where Jerome has "their splendour." Some hold that the Hyades are the Suculae [little pigs], a name not far from it; and perhaps Rabbi Jonah meant this, when he writes that in Arabic it is called סוחיל [suhail], and Jerome translates כימה in Job as Hyades. Rabbi Jonah wishes it to be a combination of stars, which in Arabic is called altudin [al-Thudin, i.e. al-Thurayya], and which the Greeks call the Bear [Ἄρκτος]; Jerome also translates this word as Hamos in Job 5:8. Ibn Ezra, on Job 38:31, records from tradition that the כימה [kimah] of the ancients was seven stars at the end of Aries (not in Aries, but on the back of Taurus), of which six are visible, and which the Latins were accustomed to call the Septentriones; but he himself thinks that there is one large star (of the first magnitude) which is the left eye of Taurus. "Chadrei teman" [the inner chambers of the south]; ταμιεῖα [tamieia, storehouses] of the South, that is, the Southern stars, so called because they are hidden and are not seen by those who inhabit our hemisphere. The holy man celebrates God as the creator of the stars, both those of the south, which flee from our sight, and those of the north, which stand ever before our eyes. All these things prove that it is by no means a new invention to divide the stars into definite figures. Pliny, Natural History, book 2, chapter 8, writes that Cleostratus was the first to give names to the signs; whether this is true I leave to others to investigate.

units.tr: CHAPTER XIX.

units.la: Signorum in Zodiaco Syllabus; multiplex distinctio, Situs, Præfectura.
units.tr: A Syllabus of the Signs of the Zodiac: their manifold division, position and rule.

units.la: SIGNORVM alia in Zodiaco; alia extra eundem. Ibi sunt duodecim, quæ Ζῴδια Græcis (causam alias indicavi) & δωδεκατημόρια, quod partes sint lati Circuli duodecimæ. Eorum quoque dispescitur in xxx. gradus; qui additi conficiunt cccLx: horum quilibet tribuitur in minutias Primas lx; Primæ in partes abeunt Secundas; hæ in totidem Tertias; Tertiæ in Quartas, & sic deinceps. Signorum autem Zodiaci nomina sunt hæc: Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpius, Sagittarius, Capricornus, Aquarius, Pisces. Ordine suo sic describit Manilius lib. i: Aurato princeps Aries in vellere fulgens, Respicit admirans adversum surgere Taurum, Summisso vultu Geminos & fronte vocantem. Quos sequitur Cancer, Cancrum Leo, Virgo Leonem. Aequato tum Libra die cum tempore noctis Attrahit ardenti fulgentem Scorpion astro. In cujus candam contentum dirigit arcum Missus Iquo volucrem missurus jamque Sagittam. Tum venit anguifo Capricornus sidere flexus. Post hunc inflexam defundit Aquarius Urnam Piscibus adsuetas aside subeuntibus undas. Quos Aries tangit claudentes ultima Signa.
units.tr: Some signs lie in the Zodiac and others outside it. There are twelve in the Zodiac, which the Greeks call Zōdia (I have given the reason elsewhere) and dōdekatēmoria, because they are the twelfth parts of the broad circle. Each is further divided into 30 degrees, which together make 360. Each degree is divided into 60 primary minutes; each primary minute into 60 second minutes; each second into the same number of thirds; the thirds into fourths, and so on. The names of the signs of the Zodiac are these: Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, Pisces. Manilius describes them in their order in Book 1: Aries, gleaming on his golden fleece, the leader, looks back in wonder at Taurus rising opposite him, and at the Twins, who call with lowered face and brow. Cancer follows them, and Leo follows Cancer, and Virgo follows Leo. Then, when day and night are equal, Libra draws in the gleaming Scorpion with its burning star. Sagittarius, having sent his bird-bearing shaft, aims his bow, its string drawn back toward the Scorpion's tail. Then comes Capricorn, its star bent like a serpent. After him Aquarius pours from its inclined urn the waters that flow down to Pisces, which are used to the stars. Aries touches them, closing the last of the signs.

units.la: Operæprecium committere hæc cum descriptionibus, partim M. Tullij in Aratum, cujusque fratris Q. Ciceronis, partim Senecæ in Thyeste. Choro Act. iiii. & undecim Scholasticorum Poëtarum, quæ leguntur in Appendice Virgiliana, Juliani, Hilasij, Palladij, Asclepiadei, Eusthenij, Maximiani, Vitalis, Basilij, Asmeni, Vomani, Eupherbi; nam Pompeiani, qui duodecimus, carmen perijt.
units.tr: It is worth comparing these with the descriptions: partly of Cicero in his translation of Aratus, and of his brother Quintus Cicero; partly of Seneca in the Thyestes, in the chorus of Act 4; and of the eleven scholastic poets read in the Virgilian Appendix: Julianus, Hilarius, Palladius, Asclepiades, Eusthenius, Maximianus, Vitalis, Basilius, Asmenus, Vomanus and Euphorbus. The poem of Pompeianus, the twelfth, has been lost.

units.la: I. Aries, Κριὸς; Signorum Princeps Manilio & Palladio, Asclepiadeo Astrorum ductor, Nubigenum Juvenum vector Maximiano, Dux gregis Vomano, Corniger Vitali, Proditor Helles Hilasio, Laniger & Celer Festo Avieno; contorta cornua imponit Cicero. Quamvis in Circulo nihil primum, nihil postremum; primus tamen plerisque nominatur: quod, ut nonnulli volunt, incipiente illo die, qui primus omnium Universo illuxit, in medio Cœli, quod quasi Mundi Vertex, fuerit, scribente Macrobio lib. i. in Somnium Scip. cap. xxi. Tendens ad Occasum, caput ad Ortum convertit. Occidit a primis pedibus; exoriens caput tenet infra Triangulum collocatum, inquit Hyginus. Stellas habet xiii; extra formam v. Nota ejus γ, Arietis referens caput cornutum.
units.tr: I. Aries (Greek Krios). Manilius and Palladius call it the chief of the signs; Asclepiades, the leader of the stars; Maximianus, the bearer of the cloud-born youths; Vomanus, the leader of the flock; Vitalis, the horned one; Hilarius, the betrayer of Helle; Festus Avienus, the woolly and swift one. Cicero gives it twisted horns. Although in a circle there is nothing first and nothing last, most writers nonetheless name it first, because, as some hold, the day on which the first light shone on the universe began when it was in mid-heaven, which is, as it were, the summit of the world, as Macrobius writes in Book 1 on the Dream of Scipio, chapter 21. Hyginus says it turns its head toward the east while stretching toward the west; it sets with its forefeet, and as it rises it holds its head, placed beneath the Triangle. It has 13 stars, and 5 outside the figure. Its mark is γ, representing the horned head of the Ram.

units.la: II. Taurus, Ταῦρος; Corniger M. Tullio, Festo Avieno & Vitali, Invencus Asmeno, Forum prænuncius Q. Ciceroni, Europæ Vector Basilio, Proditor Europæus Hilasio. Spectat Ortum. Aversus τῆ ἀνατολῆ oritur & occidit. Stellarum est xxxiv. Extra formam adsidentxi. Character ejus ϑ, Caput bubulum. Bene Manilius lib. i. Astronom.
units.tr: II. Taurus (Greek Tauros). Cicero, Festus Avienus and Vitalis call it horned; Asmenus, the unyoked; Cicero (in his Aratus) the herald of the market; Basilius, the carrier of Europa; Hilarius, the Europa-betrayer. It looks toward the east. Turned away from the east, it rises and sets. It has 34 stars. Two stand outside the figure. Its character is ϑ, the head of an ox. Manilius rightly says in Book 1 of the Astronomica:

units.la: Pleiades Hyadesque fiers pars utraque Tauri.
units.tr: The Pleiades and the Hyades, both parts of Taurus, are made.

units.la: Nam Hyades τὰ Βόκρανα huic Signo efficiunt: Pleiades vero circumcæsuram vel ἀπονεμῶ, qua Taurus finit. Est enim, ut & Equus ἱππικῷ: unde male Manilius Tauro Clunes tribuit; imprudentius cum Plinio Vitruvius Caudam, quum tamen hic cumdem paullo ante inchoatum καὶ ἡμιπλῆ fecisset. Paucis dicam de utrisque distinctius.
units.tr: For the Hyades form the head of this sign, ta Bokrana, while the Pleiades mark the cut-off point or the shoulder where Taurus ends. For it has, as the horse does, a hippikon part, and so Manilius wrongly assigns it the buttocks, and Vitruvius, following Pliny, more carelessly assigns it a tail, though a little earlier he had given it the same thing, begun and half-finished. I will say a few words about each more distinctly.

units.la: Πληάδες, quæ Mušæo Atlantis, (unde & Atlantides apud Virgilium lib. i. Georgic.) & Pleiones; Pherecydi apud Athenæum Lycurgi filiæ: dicuntur vel à Pleione matre, ut vult Ovidius lib. v. Fastor. ἀπὸ τῆς πλεῖν, quod ortu suo navigationis tempus indicent; Servius ad i. Georgic. Videndus & Vegetius lib. iv. de re militari cap. xxxix. vel ἀπὸ τῆς πλείστης, quasi πλείονες, quod plures simul, Isidorus lib. iii. cap. lxx. Sic D. Gregorius in Hijob. lib. xxix. cap. xxvii. Pleiades, inquit, Stella ἀπὸ τῆς πλείστης, id est, à pluralitate vocata sunt; ita vicinæ sibi & divisæ sunt conditæ, ut & simul sint, & tamen conjungi nequaquam possint; vel denique ὃπ πλησίον ἀλλήλων, ut in Aratum Theo. notat. Latinis Vergilius (Agell. lib. xiii. noct. Attic. cap. ix.) quod verno tempore oriantur, Ballus Comment. ad Germanicum Arati Paraphrasten; Servius ad lib. i. Georgic. Isidor. lib. iii. cap. lxx. Althoraie nonnullis, corrupta voce Arabica. אל חורים Rabi-Ionah putat esse ὄνομα Stellarum, quod Hebraeis כימה apud Hijobum cap. ix, 9. Legenda quae notavi cap. praecedente. Numero sunt (inter Tauri finitionem corporis, inquit Hyginus, & Aricis Caudam) septem: sex cum aliis contendit esse Proclus. Sed nulla ἐναντίωσις: nam Septem dici, Sex tamen esse solent, ait Ovidius; ut & Aratus ἐν Φαινομένοις: Ε᾽πάμποι δὴ πεῖ γᾶ μετ᾽ ἀνθρώπιυς ὑδίετ᾽) Ε᾽ξ εἰσὶ πρὶν ἱεσθαι ἐπιψηλα ἐ᾽ξ ἀλμεῖν, Οὐ μὴ πως δεινάλων ἐν ἀπὸ ζῆς ὅτι Διὸς Ἀστέρ.
units.tr: The Pleiades (Pleiades), which Musaeus calls the daughters of Atlas (whence also Atlantides in Virgil, Georgics 1), and Pleione; Pherecydes in Athenaeus calls them daughters of Lycurgus. They are said to be named either from their mother Pleione, as Ovid holds in Book 5 of the Fasti; or from apo tēs pleu, because their rising indicates the season of navigation (Servius on Georgics 1; see also Vegetius, Book 4 on military affairs, chapter 39); or from apo tēs pleistēs, as if pleiones, that is, many together (Isidore, Book 3, chapter 70). So St Gregory, in his Moralia on Job, Book 29, chapter 27: "The Pleiades," he says, "a star, are named from pleistē, that is, from plurality; they are created so near to one another and so separate, that they are together and yet can by no means be joined." Or finally from hop' plēsion allēlōn, near one another, as Theon notes on Aratus. To the Latins, Virgil (Gellius, Attic Nights, Book 13, chapter 9) says they rise in spring; Balbus, in his commentary on Germanicus, the paraphrast of Aratus; Servius on Georgics 1; Isidore, Book 3, chapter 70. Some call them Althoraie, a corrupted Arabic word. Rabbi Jonah thinks al Chorim is a name of the stars, which the Hebrews call Chimah (kimah) in Job 9:9. The passages I have noted should be read in the preceding chapter. Between the end of Taurus's body (says Hyginus) and the tail of the Ram, there are seven of them. Proclus contends that there are six. But there is no contradiction: Ovid says, They are called seven, yet they are usually six; and Aratus in the Phaenomena says the same, that they are seen as few by men, but are seven, though not all visible at once.

units.la: Eduntur ab eodem ejusque interpretibus nomina: ——— ἐπὶ δ᾽ κεῖναι ὀπιφρὸς καλιόντι, Ἀλκυόνη, Μεροπη, Κελαινώ τ᾽, Ἠλέκτρη. Καὶ Σπερώνη, καὶ Ταυγέτη, καὶ ποτνια Maia.
units.tr: The names of the Pleiades are given by the same poet and his interpreters: "...and upon them, bright and resplendent: Alcyone, Merope, Celaeno, and Electra, and Sterope, and Taygete, and the reverend Maia."

units.la: Earum splendidissima perhibetur Maia, scribente Servio ad viii. Aeneidos, ut non immerito Epitheto decorata; ποτνιας, ut jam auditum ex Arato, Sanctissima Ciceroni. Formosa Germanico & Festo Avieno: sic enim apud hunc non famosa legendum.
units.tr: The brightest of them, as Servius writes on the Aeneid 8, is Maia, and she is adorned with the epithet not without reason; Aratus called her potnia, and Cicero sanctissima (most holy). Germanicus and Festus Avienus call her formosa (beautiful); for in Avienus one should read formosa, not famosa.

units.la: Quidquid sit de Numero, certe nihil aliud sunt, quam Ἀστέρων συστροφή. Nam ὀλίζωνες, ut eas vocat Nicander, ἡλιόφα Φορίων), καὶ ——— ἀ μάλα πολλὸς ἀπείρους χωρῶν ἐχ.———
units.tr: Whatever the number, they are nothing other than a gathering of stars. For Nicander calls them holizones, and Phorinus ēliophaēs, and Aratus says they are very many, filling an infinite space.

units.la: inquit Aratus; & quasi in le jacent confertae & conglobatae, ut minimum spacium occupent. Et hinc Sidus parvo g. omerali ie, Manilio lib. iv. ubi de Tauro. Densos corum greges nominat Seneca in Medea, Act. i. Choro: Sic cum Sole perit Sideri lus decor, Et densi latitant Pleiadum greges.
units.tr: They lie close together and crowded into one mass, so that they occupy the smallest space; hence Manilius, Book 4, where he speaks of Taurus, calls them a small star-cluster. Seneca in the Medea, Act 1, chorus, names them the dense flocks: So with the Sun the beauty of the stars perishes, and the dense flocks of the Pleiades hide.

units.la: Spissum ignem tribuit Propertius lib. iii. Eleg. iv: Quur ferus versare boves & plaustra Bootes, Pleiadum spissö quur coit igne Chorus?
units.tr: Propertius, Book 3, Elegy 4, attributes to them thick fire: Why does the fierce Bootes turn the oxen and the wagon, and why does the chorus of the Pleiades gather in thick fire?

units.la: adeo ut propter συνδρομὴν hanc putatae Veteribus Choream, quod notat Hyginus, ducere: quam capta Troia, deseruisse; & ab Sororum exsultantium consortio se subduxisse fingitur Electra: ne lascivire videretur in publico luctu. Hinc Chorus Pleiadum non solum apud Propertium, ut jam audiimus, sed & apud Horatium lib. iv. Carminum, Ode xiv: Indomitas prope qualis undas Exercet Auster, Pleiadum choro Scindente nubes.——
units.tr: Because of this close gathering, the ancients supposed they lead a dance, as Hyginus notes; they fabled that Electra, after the capture of Troy, left the dance and withdrew from the company of her exulting sisters, so as not to seem wanton in public mourning. Hence the chorus of the Pleiades appears not only in Propertius, as we have just heard, but also in Horace, Odes Book 4, Ode 14: Like the south wind that stirs the untamed waves, when the chorus of the Pleiades parts the clouds.

units.la: Proclus Comment. quem in Opera & Dies Hesiodi scripsit, πλειάδας Sphaerarum Inferiorum Animas esse nugatur; quod Κελαινώ Saturni, Σπερώνη Iovis, Μεροπη Martis, Ἠλέκτρα Solis, Ἀλκυόνη Veneris, Μαῖα Mercurij, Ταυγέτη denique Lunae. Absurdiora addunt nonnulli, alias cum suis Planetis, alias cum aliis Diis rem habuisse; quod indicat Ovidius lib. iv. Fastorum: Pleiades incipiens humeros relevare paternos, Quae Septem dici, Sex tamen esse solent. Seu quod in amplexus Sex hinc venere Deorum, Nam Steropen Marti concubuisse ferunt. Neptuno Alcyonen: & te formosa Celeno; Maiam, atque Electram, Taygetenque Iovi. Septima mortali Merope tibi Sisyphe nupsit: Poenitet: & facti sola pudore latet.
units.tr: Proclus, in his commentary on Hesiod's Works and Days, talks nonsense in saying that the Pleiades are souls of the lower spheres: Celaeno is of Saturn, Sterope of Jupiter, Merope of Mars, Electra of the Sun, Alcyone of Venus, Maia of Mercury, and Taygete finally of the Moon. Some add still more absurd stories, that they had dealings now with their own planets, now with other gods; Ovid in Book 4 of the Fasti indicates this: The Pleiades, beginning to lift their paternal shoulders, which are called seven yet are usually six. Either because six of them came into the embraces of gods: for Sterope is said to have lain with Mars, Alcyone with Neptune, and you, beautiful Celaeno, and Maia and Electra and Taygete with Jupiter. The seventh, mortal Merope, married you, Sisyphus; she is sorry, and hides alone for shame at the deed.

units.la: Ut concludam, Athenaeus lib. ii. docet πλειάδας ab Aeschylo, Pindaro, Simonide, πελειάδας, id est πελειάδες, Columbas etiam nominari. Sufficiat audisse Simonidem: Ἐπικὰ δ᾽ Ἀτλας ἐπὶ ἰοκλαιμῶν Φίλαν Ἰυγατέρων τὴν (Μαῖαν) ἔξοχον εἰδῶν. καὶ καλέοντες πλειάδες ὑρείνας. Neque alio respicit Homerus, quum in descriptione Scyphi Nestorei πλειάδας, Columbas, Iovi canit Ambrosiam pocillari; πλειάδας intelleintellegens. Quod autem ab harum circumvolutione descriptus olim quibusdam Græciæ populis annus, πλεῶν inde solet appellari; quemadmodum videre est apud Theon. in Aratum.
units.tr: To conclude: Athenaeus, Book 2, teaches that the Pleiades are also called peleiades, that is, doves (peleiades, peleiadzes), by Aeschylus, Pindar and Simonides. It is enough to have heard Simonides: And Atlas, upon his shoulders, bore his daughters, the most excellent of forms (Maia), and they are called the Pleiades, the doves of the mountains. Homer, too, refers to nothing else when, in describing the cup of Nestor, he sings of the peleiades, the doves, as the ambrosia-pourers of Jove, understanding them as the Pleiades. The year that was once marked for certain peoples of Greece by the circling of these stars is commonly called pleōn from them, as can be seen in Theon on Aratus.

units.la: Ὑάδες, quæ in capite Tauri, Musæo Atlantis & Æthræ, nonnullis Erechthei, quibusdam Cadmi filiæ; dictæ censentur, vel ab unico fratre Hya, quem ab Læna laniatum sic scribuntur defleuisse, ut ab eo nomen sortitæ, & Astris ob pietatem inlatæ, Eustath. in Homeri Iliad. σ. vel ὑσ τῶν ὑὸν, quod ortu suo prænuncient pluvias, M. Tullius II. de Nat. Deor. Has Græci Stellas Hyades vocitare consueuerunt à pluendo. Ovidius v. Fastor.
units.tr: The Hyades, which lie in the head of Taurus, are by Musaeus, Atlas and Aethra; by some they are the daughters of Erechtheus, and by others the daughters of Cadmus. They are thought to be named either after a single brother, Hyas, whom they are written to have mourned so bitterly after he was torn apart by a lion that they got their name from him and were placed among the stars for their piety (Eustathius on Homer's Iliad, sigma); or from [ὑεῖν], because by their rising they foretell rain. Marcus Tullius, On the Nature of the Gods, book 2: The Greeks have customarily called these stars Hyades from raining. Ovid, Fasti, book 5.

units.la: Ore micant Tauri septem radiantia flammis;
units.tr: They shine at the mouth of Taurus, seven stars radiant with flames.

units.la: Nauita quas Hyades Graius ab Imbre vocat.
units.tr: Which the Greek sailor calls the Hyades from the rain.

units.la: Et hinc Tristes Horatio lib. 1. Carminum, Oda 111. Vel ab littera τ, quam ordine suo situque formant. Eustath. in Iliados σ: Αἱ δὲ Ὑάδες, Ὅτι ἐ Ταύρῳ κεῖνται κεφαλαί: ἡ ἀ ἐξ τὸν ἀδελφὸν Υἱὸν ἀ τὴν ὕτῳ ἀλληλοις; ἡ δὲ ἐπ τὸ Τ φωνήεν περιμέρεις εἰσίν. Vbi & Ὑάδες dicuntur Βακχαὶ καὶ Διονύσου. Sunt enim etiam, qui Hyades putant appellatas ab Hyc Baccho, cujus perhibentur fuisse nutrices; Apollodorus lib. 111. Latinis Suculæ, notantibus Seruio ad 1. Georgic. & Isidoro lib. 111. Etymolog. cap. LXX. Rationem nominis notant Agell. lib. xiii. cap. ix. & apud eum Tiro Ciceronis libertus, quamquam fallam: Suculæ Seruio ad finem 1. Æneid. à succo. Sidus Palilicium olim Romanis, ab Vrbis Natali die, teste Plinio lib. xviii. natural. histor. cap. xxvi. De Numero parum conuenit inter Veteres. Duas Thales Milesius putauit, quarum una Borealis, Australis altera; Tres Euripides in Phaëthonte; Quatuor Achæus: Quinarium numerum tuentur Musæus & Hesiodus; Senarium edit Proclus; Septenarium denique Aratus ejusque Interpretes, item Ovidius v. Fastor. & Hyginus in Astronomic. agnoscunt. Vere cum Musæo Hesiodus (neque enim plures quinque) cui hæc illarum nomina:
units.tr: And hence "the Sad ones" in Horace, Odes, book 1, ode 3. Or they are named from the letter upsilon, which they form by their order and arrangement (Eustathius on Iliad, sigma): "The Hyades are so called because they lie in the head of Taurus, or because they mourned their brother Hyas, or because they are arranged in the shape of the letter Υ." There the Hyades are also called the Bacchae and the nurses of Dionysus. Some indeed think they were named from Hyas, Bacchus, whose nurses they are said to have been (Apollodorus, book 3). In Latin they are called Suculae, as Servius on Georgics 1 and Isidore, Etymologies book 3, chapter 70, note. The reason for the name is given by Gellius, Attic Nights, book 13, chapter 9, and there Tiro, Cicero's freedman, though mistakenly, says it is from succus, as Servius at the end of Aeneid 1 also states. The Romans once called them the Palilician star, from the birthday of the City, according to Pliny, Natural History, book 18, chapter 26. The ancients do not agree well about their number. Thales of Miletus thought there were two, one northern and one southern; Euripides in the Phaethon says three; Achaeus says four. Musaeus and Hesiod uphold the number five; Proclus gives six; and finally Aratus and his commentators, as well as Ovid, Fasti book 5, and Hyginus in the Astronomy, recognise seven. Truly, Hesiod agrees with Musaeus that there are no more than five, and he gives their names:

units.la: Φαισύλη, ἡδὲ Κορωνίς, εὐσίφανος τὶ Κλέεια.
units.tr: Phaisyle, and Coronis, and Cleeia of the famous name [Φαισύλη, ἡδὲ Κορωνίς, εὐσίφανος τὶ Κλέεια].

units.la: Φαισώ ἱμερόεσσα, καὶ Εὐδώρη ταυνίπτσλ.
units.tr: Phaeso the lovely, and Eudore [Φαισώ ἱμερόεσσα, καὶ Εὐδώρη].

units.la: Νύμφαι, ἃς Υάδας καλέεσιν Φῦλ' ἀνθρώπων.
units.tr: "Nymphs, whom men call the Hyades" [Νύμφαι, ἃς Υάδας καλέεσιν Φῦλ' ἀνθρώπων].

units.la: Alijs alio modo nominantur. Certe inter Hyadas, quæ Orionis clypeo proxima, Arabibus; Oculus Tauri, nobis ab sicu vocatur; λαμπεδίας Græcis ab insigni splendore: est enim primæ magnitudinis.
units.tr: They are named in different ways by different writers. Certainly among the Hyades, the one nearest the shield of Orion is called by the Arabs by one name; we call it Oculus Tauri, the Eye of Taurus, from its position; the Greeks call it Lampadias from its outstanding brightness, for it is of the first magnitude.

units.la: 111. Gemini, Διόσκοροι; Fratres Iuliano, Tyndaridæ Palladio & Basilio, Sidus geminum Aclepiadio, Spartana Soboles, Prolesque Tonantis egregia Festo Avieno, Ledæ Soboles Eusthenio, Proles duplex Iouis Maximiano & Almenio, Pares Vomano, Geminum Astrum Columellæ. Occasum spectant. Occidunt directi à pedibus; exoriuntur inclinati ut jacentes: juncti quasi vinculo, quod Virgula Manilio lib. iv. & Linea, ut etiam Firmico in Myriogenesi partium, Græcis γεγαμμη: Stellis fulgent xiix; extra formam illis vii: quæ pedes illorum præcedit, Πρόστης Græcis vocatur, ut notant Geminus, Proclus, Hyginus: ὁ ἐπὶ ἡ κεφαλὴς, secundæ magnitudinis Arabibus, Caput geminorum. Alter geminorum dicitur Ἡ ἐχαλῆς, alter Α' ἀπλῶν; Arabice Abraraleus & Aphellan, vocibus fere Græcis. Nam corrupte vulgo Abracaleus & Avellar. Nota π, corpuscula duo, consertis & brachijs & cruribus.
units.tr: Third: Gemini, the Dioscuri [Διόσκοροι]. Julian calls them Fratres, the Brothers; Palladius and Basil call them Tyndaridae; Asclepiades, Sidus geminum, the twin star; Festus Avienus, Spartana soboles, the Spartan offspring, and proles Tonantis egregia, the outstanding progeny of the Thunderer; Eusthenius, Ledae soboles, the offspring of Leda; Maximian and Almenus, proles duplex Iovis, the double progeny of Jove; Vomanus, pares, the equals; Columella, geminum astrum, the twin star. They look toward the west. They set feet first and rise leaning over, like men lying down; they are joined as if by a bond, which Manilius, book 4, calls virgula, a rod, and linea, a line, as Firmicus also does in his Mathesis, and the Greeks call [γεγαμμη]. They shine with nineteen stars; seven lie outside the figure. The star that goes before their feet is called Prostes by the Greeks, as Geminus, Proclus and Hyginus note. The one at the head, of the second magnitude, the Arabs call the Head of the Twins. One of the twins is called by the Greeks [Ἡ ἐχαλῆς], and the other [Α' ἀπλῶν]; in Arabic they are Abraraleus and Aphellan, words nearly Greek, for the common forms Abracaleus and Avellar are corruptions. Their mark is π: two small bodies with arms and legs intertwined.

units.la: IV. Cancer (à quo multis olim numerandi Signa Zodiaci initium: Cicero Arati sequens ordinem:
units.tr: IV. Cancer, the Crab (from which many in the past began the numbering of the signs of the Zodiac), as Cicero does, following the order of Aratus:

units.la: Æstifer est pandens ferventia Sidera Cancer)
units.tr: Summer-bearing Cancer, which spreads out its glowing stars.

units.la: καρκίνος; Nepa torrida flammis Maximiano; Aquatile Signum nominat Iulianus, Aquarum Aluminum Almenus; fervida Brachia tribuit illi Palladius, torridum ignem Eusthenius; adustum canit Vitalis, Sole perustum Basilius, Æstus comitem Vomanus, Æstiferum Tullius, calentem denique Euphorbus. Ortum spectat. Occidit & oritur posteriore corporis parte. Stellis insignitus xiii; extra formam iv. Duæ quæ in dorso ὄνοι Græcis apud Proclum & alios, magnitudinis quartæ; Latinis Asselli, quod notat Plinius lib. xix. cap. ultimo: quæ vero non procul inde νεφελοειδῆς, nubeculam referens, οὐρα φὴ; Græcis Φάτνη, quemadmodum indicant Asterismi, Geminus & Proclus; Præsepe Latinis, Plinius ibidem. ejus Characterr ⊗, depravati ut vulgo Scaliger, Cammari figura.
units.tr: [καρκίνος]. Maximian calls it nepa torrida flammis, the scorpion scorched by flames; Julian names it signum aquatile, the aquatic sign; Almenus, aquarum alumnum, the nursling of the waters; Palladius gives it fervida brachia, burning claws; Eusthenius, torridum ignem, scorching fire; Vitalis sings of it as adustum, scorched; Basil, sole perustum, burnt by the sun; Vomanus, aestus comitem, the companion of heat; Tully, aestiferum, heat-bearing; and finally Euphorbus, calentem, hot. It looks toward the east. It sets and rises with its hinder part. It is marked by thirteen stars; four lie outside the figure. The two on its back, which Proclus and others call [ὄνοι] in Greek, are of the fourth magnitude; in Latin they are Asselli, the Donkey Colts, as Pliny notes in book 19, last chapter. The nebulous star near them, resembling a little cloud, is called [φάτνη] by the Greeks, as the star-catalogues of Geminus and Proclus show, and Praesepe (the Manger) by the Latins, as Pliny says in the same place. Its mark is ⊗, corrupted, as Scaliger says, into the shape of a crab's claw.

units.la: Quæ sic feliciter vertit Latinus ille: Idem me ille Conon cœlesti lumine vidit, F. Berenicco vertice Cæsariem, Fulgentem clare : quam multis illa Deorum Ler ia protendens brachia pollicita 'st.
units.tr: Which that Latin poet has rendered happily thus: That same Conon saw me with heavenly light, the lock of Berenice's bright hair, shining clearly, which she, stretching out her arms, promised to the many gods.

units.la: Character autem Leonis Ω, qui nihil aliud quam ejus cauda.
units.tr: The mark of the Lion is Ω, which is nothing other than its tail.

units.la: VI. Virgo, Παρθένος: Innubam scribit Iulianus; Sanctam vocat Hilasius; Almam Palladius, Eusthenius, Euphorbus; Iustam Maximianus, Vitalis, Asmenius; Piam Vomanus; Optimam Basilius; Atticam Festus Avienus. Putatur Hesiodo Jovis & Themidis; Arato Astræi & Aurorae filia, cognomine Justitia; alijs alia. Occidit capite prius, quam ceteris membris. Stellis describitur xxvi; adlocatis extra formam vi. Illarum, quæ ὅπι ἐξ ἀειστερῶν ἀκρεχωρὸν fulgida & primæ magnitudinis, Στάχυς Hipparcho in Asterismis, Gemino & Ploclo dicitur; Spica Latinis apud Hyginum & Iulium Firmicum: unde & Virginem canit Aesclepiadius, quæ Spicea munera gestat, sic Aratus, —— ἡ ῥ' ἐν χεροὶ φέρει Στάχυν αἰγλήεσσαν:
units.tr: VI. Virgo, the Virgin [Παρθένος]. Julian writes innuba, unmarried; Hilarius calls her sancta, holy; Palladius, Eusthenius and Euphorbus, alma, nourishing; Maximian, Vitalis and Almenus, iusta, just; Vomanus, pia, dutiful; Basil, optima, best; Festus Avienus, attica, Attic. She is thought by Hesiod to be the daughter of Jove and Themis; by Aratus, the daughter of Astraeus and Aurora, called Justice; others say otherwise. She sets with her head before her other limbs. She is described with twenty-six stars; six are placed outside the figure. Of her stars, the bright one of the first magnitude which is [ὅπι ἐξ ἀειστερῶν ἀκρεχωρὸν] is called [Στάχυς] by Hipparchus in his star-catalogue, and by Geminus and Proclus; the Latins call it Spica, the Ear of Grain, as Hyginus and Julius Firmicus do; hence Asclepiades also sings of the Virgin as one who spicea munera gestat, bears ears of grain as gifts. So Aratus: [ἡ ῥ' ἐν χεροὶ φέρει Στάχυν αἰγλήεσσαν], she who in her hands bears a shining ear of grain.

units.la: M. Tullius ejus Παραφέρεσθαι.
units.tr: Marcus Tullius, its [Παραφέρεσθαι].

units.la: Spicum illustre tenens splendenti Corpore Virgo.
units.tr: A Virgin holding a bright ear of grain in her shining body.

units.la: Arabica dictio, qua vocatur hodie Spica, corrupta est; emendanda fortean ex conjectura magni Scaligeri (cui vocum Arabicarum restitutionem acceptam lubens retero) سنبلة Scribit idem in lib. v. Manill. Arabes etiam appellare Stel- ℰ Iam hanc Ἀστάχυλλις, hoc est fusum: tamquam fusus sit, non Spica, quod gestat Virgo: Nam אלעדר ἡ ἐλίθερον signficare. Quæ ad dextram Virginis alam Stella Προτρυγητὴρ Græcis nominatur ut notant Asterismi, Ploclus, Hyginus, alij; Prævindemiator Latinus: videndi Plinius lib. xviii. nat. hist. cap.xxvi. & xxxi. Columella lib. xi. de re rust. cap ii. apud quos προτρυγητὴς & Vindemiator. Nota Virginis ⲙ, Ala, quæ illi duplex. Fingitur enim, nomine nota Iustitiæ, scelera mortalium auorsata in Cœlum evolasse.
units.tr: The Arabic word by which the Spica is now called is corrupted, and it should perhaps be emended by the conjecture of the great Scaliger (whose restoration of Arabic words I gladly accept and repeat), sunbulah. The same author writes in book v of his commentary on Manilius that the Arabs also call it Stel-lam. Now this is Astachyllis [Ἀστάχυλλις], that is, fusus (a spindle), as if it were the spindle and not the Spica that the Virgin carries. For al-adr [אלעדר] ... ē elitheron [ἡ ἐλίθερον] signifies... The star on the right wing of the Virgin is called by the Greeks Protrygētēr [Προτρυγητήρ], as the Asterisms, Ploclus, Hyginus and others note; the Latins call it Prævindemiator. See Pliny, Natural History book xviii, chapters 26 and 31, and Columella, On Agriculture book xi, chapter 2, where we find protrygētēs [προτρυγητής] and vindemiator. Note the sign of the Virgin, the Wing, which is double for her. For it is fabled that she, named after the sign of Justice, flew up into heaven, having turned away from the crimes of mortals.

units.la: VII. Libra, Ζυγὸς nunc, quæ prius χηλαὶ: sub configuratione quondam habita Scorpij, quem ob magnitudinem posteriores Astronomi in duo partiti sunt domicilia: alii enim tendunt brachia; alio corpus, cauda, aculeus. Hinc quod χηλαὶ Scorpij in Libra contaminantur, illæ pro hac sæpe leguntur positæ. Momen Manilio voce Lucretiana, Momentum nuncupatur Eusthenio, Æquale Iugum Euphorbo, Trutina Basilio. Stellarum est xiii. quarum quæ in medio iugo, de quo lances dependent, quæque in lance versus Virginis pedes; stellæ sunt secundæ Magnitudinis. Character ≏, Zygos ut Aristoteles vocat, Iugum cum Aasi, quæ λαβὴ Græcis, in qua Examen versatur,
units.tr: VII. Libra, now Zygos [Ζυγός], which was formerly Chelae [χηλαί]: under an earlier configuration it was part of Scorpio, which the later astronomers divided into two houses because of its size. Some of them take the arms, others the body, tail and sting. Hence, because the claws of Scorpio are contained in Libra, the name Chelae is often read for it. Manilius calls it Momen, a Lucretian word; Eusthenius calls it Momentum; Euphorbus calls it Æquale Iugum; Basil calls it Trutina. It has thirteen stars: those in the middle of the beam, from which the pans hang, and those in the pan toward the Virgin's feet. The stars are of the second magnitude. Its character is ♎. Aristotle calls it Zygos, the Yoke, together with Aasi, which the Greeks call labē [λαβή], the grip in which the Balance turns.

units.la: VIII. Scorpius; Σκορπιὸς; Cauda Animal quod dirigit ictum Iuliano; Chelæ minaces Asclepiadio; flagrante minaæ cauda Lucano lib. 1; violentus acumine cauda Hilasio; cauda tumendus adunca Eusthenio; violenta cuspide saevus Maximiano; nigrumque genus in acumine virus Vitali; armatus veneno Basilio; gerens lethale venenum Almeno; minitans ictu Vomano; cauda venenifer unca Euphorbo. Occasum spectat. Oritur erectus. Occidit curvo corpore inclinatoque capite. Stellis delineatur xxi. adpositis extra formam iii. Quæ secundæ magnitudinis in pectore, Cor Scorpij Latinis, Ἀντάρης Græcis, ut notat in Asterismus Hipparchus; Arabice dicitur قلب العقرب בלב אלעקרב. In extrema cauda positæ nomen ab loco; ubi etiam duæ, quas vocant Astronomi Scorpionis Aculeos. Nota m, quid velit notum.
units.tr: VIII. Scorpius [Σκορπιὸς]; Cauda Animal quod dirigit ictum (the tail, the creature that directs its sting), per Iulianus; Chelae minaces (threatening claws), per Asclepiadius; flagrante minaæ cauda (threatening with a blazing tail), per Lucan, book 1; violentus acumine cauda (fierce in the point of its tail), per Hilasius; cauda tumendus adunca (to be feared for its hooked tail), per Eusthenius; violenta cuspide saevus (savage with its violent point), per Maximianus; nigrumque genus in acumine virus (the dark race with poison in its point), per Vitalis; armatus veneno (armed with poison), per Basilius; gerens lethale venenum (bearing deadly venom), per Almenus; minitans ictu (threatening with its stroke), per Vomanus; cauda venenifer unca (venomous with its hooked tail), per Euphorbus. It looks toward the setting. It rises upright. It sets with its body curved and its head bowed. It is marked by 21 stars, with 3 more added outside the figure. The star of the second magnitude in the breast is called Cor Scorpii by the Latins and Antares by the Greeks, as Hipparchus notes in his Asterismus; in Arabic it is called qalb al-'aqrab [בלב אלעקרב in Hebrew]. The stars placed at the extreme tail take their name from their place; there are also two there which the astronomers call the Stings of the Scorpion. Note m: what it means is known.

units.la: IX. Sagittarius, Τοξότης; Arciteneus Festo Avieno; Sagitti potens Ciceroni ad Aratum. & ejus fratri Q. Tullio; Sagittifer Hilasio & Basilio; Senex Chiron Senecæ in Thyeste Act. iv. Choro, & Palladio, ex Theocrito cui χείρων χειρων; Semifer Arcipotens Maximiano; Centaurus biformis Vitali; geminus Chiron Almeno; Armatum arcu facit Iulianus; arcu pollentem Asclepiadius; arcu minacem Euphorbus. Spectat ad occasum. Præceps occidit; oritur directus. Stellarum est xxxi. Antepedem ejus Stellæ sunt in rotundam formam digestæ, quas Coronam, ejus ut ludentis abiectam, putant, Hygino scribente. Signum ⇢, quid signet est clarum.
units.tr: IX. Sagittarius; Toxotēs [Τοξότης]. Festus Avienus calls it the bowman; Cicero, in his translation of Aratus, and his brother Quintus Tullius call it powerful with the arrow; Hilasius and Basil call it arrow-bearer; Seneca, in the Thyestes, act 4, chorus, and Palladius, drawing on Theocritus, call it the old Chiron, where the Greek is cheirōn [χείρων]; Maximian calls it half-beast, mighty with the bow; Vitalis calls it two-formed Centaur; Almenus calls it twin Chiron; Julianus makes it armed with a bow; Asclepiadius calls it strong with the bow; Euphorbus calls it threatening with the bow. It looks toward the west. It sets headlong and rises upright. It has thirty-one stars. The stars in front of its forelegs are arranged in a round shape, which, as Hyginus writes, people think is a crown discarded by it in play. Its sign is ♐; what it signifies is clear.

units.la: X. Capricornus, Αιγόκερως; humidus Aegoceros Lucano libr. ix; Corniger Hircus Iuliano; Saxi quadrupes Hircus Asclepiadio; Caper aequoris Eusthenio; Aequoris Hircus Vomano; Corniger aequoris alti Almenio; Neptunia proles Euphorbo. geidum vocat Senecæ in Thyeste; aquosum Maximianus; ferosam speciem tribuit Avienus; Corpus semiferum & os ferum Cicero; Pelagi proceliam hic nominat Vitalis. Spectat ad Occasum. Occidit præceps; oritur directus. Stellas habet xxviii: quarum quæ in radice Caudæ, magnitudinis tertiæ, nominatur Arabice ذنب الجدي דנב אלגדי voluta, in quam hic Asterismus definit. Ejus nota ♈, extrema cauda Piscis conquam hic Asterismus definit.
units.tr: X. Capricornus, Aigokeros [Αιγόκερως]: humidus Aegoceros in Lucan, book ix; Corniger Hircus in Julianus; Saxi quadrupes Hircus in Asclepiadius; Caper aequoris in Eusthenius; Aequoris Hircus in Vomanus; Corniger aequoris alti in Almenus; Neptunia proles in Euphorbus. Seneca calls it icy in the Thyestes; Maximianus calls it watery; Avienus gives it a fierce appearance; Cicero, a half-beast body and a fierce mouth; Vitalis here names it the storm of the sea. It sets in the west. It sets headlong and rises upright. It has 28 stars, of which the one at the root of the tail, of the third magnitude, is called in Arabic Dhanab al-Jadi [דנב אלגדי], a curl at which this asterism ends. Its mark is the sign of the Goat; the asterism ends at the extreme tail of Pisces, with which it borders here.

units.la: XI. Aquarius, Υδροχόος vel Υδροχὸς; Fulsor aquæ Iuliano: Puer Armiger Hilasio; Iuvenis gestator aquæ Palladio; Urnam Nimbiferi nominat hic Asclepiadius: Deucalionis aquas Vomanus; Aureatam Urnam tribuit Avienus; Troianus puer dicitur Eusthenio; delectatusque Iovi puer Almeno; Quisquis es Senecæ, ab ritu, quo, dubitantes de certo alicujus numinis nomine, Romani Deos compellabant. Ortum spectat. Occidit & oritur capite prius, quam reliquis membris. Stellis fulget per se xxii, & cum ectusa Aqua xlii: quarum quæ postrema in ore Piscis meridionalis, primæ magnitudinis, corrupta voce Arabica nuncupatur hodie Fomahant: quum sit, indicante mihi Scaligero, פם אלחות, Os Piscis. Est enim σῶμα τοῦ ἰχθύος, τοῦ λεγομένου Νοτίου ποταμοῦ; ut videatur ex Antiquorum mente: Sidus hoc referendum potius ad Piscem Meridionalem & Solitarium, quam ad Aquarij ἀσσεμός. χύσιν ὕδατος Græcis etiam ob amfractus Ἀμπελίνον fuisse dictam, docet, quamvis corruptus, Vitruvius lib. ix. cap. vii: Arieti & Piscibus Cetus est subjectus, à cujus crista ordinate utrisque Piscibus disposita, est tenuis fusio Stellarum, quæ Græce vocatur ἐρμηδόν. Emendandum enim, magno monente Scaligero, Ἀμπελόν; Subscribit huic sententiæ Hesychius: Ἀέρεδον, inquiens, τῶν ἀμυδρῶν Ἀστέρων χύσις. Obscuras, vel potius imbecillioris lucis, appellat: quod omnes sint vel quartæ vel quintæ magnitudinis; excludens, quæ ἐν τῷ ἰχθύος primæ classis; Piscis Notij formæ potius, ut dixi, adnumeranda. Stellæ porro quatuor, quæ Aquario in summa dextra Καλῶν Græcis, ut scribit Proclus: Latinis Urnæ nomine sunt notæ. Character huius formæ ≈, Aquæ fulio, Ἀμφορέως hic iii.
units.tr: XI. Aquarius; Hydrochoos or Hydrochos [Υδροχόος, Υδροχὸς]. Julianus calls it the bright-shining water-bearer; Hilasius calls it the armour-bearing boy; Palladius calls it the young man carrying water; Asclepiadius here calls it the urn of the rain-bearer; Vomanus calls it the waters of Deucalion; Avienus ascribes to it the golden urn; Eusthenius calls it the Trojan boy; Almenus calls it the boy delighted by Jupiter; Seneca calls it Whoever you are, from the custom by which the Romans, unsure of the proper name of some deity, addressed it in that way. It looks toward the east. It sets and rises head first, before the other parts. It shines of itself with twenty-two stars, and with the Water as well with forty-two. The last of these, in the mouth of the southern fish, of the first magnitude, is now called by the corrupt Arabic name Fomahant. It is, as Scaliger indicates to me, pum al-hut [פם אלחות] in Hebrew, the mouth of the fish. For it is the body of the fish called the Southern [sōma tou ichthyos tou legomenou Notiou] river, so that the star seems, in the mind of the ancients, to belong more to the Southern and Solitary Fish than to the Aquarian urn. That Aquarius's outpouring of water was called by the Greeks ampelinon [Ἀμπελίνον] because of its winding course, is shown by Vitruvius, book 9, chapter 7, though the text is corrupt: Below Aries and the Fishes lies Cetus, from whose back, arranged evenly on both Fishes, is a thin scattering of stars, which in Greek is called ... Here, on the great authority of Scaliger, we must emend this to ampelon [Ἀμπελόν]. Hesychius agrees with this view, saying: aerédon [Ἀέρεδον] is a scattering of faint stars. He calls them faint, or rather of weaker light, because all of them are of the fourth or fifth magnitude, and he excludes those in the fish, which belong to the first class; as I have said, they should rather be counted among the figure of the Southern Fish. Four stars, which the Greeks call Kalōn [Καλῶν] at the upper right of Aquarius, as Proclus writes, are marked in Latin by the name of the Urn. The character of this figure is ♒; the Water, the Jar. Here Amphoreus has three stars.

units.la: XII. Pisces, ἰχθύες Supremos nominat Palladius: ultima Cæli Sidera Seneca in Thyeste: Postremam figuram Vomanus; Sidus Aquosum Vitalis; quibus denique Ultimus ordo datur ab Euphorbo. Ambo vocantur Βομβιχίαι; quod, quamvis corruptior, notat Festus Avienus. Alter Νότιος, alter Βορεῖος appellatur: hic (proprio nomine nonnullis etiam χιλιδονίας, quod in ejus μορφῇ caput hirundinum ei adhingant Chaldaei; Vir magnus putat inde, quod, quum Sol in extremo est Pisce, Hirundo incipiat videri, quae Veri praeludit) inter Æquinoctialem & Æstivum Circulum Arcticum polum spectat; ille, in Zodiaco Circulo extremo collocatus, occasum respicit. Oriuntur & occidunt inferiore parte. Stellae numerantur in hoc Signo xxxv; extra formam iv. Quae a Piscium Caudae partibus sita Graecis dicuntur Λίνοι, ut videre est apud Proclum; Latinis Linea & Linola, quibusdam etiam Lina; legendus Hyginus; suntque in Austrina Linea Stellae ix, in Septemtrionali v. Praefulgens autem Sidus, quod ἐν ἀκρῳ τῷ λίνῳ, inquit Proclus, Σωσίσμα Graecis; Arato σωδίσμα ἐπυρέα, M. Tullio & Festo Avieno Nodus Caelestis; significare volentibus, quod notat de Cicerone Hyginus, Nodum hunc non solum Piscium, sed totius esse Sphaerae. Nota x, Pisces duo adversi, oppositis dorsellis cum vinculo.
units.tr: XII. Pisces; ichthyes [ἰχθύες]. Palladius calls them the highest; Seneca, in the Thyestes, calls them the last stars of heaven; Vomanus calls them the last figure; Vitalis calls them the watery constellation; and Euphorbus finally gives them the last place in order. Both are called Bombichiai [Βομβιχίαι], a name which Festus Avienus records, though it is rather corrupt. One is called Notius [Νότιος], the other Boreius [Βορεῖος]. The northern one (which some also call by its proper name Chelidonias [χιλιδονίας], because the Chaldeans attach to its form the head of a swallow) faces the Arctic pole between the equinoctial and summer circles. The other, placed at the extreme edge of the Zodiac circle, looks toward the west. Both rise and set with their lower part first. Thirty-five stars are counted in this sign, with four outside the figure. The stars situated at the parts of the Fishes' tail, which are called Linoi [Λίνοι] by the Greeks, as may be seen in Proclus, are called in Latin Linea and Linola, and by some Lina; Hyginus should be read here. There are nine stars in the southern Line and five in the northern. The star that shines out most brightly, which Proclus says is at the top of the line, is called Sōsisma [Σωσίσμα] by the Greeks; in Aratus it is the fiery sōdisma; for Cicero and Festus Avienus it is the Heavenly Knot. Hyginus, writing about Cicero, notes that those who wish to indicate this say the knot belongs not only to the Fishes but to the whole sphere. The mark x: two Fishes facing each other, with their backs opposed and a bond between them.

units.la: Non autem omnibus his Signis eadem est cum Zodiaco latitudo. Alia arctiore describuntur, alia spacio latiore. Tauri pes extra Zodiacum protenditur: Piscium Australior extra eumdem multum procedit. Ut imprudenter, nobilissimus ille cum genere tum eruditione, Picus Mirandulanus lib. vii. contra Astrologos, quum didicisset Zodiaci fasciam in xii. patere gradus, scripserit unumquodque Signum xii. graduum habere latitudinem; dutiniens hanc secundum Signorum latitudines, non Planetarum, quod debebat, ᾱσονδύσεις.
units.tr: The breadth of the Zodiac is not the same for all these signs. Some are outlined within a narrower band, others within a wider one. The foot of Taurus extends beyond the Zodiac; the southern of the Fishes goes much further beyond it. Thus the very noble Pico della Mirandola, distinguished both in birth and learning, in book 7 against the astrologers, having learned that the band of the Zodiac extends over twelve degrees, wrote that each sign has a width of twelve degrees. He thought this should be reckoned by the latitudes of the signs and not of the planets, which he ought to have done. [ᾱσονδύσεις]

units.la: Quid vero dicam de variis Signorum cum apud alios, tum apud Manilium lib. ii. differentiis? Distinguuntur i. κατὰ τ φύσιν. Nam alia Ἀρρένικα: alterna ab Ariete: alia Θηλυκά ut reliqua.
units.tr: But what shall I say of the various differences among the signs, both in other authors and in Manilius, book 2? They are distinguished, first, by nature (kata tēn physin [κατὰ τὴν φύσιν]). For some are masculine (Arrhenika [Ἀρρένικα]); alternate ones, beginning from Aries; and others feminine (thēlika [Θηλυκά]), as the rest.

units.la: II. Κατὰ τὸ Εἰδος. Alia namque Λογικά καὶ Ἀνθρωπόφυή, ut Gemini; Virgo, Libra, Aquarius: alia Ἀλογα καὶ ζωομορφα; quorum Ἡμερα quidem, Aries & Taurus; Ἀνθρωπα vero, καὶ Ἀρχια, Leo & Scorpius.
units.tr: II. According to form [Κατὰ τὸ Εἶδος].
