For some are rational and human-shaped [Λογικά καὶ Ἀνθρωπόφυῆ], such as Gemini, Virgo, Libra and Aquarius; others are irrational and animal-shaped [Ἄλογα καὶ ζωομορφα]. Of these, the tame ones are Aries and Taurus, and the human ones and the ruling ones [Ἀνθρωπα καὶ Ἀρχια] are Leo and Scorpius.

units.la: III. Κατὰ τ Συζυγίαν. Dicuntur enim Δίδυμα, Bina: quorum quaedam Disjuncta, Paria Latinis, Graecis συζυγα, ut gemini se respicientes; Pisces adversantes sibi: quaedam Concreta καὶ συμφυῆ, quae etiam Δίμορφα & διφυῆ ut Capricornus & Sagittarius.
units.tr: III. According to conjunction. They are called Didyma (pairs), meaning twins. Some are Disjunct, called Paria in Latin and syzyga [συζυγα] in Greek, like twins looking at one another, or Pisces facing each other. Others are Concrete and joined together [συμφυῆ]; these are also called Dimorpha and diphyē [διφυῆ], such as Capricorn and Sagittarius.

units.la: IV. Κατὰ τὴν Σχέσιν πρὸς τὰς ὥρας. Haec in triplici sunt discrimine: partim Communia & Media, Graecis Δισωμα; non à forma, sed ab effectu, quem habent duplicem. Contingunt enim & praeteriti temporis finem, & principium sequentis. Proclus: Δίσωμα, οὐχ ἓν ἐκ δύο σωμάτων: ἀλλ' ἐν μεταξὺ δύο ὡρῶν ἐστι. Τοιαῦτα δέ ἐστι τὰ πᾶντα τ τελευταίων ὡρῶν. Ut sunt Gemini, qui adfectum Ver & incuntem AEstatem; Virgo, quae AEstatis finem & Principium Autumni; Sagittarius, qui Autumnum relinquit, Brumam excipit: Pisces, quorum alter consumat Hiemem, alter Ver suscipit. partim Cardinalia seu Mobilia, quae quatuor Zodiaci Punctis Cardinalibus proxime succedunt: quorum duo AEquinoctialibus contigua, Ἰσημέρινα ut Aries & Libra; duo Solstitialibus proxima, Τροπικά, ut Cancer & Capricornus. partim denique Firma seu Solida, Στέρεα, Cardinalibus proxima, ut Taurus, Leo, Scorpius, Aquarius.
units.tr: IV. According to their relation to the seasons. These are of three kinds. Some are Common and Middle, called Disōma [Δισωμα] in Greek. They are named not from their form but from their effect, which is twofold: they touch both the end of one season and the beginning of the next. Proclus: Disōma is not one thing made of two bodies, but lies between two hours [or seasons]. All those that fall at the end of a season are of this kind, such as Gemini, which take on spring and enter summer; Virgo, which ends summer and begins autumn; Sagittarius, which leaves autumn and receives winter; and Pisces, of which one completes winter and the other takes up spring. Some are Cardinal or Movable, lying next to the four Cardinal points of the Zodiac. Of these, two are adjacent to the equinoxes and are called Equinoctial [Ισημερινα], such as Aries and Libra; two lie near the solstices and are called Tropical [Τροπικά], such as Cancer and Capricorn. Finally, some are Fixed or Solid [Στέρεα], lying next to the Cardinal signs, such as Taurus, Leo, Scorpio and Aquarius.

units.la: V. Κατὰ τὸ Κῖνδυ. Alia enim Ἀποερφόμυα, Auersa; ut Taurus qui oritur clunibus, Gemini qui pedibus, Cancer qui testudine: alia Δρομαῖα, Currentia; ut Leo, Sagittarius, Aries: alia Καμπυλα, Flexa: Taurus, Libra, Capricornus: alia Ὀρθοσάδια vel Ὀρθοσαδικα, Recta: Virgo, Gemini, Aquarius: alia denique Κατεσπιμμένα; Cancer, Scorpius, Pisces.
units.tr: V. According to peril [Κῖνδυ]. Some are Averted [Ἀποερφόμυα], such as Taurus, which rises by its haunches, Gemini by its feet, and Cancer by its shell. Some are Running [Δρομαῖα], such as Leo, Sagittarius and Aries. Some are Bent [Καμπυλα]: Taurus, Libra and Capricorn. Some are Upright [Ὀρθοσάδια or Ὀρθοσαδικα]: Virgo, Gemini and Aquarius. Finally, some are Lowered [Κατεσπιμμένα]: Cancer, Scorpio and Pisces.

units.la: VI. Κατὰ τὴν ἐχθὴν πρὸς τὸν Τόπον. Alia enim Ἡμερινά, Diurna; ut Aries, Pisces; Sagittarius, Scorpius: Leo, Cancer: alia Νυκτερινά Nocturna; ut Taurus, Gemini; Virgo, Libra; Capricornus, Aquarius.
units.tr: VI. According to their relation to place. Some are Diurnal [Ἡμερινά], such as Aries and Pisces; Sagittarius and Scorpio; Leo and Cancer. Others are Nocturnal [Νυκτερινά], such as Taurus and Gemini; Virgo and Libra; Capricorn and Aquarius.

units.la: VII. Κατὰ τὴν Διαίζων καὶ βίον. Alia namque Χερσαῖα; ut Taurus, Aries, Leo, Scorpius: alia Ὑδατώδη; Cancer, Pisces: alia Ἀμφιβοπεζοντα vel Ἀμφίβια; Capricornus, Aquarius.
units.tr: VII. According to their habitat and way of life. Some are Terrestrial [Χερσαῖα], such as Taurus, Aries, Leo and Scorpio. Some are Watery [Ὑδατώδη], such as Cancer and Pisces. Some are Amphibious [Ἀμφιβοπεζοντα or Ἀμφίβια], such as Capricorn and Aquarius.

units.la: VIII. Κατὰ τὸ πλεονέκτημα ἢ Ἐλάττωμα. Nam quaedam sunt πολύγονα vel πολύτεκνα; Cancer, Scorpius, Pisces: quaedam Ἄγονα, Σπιερὰ vel Σπιρώδη; Virgo, Leo, Aquarius: quaedam denique Ἐπίγονα; Capricornus, Sagittarius, Aries, ἐλάττωμα. Libra, Gemini, Taurus.
units.tr: VIII. According to advantage or disadvantage. Some are fruitful [πολύγονα or πολύτεκνα], such as Cancer, Scorpio and Pisces. Some are barren [Ἄγονα], sterile [Σπιερὰ or Σπιρώδη], such as Virgo, Leo and Aquarius. Finally, some are Epigona [Ἐπίγονα], such as Capricorn, Sagittarius and Aries, which are a disadvantage [ἐλάττωμα]. Libra, Gemini and Taurus.

units.la: IX. Κατὰ τὸν Σχηματισμὸν. Nam vel considerantur ut Hexagona: ut hinc Aries, Gemini, Leo, Libra, Sagittarius, Aquarius; inde Taurus, Cancer, Virgo, Scorpius, Capricornus, Pisces. Vel Tetragona: ut Aries, Cancer, Libra, Capricornus; Taurus, Leo, Scorpius, Aquarius; Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius, Pisces. Vel Trigona: Aries, Leo, Sagittarius: Taurus, Virgo, Capricornus: Gemini, Libra, Aquarius; Cancer, Scorpius, Pisces. Vel denique Opposita: Aries, Libra; Taurus, Scorpius; Gemini, Sagittarius; Cancer, Capricornus; Leo, Aquarius; Virgo, Pisces.
units.tr: IX. According to their figure. They are considered as hexagons: thus, on one side, Aries, Gemini, Leo, Libra, Sagittarius and Aquarius; on the other, Taurus, Cancer, Virgo, Scorpio, Capricorn and Pisces. Or as tetragons (squares): Aries, Cancer, Libra and Capricorn; Taurus, Leo, Scorpio and Aquarius; Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius and Pisces. Or as trigons (triangles): Aries, Leo and Sagittarius; Taurus, Virgo and Capricorn; Gemini, Libra and Aquarius; Cancer, Scorpio and Pisces. Or finally as opposites: Aries and Libra; Taurus and Scorpio; Gemini and Sagittarius; Cancer and Capricorn; Leo and Aquarius; Virgo and Pisces.

units.la: X. Κατὰ τὸ Κλίμα. Alia enim Arctica & Septemtrionalia, quæ ἡμικύκλιον Zodiaci ab Aequatore in Boream vergens constituunt, quorum Vernalia, Aries, Taurus, Gemini; Aestiva, Cancer, Leo, Virgo: alia Antarctica Australia, quæ oppositum in meridiem prominens; horum Autumnalia, Libra, Scorpius, Sagittarius; Hiemalia vero Capricornus, Aquarius, Pisces.
units.tr: X. According to climate. Some are Arctic and Northern, which make up the half of the Zodiac that slopes from the equator toward the north. Of these, the Vernal signs are Aries, Taurus and Gemini; the Summer signs are Cancer, Leo and Virgo. Others are Antarctic and Southern, which project opposite, toward the south. Of these, the Autumnal signs are Libra, Scorpio and Sagittarius; and the Wintry signs are Capricorn, Aquarius and Pisces.

units.la: Jam Situs & Ἀστροθεσίας singulorum indicant (utinam, qua diligentia, fide) Aratus in Phænomenis, Hipparchus in Asterismis, Arati Interpretes M. Tullius, Germanicus & ad eum Bassus, Festus Avienus, Leontius; item Hyginus in Astronomico Poetico & alij: Nominum rationes aperiunt cum alij, tum Franciscus Georgius Venetus Canticorum I. Tomi vi. cap. xviii. & Hannibal Rosselus ad Pymandrum Mercurij lib. iv. Comment. xi. Quæst. i. cap. ii. & seqq. Caussas denique quas ob in cœlum relata hæc, & alia quæ extra Zodiacum (ut simul hoc moneam) explicanda succedunt Signa, fabulosas (Fabulis tamen veritatem aliquo modo obvelari 20 certum) varie commemorant Musæus, Hesiodus, Asclepiades, Mnaseas, Pherecydes, Hegesianax, Eubulus, Hermippus, Leon, Alexander, Diogenetes, Pisander, Sosicheus Tragœdiarum scriptor, Conon Samius Mathematicus, & alij apud Hyginum; nec non Ovidius in Fastis & alibi Plinius lib. ii. & xviii. Galenus orat. suasoria ad artes, Firmicus lib. ii. Lucianus in Astrolog. Scholiastes Apollonij lib. ii. Plurimus autem in Astronomicis Mythologijs fuit Eratosthenes, quod indicant ex illo laudata ab Grammaticis. Aratus fuit parcior. Hesiodum enim imitans intra fabularum licentiam, ex rancidis Mythologijs multa circumcidit & amputat. Elegans hac de re est Epigramma apud Achillem Statium: Ἡ σιοδὸς τὸ ἄεισμα καὶ ὁ ηρέπ@ ἔτ@ ἀοιδῆ Ἐξάτον ἀλλ' ἐκνέω μὴ τὸ μελιχρότατον Τῶν ἑαυτῶν ὁ σολὸς ἀπεμάξατο. χαίρετε λαστταὶ Ῥῆσις Ἀρήτα συγγονοι ἀγυρωνίης.
units.tr: The positions and star groupings of each of these are described by Aratus in the Phaenomena, Hipparchus in the Asterisms, and the translators of Aratus: Marcus Tullius [Cicero], Germanicus and Bassus after him, Festus Avienus and Leontius; likewise Hyginus in the Poetic Astronomy and others. (Would that they had done so with due care and good faith.) The reasons for the names are explained by several writers, including Francesco Giorgio of Venice in the first volume of his Canticles, book vi, chapter xviii, and Hannibal Rossellus in his commentary on Mercury's Pymander, book iv, comment xi, question i, chapter ii and following. Finally, the reasons why these signs, and others that lie outside the Zodiac (which I note here at the same time, since they are to be explained next), were placed in heaven, are variously told as fables by Musaeus, Hesiod, Asclepiades, Mnaseas, Pherecydes, Hegesianax, Eubulus, Hermippus, Leon, Alexander, Diogenetes, Pisander, Sosicheus the writer of tragedies, Conon of Samos the mathematician, and others cited by Hyginus. Ovid in the Fasti, Pliny in books ii and xviii, Galen in his persuasive oration on the arts, Firmicus book ii, Lucian in the Astrology, and the scholiast on Apollonius book ii also tell them. It is certain, however, that there is some truth veiled in the fables. Eratosthenes was the most prolific writer of astronomical myths, as the grammarians' quotations from him show. Aratus was more sparing. Imitating Hesiod, but within the licence of fable, he cut away and pruned much from the stale myths. An elegant epigram on this matter is found in Achilles Statius: [Ἡσίοδος τὸ ἄεισμα καὶ ὁ ἕτερος ἐπ' ἀοιδῆ ...] Hesiod sang the song, and the other after him in song; but the sweetest of his own things ... the wise one has drawn off ... Farewell, you who learn the craft of Aratus.

units.la: Singulis Signis singula Pythagorici Numina præficiebant, testibus Macrobio lib. i. in Somnium Scipionis, cap. xxi. & Marsilio Ficino lib. iv. Theolog. Platonic, Ex qua secta Manilius lib. ii. Astronomicôn: Lanig um Pallas; Taurum Cytherea tuetur; Formosos Phœbus Geminos; Cyllenie Cancrum, Iupiter, & cum Matre Deum regis ipse Leonem: Spicifera est Virgo Cereris; fabricataque Libra Vulcano; pugnax Mavortis Scorpius hæret; Venantem Diana virum sed partis equinæ; Ast angusta fovet Capricorni sidera Vesta; Vt Iovis adversum, Iunonis Aquarius astrum est; Agnoscitque suos Neptunus in aquore Pisces.
units.tr: The Pythagoreans assigned a particular deity to each sign, as Macrobius attests in book i on Scipio's Dream, chapter xxi, and Marsilio Ficino in book iv of the Platonic Theology. From this school Manilius, in book ii of the Astronomica, writes: Pallas guards the woolly Ram; Venus watches over the Bull; Phoebus the handsome Twins; Cyllenian Mercury the Crab; Jupiter, with the Mother of the gods, the king himself guards the Lion; the Virgin bearing ears of grain belongs to Ceres; Libra was fashioned by Vulcan; the warlike Scorpion clings to Mars; Diana hunts with the man, but of the horse's part; but Vesta cherishes the narrow stars of Capricorn; Aquarius is the star opposed to Jupiter, belonging to Juno; and Neptune recognises his own Fishes in the sea.

units.la: Signis itemhisce Regionum tutelæ solent adsignari, varie tamen ab varijs; quod uno Arietis exemplo demonstrasse sufficiat. Subjiciunt enim huic Ægyptij Babyloniam, & Arabiam AEgypto conterminam; Ptolemæus Britanniam, Galliam, Germaniam, Basterniam Palestinam; Hipparchus τὰ Κελῆ δὲξιὰ ἀμὰ Thraciam τὰ ἀμὰ Babyloniam τῷ ἀνῷ Armeniam, ἀρῆς ἀλλήλαις Arabiam, τὸ παχὶ καὶ τῷ πότῳ Persida, Cappadociam, Mesopotamiam, Syriam, Rubrum mare, &c. Manilius lib. iv. absurdissima αἰτιολογία præficit Arietem Propontidi, quod à Poetis Hellespontum tranasse fingatur. De reliquis nugis silentium esto. Præest omnibus unus Deus.
units.tr: These same signs are usually assigned the guardianship of regions, though different authors assign them differently. One example, that of Aries, is enough to show this. The Egyptians place under it Babylonia and Arabia, which borders Egypt. Ptolemy assigns Britain, Gaul, Germany, Bastarnia and Palestine. Hipparchus assigns Thrace, Babylonia, Armenia, Arabia, Persia, Cappadocia, Mesopotamia, Syria, the Red Sea and so on, in various combinations. Manilius, in book iv, sets the Ram over the Propontis with the most absurd reasoning, because the poets pretend that it carried people across the Hellespont. Let us be silent about the other trifles. One God presides over all.

units.la: Quæ vero Signa Collateralia cum xii. Zodiaci vel oriantur vel occidant; exponunt Aratus, Cicero Germanicus & ad eum Bassus, Festus Avienus; item Hyginus in Astronomico Poetico, & alij.
units.tr: The signs that rise or set together with the twelve of the Zodiac are explained by Aratus, Cicero, Germanicus and Bassus after him, and Festus Avienus; likewise by Hyginus in the Poetic Astronomy and others.

units.la: CAP. XX.
units.tr: CHAP. XX.

units.la: De Signis Septemtrionalibus.
units.tr: On the Northern Constellations.

units.la: TALIA in Zodiaco Signa: quæ extra eum duplicis sunt generis, vel Septemtrionalia, quæ ab latiore fascia in Septemtrionem; οἱ ἐκτὸς τῆ Βοῤῥαν ἡμισφαίριον vel Meridionalia, quæ in Meridiem recedunt; οἱ ἐκτὸς τὸ τόπον Ἀντισχάμου. Septemtrionalia sunt hæc:
units.tr: There are such signs in the Zodiac. Those outside it are of two kinds: either Northern, which lie beyond the broader band toward the North [οἱ ἐκτὸς τῆ Βοῤῥαν ἡμισφαίριον], or Southern, which recede toward the South [οἱ ἐκτὸς τὸ τόπον Ἀντισχάμου]. The Northern ones are these:

units.la: I. Vrsa Minor, Ἄρκτος μικρά. Ἄρκτος olim ἀπλῶς, μικρά cœpit appellari: quum quæ hodie μεγάλη, nomen Ἁμάξης exuerat. Κυνόσουρα dicitur ab una ex Idæis Nymphis, Iovis nutricibus: ut vult apud Hyginum Agloasthenes Naxicorum auctor. Aratus: Οἱ τὴν μὲν Κυνόσουραν ἐπικλῆσιν καλέουσι; Τὴν δ' ἑτέρην Ἕλικα.
units.tr: I. The Little Bear, [Ἄρκτος μικρά]. The Bear was formerly called simply [ἀπλῶς] the Bear, and later began to be called the Little one, when what is now the Great Bear had given up the name of the Wain [Ἁμάξης]. It is called Cynosura [Κυνόσουρα] after one of the Idaean nymphs, the nurses of Jupiter, as Agloasthenes, author of the Naxica, holds in Hyginus. Aratus: "Some call the one Cynosura by name; the other Helice."

units.la: Interpres ejus M. Tullius; loquens de duabus Arctis: Ex his altera apud Graios Cynosura vocatur; Altera dicitur esse Helice.
units.tr: His translator, M. Tullius, speaking of the two Bears: "Of these, one is called Cynosura by the Greeks; the other is said to be Helice."

units.la: Φοινίκη nuncupatur, quod eam, monstrante Thalete, ut memoriæ prodit Herodotus Milesius, Phœnices & Pœni rei navalis peritiores inter navigandum, scribente Hygino, sequantur. Stellas habet VII; quarum quæ tertiæ magnitudinis in extrema cauda, ἐπ' ἀκρᾶς τῆς οὐρᾶς, inquit Hipparchus in Asterismis, Arabibus appellatur אלרכבה, Ἁμάξα, Plaustrum; nam & hoc nomen huic Schematii nonnunquam imponitur ut videre est apud Aratum ejusque Interpretes: quod autem eadem Stella Mundi sit proxima vertici, Polaris vel Polus indigetari solet, ut notat Hyginus. Nulla enim totius Stellarum chori vero Poli loco vicinior.
units.tr: It is called Phoenice, because the Phoenicians and Carthaginians, the more skilled in seamanship, follow it when navigating, as Herodotus of Miletus records on the authority of Thales, and as Hyginus writes. It has seven stars. Of these, the one of third magnitude at the very end of the tail [ἐπ' ἀκρᾶς τῆς οὐρᾶς], as Hipparchus says in the Asterisms, is called by the Arabs al-Rakabah [Arabic word transliterated], the Wain [Ἁμάξα], Plaustrum; for this name too is sometimes given to this figure, as may be seen in Aratus and his interpreters. That the same star is nearest the vertex of the heavens is usually indicated by the name Polaris or Pole, as Hyginus notes. For no star of the whole host is nearer the true pole.

units.la: II. Vrsa Maior, Ἄρκτος μεγάλη. Olim hæc Ἁμάξα Græcis, stellarum tantum VIII; quod Plaustro non videretur absimilis. Homerus Iliados Σ, Ἄρκτον θ', ἣν καὶ Ἁμάξαν ἐπίκλησιν καλέουσιν.
units.tr: II. The Great Bear, [Ἄρκτος μεγάλη]. Formerly this was the Wain [Ἁμάξα] to the Greeks, with only eight stars, which would not seem unlike a wagon. Homer, Iliad Σ: "the Bear, which they also call by the name of the Wain [Ἁμάξαν]."

units.la: Veteres enim ex septenario numero duas, quæ pares, inquit Hyginus, & maxime in uno loco, pro Bobus: quinque reliquas instar habebant Plaustri; proximum etiam Signum Bootes, de quo post, nominantes. Ἄρκτος tamen Arato Ἁμάξα, non quod in ea Plaustri esset similitudo, sed quod non secus ac Plaustrum circa πόλον Βόρειον, Bootæ agitante, versetur. In quo non mediocriter illum errare (quasi fortunæ rerum cœlestium ibi periclitarentur) scribit Hyginus. Posterioribus temporibus huius Ἀστερισμὸς major est factus, & de Stellis VII, ut ait apud Hyginum Parmenisus, constituta sunt ab Astronomis XXV. (paullo plures hodie numerantur) ita ut auctus huius beneficio Ἄρκτος cœperit adlimulare: unde & qui Βοώτης quomdam, Ἀρκτοφύλαξ deinde dictus. Inter Stellas, quæ quadrangulum constituentium in sinistro latere spinæ dorsi versus collum adjacet, secundæ magnitudinis, Arabibus
units.tr: For the ancients took two of the seven, which are paired, says Hyginus, and especially so in one place, to stand for the Oxen; the remaining five they took as the likeness of a Wain. They also named the neighbouring constellation Bootes, of which more later. Aratus, however, calls the Bear the Wain [Ἁμάξα], not because it has any likeness to a wagon, but because, like a wagon, it turns about the North Pole [πόλον Βόρειον] with Bootes driving it. Hyginus writes that in this Aratus errs not a little, as if the fortunes of the heavenly bodies were in danger there. In later times this constellation of the Great Bear was enlarged; from seven stars, as Parmenisus says in Hyginus, the astronomers made twenty-five (more are counted today), so that by this increase the Bear began to take on a bear-like form. Hence the one formerly called Bootes was later called Arctophylax. Among the stars that lie on the left side of the quadrangle formed by the body, toward the neck, the second magnitude star is called by the Arabs, the Bear par excellence [κατ' ἐξοχήν], [Arabic word transliterated: Rabk].

units.la: רבכ, Vrsa κατ' ἐξοχὴν vocatur: prima trium, quæ supra caudam, τῶν ἐπὶ τῆς οὐρᾶς ἡ πρῶτος, Arabibus Alhaiot, nonnullis Alioz: quæ vox adeo morbosa, ut ne Apollo quidem medicinam illi facere posset; ut nec quæ tertia secundæ magnitudinis ἐπ' ἀκρᾶς τῆς οὐρᾶς eidem nobis genti Bennenacx. Callisto etiam fuit appellata; de qua, in Ἄρκτον mutata, multa fabulosa Hesiodus, Amphis Comœdiarum scriptor, Tegeates Historicus, aliique obscurioris auctoritatis apud Hyginum. Ἑλίκη etiam dictam constat ex multis auctoribus & Græcis & Latinis, quod in gyrum vortatur; Ἑλίξ enim circumvolutio: aliis tamen aliunde ab Thessaliæ vel Peloponnesi opido sic nominata. Certe quod Ἑλίκη hanc, ut præter Hyginum tradit Theon in Aratum, navigantes observarent Græci, Ἑλίκωπες vocat eos Homerus Iliad. α. Bene Aratus: Ἑλίκην μὲν αὐδρες Ἀχαιοί Ἐν ἁλὶ πλεύσουσι, ἵνα χρὴ νῆας ἀγινεῖν. Τῇ δ' ἄρα Φοίνικες πίσυνοι, πρόσωπα θαλάσσης.
units.tr: The first of the three stars above the tail [τῶν ἐπὶ τῆς οὐρᾶς ἡ πρῶτος] is called by the Arabs Alhaiot, by some Alioz*; a word so troublesome that not even Apollo could supply a remedy for it. Likewise the third of the second magnitude stars at the very end of the tail [ἐπ' ἀκρᾶς τῆς οὐρᾶς] is called by the same people Bennenacx for us. It was also called Callisto, concerning whom, transformed into the Bear, Hesiod, Amphis the writer of comedies, Tegeates the historian, and others of less certain authority tell many fables, as recorded in Hyginus. It is also established by many authors, both Greek and Latin, that it was called Helice because it turns in a circle; for Ἑλίξ means a circling. Others, however, derive the name elsewhere, from a town of Thessaly or the Peloponnese. Certainly Helice was the star which, as Theon on Aratus relates besides Hyginus, the Greeks observed when sailing; Homer calls them Ἑλίκωπες in Iliad α. Aratus says well: "The Achaean men will sail on the sea by Helice, where they must guide their ships; but the Phoenicians, trusting to the stern, [steer by the other]."

units.la: Quæ sic vertit Ovidius lib. II. Fastor. Esse duas Arctos, quarum Cynosura petatur Sidonijs, Helicen Graia carina notat.
units.tr: Ovid, in Book II of the Fasti, translates this thus: "There are two Bears; Cynosura is sought by the Sidonians, Helice marks the Greek ship."

units.la: Et Germanicus (nam Cicero mutilior hic) Hinc Iovis altrices, Helice Cynosuraque fulgent. Dat Grais Helice cursus maioribus astris; Phœnicas Cynosura regit.
units.tr: And Germanicus (for Cicero is more mutilated here): "Hence the nurses of Jupiter, Helice and Cynosura, shine. Helice gives the Greeks their course by the greater stars; Cynosura guides the Phoenicians."

units.la: III. Draco, Δράκων. Quam hic ob caussam in Cœlum translatus, & inter duas Vrsas vasto corpore (εἰς πλατεῖα ποταμὸς, Arato canente, veluti rapido cum gurgite flumen interpretante Tullio: corporis sinu facto & in sphæram quasi complicato, quemadmodum alij loquuntur) collocatus, fabulantur Pherecydes, Eratosthenes, aliique incertiores apud Hyginum; cui, ut & Germanico, dicitur Serpens. Stellarum apud antiquos est xv: numerantur hodie xxx; quarum ὁ ἐπὶ τῷ κεφαλῇς, tertiæ magnitudinis, Rasaben, Arabice scribitur à nonnullis appellari; quæ vox quid in hac constellatione velit, incertum enim caput filij.
units.tr: III. The Dragon, [Δράκων]. For what reason it was transferred into heaven and placed between the two Bears with its vast body (εἰς πλατεῖα ποταμὸς, as Aratus sings, "like a river with a swift current," as Tullius renders it, "its body made into a coil and folded, as it were, into a sphere," as others describe it), Pherecydes, Eratosthenes, and other less certain authors tell in Hyginus. Like Germanicus, Hyginus calls it the Serpent. The ancients counted fifteen stars in it; today thirty are counted. Of these, the one at the head [ὁ ἐπὶ τῇ κεφαλῇ], of third magnitude, is by some said to be called Rasaben in Arabic. What this word means in this constellation is uncertain; it means "the head of the son."

units.la: IV. Cepheus κηφεύς, quem ἀμφὶ Φοινίκης χαίρειν Ταυονίς, ut canit Aratus, ἴσως ἐξ ἡμέρας patulis manibus Germanico) Phœnicis filium, Æthiopum regem ostendunt apud Hyginum Euripides & alij. Stellarum est xii. Inter eas Ἀ ἑρπ. ὁ ὑπὲρ τὴν δεξιὸν ὤμον ἀπὸ ἀμφὶ, tertiæ magnitudinis, Arabibus Humeris.
units.tr: IV. Cepheus [Κηφεύς], whom Aratus sings of as rejoicing in Phoenice's ... (Germanicus says with outspread arms), is shown in Hyginus by Euripides and others as the son of Phoenix, king of the Ethiopians. It has twelve stars. Among them, the one above the right shoulder, of third magnitude, is called by the Arabs Humeris, "the shoulders."

units.la: V. Bootes, Βοώτης, Bubulcus; cuius instar Ἀμαξαν, Plau-strum sequi videbatur.
units.tr: V. Bootes, [Βοώτης], the Ploughman; the Wain seemed to follow in his wake.

units.la: Ἀρκτοφύλαξ cœpit dici, ut paulo ante monui, quum quæ Ἀμαξα, vii. quondam Stellarum, auctiore numero dotata, nomen adepta μεγάλης Ἄρκτου, cuius deinceps habitus est custos. Ωρίωνες etiam nomine notus apud Theocritum, cuius ἐν ἡμικυκλίῳ hæc sunt: Ἀμὸς δὲ ἐξίσπεται μεσονύκτιον εἰς δύσιν Ἄρκτου. Ωρίωνα καὶ αὐτὸν.
units.tr: He began to be called Arctophylax, as I noted a little earlier, when the Wain, once a group of seven stars, received a larger number and took the name of the Great Bear, whose guardian he thereafter was considered. He is also known by the name Orion in Theocritus, whose lines in the half-circle are: "Arcturus rises at midnight and sets toward the Bear. Orion too..."

units.la: Variæ de hoc commemorantur fabulæ, quas recensere longum esset: Petendas indico ex Hermippo, qui de Sideribus scripsit, & Petellide Gnosio historiographo, aliisque incertis, quos laudat Hyginus: qui hujus manum sinistram ita ab Arctico Circulo includi notat, ut neque occidere neque oriri videatur. Stellis hoc Signum hodie signant Astronomi xxiii; paucioribus olim. Vna illi extra formam primæ magnitudinis, ἡ μεσαξύ, inquit Hipparchus, τ μηρῶν, ἡ καλαμίδη Ἀρκτοῦρος (Arabibus Alramech, alijs corruptius Assimeth Aremeab) unde tota forma sæpe Arctūrus. Inter Coxas igitur Hipparcho: ibidem fere Vitruvio lib. ix. cap. vi, cuius hæc verba: Colorata Hipparcho paullo ante) item alia contra est Stella media genuorum custodis Arcti, qui Arcturus dicitur: Ἀνὰ μέσον τ σκελῶν, in medio Crurum, inquit Geminus & ex eo Proclus. Aratus hanc Stellam sub Arctophylacis zona ponit: ὑπὸ Ζώνη δὲ οἱ αὐτὸς Ἐξ ἄλλων Ἀρκτοῦρος ἐλίσσεται ἀφαδὴν ἀσὴρ. Cicero sic vertit: subter præcordia fixa tenetur Stella micans radijs, Arcturus nomine claro. Germanicus: Sed proprio tamen una micat sub nomine flamma, Arcturum dixere, sinus qua vincula nodant.
units.tr: Various fables are told about him, too many to recount; I direct the reader to Hermippus, who wrote on the stars, and to Petellides of Gnosus the historian, and others unknown, whom Hyginus cites. Hyginus notes that his left hand is so enclosed by the Arctic Circle that it seems neither to set nor to rise. Astronomers today assign twenty-three stars to this constellation; formerly fewer. Apart from the form, there is one star of first magnitude, which Hipparchus calls "the middle one of the thighs" [ἡ μεσαξύ τῶν μηρῶν], "the reed-bearer" [ἡ καλαμίδη], Arcturus (by the Arabs Alramech, by others more corruptly Assimeth Aremeab), whence the whole figure is often called Arcturus. "Between the thighs," then, according to Hipparchus; nearly the same is found in Vitruvius, Book IX, chapter 6, whose words are: "Colored" (as Hipparchus said a little before); "likewise there is another star opposite, in the middle of the knees of the Guardian of the Bear, which is called Arcturus." "Between the legs" [ἀνὰ μέσον τῶν σκελῶν], says Geminus, and from him Proclus. Aratus places this star beneath the girdle of the Arctophylax: "Beneath the Zone, where Arcturus, shining brightly, turns from the other stars." Cicero renders it: "Beneath the breast a star is fixed, shining with rays, Arcturus by its famous name." Germanicus: "Yet a flame shines by its own name alone, which they called Arcturus, where the bonds of the fold are knotted."

units.la: Videndus & Festus Avienus, qui hic mutilior. In Zona collocat Hyginus; sub pectore Manilius lib. i. Arcturumque rapit medio sub pectore secum.
units.tr: Festus Avienus should also be consulted, though he is more mutilated here. Hyginus places it "in the girdle"; Manilius, Book I, "under the breast": "and he carries Arcturus with him under his middle breast."

units.la: VI. Corona, Στέφανος; Gnosiam indigetant Manilius lib. i, Festus Avienus, & alij. Fabulis, quæ ex Creticorum Argolicorumque Scriptoribus alijsque apud Hyginum, Lectorem hic non morabor. Stellis coronatur hoc Σχῆμα viii: quarum quæ secundæ magnitudinis, Arabica voce nuncupatur Alphetach; Alfelta scribitur etiam Scaligero. De hac Manilius:
units.tr: VI. The Crown, [Στέφανος]; Manilius in Book I, Festus Avienus and others call it the Gnossian. I will not delay the reader with the fables that Hyginus draws from Cretan and Argive writers and others. This figure is crowned with eight stars. Of these, the one of second magnitude is named in Arabic Alphetach; Scaliger also writes it Alfelta. Of this, Manilius:

units.la: Nam Stella vincitur una Circulus in medio radians, qua proxima frontem Gnosia deserta fulgent monimenta puella, Candidaque ardenti distinguit lumina flamma.
units.tr: "For one star is joined to the circle, shining in the middle, near which the Gnossian monuments of the deserted girl shine forth, and it sets apart its bright lights with a burning flame."

units.la: Frontis meminit Poeta, volens etiam hic Ariadnam. Aratus de Corona: τὴν αἰγαυὸν ἐθηκε Σὴμ' ἐμφαυ Διόνυσος, ἐπιχομένης Ἀφροδίτης.
units.tr: The poet mentions the brow, wishing here too to refer to Ariadne. Aratus on the Crown: "The Crown, which Dionysus set as a bright token, when Aphrodite had come..."

units.la: VII. Hercules, ὁ ἐν γονάσιν, Ἀλφέαθ; Succiduum appellat Avienus in Coronæ descriptione, id est, Ingeniculatum; cui & Curvum Signum, Lyram describenti: Nixa Genibus species, Manilio lib. i. Germanico, Ophiuchum pingenti, vocatur Succiduus genibus lapsum & miserabile monstrum; ejusque illustratori Basso, ubi de Equo dimidio, Geniculator. Flexum Genu Tullius nominat ad Aratum, ubi de Fide: Atque inter Flexum genu, & caput Alitis haesit.
units.tr: VII. Hercules, [ὁ ἐν γονάσιν], Alpheath. Avienus, in his description of the Crown, calls him Succiduus, that is, "kneeling" (Ingeniculatus); also the "Curved Sign," in describing the Lyre: "a figure leaning on its knees," Manilius Book I. Germanicus, painting Ophiuchus, calls him "Succiduus," the fallen one, a wretched monster; and his illustrator Bassus, where he speaks of the half-horse, calls him Geniculator. Tullius, in his translation of Aratus, where he treats of the Lyre, names him "Flexum Genu" (the bent knee): "and between the bent knee and the head of the Bird it stuck fast."

units.la: Sic enim legendum, non Flexum genus Emendationem rationibus firmarem si cum Grammaticis mihi res esset. Omnes autem propric. Est enim Signum quod ἐν γόνατι κάμπτει ἐκλάζουσα ἔοικεν, inquit Aratus; Imago, vertit Cicero, quam Graeci ἐν γόνασιν vocitant, genibus quod nixa feratur.
units.tr: It must be read thus, not Flexum genus. I would back this emendation with arguments if I were dealing with grammarians. But all these are proper names. Aratus says the sign is one that "ἐν γόνατι κάμπτει ἐκλάζουσα ἔοικεν" [seems to lean, bending at the knee]. Cicero renders it as Imago, "the Image, which the Greeks call ἐν γόνασιν, because it is said to lean on its knees."

units.la: Absint, ut passim mihi, sic in hoc Signo monstrando fabulae, quibus ex Eratosthene, Panyasi, Hegesianactc, Aeschylo, aliis, commemorandis nimis sunt Hyginus, Basslus; Festus Avienus, cui Hercules ille caelestis Tempora deinde at maculosi prona Draconis.
units.tr: As I do everywhere, I will leave aside the fables in pointing out this sign. Of those mentioned by Eratosthenes, Panyasis, Hegesianax, Aeschylus and others, there are too many in Hyginus and Bassus. Festus Avienus, too, has that celestial Hercules: "Tempora deinde at maculosi prona Draconis" [then the temples of the spotted Dragon, bent low].

units.la: Stellae numerantur ejus hodie xxix; una extra formam sita. Earum quae ἐπὶ τῆς κεφαλῆς, tertiae magnitudinis, Caput Procidui vel Ingeniculati, dicitur Arabibus: quae vero quatuor in sinistra manu, Pellis Leonis nonnullis appellatur, ut notat Hyginus.
units.tr: Today it has 29 stars, one of them lying outside the figure. Of those "ἐπὶ τῆς κεφαλῆς" [on the head], of third magnitude, the Arabs call the Head of the Kneeling Man or the Kneeler. Those four in the left hand are called by some the Lion's Skin, as Hyginus notes.

units.la: VIII. Lyra, Λύρα, ut plerisque nuncupatur, χέλυς Arato & Avieno; Ciceroni Fides; Fidicula Firmico: Vulgus Corruptiore voce Arabica vocat Alohore; quam opinor factam ex Graeca Λύρα, praepositio ab Arabibus articulo. Imprudenter sane lib. v. Manilius, ut bene notat Scaliger, aliam a Lyra Fidem facit. Lyrae Cornua, ut Manilius lib. 1. nominat, vel ut Hyginus Brachia dicuntur ab Hipparcho, Cacumina Latinis Pectines ab Enarratore Germanici; cui etiam, ut & Hygino, reliquae Signi partes appellantur Humeri, vel Scapulae, Fundus, Modulus, Tympanum. Recentioribus Vultur cadens figuratur & dicitur. Fabulas de Lyra Sideribus adnumerata non recenlebo, Lectorem, qui delectatur ijs, remittens ad Eratosthenem & alios ab Germanico & Hygino laudatos. Stellis insignitum hoc Signum xi; quarum quae in Lyrae tympano, vel in Vulturis capite, primae magnitudinis, Arabice Facies; Graecis ἐμπνέοντος ὠλένη τῆς Ζωδίου Λύρα, inquiunt Geminus & Procl clus αὐτερόμενον.
units.tr: VIII. The Lyre, Λύρα, as it is commonly named; χέλυς for Aratus and Avienus; Fides for Cicero; Fidicula for Firmicus. The common people, using a corrupted Arabic word, call it Alohore. I think this was formed from the Greek Λύρα, with the Arabic article prefixed. Manilius, in book 5, rashly makes the Fides a different thing from the Lyre, as Scaliger rightly observes. The horns of the Lyre, as Manilius names them in book 1, or the Brachia (arms) as Hyginus calls them, are so called by Hipparchus; the Cacumina (peaks) by the Latins, and Pectines (combs) by the commentator on Germanicus. To him, as to Hyginus, the remaining parts of the sign are called the shoulders or blades, the bottom, the measure, the drum. Among more recent writers it is pictured and called the Falling Vulture. I will not recount the fables about the Lyre being counted among the stars, referring the reader who enjoys them to Eratosthenes and the others cited by Germanicus and Hyginus. The sign is marked by 11 stars. Of these, the ones in the drum of the Lyre or in the head of the Vulture, of first magnitude, are called Facies (the Face) in Arabic. The Greeks, as Geminus and Proclus say, call them "ἐμπνέοντος ὠλένη τῆς Ζωδίου Λύρα" [the elbow of the living Lyre of the Zodiac] and "αὐτερόμενον" [self-moving].

units.la: IX. Olor, Κύκνος, plerisque. Ὀρνις apud antiquiores Graecos absolutiore voce, ut Ales apud Ciceronem propter ignoram historiam (unde & Αἰολῶν ὄρνις Arato; varia enim de ea finguntur) teste Hygino, qui interim cum Manilio & Basso ridiculam indicat; ut nullam potius sit scire, quam talem imaginari in praestantissimis Dei creaturis. Gallina hodie indigetatur. Stellis fulget xvii. extra formam adsidení duae. ὁ ἐν τῇ ἀρᾷ Ὄρνις λαμπρὸς, secundae magnitudinis, Arabibus Cauda Gallinae, vocatur.
units.tr: IX. The Swan, Κύκνος, to most. Among the older Greeks it was Ὄρνις, the more general word, as Ales (the bird) is in Cicero, because its story was unknown. (Hence also Aratus' "bird of the Aeolians", since many things are invented about it.) Hyginus, who meanwhile points out with Manilius and Bassus how ridiculous these tales are, says it is better to know nothing than to imagine such things about the most excellent creatures of God. Today it is named the Gallina (Hen). It shines with 17 stars, two of them sitting outside the figure. "ὁ ἐν τῇ ἀρᾷ Ὄρνις λαμπρὸς" [the bright bird in the wing], of second magnitude, is called the Cauda Gallinae (Tail of the Hen) by the Arabs.

units.la: X. Cassiopeia, Καασσιέπεια. Sedet apud Hyginum in Siliquastro. Mediam eidem dividit Circulus Lacteus. Pansis brachijs ab Astronomis figuratur, vel tamquam sortem suam miserans, filiamque deplorans. Aratus: ἡδ' αὐτως ὀλίγων ἀσπαλίσωνται ὤμων ὀγυιλὼ· Φαίνης κεν ἀναίζῃ ὅτι παιδί.
units.tr: X. Cassiopeia, Καασσιέπεια. In Hyginus she sits in a Siliquastrum. The Milky Way divides her middle. Astronomers depict her with arms outstretched, either pitying her own lot or lamenting her daughter. Aratus: "ἡδ' αὐτως ὀλίγων ἀσπαλίσωνται ὤμων ὀγυιλὼ· Φαίνης κεν ἀναίζῃ ὅτι παιδί" [and so, a little from her shoulders, she spreads her arms, as a mother lamenting her child].

units.la: Germanicus ejus Interpres: Sic tendit palmas, seu sit planctura relictam Andromedam, merita non iusta piacula matris.
units.tr: Germanicus' translator: "So she stretches her palms, whether she laments Andromeda left behind, the undeserved penalty of a mother."

units.la: Neque enim & hic fabulae desunt Basso, Hygino, aliis ex Euripide & Sophocle: vel ob ἀμυδρότητα, ut tamquam atrata lugere videatur. Nam quum sit, canente Cicerone, Obscura specie Stellarum: plenilunio solet obscurari, quod indicat Aratus: Λαμπρὸν ἀδαμάντινον ἐν μάλα πολλῇ, Νυκτὶ Φαεινομένῃ παμμήνιδι:
units.tr: Here too there are no lack of fables, in Bassus, Hyginus and others, drawn from Euripides and Sophocles. She is said to mourn as if clad in black, perhaps because of her dimness (ἀμυδρότητα). For, as Cicero sings, the stars have an obscura species [dim appearance], and she is usually darkened at full moon, as Aratus indicates: "Λαμπρὸν ἀδαμάντινον ἐν μάλα πολλῇ, Νυκτὶ Φαεινομένῃ παμμήνιδι" [bright, adamantine, amid very many, in the night shining with the full moon].

units.la: Quae sic Avienus: Sed nec multa tamen, quum Caelum lumine toto Luna replet, tetram ut superet fax aurea noctem.
units.tr: Avienus says: "But not many, though when the moon fills the whole sky with its light, so that a golden torch overcomes the dark night."

units.la: Stellarum est xiii; quarum quae ἐν τῇ σηθεῖ, tertiae magnitudinis, Scheder vocatur Arabica voce corruptissima; cui ne ille quidem, qui omnibus, novit medicinam.
units.tr: It has 13 stars. Of these, the one "ἐν τῇ σηθεῖ" [in the chair], of third magnitude, is called Scheder in a most corrupted Arabic word. Not even he who knows all medicine knows a cure for that.

units.la: xi. Perseus, Περσεύς. De hujus consecratione videndi apud Hyginum & Germanicum Æschylus, Tragœdiarum scriptor, Euhemerus, alij. Κηφηνσομμον illum nonnulli faciunt: qui, quod infelicius Aratum sequuti, Pulverem in Cœlo agnoscant, reprehenduntur ab Hygino: ipso, quod multa sæpe fœdiora, quamquam aliunde petita, imaginetur in locis purissimis, majore jure reprehendendo. Stellis claret xxvi; ἀμίφωτ̃ι sunt iii. ὁ ἐν τῷ δεξιῷ πλευρᾷ λαμπρὸς, secundæ magnitudinis, Arabice אלחג Latus appellatur. Sinistra manu portat Caput Medusæ, unus ex Gorgonibus; in quo quæ secundæ Classis, Arabes vocant ⟨Arabic⟩ quod ⟨Arabic⟩ onat Δαιμονιον id est γοργόνειον. Totum autem Caput constituen-tes Aʹ ερπ̃ν, ut scribunt Geminus & Proclus, Τερτίων καλεῖται ὁ ἐν ἀκρᾳ τῇ δεξιᾷ χεῖρι & Περσέως κεφαλὴ πυκνοὶ ἀστέρες, ἐκ τῶν Ἀρπῶν, Falcem, καλυπτήρ.
units.tr: XI. Perseus, Περσεύς. On his placing among the constellations see Hyginus and Germanicus, and Aeschylus the tragedian, Euhemerus and others. Some make him Kephenssommon; these are rebuked by Hyginus for following Aratus rather unhappily when they recognise the Dust in heaven. Hyginus himself is to be rebuked with greater right, because he often imagines things far more foul, though drawn from elsewhere, in the purest places. It shines with 26 stars, three of them invisible. "ὁ ἐν τῷ δεξιῷ πλευρᾷ λαμπρὸς" [the bright one in the right side], of second magnitude, is called in Arabic the Latus (Side). In his left hand he carries the Head of Medusa, one of the Gorgons. The stars of the second class in it the Arabs call by a word which means Daemonium, that is Gorgoneion. The stars making up the whole head, as Geminus and Proclus write, "Τερτίων καλεῖται ὁ ἐν ἀκρᾳ τῇ δεξιᾷ χεῖρι" [Tertion is the name of the one at the tip of the right hand], and the dense stars of Perseus' head, from the Harpies, are called the Sickle and the Cover.

units.la: xii. Auriga, Ηνιοχος; Aurigator, Festo Avieno; Agitator, Basso; Frichtlovius, Eratosthenis & Germanico. Hunc namque Aurigam illum cœlestem fabulatur ὁ ἡνίοχος enim hic agnoscitur Arato, Fabula Avieno) apud Hyginum Eratosthenes quem dixi; & de illius nativitate putidissima narrat Euripides. Stellas habet xiv. ὁ ἡ ἀρτ̃ρ ὠμωκλεὶ ... Aἲξ sinquiunt in Asterismis Hipparchus, & in Sphæris suis Geminus & Proclus; primæ est magnitudinis. Capram vocat Hyginus. Iidem ... ἡ ἀρτ̃ρ καπρὸς, vel, ut alij ὁ ἀκρα χειρ, in summa sinistra manu formantur Ἐρῳδοὶ. Hædi: quibus in Cœlum evehendis conquirunt fabulas apud eundem Hyginum Cleostratus, Tenedius, Parmeniscus, Musæus, alij. Meminit tam Αἰγὲς quam Ἐρῳδῶν Aratus, collocans quo dixi loco; cujus etiam interpretes legendi, Tullius, Germanicus, Avienus: qui omnes Hœdos canunt,
units.tr: XII. The Charioteer, Ἡνίοχος; Aurigator for Festus Avienus; Agitator for Bassus; Frichtlovius for Eratosthenes and Germanicus. For they fable this heavenly charioteer. ὁ ἡνίοχος is what Aratus recognises here; Avienus gives the fable. Through Hyginus, Eratosthenes (whom I mentioned) has it, and Euripides tells of his most disgusting birth. It has 14 stars. "ὁ ἡ ἀρτ̃ρ ὠμωκλεὶ... Aἲξ" [the goat], as Hipparchus says in his Asterismi and Geminus and Proclus in their Spheres; it is of first magnitude. Hyginus calls it the Capram (She-goat). The same authors describe "ἡ ἀρτ̃ρ καπρὸς" [the goat], or, as others have it, "ὁ ἀκρα χειρ" [the hand's tip], formed in the top of the left hand, the Ἐρῳδοὶ (Kids). Hyginus, Cleostratus, Tenedius, Parmeniscus, Musaeus and others offer fables about the kids' being raised to heaven. Aratus mentions both the goat, Αἰγὲς, and the kids, Ἐρῳδῶν, placing them where I said. His interpreters to be read are Cicero, Germanicus and Avienus, who all sing of the Kids:

units.la: Nautis inimicum Sidus in undis.
units.tr: "A star hostile to sailors on the waves."

units.la: xiii. Serpentarius, (sic vocat Bassus) Ὀφιούχος; Anguitenens Ciceroni, Festo Avieno, alijsque Latinis scriptoribus, notante Hygino. Vulgus tamquam Arabica voce dicit Alangue, quam ex Latina scio corruptam, & convenire magis sequenti Constellationi Adsignantur Serpentario Stellæ xxiv; extra formam v. ὁ ἐπὶ τῆς κεφαλῆς, magnitudinis tertiæ, vocatur Arabice vulgo Rasalangue, dictione Arabico-Latina; enim Caput. Adeundi de hujus Anguisque, de quo mox, Consideratione Hegesianax, Polyzelus Rhodius, Eratosthenes & alij incertiores, serram inter se, quis sit, reciprocantes, apud Hyginum.
units.tr: XIII. The Serpent-holder (so Bassus calls it), Ὀφιούχος; Anguitenens for Cicero, Festus Avienus and other Latin writers, as Hyginus notes. The common people say, as if it were an Arabic word, Alangue, which I know is corrupted from the Latin, and which agrees better with the following constellation. Twenty-four stars are assigned to the Serpent-holder, five of them outside the figure. "ὁ ἐπὶ τῆς κεφαλῆς" [on the head], of third magnitude, is commonly called in Arabic Rasalangue, an Arabic-Latin word, since Rās means Caput (head). On the question of this and of the Serpent mentioned below, Hegesianax, Polyzelus of Rhodes, Eratosthenes and other less certain writers dispute among themselves which is which; see Hyginus.

units.la: xiv. Serpens, Ὄφις; quem tenet, & cui toto corpore visitur illigatus Ὀφιούχος, Anguem etiam vocant Latini. Alangue Arabice-Latine, meo judicio. Tribuuntur illi Stellæ xviii.
units.tr: XIV. The Serpent, Ὄφις, which the Serpent-holder holds, and around whose whole body he is entwined. The Latins also call it Anguis. In my judgement it is Alangue, an Arabic-Latin word. It is assigned 18 stars.

units.la: xv. Sagitta, Οἴστος; אלשהם, Alfchaham, Arabice. Nam quod vulgo fertur Alahance corruptum est. Stellas habet v. De hac multa fabulose Hyginus ex Æschylo, Eratosthene & aliis.
units.tr: XV. The Arrow, Οἴστος; Arabic Alfchaham (אלשהם). The form commonly given, Alahance, is corrupted. It has five stars. Hyginus tells many fables about it, drawn from Aeschylus, Eratosthenes and others.

units.la: xvi. Aquila, Ἀετὸς; Arabice אלטיר: Vultur etiam volans recentioribus. Hanc Cœlo beavit Ganymedis raptus, si fabulis fides. Adeundi Bassus Germanici illustrator, Hyginus & alij. Hæc, ut ex Arato canit Cicero:
units.tr: XVI. The Eagle, Ἀετὸς; Arabic Altair (אלטיר). Recent writers also call it the Vultur volans (flying vulture). If we trust the fables, the rape of Ganymede brought it its place in heaven. See Bassus, Germanicus' illustrator, Hyginus and others. Cicero sings of it, from Aratus:

units.la: grave matis
units.tr: "Heavy for ships..."

units.la: Ostendit nautis perturbans æquora signum.
units.tr: "It shows the sign that troubles the waters to the sailors."

units.la: Eleganter etiam Festus Avienus: Spumosum late mare subruit; omnia Cœli, Omnia Terrarum mox slabra procacia verrunt.
units.tr: Festus Avienus also writes elegantly: "It churns the foaming sea far and wide; soon it sweeps away all things of heaven and all things of the earth, with shameless force."

units.la: In huius laudem carmen fecit Mœro poetria Byzantina; quod primus vulgavit nobilissimus vir Josephus Scaliger ad Manilij i. Stellis pingitur ix: adsident extra formam vi. ὁ ἐπὶ τῆς μεγάλης φρένος λαμπρὸς, καλλίμωρος Αἰτὸς, κατ' ἐχοχὴν magnitudinis est secundæ.
units.tr: A Byzantine poetess, Moero, wrote a poem in its praise, which the most noble Joseph Scaliger first published in his commentary on Manilius, book 1. It is pictured with nine stars, six of them sitting outside the figure. "ὁ ἐπὶ τῆς μεγάλης φρένος λαμπρὸς, καλλίμωρος Αἰτὸς" [the bright one on the great breast, the beautiful Eagle], which is of second magnitude by eminence.

units.la: xvii. Delphinus, Δελφὶν Arabice voce Græca. Qua de caussa hic inter Astra collocatus, μυθικῶς nominant ex Eratosthene, Artemidoro, alijsque Bassus & Hyginus. Currum appellant Cicero & Avienus, cui & non inelegantér
units.tr: XVII. The Dolphin, Δελφὶν, a Greek word used in Arabic. For this reason it is placed here among the stars; Bassus and Hyginus, following Eratosthenes, Artemidorus and others, name it mythically. Cicero and Avienus call it the Currus (Chariot), and Avienus does so not inelegantly:

units.la: breve signo corpus in Astris;
units.tr: "A short body in the stars."

units.la: quod apud Aratum Δελφὶς δ' ἡ μάλα πολλὰς.
units.tr: And in Aratus, "Δελφὶς δ' ἡ μάλα πολλὰς" [the Dolphin, indeed very many...].

units.la: Oceani Cœlique decus Manilio vocatur lib. i. Stellis notus ix; unde & Musicum Signum dici scribit ad Germanicum Bassus.
units.tr: Manilius calls it "the glory of the ocean and sky" in book 1. It is known by nine stars. Hence Bassus, in his note on Germanicus, writes that it is also called the Signum Musicum (Musical Sign).

units.la: xviii. Equus prior, Equuleus vulgo: ἵππος ἀρσην̀ Hipparcho in Asterismis, & ex eo Gemino & Proclo. Stellis obscurus satis quatuor.
units.tr: XVIII. The first Equus, commonly the Equuleus (Little Horse): ἵππος ἀρσην [male horse] in Hipparchus' Asterismi, and after him Geminus and Proclus. It has four stars, rather dim.

units.la: xix. Equus καὶ ἐξοχὴν; ἵππος; Pegasus Germanico, Basso, Hygino; eidem Basso Equus dimidius. Est enim ἡμίππος, ut Taurus. Aratus: Οὐδ' ὄγε πτέρυγος ἐστιν ἀπ' ἐμφαλίοιο χαλὸς ἄεξε Μισοῦσθαι ἡμιπλὴς ἐπιπλεῖ ἱππος ἱππος. Avienus: Non hinc Equus integer aruus, Non quadrupes Cælo suflollitur, at tenus alvo Erigitur, media iam cetera pone negantur, Et quatit ætherias primis modo cruribus auras.
units.tr: XIX. The Equus by eminence, ἵππος; Pegasus for Germanicus, Bassus and Hyginus. The same Bassus calls it the Equus dimidius (Half Horse), for it is ἡμίππος, like the Taurus. Aratus: "Οὐδ' ὄγε πτέρυγος ἐστιν ἀπ' ἐμφαλίοιο χαλὸς ἄεξε Μισοῦσθαι ἡμιπλὴς ἐπιπλεῖ ἱππος ἱππος" [nor from the navel of the wing..., half-horse, horse]. Avienus: "Here is no whole horse, no four-footed one lifted up to heaven; it is raised only up to the belly, and the rest behind is denied. It shakes the ethereal breezes with its forelegs alone."

units.la: Fabulis de Equo in Cœlum elato commemorandis Lectori molestiam nolo facessere. Leguntur ex variis apud Avienum, Bassum & Hyginum. Stellarum est xx.
units.tr: I do not wish to burden the reader with the fables to be told about the Horse raised into heaven. They are read in various authors: Avienus, Bassus and Hyginus. It is one of the stars of the twentieth (?) group, with xx.

units.la: xx. Andromeda, Ἀνδρομέδα; Arabice ... quasi Mulier Catenata. Quur Astris adscripta, notant Euripides & alij apud Hyginum & Bassum. Stellas habet xxiii. ὁ ἐν τῷ δεξιῷ ὤμῳ, magnitudinis tertiae Alamac appellatur. Caput Andromedæ Pegasi, inquit Hyginus, ventri conjungitur. Eadem enim Stella, secundæ magnitudinis, & Umbilicus Pegasi & Andromedæ Caput appellatur. Unde in Sphæra Veteri: Ἵππῳ συναπτόμενος Ἀνδρομέδα τὴν κεφαλὴν ἔχει τὴν αὐτὴν Ἵππος χαλεπὸς γειῶν ἀσίεγ.
units.tr: xx. Andromeda, Andromeda in Greek; in Arabic ... that is, roughly, the Chained Woman. Why she was counted among the constellations is explained by Euripides and others, cited by Hyginus and Bassus. She has xxiii stars. The one on the right shoulder, of the third magnitude, is called Alamac. The head of Andromeda is joined to the belly of Pegasus, says Hyginus, for the same star, of the second magnitude, is called both the Navel of Pegasus and the Head of Andromeda. Hence in the Old Sphere: "Joined to the Horse, Andromeda holds the same head [Ἵππῳ συναπτόμενος Ἀνδρομέδα τὴν κεφαλὴν ἔχει τὴν αὐτὴν]."

units.la: Et Vitruvius: Lucidissima Stella finit ventrem Equi & caput Andromedæ.
units.tr: And Vitruvius: The brightest star ends the belly of the Horse and the head of Andromeda.

units.la: xxi. Triangulus (videndus Bassus ad Germanicum) Δελτωτὸν Arato. M. Tullius: Et prope Conspicies parvum sub pectore claro Andromeda signum, Δελτωτὸν dicere Graii Quod soliti, simi i quia forma littera claret.
units.tr: xxi. The Triangle (see Bassus on Germanicus), called Deltoton [Δελτωτόν] by Aratus. Marcus Tullius: "And near her you will see a small sign beneath the bright breast, which the Greeks were accustomed to call Deltoton, because its shape gleams like the letter delta."

units.la: Τεῖγων in Asterismis; Arabice ... Latera duo æqualia disparia sunt basi, quam Sedem vocat Manilius , lib. 1. Sic Aratus: — τὸ δ' ὅπη ... ἐσαθμητὸν Δελτωτὸν παλίμρητον, ἰσαμολίωνον ἐοικὸς Ἀμφοτέρης· ἡ δ' οὐκ ἐστι.
units.tr: Teigon [Τεῖγων] in the Asterisms. In Arabic ... The two sides are equal and the base unequal; Manilius, book 1, calls the base the Seat. So Aratus: "...the Deltoton, reversible, equal-sided and similar to both..." [τὸ δ' ὅπη ... ἐσαθμητὸν Δελτωτὸν παλίμρητον, ἰσαμολίωνον ἐοικὸς Ἀμφοτέρης· ἡ δ' οὐκ ἐστι]; but this is not so.

units.la: Germanicus: Tres illi Laterum ductus, æquata duorum Sunt spacia, unius brevior.
units.tr: Germanicus: "Those three lines of the sides: the spans of two are equal, one is shorter."

units.la: Festus Avienus; juvat enim hæc inter se committere: — simile est latus istud utrumque: Porrigitur summum signo caput: angulus artat, Et gemini suprema jugi vicinia mordet. Tertia, quæ stantes sustentat linea ductus, Parcior, haud similis sese sub limite tendit, Et contracta modum gemina face flammigerarum Stellarum superat.
units.tr: Festus Avienus, for it helps to set these side by side: "That side is like each of the others. The summit of the figure stretches out as a head; the angle narrows, and the nearby peak of the twin ridge bites. The third line, which holds up the drawn figure, is more sparing and not like the others; it stretches under the base, and, drawn in, surpasses in size the twin fire of the flaming stars."

units.la: Stellas habet iv. Ternam lampadem tribuit cum aliis Manilius: sed quæ in basi, media quartæ magnitudinis inter duas tertiæ obscurior est, viciniore splendore. In Cælo positum ab Mercurio fabulantur supra Caput Arietis, ut hujus obscuritas illius luce, quo loco esset, significaretur: Bassus & Hyginus, apud quos alij, de hoc Signo alia.
units.tr: It has iv stars. Manilius, with others, assigns it the triple lamp; but the middle star of the base, of the fourth magnitude, is dimmer than the two of the third magnitude beside it, because of their nearer brightness. The poets tell that it was placed in heaven by Mercury above the head of the Ram, so that the dimness of this star would signify, by the light of that one, where it was; Bassus and Hyginus, whom others follow, say other things about this sign.

units.la: CAP. XXI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXI.

units.la: Signorum Meridionalium enumeratio.
units.tr: The enumeration of the Southern Constellations.

units.la: Septemtrionalibus explicanda succedunt Signa Meridionalia, Nota: Europæis non ita, ut quæ expositi, comperta: Sunt hæc, quæ Sancto viro Hiiobo Penetralia vel interiora Austri vocantur, cap. ix: versl. 9. quod occultentur & nostros fugiant adspectus. Adeundi & Rabbini ad capitis xxxvii, versum 9. Fabulis & in horum enumeratione parcam; qui delectatur, petat ex Hesiodo, Aristomacho, Pindaro, Callimacho, Æschylo, Philarcho, Eratosthene, Athenæo, Q. Smyrnæo, Apollonij Scholiaste, Nigidio, Basso, Hygino & alijs. Catalogus igitur illorum hic est:
units.tr: After the Northern constellations come the Southern constellations, which are less familiar to Europeans, since they have only recently been observed. These are what the holy man Job calls the "inner parts" or "recesses of the South," in chapter 9, verse 9, because they are hidden and escape our sight. The Rabbis should also be consulted on chapter 37, verse 9. I will be sparing with fables in their enumeration. Whoever enjoys them may seek them in Hesiod, Aristomachus, Pindar, Callimachus, Aeschylus, Philarchus, Eratosthenes, Athenaeus, Quintus Smyrnaeus, the scholiast of Apollonius, Nigidius, Bassus, Hyginus and others. Here, then, is their catalogue.

units.la: 1. Cetus, Κῆτος, Pistrix Germanico, Nereia Pistrix Avieno. Stellarum est xxii, quarum quæ ἐπ' ἀκρας τῆς σταγόνος, inquit Hipparchus, super extremitatem Mandibulæ, tertiæ magnitudinis, Arabibus appellatur מנקאר Rostrum: quæ in Ventre posita, secundæ magnitudinis, בטן قيطوس tiæ κητος ἡ ἑσχάτη ἐπ' ἀκρα τῆς ὀράιας terr- magnitudinis, דנב יקטום Kήτος.
units.tr: 1. Cetus, [Κῆτος], the Sea-monster; Pistrix in Germanicus; Nereia Pistrix in Avienus. It has 22 stars. The one at the tip of the jaw, which Hipparchus calls "at the extremity of the mandible," is of the third magnitude and is called Rostrum by the Arabs, manqar. The star in the belly, of the second magnitude, is called by the Arabs Baṭn Qaiṭus. The last star, at the extremity of the tail, is of the third magnitude, and the Hebrews call it Kētos.

units.la: 11. Orion Ω- Arabice ὠίων, Arabibus الجارب etiam Plauti Amphitruonis Bellator dicitur ab Rabbi-Abraham-Ben-Ezra, Iugu'la Romanis, ut docent ex Plauti Ad. i. Scena i. M. Terentius Varro lib. vi. de LL. & Festus lib. ix. Vitiose legitur apud Basium Germanici enarratorem; Orion etiam Incola dici: emendandum enim Incola, ut Veteres loquebantur. Nota est cognatio litterarum C. & G, item O & V. ante L; quam pluribus docerem, si pueris hæc scriberentur. Eeotis quoque nomine insignis, ut indicat in suo Lexico Hesychius. Stellas habet xxxviii. Quę Ἡ ἡ δεξιὰ ὤμῳ λαμπρὸς, primæ magnitudinis, corruptiore Arabica voce Bed-Algenz vocatur. Quæ ἐν ἀριστερῷ ἀκρῳ ποδὶ λαμπρὸς, ὁμοῖος ὕδατι, primæ magnitudinis, Arabibus رجل الجبار Pes Gigantis, id est, Orionis, unde manat Eridanus, ut(quem- admodum eleganter Catullus ex emendatione Iani Dousæ F.) Proximus Eridano fulgeat Oarion.
units.tr: 11. Orion, [Ὠρίων]. The Arabs call him al-Jabbār, the Bellator (the Warrior), as Rabbi Abraham ben Ezra calls him. The Romans called him Iugula, as Marcus Terentius Varro in book 6 of De Lingua Latina and Festus in book 9 show from Plautus, Adelphi, act 1, scene 1. It is wrongly read in Basilius, the commentator on Germanicus: "Orion is also called Incola." It should be emended to Incola, as the ancients spoke. The interchange of the letters C and G, and likewise O and V before L, is well known; I would prove this at length if these things were written for children. He is also known by the name Eeotis, as Hesychius indicates in his Lexicon. He has 38 stars. The one on the right shoulder, bright, of the first magnitude, is called by a more corrupt Arabic name Bed-Algenz. The one on the left foot at the end, bright, of the first magnitude, "like water," is called by the Arabs Rijl al-Jabbār, that is, the Foot of the Giant or of Orion, from which the Eridanus flows, as Catullus elegantly says (following the emendation of Janus Dousa the son): "Orion shines close to Eridanus."

units.la: Dextra Clavam (Pedum & χαλέππεον, atque etiam ῥόπαλον nominant alij) tenet, sinistra, Clypeum; Calteo cinctus, à quo dependet Ensis. Lucanus lib. i.
units.tr: His right hand holds a club (some call it pedum, chalepeon, or even rhopalon); his left holds a shield. He is girded with a belt, from which hangs a sword.

units.la: Ensiferi nimium fulget latus Orionis.
units.tr: Lucan, book 1: "The side of the sword-bearing Orion shines too brightly."

units.la: Situs ejus recentioribus paullo sequior, quam Priscis; qui è regione Vrsæ collocabant, ut videre est apud Aratum & Theonem. Sic Homerus: Ἀ ἐχτὶν Ϝ' ἰὼ καὶ Λ' μαξαν Ϝπιχλησιν καλίσσιν, ἥτ' αὐτὸς σφέφεται χ' τ' Ὠίωνα δοκέει.
units.tr: His position is somewhat later for modern writers than for the ancients, who placed him opposite the Bear, as may be seen in Aratus and Theon. So Homer: "They call her the Wain, which turns about and watches Orion."

units.la: Manilius: Arctos & Orion adversis frontibus ibant.
units.tr: Manilius: "The Bear and Orion went with opposed faces."

units.la: Obsidet utrumque Hemisphærium, secundum longitudinem obtinens partes xviii; secundum latitudinem partes xxx: unde Manilius lib. i: Caput Orion excelso immersus Olympo;
units.tr: He occupies both hemispheres, covering 18 degrees in longitude and 30 in latitude. Hence Manilius, book 1: "Orion's head is sunk in the lofty heaven."

units.la: & in Sphæra Barbarica: Orion magni pars maxima Cœli.
units.tr: And in the Barbarian sphere: "Orion is the greatest part of the heaven."

units.la: iii. Flumen, ποταμὸς Alij, quemadmodum notat Hyginus, Oceanum volunt; quidam Nilum; plerique Eridanum vel Padum interpretantur. Ποταμὸς ὁ ἀπὸ τῆς Ὠίωνος non immerito apud Geminum & Proclum; quod illi ab sinistro Orionis pede fons fiet & origo. Aratus: Οἶον γὰρ καχθίνῳ ἡ τῶν ἰσὶ ἀπὸ ποσὶ φορῆτα λείψανον ἡ Δαρδανίῳ ἀλυχλαύσ ποταμοῖο. καὶ τὸ μὲν ὠίωνος ἰσὶ ἀκαίον ἀπὸ τόσῳ.
units.tr: iii. Flumen, [ποταμός], the River. Others, as Hyginus notes, take it to be the Ocean; some the Nile; most interpret it as the Eridanus or the Po. Geminus and Proclus rightly call it "the river which flows from Orion," since a spring and source arise from the left foot of Orion. Aratus: "For as the river flows from the feet of Orion, the Eridanus, so..."

units.la: Stellis depingitur xxxviii: quarum quæ postrema, primæ est magnitudinis; Arabica, sed quæ inemendatior, voce Alcarnar appellata. Hujus, ut mihi V. CL. mihique amicissimus, Petrus Plancius indicavit, nostri Nautæ diligenti crebraque dimensione Longitudinem esse deprehenderunt xli. graduum, i minutorum; Latitudinem vero vi. graduum: unde necessario sequitur, nunquam in Ægypto visam fuisse Stellam hanc Ptolemæo; cui interim, ex inconsideratione fortean, vel intellecta sequius indorum relatione, eumque sequutis hodie ejusdem longitudo graduum est xvii, minut. xviii; latitudo vero liii. graduum, minut. xxx.
units.tr: It is depicted with 38 stars. The last of them, of the first magnitude, is called by an Arabic name, though a corrupt one, Alcarnar. Its position, as my most distinguished friend Petrus Plancius, of whom I am very fond, has shown me, our sailors have discovered by careful and repeated measurement to be 41 degrees 1 minute in longitude and 6 degrees in latitude. From this it necessarily follows that this star was never seen in Egypt by Ptolemy, who perhaps through carelessness, or perhaps through misunderstanding the report of the Indians, and following him, today gives its longitude as 17 degrees 18 minutes and its latitude as 53 degrees 30 minutes.

units.la: iv. Lepus, Λαγωὸς; Δασύπους Basilo ad Germanicum; Levipes Ciceroni cognominatur. Stellis fulget xii.
units.tr: iv. Lepus, [Λαγωός]; Dasypus according to Basilius on Germanicus; Cicero calls him Levipes. He shines with 12 stars.

units.la: v. Canis Maior, Κύων: μέγας κύων Arato, Arabice الشاري الهي Alischare Aliemeni, Canis dexter. De situ ejus Aratus: ἀμφοτέροισι Κύων ἰσὶ ἀπὸ ἀστεῖ βεζηκώς.
units.tr: v. Canis Maior, [Κύων]; megas kyōn, "the great dog," in Aratus; in Arabic al-Shi'rā al-Yamāniyya, that is, the Right Canis. Aratus on its position: "The Dog stands with both feet on the ... of the stars."

units.la: Cujus hic Canis dicendus, variant auctores apud Hyginum & Basium Germanici interpretem: an Orionis, an Isidis, an Cephali. Pollux lib. v. cap 5. Icarij canem innuit fuisse. Adsentit Ovidius in Nuce: Quid si non aptas solem fugientibus umbras Finditur Icario cum cane terra, darem.
units.tr: Authors differ, as Hyginus and Basilius, the commentator on Germanicus, show, on whether this Dog should be called the Dog of Orion, of Isis, or of Cephalus. Pollux, book 5, chapter 5, implies that it was the dog of Icarius. Ovid agrees in the Nux: "If the earth were split by the Icarian dog, which does not suit the shadows fleeing the sun, I would give it."

units.la: Σημαтισμὸς ejus Stellis describitur xx. ὁ ἐν τῷ σέματι, in lingua, vel maxilla, vel, ut alij, rostro λαμπρότατον, ut utar Hipparcho, magnitudinis primæ, Græcis, quemadmodum volunt Geminus & Proclus, ἐμφανίμως ὅλῳ τῷ ζῳδίῳ Κύων dicitur: Nonnulli Ἀ ερόχυνον vocant; Σολιχὼ Ægyptij: Peculiariore voce Græcis appellatur Σείριος. Aratus in φαινομένα.
units.tr: Its muzzle is described with 20 stars. The one in the tongue, or the jaw, or, as others say, the snout, which is the brightest, in Hipparchus's words, of the first magnitude, is called by the Greeks, as Geminus and Proclus want, "the Dog" in the sense of the whole constellation, obviously. Some call it Aerokynon; the Egyptians call it Solikhō. The Greeks call it by a more particular name, Seirios, as in Aratus's Phainomena.

units.la: Stella omnium Stellarum fulgentissima, Soli ipsi claritate vix cedens: quam adferunt in speculo etiam meridie aquis impositis contra Solem cerni. Sunt & qui sine speculo vidisse se affirmant. Quæ cauda, quod Sidus hoc Soli nonnumquam commodet suum nomen. Virgilius iv. Georgic.
units.tr: It is the most brilliant of all the stars, scarcely yielding in brightness to the Sun himself. They report that it can be seen in a mirror, even at midday, when water is placed opposite the Sun. There are also those who affirm they have seen it without a mirror. Because this star sometimes lends its name to the Sun, it is called ... Virgil, Georgics 4.

units.la: Tradit etiam Suidas Σείριον ab multis exponi τὴν ἥλιον, id est, Sirium Solem. Tergo Canis adfulgent Stellæ xiv, quas mirum est nondum formam nactas. Sunt enim duæ secundæ magnitudinis, totidem tertiæ, septem quartæ, una quintæ, duæque denique sextæ. Sed exspectatur beneficium illud & absoluta meridionalium Considerationum illustratio ab V. CL. Petro Plancio. Ortu suo Signum hoc vehementissimos ciet calores & amplissimos edit effectus, ut docent cum aliis Plinius lib. ii. natur. histor. cap. 40. ix. 16. xiv. 18. Servius item ad lib. iv. Georg. & iii. Æneid. Virgilianæ; res alioquin etiam insensibili nota. Fervidum appellat Cicero; Flammigerum Sirium Avienus, cui,
units.tr: Suidas also reports that Seirios is by many explained as ton hēlion, that is, "the Sun Sirius." Around the back of the Dog shine 14 stars, which it is remarkable have not yet been given a form. For there are two of the second magnitude, as many of the third, seven of the fourth, one of the fifth, and two of the sixth. But the benefit is awaited, and the complete illustration of the Southern considerations, from the most distinguished Petrus Plancius. By its rising this constellation stirs up the most violent heats and produces the greatest effects, as Pliny in book 2 of his Natural History, chapter 40, and 9.16 and 14.18, teaches along with others, and likewise Servius on Virgil's Georgics 4 and Aeneid 3. This is otherwise a matter of common notice. Cicero calls it fervidum (burning); Avienus calls it Flammigerum Sirium, the flame-bearing Sirius, to which...

units.la: hujus Canis Occasum ejus pruinæ gelidæ frugibusque metuendæ excipiunt: Columella lib. xi. Plinius. xvii. Unde & Sophocles in Nauplio Κωνὸς ψυχρὰν δύσιν dixit. Ideoque & Oriens & Occidens, quod in utramque partem sit vehemens, diligentissime solet olim hodieque observari, canente post Aratum & alios Manilio, lib. i. & ii.
units.tr: Its setting is followed by cold frosts, dreaded for the crops: Columella, book 11; Pliny, 17. Hence Sophocles in the Nauplius said "the cold setting of the Dog." Therefore both its rising and its setting, since it is violent in either aspect, have long been and still are most carefully observed, as Manilius sings after Aratus and others, in books 1 and 2.

units.la: vi. Canis Minor, Προκύων, Quod ante Majorem Canem oriatur: Minusculus Canis Vitruvio; Arabice Antecanis Ciceroni Alschare Achemiæ, Canis sinisterior nuncupatur, Aratum interpretanti:
units.tr: vi. Canis Minor, [Προκύων], because it rises before the Greater Dog. Vitruvius calls it Minusculus Canis, the little dog. In Arabic it is Antecanis, and Cicero calls it Alschare Achemiae. It is named Canis sinisterior, the Left Dog, by one who translates Aratus.

units.la: Poeta, quem Latinum facit hoc modo:
units.tr: The poet, whom he makes Latin in this way:

units.la: Plinius dubitat an ea, quæ Προκύων vocatur, sit Canicula; quia sciebat Σείριον potius ita nominari. μέγεθος ejus, si id nomen mereatur, Stellas tantum habet duas: quarum quæ κατὰ τὴν ἐπισθίων magnitudinis primæ, totius Asterismi appellatione nota, notantibus Gemino, Proclo, aliis.
units.tr: Pliny doubts whether the star called Procyon is Canicula, since he knew that Seirios is rather so named. Its size, if it deserves that name, has only two stars: of which the one at the ... is of the first magnitude, well known by the name of the whole asterism, as Geminus, Proclus and others note.

units.la: vii. Argo, Ἀργώ; Arabibus olim xxiii. distinctum fuisse scribunt Hipparchus, Hyginus, alij; addentes non totam inter Astra videri, (divisa enim pingebatur à puppi vel gubernaculo usque ad Malum) ut quasi moneret homines, etiam fractis navibus, in alto non esse de salute desperandum. Recentiores Stellas illi tribuunt xlv. Hodie, Batavorum Argonautarum beneficio, corpus integrum Navis (remis, ut angustior pareret forma, projectis) est consequuta; eodem fere Stellarum fulgens numero. Iis ego consigno tres; quæ, extra σῶμα, secus Canis ὀπίσθια (Κωνὸς μεγάλου κατ' ἐρλὸν, ut Arati verbis utar) in lineam ex postremo, quique ad puppim, malo adscendunt; unam sextæ, reliquas duas secundæ magnitudinis. Patiatur enim grata posteritas, ut eas divinissimo consecrem Instrumento; quo, à Plancio suo accepto, peritissimus Nauclerus Petrus Theodori F. Embdanus, sedens ibi in corbe, vel, ut vocant nonnulli, galea, mensus est Siderum Meridionalium situs; ut ad fidem eos Plancio, quem ante discessum fidelissimum habuerat (ut & Vechterus quidam Guilelmi
units.tr: vii. Argo, [Ἀργώ]. Hipparchus, Hyginus and others write that the Arabs formerly divided it into 23 stars, adding that it is not seen entirely among the stars (for it was depicted divided, from the poop or the steering-oar up to the mast), as if to warn people that even when ships are wrecked, on the open sea they should not despair of their safety. Later writers assign it 45 stars. Today, thanks to the Dutch Argonauts, the whole body of the ship has been restored (the oars having been thrown out, so that it might show a narrower form), and it has nearly the same number of shining stars. I mark three of these: outside the body, beside the hind parts of the Dog (of the Great Dog, to use Aratus's words, "on the left side"), which rise in a line from the last, which is near the stern, and the mast; one of the sixth magnitude and the other two of the second magnitude. For let grateful posterity permit me to consecrate them to that most divine instrument, by which the most skilled navigator Petrus Theodori son of Embden, sitting there in the basket, or as some call it the helmet, measured the positions of the Southern stars, received from his Plancius, whom he had as the most faithful before his departure (as also a certain Vechter, son of Guilelmus, a Doctor in Astronomy), and communicated them to us through him. He died while surveying the heavens, and ascended to heaven; and having obtained immortal glory, he transmitted the inheritance of his industry to his master, from whom those eager for such things promise themselves the Southern ... and the most exact description of them.

units.la: F.) F. ) in Astronomia Doctorem, nobisque per illum communicaret. Mortuus in coelo lustrando, Cœlum conscendit; & immortalem gloriam consequutus industriæ suæ hæreditatem transmisit suo magistro, à quo Meridionales A'σρϕοσίας exactissimamque illarum descriptionem hujusmodi rerum avidi sibi polliceantur. Porro Canopus (κανωβος Græcis, cujus uberrima descriptio in navigatione Alberici Vespucij, cap. vi.) Stella fulgida, quæ plerisque hodie in uno Remorum, nostrorum consideratione locum est rursum adepta veterem, qui Gemino, Proclo, alijs ἐν πηδαλίῳ, Gubernaculo. Bene, liberius Aratum suum vertentes, & Cicero,
units.tr: ...F.) Doctor in Astronomy, and communicated them to us through him. Dying while surveying the heavens, he ascended to heaven; and, having won immortal glory, he passed the fruit of his labour on to his teacher, from whom eager readers may hope for the southern Astrophosiae and a most exact description of those things. Moreover, Canopus [κανωβος, in Greek], whose very full description is in the voyage of Amerigo Vespucci, chapter 6, is a bright star. Most people today place it in the stern of the ship, but by our reckoning it has regained its old position, which Geminus, Proclus and others called ἐν πηδαλίῳ [at the rudder], that is, Gubernaculo [the helm]. Rendering their Aratus rather freely, Cicero says:

units.la: Inde Gubernaculum desperso lumine fulgens;
units.tr: Then the Helm, its light dimmed, shines.

units.la: & Germanicus: Puppis demisso tantum flat lucida Clavo;
units.tr: And Germanicus: The Stern alone breathes its gleam from the lowered Tiller.

units.la: Avienus etiam Puppim Argus refulgentem & rutilam agnoscit. Πηλεμαῖος vocatum hoc Sidus fuisse notat ad Germanici Eridanum Bassus; addens & Terrestrem Stellam dici: quod humillime appareat & circa terram esse videatur. Loca quibus cernitur commemorant Posidonius apud Strabonem lib. iii. Plinius lib. ii. cap. 70. Geminus libro de Apparentijs, Proclus de Sphæra. Cnidij sane diu ostentarunt Turrim, ex qua Eudoxus, illorum popularis, Canopum speculari solitus; magnaque eam veneratione dignati Σκοπιὰ Ἐυδόξου nominabant. Haud procul à Canopo Stella visitur, quartæ magnitudinis, cui Βολίς vel Linea (nostrates Dieploot nuncupant) nomen nuper inditum. Bolis enim, vel, ut Lucilio vocatur, Cataprorates, illud est Nautis, quod demitti solet è navi explorandis & Fundi naturæ & Maris altitudini.
units.tr: Avienus also recognises the Stern as Argo's, shining and ruddy. Bassus, on Germanicus' Eridanus, notes that this star was called Pelemaeus, and adds that it is called the Earthly Star, which seems very apt, since it appears low and seems to be close to the earth. Posidonius, quoted by Strabo in book 3, Pliny in book 2 chapter 70, Geminus in his book on Appearances, and Proclus in his work on the Sphere, mention the places from which it can be seen. The people of Cnidus long showed a tower from which their fellow citizen Eudoxus used to watch Canopus, and they held it in such high regard that they called it the Watchtower of Eudoxus. Not far from Canopus is seen a star of the fourth magnitude, recently named by our countrymen Dieploot (the Plumb-line or Line). For the plumb, or as Lucilius calls it Cataprorates, is the sailors' name for the lead let down from a ship to sound the depth of the sea and of its bottom.

units.la: VIII. Hydra, Ἰδρα; Arato Ὑδρη; Arabice חויה; Anguis Manilio lib. i. Stellarum est xxvi: quæ μέση τῶν κάμπτων, propè colli flexuram (καμπὴ, prima scilicet, dicitur Arato & Festo Avieno, Curvatura prima Hygino) magnitudinis secundæ, Arabibus id est singularis solet dici.
units.tr: VIII. Hydra [Ἰδρα]; Aratus has Ὑδρη; in Arabic חויה; Manilius, book 1, calls it the Snake. It has 26 stars. The star in the middle of the bends, near the flexure of the neck (Aratus, Festus Avienus and others call the bend καμπὴ, the first curve; Hyginus calls it the first curvature), of the second magnitude, is usually called by the Arabs the "unique" star.

units.la: IX. Crater, Κρατὴρ; vel almo gratus Lucco apud Manilium lib. i. Locus illi μέσῃ ὕδρας σπείρᾳ, inquit Aratus; in medio sinu, Cicero. Stellis describitur vii. ὁ ἐν τῇ ἔαυτοῦ τὰς Κρατῆρος, κοινὸς τῷ ὕδρᾳ, magnitudinis quartæ, vocatur Arabibus.
units.tr: IX. Crater [Κρατὴρ]; or "the bowl pleasing to fertile Bacchus", in Manilius book 1. Aratus gives its place as μέσῃ ὕδρας σπείρᾳ, in the middle coil of the Hydra; Cicero says "in the middle bend". It is described with seven stars. The star ὁ ἐν τῇ ἔαυτοῦ τὰς Κρατῆρος, κοινὸς τῷ ὕδρᾳ, of the fourth magnitude, is called by the Arabs...

units.la: X. Corvus, Κόραξ; Phaelo sacer ales Manilio lib. i; Ὑδρας πνοῆς σπένδει, σπίλῳ κόσμου ἐπιτῶν; Arato; quem sic vertit Cicero:
units.tr: X. Corvus [Κόραξ]; Manilius book 1 calls it the sacred bird of Phoebus; Aratus has Ὑδρας πνοῆς σπένδει, σπίλῳ κόσμου ἐπιτῶν, which Cicero renders thus:

units.la: Extremumque nitens plumato corpore Corvus
units.tr: And the Crow, straining with its feathered body,

units.la: Rostro tundit.
units.tr: Pecks with its beak at the far end.

units.la: Stellas habet vii i. ὁ ἐν τῇ δεξιᾷ πτέρυγι, magnitudinis tertiæ, Arabibus est ἐμαυτῷ ὅλῳ τῷ ζῳδίῳ.
units.tr: It has seven stars. The star ὁ ἐν τῇ δεξιᾷ πτέρυγι, of the third magnitude, is called by the Arabs ἐμαυτῷ ὅλῳ τῷ ζῳδίῳ, the whole sign to itself.

units.la: XI. Centaurus Κένταυρος; Chiron cum alijs, tum Germanico; apud quem & Sonipes. De hoc Manilius Lib. i.
units.tr: XI. Centaurus [Κένταυρος]; Chiron, both among others and in Germanicus, where also Sonipes appears. Manilius, book 1, speaks of it:

units.la: duplici Centaurus imagine fulgens,
units.tr: The Centaur shining with a double image,

units.la: Pars hominis tergo pectus commissa equino.
units.tr: Half man, its chest joined to the horse's back.

units.la: Stellis depingitur xxxiv. Tenet, ut quidam apud Bassum volunt, sinistra manu Arma & Leporem; dextra Θηρίον, & Βύρσαν, id est Utrum vini plenum, tamquam libaturus in Sacrario. unde lux Gemino & Proclo; Θηρίον inquiunt, ὁ Κένταυρος, καὶ Ὑδρολόχος, ἐν χερσὶ ὁ Κένταυρος καθ' ὑπαρχον.
units.tr: It is marked with 34 stars. In its left hand, as some hold according to Bassus, it bears the Altar and the Hare; in its right hand the Θηρίον [the beast] and the Βύρσαν, that is, a skin of wine, as if about to pour a libation in the sanctuary. Hence Geminus and Proclus say: Θηρίον, the Centaur and the Hydrolochus, the Centaur holding them in hand, as it were.

units.la: XII. Fera, Θηρίον, Arato & Basso ad Germanicum: Lupus plerisque existimatur. Hosiam nominat Hyginus in Ara explicatione, Stellis fulget xix.
units.tr: XII. Fera [Θηρίον], in Aratus and in Bassus on Germanicus: most people think it is the Wolf. Hyginus calls it Hosia in his explanation of the Altar. It shines with 19 stars.

units.la: XIII. Ara, Ciceroni, Manilio, Avieno, Firmico, Hygino; Θυμιατήριον Arato; Βωμὸς in Vetere Sphæra; Sacrarium Basso ad Germanicum, Θυμιατήριον Hipparcho, Gemino, Proclo; Λιβανωτὶς quibusdam: Thuribulum Germanico, Avieno, Vitruvio, Hygino, alijs; Arabibus אלמגראמה, id est Acerra: Pharus nonnullis etiam dicitur, ut notat Bassus; nam sunt & Græci Scriptores, qui Φρυκτωρίον vocarunt: Lar Alphonso. Stellarum est vii.
units.tr: XIII. Ara (the Altar): Cicero, Manilius, Avienus, Firmicus, Hyginus; Θυμιατήριον [censer] in Aratus; Βωμὸς [altar] in the Old Sphere; Sacrarium [sanctuary] in Bassus on Germanicus; Θυμιατήριον in Hipparchus, Geminus and Proclus; Λιβανωτὶς [incense-box] according to some; Thuribulum [incense-burner] in Germanicus, Avienus, Vitruvius, Hyginus and others; among the Arabs אלמגראמה, that is, the Incense-dish. Bassus notes that some also call it the Pharos (lighthouse), for there are Greek writers who named it Φρυκτωρίον [beacon]. Alfonso calls it the Lar. It has seven stars.

units.la: XIV. Corona Australis Plinio & Hygino, Στέφανος νότιος Gemino & Proclo; quibus notantibus à nonnullis Οὐρανίσκος dicitur: κυρυκῆων secundum Hipparchum: Arabibus אכלייל Corona. Stellas habet xiii. De Στεφάνῳ asterismo sic canit Aratus: Νοτίῳ πεζὸν περίφορα τὸ ποιητικὸν Διωνὴ κυκλοι.
units.tr: XIV. The Southern Crown: Pliny and Hyginus; Στέφανος νότιος [southern wreath] in Geminus and Proclus; some call it Οὐρανίσκος [little heaven], as noted; κυρυκῆων according to Hipparchus; among the Arabs אכלייל, Crown. It has 13 stars. Of the constellation Στέφανος Aratus sings thus: Νοτίῳ πεζὸν περίφορα τὸ ποιητικὸν Διωνὴ κυκλοι [the southern wreath, round which the poet's circles of Dione turn].

units.la: Quem vertens Cicero Stellas, Coronam hodie plectentes, obscuras canit & sine nomine; quam bene non video. Nam quæ Στέφανος alijs, Arato sunt Κύκλοι; & hinc interinterpretanti poëtam Germanico sine honore Corona nominatur. Felicius Aratea illa exprimit Manilius lib. 1. ——cui iuncta feruntur Flexa per ingentes Stellarum lumina gyros.
units.tr: Translating this, Cicero calls the Crown, which is now a garland, obscure and nameless; I do not see how this is apt. For what others call Στέφανος, Aratus calls Κύκλοι [circles]; and so, in the interpretation of the poet, Germanicus calls it the Crown without honour. Manilius, book 1, expresses those Aratean lines more happily:

units.la: Sic enim legendum censeo pro flumina. Non enim possum adsentiri Viro Magno, qui per Manilliana haec censet exaudiendam χύσιν τ' ἄστρων. Reclamat omnino commissio Ciceronis, Manilij, Germanici, Avieni, Hygini cum Arato. Alioquin Aquae Fusio solet, quidquid volunt Geminus & Proclus, explicari cum Aquario, qui vere τ' ἀνθρωπίνης.
units.tr: ...to which, they say, are joined the flexed light of the stars in their great circles. [Here Manilius' reading is "flumina" (rivers).] I think this must be read as "flumina" for "flumina" ... I cannot agree with the great man who thinks that in these Manilian lines we should understand the χύσιν τ' ἄστρων [pouring of the stars]. Ciceros, Manilius', Germanicus', Avienus', and Hyginus' agreement with Aratus protests against it entirely. Otherwise, whatever Geminus and Proclus mean, the Aquae Fusio [outpouring of water] is usually explained together with Aquarius, who truly is τ' ἀνθρωπίνης [of human form].

units.la: xv. Pisces, ἰχθύες; cognomine Νότος Arato, Gemino, Proclo; Australis Ciceroni; Notus Hygino; Major Avieno; Magnus Basilo, cui & huius Nepotes (quis non ridicat?) dicuntur Pisces qui in Zodiaco: Capricorni piscis quibusdam: Arabibus אלחות. Forma Piscis Sideribus insignita xi. quibus, ut in Aquarij historia monui, adnumerarim Stellam primae magnitudinis, quae postrema χύσις ὕδατος in ore Piscis, Arabibus פום אלחות, quod non aliud quam στόμα τῆς ἰχθύος, τῆς λειομένης, scilicet rotis, μονάζοντος. Extra formam vi. μεταξὺ σπιάδια τῆς ἰχθύος καὶ τῆς πέτρας, De Signis quae hucusque commemoravi, paucis verbis, quamquam non eodem ordine (alius enim solet esse alijs) sic canit Ausonius. Ad Borea partes Arcti iunguntur & Anguis; Post has Arctophylax, paristerque Corona, Genuque Prolapsus, Lyra, Avis, Cepheus & Cassiepeia, Auriga & Perseus, Deltoton & Andromedae astrum, Pegasus & Delphinus, Telum, Aquila, Anguitenenseque.
