Signifer inde subest: bis sex & sidera complent. Hic Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpius, Arcitenens, Capricornus, & Vndam Qui tenet, & Pisces. Post hos in partibus Austri Orion, Procyon, Lepus, ardens Syrius, Argo, Hydrus, Chiron, Turibulum quoque, Piscis & ingens, Hunc sequitur Piscrix, simul Eridanusque fluenta.
units.tr: XV. Fishes [ἰχθύες]: surnamed Νότος [South] by Aratus, Geminus and Proclus; Australis [southern] by Cicero; Notus by Hyginus; Major by Avienus; Magnus by Basilius, whose grandsons (who would not laugh?) are said to be the Fishes of the Zodiac; the Fish of Capricorn according to some; among the Arabs אלחות. The form of the Fish is marked with 11 stars, among which, as I noted in the history of Aquarius, I would count the star of the first magnitude that is the last χύσις ὕδατος [outpouring of water] at the mouth of the Fish, called by the Arabs פום אלחות, which is nothing other than the στόμα τῆς ἰχθύος [mouth of the fish], of the one being pulled, that is, by the wheels, μονάζοντος [alone]. Outside the figure are six stars, μεταξὺ σπιάδια τῆς ἰχθύος καὶ τῆς πέτρας [between the Fish's shoulder and the rock]. Of the signs I have so far mentioned, briefly, though not in the same order (for one author's order is not another's), Ausonius sings thus: The Bear and the Serpent are joined towards the northern regions; after these the Keeper of the Bear, and the Northern Crown beside him, the Kneeling One fallen on his knee, the Lyre, the Bird, Cepheus and Cassiopeia, the Charioteer and Perseus, the Delta and the star of Andromeda, Pegasus and the Dolphin, the Arrow, the Eagle, and the Serpent-holder. Next lies the zodiac: twelve constellations complete the stars. Here are Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, the Archer, Capricorn, and he who holds the water, and the Fishes. After these, in the southern regions, come Orion, Procyon, the Hare, blazing Sirius, Argo, the Water-snake, Chiron, the Incense-burner also, the Fish and the great Whale; after it follows the River-fish, together with the waters of the Eridanus.

units.la: Fusius & felicius paullo Ioachimus Camerarius: Signa vocant, quibus illa vides insignia templa: Sed numerum denum quater atque octo esse dederunt. Vrsae summa tenent Aquilonis frigora: per quas Ingens, in morem fluvij, perlabitur Anguis; Hunc subit Arctophylax; sed & hunc mox gemma Corona; Inde Genu nixus, post quem Lyra; deinde Volucris; Tum Cepheus; & Cassiepe; tum Vector; & ille Falcatum extollens tela ensem Gorgone Perseus; Hinc Deltoton; & Andromede; hinc flas Pegase; sed te Delphin excipit; hunc Telum; hoc Aquila, Anguitenenseque. Signifer haec sequitur declivi Circulus orbe; In quo Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Chela, Scorpius, Arcitenens, Caper, Amphora, Pisces. At Notus undifero tenet haec simulacra sub Axe: Armatum Orionas; Canem, in quo Sirius ardet; Quis Procionque; Lepusque; & Iasonis additur Argo; Hydrusque; & Centaurus; & Ara, incognita nobis; Tum Notius Piscis; Cetusque; ac Eridani unda.
units.tr: Somewhat more fully and happily, Joachim Camerarius: They call them the signs, by which you see those famous temples; but they have given them forty-eight in number. The Bear's stars hold the cold of the North; among them the great Serpent glides like a river; next comes the Keeper of the Bear, then the Crown with its gem; then the Kneeler resting on his knee, after whom the Lyre; then the Bird; then Cepheus, and Cassiopeia; then the Charioteer, and Perseus raising his curved sword with the Gorgon's head; hence the Delta, and Andromeda; hence Pegasus, the Winged One; but the Dolphin receives you; this one the Arrow; this one the Eagle, and the Serpent-holder. The zodiac follows these in its sloping orbit, in which lie Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, the Claws, Scorpio, the Archer, the Goat, the Water-jar, and the Fishes. But the South holds these images beneath the wave-bearing axis: Orion armed; the Dog, in which Sirius blazes; then Procyon and the Hare; and Argo is added to Jason; and the Water-snake, and the Centaur, and the Altar, unknown to us; then the Southern Fish, the Whale, and the waters of the Eridanus.

units.la: CAP. XXII.
units.tr: CHAP. XXII.

units.la: De Signis in Meridiana Cœli plaga noviter inventis.
units.tr: On the Signs Newly Discovered in the Southern Quarter of the Heavens.

units.la: QVAS, præcedente Capite, μορφώσεις Austrinas, xv. numero recensui, Veteribus æque ac Nobis fuerunt cognitæ; quæ sequuntur, nostrorum Argonautarum, qui, Duce Petro Theoderi F. Embdano, remotissima in Meridiem loca anno ab Christo nato cIɔ. Iɔ. xcv, navigarunt, Cœlique ibi palatia fuerunt auli conscendere, qua fieri potuit diligentia & fide sunt communicata. Eorum Longitudines & Latitudines meis his adscripsissem, ut accuratissima consideratione mensus est peritissimus Nauclerus, ni vulgaturum se propediem mihi pollicitus fuisset V. CL. Petrus Plancius: à quo Mathesin illè, & qua arte metiundum fideliter cifet Siderum Austrinorum Longitudines, Latitudines, Declinationes, Elevationes & similia, didicerat. Sed utinam ejus progressa fuisset eo diligentia, ut in Corporum Meridionalium & formatura & nomenclatione nonnullam Naturarum, Virium, Effectorum, quæ ex Stellis, habuisset rationem; & non tam quæ Siderum esset positura, quam quæ indoles, quis genius, quæ in hæc terrena per influentias (ut artis utar voce) operatio, spectasset. Quæ omnia quum religiose servata fuerint ab antiquis Astronomis in Septemtrionalium, reliquorumque, quæ illorum non negata oculis, nominatione: tota illa novorum Nominum ratio & impositio expediri felicissime potuisset Oppositionis beneficio; uti me monuit, quum diligentius novum illud Cœlum contemplaretur, vir, cum optimus, tum doctissimus; & in Cœlestibus, si quis alius, versatissimus, meus quondam Præceptor, Rodolphus Snellius. Inventi facile in remotissimo Meridie fuisse A'ντίπυκτων, dicis gratia, & μεγάλης & μικρᾶς, facile Aὑποχάρσις, facile ex Antithesi aliorum Asterismi; non quidem Forma, sed Viribus & Effectis, quibus Forma posterior. Nihil enim saepe minus in Formis & Σχηματισμοῖς, quam quod nominantur; si Triangulus & Sagitta seponatur. Interim quæ inventa satis faciant; dum potiora certiorague exspectantur. Catalogus novorum Siderum hic est.
units.tr: The figures of the southern constellations that I listed as fifteen in the preceding chapter were known to the ancients as well as to us. The ones that follow were observed by our own Argonauts, who under the leadership of Pieter Theodorici's son, of Emden, sailed to the most remote regions of the south in the year of Christ 1595. There they were able to climb up to the heavenly palaces, and their observations were communicated with all the care and good faith possible. I would have added their longitudes and latitudes to my own, as measured with the most accurate consideration by that most skilled navigator, had not the most distinguished Petrus Plancius promised me that he would soon publish them. From these men he had learned the mathematics and the method by which the longitudes, latitudes, declinations, altitudes and similar features of the southern stars are faithfully measured. I only wish his work had gone further in taking account, both in the shaping and naming of the southern bodies, of the natures, powers and effects that proceed from the stars, and had looked less at where the stars lie than at their character, their genius, and what operation they exert on earthly things through influences, to use the language of the art. All these things were scrupulously observed by the ancient astronomers in naming the northern stars and the other stars that were not hidden from their eyes. The whole system of new names and their imposition could have been settled most happily with the help of opposition, as my former teacher Rudolf Snellius reminded me when he studied that new heaven more carefully. He is a man as excellent as he is learned, and as well versed in celestial matters as anyone. It is easy to find in the far south the Antipyctes, so to speak, and the Great and the Small [Ἀντίπυκτων, μεγάλης, μικρᾶς], easily the Hypocharsis [ὑποχάρσις], and easily other asterisms from the antithesis of the others. These are determined not by their shape but by their powers and effects, on which the shape depends. For often nothing is less true of shapes and figures than their names, if the Triangle and the Arrow are set aside. Meanwhile, let what has been found suffice, while we await more important and more certain findings. The catalogue of the new stars is as follows.

units.la: I. Columba Oliva, ifera, Περιστερὰ ἐλαιοφόρος; Noha cognominata, cujus Arcam versum videtur, rostro Ramum ferens, volitare, Αφεσία Columbæ ipsi debetur Plancio, qui eam ante aliquot annos collocari curavit in globo Cœlesti Iacobi Florentii F. Langerani; & postea etiam posuit in suo Semi-Circulo Austrino, adpicto magnæ ejus Terrarum orbis delineationi. Constituunt autem eam Stellæ xi. quas, extra Canis Majoris formam Ptolemæo, ad posteriores ejus pedes Veneris esse naturæ scribit Alphonsus: Earum, quæ in dorso duæ secundæ sunt magnitudinis, Εὐσμεσι Boni Nuncii, Ἀγγελοι, Boni Nuncij, jam cognominantur; ad alam dexteram Placatí Numinis, ad sinistram Ἀ'φεγμα, Diluvij tempore, Aquarum.
units.tr: I. The Olive-bearing Dove [Περιστερὰ ἐλαιοφόρος], surnamed Noah's dove, which is seen flying toward the Ark, carrying a branch in its beak. The Release [Αφεσία] of the dove is owed to Plancius, who some years ago had it placed on the celestial globe of Jacob Floris's son Langren, and afterwards also set it on his southern hemisphere, attached to his large map of the terrestrial globe. It is made up of eleven stars which, outside the figure of Canis Major, Alfonso writes Ptolemy placed near the hind feet of Venus. Of those on its back, the two of the second magnitude are now called by the names Good News [Εὐαγγέλιον] and Messengers [Ἄγγελοι], both meaning good tidings. On its right wing is the Appeased Divinity; on its left, the Remission [Ἄφεγμα] of the waters at the time of the Flood.

units.la: II. Aræa, χρυσόφρυς; Dorado Hispanis; Nostris Zeebraesem & Vliegendevisch. Sex descripta Stellis adnatat dextero Argus lateri, supra majorem Nubeculorum: quæ non procul inter hunc Piscem & Hydrum (de quo mox) à Polo Antarctico, χαλαξίας vel viæ Lacteæ naturam referunt; Nautæ nostri nominant Nubeculas Magellanicas. Sex Informes hic ibi sunt adpositæ, quæ dabunt aliquando Gruem.
units.tr: II. The Swordfish [χρυσόφρυς], called the Dorado by the Spanish; by our people the Zebra-fish and the Flying-fish. It is described with six stars, and lies on the right side of the Argo, above the larger Magellanic Cloud. Not far from here, between this Fish and the Hydra (of which more shortly), it stretches from the Antarctic Pole and represents hail or the nature of the Milky Way; our sailors call these the Magellanic Clouds. Six unformed stars are placed here and there, which will one day make a Crane.

units.la: III. Hirundo marina Plinio, χελιδὼν θαλάσσιος; nobis Zeezwaluwe, Piscis genus, frequens in mari Atlantico. Stellarum est vii. Adhærens Argus lateri, Navem, quæ Piscis indoles inconsiderate videtur involatura.
units.tr: III. The Sea Swallow of Pliny [χελιδὼν θαλάσσιος]; to us the Sea-swallow, a kind of fish frequent in the Atlantic Ocean. It has seven stars. It clings to the side of the Ship, which, from the nature of the fish, seems likely to fly into it carelessly.

units.la: IV. Chamæleon; χαμαιλέων versicolor ob timiditatem, ut docent Aristoteles, Plinius, alij. Stellas habet x. Caudam sinuosam faciunt tres Geminæ. Sub posterioribus Centauri pedibus, & cauda viperinis orbibus implicata contingens dexteram Hirundinis alam, Muscæ Indicæ inhiat. Nam Musca delectari & vesci scribunt Bellonius & alij: quamquam plerique Veterum nec cibo, nec potu, nec alio quam aeris alimento, vivere, memoriæ prodant.
units.tr: IV. The Chameleon [χαμαιλέων], which is many-coloured from timidity, as Aristotle, Pliny and others teach. It has ten stars, and three twin stars form its winding tail. Beneath the hind feet of the Centaur, its tail entwined in viper-like coils, touching the right wing of the Swallow, it gapes at the Indian Fly. For Bellonius and others write that the Chameleon delights in and feeds on flies, although most of the ancients record that it lives on neither food nor drink, but only on air.

units.la: V. Musca Indica, μύια Ἰνδικὴ, Ἀ'ντολική. Stellis signata quatuor quintæ magnitudinis, sub Cruce & in faucibus ferè Chamæleontis posita periculum quod imminet, volatu fugiens, Chironis implorare videtur iustitiam. vi. Crux, Σταυρὸς; Cruzero Hispanis, qui primi notarunt; Anglis Crosiers. Sub ventre collocata Centauri, supra Muscam, Stellis fulget quatuor; quarum quae in ἀκρότητι, secundae est magnitudinis, reliquae sunt tertiae, etiam Ptolemaeo sequentisque aevi Philosophis non invisae: collocatae Mathematicorum principi in posterioribus Centauri pedibus; sed deviantes ab sua & longitudine & latitudine, incuria proculdubio vel Exscribentium vel Typographorum.
units.tr: V. The Indian Fly [μύια Ἰνδικὴ], the Eastern Fly [Ἀ'ντολική]. Marked with four stars of the fifth magnitude, placed under the Cross and nearly in the jaws of the Chameleon, it flies off to escape the danger that threatens it, and seems to implore the justice of Chiron. vi. Crux, the Cross [Σταυρὸς]; Cruzero to the Spanish, who first noted it; to the English Crosiers. Placed under the belly of the Centaur, above the Fly, four stars shine, of which the one at the top [in ἀκρότητι] is of the second magnitude and the rest of the third. These were not unknown even to Ptolemy and the philosophers of the following age. They were placed by the prince of mathematicians on the hind feet of the Centaur, but they wander from their proper longitude and latitude, doubtless through the carelessness of either copyists or printers.

units.la: vii. Triangulus Australis, Τρίγωνον Νότιον. Praejacens ungulis Chironis anterioribus inter Θυμέλον & Avem Paradisi, Stellis est insignita quatuor; quarum una secundae, duae classis sunt tertiae, quibus interjacet quae magnitudinis quintae.
units.tr: vii. Triangulus Australis, the Southern Triangle [Τρίγωνον Νότιον]. Lying in front of the forefeet of Chiron, between the Thymele [Θυμέλον] and the Bird of Paradise, it is marked with four stars: one of the second magnitude, two of the third, and one of the fifth lying between them.

units.la: viii. Avis Paradisi, Ὄρνις Ἰνδική; Paradisi Vogel; Lusitanis Passaro de Sol, Soli avis; Asiaticis Manu-Codiata. Sub Triangulo Stellas habet xii; inter quas & quintae & sextae magnitudinis una est obscura in Collo. Dorso gestat Τρίγωνον Νότον μικρὸν, ex tribus Stellis quintae classis.
units.tr: viii. Avis Paradisi, the Bird of Paradise [Ὄρνις Ἰνδική]; Paradisi Vogel in German; to the Portuguese Passaro de Sol, Soli avis; to the Asians Manu-Codiata. Beneath the Triangle it has twelve stars, among which, between those of the fifth and sixth magnitudes, one is obscure, in the neck. On its back it bears a small Southern Triangle [Τρίγωνον Νότον μικρὸν], of three stars of the fifth class.

units.la: ix. Hydrus Polaris, Ὕδρος ἀρκτικός, quod Stella sit illi quintae magnitudinis in ἀκεανῇ τῆς ἐρᾶς, qua inter Meridionales nulla vero Poli Antarctici loco propior. Nostri vocant Water-Snake. Caput illi (Stellis variarum classium depictae xv.) ad finem τῆς Πολλῆς (quem absorpturus videtur) τῆς ἐξ ἀκρῶν Οὐρανοῦ (ut verbis utar ex vetere Sphaera) inde senis amfractibus caudam torquet Polum versus. Intra secundum Spiram apparet Nubecularum, de quibus dixi, minor. ἐν κεφαλῇ tertiae magnitudinis, Ὀφθαλμὸς Ὕδρα Oculus Hydri; haud procul ab ea, quae postrema Eridani, ἐσχάτης τῆς πολλῆς, vulgo Alcanar corrupte.
units.tr: ix. Hydrus Polaris, the Water-Snake of the Pole [Ὕδρος ἀρκτικός], because it has a star of the fifth magnitude in the stream of the river, where there is no star nearer to the Antarctic Pole among the southern stars. Our people call it the Water-Snake. Its head, depicted with fifteen stars of various classes, lies at the end of the great river (which it seems about to swallow), from the extremities of heaven, as the old sphere puts it. From there it coils its tail toward the Pole in six windings. Within the second coil appears the smaller of the Clouds I mentioned. In the head is a star of the third magnitude, the Eye of the Hydra [Ὀφθαλμὸς Ὕδρα], not far from the star at the end of the Eridanus, the last of the great river, commonly and corruptly called Alcanar.

units.la: x. Pavus, Ταῶν, Superstans quartae Ὑδρᾷ ἀρκτίῳ expansa cum fastu cauda, Stellis superbit xv: quarum quae secundae magnitudinis in capite Oculus Pavonis, Ὀφθαλμὸς ταῶνος; quae vero quintae classis ἐν καρπῷ τῆς τρηχήλας, Τρίδυμοι, Trigemini merito dicendi.
units.tr: x. Pavus, the Peacock [Ταῶν]. Standing above the northern Hydra, with its tail spread out proudly, it takes pride in fifteen stars. Among them, the star of the second magnitude in the head is the Oculus Pavonis, the Eye of the Peacock [Ὀφθαλμὸς ταῶνος]; and those of the fifth class at the wrist of the neck are rightly called the Trigemini, the Triplets.

units.la: xi. Indus, Ἰνδός. Praesitus Pavoni, ἡμίτομος τὰ κατώπρα unam dextra minitabundus, tres decussatim siniistra gestans Sagittas. Stellas habet xii; quarum quae quintae magnitudinis in superiore dextri brachii parte tres sunt Armilla, Ψέλλια Graecis vel Βραχιόνισμα; quibus Indorum gens solet ornari.
units.tr: xi. Indus, the Indian [Ἰνδός]. It stands in front of the Peacock, half-naked below, threatening with one raised hand and holding three arrows crosswise in the left. It has twelve stars. Among those of the fifth magnitude, three on the upper part of the right arm form the Armilla, the armlet [Ψέλλια by the Greeks, or Βραχιόνισμα], with which the people of India are accustomed to adorn themselves.

units.la: xii. Pica Brasilica Gesnero & aliis, Κίττα Βραζιλική: Indigenis ibi proprio dicta nomine Toucan, suo rostro minor. Βαλανηφάγος instat secundae Hydri ἀρκτίῳ. Stellis consignatur viii; quarum quae Rostrum fingunt, quaeque in dorso reliquis interspersae, tertiae sunt magnitudinis.
units.tr: xii. The Brazilian Magpie [Κίττα Βραζιλική] of Gesner and others; there it is called by its native name the Toucan, smaller than its own beak. The Nut-eater [Βαλανηφάγος] stands near the northern Hydra's second. It is marked with eight stars, of which those that form the beak, and those scattered over the back, are of the third magnitude.

units.la: xiii. Phoenicopterus, Φοινικόπτερος nobis dici posset Roodvleughel Martialis lib. xiii. Dat mihi penna rubens nomen, sed lingua gulosis Nostra placet: quid si garrula lingua foret?
units.tr: xiii. The Flamingo [Φοινικόπτερος], which we might call in our language the Roodvleughel, the red wing. Martial, book xiii: The red feather gives me my name, but our tongue pleases the greedy: what if the tongue were chattering?

units.la: Hispani vocant Flamengo. Expansis alis, rostro Piscem Notium, qua in arcum curvatur, appetit. Stellis fulget xiii; quarum quae in capite secundae magnitudinis (cujus classis duas alias habet, unam in dorso, in ala sinistra alteram) Ὀφθαλμὸς Φοιnicopteri; Par vero, quod in medio collo, Περιτραχήλιον, Collare vel Torquem appello.
units.tr: The Spanish call it the Flamengo. With its wings spread, it seizes the Southern Fish with its beak, where the Fish curves in an arc. It shines with thirteen stars, of which the one in the head, of the second magnitude (which has two others, one on the back and one on the left wing), is the Eye of the Flamingo [Ὀφθαλμὸς Φοινικοπτέρου]; and the pair in the middle of the neck, the Around-the-neck [Περιτραχήλιον], I call the Collare or Torquem, the collar.

units.la: xiv. Phoenix, Φοῖνιξ; Avis unica, rarenter visa; Aquilae magnitudine, auro fulgens circa collum, cetera purpuram mentiens; roseis pennis caeruleam caudam distinguentibus, cristis faciem; caputque plumeo apice cohonestante. Nido casia turisque furculis exstructo odoribusque repleto, & caloris Solis accenso; surgente utrimque fumo, superstans; Stellis distinguitur xiv. Earum quae supra collum tertiae magnitudinis, Μονάδες; tres vero quae quartae magnitudinis in pectore Ἀϊδιότητος; unica denique quae ejusdem classis paullo infra jugulum (ubi praesentiens moriendi tempus, rostro se vellicare dicitur, cruori eliciendo, unde per Vermiculum renascatur) Ἀναστασίως mihi sunt Symbola.
units.tr: xiv. The Phoenix [Φοῖνιξ]: a unique bird, rarely seen, the size of an eagle, shining with gold about the neck, otherwise resembling purple, with rosy feathers setting off a blue tail, a crest on its face, and its head adorned with a feathery tuft. It stands on a nest built of cassia and sprigs of frankincense, filled with perfumes and kindled by the heat of the sun, with smoke rising on either side. It is distinguished by fourteen stars. Of these, those above the neck, of the third magnitude, are the Monads [Μονάδες]; three of the fourth magnitude in the breast are Eternity [Ἀϊδιότης]; and finally the single star of the same class a little below the throat (where, sensing the time of its death, it is said to pluck itself with its beak to draw out blood, from which it is reborn through a little worm) is my symbol of the Resurrection [Ἀναστασίς].

units.la: L. Nihil Signorum restat. Concludam cum Manilio: Hac igitur magno divisus aethere sedes Signa tenent Mundi totum deducta per orbem. Tu modo corporeis similes ne quaere figuras, Omniaque aequali fulgentia membra colore, Ignea designat species; atque Ignibus Ignes Respondent, Media Extremis, atque Ultima Summis Cernuntur; satis est, sive non omnia celant.
units.tr: L. Nothing of the constellations remains. I will conclude with Manilius: "Hence the constellations hold their seats, divided across the great aether, spread over the whole world. You need only not seek figures like bodily forms, and all the limbs gleaming with one equal colour; a fiery appearance marks them, and fires answer to fires, the middle ones to the extremes, and the last are seen at the highest points; it is enough, whether or not they hide everything."

units.la: CAP. XXIII.
units.tr: CAP. XXIII.

units.la: De Planetis universim.
units.tr: On the Planets in general

units.la: HISTORIAM absolvi Inerrantium: succedit Errantium, qui Græcis πλανήται. Sunt illi septem cælestia Corpora, quæ certis discreta spacijs, inquit Plinius lib. II. natur. histor. cap. VI. terris proxima, præter motum primi Mobilis, quo ab ortu in occasum rapiuntur, peculiarem quamdam illique contrariam habent in proprijs orbibus conversionem.
units.tr: I have finished the history of the fixed stars. Next comes that of the wandering stars, which the Greeks call planētai. These are the seven heavenly bodies which, set apart at fixed intervals, lie nearest the earth, as Pliny says (Natural History, bk. II, ch. VI). Apart from the motion of the primum mobile, by which they are carried from east to west, they have a certain motion of their own, contrary to it, within their own orbits.

units.la: Nomen illis ἀπὸ τῆς πλανήσεως, quod Errare, unde Latinis Errantia Sidera: ab errore, inquit Macrobius; ab incessu, Plinius, quum errent nulla minus illis. Erraticas Stellas vocant Iulius Firmicus, Hyginus, alij; Errones Nigidius: Ἀλήται etiam Græcorum nonnulli. Epigrammatarius: Ἀπλανέες δ' ἱκάνεῳ, καὶ ἀντιήιοντες Ἀλήτη Ἀτροφίης ἥμεις πάσαν ἄγυσι τύχλω.
units.tr: They take their name from wandering (apo tēs planēseōs), that is, from erring (errare), whence the Latins call them errantia sidera, "wandering stars." "From error," says Macrobius; "from their gait," says Pliny, "though nothing errs less than they do." Iulius Firmicus, Hyginus and others call them erratic stars, and Nigidius calls them erones. Some of the Greeks also call them aletai. The epigrammatist says: "The fixed stars come, and the wanderers of the sky go round in their courses, opposite to them" [Ἀπλανέες δ' ἱκάνεῳ, καὶ ἀντιήιοντες Ἀλήτη Ἀτροφίης ἥμεις πάσαν ἄγυσι τύχλω].

units.la: Non autem, ut vulgo tinniunt, hæ voces sunt exaudiendæ. Sic enim dicuntur, non quod vago incertoque motu oberrent; sed quod vario & dispari circumferantur; de quo multa Macrobius lib. I. cap. XVIII. Vere Tullius lib. I. de Divin. Planeta verbo & facis Græcorum vocibus errant; revera certo lapsu spacioque feruntur. Explicatissime nuper de illis vir doctus; scribens eos progredi & retrocedere, occultari & aliquandiu delitescere; post operire se rursum, antecedere & consequi Solem; incitari & cursus vicissim veloces inhibere; tum ne moveri quidem, sed ad quoddam tempus velut insistere; à Solis itinere in Austrum alias, alias in Boream excurrere, & ad idem retorqueri exactisque & confectis itineribus, pristinos eadem lege cursus constanter repetere.
units.tr: These words, however, are not to be heard in the sense in which people commonly chatter about them. They are so called not because they wander in an aimless and uncertain motion, but because they are carried with a varied and unequal motion. Macrobius treats this at length (bk. I, ch. XVIII). Cicero rightly says in the first book of On Divination: "The planets wander in name and by the Greek word, but in truth they are carried along with a fixed gliding and a settled course." Recently a learned man explained them very fully. He writes that they advance and retrograde, are hidden and lie concealed for some time, then reappear and go ahead of or follow the Sun. They are urged on and in turn check their swift course. Then they do not even move, but for a certain time seem to stand still. They run off from the Sun's path, now to the south, now to the north, and are turned back to the same point. When their journeys are finished and completed, they constantly repeat their former courses by the same law.

units.la: Ordo Situsque Planetarum alijs alius, ut docet præter alios Macrobius lib. I. cap. XIX. Anaximander, Metrodorus Chius, Crates, Solem supremo ponunt loco; huic autem Lunam, Lunæ reliquos quinque subijciunt. Ægyptij, & qui eos sequitur Plato, Solem Lunamque reliquis omnibus inferiores agnoscunt. Platonis in Timæo verba sunt hæc: Σωμαζε δὲ αὐτὸν ἐκάστων (de Planetis loquitur) ποιήσας ὁ Θεὸς, ἔθηκεν εἰς τὰς περιφορὰς, ὡς ἡ Ἰωπίτερ περιόδῳ ἡ. Σελήνην μὲν εἰς τὴν περὶ γῆν πρῶτον, Ἥλιον δὲ εἰς τὴν δεύτερον γῆς, Ἐωσφόρον δὲ ἐκ τὴν ἱερὸν Ἑρμῆ λεγόμενον; & quæ sequuntur. Idem innuit apud Platonem Timæus Locrus de Anima Mundi: ἀ μὲν ἂν Σελήνα ... ὁ δὲ Ἀλιος μετὰ ταῦτα ... χρόνῳ τὸν αὐτὸν κύκλον ἐπιλέγει. Habet magnus Philosophus sententiæ suæ suffragatores, qui rationibus eam stabiliunt; inter eas hæc: Si Venus Mecuriusque infra Solem volverentur, necessario suo objectu atque interventu in Conjunctionibus Solis lucem terris adimerent & conspectum, ut fit, Luna Soli Terræque interposita; atqui numquam hoc accidit; ergo verisimile Venerem & Mercurium sedem suam in hac Vniversi mole Sole altiorem obtinere. Sed Platonem, & qui eum hic sequuti (inter quos & Aristoteles, si ejus sit qui de Mundo circumfertur) docte refutat Peucerus. Primo enim Veneris Mercuriique corpora tota æqualiter rara & lucida, Solis radios, si forte obijciantur, neque excludere à terra, neque impedire, quo minus in quamcumque partem libere spargantur; Lunam vero magna ex parte densam atque opacam radios Solis non solum excipere, sed & in Cœlum reflectere: Deinde Diametrum Veneris, quæ Mercurij major, ad Solis dimetientem, secundum Albategnium, esse subdecuplam, & vix centesimam posse tegere Solis partem; secundum exactiorem observationem propemodum subquadruplam esse; Solis enim Apogæi Diametrum xxxi. scrupulorum esse, Perigæi xxxiii; Veneris Apogæi Dimetientem esse vii. scrupulorum in Perigæo constitutæ x; ideoque si Solem tegeret, quum quadragesimam ejus partem vix occultaret, talem occultationem fore insensibilem: Tertio denique, quod Venus ob remotiorem distantiam tantam Latitudinis παράλλαξιν non efficiat, ut Luna. Aristarchus Samius qui ante Ptolemæum floruit annis cccc, & qui ejus voluerunt esse Sectatores, adsumtis novis Hypothematis, Solem in medio Mundi sistunt immobilem, ut reliquorum orbium centrum; Soli Mercurium & Venerem circumdantes; supra Venerem orbem magnum, qui Terram cum
units.tr: The order and position of the planets differ, as Macrobius, among others, teaches (bk. I, ch. XIX). Anaximander, Metrodorus of Chios and Crates place the Sun in the highest position, below it the Moon, and below the Moon the other five. The Egyptians, and Plato who follows them, recognise the Sun and Moon as lower than all the rest. Plato's words in the Timaeus are these: God, having made them (he is speaking of the planets), set them in their orbits, the Moon in the first orbit about the earth, the Sun in the second, and the morning star, called Hermes, in the next [Σωμαζε δὲ αὐτὸν ἐκάστων ποιήσας ὁ Θεὸς, ἔθηκεν εἰς τὰς περιφορὰς, ὡς ἡ Ἰωπίτερ περιόδῳ ἡ. Σελήνην μὲν εἰς τὴν περὶ γῆν πρῶτον, Ἥλιον δὲ εἰς τὴν δεύτερον γῆς, Ἐωσφόρον δὲ ἐκ τὴν ἱερὸν Ἑρμῆ λεγόμενον]; and what follows. Timaeus the Locrian, in his work On the Soul of the World, hints at the same thing: the Moon ... then the Sun ... in time he returns to the same circle [ἀ μὲν ἂν Σελήνα ... ὁ δὲ Ἀλιος μετὰ ταῦτα ... χρόνῳ τὸν αὐτὸν κύκλον ἐπιλέγει]. The great philosopher has supporters who confirm his view by reasons, and among these is the following. If Venus and Mercury revolved below the Sun, then at its conjunctions they would necessarily interpose themselves and take away light and sight from the earth, just as the Moon does when it is placed between the Sun and the earth. But this never happens. Therefore it is likely that Venus and Mercury hold their seat in this mass of the universe higher than the Sun. But Peucer learnedly refutes Plato, and those who have followed him here (among whom is Aristotle, if he is the author of the book On the World that circulates under his name). First, the bodies of Venus and Mercury are wholly and equally rare and bright, so that if rays of the Sun happened to strike them, they would neither shut them out from the earth nor hinder them from spreading freely in any direction. The Moon, on the other hand, is for the most part dense and opaque, and it not only receives the Sun's rays but also reflects them back into the heavens. Second, the diameter of Venus, which is greater than that of Mercury, is, compared with the Sun's diameter according to Albategnius, a tenth part, and could cover barely a hundredth part of the Sun. According to more exact observation it is nearly a quarter. For the Sun's diameter is 31 minutes at apogee and 33 at perigee, while the diameter of Venus is 7 minutes at apogee and 10 when at perigee. So if it covered the Sun, since it would hide scarcely a fortieth part of it, such an occultation would be imperceptible. Third, and finally, because Venus, owing to its far greater distance, does not produce a parallax of latitude as large as the Moon's does. Aristarchus of Samos, who flourished four hundred years before Ptolemy, and those who wished to be his followers, adopted new hypotheses. They set the Sun, immobile, in the middle of the universe as the centre of the other orbits, with Mercury and Venus encircling the Sun. Above Venus they place a great orbit, which embraces the earth with the elements and the Moon, and they leave the other places to the others, as they were thought to have held them of old.

units.la: Aristarcho. cum Elementis & Luna complectatur, constituentes; reliquis vero loca, quæ antiquitus obtinuisse existimati sunt, relinquentes. Audiendus hic Ptolemæus, qui in nona magnæ Compositionis sectione, sequutus Chaldæos, Dorotheum, Hipparchum, aliosque accuratioris notæ Astronomos, sub Octava Sphæra Saturnum, Iovem, Martem collocat; Soli medium inter Planetas locum adignat; sub Sole Venerem, Mercurium, Lunam constituit: vere & recentiorum omnium calculis comprobate. Exprimitu hunc ordinem duobus versibus Manilius lib. 1: Saturni, Iovis & Martis, Solisque; sub illis Mercurius Venerem interagit Lunamque locatus.
units.tr: Aristarchus. Here Ptolemy should be heard. In the ninth section of his Great Composition, following the Chaldeans, Dorotheus, Hipparchus and other astronomers of more accurate reputation, he places Saturn, Jupiter and Mars below the eighth sphere. He gives the Sun the middle place among the planets, and under the Sun he sets Venus, Mercury and the Moon. This view is confirmed also by the calculations of all more recent writers. Manilius expresses this order in two verses in book I: "Of Saturn, Jupiter, Mars and the Sun; beneath them Mercury, placed between Venus and the Moon."

units.la: 10 Iam cujus singuli Naturæ, Coloris, Saporis: quanti Ponderis; cujus Fortunæ; quando aucti dicantur Cursu, Numero, Lumine; quando Combusti; & alia talia rimentur, quibus est otium majus, quibusque inlicitas artes futurus istius cognitionis usus.
units.tr: Now, as for their individual natures, colours, tastes and weights; their fortunes; when they are said to be increased in course, number or light, and when they are burnt; and other such matters, let those investigate them who have more leisure, and for whom the use of such knowledge would be a forbidden art.

units.la: Adsignent etiam per me licet ijdem sua Planetis Domicilia; Saturno Capricornum & Aquarium; Iovi Sagittarium & Pisces; Arietem & Scorpionem Marti; Leonem Soli; Veneri Taurum & Libram; Mercurio Geminos Virginem; Lunæ denique Cancrum.
units.tr: Let the same men, if I may, also assign to the planets their domiciles: to Saturn Capricorn and Aquarius; to Jupiter Sagittarius and Pisces; Aries and Scorpio to Mars; Leo to the Sun; Taurus and Libra to Venus; Gemini and Virgo to Mercury; and finally Cancer to the Moon.

units.la: Docent item Saturnum exaltari in gradu xx. Librae; Iovem in xv. Cancris; Martem in xxviii. Capricorni; Solem in xix. Arietis; Venerem in xxvi. Piscium; 20 Mercurium in xv. Virginis; in iv. Tauri Lunam.
units.tr: They also teach that Saturn is exalted at the twentieth degree of Libra; Jupiter at the fifteenth of Cancer; Mars at the twenty-eighth of Capricorn; the Sun at the nineteenth of Aries; Venus at the twenty-sixth of Pisces; Mercury at the fifteenth of Virgo; and the Moon at the fourth of Taurus.

units.la: Monstrent idem denique Planetas cum Sole & Signis miscere quinque modis, ἐκ ἑξαγώνου, ἐκ τετραγώνου, ἐκ τριγώνου, ἐκ διαμέτρου, ἐκ συνόδου; omnium autem potentissimum adspectum esse ἐκ συνόδου, secundum ἐκ διαμέτρου; & ita deinceps. Ad potiora, mihi saltem, propero.
units.tr: The same men also show that the planets mix with the Sun and the signs in five ways: sextile, square, trine, opposition and conjunction. The most powerful aspect, they say, is the conjunction, and next to it the opposition; and so on. I hasten on to the more important matters, at least for my own purposes.

units.la: Errantium alii sunt Φωσφόροι, Ἀστέρες alij. Prioris classis sunt Sol & Luna; posteriores reliqui; quorum alij Sole superiores, ut Saturnus, Iupiter, Mars; alij inferiores, Venus & Mercurius. Non hæc ab aliqua temeritate Distributio. In Septenarium quidem numerum unanimi consensu conspiratum à plerisque, non nostri tantum, sed ævi quoque prisci; unde Græcus Poëta vetus: Ἐ πὶ πολυπλανεῖς κατ᾽ ὀλύμπιον Ἀστέρες ἂδον Εἰλεῖῶσιν, ἢ τοῖον ἀεὶ κατονισ᾽ αἰῶν, Νυκτοφαὴς μὴν, ςυγὸς Κρόνος, Ἠ λίος ἡδύς, Γαστροφόρος Παφίη, Ἡρᾶος Ἄρης, ἑρμῆρος Ἐ ρμῆς, Καὶ Ζεὺς δ᾽ ἐχθρυθλιος, ἀ φ᾽ ἢ φύσις ἐκλάσησεν. οἱ δ᾽ αὐτοὶ μεσόπων ἐιλέωσι ὅσιν, &c.
units.tr: Of the wandering stars, some are phōsphoroi, light-bearers, and others are asteres, stars. The first class consists of the Sun and Moon; the rest belong to the second. Of these, some are above the Sun, such as Saturn, Jupiter and Mars; others are below it, Venus and Mercury. This division is not made out of any rashness. The number seven has been agreed upon unanimously by most people, not only in our own time but also in antiquity. Hence the old Greek poet says: "Among the much-wandering stars in the Olympian sky, seven are always established in their order: the night-shining Saturn, the sweet Sun, the Cypris who bears the light, the warlike Ares, Hermes the messenger, and Zeus, the bringer of good; from these nature has formed the cycle ..." [Ἐ πὶ πολυπλανεῖς κατ᾽ ὀλύμπιον Ἀστέρες ἂδον Εἰλεῖῶσιν, ἢ τοῖον ἀεὶ κατονισ᾽ αἰῶν, Νυκτοφαὴς μὴν, ςυγὸς Κρόνος, Ἠ λίος ἡδύς, Γαστροφόρος Παφίη, Ἡρᾶος Ἄρης, ἑρμῆρος Ἐ ρμῆς, Καὶ Ζεὺς δ᾽ ἐχθρυθλιος, ἀ φ᾽ ἢ φύσις ἐκλάσησεν. οἱ δ᾽ αὐτοὶ μεσόπων ἐιλέωσι ὅσιν, &c.]. The same seven are given in a single line: "Moon, Zeus, Ares, Paphie, Kronos, Helios, Hermes" [Μλίωη, Ζεύς, Ἄρης, Παφίη, Κρόνος, Ἠ λίος, Ἑρμῆς].

units.la: & idem unico versu: Μλίωη, Ζεύς, Ἄρης, Παφίη, Κρόνος, Ἠ λίος, Ἑρμῆς: Antiquorum tamen multi Solem & Lunam (quod in his peculiaris quid contemplarentur, ut suis locis docebimur) in numerum venire Errantium nolebant; sed κατ᾽ ἐκ χαὶ φῶς vocabant, ut videre est apud Theonem Ptolemaei Commentatorem. Hinc Aratus: Οἱ δ᾽ ἕπ᾽ μιξ ἄλλει πέντ᾽ Ἀστέρες, ὠδὲν ὁμοῖοι Πάντῃ ἓν ὠδῶλων δυσκρίδεκα δίκλοντ᾽. Οὐκ αἱ ἐτ᾽ εἰς ἄλλας ὁρῶν ἐπὶ ἐπιμηφέουσ Καίνων ἔχε χίον᾽, ἐπεὶ ταῦτης μετιναῦμ.
units.tr: Many of the ancients, however, were unwilling to count the Sun and Moon among the wandering stars. (What special things they contemplated in these two, we shall be taught in their proper places.) They called them instead "lights" [κατ᾽ ἐκ χαὶ φῶς], as may be seen in Theon, the commentator on Ptolemy. Hence Aratus: "But five stars wander, unlike one another, in every direction..." [Οἱ δ᾽ ἕπ᾽ μιξ ἄλλει πέντ᾽ Ἀστέρες, ὠδὲν ὁμοῖοι Πάντῃ ἓν ὠδῶλων δυσκρίδεκα δίκλοντ᾽. Οὐκ αἱ ἐτ᾽ εἰς ἄλλας ὁρῶν ἐπὶ ἐπιμηφέουσ Καίνων ἔχε χίον᾽, ἐπεὶ ταῦτης μετιναῦμ.]

units.la: Quæ ita reddit Festus Avienus: Quinque itidem Stellæ, similis quibus haud sit imago, Nec quas formarum doctus notet adfixarum, Per biffena Poli volitant rutilantia Signa: Nullus eas alio pacto deprendere certet: 50 Tam vaga per totam cunctis via defluit æthram.
units.tr: Festus Avienus renders this thus: "Likewise five stars, to which no image is alike, and which the learned do not mark as fixed forms, fly through the twelve-fold circle of the Pole as shining signs. No one will try to grasp them in any other way; so wandering, they flow down through the whole sky by a path that is open to all."

units.la: Cicero lib. 1. de Natur. Deorum: Deos enim cælo esse dicit, quinque eos, qui in Stellis vagis nominantur: unum qui ex omnibus sideribus, quæ infixa Cælo sunt, ex dispersis quasi membris simplex sit putandus Deus; septimum Solem adjungit, cœlavamque Lunam. Idem eodem libro: Quid Solis numquidnam aut Lunæ aut quinque Errantium Siderum simile vidisti? Propertius lib. iv. Elegia 1. ex emendatione Scaligeri ad lib. iv. Manilii: Adspicienda via est cœli, versusque per Astra Limes, & à Stellis quinque petenda fides.
units.tr: Cicero, in the first book of On the Nature of the Gods: "For he says that the gods are in heaven, five of them, those named among the wandering stars. One must think of one god, made as it were from the scattered limbs of all the stars that are fixed in heaven; he adds the Sun as a seventh, and the shining Moon." In the same book: "Have you ever seen anything like the Sun, or the Moon, or the five wandering stars?" Propertius, book IV, elegy 1, following Scaliger's emendation of Manilius book IV: "The path of heaven must be watched, and the boundary through the stars, and trust must be sought from the five stars."

units.la: Manilius lib. iii. Astronomicôn: Fata quoque & Vitas hominum suspendit ab Astris, Quæ summas operum partes, quæ lucis honorem, Quæ famam adferrent, quæ numquam fessa volarent: Quæ quasi per mediam Mundi præcordia partem Disposita obtineant Phæbum, Lunamque, vagasque Fvincant Stellas, nec non vincantur ab ipsa. His Regnum Natura dedit, propriasque sacravit Vnicuique vices, sanxitque per omnia, summam Vndique ne Fati ratio traheretur in unam.
units.tr: Manilius, book 3 of the Astronomica: He also hangs the fates and lives of men upon the Stars: the stars that bring the highest parts of works, the honour of light, fame, and that fly never wearied. These, set in the midst of the Universe as it were, hold the Sun and Moon and the wandering Stars, and are themselves held by them. Nature gave them their kingdom, consecrated to each its own proper turns, and ordained through all things that the sum of Fate should not be drawn into one.

units.la: Sic Iulius Firmicus lib. i. cap. iv: In quo Sol & Luna, quinque etiam Stellæ Erraticæ, quæ πλανήτα ab Græcis vocantur, certa ac diffinita semper agitatione discurrunt. Sic Macrobius lib. i. in Somnium Scipionis, cap. xvii. Hus illud adjiciendum est, quod præter duo Lumina & Stellas quinque, quæ appellantur Vagæ, reliquas omnes alij infixas Cælo, nec nisi cum cælo moveri. Sic denique Iulius Hyginus in Poetico Astronomico: Reliquum est nobis de quinque Stellis; quas complures, ut Erraticas, ita πλανήτας Græci dixerunt. Sol igitur & Luna, principes, ut notat etiam Ptolemæus, Astrorum, & primariæ totius Vniversi Stellæ, Φῶς vocantur, Hebræis מאור, Paraphrastæ Chaldaico נהורין, φωστῆρες LXX Interpretibus, Lumina passim & Luminaria Latinis. Sol merito, quum omnium Siderum sit maximus, & ab eo augeantur minuanturque ceterarum Stellarum actiones, ejusque motus regula sit reliquorum: nec immerito Luna; quæ, quamvis, excepto Mercurio, omnium minima (quidquid, Augustino suffragante, scribat Basilius lib. i. de Genesi ad litteram, Lunam, contra Mathematicorum omnium calculos, post Solem maximum Cœli adferens astrum) oculorum tamen judicio vulgique existimatione censetur ceteris Planetis major; petere quoque solitis ab ea nonnullis gentibus temporum distinctiones, Ecclesiastici cap. xliii, verf. 6, 7. 8. Utriqué vero meritissime talem dedit Antiquitas appellationem; cum quod illorum vires & effectus in Elementis, Metallis, Stirpibus, Animantibus, humanisque Corporibus, quam reliquorum, sint insigniores; tum quod gratissima vice Diem Noctemque illustrent. Hæc enim præcipua Conditionis eorum fuit causa, quemadmodum videre est apud Moschen Genes. i. verf. 14. & seqq. & Iirmeiam cap. xxxi, 35.
units.tr: So Julius Firmicus, book 1, chapter 4: In which the Sun and Moon, and also the five wandering stars, which the Greeks call planets [πλανήτα], run their courses always with a certain and fixed motion. So Macrobius, book 1 on the Dream of Scipio, chapter 17: To this must be added that, besides the two lights and the five stars which are called wandering, all the others are fixed in the sky and move only with the sky. So finally Julius Hyginus in the Poeticon Astronomicon: It remains for us to speak of the five stars, which the Greeks, as they are wandering, so called planets [πλανήτας]. The Sun and Moon, therefore, the chief stars, as Ptolemy also notes, and the principal stars of the whole universe, are called φῶς [phōs]; by the Hebrews מאור [ma'or], by the Chaldee paraphrast nehorin, by the Seventy φωστῆρες [phōstēres], and by the Latins everywhere lumina and luminaria. The Sun rightly, since it is the greatest of all the stars, and the actions of the other stars are increased or diminished by it, and its motion is the rule of the rest; and the Moon not undeservedly, which, although it is the smallest of all except Mercury (whatever Basil writes, with Augustine concurring, in book 1 of his commentary On Genesis according to the Letter, placing the Moon, against the calculations of all mathematicians, as the greatest star after the Sun), is nevertheless judged by the eye and by popular opinion to be greater than the other planets; and some nations have customarily sought from it the divisions of time, Ecclesiasticus 43, vers. 6, 7, 8. To both, however, antiquity most deservedly gave such a name: partly because their powers and effects upon the elements, metals, plants, animals and human bodies are more notable than those of the rest, and partly because in a most welcome exchange they illumine day and night. For this was the chief cause of their appointment, as may be seen in Moses, Genesis 1, vers. 14 ff., and Jeremiah 31, vers. 35.

units.la: CAP. XXIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIV.

units.la: De Saturno, Iove & Marte.
units.tr: Of Saturn, Jupiter and Mars.

units.la: Intra Sphæras, quæ Planetis adsignatæ, supremam possidet Saturnus. Græcis Κρόνος: quod, inquit M. Tullius lib. ii. de nat. Deor. Temporis Deum finxerint Veteres: dicitur ijsdem & Φαίνων, scribente præter Hyginum Aristotele de Mundo: ὁ τῆ Φαίνοντ ἄμα καὶ Κρόνῳ καλουμένῳ κύκλῳ. Hebræis שבת, propter septimum diem. Chaldæis Molech. Ejus Stella similis illi, quæ in humero Orionis dextro, quemadmodum notat Hyginus. Gelidæ rigentisque naturæ, Plinio, lib. ii, nat. histor. cap. viii. Causa apud Ptolemæum libro i. quadripart. cap. iiii. quod, inquit, ab Solis calore, Terræque humiditate quam longissime distet. Terra major putatur nonagies semel cum octava parte. Motus, qui proprius illi, tardissimus. Cursum enim conficit annis xxx. Videndus Plinius capite, quod indicavi, octavo. Nota ejus ♄, Falx; quæ tribui Saturno solita, ut indicant Virgilius vii. Æneidos, Macrob. i. Saturn. cap. vii. Servius lib. ii. Georg. Isidorus lib. viii. Etymol. cap. xi. Et inde Falcifer, Ovidio i. Fastor, Martiali lib. xi. Epig. vii. Arnobio lib. iii. adversus gentes.
units.tr: Within the spheres assigned to the planets, the highest is possessed by Saturn. To the Greeks it is Kronos, which, as M. Tullius says in book 2 of On the Nature of the Gods, the ancients imagined to be the god of time. It is also called Phainon by the same writers, and besides Hyginus, Aristotle in On the Cosmos calls it "the circle called both Phainon and Kronos" [ὁ τῆ Φαίνοντ ἄμα καὶ Κρόνῳ καλουμένῳ κύκλῳ]. To the Hebrews it is Shabbath [שבת], because of the seventh day. To the Chaldeans it is Molech. Its star is like the one on the right shoulder of Orion, as Hyginus notes. By Pliny (Natural History, book 2, chapter 8) its nature is cold and stiff. Ptolemy (Tetrabiblos, book 1, chapter 4) gives the cause: it is as far as possible from the heat of the Sun and the moisture of the Earth. The Earth is thought to be ninety-one times the size of Saturn, with an additional eighth part. Its proper motion is the slowest, for it completes its course in thirty years. See Pliny in the chapter I have cited, chapter 8. Its symbol is ♄, the sickle, which was customarily attributed to Saturn, as Virgil (Aeneid, book 7), Macrobius (Saturnalia, book 1, chapter 7), Servius (on Georgics, book 2), and Isidore (Etymologies, book 8, chapter 11) indicate. Hence he is called "sickle-bearer" by Ovid (Fasti, book 1), Martial (Epigrams, book 11, epigram 7), and Arnobius (Against the Nations, book 3).

units.la: Iupiter secundum inter Planetas locum obtinet. Græcis Φαέθων. Aristoteles de Mundo: ἐφεξῆς δὲ ὁ τῆ Φαέθοντ κύκλῳ, Διὸς λεγόμενος. Sic appellatus à Splendore: Solus enim, φῶνις & Venere exceptis, umbram parit. Hebræis צדק, Iustitia. Chaldæis רעם פעם; βροντάς, Βροντῶ Orpheo; Tonans, Tonitrualis Latinis. Auctor vitalis & temperati caloris. Terram continet nonagies quinquies, & dimidiam fere partem. Zodiacum circumit annis fere xii, Plinio Hyginoque scribentibus, & experientia teste. Character ♄, fulmen; unde illi cognomina Κτεφανιο Orpheo, Hesychio, Phurnuto, Paulaniae: Ἀργικέραυνο Pindaro; Fulminator Apuleio; Fulgurator in antiquis marmoribus; Fulgur Festo in Provorsum.
units.tr: Jupiter holds the second place among the planets. To the Greeks it is Phaethon [Φαέθων]. Aristotle: "next in order is the circle of Phaethon, which is called Zeus" [ἐφεξῆς δὲ ὁ τῆ Φαέθοντ κύκλῳ, Διὸς λεγόμενος]. It is so named from its brightness, for apart from the Sun, Phosphorus and Venus, it alone casts a shadow. To the Hebrews it is Tsedeq [צדק], Justice. To the Chaldeans it is Ra'am Pa'am [רעם פעם]. Orpheus calls it Brontas and Bronto [βροντάς, Βροντῶ]; in Latin it is "the Thunderer" and "the Thundering." It is the giver of life and of temperate heat. It contains ninety-five and nearly a half times the Earth. It goes round the zodiac in about twelve years, as Pliny and Hyginus write, and experience confirms. Its character is ♃, the thunderbolt; hence its epithets: Ktephanios [Κτεφανιο] in Orpheus, Hesychius, Phurnutus and Pausanias; Argikeraunos [Ἀργικέραυνο] in Pindar; "Fulminator" in Apuleius; "Fulgurator" on ancient marbles; and "Fulgur" in Festus under Provorsum.

units.la: Marti tertius datus est locus. Πυρόεις Graecis ab igneo colore; vel ab effectu, quod urat & exsiccet. Aristoteles: εἰσ' ὁ Πυρόεις, ὁ Ἡφαιστος τ ἐ Ἀρεῖ ... Hebraeis מאדם, πυρόεις. Terram superat semel, & paullo plus una tertia. Duodecim percurrit signa duobus fere annis, Plinio & Hygino testibus. Fere, inquam. Cursus enim ejus Maxime inobservabilis, inquit Plinius lib. ii. nat. hist. cap. xvii, utpote numquam stationem facientis. Nota ♂, Clipeus cum Hasta. Nam utrumque illi attribuitur. Ovidius: Bellice, depositis Clipeo pauliffer & Hasta, Mars ades.
units.tr: The third place is given to Mars. To the Greeks it is Pyroeis [Πυρόεις], from its fiery colour, or from its effect, since it burns and dries. Aristotle: "Pyroeis, which is Hephaestus..." [εἰσ' ὁ Πυρόεις, ὁ Ἡφαιστος τ ἐ Ἀρεῖ ...]. To the Hebrews it is Ma'adim [מאדם], Pyroeis. It surpasses the Earth once and a little more than a third. It runs through the twelve signs in nearly two years, according to Pliny and Hyginus. "Nearly," I say, for its course is most unobservable, as Pliny says in book 2 of the Natural History, chapter 17, since it never makes a station. Its symbol is ♂, a shield with a spear, for both are attributed to it. Ovid: "Warlike Mars, lay aside the shield and spear and be present." [Bellice, depositis Clipeo pauliffer & Hasta, Mars ades.]

units.la: Tres, quos jam adumbravi, Planetae perpetua lege sic in suis moventur Epicyclis, quemadmodum peritissimi observarunt Astronomi, ut motu suo quamdam cerga Solem reverentiam praesse ferre videantur. Soli namque coniuncti ὑπόγειον Epicycli sui tenere deprehenduntur: ut veneratione tanti hospitis in extremos suae ditionis fines abgressi, regi loco quasi cedant, ex intervallo mediocri mandata virosque ab eo acceperuti: eidem ex diametro oppositos ἀντίγειον obtinere videmus, & lugere quasi regis absentiam, illiusque reditum supplices expetere. Hanc etiam Stationum legum animadvertimus eosdem indesinenter servare, ut ab Sole trium Signorum intervallo digressus Saturnus, quem quadratum adspectum vocant, tamquam immobilis subsistere videatur; Iupiter eandem σχημα φαντασίαν habeat in Trigono; Mars ultra Trigonum aliquot partibus.
units.tr: The three planets I have just outlined move in their epicycles by a fixed law, as the most skilled astronomers have observed, so that by their motion they seem to show a certain reverence toward the Sun. For when they are in conjunction with the Sun they are found to keep their epicycles underground [ὑπόγειον], so that, out of reverence for so great a guest, they withdraw to the farthest borders of his domain and, as it were, yield the place of king, receiving commands and envoys from him at a moderate distance. When they are opposite him, on the diametrically opposite side, we see them keep their epicycles above ground [ἀντίγειον], as if mourning the king's absence and humbly seeking his return. We also notice that they constantly observe the same laws of stations: Saturn, when it departs three signs from the Sun, which they call the square aspect, seems to stand still as if motionless; Jupiter has the same appearance of figure [σχῆμα φαντασίαν] in the trine; Mars, a few degrees beyond the trine.

units.la: CAP. XXV. De Sole.
units.tr: CAP. XXV. On the Sun.

units.la: Sol Locum inter Planetas nactus est medium; numero, non spatio, cujus dimensione perspecta, ipse magis ab summo, quam ab ipso recedit ima postremitas, ait Macrobius lib. i. ad Somnium Scipionis, cap. xix. Quum enim, addit, Saturni Stela, quae summa, Zodiacum xxx annis peragrat: Sol medius uno anno; Luna ultima uno mense, non integro: necesse est tantum interesse inter Solem & Saturnum, quantum inter unum & triginta; tantum inter Lunam Solemque, quantum inter duodecim & unum.
units.tr: Sol has obtained a middle place among the planets: in number, not in space. Once its extent is surveyed, the lowest extremity is further from the highest than the Sun is from it, says Macrobius, Book 1 of his Commentary on Scipio's Dream, ch. 19. "For since," he adds, "Saturn, the highest star, traverses the zodiac in thirty years, the Sun, the middle one, in one year, and the Moon, the lowest, in one month, not a full one, there must be as great a distance between the Sun and Saturn as between one and thirty, and as great between the Moon and the Sun as between twelve and one."

units.la: Dux, ut eleganter Macrobius ejusdem libri cap. xx, Princeps, Moderator Luminum reliquorum. Dux; omnes enim sui Luminis majestate praecedit: Princeps; nam ita eminet, ut quum talis solus appareat Sol vocetur: Moderator denique; quia cursus ceterorum & recursus certa spatii diffinitione moderatur. Planetarum enim Stationes ab Sole fieri censebant Veteres. Lucanus lib. x: —— Sol Tempora dividit Anni; Mutat Noctis Diem; radiisque potentibus Astra Ire vetat; Cursusque vagos Statione moratur.
units.tr: Leader, as Macrobius elegantly says in the twentieth chapter of the same book: "Prince, Governor of the other lights. Leader, for he surpasses all in the majesty of his light; Prince, for he so stands out that when he alone appears he is called Sun; and finally Governor, because he regulates the course and return of the others by a fixed definition of space." The ancients believed that the stationary phases of the planets were caused by the Sun. Lucan, Book 10: "The Sun divides the seasons of the year, changes the day for the night, and with his powerful rays forbids the stars to move, and by his station holds back their wandering courses."

units.la: Plinius lib. ii. cap. xvi: Percussa (de Stellis loquitur) in qua diximus parte & triangulo Solis radio inhibentur rectum agere cursum, & ignea vi levantur in sublime. Hoc non protinus intelligi potest visu nostro; ideoque existimatur stare: unde & nomen accepit Statio. Progreditur deinde ejusdem radii violentia & retroire cogit vapor repercussas. Vitruvius lib. ix. Architect. cap. iv. Ergo potius ea ratio nobis constabit, quod fervor, quemadmodum omnes res evocat & ad se ducit, eadem ratione Solis impetus vehemens radiis trigoni forma porrectus insequentes Stellas ad se perducit, & ante-currentes veluti refrenando retinendoque non patitur progredi, sed ad se cogit regredi & in alterius trigoni signum esse. Huc pertinet Varronis illud, Satyra, ὦ λόγος: Quam mobilem Divum lyram, (sic Mundum vocat, sequutus Orphea, Hymno in Apollinem, ubi Coelum universum Apollinis cithara temperari canit.)
units.tr: Pliny, Book 2, ch. 16, speaking of the stars: "The part where we said they were struck, and the triangle of the Sun's ray, holds them back from going on a straight course, and with the fiery force they are lifted up on high. This cannot be immediately perceived by our sight, and so they are thought to stand still, whence the name Station. Then the violence of the same ray pushes them forward again, and the vapour that is thrown back forces them to retreat." Vitruvius, Book 9 of the Architecture, ch. 4: "Therefore this explanation seems more probable to us: as heat draws out and attracts all things to itself, so by the same reasoning the violent impulse of the Sun, extended in the form of a triangle by its rays, draws the following stars to itself, and does not allow the leading ones to advance, as if by checking and holding them back, but forces them to retreat towards itself and to be in the sign of another triangle." To this belongs that line of Varro's satire, "O logos" [ὦ λόγος]: "What a mobile lyre of the gods," (thus he calls the world, following Orpheus, in the hymn to Apollo, where he sings that the whole heaven is tempered by Apollo's cithara).

units.la: Sol harmogeQuadam gubernans motibus diis vegetat.
units.tr: Sun, governing by a certain harmony the motions, gives life to the gods.

units.la: Ex quibus paret Radios esse Soli, tamquam Moderaminis, quod dixi, frena: à quorum viribus & potentia Sol saepe Radiatus Latinis; radiatum etiam Lumen illi tribuentibus. Attius in Phoenissis, citante Prisciano libro de verbibus Comicis: Sol qui micantem candido curru atque equis Flammam citatis fervido ardore explicas, Quam natum adversso augurio atque inimico omine Thebis radiatum lumen ostendis tuum.
units.tr: From these passages it is clear that the rays are, as I said, the reins of this governance for the Sun. From their strength and power the Latin writers often call the Sun Radiatus, and they also attribute radiated light to him. Attius, in the Phoenissae, as quoted by Priscian in his book on comic verbs: "Sun, you who unfold the gleaming flame with your white chariot and swift horses, with hot ardour, the light of your rays shows itself to Thebes, born under an adverse augury and a hostile omen."

units.la: Ovidius in Metamorphos. Quid nunc Hyperione nate Forma colorque tibi radiataque lumina prosunt?
units.tr: Ovid, in the Metamorphoses: "What now do your form, your colour and your radiant light avail you, son of Hyperion?"

units.la: Hinc Sol Insigne radiatum Dei, Lucretio lib. v. de rer. natura: Propterea noctes hiberno tempore longas Cessant, dum veniat radiatum Insigne diei.
units.tr: Hence the Sun is the radiant insignia of God. Lucretius, Book 5 of On the Nature of Things: "For this reason the long nights of winter cease, until the radiant insignia of day comes."

units.la: Graecis Ἥλιος ἀπὸ τῆς ἀεὶ ἑλᾶν, ab continua circumvolutione; nam perpetuo circumrotatur motu, quo Zodiacum lustrat spatio dierum cccixv, horarum sex: vel ἀπὸ τῆς ἀλαμπῆς, ut nonnulli volunt, à splendore, σ, ut saepe fieri solet, in adspirationem converso. Doribus Ἅλιος, nota Dialecto: quamquam Plato in Cratylo sic Solem huic genti dictum scribat, ἀπὸ τῆς ἀλίζειν, quod exoriens in unum homines congreget. Hebraeis חמה à calore, Hijob. cap.xxx. 28.
units.tr: In Greek, Ἥλιος comes from always turning [ἀεὶ ἑλᾶν], from its continual circling; for it is turned round perpetually in a motion by which it traverses the zodiac in 365 days and six hours. Or it comes from without brightness [ἀλαμπῆς], as some want, from its splendour, with the σ changed into the breathing, as often happens. The Dorians say Ἅλιος, in their own dialect; although Plato, in the Cratylus, writes that the Sun is so called by this people from gathering together [ἀλίζειν], because at its rising it brings men together into one place. The Hebrews call it חמה, from heat: Job cap. xxx. 28.

units.la: Solem Lampadem esse ardentem vel candens saxum, ausus olim dicere Anaxagoras, ut & Euripides eum secutus in Phaethonte Tragoedia, Glebam auream; quemadmodum refert Sotion in Successionibus: quam ob causam ille reus factus, & ab Cleone impietatis accusatus, defensusque à Pericle discipulo, talentis quinque & exilio fuit ab Atheniensibus multatus. Sic Democritus & Metrodorus Solem Ferrum ignitum voluerunt; Xenophanes Nubem igneam; sunt & qui Rotam accensam; una in parte apertam, & inde flammas vomentem: narrantibus Diogene Laertio in Philosoph. Viris, Augustino lib. xviii. de Civit. Dei, cap. xi. Theodoreto lib. iv. contra Graec. adfect. Ioanne Stobaeo in ἐκλογ. φυσικ. & aliis. Posidonius lib. xvi, Coelest. apud eundem Laertium in Zenone Cittico, Solem ait purissimum esse Ignem; quod omnia Ignis peragat munera. Parmenides, eodem scribente, putat Solem, Calidum esse ac Frigidum; ex quorum commistione constat quidquid in rerum natura. Calorem sane Soli tribuit non uno loco Sacra Scriptura, ut videre est Psalmo xix, 7. Ecclesiastici cap. xliii verf. 7. & alibi. Calidus proprie Sol ab Effectis. Nam, quamvis per se non calidus (quod alij probant validis argumentis) calefacit tamen, vel per motum, quo ipse concutit, atterit, attenuat aerem, ut innuit Aristoteles lib. Meteor. & lib. ii. de Coelo text. 42; vel, quemadmodum solidius volunt alij, sua luce (ut & reliqua Astra) quae quanto copiosior in Sole, quam in ceteris, tanto potentior illis Sol est ad calefaciendum. Obiter adscribo, qui Lampadem, Saxum, Ferrum ignitum Solem statuerunt, causam dedisse nonnullis fabulandi, eumdem, quum Oceano se mergit (nam & hoc scriptis mandant) strepitum edere & exstingui: quae opinio veterum fuit Hispanorum, ut docent Cleomedes lib. ii. & Posidonius apud Strabonem libro ii. Cosmograph, à quibus derivata ad alios, praesertim Poetas Latinos, qui de Solis se mergentis stridore multa.
units.tr: Anaxagoras once dared to say that the Sun is a burning lamp or glowing stone, and Euripides, following him in his tragedy Phaethon, called it a golden clod; as Sotion reports in his Successions. For this, Anaxagoras was made a defendant and accused of impiety by Cleon; he was defended by Pericles, his pupil, but was fined five talents by the Athenians and sent into exile. So Democritus and Metrodorus wanted the Sun to be red-hot iron; Xenophanes, a fiery cloud; and some, a kindled wheel, open in one part, and from there belching flames. This is reported by Diogenes Laertius in his Lives of the Philosophers, by Augustine in Book 18 of The City of God, ch. 11, by Theodoret in Book 4 of the Cure for Greek Maladies, by John Stobaeus in his Eclogues of Natural Things, and by others. Posidonius, Book 16 of the Celestial Matters, as reported by the same Laertius in his life of Zeno of Citium, says that the Sun is the purest fire, because fire performs all the functions of the Sun. Parmenides, according to the same writer, thinks the Sun is both hot and cold, and from the mixture of these everything in nature comes to be. Sacred Scripture, in more than one place, certainly attributes heat to the Sun, as can be seen in Psalm 19:7, Ecclesiasticus 43:7, and elsewhere. The Sun is called hot properly from its effects. For although it is not hot in itself (which others prove by strong arguments), it nevertheless warms, either through the motion by which it shakes, wears down and thins the air, as Aristotle hints in the Meteorology and in Book 2 of On the Heavens, text 42; or, as others hold with more solidity, by its own light (as also the other stars do). This light is more abundant in the Sun than in the other stars, and so the Sun is more powerful than they are in warming. I add in passing that those who held the Sun to be a lamp, a stone or red-hot iron gave some occasion to fables, namely that the same Sun, when it sinks into the Ocean (for they also commit this to writing), makes a hissing noise and is extinguished. This was the opinion of the ancient Spaniards, as Cleomedes in Book 2 and Posidonius, quoted by Strabo in Book 2 of the Geography, teach. From them it passed to others, especially to the Latin poets, who wrote much about the hissing of the setting Sun.

units.la: Solem ait Plinius lib. ii. nat. histor. cap. vi. Lumen non modo Lunae (de qua mox) sed & caeteris Sideribus faeneravi: similem enim Astris omnibus esse naturam: manifestum autem Lunae Lumen esse ab Sole; ideoque existimandum reliquas etiam Stellas inde Lumen accipere. Hugo item ad Genesin notat, soli Soli, ex Igne creato, propriam esse Lucem; ceteras Stellas ex aeria factas materia relucere potius quam lucere. Solem denique fontem esse omnis Lucis coelestis, omniaque Astra Lucem, quam habent, omnem illi ferre acceptam, visum Heraclito, Lucretio, Avicennae, Alberto Magno, Bedae, aliisque Astrologis & Theologis. Sed dicendum non esse parem Lunae caeterorumque Siderum rationem; neque vero simile, immensam illam coelestium Ignium, qui in octava sphaera, reliquarum nobilissima, mirabili pulcritudine lucent, Chorcam ab Sole suum Lumen mutuari. Augustinus lib. ii. de Genesi ad litteram, cap. xvi, ex Epistolae prioris ad Corinthios cap. xv. manifesto constare scribit, disparem esse Siderum claritatem; & Astra, quibus diuersiores vires & effectus, dissimilem etiam obtinere Lucis rationem. Stellas censendum lucere Lumine cum proprio, quod congenitum illis, Luce Solis imbecillius; tum alieno, quod ab Sole accipiunt Radiorum reflexione; sed dissimiliter, ut aliæ aliis magis sunt ὁμοιομερεῖς. Leucippus apud Laertium, contrariam superioribus ingressus viam, existimat Solem ab Sideribus, non ab Sole Sidera inflammari.
units.tr: The Sun, says Pliny in Book 2, ch. 6 of the Natural History: "I have lent my light not only to the Moon (of which I shall speak shortly), but also to the other stars." For the nature of all the stars is similar; and it is manifest that the light of the Moon comes from the Sun, so one must think that the remaining stars also receive their light from it. Hugo likewise notes on Genesis that the Sun alone has its own light, since it was created from fire, while the other stars, made of aerial matter, shine back rather than shine of themselves. Finally, the Sun is the fount of all heavenly light, and all the stars bring to us whatever light they have, received entirely from it. This seemed so to Heraclitus, Lucretius, Avicenna, Albertus Magnus, Bede, and other astronomers and theologians. But it must be said that the reason for the Moon and the other stars is not the same. Nor is it likely that that immense host of heavenly fires, which shine with wonderful beauty in the eighth sphere, the noblest of all, borrows its light from the Sun. Augustine, in Book 2 of On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, ch. 16, writes, from 1 Corinthians 15, that it is manifest that the brightness of the stars differs; and stars, which have diverse powers and effects, also have a dissimilar kind of light. The stars must be judged to shine partly with a light of their own, which is innate to them and weaker than the light of the Sun, and partly with a borrowed light, which they receive from the Sun by reflection of its rays; but in different measure, as some stars are more or less homogeneous [ὁμοιομερεῖς] than others. Leucippus, as reported by Laertius, taking the opposite road to the above, thinks that the Sun is kindled by the stars, and not the stars by the Sun.

units.la: Philostratus refert Gymnosophistas Solem pro summo Deo coluisse. Pythagoras eumdem ut & Lunam reliquaque Sidera, Deorum adscripsit numero; quum in iis superet Calor, qui vitæ auctor. Martialis lib. xii: Martis alumna dies, roscam quo lampada primum Magnaque sidera vidimus ora Dei.
units.tr: Philostratus reports that the Gymnosophists worshipped the Sun as the supreme God. Pythagoras counted him among the gods, together with the Moon and the other stars, since in them heat, the author of life, prevails. Martial, Book 12: "Day, nursling of Mars, when first we saw the dewy lamp and the great stars in the face of God."

units.la: Antiquum marmor:
units.tr: An ancient marble inscription:

units.la: DEO SOLI INVICTO P. POMPONIVS CLITVS EX VOTO
units.tr: To the unconquered God the Sun, P. Pomponius Clitus, in fulfilment of a vow

units.la: Hinc Dorylao apud Censorinum de die Natali, cap. xiii. Organum Dei, Mundus; ipsi Censorino Annus Dei, Solaris. Hinc quoque Dei propria, Soli tributa; Omnia Videre & Audire. Homerus Iliad. γ: Ἡ ἀλιος δ' ὃς πάντ' ἐφορᾷς, καὶ πάντ' ἐπακούεις.
units.tr: Hence Dorylaus, in Censorinus, On the Birthday, ch. 13, calls the world the instrument of God, and Censorinus himself calls the solar year the year of God. Hence also the attributes proper to God are given to the Sun: to see and to hear all things. Homer, Iliad 3: "The Sun, who sees all things and hears all things" [Ἡ ἀλιος δ' ὃς πάντ' ἐφορᾷς, καὶ πάντ' ἐπακούεις].

units.la: Iovis Oculum vocat Hesiodus; Pisidas; Τὸ χθονὸς ὄμμα, ἀλλ' ἀκτινοβολέων κόσμω. Fuerunt olim (ut ex Veterum patet monimentis, sacrisque litteris, Deuteron. iv. & Sapient. xiii.) suntque hodie, qui Solem, tamquam Deum, cultu & veneratione dignantur. Neque mirum. Quid enim humanis oculis adspici potest inter quae creata pulcrius? adeo ut in eo tabernaculum suum posuisse Deum canat Rex Propheta Psalmo xix, 6; addens de Sole: Et ipse tanquam Sponsus procedens thalamo suo: Exultavit ut Gigas ad currendam viam; à summo Caelo egressio ejus: Et occursus ejus usque ad summum ejus; nec est qui se abscondat à Calore ejus.
units.tr: Hesiod calls the Sun the eye of Jove; Pisidas calls it "the eye of the earth, shining with rays on the world" [Τὸ χθονὸς ὄμμα, ἀλλ' ἀκτινοβολέων κόσμω]. As the ancient monuments and the sacred letters show (Deut. 4 and Wisdom 13), there were once, and there still are, people who honour and revere the Sun as a god. Nor is this surprising. For what among created things can be seen by human eyes that is more beautiful? So much so that the Prophet King sings in Psalm 19:6 that God set his tabernacle in it, adding of the Sun: And he, like a bridegroom coming out of his chamber, rejoices like a giant to run his course. His going forth is from the end of heaven, and his circuit to the end of it; and there is nothing hidden from his heat.

units.la: Iam si quis penitius examinet, quanta Soli vis in terrena; qui potest, ut non, in summam divinissimæ Creaturæ rapiatur admirationem? Odorum, Saporum, Colorum, Calorumque, qui in fructibus, Varietates; Animalium quantitates qualitatesque; omnium Rerum Formas; diversas Terrenorum species, aliaque id genus infinita, Solis caliditate fieri certum est; adfirmantibus cum aliis, tum Diodoro Siculo lib. iii. rerum antiquarum cap. xii. & Plinio lib. xxxiv. nat. hist. cap. xiv. Homines nimia Solis vicinitate siccati, scribente Vegetio lib. i. de re militari, cap. ii. Sanguinis indigentes; Vulnera valde solent metuere: qui ab eiusdem ardoribus remotiores, sanguinis abundantia fretos nimis videmus in vulnera ferrumque præcipites. Lucanus de Orientalibus: Quidquid ad Eoos tractus mundique teporum Labitur, emollit gentes clementia Caeli. Illic & laxas vestes & fluxa virorum Velamenta vides.
units.tr: If anyone examines more closely how great the Sun's power is over earthly things, how can he not be carried away into the highest admiration of this most divine creature? That the variety of odours, flavours and colours, and of heat too, in fruits; the size and qualities of animals; the forms of all things; the diverse kinds of earthly things, and other countless things of this sort, are produced by the Sun's warmth is certain. Both others and Diodorus Siculo (Library of History, bk 3, ch. 12) and Pliny (Natural History, bk 34, ch. 14) affirm this. Men dried up by excessive nearness to the Sun, as Vegetius writes (On Military Affairs, bk 1, ch. 2), need blood and are very afraid of wounds; while we see that those who are further from its heats, relying too much on abundance of blood, rush headlong into wounds and the sword. Lucan says of the peoples of the East: "Whatever lies along the tracts of the Dawn and the warm regions of the world, the gentle sky softens its peoples. There you see loose garments and flowing veils on men."

units.la: Et de Septemtrionalibus: Populi, quos despicit Arctos, Felices errore suo: quos ille timorum Maximus haud urget leti metus: inde ruendi In ferrum mens prona viris, animaque capaces Mortis, & ignavum est reditura parcere vitae.
units.tr: And of the peoples of the North: "The peoples whom the Bear looks down upon are happy in their error; the greatest fear of dying does not press upon them. Hence their minds are prone to rush upon the sword, and their spirits are ready for death, and they think it cowardly to spare a life that will return."

units.la: De Solis Magnitudine variæ leguntur apud Plutarchum lib. xi. de Placit. Philosoph. cap. xxi. Macrobium lib. i. in Somnium Scipion. cap. xx, Diogenem Laertium, & alios, Philosophorum sententiæ. Heraclitus Ephesius & Epicurus tantum ajunt Solem, quantus apparet: pedalem tribuentes latitudinem. Anaxagoras majorem censuit Peloponneso. Anaximander Solis corpus æquale fecit Terræ; Orbem vero, in quo circumvehitur, septies vicies Terra maiorem; quod de ipso Sole notat Eratosthenes. Secundum Ptolemæum Sol major est Terra centies sexagies septies cum tribus octavis: cujus sententiam plerique sequuntur & varie stabiliunt Mathematici. Copernicus superioribus annis minorem deprehendit; ejusque corpus Terram superare centies sexagies bis, octava minus. Posidonius, nihil ausus certi, Terram dicit multo multoque sæpius multiplicatam Solis spacium efficere. Certe quantus sit Sol, quantaque illi Lucis copia, si alia deessent argumenta, paret inde, quod solus præsentia sua clarissimum faciat diem, omnibus nocturnis tenebris discussis penitus & sublatis; quod ne omnium quidem Astrorum simul præsentium lux conjuncta præstare potest: Sole etiam præsentia sua reliquorum Siderum præstinguente & occultante claritatem. Non minus elegantes quam pie Ambrosius lib. iv. ἑξαημ. cap. vi. Sivè, inquit, magnitudinem Solis non solum oculo mentis, sed etiam corporis æstimare; consydera quanti Stellarum globi Axem Cæli videantur obtexere, & innumeris insignire luminibus: non queunt tamen tenebras noctis & Cæli nubila detergere. Simul ut Solortus sui signa præmiserit, omnes Stellarum Ignes sub unius Luminaris fulgore evanescunt: aperitur Aer, Cœlique facies purpurascente rubore perfunditur. Adhuc spirans exordium, & jam momentanea celeritate pleni luminis micat; & surgentis Solis prævia aura dulcis adspirat. Similis Sol & Indis & Britannis eodem momento videtur, quum oritur: nec, quum vergit in occasum, minor adparet Orientalibus, quam Occidentalibus; nec Occidentalibus, quum oritur, inferior, quam Orientalibus æstimatur. Neque te moveat, quod tibi tanquam Orbis cubitalis videatur Solis, quum oritur: sed consydera, quantum interfit spacij inter Solem & Terras, quod adspectus nostri infirmitas sine magno sui transfire non potest dispendio. Merito igitur exclamavit Ecclesiasticus cap. xvii, 30. Quid lucidius Sole? Videndus etiam huc Dionysius libro de Divinis Nominibus. cap. 1. part. iv.
units.tr: Various opinions of the philosophers on the Sun's size are found in Plutarch (On the Opinions of the Philosophers, bk 2, ch. 21), Macrobius (Commentary on the Dream of Scipio, bk 1, ch. 20), Diogenes Laertius, and others. Heraclitus of Ephesus and Epicurus say only that the Sun is as large as it appears, ascribing to it a breadth of one foot. Anaxagoras judged it larger than the Peloponnese. Anaximander made the body of the Sun equal to the Earth, but the orbit in which it revolves twenty-seven times larger than the Earth; Eratosthenes notes this of the Sun itself. According to Ptolemy the Sun is 167 times the size of the Earth, with three-eighths added; most mathematicians follow this view and variously confirm it. In recent years Copernicus found it smaller, and its body to exceed the Earth 162 times less one-eighth. Posidonius, daring to affirm nothing certain, says that the Earth multiplied many and many times over would make up the space of the Sun. Certainly, how large the Sun is, and how great its supply of light, even if no other arguments were available, is clear from this: by its presence alone it makes the day most bright, dispelling and wholly removing all the darkness of night, which the combined light of all the stars present together cannot achieve, since the Sun by its presence also extinguishes and hides the brightness of the other stars. Ambrose, no less elegant than pious, in Hexaemeron bk 4, ch. 6, says: Or consider the size of the Sun not only with the eye of the mind but also with the eye of the body. Consider how large the globes of the stars appear to cover the axis of heaven and to adorn it with innumerable lights; yet they cannot dispel the darkness of night and the clouds of the sky. As soon as the Sun has sent forth the signs of its rising, all the fires of the stars vanish beneath the brilliance of the one luminary. The air is opened, and the face of the heavens is suffused with a purple blush. While it is still beginning to breathe, and already with momentary swiftness it glitters with full light, and a sweet breeze breathes before the rising Sun. The Sun appears alike to the Indians and to the Britons at the same moment when it rises; nor, when it sinks towards setting, does it appear smaller to the Easterners than to the Westerners; nor is it judged inferior to the Westerners when it rises, compared with the Easterners. And do not be troubled that the Sun seems to you as large as a cubit's circle when it rises; but consider how great is the space between the Sun and the Earth, which the weakness of our sight cannot cross without great loss. Rightly, therefore, Ecclesiasticus 17:30 exclaimed: What is brighter than the Sun? Dionysius, On the Divine Names, ch. 1, part 4, should also be consulted here.

units.la: Sphæræ Solis Ἀπόγειον, Ptolemæi tempore, distabat à Terra mille ducentis & decem Semidiametris; Περίγειον, mille centum viginti duabus fere: hodie mutata κεντρότητα, διπλάσιον distare deprehendunt Astronomi Semidiametris mille centum septuaginta novem. Plura hac de Plinius lib. ii. nat. hist. cap. xxi, Ptolemæus lib. v. Vitellio libr. x. Opticcs, & alij.
units.tr: In Ptolemy's time the apogee [Ἀπόγειον] of the Sun's sphere was 1,210 semidiameters from the Earth, and the perigee [Περίγειον] about 1,122. Today astronomers find that the eccentricity [κεντρότητα] has changed and that the distance is twice [διπλάσιον] 1,179 semidiameters. Pliny (Natural History, bk 2, ch. 21), Ptolemy (bk 5), Vitellio (Optics, bk 10), and others say more on this.

units.la: Maxima hodie Solis obliquitas seu declinatio xxiii. graduum, xxviii. scrupulorum. Aristarchus Samius, annis ante Ptolemæum quadringentis, deprehendit eam xxiii graduum li scrupulorum, xx. secundorum; quantam & invenisse se notat Ptolemæus. Mahometes Aratensis, anno post Ptolemæum mccxliv, graduum indicat xxiii, scrupulorum xxxv. Arzahel Hispanus cxc. annis post Albategnium, xxiii graduum, xxxiv scrupulorum. Prophatius Iudæus, ccxxx post Arzahelem anno, xxxiii graduum, xxxii scrupulorum. Dominicus Maria anno nati Redemtoris cio cccxci, graduum xxiii, scrupulorum xxix. Wernerus anno Christi cio io xiv, graduum xxiii, scrupulorum xxviii, secundorum xxx. Copernicus tandem non ita pridem maximam Solis Declinationem reperit graduum xxiii, scrupulorum xxviii, & duarum quintarum unius scrupuli. Quæ docent sensim decreuisse regulari motu æqualitatem; & decreturam adhuc, donec adsequatur extremum diminutionis terminum, quem Copernicus ponit xxiii graduum, xxviii scrupulorum: colligens post rursus accreturam; statuensque maximam, quæ fieri potest, Solis obliquitatem xxiii graduum, li scrupulorum minimam xxiii graduum, xxviii scrupulorum; differentiam denique maximæ & minimæ xxiv. scrupulorum.
units.tr: The greatest obliquity or declination of the Sun today is 23 degrees 28 minutes. Aristarchus of Samos, four hundred years before Ptolemy, found it to be 23 degrees 51 minutes 20 seconds; Ptolemy notes that he himself found the same. Mahomet of Aratensis, in the year 1244 after Ptolemy, gives 23 degrees 35 minutes. Arzahel the Spaniard, 190 years after Albategnius, gives 23 degrees 34 minutes. Prophatius the Jew, in the year 230 after Arzahel, gives 23 degrees 32 minutes. Dominicus Maria, in the year 1391 after the birth of the Redeemer, gives 23 degrees 29 minutes. Werner, in the year of Christ 1514, gives 23 degrees 28 minutes 30 seconds. Copernicus, not long ago, found the greatest declination of the Sun to be 23 degrees 28 minutes and two-fifths of a minute. These findings show that by a regular motion it has gradually decreased in equal steps, and that it will decrease still further until it reaches the extreme limit of diminution, which Copernicus puts at 23 degrees 28 minutes.
