Inferring that it will afterwards increase again, he sets the greatest possible obliquity of the Sun at 23 degrees 51 minutes, the least at 23 degrees 28 minutes, and so the difference between greatest and least at 23 minutes.

units.la: Iter autem Soli in Ecliptica; quæ, ἡλιακὸς κύκλος Græcis dicta, Ptolemæo κύκλος ΔΙΑ μεσῶν τῶν ζῳδίων, nihil aliud, quam circulus major in medio consistens Zodiaci, eumque κατὰ πλάτος in duos dirimens æquales ambitus; sex olim, hodie octo graduum spacio distinctos: quem Sol in uno perpetuo tramite oblique incedens efformat.
units.tr: The path of the Sun in the ecliptic, called by the Greeks [ἡλιακὸς κύκλος] the solar circle, and by Ptolemy [κύκλος ΔΙΑ μεσῶν τῶν ζῳδίων] the circle through the middle of the signs of the zodiac, is nothing other than a great circle lying in the middle of the zodiac, dividing it [κατὰ πλάτος] into two equal circuits, distinguished by a space of six degrees formerly, and eight today. The Sun, moving obliquely along one perpetual track, forms this circle.

units.la: Solis Defectus (ne de hoc etiam nihil dicam) alius verus & naturalis, alius prodigiosus. Verus, qui voce propria Eclipsis, est non privatio Lucis (Sol enim, Lux pulcerrima, Lucem perpetuo subministrans, numquam Lucis patitur detrimentum) sed exclusio tantum vel aversio radiorum Solis, quam facit Lunæ soliditas & densitas; collocata enim inter Solem & visum nostrum in conjunctione radios, quos dixi, spargi prohibet, & in quasdam Terræ partes pertingere. Contingit, quando Luna Soli conjungitur circa Novilunium. Investigasse primus & prædixisse perhibetur Thales Milesius, docentibus M. Tullio libro 1. de Divinat. Plinio lib. ii. nat. hist. Augustino libro de Civit. Dei vIII, cap. ii. & Eusebio. Palamedes etiam Eclipsin, Castris Græcorum formidabilem, primus naturalem esse scribitur docuisse. Imperita enim multitudo anteaquam à Philosophis Solis Lunæque Defectuum ostensa essent esset ratio, videns præstantissima Sidera deficere & quasi languore dissolvi, lugere tristiaque suo luctu portendere putabat. Propertius lib. iii. Eleg. iv, 56.
units.tr: Eclipses of the Sun (not to say nothing of this too) are of two kinds: one true and natural, the other portentous. The true eclipse, which is properly called an eclipse, is not a privation of light (for the Sun, the most beautiful light, supplying light perpetually, never suffers any loss of light), but only the exclusion or deflection of the Sun's rays, which the solidity and density of the Moon bring about; for when the Moon is placed between the Sun and our sight at conjunction, it prevents the rays I have mentioned from spreading and reaching certain parts of the Earth. It happens when the Moon is conjoined with the Sun near the new moon. Thales of Miletus is said to have first investigated and predicted it, as Cicero (On Divination, bk 1), Pliny (Natural History, bk 2), Augustine (City of God, bk 8, ch. 2) and Eusebius teach. Palamedes too is written to have been the first to teach that an eclipse, which was dreaded in the camp of the Greeks, is natural. For the unskilled crowd, before the reason for the eclipses of the Sun and Moon had been shown by the philosophers, seeing the most excellent stars fail and as it were dissolve in faintness, thought they were mourning and foretelling sorrows with their grief. Propertius, bk 3, Elegy 4, line 56.

units.la: Aut quare Perrhæbi tremuere cacumina Pindi, Solis & atratis luxerit orbis equis.
units.tr: Or why the peaks of Pindus in Perrhaebia trembled, and the orb of the Sun grew dim with its black-clad horses.

units.la: Augustinus lib. iii. de Civit. Dei cap. xv. Quasi vero, si luctus ille Solis fuisset, non magis ideo credi deberet occisus, ipsumque scelus averisime etiam diurni luminis indicatum. Excusent arcana sic opinantes συμπάθεια, quæ cœlestibus creaturis solet esse cum homine rebusque humanis: alioquin absurdum, Luctum Soli alisque in Cælo non rationalibus tale quid adfingere. Prodigiosus & ἀναλογῶ. Defectus is, qui à vaporibus & nebulis fit adeo spissis, ut visus intercipiatur, Solisque lumen appareat admodum debile. Talis accidit continuo totius pene anni pallore, quo Iulius Cæsar Dictator occisus, ut testatur Plinius lib. ii. cap. xxx. De eo Virgilius lib. i. Georgic.
units.tr: Augustine, De Civitate Dei, book 3, chapter 15: "As if, indeed, if that mourning had been the Sun's, the murder would not rather be believed on that account, and that most wicked deed would have been revealed even by the light of day." Those who hold such opinions may excuse their hidden sympathy [συμπάθεια], which heavenly creatures usually have with man and human affairs; otherwise it would be absurd to attribute such grief to the Sun and other non-rational bodies in heaven. It is a prodigy and an analogy [ἀναλογία]. The eclipse which comes from vapours and mists so thick that the sight is cut off, and the light of the Sun appears very weak, is such as happened with the almost year-long pallor in which Julius Caesar, the Dictator, was killed, as Pliny attests in book 2, chapter 30. Virgil speaks of this in Georgics book 1:

units.la: Sed tibi Signa dabit, Solem quis dicere falsum Audeat? Ille etiam cæcos instare tumultus Sæpe monet, fraudemque & operta tumescere bella. Ille etiam exsintio miseratus Cæsare Romam, Quum caput obscura nitidum ferrugine texit: Impiaque æternam timuerunt sæcula noctem,
units.tr: "But will he give you signs? Who would dare to call the Sun false? He often warns of hidden tumults, of treachery and of wars swelling up beneath the surface. He too, pitying Rome after Caesar's death, covered his shining head with dark rust; and impious ages feared an eternal night."

units.la: Ovidius lib. xv. Metamorph.
units.tr: Ovid, Metamorphoses book 15.

units.la: ——— Solis quoque tristis imago Lurida sollicitis præbebat lumina terris.
units.tr: "The sad image of the Sun too offered pale light to the anxious lands."

units.la: Tibullus lib. ii. Eleg. iii.
units.tr: Tibullus, Elegies book 2, elegy 3.

units.la: Ipsum etiam Solem defectum lumine vidit, Iungere pallentes nubibus annus equos.
units.tr: "He also saw the Sun himself deprived of light, the year yoking its pale horses to the clouds."

units.la: Nullam enim Solis defectionem, qualem Servius Virgilii interpres & reliquum Scriptorum vulgus opinatur, in nostro hemisphærio vitam anno, quo Cæsar crudeliter obtruncatus, docet calculus Astronomicus & subtilissime retro computata motuum cœlestium ratio. Talem item dicere liceat, qui contigit pendente ab arbore Crucis Christo. Nam eo tempore Sol contra naturam Lucem amisit, in medio Cœli, haud procul à capite Draconis; quum Plenilunium esset, quo Sol naturaliter deficere non poterat. Luna etiam quum, nisi ab Sole inluminetur, lucere nequeat, deficiente Sole, eodem hoc tempore in imo Cœli apud Antipodas lucem amisit, juxta caudam Draconis. Saturnus denique emergens supra horizontem adspectu quadrato malefico utrumque defectum & Solis & Lunæ adspexit. Terribilis igitur fuit tunc temporis Cœli facies. Ad prodigiosos huiusmodi Solis defectus pertinent non pauca Sacræ Scripturæ loca, quibus tales Cœlestium Corporum mœrores, ut ita dicam, & μεταφυσικῶς obfuscationes ad vivum delineantur, ut videre est apud Isaiam cap. xiii, 10. Ezech. xxxiii, 7, 8. Ioel. ii, 10, iii, 15. & alibi.
units.tr: For there was no eclipse of the Sun of the kind that Servius, Virgil's interpreter, and the rest of the common run of writers suppose in our hemisphere in the year when Caesar was cruelly cut down; the astronomical calculation and the most subtle retrospective reckoning of the heavenly motions show this. Likewise, it may be said of the one that occurred when Christ hung from the tree of the Cross. For at that time the Sun, contrary to nature, lost its light in mid-heaven, not far from the head of the Dragon, when it was full moon, at which time the Sun could not naturally be eclipsed. The Moon too, which cannot shine unless it is illuminated by the Sun, lost its light at the same time, when the Sun was eclipsed, at the lowest point of heaven among the Antipodes, near the tail of the Dragon. Finally, Saturn, rising above the horizon in a malefic square aspect, looked upon both the eclipse of the Sun and that of the Moon. The face of heaven was therefore then terrible. To such prodigious eclipses of the Sun pertain not a few passages of Holy Scripture, in which such sorrows of the heavenly bodies, so to speak, and obscurations in a metaphysical sense, are depicted to the life, as may be seen in Isaiah 13:10, Ezekiel 32:7, 8, Joel 2:10, 3:15, and elsewhere.

units.la: Fabulis de Solis Curru quatuorque Equis, quæ apud Ovidium, Tertullianum Cassiodorum, aliosque, Lectorem non morabor. Isidori, qui bonorum auctorum excerptor multa nonnunquam paucis complectitur, verba adponam ex lib. xvii r., Originum: Quadrigas Soli, Bigas Lunæ, Trigas Inferis, Sequigas Iovi, Desultores Lucifero & Hespero sacravernt; ubi mox singulorum causam exsequitur.
units.tr: I shall not detain the reader with the fables about the Chariot of the Sun and its four horses, which are found in Ovid, Tertullian, Cassiodorus, and others. I shall set down the words of Isidore, who as an excerptor of good authors often embraces much in few words, from Origines book 17: "They consecrated the four-horse chariot to the Sun, the two-horse to the Moon, the three-horse to the Underworld, the six-horse to Jupiter, and the leaping riders to Lucifer and Hesperus"; where he soon goes on to explain the reason for each.

units.la: Sol Sirii appellatione videtur exaudiendus apud Virgilium, quum inquit lib. iv. Georgic.
units.tr: The Sun is apparently to be understood under the name Sirius in Virgil, when in Georgics book 4 he says:

units.la: Iam rapidus torrens sitientes Sirius Indos Ardebat cælo.
units.tr: "Now the rapid Sirius, scorching the thirsty Indians, blazed in the sky."

units.la: Scribit etiam Sudas Σείριος à multis exponi τὸν ἥλιον, id est Sirium Solem.
units.tr: Suidas also writes that Seirios is explained by many as ὁ ἥλιος, that is, "the Sun Sirius."

units.la: Solis nota ʘ, quid velit, vident etiam pueri.
units.tr: What the symbol of the Sun ʘ means, even boys see.

units.la: Finiam, ἀναχιφαλαιωμένω quæ hactenus de pulcerrimo hoc Astro, in verbis Plinij, petitis ex lib. ii. nat. histor. cap. vi. Hunc Mundi esse totius Animum, ac planius mentem, hunc principale Naturæ regimen ac Numen credere decet, opera ejus æstimantes. Hic lucem reliquis ministrat, aufertque tenebras; hic reliqua Sidera occultat; hic vices temporum Annumque semper renascentem ex usu natura temperat; hic cœli tristitiam discutit, atque etiam humani nubila animi serenat; hic suum lumen ceteris quoque Sideribus fœnerat: præclarus, eximius, omnia intuens, omnia etiam exaudiens; ut principi literarum Homero placuisse in uno eo video.
units.tr: I shall finish, summing up what has so far been said about this most beautiful star, in the words of Pliny, taken from Natural History book 2, chapter 6: "It is fitting to believe that this is the soul and, more plainly, the mind of the whole world, this the principal governance and divinity of Nature, judging by its works. It supplies light to the others and takes away darkness; it hides the other stars; it regulates by its course the changes of the seasons and the year, ever renewed; it dispels the gloom of the sky and even clears the clouds of the human mind; it lends its own light to the other stars as well: illustrious, outstanding, seeing all things, hearing all things too; so that I see it pleased Homer, the prince of letters, in this one thing alone."

units.la: Cap. XXVI.
units.tr: Cap. XXVI.

units.la: De Venere & Mercurio.
units.tr: De Venere & Mercurio.

units.la: HÆc de Sole: sequuntur Venus & Mercurius: σωσφοροι, ἑωσφοροι, vel ὁμεδρομοι τῷ ἡλίῳ, ut Plato appellat: quorum peculiaris ratio est, neque communis cum supradictis, inquit Plinius lib. ii. nat. histor. cap. viii. pluribus id confirmans cap. xvii. Quum enim tres superiores Planetæ & Luna, ab Sole discedentes, nonnumquam per Quadratum vel per Trigonum distent; aliquando ex Adverso cernantur: Veneri Mercurioque certæ sunt metæ, quas ultra ab Sole non excurrunt. Nam Venus (cui, quam Mercurio, proprior cum Sole perhibetur copulatio: habet enim, ut alia taceam, unum idemque cum eo ⸀ tamquam blanda œconoma citra quinquagesimum; Mercurius, qui Cancellarij instar in politica Cœli administratione, citra gradum tricesimum semper Solem comitantur: perpetuoque circaeum versantes, nunc accedunt tamquam mandata accepturi; nunc rursus excurrunt, quasi speculandi gratia vias exploratum emissi; mox, ne longius ab rege evagentur ad Solem, quasi revocati, recto cursu revertuntur. Idem Planetæ, quemadmodum exactissimi notant Mathematici, in eo Solem, ceu regem suum, observant, quod quoties illi conjunguntur, semper in ⸀ vel ⸀ sui Epicycli reperiantur: suaque latitudines ita alternent, ut ab diversis regi suo lateribus adsistant & ministrent. Nam ubi vel inclinatione vel reflexione sua Venus versus Septemtrionem evagatur; ibi Mercurius ijsdem latitudinum differentijs in contrariam discedit plagam, Austrum versus; & econtra, permutatis semper vicibus.
units.tr: So much for the Sun. There follow Venus and Mercury, saviours of light (σωσφοροι), bringers of light (ἑωσφοροι), or companions of the sun (ὁμεδρομοι τῷ ἡλίῳ), as Plato calls them. Their peculiar nature is neither shared with the planets named above, says Pliny in book 2 of the Natural History, chapter 8, confirming it at greater length in chapter 17. For while the three superior planets and the Moon, as they depart from the Sun, sometimes stand at a square or a trine to it, and sometimes are seen opposite it, Venus and Mercury have fixed limits beyond which they never run from the Sun. Venus, who is said to be joined to the Sun more closely than Mercury (for she has, to pass over other things, the same ... as a gentle steward, never beyond fifty degrees), and Mercury, who in the political government of the heavens is like a chancellor, always attend the Sun within thirty degrees. Revolving constantly around it, they now draw near as if about to receive orders, now run out again, as if sent out to explore the roads for the sake of scouting, and soon, lest they wander too far from the king, they turn back on a straight course, as if recalled to the Sun. The same planets, as the most exact mathematicians observe, keep watch on the Sun as on their king in this respect: whenever they are conjoined with it, they are always found in the apex or in the epicycle of their own orbit, and they alternate their latitudes so that they stand by and serve their king from opposite sides. For when Venus wanders northward by her inclination or reflection, Mercury at the same differences of latitude departs into the opposite region, toward the south; and conversely, the roles always alternating.

units.la: Venus itaque, quintam adepta stationem, Solem annuo fere spacio, nunc antecedit, ut dixi, nunc subsequitur: quam ejus naturam primus deprehendit Pythagoras, quemadmodum indicat Plinius lib. ii. nat. histor. cap. viii. Antecedens, ut Sol alter diem maturans, docentibus Cicerone lib. ii. de natura Deorum, Varrone lib. iii. de rustica, cap. v, alijs, Φωσφόρος vel Εωσφόρος appellatur Græcis: Latinis, Lucifer; Hebræis, בֹּקֶר; Chaldæis, שפרפרא. Subsequens autem, ut prærogans lucem vicemque Lunæ reddens, Ἕσπερος Græcis, unde Latinis Vesper, & Antiquioribus, Plauto in Amphitruone aliisque. quod notant Varro lib. v. de LL. & Festus lib. ult. de verb. signif. Vesperugo. Confunduntur tamen, ut legere est apud bonos scriptores, Veneris Sidus utroque tempore Vesperi vocabulo insignitum. Horatio namque Hesperus pro Lucifero scribitur, libro Carminum ii. Od. ix. ad Valgium: Tu semper urges flebilibus modis: Mysten ademtum: nec tibi Vespero Surgente, decedunt amores, Nec rapidum fugiente Solem.
units.tr: Venus, therefore, having obtained the fifth station, now goes before the Sun, as I have said, and now follows it, at an interval of nearly a year. Pythagoras first detected this nature of hers, as Pliny indicates in book 2 of the Natural History, chapter 8. When she goes before, hastening the day like a second Sun, as Cicero in book 2 of On the Nature of the Gods, Varro in book 3 of On Rural Matters, chapter 5, and others teach, she is called Φωσφόρος or Εωσφόρος [Phōsphoros, Ōsphoros] by the Greeks; by the Latins, Lucifer; by the Hebrews, [bōqer]; by the Chaldeans, shafrafra. When she follows, however, bringing the light of the Moon and taking its place, she is called Ἕσπερος [Hesperos] by the Greeks, whence the Latin Vesper; and by the older writers, such as Plautus in the Amphitryon and others, Vesperugo, as Varro in book 5 of On the Latin Language and Festus in the last book On the Meaning of Words note. Yet, as one may read in good writers, the star of Venus is distinguished by the name Vesper at either time and so they are confused. For Horace writes Hesperus for Lucifer in book 2 of the Odes, Ode 9, to Valgius: You always urge with mournful strains the lost Mystes; nor, while Vesper rises, do your loves depart, nor when the swift Sun flees.

units.la: Ita esse scribit Lactantius Statij interpres: Lucifer & mane oritur & vesperi, equo mutato: & post pauca: Post autem quadrigas dant Soli, bigas Lunæ, Equos singulis Sideribus: eundem ergo Vesperum vult habere; ut Horatius Vesperum pro Lucifero posuit. Sic autem Plautus Noctuinus, qui idem cum Hespero, pro Lucifero capiendus: Credo ego hac noctu Nocturnum obdormisse ebrium.
units.tr: Lactantius, the commentator on Statius, writes that this is so: Lucifer both rises in the morning and in the evening, with the horse changed. And after a few words: After the quadrigas are given to the Sun and the bigas to the Moon, horses to each star; he wants the same to have Vesper, as Horace put Vesper for Lucifer. Plautus, too, Noctuinus, who must be taken as the same as Hesperus, that is, for Lucifer: I think that Nocturnus, drunk, has fallen asleep here tonight.

units.la: Continere putatur Terræ globum centies septies. Sidus tanti fulgoris, ut radiis suis reddat umbras. De claritate ejus matutina, Tiberianus apud Placiadem: Aureus subducit ignes Sydus Ora Lucifer,
units.tr: It is thought to contain a hundred and seven times the globe of the Earth. It is a star of such brightness that its rays cast shadows. On its morning brightness, Tiberianus, quoted by Placidus: Lucifer, the golden Star of the morning, draws up its fires.

units.la: De vespertina Papinius vi. Theb. Sic ubi tranquillo pellucent Sidera ponto, Vibraturque fretis Cæli stellantis imago, Omnia clara nitent: sed clarior omnia supra Hesperus exercet radios; quantumque per altum Aethera, cæruleis tantus monstratur in undis. Deutraque Seneca de morte Claudij
units.tr: On its evening brightness, Papinius in book 6 of the Thebaid: As when the stars shine through the calm sea, and the image of the starry sky quivers in the waves, all things gleam bright; but Hesperus, brighter than all, lights its rays above; and as far as it is shown through the deep aether, so far is it shown in the blue waves. And Seneca, in the Apocolocyntosis on the death of Claudius, says both things:

units.la: Qualis discutiens fugientia Lucifer astra;
units.tr: Like Lucifer, dispersing the fleeing stars;

units.la: Aut qualis surgit redeuntibus Hesperus astris.
units.tr: Or like Hesperus rising as the stars return.

units.la: Tribuunt huic Planetae quidam Currum; nonnulli Equos tantum, vespeti quidem fuscum, mane vero candidum: Tibullus lib. i. Eleg. ix, Pedo Albinavanus Elegia in Maecenatis obitum, Ovidius in Fastis. Hinc mutare dicitur equos; Statius Papinius vi. Thebaidos:
units.tr: Some assign to this planet a chariot; others only horses, dark in the evening, but white in the morning: Tibullus in book 1, Elegy 9; Pedo Albinovanus in his elegy on the death of Maecenas; Ovid in the Fasti. Hence it is said to change its horses. Statius, Papinius in book 6 of the Thebaid:

units.la: Rescida iam novies caelo demiserat astra
units.tr: Lucifer had already, for the ninth time, let down the opened stars from heaven,

units.la: Lucifer; & totidem Luna praevenerat ignes
units.tr: and the Moon had anticipated as many fires,

units.la: Mutato Nocturnus equo.
units.tr: Nocturnus, with his horse changed.

units.la: Hinc desultor esse; quod alij notarunt: hinc denique Defultatorios habere perhibetur equos. Cassiodorus lib. iii. Varior ad Faustum, de Circensibus: Biga quasi Luna Quadriga Solis imitatione reperta est. Equi defultatorij, per quos Circensium ministri missos denunciant exitus, Luciferi praecursorias velocitates imitantur. Isidorus lib. xviii. Orig. Quadrigas Soli, Bigas Lunae, Trigas Inferis, Seisugas Iovi, Desultores Luciphero & Hespero sacraverunt. Nota ♀, Speculum.
units.tr: Hence it is a desultor (a leaper between horses), as others have noted; hence, finally, it is said to have desultory horses. Cassiodorus in book 3 of the Variae, to Faustus, on the Circus games: The biga was devised on the model of the Moon, the quadriga on that of the Sun. The desultory horses, by which the attendants of the Circus announce the ending of the races when sent out, imitate the forerunning speed of Lucifer. Isidore in book 18 of the Origins: They consecrated quadrigas to the Sun, bigas to the Moon, trigas to the infernal gods, sixes to Jupiter, and desultores to Lucifer and Hesperus. Note ♀, the Mirror.

units.la: Mercurius infra venerem, Luna superior. Σὺλλᾶων Graecis apud Ciceronem, Marcianum, Apuleium. Hebraeis בכב אשף. Naturam ejus sic describit Ioannes Salisberiensis Policratici sui seu de nugis Curialium, lib. ii. cap. xix: Mercurius vero talis est, qualem vulgini Planetarum miserunt: quum & ipse convertibilis natura sit, potentioribusque cohaereat. Unde plerique eum praesulem Eloquentiae opinantur, eo quod illa iuncta Sapientiae plurimum prosit; Malitia secietata nocet plurimum. Innuit, cuicunque se conjunxerit Mercurius, cum eo vires suas communicare; & noxium fieri salutaremque, pro noxiae vel salutaris stellae adplicatione & adspectu. Hinc Communis Stella Apuleio de Mundo: Nam quum omne Caelum simplici circumactu volvatur, nocte dieque distinctum, diversis mensurarum aequalitatibus separatum, quamvis una sphaera omnia concluserit, incrementis tamen globi sui decisione, luminis menstrua tempora Luna significat, & Caeli spatium Sol annua reversione conlustrat; eiusque comites amoenus Lucifer & communis Cyllenius stella, &c Imprudeter enim genuina docti Scriptoris lectio a quibusdam ibi, tamquam falsa, solicitatur, substituta Comi stella. Hinc quod Poetis habitus Minister Deorum, notante Servio ad l. i. Georgic. quum inquit: Scendum sane, ut diximus, de Planetis quinque duos esse noxios, Martem & Saturnum: duos bonos Iovem & venerem: Mercurius vero talis est, qualis ille, cui iungitur, unde etiam fingitur minister esse Deorum, quod eorum obtemperat potestati. Hinc est quod dicit: In quos Caeli orbes erret Cyllenius ignis: id est, utrum in Septemtrionalem aut in Australem partem inclinetur; aut cui Planetarum cohaeret, ut qua tatem Mercurij exillo pos is agnoscere. Hinc denique, quod Sermonis Galeno Pergameno in Suasoria, Macrobio lib. i. Sat. cap. xix, Augustino lib. de Civit. Dei vii. cap. xiv. Horatij Commentarioribus in 1. Car. Od. x; quod Orationis, Porphyrio in Physiologia; quod Eloquentiae, veteri apud Salisberiensem Scriptoris; quod Pacis Belliquae, Ovidio v. Fastorum; quod omnium negotiorum habitus fuerit Deus, Festo lib. xi. de Verb. signif. Omnium Stellarum census minima. Anno vertente cum Sole circumagitur. Character ♀, Caduceus; de quo Servius ad iv. Aeneid. Hyginus in Lyra, Phurnutus, alij. Hinc Mercurius Ovidio Caduciferi; Arnobio libro tertio adversus gentes Caduceator. Virga dicitur Virgilio iv. Aeneid. & Horatio i. Carm. Od. x. quam torto Dracone conspicuam facit Martialis lib. vii epig. lxxii. Colubros agnoscunt alij; unde Mercurius Arnobio lib. iv. Gestator adsabilium Colubrarum. Videndus Isidorus lib. viii. Originum cap. xi, ubi elegans Mythologia.
units.tr: Mercury is below Venus, the Moon above. The Greeks call it Σὺλλᾶων [Syllaōn], as in Cicero, Martianus, and Apuleius. The Hebrews call it [בכב אשף]. John of Salisbury describes its nature thus in book 2, chapter 19 of his Policraticus, or On the Trifles of Courtiers: Mercury, indeed, is such as the common people have made him among the planets: since his own nature is changeable and clings to the more powerful. Hence most think him the patron of eloquence, because when joined to wisdom he is of great benefit; when joined to malice, he does great harm. He implies that Mercury, whatever star it joins itself to, shares its powers with it, and becomes harmful or wholesome according to the application and aspect of the harmful or wholesome star. Hence the common star in Apuleius, On the World: For though the whole heaven is turned by a single revolution, divided into night and day, separated by unequal measures of time, and though one sphere encloses all things, yet the Moon marks the monthly times of light by the waning of its globe, and the Sun illuminates the space of the heavens by its yearly return; and its companions are the pleasant Lucifer and the common star of Cyllenius, etc. For some, thinking the reading of the learned writer to be false, have unwisely altered it there, substituting Comi stella. Hence the role given to him by the poets as Minister of the Gods, as Servius notes on book 1 of the Georgics, when he says: It must certainly be understood, as we have said, that of the five planets two are harmful, Mars and Saturn, and two good, Jupiter and Venus; but Mercury is such as the one to which he is joined, whence he is also feigned to be the minister of the gods, because he obeys their power. Hence it is what he says: "Into which orbits of heaven the Cyllenian fire wanders," that is, whether it is inclined to the northern or the southern part, or to which planet it adheres, so that one may recognize Mercury's quality from that. Hence, finally, he was regarded as the god of speech (Galen of Pergamum in his Suasoria; Macrobius in book 1 of the Saturnalia, chapter 19; Augustine in book 7, chapter 14 of The City of God; the commentaries of Horace on the Odes, book 1, Ode 10); of oratory (Porphyry in the Physiology); of eloquence (an ancient writer quoted by John of Salisbury); of peace and war (Ovid in book 5 of the Fasti); and of all business (Festus in book 11 of On the Meaning of Words). The smallest census of all the stars: in the course of a year he is carried round with the Sun. The character ♀ is his caduceus, on which see Servius on Aeneid 4, Hyginus in the Lyra, Phurnutus, and others. Hence Ovid calls Mercury Caduciferus, and Arnobius in book 3 against the nations calls him Caduceator. Virgil in Aeneid 4 and Horace in Odes 1, Ode 10, call the staff a virga, which Martial in book 7, epigram 72, makes conspicuous with a twisted dragon. Others recognize serpents, whence Arnobius in book 4 calls Mercury the bearer of the lovable serpents. Isidore, Origins book 8, chapter 11, should be consulted, where there is an elegant mythology.

units.la: CAP. XXVII.
units.tr: CAP. XXVII.

units.la: De Luna.
units.tr: On the Moon.

units.la: LVNA restat explicanda, Sidus novissimum, Terrisque familiarissimum, & in tenebrarum remedium ab natura repertum; quo contemplantium oculis vicinius, eo magis eorundem multiformi sua ambage torquens ingenia: Magistra omnium, quae in Caelo pernosci potuerunt, propter Velocitatem ipsius motus unde & Ptolemæus per Lunæ locum investigavit loca Stellarum Fixarum; & rursum per hæc vera Planetarum loca; quemadmodum variis locis scribit Plinius.
units.tr: The Moon remains to be explained: the lowest of the heavenly bodies, most familiar to the Earth, and provided by nature as a remedy for darkness. The nearer she is to the eyes of those who gaze at her, the more her many-shaped appearance torments the minds of the observers. She is the teacher of all things that could be known in the heavens, because of the swiftness of her motion. For this reason Ptolemy used the Moon's position to find the positions of the fixed stars, and again, through these, the true positions of the planets, as Pliny writes in various places.

units.la: Luna, quasi lucens una; ut Sol, quod solus; aliis quod luce luceat aliena; qua de re alibi
units.tr: The Moon (Luna) is named as if it were "the one that shines" (lucens una), just as the Sun (Sol) is named because it is alone (solus). Others say it is because it shines with light borrowed from another. On this matter, see elsewhere.

units.la: De variis cognitionibus, Dianæ, Lucinæ, Proserpinæ, Hecates & similibus, dixerunt alij: sufficiat monuisse Græcis Σελήνη vel ut alij, Σελωνῖαι, quasi, σελαγονσιαι vocatam ὃτι σίλας νεόντε ἡχ ἐνωνὶ ἀέ. Nam singulis mensibus ab Sole digrediens, velut novo lumine hausto conceptoque, sensim auget, aliasque atque alias induit formas; donec Solis ex diametro obiecta orbe pleno refulgeat: inde vicissim ad Solem revertens, lumine deficiente, paullatim senescit, ac vice versa eadem figuras adquirit, donec radios Solis subiens prorsus ex oculis evanescat Hebræis appellarur יָרֵחַ, quod motu suo respirationem præbeat rebus, quæ interdiu Solis ardore inaruerant.
units.tr: Others have discussed her various names: Diana, Lucina, Proserpina, Hecate and similar ones. It is enough to note that the Greeks call her Selene, or, as others say, Selenaiai, as if from "selagonsiai," because she is the light [Σελήνη ... Σελωνῖαι ... σελαγονσιαι ... ὃτι σίλας νεόντε ἡχ ἐνωνὶ ἀέ]. For each month, as she departs from the Sun, she grows little by little, as though she had received and taken in a new light, and takes on one shape after another, until, when she is opposite the Sun on the far side of its orbit, she shines in full. Then, returning to the Sun, she loses her light and gradually grows old; and in the reverse order she takes on the same figures again, until, drawing near the Sun's rays, she vanishes entirely from our eyes. The Hebrews call her yareach [יָרֵחַ], because by her motion she gives breath to things that the Sun's heat has dried up during the day.

units.la: Lucet lumine non proprio, sed alieno, quod mutuatur à Sole: quamquam ipsa nativum quoddam habeat lumen & congenitum, sed exile & obscurum. Sententia hæc Orphei, Stoicorum & Pythagoræorum apud Laertium lib. vii. & viii; Parmenidis; ut notat Eusebius lib. iii. de Præparat. Euangelica, cap. xxxiii; Pisidæ in μηρν. & quorum non? Sic Catullus Carmine Seculari: Tu Lucina dolentibus Iuno dicta puerperis: Tu potens Trivia; & notho es Dicta lumine Luna.
units.tr: She shines not with her own light but with another's, which she borrows from the Sun, although she also has a native light of her own, which is faint and dim. This view belongs to Orpheus, the Stoics and the Pythagoreans, as reported by Laertius in books 7 and 8; to Parmenides, as Eusebius notes in book 3 of the Preparation for the Gospel, chapter 33; and to Pisides in On the Moon [μηρν.]; and who does not hold it? So Catullus in the Secular Hymn: "You, Lucina, are called Juno by women in childbirth; you are the mighty Trivia; and you are called the Moon, shining with borrowed light."

units.la: Sic Seneca Medea, Choro Actus i: Quum Phæbe solitum, lumine non suo, Orbem circuitus cornu usadigat.
units.tr: So Seneca in the Medea, in the chorus of Act 1: "When Phoebe, shining not with her own light, completes her orbit with her horn."

units.la: Addam Willerami Abbatis, à me nuper editi, illud in Cantica Canticorum de Ecclesia Christi: Stu thunket mir gelÿch therro Auroræ; Wanda fiu post tenebras infidelitatis havet sich bekeret ad verum Lumen: unde thunket mir aiso fiona, so ther Mano; Wanda fiu wole weiz thaz fiu thie pulchritudinem Virtutum von hiro selvero niet ne hatet, sunder zon Godes genashan; niet te me than ther Mano iehs lightes havet himo selvemo, secundum Physicos, noven ex inlustratione Solis. Et hæc caufla, quur, quam ceteri Sororem, Æschylus & Euripides Filiam Solis Lunam nuncuparint. Chaldæi Lunam proprij perpetuique Luminis compotem esse voluerunt, si fides Apuleio, libro de Deo Socratis. Lunam autem Lumen ab Sole per Penetrationem recipere, non per reflectionem, arbitratur Averroes: fretus cum auctoritate Avenpacis, tum ratione. Nam inquit, si posteriore modo fieret illud; totius nostri hemisphæri y universa'is non fieret in luminato: sed tanti aunta xat spaey, quanta Lunæ magnitudo. Verum ita sententi obstat, quod sic Luna semper plena viderelur lumine. Dicendum potius, partes, quæ in Lunæ ἀπ-φρέα rariores esse & puriores; eamque ob causam, quod pervia, magis ab Sole inlustrari & nitere? quæ Centri, centroque propiores, densiores esse; &, quod opacæ, lumen obtutius admittere, quum ob soliditatem densiorem penetrare Solis radij nequeant. Hinc in Luna parent intuentibus Macula: de quibus tamen varie sentiunt Philosophi, quemadmodum legere est cum apud alios, tum apud Averroem lib. ii. Cœli, Comment. xlix. & cap. ii. de subst. orbis. Sunt enim qui contingere volunt illas ex corporis inter nos & Lunam interpositione, qua plena Lunæ claritas nobis avertitur. Alij apud eundem alia. Nonnulli Campos fabulantur Elysios. Plinius lib. ii. nat. hist. cap. ix. dicit esse notas terreni humoris, ab Luna attracti. Theologorum ævo nostro quidam scribunt, indicia jam nunc esse Corruptionis Cœli, de qua non uno loco Sacra Scriptura. Verisimile autem maculas hasce, unde sint occasionem dedisse Thaleti Philosopho, sentiendi Lunam esse Terram nebula obvolutam, Anaxagoræ & Democrito Colles, Convallesque ibi somniandi; Pythagoræis, non solum Terram opinandi, sed habitari etiam ut hanc inferiorem; aliis omnia ibi, quæ apud nos inveniuntur, imaginandi. De quibus Plutarch. περὶ τῆς φιλοσ. ἀποκ. cap. xxiii. xxv. & xxx. Achilles Statius in Aratum, Ioannes Picus Comes Mirandulanus opere doctissimo & absolutissimo contra Astrologos. Et hinc Iuno apud Senecam in Hercule Furente Act. i:
units.tr: I will add a passage from the Abbot Williram, which I recently edited, on the Song of Songs, concerning the Church of Christ: It seems to me like the dawn; for she after the darkness of unbelief has turned to the true Light; and seems to me as fair as the moon; for she well knows that the beauty of her virtues does not come from herself, but from God's grace; no more than the moon has its light from itself, according to the natural philosophers, but from the illumination of the Sun. And this is the reason why Aeschylus and Euripides called the Moon the daughter of the Sun, while others called her the sister. The Chaldeans wished the Moon to possess a light that was her own and perpetual, if we trust Apuleius in his book on the God of Socrates. But Averroes holds that the Moon receives light from the Sun by penetration, not by reflection, relying both on the authority of Avempace and on reason. For, he says, if it happened in the latter way, the whole of our hemisphere would not be lit up; but there would be a dark space as large as the Moon. Yet this opinion is contradicted by the fact that the Moon would then always appear full of light. It is better to say that the parts of the Moon that are more rare and purer, and which are therefore penetrated and more brightly lit by the Sun, shine; while the parts nearer the centre are denser. Being opaque, they admit light less easily, since the denser solidity prevents the Sun's rays from penetrating. Hence spots appear in the Moon to those who look at her. Philosophers hold varied views about these, as can be read in other writers, and in Averroes, book 2 of On the Heavens, commentary 49, and chapter 2 of On the Substance of the Sphere. Some want them to be caused by the interposition of a body between us and the Moon, which takes away the full brightness of the Moon from us. Others hold other views in the same place. Some tell fables of the Elysian Fields. Pliny, book 2 of the Natural History, chapter 9, says they are marks of earthly moisture drawn up by the Moon. Some theologians of our own age write that these are already signs of the corruption of the heavens, about which Sacred Scripture speaks in more than one place. It is likely that these spots gave occasion to the philosopher Thales to think the Moon is the Earth wrapped in mist; to Anaxagoras and Democritus, that there are hills and valleys there; to the Pythagoreans, not only to suppose it is earth, but that it is inhabited as this lower world is; and to others, to imagine that everything found among us is there too. On these matters see Plutarch, On the Face in the Moon, chapters 23, 25 and 30; Achilles Statius on Aratus; and Giovanni Pico, Count of Mirandola, in his most learned and complete work against the astrologers. And hence Juno in Seneca's Hercules Furens, Act 1:

units.la: Tellus Gigante Doris excusso tremensSupposita monstri colla terrifici levet, Sublimis alias Luna concipiat Feras.
units.tr: Let the earth, trembling as the Giant Doris shakes her, raise the monstrous neck of the terrifying beast, and let the lofty Moon conceive wild beasts.

units.la: Innuit (quod & alij scribunt non solum de Leone, sed & ceteris monstris θηρίοις & praeter naturam) Nemeaeum Leonem ex orbe Lunari decidisse, alium adversus fortissimum heroem emendicans. Epimenides:
units.tr: He hints (as others also write, not only of the Lion but of the other monsters, beasts, which are contrary to nature) that the Nemean Lion fell down from the lunar sphere, sent to fight against the most valiant hero. Epimenides:

units.la: Καὶ γὰρ ἐγὼ ἡνῷ ἡμὶ Σελάνας γυνάμοιο,ἁ ἁμιν φεύξας ἀποσωσαν ἠδὲ λίοναἐν Νεμέᾳ ἀχεῖ' αὐτὴν ἀλὰ φοτιναι ἡεσν.
units.tr: For I too was once born of the womb of Selene, who once fled and gave birth to the lion at Nemea, which is cruel to the flocks [Καὶ γὰρ ἐγὼ ἡνῷ ἡμὶ Σελάνας γυνάμοιο, ἁ ἁμιν φεύξας ἀποσωσαν ἠδὲ λίοναἐν Νεμέᾳ ἀχεῖ' αὐτὴν ἀλὰ φοτιναι ἡεσν].

units.la: Claudius de Tauro ab Hercule domito:
units.tr: Claudian on the Bull, tamed by Hercules:

units.la: Taurus medio nam fidere LunaProgenitus, Dictaea Iovis possederat arva.
units.tr: For the Bull, born of the Moon in the middle of the sky, had possessed the fields of Dictaean Jupiter.

units.la: Idem de Dianae curru: Currum subiere jugales,Quos decus esse Dea primi sub limine CaeliRoscida fecundis concepit Luna cavernis.
units.tr: The same on the chariot of Diana: Yoked beasts went under the chariot, which the Moon, dewy in her fruitful caverns, conceived as an ornament of the goddess on the threshold of the first heaven.

units.la: Quum ergo opaca sit Luna, lucem admittit inaequaliter, medietate tantum sui orbis vel paullo amplius; ea parte, qua ad Solem versa. Hinc varie nostris se oculis exhibet, modo nulla, alias dimidia, interdum plena. Formae, quas Luna alias atque augendo diminuendoque induit, Graecis φάσεις atque σχήματα dicuntur, varijsque appellantur nominibus. Species enim Crescentis, suaque Cornua Orienti obvertentis (Experientia apud Plinium libro II. nat. hist. cap. xiv. docente) quarto (tertio alijs, qui in sequentibus numeris etiam paullum evariant) mensis die dicitur κεραταδὴς vel μηνοειδὴς falcata, in cornua quum cernitur curvata: Septimo die διχότομος vel ἡμίμηνος, dimidia & aequa portione divisa; Undecimo ἀμφίκυρτος, utrimque gibbosa & praetumida, quum aliquid deest integro orbi; decimoquinto πανσέληνος, plena: Senescentis autem suisque cornibus Occidentem spectantis effigies contrario ordine appellatur, decimonono die ἀμφίκυρτος; Vicesimosecundo iterum διχότομος; Vicesimosexto μηνοειδὴς: Tricesimo denique cum Sole Luna facit congressum, qui Σύνοδος Graecis & Neomenia; Latinis Conjunctio, Coitus, Novilunium, Interlunium; Virgilius & Plinius Silentia Lunae vocant. Quae dixi paucis sic notat Macrobius in Somnium Scipionis: Luna dispensatonibus septenariis luminis sui vires sempiterna lege variando disponit. Primis septem diebus dimidiata semi-orbem ostendit; vocaturque dimidia. Secundis totum orbem complet, fitque Plenilunium. Tertijs rursus efficitur dimidia. Quartis fit coitus Lunae cum Sole, quod Interlunium nominatur. Est enim tempus inter deficientem & nascentem Lunam, hoc est, tricesimus dies, in quo Luna non lucet. Nam quum Soli conjuncta sit ita obscuratur ut minime possit videri; sed eodem momento renascens, paullatim ab eo recedendo, videtur. Adeundus & Plinius lib. II. natur. histor. cap. ix & lib. xviii. cap. xxxiii. Causas harum Formarum aperit erudite Vitellio libro iv. Opticae, cap. lxxiv, & tribus seqq. Ob hanc igitur instabilitatem recte Ovidius xv. Metamorph.
units.tr: Since the Moon is opaque, she admits light unevenly, only over half her orbit or a little more, namely the part turned towards the Sun. Hence she appears to our eyes in various ways: at times not at all, at others half-lit, and sometimes full. The shapes that the Moon takes on as she waxes and wanes are called phaseis and schemata by the Greeks, and are given various names. The appearance of the waxing Moon, with her horns turned towards the east (as experience, teaching in Pliny's Natural History, book 2, chapter 14, shows), on the fourth day of the month (on the third, according to others, who vary a little in the following numbers) is called keratoeidēs or mēnoeidēs, sickle-shaped, since she is seen curved into horns. On the seventh day she is dichotomos or hēmimēnos, divided into two equal halves. On the eleventh she is amphikyrtos, gibbous and very swollen on both sides, since something is missing from the full orb. On the fifteenth she is pansēlēnos, full. But the waning Moon, whose horns face the west, takes the opposite order of names: on the nineteenth day she is amphikyrtos; on the twenty-second again dichotomos; on the twenty-sixth mēnoeidēs. Finally, on the thirtieth day the Moon meets the Sun, which is called Synodos by the Greeks and Neomenia (new moon); in Latin, Conjunction, Coitus, Novilunium, Interlunium. Virgil and Pliny call it the Silence of the Moon. What I have said is briefly summarised thus by Macrobius in his commentary on the Dream of Scipio: the Moon, by a sevenfold division, varies the strength of her light according to an eternal law. For the first seven days she shows a half-orb and is called half-moon. On the second seven she completes the whole orb, and there is the full moon. On the third seven she again becomes a half. On the fourth seven the Moon comes together with the Sun, which is called the New Moon (Interlunium). For there is a time between the waning and the new Moon, that is, the thirtieth day, on which the Moon does not shine. For, being joined to the Sun, she is so obscured that she cannot be seen at all; but at the same moment, being reborn, she is seen again as she gradually withdraws from the Sun. See also Pliny, book 2 of the Natural History, chapter 9, and book 18, chapter 33. Vitellio, in book 4 of his Optics, chapter 74 and the three following, learnedly explains the causes of these forms. Because of this instability, Ovid rightly says in book 15 of the Metamorphoses:

units.la: Nec par aut eadem nocturna forma DianaeEsse potest usquam: semperque hodierna sequente, Si crevit, minor est; major, si contrahit orbem.
units.tr: Nor can Diana's nocturnal form ever be the same or equal: and always, on the following day, if she has grown, she is smaller than she is today; if she has shrunk her orb, she is larger.

units.la: Et Horatius lib. II Carminum: Ode xi.
units.tr: And Horace, Odes, Book II, Ode 11:

units.la: Non semper idem floribus est honosVernis: neque uno Luna rubens nitetVultu, quid aeternis minoremConsilijs animum fatigas?
units.tr: The honour of spring flowers is not always the same, nor does the reddening moon shine with one face. Why do you wear out your mind with concerns too small for what is eternal?

units.la: Lunae crescentis sic decrescentisque imaginem Σελανίτης gestare, reddereque enim in dies singulos, scribunt Plinius lib. xxxvii, cap. x. ex Dioscoride, qui mutilior hodie illo loco, & Georgius Agricola lib. v. de natura Fossilium. De Quarta Luna singulare hoc legitur, quod, ex Genethliacorum doctrina & praeceptis, illa nati Laboriosam acturi sint vitam, quemadmodum de Hercule prodit Eustathius. Tales apud Sudam Τετραδίται vocantur, qui quarta Luna editi laboribus periculisque adsiduis, ut alteri Hercules, involvuntur. Herculis Sidus apud Florum i. hist. Rom. cap. xviii, nihil aliud quam quarta Luna. Adagium ἐν περάδι γνώμης ab aliis explicatur. Elegans plenae Lunae Encomium est apud Senecam Hippolito, Choro Act. II:
units.tr: Pliny (Book 37, chapter 10, drawing on Dioscorides, whose text is more mutilated at that passage today) and Georgius Agricola (Book 5, On the Nature of Fossils) write that the selenite [Σελανίτης] bears the image of the waxing and waning moon, and that it changes with each passing day. Of the fourth moon there is this peculiar notion: according to the teaching and precepts of the astrologers, those born under it are destined to lead a laborious life, as Eustathius reports of Hercules. In Suidas, those so born are called tetradites [Τετραδίται], who, being born on the fourth day of the moon, are caught up in constant labours and dangers, like a second Hercules. The "star of Hercules" in Florus, Roman History Book 1, chapter 18, is nothing other than the fourth moon. The proverb "at the fold of wisdom" [ἐν περάδι γνώμης] is explained in various ways by others. There is an elegant encomium of the full moon in Seneca's Hippolytus, Act II, in the chorus:

units.la: Pulcrior
units.tr: More beautiful

units.la: Manilius lib. III. Astronomicon: Fata quoque & Vitas hominum suspendit ab Astris, Quæ summas operum partes, quæ lucis honorem, Quæ famam adsererent, quæ numquam fessa volarent: Quæ quasi per mediam Mundi praecordia partem Dispositá obtineant Phæbum, Lunamque, vagasque Fvincant Stellas, nec non vincantur ab ipsa. His Regnum Natura dedit, propriasque sacravit Vnicuique vices, sanxitque per omnia, summam Vndique ne Fati ratio traheretur in unam.
units.tr: Manilius, Astronomica, Book III: Fate too, and the lives of men, he hung from the stars: the stars which would secure the chief parts of works, the honour of light, and fame, and which would fly without ever tiring. Those which, as if through the middle heart of the world, hold Phoebus and the Moon in their ordered place, and surpass the wandering stars, and are themselves surpassed by none. To these Nature gave a kingdom, and consecrated to each its own turns, and ordained throughout that the sum of fate should not be drawn into one reckoning from every side.

units.la: Sic Iulius Firmicus lib. I. cap. IV: In quo Sol & Luna, quinque etiam Stellæ Errantes, quæ πλανῆται ab Græcis vocantur, certa ac diffinita semper agitatione discurrunt. Sic Macrobius lib. I. in Somnium Scipionis, cap. XVII. Hæ illud adjiciendum est, quod præter duo Lumina & Stellas quinque, quæ appellantur Vagæ, reliquas omnes alij infixas Cælo, nec nisi cum cælo moveri. Sic denique Iulius Hyginus in Poetico Astronomico: Reliquum est nobis de quinque Stellis; quas complures, ut Erraticas, ita πλανήτας Græci dixerunt. Sol igitur & Luna, principes, ut notat etiam Ptolemæus, Astrorum, & primariæ totius Universi Stellæ, φῶτα vocantur, Hebraeis מאורות, Paraphrastæ Chaldaico נהיריא, φωστῆρες LXX Interpretibus, Lumina passim & Luminaria Latinis. Sol merito, quum omnium Siderum sit maximus, & ab eo augeantur minuanturque ceterarum Stellarum actiones, eiusque motus regula sit reliquorum: nec immerito Luna; quæ, quamvis, excepto Mercurio, omnium minima (quidquid, Augustino suffragante, scribat Basilius lib. I. de Genesi ad litteram, Lunam, contra Mathematicorum omnium calculos, post Solem maximum Cœli adsurgens astrum) oculorum tamen judicio vulgique existimatione censetur ceteris Planetis major; petere quoque solitis ab ea nonnullis gentibus temporum distinctiones, Ecclesiastici cap. XLIII, vers. 6, 7, 8. Utrique vero meritissime talem dedit Antiquitas appellationem: cum quod illorum vires & effectus in Elementis, Metallis, Stirpibus, Animantibus, humanisque Corporibus, quam reliquorum, sint insigniores; tum quod gratissima vice Diem Noctemque illustrent. Hæc enim præcipua Conditionis eorum fuit causa, quemadmodum videre est apud Moschen Genes. I. vers. 14. & seqq. & Ieremiam cap. XXXI, 35.
units.tr: So Julius Firmicus, Book I, chapter 4: In which the Sun and Moon, and also the five wandering stars, which are called planets [πλανῆται] by the Greeks, run on in a fixed and definite motion always. So Macrobius, Commentary on the Dream of Scipio, Book I, chapter 17: To this must be added that, besides the two lights and the five stars called wandering, all the others are fixed in the heaven and move only with the heaven. Finally, Julius Hyginus in the Poetic Astronomy: It remains for us to speak of the five stars, which the Greeks called wandering, and so planets [πλανήτας], many in number. The Sun and Moon, therefore, the chief stars and the principal lights of the whole universe, as Ptolemy also notes, are called lights [φῶτα]; by the Hebrews they are called me'orot [מאורות], by the Chaldee paraphrast nehiraya [נהיריא], by the Seventy translators lights [φωστῆρες], and everywhere lights and luminaries by the Latins. The Sun rightly so, since he is the greatest of all the heavenly bodies, and since the actions of the other stars are increased or diminished by him, and his motion is the rule for the rest. The Moon not undeservedly so either; although, Mercury excepted, she is the smallest of all (whatever Basil writes in Book I of his commentary on Genesis, with Augustine's support, that the Moon, against the calculations of all the mathematicians, is the greatest star rising in heaven after the Sun), yet by the judgment of the eyes and the estimation of the common people she is held to be larger than the other planets. Some nations also customarily take from her the distinctions of seasons, Ecclesiasticus 43, verses 6, 7, 8. Antiquity gave each of these two names most deservedly: both because their powers and effects upon the elements, metals, plants, animals and human bodies are more notable than those of the rest, and because they illuminate day and night in a most welcome alternation. For this was the principal reason for their creation, as may be seen in Moses, Genesis 1, verse 14 and following, and in Jeremiah 31, verse 35.

units.la: CAP. XXIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIV.

units.la: De Saturno, Iove & Marte.
units.tr: On Saturn, Jupiter and Mars.

units.la: Infra Sphæras, quæ Planetis adsignatæ, supremam possidet Saturnus. Græcis Κρόνος: quod, inquit M. Tullius lib. II. de nat. Deor. Temporis Deum finxerint Veteres: dicitur ipsdem & Φαίνων, scribente præter Hyginum Aristotele de Mundo: ὁ τῆς Φαίνοντος ἅμα καὶ Κρόνος καλούμενος κύκλος. Hebraeis שבתאי, propter septimum diem. Chaldaeis Moloch. Ejus Stella similis illi, quæ in humero Orionis dextro, quemadmodum notat Hyginus. Gelidæ rigentisque naturæ, Plinio, lib. II, nat. histor. cap. VIII. Causa apud Ptolemæum libro I. quadripart. cap. IIII. quod, inquit, ab Solis calore, Terræque humiditate quam longissime distet. Terra major putatur nonagies semel cum octava parte. Motus, qui proprius illi, tardissimus. Cursum enim conficit annis XXX. Videndus Plinius capite, quod indicavi, octavo. Nota ejus ♄, Falx; quæ tribui Saturno solita, ut indicant Virgilius VII. Æneidos, Macrob. I. Saturn. cap. VII. Servius lib. II. Georg. Isidorus lib. VIII. Etymol. cap. XI. Et inde Falcifer, Ovidio I. Fastor, Martiali lib. XI. Epig. VII. Arnobio lib. III. adversus gentes.
units.tr: Below the spheres assigned to the planets, Saturn holds the highest place. The Greeks call him Κρόνος [Kronos], which, as Marcus Tullius says in book II of On the Nature of the Gods, is because the ancients imagined him to be the god of time. He is also called Φαίνων [Phainon], as Aristotle in his book On the Universe writes alongside Hyginus: "the circle called both of Phainon and of Kronos" [ὁ τῆς Φαίνοντος ἅμα καὶ Κρόνος καλούμενος κύκλος]. The Hebrews call him שבתאי [Shabbetai], from the seventh day. The Chaldeans call him Moloch. His star is like the one in the right shoulder of Orion, as Hyginus notes. Pliny, in book II, chapter VIII of his Natural History, describes his nature as cold and stiff. Ptolemy, in book I, chapter IV of the Tetrabiblos, gives the cause: he is as far as possible from the heat of the Sun and the moisture of the Earth. The Earth is thought to be ninety-one times larger than Saturn... [ninety-one times, with one eighth part added]. His motion is peculiar to him and the slowest of all: he completes his course in thirty years. Pliny, in the chapter I have cited, eighth, should be consulted. His mark is ♄, the sickle, which is customarily assigned to Saturn, as Virgil in book VII of the Aeneid, Macrobius in book I of the Saturnalia, chapter VII, Servius on book II of the Georgics, and Isidore in book VIII of the Etymologies, chapter XI, indicate. Hence he is "sickle-bearing" in Ovid's Fasti I, in Martial book XI, epigram VII, and in Arnobius, book III, Against the Nations.

units.la: Iupiter secundum inter Planetas locum obtinet. Græcis Φαέθων. Aristoteles de Mundo: ἐφεξῆς δὲ ὁ τῆς Φαέθοντος κύκλος, Διὸς λεγόμενος. Sic appellatus à Splendore: Solus enim, φῶσις & Venere exceptis, umbram parit. Hebraeis צדק, Iustitia. Chaldaeis עם; βροντᾶς, βροντῶ Orpheo; Tonans, Tonitrualis Latinis. Auctor vitalis & temperati caloris. Terram continet nonagies quinquies, & dimidiam fere partem. Zodiacum circumit annis fere xii, Plinio Hyginoque scribentibus, & experientia teste. Character �given, fulmen; unde illi cognomina Κεραυνιος Orpheo, Hesychio, Phurnuto, Pausaniae: Ἀστραπαῖος Pindaro; Fulminator Apuleio; Fulgurator in antiquis marmoribus; Fulgur Festo in Provorsum.
units.tr: Jupiter holds the second place among the planets. The Greeks call him Φαέθων [Phaethon]. Aristotle in his book On the Universe: "next is the circle of Phaethon, called that of Zeus" [ἐφεξῆς δὲ ὁ τῆς Φαέθοντος κύκλος, Διὸς λεγόμενος]. He is so named from his brightness, for he alone, with the exception of the Sun and Venus, casts a shadow. The Hebrews call him צדק [Tsedeq], Justice. The Chaldeans call him עם [am]. In Orpheus he is βροντᾶς, βροντῶ [thunderer]; the Latins call him Tonans and Tonitrualis. He is the giver of life and of a temperate heat. He contains the Earth ninety-five times and nearly half as much again. He goes round the zodiac in about twelve years, as Pliny and Hyginus write, and experience bears witness. His character is the thunderbolt, fulmen; hence his epithets: Κεραυνιος [Keraunios] in Orpheus, Hesychius, Phurnutus and Pausanias; Ἀστραπαῖος [Astrapaios] in Pindar; Fulminator in Apuleius; Fulgurator on ancient marbles; and Fulgur in Festus under "Provorsum".

units.la: Martis tertius datus est locus. Πυρόεις Graecis ab igneo colore; vel ab effectu, quod urat & exsiccet. Aristoteles: εἰτ' ὁ Πυρόεις, ὁ Ἡεφαιστος ἢ Ἄρης ... Hebraeis מאדם, πυρρός. Terram superat semel, & paullo plus una tertia. Duodecim percurrit signa duobus fere annis, Plinio & Hygino testibus. Fere, inquam. Cursus enim ejus Maxime inobservabilis, inquit Plinius lib. ii. nat. hist. cap. xvii, utpote numquam stationem facientis. Nota ♂, Clipeus cum Hasta. Nam utrumque illi tribuitur. Ovidius: Bellice, depositis Clipeo paullisper & Hasta, Mars ades.
units.tr: Mars is given the third place. The Greeks call him Πυρόεις [Puroeis], the fiery one, either from his fiery colour or from his effect, since he burns and dries. Aristotle: "then the fiery one, which is Hephaestus or Ares..." [εἰτ' ὁ Πυρόεις, ὁ Ἡεφαιστος ἢ Ἄρης ...]. The Hebrews call him מאדם [Adam], and the Greek πυρρός [pyrrhos, fiery red]. He surpasses the Earth once and a little more than a third. He runs through the twelve signs in about two years, as Pliny and Hyginus attest. "About," I say, for his course is very hard to observe, as Pliny says in book II, chapter XVII of his Natural History, since he never makes a station. His mark is ♂, the shield with the spear, for both are assigned to him. Ovid: "Warlike Mars, lay aside for a little your shield and spear, and come here."

units.la: Tres, quos jam adumbravi, Planetae perpetua lege sic in suis moventur Epicyclis, quemadmodum peritissimi observarunt Astronomi, ut motu suo quamdam crga Solem reverentiam praestare videantur. Soli namque coniuncti ὑπογεῖον Epicycli sui tenere deprehenduntur; ut veneratione tanti hospitis in extremos suae ditionis fines abgressi, regi loco quasi cedant, ex intervallo mediocri mandata virosque ab eo accepturi; eidem ex diametro oppositos ἀντίχθονα obtinere videmus, & lugere quasi regis absentiam, illiusque reditum supplices expetere. Hanc etiam Stationum legum animadvertimus eosdem indesinenter servare, ut ab Sole trium Signorum intervallo digressus Saturnus, quem quadratum adspectum vocant, tamquam immobilis subsistere videtur; Iupiter eandem σημεῖον φαντασίας habeat in Trigono; Mars ultra Trigonum aliquot partibus.
units.tr: The three planets I have just outlined move, by a fixed law, in their epicycles in such a way, as the most skilled astronomers have observed, that by their motion they seem to show a certain reverence towards the Sun. For when they are in conjunction with the Sun, they are found to keep to the lower part of their epicycle [ὑπογεῖον], so that, as if out of reverence for so great a guest, they withdraw to the farthest borders of his realm and, as it were, give way to the king's place, receiving his commands and men from him at a middle distance. Again, we see them holding the position opposite him on the diameter, the antichthon [ἀντίχθονα], and as if mourning the king's absence, they humbly seek his return. We also notice that they constantly keep the same law of their stations: Saturn, when separated from the Sun by an interval of three signs, which they call the quadrate aspect, seems to stand still as if motionless; Jupiter has the same appearance [σημεῖον φαντασίας] in the trine; Mars, beyond the trine by some degrees.

units.la: CAP. XXV.
units.tr: CAP. XXV.

units.la: De Sole.
units.tr: On the Sun.

units.la: SOL Locum inter Planetas nactus est medium; numero, non spatio, cujus dimensiene perspecta, ipse magis ab summo, quam ab ipso recedit ima postremitas, ait Macrobius lib. i. ad Somnium Scipionis, cap. xix. Quum enim, addit, Saturni Stela, quae summa, Zodiacum xxx annis peragrat; Sol medius uno anno; Luna ultima uno mense, nos integro: necesse est tantum interesse inter Solem & Saturnum, quantum inter unum & triginta; tantum inter Lunam Solemque, quantum inter duodecim & unum.
units.tr: THE Sun occupies the middle place among the planets, in number rather than in space. Macrobius, in book i of his commentary on the Dream of Scipio, ch. xix, says that once its dimensions have been surveyed, the lowest limit is farther from the Sun than the Sun is from the highest. For, he adds, Saturn's sphere, which is the highest, traverses the zodiac in thirty years; the Sun, which is in the middle, in one year; the Moon, the lowest, in one month, and we in a full month. So there must be as much difference between the Sun and Saturn as between one and thirty, and as much between the Moon and the Sun as between twelve and one.

units.la: Dux, ut eleganter Macrobius ejusdem libri cap. xx, Princeps, Moderator Luminum reliquorum. Dux; omnes enim sui Luminis majestate praecedit: Princeps; nam ita eminet, ut quum talis solus appareat Sol vocetur: Moderator denique; quia cursus ceterorum & recursus certa spatii diffinitione moderatur. Planetarum enim Stationes ab Sole fieri censebant Veteres. Lucanus lib. x: Sol Tempora dividit Anni; Mutat Nocte Diem; radiisque potentibus Astra Ire vetat; Cursusque vagos Statione moratur.
units.tr: Leader, as Macrobius elegantly says in ch. xx of the same book: Prince, Ruler of the other lights. Leader, since he surpasses all of them in the majesty of his light; Prince, since he so far outshines them that when such a body alone appears he is called the Sun; and finally Ruler, since he regulates the courses and returns of the others by a fixed measure of space. For the ancients believed that the stations of the planets were caused by the Sun. Lucan, book x: The Sun divides the seasons of the year, changes day into night, and by his mighty rays forbids the stars to move, and by his station holds back their wandering courses.

units.la: Plinius lib. ii. cap. xvi: Percussa (de Stellis loquitur) in qua diximus parte & triangulo Solis radio inhibentur rectum agere cursum, & igneavi levantur in sublime. Hoc non protinus intelligi potest visu nostro; ideoque existimatur stare: unde & nomen accepit Statio. Progreditur deinde ejusdem radii violentia & retroire cogit vapor repercussus. Vitruuius lib. ix. Architect. cap. iv. Ergo potius ea ratio nobis constabit, quod fervor, quemadmodum omnes res evocat & ad se ducit, eadem ratione Solis impetus vehemens radiis trigoni forma porrectus insequentes Stellas ad se perducit, & ante-currentes velut refrenando retinendoque non patitur progredi, sed ad se cogit regredi & in alterius trigoni signum esse. Huc pertinet Varronis illud, Satyra, ὀρῶ λυσᾶς: Quam mobilem Divum lyrami.
units.tr: Pliny, book ii, ch. xvi (speaking of the stars): When the part we have mentioned is struck, and the triangle of the Sun's ray holds them back from making a straight course, they are lifted up into the sky by their fiery nature. This cannot at once be perceived by our sight, and so they are thought to stand still; hence the name station. Then the violence of the same ray pushes them forward, and the vapour thrown back forces them to retreat. Vitruvius, book ix of his Architecture, ch. iv: Therefore this explanation will rather be established for us: just as heat draws and attracts all things to itself, so the Sun's vehement force, extended in the form of a triangle by its rays, draws the following stars to itself, and, as if restraining and holding back those running ahead, does not allow them to advance, but forces them to go backward and to be in the sign of another triangle. To this belongs Varro's line in his Satire, "How mobile is the lyre of the gods" [ὀρῶ λυσᾶς].

units.la: (sic Mundum vocat, sequutus Orphea, Hymno in Apollinem, ubi Coelum universum Apollinis cithara temperari canit.) Sol harmogeQuadam gubernans motibus diis vegct.
units.tr: (Thus he calls the world, following Orpheus in his Hymn to Apollo, where he sings that the whole heaven is tempered by Apollo's lyre.) The Sun, governing with a certain harmony the motions, gives life to the gods.

units.la: Ex quibus paret Radios esse Soli, tamquam Moderaminis, quod dixi, fræna: à quorum viribus & potentia Sol sæpe Radiatus Latinis; radiatum etiam Lumen illi tribuentibus. Attius in Phœnissis, citante PriscIano libro de verbis Comicis: Sol qui micantem candido curru atque equis Flammam citatis fervido ardore explicas, Quam natum adversus augurio atque inimico omine Thebis radiatum lumen ostendis tuum.
units.tr: From these it appears that the rays are, as it were, the reins of the control I have mentioned; by their force and power the Sun is often called radiant by Latin writers, and they also ascribe radiant light to him. Attius in the Phoenissae, cited by Priscian in his book on Comic verbs: Sun, who unfold the gleaming flame with your white chariot and swift horses, with fervent heat, you show your radiant light against your son Thebes with an ill omen and hostile sign.

units.la: Ovidius in Metamorphos. Quid nunc Hyperione nate Forma colorque tibi radiataque lumina prosunt?
units.tr: Ovid in the Metamorphoses: What now do your beauty, your colour, and your radiant light avail you, son of Hyperion?

units.la: Hinc Sol Insigne radiatum Dei, Lucretio lib. v. de rer. natura: Propterea nebles hiberno tempore longa Cessant, dum veniat radiatum Insigne dei.
units.tr: Hence the Sun is the radiant emblem of God, as Lucretius says in book v of On the Nature of Things: For this reason the mists of winter last a long time, until the radiant emblem of the god comes.

units.la: Græcis ἡλιος ἀπὸ τῆς ἀει ἑλεῖν, ab continua circumvolutione; nam perpetuo circumrotatur motu, quo Zodiacum lustrat spatio dierum cccixv, horarum sex: vel ἀπὸ τῆς σίλαγης, ut sæpe fieri solet, in adspirationem conversio. Doribus ἅλιος, nota Dialecto: quamquam Plato in Cratylo sic Solem huic genti dictum scribat, ἀπὸ τῆς ἁλίζειν, quod exoriens in unum homines congreget. Hebræis חמה à calore, Hijob. cap. xxx. 28.
units.tr: The Greeks derive ἥλιος [hēlios] from ἀεὶ ἑλεῖν [aei helein], from its continual revolution, for it turns constantly in a motion by which it traverses the zodiac in 365 days and six hours; or from σίλαγης [silagēs], as often happens with a change to an aspirate. The Dorians say ἅλιος [halios], in their dialect. Plato in the Cratylus, however, writes that the Sun was so named by this people from ἁλίζειν [halizein], because at its rising it gathers men together into one. The Hebrews call it חמה [ḥammah] from heat, Job 30. 28.

units.la: Solem Lampadem esse ardentem vel candens saxum, ausus olim dicere Anaxagoras, ut & Euripides cum sequutus in Phaethonte Tragœdia, Glebam auream; quemadmodum refert Sotion in Successionibus: quam ob causam ille reus factus, & ab Cleone impietatis accusatus, defensusque à Pericle discipulo, talentis quinque & exilio fuit ab Atheniensibus multatus. Sic Democritus & Metrodorus Solem Ferrum ignitum volucrunt; Xenophanes Nubem igneam; sunt & qui Rotam accensam: una in parte apertam, & inde flammas vomentem: narrantibus Diogene Laërtio in Philosoph. Vitis, Augustino lib. xviii. de Civit. Dei, cap. xli. Theodoreto lib. iv. contra Græc. adfect. Ioanne Stobæo in ἐκλογ. φυσικ. & aliis. Posidonius lib. xvii. Cœlest. apud eundem Laërtium in Zenone Cittico, Solem ait purissimum esse Ignem; quod omnia Ignis peragat munera. Parmenides, eodem scribente, putat Solem, Calidum esse ac Frigidum; ex quorum commistione constat quidquid in rerum natura. Calorem sane Soli tribuit non uno loco Sacra Scriptura, ut videre est Psalmo xix, 7. Ecclesiastici cap. xliii vers. 7. & alibi. Calidus proprie Sol ab Effectis. Nam, quamvis per se non calidus (quod alij probant validis argumentis) calefacit tamen, vel per motum, quo ipse concutit, atterit, attenuat aerem, ut innuit Aristoteles lib. Meteor. & lib. ii. de Cœlo text. 42; vel, quemadmodum solidius volunt alij, sua luce (ut & reliqua Astra) quæ quanto copiosior in Sole, quam in ceteris, tanto potentior illis Sol est ad calefaciendum. Obiter adscribo, qui Lampadem, Saxum, Ferrum ignitum Solem statuerunt, causam dedisse nonnullis fabulandi, eumdem, quum Oceano se mergit (nam & hoc scriptis mandant) strepitum edere & exstingui: quæ opinio veterum fuit Hispanorum, ut docent Cleomedes lib. ii. & Posidonius apud Strabonem libro ii. Cosmograph, à quibus dirivata ad alios, præsertim Poetas Latinos, qui de Solis se mergentis stridore multa.
units.tr: Anaxagoras once dared to say that the Sun is a lamp that is burning, or a glowing stone, and Euripides followed him in his tragedy Phaethon, calling it a golden clod; as Sotion reports in his Successions. For this he was put on trial, accused of impiety by Cleon, and defended by Pericles, his pupil; yet the Athenians fined him five talents and sent him into exile. Democritus and Metrodorus thought the Sun was red-hot iron; Xenophanes, a fiery cloud; and some, a kindled wheel, open on one side and thence sending out flames, as Diogenes Laertius reports in his Lives of the Philosophers, and Augustine in book xviii of the City of God, ch. xli, Theodoret in book iv against the Greeks, John Stobaeus in his Eclogues on natural philosophy, and others. Posidonius, in book xvii of his work On the Heavens, as cited by the same Laertius in the life of Zeno of Citium, says the Sun is the purest fire, since fire performs all its functions. Parmenides, according to the same writer, holds that the Sun is both hot and cold, and that from the mixture of these whatever exists in nature arises. Sacred Scripture, in more than one place, ascribes heat to the Sun, as may be seen in Psalm 19. 7 and Ecclesiasticus 43. 7, and elsewhere. The Sun is called hot properly from its effects. For although it is not hot in itself (as others prove by strong arguments), it nevertheless warms, either through the motion by which it shakes, wears down and thins the air, as Aristotle hints in his Meteorology and in book ii of On the Heavens, text 42; or, as others hold with more solidity, by its light (as also the other stars do), which, being more abundant in the Sun than in the rest, makes the Sun more powerful than they are in warming. I add in passing that those who made the Sun a lamp, a stone, or red-hot iron gave some people occasion for fables, namely that it hisses and is extinguished when it sinks into the Ocean (for they also commit this to writing). This was the opinion of the ancient Spaniards, as Cleomedes in book ii and Posidonius, cited by Strabo in book ii of his Geography, teach. From them it passed to others, especially the Latin poets, who wrote much about the hissing of the setting sun.

units.la: Solem ait Plinius lib. ii. nat. histor. cap. vi. Lumen non modo Luna (de qua mox) sed & cæteris Sideribus funerari: similem enim Astris omnibus esse naturam; manifestum autem Lunæ Lumen esse ab Sole: ideoque existimandum reliquas etiam Stellas inde Lumen accipere. Hugo item ad Genesin notat, soli Soli, ex Igne creato, propriam esse Lucem; ceteras Stellas ex aeria factas materia relucere potius quam lucere. Solem denique fontem esse omnis Lucis cœlestis, omniaque Astra Lucem, quam habent, omnem illi ferre acceptam, visum Heraclito, Lucretio, Avicennæ, Alberto Magno, Bedæ, aliisque Astrologis & Theologis. Sed dicendum non esse parem Lunæ ceterorumque Siderum rationem; neque vero simile, immensam illam cœlestium Ignium, qui in octava sphæra, reliquarum nobilissima, mirabili pulchritudine lucent, Chorcam ab Sole suum Lumen mutuari. Augustinus lib. ii. de Genesi ad litteram, cap. xvi, ex Epistolæ prioris ad Corinthios cap. xv. manifesto constare scribit, disparem esse Siderum claritatem; & Astra, quibus diuersiores vires & effectus, dissimilem etiam obtinere Lucis rationem. Stellas censendum lucere Lumine cum proprio, quod congenitum illis, Luce Solis imbecillius: tum alieno, quod ab Sole accipiunt Radiorum reflexione; sed dissimiliter, ut aliæ aliis magis sunt ὁμοιομερεῖς. Leucippus apud Laertium, contrariam superioribus ingressus viam, existimat Solem ab Sideribus, non ab Sole Sidera inflammari.
units.tr: Pliny, book ii of the Natural History, ch. vi, says that the Sun extinguishes the light not only of the Moon (of which presently) but also of the other stars; for all stars have a similar nature, and it is clear that the Moon's light comes from the Sun, so one should think the other stars also receive their light from it. Hugo likewise observes on Genesis that the Sun alone, created from fire, has its own light, while the other stars, made of airy matter, shine by reflection rather than by their own light. Finally, the view that the Sun is the source of all heavenly light, and that all the stars receive from it whatever light they have, was held by Heraclitus, Lucretius, Avicenna, Albert the Great, Bede, and other astrologers and theologians. But one must say that the Moon and the other stars do not stand in the same relation to the Sun; nor is it likely that that immense host of heavenly fires, which shine with wonderful beauty in the eighth sphere, the noblest of all, borrows its light from the Sun. Augustine, in book ii of On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, ch. xvi, writes that it is clear from 1 Corinthians 15 that the brightness of the stars differs; and the stars, which have more diverse powers and effects, also have a different kind of light. The stars are to be thought to shine partly by their own light, which is innate in them and weaker than the light of the Sun, and partly by a borrowed light, which they receive from the Sun by reflection of its rays; but in different degrees, as some are more homoeomerous [ὁμοιομερεῖς] than others. Leucippus, as reported by Laertius, taking the opposite path to the earlier thinkers, held that the Sun is set on fire by the stars, not the stars by the Sun.

units.la: Philostratus refert Gymnosophistas Solem pro summo Deo coluisse. Pythagoras eumdem ut & Lunam reliquaque Sidera, Deorum adscripsit numero; quum in ijs superet Calor, qui vitæ auctor. Martialis lib. xii: Martis alumna dies, roscam quo lampada primum Magnaque sidera vidimus ora Dei.
units.tr: Philostratus reports that the Gymnosophists worshipped the Sun as the supreme God. Pythagoras counted the Sun, along with the Moon and the other stars, among the gods, since heat, the author of life, prevails in them. Martial, book xii: The day, foster-child of Mars, when first we saw the dewy lamp and the great stars of the face of God.

units.la: Antiquum marmor: DEO SOLI INVICTO P. POMPONIVS CLITVS Ex VOTO
units.tr: Ancient marble inscription: TO THE UNCONQUERED GOD SUN, P. POMPONIUS CLITUS, ACCORDING TO A VOW.

units.la: Hinc Dorylao apud Censorinum de die Natali, cap. xiii. Organum Dei, Mundus; ipsi Censorino Annus Dei, Solaris. Hinc quę Dei propria, Soli tributa; Omnia Videre & Audire. Homerus Iliad. γ: Ἡέλιός θ' ὃς πάντ' ἐφορᾷς, καὶ πάντ' ἐπακούεις.
units.tr: Hence in Dorylaus, as cited by Censorinus in his book On the Birthday, ch. xiii, the world is the organ of God, and Censorinus himself calls the solar year the year of God. Hence also what is proper to God is ascribed to the Sun: to see and hear all things. Homer, Iliad 3: "The Sun, who sees all things and hears all things" [Ἡέλιός θ' ὃς πάντ' ἐφορᾷς, καὶ πάντ' ἐπακούεις].

units.la: Iovis Oculum vocat Hesiodus; Pisidas; Τὸ κοινὸν ὄμμα, ἀὼ παντοπεῖων κόλων. Fuerunt olim (ut ex Veterum patet monimentis, sacrisque litteris, Deuteron. iv. & Sapient. xiii.) suntque hodie; qui Solem, tamquam Deum, cultu & veneratione dignantur. Neque mirum. Quid enim humanis oculis adspici potest inter quæ creata pulcrius? adeo ut in eo tabernaculum suum posuisse Deum canat Rex Propheta Psalmo xix, 6; addens de Sole: Et ipse tanquam Sponsus procedens thalamo suo: Exultavit ut Gigas ad currendam viam; à summo Cœlo egressio ejus: Et occursus ejus usque ad summum ejus; nec est qui se abscondat à Calore ejus.
units.tr: Hesiod calls the sun the "Eye of Jove," and Pisidas calls it "the common eye, the all-seeing circle" [Τὸ κοινὸν ὄμμα, ὁ παντοπεῖων κόλων]. As the ancient monuments and the sacred writings show (Deuteronomy 4 and Wisdom 13), there were once people, and there still are, who honour and revere the sun as God. This is not surprising. What created thing is more beautiful to human eyes? So much so that the Prophet King sings in Psalm 19:6 that God set his tabernacle in it, and he adds about the sun: "And he, like a bridegroom coming out of his chamber, rejoiced like a giant to run his course. His going forth is from the end of heaven, and his circuit to the end of it; and nothing is hid from its heat."

units.la: Iam si quis penitius examinet, quanta Soli vis in terrena; qui potest, ut non, in summam divinissimæ Creaturæ rapiatur admirationem? Odorum, Saporum, Colorum, Calorumque, qui in fructibus, Varietates; Animalium quantitates qualitatesque; omnium Rerum Formas; diversas Terrenorum species, aliaque id genus infinita, Solis caliditate fieri certum est; adfirmantibus cum aliis, tum Diodoro Siculo lib. iii. rerum antiquarum cap. xii. & Plinio lib. xxxiv. nat. hist. cap. xiv. Homines nimia Solis vicinitate siccati, scribente Vegetio lib. i. de re militari, cap. ii. Sanguinis indigentes; Vulnera valde volent metuere: qui ab ejusdem ardoribus remotiores, sanguinis abundantia fretos nimis videmus in vulnera ferrumque præcipites. Lucanus de Orientalibus: Quidquid ad Eoos tractus mundique teporum Labitur, emollit gentes clementia Cœli. Illic & laxæ vestes & fluxa virorum Velamenta vides.
units.tr: If anyone examines more closely how great the power of the sun is over earthly things, how can he fail to be carried away into the highest wonder at this most divine creature? It is certain that the sun's heat produces the odours, flavours, colours and warmth in fruits and their varieties, the sizes and qualities of animals, the forms of all things, the different kinds of earthly things, and countless other things of that sort. Diodorus Siculus (Book 3 of his Antiquities, chapter 12) and Pliny (Natural History, Book 34, chapter 14) both affirm this. Vegetius (On Military Affairs, Book 1, chapter 2) writes that men dried up by too close a proximity to the sun need blood and are very much afraid of wounds; while we see that those who are further from its heat, relying on an abundance of blood, rush headlong into wounds and steel. Lucan says of the peoples of the East: "Whatever lies along the eastern tracts and the warm parts of the world, the mildness of the sky softens its peoples. There you see loose garments and the flowing veils of men."

units.la: Et de Septemtrionalibus: Populi, quos despicit Arctos, Felices errore suo: quos ille timorum Maximus haud urget leti metus: inde ruendi In ferrum mens prona viris, animæque capaces Mortis, & ignavum est reditura parcere vitæ.
units.tr: And of the northern peoples: "The peoples whom the Bear looks down upon are happy in their error; the greatest fear of death does not press upon them. Hence their minds rush headlong upon the sword, and they are capable of facing death; it is cowardly to spare a life that will return."

units.la: De Solis Magnitudine variæ leguntur apud Plutarchum lib. xi. de Placit. Philosoph. cap. xxi. Macrobium lib. i. in Somnium Scipion. cap. xx, Diogenem Laertium, & alios, Philosophorum sententiæ. Heraclitus Ephesius & Epicurus tantum ajunt Solem, quantus apparet; pedalem tribuentes latitudinem. Anaxagoras majorem censuit Peloponneso. Anaximander Solis corpus æquale fecit Terræ; Orbem vero, in quo circumvehitur, septies vicies Terra maiorem; quod de ipso Sole notat Eratosthenes. Secundum Ptolemæum Sol major est Terra centies sexagies septies cum tribus octavis: cujus sententiam plerique sequuntur & varie stabiliunt Mathematici. Copernicus superioribus annis minorem deprehendit; ejusque corpus Terram superare centies sexagies bis, octava minus. Posidonius, nihil ausus certi, Terram dicit multo multoque sæpius multiplicatam Solis spacium efficere. Certe quantus sit Sol, quantaque illi Lucis copia, si alia deessent argumenta, paret inde, quod solus præsentia sua clarissimum faciat diem, omnibus nocturnis tenebris discussis penitus & sublatis; quod ne omnium quidem Astrorum simul præsentium lux conjuncta præstare potest: Sole etiam præsentia sua reliquorum Siderum præstinguente & occultante claritatem. Non minus elegantes quam pie Ambrosius lib. iv. ἑξαημ. cap. vi. Sivis, inquit, magnitudinem Solis non solum oculo mentis, sed etiam corporis æstimare; considera quanti Stellarum globi Axem Cæli videantur obtexere, & innumeris insignire luminibus: non queunt tamen tenebras noctis & Cæli nubila detergere. Simul ut Solortus sui signa præmiserit, omnes Stellarum Ignes sub unius Luminaris fulgore evanescunt: aperitur Aer, Cæliquefacies purpurascente rubore perfunditur. Adhuc spirans exordium, & jam momentanea celeritate pleni luminis micat; & surgentis Solis prævia aura dulcis adspirat. Similis Sol & Indis & Britannis eodem momento videtur, quum oritur: nec, quum vergit in occasum, minor adparet Orientalibus, quam Occidentalibus; nec Occidentalibus, quum oritur, inferior, quam Orientalibus æstimatur.
