Neque te moveat, quod tibi tanquam Orbis cubitalis videatur Sol, quum oritur: sed considera, quantum interfit spacij inter Solem & Terras, quod adspectus nostri infirmitas sine magno sui transfire non potest dispendio. Merito igitur exclamavit Ecclesiasticus cap. xvii, 30. Quid lucidius Sole? Videndus etiam huc Dionysius libro de Divinis Nominibus. cap. i. part. iv.
units.tr: Various opinions of the philosophers about the size of the sun are read in Plutarch (Book 11 of the Opinions of the Philosophers, chapter 21), Macrobius (Commentary on the Dream of Scipio, Book 1, chapter 20), Diogenes Laertius and others. Heraclitus of Ephesus and Epicurus say only that the sun is as large as it appears, ascribing to it a breadth of one foot. Anaxagoras judged it larger than the Peloponnese. Anaximander made the body of the sun equal to the earth, but its orbit, in which it travels, twenty-seven times larger than the earth; Eratosthenes records this of the sun itself. According to Ptolemy the sun is larger than the earth one hundred and sixty-seven times and three eighths; most mathematicians follow this opinion and variously confirm it. In recent years Copernicus found it smaller, and he holds that its body exceeds the earth one hundred and sixty-two times, less an eighth. Posidonius, not daring to assert anything certain, says that the earth, multiplied many and many more times, would make up the space of the sun. Certainly, if other arguments were lacking, how great the sun is, and how great its supply of light, is shown by the fact that it alone, by its presence, makes the day most bright, dispelling and wholly removing all the darkness of night; and this the combined light of all the stars present together cannot achieve, since the sun, by its presence, extinguishes and hides the brightness of the other stars. Ambrose, no less elegant than pious (Hexaemeron, Book 4, chapter 6), says: "If you wish to estimate the size of the sun not only with the eye of the mind but also with the eye of the body, consider how many globes of stars seem to cover the axis of heaven and adorn it with countless lights; yet they cannot dispel the darkness of night and the clouds of the sky. As soon as the sun has sent forth the signs of its rising, the fires of all the stars vanish beneath the brightness of that one luminary. The air is opened, and the face of the sky is suffused with a purple blush. While the sun is still breathing its beginning, it already gleams with the momentary swiftness of full light, and a sweet breeze breathes ahead of the rising sun. The sun appears the same to Indians and Britons at the same moment when it rises; nor, when it sinks towards setting, does it appear smaller to those in the East than to those in the West, nor, when it rises, is it judged smaller by those in the West than by those in the East. Do not be disturbed because the sun seems to you like a cubit-wide disc when it rises; but consider how great the space between the sun and the earth is, which the weakness of our sight cannot cross without great loss to itself." Rightly, then, Ecclesiasticus 17:30 exclaims: "What is brighter than the sun?" Dionysius, On the Divine Names, chapter 1, part 4, should also be consulted here.

units.la: Sphæræ Solis Ἀ'πύλον, Ptolemæi tempore, distabat à Terra mille ducentis & decem Semidiametris; Ἡ ἐ...ον, mille centum viginti duabus fere: hodie mutata κα-τεσ..., Ἀ...ον distare deprehenduntur Astronomi Semidiametris mille centum septuaginta novem. Plura hac de Plinius lib. ii. nat. hist. cap. xxi, Ptolemæus lib. v. Vitellio libr. x. Opticcs, & alij.
units.tr: The apogee of the sun's sphere [ἀπόγειον], in Ptolemy's time, was distant from the earth by 1210 semidiameters; its perigee [περίγειον] by about 1132. Today, with the change in the calculations, astronomers find the apogee to be 1179 semidiameters distant. Pliny (Natural History, Book 2, chapter 21), Ptolemy (Book 5), Vitellio (Optics, Book 10) and others say more about this.

units.la: Maxima hodie Solis obliquitas seu declinatio xxiii. graduum, xxviii. scrupulorum. Aristarchus Samius, annis ante Ptolemæum quadringentis, deprehendit eam xxiii graduum li scrupulorum, xx. secundorum; quantam & invenisse se norat Ptolemæus. Mahometes Aratensis, anno post Ptolemæum ıoccxliv, graduum indicat xxiii, scrupulorum xxxv. Arzahel Hispanus cxc. annis post Albategnium, xxiii graduum, xxxiv scrupulorum. Prophatius Iudæus, ccxxx post Arzahelem anno, xxxiii graduum, xxxii scrupulorum. Dominicus Maria anno nati Redemtoris cio cccxci, graduum xxiii, scrupulorum xxix. Wernerus anno Christi cio io xiv, graduum xxiii, scrupulorum xxviii, secundorum xxx. Copernicus tandem non ita pridem maximam Solis Declinationem reperit graduum xxiii, scrupulorum xxviii, & duarum quintarum unius scrupuli. Quæ docent sensim decrevisse regulari motu æqualitatem; & decreturam adhuc, donec adsequatur extremum diminutionis terminum, quem Copernicus ponit xxiii graduum, xxviii scrupulorum: colligens post rursus accreturam; statuensque maximam, quæ fieri potest, Solis obliquitatem xxiii graduum, lii scrupulorum minimam xxiii graduum, xxviii scrupulorum; differentiam denique maximæ & minimæ xxiv. scrupulorum.
units.tr: The present greatest obliquity or declination of the sun is 23 degrees and 28 minutes. Aristarchus of Samos, some four hundred years before Ptolemy, found it to be 23 degrees and 51 minutes, 20 seconds, which Ptolemy also knew he had found. Mahometes of Aratensis, in the year 1044 after Ptolemy, gives 23 degrees and 35 minutes. Arzahel of Spain, 190 years after Albategnius, gives 23 degrees and 34 minutes. Prophatius the Jew, 230 years after Arzahel, gives 23 degrees and 32 minutes. Dominicus Maria, in the year of our Redeemer 1391, gives 23 degrees and 29 minutes. Werner, in the year of Christ 1514, gives 23 degrees, 28 minutes and 30 seconds. Copernicus, not long ago, found the greatest declination of the sun to be 23 degrees, 28 minutes and two fifths of a minute. These figures show that by regular motion the obliquity has gradually decreased to equality, and will continue to decrease until it reaches the extreme limit of diminution, which Copernicus puts at 23 degrees and 28 minutes; then, reckoning that it will increase again afterwards, he sets the greatest possible obliquity of the sun at 23 degrees and 52 minutes, the least at 23 degrees and 28 minutes, and the difference between greatest and least at 24 minutes.

units.la: Iter autem Soli in Ecliptica; quæ, ἡλιακὸς κύκλος Græcis dicta, Ptolemæo κύκλος ἀ... μεσῶν τῶν ζωδίων, nihil aliud, quam circulus major in medio consistens Zodiaci, eumque κατὰ πλάτος in duos dirimens æquales ambitus: sex olim, hodie octo graduum spacio diffinitos; quem Sol in uno perpetuo tramite oblique incedens efformat.
units.tr: The path of the sun along the ecliptic, called the solar circle [ἡλιακὸς κύκλος] by the Greeks, which Ptolemy calls the circle through the middle of the signs of the zodiac, is nothing other than a great circle lying in the middle of the zodiac, dividing it by latitude into two equal circuits. Formerly this was defined by a space of six degrees, now of eight; and the sun, advancing obliquely on one perpetual track, traces it out.

units.la: Solis Defectus (ne de hoc etiam nihil dicam) alius verus & naturalis, alius prodigiosus. Verus, qui voce propria Eclipsis, est non privatio Lucis (Sol enim, Lux pulcerrima, Lucem perpetuo subministrans, numquam Lucis patitur detrimentum) sed exclusio tantum vel aversio radiorum Solis, quam facit Lunæ soliditas & densitas; collocata enim inter Solem & visum nostrum in conjunctione radios, quos dixi, spargi prohibet, & in quasdam Terræ partes pertingere. Contingit, quando Luna Soli conjungitur circa Novilunium. Investigasse primus & prædixisse perhibetur Thales Milesius, docentibus M. Tullio libro i. de Divinat. Plinio lib. ii. nat. hist. Augustino libro de Civit. Dei viii, cap. ii. & Eusebio. Palamedes etiam Eclipsin, Castris Græcorum formidabilem, primus naturalem esse scribitur docuisse. Imperita enim multitudo anteaquam à Philosophis Solis Lunæque Defectuum ostensa esset ratio, videns praestantissima Sidera deficere & quasi languore dissolvi, lugere tristiaque suo luctu portendere putabat. Propertius lib. iii. Eleg. iv, 56. Aut quur Perrhaebi tremuere cacumina Pindi, Solis & atratis luxerit orbis equis.
units.tr: Of solar eclipses (not to say nothing even of this), one is true and natural, another prodigious. The true eclipse, which is properly called an eclipse, is not a privation of light (for the sun, the most beautiful light, supplying light perpetually, never suffers any loss of light), but only the exclusion or turning away of the sun's rays, which the solidity and density of the moon produce; for when the moon is placed between the sun and our sight at conjunction, it prevents the rays I have mentioned from spreading and reaching certain parts of the earth. It happens when the moon is conjoined with the sun around the new moon. Thales of Miletus is said to have first investigated and predicted it, as Cicero (On Divination, Book 1), Pliny (Natural History, Book 2), Augustine (City of God, Book 8, chapter 2) and Eusebius testify. Palamedes too is written to have been the first to teach that an eclipse, which was dreaded in the camp of the Greeks, is natural. For the ignorant crowd, before the cause of the eclipses of the sun and moon had been explained by the philosophers, seeing the most excellent stars fail and as it were dissolve in weakness, thought they were mourning and foretold sorrow by their grief. Propertius (Book 3, Elegy 4, line 56): "Or why did the peaks of Pindus of Perrhaebia tremble, and the orb of the sun grow dim with its black-clad horses?"

units.la: Augustinus lib. iii. de Civit. Dei cap. xv. Quasi vero, si luctus ille Solis fuisset, non magis ideo credi debet eclipsim fuisse, ipsumque felius aversione etiam diurni luminis indicatum. Excutiet arcana sic opinantes συμπάθεια, quae caelestibus creaturis solet esse cum homine rebusque humanis: alioquin absurdum, Luctum Soli aliisque in Caelo non rationalibus tale quid adfingere. Prodigiosus & ἀναλογία Defectus is, qui a vaporibus & nebulis fit adeo spissis, ut visus intercipiatur, Solisque lumen appareat admodum debile. Talis accidit continuo totius pene anni pallore, quo Iulius Caesar Dictator occisus, ut testatur Plinius lib. ii. cap. xxx. De eo Virgilius lib. i. Georgic. Sed tibi Signa dabit, Solem quis dicere falsum Audeat? Ille etiam caecos instare tumultus Saepe monet, fraudemque & operta tumescere bella. Ille etiam exstincto miseratus Caesare Romam, Quum caput obscura nitidum ferrugine texit: Impiaque aeternam timuerunt saecula noctem,
units.tr: Augustine (City of God, Book 3, chapter 15): "As though, if that were the grief of the sun, one ought not rather to believe that it was an eclipse, and that the sun's face was also indicated by its turning away from the daylight." Those who think such things by hidden sympathy [συμπάθεια], which the heavenly creatures are wont to have with man and human affairs, will shake off their secrets; otherwise it would be absurd to attribute such grief to the sun and to the other non-rational bodies in heaven. The prodigious eclipse, however, is that which is caused by vapours and mists so dense that sight is cut off and the light of the sun appears very weak. Such an eclipse occurred with a pallor lasting almost the whole year, in which Julius Caesar the Dictator was killed, as Pliny attests (Book 2, chapter 30). Of this Virgil writes (Georgics, Book 1): "But who would dare to call false the signs that he will give you? He often warns of blind tumults, and of treachery and hidden wars swelling up. He, too, pitying Rome for the murdered Caesar, veiled his bright head in dark rust; and impious ages feared an eternal night."

units.la: Ovidus lib. xv. Metamorph. ——— Solis quoque tristis imago Lurida sollicitis praebebat lumina terris.
units.tr: Ovid, Metamorphoses, book 15: "...and the sad image of the sun offered pale light to anxious lands."

units.la: Tibullus lib. ii. Eleg. iii. Ipsum etiam Solem defectum lumine vidit, Iungere pallentes nubibus annus equos.
units.tr: Tibullus, book 2, elegy 3: "He saw even the sun itself deprived of its light, and the year yoking its pale horses to the clouds."

units.la: Nullam enim Solis defectionem, qualem Servius Virgilij interpres & reliquum Scriptorum vulgus opinatur, in nostro hemisphaerio visam anno, quo Caesar crudeliter obtruncatus, docet calculus Astronomicus & subtilissime retro computata motuum caelestium ratio. Talem item dicere liceat, qui contigit pendente ab arbore Crucis Christo. Nam eo tempore Sol contra naturam Lucem amisit, in medio Caeli, haud procul a capite Draconis; quum Plenilunium esset, quo Sol naturaliter deficere non poterat. Luna etiam quum, nisi ab Sole inluminetur, lucere nequeat, deficiente Sole, eodem hoc tempore in imo Caeli apud Antipodas lucem amisit, juxta caudam Draconis. Saturnus denique emergens supra horizontem adspectu quadrato malefico utrumque defectum & Solis & Lunae adspexit. Terribilis igitur fuit tunc temporis Caeli facies. Ad prodigiosos huiusmodi Solis defectus pertinent non pauca Sacrae Scripturae loca, quibus tales Caelestium Corporum moerores, ut ita dicam, & μεταφορικῶς obfuscationes ad vivum delineantur, ut videre est apud Ieschach. cap. xiii, 10. Ezech. xxxiii, 7, 8. Iohel. ii, 10. iii, 15. & alibi.
units.tr: For no eclipse of the sun such as Servius, the interpreter of Virgil, and the rest of the common run of writers suppose was seen in our hemisphere in the year in which Caesar was cruelly slain; this is shown by the astronomical calculation and by the most exact retrospective reckoning of the motions of the heavenly bodies. One may likewise say the same of the eclipse that happened when Christ hung on the tree of the Cross. For at that time the sun, contrary to nature, lost its light in the middle of the sky, not far from the head of the Dragon, although it was full moon, when the sun could not naturally be eclipsed. The moon too, which cannot shine unless it is lit by the sun, lost its light at the same time, when the sun was eclipsed, at the lowest point of the sky among the Antipodes, near the tail of the Dragon. Lastly, Saturn, rising above the horizon in a baleful square aspect, witnessed both the eclipse of the sun and that of the moon. The face of the heavens was therefore terrible at that time. To such prodigious eclipses of the sun belong not a few passages of Holy Scripture, in which such mournings of the heavenly bodies, so to speak, and obscurations described metaphorically [μεταφορικῶς], are portrayed to the life, as can be seen in Isaiah 13:10; Ezekiel 32:7, 8; Joel 2:10; 3:15, and elsewhere.

units.la: Fabulis de Solis Curru quatuorque Equis, quae apud Ovidum, Tertullianum Cassiodorum, aliosque, Lectorem non morabor. Isidori, qui bonorum auctorum exscriptor multa nonnunquam paucis complectitur, verba adponam ex lib. xviii. Originum: Quadrigas Solis, Bigas Lunae, Trigas Inferis, Sejugas Iovi, Desultores Lucifero & Hespero sacraverunt; ubi mox singulorum caulam exsequitur.
units.tr: I shall not detain the reader with the fables about the Chariot of the Sun and its four horses, which are found in Ovid, Tertullian, Cassiodorus and others. I shall add the words of Isidore, who, as a copier of good authors, often embraces much in few words, from book 18 of the Origins: "They consecrated the four-horse chariot to the Sun, the two-horse to the Moon, the three-horse to Hades, the six-horse to Jupiter, and the riders to Lucifer and Hesperus," where he soon goes through the explanation of each.

units.la: Sol Sirii appellatione videtur exaudiendus apud Virgilium, quum inquit lib. iv. Georgic. Iam rapidus torrens sitientes Sirius Indos Ardebat caelo.
units.tr: The Sun seems to be meant under the name Sirius in Virgil, when in book 4 of the Georgics he says: "Now the scorching Sirius was burning the thirsty Indians under the sky."

units.la: Scribit etiam Sudas Σείριον a multis exponi τὸν ἥλιον, id est Sirium Solem.
units.tr: Suidas also writes that Seirios is by many explained as the sun, that is, "the Sun Sirius" [τὸν ἥλιον].

units.la: Solis nota ⊙, quid velit, vident etiam pueri.
units.tr: The sign of the Sun, ⊙, what it means even boys see.

units.la: Finiam, ἀναξιφάλαιος quae hactenus de pulcerrimo hoc Astro, in verbis Plinij, petitis ex lib. ii. nat. histor. cap. vi. Hunc Mundi esse totius Animum, ac planius mentem, hunc principale Naturae regimen ac Numen credere decet, opera ejus aestimantes. Hic lucem reliquis ministrat, aufertque tenebras; hic reliqua Sidera occultat; hic vices temporum Annumque semper renascentem ex usu naturae temperat: hic Caeli tristitiam discutit, atque etiam humani nubila animi serenat; hic suum lumen ceteris quoque Sideribus faenerat: praeclarus, eximius, omnia intuens, omnia etiam exaudiens; ut principi litterarum Homero placuisse in uno eo video.
units.tr: I shall end what I have said so far about this most beautiful star with the words of Pliny, taken from book 2 of the Natural History, chapter 6, where it is fitting to believe that this is the soul of the whole world and, more plainly, its mind, the principal governance and divinity of nature, judging by its works. It gives light to the rest and takes away darkness; it hides the other stars; it regulates the changes of the seasons and the year, always renewed by the course of nature; it dispels the gloom of the sky and even brightens the clouds of the human mind; it lends its light to the other stars as well: distinguished, outstanding, seeing all things and hearing all things; so that I see it pleased Homer, the prince of letters, in this one thing alone.

units.la: Cap. XXVI.
units.tr: Chapter 26.

units.la: De Venere & Mercurio.
units.tr: On Venus and Mercury.

units.la: HÆc de Sole: sequuntur Venus & Mercurius; σωσφόροι, ἑωσφόροι, vel ὁμόδρομοι τῷ ἡλίῳ, ut Plato appellat: quorum peculiaris ratio est, neque communis cum supradictis, inquit Plinius lib. II. nat. histor. cap. VIII. pluribus id confirmans cap. XVII. Quum enim tres superiores Planetæ & Luna, ab Sole discedentes, nonnumquam per Quadratum vel per Trigonum distent; aliquando ex Adverso cernantur: Veneri Mercurioque certæ sunt metæ, quas ultra ab Sole non excurrunt. Nam Venus (cui, quam Mercurio, proprior cum Sole perhibetur copulatio: habet enim, ut alia sileam, unum idemque cum eo ϰαίγωον) tamquam blanda œconoma citra quinquagesimum; Mercurius, qui Cancellarij instar in politica Cœli administratione, citra gradum tricesimum semper Solem comitantur: perpetuoq; circaeum versantes, nunc accedunt tamquam mandata accepturi; nunc rursus excurrunt, quasi speculandi gratia vias exploratum emissi; mox, ne longius ab rege evagentur ad Solem, quasi revocati, recto cursu reverruntur. Iidem Planetæ, quemadmodum exactissimi notant Mathematici, in eo Solem, ceu regem suum, observant, quod quoties illi conjunguntur, semper in ϰατωγέων vel ἀπογέων sui Epicycli reperiantur; suaque latitudines ita alternent, ut ab diversis regi suo lateribus adsistant & ministrent. Nam ubi vel inclinatione vel reflexione sua Venus versus Septemtrionem evagatur; ibi Mercurius ijsdem latitudinum differentijs in contrariam discedit plagam, Austrum versus; & econtra, permutatis semper vicibus.
units.tr: So much for the Sun. Next come Venus and Mercury, light-bearers and dawn-bearers [σωσφόροι, ἑωσφόροι], or those running alongside the sun [ὁμόδρομοι τῷ ἡλίῳ], as Plato calls them. Their reasoning is peculiar to them and not shared with the planets already mentioned, says Pliny, Natural History, book II, chapter 8, confirming this at length in chapter 17. For while the three superior planets and the Moon, departing from the Sun, are sometimes at a square or trine from it and sometimes seen in opposition, Venus and Mercury have fixed limits beyond which they never run from the Sun. Venus, whose conjunction with the Sun is said to be closer than Mercury's (for, to say nothing of other things, she has a common point of conjunction with him [ϰαίγωον]), like a gentle housekeeper never goes beyond fifty degrees; Mercury, who in the political administration of heaven is like a chancellor, always accompanies the Sun within thirty degrees. Always moving in a circle around it, they now approach as if to receive orders, now run out again as if sent ahead to scout the roads, and soon, as if recalled so they may not wander too far from the king, they return to the Sun by a direct course. These same planets, as the most exact mathematicians note, keep watch on the Sun as on their king in this respect: whenever they are in conjunction with him, they are always found in the lower or upper [κατωγέων, ἀπογέων] part of their epicycle; and their latitudes alternate so that they stand by and serve their king from opposite sides. For when Venus wanders toward the north, by inclination or reflection, Mercury, with the same differences of latitude, departs to the opposite region, toward the south; and conversely, the roles always being exchanged.

units.la: Venus itaque, quintam adepta stationem, Solem annuo fere spacio, nunc antecedit, ut dixi, nunc subsequitur: quam ejus naturam primus deprehendit Pythagoras, quemadmodum indicat Plinius lib. II. nat. histor. cap. VIII. Antecedens, ut Sol alter diem maturans, docentibus Cicerone lib. II. de natura Deorum, Varrone lib. III. de rustica, cap. V, alijs, φωσφόρος vel ἑωσφόρος appellatur Græcis: Latinis, Lucifer; Hebræis, בוקר; Chaldæis, שפרפרא. Subsequens autem, ut prærogans lucem vicemque Lunæ reddens, ἑσπερος Græcis, unde Latinis Vesper, & Antiquioribus, Plauto in Amphitruone alijsque. quod notant Varro lib. v. de L L. & Festus lib. ult. de verb. signif. Vesperugo. Confunduntur tamen, ut legere est apud bonos scriptores, Veneris Sidus utroque tempore Vesperi vocabulo insignitum. Horatio namque Hesperus pro Lucifero scribitur, libro Carminum II. Od. IX. ad Valgium: Tu semper urges flebilibus modis: Mysten ademtum: nec tibi Vespero Surgente, decedunt amores, Nec rapidum fugiente Solem.
units.tr: Venus, therefore, having attained the fifth station, now goes before the Sun and now follows it, as I said, for nearly a year. Pythagoras first discovered this nature of hers, as Pliny shows in book II, chapter 8, of his Natural History. When she goes before, like a second Sun hastening the day, as Cicero in book II of On the Nature of the Gods, Varro in book III of On Rustic Matters, chapter 5, and others teach, the Greeks call her phosphoros or eosphoros; the Latins, Lucifer; the Hebrews, boqer; the Chaldeans, shifarfara. When she follows, bringing evening and giving back the light of the Moon, the Greeks call her hesperos, whence the Latins have Vesper, and the older writers, such as Plautus in the Amphitruo and others, Vesperugo, as Varro in book V of On the Latin Language and Festus in the last book, On the Meaning of Words, note. Yet, as one may read in good writers, the star of Venus is marked by the name Vesper at either time and is confused. For Horace writes Hesperus for Lucifer, in Odes, book II, ode 9, to Valgius: You always press on with mournful strains, mourning the lost Mystes; nor do your loves depart when Hesperus rises, nor when the swift Sun flees.

units.la: Ita esse scribit Lactantius Statij interpres: Lucifer & mane oritur & vesperi, equo mutato: & post pauca: Post autem quadrigas dant Soli, bigas Lunæ, Equos singulis Sideribus: eundem ergo Vesperum vult habere: ut Horatius Vesperum pro Lucifero posuit. Sic autem Plautus Noctuanus, qui idem cum Hespero, pro Lucifero capiendus: Credo ego hac nocta Nocturnum obdormisse ebrium.
units.tr: Lactantius, the commentator on Statius, writes that this is so: Lucifer rises both in the morning and in the evening, with the horse changed; and a little later: After the quadrigas they give to the Sun, the biga to the Moon, and horses to each of the stars; so he means the same star to be Vesper, as Horace used Vesper for Lucifer. Plautus's Noctuanus, which is to be taken as the same as Hesperus, that is, Lucifer, says likewise: I believe the Nocturnal, drunk, has fallen asleep this night.

units.la: Continere putatur Terræ globum centies septies. Sidus tanti fulgoris, ut radiis suis reddat umbras. De claritate ejus matutina, Tiberianus apud Placidem: Aureus subducit ignes Sidus Ora Lucifer,
units.tr: It is thought to contain the globe of the earth seven hundred times. It is a star of such brilliance that its rays cast shadows. On its morning brightness, Tiberianus in Placidus: The golden Lucifer, face to face, draws out its fires.

units.la: De vespertina Papinius VI. Theb. Sic ubi tranquillo pellucent Sidera ponto, Vibraturque fretis Cœli stellantis imago, Omnia clara nitent: sed clarior omnia supra Hesperus exercet radios; quantusque per altum Aethera, cæruleis tantus monstratur in undis.
units.tr: On its evening brightness, Papinius in Thebaid book VI: So when the stars shine through a calm sea, and the image of the starry sky quivers in the waves, all things gleam bright; but Hesperus, brighter than all, shoots out its rays above; and as far as it is seen across the high aether, so far it is displayed in the blue waves.

units.la: Deutraque Seneca de morte Claudij
units.tr: Both of these appear in Seneca, on the death of Claudius:

units.la: Qualis discutiens fugientia Lucifer astra; Aut qualis surgit redeuntibus Hesperus astris.
units.tr: Like Lucifer scattering the fleeing stars; or like Hesperus rising as the stars return.

units.la: Tribuunt huic Planetæ quidam Currum; nonnulli Equos tantum, vesperi quidem fuscum, mane vero candidum: Tibullus lib. i. Eleg. ix, Pedo Albinavanus Elegia in Mæcenatis obitum, Ovidius in Fastis. Hinc mutare dicitur equos; Statius Papinius vi. Thebaidos: Roscida iam novies cælo demiserat astra Lucifer; & totidem Luna prævenerat ignes Mutaco Nocturnus equo.
units.tr: Some attribute to this planet a chariot; others only horses, dark in the evening and white in the morning: Tibullus, book I, elegy 9; Pedo Albinovanus, in his elegy on the death of Maecenas; Ovid in the Fasti. Hence it is said to change its horses. Statius Papinius, Thebaid book VI: Lucifer had already, nine times, let fall the dewy stars from heaven; and the Moon had gone before as many fires, the Nocturnal one changing his horse.

units.la: Hinc desultor esse; quod alij notarunt: hinc denique Defultatorios habere perhibetur equos. Cassiodorus lib. iii. Varior ad Faustum, de Circensibus: Biga quasi Luna Quadriga Solis imitatione reperta est. Equi desultorij, per quos Circenses ministri missos denunciant exituros, Luciferi præcursorias velocitates imitantur. Isidorus lib. xviii. Orig. Quadrigas Soli, Bigas Lunæ, Trigas Inferis, Sextugas Iovi, Desultores Lucifero & Hespero sacraverunt. Nota ♀. Speculum.
units.tr: Hence Venus is said to be a desultor (a vaulter), as others have noted; hence, finally, horses are said to be desultory, for leaping. Cassiodorus, Variae book III, to Faustus, on the Circus games: The biga was devised on the model of the Moon, the quadriga on the model of the Sun. The desultory horses, by which the attendants at the Circus announce that the races are about to begin, imitate the swift forerunners of Lucifer. Isidore, Origins book XVIII: They consecrated quadrigas to the Sun, bigae to the Moon, trigae to the dead, sexjugae to Jupiter, and desultores to Lucifer and Hesperus. Note ♀. Mirror.

units.la: Mercurius infra venerem, Luna superior. Σὺλλων Græcis apud Ciceronem, Marcianum, Apuleium. Hebræis בכב ἀστὴρ. Naturam ejus sic describit Ioannes Salisberiensis Policratici sui seu de nugis Curialium, lib. ii. cap. xix: Mercurius vero talis est, qualem vicini Planetarum miserunt: quum & ipse convertibilis naturæ sit, potentioribusque cohæreat. Unde plerique eum præsulem Eloquentiæ opinantur, eo quod illa iuncta Sapientiæ plurimum profuit; Malitia secietate noceat plurimum. Innuit, cuicunque se conjunxerit Mercurius, cum eo vires suas communicare; & noxium fieri salutaremque, pro noxiæ vel salutaris stellæ adplicatione & adspectu. Hinc Communis Stella Apuleio de Mundo: Nam quum omne Cœlum simplici circumactu volvatur, necte dieque distinctum, diversis mensurarum æqualitatibus separatum, quamvis una sphæra omnia concluserit; incrementis tamen globi sui decessione, luminis menstrua tempora Luna significat, & Cœli spacium Sol annua reversione conlustrat; eiusque comites amœnus Lucifer & communis Cyllenius stella, &c Imprudêter enim genuina docti Scriptoris lectio à quibusdam ibi, tamquam falsa, solicitatur, substituta Comis stella. Hinc quod Poetis habitus Minister Deorum, notante Servio ad l. i. Georgic. quum inquit: Scriendum sane, ut diximus, de Planetis quinque duos esse noxios, Martem & Saturnum; duos bonos Iovem & venerem: Mercurius vero talis est, qualis ille, cui jungitur. unde etiam fingitur minister esse Deorum, quod eorum obtemperat potestati. Hinc est quod dicit: In quos Cœli orbes errat Cyllenius ignis; id est, utrum in Septemtrionalem aut in Australem partem inclinetur; aut cui Planetarum cohærcat, ut qua itatem Mercurij ex illo possis agnoscere. Hinc denique, quod Sermonis, Galeno Pergameno in Suasoria, Macrobio lib. i. Sat. cap. xix, Augustino lib. de Civit. Dei vii. cap. xiv. Horatij Commentariorubus in i. Car. Od. x; quod Orationis, Porphyrio in Physiologia; quod Eloquentiæ, veteri apud Salisberiensem Scriptori; quod Pacis Belliqve, Ovidio v. Fastorum; quod omnium negotiorum habitus fuerit Deus, Festo lib. xi. de Verb. signif. Omnium Stellarum centetur minima. Anno vertente cum Sole circumagitur. Character ♀, Caduceus: de quo Servius ad iv. Æneid. Hyginus in Lyra, Phurnutus, alij. Hinc Mercurius Ovidio Caduciferi; Arnobio libro tertio adversus gentes Caduceator. Virga dicitur Virgilio iv. Æneid. & Horatio i. Carm. Od. x. quam torto Dracone conspicuam facit Martialis lib. vii epig. lxxii. Colubros agnoscunt alij; unde Mercurius Arnobio lib. iv. Gestator adfabilium Colubrarum. Videndus Isidorus lib. viii. Originum cap. xi, ubi elegans Mythologia.
units.tr: Mercury is below Venus; the Moon is higher. The Greeks call it Syllon [Σὺλλων], in Cicero, Martianus and Apuleius; the Hebrews call it kokab, star [בכב ἀστὴρ]. John of Salisbury describes its nature thus in his Policraticus, or On the Trifles of Courtiers, book II, chapter 19: Mercury is such as the neighbouring planets have made him, since he is himself of a changeable nature and clings to the more powerful. Hence most think him the patron of eloquence, because when joined to Wisdom he has done the greatest good; in company with Malice he does the greatest harm. He implies that whatever Mercury joins himself to, he shares his powers with it, and becomes harmful or wholesome according to the application and aspect of the harmful or wholesome star. Hence Apuleius, in On the World, calls him the common star: For although the whole heaven turns in a single revolution, and is divided into night and day, separated by unequal measures of time, and although one sphere encloses everything, yet by the waxing and waning of its globe the Moon marks the monthly times of light, and the Sun, by its yearly return, lights up the space of heaven; and its companions are the pleasant Lucifer and the common Cyllenian star, etc. For some, wrongly thinking it false, have altered the genuine reading of that learned writer there and substituted comis stella, the friendly star. Hence the poets regarded him as Minister of the Gods, as Servius notes on Georgics book I, where he says: It must be written, as we have said, that of the five planets two are harmful, Mars and Saturn, and two are good, Jupiter and Venus; but Mercury is such as the one to which he is joined. Hence he is also imagined to be the minister of the gods, because he obeys their power. Hence what he says: "Into which orbits of the heavens the Cyllenian fire wanders," that is, whether he inclines toward the northern or the southern part, or which planet he clings to, so that from that you may know the quality of Mercury. Hence finally he is called the god of speech by Galen of Pergamum in his Suasoria, by Macrobius in Saturnalia book I, chapter 19, and by Augustine in City of God book VII, chapter 14; the god of oratory by Porphyry in his Physiology; the god of eloquence by an older writer cited by Salisbury; the god of peace and war by Ovid, Fasti book V; and his character was that of the god of all business, according to Festus, On the Meaning of Words, book XI. He is counted the least of all the stars; in the course of a year he is carried round with the Sun. His symbol is ♀, the caduceus, on which see Servius on Aeneid IV, Hyginus in Lyra, Phurnutus and others. Hence Ovid calls Mercury caduciferus, the caduceus-bearer, and Arnobius in book III, Against the Nations, caduceator, the herald. Virgil in Aeneid IV and Horace in Odes I, ode 10, call it a virga, a rod, which Martial in book VII, epigram 72, makes conspicuous with a twisted serpent. Others recognise serpents, whence Arnobius in book IV calls Mercury the bearer of affable serpents. See Isidore, Origins book VIII, chapter 11, where there is an elegant mythology.

units.la: CAP. XXVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVII.

units.la: De Luna.
units.tr: On the Moon.

units.la: LUNA restat explicanda, Sidus novissimum, Terrisque familiarissimum, & in tenebrarum remedium ab natura repertum; quo contemplantium oculis vicinius, eo magis eorundem multiformi sua ambage torquens ingenia: Magistra omnium, quæ in Cœlo pernoscí potuerunt, propter Velocitatem ipsius motus unde & Pro& Ptolemæus per Lunæ locum investigavit loca Stellarum Fixarum; & rursum per hæc vera Planetarum loca; quemadmodum variis locis scribit Plinius.
units.tr: The Moon remains to be explained: the lowest of the heavenly bodies, the most familiar to the Earth, and provided by nature as a remedy for darkness. The nearer it is to the eyes of those who gaze upon it, the more it turns their minds with its manifold wandering. It is the teacher of all the things that could be learned about the heavens, because of the swiftness of its motion. Hence Ptolemy also used the place of the Moon to investigate the places of the fixed stars, and again, through these, the true places of the planets, as Pliny writes in various places.

units.la: Luna, quasi lucens una; ut Sol, quod solus; alijs quod luce luceat alienâ; qua de re alibi
units.tr: The Moon is named as if it were "lucens una," shining alone, as the Sun is named because it is alone (solus). Others say it is because it shines with a borrowed light (alienā luce). On this matter, elsewhere.

units.la: De variis cognitionibus, Dianæ, Lucinæ, Proserpinæ, Hecates & similibus, dixerunt alij: sufficiat monuisse Græcis Σελήνη vel ut alij, Σελωνίαι, quasi, σελασνοαςια vocatam ὃα σίλας νεόντε κχ ἑινεντηζ ἀεὶ. Nam singulis mensibus ab Sole digrediens, velut novo lumine hausto conceptoque, sensim auget, aliasque atque alias induit formas; donec Soli ex diametro obiecta orbe pleno refulgeat: inde vicissim ad Solem revertens, lumine deficiente, paullatim senescit, ac vice versa eadem figuras adquirit, donec radios Solis subiens prorsus ex oculis evanescat Hebræis appellarur ירח, quod motu suo respirationem præbeat rebus, quæ interdiu Solis ardore marcuerant.
units.tr: Others have spoken about its various names: Diana, Lucina, Proserpina, Hecate and the like. It is enough to remind the reader that the Greeks call it Selene, or, as others have it, Selenaia, as if from a phrase meaning "light ever new" [σέλας νέον τε καὶ ἀεί]. For each month, as it departs from the Sun, it grows gradually, as if it had drawn in and taken up a new light, and takes on one shape after another, until it shines in full orbit, opposite the Sun across the diameter. Then, returning in turn toward the Sun as its light fails, it gradually wanes; and in the reverse order it acquires the same shapes again, until, entering the Sun's rays, it vanishes completely from sight. The Hebrews call it יָרֵחַ [yareach], because by its motion it gives breathing space to things that had wilted during the day under the Sun's heat.

units.la: Lucet lumine non proprio, sed alieno, quod mutuatur à Sole: quamquam ipsa nativum quoddam habeat lumen & congenitum, sed exile & obscurum. Sententia hæc Orphei, Stoicorum & Pythagoreorum apud Laertium lib. vii. & viii; Parmenidis; ut notat Eusebius lib. iii. de Præparat. Euangelica, cap. xxxiii; Pisidæ in ϰσ-μυρν. & quorum non? Sic Catullus Carmine Seculari: Tu Lucina dolentibus Iuno dicta puerperis: Tu potens Trivia; & notho es Dicta lumine Luna.
units.tr: It shines not with its own light but with another's, which it borrows from the Sun. Yet it has a light of its own, native and innate, but faint and dim. This opinion belongs to Orpheus, the Stoics and the Pythagoreans, as reported by Laertius in books 7 and 8; to Parmenides, as Eusebius notes in book 3 of the Preparation for the Gospel, chapter 33; and to Pisides in his work on the... [the Greek title is garbled in the scan]; and to whom not? So Catullus in the Secular Song: "You, Lucina, called Juno by women in childbirth; you, mighty Trivia; and you are called the Moon by a borrowed light."

units.la: Sic Seneca Medea, Choro Actus i: Quum Phoebe solitum, lumine non suo, Orbem circuitus cornu usadiugat.
units.tr: So Seneca in the Medea, Chorus of Act 1: "When Phoebe, shining with no light of her own, yokes the orb of her circuit to her horns..."

units.la: Addam Willerami Abbatis, à me nuper editi, illud in Cantica Canticorum de Ecclesia Christi: Siu thinket mir gelych therro Auroræ; Wanda fiu post tenebras infidelitatis havet sich bekeret ad verum Lumen: unde thunket mir aiso fiona, so ther Mano; Wanda fiu wie weiz thaz fiu thie pulchritudinem Virtutum von huo selvero niet ne havet, funder zon Godes genathan; niet te me than ther Mano iehr lights havet himo selvemo, secundum Physicos, woven ex inlustratione Solis. Et hæc causa, quur, quam ceteri Sororem, Æschylus & Euripides Filiam Solis Lunam nuncuparint. Chaldæi Lunam proprij perpetuique Luminis compotem esse voluerunt, si fides Apuleio, libro de Deo Socratis. Lunam autem Lumen ab Sole per Penetrationem recipere, non per reflectionem, arbitratur Averroes: fretus cum auctoritate Avenpacis, tum ratione. Nam inquit, si posteriore modo fieret illud; totius nostri hemisphæ ȳ universa' is non fieret in' uminatio: sed tantùm quanta Lunæ magnitudo. Verum ita sententi obstat, quod sic Luna semper plena videretur lumine. Dicendum potius, partes, quæ in Lunæ ϫφεγέα rariores esse & puriores; eamque ob causam, quod pervia, magis ab Sole inlustrari & nitere? quæ Centri, centroque propiores, densiores esse; & quod opacæ, lumen obtusius admittere, quum ob soliditatem densiorem penetrare Solis radij nequeant. Hinc in Luna parent intuentibus Maculæ: de quibus tamen varie sentiunt Philosophi, quemadmodum legere est cum apud alios, tum apud Averroem lib. ii. Cœli, Commen. xlix. & cap. ii. de subst. orbis. Sunt enim qui contingere volunt illas ex corporis inter nos & Lunam interpositione, qua plena Lunæ claritas nobis avertitur. Alij apud eundem alia. Nonnulli Campos fabulantur Elysios. Plinius lib. ii. nat. hist. cap. ix. dicit esse notas terreni humoris, ab Luna attracti. Theologorum ævo nostro quidam scribunt, indicia jam nunc esse Corruptionis Cœli, de qua non uno loco Sacra Scriptura. Verisimile autem maculas hasce, unde sint occasionem dedisse Thaleti Philosopho, sentiendi Lunam esse Terram nebula obvolutam, Anaxagoræ & Democrito Colles, Convallesque ibi somniandi; Pythagoreis, non solum Terram opinandi, sed habitari etiam ut hanc inferiorem; alijs omnia ibi, quæ apud nos inveniuntur, imaginandi. De quibus Plutarch. περὶ τ̄ ης φιλοσοφ. Αἰσ-σκοντ. cap. xxxiii. xxv. & xxx. Achilles Statius in Aratum. Ioannes Picus Comes Mirandulanus opere doctissimo & absolutissimo contra Astrologos. Et hinc luno apud Senecam in Hercule Furente Act. i: Tellus Gigante Doris excusso tremens Suppositá monstri colla terrifici levet, Sublimis alias Luna excipiat Feras.
units.tr: I will add a passage from Abbot Willeram, which I lately edited, on the Song of Songs concerning the Church of Christ: "Siu thinket mir gelych therro Auroræ [She seems to me like the dawn]; wanda fiu post tenebras infidelitatis havet sich bekeret ad verum Lumen [since she, after the darkness of unbelief, has turned to the true Light]; unde thunket mir aiso fiona, so ther Mano [and so she seems to me like the moon]; wanda fiu wie weiz thaz fiu thie pulchritudinem Virtutum von huo selvero niet ne havet, funder zon Godes genathan [since she, as is known, has the beauty of virtues not from herself but by the grace of God]; niet te me than ther Mano iehr lights havet himo selvemo, secundum Physicos, woven ex inlustratione Solis." And this is the reason why Aeschylus and Euripides called the Moon the daughter of the Sun, whom the others called her sister. The Chaldeans wished the Moon to possess a light of its own and perpetual, if we trust Apuleius in his book on the god of Socrates. But Averroes holds that the Moon receives light from the Sun by penetration, not by reflection, relying both on the authority of Avenpace and on reason: "For," he says, "if it happened in the latter way, illumination would not come to the whole of our hemisphere, but only to an area as large as the Moon itself." Yet this opinion is hindered by the fact that the Moon would then always seem full of light. It must rather be said that the parts of the Moon which are rarer and purer are more penetrated by the Sun and shine more brightly, and for this reason, because they are porous; while those nearer the centre are denser, and because they are opaque they admit light more dimly, since the rays of the Sun cannot penetrate their denser solidity. Hence spots appear to observers on the Moon, about which the philosophers hold varying views, as one may read both in other writers and in Averroes, book 2 of On the Heavens, commentary 49, and chapter 2 on the substance of the sphere. Some want them to be caused by the interposition of a body between us and the Moon, by which the full brightness of the Moon is turned away from us. Others hold other views, in the same author. Some tell fables of Elysian Fields. Pliny, Natural History, book 2, chapter 9, says they are marks of earthly moisture drawn up by the Moon. Some theologians of our own age write that these are already signs of the corruption of the heavens, of which Holy Scripture speaks in more than one place. It is likely that these spots gave occasion to the philosopher Thales to think the Moon was the Earth wrapped in mist; to Anaxagoras and Democritus, that there were hills and valleys there, which they imagined; to the Pythagoreans, not only to suppose it was an earth but that it was inhabited, like this lower one; and to others, to imagine there everything that is found among us. On these matters see Plutarch, On the Opinions of the Philosophers, chapters 33, 25 and 30; Achilles Statius on Aratus; and Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, Count of Mirandola, in his most learned and complete work against the Astrologers. And hence Juno says in Seneca's Hercules Furens, Act 1: "Let the earth, trembling, with Doris having shaken off the Giant, raise the neck of the monster, lying beneath; and let the Moon, lifted high, receive the wild beasts..."

units.la: Innuit (quod & alij scribunt non solum de Leone, sed & ceteris monstris ἐκτόπους & praeter naturam) Nemeaeum Leonem ex orbe Lunari decidisse, alium adversus fortissimum heroem emendicans. Epimenides: χαὶ γὰρ ἐγὼ ᾄδω ἐμοὶ Σελάνας ῥυκόμοιο, ἃ δλεινοι Φεῖξαο' ἀπωσάσαν Διὸς ἐξ Λεοντος ἐν Νεμέῃ ἀχεῖο' αὐτὴν Διὶ πότνια ἡγεν.
units.tr: He hints (as others also write, not only of the Lion but of the other monsters, which are out of place and contrary to nature) that the Nemean Lion fell from the Lunar sphere, begging for another to fight against the most valiant hero. Epimenides: "For I too sing of the Moon with lovely hair, which, having been cast down from the lion of Zeus, the lady of the gods led herself to Zeus in Nemea" [καὶ γὰρ ἐγὼ ᾄδω ἐμοὶ Σελάνας ῥυκόμοιο ... Διὶ πότνια ἡγεν].

units.la: Claudius de Tauro ab Hercule domito:
units.tr: Claudius on the Bull, tamed by Hercules:

units.la: Taurus medio nam sidere Luna Progenitus, Dictaea Iovis possederat arva.
units.tr: For the Bull was born under the middle star of the Moon, and had held the Dictaean fields of Jupiter.

units.la: Idem de Dianae curru: Currum subiere jugales, Quos decus esse Dea primi sub limine Caeli Roscida fecundis concepit Luna cavernis.
units.tr: Also on the chariot of Diana: The yoked team came beneath the chariot, which the goddess Moon conceived in her fruitful, dewy caverns, as the glory of the first, beneath the threshold of heaven.

units.la: Quum ergo opaca sit Luna, lucem admittit inaequaliter, medietate tantum sui orbis vel paullo amplius; ea parte, qua ad Solem versa. Hinc varie nostris se oculis exhibet, modo nulla, alias dimidia, interdum plena. Formae, quas Luna alias atque augendo diminuendoque induit, Graecis φάσεις atque Σχήματα dicuntur, varijsque appellantur nominibus. Species enim Crescentis, suaque Cornua Orienti obvertentis (Experientia apud Plinium libro II. nat. hist. cap. XIV. docente) quarto (tertio alijs, qui in sequentibus numeris etiam paullum evariant) mensis die dicitur κεραστὴς vel μηνοειδὴς falcata, in cornua quum cernitur curvata: Septimo die διχότομος vel ἡμίνομος, dimidia & aequa portione divisa; Undecimo ἀμφίκυρτος, utrimque gibbosa & praetumida, quum aliquid deest integro orbi; decimoquinto πανσέληνος, plena: Senescentis autem suisque cornibus Occidentem spectantis effigies contrario ordine appellatur, decimonono die ἀμφίκυρτος: Vicesimo secundo iterum διχότομος; Vicesimo sexto μηνοειδής: Tricesimo denique cum Sole Luna facit congressum, qui Σύνοδος Graecis & Νουμηνία; Latinis Conjunctio, Coitus, Novilunium, Interlunium; Virgilius & Plinius Silentia Lunae vocant. Quae dixi paucis sic notat Macrobius in Somnium Scipionis: Luna dispensationibus septenarys luminis sui vires sempiterna lege variando disponit. Primis septem diebus dimidia a semi-orbem ostendit; vocaturque dimidia. Secundis totum orbem complet, fitque Plenilunium. Tertijs rursus efficitur dimidia. Quartis fit coitus Lunae cum Sole, quod Interlunium nominatur. Est enim tempus inter deficientem & nascentem Lunam, hoc est, tricesimus dies, in quo Luna non lucet. Nam quum Soli conjuncta sit ita obscuratur ut minime possit videri; sed eodem momento renascens, paullatim ab eo recedendo, videtur. Adeundus & Plinius lib. II. natur. histor. cap. IX & lib. XVIII. cap. XXXIII. Causas harum Formarum aperit erudite Vitellio libro IV. Opticae, cap. LXXIV, & tribus seqq. Ob hanc igitur instabilitatem recte Ovidius XV. Metamorph. Necpar aut eadem nocturna firma Diana Esse potest usquam: semperque hodierna sequente, Si crevit, minor est; major, si contrahit orbem.
units.tr: Since the Moon is dark, it admits light unevenly, only over half its orb or a little more, on the side turned toward the Sun. Hence it presents itself to our eyes in various ways: sometimes not at all, sometimes halved, sometimes full. The forms that the Moon takes on as it waxes and wanes are called phases [φάσεις] and figures [Σχήματα] by the Greeks, and they have various names. For the crescent, with its horns turned toward the east (as Pliny in book 2 of the Natural History, chapter 14, teaches from experience), on the fourth day of the month (on the third, according to others, who also vary slightly in the following numbers) is called κεραστὴς or μηνοειδὴς, "horned," because it is seen curved into horns. On the seventh day it is διχότομος or ἡμίνομος, divided into halves in equal portions. On the eleventh it is ἀμφίκυρτος, gibbous and very swollen on both sides, since something is still lacking to the full orb. On the fifteenth it is πανσέληνος, full. But when it wanes, and its horns face the west, the figure is named in reverse order: on the nineteenth day ἀμφίκυρτος again; on the twenty-second διχότομος again; on the twenty-sixth μηνοειδής. Finally, on the thirtieth day the Moon comes together with the Sun, which is called σύνοδος by the Greeks and νουμηνία; by the Latins conjunctio, coitus, novilunium, interlunium; Virgil and Pliny call it the silence of the Moon. Macrobius in his commentary on the Dream of Scipio briefly sums up what I have said: the Moon, by its seven-day cycles, varies the strength of its light by an unchanging law. For the first seven days it shows a half-orb, and is called a half-moon. In the second seven it completes the whole orb, and there is a full moon. In the third seven it again becomes a half-moon. In the fourth, the Moon comes together with the Sun, which is called the interlunium. For there is a time between the waning and the new Moon, that is, the thirtieth day, in which the Moon does not shine. For when it is joined to the Sun it is so obscured that it cannot be seen at all; but at the same moment, being reborn, it gradually withdraws from the Sun and becomes visible. Pliny, book 2, chapter 9, and book 18, chapter 33, should also be consulted. Vitellio, in book 4 of his Optics, chapter 74 and the three following, explains the causes of these forms learnedly. Because of this instability, Ovid rightly says in Metamorphoses book 15: "Nor can Diana, the night-time goddess, remain the same anywhere, but always changes from day to day: if she has grown, she is smaller; if she has shrunk, she is larger in her orb."

units.la: Et Horatius lib. II Carminum; Ode XI. Non semper idem floribus est honos Vernis: neque uno Luna rubens nitet Vultu, quid aeternis minorem Consilius animum fatigas?
units.tr: And Horace in book 2 of the Odes, Ode 11: "The honour of the flowers is not always the same in spring, nor does the Moon shine with one blushing face. Why do you wear down your mind, which is smaller than eternal things, with your cares?"

units.la: Lunae crescentis sic decrescentisque imaginem Σελωίνῃ gestare, reddereque enim in dies singulos, scribunt Plinius lib. XXXVII, cap. X. ex Dioscoride, qui mutilior hodie illo loco, & Georgius Agricola lib. V. de natura Fossilium. De Quarta Luna singulare hoc legitur, quod, ex Genethliacorum doctrina & praeceptis, illa nati Laboriosam acturi sint vitam, quemadmodum de Hercule prodit Eustathius. Tales apud Sudam Τετραδίται vocantur, qui quarta Luna editi laboribus periculisque adsiduis, ut alteri Hercules, involvuntur. Herculis Sidus apud Florum I. hist. Rom. cap. XVIII, nihil aliud quam quarta Luna. Adagium ἐν πνεῦμά γεγονέναι ab alijs explicatur. Elegans plenae Lunae Encomium est apud Senecam Hippolito, Choro Act. II: Pulcrior tanto tua forma lucet, Clarior quanto micat orbe pleno; Quum suos ignes æquante cornu Iunxit, & curru properante pernox Exserit vultus rubicunda Phœbe, Nec tenent Stellæ faciem minores.
units.tr: Pliny in book 37, chapter 10, drawing on Dioscorides (whose text at that place is more mutilated today than it was then), and Georgius Agricola in book 5 of On the Nature of Fossils, write that the image of the waxing and waning Moon is carried by the moonstone [Selenites], which reflects it day by day. A singular belief is read about the fourth Moon: according to the teaching and precepts of the astrologers of nativities, those born under it are destined to lead a laborious life, as Eustathius reports of Hercules. Among such persons, in Suidas, are called Tetraditai, those born on the fourth Moon, who are entangled in constant labours and dangers, like Hercules. The star of Hercules in Florus, Roman History book 1, chapter 18, is nothing other than the fourth Moon. The proverb "to have been born in the breath" [ἐν πνεῦμά γεγονέναι] is explained by others. There is an elegant encomium of the full Moon in Seneca's Hippolytus, Chorus, Act 2: "Your beauty shines as much brighter as it sparkles with the full orb. When the reddening Phoebus, with a hastening chariot, has joined its fires to the equal horn and shows its face through the whole night, the lesser stars do not keep their brightness."

units.la: Simile Boetij illud: Vt nunc pleno lucida cornu, Totis fratris & obvia flammis, Condat Stellas Luna minores.
units.tr: Similar is that of Boethius: "As now the Moon, bright with its full horn, and facing the flames of its brother with its whole light, hides the lesser stars."

units.la: Easdem Lunæ, pleno Lumine lucentis, vires expressit optime Claudianus his versibus: Haud secus ac tacitam Luna regnante per Arcton, Siderea cedunt facies, quum fratre retuso Æmulus adversis flagraverit ignibus orbis. Tunc iubar Arcturi languet; tunc fulva Leonis Ira perit; Plaustro iam rara intermicat Arctos Indignata regi; iam, caligantibus armis, Debilis Orion dextram miratur inermem.
units.tr: Claudian expressed the same powers of the full-lit Moon very well in these verses: "Not otherwise, when the Moon reigns through the silent Arctos, the starry faces give way; when its brother is pushed back and the rival orb blazes with opposing fires. Then the brightness of Arcturus grows faint; then the tawny anger of the Lion dies away; the Bear, now rarely glimmering from the Wain, is indignant at the king; now Orion, with his arms dimmed, wonders at his own weak, unarmed right hand."

units.la: Lunæ Corpus Astronomi clarissimi, Ptolemæus quidem (cui omnes fere sequentes subscripserunt) Terra minus tricesies novies & unitate plus esse; Copernicus autem quadragies ter minus octava parte, deprehendisse se notant: ut falsa sint, quæ de Luna, maximum eam Cœli post Solem Astrum esse scribit ad cap. 1. Geneseos, & lib. 11. de Genesi ad litteram, cap. xvi. Basilius, quod antea monui. De Lunæ magnitudine eleganter Plinius lib. 11. nat. hist. cap. xi. & xiv.
units.tr: Regarding the body of the Moon, the most famous astronomers: Ptolemy (whom nearly all who came after him followed) observed that the Moon is smaller than the Earth by thirty-nine times and one more; but Copernicus found it forty-three times smaller, less an eighth part. Thus those things are false which Basil wrote about the Moon, that it is the greatest star of heaven after the Sun, in his commentary on Genesis chapter 1 and in book 2 of the On Genesis, chapter 16, as I noted before. On the size of the Moon, Pliny in book 2 of the Natural History, chapters 11 and 14, speaks elegantly.

units.la: De Orbibus Lunæ Eccentricis, Concentricis, & Epicyclis abunde Ptolemæus alijque Mathematici.
units.tr: On the eccentric, concentric and epicyclic orbits of the Moon, Ptolemy and other mathematicians speak at length.

units.la: Lunæ Novæ & Plenæ maximam ab terreno globo distantiam Ptolemæus indicat lxiv. semidiametr. x. scrupul. Recentiores lxv. semidiatr. xxx. scrupul. Minimam lv. semidiam. viii. scrupul. Lunæ vero ἀπογεῖον altitudinem maximam lxviii semidiametr. xx. scrupul. minimam vero semidiatr. lii. scrupul. xvii. Consulendi hac de re, præter novitios, Plinius lib. 11. cap. xxi. Ptolemæus lib. v. mag. Compos. & propos. xvii. quinti Epit. Vitellio item lib. Optic. x, propos. lix.
units.tr: Ptolemy gives the greatest distance of the Moon from the terrestrial globe at new and full moon as 64 semidiameters and 10 scruples; more recent writers give 65 semidiameters and 30 scruples. The least is 55 semidiameters and 8 scruples. The greatest altitude of the Moon at its apogee is 68 semidiameters and 20 scruples, and the least 52 semidiameters and 17 scruples. For this matter, besides beginners, one should consult Pliny, book 2, chapter 21; Ptolemy, book 5 of the Almagest, proposition 17; the fifth book of the Epitome; and likewise Vitellio, book 10 of the Optics, proposition 59.

units.la: Luna non solum in Eccentrico Circulo movetur; sed motus sui aliam etiam habet lineam; quæ deflectit hinc ad Boream, inde ad Austrum ab Ecliptica, duobus eam intersecans locis, qui Nodi Latinis, Græcis Σωδεσμοί vocantur. Eorum unus ad Boreum latus, Ἀναβιβάζων, Ascendens, recentioribus Caput Draconis; alter ad Meridionalem plagam Καταβιβάζων, Descendens, Draconis Cauda dicitur. Zodiacum adsiduo motu (unde Arnobio libro i. adversi gentes, Luna in motu indefinens, vel indefes; alterutrum enim substituendum in locum corruptioris ibi vocis Indemnis) perlustrat spacio dierum vigenti septem, horarum septem; additis scrupulis, primis quidem quadraginta tribus, secundis vero septem. Videndus Plinius lib. 11. cap. ix.
units.tr: The Moon moves not only on an eccentric circle, but also has another line of its motion, which bends from there toward the north and from here toward the south, away from the ecliptic, cutting it at two points, which are called nodes in Latin and σύνδεσμοι by the Greeks. One of them, on the northern side, is called ἀναβιβάζων, the ascending node, and by more recent writers the Head of the Dragon; the other, on the southern region, καταβιβάζων, the descending node, is called the Tail of the Dragon. By its constant motion it traverses the zodiac in twenty-seven days and seven hours, plus forty-three primes and seven seconds of scruples. (Arnobius in book 1 of Against the Nations calls the Moon "in motion, not failing" [indefinens], or "indefatigable" [indefes]; for one of these must be substituted for the corrupt word "indemnis" found there.) See Pliny, book 2, chapter 9.

units.la: Ad Lunæ Cursum Veteres Tempus Menstruum metiri solitos, innuit Theodoretus de Providentia, serm. i. Τὰ ἡμέρας ἐκ τῆς Σελήνης τὸ μέτρον λαμβάνοντας, ἐπεὶ γὰρ καὶ τῆς ἀποσπάσεως μετάλαξεν. μῆνα γὰρ ἐνεμάζοντα τῷ Σελήνῳ. Idem alij notant ex Macrobio lib. i. cap. xvi. Censorino de die Nat. & Aristophanis aliorumque Interpretibus.
units.tr: That the ancients customarily measured the course of the Moon by the monthly period is hinted at by Theodoret in his first sermon On Providence: "Those who take the measure of days from the Moon, since indeed it changed the separation, for the Moon makes a month..." [Τὰ ἡμέρας ἐκ τῆς Σελήνης τὸ μέτρον λαμβάνοντας, ἐπεὶ γὰρ καὶ τῆς ἀποσπάσεως μετάλαξεν. μῆνα γὰρ ἐνεμάζοντα τῷ Σελήνῳ.] Others note the same from Macrobius, book 1, chapter 16, from Censorinus On the Birthday, and from the commentators on Aristophanes and others.

units.la: Eclipsis Lunæ, nihil aliud, quam defectus sive privatio luminis Solaris in Lunari corpore. Fit, quoties incidit in umbram, quam in oppositam ex diametro Soli partem jacit Terra: Tunc enim necesse est Lunam, quum alieno, id est, Solis lumine luceat, obtenebrari & ἐκλείπειν pati. Incidit autem, quoties lumine plena Soli opponitur in altero Nodorum, de quibus paullo ante dixi: si quidem exacte in ipsis Nodis, fit integra; sin extra Nodos, non longe tamen ab ijs digressa intra limites defectionum manens, particulatim digitis aliquot. Vsitatissima Mathematicis utor voce. Sunt enim Digiti, quæ & Unciæ, nihil aliud quam duodecimæ Diametri Lunæ vel Solis partes. Extra Nodos & Defectionis metas Lunæ nihil accedit detrimenti. De Eclipsi, ejusque Causis & Speciebus, quare item una altera diutius duret, multa Mathematici. Paucis Macrobius lib. i. in Somn. Scip. cap. xv. & Plinius lib. 11. cap. x. Sic
units.tr: An eclipse of the Moon is nothing other than the defect or privation of the Sun's light in the body of the Moon. It happens whenever the Moon falls into the shadow which the Earth casts on the part of the Sun opposite to it on the same diameter: for then the Moon, which shines with another's light, that is, the light of the Sun, must necessarily be darkened and suffer an eclipse [ἐκλείπειν]. It falls out whenever the full Moon is opposed to the Sun at one of the nodes I spoke of a little earlier: if indeed it is exactly at the nodes themselves, the eclipse is total; but if outside the nodes, not far from them yet remaining within the limits of the defects, it is partial, by some digits. I use the most common term of the mathematicians. For "digits," which are also called "inches," are nothing other than the twelfth parts of the diameter of the Moon or the Sun. Outside the nodes and the limits of the defects, the Moon suffers no loss. Mathematicians write much about the eclipse, its causes and kinds, and why one lasts longer than another. Briefly, Macrobius in book 1 of the Commentary on the Dream of Scipio, chapter 15, and Pliny, book 2, chapter 10, treat it. Thus:

units.la: Lucanus lib. 1. Tempus & caussam Lunaris Eclipseos indicans: —— cornuque coacto Iam Phabe toto fratrem quum redderet orbe, Terrarum subita percussa expalluit umbra.
units.tr: Lucan, book 1, showing the time and cause of a lunar eclipse: "And when, her horns drawn together, Phoebe was just giving back her brother's full orbit, the earth's sudden shadow struck her and she grew pale."

units.la: Plinius etiam lib. 11. cap. xiii. ex Hipparcho docet, Lunæ defectum aliquando fieri quinto mense à priore; item contingere, utroque super Terram conspicuo Sidere: utrumque denique Sidus nonnumquam defectum pati solitum spacio xv. dierum. Quod verum esse, parebit aliquando ex meo Συγγεονσμῶ centum, qui proxime lapsi, annorum. In eo enim video annis ab Christo nato, supra sesquimillesimum, secundo, decimooctavo, & sequenti, tricesimoquarto, quadragesimoquarto, & alias, Eclipses accidisse Solis Lunæque intra spacium xv. dierum. Quo modo autem hoc fiat, perspicuis demonstrationibus aperiunt Ioannes Regiomontanus doctissima Epitoma in Almagestum, & Iacobi Zieglerus atque Milichius Commentariis suis in Plinium. Existimabant Antiqui, quum Lunam deficere viderent, Carmine Magico solicitari, & sic rubore suffundi. Seneca Hippolyto Choro Act. 11. At nos solliciti lumine turbido, Tractam Thessalicis carminibus rati, Tinnitus dedimus.
units.tr: Pliny also teaches, in book 2, chapter 13, on the authority of Hipparchus, that an eclipse of the Moon sometimes happens five months after the previous one; that it occurs when both luminaries are visible above the earth; and finally that each of the two heavenly bodies sometimes suffers an eclipse within a space of fifteen days. That this is true will sometimes appear from my Synchronismus [συγχρονισμός] of the last hundred years. In it I find that in the years after Christ's birth, above 1500, namely in the 2nd, the 18th and the following year, the 34th, the 44th and others, eclipses of the Sun and Moon occurred within fifteen days of each other. How this happens is set out in clear demonstrations by Regiomontanus in his most learned Epitome of the Almagest, and by Jacob Ziegler and Milich in their commentaries on Pliny. The ancients thought that when they saw the Moon failing she was being summoned by magic song, and so was suffused with redness. Seneca, in the chorus of the Hippolytus, act 2: "But we, anxious at the troubled light, thinking her drawn down by Thessalian charms, gave out a clanging."

units.la: Plinius: Deliquio Solis & Lunæ venificia arguente mortalitate, & ob id crepitu dissono auxiliante. Opinionem hanc tam superstitiose imbiberant Athenienses, ut eos, qui veram Eclipsis causam adferebant, tamquam impios, vivos exurerent, teste Plutarcho in Pericle. De Rubore autem, praeter alios, Ovidius lib. 11. Amor. Eleg. v: Quale Rosæ fulgent inter sua Lilia missæ, Aut ubi tantatis Luna laborat equis.
units.tr: Pliny: "When an eclipse of the Sun and Moon indicates poisonings by the death rate, and for that reason a discordant clattering comes to the rescue." The Athenians were so steeped in this superstition that they burned alive, as impious men, those who gave the true cause of an eclipse, according to Plutarch in his Life of Pericles. On the redness, besides others, Ovid, Amores book 2, elegy 5: "Like roses shining when sent among their lilies, or where the Moon labours with her harnessed horses."

units.la: Thessalis præcipue vis hæc & potentia tributa. Soliphanes in Meleagro: Μάγοις ἱπωδαῖς πᾶσι Θεσσαλὴς χθὼν, Ψιλὰς Σελήνης αὐτὴς καταβαλὰς.
units.tr: This power and might was attributed especially to the Thessalians. Soliphanes in the Meleager: "The whole land of Thessaly, with magic incantations, brings down the bare Moon herself" [Μάγοις ἐπῳδαῖς πᾶσα Θεσσαλὴ χθὼν ψιλὰς Σελήνης αὐτὴν καταβάλλει].

units.la: Seneca Medea, Act. iv: Video Triviæ currus agiles; Non quos pleno lucida vultu, Pernox agitat, sed quos facie Lurida maesta, quum Thessalicis Vexata minis, Cælum freno Propiore legit.
units.tr: Seneca, Medea, act 4: "I see the swift chariots of Trivia, not those which the bright Moon drives with full face, but those which, pale and sad of face, harassed by Thessalian threats, drives the sky with a nearer rein."

units.la: Lucanus passim lib. vi. Belli Pharsalici. Errores hujusmodi refutas eleganter, Quisquis es Antiquorum Vatum: Non illam, ut populi credunt, nigrantibus antris Infernas ululans mulier praedira subumbras Detrahit altivago è speculo, nec carmine victa Vincibilemque petit clamorem. Quippe per athram, Qua citimus limes dispescit turbida puris, Inviolata meat: sed vasto corpore Tellus, Quæ medium tenet ima polum, dum lumina fratris Detinet umbriferis metis, tum Sidere cæso, Pallescit teres umbra rotæ: dum transeat axem Aggerei velox tumuli, speculoque rosanti Fraternas reparet per Cælum libera flammas.
units.tr: Lucan, throughout book 6 of the Pharsalia. Whoever you are among the ancient poets, you refute such errors elegantly: "It is not she, as the people believe, whom a woman howling in dark caves, a fearsome sorceress, drags down from her high-wandering mirror with the aid of spells, nor does she seek a shout that she can be conquered by. For she passes unharmed through the air where the boundary of the sky divides the turbid from the pure. But the earth, with its vast body, which holds the middle place beneath the pole, while it keeps its brother's light in its shadowy bounds, then, when the Sun is struck down, her round shadow grows pale; until the swift shadow of the earth's mound passes the axis and, the mirror glowing again, the free Moon restores her brother's flames across the sky."

units.la: Obiter hic superstitio notanda Veterum, qui soliti Lunæ deficienti æreorum vasorum tinnitu, tubarumque strepitu auxiliari, quemadmodum docent Tacitus lib. 1. & Plutarch. in vita Æmilij. Sic Ovidius lib. vii. Metamorph. Te quoque Luna traho, quamvis Themesea labores Aera tuos minuant.
units.tr: Here, in passing, the superstition of the ancients is to be noted: they were accustomed to help the failing Moon with the clang of bronze vessels and the blare of trumpets, as Tacitus, book 1, and Plutarch in the Life of Aemilius teach. So Ovid, Metamorphoses book 7: "I too draw you down, Luna, though the bronze of Thessaly lessens your labours."

units.la: Tibullus lib. 1. Eleg. viii. —— è curru Lunam deducere tentat: Et faceret, si non era repulsa sonent.
units.tr: Tibullus, book 1, elegy 8: "She tries to draw the Moon down from her chariot; and she would do it, if the bronze had not sounded to drive her off."

units.la: Manilius lib. 1. Astronom. de Lunæ deliquio; quod non uno & eodem tempore ab omnibus conspicitur:
units.tr: Manilius, Astronomica book 1, on the eclipse of the Moon, which is not seen at one and the same time by all:

units.la: Ultimo Vltima ad Hesperios infectis volveris alis: Seraque in extremis quatiuntur gentibus aera, Sic Seneca paullo ante in Hippolyto: & Medea Act. iv: ——— sic face trifstem Pallida lucem funde per auras, Horrore novo terre populos, Inque auxilium Dictynna tuum Preciosa sonent aera Corinthi. Iuvenalis Sat. vi: ——— nemo aera fatiget: Vna laboranti poterit succurrere Luna. Martialis lib. xii. Epigram. lxii: Dicet quot aera verberent manus urbis, Quum secta Colcho Luna vapulat rhombo.
units.tr: "Last, you are carried to the Hesperian lands with stained wings; and late among the furthest peoples the bronze is shaken." So Seneca a little earlier, in the Hippolytus, and in the Medea, act 4: "so, pale, pour a sad light through the air, and let the peoples tremble with a new horror; and let the bronze of Corinth, precious to Dictynna, sound to bring you aid." Juvenal, satire 6: "Let no one wear out his bronze; the Moon alone can help the one who labours." Martial, book 12, epigram 62: "Who will tell how many hands of the city beat the bronze when the Moon is whipped with a Colchian rhombus?"

units.la: Alibi lego Indos Lunæ defectum & ruborem copiose fletu prosequi solitos; quod arbitrarentur, eam ab Sole ad sanguinis usque effusionem flagellatam. Lunam interdum deficere notant Scriptores, etiamsi nullam ab interposita terra patiatur obscurationem, hominibus apparens nigra vel sanguineo colore suffusa. Docet Xiphilinus in Vitellio: Θεαχης ἀν ἐ ἐ τῶ ἐ ... ἡλιῳ ... ἀλλα ... ἀλλ' ὅτι ἢ αἱματώδης ἡ μέλαινα, ἀλλα τί ἴνα χρώματα χοῖρες ἀφιέσαι ὡφθη. Quod autem cum hic & apud alios Scriptores, tum toties in sacris litteris Luna scribatur futura novissimo die, sanguinei coloris, ut Sol nigri; naturalem videtur habere causam: eventurum illud propter calidæ fumidæque, terra eductæ, Exspirationis vim maximam, oculis nostris Siderumque globis intersitam; quæ conglomerata tales colores cœlestibus corporibus est obducturæ. Videndus omnino Aristoteles lib. i. & ii. Meteororum. Intersitam, dixi; ne quis putet infici vaporibus ipsum Lunæ corpus. Nam quod cap. xv. scripsi Stellas humoribus ad se tractis non pasci: idem exaudiri volo de Luna: quod moneo, ne quem seducat Ptolemæus, qui diserte notat, Lunam ideo humectare, quod Terræ vaporibus fit vicinior; innuens non obscure Lunæ humiditatem & frigiditatem esse à Terra. Omnia supra Elementarem regionem æterna sunt; nihil obnoxium ibi corruptioni: quod abunde paret ex nostra Vniversi distributione.
units.tr: Elsewhere I read that the Indians were accustomed to accompany the Moon's failing and reddening with abundant weeping, supposing that she was being whipped by the Sun until she bled. Writers note that the Moon sometimes fails even without any obscuration caused by the interposed earth, appearing to men black or suffused with a blood-red colour. Xiphilinus, in the Life of Vitellius, teaches: "...the Sun... but because it was bloody or black, ... it appeared with such colours" [Θεαχης ἀν ἐ ἐ τῶ ἐ ... ἡλιῳ ... ἀλλα ... ἀλλ' ὅτι ἢ αἱματώδης ἡ μέλαινα, ἀλλα τί ἴνα χρώματα χοῖρες ἀφιέσαι ὡφθη]. That the Moon is written of here and in other writers, and so often in sacred letters, as to become blood-coloured on the last day, as the Sun black, seems to have a natural cause: that the great force of hot, smoky exhalation drawn up from the earth, lying between our eyes and the globes of the stars, will, when gathered together, cast such colours over the heavenly bodies. Aristotle's Meteorology, books 1 and 2, should be read in full. I said "lying between"; lest anyone think the body of the Moon itself is tainted by vapours. For what I wrote in chapter 15, that the stars are not fed by humours drawn to themselves, I want understood of the Moon as well; and I warn that Ptolemy not mislead anyone, since he clearly notes that the Moon is moist because it is nearer to the earth's vapours, thereby obscurely hinting that the Moon's moisture and coldness come from the earth. Everything above the elementary region is eternal, and nothing there is subject to corruption; this is abundantly clear from our division of the universe.

units.la: De mirabilibus Lunæ Influxibus sic loquitur Ptolemæus lib. i.c. i: Luna vero ut proxima terris manifeste in terrena influit: cum illa enim consentiunt & commutantur plerag omnia, & Animata & Inanimata: Ipsi Fluvij nunc augescunt, nunc decrescunt secundum lunari splendorem: ipsa Maria impetu diverso, pro eo ac illa oritur aut occidit, feruntur. Denique Germina ac Animantes, aut omnino aut aliqua ex parte, cum Luna incrementa ac decrementa sentiunt. Plinius lib. natur. histor. ii, cap. xli: Lunari potestate Ostrearum Conchyliorumque & Concharum omnium corpora augeri aut rursus minui. Quin & Soricum sibras respondere numero Lunæ, exquisivere diligentiores: minimumque animal Formicam sentire vires sideris, Interlunio semper cessantem. Idem Plinius ejusdem libri cap. xcvii. adfirmat Lunam motus Marium caussam esse, qua de re lib. iii. Hoc item notandum, quod Luna Terras saturet; accedensque, inquit idem cap. xcix, corpora implet, abscedens inaniat: ideo cum incremento ejus augeri Conchylia, & maxime spiritum sentire quibus sanguis non sit. Sed & sanguine Hominem etiam cum lumine ejus augeri ac minui: Frondes quoque ac Pabula sentire, in omnia eadem penetrante vi. Et hinc recte Luna Mercurio Trisincegisto Natura dicitur Miraculum, inferiorem transmutantis materiam. Plura huc referenda ex M. Porcio Catone de re rustica, cap.xxxi. & xxxvii, M. Tullio ii. de Divinatione, Plinio lib. xvi. naturalis historiæ, cap. xxxviii. & lib. xviii, cap. xxxii. Agellio lib. xx. noct. Attic. cap. vii, Vitruvio lib. ii. Architect. cap. ix, Vegetio lib. iv. de re militari, cap. xxxv.
units.tr: Ptolemy speaks thus of the wonderful influences of the Moon, book 1, chapter 1: "The Moon, being nearest the earth, plainly flows into earthly things; for almost all things, both animate and inanimate, agree with her and change with her. The rivers themselves now swell, now shrink, according to the lunar brightness; the seas themselves are carried with a varying force, according as she rises or sets. Finally, seeds and living creatures, wholly or in some part, feel the increase and decrease of the Moon." Pliny, Natural History book 2, chapter 41: "The bodies of oysters, shellfish and all shells, by the power of the Moon, grow or shrink again. More diligent observers have even found that the sinews of shrews answer to the number of the Moon; and that the smallest animal, the ant, feels the powers of the star, always ceasing between new moons." The same Pliny, in chapter 97 of the same book, affirms that the Moon is the cause of the movements of the seas, on which matter he speaks in book 3. This too is to be noted: that the Moon "saturates the lands; and as she approaches," he says in the same chapter 99, "she fills bodies, and as she withdraws she empties them. So with her increase shellfish grow, and especially those which have no blood feel the breath of life. But also man himself grows and shrinks in blood with her light; leaves too and fodder feel it, her power penetrating all things alike." And hence the Moon is rightly called "Nature" by Mercurius Trismegistus, a "miracle", transmuting the inferior matter. More to be referred here are Marcus Porcius Cato, On Agriculture, chapters 31 and 37; Cicero, On Divination, book 2; Pliny, Natural History, book 16, chapter 38, and book 18, chapter 32; Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights, book 20, chapter 7; Vitruvius, Architecture, book 2, chapter 9; and Vegetius, On Military Matters, book 4, chapter 35.

units.la: Character Lunæ Mathematicis ☽. Est enim, ut utar Horatio, Carm. Secular. Siderum Regina bicornis. Pictores, Sculptores, ceterique Formarum exprimendarum artifices, Lunæ duo semper velut parvula cornua solent affingere: cujus moris meminit Claudianus, lib. ii. de rapt. Proserp. Hic Hyperionis Solem de femine nasci Fecerat, & pariter Lunam; sed dispare forma Aurora Noctisque duces: cunabula Tethys Præbet, & infantes gremio fovetur anhelos, Caerulenfque sinus roseis radiatur alumnis: Invalidum dextro portat Titana lacerto Nondum luce gravem, nec pubescentibus alte Cristatum radijs: primo clementior aevo Fingitur, & tenerum vagitu despuit ignem; Laeva parte furor vitrei libamina potat Uberis, & parvo signantur tempora cornu.
units.tr: The mathematicians' character of the Moon is ☽. For, to use Horace's words from the Carmen Saeculare, she is the "twin-horned queen of the stars". Painters, sculptors and the other artists who portray forms are always accustomed to attach two little horns to the Moon; Claudian, in book 2 of On the Rape of Proserpina, recalls this custom: "Here he had made the Sun to be born from the seed of Hyperion, and the Moon likewise; but of unlike form, the leaders of dawn and night. Tethys offers them the cradle, and the panting infants are cherished in her bosom; the blue lap shines with its rosy foster-children. The Titan carries the weak one on his right arm, not yet heavy with light, nor crested high with growing rays; in her earliest age she is pictured as milder, and she spits out a tender fire with her wailing; on the left side, madness drinks the offerings of the glass-like breast, and her temples are marked with a small horn."

units.la: Sic Lunæ Cornua tribuuntur passim à Poëtis, Homero, Horatio, Ovidio, Lucano, Senecâ, Statio, Solino, Marciano Capella, & aliis.
units.tr: Thus the horns of the Moon are ascribed frequently by the poets: Homer, Horace, Ovid, Lucan, Seneca, Statius, Solinus, Martianus Capella, and others.

units.la: Lunæ porro varias ob causas dare cum Homero, Manilio, Tertulliano, Isidoro, aliis, Bigas, & Equos; eosque cum Ovidio Niveos, cum incertis apud Isidorum tempore matutino Album, Atrum vespertino facere: Tauros ejus currui jungere cum Fulgentio: Boves cum Prudentio; Iuvencos cum Avieno; nunc Iuvencas, nunc Vaccas cum Ausonio; Cervos cum Claudiano, ob velocitatem in cursu perficiendo: Mulas denique, ratione sterilitatis, cum Antiquis apud Festum; non est hujus loci, non nostri instituti.
units.tr: Moreover, for various reasons, the Moon is given chariots and horses by Homer, Manilius, Tertullian, Isidore and others; with Ovid they make them white, and with some unnamed authors cited by Isidore, white in the morning and dark in the evening. Fulgentius yokes bulls to her chariot; Prudentius, oxen; Avienus, bullocks; Ausonius, now heifers, now cows; Claudian, stags, on account of their speed in completing the course; and finally, on account of barrenness, the Ancients cited by Festus mention mules. This is not the place, nor the purpose of our undertaking, to discuss these.

units.la: PAVLLI G.F.P.N. MERVLÆ COSMOGRAPHIÆ PARTIS I. LIBER III.
units.tr: Of Paulus Merula's Cosmography, Part I, Book III.

units.la: De Inconstante, & quæ perpetuis obnoxia muta- tionibus, universi parte. CAP. I. De Elementis universim
units.tr: On the inconstant part of the universe, and that which is subject to perpetual change. CHAPTER I. On the elements in general.

units.la: ACTENVS fixa mens hæsit in altiore constantis æternæque & πατρὸς Partis consideratione: delabenti sentim, & Lunæ globum tramensæ, offert se totius portiuncula (quid ni quod superest sic vocem, in Universi raptus admirationem?) inconstans & perpetuis obnoxia mutationibus, in Elementis, quæ, ut eleganter Iacobus Carpentarius in Alcinoi def. molæ minima, virtute sunt maxima.
units.tr: Hitherto my mind has rested fixed on the consideration of the eternal and constant Father [πατρός]. Now, as I come down and pass beyond the sphere of the Moon, there appears a small portion of the whole (why should I not call it so, lest I be carried away in wonder at the universe?) that is inconstant and subject to perpetual change: the elements, which, as the learned Jacob Carpentarius says in his commentary on Alcinous, are very great in power though very small in mass.

units.la: Elementum Corpus est natura sua simplex, finitum, umbrosum, luce & lumine destitutum. Alij alio modo. Corpus esse scribunt Plato in Timæo, & Aristoteles apud Alexandrum Aphrodis. in 1.Meteor cap.1.text.1.Thomas ad eundem librum, c.11, Elementa negat Corpora: aliorum inquiens Corporum esse Elementa. Simplex dixi sua natura; cujus tamen præstantiam intueri mortalibus negatum. Elementa, quæ nos appellamus, nostrisque videmus oculis, simplicia non sunt, non sunt pura (Marsil. Ficin. in Platon. Phileb. c. xx) Purum enim & simplicem Aerem quis secet? Aer purus, inquit Albertus Magnus de Propriet.
