Elemen. lib. 1. tract. 1. cap. 11, occidit: qua de causa montes altissimos ascendentes Philosophi spongias aquis intinctas ante nares secum portabant, ut per has grossior esset Aer spiratus. Nihilo magis pura nobis Aqua; diffusus est per eam Aer, ut mox dicam: quam multum autem admistum illi Terræ, ne sit insipida; saporis enim expertia per se notant Elementa Aristoteles de sens. & sens. c.v, Alexander Aphrodisiensis in lib. 1. de Anima, c.xvi, Averroes ibidem, & alij. Terra denique quid dabit exse, si in se nihil humoris habeat aquei? qui provomet nobis Flumina fontesque, quibus ab Aere, Terræ verrucas penetrante, solent esse scatebræ? qui vivent sub ea Talpæ, aliaque, si viscera ejus Aere destituantur? Nihil hic miseris, & quos peccata fecit impuros, puri. Cum dolore fatendum, Elementa, quo magis ab humano consortio recedant, eo esse puriora, simpliciora, levioraque, cum per se, tum ordinis habita ratione. Videndus Averroes lib. 11. de Cœlo, text. 32. Duobus enim modis, ut scribit Albertus in 11. Meteor. tract. 1. cap. VII, considerantur vel secundum suam formam; & sic sunt absoluta, suisque distincta formis & locis: alio modo secundum viam transmutationis ad invicem; & ita non sunt determinata in suis formis, nec in suis locis. Sic Vapor nihil aliud, quam Aqua alterata ad Aeris naturam; Nubes, Vapor alteratus ad naturam Aquæ. Elementa sane, quibus utimur nos & fruimur, ex ipsis compositta quasi sunt Elementis; & inde quotidie fiunt omnia; in eadem, tamquam principiatua, Philosophis, omnia redire solita. Unde variæ variis diffinitiones. Aristoteli μεταφυσικ. δ', Σπιχεῖον λέγεται, ἐξ ὧν σύγκειται πρῶτα ἐνυπάρχοντ@ ἀδιαιρέτα τῷ εἶδει εἰς ἐτερ αὐτ@: Speusippo in Platon. diffinit. & Simplicio 1. de Cœlo, Elementum id ex quo primo quid componitur, & in quod ultimum compositum resolvitur: Averroi in Epit. Metaphysic. tract. 1, ad quod res resolvitur ratione formæ: Joanni Grammatic. 1. Physic. quod constituit rem, & fit compositi pars: Thomæ denique in 1. Physic, l. iv. text. 1. & 11. de generat. & corrupt. l. iii. cap. xvi, ex quo componitur res primo, & est in eo. Quo modo? Plene novit hoc admirandus omnium naturæ secretorum cognitor, DEVS: exercuint hic homines, quorum alij ita miscere volunt Elementa, ut ex ijs tertium fiat; alij integra manere dicunt; alij denique, mediam ingressi viam, nec integra manere statuunt, nec penitus aboleri, frangi tamen & minui sic, ut integritas formæ abeat, retenta ipsorum veritate & potestate: fusius hæc prosequente Joanne Pico Mirandulano Comite, de Element. c.
units.tr: An element is, in its own nature, a simple body, finite, shadowy, and destitute of light and brightness. Writers differ. Plato in the Timaeus, and Aristotle (as cited by Alexander of Aphrodisias on the first book of the Meteorology, chapter 1, text 1), say that the elements are bodies. Thomas, on the same book, chapter 11, denies that the elements are bodies: he says they are the elements of other bodies. I said simple in its own nature; yet it has been denied to mortals to see its excellence. The elements which we name and see with our eyes are not simple, nor pure (Marsilio Ficino on Plato's Philebus, chapter 20). For who could cut out pure and simple air? Pure air, says Albert the Great in On the Properties of the Elements, book 1, tract 1, chapter 11, is thin; for this reason philosophers, when climbing the highest mountains, used to carry sponges soaked in water before their noses, so that the air they breathed might be thicker. Water is no purer to us: air is spread through it, as I shall say presently; and how much earth is mixed into it, so that it is not insipid. For Aristotle (On Sense and Sensible Things, chapter 5), Alexander of Aphrodisias (On the Soul, book 1, chapter 16), Averroes in the same place, and others, note that the elements in themselves have no taste. Lastly, what would the earth yield if it had no watery moisture in itself? What would send forth for us the rivers and springs, which, as air penetrates the earth's hollows, are wont to bubble up? What would the moles and other creatures that live under it breathe if its inner parts were deprived of air? Nothing here is pure for wretched men whom sin has made impure. It must be admitted, with regret, that the more the elements withdraw from human company, the purer, simpler and lighter they are, both in themselves and in their order, when that order is taken into account. See Averroes, On the Heavens, book 2, text 32. For, as Albert writes in the second book of the Meteorology, tract 1, chapter 7, they may be considered in two ways: either according to their form, and so they are complete, and distinct in their forms and places; or in the other way, according to the process of their mutual transformation, and so they are not fixed in their forms or in their places. Thus vapour is nothing other than water altered toward the nature of air; and cloud is vapour altered toward the nature of water. The elements we use and enjoy are, indeed, in a manner composed of these same elements, and from them all things are made every day; and into these, as into their first principles, all things are wont to return, as philosophers hold. Hence the different definitions. Aristotle, in the fifth book of the Metaphysics: an element is said to be that from which, as first immanent constituents, a thing is composed, indivisible in form into another form [Σπιχεῖον λέγεται, ἐξ ὧν σύγκειται πρῶτα ἐνυπάρχοντα ἀδιαίρετα τῷ εἴδει εἰς ἕτερα εἴδη]. Speusippus, in the definitions of Plato, and Simplicius on On the Heavens, say: an element is that out of which a thing is first composed, and into which the final compound is resolved. Averroes, in the Epitome of the Metaphysics, tract 1: that into which a thing is resolved by reason of its form. John the Grammarian, on the Physics, book 1: that which constitutes a thing and becomes a part of the compound. Finally Thomas, on the Physics, book 1, lecture 1 and 2, and On Generation and Corruption, book 3, chapter 16: that out of which a thing is primarily composed, and which is present in it. How this is so, the wonderful knower of all the secrets of nature, God, alone fully knows. Men have argued about this: some wish the elements to be so mixed that a third thing comes from them; others say they remain whole; others, finally, taking a middle course, hold that they neither remain whole nor are utterly destroyed, but are broken and diminished in such a way that the integrity of their form is lost while their own truth and power are retained. Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, Count, treats these matters at greater length in On the Elements, chapter 11.

units.la: 11. Dum mutantur, inquit Chalcidius in Plat. Tim. non mutant essentiam, sed qualitatem, Aristoteles Elementorum circularem facit generationem, & facillimum esse motum Transmutationis: mutuam enim esse cognationem Ignis cum Aere, quum ambo calidi; Aeris cum Aqua, quum ambo frigidi; Aquæ ad Terram, quum utraque humida; Terræ ad Ignem, quum in utroque siccitas, de generat. & corrupt. summa 11. cap. 1. text. 25. Averroes etiam 111. de Cœlo, text. 51. dicit, Elementorum alicujus partis corruptionem, esse generationem alterius. Legendus & Simplicius in lib. VIII. Physic. text. 36. Finitum addidi. Ejus esse naturæ Elementa, & undique versum dimensionem habere docet, qui Naturam felicissime rimatus est, Aristoteles lib. 1. de Cœlo, text 44. & lib. 111. text. 34, 36, & 52. Infinita tamen sunt quodammodo, quod in infinitum extensa; ut idem vult lib. 111. Physic. cap. iv. text. 43. & 46; ideoque non male negantut habere quantitatem determinatam Averroi lib. 11. de Cœlo, text. 95.
units.tr: While they are changed, says Chalcidius on Plato's Timaeus, they do not change their essence, but their quality. Aristotle makes the elements a circular generation, and says that the motion of transformation is very easy: for there is a mutual kinship between fire and air, since both are hot; between air and water, since both are cold; between water and earth, since both are moist; between earth and fire, since both share dryness (On Generation and Corruption, book 2, chapter 1, text 25). Averroes also, in On the Heavens, book 3, text 51, says that the corruption of one part of the elements is the generation of another. Simplicius on the eighth book of the Physics, text 36, should also be read. I have added finite. He who searched out the nature of things most happily, Aristotle (On the Heavens, book 1, text 44, and book 3, texts 34, 36 and 52), teaches that the elements are of such a nature that they have dimension on every side. Yet they are in a way infinite, since they are extended to infinity; as the same author holds in the Physics, book 3, chapter 4, texts 43 and 46. Therefore it is not wrongly denied, as Averroes says (On the Heavens, book 2, text 95), that they have a determinate quantity.

units.la: Elementa, ut universi cetera, fecit DEVS: qua de re copiose disserui, lib. 1. cap. 11. Averroes lib. 11. de Cœlo, text. 104, & in VIII. Metaphysic. text. comment. 12. scribit Elementum omne secundum totum ingenerabile, secundum partes esse generabile: quod & legere me memini apud Joan. Grammat. in 1. Poster. cap. VIII. & Albertum Magnum in 11. de Cœlo, tract. IV cap. XIX, aliosque antiquiorisnotæ. Veteres Theologi πᾶν DEVM, ejusque μέρη vel (ut vocat Manilius lib. 1. Astronomic.) artus, Σπιχεῖα facientes; hæc, quod æternum scirent DEVM, ἀχίνητα censebant, sed κατὰ Ἀλαδεχῶ φύσεως καὶ Φθορᾶς unumquodque ζωντὸν, id est, κατὰ μέρη: Σπιχεῖα, dicis gratia, quæ in mistis, genita esse, sed ἀγενῆ Στοιχεῖων generationis expertes: Diversa enim Ἀγαθὸς esse ἡ Στοιχεῖα, ut etiam memoriæ prodit ex Zenonis Cittici sententia Diogenes Laertius. Videndus omnino Alexander Aphrodis. principio Comment. in lib. 11. Meteor.
units.tr: God made the elements, as he made the rest of the universe; I have discussed this at length in book 1, chapter 2. Averroes, On the Heavens, book 2, text 104, and in the eighth book of the Metaphysics, comment 12, writes that every element is, as a whole, ungenerated, but in its parts it is generable. I remember reading this also in John the Grammarian, on the first Posterior Analytics, chapter 8, and in Albert the Great, On the Heavens, book 2, tract 4, chapter 19, and other writers of older note. The ancient theologians made the whole God and his members (or, as Manilius calls them in the first book of the Astronomica, his limbs) into elements. They believed that, since they knew God to be eternal, these were immovable; but each living thing is subject to alternation of nature and corruption, that is, in its parts. The elements, so called for convenience, are generated in mixed bodies, but they are ungenerated, free from the generation of elements. For it is one thing to be good and another to be elements, as Diogenes Laertius also reports from the opinion of Zeno of Citium, as it is remembered. Alexander of Aphrodisias, at the beginning of his commentary on the second book of the Meteorology, should certainly be consulted.

units.la: Elementa notat Albertus in 11. de Cœlo, tract. 11.cap. 1, corpora rotunda per Accidens: locantur enim in rotundo: recta per Se: nam motus illis rectus. Utrumque patet. Quæ Aeris sursum, & quo purioris altius feruntur: quæ Aquæ Terræque, linea recta deorsum. Iam Sphærica figura, quæ reliquis, ut libro 1. cap. VI, ostendi, Elementis etiam conveniebat; quo commodissime unum ab altero contineretur: Aqua
units.tr: Albert, On the Heavens, book 2, tract 2, chapter 1, notes that the elements are round bodies per accidens, since they are located in what is round; and straight bodies per se, since their motion is straight. Both are evident. Air, which is purer, is carried upward and higher; water and earth are carried downward in a straight line. Now the spherical figure, which I showed in book 1, chapter 6, belongs to the other elements too, so that one may be most conveniently contained by another: water

units.la: Finitum. Quomodo infinitum. Efficiens. Forma. Aqua Terraque, quæ unum constituunt globum, ab ambiente & circumfuso Aere; hic ab Lunæ sphæra.
units.tr: Finite. How infinite. Efficient. Form. Water and earth, which make up one globe, are surrounded by the encompassing air; this by the sphere of the Moon.

units.la: Totam Elementorum stationem ad initium usque ætherem regionis comprehendi scribunt Mathematici semidiametris Terræ civi & scrupulis xxxiv. In ea cuique suus adtributus locus. Nam si omnibus esset idem, prohiberet se invicem in loco, inquit Averroes lib. 21. de Cœlo, text. 53. Elementa certe sub Luna esse nulli negant; at in Cœlo, Physicorum nonnulli negabant: sed, ut disserit Marsil. Ficin. in Plat. Timæum cap. xxiv, illi audiant Metaphysicos, probantes Elementa per ideas suas esse in ipso mundi Opifice; esse inde in Anima Mundi per rationes suas; esse in Natura per semina: ergo & in Cœlo per virtutes, & sub Cœlo per formas. Adeundus ad majorem horum illustrationem Franciscus Georgius Venetus de Harmonia totius mundi.
units.tr: The mathematicians write that the whole station of the elements, up to the ethereal region at the beginning, is included within a radius of the earth of about 34 minutes of arc. In that region each has its own assigned place. For if all had the same place, they would hinder one another in place, says Averroes, On the Heavens, book 2, text 53. No one denies that the elements are under the Moon; but some natural philosophers denied that they are in the heavens. However, as Marsilio Ficino argues on Plato's Timaeus, chapter 24, let them hear the metaphysicians, who prove that the elements are in the very Maker of the world through their ideas; that they are in the Soul of the World through their reasons; that they are in Nature through seeds: therefore also in the heavens through their powers, and under the heavens through their forms. For a fuller explanation of these matters one should consult Francesco Giorgi of Venice, On the Harmony of the Whole World.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: Elementa tantum tria. Ignis non vere Elementum.
units.tr: Only three elements. Fire is not truly an element.

units.la: PLERIQVE & Antiquorum & Recentiorum, variis rationibus quæ apud Platonem, Aristotelem, Galenum, Macrobium & alios, adducti, quatuor numero statuunt; duo Ignem & Aerem, recta linea sursum; totidem Aquam & Terram, deorsum tendentia. Sed revera tria tantum sunt. Aer, Aqua, Terra; ut optime multis argumentis probat vir acutissimus Hieronymus Cardanus, Medicus Mediolanensis, de Subtilitate lib. 1. quem non compilabo: consulendi & Philosophi apud Aristotelem lib. 1. Meteor. Alexander Aphrodisiensis. 11. probl. xiv. & doctissimus ille Ioannes Picus, Comes Mirandulæ, de Elementis cap. iii. Ignis enim qui putatur & Elementis connumeratur, nihil aliud est, quam Aer sub Lunæ convexo supremus, tenuissimus, purissimus, proxime accedens ad cœlestem illum benéque temperatum calorem, cujus vi & efficacia, DEO gratiam adfundente, materiam submnistrantibus Aqua & Terra (videndus Aristoteles de Anima 1, summa secunda, cap. v. text. 82.) cuncta generantur. Non existimandum Ignem istic actu flagrare. Supremus Aer, quod vicinior Sphæris cœlestibus perpetuo & velocissimo Corporum cœlestium motu calefiat, Ignis appellationem consuetudine quadam est nactus. Aristoteles: πεῖ δὲ ταῦτα καὶ τὰ ἐχόμενα τούτων, Ἀἠρ πηρ ὁ ἀληθινὸς καλούμενος πῦρ: οὐκ ἔστι δὲ τὸ πῦρ. Certe Ignis Elementum Antiquis obscurum & incognitum fuisse, testatur Leo Hebr. de Amor. Dialog. 11. Apud Moschen etiam in rerum creatarum commemoratione nulla fit Ignis hujus mentio: diversis verbis nominantur Terra & Aqua; Aerem autem magni Interpretes sentiunt non obscure indicari verbis: ורוח אלהים מרחפת על פני המים Et spiritus Domini ferebatur super faciem Aquarum. De tribus Elementis & Calore cœlesti, quem ut Causam Efficientem Igneam vocat Vim (ut & Stoici apud Ciceronem lib. iii. de natur. Deorum; Homerus πυρὸς μὴ ἀθρος, Ignis spiritum Ennius.) Eleganter Ovidius lib. 1. Metamorphoseos: Ignea convexi vis & sine pondere Cæli Emicuit, summaque locum sibi legit in arce; Proximus est Aer illi levitate locoque; Densior his tellus, Elementaque grandia traxit, Et pressa est gravitate sui; circumfluus Humor Ultima possedit, solidumque coercuit orbem.
units.tr: Many both of the ancients and of the moderns, led by various arguments such as those found in Plato, Aristotle, Galen, Macrobius and others, count four elements: two that tend upward in a straight line, fire and air, and two that tend downward, water and earth. In truth, however, there are only three: air, water, earth. This is proved very well by many arguments by the most acute man Girolamo Cardano, physician of Milan, in his book On Subtlety, Book 1, which I shall not plunder here. Those who wish to consult the philosophers may also look at Aristotle, Meteorology Book 1, and Alexander of Aphrodisias, Problems 2, problem 14, and at that most learned man Giovanni Pico, Count of Mirandola, On the Elements, chapter 3. For what is thought to be fire and is counted among the elements is nothing other than the highest air beneath the vault of the Moon, the thinnest, purest, lying closest to that heavenly and well-tempered heat. By its power and efficacy, when God pours in grace, and with water and earth supplying the matter (see Aristotle, On the Soul, Book 1, second summary, chapter 5, text 82), all things are generated. We should not suppose that fire actually blazes there. The highest air, being nearer to the heavenly spheres and warmed by their perpetual and very swift motion, has acquired the name fire by a certain custom. Aristotle: πεῖ δὲ ταῦτα καὶ τὰ ἐχόμενα τούτων, Ἀἠρ πηρ ὁ ἀληθινὸς καλούμενος πῦρ: οὐκ ἔστι δὲ τὸ πῦρ. That fire as an element was obscure and unknown to the ancients is attested by Leo the Hebrew, Dialogues on Love, 11. Nor is there any mention of this fire in Moses' account of the created things; the earth and water are named in different words. The great interpreters, however, understand that air is clearly indicated by the words [ורוח אלהים מרחפת על פני המים] And the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters. Concerning the three elements and the celestial heat, which he calls the Igneam efficient cause Vim, (as the Stoics also do in Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods, Book 3; Homer speaks of πυρὸς μὴ ἀθρος, and Ennius of Ignis spiritum), Ovid elegantly says in Metamorphoses Book 1: the fiery power of the vaulted heaven, weightless, flashed forth and took for itself the highest place in the citadel; next to it, in lightness and place, is air; denser than these is the earth, which drew to itself the great elements and was pressed down by its own weight; the surrounding moisture took the outermost place and confined the solid globe.

units.la: Quod autem in superioribus aliquoties Ignis, ut Elementi, meminerim; feci, non indicans meam hac de re sententiam, sed Philosophorum recensens opiniones. Hic tandem locus flagitabat, ut quæ mea de hoc Elemento mens esset, aperte serioque pronunciarem. Aliter quidem existimarunt Veterum non pauci: sed fuerunt homines: & ut tales se probarent, in multis singularibus aberrarunt, ἀναγωνισὰς sibique reclamantes sæpe nacti. Amicus Socrates, amicus Plato, amici ceteri; sed amica magis Veritas, cujus apud Aristotelem lib. 1. Tropicorum, tanta vis, ut propter eam etiam Philosophi, velint nolint, sibi contradicere debeant, & melius solidiusque edocti, pro quibus aliquando mordicus pugnarant, magnis animis rejicere.
units.tr: That I have several times mentioned fire among the elements in the foregoing pages, I have done without declaring my own opinion on the matter, but by setting out the opinions of the philosophers. Here at last the place demanded that I state plainly and seriously what my own view of this element is. Indeed, not a few of the ancients thought otherwise, but they were men, and in many particulars they went astray in proving themselves such, often finding themselves ἀναγωνισὰς and contradicting themselves. Socrates is a friend, Plato is a friend, the other philosophers are friends; but truth is a closer friend, whose power is so great, as Aristotle says in Topics Book 1, that because of it philosophers, whether they will or no, must contradict themselves, and, when better and more solidly taught, must with high spirit reject what they had once fought for stubbornly.

units.la: CAP. III. Elementorum Distributio. De Aere.
units.tr: CAP. III. The Distribution of the Elements. On Air.

units.la: ELEMENTVM igitur in tribus consideratum vel Pellucidum est, vel Opacum. Pellucidum voco, quod, quia rarum lumini est pervium. Cujus generis duo Aer & Aqua: Thomas de natur. luminis opusc. 51.
units.tr: An element, considered in three ways, is either transparent or opaque. I call transparent that which, being rare, lets light pass through it. Of this kind there are two: air and water. Thomas, De natura luminis, opusc. 51.

units.la: Est autem Aer Elementum pellucidum, rarius Aqua: medium spacium, quod inter globum Lunæ & terram Aquamque, ut adsignatum sibi propriumque locum, occupans; Philo Iudæus de Mundi opificio.
units.tr: Air is a transparent element, rarer than water. It occupies the middle space between the globe of the Moon and the earth and water, as its assigned and proper place. Philo the Jew, On the Creation of the World.

units.la: Pellucidum esse, id est, per medium sui lucem transmittere, nemo dubitat. Testantur nullius non oculi: qui, ni ita esset, non contemplarentur mirabilia DEI opera; non frucerentur jucundo Solis, Lunæ, Siderum, non aliarum rerum adspectu. Rariorem Aqua dixi. Docet res ipsa Raritatem ejus talem & Molliriem; ob quam Veteres eum lunoni consecrare erant soliti. M. Tullius II. de natura Deorum, Cœlum ex dictis Ennii & Euripidis, tum Augurum auctoritate, consensuque generis humani, Iovem esse tradit; Aerem autem, sicut Stoici disputant, inter Cœlum & Mare interiectum, lunonem; quæ est Soror & Conjux Iovis, quod & similitudo est Ætheris, & cum eo summa conjunctio. Effeminarunt autem eum, inquit, Iunonique tribuerunt, quod nihil est eo mollius.
units.tr: That air is transparent, that is, that it transmits light through its substance, no one doubts. The eyes of every living thing bear witness. Otherwise they would not behold the wonderful works of God, nor enjoy the pleasant sight of the Sun, the Moon, the stars, and other things. I said that air is rarer than water. The thing itself shows its rarity and softness, and for this reason the ancients were accustomed to consecrate it to Juno. Marcus Tullius, in book II of On the Nature of the Gods, says that heaven is Jupiter, on the testimony of the sayings of Ennius and Euripides, the authority of the augurs, and the consensus of the human race. Air, however, as the Stoics argue, lies interposed between heaven and sea, and is Juno, who is the sister and wife of Jupiter, because it is a likeness of the ether and has the closest union with it. They have made it effeminate, he says, and assigned it to Juno, because nothing is softer than it.

units.la: Dictus, ut vult ex Platonis Timæo Isidorus lib. Etymolog. XIII. cap. VII. ἀὴρ quod ferat terram, vel quod feratur: ut idem Plato, ἀεὶ ῥέων, quod semper fluat; ut alii censent, ab α privativa particula & ἀέρω, quod per se obscurus illuminetur a Stellis. Sed potius est, ut appellatus censeatur ab ἄνεμος, quod est spiro: Spirat enim Aeris beneficio quidquid habet vitam, & Pulmonem; aliudve Pulmonis vice, spirabile viscus.
units.tr: It is named, as Isidore says in his Etymologies book XIII chapter VII, following Plato's Timaeus, ἀήρ [aēr], either because it carries the earth or because it is carried. As Plato himself says, it is ἀεὶ ῥέων [aei rheōn], because it always flows. Others think it is named from the alpha privative and ἀέρω, because it is of itself dark and is illuminated by the stars. But it is rather thought to be named from ἄνεμος [anemos], which is to say spiro, I breathe. For by the benefit of air whatever has life breathes, and the lung, or whatever organ of breathing takes the place of the lung.

units.la: Ut Elementa reliqua, sic Aerem Lucretius, aliique apud Servium ad VI. Æneidos Physici corporeum esse probant, inde; quod Aves sustineat: sed hunc cedere vapori sulphureo: unde aves in hujusmodi locis ab Aere deniore, quo portari solent, desertæ concidunt, ponderes non odore, ut cum alijs scribit de Averno, Campaniæ lacu, Isidorus lib. Orig. XIII. cap. XIX.
units.tr: Lucretius and others, as Servius notes on Aeneid VI, prove that air is corporeal, as they do the other elements. They argue that it bears up birds. Yet it yields to sulphurous vapour, and so birds in such places, deserted by the heavier air by which they are usually borne, fall down. Their weight is not altered by the smell, as Isidore writes, along with others, about Avernus, the lake in Campania, Origins book XIII chapter XIX.

units.la: Aer apud Veteres Scriptores, Lucretium lib. IV. de Rerum natura & Virgilium lib. I. & V. Æneidos, notante Servio, aliosque, ut & Latinos Sacræ Scripturæ Interpretes, sæpe Cœlum solet nominari. Isidorus lib. XIII, cap. IV: Interdum & Cœlum pro Aere accipitur; ubi Venti & Nubes, Procellæ & Turbines fiunt; Lucretius, Cœlum quod dicitur Aer: Et Psalmus Volucres Cœli appellat; quum manifestum sit Aves in Aere volare: & nos in consuetudine hunc Aerem Cœlum appellamus, &c.
units.tr: Among the ancient writers, such as Lucretius in book IV of On the Nature of Things and Virgil in books I and V of the Aeneid (as Servius notes), and others, as well as the Latin interpreters of Holy Scripture, air is often called heaven. Isidore, book XIII chapter IV: Sometimes heaven too is taken for air, where winds and clouds, storms and whirlwinds arise. Lucretius: heaven, which is called air. The Psalm calls the birds of heaven, since it is plain that birds fly in the air. And we in common usage also call this air heaven, etc.

units.la: Diffusus autem Aer per omnia. Quod per Terram; docent respirantes Talpæ, & quæ sub terra vitam trahunt: vere Georgio Agricola scribente de Animalibus subterraneis. Nam adsentire non possum magno Cardano, notanti lib. x. Talpam adeo odisse Aerem; ut si cogatur in lucem egredi, brevissimo temporis spacio exanimetur. Et sane, quantum Aeris intra viscera sua terra cohibeat, indices sunt cum frequentes ejus motus propter spiritum intus agitatum atque conflictatum; tum Fontes & Flumina, quorum origo Aer, vel Terræ inclusus, vel intra poros ejus receptus; & in Aquam conversus. Quod vero per Aquam; ostendunt partim Pisces, de quibus Aristoteles lib. de natura Animal. VI. cap. XII, & de partib. Animal. III. cap. VI. & refutans Aristotelem, quod specialius de Balena, Delphino, Cete loquatur, Plinius lib. naturalis histor. IX. cap. VIII: partim Vrinatores, qui nisi sub Aquis Aerem, per Aquas diffusum, haurirent, quo pacto viverent? In India Occidentali passim Vrinatores, venandis margaritarum ostreis intenti, per horam integram sub Aqua latitant. Colanus Vrinator Catanie: quæ urbs Siciliæ, sub Aqua ternis ac quaternis horis, veluti Piscis quidam, delitescebat.
units.tr: Air is diffused through all things. That it is diffused through the earth is shown by moles that breathe and by those creatures which draw their life under the ground, as Georgius Agricola writes about subterranean animals. For I cannot agree with the great Cardan, who notes in book X that a mole so hates air that, if it is forced out into the light, it dies in a very short time. Indeed, how much air the earth holds within its bowels is shown both by its frequent movements, caused by the spirit stirred and struggling within, and by springs and rivers, whose origin is air enclosed in the earth or received into its pores and turned into water. That air is diffused through water is shown in part by fishes, concerning which Aristotle speaks in On the Nature of Animals book VI chapter XII and On the Parts of Animals book III chapter VI. Pliny, in Natural History book IX chapter VIII, refutes Aristotle for speaking more particularly of the whale, the dolphin, and the cetus. It is also shown in part by divers. Unless they drew in air diffused through the waters beneath the surface, how would they live? In the West Indies, divers everywhere, intent on hunting oysters for pearls, lie hidden under water for a full hour. Colanus, a diver of Catania, a city of Sicily, lay hidden under water for three or four hours, like some kind of fish.

units.la: Aer, etsi natura frigidus (quod recte sentiunt Stoici contra Aristotelem, qui natura sua calidum facit & humidum: consulendi omnino Cardanus sub initium lib. II.) lib. II. de Subtilit. & Iulius Scaliger, lectu digna ad locum illum differens) ut Elementa omnia; omnis enim Calor ab Coelestibus est & a Luce: dividitur tamen vulgo in Calidum & Frigidum: Medius propter Caloris αὐλαξεισιν frigidus est: utrimque vero extremus, calidus; Superior quidem propter perennem motum Mundi & Coelestium lucem; Inferior vero propter radiorum reflexionem a Terrae soliditate; Albertus Magnus de Passionibus Aeris. Hinc Physici tres (quinque Albertus lib. II. Meteor. tract. I. cap. III.) imaginari solent Aeris regiones, Supremam, Mediam, Infimam: scribentes in Aere Summo generari Cometas & Φασματα, ut sunt Λαμπάδες, Bολίδες, Trabes, Trajectiones, Διάστονης, Χάσματα; in Medio Fulmina, Παρηλια Παραγοηλια, Αλωνες, Τεϊδες, Tonitrua, Ventos, Nubes, Pluviam, Nivem, Grandinem; in Infimo denique Ignem Fatuum, Rorem, Pruinam. Quorum fusior explicatio quum propria sit Physici, non Cosmographi; non hic ero prolixior: legendi Aristoteles de Meteor. Plinius lib. II. natur. histor. & alij. Multa paucis Isidorus lib. XIII. Originum, cap. VII, de Aere loquens: Hic partim ad coelestem, partim ad terrenam materiam pertinet. Nam ille subtilis, ubi ventosi ac procellosi motus non possunt existere, ad coelestem pertinet partem (nihil hic de Igne, Elemento) ille vero turbulentior (intelligit ceterum & citeriorem) qui exhalationibus humidis corporescit, Terrae deputatur; qui ex se multas species reddit. Nam commotus Ventos facit; vehementius concitatus, Ignes & Tonitrua; contractus, Nubila; conspissatus, Pluviam: congelantibus nubibus, Nivem; turbulentius congelantibus densioribus nubibus, Grandinem; dissentus serenum efficit. Nam Aerem densum Nubem esse constat; Nubem rarefactam & solutam, Aerem.
units.tr: Air, though cold by nature (which the Stoics rightly hold against Aristotle, who makes it hot and moist by nature; Cardan should certainly be consulted at the beginning of book II of De subtilitate, and Julius Scaliger, who discusses that passage and is worth reading), like all the elements. For all heat comes from the heavenly bodies and from light. Yet it is commonly divided into hot and cold. The middle air is cold, because of the antiperistasis [ἀντιπερίστασιν] of heat; but at either extreme it is hot: the upper air on account of the perpetual motion of the world and the light of the heavenly bodies, the lower air on account of the reflection of the rays from the solidity of the earth. Albert the Great, On the Passions of the Air. Hence the physicists are accustomed to imagine three regions of air (Albert, in Meteorology book II tract I chapter III, makes five): the Supreme, the Middle, and the Lowest. They write that in the Supreme air comets and phantasms are generated, such as lampades, bolides, beams, trajections, diastones, and chasmata. In the Middle air come lightnings, parhelia, paraselenae, halones, teides, thunders, winds, clouds, rain, snow, and hail. In the Lowest air, finally, come will-o'-the-wisps, dew, and hoarfrost. Since a fuller explanation of these things belongs to the physicist and not the cosmographer, I shall not be longer here. Aristotle's Meteorology should be read, and Pliny, Natural History book II, and others. Isidore, Origins book XIII chapter VII, speaking of air, says much in few words: This pertains partly to the celestial matter and partly to the earthly. For that subtle part, where windy and stormy motions cannot exist, belongs to the celestial part (nothing here about fire, an element), but that more turbulent part (he means the lower and nearer air) which becomes solid from moist exhalations is assigned to the earth, and from itself produces many kinds. For when it is stirred it makes winds; when stirred more violently, fires and thunders; when contracted, clouds; when condensed, rain; when the clouds freeze, snow; when denser clouds freeze more turbulently, hail; when dissolved, it makes clear weather. For it is agreed that dense air is cloud, and cloud rarefied and dissolved is air.

units.la: Illud addam, vetustissimos Theologos totum hoc Aeris spacium sub Plutonis constituisse potestate, & inibi domicilia quasi construxisse cum Inferis, ut Proserpinae, Summano Diti, Manibus, Furijs, aliisque immundis spiritibus: tum quos merita videbantur ad loca superiora vocasse, Semideis & Heroibus. Marcianus Capella: A meditate Aeris usque in Montium Terraeque confinia Hemithei Heroesque versantur, qui ex eo quod Heram Terram veteres dixerunt, Heroes nuncupati; ibique Manes, id est, Corpori humano Praesules attributi qui parentum feminibus manaverunt. Denique hac omnis Aeris ab Luna diffusio sub Plutonis potestate consistit, qui etiam Summanus dicitur quasi summus Manium. Hic Luna, quae huic Aeri propior est, Proserpina nominatur. Verum illi Manes, quoniam corporibus eo tempore tribuuntur, quo fit prima conceptio, etiam post vitam hisdem corporibus delectantur, atque cum his manentes Lemures appellantur: qui, si vita prioris adjuti fuerint honestate, in Lares domorum urbiumque vertuntur; si autem depravantur ex corpore, Larvae perhibentur ac Mania. Manes igitur hic tam boni, quam truces sunt constituti; quos ἀγαθὸς ἢ κακὸς δαίμονας memorat Graia discretio. In his etiam locis Summanes, eorumque praesules Mana & Manuana; Dij etiam, quos Aquilos dicunt: Item Furinaque & Mater Mania Intemperiaque & alij triptes Deorum degunt. Isidorus Originum libro VIII. cap. ult. Manes deos dicunt mortuorum, quorum potestatem inter Lunam & Terram adserunt; a quibus & Mane dictum existimant, quos putant ab Aere, qui manus id est rarus est, Manes dictos; sive quia late manant per auras, sive quia mites sunt immanibus contrario nomine hoc appellantur. Et lib. V. cap. XXX: Alij Mane existimant vocari a Manibus, quorum conversatio ab Lunaad Terram est. Alij putant ab Aere, quia manus id est rarus est & persticuus. Hinc Dij Aerij apud Arnobium lib. III. adverti. gentes: Possumus si videtur summatim aliquid & de Laribus dicere, quos arbitratur vulgus Viccorum atque Itinerum Deos esse, ex eo quod Graeci Vicos cognominant Λαυρας. In diversis Nigidius scriptis, modo tectorum domuumque custodes; modo Curetas illos qui occulti adse perhibentur adibus Iovis aliquando vagitum Indigetes Samothracios, quos quinque indicant Graeci, Idaeos Dactylos nuncupari. Varro similiter hasitans; nunc esse illos Manes; & ideo Maniam matrem esse cognominatam Larum, nunc aerios rursus Deos & Heroas pronunciat appellari. Videndus & Augustinus lib. VIII. de Civitate Dei, cap. XXII. & libro de Agone Christiano: cum quo sanctisque alijs viris valere jubeamus absurdam hanc & impiam Gentilium θεολογίαν.
units.tr: I would add that the most ancient theologians placed this whole space of air under the power of Pluto, and there built, as it were, dwellings for the dead, together with Proserpina, Summanus, Dis, the Manes, the Furies, and other unclean spirits. From there they seemed to have summoned to the higher places those whom merit seemed to have deserved, namely demigods and heroes. Martianus Capella: From the middle of the air as far as the boundaries of the mountains and the earth dwell the half-gods and heroes, who were called heroes because the ancients called the earth Hera. There also dwell the Manes, that is, the lords assigned to the human body, who flowed from the seed of parents. In short, this whole diffusion of air from the Moon stands under the power of Pluto, who is also called Summanus, as the highest of the Manes. Here the Moon, which is nearer to this air, is named Proserpina. But those Manes, since they are given to bodies at the time when the first conception takes place, also delight in the same bodies after life, and remaining with them are called Lemures. If they have been aided by the honesty of their former life, they are turned into Lares of houses and cities; but if they are corrupted by the body, they are called Larvae and Mania. So the Manes are established as both good and savage, which the Greek distinction calls good or bad spirits [ἀγαθὸς ἢ κακὸς δαίμων]. In these places also live the Summanes and their lords Mana and Manuana, and gods too whom they call Aquiloni. Likewise Furina, and Mother Mania, Intempera, and other triple gods dwell there. Isidore, Origins book VIII, last chapter: They call the Manes the gods of the dead, whose power they say lies between the Moon and the Earth. From them they think the word Mane was derived, because they think the Manes were named from air, which is manus, that is, rare; or because they spread widely through the breezes; or because, being gentle, they are called by a name opposite to immanes, the savage. And in book V chapter XXX: Others think the Manes are so called from the Manes, whose dwelling is between the Moon and the Earth. Others think it is from air, because air is manus, that is, rare and thin. Hence the Air-gods of the Gentiles in Arnobius, book III: We can, if it seems fitting, say something briefly also about the Lares, whom the common people think are gods of the crossroads and highways, because the Greeks call the crossroads compita. In various writings Nigidius says that they are sometimes guardians of houses and dwellings, and sometimes those hidden Curetes who are said to have once cried out in the temple of Jupiter, the Samothracian Indigetes, whom the Greeks call the five, and who are named the Idaean Dactyls. Varro, likewise hesitating, now says that these are the Manes, and therefore that Mania is called the mother of the Lares; and now again he declares that they are called aerial gods and heroes. Augustine also should be consulted, in book VIII of The City of God, chapter XXII, and in his book On the Christian Contest. With him and other holy men we bid farewell to this absurd and impious theology of the Gentiles [θεολογίαν].

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: De Aqua.
units.tr: Of Water.

units.la: DIXI de priore Pellucidorum, Aere; alterum ejus indolis Elementum, Aquam statui. Est ea Elementum pellucidum, humidum; Aerem densitate, Terram raritate superans. Esse Pellucidum, nemo, nisi qui temerandæ contradictionibus suis veritati natus, negat. Ostendit nobis hæc Aquæ, modo nimium non fuerit vel alta, vel crassa, turbatave terrenis fæcibus, Ἀλφάνια, quæ in imis resident fundis. Alioquin Vrinatoribus perluciditatem hanc apud Plinium lib. II. natur. histor. cap. XLII, testantibus suffragantur etiam qui gemmis quæritandis alisve funditus extrahendis ævo nostro dant operam. Et quia Gemmarum mihi facta mentio; accedant & illæ probando, quod dixi. Quum enim manifestum sit, eas ex altero principaliter Elementorum, Terra vel Aqua, constarIs certo certius esse tradunt Physici, non perspicuas ex terrea crassioreque substantia generationis materiem mutuari, pellucidas vero ex aqua præsertim consistere, suaeque matris, quæ transparentior, indolem quasi referre. Aquam etiam scribit Alexander Aphrodisiensis de sensu & sensato, sect. II, quod Ignis esca & pabulum dicatur, lumine facile inlustrari. Aquam non solum humidam esse & frigidam notant Aristoteles lib. II. de generatione & corruptione, cap. III. text. 16, Magentinus Metropolita Mitylenensis, & alij ad magnum Philosophum; Aere item humidiorem, Thomas II. de generat. & corrupt. lib. III, tex. 23: verum etiam omnibus humidis esse principium & fontem, docet idem Aristoteles lib. I. Metaphysic. cap. I. Iam quod Aqua Terra sit rarior, clamat res ipsa; quod longe densior Aere, etiam obscuro, tradit Alex. Aphrodis. lib. II. de Anima, cap. XXXIII.
units.tr: I have spoken of the first of the transparent bodies, air. I now set out the second element of that kind, water. Water is a transparent element, moist, surpassing air in density and earth in rarity. No one but a man born to corrupt the truth by his own contradictions denies that it is transparent. Water shows us this quality, provided it is not too deep or too thick, or clouded with earthy dregs, so that we can see the alphania [Ἀλφάνια], the sediment lying at the bottom. Otherwise, the divers mentioned by Pliny in Book II of his Natural History, chapter 42, bear witness to this clarity, as do those who in our own age work to seek out gems or to bring other things up from the depths. Since I have mentioned gems, they too may support what I have said. For it is clear that they are made principally from one of the elements, earth or water. The natural philosophers report, quite certainly, that opaque gems draw the matter of their formation from the earthy and grosser substance, while transparent ones consist mainly of water and so, as it were, reproduce the nature of their mother, which is the more transparent. Alexander of Aphrodisias also writes in his work on sense and the sensible, section II, that water is called the food and fuel of fire, and is easily lit up by light. Aristotle in Book II of On Generation and Corruption, chapter 3, text 16, Magentinus the Metropolitan of Mytilene, and others on the Great Philosopher, note that water is not only moist and cold; Thomas, on the third book of On Generation and Corruption, text 23, notes that it is more moist than air. Moreover, Aristotle himself teaches in Book I of the Metaphysics, chapter 1, that water is the principle and source of all moist things. That water is rarer than earth the thing itself proclaims; that it is far denser than air, even dark air, Alexander of Aphrodisias states in Book II of On the Soul, chapter 33.

units.la: Aqua quemadmodum censet Isidorus lib. XIII. Originum, c. XII. quod aqua ejus supersicies; vel, quæ Latinorum, Thaletis sententiam cum apud alios tum Lactantium lib. I. de falsa religione, cap. V, sequentium mens, quasi à qua nata sint omnia.
units.tr: Isidore, in Book XIII of the Origins, chapter 12, thinks that water is so called because its surface is even. The meaning of those who follow the opinion of Thales, as reported by others and by Lactantius in Book I of On the False Religion, chapter 5, is as if all things were born from it.

units.la: Aquarum Terræque moles simul unum constituunt, ut postea dicam, globum; cujus una est supersicies convexa, scribente cum aliis Strabone lib. III: Aquis interim Terræ faciem non superantibus; Terminus enim non violandus illis positus ab suo Creatore, ut canit Propheta regius Psalmo CIV. vers. 9, quo pertinent & quæ leguntur apud Ieremiam cap. V. vers. 22, Hiiobum cap. XXXVIII, vers. 8, 9, 10. 11. Proverb. cap. VIII, vers. 29: sed vel circumdantibus, eodem Psalmo, vers. 6; vel medium quasi permanentibus, inque varias partes, velut frustra, divellentibus, nec non intra viscera illius, tamquam in utre, conclusis, Psalmo XXXIII, 7. Porro rotunditatem Aquæ, eamque propria sibi & adgenita indole sensim in tumorem adsurgere, speciaiius arguunt partim ejus partes, Guttulæ, quæ formam sphæricam plurimum adsimilare, & in parvos globari solent orbes; partim signum aliquod in littore positum, oculique in illud ex navis altius provectæ nunc prora nunc summo malo conjecti: nam quod hic contemplantibus obsertur, ibi negatur: notante Plinio lib. II. natur. histor. cap. LXV. ubi plura pro rotunditate argumenta.
units.tr: The masses of water and earth together make up one globe, as I will say later. Its one surface is convex. Strabo, among others, writes in Book III that the waters do not rise above the face of the earth, for the boundary set for them by their Creator must not be violated, as the royal Prophet sings in Psalm 104, verse 9. Related to this are the passages in Jeremiah 5:22, Job 38:8–11, and Proverbs 8:29. The waters surround the earth, as in the same Psalm, verse 6, or remain as it were in the middle, or are divided into various parts as if in vain, and they are enclosed within its bowels as in a skin bag, Psalm 33:7. Moreover, the roundness of water, and its tendency by its own and innate nature to rise gradually into a swelling, is shown especially in part by its drops, which mostly resemble a spherical shape and tend to form small round globes; and partly by a sign placed on the shore, and by the eyes of people looking at it from a ship sailing further out, sometimes from the prow and sometimes from the top of the mast. For what is seen by those looking from there is denied by those looking from here, as Pliny notes in Book II of the Natural History, chapter 65, where he gives more arguments for the roundness.

units.la: Sunt qui duplex Aquæ centrum Gravitatis & Magnitudinis ponunt; multa de constituendi utrumque necessitate colligentes, sed quæ parum firma solidaque. Ptolemæus Centrorum diuersitatem probare non videtur, quum simpliciter scribit, Terram una cum undis circumfluis Globum constituere, illamque emmere extra Aquas, veluti cespitem ex palude; & una cum undis infecti, & in globi speciem ad commune centrum inclinari. Vitruvius etiam lib. IX, Terram produc in medio positam, & una cum mari in centri loco naturaliter esse collocatam.
units.tr: Some hold that water has a double centre, of gravity and of magnitude, gathering many arguments for the necessity of positing each, but these are weak and insubstantial. Ptolemy does not seem to prove a difference of centres, since he simply writes that the earth together with the surrounding waters forms a globe, and that he has raised the land out of the waters like a turf out of a marsh, and that together with the waves it is inclined into the shape of a globe around a common centre. Vitruvius also, in Book IX, says that the earth is placed in the middle and, together with the sea, is naturally located at the place of the centre.

units.la: De varijs Aquarum Effectis Isidorus lib. XIII. Etymolog. cap. XII. ex nescio quo Scriptore (solet enim aliunde sua compilare) Aquarum, inquit, Elementum ceteris omnibus imperat. Aqua enim Cœlum temperant; Terram fœcundant; Aerem exhalationibus suis incorporant; scandunt in sublime, & Cœlum sibi vindicant: quid enim mirabilius Aquis in Cælo slantibus? Parum sit in tantam pervenisse altitudinem; rapiunt & secum Piscium examina; effusæ omnium in Terra nascentium caussa siunt; Fruges gignunt; Arbores, Frutices, Herbasque producunt; Sordes detergunt; Potum cunctis Animantibus tribuunt. Aqua omnis, licet gravitate suoque pondere ad lineam deorsum labatur, tamen non incommode partiri licet in Motam & Quietam. Mota currentisque frigidior, melior, levior subtiliorque Quieta & Stante; cui contrariae sunt Qualitates & Affectiones, ut pluribus notat Albertus Magnus 1 Meteor. tract.1.cap. ii. & lib. ii. tract. iii. cap. xx. Mota vel agitatur reciproce, cujus generis sunt Maria, quae vi Siderum imprimis Lunae, trahuntur; vel uno tantum agmine perpetuo defluit, ad quam classem pertinent Flumina, Fontes, & id genus alia. Quieta stagnans est, non nisi violentia ventorum agitari solita. Sic fere dividit Aquas Aristoteles lib. ii. Meteor. cap. i. [Greek text illegible] (fontanae) [Greek text illegible] (paludes) [Greek text illegible] (lacus) [Greek text illegible] (puteales) xaλκίδια. Propter tria haec Aquarum genera Trulentem Neptuno tribuit Antiquitas. Aeschyl. Scholiastes [Greek text illegible]. Quur autem Neptuno? Per hunc enim veteres vim Maris significabant, M. Tullius lib. i. de natura Deorum ex Chrysippi sententia prodit, Neptunum nihil aliud esse, quam Spiritum, qui Mare commovet.
units.tr: Isidore, in Book XIII of the Etymologies, chapter 12, draws on some writer unknown to us (for he is accustomed to compile from elsewhere) on the various effects of waters: The element of water, he says, rules over all the others. For water tempers the heavens, makes the earth fruitful, incorporates the air with its exhalations, climbs aloft and claims heaven for itself. For what is more wonderful than waters standing in the sky? It is a small thing for them to have reached such a height; they carry off even shoals of fish with them; they are poured out as the cause of all things that grow on the earth; they bring forth grain, trees, shrubs and herbs; they wash away filth; they give drink to all living creatures. All water, although by its weight it slides downward along a line, may nevertheless without difficulty be divided into moving and still. Moving water, which is running, is colder, better, lighter and finer than still and standing water, which has the opposite qualities and affections, as Albertus Magnus notes at length in Meteorology 1, tract. 1, chapter 2, and in Book 2, tract. 3, chapter 20. Moving water is agitated in alternation, as are the seas, which are drawn by the force of the heavenly bodies, above all the Moon; or it flows continuously in a single stream, as do rivers, springs and the like. Still water is stagnant and is not usually stirred except by the violence of winds. Aristotle, in Book II of the Meteorology, chapter 1, divides waters in much this way: spring waters, marsh waters, lake waters, well waters, and bronze basins [χαλκίδια]. Because of these three kinds of waters, antiquity assigned the trident to Neptune; the scholiast on Aeschylus gives this reason. But why to Neptune? Because through him the ancients signified the power of the sea. Marcus Tullius, in Book I of On the Nature of the Gods, reports from the opinion of Chrysippus that Neptune is nothing other than the Spirit that stirs the sea.

units.la: CAP. V. De Mari universim.
units.tr: CHAP. V. On the Sea in General

units.la: INTER Aquas primo se loco offerunt Maria. Mare nihil aliud, quam collectio reciprocantium Aquarum generalis. Isidero scribente lib. xiv. Originum, cap. xiv. dicta eidem ab Amaritudine. Collectionem diffiniens voco generalem: Nam Aqua, quae dum spacio sex dierum emolirebatur omnia potenter ex nihilo Deus, ante diem tertium universam undique terram operiebat, tertia die unum in locum est congregata; sic ut Terra apparuerit. Ita enim apud Moschen in descriptione operis tertii diei Deus nostrer infinitae potentiae: Congregentur (יקוו) Aquae, quae sub Caelo sunt ad locum unum (אל־מקום אחד) & apparebit Arida (תִּבָּשֶׁת) Addit deinde divinus Scriba: Et factum est ita. Et vocavit Deus Aridam, Terram; & Congregationem Aquarum (ואמקוה המים) appellavit Maria (ימים). Quis quaeso non legat haec & alia ibi cum stupore: Sit oscitans hic, cui sensus omnis obstructus. Nam quis hic locus, qui Aquis totam Terram paullo ante obnubentibus, in ipsa Terra factus receptaculum? Quamvis superari suos hic captus & ingenia libere fateantur viri magni, dixerunt tamen aliquid. Augustinus lib. i. de Genesi ad litteram, cap. xii. & sequuntur illum alii scribunt, Aquam prius fuisse rariorem tenuioremque, & instar materiae nebulosae terram operuisse; postea vero coactam valde densatamque minore eguisse loco. Quidam volunt Terram multis tunc partibus profunde subsedisse, alias contra plurimis in sublime sublatis extumuisse; factasque esse magnas concavitates & valles profundas, quae tantae Aquarum moli constituta quasi vasa; luculenter haec, ut nonnullorum est interpretatio, prosequente Davide, Psalmo civ, versu 6. usque ad 9. Aristoteles etiam lib. i. Meteor. quum unum corpus globosum scripsisset ex Aqua Terraque conflari; magnas simul Terrae concavitates fabricat, inque eas universum Aquae Elementum dirivat. Basilius, Ambrosius, alijque ad cap. i. Genes. & Thomas parte i, quaest. lxix. censent Aquam ante circumfusam toti Terrae, ita suisse tertio die unum in locum coactam, ut in maximam elata sublimitatem altissime extumuerit. Quidquid sit; non absurdum, si dicamus peculiarem Aquis omnibus locum tertio die factum esse Oceanum, cum quo omnia Maria (uno Caspio copulam habente secretionem) continuantur: consulendus Albertus Magnus ii. Meteor. tract. iii. cap. x. Quamvis enim videamus, tam diversa & tam longe dissita Aquarum loca in tot maribus, fluminibus, lacubus, & paludibus, ut etiam nonnulla nulla inter se communione jungi videantur; tamen locus ille, quem Aquis designat apud Moschen Deus, nihil aliud quam Stationes hic ibi, ab habitabili terra separatae; praecipue vero immensum illud spacium, quo reciprocat Oceanus, fluviorum omnium fontiumque pater & princeps; Terram vel circumeundo, vel viscera ejus per venas, conductubulos quosdam, canales & siphunculos, ingrediundo. De qua re plura suo loco Mare igitur generalis collectio Aquarum, quæ tertio die in unum congregata locum: neque interim Mare altius Terra; quod tamen voluerunt, perpensis Sacræ Scripturæ verbis, quæ modo laudavi, Theologorum non pauci; addentes Aquas in unum in locum collectas solo Dei præcepto mirandum in modum teneri: ne ad humiliora loca, quo naturaliter propendent defluentes, Terram universam operiant & obruant. Basilius Homilia iv. in ἐξαήμερ. cui adstipulantur Thomas part. 1. quæst. lxix. art. 1. & Catharinus Commentar. ad cap. 1. Genes. quod dixi, confirmare nititur adducto argumento maris Rubri, cum quo Sesostres Ægypti & Darius Persarum reges conjungere mare Ægyptiacum sunt conati: quod sane, inquit, non tentassent, nisi mare Rubrum altius esse terra Ægypti compertum habuissent. Memoria lapsus videtur, quod obiter monendum, in historiæ hujus commemoratione Basilius. Scribit enim Plinius lib. vi. nat. histor. cap. xxix, Reges, quorum meminit, non mare Ægyptiacum, sed Nilum fluvium cum mari Rubro committere voluisse, incœpto autem desistisse metu exundationis, quum excelsius tribus cubitis Rubrum mare deprehendissent, quam Terram Ægypti; qua de re legendus & Strabo lib. xvii, qui eamdem narrans historiam, notat opus illud fere fuisse absolutum, derelictum tamen ab Dario 1. cui Libratores falso persuaserant, Rubrum mare Ægypto sublimius: Inde, si intermedius Isthmus intercideretur, periculum fore, ne tota Ægyptus ab mari obrueretur. Sunt etiam qui, prolatis in medium aliquot Sacræ Scripturæ locis, eamdem opinionem tueri volunt, Psalm. xxxiii, 7. lxix, 3. civ, 6. Ecclesiastici cap. xxxix, 22. Sed refelluntur sic sentientes docte nervoseque ab Philosophis & Mathematicis, quibus certa hic & indubia docentibus plane consentiendum. Non possum non suffragari hic viris magnis. Si quis dubitat terram, quæ apparet extra aquas, esse superiorem aquis, non tam eget ratione, quam applicatione ad sensum. Cernimus enim motum Aquæ fieri semper locum versus decliviorem: quæ si altior esset Terra, profecto in eam, ut in locum humiliorem, necessario deflueret. Nam dicere Dei omnipotentia teneri Mare, ne defluat in Terram; ineptum est & puerilis insciliæ, ponere sine causa tantum & tam perpetuum miraculum. Quin & Sacra Scriptura videtur eam opinionem evertere; quum petentes ex Terra Mare dicat Descendere Psal. cvii, 33. Certe sine magno miraculo non potest Aqua, quæ natura sua gravior est Aere, quæ fluxa, quæ labilis, ita consistere, ut partes ejus, quæ Terra sublimiores, ad eam non delabantur. Accedunt huc Mathematica argumenta, quibus paullo ante probavi Aquam esse rotundam, quibusque in sequentibus sum probaturus, ex Aqua & Terra unum conflari globum. Demonstrat & quotidiana, quod dixi, experientia. Si enim Mare altius esset Terra, pari ventorum aut remigum vi & impulsu eadem navis multo velocius ferretur, ad portum seu littus tendens; quam ex portu aut littore discedens: discedens enim ex littore ascenderet, & in arduum obnitens difficiliorem haberet progressum: contra ad littus accedens, tamquam per lubrica & declivia descendens magno impetu deferretur. Facit huc & illud, quod quo magis navis ex portu discederet, eo melius commodiusque ab iis, qui sunt in portu vel littore, cerneretur, utpote quæ magis ac magis semper in locum altiorem ascenderet; quod tamen contra evenit. Benedictus porro Pererius lib. 1. in Genesin docet, quo pacto testimonia Sacræ Scripturæ, quæ pro confirmatione sententiæ prædictæ solent adferri, sint accipienda. Pergo.
units.tr: Among the waters, the seas first present themselves. The sea is nothing other than a general collection of the reciprocating waters. Isidore, writing in the Origines, book xiv, chapter xiv, says that it is so called from its bitterness. In defining it I call it "general," because the water which, while God was powerfully bringing everything out of nothing over the space of six days, covered the whole earth on every side before the third day, was gathered on the third day into one place, so that the dry land appeared. For so Moses, in the account of the work of the third day, has our God of infinite power speak: Let the waters that are under heaven be gathered [יקוו] into one place [אל־מקום אחד] and let the dry land appear [תִּבָּשֶׁת]. The divine scribe then adds: And it was so. And God called the dry land Earth, and the gathering of the waters [ואמקוה המים] he called Seas [ימים]. Who, I ask, would read these words, and others there, without wonder? Let whoever is dull and whose senses are all blocked be dull. For what place is this, which, made in the very Earth, is the receptacle of waters that a little before had covered the whole Earth? Although great men frankly confess that their grasp and their powers are overcome here, they have nonetheless said something. Augustine, in book i of On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, chapter xii, and others who follow him, write that the water was at first rarer and thinner, and covered the earth like a cloudy matter; afterwards, however, it was condensed and compacted and needed a smaller place. Some hold that at that time the earth sank deeply in many parts and rose high in others, and that great hollows and deep valleys were made, which served as vessels for so great a mass of waters; this is set out clearly, as some interpret it, in Psalm civ, verses 6 to 9. Aristotle too, in book i of the Meteorology, after writing that one globular body is formed from water and earth, at the same time fashions large hollows in the earth and drains the whole element of water into them. Basil, Ambrose and others on Genesis chapter 1, and Thomas, part i, question lxix, hold that the water, which before surrounded the whole earth, was then gathered into one place on the third day, so that it rose up into a very great height. Whatever the case, it is not absurd to say that a particular place for all the waters was made on the third day, namely the Ocean, with which all the seas are joined (the Caspian alone having a separate, enclosed basin) and continuous: Albertus Magnus, in ii Meteorology, tract. iii, chapter x, should be consulted. For although we see such diverse and far-separated places of water, in so many seas, rivers, lakes and marshes, that some seem to be joined by no communication at all with one another, yet that place which God designates for the waters in Moses is nothing other than the stations here and there, separated from the habitable earth; and above all that immense space in which the Ocean ebbs and flows, the father and prince of all rivers and springs, either by going round the Earth or by entering its inner parts through veins, certain conduits, channels and siphons. Concerning this matter more will be said in its place. The sea, then, is the general collection of the waters, which on the third day were gathered into one place. Yet meanwhile the sea is not higher than the land. Nevertheless, a good number of theologians have held that it is higher, having weighed the words of Holy Scripture just cited; adding that the waters, gathered into one place, are held there in a wonderful manner by the command of God alone, lest, flowing down to the lower places towards which they naturally tend, they cover and overwhelm the whole earth. Basil, Homily iv, On the Hexaemeron, which Thomas, part 1, question lxix, article 1, and Catharinus in his Commentary on Genesis chapter 1 support, strives to confirm what I have said by the argument drawn from the Red Sea, with which the kings of Egypt, Sesostris, and of the Persians, Darius, tried to join the Egyptian sea: which indeed, he says, they would not have attempted, unless they had found that the Red Sea was higher than the land of Egypt. It seems to be a slip of memory, which should be pointed out in passing, on Basil's part in his recounting of this history. For Pliny, in book vi of the Natural History, chapter xxix, writes that the kings he mentions wished to join not the Egyptian sea but the river Nile with the Red Sea, but gave up the undertaking out of fear of flooding, when they found the Red Sea higher by three cubits than the land of Egypt. Strabo, book xvii, should also be read on this matter; he, narrating the same story, notes that this work was almost finished but was abandoned by Darius I, because the surveyors had falsely persuaded him that the Red Sea was higher than Egypt, so that if the intervening isthmus were cut through, there would be danger that all Egypt would be overwhelmed by the sea. There are also some who, bringing forward several passages of Holy Scripture, want to defend the same opinion: Psalm xxxiii, 7; lxix, 3; civ, 6; Ecclesiasticus chapter xxxix, 22. But those who think so are learnedly and forcefully refuted by philosophers and mathematicians, whose teaching on this point is certain and indubitable, and with whom we must wholly agree. I cannot but side here with those great men. If anyone doubts that the land which appears outside the waters is higher than the waters, he needs not so much argument as an appeal to the senses. For we see that the movement of water always goes towards the lower place; and if the earth were higher, the water would certainly, of necessity, flow down into it, as into a lower place. For to say that the sea is held by the omnipotence of God lest it flow down onto the land is absurd and a sign of childish folly, to posit without cause so great and so perpetual a miracle. Indeed Holy Scripture seems to overturn that opinion too, since it says that the sea descends when those who seek it come from the land (Psalm cvii, 33). Certainly, without a great miracle, water, which by its nature is heavier than air, and which is fluid and slippery, cannot stand in such a way that the parts of it which are higher than the land do not slide down onto it. To this are added mathematical arguments, by which I proved a little earlier that water is round, and by which I shall prove in what follows that the globe is made of water and earth together. Daily experience too demonstrates what I have said. For if the sea were higher than the land, a ship would be carried much more swiftly, with equal force of winds or oarsmen and equal impulse, when heading towards a harbour or shore, than when leaving a harbour or shore. For leaving the shore it would rise, and struggling upward would have a more difficult advance; while approaching the shore it would be carried with great momentum, as if descending over slippery and sloping ground. To this also belongs the fact that the further a ship leaves the harbour, the better and more easily it would be seen by those who are in the harbour or on the shore, since it would always be rising more and more into a higher place; yet the contrary happens. Benedictus Pererius, in book i of his Commentary on Genesis, moreover teaches how the testimonies of Holy Scripture which are usually brought forward to confirm the aforesaid opinion are to be understood. I proceed.

units.la: Facta in Definitione Reciprocantium Aquarum mentione, moneor, ut de Æstu nonnihil dicam. Æstus dicitur Motus Maris, quo exundans fluit; &, exacta periodo, refluit. Species ejus: hinc Æstus speciali-ore notione, qui Maris Accessus alijs; Græcis πλήμμ, πλημμύρα, πλημμυρίς; Strabo-ni: inde Recessus vel Reciprocatio: Græcis ἀναλίρροσις, Homero κῦμα ἀναλίρροσιον, Apollonio πλημμυρίς ἀναλίνο-σ, Theophrasto ἀμπώσις, Straboni denique ἄνεσις, Cautiis ejus inquirendis operam maximam impenderunt maxima quondam ævoque nostro ingenia; Heroibus etiam hanc curam suscipientibus. Est enim illa maris Reciprocatio admiratione dignissima, & res plane divina. Bene M. Tullius lib. iii. de Natura Deorum: Quid Chalcidico Euripo in motu identidem reciprocando putas fieri posse constantius? quid freto Siculensi, quid Oceani fervore illo in loco, Europam Libyamque rapax ubi dividit unda?
units.tr: Having mentioned the reciprocating waters in the definition, I am reminded to say something about the Tide. The tide is called the motion of the sea by which it flows out in flood and, when its cycle is completed, flows back. Its kinds: hence, in a narrower sense, the tide is the advance of the sea according to others; in Greek πλήμμυρα, πλημμυρίς; according to Strabo, the retreat or reciprocation [ἀναλίρροσις]; in Homer, the wave that ebbs back [κῦμα ἀναλίρροσιον]; in Apollonius, the flood-tide of the ebb [πλημμυρίς ἀναλίρροσις]; in Theophrastus, the drawing back [ἀμπώσις]; and finally in Strabo, the slackening [ἄνεσις]. Great minds of old, and of our own age too, have devoted the greatest effort to inquiring into its causes; heroes too have taken up this care. For this reciprocation of the sea is most worthy of admiration, and a truly divine thing. Marcus Tullius rightly says in book iii of On the Nature of the Gods: What do you think can be more constant than the Chalcidian Euripus, which keeps reciprocating its motion again and again? What than the strait of Sicily, or that fervour of the Ocean in the place where the rapacious wave divides Europe from Libya?

units.la: Quid Aestus maritimi vel Hispanienses, vel Britannici, eorumque certis temporibus vel Accessus vel Recessus sine Deo fieri num possint? Caussæ vero variæ variæ, quemadmodum videre est apud Plutarchum de Placitis Philosoph. Plato, notante Strabone ἐκλογ. Quæst. lib. 1. (videndus & ipse in Phædone) ἀναφορὰ τῶν ὑδάτων, suspendium adferr Aquarum; esse enim illud per quoddam Terræ foramen, Æstum circumferens, ac Mari tumorem concilians. Aristoteles & Heraclides apud eundem Soli caussam tribuunt: plerosque Spiritus moventi ac circumferenti: quibus ingruentibus quidem, propulsum Atlanticum mare intumescat, Æstumque efficiat; cessantibus autem, retractum subsidat, Æstumque revocet. Platonici (quorum sententiam sequitur etiam Strabo lib. 1.) dixerunt Mare Animanti simile: Vt enim hoc spiritum emittit & retrahit; ita illud in se & ex se recurrenti quadam agitatione moveri. Videtur & hoc velle Vegetius lib. iv. de re militari, cap. xlii: Elementum Pelagi tertia pars Mundi est, quod præter ventorum flatum suo quoque spiramine motuque vegetatur. Non procul hinc abeunt Physicorum nonnulli apud Solinum, qui totum Mundum Animal esse somniant, nares illi constituentes in penitissimis Oceani, quibus spiritum attrahat, attractumque emittat. Physici, inquit, autumant Animal esse Mundum, eumque ex variis Elementorum corporibus conglobatum, moveri spiritu, regimente: quæ utraque diffusa per membra omnia æterna motus vigorem exerceant. Sicut ergo in Corpo illus commercia sunt spiritalia; ita in profundis Oceani nares quasdam Mundi constitutas, per quas emissi anhelitus vel reducit: modo inflent maria, modo revocent. Alij apud Pomponium lib. iii. depressos imaginati sunt Specus, in quos ingenti se mole vibrans Aquarum moles mergatur, & rursum mcatuum repagulis pulla exundet; quod agere spiritus sub Aqua conclusos Apollonius Tyaneus existimabat, ut lib. v. scribit Philostratus. Macrobius lib. ii. in Somnium Scipionis: illum Maris motum ex eo esse putavit, quod Sinus Oceani Orientalis & Occidentalis mutuo concursu sese feriant, impetuque immaniore mitceantur, ex quarum collisione nascitur, inquit, famosa illa Oceani Accessio & Recessio. Lucanus animum hic despondens ignorantiam suam fatetur, veram caussam nescire se non invitus canens: — qua littus dubium, quod Terra Fretumque Vindicat alternis vicibus: quum funditur ingens Oceanus; vel quum refugis de fluctibus aufert Ventus ab extremo pelagus sic axe volatet, Desistuatque ferens; an sidere mota secundo Tethys unda vaga Lunaribus æstuat horis; Flammiger an Titan, ut alentes hauriat undas, Eligat Oceanum, fluctuosque ad sidera tollat: Quærite quos agitat Mundi labor; at mihi semper Tu quacunque moves tam crebros caussa meatus, Vt superi volvere, lates.
units.tr: What about the tides of the sea, whether Spanish or British, and their advances and retreats at fixed times: can these happen without God? The causes are various, as can be seen in Plutarch's On the Opinions of the Philosophers. Plato, as Strabo notes (Ekloge, Quæst. lib. 1; to be consulted also in the Phaedo), held that the waters have a carrying back and forth [ἀναφορὰ τῶν ὑδάτων], a suspension of the waters. He said there is a certain opening in the earth that drives the tide back and forth, and brings about the swelling of the sea. Aristotle and Heraclides, according to the same Strabo, assign the cause to the sun, and to the many winds that move and carry it around. When these winds press on, the Atlantic sea is pushed forward and swells into a tide; when they cease, it is drawn back, subsides, and the tide ebbs. The Platonists (whose opinion Strabo also follows in book 1) said the sea is like a living creature: just as the creature breathes out and draws in again, so the sea is moved by a certain agitation of returning into itself and out of itself. Vegetius in book 4 of On Military Affairs, chapter 42, seems to hold this too: The element of the sea is a third part of the world, which, apart from the blowing of the winds, is also quickened by its own breathing and motion. Not far from this are some of the natural philosophers in Solinus, who dream that the whole world is an animal, with nostrils set in the deepest parts of the ocean, by which it draws in breath and breathes it out again. The physicists, he says, hold that the world is an animal, compacted from the various bodies of the elements, and moved by a governing spirit; both of these, diffused through all its members, exert the eternal vigour of motion. Just as in the body there are spiritual exchanges, so in the depths of the ocean certain nostrils of the world are set, through which it draws back the breath it has breathed out: now it swells the seas, now it recalls them. Others, in Pomponius book 3, imagined sunken caverns into which the huge mass of waters, swinging with great force, plunges, and then pours out again through the openings of the channels; Apollonius of Tyana thought that spirits enclosed under the water did this, as Philostratus writes in book 5. Macrobius, in book 2 on the Dream of Scipio, thought that this movement of the sea arises from the eastern and western bays of the ocean striking one another and churning with a more violent impact: from their collision, he says, arises that famous advance and retreat of the ocean. Lucan, despairing here, confesses his ignorance, singing not unwillingly that he does not know the true cause: "Where the shore is doubtful, which land and sea claim in alternating turns, when the vast ocean pours in; or when the wind, carrying the sea back from the fleeing waves, lifts it from the far edge of the sky and lets it fall again; whether the wandering tide of Tethys, moved by a favourable star, swells in lunar hours; or whether the fiery Titan chooses to draw up the nourishing waters from the ocean and raise the waves to the stars. Ask those whom the labour of the world troubles; but to me, whatever cause moves you to such frequent ebbings and flowings, you remain hidden, as the gods above have turned it."

units.la: Vbi non ofcitanter legenda, quæ de Lunaribus horis. Namque tam stupendo miraculo caussa princeps, Efficacia Motusque Corporum Cœlestium, cum primis illorum, quibus cognatio cum humidis, in quorum classe palmarium debetur Lunæ. Hæc enim Humorum omnium, ut quæ citima Terris fertur, dominatrix, eos sua Virtute ciet movetque; non solum in Animalium, quod de Luna differens monui, sed aliarum etiam rerum corporibus. Adeundi Ptolemæus ii. quadripart. cap. xii, Plinius lib. ii. natur. histor. cap. xcvii, M. Tullius lib. ii. de Divinatione, Averroes in sua Paraphr. Ambrosius lib. iv: ἐξαρμὶς. Sic Sillius lib. iii. belli Pœnici: Cynothees ea regna vaga, Pelagique labores Luna movet; Luna, immissis per cærula bigis, Fertque referetque Fretum, sequiturque reciproca Tethys.
units.tr: This is where we must read carefully what is said about the lunar hours. For the chief cause of so astonishing a wonder is the efficacy and motion of the heavenly bodies, above all those that have kinship with moisture, among whom the chief place is owed to the moon. For she, as the one that is said to be nearest to the earth, is the mistress of all humours, and by her power stirs and moves them, not only in the bodies of animals, as I noted when treating of the moon, but also in the bodies of other things. See Ptolemy, Tetrabiblos book 2, chapter 12; Pliny, Natural History book 2, chapter 97; Cicero, On Divination book 2; Averroes in his paraphrase; and Ambrose, book 4, Exarmis. So Silius in book 3 of the Punic War: "The moon moves the wandering waters of the Cynothes and the labours of the sea; the moon, driving her chariots across the blue sky, carries the sea to and fro, and the reciprocating Tethys follows her."

units.la: Præter Veteres consulendi sunt & Recentiores, Albertus de Elementorum proprietatibus, Thomas de occultis Naturæ operibus, Thimon. ii. Meteor. quæst. ii. Picus Mirandula contra Astrologos iii. cap. xv. Augustinus Niphus Suessanus super Enunciatum xxv, libri de nostrarum Calamitatum causis tertij. Quemadmodum vero Luna varias in Motu vices sustinet; ita etiam dissimilibus vicibus agitantur Æstus. Nam Lunam sequentes bis inter duos ejus exortus adfluunt, bis refluunt, vicenis-quaternis semper horis: hoc est, Maria singulis diebus naturalibus bis inundant, bis recedunt: intumescentia, adscendente Luna supra Horizontem ortivum; relabentia vero ipsa ab meridiano cœli fastigio in occasum vergente: iterum exsurgentia, recedente subter ima cœli Luna, partemque meridianæ contrariam accedente; hinc subsidentia, donec iterum exoriatur. M. Terentius Varro lib. viii. de Lingua Latina: At in Mari, credo, Motus non habent dissimilitudines geminas qui xxiv. horis Lunaribus quotidie quater se mutant. at quum sex horis Æstus creverunt, totidem decreverunt rursum. Vegetius lib. iiii. de re milit. cap. xl.ii: In diversis regionibus diverso Lunæ crescentis minuentisque statu certis horis ista variantur, &c. Vt item Luna non semper eodem tempore neque loco oritur; sed assidue aliunde, quam pridie, prodit: sic nec Æstus statis horis recurrunt; sed illo tantum tempore, quo ipsa iter facit per cœli cardines. Plinius lib. ii, cap. xcvii: Nec unquam eodem tempore quo pridie reflui, ut ancillante sidere trahenteque secum avido haustu, maria, & assidue aliunde quam pridie exoriente: paribus tamen intervallis reciproci, sentisque semper horis non cuiusque diei aut noctis aut loci, sed æquinoctialibus. Hoc etiam notandum Lunam aliter Maria movere, quum plena; aliter, quum dimidiata. Maior enim vis lumini copioso, quam debili & velut exstincto. Plinius eodem capite: Multiplex etiamnum lunaris differentia, primumque septenis diebus. Quippe modici nova ad dividuam æstus, pleni ere ab ea exundant, plenaque maxime fervent: inde mitescunt. Pares ad septimam primis: iterumque alio latere dimidio augentur. In coitu Solis pares, &c. Hinc Cæsar lib. iv. de bello Gallico: Eadem nocte accidit, ut esset Luna plena, qui dies natutinos æstus in Oceano maximos efficere solet. Tacitus lib. i. Annalium: Vitellius primum iter sicca humo, aut modice adlabente æstu, quietum habuit; mox impulsu Aquilonis, simul sidere Æquinoctii, quo maximo tumescit Oceanus, rapi agique agmen: & opplebantur terræ; eadem sicco, littora, campis facies; neque discerni poterant incerta ab solidis, brevia a profundis, &c. Nota nostratibus Plenilunii tempore vox, Sprincke loedt, quasi Æstus altius solito exsiliens. Non minus vere, quam eleganter Agellius lib. xiv, Oceanum, quasi Lunæ comitem, cum ea simul & senescere, & adulescere solere, ait. Configurationes quoque nonnullius hic momenti. Luna enim, si Venerem, dicis gratia, in idoneo adspectu respiciat, & humidas percurrat mansiones; Accessum Maris præter solitum auget; sin Martem, & siccas permeet, minuit. Observanda & hic adscensio Signorum. Luna enim si fuerit in Signis Rectarum Adscensionum, longiore tempore producit Æstus; quam si in Obliquarum. Hoc namque animadversum viris magnis, numquam Accessus Recessibus pares esse temporis duratione; nisi quum Luna in Signis Æquinoctialibus sine latitudine. Plinius paullo ante: sentisque semper horis non cuiusque diei, aut noctis, aut loci; sed æquinoctialibus &c. Neque hoc silentio prætereundum, alias Aquarum partes magis vi luminis & radiorum corporis Lunaris adfici, quam alias; vel ob rectitudinem radiorum, vel vim quamdam aliam occultiorem. Quin & alia efficacia radios suos in Aquas demittit Luna, si Septemtrionalis; alia, si Meridionalis: hic enim Accessus auget in littoribus Meridianis; ibi in Septemtrionalibus. Plinius eodem capite: Plane eadem Aquilonia & a terris longius recedente mittiores, quam quum in Austros digressa propiore nisu vim suam exercet. 40 Effectus huius Æstus alios novimus & experimur commodos, alios incommodos. Illos quidem, quod Aquas purget, ne stantes & quietæ (docet hoc experientia) situ & putrefactione corrumpantur: quod item promoveat Navigantes; Nam, ut inquit Vegetius lib. iv. de re militari; cap. xl.iii, hæc reciprocantis meatus abiquitas Cursum Navium secunda adjuvat, retardat adversa. Hos autem, Inundationum & Perruptionum violentia. Nam tanta sæpe vi terris immittitur Oceanus; ut etiam vasta flumina retroagat, mergens abluensque spaciosos campos. Scribit hoc Pomponius Mela; clamantque tot multorum seculorum calamitates. Perruptiones testantur Insulæ numerosæ; quæ Continenti quomdam adhæserunt: Sicilia Italiæ, Cyprus Syriæ, Euboea Bœotiæ, Taprobana Indiæ, aliæ aliis, ut videre est apud Strabonem lib. i. Georg. Ovidium xv. Metamorph. Senecam lib. vi, & Plinium lib. ii. cap. xxxiiix. adeo ut nonnullis Mare videatur in eo totum esse, quo terras absorbeat, & omnia pontum faciat. Sed terminum illi posuit magnus & potens Dev s, qui apud Jirmeiam cap. v: Me ergo non timebitis, ait, & a facie mea non dolebitis? Qui posui Arenam terminum Mari, præceptum sempiternum quod non præteribit: & commovebuntur & non poterunt: & intumescent fluctus ejus, & non transibunt illud. Hic enim, ut inquit Hiob. cap. xii, Si continuerit Aquas, omnia siccabuntur; & si emiserit eas, subvertent Terram. Hæc de Aestu; super quo etiam consulenda Possidonij Disputatio; ab ijs quae nobis hodie nota, non abhorrens, apud Strabonem libro iii. extremo.
units.tr: Besides the ancients, the more recent writers should also be consulted: Albert, On the Properties of the Elements; Thomas, On the Hidden Works of Nature; Thimon, book 2 of the Meteorology, question 2; Pico della Mirandola, Against the Astrologers, book 3, chapter 15; Agostino Nifo of Sessa, on the twenty-fifth enunciation of the third book On the Causes of Our Calamities. But just as the moon undergoes varied changes in her motion, so the tides are driven by unlike alternations. For, following the moon, the waters flow in twice between her two risings, and ebb twice, always in twenty-four hours: that is, the seas flood twice and recede twice in each natural day.
