They swell as the moon ascends above the eastern horizon, and sink again as she descends from the highest point of the heavens toward the west; they rise again as the moon withdraws beneath the lowest point of the heavens and approaches the meridian opposite; then they subside again until she rises once more. Marcus Terentius Varro, in book 8 of On the Latin Language: But in the sea, I believe, the motions do not have twofold differences, which change four times a day in twenty-four lunar hours. But when the tides have risen for six hours, they fall back for as many. Vegetius in book 4 of On Military Affairs, chapter 42: In different regions these vary at fixed hours according to the different state of the waxing and waning moon, etc. And just as the moon does not always rise at the same time or place, but always appears at a different hour and point from the day before, so the tides do not return at fixed hours, but only at that time when the moon itself makes its course through the poles of the heavens. Pliny, book 2, chapter 97: Nor does the sea ever ebb at the same time as the day before, as the star attends and draws the waters with greedy suction, always rising from a different point than the day before; yet they return at equal intervals, and always at the same hours, not of each day, night or place, but at equinoctial hours. It must also be noted that the moon moves the seas one way when she is full, and another way when she is half. For greater force belongs to the abundant light than to the weak and, as it were, extinguished. Pliny in the same chapter: There is still a manifold difference in the lunar influence, and first by sevens of days. For at the new moon the tides are small and almost undivided; at the full they overflow from her, and at full moon they boil most fiercely; then they grow gentle. They are equal again at the seventh day, and then increase again on the other side at the half moon. At the conjunction of the sun they are equal, etc. Hence Caesar, in book 4 of the Gallic War: It happened on the same night that the moon was full, which usually produces the greatest morning tides in the ocean. Tacitus in book 1 of the Annals: Vitellius at first had a quiet journey over dry ground, or where the tide lapped gently; but then, driven by the north wind, and at the same time by the star of the equinox, when the ocean swells most, the column was seized and driven: the lands were flooded, and the shores and plains showed the same face; nor could the uncertain be told from the solid, the shallows from the depths, etc. Our countrymen have a notable expression for the time of full moon, Sprincke loedt, as if the tide leaps higher than usual. No less truly than elegantly, Aulus Gellius in book 14 says that the ocean, as the companion of the moon, is wont to wane and wax together with her. The configurations of the planets are also of some importance here. For the moon, if she looks upon Venus, to speak figuratively, in a favourable aspect and passes through the moist mansions, increases the advance of the sea beyond its usual measure; but if she meets Mars and passes through the dry ones, she diminishes it. The ascension of the signs must also be observed here. For if the moon is in the signs of straight ascension, she produces the tides over a longer time than if she is in the signs of oblique ascension. For great men have observed that the advances and retreats are never equal in duration, except when the moon is in the equinoctial signs without latitude. Pliny, a little before: and always at the same hours, not of each day, night or place, but at equinoctial hours, etc. Nor is this to be passed over in silence: that different parts of the waters are affected more by the force of the light and rays of the lunar body than others, either because of the straightness of the rays or some other more hidden power. Indeed the moon also sends her rays into the waters with one efficacy when she is northern, and with another when she is southern: for her approach increases the tides on the southern shores, and on the northern in the other case. Pliny in the same chapter: Plainly the same northern influences, when she is farther from the lands, are milder than when, having moved toward the south, she exerts her power with a nearer effort. We know and experience other effects of this tide, some useful, some harmful. The useful ones are that it cleanses the waters, so that they do not become corrupted by stagnation and putrefaction, as experience teaches when they are still and quiet; and that it likewise helps those who sail: for, as Vegetius says in book 4 of On Military Affairs, chapter 43, this alternating movement of the returning tide helps the course of ships when favourable and holds them back when adverse. The harmful ones are the violence of floods and inundations. For the ocean is often driven into the lands with such force that it even pushes back vast rivers, drowning and washing over wide plains. Pomponius Mela writes this, and the calamities of so many ages cry it out. The many islands that once clung to the mainland testify to breaches: Sicily to Italy, Cyprus to Syria, Euboea to Boeotia, Taprobane to India, and others to others, as can be seen in Strabo book 1, Ovid Metamorphoses book 15, Seneca book 6, and Pliny book 2, chapter 93. So much so that some think the sea is entirely in this, that it swallows lands and makes everything into sea. But the great and powerful God set a limit to it, who in Jeremiah chapter 5 says: "Do you not fear me, says the LORD, and will you not tremble before my face? I who have set the sand as the bound of the sea, a perpetual decree that it cannot pass: and though its waves toss, yet they cannot prevail; though they roar, yet they cannot pass over it." For, as Job says in chapter 12: "Behold, if he withholds the waters, they dry up; and if he sends them out, they overturn the earth." These are the matters concerning the tide, on which Posidonius's discussion may also be consulted; it is not unworthy of what is known to us today, and is found in Strabo book 3, near the end.

units.la: Mare porro Salum dicitur, vel ἀπὸ τῆς ἁλὸς, ut quidam volunt, quod fluctuat; vel ab Salsedine, quam sunt qui in ipsa creatione datam Mari notant. Anaximander censuit Mare salsum esse, quod ad ipsum flumina salsa magno numero confluant: Anaxagoras & Plato, propter venas Terrae salsas: Platonici, ob nonnullas Terrae partes, quae in imo Maris salsas. Aristoteli lib. ii. Meteor. visum hoc fieri, propter Sicci terrestris usti permistionem cum ejus aquoso humido. Anaximenes & Diogenes Solis Stellarumque actioni Salsedinem attribuerunt: dixerunt enim Mare initio dulce fuisse, postea actione Stellarum saltum evasisse. Plerique Philosophi Salsedinem putant ab Exhalationibus: quas virtute Solis & Stellarum ex Mari sursum evectas, decidentes rursum ejus aquis deinde permisceri volunt. Videndus omnino Averroes in Paraphr.
units.tr: The sea is called Salum, either from ἁλός [from salt], as some hold, because it surges, or from its saltiness, which some note was given to the sea at its creation. Anaximander thought the sea was salt because a great number of salt rivers flow into it. Anaxagoras and Plato thought so because of the salty veins of the earth. The Platonists ascribed it to certain parts of the earth at the bottom of the sea that are salty. Aristotle, in book 2 of the Meteorology, thought it came from the mixing of dry, burnt earthy matter with the watery moisture. Anaximenes and Diogenes attributed the saltiness to the action of the sun and stars, for they said the sea was originally sweet and afterwards became salt through the action of the stars. Most philosophers think the saltiness comes from exhalations, which are drawn up out of the sea by the power of the sun and stars, fall back down, and are then mixed again with its waters. Averroes in his Paraphrase is well worth consulting.

units.la: Quod autem Mare non augeat, quum tot flumina, tot in se recipiat fontes, variae sint apud Isidorum lib. xiii, cap. xiv. & alios causas. i. enim adcurrentes undas ejus vastitas non sentit; ii. amarior ejus aqua dulces, quae adfluunt, consumit: iii. Nubes multum hinc Aquarum ad se attrahunt: iv. marinam Aquam partim auserunt Venti, partim Sol exiccat: v. denique Mare per occulta quaedam Terrae foramina percolatur, & ad caput amnium fontiumque revolutum recurrit. De postrema hac causa nonnihil etiam ubi de Fluminum Fontiumque ortu.
units.tr: Why the sea does not grow, although so many rivers flow into it and so many springs feed it, is explained in various ways by Isidore, book 13, chapter 14, and by others: (1) its vast size does not feel the waves that flow into it; (2) its bitter water consumes the sweet waters that run in; (3) clouds draw much of its water up to themselves; (4) the winds carry off part of the sea water, and the sun dries up part of it; (5) finally, the sea seeps through certain hidden holes in the earth and flows back to the source of rivers and springs. Something more about this last cause will be said also where we discuss the origin of rivers and springs.

units.la: Plinius lib. ii. natur. histor. cap. xcix, omnia Maria purgari notat Plenilunio; quaedam etiam stato tempore; & circa Messanam & Mylas simo similia exspui in littus purgamenta. Quur hoc? Nihil enim patiuntur foedi, nihil inquinati; quidquid violentia perit tempestatum, id omne ad littus explodunt. Respicit eo Latinus suo Panegyrico: Noster Pirata quidquid undecumque convexerat, id nobis sibique periturum in illam speluncam Charybdim congerebat. Charybdim loquor? quae quum plena navigia sorbuerit, dicitur tamen erutare naufragia, & contortas fando rates Tauromenitanis littoribus exponere.
units.tr: Pliny, Natural History book 2, chapter 99, notes that all seas are purged at full moon, and some also at a fixed season; and near Messana and Myle they cast up on the shore refuse like filth. Why is this? For the sea suffers nothing foul and nothing polluted; whatever perishes through the violence of storms, all of it it throws out onto the shore. Latinus alludes to this in his Panegyric: "Our pirate, whatever he had carried off from wherever, was piling it up for our destruction and his own in that cave, Charybdis. Do I say Charybdis? Though it has swallowed down full ships, it is nonetheless said to vomit up wrecks and to cast onto the Tauromenian shores the timbers of ships, twisted and broken."

units.la: Certe Cadavera & alia quaeque naufraga littoribus reddi, quotidie docemur, qui maris adcolae. Superstitiosius hoc, quod Magi nefas crederent, exspuere in Mare, eoque ad humanas necessitates uti. Plinius de Tyridate Mago, quem ad se Nero acciverat: Magus ad cum Tyridates venerat, Armeniacum de se triumphum adferens, & ideo provincias gravis navigare noluerat; quoniam exspuere in Maria, aliasque mortalium necessitatibus violare naturam ipsam fas non putent. Non igitur obscurum, quam ob causam marinas (Aquis omnibus tribuunt purgandi vim alij scriptores) undas usurparit Antiquitas in Purgationibus, ut videre est apud Catullum de aversis incestisque Gellii Veneribus, Senecam in Hippolyto, Apuleium libro xr. Metamorph. Lactantium lib. v. Instit. Divinar. cap. xx. Et hinc, cum apud alios tum Iulium Obsequentem de Prodigijs, leguntur Hermaphroditi Aruspicum praecepto in Mare deportari quondam soliti; quod nullis nisi aequoris undis ejusmodi Portentum lavari & expiari posse arbitrarentur. Quin Maris undas medendis morbis adhibitas innuit Diogenes Laërtius, Euripidem scribens cum Platone profectum in Ægyptum, ibique aegrotantem marina curatione ab Ægyptijs Sacerdotibus sanatum: unde postea, tamquam accepti memor beneficij, Mari hoc Encomium posuit:
units.tr: Certainly we who live by the sea are taught every day that corpses and all other wrecked things are returned to the shores. It was a superstition of the Magi to think it wrong to spit into the sea, and so they put it to human uses. Pliny writes of Tyridates the Magus, whom Nero had summoned to himself: "The Magus Tyridates had come to him, bringing news of an Armenian triumph over himself, and for that reason had been unwilling to travel through burdensome provinces, since they do not think it right to spit into the seas or to violate nature itself with other human necessities." It is therefore not obscure why antiquity used sea waves in purifications (other writers attribute purifying power to all waters), as can be seen in Catullus on the incestuous and perverted Venuses of Gellius, in Seneca's Hippolytus, in Apuleius book 11 of the Metamorphoses, and in Lactantius, Divine Institutes book 5, chapter 20. And hence, in Julius Obsequens on prodigies, among others, we read that hermaphrodites were once commonly carried out into the sea on the instruction of the haruspices, because they believed such a portent could be washed away and expiated by nothing but the waves of the sea. Indeed Diogenes Laërtius hints that sea waves were used in the treatment of diseases, writing that Euripides, having travelled with Plato into Egypt and being ill there, was cured by a sea treatment from the Egyptian priests; and that afterwards, mindful of the benefit he had received, he composed this praise of the sea:

units.la: Θάλασσα κλύζει πάντα τ' ἀνθρώπων κακά.
units.tr: The sea washes away all the ills of men. [Θάλασσα κλύζει πάντα τ' ἀνθρώπων κακά.]

units.la: Docet apud Macrobium lib. vii. Saturn. cap. xii, Difarius ab Avieno provocatus, Aquam marinam, quae amaritudine sui aspera est, numquam gelu contrahi: Herodotum Historiarum scriptorem contra omnium fere, qui haec quaesiverunt, opinionem scripsisse, mare Bosphoricum; eorumque partium mare omne, quod Scythicum dicitur, gelu constringi & consistere: aliter enim esse, quam putatur. Nam non marinam Aquam contrahi; sed, quia plurimum in illis regionibus fluviorum est, qui in ipsa Maria se exonerant, superficies Maris, cui dulces Aquae innatant, congelascere, & incolumi Aqua marina, videri in Mari gelu, sed de advenis undis coactum. Fidem deinde restatur Ponti, in quo frustra quaedam & proficiae gelidae feruntur, contractae de fluvialium undarum multitudine. Sunt qui hanc Difarij, marinam Aquam congelationis capacem negantis, disputationem rapiunt in controversiam: quod videant sequiora de Ponto scripta ab Ovidio: Ipse vides certe glacies concrescere Pontum; Ipse vides gelido flantia vina gelu;
units.tr: Difarius, challenged by Avienus, asserts in Macrobius, Saturnalia book 7, chapter 12, that sea water, which is harsh with its own bitterness, never freezes. Herodotus, the historian, wrote against almost everyone who inquired into these matters that the Bosporus and all that part of the sea called Scythian are bound and solidified by ice, and that it is otherwise than is thought. For the sea water does not contract; rather, since in those regions a great many rivers discharge themselves into the seas, the surface of the sea, on which the sweet waters float, freezes, and while the sea water remains unharmed, ice seems to form in the sea, but it is formed from the incoming waters. He then vouches for the reliability of the Pontus, in which certain icy masses are said to be carried along, formed from the great multitude of river waters. There are those who seize on Difarius's argument, which denies that sea water can freeze, and turn it into a dispute. Let them look at the later writings about the Pontus by Ovid: "You yourself certainly see the Pontus turning to ice; you yourself see the wines, flowing, bound by the icy cold."

units.la: Ipse vides onerata ferox ut ducat Iacis Per medias Istri plaustra bubulcus aquas.
units.tr: You yourself see how the fierce ploughman drives his loaded wagons through the middle of the waters of the Ister.

units.la: In Ponti naturam, an hieme obdurctur, curiosius numquam inquisivi: alioqui videri posset Ovidius talia de eo cecinisse, in littore, non in altum provectus; & ut Poëta homoque exsul, ut horribilis loci, in quem pulsus erat, delineatione misericordiam moveret cum aliis, tum Augusto principi. Certe vix esse, ut Maria (non loquor de Terrae vel infusis vel adluentibus) glacie concrescant; testamur qui adhabitamus; clamant & Argonautae nostri, qui nuperrime per fretum Vaigarium, cui Nassouium nomen indiderunt, Sinarum regna congitantes, Septemtrionale Pelagus aliquoties, semel etiam ad xxc, & quod excurrebat, Altitudinis gradum navigarunt. Inciderunt quidem non raro, cum summo navium vitaeque discrimine, in multam glaciem, sed terris adnavigantes, prope littora & portus; ut illa non tam videretur ex mari nata, marinaeque planitus connata, quam ex littoribus ventorum vehementia & undarum impetu in altum provoluta, & ex fruitris proficisque in colliculos quasi constipata. Hinc est, quod in suis Diariis passim notent; vento mutato, Mare nunc navigabile, nunc contra fuisse: hinc quod ubique littorea commemorent ab glacie pericula: hinc denique quod nullo non loco lineam a prora navigantes demittere potuerint, absque ullo obstaculo, ad explorandam Maris altitudinem; quod, si Mare congelatum fuisset, facere nequiissent. Frustra igitur Mare illud Glaciale dicitur; & ob glaciem, qua concretum non recte perhibetur, navigari posse negatur. Purum, etiam sub polo, Mare, media hieme; tempore verno, navigabile; aestate glacierum fragminibus, quae vel terris calore Solis abrupta, vel ab fluminibus eructata, obsessum: praecipue ad littora & in fretis atque angustioribus locis. Haec si vere de Septemtrionali praedicentur mari; ubi, remotissimo Sole, frigora necessario maxime penetrabilia: certe non injuria dici possunt de reliquis, quae propiora Soli; cuius calor juvare solet Maris naturam, ne in glaciem Aquae convertantur. Iam quod posteriorum temporum Scriptoris monimentis suis consignent, Mare ad aliquot milliaria subinde congelatum fuisse, arbitror ex auditu potius hoc illos tradere, quam quod viderint, & ita se res haberet: vel, si quid tale fuerit, de adventitia glacie exaudiendum. Nam quod totics illi suo tempore scribant factum; mirum ne semel quidem aevo nostro contigisse.
units.tr: I have never investigated very closely whether the Pontus freezes in winter. Otherwise Ovid might seem to have sung such things about it only from the shore, without sailing out into the deep. As a poet and an exile, he also wanted to move pity, both in others and in the emperor Augustus, by describing the horrible place to which he had been banished. It is certainly hard for seas to freeze over (I am not speaking of the lands' waters, whether poured in or flowing in). We who live here bear witness to this, and so do our own Argonauts, who lately sailed through the strait of Vaigach, which they named Nassau, while planning a route to the kingdoms of the Chinese. They have several times navigated the northern sea, once even to the eightieth degree, and further as far as the depth allowed. They did indeed often run into much ice, with great danger to their ships and their lives. But they were sailing towards land, near the shores and harbours, so that the ice seemed less born from the sea and grown together with its flat surface than heaped up from the shores, tossed out into the deep by the force of the winds and the impact of the waves, and crowded into little hills by the breakers and the floes. Hence it is that they note in their journals everywhere that, when the wind changed, the sea was now navigable, now not. Hence too they record the dangers from ice along every coast. Finally, at almost every place the sailors could drop a line from the prow without any obstacle to test the depth of the sea, which they could not have done if the sea had been frozen. It is therefore in vain that this is called the Glacial Sea, and it is wrongly claimed that it cannot be navigated because of the ice by which it is said to be solidified. The sea is clear even under the pole; in the middle of winter it is navigable in spring, and in summer it is beset with fragments of ice, which are broken off either by the heat of the sun from the lands or belched out by the rivers, especially near the shores and in the straits and narrower places. If these things are truly said of the northern sea, where, with the sun most distant, the cold must necessarily penetrate most, then they can certainly be said with no less justice of the other seas, which are nearer the sun, whose heat is accustomed to help the nature of the sea so that its waters are not turned into ice. As for the fact that writers of later times record that the sea was frozen for some miles at a time, I think they report this from hearsay rather than from what they saw, and if it was so, it should be understood of ice brought in from elsewhere. For that such things happened so often in their time, though they write it, is remarkable: in our age it has not happened even once.

units.la: Mari certum & constantem non esse Colorem, sed pro Ventorum qualitate mutari, tradunt Physici; nunc enim flavum esse, nunc atrum, nunc viridem. Videndus Isidorus lib. xiii, cap. xiv.
units.tr: Physicists teach that the colour of the sea is not fixed and constant, but changes according to the quality of the winds: for it is now yellow, now black, now green. See Isidore, book 13, chapter 14.

units.la: Maria versus Austrum esse profundiora, quam quae ad Septemtrionem, ajunt qui per utraque fecerunt huc illuc iter; quod non solum de Oceano, sed & de Mediterraneis exaudiendum, paret inde, quod, Graecis scribentibus, Pontus Ægaeo, hoc Siculo, Siculum cedat Tyrrheno & Sardoo; quae, ut etiam notat Aristoteles lib. ii. Meteor. omnium (mediterranea intellegit, homo Graecus) profundissima. Abyssum (quae Isidoro lib. xiii. Originum, cap. xx. profunditas Aquarum impenetrabilis) volunt nonnulli Mare Indicum, quod vere Austrinum. Vbi vero mensus Maris altitudinem Fabianus antiquus scriptor, nescio. Is enim apud Plinium lib. ii, cap. cii, altissimum mare tradit esse xv. Stadiorum. Æquat ejus ratio mille nongentos septuaginta quinque passus: Passus mihi spacium, quod utriusque manus extensione completur; pedes quinos continens: Vadem idiomate nostro. Hoc certum, Altitudinem Maris diversam esse, quum tamen indiscreta dorsi ejus aequalitas, inquit Isidorus lib. xiii, cap. xiv; unde Æquor appellatum ab aequitate, ut censet M. Tullius; vel quia aequaliter sursum est, ut Isidorus. Nam quamvis Aquae fluctuantes nonnumquam velut montes erigantur; tamen tempestatibus, quae commoverant, sedatis positisque ventis, rursum adaequantur.
units.tr: Those who have travelled hither and thither by both seas say that the seas are deeper towards the south than those towards the north. This must be understood not only of the Ocean but also of the inland seas. This is clear from the fact that, for Greek writers, the Pontus gives way to the Aegean, the Aegean to the Sicilian, the Sicilian to the Tyrrhenian and the Sardinian; and Aristotle, in book 2 of the Meteorology, notes (a Greek writer meaning the inland seas) that these are the deepest of all. Some hold the Indian Sea, which is truly southern, to be an abyss, which Isidore in book 13 of the Origins, chapter 20, calls water of impenetrable depth. But I do not know where the old writer Fabianus measured the depth of the sea. For he says, in Pliny book 2, chapter 102, that the deepest sea is fifteen stadia. His calculation makes it 1,975 paces. A pace is the space filled by the stretching of both arms, containing five feet; in our language, a fathom. This is certain: the depth of the sea varies, although, as Isidore says in book 13, chapter 14, its back is undivided and even. Hence, as Marcus Tullius thinks, it is called the Aequor from its evenness, or, as Isidore holds, because it lies level. For although the waves sometimes rise up like mountains, yet when the storms that stirred them have subsided and the winds have dropped, they level out again.

units.la: Maris navigantes experimur plerumque Rabiem, nonnumquam Malaciam, saepe Pellaciam. Rabiem, quoties commotum tempestatibus horrescit, caeloque confunditur; flantibus discorditer in perniciem nostram ventis, undisque longo per multa volumina tractu aestuantibus. Maris crudelitas ab Homero delineatur, Odyss. θ:
units.tr: Sailors experience the sea mostly in its rage, sometimes in its calm, and often in its treacherous smoothness. The rage is when it bristles, stirred by storms, and is thrown into confusion by the sky, when the winds blow discordantly to our destruction and the waves surge with a long swell through many coils. Homer depicts the cruelty of the sea in the Odyssey, book θ:

units.la: ἐ γὰρ ἐγωγέ τι Φημὶ κακώτατον ἄλλο Ἰαλάσσης Ἀνδρὸς τι συγχεῦσαι, εἰ κῆ μάλα καρπὸς ἐπὴ.
units.tr: ἐ γὰρ ἐγωγέ τι Φημὶ κακώτατον ἄλλο Ἰαλάσσης Ἀνδρὸς τι συγχεῦσαι, εἰ κῆ μάλα καρπὸς ἐπὴ. [For I say there is nothing more wretched for a man than to be tossed about by the sea, when the wind has pressed him hard.]

units.la: Quem Poëtæ locum Livius Andronicus apud Festum eleganter exprimit: Namque neminem peius macerat humanum, Quamde Mare saevum. Vires quoi sunt magne; Topper confrigent importune unde.
units.tr: Livius Andronicus expresses this passage of the poet elegantly, as quoted by Festus: "For no human is worn down more wretchedly than by the cruel sea, when those whose strength is great are crushed by its blows without mercy."

units.la: Tria Græci Mala agnoscebant, Ignem, Mare, Mulierem. Indicat celebratum illis Trimetrum: πῦρ καὶ θάλασσα καὶ γυνή; κακὰ τρία.
units.tr: The Greeks recognised three evils: fire, the sea and woman. They indicate this by a trimeter that was celebrated among them: fire and sea and woman; three evils.

units.la: Hinc Medea, quum apud Senecam in cognomine sibi Tragœdia, Act. II, gloriatâ esset, scelere Flammas à se vinci & Mare; paullo post in ejusdem Choro cantatur Majus Mari Malum. Quin, docente Agellio lib. xv, cap. xxi, ferocissimos & immanes, alienosque ab omni humanitate, tanquam è Mari genitos, Neptuni filios dixit Antiquitas. Audaces igitur merito primi Nautæ; de quibus multa Oppianus Halieuticôn 5, Propertius lib. III, Elegia de obitu Pœti, Seneca Medea, & alij. Sic Sophocles in Antiq. Act. II: πολλὰ τὰ δεινὰ; κοὐδὲν ἀνθρώπου δεινότερον πέλει. τῶν καὶ πολιῶ πίεσιν πῦτα χειμερίω νότῳ χωρᾶ περιβρυχίων πηρῶν ἐπὶ ἑῦ μαστ. &c.
units.tr: Hence Medea, in Seneca's tragedy named after her, boasts in Act II that by her crime she has conquered flames and the sea. Shortly afterwards, in the chorus of the same play, it is sung: "a greater evil than the sea." Indeed, as Gellius teaches in book 15, chapter 21, antiquity called the fiercest and savage men, strangers to all humanity, as if born of the sea, sons of Neptune. Sailors were therefore rightly considered bold; many things are written about them by Oppian in the Halieutica 5, by Propertius in book 3, in the elegy on the death of the poet, by Seneca in Medea, and by others. So Sophocles in the Antigone, Act II: "Many things are wonderful, yet nothing is more wonderful than man, who crosses the grey sea in the wintry south wind, through the surging waves..." etc. [πολλὰ τὰ δεινὰ; κοὐδὲν ἀνθρώπου δεινότερον πέλει. τῶν καὶ πολιῶ πίεσιν πῦτα χειμερίω νότῳ χωρᾶ περιβρυχίων πηρῶν ἐπὶ ἑῦ μαστ. &c.]

units.la: Malaciam (sic enim voce Græca Latini Scriptores Maris Molliciem nominant, ut legere est apud Cæsarem III. de bello Gallico, Senecam lib. IX. Epistolar. aliosque) experimur, quoties ferocitate depositâ tranquillum plane se præbet, placatum & certum. Pellaciam denique, quoties nos ad navigandum sua tranquillitate pellectos fallit, erumpens in horrendas subito tempestates. Lucretius lib. II. de rer. natura: Infidi Maris Insidias, Virésque, Dolumque Ut vitare velint, neve ullo tempore credant, Subdola quum ridet placidi pellacia ponti.
units.tr: We experience calm (for the Latin writers call the softness of the sea by its Greek name, as can be read in Caesar, book 3 of the Gallic War, in Seneca's Epistles, book 9, and in others) whenever, its ferocity laid aside, it shows itself perfectly tranquil, placid and steady. Finally, we experience treachery whenever it deceives us, enticed by its calm into sailing, and then bursts out into sudden horrible storms. Lucretius, book 2 of De rerum natura: "so that they may wish to avoid the faithless snares and strength of the sea, and not trust at any time, when the treacherous deceit of the calm sea smiles."

units.la: Et lib. vi Nec poterant quemquam placidi pellacia ponti Subdola pellicere in frandem ridentibus undis.
units.tr: And in book 6: "Nor could the treacherous deceit of the calm sea lure anyone into fraud, while the waves laughed."

units.la: Verum esse Senecæ illud docet experientia: Noli huic tranquillitati confidere; momento Mare vortitur; eodem die, ubi luserunt Navigia, sorbentur. Quisquis navigat tantum distat à Morte, quanta Navis est crassitudo: ad quod Anacharsis apud Laërtium Apophthegma adludit Iuvenalis in Satyris: I nunc, & ventis animam committe, dolato Confisus ligno, digitis à morte remotus Quattuor, aut septem, si sit latissima rheda.
units.tr: Experience teaches that Seneca's saying is true: "Do not trust this calm; the sea turns in an instant; on the same day on which ships have played, they are swallowed up." Whoever sails is only as far from death as the thickness of the ship's planks. To this Anacharsis' saying, reported by Diogenes Laertius, Juvenal alludes in the Satires: "Go now, and commit your life to the winds, trusting in a hewn plank, four or seven fingers from death, if the carriage is very broad."

units.la: Oraculi instar mihi Carsilidis illud, interrogati, quid Mare, quid Nauta esset; eo nil infidelius, hunc fluctuum comitem pronunciavit.
units.tr: For me, Carsilis' answer is like an oracle: when asked what the sea was and what the sailor was, he declared the sailor a companion of the waves, and nothing more faithless than the sea.

units.la: Edit Mare Murmur, nostras quotidie percutiens aures; quod, ut Veteres etiam (conferenda Aristotelis Meteorologica) notarunt, ab Mugitu non absonum Tauro: unde Græci Neptunum Μυκταῖον καὶ Ταύρειον vocarunt, Taurum illi immolantes. Solent antiqui, nosque hodie, ex hoc Murmure, si validius fuerit, Ventos augurari.
units.tr: The sea makes a murmur that strikes our ears every day. As the ancients too noted (compare Aristotle's Meteorology), this sound is not unlike the bellowing of a bull, which is why the Greeks called Neptune Myktaios and Taureios, sacrificing a bull to him. The ancients, and we today too, are accustomed to foretell winds from this murmur if it is loud enough.

units.la: Seneca in Agamemnone: — tum Murmur grave, Maiora minitans, collibus summis cadit, Tractuque longo littus ac petra gemunt: Agitata ventis unda venturis tumet.
units.tr: Seneca in Agamemnon: "Then a heavy murmur, threatening greater things, falls on the highest hills, and the shore and the rocks groan with a long tremor. The wave, stirred by the winds that are coming, swells."

units.la: Imitatus videtur M. Tullium; cujus, Aratum suum vertentis, hæc leguntur libro I. de Divinatione: Atque etiam ventos demonstrat sæpe futuros Inflatum Mare: quum subito penitusque tumescit, Saxaque cana salis niveo spumata liquore Tristificas certant Neptuno reddere voces Aut densus stridor quam celso è vertice montis Ortus adangescit scopulorum sæpe repulsu. Est autem causa Murmuris agitatio fluctuum, qui vel se impellunt & protrudunt, vel littoribus impinguntur: quorum Decimus omnium censeri solet Maximus; utroque cognomine insignis. Maximus vocatur ab Celso IC. in l. littus 96. D. de verbor. signif. restituendus lavoleno, eodem tit. ad l. 112. μέγαςι κύμα, Eclog. ii, cap. xc v. Plenius Hibernus fluctus Maximus dicitur ab Iustiniano Imp. §. 3. Instit. de rer. divis. ubi Theophilo χύμα ἐκ μέγαςι κύμα. Decimus appellant Ovidius lib. i. Tristium, & xi. Metamorph. Valer. Flaccus lib. ii. Lucanus lib. v, Seneca in Agamemnone, Sillius Italicus lib. xiiii. & alij. Latinis apud Festum nominatur Decumanus, propter Denarij numeri perfectionem. Græcis τεχνυμία, notante Hesychio: qua voce usos lego Platonem in Euthydemo, Euripidem in Agamemnone, Aristidem in Themistocl. Lucianum ἐν τῷ πεῖ τῶν ὅπι μιᾶ ψ σωέντων, & alios.
units.tr: He seems to imitate Marcus Tullius, whose lines, in his translation of Aratus, are read in book 1 of On Divination: "And the sea, swollen, often shows the winds that are about to come, when suddenly and deeply it swells, and the hoary rocks, foamed with white brine, vie in giving back to Neptune their dismal voices, or a thick roar which, rising from the high peak of a mountain, grows louder through the often-repeated echo of the crags." The murmur is caused by the agitation of the waves, which either push and thrust against each other or are dashed against the shores. Of these, the tenth is usually considered the greatest, and it is distinguished by both names. It is called the "maximus" by Celsus the jurist in l. littus 96 D. de verborum significatione, to be restored by Labeo, in the same title on l. 112; μέγαςι κύμα [great wave], Eclog. ii, chapter 95. More fully, Justinian the emperor calls it the "hibernus maximus fluctus" in §3 Instit. de rerum divisione, where Theophilus has χύμα ἐκ μέγαςι κύμα [a wave from a great wave]. They call it "decimus" (tenth): Ovid in Tristia book 1 and Metamorphoses book 11, Valerius Flaccus book 2, Lucan book 5, Seneca in Agamemnon, Silius Italicus book 14, and others. Among the Latins it is named "decumanus" in Festus, because of the perfection of the number ten. The Greeks call it τεχνυμία [tenth], as Hesychius notes; I read that Plato in the Euthydemus, Euripides in the Agamemnon, Aristides in the Themistocles, and Lucian in the work on those saved by one soul [ἐν τῷ πεῖ τῶν ὅπι μιᾶ ψ σωέντων], and others used this word.

units.la: Maria quoendam, ut indicant Plinius lib. ii. nat. hist. cap. xlvii, & Vegetius lib. iii. de re milit. cap. xxxix, Clausa dicebantur ex die iii. Eidus Novembr. usque in diem v i. Eiduum Martiarum. Vult hoc & Theodoretus de Provid. Serm. i: ἢ μὲ γὰρ χύμων ἡ λήγεντ, καὶ ἡ ἐαρ ἐκλάμπεντ, ἐνίκα τὰ λείης τ' ἀνθρώπων εἰ πεῖ τῷ ἐργασίαν ποιοῖ, εἰδεῖπερ ἡ ἐκ ἐκ ἐκβήμαι, ἡ δὲ λιμένων ἀναγαγοῦ, ἀ ἀλατ-ἀ ἱσορροπία, ἡ τῆς χειμερινῆς ἀπηλλαγμένη τεταχυμένη, & quae sequuntur. Sic Heliodus ἐργ. ἐ ἡμέρ. vetat post Virgiliarum occasum navigare. Caulam adscribit, quod eo tempore Mare, maxime infidum, tempestatibus facile solcat concitari: Εὔτ' αὖ Πληιάδες δύσ' ἐμβέμεν Ωρίωνος Φεύγοντ' πίπτωσι ἐς ἠεροειδέα πόντον, Δὴ τότε πάντοιων ἀνέμων ἐχῦσιν ἀτμῶν, Καὶ τότε μηχέτι νῆας ἐχθρὰ ὅπι ἐνοσι πόντῳ, Γλῶ δ' ἐργαζεσθαι μεμνημένῳ, ὡς ἐπ κελεύω, Νῆα δ' ἐπὶ ἠπείρῳ ἐρύσαι πυκασσαμ λίθοισι Παντὸς ἐξ φρέαρ ἱερῶ ἀνέμων μὴ ὑγρὸν αὐτῶν Χείμαρον ἐξερύσας ἵνα μὴ πίβη dies ἐμέρος.
units.tr: Certain seas, as Pliny indicates (Natural History 2, ch. 47) and Vegetius (On Military Affairs 3, ch. 39), were called closed from the third day before the Ides of November until the sixth day before the Ides of March. Theodoret also says this in his first Sermon on Providence: "For when the winter ceases and the spring shines forth, and the sea grows calm, and men resume their labours, the ships are launched and the harbours are left behind, the sea has regained its balance, and it is released from its wintry state" [ἢ μὲν γὰρ χειμὼν λήγει, καὶ ἡ ἔαρ ἐκλάμπει], and what follows. So Hesiod, in his Works and Days, forbids sailing after the setting of the Pleiades. He gives the reason that the sea, most treacherous at that time, is easily stirred up by storms: "When the Pleiades, daughter of Atlas, set into the misty sea, fleeing from Orion, then the winds of every kind rage; then no longer keep ships on the wine-dark sea, but attend to the land, as I bid you, and drag your ship up on the shore and pack it round with stones" [Πληιάδες δύσ' ἐμβέμεν Ὠρίωνος].

units.la: Clausi Maris aliquoties mentio apud Veteres Scriptores, M. Tullium ad Q. Fratrem, Cassiodorum lib. xii. Variar. cap. xxiv. & alios. Et lux hinc Horatio lib. i. Carminum, Ode iv, Suetonio in Claudii principis vita cap. xviii, & Imperatoris Constitutioni, quae est in l. civitas. C. de effic. Rectot. provinc. Ut autem instante Clausum, sic exacta solutaque hieme Apertum dicebatur Mare. Hieronymus in vita Paullæ ad Eustochium: Tandemque exacta hieme, aperto Mari, redeuntibus ad Ecclesias suas Episcopi, & ipsa voto cum eis ac desiderio navigavit. Primitiæque Navigationis Diis offerebantur. Apuleius lib. Milet. xi, ex persona Dianæ: Diem, qui dies ex ipsa nocte nascetur, aeterna mihi nuncupavit Echigo: quo sedatis hibernis tempestatibus & lenitis maris procellisis fluctibus, navigabit jam pelago, rudem dedicantes carinam, primitias commemorans libant mei Sacerdotes. Hodie numquam clauduntur Maria; fervent non minus hieme, quam æstate. Audaces hic omnia perfecti Belgæ, & inter eos loci principis Batavi; quibus in hac difficultate nihil difficile, nihil fere contra infida incertaque Maris arduum.
units.tr: Closed seas are mentioned several times by ancient writers: Marcus Tullius to his brother Quintus, Cassiodorus (Variae, book 12, ch. 24), and others. Horace also alludes to them (Odes 1, ode 4), as does Suetonius in the life of the emperor Claudius (ch. 18), and an imperial constitution, which is in the law civitas, C. De effectu rectorum provinciarum. Just as the sea was called closed when winter was approaching, so when winter was over and gone it was called open. Jerome, in the life of Paula to Eustochium: "And at last, when winter was over and the sea was open, the bishops returned to their churches, and she sailed with them with the same wish and longing." The first fruits of a voyage were offered to the gods. Apuleius, in book 11 of the Metamorphoses, speaks in the person of Diana: "The day which is born from the very night I have named eternal for myself: on it, when the winter storms have subsided and the waves of the sea are calmed, the sailors shall now sail the deep, dedicating a new keel, and my priests shall make offerings, recalling the first fruits." Today the seas are never closed; they are as stormy in winter as in summer. The Belgians, bold in everything, and among them the leading Dutch, are masters here; to them nothing in these difficulties is hard, and almost nothing is daunting in the treacherous and uncertain sea.

units.la: Possem hoc loco laudes celebrare Navigationum cum Veterum, de quibus præclara multa notat Aristides in Oratione Isthmica; tum Recentiorum, in quarum noritiam quotidie stupentes & attonitu manu quasi peritissimorum Navarchorum deducimur; nisi ad præcipuum mihi institutum, Orbis Terrarum delineationem, serio sæpe me vocaret oratio. Hoc sane monitione censui non indignum, Majorum non minorem hic industriam fuisse, quam qui ævum hodie agitant. Priscos enim illos quaesiisse etiam & adiisse per Maria Terras remotissimas, docet Sacra Scriptura, commemorans Navigationes in Indiam non solum Arabum, ut videre est in Hijobi historia; sed & Regum cum Iehudæ, tum Israelis; Schelomonis, Iehoschaphati, Ochoziæ, aliorum; eorundem etiam non obscure (quod nonnulli volunt non postremæ classis Interpretes) expeditiones in eam Orbis partem, quæ Regum Castiliæ beneficio superioribus annis rursum inventa, innuens: quum lib. ii. Paralipomen. cap. iii, 7. mentionem faciat auri Parvaim. sic enim ibi de Schelomone: Et texit domum lapide pretioso ad gloriam & aurum, aurum Parvaim, פַּרְוָיִם: & non semel Ophiriani; quod idem putatur cum Peruviano, non inamœna, ut censent, neque ingrata litterarum metathesi. Hiob cap. xxviii, 16, non æstimabitur cum auro Ophir. ro Ophir (אופיר) cum Onyche preciofo & Sapphiro. Iefaiah. cap. xiii, 11. Preciofum faciam hominem pra Obrizo, & hominem pra massa auri Ophir, מכתם אופיר. De his tamen & similibus locis, quid sentiam; quinta dicam mei operis parte. Testatur & Antiquorum hac in re diligentiam Strabo, notans lib. 1. Homeri etiam aetate (floruit autem ille Regum Albanorum temporibus, Siluii, ut vult Caffiodorus; Agrippae, ut alij) navigatum in Indiam. Ad propiora nobis veniamus. Scribit Plinius lib. 11. natur. hiftor. cap. lxvii, suo tempore totum Occidentem ab Gadibus Columnisque Herculis, Galliarum circuitu, navigatum: Septemtrionalem autem Oceanum maiori ex parte auspicijs Augusti usque ad Cimbrorum promontorium: inde ad Scythicam plagam immensum Mare fuisse cum prospectum, tum fama cognitum: ab Ortu ex Indico Mari partem totam in Caspium vergentem Macedonum armis innotuisse, Seleuco & Antiocho regnantibus, circa Caspium quoque multa Oceani littora fuisse explorata: & sic totum fere Septemtrionem hinc illinc versus Occasum & Ortum eremigatum. Addit porro, alio latere Gadium ab eodem Occidente magnam meridiani sinus portionem, ambitu Mauritaniae, suo tempore navigari solere: majorem quidem ejus, & Orientis, partem victoriis Alexandri Magni fuisse lustratam usque in Arabicum finum; Hannonem Carthaginiensem circumvectum à Gadibus ad finem Arabiae; contra Eudoxum Cyzicenum (de quo etiam Strabo libro 11.) telte Cornelio Nepote, quum Lathyrum regem fugeret, Arabico sinu egressum Gades usque fuisse perductum; Cæliun quoque Antipatrum scribere, vidisse fe, qui cum mercibus iter fecisset maritimum ex Hifpania in Æthiopiam: eumdem Nepotem tradere, Q. Metello Celeri, Galliae Proconsuli, Indos ab Suevorum Rege dono datos, qui ex patria commercij causa navigantes tempestatibus in Germaniam, necessario per Oceanum Orientalem & Septemtrionalem, fuerant abrepti.
units.tr: I could here praise the voyages of the ancients, about which Aristides in his Isthmian Oration notes many splendid things, and also those of our own time, whose knowledge astonishes us daily, and we are led along as if by the hands of most skilled navigators. But the speech often calls me back to my chief purpose, the delineation of the globe. Still, I judge it worth noting here that the industry of our forefathers was no less than that of those who live today. For Sacred Scripture shows that those early men sought out and reached the most distant lands by sea, recording voyages not only of the Arabs, as may be seen in the history of Job, but also of the kings of Judah and of Israel: Solomon, Jehoshaphat, Ahaziah, and others. Clearly, too (as some hold, interpreters of no small rank), there were expeditions to that part of the world which in recent years was found again through the good offices of the kings of Castile, the reference being to the passage in 2 Chronicles 3:7, where mention is made of the gold of Parvaim. For thus it says there of Solomon: "And he covered the house with precious stone for beauty, and the gold was gold of Parvaim" [פַּרְוָיִם], and not once "of Ophir". This is thought to be the same as Peru, which is no unpleasant or unwelcome conjecture, with a transposition of letters. Job 28:16: "It shall not be valued with the gold of Ophir, with the precious onyx and sapphire." Isaiah 13:12: "I will make a man more precious than fine gold, and a man more than the gold of Ophir" [מִכְתָּם אוֹפִיר]. What I think about these and similar passages I shall say in the fifth part of my work. Strabo also attests the diligence of the ancients in this matter, noting in book 1 that in the time of Homer (who flourished, as Cassiodorus holds, in the time of the kings of Alba, Silvius; others say in the time of Agrippa) voyages were made to India. Let us come to matters nearer to us. Pliny, in book 2 of the Natural History, ch. 67, writes that in his time the whole of the West had been sailed from Cadiz and the Pillars of Hercules around the coasts of Gaul; that the northern ocean had been sailed for the most part under the auspices of Augustus as far as the promontory of the Cimbri; and that from there the immense sea towards the Scythian region had been seen and was known by report. From the east, the whole part of the Indian sea tending towards the Caspian had been made known by the arms of the Macedonians, under the kings Seleucus and Antiochus; and many shores of the ocean around the Caspian had also been explored; and so almost the whole North had been traversed by oar, from here and there towards west and east. He adds further that on the other side of Cadiz, from the same west, a great portion of the southern bay, along the coast of Mauretania, was commonly sailed in his time; that the greater part of this coast and of the east had been explored by the victories of Alexander the Great as far as the Arabian gulf; that Hanno the Carthaginian had sailed from Cadiz to the end of Arabia; and, on the contrary, that Eudoxus of Cyzicus (about whom Strabo also speaks in book 2), as Cornelius Nepos testifies, fleeing king Lathyrus, had gone out by the Arabian gulf and had been brought as far as Cadiz; that Caelius Antipater also writes that he had seen a man who had made a sea journey with merchandise from Spain to Ethiopia; and that the same Nepos relates that to Quintus Metellus Celer, proconsul of Gaul, Indians were given as a gift by the king of the Suevi, who, sailing from their country for the sake of trade, had been carried by storms into Germany, necessarily through the eastern and northern ocean.

units.la: Hodie in omnes fere terrarum oras, & omni tempore, velis ventisque ferimur: nihil tempestatum horretur, ne quid relinquatur intactum. Quum in Indiam ex Europa Navigatio mox post Alexandri Magni tempora increbuiffet per Ægyptum, Strabone & Hieronymo notantibus; eaque aliquamdiu intermifla tandem, pace Terrarum orbi ab Augusto principe parta, fuisset repetita; ut non obscure, quae jam scripsi, docent: Veneti, qui primi palmam Europæis, longa hæc stadia decurrentibus, eripuerunt, paullo supra nostram ætatem mare Hadriaticum ingressi, devectique per Mediterraneum Alexandriam usque, & hinc aliquantum terræ spacium emensi, per finum Arabicum ad Indorum populos proficisci coeperunt: hodie, quum via, quam dixi, ab Sultano Ægyptio aliisque infestior deprehendatur, Antiochiam (quam, Syriae quondam metropolin, Aleppo vulgus nunc nominat) portati, tendunt per terrestre cccc1. milliarium iter Babylonem, Affyriae urbem; hinc milliar. ccccxxx. Balfaram; inde milliar. cc. Armuzam, quod, Ormus hodie, nobilissimum Perfiae emporium: ubi, conscensis navibus, per finum Perfticum porro in quasvis Indiae regiones vehuntur. Quod iter maritimo Lufitanorum, de quo dicam, non folum breviori compendij, ut refapta & milliarium docent computatio; delectabilius etiam, occurrentibus passim infinitis antiquarum urbium, veterumque, & quae priscis historijs scriptisque nobilitata, locorum monimentis, praeter novos indios populos, nouosque populorum ritus; verum etiam commodius, offerente fe quotidie recenti cibo potuque; tutius autem, ne cane quidem, ut sic dicam, adlatrante: quum contra maritimum, cujus memini, quod flexuosius, terrestri Venetorum triplo fit majus; cædiofius vero, cum quod nihil nisi cœlum falumque in oculos incurrant, tum quod continuo fit depugnandum cum tempestatibus, quae improvisae & inopinatae non raro solent imparatos opprimere; quodque fames plurimum levanda pane mucido, ciboque nonnumquam viliore, fitis vero sedanda potu aquae foetido vermibufque infecto, eoque modice admodum adfuso.
units.tr: Today we are carried by sail and wind to almost every shore of the earth, at all times; nothing of the storms is dreaded, so that nothing is left untouched. When the voyage from Europe to India through Egypt had grown popular soon after the times of Alexander the Great (as Strabo and Jerome note), and when this had been interrupted for a time and then, once peace had been won for the world by the emperor Augustus, was resumed (as the things I have already written show clearly), the Venetians, who first wrested the palm from the Europeans who ran these long courses, a little before our age entered the Adriatic Sea and, having sailed through the Mediterranean as far as Alexandria, and from there traversed a certain stretch of land, began to set out by the Arabian gulf to the peoples of the Indians. Today, since the route I have mentioned has been found too hostile, owing in part to the Sultan of Egypt, they are carried to Antioch (which the common people now call Aleppo, once the metropolis of Syria) and go by land a journey of 401 miles to Babylon, a city of Assyria; from there 430 miles to Basra; then 200 miles to Armuz, which today is Ormus, the most noble emporium of Persia. There, having boarded ships, they are carried further through the Persian gulf into whatever regions of India they wish. This journey is not only shorter, as the computation of distances and miles shows, but also more pleasant, since there are countless monuments of ancient cities and places everywhere along the way, made famous by old histories and writings, besides the new Indian peoples and their new customs; it is also more convenient, since fresh food and drink are offered daily, and safer, since not even a dog, so to speak, barks at them. The sea route of which I spoke, by contrast, which is more winding, is three times longer than the overland route of the Venetians; and it is more toilsome, both because nothing but sky and sea meets the eye, and because one must constantly fight with storms, which, unforeseen and unexpected, often overwhelm those unprepared; and because hunger must be relieved with mouldy bread and sometimes worse food, and thirst quenched with foul water full of worms, and that only in very small measure.

units.la: Lufitani, primos ad procul sitas nationes monstrante suis regia prole gradus, aliud in Indiam, & ad regna Sinarum iter non infeliciter sunt moliti; circumnavigata commemorando seculis omnibus ausu tota Africa, lustratisque quae Aequatori Tropicisque subiectae, terrarum oris. Hos successu temporis fequuti sunt Angli, alijque populi: & anno cio 10 xcv, Octobri mense, instructa Mercatorum quorundam aufpicijs quatuor navium classe, Batavi: qui lavam infulam circumvecti, potius quid gerendum ibi, quam quid gestum reversi docuerunt; armis, quibus gens illa nimium adsuevit, quam mercibus, expediundis promtiores.
units.tr: The Portuguese, with a royal prince showing them the first steps toward distant nations, undertook not unsuccessfully another route to India and the kingdoms of the Chinese. Through all the ages they have been remembered for sailing around the whole of Africa and exploring the shores of the lands lying under the Equator and the Tropics. In time the English and other peoples followed them. In October of the year 1595, the Dutch, with a fleet of four ships fitted out under the auspices of certain merchants, sailed around Java. On their return they reported more about what was to be done there than about what they had accomplished, being readier for arms, to which that people had grown too accustomed, than for dispatching merchandise.

units.la: Versus Occidentem primus vastum hoc pelagus ingredi fuit ausus Christophorus Columbus Genuensis; qui, oblata variis Principibus ad novas quærendum terras opera, sed à plerisque, qui rem nimis difficilem & nullius fructus arbitrabantur, rejecta: profectus tandem in Castiliam, Ferdinandi & Isabellæ mandatu, accepta paucarum navium classe, anno cıɔ ccccc xcii. Insulas in Sinu Americano positas, Cubam, Hispaniolam, aliasque invenit. Ianua sic patefacta, suscepit hoc iter Americus Vespucius Florentinus, anno cıɔ cccc xcvii; tanta cum laude, ut etiam terrae noviter repertæ suum imposuerit nomen. Hinc quum inter Lusitanos versus Orientem, Castellanos autem in Occidentem, pomeria suorum Principum promovere pro virili adnitentes, dissidium esset ortum; ne alteri alteris essent impedimento, novus ille orbis, auctoritate Alexandri vi. Pontificis & aliorum, in duas partes est distributus: scriptis legibus & conditionibus, ut quidquid instituta ab Atlantici maris insulis, quæ Hesperides solent dici, navigatione Orientem versus reperiretur, Lusitanorum esset; quidquid ad Occidentem, Castellanis cederet: sic horum beneficio pernotuit America; illorum, Orientis pleraque & Moluccæ Insulæ, ita lucri studio lapsu temporis excurrentium, ut dicerentur etiam perrumpere in adjudicatam Castellanis portionem: quæ controversia decidi non potuit, nisi Ferdinando Magellano quasi judice. Hic enim Lusitanus, odio in Emanuelem suum Principem, ob non bene pensatam, quam illi navarat & effecerat, operam, exstimulatus, docens Moluccas ex facta distributione pertinere ad Castellanos; anno cıɔ ıɔ xix, auspiciis Caroli v. ad quærendum dimissus alia via Insulas, quas dixi, ita cursum suum temperavit; ut ex Hispania in Australiora cœli spacia ad gradum latitudinis ııı. delatus, inde converså ad Occidentem Solem classe, primus fretum, quod, nomen à primo lustratore nactum, inter Americam & immensa, quæ nondum explorata navigantibus, littora, tramensus, vastissimo denique maris tractu superato, in conspectu fere Moluccarum proelio contra Barbaros cæsus, sociis suis præter Asiæ Africæque littora in patriam revectis, admirandique, & ab nemine mortalium tentati facinoris nuncijs, occasionem dederit gloriandi terræ globum ab se circinatum: quam post illos laudem proximis annis consequuti Franciscus Dracius, & Thomas Candischius, Angli; & venantur hodie Batavorum nonnulli, velit Dævs, ut eventu secundo.
units.tr: Christopher Columbus of Genoa was the first to dare to enter this vast sea toward the West. He offered his services to various princes for seeking new lands, but most of them rejected him, judging the enterprise too difficult and without profit. At last he went to Castile under the commission of Ferdinand and Isabella, and in the year 1492 set out with a small fleet of ships. He discovered the islands in the American Gulf, Cuba, Hispaniola, and others. With the door thus opened, Amerigo Vespucci of Florence undertook this voyage in the year 1497, with such renown that the lands newly found received his name. Then, since the Portuguese were striving to extend the boundaries of their princes eastward and the Castilians westward, a quarrel arose. So that they would not hinder one another, that new world was divided into two parts by the authority of Pope Alexander VI and others, under written laws and conditions: whatever was discovered by sailing eastward from the islands of the Atlantic, which are commonly called the Hesperides, should belong to the Portuguese, and whatever lay to the west should fall to the Castilians. Thus America became known through their benefit, while the greater part of the East and the Moluccas, by the passage of time, were so pursued for gain that they were said to break into the portion adjudged to the Castilians. This dispute could not be settled except with Ferdinand Magellan as judge. This Portuguese man, stung by hatred toward his prince Emmanuel, because of the service he had performed for him and which had not been properly rewarded, and teaching that the Moluccas, by the division made, belonged to the Castilians, was sent in the year 1519, under the auspices of Charles V, to seek those islands by another route. He steered his course so that he sailed from Spain into the more southern regions of the heavens, to the third degree of latitude. Then, turning the sun toward the West with his fleet, he first passed through the strait, which took its name from its first explorer, lying between America and the vast shores not yet explored by sailors. Having at last crossed the immense stretch of sea, and being slain in battle against the barbarians almost within sight of the Moluccas, he gave his companions, who returned to their homeland past the shores of Asia and Africa, the occasion of boasting that they had circled the globe, a feat marvelous and attempted by no mortal before. In the following years Francis Drake and Thomas Cavendish of England won this same praise; and today some of the Dutch are pursuing it, God willing, with a successful outcome.

units.la: Sic in omnium oculis & mente semper obversabatur Oriens, & in eo Moluccæi ideoque quum oblesla essent illuc itinera hinc ab Lusitanis, inde à Castellanis; alijs invenuendis operam varij dederunt. Casparus Cortesius versus Septemtrionem anno cıɔ ıɔ. pro Freto quod quærebat, fluvium invenit, ad lx. altitudinis gradum; & domum reversus, quum anno sequente, prosperioris successus spe, profectus eodem esset, perijt: cuius fatum sequutus non multo post Michael Cortesius, ejus frater. Sebastianus Gabottus Venetus, auspicijs Henrici VII. Angliæ regis, anno cıɔ ıɔ vii, iter ad Moluccæos & Sinas quæsivit per Septemtrionem: sed detecto Bacalaorum tractu, æquorque permensus usque ad lxvii. altitudinis gradum, in Angliam reversi fuit coactus ab adventitia glacie, quæ in angustioribus locis marinis ibi aquis innatabat. Ioannes Verasanus anno cıɔ ıɔ xxiv, nomine Francisci Galliarum regis, idem animo vorsans, ad caput Britannorum terram cum suis ingressus in cibum Barbaris est conversus. Ibidem frustra fuit anno cıɔ ıɔ xxv. Sebastianus Gomezius Hispanus: qui, parum reportans gloriæ, Barbaros aliquot inde secum abduxit. Successerunt illis Angli: & inter eos primus Hugo Willoughbæus, vir Equestris ordinis; qui, anno cıɔ ıɔ lııı. repertis aliquot ad gradum lxxii. terris, frigore aliisque incommodis cum suis periit. Eandem persequens viam triennio post Stephanus Borrovæus Anglus, Insulas aperuit Galgojeviam, Novam Zemblam, aliasque; depugnare coactus cum frigore glacie, tempestatibus, aliisque calamitatum procellis. Hos ejusdem gentis sequuti Martinus Forbisherius, Arcturus Petræus, Carolus Iackmanus, & Ioannes Davisius: quorum primus, quum anno cıɔ ıɔ lxxvi. ob glaciem parum præstitisset, sequenti Fretum invenit ad gradum lxi, quod an pervium, pernovisse nequivit; medij vero idem ad Orientem iter anno cıɔ ıɔ xxc. moliti Novæ Zemblæ littora fecerunt, quam ante id tempus fuerant, notiora; postremus deniqi anno clo lo xxcv, & sequente, patefecit borealiora Americæ, & oras Gronlandiæ: omnes, pleniore quæsitorum cognitione negata, ab glacie frigoribusque ad sedes suas repulsi. Ordo tandem in Borealis Neptuni genium inquirundi venit ad Batavos & Zelandos; qui anno clo lo xciv. auspicijs Ordinum Fœderatarum Provinciarum & Illustrissimi Comitis Mauricij, Maris Præfecti, Septemtrionale hoc iter versus Scytharum Sinarumque regna mense Iunio Pentecostes die suscepertunt.
units.tr: Thus the East was always before the eyes and in the minds of all, and especially the Moluccas. Since the routes there were blocked, on one side by the Portuguese and on the other by the Castilians, various men undertook to find other ways. In the year 1499 Caspar Corte-Real sailed northward searching for a strait and found a river at the sixtieth degree of latitude. When he returned home and set out again the following year, hoping for a more successful outcome, he perished; and not long after, his brother Michael Corte-Real followed his fate. Sebastian Cabot of Venice, under the auspices of Henry VII, King of England, in the year 1507 sought a route to the Moluccas and China through the north. But having discovered the land of the Bacalaos and sailed the sea as far as the sixty-seventh degree of latitude, he was forced by the ice that floated there in the narrower sea channels to return to England. John Verrazzano, in the year 1524, under the name of Francis, King of France, likewise turning this matter over in his mind, entered the land of the Britons with his companions and was turned into food for the barbarians. Sebastian Gomez of Spain was there in vain in the year 1525; gaining little glory, he carried off several barbarians from there with him. The English followed them, and first among them Hugh Willoughby, a man of the equestrian order, who in the year 1553, after finding some lands at the seventy-second degree, perished with his men from cold and other hardships. Following the same route three years later, Stephen Borough of England opened up the islands of Gallogeviae, Nova Zembla, and others, and was compelled to fight against cold, ice, storms, and other whirlwinds of calamity. After these came Martin Frobisher, Arthur Pet, Charles Jackman, and John Davis of the same nation. Of these, the first, in the year 1576, accomplished little because of the ice; the next year he found a strait at the sixty-first degree, but he could not learn whether it was passable. Pet and Jackman in the year 1580 attempted the eastward route and reached the shores of Nova Zembla, which were better known than before that time. The last, John Davis, in the years 1585 and 1586, opened up the more northerly parts of America and the coasts of Greenland. All of them, since fuller knowledge of what they sought was denied, were driven back to their homes by ice and cold. At last the task of searching out the genius of the Northern Neptune came to the Dutch and the Zeelanders, who, in the year 1594, under the auspices of the Orders of the United Provinces and of the most illustrious Count Maurice, Admiral of the Sea, undertook this northern voyage toward the kingdoms of the Scythians and the Chinese on the day of Pentecost in the month of June.

units.la: Quum ad Novam Zemblam (quæ Borrovæi, Petræi & Iackmani periculis jam, non plene tamen, innotuerat) junctim secundo satis flatu pervenissent; naves Aemsteldamenses, quarum cura Gulielmo Barendsonio mandata erat, versus Polum ascendentes, Insulæ, quam dixi, littora ad lxxvi. usque gradum penitius, & quam umquam antea diligentius explorarunt; reliquæ Enckhusana una, altera Zelanda, quibus præerat Ioannes Hugonis F. Linschotanus, qui septennium jam apud Indos fuerat moratus, Fretum Vaigatium pernavigantes, in altum latumque pelagus sunt delatæ, ad confinia usque Obi, nobilissimi Tartariæ fluvij, &, ut nonnullorum erat conjectura, ad Promontorium fere Tabinum: sed quum harum Argonautæ sufficere putarent Oceanum Tartaricum sç satis ad futuram navigationem rimatos; illarum vero, obstante, quæ aquis circa littora innatabat, glacie, ulterius ire nequirent; tertio mense reversi sunt incolumes. Anno deinde sequenti septem in eundem finem adornatæ fuerunt naves, quinque in Hollandia, duæ in Zelandia: quarum vectores eo-rundem, quos ante dixi, auspiciis, ductu vero variorum, inter quos primi loci Gulielmus, cujus jam memini, sublatis xiv. Kalendas Quintilis anchoris, quum iterum prospero cursu Angustias Vaigatias superassent, ab Russis, quorum nonnullis omnia ibi cognita erant, visa & sulcata, didicerunt, inter alia, Fretum certo anni tempore ab Navigantibus transiri posse; quintidui ab eo itinere versus Borcam Promontorium esse; quod transgressis occurrere, inclinans ad Eurum, ingens & spaciosum Mare. Sed quum alius alij mentis incerta, quæ ulterius in Ortum, Oceani Tartarici avorsarentur, Hollandiam repetentes Mosam quarto mense, favente D e o, sunt ingressi. Anno denique clo lo xcvi. iterum cum duabus navibus, Mercatorum adparatu, eamdem nonnulli tentantes viam, quum, itinere iii. Nonas Maij instituto, evecti essent ad gradum lxxx, minut. xi. in littora inciderunt (Insulæ dicam, an Continentis?) vasta & ampla, quæ Gronlandiæ putabantur ob viriditatem. Nam licet terra ibi, quocumque tandem nomine censenda, Polo vicinior, & eam ob causam, ut vulgo persuasum hactenus, frigidior; gramen nihilominus herbaque deprehensa fuit producere voluntarias: & pascere cervos, aliaque id genus animantia, herbis vescentia: quum à diverso in Nova Zembla, gradu lxxv & ab Arctico versus Aequinoctialem Solisque viam remotius, omnia areant; campis passim canentibus ursis, vulpibus, alijsque carnivoris bestijs omnia ibi infestantibus. Quinquagesimo sexto, postquam solverant, die, revecti ad lxxv. gradum, communibus suffragijs disiuncti; uni quidem versus Septemtrionem ad lxxx. gradum reversi, ob continuas tempestates Colam (Lapporum est opidum) salva navi remearunt: alteri vero post infinitas calamitates & inextricabiles fere periculorum ab feris, frigore, fameque casus, quum in Nova Zembla gradu altitudinis lxxxvi. exstructo, ut poterant, rugurio, novem aut circiter menses hæsissent, relicta inter glaciales Oceani montes Navi, Navarchoque Gulielmo Barendsonio ibi defuncto, cum duobus lenunculis emensi æquor quadringentorum milliarium, Colam multis difficultatibus conflictati ad Navigationis venerunt socios; cum quibus in communem navem recepti, in Hollandiam anno clo lo xcvii. Novembris initio revenerunt; quum nomina variis Portubus Insulisque, de quibus suo loco, in singularum expeditionum memoriam reliquissent.
units.tr: When they had arrived together at Nova Zembla (which had already become known, though not fully, through the perils of Borough, Pet, and Jackman) with a fairly favorable wind, the ships of Amsterdam, entrusted to the care of Willem Barentsz, sailing toward the Pole, explored the shores of that island, as I said, further and more carefully than ever before, up to the seventy-sixth degree. The remaining ships, one from Enkhuizen and another from Zeeland, under the command of John Huygen van Linschoten, who had already spent seven years among the Indians, sailing through the Strait of Vaigatz, were carried into the high and broad open sea, as far as the borders of the Ob, the noblest river of Tartary, and, as some conjectured, almost to the Tabin promontory. But when the Argonauts of these ships thought that they had sufficiently examined the Tartarian Ocean for a future voyage, and the others, because of the ice floating about the shores in the water, could go no further, they returned safely after three months. The next year seven ships were fitted out for the same purpose: five in Holland and two in Zeeland. Their passengers, under the same auspices I mentioned before, but led by various men, of whom the first place belonged to Willem, whom I have already mentioned, weighed anchor on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of July, and when they had again passed the Vaigatz Straits with a favorable course, learned from the Russians, some of whom knew all these things well, having seen and plowed them, among other things, that the strait could be passed by sailors at a certain season of the year; that five days' sail from that route there was a promontory toward the north, and that, having crossed it, there was a huge and spacious sea inclining toward the east. But since their minds were uncertain, one man differing from another about whether to go further toward the East, into the Tartarian Ocean, they returned to Holland and, God favoring them, entered the Meuse in the fourth month. Finally, in the year 1596, some, again with two ships, fitted out at the expense of merchants, attempting the same route, when on a voyage begun on the third day before the Nones of May they had been carried to the eightieth degree, eleven minutes, they came upon lands, vast and wide (islands, shall I say, or a continent?), which were thought to be Greenland because of their greenness. For although the land there, whatever name it should be given, is nearer the Pole, and for that reason, as has been commonly believed until now, colder, nonetheless grass and herbs were found there growing of their own accord, and deer and other animals of that kind feeding on herbs; whereas, in Nova Zembla, at the seventy-fifth degree and further from the Arctic toward the Equator and the path of the Sun, everything is barren, with bears, foxes, and other flesh-eating beasts roaming the fields everywhere and attacking everything there. On the fifty-sixth day after they had set out, they were carried back to the seventy-fifth degree and separated by common consent. One part, returning northward to the eightieth degree because of continual storms, came back safely to Kola (a town of the Lapps) with their ship intact. The others, after infinite calamities and almost inextricable dangers from wild beasts, cold, and hunger, having stayed about nine months in Nova Zembla at the seventy-sixth degree of altitude, in a hut built as best they could, left their ship among the icy mountains of the Ocean, and their captain Willem Barentsz died there. With two small boats they crossed four hundred miles of sea, and after struggling through many difficulties they came to Kola, to the companions of the expedition. Received with them into a common ship, they returned to Holland at the beginning of November 1597, having left names for various harbors and islands, which will be discussed in their proper place, in memory of each expedition.

units.la: Ad quid hæc omnia? ut doceam, nihil non, ut olim, sic etiam hodie vel navigari, vel posse saltem. Nihil dicam de Navigationibus Europæorum Mediterraneis. Ludus est hodie ire in Asiam, in Africam, alio. Ad Hesperidum Insulas delati, Orientem (nam in Occidentem, ad Americanos, velificari, tritius existimatur) perimus: nunc Eurum versus, Caput Bonæ Spei prætervecti; nunc Fretum Magellanicum, obversis ad Africum proris, transvecti. Quum autem immensius, flexuosius, mercibusque inimicius videretur hoc iter; emendicatus varie ad Orientales divitias aditus ab aspero duroque Septemtrione. An quid eo navigantibus versus Corum pateat itineris, an quod ibi fretum, adhuc ignoratur: Nihil enim ab Cortesio, Gabotto, Verasano, Gomezio, Willougbæo, Forbisherio, Davisio, aliisque certi. Versus Boream patere per Angustias Vaigatias, vel potius supra summa Novæ Zemblæ littora indubitatum. Alterutra sane necesse est via delatos fuisse tempestatibus in Germaniam Indos, anno ab v. c. 1Ↄc. xci, quos ab Suevorum rege dono datos Q. Cæcilio Metello, Galliæ Proconsuli, notat Plinius. Angustias enim illas non semper ab glacie obsessas esse & obturatas iterata navigatione nostrates didicerunt; cum ipsi, Augusto mense profsum vorsumque tranantes, tum ex annuis inter Russos Tartarosque, illarum beneficio utentes, commerciis. Sed tutissimum, plenioré altioreque mari decurrere, & Septemtrionaliora Novæ Zemblæ littora circumnavigare ad lxxxii, aut circiter, altitudinis gradum. Difficile hoc? tentetur modo. Non obstabunt Tenebræ; nam ut noctes ibi longæ, sic longi etiam, & ex multis compactí diebus dies: non Glacies, quæ in alto & vasto mari rarior, & prorsus ex proximis littoribus adventitia: non Frigus, quod eo loci deprehensum mitius, quam gradu lxxxvi, & circiter; intendi suctum & augeri non ob Poli vicinitatem, sed nunc in his nunc illis locis ob glacici, terris vel adhærentis vel abscissæ & cum marinis aquis mistæ, copiam: non Vada, non Syrtes; omnia enim alta & profunda docuerunt promissæ passim ab Navarchis nostris ad fundum lineæ: non Venti, qui, ut alibi, sic iis in locis nunc adversi nunc ferentes; nisi quod, quam alibi, vehementiores; Sol enim inde remotior vapores non facile consumit, sed magis eos elevans ventis præbet alimenta: non denique molestiam conciliabit Iter longum; quum enim sub Aequinoctiali Longitudinis gradui tribuantur xv. miliaria, & progrediundo vel Meridiem vel Septemtrionem versus semper minus, adeo ut loco, quem dixi, in gradum tantum tria computentur; quum item Promontorium Tabinum sit ex Veterum mente gradu Longitudinis clxxii; sequitur paullo minus ducentis esse ab Nova Zembla usque ad Promontorium, cujus facta mihi mentio, milliaribus; quæ ferente vento confici possent paucorum dierum spacio; accedente Rußorum relatione, qui quinquiduanum iter adferunt ab Freto Naßovio vel Vaigatio usque ad Promontorium quoddam, quod non nominant, Tabinum profuldubio; & inde omnia vergere in Meridiem. Sed hæc sufficiant; & putidi sit ingenii, cui æmulatione dignus censeri solet in subeundis Navigationum periculis Aglas Areas: quem, ut legitur apud veterem Iuvenalis Commentatorem ad Satyram xiv, Apollinis, quum rogaretur quis fidem verae Felicitatis implesset, Oraculum declaravit Felicissimum; ut qui numquam patrium agellum excesserat. Ita tamen huic studio indulgendum; ne Caussa Navigationis ἀναπλωκὴ videatur esse Auri sacra fames; neve verum sit, quod ait Plinius lib. xxii. natur. histor. Mare navigare coegit Avaritia; & Sophoclis illud in Scyriis; οἱ ποτιναυτῆ τῶν ταλαυπώρων βροτῶν, οἷς ἐπὶ δαίμων, ἐπὶ τῆς ζῶν νέμων, πλάστε ποτ' ἂν νεμέλαν ἀξίων χαρίν, Λεπίης ἀπιρρεπῆσαν ἰμπολὰς μαχεῖς Α᾽ἐὶ ἐωρχιπλεύνης οἱ πελύφθεροι. Η᾽ς ὡς ἂν ἡ χίρδωον, ἡ δώλεσεν.
units.tr: What is the point of all this? To show that nothing is beyond reach: as in former times, so today, sailing is either possible or at least could be made possible. I say nothing of the Mediterranean voyages of the Europeans. Today it is child's play to go to Asia, to Africa, and elsewhere. Having been carried to the Hesperides Islands, we reach the East by sailing (for sailing west, to the Americas, is thought too common). Now we have passed the Cape of Good Hope heading toward the east wind; now we have crossed the Strait of Magellan with our prows turned toward the south-west. But since this route seemed vast, winding, and unfriendly to trade, access to the eastern riches has been sought in various ways from the harsh and rugged north. Whether any passage lies open to sailors toward the Corus (the north-west wind), or whether there is a strait there, is still unknown, for nothing certain has been established by Cortés, Cabot, Verrazzano, Gomez, Willoughby, Frobisher, Davis, and others. That there is an open way north through the Strait of Vaygatz, or rather above the northernmost shores of Nova Zembla, is beyond doubt. Certainly by one or the other of these routes, Indians must have been carried by storms into Germany in the year 691 from the founding of the city, whom, given as a gift by the king of the Suebi to Quintus Caecilius Metellus, proconsul of Gaul, Pliny records. For our countrymen have learned from repeated voyages that those straits are not always beset and blocked by ice, both when they themselves crossed back and forth in the month of August, and from the yearly trade between the Russians and Tartars, who use them. But the safest course is to run on a fuller and deeper sea and sail round the more northern shores of Nova Zembla up to about the 82nd degree of latitude. Is this difficult? Let it only be attempted. Darkness will not stand in the way; for as the nights there are long, so the days are long too, each day made up of many days. Ice will not either, for it is rarer on the deep and vast sea and drifts entirely from the nearby shores. Nor will cold, which there is found milder than at about the 86th degree; it is intensified and increased not because of the nearness of the Pole, but at one place or another by the abundance of ice, either attached to the land or broken off and mixed with the sea waters. Neither shoals nor sandbanks will stop us; for our captains, lowering lines to the bottom everywhere, have found everything deep and high. Nor will the winds, which there, as elsewhere, are now adverse and now favourable, except that they are stronger than elsewhere; for the sun, being more remote there, does not easily consume the vapours, but rather lifting them up, supplies nourishment to the winds. Finally, the long journey will not bring hardship. For since under the equator fifteen miles are allotted to a degree of longitude, and going toward south or north the figure is always less, so that at the place I mentioned only three are reckoned per degree; and since, according to the ancients, the Tabin promontory lies at the 172nd degree of longitude, it follows that from Nova Zembla to the promontory I have mentioned there are a little under two hundred miles, which could be covered in a few days with a favourable wind. The report of the Russians agrees, who give a five-day journey from the Strait of Nassau or Vaygatz to a certain promontory, which they do not name, but which is doubtless Tabin; and from there everything slopes toward the south. But enough of this. It would be a foolish mind that is usually thought worthy of emulation for facing the dangers of navigation, namely Aglaus the Arcadian, of whom an ancient commentator on Juvenal's fourteenth satire reports that when he asked Apollo's oracle who had fulfilled true happiness, the oracle declared him the happiest, since he had never gone beyond his native field. Still, this pursuit must be indulged only so far, lest the cause of navigation appear to be the accursed hunger for gold, and lest what Pliny says in book 22 of his Natural History be true: "Greed has forced men to sail the sea." Sophocles in the Scyrians says something similar: O wretched seafaring mortals, for whom some god, pursuing the gain of wealth, sends them across the sea to wander, and who in the end are carried back by the ship, or lost. Likewise Alexis in Those Who Die Together: of all things, the best are... what is melancholy, what is poverty, what is prison; and of these the one who has failed to attain his end is lost. And as Euripides elegantly says in the Philoctetes: a sailor who has no cargo sails back out again.

units.la: Nec non Alexidis in Commorientibus: Ὁ᾽ης ἀλκιπλὰ ἰφιλάσσαι, ἡ μελαγχολά, Ἡ πλωχίς ἐστιν, ἡ ζωνατά. τύτων τελῶν Ἐνὸς τ᾽ ἀποτυχὴν τελέχεσιν οὐκ ἐν.
units.tr: Likewise Alexis in Commorientes: of all things, the best are... what is melancholy, what is poverty, what is prison; and of these the one who has failed to attain his end is lost.

units.la: Alioquin, ut eleganter Euripides in Philoctete; Μαχαίρᾳ ἐκ ἐπυχῶν εἶναι μόνη, Ἐνῳ δ᾽ ἐ φόρτῳ, κ᾽ ἔ πάλιν ναυτίλλεται.
units.tr: Otherwise, as Euripides elegantly says in the Philoctetes: a sailor who has no cargo sails back out again.

units.la: Porro Navigationes qualescunque conficimus beneficio Navium; quarum, ut Veteres eas habuerunt, appellationes extant cum apud Nonium, Festum & alios, tum apud Agellium lib. x. noct. Attic. capit. xxv. Plene autem de ijs Lazarus Baysius Iurisconsultus libro de re Navali, & Lilius Gregorius Gyraldus de Navigijs: qui multa lectu dignissima de hac materia collegerunt. Navium partes (præter quæ ornant, ut Acroteria, Tutela, Aplustria, & id genus alia) sunt vel Principales, puta ex quibus confiunt, ut Carina, Prora, Puppis, Tabulata, & similes; vel Adjuvantes, in quis primum dicunt agmen Malus, Antenna, Vela, quæ vere Navium alæ, linum ut eleganter Cassiodorus libro v. Variarum, volatile, quidam spiritus currentium carinarum, prænuncia mercium, auxilia quieta Nautarum, quorum beneficio conficiunt otiosi, quod à celerrimis avibus vix probatur impleri. Velorum tria genera facit Pollux, & ex eo Isidorus, Acation, Epidromon, Dolona.
units.tr: Moreover, we carry out whatever voyages we make by means of ships. The ancients had names for them, which survive in Nonius, Festus and others, and in Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights, book 10, chapter 25. Lazarus Baysius, a jurist, has written fully about them in his book On Naval Affairs, and Lilio Gregorio Giraldi in his On Ships; they have gathered many things well worth reading on this subject. The parts of a ship are either principal, those of which it is made, such as the keel, prow, stern, decks and the like, or auxiliary. Among the auxiliary parts, the first to be named are the mast, yard, and sails, which are truly the wings of ships, the linen, as Cassiodorus elegantly says in book 5 of the Variae: a kind of flying spirit of the running keels, the forerunner of merchandise, the quiet help of sailors, by whose benefit idlers accomplish what can scarcely be achieved by the swiftest birds. Pollux makes three kinds of sails, and Isidore follows him: acation, epidromon, dolona.

units.la: Ne vero Vela vento gravida & turgentia Naves quovis pro libitu quasi abripiant, opus fuit Clavo: cujus in alto pelago Magistra & fidelis Monitrix, Acus marina, punctorum altero Magnete (qui & Σιδηρῖτις & ἡραklῆ λίθος, ut notat Plinius lib. natur. hist. xxxvi. cap. xvi.) temperata; & Pyxide (ne ab aere, vento, aliove incommodo, præsertim autem alio, cum quo summa illi discordia, infestetur) ad æquilibrium libere positia. Inventor ejus avorum nostrorum memoria Flavius Melfius Neapolitanus, vir sane vel ob hoc unum beneficium omni immortalitate dignissimus.
