Temperatur autem alterum Acus Punctum Magnete in eum finem, ut veram poli Arctici stationem, tamquam indice, perpetuo monstret. Sic enim adfrictum sequace quadam virtute semper eo se convertit; quocumque loco; die noctuque; cælo & sereno & turbido; sive Stellæ appareant, seu minus. Qua vero fiat hoc ratione, ingenio humano censetur obscurum. Nam Magneticos sub Arctico polo montes imaginentur, & attractionem inde fieri contendant; quibus cerebrum alibi, quam in capite. Si Acus hoc modo temperata partes orbis Magnete abundantes naturaliter respiceret; potius apud nos in oppositam Arctico plagam se converteret; quum Magnetis copia major in Hispania & Illua vicina Corsicæ Insula, quam in Septemtrionalibus locis; quumque præstantissimus & efficacissimæ potentiæ Magnes reperiatur in Æthiopia maxime commendari solitus, qui ad cæruleum colorem inclinat, qualis ibi in Zimiri arenosa regione: legendi Dioscorides lib. v. & Plinius, loco quem indicavi. Ἀρρῆτω tribuendum hoc ἰδιότητι, & secretæ cuidam συμπαθείας quæ Magneti cum plaga Septemtrionali & Polo Arctico. Pachymerius ἐν τοῖς λεγομένοις εἰς Φιλοσοφίαν inquit, συμπαθεῖ; sic enim emendandum ibi, expuncta contrariæ notionis voce) μαγνῆτις τῶν Ελικης ἀέρων. Punctum igitur Acus Marinæ, Magnete tactum, versus Polum trahitur. Quid autem sit, quod Magnes (cui hanc ob causam natura sensum manusque quasi videtur dedite) ferrum, cujus alioquin indomita fere & pugnax natura, trahat; quique propius admotum hoc ab illo continetur, & quodam velut complexu cohæreat; serram inter se reciprocant Philosophi. Anaxagoras Magnetem facit animatum; Aristoteles περὶ ψυχῆς α, τὴν λίθον, ait, ψυχὴν ἔχει, ὅτι τὸν σίδηρον κινεῖ; Galenus περὶ φυσικῶν δυνάμεων ἰλλιλίω hic agnoscit; Clemens Alexandrinus fieri hoc censet, ἀλλὰ συγγένεια; Gregorius, ἀρρῆτω τῇ φύσεως βίᾳ; Cecropis absolute dicit, τῷ μαγνῆτι ἐρᾷ ἢ σιδήρῳ; Epicurus suis Atomis, velut uncis hoc adscribit; alij Philosophi, ἀπρόοιας πεδ ματαίωσ; quæ omnia latius apud Plutarchum: Sunt &, inter quos Lucretius lib. vi, qui Magnetem ferrum appetere volunt, tamquam cibum, quo vitam sustentet & vires renovet; eoque modo lapides omnes vivere. quas opiniones refutare non hujus est loci.
units.tr: Lest the sails, full of wind and swollen, should carry the ships off wherever they please, a rudder was needed. Its faithful guide and monitor on the deep sea is the sea needle, tempered by a magnet at one point (which is also called siderites [Σιδηρῖτις] and Heraclean stone [ἡράκλειος λίθος], as Pliny notes in book 36, chapter 16 of his Natural History), and set freely in balance in a compass box, so that it is not disturbed by air, wind, or any other inconvenience, especially by anything with which it is in complete discord. Its inventor, within the memory of our grandfathers, was Flavius Melfius of Naples, a man truly worthy of all immortality for this benefit alone. The other point of the needle is tempered by the magnet for this purpose: that it may always show the true station of the Arctic pole, as with a finger. For when rubbed with the magnet, it always turns itself toward that pole by a certain following virtue, in any place, by day and night, under clear or cloudy skies, whether or not the stars appear. How this happens is judged obscure to human understanding. For some imagine magnetic mountains under the Arctic pole and contend that the attraction comes from them; men whose brains are anywhere but in their heads. If the needle, tempered in this way, naturally turned toward the parts of the globe abounding in magnet, it would rather turn toward the region opposite the Arctic here among us; for the magnet is more plentiful in Spain and in the neighbouring island of Corsica than in northern places. And the most excellent and most powerful magnet, which is especially praised, is found in Ethiopia, inclining to a sky-blue colour, such as there in the sandy region of Zimiri. Read Dioscorides book 5 and Pliny in the place I indicated. This property must be attributed to an occult [Ἀρρῆτω] quality [ἰδιότητι] and a certain secret sympathy [συμπαθείας] which the magnet has with the northern region and the Arctic pole. Pachymeres, in the work called Philosophy [ἐν τοῖς λεγομένοις εἰς Φιλοσοφίαν], says the magnet is sympathetic [συμπαθεῖ] (so it should be corrected there, the word of contrary meaning being struck out): magnet of the Arctic airs [μαγνῆτις τῶν Ἀρκτικῶν ἀέρων]. Therefore the point of the sea needle, touched by the magnet, is drawn toward the Pole. But why the magnet, to which nature seems to have given, for this purpose, something like sense and hands, draws iron, whose nature is otherwise almost untameable and combative, and why iron brought near is held by it and clings in a kind of embrace, the philosophers debate among themselves. Anaxagoras makes the magnet animate; Aristotle, in On the Soul book 1, says the stone has a soul because it moves iron; Galen recognizes this in On Natural Faculties; Clement of Alexandria thinks it is done by kinship; Gregory by a violence of nature; Cecropis says simply that the magnet loves iron; Epicurus ascribes it to his atoms, as if they were hooks; other philosophers ascribe it to some other cause. All of these are discussed more fully in Plutarch. There are also those, among whom is Lucretius in book 6, who want the magnet to seek iron as food, by which it sustains its life and renews its strength; and in this way all stones are alive. To refute these opinions is not the business of this place.

units.la: Ut historiam Maris absolvam: Arenæ, quæ illi congenita, numerus infinitus, non re ipsa, sed nostra ignoratione. Quis enim numerabit, licet in se finitam numeroque circumscriptam? ut vere Archimedes in Psammite. Saniores Philosophi, ne absoluta quidem Dei potentia infinitam quantitatem, sive continuam, sive discretam, dari posse censent. Addo hic obiter Virgilium lib. x. Aeneid. ex interpretatione Servij, Dorsum appellare duriorem Arenam, quæ reciproco fluctuum meatu densata, & instar saxi durata: idque ab Nautis vulgo Pulvinum vocari. Nostri Zee-banck nominant, & triplicem illi statuunt ordinem.
units.tr: To complete the account of the sea: the sand that belongs to it is infinite in number, not in reality but through our ignorance. For who will count it, even though it is finite in itself and bounded by number? As Archimedes truly says in the Sand-Reckoner. The wiser philosophers hold that not even by the absolute power of God can an infinite quantity be given, whether continuous or discrete. I add here in passing that Virgil, in Aeneid book 10, according to Servius's interpretation, calls dorsum a harder sand, which is packed together by the back-and-forth movement of the waves and hardened like rock; sailors commonly call this pulvinum. Our people call it Zee-banck, and they distinguish three ranks of it.

units.la: Iam vero Arenaceæ, quas in Littoribus passim contra Maris furias & Vndarum excursiones, est videre, moles; an ab humana sint arte & industria, an vero à Natura; quæstionis est. Prior mens non paucis, ijsque in rerum antiquarum cognitione versatissimis; qui succrevisse Majorum ævo illam Arenarum vim satione Caricis volunt, non sine monitore Deo. Placet mihi magis posterior sententia. Non enim video, quorum arte Montes tales surrexerint contra Maris impetum in Littoribus, quæ nulla noverunt hominum commercia, quibusque nulla Caricis satio; esse autem ibi, docent nos variorum Navigationes: non item video, quur, cum apud nos tum alios populos, hujusmodi longi multiplicesque Montium arenaceorum rum ordines, ubi exiguum; nulli interim, ubi periculum hodie maximum. Itaque præstantissima moles has moliendi scientia nobis perijt, ut jam immanissimis sumtibus Aggeres terreos, palis valide inter se confibulatis firmatos, saxisque & alia materie laburratos, cogamur objicere Maris furoribus? eosque corruptos, exesos, haustos sæpe & absumtos, sine intermissione, reficere & mille modis corroborare? præsertim qua parte ad tria passuum millia Charybdis Scyllæque instar nobis Canina Silva, vulgo Thenf-bosch: quem locum horrisonus murmurantis maris fremitus & tristes undarum fragores perpetuis quasi latratibus longe lateque circumsonant; continuatisque nullo non tempore adsultibus tundunt, convellunt, dissipant: cum summo sæpe totius Regionis & Incolarum discrimine. Et sane, ne procul à patria discedam, si ingeniosa nostrorum Avorum industria succreverint nuper isti Colles, unde quæso denominatio illorum Ptolemæi tempore in Germaniarum Capite, Lugduno? cujus posteriori parti Etymon ab Arenaceis istis Tumulis, quod Græcum Idioma (cuius tam studiosi Majores nostri semper fuerunt; ut, præter alia, infinitos habeamus hodieque ab Doribus Infinitivos; quod docere plenius, alius erit temporis) θύρας, Hesychio & Hieronymo in cap. ix. Ieschah. & alijs notantibus, vocare solet.
units.tr: As for the sand-dune barriers that are seen everywhere on the shores, holding back the fury of the sea and the rush of the waves, the question is whether they are the work of human skill and industry or of nature. The former view is held by not a few, and those very well versed in knowledge of antiquity; they maintain that this mass of sand grew up in our ancestors' time by the sowing of marram grass, not without God as its guide. I prefer the latter opinion. For I do not see by whose skill such mountains could have risen against the onslaught of the sea on those shores, where no human settlement exists and where no marram grass is sown; yet the voyages of various men teach us that such dunes are there. Nor do I see why, both among us and among other peoples, there are such long and multiple ranks of sand-mountains where the danger is small, while none exist where the danger today is greatest. Has the most excellent art of building such barriers then perished among us, so that we must now, at enormous expense, throw up against the raging sea earthen embankments, made firm with stakes tightly bound together and faced with stone and other material, and then repair them without pause, often when they have been broken, gnawed away, swallowed and destroyed, and strengthen them in a thousand ways? This is especially so where, about three Roman miles away, like Charybdis and Scylla for us, lies the Canine Wood, commonly called Thenf-bosch [the Hague]. The horrible roar of the murmuring sea and the sad crash of the waves echo far and wide around that place as with constant barking, and with assaults that never cease they beat, tear and scatter it, often with the greatest peril to the whole region and its inhabitants. And indeed, not to stray far from my homeland: if those hills rose recently through the ingenious industry of our forefathers, I ask, whence the name Lugduno [Leiden], in the head of Germany, given in the time of Ptolemy? Its latter part has its etymology from these sandy mounds, which in Greek idiom (of which our forefathers were always so studious that, among other things, we still have infinitives from the Dorians today, a thing that will take more time to explain fully) is called thyras, as Hesychius, Jerome on chapter 9 of Isaiah, and others note.

units.la: Iam hoc loco recensere Pisces, quibus in Mari Sedes sunt attributæ, infinitum esset. Paucula dicam. Primum quidem, falsum esse, quod nonnulli volunt, totum Piscium genus esse Oviparum; nec ulla ex parte Viviparum. Pisces lego Viviparos, qui Pilosi, quique Cartilaginei. De Pilosis testatur Aristoteles lib. iii de historia Animalium; ubi tradit, Pilos habere quæ Vivipara sunt; ideoque Vitulum Marinum parere Animal. habere enim Mammas & Lac, perfectumque generare Fœtum, idem scribit lib. i. ejusdem historiæ: & lib. vi. egressum in terram eniti, non secus ac homo, omni tempore, singulos, aut geminos, plurimum etiam tres, in littore, ut terrestre: mammis, quas geminas habet, educare prolem, moreque quadrupedum lac reddere, camdemque circa duodecimum a partu diem in mare deducere. Plinius lib. ix. natur. histor. cap. xiii. Quæ pilo vestiuntur, inquit Animal pariunt, ut Prisis, Balæna, Vitulus. De Cartilagineis idem Plinius ejusdem libri cap. li: Torpedo ostogenos fœtus habens inventur; eaque intra se parit ova præmollia, in alium locum uteri transferens atque ibi excludens. Simili modo omnia quæ Cartilaginea appellavimus. Ita fit, ut sola Piscium & Animal pariant, & ova concipiant. Basilius etiam Homilia vii. in Genesin duo facit Piscium Viviparorum genera, Cartilaginata scilicet, & Cetaria, ut sunt, inquit, Delphini & Vitulus marinus. Hoc primum esto. Alterum; æque falsum esse, quod suis scriptis mandat Basilius, cujus jam memini, Homilia in Genesin viii, Pisces Memoria carere. Contrarium docet Experientia; & repugnat Ratio, qua probatur, quibuscumque Animantibus datus est Motus localis, quo necessaria vitæ quærerent & compararent, necessariam talibus fuisse Memoriam, ne motum vagum incertumque agerent. Ut merito Basilium refutarit Augustinus libro iii. de Genesi ad litteram, capite viii. Tertium, uberiorem multo & copiosiorem esse Piscium generationem, quam cæterorum animalium. Indicium, ingens Ovorum, quæ in ijs, copia. Et sic voluisse Deum, innuit haud obscure Spiritus Sanctus apud Moschen Genesi i. usus in Piscium creatione verbo שרץ, quod producere in multitudine & maximâ copiâ; Producant, inquit Deus ישרצו, Aquæ Reptile anima viventis; addita paulo post Benedictione ut crescerent & multiplicarentur: Thargum vertit per רחש, quod nihil aliud, quam erumpere, ebullire, scatere. Celebrat & Propheta Rex Psalmo civ, verf. 25, Mare Magnum & spatiosum; ubi Reptilia, quorum non est numerus. Quarcum, Multiformiora, quæ in Humore gignuntur esse, scribente Aristotele lib. iii. de generat. Animalium cap. xi, quam quæ in Terra. Humori enim naturam esse ad effingendum efformandumque habiliorem, quam Terræ. Confirmat & Plinius lib. ix. nat. hist. cap. ii. qui quum notasset, quæ in Aquis plura esse & majora terrestribus, adscribit: Caussa evidens est, humoris Luxuria: pleraque etiam Monstrifica reperiuntur perplexis, & in semet aliter atque aliter nunc flatu, nunc fluctu convolutis seminibus atque principijs; ut vera fiat Vulgi opinio, Quidquid nascatur in parte Natura ulla, & in Mari esse; præterque multa, quæ nusquam alibi. Nusquam autem in formis Piscium variandis Natura magis deprehenditur ludere, (hac utar voce) quam in Arctoum Mari. Vititur ibi ab Navigantibus Hyæna, sive Porcus marinus; animal sane monstrosissimum Ziphius, Bubonis habens caput, horrorem spectantibus incutiens: Equus marinus, quem Islandi Hrosshvalur vocant, jubatus: exitium Piscatoribus adferens: Bos marinus, Islandis Seenaut, colore cinereo: egressus aliquando mari in vicino littore pascituri naso folliculus adhaeret, cujus beneficio in aquis vivit: eo rupto, aliis bobus se non invitus coniungit: Vitulus denique, Rostunger eidem genti: quem gradi scribunt inmaris profundo pedibus quatuor, sed brevissimis; pellemque habere durissimam, & quae vix ullis ictibus potest perforari. Batavi etiam nuper, Arctoum pelagus sulcantes, prope Insulas, quas, gradu altitudinis LXXVII, ad Septemtrionaliora Novae Zemblae sitas, Orangias appellarunt, in arenam descendere & dimicare fuerunt coacti contra Belluas marinas; quae vasto corpore bovisque magnitudinem excedentes, Walrussihen vulgo dicuntur: os habent leonina specie, pellem villosiorem, quatuor pedes, duos dentes ex parte oris superna prominentes, planos, duros, candentes, ut Elephantinis precio non cedant. Quintum, prodigiosiores Animalium moles in mari esse, quam in terra. Dubitationem omnem tollunt Balaenae: quas Basilius & Theodoretus scribunt, quum dorsa super aquas exerunt, speciem ingentis insulae praebere. Docet etiam Plinius lib. IX. natur. histor. cap. XXX, Balaenas maris Indici quaternum jugerum esse; Pristes ducenum cubitorum; Anguillas trecenum pedum. Idem lib. XXXII, cap. I. Iubam laudat Regem Mauritaniae, in voluminibus ad C. Caesarem Augusti F. notantem, Ceros sexcentorum pedum longitudinis, & trecentorum sexaginta latitudinis, in Arabicum sinum intrare: cum quibus si committantur qui anno CIↃ IↃ LXXVIII, & non ita pridem iterum, in nostra littora Pisces ejecti, molis sane censendi erunt exiguae. Strabo lib. XVI. Chelonophagos ait Testudinum marinarum testis tegi; adeoque eas esse magnas, ut vel in ijs navigent. Adstipulantur Plinius & Solinus. Ille lib. IX. cap. X: Testudines tantae magnitudinis Indicum mare emittit, ut singularum superficies habitabiles casas integant; atque inter insulas Rubri praecipue maris navigent his cymbis. Hic cap. Polyhistoris LVI; Maria quoque piscationibus inquietant, marinaque Testudines capere gaudent; quarum tanta est magnitudo, ut superficies earum domos fabricat, & numerosam familiam non amplius receptet. Aristoteles Magnitudinis Piscium causam refert ad Regionum situs diversaque locorum indoles & ingenia. Addo hic Philosophos tradere, littoralibus hominibus, qui mari adcolae crebrius Piscibus vescuntur; corpora plerumque esse excelsiora; contra qui sicca sibi & a mari remota loca legerunt, minora esse & depressiora. Haec sufficiant. Nam apud alios alia. Aristoteles quinque Piscium genera ponit, lib. III. de Histor. Animalium cap. I. Σέλαχον, Α-σέλαχον, μαλακὸν, μαλακοσπερμον, & ὀστρακοδερμον. Plinius lib. IX, cap. XIII, Piscium Species inquit esse LXXIV, praeter crustis tectas, quorum XXX. species: Isidorus lib. XII, Etymolog. cap. VI. cunctorum Aquatilium Species numerat CXLIV. Nos Navigationum huc illuc beneficio multo plura, & fere dixerim infinita, novimus. Maria Reciprocantia, de quibus hactenus universim, vel Extima Terrarum amplectuntur, vel Interiora ingrediuntur. Prioris classis Oceanus; posterioris Maria sunt Interna
units.tr: To list here the fish to which seats in the sea have been assigned would be endless. I will say a few things. First, it is false, as some maintain, that the whole kind of fish is oviparous and that none is viviparous in any respect. I find that some fish are viviparous: those that are hairy and those that are cartilaginous. Concerning hairy fish, Aristotle testifies in book 3 of his History of Animals, where he states that the hairy animals are viviparous; hence the sea-calf brings forth a live young one, for it has mammae and milk and produces a fully formed foetus. The same author writes in book 1 of the same history, and in book 6, that it comes out onto land, not otherwise than a human, at all times, one or two at a time, most often even three, on the shore, as a land animal does; that it nurses its offspring with the breasts it has in pairs, gives milk in the manner of quadrupeds, and about the twelfth day after giving birth leads the young back into the sea. Pliny, in book 9 of his Natural History, chapter 13: Animals that are covered with hair, he says, bear live young, such as the seal, the whale and the calf. On the cartilaginous fish the same Pliny, in chapter 51 of the same book: The torpedo is found to have a young developed inside the womb; and it bears within itself eggs that are very soft, transferring them to another place of the womb and hatching them there. In a similar way all those we have called cartilaginous do the same. So it happens that only fish and some animals bear live young, and also conceive eggs. Basil too, in Homily 7 on Genesis, makes two kinds of viviparous fish, namely the cartilaginous and the cetaceans, such as, he says, the dolphin and the sea-calf. Let this be the first point. The second is that it is equally false, as Basil also asserts in his writings (I have already mentioned him), in Homily 8 on Genesis, that fish lack memory. Experience teaches the contrary, and reason opposes it: it is proved that to all animals to which local motion has been given, by which they seek and procure what life requires, memory has been necessary, so that they may not move aimlessly and at random. Hence Augustine rightly refuted Basil in book 3 of his On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, chapter 8. Third, the generation of fish is far richer and more abundant than that of other animals. The evidence is the vast quantity of eggs they contain. And that God willed it so the Holy Spirit clearly hints in Moses, Genesis 1, where in the creation of fish he uses the word שרץ [sharats], meaning to produce in multitude and very great abundance; God says let the waters produce [ישרצו, yishretsu] the reptile of living soul, and a little later the blessing is added, that they may increase and multiply. The Targum renders it by רחש [rachash], which means nothing other than to burst forth, to boil up, to teem. The prophet-king also celebrates it in Psalm 104, verse 25: the great and spacious sea, where there are reptiles without number. Furthermore, the things that are produced in moisture are more varied in form than those on the land, as Aristotle writes in book 3 of his On the Generation of Animals, chapter 11; for moisture is by nature more suited to shaping and forming than earth is. Pliny also confirms this in book 9 of his Natural History, chapter 2, where, having noted that in the waters there are more and larger things than on land, he adds: The cause is plain: the luxuriance of moisture. Many monsters are found too, as the seeds and first principles, tangled and rolled about in themselves in different ways, now by wind, now by wave, are turned into a true form; so that the common opinion becomes true, that whatever is born in any part of nature is also in the sea, and besides that, many things that are nowhere else. Nowhere, however, is nature seen to play more (to use this word) in varying the forms of fish than in the Arctic sea. There, according to sailors, lives the hyena or sea-hog, a truly most monstrous animal; the ziphius, with the head of an owl, which strikes horror into those who see it; the sea-horse, which the Icelanders call Hrosshvalur, maned, bringing destruction to fishermen; the sea-ox, called Seenaut by the Icelanders, of ash-grey colour, which, when it sometimes leaves the sea to graze on the nearby shore, has a little follicle attached to its nose by which it lives in the water; when this is broken, it joins itself, not unwillingly, to other oxen; and finally the calf, called Rostunger by the same people, which they write walks on the bottom of the deep sea on four feet, but very short ones, and has a skin so hard that it can scarcely be pierced by any blows. The Dutch too, recently sailing the Arctic sea near the islands which they called Orangias, situated at a latitude of 77 degrees, to the north of Nova Zembla, were forced to go down onto the sand and fight against sea monsters; these, exceeding the size of an ox in their vast bodies, are commonly called walrus [Walrussihen]. They have a lion-like face, a hairier skin, four feet, and two teeth projecting from the upper part of the mouth, flat, hard and gleaming, so that they are not inferior in value to ivory. Fifth, there are more prodigious masses of animals in the sea than on land. The whales remove all doubt: Basil and Theodoret write that when they raise their backs above the water they present the appearance of a huge island. Pliny also teaches, in book 9 of his Natural History, chapter 30, that the whales of the Indian sea are four acres in size, the sawfish two hundred cubits, and the eels three hundred feet. The same author, in book 32, chapter 1, praises King Juba of Mauretania, who, in his volumes addressed to Caesar Augustus's son, notes that ceti six hundred feet long and three hundred and sixty feet broad enter the Arabian gulf. If they are compared with these, the fish that were cast up on our shores in the year 1578, and again not long ago, will certainly be judged of small bulk. Strabo, in book 16, says that the Chelonophagi cover their huts with the shells of sea turtles, and that these are so large that men even sail in them. Pliny and Solinus agree. Pliny, book 9, chapter 10: The Indian sea produces turtles of such size that their shells form habitable huts, and they sail among the islands of the Red Sea in these boats. Solinus, Polyhistor, chapter 56: The seas also disturb fishing, and they delight in catching sea turtles, whose size is so great that their shells make houses and do not hold more than a numerous family. Aristotle attributes the size of fish to the position of regions and the diverse character and nature of places. I add here that philosophers teach that people who live on the coast and dwell by the sea, feeding more often on fish, are generally taller in body; on the other hand, those who choose dry places far from the sea are smaller and shorter. Let this suffice; for others say other things. Aristotle sets out five kinds of fish in book 3 of his History of Animals, chapter 1: selachon [σέλαχον], aselachon [ἀσέλαχον], malakon [μαλακὸν], malakospermon [μαλακοσπερμον], and ostrakoderma [ὀστρακοδερμον]. Pliny, book 9, chapter 13, says there are 74 species of fish, besides the 30 species of crustaceans. Isidore, in book 12 of his Etymologies, chapter 6, counts 144 species of all aquatic animals. We, through the help of voyages hither and thither, know many more, and I would almost say infinitely many. The Reciprocating Seas, of which we have so far spoken in general, either embrace the outer parts of the lands or penetrate the interior; the Ocean is of the former class, and the Inland Seas are of the latter.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CAP. VI.

units.la: De Oceano.
units.tr: On the Ocean.

units.la: OCEANUS proprie universa illa marinarum Aquarum moles, quae extimas principum Terrae partium oras amplectitur. Inde Iuno apud Homerum Iliados ξ, Oceanum visura, petere primo scribitur: πολυζυγοσ ... γαιης.
units.tr: The OCEAN, properly speaking, is that whole mass of sea water which washes the outermost shores of the lands of the earth. Hence Homer's Juno, in Iliad 14, is written as setting out first to visit the Ocean: πολυζυγοσ ... γαιης.

units.la: Hoc de eo potius, ut exploratissimum, non a nobis solum, sed & a Priscis dicendum erat; quam quod orbem ambiat, si de Ambitu intellexerint perfecto, quem, ut nos scimus, illi nescierunt. Nam versus Meridiem Oceanum Terram circumire per Fretum Magellanicum inter Africae, Asiae, Americaeque Australiora, & lata Terrae adhuc incognitae littora, docuerunt nos nuperae cum Lusitanorum, tum Anglorum Navigationes. An autem idem posset Oceanus Septemtrionem versus, adhuc ignoratur. Certe si liceat; duplici Aquarum falcia duo vastissimorum marium annuli & coronae inter se quasi colligantur; una quidem inter Europae Africaeque
units.tr: This should be said of it, as the best-established fact, not only by us but also by the ancients, rather than that it encircles the globe. The ancients did not know a complete circuit, as we now know. For recent voyages of the Portuguese and the English have taught us that the Ocean goes round the earth towards the south, through the Strait of Magellan, between the southern parts of Africa, Asia and America and the broad, still unknown shores of the land. Whether the same Ocean can also run round towards the north is still unknown. Certainly, if it is allowed, the two vastest seas are bound together, as it were, by a double girdle of waters, like two rings and crowns: one lies between the western parts of Europe and Africa and the western parts of America, the other between the western parts of America and the eastern parts of Asia.

units.la: v. Vafflateis Maris de I. a quam Terra.
units.tr: See on the Vafflatean Sea, concerning I.; than the earth.

units.la: Marium Reciprocantia dimittuntur.
units.tr: The reciprocating seas are let go.

units.la: Oceanus quid? Oceanum Terram ambire, nos dicimus. {a}caeque Occidentalia, Americæ vero Orientalia; altera inter hujus Occidentalia, Asiæ vero Orientalia. Quamvis verum illum circuitum ignorarint Veteres, auti tamen fuerunt multa de ambiente Terram Oceano scribere; potius quod sic ex communi quadam hominum opinione suspicarentur, quam quod ipsa re & experientia cognitum id haberent. Legendi Aristoteles de Mundo ad Alexandrum, Q. Cæcilius Metellus & Cornelius Nepos apud Pomponium Melam lib. iii. cap.v. Strabo libro i. Geograph. non recte citans isti sententiæ stabilendæ Homerum; & alij. Præivit ad hanc opinionem omnibus Orpheus in Hymnis: Ω᾽κεανὸν καλέω πατέρ᾽ ἀφθίτον αἰὲν ἑόντα, Α᾽ἰσιάτωνῆ Ἰεῶν γένεσιν, ὑπτιῶντ᾽ ἀνθρώπων; ὃς πᾶσιν μὲν ἀρχὴ γαίης πε̃ρὶ πέρμα κύκλον· ἐξ ἑπᾶ πάντα πλὰγοι καὶ πᾶσα θάλασσα.
units.tr: What is the Ocean? We say that the Ocean encircles the Earth, the western parts of Africa and of America, and the eastern parts of America; the other between the western parts of this and the eastern parts of Asia. Although the ancients did not know that true circuit, they nevertheless often wrote about the Ocean encircling the earth, more because they suspected it from a common opinion of men than because they had the thing known from experience. Read Aristotle's On the World, addressed to Alexander; Quintus Caecilius Metellus and Cornelius Nepos, cited by Pomponius Mela, book 3, chapter 5; Strabo, book 1 of the Geography, who wrongly cites Homer to establish that view; and others. Orpheus went before all others in this opinion in his Hymns: "I call upon Ocean, the immortal father, who ever is, the origin of the gods' birth and of men; from whom all rivers and every sea, the origin of the earth, flows round in a circle." [Ω᾽κεανὸν καλέω πατέρ᾽ ἀφθίτον αἰὲν ἑόντα, Α᾽ἰσιάτωνῆ Ἰεῶν γένεσιν, ὑπτιῶντ᾽ ἀνθρώπων; ὃς πᾶσιν μὲν ἀρχὴ γαίης πε̃ρὶ πέρμα κύκλον· ἐξ ἑπᾶ πάντα πλὰγοι καὶ πᾶσα θάλασσα.]

units.la: Sic Dionysius Afer. —— Ὠκεανὸς ἐπιδίδῳμι γαῖαν ἀπάσαν.
units.tr: So Dionysius the African: "Ocean encircles the whole earth." [Ὠκεανὸς ἐπιδίδῳμι γαῖαν ἀπάσαν.]

units.la: Manilius lib. iiii. Astronom. Ipsa natat Tellus Pelagi lustrata corona Cingentis medium liquidis amplexibus orbem.
units.tr: Manilius, Astronomica, book 4: The Earth itself floats, girt by the sea's crown, embracing the middle globe with liquid arms.

units.la: Seneca in Oedipo in fine Chori Actus ii. Lucida dum current annosi Sidera Mundi, Oceanus clausum dum fluctibus ambiet Orbem.
units.tr: Seneca, in the Oedipus, at the end of the chorus of Act 2: While the bright stars of the aged world run their course, and the Ocean with its waves surrounds the enclosed orb.

units.la: Oceanus quod complexu suo videatur Tellurem continere, Cyrillo Terra involucrum dicitur: nonnullis Mundi Baltheus.
units.tr: Because the Ocean seems to hold the earth in its embrace, Cyril calls it the wrapping of the earth; some call it the girdle of the world.

units.la: Dictus autem Oceanus, Solino cap. Polyhist. xxvi. Isidoro lib. xiii. Originum: cap. xv, & aliis, ab ὠκύς, quod sit citus; vel, ut idem Isidorus ex quo nescio Scriptore, quasi ὠκεανός, à purpureo colore; quo, ut Cælum nitere nonnullis putatur. Negat Herodotus lib. ii. & iv. Oceanum: non quod mare nullum arbitretur, sed quod tum temporis nomen, nondum satis notum, parum probaret.
units.tr: The Ocean is so named, as Solinus (Polyhistor, chapter 26) and Isidore (Origins, book 13, chapter 15), among others, say, from ὠκύς [swift], because it is swift; or, as Isidore says on the authority of some writer whose name he does not know, as if it were ὠκεανός [Oceanus], from its purple colour, by which some think the sky is made to shine. Herodotus, in books 2 and 4, denies that there is an Ocean. He did not mean that there is no sea, but that the name, not yet well known at that time, did not satisfy him.

units.la: Oceano passim nomen ab variis, quas abluit & amplectitur Orbis Terrarum partibus. Adeundi præter alios Solinus cap. xxvi,& Isidorus ejus Exscriptor lib.xiii. cap. xv. Nam qui citra Aequinoctialem inter Europam Africamque & Americam Septemtrionalis; qui vero ultra, inter Africam & Americam, Australis; qui Americam inter & Moluccas Insulas, Occidentalis (Pacificum Hodie vocant: quod non ita ut reliqua, exagitetur: alijs Mar del Sur nuncupatur) qui denique secus Sinarum littora, inter Moluccas & Africæ Orientalia, Orientalis vel Eous commode poterit indigetari.
units.tr: The Ocean has names everywhere, taken from the various parts of the world which it washes and embraces. Besides others, Solinus, chapter 26, and his copyist Isidore, book 13, chapter 15, indicate them. For the part on this side of the equator, between Europe, Africa and America, is the Northern Ocean; that beyond it, between Africa and America, the Southern; that between America and the Moluccas, the Western (today called the Pacific, because it is not stirred up as the others are; by others it is called Mar del Sur); and finally the part along the coasts of China, between the Moluccas and eastern Africa, may fitly be called the Eastern or Eous.

units.la: Septemtrionali varia à proximis Regionibus nomina Atlanticus, Gaditanus, Hispanicus, Ibericus, Cantabricus, Aquitanicus, Gallicus, Britannicus, Caledonius, Germanicus, Cimbricus, Arctous, Petzorke, Sarmaticus, Tartaricus, Scythicus, qui & Barbaricus Orosio lib. i. cap.ii, qui, ut & Plinius lib. vi. Pomponius Mela lib. i. quique paullo ante laudati; non obscure innuunt, Veteribus plerorum appellationes non fuisse ignotas.
units.tr: The Northern Ocean has various names from the neighbouring regions: Atlanticus, Gaditanus, Hispanicus, Ibericus, Cantabricus, Aquitanicus, Gallicus, Britannicus, Caledonius, Germanicus, Cimbricus, Arctous, Petzorke, Sarmaticus, Tartaricus, Scythicus, and also Barbaricus in Orosius, book 1, chapter 2. These names, like those used by Pliny, book 6, Pomponius Mela, book 1, and the authors praised a little earlier, make it clear that the ancients knew most of these appellations well enough.

units.la: In Australi est Aethiopicus.
units.tr: In the South is the Ethiopian.

units.la: In Occidentali, Magellanicus & Peruvianus.
units.tr: In the West, the Magellanic and the Peruvian.

units.la: In Orientali, denique Sinensis & Mare Rubrum vel Erythræum.
units.tr: In the East, finally, the Chinese and the Red or Erythraean Sea.

units.la: Alio modo admodum confuse,& (liceat illud in hac arena de Viro alioquin magno dicere) imperite dividit Albertus Magnus de Natur. Locor. distinct. iii, cap. i. & sequente. De nonnullis autem horum speciali quædam occurrunt notanda.
units.tr: Albert the Great divides it in another way, very confusedly and (may I say this of a man otherwise great, in passing) unskilfully, in his On the Nature of Places, distinction 3, chapter 1 and following. Some remarks about certain of these names need to be made.

units.la: Atlantici latissima prisicis temporibus fuit appellatio. Strabo scribit Indiam desinere ad mare Orientale & ad Austrinum, Atlantici partem; vult idem Australe & Orientale latus in Atlanticum pelagus procurrere; ait & alio loco Atlanticum mare in se coire. Quod magis, testatur Sudas omnia Maria innavigabilia, Atlantica Veteribus vocari solita. M. autem Tullius in Somn. Scipionis, omnem Terram, quæ ab Europæis colitur, Alantico Mari (qui Oceanus appellatur) tradit circumfundi. Novit denique Herodotus duo tantum Maris universi nomina, scribens Atlanticum, Rubrum, & totum illud quod Graeci navigant, unum esse; Caspium alterum: ut non immerito Zozimus ex Vetere proculdubio Scriptore Rhenum fluvium in Atlanticum mare noterse exonerare.
units.tr: Atlanticus was in ancient times the broadest name. Strabo writes that India ends at the Eastern and Southern sea, which is part of the Atlantic; he also holds that the southern and eastern flanks run out into the Atlantic main, and in another place he says the Atlantic Sea flows back into itself. Sudas further testifies that all unnavigable seas were commonly called Atlantic by the ancients. Cicero, in the Dream of Scipio, says that every land inhabited by Europeans is surrounded by the Atlantic Sea, which is called the Ocean. Herodotus, finally, knew only two names for the whole sea, writing that the Atlantic, the Red Sea and all that the Greeks sail are one, and the Caspian is the other. So Zosimus, following an undoubtedly ancient writer, not without reason, says that the river Rhine discharges into the Atlantic Sea.

units.la: Quod ad Britannicum, docet Plinius lib. iv. cap. xvi, omnes olim Europæ in Septemtrionali Oceano Insulas Britannicas fuisse appellatas, idque nomen postea inter eas omnes maximæ, quæ prius Albion dicebatur, relictum; hinc Oceanum ibi longe lateque ab Insulis tam multis nomen habuisse. Hodie Britannicus Oceanus proprie, qui Galliam inter & Angliam; Nautis Nostratibus Canale, Manche Gallis, Anglis Suife.
units.tr: As for the Britannic, Pliny, book 4, chapter 16, teaches that all the islands in the Northern Ocean of Europe were once called Britannic, and that this name was afterwards kept for the largest of them, which was formerly called Albion. Hence the Ocean there had its name, over a wide area, from so many islands. Today the Britannic Ocean properly means the sea between France and England; our sailors call it Canale, the French Manche, the English Suife.

units.la: Caledonius (ut ab Valerio Flacco vocatur; Προλεμαῖος Ptolemæo, hodie Scoticus) à Caledonijs Scotiæ olim populis, qui Silvam habebant Caledoniam, dictus.
units.tr: The Caledonian (as Valerius Flaccus calls it; Ptolemy calls it Προλεμαῖος, today it is the Scottish) is named after the Caledonians, the former people of Scotland, who had the Caledonian Forest.

units.la: Mare Arctoum appello, quod in subjectis Arctico polo locis. Glaciale nonnulli volunt & vocant ab glacie, cujus ex dulcioribus fluviorum aquis concretæ, & lapsu temporis calore Solis abruptæ violenter Terris, immensa fragmina in ejus superficie ita fluitant, ut mobilium Insularum inter se concurrentium speciem præbeant. Nam adstrictum esse ibi ipsum Mare, facilius dicitur, quam probatur: & rem sequius se habere, nobis jam innotuit Variorum in eas Oceani partes Navigationibus: ut supra etiam dixi. Qua Russiam attingit, Indigenæ vocant Myrmanskci-more, quasi Danium & Norvegicum Mare: Danos enim illi & Norvegos Mowremans appellant.
units.tr: I call it the Arctic Sea, because it lies in places subject to the Arctic pole. Some want and call it the Glacial sea, from the ice; fresh river water freezes into ice, and over time, when the sun's heat violently breaks it from the lands, huge fragments float on its surface, so that they present the appearance of moving islands colliding with one another. For it is easier to say that the sea itself is frozen there than to prove it; and that the matter is otherwise, has now become known to us from the voyages of various men into those parts of the Ocean, as I also said above. Where it touches Russia, the natives call it Myrmanskci-more, as if it were the Danish and Norwegian Sea; for they call the Danes and Norwegians Mowremans.

units.la: Scythicum Mare notat Plinius lib. vi. haustu dulce esse; Salæ nimirum influentium amnium magnitudine superato. De Caspio quod Scythici partem facit ibidem auctor, non ubique bonæ fidei; vero similiter hoc dici potest, non de Oceano Scythico: quem tamen, ne quid dissimulem, ut & reliqua Septemtrionalia, minoris Salsedinis, quam quæ versus Meridiem. Quum enim, ut alibi me monere memini, Causa Salsedinis in Mari sit adustum quoddam terrestre undis admistum, quando ab ejus summo Vapores dulces vi Solis elevantur; non potest quin, quum debilior sit radiorum Solis in Septemtrionalibus reflexio, & infirmior elevatorum resolutio, partiumque dulcium consumtio, etiam minor sit Salsedo. Notat Albertus Magnus de nat. locor. dist. 1. cap. iiii, generatim Aquam Oceani in summo dulciorem esse propter Aeris in infimo turbulentam & talsam propter Terræ admistionem; in medio insipidam.
units.tr: Pliny, book 6, says that the Scythian Sea is sweet to drink, the saltness being overcome by the great quantity of rivers flowing into it. What the same author says there about the Caspian, which he makes part of the Scythian sea, is not wholly trustworthy; but the same can be said truly, not of the Scythian Ocean, which I will not conceal is, like the other northern seas, less salty than those towards the south. For, as I recall having noted elsewhere, the cause of saltness in the sea is a certain earthy burnt matter mixed with the waters, when sweet vapours are raised from its surface by the force of the sun. It cannot be otherwise: since the reflection of the sun's rays is weaker in the north, and the resolution of the raised vapours is feebler, and the consumption of the sweet parts less, the saltness is also less. Albert the Great, On the Nature of Places, distinction 1, chapter 4, observes generally that the water of the Ocean is sweeter at the surface, because the air at the bottom is turbulent and salty from the mixture of earth, and tasteless in the middle.

units.la: Mare Rubrum, ut Latini vocant, totum illud quod inter Africæ Orientaliora & Arabiam Insulam, quæ hodie Sumatra. Rubrum dixerunt; alij Solis repercussu talem reddi colorem existimantes, quidam ab Arena Terraque, nonnulli, tali ipsius Aquæ natura, alij alunde: ut notant Strabo lib. xvi, Plinius lib. vi,cap. xxiii. & alij. Nugas, quæ de rubra Aqua finguntur, testantur qui navigarunt. Recte Curtius lib. viii. Mare certe, quo adluitur, ne colore quidem abhorret à ceteris, ab Erythro rege inditum est nomen, propter quod ignari rubere Aquas credunt. Sileant igitur, qui fuco nobis hic mentiuntur Colores; Regé cum antiquis Scriptoribus agnoscant, qui ad hoc Mare regnasse perhibetur, à quo Græcis Ἐρυθραῖον & notante Pompeio Mela, Ἐρυθραία Θάλασσα. Partes ejus principes, Persicum, qua Perlis propius: Arabicum qua radit Arabiam, ut volunt Herodotus lib. iiii, & Pomponius lib. iii. Non hic loquor de interni Persico & Arabico: quæ sequenti capite dabuntur. Utrumque tamen Arabicum, & quod Internum & quod Arabiæ Felicis exteriora lavat, est ex audiendum apud Strabonem lib. ult. ubi, frequentissimis ejus ad Indos & Troglodytas navigationibus adeo Vectigal Aegypti Regibus auctum, est auctor ut Auletæ, Cleopatræ parenti, annua talenta duodecies millena & quinquaginta obvenirent. Illud etiam monendum, hoc Mare, qua Persiam & Arabiam perfundit, Azanium Plinio nominari lib.vi. cap. xxiv. Sunt & alia Maris Rubri partes: Aethiopicum Dionysio, qua Æthyopiam; Indicum Plinio, Melæ, Orosio, qua Indiam adluit. Lusitanis Mar di India. Latissimum igitur Mare Rubrum: ut recte Seneca in Troadib. Act. i. scripserit, Tigrim rubenti freto misceri, & Eustathius Indiam ad idem pertingere; immerito eam ob causam reprehensi; hic ab Guilandino in suo de Papiro opere, ille ab Antonio Del rio in suo ad doctissimum Poetam Commentario. De Marinis hic Monstris Rufus eleganter in Periegesi ex Dionysio: fervent Erythraei marmora Ponti Tota feris: hæc, ut rigidi iuga maxima montes Nubibus attollunt, latus omne & terga tumescunt; Infar in his rupis spinæ tenor arduus adstat, Molibus in celsis scrupus quoque creber inhorret. At ne quis rapidis subvectus gurgitis unda, Hac in terga salis lembum contorqueat umquam, Aut se Monstrigenis, hostem licet, inferat assus Fluctibus, immodice late patet oris hiatus. Quippe feris antro panduntur guttura vasto, Protinus hac ipsas absorbent fauce carinas, Involvuntque simul mox Monstra vorantia nautas.
units.tr: The Red Sea, as the Latins call it, is the whole sea that lies between the more eastern parts of Africa and Arabia, and the island which today is Sumatra; they called it red. Others thought it takes that colour from the reflection of the sun; some from the sand and earth; some from the nature of the water itself; others from elsewhere, as Strabo, book 16, Pliny, book 6, chapter 23, and others note. Those who have sailed there testify to the nonsense invented about the red water. Curtius, book 8, rightly says: The sea which washes it is not at all different in colour from the others; it was named after King Erythras, and because of this name ignorant men believe the waters are red. Let those who here deceive us with false colours be silent, and let them acknowledge the king of the ancient writers, who is said to have reigned over this sea, from whom the Greeks named it Ἐρυθραῖον [Erythraian], and, as Pomponius Mela notes, Ἐρυθραία Θάλασσα [Erythraia Thalassa]. Its principal parts are the Persian, where it lies nearer Persia, and the Arabian, where it touches Arabia, as Herodotus, book 4, and Pomponius, book 3, say. I am not speaking here of the inner Persian and Arabian Gulfs, which will be dealt with in the following chapter. Still, the Arabian Sea, both the inner part and the outer part which washes Arabia Felix, should be heard from Strabo, last book, where, because of his very frequent voyages to India and to the Troglodytes, the revenue of the Egyptian kings was so increased that to Auletes, the father of Cleopatra, there came an annual sum of 12,050 talents. It should also be noted that this sea, where it bathes Persia and Arabia, is called Azanium by Pliny, book 6, chapter 24. There are also other parts of the Red Sea: the Ethiopian by Dionysius, where it washes Ethiopia; and the Indian by Pliny, Mela and Orosius, where it washes India. To the Portuguese it is the Mar di India. The Red Sea is therefore very broad, so that Seneca in the Trojan Women, Act 1, rightly wrote that the Tigris mingles with the red strait, and Eustathius that India reaches to the same sea. They were unjustly blamed for this: the former by Guilandinus in his work on papyrus, the latter by Antonius del Rio in his commentary on that most learned poet. Here Rufus, in his Periegesis after Dionysius, elegantly describes the sea monsters: The Erythraean seas, the whole sea of Pontus, teem with wild beasts: here, as rigid ridges raise the greatest mountains into the clouds, every side and back swells; here a high row of spines stands like a ridge of rock, and the crags crowd thickly upon the lofty mounds. But lest any ship, carried on the rapid waves of the flood, should ever turn its keel on these backs of the sea, a vast gaping mouth opens wide, even if an enemy of the monster-born waves should attack it. For the beasts open their throats in a huge cave, and at once with that jaw they swallow the very keels, and soon the devouring monsters swallow the sailors together with them.

units.la: Hinc & Pomponius lib. iii. Profundum notat hoc Mare & Magnorum Animalium magis, quam cetera, capax.
units.tr: Hence Pomponius, book 3, notes that this sea is deep, and holds large animals more than others do.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CAP. VII.

units.la: De Internis Maribus, & primo de Mediterraneo.
units.tr: Of the Inland Seas, and first of the Mediterranean.

units.la: INTERNA Maria vocari lego, commissis inter se bonorum Auctorum verbis, quæ ex vasto Oceano per Freta, non uno loco, Terrarum penitiora ingrediuntur.
units.tr: I read that the inland seas are so called, by the agreement of good authors, because they run from the vast Ocean through straits, in more than one place, into the more remote parts of the lands.

units.la: Inter hæc principis loci, quod per Fretum Herculeum infunditur: procurrens inter Europam Asiamque minorem, sinistras; & Africam dextram; ab Occidente in Orientem, ad oras usque Syriæ. Hinc κατ' ἐξοχὴν Mediterraneum dicitur; quod Terram, cognitam tunc temporis, quo appellationem hanc nactum, mediam quasi secaret; ut videre est apud Isidorum lib. xiii. Orig. cap. xvi. τὸ ἐσω θάλασσα nominant Græci apud Sallustium lib. i. Historiarum: cui, multisque aliis Scriptoribus qui ad Mare illud cum alibi, tum in Italia floruerunt, Nostrum nuncupatur; ut diserte notant Pomponius Mela lib. i. cap. i, & Orosius lib. i. cap. ii. Εσωτερικὸν Eustathio ab Hesperia; quo nomine nota quondam, ut alibi docebo, Hispania, Italia, & Libya, quibus interfluit. Africanum Luitprando Ticinensi, ubi Ianuensem urbem ad mare Africanum constitutam scribit; Tyrrhenum Orosio: συνεκδοχικῶς pro toto parte accipientibus, Mar di Levante vocant Hispani; quibus ut Oceanus Occidenten, hoc Orientem est versus. Augustissimum vero Cognomen ejus Magnum: vel quod nullum majus ejus adcolæ nossent, Oceanum pauciens ingressi; vel quod nullum Interrnorum majus, ut videtur velle Isidorus lib. xiii, c. quod dixi; vel in quo & alia, ut postea etiam parebit, Maria, indicante Servio ad librum iii. Aeneidos; vel denique quod omnes plagas terrasque medias interluerent, ut vult Orosius lib. i. c. ii, signans simul etymon Mediterranei. Hoc sane nomine celebratur non solum apud Latinos, quorum verba, ne hic repetam, laudo ad xvii. Annalium Ennii; verum etiam passim in Sacris Litteris, præsertim Numerorum c. xxxiv, versf. 6. & seq. Et terminus Maris erit vobis Mare Magnum (הים הגדול & terminusque erit vobis terminus Maris. Iste erit vobis terminus absconditus (צפון, Aquilonaris) a Mari Magno describetis vobis Hor-montem, & aliis eodem capite locis Iehosuah c. xv, versf. 47. Asdod. filiae ejus & villae ejus; Hazzab filiae ejus & villae ejus usque ad torrentem Ægypti & Mare Magnum (הים הגדול; legitur & הנבול, Mare termini) & terminum. Propheta Rex Psalmo civ. versf. 25: Hoc Mare Magnum (הים גדול) latum manibus; ibi Reptile & non numerus. Itali hodieque augustam hanc appellationem retinent angustiore loco, in parte Maris Ionij, qua Sinus est Tarentinus, quem Mar grande vocitant.
units.tr: Among these, the chief is the one that pours in through the Pillars of Hercules. It stretches between Europe and Asia Minor on the left and Africa on the right, from west to east, as far as the shores of Syria. For this reason it is called κατ' ἐξοχὴν Mediterraneum [the Mediterranean, par excellence], because it cut through the middle of the lands known at the time it received that name, as one may see in Isidore, Origines 13, chapter 16. The Greeks call it τὸ ἐσω θάλασσα [the inner sea], as in Sallust, Histories book 1. By Sallust and many other writers who flourished near that sea, both elsewhere and in Italy, it is called Nostrum [our sea]; as Pomponius Mela, book 1, chapter 1, and Orosius, book 1, chapter 2, clearly note. Eustathius calls it Εσωτερικὸν [the inner sea] from Hesperia, a name by which Spain, Italy and Libya, which it washes, were once known, as I will show elsewhere. Luitprand of Pavia calls it Africanum [the African sea], where he writes that the city of Genoa was built on the African sea. Orosius calls it Tyrrhenum [the Tyrrhenian sea]. Taking the part for the whole, the Spaniards call it Mar di Levante [the sea of the east], as the Ocean is to the west and this sea lies to the east. Its most august title, however, is Magnum [the Great]: either because its inhabitants knew no larger sea, having entered the Ocean only a few times; or because it is larger than the other inland seas, as Isidore, book 13, chapter cited above, seems to wish; or because it contains other seas, as will also appear later, as Servius indicates on book 3 of the Aeneid; or finally because it washes all the regions and lands in the middle, as Orosius wishes, book 1, chapter 2, which also gives the etymology of Mediterranean. This name is certainly celebrated not only among the Latins, whose words I praise, to avoid repeating them here, in the seventeenth book of Ennius' Annals, but also throughout Holy Writ, especially Numbers 34, verses 6 and following: And the border of the sea shall be to you the Great Sea (הים הגדול [ha-yam ha-gadol]: "and the border shall be to you the border of the sea"). This shall be your northern border (צפון [tsafon], northern): from the Great Sea you shall mark out for yourselves Mount Hor. Likewise in the same chapter, Joshua 15, verse 47: Ashdod with its daughters and villages; Gaza with its daughters and villages, as far as the brook of Egypt and the Great Sea (הים הגדול; some read הנבול [ha-gevul], the border of the sea) and the border. The prophet-king, Psalm 104, verse 25: This great and wide sea (הים גדול [ha-yam gadol]) in which are innumerable creeping things. Even today the Italians keep this grand name for a narrower place, the part of the Ionian sea where the Gulf of Taranto lies, which they call Mar grande [the great sea].

units.la: Oceanus igitur, ab Occasu Solis per Fretum Gaditanum gremia Terrarum irrumpens, limen aperit, ut Solini verbis utar, Interni Aequoris, quod Mediterraneum dixi; cui progressus & longe lateque diffusus, ut loquitur Pomponius Mela, vastéque sedentia littora abigens, Majores considerans partes, Ægyptum dat Asiæ, Gallicum Europæ, Africum Libyæ; Minores autem intuens & partes quasi partium (verba sunt Solini, & ex eo Isidori) varia à Provincijs, Insulis, Populis & aliunde indit nomina; ut videre est apud Manilium lib. iv. Astronomic. Solinum Polyhistor. cap. xxvi, & Isidorum lib. xiii, cap. xvi; quos semel hic, ne passim in sequentibus cogar, laudo.
units.tr: The Ocean, then, breaking in from the west through the Strait of Cádiz into the bosom of the lands, opens the threshold of the inland sea which I have named the Mediterranean. Having advanced and spread far and wide, as Pomponius Mela says, and wearing away the vast shores that lie along it, it considers the larger parts and assigns Egypt to Asia, the Gallic coast to Europe and the African coast to Libya. Looking at the smaller parts, and the parts of parts (these are Solinus' words, and Isidore's after him), it gives them various names from provinces, islands, peoples and other things. One may see this in Manilius, Astronomica book 4, Solinus, Polyhistor chapter 26, and Isidore, book 13, chapter 16. I cite these writers once here, so that I need not cite them constantly in what follows.

units.la: Ibericum Mare vocatur ab Iberia, sic enim olim Hispaniam appellabant.
units.tr: The Ibericum [Iberian sea] is so called from Iberia, for Spain was once so named.

units.la: Balearicum: qua insulas circumluit Balearicas, Majorem Minoremque; Majorca & Menorca hodie. Gallicum speciatim, qua Narbonensem Galliam attingit, Solino; inter Baleares Insulas & Sardiniam, Orosio.
units.tr: The Balearicum [Balearic sea] washes the Balearic Islands, the Greater and the Lesser, which are now Majorca & Menorca. The Gallicum [Gallic sea], specifically where it touches Narbonese Gaul, according to Solinus; between the Balearic Islands and Sardinia, according to Orosius.

units.la: Ligusticum; qua Liguriam lambit, juxta Genuam, inquit Orosius: hodie Mar di Lione, Leandro scribente.
units.tr: The Ligusticum [Ligurian sea] laps the coast of Liguria near Genoa, says Orosius; today it is the Mar di Lione [the sea of Lyon], as Leandro writes.

units.la: Sardoum; à Sardinia: quod, & sequens, omnium profundissimum docet Aristoteles lib. II. Meteor. ut alias dixi.
units.tr: The Sardoum [Sardinian sea] is named from Sardinia. Aristotle, in book 2 of the Meteorology, teaches that this sea and the following are the deepest of all, as I said elsewhere.

units.la: Tuscum; à Tuscia Italiae regione: Tyrrhenum Graecis, à Tyrrheno Lydi fratre, vel à Tyrrhenis nautis quos in hoc mare se praecipitasse tradunt Dionysius Afer in Periegesi, Pomponius Mela & Orosius. Inferum Latinis, apud Solinum; respectu Hadriatici, quod Superum, ut ex sequentibus parebit Liburnum M. Tullio; improprie: est enim Liburnia Illuridis regio, ad mare Superum. Leandro Mar Tosco: Mer de Marseille Vincentio Lupano in Tacitum.
units.tr: The Tuscum [Tuscan sea] is named from Tuscany, a region of Italy. The Greeks call it Tyrrhenum [Tyrrhenian], from Tyrrhenus, brother of the Lydian, or from the Tyrrhenian sailors who are said to have thrown themselves into this sea, as Dionysius Afer in his Periegesis, Pomponius Mela and Orosius relate. The Latins call it Inferum [the lower sea], in Solinus, in contrast to the Adriatic, which is the Superum [upper sea], as will appear from what follows. Marcus Tullius calls it Liburnum [Liburnian], but improperly, for Liburnia is a region of Illyria on the upper sea. Leandro calls it Mar Tosco [the Tuscan sea]; Vincentius Lupanus, in his commentary on Tacitus, Mer de Marseille [the sea of Marseilles].

units.la: Siculum; ab nobilissima Maris hujus Insula, Sicilia, Aristoteli, de Mundo: olim Ausonium, ut notat Strabo lib. II. Siculi suam vocabant, dulcem: quum Maria plurimum falsa; locantes, non propter dulces cibos, qui hoc mari ipsis advehebantur; qua de re videndus Eustathius, Athenaei ibi transcriptor.
units.tr: The Siculum [Sicilian sea] is named from the most famous island of this sea, Sicily, according to Aristotle, in his work On the World. It was once called Ausonium, as Strabo notes in book 2. The Sicilians called it their own sweet sea, though seas are for the most part salty; they gave it this name not because of the sweet foods which were brought to them by this sea. On this matter Eustathius, who transcribed Athenaeus there, should be consulted.

units.la: Argolicum; quod ad Peloponnesum Ptolemaeo; hodie, ut vult Nicolaus Sophianus, Golfo de Napoli; vix potest.
units.tr: The Argolicum [Argolic sea] is named, according to Ptolemy, from the Peloponnese. Today, as Nicolaus Sophianus holds, it is the Golfo de Napoli [the Gulf of Naples]; this can hardly be right.

units.la: Corinthium; à Corintho, florentissima quondam Peloponnesi urbe, ut scribit Solinus. Alcyonium mare, Straboni: Golfo de Patras, Sophiano: Ripa d'Ostria, Nautis ut notat Dominicus Marius Niger.
units.tr: The Corinthium [Corinthian sea] is named from Corinth, once the most flourishing city of the Peloponnese, as Solinus writes. Strabo calls it the Alcyonium sea; Sophianus calls it the Golfo de Patras [the Gulf of Patras]; the sailors call it the Ripa d'Ostria [the shore of Ostria], as Dominicus Marius Niger notes.

units.la: Creticum; ab Creta: hodie Mar di Candia.
units.tr: The Creticum [Cretan sea] is named from Crete; today it is the Mar di Candia [the sea of Candia].

units.la: Carpathium; ab Insula Carpatho, quae ad Orientale Cretae promontorium.
units.tr: The Carpathium [Carpathian sea] is named from the island of Carpathus, which lies off the eastern promontory of Crete.

units.la: Pamphylium; à Pamphylia Asiae Minoris regione. Emendandus hic Solinus, c. xxvi. Cyprium; ab Insula maris Mediterranei famosissima.
units.tr: The Pamphylium [Pamphylian sea] is named from Pamphylia, a region of Asia Minor. Solinus, chapter 26, needs correcting here. The Cyprium [Cyprian sea] is named from the island of Cyprus, the most famous island in the Mediterranean.

units.la: Asiaticum; Solino ab Asia, sive Minor illa sit exaudienda, quam Propriam vocabant Veteres; sive Maior.
units.tr: The Asiaticum [Asian sea] is named, according to Solinus, from Asia, whether that means the little Asia which the ancients called Proper, or the greater Asia.

units.la: Syrium: ab Syria, florentissima quondam Majoris Asiae parte, quam in quinque portiones dividit Eustathius, cuiusque undecim numerat nominatque regiones Plinius:
units.tr: The Syrium [Syrian sea] is named from Syria, once the most flourishing part of greater Asia, which Eustathius divides into five portions, and of which Pliny counts and names eleven regions:

units.la: A quarum una Phoenice, Phoenicium, apud Solinum;
units.tr: Of these regions one is Phoenicia, whence the Phoenicium [Phoenician sea], in Solinus;

units.la: Ab urbe vero Phoeniciae celeberrima, & orbis olim Emporio, Tyro; Tyrium apud eundem.
units.tr: and from the city of Phoenicia most famous, and once the market of the world, Tyre, whence the Tyrium [Tyrian sea], in the same author.

units.la: Eadem haec Aquarum Internarum moles, sui Cursus fere medio, versus Circium inter extrema Italiae & Epirum provoluta, Ionium vocatur ab Ionia, quam regiunculam in ultimis Italiae oris facit Solinus: vel ab Ionio Illuriorum Rege, ejus, à quo Hadria urbs condita fertur, filio, scribentibus Theopompo, quem Apollonij Interpres, & Autothepo, quem Tzetzes ad Lycophronem citant, quibus suffragatur & Solinus in Polyhistore, cujus jam memini; vel ab Ionibus, ut censet Archidamus apud eosdem Interpretes, in trajectu Maris ibi submersis. Fabulas (quamquam & quae dixi non prorsus ab ijs intaminata) puto narrare; qui denominatum volunt ab Ionio, Dyrrachij filio, quem interfectum Hercules eo loci in mare perhibetur dejecisse; ejus mentis Appianus: magis vero, qui ab Io Inachi filia, quae ex Dodona, ut quidam scriptis audent mandare, profugiens, Mare illud trajecit. Prometheus apud Aeschylum: Χρέων δὲ τ' μέλλοντα ποίτης μυχὸς (Σαφῶς ἀπίσσο') Ἰονίῳ κλῃσθησεται, Τῆς σῆς πορείας μίμημα πῶσι βροτοῖς.
units.tr: This same mass of inland waters, rolling forward roughly midway along its course, toward the northwest, between the extremities of Italy and Epirus, is called the Ionium [Ionian sea], from Ionia, a little region which Solinus places on the farthest shores of Italy. Or it is named from Ion, king of the Illyrians, the son of him from whom the city of Hadria is said to have been founded, as Theopompus writes (whom the commentators on Apollonius cite), and Autothepo (whom Tzetzes cites on Lycophron), to whom Solinus in the Polyhistor, which I have already mentioned, also gives support. Or it is named from the Ionians, as Archidamus holds, according to the same commentators, who were drowned there in crossing the sea. I think these are fables, though what I have said is not wholly free of them. Some want it named from Ion, son of Dyrrachius, whom Hercules is said to have killed and thrown into the sea at that spot; Appian holds this view. More likely is the view of those who name it from Io, daughter of Inachus, who, fleeing from Dodona, as some dare to write, crossed that sea. Prometheus in Aeschylus says: And the sea which shall be called Ionian, a memorial of your passage, for all mortals [Χρέων δὲ τ' μέλλοντα ποίτης μυχὸς (Σαφῶς ἀπίσσο') Ἰονίῳ κλῃσθησεται, Τῆς σῆς πορείας μίμημα πῶσι βροτοῖς].

units.la: Cronium enim & Rex Sinus antea dicebatur, ut testantur antiqui Scriptores (inter quos lego & Apollonium) notante in Lycophronem Isacio. Pars ejus Epiroticum: ab Epiro, Graeciae regione, florentissimo quondam Pyrrhi regno, apud Servium ad lib. III. Aeneid.
units.tr: For it was once called Cronium and Rex Sinus [the Royal Gulf], as ancient writers attest (among whom I read Apollonius too), as Isacius notes on Lycophron. Part of it is the Epiroticum [Epirote sea], from Epirus, a region of Greece, once the flourishing kingdom of Pyrrhus, as Servius says on book 3 of the Aeneid.

units.la: Inde versus Corum se fundens, Italiaeque lavans superiora, vocatur Hadriaticum ab Hadria oppido in finibus Piceni, quod, Romanorum olim Colonia, VII. millibus passuum distat à mari: Hadriacum Lucano, libris de bello Pharsalico: Hadrianum, M. Tullio scribenti ad Atticum, & oranti contra L. Pisonem: Hadria, simpliciter Straboni, Senecae, Tacito, Melae, aliis; sic Plutarchus in Camillo: Τὴν μὲν γὰρ Βόγεσον Θάλασσας, Ἀδρίας καλεῖν ἀπὸ Τυρρηνικῆς πόλεως Ἀδρίας: τῷ ἢ πρὸς νότῳ κεκλιμένῳ, ἀντικρυς, Τυρρηνικὸν πέλαγος. Sed opidi inglorij titulum indignatus hic Neptunus, nomen exoravit ab Vrbe magna & potente; dictus hodie Golfo di Venetia. Superum etiam Latinis; quod, si Inferum (hodie, ut dixi, Mar Tosco) spectetur, Orientalius; vel, ut alij, Arctico polo vicinius; ubi pars Mundi putatur superior. Pertinet huc jocus Crassi apud Ciceronem lib. iii. de Oratore: Hæc autem, ut ex Apennino fluminum, sic ex communi Sapientia jugo doctrinarum facta divortia: ut Philosophi tamquam in Superum mare Ionium defluerent, Græcum quidem & portuosum: Oratores autem in Inferum hoc Tuscum & Barbarum, & scopulosum atque infestum, laberentur; in quo etiam ipse Vixses erraret. Mare Hadriaticum, ut ventis & tempestatibus obnoxium damnat Horatius lib. i. Carmin. Oda xxxiii; & lib. iii. Odis iii, ix. & xxvii. iracundum, inquietum, atrum faciens; ducemque illi turbidum jungens Africum. Hinc Seneca in Thyeste: —— sævo rapidus freto Ventosi tumor Hadriæ.
units.tr: Then, flowing from there toward the northwest and washing the upper parts of Italy, it is called the Hadriaticum [Adriatic sea], from the town of Hadria in the territory of Picenum, which lies seven miles from the sea and was once a colony of the Romans. Lucan, in his books on the Pharsalian war, calls it Hadriacum; Marcus Tullius, writing to Atticus and speaking against Lucius Piso, Hadrianum; Strabo, Seneca, Tacitus, Mela and others simply Hadria. So Plutarch in the Life of Camillus: "For they call the sea beyond Tyrrhenia the Adriatic, from the Tyrrhenian city of Adria, and the one tending to the south, the Tyrrhenian sea." But Neptune, indignant at the inglorious title of a small town, begged the name from a great and powerful city; today it is the Golfo di Venetia [the Gulf of Venice]. It is also called Superum [the upper sea] by the Latins; if one looks at the Tuscan sea, Mar Tosco as I said, it lies further east, or, as others say, nearer the Arctic pole, where the upper part of the world is thought to lie. Crassus' joke in Cicero's De Oratore, book 3, belongs here: "Just as the rivers divide from the Apennine ridge, so the divisions of learning arise from the common ridge of wisdom: the philosophers flow down, as into the upper Ionian sea, Greek and full of harbours; the orators, however, slip into this lower Tuscan and barbarous sea, rocky and hostile, in which even Ulysses himself would go astray." The Adriatic Sea, as exposed to winds and storms, Horace condemns, Odes book 1, ode 33, and book 3, odes 3, 9 and 27, making it angry, restless and dark, and joining to it the stormy southwest wind, Africus. Hence Seneca in the Thyestes: The swelling of the windy Hadria, rushing over the cruel sea.

units.la: Pars Hadriatici Illyricum ab Illyrico, quæ longe lateque patens Geographis Europæ regio; meminit ex quorundam mente Apostolus epistola ab Romanos, cap. xv. ubi tamen malim ipsam regionem intelligere. Pars item Dalmaticum ab Dalmatia, quæ Illyrico conregionalis.
units.tr: The part of the Adriatic called Illyricum takes its name from Illyria, a region that spreads far and wide and is well known to the geographers of Europe. The Apostle mentions it in Romans 15, according to some authors, though I would rather take the word there to mean the region itself. Likewise the part called Dalmaticum takes its name from Dalmatia, which belongs to the same region as Illyricum.

units.la: Eadem Aquarum Maris Mediterranei vis ulterius ad Cretam Insulam, torto in Septemtrionem latere, per Orientaliora Græciæ littora & minorem Asiam, amfractibus magnis & vasto recessu, insula, nobilissimas adlambens Insulas (videndus omnino Ammianus lib. xxii.) Ægæum vocatur Pelagus. In Etymo nimium quantum variatur. Paucis indicabo, ne vel quid Lector desideret, vel ad potiora properantem hæc talia morentur. Plutarchus in Theseo, Hyginus fabula xliii, & Festus lib. i. nominatum scribunt ab Ægæo Thesei patre, qui in id se præcipitasse perhibetur: Pherecydes, ab Neptuno, qui & Ægæus: Festus iterum, ab Ægæa Amazonum regina, quam volunt in eo periisse: idem tertium, ut & Varro lib. vi. de LL. ab Insulis, quæ in hoc mari crebræ procul adspicientibus species Caprarum videntur. Plinius lib. iv. nat. hist. cap. xi. quem sequitur Isidorus lib. xiii, cap. xvi. unam Insularum figura Caprae prodit: quæ Homero dicitur Ægas, Neptuno sacra, spectris infestior, teste Nicocrate. Artemidorus dictum censet, à Promontorio Acolidis, quod Αἴγα nuncupabant adcolæ: Ἀ κεφαλῆς ἐστι, inquit, Αἰολίδῳ, ὧν Αἴγα οἱ ἀπαχώρεσοι ὀνομάζουσιν. ἀφ' ἧς καὶ τὸ πέλαγος τῷ πανταχῷ ἐπωνυμίαν περσιλήφειν. Plura huius formæ Promontoria scribit Scholiastes Apollonij in librum i. Solinus in Polyhistore ab Antandro, Asiæ Minoris opido, Capræ speciem referente, vocatum putat: Isacius in Lycophronem opinatur appellatum, quod Αἰγὲς instar valde laściviat fluctibus; alioquin Αἴγας dicere solent Dores fluctus illos, qui Latinis Decumani, Maximi. Sunt denique, qui derivant ἀπὸ τοῦ Αἰγίζειν: solet enim naves subvertere, & in brevia vada impellere, auctore Periegete, maxime circa Cycladas, ubi potissimum naves suetum adflugere & αἰγίζειν, ut ait Hesychius. Hæc de Etymo. Ipsum Mare Ægon etiam nominatur. Valerius Flaccus lib. i. Argonautic. —— quanto fremitu se sustulit Ægon:
units.tr: The same force of the waters of the Mediterranean, carried further to the island of Crete with its side turned to the north, and then along the more eastern shores of Greece and Asia Minor, with great windings and a vast recess, washing the most noble islands as it goes (Ammianus, book 22, is certainly worth consulting), is called the Aegean Sea. Its etymology varies greatly. I will point out a few explanations briefly, so that the reader does not miss anything, or so that those hurrying to weightier matters are not delayed by such trifles. Plutarch in the life of Theseus, Hyginus in fable 43, and Festus in book 1 write that it was named after Aegeus, the father of Theseus, who is said to have thrown himself into it. Pherecydes says it was named after Neptune, who was also called Aegeus. Festus again gives a third derivation, from Aegea, queen of the Amazons, whom they say perished there. The same Festus, and Varro in book 6 of On the Latin Language, derive it from the islands which, numerous in this sea, look from a distance like the shapes of goats. Pliny, book 4 of the Natural History, chapter 11, whom Isidore follows in book 13, chapter 16, reports that one of the islands has the shape of a goat; in Homer it is called Aegae, sacred to Neptune and more hostile to ghosts, as Nicocrates testifies. Artemidorus thinks it was named from a promontory of Aeolis, which the inhabitants called Aiga: "There is a headland of Aeolis," he says, "which the locals call Aiga, and from which the sea took its name all over." Scholiasts on Apollonius, on book 1, describe several promontories of this shape. Solinus in the Polyhistor thinks it was named from Antandros, a town of Asia Minor, which resembles a goat. Isaac on Lycophron supposes it was named because the goat-like sea leaps wildly with its waves; the Dorians, moreover, customarily call those waves aigas, which the Latins call the tenth and greatest waves. Finally, some derive it from aigizein, because it is accustomed to overturn ships and drive them onto shallows, as the Periegete says, especially near the Cyclades, where ships are most often driven and aigizein, as Hesychius puts it. So much for the etymology. The sea itself is also called Aegon. Valerius Flaccus, book 1 of the Argonautica: "with what a roar Aegon raised itself up,"

units.la: Et lib. iv. —— nec tantas quamvis Tyrrhenus & Ægon volvat aquas. ——
units.tr: and book 4: "nor, although the Tyrrhenian and Aegon roll such great waters."

units.la: Statius Papinius v. Thebaidos; —— quas spumifer adsilit Ægon.
units.tr: Statius Papinius, book 5 of the Thebaid: "which the foaming Aegon leaps upon."

units.la: Eidem & Ægeon eodem libro: Dys Pelagi, ventisque & Cycladas Ægeoni Amplexo. ——
units.tr: The same, in the same book, also Aegeon: "to the seas of Pelagus, and to the Cyclades embraced by Aegeon."

units.la: Sive Deus ibi marinus sit intelligendus, seu ipsum Mare. Utriusque enim notionis vox apud Eustathium; cujus hæc: Αἰγαίων ἀπὸ παμφίως ἐπάλιζε ἡμῶν, καὶ τὸ πρὸς τὰς Κυκλάδας πέλαγος. Mare Græcum Thucydidi & Polyæno. Europæis hodie Archipelago, voce Græca: Turcis Mare Album. Romani totum hoc mare duobus nominibus olim appellabant, teste Plinio lib. nat. hist. iiii, cap. xi, Macedonicum quidquid ejus Macedoniam & Thraciam attingebat; Græciense quidquid Græciam. Ægæi quoque partes Myrtoum, Icarium, Euboicum. Myrtoum, Μυρτῷον πέλαγος, Ptolemæo circa Cariam, Asiæ Minoris regionem; Castaldo Atar di Mandria: Straboni vero, Pausaniæ, Plinio, Orosio, Melæ, inter Peloponnesum & Atticam. Nomen illi à Myrtilo Mercurij filio, quem in id deturbatum ab Oenomao volunt Solinus & Isidorus: vel, ut verius sentit Plinius, ab exigua insula, non procul à Carysto Euboeæ oppido sita. Icarium Varroni, Ptolemæo, Ovidio ii. de arte amandi, Manilio lib. iv. Senecæ in Oedipo Choro Act. iv, & aliis, ab Icari nota fabula: Andreæ Tenedio in navigatione Propontidis, ab una Cycladum, quæ & Macris & Icarus: hodie Mar di Nicaria, Castaldo scribente. Euboicum ab Euboea insula; Euboicus Sinus Livio; cui, ut & Valerio lib. i. Dict. Factorumque memorabilium cap. viii, & Orosio lib. vi. cap. xv. Cœla quoque vocatur; Ptolemæo οἱπ χάλαπ: Hodie Golfo de Negroponte. Plautus Persicum indigetat Portum, apud Festum, quod in eo Classis Persarum stetisse dicatur non procul a Thebis. Horatius lib. i. Carminum, Ode xiiii. Brutum, bellum Civile reparantem monens loca naufragijs infesta non temere tentanda, ubi ait, Interfusa nitentes Vites æquora Cycladas,
units.tr: Whether a marine god is meant here, or the sea itself, is uncertain; the word is used in both senses. Eustathius, whose words are: "the Aegaeon... the sea toward the Cyclades" [Αἰγαίων ἀπὸ παμφίως ἐπάλιζε ἡμῶν, καὶ τὸ πρὸς τὰς Κυκλάδας πέλαγος]. Thucydides and Polyaenus call it the Greek Sea. Today Europeans call it the Archipelago, a Greek word, and the Turks the White Sea. According to Pliny, book 4 of the Natural History, chapter 11, the Romans once called this whole sea by two names: Macedonicum for whatever part of it touched Macedonia and Thrace, and Graeciense for whatever part touched Greece. Parts of the Aegean also have their own names: Myrtoum, Icarium and Euboicum. The Myrtoum, the Myrtoan sea (Μυρτῷον πέλαγος), is placed by Ptolemy near Caria, a region of Asia Minor; Castaldo calls it Atar di Mandria. Strabo, Pausanias, Pliny, Orosius and Mela place it between the Peloponnese and Attica. It is said to take its name from Myrtilus, son of Mercury, whom Oenomaus is said to have thrown into it, according to Solinus and Isidore; but, as Pliny more truly thinks, it was named from a small island not far from Carystus, a town of Euboea. The Icarium is named by Varro, Ptolemy, Ovid in book 2 of the Ars amatoria, Manilius in book 4, Seneca in the choral ode of Act 4 of the Oedipus, and others, from the well-known story of Icarus. Andreas of Tenedos, in his account of a voyage on the Propontis, names it from one of the Cyclades, which is also called Macris and Icarus; today it is the Mar di Nicaria, as Castaldo writes. The Euboicum is named from the island of Euboea; Livy calls it the Gulf of Euboea, and it is also called Coela by Valerius, book 1 of the Dicta et facta memorabilia, chapter 8, and by Orosius, book 6, chapter 15; Ptolemy calls it koilē. Today it is the Golfo de Negroponte. Plautus names the Persicum Portum, as Festus reports, because a Persian fleet is said to have lain there, not far from Thebes. Horatius, in Ode 14 of book 1 of the Carmina, warns Brutus, who was renewing the civil war, that places dangerous to shipwrecks should not be rashly attempted, where he says: "the waters that spread between the shining Cyclades."

units.la: Aegæum mare notat, de quo Dionysius Afer: ἃ γὰρ ᾗς ... ἐφίλης:
units.tr: He means the Aegean Sea, of which Dionysius Afer writes: "for ... loved..."

units.la: maxime circa Cyclades. Virgilius lib. iii. Aeneid. ——sparsasque per æquor Cycladas, & crebris legimus freta concita terris,
units.tr: Especially near the Cyclades. Virgil, book 3 of the Aeneid: "and we read of the Cyclades scattered over the sea, and of straits stirred by frequent lands."

units.la: Exstat Ἀνθολογ. Ἀλφάς. Ἀπιγεγμ. libro iii. cap. xxii, elegans Antipatri Carmen, cujus hoc initium: Πᾶσαι Νῆλαῖαι, Νῆλαῖαι: ὦ κυκλάδες, ἢ ςυνὸν Ἔλης Κῦμα, καὶ ὀξείας ἡλεὰ μεμφομέ-νη?
units.tr: There is an elegant poem by Antipater in the Anthologia Palatina, book 3, chapter 22, which begins: "All Nelean... O Cyclades, or the common wave of Hellas, and the sea that blames the sharp..." [Πᾶσαι Νῆλαῖαι, Νῆλαῖαι: ὦ κυκλάδες, ἢ ςυνὸν Ἔλης Κῦμα, καὶ ὀξείας ἡλεὰ μεμφομέ-νη;]

units.la: Aegæo, gracilescente paullatim Mari, succedit Hellespontus; angustiæ minus mille passuum Pomponio (septem stadia habet Plinius, quæ septingentos septuaginta quinque passus faciunt) inter Sestum Europæ & Abydum Asiæ oppida (Bogaz-Ssar hodie Turcis, ut notat Alexander Sardus) à quibus Sestiacum & Abydi Fretum; Ausonio. Hellesponti Claustra nominat antiquus Poeta, non dubito quin Ennius, in Medea apud Varronem lib. vi. de LL. Stretto de Gallipoli Italis à Callipoli Thraciæ Chersonnesi oppido: Gallis Bras de S. George, Belgis vero S. Iris Arm: ab Troadis oppido, quod hodie D. Georgio sacrum, Πιτυ Ptolemæo. Nomen ab Helle Virgine, quæ perijsse fingitur in hoc maris tractu. Ovidius in Epistola Leandri: Fluctibus immodicis Athama nitidos æquora canent, Vixque manet portu tuta carina suo. Hoc mare quum primum de Virgine nomina mersa Quæ tenet, est nactum, tale fuisse puto. Est satis amissa locus hic infimus ab Helle; Utque mihi parcat, nomine crimen habet. Invideo Phrixo, quem per freta tristia tutum Aurea lanigero vellere vexit ovis.
units.tr: After the Aegean, which gradually narrows, comes the Hellespont. Its narrowest point is less than a thousand paces according to Pomponius (Pliny gives seven stadia, which make 775 paces), between the towns of Sestos in Europe and Abydos in Asia (today the Turks call it Bogaz-Ssar, as Alexander Sardus notes), from which it is also called the Sestiacum and Abydi Fretum, as Ausonius has it. An ancient poet, I have no doubt Ennius in the Medea quoted by Varro, book 6 of On the Latin Language, calls it the Hellesponti Claustra, the bars of the Hellespont. The Italians call it the Stretto de Gallipoli, from Gallipoli, a town of the Thracian Chersonese; the French the Bras de S. George, and the Flemish the S. Iris Arm. It is named after a town of the Troad, which is now sacred to St George; Ptolemy calls it Pitys. The name comes from Helle, a virgin who is fabled to have perished in this stretch of sea. Ovid, in the letter of Leander: "With its excessive waves Athamas' ... the seas sing of the shining ... and the ship scarcely stays safe in its harbour. When this sea first got its name from the drowned virgin whom it holds, I think it was then of such a kind. This place is low enough for Helle to have lost her life here; and if it spares me, it bears the blame in its name. I envy Phrixus, whom the golden ram carried safely over the sad straits with its woolly fleece."

units.la: Hinc παρθενόχηνον πέλαγ. Lycophroni; παρθένιον Nazianzeno. Hic ex Asia in Europam contra Græcos, constrato in navibus ponte (quod hodie non solemus mirari) exercitum traduxit Xerxes Persarum rex. Ennius meus lib. xiii. Annalium: Pontibus instratis coniunxit littora Xerxes, Isque Hellesponto pontem contendit in alto.
units.tr: Hence Lycophron calls it the parthenochēnon pelagos, the sea of the maiden's goose, and Gregory Nazianzen the parthenion. Here Xerxes, king of the Persians, led his army from Asia into Europe against the Greeks, by laying a bridge of ships across the strait, a thing we no longer find remarkable today. My Ennius, book 13 of the Annals: "Xerxes joined the shores with laid bridges, and he stretched a bridge across the Hellespont in the deep."

units.la: Lycophron Alexandra: Ἀ ἀλ' αὐτὶ πάντων Παρσίως ἵνα ἀσθεῖς Σπλεῖ γίγαν ζα, τῷ ϑαλασα μὴ βατ Πεζῷ ποτ' ἐσαι; γῇ δὲ ναυσθλωθησεται Ῥῆσι ἀνδρὸς παθόις χέρσου.
units.tr: Lycophron in the Alexandra: "But above all, the Persian ... shall the sea be trodden on foot by ... and the land shall be sailed over by the ship of the man..." [Ἀ ἀλ' αὐτὶ πάντων Παρσίως ἵνα ἀσθεῖς Σπλεῖ γίγαν ζα, τῷ ϑαλασα μὴ βατ Πεζῷ ποτ' ἐσαι; γῇ δὲ ναυσθλωθησεται Ῥῆσι ἀνδρὸς παθόις χέρσου.]

units.la: Quo videndi, quos citant alij: præter, qui ex professo: Æschylus in Persis, Isocrates Panegyrico, Virgilius in Culice, Plutarch. περὶ ἀοργησίας, Juvenalis Sat. x, Ammianus lib. xxii. Arnobius lib. i. adversus gentes, Ioannes Tzetza Chiliade i. historia xxxii.
units.tr: Those who cite others on this point may be seen: besides those who treat it expressly, Aeschylus in the Persians, Isocrates in the Panegyricus, Virgil in the Culex, Plutarch in On Freedom from Anger, Juvenal, satire 10, Ammianus, book 22, Arnobius, book 1 Against the Gentiles, and John Tzetzes, Chiliades 1, history 32.
