units.la: Inde rursus modice se laxans & semiorbe, inquit Ammianus, turgescens altrinsecus, lataque aperiens terrarum devortia, facit Propontidem, inter Thraciam & Bithyniam; à qua, Bebrycia quondam, Bebrycium Mare legitur appellatum apud Tzetzam: Italis Mar di Marmora, ab Insula Proconnesso; ea enim Marmoris (quod ab urbe vicina, Cyzicenium) ferax, non hodie tantum, ut indicat Bellonius, sed & avorum nostrorum memoria, quod docet Curopalates Græcus Scriptor, Marmora dicta: unde cognominis illi Propontis.
units.tr: Then, as Ammianus says, it loosens itself somewhat and swells half-circularly on either side, and opening a wide gap in the land, it makes the Propontis, between Thrace and Bithynia. From this, called Bebrycia long ago, it is read in Tzetzes as the Bebrycian Sea. The Italians call it the Mar di Marmora, from the island of Proconnesus; for that island is rich in marble (which is named from the neighbouring city of Cyzicus), not only today, as Belon shows, but also within our grandfathers' memory, as the Greek writer Curopalates teaches, when it was called Marmora. From this the Propontis took its additional name.

units.la: Hæc mox stringitur, & in paucula stadia coartatur, fitque Bosporus Thracius: dictus ab Io Inachi filia, quæ formam Bovis induta, Mare hoc loco trajecisse fingitur. Interpres Apollonij ad lib. 11. Argonautic. Βόσπορος ὀνομάζεται Διὸς τὸ δοκεῖν τῶν Ἰὼ Βοῦς κατὰ Ἀμφιτρόπου ἀπὸ Βυζαντίου ἐς Καλχηδόνα, Διάσημα: & paulo post: ἡ Διὸς τὸ πύρταις τῆς γῆς ποθμὸς Βοσπόρως καλεῖσθαι.Promētheus apud Aeschylum: Ἐὰν δὲ ϑνητὸς εἰς ἀὰ λόγῳ μέγας Τῆς σῆς περαίας Βοσπόρου τ' ἐπωνυμῷ.
units.tr: This sea is soon narrowed and confined to a few stadia, and becomes the Thracian Bosporus. It is named after Io, daughter of Inachus, who, having taken the form of a cow, is fabled to have crossed the sea at this place. The commentator on Apollonius, on book 2 of the Argonautica: "The Bosporus is so called because Io, having become a cow, crossed from Byzantium to Chalcedon, as the story goes; and a little later: the passage of the cow across the land is called Bosporus." Prometheus in Aeschylus: "And if a mortal shall great ... in your passage and in the name of the Bosporus..." [Ἐὰν δὲ ϑνητὸς εἰς ἀὰ λόγῳ μέγας Τῆς σῆς περαίας Βοσπόρου τ' ἐπωνυμῷ.]

units.la: Bosporus Chalcedonis Herodoto; ab urbe adjacente, quæ hodieque Chalcidona, Turcis vero Caltitiu: Byzantij Portus, Incertioribus apud Stephanum ab urbe, quæ nunc Constantinopolis, olim Byzantium: Fauces Propontidis Manilio lib. iv. Astronomic. Σπμα Ποντ Εὔξεινα Pindaro; Fretum Mysium Arriano, quod tamen magis convenit Hellesponto. huic enim proxima Mysia & Minor & Maior. Græcis hodie Lamon; Turcis Bagazin, ut notat Petrus Gyllius, qui plene Bosporum describit: Italis Stretto de Constantinopoli. Bosporum Darius Hystaspis filius, Xerxis pater, rex Persarum, copias militares, facto ex Navibus ponte, traduxisse commemoratur, cum apud alios tum Herodotum lib. iv. Angustum enim ibi Mare: quinque Stadia (quæ singula cxxv. passuum) edunt Strabo & Pomponius Mela; Plinius in fine lib. v. nat. hist. quingentos passus, suspecta numeri scriptura; reponendus fortean 10 cxxv: hoc satis constat, hodieque, alituum cantus canumque latratus utrimque audiri, & fere vocis humanæ esse commercia; manente inter duos orbes, Europam Asiamque, colloquio; nisi id ipsum auferunt venti, inquit Plinius lib. natur. historiæ vi, cap. i.
units.tr: Bosporus of Chalcedon in Herodotus, from the neighbouring city, which is still called Chalcidona today, and by the Turks Caltitiu. Harbour of Byzantium. Among the less certain authorities, in Stephanus, from the city that is now Constantinople and was formerly Byzantium. Jaws of the Propontis in Manilius, Astronomica book 4. Σπμα Ποντ Εὔξεινα in Pindar. Mysian Strait in Arrian, though this name fits the Hellespont better, since Mysia, both Lesser and Greater, lies next to that. The Greeks now call it Lamon; the Turks Bagazin, as Petrus Gyllius notes, and he describes the Bosporus fully. The Italians call it Stretto di Costantinopoli. It is recorded that Darius, son of Hystaspes and father of Xerxes, king of the Persians, took his military forces across the Bosporus on a bridge made of ships, as both Herodotus (book 4) and others report. The sea is narrow there: Strabo and Pomponius Mela give its width as five stades (each of 125 paces). Pliny, at the end of Natural History book 5, gives five hundred paces, though the reading of the number is suspect and perhaps 125 should be restored. It is well established that even today the songs of birds and the barking of dogs can be heard from either side, and that there is almost a conversation of human voices, the two continents, Europe and Asia, carrying on a conversation across the gap, unless the winds carry it off, as Pliny says in Natural History book 6, chapter 1.

units.la: Hoc modo multis amfractibus fractum mare, mitescens jam in æquoream se pandit faciem, &, quantum poterat cadere sub adspectum, late diffusum & longe, Pontum aperit, qui Εὔξεινος Græcis, Euxinus Orosio lib. i. cap. ii. quondam, scribentibus Plinio, Solino, Isidoro, alijs, Ἄξεινος, Inhospitalis, ob immanem adcolarum crudelitatem & inhospitalitatem; vel, ut Theophilus tradit, latronum frequentiam; quæ expugnata fingitur ab Hercule, expurgata latrocinijs regione & hominum ibi animis cæterarum gentium commercio aliquantulum emollitis. Πόντος Πόλαγος Plutarcho in vitis Pompei & Eumenidis, Ptolemæo & Iornandi: Mare Cimmerium Herodoto & Orosio, ab Cimmerijs populis, qui adhabitabant; Caucasum, Apollonio lib. iii. à Caucaso monte inter Pontum hunc & Mare Caspium, Mare Boreale Herodoto lib. iiii. quia superioribus, quæ nominavi, ad Boream: Maurum Græcis Nautis; Maurethalassa, quasi Mare Nigrum Turcis; Mar Maiore Italis. Situm sic depingit Ammianus Marcellinus lib. xxii: Omnis ejus velut insularis circuitus littorea navigatio, viginti tribus dimensa millibus stadiorum, ut Eratosthenes adfirmat, & Hecatæus, & Ptolemæus, alyque 40 hujusmodi cognitionum scientissimi scitatores; in speciem Scythici arcus nervo coagmentati Geographiæ totius adsensione formatur. Et qua sol Oceano exsurgit Eoo, Paludibus clauditur Mæotidos: qua declinat in vesperum, Romanis provincijs terminatur: unde suspicit fidus Arctoum, Homines alij linguis & moribus dispares: latus ejus Austrinum molli devexitate subductum. Mare hoc dulcius, quam cetera, ex multitudine fluminum, Isidorus lib. xiii. cap. xvi, ex Sallustij historijs. Sic Seneca in Medea Act. ii: Quodcumque placidis flexibus Phasis rigat; Pontusque quidquid Scythicus à tergo videt, Palustribus qua maria dulcescunt aquis.
units.tr: Once the sea has been broken by many twists and turns, it grows calm and spreads into a level surface, and it opens out into the Pontus, which stretches wide and far as far as the eye can reach. The Greeks called it Εὔξεινος and Orosius (book 1, chapter 2) Euxinus. Earlier, as Pliny, Solinus, Isidore and others write, it was called Ἄξεινος, Inhospitable, because of the savage cruelty and inhospitality of its inhabitants; or, as Theophilus relates, because of the number of robbers there. It is said that Hercules conquered it, clearing the region of brigands and softening the minds of the people there somewhat through contact with other nations. Plutarch in the lives of Pompey and Eumenes, and Ptolemy and Jordanes, call it Πόντος and Πόλαγος. Herodotus and Orosius call it the Cimmerian Sea, from the Cimmerian peoples who lived there. Apollonius (book 3) calls it Caucasus, from the Caucasus mountain between this Pontus and the Caspian Sea. Herodotus (book 4) calls it the Boreal Sea, because the names I have mentioned point towards the north wind. Greek sailors call it Maurum; the Turks Maurethalassa, that is, the Black Sea; the Italians Mar Maggiore. Ammianus Marcellinus describes its situation thus, in book 22: "All its circuit, like an island's, is a coastal voyage measured at twenty-three thousand stades, as Eratosthenes affirms, and Hecataeus, and Ptolemy, and other most learned investigators of such matters. It is formed, by the agreement of all geographers, in the shape of a Scythian bow strung with its cord. Where the sun rises from the Eastern Ocean, it is closed off by the marshes of the Maeotis; where it sinks towards evening, it is bounded by Roman provinces; from there it looks up to the Bear constellation, and its inhabitants differ in languages and customs; its side towards the south slopes gently down." Isidore (book 13, chapter 16), from the histories of Sallust, says this sea is sweeter than others because of the number of rivers. So Seneca in the Medea, act 2: "Whatever the Phasis waters with its gentle windings, and whatever the Scythian Pontus sees behind its back, where the seas grow sweet with marsh waters."

units.la: Rationem reddit Ammianus, cujus jam memini. Verba, quod lectu digna, adscribam: Omnis autem circumfluo ambitu Pontus & nebulosus est, & dulcior æquoribus cæteris & vadosus; quod concresçit aer ex humorum spiramine, sæpe densatus & irruentium undarum multitudine temperatur, & consurgit in brevia dorsuosa; limum globosque aggerente multitudine circumvenientium fluentorum. Piscosus admodum est Pontus: cujus rei causæ: cum quod, præter Phocas, Thynnos & Delphinos, eosque non grandes & innoxios, belluas majores non patiatur, ut cum alijs Isidorus notat; notum autem rem tem Majoribus Minores esse plerumque escam, hosque ab illis devorari: tum quod ex vastiore pelago pisces minorum gentium eo, tamquam in tutum quemdam recessum, confluant ad profundendos foetus, aquarum adlecti partim suavitate, partim tranquillitate. Ammianus loco jam indicato: Et constat ab ultimis Nostri finibus maris agminatim ad hunc secessum pariendi gratia petere pisces, ut aquarum suavitate salubrius foetum educant, in receptaculis cavis, quae sunt ibi densissima, securi voracium belluarum: nihil enim in Ponto huiusmodi aliquando est visum, praeter innoxios Delphinas & parvos. Aelianus lib. ix. cap. lix. Ἰχθύες ἐστὶ πολλῶν γεννῶν τῇ θαλάττῃ σωτηρίᾳ κίκτηνται, ἡ καὶ λίμνῃ ἰσὰ. ὅταν μέλλωσι ἰχθύειν, ἐκπίπτουσι τὰ ἄλμης, καὶ τῶν κυμάτων τὸ ἀκλυσεῖ ὕδωρ ἀπαγαγὼν. Ἀ γαθὴ γὰρ αὐτοῖς ἡ τῶν ὑδάτων εἰρήνη λοχείαι ἰσχὺς ἐξ ἀπόδειξις, ἡ Φυλάξαι αὐτὸν τὴν ἀνεπιβούλευτα τῶν ἰχθύων τὰ ἐρεῖφη. Φιλάσπα δὲ ... Iam quod Color Aquae Pontice albus, de quo caussisque Aristoteles in Problemat. sect. xxiii, Theocritus Eidyll. xxiii, ἠφόεντα vocat. In Ponto Peninsula est nobilissima, quae Taurica vel Scythica Chersonesus; de qua alibi suo loco. Ad Occidentaliora (ubi & pars Ponti Hylaeum mare, ab Hylaea, Taurosycytharum regione) Isthmi, Carcinetes vocatur Sinus, Ammiano & Pomponio Mela sic nominantibus, καρκινῖτης Ptolemaeo; καρκινῖτης Arriano; καρκινῖτης Straboni, inemendatius; nam ab opido, quod Carcina hodieque ad ostia fluviorum Hypacyris & Gerrhi. Strabo lib vii, sinum hunc Tamaracen vocat à Promontorio, quod in eum ab Occasu Ortum versus procurrit. Periplum Euxini Ponti scripsit eleganter & docte Arrianus.
units.tr: Ammianus, whom I have already mentioned, gives the reason. I shall add his words, since they are worth reading: "The whole Pontus, with its surrounding circuit, is misty and sweeter than the other seas and shallow; this is because the air thickens from the breath of moisture, often condensed and tempered by the multitude of rushing waves, and it rises into ridged shallows, with the multitude of surrounding currents piling up silt and clods." The Pontus is very abundant in fish. The reasons for this are, first, that apart from the Phocae, tunnies and dolphins, and those not large or harmful, it allows no larger monsters, as Isidore notes along with others; and it is well known that for the greater creatures the smaller are mostly food, and are devoured by them. Second, fish of the smaller kinds flock there from the wider sea, as into a safe retreat, to lay their spawn, drawn partly by the sweetness of the waters and partly by their calm. Ammianus, in the passage already cited: "It is established that fish come in flocks from the furthest parts of our sea to this retreat to bear their young, seeking the sweetness of the waters, which nourish the young more healthily, in hollow hiding places, which are very dense there, safe from voracious monsters; for nothing of that kind has ever been seen in the Pontus, except harmless dolphins and small fish." Aelian, book 9, chapter 59: "Fish of many kinds, which possess safety in the sea, or in a lake likewise, when they are about to spawn, come out of the brine and draw away from the unquiet water of the waves. For peace of water is good for them, both for their strength in breeding and for guarding the young from the plotting of predatory fish." [Ἰχθύες ... ἰχθύων τὰ ἐρεῖφη.] Next, the colour of the water of the Pontus is white, concerning which Aristotle in the Problems (section 23) gives the causes, and Theocritus in Idyll 23 calls it ἠφόεντα. In the Pontus is the most famous peninsula, which is called the Taurica or Scythian Chersonese, about which I shall speak in its own place. Towards the west (where the part of the Pontus called the Hylaean Sea lies, named from Hylaea, the region of the Tauro-Scythians), the bay at the isthmus is called Carcinetes, as Ammianus and Pomponius Mela name it; Ptolemy calls it καρκινῖτης, Arrian καρκινῖτης, and Strabo, less correctly, καρκινῖτης; for it is named from the town of Carcina, which still stands at the mouths of the rivers Hypacyris and Gerrhus. Strabo (book 7) calls this bay Tamaraces from the promontory that juts out into it from the west towards the east. Arrian wrote an elegant and learned Periplus of the Euxine Pontus.

units.la: Succedit postremo Maeotis Palus, ab Maeotis populis apud Ptolemaeum & Pomponium Melam, qui hodie Tartarorum pars. Fretum ejus ad Orientaliora Peninsulae littora Bosporus Cimmerius vel Maeoticus, ter mille passuum latitudine. Ab Scythis vocatur haec Palus, ut notat Tzetza. καρπαλὴκ; & ut Plinius, Temerinda, addens hac voce Matrem Maris (ut eam etiam nominat Dionysius Alexandrinus) designari, quod perpetuo agmine defluat, numquam recurrens, aquas quasi subministrans absque intermissione subsequentibus, Euxino, Propontidi, Aegaeo, Magnoque Mari. Hinc est, quod Lucanus libro iii. de bello Pharsalico canat, imminui laudem immissi in terras ab Hercule, scissis montibus, Oceani; quum Mare Mediterraneum quibusdam videretur non tam oriri ex Oceano, quam ex Maeotide Palude, & Ponto Euxino, semper decurrentibus in Propontidem, & hinc porro in Pelagi Interni vastiora. Verba ejus haec: Quaque foetum torrens Maeotidas egerit undas Pontus, & Herculeis auferatur gloria metis, Oceanumque negat solas admittere Gades.
units.tr: Lastly comes the Maeotian Marsh, named after the Maeotian peoples by Ptolemy and Pomponius Mela, who are today a part of the Tartars. Its strait, towards the eastern shores of the peninsula, is the Cimmerian or Maeotian Bosporus, three thousand paces wide. The Scythians call this marsh, as Tzetzes notes, καρπαλὴκ; and Pliny calls it Temerinda, adding that by this word is meant the Mother of the Sea (as Dionysius of Alexandria also names it), because it flows down in an unbroken stream, never returning, and supplies its waters without interruption to the Euxine, the Propontis, the Aegean and the Great Sea. Hence Lucan in book 3 of the Civil War sings that the praise of the Ocean which Hercules let in upon the lands, by splitting the mountains, is diminished; since the Mediterranean seemed to some people to rise not so much from the Ocean as from the Maeotian Marsh and the Euxine Pontus, which always flow down into the Propontis and from there further into the vaster reaches of the inland sea. His words are these: "Where the Pontus, sending forth its waters, pours the Maeotian streams, and the glory of Hercules' pillars is taken away, and it denies that Gades alone admits the Ocean."

units.la: Sed vero similius, quod indicat Abrahamus Ortelius, nuper maximo reip. litterariae detrimento nobis sublatus, vocem quae apud Plinium, mere Germanicam esse, eaque significari Mari Finem, quum Meer Mare, Ende Finis, Et vero sive Het articulus sit, qui in vocis capite metathesi litterarum, quod non infrequens apud Germanos, scribitur. Non male. Nam Mari Mediterraneo, per fretum Herculeum immisso, Finis in Maeotide, ut quidem oculi nostri testantur. Caspio enim secretior est cum superioribus copula, ut jam parebit. Vera & genuina vocis scriptura forte Tesmerinda, ut sic quasi Das Meers Enda, ut Majores nostri pronunciabant. Hodie Mar Tanaich à Circassis (sic Tatrari Turcaeque vocant Sarmatiae Asiaticae populos, qui Plinio Ziga, Stephano ζυγὸι) nominatur: Italis Mar della Tana, ab Tanai fluvio, qui duobus ostiis huc influit: item Mar bianco, Mare album Palus haec non altior quinque; &, ubi profundissima, septem ulnis; habetque in ambitu septingenta, vel, ut alij, nongenta millia passuum. Videndi Polybius lib. iiii. & Strabo lib. ii. Ego scio circuitum ejus usque ad insulam in ostio Tanais esse centum nonaginta aut circiter milliar. Germanicorum, quorum singula xxxii. statuunt stadia. De Frigore Maeotico legendus Strabo lib. vii. dicitur adeo indurari gelu, ut vehicula super eam adcolae ducant. Lucanus lib. ii. belli Pharsal. ubi de gentibus ad bellum civile excitandis: quas tenet æquore denso Pigra Palus Scythici patiens Mæotica plaustri. Non adeo mirum. Mitiores tamen hiemes ibi, quam apud nos, quum Palus hæc ad gradus Altitudinis xlviii, xlix, l. & li, Auctores tam Romani, quam Græci externa: & quæ de quarundam Regionum malis atque incommodis auditu tantum intellexerant, intendere & verbis solent mirum quantum exaggerare: quod exemplis adductis probare, hominis sit ocio bono non bene utentis.
units.tr: But more likely is what Abraham Ortelius indicates, who was lately taken from us to the great loss of the republic of letters. He says that the word found in Pliny is purely German, and that it means Sea's End: Meer is sea, Ende end, and Et, or Het, is the article, which is written in the head of the word with a transposition of letters, something not uncommon among the Germans. He is not wrong. For the Mediterranean, let in through the Strait of Hercules, has its end in the Maeotis, as our own eyes indeed testify; for it is more remote from the upper waters by a link, as will appear. The true and genuine spelling of the word is perhaps Tesmerinda, so that it is as if Das Meers Enda, as our ancestors pronounced it. Today it is called Mar Tanaich by the Circassians (so the Tartars and Turks call the peoples of Asiatic Sarmatia, whom Pliny calls Ziga and Stephanus ζυγοί); by the Italians Mar della Tana, from the river Tanais, which flows into it by two mouths; and likewise Mar bianco, the White Sea. This marsh is not more than five fathoms deep, and where it is deepest, seven ells; it has a circuit of seven hundred or, as others say, nine hundred thousand paces. See Polybius book 4 and Strabo book 2. I know that its circuit as far as the island at the mouth of the Tanais is about one hundred and ninety German miles, each of which is reckoned at thirty-two stades. On the Maeotic cold, read Strabo book 7: it is said to be so hardened by frost that the inhabitants drive wagons over it. Lucan in book 2 of the Civil War, where he speaks of the peoples to be stirred up for civil war: "whom the sluggish Maeotian marsh holds in its dense sea, enduring the Scythian wagon." This is not so surprising. Yet the winters there are milder than with us, although this marsh lies at latitudes 48, 49, 50 and 51; Roman and Greek authors, and those who knew only by hearsay of the evils and discomforts of certain regions, are wont to stretch and exaggerate their words wonderfully. To prove this with examples would be the work of a man who does not make good use of his leisure.

units.la: Quæ commemoravi, Moribus conjungam non immerito Caspium; quod cum Euxino per occultos Cuniculos unum. Affirmate loquor. Alioqui pars sit Oceani Scythici, nec ne; diversa Veterum sententia. Ajunt Dionysius de situ orbis, Manilius lib. iv. Astronom. Plinius lib. vi. nat. histor. cap. xiii, Pomponius Mela lib. iii. cap. v, Orosius lib. i. cap. ii, Basilius ad cap. i. Genescos, & alij. Notat etiam Strabo lib. xi. Patroclem nobilem Scriptorem in ea fuisse sententia, ex India navigari posse ad Hircanos. Negat Herodotus lib. i. scribens Caspium alterum ac per se ipsum, Mare esse. Eiusdem mentis Aristotelis lib. ii. Meteoror. cap. i. Hos alij multi sequuti quorum princeps Ptolemæus in sua Geographia accuratioris locorum cognitionis beneficio. Ipse Strabo, nisi, ut notavit Vir magnus, planis expressisque verbis fallam subdidisset sententiam, potuisset absque negocio ex prioribus persuadere Lectori, credidisse se litoribus circumseptum Caspium exitu carere. Sic enim ait: κυκλῳ δὲ περὶ τὴν θάλατταν. Sed mox omnia corrumpit, & in aliam imprudens trahitur opinionem, illis præcipue verbis; τὸν Ὠκεανὸν τὴν πλησιόν τὴν Κάσπιον. Illud verum, Aquas Oceani Caspium excipere subterraneo meatu, & exonerari occultis sub terram alveis & cryptis in Euxinum. Quum enim maxima flumina Caspium influant (inter quæ ab Septemtrione, Rha, hodie Volga; & Rhymnus, Iaick; ab Ortu, Iaxartes, Chefel; à Meridie, Oxus, Abiamu; ab Occasu denique alia non pauca) necesse sane fuit infusa, præsertim quum marinas stationes Flumina naturaliter adpetant, aliqua exire. Nam qui recipiendis quotidie tot fluminum aquis alveus hujus maris suffecisset; hodieque sufficeret? Quæ igitur labuntur in Caspium voragine quadam subterranea ex illis carceribus recipiuntur in Pontum: qui etiam terræ conclusus per Hellesponti & Abydenorum freta in Archipelagum; inde per mediam Europam & Africam ad Herculeum fretum, qua patet exitus, decurrit. Mare Caspium, ut delineat Pomponius lib. iii, in tres sinus diffinditur: contra os ipsum & alvei fauces, in Hyrcanum, ubi Georgiani: ad sinistram versus Septemtrionem in Scythicum, qua parte Zibierairorum & Zagataiorum sunt Hordæ: ad dextram vel oram meridianam, qua nobilissima urbs Tauris, in eum, quem proprie & totius nomine Caspium à Caspijs ibi populis appellant; Parthis hodie à proximo opido Bacau. Georgianis Chelucelam. Aristoteles Caspium & Hyrcanum lib. ii, Meteorolog. duo Maria numerat; quum unius rei duo sint nomina. Plurimis alijs nominibus (quod & Plinius scribit) ab adcolis appellatum: Rhutenis & Tartaris hodie Chunalinsko-morie vocatur: Mauris Bahar Curfan, id est mare clausum, indicant quæ dixi; Georgiam dicitur ab Georgianis, qui quondam Iberes & Albani Asiæ populi: Ab alijs Mare de Sala, ab opido Tartariæ cognomine; Item Therbessam alijsque modis pro vario gentium idiomate vel regionibus illi adpositis, ut se observasse scribit ex tabulis & scriptis peregrinationibus V. CL. Abrahamus Ortelius. Variatur inter Auctores de Maris hujus magnitudine: inter eos Herodotus in Clio longitudinis esse tradit quindecim dierum cursu navis, quæ remis utatur; latitudinis, ubi spaciosissimum est, dierum octo. Fidendum magis, qui quotidie transmittunt, Mercatoribus, non amplius duodecim diebus universum expleri ambitum testantibus. In eo Mari Pisces, ut prodit Iulius Cæsar Scaliger de Subtilitate adversus Cardanum, exercitat. i. capiuntur Siluri, & Moroni; quos, vulgari nomine sic appellatos, non audet Glanios vel existimare vel negare: præterea Caniculæ, canino prorsum capite, cauda, pedibus: adhæc Piscis teres totus sine capitis exprella figura, longitudine circiter pedum quatuor: ex quo ad lucernarum usum exemtus adeps vices præstat olei, frequenti mercatu expetitus.
units.tr: I will rightly join Moscovy with the Caspian, which is connected to the Euxine by hidden channels. I state this positively. Otherwise, whether it is part of the Scythian Ocean is a matter on which the ancients disagreed. Dionysius in his On the Position of the World, Manilius in book 4 of the Astronomica, Pliny in book 6, chapter 13, of the Natural History, Pomponius Mela in book 3, chapter 5, Orosius in book 1, chapter 2, Basil on Genesis chapter 1, and others say that it is. Strabo, book 11, also notes that the noted writer Patrocles held the view that one can sail from India to the Hyrcanians. Herodotus, in book 1, denies that the Caspian is a sea in its own right and separate, and Aristotle, in book 2, chapter 1, of the Meteorologica, shares this opinion. Many others followed them, the chief of whom was Ptolemy in his Geography, thanks to a more accurate knowledge of places. Strabo himself, unless, as a great man has observed, he had subjoined an opinion contrary to his earlier words in plain and express terms, could easily have persuaded the reader from what he said earlier that he believed the Caspian, surrounded by shores, has no outlet. For he says: in a circle around the sea [κυκλῳ δὲ περὶ τὴν θάλατταν]. But soon afterwards he undoes everything, and, unwittingly, is drawn into another opinion, especially by these words: the Ocean, neighbouring the Caspian [τὸν Ὠκεανὸν τὴν πλησιόν τὴν Κάσπιον]. That is true: the waters of the Ocean are received by the Caspian through an underground passage and are discharged through hidden channels and caverns under the earth into the Euxine. For since the largest rivers flow into the Caspian (among which from the north are the Rha, today the Volga, and the Rhymnus, the Iaick; from the east the Iaxartes, the Chefel; from the south the Oxus, the Abiamu; and finally from the west a good many others), it was surely necessary that some outflow should occur, especially since rivers naturally seek out seas where they can discharge. For would the bed of this sea have sufficed to receive the waters of so many rivers every day, and would it suffice even now? Therefore what flows into the Caspian sinks into a kind of subterranean abyss and is received from those prisons into the Pontus. This, also enclosed by land, runs through the straits of the Hellespont and of Abydos into the Archipelago; then through the middle of Europe and Africa to the Pillars of Hercules, where its outlet lies open. The Caspian Sea, as Pomponius describes it in book 3, is divided into three bays. Opposite the mouth itself and the throat of the channel is the Hyrcanian bay, where the Georgians live. To the left, towards the north, is the Scythian bay, where the Hordes of the Zibierairi and Zagataians are. To the right, or on the southern shore, where the most noble city of Tauris lies, is the bay which is properly and by the name of the whole sea called the Caspian by the Caspian peoples there; by the Persians today it is called Bacau from the nearby town; by the Georgians, Chelucela. Aristotle, in book 2 of the Meteorologica, counts the Caspian and the Hyrcanian as two seas, although one thing has two names. It is called by many other names by its neighbours (as Pliny also writes): by the Russians and Tartars today it is called Chunalinsko-morie; by the Moors Bahar Curfan, that is, a closed sea. These names indicate what I have said. It is called Georgiam by the Georgians, who were formerly the Iberians and Albanians, peoples of Asia. By others it is called Mare de Sala, from a town of Tartary of the same name; likewise Therbessam, and in other ways according to the varied idiom of the peoples or the regions adjoining it, as the most distinguished Abraham Ortelius writes that he observed from maps and written accounts of travellers. Authors differ about the size of this sea. Among them Herodotus, in Clio, says that its length is a fifteen days' journey for a ship that uses oars, and its breadth, where it is widest, eight days'. More trust should be placed in those who cross it every day, the merchants, who testify that the whole circuit is completed in no more than twelve days. In this sea fish are caught, as Julius Caesar Scaliger reports in his On Subtlety against Cardano, exercise 1: sheatfish and moroni, which, being called by these common names, he does not dare either to identify with the glanis or to deny that they are such. There are also little dogfish, with the head, tail and feet of a dog; and a smooth fish entirely without a distinct head, about four feet long. From this fish, when it is taken out, the fat serves in place of oil for lamps and is eagerly sought in frequent trade.

units.la: CAP. VIII. De reliquis Internis Maribus.
units.tr: CAP. VIII. Of the other Internal Seas.

units.la: PRæter Mediterrancum illud (quod optimo jure Magnum, quum si commissio fiat, reliqua non tam Maria, quam Sinus, censenda) & alia sunt Interna, quæ per sua Freta terras irrumpunt ex Oceano; Orientali quidem, Persicum & Rubrum; Septemtrionali vero, Balticum.
units.tr: Besides that Mediterranean (which by the best right is called the Great Sea, since if it is compared with the rest, they should be reckoned not so much seas as gulfs), there are other Internal Seas, which force their way into the lands through straits from the Ocean: on the east, the Persian and the Red; on the north, the Baltic.

units.la: Persicum inter Persiam est, unde illi nomen, & Arabiam Felicem: primo Sinus (ut & multis habetur) quem inter Promontorium Asoborum (hodie Cabo Mochandan) & Armuziam (Ormus nunc, nobilissimum in Insula ferace Emporium) excipit Fretum, quod vulgo Basora: mox Mare, quod etiam Plutarcho in vita Luculli Babylonium, ab urbe Mesopotamiæ versus Caurum illi adlocata, quam Bagdet hodie dicunt, ad Euphratem. Mar Fleatif & Mesendin vulgo nominari testantur Tabulæ Geographicæ. Tumach-cama ab Mesopotamijs vocari, ab aliis item Bein elnaharin, scribit vel fingit potius Thevetus; quem non in Geographicis tantum, sed & alijs familiariter aliquando Parisius novi, & mecum alij, fluxissimæ fidei. Semel hoc dicendum erat, Lector: ne, si passim non laudem, a me negligentia factum arbitrere.
units.tr: The Persian lies between Persia, from which it takes its name, and Arabia Felix. First comes the gulf (as many also hold), which the strait commonly called Basora receives between the promontory of the Asoborae (today Cabo Mochandan) and Armuzia (now Ormus, a most noble trading-place on a fertile island). Then comes the sea, which Plutarch in the Life of Lucullus also calls the Babylonian, after the city of Mesopotamia lying to the northwest of it, on the Euphrates, which they today call Bagdet. Geographical tables testify that it is commonly named Mar Fleatif and Mesendin. Thevet writes, or rather invents, that the Mesopotamians call it Tumach-cama, and others Bein elnaharin. I once knew him well in Paris, not only in geographical matters but otherwise too, and others with me found him of most fluid faith. This had to be said once, reader, so that you do not think I was negligent if I fail to praise him everywhere.

units.la: Rubrum id: specialiore notione, (κατ' ἐξοχὴν) Europæis hodie, quod olim Arabicus Sinus, Plinio scribente lib. nat. historiæ II, cap. LXVII & sequente; inter Arabiam Felicem & Africam. Sinus primo, ubi ad dextram Aden urbs, olim Arabia: deinde Fretum, quod nostro tempore Babelmandel. hinc Mare, quod ab adcolis hodie Mar di Mecha, ab Arabiæ Felicis urbe, quæ μεγάλη Ptolemæo; ab alijs Mar Rosso. Sunt qui scribunt appellari etiam Tohar-Corsun, Mare clausum; quod Caspio verius convenit. Thevetus, nisi, quod plerumque solet, nugas (quibus hoc lucratus, ut nusquam fidem mereatur) vendat, ab Arabibus vocari notat Zocoroph vel Beharzocoroph; ab alijs Zahara. סוּף mare Caricosum passim in Sacris litteris: סוּף enim lunci genus, crescentis in extremitatibus Maris vel Fluminis: unde ים־סוף Mare Caricis, quod eo lunci genere abundet. Stephano Βεγγα dicitur. De Persico & Arabico Internis junctim Manilius lib. IV. Astronomic. Altera sub medium Solem duo bella per undas Intulit Oceanus Terris. Nam Persica fluctus Arva tenet, titulum Pelagi prædatus ab ysdem, Qua rigat ipse, locis; latoque infunditur Orbi. Nec procul in molles Arabas, Terramque ferentem Delicias, variaque novos radicis odores, Leniter adfundit gemmantia littora Pontus, Et Terra Mare nomen habet.
units.tr: The Red Sea, in its more special sense (κατ' ἐξοχὴν [kat' exochēn]), is what Europeans today call it; formerly it was the Arabicus Sinus, as Pliny writes in Natural History book II, chapter LXVII and following, between Arabia Felix and Africa. First there is the gulf, where Aden, a city once in Arabia, lies on the right. Then comes the strait, which in our time is Babelmandel. Then comes the sea, which the inhabitants today call Mar di Mecha, after the city of Arabia Felix that Ptolemy calls μεγάλη [megalē], and others call Mar Rosso. Some write that it is also called Tohar-Corsun, the closed sea, a name that suits the Caspian more truly. Thevet, unless he is selling trifles, as he usually does (by which he has gained that he never deserves belief), notes that the Arabs call it Zocoroph or Beharzocoroph, and others Zahara. In Sacred letters it is frequently called the Sea of Reeds: sof [סוּף] is a kind of reed growing at the edges of a sea or river, whence yam-suf [ים־סוף], the Sea of Reeds, because it abounds in that kind of reed. Stephanus calls it Βεγγα [Bengga]. Manilius, in book IV of the Astronomica, describes the Persian and Arabian together: the Ocean brought two wars upon the lands beneath the middle sun. For the Persian waves hold the fields, having taken the name of the sea from the same places which they water, and pour themselves into the wide world. Not far off, the sea gently pours its gem-bright shores upon the soft Arabians and the land that bears delights and the fragrant odours of many new roots, and the land takes its name from the sea.

units.la: Balticum (ut appellat Xenophon; vel, ut alij, Baltæum, unde Belts hodie, præcipue prope Insulam Langlandiam, ubi Lagnus Sinus Plinio lib. nat. histor. IIII, cap. XIII.) id mihi; quod angustiore primum & sinuoso ore Caput Cimbricæ Chersonnesi prægressum, factis aliquot Danorum Insulis, per Sundam, nobilissimum Daniæ Fretum (ubi quondam Baunos Ptolemæi) infunditur versus Orientem; inter hinc Germaniæ, Prussiæ, Lituaniæ, Livoniæ, Russiaque, inde Gothiæ & Sueciæ littora: Morimaruza Philemoni; Amalchium Hecatæo apud Plinium: Suevicum à populis, qui adhabitant; Pigrum nominat Tacitus, quod non, ut bene Ortelius, veluti cetera Maria, moveatur. Nam Aestus ejus, quod etiam qui quotidie navigant, testantur, vix deprehenditur. Venedicus Sinus eidem ab Venedis populis; Codanus Plinio lib. IV, cap. XIII, & Pomponio Melæ lib. III. Germanis Oost-zee; quod Oceano versus Ortum: Rutenis Warezkovic-morie. Excurrens porro in duo brachiæ dispescitur: faciens à sinistra: inter hinc Sueciam & Boddiam, inde Finlandiam Sinum prius Finnicum, Finnisch-zee; post, freto discriminante, Boddicum, Bodner zee: à dextra inter Finlandiam & Livoniam alium, qui item Finnicus. Alia minorum gentium prætereo:
units.tr: The Baltic (as Xenophon calls it; or, as others do, Baltaeum, whence the Belts today, especially near the island of Langeland, where Pliny's Lagnus Sinus lies, Natural History book IV, chapter XIII) is, to my mind, a sea which first enters through a narrower and winding mouth, passing the head of the Cimbric Chersonese, with several islands of the Danes lying in its path, and through the Sound, the most famous strait of Denmark (where once stood Ptolemy's Baunos), it pours itself out towards the east. Between it and the shores of Germany, Prussia, Lithuania, Livonia and Russia on one side, and those of Gothia and Sweden on the other, lie: Morimaruza, according to Philemon; Amalchium, according to Hecataeus in Pliny; and Suevicum from the peoples who dwell there. Tacitus calls it Pigrum, the sluggish, because it is not moved as the other seas are, as Ortelius rightly notes. For its tide, as even those who sail on it every day testify, is scarcely perceived. The same sea is called the Venedicus Sinus, from the Veneti; the Codanus in Pliny, Natural History book IV, chapter XIII, and in Pomponius Mela, book III. The Germans call it Oost-zee, because it lies toward the east of the Ocean; the Russians Warezkovic-morie. Running further out, it divides into two arms. The one on the left, between Sweden and Bothnia on one side and Finland on the other, forms first the Finnicum gulf, called Finnisch-zee, and then, separated by a strait, the Boddicum, called Bodner zee. On the right, between Finland and Livonia, it forms another, which is likewise the Finnicus. I pass over the other smaller parts.

units.la: Album, quod Arctoum Pelagus Terris immittit inter Russiam, Moscovitarumque & Lapporum fines: ad cuius interiora Fanum D. Nicolai, quo plerumque cum Moscovitis commercia facturi Mercatores nostri adpellunt. Witte-zee Batavis, qui plurimum hoc Mare navigant, appellatur.
units.tr: The Album, which the Arctic sea pours into the lands, lies between Russia and the borders of the Muscovites and the Lapps. Near its inner parts is the shrine of St. Nicholas, where our merchants, who are about to trade with the Muscovites, usually put in. The Dutch, who sail this sea most, call it Witte-zee.

units.la: Illud etiam non magni præ ceteris momenti, quod inter Americam & Mexicanam primis lustratoribus Mar Vermejo nominatum.
units.tr: This also, though not of great importance compared with the others, is worth noting: between America and Mexico it was named Mar Vermejo by the first explorers.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: De Euripis.
units.tr: Of the Euripus.

units.la: MARIBVS Reciprocantibus addiderim Furipos. Εὔριπος, inquit Sudas, νίλαγος ἐστὶν; ἥ πττ ὑδατώδης μεταξὺ δυο χωρῶν, τὴν τῆς Βοιωτίας, καὶ Αἰτικῆς. ἐπέχως δὲ τὰς ἡμέρας τὸ ἱκανὸν ὕδωρ τρεπόμενον. Describit mare, quod inter Atticam & Euboeam, Euboicus Euripus aliis, nonnullis Chalcidicus ab urbe Chalcide, Italis Strecho de Negroponte; sic enim illis hodie Euboea dicitur. De eo sic Pomponius Mela lib. II. cap. VII. Mare rapidum, & alterno cursu septies die ac septies nocte, fluctibus invicem versis, adeo immodice fluens, ut ventos etiam ac plenis velis navigia frustretur. Strabo tamen lib. IX, Plinius lib II. cap. XCVII, & alij (quibus adscribendus fortean & Sudas) tantum die ac noctu simul septies fluere contendunt. Sic Seneca in Hercule Octæo, Act. II. Sc. I. profugë: Euboica tellus, vertice immenso tumens, Pulsatur omni parte; Phryxeum mare Scindit Capharcus: servit hoc Austro latus; At qua nivosi patitur Aquilonis minas, Euripus undas flectit instabi is vagas, Septemque cursus flectit & totidem refert, Dum lassum Titan mergat Oceano jubar.
units.tr: To the reciprocating seas I would add the Furipos (Euripus). Suidas says: "The Euripus is a sea-channel, or a watery passage between two regions, Boeotia and Attica; the sufficient water is held back for the days and turned round" [Εὔριπος νήλαγος ἐστίν· ἢ πηγὴ ὑδατώδης μεταξὺ δύο χωρῶν, τῆς Βοιωτίας καὶ Ἀττικῆς· ἐπέχεται δὲ τὰς ἡμέρας τὸ ἱκανὸν ὕδωρ τρεπόμενον]. He describes the sea that lies between Attica and Euboea, which some call the Euboicus Euripus, others the Chalcidicus after the city of Chalcis, and the Italians the Strecho de Negroponte, for so Euboea is called today. Pomponius Mela says of it (book 2, chapter 7): The sea is rapid, and with an alternating current, flowing back and forth seven times by day and seven times by night, its waves turned against each other, so immoderately that it defeats even the winds and ships under full sail. Strabo (book 9), Pliny (book 2, chapter 97) and others (perhaps Suidas too) maintain that it ebbs and flows only seven times in the day and night together. So Seneca in the Hercules Oetaeus, Act 2, Scene 1, speaks: The land of Euboea, swelling with its immense peak, is beaten on every side; the Phrixean sea is cut by Capharus; the flank of this sea serves the south wind; but where it suffers the threats of the snowy north, the Euripus bends its restless wandering waves, and it bends seven courses and turns back as many, until the Sun sinks his weary light in the ocean.

units.la: Antiphilus Byzantius quodam Epigrammate senarium prodit numerum: Εὔβοια κλήμις παλιώδινη θάλασσα, Πλαγκτὴν ὕδωρ, ἰδίως ῥέμασιν αὐτὴ παλον, Ἡ ἡλίῳ κήν νυκτὴ πτερυμόν, ἐς τέλος ἀπίγεν Ναυσὶν ἐσὼν πτεροῖς χείμα δαιέζωμεν, Θαῦμα βίω, ἑαυβώ σὺ τὸ μυγλον, ἰδὲ μαχόμω Σλῶ ςίσιν. ἀρρήτω ταῦτα μέμηλε Φύσει.
units.tr: Antiphilus of Byzantium, in a certain epigram, sets out the number six: "Euboea, the rocky sea of the Euripus, wandering, moved by its own rushing, the sun and night, a sign of the sea, to the end it moves; with ships and sails we make the storm; a wonder to life, let it be, and it is hard to fight with the wind; these things are a care to unclear nature." [Εὔβοια κλήμις παλιώδινη θάλασσα ... ἀρρήτω ταῦτα μέμηλε φύσει]

units.la: Alium alij. Ab omnibus, nisi mens mea me fallit, certus numerus positus pro incerto. Livius lib. xxxviii veritatis, quam superiores, convenientius, Fretum ipsum, inquit, Euripi sen septies die, sicut fama fert, temporis vus flatus reciprocat; sed temere in modum venti nunc huc nunc illuc, verso mari, velut monte præcipiti devolutus torrens, rapitur. Videndus & Thucydides lib. vi. Caussam huius Fluxus & Refluxus quum nequisset adsequi Aristoteles, mœrore contabuisse scribitur ab Iustino Philosopho & Martyre Admonitor ad Gentes, & Gregorio Nazianzeno oratione 1. in Iulianum Apostatam. Hinc certe Proverbium, ut Euripo dicatur mutabilius, quidquid instabile. Aeschines Κτησιφῶντ, Calliam mutabiliorem esse notat Euripo, cui vicinus. Eleganter & Plato in Phædone: πάντα τὰ ὄντα ἀπχνῶς ὥσπερ ἐν Εὐρίπῳ ἄνω καὶ κάτω φέρεται. ἐ χρόνου ἐδίνα ἐν ἐδένι μηδ. Aristoteles Ethic. ix. cap. vi. ἐ μεταβολὴ ὥσπερ Εὔριπος. Committit & eleganter M. Tullius oratione pro Mur. cum Euripi fluxu & refluxu inconstantiam populi & incertam Comitiorum rationem. Instabilis enim Euripus; & inde inter ἀδιάνατα apud Senecam in Hercule Octæo, Act. II. Sc.III: — prius Exstinguet ortus, referet occasus, diem: Pax ante fida nivibus & flammis erit: Et Scylla Siculum jungat Ausonio latus: Priusque multo vicilius alternis fugax Euripus, unda flabit Euboica piger.
units.tr: Others give other numbers. Of all of them, unless my memory deceives me, a certain number is put in place of an uncertain one. Livy (book 38) states the truth more fittingly than the earlier writers: The strait itself, the Euripus, as report has it, is turned back by the tide and the winds seven times a day; but rashly, in the manner of a wind, now here, now there, with the sea turned over, it is carried along like a torrent rushing down a steep mountain. Thucydides (book 6) should also be consulted. Aristotle, not being able to grasp the cause of this ebb and flow, is said by Justin the Philosopher and Martyr (in his Address to the Greeks) and by Gregory Nazianzen (Oration 1 against Julian the Apostate) to have pined away from grief. Hence the proverb that whatever is unstable is said to be "more changeable than the Euripus." Aeschines, in his speech against Ctesiphon, notes that Callias is more changeable than the Euripus, which lies near him. Plato too says elegantly in the Phaedo: all things are carried up and down as in the Euripus [πάντα τὰ ὄντα ἀπὸ ... ὥσπερ ἐν Εὐρίπῳ ἄνω καὶ κάτω φέρεται]. Aristotle (Nicomachean Ethics, book 9, chapter 6) says: change is like the Euripus [ἡ μεταβολὴ ὥσπερ Εὔριπος]. Marcus Tullius, in his speech for Murena, elegantly compares the fickleness of the people and the uncertain nature of the assemblies with the ebb and flow of the Euripus. The Euripus is indeed unstable; and hence, among the impossibilities in Seneca's Hercules Oetaeus, Act 2, Scene 3: Sooner shall the rising sun be quenched, the setting sun bring back the day; peace shall be kept faithfully between snows and flames; Scylla shall join the Sicilian and the Ausonian flank; and sooner the Euripus, restless in its alternating flow, shall blow with the slow Euboean wave.

units.la: Euripus Tauromenitanus Plinio lib. II. cap. XCVII. illa maris reciprocatio, in quam delabi ferunt Charybdim; quæ, vorticosum mare inter Siciliam & Italiam in freto Mamertino, Garofaro dicitur hodie, Fazello & Arctio notantibus. Exaudiendus de eo Seneca in Epistolis, Charybdis an respondeat fabulis, perscribi mihi desidero: & si forte observaris (dignum est autem quod observes) fac nos certiores, utrum uno tantum vento agatur in vortices, an omnis tempestas mare illud contorqueat; & an verum sit, quidquid illo freti turbine arreptum est, per multa millia trahi, & circa Tauromini anum littus emergere.
units.tr: The Euripus of Taormina, in Pliny (book 2, chapter 97), is that reciprocation of the sea into which they say Charybdis sinks; this whirling sea between Sicily and Italy, in the Strait of Messina, is called Garofaro today, as Fazello and Arctius note. Seneca's letters should be heard on this matter: I want it fully written out to me whether Charybdis answers to the fables; and if perhaps you observe it (and it is worth observing), let us know whether the whirlpools are driven by one wind only, or whether every storm twists that sea; and whether it is true that whatever is caught up in the whirl of that strait is carried along for many miles and comes to the surface near the shore of Taormina.

units.la: Euripos quatuor, vastissimis Insulis interpositis, sub Arctico polo comminisci fuit author quidam Minorita Anglus Oxoniensis, Mathematicus, ut scribit in suo Itinerario Iacobus Cnoxen Buloducensis: eosque tanto impetu versus Voraginem, quae ad Euriporum concursus, (ubi & Rupem sub ipso Polo nigram statuit, cuius ambitus xxxiii circiter leucarum) rapi, ut naves semel ingressae vento retrogi non possint: neque unquam tantum ibi ventum esse, ut molae frumentariae circumagendae sufficiat. Alia ejus praetereo. Hunc sequuti temere sunt alii; inter quos Giraldus Cambrensis libro de Mirabilibus Hiberniae; qui addit, ad Voraginem hanc omnes undique ab remotissimis orbis partibus marinos fluctus, tamquam ex condicto, confluere, & in secreta Naturae penetralia se transfundentes quasi in Abyssum vorari; naves hac forte transeuntes tanta rapi & attrahi fluctuum violentia, ut eas statim irrevocabiliter vis voracitatis absorbeat. Additur, ne quid desideremus ad plenam loci stupendi cognitionem, Ostiorum, quae singulis Euripis, numerus: septem illi, qui freto Anano obversus; quinque, qui Septemtrionaliora Novae Zemblae respicit, ea autem propter angustiam & celerem cursum numquam congelari; tria, qui Groenlandiae vicinus; quatuor denique, qui proxime succedit: omnibus vero Ostiis initia describuntur ad gradum lxxviii. Belle mehercules. Tam adeveranter de his differunt, quasi vel ibi nati educatique, vel eo delati suis oculis omnia fideliter & diligenter notassent; Rupem etiam mensi. Si loco tam mirando nati; non video, quibus adminiculis quarumque Aquarum beneficio venerint ad nos, tantam περιφυσικῶν nunciaturi: quum Fluctus ex quatuor Orbis partibus, ut dicunt, eo se rapientes tanta vehementia obnitantur, & ventus ibi numquam tam validus, ut molae versandae (qui vero navi huc inde contra Fluctus reluctantes promovendae?) sufficiat. Sin eo delati, magna certe praerogativa munitos fuisse necesse fuit, quod adeuntes horrida, tetra & inaccessa loca, non fuerint cum navibus, ut omnibus evenire volunt, absorpti; at placidissime portati ita Rupi adhaeserint, ut non solum ejus colorem cognoscere, verum & magnitudinem metiri potuerint. Sistebat, credo, terribilis ille Aquarum raptus; dum ibi docenda nos illi discebant: ne scilicet quid quod uspiam in rerum natura nesciremus. Sed abesto jocus, & vana vanis relinquamus. Quisquis fuit primus hujus commenti auctor, amicus fuit non Veritatis, sed Platonis. Hic namque, quum excogitare non valeret veram Fluxus Refluxusque Maris causam, in Phaedone somniavit, χάσμα esse μέγιστον, καὶ ἀξιομνήστον, πηγὴ ἀρῶν δὲ ὅλης τῆς γῆς; ejus mentionem facere Homerum.
units.tr: A certain English Minorite of Oxford, a mathematician, invented four Euripi, with the most vast islands placed between them, beneath the Arctic pole, as James Cnoxen of Buloduc writes in his Itinerary. These, he says, are drawn with such force towards an abyss, which lies where the Euripi meet (and he places there a black rock beneath the very pole, with a circuit of about thirty-three leagues), that ships once caught in them cannot be turned back by the wind; and that there has never been so much wind there as would suffice to turn a grain mill. I pass over his other claims. Others have rashly followed him, among them Giraldus Cambrensis in his book on the Marvels of Ireland. He adds that to this abyss all the sea waves from the most remote parts of the world flow together as if by agreement, pouring themselves into the secret recesses of Nature and being swallowed up as into an abyss; that ships passing by chance are seized and drawn in by such violence of the waves that the force of the vortex irrevocably swallows them at once. To leave nothing lacking for a full knowledge of this astonishing place, he adds the number of mouths of each Euripus: seven of them face the strait of Anian, five look toward the more northern parts of Nova Zembla (which, because of their narrowness and swift current, never freeze), three lie near Greenland, and finally four lie next to these; and the beginnings of all these mouths are described at the seventy-eighth degree. Splendid, by heaven! They differ about these things so confidently, as if they had been born and brought up there, or had been carried there and had noted everything faithfully and diligently with their own eyes; they have even measured the rock. If they were born in so marvellous a place, I do not see by what aids, or by the help of what waters, they came to us to announce such περιφυσικά (marvels beyond nature); since the waves, as they say, rushing there from the four quarters of the world, struggle against each other with such violence, and the wind there is never strong enough to turn a mill (but what of the ship, pushed here and there against the waves that resist it?). But if they were carried there, they must certainly have been protected by some great privilege, since, going to such horrid, foul and inaccessible places, they were not swallowed up with their ships, as they wish to make it happen to everyone; rather, carried most gently, they clung to the rock so that they could know not only its colour but also measure its size. That terrible rush of waters, I suppose, stopped for them while they taught us these things, so that we should not be ignorant of anything that exists in nature. But let the joke be off, and let us leave vain things to the vain. Whoever was the first author of this fiction was a friend not of Truth but of Plato. For Plato, when he could not devise the true cause of the ebb and flow of the sea, dreamed in the Phaedo that there is a very great chasm, and one worth remembering, which is the source of all waters of the whole earth; and he says that Homer makes mention of it.

units.la: τὰς μὲν γὰρ ἐξ βάθιστον ἀπὸ χθονὸς εἰς Βέρεθρον
units.tr: For from the deepest depth below the earth into the pit [τὰς μὲν γὰρ ἐξ βάθιστον ἀπὸ χθονὸς εἰς Βέρεθρον]

units.la: alibi vero Homerum aliosque Poetas hoc χάσμα Ταρτάρον appellare; ad hiatum denique illum omnes fluvios, atque adeo totum Aquarum corpus universae Terrae circumfusum, confluere, & ex eo Aquas omnes vicissim effluere: surlumque ad nos motas, deorsum autem ad Antipodas Rheumatibus effusionem facere. Sed hanc Platonis (cuius Eloquentiam & Orationis flumen magis saepe mirari venerarique soleo, quam Philosophiam) opinionem, quod absurda esset & omni careret ratione, merito refutat Aristoteles lib. ii. Meteor. cap. ii; cujus Argumenta legenda. Docuerunt & haec falsa esse, nuper Argonautae nostri; qui ad lxxx. Altitudinis gradum delati, nullas Aquarum versus loca, quae ad perpendiculum Polo subjacent, attractiones, quales foede finguntur, deprehenderunt; quum tamen initium attrahendi in pictis ad illorum mentem tabulis scribatur ad gradum lxxviii. Alioquin videri sub ipso Polo habitationes esse commodiores, quam quae aliquot inde gradibus propiores Aequinoctiali, jam dixi; & dicam plenius, ubi ad istorum locorum historiam mea me deduxerit Methodus.
units.tr: Elsewhere Homer and other poets call this chasm Tartarus [χάσμα Ταρτάρον]; and that all rivers, and indeed the whole body of waters surrounding the whole earth, flow together into that gaping hole, and from it all waters flow out again in turn, rising up to us and, downwards, pouring out to the Antipodes through subterranean channels. But this opinion of Plato's (whose eloquence and flow of speech I am more often wont to admire and venerate than his philosophy) Aristotle rightly refutes, because it is absurd and lacks all reason (Meteorology, book 2, chapter 2), and his arguments should be read. Our own Argonauts, recently, have also shown these things to be false: they were carried to the eightieth degree of altitude, and there they found no attractions of the waters towards the places which lie directly beneath the pole, such as are foully invented; yet in the maps drawn according to their judgement, the beginning of the attraction is marked at the seventy-eighth degree. Otherwise, I have said already that habitations directly under the pole seem more convenient than those a few degrees nearer the equator; and I shall say more fully when my method leads me to the history of those places.

units.la: Cap. X.
units.tr: Chapter X.

units.la: De Aquis perpetuo defluentibus.
units.tr: On Waters That Flow Perpetually.

units.la: SVFFICIANT hæc de Aquis, quæ reciproco motu agitantur; historia succedit earum, quæ perpetuo defluunt: eo numero sunt Fontes, Fluvii, Rivi, Torrentes, & id genus aliæ; quæ gravitate sua per declivia feruntur, donec tandem in mare se exonerant.
units.tr: So much for the waters that move with a back-and-forth motion. The account now turns to those that flow on without ceasing. These include springs, rivers, streams, torrents and similar kinds, which are carried down slopes by their own weight until at last they discharge themselves into the sea.

units.la: Fons Isidoro lib.xiii. Originum, cap.xxi, caput aquæ nascentis: quasi fundens aquas. Fluvius perennis aquarum, quæ in unum alveum ex variis fontibus confluctæ, decursus; Flumen ipsa aqua; Gurges altus in eo locus. Rivus fluviolus perennis, natura & arte coactus; sic dictus, quod diriveretur ad irrigandum, id est inducendum aquas agris. Torrens fluentum non perenne; quod æstate exsiccari solitum, augeri vero solutarum nivium aut ingruentium imbrium accessione: à torrendo, ut idem Isidorus notat, laudans hoc Pacuvii: Flammeo vapore Torrens torret.
units.tr: Isidore, in the thirteenth book of the Origins, chapter 21, says that a spring is the head of water as it rises, as if it were pouring out waters. A river is a perennial flow of water gathered from various springs into a single channel; a stream is the water itself; a whirlpool is a deep place within it. A brook is a small perennial stream, made by nature or constrained by art; it is so called because it is diverted [derivatur] to irrigate, that is, to lead water onto the fields. A torrent is a stream that does not flow perennially: it is accustomed to dry up in summer and to swell from melted snows or the onset of storms. It is named from torrere, "to scorch," as Isidore also notes, quoting the line of Pacuvius: "The torrent scorches with a fiery vapour."

units.la: Amnis fluvius nemore ac frondibus redimitus; ab amœnitate Isidoro: alijs ab ambiendo: unde & Tiberim à quibusdam Amnem volunt appellatum, quod, docente Varrone, Romam ambiret; falso. Numquam enim ambijt Vrbem, sed adluit: nisi Ambire viro docto non totum circumire, sed partem tantum.
units.tr: An amnis is a river fringed with groves and foliage; Isidore derives the name from its pleasantness, while others derive it from ambire, "to go round." Some for this reason claim that the Tiber was also called Amnis, because, as Varro teaches, it flows around Rome; but this is false. For it never went round the city, but only washed past it; unless "to go round" in the learned sense means not to circle the whole thing, but only a part of it.

units.la: Veterum Philosophorum, qui aliquin Physicæ in dias luminis auras efferendæ singularem navarunt operam, illa semper fuit, estque hodie opinio; decurrentes jugiter aquas generari ab Aere vel Vapore calido & humido; quem, adiuvante loci natura, per Terræ poros receptum, & in ejusdem cavernis coactum, ibi volunt in Aquam ab circumstante Frigore sensim converti. Multas enim ajunt passim esse sub terra concavitates; in quas, quum natura non patiatur Vacuum, Aerem per meatus & poros necesse est ingredi; qui condensatus loci frigore in Aquam abit: ideoque Fontes esse perennes & perpetuos, quum caulla sit illis perpetua, Aere Frigoreque, à quibus generantur, numquam deficientibus. Seneca: Subterra quidquid est, quod illum in Aquam convertat, id semper est umbra perpetua, frigus æternum, inexercitata densitas: semper ergo præbebit perennes caussas Fontium. Hæc Aristotelis (qui contradicendi studio sæpe totus in Antiquorum Placitis, quamvis ea bona solidaque, convellendis) lib. ii. Meteor. cap. ii; hæc, qui eum sequuti, (videndi Seneca lib. iii. nat. quæstionum, Georgius Agricola de ortu & caus. Subterran. i, Antonius Galataeus de fluminum origine, & alij) de generatione decurrentium perpetuo Aquarum mens; cui enervandæ non pauca. Ut alia omittam: qui quæso fieri potest, ut Aer sive Vapor, intra Terræ Venas receptus, tanta corrumpatur celeritate, quanta fluunt Aquæ? Nam si vel momento μεταμόρφωσις illa fieret, quidquid in rerum natura est, Aeris, quem suapte natura scimus rarissimum; numquam ad eam Aquarum, quæ vel uno die fluunt, molem emoliendam sufficeret; neque altissimi Oceani gurgites, si vacuarentur, tantam Aquarum vim caperent. Certe infinita Fluviorum multitudo, quæ tot jam sæculis infinitam Aquarum copiam in Oceanum infundit, jampridem elementarem hanc Mundi partem Aquis obruisset, ac Cœlestes orbes attigisset; quum vel continui quadraginta dierum imbres tantas olim eluviones effuderint, ut Aquæ Montes altissimos, cubitis quindecim superarent. Divinior itaque, & naturæ legibus consentanea magis, hac de re sententia Philosophorum; qui decurrentes Aquas ab Oceano, Terræ meatus quibus percolatur, subeunte; & nunc in planis patentibusque campis coacto, nunc versus editissimorum montium juga (quo modo, consulendus Iulius Cæsar Scaliger de Subtilitate, exercit. xlvi.) per concavas speluncarum altitudines variasque terrarum (sua etiam gravitate prementium) venas exilientes: sicque rursus, unde venerat, refluente dirivari censuerunt; & inde esse, quod Maria (quum quæ data recipiant, receptaque mox reddant) nec augeant, nec minuantur. Sic Plato, Philo de Mundi opificio, Seneca lib. iii. Nat. quæst. cap. ix, & nostri temporis alij: subscribentes arcanis Hebræorum Dogmatibus. Ecclesiastes cap. i: Omnia flumina intrant in mare; & mare non redundat: redundat: ad locum, unde exeunt, flumina revertuntur, ut iterum fluant: quibus consona Homeri illa, de Oceano loquentis: Ε᾽ ξ ὕπερ πάντης Ποταμοὶ, καὶ πῆγαι Θάλασσα, Καὶ πηγαὶ Κρήνη, ἡ Φρέατα μάκρα ταῦτα.
units.tr: The ancient philosophers, who took especial pains to bring natural philosophy out into the light of day, always held, and the opinion is still held today, that flowing waters are generated from air or warm, moist vapour. They hold that this vapour, aided by the nature of the place, is drawn in through the pores of the earth, gathered in its hollows, and there gradually turned into water by the surrounding cold. They say that there are everywhere many hollows beneath the earth, and since nature does not tolerate a vacuum, air must necessarily enter them through passages and pores. This air, condensed by the cold of the place, turns into water. For this reason, they say, springs are perennial and perpetual, since the cause is constant: the air and cold from which they are generated never fail. Seneca: Whatever is beneath the earth that turns air into water is always in perpetual shade, eternal cold, and unvarying density; it will therefore always supply the perennial causes of springs. This is the view of Aristotle (who, in his eagerness to contradict, often overturned the opinions of the ancients, even sound and solid ones), Meteor. ii, chap. ii. The same view, held by those who followed him (see Seneca, Nat. quaest. iii; Georgius Agricola, De ortu et causis subterraneorum i; Antonius Galateus, De fluminum origine; and others), is the opinion about the generation of rivers that flow perpetually. Not a few arguments can be brought against it. To leave aside others: how can it be that air or vapour, received into the veins of the earth, is changed so quickly as the waters flow? For if that transformation took place in a moment, whatever air there is in nature (which we know by its own nature to be very rare) would never be enough to produce the mass of water that flows in a single day; nor would the deepest gulfs of the ocean, even if they were emptied, hold so great a volume of water. Certainly the infinite multitude of rivers, which for so many ages has poured an infinite quantity of water into the ocean, would long ago have overwhelmed this elemental part of the world with water and reached the heavenly spheres; since even continual rains of forty days once poured out such floods that the waters rose fifteen cubits above the highest mountains. So the view of the philosophers is more divine, and more in harmony with the laws of nature, on this matter: they judged that the rivers flow down from the ocean, which sinks into the passages of the earth through which it is filtered, and then, now gathered in flat and open plains, now toward the ridges of the highest mountains (on which see Julius Caesar Scaliger, De subtilitate, exercit. xlvi), leap forth through the deep caverns and the various veins of the earth (which press down with their own weight), and so flow back again to where they came from. They hold that this is why the seas neither grow nor shrink, since they receive what is given to them and soon give back what they have received. So Plato, Philo in De opificio mundi, Seneca, Nat. quaest. iii, chap. ix, and others of our own time have taught, agreeing with the hidden doctrines of the Hebrews. Ecclesiastes 1: All the rivers run into the sea; yet the sea is not full: unto the place from whence the rivers come, thither they return again. In agreement with this is Homer's line about the ocean: [Ἐξ οὗ πάντες ποταμοὶ καὶ πᾶσα θάλασσα, καὶ πηγαὶ κρῆναι τε καὶ φρέατα μακρά] (from which all rivers and all the sea, and all springs, fountains and long wells, come).

units.la: Haec ut paucis dicam, Aquas omnes à Mari & ad Mare, signant. An absurde, & contra Naturae Decreta? Suffragatur, quod nos docet Experientia, non paucas esse Aquas: quae, quamvis dulces, aestum tamen Oceani sequuntur. Fontem Gadibus indicat Plinius lib. II. motibus Oceani consentientem: alium in Tenedo (Insula est in Hellesponto, nomen hodieque retinens) semper à tertia noctis hora in sextam ab aestivo solstitio exundantem: contra Timavum amnem Insulam in mari parvam; & in ea Fontes calidos, pariter cum aestu maris crescentes minuentesque. Aliam à Percolatione notans hujus rei causam Seneca, prodit suam hic (ut & alibi saepe) in rebus Physicis infantiam. Festiva sunt ejus verba: Quemadmodum, inquit, quartana ad horam venit; quemadmodum podagra ad tempus non respondet; quemadmodum purgatio, si nihil obstiterit; statum diem servat; quemadmodum praeco est ad mensem suum partus: sic Aquae intervalla habent, quibus se retrahant, & quibus redeant; quaedam autem intervalla, quia minora sunt, ideo notabilia: quaedam majora, & minus certa. Et hoc, quod de Percolatione dixi, juvat: in Alpheum Peloponnesi fluvium olim casu delapsa, longissimo Maris intervallo in Arethusa Syracusarum fonte, qui in Sicilia, postea fuisse reperta. Quo modo? beneficio Percolationis. Dicere enim Alpheum, prope Elidem civitatem ortum, non se consociare Pelago; sed subter mare Ionium defluere, & in Arethusam erumpere; supra fidem est: & tamquam rem omnino fabulosam agnoscit Strabo lib. VI; ut & non obscuris indiciis Virgilius lib. III. Aeneidos, Ovidius lib. V. Metamorph. Seneca in natur. quaest. Pomponius Mela lib. II, & si qui alij; contra Oraculum, quod citat Pausanias lib. I, Moschum Pindarumque Poetas, & Timaeum Philosophum; quos sequuti Plinius lib. II. & Lucianus in Marinorum Deorum Dialogis: ut, quum de Sicilia erit sermo, videbimus.
units.tr: To say it briefly: all waters come from the sea and go back to the sea. Is this absurd, and contrary to the decrees of nature? Experience teaches us that it is not, since there are not a few waters which, although sweet, nevertheless follow the tide of the ocean. Pliny, in the second book, reports a spring at Gades which agrees with the movements of the ocean; another on Tenedos (an island in the Hellespont that still keeps its name), which from the third hour of the night to the sixth overflows at the summer solstice; and, against this, the river Timavus, and on a small island in the sea, warm springs which grow and diminish together with the tide of the sea. Seneca, giving a different cause for this, namely percolation, reveals here (as he often does elsewhere) his childish ignorance in physical matters. His words are amusing: As a quartan fever comes at its hour, as gout does not keep to its time, as a purgation, if nothing hinders it, keeps its appointed day, as a herald is punctual at his month of delivery: so waters have intervals at which they withdraw and at which they return; but some intervals, because they are shorter, are therefore noticeable; others are longer and less certain. And what I have said about percolation is confirmed by the following: the Alpheus, a river of the Peloponnese, once fell by chance into the sea and, after a very long underwater course, was later found to emerge at the spring of Arethusa at Syracuse, in Sicily. How so? By the benefit of percolation. For that the Alpheus, rising near the city of Elis, does not join the deep, but flows beneath the Ionian sea and bursts out at Arethusa, is beyond belief; and Strabo, in book 6, recognises it as an entirely fabulous story, as do Virgil in the third book of the Aeneid, Ovid in the fifth book of the Metamorphoses, Seneca in the Natural Questions, Pomponius Mela in book 2, and others. Pausanias, in book 1, quotes an oracle against it, as well as the poets Moschus and Pindar and the philosopher Timaeus, whom Pliny in book 2 and Lucian in his Dialogues of the Sea-Gods followed; as we shall see when the discussion comes to Sicily.

units.la: Sed objiciet quis forte; quum omnium defluentium Aquarum origo sit ab Oceano, eoque salso: qui fiat, ut pleraque sint dulces; nonnullae autem bituminatae, sulphuratae, aluminosae, nitratae, aliisque saporibus imbutae percipiantur: quum item natura sua omnes fere cum matre frigeant, unde tantus non paucis Ardor?
units.tr: But perhaps someone will object: since the origin of all flowing waters is the ocean, and that is salt, how does it happen that most are sweet, while some are found to be bituminous, sulphurous, aluminous, nitrous, and imbued with other tastes? Likewise, how is it that almost all of them are naturally cold, like their mother, while some are very hot?

units.la: Naturalem Qualitatem, id est, Dulcedinem conciliat Aquis generatim Percolatio, de qua dixi; eo majorem semper, quo ductus Percolationis longior, & locus Eruptionis à Mari remotior.
units.tr: Percolation, of which I have spoken, gives waters in general their natural quality, that is, their sweetness; and it is always greater the longer the course of percolation and the farther the place of eruption is from the sea.

units.la: Sapores ceteros aliaque Accidentia infundunt; partim Terrarum, quibus percolantur Aquae, natura & genius: partem variae primarum Qualitatum permistiones, & Influentiarum, ut artis utar voce, concursus. Nam in confesso est apud omnes, Aquas Subterraneas per Venas currentes, earum rerum naturam easque Qualitates imbibere, quas perfluunt: sive Herbae latentes fuerint; seu Metalla, ut Aurum, Argentum, Aes, Ferrum, Plumbum, Cuprum, Argentum vivum, Auripigmentum vel Arsenium, Sandaracha; seu Lapides, ut Gemmae, Saxum Calcarium, Marmora, Arena; seu Succi concreti, ut Sulphur, Bitumen, Alumen, Chalcitis, Nitrum, Sal, Viscum; seu diversa Terrarum genera, ut Creta, Argilla, Marga, Ampelitis, Pignitis, Sinopis, Ochra; seu denique infecti Halitus & Vapores.
units.tr: The other tastes and accidental qualities are imparted partly by the nature and character of the earths through which the waters percolate, and partly by the various mixtures of the primary qualities and by the concurrence of influences, to use the language of the art. For it is generally agreed that subterranean waters, running through veins, take on the nature and qualities of the things through which they flow: whether these are hidden herbs; or metals, such as gold, silver, bronze, iron, lead, copper, quicksilver, orpiment or arsenic, and sandarach; or stones, such as gems, limestone, marble and sand; or concrete juices, such as sulphur, bitumen, alum, chalcitis, nitre, salt and bird-lime; or different kinds of earth, such as chalk, clay, marl, ampelitis, pignitis, sinopis and ochre; or, finally, infected exhalations and vapours.

units.la: Quod quaedam Aquae cum hominibus tum aliis animantibus Salutiferae, quaedam Morbidae, quaedam etiam Lethales: faciunt & Herbarum, quae latent vel ad juvandum vel ad nocendum, potentia; & Metalla, quibus perlabendo attactis affrictisque vis inest occulta, stupendorum effectuum generatrix.
units.tr: That some waters are healthful to humans and other animals, some harmful, and some even deadly; and that herbs lying hidden have power either to help or to harm; and that metals have a hidden force which touches and rubs whatever flows over them, producing astonishing effects.

units.la: Salutiferas quis quaerit? Albula Aquae, teste Isidoro, juxta Romam vulneribus medentur: Fons Ciceronis in Italia scissuras oculorum sanat, & sauciationes: in Sardinia etiam calidi Fontes, qui oculis medicinam adferunt; exceptis eorum, qui furti se alligarunt; horum enim facinus caecitate detegitur: Lechnus Arcadiae fons Abortus fieri non patitur. Zamae fons, apud eundem Isidorum, in Africa canoras facit voces.
units.tr: Who looks for healthful ones? According to Isidore, the Albula waters near Rome heal wounds. The Fountain of Cicero in Italy cures cracks and inflammations of the eyes. In Sardinia there are also warm springs that bring medicine to the eyes, except for those who have bound themselves to theft, for their crime is revealed by blindness. The spring Lechnus in Arcadia does not allow abortion to take place. The spring Zama, according to the same Isidore, in Africa makes voices tuneful.

units.la: Morbidas indicandum? Meminit Seneca Fontis, qui furere facit bibentes: Alius, qui Phreneticos. Isidoro scribente, in Chio insula Fons, quem qui bibunt fiunt hebetes: in Aethiopia fonte rubro qui bibunt, fiunt Limphatici. His adcensuerim illas, quae bibentibus Strumas in collo generant: fit illud (ut Iulio Caesare Scaligero de Subtilit. adversus Cardanum utar) ab Aqua è nivibus liquefactis; quæ multum terrestris & crudi continet. Crudum repugnat resolutioni: Gutturis hærent musculis & glandibus terrestre, quod propter aqucum se insinuavit, ibique concretum durescit. Idcirco qui ad Alpes habitant & Pyrenæos atque in Arvernis, hoc patiuntur. In locis autem frigidioribus nives rarius ac serius solvuntur: & quæ solvuntur, pusillo temporis spacio cedunt aliis cito subituris. Celsus, quem alij sequuntur, Aquam Frigidam Strumas excitare scribit ἀπλῶς. Sed non omnis Frigida gignit hoc malum. Nullos enim hujusmodi Tumores novit Asia, nullos Africa, nullos potissima pars Europæ: quibus omnibus tamen Aquæ frigidissimæ. In Germania familiare hoc perexiguo Alpium tractu; ubi qui nascuntur, nemo caret eo malo: quod etiam de ea parte agri Taurini, quæ Valdocca, id est vallis Anseris appellatur, notat Vir nobilissimus quem dixi. Ego ex Italia reversus in Alpibus vidi strumosissimos, & ad loquendum incredibile, quam ineptos. Legendus & de Caulla Strumas generante Albertus Magnus 11. Meteor. tract. iii. cap. xix.
units.tr: Shall I point out harmful ones? Seneca mentions a spring that makes its drinkers mad, and another that affects phrenetics. Isidore writes that on the island of Chios there is a spring whose drinkers become dull, and in Ethiopia drinkers of the red spring become lymphatic. To these I would add those waters that produce goitres in the necks of those who drink them. This happens (to use the words of Julius Caesar Scaliger in his De subtilitate against Cardan) from water of melted snow, which contains much earthy and crude matter. What is crude resists dissolution: the earthy matter, which has crept in with the water, lodges in the muscles and glands of the throat and there hardens into a lump. For this reason those who live among the Alps and Pyrenees, and in Auvergne, suffer from it. In colder places snows melt more rarely and more slowly, and those that do melt yield in a short space of time to others that will soon melt in turn. Celsus, whom others follow, writes that cold water simply [ἀπλῶς] produces goitres. But not every cold water causes this disease. Asia knows no such swellings, nor Africa, nor the greater part of Europe, though all of these have very cold waters. In Germany it is common in a very small stretch of the Alps, where whoever is born there is never free of this affliction. The most noble man I mentioned notes the same of that part of the Turin territory called Valdocca, that is, Goose Valley. I, returning from Italy, saw in the Alps very many goitrous people, and it is incredible to say how stupid they are. Albertus Magnus, Meteor. 11, tract. iii, cap. xix, should also be read on Caulla producing goitres.

units.la: In nos armatas & Lethales quis avet novitle? Seneca dicit esse quosdam fontes, qui bibentes venenando occidant. In Berofo Taurorum colle tres apud Plinium feruntur fontes; sine remedio, sine dolore mortiferi. In Arcadia, ut scribunt Plinius & Vitruvius (ex quibus Isidorus emendandus) juxta Nonacrin Aqua profluit e saxis, Styx appellata: quæ potata necat illico.
units.tr: Who wishes to learn about harmful and deadly ones? Seneca says there are certain springs which kill their drinkers by poisoning them. On the Taurus hill of Berosus, Pliny reports three springs which are deadly without remedy and without pain. In Arcadia, as Pliny and Vitruvius write (and Isidore must be corrected by them), near Nonacris a water flows from rocks, called Styx, which kills at once anyone who drinks it.

units.la: Ab alijs alia capiuntur Commoda & Incommoda. Apud Senecam fons est, qui memoriam confert: alius qui oblivionem inducit; quem in Boeotia ponit Isidorus: cui & in Sicilia duo Fontes, quorum unus fœcundat sterilem, alter contrariæ naturæ. Nominat idem Aquas in Campania, quæ sterilitatem fœminarum, & virorum insaniam abolere dicuntur. Iterum apud Senecam, fons Salmacis in Caria libidinem incendit: Cizici fons contra, apud Isidorum, Veneris tollit amorem.
units.tr: Different waters bring different advantages and disadvantages. In Seneca there is a spring that improves memory, and another that brings on forgetfulness; Isidore places the latter in Boeotia. In Sicily there are two springs, one of which makes a barren woman fruitful, the other of the opposite nature. The same author names waters in Campania said to abolish women's sterility and men's madness. Again in Seneca, the spring Salmacis in Caria kindles lust; the spring of Cyzicus, on the contrary, according to Isidore, takes away love of Venus.

units.la: Quod epotæ quædam insignes corporibus adferant mutationes, sine tamen corruptione naturæ: Caulla proculdubio manat ab variis Terræ, quam perlabitur, qualitatibus; quibus colores nunc hos nunc illos efficiundi vis inest. Plinius lib. 11. nat. hist. cap. cIII: In Fulfio omnis Aqua potata candidos boves facit; in Boeotia amnis Melas oves nigras; Cephisus ex eodem lacu profluens albas; rursus nigras Penius; russasque iuxta Lium Xanthus, unde & nomen amni. In Ponto fluvius Asacs irrigat campos; in quibus pastæ nigro lacte equæ gentem alunt. Seneca de natur. quæst. Quibusdam fluminibus vis inest mira: alia enim sunt; quæ potæ inficiunt greges ovium; intraque certum tempus, quæ fuere nigræ, albam ferunt lanam; quæ albæ venerant, nigræ abeunt. Hoc etiam in Boeotia amnes duo efficiunt: quorum alteri ab effectu Melas nomen est; uterque ex eodem lacu exeunt diversa facturi. In Macedonia quoque, ut ait Theophrastus, est flumen, ad quod qui facere albas oves volunt, adducunt; quod ut dimitus potavere non aliter quam infecta mutantur: at si illis lana fuerit opus nigra, pullis paratus gratuitus insector est: ad Penium eundem gregem adpellunt. Auctores habeo, esse in Calatia flumen, quod idem in omnibus efficiat. Est in Cappadocia, quo pato equis nec ulli præterea animali, color mutatur & spargitur alba cutis.
units.tr: That some remarkable waters, once drunk, bring about changes in the body without any corruption of nature: Caulla doubtless arises from the various qualities of the earth through which it flows, by which there is a power to produce now these colours, now those. Pliny, Natural History, book 11, chapter 103: "In Fulfium every water drunk makes white oxen; in Boeotia the river Melas makes black sheep; the Cephisus, flowing from the same lake, makes white ones; the Penius again makes black ones; and near Lium the Xanthus makes red ones, whence the river takes its name. In Pontus the river Asacs waters fields, on which mares pastured give black milk, and nourish a people." Seneca, Natural Questions: "Some rivers have a remarkable power: for there are some which, when sheep drink them, stain the flocks; and within a certain time, those that were black bear white wool, and those that were white turn black. This too two rivers in Boeotia produce, of which one takes the name Melas from its effect; both flow out of the same lake yet produce different results. In Macedonia too, as Theophrastus says, there is a river to which those who want white sheep bring their flocks; when they drink it, they are changed no otherwise than as if dyed; but if they need black wool, they take them to the Penius, the same river as before. I have authorities that in Galatia there is a river which does the same thing in all animals. In Cappadocia there is a river by which horses, and no other animal, have their colour changed and white marks spread over their skin."

units.la: Quod in quibusdam, ut de Rubro Mari notat Plinius, Oleæ nascantur & fruticcs virentes; facit Aquarum spiritus, quæ aliquid pingue & naturalis seminis seu caloris continent.
units.tr: That olives and shrubs grow green in some places, as Pliny notes of the Red Sea, is due to the spirit of the waters, which contain something oily and of a natural seed or heat.

units.la: Quod quidam fontes oleo perfusi; facit Bitumen pinguius, quod oleum in se habere extra omnem est controversiam. Tales: in Scotia, haud procul urbe regia; in Saxonia, prope Brunsvicum; alij alibi: ut mirum non sit, mandatum scriptis ab Ariano, ad Alexandri tabernaculum Fontem Olei (totum ex oleo, ablit ut credam) prorupisse: ab alijs vero, idem Augusti principatu Romæ contigisse.
units.tr: That some springs are soaked with oil is caused by bitumen richer in oil, and there is no controversy that bitumen contains oil. Such springs are found in Scotland, not far from the royal city; in Saxony, near Brunswick; and elsewhere. So it is not surprising that, as Arrian wrote, a Fountain of Oil burst forth at Alexander's tent (entirely of oil, far be it from me to believe that), and others say the same happened at Rome under the principate of Augustus.
