units.la: Quod quædam Aquæ injecta corpora agglutinent & indurent, facit limi copia & viscosa earum natura. Quemadmodum enim Pulvisculus Puteolanus, ut est apud Senecam, si aquam attingit confestim fit Saxum; sic contra sunt Aquæ quæ si solidum contingant, hærent & adfiguntur. Et adscribit ille constare quosdam esse Fontes, qui ligna injecta in lapideam substantiam convertunt, & ex hujusmodi lapidibus optimas fieri cotes. Exempla alia subministrant alij. Memoriæ prodit Plinius, in Ciconum flumine lignum dejectum lapideo cortice obduci. De eo Ovidius in Metamorph. Flumen habent Cicones: quod potum saxea reddit Viscera, quod tactis inducit marmora rebus. Apud eundem Plinium, in flumine Silari ultra Surrentum non Virgulta modo immersa, sed & folia lapidescunt: alias salubri aquae ejus potu. Similem omnino vidi in Arduenna silva juxta Malmundarium, quamvis lapidescentem, potui tamen aptum; qui in lacunas & incilia ductus instar tophi coalescit, ex quo camini & fornaces fieri solent. In Allicnsi fonte Arvernorum ligna, calamos, quisquilias lapidescere, trium horarum spacio, docet in suo universa naturae Theatro Ioannes Bodinus, testis oculatus. Refert in suis Mineralibus Albertus Magnus, inventum esse suo tempore ramum Arboris in portu Lubecensi, in quo erat avium nidus una cum pullis, conversis omnino in lapidem paullulum subrufum & durum. Addam huc; in Hungaria rivulum esse, in quem ferrum injectum Cuprum redditur: In Marsida Phrygiae fonte, quod scribit Isidorus, Saxum crescere.
units.tr: That some waters bind and harden the bodies put into them is due to the abundance of silt and the viscous nature of the water. For just as Puteolan dust, as Seneca says, immediately becomes stone when it touches water, so conversely there are waters which, when they touch something solid, cling to it and attach themselves. Seneca adds that it is well established that some springs turn wood thrown into them into a stony substance, and that excellent whetstones are made from such stones. Others supply other examples. Pliny records that in the river of the Cicones a piece of wood thrown in is covered with a stony bark. Ovid, in the Metamorphoses: "The Cicones have a river which, when drunk, turns the innards to stone, and which turns whatever things it touches to marble." In the same Pliny, in the river Silarus beyond Surrentum, not only immersed twigs but also leaves turn to stone; yet its water is healthful to drink. I have seen a wholly similar water in the Ardennes forest near Malmedy, which, although it petrifies, is nonetheless fit to drink; it spreads into pools and channels and hardens like tufa, from which hearths and furnaces are commonly made. In the spring Allier of the Arverni, wood, reeds and rubbish turn to stone within three hours, as Jean Bodin, an eyewitness, teaches in his Universae naturae theatrum. Albertus Magnus reports in his Mineralia that in his time a branch of a tree was found in the harbour of Lübeck, with a bird's nest and its chicks in it, all turned into a somewhat reddish and hard stone. I will add here: in Hungary there is a stream into which iron thrown is turned into copper; and at the spring Marsida in Phrygia, as Isidore writes, stone grows.

units.la: Non obscurum igitur, quod quidam fluvij trahant Metalla, per quae fluunt. Auriferi sane gemmiferique, ut de aliis sileam, celebrantur Ister, Hermus, Pactolus, Hebrus, Tagus, Hydaspes, Ganges, & alij; de quibus simul Seneca in Hercule Oetaeo, Act. II. Choro: Cupit hic gazis implere famem: Nec tamen omnis plaga gemmiferi Sufficit Istri; nec tota sitim Lydia vincit; nec, qua Zephyro Subdita tellus, slupet auro Flumine clarum radiare Tagum; Necsi totus serviat Hebrus; Ruraque dives cingat Hydaspes; Intraque suos currere fines Spectet toto flumine Gangem.
units.tr: It is therefore not unclear that some rivers carry away metals through the lands they flow through. Rivers rich in gold and gems, to say nothing of others, are famous: the Ister, Hermus, Pactolus, Hebrus, Tagus, Hydaspes, Ganges and others. Seneca speaks of them together in the Hercules Oetaeus, Act II, chorus: "Here he desires to fill his hunger with treasures; yet not every region of the gem-bearing Ister suffices, nor does all Lydia quench his thirst; nor the land that lies under the West Wind, dazzled by the gold of the bright Tagus river; nor, if the whole Hebrus were to serve him, and rich Hydaspes were to surround the fields, and he were to watch the Ganges running within its own bounds with its whole stream."

units.la: Sic Claudianus: Non Tartessiacis illum sariaret arenis / Tempestas preciosa Tagi; non stagna rubentis / Aurea Pactoli, totumque exhauserit Hermum: / Ardebit majore siti.
units.tr: Claudian says thus: "Not even the precious storm of the Tagus, with its Tartessian sands, would sate him; nor the golden pools of the reddish Pactolus, nor would he have drained the whole of Hermus: he will burn with a greater thirst."

units.la: De his univer sim Seneca. lib. de Consolatione ad Marciam: Quid lapidum gemmarumque fulgor, & inter rapidorum torrentium arenas aurum interfluens!
units.tr: Seneca writes of this same matter in his book to Marcia, On Consolation: "What is the glitter of stones and gems, and gold flowing between the sands of rushing torrents!"

units.la: Dicendum & hic nonnihil de Colorum, Saporumque varietate, & Ardore. Quod Diversicolores; facit varians etiam passim in coloribus Terra. Notat Cardanus Aquam candidam ad secundum à Glauca Milenae opido lapidem, rubeam Raderae, Milenae fluvij juxta Radeburgum; viridem in Carpatho monte, juxta Neusolam; caeruleam Blavae, inter Feltrium & Tarvisium; nigerrimam Alterae, fluvij Saxoniae, ubi in Visurgim se exonerat. Referunt & alij vix credibile in Idumaea fontem esse (cui cognomen Iob tribuitur ab Isidoro) tribus mensibus turbidum, tribus sanguineum, tribus viridem, tribus denique limpidum.
units.tr: Something should also be said here about the variety of colours and tastes, and about heat. That waters are of different colours is due to the fact that the earth itself varies in colour in many places. Cardanus notes that the water is white about a mile from the town of Milena at Glauca; red at Radera, the river Milena near Radeburg; green on the mountain Carpathus, near Neusohl; blue at the Blava, between Feltre and Treviso; and very black at the Altera, a river of Saxony, where it empties into the Weser. Others also report what is hardly credible: that in Idumaea there is a spring (to which Isidore gives the name of Job) which is turbid for three months, bloody for three, green for three, and finally clear for three.

units.la: Sunt & quae bibentes inebriant: causa est, quod multum spirituum ex sulphureis meatibus contineant: quos certum est fumis replere cerebrum. Lyncestis aqua, quae vocatur Acidula, vini modo temulentos facit; ut & alij in Paphlagonia, & in agro Caleno; notante Plinio lib. II. Multos etiam in Germania & Helvetia fontes hausi, vini semper sapore fluentes: Incolae Saurbrun appellant, ab acido sapore. In Boemia, prope opidum, quod Brelen indigetant, distans à Ponte (Brugs vulgo) miliare, fons esse dicitur; cujus Aqua matutino tempore utuntur pro Vino adusto. Aristoteles adfirmat in Sicilia fontem esse acetosum: quo indigenae utuntur pro Aceto: in Scythia amarum esse, cujus defluxus amnem etiam proximum eodem inficit sapore. Semper-saporis voce paullo ante sum usus. Nam me latet causa, unde apud Plinium fonti cuidam in Andro, (Insula Cycladum principe, nomen hodieque retinente) in templo Liberi Patris talis sapor Nonis solum Ianuarij. Ludebat olim saepe in his & talibus ad obcaecandum hominum animos humani generis hostis Diabolus. Poterant & hoc astu quodam templi Antistites: ut ad Alicea sive Ἀμξέια, Bacchi festa (quae, docente Aristophanis Interprete, in Ταμηλιῶνα, qui Latinorum Ianuario respondebat, incidebant) majorem hominum multitudinem, vana tractam superstitione, adlicerent; locoque, suis commodis invigilantes, majorem conciliarent religionem.
units.tr: Some waters also intoxicate those who drink them. The cause is that they contain much spirit from sulphurous passages, which certainly fill the brain with fumes. The water of Lyncestis, called Acidula, makes drinkers drunk just like wine; so do others in Paphlagonia and in the territory of Calenum, as Pliny notes in book 2. I have also drunk from many springs in Germany and Switzerland that always flow with the taste of wine. The locals call one of them Saurbrun, from its sour taste. In Bohemia, near the town which they call Brelen, a mile from Pont (commonly Brugs), there is said to be a spring whose water is used in the morning in place of burnt wine. Aristotle affirms that in Sicily there is an acidic spring, which the natives use in place of vinegar; in Scythia there is one that is bitter, and its outflow infects even the nearby river with the same taste. I have just used the phrase "ever-tasting". For I do not know the reason why, according to Pliny, a certain spring on Andros (the chief island of the Cyclades, still keeping its name) has such a taste only on the Nones of January, in the temple of Father Liber. The enemy of the human race, the Devil, used to play often with such things, and with others like them, to blind men's minds. The priests of the temple could also, by some such trick, lure a greater crowd of people, drawn by empty superstition, to the Alicea, or Ἀμξέια [Amzeia], the festival of Bacchus (which, as the interpreter of Aristophanes teaches, fell in the month of Thamelion [Ταμηλιῶνα], which corresponded to the Roman January); and the priests, watching over their own advantage, would thereby win greater reverence for their religion.

units.la: Ardor, ut mihi vero videtur simile, multis aquis fluentibus non aliunde, quam à perpetua jactatione; qua in interioribus Terræ visceribus per abrupta loca longissimasque cataractas eæ feruntur. Satis enim constat, quæcumque violenter agitantur, præsertim si temporis longinquitas comitetur, mirum in modum incalescere. Indignam censeo solidioris scientiæ Philosopho sententiam; fieri hoc ab aliquo Igne subterraneo, eoque sulphureo. Ignis consideretur natura. Non potest ille diu vivere, non vigere, in subterraneis: conclusus artius angustiusque constipatus exstinguitur, nisi eruptioni detur locus: ut vivat vigeatque, quærit semper libertatem, apertum aërem, superiora & homogenea sibi loca: ubi supra Aërem non aliquis actu Ignis, sed primigenius ille cœlestis Calor. An quæ hujusmodi Ignium Eruptiones alicubi (argumentum enim subministret & exemplum nobilissima regio, Mundi ocellus) in Italia hodie? ubi tamen paullo minus sexaginta calidarum Aquarum sontes notarunt naturalium ibi rerum scrutatores: quorum etiam scripta, nenos contra vulgus hic sentientes dejuvent) nusquam ignes fontibus, fontesve ignibus commiscieri loquuntur. Deinde quum Ignis quidquid Aqueum exsiccet, Aqua vero quidquid igneum exstinguat, simulac alterum alteri dominari possit: proculdubio paullatim vel tam violenta Flammarum vis Aquas perlabentes exsiccaret, Terramque suis deflagrationibus in cineres redegisset; vel tam inexhausta Aquarum, tot seculis adfluentium, copia iam pridem Ignes illos subterraneos exstinxisset. Nam non credendum tam æquales esse Igni Aquæque sub terra vires, tamque concordem discordiam; ut vel ille non consumat percolantem, vel hæc incalfacientem non suffocet. Fieri non potest. Et sane quis unquam vidit, vel fando audivit, Aquas ferventes erumpere ex Vesuvio Italiæ, ex Ætna Siciliæ, alijsque alibi: ut vere possit dicere, fervorem illum ab Ignivomis esse Montibus? Quin, quod argumentum etiam non insuper habendum, Aquas in Helvetia alijsque in locis gustavi ferventes, quæ profsus erant insipidæ; ut plane mihi persuaderent calorem inditum sibi non ab Sulphure; cujus indolem noveram, liquidis facile saporem suum communicare.
units.tr: Heat, as it truly seems to me likely, arises in many flowing waters from nothing other than their constant agitation, as they are hurled through the inner bowels of the earth over precipitous places and very long cataracts. For it is well established that whatever is violently stirred, especially if the stirring lasts a long time, grows hot in a marvellous way. I judge the view of a philosopher of sounder learning to be unworthy: that this happens from some subterranean fire, and a sulphurous one at that. Let us consider the nature of fire. It cannot live or flourish for long underground: when it is shut in and packed too tightly and narrowly, it goes out, unless a way of escape is given to its eruption. In order to live and flourish, it always seeks freedom, open air, and places above and akin to itself; where, above the air, there is not some active fire, but that primeval heavenly heat. But what of the eruptions of such fires, which occur somewhere (for the most noble region, the eye of the world, Italy, provides both the argument and the example) today? Yet although the natural investigators there have noted a little under sixty sources of warm waters, their writings (which help those who here think otherwise against the common view) nowhere speak of fires mixed with springs, or springs with fires. Next, since fire dries up whatever is watery, and water extinguishes whatever is fiery, as soon as one could rule over the other: without doubt either the violent force of the flames would gradually dry up the waters flowing through, and reduce the earth to ashes by its conflagrations; or the inexhaustible abundance of waters, flowing in for so many ages, would long ago have put out those subterranean fires. For we must not believe that the powers of fire and water under the earth are so equal, and their discord so harmonious, that the one neither consumes the water that filters through it, nor does the water suffocate the fire that heats it. It cannot happen. And indeed, who has ever seen, or heard by report, boiling waters bursting out of Vesuvius in Italy, out of Etna in Sicily, or elsewhere, so that one could truly say that this heat comes from the fire-spewing mountains? Indeed, and this argument is not to be scorned either: I have tasted waters in Switzerland and elsewhere that were boiling, yet entirely insipid; so that they fully persuaded me that the heat within them did not come from sulphur, whose nature I knew to communicate its taste easily to liquids.

units.la: Iam quod nonnullis Aquis Miracula potius tributa, quam singulariæ Qualitates: unde nisi ab magno illo & potente Deo? Valeant, qui rationes alias excogitant. Feliciter enim hoc agere solideque, homini non dicam difficillimum, sed ἀδύνατον omnino. Cæcutimus hic mortale genus.
units.tr: As for the fact that some waters are attributed to miracles rather than to particular qualities, whence could this come except from that great and powerful God? Let those who devise other explanations fare well. For to do this successfully and soundly is not, I will not say very difficult for man, but altogether impossible. Here mankind is blind.

units.la: Sunt quæ per minima & dilucida intervalla calent & frigent. Fons apud Garamantas, indicantibus Augustino lib. xxi. de Civit. Dei, & Isidoro lib. xiii. Orig. qui in die tam frigidus, ut bibi non possit; nocte tantæ caliditatis, ut tangi nequeat. Plinius lib. v. nat. histor. cap. v: Ultra eum Deserta; Atarelæ, oppidum Garamantum; itemque Debris, adfso fonte, à medio die ad mediam noctem aquis ferventibus, totidem horis ad medium diem rigentibus. Ejusdem ingenij fons Iovis Hammonis celebratissimus: de quo idem Plinius; item Diodorus, Solinus, Arrianus, Pomponius Mela, & alij. Sic Lucretius: Est apud Hammonis fanum fons luce diurna Frigidus, at calidus nocturno tempore fertur.
units.tr: Some waters grow hot and cold again at very short and clear intervals. There is a spring among the Garamantes, as Augustine in book 21 of The City of God and Isidore in book 13 of the Origins indicate, which is so cold by day that it cannot be drunk, but at night is of such heat that it cannot be touched. Pliny in book 5 of the Natural History, chapter 5: "Beyond it lies the desert; Atarelae, a town of the Garamantes; and likewise Debris, where by the spring, from midday to midnight, the waters are boiling, and for as many hours they grow cold again until midday." Of the same kind is the spring of Jupiter Ammon, very famous; Pliny speaks of it, and likewise Diodorus, Solinus, Arrian, Pomponius Mela and others. So Lucretius: "At the shrine of Ammon there is a spring which is cold by day, but is said to be hot at night."

units.la: Ovidius lib. xv. Metamorphos.
units.tr: Ovid, Metamorphoses, book 15

units.la: medio tua corniger Hammon Unda die gelida est, ortuque obituque calescit.
units.tr: At midday the horned Hammon's water is cold, and at sunrise and sunset it grows warm.

units.la: Caussam post Lucretium tentat indicare Pontanus in Meteoris; Caussa quidem vel certa subest: nam frigora noctis Intus alunt Ignes, nocte & vapor æstuat intus; Unde fluunt calidi noctis per tempora rivi: Luce autem quum Sol Terras populatur, & ardens Exhalat vis; tum vena recreantur hiantes, Unde redit gelidus sua per vestigia torrens.
units.tr: After Lucretius, Pontanus in his Meteora tries to indicate the cause. Indeed a cause lies ready to hand: by night the fires within feed the cold, and by night the vapour seethes inside, whence warm streams run through the hours of darkness. But by day, when the Sun lays waste the lands and its burning force breathes out, the gaping veins are refreshed, and so the cold torrent returns along its own tracks.

units.la: Sollicitari nolite Viri magni Manes, quod hic differentiam. Si enim Frigoris nocturni, calores sub terra constringentis & augentis: vel Aestus diurni, eosdem, ut Frigori detur locus, dispergendo minuentis, ἀντιθεσεως causa sit tantæ Mutationis: quur non idem fit in aliis Fontibus cum calentis Libyæ, tum aliarum regionum? An quod alibi non tantus Aestus? atqui in Libya non tantum Frigus. Et vero demus ἀντιθεσεως Calorum nocturno, Frigorum vero diurno tempore caussam esse; quod in Subterraneis passim fieri novimus: illud velim scire, an ab ea duo illa summe contraria; Mutatio, inquam, illa violentissima tam brevi temporis spacio: nocte enim dicunt adeo calere, ut tangi; die tantopere frigere, ut bibi nequeat. Experimur quotidie Contraliftentiam (hac enim voce utar) Aquarum qualitates tantillo tempore alternantem, omnia operari moderata; non tantas inducere Metamorphoses. Aliud igitur latet, quod me, quod, scio, latet multos: uni D E O, qui creatarum à se Rerum novit Vires & ingenia, manifestum. Miranda non minus, quæ sequuntur.
units.tr: Let not the great spirits of the dead be troubled that I raise a difficulty here. For if the cause of the change is that the cold of night constricts the heat beneath the earth and increases it, or that the heat of day disperses the same heat and diminishes it, so that room is given to the cold, by a contrary action, then why does the same not happen in other springs, both in hot Libya and in other regions? Is it because elsewhere the heat is not so great? But in Libya there is not so much cold. And let us grant that the contrariety of heat at night and cold by day is the cause, as we know happens everywhere in subterranean places. I would still like to know whether this change, so violent in so brief a span of time, arises from those two utterly opposed things. For they say that at night the water grows so hot that it can hardly be touched, and by day it grows so cold that it cannot be drunk. Every day we experience the contrariety (for so I shall call it) of waters alternating in quality in a short time, and all of these work in moderation; they do not bring about such great metamorphoses. Something else therefore lies hidden, which, I know, is hidden from many: it is manifest to GOD alone, who knows the powers and natures of the things he has created. The things that follow are no less wonderful.

units.la: Sunt enim quæ inflammant & exstinguunt. Fons apud Augustinum, loco à me laudato, & Isidorum, in Epiro, qui accensam facem exstinguit, exstinctam accendit. Scribitur & à Plinio fons in Dodone Iovis, quum sit gelidus, immersas tamen faces exstinguere; si exstinctæ admoveantur, accendere. De eo Lucretius lib. VI. de natur. rerum: Frigidus est etiam Fons, supra quem sita sape Stuppa jacit flammas, concepto proximus igni; Tedaque consimili ratione accensa per undas Conlucet, quocumque natans impellitur auris:
units.tr: For there are springs that both kindle and extinguish. Augustine, in the passage I cited, and Isidore mention a spring in Epirus which extinguishes a lighted torch and relights an extinguished one. Pliny also records a spring of Jupiter at Dodona which, though cold, extinguishes torches dipped in it, and if extinguished ones are brought near, kindles them. Lucretius, in book 6 of On the Nature of Things, speaks of it: Cold too is the spring above which tow, placed near the fire, often throws up flames; and a torch kindled in the same way shines through the waves, wherever the blowing breeze drives it floating.

units.la: Et causam audet scribere: Nimirum quia sunt in aqua permulta vaporis Semina, de terraque necesse est fundittus ipsa Ignis corpora per totum consurgere fontem, Et simul exspirare foras, exireque in auras: Non tam viva tamen, calidus queat ut fieri fons.
units.tr: And he dares to give the cause: surely because there are very many seeds of heat in the water, and it is necessary that fires rise up from the bottom of the earth through the whole spring, and breathe out and escape into the air at the same time; yet they are not so living that the spring can become warm.

units.la: Quid illud? Ignis ex Fontis fundo consurgit ad superiora, & foras exit; qui quidem stuppam, qui tedam accendat; non tamen Fontis aquam sensim calefaciat. Si tantarum virium Ignis, ut perrumpens Aquæ molem tanti miraculi sit effector: qui potest, ut Aquam paullatim non reddat calidam? Si contra tam debilis potentiæ, ut ab imis penetrans in auras Aquam non mutet: qui fit, ut non exstinguatur, sed ita vires adquirat eundo, ut libertatem nactus accendat vel Stuppam virginem, vel exstinctam tedam? Aliud hic, longe aliud; quod uni DEO clarum humanis oculis videri nequit.
units.tr: What of that? Fire rises from the bottom of the spring to the surface and goes out, and it can indeed set tow or a torch alight, yet it does not gradually warm the water of the spring. If the fire has such power that, breaking through the mass of water, it is the agent of so great a marvel, how can it fail to make the water gradually warm? And if on the contrary its power is so weak that, penetrating from the depths into the air, it does not change the water, how does it happen that it is not extinguished, but gathers strength as it goes, so that once it is free it kindles either a virgin tow or an extinguished torch? Here is something else, something far different, which can appear clear to God alone and not to human eyes.

units.la: Quin & miraculo mihi Iudææ quidam Rivus; quem notat Isidorus Sabbatis omnibus siccari solitum.
units.tr: Indeed, to me also a certain stream of Judaea is a wonder, which Isidore notes used to dry up on every Sabbath.

units.la: Sed & nonnullæ; quæ quid futurum prænunciant. In Monte Anthracio Fontem novit Plinius, qui summe plenus & redundans anni fertilitatem significabat; subsidens caritatis indicium: in Reatino vero agro Fontem Neminiæ; qui, alio atque alio loco exoriendo, mutationem Annonæ Incolis præaugurabatur.
units.tr: There are also some springs which foretell what is to come. Pliny knows of a spring on Mount Anthracium which, when it is very full and overflowing, signifies a fertile year, and when it subsides, is a sign of dearth. In the land of Reate there is the spring of Neminia, which, breaking out now in one place and now in another, used to forewarn the inhabitants of changes in the price of grain.

units.la: Mirabile quod de Rheno nostro commemorat Antiquitas, cum Castitatis fuisse Indicem & ludicem. Aiunt enim, Celtarum Infantes intra sinum suum conjectos, si læsa matris pudicitia essent suscepti, fluvium hunc, tamquam impuri lecti vindicem, rapidis vorticibus suffocare; quos autem legitimo & impolluto matrimonio natos noverat, in portum placidis aquis solitum efferre. Sed hodie talia pericula in recens natis neque, & prudenti consilio, audentur; neque, edoctis meliora sanioraque qui adhabitant, adeuntur.
units.tr: Remarkable is what antiquity records of our Rhine, that it was an indicator and judge of chastity. For they say that the infants of the Celts, when thrown into its bosom, if the mother's chastity had been violated, were taken up by this river, as avenger of the impure bed, and suffocated in its rapid whirlpools; but those known to have been born of lawful and unpolluted marriage it used to carry out into harbour on its calm waters. But today such dangers are neither risked with newborns, nor by prudent counsel; nor are they encountered, since the inhabitants have been taught better and saner things.

units.la: Quod autem de Matrona (qui Celtas à Belgis dirimit, hodie Marne) perhibetur, esse ejus fati, ut quotidie prædam aliquam ad mare secum conripiat: hoc facile de omnibus majoribus fluviis dixerim.
units.tr: What is said of the Matrona (which divides the Celts from the Belgians, today the Marne), that it is so fated as to carry off some prey to the sea every day, I could easily say of all the larger rivers.

units.la: Monendum & illud hoc loco, Fluvios quosdam in cavernas & antra Terræ devolvi & absorberi: quærentes contra montana, quibus liberior cursus prohibetur, per subterranea progressum; &, ubi, in remotissimis sæpe locis, planiora rursus deprehendunt, repetito nomine erumpentes. Tales, indicante Plinio, Lycus in Asia, Erasinus in Argolica, Tigris in Mesopotamia. De postremo Seneca in Nat. quæst. Age, inquit, quum vides Tigrim in medio itineris siccari, & non universum averti: sed paullatim, non apparentibus damnis, minui primum, deinde consumi: quo illum putas abire, nisi in obscura terrarum? utique: quum videas emergere iterum, non minorem eo, qui prior fluxerat. De prioribus Ovidius lib. XV. Metamorph. Sic ubi terreno Lycus est epotus hiatu Exsilit procul hinc, alioque renascitur ore: Sic modo quum bibitur, tacito modo gurgite lapsus Redditur Argolicis ingens Erasinus in undis.
units.tr: It should also be noted here that some rivers roll down into the caverns and caves of the earth and are swallowed up, seeking through underground channels a passage past the mountains that block their freer course; and where, often in very remote places, they find flatter ground again, they burst forth once more under the same name. Such, as Pliny points out, are the Lycus in Asia, the Erasinus in Argolis, and the Tigris in Mesopotamia. Of the last, Seneca says in the Natural Questions: "Come, when you see the Tigris drying up in the middle of its course, and not turned away entirely, but little by little, with no visible loss, first diminishing and then being consumed: where do you think it goes, except into the hidden places of the earth? Certainly; when you see it emerge again, no less than it was before it flowed." Of the former, Ovid, Metamorphoses book 15: "So where the Lycus is swallowed by the gaping earth, it leaps forth far away and is reborn from another mouth. So too, when it is drunk, the Erasinus, slipping with a silent current, is given back in the Argolic waves, mighty as it was."

units.la: Talis item, ut alios hoc loco praeteream, Anas in Hispania, hodie Rio Guadiana; qui infra Castra Vnelliana (Medelino vulgo) se condit, progressusque per meatus quosdam subterraneos ad decem circiter milliaria erumpit rursus paulo supra oppidum Villarta.
units.tr: Such also, to pass over others here, is the Anas in Spain, today the Guadiana. Below the Castra Vnelliana (commonly Medellín) it hides itself, and having advanced through certain underground passages, it bursts out again about ten miles away, a little above the town of Villarta.

units.la: Ex Fluviis porro tanta rerum omnium abundantia terris adjacentibus subministratur, tam multa bona, tam infinitae provenium mortalibus utilitates; ut eos sacros habuerint Prisci, vel Ovidio teste libr. 11. & viii. Metamorph. eorumque Fontes & Capita Dis sacrarint, & magna semper veneratione fuerint dignati. Seneca Epistola xii: Magnorum Fluminum Capita veneramur; subita exabdito vasti Amnis eruptio Aras habet: volunt Aquarum calentium fontes: & Stagna quaedam vel opacitas vel immensa altitudo sacra: 11. Servius ad Eclogam 1: Omnes Aquis Nymphae sunt praesidentes. Aelianus Περὶ Ζώων lib. 11. cap. xxxiii: Τῶν τῶν ποταμῶν Φύσιν... Quin & nefas habebant in quibusdam natare. Tacitus lib. xiv. Annal. Isdem diebus nimia luxus cupido in famam & periculum Neroni tulit: quia fontem Aquae Martiae ad urbem deductae nando inquinaverat; videbaturque potus sacros & carimoniam loci loto corpore polluisse: sequutaque anceps valitudo iram Deum adfi marit. Plinius lib. viii. natur. histor. de Clitumno: Pons terminus Sacri Profanque, in superiore parte navigare tantum, infra etiam natare concessum. Quae innuunt in quibusdam etiam navigare non licuisse: & plenius loquuntur ejusdem Plinii, quae de Lacu Vadimonis: Nullis in hoc navis (sacer enim est) sed innatant Insulae. Addo fluvium aliquem transituros adorare, manuque lavare solitos. Hesiodus lib. 11: Μηδὲ πὰρ' ἀσινάων ποταμῶν καλλίρροον ὕδωρ Ποσὶ πρὸς γε, πρὶν γ' ἂξη ἰδῶν ἰς καλὰ ῥέεθρα, Χεῖρας νιψάμενος πολυηράτῳ ὕδατι λούειν.
units.tr: Moreover, from rivers such abundance of everything is supplied to the neighbouring lands, so many goods and such endless advantages come to mortals, that the ancients held them sacred, as Ovid testifies in books 11 and 8 of the Metamorphoses, and consecrated their springs and sources to the gods and always deemed them worthy of great veneration. Seneca, Letter 12: "We venerate the sources of great rivers; a sudden outburst of a vast stream from a hidden place has altars. They consider the springs of warm waters sacred, and certain pools, either because of their gloom or their immense depth." Servius on Eclogue 1: "Nymphs preside over all waters." Aelian, On Animals, book 11, chapter 33: [Τῶν τῶν ποταμῶν Φύσιν...]. Indeed they even thought it wrong to swim in some of them. Tacitus, Annals book 14: "In the same days an excessive desire for luxury brought Nero into fame and danger, because by swimming he had polluted the spring of the Aqua Martia, which had been brought into the city; and it seemed that by bathing his whole body he had defiled the sacred water and the sanctity of the place; and a serious illness that followed showed the anger of the gods." Pliny, Natural History book 8, on the Clitumnus: "The bridge is the boundary between the sacred and the profane: upstream it is allowed only to sail, downstream even to swim." These words imply that in some places even sailing was not permitted; and Pliny speaks more fully of what he says about the Lake Vadimo: "No ship is used on this lake (for it is sacred), but islands float upon it." I add that those about to cross a river used to worship it and wash their hands in it. Hesiod, book 2: [Μηδὲ παρ' ἀσινέων ποταμῶν καλλίρροον ὕδωρ / ποσὶ προσελθών, πρὶν γ' ἂν ἴδῃς ἐς καλὰ ῥέεθρα, / χεῖρας νιψάμενος πολυηράτῳ ὕδατι λούειν.] Do not go to wash your feet in the fair-flowing water of undefiled rivers before you have seen their fair channels, and you must first wash your hands in water that is much desired.

units.la: Quia Fluvij, ut Theocritus canit, Ἰχθύες. Quod autem Aelianus paullo ante 30 Βοῶν εἰδῶν; alij Taurorum speciem fluminibus tribui solitam scribant: varie varij interpretantur illam Veterum consuetudinem. Festus, quod sint atrocia, ut Tauri: Acron ad lib. iiii. Carm. Horat. Odam xiv, quod mugiant: alias etiam causas indicant Interpretes Graeci, Hesiodi quidem ad Ἀσπίδα: inquit in illa ταῦρος ...
units.tr: Because rivers, as Theocritus sings, [have] fishes [Ἰχθύες]. But as to what Aelian says a little earlier (ch. 30) [Βοῶν εἰδῶν], others write that the form of bulls was usually attributed to rivers. Interpreters explain that ancient custom in various ways. Festus says it is because they are fierce, like bulls; Acron, on Horace's Odes book 4, ode 14, says it is because they bellow. The Greek commentators indicate other reasons too, Hesiod's indeed in his commentary on the Shield, where he says that in it [ταῦρος ...] the bull ...

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CAP. X.

units.la: De Aquis natura sua Quietis.
units.tr: On the Natural Quietness of Waters.

units.la: SIc se habet Aqua moveri solita: species altera erat Quieta. Stantem Aquam appello, quaeque non nisi Vento agitatur. Hic in genere monendum Aquam Currentem meliorem, leviorem & subtiliorem esse Stante; hanc autem Illa calidiorem ab Solis radiis, in unam eamdemque totos dies fixis, suaque vires infundentibus: ideoque Stantem Plantis magis conducere, quam Currentem, legendus Albertus Magnus lib. 1. Meteoror. cap. xi. & lib. 11. tract. iii. cap. xx, nec non de Veget. & Plant. vii. tract. 1, cap. iii.
units.tr: This is how water is described when it is moving; the other kind is still water. I call standing water that which is stirred only by the wind. Here it must be noted in general that running water is better, lighter and finer than standing water. Running water is also warmer, since it is not fixed in one place all day under the rays of the sun, which pour their strength into it. For this reason standing water is more suitable for plants than running water. Albertus Magnus should be read: Meteorology book 1, chapter 11; book 2, tractate 3, chapter 20; and also On Vegetables and Plants, book 7, tractate 1, chapter 3.

units.la: Species Aquae Quietae, Lacus, Stagnum, Palus, & similes: quae, ut Flumina, passim in hoc Globo: quemadmodum suis locis parebit.
units.tr: The kinds of still water are lakes, pools, marshes and the like. Like rivers, they are found everywhere on this globe, as will appear in their proper places.

units.la: Lacus locus profundus vel receptaculum, in quo Aquae perpetuae ibidem natae; Varroni, Lacuna magna, ubi Aqua contineri potest. Ab voce Graeca λάκκος: Isidoro, quasi Aquae locus.
units.tr: A lake is a deep place or basin in which water is perpetually produced. Varro calls it a great hollow in which water can be held. The word comes from the Greek λάκκος. Isidore says it is as if it were a place of water.

units.la: Lacibus quibusdam singulariæ sunt Qualitates ab ipsdem causis, quas in Aquarum perpetuo decurrentium historia aperui.
units.tr: Some lakes have singular qualities, arising from the same causes which I have explained in the history of running waters.

units.la: In Æthiopia Lacum esse ajunt nescio qui apud Isidorum, quo perfusa corpora velut oleo nitescant. In Suevia juxta Cœnobium cui Degere lacus nomen est, Aquas vidi Oleo perfusas.
units.tr: In Ethiopia, someone reports in Isidore, there is a lake in which bodies bathed in it shine as if anointed with oil. In Swabia, near the monastery called Degere, which takes its name from the lake, I have seen waters drenched in oil.

units.la: Clitorius Italiæ lacus, inquit Isidorus, Vini tædium parit.
units.tr: The Clitorius, a lake of Italy, says Isidore, produces a distaste for wine.

units.la: Bœotiæ quidam lacus, eodem scribente, furialis est: de quo qui biberit ardore libidinis exardescit.
units.tr: According to the same writer, a certain lake in Boeotia is maddening: whoever drinks from it is inflamed with the heat of lust.

units.la: In Velino lacu (qui hodie Lago de Terni, vel Lago de pie de Luco) dejectum lignum lapideo, quod notat Plinius, cortice obduratur. Sic in Cappadocia, inquit Vitruvius, lacus est, in quem pars arundinis si demissa fuerit, & postero die exempta, invenitur lapidea; pars autem, quæ extra lacum manserat, in sua permanet proprietate.
units.tr: In the lake Velinus (today Lago de Terni, or Lago de pie de Luco) a stick thrown in is hardened by a stony crust, as Pliny notes. So in Cappadocia, says Vitruvius, there is a lake into which, if part of a reed is lowered and taken out the next day, it is found to be stone; the part which had remained outside the lake keeps its own nature.

units.la: Notat Isidorus in Troglodytis lacum esse; qui ter in die fit amarus, deinde toties dulcis.
units.tr: Isidore notes that in the land of the Troglodytes there is a lake which becomes bitter three times a day and then sweet as often.

units.la: Quod nonnullis innatent gravia, & ad fundum in aliis ire solita; facit Bitumen & multa Pinguedo, quæ in Aquis gignitur à pinguibus Terræ, quæ tenax, lenta, picique non absimilis, venis: ex quibus scaturiunt vel per quas labuntur. Scribit Seneca libro vii. natural. Quæst. quosdam esse lacus, qui natandi imperitos ferant: item in Syria Stagnum esse, in quo lateres natant, & mergi projecta non possunt; licet sint graviora. Loquuntur posteriora de Asphaltite (cui nomen ἀσφάλτης, quod Bitumen Syriæ lacu; in quo, ut scribit variis locis Plinius, & ex eo Isidorus, nihil mergi potest, quod animam habet. De eo sic scribit ex Trogi Pompei lib. xxxvi. Iustinus: In ea regione Lacus est, qui propter magnitudinem & aquæ immobilitatem Mortuum Mare dicitur. Nam neque Ventis movetur, resistente turbinibus Bitumine, quo aqua omnis stagnatur: neque navigationis patiens est, quoniam omnia vita carentia in profundum merguntur, nec materiam ullam sustinet, nisi quæ alumine illinatur. Sic Solinus cap. Polyhist. xxxviii: Asphaltites gignit Bitumen: Animal non habet: nihil in eo immergi potest. Tauri etiam Camelique ibi fluitant. Nos ibi novimus admiranda Dei Opt. Max. iudicia; ut suo loco dicam.
units.tr: That some heavy things float on some lakes, while in others they usually sink, is caused by bitumen and much oily matter. This is produced in the waters from the fatty parts of the earth, which are tenacious, sluggish and not unlike pitch, and from the veins through which the waters well up or flow. Seneca, in book 7 of the Natural Questions, writes that there are some lakes which bear up those who cannot swim. Likewise in Syria there is a pool in which bricks float, and they cannot be made to sink when thrown in, though they are heavier. The latter remarks concern the Asphaltites (from the Greek ἀσφάλτης, bitumen), the lake of Syria in which, as Pliny writes in various places and Isidore after him, nothing that has life can sink. Of it Justin writes thus, from book 36 of Trogus Pompeius: "In that region there is a lake which, on account of its size and the immobility of its water, is called the Dead Sea. For it is not moved by the winds, the bitumen by which all its water is held still resisting the whirlwinds; nor is it fit for navigation, since all things lacking life sink to the depths, and it supports no material except what is smeared with alum." Likewise Solinus, Polyhistor chapter 38: "The Asphaltites produces bitumen; it has no animal life; nothing can be submerged in it. Even bulls and camels float there." We have learned there the wonderful judgments of God, the Best and Greatest, as I shall say in its place.

units.la: Est in Carnia lacus, qui singulis annis Meslem, Piscationem & Venationem præbet. Adcolæ Zircknitzerfee nominant ab opido Zircknitz, quod in ejus ora situm. Straboni, locus hic an lacus dicam? vocari putatur λίμνον, in Pannonia descriptum. Delineat Georgius Wernherus in aureo isto libello de admirandis Hungariæ Aquis.
units.tr: In Carniola there is a lake which every year yields a hay harvest, fishing and hunting. The inhabitants call it the Zirknitz lake, after the town Zirknitz, which lies on its shore. Whether I should call this a place or a lake is a question. It is thought to be the λίμνον [limnon] described by Strabo in Pannonia. Georgius Wernherus depicts it in that golden little book on the wonderful waters of Hungary.

units.la: In Helvetia haud procul Lucerna in editissimo monte lacus est Pilati cognomine, angustus admodum & Palus verius, quam Lacus: in quem quæ de industria injiciuntur maximas ciere tempestates, omniaque undis opplere adfirmant, qui sæpe tentarunt & experti: quæ vero casu incidunt nihil ad ferre periculi; quasi Lacus humano sensu intelligeret, culpa carere quod fit casu. Capit res fidem; quod pacatum irritare ausos, mox capitali fuisse adfectos supplicio ob inlatam adcolis calamitatem commemorent Lucernates.
units.tr: In Switzerland, not far from Lucerne, on a very high mountain, there is a lake called Pilatus. It is very narrow, and is more a marsh than a lake. Those who have often tried it affirm that whatever is thrown in deliberately raises the greatest storms and fills everything with waves, but whatever falls in by chance brings no danger; as if the lake perceived with human sense and was not at fault for what happens by chance. The matter gains credibility because the people of Lucerne report that those who dared to provoke the quiet lake were soon punished with capital punishment for the calamity brought upon the inhabitants.

units.la: Stagnum nihil aliud quam locus, in quo Aqua reses perpetuo stat; plurimum hieme colligi, æstate vero siccari solita. Nomen illi apud Servium ad i. Aeneid. & Isidorum lib. xv. à stando; vel, ut Varro innuit, quod Græce σταγνὸν. Utrumque Etymon indicat Festus, qui corruptior; emendandus facile ex superioribus. Τὸ ὕδωρ σταγνὸν vocat Dioscorides. Neque Stagna suis carent vel virtutibus, vel vitiis. Dicis gratia: Stagnum, inquit Solinus, Pentasium serpentibus noxium, hominibus salutare: Gelonium Siciliæ stagnum, Isidoro scribente, tetro odore proximantes abigit.
units.tr: A pool is nothing other than a place where still water stands perpetually, usually gathered mostly in winter and dried up in summer. Its name, in Servius on Aeneid 1 and in Isidore book 15, comes from standing; or, as Varro hints, because in Greek it is σταγνόν. Festus indicates both etymologies, though in a more corrupt form, which can easily be emended from what was said above. Dioscorides calls it "stagnant water" [τὸ ὕδωρ σταγνὸν]. Pools have their own virtues and vices too. For example, Solinus says the pool Pentasium is harmful to serpents and healthful to men; and Isidore writes that the Gelonian pool of Sicily drives away with its foul odour those who come near it.

units.la: Palus paullulum Aquæ in altitudinem & palam latius diffusæ, ait Varro lib. iv. de LL. Isidoro lib. xv. Orig. cap. xiii. à Pale Dea Pastorali; vel quod paleam, id est pabula nutriant jumentorum. Et his secretiorem inesse sæpe potentiam loquuntur vel Reatinæ Paludes; quibus lumentorum ungulæ perhibentur indurari, apud Isidorum: in earundem exitu Saxum crescere notat Plinius.
units.tr: A marsh is a little water spread out to some depth and over a broad surface, says Varro in book 4 On the Latin Language. Isidore, in Origins book 15, chapter 13, derives it from Pales, the goddess of pastures, or because it nourishes the fodder (palea, that is, the pasture) of cattle. That a more hidden power often lies in these is shown by the Reatine marshes, in which the hooves of beasts of burden are said to harden, according to Isidore. Pliny notes that a stone grows at their outlet.

units.la: CAP. XI. De Terra.
units.tr: CAP. XI. Of the Earth.

units.la: HÆc de Pellucidis Elementis: sequitur Opacum, Terra.
units.tr: So much concerning the transparent elements; there follows the opaque one, Earth.

units.la: Terra Elementum est opacum; quod, ut legere est apud Hyginum, Isidorum, alios, in media Mundi regione collocatum, omnibus partibus æquali passim intervallo diffidens, centrum obtinet Sphæræ: dicta, quod superiora ejus nostris pedibus terantur. Latinis etiam Humus; quod interiora ejus humeant, cum aliunde, tum ab Oceano percolante; unde eduxi paullo ante Fontes, Flumina, aliasque id genus Aquas: alioquin sua natura & indole est Arida; qua voce sæpe nota Sacris Litteris, יבשה, יבשה, יבשה, Genes. cap. 1. verf. 9. & 10, Psalm. xcv, 5. Ieichah xliv, 3. Ezech. xxxvii, 1. Tellus appellatur, quod quæ ad umbratilem hanc & acerbam vitam transfigendam homines inde tollamus. Multis aliis Nominibus & Cognominibus (aliarum Dearum non absurde ad hanc, ut scribit Varro apud Augustinum lib. vii. de Civitate Dei, cap. xiiii, revocatis) nuncupabatur. Ops cum alias ob causas, tum quod opera nostra fiat melior, vel potius, quod miseris nobis & calamitosis, Deo sic disponente, ferat opem; perituris, nisi sic ordinarie opitularetur. Varro lib. iv. de LL. (videndus idem apud Augustinum) Terra, Ops; inquit, quod hic omne opus ad vivendum. Et ideo dicitur Ops-Mater; quod Terra nutriat. Hæc enim Terræ gentes omnes peperit, & resumit denuo. Sic Macrobius Terram notat nominatam Opem, quod ejus ope vitæ humanæ alimenta quærantur: vel ab Opere, per quod fructus frugesque nascantur. Festus denique, Opis, ait, dicta est Conjux Saturni; per quam volunt Terram significari; quia omnes opes humano generi Terra tribuit. Δημήτηρ à Platone alijsque Philosophis & Poetis vocari scribit Theodoretus lib. iii. curat. Græc. ὡς δὴ μητέρα (alijs Δημήτηρ, quasi γῆ μήτηρ, legendus Cicero lib. ii. de nat. Deor.) καὶ τεο-φὸν θεων, τ ἐν αὐτῇ Δημιτωρῶν ἀπάντων. Orpheus: Γῆ μήτηρ πάντων, Δημήτηρ πλουτοδότειρα.
units.tr: Earth is the opaque element which, as one may read in Hyginus, Isidore and others, is placed in the middle region of the World, standing at an equal distance from all parts everywhere, and holds the centre of the sphere. It is so called because its upper surface is trodden by our feet. It is also called Humus in Latin, because its inner parts are moist, both from elsewhere and especially from the Ocean percolating through it; from which, a little earlier, I drew forth springs, rivers and other waters of that kind. Yet by its own nature and disposition it is dry; a word often noted in Sacred Letters: יבשה, יבשה, יבשה (Gen. 1:9–10; Ps. 95:5; Isa. 44:3; Ezek. 37:1). It is called Tellus, because by it we bear off what we need to pass this shadowy and bitter life. It was named by many other names and surnames (and those of other goddesses, not absurdly, are referred to this one, as Varro writes in Augustine, City of God, bk. 7, ch. 14). It was called Ops, both for other reasons, and because our work is made better by it, or rather because it brings help, by God's disposing, to us wretched and afflicted people, who would otherwise perish, unless it ordinarily helped in this way. Varro, On the Latin Language, bk. 4 (to be seen also in Augustine): Earth, Ops, he says, because all work for living is here. And therefore she is called Ops-Mother, because the Earth nourishes. For she has borne all the peoples of the earth, and takes them back again. So Macrobius notes that the Earth was named Ops, because by her aid the nourishments of human life are sought; or from Opus (work), through which fruits and crops are born. Festus, lastly, says: Ops was named the wife of Saturn; by whom they wish the Earth to be signified, because the Earth gives all riches to the human race. Theodoret, in the third book of his Cure of Greek Maladies, writes that Plato and other philosophers and poets called her Demeter, as if mother (others read Demeter as if γῆ μήτηρ, Earth Mother; see Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods, bk. 2): ὡς δὴ μητέρα καὶ τροφὸν θεῶν, ἐν αὐτῇ δημιουργῶν ἁπάντων [as the mother and nurse of the gods, in whom all creators are]. Orpheus: Earth, mother of all, Demeter the wealth-giver [Γῆ μήτηρ πάντων, Δημήτηρ πλουτοδότειρα].

units.la: Hinc est quod nonnullis ea fuerit habita Rerum omnium Principium, Xenophani, Hesiodo, aliis, ut libro primo monui. Hinc quod Mater: nam scribente Varrone, plurima parit; Cognomine etiam honorata Magna, apud Latinos veteres; cuius effigiem sic describit Varro apud Augustinum: Eamdem dicunt Matrem Magnam, quod Tympanum habeat, significari, esse Orbem Terræ, quod Turres in Capite, Oppida; quod Sedes fingantur circa eam, quum omnia moveantur, ipsam non moveri; quod Gallos, huic Deæ ut servirent, secerunt, significat eos, qui femine indigeant, Terram sequi oportere, in ea quippe omnia reperiri; quod se apud eam jactant, præcipitur, qui Terram colunt, ne sedeant, semper enim esse quod agant; Cymbalorum sonitus, ferramentorum jactandorum, ac manuum & cujusque rei crepitus in colendo agro, quid sit, significat, quod ferramenta illa erant ideo ex ære; quod antiqui colebant eam ære, anteaquam ferrum esset inventum. Leonem adjungunt solutum ac mansuetum; ut ostendant esse nullum genus Terræ tam remotum, ac vehementer ferum, quod non subigi colique conveniat. Quin Mater Deorum hominumque Priscis dicebatur. Orpheus: Γαῖα, θεῶν μήτηρ μακάρων, θνητῶν τ' ἀνθρώπων.
units.tr: Hence it is that by some she was held to be the Principle of all things, by Xenophanes, Hesiod and others, as I noted in the first book. Hence also she is Mother: for, as Varro writes, she bears very many things; she was honoured also with the surname Great among the ancient Latins. Varro, as cited by Augustine, describes her image thus: They say that the same is called the Great Mother, because she has a drum, which signifies that the Earth is a globe; that towers are on her head, which signify cities; that seats are imagined around her, since all things are moved while she herself is not moved; that the Galli were made to serve this goddess, which signifies that those who lack seed ought to follow the Earth, since in her all things are found; that they boast of themselves before her, and it is commanded that those who cultivate the Earth should not sit idle, for there is always something to do; the sound of cymbals, the clashing of tools and the din of hands and of each thing in tilling the field, signifies this, that those tools were of bronze, because the ancients cultivated her with bronze before iron was discovered. They attach a lion, loosed and tame, to show that there is no kind of earth so remote and so fiercely wild that it does not fit to be subdued and tilled. Indeed, among the ancients she was called Mother of gods and men. Orpheus: Earth, mother of the blessed gods and of mortal men [Γαῖα, θεῶν μήτηρ μακάρων, θνητῶν τ᾽ ἀνθρώπων].

units.la: Apollonius libro iii. Argonautic. Γαῖα, θεῶν μήτηρ, ὅσσον ἀνέχω ἐστὶν ἰμείο.
units.tr: Apollonius, book 3 of the Argonautica: Earth, mother of the gods, as far as I am able [Γαῖα, θεῶν μήτηρ, ὅσσον ἀνέχω ἐστὶν ἰμείο].

units.la: Plinius lib. ii. natur. hist. Sequitur Terra, cui uni rerum Natura partium eximia propter merita Cognomen indidimus materna venerationis. Nos nascentes excipit, natos alit, semel editos sustinet, & semper novissime complexa gremio, jam ab reliqua natura abdicatos, tum maxime, ut Mater operiens. Vesta Varroni, quod vestiatur herbis: vel quod vi sua stet, ut canit Ovidius in Fastis: Stat vi Terra sua, vi stando Vesta vocatur.
units.tr: Pliny, Natural History, bk. 2: Next comes the Earth, to whom alone Nature of things, for her outstanding merits, we have given the surname of maternal reverence. She receives us as we are born, nourishes those born, sustains those once brought forth, and, always embracing us last in her lap, as Mother covers us when we are already disowned by the rest of nature, most of all then. Vesta, according to Varro, because she is clothed with herbs; or because she stands by her own strength, as Ovid sings in the Fasti: The Earth stands by her own strength, and from standing by strength she is called Vesta.

units.la: Cicero dirivat ab Græcis; Ea enim est, inquit in libris de Natur. Deor. quæ ab illis Ἑστία dicitur: Vis autem eius omnis ad aras & focos pertinet. Alij volunt Hebræx esse originis nomen, compositum ex אש, quod Ignis, & יה quod unum ex nominibus Dei. Γῆ ἀπὸ ... cadem Terra nominatur; quod rebus omnibus adiuvat. Ceres ab Græca voce τῆρυς; ita enim prius,ut quidam censent,appellabatur. Hesychius: Ἀ-χερὼ ἓ Ω᾿αις, ἡ Ἐλλὴ, ἡ Τῆρυς, ἡ Γῆ, ἡ Δημήτηρ, ἡ αὐτή: Ciceroni non inconvenienter à Creando vel Gerendo, lib. iii. de natura Deorum. Proserpina Varroni apud Augustinum, Terra; quod fruges inde proserpant.
units.tr: Cicero derives it from the Greeks; for she is, he says in the books On the Nature of the Gods, the one called by them Hestia; and her whole power pertains to altars and hearths. Others wish the name to be of Hebrew origin, compounded from אש, which means fire, and יה, which is one of the names of God. Γῆ, from ... she is named Earth, because she helps all things. Ceres comes from the Greek word τῆρυς (for so, as some think, she was first called). Hesychius: Ἀχερὼ, Ὠαις, ἡ Ἑλλὴ, ἡ Τῆρυς, ἡ Γῆ, ἡ Δημήτηρ, ἡ αὐτή. Cicero, in the third book On the Nature of the Gods, not inappropriately derives it from creare or gerere. Proserpina, according to Varro in Augustine, is the Earth, because fruits creep forth from her (proserpere).

units.la: Fecit, ut alia omnia, & hanc Deus; & fecit ex Nihilo: quod pluribus explicatum libro primo.
units.tr: God made this one, as all other things, and he made it out of nothing; this has been explained at more length in the first book.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CAP. XII.

units.la: De Forma Terræ.
units.tr: On the Form of the Earth.

units.la: INN Forma Terræ describenda variatum olim, ut videre est cum apud alios, tum apud Plutarchum ... Leucippo putabatur Τυμπανοειδής; Heraclito, Σκαφοειδής; Anaximandro, Κυλινδροειδής; Democrito, Κοίλη; Empedocli & Anaximeni, ὁμαλὸς; Aliis etiam Πυραμοειδής; Nonnullis, Κυδοειδής: quorum omnium opiniones doctissime refutant non solum Veteres,sed & Recentiores. Fuerunt & qui Terrarum orbem in formam litteræ Græcæ ω effigiarunt; ut extremum lineamentum, quod O litteram ambit, Oceanum referat designetque; quem ζωσηρα κόσμος, Mundi Baltheum, quidam dixerunt,ut Probus Grammaticus testatur.
units.tr: In describing the form of the earth, opinions varied in former times, as may be seen both in other writers and in Plutarch. Leucippus was thought to hold it drum-shaped [Τυμπανοειδής]; Heraclitus, boat-shaped [Σκαφοειδής]; Anaximander, cylinder-shaped [Κυλινδροειδής]; Democritus, hollow [Κοίλη]; Empedocles and Anaximenes, level [ὁμαλὸς]; others, pyramid-shaped [Πυραμοειδής]; some, wedge-shaped [Κυδοειδής]. The older and the more recent writers alike refute all these opinions very learnedly. There were also those who fashioned the orb of the lands in the form of the Greek letter omega, so that the outermost line, which encircles the O, represents and marks the Ocean, which some have called the girdle of the world [ζωσηρα κόσμος], as the grammarian Probus testifies.

units.la: Terra, non σφαῖρα, quæ ubique ὁμαλὴ; sed revera σφαιροειδὴς habens ἀσοχὰς καὶ σφαιροειδὴς: quæ tamen in tanta mole vix deprehenduntur; ut non immerito Pilæ simili Ovidio,quaqua versum rotundam adsimilans figuram, circumfluo mari præcincta globosum constituens corpus & unam superficiem.
units.tr: The earth is not a sphere [σφαῖρα], which would be level [ὁμαλὴ] everywhere, but is truly spheroidal [σφαιροειδὴς], having hollows and prominences. Yet these are scarcely detected in so great a mass; so, not without reason, Ovid likened it to a ball [pilae simili], rounded in every direction, girt about by the encircling sea, and so forming one globular body with a single surface.

units.la: Formam hanc cum circumfusis Aquis habere Terram, ostendit partim Universi, cui Partes omnes amica quadam concordia consentiunt, rotunditas; de qua ego alibi: deinde (quid enim evidentius?) Lunæ Defectio, in qua ejus umbra non quadrangula, non triangula, non multiangula; sed absoluta rotunditate cernitur. Evincunt idem alia non pauca cum secundum Longitudinem, tum Latitudinem. Illius quidem habita ratione: 1. Solis,Lunæ, Stellarum non eodem Ortus, non eodem Occasus omnibus tempore. Prius enim inlucescunt habitantibus ad Orientem, inde qui ad Occidentem. 11. Eclipses, quæ,licet eadem, aliis tamen horis in Oriente videntur, aliis in Occidente; circuitu globi scilicet eas nunc his detegente, nunc illis occultante: ut nobili apud Arbela Alexandri Magni victoria Luna defecisse noctis hora quinta prodita est, quæ Karthagine secunda, ut est apud Ptolemæum lib. 1. cap. iv. Sic Solis Defectum,C. Vipsanio Poplicola Aproniano & C. Fonteio coss. anno ab V.C. 10 ccccxii, factum pridie Kal. Maias Campania hora diei inter septimam & octavam sensit;Corbulo Dux in Armenia inter horam diei decimam & undecimam prodidit risum: quemadmodum memoriæ tradit Plinius lib. 11. c. lxx. natur. histor.iii. Variantia Noctium Dierumq; diversis Terræ locis Initia & spacia. Sidera enim non simul omnibus in conspectum veniunt; sed paullatim evehuntur successione quadam & serie, apparentque Orientalibus prius,deinde occidentalibus post evictum superatumque Terræ tumorem, qui inter utrosque eminens Occidentalibus objiciebatur,& stellas ab eorum conspectu diutius abscondebat. Secundum Latitudinem; inæqualia Poli Ἐξάρματα sive Elevationes. Hæ namque nonnullis in locis sunt nullæ; ut exempli gratia;in Insulis Moluccæis, media Taprobana, Insula D. Thomæ; quæ sub Æquinoctiali, ideoque Poli sunt illis in Finiente:Alibi Majores,ut Syene(quæ Ægypti urbs Ptolemæo,hodie China,ut notat Niger)23½,quia sub Cancri Tropico; Alexandriæ 31-0; inRhodo 36-0; Romæ 41-50; Venetijs 45-0; Dordraci (quæ urbs Hollandiæ primaria & metropolis,carissima mihi patria)52-30. Alibi tursum,sed alio modo, nullæ; ubi scilicet Polus ad perpendiculum verticibus imminet.
units.tr: That the earth has this shape, with the waters poured around it, is shown partly by the roundness of the universe, in which all the parts agree in a certain friendly harmony (of which I speak elsewhere); then by the eclipse of the moon, which (what could be more evident?) shows its shadow not square, not triangular, not many-angled, but of perfect roundness. Many other things prove the same, both with respect to longitude and to latitude. As to longitude, the following considerations apply: (1) The rising and setting of the sun, moon and stars do not occur at the same time for all. For they shine first on those who dwell to the east, and afterwards on those to the west. (2) Eclipses, which are the same in every case, nevertheless are seen at different hours in the east and in the west, since the circuit of the globe reveals them now to these, now to those, and hides them from others. Thus the eclipse of the moon at the famous victory of Alexander the Great at Arbela is recorded as having occurred in the fifth hour of the night, whereas at Carthage it was the second, as Ptolemy has it, book 1, chapter 4. Likewise the eclipse of the sun, in the consulship of C. Vipsanius Poplicola Apronianus and C. Fonteius, in the year 10 ccccxii from the founding of the city, which occurred on the day before the Kalends of May, was felt in Campania between the seventh and eighth hours of the day; while the general Corbulo, in Armenia, reported a darkening between the tenth and eleventh hours of the day, as Pliny records in book 2, chapter 70 of his Natural History. (3) The beginnings and lengths of nights and days vary in different places of the earth. For the stars do not come into view for all at the same time, but rise gradually in a certain succession and series, appearing first to those in the east and afterwards to those in the west, once the swelling of the earth, which rose between the two and blocked the western peoples, has been surmounted and overcome, and which kept the stars hidden from their sight for longer. As to latitude, the elevations of the pole [Ἐξάρματα], that is, its heights, are unequal. In some places they are none at all: for example, in the Moluccas, in the middle of Taprobane, in the island of St. Thomas, which lie under the equator, and where the pole is therefore on the horizon. Elsewhere the elevations are greater: at Syene (which for Ptolemy is a city of Egypt, but today is China, as Niger notes) 23½, because it lies under the Tropic of Cancer; at Alexandria 31; at Rhodes 36; at Rome 41 50′; at Venice 45; at Dordrecht (the chief city and metropolis of Holland, my dearest homeland) 52 30′. Elsewhere, again in another way, there are none, namely where the pole hangs directly over the zenith.

units.la: Suffragantur huic sententiæ principes Philosophi; cum primis Plato in Timæo, Aristoteles lib. 11. de Cœlo, text.104, & lib. 1. Meteoror. & tota Stoicorum schola. Sic M. Tullius lib. de natura Deorum 11: Fademque ratione Mare, quum supra Terram sit, medium tamen Terræ locum expetens, conglobatur undique æqualiter, neque redundat unquam, neque effunditur. Strabo lib. iii: Τ' ποκείσθω δὲ σφαιροειδὴς ἡ γῆ, σωῷ τῇ ἁλάττῃ, μίας ἡ τῶν αὐτῶν ... ἐχυρᾶ τῆς πλάγια. Manilius etiam lib. 1. Astronomic nomic. multis Terræ rotunditatem adstruit: quæ brevitati studens, lubens præterco. Homerus idem videtur sensisse; quum Terram Ἀ'πείρονα, id est σφαιροειδῆ, dixerit; propter orbicularem figuram, initio pariter ac fine carentem: ut exponunt Heraclides, Eustathius, & Ioannes Grammaticus Aristotelis enarrator. Sic Numa Pompilius, secundus Romanorum Rex, Terram Pilæ forma credens esse, quemadmodum Sex. Pompeius Festus notat, Aedem Vestæ rotundam consecravit, ut sui simili li templo Dea coleretur.
units.tr: This view is supported by the leading philosophers, above all Plato in the Timaeus, Aristotle in book 2 of On the Heavens, text 104, and book 1 of the Meteorology, and the whole school of the Stoics. So Marcus Tullius in book 2 of On the Nature of the Gods: And by the same reasoning the sea, although it lies above the land, yet seeking the middle place of the earth, is rounded evenly on all sides, and never overflows or spills out. Strabo, book 3: Let the earth be supposed spherical, with the sea... [Τ' ποκείσθω δὲ σφαιροειδὴς ἡ γῆ, σωῷ τῇ ἁλάττῃ]. Manilius also, in book 1 of his Astronomica, asserts the roundness of the earth in many passages; but I, wishing to be brief, gladly pass them over. Homer seems to have held the same view, when he called the earth boundless [Ἄπειρον], that is, spherical, because of its orbicular shape, having neither beginning nor end, as Heraclides, Eustathius and John the Grammarian, the commentator on Aristotle, explain. So Numa Pompilius, the second king of the Romans, believing the earth to be of the form of a ball, as Sextus Pompeius Festus notes, consecrated a round temple to Vesta, so that the goddess might be worshipped in a temple like the earth.

units.la: Quæ dixi non obscure confirmat Sacra Scriptura. Hæc enim sæpe Terram nominat תבל orbem. Propheta Rex Psalm. ix, 9: Et ipse judicabit orbem (תבל) Idem Psalmo xxiv. 1. Domini Terra & plenitudo ejus: orbis (תבל) & habitantes in eo. Legend. & Psalm. xlviii, 7, 9, l, 12, lxxvii, 19. lxxxix, 12, xcvi, 13. Nach. i, 5. Sic Iesaiah. cap. xxxiv, 1. Accedite Gentes ad audiendum, & Populi attendite: audiat Terra & plenitudo ejus; orbis (תבל) & omnia germina ejus. Augustius Schelom. Proverbior. cap. viii; ubi Sapientia: Ludens in Orbe Terræ (בתבל ארצו) & delectationes meæ in filiis hominum. Quin &, ne quis dubitationi locus relinquatur, Iesaiah. cap. xl, 22. Qui sedes super globum Terræ (על-חוג הארץ) & habitatores ejus ut Locustæ.
units.tr: Sacred Scripture plainly confirms what I have said. For it often calls the earth tebel [תבל], the world. The prophet-king in Psalm 9:9: And he himself shall judge the world [tebel]. The same in Psalm 24:1: The earth is the Lord's, and the fullness thereof; the world [tebel] and they that dwell therein. See also Psalm 48:7, 9; 50:12; 77:19; 89:12; 96:13; Nahum 1:5. So Isaiah 34:1: Draw near, ye nations, to hear, and hearken, ye peoples; let the earth hear, and the fullness thereof, the world [tebel] and all the things that spring from it. In Proverbs 8, where Wisdom speaks, rejoicing in the habitable part of the earth [bethebel arzo] and my delights are with the sons of men. Moreover, lest any room for doubt be left, Isaiah 40:22: He that sits upon the circle of the earth [al-chug ha-arets] and its inhabitants are as grasshoppers.

units.la: Terra igitur est rotunda, huc illuc in æquabilem tumorem adsurgens. Nam excelsi Montium vertices, declivesque Vallium descensus cum totius Terræ vastitate commisti inæqualitatem nullam pariunt aut diversitatem; habentque se in hac mole Montes altissimi verrucarum instar in manu; Valles autem, etiam profundissimæ, ut rimæ in magno globo. Quod magis: Inæqualitas, si ita appellanda, Montiumque & Vallium distinctio mirum est quam faciat ad decorem, ornatum, commoditatem Terræ. Ejus enim beneficio temperatior Aeris salubritas, laetior Frugum Herbarumque fertilitas, major rerum omnium maturitas; franguntur Maris impetus; Ventorum furor refrænatur; Fontes Fluminaque versus declivia provomuntur, & ad varia longinquaque loca decurrunt. Eleganter Rupertus lib. 1. de Trinitate & ejus operibus, cap. xxxiv: Quid opus erat, inquit, eidem Aridæ ita ut Terræ, ut ascenderent Montes, & descenderent Campi in locum, quem fundasti eis? Hic planè illud sciendum est: quia si Terra æqualis ubique jaceret; non lexior, quam in Mari, ventorum tempestas in ea regnaret. Nam solet & nunc in locis illis, qui Montibus carent, videlicet maxime in Libya, tempestas, non minus quam in Pelago, turbare foris deprehensos quoscumque tam Pedites, quam equo sedentes. Etenim ubi per loca æqualia & nuda Ventus coortus arenam humo excitavit, magna vi agitat ora oculosque implet; & ita progressum incessumque impedit, ut in nullo Mari Malus fiat naufragium. Quid si nulli usquam Montes ascendissent si cuncta in planum Terra descendisset? Si, ubi paululum Ventus currere licet, tantas vires brevi colligunt: quid possent, si nullum in toto Mundo haberent repagulum? Ergo nec istud magnificis DEI laudibus deesse debuit, quod ascendunt Montes & descendunt Campi in locum, quem ille fundavit eis: fundavit, inquam, videlicet ut neque Montes, semel ascendere jussi, descendant; neque Campi, semel depressi, consurgant. Quum ita Terræ fundatur Abyssum, quæ sicut Vestimentum amictus ejus erat, dispulit; eadem ipse potentia competens Aquarum subsidium large diffudit, &c.
units.tr: The earth is therefore round, rising here and there into an even swelling. For the highest peaks of mountains and the deepest descents of valleys, when mixed with the vast extent of the whole earth, produce no inequality or diversity worth mentioning; and in this mass the highest mountains stand like warts on a hand, while the valleys, even the deepest, are like cracks in a great globe. What is more, this inequality, if it must be so called, and the distinction of mountains and valleys, is marvellously useful for the beauty, adornment and convenience of the earth. For by its benefit the air is more temperate and healthful, the fruits and herbs more fertile and abundant, and everything matures more fully. The assaults of the sea are broken, the fury of the winds is curbed, and springs and rivers are sent down the slopes and run to various distant places. Rupert writes elegantly in book 1 of On the Trinity and its Works, chapter 34: What need was there, he says, for mountains to rise and plains to sink into the place which you have founded for them, to the same dry land as the earth? Here it must be clearly understood that if the earth lay level everywhere, the storm of the winds would reign over it no less than on the sea. For even now, in those places which lack mountains, namely chiefly in Libya, a storm disturbs no less than on the open sea any who are caught out there, whether on foot or on horseback. For wherever the wind, arising over level and bare ground, stirs up the sand from the soil, it drives it with great force, fills the mouth and eyes, and so hinders the progress and passage that no ship is wrecked in such a sea. What if mountains had nowhere risen, and the whole earth had sunk into the plain? If the wind, where it is allowed to run only a little, gathers such strength in a short space, what could it do if it had no barrier anywhere in the whole world? Therefore this also ought not to be lacking from the magnificent praises of God, that mountains rise and plains sink into the place which he founded for them: founded, I say, so that the mountains, once bidden to rise, do not sink again, and the plains, once depressed, do not rise again. When he had thus founded the earth, he drove back the abyss, which was as a garment for its covering; by the same power he poured out abundantly the help of the waters, etc.

units.la: In memoriam hic inducor stultæ quorumdam Opinionis, existimantium, Terram ante Diluvium, totam æqualiter rotundam fuisse, nulla celsiorum humiliorumque Locorum inæqualitate; post Diluvium autem hanc, quam in Terra conspicimus, Montium Vallumque distinctionem inductam fuisse. Adversatur manifesto Sacra Scriptura: quæ Genef. cap. vii, docet Aquas Diluvii quindecim cubitis omnes Terræ Montes supergressas. Propheta David Psalmo lxxvi, 5. Montes nominat æternos. Sapientia etiam apud Schelomon. Proverb. viii, demonstrandæ suæ Antiquitati, dicit se fuisse, priusquam in prima rerum creatione, Montes gravi mole consisterent.
units.tr: Here I am reminded of the foolish opinion of some, who think that before the Flood the whole earth was equally round, with no inequality of higher and lower places, and that after the Flood the distinction of mountains and valleys which we see in the earth was introduced. Sacred Scripture plainly contradicts this, for Genesis 7 teaches that the waters of the Flood rose fifteen cubits above all the mountains of the earth. The prophet David, in Psalm 76:5, calls the mountains eternal. Wisdom also, in Proverbs 8, to show her antiquity, says that she existed before the mountains were settled in their heavy mass at the first creation of things.

units.la: Aquam porro, cum qua Terram sphæricum dixi constituere corpus, sua natura conglobari & habere κυρτότητα, superioribus demonstravi; ideoque ejus nihil hic repetendum: illud autem hinc perspicuum; Terram simul & aquam uni Centro initi, ijsdem concludi Verticibus; dehiscentes Terræ partes Aqua subeunte atque explente.
units.tr: I have shown above that water, with which I said the earth forms a spherical body, is by its nature gathered into a globe and has convexity [κυρτότητα]; therefore nothing of that need be repeated here. This, however, is clear from it: the earth and the water together tend to one centre and are bounded by the same poles, the parts of the earth that open up being filled as the water flows in and fills them.

units.la: CAP. XIIII.
units.tr: CAP. XIIII.

units.la: De Fine creati Terrarum Orbis.
units.tr: Concerning the end for which the orb of the earth was created.

units.la: TERRÆ totius dominium, jus & gubernatio DEI Creatoris est propriè: usus vero hominum, maximè Piorum Iustorumq;, Injustorum autem & Impiorum usurpatio est & abusus. Psalm. xxiv, 1: Domini est Terra & plenitudo ejus: orbis Terrarum, & universi qui habitant in eo. Et cxv, 16: Cælum Cæli Domino; Terram autem dedit filijs hominum. Item xxxvii, 9. Quoniam qui malignantur, exterminabuntur: sustinentes autem Dominum ipsi hereditabunt Terram: & paulo post: Mansueti autem hereditabunt Terram, & delectabuntur in multitudine pacis. Ius illud Potestatemque sibi perpetuo servatam notat ipse DEus, apud Iesaiam, cap. lxvi, his verbis: Cælum, Sedes mea: & Terra, Scabellum. Si in Scabellum à DEO occupata: facile quisquis es intellegis, sanctam esse habendam; neque vel verbo vel facto temerandam: quo pertinet IESV CHRISTI monitum apud Matthæum cap. v, Neque per terram jurabitis.
units.tr: Dominion over the whole earth, its right and government, belong properly to God the Creator. The use of it by men, above all by the pious and just, is theirs; the seizing and abuse of it belongs to the unjust and impious. Ps. xxiv. 1: The earth is the Lord's, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein. And cxv. 16: The heaven, even the heavens, are the Lord's: but the earth hath he given to the children of men. Likewise xxxvii. 9: For evildoers shall be cut off: but those that wait upon the Lord, they shall inherit the earth. And a little after: But the meek shall inherit the earth; and shall delight themselves in the abundance of peace. God himself marks this right and power, reserved to himself for ever, in Isaiah lxvi, in these words: Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool. If the earth is taken by God as his footstool, you easily understand, whoever you are, that it is to be held holy and not to be profaned by word or deed. To this belongs the admonition of Jesus Christ in Matthew v: Neither shalt thou swear by the earth.

units.la: Terra igitur vel in Terra Sedes hominum; ut ibi crescerent & multiplicarentur, eamque replerent & subjicerent; Piscibus Maris, Cœli Volatilibus, omnibusque Terræ Animantibus dominando, Geneseos cap. i, verf. 26. & 27, & cap. viii, verf. 17.
units.tr: The earth, then, or a place on the earth, is the dwelling of men, so that there they might grow and multiply, fill the earth and subdue it, having dominion over the fish of the sea, the birds of the air, and every living thing that moves upon the earth: Genesis i. 26, 27, and viii. 17.

units.la: Sedes hæc initio angustior finibusque descripta contractioribus. Terra enim primo cœpit habitari, ubi in Syria Damascenus Ager: inde itum, non admodum remote, versus Orientaliora; ubi Urbem Cainus condidit, indito filij Henoch nomine, Genes. cap. iv, 16, 17. Augustiora, prolatis longe lateque Pomœrijs, facta sunt omnia post Diluvium: quo, ob hominum intemperantiam & contaminata per impiarum mulierum consortium matrimonia, terribili cataclysmo cuncta Terrarum inundarunt, universumque genus humanum horrendum in modum perierat; Noæo cum Uxore, tribus filijs Iapheto, Schemo & Chamo, eorumque Conjugibus servato. Ab his horumque posteris divina providentia, in diebus Peleg (הַפְלֵג Dividere est) ex Schemi posteritate, divisus est totus Terrarum orbis, missis huc illuc in omnes Mundi partes Colonis: His omnium Gentium origines debentur: Hi Majores nostri & Progenitores. Cyprianus in libro de Sina & Sion adversus Iudæos (suppositititius tamen mihi semper visus hic liber, Cypriani nomen, ut Lectorem invitet, præferens) & Augustinus tract. ix. & x, in Euangel. Ioannis, tradunt, si nomen Adam Græce scribatur, quatuor constare litteris; à quibus quatuor voces incipiunt, significantes quatuor Mundi partes, Ἀνατολή, Oriens; Δύσις, Occidens: Ἄρκτος Septemtrio; Μεσημβρία Meridies: quod Adami posteritas per omnes Orbis plagas esset dispergenda. Sed acutum hoc magis censeo, quam verum. De prosemimato ab his humano genere Terraque habitatoribus completa, scribunt universum Iosephus & Epiphanius. Ille quidem lib. i. Antiquit. Iudaicar. Iapheto septem fuisse filios: horum sedes, à Tauro & Amano montibus incipientes, pertinuisse in Asiam ad amnem usque Tanaim; in Europa usque Gades: Chami vero filios Syriam, & regionem Amano Libanoque montibus hærentem obtinuisse: quidquid ejus ad Mare vergit occupando, & Oceanum usque ditionis terminos proferendo: Schemo denique filios fuisse quinque, colsque Asiam usque ad Oceanum Indicum incoluisse; ab Euphrate propagandæ ditionis initio facto. Epiphanius vero (& ex eo Zonaras) libro ii. contra hæreses in refutatione Errorum ab Manichæis factorum; Noæum, velut hæredem Mundi ab DEO constitutum, tribus filijs suis divisisse universum Mundum sub sortem missum, & unamquamque partem juxta sortem singulis distribuisse: Schemo quidem primogenito (fatum hoc, ut mox monebo) sortem cecidisse à Persida & Bactris usque in Indiam, usque ad regionem Rhinocorurorum sitam; hanc esse in medio inter Ægyptum & Palæstinam: Chamo obtigisse terram ab Rhinocorurorum regione usque ad Gadira in Meridiem: Iapheto denique forte fuisse adsignatum quidquid spectat in Aquilonem, à Media usque ad Rhinocoruros.
units.tr: This dwelling was at first narrower and bounded by smaller limits. For the earth first began to be inhabited where the Damascene field lies in Syria; from there men moved, not very far, towards the east, where Cain founded a city and named it after his son Enoch: Genesis iv. 16, 17. Everything became more confined after the Flood, though the boundaries were later extended far and wide. Because of human intemperance, and marriages polluted by the fellowship of ungodly women, the Flood with its terrible cataclysm overflowed all the lands, and the whole human race perished in a dreadful manner, save Noah with his wife, his three sons Japheth, Shem and Ham, and their wives. From these and their descendants, by divine providence, in the days of Peleg (פֶּלֶג, "division"), the whole orb of the earth was divided, from the posterity of Shem, colonists being sent hither and thither into all parts of the world. To them the origins of all nations are owed; they are our ancestors and progenitors. Cyprian, in his book On Sinai and Zion, against the Jews (a book I have always thought spurious, though it bears Cyprian's name to attract the reader), and Augustine in tractates ix and x on the Gospel of John, report that if the name Adam is written in Greek it consists of four letters, with which four words begin that signify the four quarters of the world: Ἀνατολή, East; Δύσις, West; Ἄρκτος, North; Μεσημβρία, South, because Adam's posterity was to be scattered through all the regions of the earth. But I judge this to be more clever than true. Concerning the early spreading of the human race, and the filling of the earth with its inhabitants, Josephus and Epiphanius write at length. Josephus, in book i of the Jewish Antiquities, says that Japheth had seven sons, whose dwellings, beginning from the Taurus and Amanus mountains, extended in Asia as far as the river Tanais, and in Europe as far as Gades. The sons of Ham took Syria and the region clinging to the mountains Amanus and Lebanon, occupying whatever slopes towards the sea and extending their borders as far as the Ocean. Lastly, Shem had five sons, who inhabited Asia as far as the Indian Ocean, having begun the spread of their rule from the Euphrates. Epiphanius (and Zonaras after him), in book ii of his Against Heresies, in the refutation of the errors of the Manichaeans, says that Noah, appointed by God as heir of the world, divided the whole world among his three sons, sending each by lot, and that he assigned each part to each by lot: to Shem the firstborn (a fate, as I will shortly note) fell the region from Persis and Bactria as far as India, as far as the region of the Rhinocorurans; this lies midway between Egypt and Palestine. To Ham fell the land from the region of the Rhinocorurans southward as far as Gadira. Lastly, to Japheth perhaps was assigned whatever lies towards the north, from Media to the Rhinocorurans.

units.la: Ordiar igitur ab Iapheto, unde & Sacra Scriptura; ut qui primogenitus. Nam maximum hunc esse natu: Schemum medium; minimum vero Chamum: Schemum autem primo loco nominari Electionis & Benedictionis prærogativa, multis argumentis contra Epiphanium loco paullo ante laudato, & Aurelium Augustinum lib. vi. de Civitate Dei cap. iii. aliosque probare, non est vel hujus loci vel mei instituti. Illud in præsentia Lectori sufficerit: quod Chamus sit postremus Noæi filiorum, apparere ex cap. Genes. ix. verf. 24: ubi dicitur Noæus rescivisse, quæ in se admisisset Chamus filius ipsius natu minimus: Schemum vero non esse liberorum Noæi natu maximum; ex eo constare, quod liberos coeperit tollere Noæus, quum annum ageret quingentesimum; cujus anno postea sexcentesimo terras occupavit Diluvium, ut docent quæ leguntur Genes. v, 32, & vii, 6: biennio autem post diluvium Schemum genuisse Arpacshad, tum quum annum ageret centesimum, ut scribitur Genes. cap. xi, 10. ideoque nondum centum fuisse annorum ipso Diluvij tempore; ex eo demique sequi, natum ipsum Schemum; biennio post annum patris quingentesimum; & necessario relinqui, Iapetum liberorum Noæi natu maximum sive primogenitum, & patris anno quingentesimo fuisse procreatum: postremo convinci hinc versum 21.c. x.
