Genes. וּלְשֵׁם יָלַד נָם יְרוּא, sic esse vertendum; Ipsi quoque Scheme nati sunt liberi, qui parens est generis Hebrei, & frater Iapheti librorum Noæ natu maximi: non ut vulgo; Dei Sem quoque nati sunt patre omnium filiorum Heber, fratre Iapheti majore. Alia huic rei probandæ argumenta prætereo. Ad rem nostram.
units.tr: I will begin, then, with Japheth, as Sacred Scripture does, since he was the firstborn. For this one was the eldest, Shem the middle, and Ham the youngest. That Shem is named first, with the privilege of election and blessing, I leave to be proved against Epiphanius in the passage cited a little above, and by Augustine in City of God book vi, chapter 3, and others; this is neither the place nor the purpose of my work. For the reader it will suffice at present to note the following: that Ham was the youngest of Noah's sons appears from Genesis ix. 24, where it is said that Noah learned what his youngest son Ham had done to him; and that Shem was not the eldest of Noah's children is clear from the fact that Noah began to have children when he was five hundred years old, and in the six hundredth year of his life the Flood covered the earth, as Genesis v. 32 and vii. 6 teach. Shem begot Arpachshad two years after the Flood, when he was a hundred years old, as is written in Genesis xi. 10; therefore he was not yet a hundred at the time of the Flood. From this it follows that Shem himself was born two years after his father's five hundredth year. It must necessarily be concluded that Japheth was the eldest or firstborn of Noah's children and was born in his father's five hundredth year. Finally, this is confirmed from verse 21 of Genesis x, where the Hebrew וּלְשֵׁם יָלַד גַּם הוּא (ulshem yalad gam hu) must be rendered: To Shem also children were born, who is the father of the whole Hebrew race, and the brother of Japheth the eldest son of Noah; not as commonly rendered: To Shem also, the father of all the sons of Eber, the brother of the elder Japheth, sons were born. I pass over other arguments for proving this. Back to our matter.

units.la: Iaphetus (יֶפֶת) maximam totius orbis partem obtinuit; occupatis Maris Magni vel Mediterranei Insulis, & tota Europa, cum maxima Asiæ parte. Quod futurum præsciens Noæus, bene feliciterque illi precatur, Genes. cap. x. verf. 27, his verbis: יַפְתְּ אֱלֹהִים לְיֶפֶת וִישְׁכֹּן בְּאָהֳלֵי שֵׁם: Septuaginta Interpretes sic convertunt: πλατύναι ὁ Θεὸς τῷ Ἰαφὲθ, καὶ κατοικησάτω ἐν οἴκοις Σήμ; Dilatet Deus Iapheturn, & habitet in Tabernaculis Sem: innuens amplissimas ab hoc filio suo regiones occupandas esse, eumque inserendum quasi in Semi fratris familiam. Et sane factum illud. Non enim solum receptus fuit in partem bonorum Semi, missis in Asiam Africamque Colonis; verum etiam locum adeptus est singulari beneficio, in Ecclesia & Domo Dei: notus, ut primus Europæorum parens, Græcis Latinisque Scriptoribus; qui de eo multa confinxerunt mendacia, prorsus quæ legantur indigna; petita ex Satanæ, qui vera falsorum adspersione solet, quantum potest, obscurare, & paullatim supprimere, scrinijs & officina. Illud non absurdum neque ofcitanter excogitatum, unum ex Iapheti filijs fuisse Promethcum; ab eo hominem ex limo Terræ fictum; Ignemque Iovis ad homines ex Cœlo delatum: hanc fortean ob causam: quod ex ipsius sermonibus doctrina de Creatione προνοήσει ad Gentes emanarit: quodque veram Sapientiam, quæ est radius Lucis divinæ, Doctrinam nimirum de Deo, Præcepta de Moribus, & Leges Motuum cœlestium alijs tradiderit. Unde ab Hesiodo nominatur; Ἰαπετιονίδης πάντων τῶν μήδεα εἰδώς.
units.tr: Japheth (יֶפֶת) obtained the greatest part of the whole world: he occupied the islands of the Great or Mediterranean Sea and all of Europe, together with the greater part of Asia. Foreseeing this, Noah blessed him well and happily, in Genesis x. 27, in these words: יַפְתְּ אֱלֹהִים לְיֶפֶת וִישְׁכֹּן בְּאָהֳלֵי שֵׁם (yaft Elohim leYefet veyishkon be'ohalei Shem). The Seventy translate thus: πλατύναι ὁ Θεὸς τῷ Ἰαφὲθ, καὶ κατοικησάτω ἐν οἴκοις Σήμ: May God enlarge Japheth, and let him dwell in the tents of Shem. This signifies that the most extensive regions were to be occupied by this son, and that he was to be grafted, as it were, into the family of his brother Shem. And indeed that happened. For he was not only received into a share of Shem's goods, colonists being sent into Asia and Africa; he also obtained a place by a singular favour in the Church and the house of God. He is known, as the first parent of the Europeans, to Greek and Latin writers, who have invented many lies about him, altogether unworthy of being read. These were drawn from Satan, who is accustomed to obscure the truth, as far as he can, by sprinkling it with falsehoods, and to suppress it gradually in his cabinets and workshops. It is not absurd or carelessly devised that one of Japheth's sons was Prometheus, who, they say, formed man from the clay of the earth and brought the fire of Jove from heaven to men; perhaps for this reason: that from his discourses the doctrine of creation by providence spread to the Gentiles, and that he taught others true wisdom, which is a ray of divine light, namely the doctrine concerning God, precepts concerning morals, and the laws of the heavenly motions. Hence Hesiod calls him: Ἰαπετιονίδης πάντων τῶν μήδεα εἰδώς (Iapetionides, who knew all the cunning arts).

units.la: Iapheti genus sic proponit Spiritus Sanctus Genes. x, 2. Filij Iapheti: Gomer, & Magog, & Madai, & Iavan, & Tubal, & Meschec, & Tiras.
units.tr: The Holy Spirit thus sets out Japheth's family in Genesis x. 2: The sons of Japheth: Gomer, and Magog, and Madai, and Javan, and Tubal, and Meshech, and Tiras.

units.la: Gomer, גֹּמֶר, pater Gomeritarum, qui populi Asiatici, Iudæis ad aquilonem siti. Horum auxilia Gogo rei contra Dei populum adducenda recensit Iechezkel cap. xxxviii, verf. 6. Gomer & universa agmina ejus, domus Togorma, latera Aquilonis (יַרְכְּתֵי צָפוֹן) & totum robur ejus, populique multi tecum: ubi latera Aquilonis indicant, quas habuerint regiones. Non abludit ab Gomeritis Cimmeriorum appellatio; quos circa Mæotidem Paludem & Bosporum Cimmerium (sic ab his cognominatum, ubi & opidum Cimmerium Straboni, Plinio, alijs) & circa Colchidem locant Herodotus lib. iiii, & Ptolemæus lib. v: quosque cum Georgijs juxta mare Caspium nominat Plinius. Ab his ortos volunt nonnulli Cimmerios Campaniæ circa Baias apud Strabonem, & Cimbros Germaniæ populos Septemtrionales apud eumdem, à quibus Cimbrica Chersonesus, quæ nunc Holsatiam, Iutiam, aliasque ditiones complectitur. Plerique Josephum sequuti ab Gomero progenitos volunt Comeritas, quos postea Græci Galatas dixerunt. Atque Græcis Galatæ sunt Galli; à quibus profecti ij, qui Delphos spoliarunt, & postea in Asia haud procul Troade consederunt, dicti sunt Gallograeci, & Galatæ Asiani, qui Phrygiæ partem maiorem occuparunt, ut suo loco dicam. Refutandis, quæ de gentium Originibus, cum in Biblicis Indicibus nullo judicio scripta, tum sub Berosi, qui nuper nobis ab audacula quodam obtrusus, nomine vulgata leguntur, tempus non teram, Lectoremque non morabor. Vana sunt ibi omnia putidaque; & quod Berosum illum suppositicium ejusque Commentatorem attinet, mendaciorum plaustra meraeque Viterbiensium nugae.
units.tr: Gomer, גֹּמֶר [Gomer], father of the Gomerites, who were Asiatic peoples living north of the Jews. Ezekiel lists their auxiliaries whom Gog was to bring against God's people, in chapter 38, verse 6: Gomer and all its hordes, the house of Togarmah, the sides of the north (יַרְכְּתֵי צָפוֹן) and all its might, and many peoples with you. Here the sides of the north indicates the regions they held. The name Cimmerians does not differ from Gomerites. Herodotus (book 4) and Ptolemy (book 5) place the Cimmerians around the Maeotian Marsh and the Cimmerian Bosporus (so named by them, where Strabo, Pliny and others also mention the town Cimmerium), and around Colchis. Pliny names them together with the Georgians near the Caspian Sea. Some hold that the Cimmerians of Campania around Baiae, according to Strabo, and the Cimbri, northern peoples of Germany, according to the same author, were descended from them, and that from them comes the Cimbric Chersonese, which now includes Holstein, Jutland and other territories. Most, following Josephus, hold that the Comeritae, whom the Greeks later called Galatians, were descended from Gomer. To the Greeks the Galatians are the Gauls. Those who came from them, who plundered Delphi and afterwards settled in Asia not far from Troas, were called Gallo-Greeks, and the Galatians of Asia, who occupied the greater part of Phrygia, as I shall say in its place. I will not waste time refuting what is written about the origins of the nations in the biblical indexes, without any judgment, and under the name of Berosus, which is read in the common editions, having been foisted on us lately by some audacious fellow; nor will I detain the reader. All of it is empty and foul. As for that spurious Berosus and his commentator, they are wagonloads of lies and pure Viterbo trifles.

units.la: Gomero tres fuerunt filij, ut eodem capite vers. 3. docemur: Porro filij Gomer Aschenaz, Riphath, Togorma.
units.tr: Gomer had three sons, as we are taught in the same chapter, verse 3: Moreover the sons of Gomer: Ashkenaz, Riphath, Togarmah.

units.la: Aschenaz, אשכנז: LXX. Interpretibus, Ἀσχανάζ. Ab eo populi Asiatici, in Medorum regnis conlocati, vel certe Medis finitimi; quod manifestum ex Iechezkelis cap. L. vers. 27. ubi Aschenaz commemorantur aliis Gentibus, ad Medorum regna pertinentibus. Sic enim ibi scriptum: Levate signum in terra, clangite in Gentibus, significate super eas Gentes, annunciate contra illam Regibus Ararat, Menni, Aschenaz. Agitur de Excidio Babylonis; & Medis eorumque sociis & auxiliariis, in quis Aschenazei, per quos Chaldaeorum imperium esset exstirpandum. Iosephus Aschenaz appellari scribit ab Graecis Rheginos; Eusebius dissentiens Gentes ait esse Gothicas; aetatis nostrae Iudaei Alemannos vocant Aschenazim: omnes levibus usi conjecturis, de quibus alias. Sunt etiam, qui volunt ab Aschenaz denominatam cum Asciniam Asiae Minoris regionem, cujus meminit Homerus 6 & 7 Iliados, ubi & Ascania Palus, ex qua fluvius Ascanius Troiae vicinus, Ptolemaeo & Straboni: tum Siciniam, quae hodie Sicilia apud Solinum & alios. Quin & quidam Hiftiam hinc derivant, & Saxoniam ob vocum similitudinem.
units.tr: Ashkenaz, אשכנז: in the Septuagint, Ἀσχανάζ [Aschanaz]. From him came Asiatic peoples, settled in the kingdoms of the Medes or at least neighbouring the Medes. This is clear from Ezekiel chapter 50, verse 27 (as printed), where the Ashkenazites are mentioned along with other nations belonging to the kingdoms of the Medes. For there it is written: Lift up a standard in the land, sound the trumpet among the nations, sanctify the nations against her, summon against her the kingdoms of Ararat, Minni, and Ashkenaz. The passage concerns the destruction of Babylon, and the Medes with their allies and auxiliaries, among whom were the Ashkenazites, through whom the empire of the Chaldeans was to be overthrown. Josephus writes that Ashkenaz is called by the Greeks Rheginoi. Eusebius, disagreeing, says the peoples are Gothic. Jews of our own age call the Alemanni Ashkenazim. All of them use slight conjectures, about which more elsewhere. There are also those who hold that the region of Asia Minor called Ascinia was named from Ashkenaz, which Homer mentions in Iliad 6 and 7, where also is the Ascanian marsh, from which the river Ascanius near Troy flows, according to Ptolemy and Strabo. Then there is Sicinia, which today is Sicily, according to Solinus and others. Indeed some derive Hesse from it, and Saxony because of the similarity of the words.

units.la: Riphath, רפת, secundus Gomeri filius. Ab hoc qui descenderint, historia sacra non docet. Iosephus lib. 1. Antiquit. Iudaicar. cap. xi. & D. Hieronymus putant nomen hunc dedisse Riphatis (vel, ut Mela lib. 1. Riphatibus) qui postea Paphlagones nuncupati. Riphaeos etiam Montes nominant Ptolemaeus, Mela, & alij, in Sarmatia & Scythia: qui quamquam ibi nulli, videntur tamen ab Riphath appellationis originem invenisse.
units.tr: Riphath, רפת, the second son of Gomer. Sacred history does not teach who descended from him. Josephus (Antiquities of the Jews, book 1, chapter 11, as printed) and St Jerome think this name gave rise to the Riphathi (or, as Mela says in book 1, the Riphathibus), who were later called Paphlagonians. Ptolemy, Mela and others also name the Riphaean Mountains in Sarmatia and Scythia. Although no such people are found there, they seem nonetheless to have found the origin of the name in Riphath.

units.la: Togorma תוגרמה, tertius. Ab eo genus ducunt Togormei populi Asiatici; Iudaeis ad Aquilonem; qui Syriae Asiaeque Regibus paruerunt. Nam Ezechieli cap. xxxviii, vers. 6. Togormaei, Iudaeorum respectu, תרבת צפון, Latera Aquilonis describuntur inter eos, quos Gogus Syrarum Gentium dux, secum adversus Israelitas trahit ad bellum. Conjectura est, Togormaeos fuisse, qui deinde Cappadoces. Sic enim Iechezkel cap. xxvii. versu 14: De domo Togorma Equos, Equites & Mulos (פרדים) adduxerunt ad forum tuum. habet enim Cappadocia Mulas, quae pariant, ut notat Theophrastus, quod ibi sit animal sui generis, quemadmodum scribit Plinius lib. viii. natur. histor. cap. xliv. Alij volunt Togormam progenitorum esse Populorum Armeniae, quorum Reges Tigranes; quibusque opida non pauca Τιγρανοκέρτα, quas Appianus lib. de bellis Mithradaticis & alij Graece scribunt sonare Tigranopoles, Κέρτα enim Parthorum lingua πόλις, docente Stephano; apud quos denique fons nobilissimi fluvij Tigris. Alij, inter quos Zonaras, litteris mandant ad Togormam referre genus Tigranos, qui deinde Phryges dicti. Nonnulli Togormaeos Tartaros interpretantur; alij Turcas, & inde hodieque Iudaeis Turcarum Imperatorem Togar nominari. Alijs Togorma censetur Germania quod Chaldaeus interpres Iechezkelis illa cap. xxvii, vers. 14, quae paullo ante laudavi, sic reddiderit: Gomer & omnis exercitus ejus, provincia Germanica, (מדינת גרמניא, proprie regio Germaniae) fines Aquilonis. Priorum conjecturae ex vocis tantum similitudine sunt natae: posteriori nullus locus, quod nihil commercii potuerit esse Germanis cum Tyrijs, tanto terrarum intervallo dissitis. Interim quid apud Chaldaeum Paraphrastem גרמניא fateor, nondum liquet, & ampliandum hic censeo. Est quidem apud Plinium Germanicopolis, quae & Boofcatae, & Helgas, Asiae Minoris urbs; est item Germanicia, Galatiae, scribente Paulo Diacono; tertia denique ejusdem nominis, ut indicat Ptolemaeus, in Syria juxta Amanum Montem: sed, quod nomina illarum recentiora, ut alibi probabo, nihil ad Togormaeos. Incertior illorum divinatio, quibus Togormaei Moscovitae, qui & Albi Rutli. Pergo incoepta paullo ante prosapia.
units.tr: Togorma, תוגרמה [Togarmah], the third son. From him trace their descent the Togarmites, Asiatic peoples north of the Jews, who obeyed the kings of Syria and Asia. For in Ezekiel 38, verse 6, the Togarmites, from the Jews' point of view, the sides of the north (תרבת צפון as printed), are described among those whom Gog, leader of the Syrian peoples, takes with him to war against the Israelites. It is a conjecture that the Togarmites were those who afterwards were called Cappadocians. For Ezekiel 27, verse 14: From the house of Togarmah they brought horses, riders and mules (פרדים) to your market. Cappadocia has mules that bear young, as Theophrastus notes, because there is a peculiar animal there, as Pliny writes in Natural History, book 8, chapter 44. Others hold that Togarmah was the ancestor of the peoples of Armenia, whose kings were Tigranes, and whose many towns were called Τιγρανοκέρτα [Tigranokerta]. Appian, in his book on the Mithridatic wars, and others write in Greek that this means Tigranopolis, for κέρτα means city in the language of the Parthians, as Stephanus teaches. Among these peoples is the source of the very famous river Tigris. Others, among whom is Zonaras, record in writing that the family of Tigranes, who were afterwards called Phrygians, traces back to Togarmah. Some interpret the Togarmites as Tartars, others as Turks, and hence even today the Jews call the emperor of the Turks Togar. Others think Togarmah is Germany, because the Chaldee paraphrast rendered Ezekiel 27, verse 14, cited a little earlier, thus: Gomer and all its army, the German province (מדינת גרמניא, properly the region of Germany), the borders of the north. The former conjectures arose merely from similarity of the word. The latter has no basis, since the Germans could have had no commerce with the Tyrians, separated from them by so great a distance of lands. Meanwhile I confess that it is not yet clear what גרמניא means in the Chaldee Paraphrast, and I think it should be examined further here. There is indeed in Pliny Germanicopolis, which is also called Boscata and Helgas, a city of Asia Minor. There is also Germanicia in Galatia, according to Paul the Deacon, and a third of the same name, as Ptolemy indicates, in Syria near Mount Amanus. But since those names are more recent, as I will prove elsewhere, they have nothing to do with the Togarmites. Less certain is the guess of those who make the Togarmites the Muscovites, who are also called White Ruthenians. I return to the line of descent I began a little earlier.

units.la: Magog, מגוג, secundus Iepheti filiorum. Ab hoc populus Coelesyriae, Magog. Plinius lib. v. natur. histor. cap. xxiii. in Syriae descriptione: Nunc interiora dicuntur. Coele habet Apamiam, Marsyam amne divisam ab Nazerinorum Tetrarchia. Bambycem, quae alio nomine Hierapolis, vocatur; Syris vero Magog. Notat distinctis verbis Magog Cœlesyriæ populum: quem Gentium illarum fuisse primum, arguit nomen Græcum Hierapolis, sacra augustaque Syrorum urbs: cujus, vel regionis potius, principem vocat Iechezkel Gogum cap. xxxviii, verf. 1: Et factus est sermo Domini ad me, dicens: Fili hominis, pone faciem tuam contra Gog. & terram Magog principem Capitis Meschec & Tubal. Imperat summus ille Imperator; Propheta se convertat ad Gogum, qui habitabat regionem Magog, summusque regnator erat Meschec & Tubal. Magog enim regionem apud Prophetam denotare, paret (ut bene doctèque notat Matthæus Beroaldus Chronici sui libro. iiii, cap. vi, qui, quod lubens agnosco, magnus & certus mihi dux fuit ad explorandum veras Patrum istorum migrationes.) ex Hebraica voce המגוג. ה enim illud Emphaticum proprijs Virorum nominibus numquam præjicitur; Locorum, frequenter. Gog igitur rex trium populorum Magog, Meschec, Tubal. Indicat hoc & alius Prophetæ locus cap. xxix: Tu autem fili hominis, vaticinare adversus Gog; & dices, Hæc dicit Dominus DEVS: Ecce ego super te Gog, principem capitis Mesechec & Tubal. Sic in Apocalypsi cap xx. verf. 8. nominantur Gog & Magog excitandi ab Satana adversus Civitatem sanctam: Gog enim ibi Reges & Principes, capitales populi DEi hostes, Magog autem, qui auxiliares illis ad injuriam & vim faciendam. Iosephus, ne aliorum sententias prætereat, & sequutus eum Zonaras, ab Magogo Magogas deducunt; quos Græci Scythas Νομάδας & Αμαξοίας nominant. Alij; Massagetas & Getas hinc trahunt.
units.tr: Magog, מגוג [Magog], the second of Japheth's sons. From him comes the people of Coele-Syria, Magog. Pliny, book 5, chapter 23, in his description of Syria: Now the inland parts are called... Coele has Apamea, divided by the river Marsyas from the tetrarchy of the Nazerini. Bambyce, which by another name is called Hierapolis; but by the Syrians, Magog. He clearly names Magog as the people of Coele-Syria. That this was the first of those nations is shown by the Greek name Hierapolis, a sacred and venerable city of the Syrians. Ezekiel calls its prince, or rather the prince of the region, Gog, in chapter 38, verse 1: And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, set your face against Gog, and the land of Magog, the chief prince of Meshech and Tubal. The supreme commander gives the order: the prophet is to turn to Gog, who inhabited the region of Magog and was the supreme ruler of Meshech and Tubal. That Magog in the prophet denotes a region is evident (as Matthaeus Beroaldus notes well and learnedly in book 4, chapter 6 of his Chronicle, who, as I gladly acknowledge, was a great and reliable guide to me in establishing the true migrations of those fathers) from the Hebrew word המגוג. For that ה is emphatic and is never prefixed to the proper names of men, though it frequently is to the names of places. Gog, therefore, is king of the three peoples, Magog, Meshech and Tubal. Another passage of the prophet indicates this, chapter 29 (as printed): But you, son of man, prophesy against Gog, and say: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against you, Gog, prince of the chief of Meshech and Tubal. So in Revelation chapter 20, verse 8, Gog and Magog are named as those to be stirred up by Satan against the holy city. For Gog there denotes the kings and princes, the chief enemies of God's people, while Magog denotes those who serve as their auxiliaries in doing injury and violence. Josephus, not to pass over the opinions of others, and Zonaras following him, derive the Magogites from Magog; the Greeks call them Scythians, Νομάδας [Nomadas] and Ἁμαξοίας [Hamaxoias]. Others derive the Massagetae and the Getae from this name.

units.la: Madai, מדי, natu tertius, nomen dedit Medis Imperij Babyloniorum eversoribus, qui passim in Sacris Monimentis appellatione מדי significantur: lib. ii Regum, capite xvii, 6. Ieschahih. cap. xiii, 17. Iirmeiæ cap.xxv. 25. & Li, 11,25. Danielis cap. vi. 8. 12, 15. viii,20. ix, 1.
units.tr: Madai [מדי], the third son, gave his name to the Medes, the conquerors of the Babylonians. In the Sacred Monuments they are everywhere designated by the name מדי: 2 Kings 17:6; Isaiah 13:17; Jeremiah 25:25 and 51:11; Daniel 6:8, 12, 15; 8:20; 9:1.

units.la: Iavan, יון Hinc Iones, qui postea cum aliis gentibus concesserunt in nomen Græcorum. Quæ causa; quod, quum Ieschahih. cap lxvi, verf. 19, יון, Interpretes Septuaginta dixerint Ἑλλάδα: quod apud Iechezkel cap. xxvii. verf. 19. vox יון, Latino Interpreti versa sit Græcia, ijsdem vero Interpretibus ἰάδες: quod in Prophetia Ioelis cap. iii. verf. 6. יוני ijsdem sint Ἕλληνες, Latinis Græci: quod denique Alexander Magnus Danieli cap. viii, 21. מלך יון, Septuaginta dicatur Βασιλεὺς Ἑλλήνων, Latino Interpreti Græcorum Rex; & cap x, verf. 20. יון Septuaginta ἀρχων τῶν Ἑλλήνων, Latino Princeps Græcorum. Nondum me pœnitet conjecturæ, Ianum Latinis eundem esse, qui Hebraïs יון: &, quum Iapheto pars orbis, quæ Europa hodie, forte obtigisset, esse verisimile Iavano (κατὰ συναίρεσιν, Iano) quidquid sequentibus sæculis Græciæ, Italiæ, vicinarumque Regionum innotuit appellatione, fuisse adsignatum. Græci, qui multo post tempore sequuti, quum putarent Progenitorem suum nominatum ab Hebraica voce יון quæ illis οἰν@, Iavanum suo Idiomate Οὐνοτρὸς; Terram vero, quam imperio regebat, eam præcipue quæ in Italia Sedes illi regia, Οἰνωτρία; Incolas οἰνωτρίους appellarunt. Videndi Dionysius lib. i. Antiquitat. Romanar. Virgilius lib. i. Æneidos, & ibi Servius. Non immerito igitur Ianus Antiquissimus Divum, respectu Italiæ, apud Iuvenalem, Satyra vi. Deorum Deus, Salijs apud Macrobium lib. i. Saturnalior. cap. ix; ubi etiam Mundus, ut & Incertioribus apud Arnobium lib. iii, adverf. gent. & Augustinum lib. vii, de Civit. Dei, cap. vii, viii, & ix; Mundi Sator, Martiali lib. x. epigr. xxviii: fingiturque jure primus in Italiam Colonias duxisse, scribente Dionysio Halicarnassi. lib. i. Antiquit. Roman. primus Diis Templa fecisse, Ritus instituisse Sacrorum, à Xenone apud Macrobium loco laudato; Aes signasse, eidem Macrobio cap. vii; primus Navigia, tumultuarios pontes & alia invenisse, ut notat Dracon Corcyræus apud Athenæum lib. xv. Ἀδηνομφις. Bifrons denique pingitur cum ob alia, tum quod duorum esset Populorum progenitor, Græcorum Latinorumque; quibus initio multa fuerunt communia, in primis Lingua: nam in Latina Græcæ non pauca vestigia. Clamant & aperte Græcam originem non solum, in ipsa Italia, Magna Græcia: sed infinitæ etiam locorum opidorumque passim appellationes.
units.tr: Javan [יון]. From him came the Ionians, who afterwards, together with other peoples, passed into the name of the Greeks. The reason is this. In Isaiah 66:19 the Septuagint rendered יון as Hellada [Ἑλλάδα]. In Ezekiel 27:19 the Latin translator rendered the word יון as Greece [Græcia], while the same Septuagint translators rendered it as Iades [ἰάδες]. In Joel 3:6 the Hebrew יוני is rendered by the Septuagint as Hellenes [Ἕλληνες] and by the Latin as Greeks [Græci]. Finally, in Daniel 8:21, where the Hebrew reads מלך יון, the Septuagint has king of the Hellenes [Βασιλεὺς Ἑλλήνων] and the Latin translator king of the Greeks [Græcorum Rex]; and in Daniel 10:20 the Septuagint has ruler of the Hellenes [ἀρχων τῶν Ἑλλήνων] and the Latin prince of the Greeks [Princeps Græcorum]. I still do not regret the conjecture that Janus among the Latins is the same as the Hebrew יון. Since the part of the world which is today Europe probably fell to Japheth, it is likely that whatever became known in the following centuries under the name of Greece, Italy and the neighbouring regions was assigned to Javan (by contraction, Ian). The Greeks, who came much later, supposing that their forefather was named from the Hebrew word יון, which for them was οἰν@, called Javan in their own idiom Οὐνοτρὸς; and the land he ruled, especially that part in Italy where his royal seat was, they called Οἰνωτρία, and its inhabitants οἰνωτρίους. See Dionysius, book 1 of the Roman Antiquities, and Virgil, book 1 of the Aeneid, with Servius there. Not without reason, then, is Janus called the most ancient of the gods [Antiquissimus Divum] with respect to Italy by Juvenal, Satire 6; the god of gods [Deorum Deus] by the Salii in Macrobius, Saturnalia 1.9; where also the World [Mundus] (as also in the Incertiores cited by Arnobius, Against the Nations, book 3, and by Augustine, City of God 7.7–9), and maker of the world [Mundi Sator] in Martial 10.28. And he is fabled, rightly, to have first led colonies into Italy, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus writes in book 1 of the Roman Antiquities; to have first built temples to the gods and instituted rites of worship, according to Xenon in Macrobius, cited above; to have struck bronze coinage, in the same Macrobius, ch. 7; and to have invented ships, makeshift bridges and other things, as Dracon of Corcyra notes in Athenaeus, book 15. Finally he is painted two-faced, both for other reasons and because he was the progenitor of two peoples, the Greeks and the Latins, among whom at the beginning there was much in common, above all language: for in Latin there are not a few traces of Greek. Moreover, not only in Italy itself but also in countless names of places and towns, they proclaim a Greek origin, Magna Graecia.

units.la: Iavani progenies sic nobis describitur eodem capite x, verf. 4. Filij autem Iavan Elisha, Tarschisch, Kittim, Dodanim.
units.tr: The progeny of Javan is described for us thus in the same chapter 10, verse 4: And the sons of Javan: Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim, and Dodanim.

units.la: Elisha, אלישה, posteri videntur occupasse Insulas Maris Mediterranei. Persuadet Propheta Iechezkel cap. xxvii, 7. Hyacinthus & Purpura de Insulis Elisha (מאיי אלישה: Septuaginta Interpret. ἐκ νήσων Ἑλισα) facta sunt operimentum tuum. Quid moveric Chaldæum Paraphrasten, ut pro אלישה verteret איטליא, nondum video. Sic enim ait: Byssus & varia tinctura de Ægypto fuit tibi velum, ut esset tibi in signum. Hyacinthus & purpura מדינת איטליא, id est, de provincia Italia, fuit operimentum tuum. Intelligit certe Iechezkel Cycladas Ægæi maris Insulas: è quibus, ut suo loco dicam, Purpura prioribus sæculis, multo antea quam Tyrijs, Getulis, aliisque nota esset, petebatur. Insulæ igitur Maris Mediterranei peculium Elischæ nepotum, quorum etiam nonnulli, Magnum emensi Mare, Fretumque inter Africam Europamque pervecti, videri non incommode possunt ad Insulas illas Fortunatas, quas ab Elischa suo Græci Campos Eliseos nuncuparunt, profecti: quorum longinquam à primis sedibus navigationem in majus deinde posteri, falsa veris admiscentes, extulerunt. Nomen Elischæ mansisse videtur aliquibus non solum in Æolo, qui Ventorum, id est Insularum in Mari Ægæo, Rex celebratur: sed & in Aeolide, quæ regio Minoris Asiæ ad Orientaliora Maris, quod dixi, Hul Hebræis hodieque. Quin Strabo notat Aeoles habitos olim omnes populos extra Isthmum, præter Athenienses & Megarenses. Sunt etiam, qui volunt ab Elischa ἡλέασ, Peloponnesi regiunculam apud Strabonem, quæ ἡλας Ptolemæo; Græcosque omnes ΕʹΑλωας denominatos.
units.tr: Elishah [אלישה]: his descendants seem to have occupied the islands of the Mediterranean Sea. Ezekiel 27:7 confirms this: Blue and purple from the isles of Elishah (מאיי אלישה; the Septuagint, ἐκ νήσων Ἑλισα) were your covering. I do not yet see what moved the Chaldee paraphrast to render אלישה as איטליא. For he says: Fine linen and varied dye from Egypt was your sail, that it might be a sign to you. Blue and purple from the province of Italy (מדינת איטליא), that is, from the province of Italy, was your covering. Ezekiel certainly means the Cyclades, the islands of the Aegean Sea; from these, as I shall say in its place, purple was fetched in earlier centuries, long before it was known to the Tyrians, Getulians and others. The islands of the Mediterranean, then, may not inappropriately be regarded as the portion of Elishah's descendants, some of whom, having crossed the great sea and passed through the strait between Africa and Europe, may be thought to have set out for those Fortunate Isles, which the Greeks from their Elisha called the Elysian Fields. Their long voyage away from their first homes later generations magnified, mixing false things with true. The name Elishah seems to have remained for some not only in Aeolus, who is celebrated as king of the winds, that is, of the islands in the Aegean Sea, but also in Aeolis, the region of Asia Minor toward the eastern parts of the sea I mentioned, which the Hebrews still call Hul today. Indeed Strabo notes that all peoples outside the Isthmus were once considered Aeolians, except the Athenians and the Megarians. There are also those who wish that Elis (ἡλέασ), a little region of the Peloponnese in Strabo, which is ἡλας for Ptolemy, and all Greeks, were named from Elishah.

units.la: Tarschisch, תרשיש, dedit nomen Tarsensibus, qui Tarsum Cilicum metropolin incolunt. Psalmo. lxxii. vers. 10. Reges Tarsis (מלכי תרשיש) & Insulæ munera offerent; ubi Chaldæus Paraphrastes, מלכיא דמרסים, Reges Tharsensium, id est, Cilicum & conregionalium populorum. Sunt etiam, qui putant Karthaginiensibus originem hinc esse, quum credo viderent Septuaginta Interpretes illa Ieschahih. xxiii. 1. הילילו אניות תרשיש, Vlulate Naves Tarsis, vertere, ὀλολύζατε πλοῖα Καρχηδόνος, Vlulate Navigia Karthaginis: Iechezkelis item cap. xxvii, 13: Seba & Deda & Negociatores Tarsis, סחרי תרשיש; dicere, Σαβὰ καὶ Δαυδὰν καὶ Ἐμπορoι Καρχηδόνιοι: Iirmeiæ denique verba cap. x, 9: Argentum involutum de Tarsis (מתרשיש) adfertur, & aurum de Ophir. Chaldæum Paraphrasten interpretari מאפריקא, Africam. Sed quam late pateat vox תרשיש, & quo modo sint, quæ ex Prophetis citantur, accipienda, doctissime docet Matthæus Beroaldus, quem paullo ante laudavi. Porro Tarschisch, vel ut alii, Tubalis Nepotes putantur fuisse Sepharad & Sarphad: & ab illo quidem Hesperia, quam nunc Hispaniam dicimus; ab hoc vero Gallia, denominatæ: quæ, ut ambigua & parum explorata, in medio relinquenda censeo.
units.tr: Tarshish [תרשיש] gave its name to the Tarsians, who inhabit Tarsus, the metropolis of Cilicia. In Psalm 72:10: The kings of Tarshish (מלכי תרשיש) and the isles shall bring gifts; where the Chaldee paraphrast has מלכיא דמרסים, the kings of the Tarsians, that is, of the Cilicians and peoples of the same region. There are also those who think the Carthaginians have their origin here, since they believe the Septuagint translators rendered Isaiah 23:1, הילילו אניות תרשיש, Howl, ships of Tarshish, as ὀλολύζατε πλοῖα Καρχηδόνος, Howl, ships of Carthage; likewise Ezekiel 27:13: Sheba and Dedan, and the merchants of Tarshish (סחרי תרשיש), they rendered as Σαβὰ καὶ Δαυδὰν καὶ Ἐμπορoι Καρχηδόνιοι; and finally the words of Jeremiah 10:9: Silver beaten into plates (מתרשיש) is brought from Tarshish, and gold from Uphaz. The Chaldee paraphrast renders it as מאפריקא, from Africa. But how widely the word תרשיש extends, and how the passages cited from the Prophets are to be understood, is most learnedly taught by Matthew Beroaldus, whom I praised a little earlier. Further, Tarshish, or as others hold, the descendants of Tubal, are thought to have been Sepharad and Sarphad; and from the former indeed Hesperia, which we now call Spain, and from the latter Gaul, were named. These names, as ambiguous and not sufficiently ascertained, I think should be left undecided.

units.la: Kittim, כתים, tertio loco inter filios Iavani: qua voce non tam ejus filius, quam ab filio descendentes designantur: quos Interpretes Septuaginta nunc Κιτιαίους, nunc χιτιεῖμ, retento Hebraico vocabulo, nominant. Kittimos esse Italos, Romanos, illisque confinales populos (ubi & Caieta, quidquid fabulantur Poetæ & ex ijs alij, vetus nomen tueri putatur) docent varij variarum, quæ passim in Sacra Scriptura, Prædictionum eventus. Et hinc Interpretes semper Gentes illas in animo oculisque quasi habuerunt. Numeror. cap. xxiv, 24. Venient in Trieribus, כתים, de Italia, superabunt Assyrios, vastabuntque Hebræos, & ad extremum etiam ipsi peribunt. Chaldæus Paraphrastes, ne quis dubitet de Romanis exaudienda: Et naves venient ab Romanis, מן רומאי, & adfligent Assyriam &c. Iechezkel xxvii, 6: Quercus de Basan dolaverunt in remos tuos, & transtra tua fecerunt tibi ex Ebore Indico, & Pratoriola de Insulis כתים, Latin. Interp. Italiæ; Chald. Paraphrast. מדינת אפליא de Provincia Apuliæ, quæ Italiæ pars. Daniel denique cap.xi, 30: Et venient super eum Trieres, & כתים, Latinus Interpres, Romani, (quos & Hebræi ipsi atque Rabbini ibi censent intelligendos) & percutietur, & revertetur, & indignabitur contra testamentum sanctuarij, & faciet: reverteturque, & cogitabit adversum eos, qui dereliquerunt testamentum Sanctuarij. Nonnulli per כתים intelligunt cum Italis Romanisque etiam Macedonas. Nam, vastator Tyri, Alexander Magnus educitur apud Ieschahih. cap. xxiii, ex terra כתים: Idem lib. 1. Machab. cap. i. scribitur egressus ex terra כתים. Sic Philippus & Perseus Macedoniæ principes, quos vicerunt Romani, Reges nominantur Cethæorum lib.Machab. eodem, cap. viii. Ad hæc, Macedoniæ partem Maxetia (in cujus posterioribus latere videtur nonnihil vocis כתים) fuisse dictam, scribunt Stephanus & Hesychius; idemque nomen paullatim totam regionem accepisse, refert Eustathius in Dionysium; unde & ipsi populi nunc Macedones, nunc Maxim, apud eundem Stephanum in Geographico Lexico, vel Macetes, ut eos vocant Ausonius, & Vegetius lib.iii, de re militari, cap.xxii. Iosephus כתים vult esse Cyprum, scribens veteris appellationis vestigium ibi servari in urbe Kitiæ: quam veteres Tabulæ mihi monstrant ad Euroaustrum in Sinu, quem faciunt duo Promontoria Throni & Dades: recentiores vero opidum Chiti nominant ad Promontorium Occidentalius; quod Dades olim, ut dixi, hodie ab ipsa urbe, Capo Chiti. Est tamen, ne quid dissimulem, ubi vetus quondam, si Tabulæ Geographicæ non fallant, Kinev, & nunc fere (nam paullo versus Septemtrionem & Mediterranea) opidum Chidia: sed plenius hæc in mea Cypro. Alij simpliciter כתים interpretantur Kinoῶ, regionis apud Ptolemæum in Cilicia; Incolas. Quidquid sit, כתים non solum Cyprij, Macedones, Itali, Romani Sudas in voce Λαπιvε, Cereos in Italiam ductos indicat ab Latino Telephi filio; sed omnes, quæ Hebræis Transmarinæ Gentes, videntur explicandi.
units.tr: Kittim [כתים], third in order among the sons of Javan: by this word not so much his son as those descending from the son are designated. The Septuagint translators render them now as Κιτιαίους, now as χιτιεῖμ, keeping the Hebrew word. That the Kittim are the Italians, the Romans, and the peoples bordering on them (where also Caieta, whatever the poets fable and others after them, is thought to preserve the old name) is shown by the various outcomes of various predictions found everywhere in Sacred Scripture. And from this the interpreters always had those nations, as it were, before their minds and eyes. Numbers 24:24: Ships shall come from the coasts of Chittim (כתים), from Italy; they shall overcome Assyria, and afflict the Hebrews, and at last they too shall perish. The Chaldee paraphrast, lest anyone doubt that the Romans are to be understood: And ships shall come from the Romans (מן רומאי), and shall afflict Assyria, etc. Ezekiel 27:6: Oaks of Bashan they have hewn for your oars, and your benches they have made of ivory of India, and your decks from the isles of Chittim; the Latin translator has of Italy; the Chaldee paraphrast has מדינת אפליא, from the province of Apulia, which is part of Italy. Finally Daniel 11:30: And ships shall come against him, and Chittim, which the Latin translator renders Romans (whom the Hebrews themselves and the rabbis there judge should be understood), and he shall be struck down and return, and be indignant against the covenant of the sanctuary, and shall act: and he shall return and take thought against those who have forsaken the covenant of the sanctuary. Some understand by כתים, along with the Italians and Romans, also the Macedonians. For Alexander the Great, the destroyer of Tyre, is brought out of the land of Chittim in Isaiah 23; the same is written in 1 Maccabees 1, that he came out of the land of Chittim. So Philip and Perseus, princes of Macedonia, whom the Romans conquered, are called kings of the Cittaeans in 1 Maccabees 8. Besides, Stephanus and Hesychius write that a part of Macedonia was called Maxetia (in whose later part something of the word כתים seems to lie), and Eustathius on Dionysius reports that this name gradually came to be applied to the whole region; whence the peoples themselves are now called Macedonians, now Maximi, or Macetae, as Ausonius and Vegetius (On Military Affairs, book 3, ch. 22) call them, according to the same Stephanus in his Geographical Lexicon. Josephus wants כתים to be Cyprus, writing that a trace of the old name survives there in the city Kitiae. Old maps show me this town to the southeast, in the gulf made by the two promontories Throni and Dades; more recent ones call the town Chiti, on the western promontory, which Dades formerly was, as I said; today it is called Capo Chiti, from the town itself. There is, however, lest I conceal anything, a place where, if the geographical tables do not deceive, there was once Kinev, and now almost (for a little toward the north and inland) the town Chidia*; but these matters are treated more fully in my work on Cyprus. Others simply interpret כתים as Kinoῶ, the region in Cilicia in Ptolemy, and its inhabitants. Whatever the case, כתים seems to indicate not only the Cyprians, Macedonians, Italians and Romans, but all the overseas peoples to the Hebrews, as well as Sudas, under the word Lapiven (Λαπιvε), who says that the Cereans were led into Italy by the Latin son of Telephus.

units.la: Dodanim, דודנים, capite Genes. x, posteri à quarto Iavani filio, qui lib. 1. Paralipom. cap. 1. vers. 7. nunc דודנים, nunc vero דודנים nuncupantur: utramque lectionem vel scripturam arripientes, posterioris vocis vestigium indicant in celeberrimo Galliæ fluvio Rhodano; & qui non tam longe profectos דודנים volunt Rhodios interpretantur: prioris vero putant exstare in antiquo Provinciæ, quæ deinde Epirus appellata, nomine. Eam enim Dodonam olim vocatam ex Dionysio & Thrasybulo: Incolas autem Dodoneos ex Plinio Stephanoque constat. Satis certum, fuisse in Chaonia, quæ Epiri pars, Dodonam urbem, cui propinquum erat Nemus Dodonæum, ubi Dodonæus Iupiter, in templo sibi cognomine colebatur. Legendi Strabo lib. v. Pomponius Mela lib. 11, Solinus in Polyhist. Stephanus, Aëcon. Pædianus, Hyginus, & alij.
units.tr: Dodanim, דודנים, in Genesis 10, are the descendants of the fourth son of Javan, who in 1 Chronicles 1:7 are called now Dodanim and now Rodanim [דודנים; רודנים]. Taking up either reading, they find a trace of the second form in the famous river of Gaul, the Rhone. Those who do not want the Dodanim to have travelled so far take them to be the Rhodians. Others think the first form survives in the name of the ancient province later called Epirus. For that region was once called Dodona, according to Dionysius and Thrasybulus, and its inhabitants Dodoneans, as Pliny and Stephanus establish. It is quite certain that in Chaonia, part of Epirus, there was the city of Dodona, near which lay the Dodonaean grove, where Dodonaean Jupiter was worshipped in a temple named after him. Read Strabo, book 5; Pomponius Mela, book 2; Solinus in the Polyhistor; Stephanus; Aëcon.; Pædianus; Hyginus; and others.

units.la: Tubal, תובל, quintus filiorum Iavani. Huius Posteri Tubalæi (sic enim Latine vocentur) conjungitur Populis Meschechæis; ut docent, quæ paullo ante scripta mihi ex Iechezkelis cap. xxxvIII. & seq. ubi de Magogæis: connumerati apud eundem Prophetam cap. xvII & xxxII non solum ijs, quos dixi, sed & Assyrijs, Ælamitis, Edomitis, Sidonijs, alijsque ad Aquilonem Asiæ incolis: cum quorum plerisque pertinebant ad Imperium Gogi, quo nomine Reges complectitur Sacra Scriptura Asiaticos & Syriacos. Tubalei igitur populi Asiatici; non Europæi. Quod addo, non sine causa. Tubaleos enim Iberos vel Hispanos censet esse Iosephus: & accedunt alij; quum audiant in Hispania Bætica opidum esse, quod Setubal hodie, vetus nomen præferens. Zonaras Iberes ab eo deducit, qui in Asia Chalybibus vicini, iuxta Mæotidem Paludem, apud Pomponium Melam: Alij Italos arbitrantur; nulla ratione. Interpretes Chaldæus, Septuaginta, Latinus, quum ignorarent quarum gentium progenitor esset Tubal, nomen passim ejus retinuerunt.
units.tr: Tubal, תובל, the fifth son of Javan. His descendants, the Tubalites (for so they are called in Latin), are joined with the Meshech peoples, as is shown by what I wrote a little earlier from Ezekiel 38 and following, where Gog and Magog appear. The same prophet, in chapters 17 and 32, also counts among them not only those I have named but also the Assyrians, Elamites, Edomites, Sidonians, and other inhabitants of the north of Asia. Many of these belonged to the empire of Gog, a name under which Sacred Scripture includes the Asiatic and Syrian kings. The Tubalite peoples were therefore Asiatic, not European. I add this deliberately. Josephus thinks the Tubalites were the Iberians or Spaniards, and others agree, since there is a town in Spanish Baetica that is called Setubal today, preserving the old name. Zonaras derives the Iberians from Tubal, but they lived in Asia, near the Chalybes, beside the Lake Maeotis, according to Pomponius Mela. Others think the Italians are meant, without any good reason. The Chaldee paraphrast, the Septuagint, and the Latin translator, not knowing which nations descended from Tubal, retained his name throughout.

units.la: Meschec משך. Ab hoc qui prognati; & progenitos fuisse sub Imperio Gogi, id est Regum Asiaticorum & Syrorum, testantur quæ dixi. Sic Chaldæus Paraphrastes, vertens Querimoniam Davidis profugi, Psalmo cxx, vers. 5. Heu mihi, quia peregre ago in Meschec (משך) habito in tabernaculis Cedar; satis indicat populum hunc Asiaticis conscribendum, & vicinum Arabiæ: Sic enim explicat; Hei mihi, quoniam peregrinatus sum cum Asiaticis (עם אוכאי) habitavi in tabernaculis Arabum (ערבאי) Male Septuaginta: οἱ μοι, ὅτι ἡ παροικία μου ἐμακρύνθη: quos sequutus Interpres Latinus; Hei mihi, quia incolatus meus prolongatus est. Vicini igitur fuerunt Arabibus Cedræis: quibus nomen ab Cedro Ismaelis filio, ut legere est Genes. xxv, 13. Cedræos Nabataeis finitimos facit Plinius lib. nat. histor. v, cap. xi. Alij ob vocis adfinitatem ad Meschec referunt Mysos: alij Moschos, Ammiano Marcellino notos; quos hodie Moscovitas indigetamus; præsertim quum Septuaginta Moσχ dixerint. Alij denique quod in Cappadocia, scribentibus Iosepho, Eutropio, Suda, urbs Mazaca (cuius Incolæ; μάζυες, Herodoto: Ptolemæo & Ammiano, μαζικες; Stephano, μάζης; μάζηκες, Oppiano; Mazaces denique Lucano lib. iiii. belli Pharsalici, Claudiano Panegyrico i. in consulat. Stilliconis & Aurelio de venatione) quodque in finibus Cappadociæ & Colchidis Moschii montes & populi ab Apollonio lib. ii. Argonautic. celebrentur; Cappadoces ab Meschec ortos tradunt.
units.tr: Meshech, משך. Those descended from him, and the fact that they were under the empire of Gog, that is, of the Asiatic and Syrian kings, are attested by what I have said. So the Chaldee paraphrast, translating David's lament as a fugitive in Psalm 120:5, "Woe is me, that I sojourn in Meshech and dwell among the tents of Kedar," makes it sufficiently clear that this people is to be counted among the Asiatics and is near Arabia. He explains it thus: "Woe is me, that I have lived among the Asiatics [am Ukhai] and dwelt among the tents of the Arabs [Araboi]." The Septuagint translates badly: "οἴμοι, ὅτι ἡ παροικία μου ἐμακρύνθη" [Woe is me, that my sojourning has been prolonged], and the Latin translator follows them: "Woe is me, because my sojourning has been prolonged." So Meshech was near the Kedarite Arabs, who take their name from Kedar, son of Ishmael, as can be read in Genesis 25:13. Pliny, Natural History 5.11, makes the Kedarites neighbours of the Nabataeans. Others, on account of the similarity of the words, refer Meshech to the Mysians, or to the Moschi, known to Ammianus Marcellinus, whom we today call the Muscovites, especially since the Septuagint wrote Mosch. Finally, others trace the Cappadocians from Meshech, because in Cappadocia there is the city of Mazaca, as Josephus, Eutropius, and Suidas write (its inhabitants are the Mazyes [μάζυες] in Herodotus, the Mazaci [μαζικες] in Ptolemy and Ammianus, the Mazes [μάζης] in Stephanus, the Mazeces [μάζηκες] in Oppian, and finally the Mazaces in Lucan, book 4 of the Civil War, in Claudian's first Panegyric on the consulship of Stilicho, and in Aurelius on hunting). Also, on the borders of Cappadocia and Colchis, the Moschian mountains and peoples are celebrated by Apollonius, Argonautica 2.

units.la: Tiras, תירש, postremus Iapheti filiorum nominatur. De huius posteris nihil ex Sacra Scriptura certi: ideoque remotiora ab alijs videntur petijsse loca. Iosephus putat Thracas ab eo dictos: apud quos etiam, notante Ptolemæo, Αʼ̓νεγς fluvius, quem Astiram scribunt Plinius & Pomponius Mela. Sic in Sarmatia Europæa fluvius est Tυγες Ptolemæo, Τυρης Herodoto, Tyra Plinio, Tυεας Hesychio; hodie Nester; cuius ostium inter Istrum & Borysthenem fere medium. Sunt qui Tyrum Phoeniciæ urbem nonnulli Thyrrenium Italiæ regionem; quidam Turingos Germaniæ populos hinc deducunt. Alij Thuras apud Plinium, vel Θύρεον, ut Ptolemæus, vel Θυρίαν ut Strabo notat, Messeniæ, quæ Peloponnesi australior regio, urbem hinc trahunt. Neque innoratum abit quibusdam Thurium, quæ Magnæ Græciæ apud Ptolemæum & Stephanum urbs, in Sinu Tarentino: ubi & Thuria fons. Alia prætereo: malens, veteres formula, N. L. usus, sententiam hic suspendere; quam temerariam pronunciare.
units.tr: Tiras, תירש, is named last of the sons of Japheth. Nothing certain is known from Sacred Scripture about his descendants, so others have seemed to look for them in more distant places. Josephus thinks the Thracians were named after him. Among them, as Ptolemy notes, there is the river Anes [Ἀνέγς], which Pliny and Pomponius Mela call Astira. Likewise in European Sarmatia there is a river Tyges [Τυγες] in Ptolemy, Tyres [Τυρης] in Herodotus, Tyra in Pliny, and Tyeas [Τυεας] in Hesychius, today the Dniester, whose mouth lies roughly midway between the Danube and the Borysthenes. Some derive the name from Tyre, the Phoenician city; some from the Tyrrhenian region of Italy; some derive the German Thuringians from it. Others derive it from the town of Thuras, which Pliny mentions, or Thyreon [Θύρεον], as Ptolemy writes, or Thyrian [Θυρίαν], as Strabo writes, in Messenia, the southernmost region of the Peloponnese. Nor is it unknown that some derive it from Thurium, a city of Magna Graecia in the Gulf of Tarentum, mentioned by Ptolemy and Stephanus, where there is also a spring called Thuria. I pass over other suggestions. Following the old formula, N.L. (non liquet), I prefer to leave the matter undecided here, rather than rashly pronounce on it.

units.la: De Iapheти liberis dixi: succedunt Schemi secundo-geniti, cujus progeniem sic describit Sp. Sanctus: Filij Schemi Hhelam, & Aschur, & Arpacshad, & Lud, & Aram. Hos notat Zonaras, ut universim hoc præmoneam, loca Armeniæ, vicina Euphrati fluvio, id est Syriam, Persiam & reliquum Orientem occupasse, usque ad Oceanum Indicum: quod an verum, docebunt dicenda.
units.tr: I have spoken of the sons of Japheth. Next come the sons of Shem, the second-born, whose descendants the Holy Spirit describes thus: "The sons of Shem: Elam, and Asshur, and Arpachshad, and Lud, and Aram" (Genesis 10:22). Zonaras notes these. I give this general warning in advance: the places of Armenia near the river Euphrates, that is, Syria, Persia, and the rest of the East as far as the Indian Ocean, were occupied by these men. Whether this is true, what follows will show.

units.la: 1. Hhelam, עילם: Septuaginta Interpretibus Αιλάμ, pater fuit Hhelamitarum (Ἐλυμαίας appellat Iosephus) à quibus originem ducunt Persæ; qui, constituta Monarchia, nomen hoc obscurarunt. Est apud Danielem Prophetam, cap. viii. in principio, Schuschan Castrum in regione Hhelam: Ego Daniel, inquit, post id quod videram initio, vidi in visione mea, quum essem בשושן הבירה אשר בעילם הדיסה, in Schuschan metropoli, quæ in Hhelam provincia; vidi autem in visione, esse me super portam Vlai. Sic Ieschach. cap. xxi,6: Et Hhelam susumpsit Pharetram &c. Lucas Euangelista in Actis Apostolorum cap. ii. 9: Πάρθοι, Μήδοι, Ἐλαμῖται &c. Elymæos describit Strabo lib. xvi. Apud Plinium etiam Elamita in Arabia Felice, Maris adcolæ; ubi & oppidum ejusdem nominis. Xenophon denique in Historia Cyri, Persarum regis, mentionem facit Tribus Elamidos.
units.tr: 1. Elam, עילם. The Septuagint call him Ailam [Αιλάμ]. He was the father of the Elamites (Josephus calls them Elymaeans [Ἐλυμαῖας]), from whom the Persians trace their origin; after the Persian monarchy was established, they obscured this name. In Daniel 8:2, at the beginning of the chapter, there is the castle of Shushan in the region of Elam: "I, Daniel," he says, "after what I had seen at first, saw in my vision, when I was in Shushan the palace, which is in the province of Elam, and I saw in the vision that I was by the gate of the Ulai." So Isaiah 21:2: "Elam took up the quiver," and so on. The evangelist Luke in Acts 2:9 writes: "Parthians, Medes, Elamites [Πάρθοι, Μήδοι, Ἐλαμῖται]," and so on. Strabo, book 16, describes the Elymaeans. In Pliny there is also an Elamite people in Arabia Felix, neighbours of the sea, where there is also a town of the same name. Finally, Xenophon, in his history of Cyrus, king of the Persians, mentions the tribe of the Elamidae.

units.la: II. Aschur, אשור, nomen dedit Asserijs, condita Metropoli Ninive, Genes.x, 11; quam gloriam historiæ prophanæ tribuunt Nino.
units.tr: II. Asshur, אשור, gave his name to the Assyrians, who founded the metropolis of Nineveh (Genesis 10:11). Profane history attributes this glory to Ninus.

units.la: III. Arpacshad ארפכשד, Quidam quum in ארפכשד viderent latere Thema, à quo deducuntur כשדים Chaldæi, hos nulla Scripturæ Sacræ auctoritate sunt ausi ab eo derivare; sequuti Iosephum: qui addit Χαλδαίως dictos olim Ἀρφαξαδαίως. Alij Susiorum quorum regio Susiana, patrem arbitrantur.
units.tr: III. Arpachshad, ארפכשד. Some, seeing in the word Arpachshad the root Kesed, from which the Chaldeans (כשדים) are derived, dared to derive the Chaldeans from him, though no authority of Sacred Scripture supports this. They followed Josephus, who adds that the Chaldeans were formerly called Arphaxadeans [Ἀρφαξαδαῖοι]. Others think he was the father of the Susians, whose region is Susiana.

units.la: Arpacshadi posteritatem sic docet Spiritus Sanctus, Genes. x, 24: At vero Arpacshad genuit Schelach de quo ortus Hheber. Natique sunt Hheber Filij duo: nomen uni Peleg, eo quod in diebus ejus divisa sit terra; & nomen fratris ejus Iokatan. Qui Iokatan genuit Almodad, & Scheleph, & Chatzar-maveth, & Ierach, & Hadoram, & Vzal, & Diklah, & Hhobalez, & Abimael, Scheba, & Ophir, & Chavila, & Iobab: omnes isti filij Iokatan. Hi notantur ibidem Regiones obtinuisse, quæ sunt à Mesla pergentibus ad Sephar, montem Orientalem. Iosephus censet eos invasisse omnia, quæ sunt à Cophene flumine Indiæ (de quo alibi) usque ad Assyriam. Alij Indiam habuisse scribunt. Benedictus Arias Montanus in Adparatu Biblico specialiora rimatus, ab Almodad, אלמודד, Themeotes deducit, Sarmatiæ Asiaticæ populos, apud Ptolemæum & Pomponium Melam: à Scheleph, שלף Selebios: à Chatzarmaveth, חצרמות, Sarmatas: ab Iarach, ירח, Ariam & Arachosiam: ab Hadoram, הדורם, Hircaniam: ab Vzal, אוזל, Oxiam Bactrianam, cujus cultoris Oxy Ptolemæo: ab Dicklah, דקלה, Scythiam intra Imaum: ab Hhobalez חובל, Bolitas, sive Obolitas intra Caucasum & Paropanysum Montes: ab Abimael, אבימאל, Imaenses sive Imaos; apud quos mons nobilis Imaus: ab Scheba, שבא, Sacas, Ptolemæo & Pomponio notos. Sed derivandi potius hinc Sabei Indici; quorum meminit Dionysius de Situ Orbis: Τ ἢ μίσοι ναίνσι Σάβαι, κ' Ταξίλοι ἀνδρες.
units.tr: Holy Spirit describes the posterity of Arpachshad thus, Genesis 10:24–29: "And Arpachshad begat Shelah, and Shelah begat Eber. And to Eber were born two sons: the name of one was Peleg, because in his days the earth was divided; and the name of his brother was Joktan. And Joktan begat Almodad, and Sheleph, and Hazarmaveth, and Jerah, and Hadoram, and Uzal, and Diklah, and Obal, and Abimael, and Sheba, and Ophir, and Havilah, and Jobab; all these were the sons of Joktan." Here it is noted that they held the regions stretching from Mesha, going towards Sephar, the eastern mountain. Josephus thinks they occupied everything from the river Cophen of India (of which more elsewhere) to Assyria. Others write that they held India. Benedictus Arias Montanus, in his Apparatus Biblicus, searching more closely into details, derives from Almodad (אלמודד) the Themeotes, a people of Asiatic Sarmatia, mentioned by Ptolemy and Pomponius Mela; from Sheleph (שלף) the Selebi; from Hazarmaveth (חצרמות) the Sarmatians; from Jerah (ירח) the Arians and Arachosians; from Hadoram (הדורם) the Hyrcanians; from Uzal (אוזל) the Bactrian Oxus, whose inhabitants were called Oxi by Ptolemy; from Diklah (דקלה) Scythia within the Imaus; from Obal (חובל) the Bolitae, or Obolitae, between the Caucasus and the Paropamisus mountains; from Abimael (אבימאל) the Imaeans, or Imaï, among whom is the famous mountain Imaus; from Sheba (שבא) the Sacae, known to Ptolemy and Pomponius. But it is more likely that the Indian Sabaeans derive their name from this source. Dionysius, On the Situation of the World, mentions them: "Τ ἢ μίσοι ναίνσι Σάβαι, κ' Ταξίλοι ἀνδρες" [The Sabaeans and the Taxili men dwell in the middle...].

units.la: Nam Sabæi, Persis proximi ab Abrahami filio orti. De his idem Dionysius: Πρῶτοι Σάβαι, μετὰ τὰς ἢ Πασιγάρδαι, ἄγχι ἢ Τάσκοι.
units.tr: For the Sabaeans, who were neighbours of the Persians, descended from a son of Abraham. Of these the same Dionysius writes: "The Sabaeans first, after the Pasigardae, and near the Tasci." [Πρῶτοι Σάβαι, μετὰ τὰς δὴ Πασιγάρδαι, ἄγχι δὲ Τάσκοι]

units.la: Ophir אופיר, appellationem dedit Regioni Ophir; ex qua Schelomo Rex, instructa & missa classe, singulis triennijs magnam auri vim petebat; ut legere est lib. iii. Regum, cap. ix, 26, & lib. ii. Paralip. cap. ix. Auri Ophyriani mentio apud Hijobum, cap. xxii, 24: Davidem Psalmo xlv, 10; & i. Paralipom. xxxix, 4. ut quidem Hebraica tinniunt: obscurior enim apud Interpretes & Græcos Septuaginta, & Latinos. Vbi autem Ophir, & quod hodie Regioni nomen, variatur. Iosephus eam in India ponit. χρυσω γῆν suo tempore nominatam scribens: suffragatur illi Marius Niger, Aureum putans Chersonnesum; quæ cum illa Iosephi eadem. Gaspar Varrerius, Ophiriana Pomœria proferens, non solum Chersonnesum existimat esse, sed omnem etiam oram, quæ Pegufiis, Malacca, Sumatra continetur. Sed Regiones hasce ab auro non esse fœcundas, didicimus plene cum ex Lusitanorum, tum Nostratium navigationibus. Varablus Insulam arbitratur, quæ Hispaniola hodie. Postellus, Goropius Becanus, Arias Montanus, Michael Neander, & alij Peris interpretantur, ξῆ μετ-αξῆνν. Sunt quidem ibi copiosissimæ Auri venæ: sed quis credet, tam longinquas provincias tunc temporis, tanto Pelagi periculosissimi intervallo separatas ab Erythræo mari, petitas? cui persuadebitur, Populos istos, si jam tum cum ijs agi coeperit, tam parum frequentium commerciorum beneficio didicisse, ut pro Hominibus immanes Belluas in posteris reliquerint? Mitigari solent, & ad comitarem revocari ferociores immitium nationum mores, aliorum, qui humaniores, aditu & consuetudine. Fieri hoc facile quotidiana docet experientia. Saevissimos tamen fuisse, & efferatissimæ vitæ illorum plerosque, deprehensum ab ijs, qui primi Terras eorum ante centum aut circiter annos ingressi. Matthæus igitur Beroaldus Chronici sui lib. iiii. cui cum Abrahamo Ortelio subscribo, censet, quamuis timidior, Ophir esse Africæ regionem, quam Zaffalam hodie dicunt vel Cephalam; quæ aurifera admodum, teste Ioanne Baroso: nihil etiamnum, ut Lusitanorum peregrinationes loquuntur, præter Aurum Mercatoribus exteris communicans, quum ibi sint Aurifodinæ fertiles facilesque effossu. Accedit, quod in Indica sua navigatione memoriæ prodat Thomas Lopezius, Zaffolenses habere libros, patria lingua scriptos, in quibus legitur, Schelomonem Regem tertio quoque anno Aurum hinc tulisse. Potest & illud probare regionem horum esse Ophir, vel saltem Peruanam non esse: quod Sacræ literæ tradant ex Ophir etiam, præter Aurum, Ebur Schelomonem petijsle. At in Peruana Elephantem nemo adhuc dixit, scripsit, pinxit. Quidquid sit: ab Ophir dictum nonnulli volunt Aurum Obrizum, quasi Ophirizum, ab Ophir petitum: quod ita describit Plinius lib. xxxiii. natur. histor. cap. iii: Auri experimento ignis est, ut simili colore rubeat, quo Ignis: atque ipsum Obrizum vocant. Chavila, חוילה, qui duodecimus Ioktanis filiorum, posteros Indiam omnem & Gangeticas Regiones possedisse judicat post alios Arias Montanus, cujus sæpe memini: ut, qui ab Iobab, יובב, posterno liberorum, Novi Orbis partem; quæ Parias vocata, auro margaritisque abundans.
units.tr: Ophir gave its name to the region of Ophir, from which King Solomon, having fitted out and sent a fleet, used to fetch a great quantity of gold every three years, as can be read in 1 Kings 9:26 and 2 Chronicles 9. A mention of Ophirian gold occurs in Job 22:24, and in David at Psalm 45:10, and in 1 Chronicles 29:4, as the Hebrew indeed rings out; for the Interpreters, both the Septuagint Greeks and the Latins, are more obscure. But where Ophir was, and what region is called by that name today, is disputed. Josephus places it in India, writing that in his time it was called the land of gold. Marius Niger agrees with him, thinking it the Golden Chersonese, which is the same as Josephus's. Gaspar Varrerius, bringing forward the Ophirian Pomeria, thinks it is not only the Chersonese but also the whole coast that contains Pegu, Malacca and Sumatra. But we have learned fully, both from Portuguese and from our own countrymen's voyages, that these regions are not rich in gold. Varablus thinks it was the island which is today Hispaniola. Postellus, Goropius Becanus, Arias Montanus, Michael Neander and others interpret Peru as the name, ξῆ μετ-αξῆνν. There are indeed very rich veins of gold there; but who will believe that such distant provinces, separated by so dangerous a stretch of sea from the Red Sea, were sought out at that time? Who will be persuaded that those peoples, if contact with them had begun even then, learned so little from the benefit of such infrequent commerce that they left behind them, for their descendants, beasts rather than men? The fiercer customs of savage nations are usually softened and brought back to humanity by the approach and familiarity of more civilised peoples; daily experience shows that this happens easily. Yet it was discovered by those who first entered their lands, about a hundred years ago, that most of them were very savage and lived a most brutish life. Matthaeus Beroaldus therefore, in book 4 of his Chronicle, with whom I agree along with Abraham Ortelius, though more timidly, thinks Ophir is the region of Africa which is today called Zaffala or Cephala; this is very rich in gold, according to John Barros, who says that, as the Portuguese voyages report, it still supplies nothing but gold to foreign merchants, since there are fertile gold mines there that are easy to dig. In addition, Thomas Lopez, in his account of the Indian voyage, records that the people of Zaffala have books written in their native language, in which it is read that King Solomon brought gold from there every third year. It can also prove that the region of these people is Ophir, or at least that it is not Peru: the Sacred Letters report that Solomon sought ivory from Ophir as well as gold. But no one has yet spoken of, written about, or painted an elephant in Peru. Whatever the case, some want obrizum gold to be named from Ophir, as if Ophirizum, because it was brought from Ophir; Pliny describes it thus in book 33 of his Natural History, chapter 3: "The test of gold is fire: it reddens with the same colour as fire, and they call it obrizum." Chavila, the twelfth of the sons of Joktan, is judged by Arias Montanus, whom I often mention, after others, to have possessed all India and the regions of the Ganges; just as Iobab, the youngest of the children, possessed a part of the New World, which is called Paria, abounding in gold and pearls.

units.la: iv. Lud. לוד, quartus ordine Schemo natus: à quo, ut notant Eusebius & Zonaras, Lydi, Minoris Asiæ populi, bellicæ virtutis laude quondam præsignes. Legendi Iefchah. cap. lxvi, 19. & Iechezkel cap. xxvii, 10.
units.tr: iv. Lud, the fourth in order, son of Shem; from whom, as Eusebius and Zonaras note, came the Lydians, a people of Asia Minor once distinguished for the praise of martial valour. See Isaiah 66:19 and Ezekiel 27:10.

units.la: v. Aram, ארם, postremus inter Schemi filios. Varios ab eo populos in Asia, præsertim Syria, scribente Hieronymo, fuisse dispersinatos, paret ex variis appellationibus. Nam cognominati leguntur: Aram Naharaim, ארם נהרים, id est fluminum, vel Interamnis, ut Ammianus loquitur, Græcis μεσοποταμία; quod media inter Euphratem & Tigrin; Deuteronom. xxiii, 4. & Iudicum cap. iii, 8: Aram Padua, ארם פדנה; Genef. xxxiii, 18, xlviii, 7. & alibi; hæc eadem videtur fuisse cum Aram Naharaim, aut certe ejus pars: Aram Damasci, ארם דמשק; lib. ii. Schemuel. cap. viii, 6, & Iefchah, cap. vii, 8: Aram Mahachah, ארם מעכה; lib. i. Paralip. cap. xix, 6. Aram Sobah, ארם צובה: eodem cap. xix, & lib. ii. Schemuel. Alia praeterea. Plinius, ut & hoc addam, lib. vi. natur. histor. cap. xvii, scribit Scythas olim Aramaeos fuisse nuncupatos. Alij, quos inter Arias Montanus, ab Aram Armenios derivat. Arama etiam Palæstinæ locus, Ichoschuhhæ libro, cap. xix, 36.
units.tr: v. Aram, the last of the sons of Shem. That various peoples were scattered from him throughout Asia, especially Syria, as Jerome writes, is clear from the various names. For they are called by surnames: Aram Naharaim, that is, of the rivers, or of the Interamnes (as Ammianus puts it), which the Greeks call Mesopotamia, because it lies between the Euphrates and the Tigris (Deut. 23:4 and Judges 3:8); Aram Padan (Gen. 33:18, 48:7 and elsewhere), which seems to have been the same as Aram Naharaim, or at least a part of it; Aram Damascus (2 Samuel 8:6 and Isaiah 7:8); Aram Maacah (1 Chronicles 19:6); Aram Zobah (in the same chapter 19 and in 2 Samuel). There are others besides. Pliny, to add this too, in book 6 of his Natural History, chapter 17, writes that the Scythians were once called Arameans. Others, among whom Arias Montanus, derive the Armenians from Aram. Arama is also a place in Palestine, in the book of Joshua, chapter 19:36.

units.la: Arami posteritatem sic legimus Genef. cap. x, 23. Filij Aram: Hhutz, & Chul, & Gether, & Mesch.
units.tr: We read the posterity of Aram as follows, Gen. 10:23: "The sons of Aram: Uz, and Hul, and Gether, and Mash."

units.la: A primo Hhutz, עוץ, Regio dicta Hhutz; cuius incola Hijobus, ut scribitur in ejus historia cap, i, 1. adcensa Syriæ vel Arabiæ, quæ Scenitis, cujus pars Idumæa apud Iirmeiam Lamentat. cap. iv, 21, vergens ad Chaldæam & Sabæam; quarum Incolæ Hijobi bona deprædantur; c. 1,15 & 17, Iosephus & Zonaras ajunt Hhutz condidisse Traconitiden & Damascum, quæ inter Palæstinam & Cœlesyriam. Chul, חול. Ab ejus posteris, quod censet Arias Montanus, Aeolis occupata, Asiæ Minoris regio in littore Maris Ægæi: Hieronymus Chul Armeniorum stirpem opinatur. Gether, גתר. Ab hoc qui prognati locis insedisse putantur eidem Montano, quæ postea Aetolia appellatione innotuerunt: Nonnullis Getuli & Getæ cū vicinis Massagetis & Samogetis hinc trahuntur. Zonaras Bactrianos condidisse censet Getherum: cujus etiam mentio lib. i Paralip. c.
units.tr: From the first, Uz, the region was called Uz, whose inhabitant was Job, as is written in his history, chapter 1:1; it lay on the edge of Syria or Arabia, which is called Scenitis, part of which was Idumaea, as Jeremiah says in Lamentations 4:21, bordering on Chaldaea and Sabaea; the inhabitants of these plundered Job's goods (Job 1:15, 17). Josephus and Zonaras say that Uz founded Trachonitis and Damascus, which lie between Palestine and Coele-Syria. Hul: Arias Montanus thinks that the Aeolians occupied the region from his posterity, a region of Asia Minor on the coast of the Aegean Sea; Jerome thinks Hul was the stock of the Armenians. Gether: Montanus thinks that those descended from him settled in places that were later known by the name Aetolia; some derive the Getuli and Getae from him, together with the neighbouring Massagetae and Samogetae. Zonaras thinks Gether founded the Bactrians. He is also mentioned in 1 Chronicles, chapter 7:1. Mash, the parent of the Mysians, as Montanus holds, a name not far from it; Juvenal, he says, calls them Meses. Josephus thinks Mash was the progenitor of the Arabs of the Mesjani.

units.la: 1. Mesch, משׁ, Misiorum parens, ut vult Montanus; voce non abludente: quos Iuvenalis, inquit, Meses vocat. Iosephus Mesjanorum Arabum progenitorem putat.
units.tr: 1. Mesch [משׁ], the father of the Misians, as Montanus holds, the name being not dissimilar: Juvenal, he says, calls them Mesi. Josephus thinks he was the ancestor of the Arab Mesjani.

units.la: Sic se habuit in Terræ distributione Schemi Posteritas: sequitur Chami; cujus hæc propago, Genes. x, 6: Filij autem Chami: Cusch, & Mitzraim & Put, & Cenahhan.
units.tr: Such was the order of Shem's posterity in the division of the earth. Next comes Ham's line, whose offspring is listed in Genesis 10:6: "The sons of Ham: Cush, and Mizraim, and Put, and Canaan."

units.la: 1. Cusch כוש. Ab eo Cusch, Arabia; hinc Cananæ, inde Ægypto finitima. Paret partim ex Plinij lib. II. natur. hist. cap. xi: partim quod Cusch & Mitzraim in Sacris litteris non uno loco jungantur, ut omnino vicinas sibi regiones duo fratres videantur sortiti: Mitzraim quidem, quæ post Ægyptus; Cusch vero, quæ confinalis illi ad Sinum Arabicum. Alij nunc infeliciorem Septuaginta versionem, nunc vero nugas & putida Iosephi mendacia, quæ leguntur lib. II. cap. x, sequuti, ab Cuscho notant originem Æthiopiæ Gentibus, quæ in ultima ora Africæ ad Nili fontes. Hinc ubi כוש, & ab eo derivata in Sacra Scriptura, vertentibus, semel gnaviter deceptis, semper in oculis & mente fuerunt Æthiopia, ejusque Incolæ; quum respiciendum ijs fuisset ad Arabiam & Arabas. Sic, dicis gratia, Tzippora Cushæa, הכושית, Rehhuelis Midianitarum Sacerdotis filia, quam Moschè uxorem ducit, Exod. cap. III; Æthiopissa male ijs vertitur, Numerorum cap. xii, 1. Sic Zerach Cushæus, הכושי Midianitarum Rex male Æthiops vocatur, quum Arabs: II. Paralipom. cap. xiiii, 9. sic כוש, id est Arabia, subsidia submittens populo DEI, male dicitur Æthiopia apud Iesahh. cap. xx, 5: Nam quid auxilij potuisset sperari & exspectari populo DEI ab gente tam remota, & cui sedes sub alio cœlo? Sic denique Sephaniæ cap. II, 12. Chusæi, כושים, Arabes interfecti gladio Domini male scribuntur nonnullis Æthiopes. Quid quod Nebucad-nezar, ut paret ex Ieckezkel. cap. xxix, 10 xxx, 6; & Iirmeiæ cap. xxv, Chusæos, כושים, subegerit: quis autem umquam legit ingressum Æthiopiam? quis aliquem ejus auspiciis in remotissimas terras missum? Victoriarum ejus limitem statuunt Prophetæ Syenen, postremam Ægypti oram; legenda quæ scribuntur apud Iechezkelem cap. xxx, 6. & Iirmeiam cap. xxv.
units.tr: 1. Cush [כוש]. From him come Cush, Arabia; on one side it borders Canaan, on the other Egypt. This appears partly from Pliny, Natural History, book 2, chapter 11; and partly because Cush and Mizraim are joined together in the sacred writings in more than one place, so that the two brothers seem to have been allotted wholly neighbouring regions: Mizraim, which later became Egypt, and Cush, which bordered it on the Arabian Gulf. Others, following now the less reliable version of the Seventy, and now the trifles and foul lies of Josephus, which are read in book 2, chapter 10, derive from Cush the origin of the Ethiopian peoples, who dwell on the furthest shore of Africa near the sources of the Nile. Hence, wherever Cush [כוש] and the words derived from it occur in Sacred Scripture, translators, having once been thoroughly misled, always had Ethiopia and its inhabitants in their eyes and minds, whereas they should have looked to Arabia and the Arabs. Thus, for instance, Zipporah the Cushite [הכושית], daughter of Reuel, priest of Midian, whom Moses married (Exod. 3), is wrongly rendered as an Ethiopian woman; and likewise in Numbers 12:1. So Zerah the Cushite [הכושי], king of the Midianites, is wrongly called an Ethiopian, when he was an Arab (2 Chron. 14:9). So too Cush [כוש], that is Arabia, sending help to the people of God, is wrongly called Ethiopia in Isaiah 20:5: for what help could the people of God have hoped for and expected from a nation so remote, and whose seat lay under another sky? Likewise in Zephaniah 2:12, the Cushites [כושים], Arabs slain by the sword of the Lord, are wrongly described by some as Ethiopians. What of the fact that Nebuchadnezzar, as appears from Ezekiel 29:10 and 30:6 and from Jeremiah 25, subdued the Cushites [כושים]? But who has ever read of his entering Ethiopia? Who has read of anyone sent into the most remote lands under his auspices? The prophets set the limit of his victories at Syene, the furthest edge of Egypt; read what is written in Ezekiel 30:6 and Jeremiah 25.

units.la: Genus Cuschi tale Genes. x, 7: Filij autem Cusch: Seba, Chavila, & Sabtha & Rahhema, & Sabteca. Filij Rahhema: Scheba & Dedan. Porro Cusch genuit Nimrod. &c.
units.tr: The family of Cush, Genesis 10:7: "And the sons of Cush: Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah, and Sabteca. And the sons of Raamah: Sheba and Dedan. And Cush begat Nimrod," etc.

units.la: Seba, סבא (alius ab שבא Scheba, qui decimus Ioktanis; alius item ab שבא Scheba filio Rahhemæ; de illo dixi, de hoc postea dicturus) nomen dedit סבאים Sabæi felicem Arabiam ad Sinum Arabicum colentibus; de quibus Plinius lib. vi. natur. historCap. xxviii. Apud Iesahih. cap. xliii, 3, & xlv, 14. Cush, Sela כבא & Mitzraim, id est, interior Arabia male Æthiopia vertitur) Sebæa & Ægyptus junguntur ob sedium vicinitatem. Mentio apud Davidem Psalmo lxxii, 10. Chavila חוילה (alius ab eo, qui Ioktanis filius) Chavilæorum pater; quibus prope Scheba versus Sinum Persicum fuerunt sedes, pertinentes usque ad Ismaelitas, deserti Pharan aliorumque in Arabia Petræa locorum incolas, uti constat ex Genesios capitis vigesimiquinti versu decimooctavo, & lib. I. Schemuel. cap. xv, 7. Iosephus, eique suffragantes alij, Chavilæos Africæ faciunt populos, qui sequentibus sæculis Getuli; nonnulli Indos: fallissime, & omnino contra Sacræ Scripturæ auctoritatem. Sabtha, סבתח: ab hoc Sabthæi, Arabiæ felicis incolæ; quo loco Metropolis Sabbatha collocatur Ptolemæo. Iosepho Σαβαβλωοί (qui Græcis Α᾿σαβαρρίοι) nominantur; sed ubi sint, non adscribit: an ad Aftaboram fluvium habitantes? Est & Sabatha urbs xxx. stadijs ab Seleucia Mediæ distans apud Zosimum; quæ Plinio Sabata. Alia item Metropolis Æthiopiæ; cui Ptolemæus lib. iiii. tribuit Longitudin. 68-20; Latitud. 12-20. Hinc confirmatiores facti, qui Sabtha posteros in Æthiopiam ultra Atlantem emoverunt. Rahhema, רעמה: ab eo populi Arabiarum incolæ, vicini Schebæis. Conjunguntur enim apud Iechezkel. cap. xxvii, 21. Carmaniam hinc dictam putat Montanus. Filij Rahhemæ Scheba & Dedan. Scheba, שבא, Schebæorum pater ad Sinum Persicum vergentium: quos nobilitarunt apud Græcos Latinosque partim Aurum, Tus, Gemmæ, quibus abundabant, Iesahih. cap. ix, 60. Iirmeiæ cap. vi, 20, Plin. lib. vi, cap. xviii. natur. historiæ; partim Prædæ & Latrocinia, Hijob cap. i, 15. Plin. ibidem. שבא, Scheba Regina potens & dives (quæ recte respectu Iudææ Βασίλισσα dicitur Νότη, Austri Regina, Matthæi cap. xii. 41, & Lucæ cap. xi, 31.) magna pompa venisse scribitur ad audiendam Schelomonis sapientiam. Iosephus male Æthiopes ab hoc Scheba natos asserit: quem oscitanter alij sequuntur. Nam si Æthiopes Schebæi, qui tam procul distiti potuerunt infestare Hijobum? Dedan, דרן. ab eo populus Idumææ, uti liquet ex Iechezkele cap. xxv, 15. & Iirmeia cap. xlix, 8. Sunt qui Iosephi delirijs adhærentes parum considerate statuunt parentem esse nescio cujus gentis in Aethiopia Occidentali. Quod si verum; non video, quo praemio vel lucro excitati, infinitis Terrarum spacijs superatis, ad Mercatum venerint Tyriorum: Venisse enim eo cum Tapetibus discimus ex Iechezkele xxvii, 15. & 20. Dedanijs Palmyrenam regionem, Ptolemaeo nomen, in qua Alsadanus mons magnus, adsignat Montanus. Sabteca סבתכא quintus filiorum Chusi, cui genti nomen suum impartierit, non docet Sacra Scriptura.
units.tr: Seba, סבא (not to be confused with Sheba, שבא, the tenth son of Joktan, nor with another Sheba, son of Raamah; of the first I have spoken, of the second I shall speak later), gave his name to the Sabaeans, סבאים, who inhabited Arabia Felix by the Arabian Gulf. Pliny speaks of them in Natural History, book 6, chapter 28. In Isaiah 43:3 and 45:14, where Cush, Seba (כבא) and Mitzraim are named, the phrase is wrongly rendered as Ethiopia; that is, inner Arabia. Seba and Egypt are joined because their settlements were neighbouring. There is mention of them in David's Psalm 72:10. Havilah, חוילה (not the one who was a son of Joktan), was the father of the Havilahites, whose seats lay near Sheba towards the Persian Gulf, extending as far as the Ishmaelites, the inhabitants of the desert of Paran and of other places in Arabia Petraea, as is clear from Genesis 25:18 and 1 Samuel 15:7. Josephus, and other writers who follow him, make the Havilahites the peoples of Africa, who in later centuries were called Getuli; some make them Indians. This is most mistaken and entirely contrary to the authority of Holy Scripture. Sabtah, סבתח: from him come the Sabtheans, inhabitants of Arabia Felix; Ptolemy places the metropolis Sabbatha there. Josephus calls them Sabablooi (Σαβαβλωοί), which the Greeks name Asabarrioi (Α᾿σαβαρρίοι), but he does not say where they are; were they dwelling by the river Aftabora? There is also a city Sabatha, thirty stadia from Seleucia in Media, according to Zosimus, which Pliny calls Sabata. There is likewise another metropolis of Ethiopia, to which Ptolemy in book 4 assigns longitude 68°20′ and latitude 12°20′. From this, those who moved the descendants of Sabtah into Ethiopia beyond the Atlas have grown more confident. Raamah, רעמה: from him come the peoples of the Arabians, neighbours of the Sabaeans; for they are joined together in Ezekiel 27:21. Montanus thinks Carmania took its name from him. The sons of Raamah, Sheba and Dedan. Sheba, שבא, father of the Sabaeans who lie towards the Persian Gulf, who became famous among Greeks and Latins, partly for their gold, frankincense and gems, of which they had abundance (Isaiah 60:6; Jeremiah 6:20; Pliny, Natural History, book 6, chapter 18), and partly for their plunder and robberies (Job 1:15; Pliny, ibid.). The Queen Sheba, שבא, a powerful and wealthy queen (who is rightly called the Queen of the South, Basilissa Notē (Βασίλισσα Νότη), in relation to Judea, Matthew 12:42 and Luke 11:31), is written of as having come with great pomp to hear Solomon's wisdom. Josephus wrongly asserts that the Ethiopians were descended from this Sheba, and others carelessly follow him. For if the Ethiopians were Sabaeans, how could they have been so far away and yet have been able to harass Job? Dedan, דדן: from him comes the people of Edom, as is clear from Ezekiel 25:13 and Jeremiah 49:8. Some, adhering to the fancies of Josephus, rashly hold that he was the ancestor of some people in Western Ethiopia, I know not which. If this is true, I do not see for what reward or gain they would have been roused, crossing such vast tracts of the earth, to come to the market of the Tyrians; for we learn from Ezekiel 27:15 and 20 that they came there with rugs. Montanus assigns to the Dedanites the region of Palmyra, which Ptolemy calls Palmyrene, in which is the great mountain Alsadanus. Sabteca, סבתכא, the fifth of the sons of Cush, whose name he gave to his people, is not taught by Holy Scripture.

units.la: Nimrod נמרד postremo loco nominatur inter Chusi liberos. Hunc discimus Genef. x,10. primum Babilone coepisse regnare, deinde vero longius Imperij fines protulisse.
units.tr: Nimrod, נמרד, is named last among the children of Cush. We learn from Genesis 10:10 that he first began to reign in Babylon, and afterwards extended the bounds of his empire further.

units.la: II. Mitzraim, מצרים Septuaginta μεσραιμ. Ab eo Mitzraim, qui postea ab Aegypto Danai fratre, ut nonnulli volunt, Aegyptij; Chusaeis, id est, Arabibus (non, ut male vertunt, Aethiopibus, quemadmodum antea plene dixi) conterminis; Iesaiah. cap. xviii. 1. non obscuris indicijs innuente, ubi Aegypti, quod parte mei Operis iiii. docebo. Hodie nomen perseverat. Aegyptum enim Arabes & Turcae Mizri & Mizra dicunt. Latere videtur & Hebraica nomenclatura in μυαεφι qua, vitiose fortean, Aegyptus appellatur apud Stephanum.
units.tr: II. Mitzraim, מצרים, in the Septuagint Mesraim (μεσραιμ). From him, who was afterwards called Egypt, the brother of Danaus, as some hold, come the Egyptians, Mitzraim; they bordered on the Chusites, that is the Arabians (not, as they wrongly translate, the Ethiopians, as I have fully said before). Isaiah 18:1 hints at this, not obscurely, where Egypt is meant, which I shall show in part four of my work. The name persists today: for the Arabs and Turks call Egypt Mizri and Mizra. The Hebrew name seems also to lie hidden in Myaefi (μυαεφι), by which Egypt is called, perhaps wrongly, in Stephanus.
