units.la: De hujus progenie sic Moschaeus Genef. cap. x. 13. At vero Mitzraim genuit Ludim, & Hhanamim, & Lehabim, & Naphtuchim, & Patrusim, & Casluchim; de quibus egresisi sunt Pelischtim & Caphtorim: omnes non tam generis auctores, quam populi ab ipsis auctoribus orti. Videntur hi reliquam Africae ab Aegypto oram incolis complesse, & sedes quaesitum profecti longius. Rara enim eorum, imo nulla, mentio; praeterquam Pelischtim, & Caphthorim qui conregionales populo Dei terras occuparunt.
units.tr: Concerning his descendants, Moses writes thus in Genesis 10:13: "But Mitzraim begat Ludim, and Anamim, and Lehabim, and Naphtuhim, and Pathrusim, and Casluhim, from whom came the Philistines and the Caphtorim." These were not so much founders of families as peoples arising from those founders. They seem to have filled the remaining coast of Africa from Egypt onwards, and to have gone further afield seeking settlements. For there is little, indeed no, mention of them, except of the Philistines and Caphtorim, who as neighbours occupied lands of the people of God.

units.la: Ludaeorum, לודים meminit Iirmeias cap. xlvi. 9, & alibi; ubi non satis proprie Latinus Interpres vertit Lidos, qui Asiae Minoris populi, a לוד quarto Schemi filio. Montanus Libyos ab Ludim dirivat: & ab Hhanamim, ענמים, Trog.odytas; alij Pentapolitanos circa Cyrenaicum, & Anaitas in Aethiopia: ab Lehabim, לחבים idem Montanus Libyos Cyrenaicos sive Libyes Aegyptios: ab Naphtuchim, נפתוחים, Africam minorem, & huic subjacentes Numidas; alij Naphtutas in Numidia & Lusitanos: à Patrusim, פתרוסים, Petrosos unde Arabiae Petraeae nomen, cujus Metropolis Patras; nonnulli Pelusiacos ad Nilum: ab Casluchim, כסלחים, Sarracenorum gentem. Accessisset facile Magno viro, si solidioribus argumentis sua probasset. Pelischtim, פלשתים Philistim Latino Interpreti, Septuaginta nonnumquam Αλλοφυλοι, quasi externi generis homines, Latinis Geographis Palestini; oram Cananaeae maritimam tenuerunt, quae vergit in Aegyptum. Eorum frequentissima in Sacris Libris mentio. Fines Palaestinorum describuntur in Iehoschuhhae historia cap. xiii, 3. Origo fuisse videtur illis ab Caphtoreus, uti colligere est ex Iirmeiae cap. iiii, 4. & Amos cap. ix. 7. Caphtorim, כפתרים, sedes ubi fuerint, docemur ex Deuteronom. cap. ii, 23: Hhevaeos quoque, qui inhabitabant Chatzerrima Hhazzam usque Caphtorai, כפתרים qui prodierunt e Capthore מכפתר perdiderunt, & inhabitant loca illorum. Septuaginta, eisque fidens Latinus male Cappadoces & Cappadociam vertunt; ut & Chaldaeus Paraphrastes קפוטקיא & מן קפוטקיא.
units.tr: The Ludim, לודים, are mentioned in Jeremiah 46:9 and elsewhere, where the Latin translator not quite properly renders them Lydians, Lidos, the peoples of Asia Minor, from Lud, the fourth son of Shem. Montanus derives the Libyans from Ludim, and from Anamim, ענמים, the Troglodytes; others the Pentapolitans around Cyrenaica, and the Anaitae in Ethiopia. From Lehabim, לחבים, the same Montanus derives the Cyrenaic Libyans, or the Libyans of Egypt. From Naphtuhim, נפתוחים, Lesser Africa and the Numidians subject to it; others the Naphtutae in Numidia and the Lusitanians. From Pathrusim, פתרוסים, the Petrosi, whence comes the name of Arabia Petraea, whose metropolis is Patras; some make them the Pelusiacs by the Nile. From Casluhim, כסלחים, the nation of the Saracens. It would have been easy for so great a man to have supported these conjectures, had he proved them with firmer arguments. The Philistines, פלשתים, Philistim to the Latin translator, sometimes Allophyloi (Αλλοφυλοι) in the Septuagint, as if men of foreign race, Palestini to the Latin geographers, held the maritime coast of Canaan, which faces towards Egypt. They are very frequently mentioned in the Holy Books. The boundaries of the Palestinians are described in Joshua 13:3. They seem to have originated from the Caphtorites, as may be gathered from Jeremiah 4:4 and Amos 9:7. Where the Caphtorim, כפתרים, were settled, we are taught by Deuteronomy 2:23: "The Avvim also, who dwelt in villages as far as Gaza, the Caphtorim, who came out of Caphtor, destroyed them and dwelt in their place." The Septuagint, trusting it, and the Latin translator too, wrongly render this as Cappadocians and Cappadocia; as does the Chaldee paraphrast, with Kapputkia (קפוטקיא) and from Kapputkia (מן קפוטקיא).

units.la: III. Put, פוט, pater Putaeorum, quos Aegyptiorum socios innuit Iechezkel cap. xxvii. 10. ut & Iirmeias xlvi. 9. ubi Septuaginta & Latinus pro פוט Libyam & Libyes reddiderunt. Alij Numidas; alij Mauritanos interpretantur, apud quos Ptolemaeus l.iii. & Plinius lib. v. natur.historiae cap. i, Phtuth fluvium nominant. Hunc Phaethonicm quidam augurantur, quem cognitione motuum coelestium claruisse, & inusitatos adores ex Astris praedixisse, canit, tecta Fabularum involucris Veritate, Antiquitas.
units.tr: III. Put, פוט, father of the Putites, whom Ezekiel 27:10 indicates as allies of the Egyptians, and likewise Jeremiah 46:9, where the Septuagint and the Latin translator rendered Put as Libya and Libyans. Others interpret it as Numidians; others as Mauritanians, among whom Ptolemy in book 3 and Pliny in Natural History, book 5, chapter 1, name a river Phtuth. Some conjecture that this man was Phaethon, who, famous for his knowledge of the heavenly motions, foretold unusual disasters from the stars; antiquity, veiling truth in the wrappings of fables, sings of this.

units.la: IIII. Cenahhan כנען regioni Cenahan nomen à se dedit; quam postea Filijs Israel, ex Aegypto reducibus, Deus singulari beneficio adtribuit.
units.tr: IV. Canaan, כנען, gave his own name to the region of Canaan, which God afterwards assigned to the sons of Israel returning from Egypt by a singular benefit.

units.la: De Posteris ejus Moschaeus Genef. cap. x. 15: Cenahhan autem genuit Tzidonem primogenitum suum, & Chetaeum, Iebusaeum quoque, & Emoraeum, & Girgasihaeum, & Chivvaeum, & Hharkaeum, & Sinaeum, & Arvadaeum, & Tzemaraeum, & Chamathaeum. Sic enim Latine posiunt commode verti. Populorum, qui ab his descenderunt, passim in Biblijs mentio. Tzidon צידון Σιδων Interpretibus Lxx, parens Sidoniorum, quibus Sidon, Σιδων, nobilissima Phoeniciae urbs, ad Mare Magnum vel Mediterraneum habitata; said. hodieque, ut Marius Niger & Gulielmus Postellus notant: Chet, חת, χετταιων (qui condidisse scribitur Hebron, ubi Abraham habitavit) Chetaeorum: Iebusi, יבוסי, Ιεβουσαιων (qui Gabea & Ierusalem, antiquis Iebus, tenuit) Iebusaeorum: Hemori, אמורי, Αμορραιων, Hemoraeorum: Girgasi, גרגשי, Γεργεσαιων, Girgasihenorum Chivvi Chivvi, חיוי, Εὐαῖοι, tenuit Sichem, Gazam & Mizphe, Genef. cap. xxxiv, Deuterononom. cap. 11. & Iehoschuh. cap. x i. Hharki, ערקי, Α᾿ρκαῖοι, perhibetur auctor Arces opidi, quod è regione Tripolis, ad radices Montis Libani. Sini, סיני, Chaldæo Paraphrasti evarianti אנתיוסא, Septuaginta Α᾿συαῖοι, Incola fuisse videtur Deserti Sinai. Arvadi, ארודי, Α᾿γαδῖοι, Arado Insulæ, cujus mentio apud Iechezkel. cap.xxvii,8. in deploratione excidij Tyri, dedit nomen: alij ferunt in finibus Iudææ & Arabiæ Petræ urbem condidisse. Tzemari, צמרי, Chaldæo צלמורא, Σαμαραῖοι, nomen, quod mihi vero simile, imposuit urbi צמרים; Tzemaraim in Tribu Beniamin, cuius mentio cap. Iehoschuhhæ xviii, 22. & 11. Paralipom. cap. xiii, 4. Chamathi, חמתי, Α᾿μαθι Septuaginta, Latinis Emath vel Hemath, regionem occupavit Iturææ, quæ limes Terræ promissæ, qua vergit Damascum versus, ad Trachonos montes, ut sentiunt & probant ex Numerorum capite xxxiv,8; Iehoschuh. xiii,5; lib.1. Paralipom. cap. xviii, 10. & Iirmeiæ cap. xlix, 23. Zieglerus & Beroaldus contra Iosephum & D. Hieronymum; qui Emath putarunt esse Antiochiam, cognomine Epiphaniam, & pertinuisse ad Tribum Nephthali. Zonaras etiam arbitratur Emath auctorem esse urbis Amathæ, Macedonibus habitatæ; cujus nomen Ptolemæus Epiphanius in Epiphaniam commutavit: hinc autem ortos Macedonas, qui Emathij; quorum campos nominat, ut alij addunt, Lucanus lib. 1. belli Pharsalici.
units.tr: Concerning his descendants, Moses writes in Genesis 10:15: "And Canaan begat Sidon his firstborn, and Heth, and the Jebusite also, and the Amorite, and the Girgashite, and the Hivite, and the Arkite, and the Sinite, and the Arvadite, and the Zemarite, and the Hamathite." For so these may conveniently be rendered in Latin. The peoples who descended from them are mentioned throughout the Bibles. Zidon, צידון, Sidon, Σιδων, in the Seventy, the father of the Sidonians, to whom belongs Sidon, the most noble city of Phoenicia, inhabited by the Great or Mediterranean Sea, and still so today, as Marius Niger and Guillaume Postel note. Heth, חת, Chettaion (χετταιων), of the Hittites (who is said to have founded Hebron, where Abraham dwelt). Jebusi, יבוסי, Iebousaion (Ιεβουσαιων), of the Jebusites (who held Gibeah and Jerusalem, anciently called Jebus). Hemori, אמורי, Amorraion (Αμορραιων), of the Amorites. Girgasi, גרגשי, Gergesaion (Γεργεσαιων), of the Girgashites. Chivvi, חיוי, Euaioi (Εὐαῖοι), held Shechem, Gaza and Mizpeh (Genesis 34; Deuteronomy 11; Joshua 11). Harki, ערקי, Arkaioi (Α᾿ρκαῖοι), is said to be the founder of the town of Arca, which lies opposite Tripoli, at the foot of Mount Lebanon. Sini, סיני, Asuaioi (Α᾿συαῖοι) in the Septuagint, and in the Chaldee paraphrast, who varies it as Antiusa (אנתיוסא). He seems to have been an inhabitant of the desert of Sinai. Arvadi, ארודי, Agadioi (Α᾿γαδῖοι), gave its name to Arados, an island mentioned in Ezekiel 27:8, in the lament over the fall of Tyre. Others report that he founded a city in the borders of Judea and Arabia Petraea. Zemari, צמרי, in the Chaldee צלמורא, Samaraioi (Σαμαραῖοι), a name which, as seems to me likely, he gave to the city Zemaraim, צמרים, in the tribe of Benjamin, mentioned in Joshua 18:22 and 2 Chronicles 13:4. Chamathi, חמתי, Amathi in the Septuagint, to the Latins Emath or Hemath; he occupied the region of Iturea, which was the border of the Promised Land, towards Damascus, as far as the mountains of Trachon, as they think and prove from Numbers 34:8; Joshua 13:5; 1 Chronicles 18:10 and Jeremiah 49:23. Ziegler and Beroaldus, against Josephus and St Jerome, who thought Emath was Antioch, surnamed Epiphania, and belonged to the tribe of Naphtali. Zonaras also holds that Emath was the founder of the city Amathe, inhabited by Macedonians, whose name Ptolemy Epiphanius changed to Epiphania; and that from there came the Macedonians, who are called Emathii, whose plains, as others add, Lucan names in book 1 of the Civil War (Pharsalia).

units.la: Sic igitur partiti sunt inter se Terram hanc, hominibus, ut dixi, ab Deo datam ad inhabitandum, Noxi filij nepotesque; quum frustra moliti essent Turrim Babylonicam, à Terra Sennaar locisque vicinioribus digressi versus omnes Orbis partes: ulteriora semper, quum sensim augerent, petentes. Nam quidquid uspiam terrarum occupatum in prima illa distributione fuisse, ut nonnulli censent, nequaquam existimandum. Crediderim facile proximis primisque à Divisione annis in omnes Orbis regiones, præsertim Orientalem & Occiduam, ut reliquis temperatiores, fuisse procursum: quamdiu Terra fuit: at primis istis (ut sic loquar, nam & multi sic volunt) momentis ad extrema vel Septemtrionis itum, vel Meridiei; nemo mihi persuaserit, nisi probandis suis validissima in medium protulerit argumenta.
units.tr: Thus, as I have said, the sons and grandsons of Noah divided this earth among themselves, the earth that God had given to men to inhabit. After they had attempted in vain to build the Tower of Babel, they departed from the land of Shinar and the nearer places and spread out to all parts of the world, always seeking farther regions as they gradually increased. As for the view of some that every land anywhere was occupied in that first distribution, it should not be accepted at all. I would readily believe that in the years immediately following the Dispersion, people advanced into all regions of the world, especially the eastern and western ones, which are milder than the others, for as long as the earth lasted. But whether in those first moments (if I may put it so, for many also hold this) they went toward the extremes of the north or of the south, no one will persuade me unless he brings forward very strong arguments to prove his case.

units.la: Sic sentio: Loca quæ vel immigratu ob interjacentes Marium vastitates erant difsicilia, vel habitatu ob nimietatem Frigorum Calorumve molestiora, tardius, & non nisi urgente summa necessitate, fuisse adita & inventis antea habitatisque addita. Quod etiam de illa Orbis parte velim dictum, quam hodie Americam ab Inventore dicimus. Scribunt quidem viri docti Ophirum & Iobabum Ioktanis filios eo profectos; sed scribunt tantum, non probant. Primi, quos enumeravi, Coloni contractius, quam multi diffiniunt, habitarunt: sed copiosiore adaucti prole perpetuo remotiora quæsiverunt loca. Sic tandem enavigatum & ventum (ab Occidentalioribus, quæ notiora nobis, sumamus exemplum) versus Africum, in eam, cui Americæ nomen nuper inditum; versus Zephyrum, in Britannias; Corum Circiumque versus, in Islandiam & alias Arctoi maris Insulas. Et quum progrediundo in Globi huius vel Latitudinem vel Longitudinem, nihil amplius occurreret occupandum; reversum est quasi ad priora loca & Progenitorum sedes. In hoc migrandi remigrandique studio principem facile tenuerunt locum Nationes, quæ Septemtrionem versum concesserant. Hæ namque non semel coactæ leguntur, sortitione facta, numerosiorem partum, suorum partem, extrudere; & ad nova quærendum domicilia, patrijs relictis sedibus, animare. Cautas habebant nunc has, nunc illas; in primis, ut jam innui, fœcunditatem suorum nimiam. Nam Aere fruentes hi populi saluberrimo, & constipato per frigus externum intus calore, generandis liberis aptissimi in maximam sæpe excrescebant multitudinem: cui alendæ, quum proprias terras animadverterent ob horrorem Cœli sterliores non sufficere; suis nulla difficultate aliarum Regionum instillabant amorem: qui facili negocio ubertatem persuasi atque aeris temperiem, avitum solum mutantes, extorresc passim per alias gentes, velut examina, diffundebant. Sic Germani, Marcomanni, Gothi, Heruli, Rugij, Langbardi, & qui non? Italiam invaserunt; Cimbri, Franci Sugambri cujusque prænominis alij, Nortmanni, Galliam; Tungri, Nervij, Atrebates, Eburones, Veromandui, Condrusi, Verocasses, Cæresi, Pæmanni, Vbij, & alij, Trans-Rhenanas Provincias; Triboci, Mediomatricum agros; Baravi, propinquiora Occano, versus Rheni ostia; Carpi & Suevi, Pannoniam; Vandali, Catti, Alani, Hispaniam. Aliorum in alias Regiones inruptiones praetereo. Nam haec omnia suis locis plenius. Paucis multa generatim Tertullianus libro de Anima: Invenimus, inquit, apud Commentarios etiam Humanarum Antiquitatum paullatim humanum genus exuberasse, dum Aborigines vel vagi, vel extorres, vel gloriosi quique occupant Terras: ut Scythae, Parthicas; ut Menidae, Peloponnesum; ut Athenienses, Asiam; ut Phryges, Italiam; ut Phoenices, Africam: dum solemnes Nationum migrationes, quas µετοικίας appellant, consilio exonerandae popularitatis, in alios fines examina gentis eructant. Nam & Origines nunc in suis sedibus permanent; & alii amplius gentilitatem suam funeraverunt. Et de Pallio: Transfer avere redundantium gentium examina; Scytha exuberant Persas; Phoenices in Africam eructant; Romanos Phryges pariunt; Chaldaeum semen in Aegyptum educatur; dehinc, quum inde transducitur, Iudaea gens est.
units.tr: This is my view. Places that were either hard to reach because of the intervening deserts of the sea, or less pleasant to live in because of the excess of cold or heat, were approached more slowly, and only under great necessity, and were added to the places already found and inhabited. I would wish this said also of that part of the world which we today call America after its discoverer. Learned men write that Ophir and Jobab, the sons of Joktan, went there; but they only write it, they do not prove it. The first settlers I have listed lived in a smaller area than many define, but as they grew through a larger offspring they continually sought more distant places. So at last, sailing and arriving (let us take as our example the western lands, which are better known to us) toward Africa, into that land which has recently been given the name America; toward the west, into the British Isles; toward the northwest and north, into Iceland and the other islands of the Arctic sea. And since, in advancing, nothing more remained to be occupied in the breadth or length of this globe, they turned back, as it were, to the earlier places and the seats of their forefathers. In this eagerness to migrate and to return, the nations that had gone toward the north easily held the first place. For it is recorded that these were not once but many times compelled, by drawing lots, to thrust out the more numerous part of their people, and to urge them to seek new homes after leaving their ancestral seats. They had different reasons at different times; above all, as I have already hinted, the excessive fertility of their people. For these peoples, enjoying a most healthful air, and with an inner heat compressed by the outer cold, were very apt for bearing children and often grew into a great multitude. When they saw that their own lands, because of the harshness of the sky, were too barren to feed such a multitude, they easily instilled in their people a love of other regions. Changing their ancestral soil with little difficulty, for the sake of fertility and a milder climate, they poured out in swarms, like bees, among other peoples. So the Germans, Marcomanni, Goths, Heruli, Rugians, Lombards, and who not, invaded Italy; the Cimbri, Franks, Sugambri and others of each name, and the Northmen, invaded Gaul; the Tungri, Nervii, Atrebates, Eburones, Veromandui, Condrusi, Veromasses, Caeresi, Paemani, Ubii and others, the provinces beyond the Rhine; the Triboci, the fields of the Mediomatrici; the Baravi, the regions nearer the ocean toward the mouths of the Rhine; the Carpi and Suevi, Pannonia; the Vandals, Chatti, Alans, Spain. I pass over the other invasions of different peoples into other regions, for all these will be treated more fully in their proper places. Tertullian has briefly summed up many things in general in his book On the Soul: "We find, he says, in the commentaries of human antiquities also, that the human race gradually overflowed, while the Aborigines, either wandering or driven out, or certain proud men, occupied lands: as the Scythians occupied Parthia; the Menidae, the Peloponnese; the Athenians, Asia; the Phrygians, Italy; the Phoenicians, Africa; while solemn migrations of nations, which they call migrations [µετοικίας], for the sake of relieving overcrowding, belched forth swarms of the race into other territories. For the Origines now remain in their own seats, and others have much more completely lost their own nationality." And in his On the Pallium: "Transfer the swarms of overflowing peoples: the Scythians overflow into Persia; the Phoenicians belch forth into Africa; the Phrygians bring forth the Romans; the Chaldean seed is led out into Egypt; then, when it is carried thence, it becomes the Jewish nation."

units.la: Per Migrationes autem, de quibus hactenus, & has modo, modo illas, etiam ad remotissima, profectiones, qui paullatim promigrarunt à Progenitoribus suis evariarunt quidem, pro natura genioque locorum; sed ita, ut semper principes, quibus corpus humanum constituitur, partes retinuerint. Falsa sunt enim, quae apud Plinium lib. vii. natur. histor. cap. ii, & Augustinum lib. de Civitate Dei xvi, cap. viii. (qui tamen non Scriptorum laudat nomina, sed maritimam Carthaginis plateam; ubi multivo opere multa monstra erant picta) scribunt Herodotus & Aristeas Proconnesius: esse ad Septemtrionem, haud procul ab ipso Aquilonis exortu, Arimaspos, uno oculo in fronte media insignes; cum Gryphis adiudue circa Metalla bellantes: quae Beton, esse supra Anthropophagos Scythas in magna quadam Imai montis convalle regionem, cui nomen Abarimon; in eaque silvestres vivere homines, aversis post crura plantis, eximiae interim velocitatis; passim cum feris vagantes, non alio spirare caelo, ideoque ad finitimos reges non pertrahi, neque etiam ad Alexandrum Magnum perractos: quae Calliphanes, esse supra Nalamonas, confinesque illis Machias, Androgynos (Latini Semimares vocant) utriusque naturae, eosque inter se vicibus alternis coeuntes & gignere & parere; atque, ut adjicit Aristoteles, dextram mammam ijs esse virilem, laevam muliebrem. Commentitia sunt, quae apud eosdem tradit Megasthenes, esse in monte, cui nomen Milo, homines aversis plantis, octonos digitos in singulis pedibus habentes: quae Ctesias, esse in multis montibus genus hominum, capitibus caninis, pro voce latratum edere, unguibus armatum, venatu & aucupio vesci; alios item homines, qui Monosceli Graecis dicti, singulis cruribus: mirae pernicitatis, eosdemque Sciopodas (Umbripedes quidam vertunt) vocari, quod per majorem aestum in terra supini jacentes umbra se pedum protegant, non longe eos ab Troglodytis abesse; rursumque ab his Occidentem versus esse quosdam sine cervice, oculos in humeris habentes; & Choromandae sine voce stridoris horrendi, hirtis corporibus, oculis glaucis, dentibus caninis: quae Eudoxus, in Meridianis Indiae locis Plantas esse viris cubitales; feminis adeo parvas, ut Struthopodes appellentur. Nugae; quae scriptis mandant ibidem Megasthenes, cuius jam memini, gentem esse inter Nomadas Indos narium loco foramina tantum habentem, anguium modo loripedem, vocari Syrittas; ad extremos fines Indiae ab Oriente circa fontem Gangis Astomorum gentem reperiri, sine ore, corpore toto hirtam, vestiri frondium lanugine, halitu tantum viventem & odore, quem naribus trahant, nullum illis cibum, nullum potum, tantum radicum florumque varios odores & silvestrium malorum, quae secum portant longiore itinere, ne desit olfactus, graviore paullum odore haud difficulter examinari: quae Duris, nasci in quibusdam Indiae locis homines cauda villosa, pernicitatis eximiae; alios auribus ad pedes usque propendulis, quae tegendis corporibus sufficiant: quae denique Diodorus lib. iii. de fabulosis Antiquorum gestis, homines esse nescio qua Insula bisulcis linguis. ait enim Iambolum quemdam Mercatorem cum Conservo captum ab Æthiopibus maritimis, navim ingredi fuisse jussum, & versus Meridiem navigando pergere, donec ad Insulam quamdam Felicem pervenisset: hunc enim Aethiopibus fuisse morem antiquissimum, ut duos alienigenas expiationis gratia illuc mitterent singulis annis: Iambolum post quatuor menses ad Insulam appulisse, & in ea homines invenisse benignos, corpore agili & robusto; ossibus instar nervorum flexibilibus; linguam ijs datam ab natura in inferiore parte scissam, ut ab radice duplex esse videretur; ita autem varia uti loquela, ut non solum voce hominum loquerentur, rentur, sed Avium etiam diversarum imitarentur cantus; & quod admirabilius, una cum duobus hominibus perfecte simul loqui, respondendo & disputando; unam enim illos dare linguam uni, alteram alteri. Buttubata Nævij; & quæ, mihi saltem, nullius dignationis. Quid non ausi quondam in historia mendaces Græci? Impunita fuit illis vanitas, & nihil non excogitandi licentia. Non habebant qui veritatem contra putidissima illorum mendacia scriptis tuerentur; & post unam alteramque ætatem summa tribuebatur commentis illorum fides. Certe Mercatores nostrorum temporum nullas non adierunt Terras, nulla non viderunt loca: at hujusmodi monstra nasci aspiam, illorum nusquam loquuntur Ephemerides. Confecit, credo, cum reliquis Hercules. Sed serio. Hominum sæpe nata fuisse Monstra, hodieque ex vehementi Concipientis imaginatione (nam ex cœlesti, ut Abincenna vult lib. xviii. de Animalibus, impressione; vel fato, quod censet Vlpianus in l. quærct aliquis. D. de verb. signif. vel casu, quemadmodum putat Aristoteles lib. ii. Physicorum, edi, parum mihi probatur) nasci in singulis quibusque gentibus, non nego: at in universo genere humano quædam gentium esse Monstra, pernego. Omnia hominum genera, quæ perhibentur esse, esse credere non est necesse, præsertim quum contrarium adferant experimenta. Accedit huc, quod, quæ (de nonnullis hoc velim dictum) Veteres putarunt esse monstrosas hominum species; nos, certiora edocti, didicimus esse, cum alia Animalia, tum præcipue varia Simiarum genera; Cynocephalos, quos Canicipites interpretatur Augustinus: Cercopithecos, vel Caudatas Simias: Sphinges, animalia vulgaribus Simijs non absimilia, nisi quod majora, geminis à pectore mammis propendulis, mulicbri facie, in Æthiopia nasci solita, docilia, ut scribit Solinus, ad feritatis oblivionem. De ipsa certe Simia meus Ennius in Annalibus:
units.tr: Through the migrations of which I have spoken so far, and these or those journeys even to the most remote places, those who gradually migrated from their forefathers did indeed vary, according to the nature and character of the places; but in such a way that they always kept the principal parts by which the human body is constituted. For what Pliny writes in book 7 of his Natural History, chapter 2, and what Augustine writes in book 16 of The City of God, chapter 8 (though he does not name the authors, but mentions the seafront of Carthage, where many monsters were painted in a costly work), is false: that Herodotus and Aristeas of Proconnesus write that to the north, not far from the very rising of the North Wind, there are the Arimaspi, distinguished by one eye in the middle of the forehead, who fight constantly with the griffins over metals; that Beton says that above the man-eating Scythians, in a certain large valley of Mount Imaus, there is a region called Abarimon, in which wild men live with their feet turned backward behind their legs, of remarkable speed, wandering everywhere with the wild beasts, and breathing no other air, and therefore are not brought before the neighbouring kings, nor even before Alexander the Great; that Callisthenes says that above the Nalamonae, and bordering them, the Machiae, Androgyni (the Latins call them Semimares), of both natures, who by turns couple with each other and both conceive and bear; and, as Aristotle adds, that their right breast is male and their left female. Fictions are those that Megasthenes hands down in the same writers: that on a mountain called Milo there are men with feet turned backward, having eight toes on each foot; that Ctesias says that in many mountains there is a race of men with dog's heads, who utter barking for speech, armed with claws, and feed on hunting and fowling; likewise other men, called Monoscelei by the Greeks, with a single leg each, of remarkable swiftness, and these are called Sciopodae (some translate Umbripedes), because in the greater heat they lie on their backs on the ground and shelter themselves with the shadow of their feet; that they are not far from the Troglodytes; and again, that from these toward the west there are some without necks, having their eyes in their shoulders; and Choromandae, without voice, of horrible screeching, with hairy bodies, grey eyes and dog's teeth. Eudoxus says that in the southern regions of India the feet of the men are a cubit long, and of the women so small that they are called Struthopodes. These are trifles, which Megasthenes, whom I have just mentioned, commits to writing in the same place: that there is a people among the Indian nomads who have only holes instead of nostrils, who walk with legs like serpents, and are called Syrittae; that at the far borders of India, to the east, near the spring of the Ganges, there is found a race of Astomi, without a mouth, their whole body hairy, clothed in a down of leaves, living only by breath and by the smell they draw in through their nostrils, having no food or drink, only the various scents of roots and flowers and of wild fruits, which they carry with them on a longer journey so that the sense of smell may not fail, and which are easily tested by a rather heavier smell. Duris writes that in certain places of India there are men with hairy tails, of remarkable swiftness, and others with ears hanging down to their feet, which suffice to cover their bodies. Finally, Diodorus, in book 3 of his work on the fabulous deeds of the ancients, reports men on I know not what island with forked tongues. For he says that a certain merchant named Iambulus, taken captive with a fellow slave by the seafaring Ethiopians, was ordered to board a ship and sail southward until he reached a certain fortunate island; for it was the most ancient custom of the Ethiopians to send two foreigners there every year for the sake of expiation. He says that after four months Iambulus landed at the island and found there kindly men of agile and robust body, with bones as flexible as sinews; their tongue was given them by nature, split in the lower part, so that from the root it seemed double; and they used speech in such a varied way that they not only spoke with human voices but also imitated the songs of various birds; and, what is more remarkable, they could speak perfectly at the same time with two men, answering and disputing, for they gave one tongue to one and the other to the other. The Buttubata of Naevius, and other things which, to me at least, are of no worth. What lies did the Greeks once dare to tell in history! Their vanity went unpunished, and they had licence to invent anything. There were no people to defend the truth in writing against their most foul lies; and after a generation or two their fictions were given the highest credit. Surely the merchants of our own time have visited every land and seen every place; yet the daily records nowhere speak of such monsters being born anywhere. Hercules, I suppose, has finished them off along with the rest. But seriously. That monsters were sometimes born of men, and are still born today in every nation from the strong imagination of the conceiving woman (for I do not much approve that they arise from a heavenly impression, as Avicenna holds in book 18 of On Animals, or from fate, as Ulpian thinks in the law "Quaeret aliquis," D. de verborum significatione, or from chance, as Aristotle thinks in book 2 of the Physics), I do not deny; but that in the whole human race there are certain monstrous peoples, I flatly deny. It is not necessary to believe that all the kinds of men that are said to exist do exist, especially since experience brings the contrary. Add to this that those forms of men which the ancients thought monstrous (I would wish this said of some of them), we, better instructed by more certain knowledge, have learned to be other animals, and above all various kinds of apes: the Cynocephali, whom Augustine interprets as Canicipites; the Cercopitheci, or tailed apes; the Sphinges, animals not unlike common apes, except that they are larger, with two breasts hanging from the chest, a female face, which are said to be found in Ethiopia, and, as Solinus writes, tame enough to forget their wildness. Of the ape itself, certainly, my Ennius says in the Annals:

units.la: Simia quam similis turpissima bestia nobis.
units.tr: The ape, how like us, the most hideous of beasts.

units.la: Fecit similitudo, ut Antiquitas putarit esse homines, sibique (ô crassos & non tolerandos errores!) congeneres.
units.tr: It was the likeness that made the ancients think they were men, and (O gross and intolerable errors!) their own kin.

units.la: Evariarunt igitur homines qui huc illuc profecti, ab suis progenitoribus; non quidem violente, ut alias formas, quales jam delineavimus, induerint; sed pro locorum, quibus insederant, genio; cum in alijs, ut Coloribus, Ingenijs, Ritibus, Moribus & similibus, quæ suis locis explicantur; tum in Statura & Linguarum Dialectis, de quibus hic in genere pauca.
units.tr: Men who travelled hither and thither therefore departed from their forefathers in appearance. They did not take on other forms by force, of the kind we have already described, but changed according to the disposition of the places where they settled. This happened in other respects, such as colour, intellect, customs, manners and the like, which are explained in their proper places, and also in stature and in the dialects of languages. I will say a few things here in general about these last two.

units.la: Quod ad Staturam: proceriores alijs videmus esse, & augustioris formæ plerumque Septemtrionaliores. Faciunt hoc ibi, cum abundantia sanguinis (docente Vitruvio lib. vi. Architect. cap. i.) tum cohibitus intus ab frigore circumstante Calor (de quo Aristoteles lib. ii. de Part. Animal. cap. vi.) qui in Regionibus ab Septemtrione remotioribus dissipatur, meatibus usquequaque hiantibus. Quo modo tamen & calidas habitantibus regiones corpora nonnumquam in molem adolescant: notat ex Aristotele aliisque Hieronymus Magius lib. Miscellaneor. i, cap. v. & alibi forte dicam. Sunt qui vastiora multo, passim & universim, quondam, quam hodie, perhibent humana fuisse corpora. Legerant enim, quæ de Corporibus humanis sensim, & sine sensu decrescentibus scripserant Esdras lib. iv. cap. v; Homerus Iliad. v, ubi de Aenea ab Diomede vulnerato, & libro xii. ubi de Ajace & Hectore, eoque respiciens Virgilius lib. Aeneid. xii, ubi de Turno; item quæ Lucretius lib. ii. de natur. rerum; Plinius libro natur. histor. vii, cap. xvii; Agellius lib. iii. Noct. Atticar. cap. iii; & Iuvenalis Satyr. xv. Viderant ijdem Arma Veterum ab hujus ævi hominibus vix tractari: gradus Cochlearum antiquarum hodie difficillime superari posse; neminemque reperiri, qui Pyramidis Aegyptiacæ; ejus quæ maxima est, gradus queat ascendere. Hominum, qui quondam ævum agitarunt, longitudinem & robur; Nostrorum autem hodie brevitatem & impotentiam, ad quam paullatim ventum, facile tamquam Mundi senescentis, & qui brevi interiturus, argumenta concedo: sed nimium illum generatim hic ibive in corporibus vel Excessum vel Defectum, id est, fuisse, vel esse Giganteas vel Pygmæas gentes, ægrius admitto. Exorbitat (sic loquar) hic pro incomprehensibili sua sapientia summus opifex: sed raro, & in paucis. Nota sunt, quæ de Goliath Sacræ litteræ: de Pallantis cadauere Martinus Polonus in Chronicis, & Galeotus Marrius de doctrina promiscua cap. xxxvi. de Mulicre quadam Cælius Rhodiginus lib. ii. Antiquar. Lect. cap. vi; de Iohanne ejus nominis Octavo, Arkulei Dinasta, Nicolao Kyerhenio Spartne woudano, & Zelanda quadam Hadrianus Iunius in Batavia; de Mediolanensi Iulius Cæsar Scaliger; de Pedemontano quodam M. Antonius Delrio ad Oedipum Senecæ: de multis simul Hieronymus Magius libro Miscellan. 1. cap. iv. deque aliis alij, vt Paufanias in Atticis, Herodotus lib. 1, Philostratus lib. v, Plinius lib. natur. histor. vii. cap. xvi & xx, Solinus cap. v, Polyhistor. & xiv, Glycas parte iv. ad Anastasij imperium, Zonaras Tom. ii, August. lib. ix de Civitate Dei, cap. xv. & xxiii, Nicephorus lib. xii. Ecclesiast. histor. cap. xxxvii, Saxo Grammaticus in Præfat. histor. Danicæ, Hector Boëthus Scoticæ Historiæ lib. ii. memoriæ prodiderunt. Et ego (vt ἀντιλία, cui magna solet esse fides, testem etiam faciam) Belgam (Antverpianum se ferebat) in Galliis, anno cIↄ Iↄ LXXXIII, vidi novem pedes altitudine excedentem; quem audivi paulo post, quum magna pecuniæ vi conquisita in patriam pararet reditum, ab viarum obsessoribus obtruncatum. Sed rariores vt dixi, sunt huiusmodi formæ, & paucorum hominum; non totarum gentium. Monendum hoc loco succurrit, Ioannem Lucidum lib. 1. de Emendat. Temp. cap. iiii. scriptis prodere, Adamum etiam fuisse non solum Gigantem: sed omnium Gigantum, qui fuerint umquam, maximum, ex libro Iehoschuhhæ cap. xiiii, 15: sed docte & neruose refutatur à Benedicto Pererio lib. iv. in Genef. quæst. iii, qui addit, non ibi significari Adamum primum omnium hominum parentem, sed alium: illum enim perfecta corporis statura fuisse creatum. Atqui obiiciet quis, Gigantéas Gentes nominari Genes. cap. vi, 4. ubi Moyses sic scribit: Gigantes autem (Hebr. נפלים; Chaldæo Paraphrasti, גבריא; Septuaginta γίγαντες) erant super terram, & quæ sequuntur: Gigantes enim ibi נפלים dici, ab נפל cadere; quod caderet, ut Rab. Abraham interpretatur, cor videntis illos. Nominari ab Latino Græcisque Interpretibus fateor, designari in Hebræo textu & ab Chaldæo Paraphraste differeor. נפלים ibi, non qui insolita statura; sed, ut bene notant ad laudatum à me caput Geneseos, Gennadius Archiepiscopus Constantinopolitanus, Theodoretus Cyri Episcopus, Io. Damascenus Monachus, alij; qui feri, audentes, robusti: unde & Chaldaice גבריא: nam גבור fortis, potens, robustus. Adposite Chrysostomus: γίγαντες, ἐξίνλω πλάσιν, ὁ δὲ ξίνλω μορφῷ; ἀλλὰ τὰς Ἡρωας, τὰς πολεμικὰς, τὰς ἰσχυρὰς. נפלים, qui superbi, qui fortissimi, ut censet Augustinus in Psalmos xxxii & xcvii, qui inexpugnabiles, rebelles, contumaces, scribentibus D. Hieronymo & ejus discipulo Philippo Presbytero in Hijobum lib. ii. cap. xxvi: Gigantes appellat Scriptura Divina homines superbos, rebelles & contumaces, ut fuit ille Nemroth Gigas, Venator contra Dominum. Diabolus quoque & sui, translato nomine, Gigantes propter superbiam nuncupantur. Eleganter & Macrobius lib. ii. Saturnaliorum cap. xxvi: Quid aliud fuisse (Gigantes) credendum est, quam hominum quamdam impiam gentem, Deos negantem, & ideo existimatam Deos pellere de cœlesti sede voluisse: horum pedes in Draconum volumina desinebant; quod significat, nihil rectum, nihil eos superum cogitasse, totius vita eorum gressu atque processu in inferna vergente: de Pedum significatione consulendi Petrus Crinitus lib. ii. de honesta disciplina, cap. xi. & Georgius Fabricius ad Romanum Martyrem Prudentij; nonnihil & Ego ad 1. Annalium Ennij. נפלים deniq; vel γίγαντες illi; qui, D E I desertores, quidquid rerum divinarum, quidquid cœleste insuperhabentes, Naturæque duci reluctantes, ut Terra nati, quæ Terræ sapiunt & somniant. Confirmat hoc Etymon, cum apud Hebræos; נפלים enim derivati ab Deficiendi vel Desciscendi verbo, ut accipitur lib. ii. Regum, cap. xxv, 11, & Iirmejæ cap. xxxvii, 13: tum apud Græcos; Sic enim Orpheus: οὓς καλέιση γίγαντας ἱπωνυμον ἐν μαχάρεσιν οὐνεκα γῆς ἐνφοιτο ἡδὴ αἵματ᾽ ἀρξιοιο.
units.tr: As to stature: we see some peoples taller than others, and those further north are generally of larger and more massive build. This happens there partly because of the abundance of blood (as Vitruvius teaches, Architecture book 6, chapter 1), and partly because the heat, held in by the surrounding cold (on which see Aristotle, On the Parts of Animals book 2, chapter 6), is dispersed in the regions farther from the north, whose passages are open on every side. Yet how it is that in hot regions bodies sometimes grow to a huge size, Hieronymus Magius notes from Aristotle and others, in Miscellanea book 1, chapter 5, and I may perhaps say more elsewhere. Some maintain that human bodies were once far larger, everywhere and generally, than they are today. For they had read what was written about human bodies gradually and imperceptibly shrinking: by Esdras (4 Esdras 5); by Homer (Iliad 5, where Aeneas is wounded by Diomedes, and Iliad 12, where Ajax and Hector are described); by Virgil, who alludes to this in Aeneid 12 where Turnus is described; likewise by Lucretius (On the Nature of Things book 2); by Pliny (Natural History book 7, chapter 17); by Aulus Gellius (Attic Nights book 3, chapter 3); and by Juvenal (Satire 15). The same writers had observed that the weapons of the ancients can hardly be handled by the men of this age, that the steps of the ancient snail-shell staircases can be climbed only with great difficulty today, and that no one can be found who can climb the steps of the Egyptian pyramid, the largest of them. I readily concede these as proofs of the length and strength of the men who once lived, and of the brevity and weakness of ours today, which has gradually come about, as is easily understood, as the world grows old and is about to perish. But I more reluctantly admit that there were, or are, giant or pygmy peoples, that is, an excess or deficiency in bodies. In his inscrutable wisdom, the supreme Maker, so to speak, goes beyond the usual measure, but rarely and in a few cases. Those things which Holy Letters tell of Goliath are well known; Martinus Polonus in his Chronicles tells of the corpse of Pallas; Galeotus Marius in On Promiscuous Learning, chapter 36, tells of a certain woman; Caelius Rhodiginus in Ancient Lessons book 2, chapter 6, tells of the same; of John, the eighth of that name, lord of Arkel, Nicolaus Kyerhenius of Spaarndam, and a certain woman of Zeeland, Hadrianus Junius writes in his Batavia; of a man from Milan, Julius Caesar Scaliger; of a certain Piedmontese, M. Antonius Delrio in his commentary on Seneca's Oedipus; and Hieronymus Magius, in Miscellanea book 1, chapter 4, reports many of these together. Others have recorded other such cases: Pausanias in Attica, Herodotus book 1, Philostratus book 5, Pliny Natural History book 7, chapters 16 and 20, Solinus chapter 5 and chapter 14 of his Polyhistor, Glycas part 4 under the reign of Anastasius, Zonaras volume 2, Augustine On the City of God book 9, chapters 15 and 23, Nicephorus Ecclesiastical History book 12, chapter 37, Saxo Grammaticus in the preface to the Danish History, and Hector Boece in Scottish History book 2. I too (since the testimony of an eyewitness is usually held in high regard, I shall call myself as a witness) saw in Gaul, in the year 1583, a Belgian who called himself a native of Antwerp, exceeding nine feet in height. I heard shortly afterwards that, when he was preparing to return home with a large sum of money collected, he was cut down by highway robbers. But such forms, as I have said, are rarer and belong to a few men, not to whole nations. It occurs to me to note here that John Lucidus, in On the Emendation of Times book 1, chapter 4, writes that Adam was not only a giant but the greatest of all giants who ever existed, citing the book of Jehoshua chapter 14, verse 15. But Benedictus Pererius, in his commentary on Genesis book 4, question 3, refutes this learnedly and vigorously, adding that Adam, the first parent of all men, is not what is meant there, but another man; for Adam was created with the perfect stature of a body. But someone will object that Gigantean peoples are named in Genesis chapter 6, verse 4, where Moses writes thus: The giants (Hebrew נפלים; Chaldee Paraphrast גבריא; Septuagint γίγαντες) were upon the earth, and so on. For the giants are there called נפלים, from נפל, to fall; they were so called, as Rabbi Abraham explains, because the hearts of those who saw them fell. I admit that they are named by the Latin and Greek translators, but I differ as to what is designated in the Hebrew text and by the Chaldee Paraphrast. The נפלים there are not men of unusual stature, but, as Gennadius, Archbishop of Constantinople, Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrus, John Damascene, the monk, and others, rightly note in the chapter of Genesis I have cited, were fierce, bold and robust men; hence also the Chaldee gabria, for גבור means strong, powerful, robust. Chrysostom aptly says: giants are not men of huge size but heroes, warlike and strong men. The נפלים were proud and very strong men, as Augustine thinks (on Psalms 32 and 97), men who were invincible, rebellious and obstinate. Jerome and his disciple Philip the presbyter, in their work on Job book 2, chapter 26, write: Holy Scripture calls proud, rebellious and obstinate men giants, as that giant Nimrod was, a hunter against the Lord. The devil and his followers too are called giants, by a transferred name, because of their pride. Macrobius also elegantly says, in Saturnalia book 2, chapter 26: What else are we to believe the giants were than an impious race of men who denied the gods, and who therefore were thought to have wished to drive the gods from their heavenly seat? Their feet ended in coils of serpents, which signifies that they thought nothing upright, nothing of the heavenly things, and that the whole course of their life, in its step and advance, tended towards the underworld. On the meaning of the feet, consult Petrus Crinitus, On Honest Learning book 2, chapter 11, and Georg Fabricius on Prudentius's Roman Martyr; I too have said something on the first book of Ennius's Annals. Finally, those נפלים or γίγαντες were, as the deserters of God, despising whatever is divine and heavenly and resisting being led by nature, born of the earth, and they savour of the earth and dream of it. The etymology confirms this: among the Hebrews, נפלים derives from the verb meaning to fail or to revolt, as it is used in 2 Kings chapter 25, verse 11, and Jeremiah chapter 37, verse 13; and among the Greeks, for so Orpheus says: [οὓς καλέουσι γίγαντας ἐπωνύμους ἐν μακάρεσιν, οὕνεκα γῆς ἐνέφυσαν ἡδὲ αἵματος ἀρχῆ] (those whom they call giants, named after the earth, because they were born of the earth and of the blood of the beginning).

units.la: Cui consonans Homerus in Batrachomyomachia dixit γηγενέων αὐδρῶν ἔρα Γιγάντων. בני ארץ, Terræ filios, etiam nominare videtur Chaldæus Paraphrast. ad cap. Proverbior. xxi, 16. Sic enim ibi: Homo errans de via Intellectus, in concione רפאים, Manium (id est Mortuorum. Latinus Interpres, Septuaginta sequutus, Gigantum; Chaldæus בני ארץ cum filijs Terræ) requiescet. Atqui urget quis, Giganteas gentes non tantum nominari, sed & designari Numeror.cap. xiii, 33. Nam ita Exploratores eo loco: Populus, quem vidimus, procera statura est: ibi vidimus monstra quaedam filiorum Henak de genere Gigantéo (מן-הנפלים; Chaldæus Paraphraft. ית גיבריא: Septuaginta τὰς γίγαντας) quibus commessi, quasi Locustæ videbamur. Neque hic Gigantææ gentes. Populus, quem viderant Exploratores, procerae staturae erat prae Israelitis: qui Ægyptiorum iam indolem ex ducentorum & sedecim annorum convictu & consuetudine induerant: quemadmodum saepe gens una, ut dixi, procerior altera; adeo ut Romani legantur apud Caesarem Gallis ob brevitatem fuisse derisui: sed erat inter Chaananitas, alioquin proceros, familia Enakaea, cui augustior ceteris forma propria erat, & quasi hereditaria. Nationes igitur GigantEae, id est monstrosae magnitudinis, nusquam: & esse hodie in America Australi, quos Patagonas ab immanitate Pedum Victores Hispani nominarunt, malo simpliciter credere nudis quorundam, inter quos Gomaras Historiae Indicae cap. xci. adseverationibus, quam, an res sic se habeat, periculosa peregrinatione experiri.
units.tr: Homer, in the Battle of the Frogs and Mice, agreeing with this, said [γηγενέων ἀνδρῶν ἔρα γιγάντων] (the earth-born men, the giants). The Chaldee Paraphrast also seems to call them sons of the earth [bene arca] in his comment on Proverbs chapter 21, verse 16. For there he says: A man wandering from the way of understanding shall rest in the assembly of the rephaim [רפאים], that is, of the dead. The Latin translator, following the Septuagint, has of the giants; the Chaldee has with the sons of the earth [bene arca]. But someone presses that Gigantean peoples are not only named but also designated in Numbers chapter 13, verse 33. For the spies there say: The people whom we saw are of great stature. There we saw certain monsters, the sons of Anak, of the giant race (Hebrew מן־הנפלים; Chaldee Paraphrast yit gabria; Septuagint τὰς γίγαντας), in comparison with whom we seemed like grasshoppers. But here there are no Gigantean peoples. The people whom the spies had seen were of great stature compared with the Israelites, who had by then taken on the character of the Egyptians through two hundred and sixteen years of living together and custom, just as, as I have said, one people is often taller than another. So much so that the Romans are read, in Caesar, to have been a laughing stock to the Gauls because of their small stature. But among the Canaanites, who were otherwise tall, there was a family of Anakim, whose form was more majestic than the others and, as it were, hereditary. Therefore Gigantean nations, that is, of monstrous size, are nowhere; and that there are today in South America, whom the Spaniards, victors, named Patagonians from the vastness of their feet, I prefer simply to believe on the bare assertions of certain men, among whom is Gomara in his History of the Indies, chapter 91, than to test by a dangerous journey whether the matter is really so.

units.la: Ut autem nusquam Gigantes, sic nusquam Pygmaei, homines monstrosae brevitatis (Graeci vocant ἀνθρωπάκια μικρὰ, Νάνος, Σκωπαίως & Σπιλπωνας) quibus πυγών, id est; Cubitus, sesquipedem capiens vel digitos xxiv, nomen, ut Eustathius Homeri Interpres notat, indidit. Iuvenalis poeta, ut homunciones faceret magis ridiculos. Pygmaeam cohortem pede uno non esse altiorem dixit. Nusquam, inquam, vel fuerunt, vel sunt. Ausi tamen eos statuere varii variis locis. Aristoteles, Philostratus & Ammianus in Æthiopia Troglodytarum Regionem ijs adsignant; ibique in Terrae cavernis, formicarum instar, volunt degere: Strabo etiam Homerum interpretatus ad meridiem Terrae Pygmaeos agere scribit. Scholiastes ejusdem in Aegypto penita ponit: Plinius, nunc hos nunc illos sequutus, lib. vii. natur. histor. cap. ii. & lib. iv. cap. xi. collocat in Thracia ad Geraniam; lib.v. cap. xxix. in Asia ad Eudonem Cariae fluvium; lib.vi. cap.xxx. in Aethiopia; ejusdem libri cap. xix. in Prasiorum Montanis, quae sunt in India: Mela in Arabia Interiore fuisse memoriae prodit: Paullus Iovius lib.de Moscovitic.Legat.ultra Iapones statuit; & magis ad Simias, quam Homines (argumentum hoc, quo quis facile persuaderetur esse Pygmaeos) accedere docet. Quidam aevi nostri locum ijs dant sub Polo Arctico. Albertus Magnus lib. i. Animal. cap. iii. ait esse homines silvestres, & nonnihil humanae naturae, quo ad primos motus deliberativos, obtinere; sed cap. xxi. omnem ijs rationis scintillam adimit. Peperit primum Pygmaeos, & o'ενθρομαχίαν (cum Gruibus enim pugnare dicuntur) Homerus, cujus Iliados γ sunt haec: Τρῶες μὲν κλαγγῇ τ' ἰνοπῇ τ' ἰοαν, ὁρνίθες ὡς. Ἡ ὑπ' ἡμ κλαγγὴ γερανων πηλὸς ἀεχνέθη ἀσὶ, Αἴτ' ἐπεὶ ἀν χειμῶνα Φύγον καὶ ἀθεσφατον ὀμβρον, Κλαγγῇ τεῖχε πάντως ἐπ' Ωκεανοῦ ῥοαῶν, Ἀνδρέσιν Πυγμαίοισι Φόνον ἡ κῆρα Φέρουσι.
units.tr: But just as there were never any giants, so there were never any Pygmies, men of monstrous smallness (the Greeks call them "little manikins" [ἀνθρωπάκια μικρά], Nanos, Skōpaiōs and Spilpōnas), to whom the name pygōn, that is "cubit," measuring a cubit and a half or twenty-four fingers, was given, as Eustathius, the interpreter of Homer, notes. The poet Juvenal, to make these little men more ridiculous, said that the Pygmy cohort was not a foot taller than a man. I say that they never existed, or do not exist. Yet various writers have dared to place them in various regions. Aristotle, Philostratus and Ammianus assign to them the region of the Troglodytes in Ethiopia, and they want them to live in holes in the earth, like ants. Strabo, too, in interpreting Homer, writes that the Pygmies live in the south of the earth. Homer's scholiast places them in remote Egypt. Pliny, now following one authority and now another, places them in Thrace near Geranea (Natural History 7.2 and 4.11); in Asia by the river Eudon in Caria (5.29); in Ethiopia (6.30); and in the mountains of the Prasii, which are in India (6.19). Mela reports that they were in inner Arabia. Paulus Iovius, in his work on the embassy to Muscovy, places them beyond the Japanese, and teaches that they approach apes more than men, an argument by which one might easily be persuaded that they are Pygmies. Some of our own age give them a place under the Arctic Pole. Albertus Magnus, in Animals 1.3, says that they are wild men who keep something of human nature as far as their first deliberate movements go; but in chapter 21 he takes away from them every spark of reason. Homer first produced the Pygmies, and their battle with the cranes (for they are said to have fought with cranes), in the third book of the Iliad, which reads: "The Trojans went forth with clamour and shouting, like birds, as when the cry of cranes rises in the sky, which, after escaping winter and boundless rain, fly off with a clamour over the streams of Ocean, bringing death and destruction to the Pygmy men" [Τρῶες μὲν κλαγγῇ τ' ἰνοπῇ τ' ἰοαν, ὁρνίθες ὡς. Ἡ ὑπ' ἡμ κλαγγὴ γερανων πηλὸς ἀεχνέθη ἀσὶ, Αἴτ' ἐπεὶ ἀν χειμῶνα Φύγον καὶ ἀθεσφατον ὀμβρον, Κλαγγῇ τεῖχε πάντως ἐπ' Ωκεανοῦ ῥοαῶν, Ἀνδρέσιν Πυγμαίοισι Φόνον ἡ κῆρα Φέρουσι].

units.la: Peperit, inquam, primus & finxit Homerus. Pygmaeorum quidem meminit Latinus Sacrae Scripturae Interpres apud Iechezkel. cap. xxvii,11: Filij Arvad & virtus tua super muros tuos undique, & Pygmaei in turribus tuis fuerunt. Sed ipsi Prophetae dicuntur נמדים: quos Chaldaeus Paraphrastes vertit קפוטקאי, Cappadoces; Septuaginta μῆ-δες. נמדים Latinis Gammadei. Fortean genuina Scriptura fuit נמליס, ut sint Gammalei. Γάμαλα urbs Stephano Ναυλαυίνδ, quae Egesippo Syriae regio: Gamalam urbem Iudeae in potestatem suam redegit Titus Vespasiani Imperatoris filius, scribente Suetonio: Plinius etiam Gamalen, urbem Phoeniciae, terra absorptam scribit lib. ii. natur. hist. cap. xci. Si quis piaculum putet mutare quid in textu Hebraico, per me licet legat apud laudatos auctores Γάμαδα. Latinus autem Interpres נמדים Pygmaeos vertit, quod נמד Cubitus brachii & mensura Cubiti, Iudic. cap. iii, 16; unde נמד Cubitalis: Septuaginta μῆδες interpretantur, quod posteriores Hebraicae vocis syllabae ab illa gente non prorsus abludere viderentur: ut hinc suspicio mihi nascatur, Scripturam vulgarem probam esse & germanam. Quam autem ob causam Chaldaeus Paraphrastes Cappadoces Gammadaeis substituerit, nondum liquet: nisi forte populi fuerint inter se Conregionales; & notiores positi pro Confinalibus, quorum nomen, absorpta Terrae motu Metropoli, erat exstinctum. Non inficiandum interim quosdam hic ibi valde breves reperiri. Notus Canopas, homuncio ille duorum pedum & palmi; Iuliae, Neptis Augusti, cura & amor, apud Plinium lib. vii, cap. xvi. Notus apud Suetonium in Augusto cap. xliii. adolescentulus Lucius bipedalis, ac vocis immensae. Notus Aegyptius ille perdici similis, apud Nicephorum lib. Ecclesiast. histor. xii, cap. xxxvii. Celebrat Diophantum quemdam, Atomos etiam sua brevitate vincentem, Lucilius lib. ii. Græcor. Epigrammat. tit. xxxii. ὡς λεπτὸς: Ἐξ Ἀτόμων Ἐπικύρος ὅλον τὸν κόσμον ἐγραψεν, Εἶναι τῶν δοxῶν, Ἀ λκιμε, λεπτότατον. Εἰ δὲ τίς τῶ Διοφάντῳ, ἐγραψεν ἂν ἐκ Διοφάντα, Τῆ καὶ τῶν Ἀτόμων πτελυ τι λεπτότερα. Ἡ τὰ μὲν ἀλλ᾽ ἐγραψε σωτεῖναι ἐξ Ἀτόμων ἂν, Ἐκ τότε δ᾽ αὐτὸς, Ἀ λκιμε, τας Ἀτόμας.
units.tr: I say that Homer first produced and invented them. Indeed, the Latin translator of Holy Scripture mentions Pygmies in Ezekiel 27:11: "The sons of Arvad and your strength were upon your walls round about, and the Pygmies were in your towers." But the Hebrew word itself is נמדים [nimdim], which the Chaldee paraphrast renders קפוטקאי [Qappoṭqai], Cappadocians, and the Septuagint μῆδες [mēdes]. The Latins render נמדים as Gammadim. Perhaps the genuine reading of Scripture was נמליס, so that they were Gammalites. Gamala, which Stephanus calls Naulaunited (?) and Hegesippus a region of Syria, was a city of Judaea, which Titus, son of the Emperor Vespasian, brought under his power, as Suetonius writes. Pliny, too, writes in Natural History 2.91 that Gamala, a city of Phoenicia, was swallowed up by the earth. If anyone thinks it sacrilege to change anything in the Hebrew text, let him read Γάμαδα in the authors cited, as far as I am concerned. But the Latin translator rendered נמדים as Pygmies, because נמד means a cubit, the measure of the forearm, Judges 3:16, and hence נמד means cubital. The Septuagint translated μῆδες, because the later syllables of the Hebrew word did not seem to differ much from that people's name. Hence the suspicion arises in my mind that the common Scripture reading is sound and genuine. Why the Chaldee paraphrast put Cappadocians in place of Gammadim is not yet clear, unless perhaps the peoples were neighbours, and the better-known people was put in place of the people living nearby, whose name was extinguished when their metropolis was swallowed up by an earthquake. Meanwhile, it must not be denied that some very small people are found here and there. Canopas is well known, that little man two feet and a palm tall, the care and love of Julia, granddaughter of Augustus (Pliny 7.16). Known too is the boy Lucius, two feet tall but with a voice of immense volume, in Suetonius, Augustus 43. Known too is that Egyptian like a partridge, in Nicephorus, Ecclesiastical History 12.37. Lucilius, in the second book of the Greek Epigrams, title 32, celebrates a certain Diophantus, who surpassed even atoms in his smallness: "Epicurus wrote the whole world out of atoms, which, most foolish man, are the most minute of opinions. But if anyone wrote the world out of Diophantus, he would have written something even smaller than atoms. Yet Epicurus wrote the world from atoms; but Diophantus, most foolish man, is smaller than atoms."

units.la: Alios alij commemorant. Ipse nonnullos utriusque sexus vidi inter ministeria Principum; non solum Nanos, sed & mire graciles, vocisque gravis & sonoræ. Hi non solum nascuntur, sed etiam fiunt ab Mangonibus; quorum hac in re artem sic describit Longinus, in eo, quem ὡς ὕψος edidit: τὰ γλωττικὰ, ἐν οἷς οἱ Πυγμαῖοι Νάνοι τρέφονται, ἃ μόνον καλυὶ τ᾽ ἐγκεκλεισμένων τὰς αὐξήσεις, ἀλλὰ ἡ σωμάτων δεσμόν.
units.tr: Others mention others. I myself have seen several of both sexes among the attendants of princes: not only dwarfs, but also remarkably slender ones, with deep and sonorous voices. These are not only born that way but are also made by the dwarf-keepers. Longinus, in the work he published on the sublime, describes their craft in this matter: the fattening rooms in which the dwarfish Pygmies are reared, which not only stop their growth by confinement but also bind their bodies.

units.la: In statura quo modo & quatenus evariatum hodie à Priscis illis, Progenitoribus nostris per varias Migrationes, docui: sequitur, ut de Linguarum Dialectis nonnihil dicam. Inciderat Linguarum confusio in annum ab Diluvio centesimum & primum: quam sequuta statim, D e o, qui volebat totum orbem Colonis sensim impleri & latissime coli, sic ordinante, ipsa Terræ Partium Distributio. Causam quis quærit tam memorabilis, vel miseræ potius, commutationis? Aliam nemo dabit homo, quam hominum Insolentiam tunc temporis, & Dei contemtum. Testatur ipsa Veritas. Unus fuerat, idemque omnibus sermo ab initio mundi ad annum usque cio io cc, & qui excurrebant: qua tempestate id inter se miselli agitare coeperunt; ut, obscurata D e i gloria, suum æternarent nomen. Quid factum? Soluta fuit & oppressa mirando Dei judicio, ejusque nutu simplici (Origenes Angelorum operam huc advocat) furialis illa & luctuosa conspiratio, Linguarum confusione & insolentium vocum novitate. Sic tunc temporis intellectum, non esse modo stulta, sed & impia maledictaque consilia, quæ obfuscandæ D e i gloriæ & perfectissimæ, supremæque divinæ voluntatis rationi enervandæ conta explicantur. Manebit perpetuum; & amentissimam Structorum suorum temeritatem immortalitati commendabit miserum & infelix Babylonis nomen: non in una tantum Syria cognitum, sed ubique gentium, ubique locorum. Quid relatum laudis tam imprudenter captis? Babel, venit Confusio. Gloriam Operis tanti molitores, Dei securi, somniabant & venabantur: sed justa Dei, qui videt, audit, judicat omnia, modisque justissimis gubernat, vindicta summi dedecoris & ignominiæ numquam delendæ facti sunt hæredes. Quum qui eodem antea sermone fuerant usi, jam autem alienas atque adeo insolitas ederent voces, inexspectato perculsi miraculo, simul agere non possent: facto quasi gravissimo schismate, ad solennem discessionem necesse fuit venire, singulosque ijs se consociare, à quibus intelligi poterant. Quot autem natæ tunc Linguæ, quis dicet? Nemo hercle, nemo. Frustra Euphorus, frustra Scriptores alij, Gentes & Linguas ausi dicere lxx. quo argumento? quod in Genesi scriptum cap. xlvi, Animas ex Iacob lxx. in Ægyptum descendisse. Quæ Analogia inter hos & Principes Linguas? De Numero (quem minorem, quam Euphorus ceterique edunt, fuisse censeo) non laboremus: hoc certum, primigenias illas post Hebraicam multas Dialectos, Migrationum huc illuc ope, peperisse; quemadmodum in singulis arguunt Litterarum numerus, series, potestas; ordo scribendi; Origines Vocum, Verborum Radices & Themata; Inflectendi formulæ & Analogiæ; aliaque id genus infinita. De Tribus obiter dicam. Nam postulant hæc alium locum. Hebraica, quæ, ut prima & quasi parens, suo loco manserat incorrupta, pura, syncera, propagines fuerunt, Chaldaica, Arabica, Samaritana, Æthiopica, veteres Medica, Persica, Armenica, Ægyptia, Punica: quibus tanta inter se adfinitas, ut rara sit vox in una, quæ non in aliarum aliqua, leni inflexione. Græca lingua non in Hellade sola legitur quondam habita; verum etiam, farcta passim adventitiis vocibus (ut suis locis docebimur) in Epiro, Peloponnesio, Illurico, Macedonia, Thracia, Asia Minore, Syria, Cilicia, Ægypto, Italia, quæ inde Magna Græcia, Gallia (nam nemo non novit Massiliæ floruisse; & Druidas, Gallorum Sacerdotes, ea in rebus divinis usos) Helvetia (quod ex Cæsaris paret Ephemeridibus de Bello Gallico) Germania Superiore & Inferiore (quod vocum fere Myrias clamat) Ad contractiores limites vocata principes novit praeter quae Communis, Atticam, Ionicam, Doricam, Aeolicam; & his adnumerari solitas, Chalcidicam, Baoticam, Cypriam, Pamphiliçam, Siculam, Rheginam, Cretensem, Tarentinam, Rhodianam, Lacedaemonicam, Argivam, Laconicam, Libycam, Macedonicam, Syracusanam & Thessalicam, principibus conformes & in sermone convenientes. Priores enim ex adnumeratis quatuor Atticismum expressisse, non quidem omnino, sed ex parte, satis docent Herodotus, Demosthenes, Libanius Sophista, aliique: reliquas undecim ad Dorienium proxime accessisse Dialectum, in nonnullis tamen differentes fuisse, testatur Corinthus: Thessalicam denique ad Ionum simul & Dorum idioma pertinuisse Trypho adfirmat. Latina Lingua, quae nobis nunc in usu, non est vere primigenia, sed ab ea prognata. Varias enim passa est mutationes. Nam veluti saecula quaedam sunt, ut Rerum omnium, sic Sermonis. Prima, quam Casam vel Priscam vocare licet, quaeque haud absimilis Doricae fuisse dicitur, vetustissimis Italiae populis usurpata sub primis, quicumque illi fuerint, Regibus. Ejus reliquiae quaedam, ne ignoremus qualis fuerit, servantur hodieque apud Grammaticos Varronem, Festum, & alios; cum in quibusdam, inconditis sane parumque intellectis, Saliorum Antiquorumque Vatum Carminibus, tum singularis aliquot Dictionibus: quemadmodum nulli non notant Critici; &, si quid mihi, quondam etiam insaniam illam insanienti, inter eos loci, ego ad librum 1. Annalium Ennij. Expurgatior facta Latina nomen adquisivit; ab Latino rege, quod nonnulli volunt. Qualis illa; conspici potest, cum aliunde, tum ex fragmentis Regiarum Legum, & censim duodecim Tabularum; nec non Inscriptione C. Duilii Cos. quae hodieque, sed mutila, Romae visitur; posita anno ab V. C. ccccxciv. Et haec cultior reddita ab Romanis; merito Romana nomen nacta: quam, varie tamen Poetae, Historiographi, Oratores, aliis alii, prioribus posteriores, semper felicius, cum primis Ennius (qui merito dixisse Linguam Latinam, & nova rerum vocabula finxisse ab Horatio canitur) maxime coluerunt. Inrepsit postremo loco Misa: quam, aucto Imperio & Libertate amissa, condiderunt cum ipsi Cives Romani; tum varij Populi, in Ius Civitatis & usum Romanae Linguae (nam illud beneficij loco habebatur) admissi. Hi enim sua 30 verba suaque loquendi proprietates admiscuerunt.
units.tr: I have explained how, and to what extent, the stature of men has changed today from that of those early ancestors of ours through their various migrations; it follows that I should say something about the dialects of languages. The confusion of tongues occurred in the hundred and first year after the Flood; and immediately after it, God, who willed that the whole earth should be filled gradually by colonists and widely inhabited, ordained the division of the parts of the earth in this way. Who asks for the cause of so memorable, or rather wretched, a change? No man will give another cause than the arrogance of men at that time and their contempt of God. Truth itself bears witness. There was one and the same speech for all from the beginning of the world until the year 1 to 100 (?), and they were moving about; at that time those poor wretches began to plot among themselves, so that, with the glory of God obscured, they might make their own name eternal. What happened? By the wonderful judgment of God, and by his simple command (Origen calls in the work of the angels here), that furious and disastrous conspiracy was dissolved and crushed, by the confusion of tongues and the novelty of unfamiliar words. Thus it was understood at that time that the counsels were not only foolish but also impious and cursed, which were devised to obscure the glory of God and to weaken the reasoning of his most perfect and supreme will. The wretched and unhappy name of Babylon will remain forever, and will commend the most insane rashness of its builders to immortality: known not only in Syria alone but among all nations and in all places. What reward of praise was gained by men so imprudently engaged? Babel, confusion has come. The builders of so great a work, careless of God, dreamed of and sought glory; but by the just vengeance of God, who sees, hears and judges all things and governs them by most just means, they became heirs of a shame and disgrace that can never be erased. Those who had previously used the same speech, now uttering strange and even unfamiliar voices, struck by an unexpected miracle, could no longer act together; as if a very grave schism had occurred, it was necessary to come to a formal separation, and each joined himself to those by whom he could be understood. How many languages arose then, who can say? No one, by Hercules, no one. In vain did Euphorus, in vain did other writers, dare to say there were seventy nations and languages; on what argument? Because it is written in Genesis 46 that seventy souls descended from Jacob into Egypt. What analogy is there between these and the primary languages? Let us not trouble about the number (which I think was smaller than Euphorus and others state). This is certain: those first languages, after Hebrew, produced many dialects by the means of migrations hither and thither; as the number, sequence and values of the letters, the order of writing, the origins of words, the roots and stems of verbs, the forms and analogies of inflection, and other countless things of this kind, show in each language. I will say something about the three in passing, for these demand another place. Hebrew, which, as the first and as it were the parent, had remained uncorrupted, pure and unmixed in its place, produced offshoots: Chaldaic, Arabic, Samaritan, Ethiopic; the ancient Median, Persian, Armenian, Egyptian and Punic; between which there is such affinity that there is hardly a word in one that does not occur in some other with a slight inflection. The Greek language is not read only in Hellas, where it was once held; but also, filled everywhere with foreign words (as we shall be taught in their places), in Epirus, the Peloponnese, Illyricum, Macedonia, Thrace, Asia Minor, Syria, Cilicia, Egypt, Italy (from which came Magna Graecia), Gaul (for everyone knows that Massilia flourished, and that the Druids, the priests of the Gauls, used it in their sacred rites), Helvetia (as appears from Caesar's Commentaries on the Gallic War), and Upper and Lower Germany (as a myriad of words almost cries out). Narrowed to more limited boundaries, it knows the principal dialects: Common, Attic, Ionic, Doric and Aeolic; and to these are usually added Chalcidian, Boeotian, Cyprian, Pamphylian, Sicilian, Rhegian, Cretan, Tarentine, Rhodian, Laconian, Argive, Libyan, Macedonian, Syracusan and Thessalian, which conform to the principal ones and agree in speech. For Herodotus, Demosthenes, Libanius the Sophist and others sufficiently show that the first of the four named expressed Atticism, not entirely but in part; Corinthus testifies that the remaining eleven came very near to the Doric dialect, though they differed in some respects; and Tryphon asserts that Thessalian belonged to both the Ionic and the Doric idiom at once. The Latin language, which is now in use among us, is not truly primitive, but was born from that. For it underwent various changes. For as there are certain ages of all things, so there are of speech. The first, which one may call the Old or Early Latin, and which is said to have been not very unlike Doric, was used by the most ancient peoples of Italy under their first kings, whoever they were. Some remnants of it, so that we may not be ignorant of what it was like, are preserved to this day among the grammarians, Varro, Festus and others; partly in some of the songs of the Salii and the ancient bards, which are indeed crude and little understood, and partly in some single words, as all critics note; and, if I may add anything of my own, I too have once, when I was mad with that madness, noted them in my commentary on the first book of Ennius's Annals. Latin, made more refined, acquired its name, from a Latin king, as some want. What it was like can be seen, both from elsewhere and from the fragments of the royal laws and the censorial Twelve Tables; as well as from the inscription of Gaius Duilius, consul, which is still seen at Rome, though mutilated, set up in the year 494 from the founding of the city. And this, made more polished by the Romans, rightly acquired the name Roman; though poets, historians and orators in various ways, one after another, later ones after earlier, always with more success, and especially Ennius above all (who, as Horace sings, rightly said that the Latin language and invented new words for things), cultivated it. Last of all came in the Misc (?) language, which the citizens of Rome themselves established when their empire had grown and their liberty was lost, together with various peoples admitted to the rights of citizenship and the use of the Roman language (for that was regarded as a benefit). For these mixed in their own words and their own peculiarities of speech.

units.la: Ab ingenti, quae varijs in Linguis, Dialectorum, ut alibi dicam fusius, numero, memoriae, ni fallor, produnt; Timosthenes quidem, Diocuriadem Colchorum urbem nunc delertam, quondam adeo claram, ut in eam trecentae nationes, quae dissimilibus utebantur Linguis, descendere fuerint solitae: Plinius vero lib. vi. natur. histor. cap. v, Romanos ibi negocia gessisse per centum triginta Interpretes; Mithradatem autem Ponti Regem, solum Mortalium, xxii. Linguis fuisse loquutum, nec subjectarum gentium ullum hominem per Interpretem appellatum ab eo, annis quinquaginta sex, quibus regnavit. Nam trecentas Linguas Diocuriadem, quae Primigeniae dici poterant, aliquando audivisse; Mithradatem vero xxii. ex Primigenijs loquutum fuisse; credant alij, non ego. Si quis me, dicis gratia, audiat loqui Belgice, Germanice, Gallice, Hispanice, Italice: an vere dici merebor Multilinguis? Callens Hebraeam, Graecam, Latinam, sum Trilinguis; quod Primigeniae quamvis hodie, praesertim Latina, non parum evariarint: accedente Germanica, etiam cum infinitis suis Dialectis, inter quas Belgica, quatuor vere teneo: si comitentur Gallica, Italica, Hispanica: quinque; quod qui unam, reliquas fere noverit, juvante praecipue Latina: quum denique nec Anglica nec Scotica desint, quod haec ab illa parum abeat; sex. Essent tamen hic, qui, Suffeni sibi, inita Hebraicae, Graecae, Germanicaeque Dialectorum ratione, Linguarum supra triginta cognitionem jactarent. Ita nos vana titillat gloria.
units.tr: Concerning the vast number of languages and dialects, which, as I will explain more fully elsewhere, is recorded in the memory of writers, if I am not mistaken: Timosthenes reports that Dioscurias, the city of the Colchians, now destroyed but once so famous that three hundred nations speaking different languages used to resort to it. Pliny, in book 6, chapter 5 of his Natural History, says that the Romans conducted business there through a hundred and thirty interpreters. He also says that Mithridates, king of Pontus, was the only mortal who spoke twenty-two languages, and that during the fifty-six years of his reign he never addressed any man from the subject peoples through an interpreter. I will let others believe that the three hundred languages heard at Dioscurias were all original ones, and that Mithridates spoke twenty-two of the original languages; I do not. If someone hears me, for example, speaking Dutch, German, French, Spanish and Italian, would I truly deserve to be called multilingual? I know Hebrew, Greek and Latin, so I am trilingual, although the original languages, Latin especially, have today diverged not a little. Add German, with its countless dialects, among which is Dutch, and I truly hold four; if French, Italian and Spanish accompany them, five. Whoever knows one of these will know nearly all the rest, chiefly with the help of Latin. Finally, since neither English nor Scots is missing, and these differ little from each other, that makes six. There would nevertheless be some who, like Suffenus himself, having worked out the principles of Hebrew, Greek and German dialects, boast of knowing more than thirty languages. Thus empty glory tickles us.

units.la: Quemadmodum autem pars Infelicitatis humanae magna fuit Linguarum Confusio: ita nostris temporibus Donum vere divinum, totum fere Terrarum orbem Tribus, quae in Cruce Christi consecratae, Linguis denuo conjungi; atque harum cognitione non ea modo, quae ad mutua hominum commercia, quaeque ad adquirendum Sapientiam humanam pertinent: sed Pietatem & quidquid ad DEVM, ubertim innotescere. Satis enim constat maximum esse per universam Europam Latinae Graecaeque Linguarum usum: Hebraicae vero, &, quae adfinis illi, Arabicae per totam Asiam Africamque. Arabica sane, quod bene notat Guilielmus Postellus
units.tr: Just as the confusion of languages was a great part of human misfortune, so in our own times a gift truly divine is being restored: the whole round of the earth's tribes, consecrated in the Cross of Christ, is being joined together again by languages. Through knowledge of them, not only are the things made known that serve human intercourse and the acquisition of human wisdom, but also piety and whatever pertains to God, and these are made known abundantly. It is well established that the use of Latin and Greek is greatest throughout Europe, and that of Hebrew, and of Arabic, which is akin to it, throughout Asia and Africa. Arabic certainly, as William Postel well observes:

units.la: Postcllus omnibus Mahumedicæ superstitionis cultoribus nota est & familiaris: paterque latius hodie, quam ulla alia. Possidet quidquid est Asiæ, etiam Moluccas Insulas. Habet Africam totam, ut dixi, præter Nubianam Regionem. In Europa tenet Græciam, Macedoniam, Thraciam, Daciam, Hungariæ partem, Serviam, non exiguam Pannoniæ Superioris portionem. Ejus beneficio versari licet sine Interprete cum Mauris, Ægyptiis, Syris, Persis, Turcis, Indis, (quod nuper etiam Nostrates experti) &, ut compendio dicam, cum omnibus Totius Incolis; Europa sane tanto ceteris æstimanda felicior; quod, quum locis aliis Sapientiæ studiosi singulas tantum Linguas addiscant, in ipsa Tres, quas dixi, excolantur: Subit animum meum hoc loco, quod admiratione semper censui dignissimum; quum quidquid olim, exceptis quæ plane perierunt, quidquid hodie Linguarum fixum possideat in hoc globo domicilium, Principes illas, quibus causa nostri Capitis in Cruce fuit signata, certa sede, quod illa luce clarius, carere. Scilicet exturbatæ quasi sunt sua Possessione, ut deinceps possiderent omnia. Nam Trigam illam ab infinitis Scriptorum ingeniis, adspirante Deo, mirum in modum excultam Christus, accepto in gentes omnes a Patre cœlesti Imperio, suæ Civitati suoque Regno consecravit. Trigæ tam felicis ope, præterquam quod fores, illarum clave, nobis aperiantur omnium Disciplinarum & Artium (nam nulla Lingua labore propter seipsam digna, si nihil aliud quæratur) Religio Christiana quovis terrarum propagatur, Ovesque fideles Linguarum confusione dolenter dispersæ divinis auspiciis ad unum Pastorem, Animæ pro Suis prodigum, inque unum, & id æternum Ovile convehuntur; &, submota ex animis hostilitate, ad sanctam Societatem conciliandam, fovendam, magisque & magis confirmandam animantur: quo tandem unus Deus, qui creavit omnia per Filium cum Spiritu Sancto, qui ab utroque procedit, una quasi Lingua, unoque ore ametur, colatur, invocetur. In hac enim Triga Labium illud electum (שפה ברורה) quod Populis daturum se pronunciavit Deus apud Sophanjah cap. iii, 9, ut invocarent omnes Nomen suum, sibique servirent uno humero.
units.tr: Postel is known and familiar to all the followers of the Mahometan superstition, and it is spoken more widely today than any other language. It holds all of Asia, even the Moluccas. It holds all of Africa, as I said, except the region of Nubia. In Europe it holds Greece, Macedonia, Thrace, Dacia, part of Hungary, Serbia, and a not inconsiderable portion of Upper Pannonia. By its help one may converse without an interpreter with Moors, Egyptians, Syrians, Persians, Turks, Indians (as our own countrymen have recently experienced), and, to sum up, with all the inhabitants of the whole world. Europe is certainly more fortunate than the rest, and to be valued all the more highly, because, while scholars in other places learn only single languages, here the three I have mentioned are cultivated. My mind is drawn at this point to something I have always judged most worthy of wonder: whatever languages have fixed their home on this globe, whether they have perished completely or survive today, those princes of languages, in whose case the cause of our Head was inscribed on the Cross, lack a secure seat, which is clearer than daylight. They have been, as it were, driven out of their possession, so that others may possess everything in their place. For Christ, having received from the heavenly Father dominion over all nations, has consecrated that triad, wonderfully refined by the countless wits of writers through the breath of God, to his city and his kingdom. By the help of this so fortunate triad, besides the fact that its keys open to us the doors of all disciplines and arts (for no language is worth the labour for its own sake, unless something else is sought through it), the Christian religion is spread to every part of the earth, and the sheep, scattered sorrowfully by the confusion of tongues, are brought under divine guidance to one Shepherd, who gave his soul for his sheep, and into one everlasting fold. Hostility being removed from their minds, they are encouraged to be drawn together, cherished, and more and more confirmed in the holy fellowship, so that at last the one God, who created all things through the Son with the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from both, may be loved, worshipped and invoked with one tongue, as it were, and one mouth. For in this triad is that pure lip [שפה ברורה] which God declared he would give to the peoples, in Zephaniah chapter 3, verse 9, so that all might call upon his name and serve him with one shoulder.

units.la: CAP. XV.
units.tr: CHAP. XV.

units.la: Terra medium obtinet Mundi Locum, esque Centrum Universi.
units.tr: The earth holds the middle place in the world and is the centre of the universe.
