units.la: EFFICIENTEM Materiam, Formam & Finem creati Terrarum Orbis indicavi: succedit quærendum illi in hac mole Subjectum, locusque monstrandus. Terræ Medium Universi tribuendum esse varia docent φαινόμενα, Stellarum Fixarum Ortus & Occasus, Æquinoctia, Dierum augentium & deficientium vices, Eclipses & Umbræ.
units.tr: I have set out the efficient matter, the form and the end of the created orb of the earth. Next, I must inquire what its subject is in this mass, and show where its place is. That the earth should be assigned the middle of the universe is taught by various appearances: the rising and setting of the fixed stars, the equinoxes, the alternation of lengthening and shortening days, eclipses and shadows.

units.la: Non est magis ad Ortum. Sic enim surgente Sole orientia nobis, ut Ortui vicinioribus, majora viderentur; Occidente vero, ut remotioribus, minora. Deinde Tempus ab ortu ad Meridiem non esset æquale Tempori, quod ab Meridie ad Occasum: Nam priores sex horæ Dici essent, Sole subito verticem superante, brevissimæ; posteriores, spacio quod ad Occasum percurrendum majore, longissimæ: Sed nihil tale adparet: ergo non Ortum magis. Neque etiam ad Occasum: evenirent enim omnia prædictis contraria. Non etiam magis accedit ad alterutrum Polorum. Nam si ad Arcticum; in omni ortu & Occasu Umbræ essent Septemtrionales: sin ad Antarcticum, ad Meridiem Umbræ vergerent, & Oriente & Occidente Sole: Neutrum autem fit; ergo nec in has partes inclinare Terram, dicendum. Non item medio est sublimior: sic enim, Horizonte Æquinoctialem non secante, pars Mundi dimidia supra Terram non adpareret; neque sex Signa, neque Æquinoctialis dimidium: unde & Noctes semper majores haberemus Diebus. Sin medio humilior; ijs, quæ dixi, contingerent contraria; quum majus supra Terram esset hemisphærium. Si igitur sit nec ad latera, nec supra, nec infra: sequitur esse & in Medio, & Centrum Universi. Pluribus hæc apud Cleomedem lib. i. de Mundo, & Ptolemæum lib. μεγαλ. συντάξ. i. cap. iv. Probant naturalem hunc Mundi situm & Sacra Scriptura; Sursum adlignans cœlo, Terræ deorsum. Deuteron. cap. iv, 39: Et 39: Et scito hodie, & reducito ad cor tuum; quia Dominus ipse DEUS in Caelis desuper (ממעל) & super Terram deorsum (מתחת) & non sit alius. Proverb. xxv, 3: In altitudine (לרום) Caelorum & in Terra profunditate (לעמק) & cordis Regum non est investigatio: ubi LXX Interpretes; Οὐρανὸς ὑψηλὸς, γῆ δὲ βαθεῖα; Caelum excelsum, Terra autem profunda. Rex etiam Propheta eundem situm volens exprimere, sic canit Psalmo ciii, 11: Quoniam secundum altitudinem (כגבה, LXX Interpret. ὡς τὸ ὕψος) Caeli super Terram, roborata est misericordia ejus super timentes eum. Qui enim posset esse maxima inter Caelum Terramque distantia: nisi Terra in medio Mundi esset posita? Loquuntur & Philosophi aliique Scriptores. Sic Eratosthenes:
units.tr: It is not more inclined to the east. For if the sun rose, the things rising toward us would seem larger as they approached the rising, and smaller as they were more remote in the west. Moreover, the time from sunrise to noon would not equal the time from noon to sunset. For the first six hours of the day would be very short, since the sun would suddenly pass the zenith, and the later hours very long, since the sun would have a greater distance to traverse to the west. But nothing of the kind appears; therefore the earth is not more inclined to the east. Nor is it inclined to the west, for everything would then happen contrary to what has been said. Nor is it nearer to either pole. For if it were nearer the Arctic pole, the shadows would fall northward at every rising and setting; if nearer the Antarctic, the shadows would tend southward, whether the sun was rising or setting. But neither happens; therefore we must say that the earth does not incline toward these parts either. Nor is it higher in the middle. For if so, the equator would not cut the horizon, and half of the heavens would not appear above the earth, neither six signs nor half the equator; and so we would always have nights longer than days. But if it were lower in the middle, the contrary of what I have said would follow, since the hemisphere above the earth would be the greater. If, then, it is neither at the sides, nor above, nor below, it follows that it is in the middle and is the centre of the universe. Much more on this may be found in Cleomedes, On the World, book 1, and in Ptolemy, Megale Syntaxis, book 1, chapter 4. Holy Scripture also proves this natural position of the world, assigning upward to heaven and downward to the earth. Deuteronomy 4:39: And know this day, and lay it to your heart, that the LORD himself is God in heaven above [ממעל], and upon the earth beneath [מתחת], and there is no other. Proverbs 25:3: The heaven for height [לרום], and the earth for depth [לעמק], and the heart of kings is unsearchable. Here the Seventy translate: "The heaven is high, but the earth is deep"; heaven high, earth however deep. The king and prophet, wishing to express the same position, sings thus in Psalm 103:11: For as the height [כגבה; Seventy: ὡς τὸ ὕψος] of the heaven above the earth, so is his mercy great toward them that fear him. For how could there be so great a distance between heaven and earth, unless the earth were placed in the middle of the world? The philosophers and other writers also speak so. Thus Eratosthenes:

units.la: Αὐτὸς μὲν μὴν ἔπτα μεσηρία πάντῃ ὅλυμπον
units.tr: He himself, having fixed the sphere of Olympus in the midst on every side, [Αὐτὸς μὲν μὴν ἔπτα μεσηρία πάντῃ ὅλυμπον]

units.la: Κίνεω ἀπὸ σφαίρας. Ἀλλ' ἀξονα ἀφῆρησεν.
units.tr: set it moving from the sphere; but he took away the axis. [Κίνεω ἀπὸ σφαίρας. Ἀλλ' ἀξονα ἀφῆρησεν.]

units.la: Parmenides ταὶ ξ ὅλως:
units.tr: Parmenides, in the same vein, says:

units.la: Πάντῃθεν ἰσοπαλὲς σφαίρας εὐκύκλου ὄγκῳ
units.tr: On every side, equal in weight, like a well-rounded sphere, [Πάντῃθεν ἰσοπαλὲς σφαίρας εὐκύκλου ὄγκῳ]

units.la: Μεσσόθεν ἰσοπαλὲς πάντῃ. τὸ γὰρ ἔτε τι μέζον,
units.tr: equal from the middle in every direction; for there is nothing greater [Μεσσόθεν ἰσοπαλὲς πάντῃ. τὸ γὰρ ἔτε τι μέζον,]

units.la: Οὔτε γε βαιότερον πηλάν χρεῶν ἐστι τῆ, ἡ τῆ.
units.tr: nor anything smaller that it must be here rather than there. [Οὔτε γε βαιότερον πηλάν χρεῶν ἐστι τῆ, ἡ τῆ.]

units.la: Τοιοῦτόν γε τὸ ὂν μέσον τε ἡ ἐκατονταχῇ.
units.tr: Such is what-is, in the middle and at the extremities alike. [Τοιοῦτόν γε τὸ ὂν μέσον τε ἡ ἐκατονταχῇ.]

units.la: Cicero lib. II. de Nat. Deorum: Nec vero haec solum admirabilia, sed nihil majus, quam quod ita stabilis est Mundus, atque ita cohaeret ad permanendum, ut nihil ne excogitari quidem possit aptius: omnes enim partes ejus undique medium locum capessentes nituntur aequaliter; maxime autem corpora inter se juncta permanent, quum quodam quasi vinculo circumdata colligantur: quod facit ea natura, quae per omnem Mundum omnia Mente & Ratione confecta funditur, & ad medium rapit & convertit extrema, &c. Manilius lib. I. Astronomic. de Terra:
units.tr: Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods, book 2: Nor indeed are these things alone admirable, but nothing is greater than that the world is so stable and so cohering to endure that nothing more apt could be conceived. For all its parts, from every side, strive equally to occupy the middle place; and bodies joined together endure most of all when they are held in a kind of bond, binding them. This is done by that nature which, through the whole world, is poured through all things made by mind and reason, and draws the extremes to the middle and turns them, etc.

units.la: Imaque de cunctis mediam tenet undique sedem.
units.tr: Manilius, Astronomica, book 1, on the earth: And the lowest of all things holds the middle seat on every side.

units.la: Plinius lib. II. natur. histor. cap. v: Hujus vi suspensam cum quarto Aquarum Elemento, librari medio spacio Tellurem: ita mutuo complexu diversitatis effici nexum; & levia ponderibus inhiberi, quo minus evolent; contraque gravia, ne ruant, suspendi levibus in sublime tendentibus,&c.
units.tr: Pliny, Natural History, book 2, chapter 5: By its power the earth is suspended with the fourth element of water and balanced in the middle space; thus by mutual embrace of unlike things a bond is made, and light things are held back by weights, so that they do not fly away; and on the contrary heavy things are suspended by light things tending upward, lest they fall, etc.

units.la: Sed suffragata Rationibus, quas indicavi, validissimis Sacrarum Litterarum Philosophorumque auctoritas ita tutari Veritatem hac in re nequivit, ut interea quondam non fuerint, hodieque desint, qui ausu magno vimque Rerum naturae facientes oppugnatum illam irent. Inter eos Aristarchus Samius; qui Terram Medio Mundi immotam orbique peculiari inclusam intra Martis & Veneris sphaeras collocat, suisque & proprijs circumagi motibus, circa Solem in Medio Mundi immotum, Stellarum instar finxit. Ejus Hypotheses ad suas Demonstrationes adsumsit superioribus annis Nicolaus Copernicus.
units.tr: But although the authority of Holy Scripture and of the philosophers, supporting the most powerful reasons I have indicated, has not been able to defend the truth so well in this matter that there have not been, and are not even now, some who with great boldness and in defiance of the nature of things have gone to attack it. Among them is Aristarchus of Samos, who places the earth, motionless, in the middle of the world, enclosed in its own orb between the spheres of Mars and Venus, and imagined that it moves with its own motions around the sun, which stands motionless in the middle of the world, like the stars. In recent years Nicolaus Copernicus took up his hypotheses to support his own demonstrations.

units.la: Terra porro in Medio Mundi, infimo Universitatis loco, fixa & immota quiescit. Probant Physicorum Dogmata. Unius Corporis, quod Simplex, unus tantum isque Simplex est Motus: Terra Corpus est Simplex: Ergo Motus unus, qui Simplex, illi convenit. Porro Simplicium Motuum unus Rectus est, alter Circularis: Rectum aut Sursum tendere videmus, aut Deorsum: Terrae autem Partibus, isque, quae ex Terra constant, Rectus competit Motus, quod planum ab experientia, deorsum ad Medium quo delatae conquiescunt: Ergo idem competit Terrae Motus: non Circularis. Quod enim de Parte, praedicatur idem de Toto. Sane si Terra moveretur; vel Recto necesse esset eam ferri Motu, vel Circulari: Si Recto, quum sit omnium gravissima, celeritate sua quidquid gravium reliquorum anteuorteret, & Animantia ceterasque res sibi innixas destituerent, inque aere pendentes relinquerent: Si Circulari Motu ageretur diurnaque conversione circa Axem ab Occasu in Ortum, vel sola vel cum primo orbe, volveretur; singulis diebus multa acciderent absurda, & quae experientiae contraria. Nam quis non animadvertit, quum Motus hic futurus concitatissimus & Celeritas insuperabilis, qua xxiv. horarum curriculo terrenus orbis totus in gyrum esset contorquendus, subitam illam concitatamque vertiginem collectioni & cohaesioni, quae Rebus necessariis nascentibus, obfuturam? Quin si sic Terra rapiatur, Animantia, quae ejus superficiei insistunt, qui manebunt inconcussa? in altum projecta quo pacto, quo decidere videmus, relabentur? μετέωρα denique, ut Nubes; item volitantia in Aere, ut Aves, quando ferri deprehenderemus ad Ortum? Omnia Terrae circumactu prævorterentur longoque relinquerentur intervallo: si circa Axem Mundi tanta pernicitate Terra rotaretur. Quibus & quæ solent adferri alia, bene perpensitatis, sequitur Terram quiescere; non moveri.
units.tr: Furthermore, the earth lies fixed and motionless in the middle of the world, in the lowest place of the universe. This is proved by the doctrines of the natural philosophers. A simple body has one simple motion only: the earth is a simple body; therefore one motion, which is simple, belongs to it. Of simple motions, one is straight and the other circular. We see that straight motion tends either upward or downward; and straight motion belongs to the parts of the earth, and to those things which are made of earth, as is plain from experience: they are carried downward to the centre and come to rest there. Therefore the same motion belongs to the earth as a whole, and not circular motion. For what is predicated of a part is predicated of the whole. Certainly, if the earth were moved, it would have to be carried either by straight motion or by circular motion. If by straight motion, since it is the heaviest of all bodies, by its speed it would outrun all the other heavy things, and would leave animals and other things resting on it, and leave them hanging in the air. If it were carried by circular motion, turning daily about its axis from west to east, either alone or together with the outermost sphere, many absurd things would happen every day, contrary to experience. For who does not notice that, since this motion would be most violent and its speed insurmountable, by which the whole terrestrial globe would have to be turned around in a course of twenty-four hours, that sudden and violent whirling would hinder the gathering and cohesion of things that are necessary for their birth? Indeed, if the earth were so snatched along, how would animals standing on its surface remain unshaken? Why would things thrown up into the air fall back to the place from which we see them descend? Moreover, things suspended in the air, like clouds, and things flying in the air, like birds, would be found carried toward the east. All things would be outstripped by the turning of the earth and left far behind, if the earth were rotated about the axis of the world with such great speed. Having weighed these things well, along with the other objections usually brought forward, it follows that the earth rests and does not move.

units.la: Quictem firmant & Sacræ, quis optima spectatissimaque fides, Litteræ. Divinissimum illud Psalmorum volumen, non uno loco. Psalm. xxiv, 2: Quia ipse super Maria (על־ימים; lxx Interpretes, ὅτι αὐτὸς ἐπὶ θαλασσῶν) fundavit (ישדה; lxx, ἐθεμελίωσεν) eam, & super Flumina (על־נהרות, ὅτι ποταμῶν) firmavit eam (יכוננה; lxx, ἐστήριξεν αὐτὴν; Chaldæus Paraphrastes, אתסנחה, confirmavit eam) Sic lxxv, 4: Liquefacta est Terra, & omnes Habitatores ejus: Ego direxi (Chaldæus אתקבית, firmavi) Columnas ejus, (עמודיה; lxx. τὰς σύλας αὐτῆς) Psalmo xciii, 1: Dominus regnavit, Celsitudinem induit, induit Dominus fortitudinem; accinxit se: etiam firmabitur (תכון; lxx Interpr. ἐστερέωσε, firmavit) orbis, ne nutet (Hebr. בל־תמוט; ἀσαλεύθησεται, non commovebitur, lxx Interpr.) Psalmo civ, 5: Fundavit (יסד; lxx, ὁ θεμελιῶν) Terram super Bases ejus (על־מכוניה; lxx. ὅτι τῷ ἀσφαλείᾳ αὐτῆς, super stabilitatem suam ne nutet בל־תמוט; ἀ κλιθήσεται) in seculum & in seculum. Psalmo denique cxxxvi, 6: Expandentis (lxx Interp. τῷ στερεώσαντι, firmanti) Terram super Aquas: quoniam in seculum Misericordia eius. Sic Schelomo Ecclesiast. 1, 4: Generatio vadens, & generatio veniens; & Terra in seculum stans; עמדת, lxx, ἔστηκε, stetit. Paralipomen. cap. xvi, 30: Parete à facie bus eius omnis Terra, & firmabitur Orbis, ne nutet; Hebr. אף־תכון תבל בל־תמוט. Solem autem, quem qui Terræ tribuunt Motum, volunt Quiescere, moveri canit. Propheta Psalmo xix, 6. Et ipse tamquam Sponsus egrediens (יצא; lxx, ἐκπορευόμενος) de Thalamo suo gaudebit, ut potens, ad currendum viam (לרוץ-ארח, δραμεῖν ὁδὸν) ab extremo Cælorum egressio ejus (מוצאו; lxx, ἐξοδος αὐτοῦ; Chaldæus Interp. in hanc sententiam: Et ipse mane sicut Sponsus, qui egreditur velut de Thalamo suo desiderabili, & in dimidio dici letabitur, ut Gigas, qui pervenit, ut currat viam occasus sui sub vespera.) Notum etiam, connumerari Miraculis; quod D e v s Solem voluerit consistere. Ichosuah. cap. x; 12: Tunc loquutus est Ichosuah Domino, in die, qua tradidit Dominus Emorraum coram filiis Israel; & dixit in oculis Israel: Sol in Gibbon exspecta (רום, sile; Chaldæus Paraphrast. אורך; lxx Interp. στῆτω) & Luna in Valle Aialon.
units.tr: Holy Scripture, the most excellent and most trustworthy witness, also confirms this rest, in more than one place. Here is the most divine book of the Psalms. Psalm 24:2: For he has founded it [ישדה; Seventy: ἐθεμελίωσεν] upon the seas [על־ימים; Seventy: ἐπὶ θαλασσῶν], and established it [יכוננה; Seventy: ἐστήριξεν αὐτὴν] upon the floods [על־נהרות; Seventy: ποταμῶν]; the Chaldee paraphrast renders: he has confirmed it [אתסנחה]. So in Psalm 75:3: The earth is dissolved, and all its inhabitants; I have set up [Chaldee: אתקבית, I have firmed] its pillars [עמודיה; Seventy: τὰς σύλας αὐτῆς]. In Psalm 93:1: The LORD reigneth, he is clothed with majesty; the LORD is clothed with strength, wherewith he hath girded himself; the world also is stablished [תכון; Seventy: ἐστερέωσε, he established], that it cannot be moved [בל־תמוט; Seventy: ἀσαλεύθησεται, it shall not be shaken]. In Psalm 104:5: He laid the foundations of the earth [יסד; Seventy: ὁ θεμελιῶν] upon its bases [על־מכוניה; Seventy: ἐπὶ τῇ ἀσφαλείᾳ αὐτῆς, upon its stability], that it should not be removed [בל־תמוט; Seventy: οὐ κλιθήσεται] for ever and ever. Finally, in Psalm 136:6: To him that stretched out the earth above the waters [Seventy: τῷ στερεώσαντι, to him that established], for his mercy endureth for ever. So Solomon in Ecclesiastes 1:4: One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh; but the earth abideth for ever [עמדת; Seventy: ἔστηκε, stood]. In 1 Chronicles 16:30: Fear before him, all the earth; the world also shall be stable, that it be not moved [Hebrew: אף־תכון תבל בל־תמוט]. But the sun, which those who assign motion to the earth wish to rest, the prophet sings as moving. Psalm 19:6: And he, like a bridegroom coming out [יצא; Seventy: ἐκπορευόμενος] of his chamber, rejoices as a strong man to run his course [לרוץ-ארח; Seventy: δραμεῖν ὁδόν]; his going forth [מוצאו; Seventy: ἔξοδος αὐτοῦ] is from the end of the heavens. The Chaldee paraphrase to this effect reads: And he rises in the morning like a bridegroom who goes forth as from his desirable chamber, and at midday rejoices, like a giant who comes to run the road of his setting toward evening. It is also well known that God willed the sun to stand still, which is counted among the miracles. Joshua 10:12: Then spake Joshua to the LORD in the day when the LORD delivered up the Amorites before the children of Israel, and he said in the sight of Israel: Sun, stand thou still [רום, Chaldee: אורך; Seventy: στῆτω] upon Gibeon; and thou, Moon, in the valley of Ajalon.

units.la: Nec alius mentis summi Philosophi, magnique Scriptores; Plato in Phædro & Phædone (nam non obstat locus in Timæo: ibi enim loquitur non ex sua, sed Timæi Locri, qui Pythagoricus erat, mente; frustra se ad eruendam conciliationem torquentibus Proclo, Alcinoe, Iamblicho, Diogene Laertio, & Nuperorum non paucis) Aristoteles lib.ii. de Cœlo, cap.xiii. & xiv, & ibi Lucilius Philaltheus; Ptolemæus lib. 1. Almagest. cap. v. & seq. M. Tullius lib.1. de nat. Deor. Manilius lib.1. Astronomic. Plinius lib.ii.nat. hist. Macrob. lib. 1. in Somnium Scipionis cap. xxii, Alfragan. Differ. iv, Ioannes Sacrobust. cap.1. Sphæræ; & in eum Capuanus & Clavius. Adscribam polita illa elegantissimi Poetæ Ovidii ex libro vi. Fastorum: Terra Pilæfimi'is, nullo fulcimine nixa, Aere subjecto tam grave pendet onus. Ipsa volubilitas libratum sustinet Orbem; Quisque premat partes angulus omnis abest. Quumque sit in media rerum regione locata, Et tangat nullum plusve minusve latus: Ni convexa foret, parti vicinior esset, Nec medium Terra Mundus haberet onus. Arte Syracusia suspensus in aere clauso Stat globus, immensi parva figura Poli: Et quantum à summis, tantum secessit ab imis Terra, quod ut fiat, forma rotunda facit.
units.tr: Nor do the minds of the greatest philosophers and the great writers disagree. Plato in the Phaedrus and Phaedo holds this. (The passage in the Timaeus is no obstacle, for there he speaks not in his own mind but in that of Timaeus the Locrian, who was a Pythagorean. Proclus, Alcinous, Iamblichus, Diogenes Laertius, and not a few modern writers have tormented themselves in vain trying to reconcile it.) So too Aristotle, On the Heavens book 2, chapters 13 and 14, with Lucilius Philalthaeus on that passage; Ptolemy, Almagest book 1, chapter 5 and following; Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods book 1; Manilius, Astronomica book 1; Pliny, Natural History book 2; Macrobius, On the Dream of Scipio book 1, chapter 22; Alfraganus, Differentia 4; John of Sacrobosco, On the Sphere chapter 1, and on it Capuanus and Clavius. I shall add the polished lines of that most elegant poet Ovid from book 6 of the Fasti: The earth, shaped like a ball, rests on no prop; it hangs with its heavy weight in the air beneath it. Its very whirling keeps the globe balanced; every corner is far from pressing on any part. And since it is set in the middle region of things, touching no side more than another, if it were not curved it would be nearer one part, and the world would not have the earth as its middle burden. Suspended in the enclosed air by Syracusan art, the globe stands, a small figure of the vast heavens; and the earth has withdrawn as far from the highest point as from the lowest, and its round form makes this so.

units.la: Et hinc Terra Veteribus Latinis Vesta; quod vi stet & quiescat: Idem poeta: Vi stat Terra sua, Vi stando Vesta vocatur.
units.tr: And from this the Latins of old called the earth Vesta, because it stands firm (vi stet) and is at rest. The same poet: The earth stands by its own strength, and by standing firm it is called Vesta.

units.la: Causa vero Stabilitatis & Firmitatis est Naturalis Terræ gravitas; quæ quum summa sit, suopte pondere petit infimum Mundi locum, hoc est, Centrum: in quo locata naturaliter quiescit. Ab naturali, inquam, gravitate nata Terræ מכונה, ἀσφάλεια, Stabilitas illa, quæ celebratur Psalmo civ, 5; hæc autem ab uno Deo. Hic enim; de quo sanctissimus Vir Hijobus, cap. xxvi, 7. Extendens Aquilonem super Vacuum; suspendens (תלה; Chaldaeus Paraphrast. זקף, sublevat, lxx. Interpret. κρεμάζων) Terram super Nihilum (Hebr. על־בלימה; lxx, ἐπὶ μηδενός; Chaldaeus Paraphrastice, רסמיך לה על־מיא מדעם, super Aquas, nullo sustinente eam) Falleris homo, alia pulcerrimae machinae moliens fundamenta, alia fulcra: frustra si quae Deus fecit facitque quotidie metiaris ex ijs, quae potest homo. Exclamemus cum Davide Psalmo laudato: Quam magnificata sunt opera tua Domine! omnia in sapientia fecisti, Et paullo post: Laetabitur Dominus in Operibus suis. Cum his enim quae decantantur Orbis miracula, cum his superba Regum Palatia, cum his denique quidquid humanorum Operum & luventorum non venit committendum. Parva sunt omnia prae his, nullisque rei. Ea divinis Operibus est indoles; ut millesimum etiam intuito novam semper pariant delectationem: quum e diverso natura sit humanorum, quam etiam fuerint preciosa, quam egregia, quamque artificiose fabrefacta, ut semel iterumque contemplato plerumque adferant fastidium. Quis igitur non erumpat in illud regii Prophetae, Psalmo xciii, Delectasti me Domine in factura tua: in Operibus manuum tuarum exsultabo?
units.tr: The cause of its stability and firmness is the natural heaviness of the earth. Since this is greatest, it by its own weight seeks the lowest place of the world, that is, the centre, and there, placed by nature, it rests. It is from this natural heaviness, I say, that the stability celebrated in Psalm 104:5 arises for the earth (מכונה, ἀσφάλεια), but this comes from the one God alone. He is the one of whom the most holy man Job speaks, chapter 26:7: He stretches out the north over the empty place; he hangs (תלה; the Chaldee paraphrast זקף, raises up; the Septuagint κρεμάζων) the earth upon nothing (Hebrew על־בלימה; Septuagint ἐπὶ μηδενός; the Chaldee paraphrase, רסמיך לה על־מיא מדעם, upon the waters, with nothing sustaining it). You are mistaken, O man, when you lay other foundations and other supports for that most beautiful machine. It is vain to measure by what man can do the things God has made and continually makes. Let us cry out with David in the psalm already cited: How magnificent are your works, O Lord! You have made all things in wisdom. And a little after: The Lord shall rejoice in his works. For compared with these the wonders of the world which men sing about, compared with these the proud palaces of kings, indeed with whatever works and inventions of men, all are small and cannot be weighed against them. It is the nature of divine works that even when they have been seen a thousandth time they always bring forth fresh delight; whereas the nature of human works is the reverse, however precious, however excellent, however skilfully made they are, for they commonly cause weariness when contemplated once or twice. Who then would not burst out into the words of the royal prophet in Psalm 92: You have delighted me, O Lord, in your work; I will exult in the works of your hands?

units.la: Sic autem Terra in Universi quiescit medio, ut tota Aere circumfundatur. Tibullus cum alibi, tum lib. iv, Eleg. i:
units.tr: Thus the earth rests in the middle of the universe, and is surrounded on all sides by air. Tibullus, here as elsewhere, in book 4, elegy 1:

units.la: Nam circumfuso consistit in Aere Tellus.
units.tr: For the earth stands fixed in the surrounding air.

units.la: Claudianus de quarto Consulatu Honorii:
units.tr: Claudian, on the Fourth Consulship of Honorius:

units.la: Et qui perpetuo Terras ambitque vehitque, Nec premat incumbens oneri, nec cesserit Aer.
units.tr: "And he who encircles and bears up the lands forever, Neither presses them with his weight as he rests upon them, nor yields; the air."

units.la: Vbi quasi Pendere, absque Motu, videtur. Plinius lib. ii. nat. histor. cap. lxv: Sed quid hoc refert, alio miraculo exoriente? Pendere ipsam ac non cadere nobiscum, ceu spiritus vis Mundo praesertim inclusi, dubia sit: aut possit cadere, Natura repugnante; & quo cadat, negante. Nam sicut Ignium sedes non est nisi in Ignibus; Aquarum nisi in Aquis; Spiritus nisi in Spiritu: ita Terra, arcentibus cunctis, nisi in se locus non est. Ovidius non modo vi. Fastor. ut paullo ante vidimus, sed & lib. i. Metamorph.
units.tr: Here it seems to hang, without motion. Pliny, Natural History book 2, chapter 65: "But what does it matter, when another wonder arises? Whether the earth itself hangs and does not fall with us, as the force of a spirit, especially enclosed in the world, is doubtful: or whether it could fall, nature resisting, and whether it has anywhere to fall, nature denying. For just as the seat of fires is only in fires, of waters only in waters, of spirit only in spirit, so the earth, since all things hold it back, has no place except in itself." Ovid too, not only in book 6 of the Fasti, as we saw a little before, but also in book 1 of the Metamorphoses:

units.la: Nec circumfuso pendebat in Aere Tellus.
units.tr: Nor did the earth hang in the surrounding air.

units.la: Sic Manilius libro i. Astronomic. Nec vero tibi Natura admiranda videri Pendentis Terrae debet, quum pendeat ipse Mundus, & in nullo ponat vestigia fundo: Qua caderet, subeat Caelum, rursusque resurgat. Quod patet ex ipso motu, curvusque volantis: Quum suspensus eat Phoebus, curvumque reflectat Huc illuc, agiles & fervet in aethere metas: Quum Luna & Stellae volitent per inania Mundi, Terra quoque aethereas leges imitata pependit. Est igitur Terra mediam sortita cavernam Aeris, & toto pariter, suspensa profundo, Nec patulas dissenta plagas, sed condita in orbem Undique surgentem pariter, pariterque cadentem.
units.tr: So Manilius in book 1 of the Astronomica: "Nor should the hanging of the earth seem wonderful to you, since the world itself hangs and sets its feet on no bottom. If it fell, the sky would sink and then rise again. This is plain from the motion itself and the curve of the flying [sun]: when Phoebus goes on high and turns his curving course this way and that, the swift goals burn in the aether. When the moon and the stars fly through the emptiness of the world, the earth too, imitating the ethereal laws, hangs. The earth, then, has obtained the middle hollow of the air, and, suspended in the whole deep, is not spread out in open regions, but set together so as to rise and fall equally on every side."

units.la: In Universi igitur medio quiescit. Moveri tamen adferunt: in Mundi quidem Centro, Heraclides & Ecphantus Pythagorici, apud Plutarchum lib. iii. cap. xiii; Nicetas Syracusanus apud Ciceronem lib. ii. Academicar. Quaest. Cleanthes Samius apud eundem Plutarch. libello de forma, quae visitur in orbe Lunae: circa Centrum autem, extra Medium, alij: Philolaus circa Ignem, sub Zodiaco, instar Solis & Lunae; quemadmodum idem docet Plutarchus: Aristarchus Samius inter Martis & Veneris Sphaeras; qui Solem collocat, ut Centrum, in Totius medio. Et sententiam de Terrae Motu Patrum nostrorum memoria conati sunt defendere Caelius Calcagninus libro de perenni Terrae Motu, & Nicolaus Copernicus de Revolutionibus: quorum argumenta probabilia censuit Pontus Thyardeus in eo qui de Universitate: videtur etiam idem voluisse Gemma Frisius in Praefatione Tabularum Bergensium Ioannis Stadij, qui in hanc quoque propendebat opinionem. Fuerunt item multi Veterum, qui Terram in medio κυλίεσθαι, ac circumjecto humore portari crediderunt, velut grande aliquod & grave navigium. Eius sententiae auctor putatur Thales apud Aristotelem lib. ii. de Cœlo text. 78. Thaleti favere videtur non uno loco Sacra Scriptura. Psalmo xxiii, 2: Quia ipse super Maria (על־ימים, ὅτι ἐπὶ θαλάσσῶν) fundavit eam, & super flumina (על־נהרות, ὅτι ἐπὶ ποταμῶν) firmavit eam. Et Psalmo cxxxvi, 6: Qui firmavit Terram super Aquas, (על־המים, ὅτι τῶν ὑδάτων. Sequuntur hanc sententiam Auctor Libri iii. Esdræ, cap. ult. & Iustinus Martyr in responsione ad Quæstionem Orthodoxorum cxxx. Sic Virgilius in Aetna: Quacumque immensus Terra se porrigit orbis Extremique maris curvis agitatur ab undis.
units.tr: Therefore it rests in the middle of the universe. Yet some report that it moves: at the centre of the world, Heraclides and Ecphantus the Pythagoreans, according to Plutarch book 3, chapter 13; Nicetas of Syracuse, according to Cicero, Academica book 2. Cleanthes of Samos, according to the same Plutarch in his little work On the Form that Appears in the Orb of the Moon; around the centre but outside the middle, others; Philolaus around fire, beneath the zodiac, like the sun and moon, as Plutarch likewise teaches; Aristarchus of Samos between the spheres of Mars and Venus, who places the sun as the centre in the middle of all. In our fathers' time, Caelius Calcagninus in his book On the Perpetual Motion of the Earth and Nicolaus Copernicus in On the Revolutions have tried to defend the opinion of the earth's motion; Pontus Thyard in his work on the universe judged their arguments probable. Gemma Frisius seems to have held the same view in the preface to the Bergen Tables of John Stadius, who also inclined to this opinion. There were also many of the ancients who believed that the earth rolls (κυλίεσθαι) in the middle and is carried by the surrounding moisture, like some great and heavy ship. The author of this opinion is thought to be Thales, according to Aristotle, On the Heavens book 2, text 78. Holy Scripture seems to favour Thales in more than one place. Psalm 24:2: For he founded it upon the seas (על־ימים, ὅτι ἐπὶ θαλάσσῶν) and established it upon the rivers (על־נהרות, ὅτι ἐπὶ ποταμῶν). And Psalm 136:6: He who established the earth upon the waters (על־המים, ὅτι τῶν ὑδάτων). The author of the third book of Esdras, in the last chapter, and Justin Martyr in his answer to the 130th Question of the Orthodox follow this opinion. So Virgil in the Aetna: Wherever the immense orb of the earth extends, it is stirred by the curved waves of the farthest sea.

units.la: Sic enim Veteres Editiones. Sed ubi in Sacris Literis Terra fundata vel firmata dicitur super Aquas vel Flumina, notandum Cavernas esse Terræ, Meatus, & Poros; per quos Maria in penitissima ejus Viscera ingrediuntur; unde egressa Fontium Fluminumque sunt causæ: ut Terra quasi Aquis innatare, & super Aquas passim fundata videatur, quemadmodum alibi dixi. Alij alio modo exponunt: videndi Basilius & Chrysostomus apud Euthymium in expositione Psalmi xxiii. Merito igitur Thaletis opinionem, ante Senecam libro vi. nat. quæst. cap. vi, refutat Aristoteles loco, quem nominavi, ubi & nonnullas aliorum Veterum sententias commemorat de causa Firmitatis & Stabilitatis Terræ, quas prudens prætereo. Nam, ut concludam, Terra in medio Totius, cujus est Centrum, quiescit.
units.tr: This is how the old editions read. But where Holy Writ says that the earth is founded or established upon the waters or the rivers, it should be noted that the earth has caverns, passages, and pores, through which the seas enter into its innermost viscera, whence the sources and causes of rivers come forth; so the earth seems to float upon the waters and to be founded upon them everywhere, as I have said elsewhere. Others explain it in other ways; see Basil and Chrysostom, as cited by Euthymius in his exposition of Psalm 23. Aristotle rightly refutes the opinion of Thales in the place I named, and so before him does Seneca in book 6 of the Natural Questions, chapter 6; there Aristotle also mentions some other opinions of the ancients about the cause of the earth's firmness and stability, which I prudently pass over. For, to conclude, the earth rests in the middle of the whole, of which it is the centre.

units.la: CAP. XVI.
units.tr: CAP. XVI.

units.la: De Terræ Quantitate.
units.tr: On the Quantity of the Earth

units.la: TERRARUM Orbis per se, καθ' αὑτὸ, & cum Sole Lunaque comparatus vastus sane est & immensus; cum Universo vero, præsertim autem cum octava sphæra, si committatur, quid aliud, quam Punctum? Quod Terræ sensibilis sit ad Solem Lunamque quantitas, ostendunt evidentissime Sideris utriusque Parallaxes; quæ neutri contingerent, nisi globus hic suam, eamque conspicuam, utriusque comparatione haberet magnitudinem. Ex umbra etiam, quam in oppositam Soli partem Terra semper ejaculatur, colligi, quod dixi, quodammodo posse, plene demonstrant alij.
units.tr: The orb of the earth, considered in itself [καθ' αὑτό] and compared with the Sun and Moon, is certainly vast and immense. But when set beside the Universe, especially if it is joined with the eighth sphere, what is it but a point? That the earth's quantity is perceptible in relation to the Sun and Moon is shown most clearly by the parallaxes of each of those bodies, which would not occur unless this globe had a size of its own, and a noticeable one, in comparison with them. Others also fully demonstrate that this can to some degree be inferred from the shadow which the earth always casts on the side opposite the Sun.

units.la: Ambitum Terrestrem Veteribus varie diffinitum, variis locis apud Aristotelem, Ptolemæum, Cleomedem, Strabonem, Plinium, Macrobium, & alios lego. Eratostheni, quem Strabo sequitur, & Veterum plerique, Auctor item de Sphæra, stadiis 250000; Posidonio, 240000; Hipparcho, 277000; Dionysodoro, 264000; Plinio, 252000; Ptolemæo denique, 180000. Unde tanta varietas? quod hi majoribus, minoribus illi fuerint usi stadiis. Nam uni gradui terrestris Circuli maximi tribuenda juxta rationem, Eratosthenis quidem, 694 cum quatuor nonis; Posidonij vero, 666 cum duabus tertiis; Hipparchi, 774; Dionysodori, 733 cum tertia parte; Plinii, 700; Ptolemæi denique, 500: sic Diameter seu crassitudo Terrenæ molis Eratosthenis stadiorum est 79545; Posidonio, 76363 cum duabus fere tertijs, Hipparcho, fere 88132; Dionysodoro, 84000; Plinio, fere 80182; Ptolemæo, fermè 57273. Sed Eratosthenis Posidonij & Ptolemæi, ut in hac re principum, rationes paullo fusius in sequentibus explicabuntur. Hodie Geographi plerique uni gradui (numerus autem 360) Terrestris Circuli tribuunt milliaria xv. Germanica; Italica vero lxii: sicque Globi totius ambitum statuunt milliar. Germanic. 5400; Italicorum 22320: Diametrum Germanicor. 1718, Italicorum autem 7556 cum quatuor undecimis. Quæ Veterum Recentiorumque de Terrenæ Machinæ magnitudine parum consentientes inter se Opiniones satis confirmant esse verum, cum ipsius summi Numinis verba apud Virum sanctum Hijobum cap. xxxviii, 18: Numquid intellexisti usque ad Latitudines Terræ? indica mihi, si nosti totam ipsam. tum quod Ecclesiasticus exclamat initio sui libri: Α᾽ μμον γελασῶν, ἡ σειγέτας νέτα, ἡ ἡμέρας αἰῶνΘ τῆς ἐξαγλημοῦ? ὑψΘ ἡμάνς καὶ πλάτΘ γῆς, Terra Latitudinem, καὶ ἄβυσσον, καὶ σοφίαι τῆς ἐξιχνιασοῦ? Innuunt neminem prorsus tam exactam adsequutum cognitionem tantæ rei, ut eam acu tetigisse dici potuerit. Raritas scilicet & difficultas inculcatur ipsissimæ Veritatis, hac de re feliciter eruendæ, mortalibusque communicandæ.
units.tr: I have read that the circumference of the earth has been variously defined by the ancients in various places in Aristotle, Ptolemy, Cleomedes, Strabo, Pliny, Macrobius and others. Eratosthenes, whom Strabo follows, and most of the ancients, and also the author of the work On the Sphere, put it at 250,000 stadia; Posidonius at 240,000; Hipparchus at 277,000; Dionysodorus at 264,000; Pliny at 252,000; and Ptolemy at 180,000. Whence such great variety? Because these men used larger stadia and those smaller ones. For, reckoning by the proportion, one degree of a great circle of the earth is taken as 694 and four ninths by Eratosthenes; by Posidonius 666 and two thirds; by Hipparchus 774; by Dionysodorus 733 and a third; by Pliny 700; and by Ptolemy 500. So the diameter, or thickness, of the earthly mass is 79,545 stadia by Eratosthenes; 76,363 and nearly two thirds by Posidonius; nearly 88,132 by Hipparchus; 84,000 by Dionysodorus; nearly 80,182 by Pliny; and nearly 57,273 by Ptolemy. But the reasoning of Eratosthenes, Posidonius and Ptolemy, as the leaders in this matter, will be explained somewhat more fully in what follows. Today most geographers assign to one degree of the earth's circle (the number of degrees being 360) fifteen German miles, or sixty-two Italian miles. Thus they reckon the circumference of the whole globe at 5,400 German miles, or 22,320 Italian miles, and its diameter at 1,718 German miles, or 7,556 and four elevenths Italian miles. These opinions of the ancients and moderns about the size of the earthly machine, which differ little from one another, sufficiently confirm that it is true, since the very words of the supreme Deity to the holy man Job (ch. 38:18) are: "Hast thou understood the breadth of the earth? Tell me, if thou knowest it all." Likewise Ecclesiasticus cries out at the beginning of his book: "Who shall number the sand of the sea, and the drops of rain, and the days of eternity? Who shall search out the height of heaven and the breadth of the earth, and the deep, and wisdom?" [Ἄμμον θαλασσῶν καὶ σταγόνας ὑετοῦ καὶ ἡμέρας αἰῶνος τίς ἐξαριθμήσει; ὕψος οὐρανοῦ καὶ πλάτος γῆς καὶ ἄβυσσον, καὶ σοφίαν τίς ἐξιχνιάσει;] They hint that no one has ever attained so exact a knowledge of so great a thing that he could be said to have touched it with a needle. Clearly the rarity and difficulty of finding out this very truth, and of happily bringing it to light and sharing it with mortals, is being impressed upon us.

units.la: Proportionem etiam Quantitatis & Distantiae, quae Soli, Lunae, Terraeque inter se, pulcerrime monstrat ex Parallaxium atque Apparentium Solis, Lunaeque diametrorum observatione, Nicolaus Copernicus libro quarto Revolutionum, via & ratione Geometrica. Notat enim Lunae silentis ac plenae maximam a Terra distantiam sexaginta quinque partium cum semisse; Dimidiatae vero sexaginta & octo, qualium semidiameter Terrae est una; Solis autem apogei similium partium mille, centum septuaginta novem. Monstrat deinde Terram Luna quadragesies ter fere majorem: eandemque Solem centies sexagesies bis; ita ut Sol major existat Luna sex millies nongenties triginta octo. Utrius autem Terrae an Aquae moles sit major, aperit docte Ioannes Bodinus in suo Naturae Theatro.
units.tr: Nicolaus Copernicus, in the fourth book of the Revolutions, by a geometrical method and reasoning, also shows most beautifully the proportion of the quantity and distance of the Sun, Moon and Earth to one another, from the observation of the parallaxes and apparent diameters of the Sun and Moon. For he notes that the greatest distance of the Moon, when it is new or full, from the Earth is sixty-five and a half parts (of which the Earth's semidiameter is one), and when it is half-lit sixty-eight; while the greatest distance of the Sun at apogee is one thousand, one hundred and seventy-nine such parts. He then shows that the Earth is about forty-three times larger than the Moon, and the Sun about one million, two hundred and sixty times larger than the Earth, so that the Sun is six thousand, nine hundred and thirty-eight times larger than the Moon. Whether the mass of the Earth or of the Water is greater, learned John Bodin explains in his Theatre of Nature.

units.la: Tanta igitur Terra: sed collata cum Toto imprimis autem cum octavo Orbe, Particulam esse & σημεῖον, instarque Puncti, loquuntur illustria, quae Philosophi passim, praesertim Ptolemaeus lib. 1. μεγ. συντ. cap. v, notant φαινόμενα. Primo, quod ex quavis orbis Terreni parte Magnitudines Distantiaeque Stellarum isdem temporibus aequales similesque ubique cernantur. Deinde, quod Gnomones & Centra Armillarum sphaericarum, quocumque Terrae loco ponantur, tantundem, quantum in vero Terrae centro, valeant: conserventque considerationes & circumductiones Umbrarum adeo regulares & consentientes Hypothesi Apparentiarum, ac si ipsa in medio Terrae puncto collocarentur. Tertio quod Horizon ubique dividat totum Caelum in aequales portiones. Nam quod dari potest momentum, quo non sex Zodiaci signa supra Horizontem eminent, & noctu coelo sereno cernantur? quod, quo non totidem infra lateant; continuo Caeli circumactu aliis quidem signis productis, aliis autem e regione sub occasum devolutis: Sane si Terrae magnitudo alicuius esset momenti ad Caelum, tantum ex Centro educta undiquaque superficies coelum in aequalia dispesceret Hemisphaeria; reliquae a quacumque superficiei parte extensae, idem in segmenta dirimerent inaequalia: nec dimidius semper appareret Zodiacus; sed portio dimidio Zodiaci multo minor exstaret; major Terrae solidi tate exclusa ac contecta delitesceret. Quarto quod Umbrae aequinoctialis Orientis & Occidentis Solis constituant unam rectam lineam, perinde ac si jacerentur in planum per Centrum Terrae transmissum. Haec omnia non fierent, si Caeli respectu Terrae magnitudo sensibilis aut alicuius esset quantitatis. Et hinc recte Ptolemaeus pro Centro Universi semper usurpat τὴν ὀφιν τ' ἐρώντων; nec superficiem Terrae discernit ab ejus intimo. Accedit his quod quidam affirmant, unum in Caelo gradum cuiuscumque maximi Circuli milliaria complecti Germanica (de Communibus loquor) 570581; qualium quindecim unus terreni alicuius Circuli gradus in Terrae superficie occupat: Unum vero scrupulum gradus Caelestis, 9509 explere milliaria.
units.tr: So the Earth is great; but when compared with the whole, and especially with the eighth orb, the illustrious facts which the philosophers, Ptolemy above all (Almagest, book 1, ch. 5), point out show that it is a small part and a point, like a dot. First, that from any part of the terrestrial orb the magnitudes and distances of the stars are seen everywhere equal and similar at the same times. Second, that gnomons and the centres of spherical armillary spheres, wherever they are placed on the earth, have the same value as they would at the true centre of the earth; and the considerations and circuits of shadows keep so regular and consistent with the hypothesis of appearances as if they were placed at the very midpoint of the earth. Third, that the horizon everywhere divides the whole heaven into equal portions. For what moment can there be at which six signs of the zodiac do not stand above the horizon and are not seen at night in a clear sky? Or at which the same number do not lie hidden below it, as the continual turning of the heaven brings some signs forward while others sink down opposite them at sunset? Certainly, if the magnitude of the earth had any significance in relation to the heaven, the surface extended everywhere from the centre would divide the heaven into equal hemispheres; the remaining parts, extended from any part of the surface, would divide it into unequal segments; and half of the zodiac would not always appear, but a portion much smaller than half would stand out, while the larger part, shut out and covered by the bulk of the earth, would remain hidden. Fourth, that the shadows at the equinox of the rising and setting Sun form one straight line, just as if they were cast on a plane passed through the centre of the earth. None of this would happen if the magnitude of the earth were perceptible or of any quantity in relation to the heaven. And hence Ptolemy rightly always takes as the centre of the universe the eye of the beholders [τὴν ὄψιν τῶν ὁρώντων], and does not distinguish the surface of the earth from its inmost part. To these things is added what some affirm: that one degree of any great circle in the heaven contains (I speak of common German miles) 570,581 miles, of which fifteen make up one degree of some terrestrial circle on the surface of the earth; and one minute of a heavenly degree fills 9,509 miles.

units.la: Haec omnia si certa & explorata: quis non videt Terram Caeli ratione instar censendam Puncti? In hoc Puncto, vel in ejus potius medio, nemo non collocatus homo, ut nusquam non, numquam non opera contempletur Dei; cujus ille εἰκὼν, ut est in Sibyllinis, νῦν ἐξῆν ἔχωσα; cujus ωδὲ ... μικρόκοσμος ille, in quo uno, quidquid in Universo.
units.tr: If all these things are certain and established, who does not see that the earth, in relation to the heaven, must be regarded as a point? In this point, or rather in its midst, man has been placed, so that he may everywhere and always contemplate the works of God; he is the image of God, as the Sibylline books say, [...] and that little world in which, in one being, is whatever is in the Universe.

units.la: Terra, inquam, Punctum: cui tamen post Deum quid non debemus? Recens in lucem editos, Vitamque incertam, brevem, precarioque datam, & citato cursu properantem victuros suscipit suscepstas educat & nutrit; variaque tentantes gestat usque ad Mortem: cui ut Ligna Igni, Arista Falci, nemo non homo natus, sedente semper & passim in primis quasi labris anima: at Morte confectos eadem benigno sinu, ut communis mater, recipit, receptos servat in Iudicii diem. Hic qua inquieta quam tumultuosa nobis universim, publice privatimque, vita; cujus initium Caecitas possidet, progressum Labor, Dolor exitum, Error omnia. Hoc Punctum Potentiae nostrae Campus; Dominationis nostrae Sedes, nostrae Materia Gloriae.
units.tr: The earth, I say, is a point: yet what do we not owe to it after God? It receives us, newly brought into the light, with a life uncertain, brief and given on loan, and hastening on a swift course; it takes us up when we are received, nourishes and raises us, and carries us, trying various things, to death; to which, as wood to fire and grain to the sickle, every man born goes, the soul always sitting, and everywhere as it were on the very lips. Then, as a common mother, it receives those worn out by death into its kindly bosom, and keeps those received until the day of judgment. Here, how restless and how tumultuous is our life, in general, public and private; whose beginning is held by blindness, whose progress by toil, whose end by pain, and all of it by error. This point is the field of our power, the seat of our dominion, the matter of our glory.

units.la: Sunt hic, qui Numina nobis terrestria, & Divi nobiscum habitantes, Imperatores, Reges, Principes. Hic in nostrum nonnullos primas tenet Monarchia; sub ditione quosdam habet Aristocratia; dominatur plurimis Democratia: multos exagitant Tyrannides, Oligarchiae, & Ochlocratiae; vexant etiam non paucos Anarchiae. Hic qui gubernant suis, sed quae, magna licet, ferenda essent, vitiis; qui gubernamur, nostris quae majora, quae pluria, laboramus.
units.tr: Here are those who are for us earthly deities and gods dwelling among us: emperors, kings, princes. Here monarchy holds the first place over some of us; aristocracy has some under its sway; democracy rules over many; tyrannies, oligarchies and mob rule torment many; and anarchy harasses not a few. Here those who govern us bear with their vices, which, however great, must be endured; we who are governed suffer from our own faults, which are greater and more numerous.

units.la: Hic Iudices jus pervortunt, adfuso mentibus illorum ab ἀνομία, πολυπολλία, δωροφαδωροφαγία, veneno. Hic Advocati, Procuratores, alijque forenses homines canina freti facundia, clamosi fori vendunt jurgia: ibique Clientes, ut Vulturij quidam & immanes feræ, pro virili deglubunt, exsucto etiam sanguine, extractisque medullis; quibus depauperatis post crudeles torturas fero favéntes, calore quodam & impetu abrepti, seu agendum seu scribendum, contumeliis lacessunt Adversarios, inopiaque pretii muniendarum Allegationum, ad effrenatam deflectunt conviciandi licentiam: insano denique foro litibus eorum longe lateque mugiente, primas tenent partes qui linguæ fremitu impudentissimi, qui ab alijs allegata noverint novis opinionibus enervare, qui inventas bene leges ambiguis interpretationibus ad sua figmenta adaptare.
units.tr: Here judges pervert the law, the poison of lawlessness, much-talk and bribe-taking [ἀνομία, πολυπολλία, δωροφαγία] being poured into their minds. Here advocates, procurators and other men of the forum, trusting in dog-like eloquence, sell quarrels in the noisy courts; and there clients, like vultures and savage beasts, flay their victims as far as they can, sucking out their blood and draining their marrow; and when these have been impoverished by cruel torments, the advocates, carried away by a kind of heat and passion, whether in pleading or writing, assail their opponents with insults; and, lacking the money to fortify their pleas, they turn to an unbridled licence of abuse. Finally, when the mad forum roars far and wide with their lawsuits, the first place is held by those most shameless in the din of their tongues, who know how to weaken what others have alleged by new opinions, and who adapt well-made laws, by ambiguous interpretations, to their own fabrications.

units.la: Hic quid non scitur, quid non discitur ad factum, ad quæstum? Theologi sacro DEI verbo vim facientes, insana quadam sapientia miras & deploratas movent quæstiones, absurdas pravasque fabricant opiniones, intricatis verbis alienum sensum scripturis obducunt: paratiores ventilare, quam examinare; ingenium in non necessarijs labyrinthis exercentes, ætatemque jurgijs perpetuis & prodigiosis contentionibus terentes.
units.tr: What is not known here, what is not learned for gain and profit? Theologians, doing violence to the sacred Word of God, with a certain mad cleverness raise wonderful and desperate questions, fabricate absurd and perverse opinions, and cover the sense of Scripture with intricate words that are foreign to it. They are readier to stir up disputes than to examine them. They exercise their wits in unnecessary labyrinths and waste their lives in perpetual quarrels and monstrous contentions.

units.la: Hic Iurisconsulti perniciosissima Iuris Naturalis inculcamus Axiomata: Vim vi repellendam esse, Frangenti Fidem frangendam; Fallentem fallere non esse fraudem; Culpam cum Culpa compensare fas esse; Volenti non fieri Iniuriam; Permissum contrahentibus se decipere; Tanti rem esse, quanti potest vendi; Licere sibi consulere cum alterius etiam detrimento; & similia. Hic Ius Gentium infelici fœcunditate Bella, Cædes, Servitutes peperit; Civile vero infinita disseminavit in omnes homines Litigia, ingeniosa Avaritiæ Præcepta, & mille rapiendi formulas; præterea Opinionum maria, Consiliorum Silvas, Cautelarum procellas, quibus Advocatorum instrui solent & nutriri nequitiæ.
units.tr: Here we jurists teach the most pernicious axioms of natural law: force is to be repelled by force; faith is to be broken with one who breaks faith; deceiving the deceiver is not fraud; it is lawful to repay fault with fault; no injury is done to one who consents; contracting parties are permitted to deceive one another; a thing is worth as much as it can be sold for; it is lawful to look after one's own interest even to another's loss; and the like. Here the law of nations, with unhappy fertility, has brought forth wars, slaughters and slaveries. The civil law has scattered endless lawsuits among all men, clever precepts of greed, and a thousand formulas for plunder. Besides these there are seas of opinions, forests of counsels and storms of cautions, with which the wickedness of advocates is usually trained and nourished.

units.la: Hic Medici Artem callentes & colentes non tam beneficam, quam veneficam, difficilem scilicet & fallacem, quaque nulla inconstantior, sæpe plus male habentibus periculi concinnant, quam ipsi morbi; sumtuosis exitiosisque mistionibus divinam scientiam non nisi casum & conjecturam facientes; illudque in omnem curant eventum, ut nemo laborans, nisi propria culpa, vel altem naturæ inopia maliariave morbi, periisse; nemo, nisi suo beneficio suaque peritia fideque restitutus videatur.
units.tr: Here physicians who cultivate and practise an art that is not so much beneficial as poisonous, difficult and deceptive, and than which none is more inconstant, often prepare more danger for the sick than the diseases themselves do. By costly and deadly mixtures they reduce divine science to nothing but chance and guesswork. They so manage every outcome that no patient seems to have died except through his own fault, or at least through the weakness of nature or the malignity of the disease, and no one seems to have been restored except by their kindness, skill and good faith.

units.la: Hic Historici quam varia diversaque de ijsdem tradunt: narrantes quæ argumento suo institutoque maxime conducunt, ceteris dissimulatis, præteritis, exten-uatis: verbosa novitate nugas elegantes & monstrosa mendacia ad recreandum lectorem effutientes; nonnumquam Veritati nonnihil adfabulantes, plerumque vero eidem metu, simulate, odio corrupti detrahentes; non quod est, sed quod volunt, quodque jubet adfectus, scribentes.
units.tr: Here historians hand down how varied and diverse their accounts of the same things are. They relate what most serves their subject and purpose, passing over, omitting or belittling the rest. With verbose novelty they babble elegant trifles and monstrous lies to entertain the reader. Sometimes they add fictions to the truth, but for the most part, corrupted by fear, flattery or hatred, they disparage the same things, writing not what is, but what they wish, and what passion commands.

units.la: Hic Critici (sæpe temerarij Adolescentes, similesque Adolescentum Senes; raro viri, serij, germanique) proprium habentes pervolitare & pervolutare omnia, certatim Libros effundunt magna mole Commentarios, Adversaria, Adnotationes, Scholia, Observationes, Animadversa, Castigationes, Disquisitiones, Miscellanea, Centurias, Syntagmata, Conlectanea, Catalecta, Additiones, Appendices, Verisimilia, Conjecturas, Præcidanea, Spicilegia, Lectiones Varias, Succisivas, Novas, Antiquas, & quasi nihil prætermissuri Nov. Antiquas; inficiunt sæpe industria quadam audaci quod sanum; quod receptum cum novis & commentitijs commutant; quidquid lubet, tamquam pristinum nitorem reconciliaturi, inducunt: saucium, lacerum, mutilum, depositum, corruptum, male adfectum nihil non pronunciantes; ostentando ingenio: plurimum non correctores, sed corruptores bonorum Auctorum, vulnera facientes, dum mederi se credunt: interea passim Litterarum apices, Voculas, Tropulos, & similia, tamquam res magni momenti, plerumque sectantes; Fluctus in simpulo excitantes; invecti ubique (solennis enim & φιλάργυρος huic ordini morbus, præter Pruriginem, Litigium) in viros ignotos, ijs sæpe multo & meliores & doctiores.
units.tr: Here critics (often rash young men, and old men who are like young men; rarely serious and genuine men), having the habit of flitting and rolling through everything, pour out books in great bulk: commentaries, adversaria, annotations, scholia, observations, animadversions, corrections, disquisitions, miscellanies, centuries, syntagmas, collections, catalecta, additions, appendices, probabilities, conjectures, leftovers, gleanings, various readings, selected readings, new and old, as though they would omit nothing. They often spoil with a bold industry what is sound, and exchange what is accepted for new and fabricated things. Whatever pleases them they introduce, as if they were going to restore the former lustre. They pronounce everything wounded, torn, mutilated, displaced, corrupted and badly affected, and they display their wit. For the most part they are not correctors but corruptors of good authors, inflicting wounds while they believe they are healing. Meanwhile everywhere they chase after letters, little words, tropes and the like as matters of great moment, stirring up storms in a teacup. They attack, as is the customary disease of this order (apart from itching, litigiousness and a love of money), men they do not know, often far better and more learned than themselves.

units.la: Hic Astronomi, tamquam è Cœlo nuper delapsi, magna temeritate pro libitu Veteres & Recentiores fabricant nunc hoc nunc illo numero sphæras & orbes cælestes; differunt de Siderum mensuris, motibus, figuris, imaginibus, numeris & concentibus; dumque Cœli scrutantur plagas, non spectant quod ante pedes.
units.tr: Here astronomers, as if they had newly fallen from heaven, with great rashness fabricate at their pleasure now this, now that number of spheres and celestial orbits, both ancient and modern. They dispute about the measures, motions, shapes, images, numbers and harmonies of the stars. And while they scrutinize the regions of the sky, they do not look at what is at their feet.

units.la: Hic Astrologi, bene constitutis rebuspublicis pestilentes, Principibus infidi, credentibus fallaces, vanissimis vaticinijs nunc alijs Coniugium, Subolem, Amicos, Vitam, Salutem, Honores, Magistratus, Potentiam, Opes, Victoriam pollicentur: alijs, arte scelerata, prædicunt Orbitates, Cladés, Exilia, Dedecora, Mortes: præposterum hominum genus, Futura se præscire qui gloriantur, Præteritorum & Præsentium miserægue suæ Sortis ignari.
units.tr: Here astrologers, pestilent to well-ordered commonwealths, unfaithful to princes and deceitful to believers, with most empty prophecies promise some people marriage, offspring, friends, life, health, honours, offices, power, wealth and victory. To others, by a wicked art, they foretell bereavement, disasters, exile, disgrace and death. They are a perverse race of men who boast that they foreknow the future, while they are ignorant of the past and present and of their own wretched lot.

units.la: Hic Geometræ de Punctis, Lineis, Superficiebus adhuc disputant; veramque Circuli Quadraturam adhuc quærunt, Priorum præceptis numquam adquiescentes in maximam aguntur nova semper rimandi insaniam.
units.tr: Here geometers still dispute about points, lines and surfaces, and still seek the true squaring of the circle. Never content with the precepts of their predecessors, they are driven into the greatest madness of always seeking new things.

units.la: Hic Optici Lucem quærentes in Tenebras deviant; Rebusque ipsis amissis de Umbris disceptant: Intervalla docentes longis intervallis quæ maxime discenda relinquunt.
units.tr: Here opticians, seeking light, wander into darkness; having lost the things themselves, they argue about shadows. Teaching intervals across long intervals, they leave the most important things to be learned.

units.la: Hic Cosmographi pugnant adhuc de Limitum, Longitudinum, Latitudinum, Distantiarum, Climatum veritate; dumque Terram immensam, Maria magna, Regionum & Insularum situs, Gentium origines ritusque rimantur, aliena avidius pervestigantes, seipsos ignorare discunt; & admiratum euntes quæ non sua, se in periculosissimam sui præcipitant ignorantiam.
units.tr: Here cosmographers still fight over the truth about limits, longitudes, latitudes, distances and climates. And while they search out the immense earth, the great seas, the positions of regions and islands, and the origins and customs of peoples, investigating foreign things too eagerly, they learn to be ignorant of themselves. Going to admire what is not their own, they plunge themselves into the most dangerous ignorance of themselves.

units.la: Hic Arithmetici de Rebus futilibus, frigidissimis inquam & insensatis numeris, magna contentione jurgantur.
units.tr: Here arithmeticians wrangle with great contention about futile things, very cold and senseless numbers, I say.

units.la: Hic Musici aliorum animis effeminandis conducuntur pluris, ut desinant, quam ut canant; Auditorum aures venenata quadam & dulci numerorum varietate, veluti Sirenes, adsonante læta vocum sonorumque lascivia, corrumpentes: præsertim si comitetur Chorearum licentia: qua permissa, fit ut Matronæ quidem servatum diu decus amittant; infelices autem Virgunculæ discant quod satius fuerat ignorare: multi denique per inconditos gestus monstrosumque pedum ad molles pulsationes strepitum famam perdant & pudorem.
units.tr: Here musicians are hired more to unman men's minds than to sing, and more to make them stop than to sing. With a certain poisonous and sweet variety of numbers, like Sirens, and with the joyful wantonness of voices and sounds blending together, they corrupt the ears of listeners. This is especially so if the licence of dancing accompanies it. Once that is allowed, matrons lose the honour they have long kept, while unhappy young girls learn what it would have been better to be ignorant of. Finally, many lose their reputation and modesty through unseemly gestures and the monstrous stamping of feet to soft beats and noise.

units.la: Hic unum hoc agunt Dialectici, ut altercando & perpetuis digladiationibus explicandam veritatem vel obscuriorem reddant, vel amittant; gloriaque in convicijs & tumultu posita, non tam victoriam appetant, quam certamen.
units.tr: Here dialecticians aim at one thing only: by wrangling and perpetual sword-fights they either make the truth to be explained more obscure or lose it altogether. Placing their glory in insults and uproar, they seek not so much victory as contention.

units.la: Hic Rhetores magna Proœmiorum, Insinuationum, Figuratum, Colorum, aliorumque id genus Artificiorum, captandæ benivolentiæ & Auditoribus persuadendis, excogitata mole, quod rei veritate nequeunt, Orationis fuco & dumnifica loquacitate conantur efficere: in eo sæpe toti, ut alios inepte cavillentur, & in innocentes tyrannidem quamdam usurpent, noxiaque eloquentia totas: Respublicas evertant; Verum ampullis insanisque declamationibus Bonorum tranquillitatem, quantum in se est, perturbantes, homınesque, quo volunt; dicendo seducentes.
units.tr: Here rhetoricians, with a great mass of prologues, insinuations, figures, colours and other devices of this kind contrived to win goodwill and persuade hearers, try by the paint of oratory and harmful wordiness to achieve what they cannot by the truth of the matter. They are often wholly intent on silly sneering at others, assume a kind of tyranny over the innocent, and with harmful eloquence overturn whole commonwealths. With bombastic and mad declamations they disturb, so far as in them lies, the tranquillity of good men, and by speaking they lead men wherever they will.

units.la: Hic Poetæ quid agunt? fabulis suis nunc ut adulatores blandiuntur, nunc Satyrici mordent & accusant: inque omnes dentati, Lucianos mere exprimunt; à carpendis alienis moribus numquam sibi temperantes; in aliena vitia acutiores, quam in sua.
units.tr: Here what do the poets do? In their fables they now flatter like sycophants, now as satirists bite and accuse. Biting at everyone, they express pure Lucians, never restraining themselves from carping at other people's morals, and being sharper against the vices of others than against their own.

units.la: Quam autem hic absurdæ de Magno Numine, de Anima, de Summo Bono conceptæ quondam à Philosophis, & utinam hodie non conciperentur, opiniones? Diagoras Milesius & Theodorus Cyrenaicus nullum prorsus esse DEVM, non erubuerunt dicere: Epicurus esse quidem, sed nulla inferorum cura tangi: Protagoras esset nec ne, sciri non posse: Antisthenes multos Deos populares esse; sed unum naturalem, summum Totius artificem. Alcmæon Solem, Lunam, reliquaque Sidera Deos dixit. Quod ad Essentiam Divinam: Thales Milesius Νῶν τῶ Κόσμῳ opinatus est DEVM; à quo quidquid in Universo ex Aqua formatum: Cleanthes & Anaximenes τὸν Ἀέρα: Archelaus Ἀέρα καὶ Νοῦν; ἀ μὴ πι κοσμοποιὸν τὸν Νοῦ: Anaxagoras Νοῦν κόσμου ποιόν: Democritus Νοῦν ἐν πυρὶ σφαιροειδὲς: Diogenes & Oenopides τῷ τῶ κόσμῳ ψυχῶ: Pythagoras Μονάδα καὶ τ' Ἀόριστον, τῆς Νοῦς Φύσιν: Posidonius Πνεῦμα νοερὸν καὶ πυρώδες, οὐκ ἔχον μὲν μορφὴν, μεταβαλλὸν δὲ εἰς ὁ βάλλετο: Speusippus τὸν Νοῦν ἐπὶ τῷ Ἑνὶ ἐπὶ τῷ Ἀγαθῷ τ' αὐτὸν; idioφυῆ δὲ: Critolaus & Diodorus Tyrius Νῶν ἀπ' Αἰθέρος ἀπαθῆς: Heraclitus τὸ πυρώδικον: Zeno Stoicus Νῶν κόσμου πνεῦμα: Mnesarchus τὸν Κόσμον, τῷ πρώτῳ οὐσίαν ἔχοντα ὅπ' Πνεύματος: Boethus Αἰθέρα: Parmenides τὸ ἀκίνητον πᾶν περιέχον σφαιροειδὲς: Melissus τὸ Ἐν εἶναι ... ἀεὶ καὶ ἄπειρον: Xenophanes denique quidquid esset Deum voluit.
units.tr: How absurd are the opinions, once conceived by philosophers (and would that they were not conceived today), about the Great Divinity, the soul and the highest good! Diagoras of Melos and Theodorus of Cyrene did not blush to say that there is absolutely no God. Epicurus said there is one, but that he is untouched by any care for lower things. Protagoras said that whether he exists or not cannot be known. Antisthenes said there are many gods of the people, but one natural God, the supreme craftsman of the whole. Alcmaeon said the Sun, Moon and the other stars are gods. As to the divine essence: Thales of Miletus thought God was the mind of the world [Νοῦν τῷ κόσμῳ], from whom whatever is formed in the universe comes from water. Cleanthes and Anaximenes said air [τὸν ἀέρα]. Archelaus said air and mind [ἀέρα καὶ νοῦν]. Anaxagoras said mind, the maker of the world [νοῦν κόσμου ποιητήν]. Democritus said mind in spherical fire [νοῦν ἐν πυρὶ σφαιροειδές]. Diogenes and Oenopides said the soul of the world [τὴν τοῦ κόσμου ψυχήν]. Pythagoras said the monad and the indefinite, the nature of mind [μονάδα καὶ τὸ ἀόριστον, τῆς νοῦ φύσιν]. Posidonius said an intelligent and fiery spirit, without form but changing into whatever it is turned into [πνεῦμα νοερὸν καὶ πυρῶδες, οὐκ ἔχον μὲν μορφήν, μεταβαλλὸν δὲ εἰς ὃ βάλλετο]. Speusippus said mind in the One, in the Good itself, and self-existent [τὸν νοῦν ἐπὶ τῷ ἑνὶ, ἐπὶ τῷ ἀγαθῷ τὸ αὐτὸ, ἰδιοφυῆ δέ]. Critolaus and Diodorus of Tyre said mind from impassive aether [νοῦν ἀπ' αἰθέρος ἀπαθῆ]. Heraclitus said the fiery [τὸ πυρῶδες]. Zeno the Stoic said the mind, the spirit of the world [νοῦν κόσμου πνεῦμα]. Mnesarchus said the world, which has substance in the first place from spirit [τὸν κόσμον, τῷ πρώτῳ οὐσίαν ἔχοντα ὑπὸ πνεύματος]. Boethus said aether [αἰθέρα]. Parmenides said the immovable all, encompassing, spherical [τὸ ἀκίνητον, πᾶν περιέχον, σφαιροειδές]. Melissus said the One is always and infinite [τὸ ἕν εἶναι ... ἀεὶ καὶ ἄπειρον]. Xenophanes, in short, wanted whatever there is to be God.

units.la: Animam autem, præstantissimam μικροκόσμου portionem, & divinæ particulam auræ, Crates Thebanus Nihil esse, autus est aliquando dicere. Eorum qui quid esse sunt fassi: Hipparchus, Parmenides & Leucippus censuerunt πυρώδη: Stoici Πνεῦμα νοερὸν, θερμόν: Democritus πυρώδες Σύγκριμα ἐκ τῶν Λόγων θεωρικῶν, σφαιρικὰς μὲν ἔχοντας τὰς ἰδέας, πυρίνλω δὲ τῷ δυνάμει. ὅπερ σῶμα εἶναι: Heraclitus Φυσικὴ esse: Hippo ἐκ τῶν ὕδατος constare: Xenarchus Peripateticus alijque ejus sectæ τῶν κατὰ τὸ αὐτὸ πλεῖστα ἐν ἰδίᾳ ... esse, καὶ ἑαυτὸ ἔχειν ἅμα ἐκ μετὰ τὰ σώματα συνπεζομένη: Epicurus χρῆμα, mistionem rerum quatuor, Igneæ, Aereæ, Spiritalis, & quartæ nominis carentis; qua Sentiendi vim, τὸ αἰσθητικὸν, indicat: Anaxagoras, Anaximenes, Archelaus, Diogenes Apolloniates, Critias, M. Terentius Varro, Ἀέροειδὴ sunt Animam opinati: Hesiodus, Thales, Anaximander Terreum quid dixerunt: Empedocles & Circias Sanguineum quid voluerunt: Hippocrates Medicus Spiritum tenuem, qui per Corpus diffusus: Asclepiades Carnem cum Sensuum exercitio: Zeno Citticus, Dicæarchus, Alexander Aphrodisæus Animam composuerunt ex quatuor Elementis: Cleanthes, Antipater, Posidonius, Galenus Complexionem dixerunt calidam: Chrysippus & Heraclitus Animam vocarunt Lucem: Critolaus quintam Essentiam dixit: Xenocrates moventem se Numerum: Ægyptii vim quamdam in omnia corpora transmeantem: Chaldæi Virtutem absque determinata forma, omnes exteras suscipientem: Aristoteles nova voce appellavit Ἐντελέχειαν: Zoroastes, Hermes Trismegistus, Orpheus, Pythagoras, Eumenius, Ammonius, Plutarchus, Porphyrius, Timæus & Plato Animam dixerunt divinam quamdam Substantiam, totam & individuam, toti & cuique Corporis parti præsentem; ita productam, ut ex sola Agentis Virtute, non ex Materia dependeat: Eumonius Episcopus Animam ait esse Substantiam incorpoream in Corpore factam: M. Tullius, Seneca, Lactantius quid sit Anima, fatentur se ignorare. Quam autem de Sede ejus controvertitur? Ea Hippocrati in Cerebri Ventriculis: Democrito, Platoni, Aristoteli, alijsque nobilioribus Philosophis in toto Corpore: Erasistrato circa Membranam Epicranidem: Stratoni in Superciliorum interstitio: Epicuro in toto Corpore: Diogeni in arteriato Cordis Ventriculo: Stoicis, Chrysippo, Bedæ ad Marium scribenti in toto corde ac Spiritu circa Cor versante: Empedocli in Sanguine: Galenus cuivis Corporis particulæ suam Animam esse ait. Eamdem, quum omnium fere Nationum Sapientissimi, omnes fere Philosophi, in quibus sana Mens fuit, plerique denique Scriptores Animam dixerunt Immortalem: Zeno, Democritus, Epicurus, Cleanthes, Lucretius, Seneca, Plinius cum Corpore interituram scripserunt: Pythagoras & Plato Immortalem dixerunt; sed egressam corpus ad sui generis naturam avolare: Stoici, mediam inter hos viam ingressi, Animam censuerunt Corpus reliquram; ita tamen, ut quæ nullis prædita Virtutibus infirmior, una cum illo emoriatur; heroica autem & Virtutibus ornata ad sublimiores sedes evolet.
units.tr: Crates the Theban once ventured to say that the soul, the most excellent portion of the microcosm and a particle of the divine breath, is nothing. Of those who professed what it is: Hipparchus, Parmenides and Leucippus thought it fiery [πυρώδη]. The Stoics thought it a mind-like, warm spirit [πνεῦμα νοερὸν, θερμόν]. Democritus thought it a fiery compound from theoretical reasons, having spherical forms and a fiery power, which is a body [πυρῶδες σύγκριμα]. Heraclitus thought it natural [φυσικήν]. Hippo held that it consists of water [ἐκ τοῦ ὕδατος constare]. Xenarchus the Peripatetic and others of his school said it is a thing that has many parts in one, and holds itself together along with the bodies [συμπεζομένη]. Epicurus said it is a mixture of four things, the fiery, the airy, the spiritual, and a fourth nameless thing, which indicates the power of sensation [τὸ αἰσθητικόν]. Anaxagoras, Anaximenes, Archelaus, Diogenes of Apollonia, Critias and M. Terentius Varro thought the soul airlike [ἀεροειδῆ]. Hesiod, Thales and Anaximander said it is something earthy. Empedocles and Circias meant something bloody. Hippocrates the physician meant a thin spirit diffused through the body. Asclepiades meant flesh together with the exercise of the senses. Zeno of Citium, Dicaearchus and Alexander of Aphrodisias composed the soul of the four elements. Cleanthes, Antipater, Posidonius and Galen said it is a warm complexion. Chrysippus and Heraclitus called the soul light. Critolaus called it a fifth essence. Xenocrates called it a self-moving number. The Egyptians held it a certain power passing through all bodies. The Chaldeans held it a power without determinate form, receiving all external forms. Aristotle called it by a new word, entelechy [Ἐντελέχειαν]. Zoroaster, Hermes Trismegistus, Orpheus, Pythagoras, Eumenius, Ammonius, Plutarch, Porphyry, Timaeus and Plato said the soul is a certain divine substance, whole and undivided, present to the whole body and to each part of it, produced in such a way that it depends on the power of the agent alone, not on matter. Eumenius the bishop says the soul is an incorporeal substance made in the body. Cicero, Seneca and Lactantius confess that they do not know what the soul is. But where is its seat disputed? Hippocrates placed it in the ventricles of the brain; Democritus, Plato, Aristotle and other more noted philosophers in the whole body; Erasistratus around the epicranial membrane; Strato in the space between the eyebrows; Epicurus in the whole body; Diogenes in the arterial ventricle of the heart; the Stoics, Chrysippus and Bede writing to Marius, in the whole heart, with the spirit dwelling around the heart; Empedocles in the blood; and Galen says every particle of the body has its own soul. Nearly all the wisest men of all nations, nearly all philosophers in whom there was sound judgement, and most writers, have called the soul immortal. Zeno, Democritus, Epicurus, Cleanthes, Lucretius, Seneca and Pliny wrote that it perishes with the body. Pythagoras and Plato said it is immortal, but that when it leaves the body it flies away to its own kind of nature. The Stoics, taking a middle way between these, held that the soul survives the body; yet only so that the weaker soul, endowed with no virtues, dies together with the body, while the heroic soul, adorned with virtues, flies up to higher seats.

units.la: De Summo denique Bono quam hic à Philosophis varie decepticatum? In Voluptate posuerunt Epicurus, Aristippus, Eudoxus & Philoxenes: in eadem comitante Honestate, Dinomachus & Calipho: in Primigeniis Naturæ Carneades & Hieronymus Rhodius: in Virtutibus earumque Connexione Pythagoras, Socrates, Ariston, Empedocles, Democritus, Zeno Citticus, Cleanthes, Hecaton, Posidonius, Dionysius Babylonius, Antisthenes, Stoici omnes: Indolentiam illud esse censuit Diodorus: Fortunam Theophrastus: eamdem, sed cum Primigeniis Naturæ Virtutibusque conjunctam, Aristoteles: Scientiam Herillus: multique Socratici: Speculationem hic imaginantur Peripatetici: Vnionem Plato ejusque sectatores: Sapientiam Bias Prienæus; Prudentiam Bion & Boryslhenes; utramque Thales Milesius: Omnium Rerum Vacationem M. Tullius. Agentem bene ab Summo Bono proxime abesse dixit Pittacus Mitylenæus.
units.tr: Finally, how variously have the philosophers disputed the Chief Good! Epicurus, Aristippus, Eudoxus and Philoxenes placed it in pleasure; Dinomachus and Calipho placed it in pleasure accompanied by honour; Carneades and Hieronymus of Rhodes placed it in the primary things of nature; Pythagoras, Socrates, Ariston, Empedocles, Democritus, Zeno of Citium, Cleanthes, Hecaton, Posidonius, Dionysius of Babylon, Antisthenes and all the Stoics placed it in the virtues and their connection. Diodorus held that it is freedom from distress; Theophrastus, fortune; Aristotle, the same, but joined to the primary things of nature and the virtues; Herillus, knowledge; and many of the Socratics likewise. The Peripatetics imagine it to be contemplation; Plato and his followers, union. Bias of Priene placed it in wisdom, Bion and Borysthenes in prudence, Thales of Miletus in both, and Marcus Tullius in freedom from all cares. Pittacus of Mytilene said that one who acts well is very close to the Chief Good.

units.la: Quam vero fœdis hic domi forisque vivitur & inquinatis moribus? Pauci bene, multi male faciunt: bene; insolenter & laboriose: male; crebro, sine duce, sine magistro.
units.tr: And how foully, at home and abroad, do men live, with what polluted morals! Few do well, many do ill: they do well with arrogance and toil, ill often, without a leader, without a teacher.

units.la: Hic ἀταξία regnat, & Vincula inter Parentes & Liberos, inter Coniuges, Cognatos, Adfines disrupta jacent: Parentes fe suaque Officia Liberis negant; Liberi Amorem, Obedientiam, Gratitudinem Parentibus: inter fe dissentiunt, pulsis Amore, Fide, E'mexeía Conjuges: exsulante φιλαδελφία, rara Fratrum hic Concordia; Odijs certant reliqui.
units.tr: Here disorder [ἀταξία] reigns, and the bonds between parents and children, between spouses, kinsfolk and in-laws lie broken. Parents deny themselves and their duties to their children; children deny love, obedience and gratitude to their parents. Spouses quarrel among themselves, love and faith having been driven out, and forbearance with them. Brotherly love [φιλαδελφία] is banished, and harmony among brothers is rare here; the rest contend in hatred.

units.la: Hic Benificijs adfecti Ingratitudinis fe constituunt reos.
units.tr: Here men who have been loaded with benefits make themselves guilty of ingratitude.

units.la: Hic Liberalitati antistant ex una Prodigentia; profundens omnia in Luxum, reliquae non neceflarias, Pomparum inanitatem, splendorem Vestium, monstra Conviviorum, & similia: ex altera parte, malorum omnium radix, Avaritia: sibi canens, nemini benefaciens, possessos horrenda inflammans habendi rabie, victuque eosdem defraudans: Opes cumulans quocumque modo, fuerit etiam cum aliorum dispendio & jactura. Hic nullus aedificationibus statuitur modus: rupes abfcinduntur; complentur valles; aguntur in planum montes; saxa perforantur; excavantur Terrae viscera; flumina deducuntur; Maribus Maria junguntur; exhauriuntur lacus; paludes exsiccantur; coercentur aequora; profunda peruntur Maris; novae fiunt Infulae, aliaeque restituuntur Continenti; Labyrinthi, Pyramides, Colossi, Obelifci, aliaque insana opera, omnia ad stultam opum ostentationem, fabricantur. Hic Metallici majore studio praecipitant fe in Terrae penetralia, quam ad Coelestia feruntur: ad Inferos vivi descendentes, magna Naturae ruina, in sedibus Manium quaerunt divitias; vim Terrae facientes, ejusque viscera extrahentes, ut auro pauci fulgeant, argento sint fplendidiores, digitis gestent gemmas; attritis multorum manibus, ut unus niteat articulus.
units.tr: Here generosity is opposed by one kind of prodigality, which pours everything into luxury, into unnecessary things, the vanity of processions, the splendour of clothing, the monstrous feasts and the like. On the other side, the root of all evils, avarice, reigns: it sings only to itself, does good to no one, and, inflaming its possessors with a dreadful rage for having, cheats them of their food. It piles up wealth by any means, even at the expense and loss of others. Here no limit is set to building: cliffs are cut away, valleys filled, mountains levelled, rocks bored through, the bowels of the earth hollowed out, rivers diverted, seas joined to seas, lakes drained, marshes dried up, the waters restrained, the depths of the sea traversed; new islands are made, and others joined back to the mainland. Labyrinths, pyramids, colossi, obelisks and other mad works are all built for the foolish display of wealth. Here miners hurl themselves into the recesses of the earth with greater zeal than men aspire to heaven.
