Going down alive to the underworld, to the abodes of the dead, they seek riches with great ruin to nature, forcing the earth and dragging out its bowels, so that a few may glitter with gold, be more splendid with silver, and carry gems on their fingers, while many hands are worn away so that a single joint may shine.

units.la: Hic multi, quae Deus largitus est, non contenti, aliena attrectant, fraudibus Contractus foedant, Vsurarum vi medullas ossibus tenuiorum exturbant; rapinis & expilationibus immoderatis alios inquietantes.
units.tr: Here many men, not content with what God has granted them, lay hands on what belongs to others, defile their dealings with fraud, and by the violence of usury drain the marrow from the bones of the poor; they harass others with immoderate robberies and plunderings.

units.la: Opes hic quantae quales inexplebilem multorum aviditatem non saturant; majores perpetuo (nam semper avari egent) maximis expetunt votis, omnem animi tranquillitatem mille curis dilaniantes. Hic Mercatoribus, qui numquam habendi fructu felices, semper quaerendi cupiditate miserrimi, proprium est & perpetuum mentiri, pejerare, fallere; dignas supplicio fraudes struere; contra jus falsque Monopolia exercere; nullam lucrandi rationem turpem inlicitamque aestimare; Monetam intendere, remittere; mores inquinare: nullam Animae, Corporis, Fortunae periculum, modo lucrum adfulgeat, excludere: tandem autem (in bonos nulla mihi Satyra) magno aere alieno conflato, prostituta fide solum vertere, & Creditores fraudare.
units.tr: Here the wealth, however great, does not satisfy the boundless greed of many; always seeking more (for the avaricious are always in want), they pursue the greatest things with their vows, tearing all tranquillity of mind to pieces with a thousand cares. Here it is characteristic and constant for merchants, who are never made happy by the enjoyment of having, but always miserable in their desire to get, to lie, to perjure themselves and to deceive; to contrive frauds worthy of punishment; to practise monopolies against law and right; to judge no way of gain shameful or unlawful; to tamper with the coinage, debasing and adulterating it; to corrupt morals; to exclude no danger to soul, body or fortune, provided that profit shines forth. And finally (I am no satirist against good men), with a great debt contracted, and faith prostituted, they flee the country and defraud their creditors.

units.la: Hic (quum Naturae Communis vinculum suaderet modum adhibendum Iracundiae; remittendum Offensiones; Injuriasque, etiam veras, condonandum) Phalaride crudelius multi saeviunt, saepe etiam in innocentes; justas poenas nimium exasperant; ingentes Irarum motus concipiunt; poenitenda saepe & pudenda decernunt; Vindictam bonum clamantes, Vitaque ipsa jucundius, nusquam magis memoria valentes.
units.tr: Here (although the bond of common nature would advise a measure to be kept in anger, offences to be remitted, and injuries, even true ones, to be forgiven), many rage more cruelly than Phalaris, often even against the innocent. They exaggerate just punishments beyond measure, conceive huge movements of wrath, and often decree things that are to be regretted and are shameful. Crying out that vengeance is a good, they are more eager for it than for life itself, and nowhere is their memory stronger.

units.la: Hic Venena propinantur in auro, Aconita poculis offeruntur gemmatis, in mutuam perniciem omnes excogitantur machinae, Majores praedam rapiunt Minores. Hic Ditiorum ambiuntur Amicitiae, Pauperum cognatio non numeratur.
units.tr: Here poisons are administered in gold, aconites are offered in jewelled cups, all sorts of machines are devised for mutual destruction, the greater plunder the lesser. Here the friendships of the richer are courted, and the kinship of the poor is not counted.

units.la: Hic infracta Veritate, niveo Animi Candore, prudentique Simplicitate potiora ducuntur, hinc prodigiosa Mendacia, Nocendi cupiditas, impudentes Obtrectationes, foeda Convicia, Calumniae forenses, audax & scelerosa Perfidia; inde insanis & insolens Iactatio, inconstans Vanitas, Adsentatio denique Simulandi Dissimulandique docta.
units.tr: Here, truth being broken, the candour of a pure mind and prudent simplicity are esteemed less, whence come monstrous lies, the lust to harm, shameless detractions, foul abuse, forensic slanders, and bold and wicked treachery; whence come mad and insolent boasting, unstable vanity, and finally flattery skilled in pretending and dissembling.

units.la: Hic (quum fideliter, constanter, diligenter cuique quod suum, proprium, quodque necessarium esset curandum) inrumpitur in alieni Muneris functionem; tantum ocij ab re sua putatur, aliena ut curari queant; παρέργα & inutilia tractantur bonae rerum bene gerendarum occasiones negliguntur.
units.tr: Here (when each man should faithfully, constantly and diligently attend to what is his own, what is proper to him and what is necessary) men break into the office of another; so much leisure is thought to be left over from one's own affairs that other people's can be looked after. Trifles and useless things are handled, and the good opportunities for doing well what ought to be done are neglected.

units.la: Nitimur in Vetitum hic semper, cupimusque negata: & (quum retinenda passim omnibus in rebus & actionibus esset Constantia, Aequabilitas, & Animi Firmitas) Vortumnos induimus; Euripo mutabiliores nunc ad levem Inconstantiam, nunc ad stultam Pertinaciam, ἀψιχαγοι & arefacto rubo praefractiores, mirum quam prono lapsu, declinamus.
units.tr: We always strive here after what is forbidden, and desire what is refused; and (when constancy, evenness and firmness of mind ought to be maintained everywhere in all our affairs and actions) we put on the character of Vertumnus. More changeable than the Euripus, now toward light inconstancy, now toward foolish obstinacy, more stubborn than a withered bramble and [ἀψιχαγοι], we decline with a wonderfully ready slide.

units.la: Hic (quum, mutato nonnumquam Vitae statu, Adversa patienter & moderate tote toleranda; Dolor, si forte vinci non potis, temperandus: & auxilium in rebus adflictis ab uno Deo, Calamitates nostras, quæcumque sint, vel mitigaturo, vel, si expedit, aversuro, esset exspectandum; castiganti murmurantes, qui non irascuntur? imputantes illi, quod ab alijs derideantur; quod immites & malignæ de se voces in Vulgus spargantur; quod, omnium rerum egeni, pauperie premantur; quod capitalia in se Odia exerceantur: quod mari terraque tam sævis sæpe iactentur periculis; quod terrore metuque toties concutiantur; quod denique varijs supplicijs mactentur.
units.tr: Here (when, the state of life sometimes having changed, adversity must be borne patiently and moderately throughout, grief tempered if it cannot be overcome, and help in afflictions expected from God alone, who will either lessen our calamities, whatever they are, or, if it is expedient, turn them away) — who does not grumble when chastised? They blame him because they are mocked by others; because bitter and malicious words about them are spread among the common people; because, lacking everything, they are oppressed by poverty; because deadly hatreds are stirred up against them; because they are so often tossed about by such savage dangers on sea and land; because they are so often shaken by terror and fear; because, finally, they are slaughtered with various torments.

units.la: Hic præ laudandis quantam moliuntur multi Dedecorum molem? Mira nos habet Auræ popularis fames, Famæque aviditate præcipites ferimur; humillimi quique, ubi alia accesserimus, Superbia & Ambitione fumus immodici.
units.tr: Here, before what is praiseworthy, how great a mass of disgraces do many build up! A strange hunger for popular applause possesses us, and we are carried headlong by the greed for fame; the humblest of men, when other vices have joined them, swell immoderately with pride and ambition.

units.la: Hic alij pallent ex studijs; alij res fugiunt laboriosas, & præter propter vitam vivunt; otioque & desidia torpent, indigentes nasturtio.
units.tr: Here some grow pale over their studies; others shun laborious tasks and live a life that is somewhat just getting by, and are numbed by idleness and sloth, lacking even cress.

units.la: Hic Animis fidunt homines, hic Annis; adgenitamque Infirmitatem non agnoscentes, obcæcati sibi blandiuntur, suaque admirantur; Dotes Animi Corporisque, Sapientiam, Potentiam, Doctrinam, Formam, Fortunam, tamquam perpetuas sibi & proprias, arroganti persuasione magni pendunt; majoresque, quam revera sunt, somniant: alios, quibus (ut quidem oculis judicioque sæpe fallentibus videtur) talia negata, despicientes.
units.tr: Here men trust in their minds, here in their years; not recognising the infirmity that clings to them, blinded, they flatter themselves and admire their own qualities. They esteem highly, with an arrogant conviction, the gifts of mind and body, wisdom, power, learning, beauty, fortune, as though they were perpetual and their own; they dream them to be greater than they really are, and despise others to whom such things are denied (as, indeed, the eyes and judgement often deceive, it seems so).

units.la: Hic quidquid humile, quidquid modestum in Verbis, Gestu, quacumque Actione detestati, cristas plerique tollunt, fastu superbiunt, scurrantur, inepte semper nescio quid grave secum cornicantur, ampullas & sesquipedalia projiciunt verba.
units.tr: Here most men spurn whatever is humble or modest in words, gesture or any conduct; they raise their crests, swell with haughtiness, play the buffoon, and always foolishly bluster with some solemnity they do not understand, and throw out bombastic and long-winded words.

units.la: Hic, quum Gulæ numquam satis, Temperantiam plerique ridentes, insana luxuria palatis ad fastidium usque multa Ferculorum genera, multaque Obsoniorum instrumenta & condimenta conquirunt, & in Ebrietatis castris nomina profitentur; diligentem Voracitati, Crapulæ, Heluationi, curandæque Cuti daturi operam, & omni Luxuriæ Corpora mancipaturi.
units.tr: Here, since the throat is never satisfied, many, mocking temperance, seek out with insane luxury, for their palates to the point of disgust, many kinds of dishes, many implements and seasonings for delicacies, and in the camps of drunkenness they profess their names, giving their bodies wholly over to gluttony, excess, indulgence, and care for the skin, and to every kind of luxury.

units.la: Hic Castitatem, cum communem, tum conjugalem, exosi, blandas & perniciosas æstimant magni Pestes; vagas spurcasque sectantur Libidines; Adulteria committunt: Stupris sese contaminant, infra Pecudum conditionem dejecti; ab Incestu non abhorrent, obscænis sermonibus aliorum aures offendunt: quamvis ad summa divinaque nati, in tota tamen vita molles & voluptuarij; &, verbo dicam, nihili, toti luxu diffluentes, omnis amentiæ socij, omniumque scelerum mancipia; in quorum animos, ut in cœnosam cloacam, omnia prorsus confluxerunt flagitia.
units.tr: Here they hate chastity, both general and conjugal, and consider it a pernicious and seductive plague of great magnitude; they pursue vagrant and filthy lusts; they commit adulteries; they defile themselves with debaucheries, cast down below the condition of beasts; they do not shrink from incest, and offend the ears of others with obscene talk. Though born for the highest and most divine things, they are nevertheless soft and voluptuous through their whole life; and, to say it in a word, they are worthless, dissolved in complete luxury, companions of every madness and slaves of every crime, into whose minds, as into a muddy sewer, all shameful acts have flowed together.

units.la: Hic, ut multa paucis complectar, novissimam jam Mundi videmus ætatem, Virtutum sterilem, Vitiorum fœcundam: ideoque Beatus in hoc puncto, qui hoc agit, ut bene dicat, agat, sapiat; qui vivit, ut post vivat, Seipsum superans, contemnens Solum, Cælum suspiciens: Beatus, cui, Sorte sua contento, edoctoque Castitatem periclitari in Delicijs, in divitijs Humilitatem, Pietatem in multis Negocijs, in Loquacitate Veritatem, Virtutes omnes in hoc nequam Seculo, cui, inquam, magnus ille Deus suus Deus, in quo, cum quo Uno Omnia; cui persuasum, non esse, quaeundum, nisi per Christum; non esse, quo eumdum nisi ad Christum: Beatus denique, cui, Socias Vitæ Virtutes, Gloriam autem Mortis nacto Comitem bono jure cum Synesio datum exclamare: Τί γὰρ ἄλκα, τί δὲ Κάλλος, Τί δὲ Χρυσὸς, τί δὲ Φάμα, Βασιλῆοί τε Τιμαί, Παρὰ τᾶς ΘΕΟΥ μεφίμνας; Ο᾽ μὲν ἵππων ἀὶ δρώκει. Ο᾽ δὲ πῆχυν ἀὶ πλαίνοι, Ο᾽ δὲ ἡμέρα Φυλάσσων Κτεάνων, χρύσιον ὄλβον. Ἐ᾽πρῶ δ᾽ ἀχάλμα χαίτη Καλλιμένη Τενόντων. Πολύυμνος δίκεν εἴη Παρὰ κύρεις, παρὰ κύρεις, Ἀμαρύγματα
units.tr: Here, to embrace many things in few words, we see the last age of the world now, sterile of virtues and fertile of vices. Therefore blessed in this situation is the one who takes care to speak, act and be wise well; who lives so that he may live afterwards, surpassing himself, despising the earth alone, looking up to heaven. Blessed is he who, content with his lot, and taught that chastity is endangered by delights, humility by riches, piety by many businesses, and truth by loquacity, holds all the virtues in this worthless age; to whom, I say, that great God is his God, in whom and with whom is all things, to whom it has been persuaded that one must not go, except through Christ, nor go anywhere except to Christ. Finally, blessed is he who, having obtained the virtues as companions of life and glory of death as his comrade, may rightly exclaim with Synesius: "For what is strength, what is beauty, what is gold, what is fame, and royal honours, apart from the favour of God? The one rejoices in horses, the other in ships, another in guarding his stores and golden wealth; ... [Τί γὰρ ἄλκα, τί δὲ Κάλλος, Τί δὲ Χρυσὸς, τί δὲ Φάμα, Βασιλῆοί τε Τιμαί, Παρὰ τᾶς ΘΕΟΥ μεφίμνας; Ο᾽ μὲν ἵππων ἀὶ δρώκει. Ο᾽ δὲ πῆχυν ἀὶ πλαίνοι, Ο᾽ δὲ ἡμέρα Φυλάσσων Κτεάνων, χρύσιον ὄλβον.]

units.la: Α᾽μαϱύγμαοι ꞷεσοϣ́πων· Ε᾽μὲ δ᾽ ἀψόφητον ἐὴ Βιοτὴν ἄσημον ἴλαχεν, Τὰ μὲν εἰς ἄλλας ἄσημον, Τὰ δὲ πεὸς ΘΕΟΝ εἰδότα.
units.tr: Glimmerings of ... But me [the god] has allotted an unnoticed and obscure life: some things belong to others, obscure, but some things are directed toward God, knowing [Ἀμαρύγματα ... Ἐμὲ δ' ἀψόφητον ἐᾶ βιοτὰν ἄσημον ἴλαχεν, τὰ μὲν εἰς ἄλλας ἄσημον, τὰ δὲ πρὸς θεὸν εἰδότα].

units.la: CAP. XVII. De Circulis.
units.tr: CAP. XVII. On Circles.

units.la: SIc finis esto tandem ijs, quæ Terræ consentiunt, vel absolute, per Causas: vel quodam modo, per Subjectum & Adjunctum: offerunt se, Methodo flagitante, Dissentanea, quæ duplicem Terræ pandunt Divisionem; priorem, Adjunctorum respectu; posteriorem, Partium. Adjuncta voco, quæ Terræ accidunt ratione vel Superiorum, vel inferiorum: Partes vero, partim Continentem Hemisphærij, intermedio primo Meridiano, tam Eoi, quam Occidui; partim Insulas, & Oceani & Maris Mediterranei. Respectu Superiorum Terra dividitur in Circulos.
units.tr: So let there at last be an end to those matters which concern the Earth, whether absolutely, through causes, or in some manner, through subject and adjunct. As method requires, the matters that follow present themselves, and these open up a twofold division of the Earth: the first with respect to its adjuncts, the second with respect to its parts. I call adjuncts those things which belong to the Earth by reason of either the superior or the inferior things. The parts are partly the continent of each hemisphere, with the first meridian lying between, both eastern and western; partly the islands, both of the ocean and of the Mediterranean Sea. With respect to the superior things, the Earth is divided into circles.

units.la: Hos si quis, ut cl. v. Rudolphus Snellius judicat, Animam Geographiæ vocitarit, nihil aberraverit à Vero. Ab his enim, tamquam primis principijs, quidquid est Geographiæ dependet. Sine his Errorem perpetuo trahit comitem aliosque in crassas & fallaces præcipitabit tenebras, quicumque delineare Terram, ejusque Partes, Partiumque Partes aggreditur. Hinc ortæ Refutationes & Disputationes cum aliorum, tum Strabonis, Plinij, Ptolemæi contra Eratosthenem, Megasthenem, Hipparchum, Marinum, Posidonium, aliosque veteres Geographos: quorum quidam in Longitudine, quidam in Latitudine, nonnulli in utraque describenda turpiter sunt hallacinati.
units.tr: If anyone, as the most learned Rudolphus Snellius judges, should call these the soul of Geography, he would hardly stray from the truth. For everything in Geography depends upon them as its first principles. Whoever sets out to map the Earth, its parts, and the parts of its parts, without them will always drag error along as a companion, and will plunge himself into thick and deceptive darkness. Hence arose the refutations and disputes, both of others and of Strabo, Pliny and Ptolemy, against Eratosthenes, Megasthenes, Hipparchus, Marinus, Posidonius and other ancient geographers. Some of these were shamefully mistaken in describing longitude, some in latitude, and some in describing both.

units.la: Astronomos autem imitantur in Circulorum notatione Geographi. Quibus enim illi Corpus Cœli finitum quidem, sed infiniti simile, distinguunt Circulis; ijsdem etiam hi Terram. Illi, media inter Mundi Polos regione, Circulum ducunt, quem Sol Æquinoctij die suo motu notat; duobus deinde alijs Zodiaci λοξότης terminant, eosque Tropicos vocant, quod illic Solis fiant Conversiones: idem faciunt in Terra Geographi; quod, quo tempore Sol in ea incidit loca, nullam faciat Umbram. Astronomi Meridianis & Finientibus Cœlum redimitum fingunt propter Ortus & Occasus Siderum, item ad Diem Noctiumque Medietatem diffiniendam: idem multo majore jure potuerunt Geographi. Nam in Cœlo nec Dies, neque Nox; sicque nec Ortus neque Occasus: accidunt autem quæ dixi Terræ, Corpori denso & opaco, quodque lucido oppositum Umbram projicit. Ad Molem igitur Terræ suas in Partes diducendam, Cœli Circulis fuit opus; quos ab Astronomis sumunt Geographi, suisque Terræ Dimensionibus adplicant.
units.tr: Geographers, moreover, imitate the astronomers in marking the circles. Just as the astronomers divide the body of the heavens, which is finite yet resembles the infinite, by circles, so too do the geographers divide the Earth. The astronomers draw a circle in the middle region between the poles of the world, which the Sun marks by its own motion on the day of the equinox; then they bound it on either side by the obliquity of the zodiac, and call these the tropics, because the turnings of the Sun take place there. Geographers do the same on the Earth, since at the time when the Sun falls upon those places it casts no shadow. The astronomers imagine the heaven girded with meridians and finite circles, on account of the risings and settings of the stars, and likewise to define the halving of day and night. Geographers could have done the same with much greater right. For in the heavens there is neither day nor night, and so neither rising nor setting; but the things I have mentioned happen to the Earth, a dense and opaque body, which casts a shadow opposite to the luminous one. Therefore, to divide the mass of the Earth into its parts, circles of the heavens were needed; geographers take these from the astronomers and apply them to their own measurements of the Earth.

units.la: Circulum autem quemque in cccLx, Partes; Partem porro quamlibet in lx. Scrupula partiri solent: numeris istis delectati, quod multas exactas caperent Divisiones, & ad quamplurimos essent compositi, ideoque cum illis ad primos reduci possent: quod magno sæpe compendio & emolumento numerantibus.
units.tr: Each circle is usually divided into 360 parts, and each part further into 60 minutes. They were delighted with these numbers because they admit many exact divisions and are composed for the most part so that they can be reduced to the first numbers, which is often a great saving and advantage to those who count.

units.la: Denique ex Circulis, Circulorumque segmentis, Anticipationes Ortuum & Occasuum, Longiorum Contractiorumque Dierum Æstivorum Hibernorumque dependent: quæ discrimina pro segmentis Circulorum Horis diffiniuntur.
units.tr: Finally, the anticipations of risings and settings, and the longer and shorter summer and winter days, depend upon the circles and their segments; and these differences are defined in hours according to the segments of the circles.

units.la: De Circulis quædam dicam separatim, quædam junctim. Separatim inquam. Nam Circulorum alij ad Æquatorem sunt Paralleli, alij in Polis se secantes: Illi Longitudinis, μήκυς; hi Latitudinis, πλάτυς appellantur. Nomina hæc placuerunt; quod, ut in sequentibus parebit, plus Terrarum Veteribus cognitum esset inter Occasum & Ortum, quam inter Meridiem & Septemtrionem. Ibi enim Gradus numerabant cLxxvii; hic vero lxx. Pertinet huc Strabonis locus lib. ii: ἐκ τῆς λόγῳ τ᾽ Παραλλήλων τῶν πεὸς τ᾽ ἰσημερινὸν δῆλον, ὡς πλέον ἡ διπλασίον ἐστι τῆς πλάτυς τὸ μῆκος, &c. Ex aliorum deinde sententia, confirmandis quæ dixerat, Chlamydi Terram comparat: Λέγεται δὲ ἡ γῆ χλαμυδοειδῆς, inquit, τὸ σχῆμα· πολλῇ γὰρ σωαγωγῇ τῆς πλάτυς πεὸς τῆς ἄκρους διέχοντα, ἡ μάλιστα τῆς Εὐσεβείας, τὸ καθ᾽ ἕκαστον ἐπιον τῶν ἡμῶν. Manent hodie
units.tr: I shall speak about the circles partly separately and partly together; separately, I say, for some of the circles are parallel to the equator, while others intersect at the poles. The former are called longitude (μήκυς), the latter latitude (πλάτυς). These names were chosen because, as will appear below, the ancients knew more of the lands between west and east than between south and north: for there they counted 177 degrees, but here only 70. Strabo's passage in book ii pertains here: "From the ratio of the parallels to the equator it is clear that the length is more than double the breadth, &c." [ἐκ τῆς λόγῳ τ᾽ Παραλλήλων τῶν πεὸς τ᾽ ἰσημερινὸν δῆλον, ὡς πλέον ἡ διπλασίον ἐστι τῆς πλάτυς τὸ μῆκος, &c.] Then, to confirm what he had said, drawing on the opinions of others, he compares the Earth to a cloak: "The Earth is said," he says, "to be cloak-shaped in form; for it stretches far in length, and narrows greatly in breadth toward the extremities, and this is most of all so in each of the inhabited parts." [Λέγεται δὲ ἡ γῆ χλαμυδοειδῆς, inquit, τὸ σχῆμα· πολλῇ γὰρ σωαγωγῇ τῆς πλάτυς πεὸς τῆς ἄκρους διέχοντα, ἡ μάλιστα τῆς Εὐσεβείας, τὸ καθ᾽ ἕκαστον ἐπιον τῶν ἡμῶν.] These names remain today, although on either side there are equally 360 degrees, for this terrestrial globe is round.

units.la: P Nomina, quamvis æqualitas utrimque Graduum ccclx. Rotundus enim terrenus hic Globus. Præmissis igitur quibusdam de Circulorum natura spectalioribus; mox de ijs junctim agam, & loca dimetiendi rationem aperiam.
units.tr: Names remain. Having therefore first set out certain more notable matters about the nature of the circles, I shall next treat of them together and explain the manner of measuring places.

units.la: CAP. XVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVIII.

units.la: De Circulis Longitudinis.
units.tr: On the Circles of Longitude.

units.la: LONGITVDO Terræ inter Ortum est & Occasum porrecta: quam Ptolemæus lib. 1. cap. xii, habitatæ Terræ graduum esse scribit 177-15. Nam ab Insulis Fortunatis (ubi hodieque Longitudinis principium ex Veterum mente, qui ultra has vastum & perpetuum mare imaginabantur; nullas reperiri amplius Insulas, aut sicubi essent, desertas tamen rati) ad Euphratem usque notat 72-0; ab Euphrate autem ad Seram 105-½: Hodie, prolatis pomœriis, Longitudinis spacium gradus complectitur 180: qui ab infero Hemisphærio & peregrino, ut Manilius vocat, orbe duplicati Terræ circuitum ostendunt graduum esse 360; qui per 15 multiplicati terrenæ molis ambitum edunt Germanicorum Milliar. 5400, ut antea dixi.
units.tr: Longitude is the extent of the earth from east to west. Ptolemy, book 1, chapter 12, writes that the inhabited earth has 177-15 degrees of it. For from the Fortunate Islands (where even today the reckoning of longitude begins, following the view of the ancients, who imagined that beyond these lay a vast and endless sea, and who thought that no islands were found there any more, or if there were any, that they were deserted) he reckons 72-0 degrees to the Euphrates, and from the Euphrates to the Seres 105-½. Today, with the boundaries pushed outward, the extent of longitude takes in 180 degrees. Those who measure the circuit of the earth by the lower hemisphere and the distant world, as Manilius calls it, double the earth's circuit and show that it has 360 degrees. Multiplying these by 15 gives the circumference of the earth's mass as 5400 German miles, as I said before.

units.la: Longitudinem Æquinoctiali aut Circulo ad Æquinoctialem parallelo mensus est Ptolemæus, & sequuti illum alij; initio sumto ab Insulis, quas jam nominavi, quæque hodie Canariæ dicuntur ab una omnes, progressu autem facto versus extrema Indiæ Orientalis. Rationes vero, quod ab Occasu Longitudinem inchoarint Ortum versus variæ: inter quas principis loci duæ: prior, quod Occidentaliores Terræ partes, partim Herculis (fertur enim hoc) expeditione; partim Phœnicum navigationibus habuerint magis exploratas; Facilis enim erat navigatio per Mare Magnum Gades usque, ab Gadibus autem in vastum Oceanum: posterior, quod Planetarum hic esset motus, hoc est, ab Occasu in Ortum & Cardinem oppositum; in primis Solis & Lunæ, quorum Defectus indices sunt Longitudinis. Quum enim Eclipsis una eademque omnibus cernatur populis eodem momento: tamen non omnibus eadem est ab Ortu & Occasu. Lunæ Defectus qui apud Arbela hora noctis v, visus est Karthagine ii. Solis autem, qui in Armenia inter horam diei x & xi, in Campania inter vii & viii conspectus: quod fieri nullo modo potuisset, si locis nominatis eadem fuisset longitudo, & æqualis ab Ortu vel Occasu distantia. Cognita autem Horarum Differentia, quam Subductione non difficile est indagare, Longitudo inter ea Loca, ubi Defectus notati sunt & observari negocio facili, Proportionis Geometricæ regula poterit inveniri. Nam quum Æquinoctialis (cui Partes sunt, ut dixi, 360) mensura sit diei, qui ex xxiv constat horis: si 360 dividantur per 24 quorum dabunt 15 partes Æquinoctialis, quibus unam horam metimur. Loca igitur, quorum differentia hora una, distant partibus quindecim; quorum duæ, dissident triginta; quorum denique tres horæ, ut in exemplo de Karthagine & Arbelis, abeunt inter se gradibus quadragintaquinque; & sic de aliis dicendum. Iam si Horis horaria cohæreant Scrupula: quatuor unum constituunt gradum; si plura, si pauciora, Proportio rem expedit. Porro Partes etiam ad Horas, contraria via, itidem Proportione, solent redigi, ut lib. vi. cap. 1. Ptolemæus Arbelæ Longitudinem 80-0 esse prodidit, Karthaginis vero, lib. iiii. cap. iii, 34-50: differentia est 36-10: dicendum igitur quindecim Partes esse mensuram unius Horæ; ergo 36 ½ esse horas 2 ½, id est 2-24'-4 0.
units.tr: Ptolemy measured longitude along the equinoctial, or along a circle parallel to the equinoctial, and others after him did the same. They began from the islands I have just named, which are now all called the Canaries together, and proceeded toward the far parts of East India. The reasons why they began longitude in the west and counted eastward differ. Among them two are the principal ones. The first is that the western parts of the earth were better explored, partly through Hercules' expedition (as is said) and partly through the voyages of the Phoenicians; for navigation through the Mediterranean as far as Gades was easy, and from Gades out into the vast Ocean. The second is that the motion of the planets runs this way, that is from west to east, and the opposite pole; especially that of the Sun and Moon, whose eclipses are the signs of longitude. For although one and the same eclipse is seen by all peoples at the same moment, yet it is not the same for all from east and west. The eclipse of the Moon, seen at Arbela at the fifth hour of the night, was seen at Carthage at the second. The eclipse of the Sun, seen in Armenia between the tenth and eleventh hours of the day, and in Campania between the seventh and eighth, could in no way have happened if the named places had the same longitude and an equal distance east or west. Once the difference in hours is known, which is not hard to work out by subtraction, and the times of the eclipses at those places are observed without much difficulty, the longitude between those places can be found by the rule of geometric proportion. For since the equinoctial (whose parts are, as I said, 360) is the measure of the day, which consists of 24 hours, dividing 360 by 24 gives 15 parts of the equinoctial, by which we measure one hour. Places whose difference is one hour are therefore 15 degrees apart; those two hours apart are 30 degrees apart; and those three hours apart, as in the example of Carthage and Arbela, are 45 degrees apart; and the same is to be said of others. Now if scruples are attached to the hours, four make one degree; if there are more or fewer, proportion settles the matter. Conversely, degrees are also reduced to hours, by the same proportion, as in book 6, chapter 1. Ptolemy gave the longitude of Arbela as 80-0, and that of Carthage, in book 4, chapter 3, as 34-50. The difference is 36-10. So, taking fifteen degrees as the measure of one hour, 36½ degrees make 2½ hours, that is 2-24'-40".

units.la: Partes Maioris Circuli diffinivit Eratosthenes 697 ⅓ stadijs, pro quibus vulgo usurpant 700 Stadia. Quum enim, ut ejus hac de re mentem explicat Cleomedes, Alexandriæ Latitudo deprehenderetur 31-0; Syenes vero 23-50. (urbes hæ postillimum placuerunt; quod quamproxime ejusdem essent Longitudinis: Differentia enim 1 grad. 30. minut.) at Viatores hoc terrestre Intervallum 5000 stadijs fuisse dimensi: conclusit Philosophus: Si 7-12 (hæc enim Latitudinis differentia) sunt 5000 Stadia; ergo totus Ambitus Terræ, hoc est 360 Partes sunt 250000 Stadiorum; singulæ vero 694 ⅓. Et hæc quidem Eratosthenis ratio (ut, quod res est, fateamur) laudanda plurimum. Primus enim Terræ Ambitum diffinire, & Circuli Partes ad Terrestria spacia adcommodare fuit conatus: non tamen quod sequutus est, est, consequutus fuit visus Posterioribus. Sed numquam quid inventum & perfectum simul. Artibus sua sunt Initia & Incrementa, Aetas adulta, Senium. Successit enim Posidonius: qui, Terram eadem ratione, sed inter alia mensus loca, maximum Orbis Ambitum 240000 Stadiis definivit hoc modo. Canopum (qui, ut libro II. dixi, Veteribus Ἀ᾽φ᾽ ... ) & Rhodi & Alexandriae observavit, quum motu Mundi ad Meridianum devectus esset: Hic Rhodi quidem Horizontem tangens tantummodo, statim vertigine Mundi abripitur; (...) Alexandriae vero ad Signi quadrantem (...) altus conspicitur sub Meridiano Circulo: at Intervallum inter Rhodum & Alexandriam ex communi opinione 5000 habetur Stadiorum: Quum igitur omnes Circuli similes sint, si ex Terrae Centro duas rectas educi singamus, alteram per Canopum in Rhodo, alteram per eundem in Alexandria; segmentum terrestris Circuli se habebit ad suum Totum, quemadmodum Pars Coelestis: at segmentum 7½ est 1/V Totius, ut constat Divisione Partium 360 per 7½; erit igitur & Intervallum Terrestre 5000 Stadia inter Rhodum & Alexandriam; itidem 1/V ambitus terrestris: totusque Ambitus Stadiorum 240000. Ptolemaeus denique lib. I. cap. III, quum aliquid in Hipparcho, Eratosthene, Posidonio desideraret, per Astrolabia & ... Polorum ... & Eclipses diversis locis exactius observavit; observatas contulit, & per Geometricam doctrinam Triangulorum ... Latitudines & Longitudines, emendavit; tandemque per rectissima quam potuit itinera deprehendit, unam partem 500; universum autem Ambitum 180000 Stadijs definiri. Et haec quidem Aequinoctialis terrestris Mensura est. Longitudines autem non solo Aequinoctiali; sed etiam ... ad Aequinoctialem parallelis metiri solemus: ut in ijs locis, quae ab Aequinoctiali alterum Polorum versus vergunt. Quum autem Terra propter figuram rotundam & globosam, quae sibi ubique similis, paullatim à medio Polos versus artatur & contrahitur; necesse est, ipsas quoque ... artari & imminui: quumque omnes in 360 Partes distinguantur, Partes etiam singulae pro ratione Circulorum solent minui. Geographi igitur Tabulam Geometricis rationibus & demonstrationibus efformarunt huiusmodi:
units.tr: Eratosthenes defined the parts of the greatest circle as 697⅓ stadia, for which 700 stadia is commonly used. For when, as Cleomedes explains his view on this matter, the latitude of Alexandria was found to be 31-0, and that of Syene 23-50 (these cities were chosen most of all because they lie almost on the same longitude, the difference being 1 degree 30 minutes), and travellers had measured this land distance as 5000 stadia, the philosopher concluded: if 7-12 (for this is the difference of latitude) are 5000 stadia, then the whole circuit of the earth, that is 360 parts, is 250000 stadia, and each part is 694⅓. Indeed, this is Eratosthenes' reasoning, which (to confess the truth) deserves great praise. For he was the first to try to define the circuit of the earth and to fit the parts of the circle to earthly distances. Yet what he attempted was not what later writers achieved. But nothing is ever at once discovered and perfected. Arts have their beginnings and growth, their mature age and their old age. For Posidonius succeeded him; he measured the earth by the same method, but among other places, and fixed the greatest circuit of the globe at 240000 stadia in the following way. He observed Canopus (which, as I said in book 2, the ancients...) at Rhodes and at Alexandria, when it had been carried by the motion of the world to the meridian. At Rhodes it merely touched the horizon and was at once swept away by the rotation of the world; but at Alexandria it was seen high, at a quadrant of the sign, under the meridian circle. The distance between Rhodes and Alexandria, by common opinion, is held to be 5000 stadia. Since therefore all circles are similar, if we imagine two straight lines drawn from the centre of the earth, one through Canopus at Rhodes and the other through the same star at Alexandria, the segment of the terrestrial circle will bear the same relation to its whole as the celestial part does: and the segment of 7½ is 1/V of the whole, as is clear from dividing the 360 parts by 7½. So the terrestrial distance between Rhodes and Alexandria will also be 5000 stadia, and likewise 1/V of the terrestrial circuit; and the whole circuit will be 240000 stadia. Finally, Ptolemy, book 1, chapter 3, since he found something lacking in Hipparchus, Eratosthenes and Posidonius, observed the poles and eclipses at various places more exactly with astrolabes ..., compared his observations, and by the geometrical doctrine of triangles corrected the latitudes and longitudes. At last, by the most direct routes he could find, he determined one part as 500 stadia and the whole circuit as 180000 stadia. This is the measure of the terrestrial equinoctial. We usually measure longitudes not only along the equinoctial, but also along parallels to the equinoctial, in those places which tend toward one or the other pole from the equinoctial. Since the earth, on account of its round and globular figure, which is everywhere like itself, gradually narrows and contracts from the middle toward the poles, it is necessary that these parallels too be narrowed and diminished. And since all are divided into 360 parts, the individual parts also are usually reduced in proportion to the circles. Geographers therefore drew up a table of this kind, using geometrical rules and demonstrations:

units.la: Tabula exhibens quot Germanica Milliaria, nimirum XXXII. Stadiorum, singulis 360 Partibus Circulorum Longitudinis, & ad Aequinoctialem parallelis, respondeant:
units.tr: A table showing how many German miles, namely 32 stadia each, correspond to each of the 360 degrees of longitude, along the parallels to the Equator:

units.la: Graduus | Milliar. | Stadior. (table of degrees, miles and stadia, columns of Roman numerals and Arabic numbers, reproduced as printed in the table below)
units.tr: Degree | Miles | Stadia (table of degrees, miles and stadia, columns of Roman numerals and Arabic numbers, reproduced as printed in the table below)

units.la: CAP. XIX.
units.tr: CAP. XIX.

units.la: De Latitudinis Circulis.
units.tr: On the Circles of Latitude.

units.la: TERRÆ Longitudinem explicavi: Latitudinem voco, quæ inter Æquinoctialem & Mundi Vertices porrecta: quam Ptolemæus versus Septemtrionem ad lxiii. usque gradum extendit; termino in Thule Insula, quæ fuit ultima cognitarum Veteribus ad Boream Terrarum, constituto; versus Meridiem autem ad gradum usque xvii, præfixo termino in Prasso, Agysimbæ Æthiopum regionis Promontorio; ideoque tota Terræ Latitudo Veteribus visa fuit graduum lxxx, hoc est Milliar. cıɔ cc. Prorogarunt hæc Pomœria centum ab hinc annis quoquovorsum: illuc quidem, ultra Æquinoctialem, ad gradum lv, ubi Fretum Magellanicum, Lusitani & Castellani: huc vero, citra Æquatorem, Franci, Angli, & nuperrime summa cum gloria, evecti ad lxxxi. Altitudinis gradum quodque excurrebat, Batavi.
units.tr: I have explained the length of the earth. Latitude I call the extent running between the Equinoctial and the poles of the world. Ptolemy extends it northward to the 63rd degree, taking as the limit the island of Thule, which was the furthest northern land known to the ancients. Southward he extends it only to the 17th degree, with the limit set at Prasum, a promontory of the Ethiopian region of Agysimba. So the whole latitude of the earth seemed to the ancients to be 80 degrees, that is, 1200 miles. In the last hundred years these boundaries have been pushed out on every side. To the south, beyond the Equinoctial, the Portuguese and Spanish, sailing to the Strait of Magellan, reached the 55th degree. To the north, on this side of the equator, the French and English, and most recently the Dutch, with great glory, have reached the 81st degree of altitude.

units.la: Quia vero gradu Latitudinis Australis lv, pernavigantibus Fretum, quod dixi, ad sinistram sese vasta aperuerit Terra, quæ hodieque incognita; compertumque satis sit Nostratium Navigationibus, ultra gradum Latitudinis Borealis lxxxi. vastum adhuc sese pandere Pelagus; non male cum Recentioribus Terræ Latitudinem finiemus ad utrumque Polum, gradu xc; qui numerus per Quaternarium multiplicatus Factum dabit ccclx, si Latitudo spectetur, gradus: quibus per xv auctis provenient Germanica 5400: siccque Latitudine Longitudineque æqualibus; certum erit, quod monui sæpe, Terrenam hanc molem esse plane rotundam.
units.tr: But since the vast land opened up to the left of those sailing through the strait I mentioned, at the 55th degree of southern latitude, and that land is still unknown today, and since it is well enough established by the voyages of our countrymen that beyond the 81st degree of northern latitude a vast sea still stretches out, we shall not be wrong, with the more recent writers, to set the latitude of the earth at 90 degrees to each pole. This number multiplied by four gives 360 degrees of latitude, and if these are multiplied by 15 they come to 5400 German miles. Thus, with latitude and longitude equal, it will be certain, as I have often said, that this earthly mass is perfectly round.

units.la: Quemadmodum autem Longitudinis initium sumitur ab Meridiano per Fortunatas ducto; numeratur tamen in Æquinoctiali & Circulis illi Parallelis: sic Latitudo ab Æquinoctiali numeratur in Meridiano.
units.tr: Just as the starting point of longitude is taken from the meridian drawn through the Fortunate Isles, yet it is counted along the Equinoctial and the circles parallel to it, so latitude is counted from the Equinoctial along a meridian.

units.la: Est itaque Latitudo segmentum Meridiani, quod inter Æquatorem & Punctum Verticale; ἐπιθέτων κατὰ κορυφὴν vocant Græci Scriptores. Est autem tanta cuiusque loci Latitudo, quanta Poli Altitudo; ut Vnius, notitia sit utriusque. Vt autem Solis Lunæque Defectus Longitudinis, ita Poli ἔξαρμα Latitudinis est index. Ἐξαρμα Poli variis modis indagari potest: partim Stellarum observatione, Solisque Æquinoctiali, vel etiam Solstitiali, aut Brumali Meridie; partim ex Vmbris Meridianis. Quæ enim loca umbras habent æquales, æqualiter ab Aequinoctiali distant. Οὐ λόγον ὑφηκε, inquit Strabo lib. i. de Eratosthene, τῷ ἐν μεσημβρίᾳ γνώμονες πρὸς τὴν σκιὰν, τὴν αὐτὴν καὶ ἴσην πρὸς τὴν ὁμοίαν καιρὸν ἔχειν ἐν τῇ Βυζαντίῳ Φησίν. Massilia igitur & Bizantium æque ab Aequinoctiali distant: unde & Ptolemæus Massiliæ & Bizantio latitudinis Partes 43-6 attribuit, huic cap. xi. libri iii, illi cap. x. libri ii. Quibus porro inæquales sunt Vmbræ, dissident ab Aequinoctiali inæqualiter; majores Vmbræ Altiorem, Minores Humiliorem habent Polum. Strabo in fine libri ii: Ἐν τῇ Ἀλεξανδρείᾳ ὁ γνώμων λόγον ἔχει πρὸς τὴν ἰσημερινὴν σκιὰν, ὃν ἔχει τὰ πίντ πρὸς ἴπΓ (Vitruvius tamen lib. ix. cap. viii. 5 ad 3) Καρχηδόνι δὲ τοπώποροι σίσι χιλίοις καὶ τρισαχοσίοις σταδίοις, καὶ Ἀλεξανδρείας δὲ τοπώποροι. ἔπειρ ἐν Καρχηδόνι ὁ γνώμων λόγον ἔχει πρὸς τὴν ἰσημερινὴν σκιὰν, ὃν ἔχει τὰ ἑνδεκα πρὸς τὰ ἴπΓ. Sic in Rhodo rationem habet Vmbilicus (sic enim vocat Plinius lib. vi. cap. ult. & alibi) ad umbram Aequinoctialem; quam habent 7 ad 5: Tarenti; quam 11 ad 9: Romæ; quam 9 ad 8: Anconæ; quam 36 ad 35: Venetijs æquatur Gnomoni: apud Nos paullo major, quam 10 ad 13: cæterisque locis omnibus aliæ alio modo Vmbræ Gnomonum Aequinoctiales inveniuntur disparatæ.
units.tr: Latitude is therefore the segment of the meridian lying between the equator and the point overhead, which the Greek writers call the zenith [ἐπιθέτων κατὰ κορυφὴν]. The latitude of each place is exactly as great as the height of the pole there, so that knowing the one gives knowledge of the other. Just as eclipses of the sun and moon are an indication of longitude, so the elevation of the pole is an indication of latitude. The elevation of the pole can be investigated in various ways: partly by observing the stars, or the sun at the equinox, or at midday at the solstice or the winter solstice; partly from meridian shadows. For places whose shadows are equal are equally distant from the Equinoctial. Strabo, in book 1, on Eratosthenes, says that Eratosthenes did not state that gnomons at midday cast shadows that have the same ratio and are equal at the same time at Byzantium [Οὐ λόγον ὑφηκε ... τῷ ἐν μεσημβρίᾳ γνώμονες πρὸς τὴν σκιὰν, τὴν αὐτὴν καὶ ἴσην πρὸς τὴν ὁμοίαν καιρὸν ἔχειν ἐν τῇ Βυζαντίῳ Φησίν]. Therefore Marseille and Byzantium are equally distant from the Equinoctial. Hence Ptolemy also assigns to Marseille and to Byzantium 43 degrees 6 minutes of latitude: the former in chapter 11 of book 3, the latter in chapter 10 of book 2. Where the shadows are unequal, places differ from the Equinoctial unequally: larger shadows indicate a higher pole, smaller shadows a lower one. Strabo, at the end of book 2: at Alexandria the gnomon has to the equinoctial shadow the ratio which the 5 parts have to the 3 [Ἐν τῇ Ἀλεξανδρείᾳ ὁ γνώμων λόγον ἔχει πρὸς τὴν ἰσημερινὴν σκιὰν, ὃν ἔχει τὰ πίντ πρὸς ἴπΓ] (though Vitruvius, book 9, chapter 8, gives 5 to 3). Carthage is 1300 stadia from Alexandria, and there the gnomon has to the equinoctial shadow the ratio which the 11 parts have to the 3 [Καρχηδόνι δὲ τοπώποροι σίσι χιλίοις καὶ τρισαχοσίοις σταδίοις, καὶ Ἀλεξανδρείας δὲ τοπώποροι. ἔπειρ ἐν Καρχηδόνι ὁ γνώμων λόγον ἔχει πρὸς τὴν ἰσημερινὴν σκιὰν, ὃν ἔχει τὰ ἑνδεκα πρὸς τὰ ἴπΓ]. Thus at Rhodes the navel (for Pliny calls it so in book 6, last chapter, and elsewhere) has to the equinoctial shadow the ratio 7 to 5; at Taranto, 11 to 9; at Rome, 9 to 8; at Ancona, 36 to 35; at Venice the gnomon equals the shadow; among us it is a little larger, about 10 to 13. In all other places the equinoctial shadows of gnomons are found to differ in other ways.

units.la: CAP. XX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XX.

units.la: De Locorum Dimensionibus.
units.tr: On the Dimensions of Places.

units.la: HÆc de Circulis separatim: flagitat ordo, ut quædam de ijs junctim dicam, & Locorum inde ducam Dimensiones. Loca, de quorum Intervallis est quæstio, vel versus eundem vergunt Polum: vel, Æquinoctiali intermedio, diversos; alter Borealem, Australem versus alter. Quæ eundem habent Polum; vel una Dimensione differunt, vel duplici. Una quidem, quum sola differunt vel Latitudine, vel Longitudine.
units.tr: So much for circles taken separately. The order of the subject requires that I now say something about them together, and from them derive the dimensions of places. Places whose distance from one another is in question either tend towards the same pole, or, lying on either side of the equinoctial, they are opposite, one towards the north and the other towards the south. Those that have the same pole differ either by one dimension or by two. They differ by one when they differ only in latitude or only in longitude.

units.la: In sola Latitudine discrepantibus, si Locorum, quæ proposita, Latitudo minor à majori fuerit subducta; Reliquus, Latitudinis est Differentia: quum autem Gradibus singulis respondeant Milliaria quindecim Germanica, quatuor vero Minutis Unum; Gradus Differentiæ per quindecim multiplicati, Minuta vero per quatuor divisa, numerum ostendunt Milliar. Germanicorum, & Distantiam Locorum quæsitam.
units.tr: For places that differ only in latitude: subtract the smaller of the proposed latitudes from the greater, and the remainder is the difference of latitude. Since fifteen German miles correspond to each single degree, and one mile to four minutes, multiply the degrees of the difference by fifteen and divide the minutes by four. The results show the number of German miles, that is, the sought distance between the places.

units.la: In ijs quæ sola differunt Longitudine; inventa, Subtractionis beneficio, Longitudinis Differentia, cum gradibus communis utrique loco Latitudinis ingrediundum ante omnia Tabulam, quæ, ut cap xrix vidimus, perscripta habet Milliaria Gradibus cœlestibus extra Æquinoctialem in proposita Latitudine respondentia. Deinde Gradus inibi oblatos (quos, docendi gratia, vocemus Inventum Prius) multiplicari necesse est per Differentiam Longitudinis. Si Gradibus communis Latitudinis Minuta, præsertim plura, adhæserint; milliaria sequentis Gradus ab Invento Priore sunt subtrahenda; Reliquum hic appellemus Inventum Posterius. Hinc veniendum ad Proportionum regulam; ubi primum numerum semper esse oportet 60; Medium semper Inventum Posterius, Tertium denique Minuta adhærentia: Productum ex Regula Proportionum à Priore Invento subtrahendum, Reliquum per Differentiam Longitudinis multiplicandum; Factus ostendet Distantiam quæsitam: ubi 60 Secunda unum Minutum, & 60 Minuta Milliare Germanicum unum constituunt.
units.tr: For places that differ only in longitude: first, by subtraction, find the difference of longitude. Then, with the degrees of the latitude that the two places share, one must first enter the table which, as we saw in chapter xix, lists the miles corresponding to celestial degrees away from the equinoctial at the given latitude. Next, the degrees found there (which, for the sake of teaching, we will call the First Finding) must be multiplied by the difference of longitude. If the minutes of the common latitude are attached to the degrees, especially a large number of them, the miles of the next degree must be subtracted from the First Finding; we will call the remainder the Second Finding. Here one must come to the rule of proportion, in which the first number must always be 60, the middle always the Second Finding, and the third the attached minutes. The product of the rule of proportion is to be subtracted from the First Finding, and the remainder multiplied by the difference of longitude. The result shows the distance sought, where 60 seconds make one minute and 60 minutes make one German mile.

units.la: Talis ratio dimetiendi loca, quæ una differunt dimensione, vel Latitudine, vel Longitudine: operosius paullo negocium hoc si duplici differunt, id est utraque. Hic subducenda Minor Latitudo à Maiore; Differentiæ dimidium Minori addendum; Totus ex illis Parallelus erit Longitudinis; cum quo Tabula Longitudinum consulenda; ubi se offerunt Milliaria uni Parti congruentia: Dehinc Numerus hic per se multiplicatus Factum edit Quadratum Longitudinis: Post Differentia Latitudinum multiplicanda per quindecim, & si scrupula adhæserint dividenda per quatuor: illic Factus; hic Quotus dabunt Milliara Latitudinis: Totus illorum erit Quadratum Basis; cuius radix ostendet Distantiam quæsitam.
units.tr: That is the method for measuring places that differ by one dimension, either latitude or longitude. This task is a little more laborious if they differ in both dimensions. Here the smaller latitude is subtracted from the greater, and half the difference is added to the smaller latitude; the whole of this gives the parallel of longitude, and with it the table of longitudes must be consulted, where the miles that agree with one part are found. Then this number multiplied by itself produces the square of the longitude. After that the difference of latitudes is multiplied by fifteen, and if there are scruples attached, they are divided by four. The former result and the latter quotient give the miles of latitude. The sum of these will be the square of the base, and its root will show the distance sought.

units.la: Iam si datorum Locorum alter Latitudinem habeat Borealem, alter Australem: inprimis quærenda utriusque Intervalli Differentia; Longitudinis quidem, Minore Longitudine subducta ex Majore; Latitudinis vero, coniuncta utriusque Loci Latitudine. Hic Situs considerandus; utrum Loca sint sita sub æqualibus, & quæ eodem spacio utrimque ab Æquarore distant Parallelis, an inæqualibus. Si æqualibus: in alterutro numeranda Longitudinis Differentia: sin inæqualibus; dimidium Latitudinis Majoris adpositum Minori Latitudini demonstrabit Parallelum; qui huic instituto aptus & idoneus. Cum eo Parallelo Gradus unius Gradui respondentes depromendi ex Tabula, cujus memini, reliquumque peragundum, ut in præcedentibus monui.
units.tr: Now, if one of the given places has north latitude and the other south latitude, first the difference of the two intervals must be sought: of longitude, by subtracting the smaller longitude from the greater; of latitude, by adding together the latitudes of the two places. Here the situation must be considered: whether the places lie under equal parallels, that is, at the same distance from the equator on either side, or under unequal ones. If equal, the difference of longitude is to be counted in either of them. If unequal, half of the greater latitude added to the smaller latitude will show the parallel which is suitable and fit for this purpose. With that parallel, the degrees corresponding to one degree are to be taken from the table I mentioned, and the rest carried out as I have said in the preceding sections.

units.la: Exempla singulorum, ne sim adscribendis ijs prolixior, sunt cum apud alios, tum Petrum Appianum, Caspar um Peucerum, Victorinum Strigelium.
units.tr: Examples of each, so that I do not run on too long in adding them, are to be found both in others and in Petrus Appianus, Caspar Peucer and Victorinus Strigelius.

units.la: Cap. XXI. De Amphiscijs, Heteroscijs, Periscijs.
units.tr: Chapter XXI. On the Amphiscians, Heteroscians and Periscians.

units.la: HÆc de Circulis, & Separatim & Iunctim, tam Latitudinis, quam Longitudinis: quos accidere dixi Terræ, ratione Superiorum, id est, Cœlestium: jam Inferiorum respectu, Terra dividitur in portiones & Majores, & Minores. In illas quidem, causa vel Umbræ, in Ἀμφισκίας, Ἑτεροσκίας & Περισκίας; vel Aeris Temperiei, in Zonas: in has autem, ob Horas variantes, in Climata.
units.tr: These things have been said about the circles, both separately and together, both of latitude and of longitude, which I said belong to the earth in relation to the superior things, that is, the heavenly bodies. Now, with respect to the inferior things, the earth is divided into portions, both larger and smaller. The larger portions are, on account of the shadow, called Amphiscians, Heteroscians and Periscians [Ἀμφισκίας, Ἑτεροσκίας, Περισκίας]; or, on account of the temperature of the air, Zones. The smaller portions, on account of the varying hours, are called Climates.

units.la: Ἀμφίσκια Terra dicitur, ubi Gnomones sive Umbilici Meridianam Umbram & Meridiem & Septemtrionem Versus projiciunt; illam, quum Sol decurrit Septemtrionale Zodiaci latus; hanc, quum Austrinum: tale Terræ spacium, quod duobus inclusum Tropicis.
units.tr: The land is called Amphiscian where the gnomons, or pointers, cast their meridian shadow both towards the south and towards the north: the former when the sun runs through the northern side of the zodiac, the latter when it runs through the southern side. Such a stretch of land is enclosed by the two tropics.

units.la: Ἑτεροσκία vocatur, ubi Gnomones alteram tantum Umbram meridie projiciunt: Septemtrionalem, ut apud Nos; Austrinum apud eos, qui ultra Brumalem Solis Cursum habitant: tale illud Terræ spacium, quod est à Tropicis usque ad LXVII. Parallelum.
units.tr: It is called Heteroscian where the gnomons cast only one shadow at midday: the northern shadow, as with us, and the southern shadow among those who live beyond the course of the sun at the winter solstice. Such a stretch of land is that which lies from the tropics as far as the 67th parallel.

units.la: vel Περισκία denique appellatur, ubi Umbra in Orbem agitur & gyratur; quod accidit illi Terræ portioni, quæ inclusa LXVII. Parallelo: ubi scilicet Arcticus Circulus æqualis, vel major est Tropico, ut cum Strabone loquar: qui videndus lib. II. extremo; ut & Cleomedes lib. I, Macrobius lib. II. in Somnium Scipionis cap. VII; & alii.
units.tr: Finally, it is called Periscian, where the shadow is driven and turns in a circle. This happens to that portion of the earth which is enclosed beyond the 67th parallel, where, namely, the Arctic circle is equal to or greater than the tropic, as I shall speak with Strabo, who is to be consulted at the end of book II; likewise Cleomedes, book I, Macrobius, book II, on the Dream of Scipio, chapter VII; and others.

units.la: Cap. XXII. De Zonis: primo universim; deinde an & quomodo habitentur Intemperatæ.
units.tr: Chapter 22. On the Zones: first in general; then whether and how the Intemperate zones are inhabited.

units.la: AB Aeris Temperie Terra distinguitur in quinque Zonas: Latini Cingulos, Fascias, Plagas, Circulos (hæc enim unius Rei plura Nomina) nuncupant.
units.tr: By the temperature of the air, the earth is divided into five zones, which the Latins call girdles, bands, regions, circles (these are several names for one thing).

units.la: Aeris Qualitas vel est Æstuosa, vel Temperata, vel denique Frigida. Æstuosa quidem Plaga ijs, quibus Sol supra verticem ad perpendiculum ipso Meridie consistit. Zona Torrida καυματώδης vocatur. Torretur enim perpendicularibus Solis radijs; ut Terra duobus Tropicis inclusa, Gradibusque XLVII comprehensa. Intelligit Seneca in Hercule Oetæo, Act. III. Sc. Pro lux acerba. Sic enim ibi Hercules: Video nitentem Regiam clari Aetheris, Phœbique tritam flammea Zonam rota.
units.tr: The quality of the air is either scorching, temperate, or cold. The scorching region belongs to those under whose zenith the sun stands directly overhead at midday. It is called the torrid zone [kaumatōdēs]. It is scorched by the sun's perpendicular rays. It is the earth enclosed by the two Tropics and spanning 47 degrees. Seneca means this in Hercules Oetaeus, Act III, Scene Pro lux acerba. There Hercules says: "I see the gleaming palace of the bright sky, and the zone of Phoebus scorched by the fiery wheel."

units.la: Temperata, Εὔκρατος, ubi nimirum, ut cum Poeta loquar, missa est cum Frigore Flamma; ijs, quorum Verticem Sol ita non accedit, ut eam torreat: nec tantum abest, ut perpetuo gelu rigeat. Talis Terra, quæ à Tropicis est usque ad LXVII usque utrimque Parallelum: quæ tamen tota Plaga non æquabiliter temperata est; sed vel calidior, vel frigidior, ut proprius vel longius à Tropico abest. Legendus omnino Macrobius lib. II. in Somnium Scipionis, cap. VII. Dixi autem, utrimque. Est enim Temperata duplex: Aquilonaris, quæ inter Cancri Tropicum & LXVII Parallelum versus Arctos, Austrina vero, quæ à Capricorni Tropico usque ad LXVII Parallelum versus Polum Antarcticum.
units.tr: The temperate zone [eukratos] is where, as the poet says, the flame is mixed with the cold. It is for those whose zenith the sun does not approach so closely as to scorch it, yet it is far from being stiff with perpetual frost. This is the earth from the Tropics as far as the 67th parallel on each side. Yet this whole region is not evenly tempered: it is warmer or colder according as it lies nearer to or farther from the Tropic. Macrobius, Book II on the Dream of Scipio, chapter VII, should certainly be read. I say "on each side", for the temperate zone is twofold. The northern one lies between the Tropic of Cancer and the 67th parallel towards the Bear. The southern one lies from the Tropic of Capricorn to the 67th parallel towards the Antarctic pole.

units.la: Frigida denique, quæ, quum Sol ibi plurimum à Vertice remotus, perpetuo riget gelu & æterno premitur rigore: LXVII, vel, ut distinctius alij, LXVI gradu scrupulisque XXXI. Latitudinis & Polis utrimque inclusa. Duplex & hæc: Arctoa, sub Arctico polo; & quæ huic sub Antarctico oppolita.
units.tr: Finally, the cold zone is where the sun, being very far from the zenith, is perpetually stiff with frost and pressed by eternal rigour. It lies beyond the 67th degree, or, as others more exactly say, the 66th degree and 31 minutes of latitude, enclosed between the poles on each side. This zone too is twofold: the Arctic, under the Arctic pole, and the one opposite to it under the Antarctic pole.

units.la: Zonarum Discrimen Probus Grammaticus scribit è Manu sumi posse, si lævam contra ora nostra, in Ortum Solis versa, digitis expansis introspexerimus. Vbi enim Pollex est, ibi Zonam ait esse Arcticam, quæ & Septemtrionalis: nimio rigore inhabitabilem: Pollici proximo digito Temperatam nostram, quam Australem nominat, indicari: Medium digitum Aequinoctiali adustæ & inhabitabili respondere: Quartum alteram Temperatam ostendere, quam Hiemalem nominat, quod Sol in eam inclinans nobis Hiemem relinquat: sicut in nostram ascendens Æstatem aperit, Digitque longiores facere solet: Digitum denique Minimum Quintam Zonam referre, Notiam & Australem dictam, ob gelu perpetuum, sicut Septemtrionalis nostra, inhabitabilem.
units.tr: Probus the grammarian writes that the distinction of the zones can be learned from the hand. Turn the left hand towards the rising sun, facing us, and spread the fingers. Where the thumb is, he says, lies the Arctic zone, also called the northern, uninhabitable on account of its excessive cold. The finger next to the thumb indicates our temperate zone, which he calls southern. The middle finger corresponds to the equinoctial zone, scorched and uninhabitable. The fourth finger shows the other temperate zone, which he calls wintry, because the sun, inclining towards it, leaves us winter; and as it rises into ours it brings summer, and tends to lengthen the fingers. Finally, the little finger represents the fifth zone, called Notian and Antarctic, uninhabitable because of its perpetual frost, just as our northern one is.

units.la: De Zonis M. Tullius Somnio Scipionis: Cernis eamdem Terram quasi quibusdam redimitam & circumdatam Circulis: è quibus duos maxime inter se diversos, & Cæli verticibus ipsis ex utraque parte subnixos obriguisse pruina vides; Medium autem illum & Maximum Solis ardore torrent: duo sunt habitabiles: quorum Australis ille, in quo qui insistunt adversa nobis urgent vestigia, nihil ad vestrum genus; hic autem alter subjectus Aquiloni, quem incolitis, cerne quam tenui vos parte contingat, &c. Sic Virgilius lib. Georgic. I: Quinque tenent Cælum Zonæ: quarum una corusco Semper Sole rubens, & torrida semper ab igni; Quam circum extrema dextra lævaque trahuntur, Cærulea glacie, concreta atque imbribus atris; Has inter media que dua Mortalibus ægris Munere concessa Divum.
units.tr: Marcus Tullius writes of the zones in the Dream of Scipio: You see the same earth as if it were encircled and surrounded by certain circles. Of these, you see that the two most unlike one another, which rest on the very poles of heaven on either side, are stiff with frost; but the middle one and the greatest is scorched by the heat of the sun. Two are habitable. Of these, the southern one, whose inhabitants set their feet opposite to yours, has nothing to do with your race. But this other one, lying under the north, which you inhabit, see how small a part of it touches you, and so on. So Virgil, Georgics I: Five zones hold the sky: one of them, always red with the flashing sun and always scorched by fire, is the torrid one; around it, on the right and left, are drawn the two extremes, held fast in blue ice and dark storms. Between these and the middle zone, the two granted by the gods' favour to sickly mortals.

units.la: Cingulos Cicero Terræ, Virgilius Cælo adsignant; docentes non discrepantia; sed consona eademque. Natura enim Cæli hanc (inquit Macrobius lib. II. in Somn. Scip. cap. VII) in diversis Terræ partibus Temperiem Nimietatemque distinxit: & qualitas vel Frigoris vel Caloris, quæ cuilibet Ætheris parti semel inhæsit, eamdem infert partem Terræ, quam despicit ambiendo. Et quia has diversitates, quæ certis finibus terminantur, Cingulos in Cælo vocarunt, necesse est totidem Cingulos & hic intelligi &c. Et sane μεταφορικῶς illa Virgilium scripsisse notat Servius; addens propriè Zonas in Terra dici. Operæprecium & hic audire Tibullum lib. IV. Eleg. I: Et quinque in partes totus disponitur Orbis: Atque duæ gelido vastantur Frigore semper; Illic & densa Tellus abscondítur umbra, Et nulla incepto perlabitur unda liquore; Sed durata riget densam in glaciemque nivemque; Quippe ubi non umquam Titan superegerit ortus: At Media est Phæbi semper subjecta calori, Seu propior Terris æstivum fertur in orbem, Seu celer hibernas properat decurrere luces; Non ergo presso Tellus consurgit aratro; Nec Frugem Segetes præbent, nec Pabula Terræ; Non illic colit Arva Deus, Bacchusve, Cereseve; Nulla nec exustas habitant Animalia Partes: Fertilis hanc inter posita est interque Rigentes, Nostraque & huic adversa solo pars altera nostro; Quas similis utrimque tenens Vicinia Cæli Temperat; alter & alterius vires necat Aeri; Hic placidus nobis per Tempora labitur Annus.
units.tr: Cicero assigns the girdles to the earth, Virgil to the sky. They teach things that do not disagree, but agree and are the same. For the nature of heaven (says Macrobius, Book II on the Dream of Scipio, chapter VII) has distinguished temperature from excess in different parts of the earth; and the quality of either cold or heat, once it has settled in any part of the sky, brings the same quality to that part of the earth which it looks down upon as it surrounds it. And because these differences, which are bounded by fixed limits, they called girdles in the sky, it is necessary that the same number of girdles be understood here, and so on. Servius notes that Virgil wrote those words metaphorically, adding that zones are properly so called on the earth. It is worth hearing Tibullus too, Book IV, Elegy I: The whole world is divided into five parts. Two are always laid waste by gelid cold. There the earth is hidden in dense shade, no wave glides through with its liquid course, but it hardens and stiffens into dense ice and snow, since Titan never rises there to bring the sun. But the middle zone is always subject to the heat of Phoebus, whether he is carried in summer's orbit nearer the earth, or hurries to run through the winter days. So the earth does not rise under the pressing plough; the crops do not give grain, nor the land fodder. There neither god nor Bacchus nor Ceres tends the fields; nor do any living creatures inhabit the scorched parts. The fertile zone lies between the frozen ones, and the other part lies opposite to ours on the other soil. Such neighbourhood of the sky, similar on both sides, tempers them; each destroys the strength of the other in the air. Here the year glides by pleasantly for us.

units.la: Et quæ sequuntur alia de commoda Temperaturarum habitatione. Sic Ovidius lib. I. Metamorph. Utque duæ dextra Cælum totidemque sinistra Parte secant Zonæ; quinta est ardentior illis: Sic onus inclusum numero distinxit eodem Cura Dei; totidemque Plagæ tellure premuntur: Quarum quæ media est, non est habitabilis æstu; Nix tegit alta duas; totidem inter utramque locavit, Temperiemque dedit, mista cum Frigore Flamma.
units.tr: And what follows is about the convenient habitation of the temperate zones. So Ovid, Metamorphoses I: As two zones on the right and two on the left divide the sky, and the fifth is hotter than these, so the care of God divided the burden enclosed in the same number, and the same number of regions are held by the earth. Of these, the middle one is uninhabitable because of its heat; deep snow covers two; between these two he placed the same number, and gave them temperature, a flame mixed with cold.

units.la: Elegantér & Marcianus Capella lib. VI: Orbis Terra in quinque Zonas, sive melius Fasciás dico, pro rerum diversitate discernitur: quarum tres Intemperies multa ob Contrariorum rum nimietatem relegavit: Nam dua Axi utrimque confinales algore immenso & frigoribus desertionis causssas, pruinis urgentibus, prabuere: Media vero flammis & anhelis ardoribus torridata propinquantes Animantium inurit accessus. Alia autem dua, vitalis Aura halitu temperata, habitationem Animalibus indulserunt, qua quidem per totius rotunditatem Telluris incurua tam supernum Hemisphærium, quam inferius ambierunt. Legendus &, præter alios, Macrobius lib.11. in Somnium Scipionis, cap. v.
units.tr: Martianus Capella also says elegantly, Book VI: The earth's orb is divided into five zones, or, to speak better, bands, according to the diversity of things. Of these, excessive contraries have cast three out as intemperate. For the two bordering the axis on either side have offered causes of desolation through immense cold and pressing frosts; but the middle one, parched by flames and panting heats, burns the approaches of living creatures that come near. The other two, tempered by the breath of the life-giving air, have granted habitation to living things; these, curving through the whole roundness of the earth, surround both the upper and the lower hemisphere. Macrobius, Book II on the Dream of Scipio, chapter V, should also be read, among others.

units.la: Hæc de Zonis universim. Solet autem in earum historia moveri Quæstio; num, ut Temperatæ, sic etiam Intemperatæ sint Hominum habitationi commodæ. De Torrida prius agam.
units.tr: These things are said about the zones in general. In their history, however, a question usually arises: whether the intemperate zones, as well as the temperate ones, are suitable for human habitation. I will deal first with the torrid zone.

units.la: Habitari negarunt olim Thales, Pythagoras, Aristoteles, Hipparchus, Artemidorus, Posidonius, Eratosthenes, Ovidius, Strabo, Plinius, Pomponius Mela, Macrobius, Marcianus Capella, aliique Latini & Græci Scriptores; ut nonnullorum verba jam indicarunt. Iis ex lib. 11. Sententiar. ubi de Paradisi situ, addiderim, qui avorum nostrorum temporibus floruerunt, Scotum, Durandum & alios. Accedunt & speciatim de Tropico Capricorni loquentes, Petrus Cameracensis xii. Quæst. Astronomi & Rupertus Linconiensis Compendiosus de Sphæra. Ejusdem classis esto & Albatignius Astronomus, qui suo de Siderum motu opusculo scribit sub Æquatore temperatam quidem esse regionem, neminem tamen ibi habitare. Et hodie nondum adeo victoria est potita Veritas, ut desint, qui Veterum sententiam suis etiam calculis cant comprobatum. Omnia namque hominum commercia Torridam ob immanes Solis, perpendiculares ibi radios proverberantis, ardores & nimios æstus avorsari; inde enim siccitatem provenire; hinc Aquarum inopiam; Aquarum deniique beneficio & subsidio destitutos vitam agere non posse.
units.tr: Thales, Pythagoras, Aristotle, Hipparchus, Artemidorus, Posidonius, Eratosthenes, Ovid, Strabo, Pliny, Pomponius Mela, Macrobius, Martianus Capella, and other Latin and Greek writers once denied that it was inhabited, as some of their words have already shown. To these, from Book II of the Sentences, where he discusses the situation of Paradise, I would add Scotus, Durandus and others who flourished in our fathers' times. Speaking particularly of the Tropic of Capricorn, Peter of Cambrai in his twelfth Question as astronomer, and Robert of Lincoln in his Compendium on the Sphere, join them. Albategnius the astronomer belongs to the same class, who in his little work on the motion of the stars writes that the region under the equator is temperate, yet that no one lives there. Even today Truth has not so far prevailed that there are no men who think they have confirmed the opinion of the ancients by their own calculations. For all human intercourse is kept away from the torrid zone by the huge, perpendicular rays of the sun striking there, and by its excessive heat and burning; for from this comes dryness, and from dryness a lack of water; and men deprived of the benefit and help of water cannot live.

units.la: Sed rem aliter habere se primus, non dicam deprehendit (nam, ut de aliis sileam, Plato in Timæo & aliis locis suam Atlantidem, quam sub Torrida locat, facit, vel, si quis ita malit me loqui, fingit, temperatam admodum & incolis rebusque omnibus ad Vitam bene commodeque agendam necessariis divitem) sed, ni fallor, diserris verbis tamquam indubitatum docuit princeps in hoc Studiorum stadio Ptolemæus; quemadmodum apud eum est legere, de locis quidem Æquatori subjectis lib. 1. Cosmograph. cap. v; Tropicis autem, libro de Sphæræ dispositione. Subscribunt Hali Rhodoan Astronomus, Nicolaus aliique ejus Interpretes. Neque sequior hic mens Avicennæ, Alberto Magno de natura Distinct. 1. cap. vi. & seq. Thomæ Argentinensi libro Sententiarum 11, ubi de Paradiso, Contareno Cardinali libro 11. de Elementis, Clavio Comment. in Sacrobosci Sphæram.
units.tr: But the first man to discover, I will not say, that things stand otherwise (for, to say nothing of others, Plato in the Timaeus and elsewhere makes his Atlantis, which he places under the torrid zone, or, if one prefers me to speak thus, invents it as quite temperate and rich in inhabitants and in all things necessary for living well and comfortably), but who, unless I am mistaken, taught it in express words as beyond doubt, was Ptolemy, the leader in this field of study. As one can read in him, he taught this of places lying under the equator in the first book of the Cosmography, chapter V, and of the Tropics in his book on the arrangement of the sphere. Hali the Rhodian astronomer and Nicolaus and his other interpreters agree with him. Nor is the mind of Avicenna different here, nor that of Albertus Magnus in On Nature, Distinction 1, chapter VI and following; nor that of Thomas of Strasbourg in Book II of the Sentences, where he discusses Paradise; nor that of Cardinal Contarenus in Book II on the elements; nor that of Clavius in his commentary on Sacrobosco's Sphere.

units.la: Hodie habitari Zonam Torridam exploratissimum. Variæ Temperiei sunt causæ: quarum quædam toti Zonæ communes, quædam speciales. Communes mihi sunt: Aquarum ibi Cœlestium copia & Nocturnum Frigus. Has priore loco aperiam, reliquas mox explicaturus.
units.tr: It is most thoroughly established that the Torrid Zone is inhabited today. There are various causes of its temperature: some common to the whole Zone, some particular. The common ones, in my view, are the abundance of celestial waters there and the cold of the night. I shall set out these first, and explain the rest shortly.

units.la: Quod ad Aquas Cœlestes: ut animadversum sæpe ideoque compertissimum scribitur ab ijs, qui loca Zonæ Torridæ suppositia annos aliquot habitarunt, numquam majorem ibi vim Nubium glomerari, numquam ex Nubibus vel resolutis validiores Pluviarum incursus fieri, vel congelatis plus Nivium, ubi tamen solet, cadere, quam quum Sol maxime vicinus & verticalis, habens scilicet efficaciam potentissimam Vaporibus in mediam Aeris regionem subvehendis: ediverso Cœli convexa numquam ibi esse sereniora, numquam minus varia; quam Sole versus alterutrum Tropicorum maxime remoto. Dicis gratia: Peruani, qui Polum respiciunt Antarcticum, Solem habent remotissimum, quum mensibus Maio, Iunio, Iulio & Augusto Tropicum Cancri perambulans, Europæis est proximus; quo tempore Cœli tractus ibi purus, liquidus, liberque, & vix ullis mutationibus obnoxius; suppressis item fontibus, fere est, ut areant fluvii: contra quum ab Octobri usque ad Decembrem revisit Sol ad Capricornum, Aer sensim mutat, fitque paullatim caliginosus & turbidus, hic pluvius, ibi nivalis: simulac denique ab Ianuario usque ad adultum Martium suum iter flectit a Capricorno versus viam mediam, & perpendicularibus lancinat radiis Peruanos, quos dixi; redeunt immanes aliquotque mensium Pluviæ; a quibus aucta Terras ibi inundant, &, ut Ovidio utar, Exspatiata ruunt per apertos flumina campos;
units.tr: As to the celestial waters: it is written, as something often observed and therefore very well established, by those who lived for some years in places supposed to lie under the Torrid Zone, that never are greater masses of clouds gathered there, never do heavier downpours of rain fall from the clouds, whether dissolved or frozen into more snow where snow does fall, than when the Sun is very near and directly overhead, since it has the most powerful efficacy for raising vapours into the middle region of the air. Conversely, the vault of the heavens is never clearer there, never less varied, than when the Sun is most remote from either of the Tropics. To give one example: the Peruvians, who face the Antarctic Pole, have the Sun most remote when, passing through the Tropic of Cancer in the months of May, June, July and August, it is nearest to Europeans. At that time the tract of the sky there is pure, clear and free, and hardly subject to any changes; the springs are dried up, and the rivers nearly run dry. On the other hand, when from October until December the Sun returns to Capricorn, the air gradually changes and becomes by degrees misty and turbid, here rainy, there snowy. Then, as soon as from January until the early part of March the Sun turns its course from Capricorn towards the middle path and strikes the Peruvians I mentioned with vertical rays, the huge rains return and last for several months; swollen by them, the rivers flood the lands there and, to use Ovid's words, rush out over the open fields, spread far and wide.

units.la: adeo ut Diluvium pene facies rerum sit ibi multis in locis. Quid enim dicam (ut novus ille nobis Orbis in exemplum veniat) de Parana? Hic (Europæis Rio de la Plata dictus, quasi Argenteus) tam immanis, ut Confluentes etiam Nilum. Gangen & Euphraten facile sua magnitudine vincat. Qui adcolunt, simulac animadvertunt minacem, alveo quasi relicto, increscere, in suas se conjiciunt scaphas, quas Canoas dicunt; manSuri inibi ad tris menses, donec iterum subsidens in locum suum revertitur. Quid de Magdalena fluvio? Hic, inter fanum D. Mariæ & Carthagenam in Oceanum se exonerans, optimo jure gaudet Magni (dicitur enim nobis Rio grande) cognomine. Auctus enim & cum auctu ingressus ad aliquot milliaria mare, Vires servat & Colorem. Quid denique de Amazonum fluvio, qui quibusdam Marannon, nonnullis Orgliana, fluviorum ibi merito rex? Sub Iudice adhuc lis est; utrum, pluviis aquis tumidus, fluviis sit adscensendus, an vero Maribus connumerandus internis. Si quod illi vastum ostium, fretum esset angustius, nullam res haberet controversiam. Hæc de Aquis Cœlestibus: quod ad Nocturnum Frigus; Sole remoto, non tantum Aer ibi, quod passim naturaliter fieri solet, abunde xii. horarum spatio (hoc addo, ne ignoremus maximi hic momenti esse æqualitatem Dierum & Noctium) perfrigeratur: verum etiam, quæ collectæ surlumque diurnis æstibus evectæ, & ab Sole post occasum destitutæ in Aere restiterunt, Exhalationes maxima copia, nocturno Frigore circumventæ densataque largissimo coque frigidissimo rore Terram conspergunt, & imbuunt Pluviarum instar: quumque novus Sol exoriens nec Frigus, quod Aeri impressum, subito discutere atque evincere; nec, qui Terræ Rebusque nascentibus adspersus, Rorem evestigio exhaurire potis sit & consumere; sit, ut totum post mediam noctem & matutinum ante meridiem tempus sufficiat corporibus refrigerandis, aliisque rebus, quantum flagitat necessitas, inrigandis & reficiundis. Quod eo magis fit, quum etiam accedat celerior Solis in Aequatore Motus. Licet enim ejus Radij bis anno sint illic perpendiculares, & in seipsos reflectantur; non tamen tam diu eidem infiguntur loco, ut alius Calor alium inveniat. Solis namq; Circulus ibi est extensus, rectoque fere cursu recedit ab Aequinoctiali; quem rursum Sol non adit, nisi interpositis quatuor minimum signis: magno sic intervenicnte tempore inter Solis calorem, quem accedendo, quemque facit idem regrediundo. Hæc de Caussis Temperiei Communibus. Sed, quum objicere quis posset, quæ dicta sunt sequius habere se, nunc his nunc illis in locis, neque universim esse vera: alias enim alijs plagis esse sub eodem etiam Climate, eodemque tempore, ferventiores; alias Aquis abundare, destitui alias: in alijs Homines esse fusci, in alijs coloris albi; in quibusdam Corpora hominibus esse, ut nobis, boni habitus; in nonnullis plane alius esse naturæ, Capita dura quidem, sed exsucca, flaccida Cerebra, Capillos crispos, Sensus hebetes ac stupidos, minuta, arida, contorta omnia; quod alias docebimur: unde dicemus hanc variationem sub Zona Torrida procedere, si ab Aquarum copia, Nocturno Frigore, alijsque Caussis omnia ibi sint temperata, & per Temperiem læti perfectique Corporum habitus? Specialiores quærendæ sunt Caussæ, quæque non omnibus Torridæ Zonæ incolis generatim conveniunt. Tales meo judicio censeri possunt Oceani vicinitas, & Terrestrium Aquarum copia, Regionis situs & Montium altitudo, Ventorum proprietas, & si quæ aliæ. Oceanus natura frigidus, proculdubio mirum in modum Æstus Zonæ Torridæ nimios temperat; præsertim ubi profundior, quam ut ab Radiis Solaribus incalescat. Docet alioquin hoc Experientia, Mare non solum Terra frigidius esse: verum etiam Loca Mari adposita magis, quam Mediterranea, algere. Idem pronunciavero de Locis, quæ, quamvis procul à Mari, magnis tamen latisque rigantur Fluminibus, quæ Fontibus scatent largissimis, quæ tumidos habent Torrentes, altas Paludes, Lacus denique profundos. Nam, ut semel dicam, Aquarum natura & indoles est, Frigefacere. Iam Temperiem his, quam illis, sub eodem etiam Climate locis majorem conciliat ipse Regionis alicuius cum genius, tum situs. Loca alta & montosa docent quod volo. Summa certe Montium, qui sub Zona (cujus veram naturam scrutor) frequentissimi, cacumina algent; pertingunt enim plurimum ad mediam Aeris regionem: Valles & Intermontia fervent; Nam infixi ijs Solares radij condensantur ob angustiam, & majores adquirunt vires: Media denique sunt temperatiora; quod utrimque participent. Nec minus nunc hæc nunc illa Zonæ hujus loca speciatim juvat & recreat Ventorum Proprietas.
