Deus enim, qui sapientissimus Rerum omnium conditor, singulari sua providentia Regioni, quam continuo cursu peragrat Sol, & suo æstu sensim vastaturus videbatur, præter alia, quibus incommoda huiusmodi averruncarentur, Ventos adtribuit, temperata Frigora præ se quasi agentes, fervoremque Solis sua natura mirifice temperantes.
units.tr: So much so that in many places there the face of things is almost a Deluge. For why should I speak (so that that new world of ours may serve as an example) of the Parana? This river (called Rio de la Plata by Europeans, as if Silver) is so immense that by its size it would easily surpass even the Nile, the Ganges and the Euphrates combined. Those who live beside it, as soon as they notice it rising threateningly, as if leaving its bed, throw themselves into their boats, which they call canoes, and remain in them for about three months, until it subsides again and returns to its place. What of the river Magdalena? This one, discharging itself into the Ocean between the shrine of St Mary and Cartagena, rightly enjoys the surname Great (for among us it is called Rio grande). For swollen, and entering the sea with its swelling for several miles, it keeps its force and its colour. Finally, what of the river Amazon, which some call the Marannon, others the Orellana, and which is rightly the king of the rivers there? The question is still before the court: whether, swollen with rain waters, it should be counted among the rivers, or rather among the inland seas. If its vast mouth were narrower, there would be no dispute. So much for the celestial waters. As to the cold of the night*: when the Sun is removed, the air there is not only chilled, as commonly happens naturally, over a span of twelve hours (I add this so that we do not forget that the equality of days and nights is of the greatest importance here); but also the exhalations, gathered and carried up by the daytime heats, and left behind in the air when the Sun has withdrawn after setting, are caught by the night's cold in the greatest quantity, and, condensed, sprinkle and steep the earth with a very copious and very cold dew, like rain. And since the new rising Sun can neither immediately dispel and overcome the cold impressed on the air, nor is it able at once to draw off and consume the dew sprinkled on the earth and on the growing things, it happens that the whole time after midnight and the morning before noon suffices for cooling bodies and for watering and refreshing other things as much as necessity requires. This happens all the more because the Sun's motion over the Equator is quicker. For although its rays are there perpendicular twice a year and are reflected back upon themselves, yet they do not fix themselves on the same spot so long that another heat finds another. For the Sun's circle there is extended and withdraws from the Equinoctial along an almost straight course, which the Sun does not approach again except after at least four intervening signs. Thus a long interval comes between the heat of the Sun, which it produces by approaching, and that which it produces by returning. So much for the common causes of temperature. But since someone could object that what has been said is otherwise in this place and that, and is not true universally (for in some regions, under the same climate and at the same time, there are hotter places; some abound in waters, others lack them; in some places men are dark, in others of a white colour; in some bodies are of a good habit, as with us; in some there is a quite different nature, heads hard indeed but dry, brains flabby, hair frizzy, senses dull and stupid, all things small, withered and twisted, which we shall be taught elsewhere): from which we shall say that this variation proceeds under the Torrid Zone, if everything there is tempered by the abundance of waters, the cold of the night and other causes, and bodies have a happy and perfect habit through temperance? More particular causes must be sought, which do not apply generally to all the inhabitants of the Torrid Zone. In my judgment these can be reckoned the nearness of the ocean and the abundance of terrestrial waters, the situation of the region and the height of mountains, the character of the winds, and any others. The Ocean, being cold by nature, undoubtedly tempers in a marvellous way the excessive heats of the Torrid Zone, especially where it is too deep to be warmed by the Sun's rays. Experience otherwise teaches this: the sea is not only colder than land, but places lying close to the sea are colder than inland ones. I would say the same of places which, though far from the sea, are watered by great and broad rivers, which abound in very copious springs, which have swollen torrents, high marshes, and finally deep lakes. For, to say it once for all, it is the nature and property of waters to make cold. Now the very situation of one region, both its nature and its position, brings a greater temperance to some places than to others under the same climate. High and mountainous places show what I mean. The summits of mountains, which are very frequent under the Zone (whose true nature I am investigating), are cold, for they reach largely into the middle region of the air; the valleys and the places between mountains are hot, since the Sun's rays, fixed in them, are condensed by the narrowness and acquire greater force; the middle places finally are more temperate, because they share in both. Nor less does the nature of the winds bring help and refreshment now to this place of the Zone, now to that. For God, the wisest creator of all things, with his singular providence, assigned winds to the region which the Sun traverses in continuous course and which seemed about to be laid waste by its heat, besides other things by which such inconveniences might be averted; these winds, as it were, bring cool temperatures with them and wondrously temper the Sun's fervour by their nature.

units.la: His omnibus non obstat, quod quidam volunt, inter duo calidissima nullum esse Temperamentum. Nam duo Tropici (hos enim designant) numquam simul sint calidissimi; quum numquam simul eodem tempore Solis habeant præsentiam. Sole enim Capricorni Solstitium occupante, non dubium, quin temperatior sit sub Cancro habitatio: ut contra sub Capricorno, quum Cancrum perambulat. Recessus Solis efficit Frigus, ut Calorem Accessus.
units.tr: None of these things is undermined by what some maintain, that between two most hot places there is no temperate one. For the two Tropics (for these are what they mean) are never most hot at the same time, since the Sun is never present to both at the same time. For when the Sun occupies the solstice of Capricorn, there is no doubt that a habitation under Cancer is more temperate; and conversely under Capricorn when it passes through Cancer. The Sun's withdrawal produces cold, as its approach produces heat.

units.la: Porro si quæ dicta bene perpendantur, & in suas portiones Torrida diducatur, diffiniendum erit sub Aequatore commodissime jucundissimeque, & tamquam in terrestri Paradiso (quem hic quidam ausi ponere) vitam homines transigere. Inter Avicennam & Albertum, magnos in Philosophia Viros, hanc video diversitatem; quod Habitationem ibi censeant, ille quidem omnium temperatissimam, <bl>ἁπλῶς</bl> & simpliciter; hic autem eandem, sed habito Tropicorum respectu. Sub Tropicis autem dicendum molestius, quam sub Aequinoctiali, habitari. Nam loca, quæ ijs subsunt, majores habent dies, quam quæ sub Æquatore: deinde Solis ibi declinatio secundum gradus Latitudinis non cito variatur. Ægrius denique paullo sub Capricorni, quam sub Cancri Tropico; ob peculiarem ijs in locis Caloris causam. Nam Solis illic oppositum est Augis, & ideo major ejus ad Terram propinquitas; unde ardentior Æstus. Franciscus tamen Capuanus de Manfredonia huic Solis vicinitati præter Radii perpendicularem incidentiam (utar ejus verbis) non multum ad Caloris productionem tribuit.
units.tr: Furthermore, if what has been said is weighed carefully, and the Torrid Zone is divided into its parts, it must be determined that under the Equator men live most conveniently and most pleasantly, and as it were in an earthly Paradise (which some have ventured to place here). I see this difference between Avicenna and Albertus, great men in philosophy: that the former judges habitation there to be the most temperate of all, <bl>ἁπλῶς</bl> and simply; the latter, the same, but with regard to the Tropics. Under the Tropics, however, it must be said that habitation is more troublesome than under the Equinoctial. For the places lying under them have longer days than those under the Equator; then the Sun's declination there does not quickly vary according to the degrees of latitude; finally it is somewhat harder under Capricorn than under the Tropic of Cancer, because of a peculiar cause of heat in those places. For the Sun there is at its apogee opposite, and therefore its approach to the Earth is greater, whence the heat is fiercer. Franciscus Capuanus of Manfredonia, however, attributes not much to this nearness of the Sun, apart from the perpendicular incidence of the rays (to use his words), in producing heat.

units.la: Sed quid Rationibus, quid Argumentis, quid indicio Causarum opus in re tam manifesta, quaque nobis hodie Navigationum variarum beneficio nihil certius? Loquuntur edita nuper ab Navarchis Hispanis, Anglis, Gallis, Nostratibus, qui suis viderunt oculis, scripta, Populos innumerabiles in locis, quæ Zonæ Torridæ subdita agere, neque incommode, ut hactenus creditum; non solum littoreis, verum etiam mediterraneis. Sub Æquatore conjacet Asiæ (præter Moluccæas, & adjacentes ijs Borneo & Ceiram) Insularum nobilissima Taprobana (Sumatra dicitur Indigenis) quam Pomponius Mela lib. iii. ex Hipparchi testimonio primam ait partem alterius orbis, Austrini scilicet; Plinius lib. vi. nat. histor. cap. xxii. frequentissimæ tradit habitationis; Nostrates Incolis notant refertissimam. Sub eodem in Africæ litoribus (nam mediterranea parum innotuerunt) Orientalioribus quidem Melinde cum aliis; Occidentalioribus autem est celebratissimum illud magni Viri scriptis regnum Manicongo, & objecta fluvio S. Dominici Insula Divo Thomæ sacrata. Sub eodem denique in America, hinc quidem amplissimus Caribanorum tractus; inde vero aurifera Peruanorum Terræ. Et quæ non loca sub Tropicis? De ijs quæ sub Cancri, nimis omnia nota. Testantur mille Ephemerides. Quum vero sub Capricorno molestior, quam alibi, sit habitatio; degunt tamen ibi in America Tonou pinambaultij, Toupinikini, & alij; subjacet illi Insula D. Laurentij, Madagascer; alia prætereo.
units.tr: But why should we argue from reasons, arguments, or evidence of causes in a matter so plain, and one that, thanks to the various voyages of our own day, nothing makes more certain? Recently published accounts by Spanish, English, French and our own naval commanders say so, written by men who saw with their own eyes that countless peoples live in places lying under the Torrid Zone, and not unpleasantly, as has hitherto been believed; and not only on the coasts but also inland. Under the Equator in Asia lies Taprobana, the noblest of the islands (apart from the Moluccas and the islands near them, Borneo and Ceram), which is called Sumatra by its natives. Pomponius Mela, in book 3, on the testimony of Hipparchus, calls it the first part of the other, that is the southern, world. Pliny, Natural History book 6, chapter 22, describes it as very densely inhabited, and our own men note that its people are very numerous. Under the same line on the African coasts (for the inland parts are little known), to the east there is Melinde with others, and to the west the famous kingdom of Manicongo, described by a great man in his writings, and, across the river of St Dominic, the island consecrated to St Thomas. Under the same line in America, on one side there is the vast tract of the Caribanorum, and on the other the gold-bearing lands of the Peruanorum. And what places are not under the Tropics? Of those under the Tropic of Cancer everything is too well known; a thousand almanacs bear witness. Under the Tropic of Capricorn, although living there is more troublesome than elsewhere, people nevertheless dwell there in America: the Tonou pinambaultij, the Toupinikini and others. The island of St Lawrence and Madagascer lie under it. I pass over other examples.

units.la: Nusquam autem, quod hic addendum, Montes ab ijs, qui nostris temporibus peragrarunt, qui navigarunt omnia, reperti; quibus, in media Torrida collocatis, incredibilem inesse vim Magnetis, magna temeritate sunt fabulati Veteres, trahentis ad se avidissime carnem humanam: ideoque Temperatam alteram nobis omnino esse inaccessam. Nihil occurrit tale per totam Torridam navigantibus. Nusquam etiam hodie Æstus obest; & ne perpendicularis quidem Radius in se reflexus adeo subeuntes infestat, ut minus expedita sit Navigatio. Nusquam denique Austrinum orbem ita ab hoc Nostro intercipit Oceanus (quod crediderunt nonnulli) ut in eum pervenire non liceat. Quæ quanta sint futilitate chartis mandata, clamant etiam Variorum ævi prisci navigationes. Nam si sub Zona Torrida sæviret intolerabilis Æstus; si Temperatam alteram vastior, iniquior, & arte nulla superandus Oceanus ab nostra disjungeret; qui potuerunt, notante Plinio lib. vi. nat. tur. histor. cap. xxii, Onesicritus, Classis Alexandrinæ Præfectus, hinc eo penetrare, inde autem in nostrum hunc orbem; qui ad Claudium Imperatorem quatuor, principe Rachia, Legati ; qui Eudoxus Lathuri regis tyrannidem fugiens, Arabico sinu egressus per vastissimum pelagus, ut Cornelius Nepos apud Plinium lib. II. cap. LXVII adfirmat, Gades usque pervehi ; qui contra Hanno, quod idem Plinius docet ejusdem libri capite LXIX, Fretum transiens Gaditanum immensum illud Aequor emetiri, & Arabiam feliciter contingere ; Solinus habitantibus sub Zona Torrida aetatem annosam tribuit, & prope ultra mortalium fragilitatem extendi Vitam ait. Pomponius Mela scribit lib. III. supra Aegyptum Meroenos esse, quorum pars Macrobii nominantur ; quod ipsorum vitae spacium nostram aetatem, inquit, dimidio superet : Meroenos autem intra Cancri Tropicum & Aequatorem esse, Ptolemaeus est auctor : Plinius denique lib. II, nat. hist. cap. XVI, nihil habitari in Terris adserit, quam quod Zodiaco subjacet ; scimus autem terminos Obliquitatis Zodiaci esse Parallelos Tropicis : ut ex Plinii mente sub Ardore unica sit Mortalium habitatio, quibus contraria idem, ante scriptorum parum memor, tradit ejusdem libri capite LXXII.
units.tr: Nowhere, and this is worth adding here, have those who have travelled in our times and sailed everywhere found mountains in the middle of the Torrid Zone with the incredible magnetic power that the ancients foolishly invented, drawing to themselves most eagerly the flesh of men; and so they claimed that the other Temperate Zone was altogether inaccessible to us. Nothing of the sort is encountered by those who sail through the whole Torrid Zone. Nowhere today does the heat hinder them, and even the vertical ray, reflected back upon those who go through it, does not trouble them so much as to make the voyage less convenient. Nowhere finally does the ocean cut off the southern world from this world of ours so that it cannot be reached, as some have believed. How empty these notions are, the voyages of the ancient sailors cry out. For if intolerable heat raged under the Torrid Zone; if an ocean wider, more hostile, and impossible to overcome by any skill separated us from the other Temperate Zone, how could Onesicritus, prefect of the Alexandrian fleet, have got there from one side and returned to our world on the other, as Pliny reports in book 6, chapter 22? How could the envoys of the emperor Claudius, under the leadership of Rachias, have come to him? How could Eudoxus, fleeing the tyranny of King Lathurus, have set out from the Arabian gulf and sailed across the vast sea as far as Gades, as Cornelius Nepos affirms in Pliny, book 2, chapter 67? Or how could Hanno, as the same Pliny teaches in chapter 69 of the same book, have crossed the Strait of Gibraltar and measured that immense sea and successfully reached Arabia? Solinus attributes long life to the inhabitants under the Torrid Zone, and says that their life is extended almost beyond human frailty. Pomponius Mela writes in book 3 that beyond Egypt there are the Meroë people, part of whom are called the Macrobii, because, he says, the span of their life exceeds our age by half. Ptolemy is the authority that the Meroë people lie between the Tropic of Cancer and the Equator. Finally, Pliny, Natural History book 2, chapter 16, asserts that nothing is inhabited on the earth except what lies beneath the Zodiac. We know, however, that the limits of the obliquity of the Zodiac are parallels to the Tropics; so, according to Pliny's view, there would be only one place of human habitation under the Ardor, although the same writer, forgetful of his earlier writings, states the contrary in chapter 72 of the same book.

units.la: Sed sufficiant haec de Intemperatis ob Solis praesentiam : Reliquas ob ejusdem absentiam aeterno damnatas Frigore, unde & nomen illis, & perpetuis horridas tenebris, non secus ac Torridam ; esse inhabitabiles, Antiqui Scriptores, quorum ante mentio mihi facta, tradiderunt. Ejusdem mentis, prolaris in medium non frivolis (ut, nisi argumenta in contrarium hodie essent, prima lectione videntur) rationibus, est Albertus Magnus cap. de natura locorum VIII ; existimans inter alia omnibus his, quibus dies ad mensis spacium, Sole hic Cancrum, ibi Capricornum tenente, extenditur, in hieme habitationem ob molestissimum frigus negari. De Frigida, quae sub Arcto, certiora doceri possunt ; quam de Opposita. An enim quae sub Polo Antarctico habitetur, nondum satis exploratum : quum nihil adhuc ultra LVII, aut circiter, Latitudinis Australis gradum innotuerit. Ejusdem tamen esse naturae vero simile est cum hac nostra. De qua ut quid dicam ; cum primis notandum Latitudinem commodae Habitationis juxta Polum certam non esse neque diffinitam. Ea enim, quum Sol, ad cujus praesentiam omnia referenda, Cancrum perambulat, major ; minor autem, quum Capricornum. Quid enim virium habere potest obliquitas Radiorum, quos Sol longe amotus illuc projicit? Quemadmodum fortean (putandum enim Regulas, quae generales paullo ante indicatae, nonnihil subinde exceptionis admittere) sub Zona Torrida nunc his, nunc ijs locis per Solis praesentiam aut molesta sit, aut etiam nulla habitatio : quae, Sole rursum abeunte, permittitur : ita etiam usu venit sub Zonis Frigidis : ut hiberno tempore, Sole Calorem ijs aliquot mensis negante, Loca multa vel sint inhabitata, vel moleste habitentur ; aestivo autem Temperiem ab ejusdem Solis quali-quali Calore recuperantia habitantes admittant. Docuerunt nos nostrates nuperis suis versus Septemtrionaliora navigationibus, in nova Zembla (insula est, cujus ab Aequatore initium ad gradum Latitudinis LXX ; finis vero ad LXXVII) se in rudera quaedam Tuguriorum incidisse, Navigiorum invenisse fragmenta, Pedum denique humanorum majoris minorisque aetatis vidisse vestigia ; quum tamen totos illos septem menses, quibus in Insula fuerant concluti, continuas ibi hominum nusquam deprehenderint Habitationes : ut dubium non sit, quin per aetatem & longiores dies ibi, quae dixi, fuerint aedificata ab Russis, Lappis, vicinisque populis, Vtiorum aliarumque Ferarum venatui operam datum eo ex Continenti Alia Europaque proficisci solitis. Frigus igitur, quod ex longa Solis absentia locis Polo proximis, causla princeps est, quod pauciens & fortean non habitentur. Frigus autem illud intendi tuetur, in alto quidem Pelago ab ipsius Aquae, quam Frigidam novimus natura : acrius autem in Terris ab Nivibus, quae ijs insulae non facile liquescunt ; & Glacie, quam ex dulcioribus & Mediterraneis Aquis generatam flumina solent trudere, & in Oceanum provomere : ubi non tam alta petunt maria, quam littoribus adhaerescunt. Hinc nostri, quod alibi dicere me memini, subpolare parum abfuit Pelagus sulcantes, semper littoralia ab Glacie commemorant discrimina. Nulla Nix, rara in alto ibi Pelago Glacies. Nive conspersae jacent Insulae : Nives, quum Sol Horizontem nostrum scandit, praesertim autem quum Cancrum premit, liquefactae generant Aquas dulces ; quae cum Aquis Naturalibus versus Oceanum delapsae, & in Glaciem ob excellens ibi Frigus conversae immanissimos Terris ibi potius, quam mari liberiori, conciliant algores. Ob Frigus ergo rarum arbitror, ut illa loca habitentur; eo magis, quod & Tenebrarum aliquot Mensium accedat incommoditas. Quum enim Sol in Meridianis Signis, præsertim Capricorno, Cursum suum conficit, diu abest, Noctemque Locis, quæ sub Polo nostro, sex mensium relinquit: augentibus etiam Tenebras continuas Vaporibus frigidis: quum non solum Radij Solis halitus ex Aquis elevent, nihil tamen eorum, quod infirmiores, consumant, verum etiam immodicum ipsius Regionis Frigus Acrem frequenter spisset, reddatque tenebrosum, & ipsum perpetim convertat in Aquam. Et hinc merito Aquosa plerumque sub Polis loca. Nam Maria magis ibi, quam Terræ: adeo ut sint, qui perpetuam Aquarum generationem ijs locis statuant; providente scilicet Natura, quod illic ob vicissitudinis temporum penuriam incommodum fuisset vivere, etiamsi Terra fuisset. Naturam tamen eamdem non negaverim, ut aliis, sic illis etiam locis aliquando Ἀντεφύσεα quædam moliri: non quidem Voraginem illam Platonicam cum quatuor suis Euripis, quos emovi inde, quum de Arctoo Pelago scriberem; sed loca, quæ Polo vicina (quis hoc credat?) temperatiora, quam quæ aliquot inde gradibus versus Cancri Tropicum. Discimus ex nostrorum Argonautarum Diarijs, majorem esse Temperiem gradu Latitudinis lxx, quam lxxvi. & circiter. Loquuntur enim in Insula quadam, in quam gradu lxxx. & minut. xi. delati fuerunt, omnia virere, & Animantia herbis pascentia vivere; quum contra in Nova Zembla, ubi ad gradum lxxvi. diu morati, omnia arerent, & Vrsis, Vulpibus, aliisque carnivoris 20 feris essent infamia. Caussa forte (divinare mihi liceat) quod Nova Zembla intensiore feriatur & infestetur frigore, quam Insula, cujus memini. Huic enim remissius est proculdubio; quod sola, magnoque intervallo ab Continente dissita, proprio tantum & simplici quasi algore laboret, ex propria vel nive vel glacie collecto: illi autem acrius est & penetrabilius; quod, Freto satis angusto interjecto, Continentem Terram habeat valde vicinam, ex cuius copiosa nive glacieque Frigus illud Zemblanum nimium quantum augetur: præsertim si vehementius ab Meridionali plaga consurrexerint venti, qui sæpe brumaliores ibi, quam si aliunde. Quidquid sit, docet duarum Insularum inter se commissio, non plane fabulosa esse, quæ leguntur apud Pomponium Melam & Plinium, locis haud procul à Polo nostro 30 distantibus Riphæos esse Montes; ad eosque degere Arymphæos populos nudis capitibus, vesci Baccis, Nemora pro Domibus habitare, Moribus vero præditos justissimis & pientissimis. Nam qui possent nisi loco paullo amœniore? Si tamen ibi quædam talia; certe sunt rara. Censendum enim pleraque frigoribus illic aduri, squalere, horrere, nebulisque caligare: accedente, quod non postremi loci censendum, & hoc argumento: quod grandia pusillaque Animalia, ut plurimum hirsuta quæque ad frigoris acumen tolerandum apta, sapientissimus Naturæ artifex DEVS in hæc destinavit loca, de quibus recte dixero, quod de Cimmerijs vicinis Poeta: Ἠέρα κὰι νεφέλη κεκαλυμμένοι ἤδε μὰν αὐτὰς Ἠέλιος φαεσβων ὑπὸ ἰρκετὴν ἀχλύεσσιν.
units.tr: But let these remarks suffice concerning the Intemperate zones, on account of the presence of the sun. The remaining zones, condemned to eternal cold because of the sun's absence, whence they have their name and are dreadful with perpetual darkness, just as the Torrid Zone is, the ancient writers, whom I mentioned before, have taught are uninhabitable. Albertus Magnus, in chapter 8 of his work on the nature of places, holds the same opinion, and brings forward reasons which are not trivial (as they seem at first reading, unless there were arguments to the contrary today); he thinks that among other things habitation is denied in winter in all those places where the day extends to a month's length while the sun holds Cancer here and Capricorn there, on account of the most severe cold. Concerning the Frigid Zone which lies beneath the Arctic, more certain things can be taught than concerning the opposite one. For it is not yet sufficiently established whether the zone beneath the Antarctic Pole is inhabited, since nothing has yet become known beyond the fifty-seventh degree of southern latitude, or thereabouts. It is nevertheless likely that it has the same nature as this one of ours. Concerning this one, to say what I can: first of all it should be noted that the latitude of comfortable habitation near the Pole is neither fixed nor defined. For it is greater when the sun, to whose presence all things must be referred, traverses Cancer, and smaller when it traverses Capricorn. For what strength can the obliquity of the rays have, which the sun, far removed, projects there? Just as perhaps (for we must think that the general rules indicated a little earlier admit some exceptions at times) under the Torrid Zone habitation is at one time or another in some places troublesome or even impossible, owing to the sun's presence, and is again permitted when the sun withdraws, so also it happens under the Frigid Zones: in winter, when the sun denies them warmth for some months, many places are either uninhabited or inhabited with difficulty; but in summer the inhabitants, recovering a mild temperature from the sun's heat, such as it is, are able to remain. Our countrymen, in their recent voyages towards the north, have taught us that in Nova Zembla (an island whose extent runs from the Equator to the seventieth degree of latitude at its beginning, and to the seventy-seventh at its end) they came upon certain ruins of huts, found fragments of ships, and saw the traces of human feet of both adults and children; yet during all those seven months in which they were shut up on the island, they nowhere encountered any continuous human dwellings. So there is no doubt that, in the course of time and during the longer days, what I have described was built by Russians, Lapps and neighbouring peoples, who were accustomed to set out from that continent of Asia and Europe to hunt the otter and other wild animals. Cold, therefore, which is the principal cause, owing to the long absence of the sun, makes the places nearest the Pole rarely and perhaps never inhabited. That cold is increased, on the open sea, by the very nature of the water, which we know to be cold; but more sharply on the land by the snows, which do not easily melt on those islands, and by the ice which the rivers generated from fresher and inland waters are accustomed to push out and throw into the ocean, where they do not so much make for the deep seas as cling to the shores. Hence our men, as I remember saying elsewhere, sailing the sub-polar seas, always report the boundaries of the coasts by the ice; there is no snow in the open sea there, and little ice. The islands lie covered with snow; the snows, melted when the sun climbs above our horizon, and especially when it presses on Cancer, produce fresh waters, which, falling with the natural waters towards the ocean and turned into ice by the excessive cold there, bring on the most monstrous frosts on the lands there rather than on the freer sea. Therefore I think it is rare that those places are inhabited, the more so as the inconvenience of several months of darkness is added. For when the sun completes its course in the southern signs, especially Capricorn, it is absent for a long time, and leaves the places under our Pole with six months of night; the continual darkness is increased by the cold vapours, since the rays of the sun not only raise exhalations from the waters, but none of them is consumed, being too weak; moreover the excessive cold of the region frequently thickens the air, makes it gloomy, and turns it entirely into water. And hence places near the Poles are generally watery; for there is more sea there than land, so much so that some think there is a perpetual generation of waters in those places, Nature providing, of course, against the inconvenience which would have been there, owing to the lack of alternation of seasons, even if there were land. Nevertheless I would not deny that the same Nature sometimes contrives, in those places as in others, some counter-natural effects: not indeed that Platonic whirlpool with its four channels, which I removed from there when I was writing about the Arctic sea, but places which are near the Pole, and (who would believe it?) are more temperate than those a few degrees from there towards the Tropic of Cancer. We learn from the diaries of our Argonauts that there is a greater mildness at the seventieth degree of latitude than at the seventy-sixth or thereabouts. For they report that on a certain island, to which they were carried at the eightieth degree and eleven minutes, everything was green and the animals lived on grass; whereas on Nova Zembla, where they stayed a long time at the seventy-sixth degree, everything was parched, and was infested with bears, foxes and other flesh-eating beasts. The reason is perhaps (I may be permitted to guess) that Nova Zembla is struck and afflicted by a more intense cold than the island I mentioned. For that island is certainly milder, because, lying alone and far separated from the continent, it suffers only from its own peculiar and almost simple cold, gathered from its own snow or ice; whereas the cold on the other is sharper and more penetrating, because, with a fairly narrow strait lying between, it has the mainland very close, and from its abundant snow and ice that Zemblan cold is increased beyond measure; especially if the winds rise more violently from the southern quarter, which are often more wintry there than from any other direction. Whatever the case, the coming together of the two islands shows that what is read in Pomponius Mela and Pliny is not altogether fabulous: that the Riphaean mountains lie in places not far from our Pole, and that the Arimphaei people live near them with bare heads, feed on berries, dwell in groves instead of houses, and are endowed with the most just and pious morals. For how could they live otherwise, unless in a rather pleasant place? If there are indeed some such places there, they are certainly rare. For it must be supposed that most of those regions are scorched by the cold, neglected, bristling, and shrouded in mist; and there is another consideration which should not be counted least: that God, the most wise Artificer of Nature, has appointed to those places large and small animals, mostly hairy, suited to bearing the keenness of the cold. Of them I may fitly say what the poet said of the neighbouring Cimmerians: [Ἠέρα κὰι νεφέλη κεκαλυμμένοι, ἤδε μὰν αὐτὰς Ἠέλιος φαεσβων ὑπὸ ἰρκετὴν ἀχλύεσσιν] "shrouded in air and cloud, nor does the shining sun ever look down upon them with its rays, but dismal mist lies spread over them."

units.la: Paret igitur ex iis, quæ dixi, omnes Zonas habitationis esse patientes; non solum Temperatas, quod extra omnem semper fuit controversiam; verum etiam intemperatas, earum autem Aestuosam magis, quam Frigidas.
units.tr: It is therefore clear from what I have said that all zones are habitable: not only the Temperate zones, which has always been beyond dispute, but also the intemperate zones, the Torrid more than the Frigid.

units.la: Zonarum autem, id est, Terræ totius, Incolis varia Veteres indiderunt Nomina: partim Vmbrarum ratione: Nam Aestuosam Ἀμφίσκιοι, Temperatas Ἑπρέσκιοι, Frigidas denique colunt Περίσκιοι: videndi Cleomedes lib. i. κυκλικῆς θεωρίας μεθωμεξῶν, Strabo lib. ii. extremo Geograph. & alij; legenda & quæ cap. xxi. scripsi: partim vero Situs respectu & mutuæ comparationis; alij enim sunt. Περίσκιοι, alij Ἀντίσκιοι, alij denique Ἀντιποδες: de quibus omnibus multa disserit V. CL. Ioachimus Vadianus doctissimis suis in Pomponii Melæ lib. i. Castigationibus. Περίσκιοι (non male quis Latine dixerit Circumcolus) appellantur, qui in eadem degunt Zona sub eodem Parallelo & Meridiano; sed oppositis Hemisphærijs, interjacente Verticibus illorum Mundi Polo: id est, qui æqualem ejusdem Partis Latitudinem, Longitudinem semicirculo differentem, habent: Hi eadem fruuntur Cœli constitutione; Anni tempora pariter agunt; medium autem Diem & Noctem horis vident contrarijs. Ἀντίσκιοι, qui in diversis & positis è regione Zonis, intercedente Verticibus Æquatore, sub eodem Meridiano, sed non ijsdem Parallelis, æqualiter tamen ab Aequinoctiali remotis, habitant; Latitudine obsiti; Longitudine pares: His Nox & Dies communes; sed oppositio tempore Aestas & Hiems. Ἀντίποδες (Ἀντίχθονες etiam Ἀντιπεab contraria, quam inhabitant, Terra vocantur) sunt, qui ex Diametro secundum ἀξ. rectissimam Lineam, per Terrae Centrum trajectam, Partes colunt oppositas: Pedes obversos invicem habentes (unde & Adversipedes Glossarium vetus interpretatur) hoc est, qui eumdem Meridianum & Horizontem, sed diversos Parallelos, aequaliter tamen ab Aequatore remotos, obtinent; ac distant inter se medietate Circuli Maximi, nempe gradibus CLXXX. Hi nihil habent commune; non Anni tempora, non Dies, non Noctes; illis exceptis, qui sub Aequinoctiali sunt siti. Nam omnia illis, praeter Diem & Noctem, quas alternatim habent, sunt communia. Exempla suppeditant Sphaerae Terrestres & Tabulae Geographicae. Ἀντίποδες & Περίοικοι vario respectu Ἀντίποδες dicuntur. Nos Ἀντικῶν nostrorum Περιοίκοις Ἀντίποδες sumus; nostri Περίοικοι Ἀντικοῖς nostris sunt Ἀντίποδες. Marcianus Capella lib. VI. (ignoranter dicam, an imprudenter?) quae Περίοικων sunt Antipodibus tribuit, & Περίοικας Antipodas nominat. Antipodes autem Veterum quidam esse, quidam non esse, tradiderunt. Esse scripserunt; absolute quidem, Strabo lib. I. Geograph. Cleomedes lib. I, Manilius lib. I. Astronomic. Pomponius Mela lib. I, Plinius lib. II. nat. hist. cap. LXVII, & lib. VI, cap. LXVI, Solinus in Polyhist. & alij: quorum argumenta cum alibi, tum apud Lactantium lib. III. Divinar. Instit. cap. XXIII, & Augustinum lib. XVI de Civitate Dei, cap. IX: re-
units.tr: The ancients gave various names to the inhabitants of the zones, that is, of the whole earth. Some names are based on shadows: the inhabitants of the Torrid zone are called Amphiscii [Ἀμφίσκιοι], those of the Temperate zones Heteroscii [Ἑπρέσκιοι], and those of the Frigid zones Periscii [Περίσκιοι]. See Cleomedes, book I of his Κυκλικὴ θεωρία μετεώρων, Strabo, end of book II of the Geography, and others; and what I wrote in chapter XXI should also be read. Other names are based on position and mutual relation, for there are Periscii, others Antiscii [Ἀντίσκιοι], and others finally Antipodes. On all of these matters the most learned V. CL. Joachim Vadian discusses at length in his Castigationes on Pomponius Mela, book I. Periscii (one might fairly call them in Latin Circumcolus, "dwellers around") are those who live in the same zone, under the same parallel and meridian, but on opposite hemispheres, with the pole of the world lying between their zeniths. That is, they have the same latitude in the same part, and longitudes differing by a semicircle. These enjoy the same state of the sky, experience the seasons alike, but see midday and midnight at opposite hours. Antiscii are those who live in zones situated opposite each other, with the equator lying between their zeniths, under the same meridian but not the same parallels, yet equally distant from the equinoctial. They share the same longitude but differ in latitude. For them night and day are common, but the seasons are opposite: summer for one is winter for the other. Antipodes (also called Antichthones [Ἀντίχθονες], from the opposite earth they inhabit) are those who, along a diameter, that is, the most direct line drawn through the centre of the earth [ἄξων], inhabit opposite parts, with their feet turned towards each other (whence an old glossary translates them as Adversipedes). That is, they share the same meridian and horizon but have different parallels, equally distant from the equator, and are separated by half a great circle, namely 180 degrees. These have nothing in common: neither seasons, nor days, nor nights, except those who are situated under the equinoctial. For all things are common to them except day and night, which they have in turn. Terrestrial globes and geographical maps supply examples. Antipodes and Perioeci [Περίοικοι] are called Antipodes in different respects. We are Antipodes to the Perioeci of our Antiscii, and our Perioeci are Antipodes to our Antiscii. Marcianus Capella, book VI (I say this ignorantly, or rather carelessly?), assigns to the Antipodes what belongs to the Perioeci, and calls the Perioeci Antipodes. Some of the ancients held that Antipodes exist, others that they do not. Those who wrote that they exist: without qualification, Strabo, book I of the Geography; Cleomedes, book I; Manilius, book I of the Astronomica; Pomponius Mela, book I; Pliny, book II of the Natural History, chapter 67, and book VI, chapter 66; Solinus in the Polyhistor; and others. Their arguments are set out elsewhere, and also in Lactantius, Divine Institutes, book III, chapter 23, and Augustine, City of God, book XVI, chapter 9.

units.la: stricte vero & cum exceptione quasi, M. Tullius lib. VI. de repubi. Macrobius lib. I. in Somnium Scipionis, Marcianus, & inter recentiores Albertus Magnus cap. XII. de Natura Locorum; censentes, quum quidem sint, Commercia tamen cum illis Nobis, & Nobiscum Illis omnino denegari: partim propter immensam Oceani, qui interjacet undique per circuitum circa Terrae globum quantitatem, & insuperabilem Locorum distantiam; partim propter intolerabiles Aestus, & nimios Solis sub Zona Torrida, quae, si ad Antipodes eundum, peragranda esset, ardores. Non esse voluerunt variis argumentis Lactantius & Augustinus: dignus uterque qui audiatur. Illius loco, quem indicavi, verba sunt haec: Quid illi, qui esse contrarios Vestigiis nostris Antipodas putant, num aliquid loquuntur? aut est quisquam tam ineptus, qui credat esse homines, quorum Vestigia sint superiora quam Capita? aut ibi, quae apud nos jacent, inversa pendere? Fruges & arbores deorsum versus crescere? Pluvias & Nives & Grandinem sursum versus cadere in terram? Et miratur aliquis Hortos pensiles inter septem mira narrari, quum Philosophi & Agros, & Maria, & Urbes, & Montes pensiles faciant? Philosophos deinde, qui contrarium adserebant, falsae carpit: in multa, inquiens, incidere ridicula; quum semel aberrarint, constanter in stultitia perseverare, & vanis vana defendere; interdum joci causa Philosophari; saepe prudentes & scios Mendacia defendenda suscipere, ut Ingenia sua in malis rebus exerceant & ostentent. Augustinus autem cap. jam nominato, Quod vero & Antipodas esse fabulantur, ait, id est homines a contraria parte Terrae, ubi Sol oritur, quando occidit nobis, adversa pedibus nostris calcare Vestigia, nulla ratione credendum est. Neque hoc nulla historica cognitione didicisse se affirmant; sed quasi ratiocinando conjectant, eo quod intra convexa Coeli Terra suspensa sit, eundemque locum Mundus habeat & infimum & medium; & ex hoc opinantur alteram Terrae partem, quae infra est, habitatione hominum carere non posse. Et post pauca: Nimis quam absurdum est, ut dicatur aliquos homines ex hac in illam Partem, Oceani immensitate trajecta, navigare ac pervenire potuisse: ut etiam illic ex uno illo primo homine genus institueretur humanum. Videndus idem lib. Categoriar. cap. x. Condonandum utrique, Theologiae sacraria penitius, quam Philosophiae ingressis; magis autem alteri. Lactantius enim risu jocoque sanam de Antipodibus opinionem prosequitur: nihil validi contra adferens: Augustinus vero eamdem rejicit, non levem ob causam; ne cogeretur fateri, illos de genere Adae primi hominis non esse; quum jam, ut audivimus, praejudicasset Cicero, & sequuti illum alij, nullum hinc ad eos esse aditum. Sed Antipodas esse tam certum est, ut negari non posslit, & insensatus audiret meritissimo, qui diversum sentiret. Hinc ad illos, illinc huc Viam esse compertissimum hodie nobis; etiam non paucis Antiquorum: quod docent variarum Navigationum & Expeditionum exempla; quae in praecedentibus fusius sunt commemorata. Iam qua via venerint in oppositum nobis Orbem primi homines, quod capere non potuerunt Antiqui, quaeram, ubi ad Americae delineationem & historiam erit deventum.
units.tr: Those who wrote more strictly, and with a kind of exception, were Marcus Tullius Cicero, De re publica, book VI; Macrobius, commentary on Scipio's Dream, book I; Marcianus; and among more recent writers Albertus Magnus, On the Nature of Places, chapter 12. They held that, although the Antipodes exist, all dealings between them and us, and between us and them, are altogether impossible. This was partly because of the immense extent of the ocean that lies all round the globe of the earth and the insuperable distance between places, and partly because of the intolerable heat and the excessive burning of the sun under the Torrid zone, which would have to be crossed on the way to the Antipodes. Lactantius and Augustine, each with various arguments, held that they do not exist. Both deserve to be heard. In the passage I have cited, Lactantius writes: What of those who think there are Antipodes whose feet are set against ours? Do they say anything at all? Or is anyone so foolish as to believe there are men whose feet are higher than their heads? Or that things lying among us hang upside down there? That crops and trees grow downwards? That rain and snow and hail fall upwards to the earth? And does anyone wonder that hanging gardens are counted among the seven wonders, when the philosophers make fields and seas and cities and mountains hang as well? He then criticises the philosophers who maintained the opposite, saying: They fall into many ridiculous things; once they have gone astray, they persist constantly in folly, and defend vain things with vain arguments; sometimes they philosophise for the sake of a joke; often clever and learned men undertake to defend lies, so that they may exercise and show off their wits on bad subjects. Augustine, in the chapter already named, says: As for their fable that there are also Antipodes, that is, men on the other side of the earth, where the sun rises when it sets for us, treading the ground with feet opposite ours, it must by no means be believed. Nor do they claim to have learned this from any historical knowledge; rather, they conjecture it by reasoning, because the earth is suspended within the vault of heaven, and the world has the same place for both its lowest and its middle point. From this they think that the other part of the earth, which lies below, cannot lack human inhabitants. A little later he says: It is far too absurd to say that some men could have crossed the immensity of the ocean from this part to that, and arrived there, so that the human race could have been established there too from that one first man. The same book may be consulted, and also the Categories, chapter 10. Both men should be pardoned, since they had entered more deeply into the sanctuaries of theology than of philosophy, but the latter more than the former. For Lactantius pursues his sound opinion about the Antipodes with mockery and jokes, bringing forward nothing of weight against them; but Augustine rejects the same opinion for no slight reason: he did not want to be forced to admit that they are not descended from Adam, the first man. Since Cicero, as we have heard, had already prejudged the question, and others had followed him, there was no way in for them. But that Antipodes exist is so certain that it cannot be denied, and anyone who thought otherwise would rightly be deemed a fool. Today we know most clearly that there is a way from there to here and from here to there, and not a few of the ancients knew it too. The examples of various voyages and expeditions, which were described more fully above, teach this. By what route the first men came to the world opposite us, which the ancients could not grasp, I shall inquire when we arrive at the description and history of America.

units.tr: CHAPTER XXIII. Of Climates.

units.la: HÆc de Terræ Divisione, Inferiorum respectu, in Partes Majores, caussa vel Umbræ; vel Aeris Temperiei: succedit Distributio in Partes Minores, Horarum variantium ratione, in Climata scilicet.
units.tr: So much for the division of the earth into the major parts, according to the inhabitants, by reason of shadow or the temperature of the air. Next comes the distribution into minor parts, according to the varying length of the hours, namely into climates.

units.la: Clima Terræ spacium definiunt, duobus Parallelis comprehensum; cujus finis Diem Solstitialem dimidia hora majorem habet, quam initium: unde paret, quorum aliquod Clima fuerit ab Aequatore; tot semihoris maximum ejus diem superare Diem Aequinoctialem.
units.tr: A climate is a space of the earth enclosed by two parallels, whose end has a solstitial day half an hour longer than its beginning. Hence it is clear that, whichever climate lies at a given distance from the equator, its longest day exceeds the equinoctial day by that many half-hours.

units.la: De Numero Climatum utrinque (nam quod de Septemtrionalibus, idem de Meridionalibus judicium esse debet) variant Scriptores. Auctor Sphærae vetustissimam distinctionem sequutus, septem Climata recenset. Nam ultra Septimum Prisci vel non putarunt Habitationem esse commodam, vel ob longinquiorem Distantiam adire Loca, quæ ulterius posita, & explorare nequierunt. Eorum hæc est Tabula:
units.tr: Writers differ on the number of climates in each direction (for whatever judgement is made of the northern climates should be made of the southern too). The author of the Sphere, following the most ancient division, lists seven climates. For the ancients either did not think habitation beyond the seventh was convenient, or, because of the greater distance, they could not reach and explore the places lying further out. units.tr: Ptolemy bounds the inhabited earth toward the north from the equator at the twenty-ninth parallel. Of these, he separates the first twenty-five by intervals as large as the longest day increases by a quarter of an hour; the remaining four he marks off with a somewhat larger space, less exactly, and he notes the differences in meridian shadows. units.tr: In our own age, since both the greatest declination of the sun has been changed and most places up to the 72nd degree of latitude, and beyond toward the north, have come to be known, another notation of the climates has been devised. An example of it is found in Glareanus, but it is more obscure. In it the first column gives the names of the inhabitants throughout, by reason of the shadows; the second the number of climates, which are nineteen; the third the parallels, which in all are thirty-nine; the fourth the hours with parts, proceeding from twelve hours up to the middle of the year; the fifth explains how many degrees each parallel lies from the equator, until the 90th degree is reached; the sixth, seventh and eighth exhibit the ratio of shadows on gnomons, of which the one described first in place indicates the summer shadow, the second the equinoctial, and the third the winter shadow, up to the 25th parallel. Beyond that the ratios of the shadows fail, on account of proximity, which Ptolemy says is too narrow. The ninth and last notes the places through which the parallels pass. units.la: Sub Aequatore habitantibus; Sole bis singulis annis ad verticem veniente, primaque contingente Arietis, Librae, Cancri & Capricorni Puncta, quatuor sunt Solstitia: Alta duo, totidem Ima. His item duae Aestates, quum Sol ad vertices accedens in alterutro Punctorum est Aequinoctialium, vel prope duaeque Hiemes quum ad Tropicos deflectens in primis est Punctis Cancri vel Capricorni vel circiter. His quadruplices in anno sunt Umbrae. Quum enim Sol in alterutro versatur Punctorum Aequinoctialium tempore matutino, Umbra jacitur illis versus Occidentem; vespertino, in Orientem: Meridie Perpendicularis est; quum in Signis Septemtrionalibus, versus Austrum; quum in Australibus, in Septemtrionem. His denique oriuntur occiduntque Stellae quae juxta Polos. I | II | III | 12½ | 12½ | 4½ | 8½ | 21 | 16½ | 4 | 8½ | 32 | 37½ | Per Septemtrionalium Taprobanam. Per Australium Sinum.
units.tr: For those living under the Equator, the Sun comes twice a year to the zenith and touches the first points of Aries, Libra, Cancer and Capricorn. There are therefore four solstices: two high and two low. There are likewise two summers, when the Sun, approaching the zeniths, is at or near one of the equinoctial points, and two winters, when it turns toward the tropics and is at or about the first points of Cancer or Capricorn. Hence there are four kinds of shadow in the year. When the Sun is at one of the equinoctial points, the shadow falls to the west in the morning and to the east in the evening, and at midday it is perpendicular. When the Sun is in the northern signs, the shadow falls toward the south; when in the southern signs, toward the north. Finally, from these positions the stars near the poles rise and set. units.tr: For those who are between latitude 67 and the Arctic Pole, the horizon cuts the zodiac at two points equidistant from the beginning of Cancer, and the portion of the zodiac cut off always remains above the horizon. While the Sun passes through that portion, they have continuous day without night: so that if the cut-off portion equals one sign, the day lasts one month without night; if two signs, as many months, and so on. units.la: Hic manendi loca sortitis (si qui tamen sient) Horizon est Æquator; qui quum intersecet Zodiacum in duas partes æquales, quarum una relinquitur supra, altera infra; quum Sol superiorem medietatem à principio Arietis usque ad finem Virginis decurrit, Dies est sex Mensium; quum inferiorem à principio Librae ad finem Piscium, Nox totidem.
units.tr: Here, for those who have been allotted a dwelling place (if there are any such), the horizon is the Equator. It cuts the zodiac into two equal parts, one of which remains above and the other below. When the Sun runs through the upper half, from the beginning of Aries to the end of Virgo, the day lasts six months; when through the lower, from the beginning of Libra to the end of Pisces, the night lasts as many.
