units.la: De Terræ, respectu Adjunctorum, Divisione dixi: sequitur, quæ ratione Partium. Hujus Explicationem priusquam opere meo reliquo adgrediar, haud abs re fore duxi, aliorum sequutus consuetudinem, Voces quasdam Geographicas, quæ passim in sequentibus occurrent, præter jam indicatas, notare: priore quidem loco, quæ Maris; posteriore, quæ Terræ Maris sunt Fretum & Sinus.
units.tr: I have spoken of the division of the Earth with respect to its adjuncts; what follows is its division with respect to its parts. Before I take up the explanation of this in the rest of my work, I have thought it not out of place, following the custom of others, to note certain geographical terms that will occur everywhere in what follows, beyond those already indicated: first those of the sea, and then those of the land that are of the sea, namely Strait and Gulf.

units.la: Fretum angustissimum Pelagus est inter duas Continentes: ab Aquarum fremitu nonnullis: vel, ut Isidorus lib. xiii. Etymolog. cap. xviii ratiocinatur, quod ibi semper Mare ferveat: πορθμὸς Græcis: Θαλάττης Αὐλὼν Polluci: Belgæ vocant Hoffden; quod duo utrimque Capita Continentis & Promontoria excurrant: quod autem strictius ibi & angustius Mare, Galli dicunt Estroit, Itali Stretto, Hispani Estrecho. Fretorum alia primos in hoc globo ducunt ordines, alia secundos: illa Oceani, hæc Maris sunt Mediterranei. Oceani ultra Æquatorem duo sunt nobilissima, quæ Antarcticas terras, quales quales sint (nondum enim plene innotuerunt) separant a Continente; ab America quidem Australiore, Magellanicum; ab extremis autem Africæ, id quod inter Caput Bonæ Spei & Regionem Psittacorum, priore multo latius: liceat enim & hanc ibi Maris angustiam Fretis adcensere. Totidem, tamquam nominatis oppositia, cis Æquatorem, quæ Arcticas desiungunt ab eadem Continente: ab Asia quidem, Vaigatium, quod hodie Nassovium à Principe Mauritio Nassovio, vel si quod aliud ulterius; ab America vero Septemtrionaliore (auguror enim hoc ex Partium orbis positu) id, quod ab Inventore primo Davisium cœpit audire, nondum plene perlustratum; non dubito quin pervium vir audax nunciasset, nisi ab glacie fuisset repulsus. Quemadmodum ex Oceano, quem Australem dixi cap. vi, per Magellanicum Fretum in Occidentalem (Pacificum quidam appellant) pervium est iter: per id vero, quod Capiti Bonæ Spei adfremit, ex eodem in Eoum: sic citra Æquinoctialem ex Oceano Septemtrionali per Vaigatias Angustias in Eoum quem dixi, transitus patet; per Davisias autem in Oceanum, cujus memini, Occidentalem. Priora, nunquam ab glacie obsessa, semper sunt pervia hinc inde: fluctus enim Magellanici freti semper ab Oriente in Occidentem ferri, ideoque transitum ex Occidente in Orientem negari falso nonnulli ferunt, ut alibi ex nuperis Navigationibus docebo. Posteriora, ab glacie plerumque obstructa, non nisi æstivis anni temporibus, Sole Tropicum Cancri scandente, penetrari possunt. Nassovium enim gradu altitudinis Borealis 69½; Davisium autem 67 aut circiter. De Nassovio certum est: Nostrates enim Argonautæ bis prorsum vorsum navigarunt; Russi autem singulis tranant annis. De Davisio (ni futurum ita, falsus dicar Augur) docebit suo tempore audax Iapeti genus. Hæc de principum Fretorum inter se commissione obiter, & hic potius, quam nusquam. Quatuor his adnumerarim Britannicum & Herculeum: de quibus, us& de alijs, quæ varijs locis in Mari Mediterraneo, suis dicam locis.
units.tr: A strait is a very narrow stretch of sea between two continents. Some derive the name from the roaring of the waters, or, as Isidore reasons in Etymologies book 13, chapter 18, because the sea there always seethes. The Greeks call it πορθμός [porthmos]; Pollux calls it Θαλάττης Αὐλών [Thalattes Aulon]; the Belgians call it Hoffden, because two capes of the continent and promontories jut out on either side. The Gauls call a sea that is narrower and tighter there Estroit, the Italians Stretto, the Spanish Estrecho. Some straits hold the first rank on this globe, others the second: the former belong to the Ocean, the latter to the Mediterranean Sea. Beyond the Equator there are two most noble straits of the Ocean, which separate the Antarctic lands, whatever they are like (for they are not yet fully known), from the continent. From the more southern America it is the Magellanic; from the extremities of Africa it is the one between the Cape of Good Hope and the Region of the Parrots, which is much wider than the former, for we may count this narrowing of the sea there among the straits too. Equally many, set opposite to those named, lie on this side of the Equator, separating the Arctic lands from the same continent: from Asia, the Vaigatz Strait, which today is called Nassau after the Prince Maurice of Nassau, or whatever other name it may have further on; and from the more northern America (for I conjecture this from the position of the parts of the globe) the one whose first discoverer Davis began to be heard of, not yet fully explored. I do not doubt that the bold man would have reported it passable, had he not been driven back by ice. Just as from the Southern Ocean, which I called southern in chapter 6, a passage lies open through the Magellanic Strait into the Western Sea (some call it the Pacific), and through the strait that roars against the Cape of Good Hope from the same Ocean into the Eastern, so on this side of the Equinoctial a passage lies open from the Northern Ocean through the Vaigatz Narrows into the Eastern Sea I mentioned, and through the Davis Strait into the Western Ocean I spoke of. The former, never beset by ice, are always passable from either side, for the currents of the Magellanic Strait always run from east to west, and so some falsely claim that passage from west to east is denied, as I shall show elsewhere from recent voyages. The latter, for the most part blocked by ice, can be entered only in the summer months of the year, when the Sun climbs toward the Tropic of Cancer. For Nassau lies at 69½ degrees of northern altitude, and Davis at about 67 degrees. About Nassau there is no doubt: our own Argonauts sailed through it twice, going and returning, and the Russians cross it every year. About Davis (unless it turns out otherwise, and I am proved a false prophet) the bold race of Iapetus will teach us in its time. These remarks on the joining of the principal straits with one another I have made in passing, and here rather than nowhere. To these four I would add the British and the Herculean; of these, and of others which I shall discuss in their places, where they lie in the Mediterranean Sea, I shall speak in due course.

units.la: Sinus Isidoro lib. xiii. Etymolog. cap. xvii, dicitur maior Maris Recessus: alijs Aqua Terris se insinuans: Græcis κόλπος, qua notione & Gremium Plinio lib. iiii. natur. histor. cap. x, Pomponio lib. ii. Geogr. cap. iii, alijs: Ab Græca voce Italis Hispanisque Golfo; Gallis Goulfe. Belgis Natitis vocatur Inkam. Nam Golve Fluctus nobis vel unda Sinus, ut Freta, vel Oceani sunt, vel Maris Mediterranei: Ab utroque Sinus in omnes Mundi partes, Europam, Scythiam, Asiam, Africam & Americam, quin & in Insulas, innumeri: quibus quum nomina ab Locis vicinis, vel Regionibus vel opidis; earum descriptiones variasque nomenclaturas, ubi Methodus me poscet, designabo.
units.tr: Sinus, according to Isidore (Etymologiae, book 13, chapter 17), is a larger recess of the sea; for others it is water insinuating itself into the land. The Greeks call it κόλπος [kolpos], and in this sense Pliny (Natural History, book 4, chapter 10) and Pomponius (Geography, book 2, chapter 3), among others, use Gremium, "bosom". From the Greek word the Italians and Spaniards say Golfo, the French Goulfe. The Belgians call it Inkam, while Golve among us means a wave or surge of water. Bays, like straits, belong either to the Ocean or to the Mediterranean Sea. Bays of this kind are innumerable, running into every part of the world: Europe, Scythia, Asia, Africa and America, and even into islands. Since they take their names from nearby places, whether regions or towns, I shall describe them and their various names where the plan of this work requires it.

units.la: Tales sunt Voces Geographicæ Maris: Terræ dicuntur Isthmus, Promontorium, Regio, & similes.
units.tr: These are the geographical terms for the sea and the land: Isthmus, Promontorium, Regio, & similes.

units.la: Isthmus angusta est terra inter duo Maria. Hinc Bimaris quod Epitheton convenit non solum Peloponnesiaco, sed reliquis etiam omnibus; ut & quæ de eodem apud Ovidium in Epistola Medeæ,
units.tr: An Isthmus is a narrow strip of land between two seas. Hence the epithet "two-sea" (Bimaris) fits not only the Peloponnese but all the others as well, as in what Ovid says of it in Medea's Letter:

units.la: Quique Maris gemini distinet Isthmos aquas;
units.tr: Quique Maris gemini distinet Isthmos aquas;

units.la: quæque apud Lucanum lib. i. belli Pharsalici,
units.tr: and as Lucan says in book 1 of the Pharsalia:

units.la: qualiter undasQui secat, & geminum gracilis mare separat Isthmos. Nec patitur conferre Fretum.
units.tr: in the manner in which the slender Isthmus cuts through the waves and separates the twin seas. Nor does it allow the strait to be compared.

units.la: ῥῆ ἀμφιβάλλων nonnullis.
units.tr: ῥῆ ἀμφιβάλλων [rhē amphiballōn], as some call it.

units.la: Promontorium, Ἄκρον Græcis, mons in Mari prominens, Isidoro libro decimo quarto, capite vii, & quædam Terræ ad Littus extuberatio. Quum passim multa: nullum tamen nobilius, quam quod in extrema Africa, cui à Bona Spe nomen est inditum.
units.tr: Promontorium, in Greek Ἄκρον [akron], is a mountain jutting out into the sea (Isidore, book 14, chapter 7), or any projection of land onto the shore. Many occur everywhere, but none is more famous than the one at the far end of Africa, which has been given the name Cape of Good Hope.

units.la: Regio, χώρα, ab Rego; quod, priusquam Provinciæ fierent, Regiones ab Regibus regerentur; Tractus quibusdam; nonnullis Plaga; non indoctis etiam Scriptoribus Terra, speciliore notione; unde Terra Italia, apud Lucretium libro primo de natura rerum, & Agellium libr. i. noctium Atticar. cap. i; Terra Latium, apud Ennium libr. i. Annalium; Terra Sicilia apud Catonem in Originibus, cujus verba recitat Agellius lib. iii. cap. vii; Terra denique Thracia, apud eundem Ennium, laudante Varrone; me vero in meo ad doctum poetam commentario emendante.
units.tr: Regio, χώρα [chōra], comes from rego, "to rule", because before they became provinces, regions were ruled by kings. Some call it Tractus, others Plaga, and even learned writers use Terra in a narrower sense: thus Terra Italia in Lucretius, book 1 of On the Nature of Things, and in Gellius, Attic Nights, book 1, chapter 1; Terra Latium in Ennius, book 1 of the Annals; Terra Sicilia in Cato's Origines, whose words Gellius quotes in book 3, chapter 7; and finally Terra Thracia in the same Ennius, as Varro praises it, though I have corrected this in my commentary on that learned poet.

units.la: Regnum, βασιλεία, quod Regionibus Regi parentibus continetur. Regis nomen in Terris Imperij primum fuit, scribente Sallustio in Conjuratione Catilinaria.
units.tr: Regnum, βασιλεία [basileia], is the territory contained in regions obedient to a king. The title of king was first used of the lands of an empire, as Sallust writes in the Catilinarian Conspiracy.

units.la: Satrapia, vox Persica, Plinio lib. vi, cap. xx, regio quæ ab uno administratur Præsecto. Herodotus Νόμον vocat, quod peculiares illi leges.
units.tr: Satrapia is a Persian word (Pliny, book 6, chapter 20) for a region governed by one prefect. Herodotus calls it νόμος [nomos], because those peoples have their own laws.

units.la: Provincia Regio porro, vel procul, victa & bello adquisita, ut scribunt Hegesippus, Donatus, Isidorus, & alij. Regionem autem victam in Provinciæ formam redigendi ratio apud Veteres Romanos talis erat: Senatus populi Romani, acceptis ab Imperatore de superatis hostibus & Regione in potestatem addubta, litteris; secum de victis consultabat, & quid fieri placeret, per SC Imperatorem admonebat: decem aut quinque Legatis Senatoribus ad eum missis, ut ex eorum sententia de hostibus hostiumque Regione statueret. Imperator, mandatis acceptis, aut ex certa Senatus, si ita placuerat, voluntate, aut de communi Legatorum sententia, victis hostibus ignoscebat, vel Regionem illorum in Provinciæ formam redigebat. Ignoscere dicebatur; si liberos relinqueret, si suis uti Legibus, suosque creare, more patrio, Magistratus permitteret: in Provinciæ vero formam redigere; quum, ademtis vel immutatis Legibus, eos omnino Magistratui Romano, quotannis ab Urbe mittendo, subjiceret; & Vectigalia Conventusque constitueret. Quemadmodum autem Imperatores aut Duces exercituum Romanorum nomina sibi sumebant ex Regnis vel Provinciis: sic etiam ipsas sæpe Provincias subjugatas nomen suum ferre volebant: quod Opidis quoque evenisse docebunt in sequentibus exemplis. Territorium, apud Ciceronem & alios, universitas Agrorum, inquit Pomponius I.C, intra cuiusque Civitatis fines: dictum, quod maxime teratur; vel à Terrore, quo Iudex utitur in Iure dicundo. Ejusdem cum eo notionis Diæcesis; quæ tamen vox nunc fere usurpatur pro eo tractu, in quem jus suum exercet Episcopus.
units.tr: A Provincia is a region won and acquired by war, whether near or far, as Hegesippus, Donatus, Isidore and others write. The method by which the ancient Romans reduced a conquered region into the form of a province was as follows. The Senate of the Roman people, having received from the commander a letter about the defeated enemies and the region brought under their power, consulted with itself about the conquered and, by decree, advised the commander what it wished done. Ten or five senators were sent to him as legates, so that he might decide about the enemies and their region in accordance with their opinion. The commander, having received his instructions, either by the explicit will of the Senate, if that was its pleasure, or by the common opinion of the legates, pardoned the defeated enemies or reduced their region into the form of a province. They were said to be pardoned if he left them free, and allowed them to use their own laws and to create their own magistrates according to ancestral custom; but they were reduced into the form of a province when, their laws being taken away or altered, he made them wholly subject to a Roman magistrate sent yearly from the City, and fixed tributes and assize-courts. Just as the commanders or generals of the Roman armies took their names from kingdoms or provinces, so also they often wished the provinces they had subdued to bear their own name, as examples in what follows will show of towns too. Territorium, in Cicero and others, is the whole body of fields within the boundaries of each city; Pomponius the jurist says it was so called because it is greatly worn down (teratur), or from the terror (terror) which a judge uses in administering justice. Diæcesis has the same meaning, though this word is now used almost only of the district over which a bishop exercises his jurisdiction.

units.la: Vrbs ab orbe; quod, ut post Varronem vult Isidorus, in orbem antiquitus fierent Vrbes: vel, ut idem, ab Vrbo, Aratri parte, quo Muri describebantur; hoc quo modo quibusque ritibus, saltem in Latio, fieri solitum, explicant Varro libro iv. de LL, Plutarchus in Romulo, Dionysius lib. i. Antiquit. Romanar. Livius libro i. ab V.C, Isidorus lib. xv. Originum, cap. ii, Servius ad Aeneidem Virgilianam, & alij.
units.tr: Vrbs (city) comes from orbis, because, as Isidore prefers after Varro, cities were formerly built in a circle; or, as he also says, from urbo, the part of a plough by which the walls were marked out. How this was done, and with what rites, at least in Latium, is explained by Varro in book 4 of On the Latin Language, Plutarch in his Life of Romulus, Dionysius in book 1 of the Roman Antiquities, Livy in book 1 from the founding of the City, Isidore in book 15 of the Origines, chapter 2, Servius on Virgil's Aeneid, and others.

units.la: Quemadmodum autem Ἀστυ proprie de Athenis; de Alexandria vero Ægypti, πόλις: sic Vrbs per Antonomasiam, inquit Quintilianus lib. viii. Oratoriarum Institut. cap. ii, de Roma; quum cetera dicantur Opida. Civitas conlecta Civium multitudo. Opidum Ciceroni, Varroni, Festo, Isidoro, aliis, ab Ope; munitur enim Opis & auxilij causa; vel quod opus eo sit ad vitam tuto & absque periculo transigendam; vel quod Opere muniantur Mœnia, quo munitius sit opidum; vel denique ab Oppositione Murorum contra vim & incursiones hostium. Opidorum originem sic indicat Isidorus lib. xv, capite jam indicato (proculdubio ex libro M. Tullij i. de Gloria; innuente, ex Verrio Flacco, Festo lib. xiii. de Verbor. Significat.) Homines, inquit, primum, tamquam nudi & inermes, nec contra belluas præsidia habebant, nec receptacula frigoris & caloris; nec ipsi inter se homines ab hominibus satis erant tuti. Tandem naturali solertia speluncis silvestribusque tegumentis Tuguria sibi & Casas virgultis arundinibusque contexuerunt; quo esset vita tutior, nec ys, qui nocere possent, aditus esset. Hæc est origo Opidorum; quæ, quod opem darent, idcirco Opida nominata dixerunt. Vrbes Nomina, cum aliunde, tum ab Conditoribus sumere solitas, testatur Caput Orbis, Roma; quam sic, non Romulam, dixit Romulus, ut, quemadmodum scribit ex Festo Paullus Diaconus, ampliore vocabuli significatu prosperiora suæ Patriæ ominaretur: Item ab ijs, per quos erant vel amplificatæ, teste Vegetio lib. iv. de re militari Prologo; vel restauratæ, quod notat D. Hieronymus principio sui Chronici, de Helenopoli. Exempla suppeditat Isidorus lib. xv. Orig. cap. i, De Vrbe, Opido, Civitate sic eleganter M. Tullius i. de Republ. Quam quum locis manuque sepsissent, ejusmodi conjunctionem tectorum Opidum vel Vrbem appellarunt, delubris distinctam spaciisque communibus. Omnis ergo populus, qui est talis cætus multitudinis, qualem expososui, Civitas est.
units.tr: Just as Ἀστυ [astu] properly refers to Athens, and πόλις [polis] to Alexandria in Egypt, so Vrbs, by antonomasia, refers to Rome, as Quintilian says in book 8, chapter 2 of the Institutes of Oratory, while all other places are called towns (opida). A Civitas is a gathered multitude of citizens. Cicero, Varro, Festus, Isidore and others derive Opidum from ops (help): a town is fortified for the sake of help and protection, or because it is needed for living safely and without danger, or because its walls are fortified with works, so that the town is more strongly defended, or finally from the setting of walls against the force and attacks of enemies. Isidore, in book 15, in the chapter already cited (no doubt drawing on Cicero's book On Glory, book 1, as Verrius Flaccus and Festus, book 13 of On the Meaning of Words, suggest), describes the origin of towns thus: "At first men, as if naked and unarmed, had no defences against beasts, no shelter from cold and heat, and men were not safe from one another. At last, by natural skill, they built for themselves huts (tuguria) in caves and forest coverings, and houses (casae) woven of twigs and reeds, so that life might be safer and there might be no access for those who could do harm. This is the origin of towns, which, because they gave help (opem), were called opida." That cities have often taken names both from other places and from their founders is shown by the capital of the world, Rome, which Romulus called not Romula, so that, as Paulus the Deacon writes from Festus, he might augur better fortunes for his country from the wider meaning of the word. Cities were also named after those by whom they were enlarged, as Vegetius attests in the Prologue to book 4 of On Military Affairs, or restored, as St Jerome notes at the beginning of his Chronicle concerning Helenopolis. Isidore, in book 15 of the Origines, chapter 1, On the City, Town and Civitas, supplies examples, and Marcus Tullius puts it elegantly in book 1 of On the Republic: "When they had surrounded their houses with place and hand, they called such a joining of dwellings an oppidum or urbs, distinguished by temples and common spaces. Therefore every people which is such a gathering of a multitude, as I have described, is a civitas."

units.la: Municipium urbs erat, quæ Civitatis Romanæ gaudebat Privilegijs. Municipiorum duo erant genera; quædam, quæ omnia, quorum memini, Priuilegia habebat præter Suffragii lationem; quædam, quæ Civitatem ipsam cum Suffragio obtinuerant. De priore genere Servius, Municipium, inquit, id genus hominum dicitur, qui, quum Romam venissent, neque Cives Romani essent; participes tamen fuerunt omnium rerum ad Munus fungendum una cum Romanis Civibus, præterquam de Suffragio ferendo, aut Magistratu capiendo. Sic Festus lib. xi de verbor.significc. Municipes erant, qui quum ex alijs Civitatibus Romam venissent (hoc est; ut docti Viri interpretandum censent, Civitate donati essent) eis non licebat Magistratum capere, sed tantum Muneris partem. De posteriore genere Agellius lib. xvi Noct. Attic. cap. xiii. Municipes sunt Cives Romani ex Municipys suo jure & legibus utentes, Muneris tantum cum Populo Romano honorarij participes: a quo Munere capessendo appellati videntur, nullis aliis necessitatibus adstricti, neque ulla Populi Romani lege, quum numquam Populi eorum fundus factus esset. His sua erant in suis Municipijs Sacra quæ Municipalia dicebantur, de quibus sic Festus: Municipalia Sacra vocantur, quæ ab initio habuerunt ante Civitatem Romanam acceptam, quæ observare eos voluerunt Pontifices, & eo more facere, quo fecissent antiquitus. De Municipibus Vlpianus IC. lib. i: Municipes aut Naturitas facit, aut Manumissio, aut Adoptio: & proprie quidem Municipes appellantur Muneris participes, recepti in Civitatem, ut Munera nobiscum facerent. In Municipijs porro, quemadmodum Romæ, tres Ordines fuisse, Decuriones, Equites & Plebem; Consilia publica duo, Senatus & Populi; Magistratus item, Dictatorem, Duumviros, Quatuorviros, Censores, Ædiles & Quæstores; Sacerdotes denique Flamines Municipiorum: ex Decurionum etiam ordine Decemprimos legi solitos, qui, ut scriptum est apud Hermogenianum, Tributorum exactioni ita præerant, ut, si quæ detrimenta Fisco mortuorum causa contraheret, ipsi suis sumtibus resarcirent: plene notant ex varijs Scriptoribus in Antiquitatum Romanarum historia alij.
units.tr: A Municipium was a town which enjoyed the privileges of Roman citizenship. There were two kinds of municipalities: some had all the privileges I have mentioned except the right to vote; others had obtained full citizenship with the vote. Of the first kind Servius says: "Municipium is the name given to people who, having come to Rome, were not Roman citizens, yet shared in all things relating to the performance of public duties together with the Roman citizens, except voting and holding magistracies." So Festus, book 11 of On the Meaning of Words: "Municipes were those who, having come to Rome from other states (that is, as learned men think it should be understood, having been granted citizenship), were not allowed to hold magistracies, but only a share of the public duties." Of the second kind, Gellius, Attic Nights, book 16, chapter 13: "Municipes are Roman citizens who, by their own right and laws, live in their municipalities, sharing with the Roman people only the honorary duties, from the performance of which they seem to have been named, bound by no other obligations, and by no law of the Roman people, since their land never became the land of that people." These municipalities had their own sacred rites, called Municipalia, of which Festus says: "The Municipalia Sacra are those which they had from the beginning, before receiving Roman citizenship, which the pontiffs wished them to observe, and to perform in the manner they had performed them in ancient times." On municipes, the jurist Ulpian, book 1, says: "Municipes are made so either by birth, or by manumission, or by adoption; and properly they are called municipes, as sharers in public duties, received into the citizenship so that they might perform public duties with us." In the municipalities, moreover, as at Rome, there were three orders: decurions, knights and commons; two public councils, of the Senate and of the People; magistrates likewise, a dictator, duumvirs, quattuorvirs, censors, aediles and quaestors; and finally priests, the flamines of the municipalities. From the order of the decurions were also chosen the so-called decemprimi, who, as is written in Hermogenianus, presided over the collection of tributes in such a way that, if they incurred any loss to the treasury through the death of taxpayers, they made it good from their own resources. Others, from various writers, fully note these matters in their histories of Roman antiquities.

units.la: Coloniæ
units.tr: Colonies

units.la: Colonia Isidoro urbs, quæ ob Indigenarum inopiam novis Cultoribus impletur; vel aliunde deportatis Opidanis nova exstruitur. De iis sic Agellius loco jam indicato, ubi eas committit cum Municipiis: Sed Coloniarum alia necessitudo est. Non enim veniunt extrinsecus in Civitatem, nec suis radicibus nituntur, ut Municipia; sed ex Civitate quasi propagatæ sunt, & Iura Institutaque omnia Populi Romani, non sui arbitrij, habent. Magis igitur Coloniarum, quam Municipiorum, conditio obnoxia erat minusque libera; potior tamen & præstabilior propter amplitudinem & majestatem Populi Romani: cujus, ut scribit Onuphrius Panuinius, Coloniæ quasi parvæ quædam erant effigies. Deducendi Colonias mos ab Romulo; primo Romanorum rege, institutus, frequentissimus deinde perseveravit apud Romanos. Nam, ut late scribit Dionysius Halicarnass. lib. II. Antiquit. Romanarum, hostibus victis agrique & regionis parte multatis, in agris captis vel novas urbes condebant; vel in antiquitus conditas, veteribus colonis alio migrare jussis, cum novorum ex urbe Civium per III Viros, ad id creatos, deducebant numerum, qui agro capto colendo sufficere posset. Hi in Coloniam deducti evestigio novam instituebant reip. administrandæ rationem, Romanæ plane similem. Coloniarum Resp. in Legibus Legumque Curatoribus posita erat. Leges vel à Populo Romano accipiebant, vel ipsæ sibi per Senatum aut Populum condebant. Legum Curatores vel Magistratus erant, vel Sacerdotes: hi Divinarum; illi Humanarum. Sacerdotes erant Pontifices & Augures; quorum sæpe mentio in antiquis marmoribus. Magistratus, ut Decuriones, Duumviri, Quatuorviri, Ædiles, Quæstores creari soliti ex Colonis. Quum enim, ut Romæ Senatores erant & Populus, in Colonijs essent Decuriones & Plebs; ex Decurionibus singulis annis duo vel Quatuorviri Iuri dicundo creabantur, pro Coloniæ quantitate. Hi Consulum erant instar Romanorum. Creabatur & Ædilis, qui Viarum, Ædificiorum publicorum, Annonæ, & locandorum Redituum; item Quæstor, qui Ærarij publici curam habebat: in reliquis omnibus more, legibus & institutis Romanis vivebant. Censores etiam in Coloniis erant, ibique Censum agebant, uti constat ex non uno Livii loco. Leguntur & fuisse Coloniarum Patroni: sic Bononienses in Antoniorum Clientela fuisse prodit Suetonius in Augusti vita cap. xvi; Lacedæmonios in Claudiorum, idem in Tiberio cap. v i; Puteolanos in Cassiorum, M. Tullius in Philippicis; alios in aliorum fuisse tutela loquuntur alij Scriptores & vetusta Lapidum Monimenta.
units.tr: Colonia is, according to Isidore, a city that is filled with new inhabitants because of a lack of natives, or a new town built from citizens brought in from elsewhere. Agellius, in the passage already cited, where he compares colonies with municipalities, says of them: But colonies stand in a different relation. They do not come into the state from outside, and they do not rest on their own roots as municipalities do; rather they are, as it were, offshoots of the state, and they have all the laws and institutions of the Roman people, not of their own choosing. The condition of colonies was therefore more dependent and less free than that of municipalities, yet it was the more favoured and more distinguished, on account of the greatness and majesty of the Roman people, of which, as Onuphrius Panvinius writes, the colonies were, as it were, small likenesses. The practice of founding colonies was instituted by Romulus, the first king of the Romans, and it continued very frequently among the Romans afterwards. For, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus writes at length in the second book of his Roman Antiquities, when the enemy had been defeated and a part of their land and territory had been taken away, they either founded new towns on the captured land or, in towns founded long before, ordered the old colonists to move elsewhere; and they then led out, with three men appointed for this purpose, a number of new citizens from the city sufficient to cultivate the conquered land. Once led out into the colony, these settlers at once set up a system of government quite like the Roman one. The government of a colony rested on its laws and on the guardians of the laws. The laws were received either from the Roman people, or the colonists made them for themselves through the Senate or the people. The guardians of the laws were either magistrates or priests: the priests were for divine matters, the magistrates for human ones. The priests were the pontiffs and augurs, who are often mentioned in ancient inscriptions. The magistrates, namely the decurions, duumvirs, quaestors and aediles, were usually chosen from among the colonists. For since at Rome there were senators and the people, so in the colonies there were decurions and the common people; from among the decurions, two or four men were appointed each year to administer justice, according to the size of the colony. These served as consuls did among the Romans. An aedile was also appointed, who had charge of the roads, public buildings, the grain supply and the letting of revenues; likewise a quaestor, who had the care of the public treasury. In all other matters they lived by Roman custom, laws and institutions. There were also censors in the colonies, and they carried out the census there, as is clear from more than one passage of Livy. We also read that colonies had patrons: thus Suetonius, in the life of Augustus, chapter 16, reports that the people of Bologna were under the protection of the Antonii; that the Lacedaemonians were under that of the Claudii, as he says in the life of Tiberius, chapter 6; that the people of Puteoli were under that of the Cassii, as Marcus Tullius says in the Philippics; and other writers and ancient monuments of stone speak of others being under the protection of others.

units.la: Præfecturæ erant Opida Italiæ, in quibus qui habitabant nec suis Legibus, ut Municipes, vivebant; nec ullis de suo corpore Magistratus creare poterant, ut Coloni; sed à Magistratibus Roma missis regebantur ijs Legibus, quas Romanus Magistratus dixisset: qui quum Præfectus diceretur, eam ob causam appellabantur Præfecturæ. De iis Festus lib. xiv de verb. signif. Præfecturæ hæ vocantur in Italia, in quibus & ius dicebatur, & Nundinæ agebantur: & erat quædam earum Respublica; neque tamen Magistratus suos habebant: In quas Legibus Præfecti mittebantur quotannis, qui jus dicerent: Quarum genera fuere duo: alterum, in quas solebant ire Præfecti decem, Populi suffragio creati; & erant hæc opida, Capua, Cumæ, Casilinum, Vulturnum, Linternum, Puteoli, Acerræ, Suessula, Atella, Calatia; alterum, in quas Prætor Urbanus quotannis Præfectos ex legibus mittebat, ut Fundi, Formiæ, Cære, Venafrum, Allisæ, Privernum, Anagnia, Frusino, Reate, Saturnia, Nursia, Arpinum, & alia complura. Exemplum in Capua, quam nominat Festus, apud Livium lib. xxvi; ubi inter alia, post varias in Senatu de Urbis victæ statu disceptationes, sic inquit: Ceterum habitari tantum, tamquam Urbem, Capuam, frequentariique placuit: nullum corpus Civitatis, nec Senatus, nec Plebis Concilium, nec Magistratus esse. Sine Consilio publico, sine Imperio; multitudinem nullius rei inter se sociam ad consensum inhabilem fore: Præfectum ad jura reddenda Roma quotannis missuros. Illud satis constat ex variis Veterum Auctorum scriptis, in Præfecturis tres fuisse Ordines, Summum, Medium, Infimum: Summum Ordinem Conventum dici solitum; Medium Equitum; Tertium fuisse Populi vel Plebis: Magistratus inibi fuisse duplices: alios Roma mitti, alios è Præfectura creari solitos: qui Roma mittebantur, Præfectos appellatos, jus dixisse; qui è Præfectura creabantur, ut Ædiles & Quæstores, publicæ alicui curationi præfuisse. Præfectos Festus Quatuorviros aut Sexviros dictos tradit. Nominantur & à Cicerone lib. III de Nat. Deor. Sexprimi in Præfecturis; qui fortean Decemprimis Municipalibus respondebant. Occurrit etiam frequenter apud Geographos aliosque Scriptores in Locis, Opidis praecipue, designandis Fori vocabulum. Fora in Italia & Provincijs erant, partim ubi Praetores juris dicundi causa Conventum habebant, partim quae Nundinationis gratia erant instituta. De utraque Vocis notione ex Festi lib. vi. de Verbor. signif. Paullus Diaconus in rutis cavis: Forum sex modis intelligitur. Primo Negociationis locus, ut Forum Flaminium, Forum Iulium, ab eorum nominibus, qui ea Fora constituenda curarunt. Et paullo post: Tertio, quum is, qui Provincia praeft, Forum agere dicitur; quum Civitates vocat, & de controversiis eorum cognoscit. Ad posteriorem respicit etiam Nonius Marcellus, quum inquit, Fora fuisse Loca, in quibus jus dicebatur.
units.tr: Præfecturæ were towns of Italy whose inhabitants lived neither under their own laws, as municipal citizens did, nor could they appoint any magistrates from their own body, as colonists could; instead they were governed by magistrates sent from Rome, under the laws that the Roman magistrate had pronounced. Because such a magistrate was called a prefect, these towns were named prefectures for this reason. Festus speaks of them in the fourteenth book of his work on the meaning of words: These are called prefectures in Italy, in which justice was administered and markets were held, and which had a certain public organisation, yet had no magistrates of their own. Prefects were sent to them every year under the laws to administer justice. There were two kinds of these: one kind, to which ten prefects used to go, chosen by the vote of the people, and these towns were Capua, Cumae, Casilinum, Vulturnum, Linternum, Puteoli, Acerrae, Suessula, Atella and Calatia; the other kind, to which the urban praetor sent prefects every year under the laws, such as Fundi, Formiae, Caere, Venafrum, Allifae, Privernum, Anagnia, Frusino, Reate, Saturnia, Nursia, Arpinum, and many others. An example is Capua, which Festus names, in Livy, book 26, where, among other things, after various debates in the Senate about the condition of the defeated city, he says: But it was decided that the city of Capua should be inhabited only as a city, and be kept full: that there should be no corporate body of the state, neither Senate nor assembly of the people nor magistrates. Without a public council and without authority, the multitude, having no common interest, would be unfit for agreement; the prefect would be sent from Rome every year to administer justice. It is quite certain from various writings of the ancient authors that in the prefectures there were three orders: the highest, the middle and the lowest. The highest order was usually called the Conventus; the middle, that of the knights; the third was that of the people or commons. There were two kinds of magistrates there: some were sent from Rome, others were usually chosen from within the prefecture. Those sent from Rome were called prefects and administered justice; those chosen from within the prefecture, like the aediles and quaestors, presided over some public charge. Festus says that the prefects were called quattuorviri or sexviri. They are also named by Cicero in the third book of On the Nature of the Gods as the six chief men in the prefectures, who perhaps corresponded to the municipal decemprimi. The word Fori also frequently occurs in the geographers and other writers when places, especially towns, are described. Fora in Italy and the provinces were partly places where the praetors held assize for the sake of administering justice, and partly were established for the sake of a market. Paulus Diaconus, in his epitome of Festus, gives both meanings of the word: Forum is understood in six ways. First, a place of trade, such as the Forum Flaminium or the Forum Julium, named after the men who took care to establish those fora. And a little later: Third, when the man who presides over a province is said to hold a forum, when he summons the states and hears their disputes. Nonius Marcellus also looks to the latter meaning when he says that fora were places in which justice was administered.

units.la: Legionis etiam nomen Opida saepe gerere leguntur. Quum enim Augustus Imperator bellis civilibus confectis, & pace cum Populo Romano terra marique parta, rerum potitus esset; multas militum Legiones legit, easque certis auctoramentis habuit mercenarias; quae certis stationibus ad Imperii Romani limites contra barbaras nationes, earumque incursiones, dispositae; &, vel Fluviorum, ut Rheni, Danubii, Euphratis magnitudine, vel montibus asperrimis, vel desertis & impervijs locis munitae, paullatim in Opida vel vicos degenerarunt: quemadmodum passim in reliquo meo Opere videbimus. Legionibus huiusmodi (nam & hoc in genere monendum hic) nomina erant ex variis causis: ab Ordine, quo unaquaeque earum in aliquo loco constituta fuerat, ut Prima, Secunda, Tertia, Decima, Vicesima; quumque saepe fieret, ut duae vel tres variis in locis constitutae, omnes Primae vel Secundae, vel Tertiae appellarentur, visum est eas inter se cognominibus distinguere, ut una quidem esset Prima Adjutrix, alia Prima Minervia, alia, dicis gratia, Prima Parthica. Vel ab Nominibus vocabantur eorum, qui eas instituerant: ut Augusta, Claudiana, Galbiana, Flavia, Ulpia, Trajana: vel a Provincijs devictis; ut Parthica, Scythica, Gallica, Arabica, Hispanienses: vel ab locis, in quibus primo institutae manserunt; ut Italica, Fretensis, Cyrenaica: vel ab Nominibus Deorum Dearumque, quibus earumdem auctores erant addicti; quales Minervia, Apollinaris, Veneria: vel denique ab alijs Eventibus; ut Gemina, Adiutrix, Martia, Victrix, Fulminatrix, Rapax, Alauda, Primigenia, &c id genus aliae.
units.tr: The name of legion is also often read as borne by towns. For when Augustus, as emperor, having finished the civil wars and having secured peace with the Roman people by land and sea, had taken control of affairs, he enlisted many legions of soldiers and kept them as paid troops with fixed pay. These were posted at fixed stations along the limits of the Roman Empire against the barbarian nations and their incursions; and, fortified either by the size of rivers such as the Rhine, the Danube and the Euphrates, or by very rugged mountains, or by deserted and impassable places, they gradually declined into towns or villages, as we shall see everywhere in the rest of my work. The legions of this kind (for this also should be noted here) had their names from various causes: from the order in which each of them had been stationed in some place, such as First, Second, Third, Tenth, Twentieth; and since it often happened that two or three legions stationed in different places were all called First, or Second, or Third, it was thought fit to distinguish them from one another by surnames, so that one was the First Adjutrix, another the First Minervia, and another, for the sake of example, the First Parthica. Or they were named after the men who had founded them, such as Augusta, Claudiana, Galbiana, Flavia, Ulpia, Trajana; or after the provinces they had conquered, such as Parthica, Scythica, Gallica, Arabica, Hispaniensis; or after the places where they first remained, such as Italica, Fretensis, Cyrenaica; or after the names of gods and goddesses to whom their founders were devoted, such as Minervia, Apollinaris, Veneria; or finally after other events, such as Gemina, Adiutrix, Martia, Victrix, Fulminatrix, Rapax, Alauda, Primigenia, and other names of that kind.

units.la: Emporium locus Mercatus, vel Nundinarum, ἐμπόριον. Talis Barn. Mesopotamiae Municipium, de quo sic loquitur Ammianus lib. xiv: Refertum, inquit, Mercatoribus opulentis; ubi annua solennitate prope Septembris initium ad Nundinas magna promiscua fortuna convenit multitudo; ad commercanda, quae Indi mittunt, & alia plurima: quae terra marique consueta.
units.tr: Emporium [ἐμπόριον] is a place of trade or of a market. Such was Barna, a municipal town of Mesopotamia, of which Ammianus speaks thus in book 14: It is crowded, he says, with wealthy merchants, where, at a yearly festival near the beginning of September, a great and mixed crowd of people gathers at the market to trade in what the Indians send and in many other things that are usual by land and sea.

units.la: Porro Vici, Castella, Pagi sunt ij, inquit Isidorus lib. xv. cap. ii, qui nulla dignitate Civitatis ornantur; sed vulgari hominum conventu incoluntur, & propter parvitatem sui majoribus civitatibus attribuuntur. Castellum apud M. Ciceronem & Caesarem, Opidulum muro cinctum. Vicus locus pluribus Villis domibusve rusticis coagmentatus, spacio aliquantulo ab Urbe remotus, nullis moenibus circumdatus, dictus Isidoro ab vicinis tantum habitatoribus; vel quod Vias habeat tantum sine Muris; vel quod vice sit Civitatis. Dicitur & Pagus, χώρα τών πρυγών: circa Fontes enim habitare gaudent Rustici, ut facilis sit aquatio, inquit Festus. Plura de his apud Aldum Manutium lib. ii. Quaesitorum, Epist. viii.
units.tr: Further, Vici, Castella, Pagi are, says Isidore in book xv, chapter ii, those which are adorned with no dignity of a city, but are inhabited by a common gathering of people, and on account of their smallness are assigned to the larger cities. Castellum in Cicero and Caesar is a small town (opidulum) surrounded by a wall. Vicus is a place put together from several villas or country houses, set some little distance from the city and surrounded by no walls; Isidore says it is so called only from its neighbouring inhabitants, or because it has streets but no walls, or because it stands in place of a city. It is also called Pagus, χώρα τών πρυγών: for country folk like to live around springs, so that watering is easy, says Festus. More on these things in Aldus Manutius, book ii of the Quaesita, letter viii.

units.la: Silva, quae ὕλη, id est, materia lignisque abundat. Saltus densior silua & opacior; in qua aestivare pascique solent ferae, quod, ut notat Isidorus, arbores ibi saliant in altum: videndus & Aelius lib. ii. significationum, quae ad ius pertinent, apud Festum. Nemus locus arboribus consitus, amoenus, ut Festus scribit, virens, opacitate umbrosa, frigore gratus. Lucus densa intactis arboribus Silua, Numini alicui consecrata, eamque ob causam incidua: dicta Servio per antiphrasin, quod non luceat; vel, ut censet Isidorus, quod Soli lucem detrahat; idem & ab collucendo derivat, quod crebra ibi lumina lucerent ob religionem cultumque Gentilium. Roboretum Agellio lib. ii. cap. xx: septum e robusteis tabulis, intra quod Cervi & Ferae includuntur. Arbustum locus amoenitatis vel utilitatis gratia arboribus consitus. Tesqua Accio, Ciceroni alijsque, inculta, deserta, inhospita, aspera, difficilia loca; ipso situ silentioque religionem & horrorem incutientia. Varroni quasi Tuesca a tuendis sacris.
units.tr: Silva, which is ὕλη, that is, abounds in timber and wood. Saltus is a denser and darker wood, in which wild beasts are wont to spend the summer and graze, because, as Isidore notes, the trees there leap up on high; see also Aelius, book ii of the Significations that pertain to law, in Festus. Nemus is a place planted with trees, pleasant, as Festus writes, green, shady with dense cover, and pleasing for its coolness. Lucus is a dense wood of untouched trees, consecrated to some deity, and for that reason not to be cut; Servius says it is so called by antiphrasis, because it gives no light; or, as Isidore thinks, because it takes light from the sun; he also derives it from collucere, because many lights shone there on account of Gentile religion and worship. Roboretum (Agellius, book ii, chapter xx) is an enclosure made of stout boards, within which stags and wild beasts are shut up. Arbustum is a place planted with trees for the sake of pleasure or use. Tesqua, in Accius, Cicero and others, are uncultivated, desert, inhospitable, rough, difficult places, which by their very situation and silence inspire religious awe and dread. For Varro it is as if Tuesca from guarding sacred things.

units.la: Campus amplum Terrae spacium, a Capiendo, ut vult Varro: vel, ut Isidorus, ab Graeca voce καμπός, humi. Ager, quod, ut cum M. Terentio Varrone censet Aelius
units.tr: Campus is a wide expanse of land, from capiendo (taking), as Varro would have it; or, as Isidore has it, from the Greek word καμπός, a bending of the ground. Ager, which, as Aelius thinks along with Marcus Terentius Varro,

units.la: Donatus, in eo multa agenda. Pascuum, ubi pecora pascunt. Pratum, in quo ad percipiendum fructum falce duntaxat opus est; quod sine ope, ut scribunt Varro & Columella lib. ii. de re rustica cap. xvii, paratum sit. Arvum Varroni i. de re rustica, cap. xxix, & Festo; quod aratum necdum satum est: Seges quod aratum & satum.
units.tr: Donatus, is a place where much has to be done. Pascuum is where flocks graze. Pratum is a place in which only the scythe is needed to gather the crop; as Varro and Columella write in book ii of On Farming, chapter xvii, it is ready without human labour. Arvum, according to Varro, On Farming, book i, chapter xxix, and Festus, is land that has been ploughed but not yet sown: seges is what has been both ploughed and sown.

units.la: Mons tumor, inquit Isidorus lib. xiv. Orig. cap. viii, terrarum altissimus; quasi eminens: Ejus partes Iugum vel Cacumen; Supercilium eminentior montis vertex; Dorsum vel Clivus, montis latus; Radix, vel, ut Caesari aliisque dicitur, Pes; quam vocem hac notione multi populi in suo idiomate agnoscunt. Collis minor mons a colendo Varroni; quasi Collum, Isidoro. Tumulus Isidoro mons brevis, quasi tumens tellus. Vallis planicies duobus lateribus inclusa, hinc inde montibus vallata: Valles vocat Isidorus humilia loca, quasi vulsa; hinc Convallis, Vallis undique montibus circumdata. Rupes, quae & Petra vel Cautes, praeruptum & inaccessum saxum, a rumpendo: ejus extremitas Crepido. Scopulus mons saxeus vel rupes e mari eminens, cujus acumen Murex. Fauces Isidoro angustorum locorum aditus inter arduos montes ab Faucium similitudine. Sed minutiora sunt haec, quam ut diutius immorer.
units.tr: Mons, says Isidore in book xiv of the Origines, chapter viii, is a swelling of the earth, the highest of lands, as if standing out. Its parts are the Iugum or Cacumen (ridge or summit); Supercilium is the more prominent peak of a mountain; Dorsum or Clivus is the flank of a mountain; Radix, or, as Caesar and others say, Pes (foot), a word which many peoples recognise in this sense in their own language. Collis is a smaller mountain, from colere according to Varro; as if Collum (neck), according to Isidore. Tumulus is, for Isidore, a short mountain, as if a swelling of the earth. Vallis is a plain enclosed on two sides, walled in by mountains on either side; Isidore calls valles low places, as if torn out; hence convallis, a valley surrounded on all sides by mountains. Rupes, which is also petra or cautes, is a steep and inaccessible rock, from rumpere (to break); its edge is the crepido. Scopulus is a rocky mountain or cliff standing out of the sea, whose pointed top is the murex. Fauces, for Isidore, are the approaches of narrow places between steep mountains, named from the likeness to a throat. But these are too minor matters for me to dwell on longer.

units.la: Vnum, quod huic loco non male convenit, adscribam: DEVM Providentia sua singulari singulis Ecclesijs, Populis, Regnis, Provincijs suos speciatim Angelos, a quibus custodiantur, adsignasse: quod ex cap. Iehof. v, 13. Danijel. x. 13, & alijs Sacrae Scripturae locis colligunt Patres, Clemens Romanus lib. ii. Recognit. Clemens Alexandrinus lib. vi. Stromat. Theodosius Orat. x. in Danijel. D: Isidorus lib. i. de Summo Bono cap. ii; & ex Philone atque Nazianzeno Arethas in i. & ii. cap. Apocalypf. Quin, antea quam caperentur ab Tito Romanorum principe Hierosolymae, auditam vocem, quae testabatur migrare Numen urbis, memoriae produnt non modo Tacitus lib. iv. Histor. sed & Iosephus lib. vi. de bello Iudaico, & Nicephorus lib. iii. Histor. Ecclef. cap. iv. Gentiles, qui Sacrarum Litterarum lectionem non omnino avorsabantur; veram mentem non adsequuti, ut alia multa, sic sacrosanctam illam de Angelorum praesidio sententiam inibi animadversam plane pervorterunt quosdam Genios commenti Provinciarum, Urbium, Coloniarum; ut testatur Tertullianus libro de Idololatr. & legere est apud Symmachum in libello ad Theodosium Imperatorem, Varios, inquit, Custodes urbibus Mens Divina destribuit; ut Anima Nascentibus; ita Populis Fatales Genij dividuntur. Eo pertinent Poetae illa: Dodone tibi Iupiter sacrata est; Iunoni Samos & Mycenae diti; Vnde Tenaros Aequorisque regi; Pallas Cecropias tuetur arces; Delphos Pythius Orbis umbilicum; Creten Delia Cynthiosque colles, Faunus Manalon, Arcadumque silvas, Est tutela Rhodos beata Solis; Gades Herculis humidumque Tybur, Cyllene celeri Deo nivosa; Tardo gratior astuosa Lesbos: Aetnaea Cererem nurus frequentant; Raptam Cyzicos ostreosa Divam; Formosam Venerem Cnidos Paphosque,
units.tr: One thing, which fits this place not badly, I shall add: that God, by his singular providence, has assigned to individual churches, peoples, kingdoms and provinces particular angels by whom they are guarded; the Fathers gather this from Joshua 5:13, Daniel 10:13, and other places of Holy Scripture: Clement of Rome, book ii of the Recognitions; Clement of Alexandria, book vi of the Stromata; Theodoret, Oration x on Daniel; Isidore, book i On the Supreme Good, chapter ii; and from Philo and Nazianzen, Arethas on chapters i and ii of the Apocalypse. Indeed, before Jerusalem was taken by Titus, the Roman emperor, a voice was heard testifying that the divinity of the city was departing; this is recorded not only by Tacitus, book iv of the Histories, but also by Josephus, book vi of the Jewish War, and Nicephorus, book iii of the Ecclesiastical History, chapter iv. The Gentiles, who did not altogether shun the reading of Holy Writ, not having attained the true sense, as in many other things, so in that most sacred opinion about the protection of angels, which they noticed there, they utterly perverted, devising certain Genii of provinces, cities and colonies; as Tertullian testifies in his book On Idolatry, and one may read in Symmachus in his little book addressed to the Emperor Theodosius: "The Divine Mind," he says, "assigns various guardians to cities; as souls are given to those being born, so Fated Genii are divided among peoples." To this pertain those verses of the poets: "Dodona is sacred to you, Jupiter; Samos and Mycenae to Juno, rich in gold; from there Tenarus and the ruler of the sea; Pallas guards the Cecropian citadels; Pythian Delphi the navel of the world; Crete Delia and the Cynthian hills; Faunus Manalus, and the woods of Arcadia; Rhodes is the blessed charge of the Sun; Gades of Hercules and damp Tibur; Cyllene snowy to the swift god; Lesbos, hot, more pleasing to the slow god; the daughters-in-law of Aetna frequent Ceres; Cyzicus, rich in oysters, the goddess who was carried off; Cnidos and Paphos beautiful Venus."

units.la: Sic Ovidius lib. iii. Fastorum: Pallada Cecropia, Minoia terra Dianam, Vulcanum Tellus Hypsipilaea colit, Iunonem Sparta, Pelopeiadesque Mycenae, Pinigerum Fauni Manalis ora caput: Mars Latio venerandus erat.
units.tr: So Ovid in book iii of the Fasti: "Pallas the Cecropian land, Diana the Minoan land, Vulcan Hypsipylean Tellus worships; Juno Sparta, and Mycenae of Pelops' line; the pine-bearing head of Faunus at Manalus; Mars was to be revered in Latium."

units.la: Seneca in Agamemnone, Act. i: Choro: Ades o magni Soror & Coniux consors sceptri Regia Iuno: tua te colimus Turba, Mycenae: tu sollicitum Supplexque tui Numinis Argos Sola tueris. Tertullianus in Apologet. cap. x. Genios hosce vocat Proprios; nonnullos enumerans cap. xx : Vnicuique, inquit, Provincia & Civitati suus est Deus: ut Syria, Astarte; ut Arabia, Difares; ut Norici, Belenus; ut Africa, Caelestis; ut Mauritania, Reguli sui: & paullo post: Cruftuminienfium, Belventinus; Narnicenfium, Vividianus; Afculanorum, Ancaria; Volfinienfium, Narfia; Ocriculanorum, Valentia; Sutrinorum, Nortia; Faliscorum in honore est pater Curis. Patrios Deos nominant hos Genios Cicero orat. pro Sestio, Virgilius lib. i. Georgic. Silius Italicus lib. iv. de bello Poenico, & alij. Hujusmodi Genii saepe occurrunt in antiquis monimentis: Genius Coloniae, in Inscriptione quadam Neapolitana & Tarraconensi; Genius Coloniae Puteo'anorum, in alia Neapolit. Genius Conventus Asturicensis, in alia Tarraconensi: Genius Loci in duobus lapidibus Cantharopoli, opido Nechari in Germania. Credebant autem Veteres Genios tales urbes expugnandas vel sponte deserere, vel solenni prece evocatos alio migrare. De spontanea desertione Virgilius lib. ii. Aeneid. Excesserre omnes adytis, Sacrisque relictis Dii, quibus Imperium hoc steterat. Peritura Troia perdidit primum Deos.
units.tr: Seneca in Agamemnon, Act i, Chorus: "Come, O Juno, sister and wife, partner of the great sceptre, royal one: your crowd, Mycenae, worships you; you alone protect anxious Argos, a suppliant of your divinity." Tertullian in the Apologeticus, chapter x, calls these Genii proprii (their own); listing some in chapter xx he says: "Each province and city has its own god: as Syria has Astarte; Arabia, Dusares; Noricum, Belenus; Africa, Caelestis; Mauretania, its own petty kings"; and a little later: "of the Cruptuminians, Belventinus; of the Narnians, Vividianus; of the Aesculans, Ancharia; of the Volsinians, Nortia; of the Ocriculans, Valentia; of the Sutrians, Nortia; the Faliscans honour the father Curis." Cicero in his speech for Sestius, Virgil in book i of the Georgics, Silius Italicus in book iv of the Punic War, and others call these Genii Patrios Deos (ancestral gods). Such Genii often occur in ancient monuments: Genius Coloniae in a Neapolitan and a Tarraconensian inscription; Genius Coloniae Puteolanorum in another Neapolitan; Genius Conventus Asturicensis in another Tarraconensian; Genius Loci on two stones at Cantharopolis, a town on the Neckar in Germany. The ancients believed that such Genii either abandoned cities to be taken of their own accord, or, called out by a solemn prayer, migrated elsewhere. Of spontaneous desertion Virgil writes in book ii of the Aeneid: "The gods, by whose power this empire had stood, departed from the shrines and abandoned the sacred places. Troy, doomed to perish, first lost its gods."

units.la: Petronius Arbiter:
units.tr: Petronius Arbiter:

units.la: Æschyli Scholiastes: Αἰγὶ γὰρ ὅτι, ὅταν ἐμελλε πορθηναι ἡ Τροία, ἐφάνησαν οἱ Θεοὶ τῶν Τρῶων, ἀπολιπόμενοι ἐκ τῶν ναῶν τὰ ἀγάλματα αὐτῶν. Solennis Evocationis ritus ab Sammonico Sereno lib. v. rerum reconditarum ex Furio scriptore prisco refertur apud Macrobium lib. iii. Saturnal. cap. ix : exemplum autem est apud Livium lib. v. ab V. C. ubi de Vejentium oppugnatione. Ne vero contra Romam ab hostibus Tutelaris Romae Deus evocaretur, Romani verum ejus nomen ignotum esse vulgo volebant. Plinius lib. xxviii. nat. histor. cap. ii: Verrius Flaccus auctores ponit, quibus credat in Oppugnationibus ante omnia solitum a Romanis Sacerdotibus evocari Deum, cujus in tutela id opidum esset: promittitque illi eumdem, aut ampliorem locum apud Romanos, cultumve. Durat in Pontificum disciplina id Sacrum: canstatque ideo occultatum, in cujus Dei tutela Roma esset, nomen, ne qui hostium similis modo agerent. Legendi & Solinus in Polyhistore, Plutarchus ἐν Αἰτίοις, Servius ad librum i. Georgic. Ab hujusmodi etiam Genijs & Diis Topicis orta Veteribus Consuetudo, ut qui primum ingrederentur aliquam Regionem vel Urbem, ad eamve ex intervallo aliquo reverterentur, religiosa prosequerentur salutatione; cuique loco suum Genium arbitrati praesse. Scholiastes in Apollonij ii: τὰς Παιδημιούργους ἐθω ἡν ἐν τῇ ἀλλοδαπῇ ... τὴν Φαοι ἡ Αλέξανδρος πέμπει τὸν Μακεδόνα ἐν Γλίω. Exempla huic ritui probando multa congerunt ex Plauto Bacchid. Act. ii. Sc. i, Stich. Act. v. Sc. ii; Virgilio vii. Aeneidos; Ovidio i. Fastorum; Seneca Agamemn. Act. iiii. Sc. i; Claudiano de raptu Proserpinae; & alijs, Antonius Muretus in Variis Lectionibus, Barnabas Brissonius lib. i. de Antiq. Romanorum Formulis, M. Antonius Delrio in Agamemnon. Senecae. Sufficiant haec: pergam ad Partem Operis mei secundam; si memoriae & intellegentiae juvandae subtexuero praecedentium Librorum Tabulam.
units.tr: The scholiast on Aeschylus: "For it is said that when Troy was about to be sacked, the gods of the Trojans appeared, leaving their statues behind in the temples." The solemn rite of evocation is reported by Sammonicus Serenus in book v of his Recondite Matters, from the ancient writer Furius, and in Macrobius, book iii of the Saturnalia, chapter ix; there is an example in Livy, book v, concerning the siege of Veii. Lest the Tutelary God of Rome be called out from Rome by the enemy, the Romans wanted his true name to be unknown to the common people. Pliny, Natural History, book xxviii, chapter ii: "Verrius Flaccus gives authorities by whom he believes that in sieges it was above all the custom of the Roman priests to call out the god under whose protection the town was, and they promise him the same or a greater place and worship among the Romans. This sacred rite endures in the discipline of the Pontiffs; and it is agreed that the name of the god under whose protection Rome was is therefore hidden, lest any of the enemy do the same." Solinus in his Polyhistor, Plutarch in the Aetia, and Servius on book i of the Georgics are also to be read. From such Genii and local gods the custom arose among the ancients that those who first entered some region or city, or returned to it after some interval, greeted it with a religious salutation, thinking that each place had its own Genius presiding over it. The scholiast on Apollonius, book ii: ... (the Macedonian sent to Pheneus by Alexander). Many examples supporting this practice are gathered from Plautus, Bacchides Act ii, Scene i, and Stichus Act v, Scene ii; from Virgil, Aeneid vii; from Ovid, Fasti i; from Seneca, Agamemnon Act iv, Scene i; from Claudian on the rape of Proserpina; and from others: Antonius Muretus in his Variae Lectiones, Balthasar Bonifacius? Barnabas Brissonius, book i, On the Ancient Formulas of the Romans, and Martin Antonius Delrio on Seneca's Agamemnon. These will suffice: I shall go on to the second part of my work, if I append a table of the preceding books to help memory and understanding.

units.la: BREVIARIVM PARTIS I.
units.tr: Summary of Part I.

units.la: Libri I.
units.tr: Book I.

units.la: De Vniverso agitur vel Generatim, de Creatione. Hic perpendenda Diffinitio. Quid sit Mundus. Cap. 1. Causa: quarum alia Antecem, ut Efficiens. DEVS quidquid est creavit. II. Materia, que In Principio quidem Nihil, III; Deinde vero Chaos quoddam, id est, Materia prima informis omnino, cui tamen inerat quaedam ad Formas futuras suscipiendas Potentia. Videndum hic, Quo ordine sex Dierum spatio DEUS ex Chao singula potenter eduxerit. IV. Quo modo singula ordine creata in unum, ideoque Finitum coaluerint. V Cum Re, quales sunt Forma. Est illa vel in Figura ipsa. Mundus enim plane rotundus. VI. Concentu, quo Creata omnia mirandum in modum inter se consonant. VII. Finis, respectu Sui. Creata enim hac Moles, ut, quemadmodum Tota in tempore coepit: VIII. sic Partes ejus Inferiores, quum magna Dies advenerit, pereant. IX. Aliorum. Mundus enim creatus, ut primario propter DEUM, sic secundario Hominum causa; quo ex creata Mole adspectu DEUM esse fiiret & crederet, tanquam ex Magno Libro. X. Gubernatione. DEUS enim non solum quidquid est creavit, sed creata etiam conservat & gubernat, omnia, etiam Minima, non immediate solum, sed & mediate. XI.
units.tr: Here the subject is the universe in general, that is, its creation. The definition must be weighed here: what the world is. Chapter 1. Causes, of which some are prior, such as the efficient cause: God created whatever exists. II. Matter, which at the beginning was nothing. III. Then a certain chaos, that is, matter wholly formless, yet containing a certain power to receive the forms to come. Here one must consider in what order God, within the space of six days, powerfully brought each thing out of chaos. IV. How the individual things, created in order, came together into one whole, and so into something finite. V. With respect to the thing itself, what sort of form it has: it lies in the figure itself, for the world is perfectly round. VI. Harmony, by which all created things agree with one another in a wonderful manner. VII. The end, with respect to itself. For this created mass, just as the whole began in time, VIII. so its lower parts will perish when the great day comes. IX. The end with respect to others. For the world was created primarily on account of God, and secondarily for the sake of men, so that from the sight of the created mass people might know and believe that God exists, as from a great book. X. Government. For God not only created whatever exists, but also preserves and governs created things, all things, even the smallest, not only immediately but also mediately. XI.

units.la: Libri II.
units.tr: Book II.

units.la: Speciatim. Universi aliud hic est Coelestis & aeternum, ut Coelum; cujus nomine donamus quidquid ab Luna sursum est; ut est totum illud expansum, quantumquantum est, quod Elementarem Regionem ambit & circumamplectitur. Cap. I. Estque vel Firmum & Stabile, ut Empyreum, DEI & Beatorum Genitorum sedes & διαπνοα; nonnullis ante omnia creatum, aliis increatum; Veteribus etiam cognitum Ἀνάρχω appellatione. II. Volubile circa Axem; quem terminantes Puncta dicuntur Πόλοι Graeci, Vertices Latinis, &c. Vide ad litteram A. Stella, quae nihil aliud quam densior Orbis Coelestis pars. B.
units.tr: In particular. Of the universe, one part is heavenly and eternal, such as the heaven. By this name we designate whatever lies above the moon, that is, the whole vast expanse that surrounds and encloses the elemental region. Chapter I. This heaven is either firm and stable, like the Empyrean, the seat of God and the blessed, and the breathing-space [διαπνοα]; some hold it to have been created before all things, others hold it uncreated; the ancients too knew it under the name Anarchos [Ἀνάρχω]. II. Revolving about an axis; the points that terminate the axis are called Poles by the Greeks and Vertices by the Latins, etc. See under letter A. A star is nothing other than a denser part of the heavenly sphere. B.

units.la: Libri II- I.
units.tr: Book II, chapter I.

units.la: Inconstans & perpetuis obnoxium Mutationibus; ut Elementa. C. A Volubile circa Axem. Hic consideranda Coeli huius Puncta, quae Graeci Πόλοι, Vertices Latinis, quorum alter Boreus, Notius alter Cap. III. Distributio. Est enim vel Vniversim, ubi de Circuli Diffinitione, & aliis IV. Speciatim. Est enim vel Circuli infinitum. De Circulis dicta Maior. Hic in Aequalia segmenta Mundum partitur. Estque vel Idem ubique. Hic intelligitur secundum Mundi vel Longitudinem; quae consideratur secundum Mundi Motum ab Ortu in Occasum; & inde in Ortum. Est autem vel Rectus, ut Aequinoctialis, aequaliter Polos interiacens. V. Obliquus, λοξὸς, Zodiacus, inaequaliter inter Polos locatus. VI. Latitudinem. Hi Circuli in Polis ad Angulos rectos se mutuo bisecant: Zodiacum autem vel potius Eclipticam quadripartiuntur in Aequinoctiorum Solstitii & Brumae Punctis, pro anni quadripartita vicissitudine. Vocantur autem Coluri, hoc est, mutilati; quorum alter est Aequinoctialis Solstitialis utrumque, ab loco motum sertitus VII. Alius alibi. Estque vel Horizon; cuius duplex Divisio I. quae mutuata ab varia Polorum elevatione. Est enim II. ab hominis sumta sensu & ratione. Hic vel Rectus, Obliquus, Sensibilis, Rationalis. VIII. Meridianus IX. Minor. qui Mundum dividit in sequenta inaequalia, Minorum sunt in duplici discrimine. Aly in Sphaera usum praestant. Hic Minor Circulus est vel ubique Idem, ut Circulus Tropicus Cancri, ubi Solstitium est; Capricorni, ubi Bruma. X. Alius alibi; Polaris. Mutatur enim pro Poli examinate. Estque Arcticus, Antarcticus. Nam describuntur a Puncto sectionis, qua Meridianus & Horizon se secant mutuo. XI. nullius sunt usus, quales sunt cum aliy, tum Lacteus Circulus XII. Globus & Circuli diremtum. Huius Historiam duobus includo capitibus; quorum I. de Numero Caelestium Orbium, qui varius; vere octonarius XIII. II. de eorundem Motu XIIII.
units.tr: Inconstant and subject to perpetual changes, like the elements. C. Revolving about an axis. Here the points of this heaven are to be considered, which the Greeks call Poles and the Latins Vertices, of which one is the Arctic and the other the Antarctic. Chapter III. Division. It is either general, where the definition of a circle and other matters are discussed. IV. Particular. Circles are either infinite... The greater circles are so called. Here the world is divided into equal segments. A circle is either the same everywhere. This is understood with respect to the length of the world, which is considered according to the motion of the world from east to west and thence back again to east. A circle is either right, like the equinoctial, lying equally between the poles. V. Oblique, slanting [λοξὸς], like the zodiac, placed unequally between the poles. VI. Latitude. These circles bisect one another at the poles at right angles. The zodiac, or rather the ecliptic, is divided into four parts at the points of the equinoxes, the solstices and the winter point, according to the fourfold alternation of the year. They are called coluri, that is, mutilated. VII. Another, elsewhere. The horizon is either of a double division: I. derived from the varying elevation of the poles; II. taken from human sense and reason. Here it is either right, oblique, sensible or rational. VIII. The meridian. IX. The lesser circles, which divide the world into the following unequal parts. The lesser circles are of a twofold distinction. Some serve a purpose in the sphere. Here a lesser circle is either the same everywhere, like the Tropic of Cancer, where the summer solstice is, or the Tropic of Capricorn, where the winter solstice is. X. Another, elsewhere: the polar circles. For they change according to the pole in view. They are Arctic and Antarctic, for they are described from the point of intersection where the meridian and the horizon cut each other. XI. Some are of no use, such as both others and the Milky Way. XII. The globe and the divided circles. I include its history in two chapters, of which I deals with the number of the heavenly spheres, which varies, but is truly eightfold. XIII. II. deals with their motion. XIV.

units.la: Generatim; hic queramus
units.tr: In general; here we inquire

units.la: {a} ... Singulatim. Singularem Siderum consideration pandet Distributio. Sunt enim alia Fixa, ve[?] Inerrantia in Coelo Stellifero vel Firmamento. Ha describuntur mihi quatuor Errantia, id est Planeta, singuli in suis Orbibus; qui extimo id est Stellifero, sunt citeriores. De his item in 1. Stellarum Descriptionem. cap. xv. 11. An Astrologia & quatenus licita. xvi. Αʼ σωώθετα. Hic explico, quis illis Motus: quis Numerus, quæ secundum Magnitudinem Classes. xvii. Σωώθε-τα, id est, ut Signa constituentia & μορφώσεις. De quibus in Genere. Nomina Signis non nuper imposita, sed ante aliquot secula. xix. In Zodiaco, ut Aries, Taurus, Gemini, &c. xix. Extra Zodiacum: quorum alia Septemtrionalia. xx. Australia. Hæc duplicis generis, Alia quæ Veteribus æque ac Nobis cognita. xxi. Nobis nuper innotescere capta. xxii.
units.tr: {a} ... Individually. The distribution will reveal the separate consideration of the stars. For some are fixed, or unmoving, in the starry heaven or firmament. These I describe; four are wandering, that is, planets, each in its own orbit, which, in the outermost sphere, that is the starry one, are nearer. On these also in the first book, the description of the stars, chapter 15. 11. Whether astrology is lawful and how far. 16. Fixed [ἀπλανῆ]. Here I explain what their motions are, what their number, and what classes according to magnitude. 17. Wandering [πλανῆται], that is, as constituting signs and figures. Of these in general. Names not recently imposed on the signs, but some centuries ago. 19. In the zodiac, such as Aries, Taurus, Gemini, etc. 19. Outside the zodiac, of which some are northern. 20. Southern. These are of two kinds: some known to the ancients as well as to us, 21. and some recently discovered and only now becoming known to us. 22.

units.la: Genere, unde dicti, quis Motus, quis Ordo, Situsque, qua Affectiones, Domicilia, Exaltationes, Adspectus, Distributio. xxiii. Species sunt enim vel Φωσφόρος, Tenebras discutientes, & umbras facientes, ut Sol, in Planetas medius. Luna, Terræ citima: Αʼ στέρες; quorum alij Sole sunt Superiores Saturnus, Iupiter, Mars: Inferiores Venus, Mercurius. His in Universo talis ordo Situsque Saturnus, Iupiter, Mars, xxiv. Sol, xxv. Venus, Mercurius, xxvi. Luna, xxvii.
units.tr: By kind, whence they are named, what their motion, what their order and position, what their affections, dwellings, exaltations, aspects and distribution. 23. For the species are either luminaries [φωστῆρες], dispelling darkness and casting shadows, like the Sun, which is in the middle of the planets, and the Moon, nearest to the Earth; or stars [ἀστέρες], of which some are superior to the Sun: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars; and inferior: Venus, Mercury. In the universe they have this order and position: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, 24. the Sun, 25. Venus, Mercury, 26. the Moon. 27.

units.la: LIBRI III.
units.tr: BOOK III.

units.la: C. Inconstans & perpetuis obnoxium mutationibus, ut Elementum: de quo Universum; de Definitione; Corpus esse Simplex, Finitum, Vmbrosum, Luce & Lumine destitutum Cap. 1. Numero. Tria tantum esse, quum Ignis non sit Elementum. II. Particulatim. Est enim Elementum vel Pellucidum; quod, quia rarum, lumini est pervium, ut Aer. III. Aqua; de qua in Genere: Quid, unde dicta; unum formare cum Terra Globum; quod eius Centrum; quae Effecta; Divisio. IV. Specie. Est enim vel reciproco motu agitatur; ut Maria; quorum explicantur hic Communes Adfectiones, ut Diffinitio, Aestus, Salsedo, congelatio, color, Profunditas, & similia. V. Mota. Haec vel Species, ut sunt Oceanus. VI. Mediterranea, Maiora. VII. Minora. VIII. Euripi. IX. uno tantum agmine perpetuo defluit; ut Fons; Fluvius, Rivus, Torrens. X. Quieta, ut Lacus, Stagnum, Palus. XI. Ante Rem, ut Efficiens, Materia. XII. Cu re, ut Forma. Est enim, ut Totum, σφαιροειδής, XIII. Finis. Terra dominium Dei; usus hominum. XIV. Modo quodam, ut sunt Subiectum. Locus. Terra Centrum Universi. XV. Adiunctum. Quantitas. Terra ad Caelum, instar Puncti; ad Nos immensa Globositas, XVI. Generalia praemittuntur, ut quae consentiunt illi vel Absolute, quales Causae, vel Opacum, Terra, De qua quaedam Specialia explicantur, ut variae Divisiones, ratione vel Adiuncto-rum. Ea voco, quae Terra accidunt ratione Superiorum vel Coelestium in Circulos, quorum describuntur Necessitas & Partes. XVII. Separatim, Sunt enim Iunctim. Hic de Locorum Dimensionibus. XX. Longitudinis. XIX. Latitudinis. XIX. Species; De his Inferiorum. Hic Terra dividitur in Portiones Maiores, respectu Umbra, in Aeris Temperies, in Zonas. XXII. Amphiscii, Heterosciai, Periscii. XXI. Minores, horarum variantium ratione, in Climata. Hic Corollarij loco describuntur voces Geographicae. Partium. Terra distribuitur ratione nostra Scientia, sed Essentia. Est enim vel Continens, Haec primo Meridiano, qui per Canarias ducitur, dividuntur in Hemisphaerium Eorum, quod veteribus cognitum. Hoc in latus dividitur Boreum; cuius Partes flatuo Evrop. Pars II. Scythiam Pars. III. Australis huius Asiam Pars IV. Africam Pars V. Occiduum, quod iam ante C. annos detegi coepit: America dicitur ab Inventore. Pars. VI. Insula maris tam Oceani, quam Mediterranei Pars. VII.
units.tr: C. Inconstant and subject to perpetual change, like an element. Concerning which the Universe; on the definition: that it is a simple, finite body, shadowy, and destitute of light and luminosity. Chapter 1. In number: there are only three, since fire is not an element. II. Particularly: an element is either transparent, which, being rare, is permeable to light, as air. III. Water, concerning which in general: what it is and whence it is named; that it forms one globe with the earth; what its centre is; its effects; its division. IV. In species: water is either stirred by a reciprocal motion, as the seas, of which the common affections are explained here, such as definition, tides, saltness, freezing, colour, depth, and the like. V. Moved waters. These are either species, as the Ocean. VI. The Mediterranean, the greater ones. VII. The lesser ones. VIII. Straits. IX. Those which flow down in a single, perpetual channel, such as a spring, a river, a brook, a torrent. X. Still waters, such as lakes, pools, and marshes. XI. Before the thing, as efficient cause and matter. XII. With the thing, as form. For it is spherical as a whole [σφαιροειδής]. XIII. End. The earth is God's dominion; for the use of men. XIV. In a certain manner, as subject and place: the earth is the centre of the universe. XV. Attributes: quantity. The earth, compared with heaven, is like a point; to us it is a vast globe. XVI. General matters are set out first, such as those that agree with it either absolutely, like causes, or as opaque, the earth. Concerning it certain special matters are explained, such as the various divisions by reason of its attributes. I call those things which befall the earth by reason of the superior or heavenly bodies, in circles, whose necessity and parts are described. XVII. Separately, for they are joined together. Here concerning the dimensions of places. XX. Of longitude. XIX. Of latitude. XIX. Kinds; concerning these, of the lower regions. Here the earth is divided into larger portions with respect to shadow, into temperatures of the air, into zones. XXII. Amphiscians, heteroscians, periscians. XXI. Smaller portions, by reason of the varying length of hours, into climates. Here, by way of a corollary, geographical terms are described. Of parts: the earth is divided with respect to our knowledge, not by its essence. For it is either continent; these, by the first meridian, which runs through the Canaries, are divided into the hemisphere of those parts known to the ancients. This is divided into the northern side, whose parts I set down as: Europe, part II; Scythia, part III; of the southern side of this, Asia, part IV; Africa, part V; the western, which began to be discovered about a hundred years ago, is called America after its discoverer, part VI; islands of the sea, both of the Ocean and of the Mediterranean, part VII.

units.tr: The Ancients, to whom the earth was not known as it is known to us today, divided the terrestrial globe at one time into two parts and at another into three.

units.tr: Those who made two parts, I read, included Africa under Asia, and others under Europe.

units.tr: Some divide it into two parts, Asia and Europe, and others into Africa and

units.la: comprehendisse lego sub Asia, alios sub Europa. Sub Asia
units.tr: I have read that some have included Africa under Asia, and others under Europe. Under Asia indeed the most ancient writer Eratosthenes includes it,

units.la: quidem complectuntur Scriptor Antiquissimus Eratosthenes,
units.tr: (I cannot be sure which of the two places it is in). The most ancient writer, Eratosthenes, is one of those who place it under Asia,

units.la: de quo M. Terentius Varro lib. 1. de Re Rustica,
units.tr: of whom Marcus Terentius Varro writes in book 1 of On Agriculture,

units.la: cap. 11; Primum quum Orbis Terra divisus sit in duas Partes ab
units.tr: chapter 11: First, since the orb of the earth was divided into two parts by Eratosthenes, chiefly according to nature, towards the south and towards the north;

units.la: Eratosthene, maxime secundum naturam, ad Meridiem versus, & 10
units.tr: and 10 and towards the north.

units.la: & ad Septemtriones; Et sine dubio, quoniam salubrior pars Septemtrionalis est quam Meridiana, & quae
units.tr: And undoubtedly, since the northern part is healthier than the southern, and what is healthier is also more fruitful, it must be said that Europe was more suitable for cultivation than Asia,

units.la: salubrior, illa fructuosior; dicendum magis Europam fuisse oportunam ad colendum, quam Asiam,
units.tr: and there Italy, first because it lies in Europe, and second because this part is more temperate than the interior;

units.la: ibique Italiam; primum, quod est in Europa, secundo, quod haec temperatior pars est, quam interior;
units.tr: for inland there are almost everlasting winters. And Varro himself, in book 1 of On the Latin Language: As all

units.la: nam intus pene sempiternae hiemes: & ipse Varro lib. 1. de Lingua Latina: Ut omnis,
units.tr: nature, he says, is divided into Heaven and Earth, so Heaven is divided into regions and Earth into Asia and Europe. For Asia

units.la: inquit, natura in Caelum & Terram divisa est: sic Caelum in Regiones, Terra in Asiam & Europam. Asia enim
units.tr: lies towards the south and the east wind; Europe towards the north and the north wind. He has in view

units.la: iacet ad Meridiem & Eurum; Europa ad Septemtriones & Aquilonem. Respicit
units.tr: here Silius Italicus, book 1 of the Punic War:

units.la: eo Silius Italicus lib. 1. Belli Poenici:
units.tr: Libya, placed beneath the summer Cancer, is scorched,

units.la: Aestivo Libye torquetur subdita Cancro,
units.tr: Libya, lying under the summer Crab, is tormented, either the vast flank of Asia or the third part of the world.

units.la: Aut ingens Asiae latus, aut pars Tertia Rerum.
units.tr: Or the vast flank of Asia, or the third part of the world.

units.la: Sub Europa vero locant Africam, praeter Isocratem in Panegyrico, Incertiores cum apud Sallustium in Bello Iugurthino, In divisione Orbis Terra plerique in Parte Tertia Africam posuere: pauci tantummodo Asiam & Europam esse, sed Africam in Europa; & Lucanus lib. ix. Belli Pharsalici; Tertia Pars rerum Libye, si credere fama Cuncta velis; at, si ventos Caelumque sequaris; Pars erit Europa; neque enim plus littora Nili, Quam Scythicis Tanais, primis a Gadibus absint:
units.tr: But they place Africa under Europe, except Isocrates in the Panegyricus and some less certain writers. Sallust in the Jugurthine War says: "In the division of the world, most people have placed Africa in the third part; only a few say that there are only Asia and Europe, but that Africa is in Europe." Lucan, in book 9 of the Pharsalia, says: "Libya is the third part of the world, if you wish to believe common report in everything; but if you follow the winds and the sky, it will be Europe. For the shores of the Nile are no farther from the nearest Gades than the Scythian Tanais is."
