units.la: tum apud Augustinum lib. xvi. de Civitate Dei cap. xvii, & Orosium lib. i. cap. ii. Quasi Sallustius etiam ejusdem fuisset sententiae, canit apud Ausonium Pontius Paullinus: Europamque Asiamque, duo vel Maxima Terra Membra: quibus Libyam dubie Sallustius addit Europa adjunctam, posset quum Tertia dici.
units.tr: Then in Augustine, City of God book 16, chapter 17, and in Orosius book 1, chapter 2. As if Sallust too had held the same opinion, Pontius Paulinus sings in Ausonius: "Europe and Asia, the two very large limbs of the earth; to which Sallust doubtfully adds Libya, joined to Europe, so that it could be called the third."

units.la: In tres partes distributio quondam maxime celebris, Europam, Asiam, Africam vel Libyam. Videndi Aristoteles variis locis, Plinius cum alibi, tum lib. iii Prooemio, Ptolemaeus, Strabo initio lib. xi, Mela lib. i. cap. i, Orosius quem dixi lib. i. cap. ii, Festus Avienus in Orbis Terrae descriptione, & qui non? Tripartitam hanc Orbis Terrarum Distributionem primum per Chorographiam ostendisse Divum Augustum, scribit Incertus Auctor Libri de Mensura Orbis Terrae; quem Manuscriptum mihi transmissione liberali communicavit Vir, cum Nobilissimus, tum Doctissimus & Rerum Geographicarum aliarumque, quod Monimenta ab ipso edita plene loquuntur, peritissimus, Marcus Velserus Patricius & vii-Vir Augustanus. Sunt qui Tres illas Partes totidem faciunt Insulas apud Aelianum lib. iii Var. histor. cap. xxii. Falso. Europam enim ipsorum Asiae magno Terrarum spatio ab Fontibus Tanais ad Grandvicum usque Sinum; hanc autem Africae Isthmo inter Maria Mediterraneum & Erythraeum adhaerere, vel Pueri noverunt. America potius Insula, quam separari ab locis Europae, parum adhuc sub Polo notis, aliquo Freto, sunt qui Scriptis produnt.
units.tr: The division into three parts was once very widely known: Europe, Asia, and Africa or Libya. See Aristotle in various places; Pliny, both elsewhere and in the preface to book 3; Ptolemy; Strabo at the start of book 11; Mela, book 1, chapter 1; Orosius, whom I have mentioned, book 1, chapter 2; Festus Avienus in his description of the earth; and who else? The unknown author of the book On the Measurement of the Earth writes that the deified Augustus was the first to show this threefold division of the world on a map. I received this manuscript by the generous loan of a man who is both most noble and most learned, and most expert in geography and other subjects, as his published works fully show: Marcus Welser, patrician and member of the Seven of Augsburg. Some make these three parts into three islands, in Aelian, Varia Historia book 3, chapter 22. This is false. For Europe is joined to their Asia by a great stretch of land from the sources of the Tanais as far as the Grandvicum gulf, and Africa is attached to these by the isthmus between the Mediterranean and the Erythraean Sea; even boys know this. America is rather an island, separated from the lands of Europe by some strait, as some writers report, though it is still little known under the Pole.

units.la: Mihi, quod instituto meo putavi convenientissimum, Terra vel Continens est, vel Insula. Continentem Primo Meridiano, qui per Canarias ducitur, divido in Hemisphaerium Eoum, & Occiduum. Illud Veteribus, non tamen ut hodie Nobis, cognitum: Hoc iam ante centum, & qui excurrunt, annos detegi coeptum; lapsu temporis, si Europaeis bonum hoc felix & salutare censeat Deus, detegendum plenius. Eum Mari Mediterraneo & Tauro Monte (qui, ut inquit Strabo lib. xi. Μἠκ habet ... ad dextram, καὶ Σκυθίας, ad sinistram, ...) sub xxxvi fere Parallelo, dirimitur in latus Boreum & Austrinum. Boreum Aegaeo Pelago, Hellesponto, Propontide, Bosporo Thracio, Ponto Euxino, Bosporo Cimmerio, Maeotide Palude, Tanai Fluvio, ductaque ab eius Fonte in Oceanum usque Septemtrionalem Lineam, in Europam, quae Borea pars Occidentalis, & Scythiam, quae Orientalis, dispescitur. Austrinum Arabico Sinu & Isthmo inter ipsum & Mediterraneum, in Africam partio & Asiam. Occiduum Hemisphaerium (quod Veteribus omnino incognitum fuerit, nec ne; alibi dicam) ab Inventore (sic enim nunc loquar) nupero vocatur America, quam Isthmus nobilissimus, & Septemtrionalem facit & Meridionalem. In hac mea distributione primo loco sese offert Europa; quam aperit Pars Operis mei Secunda.
units.tr: For my purpose, which I judged most suitable, the earth is either a continent or an island. I divide the continent, by the First Meridian drawn through the Canaries, into an eastern and a western hemisphere. The eastern was known to the ancients, though not as it is known to us today. The western began to be discovered more than a hundred years ago, and in time, if God judges this to be a good, happy and salutary thing for Europeans, it will be discovered more fully. This continent is divided by the Mediterranean and the Taurus mountains (which, as Strabo says in book 11, lies [...] on the right, and Scythia [...] on the left) at about the 36th parallel into a northern and a southern side. The northern side is marked off by the Aegean Sea, the Hellespont, the Propontis, the Thracian Bosporus, the Euxine Sea, the Cimmerian Bosporus, the Maeotic marsh and the river Tanais, and, drawn from the source of that river to the Ocean as far as the northern line, it is divided into Europe, which is the western part of the north, and Scythia, which is the eastern. The southern side is divided, by the Arabian Gulf and the isthmus between it and the Mediterranean, into Africa and Asia. The western hemisphere (whether it was entirely unknown to the ancients I shall say elsewhere) is called America by its recent discoverer (for so I shall call him now), and the noble isthmus makes it both northern and southern. In this my division, Europe presents itself first, and it is with Europe that the second part of my work opens.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CAP. II.

units.la: Ab Europa quur ordiundum.
units.tr: Why Europe is to be treated first.

units.la: IN Europa explicanda considerabo vel Totam vel ejus Partes. Totam quidem Universim primo, deinde Speciatim. Universim aperiam cum Ordinis ratione, quur Europa ante alias Orbis Partes explicari consueuit; tum ipsius Etymon & Appellationes. Quod ad Ordinem: ab Europa Principium mihi, quemadmodum modum & potissimis Terrestris Globi Delineatoribus. Semper enim reliquis partibus notior fuit & culta magis; celebratissima variis magnorum Scriptorum Monimentis, cum ob admirandum illud Macedonum Imperium, tum summam Romanorum potentiam. Alias confert Ordini stabiliendo Rationes Strabo lib. ii. ἐπὶ πολυχρήμων τε, καὶ ταῖς ἀρετῶν ἀνδρῶν δ᾽ Φυσικὴ καὶ πολιτῶν, καὶ τὰς ἀλλας τ᾽ ἀλλὰς μεταδιδωκίας τῶν οἰκείων ἀγαθῶν: ἀλλὰ ψυχῶν, &c. Et paulo post: ἀεὶς ἐιφωνὰ καὶ ἀεὶς πόλεμον αὐτερχεσθαι: καὶ γὰρ τὸ μάχιμον πλῆθος ἀφθονον ἔχει, καὶ τὸ ἐργαζόμενον τῶν γῆ καὶ τὸ τῆς πόλης σωίεχον. Addit deinde Partem hanc ferendis passim Fructibus, qui optimi Vitaeque necessarij, excellere; Metallis item, quae hominibus maximo usui; esse praeterea hic, ut incredibilem βοοχημάτων copiam, sic magnam ἡμέων raritatem. Paucis idem Strabo eodem libro: Εὐρώπη, inquit, ἔχει πολύ τὸ ἀφὸν, καὶ ἐπέχων ἡ βίᾳ. Plinius lib. iii. s.p.q.r. adblanditus Europam dicit, Altricem Victoris omnium Gentium Populi, Terrarumque pulcherrimam. Europam sane compertissimum est Asiae, Africae, Americaeque, non quidem magnitudine (sunt enim hae longe ampliores) sed Religione Christiana (cuius illa unicum fere domicilium) Incolarum virtute, Moribus, Diligentia, Vivendi Consuetudine; Urbium, Pagorumq; frequentia; Rerumque, quae ad Vitam commode sustentandam necessariae, abundantia; praesigni denique Coeli Solique Temperie, multis intervallis anteponi. Superbivit olim Africa unica fere sua Karthagine; tumuit vix tribus Asia Urbibus, Babylone, Ninive & Hierosolymis: Gloriantur hodie America Cusco; Mexicoque Nova Hispania: at vero quis hoc tempore non videt pares majoresque in singulis Europae Regionibus? Perambulet quis cogitatione solum sua in Italia (exemplum enim subministret hic unus ille Mundi Ocellus) sumtuosam Romae Magnificentiam, regales Venetiarum Divitias, suspiciendam Neapolis Nobilitatem, ferventia Genuae Commercia & Negociationes, felicem illam & beatam Mediolani Amoenitatem, aliarum denique alia cum Miracula, tum Commoda: Sileant sua, clamare cogetur, sileant Partes Orbis ceterae: Par nihil Europae, nihil est secundum. Haec hodie vere Imperatorum, Regum, Principumque Mater; haec laudatissimarum Rerumpublicarum Genitrix; haec felicissimorum Ingeniorum Nutrix: Sedes unica Rebus Mortalium bono dextre inveniendis, solaque praeclaris Artibus excogitandis consecrata. Potem tem non semel nominat Statius in Achilleide: Maxima Terra Viris & fecundissima doctis Vrbibus
units.tr: In explaining Europe I shall consider either the whole of it or its parts. I shall take the whole first, in general, and then in particular. In general I shall set out the reason for the order, why Europe is customarily explained before the other parts of the world, and then its etymology and names. As to the order: I make Europe my starting point, as do most of the chief makers of maps of the terrestrial globe. For it has always been better known and more cultivated than the other parts, and it is celebrated in the records of many great writers, both because of the admirable empire of the Macedonians and because of the supreme power of the Romans. Strabo, in book 2, gives other reasons for fixing this order: ἐπὶ πολυχρήμων τε, καὶ ταῖς ἀρετῶν ἀνδρῶν δ᾽ Φυσικὴ καὶ πολιτῶν, καὶ τὰς ἀλλας τ᾽ ἀλλὰς μεταδιδωκίας τῶν οἰκείων ἀγαθῶν: ἀλλὰ ψυχῶν, and so on. A little later: ἀεὶς ἐιφωνὰ καὶ ἀεὶς πόλεμον αὐτερχεσθαι: καὶ γὰρ τὸ μάχιμον πλῆθος ἀφθονον ἔχει, καὶ τὸ ἐργαζόμενον τῶν γῆ καὶ τὸ τῆς πόλης σωίεχον. He then adds that this part bears fruits everywhere, which are the best and most necessary for life, and that it excels in metals, which are of the greatest use to men; moreover, that it has an incredible abundance of livestock and a great scarcity of wild beasts. In a few words, the same Strabo in the same book says: Εὐρώπη, inquit, ἔχει πολύ τὸ ἀφὸν, καὶ ἐπέχων ἡ βίᾳ. Pliny, in book 3, calls Europe the nurse of the victorious peoples of all nations and the most beautiful of lands. It is quite certain that Europe is far inferior to Asia, Africa and America in size (for these are much larger), but it surpasses them by many degrees in Christian religion (of which it is almost the only home), in the virtue, morals, diligence and manner of living of its inhabitants, in the number of its cities and villages, in the abundance of things necessary for a comfortable life, and finally in the outstanding mildness of its climate and sunshine. Africa once took pride in its almost only city, Carthage; Asia scarcely swelled with its three cities, Babylon, Nineveh and Jerusalem. Today America boasts of Cusco and Mexico in New Spain. But who does not see at this time equal and greater cities in each region of Europe? Let anyone go through in thought alone the sights of Italy (for this one jewel of the world will serve as an example): the sumptuous magnificence of Rome, the royal riches of Venice, the admirable nobility of Naples, the busy trade and business of Genoa, and the happy and blessed pleasantness of Milan; in short, one wonderful and useful thing after another. He will be forced to cry out that the other parts of the world should keep silent about their own things. Nothing is equal to Europe, nothing comes second. This is truly the mother of emperors, kings and princes today; the parent of the most praised commonwealths; the nurse of the most fortunate minds; the only seat consecrated to finding the good things of mortal life and to devising noble arts. Statius, in the Achilleid, calls it more than once Maxima Terra Viris & fecundissima doctis Vrbibus, the greatest land, most fertile in men and in learned cities.

units.la: canit de ea Manilius: Salubriorem, quam Africam, scribit Varro: Mardonius, apud Xerxem verba faciens, Regionem esse admodum speciosam adiserebat, omniaque genera felicium Arborum gerentem, & summae bonitatis, uti de eo scribit Herodotus: ejus habitatores Animi Ardorisque plenos laudat Aristoteles. Principium igitur del has aliasque ob causas Europa; nobilissima Haereditatis Iapheti (qui primogenitus Noxi liberorum sua pomeria produxit etiam in Fratrum Semi Chamique Terras) Portio.
units.tr: Manilius sings of it. Varro writes that it is healthier than Africa. Mardonius, addressing Xerxes, declared that the region was very beautiful, bearing every kind of fruit-bearing tree and of the highest quality, as Herodotus writes of him. Aristotle praises its inhabitants as full of spirit and courage. Europe is therefore the starting point, for these and other reasons: it is the most noble portion of the inheritance of Japheth, who, as the firstborn of Noah's sons, extended his boundaries even into the lands of his brothers Shem and Ham.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: Europae varia indicantur Nomina.
units.tr: Various names of Europe are indicated.

units.la: HÆc de Ordinis Ratione: jam nunc Etymon succedit explicandum. Europae quidem Etymon a nemine Mortalium compertum esse notat Herodotus lib. iv; aliis tamen ab Europa Tyria dici, Agenoris Phoenicum (Libyae, inquit Isidorus) regis filia: quam Iovem in Bovem conversum rapuisse tergoque impositam Sydone in Cretam, vel Cyprum, avexisse, fingunt Veteres. Legendi Homerus Iliados ξ, Moschus in Europa, Lycophron Cassandra, Theocritus, Apollodorus lib. iii. in princ. Horatius iii Carm. Oda xxvii, Ovidius lib. v. Fastor. & vi. Metamorph. Seneca Herc. Furente Actus i. Sc. i. & Herc. Oeta Act. ii. Sc. ultima, Varro lib. iv. de LL. & apud eum Manlius, Festus lib. v. de Verb. signific. Isidorus lib. viii. Originum, cap. xi, & lib. xiv, cap. iv, Calpurnius Bassus commentar. Phaenomen. Caesaris Germanici, & apud eum Nigidius Grammaticus, qui Iovem in hoc raptu opera Neptuni scribit usum. Videndi & Clemens Alexandrinus ἀρπαγή λεγ. Iustinus
units.tr: So much for the order of the discussion. Now the etymology of the name comes next to be explained. Herodotus, in book 4, notes that no mortal has discovered the origin of the name Europe. Others, however, say that it is called after Europa the Tyrian, daughter of Agenor, king of the Phoenicians (of Libya, says Isidore). The ancients feign that Jupiter, changed into a bull, carried her off and, setting her on his back, bore her from Sidon to Crete or Cyprus. Read Homer, Iliad 20 [ξ]; Moschus, On Europa; Lycophron, Cassandra; Theocritus; Apollodorus, book 3, at the beginning; Horace, Odes 3, ode 27; Ovid, Fasti book 5 and Metamorphoses book 6; Seneca, Hercules Furens, act 1, scene 1, and Hercules Oetaeus, act 2, last scene; Varro, On the Latin Language, book 4, and Manilius, who is cited by him; Festus, On the Meaning of Words, book 5; Isidore, Origins, book 8, chapter 11, and book 14, chapter 4; Calpurnius Bassus, Commentary on the Phaenomena of Caesar Germanicus, and Nigidius Grammaticus cited there, who writes that Jupiter used the help of Neptune in this abduction. See also Clement of Alexandria, ἀρπαγή λεγ. [arpagē, used only once], and Justin.

units.la: Europae nomen indunt alii ab Europa Agenoris filia, ab Iove Tauro rapta. nus Martyr 11 ad Græcos, Arnobius lib. iv. adversus Gentes, Augustinus lib. iv. de Civitate Dei cap. xxvii, Lactant. lib. Divinar. Instit. 1. cap. xi. Prudentius adversus Symmachum de Iove. Scriptores apud Pollucem, lib. 1. cap. ix. non nominati, Fabulis rejectis, raptam volunt Navi Tauriformi: Incerti apud Festum Navem hic agnoscunt, cujus Tutela effigiem habebat Tauri: Palephatus virum quemdam Cretensem Taurum nominatum fuisse scribit, qui ex Tyrrhena Regione cum ceteris Puellis Europam quoque Regis Filiam abduxit Captivam: Sunt qui Legionem Militarem fuisse censent, cui inter Signa Insigne erat Tauri: Quidam, ut addit Festus, ob pulcritudinem Regionis, per similitudinem raptæ Filiæ, sic nuncupatam narrant.
units.tr: Others take the name Europe from Europa, daughter of Agenor, carried off by Jove in the form of a bull: Justin Martyr, To the Greeks 11; Arnobius, Against the Gentiles, book 4; Augustine, City of God, book 4, chapter 27; Lactantius, Divine Institutes, book 1, chapter 11; Prudentius, Against Symmachus, on Jove. Writers not named by Pollux, book 1, chapter 9, reject the fables and hold that she was carried off on a ship in the shape of a bull. Unnamed writers cited by Festus recognise here a ship whose figurehead bore the image of a bull. Palephatus writes that a certain Cretan called Taurus, who came from the Tyrrhenian region, carried off with the other girls also Europa, the king's daughter, as a captive. Some think she was a military legion, whose standard bore the sign of a bull. Others, as Festus adds, tell that the region was named in this way on account of its beauty, by likeness to the daughter who was carried off.

units.la: Taurus sane, quo vecta fingitur Europa, non inconcinne mores & indolem quodam modo refert Europæorum. Elatioris est animi, exsultans, speciosus cornibus, colore niveo, lato gutture, cervice crassa, Dux & Armentis imperitans; summæ continentiæ, sed si ad dissimilem sexum adducatur, calidissimus inguineque potens, post casus modestiæque servantissimus. Tales fere Europæi, præsertim qui Septemtrionaliores. Andron Teius putat Oceano duas nupsisse Nymphas; ex quarum una natæ Asia & Africa, ex altera Europa: has autem tribus Orbis Partibus nomina imposuisse. Ab Europo sic vocatam non male quis dixerit, quem in hac Orbis Terrarum Parte aliquando Regnum tenuisse scribunt Pompeius Trogus & Eustathius in Lycophronem; quorum etiam hic eundem Europum cuiusdam Himeri facit Filium.
units.tr: The bull, indeed, on which Europa is feigned to have been carried, somewhat aptly reflects in a way the character and disposition of the Europeans. It is high-spirited, exultant, proud in its horns, snow-white in colour, broad in the throat, thick in the neck, a leader that rules the herd. It is of the greatest self-restraint, but if it is brought near the other sex it is very hot and potent in its loins, yet after its conquests it is most moderate and reserved. Such, for the most part, are the Europeans, especially those who live further north. Andron of Teos thinks that Ocean married two nymphs, from one of whom Asia and Africa were born, and from the other Europe; and that they gave their names to the three parts of the world. It would not be wrong to say that the name comes from Europus, whom Pompeius Trogus and Eustathius on Lycophron write once ruled in this part of the earth; Lycophron also makes this same Europus the son of a certain Himerus.

units.la: Quin & Europen Sicyniorum Regem statuunt Pausanias & Eusebius in Chronicis; eumque tempore Abrahami Patriarchæ. Geropius Becanus persuaderi nolens Europam Græcam habere nomenclaturam, quum prius ab Cimmeriis sit habitata, quam ab Græcis, ipsque alia, quam his, fuerit Lingua; sic vocatam arbitratur ab Gentis præstantia: Ver enim monosyllabum per Diphthongum elatum nihil aliud esse, quam magnum quid & excellens, quodq; in quaque re præstantissimum; Hop autem hominum multitudinem designare. Idem Goropius in Codice quodam edito, quo uti solitus erat, cuiusque marginibus, secundam parans editionem, sua manu passim multa adscripserat, novam de Europæ Etymo sententiam notarat his verbis: Verum diligentius mihi nomen cum Sacris Litteris conferenti, altera ratio in mentem
units.tr: Moreover, Pausanias and Eusebius in his Chronicle make Europen king of the Sicyonians, and place him in the time of the patriarch Abraham. Goropius Becanus, unwilling to be persuaded that the Greek word Europe has its origin in Greek, since the region was inhabited by the Cimmerians before it was by the Greeks, and since they had a different language from these, thinks it was so called from the excellence of the people. For Ver, he says, a monosyllable lengthened by a diphthong, means nothing other than something great and excellent, and what is most outstanding in any thing; and Hop designates a multitude of men. The same Goropius, in a certain edition which he used, and in whose margins, while preparing a second edition, he had written many notes in his own hand here and there, noted a new opinion on the etymology of Europe in these words: "But when I compared the name more carefully with the Sacred Letters, another explanation came into my mind,

units.la: venit, longe præstantior & felicius omen proferens. Iapeto dilationem, & ut alij interpretantur, Gaudium promitti videmus, quod tum consequuturus erat, quum Christus Morte sua nos redemisset. Et igitur legitimum Connubium denotat; Ur/ excellens; Hop spem: quo fit, ut Europ Legitimi Connubij excellens spes sit, quæ propria ejus Terrarum portionis fuit, quam Noachus Iapeto dedit habitandam. Quamvis enim Semi posteritas per Abrahamum multis sæculis Deo fuerit conjugata, tamen repudiata est. Conjugium vero, quo Christus Europam Ecclesiam suam copulavit, numquam dissolvetur; adeo ut optimo jure Iapeti portio Europa dicatur.
units.tr: far more excellent, and bringing a happier omen. We see that enlargement is promised to Japheth, and, as others interpret, joy, which he was to obtain when Christ had redeemed us by his death. So Ur denotes lawful marriage, Ur excellent, and Hop hope. It follows that Europe is the excellent hope of lawful marriage, which was the proper portion of that part of the earth which Noah gave to Japheth to inhabit. For although the posterity of Shem, through Abraham, was wedded to God for many centuries, yet it was repudiated. But the marriage by which Christ joined Europe to himself as his Church will never be dissolved; so that with the best right Europe is called the portion of Japheth."

units.la: Cap. IV.
units.tr: Chapter IV.

units.la: Europæ diversa panduntur vel Nomina vel Cognomina.
units.tr: The various names and surnames of Europe are set out.

units.la: ETymon Europæ indicavi: nonnullas pandam ejusdem varias Appellationes. Tyriam vocant hanc Orbis partem nonnulli, inter quos Theocritus, à Tyria, quam Puellæ raptæ, quidam Matrem, Patriam alij perhibent. Scriptorum Sacrorum non pauci Iapetiam nominant ab Iapeto, de quo dixi. Ptolemæus 11 Quadripartiti Celticam communi nomine vocari scribit, à Populis eam incolentibus. Sed ubi? Passim. Nam ubi non in ea Orbis Parte, quam nunc Europam dicimus, fuere Celta? Si Hispaniæ antiquiora rimemur; Celtos vel Celticos indicabit circa Bætin Fluvium Strabo; partim Bæticæ, Lusitaniæ partim Incolas Ptolemæus; extra Cippos Herculis, Cynesijs finitimos, omniumque, qui ad Occasum habitant, ultimos, Herodotus; Citerioris Hispaniæ Populos Plinius, eosque duplices, Nerias & Præsamarcos; circa Promontorium, quod ab ijs Celticum (olim etiam Artabrum & Nerium, hodie Cabo de Finisterre) Pomponius: Celtas insuper nominatos fuisse Cantabros & Asturæs, docebunt Dio & Xiphilinus: aperiet item Celticam, Conventus Hispalensis Civitatem, Plinius, quæ Celsum Antonino inter Hispalim & Augustam Emeritam: Celtiberos denique vel Celtiberes dabunt cum alij, tum Ptolemæus, Hispaniæ Tarraconensis conensis Populos. Si veterem Galliam Germaniamque consideremus: Gallos & Germanos Celtas appellatos omnium Historicorum vnanimis loquetur sententia; Celtas utramque Rheni Ripam & Gallicam & Germanicam (quo loco hodieque antiquum nomen non obscure servatur Gelri) habitasse dicet Dio lib. xxxix. Celtas Rheni adcolas facit Sudas; Galliam quidem Latinis, Ptolemæo autem aliisque Græcis Scriptoribus Celto-Galatiam vocari discemus: Strabo prolatos ex parte illa, quæ Narbonensis, Celtas adferet nomen etiam ceteris Gallis indidisse: Celto-Ligures monstrabit Aristoteles in Admir. qui Celto-Ligures Straboni, quorumque sedes, ubi hodie Provincia circa Massiliam. Si calcos Italos examinemus, Celtas in Gallia Cisalpina vel Italica & ad mare Ionium vel Adriaticum (quod & Celticum Apollonij Scholiasti) monstrabunt Appianus & Strabo; ad Eridanum fluvium Silius Italicus. Si remotiores hinc Partes perambulare lubebit, Celtas in Cassiteridibus Britanniæ Insulis sistet Pomponius; in Epiro, Antonius Liberalis; ad Hemum Montem, Stephanus; ad Danubij ostia, Arrianus in Mœsia, in Illurico, in Thracia, ad Borysthenem, Strabo; in Scythia, Aristoteles de Mundo, idem Strabo, & Plutarchus: Omnes versus Septemtrionem Gentes Celtas nuncupatos, docebit, quem sæpe dixi, Strabo: Plutarchum etiam deprehendemus in Mario Celticam diffinire ab exteriore Mari vel Atlantico versus Septemtrionem, indeque ad Mœotidem usque Paludem: accedet & Lycophron Celtes Stagnum describens prope Istri ostium. Sed Europam merito Celticam nominari debere, manifeste innuit apud Strabonem Ephorus, ubi Terræ totius loca in quatuor partes diducens, dicit eam, quæ versus Subsolanum est, habitari ab Indis, quæ versus Austrum, ab Æthiopibus, quæ ad Aquilonem, ab Scythis, quæ in Occasum vergit, ab Celtis.
units.tr: I have given the etymology of Europe; now I shall set out some of its various appellations. Some call this part of the world Tyria, among them Theocritus, after Tyria, which some say was the mother of the abducted girl and others her homeland. Not a few writers of sacred matters call it Iapetia, after Iapetus, of whom I have spoken. Ptolemy (Quadripartitum, book 11) writes that it was commonly called Celtica, after the peoples who inhabited it. But where? Everywhere. For where in that part of the world which we now call Europe were the Celts not? If we examine the more ancient parts of Spain: Strabo will show Celts or Celtici around the river Baetis; Ptolemy shows them among the inhabitants of Baetica and of Lusitania; Herodotus places them beyond the Pillars of Hercules, neighbours of the Cynesii and the furthest of all who dwell towards the west; Pliny names the peoples of Hither Spain, and these in two groups, the Nerii and the Praesamarci; Pompónius shows them around the promontory called Celtic by them (formerly also Artabrum and Nerium, today Cabo de Finisterre); Dio and Xiphilinus will teach that the Cantabrians and the Asturians were also called Celts; Pliny likewise reveals a Celtica, a town in the assize district of Hispalis, which Antoninus calls Celsa, between Hispalis and Augusta Emerita; and finally, both others and Ptolemy will give us the Celtiberians or Celtiberes, peoples of Tarraconensis. If we consider old Gaul and Germany: the unanimous opinion of all the historians will tell us that the Gauls and Germans were called Celts; Dio, book 39, says that the Celts inhabited both banks of the Rhine, Gallic and German (in which place the ancient name is still plainly preserved today in Gelri). Suidas makes the Celts neighbours of the Rhine; we shall learn that Gaul is called by the Latins, but by Ptolemy and other Greek writers, Celto-Galatia. Strabo will show that the Celts, sprung from that part which is Narbonensis, also gave their name to the other Gauls. Aristotle, in the De mirabilibus, will point out the Celto-Ligures, whom Strabo mentions, and whose seat, where the province around Massilia now lies. If we examine the Italian lands, Appian and Strabo show the Celts in Cisalpine or Italian Gaul and by the Ionian or Adriatic sea (which is also the "Celtic" sea of Apollonius' scholiast); Silius Italicus places them by the river Eridanus. If we wish to wander through more remote regions, Pompónius sets the Celts in the Cassiterides islands of Britain; Antoninus Liberalis in Epirus; Stephanus by Mount Haemus; Arrian by the mouths of the Danube, in Moesia, in Illyricum and in Thrace; Strabo places them by the Borysthenes; Aristotle (De mundo), Strabo again, and Plutarch place them in Scythia. Strabo, whom I have often cited, teaches that all the nations toward the north are called Celts. In Marius, Plutarch is found defining Celtica as extending from the outer or Atlantic sea toward the north, and thence as far as the Maeotian marsh. Lycophron, describing the lake of the Celts near the mouth of the Ister, also joins in. But that Europe ought rightly to be called Celtica is plainly hinted by Ephorus in Strabo, where, dividing the whole earth into four parts, he says that the part facing the east is inhabited by Indians, that facing the south by Ethiopians, that facing the north by Scythians, and that which tends to the west by Celts.

units.la: Europæos hodie Francos universim appellant Asiatici. Turcis Franki vocantur Religionis Romanæ Cultores, ut Romei, qui Græcæ addicti. Abissini, quod restantur variorum Ephemerides, in Africa, Nos etiam Alfranguēs, Christianorum autem Regionem Frankiam nuncupant.
units.tr: Today Asians generally call all Europeans Franks. By the Turks, worshippers of the Roman religion are called Franks, as are the Romei, who adhere to the Greek rite. The Abyssinians, as the journals of various writers attest, in Africa also call us Alfranguēs, and they name the region of the Christians Frankia.

units.la: Græcis hæc Pars Εὐρώπη & Εὐρωπέα; Sophocli item & Euripidi tante Stephano, Ἀλφ Ἐ ἡ Εὐρωπία. De Specialiore vocis notione dicam, ubi de Asia.
units.tr: To the Greeks this part is Εὐρώπη and Εὐρωπέα [Europē, Europea]. Sophocles and Euripides likewise, and Stephanus, call it ἡ Εὐρωπία [hē Europia]. I shall speak of the more specific sense of the word when I come to Asia.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: Chapter V.

units.la: Europæ Situs Cœlestis, ejusque Longitudo & Latitudo.
units.tr: The Celestial Position of Europe, and its Longitude and Latitude.

units.la: DE Europa dixi universim: speciatim quæ ipsi Quantitas, quæ Qualitas, docebo. Quod illam attinet, sciendum cum primis Ptolemæum Aliosque veteres Europam collocare inter Climata iv & ix; inter Parallelos xl & xxx; inter Gradus Latitudinis xxxvi & liv, Longitudinis xvii & lxi: nostra ætate, quum & Solis Declinatio, quemadmodum Partis i lib. iii. cap. xxiii notavi, mutata sit, & plurima Loca, Europæ Nostræ adcensenda, ad lxxii. usque Latitudinis gradum versus Septemtrionem in notitiam venerint; eamque ob causam ulterior Climatum Parallelorumque Notatio fuerit excogitata; sitam conspicimus Europam inter Climata iv & xiix; Parallelos x i & xxxvi; Gradus denique Latitudinis quidem xxxvi & lxxii, Longitudinis autem, si, qua longissime se expandit, considerentur à Promontorio Hispaniæ, quod Cabo S. Vincenty hodie vocant, usque ad Lineam rectam à Tanais fonte ad Oceanum Borealem ductam, inter Gradus fere xvii & lxxi; qua vero brevissima, ab eodem Hispaniæ Promontorio usque ad Malcam Peloponnesi Caput, exclusis Ægæi maris, quæ Europæ adnumerari possunt, Insulis (de quibus speciatim ago Parte mei Operis vii) inter Gradus xvii & lviii: adeo ut Meridionalissima Europæ sint gradu Latitudinis xxxvi, Hispaniæ Mons Calpe, quem unam Herculis Columnarum faciunt, Promontorium Siciliæ Austrinum, Odyssia olim dicebatur, & Peloponnesi, hodie Morea, Caput, quod ad Messeniacum Sinum Tænaria Veteribus, nunc Cabo Maini, dicitur; quibus locis maximus dies horarum xiiii, minut. xxx: Septemtrionalissimus autem Limes sit, gradu lxxi & dimidio, Scandiæ Promontorium, versus Boream ultimum, quod hodie wardhuys dicunt, ubi maximus dies ii est mensium, xxii dierum, horarum vii. Ex quibus, quot miliaria vel Germanica vel Italica sit aut longa aut lata Europa, facile docebit Caput libri iii, Partis Primæ, xx.
units.tr: I have spoken of Europe in general; now I will set out its particular extent and character. As to its extent, it should first be noted that Ptolemy and the other ancients place Europe between the 4th and 9th climates, between the parallels of 40 and 30, and between the degrees of latitude 36 and 54 and of longitude 17 and 61. In our own age, since the solar declination has changed (as I noted in Part I, book 3, chapter 23), and since very many places that belong to our Europe have become known as far north as the 72nd degree of latitude, a further notation of climates and parallels has been devised for this reason. We now see Europe lying between the climates 4 and 18, the parallels 11 and 36, and, finally, between the degrees of latitude 36 and 72. As to longitude, if one measures it along the greatest extent of Europe, from the promontory of Spain that is now called Cabo S. Vincenty to the straight line drawn from the source of the Tanais to the Northern Ocean, it lies between about the 17th and 71st degrees. Measured by the shortest line, from the same promontory of Spain to Malea, the cape of the Peloponnese, leaving out the islands of the Aegean Sea (which may be counted as part of Europe, and which I treat in particular in Part VII of my work), it lies between the 17th and 58th degrees. So the most southerly points of Europe lie at 36 degrees of latitude: Mount Calpe in Spain, which together with Abyla makes up one of the Pillars of Hercules; the southern promontory of Sicily, once called Odyssia; and the cape of the Peloponnese, now Morea, which the ancients called Tænaria and which is now called Cabo Maini, on the Messenian Gulf. In these places the longest day is 14 hours and 30 minutes. The northernmost limit, at 71 and a half degrees, is the promontory of Scandia furthest north, which they now call wardhuys; there the longest day is 2 months, 22 days and 7 hours. From these figures, the third book of the first Part, chapter 20, will easily show how many German or Italian miles Europe is in length and in breadth.

units.la: Lineam porro, a Tanais fonte versus Septemtrionem recta in Oceanum ductam, Orientalem Europæ Limitem statui, communes, à quibus dissentire religio mihi est, sequutus Calculos. Quis enim Europa Limitibus sit versus Orientem distinguenda, inter veteres Scriptores parum convenit. Quid sit, quod Seneca lib. vi. Natural. Danubium scribat Europam Asiamque distinguere, alibi erit aperiendi locus. Aristoteles, Plato, Herodotus, & alij, qui his suffragantur, Europam ab Asia separant Phasi flumine sive Isthmo, qui est inter Pontum Euxinum Mareque Caspium. Dionysius, Arrianus, Diodorus, Polybius, Iornandes, Tanai flumine simpliciter. Abrahamus Ortelius Fines Europæ versus Ortum statuit, primo Fluvium Tanaim, hinc Isthmum inter eundem Tanaim & Rhaam, mox Rhaæ versus Orientem Divertigium; postremo Obium fluvium ad Ostium usque. Novi, qui Moscoviam in Asia (quæ mihi eo loco Scythia) positurus, Terminos Europæ versus ortum sacraret primo Arcum, cuius Medio Livoniam attingente, extremitas una in Grandvico Sinu, altera in Borusthenis Ostio collocaretur; hinc, lectis Occidentalioribus Euxini Ponti littoribus, Bosporum Thracium, Propontidem, Hellespontum & Ægæum Pelagus. Ptolemæus eodem Tanai flumine finit ab Asia Europam, ductaque ab ejus fonte versus Boream ad Mare usque Linea. Huic cum peritissimis Geographis subscribens, descensu ab Linea Tanaique flumine versus Austrum facto, metas porro cum aliis Orientales signo in Palude Mœotide, Bosporo Cimmerio, Ponto Euxino, Bosporo Thracio, Propontide, Marique Ægæo usque in Mare Mediterraneum, quo Meridiem versus ab Africa separatur: ad Occidentem vastissimus eam pullat & apertissimus Oceanus; ad Septemtrionem denique Mari clauditur Boreali. Videndi huc Strabo lib. ii. Dionysius de Situ Orbis, Plinius lib. iii. in Præfat. item lib. iv. cap. xi, lib. v. cap. xxxii, alisque locis, Pomponius Mela lib. i. cap. iii, Rufus Festus Avienus in descriptione Orbis Terræ, Orosius lib. i. cap. ii; Isidorus lib. xiv. cap. iv.
units.tr: Next, I have taken as the eastern boundary of Europe the line drawn straight from the source of the Tanais northward into the ocean, following the calculations commonly accepted, from which I think it wrong to depart. For there is little agreement among the ancient writers about how Europe is to be divided from the east. Why Seneca, in book 6 of the Natural Questions, writes that the Danube separates Europe from Asia will be explained in another place. Aristotle, Plato, Herodotus and others who agree with them separate Europe from Asia by the River Phasis or by the isthmus between the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea. Dionysius, Arrian, Diodorus, Polybius and Jordanes use simply the River Tanais. Abraham Ortelius set the eastern limits of Europe as follows: first the river Tanais, then the isthmus between the same Tanais and the Rha, then the watershed of the Rha towards the east, and finally the river Ob as far as its mouth. Some who wished to place Moscovy in Asia (which for me is Scythia in that place) marked the eastern limits of Europe by first an arc, whose middle touches Livonia, with one end at the Gulf of Riga and the other at the mouth of the Borysthenes; then, following the western shores of the Black Sea, the Thracian Bosporus, the Propontis, the Hellespont and the Aegean Sea. Ptolemy divides Europe from Asia by the same River Tanais, drawing a line from its source to the ocean northward. Agreeing with the most learned geographers, after going down from this line along the Tanais southward, I mark the remaining eastern boundaries, with others, through the Maeotian Marsh, the Cimmerian Bosporus, the Black Sea, the Thracian Bosporus, the Propontis and the Aegean Sea, as far as the Mediterranean, which separates Europe from Africa to the south. To the west it is bounded by the vast and open Ocean; to the north it is finally enclosed by the Northern Sea. On these matters see Strabo, book 2; Dionysius, On the Situation of the World; Pliny, book 3, in the preface, and also book 4, chapter 11, book 5, chapter 32, and elsewhere; Pomponius Mela, book 1, chapter 3; Rufus Festus Avienus, in his description of the earth; Orosius, book 1, chapter 2; and Isidore, book 14, chapter 4.

units.la: Europæ sic distinctæ formam Strabo tribuit, quæ Draconis fere effigiem æmulatur, Capite Occidentem spectante, Alis utrimque expansis; referentibus eas ad Austrum quidem Italia, ad Septemtrionem Cimbrica Chersonneso. Placet: ea tamen lege, ut Ala dexterior, multo jam quam Strabonis ævo sinisteriore sit major, quod, ut sæpe monui, multa supra Cimbricam Chersonnesum versus Septemtrionem nobis Loca, de quibus nihil Veteres compertum habuerunt, in notitiam venerint.
units.tr: Strabo ascribes to Europe, so divided, a shape that closely resembles a dragon: its head faces west, and its wings are spread out on either side. Italy is taken to correspond to the wing toward the south, and the Cimbrian Chersonese to the wing toward the north. I agree, with this proviso, that the right wing is now much larger than the left was in Strabo's day, because, as I have often pointed out, many places north of the Cimbrian Chersonese have become known to us, of which the ancients had learned nothing.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CAP. VI.

units.la: Europæ Qualitas.
units.tr: The Quality of Europe.

units.la: Sic se habet Quantitas: sequitur illustranda Qualitas, cum ipsius Terræ, tum Incolarum, quo ad Mores & Linguam. Europa quanta quanta est habitatur, quamuis quicquid locorum supra lx Latitudinis gradum, propter Frigora cum incommode, tum laboriose. Addit Strabo lib. ii, τὴν Εὐρώπην συμπάσαν οἰκήσιμον εἶναι, πλὴν ἐλίγης τῆς ἀοικήτου ... περὶ τὴν Τάναιν καὶ τὴν Μαιώτην, καὶ τὴν Βοσπόρον. Quod mirum alicui merito censeri posset, quum loca, quæ nominat Strabo, incidant in xlvii, xlviii & xlix Latitudinis gradus; & ex Situ cælesti sub Octavo Climate non inclementiore videantur frui Aëre, quam in Gallijs Biturigum, Aurelianensium, Parisiensiumque Agri. Sed faciunt passim in hac Mole Montes; ut quæ loca suo situ futura essent calida, habitationique commodissima, si plana vastioribus istis huius Orbis Verrucis carerent; eadem, quacumque Terrarum parte, propter impositia Tubera, Nivibus numquam non cana, Intermontiaque ab Ventis, semel ingressis, ibique conclusis, & ut maiorum essent virium, contractis, præcipue si ab Arctoo Orbe ingruerint, infestari supra modum solita, sint frigida, efficianturque aspera, inculta, horrida, deserta, & Domiciliis figendis, Pagis struendis, Opidis condendis inimica. Nota sane quæ commemorantur de Frigoribus etiam media æstate Montium Pyrenæorum gradu xliii, Alpiumque gradu xlvii aut circiter; quin & illorum, quos in Orbe Novo gradu x gerit Isthmus, Americam Meridionalem ab Septemtrionali separans. Alia præterea: singula enim suis locis explicabuntur. Hoc certum; Nihil hodie non in Europa habitari; neque adeo ipsos Montes, licet perpetuis fere Nivibus obsitos Incola, frequentiore tamen, carere. Summo igitur merito reliquas Orbis Terræ Partes stupenda Cœli clementia, temperie, amœnitate; benigna Soli fertilitate; maxima Incolarum incredibilis humanitatis, Indolisque supra, quam dici potest, tractabilis frequentia; Urbium ingentium pulcherrimarumque, Opidorum, Arcium, Pagorum, Fluminum, Stagnorum, Lacuum, Aquarumque, quis variæ vires, Omnis item generis Animantium, Arborum, Frugum, Plantarum, Metallorum, & aliarum, quæ sustentandæ hominum Vitæ sunt necessariæ, Rerum copia longe superat. Cetera, quibus caret, Gemmas Preciososque lapides, Aromata, aliaque odorifera, tam cumulate, tamque liberali manu ab Asia importata accipit, imo ut generalius cum Strabone loquar, neve quam Orbis particulam excludam, ξω̃ν μίσον, ut nusquam major fit affluentia. Orbis Domitorum (nam nec hic ab ejus temperare possum laudibus) Genitrix. Quid ni? Produxit quidem hic olim Alexandrum Macedonia, Italia Romanos; qui successione quadam; quam Deus æterna sua Providentia decreverat, Terrarum Orbem, quousque notum habebant, domuerunt: producit autem hodieque Germania Principes, qui Quartæ Romanorum Monarchiæ jura, quantum per Immanissimorum Hostium potentiam & impressiones licet, sarta tecta tuentur. Nunquid & Magni, quos Avorum adorarunt tempora, Europæ Heroes incognitam, ut plerorum est opinio, Veteribus Americam, potioresque & validiores Africæ Asiæque Partes suo adjecerunt Imperio? Numquid & Sedes Summi est Pontificis? Numquid Mater tot Regum, tot Principum, Christo, quod alibi rarius, militantium? Quin & Turcarum Imperator, neglecta quasi & relicta suis Ducibus Præfectisque Asia, in hanc Orbis Partem extremis usus viribus, migravit: omnem adhibens operam, ut singulis annis in penitiora, etiam magna Suorum clade & internecione, se insinuet.
units.tr: Such is the quantity of Europe. Its quality must now be set out, both of the land itself and of its inhabitants, in respect of their manners and language. Europe is inhabited throughout its whole extent, although whatever lies beyond the sixtieth degree of latitude is inhabited with difficulty and hardship, because of the cold. Strabo adds in book 2 that the whole of Europe is habitable, except for a small uninhabited tract around the Tanais, the Maeotis and the Bosporus [τὴν Εὐρώπην συμπάσαν οἰκήσιμον εἶναι, πλὴν ἐλίγης τῆς ἀοικήτου ... περὶ τὴν Τάναιν καὶ τὴν Μαιώτην, καὶ τὴν Βοσπόρον]. This might rightly strike someone as remarkable, since the places Strabo names lie at the forty-seventh, forty-eighth and forty-ninth degrees of latitude, and by their position under the eighth climate they seem to enjoy no harsher air than the fields of the Bituriges, the Aurelians and the Parisians in France. But throughout this mass there are mountains, which make places that would otherwise be warm and most suitable for habitation, were they flat and free of those vast warts of the globe, into something cold, rough, uncultivated, bristling and deserted, hostile to settling homes, building villages and founding towns. The mountains are always white with snow, and they lie between high ridges, and once the winds have entered and been shut in there, they grow stronger through confinement. Where these winds rush in from the northern regions, the land is especially plagued beyond measure. Indeed, the facts reported about the cold even in midsummer are well known: in the Pyrenees at about the forty-third degree, in the Alps at about the forty-seventh, and likewise in the mountains that the Isthmus in the New World, at the tenth degree, carries, separating South America from North. There are other examples too, for each will be explained in its place. This much is certain: today nothing is left in Europe uninhabited, and even the mountains themselves, though the inhabitants keep them almost always covered with snow, are nonetheless quite densely settled. Rightly, then, does Europe far surpass the other parts of the world in the astonishing mildness and temperateness of its climate and its pleasantness; in the kindly fertility of its soil; in the greatest and incredible humanity of its people and their disposition, more tractable than can be said; and in the abundance of its great and most beautiful cities, towns, fortresses, villages, rivers, pools, lakes and waters, each with its own virtues, and of every kind of living creature, trees, crops, plants, metals and other things necessary to sustain human life. As for the things it lacks, such as gems and precious stones, spices and other fragrant goods, Europe receives them in such abundance and with such generous hands imported from Asia that, to speak more broadly with Strabo, and so as not to exclude any part of the world, it is "in the middle of the living world" [ζῴων μέσον], so that nowhere is there a greater flow of goods. It is the mother of the conquerors of the world (for I cannot refrain from praising it here too). Why not? Macedonia once produced Alexander, and Italy the Romans, who by a certain succession, which God in his eternal providence had decreed, subdued the orb of the earth as far as they knew it. And even today Germany produces princes who, so far as the power and assaults of the most savage enemies allow, preserve the rights of the Fourth Monarchy of the Romans whole and intact. Did not the great men whom the times of our forefathers worshipped, the heroes of Europe, add to their empire America, unknown to the ancients as most people think, and the more important and stronger parts of Africa and Asia? Is not the seat of the supreme Pontiff here? Is it not the mother of so many kings and princes, who fight for Christ more rarely elsewhere? Indeed, the emperor of the Turks, as if he had neglected and abandoned Asia to his commanders and prefects, has migrated into this part of the world, using his utmost strength, and makes every effort to insinuate himself further in each year, even at great slaughter and destruction of his own people.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CAP. VII.

units.la: Europæorum Mores.
units.tr: The Morals of the Europeans

units.la: EA Terræ est Qualitas: sua etiam est Incolis. Sed ego non is sum, qui nulla coactus necessitate summas mihi parare velim molestias, & certissimam ab aliis Invidiam. Præstare difficile est, quod Titulus pollicetur. Non ubique fui, ut Europæorum omnium genios & ingenia fideli penicillo depingam. Faciat hoc, qui πολλῶν ἀνθρώπων ἴδεν ἄστα καὶ νόον ἔγνω.
units.tr: Every land has its own quality, and its inhabitants have their own. But I am not one who, without any compelling necessity, would wish to bring great trouble on myself and certain hostility from others. It is hard to deliver what the title promises. I have not been everywhere, so as to paint faithfully the genius and character of all Europeans. Let him do that who "saw the cities of many men and knew their minds" [πολλῶν ἀνθρώπων ἴδεν ἄστα καὶ νόον ἔγνω].

units.la: Et fuerim etiam multis in locis, multaque multo usu & longa consuetudine didicerim, numquid omnia temporis lapsu adventitioque commercio crebris Mutationibus sunt obnoxia? Vni prodeant in arenam Populares mei. De Batavis scripserat, Domitiano Imperante, Poeta festivus, Tune es, tune, ait, ille Martialis? Cujus Nequitias locosque novit, Aurem qui modo non habet Batavam.
units.tr: Even though I have been in many places, and have learned much from long experience and lasting acquaintance, do not all things change with the passing of time and through the frequent mutations of outside commerce? Let my fellow countrymen come forward into the arena first. The witty poet wrote about the Batavians under Domitian: "Are you really that Martial, you who know his wickedness and the places where he lives, the one who scarcely has a Batavian ear?"

units.la: Rusticitatis, si genuina sit & vera Scriptura (nam Batavam sunt qui mutant ex Membranis in severam) Inelegantiæ, Frontisque tetricæ Maiores nostros insimulat: an vere, non libet inquirere. Esto tamen. Sed quis hæc talia non etiam de aliis aliquando canere potuit Populis? Nam qui non quandoque fuerunt rudiores? Quum Romani, Rerum post Domini, nihil noscent præter Agriculturam & Militiam fortean, Auris cui modo non erat Quiritum,
units.tr: He accuses our forebears of rusticity, of inelegance and a grim brow, if the text is genuine and true (for some change "Batavam" to "severam" in the parchment copies). Whether this is really so, I do not care to inquire. Granted, let it be so. But who could not sing such things about other peoples at some time? For were not all peoples at some time ruder? When the Romans, after the age of the Lord, knew nothing except farming and perhaps soldiering, an ear like that of the Quirites, which was not yet cultivated,

units.la: Elegans, festivis moribus, & exploratæ censebatur facilitatis. Fuerint igitur Domitiani principatu, atque etiam multo post, cum ab impuritate Martialis aversiores, tum rudiores, crassioresque & auris & naris Batavi. Prius Objectum lubentes patiuntur, tiuntur, adgenitam sibi gratulantes Probitatem Morumque sanctitatem: si Posterius discutiatur, quam hodie mutarunt! Quid enim Batavis humanius, quid candidius, quid ad omne Disciplinarum Artiumque genus capiendum pronius, paratius, promptius? Nihil non ab ijs, etiam hac belli tempestate, cum publice, tum privatim discitur, vel ad Remp. prudenter administrandam, vel ad Bellum caute suscipiendum, fortiter gerendum, feliciter finiendum, vel ad Bellorum nervos valide cumque optato fructu concinnandos, vel ad Oeconomicas res dextre nitideque instituendas. Dicant, quae viderint audierintque cum alij, tum Mercatores, qui ipsos adierunt: Velint nolint, fateri cogentur quae dixi. Quid Vitiorum in aliis Populis non aperiam. Vestigia terrent. Scio quid valeant Tela Westphalorum in Brabantos. Hoc saltem liceat, ut ab Magno viro (cui Scientiae omnes vanae erant & incertae) Commissionem videamus, institutam inter quatuor, quae in nostra Distributione primo se loco obserunt, Gentes; Hispanos, Gallos, Italos, & Germanos: Habent singulae Nationes, inquit, a Superis adgnata sibi Morum discrimina, per quae facile a se invicem discernantur, ut cujus quisque nationis sit oriundus, a Voce, a Sermone, ab Oratione, a Consilio, a Conversatione, a Victu, a Negocio, ab Amore & Odio, ab Ira & Militia, similibusque Exercitys facile cognoscatur. Quis enim videns hominem ingredientem incessu gallinaceo, gestu gladiatorio, vultu effreno, voce bubula, sermone austero, moribus ferocem, habitu dissoluto laciniatove, non mox judicet esse Germanum? Nonne Gallos cognoscimus ab Incessu moderato, gestu molli, vultu blando, voce dulcisona, sermone facili, moribus modestis, habitu laxo? Hispanos autem ab ingressu, & moribus gestibusque festivis, vultu claro, voce flebili, sermone eleganti, habitu exquisito: Italos vero videmus incessu tardiusculos, gestu graves, vultu inconstantes, voce remissos, sermone captiosos, moribus magnificos, habitu compositos. Iamque scimus etiam, quia in Cantu balant Itali, gemunt Hispani, ululant Germani, modulantur Galli: sunt in Oratione graves, sed versuti Itali: culti, sed jactabundi, Hispani; prompti, sed superbi, Galli; duri, sed simplices, Germani: in Consilys est providus Italus, astutus Hispanus, inconsideratus Gallus, utilis Germanus: in Victu est mundus Italus, delicatus Hispanus, copiosus Gallus, inconditus Germanus: sunt erga Exteros officiosi Itali, placidi Hispani, mites Galli; agrestes inhospitalesque (non tamen passim) Germani: in Conversationibus sunt prudentes Itali, cauti Hispani, mansueti Galli, imperiosi intolerabilesque Germani: sunt in Amore Zelotypi Itali, impatientes Hispani, leves Galli, ambitiosi Germani: in Odys vero sunt occulti Itali, pertinaces Hispani, minaces Galli, ultores Germani: in gerendis Negocijs sunt circumspecti Itali, laboriosi Germani, vigiles Hispani, solliciti Galli: in Militia sunt strenui, sed crudeles Itali; Hispani callidi, & rapaces; Germani truces & venales; Galli magnanimi, sed precipites: insignes sunt Litteratura Itali, Navigatione Hispani, Civilitate Galli, Religione & Mechanicis Artificijs Germani: & habet unaquaeque Natio, quantumcunque etiam sive civilis sive barbara, peculiares Mores Ritusque, sibi a Caeli influxu a ceteris diversos, &c.
units.tr: was thought elegant, of polished manners, and of proven refinement. So in Domitian's reign, and long after, the Batavian ear and nose were both more averse to Martial's filth, and ruder and coarser. The former charge they bear willingly, rejoicing in the probity and holiness of manners natural to them. But if the latter is examined, how much have they changed today! For what is more humane than the Batavians, what more candid, what more inclined, ready and prompt to take up every kind of learning and art? Nothing is not learned among them, even in this storm of war, both publicly and privately: either to administer the state wisely, or to undertake war cautiously, wage it bravely and end it successfully, or to put together the sinews of war vigorously and with the desired result, or to arrange household affairs skilfully and neatly. Let those who have seen and heard them say so, both others and merchants who have visited them: whether they want to or not, they will be forced to admit what I have said. Why should I not reveal the vices of other peoples? Their traces are frightening. I know what the weapons of the Westphalians can do against the Brabanters. Let us at least allow this, that we see a commission set up by a great man (to whom all sciences were vain and uncertain) among the four nations which appear first in our division: the Spaniards, the French, the Italians and the Germans. Each nation, he says, has its own distinctive manners, bestowed by the heavens, by which they are easily distinguished from one another, so that from voice, speech, discourse, counsel, conduct, food, business, love and hatred, anger and warfare, and similar practices, one can readily recognise of what nation each man is born. For who, seeing a man walk with a cock's strut, with a gladiator's gesture, with a wild face, a bellowing voice, a harsh speech, fierce manners, and a loose or ragged dress, would not at once judge him to be a German? Do we not recognise the French by a moderate walk, a soft gesture, a gentle face, a sweet voice, an easy speech, modest manners and a loose dress? The Spaniards, however, by their entrance, their festive manners and gestures, their bright face, plaintive voice, elegant speech and exquisite dress; while the Italians we see walking rather slowly, grave in gesture, inconstant in face, relaxed in voice, crafty in speech, magnificent in manners, and composed in dress. And we now know too that Italians bleat in singing, Spaniards moan, Germans howl, and French warble. The Italians are grave in speech but crafty; the Spaniards refined but boastful; the French ready but proud; the Germans hard but plain. In counsel the Italian is prudent, the Spaniard shrewd, the Frenchman thoughtless, the German useful. In food the Italian is neat, the Spaniard delicate, the Frenchman abundant, the German unrefined. Towards foreigners the Italians are obliging, the Spaniards calm, the French gentle; the Germans are rustic and inhospitable (though not everywhere). In conversation the Italians are prudent, the Spaniards cautious, the French mild, the Germans domineering and intolerable. In love the Italians are jealous, the Spaniards impatient, the French fickle, the Germans ambitious. In hatred the Italians are secretive, the Spaniards stubborn, the French threatening, the Germans vengeful. In carrying on business the Italians are circumspect, the Germans hard-working, the Spaniards watchful, the French anxious. In war the Italians are vigorous but cruel; the Spaniards clever and rapacious; the Germans fierce and venal; the French magnanimous but rash. The Italians are distinguished in literature, the Spaniards in navigation, the French in courtesy, the Germans in religion and mechanical arts. And every nation, however civilised or barbarous, has its own peculiar manners and customs, different from others by the influence of the heavens, and so on.

units.la: Si quis in hac Comparatione vehementius quid in se dictum arbitretur, non Mihi, sed pedibus primo prodeuntibus Nato Aegreque Parto imputet; modeste tamen & sic, ut Manes ejus non solicitet; Me vero habeat insontem. Quidquid sit, non tam in liberum mihi est ingenium, ut alicujus Odio Gratiave Veritati velim vel Vim vel Fucum facere.
units.tr: If anyone in this comparison thinks something has been said against himself more harshly than it should be, let him blame not me but the fate of one born feet first and born with difficulty; yet let him do so modestly, and in a way that does not disturb his shade. Let him consider me innocent. Whatever the case, my nature is not so free that I would wish, out of hatred or favour toward anyone, to do violence to or disguise the truth.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CAP. VIII.

units.la: Europaeorum Linguae.
units.tr: The Languages of Europe.

units.la: MORES aliciniore potius, quam meo, eoque rudiore penicillo depinxi: Linguas Europaeorum jam videamus. De Linguis quaedam universim & in genere dixi Partis 1 lib. iii. cap. xiv: specialius quid de Europaeorum Matricibus & Majoribus iv & Minoribus vii, unde reliquae omnes ibidem propagarunt, malo, Lector, discas ex Magni Scaligeri Litteris ad me anno clo lc xcix. mense Martio scriptis, quam aliunde. Praefatus Vir cum multis aliis, tum Eruditione variarumque Rerum scientia maximus, sic inquit: Linguas Matrices vocare possumus, ex quibus multae Dialecti, tamquam Propagines, deductae sunt. Propagines quidem unius Matricis Linguae commercio inter se aliquo conjunctae sunt: Matricum vero inter se nulla Cognatio est, neque in Verbis, neque in Analogia. Sunto igitur Matrices ea, quæ per omnia inter se difsi repant; cujusmodi undecim, non amplius, hodie supersunt in universa Europa: quarum quatuor amplissimæ sunt; reliquæ septem longe Inferiores. Itaque illis quatuor Majores Matrices, reliquas Minores vocabimus. Eadem Verba faciunt unam Linguam videri: sed eorundem Verborum Trajectio, Immutatio, Inflexio aliam atque aliam Propaginem facit. Nam Italicam, Hispanicam & Gallicam Latinam vocamus propter unum Verbum Latinum, quamquam varie immutatum in illis tribus. Exempli gratia: Gener Latinum Italis Genero, Hispanis Yerno, Gallis Gendre: Latina sunt, si originem spectes; sin distortionem, unaquæque natio harum trium illud vindicat sibi. Itaque possumus deligere unum Verbum Matricis, quod commune sit Propaginibus sive Dialectis a quo nomen ipsa Matrix habere possit. Sunto igitur quatuor hæc Verba, Deus, ΘΕΟΣ, Godt, Boge, nota quatuor Majorum Matricum, Latinæ, Græcæ, Teutonicæ, Slavonicæ. Hæ, ut diximus, supra reliquas septem Minores latissime patent. Linguæ Boge duplices Characteres sunt, Rutenici sive Moschovitici, è Græcis depravati, totidem numero, & figura pene similes, adjunctis paucis Barbaris: item Dalmatici, qui & Hieronymiani, eadem potestate, totidem numero, sed figura longe dissimillimi. Atque adeo duplex Sacrorum Librorum Translatio, Rutenica recentior, & Hieronymiana vetustior. Hæc Matrix sive Lingua Boge in multas propagines diffusa est, Rutenicam, Polonicam, Boemicam, Illuricam, Dalmaticam, Windicam, & alias, quas unusquisque potest adjicere. Matricis Godt Propagines sive Idiomata præcipua sunt tria, Teutonismus, Saxonismus, & Danismus. Rursus Teutonisti Idiomata duo, Superior Teutonismus, quæ est Lingua Waffer; Inferior Teutonismus, sive Lingua Water: Reliqua duo Idiomata & ipsa quidem sunt Lingua Water: sed Saxonismi Propagines sunt Nord-Albingorum & Frisiorum, item Anglorum Dialectus: quæ tamen veterum Nord-Albingorum & Turingiorum Dialecti sint Anglismus & Scotismus. Danismi tria discrimina sunt, Lingua scilicet Danorum Limitancorum, quos Denemarkos vocant; Danorum Austrolium, qui Suedan, Suedi & Sueones ab Austrodicti: denique Danorum Septemtrionalium, qui Nordan, Normanni & Norwegi vocantur: a quorum idiomate propagatum est Islandicum hodiernum, quod ita intelligitur ab Norwegis, ut Hollandica Lingua a Germanis, Italica a Gallis. Matrix Deus peperit Italicam, Gallicam & Hispanicam: quæ omnes uno nomine Romansæ, id est Romanenses sive Romanæ vocantur, quam appellationem Victores Barbari induxerunt. Nam in eorum Legibus duplex Conditio Ingenuorum; deterior Romanorum, ut Latinorum Romæ. In Gallia olim Franci & Burgundiones, in Italia Longobardi, in Hispania Gotthi distinguuntur a Romanis, ut Quirites a Latinis Civibus. Hinc Luitprandus Tiotiscam Galliam ab Romana distinguit. Matricis ΘΕΟΣ pluria sunt Idiomata, quod non mirum in tot Insularum intervallis, quæ ut loco, ita Lingua commercio valde dissident. Atque de quatuor Majoribus Matricibus hactenus. Reliquæ septem Minores sunt hæ: Epirotica, quam Albanam vocamus in Montanis Epiri, ubi gens studys asperrima belli; Indigenæ, an Advenæ, incertum. Secunda Cosacorum & Præcopiensium, id est Tartarica. Tertia Hungarorum, quam ex Asia in Europam transeverunt crudelissimæ duæ gentes, Hunni & Avares. Quarta Finnonica, cujus propago est Lapponica, in Septemtrionalibus Scandinaviæ Suedorum. Quinta Hirlandica, cujus pars, quæ hodie in usu Scotis Silvestribus. Sexta Vetus Britannica, in Montibus, Anglis: item in Aremorica Gallis, quam Britonnantem Linguam Galli vocant. Septima Cantabrorum, quos Biscainos Galli & Hispani nominant, quæ sunt reliquiæ Veteris Hispanicæ: patet ut minimum itinere septem dierum cis & uls Pyrenæos, a Baionensi usque Agro, quem tractum in Tarbellis Lapurdensem vocant Sidonius & aly Veteres. Hæ sunt Undecim Matrices nullo inter se cognationis vinculo conjunctæ: atque has inter se divisserant Ecclesiæ Constantinopolitana & Romana; Et quidem commercio Characterum quintuplicis generis, Latinorum, Græcorum, Hieronymianorum, Rutenicorum & Gotthorum. Nam & ipsi veteres Gotthi suos Characteres habent, Sacra alioquin Græco ritu celebrantes, Lingua Veteri Gotthica: in usu autem quotidiano magna ex parte Teutonissant. Hæc Europæus ille noster Mithridates: quo nemo potuisset de his talibus solidius, distinctius, elegantius. Ego quid his adponerem? Nihil. Singularum specimina tuis conabor dare locis.
units.tr: I have painted the customs with a rather lively and therefore rougher brush than my own. Now let us look at the languages of Europe. I have said some things about languages in general in Part 1, book 3, chapter 14. As for the more detailed matter of Europe's mother tongues, four major and seven minor, from which all the rest have spread, I would rather you, reader, learn it from the letter the great Scaliger wrote to me in March 1599 than from elsewhere. That man, very eminent both in learning and in his knowledge of many subjects, says this: "We may call them mother languages, from which many dialects have been derived as offshoots. Offshoots are joined to one another by some kinship with a single mother language, but the mother languages have no kinship with one another, either in vocabulary or in grammatical pattern. Those are mother languages which differ from one another in every respect. Only eleven of this kind survive today in the whole of Europe, four of them very extensive and the other seven far less so. So we shall call those four the major mother languages and the rest the minor. The same words make a language seem to be one, but the transposition, alteration and inflection of the same words make one offshoot differ from another. For we call Italian, Spanish and French Latin because of one Latin word, though it has been variously altered in those three. For example, the Latin gener (son-in-law) is genero in Italian, yerno in Spanish, gendre in French. These are Latin if you look at their origin, but if you look at their distortion, each of the three nations claims the word for itself. So we can choose one word of the mother tongue that is common to the offshoots or dialects, from which the mother tongue itself may take its name. Let these four words then be the marks of the four major mother tongues: Deus, ΘΕΟΣ [God], Godt, Boge: Latin, Greek, Teutonic and Slavonic. These, as we said, extend most widely of all, beyond the other seven minor ones. The language of Boge has two alphabets, the Russian or Muscovite, corrupted from the Greek, with the same number of letters and nearly similar shapes, with a few foreign additions; and the Dalmatian, also called Hieronymian, with the same sound values and the same number of letters but very different shapes. Hence there are two translations of the Holy Books, the more recent Russian and the older Hieronymian. This mother tongue or language of Boge has spread into many offshoots: Russian, Polish, Bohemian, Illyrian, Dalmatian, Windic and others that anyone may add. The chief offshoots or idioms of the mother tongue Godt are three: Teutonism, Saxonism and Danism. Teutonism again has two idioms: the Upper Teutonism, which is the language of Waffer, and the Lower Teutonism, or the language of Water. The other two idioms are also the language of Water, but the offshoots of Saxonism are those of the North Albingians and Frisians, and likewise the dialect of the English; yet these are dialects of the old North Albingians and Thuringians. The varieties of Danism are three: the language of the Danes of the frontier, whom they call Denemarkos; the Danes of the south, who are called Suedan, Suedi and Sueones from the south; and finally the Danes of the north, who are called Nordan, Normanni and Norwegi. From their idiom has descended the present Icelandic, which the Norwegians understand as Dutch is understood by Germans, and Italian by the French. The mother tongue Deus gave birth to Italian, French and Spanish, which are all called by the one name Romance, that is, Romanic or Roman, a name the conquering barbarians introduced. For in their laws there was a double status of freemen, the inferior that of the Romans, as of the Latins at Rome. In Gaul the Franks and Burgundians, in Italy the Lombards, in Spain the Goths were distinguished from the Romans, as Quirites were from the Latin citizens. Hence Liutprand distinguishes Teutonic Gaul from Roman. The mother tongue ΘΕΟΣ [God] has many idioms, which is not surprising given the great distances between so many islands, which differ as much in language as in place. So much for the four major mother tongues. The remaining seven minor ones are these: the Epirote, which we call Albanian, in the mountains of Epirus, where the people are very fierce in war; whether they are natives or newcomers is uncertain. The second is that of the Cossacks and the Precopians, that is, Tartar. The third is that of the Hungarians, whom two most cruel peoples, the Huns and the Avars, brought from Asia into Europe. The fourth is Finnish, whose offshoot is Lapp, in the northern parts of Scandinavia among the Swedes. The fifth is Irish, of which the part now in use among the Scots is the Wild Scots. The sixth is the old British, among the Welsh in the mountains, and among the Gauls in Armorica, which the Gauls call the Britonnic language. The seventh is that of the Cantabrians, whom the French and Spanish call Biscayans, which are the remnants of old Spanish; it extends at least a seven days' journey on this and that side of the Pyrenees, from Bayonne to the district which Sidonius and other ancients call Lapurdum in the land of the Tarbelli. These are the eleven mother tongues, bound to one another by no tie of kinship; and the Constantinopolitan and Roman Churches have divided these among themselves, indeed by means of five kinds of letters: Latin, Greek, Hieronymian, Russian and Gothic. For the ancient Goths too have their own letters, celebrating their sacred rites otherwise in the Greek manner, in the old Gothic language, but in daily use they largely speak Teutonic. So much for that Mithridates of ours, the European, than whom no one could have spoken on such matters more solidly, more clearly or more elegantly. What could I add to these? Nothing. I shall try to give specimens of each in their proper places."

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CAP. IX.

units.la: Europa Divisio.
units.tr: The Division of Europe.

units.la: EVROPÆ nostræ Totum ut considerandum monstravi: Partium doctrinam & indicium nostra jam flagitat Methodus. Partes Majores Minoresque Orbis Terrarum alij alio modo soliti sunt dividere: nunc φυσικὰς, prout sese osserunt vel Montes vel Flumina; nonnumquam ἐθνικὰς, secundum habitationes & Linguas; aliquando πολιτικὰς, vel quemadmodum Strabo loquitur, μικίλως, juxta voluntatem & Jurisdictionem Principum. Mihi non censeo curiosius inquirendum, quæ Distributionis ratio Trium optima, Regionibusque fideliter depingendis sit convenientissima. Aliis lubens laudem, quæ veram istius difficultatis definitionem sequi potest, relinquo. Ego, non ignorans, ut hoc saltem dicam, quam firma validaque in medium adduci queant argumenta, cum Primæ, ut quæ aptissima, stabiliendæ; tum enervandæ, quum obnoxia valde sit mutationi, Tertiæ, mediam ingrediar viam; hunc nostrum Terrarum Orbis Ocellum partiturus, & penicillo, licet quam velim rudiore, delineaturus secundum Matrices, de quibus præcedenti capite dixi; Linguas: non quidem omnes, sed Majores illas latissimeque patentes: quarum aliæ usurpantur in Europa Occidentaliore, aliæ in Orientaliore.
units.tr: Having shown that our Europe is to be considered as a whole, our method now calls for a account and description of its parts. Writers have customarily divided the greater and lesser parts of the world in various ways: sometimes physically (φυσικὰς), according as mountains or rivers present themselves; sometimes ethnically (ἐθνικὰς), according to habitations and languages; and sometimes politically (πολιτικὰς), or, as Strabo puts it, by the mixed method (μικίλως), according to the will and jurisdiction of princes. For my part, I do not think it necessary to inquire too closely which method of division is the best of the three and most suitable for depicting the regions faithfully. I leave the praise to others who can follow the true definition of that difficulty. I, not unaware of how firm and strong the arguments are that can be brought forward on each side (the first being the most apt to establish, and the third being very liable to change and therefore easy to weaken), will take the middle way. I shall divide this little jewel of our world's orb and sketch it, though with a rougher brush than I would like, according to the matrices of which I spoke in the previous chapter: the languages. Not all of them, but the greater ones which are spread most widely. Some of these are used in Western Europe, others in Eastern Europe.

units.la: In Occidentaliore quidem versus Meridiem Latina, cujus, varie admodum mutatæ distorteque, Propaginibus utuntur Hispania, Gallia, Italia: versus Septemtrionem Teutonica, cujus Dialecti Teutonismus specialioris notionis, & Danismus. Prioris usus, non exiguo tamen discrimine, in Germania tam Superiore quam Inferiore. Posterioris tres sunt differentiæ Danorum Limitancorum, qui Daniam; Austra-lium, Sueciam; Septemtrionalium, qui Norvegiam habitant. His adhæret Finmarchia, cui peculiare est Idioma, Propaginem habens Lapponicum, quo utitur Lappia.
units.tr: In Western Europe, to the south, there is Latin, whose offshoots, variously and quite considerably changed and distorted, are used in Spain, France and Italy; to the north, there is German, whose dialects are Teutonism in the narrower sense, and Danish. The former is used, though with no small difference, both in Upper and in Lower Germany. The latter has three varieties: that of the Danes of the border, who inhabit Denmark, Austrasia and Sweden; and that of the northerners, who inhabit Norway. To these is attached Finmark, which has its own idiom, having an offshoot of Lapp, which is used in Lapland.

units.la: In Orientaliore vero ad Septemtrionem Slavonica, quæ in multas Propagines est diffusa. Nam in quibus ibi Regionibus non ejus Usus? Gaudent ea Populi, quos fere Majorum nostrorum temporibus longe lateque habuisse constat Superiorem Inferioremque & Mœsiam & Pannoniam, Daciam, Illuricum, Dalmatiam, Sarmatiam & alias: qui hodie Poloni, Hungari, Transilvani, Walachi, Livones, Lituani, Podolj, Moldavi, Bulgari, & alij; quos omnes, exceptis Primis, uno complectar libro. Hispaniam igitur, cui in nostra Distributione princeps tribuitur locus, & merito, quum in Europa Terræ Continentis proxima sit Fortunatis Insulis, unde hodieque ex Veterum mente Longitudinis initium ducitur, quod felix faustumque sit, ingrediamur.
units.tr: In Eastern Europe, to the north, there is Slavonic, which has spread into many offshoots. For in what regions is its use absent? Those peoples enjoy it who, as is established, in the times of our forefathers held far and wide both Upper and Lower Moesia and Pannonia, Dacia, Illyricum, Dalmatia, Sarmatia and others; who today are the Poles, Hungarians, Transylvanians, Walachians, Livonians, Lithuanians, Podolians, Moldavians, Bulgarians, and others. I shall embrace all of these in one book, except the first. So let us enter Spain, to which the first place is rightly given in our division, since in Europe it is the mainland region nearest to the Fortunate Islands, from which even today, according to the mind of the ancients, longitude takes its beginning, that it may be fortunate and auspicious.

units.la: PAVLLI G.F.P.N. MERVLÆ COSMOGRAPHIÆ PARTIS II, LIBER II. DE HISPANIA.
units.tr: Of Paul Merula's Cosmography, Part II, Book II: Of Spain.

units.la: CAPVT I. Hispania unde dicta, queque varia ejus Nomina.
units.tr: CHAPTER I. Whence Spain takes its name, and its various names.

units.la: N delineanda Terrarum Orbis Parte illa, quæ L. Floro Viris Animisque Nobilis dicitur, quædam generatim explicabo, quædam speciatim. Generatim Nomen & Res. In Nomine quod Etymon sit Hispaniæ, scrutabor, quæque varia Appellationes.
units.tr: Now, in describing that part of the globe which Florus calls noble in its men and in its spirit, I will set out some things in general and some in particular. In general: the name and the thing. Regarding the name, I will examine what the etymology of Hispania is and what its various appellations are.

units.la: Hispaniam Iustinus ex Trogi Pompei Historiarum Philippicarum lib. xliv. dictam notat ab Hispano Rege.
units.tr: Justin, from Trogus Pompeius' Philippic Histories, book 44, notes that Hispania was named after King Hispanus.

units.la: Alij sic nominatam volunt ab Hispali urbe nobilissima; quam hodie Sevilliam appellant.
units.tr: Others want it named after Hispalis, a most noble city, which people now call Seville.

units.la: Abrahamus Ortelius, Vir quo nullus in Palæstra Geographica fuit operosior, quum Iberiam Asiæ Regionem olim Paniam à Pane, quem Iberis Dionysius, victoria potitus, præfecerat, inde vero Spaniam ab Iunioribus vocatam fuisse, legisset apud Auctorem de Fluminibus & Montibus, fidem sequutum Sosthenis lib. iii. rerum Ibericarum: Scriptoresque fere omnes animadvertisset primos Hispaniæ Incolas ex Iberia usque dirivare: adductus est, ut ab Spania potius illa, quam ab Hispano vel Hispali nomen Regioni inditum, crederet. Sane Spania nominat D. Paulus Epistola ad Romanos, cap. xv: Apud Iustinum, ubi in Vulgatis Hispania exstat, in membranis Spania legitur: In optimis Q. Curtij Codicibus Spaniam esse notat Bongarsius: Spaniam vocat D. Hieronymus ad Ieschahihiae caput lxiv: D. Eulogius, qui ante septingentos annos floruit, Spaniam appellat: Vetus in Iuvenalem Glossographus Tagum Spanie facit fluvium: in Glossario D. Benedicti Græco-Latino αραύη est pro Hibera, αραvia pro Hispania: Spaniam ab Chaldæis dici scribit Arias Montanus Commentariis in Abdiam: Galenus v i. Simpl. cap. i v. Spanum vocat oleum ex Iberia (sic Hispaniam nuncupat) advectum: Consonat denique hodierna appellatio. Incolis enim Ffpana nominatur. Nam Ffpania & Spania scriptione tantum differunt; quum Hispani Gallicque vocibus Latinis, quibus ab S littera initium, E præponere suaque facere consueverint.
units.tr: Abraham Ortelius, a man than whom no one was more diligent in the field of geography, having read in the author On Rivers and Mountains that Iberia, a region of Asia, was formerly called Paniam after Pan, whom Dionysus had set over it after his victory, and afterwards Spaniam by the Iuniores, and following the authority of Sosthenes in book 3 of the Iberian Affairs, and having observed that almost all the writers derive the first inhabitants of Spain from Iberia, was led to believe that the region took its name from Spania rather than from Hispanus or Hispalis. Indeed, St Paul names Spania in the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 15. In Justin, where the Vulgate has Hispania, the manuscripts read Spania. Bongarsius notes that Spaniam is found in the best manuscripts of Quintus Curtius. St Jerome calls it Spaniam in his commentary on Isaiah, chapter 64. St Eulogius, who flourished seven hundred years ago, calls it Spaniam. An old glossator on Juvenal makes the Tagus a river Spanie. In the Greek-Latin glossary of St Benedict, "araue" [αραύη] stands for Hibera, and "aravia" [αραvia] for Hispania. Arias Montanus writes in his commentary on Obadiah that the Chaldeans call it Spaniam. Galen, in book 6 of the Simples, chapter 4, calls the oil brought from Iberia (as he names Hispania) Spanum. Finally, the modern name agrees: the inhabitants call it Ffpana. Ffpania and Spania differ only in spelling, since the Spanish and the French are accustomed to prefix an E to Latin words beginning with S and make them their own.

units.la: Quam Hispaniam Latini Scriptores, Ptolemæus autem, Stephanus, Authorque Librorum de Machabæorum gestis Ιαραvίαν vocant, rejecta aspiratione, temporibus antiquissimis Iberiam & Hesperiam nominatam memoriæ produnt Strabo, Plinius, alij.
units.tr: Latin writers call it Hispania, but Ptolemy, Stephanus, and the author of the Books of the Maccabees call it Ἰσπανίαν [Ispanían], with the aspiration dropped. Strabo, Pliny, and others record that in very ancient times it was called Iberia and Hesperia.

units.la: Iberia quidem ab Iberia Asiæ Regione, unde primos Hispaniæ Incolas non pauci deducunt: Strabo tamen, quamvis alibi propter Linguæ diversitatem hæsitet, ex Apollodoro, Socrate, aliisque; Dionysius item Alexandrinus & Priscianus malunt Iberos ex Hispania in Asiam migrasse, ibique Provinciæ, quam occuparant, patrium nomen imposuisse. Appianus quoque tres refert sententias; primam Europæos Iberos ab Asiaticis deducentium; secundam, Asiaticos ab Europæis; tertiam, nihil illis præter nomen commune volentium. Alij Iberiam ab Ibero Rege trahunt; alij ab Ibero flumine; Avienus ab Ibera Bæticæ opido.
units.tr: Iberia is indeed named from Iberia, a region of Asia, from which not a few derive the first inhabitants of Spain. Yet Strabo, although elsewhere he hesitates because of the difference of language, follows Apollodorus, Socrates, and others. Dionysius of Alexandria and Priscian likewise prefer to say that the Iberians migrated from Spain into Asia and there gave their native name to the province they had occupied. Appian also reports three opinions: the first, of those who derive the European Iberians from the Asiatic; the second, of those who derive the Asiatics from the Europeans; the third, of those who wish that they had nothing in common but the name. Others derive Iberia from King Iberus, others from the river Iberus, and Avienus from the town of Ibera in Baetica.

units.la: Hesperiam vero, ab Hesperio, ut quidam memorant.
