Atlantis fratre vel ut Horatius putat, ab Hesperia Hesperi filia, vel potius ab Hespero Stella Occidentali: quia in Europæ Continente nihil est hac Regione Occidentalius; unde à Seneca in Hercule Octæo, Zephyro subdita tellus. Quumque & Italiæ nomen idem esset, Horatius lib. 1. Carm. hanc Ultimam canit.
units.tr: Hesperia, however, is said to be named from Hesperus, the brother of Atlas, as some report, or, as Horace thinks, from Hesperia, the daughter of Hesperus, or rather from Hesperus, the western star, because nothing in the continent of Europe lies farther west than this region. Hence Seneca, in the Hercules Oetaeus, speaks of "the land under the west wind." And since the name of Italy was also the same, Horace in book 1 of the Odes sings of this as "the ultimate" [Hesperia].

units.la: Hesperia Iberia vocatur Dioscoridi lib. v. cap. cii, tamquam Iberia Occidentalis, ad differentiam Orientalis, quæ in Asia.
units.tr: Hesperia is called Iberia by Dioscorides in book 5, chapter 102, as Western Iberia, to distinguish it from the Eastern, which is in Asia.

units.la: Celtiberiam quondam fuisse nominatam tradit Appianus Alexandrinus: quæ tamen pars Hispaniæ (quam Celticam olim dixerunt teste Varrone) potius censenda, cujusque Incolæ nunc Celti nunc Celtiberi, Plinio etiam Celtici.
units.tr: Appian of Alexandria records that Celtiberia was once its name. That part of Spain, however, which they once called Celtic, according to Varro, should rather be considered as such, and its inhabitants are now called Celti and now Celtiberi, and by Pliny also Celtici.

units.la: Pannoniam quoque nominat Stephanus, Παννονία πόλεον.
units.tr: Stephanus also names Pannonia, Παννονία πόλις [Pannonia, a city].

units.la: Γαλάται Regionis Incolas olim nuncupatos ex Asclepiade Myrleano scribit Strabo.
units.tr: Galatae [Γαλάται]: Strabo writes that the inhabitants of the region were formerly so called, according to Asclepiades of Myrlea.

units.la: Sepharad (ספרד) Hebræis dici notant Gulielmus Postellus & Benedictus Arias Montanus Commentario in Abdiam.
units.tr: Hebrews call it Sepharad [ספרד], as Guillaume Postel and Benedictus Arias Montanus, in his commentary on Obadiah, note.

units.la: An Iosepho vere ab Tubale progeniti scribantur, vereque Τοβηλεοι vocentur, dixi Partis 1. lib. iii. cap. xiv.
units.tr: I discussed in Part 1, book 3, chapter 14, whether Josephus truly writes that they were descended from Tubal, and whether they are truly called Tobeleans [Τοβηλεοι].

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: Hispaniæ Fines, Longitudo, Latitudo, Circumitus, Forma.
units.tr: The Boundaries, Length, Breadth, Circuit and Shape of Spain.

units.la: NOMEN dedi: offerunt se Res; ipsa, inquam, Regio & Incolæ. Regionis primum examinabo Adjuncta, inde Partes. Illa mihi sunt Quantitas & Qualitas. Quantitas consistit in Finibus & Circuitu, quæque inde quasi nascitur, Forma vel Figura. Quod igitur ad Fines: adluit Hispaniæ duo quidem latera Oceanus: Aquilonare, Cantabricus; Occidentale, Atlanticus: Tertium, quod ad Meridiem, ubi Fretum Herculeum, mare pulsat Ibericum, quod & Balearicum: Versus Orientem Pyrenæos habet Montes, perpetuis jugis ab Oceano, ubi Flaviobriga, hodie Fuentarabia, tendentes ad Mare Mediterraneum; duobus insignes Promontoriis, uno, quod Olarso cognominatum, in Oceanum projecto; altero, quondam ab Veneris templo, nunc vero Religione mutata, ab S. Cruce denominato, in Mediterraneum.
units.tr: I have given the name; the things themselves now present themselves: I mean the region and its inhabitants. I shall first examine the region's attributes, and then its parts. The attributes are quantity and quality. Quantity consists in the boundaries and the circuit, and in the form or figure that arises from these. As to the boundaries: the Ocean washes two sides of Spain, the northern, which is the Cantabrian, and the western, which is the Atlantic. The third side, facing south, is where the Herculean Strait meets the Iberian Sea, which is also called the Balearic. On the east it has the Pyrenees, with unbroken ridges running from the Ocean, where Flaviobriga, today Fuentarabia, lies, down to the Mediterranean. It is marked by two notable promontories: one, called Olarso, projects into the Ocean; the other, once named from the temple of Venus but now renamed after the change of religion Holy Cross, projects into the Mediterranean.

units.la: Hispaniæ Longitudo, Straboni libro Geograph. iii. σταδίων ἐξακισχιλίων, Latitudo, qua maxima, μυριαχιλίων, qua minima, τεισχιλίων: quæ, si cogitemus Stadium Græcum centum, Latinum centum viginti quinque passus continere, quatuor autem Passuum millia Leucam, qua Hispani cum aliis Conregionalibus hodie utuntur, tur, conficere, nihil erit difficultatis ad hodiernæ mensuræ rationem revocare. Ioannes Valæus in Hispaniæ Chronico, cap. viii. memoriæ prodit, Hispaniam ad Pyrenæos tam augustam esse, ut, quum per eos iter faceret, in Monte D. Hadriani, Ferdinando Colone rerum istarum peritissimo commonstrante, nisi fefellerit adspectus, utrumque viderit mare: Oceanum scilicet, cui peregrinantes erant proximi, atque eminus, quousque oculorum acies ferre poterat, albicantes Maris Mediterranei fluctus.
units.tr: Strabo, in Book 3 of his Geography, gives the length of Spain as 6,000 stadia [σταδίων ἐξακισχιλίων], and its greatest breadth as 10,000 stadia [μυριαχιλίων], and its least breadth as 3,000 stadia [τεισχιλίων]. If we reckon the Greek stadium as containing 100 paces, and the Latin as containing 125, and if we take four Roman miles as one league, which the Spaniards today use along with other peoples of the same region, it is no difficulty at all to reduce these to modern measure. John Vaseus, in his Chronicle of Spain, chapter 8, records that Spain near the Pyrenees is so lofty that, when he travelled through them, on Mount Saint Adrian, with Ferdinand Colon, a man most expert in these matters, pointing it out, he saw both seas, if his sight did not deceive him: the Ocean, to which the travellers were close, and, in the distance as far as the eye could reach, the whitish waves of the Mediterranean.

units.la: Circumitum Hispaniæ dimetiuntur per maritima littora & Pyrenæum Ioannes Episcopus Gerundensis lib. 1 Paralipomenon Hispaniæ, & Ioannes Mariana lib. 1. Historiæ cap. 11.
units.tr: John, Bishop of Girona, in Book 1 of his Paralipomena of Spain, and John Mariana, in Book 1 of his History, chapter 11, measure the circuit of Spain along the coasts and the Pyrenees.

units.la: Formam Hispaniæ quadratam nonnulli (inter quos Iustinus ex Trogi Pompei lib. xliv) statuunt; nisi quod Aquilonem versus sensim in Pyrenæum angustius coëat. Trigonam imperite facit Æthicus. Strabo, Pomponius Mela, Ptolemæus & alij Hispaniam comparant Corio Bubulo (Βύρση Βοεία) humi protenso: cujus partes ad collum pertinentes in adhærentem ipsi Galliam porriguntur. Collum inquam, quantum protenditur Mons Pyrenæus ab Mediterraneo Mari ad Oceanum Britannicum: inde dilatatur ad Brachia, ab Nova Karthagine usque ad Cantabros: Crura à Freto Herculeo usque in Galliaciam & Mare Britannicum: ultimum Corij ad modum Caudæ, Promontorium Sacrum, hodie S. Vincentij, quod extenditur in Oceanum Atlanticum, longe ultra omnem Hispaniam.
units.tr: Some (among them Justin, from Trogus Pompeius, Book 44) hold that the shape of Spain is square, except that toward the north it narrows gradually into the Pyrenees. Aethicus unskilfully makes it triangular. Strabo, Pomponius Mela, Ptolemy and others compare Spain to an ox hide [Βύρση Βοεία] stretched out on the ground, whose parts corresponding to the neck extend into Gaul, which adjoins it. I mean the neck, as far as the Pyrenees stretch from the Mediterranean Sea to the British Ocean; from there it widens into the arms, from New Carthage as far as the Cantabrians; the legs run from the Herculean Strait to Galicia and the British Sea; and the tail of the hide, the Holy Promontory, today Cape Saint Vincent, which juts out into the Atlantic Ocean, far beyond all of Spain.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CAP. III.

units.la: Clima Hispaniæ, ejusque ex Situ Cœlesti Qualitas, & quæ inde commoda.
units.tr: The climate of Spain, the quality arising from its heavenly position, and the advantages that follow from it.

units.la: EXPOSITA Quantitate, in medium prodit Qualitas, cujus causa plurimum in Climate, Situque Cœlesti. Subest Hispania medio Quarti, totique Quinto, parti etiam Sexti Climatis; inter Gradus, Latitudinis quidem xxxv & xlv, Longitudinis autem inter xvi (ut nunc, capto ab Azoribus Insulis initio, notari solet: quam rationem deinceps sequar) & xxxi; ubi optima ad res omnes Temperies. Hinc merito Iustinus ex Trogo, fertiliorem facit Hispaniam Africa aut Gallia, quum neque, ut illa, violento Sole torreatur; neque, ut hæc, adsiduis Ventis fatigetur; sed media inter utramque, hinc temperato calore, inde felicibus Imbribus in omni frugum genere sit fœcunda. Maxima Dies Æstatis in Parallelo Australi, qui distat ab Æquinoctiali Linea xxxvi gradibus, horarum est xiv-30: in Boreali, qui abest ab Æquatore gradibus xliv. semi, horarum est xv-30. Hispaniæ igitur, quod monere jam cœpi, non eadem passim est Qualitas, non idem Solo genius. Qua Arcton spectat, plerisque scribentibus, frigidior est, nonnulliusque asperitatis; Oceano semper obnoxia, interiorum aquarum indiga, malignæque inde habitationis: quum etiam Rupibus, Saltibus, Locisque Silvestribus pleraque obsessa. Qua, Montibus fere perpetuum intercurrentibus, in Austrum declinat, tota felix, tota beata, ut multis magnisque Fluminibus irrigari, sic tempestivis pluviis, quantum sufficit, recreari solita; & hinc omne genus, ea præcipue parte, Frugum, Animaliumque non benigna solum Mater, sed & Nutrix solicita. De Hispaniis universim quæ scripserit ex Trogo Iustinus, capite præcedenti audivimus. Addam alios. Memoriæ mandat Philostratus: hic Cœli temperiem esse talem, qualis Autumni tempore solet esse in Attica. Leguntur & hæc apud Solinum: Terrarum plaga comparanda optimis, nulli posthabenda, Frugis ac Soli copia; sive vinearios Proventus respicere, sive arborarios velis. Omni materia adfluit, quacumque aut precio ambitiosa est, aut usu necessaria. Argentum & Aurum si requiras, habet: Ferrarijs numquam deficit, nec cedit Vitibus, vincit Olea. Nihil in ea otiosum, nihil sterile, quidquid cujuscunque negat Messem, viget Pabulis: etiam quæ arida sunt ac sterilia, Rudentum materiam nauticis submi-nistrant. Verba denique sunt hæc Pomponij: Viris, Equis, Ferro, Plumbo, Argento, Auro tam abundans, & adeo fertilis; ut, sicubi ad penuriam aquarum effœta & sui dissimilis est, Linum tamen aut Spartum alat.
units.tr: Having set out its size, I now come to its quality, which depends chiefly on its climate and its position in the heavens. Spain lies in the middle of the fourth climate, all of the fifth, and part of the sixth. It lies between latitudes 35 and 45 and between longitudes 16 (counted, as is now customary, from the Azores, which is the reckoning I shall follow from here on) and 31. Its temperature is excellent for all purposes. For this reason Justin, following Trogus, rightly makes Spain more fertile than Africa or Gaul, since it is not scorched by a violent sun like the one, nor worn down by constant winds like the other. It lies between the two, with a temperate heat on one side and seasonable rains on the other, and so it is fruitful in every kind of crop. The longest summer day on the southern parallel, which is 36 degrees from the equinoctial line, has 14 hours and 30 minutes; on the northern parallel, which is 44 and a half degrees from the equator, it has 15 hours and 30 minutes. As I have already begun to point out, then, Spain does not have the same quality everywhere, nor the same nature of soil. The part that faces the north, according to most writers, is colder and rather rough. It is always exposed to the ocean, lacks inland waters, and is therefore a poor place to live, and much of it is also beset by rocks, thickets and wooded places. The part that inclines towards the south, where the mountains run more or less continuously, is wholly fertile and wholly blessed. It is customarily watered by many large rivers and refreshed by timely rains as much as needed, and so it is not only a kindly mother of every kind of crop and animal but also a careful nurse, especially in that region. What Justin wrote about Spain in general, following Trogus, we heard in the previous chapter. I shall add others. Philostratus records that its air is of such a temperature as Attica usually has in autumn. These words are also read in Solinus: A region to be compared with the best, inferior to none, rich in crops and in soil, whether you look to its yield of vines or of trees. It abounds in every material, whatever is either costly for its price or necessary for use. If you ask for silver and gold, it has them; the iron mines never run dry; it does not yield to vines, and it surpasses the olive. Nothing in it is idle or barren; whatever land does not yield a harvest flourishes with pasture; even what is dry and sterile supplies sailors with material for ropes. And finally these are the words of Pomponius: So abundant in men, horses, iron, lead, silver and gold, and so fertile, that wherever it is worn out and unlike itself for lack of water, it still feeds flax or broom.

units.la: Admirandam eorum, cum quæ ex terra proveniunt, tum quæ in Terræ visceribus generantur & latent, fertilitatem; Animantium item, quæ Terra Marique nascuntur, præstantiam, quis digne, utque singula flagitant, commemorabit?
units.tr: Who could worthily and as each detail demands recount the wonderful fertility of the land, both in what it produces on its surface and in what is generated and lies hidden in the bowels of the earth, and likewise the excellence of the living creatures that are born on land and in the sea?

units.la: Incredibilis per omnem Hispaniam Frugum Ubertas; & plenique Agri tantæ sunt liberalitatis, ut pro accepto uno Tritici Modio triginta plurimum Colonis reddant; sæpe etiam quadraginta in Bætica præsertim.
units.tr: The fruitfulness of the crops throughout all of Spain is incredible, and the fields are so generous that for one measure of wheat sown they usually return thirty, and often forty, especially in Baetica.

units.la: Herbarum, cum Sativarum, tum Voluntariarum, quæ citra sementem erumpunt quibusque insignes sunt & peculiares vires, (videndus Plinius lib. xxv. cap. viii.) passim, cum primis in montosis locis, est feracissima: ubi sui dissimilis, inquit Pomponius, Linum aut Spartam alit. Strabo lib. iii. ἀναρπάςιον nominat Campum, circa Karthaginem Novam, spaciosum admodum & Aquarum indigentem, quem Manxam ab Arabibus vocari scribunt Hieronymus Surita & Ioannes Mariana. Idem Iuncarium Campum habet in Emporiensium agris. Ἀνυρχόι δὲ ἰχαῶς, inquit, οἱ Ε' μπε-ξίτης, χώρης δὲ τὴν μεσόγαιαν ἔχει, τῶν μὲν ἀγαθῶν, τῶν δὲ σπερμοφόρων, τῆς ἀρχαιότητος καὶ ἐλαίας ἀφθονίαν. καλῶς δὲ ἰσχυρότερον τιθέν. Faciunt hæc Strabonis & appellationis Latinæ ratio, ut apud Ptolemæum legendum censeam ἰσχυραίας; quemadmodum etiam dicitur Antonino Iuncaria, pro ejus Loci opido, quod hodie Iunquera.
units.tr: Its herbs, both cultivated and wild, which spring up without sowing and have their own remarkable and distinctive powers (see Pliny, book 25, chapter 8), are everywhere very productive, especially in hilly places, where, unlike itself, says Pomponius, it feeds flax or broom. Strabo, book 3, calls the Campus near New Carthage, a very spacious plain lacking water, ἀναρπάςιον (the one that is snatched away), and Hieronymus Surita and Juan de Mariana write that the Arabs call it Manxa. He also has the Iuncarian Plain in the territory of the Emporitani. Strabo says: "The Emporitans ... and the inland region they hold has abundant good land, some of it producing grain, and of olives ..." [Ἀνυρχόι δὲ ἰχαῶς, inquit, οἱ Ε' μπε-ξίτης, χώρης δὲ τὴν μεσόγαιαν ἔχει, τῶν μὲν ἀγαθῶν, τῶν δὲ σπερμοφόρων, τῆς ἀρχαιότητος καὶ ἐλαίας ἀφθονίαν. καλῶς δὲ ἰσχυρότερον τιθέν.] The reasoning of Strabo and of the Latin name leads me to think that in Ptolemy we should read ἰσχυραίας; in the same way Antoninus also has Iuncaria, for the town of that place, which is today Iunquera.

units.la: Siluis, Nemoribus, Arboribusque singulares ferentibus fructus ubique est plena. Longum esset omnia commemorare. Nemus est apud Opidum, cui ab Monte Majore nomen, in quo Quercus, Castaneas, Ilices, Nuces, Corylos, Cerasos, Prunos, Pyros, Ficus, Labruscas, & omne genus Arborum fructiferarum sola Natura plantavit, altitudinis ingentis & latitudinis. Haud procul opido Beierano Nemus est amœnissimum, ubi Castaneæ Arboris ambitum se mensum scribit Lucius Marineus Siculus pedum circiter quadraginta. Quid Mala referam? Inter ea melioris notæ sunt duo, Cannsium & Regium. Quid Pyra? In ijs supremæ classis quatuor, quæ odore gustuque suavissima: Apianum, quod Muscatum vocant, omnium Pyrorum minimum, Vinosum, Pintum, Quartumque, quod Hispanis Sine Regula nominatur. Quid Olivas? In harum numero primas obtinent Hispalenses, quæ magnitudine Iuglandes excedunt. Hinc Oleastrum in ea ora circa Sinum Gaditanum, Lucus ab Arbore quam alit, apud Pomponium Melam lib. iii. Dives enim Olivetis tota Bætica. Silius Italicus lib. iii: Palladio Bætis umbratus cornua ramo,
units.tr: It is full of woods, groves and trees that bear special fruits everywhere. It would take too long to mention them all. There is a grove near the town named after Monte Mayor, in which nature alone has planted oaks, chestnuts, holm oaks, walnuts, hazels, cherries, plums, pears, figs, wild vines and every kind of fruit tree, of great height and breadth. Not far from the town of Beiera there is a very pleasant grove, where Lucius Marineus Siculus writes that a chestnut tree has a girth of about forty feet. Why mention apples? Among them, two are of better note, the Cannsian and the Regian. And pears? Among them are four of the highest class, very sweet in smell and taste: the Apian, which they call Muscat, the smallest of all pears; the Vinous; the Pintan; and a fourth, which the Spaniards call Sine Regula. And olives? Among these the Hispalensian olives take first place, exceeding walnuts in size. Hence the Oleaster on that coast near the Gaditan bay, a grove named after the tree it nourishes, in Pomponius Mela, book 3. For all of Baetica is rich in olive groves. Silius Italicus, book 3: Baetis, shaded with a branch of Pallas' tree, ...

units.la: Quin de Hispania canit universa libri; Nullaque Palladia sese magis arbore tollit.
units.tr: Indeed the whole book sings of Spain, and none rises more proudly than the tree of Pallas.

units.la: Hinc Oleastrum Antonino, opidum inter Tarraconem & Dertosam; hinc ἐλαίφος Straboni circa Saguntum; hinc alia aliis locis. Quid de reliquis dicam Fructibus? Plene decantata sunt non paucis Mala Hesperia vel Citrea; Cydona, quæ vulgo Membrillos: Granata, suis etiam Coriis medicinam facientia. Nucem Iuglandem primus in Hispaniam intulit Pomponius Flaccus, Eques Romanus, quum sub Vitellio Imperatore militaret. Testatur Plinius lib. xv. natural. histor. cap. xxii.
units.tr: Hence Antoninus' Oleaster, a town between Tarraco and Dertosa; hence Strabo's ἐλαίφος near Saguntum; and other names in other places. What shall I say of the remaining fruits? The Hesperian or Citron apples have been fully celebrated by many writers; the quinces, commonly called membrillos; and the pomegranates, which also serve as medicine with their rinds. The walnut was first brought into Spain by Pomponius Flaccus, a Roman knight, while he was serving under the emperor Vitellius. Pliny attests this in Natural History, book 15, chapter 22.

units.la: Quid Vina commemorabo, optimi saporis odorisque? Passim quidem generosa admodum leguntur, alijs tamen & alijs locis præstantiora, quæ Marineus Siculus indicat lib. i. de Rebus Hispaniæ. Vinum ex Turdetania multum exportari, præter alia, scribit Octaviani Augusti tempore Strabo lib. Geograph. iii: quod quo modo intelligemus, quum memoriæ prodat Fl. Vopiscus Syracusanus Probum Imperatorem Hispanis, ut & Gallis Britannisque, primum Vineas ut haberent, Vinumque conficerent, permisisse? Singulare scilicet jam fuerat multos annos Turdetanis Turdulisque, quos Hispanorum omnium cultisimos sapientissimosque noverant Romani, quod tandem commune factum & generatim concessum omnibus (hanc enim vocem addit Vopiscus) sub Probo. Vites Germanicæ superioribus annis in Hispaniam à Belga quodam Petro Simonis F. transportatæ, Hispanicoque solo insitæ, jamque mirum in modum multiplicatæ, experimur quotidie, quam grata producant Vina; nomen ejus, qui transflevit, retinentia. Asperitatem, quam conciliare Soli solet natura, frangit, emollit, jucundoque condit sapore adgenitus jam in aliena terra sub alio Climate genius.
units.tr: Why should I mention the wines, of the finest taste and smell? They are read of everywhere as very noble, yet some are superior in some places and others in other places, which Marineus Siculus indicates in book 1 of his work on the affairs of Spain. Strabo, in book 3 of his Geography, writes in the time of Octavian Augustus, among other things, that much wine is exported from Turdetania. How are we to understand this, when Flavius Vopiscus of Syracuse records that the emperor Probus allowed the Spaniards, and likewise the Gauls and Britons, to have vineyards and make wine? Clearly it had already been a special privilege for many years of the Turdetani and Turduli, whom the Romans knew as the most cultivated and wisest of all the Spaniards, and at last under Probus it became a common practice and was granted generally to all (for Vopiscus adds this word). In recent years vines from Germany were brought into Spain by a certain Belgian, Peter son of Simon, and grafted into Spanish soil, and they have multiplied in a remarkable way. We experience every day how pleasant the wines they produce are, and they keep the name of the man who transplanted them. The nature that a soil tends to impart in its harshness is broken and softened, and a character that has taken root in a foreign land under a different climate is seasoned with a pleasant flavour.

units.la: Hispania Dives quondam universum, ut nunc quoque variis in locis, preciosissimis Auri, Argenti, Æris, Ferri, Plumbi, aliorumque Metallorum Thesauris; de quibus videnda, quæ multis adfert cum ex Posidonio, tum ex aliis Strabo lib. iii: quæ item tradunturab Diodoro Siculo, Solino in Polyhistor. Iustino libro ultimo ex Trogo Pompeio, Panegyrista Theodosij, & aliis. παρ ἐκείνοις, ὡς ἀληθῶς, inquit inter cetera Posidonius, de Hispanis, τὴν ὑπογεγνυμένην τιμὴν ὑχ ὁ Ἀδης, ἀλλ' ὁ Πλούτων καταιχεῖ. Qui potuisset, oratoria quadam Eloquentiæ vi latius se expandens, insignem Metallorum fœcunditatem explicare commodius? De Auri Argentique copia fidem etiam faciunt, præter alios Auctor Librorum de Gestis Machabæorum, i. cap. viii, & Iosephus lib. ii. Belli Iudaici, cap. xvi. In Montibus circa Baßetaniam & Oretaniam Auri Metalla describit Strabo. Nam avidi sterilesque, & in quibus nihil aliud gignitur, Auri bono coguntur, ut Plinii verbis utar, fertiles esse. Ab Argenti-fodinis, Mons Argenteus, Ἀργυρῶν Straboni. Argentarius Avieno: hodie Incolis Sierra Segura, vel, ut alij censent, Sierra d' Alcara. non procul à Castulone, nunc Castulo na la veja. Argentum item fodi scribunt circa Ilipam (Calamea en la Serena) & utramque Sisaponem, Strabo; circa Babylam Polybius libro x: in Meleßum finibus, ubi Oringis urbs, Livius, lib. xxviii. Ad Tagum quoque in Montibus Sedturas esse Metallicas, apud Cotinam item circa Bætim Aes Aurumque nasci, notat Strabo. Galleciæ Regio, ait Trogus, vel ex Trogo Iustinus, Aeris ac Plumbi uberrima, Auro quoque dissimilis, adeo ut etiam aratro frequenter glebas aureas exsindant Agricolæ. Commemorat & hic Seram in ejusdem finibus esse Montem; cum ferro violare, nefas haberi; si quando fulgure Terra proscissa est (hoc autem in his terris frequens esse) detectum Aurum, velut Deûm Munus, colligi. Eandem Galleciam, Asturiam & Lusitaniam æque omnium Metallorum fœcundam prædicat Plinius. Inter Auri ramenta selibras aliquando glebas fuisse inventas, scriptum reliquit Strabo. Apud Ibyllam, Tartesiæ urbem (quid si Ilipam de qua ante?) Auri Argentique Fodinas collocat Stephanus. Maximam Argenti Fodinam quondam apud Novam Karthaginem fuisse, ab Urbe ad xx Stadia difficam; ibique quadraginta hominum millia in labore versari, & singulis diebus Populo Romano viginti quinque millia drachmarum inde tribuere solitos, ex Strabone discimus. Vicena millia Pondo Argenti annis singulis Asturiam, Galleciam & Lusitaniam præstitisse, tradit ex aliorum fide Plinius. Apud eundem Bebelo est, Argenti Puteus, ab Annibale inchoatus, Auctori suo ccc indices pondo subministrare solitus: sine dubio haud procul Pyrenæis montibus. Addit enim Aquitanos, Galliæ populos, Pyrenæo vicinos, hujus Putei aquas egerere. Forte circa Ofiam in Ilergetibus. Nam Ofcensis Argenti non semel mentionem facit Livius. Argenti ex Pyrenæorum nati incendio, quemadmodum referunt Diodorus & Strabo, tanta fuit copia, ut Phœnices, quum illud aveherent, atque Argentum, onustis jam Navibus, superaret, loco Plumbi Anchoris illud subdiderint; imo, ut Aristotelii placet, circa Tartessum ipsas inde Anchoras fabricarint. Turdetanos Argenteis Lacunaribus Doliisque usos, notat Strabo. Non pauca etiam hujus Regionis Flumina Aurum ferre, docebunt sequentia. Montem præruptæ altum in Cantabriæ ora maritima totum ex Ferro constantem habet Plinius. Probat Metallorum, Auri cum primis & Argenti, copiam inlata in Romanum Ærarium ab Triumphantibus vis admiranda. Testatur infinitis locis Livius Triumphos delineans c n. Cornelii Lentuli, M. Helvii, Blasionis, Q. Minucii Thermi, M. Porcii Catonis. M. Fulvii Nobilioris, C. Calpurnii Pisonis, L. Quinctii Crispini, Q. Fluvii Flacci, Ti. Sempronii Gracchi, L. Postumii Albini, aliorumque: ut merito dixerit & vere Antonius Augustinus, Hispaniam id temporis Romanis eo fuisse loco, quo nunc Hispanis America: inde, alijsque ex locis hac tempestate potentissimi Hispaniæ Reges, ex Metallis apud se domique nasci solitis contenti vilioribus, Aurum & Argentum petere malunt; quam penitiora Regnorum suorum Viscera, Necessitate non cogente, eam ob causam inquietare. Pergamus ad alia. Strabo lib. iii. memoriæ prodit, in Hispania Electrum fieri solere. Nam Auro ecfoso, Terraque aluminosa abluto, id quod tunc purgando rejicitur, Electrum esse, ex Auri Argentique mixtura conflatum. Hinc Silius Italicus in libris de bello Poenico:
units.tr: Spain was once rich throughout, as it still is in various places, with the most precious treasures of gold, silver, copper, iron, lead and other metals. On these matters one should consult what Strabo, book 3, brings forward from Posidonius and from others. The same things are related by Diodorus Siculus, by Solinus in his Polyhistor, by Justin in the last book, drawn from Trogus Pompeius, by the panegyrist of Theodosius, and by others. Among other things Posidonius says of the Spaniards, truly, "παρ ἐκείνοις" [among them], "τὴν ὑπογαῖον τιμὴν οὐχ ὁ Ἀΐδης, ἀλλ' ὁ Πλούτων κατέχει" [it is not Hades but Pluto who holds the precious wealth beneath the earth]. What writer could set forth more fittingly the remarkable fertility of the metals, spreading wide with a certain oratorical power of eloquence? The abundance of gold and silver is also attested, apart from others, by the author of the Books of the Maccabees, 1 Maccabees chapter 8, and by Josephus, Jewish War, book 2, chapter 16. Strabo describes gold mines in the mountains around Baetia and Oretania. For, as Pliny puts it, the barren and sterile lands, in which nothing else is produced, are compelled by the goodness of gold to be fertile. From the silver mines comes Mons Argenteus (Argyrôn [Ἀργυρῶν] in Strabo), called Argentarius by Avienus; today the inhabitants call it Sierra Segura, or, as others think, Sierra d' Alcara, not far from Castulo, now Castulo na la veja. Strabo also writes that silver was dug near Ilipa (Calamea en la Serena) and both Sisapo; Polybius, book 10, near Babyla; Livy, book 28, in the territory of Melesum, where the city of Oringis is. Strabo notes that there are metal-bearing mines on the mountains by the Tagus too, at Sedturas, and that copper and gold are likewise found near Cotina around the Baetis. Trogus, or Justin from Trogus, says of the region of Galicia: "It is very rich in copper and lead, and unlike other lands in its gold as well, so that the farmers often turn up golden clods even with the plough." Here too he mentions that there is a mountain called Sera within its borders; it was considered sacrilege to break it with iron, but when the earth was split by lightning (which often happens in these lands), gold was uncovered and gathered up as a gift of the gods. Pliny declares that Galicia, Asturia and Lusitania are equally fertile in all metals. Strabo has left it in writing that lumps weighing a pound were sometimes found among the grains of gold. Stephanus places gold and silver mines near Ibyla, a city of Tartessus (or is it Ilipa, mentioned above?). Strabo tells us that there was once a very large silver mine near Nova Carthago, twenty stadia from the city, where forty thousand men worked, and that they used to pay the Roman people twenty-five thousand drachmas every day from it. Pliny, on the authority of others, relates that Asturia, Galicia and Lusitania yielded twenty thousand pounds of silver each year. In the same author there is a silver well at Bebelo, begun by Hannibal, which used to supply its founder with three hundred Indian pounds; no doubt it was not far from the Pyrenees, for he adds that the Aquitanians, a people of Gaul neighbouring the Pyrenees, drained the waters of this well. Perhaps it was near Ofia among the Ilergetes, for Livy mentions the silver of Ofca more than once. From the fire that broke out among the Pyrenean mountains, as Diodorus and Strabo report, there was such an abundance of silver that the Phoenicians, when they were carrying it away and the ships were already loaded and the silver still remained, put it under their anchors in place of lead; indeed, as Aristotle thinks, they made their anchors from it near Tartessus. Strabo notes that the Turdetani used silver panels for their ceilings and silver casks. The following examples will show that not a few rivers of this region also carry gold. Pliny reports a high steep mountain on the sea coast of Cantabria made entirely of iron. The wonderful quantity of metals, especially gold and silver, brought into the Roman treasury by triumphing generals proves it. Livy, in describing the triumphs of Gnaeus Cornelius Lentulus, Marcus Helvius, Blasio, Quintus Minucius Thermus, Marcus Porcius Cato, Marcus Fulvius Nobilior, Gaius Calpurnius Piso, Lucius Quinctius Crispinus, Quintus Fulvius Flaccus, Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus, Lucius Postumius Albinus and others, bears witness to this in countless places. So Antonius Augustinus rightly and truly said that at that time Spain stood to the Romans in the position America now stands to the Spanish. Hence the most powerful kings of Spain in these days, content with the cheaper metals usually produced at home, prefer to seek gold and silver from elsewhere, rather than disturb the inner depths of their kingdoms without any compelling necessity. Let us proceed to other matters. Strabo, book 3, records that electrum is usually made in Spain. For when gold is melted and the aluminous earth washed away, what is then cast off in the cleansing is electrum, formed from a mixture of gold and silver. Hence Silius Italicus, in his books on the Punic War:

units.la: Electri gemino pollent de femine Vena.
units.tr: Electrum is strong from the twin veins of its source.

units.la: Gemino, Auri & Argenti. Specularem Lapidem, in quamlibet tenues crustas sindi consuetum, Hispaniam olim Citeriorem tantum dedisse, nec totam, sed intra centum millia passuum circa Sigobrigam (Segerbia) urbem, scribit Plinius lib. xxxvi. nat. hinatur. histor. cap. xxii. Minium in Hispania gigni, celeberrimumque peti ex Sisaponensi Baeticae Regione; inde Romam perferri, ibique perfici, excoqui, vendi, adulterari etiam, docet Plinius lib. xxxiii, cap. vii. Ab cujus verbis Lux M. Tullio Philippica ii. Quid erat in terris ubi in tuo pedem poneres, praeter unum Mifenum, quem tu cum Socys, tamquam Sisaponem, tenebas. De his Sisaponensium Miniariis loquitur Vitruvius lib. vii: Quae autem, inquit, in Ephesiorum metallis fuerunt Officina, nunc trajectae sunt ideo Romam, quod id genus vena postea est inventum in Hispaniae Regionibus; quibus metallis glebae portantur & per Publicanos Romae curantur. Eae autem Officinae sunt inter aedem Florae & Quirini.
units.tr: "Twin" refers to gold and silver. Pliny, book 36 of the Natural History, chapter 22, writes that Spain, formerly only Hither Spain, and not all of it but within a hundred thousand paces around the city of Segobriga (Segorbe), gave the specular stone, which is accustomed to split into very thin plates. Pliny, book 33, chapter 7, teaches that minium is produced in Spain and is most highly sought from the Sisaponensian region of Baetica; from there it is carried to Rome, and there it is refined, smelted, sold and even adulterated. Cicero, in the second Philippic, alludes to this: "What land was there where you could set your foot, except the single Misenum, which you held with your companions as if it were Sisapo?" Vitruvius, book 7, speaks of these Sisaponensian mineral workshops: "The workshops which were in the mines of the Ephesians," he says, "have now been moved to Rome, because this kind of vein was later discovered in the regions of Spain; the lumps of ore are carried from those mines and are processed at Rome by the tax-farmers. These workshops are between the temple of Flora and that of Quirinus."

units.la: Quid jam dicam de Salinis? Sal in Hispania non modo coqui, verum etiam plurimum effodi, hoc est, & fieri & gigni, tradit Solinus. Fit in multis Hispaniae locis ex Aquis puteanis, ut apud Seguntiam & alibi: unde Regibus magnum exigitur Vectigal. Gignitur in extremis Maris littoribus, ceteris candidior. Sunt & Montes Hispaniae, ii fides Marinco Siculo, nativi Salis, ut apud Pitagorciam; in quibus lapidicinarum modo Sal caeditur, & Arborum modo postea pullulat ac renascitur. Apud opidum Antiqueram Vallis est amoenissima, cujus longitudo passuum mille quingentorum, ex omni parte montium clausa jugis, quae hieme pluvialibus Aquis impletur, & in formam magni Lacus efficitur, cujus Aquae calore Solis, adjuvante Soli genio, in Salem candidum convertuntur. Alias silentio praetereo Salinas. Sed Miracula etiam audiamus, quae tamen hodie evanuerunt. Memorat Strabo, Sal purpureum inveniri in Lusitania: dulcedine quadam temperatum in jugis Tarraconensibus caedi, Solinus ad Oresium; ex Varrone Agellius, Montem Magnum circa Iberum, ex mero Sale, eique quantum demas, tantum adcrescere.
units.tr: What shall I now say of the salt pans? Solinus reports that in Spain salt is not only boiled but also dug up in great quantities, that is, it is both made and generated. It is made in many places in Spain from well water, as at Segontia and elsewhere, whence a large revenue is raised for the kings. It is generated on the far shores of the sea, whiter than the rest. There are also mountains of Spain, as Marcianus of Sicily believes, of native salt, as near Pitagorcia; in these the salt is cut like stone from a quarry, and afterwards it sprouts again and regrows like trees. Near the town of Antiquera there is a most pleasant valley, one thousand five hundred paces long, enclosed on every side by mountain ridges, which in winter is filled with rainwater and becomes like a great lake; by the heat of the sun, with the help of the genius of the sun, its waters are turned into white salt. I pass over other salt works in silence. But let us also hear the marvels, which nevertheless have today vanished. Strabo records that purple salt is found in Lusitania; that it is cut in the ridges of Tarragona, tempered with a certain sweetness, as Solinus reports about Oresius; and, according to Varro, as Agellius reports, that there is a great mountain near the Ebro made of pure salt, which grows back as much as you remove from it.

units.la: Iuxta Antiqueram, de qua dixi, Montes inexhaustas habent Fodinas, ex quibus praestantissimi Lapides, ad sumtuosissimorum Operum & Aedificiorum ornamenta idonei, eruuntur; qui late patenti & amplissimae Negociationi occasionem praebent. Quin & ijdem Montes alterius quoque Lapidis foecunditate praestant, quem Hiessó vulgare Hispanorum Idioma nuncupat; ex quo Calcem, imo notae singularis Glutcn conficiunt, quod usitato nunc nomine Architecti Tarram appellitant, Muris consolidandis firmandisque Aedificiis maximam vim habens. Hoc siquidem Lapidis genus igne concoctum, contusum, perque Incerniculum cribratum, aqua deinde maceratum Calcem & tenacissimum reddit Caementum, quod in priorem soliditatem mox coalescit: quo structuras tanta industria componunt, & tenacissimas Muris Incrustationes superinducunt, ut Aedificia continuo ex lapide nata, non manu facta aut compositia, esse videantur. Eadem etiam Calce, seu potius Gypso, Glutinatores utuntur in obturandis ligneis fictilibusque Vasis, quae Condimentis & vario foeta liquore in Indiam Belgicaque Regiones & alio transmittuntur.
units.tr: Near Antiquera, which I have mentioned, there are mountains with inexhaustible quarries, from which the finest stones, suitable for the adornment of the most sumptuous works and buildings, are dug out; these offer an occasion for a wide and very ample trade. Indeed the same mountains are also remarkably fruitful in another stone, which the Spanish vernacular calls Hiessó; from it they make lime, indeed a glue of a singular kind, which architects now commonly call tarra, and which has the greatest power for consolidating and strengthening walls. For this kind of stone, when burnt, crushed and sifted through a sieve, then soaked in water, yields lime and a very tenacious mortar, which soon hardens into its former solidity. With it builders put together structures with such great skill and lay on such tenacious coats of plaster on walls that the buildings seem to have grown continuously out of the rock, not made or assembled by hand. The glaziers also use the same lime, or rather gypsum, for sealing wooden and earthen vessels, which are sent to India, the Netherlands and other regions, filled with condiments and liquors of various kinds.

units.la: Iam vero quod Pecorum omnis generis mugitu balatuque Nemora; Silvae, Montes, Prata, Campi, Saltus ubique resonent?
units.tr: Now what of the fact that the groves, woods, mountains, meadows, plains and pastures everywhere resound with the bellowing and bleating of herds of every kind?

units.la: Equos alunt Hispaniae optimos: Ceteris Baetica plures; Asturia fortiores; Asturcones inde nominatos. De quibus sic Plinius lib. viii cap. xlii: In eadem Hispania Callaica gens & Asturica, equini generis, quos Thieldones vocamus, minori forma, appellatos Asturcones gignunt; quil un non vulgaris in cursu gradus; sed mollis alterno crurum expilicatu glomerasio: unde equus tolutim carpere incussus traditur arte. Martialis: Hic brevis ad numerum rapidos qui colligit ungues, Venit ab armiferis Gentibus Asturequus.
units.tr: Spain rears the finest horses; Baetica more than the others, and Asturia the stronger ones, from which the Asturcones take their name. Pliny speaks of them thus in book 8, chapter 42: In the same Spain the Callaecian and Asturian peoples breed a horse of the equine kind, which we call Thieldones, of smaller size, known as Asturcones; their gait in running is not ordinary, but a soft ambling, with a rhythmic alternating movement of the legs; whence the horse is said to be trained by art to carry its rider at a tolt. Martial: This short horse, which gathers up its swift hooves to a measure, has come from the armed peoples, the Asturian horse.

units.la: Silius Italicus lib. iii de Bello Poenico: Hic parvus Sonipes, nec Marti notus; at idem Aut inconcusso glomerat vestigia dorso, Aut molli pacata celer trahit esseda collo.
units.tr: Silius Italicus in book 3 of the Punic War: Here is the small steed, unknown to Mars; yet the same either gathers its footsteps on an unshaken back, or, quick and calm, draws the chariot with a soft neck.

units.la: Recte: commodissimam enim praebet Sellori vectationem. Omnis abest Succussatio. Hinc Εὐδρομος, Polluce teste, Graece vocatur. In vetere quodam Glossario, Asturco, Equus exponitur Ambulatorius. Gradarius aliis dicitur. Tolutarium item appellant Latini, a pedibus tolutim (quam vocem ex variis Scriptoribus explicat Nonius) id est, volubiliter & molliter glomerandis. Negat autem Silius Asturconem Marti notum (nam sic contra vulgatos quosdam codices legendum) de eo igitur exaudiendum illud Gratij, Non tamen Hispano Martem tentare minacem Ausim.
units.tr: Rightly so: for it offers the most comfortable riding for the rider, and there is no jolting at all. Hence it is called in Greek Eudromos [Εὐδρομος], as Pollux testifies. In an old glossary, asturco is explained as equus ambulatorius, a horse that ambles. Others call it gradarius. The Latins also call it tolutarium, from the feet moving tolutim (a word Nonius explains from various writers), that is, gathered smoothly and softly. Silius, however, says the Asturco is unknown to Mars (for so it must be read, against certain vulgar codices); that line of Gratius, Yet I would not dare to challenge the Spanish Mars, threatening, is therefore to be understood of this horse.

units.la: Equos enim ad bellum alibi suppeditat Hispania; quos Feros vocant Varro, Oppianus, Strabo; Probos, Olympius Nemesianus: Quinetiam gens ampla jacet trans ardua Calpes Culmina, Cornipedum late fœcunda proborum, &c.
units.tr: For Spain supplies horses for war elsewhere; Varro, Oppian and Strabo call them feri (wild); Olympius Nemesianus calls them probi (sound): Moreover, beyond the steep heights of Calpe there lies a wide people, richly fruitful in good stallions, &c.

units.la: De his etiam Silius, quem sæpe nominavi; Martius hic Sonipes campos hinnitibus implet, Hinc juga Cornipedes evecti bellica captant.
units.tr: Silius, whom I have often named, also speaks of these: Here the Martian steed fills the plains with neighing; from here the stallions, carried forth for war, seize the yokes.

units.la: Equi nonnullis Hispaniæ locis tantæ velocitatis agilitatisque generantur, ut Vento conceptos fabularetur, imo crederet Antiquitas? Tribuunt hanc vim locis ad Oceanum circa Olisipponem (videndum cap. xxvi. hujus libri) cum Plinio plerique; Vettonibus, Silius; Tagro Monti, Varro; Sacro, Columella, ex quo corrigendus fortean Varro, Ventum autem nominant Favonium aut Zephyrum omnes. Multorum vicem obeat Vergilius Georgic. iii: Ore omnes versa in Zephyrum stant rupibus altis, Exceptantque leves auras, & sæpe sine ullis Coniugiis Vento gravida (mirabile dictu)
units.tr: Are there horses in some parts of Spain of such speed and agility, that antiquity would have fabled them conceived by the wind, or even believed it? Most writers, with Pliny, ascribe this power to places on the ocean near Olisipo (see chapter 26 of this book); Silius to the Vettones; Varro to Mount Tagus; Columella to the Sacred (Promontory), from which Varro perhaps should be corrected. All name the wind as Favonius or Zephyrus. Virgil in Georgics book 3 takes the place of many: All turn their faces to the Zephyr, standing on the high rocks, and they catch the light breezes, and often, without any mating, pregnant by the wind (a marvel to tell).

units.la: Homerus iugales Achillis Equos ad Oceanum Zephyro Patre genitos, tradit, littoralia Iberiæ loca versus Occidentem designans. Pullos ex his natos non plus Triennio vivere perhibent M. Terentius Varro lib. iii. de re Rustica, Solinus in Polyhist. Plinius viii. cap. xlii, Columella lib. vii. rei Rusticæ, & alij; Septimam ferre ætatem canit Silius lib. iii, cujus locus operæ, qui adscribatur: At Vettonum alas Balarus probat æquore aperto. Hinc adeo, quum Ver placidum Flatusque tepescit, Concubitus servans tacitos Grex prestat Equarum, Et Venerem occultam genita concipit aura: Sed non multa dies Generis properatque senectus; Septimaque his stabulis longissima ducitur ætas.
units.tr: Homer tells that the yoked horses of Achilles were begotten on the ocean by the father Zephyrus, pointing to the coastal regions of Iberia toward the west. Foals born of these, they say, live no more than three years: Marcus Terentius Varro in book 3 of On Farming, Solinus in his Polyhistor, Pliny in book 8, chapter 42, Columella in book 7 of On Farming, and others. Silius, in book 3, sings that they bear a seventh age; his passage is worth quoting: But Balarus proves the wings of the Vettones on the open sea. Hence, when spring is calm and the breezes grow warm, the herd keeps its secret couplings with the mares, and the hidden love is conceived by the born breeze: but the day is not long, and old age hastens on this race; and the seventh age is reckoned the longest for these stables.

units.la: Septem annos dat illis Poëta, quibus alij vix tres. Nam Tertiam hic substituere pro Septima, nimis violentum. Tamquam notissima, hæc de Equis vento concipi solitis, scribit Columella; pro re incredibili, sed vera, recitat Varro; addens Equas ex Vento ibi concipere, ut hic Gallinæ solent, quarum Ova Hypenemia vocat, Zephyria Plinius. Iustinus ex libro Trogi ultimo natam credit Fabulam ex Equarum fœcunditate, Equorumque pernicitate. Hæc sane causa fuit, quod ex Hispania Equos ad Curules Ludos & Saltationes petere consueverint Veteres Romani: cujus rei amplissima sunt testimonia apud Q. Aurelium Symmachum, lib. iv. Epist. lx, lxi, & lxiv, lib. vii epist. cv. & cvi. lib. ix. epist. xii, xiix, xix, xx, xxii; & xxiii. Ut huic Qualitatis Membro finem imponam. Celtiberorum Equi, Strabonis indicio, subalbi fi in Ulteriorem traducuntur Hispaniam, colorem permutant: suntque Parthicorum similes.
units.tr: The poet gives them seven years, where others give scarcely three. For to read tertiam in place of septimam here is too violent. As well-known matters, Columella writes that these are the mares accustomed to conceive from the wind; Varro recites it as an incredible but true thing, adding that the mares there conceive from the wind as hens here do, whose eggs he calls hypenemia, Pliny calls them zephyria. Justin, from the last book of Trogus, believes the fable arose from the fecundity of the mares and the swiftness of the horses. This was certainly the reason why the ancient Romans were accustomed to seek horses from Spain for the Circus Games and the dances; there are very ample testimonies of this in Quintus Aurelius Symmachus, book 4, letters 60, 61 and 64; book 7, letters 105 and 106; book 9, letters 12, 13, 19, 20, 22 and 23. To bring this section on the qualities to an end: the horses of the Celtiberians, according to Strabo, are somewhat whitish, but when they are taken into farther Spain they change colour, and they are like the Parthian horses.

units.la: In Lusitania Sus quum esset occisus, inquit Varro lib. ii. de Re Rust. cap. iv, Attilius Hispaniensis, minime mendax, & multarum rerum peritus in doctrina dicebat L. Volumnio Senatori Missam esse offulam cum duabus costis, qua penderet iii & xx pondo; eiusque Suis a cute ad os pedem & tres digitos fuisse.
units.tr: "In Lusitania a pig was killed," says Varro in book 2, chapter 4 of On Farming, "and Attilius of Spain, not at all a liar, and skilled in many matters of learning, used to tell Lucius Volumnius, a senator, that a piece of meat with two ribs had been sent, which weighed 23 pounds; and from the skin to the snout of that pig there were a foot and three fingers."

units.la: Hispaniæ Canes laudant Oppianus & Iulius Pollux; item Nemesianus, quorum proles de sanguine manat Ibero.
units.tr: Oppian and Julius Pollux praise the dogs of Spain; so too Nemesianus, whose offspring flows from Iberian blood.

units.la: Ad Venationes exstimulant cum alia, tum in Montibus, Vallibus, Silvisque Damæ, Cervi, Apri, Vrsi. Lepores, Cuniculi. His sane abundantem docet Hispaniam versiculus Catulli; Cuniculosæ Celtiberiæ fili;
units.tr: For hunting, Spain invites with its deer, fallow deer, roe deer, boars and bears in the mountains, valleys and woods, and also with hares and rabbits. A line of Catullus clearly shows that Spain abounds in these: sons of rabbit-rich Celtiberia.

units.la: & Nummus Hadriani Imperatoris, in cujus una facie, HADRIANVS AVG. COSS. III. P. P. cum Imperatoris capite; in altera HISPANIA. S. C. cum ipsius, Olivarum Ramulos aliquot dextra tenentis, effigie, adpicta ad pedes hoc animalculo.
units.tr: And a coin of the Emperor Hadrian, on one face of which is HADRIANVS AVG. COSS. III. P. P. with the emperor's head; on the other HISPANIA. S.C., with the figure of Spain holding some sprigs of olive in her right hand, and this little animal at her feet.

units.la: Ad Aucupia invitant cum Aves aliæ, tum Aquilæ, Ardeæ, Accipitres, Atagines item, eo nuper ex Sicilia allati. Peculiare Hispaniæ esse Posidonius apud Strabonem adscrit, τὰ τῆς χερσαίας μελάνας ὄναι. Ad Piscationes denique incitant in Mari quidem cum Pisces ipsi, ut Cetae, Balenae, Congri, Murenae, Thynni, Savali, Lampetrae, & alij, tum Ostrea Conchylia que; in Fluminibus autem & Mediterraneis, ut alijs commemorandis superseded am, Turtures, Iuvenali etiam decantati, aureis maculis insigniti: Truchas vocat Vulgus Hispanicum, Trochus Itali Siculique; saporis jucundissimi, optimi nutrimenti, Senibus Aegrotantibusque ab Medicis concedi soliti. Legisse se scribit Lucius Marineus Siculus de rebus Hispaniae lib. 1, in Hispania Polypum olim captum suisse tantae magnitudinis ut ejus caput ostensum Lucullo xv. amphorarum capax fuerit, crines quidvis utroque brachio comprehenderint, caliculi instar pelvium urnam aequaverint, reliquiae ejus miraculo adservatae septingenta pondo penderint. Memoriae prodit idem Marineus Valentiae se piscem vidisse, quem Piscatores mari captum portaverant, & Torculari magno locaverant Aquae pleno, crassitudine & longitudine magnae Mulae, cujus Caput, Os, Nares, Oculi Bovis esse videbantur; praeter Cornua, quibus carebat; Mammas habebat muliebres, & Manus Mamillis adpositas, Vulvam quoque mulieris: addit postero die peperisse Piscioulum ipsi persimilem, longitudine trium pedum, crassitudine Colli Canis Gallici, Matremque cum quatriduo post fame fortean coactam, devorasse.
units.tr: For fowling, Spain invites with other birds, and with eagles, herons, hawks, and also the goshawks, recently brought from Sicily. Posidonius, quoted by Strabo, asserts that the land-birds of black colour are peculiar to Spain. Finally, for fishing, they invite both in the sea, with the fish themselves, such as whales, sea-monsters, conger eels, moray eels, tunnies, shad, lampreys and others, and with oysters and shellfish; and in the rivers and inland waters, to mention others while omitting many, with turtles, celebrated even by Juvenal, marked with golden spots: the Spanish people call them trucha, the Italians and Sicilians trocus; of most pleasant flavour and excellent nourishment, which doctors are accustomed to allow to the old and the sick. Lucius Marineus of Sicily writes that he has read in book 1 of his work on the affairs of Spain that a polyp was once caught in Spain of such size that its head, shown to Lucullus, could hold fifteen amphorae; its tentacles would be grasped by either arm, its suckers matched the size of a basin in the shape of a cup, and its remains, preserved as a wonder, weighed seven hundred pounds. The same Marineus records that he saw at Valencia a fish which fishermen had brought from the sea and placed in a great press full of water, as large in thickness and length as a mule, whose head, mouth, nostrils and eyes seemed those of an ox, except that it lacked horns; it had female breasts and hands placed against the breasts, and also the womb of a woman. He adds that on the next day it gave birth to a little fish very like itself, three feet long, the thickness of a Gallic dog's neck; and the mother, after four days, perhaps forced by hunger, devoured it.

units.la: Sed ego haec paucis: pluribus explicantur ab Caesare lib. iii. de bello Civili, Appiano, Strabone, Iustino, Solino, & aliis probatis Scriptoribus: quibus addendi, ut certiora tradentes omnia, & oculis visa, L. Marineus Siculus lib. 1, Rodericus Sanctius Historiae Hispan. Part. 1. cap. ii, Ioannes Vasaeus cap. ix. Marius Aretius Patricius Syracusanus Dialogo, cui nomen Calipho, & si qui his adcensendi.
units.tr: But I touch on these things briefly: they are explained at greater length by Caesar in book 3 of the Civil War, Appian, Strabo, Justin, Solinus and other approved writers. To these should be added, as writers who hand down more certain things, having seen them with their own eyes: Lucius Marineus of Sicily in book 1; Rodericus Sanctius, Historia Hispaniae, part 1, chapter 2; Joannes Vasaeus, chapter 9; Marius Aretius, a Syracusan patrician, in the dialogue called Calipho; and any who may be counted with these.

units.la: Talis igitur Hispania & Vetus & Nova; Terris omnibus Terra felicior; cui excolendae ditandaeque impensius, quam ceteris gentibus, ut ait Latinus Pacatus, supremus ille Fabricator indulsit.
units.tr: Such, then, is Spain, both old and new; happier than all lands on earth, to which, as Latinus Pacatus says, that supreme Craftsman has granted more lavishly than to other nations the gifts of cultivation and enrichment.

units.la: Tanta autem hujus Regionis fertilitas, tamque laeta rerum omnium copia facit hodie, ut larga manu Confinalibus suis, alijsque remotioribus Populis infinita cum apud se nata, tum etiam aliunde advecta submini-stret, Sericum, Lanas, Pannos omnis generis, Sal, Saccharum, Mel; Mala, Medica; Citrea, Granata, Cydonea; Olivas conditas; Cappares; Vvas, Ficus, Pruna passa; Amygdala, Castaneas, Glycyrrhizam, Anisum, Cuminum, Coriandrum, Oryzam, Crocum, Oleum, Ceram, Alumen, Smegma, Minium, Purpuram; Thynnos, Balenasque salitas. Baccas Laurinas; Fructus diversorum generum, Saccharo adspersos; Alabastrum, Coralium: Aurum, Argentum, Ferrum, Chalybem, Stannum, Cuprum, Plumbum, Rubiam Tinctorum, Argentum Vivum, Gossipium; Gemmas item preciososque Lapides & Aromata ab alijs, tum ab Indis accepta. De quibus omnibus, praeter Strabonem lib. iii, plene Damianus a Goes, Eques Lusitanus, libello, brevi quidem, sed nervoso; quo Patriae fertilitatem & potentiam suis coloribus delineare est conatus.
units.tr: Indeed, the fertility of this region and so generous an abundance of all things make it today that, with an open hand, it supplies its neighbours and more distant peoples with endless goods, both those born at home and those brought in from elsewhere: silk, wool, cloths of every kind, salt, sugar, honey; apples, quinces; citrons, pomegranates, quinces (cydonia); preserved olives; capers; grapes, figs, raisins; almonds, chestnuts, liquorice, aniseed, cumin, coriander, rice, saffron, oil, wax, alum, cosmetic ointment, red lead, purple; tunny and salted whales. Laurel berries; fruits of various kinds sprinkled with sugar; alabaster, coral; gold, silver, iron, steel, tin, copper, lead, dyers' madder, quicksilver, cotton; likewise gems, precious stones and spices received from other peoples and from the Indies. Concerning all these things, besides Strabo, book 3, Damianus a Goes, a Portuguese knight, has written fully in a little book, indeed brief but vigorous, in which he has tried to portray his country's fertility and power in its own colours.

units.la: Pro ijs autem omnibus grata quadam commutatione certatim ab Europaeis, Africanis, Asiaticis, Americanis accipiunt eas Hispani merces, quas Natura Coelique & Soli genius ipsis negare solet.
units.tr: In return for all these things, the Spanish receive from Europeans, Africans, Asians and Americans, eagerly and in a certain welcome exchange, those goods which Nature and the genius of the heavens and soil are wont to deny them.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: Hispaniae Montes.
units.tr: The Mountains of Spain.

units.la: ITA se habent Regionis Adjuncta: succedunt Partes. Eas hic appello, Terra quidem, Montes & Promontoria; Aqua vero, Sinus, Portus, Flumina & similia. Inter Hispaniae Montes Pyrenaeus principem obtinet locum, Hispanos ab Gallis dividens; qui Ptolemaeo & reliquis, Πυρήνα; Stephano, Πυρήν; Tibullo lib. 1. & Silio Italico lib. iii, Pyrene; Livio lib. xxi, Caesari lib. 1. de bello Civili, Suetonio in Caesare cap. xxv, Aemilioque Probo in Annibale, Saltus Pyrenaeus: Hispanis, Los Pireneos universim; nam pro ratione Locorum varia sortitur nomina, ut docet Olivarius. Ad Templum Veneris dicitur Puig cerda; inde Montes de Iacque & Roncevalles; ad Navarrae demum regnum, Mons S. Hadriani. Dictum volunt plerique Ἀπὸ τῆς πυρὸς, ab Igne: vel quod crebris fulminum ictibus feriatur; vel quod ejus silvae (scribente Diodoro libro vi) injecto à Pastoribus Igne, quomdam universæ conflagrarint. Certe ab Græca voce nuncupatum, non est mirandum; quum ex Antiquis Monimentis, Græcos tam Occidentale, quam Orientale hujus montis latus habitasse quondam, satis superque constet. Silius Italicus Denominationis honorem tribuit Pyrene puellæ, Bebrycis, qui rerum ibi gubernacula tenebat, filiæ; in eo monte ab Hercule, violato Hospitij iure compressæ; ibique, quum ab feris laniata esset, sepultæ. Pomponius Mela lib. iii. Dion. lib. lxiii, & Orosius lib. vi. cap. xxi, Pyrenæos appellant non tantum, qui Hispaniam inter & Galliam; sed & qui ab Oriente in Oceanum usque excurrunt Occidentalem. Quin & ad Artabrum vel Celticum Promontorium, quod hodie Cabo de Finis terræ, Pyrenæos hactenus ab Adcolis appellari testatur apud Ortelium Georgius Austriacus, Præpositus Harlebecensis. Quidquid sit, perpetuus ille Pyrenæi ab Ortu in Occasum procursus Hispanorum alios facit Citramontanos versus Meridiem, Ultramontanos ad Septemtrionem. Pyrenes latus, ut notat Strabo lib. iii. in Hispaniam vergens variis consitum est arboribus, ijsque semper virentibus; alterum autem Galliam spectans, omnino nudum: media Loca Convalles continent, ab frequente Incola habitatas. Mutata nonnihil hodie Loci facies.
units.tr: Such are the adjuncts of the region. Next come the parts. I call these, namely the land, mountains and promontories; and the water, bays, harbours, rivers and the like. Among the mountains of Spain the Pyrenees hold the chief place, dividing Spain from Gaul. Ptolemy and the others call it Πυρήνα; Stephanus, Πυρήν; Tibullus in book 1 and Silius Italicus in book 3, Pyrene; Livy in book 21, Caesar in book 1 of the Civil War, Suetonius in the Life of Caesar chapter 25, and Aemilius Probus in the Life of Hannibal, the Pyrenaean pass (saltus Pyrenaeus). The Spanish call it Los Pireneos in general, for it takes various names according to the places, as Olivarius teaches. Near the temple of Venus it is called Puig Cerda; then the Mountains of Jacque and Roncevalles; and finally, at the kingdom of Navarre, Mount St. Adrian. Most hold that it is named from the Greek ἀπὸ τῆς πυρός, from fire, either because it is often struck by lightning-bolts, or because its woods (as Diodorus writes in book 6) were at one time all burned up when shepherds set fire to them. That it was named from a Greek word is no cause for wonder, since from ancient monuments it is abundantly clear that the Greeks once inhabited both the western and the eastern side of this mountain. Silius Italicus attributes the honour of the name to Pyrene, the daughter of Bebrycus, who ruled there; she was violated on that mountain by Hercules, in breach of the right of hospitality, and after being torn to pieces by wild beasts she was buried there. Pomponius Mela in book 3, Dio in book 63, and Orosius in book 6 chapter 21 call the Pyrenees not only the range between Spain and Gaul, but also the range that runs from the east to the western ocean. Indeed, as far as Artabrum or the Celtic promontory, which today is Cabo de Finisterre, Georgius Austriacus, provost of Harlebeke, testifies in Ortelius that the range has been called the Pyrenees by the inhabitants up to now. Whatever the case, that unbroken course of the Pyrenees from east to west divides the Spanish mountains into those on this side toward the south and those beyond toward the north. As Strabo notes in book 3, the side of the Pyrenees facing Spain is planted with various trees, and these always green; the other side, facing Gaul, is wholly bare; the middle places contain valleys inhabited by many people. The appearance of the place is somewhat changed today.

units.la: Pyrenæus, non ut Galliam separat ab Hispania, sed ut ab Ortu in Occasum ad Promontorium usque Celticum prolatatus Hispanos dividit in Cismontanos & Ultramontanos, alium ad Iberi fontes Montem protrudit versus Meridiem per Hispaniæ latitudinem. Nomen illi Ἰδύβεδα apud Strabonem & Ptolemæum: Saltus Aucensis, vulgo Monte d'Oca hodie vocatur, ab Auca Urbe vetere, cujus ad Villam-Francam, vigesimo supra Burgos milliari, vestigia monstrantur. Hujus progressum sic describit Ioannes Mariana lib. 1. de rebus Hispaniæ, cap. iii. Ex his Montibus (eos designat, qui ab Ortu abeunt in Occasum per Hispaniæ longitudinem) Idubeda Mons versus Austrum ad Iberi fontes in Pelendonibus derivatur & per Virvessam Arevacesque, ubi Orbionis cacumina surgunt, neque procul Cauno, qui hodie Moncaius est, Bilbilim Darocamque praetervectus, Mare Mediterraneum attingit, non procul Dertusa Urbe; unde extremæ ejus montis partes hodie etiam nomen habent. Iberum Amnem, contra quam reliqui insigniores Hispaniæ fluvij faciunt, ad Occasum ire Idubeda mons prohibet, &c.
units.tr: The Pyrenees do not separate Gaul from Spain in the sense that they run from east to west to the Celtic promontory and divide the Spanish into Cismontane and Ultramontane; they also send out another mountain southward across the breadth of Spain to the sources of the Ebro. Strabo and Ptolemy call it Ἰδύβεδα (Idubeda). Today it is commonly called Saltus Aucensis, the Monte d'Oca, from the ancient city Auca, whose remains are shown near Villam-Francam, twenty miles beyond Burgos. Juan de Mariana describes its course thus in book 1 of his De rebus Hispaniae, chapter 3: Of these mountains (he means those that run from east to west through the length of Spain) the Idubeda range runs south to the sources of the Ebro among the Pelendones, and passing through the Verrusa and Arevaci, where the peaks of Orbio rise, and not far from Caunus, which is today Moncayo, past Bilbilis and Dercon, it reaches the Mediterranean sea, not far from the city of Dertosa; whence the farthest parts of this mountain still bear the name today. The Idubeda range prevents the Ebro river from flowing west, contrary to what the other more notable rivers of Spain do, and so on.

units.la: Orospeda Idubedæ proles: Ὀροσπέδα Straboni, Ὀρεσπέδα Ptolemæo. Toti hodie certum non est nomen: nam quod Alvaro Gomecio censentur Sierra Vermigia, quod Floriano Sierra Molina, quod Clusio Sierra Morena; Partes ejus sunt; quibus alias addit pro ratione locorum Navagierus in suo Itinerario: Puerto de la Tablada, di Ponfria, Tofria, del Pico, di Soma Sierra, Palomera de Avila, &c. Describit eleganter meo judicio Ioannes Mariana, loco quem indicavi: Paullo infra Caunum (Moncayo hodie, ut ante dictum) ex Idubeda emissus Orospeda, mollibus initio jugis, ut vix adsurgere videatur, sensim tamen se efferens, ulteriusque progressus, Molina primum montes (Sierra Molina hodie) erigit; Concha deinde, ubi Sucronem ad laevam, ad dextram Tagum emittit. Inde Consaburonis seu Consiegra montibus constitutis, & in Campis Laminitanis Ana fontes emixus, ad Alcaraßum (Ἀλκαράσσα Ptolemæi putatur, Ilergetum urbs: hoc loco Orospeda, Sierra de Alcaraz; Ἀργυρεῖς, Argenteus Mons, dicitur Straboni) Seguramque procedens in diversas partes mariaque diversa Taderem (hic hodie Segura fluvius est) Batimque in Saltu Tigensi non longe à Caforla opido fundit; ab Ana fontibus remotum amplius centum millibus passuum: unde in duo brachia scissus, parte una è regione Murcia factus ad Murgim, hoc est Muxacram, mareque terminatur, relictis ad occasum Bastitanis à Basta Urbe, quae hodie Baza est; ad ortum vero Contestanis, veteris Hispaniæ populis: parte altera versus Malacam porrectus, & Eliberritanis jugis sese adnectens ultra Calpem ultraque Tartessum tanta procurrit aviditate, ut penetrato mari Fretique angustiis tantum non obturatis, Africa complexum non semel appetere videatur. Orospedæ adienseri solet Calpe. Sic Ptolemæo aliisque Mons vocatur ad Fretum Herculeum; qui Gibraltar vulgo. Vere notatur pronunciaturque Gebal Tarik: sic nominatus ab strenuissimo Duce Tarik, filio Abdallæ, filij Wenemu Renathæi, quem Mules filius Nutzir ex genere Marawanæorum, quo tempore (annus is erat 1occix) ex Africa in eam Hispaniæ partem, quæ Andalusia nunc dicitur, irrumperet, secum habebat. Testatur Auctor Geographiæ Arabs, qui quum de subacta Insula Chadhar verba fecisset, hæc subjungit : وكان وصن لهم البهـــا من جبل طارق وانما سمي جبل طارق لان طارق بن عبد الله بن وئن الرباني امـــا جامر بن معد من البرابر وتحصنوا بهذا الجبـــــــل *
units.tr: Orospeda is the offspring of Idubeda: Ὀροσπέδα in Strabo, Ὀρεσπέδα in Ptolemy. Today its name is not fixed for the whole range. For what Alvaro Gomez reckons as the Sierra Vermigia, Florian as the Sierra Molina, and Clusius as the Sierra Morena, are parts of it; Navagerius in his Itinerary adds others according to the places: Puerto de la Tablada, di Ponfria, Tofria, del Pico, di Soma Sierra, Palomera de Avila, and so on. In my judgment, Juan de Mariana describes it elegantly in the passage I have indicated: A little below Caunus (today Moncayo, as said above), the Orospeda, sent out from Idubeda, with gentle ridges at first, so that it hardly seems to rise, yet gradually lifting itself higher and advancing further, first raises the mountains of Molina (today the Sierra Molina); then, at Concha, it sends out the Sucro on the left and the Tagus on the right. Thence, with the mountains of Consaburo or Consiegra set up, and after the springs of the Anas have gushed out in the plains of Laminium, it proceeds to Alcaraz (thought to be the Alkarassa of Ptolemy, a city of the Ilergetes; here the Orospeda is the Sierra de Alcaraz; Strabo calls it Ἀργυρεῖς, the Silver Mountain), and then to the Segura, and in various directions and into various seas it pours out the Tader (today the river Segura) and the Bastis in the forest of Tigis, not far from the town of Caforla, a distance of more than a hundred miles from the springs of the Anas. Thence, split into two arms, one part, facing Murcia, runs to the Murgis, that is, the Muxacra, and ends in the sea, leaving to the west the Bastitani from the city of Basta, which today is Baza, and to the east the Contestani, an ancient people of Spain; the other part, stretching toward Malaca and joining the Eliberritan ridges, runs beyond Calpe and beyond Tartessus with such eagerness that, having penetrated the sea and nearly closed the narrows of the strait, it seems more than once to aim to embrace Africa. Calpe is usually added to the Orospeda. So it is called by Ptolemy and others the mountain at the Pillars of Hercules, which is commonly called Gibraltar. It is truly written and pronounced Gebal Tarik, named after the most valiant leader Tarik, son of Abdallah, son of Wenemu Renathaeus, whom Mules, son of Nutzir, of the family of the Marawanaei, brought with him when, in the year 1 occix (that is 711), he broke from Africa into that part of Spain now called Andalusia. The Arab author of a Geography testifies to this; when he had spoken of the subjugated island Chadhar, he adds these words:

units.la: id est : Applicarunt autem ad eam Gebal Tarik (Monte Tarik.) Vocatus est autem Gebal Tarik, ideo quod Tarik filius Abdalle, filij VVenemu Renathai, postquam trajecit quos secum habebat Barbaros, & muniverunt sese intra hunc montem. Orospedæ item pars Rupes præcelsa, quæ ex Hispalensi urbe Granatam euntí prope Archidonam se conspiciendam offert. Nomen habet famamque meretur ex memorabili ; quòd in omne ævum est duraturum, Amoris exemplo. Hispanis dicitur, La Penna de ios Enamorados, Amantium Rupes. Res, ut paucis dicam, ita habet: Quum Regnum Granatense Mauris adhuc pareret, graveque inter ipsos & Christianos bellum flagraret, quodam in conflictu inter alios captus est Christianus, quem Maurorum Rex ob formæ venustatem facilitatemque morum libertate donavit, eumdem apud se in palatio retinens. Inter hunc porro Filiamque Regis tanta tamque casta coaluit familiaritas; ut Articulis hæc Christianæ Fidei præcipuis imbuta, Christianisque commorari deinceps avens & commori, Torum Conjugalem pollicita, fugam cum Captivo fuerit molita. Quum autem Rex diligenter illos persequeretur; in Rupem, quam dixi, ut ibi delitescerent, fugerunt: videntes autem se detectos, & Rupem ab Mauris undique circumseptam animadvertentes, cacumen conscenderunt: seque, supplicio, quod ab Rege exspectabant, territi, mutuo complexu præcipites inde dederunt. Ad cujus rei memoriam in ejusdem Rupis dorso, inque via publica Cruces erectæ videntur.
units.tr: That is: They landed there at Gebal Tarik (Mount Tarik). Gebal Tarik is so called because Tarik, son of Abdallah, son of Wenemu Renathai, after he had ferried over the Berbers whom he had with him, fortified themselves within this mountain. Also part of the Orospeda is the very steep rock which, on the way from the city of Seville to Granada, presents itself to be seen near Archidona. It has its name and fame from a memorable event, an example of love that will last forever. The Spanish call it La Penna de los Enamorados, the Rock of the Lovers. The matter, to tell it briefly, is this. When the kingdom of Granada was still under the Moors, and a grievous war was blazing between them and the Christians, in a certain clash a Christian was captured among others, and the king of the Moors, on account of his beauty and his easygoing manners, granted him his liberty, keeping him in his palace. Between this man and the king's daughter there grew up such a close and chaste friendship that she, instructed in the principal articles of the Christian faith, desiring thereafter to stay and die among Christians, and promising him her marriage bed, contrived to flee with the captive. When the king pursued them diligently, they fled to the rock I have mentioned, to hide there; but seeing themselves discovered, and noticing that the rock was surrounded on all sides by Moors, they climbed to the summit, and terrified at the punishment they expected from the king, they threw themselves headlong from it in a mutual embrace. In memory of this event, crosses are seen erected on the ridge of the same rock and on the public road.

units.la: Paullinus Bimarem nominat. Respicit enim duo Maria, Internum & Externum. Strabo libro Geographicorum tertio Calpen montem esse, ait, Circuitu quidem non magnum admodum, altitudine autem ingentem & arrectum, ut remotioribus Insulæ formam præferat. Vnam Herculis Columnarum sunt qui fabulantur, alteramque ex adverso Abylam in Africa, Laborum Herculis metas. Addunt unum fuisse quondam Montem; sed ab Hercule perfossum: ut, mutata rerum facie, exclusa ante Maria in Mediterraneas Terras, Aquarum indigas, admitterentur. Videndi, præter alios, Plinius lib. iii, & Pomponius Mela lib. i. ubi de Mauritania & lib. ii. ubi de Hispania: Calpe, inquit inter alia, facta cum Abyla commissione, magis & pene totus in Mare prominens. Is mirum in modum concavus, ab ea parte, qua spectat occasum, medium fere latus aperit, atque inde ingressus totus admodum pervius prope, quantum patet Sinus & specus, ultra est. Diodorus etiam, agens de Perfossione, quam dixi, scribit Herculem Fretum tam angustum reliquisse, ne grandia Cete intrarent. Alij de Columnis Herculis tradunt alia; quæ ad meum nihil faciunt institutum.
units.tr: Paulinus calls it Bimarem, for it looks to both seas, the inner and the outer. Strabo in book 3 of his Geography says that Calpe is a mountain not very large in circuit, but huge and steep in height, so that from a distance it presents the shape of an island. Some who tell fables say that it was one of the Pillars of Hercules, and the other, opposite, was Abyla in Africa, the limits of the labours of Hercules. They add that it was once a single mountain, but was pierced through by Hercules, so that, the face of things being changed, the seas were let in from outside into the inland lands, which lacked water. Among others, Pliny in book 3 and Pomponius Mela in book 1, where he speaks of Mauretania, and in book 2, where he speaks of Spain, are worth consulting: Calpe, he says among other things, made by its junction with Abyla, juts out into the sea more and almost wholly. It is remarkably hollow, and on the side that faces the west it opens up roughly half its side, and from there the entrance is almost wholly passable, as far as the bay and cave extend. Diodorus too, speaking of the piercing I mentioned, writes that Hercules left the strait so narrow that huge whales could not enter. Others hand down other things about the Pillars of Hercules, which have nothing to do with my present purpose.

units.la: Ex Orospeda prope Alcarassum Mariani Montes surgunt. Sic nominat Plinius lib. iii, cap. i. qui singulariter Prolemæo, & Mons Mariorum Antonino, hodie Sierra Morena: Radices horum montium adluit ad lævam perpetuo fere ad Oceanum usque nobilissimus fluvius Bætis.
units.tr: From the Orospeda near Alcarassum rise the Marian Mountains. So Pliny names them in book 3, chapter 1, where Ptolemy calls them singularly the Mountains of Mars and Antoninus the Mountain of the Marians; today they are the Sierra Morena. The most noble river Baetis washes their foot on the left, almost all the way to the Ocean.

units.la: Haud procul ab eo loco, quo Orospeda ab Idubeda prodit, prope Caunum è media Camporum vastitate atque planicie Montes alij videntur oriri; ceterum in Pyrenæi brachiis quibus universa innectitur Hispania, numerandos esse, nemini dubium est. Eorum apud Veteres Scriptores nulla mentio: nunc multis nominibus ab vicinis Civitatibus sunt noti. Numantia, Segobia, Abulaque lustratis, Castellam in Veterem Novamque secernunt; præterque Caurium & Placentiam Tagi ductum, quo ad lævam adluuntur, sequentes, Portugalliam in duas ferme æquas partes secant. Ad opidum Sintram demum, Tagro Monti viginti octo millibus passuum ad Septemtrionem ab Olisippone impositum, Occiduum attingunt Oceanum, desinuntque Promontorio in Mari constituto, cui Magno vel Olisipponensi cognomen.
units.tr: Not far from the place where the Orospeda branches off from the Idubeda, near Caunus, other mountains seem to rise out of the middle of the vast, flat plains. That they should be counted among the arms of the Pyrenees, by which the whole of Spain is bound together, is beyond doubt. The ancient writers make no mention of them; now they are known by many names from the neighbouring cities. Passing by Numantia, Segobia and Abula, they separate Old Castile from New Castile; and following the course of the Tagus, which they border on the left, past Caurium and Placentia, they cut Portugal into two roughly equal parts. Finally, reaching the town of Sintra, which lies twenty-eight thousand paces north of Olisipo on the mountain Tagro, they touch the western Ocean and end in a promontory projecting into the sea, which bears the surname Great or Lisbon.

units.la: Iuxta Barcinonem Mons est, quem Mon-Iui vocant adcolæ: sunt qui interpretantur Montem Iovis; alij melius Montem Iudæorum, qui quondam illic sepelicbantur, quorumque plura adhuc ibi Sepulcreta & Signa. In vertice Turris est; unde Speculator die quidem Linteo Velo, noctu vero Facibus Navigiorum adventum Barcinonæ Civibus ostendit. De Montibus Fluminibusque Hispaniarum libellum edidit Hieronymus Paullus Barcinonensis. T CAP. V.
units.tr: Near Barcino there is a mountain which the inhabitants call Mon-Iui. Some interpret this as Mount Jupiter; others, more plausibly, as Mount of the Jews, since Jews were once buried there, and many of their sepulchres and monuments are still to be seen there. On the summit is a tower, from which a watchman signals to the citizens of Barcino the arrival of ships, by a linen sail by day and by torches at night. Hieronymus Paullus of Barcino published a little book on the mountains and rivers of Spain.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAP. V.

units.la: Hispaniæ Promontoria.
units.tr: The Promontories of Spain.

units.la: HÆc de Montibus: Promontoria sunt in Hispaniæ ambitu ad utrumque Mare nobilissima; quæ paucis recensebo; capto ab ijs, quæ ad Oceanum, initio.
units.tr: So much for the mountains. The promontories around the coasts of both seas are the most notable in Spain. I shall list a few of them, beginning with those on the Ocean.

units.la: Scythicum in Cantabris Melæ libro iii. cap. i. Geograph. Olivario dicitur Cabo del Rigo; Floriano Penas de Hufon; alijs Cabo de Peñas. Credunt nonnulli esse, quod Λαπαπία κάρη & τείλλιον Ptolemæo.
units.tr: The Scythicum, in the land of the Cantabrians, is in Mela, book iii, chapter 1 (Geography). Olivarius calls it Cabo del Rigo, Florianus Penas de Hufon, and others Cabo de Peñas. Some believe it is what Ptolemy calls Λαπαπία κάρη [Lapapia kare] and τείλλιον [teillion].

units.la: Artabrum, quod & Celticum Plinio, à Populis Artabris & Celticis, Promontorio adhabitantibus; Νέγον Ptolemæo & Straboni, apud quem libro iii. male, μετὰ τὰς αὐτὰς Ἀρτάβριος Ἀκρας, ἥν καλοῦσιν ἱερὴν: legendum enim, inversis litteris, νέγον, ut & ipse alibi appellat. Speculum Britanniæ vocant Æthicus & Orosius. Hodie Nautis appellatur Cabo de Finis Terræ, in Galecia.
units.tr: The Artabrum, also called the Celticum by Pliny after the Artabri and Celtici peoples who lived near the promontory. Ptolemy and Strabo call it Negon. In Strabo, book iii, the text reads wrongly, "after the same Artabrian headland, which they call holy" [μετὰ τὰς αὐτὰς Ἀρτάβριος Ἀκρας, ἥν καλοῦσιν ἱερὴν]. One should read, with the letters inverted, νέγον [negon], as he himself calls it elsewhere. Aethicus and Orosius call it the Mirror of Britain. Today sailors call it Cabo de Finis Terræ, in Galicia.

units.la: Magnum, in Lusitania, Pomponio & Plinio: hodie Cabo de Casias, ab vicino opido; ad dextram Tagi fluminis. Plinium maximo errore, quemcumque tandem Auctorem est sequutus, se involuere, notat Ioachimus Vadianus Commentario in Pomponium Melam, quum lib. iv. natur. histor. cap. xxi. scribat, Olisipponensi Promontorio oram Hispaniæ occiduam finiri, & Septemtrionalis lateris flexum incipi. Verba ponam; ut, an vere notetur, pareat: Excurrit deinde, inquit, in aliud vasto cornu Promontorium, quod alij Artabrum appellavere, alij Magnum, multi Olisipponense ab opido: Terras, Maria, Cælum disterminans. Illo finitur Hispaniæ Latus, & à circuitu eius incipit Frons. Vox, illo, Artabri respicit appellationem, non Olisipponensis. Dicit enim Artabro finiri Hispaniæ Latus, & ab ejus circuitu incipere Frontem. Artabrum autem, obiter addit, Olisipponense multis vocari. Hoc non Plinij, sed aliorum dogma; salsum omnino. Nam si Olisipponensi nomen ab Olisippone, clarissima Lusitaniæ Urbe; non idem poterit esse cum Artabro, sed cum Magno, cuius jam memini, quodque in Frontis medio. Eodem modo, eademque interpretatione juvandus C. Iulius Solinus in Polyhist. cap. xxvi.
