units.tr: The Magnum, in Lusitania, according to Pomponius and Pliny. Today it is Cabo de Casias, named from the nearby town, on the right bank of the Tagus river. Joachim Vadian, in his commentary on Pomponius Mela, notes that Pliny entangled himself in a very great error, whichever authority he followed. In book iv, chapter 21 of the Natural History, Pliny writes that the western coast of Spain ends at the Olisipponensian promontory, and the bend of the northern side begins there. I shall give his words, so that it may be seen whether the charge is true: "Then it runs out into another promontory with a vast horn," he says, "which others have called Artabrum, others Magnum, and many Olisiponense from the town, dividing lands, seas and sky. At that point the side of Spain ends, and from its circuit the front begins." The word "illo" (there) refers to the name Artabrum, not to Olisiponense. For he says that the side of Spain ends at the Artabrum, and that the front begins from its circuit. He adds in passing that the Artabrum is called Olisiponense by many. This is not Pliny's doctrine but that of others, and altogether absurd. For if the name Olisiponense comes from Olisippo, the most famous city of Lusitania, it cannot be the same as the Artabrum, but only the same as the Magnum, which I have already mentioned, and which lies in the middle of the front. In the same way, and with the same interpretation, C. Julius Solinus in the Polyhistor, chapter 26, is to be helped.

units.la: Barbarium, Βαρβάριον ἄκρα Ptolemæo: hodie, ut volunt Clusius & Taraffa, Cabo de Spichel, ad sinistram Tagi ripam oppositum Magno vel Olisipponensi.
units.tr: The Barbarium, Βαρβάριον ἄκρα [Barbarion akra] for Ptolemy. Today, as Clusius and Tarafa think, it is Cabo de Spichel, on the left bank of the Tagus, opposite the Magnum or the Olisiponense.

units.la: Sacrum ἱερὸν Ptolemæo & Straboni, cui etiam Κάλλιον lib. i: Sacer Mons Columella: Caput Europæ Eustathio: hodie Cabo de S. Vincente. In Algarbiæ regno.
units.tr: The Sacrum, ἱερὸν [hieron] for Ptolemy and Strabo, to whom also belongs the Κάλλιον [Kallion] of book i. Columella calls it the Sacred Mountain, and Eustathius the Head of Europe. Today it is Cabo de S. Vincente, in the kingdom of the Algarve.

units.la: Charidemo, χαρίδημος Ptolemæo ad Mare Mediterraneum: hodie, recte Clusio, Cabo de Gates; vel ut scribendum censet Florianus, Cabo de Agatas, ab Achate Lapide, qui ibi effoditur.
units.tr: The Charidemo, χαρίδημος [charidemos] in Ptolemy on the Mediterranean. Today it is Cabo de Gates, correctly according to Clusius, or, as Florianus thinks it should be written, Cabo de Agatas, from the agate stone that is dug there.

units.la: Scombraria, Σκομβραγία, Ptolemæo, Tarraconensis Hispaniæ; Plinio, Saturni, hodie Cabo de Palos, scribente Clusio.
units.tr: The Scombraria, Σκομβραγία [Skombragia], in Ptolemy, of Hispania Tarraconensis. Pliny calls it Saturni. Today it is Cabo de Palos, according to Clusius.

units.la: Ferraria, apud Pomponium Melam; Dianium, Ciceroni & Plinio; Ἀρημίσιον & ἡμερόσκοπεῖον Straboni; qui de eo sic scribit: Τῶν δ' ἐπὶ γνωμόνων, τὸ ἡμεροσκοπεῖον, ἔχον δὲ τὴν ἀκραν τῆς ἐφέσιας Ἀρτεμίδος ἱερὸν σφόδρα πυρώδες. Ἐρυμνὸν γὰρ ἐπὶ καὶ λιγυρόν, κάπητον δὲ ἐκ πλὴν τῆς παραλίου. καλεῖται δὲ Διάνιον, οἷον Ἀρτεμίσιον, ἔχον σιδήρεα ὕλην πολλήν. Ferraria igitur à Ferro.
units.tr: The Ferraria in Pomponius Mela; the Dianium in Cicero and Pliny; Strabo gives Ἀρημίσιον [Aremision] and ἡμερόσκοπεῖον [hemeroskopeion]. He writes of it thus: "Of the places on the gnomons, the hemeroskopeion, which has the headland of Ephesian Artemis, a sanctuary very fiery. For it is steep and clear, and bare except along the shore. It is called Dianium, as if Artemision, having much iron ore" [Τῶν δ' ἐπὶ γνωμόνων, τὸ ἡμεροσκοπεῖον, ἔχον δὲ τὴν ἀκραν τῆς ἐφέσιας Ἀρτεμίδος ἱερὸν σφόδρα πυρώδες. Ἐρυμνὸν γὰρ ἐπὶ καὶ λιγυρόν, κάπητον δὲ ἐκ πλὴν τῆς παραλίου. καλεῖται δὲ Διάνιον, οἷον Ἀρτεμίσιον, ἔχον σιδήρεα ὕλην πολλήν]. The Ferraria is therefore so named from iron (ferrum).

units.la: Tenebrium Τενέβριον Ptolemæo; hodie Cabo de Alfaques.
units.tr: The Tenebrium, Τενέβριον [Tenebrion], in Ptolemy. Today it is Cabo de Alfaques.

units.la: Lunarium, Λυνάριον Ptolemæo; Hodie Cabo de Vallis, ut putat Cl. Aretius; vel, ut Coquus Palafigel.
units.tr: The Lunarium, Λυνάριον [Lynarion], in Ptolemy. Today it is Cabo de Vallis, as Cl. Aretius thinks, or, according to Coquus, Palafigel.

units.la: Aphrodisium, Ἀφροδίσιον Ptolemæo: ad Pyrenæi radices; Πυρηναία Ἀφροδίτη, Straboni lib. iv. Pyrenæa Venus Plinio. Μαστλιωνὸν etiam appellatum scribit idem Strabo libro, quem nominavi. Hodie Cabo de Cruz.
units.tr: The Aphrodisium, Ἀφροδίσιον [Aphrodision], in Ptolemy, at the foot of the Pyrenees; Πυρηναία Ἀφροδίτη [Pyrenaia Aphrodite] in Strabo, book iv; Pyrenaea Venus in Pliny. The same Strabo, in the book I have named, writes that it was also called Μαστλιωνὸν [Mastlionon]. Today it is Cabo de Cruz.

units.la: In horum enumeratione nihil dixi de minorum gentium, præcipue, quæ ad Oceanum, Promontorijs, quæ quamvis ab Veteribus scriptoribus non nominentur, suis tamen hodie appellationibus non carent. Si quis Latus Hispaniæ, quod Septemtrioni obversum jacet, legat, anteaquam à Pyrenæis montibus ad Scythicum Promontorium, quod primo loco posui, perveniat, praetervehatur, necesse est illud, quod vulgo Cabo Matiaco, versus ortum ab ingressu Portus Bermeensis paullo amplius quatuor distans milliaribus. Scythico proxime succedit Cabo d' Aviles, sic dictum ab adjacente opido. Sequuntur Cabo de Brilo, de Ortegal, de Prior, quod Corunnae Portum ingredienti ad sinistram; tribus semimiliaribus Ferolio: mox Cabo de Belem, de Corrian, de Conte, confusa omnia cum Artabro vel Nerio Promontorio, quod Finis Terrae vulgo: inter quod & Olyssiponense sunt etiam Cabo de Phalselis, duobus Baiona milliaribus, & Cabo de Montego.
units.tr: In this enumeration I have said nothing of the smaller headlands, especially those on the Ocean. Although the ancient writers do not name them, they nonetheless have their own names today. If anyone reads the side of Spain that faces north, he must pass by, before he reaches the Scythicum promontory, which I placed first, the one commonly called Cabo Matiaco, a little more than four miles east of the entrance to the port of Bermeo. Next to the Scythicum comes Cabo d'Aviles, so called from the town beside it. Then follow Cabo de Brilo, de Ortegal, and de Prior, which lies on the left for one entering the harbour of Corunna, three half-miles from Ferrol. Then come Cabo de Belem, de Corrian, and de Conte, all confused with the Artabrum or the Nerio promontory, which is commonly called Finis Terrae. Between it and the Olisiponense are also Cabo de Phalselis, two miles from Bayonne, and Cabo de Montego.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CAP. VI.

units.la: Hispaniae Sinus & Portus.
units.tr: Harbours and Bays of Spain.

units.la: PARTES, quae Terra, absolvi: restant quae Aqua, ut sunt Sinus & Portus. Sinus Hispaniae celeberrimi sunt tres: omnes ad Mare Mediterraneum, Sucronensis, Illicitanus, Virgitanus.
units.tr: Having dealt with the parts that are land, what remains are the parts that are water, namely gulfs and harbours. There are three famous gulfs of Spain, all on the Mediterranean Sea: the Sucronensis, the Illicitanus, and the Virgitanus.

units.la: Omnium vastissimus est Sucronensis, magno satis ore Pelagus, inquit Mela, acci- piens; & quo magis penetratur, angustior. Hunc ab Illicitano separat Promontorium Artemisium, cujus antea facta mentio. Nomen illi ab Sucrone, vel Huvio (notus ille Plinio. Ptolemaeo & Silio Italico lib. iii.) nunc Xucar; vel opido (quod apud eundem Plinium & Strabonem) in sinistra fluminis ripa, quod hoc tempore Cullera.
units.tr: The Sucronensis is the largest of all. Pomponius Mela says that it takes in the sea through a fairly wide mouth, and that it narrows the farther one goes in. It is separated from the Illicitanus by the Artemisium promontory, which I mentioned earlier. It takes its name either from the river Sucro, or Hiberus (the river well known to Pliny, Ptolemy and Silius Italicus, book 3), now the Xucar, or from the town (mentioned by the same Pliny and by Strabo) on the left bank of the river, which is now called Cullera.

units.la: Mediae magnitudinis est Illicitanus, ab Illice opido, ut notat Pomponius Mela, quod Illici Plinio: Ἰλλικίας Ptolemaeo; hodie, ut quibusdam placet, Elche; ut aliis, Alicante; unde & Sinus nunc Puerto d' Alicante.
units.tr: The Illicitanus is of medium size. Pomponius Mela says it is named from the town of Illice, which Pliny calls Illici and Ptolemy Illicias [Ἰλλικίας]. Today, as some think, it is Elche; as others think, Alicante, whence the bay is now called Puerto d' Alicante.

units.la: Minimus est Virgitanus ab Opido, ut scribit Mela, Virgi, hodie Vera vel Bera. Corrupte apud Ptolemaeum, pro vel: nec emendatius apud Antoninum Vrci, ut nec apud Plinium Vrgi.
units.tr: The Virgitanus is the smallest, named by Mela from the town of Virgi, today Vera or Bera. Ptolemy has it corruptly, and Antoninus has no more accurate form, Vrci, just as Pliny has no better form, Vrgi.

units.la: Nominatur & Gaditanus Sinus Melae lib. iii. ab Gadibus. Hodie Baia de Cadix. Ταρρακωνίς etiam in κόλπῳ jacet Straboni; quem & hodie sinum habet Tarragona.
units.tr: Mela, book 3, also names the Gaditanus Sinus, from Gades. Today it is the Baia de Cadix. Strabo also places the Tarraconensis in a gulf [κόλπος], which the town of Tarragona still has as its bay.

units.la: Inter Portus, quos Hispania habet, primi est loci qui Magnus Veteribus, μέγας λιμήν Ptolemaeo inter Nerium & Scythicum Promontoria: Coruña hodie. Sunt & Annibalis Portus, apud Pomponium, Albor hodie in Algarbiae regno: Amanum, Plinio; nunc Fuentaribie, ut Villanovanus, vel Bermeo, ut Moralis censet: Gaditanus, Melae & Antonino, circa Gades: Tarraconensis, de quo Silius Italicus lib. xv. ——Tunc hospita Tarraco Baccho Confidunt portu, & secura gurgite clauso Stant Puppes, positusque labor, terrorque profundi:
units.tr: Among the harbours that Spain has, the first in rank is the one that the ancients called Magnus, and which Ptolemy calls the Great Harbour [μέγας λιμήν], between the Nerium and Scythicum promontories. Today it is Coruña. There are also the Annibalis Portus, in Pomponius, today Albor in the kingdom of the Algarve; the Amanum of Pliny, now Fuentaribie, as Villanovanus holds, or Bermeo, as Moralis thinks; the Gaditanus of Mela and Antoninus, near Gades; and the Tarraconensis, of which Silius Italicus writes in book 15: "Then the hospitable Tarraco trusts its harbour to Bacchus, and with the current enclosed and secure, the ships stand still, the toil is over, and the terror of the deep."

units.la: Veneris denique Melae nominatus ad radices Montis Pyrenaei. Sed de Sinibus Portubusque, eorumque latitudine & profunditate multis felicissime scribit Lucas Augustinus Rigarius in suo Navigationis Speculo, Chartis, quod ad Hispaniam, decima novemque sequentibus.
units.tr: Finally, there is the Veneris named by Mela, at the foot of the Pyrenean mountains. But Lucas Augustinus Rigarius writes most fortunately of the bays and harbours, and of their breadth and depth, in his Navigation Mirror, in the charts for Spain, the nineteenth and following ones.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CAP. VII.

units.la: Hispaniae Flumina, Lacus, Stagna, Fontes, &c.
units.tr: The Rivers, Lakes, Pools, Springs, etc. of Spain

units.la: SINVS Portusque demonstravi: Flumina, me vocant, & quae cum ijs censeri solita. Hispania multis irrigatur passim Fluviis. Sunt qui centum & quinquaginta numerant, & in ijs Pontes ultra septingentos, inter quos nobilissimi Segoviae & Alcantarae. Alij alijs sunt nobiliores.
units.tr: I have described the bays and harbours. Now the rivers come to my mind, together with the streams usually counted among them. Spain is watered everywhere by many rivers. Some count a hundred and fifty of them, and in these more than seven hundred bridges, among which the most famous are those at Segovia and Alcántara. Some rivers are more famous than others.

units.la: Iberus, ab Ibera opulentissima quondam Urbe, quae Elix hodie putatur, circa Karthaginem Veterem: in cujus agro P. Cornelius Scipio vicisse Poenos, totamque Hispaniam Imperio populi Romani adjecisse scribitur. Ἴβηρ Ptolemaeo & aliis Ebro hodie. Erumpit apud Cantabros (Provincia de Campo) ex Idubeda Montibus, duobus Fontibus, quorum dexter in Saltu Aucensi (Monte d' Oca) sinister ad Opidum Opidum, quod Incolis Fuentibre. Inde, magnis crescens Amnibus, primo Calaguritanis exceptus arvis (Callahorra) Iuliobrigam & Tubellam petit, Navarrae opida; Iuliamque & Celsam, Ponte quondam celebrem, inde Cæsar-Augustam adluit. Illinc digressus in Austrum, & mox versus Euronotum (nam quo minus, ut reliqui celebriores Hispaniae fluvii, ad Occasum tendat, facit Mons Idubeda) labitur per Laletaniæ populos, qui nunc Catalani, Dertusam opulentam urbem praeterlabitur, Postremo auctus Raia, Cadora, Tirone, Naierilla, Fruega, Letia, Melero, Ega, Arga (Aragus Antiquis) Aragonibus duobus (unde Aragonia nomen, Gallico) Salone, Congedo, (Cogedus Martiali) Cinga, (cujus, nomen retinentis, mentio apud Cæsarem de bello Civili, & Lucanum lib. I. & IV) Sicori (Segre vulgo, Dioni; notus Plinio, Cæsari, Vibio) alijsque, peracto quadringentorum sexaginta millium passuum cursu, in Mediterraneum, cognomine ipsi, Pelagus tam violenter duobus Ostijs (facta Alphacia Insula) ingreditur, ut quinquaginta passus in mare profusus dulcis hauriatur. Sequior ille, quam aliorum Hispaniæ Fluviorum, Iberi cursus, cujus facta mihi mentio, eleganter describitur, in Urna Marmorea, quæ in ædibus hortisque Cardinalis Cæsij servatur, in Vaticano; ubi inter alia: IAM. DATVS. EST. FINIS. VITÆ. IAM. FAVSSA. MALORVM VOBIS. QVAS. HABET. HOC. GNATAM. MATREMQ. SEPVLCHRVM LITTORE. PHOCAICO, PELAGI. VI. EXANIMATA ILLIC. VNDE. TAGVS. ET. NOBILE. FLVMEN. IBERV VORSVM. ORTVS. VORSVM. OCCASVS. FLVIT. ALTER. ET. ALTER STAGNA. SVB. OCEANI. TAGVS. ET. TYRRHENICA. IBERV
units.tr: The Iberus, named after Ibera, a once very wealthy city, which today is thought to be Elix, lies near Old Carthage. It is written that Publius Cornelius Scipio defeated the Carthaginians in its territory and added all of Spain to the empire of the Roman people. Ptolemy and others call it Ἴβηρ [Ibēr]; today it is the Ebro. It breaks out among the Cantabrians (Provincia de Campo) from the Idubeda mountains, from two springs, of which the right one is in the Aucensian forest (Monte d' Oca) and the left one near the town called Opidum, which the locals call Fuentibre. From there, swelling with large tributaries, it first passes through the fields of Calagurris (Callahorra), then heads for Iuliobriga and Tubella, towns of Navarre; it washes Iulia and Celsa, once famous for its bridge, and from there Caesaraugusta. Turning away from there to the south, and soon toward the southeast (for the Idubeda mountains keep it from running due west, as the other more famous rivers of Spain do), it flows through the peoples of Laletania, now Catalonia, and passes by the wealthy city of Dertosa. Finally, enlarged by the Raia, Cadora, Tirone, Naierilla, Fruega, Letia, Melero, Ega, Arga (Aragus among the ancients), Aragon rivers (from which the name Aragon derives, in the French form), Salone, Congedo (Cogedus in Martial), Cinga (whose name is still kept, and which Caesar mentions in his Civil War, and Lucan in books I and IV), Sicoris (Segre in common use, Dionis; known to Pliny, Caesar and Vibius) and others, after a course of four hundred and sixty thousand paces, it rushes into the Mediterranean, which bears its name, through two mouths (forming the island of Alphacia) so violently that fresh water can be drawn up fifty paces out into the sea. The course of the Ebro, which I have mentioned, is more gracefully described than that of other rivers of Spain, on a marble urn kept in the house and gardens of Cardinal Cesi in the Vatican, where, among other things, it reads: NOW THE END OF LIFE IS GIVEN TO YOU, NOW THE EVILS THAT SHE HAS ARE FAR FROM YOU. THE DAUGHTER AND MOTHER HAVE A TOMB ON THE PHOCAEAN SHORE, LIFELESS, TORN BY THE FORCE OF THE SEA. THERE THE TAGUS AND THE NOBLE RIVER EBRO FLOW, ONE RISING TOWARD THE EAST, THE OTHER TOWARD THE WEST. THE TAGUS AND EBRO FLOW BENEATH THE OCEAN AND THE TYRRHENIAN LAKES.

units.la: Et quæ sequuntur. Fluviolum etiam in Bætica, qui hodie Rio Tinto & Azeche, scribit Florianus à Campo appellatum quondam Iberum: unde nomen Iberi inditum canit Sex. Avienus: Iberus inde manat amnis; & locos Fœcundat unda. Plurimi ab ipso ferunt Dictos Iberos; non ab illo flumine, Quod inquietos Vasconès prælabitur.
units.tr: And what follows. Florian del Campo writes that a small river in Baetica, today the Rio Tinto and Azeche, was once called the Iberus; from this, Sextus Avienus sings, the name Iberi was given: The river Iberus flows from there, and its waters make the places fruitful. Most people say the Iberians were named from it, not from that river which flows past the restless Basques.

units.la: Durius maximus (concurrentibus in eum tot Amnibus, quos enumerare longum esset) Hispaniæ fluvius ex Idubeda, ubi nomen illi Sierra de Coçollo (apud Cantabros juxta Numantiam, ut notant Strabo & Plinius) scaturiens, Vectones ab Asturibus, Lusitanos ab Gallecis Veteribus disterminat. Turrem Sullanam (Tordesillas) Sarabrim, Mirandam, & alia opido contemplatus, decimoquinto fere infra Lamecam milliari, apud opidum Portugalliæ, quod Portus dicitur, rapidissimo cursu Occidentali se miscet Oceano. Δωρὶς, Ptolemæo; Δωρίας, Straboni; Δέρ, Appiano Alexandrino; Duero hodie.
units.tr: The Durius, the largest river of Spain (many streams flow into it, too many to list), rises in the Idubeda, where it is called the Sierra de Coçollo (among the Cantabrians near Numantia, as Strabo and Pliny note). It separates the Vettones from the Asturians and the Lusitanians from the ancient Gallaeci. It passes by Turris Sullana (Tordesillas), Zamora, Miranda and other towns, and about fifteen miles below Lamego, near the Portuguese town called Portus, it joins the western ocean with the swiftest current. Δωρὶς [Dōris] for Ptolemy, Δωρίας [Dōrias] for Strabo, Δέρ [Dér] for Appian of Alexandria; today the Duero.

units.la: Tagus (Τάγος Ptolemæo ceterisque) nascitur in altissimis Orospedæ jugis, stadijs quinquaginta ab Opido parvo, cui nomen Tragacet, haud procul ab Urbe Concia, nunc Cuenca, Per Carpentanos lapsus Toletum, regalem Urbem, petit, Pontequeque accepto, Talaveram, Augustobrigam, Alcantaram, aliasque Urbes non ignobiles adluens, mediam fere secans Portugalliam, ultra Olisipponam in Occiduum se exonerat Oceanum; Ostio bis millium, ut quidam notant, quinquaginta passuum latitudine. De Ostio Tagi scribit hæc Strabo lib. III. ὁ δὲ Τάγος καὶ τὸ πλάτος ἔχει τὰ ςόματος, ὑπὸ πε ςαδίων, καὶ τὸ βάθος μίχε, ὡς μυριαγωγοῖς ἀναπλεῖσθαι: & quæ ibi alia. Quod ad Ostij Latitudinem, si censenda illa inter duo Promontoria, quæ vulgo nominari solita dixi, Cabo de Roxent & Cabo de Spichel; Nostrates Nautæ, quibus hæc notissima, numerant decem fere Leucas; sin, qua maxima angustia, inter duo interiora Promontoriola, quorum Borealius S. Giaon, Nostris S. Gielis, Australius Trafuria, unius tantum & semis est Leucæ. Quod ad Altitudinem; ea quidem duobus pulvinis, quibus infaustum nomen Malechepos, est infesta, sed inter quos Profunditas satis fida, XII, ubi minima passuum. Adcolis hic fluvius hodieque Tajo, Lusitanis Tejo. An quod aliud habuerit olim nomen, disputat M. Antonius Del Rio Commentario in Senecæ Tragœdiam, Thyestem. Tagus auriferis Arenis copiosus reliquis Hispaniarum fluminibus, uti testantur Solinus in Polyhistore & Isidorus lib. XIII. Etymolog. cap. XXI, præferebatur. Eo respiciunt Ovidius XI. Metamorph. Quodque suo Tagus amne vehit, fluit ignibus Aurum.
units.tr: The Tagus (Τάγος [Tagos] for Ptolemy and the others) rises on the highest ridges of the Orospeda, fifty stadia from a small town called Tragacete, not far from the city of Concia, now Cuenca. Flowing through the Carpetani, it makes for Toledo, the royal city, and taking on bridges, it washes Talavera, Augustobriga, Alcántara and other towns not without distinction. Cutting through the middle of Portugal, it empties itself into the western ocean beyond Lisbon. Its mouth is, as some note, two miles across, or fifty paces wide. Strabo writes this about the mouth of the Tagus in book III: "The Tagus has a width at its mouth of about five stadia, and a depth so great that ships carrying ten thousand measures can sail up it," and more besides there. As for the width of the mouth: if it is measured between the two headlands I said are commonly named, Cabo de Roxent and Cabo de Spichel, our sailors, for whom these are best known, count nearly ten leagues. But if measured at its narrowest, between the two inner headlands, of which the northern is S. Giaon, called S. Gielis by our people, and the southern is Trafuria, it is only one and a half leagues. As for depth: the bar with the ill-omened name Malechepos is dangerous, but between the two sandbanks the depth is quite reliable, twelve passus at its least. The local people still call this river the Tajo, and the Lusitanians the Tejo. Whether it had some other name in the past, M. Antonius del Río discusses in his commentary on Seneca's tragedy Thyestes. The Tagus, rich in gold-bearing sand, was preferred to the other rivers of Spain, as Solinus in his Polyhistor and Isidore in book XIII of the Etymologies, chapter 21, attest. Ovid in book XI of the Metamorphoses refers to this: "And the gold which the Tagus carries in its waters flows with fire."

units.la: Iuvenalis Satyra IV: ——tanti tibi non sit opaci Omnis arena Tagi, quodque in mare volvitur Aurum.
units.tr: Juvenal, Satire IV: "Let all the sand of the shadowy Tagus, and the gold that rolls into the sea, not be worth so much to you."

units.la: Statius Papinius Silvarum lib. I: Huic Hermum, fulvoque Tagum decurrere limo.
units.tr: Statius Papinius, Silvae book I: "To him the Hermus and the Tagus, with its tawny mud, run down."

units.la: Claudianus denique (nam alios praetereo) libro I. in Rufinum: Non Tartesfiacis illam satiaret Arenis Tempesfas pretiosa Tagi; non flagna rubentis Aurea Pactoli: rotumque exhauserit Hermum, Ardebit majore siti.
units.tr: Claudian finally (for I pass over others), in book I against Rufinus: "The precious storm of the Tagus with its Tartessian sands would not satisfy her; nor the golden pools of the reddening Pactolus; and even if she drained the Hermus dry, she would burn with a greater thirst."

units.la: Auriferum hodieque, ut & alios multos Lusitaniae fluvios esse adfirmat apud Ortelium, vir fide dignus Emanuel Enricus. Piscium item Ostreorumque feracissimum, Gemmaque generantem memoriae prodit Pomponius Mela.
units.tr: Emmanuel Henricus, a trustworthy man, asserts that the Tagus is still gold-bearing today, as are many other rivers of Lusitania, as reported by Ortelius. Pomponius Mela also records that it is very rich in fish and oysters, and produces gems.

units.la: Anas, Ἀνας, Latinis Graecisque Scriptoribus satis notus, Originem (ubi Reydera vocari tradit Garibaius lib. III. cap. II. Hispanicae Historiae) habet ex vastis Stagnis, in Laminitano Agro, ut scribit Plinius lib. III. Naturalis histor. cap. I. qui hodie Campo de Montiel, circa Opidum, quod Hispanis Cagnamares vocatur. Oretanos praeterlapsus ad Metallinam, ubi Castra fuisse Vicelliana docent Antiquae ejus loci Inscriptiones, Terrae se penetralibus condere putatur (Nam ex Vulgi opinione magis, quam ex veritate haec esse, testis est apud Ortelium oculatus Georgius ab Austria, Praepositus Harlebeccensis) mox post aliquod leucas, quasi saepius nasci gaudens, inquit Plinius, ad Villarram eruptione facta, Augustam Emeritam, ubi longissimo Ponte lapideo transitur, Pacem Iuliam, & Austrum versus alias Urbes praetergressus ad Castrum Marinum in Oceanum evolvitur. Hispanis hodie vocatur Rio Guadiana, recepta ab Arabibus voce. Iis enim Guad Fluvius. Duo quondam habuit Ostia, quemadmodum notat Strabo lib. III. Quod verum fuisse arguunt satis cum Insulae adjacentes, tum Loca ad ingressum vadosa, & vix duorum trium vel passuum altitudinis.
units.tr: The Anas, Ἀνας [Anas], well known to Latin and Greek writers, has its source (where Garibay in book III, chapter 2 of his Spanish History says it is called Reydera) in vast marshes in the territory of Laminium, as Pliny writes in book III, chapter 1 of his Natural History. These are today the Campo de Montiel, near a town which the Spanish call Cagnamares. Flowing past the Oretani to Metallinum, where the ancient inscriptions of that place show there was a camp of the Vicelli, it is thought to hide itself in the depths of the earth (for that this is more the common opinion than the truth is attested by George of Austria, provost of Harlebeke, an eyewitness reported by Ortelius). Some miles later, as Pliny says, delighting to be born again and again, it breaks out again near Villarrica, passes Augusta Emerita, where it is crossed by a very long stone bridge, Pax Julia, and other cities to the south, and flows out into the ocean at Castrum Marinum. Today it is called the Rio Guadiana, the Arabic word having been adopted, for guad means river in their language. It once had two mouths, as Strabo notes in book III. That this was true is shown well enough both by the islands lying off it and by the places at its entrance that are shallow and only two or three passus deep.

units.la: Batis (Βαῖτις Ptolemaeo) oritur prope Castaonem ex Orospeda Monte, ut scribunt Strabo & Stephanus, qua parte Sierra d' Alcaraz nominatur. Ab Fonte in Occasum vergens Cordubam, tot claris nobilem ingeniis, aliaque Opida praeterlapsus, ad Hilpalim, illius orae caput, in Austrum declinans, Ostio satis amplo (unius enim Leucae est) sed quod Vadosius haud procul Gadibus in Atlanticum Mare se exonerat. Tribuit & huic duo ostia Strabo lib. III, inter utrumque locans Insulam, in qua Menesthei erat oraculum & Capionis Turris in Petra, quam circumcirca Pelagus alluebat. Alveus, qui Nebrissam & Astam praeterfluebat, oblimatus est; sic tamen, & illius vestigia hodie visantur cum Aestuariis atque Diorygibus manu factis, ut inquit Strabo, ad exportandas scaphis lintribusque fruges ex agris in vicinas urbes. Batis Isidoro lib. XIII. Originum, quasi βαθύς, quod humili solo decurrat. Batis nobilis Auro Veteribus est, & Olivetis. De Auro Aristoteles in Admirand. Audit. & Stephanus de Urbibus, ubi de Βυττα. De Olivetis Silius lib. III. ——genuit quos ubere ripa Palladio Batis velatus cornua ramo.
units.tr: Batis (Baitis [Βαῖτις] in Ptolemy) rises near Castaon, on the Orospeda mountain, as Strabo and Stephanus write, in the part called the Sierra d'Alcaraz. Flowing west from its source, it passes Cordoba, a city made famous by so many distinguished minds, and other towns. It then turns south toward Hispalis, the chief city of that coast, and discharges into the Atlantic Sea near Gades, through a mouth that is fairly wide (about a mile across) but shallow, and not far from Gades. Strabo, in book III, also gives this river two mouths, placing between them an island on which stood the oracle of Menestheus and the tower of Capion on a rock, washed on all sides by the sea. The channel that flowed past Nebrissa and Asta has silted up, yet its traces can still be seen today, together with the estuaries and canals made by hand, as Strabo says, for carrying crops from the fields to the neighboring cities by boats and barges. Isidore, in book XIII of the Origins, derives the name Batis, as if from [βαθύς], deep, because it runs over low ground. The Batis was famed among the ancients for its gold and its olives. On the gold, see Aristotle in the Wonderful Things Heard, and Stephanus in his work on cities, under Butta [Βυττα]. On the olives, see Silius, book III: "the Batis, whose fertile banks are wreathed with the olive bough of Pallas."

units.la: Martialis in Epigrammat. Batis olivifera crinem redimite corona, Aurea quae nitidis Vellera tingis aquis.
units.tr: Martial, in his Epigrams: "Batis, crowned with olive wreaths about your hair, you who dye the golden fleeces in your bright waters."

units.la: Statius Papinius lib. XI. Silvarum: Vnctis Batica provocas Tapetis Lucanum potes imputare terris.
units.tr: Statius Papinius, Silvae, book 11: "You vie with the Baetican rugs, drenched in oil; you could make Lucan's lands your own."

units.la: Et mox: Attollat refluos in Astra fontes Graio nobilior Melete Batis. Batim Mantua provocare noli.
units.tr: And soon after: "Let Melete, nobler than any Greek river, lift its waters back up to the stars. Do not try to outdo Batis with Mantua."

units.la: Nomen dedit, quam mediam secat, Baeticae Provinciae; testantur cum alii, tum Seneca in Medea Actus IV. Scena I. Nomenque Terris qui dedit Batis suis, Hesperia pulsans Maria languenti vado.
units.tr: It gave its name to the Province of Baetica, which it cuts through the middle. Other writers attest this, and so does Seneca in Medea, Act 4, Scene 1: "Batis, who gave its name to the lands of Spain, striking the Hesperian seas with its languid shallows."

units.la: Anas Recte, Languenti Vado. Nam quum spaciosum sit Ostium, languidior & minore cum impetu Oceanum ingreditur: adeo ut metus sit, ne aliquando non obturetur quidem nobilissimus Portus, sed difficiliorem præbeat grandioribus Navigiis adscensum; quum nonnullis locis trium-semis tantum passuum sit altitudinis. Straboni etiam & Pausaniæ Ταρτησὸς nominatur. Apud Strabonem Stesichorus, antiquus Poëta: Διότι ἓλκηθείη ἀγεδὸν ἀντιπέρων ϰλεινὰς Εὐβοίας Ταρτησσὸν πλαμὺ ἐπὶ ἡ πηγὰς ἀπείρονας δεγμοεί ζας.
units.tr: Anas reads "languenti vado" correctly. Since its mouth is wide, it enters the Ocean more sluggishly and with less force. So there is a fear that the famous harbour may someday be silted up altogether, or at least offer a harder passage to larger ships, since in some places it is only three and a half paces deep. Strabo and Pausanias also call it Tartessus. In Strabo, the ancient poet Stesichorus says: "Since ... the famous Euboea, Tartessus, the sea, from the boundless springs..." [Διότι ἓλκηθείη ἀγεδὸν ἀντιπέρων ϰλεινὰς Εὐβοίας Ταρτησσὸν πλαμὺ ἐπὶ ἡ πηγὰς ἀπείρονας δεγμοεί ζας.]

units.la: Stephano Πέρκης; apud quem levi fortean mutatione scribendum Κίρκης. Livius enim Circen ab Incolis nominari notat: quam appellationem aliquandiu retinuerunt, scribente Mario Nigro, Hispania potiti Afri; quibus tandem Guadalquivir, vel, ut alij scribunt Guadalchebir, tamquam Fluvius Magnus, fuit dictus. Ab hoc Fluvio Baticola apud Silium lib. i. Excipit præter alios Singulim, ut eum vocat Plinius, qui hodie Xenil vel Guadaxenil: Singilius Isidoro.
units.tr: Stephanus gives it as Πέρκης, though perhaps with a slight change it should be written Κίρκης. Livy notes that the inhabitants call it Circe. The Africans who held Spain kept this name for some time, as Marius Niger writes. Later it was called Guadalquivir, or as others write Guadalchebir, meaning "great river." Silius, book 1, calls the river Baticola. Besides others, the Singulis receives it, as Pliny calls it. It is today Xenil or Guadaxenil; Isidore calls it Singilis.

units.la: Minius Hispaniæ Terraconensis fluvius, ortum habens sexto supra Aras Sextianas, quibus hodie Lugo nomen, miliari ad opidum quod vulgo Castel-Verde, Portum Marinum secans, Pontemque Belsarium & Orensem Civitatem perlapsus, facto ad Valentiam cum Avia congressu, sex milliaria procurrens in Oceanum se præcipitat. Hunc Lusitaniæ maximum & Bαῖνις etiam appellari notat Strabo. Ptolemæo Μινίω. Apud Appianum incmendatius Νίμις legitur, pro Minis. Minio etiamnum dici, docent Tabulæ.
units.tr: Minius is a river of Hispania Tarraconensis. It rises six miles above the Sextian Altars, which are today called Lugo, and flows past the town commonly called Castel-Verde, cutting through the Marine Port and passing the Bridge of Belsarius and the city of Orense. Near Valentia it joins with the Avia, and running six miles further it plunges into the Ocean. Strabo notes that this is the largest river of Lusitania, and that it is also called Bainis. Ptolemy calls it Minius. Appian reads the less correct Nimis, for Minis. The tables show that it is still called Minio today.

units.la: Lethe Bæticæ fluvius. Veterem appellationem videntur illi reliquisse Arabes; qui, præposita in Fluviis nominandis usurpari solita voce, Guadalete dixerunt. Meminit fortean Silius Italicus lib. xvi: Et Theron potator Aqua sub nomine Lethes.
units.tr: Lethe is a river of Baetica. The Arabs seem to have kept its old name, though they used their customary prefix in naming rivers and called it Guadalete. Perhaps Silius Italicus, book 16, mentions it: "Theron, the drinker, in the water under the name of Lethe."

units.la: Mauris Bedalac nuncupatum fuisse, memoriæ prodit P. de Medina.
units.tr: Pedro de Medina records that the Moors called it Bedalac.

units.la: Turius Plinio; Turias Sallustio, PriscIano & Vibio; Duria Pomponio & alijs; hodie, mutuata ab Arabibus voce, Guadalabiar, quasi pura & Limpida Aqua. Habet amoenissimas Ripas, Rosis semper varioque florum genere coronatas. Vestitur utrimque Nemoribus ab Fonte (qui in Aragonia haud procul Opido Tervelo) ad Ostia usque, aspectu pulcherrimo gratissimoque; ubi Vitex, Platanus, Pinus, aliæque numquam carentes fronde Arbores: ut non immerito Claudianus in laude Serenæ: Floribus & roseis formosus Duria ripis.
units.tr: Pliny calls it Turius; Sallust, Priscian and Vibius call it Turias; Pomponius and others call it Duria. Today, with a word borrowed from the Arabs, it is Guadalabiar, as if meaning "pure and clear water." It has very pleasant banks, always crowned with roses and many kinds of flowers. Both sides are clothed with groves from its source (which lies in Aragon, not far from the town of Tervel) down to its mouths, a most beautiful and pleasing sight, where the vitex, plane, pine and other trees that never lose their leaves grow. So Claudian, in his praise of Serena, not undeservedly says: "Duria, beautiful with flowery and rosy banks."

units.la: Est item prope Minium versus Meridiem Limaea Plinio, Λιμαῖα Straboni, Λίμιῶ Ptolemæo, Limia Pomponio, Limas hodie. Λήθη quoque Straboni. Lethe Silio Italico lib. i, qui populos illi adlocat Gravios: Quiqve super Gravios lucentes volvit arenas Inferna populis referens oblivia Lethes.
units.tr: Near Minius, toward the south, is also Limaea, which Pliny names; Limaia in Strabo; Limius in Ptolemy; Limia in Pomponius; and today Limas. Strabo also gives Lethe. Silius Italicus, book 1, calls it Lethe, and places the Gravii peoples beside it: "And he who rolls his shining sands past the Gravii, bringing to the peoples the forgetfulness of the underworld, Lethe."

units.la: Quibus verbis Poëta ad oblivionis appellationem respicit. Sic enim Latinis etiam fuit dictus, ut videre est apud Plinium lib. iv. natur. histor. cap. xxii, Pomponium lib. iii, L. Florum Epitoma Liviana lib. lv. Oblivionis Nomen corruptum video apud Strabonem lib. iii. Εἰσ' ἄλλοι πλαμοὶ, καὶ μὴ τότας ὁ τῆς λήθης, ὃν τινες Λιμαῖαν, εἰ δὲ βλιῶνα καλῶσι. Legendum enim Ὀβλισιώνα. Aeminium etiam dictum fuisse scribit Plinius loco, quem paullo ante indicavi. Hunc Amnem designat Pluto apud Claudianum: ——sunt altera Lethes Flumina.
units.tr: With these words the poet alludes to the name "oblivion." For it was so called by the Latins as well, as can be seen in Pliny, Natural History, book 4, chapter 22; Pomponius, book 3; and Florus's Epitome of Livy, book 55. I find the name of Oblivion corrupted in Strabo, book 3: "There are other rivers, not these, [and] that of Lethe, which some call Limaea, but others call Blison." For it should be read Oblisiona [Ὀβλισιώνα]. Pliny, in the passage I cited a little earlier, writes that it was also called Aeminium. Pluto, in Claudian, points to this river: "There are other rivers of Lethe."

units.la: Sicoris (à quo Sicanos & Sicaniam nonnulli dirivant) Ibero se commiscet. Aureas defert arenas. Potus valde salubris. Σίκοςις Græcis. Meminerunt Plinius, Cæsar, Vibius, Dion, alij. Hodie Segre nuncupatur. Notat Beuterus Cathalonica lingua vocari Agua naval.
units.tr: The Sicoris (from which some derive Sicani and Sicania) mingles with the Ebro. It carries golden sands and is a very healthy drink. The Greeks call it Sikoris [Σίκοςις]. Pliny, Caesar, Vibius, Dion and others mention it. Today it is called Segre. Beuter notes that in the Catalan language it is called Agua naval.

units.la: Chalybs apud Vasconos oritur, cujus Aqua ad Ferri temperamentum plurimum valet; adeo ut Hispani non alia Arma, nisi quæ hujus liquore temperata, adprobent, Ab hoc Flumine Populos Chalybes Iustinus lib. xliv. ait appellatos.
units.tr: The Chalybs rises among the Vascones, and its water is very effective in tempering iron. So much so that the Spaniards approve no weapons except those tempered in its water. Justin, book 44, says that the Chalybes people were named after this river.

units.la: Apud Gallecos nascitur Aflura, Amnis non obscuri nominis: à quo Aflures nominati. Mentio apud Orosium lib. vi. cap. ii, Romanæ historiæ. Reliquos minorum gentium alijs explicandos relinquo.
units.tr: Among the Gallaeci rises the Aflura, a river of no obscure name, from which the Afluri are named. It is mentioned in Orosius, Roman History, book 6, chapter 2. I leave the remaining peoples of lesser note to be explained by others.

units.la: Prope opidum Beiarum Lacus est non utilis minus, quam admirabilis: qui & Turtures, Pisces subnigros & excellentes, gignit, & futuram pluviam turbinemque, ut scribit L. Marineus Siculus lib. 1. de reb. Hisp. magno aëris sonitu prænunciat: adeo ut ejus murmur quasi Tauri mugitus saepenumero ad duodeviginti millia passuum fuerit auditum. In summo Montis Stellæ cacumine Lacus quidam est, scribente Vasæo, in quo fragmenta navium subinde reperiuntur, quum tamen à mari plus xii leucis abest: quin quod exæstuet & Tempestates ibi audiantur, affirmare Incolas, quoties intumescit Mare, idem notat. In Cantabriæ Lacum fulmen decidisse, & repertas duodecim Securès, ait in Galbæ vita diligentissimus Scriptor Suetonius.
units.tr: Near the town of Beiarum there is a lake that is as remarkable as it is useful. It produces turtles and dark, excellent fish, and, as Lucius Marineus Siculus writes in book 1 of his work on the affairs of Spain, it announces coming rain and storms with a great sound in the air. Its murmur is often heard, like the bellowing of a bull, as far as eighteen thousand paces. On the summit of Mount Stella there is a certain lake, according to Vasaeus, in which fragments of ships are found from time to time, although it is more than twelve leagues from the sea. The locals also say that it swells and that storms are heard there whenever the sea rises. In the life of Galba, the most diligent writer Suetonius says that lightning struck a lake in Cantabria, and that twelve axes were found there.

units.la: Amænum Stagnum est apud Plinium lib. iii. natur. histor. cap. iii, haud procul Valentia: hodie Albufera.
units.tr: The "pleasant lake" is in Pliny, Natural History, book 3, chapter 3, not far from Valentia. Today it is called Albufera.

units.la: Fontes ibi in Montibus, Vallibus, Opidis, Pagis, privatis Ædificiis innumerabiles. Ager solus Xericij in Territorio Pacis Augustæ Fontes habet c Io Io. Sunt & nonnullis sua Miracula. Prope Orientem opidum Fons est nomine Burga in altum scaturiens, ita fervens ut in eo & ova coquantur, & Sues immersi facile depilentur. In opidulo Lusitaniæ Villa Nova Fons non solum oritur, sed & occidit. Oritur Kalendis Maii, & ad Kalendas usque Novembris aquas Villænovanis abunde adfundit; postea vero occultatur latetque hieme tota, & ad statutum tempus renascens adcolas revisit; quod quidem singulis annis fieri compertum scribitur. Octo leucis à Conimbrica visitur hodieque Fons Ferventia, vere admirabilis, quem Plinius in Catinensi Hispaniæ agro (Cadima hodie dicitur, haud procul à Teutagallensi Municipio) ponit: qui quidquid admotum fuerit, absorbet. Cujus rei factum periculum se præsente, adserit apud Io. Vasæum Henricus Cardinalis & Princeps coram Joanne Rege Lusitaniæ & ceteris Fratribus regiis, cum in Arborum truncis & ramis, tum in Iumento, quod Fonti admotum pede paullatim absorberi cœptum, ægre tandem ab famulis extractum est. Affirmat Plinius alterum juxta fluere, qui omnia respuat. Is hodie si exstat, saltem ignoratur. Supra Burgensem Civitatem ad passuum millia circiter viginti versus Orientem Pagus est nomine Boetius, sub altissima rupe positus, ex qua Fonticulus effluens in planiciem apud Pagum, cujus memini, descendit, duoque in Lacus ingressus tantam ijs virtutem vimque salubritatis infundit, ut quicumque fluxum sanguinis patiuntur, hac aqua loti è vestigio liberentur. In Bætica Provincia juxta opidum Antiqueram Fons potus Calculos dissolvit; à Petra, quam per urinam extrahit, cognominatus. In Cantabrica Fontes Tamaricos tres describit Plinius, qui singulis siccantur duodecies diebus, aliquando vicies, citra suspicionem ullam Aquæ, quum sit vicinus illis Fons, sine intermissione largus. Videndus Marineus Siculus lib. 1. de Reb. Hisp.
units.tr: There are countless springs there, on the mountains, in the valleys, in towns, in villages, and even in private houses. The field of Xerez alone, in the territory of Pax Augusta, has 1,100 springs. Some also have their own wonders. Near the eastern town there is a spring called Burga, gushing up so hot that eggs can be cooked in it and pigs dipped in it are easily depilated. In the small town of Villa Nova in Lusitania, a spring not only rises but also sinks. It rises on the first of May and pours out plenty of water for the people of Villa Nova until the Kalends of November. After that it disappears and stays hidden the whole winter, and then, reborn at the appointed time, it returns to the residents. This is recorded as happening every year. Eight leagues from Coimbra, the spring called Ferventia can still be seen today. It is wonderful in spring, and Pliny places it in the Catinensian district of Spain (today called Cadima, not far from the municipality of Teutagallensis). Whatever is put to it, it absorbs. Henry the Cardinal and Prince, in the presence of John, King of Lusitania, and his other royal brothers, asserts to John Vasaeus that a test of this was made in his presence, both with tree trunks and branches and with a beast of burden. When the animal's foot was placed against the spring, it began to be gradually drawn in, and was at last pulled out with difficulty by the servants. Pliny affirms that another spring flows nearby which rejects everything. If it still exists today, it is at least unknown. Above the city of Burgos, about twenty miles to the east, is a village called Boetius, set under a very high rock. From this rock a little spring flows out and descends into the plain near the village I mentioned, and it enters two lakes. It pours into them such a power and virtue of healing that whoever suffers from a flow of blood is immediately freed by bathing in this water. In the province of Baetica, near the town of Antiquera, there is a drinkable spring that dissolves stones in the bladder, and it is named after the stone it draws out in the urine. Pliny describes three Tamaric springs in Cantabria, which dry up every twelve days, sometimes every twenty, without any apparent cause, although a spring nearby flows without interruption and abundantly. Marineus Siculus, book 1 of his work on the affairs of Spain, should be consulted.

units.la: Quod ad Balnea, celebrat cum primis Marineus, quem dixi, quod in ripa Thormis Amnis. Huic addit, quod ad Opidum Beiaram; quæque apud Callæcos prope Minij fluminis ripam & Orensem urbem. Alia prætereo.
units.tr: As for baths, Marineus, whom I mentioned, celebrates those above all, such as the one on the bank of the river Thormis. To this he adds the one near the town of Beiara, and those among the Callaeci near the bank of the river Minius and the city of Orense. I pass over the others.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CAP. VIII.

units.la: Hispanorum Genius, Mores, Lingua.
units.tr: The Character, Customs and Language of the Spaniards

units.la: Regionem generatim perlustravi: Incolæ succedunt considerandi. Hic investigabo primo quis ipsis Genius & indoles; inde qui gubernentur vel Politice, vel Ecclesiastice. Quales hodie, depingere conabor: si, quis antiquis Hispaniæ incolis genius, quales vivendi cum domi, tum militiæ ritus fuerint, fideliter ex Veterum Scriptorum monimentis demonstraro.
units.tr: I have now surveyed the region in general terms; next come its inhabitants. Here I will first examine what their character and disposition are, and then how they are governed, both in civil and in ecclesiastical affairs. I will try to describe what they are like today. As for the character of the ancient inhabitants of Spain, and the manner of life both at home and in war, I will set these out faithfully from the records of the ancient writers.

units.la: Elatos jactantiæ animositate præposteros vocat Hispanos Iulius Firmicus. Astutam dicit hanc gentem Vopiscus; Velocem Corpore, Inquietam, avidam in res novas, Ingenijs præditam, quæ Feris propiora, quam Hominibus, Iustinus ex Trogo & Livius appellant. Brevi utebantur, scribente Diodoro, veste, ac nigra Hispani. Striges Hispanorum Vestes nominantur apud Isidorum lib. xix. cap.xxiii. Munditiei amantes faciunt Ptolemæus ii Quadripartit. & Diodorus: quorum tamen hic una in re eos Spurcitici notat, quod Vrina totum Corpus lavarent, Dentesque fricarent. Cantabris, alijsque qui confinales illis, hoc tribuit Strabo lib. iii: Ει μὴ πᾶς εἰσπ̣ τοὺς Δαγωγὶ ζῶ, τὰς ἀφωλοιδῆς ἐν δεξαμδρᾶς παλαιαμδρῷ, καὶ τὰς ἐδίνας σμηχομένας καὶ αὐτὰς καὶ τὰς γυναῖκας αὐτῶν, καθάπερ τὰς Καντάβρας φασὶ, καὶ τὰς ὀμέρας αὐτῆς.
units.tr: Julius Firmicus calls the Spaniards conceited and foolish, puffed up with the arrogance of pride. Vopiscus calls this people crafty. Justin, following Trogus, and Livy describe them as swift of body, restless, eager for revolution, gifted in intellect, and nearer to wild beasts than to men. According to Diodorus, the Spaniards wore short black clothes. Their garments are called striges in Isidore, book 19, chapter 23. Ptolemy in his Quadripartitum and Diodorus make them lovers of cleanliness, though Diodorus notes them for one filthy habit in this respect: they washed their whole body with urine and scrubbed their teeth with it. Strabo, in book 3, ascribes this practice to the Cantabrians and their neighbours: they rinse their mouths and teeth with urine, which they collect in tubs, and they say the Cantabrians and their women do the same [ὅπερ ... τὰς ὀδόντας σμηχομένας ... καθάπερ τοὺς Καντάβρους φασί].

units.la: Celtiberis adscribit Catullus, his versibus: Nunc Celtiber in Celtiberia terra Quod quisque minxit, hoc sibi solet mane Dentem atque rufam defricare gingivam.
units.tr: Catullus ascribes the same habit to the Celtiberians, in these verses: "Now the Celtiberian in Celtiberian land cleans his teeth and reddish gums each morning with whatever he has passed."

units.la: Spurcissimum hunc ritum appellat Apuleius Apologia 1, Quem multo aquius erat spurcissimo ritu Hiberorum, ut ait Catullus ——sua sibi urina Dentem atque russam pumicare gingivam.
units.tr: Apuleius, in his Apology 1, calls this a most filthy custom: "It would have been much fairer to use the most filthy custom of the Iberians," as Catullus says, "to scour his teeth and reddish gums with his own urine."

units.la: Virorum Mulierumque communem fuisse ad Robur exercendum utilitatem, memoriae prodit Strabo: consuevisse autem Mulieres Rem Rusticam exercere; Puerperasque Maritis suis in Lecto conlocatis ministerium exhibere. Adfluenter Carnibus variis nutriri solitos, Potum ex Melle conficere, Vinum emtum bibere, apud Diodorum legimus. Potum ex Frumento confectum largiuntur Florus, Plinius, qui Celiam & Cerium nominat, & Dioscorides, qui Curmi dicitur. Hispanos certe Gentibus inebriari solitis connumerat Athenaeus. Duram omnibus & adstrictam Parsimoniam tribuit ex Trogo Iustinus: & quamvis ditissimi, ut videre est apud Athenaeum, Aquam bibebant, Soli Cibum capiebant, ut sumtuose incederent. 10 Neque in festos dies ullus Epularum adparatus, teste Trogo. Erucae silvestris semine uti solitos Sinapi loco, tradit Dioscorides. Plinius scribit eos aevo suo Glandem in secundis Mensis habuisse; quin ex Glandium farina Panem etiam confecisse, docet Strabo. Humi eos decumbere solitos, idem Plinius testatur. Aqua calida lavari post Secundum Bellum Punicum ab Romanis didicere. Quid, ait, quem saepe dixi, Plinius lib. xxxv. cap. xiv, non in Hispania ex Terra Parietes, quos appellant fornaceos, quoniam fornacum modo circumdati utrimque duabus Tabulis infarciuntur versus, quam instruuntur, aevi durant, incorrupti Imbribus, Ventis, Ignibus, omnique cemento firmiores? Gens, ut hodie, sic olim belli avida. Hinc audax Tibullo lib. iv; ferocissima, jugiqueimpatiens, Floro; Viribus corporis Romanos superans Vegetio: Prodiga gens animi, & properare facillima mortem: Namque ubi transcendit florentes viribus annos, Impatiens aevi spernis novisse senectam, Et fati modus in dextra est, Silio Italico.
units.tr: Strabo records that the exercise of men and women alike was useful for building strength, and that the women customarily did country work and waited upon their husbands when they had given birth, laying them in bed. We read in Diodorus that they were in the habit of being fed plentifully on various meats, of making a drink from honey, and of buying wine to drink. Florus and Pliny, who names it celia and ceria, and Dioscorides, who calls it curmi, mention a drink made from wheat. Athenaeus certainly counts the Spaniards among the peoples accustomed to get drunk. Justin, following Trogus, ascribes to them a hard and strict thrift of all kinds; and although they were very rich, as may be seen in Athenaeus, they drank water and ate only what the sun had cooked, so that they could walk about in splendour. 10 According to Trogus, they had no elaborate preparations for banquets even on feast days. Dioscorides reports that they used the seed of wild rocket in place of mustard. Pliny writes that in his own time they regarded acorns as a delicacy at table; and Strabo teaches that they even made bread from acorn flour. Pliny also attests that they were accustomed to lie down on the ground. The Romans learned to bathe in warm water from the Spaniards after the Second Punic War. "What," says Pliny, whom I have often cited, in book 35, chapter 14, "are those walls made of earth, which they call fornaceos, since they are surrounded on both sides like furnaces with two boards and packed in, and when built they last for ages, uncorrupted by rain, wind and fire, and firmer than any mortar?" The people, now as then, were eager for war. Hence Tibullus in book 4 calls them audax (bold); Florus calls them ferocissima, jugiqueimpatiens (most fierce and always impatient of rule); Vegetius says they surpass the Romans in bodily strength; and Silius Italicus says: "A people prodigal of spirit, most ready to hasten to death. For when they pass their years of flourishing strength, impatient of life, you scorn to know old age, and the limit of their fate lies in their own right hand."

units.la: Corpora ad inediam & laborem, Animos ad mortem paratos ijs fuisse, notant Valerius Maximus & Iustinus. Impacatos vocat Iberos Virgilius in Georgicis; quod Abactores essent, ut interpretatur Servius: quod in latrociniis praeponderarent, ut Iunius Philargyrius; quod supra modum sua Virtute Veteres Romanos inquietarent, ut alij. Bellum, quam Ocium malebant: si extraneus deesset, domi Hostem quaerebant, Trogo scribente. In bello non Equites modo, sed & Pedites robore manorum tolerantia ceteris habebant excellentiores. Praelia adgrediebantur Carminibus, eodem teste. Respicit eo Silius, quum inquit: —— ritu jam moris Iberi Carmina pulsata fundentem barbara cetra.
units.tr: Valerius Maximus and Justin note that they were prepared for hunger and toil in body and for death in spirit. Virgil in the Georgics calls the Iberians impacatos (unappeased); Servius explains this as meaning that they were robbers; Junius Philargyrius that they were more prominent in brigandage; others that they harassed the ancient Romans beyond measure by their valour. Trogus writes that they preferred war to peace: if no foreign enemy was at hand, they looked for an enemy at home. In war they excelled others, not only their cavalry but also their infantry, in the strength and endurance of their hands. They used to join battle with songs, according to the same writer. Silius alludes to this when he says: "...in the manner of the Iberians, who now pour out barbarous songs while beating their shields."

units.la: Duobus Gladijs fulti, quum equestri certamine superiores evasissent, ex equis, si eundem Diodorum audiamus, desiliebant, Peditesque pugna juvabant. Gladij, ut ex Livio Polybioque constat, brevitate agiles erant, ad propiorem pugnam habiles; cum Mucronibus, ita ut punctim, non caesim, ferirent. Machaeram etiam Hispanicam nominat Seneca de Beneficijs libro quinto circa finem. Eam sic describit Polybius lib. vi. ἅμα ἡ τῶν Ιυρεῶν Μάχαιραν, πιστῶς δὲ τὴν δεξιὸν φέρει μηρὸν: καλῶς δ' αὐτῷ ἐγ-ἐχλῶ. ἐχὶ δ' αὐτῆ κινυμα Διάφορον, ἔ καὶ φορὸν ἐξ ἀμφοῖν τὴν μηρὸν βιαιον, Διὰ τὸ τὸν ὀσ-λίσχον αὐτῆς ἰσχυρὸν καὶ μόνιμον εἶναι. Gaeis usos fuisse, docet, Athenaeus; Galeas tulisse aereas, Cruribusque Ocreas ex pilis factas advolvisse, Diodorus; levi Armatura, Peltis, Iaculis, Fundis uti consuevisse, Strabo; Linteis purpura praetextis & candidissimis Tunicis indutos praelia inisse, Polybius. Et quamvis tragicis Stolis atque variis amicti Tunicis, etiam ad pedes demissis in publicum prodirent, ut auctor est Athenaeus, nihilo tamen ad bella gerenda erant ignaviores ac minus fortes. Iuvenibus nibus in bellum euntibus Parentum facta memorabant Matres, ut notat in Historiis Sallustius. Tot Columellas circa defunctorum Sepulcra statuebant, quot quisquis hostes occiderat: testis Aristoteles lib. vii. Politicor. Proclive eis fuisse transnare flumina, ait Cæsar; isque omnibus in more positum, addit, sine Utribus ad exercitum non ire. Plurimis militares Equos & Arma ipsorum sanguine cariora fuisse, tradit ex Trogo Iustinus. In Hostes crudeles fuisse; erga Advenas humanos & hospitales, ait Diodorus. Regibus se devovere, postque eos vitam acerbam censere, prodit ex Sallustio Servius ad x Georgic. Tantus ipsis innatus legitur apud Strabonem Amor fuisse Libertatis, ut bello Cantabrico Matres Liberos suos necarint, ne in hostium manus pervenirent: Puer, mandatu Patris, Parentes Fratresque omnes captos, ferrum nactus, interfecerit: Mulier quædam una secum vinculis mancipatos obtruncarit. Quosdam captos & in crucem suffixos Pæana cecinisse, tradunt apud eumdem Strabonem incerti: stupendus hic Mortis contemtus: Quid jam dicam de insigni ipsorum Fortitudine? Celebratur apud Iustinum Servi Bello Punico Patientia, qui ultus Dominum, inter Tormenta risu exsultavit, serenaque lætitia crudelitatem torquentium vicit. Fidelitatem Veterum Hispanorum commendat, quod custodijs ipsorum, cum gladijs insectantium se, fuerit usus Cæsar, teste Suetonio in ejus vita cap. xxcvi. Hispanum & illud, inquit Strabo, ut de more Toxicum adponeretur, ex olere, quod Apio adsimile, confectum; nullum adferens dolorem: ut si quid imminceret invitis, in promtu illud haberent. Hoc item eorumdem erat, ut sese proijs, quibus conciliarentur, immolarent, morteque devoverent. Quo modo autem Mortuos suos habuerint, docet Silius Italicus lib. xiii:
units.tr: Armed with two swords, when they had won in a cavalry contest, they dismounted, if we may trust the same Diodorus, and aided the infantry in the fighting. The swords, as is clear from Livy and Polybius, were light and handy for close combat; they had points and were used to thrust, not to hack. Seneca, in the fifth book of De Beneficiis near the end, also names the Spanish machaera (sword). Polybius describes it in book 6: they carry the Iberian sword at the right thigh, and it cuts on either side with a strong and unbroken blade [τὴν Ἰβηρικὴν μάχαιραν ... τὴν δεξιὰν μηρὸν]. Athenaeus teaches that they used the gaesum (javelin); Diodorus that they wore bronze helmets and drew up greaves made of hair on their legs; Strabo that they were accustomed to light armour, shields, javelins and slings; Polybius that they went into battle clad in linen edged with purple and in shining white tunics. And although they went out in public in tragic robes and varied tunics that reached down to their feet, as Athenaeus reports, they were none the less no cowards or weaklings in waging war. When young men went off to war, mothers reminded them of their fathers' deeds, as Sallust notes in his Histories. They set up as many columns around the graves of the dead as the number of enemies each man had killed; Aristotle attests this in book 7 of the Politics. Caesar says it was easy for them to swim rivers, and adds that it was the custom for all of them not to go to the army without inflated skins. Justin, following Trogus, relates that most of them held their military horses and arms dearer than their own blood. They were cruel to enemies, but humane and hospitable to strangers, says Diodorus. Servius, on Georgics 10, records from Sallust that they devoted themselves to their kings and afterwards considered life bitter. So great was the love of liberty innate in them, as Strabo reads, that in the Cantabrian war mothers killed their own children so that they would not fall into enemy hands; a boy, at his father's command, got a sword and killed all his captured parents and brothers; a certain woman slew with her own hand the men who had been bound in chains alongside her. Some writers, quoted by the same Strabo, say that some who were captured and fixed to a cross sang a paean: a remarkable contempt for death. Why should I now say more about their outstanding courage? Justin celebrates the patience of the slave in the Second Punic War, who, having avenged his master, leapt for joy amid the torments with a laugh, and by his serene cheerfulness overcame the cruelty of his torturers. Suetonius, in his life of Caesar, chapter 36, commends the loyalty of the old Spaniards, since Caesar used their guards when they pursued him with swords. Strabo adds that the Spaniards also had this custom: that poison, should it be served as usual, was made from a herb like parsley, causing no pain, so that if anything threatened against their will, they would have it ready to hand. It was also a custom of the same people to sacrifice themselves to those by whom they were befriended, and to devote themselves to death. How they treated their dead, Silius Italicus shows in book 13:

units.la: Ælianus hoc peculiariter de Barcæis scribit; & tantummodo de ijs, qui in bello perierant: qui autem ex morbo, igne cremari solitos addit. Sed Hispanorum Veterum mores pluribus delineant Diodorus Siculus lib. v. Strabo lib. iii, alijque antiqui Scriptores.
units.tr: Aelian writes this about the Barcaeans in particular, and only about those who had died in war; he adds that those who died of disease were customarily cremated with fire. But the customs of the ancient Spaniards are described at greater length by Diodorus Siculus in book 5, by Strabo in book 3, and by other ancient writers.

units.la: Quales hodie, dicam, ipsis verba præeuntibus. Hispanis Natura calida est & sicca: Color subobscurus: cui juvando Feminæ Collyrio plurimum ex Cerusla Minioque utuntur: duriora & bene compacta Membra. Magna Mortales omnes Superstitione superant: ad Cerimonias, Adulationes, amplos Titulos Populis alijs duces. Animi concepta dexteritate singulari tacendo, simulando, dissimulandoque celare norunt. Gravitatem servant cum adfectata quadam Severitate: quæ facit, ut odium sustineant Nationum omnium, gravissimum, quemadmodum ipse Mariana prædicat, atque individuum magnorum Imperiorum adseclam. Mulieres non admodum fœcundæ paucos pariunt: priscas Romanas æmulantes Vino plurimum abstinent: raro se conspiciendas præbent; & Nobiles quidem domo non egrediuntur, nisi comitante satis grandi Famulorum præcedentium, sequentiumque Ancillarum numero. In Conviviis domi quidem frugales, sobrij, paucisque contenti; foris Ciborum, præsertim delicatiorum, adpetentiores. Advenas inhumaniter excipiunt. Apud exteros alter alterum colit, veneratur, laudat, extollit; Nobilitatem, Plebeio etiam, si quo potest modo, concilians. Iustitiæ cultores maximi: Summis, Mediis, Imis æquale Ius administratur. Facit Magistratuum industria, ut pauca, imo nulla ibi sint latrocinia. Plerorum manus purae ab cædibus, aliisque flagitijs. Nemini impune est, qui vel Sacro-sanctas Leges, vel quemcumque, etiam minimi loci, violare fuerit ausus. Inquieti Magna semper moliuntur. Pulsis intestinis Hostibus, profligatisque Saracenis, pulcherrimas Orbis Terrarum partes suis Regibus adquirere student. Ubi duo tresve convenerint, cujuscumque loci & conditionis, de Rep. gravissimisque Rebus differunt; ad enervandas Hostium vires vias quærunt, Strategemata excogitant, mille Machinas fabricant; suisque Ducibus, si quid utiliter inventum, aperiunt. In Castris Famis, Sitis, Laborum patientissimi. In acie conflictuque majori illis Ars, quam Ferocitas. Levi corpore, Levibusque Armis induti Hostem facile sequuntur, facileque, quum opus, fuga sibi consulunt; nusquam non, numquam non militaribus operam dantes Meditationibus: concessaque unis Batavis hodie contra se non inlubenter palma, reliquos omnes
units.tr: As for what they are like today, I shall speak, following the words that go before. The Spanish nature is hot and dry; their complexion is somewhat dark, and to improve it the women use a great deal of eye-salve made from white lead and red lead; their limbs are harder and well put together. All mortals surpass them in superstition: they are fond of ceremonies, flattery, and grand titles, and they call the leaders of other peoples dukes. Having a singular dexterity of mind, they know how to conceal their feelings by silence, simulation and dissimulation. They keep a dignity mixed with a certain studied severity, which makes them suffer the hatred of all nations, the gravest kind, as Mariana himself declares, and the inseparable companion of great empires. Their women, not very fertile, bear few children; imitating the ancient Roman women, they abstain greatly from wine; they seldom show themselves in public; and the nobles do not go out of doors unless accompanied by a fairly large number of servants going before and maidservants following. At home at banquets they are frugal, sober and content with little; abroad they are more eager for food, especially for the more delicate kinds. They receive strangers inhumanly. Among foreigners each one cultivates, honours, praises and exalts the other, and wins over the nobility, even the commoners, in whatever way he can. They are the greatest cultivators of justice: the same law is administered to the highest, middle and lowest alike. Through the diligence of the magistrates there are few or rather no robberies there. Most of them have hands clean of murder and other crimes. No one goes unpunished who has dared to violate the sacred laws or anyone at all, even of the lowest rank. The restless always plan great things. Having driven out the internal enemies and routed the Saracens, they strive to acquire for their kings the most beautiful parts of the world. When two or three meet, of whatever place or condition, they debate about the commonwealth and the most serious matters; they seek ways of weakening the strength of their enemies, devise stratagems, and fabricate a thousand machines; and if they have discovered something useful, they reveal it to their leaders. In camp they are most patient of hunger, thirst and labour. In the line of battle and in larger engagements they rely more on skill than on fierceness. Clad in light bodies and light armour, they easily follow the enemy and easily, when necessary, look to their safety by flight; they are always and everywhere devoted to military meditations. Today the Dutch alone, not unwillingly, have been granted the palm over them in this respect; but all the other peoples, they boast, they surpass by far and in many steps in such matters, and not without reason. Gifted in intellect, they learn unhappily; the half-learned think themselves learned. They are very fond of the subtleties of the sophists. In the academies they take more pleasure in speaking Spanish than Latin, mixing in not a few words of the Moors.

units.la: Populos in his talibus longe multisque gradibus superare se, gloriantur, non frustra. Felices Ingenio, infeliciter discunt: semidocti Doctos se censent. Sophistarum Astus plus satis amant. In Academijs Hispanice magis, quam Latine loqui gaudent; voces etiam Maurorum non paucas admiscentes. Suos Fœtus Ingeniique monimenta ad posteritatem raro, rarius ad Exteros, ob Linguæ defectum, producunt. Fuerunt tamen, suntque hodie non vulgariter docti, qui præclara eruditione lectissimisque Scriptis patriam inlustrarunt, varijsque Operibus apud remotissimos etiam clariorem fecerunt. Si Theologi postulantur: prodibunt Vigilantius, Presbyter Barcinonensis; Aquilius Severus; Prudentius, Episcopus Armentiæ; Olius Cordubensis; Avitus Presbyter; Marcianus, Episcopus item Barcinonensis; Paullus Orosius; Pacianus, ejusque filius Dexter; Audentius; Isidorus, Apocalypseos Interpres; Iustinianus, Valentinæ Ecclesiæ Antistes; Leander, Hispalensis Episcopus; Martinus, Præsul Mandovensis; Fulgentius, Episcopus Karthaginensis; Eladius, Archiepiscopus Toletanus; Isidorus, Episcopus Hispalensis; Ioannes, Gerundensis Præsul; Eutropius, Valentinus Antistes; Franciscus Ximenes, Cardinalis & Archiepiscopus Toletanus, Academiæ Complutensis pater, qui variis Linguis Sacra Biblia, Complutensium appellatione notissima, curavit imprimenda; & alij: hisque connumerandi, quamvis adventitiæ stirpis, Paullus Episcopus Burgensis, Iudæus; Rabbi Aben-Ezra; Rabbi Moyses; Rabbi David Chimhi; Moses Cordubensis; Rabbi Camora. Si Canonici Iuris periti; Bernardus Compostellanus; Raimundus de Pennya Forti; Hugo Barcinonensis. Si Iurisconsulti: Calixtus III. Pontifex Maximus; Fortunius Garcia; Gomesfius; Didacus Covarruvias; silentioque minime prætereundus Antonius Augustinus, domo Cæsar-augustanus, XII-vir Romæ S.Iit. Iudicandis, inde vero ex Allifano & Ilerdensi Episcopo, Tarraconensis Archiepiscopus, Vir Romanarum Antiquitatum & melioris litteraturæ peritissimus, qui septuagenarius obiit anno MDXCVI pridie Kalendas Iunij. Si Medici licet non patrij, sed infitiij: aderunt Abincenna, Averrois, Rasis Almançor, Messahallah. Si Historici: Trogus Pompeius; Iustinus; & qui non hoc ævo, passim hoc libro à me laudati? Si Philosophi; L. Annæus Seneca; ejusque filij, Seneca Novatus, & Mela; L. Iunius Moderatus Columella; C. Iulius Hyginus; Sotion; Ioannes Vives Valentinus. Si Mathematici: Pomponius Mela; Abrahamus; Cacutius; Alphonsus Rex Castellæ, cujus sunt Tabulæ, quæ dicuntur Alphonsinæ; Henricus, Infans Portugalliæ; Henricus, Marchio Villenensis; Arnoldus Villanovanus, ejusque Discipulus Raimundus Lullius. Si Oratores: præter Senecam, Porcius Latro & M. Fabius Quintilianus. Si denique Poëtæ in medium producendi: sistent se Sextilius Hena, LL. Annæi Seneca & Lucanus, Patrucles; M. Valerius Martialis; Rufus Festus Avienus, Aurelius Prudentius; Damasus, Pontifex Maximus; Iuvencus, Arator; Cælius Sedulius. Iuniores, ne tædium pariam, omitto. De Poëtis hoc addam; Cordubenses, Ciceronem scriptum reliquisse, ætate ipsius pingue quid redolere solitos.
units.tr: They boast that in such matters they far surpass other peoples, and not without reason. They are fortunate in their natural talent, yet they learn unfortunately: the half-learned consider themselves learned. They love the tricks of the sophists far too much. In their academies they take more pleasure in speaking Spanish than Latin, mixing in not a few words of the Moors. They rarely bring their offspring and monuments of their talent before posterity, and more rarely before foreigners, because of their lack of language. Yet there have been, and there are today, men of no ordinary learning, who have distinguished their country by outstanding erudition and most select writings, and by various works have made it more famous even among the most remote peoples. If theologians are wanted, there will come forward: Vigilantius, presbyter of Barcelona; Aquilius Severus; Prudentius, bishop of Armentia; Olius of Córdoba; Avitus, presbyter; Marcianus, likewise bishop of Barcelona; Paulus Orosius; Pacianus and his son Dexter; Audentius; Isidore, interpreter of the Apocalypse; Justinian, bishop of the Church of Valencia; Leander, bishop of Seville; Martinus, prelate of Mandovo; Fulgentius, bishop of Carthage; Eladius, archbishop of Toledo; Isidore, bishop of Seville; John, prelate of Gerona; Eutropius, bishop of Valencia; Francisco Ximenes, cardinal and archbishop of Toledo, father of the Academy of Alcalá, who had the Holy Bibles printed in several languages, known by the name of the Complutensian Polyglot; and others. To these may be added, although of foreign stock, Paulus, bishop of Burgos, a Jew; Rabbi Aben Ezra; Rabbi Moses; Rabbi David Kimchi; Moses of Córdoba; Rabbi Camora. If canon lawyers are wanted: Bernard of Compostela; Raymond of Peñafort; Hugo of Barcelona. If jurists: Pope Callixtus III; Fortunius García; Gomesius; Diego Covarrubias; and not to be passed over in silence, Antonio Agustín, a native of Zaragoza, one of the Twelve Men in Rome for judging, then bishop of Alife and Lleida, and archbishop of Tarragona, a man most skilled in Roman antiquities and in better literature, who died at the age of seventy, on 31 May 1586. If physicians, though not native but foreign: there will be Avicenna, Averroes, Rhazes, Almansor, Masallah. If historians: Trogus Pompeius; Justin; and those who, though not of this age, I have praised here and there in this book? If philosophers: Lucius Annaeus Seneca; his sons, Novatus Seneca and Mela; Lucius Junius Moderatus Columella; Gaius Julius Hyginus; Sotion; Juan Vives of Valencia. If mathematicians: Pomponius Mela; Abraham; Cacutius; Alfonso, King of Castile, whose are the tables called Alphonsine; Henry, Infante of Portugal; Henry, Marquis of Villena; Arnold of Villanova, and his disciple Raymond Lull. If orators: besides Seneca, Porcius Latro and Marcus Fabius Quintilian. Finally, if poets are to be brought forward: there will present themselves Sextilius Hena, Lucius Annaeus Seneca and Lucan, Patrocles; Marcus Valerius Martialis; Rufus Festus Avienus, Aurelius Prudentius; Damasus, Pope; Juvencus, Arator; Caelius Sedulius. I omit the later writers, lest I weary the reader. About the poets I will add this: the people of Córdoba are said to have left behind Cicero's writing, which they used to say smelled somewhat of fat from their own time.

units.la: Sed de Moribus hæc sufficiant: Linguam Antiquis Hispaniæ Cultoribus fuisse eam, qua hodieque utuntur Cantabri Vasconesque (A quibus Vazquense vulgo dicitur) est Coniectura. Hos namque scribunt, qui penitissima Hispanorum Sacraria sunt ingressi, & Linguam & Mores in tot rerum vicissitudinibus, mordicus, maximam partem, retinuisse: Reliquos autem Idioma illud, ad Turrim etiam Babylonicam natum, cum per variorum Populorum Commercia, tum per Karthaginiensium, præcipue vero Romanorum & Irruptiones & Victorias, non quidem mutasse, sed omnino rejecisse, inque locum ejus Latinam, Victorum suorum Linguam, corruptam varieque inflexam suffecisse: ut Hispanis fere omnibus hodie communis sit ea Lingua, quæ Vulgar vulgo, quibusdam Espanola, multis etiam Castellana nuncupatur. Vulgaris quidem & Hispana, quod universum per totam fere Hispaniam intelligatur; sedem nihilominus propriam habens in Regnis Aragoniæ, Murciæ, Andaluziæ, Castellæ, Novæ & Veteris, Legionis, inque pleraque Portugallia. Castellana vero ab Castella, cujus Incolæ Linguam hanc purissime loqui perhibentur. Alij tamen illud negant, gloriam ejus rei, variis adductis rationibus, nunc Legioni, nunc Aragoniæ tribuentes. Sunt qui Romanciam appellant, quod fons illi ab Lingua Romana vel Latina degenerante. Exemplum nobis sit præter Orationem Dominicam (quæ perpetuo reliquorum omnium Idiomatum suis locis specimina suppedi-
units.tr: But let these remarks on customs suffice. That the language of the ancient cultivators of Spain was the one still used today by the Cantabrians and Basques (from whom it is commonly called Vascuence) is a conjecture. For those who have entered the most hidden sanctuaries of Spain write that these people have retained their language and customs, through so many changes of fortune, most stubbornly and for the greater part. As for the rest, that idiom, which came into being even at the Tower of Babel, was not indeed changed but utterly rejected, both through the dealings of various peoples and through the invasions and victories of the Carthaginians, and above all of the Romans; and in its place there came Latin, the language of their conquerors, corrupted and variously inflected; so that this language, called Vulgar by some, Espanola by others, and by many also Castellana, is today common to nearly all Spaniards. It is indeed vulgaris and Hispana, because it is understood throughout almost all of Spain; nevertheless it has its own proper seat in the kingdoms of Aragon, Murcia, Andalusia, Castile, New and Old, León, and in most of Portugal. It is called Castellana from Castile, whose inhabitants are said to speak this language most purely. Others, however, deny this, and assign the glory of the thing, on various grounds, sometimes to León, sometimes to Aragon. There are those who call it Romanciam, because it derives from the Roman or Latin language as it degenerated. Let the Epistle of King Artaxerxes, written in the provinces, serve as an example, besides the Lord's Prayer (which will always supply the reader with specimens of all the other idioms in their places).

units.la: HISPANICE.
units.tr: SPANISH.

units.la: EL grand Rey Artaxerxes, y Rey de ciento y veynte y siete provincias, desde la India hasta la Ethiopia, à todos los Governadores, y Principes, que están sujetos à nuestro Mandamiento, Salud. Muchos han mal usado de la clemencia de los Principes, y de la honrra, que se les ha hecho han se ensober vecido de tal manera, que non solamente maltratan à los Vasallos de los Reyes, pero tambien de la mucha honrra, que tienen, toman occasion para armar alguna traicion à los, que les dieron aquella honrra. Ne se contentan con quebrantar los derechos de naturaleza, no haziendo gracias de los beneficios recebidos: pero aun piensan poder huir la sentencia de Dios, que vée todas las cosas; y hallegado su locura à táto, que trabajan de derribar con mentiras y falsedades aquellos, que administran con grande diligécia todo lo que seles encomienda, y de tal manera, que merecen de todos ser alabados, &c.
units.tr: The great King Artaxerxes, king of one hundred and twenty-seven provinces, from India to Ethiopia, to all governors and princes who are subject to our command, greeting. Many have abused the clemency of princes and the honour shown them; they have become so puffed up that they not only mistreat the vassals of kings, but also, from the great honour they hold, take occasion to plot treason against those who conferred that honour upon them. Not content with breaking the laws of nature, failing to give thanks for benefits received, they even think they can escape the judgement of God, who sees all things; and their folly has reached such a pitch that they labour to overthrow, by lies and falsehoods, those who administer with great diligence all that is entrusted to them, in such a way that they deserve to be praised by all, etc.

units.la: Y no nos metas en tentacion: mas libranos de mal.

units.tr: Porque tuyo es el reino, y la potencia, y la gloria, por todos los siglos. Amén. This was given for the Jews, and for all the provinces of his kingdom.
