units.la: REx Magnus Artaxerxes, Rex centum & viginti & septem Provinciarum ab India usque Æthiopiam, omnibus Gubernatoribus & Principibus, qui sunt subjecti nostro Mandato, salutem. Multi male usi sunt clementia suorum Principum, atque etiam honore, qui in eos collatus est; tali modo, ut non solum maletractent eos, qui Regibus subditi, verum etiam ex multo honore, quo decorantur, capiant occasionem struendi quasdam insidias iis, qui honore ipsos impertiverunt. Nec contenti sunt humanitatis in se Iura violare, nullas agentes gratias pro acceptis beneficiis, verum arbitrantur etiam se posse fugere sententiam Dei, qui quidquid est videt: & in tantum Vesania proruperunt, ut laborent subvertere mendacijs falsisque testimonijs eos, qui administrant magna diligentia quidquid ipsis injunctum, & ita cuncta agunt, ut digni sint, qui ab omnibus laudentur, &c.
units.tr: King Artaxerxes the Great, to all the governors and princes of the one hundred and twenty-seven provinces from India to Ethiopia, who are subject to our command, greeting. Many have misused the clemency and even the honour shown to them by their princes. They have done so in such a way that they not only mistreat those who are subject to the kings, but also take occasion from the great honour with which they are adorned to lay certain snares for those who have bestowed the honour on them. Not content to violate the rights of humanity, and making no return of thanks for benefits received, they even think they can escape the judgment of God, who sees all things. Their madness has gone so far that they labour to overthrow, by lies and false testimonies, those who administer with great diligence whatever is entrusted to them, and who act in such a way that they deserve to be praised by all, etc.

units.la: Oratio Dominica.
units.tr: The Lord's Prayer.

units.la: PATER noster, qui es in Cælis, Sanctificetur tuum Nomen. Veniat tuum Regnum. Fiat tua voluntas, quemadmodum in Cælo, sic etiam in Terra. Da nobis hodie nostrum panem quotidianum. Et remitte nobis nostra debita, sicut nos remittimus Debitoribus nostris. Et ne nos inducas in tentationem: sed libera nos à malo. Quia tuum est Regnum, & Potentia, & Gloria, per omnia secula, Amen. Ex multis conflatam dixi. Nam qui exactam ejus habent cognitionem, non ignorant innumeras in ea esse Maurorum Gothorumque (utrorumque enim in Hispania fuit Imperium) voces, quas colligere infiniti esset laboris: non paucas item esse Græcorum, una cum Latinis, vel ab ipsorum Græcorum commercio invectas. Nihil dicam de Arabicis, quibus mirum quam scatet. Quum autem Hispania lata sit Regio, variaque habeat Regna & Principatus, etiam Lingua, ut fieri solet, varias patitur Dialectos. Omnium purissima fertur esse, ut paullo ante indicavi, Castellana; qua quidquid æternitatem meretur, quidquid memoria dignum, hodie conscribitur. Eam enim volunt proxime ad Latinam accedere. Viros quosdam novi eruditos; qui, ut quam prope abesset ab Matrice sua hæc Propago, qualisque ante fœdiorem fuerit depravationem, monstrarent, dexteritate quadam scriptis Epistolis, & Latine & Hispanice loquerentur, eademque animi sensa explicarent; ita ut Latinis Latini, Hispanis Hispani essent; servata passim utriusque Linguæ vi, natura & proprietate. Unum ex nonnulla mole adscribam exemplum, illud; quo succinte Hispania suis coloribus depingitur.
units.tr: Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth. Give us today our daily bread. And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever and ever, Amen. I have said that the language is compounded of many sources. Those who have an exact knowledge of it are not unaware that it contains countless words from the Moors and the Goths (for both held power in Spain), words whose collection would be an endless labour; and that there are not a few Greek words, along with Latin ones, brought in either from Greek or Latin trade. I say nothing of the Arabic words, with which it teems in a remarkable way. Since Spain is a wide region with various kingdoms and principalities, its language, as usually happens, has also taken on various dialects. The purest of all is said to be Castilian, in which whatever deserves to be remembered and to last is written today. For they want it to come closest to Latin. I have known certain learned men who, to show how near this offshoot stands to its mother, and what it was like before its more foul corruption, wrote letters with a certain skill, in both Latin and Spanish, and expressed the same thoughts in each, so that in Latin they were Latin and in Spanish they were Spanish, the force, nature and character of each language being preserved throughout. I shall add one example, out of a considerable number, in which Spain is briefly depicted in its own colours.

units.la: Epistola Latina-Hispanica.
units.tr: Latin-Spanish letter.

units.la: SCRIBO & supplico rogando te Francia, des & respondeas tales probationes, tractando de tua eloquentia, loquela & excellentia, quales scribo de Hispania; comparando gentes, nationes & provincias: quales manifesto dictando Epistolas puras Latinas & Hispanas. Hispania (antiquissima corona) perseveró (cessante memoria de contrario) duro & regno, Provincia Christiana. Tu Francia principias à Meroveo, & regnas continuando quasi mille annos Christiana; prædicante Sancto Remigio, & Regnando Clodoveo: Et Hispania quasi ante quatercentum annos, prædicante Sancto Iacobo Apostolo. Respondè Francia, & da & propone contra nos tam grandes nationes, tam fertiles, tam fructuosas Provincias & tantas; tales gentes tam ingeniosas, tam scientificas, tam virtuosas, prudentes, justas, modestas, liberales, graciosas & magnificas: Non monstras tu Francia tam grandes resistentias, & tantas victorias contra Romanos. Tu Francia subjecta per Cæsarem subito quasi ante tres annos: & Hispania subjecta per Catones, Scipiones, Sertorios, Pompejos & Cæsares non ante ducentos annos. De perseverantia & Constantia da testimonia Sagunto, Calaguria, Numantia, gentes feroces, constantes & magnificas. Præsenta tu Francia, & da tales Campos, Montes, Valles; tales Bestias feras & domesticas, tantos & tam excellentes Caballos, tales Vaccas, Aves, Carnes suavissimas, Lanas preciosas; Panes albissimos; tales Plantas, tam odoriseras; tales Arbores, tam fructiferas & fertiles, fructuosas in copia abundante & copiosa; tantas Mineras & tam abundantes, tantas & diversas persectiones. Provincia manante Vino clarissimo, Oleo dulcissimo, Auro purissimo, Argento claro, Plumbo, Ferro, Stagno. Non cognoscos tu Francia Plantas, Arbores, Bestias & Perfectiones, quales de Hispania majores Nos demonstramus. Et cognosco de Hispania infinitas, quales tu Francia non cognosces. Si exaltas & celebras Principes & Imperatores Romanos; demanda & inquire de Bruto, de Fabio, de Hadriano, de Honorio, de Theodosio, de Traiano inclito & gloriosó Hispano. Si amas Poetas & Oratores, & Historias veras; demanda de Seneca, de Quintiliano, de Lucano, de Martiale, de Trogo Pompeio. Si honoras Astrologos, inquire de Alfraiano, de Albumazar, de Pedragio, Alquibicio, & Abenazara, & de grande Alfonso. Si Medicos, Physicos & Philosophos; roga de Avicenna, Abeuron, Algabar, Alfrabio. . Si canonizas & sanctificas Theologos, inquire de Alfonso Sancto, Isidoro, Leandro & Fulgentio, & de divino & sanctissimo Laurentio & Vincentio. Si demandas Eloquentia tam propinqua Latina: Respondé dictando, & compone Libros. Chartas tam Latinas & vulgares contra unas Hispanas & Latinas tales.
units.tr: I write and beg you, France, to give and to offer proofs of the same kind, treating of your eloquence, speech and excellence, as I write of Spain, comparing peoples, nations and provinces, as I plainly do in writing pure Latin and Spanish letters. Spain, the most ancient crown, has remained (with no memory to the contrary) hard and kingdom-like, a Christian province. You, France, begin from Merovech and reign as Christian for almost a thousand years, Saint Remigius preaching and Clovis reigning; and Spain, almost four hundred years earlier, Saint James the Apostle preaching. Answer, France, and set against us such great nations, such fertile, fruitful and numerous provinces, such peoples so ingenious, so learned, so virtuous, prudent, just, modest, generous, gracious and magnificent. Do you, France, show such great resistance and so many victories against the Romans? You, France, were subjected by Caesar only about three years ago; but Spain was subjected by the Catos, Scipios, Sertorius, Pompeys and Caesars not less than two hundred years ago. For perseverance and constancy, bear witness to Saguntum, Calagurris, Numantia, fierce, steadfast and magnificent peoples. Present, France, such fields, mountains and valleys; such wild and domestic beasts, so many and such excellent horses, such cows, birds, most delicate meats, precious wool, very white bread; such plants, so fragrant; such trees, so fruitful and productive, abounding in plenty; so many and such abundant mines, so many and diverse perfections. A province flowing with the clearest wine, the sweetest oil, the purest gold, bright silver, lead, iron, tin. You, France, do not know the plants, trees, beasts and perfections which we show to be greater in Spain. And I know of infinite ones in Spain which you, France, do not know. If you exalt and celebrate Roman princes and emperors, ask and enquire about Brutus, Fabius, Hadrian, Honorius, Theodosius, Trajan, the famous and glorious Spaniards. If you love poets and orators and true histories, ask about Seneca, Quintilian, Lucan, Martial, Trogus Pompeius. If you honour astrologers, enquire of Alfraganus, Albumasar, Pedragius, Alquibicius, Abenazra, and of the great Alfonso. If physicians, natural philosophers and philosophers, ask of Avicenna, Abeuron, Algabar, Alfrabius. If you canonise and sanctify theologians, enquire of Saint Alfonso, Isidore, Leander and Fulgentius, and of the divine and most holy Laurence and Vincent. If you seek eloquence so near to Latin, answer by dictating and compose books. Charters so Latin and vernacular, set against Spanish and Latin ones of such a kind.

units.la: Ab Castellanae elegantia reliquae, Portugallica, Andaluzica, Granatensis & aliae nonnihil abeunt. Portugallos sane Dominicam Orationem, quam puriorem antea posui, sic solitos scribere disco:
units.tr: The rest of the Castilian elegance, Portuguese, Andalusian, Granadan and others, depart somewhat from it. Indeed I have learned that the Portuguese customarily write the Lord's Prayer as follows, which I gave earlier in its purer form:

units.la: Oratio Dominica.
units.tr: The Lord's Prayer.

units.la: PORTVGALLICE. | LATINE. PADRE nosso, que stas nos Ceos, Santificado seja o teu Nome. | PATER noster, qui es in Caelis, Sanctificetur Nomen tuum. Venha a nos o teu Reino. | Veniat nobis Regnum tuum. Seia feita a tua volontade, assi nos Ceos, come na terra. | Fiat voluntas tua, quemadmodum in Caelis, sic etiam in Terra. O Pao nosso de cadadia dano lo oie nesto dia. | Panem nostrum quotidianum da nobis hodie. Et perdoa nos sennoras nossas dividas, assi comme nos perdoamos aos nossos dividores. | Et remitte nobis Domine Debita nostra, sicut nos remittimus nostris Debitoribus. Et nao nos dexes cahir in tentacao: mas libra nos do mal. Amen. | Et ne nos inducas in tentationem; sed libera nos a malo. Amen.
units.tr: PORTUGUESE | LATIN. Our Father, who art in Heaven, hallowed be thy Name. | Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. | Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. | Thy will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth. Give us this day our daily bread. | Give us today our daily bread. And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. | And forgive us, Lord, our debts, as we forgive our debtors. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. Amen. | And lead us not into temptation; but deliver us from evil. Amen.

units.la: Extremis Portugallis peculiare est Idioma ex Gallico Castellanoque confusum; non inelegans, neque auditu ingratum. Valentini & Catalani (a quibus Catalana vocatur) Lingua Progenitorum, cui cum Narbonensi (adeo ut nonnullis etiam Francesa nominetur) nonnihil adfinitatis, uti dicuntur. Granatenses, Barbaricae gentis & Originis, qui quidem ab Catholicis Principibus devicti, Christianorum consuetudine convictuque Castellanam didicerunt; Vernaculae Proprieque, parum abest, obliti: qui vero Montes asperos & inaccessibiles, quos Alpuxarras vocant, incolunt, & ad quos Victorum arma pertingere nequierunt, suis adhuc moribus Linguaque, quae vix alia, quam Syrorum, Arabum, Maurorum, utuntur. Araviga ab Arabibus vulgo nominatur: duratque ejus usus non solum in Granatae ut dixi montanis, verum etiam in multis Andaluziae, Valentiae, Aragoniaeque locis. Cantabri, ut ad eos redeam, primigeniam illam antiquissimam (quam ab Chaldaea ortam volunt nonnulli) servant, ab reliquis omnino discrepantem: ut & olim a Latina. Docent hoc Plinij & Pomponij Melae verba: Illius quidem lib. iii. cap. i. natur. histor. Ex his digna memoratu, aut Latiali sermone dictu facilia, &c. Hujus autem lib. iii, ubi extima Hispaniae Littora, & inter ea Borealiora, explicat; Cantabrorum, inquit, aliquot populi, Amnesque sunt, sed quorum Nomina Nostro ore concipi nequeunt. Accedit & apud Ennium meum nescio quis: Hispane, non Romane memoreti' loqui me.
units.tr: The far Portuguese have a peculiar idiom, mixed from French and Castilian; it is not inelegant, nor unpleasant to hear. The language of the Valencians and Catalans (by whom it is called Catalana) is said to have some affinity with the Narbonese language, so that by some it is even called Francesa. The Granadans, of Berber stock and origin, who were indeed conquered by the Catholic princes, learned Castilian from Christian custom and intercourse, and have almost entirely forgotten their own native tongue. But those who inhabit the rough and inaccessible mountains, which they call Alpuxarras, and to which the victors' arms could not reach, still keep their own customs and language, which is hardly other than that of the Syrians, Arabs and Moors. Araviga is the common name given to it by the Arabs; its use survives not only in the mountains of Granada, as I said, but also in many places in Andalusia, Valencia and Aragon. The Cantabrians, to return to them, keep that primeval and most ancient language (which some believe came from Chaldea), entirely different from the rest, as it once was from Latin. The words of Pliny and Pomponius Mela show this. Of the former, book iii, chapter i of the Natural History: Of these, things worth recording, or easy to express in the Latin speech, and so on. Of the latter, in book iii, where he describes the outermost coasts of Spain and those more northerly among them: The Cantabrians, he says, are several peoples and rivers, but their names cannot be pronounced by our mouth. Moreover, in Ennius, my author, someone says: "I seem to speak Spanish, not Roman."

units.la: Non immerito igitur Cantabricam Matricibus in Europa Minoribus connumerat Magnus ille Scaliger, quod ejus ad me docent Litterae, fideliter & bona fide libro hujus Partis Primo, capite octavo posita. Ratio servatae per inlata totiens ab Romanis aliisque Populis arma, Linguae non alia videtur, quam partim, quod Irruptiones pleraque cum ex Africa, tum ex Orbe Romano per Mare Mediterraneum factae fuerint in eas partes, quae hodie Catalonia, Valentia, Murcia, Granada, Andaluzia; non per montana illa aspera, & tunc temporis, ut hodieque, inaccessa fere loca: partim, quod per faciliora & maritima, quae commemoravi, loca Hispaniam ingressis, quo minus Cantabros, ut & Asturcs Callaicosque suis armis adgrederentur & inquietarent, obstiterint Montes illi, qui perpetuis jugis ab ipso Pyrenaeo per mediam Hispaniam procurrunt ad Artabrum usque Promontorium (Caput hoc tempore, Finis Terra) quique Populos, quos dixi faciebant, ut & nunc, Ultramontanos, adgressu ex Meridionalibus locis difficiles; quum reliqui versus Austrum Cismontani adventantium Armis, prædæ, libidini omnino essent expositi. Intulerunt quidem Cantabris aliquoties arma Romani; sed tales semper debellatos fuerunt experti, ut eos vel sub jugo imperioque servare, vel ad Morum Linguæque mutationem adducere nequiérunt. Accedebat & quod apud eos diu morari parum adriderel Imperatoribus, qui vicerant; & Stativa perpetuare injucundum esset, qui porro victos in officio continerent, Militibus. Nam quidquid Locorum occurreret, horridum & incultum; quidquid hominum, erat indomitum Libertatisque suæ tenacissimum. Sane de Ultramontana Hispania sic Strabo libro III in principio: ἡ δὲ ἀσόσοφ ψυχρά τι ἐν πλέως ... οἰκήσεως. Non difficultatem interim antiquum illud Hispanorum Idioma, Cantabricum inquam, nonnihil etiam hoc tempore, peregrinorum aliquot Vocabulorum, præcipue Castellanorum, admissione esse deformatum, ut cuilibet constare potest vel ex vna Oratione Dominica, quæ sic sonat:
units.tr: Not without reason, then, that great Scaliger counts the Cantabrian among the minor mother-tongues of Europe, as his letter to me shows, which I have set out faithfully and in good faith in the first book of this Part, chapter eight. The reason why this language was preserved through so many invasions by the Romans and other peoples seems to be partly this: most of the incursions were made into those regions which are today Catalonia, Valencia, Murcia, Granada and Andalusia, both from Africa and from the Roman world across the Mediterranean, and not through those rough mountains, places then as now almost inaccessible. And partly this: those who entered Spain by the easier maritime places I have mentioned were prevented from attacking and disturbing the Cantabrians, and likewise the Asturians and Gallaecians, by those mountains which run in unbroken ridges from the Pyrenees through the middle of Spain as far as the Artabrian Promontory (now called Finis Terrae). These mountains made the peoples I have named, as they still do, hard to approach from the southern regions, and so they were called Ultramontane; while the others towards the south, on this side of the mountains, were wholly exposed to the arms, plunder and lust of those who came. The Romans did indeed make war on the Cantabrians several times, but they always found them so stubborn that they could neither keep them under the yoke and rule, nor bring them to change their customs and language. Moreover, it was not pleasant for the victorious commanders to stay long among them, and it would have been irksome for soldiers to keep up permanent camps to hold the defeated in obedience. For whatever places they came to were rough and uncultivated, and whatever people there were, they were untamed and most tenacious of their liberty. Indeed, Strabo speaks thus of Ultramontane Spain at the beginning of book III: [ἡ δὲ ἄλλη ... ψυχρὰ ... οἰκήσεως] (the rest is cold and ... unfit for habitation). Meanwhile, that ancient Spanish language, I mean the Cantabrian, has not a little been deformed even at this time by the admission of some foreign words, chiefly Castilian, as anyone may see from the Lord's Prayer alone, which sounds thus:

units.la: Oratio Dominica.
units.tr: The Lord's Prayer.

units.la: CANTABRICE. GVRE Aita ceruëtan aicena, Sanctifica bedi hire icena. Ethor bedi ire Resuma. Eguin bedi hire Vorondarea, cetuän beçala lurrean ere. Gure eguneco oguia iguc egun. Eta quita ietzaguc gure çorrac, nola guçere çorduney quittazen baitrauegu. Eta ezgaitzala sar eraci tentationetan, baina delura gaitzac gaichtotic. Ecen hirea duc Resuma, eta Puissança, eta Gloria seculacotz. Amen.
units.tr: Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread. And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever. Amen.

units.la: LATINE. PATER noster, qui es in Cælis, Sanctificetur nomen tuum. Veniat Regnum tuum. Fiat voluntas tua, quemadmodum in Cœlo, sic etiam in Terra. Panem nostrum quotidianum da nobis hodie. Et remitte nobis debita nostra, sicut & nos remittimus debitoribus nostris. Et ne nos inducas in tentationem; sed libera nos a malo. Quia tuum est Regnum, & Potentia, & Gloria in secula. Amen.
units.tr: LATIN. Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth. Give us this day our daily bread. And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory for ever. Amen.

units.la: In qua quis non videt Voces illas; Sanctifica, Resuma, Vorondatea, quitta, quittazen, tentationetan, deliura, puissança, gloria, seculacotz, Romanensis esse Linguæ, ad Cantabricam Dialectum inflexas? Idem deprehendere erit in Symbolo Apostolico, quod in generali meæ Galliæ Descriptione ponam. Lucius Marinæus Siculus lib. IV. de reb. Hispanic. proprium, hujus Idiomatis esse notat, in compluribus Dictionibus Singularem Numerum in A Litteram, Pluralem in Ac terminare: ut dicis gratia, Lurra terra, Lurrac terræ. Adscribit deinde alia quædam Exempla. Vocant, inquit, Vasconcs Cælum Cerva: Terram, Lurra; Solem, Eguzquia; Lunam, Irarguia; Stellam, Izarra; Nubem Odéya; Panem, Oguia; Vinum, Ardaoa; Carnem, Araguia; Maritum, Scnarra, Flumen, Ibáya: Bibo, Edatendòt; Lego, Iracurtendot: Domum, Echea; Villam, Uria; Lectum, Ocea; Interulam, Alcandórea; Senem, Zarra; Album, Zuria; Nigrum, Belza; Rubrum, Gorria; Piscem, Arraya; Amare, Oncréxtea; Dormio, Lonazá; Video, Bacúst; Hominem, Guizona; Mulierem, Emaztéa; Filium, Semèa; Filiam, Alauéa; Patrem, Aytéa; Matrem, Améa; Fratrem, Anagea; Sororem Arreuéa; Corpus, Gorpuza (quod ab Latinis mutuatum, addita Vasconica terminatione; ut alia nonnulla ab aliis) Ignem, Suá; Formosum Ederrà; Comedere, Ian; Curro, Lasteregnitendot. Habent etiam Numerandi modum, dicentes: Vnum, Bat; Duo, Bi; Tria, Irù; Quatuor, Lau; Quinque, Bost; Sex, Sey; Septem, Zaspì; Octo, Zorzì; Novem, Vedrazì, Decem, Amarr, Viginti, Oguèy; Triginta, Oguéytamar; Quadraginta, Berroguéy; Quinquaginta, Berroguéytamar; Sexaginta, Yruroguéy; Septuaginta, Iruroguéytamar; Octoginta, Lauroguéy; Nonaginta, Lauroguéytamar: Centum, Eun. Iam quod hic restat, supra meas vires est, fateor, explicare Strabonis illud libro Geograph. tertio, ubi dicit, non unum genus Litterarum, vel unius speciei Grammaticam: neque Linguam unam Hispanis omnibus fuisse. Sic enim ait; quum scripsisset Tardulos inter Hispaniæ Populos sapientia excellere, Grammatices Præceptis uti, & memorandæ Vetustatis Volumina habere, Poëmata, Leges quoque versibus conscriptas è sex annorum millibus: Καὶ οἱ ἄλλοι δ' ἱ Ἐηρης χρῶνται γραμματικῇ, ὁ μὲν ἰδίᾳ, ὁ δὲ γλώσσῃ ἰδίᾳ. Quis in re antiqua, tamque ab aevo nostro remota, certi quid de variis Hispanorum Veterum Linguis divinarit? Non ego, nisi varias antiquas, id est Cantabricae Dialectos exaudiat Strabo. Voces nonnullas Veteribus Hispanis usurpatas laudant Grammatici Latini. Dureta, ligneum Solium est apud Suetonium in Augusto cap. LXXXIII; Necys, Mars apud Macrobium lib. 1. Satur. cap. xix: Striges, genus vestium apud Isidorum lib. xix. Etymol. cap. xxiii. Gurdus, stolidus, scribente Quintiliano lib. 1. cap. v. Lanceae, Teli genus, ut notat Agellius lib. x. cap. xxx. Alias his apponendas aliis relinquo. Hoc unum monendum hic in genere duxi, vocem Briga, vel ut aliis scribitur, Brica, quae multas non in Hispania solum, sed in Gallia etiam & Germania, Urbes terminat, Opidum significare. Hinc Juliobriga, Caesarobriga, Augustobriga, Flaviobriga, & aliae. Putant quidam Brigam nihil aliud esse, quam transposita Canina littera, Burgum, quo quamplurima Germaniarum Opida hodieque finiuntur. Ejusdem notionis Βέϊα apud Thracas, ut notant Strabo & Stephanus; ut in Selymbria, Mesembria, Poltiobria. Sunt qui diiquirendum monent an non pro Βέϊα legendum sit Βέϊχα. Sic Certa apud Parthos in Dadocerta, Tigranocerta, Vologesocerta, & id genus aliis. Sic denique πόλις apud Graecos. Exempla suis locis videbimus infinita.
units.tr: In which who does not see that those words, Sanctifica, Resuma, Vorondatea, quitta, quittazen, tentationetan, deliura, puissança, gloria, seculacotz, are of Romance speech, bent to the Cantabrian dialect? The same will be found in the Apostles' Creed, which I shall set out in my general description of Gaul. Lucius Marineus of Sicily, in book IV of his On the Affairs of Spain, notes that it is a peculiarity of this idiom that in many words the singular ends in A and the plural in AC, as, to give an example, Lurra, earth, Lurrac, the earths. He then adds some other examples. The Basques, he says, call heaven Cerva; earth, Lurra; sun, Eguzquia; moon, Irarguia; star, Izarra; cloud, Odéya; bread, Oguia; wine, Ardaoa; meat, Araguia; husband, Senarra; river, Ibáya. To drink, Edatendòt; to read, Iracurtendot; house, Echea; village, Uria; bed, Ocea; shirt, Alcandórea; old man, Zarra; white, Zuria; black, Belza; red, Gorria; fish, Arraya; to love, Oncréxtea; to sleep, Lonazá; to see, Bacúst; man, Guizona; woman, Emaztéa; son, Semèa; daughter, Alauéa; father, Aytéa; mother, Améa; brother, Anagea; sister, Arreuéa; body, Gorpuza (which, borrowed from the Latins with a Basque ending added, as some others were by others); fire, Suá; beautiful, Ederrà; to eat, Ian; to run, Lasteregnitendot. They also have a way of counting, saying: one, Bat; two, Bi; three, Irù; four, Lau; five, Bost; six, Sey; seven, Zaspì; eight, Zorzì; nine, Vedrazì; ten, Amarr; twenty, Oguèy; thirty, Oguéytamar; forty, Berroguéy; fifty, Berroguéytamar; sixty, Yruroguéy; seventy, Iruroguéytamar; eighty, Lauroguéy; ninety, Lauroguéytamar; a hundred, Eun. What remains here is, I confess, beyond my powers: to explain that passage of Strabo in the third book of his Geography, where he says that the Spaniards did not all have one kind of letters or one grammar, nor one language. For he says this: after writing that the Turdetani excelled among the peoples of Spain in wisdom, used the rules of grammar, and had books of ancient memory, poems, and laws written in verse covering six thousand years: [Καὶ οἱ ἄλλοι δ' οἱ Ἴβηρες χρῶνται γραμματικῇ, ὁ μὲν ἰδίᾳ, ὁ δὲ γλώσσῃ ἰδίᾳ] (and the other Iberians use letters, one in one way, another in its own tongue). Who could divine anything certain, in a matter so ancient and so remote from our age, about the various languages of the ancient Spaniards? I could not, unless Strabo means the various ancient dialects, that is, the Cantabrian ones. Some Latin grammarians praise words used by the old Spaniards. Dureta, a wooden throne, is in Suetonius, Augustus, chapter 83; Necys, Mars, in Macrobius, Saturnalia, book 1, chapter 19; Striges, a kind of garment, in Isidore, Etymologies, book 19, chapter 23; Gurdus, stupid, as Quintilian writes in book 1, chapter 5; Lanceae, a kind of javelin, as Gellius notes in book 10, chapter 30. I leave other examples to be added to these by others. One thing I thought should be noted here in general: the word Briga, or as others write it, Brica, which ends many town names not only in Spain but also in Gaul and Germany, means a town. Hence Juliobriga, Caesarobriga, Augustobriga, Flaviobriga, and others. Some think that Briga is nothing but Burgum with the letters transposed, the ending by which very many German towns are still named. Of the same meaning is Βρίγα among the Thracians, as Strabo and Stephanus note, as in Selymbria, Mesembria, Poltiobria. Some advise inquiring whether we ought not to read Βρίγχα instead of Βρίγα. So Certa among the Parthians in Dadocerta, Tigranocerta, Vologesocerta, and similar names. So finally πόλις among the Greeks. We shall see countless examples in their places.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CHAP. IX.

units.la: Hispaniarum Gubernatio Politica.
units.tr: The Political Government of Spain.

units.la: EIvs cum Genij, tum Idiomatis fuerunt olim, suntque hodie Hispaniarum Incolae. Convertendus jam-nunc sermo ad delineandam aliquo modo Gubernationem per Statum & Politicum & Ecclesiasticum.
units.tr: Its people, both in character and in language, were once what the inhabitants of Spain are today. The discussion must now turn to sketching in some way the government, both civil and ecclesiastical.

units.la: Non animus hic mihi recensendis cum ex aliis, tum Justino, Diodoro, Josepho, Eusebio, Hieronymo, suppositicio. Beroso, & Interprete ejus Annio Viterbiensi, Antiquis Hispaniae Regibus, Rebusque ab ijs domi militiaeque gestis, Lectorem morari. Morari hoc esset & ineptire cum multis. Tubal an in Hispania fuerit parte prima diflerui. Huic qui sufficiuntur, Iberus, Iubalda, Brygus, Tagus, Batus, & alij, Regesne censendi? Absit, nisi quis Fluviis alijsque rebus Inanimatis nasci tunc temporis solitos Reges concedat. Qui fictum illud agmen sequuti, non melioris sunt conditionis. Incerta omnia: ut & vix certiora, quae successione quidam gestisse scribuntur in Hispania, Regibus quasi exactis, varia fortuna, multisque & Populis a se seminatis & Opidis conditis, Lydi, Thraces, Rhodij, Phruges, Cyprij, Phoenices, Aegyptij, Milesij, Cares, Lesbij & Chaldaei. Exploratiora censeri solent, quae ab Karthaginiensibus, Romanis, multoque post Gothis, Vandalis, Alanis, Suevis, Hunnis, eorumque Regibus patrata memoriae produnt Scriptores, qui partim rebus gerendis adfuiterunt, partim ex fidelissima aliorum cognoverunt relatione. Ea, paucis dicam, sic habent. Quum in Hispania longe lateque dominarentur & pleraque sub ditione sua haberent Poeni, alijque Africae populi, contra eos primi omnium cum armatis exercitibus ab S.P.Q.R. missi sunt Cn. & P. Cornelij Scipiones, belli Punici II initio: qui septimo ejus belli anno sunt caesi, Q. Fulvio Flacco & Ap. Claudio Polcro coss. Submissus anno sequenti Patri Patruoque P. Cornelius Scipio Africanus Major multa prospere gessit, primusque ibidem Provinciam fecit, Q. Caecilio Metello & L. Veturio Philone coss. anno ab V.C.IOXLII: Hic Asdrubale & Magone, Karthaginiensium Ducibus, acie ad Baerulam urbem (quae, quo loco hodie in Andaluzia visuntur Baeça & Vbeda, fuisse creditur) fugatis, atque inde ex tota Hispania pulsis, vindicatisque armis Hispanijs, amicitiam cum Syphace Masfylorum (hodie Bilediulgerid) Rege, icto foedere, firmavit. Paullo post rebellantes Hispaniae populos ad deditionem compulit, Foedereque cum Masanissa Masaesulorum (fuerunt, ubi nunc Regnum Tremissenum) Rege & Gaditanis facto, Provincia L. Lentulo & L. Manlio Acidino tradita, Romam reversus est. Post Scipionem Hispaniam L. Cornelius Lentulus Proconsule obtinuit; qui, rebus bene feliciterque gestis, ovans Urbem ingressus est, anno ab V.C.IOLIV. Triennio post C. Cornelio Cethego, Q. Minucio Rufo coss. Hispaniae primum sunt terminatae,
units.tr: I have no wish here to detain the reader by listing the kings of old and the deeds they did at home and in war, drawn from Justin, Diodorus, Josephus, Eusebius, Jerome, the spurious Berosus and his interpreter Annius of Viterbo, among others. To do so would be to dawdle and to play the fool along with many others. I deferred the question of whether Tubal was in Spain to the first part. Are Iberus, Iubalda, Brygus, Tagus, Batus and the others who are brought forward to be counted as kings? Far from it, unless one grants that rivers and other inanimate things were then accustomed to being kings. Those who follow that fictitious line are no better off. All of it is uncertain, and scarcely more certain are the things some writers record as done in Spain by a succession of rulers, after the kings had been, as it were, driven out: by Lydians, Thracians, Rhodians, Phrygians, Cypriots, Phoenicians, Egyptians, Milesians, Carians, Lesbians and Chaldeans, with varied fortune, and with many peoples sown by them and towns founded. Those things are usually judged more reliable which the writers hand down as done by the Carthaginians, the Romans, and, much later, the Goths, Vandals, Alans, Suevi and Huns, and their kings. Some of these writers were present at the deeds, and others learned of them from the most trustworthy report of others. To speak briefly, the matter stands thus. When the Carthaginians and the other peoples of Africa held sway far and wide in Spain and held most of it under their control, the first to be sent against them with armed forces by the Senate and People of Rome were Gnaeus and Publius Cornelius Scipio, at the beginning of the Second Punic War. In the seventh year of that war they were slain, in the consulship of Quintus Fulvius Flaccus and Appius Claudius Pulcher. The following year Publius Cornelius Scipio Africanus the Elder, who had been sent to help his father and uncle, achieved much success, and was the first to make it a province there, in the consulship of Quintus Caecilius Metellus and Lucius Veturius Philo, in the year 542 from the founding of the city. Here, after Hasdrubal and Mago, the Carthaginian commanders, had been routed in battle near the town of Baerula (which is believed to have stood where Baeza and Úbeda are seen today in Andalusia), and had been driven out of the whole of Spain, and after Spain had been won back by arms, he strengthened by treaty his friendship with Syphax, king of the Masaesyli (today Bilediulgerid). Shortly afterwards he forced the rebellious peoples of Spain to surrender. Then, having made a treaty with Masinissa, king of the Masaesuli (whose lands are where the Kingdom of Tremecen now lies), and with the people of Gades, he handed over the province to Lucius Lentulus and Lucius Manlius Acidinus and returned to Rome. After Scipio, Lucius Cornelius Lentulus held Spain as proconsul; having conducted affairs well and successfully, he entered the City in triumph in the year 574 from the founding of the city. Three years later, in the consulship of Gaius Cornelius Cethegus and Quintus Minucius Rufus, the Spanish provinces were first divided.

units.la: Fortean explicatus. minatæ, atque in eas duo Novi Prætores missi C. Sempronius Tuditanus in Citeriorem, M. Helvius Blasio in Ulteriorem. Vix duobus elapsis annis, quum tantum glisceret in Hispania Bellum, ut jam Consulari & Duce & Exercitu opus esset, M. Porcius Cato Consul Citeriorem sortitus, bello ab Emporijs (retinetur hodieque nomen in Ampurias) coepto, rebellantem ita pacavit, ut Proconsule ex ea triumpharit, anno 195 x. Hic est ille Cato, qui miro strategemate multarum Hispaniæ Urbium muros uno die diruit, scribentibus Livio lib. xxxiv, Auctore de V V. Inlustribus cap. xlvii, & Iulio Frontino lib. 1. Strategemat. cap. 1. Post Catonis victoriam Hispaniæ varie possessæ, sæpeque nunc hic nunc ibi a missæ; ita ut supra xxx Triumphi postea ex his relati memorentur. Stipendium pendere non prius coeperunt, quam Augusto Principe; qui, quum Hispaniam omnem, debellatis Cantabris & Asturibus, qui omnium diutissime restiterant, multo varioque Marte perdomuisset, uniuersam in tres Provincias divisit, Baeticam, Lusitanicam & Tarraconensem. Singulis inde sui sunt adtributi Conventus; Baeticæ iv, Gaditanus, Cordubensis, Astigitanus, & Hispalensis; in iis Opida centebantur clxxv: Lusitania tres habuit Emeritensem, Pacensem, & Scallabitanum; & in iis Opida xlv: Tarraconensi denique dati Conventus vii. Carthaginiensis, Tarraconensis, Cæsar-Augustanus, Cluniensis, Asturum, Lucensis, & Bracarensis; in quibus opida numerabantur ccxciv. Videndi Plinius lib. iii, Strabo lib. iii. & alij. Sic, Rebus subinde paullum mutantibus, Provinciæ nobilissimæ Romanis parucrunt usque ad Imperatores Honorij & Theodosij iii Consulatum, qui incidit in annum Christi cccccx: quo tempore Vandali, Suevi & Alani, ab Stilicone in Gallias evocati, quum eas, Rheno trajecto, omnes pene occupassent, & in iis jam romanum Barbarorum more debaccharentur: ab Gothis, Adolpho & Vallia Regibus, quos ad liberandas Gallias Honorius Imperator miserat, exacti, transgressi Pyrenæos montes, Hispaniam Romanis ereptam multos annos obtinuerunt. Post aliquot annos Gothi, Galliam incolentes, ab Francis bello petiti in Vandalos vice versa arma movent. Franci Gothos ex Gallijs, Gothi Vandalos & Alanos ex Hispanijs ejiciunt; Suevis ad internecionem cæsis. Quo tempore Vandali & Alani à Bonifacio in Africam, cui pro Imperatore præerat, evocati Hispanias Gothis possidendas reliquerunt. Gothi Hispaniam, Romanis Præsidijs omnino expulsis, quum sui juris fecissent, eaque sub suis Regibus longo jam tempore fuissent potiti; tandem ingenti bello ab Sarracenis Arabibus profligati, Rege Roderico occiso, Hispaniam fere omnem amiserunt. Bello superstites quum in Asturum, Cantabrorum & Gallæcorum montibus sese muniissent, paullatim amissas Regiones, Urbes & Castella recuperare coeperunt; & postremo, quum Sarracenorum res in Baetica Hispania se contraxissent, omnemque Hispaniam Gothi recuperassent, ijs etiam ab Ferdinando Aragoniæ Rege cognomine Catholico (quod hæreditarium deinceps esse coepit Successoribus) victis atque omni Hispania cum Mele, qui se Granatæ Regem scribebat, exturbatis, universa Regio Dominis antiquis est restituta. Accuratiorem Regum omnium, rerumque ab ijs gestarum narrationem, quum non Cosmographi sit, sed Historiographi, videre est cum apud Veteres Scriptores & Latinos & Græcos, tum apud eos, qui ævo medio nostraque tempestate ex professo Hispanorum acta contexuerunt; quales sunt Idacinus Gallecię Episcopus, qui à primo Theodosij Consulatu scripsit usque ad annum ccccxc, Ioannes Abbas Biclarienis Monasterij & Episcopus postea Gerundensis, cui initium ab anno Iustini Ioioris Imperatoris 1 usque ad viii Mauricij Principis; Maximus, Cæsar-Augustanus Episcopus, qui Historiam composuit de ijs, quæ Gothorum temporibus in Hispania contigerunt, Isidorus Hispalensis Archiepiscopus, qui Gothorum, Vandalorum, Suevorumque historiam ad sua usque tempora paucis est complexus; Iulianus Archiepiscopus Toletanus, cujus Historia de Rebus sub Bamba Rege gestis exstat Salmanticæ in Bibliotheca Ecclesiæ Cathedralis; Lucas Tudensis, qui Chronicon scripsit jussu Berengariæ Reginæ, Matris Regis Ferdinandi iii; Roderic[us] Ximenez Navarrus, Archiepiscopus Toletanus, qui Res in Hispania gestas novem libris comprehendit, subjuncta compendiosa Ostrogothorum, Suevorum, Alanorum & Vandalorum Historia; Ioannes Episcopus Gerundensis, cujus sunt Paralipomenon, id est Rerum Hispaniæ ab alijs omissarum, Libri x; Hic Hispaniæ primordia, progressus, incrementa, variasque vicissitudines prosequutus est usque
units.tr: Fortean explicatus. Two new praetors were sent into them: Gaius Sempronius Tuditanus to Hither Spain and Marcus Helvius Blasio to Further Spain. Less than two years had passed when the war in Spain blazed up so much that a consular, a general and an army were needed. Marcus Porcius Cato, as consul, drew Hither Spain by lot; beginning the war at Emporiae (the name is still kept today in Ampurias), he so pacified the rebels that he celebrated a triumph over them as proconsul, in the year 195. This is that Cato who, by a remarkable stratagem, tore down the walls of many towns of Spain in a single day, as Livy records in book 34, the author of On Illustrious Men in chapter 47, and Julius Frontinus in book 1 of the Stratagems, chapter 1. After Cato's victory, Spain was held in various ways and was often sent now here, now there, so that more than thirty triumphs over it are afterwards recorded. They did not begin to pay tribute until the time of the Emperor Augustus, who, after he had subdued the whole of Spain, crushing the Cantabrians and Asturians, who had resisted longest of all, in a long and varied campaign, divided the entire region into three provinces: Baetica, Lusitania and Tarraconensis. To each of these were assigned its own assize-districts. Baetica had four: Gades, Corduba, Astigi and Hispalis; in these were counted 175 towns. Lusitania had three: Emerita, Pax Julia and Scallabis, and in these 45 towns. Tarraconensis was finally given seven assize-districts: Carthago Nova, Tarraco, Caesaraugusta, Cluniensis, Asturica, Lucus and Bracara, in which 294 towns were counted. See Pliny, book 3, and Strabo, book 3, and others. So, with affairs changing a little from time to time, these most noble provinces obeyed the Romans until the third consulship of the Emperors Honorius and Theodosius, which fell in the year of Christ 410. At that time the Vandals, Suevi and Alans, summoned into Gaul by Stilicho, had after crossing the Rhine occupied almost all of it, and were now running riot there in barbarian fashion. Driven out by the Goths, under their kings Adolphus and Walia, whom the Emperor Honorius had sent to free Gaul, they crossed the Pyrenees and held Spain, which had been taken from the Romans, for many years. After some years the Goths, who inhabited Gaul, were attacked in war by the Franks, and in turn turned their arms against the Vandals. The Franks drove the Goths out of Gaul, and the Goths drove the Vandals and Alans out of Spain, the Suevi being cut down to utter destruction. At this time the Vandals and Alans were summoned into Africa by Boniface, who was in charge there as commander, and they left Spain to be possessed by the Goths. The Goths, with the Roman garrisons entirely expelled, made Spain their own, and for a long time held it under their own kings. At last, after a great war, they were overthrown by the Saracen Arabs, King Roderic was killed, and they lost almost all of Spain. The survivors of the war entrenched themselves in the mountains of the Asturians, Cantabrians and Gallaecians, and gradually began to recover the regions, towns and fortresses they had lost. Finally, when the affairs of the Saracens had contracted into Baetica, and the Goths had recovered all of Spain, the Saracens were also defeated by Ferdinand, King of Aragon, surnamed the Catholic (a title that thereafter began to be hereditary among his successors). With Muley, who styled himself king of Granada, driven out of all Spain, the whole region was restored to its ancient lords. A fuller account of all the kings and of the deeds done by them belongs to the historian, not to the cosmographer. It may be found both among the ancient Latin and Greek writers, and among those who in the Middle Ages and in our own time have professedly composed the acts of the Spaniards. Such are Idacius, bishop of Gallaecia, who wrote from the first consulship of Theodosius to the year 490; John, abbot of the monastery of Biclaro and later bishop of Gerona, whose work begins with the first year of the Emperor Justin the Younger and runs to the eighth year of the Emperor Maurice; Maximus, bishop of Caesaraugusta, who composed a history of what happened in Spain in the time of the Goths; Isidore, archbishop of Seville, who briefly embraced the history of the Goths, Vandals and Suevi down to his own time; Julian, archbishop of Toledo, whose history of the deeds done under King Wamba survives in the library of the cathedral church at Salamanca; Lucas of Tuy, who wrote a chronicle at the command of Queen Berengaria, mother of King Ferdinand III; Roderic Ximenez de Rada, a Navarrese, archbishop of Toledo, who comprised the deeds done in Spain in nine books, with a brief history of the Ostrogoths, Suevi, Alans and Vandals appended; John, bishop of Gerona, whose work is the Paralipomena, that is, ten books of things of Spain omitted by others. He followed the beginnings, progress, growth and varied vicissitudes of Spain as far as

units.la: Inde in Extiticam. Lusitanicam, & Tarraconensem: quibus sui erant Conventus.
units.tr: Thence into Baetica, Lusitania and Tarraconensis, each of which had its own assize-districts.

units.la: Res ab Germania Pontis in Hispania gestæ.
units.tr: Deeds done in Spain by the Germans.

units.la: Sarracenorum gesta.
units.tr: The deeds of the Saracens.

units.la: Penes quos hodie Hispania.
units.tr: Those in whose hands Spain is today.

units.la: Hispaniæ Scriptores, qui res gestas memoriæ consecraverunt. usque ad Honorij Arcadiique Augustorum tempora; Alphonsus Karthaginiensis, Episcopus Burgensis, qui inter alia scripsit Anacephalæosin Regum Hispaniæ; Franciscus Tarapha, cujus omnium Historiarum Regumque Hispaniæ ab Orbe fere condito usque ad Karolum Imperatorem Brevis circumfertur Epitome; Michael Riccius Neapolitanus, cujus de Regibus Hispaniæ Libros tres habemus, ab Gargori Rege usque ad Philippum Karoli Imperatoris Patrem; Lucius Marineus Siculus, cui de Rebus Hispaniæ Libros xxii debemus; Joannes Vasæus Brugensis, qui Hispaniæ Chronicon edidit summa fide diligentiaque conscriptum; Antonius Nebrissensis, qui res ab Ferdinando gestas æternitati consecravit. Joannes Mariana Hispanus, à Societate Iesu, qui Historiam de Rebus Hispaniæ scripsit libris xx ab ipso Tubale ad annum Christi cIↄ ccccxxix. Nec prætereundi, qui Hispanica lingua posteris præclara suorum Acta communicarunt, Petrus Antonius Rodericus Palentinus, Petrus Medimna. Dicitur & Ferdinandus à Pulgar sermone vernaculo Catholicorum Regum Ferdinandi & Isabellæ res gestas quatuor Tomis complexus. Quin & Alphonsus Rex ejus nominis x, cognomine Sapiens, ex Auctoribus probatis Historiam Hispanam jussit in quatuor partes redigi, opus copiosum, & antiquo temporis istius Idiomate venerandum; & Alphonsus xi secundo mandavit colligi atque in ordinem digeri Hispanorum historias. Salmanticæ item in Bibliotheca Franciscana repositas intelligo Antiquorum Hispaniæ Regum Historias. Diegus à Valera Historiam Hispaniæ generalem in compendium contraxit, mandatu Isabellæ Reginæ. Didici & Joannem Aegidium Zamorensem de rebus Hispanorum scripsisse. Florianus denique à Campo res omnes Hispaniæ memorabiles quatuor Tomis delineandas susceperat: sed eorum Primus tantum est editus; in quo quæcumque de Primordijs hujus Regionis potuerunt inveniri, studiose sunt collecta.
units.tr: Spanish writers who have preserved the deeds of nations in memory, down to the time of the emperors Honorius and Arcadius: Alphonsus Karthaginiensis, Bishop of Burgos, who among other works wrote a summary of the kings of Spain; Franciscus Tarapha, whose brief epitome of all histories and kings of Spain, from almost the creation of the world down to the Emperor Charles, is in circulation; Michael Riccius Neapolitanus, whose three books on the kings of Spain we have, from King Gargoris down to Philip, father of the Emperor Charles; Lucius Marineus Siculus, to whom we owe twenty-two books on the affairs of Spain; Joannes Vasaeus Brugensis, who published a chronicle of Spain written with great fidelity and diligence; Antonius Nebrissensis, who immortalised the deeds of Ferdinand. Joannes Mariana Hispanus, of the Society of Jesus, wrote a history of the affairs of Spain in twenty books, from Tubal himself to the year of Christ 1429. Nor should I pass over those who have handed down the illustrious deeds of their countrymen to posterity in the Spanish language: Petrus Antonius Rodericus Palentinus and Petrus Medimna. It is said that Ferdinandus à Pulgar also embraced in four volumes, in the vernacular, the deeds of the Catholic kings Ferdinand and Isabella. Indeed, Alphonsus, the tenth king of that name, surnamed the Wise, ordered that the Spanish history, drawn from approved authorities, be reduced to four parts, a copious work and venerable for the old language of that age; and Alphonsus xi ordered a second collection and arrangement of the histories of the Spaniards. I understand that the histories of the ancient kings of Spain are also kept in the Franciscan library at Salamanca. Diegus à Valera condensed a general history of Spain into an abridgment, by command of Queen Isabella. I have also learned that Joannem Aegidium Zamorensem wrote about the affairs of the Spaniards. Finally, Florianus à Campo had undertaken to set out all the memorable things of Spain in four volumes, but only the first of these has been published, in which whatever could be found about the beginnings of this region has been carefully collected.

units.la: Quum autem Maurorum temporibus à quinque Regibus Castellæ, Aragoniæ, Portugalliæ, Granatæ & Navarræ, Hispania fuerit possessa, Solus hodie Imperium in eam exercet Philippus iii, Philippi Magni F, Karoli Imperatoris ter-Maximi N.
units.tr: Since in the time of the Moors Spain was held by five kings, of Castile, Aragon, Portugal, Granada and Navarre, today only one rules over it: Philippus iii, son of Philip the Great and grandson of the thrice-greatest Emperor Charles.

units.la: PHILIPPI III.
units.tr: PHILIP III.

units.la: HISPANIARVM REGIS POTENTISSIMI MAIORES NVPERI.
units.tr: THE MOST POWERFUL KING OF SPAIN'S RECENT ANCESTORS.
