Karolus v Imperator Romanorum, obiit cIↄ Iↄ lviii. | Isabella Lusitana, obiit cIↄ Iↄ xxxix. | Maximilianus Imperator Romanorum, obiit cIↄ Iↄ lxxvii. | Maria Austriaca. | Philippus ii Rex Castellæ, Legionis, Arag. &c. obiit cIↄ Iↄ xcviii. | Anna Austriaca, obiit cIↄ Iↄ lxxx.
units.tr: Philip I | Joanna | Emanuel | Maria | Ferdinand | Anna | Charles | Isabella (genealogical table; see the scan). Charles V, Emperor of the Romans, died 1558. Isabella of Portugal died 1539. Maximilian, Emperor of the Romans, died 1577. Maria of Austria. Philip II, King of Castile, León, Aragon, etc., died 1598. Anna of Austria died 1580.

units.la: PHILIPPVS
units.tr: PHILIP

units.la: HISPANIARVM REX POTENTISSIMVS.
units.tr: PHILIP, MOST POWERFUL KING OF THE SPANIARDS.

units.la: Status porro Principalis in tria summa distribui solet Regna, Castellæ, Aragoniæ & Portugalliæ. Primum quidem, præter Castilias, continet Regna Legionis, Granatæ, Navarræ, Galeciæ, Toleti, Sivilia (vel Andaluziæ) Cordubæ, Iaënis, Murcia, Carteia, (vel Algezira) & Gebal-Taricis: Insulas Canarias, Philippinas, & alias, totamque Indiam Occidentalem: Principatum Austriæ, Ducatum Mediolanensem; Dominatus Cantabricum (vulgo Gerundensis (vulgo Girona) Vrgellensis (vel Vrgellitanus) & Vicquensis (vel Vicensis olim etiam Aufonensis.)
units.tr: The principal state is usually divided into three great kingdoms, Castile, Aragon and Portugal. The first, besides the Castiles, contains the kingdoms of León, Granada, Navarre, Galicia, Toledo, Seville (or Andalusia), Córdoba, Jaén, Murcia, Carteia (or Algeciras) and Gibraltar; the Canary Islands, the Philippines and others, and the whole of the West Indies; the Principality of Austria, the Duchy of Milan; the Lordship of Cantabria (commonly Gerona), Urgel (or Urgellitanus) and Vich (or Vicensis, formerly also Ausonensis).

units.la: Septimus denique Cæsaraugustanus. Episcopatus antiquissimus, cuius Præsulem Felicem ab sanctitate & orthodoxa fide laudat D. Cyprianus lib. 1. cap. v. Eum in sacris agnoscunt Pampilonensis (vel Pampelonensis) Calagurritanus (vulgo Calahorrensis) Oscensis (quem & Huescensem quidam vocant) & Balbastiensis.
units.tr: Seventh and last is Zaragoza, a very ancient bishopric whose bishop Felix is praised by St Cyprian for his holiness and orthodox faith (book 1, chapter 5). Its suffragans are acknowledged as Pamplona (or Pampelona), Calahorra (commonly Calahorrensis), Huesca (which some also call Huescensis) and Barbastro.

units.la: Nulli subsunt Leonensis & Ovetensis, Leonensis, quæ & Legionensis, jam inde à Gothorum temporibus Sedi tantum Apostolicæ subiecta fuit; nullum agnoscens Episcopum Metropolitanum. Ovetensem Ecclesiam Froila, quartus ab Hispaniæ recuperatione Rex, ædificasse & Cathedralem constituisse dicitur. Metropolitanæ jus illi tributum ab Ioanne VIII P. M. sub Alphonso Magno Rege, uti litteræ docent Apostolicæ.
units.tr: León and Oviedo are subject to no one. León, also called Legionensis, has been subject from Gothic times to the Apostolic See alone and recognizes no metropolitan bishop. Froila, the fourth king after the recovery of Spain, is said to have built the church of Oviedo and made it a cathedral. The right of a metropolitan was granted to it by Pope John VIII in the reign of King Alphonso the Great, as the apostolic letters attest.

units.la: Habet & tres Archiepiscopos Portugallia, Bracarensem, Olisiponensem & Funchalensem: subque iis Episcopos Eborensem, Viscensem, Guardensem, Conimbricensem, Portugallensem, Lamecensem, Silvensem, Ceppetensem. Lerienses. Eborensis Episcopatus antiquissimus: quod B. Mancinus Christi Discipulus, primus Eboræ Divini verbi præco, primusque, ut nonnulli autumant, Episcopus fuisse dicatur. Eborensem Ecclesiam Metropolitanam fecit Paullus III P. M. primumque ibi Archiepiscopum nominavit serenissimum Principem, S. R. E. Cardinalem, Henricum Portugalliæ Infantem. Silvensis in regno Algarbiorum, mutata Sede, Osonobensi successit. Lerienses Episcopatus nuper institutus auctoritate Paulli III P. M. De reliquis Episcopatibus consulendus Vasæus, loco, quem indicavi.
units.tr: Portugal also has three archbishops, of Braga, Lisbon and Funchal, and under them the bishops of Évora, Viseu, Guarda, Coimbra, Porto, Lamego, Silves, Ceuta and Leiria. The see of Évora is very ancient: Blessed Mancinus, a disciple of Christ, is said to have been the first preacher of the divine Word there and, as some think, its first bishop. Paul III made the church of Évora a metropolitan church and named as its first archbishop the most serene Prince Henry, Infante of Portugal, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church. The see of Silves, in the kingdom of the Algarves, moved from its former seat and succeeded Ossonoba. The bishopric of Leiria was lately founded by the authority of Paul III. Concerning the other bishoprics, consult Vasaeus in the place I have indicated.

units.la: His omnibus, ut & Abbatibus, Monasteriisque quanti sint annuatim Reditus, notant curiose Lucius Marineus Siculus, Damianus à Goes, Eques Lusitanus, & alij.
units.tr: Lucius Marineus Siculus, Damião de Góis, the Portuguese knight, and others have carefully noted how much each of these, and likewise the abbots and monasteries, yields in income every year.

units.la: Ad statum Ecclesiasticum pertinent etiam Fidei Inquisitores, in Sarracenos, Maranos & Iudæos primum creati, qui lapsu temporis vires suas & auctoritatem extendere cœperunt in omnes, quibus alieniores ab Ecclesia Romana mentes: de quorum Institutione Potestateque ego in Historia Belgica, quam Posteritati paro auctoritate mandatoque Ordinum Fœderatarum Provinciarum.
units.tr: Among the ecclesiastical institutions are also the Inquisitors of the Faith, first appointed against Saracens, Marranos and Jews, who in the course of time began to extend their powers and authority over all whose minds were more estranged from the Roman Church. On their institution and power I am preparing a account for posterity in my Belgian History, by the authority and commission of the States of the United Provinces.

units.la: Non alienum duxi hoc loco obiter monere, claruisse quondam Hispaniam Viris tam pijs, quique adeo solam rerum divinarum Cœlestiumque meditationem animo visi fuerunt gessisse, ut pro adserenda. Fide Christiana mortuos Posteritas censuerit dignos, qui in Divorum numerum referrentur. Tales fuerunt, ut ipsorum notant Fasti, sub Alexandro Cyriacus; sub Decio Parmenus, Helmienas, Chrysotolus, Lucas & Mucius: sub Valeriano Laurentius. Fructuosus, Eugurius, Eulogius Emitherius & Chelidonius: sub Diocletiano, Vincentius, Valerius, Optatus, Lupercius, Successus, Martialis, Vrbanus, Iulius, Quintilianus, Publius, Frontonus, Felix, Cæcilianus, Euotus, Primitivus, Apodemus, Saturnini quatuor, Calpophorus, Abuntius, Marcellus cum XI filijs: sub Genserico Vandalorum Rege, Arrianis addictiore, Arcadius, Probus, Pafchasius & Eutychius. Theodorici Gothorum Regis tempore, Turibius, Heimrichii Theodorici fratris, Sabinus; Raimiri Regis, Victor aliique ducenti. Dominicum Calarogitanum (sic dictum ab Calaroga Oxomensis Dioecesis opido: fallo enim Calagurritanus nominatur à Calagurris, hodie Calahorra) Prædicatorum Ordinis parentem Principatus vidit Alphonsi IX Castellæ Regis: Antonium vero Paduanum, Ferdinandi III tempora sunt venerata. Neque suis caruit alter sexus. Nam Divarum classi leguntur adscriptæ sub Alexandro Imperatore Iulitta: sub Diocletiana autem Eulalia, tam Barcinonensis, quam Emeritensis, Iulia, Leucadia, Sabina, Christina & Engratia. Nunilonem & Alodiam supplicio adfecit, quod Christi militiam sequerentur, Maurorum Rex Ayola. Sed de his omnibus & pluribus legendi Laurentius à Padilla Archidiaconus Rondensis in Ecclesia Malacitana, qui librum de Sanctis Hispaniæ emisit; Marineus lib. v. de Reb. Hisp. Franciscus Tarapha, & Damianus à Goes. Marineus item eodem libro non pauca commemorat de Sacris Ædibus Locisque in Hispania, quæ Religiosa & miraculis celebrata. Ionas Aurelianensis Episcopus, qui tempore Karoli Calvi Galliarum Regis floruit, adfirmat Hispaniam, invictos & difertissimos Apostolicæ & Catholicæ Fidei Defensores produxisse; dolens nihilominus lominus multos quoque Hæreticos dedisse. Legendus ille lib. 1. de Cultu Imaginum. Erasinus etiam in Panegyrico ad Philippum 1. Hispaniam vocat fatalem Fidei nostræ murum, unicumque Christianæ Regionis Propugnaculum.
units.tr: I think it not out of place to remark here in passing that Spain once shone with men so pious, and who seemed to devote themselves so wholly to divine and heavenly contemplation, that posterity judged them worthy, for their defence of the Christian faith even unto death, to be counted among the saints. Such were, as the calendars note: under Alexander, Cyriacus; under Decius, Parmenius, Helmienas, Chrysotolus, Lucas and Mucius; under Valerian, Laurentius, Fructuosus, Eugurius, Eulogius, Emitherius and Chelidonius; under Diocletian, Vincentius, Valerius, Optatus, Lupercius, Successus, Martialis, Urbanus, Julius, Quintilianus, Publius, Fronto, Felix, Caecilianus, Euotus, Primitivus, Apodemus, the four Saturnini, Calpophorus, Abuntius, and Marcellus with eleven sons; under Gaiseric, king of the Vandals, a man more given to Arianism, Arcadius, Probus, Paschasius and Eutychius. In the time of Theodoric, king of the Goths, Turibius and Sabinus, brother of Heimrich, Theodoric's brother; in the reign of King Raimir, Victor and two hundred others. Dominic of Calaroga (so called from Calaroga, a town in the diocese of Osma, for he is wrongly named Calagurritanus from Calagurris, today Calahorra), father of the Order of Preachers, was seen in the principality of Alphonso IX, King of Castile; Anthony of Padua was venerated in the times of Ferdinand III. Nor has the other sex lacked its saints: among the company of holy women are enrolled, under the Emperor Alexander, Julitta; under Diocletian, Eulalia (both of Barcelona and of Mérida), Julia, Leucadia, Sabina, Christina and Engratia. Nunilo and Alodia were put to death by the Moorish king Ayola because they followed the warfare of Christ. But concerning all these and many more, read Lorenzo de Padilla, archdeacon of Ronda in the church of Málaga, who published a book on the saints of Spain; Marineus, book 5 of his De rebus Hispaniae; Francisco Tarapha; and Damião de Góis. Marineus likewise in the same book recounts not a few things about the sacred buildings and places in Spain that are celebrated for religion and miracles. Jonas, bishop of Orléans, who flourished in the time of Charles the Bald, King of the Franks, affirms that Spain has produced unconquered and most eloquent defenders of the apostolic and Catholic faith, though he grieves that it has also given many heretics. Read him in book 1 On the Cult of Images. Erasmus too, in his Panegyric to Philip I, calls Spain the fated wall of our faith and the one bulwark of the Christian region.

units.la: Habeat & locum hic Notatio cum Academiarum, quas in Hispania circiter viginti duas numero; interque eas primi loci Salmanticensem, Complutensem, Conimbricensem, Pericianensem, Saguntinam, Oscensem & Ilerdensem: tum Romanorum Pontificum, quorum Hispania fuit genitrix. Eos reperio Damasum, Ioannem xxi, Benedictum xiii, Calixtum iii & Alexandrum vi.
units.tr: Here also a note should be given on the academies, about twenty-two in number in Spain, and among them, in the first rank, those of Salamanca, Alcalá (Complutensis), Coimbra, Perpignan (Pericianensis), Sagunto, Huesca and Lleida; and then of the Roman pontiffs, of whom Spain was the mother. I find these to be Damasus, John XXI, Benedict XIII, Callixtus III and Alexander VI.

units.la: Accipe & hoc loco potius, quam nusquam, Imperatores quos apud se natos Romæ dedit Hispania, Vespasianum, Titum ejus Filium, Nervam, Traianum, Hadrianum, M. Aurelium Antoninum Philosophum, Theodosium Iuniorem. Alphonsum Legionis & Castellæ Regem, ejus nomenclaturæ x, Ferdinandum Austriacum. Quos quidam adnumerant, Maximilianus & Karolus; hic Gandavi, ille Neapoli est natus.
units.tr: Take here also, rather than nowhere, the emperors whom Spain produced and who were born at Rome: Vespasian, his son Titus, Nerva, Trajan, Hadrian, Marcus Aurelius Antoninus the philosopher, and Theodosius the Younger; Alphonso, King of León and Castile, the tenth of that name; and Ferdinand of Austria. Some also count Maximilian and Charles, the one born at Ghent, the other at Naples.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CAP. XI.

units.la: Variæ Hispaniarum Distributiones. Biscaia.
units.tr: Various Divisions of Spain. Biscay.

units.la: GENERATIM quæ dicenda habui de Hispania, absolvi: postulat Methodus, ut speciatim & per partes eam perambulem. Hispaniam ab se debellatam Romani primo, anno ab v. c. 1LVI. C. Cornelio Cethego & Q. Minucio Rufo coss. diviserunt in Citeriorem & Ulteriorem. Citeriorem dicebant, quæ Principi Urbi Imperijque terris proximior erat, inter Iberum sita fluvium & Pyrenæos montes: Ulteriorem vocabant, quæ remotior, ultra Iberum, ad Oceanum vsque extensa. Consulendus Livius lib. xxxii ab v. c.
units.tr: I have now finished what I had to say about Spain in general; method requires that I go through it in detail and part by part. The Romans, when they first subdued Spain in the year 156 from the founding of the city, in the consulship of Gaius Cornelius Cethegus and Quintus Minucius Rufus, divided it into Hither and Further Spain. They called Hither Spain the part that lay nearer to the Prince, the City and the lands of the Empire, situated between the river Ebro and the Pyrenees; Further Spain was the more distant part, beyond the Ebro, extending as far as the Ocean. Livy, book 32 from the founding of the city, should be consulted.

units.la: Postea in tres partiti sunt partes, Citeriorem, multo amplioribus dotatam ultra Iberum finibus, appellantes Tarraconensem: Ulteriorem autem in Baticam & Lusitaniam distinguentes. Tarraconensis, cui nomen ab nobilissima Urbe Tarracone, potiorem complexa Hispaniam, à Pyrenæis, ubi Ortum spectabat, incipiens Montibus, Septemtrionalem partem inter Britannicum vel Cantabricum Oceanum Duriumque fluvium ad Nerium usque promontorium, & Mare Atlanticum vel Externum; Australiorem vero ab ipsdem Pyrenæis, ad Castalonem, ultimam Oretanorum Urbem, milliaribus aliquot infra Bætis fontem, ubi initium erat Baeticæ, inter hanc & Borealis sui procursus brachium Lusitaniam relinquens, protendebat; cui spacio Plinius Ixcvii millia passuum adsignat: Latera utrimque Mari objiciebat, qua quidem Meridiei obversa, Mediterraneo; qua vero Septemtrionibus, Oceano. Baetica, quam Bætis (unde nomen) mediam fere secabat, ad Septemtrionem & Occasum Anam habebat fluvium, quo ab Lusitania separabatur: ad Meridiem Mare spectabat, extra Columnas quidem Gaditanum, intra Columnas Ibericum, quod pars Mediterranei, ut illud Oceani: ad Ortum à Tarraconensi distinguebatur Castalonis fine, vel Saltu Castulonensi, fluvioque, qui hodie Guadelentin, Veteribus Tader fuit appellatus. Plinius huic spacio tribuit ccl millia passuum. Lusitania ad Septemtrionem Durio fluvio terminabatur à Tarraconensi, ad Occidentem & Meridiem Oceano adluebatur; ad Ortum limitem habebat, contra Baeticam, Anam fluvium, Lineamque ductam ab Castris Vicellanis Septemtrionem versus per Augustobrigam ad Manlianum Saltum, ubi Fons erat Tormeis in cujus ripa siniistra visitur Salamantica; vel, ut alij, ad Albocellam Vaccæorum opidum & Ocellum Amnem, cujus alvei vestigia conspiciuntur hodie ad Durij ripas juxta Fermoselium. Videndi de his Finibus Plinius lib. 1 v. natur. histor. cap. xxi, Pomponius Mela lib. 11, Strabo lib. iii, Ptolemæus, Cæsar & alij.
units.tr: Later they divided the country into three parts. Citerior, which had much larger boundaries beyond the Ebro, they named Tarraconensis. Ulterior they distinguished into Baetica and Lusitania. Tarraconensis, named after the most noble city of Tarraco, embraced most of Spain. Beginning at the Pyrenees, where it faced east, with the mountains, it extended along the northern part between the British or Cantabrian Ocean and the river Durius, as far as the promontory of Nerium, and the Atlantic or Outer Sea. Its southern side ran from the same Pyrenees to Castalo, the last city of the Oretani, a few miles below the source of the Baetis, where Baetica began. Leaving Lusitania between itself and the northern arm of its own stretch, it reached that far. Pliny assigns this stretch 197,000 paces. On both sides it faced the sea: the southern side the Mediterranean, the northern side the Ocean. Baetica, which the Baetis (from which it takes its name) cut almost in the middle, had on the north and west the river Anas, by which it was separated from Lusitania. On the south it faced the sea, outside the Pillars the Gaditan sea, and inside the Pillars the Iberian sea, which is part of the Mediterranean, as the other is of the Ocean. On the east it was marked off from Tarraconensis by the boundary of Castalo or the Castulonian forest, and by the river which is today the Guadalentin and was called Tader by the ancients. Pliny assigns this stretch 250,000 paces. Lusitania was bounded on the north by the river Durius, which separated it from Tarraconensis, and was washed on the west and south by the Ocean. On the east it had as its boundary, facing Baetica, the river Anas, and a line drawn from the camp of Vicelle northward through Augustobriga to the Manlian pass, where the spring of the Tormes is, on whose left bank Salamanca is seen; or, as others say, to Albocella, a town of the Vaccaei, and the river Ocellum, whose channel traces can be seen today on the banks of the Douro near Fermoselle. On these boundaries see Pliny, book 4, chapter 21 of the Natural History; Pomponius Mela, book 2; Strabo, book 3; Ptolemy, Caesar and others.

units.la: Sequentibus temporibus Hispaniam in sex fuisse distributam Provincias legimus in Breviario Rufi Festi, quod Valenti Imperatori dicatum: Ac per omnes, inquit, Hispanias sex sunt nunc Provinciæ Tarraconensis, Karthaginiensis, Lusitania, Galliæa, Baetica, Trans-Fretum etiam in solo Terræ Africæ Provincia Hispaniarum est, quæ Tingitanica Mauritania cognominatur. Ex iis Baetica & Lusitania Consulares; cetera, Præsidiales sunt.
units.tr: In later times we read that Spain was divided into six provinces, in the Breviary of Rufus Festus, which was dedicated to the Emperor Valens: "Throughout all the Spains," he says, "there are now six provinces: Tarraconensis, Carthaginiensis, Lusitania, Gallaecia, Baetica; and across the strait, on the African mainland, there is also a province of the Spains, which is called Mauretania Tingitana. Of these, Baetica and Lusitania are consular; the rest are governed by presidents."

units.la: Marianus Scotus, Auctor Notitiæ Provinciarum, Baleares addit Insulas: Sub dispositione, inquit, Viri spectabilis Vicarij Hispaniarum, Consulares Baticæ, Lusitaniæ, Galliciæ; Præsidiales, Tarraconensis, Karthaginiensis, Tingitaniæ, Insularum Balearium.
units.tr: Marianus Scotus, author of the Notitia of the Provinces, adds the Balearic Islands: "Under the authority," he says, "of the distinguished Vicar of the Spains: consular, Baetica, Lusitania, Gallicia; presidial, Tarraconensis, Carthaginiensis, Tingitania, of the Balearic Islands."

units.la: Videtur & aliquando divisa fuisse Hispania in Superiorem & Inferiorem; quum hujus fiat mentio in tabula Marmorea antiqui Sepulchri, quæ in Agro Tiburtino, subque ipso Tibure, ad Pontem Lucanum; sic de Ti. Plautio Silvano inter alia honorifice loquens: PRIMVS. EX. EA. PROVINCIA. MAGNÓ. TRITICI. MODO ANNÓNAM. P. R. ADLEVAVIT. HVNC. LEGATVM, IN IN. HISPANIAM. AD. PRÆFECTVR. VRBIS. REMISSVM SENATVS. IN. PRÆFECTVRA. TRIVMPHALIBVS ORNAMENTIS. HONÓRAVIT. AVCTÓRE. IMP. CÆSARE. AVGVSTO. VESPASIANO. VERBIS. EX ORATIONE. EIVS. Q. I. S. S. &c.
units.tr: Spain also seems at one time to have been divided into Upper and Lower. This is mentioned on a marble tablet from an ancient tomb, which is in the territory of Tibur, just below Tivoli, at the Lucan Bridge. There, speaking honourably of Ti. Plautius Silvanus among other things, it says: "He first, out of that province, relieved the city of Rome's grain supply with a great quantity of wheat. The Senate sent him as legate into Spain, and then to the prefecture of the City, and in the prefecture honoured him with triumphal ornaments, the Emperor Caesar Augustus Vespasian being the author, by the words of his speech..." and so on.

units.la: nisi vitiose Sculptor (nam his talibus non, quantam nonnulli volunt, fides semper est adhibenda) vocem IN geminarit.
units.tr: Unless the sculptor doubled the letter IN by mistake. For inscriptions of this kind one must not always put as much trust as some would like.

units.la: In Majorem etiam & Minorem partitur Stephanus. Alias quæ Gothorum temporibus institutæ, Divisiones, brevitatis gratia, omitto. Videndi Io. Gerundensis Episcop. Paralipomenon Hispaniæ lib. 1. & alij Rerum Hispanicarum Auctores.
units.tr: Stephanus also divides it into Major and Minor. I omit, for brevity's sake, the other divisions made in the time of the Goths. On these see John of Girona, bishop, Paralipomena of Spain, book 1, and the other writers on Spanish affairs.

units.la: Hodie in multa Regna, multosque Principatus distribuitur. Quæ enim Citerior olim, & Tarraconensis postea Romanis, nunc alia est, ad Iberi ripam Borealem, alia ad Africanam. Ad Borealem quidem in Ultramontanis sunt Biscaia & Guipuscoa, in Cismontanis autem cis Cingam Navarra & Aragonia, trans Cingam Catalonia. Africana vel est Cis-Tagana vel Trans-Tagana: Illa in Durij ripa dextra versus Occidentem habet Galliciam, versus Ortum Austriam & Legionem; in sinistra Castiliam & Veterem & Novam. Trans-Taganæ adcensentur Volentia & Murcia. Quæ Ulterioris Baticæ quondam Romanis, comprehendit hodie trans Bætim Granadam & Andaluziam, cis Bætim Extremaduram. Lusitania Romanorum hodie fere Portugallia dicitur. Harum omnium Partium, quo ordine methodoque commemoravi, delineationem, quam potero fidelissime, proponam. Offert se primo loco Biscaia.
units.tr: Today it is divided into many kingdoms and many principalities. What was once Citerior and later Tarraconensis for the Romans is now one part on the northern bank of the Ebro and another on the African side. On the northern side, beyond the mountains, are Biscay and Guipuzcoa; on this side of the mountains, on the near side of the Cinca, Navarre and Aragon; beyond the Cinca, Catalonia. The African side is either on this side of the Tagus or beyond it. The former, on the right bank of the Douro, has to the west Galicia and to the east Austria and León; on the left, Castile, Old and New. Beyond the Tagus are reckoned Valencia and Murcia. What was once Ulterior Baetica for the Romans now comprises, beyond the Baetis, Granada and Andalusia, and on this side of the Baetis, Estremadura. Lusitania of the Romans is today mostly called Portugal. I shall set out a delineation of all these parts, in the order and method in which I have mentioned them, as faithfully as I can. The first to present itself is Biscay.

units.la: BISCAIA Hispaniæ Regio ad Oceanum Montibus obtusa, Arboribusque, quæ Navibus fabricandis idoneæ, referta. Novit hoc præter alias Provincias tota Hispania, cui integræ nonnunquam Classes hinc subvehuntur. Castanearum rum, Nucum, Pomorum, quæ Aurea cognominantur, Resinæ, Metallorum omnis generis, præcipue Ferri, Nigrique Plumbi, & aliarum rerum feracissima. Vino carenti potum subministrant Poma saporis optimi, presła. Margaritas marinæ nō negant conchæ; sed quæ ignobiliores. Temperatius hic clementiusque est Cælum, quam in reliqua Hispana. Magnis enim Montibus circumdata nec frigore nimio infestatur, nec calore nimio torretur. Animalium hic Terrestrium, Marinorum, Volatilium; Fructuum, omniumque, quæ vitæ hominum commodius agendæ necessaria, ingens copia. Magna itidem Hispanis hic (sunt enim portus nobilissimi) cum Gallis, Belgis, Anglis, aliisque Populis commercia. Lana præcipue facit, ut omnia Fora Locaque ab Emtore Venditoreque ferveant. Virginibus Biscainis mos, quamdiu innuptæ sunt, nec Capillos alere, nec velari.
units.tr: BISCAY is a region of Spain on the Ocean, closed in by mountains, and full of trees suitable for building ships. The whole of Spain knows this, beyond the other provinces, since whole fleets are sometimes sent out from here. It is very rich in chestnuts, walnuts, and apples, which are called golden; in resin; and in metals of every kind, especially iron and black lead, and other things. Its apples of the best flavour and its pears supply drink to those who lack wine. The sea shells do not refuse pearls, though they are of lesser quality. The sky here is milder and more temperate than in the rest of Spain, for being surrounded by great mountains it is neither troubled by excessive cold nor scorched by excessive heat. Here there is a great abundance of land animals, sea animals and birds, and of fruits and everything needed for living a more comfortable life. The Spaniards here also have great trade with the French, Flemings, English and other peoples, for it has very famous harbours. Wool above all makes every market and place bustle with buyers and sellers. It is the custom among Biscayan maidens, as long as they are unmarried, neither to grow their hair nor to cover it.

units.la: Quam Biscaiam hodie dicimus, habitarunt olim Cantabri; latius tamen, quam ipsa Biscaia patet, occupatis etiam locis ijs, ubi nunc Guipuscoa & Navarra. Populi celeberrimi multorumque scriptis decantati. De moribus illorum nonnulla tradit Strabo lib. iii. Hi vitam nullam sine Armis esse existimabant. Eleganter Silius Italicus lib. iii: Cantaber ante omnes hiemisque, æstusque, famisque Invictus, palmamque ex omni ferre labore. Mirus amor Populo, quum pigra incanuit ætas, Inbelles jamdudum annos prævertere saxo: Nec vitam sine Marte pati; quippe omnis in armis Lucus caussa sita, & damnatum vivere paci.
units.tr: The people whom we now call Biscayans were formerly the Cantabri, though they occupied a wider area than Biscay itself, including also the places where Guipuzcoa and Navarre now are. They were a most famous people, celebrated in the writings of many. Strabo, book 3, gives some account of their customs. They thought that life was nothing without arms. Silius Italicus, book 3, puts it elegantly: "The Cantabrian, unconquered before all others by winter, heat and hunger, and bearing away the palm from every labour. Strange is the people's love: when its sluggish age has grown grey, they have long since passed their years with the rock, unfit for war; nor can they endure life without Mars, for every grove is set in arms, and they are condemned to live in peace."

units.la: Omnibus Hispaniæ Populis subactis, & in Populi Romani potestatem adductis, soli cum Asturibus aliisque Conregionalibus vinci non potuerunt; unde Horatius lib. ii. Od. vi: Cantabrum indoctum juga ferre nostra.
units.tr: When all the peoples of Spain had been subdued and brought under the power of the Roman people, the Cantabrians alone, together with the Asturians and other neighbouring peoples, could not be conquered. Hence Horace, book 2, Ode 6: "The Cantabrian, untaught to bear our yoke."

units.la: Ultra Montes enim, qui à Pyreneis perpetuo procurrunt ad Nerium usque Promontorium, habitabant, neque, nisi cum maxima difficultate summoque periculo adiri poterant. Debellavit tandem ferocissimam gentem, bello fere quinquennali fractam & defatigatam, C. Cæsar Octavianus Augustus; ipse contra eos, reliquosque Romanis nondum parentes profectus. Horatius lib. iii Carm. Od. viii: Servit Hispanus vetus hostis ora Cantaber sera domitus catena.
units.tr: For they lived beyond the mountains which run continuously from the Pyrenees to the promontory of Nerium, and could be approached only with the greatest difficulty and at the greatest risk. At last the most ferocious nation, worn down and exhausted by a war of nearly five years, was subdued by Gaius Caesar Octavianus Augustus, who himself set out against them and the others who did not yet obey the Romans. Horace, book 3, Ode 8: "The Spaniard, the old enemy, serves, and the Cantabrian, late tamed, wears chains on his neck."

units.la: Et lib. iv Ode xiv, Augustum ipsum adloquens: Te Cantaber non ante domabilis, Medusque & Indus, te profugus Scythes Miratur, o Tutela præsens Italia, Domineque Roma.
units.tr: And book 4, Ode 14, addressing Augustus himself: "The Cantabrian, not previously to be tamed, the Mede and the Indian, and the Scythian in exile, admire you, O present guardian of Italy and mistress Rome."

units.la: Subjungavit autem Cantabros Augustus Vipsanij Agrippæ, ceterorumque Legatorum quos secum duxerat, industria & fortitudine. Horatius lib. i, Epistol. ad Iccium: Cantaber Agrippa, Claudi Virtute Neronis Armenius cecidit.
units.tr: Augustus, however, brought the Cantabrians under his rule through the diligence and courage of Vipsanius Agrippa and his other legates, whom he had taken with him. Horace, book 1, Epistle to Iccius: "Agrippa the Cantabrian, through the valour of Claudius Nero, fell to the Armenian."

units.la: Cantabrorum gentes hac Hispaniæ parte lego & Salenos, quos nominat Pomponius Mela, & Concanos, qui apud Silium Italicum lib. iii. Posteriores male video adfectos apud Strabonem lib. iii. Ubi enim in vulgatis legitur; ἡ ἀπὸ τὰ πρὸς τὰς τῶν Ῥωμαίων συμμαχίας, σεσταλκότες γὰρ ὑπὲρ τῶν Ῥωμαίων οἱ πανιακοὶ καὶ οἱ ἄρκες τῆς παγαῖς & ἰστορίαν οἰκηνῆς, ἀλλὰ Τυίσι. Emendandum Κογκανοὶ. Quidam hos Populos male confundunt cum Coneis, qui ad Fretum Herculeum. De Concanis Horatius lib. iii. Car. Ode iv: Visam Britannos hospitibus feros, Et lætum equino sanguine Concanum.
units.tr: The Cantabrian peoples in this part of Spain, as I read, are also the Saleni, whom Pomponius Mela names, and the Concani, who appear in Silius Italicus, book 3. I see the latter are badly handled in Strabo, book 3. For where the printed texts read ἡ ἀπὸ τὰ πρὸς τὰς τῶν Ῥωμαίων συμμαχίας, σεσταλκότες γὰρ ὑπὲρ τῶν Ῥωμαίων οἱ πανιακοὶ καὶ οἱ ἄρκες τῆς παγαῖς & ἰστορίαν οἰκηνῆς, ἀλλὰ Τυίσι, the reading should be emended to Κογκανοὶ. Some men wrongly confuse these peoples with the Cones, who lived by the Pillars of Hercules. About the Concani, Horace in book 3, Ode 4 of the Odes: "I shall see the Britons, fierce to their guests, and the Concanian, glad in horses' blood."

units.la: Est in Biscaia, præter alia, opidum nobile Bilbao, quod quomdam, uti censent Vilanouanus & Henricus Coquus, Φλαυιοραγια, ut quidem in Græcis Ptolemæi Codicibus legitur. Bilbao dictum, ut quidam opinantur, quasi, commutatione litterarum Hispanis familiari, Bilvao, id est Bellum-vadum. Condidit Didacus Lopcus de Hazo, Cantabrorum Princeps anno ab Christo nato cIɔ cccɔ, aut circiter. Tria cum primis hoc opidum commendant, Situs oportunitas, Annonæ copia, mirabilisque Negociorum Hominumque varietas & multitudo. Situm est in loco plano duobus ab mari milliaribus. Panis habet genus, singularis excellentiæ & bonitatis, quod Incolis Pan del Fuego, vel de Arregoriaga vocitatur. Per hoc Opidum in reliquam Hispaniam importatur, quidquid Anglia, Gallia, Belgica mittunt; per idem ipsum exportatur quidquid cum ijsdem aliisque Regionibus communicandum censet Hispania. Reperire hic est Cives, qui soli quotannis sua pecunia tres quatuorque naves ædificari curant. Hæc & plura Petrus Medinensis, qui sua lingua Hispaniam descripsit.
units.tr: In Biscay, among other places, there is the noble town of Bilbao, which was once, as Vilanova and Henricus Coquus think, called Flavioragia, as is indeed read in the Greek codices of Ptolemy. Bilbao is said, as some suppose, to be named from Bilvao, that is, Bellum-vadum (the fair ford), through a change of letters familiar to the Spanish. Didacus Lopez de Haro, prince of the Cantabrians, founded it in the year 1300 after the birth of Christ, or about then. Three things above all commend this town: the advantage of its situation, the abundance of provisions, and the remarkable variety and quantity of its trade and people. It lies on level ground two miles from the sea. It has a kind of bread of singular excellence and quality, which the inhabitants call "Pan del Fuego" or "de Arregoriaga." Through this town is imported into the rest of Spain whatever England, France and the Low Countries send; through it is exported whatever Spain judges should be shared with those same and other regions. Here one finds citizens who alone each year have three or four ships built at their own expense. These and more things are related by Pedro de Medina, who described Spain in his own language.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CAP. XII.

units.la: Guipus- coa.
units.tr: Guipuscoa.

units.la: GVIPVSCOA Cantabrorum etiam olim erat regio. Nonnulli Lipuscam & Lepuiscam vocant: corrupte, ut notat Stephanus Garybaius ejus Incola, Concluditur ad Ortum Amne Vidasone (qui & Vidorso, Alduida, Iiurta & Beoyvia, medius inter Galliam & Hispaniam) Pyrenaisque Montibus; ad Meridiem Navarræ Regno, ad Occasum Biscaia, de qua præcedenti capite dixi; ad Septemtrionem Mari Cantabrico. Incolæ ijsdem cum Biscainis sunt moribus eademque utuntur lingua, de qua disserui cap. viii. Vulcani officina, Martisque Armamentarium ab Natura videntur hic conlocata: tantam ibi videre est Ferri, Chalybis, factorumque inde Armorum copiam: ut non immerito Murus sive Propugnaculum Regnorum Castellæ & Legionis in quibusdam Regionis Archivis cognominetur. Scribit Navagierus hoc tractu tantum Ferri Chalybisque ecfodi, ut singulis annis xxc millium Ducatorum inde quæstus fiat. Non igitur sine causa Montem ibi scribit Plinius lib. xxxiv. cap. xiv, totum ex Ferro: Cantabria, inquit, maritima parte, Mons praerupte altus, incredibile dictu, totus ex ea materie est. Maris Adcolæ Navigationi Piscibusque, cum aliis, tum quos Baccalaos appellant, capiundis, magno lucro, dant operam.
units.tr: Guipuscoa was also once a region of the Cantabrians. Some call it Lipuscam and Lepuiscam, wrongly, as its inhabitant Stephanus Garybaius observes. It is bounded on the east by the river Vidasone (also called Vidorso, Alduida, Iiurta and Beoyvia, lying between France and Spain) and by the Pyrenean mountains; on the south by the kingdom of Navarre; on the west by Biscay, of which I spoke in the preceding chapter; and on the north by the Cantabrian Sea. The inhabitants have the same customs as the Biscayans and use the same language, which I discussed in chapter viii. Here the workshop of Vulcan and the armoury of Mars seem to have been placed by nature: so great is the abundance of iron, steel and weapons made from them that it is not without reason that in some of the regional archives it is called the Wall or Bulwark of the kingdoms of Castile and Leon. Navagierus writes that so much iron and steel is dug out in this tract that a yearly profit of two hundred thousand ducats is made from it. Not without cause, then, Pliny in book xxxiv, chapter xiv, writes of a mountain there made wholly of iron: In the maritime part of Cantabria, he says, there is a mountain steeply high, incredible to say, wholly made of that material. The dwellers by the sea busy themselves with navigation and with catching fish, among them those they call Baccalaos (cod), to great profit.

units.la: Conlocantur hic à Ptolemæo, Pomponio, Plinio, aliisque, Populi Oregeviones, Autrigones & Varduli: Primorum memoria videtur etiamnum servari in Opidis Orendsin, Oresa & Orio, cujus appellationis ibidem etiam Fluvius est non ignobilis.
units.tr: Here Ptolemy, Pomponius, Pliny and others place the peoples Oregeviones, Autrigones and Varduli. The memory of the first seems still to survive in the towns Orendsin, Oresa and Orio, and there is also a not unknown river bearing this name.

units.la: Metropolis est Tolosa, ad Confluentes sita Araxin & Oriam. Sunt & alia Opida: Placentia, ubi Fabrorum Ferrariorum incredibilis copia: Motrico, vel, ut alij scribendum censent, Monte de Trico, ab scopulo cognomine, qui opido imminet: Fuentarabia, Ptolemæo Φλαονίσαρια: Fanum D. Sebastiani; olim Hiçuru, postea Don-Baitia, & corrupte hodie Donaftien, idem sonans, quod D. Sebastianus. Don enim Cantabris nihil aliud, quam quod Latinis Sanctus, Castellanis Santo. Loca namque in Cantabrorum agris varia plerumque habent nomina, ob Linguarum differentias. Aliter ipsi Cantabri, aliter Hispani reliqui, aliter Galli, qui ipsis Confinales, vocant. Situm est hoc opidum ad ostium Fluminis, quod Menascus Pomponio Melæ, Ptolemæo Μηνόσα, hodie Rio Gurumea, vel Vramea. Portum habet amplissimum, non arte humana, sed sagacis naturæ providentia factum, in quo Naves ab sævientibus undis Ventisque parum faventibus securam & tutissimam inveniunt Stationem. Ingressus patet inter duo Castella; quorum quod ad Orientem, in edito Monte exstructum, Occidentaliore, quod in Rupe, est eminentius. Describit plenissime hanc Regionem Stephanus Garybaius, qui consulendus libro xv. capite ix & quinque sequentibus. Videndus & Florianus del Campo libro i. capite ii.
units.tr: The metropolis is Tolosa, situated at the confluence of the Araxis and the Oria. There are also other towns: Placentia, where there is an incredible number of blacksmiths; Motrico, or, as others think it should be written, Monte de Trico, named after the crag of the same name that overhangs the town; Fuentarabia, called Φλαονίσαρια by Ptolemy; and the Shrine of St. Sebastian, formerly Hiçuru, later Don-Baitia, and corruptly today Donaftien, which sounds the same as D. Sebastianus. For don among the Cantabrians means nothing other than what Sanctus means in Latin and Santo in Castilian. Indeed, places in the lands of the Cantabrians mostly have various names because of differences of language: the Cantabrians themselves have one name, the other Spaniards another, and the French, who border them, another. This town lies at the mouth of the river which Pomponius Mela calls Menascus, Ptolemy Μηνόσα, and which is today the Rio Gurumea or Vramea. It has a very spacious harbour, made not by human skill but by the providence of a keen nature, in which ships find a safe and very secure anchorage from the raging waves and winds that do not favour them. The entrance lies between two castles: of these, the one to the east, built on a high mountain, is the less lofty; the western one, on a rock, is the more prominent. Stephanus Garybaius describes this region most fully; he should be consulted in book xv, chapter ix and the five following. Florianus del Campo, book i, chapter ii, should also be seen.

units.la: CARVT
units.tr: CARVT

units.la: CAPUT XIII.
units.tr: CAPUT XIII.

units.la: Navarra.
units.tr: Navarra

units.la: NAVARRA nomen novum est, recensque natum. Sic enim dicitur, ut quorundam est conjectura, quod Hispani Navas vocent Areas Camporum planas, arboribusque purgatas; quibus tamen in circuitu Silvæ sunt & Dumeta; unde Navarra regio, quæ complures habet Navas. Pecori est agriculturæque valde commoda: &, quamvis Pyrenæis opposita, atque adeo montibus undique conclusa, finitimas tamen versus Hispaniæ interiora Provincias Acris clementia superat. De Navarrorum gente multa Ioannes Gerundensis Episcopus Hispaniæ Paralipomen. lib. v. Rodericus Sanctius part.i. cap. xii, & alij.
units.tr: Navarra is a new name, of recent origin. According to some conjecture, it is so called because the Spaniards call the flat, tree-cleared plains of the fields Navas, though these are still surrounded by woods and thickets; hence the region of Navarra, which has many Navas. It is very suitable for pasturage and farming. Although it lies opposite the Pyrenees and is therefore enclosed on every side by mountains, its mildness surpasses that of the neighbouring inland provinces of Spain. Much about the people of Navarre is found in John, Bishop of Girona, Paralipomenon book 5, and in Rodrigo Sánchez, part 1, chapter 12, and others.

units.la: Habitarunt hic olim, qui Vascones Plinio Tacitoque; Ptolemæo Οὐάσκονες: quos postea in Galliam transmigrasse constat. Berones, Βήρωνες Straboni & Ptolemæo, quos ille antea Tyrios notat vocatos: nomen manere putatur hodieque in Opido Briones apud quos Bero fluvius, qui Vero Martiali, corrupte dicam, an consueta genti commutatione Litterarum B & V? Suessitani, Livio; quorum appellationem adhuc superesse volunt quidam in Sanguessa opido. Bergistani, qui apud eundem Livium lib. xxxvi, Καρίσιοι denique, quorum apud Ptolemæum est mentio.
units.tr: Here once lived the Vascones, as Pliny and Tacitus call them, and Ptolemy calls them Οὐάσκονες [Ouaskones]; it is established that they later migrated into Gaul. The Berones, Βήρωνες [Bērōnes] in Strabo and Ptolemy, whom Strabo earlier notes were called Tyrians; their name is thought to survive today in the town of Briones, near which flows the river Bero, which Martial calls Vero. Should I say this is a corruption, or is it the customary interchange of the letters B and V in that people's speech? The Suessitani (Livy), whose name some wish to survive in the town of Sanguessa. The Bergistani, who in Livy book 36 are mentioned by the same name, and finally the Καρίσιοι [Karisioi], who are mentioned in Ptolemy.

units.la: Regionis Caput hodie Pompelon; Πομπήλων apud Ptolemæum & Strabonem: nomen & nunc servans, Pampelona vulgo dicta. Vocemhanc per Ae diphthongon scribendam innuit Lapis Tarraconensis, nisi Sculptoris manus aberrarit:
units.tr: The capital of the region today is Pompelon, Πομπήλων [Pompēlōn] in Ptolemy and Strabo, which also keeps its name, commonly called Pampelona. That the word should be written with the diphthong Ae is suggested by a stone from Tarragona, unless the hand of the carver went astray:

units.la: SEMPRONIAE
units.tr: SEMPRONIAE

units.la: LVCI. F. FLACIDAE POMPAELONENSI FLAMINICAE. CONSENSV CONCILII. P. H. C. CORNELIVS. VALENS MARITVS. S. P. F.
units.tr: To Sempronia Flacida, daughter of Lucius, of Pompaelo, flaminica, by decree of the council. Cornelius Valens, her husband, erected this at his own expense.

units.la: Euci legit Clusius. P. E. Clusius.
units.tr: Clusius read it as "Euci". P. E. Clusius.

units.la: Quibusdam Pompeiopolis (quod à Cn. Pompeio Magno condita) & Martua dicitur: Olim etiam Athanagiam fuisse nuncupatam, cujus Livius meminit, memoriæ prodit Io. Gerundensis Episcopus lib. v. Paralip. Hisp. Athanagia tamen Floriano Manresa est, aliis Tarrega, nonnullis Sanahuja. Secundæ Classis sunt Iturissa Pomponio Melæ; Ἰτουρίσσα, Ptolemæo; Iurissa Antonino, corrupte, hodie Sanguessa, cujus jam memini; Suessam olim nominatam scribit intellexisse se ex Archivis publicis Florianus del Campo. Cascantum, ut Antoninus vocat: Cascantenses habet Plinius: corrupte apud Ptolemæum Βασκάντων pro Κασκάντων: Ejus mentio in Nummo Tiberij Imperatoris; TI. CÆSAR DIVI AVG. F, AVGVSTVS; & in aversa parte supra Tauri effigiem MVX NIOIP. NIC IP. & infra CASCANTVM. Logronium, quod, ut censent Clusius & Tarapha, Plinio & aliis Iuliobriga, Cantabrorum opidum: Inscriptio Tarraconensis: C. ANNIO. L. F. QVIR. FLAVO. IVLIOBRIGENS EX. GENTE. CANTABRORVM PROVINCIA. HISPANIA. CITERIOR. OB. CAVSAS. VTILITATESQVE PVBLICAS. FIDELITER. ET CONSTANTER. DEFENSAS
units.tr: Some call it Pompeiopolis, because it was founded by Gnaeus Pompey the Great, and Martua. Once it was also called Athanagia, which Livy mentions; John, Bishop of Girona, Paralipomenon book 5 on Spain, records this. Athanagia, however, is Manresa according to Florian, Tarrega according to others, and Sanahuja according to some. Of the second class are Iturissa in Pomponius Mela, Ἰτουρίσσα [Iturissa] in Ptolemy, and Iurissa in Antoninus (wrongly), today Sanguessa, which I have already mentioned. Florian del Campo writes that he understood from the public archives that it was formerly called Suessa. Cascantum, as Antoninus calls it; Pliny has the Cascantenses; in Ptolemy it is wrongly given as Βασκάντων [Baskantōn] for Κασκάντων [Kaskantōn]. It is mentioned on a coin of the Emperor Tiberius: TI. CAESAR DIVI AVG. F. AVGVSTVS; and on the reverse, above the figure of a bull, MVX NIOIP. NIC IP., and below, CASCANTVM. Logronium, which Clusius and Tarafa think is Iuliobriga of Pliny and others, a town of the Cantabrians. Inscription from Tarragona: To Gaius Annius Flavus, son of Lucius, of the Quirina tribe, of the Iuliobrigenses, of the people of the Cantabrians, of the province of Hispania Citerior, who on account of public causes and advantages was faithfully and steadfastly defended.

units.la: Floriano tamen Iuliobriga est Oliva; Henrico Coquo Aguilar del Campo. Calagurris Livio, Ausonio & Antonino, in cujus tamen nonnullis exemplaribus Calagorra & Calagurra; Καλάγυρις Straboni; Καλαγορρα Ptolemæo, vitiose; hodie Calahorra, ut volunt Ambrosius Moralis, Varrerius & Marineus: in Iberi ripa. Plinio duplices sunt Calagurritani, & Fibularenses & Nassici; hi ad Ilergetes pertinebant, ut postea dicam; illi ad Vasconés & Navarram nostram. Fibularenses fuerunt Calagurritani Martyres Hemeterius & Chelidonius, de quibus Prudentius. Vasconum enim ibi mentio & Iberi Fluminis, ad quod Calagurritani Fibularenses habitabant, quum Nassici procul inde ad Pyrenæos montes prope Gallicum fluvium, qui hodie Gallego. Vtra autem Calagurris patria sit censenda Quintiliani Oratoris, non facile quis diffinierit. D. Hieronymus ex Eusebij Chronico: Quintilianus ex Hispania Calagurritanus, primus Romæ publicam Scholam tenuit, & Salarium à Fisco accepit, & claruit. Ausonius in commemoratione Rhetorum Burdigalensium: Primus Burdigalæ columen dicere Minervæ Alter Rhetoricæ Quintiliane Togæ: Adferat vsque licet Fabium Calagurris Alumnum, Non fit Burdigalæ dum Cathedra inferior.
units.tr: According to Florian, however, Iuliobriga is Oliva; according to Henricus Cocus, Aguilar del Campo. Calagurris in Livy, Ausonius and Antoninus, though in some copies of Antoninus it is Calagorra and Calagurra; Καλάγυρις [Kalagyris] in Strabo; Καλαγορρα [Kalagorra] in Ptolemy (incorrectly); today Calahorra, as Ambrosio Morales, Varrerius and Marineo maintain, on the bank of the Ebro. In Pliny there are two kinds of Calagurritani: the Fibularenses and the Nassici. The latter belonged to the Ilergetes, as I shall say later; the former to the Vascones and to our Navarra. The Fibularenses were the Calagurritani martyrs Hemeterius and Chelidonius, of whom Prudentius writes. Mention is made there of the Vascones and of the river Ebro, by which the Calagurritani Fibularenses lived, while the Nassici lived far from there, near the Pyrenean mountains, close to the Gallic river which today is the Gallego. Which Calagurris should be considered the homeland of the orator Quintilian is not easy to determine. Saint Jerome, from Eusebius's Chronicle: "Quintilian, a Calagurritan from Hispania, first held a public school at Rome, received a salary from the treasury, and flourished." Ausonius, in his commemoration of the rhetoricians of Bordeaux: "First at Bordeaux, the pillar of Minerva's speech; second, Quintilian, in the toga of rhetoric. Let Calagurris bring forward Fabius as her son; while the chair at Bordeaux is not lower."

units.la: Beronum etiam urbem Variam nominat Plinius, Iberus, inquit, amnis navigabilis commercio dives ortus in Cantabris, haud procul opido Iuliobriga, CCCCL. M. P. fluens; navium per CCLX. M. P. à Varia opido capax. Est item Ναεία Ptolemæo in Beronibus, qui infra Autrigones sunt. Vicus est juxta Logronium in Variæ Vrbis vestigijs, qui nomen retinet. Varcam enim nuncupant. In Beronibus etiam locat Ptolemæus Τείτιον μεγάλον. Plinius autem Tritium inter decem Autrigonum Civitates numerat. Hodie juxta Haiaram urbem Tritium nomen adhuc suum tuetur, sed in Vici formam redactum.
units.tr: Pliny also names the city of the Berones Varia. "The Ebro," he says, "is a navigable river, rich in trade, which rises among the Cantabrians, not far from the town of Iuliobriga, flowing 450 miles; ships of capacity can sail 260 miles from the town of Varia." Ptolemy also has Ναεία [Naeia] among the Berones, who are below the Autrigones. There is a village near Logroño, on the remains of the city of Varia, which keeps the name, for they call it Varca. Ptolemy also places Τείτιον μεγάλον [Teition megalon] among the Berones. Pliny, however, counts Tritium among the ten cities of the Autrigones. Today near the city of Haro, Tritium still keeps its name, but has been reduced to the form of a village.

units.la: Navarram porro suis Hispaniæ Regnis primus adscribere cœpit Ferdinandus Catholicus, pulso Ioanne Alani F. Dynasta Albretano. Hic, ducta Catharina Galtonis F. Navarræ regina, Comite Fecensi, Bearnij, Bigorræ ac Viennæ Principe, cum Ludovico XII Francorum Rege arma junxerat contra Venetos, Hispanos, Germanos, Iuliumque II. P. M. Indignatus Pontifex Regem proscripsit & excommunicavit; Regnumque ipsius, quasi in commissum cecidisset, occupandum dedit Ferdinando; qui, expugnatis Pompelone & universa pene, paucis Opidis Arcibusque exceptis, Navarrea Ditione, profligatisque Veris Dominis, ante nonaginta circiter annos usurpare cœpit, & defunctus ad Successores transmisit nomen regium: quo jure, multis exponit Ælius Antonius Nebrissensis de bello Navarreo lib. I. cap. I. & seqq. Retinuerunt Nomen nihilominus pultorum Principum heredes: quorum hæc series:
units.tr: Ferdinand the Catholic first began to add Navarre to his Spanish kingdoms, after expelling John, son of Alan, lord of Albret. He, having married Catherine, daughter of Gaston, queen of Navarre, count of Foix, prince of Béarn, Bigorre and Vienne, had joined arms with Louis XII, king of the Franks, against the Venetians, the Spaniards, the Germans and Julius II, supreme pontiff. Indignant, the Pontiff proscribed and excommunicated the king, and gave his kingdom, as though it had fallen forfeit, to be seized by Ferdinand. Ferdinand, having stormed Pamplona and nearly the whole of Navarre, except a few towns and citadels, and having overthrown the rightful lords, began to usurp it about ninety years ago, and on his death passed the royal title to his successors. Antonio de Nebrija, in his De bello Navarreo book 1, chapter 1 and following, sets out the right by which this was done. Nevertheless, the heirs of several princes kept the name, and their line is as follows:

units.la: IOANNES Alani F. Dynasta Albretanus. Vxor KATHARINA Galtonis F. Galtonis N. Navarræ Regina, Comes Fecensis, Bearnii Bigorræ & Viennæ.
units.tr: John, son of Alan, lord of Albret. Wife Catherine, daughter of Gaston, king of Navarre, count of Foix, of Béarn, Bigorre and Vienne.

units.la: HENRICVS Albretanus Rex Navarræ, Comes Bearnii, Foxii, Bigorræ & Armigniaci. Vxor MARGARETA Valesia, Soror Germanæ Francisci I Galliarum Regis, Katolii Alenconii vidua.
units.tr: Henry of Albret, king of Navarre, count of Béarn, Foix, Bigorre and Armagnac. Wife Margaret of Valois, sister of Francis I, king of the French, widow of Charles, duke of Alençon.

units.la: IOANNA Albretana Navarræ Regina, &c. Nupsit Antonio Borbonio Duc.
units.tr: Joan of Albret, queen of Navarre, etc. She married Antoine de Bourbon, duke.

units.la: HENRICVS Borbonius Rex Galliæ Navarræque Christianissimus.
units.tr: Henry of Bourbon, most Christian king of France and Navarre.

units.la: Navarræ Historiam composuit Karolus Infans istius Regni, quæ nondum est evulgata.
units.tr: Charles, the infant of this kingdom, composed a history of Navarre, which has not yet been published.
