units.la: CAPVT XIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV.

units.la: Arago- nia.
units.tr: Aragonia.

units.la: ARAGONIÆ adhærent ad Caurum Navarra; ad Vulturnum Catalonia; qua Africo exposita, Caftiliam spectat; qua Aquiloni, Pyrenæos habet montes. Aragonenses corrupta voce à Tarraconensibus dici non inconcinne opinatur Antonius Nebrissensis. Subscribit illi Ioannes Vasæus in Hispaniæ Chronico. Et ego lubens. L. Vallæ placet Aragonia nomen esse ab Autrigonibus, Hispaniæ populis. Alij ab Aragone fluvio, qui illic ortus Iberum influere perhibetur. Nonnulli ab Herculis Ara Agonalibusque Ludis derivant: quod si verum, mirum tam altum obstinatumque apud Veteres Scriptores de Aragonia esse silentium.
units.tr: Aragon borders on Navarre to the north-west and on Catalonia to the south-east. Where it faces south-west it looks towards Castile, and where it faces north it has the Pyrenees. Antonius Nebrissensis thinks, not unreasonably, that the Aragonese are so called from the Tarraconenses, the name having been corrupted. John Vaseus agrees with him in his Chronicle of Spain, and I gladly do too. Lorenzo Valla prefers that the name Aragonia comes from the Autrigones, a people of Spain. Others derive it from the river Aragon, which is said to rise there and flow into the Ebro. Some derive it from the altar of Hercules and the Agonalian Games. But if that were true, it would be strange that the ancient writers are so deep and stubborn in their silence about Aragonia.

units.la: Sedes hic habuerunt olim suas Iaccetani, Ἰακκητανοὶ apud Ptolemæum, à quibus hodie Iacca urbs: corrupte Lacetani, nisi alij sint populi, apud Plinium, Cæsarem & Livium videntur appellari; nec minus fortean emendate Acitani vel Accitani apud Macrobium lib.1.cap.xix, qui eos Martis Simulacrum, radijs ornatum, maxima religione colere scribit, Necynqi nominare. Sedentani Livio Plinioque; Σιδηνοὶ Straboni: Sedentana Co-hors etiam est apud Silium Italicum lib.iii. Nescio an ijdem qui Hedetani alijs, de quibus vide ad Valentiam. Surdaones Plinio; quorum loco Sardones Caspar Varrerius substituit; addens, memoriam eorum conservari in Sardonum Campo, qui vulgo Campos de Serdania. Ilergetum etiam magna pars hic quondam habuit: de quibus ad Cataloniam.
units.tr: The Iaccetani once had their seats here, Ἰακκητανοὶ [Iakkētanoi] in Ptolemy, and from them the town of Jaca takes its name today. The form Lacetani, found in Pliny, Caesar and Livy, seems to be a corruption, unless these are different peoples. Perhaps no less correctly, Acitani or Accitani appears in Macrobius (book 1, chapter 19), who writes that they worshipped with the greatest reverence an image of Mars adorned with rays, and calls it Necyn. The Sedentani are in Livy and Pliny; Σιδηνοὶ [Sidēnoi] in Strabo. A Sedentana cohort also occurs in Silius Italicus, book 3. I do not know whether they are the same as the Hedetani mentioned by others, on whom see under Valencia. Pliny has the Surdaones, for whom Caspar Varrerius substitutes the Sardones, adding that their memory is preserved in the Plain of the Sardones, commonly called the Campos de Serdania. A great part of the Ilergetes also once lived here; on them see under Catalonia.

units.la: Metropolis & Regni caput Cæsaraugusta Plinio alijsque; Καισάρεια Αὐγούστα Ptolemæo. Nominatur sæpe in Nummis Veterum. In duobus æneis Augusti Vexillum erectum visitur, hasta in basi adfixa: quod signum erat deducendæ Coloniæ: in uno eorum adparet Augusti effigies, & hic titulus, DIVI F. AVGVSTVS; in aversa parte, qua Vexillum est, CÆSARAVGVSTA L. CASSIO CN. F. L. N. II VIR: In altero circum Augusti effigiem AVGVSTVS DIVI F; & averså parte, CÆSARAVGVSTA M. POR. CN. F. A. N. II VIR. Alios alijs legendos relinquo. Sic Prudentius de Martyribus Cæsar-Augustanis:
units.tr: The metropolis and capital of the kingdom is Caesaraugusta, according to Pliny and others; Καισάρεια Αὐγούστα [Kaisareia Augoustā] in Ptolemy. It is often named on ancient coins. On two bronze coins a standard is seen erected, with a spear fixed in its base; this was the sign of the founding of a colony. On one of them appears the effigy of Augustus with this inscription: DIVI F. AVGVSTVS. On the reverse, where the standard is, is CAESARAVGVSTA L. CASSIO CN. F. L. N. II VIR. On the other, around the effigy of Augustus, is AVGVSTVS DIVI F; and on the reverse, CAESARAVGVSTA M. POR. CN. F. A. N. II VIR. I leave it to others to read them differently. So Prudentius, on the martyrs of Caesaraugusta:

units.la: Cæsar-Augustam vocitamus Vrbem:
units.tr: We call the city Caesar-Augusta:

units.la: Hodie Carragoça, Academia nobilis. Conditorem ejus ferunt Iubam Mauritaniæ Regem, & ab eo Saldybam appellatam, quasi Iubæ domum: postea vero, priore repudiato nomine, Cæsaris Augusti nomen illi fuisse inditum. Sita est in ripa Fluminis Iberi, loco plano, ex quo Iberus insigni Ponte lapideo longoque (cujus etiam Strabo facit mentionem lib. iii) trajicitur. Urbis autem Situs Soleæ Calcei formam refert. Portas habet quatuor ad totidem Mundi partes spectantes. Validissimis muris cincta, crebrisque Turribus probe munita. Extra Muros priores quamplurimæ sunt Domus, & quasi altera Civitas, quas Cæsar-Augustani Populationes appellant. Duo sunt ibi memoratu dignissima: Xenodochium inter alia Christiani orbis opera loci non postremi; alterum Domus prope Urbem in Campo amœnissimo satis grandis & insignis, quæ vulgo Alia pharia nuncupatur, de qua consulendus Marineus Siculus. In hac Urbe Reges Aragoniæ ab ejus Archiepiscopo, qui Primus Regni, Diadema foliti accipere. Ab eadem Iter ducit Benebarnum, Antoninus per Pyrenæum in Galliam Aquitanicam. Civitates reliquæ: Osca Latinis, Oxa Ptolemæo & Plutarcho in Sertorio: Hodie Huesca: Cives ejus Osicenses Cæsari nominantur: Oscensis Argenti meminit Livius lib. xxiv: Plutarchus auctor, Sertorium hanc Urbem delegisse, in quam Filii Principum Virorum, Hispaniarum Obsides, studiorum specie, accitis Disciplinarum Magistris, mitterentur. Est ibi hodieque non ignobilis Academia: Ecteosia mendose vocatur Velleio Paterculo: ubi Sertorium interemtum scribit: In Vetustis Nummis Urbs Victrix videtur cognominari; si ita notas vv. osca liceat cum Antonio Augustino interpretari. Tyriaffona Civitas apud Montem Caci, quam à Tyriis & Ausonijs conditam fuisse nonnulli opinantur. Iacca, jacens in Convallibus, Iaccetanorum quondam, ut monui, sedes, Iaxa Ptolemæo. Catalajuta, in campestri loco, ex ruinis nata Bilbilitanis, quæ cum multis aliis Antiquitatum monimentis, medio Miliari Hispanico ab hoc opido hodie visuntur, in Colle, qui vulgo Bamboía vel Baubola, adludente ad Urbis jacentis appellationem nomine: Cingitur Mons ille in orbem fere ab Salone flumine; quem situm Bilbili tribuit alumnus ejus & Civis (vide lib. Epigr. lxii) Valerius Martialis lib. x. Epigram. cıııı: Municipes Augusta mihi quos Bilbilis acri Monte creat, rapidis quem Salo cingit aquis.
units.tr: Today it is Zaragoza, a noted university town. Its founder is said to have been Juba, King of Mauretania, and it was called by him Saldyba, as if "Juba's house". Later, that name being rejected, it was given the name of Caesar Augustus. It lies on the bank of the river Ebro, on a flat site, and the Ebro is crossed there by a famous long stone bridge (Strabo also mentions it, book 3). The shape of the city resembles a sole of a sandal. It has four gates facing the four quarters of the world. It is surrounded by very strong walls and well protected by frequent towers. Outside the older walls there are very many houses, almost a second city, which the people of Zaragoza call the Populationes. Two things there are most worthy of mention: the hospice, one of the works of the Christian world, outstanding among others for its place; and another, a fairly large and notable house near the city in a most pleasant field, commonly called Alia Pharia, about which Marineus Siculus should be consulted. In this city the kings of Aragon were accustomed to receive the diadem from its archbishop, who is the first of the kingdom. From it a road leads to Benabarnum, which Antoninus gives through the Pyrenees into Aquitanian Gaul. Other cities: Osca for the Latins, Oxa for Ptolemy and for Plutarch in his Life of Sertorius; today Huesca. Its citizens are called Osicenses by Caesar. Livy, book 24, mentions the Oscensian silver. Plutarch, the author, says that Sertorius chose this city, to which the sons of the leading men of Spain, as hostages, were sent under the pretext of study, with teachers of the arts summoned to them. There is still a not unimportant university there today. Ecteosia is a wrong form in Velleius Paterculus, where he writes that Sertorius was killed there. On ancient coins the city seems to be surnamed Urbs Victrix, if one may so read the letters osca, following Antonio Augustino. Tyriaffona is a city near Mount Caci, which some think was founded by the Tyrians and Ausonians. Jaca, lying in the valleys, was once, as I have noted, the seat of the Iaccetani; Iaxa in Ptolemy. Catalayuta lies in a plain, arising from the ruins of the Bilbilitani. Together with many other monuments of antiquity, it is seen today a Spanish mile from this town, on a hill commonly called Bamboía or Baubola, the name playing on the name of the lying city. That hill is almost encircled by the river Jalón (Salo), and its situation at Bilbilis is attributed by Valerius Martial, its nursling and citizen (see the book of Epigrams, lxii), in book 10, epigram 103: "The townsmen whom Bilbilis, on its sharp mountain, bears to me, which the Salo girds with its swift waters."

units.la: Sic Paullinus ad Ausonium, Bilbilim acutis scopulis pendentem, prodit. Quod autem in Monte, Altam vocat idem Martialis scribens ad Licinianum lib. i. Epigram. i, quod quia multorum Hispaniæ locorum meminerit, semel adscribam: Vir Celtiberis non tacende Gentibus, Nostraque laus Hispaniæ, Videbis altam Liciniane Bilbilim, Equis & Armis nobilem: Sterilemq; canum nivibus effractis sacrum a Vadaveronem montibus: Et delicati dulce b Botrodinemus, Pomona quod felix amat: Tepidum natabis lene c Congedi vadum, Mollesque Nym1>harum d lacus, Quibus remissum corpus adstringas brevi e Salone, qui ferrum gelat. Praestabit illic ipsa figendas prope f Voberta prendenti feras: Aestus serenos aureo franges Tago, Obscurus umbris Arborum: Avidam vigens g Dircenna placabit sitim, Et Nemea, quæ vincit nives. At quum December canus, & Bruma impotens Aquilone rauco mugiet: Aprica repetes Tarraconis littora, Tuamque Laletaniam, &c.
units.tr: So Paulinus, in his letter to Ausonius, speaks of "Bilbilis hanging on sharp crags". That Martial calls it "high" in the mountain, writing to Licinianus in book 1, epigram 1, I will quote once in full, since he mentions many places of Spain: "Licinianus, you shall see high Bilbilis, a man not to be silent about among the Celtiberians, the praise of our Spain, famous for horses and arms; and the barren Vadaveron, sacred to the dogs, with its mountains broken by snows; and the sweet Botrodinemus, of the delicate, which fruitful Pomona loves; you shall swim in the mild, gentle ford of the Congedus, and the soft lakes of the Nymphs, by which you may relax your body in a short time; Salo, which chills iron. There, Voberta itself will provide wild beasts for you to hunt nearby; you will break the clear heat with the golden Tagus, dark with shadows of trees; the lively Dirce will satisfy your eager thirst, and Nemea, which surpasses snow. But when grey December and impotent Winter bellow with the hoarse north wind, you will seek again the sunny shores of Tarraco, and your Laletania, etc."

units.la: Sic idem Martialis lib. x. epig. civ, ad Librum suum: Hispana pete Tarraconis Arces: Illinc te rota tollet, & citatus
units.tr: So the same Martial, book 10, epigram 104, to his book: "Seek the citadels of Spanish Tarraco; from there the wheel will carry you off, and swiftly..."

units.la: a Sic ex MS. legit Turnebus, quum in Vulpatis divisum legatur Vada Verrarum; agnoscens Montis nomen. Pettancut hoc quæ scribit Hieronymus Paullus Barcinonensis libro de Fluminibus & Montibus Hispaniæ: Quidam non temere Certaminum montes et crepitant ab alio effractum aliquo in loco ... quem nunc Vada vocatum corrupte vocant.
units.tr: a Turnebus reads this from a manuscript, whereas in the printed editions it is divided as Vada Verrarum; he recognizes the name of a mountain. Hieronymus Paulus of Barcelona, in his book on the rivers and mountains of Spain, writes this: "Some mountains are not without reason called the 'crags of contests', and they rattle when broken by another ... which, now called Vada, they wrongly call."

units.la: b Oppidum quondam, hodie Vicus haud procul Segobriga: ab Græcho dictum notat Polybius. Meminit & Martial. lib. xiii, epig. xxviii.
units.tr: b A former town, today a village not far from Segobriga. Polybius notes that it was named after Grecchus. Martial also mentions it, book 13, epigram 28.

units.la: c Fluvii nomen prope Bilbilim: hodie Congeda, vel, ut alij, Rio de Sedes.
units.tr: c The name of a river near Bilbilis: today the Congeda, or, as others say, the Rio de Sedes.

units.la: d Ex duplici enim Lacu videbatur Congedus profluere.
units.tr: d For the Congedus seemed to flow out of a double lake.

units.la: e Hodie Xaxan Bilbilis Iusti no lib. xliv ab urbe adjacente; Aqua fortean Bilbilitana Antonino.
units.tr: e Today Jaján. Bilbilis, in Justin book 44, is named from the neighbouring city; perhaps the Aqua Bilbilitana of Antoninus.

units.la: f melius Voberta: hodie Bobleta.
units.tr: f Better Voberta; today Bobleta.

units.la: g fontis videtur nomen. Altam Bilbilin, & tuum Salonem Quinclo forsitan essedo videbis.
units.tr: g This seems to be the name of a spring. You will see "high Bilbilis" and "your Salo" perhaps from a Quinctian chariot.

units.la: An per Quinctium Essedum notat iter inter Tarraconem & Bilbilim quintiduanum? Sunt hodie Leucæ Hispanicæ xlviii, aut circiter. Auro ferroque superbam facit Bilbilim idem Poëta lib. xii. Epig. xviii: Me multos repetita post Decembres Accepit mea, rusticumque fecit, Auro Bilbilis & superba Ferro: Hic pigri colimus labore dulci Botrodum, a Plateamque: Celtiberis Hæc sunt nomina crassiora terris:
units.tr: Does "Quinctian chariot" perhaps denote a journey of five days between Tarraco and Bilbilis? Today there are about forty-eight Spanish leagues. The same poet, book 12, epigram 18, makes Bilbilis "proud of gold and iron": "My Bilbilis, proud of gold and iron, after many repeated Decembers, received me and made me rustic. Here we cultivate with sweet toil Botrodum and Platea; these are the names too coarse for the Celtiberian lands."

units.la: Inter Bilbilim & Segobrigam (quæ hodie Segorbia putatur) Sertorius & Metellus memorabili prælio conflixerunt, ut apud Appianum & alios est legere. Βίλβις Ptolemæo corrupte. Augusta Bilbilis cognominatur Martiali, ut jam vidimus; quemadmodum & in multis Veterum Numismatum Inscriptionibus. Sunt & alia Aragoniæ Opida: Barbastrum, Arcubus ferreis nobile; Βαρτίνα Ptolemæo; Bortina Antonino, ut nonnulli censent: Putat tamen Surita Bortinam sua nunc ostentare vestigia ad Almuderar opidum, ibique inter alia conspici quasdam Viæ erutæ Substructiones Monsonium in Regni situm umbilico, ad Cingæ ripam, cui Collis imminet, à quo nomen opido: Conventibus Regnorum Aragoniæ, Valentiæque & Principatus Cataloniæ celebris sedes. Fere est, ut Hieronymus Surita, cui emendatius debemus Itinerarium, quod sub Antonini Augusti nomine circumfertur, censeat esse Toloum Antonini: ait enim inter Barcinonem & Cæsaraugustam nullum exstare opidum, quod isti adplicare mansioni certo audeat: Vulgo Monçon: fertilis agri & aprici situs. Fraga, inter Ilerdam & Cæsaraugustam: Φραγα Ptolemæo; Gallicum Antonino, ut Varrerius censet; Alij Gallicum locant, ubi nunc Zuera, in cujus agro vetustorum Pavimentorum vestigia visuntur: Fluvius ibi nomen retinet, qui Gallego nominatur: cui jure vetustas Gallici nomen tribuit; quod, summo transcenso Pyrenæo supra opidum, cui Salientis nomen impositum, in ipsa terra Gallia oriatur. Gurrea olim Forum Gallorum, Antonino inter Cæsaraugustam & Pyrenæos. Aierbium, in cujus solo quondam stetisse creditur Ebellinum, Antonino cum aliis nominatum. Vrgella, Orgellum Aimonio; Ορελλα forte Ptolemæo, opidum haud procul Sicoris fonte. Fuerunt & alia Opida, sed quæ diruta, quorumque nulla hodie vestigia. Inter illa non ignobilis Calagurris Nassica, alia ab ea, quam in Navarra descripsi. Hanc Iulia cognomine decoratam fuisse loquuntur Veteres Nummi: In æreo quodam effigies est Juvenis Augusti, cum hac Inscriptione NASSICA; in aversa facie, Taurus est sculptus, insigne Municipiorum, cum Inscriptionibus, supra quidem Taurum CALAG. infra vero IVLIA: in alio cum Augusti imagine AVGVSTVS. MV. CAL. IVLIAS; in aversa parte supra Tauri effigiem, L. BÆB. PRISCO C. CRAV. BROG. II VIR: in tertio cum Augusti effigie MVN. CAL. IVL. in aversa facie supra Taurum II VIR. L. CRAVIO; infra alterius Duum-viri nomen est vetustate extritum. Posteriores Nummi docent hanc Calagurrim Municipij nomen obtinuisse. Cives ejus Calagurritani nominantur ab Cæsare i belli Civilis Commentario: eosque Corporis sui Custodes habuisse Augustum notat Suetonius in ejus vita cap. xlix. Plinius Nassicos cognominat. Addantur hic Coronidis loco
units.tr: Between Bilbilis and Segobriga (which is thought to be today's Segorbe), Sertorius and Metellus fought a memorable battle, as one may read in Appian and others. Βίλβις [Bilbis] is a corrupt form in Ptolemy. Augusta Bilbilis is its surname in Martial, as we have seen, as also in many inscriptions on ancient coins. There are also other towns of Aragon: Barbastro, famous for its iron arches; Βαρτίνα [Bartina] in Ptolemy; Bortina in Antoninus, as some think. Surita, however, thinks that Bortina still displays its traces at the town of Almudévar, where, among other things, some excavated substructures of a road can be seen. Monzón, situated in the middle of the kingdom on the bank of the Cinca, which a hill overhangs and from which the town takes its name, is a famous seat for the assemblies of the kingdoms of Aragon, Valencia and the Principality of Catalonia. Surita, to whom we owe a more accurate Itinerary, which goes around under the name of the Emperor Antoninus, almost thinks that Monzón is the Toloum of Antoninus. For he says that between Barcelona and Caesaraugusta there is no town which one could confidently assign to that station. Commonly called Monzón: a place of fertile land and sunny situation. Fraga, between Lleida and Caesaraugusta: Φραγα [Phraga] in Ptolemy; Gallicum in Antoninus, as Varrerius thinks. Others place Gallicum where Zuera now is, in whose territory traces of ancient pavements are seen. A river there keeps the name, called the Gállego, to which antiquity rightly gave the name Gallicus, because it rises in the land of France, after crossing the high Pyrenees above the town to which the name Salientis was given. Gurrea was once Forum Gallorum, in Antoninus between Caesaraugusta and the Pyrenees. Ayerbe, in whose soil Ebellinum is believed once to have stood, is named by Antoninus along with others. Urgel, Orgellum in Aimoinus; perhaps Ορελλα [Orella] in Ptolemy, a town not far from the source of the Segre. There were also other towns, but they have been destroyed, and no trace of them remains today. Among these, not unimportant was Calagurris Nassica, different from the one I described in Navarre. Ancient coins tell that this one was adorned with the surname Julia. On one bronze coin there is an effigy of a young Augustus with this inscription: NASSICA; on the reverse is a bull, the emblem of the municipalities, with inscriptions: above the bull CALAG, below it IVLIA. On another, with an image of Augustus: AVGVSTVS. MV. CAL. IVLIAS; on the reverse, above the image of the bull, L. BAEB. PRISCO C. CRAV. BROG. II VIR. On a third, with an effigy of Augustus: MVN. CAL. IVL. On the reverse, above the bull, II VIR. L. CRAVIO; below, the name of the other duumvir has been worn away by age. Later coins show that this Calagurris obtained the name of a municipality. Its citizens are called Calagurritani by Caesar in the commentary of his Civil War; Suetonius notes that Augustus had them as the guards of his body, in his life, chapter 49. Pliny surnames them Nassici. Let these be added here by way of conclusion.

units.la: REGES ARAGONIÆ NVPERI:
units.tr: THE RECENT KINGS OF ARAGON:

units.la: Petrus iv. Alphonsi iv ex Tyrefia Gulielmi Dantensij F. Iacobi ii N. Rex Aragoniæ, ab Ranimiro, quem omnium Scriptorum Calculi Primum faciunt, Decimusquartus. Obiit MCCCXXCVII. Vxor Lemora, Petri Siculorum Regis F. ordine tertia.
units.tr: Peter IV, son of Alphonso IV and Teresa, daughter of William of Entença, grandson of James II. King of Aragon, the fourteenth in the count from Ramiro, whom all writers of catalogues make the first. He died in 1387. His wife Leonora, daughter of Peter, king of Sicily, was his third.

units.la: Marinus Rex Aragoniæ xvi. Obiit MCCCCX. Vxor Maria Lunæ Comitis F.
units.tr: Martin, king of Aragon, the sixteenth. He died in 1410. His wife Maria, daughter of the Count of Luna.

units.la: Leonora. Nupsit Ioanni i. Regi Legionis & Castellæ.
units.tr: Leonora. She married John I, king of Leon and Castile.

units.la: Ioannes i Rex Aragoniæ xv. Obiit MCCCCXXI. Vxor Violanta Ducis Ebaus F.
units.tr: John I, king of Aragon, the fifteenth. He died in 1421. His wife Violant, daughter of the Duke of Bar.

units.la: Iacobus Gemundæ Delphinus. Obiit ante Patrem.
units.tr: James, Dauphin of Girona. He died before his father.

units.la: Martinus Ante Patrem obiit MCCCCIX.
units.tr: Martin died before his father, in 1409.

units.la: Henricus Rex Castellæ.
units.tr: Henry, king of Castile.

units.la: Ferdinandus Rex Aragoniæ xxvii. Obiit MCCCCXVI.
units.tr: Ferdinand, king of Aragon, the twenty-seventh. He died in 1416.

units.la: Alphonsus v. Rex Aragoniæ xviii.
units.tr: Alphonso V, king of Aragon, the eighteenth.

units.la: Ioannes ii. Rex Aragoniæ xix. FERDINANDVS V. Rex Aragoniæ XX, CATHOLICVS cognominé. Obiit MDXVI. uxor ISABELLA Castellæ & Legionis Regina. IOANNES, post confectas cum Margareta Austriaca Maximiliani I. Imper. F. nuptias. Obiit anno, ante Patrem, MDCCCXVII. ISABELLA Alphonso IV, inde Emanuelis Lusitaniæ Regibus nupta. Obiit MCCCCXCVIII. IOANNA Aragoniæ, &c. Regina XXI. Obiit MDLV. Nupsit Philippo Austriaco, Burgundiæ Duci, Belgarum Principi. Aliæ Filiæ. KAROLVS V. IMPER. Rex Aragoniæ XXII, obiit MDLVIII. Uxor Isabella Lusitana. FERDINANDVS Imper. PHILIPPVS II. Rex Aragoniæ XXIII, Obiit MDXCVIII. uxor Anna Austriaca. PHILIPPVS III Rex Aragoniæ XXIV, potentissimus.
units.tr: John II, king of Aragon, the nineteenth. FERDINAND V, king of Aragon, the twentieth, surnamed the Catholic. He died in 1516. His wife Isabella, queen of Castile and Leon. JOHN, who after his marriage to Margaret of Austria, daughter of the Emperor Maximilian I, died before his father in 1497. ISABELLA, married first to Alphonso IV and then to Emanuel, kings of Portugal. She died in 1498. JOAN of Aragon, queen, the twenty-first. She died in 1555. She married Philip of Austria, Duke of Burgundy, Prince of the Belgians. Other daughters. CHARLES V, emperor, king of Aragon, the twenty-second; he died in 1558. His wife Isabella of Portugal. FERDINAND, emperor. PHILIP II, king of Aragon, the twenty-third; he died in 1598. His wife Anne of Austria. PHILIP III, king of Aragon, the twenty-fourth, most powerful.

units.la: De Origine Regni Regumque Aragoniæ, Valentiæ & Cataloniæ, à quibus & quo modo initium habuerint, deque unione eorum, legendi Rodericus Sanctius Historiæ Hispanicæ Parte 1. cap. xiii, Lucius Marineus Siculus lib. viii de Regibus Hispan. & alij. Historiam etiam Aragonum scripsit Frater Gilbertus Monachus Ordinis S. Bernardi; sed quæ, si laudes immodicæ, quæque parum ad rem, detrahantur, in exiguum redigi posset opusculum.
units.tr: For the origin of the kingdom and of the kings of Aragon, Valencia and Catalonia, from whom and how they had their beginning, and on their union, read Rodericus Sanctius, Spanish History, part 1, chapter 13; Lucius Marineus Siculus, book 8 On the Kings of Spain; and others. Brother Gilbert, a monk of the Order of St Bernard, also wrote a history of the Aragonese; but if its immoderate praises and whatever is of little relevance were removed, it could be reduced to a small work.

units.la: CAP. XV.
units.tr: CHAP. XV.

units.la: Catalonia.
units.tr: Catalonia.

units.la: CATALONIA, vulgo Catalūna, Pyrenæis Montibus, Mari Mediterraneo, Fluminibusque Ibero & Cinga, qui inter hanc est & Aragoniam, terminatur. Nomen illi impositum putat Volaterranus ab Gothis & Alanis, scribendamque esse Gothalaniam. Beatus Rhenanus lib. 1. Rer. Germanic. Cattalaniam arbitratur appellatam ab Cattis & Alanis, qui junctim in eam Hispaniæ portionem proruperunt. Alij ab Castellanis, antiquis Hispaniæ populis, qui hisce locis sua habuerunt domicilia, denominatam judicant. Sunt etiam, qui nuncupatam Cathaloniam tradunt ab Othogerio Cathalone; de quo multa præter alios, Marineus Siculus lib. ix de Reb. Hispan. & L. Valla de Ferdinando Aragon. Rege lib. 1.
units.tr: Catalonia, commonly called Catalūna, is bounded by the Pyrenean Mountains, the Mediterranean Sea, and the rivers Ebro and Cinca, which lies between it and Aragon. Volaterranus thinks the name was given to it by the Goths and Alans, and that it should be written Gothalonia. Beatus Rhenanus, in book 1 of his Germanic Affairs, thinks it was called Cattalonia from the Catti and Alans, who together broke into that part of Spain. Others judge that it takes its name from the Castellani, an ancient people of Spain who had their homes in these places. Some also report that it was named Cathalonia after Othogerius the Catalan. On him, besides others, see Marineus Siculus, book 9 of On the Affairs of Spain, and L. Valla, On Ferdinand, King of Aragon, book 1.

units.la: Collocantur hac Hispaniæ Parte ab Veteribus varij Populi. Castellani, Καστελλανοὶ Ptolemæo, Ducatum Cardone interpretantur Villanouanus & Varrerius. Indigeti, Avieno; Ἐνδιγέτι Ptolemæo; Ἰνδιγέτι Stephano, qui & Indicam urbem ibi nominat. Ilergetes Livio, & Ptolemæo; Ἰλεργῆται Polybio lib. iii. Laletani Plinio, unde Laletania Martiali lib. 1. epig. xxvii; Λαλητανοὶ Ptolemæo; Λεητανοὶ Straboni, cui & Ἐλητανοὶ; omnia corrupte pro Λαλητανοί: his adhærebant, notante Strabone, Λαγτολαυητανοὶ. Cempsi Aimonio; Κεμψοὶ Dionysio & Eustathio. Cerretani Plinio, qui eosdem & Iulianos & Augustanos cognominat; Κερρετανοὶ Ptolemæo; Κερρητανοὶ Straboni; Ceretani Silio; Ceretes Avieno; Κέρετες Stephano: horum vestigia latere adhuc videntur in Cerveira, Puigcerda, Condado de Cerdania. Vetteres, sic enim Xilander interpretatur Hispaniæ Tarraconensis populos, qui inter Iberum & Pyrenæos ad Mare, Βέττηρες Straboni: Isaacus Casaubonus mallet Antonini Secerras. Ligyes, Λίγυες ad Sicanim fluvium Thucydidi lib. vi, & Halicarnass. lib. 1; forte qui Avieno Ligures. Ausetani Livio & Plinio; Αὐσητάνοι Ptolemæo. Larnenses Plinio ad Larnum fluvium ad Pyrenæi radices. Ἰλερκαόνες Ptolemæo, apud quos Dertosa urbs; Livio Ilercaonenses, & Cæsari fortean Ilurgavonenses: Μαρχαβῶν & item Ηεδίον, Fæniculariuum Campum, ponit hoc loco Strabo.
units.tr: Various ancient peoples were located in this part of Spain. The Castellani (Καστελλανοί in Ptolemy); Villanovanus and Varrerius interpret this as the Duchy of Cardona. The Indigetes (Avienus; Ἐνδιγέτι in Ptolemy; Ἰνδιγέτι in Stephanus, who also names an Indican city there). The Ilergetes (Livy and Ptolemy; Ἰλεργῆται in Polybius, book 3). The Laletani (Pliny, whence Laletania in Martial, book 1, epigram 27; Λαλητανοί in Ptolemy; Λεητανοί in Strabo, who also has Ἐλητανοί; all are corruptions of Λαλητανοί, and, as Strabo notes, the Λαγτολαυητανοί adhered to them). The Cempsi (Aimonius; Κεμψοί in Dionysius and Eustathius). The Cerretani (Pliny, who also surnames them Iulians and Augustans; Κερρετανοί in Ptolemy; Κερρητανοί in Strabo; Ceretani in Silius; Ceretes in Avienus; Κέρετες in Stephanus). Traces of these people still seem to survive in Cerveira, Puigcerda and Condado de Cerdania. The Vettones, for so Xylander renders the peoples of Hispania Tarraconensis who lived between the Ebro and the Pyrenees by the sea (Βέττηρες in Strabo); Isaac Casaubon would prefer Antoninus's Secerras. The Ligyes (Λίγυες by the river Sicanus, Thucydides book 6, and Halicarnassensis book 1; perhaps the Ligures of Avienus). The Ausetani (Livy and Pliny; Αὐσητάνοι in Ptolemy). The Larnenses (Pliny, by the river Larnus at the foot of the Pyrenees). The Ilercaones (Ἰλερκαόνες in Ptolemy, among whom lies the city Dertosa; Livy has Ilercaonenses, and Caesar perhaps Ilurgavonenses). Strabo places here Μαρχαβῶν and likewise Ηεδίον, the Fenicularian Plain.

units.la: Metropolin habet hodie Barcelonam, Vrbem pulcherrimam, quæ in Maris Mediterranei littore sita meram redolet Antiquitatem, complures servans rei probandæ lapides vetustos. Conditor ejus fertur à plerisque Hispaniarum Inlustratoribus Amilcar Barcha cognomine, filius Annibalis Karthaginiensium Ducis; qui, victa classe, à Militibus in crucem fuit sublatus; pater autem Annibalis, Magni istius Imperatoris: Βαρκίνων Ptolemæo; Barcinnus Paullino in Epistolis; Barcilona Iornandi: Faventia etiam quondam, teste Plinio. Recp. Barcinonensis mentio in Lapide, qui ibidem visitur pro æde Divorum Iusti & Pastoris. Extat inter Smetianas Inscriptiones sol. clviii, numero 11. Antonius Augustinus Dialogo vii de Nummis Antiquis Numismata Galbæ habet, in quo col. f. i. a. barc. quæ interpretatur COLONIA FAVENTIA IVLIA AVGVSTA BARCINO. Laudat hanc Urbem multis verbis Marincus Siculus Rer. Hisp. lib. xiii, qui & Situm ejus describit lib. xv. Fuit olim multo minor, quam hodie conspicitur, ab Littore Maris uno fere stadio remota. Habebat Portas quatuor, quæ totidem Mundi plagas spectabant, æquo fere omnes spatio inter se distantes, quæ adhuc in ipso pene umbilico Urbis visuntur; cæleta gerentes Capita Bubula, altæ Pacis, ut nonnulli volunt, & quietæ Agriculturæ Symbola. Lapsu temporis bis prævalidis Muris superbisque Turribus est cincta, inque tantam paullatim magnificentiam excrevit, ut multo merito Caput hodie censeatur Cataloniæ. De Barcinonis Comitibus, eorumque origine consulendi Rodericus Toletanus lib. vi. de Rebus Hispaniæ cap. iii. & L. Marineus Siculus lib. ix. Prope Barcinonem locus, qui dicitur S. Locat, ubi olim Castrum; ut vult Ambrosius Moralis, fuisse perhibetur Octavianum. Sequuntur hanc Tarraco; Ταρράκων Ptolemæo & Straboni: Tarragona hodie; Colonia Tarraconensis apud Tacitum lib. i. Annal. Legō & in antiquo Lapide, COL. I.IV. TARRAC. fortean; COLONIA IVLIA VICTRIX TARRACO. Opus existimatur Scipionum. Vrbs olim tam celebris, ut potiori Hispaniæ parti nomen dederit. Maritimarum opulentissima Melæ lib. ii. De ea sic Strabo lib. iii: Πρῶτη Ταρράκων πόλις, ἀλλὰ ... ἐν κλίπῳ δὲ ἱδρυμένη, καὶ καταλυσμὸς τῆς ἄλλης ἱκανῶς, καὶ ἐκ τῆς Καρχηδόνος. Πρὸς γὰρ τὰς τῶν ἡγεμόνων, ἀπιδημίας ἐφυῶς ἔχει. καὶ ἐστιν ὥσπερ μητρόπολις ἡ τῆς ἐντὸς Ἰβηρίας μέρος, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῆς ἐκτὸς τῆς πόλεως. Sic Silius lib. iii. de bello Punico: Dat Tarraco Pubem Vitifera. & Latio tantum cesura Lyæo.
units.tr: The metropolis today is Barcelona, a very beautiful city, lying on the shore of the Mediterranean, which smells strongly of antiquity and keeps several old stones to prove it. Most of the illustrators of Spain report that its founder was Hamilcar, surnamed Barca, son of Hannibal, leader of the Carthaginians, who after his fleet was defeated was crucified by his soldiers. His father was Hannibal, that great commander. (Βαρκίνων in Ptolemy; Barcinnus in Paulinus's Letters; Barcilona in Jordanes.) It was also once called Faventia, according to Pliny. Barcinonensis is mentioned on a stone that can be seen there in the church of Saints Justus and Pastor. It is among the Smetian inscriptions, page clviii, number 11. Antonius Augustinus, in Dialogue 7 of On Ancient Coins, has a coin of Galba on which is COL. F. I. A. BARC., which is read as COLONIA FAVENTIA IULIA AUGUSTA BARCINO. Marineus Siculus praises this city at length in book 13 of his Affairs of Spain, and describes its site in book 15. It was formerly much smaller than it appears today, about one stadium distant from the shore of the sea. It had four gates, facing the four quarters of the world and almost equally spaced apart; they can still be seen almost at the very centre of the city, bearing carved bulls' heads, which some hold to be symbols of lofty peace and quiet agriculture. With the passage of time it was surrounded by very strong walls and proud towers, and grew little by little into such magnificence that it is rightly considered today the head of Catalonia. On the counts of Barcelona and their origin, consult Roderic of Toledo, book 6 of On the Affairs of Spain, chapter 3, and L. Marineus Siculus, book 9. Near Barcelona there is a place called S. Locat, where it is said there was once a castle, which Ambrosius Morales holds was Octavian's. Next comes Tarraco (Ταρράκων in Ptolemy and Strabo): today Tarragona; Colonia Tarraconensis in Tacitus, Annals book 1. I also read on an ancient stone COL. I.IV. TARRAC., perhaps COLONIA IULIA VICTRIX TARRACO. It is thought to be the work of the Scipios. The city was once so famous that it gave its name to the greater part of Spain; it is the richest of the maritime cities (Mela, book 2). Strabo, book 3, says of it: "Tarraco is the first city..." [Πρῶτη Ταρράκων πόλις, ἀλλὰ ... ἐν κλίπῳ δὲ ἱδρυμένη, καὶ καταλυσμὸς τῆς ἄλλης ἱκανῶς, καὶ ἐκ τῆς Καρχηδόνος. Πρὸς γὰρ τὰς τῶν ἡγεμόνων, ἀπιδημίας ἐφυῶς ἔχει. καὶ ἐστιν ὥσπερ μητρόπολις ἡ τῆς ἐντὸς Ἰβηρίας μέρος, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῆς ἐκτὸς τῆς πόλεως.] Likewise Silius, book 3 of the Punica: "Tarraco gives its youth, rich in vines, and yields only to Latin Lyaeus [Bacchus]."

units.la: Multa hic Antiquitatum vestigia; innumeri quotidie reperiuntur Nummi in Agris & Vinetis: unde conjicere licet olim multo fuisse majorem. Tarracone Templum Augusto fuit conditum Principatu Tiberij, scribente Tacito lib. i. Annal. Mantic illud ad ævum usque Hadriani, qui conlapsum restauravit. Spartianus in ejus vita. Laudat & Nummum æreum Augusti Imperatoris Abrahamus Ortelius: in cujus aversa parte Templum erat cum Inscriptione ÆTERNITATIS AVGVSTÆ, & litteris singularibus C. V. T. T. COLONIA, VICTRIX, TOGATA (vel TYRRHENICA) TARRACO. Viqua, Vicque vulgo, vel Vich; Ἀ'vσυ Ptolemæo, Authetanorum Vrbs. Girona, Gerunda Plinio & Antonino; Γερόνδα Ptolemæo: Gerundenses etiam Plinio noti. Sic Inscriptio Tarraconensis: C. MARIO. C. FIL PAL. VERO GERVNDENS OMNIBVS. HONORIB IN RE. P. SVA. FVNCTO FLAMINI. PROV. HISP CITER. P. H. C.
units.tr: There are many traces of antiquity here; countless coins are found every day in the fields and vineyards, whence one may conjecture that it was once much larger. A temple to Augustus was built at Tarraco in the principate of Tiberius, as Tacitus writes in Annals book 1. It remained standing until the age of Hadrian, who restored it after it had collapsed (Spartianus in his life). Abraham Ortelius also cites a bronze coin of the Emperor Augustus, on whose reverse was a temple with the inscription AETERNITATIS AVGVSTAE, and the separate letters C. V. T. T., COLONIA VICTRIX TOGATA (or TYRRHENICA) TARRACO. Vic, commonly Vique or Vich (Ἀ'vσυ in Ptolemy), was a city of the Ausetani. Girona, Gerunda in Pliny and Antoninus (Γερόνδα in Ptolemy); the Gerundenses are also known from Pliny. So too the Tarragona inscription: C. MARIO C. FIL. PAL. VERO GERVNDENSI OMNIBVS HONORIB. IN R. P. SVA FVNCTO FLAMINI PROV. HISP. CITER. P. H. C.

units.la: Tortosa, quæ Δέρτωσα Ptolemæo; Dertosa Vetusto Lapidi, qui ibi exstat: Derdosa Antonino, Δέρτοσα Straboni. Dertosani (sic enim legendum) Populi sunt apud Plinium. Dertosa Ilercavonia cognominatur à Populis, quorum hæc Vrbs erat Caput, in Nummo Tiberij Imperatoris: TI. CÆSAR DIVI AVG. F. AVGVSTVS; & in aversa parte infra navis carinam, DERT. ILERGAONIA. Situm ejus ita paucis notat Strabo lib. iii: ἐπ' αὐτῆ δὲ τῆ Ἰβηρίας ... Ἰλέρδα κατοικία. Lerdi, quæ Ptolemæo, Stephano & aliis Ἰλέρδα, Ilergetum Vrbs. De ea Strabo: ... Ἰλέρδα ... Situs ita delineatur ab Lucano lib. iv. belli Pharsalici: Colle tumet modico, lenique extrevit in altum Pingue solum tumulo: super hunc fundata vetusta Surgit Ilerda manu; placidis pralabitur undis Hesperios inter Sicoris non ultimus amnes: Saxeus ingenti quem pons amplectitur arcu, Hibernas passurus aquas:
units.tr: Tortosa: Δέρτωσα in Ptolemy; Dertosa on an ancient stone that stands there; Derdosa in Antoninus; Δέρτοσα in Strabo. The Dertosani (so it must be read) are a people in Pliny. Dertosa is called Ilercavonia after the peoples of whom this city was the head, as on a coin of the Emperor Tiberius: TI. CAESAR DIVI AVG. F. AVGVSTVS; and on the reverse, below the keel of a ship, DERT. ILERGAONIA. Strabo, book 3, notes its situation briefly in these words: "on the Ebro itself ... the dwelling of the Ilerda." Lérida, which in Ptolemy, Stephanus and others is Ἰλέρδα, was a city of the Ilergetes. Of it Strabo says: "... Ilerda ..." Its site is described thus by Lucan, book 4 of the Pharsalia: It swells on a gentle hill, and the rich soil rises into a high mound; upon this old Ilerda rises, built by hand; the Sicoris, not the least of the rivers of the West, flows past with gentle waters, which a stone bridge embraces with a huge arch, about to bear the winter floods.

units.la: & quæ alia ibi de devictis ad Ilerdam ab C. Cæsare Cn. Pompei Legatis, M. Petreio & L. Afranio: qua de re plene Cæsar lib. 1. Belli Civilis, qui etiam opidum in Monte positum notat, Pontis item faciens mentionem. Academiam habet celebrem & insignis antiquitatis, quam Horatius putatur intellexisse lib. 1. Epist. ult.
units.tr: Also what else is told there about those defeated at Ilerda by Gaius Caesar: the legates of Gnaeus Pompey, M. Petreius and L. Afranius. Caesar gives a full account of this matter in book 1 of his Civil War, where he also notes that the town stands on a hill, and mentions its bridge. It has a famous academy of notable antiquity, which Horace is thought to have meant in the last epistle of book 1.

units.la: Aut fugies Vticam aut unctus mitteris Ilerdam.
units.tr: Either you will flee to Utica, or you will be sent, anointed, to Ilerda.

units.la: Hic Calixtus III. P. M. publice Iurisprudentiam docuit teste Platina. Emporia Silio lib. III, Ἐμπορίον Polybio lib. III, & Ptolemæo: Ἐμπόριον Stephano; Empurias vel Ampurias vulgo. Emporienses prius Insulam oppositam habitasse, quæ Παλαιόπολις dicebatur, & Emporium ab Massiliensibus fuisse conditum auctor est Strabo. Emporiæ Phocaicas cognominat Silius libro, qui à me laudatus. Blanda Pomponio; Βλάνδα Ptolemæo; Blanes vulgo, ut volunt Beuterus, Florianus & Navagierus Manresa, quam Florianus, ut antea dixi, Athanagiam ab Livio vocari censet. Rosa, Roses vulgo: Rhoda Livio; ῥόδη Stephano, ῥοδίνη Straboni; ῥοδιμλις Ptolemæo, apud quem Casaubonus ῥόδη πόλις legit, divisim. Colibra, Ἰλίβεγις Ptolemæo; Iliberis Livio & Plinio: Ἰλουβέρρις Straboni: Eliberri Pomponio, Vicus magnæ quondam Urbis & tenue magnarum opum, addenti, vestigium; Cliberra Tabulæ Peutingerianæ, in quis emendandum Eliberri, nisi quis velit hodiernam appellationem in Tabulis expressam, ut etiam Theodosij principatu Colibra fuerit nominata. Alij tamen Iliberim non Colibram, sed aliud opidum volunt; Salsulas, Poldus; Eunam, Petrus Olivarius; Illam, Mercator. Prope Salsas sane sub Pyrenæis montibus fuerunt, quarum meminerunt Pomponius Mela & Antoninus. Salsulæ lacus prope Narbonem Galliæ. Is est, quem Strabo juxta Ruscinonem locat paullum supra mare, Salinis nobilem & κῆρας ὀρυκτὰς habentem, Mugiles fossiles; cujus rei Ælianus ex Polybio facit mentionem. Fuit &, ubi nunc Catalonia, quondam Iulia Libyca, cujus rudera putantur esse haud procul Linca opido. Item apud Pyrenæos Cinniana Antonino, corrupte Cegnama Tabulæ Peutingerianæ; Deciana, Δεκίανα Ptolemæo, Declana eidem Tabulæ mendose. Hispaniæ sub Catolonia adcenseri Terram Ruscilionis in Pyrenæis montibus, disputat varie Io. Gerundensis lib. 1. Paralipom. Hispaniæ: sic dictam ab opido, quod Plinio Ruscino, Straboni Ῥοσκινών; Ptolemæo Ῥούσκιον; Ruscinus Avieno. Urbis vestigia exstant haud procul opido Perpigniano juxta Turrim, quæ nomen ejus retinet. Vocant enim Turrim Rusciltionis. De Iunquera, quæ olim Iuncaria, dixi cap. III. Iter (ut hoc Coronidis instar, tribus, quæ præcedunt, Capitibus adjiciam) quod Vapinco (opidum illud est Delphinatus in Gallijs, quod hodie Gap) describit Antoninus, vel quicumque Itinerarij vulgati est auctor, ad Legionem VII Geminam, continet præcipua Cataloniæ, Aragoniæ, Navarræ, Castellæ Veteris & Legionis loca, ad initium usque Galleciæ. Non potui, quin illud Lectori proponerem; facta commissione non solum cum ijs, quæ ad idem iter exstant in Tabula Peutingeriana (publici nuper juris facta, beneficio Magni Viri, Marci Velseri Patricij & VII-VIRI Augustani) verum etiam cum hodiernis Urbium Opidorumque, quantum in re tam ab ævo nostro remota fieri potest, nomenclaturis. Unum prius, ut semel Numerorum ratio recte intelligatur, monendum duxi. In Antonini Itinerario Numerus alicui Urbi vel opido subjectus, tantum notat spacium vel tot passuum esse millia inter Stationem cui subjicitur, & præcedentem. In Tabula Peutingeriana secus se res habet. Quum enim pleraque Itinera producantur (subinde satis imperite & confuse, Nominibusque & Numeris sæpe vitiosissimis) ab Occasu in Ortum; nonnulla etiam, si cum Antonino fit Comparatio instituenda, ab Ortu in Occasum: illud fere animadverti & didici; si ab Occasu in Ortum Itineris collectio fit facienda, Numerum loco subjectum indicare spacium inter eum, cui subjicitur & sequentem: ideoque in Auferendi casu pleraque esse expressa: sin ab Ortu in Occasum, Numerum inter duo Loca positum eorumdem edere intervallum. Iter, quod dixi, sic se habet:
units.tr: Here Pope Calixtus III publicly taught law, according to Platina. Emporia in Silius, book 3; Ἐμπορίον in Polybius, book 3, and Ptolemy; Ἐμπόριον in Stephanus; commonly Empurias or Ampurias. The people of Emporiae, as the author says, previously inhabited an island opposite, called Palaeopolis, and Emporium was founded by the Massilians, according to Strabo. Silius calls Emporiae "Phocaean", in the book I have already praised. Blanda in Pomponius; Βλάνδα in Ptolemy; commonly Blanes, as Beuter, Florian and Navagero think; Manresa, which Florian, as I said before, judges to be the Athanagia named by Livy. Rosa, commonly Roses: Rhoda in Livy; ῥόδη in Stephanus, ῥοδίνη in Strabo; ῥοδιμλις in Ptolemy, where Casaubon reads ῥόδη πόλις as two separate words. Colibra: Ἰλίβεγις in Ptolemy; Iliberis in Livy and Pliny; Ἰλουβέρρις in Strabo; Eliberri in Pomponius, a village of a once great city and a meagre remnant of great wealth, he adds, a vestige. Cliberra in the Peutinger Table, where Eliberri should be emended, unless one prefers to think the modern name is expressed in the Table, just as Colibra was also the name in the reign of Theodosius. Others, however, hold that Iliberis, not Colibra, was another town: Salsulas, Poldus; Eunam, Petrus Olivarius; Illam, Mercator. Near Salsae, indeed, under the Pyrenees, there were places mentioned by Pomponius Mela and Antoninus. Salsulae is a lake near Narbo in Gaul. This is the one Strabo places near Ruscino, a little above the sea, noted for its salt-pans and having dug-out pits and fossil mullets; Aelian mentions this fact from Polybius. Where Catalonia now lies there was once also Iulia Libyca, whose ruins are thought to be not far from the town of Linca. Likewise near the Pyrenees, Cinniana in Antoninus, corruptly Cegnama in the Peutinger Table; Deciana, Δεκίανα in Ptolemy, Declana in the same Table by mistake. John of Gerona, in book 1 of his Paralipomena of Spain, argues variously whether the land of Roussillon, in the Pyrenees, is to be counted among the Spanish parts under Catalonia. It is so called from the town which Pliny calls Ruscino, Strabo Ῥοσκινών, Ptolemy Ῥούσκιον, and Avienus Ruscinus. Traces of the city survive not far from the town of Perpignan, beside a tower which keeps its name; they call it the Tower of Roussillon. I spoke of Iunquera, once Iuncaria, in chapter 3. The route (I shall add it as a kind of crown to the three chapters that precede), which Antoninus, or whoever is the author of the published Itinerary, describes from Vapincum (a town of Dauphiné in France, now Gap) to Legio VII Gemina, contains the chief places of Catalonia, Aragon, Navarre, Old Castile and León, up to the beginning of Galicia. I could not refrain from setting it before the reader, after comparing it both with what appears on the same route in the Peutinger Table (recently published through the kindness of the great man Marcus Welser, patrician and decemvir of Augsburg), and with the modern names of cities and towns, as far as can be done in a matter so remote from our age. I thought one point should first be noted, so that the system of numbers is rightly understood. In Antoninus's Itinerary, a number placed under a city or town only indicates how many miles lie between the station to which it is subjoined and the preceding one. In the Peutinger Table it is otherwise. For since most routes are drawn out (sometimes rather clumsily and confusedly, with names and numbers often very faulty) from west to east, and some, where a comparison with Antoninus is to be made, from east to west, I have generally observed and learned this: if the route is to be collected from west to east, the number placed under a place indicates the space between it and the one following; hence in most cases it is so expressed. But if from east to west, the number placed between two places gives the interval between those same places. The route I mentioned stands thus:

units.la: Galecia.
units.tr: Galicia.

units.la: GALECIA (quæ & Galicia vel Gallecia scribitur, cuique nomen ab Antiquis populis Callaicis) ad Septemtrionem & Occidentem Oceanus est; ad Meridiem Portugallia, interfluente Durio; ad Ortum Asturia. Huic Regioni, quum sexta quondam fuerit Hispaniæ Provincia, ut supra dixi, majores olim, quam hodie, fuerunt fines. Adcensebatur illi versus Meridiem pars illa Portugalliæ, quæ inter Durium & Minium fluvios; consulendus Strabo lib. iii: versus ortum multo longius se extendebat ad Pyrenæos fere Montes, Asturibus & Cantabris Galeciæ connumeratis. Antonini Itinerarium Legionem VII (hodie Leon) in Galecia ponit. Scotus etiam, Notitiæ Provinciarum auctor, in eadem Provincia Præfectum Legionis vii Gemina constituit. Quin & Paullus Orosius Mnemantiam, celebrem olim Pelendonum Regionis Vrbem, in capite Galeciæ sitam scribit. Rodericus denique Santius Parte i. Historiæ Hispanicæ, cap. vi, Galeciæ tribuit Biscaiam, Lepusinum vel Gutpuscoam, & eas partes, quas hodie Castellum Antiquam vocamus: Gallecia, quod ob montes nimis lit aspera, Aquilique careat, rarenter habitatur. Equis adeo abundat, ut Vento concipi dicantur: qua de re antea dixi. Plinius hic locat Mineras Auri ditissimas. Niger scribit in Artabris Amnes Terram Auro, Argento, Stanno mistam ferre; Solumque Auri, Æris ac Plumbi uberrimum esse, adeo ut aureæ glebæ sæpe aratro exfodiantur. Montes magnam Lignorum copiam Navibus ædificandis suppeditant. Piscibus Galecia supra modum abundat. Salmonibus præcipue, Congris, cujusque generis, quos vulgo Pescadas appellant; aliis item multis lautissimis, qui sale conditi varias in Hispaniæ partes distrahuntur. Novembri Decembrique mensibus infinita Piscium, quos vulgus Sardinas nominat, vis capitur, duarum aut circiter librarum: recentes in totam Castiliam venum exportantur: facit enim adstringens frigus, ut facile serventur: saporis sunt gratissimi; gratioris tamen qui in Oceano, quam qui in Mediterraneo mari capiuntur. Algor enim Oceani Pisces impinguat; ideoque quo propiores sunt Septemtrionibus, eo solent esse meliores. Potissima huius Regni Incolarum pars in Montibus degit; in quibus Domicilia satis commoda passim visuntur exstructa.
units.tr: GALICIA (also written Galicia or Gallecia, and named after the ancient Callaici peoples) is bounded to the north and west by the Ocean; to the south by Portugal, with the Durius flowing between; to the east by Asturias. This region, since it was once the sixth province of Spain, as I said above, had formerly greater borders than it has today. On its southern side that part of Portugal lying between the rivers Durius and Minius was counted in it; see Strabo, book iii. To the east it extended much further, almost to the Pyrenean mountains, with the Asturians and Cantabrians counted as part of Galicia. Antoninus' Itinerary places Legio VII (today León) in Galicia. Scotus, the author of the Notitia of the Provinces, likewise sets the Prefect of Legio VII Gemina in the same province. Indeed Paulus Orosius writes that Mnemantia, once a famous city of the Pelendones, lay at the head of Galicia. Finally Rodrigo Sánchez, in Part i of his Spanish History, chapter vi, assigns to Galicia Biscay, Guipúzcoa, and those parts which we today call Old Castile. Galicia, because it is very rough on account of its mountains and lacks eagles, is thinly inhabited. It abounds in horses to such an extent that they are said to be impregnated by the wind; I have spoken about this matter earlier. Pliny here places very rich gold mines. Niger writes that the rivers in the Artabri carry down earth mixed with gold, silver and tin, and that the soil is very rich in gold, copper and lead, so that golden clods are often dug up by the plough. The mountains supply a great quantity of timber for building ships. Galicia abounds in fish beyond measure: especially salmon, conger eels, and every kind of fish, which they commonly call pescadas, and many other very choice kinds, which are salted and sent off to various parts of Spain. In the months of November and December an endless quantity of fish, which the common people call sardines, about two pounds each, is caught; the fresh ones are exported to all of Castile for sale, since the cold that prevails keeps them easily. They are very pleasant in flavour, though those caught in the Ocean are more pleasing than those caught in the Mediterranean. For the coldness of the Ocean fattens the fish, and so the nearer they are to the north, the better they are wont to be. The greater part of the inhabitants of this kingdom live in the mountains, where fairly comfortable dwellings are seen built here and there.

units.la: Floruerunt hic olim Triginta, ut Strabo refert, Populi, quorum præcipui nominantur Callaeci multis & Gallaeci; Καλλαικοι Ptolemæo & Straboni; Gallegi Eutropio. Καλλαικιαν hic ponit Strabo lib. iii: Gallaeiam Iustinus lib. xliii. Callaicum Oceanum facit hinc Martialis. De Callaicorum origine & nomine (quidam enim ab Galatis Græciæ populis; nonnulli ab Galathe Herculis filio dirivant) videat Lector, si otium, Io. Gerundensem Episcopum Paralipomen. Hispaniæ lib. ii, Rodericum Toletanum lib. x. de Rebus Hispaniæ cap. iv, & alios. De Callaicis, inter alia, sic scribit Strabo lib. iii: Καλλαικοι δ' ὑψηλοι τ' ὁρεινῆς ἐπίχωνοι πλείω; διὸ ἢ δυσμαχώτατοι εἰσι, τῷ τε καταπολεμήσαντι τῆς Ανστασιας αὐτοῖς πρείζων τῶν ἐπιγωμίαν. Verum illud. Cognomen enim Callaici habuit D. Iunius Brutus cos. anno Ab v. c. Ioxcvii, Callaicorum & Lusitanorum ad Oceanum usque Domitor: quo tempore, quum Exercitus Fluvium mali ominis Oblivionem, de quo alibi, transire nollet, ereptum Signifero signum ipse transportavit, militesque, ut sequerentur; animoso strategemate incitavit. Legendus Livius lib. lv. & sequenti. Ab hoc Bruto Templum Romæ in ix. Urbis Regione, Bruti Callaici; cujus meminerunt Victor & Plinius lib. nat. hist. xxxvi. cap. v, qui notat in eo fuisse Colossum Martis & statuam Veneris Gnidiæ nudæ. Callaicos nihil de Diis sensisse, sunt qui scribunt apud Strabonem. De iisdem & Silius lib. iii: Fibrarum & Pennæ, Divinarumque sagacem Flammarum, misit dives Gallecia pubem: Barbara nunc patrijs ululantem carmina linguis, Nunc pedis altero percussa verbere terra Ad numerum resonas gaudentem plaudere Cetras: Hæc requies, ludusque viris, ea sacra voluptas: Cetera fœminea peragit labor: addere sulco Semina, & impresso Tellurem vertere aratro; Segne Viris, quid apud Auro sine Marte gerendum est, Callaici connubio obiit inrequieta Mariti.
units.tr: Thirty peoples, as Strabo reports, once flourished here, of whom the principal are called the Callaici, also written Gallaici: Καλλαικοι [Kallaikoi] for Ptolemy and Strabo; Gallegi for Eutropius. Strabo, book iii, calls the region here Καλλαικία [Kallaikia]; Justin, book xliii, calls it Gallaecia. From here Martial makes the Callaecian Ocean. Whoever has leisure may consult about the origin and name of the Callaici (some derive them from the Galatians, a people of Greece; others from Galates, a son of Hercules) John of Girona, Bishop, Paralipomena of Spain, book ii; Rodrigo of Toledo, book x, On the Deeds of Spain, chapter iv; and others. Among other things Strabo writes about the Callaici in book iii: [Καλλαικοι δ' ὑψηλοι τ' ὁρεινῆς ἐπίχωνοι πλείω; διὸ ἢ δυσμαχώτατοι εἰσι, τῷ τε καταπολεμήσαντι τῆς Ανστασιας αὐτοῖς πρείζων τῶν ἐπιγωμίαν.] That is true. For D. Junius Brutus, consul in the year 617 from the founding of the city, was given the surname Callaicus, as conqueror of the Callaici and Lusitanians as far as the Ocean. At that time, when the army refused to cross the river of ill omen, Oblivion, of which I speak elsewhere, he himself carried the standard, seized from the standard-bearer, and by a bold stratagem roused the soldiers to follow him. Livy, books lv and following, should be read. From this Brutus there was a temple at Rome in the ninth region of the city, the Temple of Brutus Callaicus, which Victor and Pliny, Natural History, book xxxvi, chapter v, mention, who notes that in it there was a colossus of Mars and a statue of the naked Venus of Cnidos. Some writers in Strabo say that the Callaici thought nothing of the gods. Silius also speaks of them in book iii: The rich Gallaecia sent forth its youth, skilled in reading entrails and feathers and the flames of divination: now a barbarian chanting songs in their native tongue, now beating the earth with one foot stamping, and delighting to clap their sounding shields to the rhythm. This is their rest and sport, this their manly pleasure; the rest of the work is done by women: to scatter seed in the furrow and turn the earth with the ploughshare. Idle for men, when there is nothing to be done with gold and no war, the restless Callaici wife undertakes the husband's labour.

units.la: Amphilochi, quos Galleciæ portionem facit Iustinus lib. xliii. Cilini vel Celeni, ut in aliis Exemplaribus scribuntur: Plinio; Κιλινοι Ptolemæo. Celtici Pomponio Mela, circa Celticum Promontorium; Κελτικοι Ptolemæo; Κελτοι Straboni: eorum alteros Nervas, alteros Præsammarcos cognominat Plinius; vocibus Germanicis, quarum illa Inferiores Celticos notat, hæc admarinos & Oceano adcolas: habitarunt enim olim longe lateque loca illa Germani. Tamarici ad Tamarin fluvium, qui μαγα Ptolemæo: hodieque Tamar. Capori Plinio; Καπορoι Ptolemæo. Arotreba Plinio; Αρταβροι & Αρογείβαι Straboni ad Artabrum Promontorium. Lucentes Plinio, Καλλαικοι Λυκιονιοι Ptolemæo; ab his hodieque Lugo ad Minium amnem. Zeela Plinio, qui & Zeelici Lini facit mentionem. Alios aliis indagandos, suisque & certis locis sistendos relinquo.
units.tr: The Amphilochi, whom Justin in book 43 makes a part of Galicia; the Cilini or Celeni, as other copies have it (Pliny); Κιλινοι [Kilinoi] (Ptolemy). The Celtici (Pomponius Mela), near the Celtic Promontory; Κελτικοι [Keltikoi] (Ptolemy); Κελτοι [Keltoi] (Strabo). Pliny calls one of these people the Nervae and the other the Praesammarci. The names are German: the first denotes the Lower Celts, the second those who live by the sea and on the Ocean, for that region was long and widely inhabited by Germans. The Tamarici, on the River Tamaris, which is Μαγα [Maga] for Ptolemy and is today the Tamar. The Capori (Pliny); Καπορoι [Kaporoi] (Ptolemy). The Arotreba (Pliny); Αρταβροι [Artabroi] and Αρογείβαι [Arogeibai] (Strabo), at the Artabrian Promontory. The Lucentes (Pliny), Καλλαικοι Λυκιονιοι [Kallaikoi Lykionioi] (Ptolemy); from these comes today's Lugo on the River Minius. The Zeela (Pliny), who also mentions the Zeelician linen. I leave others to track down the rest and fix them in their proper places.

units.la: Metropolis Galeciæ Compostella: ubi Corpus D. Iacobi religiosè dicitur, à quo ipsa Vrbs, nonnullam etiam ab Academia sua celebritatem habens, hodie Santiago: Brigantium olim, uti censent Franciscus Tarapha, Ambrosius Moralis & Villanovanus. Brigantium autem dicitur Antonino; Dioni Βεργάντιον; Brigantia Orosio, qui ibi Pharum altissimam exstare addit: Ptolemæus cognomen addit, Φλαϊον Βεργάντιον. Flavium tamen Brigantium Beutero, Coquo & Io. Marianæ Betanços est; Floriano & Gomecio Coruna. Compostellam autem Io. Gerundensis Hisp. lib. 1. dictam scribit, tamquam Compotem Stellam: sic enim appellatum fuisse Hesperum, Regionibus illis salubrem. Ego hoc in medio relinquo. Extat Salmanticæ in Bibliotheca Collegij S. Salvatoris Historia Compostellana, in duos libros digesta jussu Didaci primi Archiepiscopi Compostellani: in quibus Primordia, Successus, Incrementa Ecclesiæ Compostellanæ late describuntur. Consulendus & L. Marineus Siculus de Rebus Hispaniæ lib. v. cap. de Sacris Ædibus & Locis in Hispania religiosis, miraculisque celebratis. Minorum gentium sunt Orensium ad Minium fluvium vrbs; Οὐάλα Ἰππέα Ptolemæo, ut putat Gomecius in vita Francisci Ximenij; addens eam ab Suevis Germaniæ populis, qui quondam hanc oram sibi subjugarunt, proprio idiomate Warense appellatam. Ortelius scribendum monet Warmsee, quod nihil aliud, quam Calidus Lacus; Aquæ Cilinæ dicuntur Antonino, ab Cilinis populis, credo. Lucus Latinis id in Galecia opidum, quod Lugo hodie dicitur; Αὔγουστος Ptolemæo; Turris Augusti Pomponio; Ara Sextiana Plinio; Σηστ etiam Ἔμπόριον, Ara Sestij, Promontorium Ptolemæo ad Oceanum Cantabricum in Artabris. Pons Vetus, Ponte Vedra; Ἐ̓πίλλωσ Straboni, ut putat Io. Mariana. Ribadeum, vulgo Ribadeo; Δαχηνον Cilinorum gentis Ptolemæo, ut vult Coquus. Arzua, Araduca Ptolemæo, judice Moletio; Florianus tamen opinatur esse Aradutam opidum illud, quod hodie Gummarez. Fuit ibidem & Ἰ̓ἐρα Φλαϊα Ptolemæo; quæ Padron (Patronum Peregrinantibus notissimum) Clusio videtur & Morali (cui & alibi Fuente encalada) quibusdam, inter quos L. Marineus libro iii. Sancta Maria in finibus Terræ. Commemorat reliqua Opida idem L. Marineus Siculus initio libri tertij.
units.tr: The metropolis of Galicia is Compostella, where the body of St James is devoutly said to lie, and from which the city itself takes its name; it now has some renown also from its university, and is today Santiago. It was formerly Brigantium, as Francisco Tarapha, Ambrosio Morales and Villanueva think. Brigantium is the name given by Antoninus; Βεργάντιον [Bergantion] by Dio; Brigantia by Orosius, who adds that a very tall lighthouse stands there. Ptolemy adds the epithet Φλαϊον Βεργάντιον [Flaion Bergantion]. However, Flavium Brigantium is Betanços for Beuter, Cocus and Juan de Mariana; for Florian and Gómez it is Coruña. Juan of Gerona, in book 1 of his History of Spain, writes that Compostella was so called as if Compotem Stellam, a star-possessing place, since the evening star was called that in those regions, which were healthy. I leave this open. In the library of the College of St Saviour at Salamanca there is the Historia Compostellana, arranged in two books at the command of Diego I, Archbishop of Compostella, in which the beginnings, successes and growth of the Church of Compostella are widely described. L. Marineus Siculus, On the Affairs of Spain, book 5, the chapter on the sacred buildings and places in Spain that are religiously regarded and famous for miracles, should also be consulted. Of the lesser peoples, the Orensium are the city on the River Minius; Οὐάλα Ἰππέα [Oualla Hippea] for Ptolemy, as Gómez thinks in the life of Francisco Ximénez, adding that the Suevi, a German people who once subjected this coast to themselves, called it Warense in their own language. Ortelius advises that it should be written Warmsee, which means nothing else than warm lake. The Aquae Cilinae are named by Antoninus, I suppose after the Cilini people. Lucus is the Latin name of the Galician town now called Lugo; Αὔγουστος [Augoustos] for Ptolemy; Turris Augusti for Pomponius; Ara Sextiana for Pliny. Also Σηστ Ἔμπόριον [Sest Emporion], Ara Sestij, is a promontory on the Cantabrian Ocean among the Artabri, for Ptolemy. Pons Vetus is Pontevedra; Ἐ̓πίλλωσ [Epillos] for Strabo, as Juan de Mariana thinks. Ribadeum, commonly Ribadeo; Δαχηνον [Dachenon] of the Cilini people for Ptolemy, as Cocus holds. Arzua, Araduca for Ptolemy, in the judgement of Moletius; Florian, however, thinks that the town now called Gummarez is Aradutam. There was also there Ἰ̓ἐρα Φλαϊα [Hiera Flaia] for Ptolemy; this is thought by Clusius and Morales (who elsewhere calls it Fuente encalada) to be what is now Padrón, well known to pilgrims as Patronum; by some others, among them L. Marineus in book 3, it is Sancta Maria in finibus Terrae. The same L. Marineus Siculus mentions the other towns at the beginning of book 3.

units.la: Galecia Regni titulum adepta est circa annum ab Christo nato cIↄ lx. Eo enim Ferdinandus Sanctij Majoris Regis Navarræ F. Rex Castellæ, quum Vxorem duxisset Sanctiam Alphonsi v. F. Veremundi iii. Legionis Regis Sororem & heredem; sicque Regna duo Castellanum & Legionense uniisset, tres habens filios, Sanctius quidem Testamento Castellæ Regem; Alphonsum Legionis & Asturum; Garciam denique Galeciæ (quæ ab Conjugis Majoribus adquisita Comitatus ad illud usque tempus fuerat) & Portugalliæ nominavit. Sanctius, Divisionis paternæ impatiens, Fratres, Alphonsum quidem Regno deturbavit, Garciam autem occidit. Quum jam Sanctius circiter sex annos regnasset, & ab Vellido per fraudem esset obtruncatus, Alphonsus, qui Toleti apud Maurorum regem exsul vixerat, non solum Legionis, quod ex Patris voluntate obtinebat, recuperavit; sed & Castellæ, Galeciæ, Portugalliæque regna est consequutus. Alphonso tres liberi fuerunt legitimi ex totidem Conjugibus: ex Isabella quidem Franciæ Regina, Sanctia, nupta Roderico Comiti, qui novas Colonias duxit in Civitatem, quæ vulgo Ciudad Rodrigo: ex Zaida Maura, Sibiliæ Regis filia, Sanctius, qui acie adversus Saracenos cecidit; ex Constantia denique Urraca, quæ Sanctio Sanctiqué inprolibus superstes, post Raimundum Berengarium Tolosæ Comitem, nupsit Alfonso Aragoniæ Regi; heredemque ex se reliquit Alphonsum vii. Regem omnium, qui ante ipsum fuerant, potentissimum, Hispaniæque Imperatorem nuncupari meritum. Ab eo tempore Galecia unum semper habuit cum Castella Legioneque Regem & Principem.
units.tr: Galicia obtained the title of kingdom around the year of Christ 1060. For then Ferdinand, son of Sancho the Great, King of Navarre, became King of Castile, having married Sancha, sister and heiress of Alfonso V and of Veremund III, King of León; thus he had united the two kingdoms of Castile and León and had three sons. Sancho he named King of Castile in his will, Alfonso King of León and the Asturias, and finally Garcia he named over Galicia (which had been acquired by the Conjugal line from the Greater Kings and had until then been a county) and over Portugal. Sancho, impatient of his father's division, drove Alfonso from his kingdom, and killed Garcia. When Sancho had now reigned about six years and had been cut down by treachery by Vellido, Alfonso, who had lived in exile at Toledo at the court of the Moorish king, not only recovered León, which he held by his father's wish, but also obtained the kingdoms of Castile, Galicia and Portugal. Alfonso had three legitimate children by three wives. By Isabella, Queen of France, he had Sancha, who married Count Roderick, who led new colonies into the city now commonly called Ciudad Rodrigo. By Zaida, a Moorish woman, daughter of the King of Seville, he had Sancho, who fell in battle against the Saracens. Finally, by Constance he had Urraca, who, after the death of Sancho and the childless Sancho's ... survived, married after Raymond Berengar, Count of Toulouse, to Alfonso, King of Aragon; and she left as her heir Alfonso VII, deservedly called the most powerful of all the kings who had gone before him and Emperor of Spain. From that time Galicia always had one king and prince in common with Castile and León.
