units.la: Asturia.
units.tr: Asturia.

units.la: ASTVRIA ad Septemtrionem habet Oceanum; ad Ortum, Biscaiam; ad meridiem, Castellam Veterem; ad Occasum, Galeciam. Auri, variorumque Colorum est ferax: alioquin parum culta maleque habitata; locis, quæ ad mare, exceptis.
units.tr: Asturia borders the Ocean to the north; Biscay to the east; Old Castile to the south; and Galicia to the west. It is rich in gold and in ores of various colours. Otherwise it is little cultivated and poorly inhabited, except for the places along the coast.

units.la: Veterum hic sedes Asturum: qui sic dicti, ut scribit Isidorus lib. ix. Etymolog. cap. ii. ab Astura (dicenim emendandum) Fluvio; cujus mentio etiam apud Florum lib. iv. Hist. Romanae, & alios. Ab his ipsa Regio Ἀστουρία, Ptolemaeo: Latinis Asturia, ut & antiquis Marmoribus: in quibus etiam Asturum lego nominatam. Romae in pavimento Sacelli, quod est ad templum S. Gregorii in Caelio monte, Tabula confracta: ACONTII L. RANIO. OPTATO. V. C. COS CVRATORI. REIP. MEDIOLANENSIVM CVRAT. REIP. NOLANORVM. PROCOS. PROVINCIAE NARBONENSIVM. LEGATO. AVG. ET. IVRIDICO ASTYRIAE. ET. GALAECIAE. CVRATORI. VIAE SALARIAE. &C.
units.tr: This was the ancient seat of the Asturs, who were so called, as Isidore writes in Etymologies, book ix, chapter ii, from the river Astura (for so it should be emended). The river is also mentioned by Florus, Roman History, book iv, and by others. From these people the region itself is called Ἀστουρία by Ptolemy, and Asturia in Latin, as also on ancient marbles, where I also read the name Asturum. At Rome, on the pavement of the chapel beside the church of S. Gregory on the Caelian hill, there is a broken tablet: "To Lucius Ranius Optatus, of consular rank, curator of the state of the Milanese, curator of the state of the Nolans, proconsul of the province of Narbonensis, imperial legate and juridical officer of Asturia and Galicia, curator of the Salarian Way, etc."

units.la: Quin & Asturicam video nuncupatam in Tabula Marmorea, quae trans Tiberim Romae legitur in domo Privata Civis Romani. Verba ponam ad Italiae Delineationem, ubi de Alpibus Maritimis. Asturas hodieque. Astures Plinius lib. iii. cap. iii. dividit in Augustanos & Transmontanos. Illi cis montes versus Meridiem: hi ultra montes versus Septemtrionem ad Oceanum. De Asturibus Silius Italicus lib. i. — Astur avarus Viscieribus latera Telluris mergitur imis, Et redit infelix effosso concolor Auro.
units.tr: Indeed, I see Asturica also named on a marble tablet, which is read across the Tiber at Rome in the private house of a Roman citizen. I will set out the words in my description of Italy, where I treat the Maritime Alps. The Asturas still exist today. Pliny, book iii, chapter iii, divides the Astures into the Augustani and the Transmontani: the former dwelt on this side of the mountains towards the south, the latter beyond the mountains towards the north, at the Ocean. Silius Italicus, book i, writes of the Asturians: "The greedy Asturian digs down into the deepest veins of the earth, and returns unhappy, the same colour as the gold he has dug out."

units.la: Asturum Equorum antea memini. Ipsorum Equitum, Romanis militantium, mentio in Monumento quod vilitur ad primum ab Æmilia lapidem: SEXTO. CLASENO. SEX. F. SEX. NEP. SEX. PRON. CLV. ALLIANO. PONTIFICI. FLAMINI. VICTORIAE. ET. FELIC. CAESAR. PERPETVO. PRAEF. COH III. ASTVR. EQ. C. A. TRIB. LEG II. ITALIC. &C.
units.tr: I have already mentioned the Asturian horses. The Asturian cavalry themselves, serving under the Romans, are mentioned on the monument found at the first milestone from Aemilia: "To Sextus Clasenius Alianus, son of Sextus, grandson of Sextus, of the Pronian tribe, pontiff, flamen of Victoria and of Felicitas, Caesar's perpetual prefect of the third cohort of Asturians, cavalry, C. A., military tribune of the second legion Italica, etc."

units.la: Asturum Populos xii. fuisse, memoriae prodit Plin. iii. cap. iii. In iis, ut idem notat, erant Giguri, vitiose fortean, quum Ptolemaeo sint Ἡγέρρει: Pefici; qui Ptolemaeo Παίονες & alij. Narbafes item, ut eos appellat Isidorus, hic habitarunt; qui Νάρβαοι Ptolemaeo, ubi hodie inter Legionem & Ovetum, Arvas, Forum Narbasorum antiquis Scriptoribus; apud quos & Montes Arvases. Alios praetereo.
units.tr: Pliny, book iii, chapter iii, records that the Asturians had twelve peoples. Among them, as he also notes, were the Giguri, perhaps wrongly named, since in Ptolemy they are Ἡγέρρει; the Pefici, who in Ptolemy are Παίονες, and others. The Narbafes, as Isidore calls them, likewise lived here; they are Νάρβαοι in Ptolemy. Today between León and Oviedo lie the Arvas, known to ancient writers as the Forum Narbasorum, and there are also the Arvases mountains. I pass over the others.

units.la: Provinciae Metropolis est Ovetum; quod, ut censet Moletius & Coquus, Ἀστ Ἀστυρῶν Ptolemaeo. Tarapha Ῥεγαικον Ptolemaei olim dictum putat; quod tamen potius Β ἰδιεῖα nunc esse monet Moletius, unde & Brigacini Populi apud Ptolemaeum. De Oveto multa Rodericus Toletanus lib. iv. de Rebus Hispaniae cap. xviii. ubi etiam exponitur, quam ob causam Civitas Episcoporum fuerit nominata. Est & ibidem Asiorga; quae Asturica Plinio & Antonino; quorum ille Urbem Magnificam vocat; hic quatuor inde Itinera Consularia describit; priora quidem Caesaraugustam, cum per Betunam, tum per Brigecum; Tertium Tarraconem; quartum Burdigalam in Gallias. Ἀστέγκα Αὐγέστ Ptolemaeo dicitur: Coloniam appellant Augusti Nummi.
units.tr: The metropolis of the province is Ovetum (Oviedo), which, as Moletius and Coquus think, is Ptolemy's Ἀστυρῶν. Tarapha holds that it was formerly called Ptolemy's Ῥεγαικον, though Moletius advises that this is rather the place now called Ἰδιεῖα, whence also the Brigacini people in Ptolemy. Rodericus Toletanus, History of Spain, book iv, chapter xviii, says much about Oveto, and there explains why it was named the Civitas Episcoporum (City of Bishops). There is also Asiorga, which is Asturica to Pliny and Antoninus. Pliny calls it a Urbem Magnificam (magnificent city). Antoninus describes four consular routes from it: the first two to Caesaraugustam, one through Betunam and one through Brigecum; the third to Tarraconem; and the fourth to Burdigalam in Gaul. In Ptolemy it is called Ἀστέγκα Αὐγέστ. The coins of Augustus call it Coloniam.

units.la: CAP. XVIII.
units.tr: CAP. XVIII.

units.la: Legio.
units.tr: Legio.

units.la: LEGIONI conregionales ad Boream, Asturia; ad Occidentem, Gallecia: ad Meridiem & Ortum fere, Castella Vetus. Nomen illi ab Legione vii Germanica, quæ hic olim (Nervæ Imperatoris principatu, ut quidam autumant stativa habuit. Ioannes Gerundensis Paralipom. Hispaniæ lib. iii, initio Eleonam dictam scribit ab Elrona Provincia Libyæ, propinqua Syriæ & Æthiopiæ, in qua, ne scilicet appellationis causam ignoremus, maxima Leonum copia invenitur.
units.tr: The regions neighbouring LEON lie: to the north, Asturias; to the west, Galicia; to the south and east, roughly Old Castile. It takes its name from the Seventh Legion, Germanica, which, as some think, had its winter quarters here in the reign of the Emperor Nerva. John of Gerona, in the beginning of the third book of his Paralipomena of Spain, writes that it was called Eleona from Elrona, a province of Libya near Syria and Ethiopia, where, so that we do not miss the reason for the name, a great number of lions is found.

units.la: Hanc Hispaniæ partem qui hodie habitant, eos plerique fuisse volunt, qui Vettones Plinio; Ptolemæo, Straboni, Appiano; Vergones male in Latinis Exemplaribus. Vettonia etiam mentio apud Prudentium. Hi populi, quo tempore primum in Romanorum venerant potestatem, quum quosdam Centuriones viderent deambulandi causa hac illac se flectere, opinati eos (magnum hoc simplicitatis indicium) insanire, Duces se, ut refert Ælianus lib. ii. Variarum cap. v. ad Tabernacula eis præbuere: putabant enim aut in Tabernaculo quiete sedendum, aut pugnandum esse.
units.tr: Those who now inhabit this part of Spain are mostly thought to be the people whom Pliny calls Vettones, Ptolemy, Strabo and Appian call by other names, and whom the Latin copies wrongly name Vergones. Vettonia is also mentioned by Prudentius. When these people first came under Roman power, they saw some centurions strolling about here and there for exercise, and, supposing (a great sign of simplicity) that they were out of their minds, they gave them their tents, as Aelian reports in the fifth chapter of the second book of his Miscellany. For they thought that one should either sit quietly in a tent or fight.

units.la: Metropolis, Urbs illa clarissima Regioni cognominis, quæ Ἀεγίων ζ Γερμανικὴ Ptolemæo; Legio Gemina, Antonino; Leon hodie vulgo; quod nomen, quur ab Leonogildo Gothorum Rege malit, quam ab Legione ipsa Franciscus Tarapha derivare, mihi nondum liquet. Moralis tradit etiam Sublantiam olim dictam, adscribens ejus nominis vestigia etiamnum exstare in loco, qui sesquimiliari distans Legione, dicitur Sollanço. Consulendum moneo hac de re Thesaurum peritissimi rerum Geographicarum Abrahami Ortelij. Illud præterea minime omittendum suggerit Hieronymus Surita Cæsaraugustanus Commentario Antonini Augusti Itinerarium, exstare Auctores, qui ante cccc annos id prodiderint, huic Urbi quondam Floris nomen fuisse inditum. Præfectum Legionis vii Geminæ Legione constituit Scotus, Auctor Notitiæ Provinciarum. De Templo Legionensi sic scribit L. Marineus Siculus lib. iii. de Rebus Hispaniæ: Etsi Templum, quod ætate nostra Civitas Hispalensis ædificat, alia omnia magnitudine præstat; etsi Toletanum cunctis aliis decoris, ornamentis & speculariibus fenestris est illustrius; etsi denique Compostellanum fortioribus ædificiis & S. Iacobi miraculis, & rebus aliis memorabilibus est: Legionense tamen artificio mirabili, meo quidem judicio, omnibus est anteponendum: in cujus Claustro Sacellum est, in quo jacent Reges septem & triginta, & unus Hispaniæ Imperator.
units.tr: The metropolis, that most famous city of the region of the same name, which Ptolemy calls Aegion VII Germanica, and the Antonine Itinerary Legio Gemina, is now commonly called Leon. I am not yet clear why Francisco Tarapha prefers to derive this name from Leovigild, king of the Goths, rather than from the legion itself. Morales also reports that it was formerly called Sublantia, adding that traces of this name still survive in a place about a mile and a half from the legion, which is called Sollanço. On this matter I advise consulting the treasury of Abraham Ortelius, a most skilled expert in geography. Hieronymus Surita of Zaragoza, in his commentary on the Antonine Itinerary, also suggests that one should not pass over the authors who, four hundred years ago, stated that this city was once named Floris. Scotus, the author of the Notitia of the Provinces, placed the prefect of the Seventh Gemina Legion at Legio. L. Marineus Siculus writes thus about the cathedral of León in the third book of his On the Affairs of Spain: Although the temple which the city of Seville is building in our age surpasses all others in size; although the Toledan is more famous than all others for beauty, ornaments and windows of glass; although finally the Compostela is notable for its sturdier buildings, the miracles of St James and other memorable things: nevertheless the León cathedral, in my judgement, is to be preferred to all others for its wonderful workmanship; in its cloister there is a chapel in which lie thirty-seven kings and one emperor of Spain.

units.la: Illud autem memoria dignissimum est, quod ab hac Vrbe cœperit circa annum Icccxvi Recuperatio Hispaniæ, quam totam fere Maurorum & Saracenorum gens occuparat. Pelagius enim, ut cum alijs referunt Rodericus Toletanus lib. de Rebus Hispaniæ vi per multa capita, & Rodericus Sanctius part.1. Hist. Hisp. cap.xi, ex regio Gothorum sanguine, Fafilæ Cantabriæ Ducis filius, ab Christianorum, qui in Montes Asturiæ confugerant, reliquijs Rex consalutatus, magna strage Maurorum edita, vix Regnum rursus, hosti Legionem eripuit; ibiq; sedem sui principatus figens, novum Castellum, quasi propugnaculum adversus Barbarorum vim & incursiones, exstruxit; unde Comites deinceps Castellæ dicti, de quibus postea: rejectis autem Gothorum Regum Insignibus Leonem sumsit Rubrum in albo Campo ferocientem; quo hodieq; Reges Legionenses utuntur. Pelagium in Regno sequutus est Fafila filius: huic autem Improlem Alphonsus Catholicus, Petri Cantabriæ Ducis filius, ex genere Ricaredi Catholici Gothorum Regis oriundus: qui uxorem duxerat Ormisendam Fafilæ Sororem unicam & hæredem. In Alphonsi familia posteriisq; Legionis principatus mansit usq; ad Veremundum, Regem Legionis xxiv: quo, anno cIↄ. xx sine successore defuncto, Sanctia Soror, Ferdinando Navarreo, de quo dixi cap.xvi, Castellæ Regi nupta Legionense Regnum ad Castellanum transtulit.
units.tr: It is especially worth remembering that from this city, around the year 1116, the recovery of Spain began, for almost all of it had been occupied by the Moorish and Saracen people. For Pelayo, as Rodrigo of Toledo in the sixth book of his History of Spain, in many chapters, and Rodrigo Sánchez, in the first part of his Spanish History, chapter 11, report along with others, was the son of Fáfila, duke of Cantabria, of the royal blood of the Goths. Acclaimed king by the remnants of the Christians who had fled to the mountains of Asturias, and after a great slaughter of the Moors, he scarcely recovered the kingdom and snatched León from the enemy. Settling there as the seat of his rule, he built a new castle, as a bulwark against the force and raids of the barbarians; hence the later counts, who were called counts of Castile, of whom more below. Having laid aside the insignia of the Gothic kings, he took as his emblem a red lion rampant on a white field, which the kings of León still use today. Pelayo was succeeded in the kingdom by his son Fáfila; after him came Alfonso the Catholic, son of Pedro, duke of Cantabria, descended from the line of Ricared the Catholic, king of the Goths, who had married Ormisenda, the only sister and heir of Fáfila. The rule of León remained in Alfonso's family and his descendants until Veremund, the twenty-fourth king of León. When he died without an heir in the year 1037, his sister Sancha, married to Ferdinand of Navarre, of whom I spoke in chapter 16, king of Castile, transferred the kingdom of León to the Castilian crown.

units.la: CAP. XIX.
units.tr: CAP. XIX.

units.la: CASTELLAM (cui nomen ab Castello, quod Pelagius Rex, Legione ab Mauris recuperata, ut Propugnaculum, contra hostes exstruxerat) duplicem faciunt Hispaniarum Delineatores, Veterem & Novam. VETEREM circumdant ad Boream Asturia & Biscaia; ad Occasum Portugallia; ad Meridiem Castella Nova, Montibus qui fere per Longitudinem Hispaniæ incedunt, intercurrentibus; ad Ortum Aragonia & Navarra.
units.tr: The map-makers of Spain divide Castile, named from the castle (which King Pelayo built as a bulwark against the enemy when he had recovered León from the Moors), into two parts, Old and New. Old Castile is bounded on the north by Asturias and Biscay; on the west by Portugal; on the south by New Castile, the mountains which run through almost the whole length of Spain lying between them; on the east by Aragon and Navarre.

units.la: Fuerunt hic olim cum alijs Populi Carietes, ut eos vocat Plinius in Conventu Clunienfi: de quibus & Vetus Brixiæ Inscriptio; Vestigia exstant in Ciria opido, ut Pineto videtur: μαγεόγοι, quos nominat Ptolemæus: Pelendones Plinio, πελένδονες Ptolemæo; ubi hodie Medina Cœli, Reuilla del Campo, S. Pedro d'Arlança, Salas, ijsq; vicíniora opida, scribentibus Pineto & Floriano: Vaccei Plinio, βακκαῖοι Ptolemæo, Βακκαῖοι Stephano: Arevaci Plinio, Αρεβακοι Straboni, Αρεβακαι Ptolemæo; Αρεβάκκοι Appiano Alexandrino; Arbachi corrupte Auctori de VV Illustr. cap. lxi: Memoria Arevacorum servari videtur in Pago Aravacca, qui tribus passuum millibus distat Madrito Septemtrionem versus: Navagierus putat Vrbem Arevalo nomen antiquum Arevacorum retinere: eorum Vrbem
units.tr: There were also here, along with other peoples, the Carietes, as Pliny calls them in the Conventus Clunienses; there is also an ancient inscription from Brixia concerning them. Traces of them survive in the town of Ciria, as Pineda thinks: the Magegoi [μαγεόγοι], whom Ptolemy names; the Pelendones for Pliny, Pelendones [πελένδονες] for Ptolemy. Where today stand Medina Cœli, Reuilla del Campo, S. Pedro d'Arlança, Salas, and the towns nearer to them, according to Pineda and Florian: the Vaccei for Pliny, Bakkaioi [βακκαῖοι] for Ptolemy, Bakkaioi [Βακκαῖοι] for Stephanus; the Arevaci for Pliny, Arevakoi [Αρεβακοι] for Strabo, Arevakai [Αρεβακαι] for Ptolemy; Arebakkoi [Αρεβάκκοι] for Appian of Alexandria; Arbachi, corruptly, in the author of De Viris Illustribus, chapter 61. The memory of the Arevaci seems to be preserved in the district of Aravacca, which lies three Roman miles north of Madrid. Navagero thinks the town of Arevalo retains the ancient name of the Arevaci. Their city

units.la: Y bem hoc tempore Marquesiam dici colligit ex antiquis ruinis Carolus Clusius: Areva. cis,inquit Plinius lib.iii. nomen dedit Fluvius Areva (hodie Eresma nominatur Navagiero in Itinerario,quod Italica lingua conscripsit.)Horum sex Populi,Segontia & Vxama:quae nomina crebro aliis in locis usurpantur: praeterea Segovia & Nova Augusta,Termes ipsaq. Clunia. Eandem Vrbes in Arevacus recensentur à Ptolemæo: cui,ut & Appiano τὴρμισον, quod Plinio Termes, à quo Termestini apud Sallustium ; Hi Saltibus inquit occupatis Termestinorum agros invasere: sic emendat v. cl. Iustus Lipsius, commentario ad lib. i v Annalium Taciti, quum antea corrupte legeretur, tum externorum agros. Termestinorum etiam & Termestina nationis mentionem facit Tacitus libro, quem indicavi.
units.tr: And that city is at this time called Marquesia, Carolus Clusius gathers from its ancient ruins. "Arevacis," says Pliny in book 3, "gave its name to the river Areva (today called Eresma by Navagero in his itinerary, which he wrote in Italian). Of these there were six peoples: Segontia and Uxama, names often used elsewhere; besides these, Segovia and Nova Augusta, Termes and Clunia itself." The same cities are listed under the Arevacus by Ptolemy, and by Appian the Termes, which Pliny calls Termes, from which come the Termestini in Sallust: "These, having seized the passes, invaded the fields of the Termestini." So the most learned Justus Lipsius emends it, in his commentary on book 4 of Tacitus's Annals, where previously it was corruptly read as "then the fields of foreigners." Tacitus too mentions the Termestini and the Termestine nation in the book I have indicated.

units.la: Metropolis Veteris Castellæ Civitas Burgensis, vulgo Burgos putatur Ptolemæo. Vrbs antiquissima,multisq; rebus insignis, & inter primarias Hispaniæ merito referenda; cl. sub se habens minorum gentium oppida; magnis, pulchris, commodisque ædificijs passim adornata; Foris venalibus,Plateis, Vicis, Pontibus, Templis, Cœnobijs, Amnibus exculta; ob incredibilem Incolarum cujuscumq; ætatis, sexus, conditionis,industriam & diligentiam memoranda.Laudat eam lib.iii de reb. Hisp. L. Marineus Siculus; qui & ibi multa de Monasterio Monialium, quod Huelgas vulgo, ejusque divitijs & ampla Iurisdictione. Scribunt nonnulli hanc Vrbem olim nomen etiam habuisse Masburgi; quorum auctoritate freti, nescio: nisi forte ex lecto parum caute Ptolemæo, qui Bravum Mourbogis adcenset: ex Mourbogis enim Masburgum arbitror exstructum ab ijs, qui parum Græce noverant. Circumdant suam Metropolin jucundissimo commodissimoque situ: Palencia ad Carrionis marginem sita : Palantia Plinio & Pomponio Melæ: Παλαντία Ptolemæo & Appiano; Παλλαντία Straboni; Peralancia corrupte apud Antoninum. Hanc alij Vaccæorum, alij Arevacorum opidum faciunt. Strabo: τὰν δ' Ἀρευακῶν ἐςι κὴ Σιγίδα κὴ Παλλαντία; nam statim ab eodem auctore Vaccæorum fit mentio. A Palantia Palantini apud Frontinum de Limitibus Agrorum ; male in Vulgatis Codicibus Palatini: ab eadem Palantini Campi Orosio, qui item Gothici nuncupati, quæ nunc Regio Gothorum dicta. Palantiam ab Rege Hispaniæ Palatuo conditam quidam fabulantur. Hic olim Academiam fuisse volunt, quæ nunc Salamanticæ. In Palantina Diœcesi Sacerdotia Gentilitia, quæ Iuris-Patronatus vocant, quadringenta esse memoriæ prodit Marineus Siculus lib. iii de Reb. Hispaniæ. Valdoledum, Sedes olim Regia; locus in amœnissima Pisuergæ ripa, non Hispaniæ solum, sed Europæ totius pulcherrimus; cui quæ Vrbs anteponatur, non invenitur: agro beatus fertili Frugum, Animalium, Vini, omnisque generis fructuum: Forum ibi pulcherrimum amplissimumque; cujus ambitus Io c c passuum: quumque multis alijs de caussis hoc opidum valde fit nobilitatum, multo tamen magnificentius illud reddidit inlustrissimus Philippi Regis Hispaniarum ortus. Vulgo Valladolid: quod Vallem Oleti sunt qui interpretantur. νῦν Ptolemæo, Pintia Antonino, ut censet Carolus Clusius. Videndus tamen Hieronymus Surita ad Antonini Itinerarium , qui notat multo plura milliaria Valle Oleti Randam (ea autem Aranda ad Durij ripas est) interesse, quam isthoc itinere proponuntur ab Antonino Pintia Randam: Vallem enim Oleti dextrorsus per aliquot milliaria derelinqui. Simanca, Antonino Septimanca. Camora, Ptolemæo Σαραβρῖς, ut Clusio videtur: quæ vitiose Sabaria apud Antoninum: Sarabrim tamen esse putant Florianus del Campo & Gomerius opidum illud, quod vulgo vocatur Toro, Latinis Taurus, ad Durium fluvium. Non autem postremi hic visitur loci Salmantica Antonino, Σαλμαντικα Ptolemæo, Σαλμάτις Polyæno lib. vii de Annibale: Salamanca vulgo. Hinc Salmaticensis apud Iulium Frontinum de Limitibus Agrorum; & in vetusto lapide, qui in templo ibi S. Pelagij.
units.tr: The metropolis of Old Castile, the Civitas Burgensis, commonly thought to be Burgos, is Ptolemy's city. It is a very ancient city, notable for many things and rightly counted among the foremost in Spain; it has under its authority many towns of lesser peoples, is everywhere adorned with large, handsome and convenient buildings, and is furnished with markets, squares, streets, bridges, temples, monasteries and rivers; it is worth remarking on account of the incredible industry and diligence of its inhabitants of every age, sex and condition. L. Marineus Siculus praises it in book 3 of De rebus Hispaniae, and there he also says much about the convent of nuns commonly called Huelgas, and its riches and wide jurisdiction. Some write that this city once also had the name Masburgi; I do not know on what authority they rely, unless perhaps from a text of Ptolemy read rather carelessly, who lists Bravum among the Mourbogis; for I think Masburgum was formed from Mourbogis by those who had little Greek. Its metropolis is surrounded by a most pleasant and convenient site: Palencia, situated on the bank of the Carrion, called Palantia by Pliny and Pomponius Mela; Παλαντία [Palantia] in Ptolemy and Appian; Παλλαντία [Pallantia] in Strabo; Peralancia, corruptly, in Antoninus. Some make this a town of the Vaccaei, others of the Arevaci. Strabo: "And of the Arevacans are Segida and Pallantia" [τὰν δ' Ἀρευακῶν ἐστι καὶ Σιγίδα καὶ Παλλαντία]; for mention of the Vaccaei is made immediately afterwards by the same author. From Palantia come the Palantini in Frontinus, On the Limits of Fields; wrongly in the common editions Palatini. From the same place come the Palantine Plain in Orosius, which are also called Gothic, and which is now called the Region of the Goths. Some fabulously tell that Palantia was founded by Palatuus, a king of Spain. They hold that it once had the academy which is now at Salamanca. Marineus Siculus, book 3 of De rebus Hispaniae, records that there are four hundred hereditary benefices in the diocese of Palencia, which they call Iuris-Patronatus. Valladolid, a royal seat in former times, is a place on the most pleasant bank of the Pisuerga, the most beautiful not only in Spain but in all Europe; no city can be found that is preferred to it; it is blessed with fertile land for crops, animals, wine and every kind of fruit. There is a very handsome and very large marketplace there, whose circuit is 1,000 paces. Although this town has been greatly ennobled for many other reasons, the most illustrious birth of King Philip of Spain has made it far more magnificent. Commonly Valladolid, which some interpret as "Vallem Oleti" (the valley of the olive). Pintia is Ptolemy's nyn [νῦν], according to Carolus Clusius. Yet Hieronymus Surita, on Antoninus's Itinerary, should be consulted; he notes that the distance between Pintia and Aranda (which Aranda lies on the banks of the Duero) is much greater than the mileage given in this route by Antoninus from Pintia to Randa, since Valle Oleti is left some miles off to the right. Simanca is Antoninus's Septimanca. Camora is, in Ptolemy, Σαραβρῖς [Sarabris], as it seems to Clusius, which is corruptly Sabaria in Antoninus; yet Florian del Campo and Gomez think that town is Sarabrim, which is commonly called Toro, in Latin Taurus, on the river Duero. Nor is the last place here Salmantica in Antoninus, Σαλμαντικα [Salmantika] in Ptolemy, Σαλμάτις [Salmatis] in Polyaenus, book 7, on Hannibal; commonly Salamanca. Hence Salmaticensis in Julius Frontinus, On the Limits of Fields, and on an ancient stone which is in the church of S. Pelagius there.

units.tr: TO THE SPIRITS OF THE DEAD. JULIUS CAPITO OF SALAMANCA, AGED 70 YEARS. JULIA RUSTICILLA, HIS MOST DUTIFUL SISTER, SET THIS UP. MAY THE EARTH LIE LIGHTLY ON YOU.

units.la: Salmaticenses proprie Vicanos dici scribit Aggenus Urbicus. Salmanticam à Salaminis & Atticis, Græciæ Populis, conditam notant Ioannes Gerundensis Paralip. Hispan. lib. 11, ubi de Aduentu Teucri & aliorum Græcorum in Hispaniam, deque Vrbibus ab ijs conditis, & Ioannes Vasæus Hispaniæ Chronico ad annum post Diluvium cIɔ cxxxix. Clarissimam habet hæc Vrbs Academiam, variis Pontificum Regumque Privilegijs ornatam, Disciplinarum omnium genitricem: à qua omnes fere Hispaniæ Vrbes & Populi, tamquam à Domina, Leges petunt & Iura. Hinc Consiliarij, Theologi, Iurisconsulti, Medici, reliquarumque Scientiarum Magistri in varias Hispaniarum Provincias & Regna peti proficiscique consueverunt.
units.tr: Aggenus Urbicus writes that the Salmaticenses are properly called Vicanos. Ioannes Gerundensis, in the eleventh book of his Paralipomena Hispaniae, where he treats of the arrival of Teucer and other Greeks in Spain and of the cities they founded, and Ioannes Vasaeus, in his Chronicle of Spain for the year 1139 after the Flood, note that Salmanticam was founded by the Salaminians and Athenians, peoples of Greece. This city has a most famous university, adorned with many privileges granted by popes and kings, the mother of all the disciplines. Almost all the cities and peoples of Spain seek their laws and rights from it, as from a mistress. From here counsellors, theologians, jurists, physicians and masters of the other sciences are wont to be sought out and sent to the various provinces and kingdoms of Spain.

units.la: Iura ibi sunt professi Didacus & Antonius Covarruviæ; uti ipse Didacus in Varijs Resolutionibus testatur, non uno loco. Dominicus à Soto lib. 1. de justitia & jure suam vocat Academiam. Haud procul hinc ad fluvium, qui vulgo Gada, Civitas Roderici Comitis, de quo dixi cap. xvi, Ciudad Rodrigo; quæ, ut putant Vasæus & Clusius, Μυροβρίγα Ptolemæo, Celticorum opidum in Lusitania; à quo Mirobrigenses Celtici apud Plinium, quos Civitatis ejusdem Incolas interpretatur Iacobus Delgadus, quasi Rodrigo corruptum esset nomen ex Mirobriga. Tendentibus hinc versus Meridiem occurrit Coria, Caurita quondam, ut scribit, nullo nominato auctore, Clusius: Cauriam ab Latinis Iunioribus appellari tradit Andr. Schottus. Cauriæ versus Ortum ad nonam circiter Leucam est Placentia, urbs pulcherrima; cujus
units.tr: Didacus and Antonius Covarruvias taught law there, as Didacus himself attests in his Various Resolutions in more than one place. Dominicus a Soto, in the first book of his work On Justice and Law, calls it his own academy. Not far from here, on the river which is commonly called the Gada, lies Civitas Roderici (the city of the Count Roderick, of whom I spoke in chapter 16), now Ciudad Rodrigo. Vasaeus and Clusius think this is the Ptolemaic Myrobriga [Μυροβρίγα], a Celtic town in Lusitania, from which Pliny's Mirobrigenses Celtici take their name; Iacobus Delgadus interprets them as the inhabitants of this same city, and holds that the name Rodrigo was corrupted from Mirobriga. Heading south from here one meets Coria, once called Caurita, as Clusius writes, without naming any author. Andreas Schottus reports that the Later Latins called it Cauria. About nine leagues east of Cauriam is Placentia, a very beautiful city.

units.la: Citria, cæterisque Arborum fructus, nec non Panis candidissimus maximè solent commendari & expeti: Plazencia vulgo. Ambrosium Pagum ibi quondam fuisse scribit Ioannes Mariana de Rebus gestis Hispaniæ. Habet Placentia sub sua ditione Opida amœnissima, in quis est Xavahicium Nemoribus superbiens, & Pisaro in Convalle jacens, velut altare, ut Marineus notat in Testudine templi. Montes Placentiæ adjacentes ab ipsa Urbe Vera de Plazencia cognominantur. Quæ Avila hodie, Ptolemæo Ἀβύλα nuncupatur, ut vult Clusius. Haud procul fontibus Areva, cujus antea memini, Segobia jacet, quæ Plinio & Antonino Segovia, ut hodieque, Ptolemæo Σεγοβία. Sunt vetustissimi Nummi ærei, qui ex vna parte Caput decora facie juvenis præferunt, cum litteris ad sinistram C, dextram autem I; ex altera vero Viri effigiem cum hasta, celeri impetu velociter equo currentis, subscripta pedibus SEGOVIA. Vrbs est lanificio & Aquæductu visendo Romani operis nobilis: in qua, ut Vasæus scribit, illud memorabile, quod illic nemo conspiciatur ociosus, nemo mendicus, nisi qui per ætatem aut morbum opus facere non possit: quum nulli desit, unde victum quærat, aut in quo se exerceat. Quæ nunc Aranda ad Durium flumen, Ῥαύδα Vaccæorum urbs est Ptolemæo in Hispania Tarraconensi; Rauda Antonino ex emendatione Hieronymi Suritæ; nam antea Raudaclunia cum altera mansione mista legebatur. Raudam etiam Regum Legionensium tempore vocatam fuisse constat ex Vetusto Exemplari, in quo descriptæ leguntur ab nescio quo Auctore Res ab Legionensibus gestæ. In eo ubi de Ranimiro Legionensi Rege, qui Cæsaraugustam Saracenis vi eripuit, hæcinter alia commemorantur: Tunc temporis populavit Roderic[?] Comes Amaiam. Didacus etiam Comes populavit Burgis per jussionem Regis. Populavit etiam Munio Alunia Raudam, & Gondisalvus tollit Exomam, & Gondisalvus Ferdinandi Axiam, Duniam (emendandum Cluniam, de qua paullo post) & S. Stephanum. Quæ incerto scriptori Exoma, Vxama Plinio est, qui addit nomen hoc crebro alijs in locis vsurpari: cognomen adscribit Ptolemæus; cui Ὀξάμα Ἀρεβακορῶν vocatur, Arevacorum urbs: Vxama per S. in antiquo marmore legitur: Osma hodie dicitur. Reliquas nominatis à me adponendas Curiosioribus relinquo.
units.tr: Citrons and the other fruits of trees, and also the whitest bread, are most often praised and sought after there: Plazencia in the vernacular. Juan de Mariana, in his work on the deeds of Spain, writes that Ambrosium Pagum once stood there. Placentia has under its rule very pleasant towns, among them Xavahicium, which takes pride in its groves, and Pisaro, lying in a valley, like an altar, as Marineus notes in his description of the temple's vault. The mountains adjoining Placentia are called Vera de Plazencia after the city itself. The town that today is Avila is called Ἀβύλα [Abyla] by Ptolemy, as Clusius holds. Not far from the springs of the Areva, which I mentioned earlier, lies Segobia, which Pliny and Antoninus call Segovia, as it still is today, and which Ptolemy calls Σεγοβία [Segobia]. There are very old bronze coins which on one side bear the head of a young man of comely face, with the letter C on the left and I on the right; on the other side is the figure of a man with a spear, riding a horse that runs at swift speed, with the word SEGOVIA written beneath the feet. The city is famous for its wool-making and for its aqueduct, worth seeing, a noble work of Roman construction. Of it Vasaeus writes this remarkable thing: that there no one is to be seen idle, and no one a beggar, except those who by age or sickness cannot work, since no one lacks a means of getting a living or a trade in which to occupy himself. The town now called Aranda, on the river Duero, is Ῥαύδα [Rhauda], the city of the Vaccaei, in Ptolemy's Hispania Tarraconensis; Rauda in Antoninus, following the correction of Jerónimo Zurita; for previously it was read as Raudaclunia, mixed up with another station. That it was also called Raudam in the time of the kings of León is established from an old manuscript, in which the deeds of the Leonese are written down by some unknown author. In it, where it speaks of Ramiro, king of León, who wrested Caesaraugusta from the Saracens by force, these things are recorded among others: At that time Roderic[?] the count plundered Amaia. Count Diego also plundered Burgos by the king's command. Munio likewise plundered Alunia and Rauda, and Gonzalo takes Exoma, and Gonzalo Ferdinand's Axia, Dunia (to be corrected to Cluniam, of which a little later) and San Esteban. The town that the unknown writer calls Exoma is Uxama to Pliny, who adds that this name is often used in other places as well; Ptolemy assigns it a surname, calling it Ὀξάμα Ἀρεβακορῶν [Oxama Arebakoron], the city of the Arevaci. Vxama with an S is read in an ancient marble inscription; today it is called Osma. I leave the remaining names, which I have cited here, to the more curious readers.

units.la: Fuerunt olim hic etiam aliæ Vrbes nobilissimæ; sed quæ vel dirutæ, vel tantam
units.tr: There were also formerly here other most noble cities; but these, having either been razed or having suffered so great a calamity, that their exact location is little known.

units.la: passæ calamitatem, ut de loco certo parum constet. Inter eas principem facile locum tuebatur Numantia, totius quondam Hispaniæ robur, fortiumque Militum genitrix; quantum, inquit Florus lib. 11. histor. Rom. cap. xviii, Karthaginis, Capua, Corinthi opibus inferior, ita Virtutis nomine & honore par omnibus, summumque, si viros æstimes, Hispaniæ decus: quippe quæ sine Muro, sine Turribus, modice edito in tumulo apud flumen Durium sitacta, quatuor millibus Celtiberorum xl. millium exercitum per annos xiv sola sustinuit: nec sustinuit modo, sed sævius aliquanto perculit, pudendisque fœderibus adsecit. Novissime quum invictam esse conslaret, opus quoque eo fuit, qui Karthaginem everterat. Bellum Numantinum, Reliquæ ab Numantinis contra Romanos variosque eorum Duces, præcipue vero P. Cornelium Scipionem Africanum, per annos xiv, vel ut Strabo xx, gestas describunt L. Iulius Florus loco, quem dixi, & Epitomis librorum Livij lv quatuorque sequentium, Appianus de bello Hispan. Eutropius lib. iv, Paterc. lib. ii, Strabo lib. iii, Valerius Max. lib. vii. cap. vi, Auctor de VV. Inlustr. cap. lviii, Veget. lib. iii cap. x. Orosius lib. v. cap. vi, Augustinus lib. iii de Civit. Dei, cap. xxi, & alij. Deleta est anno ab v. c. Io cxxi, P. Mucio Scævola & L. Calpurnio Pisone coss. De Interitu ejus fama duplex. Alij Cives ipsos ad incredibilem famem, humanarumque Carnium Dapes & ipsissimam Desperationem adactos Sc, Patriamque ferro, veneno, subjectoque undique igne peremisse produnt; ne quid præter nudum nomen Victoribus esset, quo triumpharent: Alij à Scipione deletam narrant, etiam sine Senatus auctoritate; vel quod Victor id è republica esse censeret, vel quod natura crudelis in eos esset, quos vi caperet; vel certe quod maximis urbium eversionibus clarius se nomen suum esse redditurum putaret: sane ab Vrbe debellata Numantini cognomen sibi sumsit, testibus Auctore de VV. Inlustr. & Plinio lib. xxxiii natur. hist. cap. xr, ubi & de Scipionis Triumpho. Tanti erat Numantia victa momenti, ut mox Scipio reliquam Regionem in fidem accepeit; ceterasque, quæ defecerant, Civitates Hispaniæ, partim vi, partim deditione in potestatem suam redegerit. Agri Numantinorum, post eam Victoriam, Vrbibus vicinis sunt distributi. Νομαντια Ptolemæo & Græcis, Νομαντια Strephano inter Arevacos & Durium flumen: Garrai hodie, ut vult Ambrosius Moralis; Soria, ut Tarapha & Antonius Nebrissensis lib. v. Dec. i. cap. iv; Haud procul Soria fuisse, censet Clusius: quatuor millibus supra Soriam ad Garai pontem non longe abortu Durij fluminis rudera Numantiæ monstrari notat Ioannes Mariana lib. iii. cap. i. Plinius lib. iii. nat. hist. cap. iii Numantinæ: Pelendonibus, Celtiberorum populis, attribuit; Ptolemæus Arevacis. Strabo Numantiam ab Cæsaraugusta abesse perhibet stadiis octingentis: quorum rationem cum numeris Mansionum, quæ apud Antoninum sunt in Itinerario, conferre non oportet: quod apud hunc viæ per Diverticula quædam Mansionum sæpe ducantur. Numantiam quasi coronabant præsignes aliæ Vrbes. Graccurris Antonino, Τεγινεης Ptolemæo, Gracuris etiam nonnullis. Graccurrim scribi debere comp lures ærei nummi testantur; ex quibus unum profert Surita cum hac Inscriptione TI. CÆSAR DIVI AVG. F. AVGVSTVS; in aversa autem facie cum Tauri effigie mitrati, infra cujus pedes GRACCVRRIS. Agridam hodie appellari opinantur Clusius & Moralis: subdubitat Antonius Augustinus an sit Grati. Grachurim Iberæ Regionis Vibem antea Illurcim denominatam tradit Festus lib. vii de verbor. signific. Plinius Cassantenses, Ergavicenses & Graccuritanos Cæsaraugustanum conventum adire memorat. Graccurrim a Ti. Graccho conditam dictamque ex Epitoma Liviana lib. xli paret: Ti. Sempronius Gracchus, inquit, Proconsule Celtiberos victos in deditionem accepit: monimentumque operum suorum Graccurrim opidum in Hispania constituit. Strabo perhibet Polybium prodere trecentas Celtiberorum Vrbes à Ti. Graccho esse subversas, quod ritu Comico in Ti. Gracchi gratiam dictum intelligi vult ab Auctore, qui Turres Vrbes appellavit, ut in Triumphalibus Pompis fieri solitum. Turiaso Antonino, Τυριασω Ptolemæo; urbs olim celebris, quam Taraconam hodie dici volunt Clusius, Florianus & Varrerius; alij aliam censent. Surita duos profert Nummos: in quorum uno Capitis Feminæ visitur effigies, cum hac Inscriptione SILBIS, quod Numinis alicujus videtur esse nomen; in aversa facie Viri equitantis imago, protenta dextera, habitu Pacificatoris; & infra equi pedes TVRIASO: in altero Augusti facies cum Inscriptione IMP. AVGVSTVS P. P. & in aversa parte, in media Coronæ Civicæ area MVN. litteræ, quæ Municipium fuisse docent: sub corona denique TVRIASO: à qua Turiasonenses apud Plinium. Augusstobriga Antonino, Αυγουστοβριγα Ptolemæo Pelendonum urbs: opidulum esse, quod hodie Aldea el muro vocant, tradit Ambrosius Moralis: ruinas ejus in opido Muro VIII M. P. supra Vrbem Agredam conspici notat Hieronymus Surita: qui & lapides Augusstobriga mentionem facientes producit, anno clɔ lɔ xlvii Via Consulari inter eamdem urbem & Numantiam eruetos: quorum in
units.tr: that little is certain about their exact location. Among them, Numantia easily held the first place, once the strength of all Spain and the mother of brave soldiers. "As much," says Florus in book 2 of his Roman History, chapter 18, "as it was inferior to Carthage, Capua and Corinth in wealth, so it was equal to them all in the name and honour of courage, and, if you judge by men, the highest glory of Spain. For without a wall, without towers, set on a modest hill by the river Duero, it alone, with four thousand Celtiberians, held out for fourteen years against an army of forty thousand. Nor did it merely hold out; it struck back rather more fiercely and forced shameful treaties upon the enemy. At last, when it was plain that it could not be conquered, it needed the man who had overthrown Carthage." The Numantine War, the deeds of the Numantines against the Romans and their various commanders, especially Publius Cornelius Scipio Africanus, over fourteen years (or, as Strabo says in book 20, [some other span]), are described by Lucius Julius Florus in the passage I have cited, by the epitomes of the fifty-fifth and following books of Livy, by Appian in his work on the Spanish war, by Eutropius book 4, Paterculus book 2, Strabo book 3, Valerius Maximus book 7 chapter 6, the author De viris illustribus chapter 58, Vegetius book 3 chapter 10, Orosius book 5 chapter 6, Augustine De civitate Dei book 3 chapter 21, and others. It was destroyed in the year 621 from the founding of the city, in the consulship of Publius Mucius Scaevola and Lucius Calpurnius Piso. There are two accounts of its end. Some report that the citizens themselves, driven to incredible famine, to eating human flesh and to utter despair, killed themselves with the sword, poison, and fire set on every side, so that nothing but the bare name would be left for the victors to triumph over. Others say that it was destroyed by Scipio, even without the authority of the Senate, either because the victor thought this was for the good of the republic, or because he was by nature cruel towards those he took by force, or certainly because he thought his name would be made more famous by the greatest overthrows of cities. Certainly, after the city was conquered, he took the surname Numantinus, as witnessed by the author De viris illustribus and by Pliny in book 33 of his Natural History, chapter 11, where he also speaks of Scipio's triumph. So great was the importance of conquered Numantia that Scipio soon took the rest of the region under his protection and brought the other cities of Spain that had revolted under his power, some by force, some by surrender. After that victory the lands of the Numantines were distributed to the neighbouring cities. Numantia in Ptolemy and the Greeks, Nomantia [Νομαντια] in Stephanus, lay between the Arevaci and the river Duero. It is today Garray, as Ambrosio de Morales holds, or Soria, as Tarapha and Antonio de Nebrija think in book 5, decade 1, chapter 4. Clusius thinks it was not far from Soria. Juan de Mariana, book 3 chapter 1, notes that ruins of Numantia are shown four miles above Soria, at the bridge of Garray, not far from the source of the Duero. Pliny in book 3 of his Natural History, chapter 3, assigns Numantina to the Pelendones, a people of the Celtiberians; Ptolemy assigns it to the Arevaci. Strabo says that Numantia is eight hundred stadia from Caesaraugusta; this distance should not be compared with the numbers of the stations which are in the Itinerary of Antoninus, because on that road the routes often lead through certain side branches between stations. Numantia was almost encircled by other notable cities. Graccurris in Antoninus, Tegineës [Τεγινεης] in Ptolemy, Gracuris for some. That the name should be written Graccurris is attested by several bronze coins, one of which Zurita publishes, with this inscription: TI. CAESAR DIVI AVG. F. AVGVSTVS; on the reverse a figure of a mitred bull, beneath whose feet is GRACCVRRIS. Clusius and Morales think it is today called Agrida; Antonius Augustinus doubts whether it is Grati. Festus, book 7 of De verborum significatione, says that the city of Iberian territory, Grachurim, was formerly named Illurcis. Pliny records that the Cassantenses, Ergaviçenses and Graccuritani resorted to the assembly of Caesaraugusta. That Graccurris was founded and named after Tiberius Gracchus is clear from the Epitome of Livy, book 41: "Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus, as proconsul, received the Celtiberians into surrender after defeating them, and set up Graccurris, a town in Spain, as a memorial of his works." Strabo reports that Polybius records that three hundred Celtiberian towns were overthrown by Tiberius Gracchus; he wishes this to be understood, in the manner of comedy and in favour of Tiberius Gracchus, of the author who called the towers "cities", as was customary in triumphal processions. Turiaso in Antoninus, Tyriaso [Τυριασω] in Ptolemy, a city once famous, which Clusius, Florián de Ocampo and Varrerius want to be called Tarazona today; others think otherwise. Zurita publishes two coins. On one of them is the figure of a woman's head with this inscription, SILBIS, which seems to be the name of some divinity; on the reverse is the image of a horseman with his right hand outstretched, in the manner of one bringing peace, and beneath the horse's feet TVRIASO. On the other is the face of Augustus with the inscription IMP. AVGVSTVS P. P., and on the reverse, in the middle of the field of a civic crown, the letters MVN, which show it was a municipium; finally, beneath the crown, TVRIASO. From this come the Turiasonenses in Pliny. Augustobriga in Antoninus, Augoustobriga [Αυγουστοβριγα] in Ptolemy, a city of the Pelendones. Ambrosio de Morales says that it is a small town which is today called Aldea del Muro. Jerónimo Zurita notes that its ruins can be seen in the town of Muro, eight Roman miles above the city of Agreda, and he also brings forward stones mentioning Augustobriga, dug up in the year 1547 along the consular road between that city and Numantia, of which one is in

units.la: 10 Clunia, cujus meminerunt Plinius lib. iii, cap. iii, & Suetonius in Galba cap. ix: Plutarcho in Galba; Dioni lib. xxxix, & Ptolemæo Κλυνία vocatur, Arevacorum opidum: hodie, ut volunt Antonius Nebrissensis, Clusius & Florianus, Coruña; ut alij, Cruna. Coruña hæc cognominatur del Conde ad differentiam ejus, quæ est in Galecia. Cluniam corruptam esse ex Coronia verisimile est. Nam Colonia Suipucia dicitur in Nummo Galbæ. Nebrissensis Comitem illius opidi Cluniacensem appellat. Vasæus Corunnam non vere Cluniam esse, sed quæ olim Clunia, fuisse ab Corunna quarta Leucæ parte docet; ibique esse antiquæ Urbis vestigia, & Sacellum D. Virgini sacrum, appellarique Castro. Extant ibi Amphitheatri aliæque Antiquitatum reliquiæ: quin & Sigillum Conventus Cluniensis (tam enim celebris fuit olim Clunia, ut multarum Civitatum Conventus illi fuerit attributus, de quo dixi cap. ix) ante aliquot annos repertum, penes Comitem Clunienscm hodie asservatur. Segisamunclum Antonino; Σεγισαμόνκλον Ptolemæo; Σεγισαμα Vaccæorum urbs Straboni; Segisamonenses Plinio: hodie, ut videtur Pineto, Segura; ut Garybaio, Veigama. Alia item Σεγίσαμα Ιουλία Ptolemæo est; unde Segisamcinlienses apud Plinium; ea Segesamo simpliciter nominatur Antonino. Haud procul Palantia stetit floruitque Intercatia, nota cum Geographis Straboni & Antonino; tum aliis scriptoribus, ut Polybio, Appiano, Auctori de V V. Illustribus, & aliis. Ptolemæus duas habet Intercatias, unam in Orniacis, alteram in Vaccæis. Hinc Intercatienses apud Plinium lib. xviii. Ex horum numero fuit, quem singulari certamine Provocatorem superavit P. Cornelius Scipio Æmilianus. Epitoma Liviana lib. lxviii: Vaccæos Cantabros & alias adhuc incognitas nationes in Hispania subegit. Ibi P. Cornelius Africanus Scipio Æmilianus L. Pauli F. Africani N. sed adoptivus, Provocatorem Barbarum Trib. militum occidit: & in expugnatione Intercatiæ Urbis majus etiam periculum adiit. Ita in MS. legitur. Librariorum imperitia Intercatiæ vocem Intercaptæ substituerat. Sic Plinius libro xxxvi cap. i: Ipse apud auctores & Intercatienses illum, cujus patrem Scipio Æmilianus ex Provocatione interfecerat, pugnæ ejus effigie significe, vulgato stilo, plerumque Incommodum valere aliquid: non enim hoc fuisse actarum eum, si Scipio a Patre ejus interemtus esset. Adeundus & Auctor de VV. Illustr. cap. lviii. Marmor Intercatiensi positum in radice turris Ecclesiæ D. Mariæ, cognomine de Rebilla, extra Cruniam, legitur apud Hieronymum Suritam doctissimis in Antonini Itinerarium Emendationibus. Pluribus commemorandis, ne molestus sim Lectori, supersedebo.
units.tr: 10 Clunia, which is mentioned by Pliny in book iii, chapter iii, and by Suetonius in Galba, chapter ix; by Plutarch in Galba; by Dio in book xxxix; and by Ptolemy as Κλυνία, a town of the Arevaci. Today, as Antonio de Nebrija, Clusius and Florian think, it is Coruña; as others think, Cruna. This Coruña is called del Conde to distinguish it from the one in Galicia. It is likely that Cluniam was corrupted from Coronia, for Colonia Suipucia is the name on a coin of Galba. Nebrija calls the count of that town Cluniacensem. Vasaeus teaches that Corunnam is not truly Clunia but was once Clunia, lying a quarter of a league from Corunna; there are traces of the ancient city there, a chapel sacred to the Virgin, and the place is called Castro. Remains of an amphitheatre and other antiquities survive there. Moreover, a seal of the Conventus Cluniensis (for Clunia was once so famous that the assize of many cities was assigned to its conventus, as I said in chapter ix), found some years ago, is kept today by the Count of Clunia. Segisamunclum in Antoninus; Σεγισαμόνκλον in Ptolemy; Σεγισαμα, a town of the Vaccaei, in Strabo; Segisamonenses in Pliny: today, it seems, Pineto, Segura; according to Garibay, Veigama. There is also another Σεγίσαμα Ιουλία in Ptolemy, whence the Segisamcinlienses in Pliny; Antoninus simply calls it Segesamo. Not far from Palantia stood and flourished Intercatia, known to the geographers Strabo and Antoninus, and to other writers such as Polybius, Appian, the author of De viris illustribus, and others. Ptolemy has two Intercatiae, one among the Orniaci and the other among the Vaccaei. Hence the Intercatienses in Pliny, book xviii. Of their number was the man whom P. Cornelius Scipio Aemilianus overcame in single combat as challenger. The Epitome of Livy, book lviii: "He subdued the Vaccaei, the Cantabri and other nations still unknown in Spain." There P. Cornelius Africanus Scipio Aemilianus, son of L. Paulus and grandson by adoption of Africanus, killed a barbarian challenger as a military tribune, and in the storming of "the city of Intercatia" he faced an even greater danger. So it is read in the manuscript; through the ignorance of copyists the word Intercatiae had been replaced by Intercaptae. Pliny likewise, book xxxvi, chapter i: "Among the authors and the Intercatienses, he himself, whose father Scipio Aemilianus had killed in single combat, is marked by the image of that fight, in the common style, which generally means that something has value; for he would not have been a fighter, had Scipio been killed by his father." The author De viris illustribus, chapter lviii, should also be consulted. An inscription on marble, set at the base of the tower of the church of St Mary, surnamed de Rebilla, outside Cruna, is read in Hieronymus Surita's very learned emendations to the Antonine Itinerary. I shall pass over further examples, so as not to weary the reader.

units.la: Castellæ porro Regno tale legitur fuisse initium. Pelagius, ut capite xviii ex probatissimis Veterum scriptorum monimentis narravi, erepta rursum Mauris Legione, Castellum quasi Propugnaculum adversus Barbarorum vim exstruxerat: cui qui Præfecti, Comites Castellæ nuncupati, Regem Legionensem, ut Principem, diu agnoverunt usque ad Ordonium II, decimumquartum Asturum Legionisque Regem: qui quum Comites Procerebique Castellæ per speciem Colloquij ad se evocatos obtruncassent, Castellani pessimo scelere indignati, projecto Regum Legionis jugo, ex suo corpore duos, ut Rodericus Sanctius scribit Parte I Histor. Hispaniæ cap. xi. & part. iii multis capitibus, elegerunt Iudices Nunium Rasuram & Lainum Calvum; unum, qui Iuridicundo, alterum qui rebus Bellicis præesset: quorum Liberi horumque Posteri (indicati ab Alphonso Karthaginiensi in Regum Hispan. Anacephal. cap. lxx.) Comites Castellæ sunt appellati usque ad Sanctium Majorem Navarræ Regem, qui quum bello fortis Cordubam & Toletum Saracennis eripuisset. Mauros omnes Navarra, Aragonia, Castella, Legione, Portugallia, alijsque Hispaniæ locis exturbasset, totamque Hispaniam Christiano Nomini restituisset, ducta Elvira Sanctij Castellæ Comitis filia, Garliæque postremi Comitis Sorore & ex Asse heredé, Se dotis nomine non Comitem, sed Regem Castellæ scripsit, Regnumque ad Ferdinandum Filium, Legionis etiam Regno per Coniugem Sanctiam, ut capite xvi dixi, locupletatum, transmisit. Ferdinando successit Filius Sanctius; huic Frater Alphonsus; cujus Filia Vrraca (nam Stirps masculà obierat) quum, post Raimundum Berengarium Tolosæ Comitem, Alphonso Regi Aragoniæ nupsisset, Aragoniæ, Castellæ & Legionis Regna fuerunt unita. Videndi & Rodericus Toletanus de Rebus Hispaniæ lib. vi, cum alijs, tum præcipue cap.ix, & Ioannes Vasæus Hispaniæ Chronico ad annos MCCCXCVI, MCCCXVIII, CIOXI, & alios.
units.tr: The beginning of the Kingdom of Castile is recorded as follows. Pelagius, as I related in chapter xviii from the most trustworthy monuments of the ancients, having won back the Legion from the Moors again, built Castile as a kind of bulwark against the violence of the barbarians. The commanders of it, called Counts of Castile, long acknowledged the King of León as their prince, down to Ordoño II, the fourth King of the Asturians and León. When he had lured the Counts and nobles of Castile to himself under the pretext of a conference and slaughtered them, the Castilians, outraged at this wicked crime, threw off the yoke of the Kings of León. From their own body they chose two judges, as Rodrigo Jiménez de Rada writes in part I of his History of Spain, chapter xi, and in part III in many chapters: Nuño Rasura and Laín Calvo, one to administer justice and the other to command in war. Their descendants (listed by Alfonso of Carthagena in the Anacephalaeosis of the Kings of Spain, chapter lxx) were called Counts of Castile down to Sancho the Great, King of Navarre, who, having by war won Córdoba and Toledo from the Saracens, drove the Moors out of Navarre, Aragon, Castile, León, Portugal and other places in Spain, and restored all Spain to the Christian name. He married Elvira, daughter of Count Sancho of Castile and sister and sole heir of the last Count, García, and in the dowry settlement he styled himself not Count but King of Castile. He passed the kingdom to his son Ferdinand, who was also enriched with the Kingdom of León through his wife Sancha, as I said in chapter xvi. Ferdinand was succeeded by his son Sancho, and Sancho by his brother Alfonso. Alfonso's daughter Urraca (for the male line had died out), after Raymond Berengar, Count of Toulouse, had married Alfonso, King of Aragon, saw the kingdoms of Aragon, Castile and León united. Rodrigo of Toledo, On the Affairs of Spain, book vi, especially chapter ix, and John Vasaeus in his Chronicle of Spain for the years 1396, 1318, 1011 and others, should also be consulted.

units.la: CAP. XX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XX.

units.la: Castella Nova.
units.tr: New Castile.

units.la: CASTELLA NOVA, ad Septemtrionem adhærens Veteri, reliquis lateribus claudítur Portugallia, Extremadura, Andaluzia, Granada, & Valentia. Abundat Tritico aliisque Segetibus, ad utramque Tagi ripam sita.
units.tr: NEW CASTILE, bordering on Old Castile to the north, is bounded on its other sides by Portugal, Extremadura, Andalusia, Granada and Valencia. It abounds in wheat and other grain, lying on both banks of the Tagus.

units.la: Nobilitarunt quondam hanc Hispaniæ partem Carpitani, Καρπητανοὶ Ptolemæo; Καρπητανοὶ Straboni: quos etiam Villanovanus & Moralis Regnum Toletanum interpretantur: Καρπησιυς vocat passim Polybius; ut & Livius: apud quem etiam, ut item apud Plinium, Carpetania legitur Regio. Horum pars videntur fuisse Caraccitani, vel, ut Plutarch. nominat Χαρακιτανοὶ; quum eorum Vrbs Καρρακα ponatur à Ptolemæo in Carpitanis. Confaburenses Plinio, ubi hodie, scribente Morali, Confuegra, florentis quondam Vrbis servans etiamnum ruinas; vel, uti placet Pineto, Contabra: Non abludit etiam nomen opidi Cosarubios: Confabrum Antonino scribitur inter Laminium & Toletum: Laminitani Plinio: quos Pinetus Alambra vertit: Horum Ager, Liminitanus, ubi Anas oritur; P. Methymnæo & Clusio, Campo de Montiel: Mancha d'Aragon, Varrerio; Manchaçiega, Coquo: Laminium in Carpitanis nobile quondam opidum à Ptolemæo locatur: eius mentio est & apud Antoninum: Cotes Laminitanas ex Hispania Citeriore invenio apud Plinium nat. historiæ lib. xxxvi, ubi male Flaminitanæ: Laminiobrensem Episcopum cum alijs Hispaniarum Præsulibus subscripsisse Concilijs quibusdam lego. Oretani Ὠρητανοὶ Ptolemæo & Straboni; Germani Plinio: unde Vrbs eorum Ptolemæo Ὠρηπν Τεμεανῶν; Stephano simpliciter Ὠρεια, Straboni forte n inemendatius Ὠρεια: hodie Oreto, ut scribit Moralis: Clusio tamen Oretum est Calatrava. Quum vero magna veteris Lusitaniæ portio versus Ortum hodie Castellæ cum Veteri, tum Novæ adcreverit: putantur & nonnulli eius Populi habuisse loca illa, quæ in Occidentalioribus sunt Castellis, ubi Portugalliæ adhærent: præcipue vero quos Vetus loquitur Inscriptio stipem contulisse Ponti, qui Norbæ Cæsariæ (hodie Alcantara) perficiendo; in cujus arcu Tabulæ quatuor marmoreæ quondam fuerunt; quarum una hæc superest, verba, quæ sequuntur, præferens: MVNICIPIA PROVINCIAE LVSITANIÆ. STIPE CONLATA. QVÆ. OPVS PONTIS. PERFECERVNT ICAEDITANI LANCIENSES OPIDANI TALORI INTERANNIENSES LANCIENSES. TRASCVDANI ARAVI MEIDVBRIGENSES ARABRIGENSES BANIENSES PAESVRES
units.tr: This part of Spain was once made famous by the Carpetani, Καρπητανοί [Karpetanoi] in Ptolemy and Καρπητανοί in Strabo. Villanovanus and Morales take them to be the people of the Kingdom of Toledo. Polybius calls them Καρπησιοί [Karpesioi] throughout, as Livy does too, and in Livy, as in Pliny, the region is read as Carpetania. Some of them seem to have been the Caraccitani, or, as Plutarch calls them, Χαρακιτανοί [Charakitanoi], since Ptolemy places their city Καρρακα [Karraka] among the Carpetani. Pliny's Confaburenses are where Confuegra now stands, according to Morales, still preserving the ruins of a once flourishing city; or, as Pinetus prefers, Contabra. The name of the town Cosarubios is not far off. Antoninus writes Confabrum between Laminium and Toledo. Pliny's Laminitani, whom Pinetus renders as Alambra, had their territory, Liminitanus, where the Anas rises: according to P. Methymnaeus and Clusius this is Campo de Montiel, according to Varrerius Mancha d'Aragon, and according to Cocquus Manchaçiega. Laminium, once a famous town among the Carpetani, is located by Ptolemy and also mentioned by Antoninus. I find in Pliny's Natural History, book 36, the Cotes Laminitanae from Hither Spain, where it is wrongly given as Flaminitanae. I read that a bishop of Laminiobriga subscribed to certain councils with other prelates of Spain. The Oretani are Ὠρητανοί [Oretanoi] in Ptolemy and Strabo, and Germani in Pliny. Hence Ptolemy gives their city as Ὠρηπν Τεμεανῶν; Stephanus simply as Ὠρεια [Oreia], and Strabo perhaps, less correctly, as Ὠρεια. It is today Oreto, as Morales writes, though Cluverius places Oretum at Calatrava. Since a large part of old Lusitania to the east has now been added to Castile, both Old and New, some think the people of that region also held the places lying in the western parts of Castile, where it borders Portugal. This is especially so of those whom the ancient inscription says contributed alms toward completing the bridge at Norba Caesarea (today Alcántara). Four marble tablets once stood on its arch, and one of them survives, bearing these words: "The municipalities of the province of Lusitania, by contributed alms, completed the work of the bridge: the Icaeditani, the Lancienses Oppidani, the Talori, the Interannienses Lancienses, the Trascudani, the Aravi, the Meidubrigenses, the Arabrigenses, the Banienses, the Pesures."

units.la: Icaeditanorum, quos habet Marmor, memoriam servari notat Ioannes Vasæus in obscuro Vico Edania: Varrerius scribit vulgo Idanhas dici, & nova voce Latina Odoniam: Morali est hodie Idania la veja. Quod ad Lancienses Opidanos, Λαγκια Oppidum est apud Ptolemæum in Lusitania: Lancia item apud Dionem libro liii, & Orosium lib.vi. cap. xxi: Lancienses etiam Ocellenses appellatos scribit Plinius; Ptolemæo tamen Lancia & Ocellum diversa sunt opida Vettonum: cognominantur & Trasscudani in Lapide. Meidubrigenses, apud Plinium v cap. xxii sunt Medubricenses Plumbarij cognominati (ad quorum differentiam, ignoro) ab Medobriga, quæ Lusitaniæ urbs A. Hirtio; Armena hodie Vasco. Arabrigenses ab Arabriga, Ptolemæo Lusitaniæ urbe; Rabida, Ariæ Montano, vel, ut legit Varrerius, Arrabida. De Talorù, Interannienfibus, Aravis, Banienfibus & Pesuribus præterea nihil reperio. Interamnum quidem & Lancia sunt in Asturia: quorum illud Ponferrada Coquo est, Morali Fuente Encelada; hæc autem maxima Asturiæ Vrbs Floro lib. iv: sed remotiora hæc oppida, quam ut ad Occidentaliores Castellas pertinere possint. Alij proculdubio tam in Veteri, quam Nova Castella fuerunt olim populi, sed quorum memoria periit.
units.tr: John Vasaeus notes that the memory of the Icaeditani, named on the marble, is preserved in the obscure village of Edania. Varrerius writes that it is commonly called Idanhas and, in a new Latin term, Odonia; today it is Idania la veja, according to Morales. As for the Lancienses Oppidani: Λαγκια [Lagkia] is a town in Lusitania in Ptolemy, and Lancia is likewise in Dio, book 53, and in Orosius, book 6, chapter 21. Pliny writes that the Lancienses were also called Ocellenses, though in Ptolemy Lancia and Ocellum are separate towns of the Vettones. The Trascudani are also named in the inscription. The Meidubrigenses in Pliny, book 5, chapter 22, are the Medubricenses, surnamed Plumbarii (I do not know why they are distinguished), named after Medobriga, a city of Lusitania (A. Hirtius), today Armena or Vasco. The Arabrigenses take their name from Arabriga, a city of Lusitania in Ptolemy; it is Rabida according to Arias Montanus, or, as Varrerius reads it, Arrabida. About the Talori, the Interannienses, the Aravi, the Banienses and the Pesures I find nothing further. Interamnium and Lancia are indeed in Asturias. Of these, the former is Ponferrada according to Cocquus and Fuente Encelada according to Morales; the latter is the greatest city of Asturias, according to Florus, book 4. But these towns are too remote to belong to western Castile. Other peoples, undoubtedly, once lived in both Old and New Castile, but their memory has perished.

units.la: Metropolis Castellæ Novæ Toletum, ut Latini vocant; Τολητον Ptolemæo: hodie Toledo. Toletanos nominat Plinius: Colonia Toletana est in Nummis Augusti apud Hubertum Goltzium: Serezolam etiam scribit appellatam fuisse Villanovanus ad Ptolemæum. De Conditoribus, nunc Hercule, nunc alijs, quæ adferuntur, fabulosa magis sunt, quam vera. Centrum est & quasi umbilicus Hispaniæ: Situs clivosi, inæqualis, & asperioris, ascensus ambulationisque difficilis. Majorem partem adluit & contra hostes tuetur Tagus: qua Arcticum spectat Polum, muris munitum est validissimis Turribus; c 1; quarum auctorem memorant circa annum 1o cc lxxiii Bambam Regem, quem etiam hos Versus in Turri quadam, nitido lucidoque marmore, insculpendos curasse, scribunt Rodericus Toletanus Archiepiscopus lib. iii, de reb. Hispaniæ cap. xi, & in Chronico Ioannes Vasæus:
units.tr: The metropolis of New Castile is Toletum, as the Latins call it; Τολητον [Tolēton] in Ptolemy; today Toledo. Pliny names the Toletani, and the Colonia Toletana appears on coins of Augustus in Hubert Goltzius. Villanovanus, on Ptolemy, writes that it was also called Serezola. The stories about its founders, now Hercules and now others, are more fabulous than true. It is the centre and almost the navel of Spain. Its site is hilly, uneven and rough, so the ascent and walking are difficult. The Tagus washes most of it and defends it against enemies. On the side facing the north pole it is fortified with very strong walls and towers. Its builder, they relate, was King Bamba, around the year 673, and they also say he had these verses carved on a certain tower in shining white marble, as Roderic of Toledo, archbishop, writes in book 3 of his De rebus Hispaniae, chapter 11, and John Vasaeus in his Chronicle:

units.la: EREXIT, TAVTORE DEO REX INCLYTVS VRBEM BAMBA, SVÆ CELEBREM PROTENDENS GENTIS HONOREM.
units.tr: KING BAMBA, RENOWNED, BY GOD'S GUIDANCE, RAISED THIS CITY, EXTENDING THE FAMOUS HONOUR OF HIS PEOPLE.

units.la: Visuntur hodie extra Muros Septemtrionem versus Theatri magni, sed diruti, complanatique rudera. Nobilium ingens in hac Vrbe numerus: Cives admodum sunt industrij: Disciplinis omnibus (Academiam enim habet florentem) Artibusque Mechanicis magnus ibi honos: Lanificio Sericoque vitam quærunt hominum milia fere decem. Vrbs Regia cognomen adeptum est Toletum post adventum Gothorum, qui sedem Regni illuc transtulerunt, quum antea, ut Rodericus Toletanus tradit, ab Vandalis, alijsque Germaniæ populis, qui una in Hispaniam commigrarant, Hispalis Vrbs Regia & vocata fuerit & habita. Cum alijs amplissimis ædificiis, tum templo nobilitatur augustissimo, pulcherrimo, ditissimo: cujus Archiepiscopum Vrbanus 11. Pont. Max. Hispaniæ totius instituit Primatem. Est idem secundus ab Rege, maximusque Regni Cancellarius: quo inconsulto, nihil fieri solitum, nihil decerni. Sententiam statim dicit post Regem: tantæque est non solum dignitatis & auctoritatis, verum etiam potentiæ, ut sub se præter pagos infinitos opida celebria habeat septemdecim, exque iis alijsque Vectigalibus Reditum annuum ducentorum millium Ducatorum: quæ quum Regibus parum grata, Viriplerumque, ut Rerum Hispanicarum Scriptores produnt, mediocris quidem fortunæ paucorumque Clientum, sed qui Virtutis Probitatisque spectatæ, ad hanc dignitatem ex instituto Ferdinandi & Isabellæ Regum evehuntur. Multa Toleti Concilia leguntur celebrata: certe ultra xvii numerantur, quot alibi nusquam. Est ibi celeberrimum Palatium ab Carolo v. restauratum, novisque structuris regio adparatu exornatum: in quo, præter alia multa singularia, Machina visitur hydraulica, miro Italorum ingenio fabricata, quæ ex Tago flumine, opera magnæ versatilis & excavatæ rotæ, Aquas in Fistulas & Tubos per Canales in summitatem Arcis & Montis artificioso impetu cogit & impellit: ubi unum in locum & amplum receptaculum collectæ in varios Arcis Vrbisque totius usus dilapsæ distribuuntur; quæ rivulos deinde & fontes Hortis, Magnatum ædibus, Balneis, Fullonibus, Civiumque necessitatibus abunde suppeditant. Pons ad Vrbem est super Tagum, quem unus Arcus opere mirando sustinet. Describunt Toletum Gomecius lib. vi de rebus Iacobi Aragoniæ Regis, Navagierus in Itinerario, Petrus Medinensis, L. Marineus Siculus lib. ii. de Rebus Hispaniæ, ubi de Lusitania. Toletum, ut Matrem Reginamque suam, venerantur Madritum, vulgo Madrid: aëris salubris- simi; ubi Carolus V. Imperator dies paucos commoratus, Morbo Quartanæ, quo diu laboraverat, est liberatus: Rebus omnibus abundans gratum nunc est Hispaniæ Regibus Domicilium; Incolis hinc plenum, multisque primæ nobilitatis & equestris dignitatis viris, illustribusque familijs nobilitatum. Silicum illi sunt in Circuitu Lapidicinæ: unde Cinctum Igne cecinit Hispanus Poeta Ioannes Mena. Terminos habet latissimos, Campos-que fertilissimos, quos Matricios Lumbos appellant. Non procul hinc Villamanta est; quæ, ut volunt Montanus, Tarapha, & Villanovanus, μάττωα est Prolemæo, Carpetanorum in Tarraconensi Hispania opidum. Quinta Madrito leuca versus Occidentem conspicitur magnificum illud & sumtuosum Monasterium S. Laurentij in Escuriali vulgo, Ordinis D. Hieronymi:
units.tr: Outside the walls to the north can be seen the ruins, now levelled, of a great theatre. The nobility in this city is very numerous, and the citizens are very industrious. In all the disciplines (for it has a flourishing academy) and in the mechanical arts there is great honour. Some ten thousand people earn their living by wool and silk. Vrbs Regia, the royal city, is the title Toledo acquired after the Goths arrived and moved the seat of the kingdom there. Before that, as Roderic of Toledo reports, Hispalis had been both called and regarded as the royal city, under the Vandals and other German peoples who had migrated into Spain together. Besides other very large buildings, it is distinguished by a most august, beautiful and rich temple, whose archbishop Pope Urban II made primate of all Spain. He is also second to the king and the greatest chancellor of the kingdom; nothing is customarily done or decreed without his advice. He gives his opinion immediately after the king. His dignity, authority and power are so great that, besides countless villages, he has seventeen notable towns under him, and from these and other taxes an annual revenue of two hundred thousand ducats. Since these posts are not very welcome to kings, they are generally held, as the writers on Spanish affairs report, by men of moderate means and few clients, but of tested virtue and integrity, who are raised to this dignity by the regulation of Kings Ferdinand and Isabella. Many councils are read of as having been held at Toledo: more than seventeen are counted, more than anywhere else. There is a very famous palace, restored by Charles V and adorned with new structures in royal style. In it, besides many other singular things, is seen a hydraulic machine, made with wonderful Italian ingenuity. By means of a large turning, hollowed wheel worked from the Tagus, it forces water through pipes and tubes along channels, with artful force, up to the top of the citadel and hill. There the water is collected in one place and a large reservoir, and then flows down to be distributed for the use of the citadel and the whole city. These supply streams and fountains abundantly for gardens, the houses of magnates, baths, fullers, and the needs of the citizens. There is a bridge over the Tagus to the city, which a single arch of wonderful workmanship supports. Gomecius, in book 6 on the deeds of James, King of Aragon, Navagierus in his Itinerary, Peter of Medina, and L. Marineus Siculus, in book 2 of his On the Affairs of Spain (where he treats of Lusitania), describe Toledo. Madritum, commonly Madrid, venerates Toledo as its mother and queen. It has very healthy air. Here Emperor Charles V stayed a few days and was freed from the quartan fever from which he had long suffered. Abounding in all things, it is now a pleasant home for the kings of Spain. It is full of inhabitants and ennobled by many men of the first nobility and knightly rank, and by illustrious families. All around it are flint quarries, whence the Spanish poet John Mena sang of it as "girt with fire". It has very wide boundaries and very fertile fields, which people call the Matrician Loins. Not far from here is Villamanta, which, as Montanus, Tarapha and Villanovanus think, is the μάττωα [mattōa] of Ptolemy, a town of the Carpetani in Tarraconensian Spain. Five leagues west of Madrid stands the magnificent and sumptuous monastery of St Lawrence in the Escorial, commonly of the Order of St Jerome:

units.la: PHILIPPI II Hispaniarum Regis opus; quod merito certare potest cum Ægyptiorum Pyramidibus, cum Veterum Græcorum Romanorumque Templis, Theatris, Amphitheatris, Ludis, Circis: Thermis item, Balneis, Sepulchris; cum aliis denique variorum Regum & Principum Monimentis. Operi tanto vix quid est par, vix quid secundum. Frontispicium ejus, Occasum spectans, tribus superbit portis: quarum quæ media primariaque in Templum augustissimum, Cœnobium, Collegiumque ducit: quæ ad dextram, in Officinas Monasterio consecratas; quæ ad sinistram in Domos Scholæ destinatas. Quatuor Angulos totidem exornant mirabiles arte sua Turres; quas etiam duæ superant, ad ipsius Templi pedem hinc inde fastu quodam consurgentes. Supra Ostium Templi magnisicæ Stylobatæ Statuas sustinent ex Marmore Tophoque sex Israelhelis Regum, pedes altas xviii. Ad Septemtrionem Palatium Templo adjitum visitur, Regi Regioque Comitatui commodissime excipiendo paratum. Ad Meridiem variæ sunt Porticus; Hortus omnis generis instructus Herbis Floribusque, & pluribus ornamentis; Pomarium gratissimis constitum fructibus: item Nosocomium, Pharmacopolium, & alia. Videre ibi est inter alia depictum artificiose Conflictum inter Ioannem II Legionis Regem & Mauros Granatenses; extractum ex Linteo cxxx pedum, quod totam Historiam continens repertum fertur Segoviæ in pervetusta Turre. Quid superest? quidquid ibi occurrit, stuporem incutit spectanti: ideoque de iis, quæ dicenda restant, silere cum modestia præstat, quam jejune pauca in medium proferre. Ad reliquas Vrbes opidaque pergo. Quæ vulgo, voce Arabica, Hispanis hodie Alcala de Henares, tam certo creditur Κομπλυτον Ptolemæi, ut Latine etiam non aliter in publicis Actis & Monimentis audiat. Situm est in loco plano, ad Fluvium, quem Henarem vocant; rerum omnium, quibus humanus usus indiget, copia, suisque proventibus adeo abundans, ut nullis aliunde bonis opus habeat. Ecclesia ibi, cujus omnes Canonici sunt Theologi. Facit hoc omnium Disciplinarum Academia; qua nobilitatum est Complutum ab Francisco Ximenio Cardinali, Archiepiscopo Toletano; cujus & auspiciis sumtibusque (qui superasse dicuntur ix millia Ducatorum) Biblia ibi edita, anno clo Io xv, quæ ab loco Complutensia. Erasmus Epistola ad Franciscum Vergaram Græcarum litterarum ibi Professorem, Gratulor, inquit Complute, quod duorum Præsulum Francisci & Alphonsi Alphonsi felicibus auspiciis sic efflorescit omni genere Studiorum, ut jure optimo πανσοφίας appelletur. D. Isidorus Complutum dicit esse sexagesimo milliario à Toleto. Segoncia Antonino inter Complutum & Caesaraugustam medio fere itinere; Siguença nunc appellatur Varrerio & Morali judicibus. Alcantaram in ripa Tagi scribunt Varrerius, Tarapha & Clusius esse, quae Νώρβα Καισαρέα Ptolemaeo; Norbensis Colonia Plinio. Opidum est insigni conspicuum Ponte, venerandae & antiquitatis & majestatis, in cujus ingressu extat Sacellum, hodie D. Juliani appellatum, habens limen superius sic inscriptum:
units.tr: Philip II, King of the Spains, built this work, which may rightly vie with the Pyramids of the Egyptians and with the temples, theatres, amphitheatres, games, and circuses of the ancient Greeks and Romans, and likewise with their baths and tombs; in short, with the monuments of various kings and princes. Hardly anything is equal to so great a work, and hardly anything is second to it. Its façade, facing west, is proud of three gates. The middle and chief of these leads into the most august temple, the monastery, and the college; the one on the right leads into workshops consecrated to the monastery; the one on the left leads into houses set aside for the school. Four corners are adorned by as many towers, wonderful in their craftsmanship, and two more rise with a certain pride at the foot of the temple itself, one on each side. Above the door of the temple, magnificent pedestals support statues of six kings of Israel, eighteen feet high, made of marble and tufa. To the north a palace joined to the temple is seen, prepared to receive the King and his retinue most conveniently. To the south there are various porticoes, a garden furnished with herbs and flowers of every kind and with many ornaments, an orchard planted with most pleasant fruit trees, and also a hospital, a pharmacy, and other buildings. There one sees, among other things, a battle skilfully depicted between John II, King of León, and the Moors of Granada, taken from a linen cloth of 130 feet, which, containing the whole history, is said to have been found at Segovia in a very ancient tower. What more is there to say? Whatever meets the eye there strikes the beholder with amazement, so it is more becoming to keep modestly silent about the things that remain to be said than to bring forward a few poor remarks. I now pass on to the other cities and towns. The place which in the vulgar tongue, using an Arabic word, is now called Alcalá de Henares by the Spaniards is so certainly believed to be the Complutum of Ptolemy that even in Latin it is called so in public records and monuments. It lies on a level site by a river which they call the Henares, and it is so abundant in every kind of thing that human use requires, and in its own produce, that it needs no goods from elsewhere. There is a church there whose canons are all theologians. This is brought about by the academy of all the disciplines, by which Complutum has been made famous by Cardinal Francisco Ximenes, Archbishop of Toledo, under whose auspices and at whose expense (which is said to have exceeded 9,000 ducats) the Bibles were printed there in the year 1515, which are called the Complutensian. Erasmus, in his letter to Francisco Vergara, Professor of Greek literature there, says: I congratulate you, Complutum, that under the happy auspices of the two prelates Francisco and Alfonso you flourish in every kind of study, so that you rightly be called all-wise. St Isidore says that Complutum is sixty miles from Toledo. Segontia lies between Complutum and Caesaraugusta, about halfway along the road, according to Antoninus; it is now called Sigüenza, according to the judgements of Varrerius and Moral. Varrerius and Tarapha and Cluverius write that Alcántara on the bank of the Tagus is the Norba Caesarea of Ptolemy; Norbensis Colonia is the name Pliny uses. It is a town conspicuous for its famous bridge, venerable both for its antiquity and its majesty, at whose entrance stands a little shrine, now called St Julian's, having a lintel above it inscribed thus:
