ICÆDITANO
units.tr: A TEMPLE ON THE BANK OF THE TAGUS, FULL OF THE GODS ABOVE AND OF CAESAR. WHERE SKILL IS OVERCOME BY ITS OWN MATERIAL. WHAT SORT OF VOW HE GAVE, PERHAPS THE CARE OF TRAVELLERS WILL ASK, WHOM THE NEW FAME DELIGHTS. LACER, WHO BUILT THE VAST BRIDGE, MADE IT WITH ITS HUGE MASS, FOR THE SACRIFICE TO BE OFFERED WITH SACRED HONOUR. LACER, WHO BUILT THE BRIDGE, ALSO DEDICATED NEW TEMPLES. THERE THEY OFFER VOWS AND SACRIFICES. LACER, NOBLE, MADE THE BRIDGE BY DIVINE ART, TO LAST FOREVER THROUGH THE AGES OF THE WORLD. THE SAME LACER ESTABLISHED A TEMPLE TO THE ROMULEAN DEIFIED ONES, WITH CAESAR. BOTH CAUSES OF THE SACRED WORK ARE HAPPY. GAIUS JULIUS LACER, WHO IS OF HIGH STATION, MADE IT AND DEDICATED IT TO HIS FRIEND CURIUS LACO OF ICAEDITUM.

units.la: Quæ Talavera nunc, Livio lib. xl. Aeburam nominari opinantur Beuterus & Moralis. Caucensium, quos Hispaniae populos habet Plinius, memoriam adhuc extare in opido, quod vulgo Cuença, Pinetus arbitratur. Opidulum, quod Lebazuza, vel, ut alij, Lenuza, hodie nuncupatur, circa Alcarez urbem, Libisosam Antonini esse non est dubium; & monent illud, adduc etiam antiquo Lapide, Moralis & Frias Albornozius, suffragatorem habens Hieronymum Suritam: Aιβισσα apud Ptolemaeum est pro Aιβισσοῦ: Libisosona cognomine Ferougustana dicitur Plinio lib. iii. cap. iii. Docent ibi ruinae celebrem olim fuisse locum. Castulonem ejusdem Antonini, quae Κασταλών Appiano & Ptolemaeo, Κασταλών Polybio lib. x, Florianus & Moralis esse censent, quae hodie Caslona la vieja. Apud Strabonem lib. iii nomen hujus Urbis aliquoties depravatum est, Κασσών pro Κασταλών. Apud Stephanum Regio, cui Castulo solet adcenseri, male habet; Κασταλών, inquit, μεγίστη πόλις Ἰβηρίας: reponendum enim Ὀρητανίας: De Oretanis antea dixi. Silius Italicus Parnassiam cognominat, quasi Castaliam. Strabo etiam Baeticae terminos ad Ortum Castulonem usque Veteres constituisse, memoriae prodit. Ab hac urbe Saltui Castulonensi nomen: is hodie nonnullis, qui Portus S. Stephani, Santisteban vulgo. Caesar Commentario Belli Civilis i. M. Terentium Varronem, Cn. Pompei Legatum, Hispaniae Baeticae Regiones tenuisse ab Castulonensi Saltu ad Anam scribit. C. Asinius Pollio Ciceroni indicat suos Tabellarios tenuisse semper Saltum Castulonensem. Castulonenses habet Plinius, quos Caesari Venales vocari ait.
units.tr: What is now Talavera, which in Livy, book 40, they think is called Aebura, is the view of Beuterus and Moral. The memory of the Caucenses, a people of Spain which Pliny mentions, is thought by Pinetus to survive still in the town commonly called Cuenca. The little town now called Lebazuza, or, according to others, Lenuza, near the city of Alcaraz, is undoubtedly Antoninus' Libisosa; Moral and Frías Albornoz, who have the support of Jerome Surita, point this out, and an ancient stone still bears witness to it. The Aιβισσα in Ptolemy stands for Aιβισσοῦ. Pliny, book 3, chapter 3, calls Libisosona by the surname Ferougustana. The ruins show that it was once a famous place. Florian and Moral consider Castulo, the same as Antoninus' town, which is Κασταλών for Appian and Ptolemy, and Κασταλών for Polybius, book 10, to be what is now called Caslona la Vieja. In Strabo, book 3, the name of this city is corrupted in several places, Κασσών for Κασταλών. In Stephanus of Byzantium, Regio, to which Castulo is usually reckoned, is in a bad way: Κασταλών, he says, is the greatest city of Iberia; but we must read Ὀρητανίας, that is, of the Oretani, about whom I spoke earlier. Silius Italicus calls it Parnassian, as if it were Castalian. Strabo also records that the ancients set the boundaries of Baetica at Castulo towards the east. From this city the Castulonensian forest takes its name; today some call it the Port of St Stephen, commonly Santisteban. Caesar, in the first book of his Commentary on the Civil War, writes that Marcus Terentius Varro, legate of Gnaeus Pompey, held the regions of Hispania Baetica from the Castulonensian forest to the Anas. Gaius Asinius Pollio tells Cicero that his couriers always kept to the Castulonensian forest. Pliny mentions the Castulonenses, whom he says were called Venales by Caesar.

Castra Cecilia, 20 miles. | Cárceres. | Miacum, 24 miles. | Vanneuva. Turmulos, 20 miles. | Cannaveral, or not far from there. | Titulcia, 24 miles. | Perhaps Getafe. units.la: VALENTIA ad Meridiem Murciam respicit; ad Occasum utramque Castellam; ad Septemtrionem Aragoniam; ad Ortum littora ejus pulsat Mare Internum. Nomen illi ab Valentia, Emporio Nobilissimo, venerandæque Antiquitatis. Habet Valentia duos Montes, quibus nomen Mariola & Penna golosa (Rupes cupedinaria Latine sonant) in quos, quum Stirpibus rarioribus Herbisque variis abundant, quotidie magnus Medicorum & Herbariorum numerus ex diversis Hispaniæ partibus confluit. Numquam non rari quid ibi se offert. Qua Tortosam itur, & Iberum versus ascenditur, Argenti sunt Fodinæ: locus, ubi præcipuæ, Buriel ab Incolis dicitur. Reperiuntur & Lapides aureis venis lineolisque interstincti in loco, qui Aioder nominatur. Ad Promontorium Finistratum sunt ferri Mineræ: circa Segorbiam Lapidicinæ vestigia in Piacento Alabastrum ecfoditur. Passim Alumen, Rubia, Calx, Gypsum. Maximum Incolæ quæstum faciunt ex Fictilibus, quæ ipsis Porcellanæ vocantur, elegantia admirabili confectis. Plura de hoc Regno videat Lector apud Bernardinum Gomecium ix, xii & xiii libr. Vitæ Iacobi i. Aragonum Regis. Petrus etiam Antonius Beuterus Theologus Valentinus Res Hispaniæ memorabiles tribus Tomis se complexum profitetur: cujus præcipuus videtur fuisse scopus, ut Valentiam Patriam suam quam maxime inlustraret.
units.tr: Valentia faces south towards Murcia, west towards both Castiles, north towards Aragon, and to the east its shores are washed by the Mediterranean Sea. It takes its name from Valentia, a most noble emporium of venerable antiquity. Valentia has two mountains, called Mariola and Penna golosa (in Latin, Rupes cupedinaria, "delicacy rocks"). Because they abound in rarer plants and various herbs, a great number of physicians and herbalists gather there every day from different parts of Spain. Something rare always presents itself there. On the road to Tortosa, where one climbs towards the Ebro, are the silver mines; the chief of them is called Buriel by the locals. Stones streaked with golden veins and lines are also found in a place called Aioder. Near the promontory Finistratum are iron mines; near Segorbe there are traces of a quarry, and at Piacento alabaster is dug out. Alum, madder, lime and gypsum are found everywhere. The inhabitants make their greatest profit from earthenware, which they call Porcellanæ ("porcelain"), made with remarkable elegance. The reader may consult Bernardino Gomez, books 9, 12 and 13 of the Life of James I, King of Aragon, for more on this kingdom. Pedro Antonio Beuter, a Valencian theologian, also professes that he has embraced the memorable affairs of Spain in three volumes; his chief aim seems to have been to do as much honour as possible to Valentia, his homeland.

units.la: Valentiam habitasse quondam præter alios deprehenduntur Hedetani, Ἡδητανοὶ Ptolemæo forte non alij ab Sedetanis. de quibus ad Aragoniam mihi dictum: Est & Regio Hedetania apud Livium & Plinium. Bisargitani; hic ex membranis lego apud Plinium: Metropolis ipsorum Bisargis, cujus mentio in Nummo Germanici Cæsaris, teste Huberto Goltzio: videntur pars fuisse Heditanorum, quum in ijs Βισταςγὶ nominet Ptolemæus. Leonicenses Plinio; quorum Metropolis Ἀεονίκα etiam à Ptolemæo in Heditanis collocatur: Mentio ejus in Goltzij Thesauro. Contestani, Κεντεσάνοι Ptolemæo; à quibus Contestania Hispaniæ Tarraconensis Regio apud Plinium: horum memoria servatur hodieque in Opido Contayna, vel ut aliis effertur, Contentaina ad fontem ejus amnis, cujus ostio adpositum videtur opidum Oliva contra Pytiusas Insulas. Lusones; quos ad Iberum fluvium ponit Appianus in Ibericis, Numantinis vicinos: ad Tagi fontes pertingere scribit Strabo. Lobetani, quorum Metropolis Ἀόβητιν Ptolemæo; quam Beuterus scribit antea Turiam, postea Averazin, tandemque, ut hodieque, Albarrazin dictam. Τεζόλιπχ Appiano in Ibericis, Saguntinis vicini,
units.tr: Among others, the Hedetani are found to have once inhabited Valentia; Ptolemy's Ἡδητανοὶ [Hedetanoi] are perhaps no different from the Sedetani, about whom I have spoken under Aragon. There is also the region Hedetania in Livy and Pliny. The Bisargitani: here I read from the manuscripts in Pliny. Their metropolis was Bisargis, mentioned on a coin of Germanicus Caesar, according to Hubert Goltz. They seem to have been part of the Heditani, since Ptolemy names them Βισταςγὶ [Bistasgi]. The Leonicenses in Pliny; their metropolis Ἀεονίκα [Aeonika] is also placed by Ptolemy among the Heditani. It is mentioned in Goltz's Thesaurus. The Contestani, Κεντεσάνοι [Kentesanoi] in Ptolemy; from them comes Contestania, a region of Hispania Tarraconensis, in Pliny. Their memory is preserved to this day in the town of Contayna, or as others give it, Contentaina, near the source of that river at whose mouth the town of Oliva seems to lie, opposite the Pityusic Islands. The Lusones, whom Appian in his Iberica places on the Ebro river, neighbours of the Numantines; Strabo writes that they reach to the sources of the Tagus. The Lobetani, whose metropolis is Ἀόβητιν [Aobetin] in Ptolemy; Beuter writes that it was formerly called Turia, later Averazin, and at last, as today, Albarrazin. Τεζόλιπχ [Tezolipch] in Appian's Iberica, neighbours of the Saguntines.

units.la: Lusones, Lobetani, Torbolete. vicini, à quibus Turbula Ptolemæo, Torres hodie fortean. Celtiberos, ut eos appellant Plinius iii cap.iii, Pomponius Mela lib. iii, cap. i ceterique Latini; qui Κελτιβηρες Ptolemæo; quidam Castellæ Veteri adscribunt, plerique Valentiæ. Illud satis constat Celtiberorum Pomeria huc illuc longe lateque se extendisse. Clunia, de qua dixi cap. xix, Celtiberiæ finis Plinio vocatur. Posidonius apud Strabonem lib. iii. auctor est M. Claudium Marcellum Tributum ex Celtiberia exegisse Talentum loc: ex quo conjecturam facere licet, inquit, quod Celtiberorum natio frequentissima fuerit, & aurī atque argenti copia excellens, tamethi agrum incolerent steriliem. Nomen compositum ex Celtis & Iberis. Lucanus lib. iv: profugique à gente vetusta Gallorum Celtæ, miscentes nomen Iberis.
units.tr: The Lusones, Lobetani, and Torbolete neighbours, from whom Turbula in Ptolemy, perhaps today Torres. The Celtiberi, as Pliny (book 3, chapter 3), Pomponius Mela (book 3, chapter 1) and the other Latin writers call them, who are Κελτιβηρες [Keltiberes] in Ptolemy; some assign them to Old Castile, most to Valencia. This much is certain: the territories of the Celtiberians extended far and wide in various directions. Clunia, of which I spoke in chapter 19, is called the boundary of Celtiberia by Pliny. Posidonius, in Strabo book 3, is the authority that Marcus Claudius Marcellus exacted a tribute of a talent from Celtiberia. From this, he says, one may conjecture that the Celtiberian people were very numerous and abounding in gold and silver, although they inhabited a barren land. The name is compounded from Celts and Iberians. Lucan, book 4: "and the Celts, Gauls of an ancient race, having fled, mixing their name with the Iberians."

units.la: Sic Silius Italicus lib. iii Belli Pœnici ii: Venere & Celtæ, sociati nomen Iberis, Iis pugna cecidisse decus, corpusque cremari. Tale nefas cælo credunt Superisque referri, Impastus carpat si membra jacentia vultur.
units.tr: So Silius Italicus, book 3 of the Punica, line 2: "The Celts, allied with the Iberians in name, fell in battle with the glory of Venus; and their bodies are to be burned. They believe that such an outrage is reported to heaven and the gods, if a vulture should tear at their limbs lying there unfed."

units.la: Celtiberi, apud eundem Strabonem, & confinales ipsis Boream versus habitantes Deo cuipiam, cujus nomen ignoratur, plena Luna, tempore nocturno Pervigilium celebrant, choreas ducendo. In Celtiberis vicinos Urbi Segedæ ponit Appianus in Ibericis Titthos populos.
units.tr: The Celtiberi, according to the same Strabo, and their neighbours who dwell towards the north, celebrate a vigil at night under the full moon, dancing, to some god whose name is unknown. In Appian's Iberica he places the Tittho peoples among the Celtiberians, neighbours of the city of Segeda.

units.la: Metropolis Valentia, Valencia vulgo: cujus antea memini. Hanc Contestanis Ptolemæus (cui ΒΑΛΕΝΤΙΑ) Hleditanis autem adscribit Plinius. In Numino quodam æreo apud Goltzium est COL. IVL. VAL, id est COLONIA IULIA VALENTIA. Habet etiam Nummum Surita in cujus una facie Mercury videtur esse Caput, cum Inscriptione C. LVCIEN. C. MVN. I. Q: altera vero Cornucopiæ figura, fulmine transverso; & infra cornu, VALENTIA. Mirum est Strabonem nullam facere hujus Urbis mentionem, quum Cherronesji, Oleastri, Dertosæ ad Iberi transitum meminerit; eaque celeberrima fuerit bello Sertoriano; conflictu, quo Cn. Pompeius juxta eamdem urbem Herennium & Perpennam, magnos Sertorij Duces, devicit. M. Tullius Prælium illud Turiense vocat: quod inter lœva mœnium & dextrum flumen Turiam, ut Sallustius scribit lib. ii Historiarum, fuerit commissum. Urbs Hispaniæ primarijs, ut olim, sic & hodie, conlocanda: duodecim ædificiorum habens millia; præter quæ in Suburbijs & Hortis, Urbana suo numero fere exæquantia. Sita est in intimo Sinus Sucronensis recessu ad dextram fluvij Turiæ ripam: à mari remotam tribus passuum millibus tradit Plinius. Valentia Moribus & Institutis clara. Disciplinis liberalibus exculta; Mechanicis Artibus nobilis; magnis Ingenijs felix: Pacis Concordiæque Cives inter servandæ studiosissima: Multorum Equitum splendore illustris: Mercatorum Commercijs dives. Academiam habet celebrem, in qua S. Dominicus, Ordinis Prædicatorum auctor, bonis Artibus Sacraæque Theologiæ operam dedisse scribitur. Præter hanc in regno Valentiæ est & Academia Gandiana, quam non ita pridem erexit Illustrissimus Gandiæ Dux; ut ibi præcipue Patres Societatis Iesu, ad quam scipsum quoque contulisse fertur, philosopharentur. Silentio non prætereundum, quod de Valentinis notat L. Marineus Siculus: ijs in more positum esse singulis annis, Festo D. Matthiæ, fusis precibus factisque obtestationibus, ad locum Supplicijs destinatum ire, ibique Damnatorum Corpora, sive suspensa sint, sive humi jaceant, suscipere, ossaque sparsa colligere; mox autem omnia feretris impositia ad commune Civibus omnibus Sepulchretum devecta honorifice, Sacrificijs Orationibusque peractis, Terræ mandare. Memoriæ prodit Petrus Medinensis esse in hac Urbe supra decem millia Puteorum Aquæ Vivæ. Tritum est apud Hispanos Proverbium, quo Barcino fertur dives, Cæsaraugusta satura, Valentia formosa. Infinita hic Antiquitatum Romanarum rudera & plurimæ Inscriptiones: quarum quædam apud Beuterum, Ambrosium Moralem, Hotomannum in Cæsaris Ephemerides, & alios. Exacta ejus descriptio Lausque apud Ioannem Marianam lib. xii. cap. xix & Marineum Siculum lib. iii extremo. Stetit olim ad ripam Turiæ sinistram, haud procul Valentia (Strabo lib. iii. Pliniusque iii. cap. iii, mille passibus ab Mari separant) Saguntum; Heditanorum urbs; Σαγῦντ Ptolemæo; Σάγυντ Straboni; Ζάκυνθ & Ζακανθ Stephano:
units.tr: The metropolis is Valentia, commonly Valencia, of which I spoke earlier. Ptolemy (who gives it as ΒΑΛΕΝΤΙΑ [Valentia]) assigns it to the Contestani, but Pliny assigns it to the Heditani. On a bronze coin in Goltz there is COL. IVL. VAL, that is, COLONIA IULIA VALENTIA. Surita also has a coin, on one side of which is a head that seems to be Mercury, with the inscription C. LVCIEN. C. MVN. I. Q; on the other side a cornucopia with a transverse thunderbolt, and below the horn, VALENTIA. It is remarkable that Strabo makes no mention of this city, although he mentions Cherronesus, Oleaster and Dertosa at the crossing of the Ebro; and yet it was very famous in the Sertorian War, in the battle in which Gnaeus Pompey defeated Herennius and Perperna, great leaders of Sertorius, near this same city. Marcus Tullius calls that battle the Turiense ("of Turia"), because, as Sallust writes in book 2 of the Histories, it was fought "between the left of the walls and the right river Turia." A city to be counted among the foremost of Spain, then as now; it has twelve thousand buildings, not counting those in the suburbs and gardens, which nearly equal the city in number. It lies at the innermost recess of the Gulf of Sucro, on the right bank of the river Turia; Pliny reports that it is three miles from the sea. Valencia is famous for its manners and institutions, cultivated in the liberal disciplines, noted for the mechanical arts, blessed with great talents, most diligent in keeping peace and concord among its citizens, illustrious for the splendour of its many knights, and rich in the commerce of its merchants. It has a famous university, where St Dominic, the founder of the Order of Preachers, is written to have studied the good arts and sacred theology. Besides this, in the kingdom of Valencia there is also the Gandia academy, which the most illustrious Duke of Gandia established not long ago, so that the Fathers of the Society of Jesus, to which he is also said to have devoted himself, might teach philosophy there chiefly. It must not be passed over in silence what Lucius Marineus Siculus notes about the Valencians: it is their custom every year, on the feast of St Matthias, after pouring out prayers and making supplications, to go to the place appointed for executions, and there to take up the bodies of the condemned, whether they are hanging or lying on the ground, and to gather their scattered bones; then, having placed everything on biers, they carry it honourably to the common burial ground for all citizens, and, when the sacrifices and orations are finished, commit it to the earth. Pedro Medina records that in this city there are more than ten thousand wells of living water. A common proverb among the Spaniards goes: "Barcelona is rich, Zaragoza is sated, Valencia is beautiful." Here there are countless ruins of Roman antiquities and very many inscriptions, some of which are in Beuter, Ambrosio Morales, Hotman in the Ephemerides of Caesar, and others. Its exact description and praise are found in Juan de Mariana, book 12, chapter 19, and in Marineus Siculus, at the end of book 3. Once, on the left bank of the Turia, not far from Valencia (Strabo book 3, and Pliny book 3, chapter 3, place it a thousand paces from the sea), stood Saguntum, a city of the Heditani; Σαγῦντ [Sagunt] in Ptolemy; Σάγυντ [Sagunt] in Strabo; Ζάκυνθ and Ζακανθ [Zakunth, Zakanth] in Stephanus:

units.la: Z phano: Secundum & Secuntum vitiose apud Antoninum. Hodie putatur à plerisque Morvedre, sic dictum, ut quidam censent, ab Muris Veteribus. Theatrum certe & nunc ibi, cum Scena, aliaque multa Antiquitatis vestigia. Zacynthorum Coloniam facit Appianus: Σαγυντ@, χωρμα, inquit Strabo lib. iii, zaxwθιων: quidam Saguntum Herculis filium conditorem opinantur: sunt & qui ab Saguis Iberico nomen accepisse volunt. Situm describit Silius Italicus lib. i. Saguntt Muris Carmenta tribuit Livius lib. xxx: quæ calce durata erant, sed interlita luto, structuræ antiquæ genere. Constat ex Plinio Saguntinos olim coluisse Dianam, eodem ab Zacynthys, iplorum Progenitoribus, advectam; annis ducentis ante excidium Troiæ. Saguntum, Fide & ærumnis inclusa, Pomponio Melæ. De expugnatione Vrbis nobilissimæ, Cladeque, quæ ob admirabilem constantiam & egregiam in Romanos fidem incidit in annum ab u. c. lxxxv. M. Livio Salinatore, L. Æmilio Paullo cos. consulendi Livius lib. xxi, Polybius lib. iii, Orosius lib. iv. cap. xiv, Eutropius lib. iii, Florus lib. ii, histor. Român. cap. vi, Silius Ital. lib. i, Valerius Maximus lib. v, cap. vi. Augustinus lib. iii. de Civit. Dei, cap. xx, Auctor de VV. Illustr. cap. xliii, Æmilius Probus in Annibale, Cicero in Philippicis, & qui non' Superest memoria Senatus Populique Saguntini, quo loco Vrbs fuit, in Muro Veteri his verbis: SENATVS. ET. POPVLVS. SAGVNTINORVM CLAVDIO. INVICTO. PIO. FELICI. IMP. CÆS. PONT. MAX. TRIB. POT. P. P. PROCOS
units.tr: (Stephanus, as in Z phano.) "Secuntum" and "Secundum" are wrongly written in Antoninus. Today it is commonly thought to be Morvedre, so called, as some think, from the old walls. Certainly there is still a theatre there, with its stage, and many other traces of antiquity. Appian makes it a colony of the Zacynthians; Strabo, book 3, calls it Σαγυντ@ [Sagunt@], χωρμα [chorma], ζαχωθιων [zachōthiōn]; some believe Saguntum was founded by a son of Hercules; some want it to have received its name from the Iberian word Saguis. Silius Italicus, book 1, describes its site. Livy, book 30, attributes the walls of Saguntum to Carmenta: they were hardened with lime but plastered over with mud, in the ancient style of building. From Pliny it is clear that the Saguntines once worshipped Diana, brought there by the Zacynthians, their ancestors, two hundred years before the fall of Troy. Pomponius Mela calls Saguntum "shut in by faith and hardships." Of the taking of this most noble city, and of the disaster that befell it, owing to its remarkable constancy and outstanding loyalty to the Romans, in the year from the founding of the city 585, in the consulship of Marcus Livius Salinator and Lucius Aemilius Paulus, see Livy, book 21; Polybius, book 3; Orosius, book 4, chapter 14; Eutropius, book 3; Florus, book 2 of the Roman history, chapter 6; Silius Italicus, book 1; Valerius Maximus, book 5, chapter 6; Augustine, City of God, book 3, chapter 20; the author On Illustrious Men, chapter 43; Aemilius Probus in his Hannibal; Cicero in the Philippics, and others. The memory of the Senate and People of Saguntum survives, in the place where the city was, on an old wall, in these words: "THE SENATE AND PEOPLE OF THE SAGUNTINES TO CLAUDIUS, UNCONQUERED, PIOUS, FORTUNATE, EMPEROR CAESAR, PONTIFEX MAXIMUS, HOLDING TRIBUNICIAN POWER, FATHER OF THE COUNTRY, PROCONSUL..."

units.la: Non ignobilis in Valentia loci sunt hodieque Segorbia, Σεγόβριγα Ptolemaeo & Straboni, uti placet Vasæo, Clusio, Taraphæ, Emanueli Enrico, & aliis: Segobrigam habent Nummi Augusti. Incolæ Plinio Segobricenses; eos in capite Celtiberiæ ponenti. Segobriga tamen Morali censetur Injesta, vel Cabeça el Griego cujus sententiæ est & Ioannes Mariana. Hieronymus Surita, ubi fuerit Segorbia, dicit se ignorare. Segobrica meminit antiquum Marmor, quod Tarraconæ: L. ANNIO. L. F. GAL CANTABRO FLAM. ROMÆ. ET. DIVOR AVGVST. P. H. C OMNIBVS. HONORIBVS GESTIS. SEGOBRICAE DECRETO. ORDINIS. FECV NIA PVBLICA SEGOBRICENSES
units.tr: Not unimportant places in Valentia still exist today: Segorbia, which is Segobriga [Σεγόβριγα] for Ptolemy and Strabo, as Vasaeus, Clusius, Tarapha, Emanuel Henricus and others think. The coins of Augustus have Segobriga. Pliny calls its inhabitants the Segobricenses and places them at the head of the Celtiberian region. Moralis, however, thinks Segobriga is Injesta, or Cabeça el Griego, and John Mariana agrees. Hieronymus Surita says he does not know where Segorbia is. An ancient marble at Tarragona mentions Segobrica: "To Lucius Annius, son of Lucius, of the Galerian tribe, a Cantabrian, flamen at Rome and of the deified Augustus, who held all the offices, by decree of the council at Segobrica; the public of the Segobricenses erected this at public expense."

units.la: Denia, Dianium (ut volunt Florianus, Moralis, Clusius) apud Ciceronem & Plinium, qui Stipendiarium cognominat: Ἀρπμίσον & Πιρεσοκοπᾶς est Straboni, haud procul Ferraria Promontorio. Castrum Altum, arx Hispaniæ Citerioris valida, Amilcaris Pœni cæde insignis apud Livium; hodie, ut vult Beuterus, Castralla vocatur; Floriano est Castel-Seras. Incibilis Livij; quæ Indibilis Frontino, ubi Annonem Carthaginiensium Ducem ab Scipione fugatum narrat, Chelua censetur Floriano, subdubitanti tamen. Ilici Plinio, Ἰλικίας Ptolemaeo, Illice Pomponio, Ilce Colonia Nummis, Ἰλικιτανῶν etiam Ptolemaeo (unde Illicitanus Sinus) hodie aliis Alicanta, aliis Elche, quod propius accedit. Belgida Celtiberiæ Vrbs, quam Orosius lib. v. cap. xxiii scribit à Cn. Pompeio Magno captam, nomen adhuc retinet. Ἀεύγια, quæ & Ἐδρτα Ptolemaeo (unde Hleditani populi) Lirta hodie est Clusio & Morali; Floriano autem. Oliete Ὀρυαλις Ptolemaei, Horiuela & Oriola Gomecio est & Clusio; Zamora Nebrissensi. Bigerra Livij, Βιγερρα Ptolemaei; hodie Bejar Beutero & Vasæo; Clusio Villena est. Quæ Σέταβις Straboni, vel Setabis antiquis Lapidibus, teste Clusio; hodie Floriano judice, Xativa cluit. Sed hæc sufficiant; ne proferendis in medium omnibus in immensum excrescat volumen; tædiumve pariatur Lectori.
units.tr: Denia is Dianium (as Florian, Moralis and Clusius hold), in Cicero and in Pliny, who gives it the surname Stipendiarium. Harpision and Pyresocopas [Ἀρπμίσον & Πιρεσοκοπᾶς] are in Strabo, not far from the Promontory of Ferraria. Castrum Altum, a strong fortress of Hispania Citerior, is notable in Livy for the slaughter of Hamilcar the Carthaginian; today, according to Beuterus, it is called Castralla, while for Florian it is Castel-Seras. Livy's Incibilis is the Indibilis of Frontinus, where he tells how Hanno, the Carthaginian commander, was put to flight by Scipio. Florian thinks it is Chelua, though with some doubt. Ilici is in Pliny, Ἰλικίας [Ilikias] in Ptolemy, Illice in Pomponius, and Ilce is the colony on the coins; Ἰλικιτανῶν [Ilikitanon] is also in Ptolemy, whence the Illicitanian Gulf. Today some call it Alicante and others Elche, which comes closer. Belgida, a city of Celtiberia, which Orosius (book 5, chapter 23) writes was captured by Gnaeus Pompey the Great, still keeps its name. Ἀεύγια [Aeugia], which in Ptolemy is also Ἐδρτα [Edrta], whence the people of the Hleditani, is today Lirta for Clusius and Moralis; for Florian, however, it is something else. Oliete is Ptolemy's Ὀρυαλις [Oryalis]; Horiuela and Oriola are Gomecius's and Clusius's; Zamora is Nebrissensis's. Bigerra is Livy's, Βιγερρα [Bigerra] in Ptolemy; today it is Bejar for Beuterus and Vasaeus, but for Clusius it is Villena. Which is Σέταβις [Setabis] in Strabo, or Setabis on ancient stones, as Clusius attests, is today Xativa, in Florian's judgment. But these will suffice, lest by bringing forward all of them the volume grow to an immense size and cause weariness to the reader.

units.la: Regni porro Titulum accepit Valentia circa annum loccxcviiix, uti auctores sunt Petrus Medinensis & Petrus Antonius Beuterus; qui omnino, cum aliis, legendi.
units.tr: The title of kingdom was received by Valentia around the year 1098, as Peter of Medina and Peter Antony Beuterus report; both of them, along with others, are worth reading in full.

units.la: CAP. XXII.
units.tr: CHAP. XXII.

units.la: Murcia.
units.tr: Murcia.

units.la: MVRCIA Regnum ab Occasu Granatam tangit; ad Septemtrionem Castellam Novam: cetera claudit Mare Mediterraneum: olim, ut ex Strabonis colligitur delineatione, Spartarium Campus, de quo dixi cap. iii. Nomen habet ab Murcia, Urbe Regni primaria. Optima in hac Provincia fiunt Vasa ex Creta, miraque hic Serici quantitas.
units.tr: Murcia borders Granada on the west and New Castile on the north; the Mediterranean Sea closes it on the other sides. Formerly it was the Spartarian Plain, of which I spoke in chapter iii, as can be gathered from Strabo's description. It takes its name from Murcia, the chief city of the kingdom. The finest vessels from Crete are made in this province, and there is a remarkable quantity of silk here.

units.la: Obtinuerunt quondam haec Loca Basitani Βαστιανοὶ Ptolemaeo; Vasetani, corruptius in prima littera, Livio: Bateflanij Antiquae Inscriptioni in Agro, qui hodie Madrigal; ubi Boves quinque Marmorei, singuli cum sequentibus Titulis: Primus habet in Latere dextro, LONGINVS. PRISCO. CALVO in sinistro; LAVINIO. PRI. F. C Secundus in Latere dextro; CAECILIO. METELLO in sinistro; CONS. II. VICTORI Tertius in Latere dextro, EXERCITVS. VICTOR in sinistro; HOSTIBVS. FVSIS Quartus in dextro, I. PORCIO. OB. TROV. OPT in sinistro; ADMINISTRATAM BATESTANI. POPVLI. F. C Quintus habet BELLVM. CAESARIS ET. PATRIAE. EX. MAGNA. PARTE CONFECTVM. SEX. ET. CN MAGNI. POMPEI. FILIIS. HIC IN. AGRO. BATESTANIORVM PROFLIGATIS
units.tr: These places were once held by the Basitani (Ptolemy's Βαστιανοί), by the Vasetani (Livy's form, more corrupt in its first letter), and by the Bateflani of the ancient inscription in the district that is today called Madrigal. There are five marble oxen there, each with the following inscriptions. The first has on its right side LONGINUS PRISCUS and on its left CALVUS LAVINIUS, son of Primus, C(…). The second has on its right side CAECILIUS METELLUS and on its left CONSUL for the second time, VICTOR. The third has on its right side EXERCITUS VICTOR and on its left HOSTIBUS FUSIS (the enemy having been routed). The fourth has on its right side I. PORCIUS, OB TROV(…), OPTIMUS, and on its left ADMINISTERED BY THE BATESTANI, the people of ... (the rest of the inscription is unclear). The fifth bears: THE WAR OF CAESAR AND OF THE COUNTRY, LARGELY FINISHED BY THE SONS OF SEXTUS AND GNAEUS MAGNUS POMPEY, WERE DEFEATED HERE IN THE FIELD OF THE BATESTANI.

units.la: Eorum Regio Bastitanis apud Plinium. Videntur illi esse, qui hodie Baza oppidum colunt. Nam & Basti Antonino Basteraniae urbs. De Basletanorum moribus singularia quaedam commemorat Strabo lib. iii. Praeter Bastitanos fuerunt & Belli Appiano in Ibericis; qui Bellitani à Plinio videntur appellari. Item Deitani, quorum regionem Deitaniam circa Carthaginem Novam collocat Plinius.
units.tr: Their region is called Bastitani by Pliny. They seem to be the people who now inhabit the town of Baza, for Basti in Antoninus is a city of the Basteraniae. Strabo, in book iii, records certain particular customs of the Basletani. Besides the Bastitani there were also the Belli, mentioned by Appian in his Iberica; these seem to be the Bellitani of Pliny. Likewise the Deitani, whose region, Deitania, Pliny places near New Carthage.

units.la: Metropolis Murcia, sita ad Fluvium, qui Ptolemaeo. Ipsum Oppidum Murgis Plinio, Μύργις Ptolemaeo, cujus populos Murgos vocat Antoninus. Alijs tamen Murgis Plinij Muxacra putatur; Μύργις autem Ptolemaei Murga. Sepultus hic est Alphonsus Ferdinandi Regis filius: qui ex Rege Castellae Romanorum Rex Imperij Occidentis creatus est in Schismate contra Richardum, Ioannis Anglorum Regis Filium, pridie Calendas Aprilis anno MCCCCLVIII; regnavitque annos xv, menses vi. Quum autem anno MCCCCLXXIIII sponte Imperij molem depositisset, in Hispaniam reversus parum gratus fuit filio Sanctio; passimque exclusum sola recepit Murcia, Privilegium inde consequuta, ut septem coronas Insignibus suis imponeret. Summus fuit Astrologus, & Sideralis Scientiae peritissimus; ejusque extant Tabulae, quae Alphonsinae ab eo dictae. Est ibi & Carthago Nova, ab Asdrubale, Poenorum Duce, ut Strabo lib. iii. notat, quo tempore contra Romanos bellum gerebat, condita. Haec Appiano, Plinio, Antonino, Isidoro, alijs Spartaria, Σπάρταρια, cognominatur, à Spartario Campo. Καινόπολις etiam ad differentiam Veteris appellatur Polybio lib. iii. & Strephano. Phoenissa dicitur Polyaeno, instar istius in Africa, quae à Phoenicibus condita. Idem Appianus censet prius Saguntum nominatam; sed postea ab Annibale excisam, & Carthaginiensium Coloniam factam, Carthaginem Spartagenam fuisse nuncupatam. Sed Carthaginem & Saguntum duo diversa esse Opida, nimis est notum. Labitur & alias in Hispania Appianus, Iberum in Septemtrionalem Oceanum evolvi scribens, quum in Mediterraneum erumpat. Novam autem dictam scribit Ioannes Gerundensis Episcopus Paralip. Hispaniae lib. i. sub finem, & lib. iii, non ob Africanam illam, sed Veterem aliam in ipsa Hispania.
units.tr: The metropolis is Murcia, situated on a river which Ptolemy names. The town itself is Murgis in Pliny, Μύργις in Ptolemy, and Antoninus calls its people the Murgi. Others, however, think that Pliny's Murgis is Muxacra, while Ptolemy's Μύργις is Murga. Here lies buried Alphonsus, son of King Ferdinand, who was created King of the Romans and Emperor of the West, from King of Castile, during the schism against Richard, son of John, King of the English, on 31 March 1458. He reigned fifteen years and six months. When in 1474 he voluntarily laid down the burden of the Empire and returned to Spain, he was little favoured by his son Sancho, and, shut out almost everywhere, Murcia alone received him; from this it obtained the privilege of placing seven crowns on its arms. He was a very great astrologer and most skilled in the science of the stars, and his Tables, called Alphonsine after him, survive. There is also here New Carthage, founded by Hasdrubal, the Carthaginian general, at the time when he was waging war against the Romans, as Strabo notes in book iii. It is called Spartaria (Σπάρταρια) by Appian, Pliny, Antoninus, Isidore and others, from the Spartarian Plain. It is also called Καινόπολις, to distinguish it from the Old city, by Polybius in book iii and by Stephanus. Polyaenus calls it Phoenissa, like that city in Africa founded by the Phoenicians. Appian also thinks that it was formerly called Saguntum, but was afterwards destroyed by Hannibal and made a colony of the Carthaginians, and was then named Carthage Spartagena. But that Carthage and Saguntum are two different towns is too well known to need discussion. Appian also errs elsewhere in Spain, writing that the Ebro flows out into the northern Ocean, whereas it empties into the Mediterranean. John, Bishop of Girona, in the Paralipomena of Spain, book i, near the end, and book iii, says that it was called New not from that African city but from another, older one in Spain itself.

units.la: {z} Murcia Regni primaria.
units.tr: {z} Murcia, the chief city of the kingdom.

units.la: Hispania. Certe Carthago Vetus Ptolemæo est Elarcaonum urbs in Hispania Tarraconensi; quam Pænorum cognominat Plinius; cujusque mentio apud Ciceronem de Lege Agraria: Cantavilla hodie, ut scribunt Varrerius & Beuterus: Canta Vera Antonio Augustino; Villa Franca Gerundensi. Καρχηδὼν ἡ νέα, scribitur Straboni lib. iii. χερσίῳ πολὺ τῶν ταύτῃ πόλεων. Καὶ γὰρ ἐφυμνοτάτη, καὶ τέχνῃ καζασκευασμένῳ καλῶς, καὶ λιμένι καὶ λίμνῃ ἀεκόσμητος· καὶ τῆς τῶν δεχομένων μεταλλεῖς, ὅθι ὢν ἐρήμωμεν.
units.tr: Hispania. Certainly Old Carthage is, for Ptolemy, the city of the Elarcaones in Tarraconensian Spain, which Pliny calls the city of the Poeni, and which Cicero mentions in his De Lege Agraria. Today it is Cantavilla, as Varrerius and Beuterus write; Antonio Augustino calls it Canta Vera, and Girona calls it Villa Franca. Strabo, in book iii, writes of New Carthage: it is far superior to the other cities of this region, being very well placed and well built, and adorned with harbour and lagoon, and with mines of the things it receives... [Καρχηδὼν ἡ νέα, χερσίῳ πολὺ τῶν ταύτῃ πόλεων. Καὶ γὰρ ἐφυμνοτάτη, καὶ τέχνῃ καζασκευασμένῳ καλῶς, καὶ λιμένι καὶ λίμνῃ ἀεκόσμητος· καὶ τῆς τῶν δεχομένων μεταλλεῖς, ὅθι ὢν ἐρήμωμεν.]

units.la: Addit deinde, Ibi & propinquis locis frequentissima esse Salsamenta: item amplissimum esse Emporium, sive rebus e mari ad Mediterranea inportandis, sive ex penitioribus Hispaniæ locis ad transmarinas Provincias exportandis. Silius Italicus lib. xv ita describit:
units.tr: He then adds that in the nearby places there are very many salt-fish preserves; and that it is a very large emporium, both for bringing in goods from the sea for the inland regions and for shipping out goods from the more remote parts of Spain to the overseas provinces. Silius Italicus, in book xv, describes it thus:

units.la: Vrbs colitur Tencro quondam fundata vetustoNomen Carthago, Tyrius tenet Incola muros.
units.tr: The city, founded long ago by the Tyrians, is tended by the Tyrians, who hold its walls, and it bears the name Carthage.

units.la: Vt Libya sua, sic terris memorabile IberisHæc Caput est: non ulla opibus certaverit auri,
units.tr: As Libya is famous for its own, so for Iberia this is the chief city; no other place has rivalled it in the wealth of gold,

units.la: Non portu celsove situ, non dotibus arviVberis, aut agili fabricanda ad tela vigore.
units.tr: nor in harbour or lofty site, nor in the gifts of the fertile Iberian fields, or in the sturdy vigour for forging weapons.

units.la: Invade adversis nate hanc ductoribus Vrbem. Nulla acies fama tantum, prædæve paravit.
units.tr: Born of an unfavourable line, invade this city. No army prepared it, only fame and plunder.

units.la: Carthago impenso Natura adjuta favoreExcelsos tollit Pelago circumfluæ muros;
units.tr: Carthage, aided by nature with lavish favour, lifts its lofty walls, surrounded by the sea.

units.la: Arctatas Ponti Fauces modica Insula claudit,Qua Titan ortus terras aspergit Eoo.
units.tr: A small island closes the narrowed straits of the Pontus, where the rising Sun sprinkles the lands with eastern light.

units.la: At qua prospectat Phœbi juga fera cadentis. Pigram in planiciem flagnantes egerit undas,
units.tr: But where it looks toward the wild ridges of the setting Phoebus, it drives its sluggish waters into a flat plain, stagnant,

units.la: Quas auget veniens, refluusque reciprocat æstu.Sed gelidas à fronte sedet sublimis ad Arctos
units.tr: which the incoming tide increases and the ebb drives back again. But high from its front it sits toward the cold Bear,

units.la: Vrbs impolita jugo, pronumque excurrit in aquor. Et tuta æterno defendit mœnia fluctu.
units.tr: a city unfenced on its ridge, running out steeply over the sea, and it defends its walls safe by its eternal wave.

units.la: Hanc P. Cornelius Scipio Africanus, anno ab V. C. Ioxiv M. Claudio Marcello iv, M. Valerio Lævino ii. coss. belli Punici ii. anno ix, oppugnatam uno die cepit; Magone mox Se, Arcem & Præsidium dedente, scribentibus Livio lib. xxvi, Eutropio iii, Orosio iv. cap. xviii, Polybio lib. x, Silio lib. xv, Auctore de VV. Illustribus cap. xlix, Plutarch. in Vitis, Plinio lib. xxvi. cap. iv, Appiano de reb. Hisp. Floro lib. ii, cap. xvii, & aliis: Hic idem Scipio Captivam Virginem eximiæ formæ Sponso Allucio Celtiberorum Principi intactam reddidit; ijsdem testantibus, cum Valerio Maximo lib. iv. cap. iii & Agel. vi. cap. viii: hic denique in Ludis, ab ipso Scipione factis, duo Hispani Principes Corbis & Orsua Patrueles, de Regno dissidentes, impetu facto, perierunt; quod superiorum plerique memoriæ produnt.
units.tr: This city was taken in a single day, after assault, by P. Cornelius Scipio Africanus, in the year 214 from the founding of the city, when M. Claudius Marcellus (for the fourth time) and M. Valerius Laevinus (for the second time) were consuls, in the ninth year of the Second Punic War; Mago soon surrendered himself, the citadel and the garrison. So write Livy in book xxvi, Eutropius in book iii, Orosius in book iv, chapter xviii, Polybius in book x, Silius in book xv, the author of De Viris Illustribus, chapter xlix, Plutarch in the Lives, Pliny in book xxvi, chapter iv, Appian in De rebus Hispanicis, Florus in book ii, chapter xvii, and others. This same Scipio restored intact to Allucius, prince of the Celtiberians, to whom she was betrothed, a captive virgin of outstanding beauty; the same authors attest this, together with Valerius Maximus in book iv, chapter iii, and Gellius in book vi, chapter viii. Finally, in the games held by Scipio himself here, two Spanish princes, Corbis and Orsua, cousins who disagreed about the kingdom, perished after making an attack; most of the earlier writers record this.

units.la: Hactenus Citerioris vel Tarraconensis Hispaniæ, quæ in antiqua Romanisque usitata Distributione principem facile locum tuebatur, partes recensui; sequuntur, quæ Betica attribui solitæ: quas antea quam ingrediar, operæprecium me facturum arbitror, si prius Iter illud nobilissimum, quod ex Gallia Narbonensi in Bæticam usque per maritimas ejusdem Tarraconensis Stationes Antonini Itinerarium ducit, proponam conlatum magna parte cum Itineraria Peutingeri Tabula, cujus antea memini, cumque hodiernis Vrbium Opidorumque appellationibus. Itinerarium Antonini. | Itineraria Peuting. Tabula. | Hodierna Nomina. Nemausum, M.P.XIIII. | Nemuso, Leg. Nemauso, XV. | Nismes. Ambrussum, M.P.XV. | Ambrusium, XX. | Sambres. Sextationem, M.P.XV. | Serratione, Leg. Sextatione, XV. | Saas. Forum Domitij, M.P.XV. | Foro Domitij, XVIII. | Gigean, aut circiter. Ceseronem, M.P.XVIII. | Cesse Rone: Voces cojunge, XII | Sainct Hubert, alijs S. Tubert. Beterras, M.P.XII. | Beteris, XXI. | Befieres. Narbonem, M.P.XII. | Narbone, | Narbona. Ad Vigesimum, M.P.XX. | | Combustam, M.P.XIIII. | | Quid sit, nihil opus divinare.
units.tr: So far I have reviewed the parts of Hispania Citerior, or Tarraconensis, which in the ancient and Roman division rightly held the first place. What follows are the parts usually assigned to Baetica. Before I enter upon them, I think it will be worth my while to set out first that most noble road which runs from Gallia Narbonensis into Baetica through the coastal stations of the same Tarraconensis, as given in Antoninus' Itinerary, compared for the most part with the Peutinger Table, which I mentioned earlier, and with the modern names of the cities and towns.
