units.la: GRanatæ Conregiones sunt ad Ortum Murcia ; ad Septemtrionem Castella Nova; ad Occasum Andaluzia : Meridionale Latus ab Iberico Mari abluitur, oppositas habens oras Africanas. Nomen illi ab Vrbe Granata, Metropoli. Longitudo Granatæ, inquit L. Marineus Siculus lib. xx. de rebus Hispaniæ, est passuum millium circiter ducentorum, & latitudo fere centum; paretque circuitu ad passuum millia septingenta. Est enim Longitudo ab Ronda usque ad Oscam; Latitudo vero ab opido Cambili usque ad Mare Mediterraneum & Portum Almugnecaris. Qua Meridiem spectat, ex una parte planicies habet amplas & fertiles Campos; ex altera, Bastanos Montes altos, & ascensu difficiles : Vulgus Alpuxarras appellat. Est ibi omnium Rerum, quæ sunt ad hominum vitam degendam necessariæ, magna fertilitas: saluberrima semper aëris cœlique temperies, ubi neque Tellus nimio Solis ardore torretur, neque frigore contrahitur: hominibus perpetuo temperamento perfruentibus.
units.tr: The regions of Granada lie: to the east, Murcia; to the north, New Castile; to the west, Andalusia. Its southern side is washed by the Spanish Sea, and the African shores lie opposite it. It takes its name from the city of Granada, its metropolis. The length of Granada, says L. Marineus Siculus in book 20 of his work On the Affairs of Spain, is about two hundred miles, and its breadth nearly one hundred; its circuit comes to about seven hundred miles. Its length runs from Ronda as far as Osca, and its breadth from the town of Cambil to the Mediterranean Sea and the port of Almuñécar. On the side facing south it has, on one part, wide plains and fertile fields; on the other, the high Bastan mountains, which are hard to climb and which the common people call the Alpujarras. There is there a great abundance of all the things needed for living a human life. The air and sky always have a most healthful temperature: the land is neither scorched by the excessive heat of the sun nor chilled by cold, and the people enjoy a constant mildness.

units.la: Commoratos olim in hac Hispaniæ parte lego, cum aliis proculdubio, Sexitanos: quorum opidum Sex Plinio: Σίξ Ptolemæo post Manocam & Menobam in Bastulis; quod τῶν Ἐξιτανῶν πόλις, Straboni; Sexitanum (alia Exemplaria habent Saxetanum; Saxetani etiam Lacerti meminit Martialis lib. vii.) Antonino: Hexi apud Pompon. Melam: Floriano Motrel hodie; Coquo & Pineto Velez Malaga; Clusio Salobrenna ad mare: Σιξιτανία legitur apud Athenæum lib. iii. Sexitanis vicini fuerunt Bastuli: Βαστύλοι, qui & Ποένοι, cognominantur Ptolemæo, Populi Hispaniæ Baeticæ ad Fretum Gaditanum. Certe Pœnis suas ab utraque Freti parte Sedes fuisse, testantur etiam Seneca de Consolatione, Plinius lib. iii. nat. hist. cap. i. & Pomponius lib. ii. cap. vi. Eo, ut bene censet, etiam contra Criticorum illum Parentem Hadrianum Turnebum, Abrahamus Ortelius, respicit in Odis Horatius lib. ii. Od. ii: Latius regnes, avidum domando Spiritum, quam si Libyam remotis Gadibus jungas, & uterque Poenus Serviat uni.
units.tr: I read that the Sexitani once dwelt in this part of Spain, along with others, no doubt. Their town is called Sex by Pliny; Six by Ptolemy, after Manoca and Menoba among the Bastuli [Σίξ]; the city of the Exitani by Strabo [τῶν Ἐξιτανῶν πόλις]; Sexitanum by Antoninus (other copies have Saxetanum, and Martial in book 7 also mentions the Saxetani Lacerti); Hexi by Pomponius Mela. Today Florianus identifies it as Motrel, Cook and Pinetus as Vélez-Málaga, and Clusius as Salobreña, on the sea. Athenaeus in book 3 reads Sixitania [Σιξιτανία]. Neighbours of the Sexitani were the Bastuli [Βαστύλοι], who are also called Poeni by Ptolemy, a people of Hispania Baetica by the Strait of Gades. Certainly that the Phoenicians had their seats on both sides of the strait is attested by Seneca in his Consolation, by Pliny in book 3 of his Natural History, chapter 1, and by Pomponius in book 2, chapter 6. In this, as he rightly judges, Abraham Ortelius agrees, and against that father of critics, Hadrianus Turnebus. Horace also has this in view in Odes book 2, ode 2: You would reign more broadly by mastering your greedy spirit than if you joined Libya to the distant Gades, and both Carthaginians served one master.

units.la: Metropolis Granata; sic dicta ab Malo Punico, quod Granatum vocatur. Nam ut Malum Punicum granosum est, & Acinis, hoc est Granis, densissimis refertum; sic & (inquit Georgius Hoffnagel, Civis Antverpianus, qui hanc Vrbem coloribus suis optime delineauit) Vrbs Granata densissimas domos, & dehiscentis Granati similitudinem habet. Alij aliunde dirivant: quidam Granatam appellari perhibentes, à Cocco; cujus in ea Provincia ingens copia legi solita, quam rem Granam Hispani dicunt; quidam, quasi Gar Nata, ab Gar, quod lingua Punica Antrum, & Nata Nympha, cui in isthoc Antro Domicilium erat, quaeque ijs in locis ab Incolis olim colebatur. Ἰλιβέρις (ab Illiberia Hispani Regis filia, ut quidam somniant) Ptolemaeo multorum judicio; Illiberi vel Liberini Plinio; Ἐλιβέργη Stephano. Vasaeus tamen Granatam Illiberi recentiorem censet, & ab ea duabus leucis distare. Suffragatur Moralis, scribens Illiberim non procul Granata fuisse in eo Colle: qui vulgo nunc Elvire, immutata nonnihil antiqua voce; ubi Elvira erat opidum; ab eoque & hodie Granatae Portam esse Elveriam. Illiberim hac aetate Almariam nominari putat Episcopus Gerundensis; Granatam autem esse, quae Ptolemaeo Ἀιχνλα μεγάλα; Plinio Iupula simpliciter. Circuitus Granatae passuum millium circiter est duodecim. Moenibus undique cingitur; tuentibus eam mille triginta Propugnaculis. Portae, quae sunt numero duodecim, ad Occidentem faciles habent exitus, & Campos amoenos; ceterae vero ad Orientem, subdifficiles. Vrbs communi nomine Granata dicitur, Academia nobilis, duos comprehendens, praeter minores alios, nonnullius altitudinis Colles, quos Darrus fluvius (Duurum Bernardus Gentilis Poeta nominat, quasi dantem Aurum, quod in eo quam optimum legi consuevit, unde & vulgo El Rio del Oro) per Vallem mediam fluens dividit. Vrbs in quatuor hodie distributa est Partes, sicut separatas, suisque appellationibus distinctas. Prima peculiari voce Granata nuncupatur, Loca declivia & Valles occupans. Habitant hic Ecclesiastici, Nobiles plerique, potentiores Mercatores; in Aedificijs omnes magnificis, quibus Horti conjacent amoenissimi. Templo decoratur longe maximo, sumtuosissimi mirabilisque operis; in quo Sacellum splendidissimum, corpora servans Ferdinandi & Isabellae, qui Granatam Maurorum tyrannidi ante centum, & qui excurrunt, annos ceperunt. Iuxta est perantiquum Maurorum Fanum, Mesquita eorum lingua nuncupatum. Est in eadem Vrbis Regione Summum Iudicum Tribunal, ad quod supremae Iudiciorum omnium Appellationes devolvuntur: cui qui praesunt Oidores appellantur. Est ibidem Platea vel Forum Venale, conspicuae magnitudinis, nuper à Christianis instructum; Bizatamblam Mauri vocant, Arenariam significari dicentes. Forma est quadrangularis, ad mensae similitudinem: Longitudo pedum est quadringentorum, Latitudo ducentorum. Ibi Fons est excelsus & insignis. Foro coniuncta est domus Alcaceria, Tabernulas habens fere ducentas, in quibus sericí panni ceterarumque rerum merces quotidie venduntur. Secunda Vrbis Regio in altiore sita Colle, qui Solis spectat exortum (unde & Sierra del Sol) voce Maura Alhambra dicitur: Mauri Rubram significari notant, sicque nominari vel ab Conditore, homine rufo; vel ab rubra Terra, quae nunc etiam conspicitur in aedificijs. Habitatur mistim ab Mauris & Hispanis. Occurrunt ibi multa singularia cum primis Arx Nova, ab Philippo II. Hispaniarum Rege, forma quadrata, ex caeruleo lapide, qui singulari Architecturae artificio ad normam sectus, condita: Aream habet rotundam, valde elegantem, & amplam; Ambitum autem, triplicibus Menianis (quae Columnis Marmoreis, venusto ordine dispositis, sustentantur) laetaque ambulatione distinctum: Multa ac varia ibi Conclavia; in quorum interiore ornatu Ars & Sumtus decertare videntur. Tam amoenus illi undique prospectus, ut oculi incredibili oblectatione sese pascant; nusquam non, quoquo se vertant, habentes, quo Dei ac Naturae bonitatem, Agrique Granatensis felicitatem admirentur. Opus sane, dignum, quod decantatis totius Universi Miraculis non adnumeretur modo, verum etiam optimo jure praeferatur. Est & in eadem Vrbis Regione antiquum Maurorum Regum Palatium vastitate visenda: Defensores commode admittens ad quadraginta millia. Hoc unicum, si alia deessent indicia, quanta magnificentia, quantoque fastu gens barbara Granatensie Regnum possederit, manifeste loquitur. Interior Structura valde sumtuosa est, valde superba; ex Porphyrite constans, Iaspide & Marmore: Muri, Trabes, Tabulata auro sunt obducta: videre passim est Emblemata, Hieroglyphicas Notas, Arabicas Litteras, varia Signa, Musivo opere incrustata. Quae quum sint exquisita, & rarae notae ornamenta, magnaque Mauritaniae gentis opes & singularem magnificentiam contestantia; magna Christianorum cura diligentiaque ab situ & interitu, quantum fieri potest, conservantur, collapsaque restaurantur. Locus est in eadem arce elegans & spaciosus, forma quadrata, vulgo El Quadro, aut Los Leones: in cujus medio duodecim Leones Labrum admodum capax ex candido Marmore in dorso sustinent: medium spacium Fons exornat limpidissimæ aquæ, in altum ad instar erectæ hastæ rapidissimo motu prosiliens, & in idem Labrum deinde recidens; unde Canales mox & delectabiles Aquationes promanant, in quibus Maurorum Reges cum Reginis æstivos Calores ludendo lauandoque mitigare perhibentur soliti. Locum hunc Meniana, quæ marmoreis innituntur Columnis, cingunt. Ex hac Arce, in quantum oculorum acies extendere se potest, universa propemodum Granata videtur; læta etiam Arva, La Vega de Granada nuncupata: Montes insuper conspiciuntur, perpetuis Nivibus candentes, La Sierra Nevada vulgo; Ferarum quoque Vivarium, in eoque omnis generis Animalia; Cervi præcipue, Damæ & Capreoli. Ultra hanc Arcem paullulum ascendendo elegans & splendida Domus, Generalipha, se offert; natura, arte, situ ad venustatem & recreationem composita. Aëre sereno semper gaudet. Multis abundat Fontibus, suavissimo Murmure undique discurrentibus: quorum unus, mirabile & jucundissimum visu, Aquas in miram altitudinem copiosissima eructatione, brachij crassitudine evomit, quod extra istius domus muros longissime prospici potest, maxime splendente Sole. Præterea hic consitas arte Siluulas; Arbores patentibus ramis generosis fructibus graves; Sepimenta reticulata; inque ijs feras magno numero bestias. Ij fissima videtur Sedes Voluptati Delicijsque ab Maurorum Regibus consecrata. In Verticem porro Montis eminenti occurrit ætate multa conlapsum fere Maurorum Fanum, ab Christianis S. Helena nunc dedicatum: ad quod fere omnes, qui Granatæ videndæ desiderio flagrant, conscendunt ut ejus Templi Muro suum Patriæque nomen inscribant: quod quidem ea consuetudine Vulgiqué opinione receptum, ut is Granatam non censeatur vidisse, qui id non præstiterit. In eodem hoc Monte Maurorum Reges suos olim habuerunt hortos, vario Florum & Herbarum genere decenter vestitos; quorum nunc etiam manifesta satis superstant indicia. Iuxta Cisterna est publica, Algibe dicta; Imbribus colligendis quomdam ab Romanis parata: Aqua inibi non solum nullum Putredinis incommodum sentit, verum etiam medendi vim habet & facultatem: quod Hispani longa experientia sunt docti. Nam pota Ventris fluxum sedat. In Latere ejusdem Montis Ædicula Sacra est, multa antiquitate & Veneranda Martyrum memoria nobilis; Los Martyres vulgo: vbi Putei & Antra in Rupibus excisa, & scalpellis excavata conspiciuntur: quorum ut Ingressus sunt angustiores, ita interiores recessus latioris sunt spacij: in hac Mauri Christianos, quos ingenti numero captivos tenebant, crudeliterque tractabant, noctu protrudere & funibus demittere so-lebant, diuturnis laboribus fractos & confectos. Hispanis Mafmoros dicitur. Tertia Vrbis Regio, El Alvejin, duos complectitur Colles, admiranda ædium frequentia cultos. Hæc, quia à solis Mauris quondam habitabatur, non altera Civitatis Regio, sed diversa plane Natio habita & Idiomate ab reliquis Granatæ Incolis separata esse videbatur: Agricultura & Serici Textrinis ut plurimum victum quærebant; & quantum Vxorum luxui Serico, aureoque & argenteo vestitu indulgere, tantum sibi viliore habitu Viri solebant adimere; sacco semper onusti, etiam si prædivites, incedentes, ut qualiacumque onera, Mercedis consequendæ gratia, petentibus ferrent. Nomen Fidemque Christo cum pietate exstimulati, tum Poenarum adducti metu dederunt. Hujus Partis Porta est illa, per quam Maurorum Rex, Il Ro Cicho, Rex Parvulus nuncupatus, Se, Granatam, & Arcem tradens Ferdinando Regi, exivit, & expugnati Granatensis Regni memoriam sempiternam remanere flagitavit hanc, ut nemini post se ea umquam pateret. Quod ab Ferdinando facile impetravit: ideoque ab eo tempore semper clausa mansit: &, ne unquam aperiretur, firmum illi oppositum fuit Propugnaculum. Fertur Rex Maurorum egressus, inque Colle constitutus, quum magnificam, quam deserere cogebatur, Vrbem tristis intueretur, inlacrumari cœpisse. Quod ubi Mater ejus videret, quæ & ipsa in fuga salutem quærebat, Filium adfata, Merito, ajebat, nunc extra Vrbem pueriles emittit lacrumas, in qua, tamquam Vir, cordate pro Aris & Focis pugnare voluisti. Quarta denique Vrbis Pars, quæ temporis successu ob majorem Civium frequentiam adnata, Antiquerula nominatur, praestans etiam & populosa; situ plano. Incolæ Antiquerulani vocantur ab Antiquera opido, unde huc profecti memorantur. Hi Byssum, Holosericum, Karmesinum, Bambacium, Damascenam, variasque praestantioris pretij telas magna copia neque contemnendo quæstu conficiunt. Sed ad Metropolis hujus Regni delineationem hæc sufficiant: perlustremus alia nonnulla ejusdem Opida. Quod ab Interni Maris littus hodie Malaga; μαλάκα Straboni & Ptolemæo vocatur; μαλάκη Stephano; Malaca Antonino; Malacha corrupte & contra Veterum Codicum fidem, cum adspiratione in Vulgatis Plinij Exemplaribus; Malecha corruptius Gratiano in Decretis. Vrbs est Episcopalis, Situ, Civium frequentia, Rerumque omnium copia celebris. Eo variarum nationum Mercatores, potissimum vero Belgæ, magno numero singulis annis confluunt, ad exportandos, quos Vindemia hoc loci suppeditat, delicatissimos fructus. Portum enim habet commodissimum; cujus etiam Festus Avienus meminit in Maritimis:
units.tr: The metropolis is Granada, so called from the pomegranate, which in Latin is Granatum. For as the Malum Punicum is full of seeds, that is, Grains, packed very tightly together, so too (says Georgius Hoffnagel, a citizen of Antwerp, who drew this city very well in its colours) the city of Granata has very dense houses and resembles a split pomegranate. Others derive the name from elsewhere. Some say that Granada is called after the kermes (coccus), which was usually gathered in great quantity in that province, a thing the Spaniards call Grana. Some say it is named as if Gar Nata, from Gar, which in the Punic language means a cave, and Nata, a nymph, who had her home in this cave and was once worshipped by the inhabitants of those parts. Ptolemy, in the judgment of many, calls it [Ἰλιβέρις] Ilibéris (said to be from Illiberia, daughter of a Spanish king, as some dream); Pliny calls it Illiberi or Liberini; Stephanus calls it [Ἐλιβέργη] Elibérgē. Vasaeus, however, holds that Granada is a more recent town than Illiberis, and that it lies two leagues from it. Moralis supports him, writing that Illiberis was not far from Granada on that hill which is now commonly called Elvire, the ancient name being somewhat changed; there was a town of Elvira, and from it the gate of Granada is still called Elveria. The bishop of Girona thinks that in our own age Illiberis is called Almaria, and that Granada is the place which Ptolemy calls [Ἀιχνλα μεγάλα] Aichnla megala, and Pliny simply Iupula. The circuit of Granada is about twelve miles. It is enclosed on every side by walls, which are defended by a thousand and thirty bastions. Its gates, twelve in number, open on the west onto easy roads and pleasant fields; those on the east are somewhat more difficult. The city, taken as a whole, is called Granada. It is a famous university, and it includes two hills of some height, besides other smaller ones, which the river Darrus (Bernardus Gentilis the poet calls it Duurum, as if giving gold, because the finest gold was usually found in it, whence it is also commonly called El Rio del Oro) divides as it flows through the middle valley. The city is today divided into four parts, separate from one another and distinguished by their own names. The first, by its own name, is called Granata, and occupies the sloping places and valleys. Here live the churchmen, most of the nobles, and the wealthier merchants, all in splendid buildings, around which lie the most pleasant gardens. It is adorned with a temple by far the largest, of the most sumptuous and wondrous workmanship, in which is a most splendid chapel holding the bodies of Ferdinand and Isabella, who took Granada from the tyranny of the Moors a hundred and some years ago. Near it is a very ancient mosque of the Moors, called Mesquita in their language. In the same region of the city is the supreme court of judges, to which the final appeals of all courts are referred; those who preside over it are called Oidores. There is also a square or public market of notable size, recently laid out by the Christians; the Moors call it Bizatamblam, saying it means sandy place. It is rectangular, like the shape of a table. Its length is four hundred feet, its breadth two hundred. There is a tall and remarkable fountain there. Joined to the market is the building Alcaceria, with about two hundred little shops, in which silk cloths and the wares of other goods are sold every day. The second region of the city lies on the higher hill that faces the rising sun (hence also Sierra del Sol), and is called by the Arabic name Alhambra; the Moors note that this means red, and that it was so named either after its founder, a red-haired man, or after the red earth which can still be seen in the buildings. It is inhabited by Moors and Spaniards together. Many remarkable things are to be seen there, above all the New Citadel, built by Philip II, king of the Spains, square in form, of blue stone, which was cut to a rule with singular skill in architecture. It has a round courtyard, very elegant and spacious, and its circuit is marked off by triple porticoes (supported by marble columns arranged in a graceful order) and a pleasant walkway. There are many and varied chambers there, in whose interior decoration art and expense seem to vie with each other. The view on every side is so pleasant that the eyes feed on it with incredible delight; wherever one turns, one has something on which to marvel at the goodness of God and of nature and at the fertility of the land of Granada. It is indeed a work worthy not merely to be counted among the celebrated wonders of the whole world but to be placed before them by the best right. In the same region of the city there is also an ancient palace of the Moorish kings, worth seeing for its vastness; it can comfortably admit up to forty thousand defenders. This alone, even if no other evidence existed, clearly shows with how much magnificence and how much pride the barbarian people possessed the kingdom of Granada. The interior structure is very sumptuous and very splendid, made of porphyry, jasper and marble; the walls, beams and ceilings are overlaid with gold; everywhere one sees emblems, hieroglyphic signs, Arabic letters and various symbols inlaid in mosaic work. Since these are exquisite and rare ornaments, bearing witness to the great wealth and singular magnificence of the Mauritanian people, the Christians take great care and diligence to preserve them, as far as possible, from decay and ruin, and to restore what has fallen. In the same citadel there is an elegant and spacious place, square in form, commonly called El Quadro or Los Leones. In its middle twelve lions support on their backs a very large basin of white marble. In the central space a fountain adorns it with the clearest water, which leaps up with the swiftest motion, like an upright spear, into the air, and then falls back into the same basin; from there channels and delightful streams soon flow out, in which the Moorish kings, with their queens, are said to have been accustomed to relieve the summer heat by playing and bathing. This place is surrounded by porticoes that rest on marble columns. From this citadel, as far as the sight can reach, almost the whole of Granada is visible, and also the joyful fields called La Vega de Granada. Moreover, there are seen the mountains glittering with perpetual snows, commonly called La Sierra Nevada; and also a game park, containing animals of every kind, especially stags, does and roe deer. A little way above this citadel there presents itself an elegant and splendid house, Generalipha, composed by nature, art and situation for beauty and recreation. It always enjoys a clear air. It abounds in many fountains, which run everywhere with a most sweet murmur; one of them, wondrous and most pleasing to see, throws its water up to a remarkable height with the greatest abundance, as thick as an arm, so that it can be seen from very far outside the walls of this house when the sun shines brightly. Besides this, there are woods planted by art, trees laden with generous fruit on their spreading branches, hedges of latticework, and in them wild beasts in great number. This is indeed seen to be the seat consecrated by the Moorish kings to pleasure and delight. Further, on the top of the mountain, there stands the Moorish temple, now almost collapsed with age, now dedicated by the Christians to S. Helena; almost everyone who burns with desire to see Granada climbs up to it, to inscribe his own name and that of his homeland on its wall. This custom and popular belief is so established that a person is not considered to have seen Granada unless he has done this. On this same mountain the Moorish kings once had their gardens, decently clothed with a varied kind of flowers and herbs, and clear traces of them still survive. Next to it is a public cistern, called Algibe, prepared by the Romans for collecting rainwater. Its water not only causes no harm of putrefaction but even has the power and property of healing, as the Spaniards have learned by long experience; for when drunk it stops the flux of the belly. On the side of the same mountain is a sacred little chapel, noted for its great antiquity and the venerable memory of the martyrs, commonly called Los Martyres. There can be seen wells and caves hollowed out of the rocks and dug out with chisels; the narrower their entrances, the wider the spaces within their recesses. Into these the Moors used to thrust down, and let down by ropes, the Christians whom they held captive in great number and treated cruelly, worn out and exhausted by long labours. Among the Spaniards it is called Mafmoros. The third region of the city, El Alvejin, takes in two hills, cultivated with a remarkable number of buildings. Because this region was formerly inhabited by Moors alone, it seemed not another region of the city but a quite different nation, separated from the other inhabitants of Granada by their language. They mostly sought their living by agriculture and the silk weaving-houses; and just as much as they allowed their wives indulgence in silk and in gold and silver clothing, so much did the men use to take away from themselves by wearing cheaper dress; they always walked about loaded with sacks, even when very rich, so that they might carry whatever burdens they were asked to carry for the sake of earning a wage. They gave their name and faith to Christ, partly stirred by piety, partly moved by fear of punishments. The gate of this region is that through which the Moorish king, Il Ro Cicho, called Rex Parvulus, went out, surrendering himself, Granada and the citadel to King Ferdinand; and he asked that this gate, as a perpetual memorial of the conquered kingdom of Granada, should never be opened to anyone after him. This Ferdinand readily granted; and so from that time it has always remained closed, and, lest it ever be opened, a strong bastion was built in front of it. It is said that the Moorish king, having gone out and taken his stand on the hill, began to weep when he gazed sadly at the magnificent city which he was forced to abandon. When his mother saw this, she too was seeking safety in flight, and she addressed her son: Rightly, she said, now you shed childish tears outside the city, you who wished to fight within it like a man, bravely, for your altars and hearths. Finally, the fourth part of the city, which by the progress of time was added on account of the greater crowd of citizens, is called Antiquerula; it is also distinguished and populous, and lies on level ground. Its inhabitants are called Antiquerulani, from the town of Antiquera, whence they are recorded to have come here. They make fine linen, silk brocade, crimson cloth, cotton, Damascene cloth and various fabrics of greater value, in no small quantity and for no small profit. But let these details suffice for the description of the metropolis of this kingdom; let us now survey some other towns of the same. The town which on the shore of the inland sea is today called Malaga; by Strabo and Ptolemy [μαλάκα] malaka, by Stephanus [μαλάκη] malakē, by Antoninus Malaca, and wrongly, and contrary to the testimony of the old manuscripts, Malacha with an aspirate in the printed copies of Pliny, and more corruptly Malecha in Gratian's Decretum. It is an episcopal city, famous for its situation, the crowd of its citizens and the abundance of all things. Merchants of various nations gather there in large numbers every year, above all the Belgians, to export the most delicate fruits which the vintage supplies in that place. For it has a very convenient harbour, which Festus Avienus also mentions in his Maritima:

units.la: Et rursus inde si petat quisquam pede
units.tr: And if anyone should go from there on foot,

units.la: Tartesiorum littus exsuperet viam
units.tr: he would cross the road to the shore of the Tartessians

units.la: Vix luce quarta. Si quis ad nostrum Mare
units.tr: scarcely by the fourth day. If anyone makes for our sea

units.la: Malacaque portum semitam tetenderit
units.tr: and sets out by path for the harbour of Malaca,

units.la: In quinque Soles est iter.
units.tr: the journey takes five days.

units.la: Vrbs contra hostiles insultus usque adeo munita, firmisque mœnibus est selta, ut Valli invictique Propugnaculi vicem contra Africam obtineat: ideoque ab Rege Armamentarium totius fere Hispaniæ hic locatum; omni Armorum, Machinarum bellicarum, Commeatusque genere instructissimum; ex quo maximis impensarum sumtibus perpetuum Præsidium in suis Africæ opidis sustentat atque communit. A Phœnicibus conditam nonnulli adserunt, anno ante Christum natum 1occcxxxx. Fictilia Vasa conficiuntur hic nitidissima. Cives Malacitani in antiquo Marmore, quod Romæ. Flumen ejusdem cum Urbe nominis, memorat Avienus, quem dixi:
units.tr: The city is so well fortified against hostile attacks, and so strongly walled, that it serves as a rampart and an unconquerable bulwark against Africa. For this reason the king has placed here an arsenal for almost the whole of Spain, very well stocked with every kind of weapon, siege engine and provision. From it he maintains and secures a permanent garrison in his towns in Africa at very great expense. Some maintain that it was founded by the Phoenicians in the year 1230 before the birth of Christ. Very fine earthenware vessels are made here. The citizens are called Malacitani, as is shown on an ancient marble in Rome. The river of the same name as the city is mentioned by Avienus, whom I have quoted:

units.la: At propter hos mox est Iugum Barbetium;
units.tr: But near these is the Barbetian ridge,

units.la: Malacaque flumen Urbe cum cognomine.
units.tr: and the river Malaca, with the city of the same name.

units.la: De Malaca etiam auctor Commentarij belli Alexandrini: Ipse omnibus rebus celeriter correptis, Malacam contendit. Ab hac Urbe Gados usque iter describit Antoninus, cxlv millium passuum, per hæc opida, Sivel (σὺν Ptolemæo, Molena vulgo putatur) Cilnianam, Barbarianam, Calpe-Carteiam, Portum Album, Mellariam (Beiar de Melena, vel Beiar de la miel, alijs Tariffa) Belonem Claudiam (Tariffa, quibusdam Brabate) Baesippomem, Mergablum, Ad Herculem & Gades. Quinto hinc lapide, versus Solis ortum, distat Velis Malaga, haud procul Mari Mediterraneo: opidum amœnissimis cinctum campis, fructiferisque Collibus, in quibus Arx ab Afris olim condita conspicitur. Ibi Vuæ passæ, tam quæ vulgo Passa de Lexia quam quæ cæruleo colore Passa de Sol, colliguntur. Aspera Montium iuga tam hic sunt præcelsa, ut ex eorum cacuminibus Herculeum non solum Fretum, verum etiam Barbariæ (ut vulgo vocatur) littora, ac Montes, atque adeo Africæ Opida Ceuta & Tingis, in faucibus Freti sita, commodissime conspici queant. Incredibilem Pagorum frequentiam soli fere Mauri, ex postrema profligatione superstites, inhabitant: Christianam Fidem professi peculiari suo, ex antiqua consuetudine, utuntur vestitu & Lingua: Montes Vitibus Arboribusque fructiferis conserunt, vicinaque loca tam decenter suo labore exornant, ut spectatu valde sit jucundum, uberrimosque annuo proventu fructus colligant; quos hujus opidi Incolis divendunt; à quibus deinde Mercatores exteri coemtos, navibusque onerarijs impositos in varias totius Vniversi partes exportant. Ad maris littus amplissima est Domus, La Torre de Velis, appellata; in qua varia sunt loca peropportune dispolita, in quæ omnia, quæ vicinū Territorium suppeditat, Bona comportata, antea, quam evehantur, Vectigal Regi persoluunt. Almeria etiam Littori est adpolita; Ἀβδαγα Ptolemæo, & Ἀυδηγα Straboni; μίγας etiam λιμὴν Ptolemæo, Magnus Portus, ut vult Coquus: Condita putatur ab Thracibus, nomenque adepta ab Abdera Thracum Urbe, quam Diomedis Soror Abdera condidisse scribitur, conditæque ab se nomen imposuisse. Alhama, Ἀ(ψ)τιγις Ptolemæo, Artigi Plinio, qui eos Iulienses cognominat; Opidum septem distans Granata milliaribus; ab Mauris, ut Historiæ loquuntur, conditum, situ amœnissimo;
units.tr: The author of the Commentary on the Alexandrian War also mentions Malaca: He himself, having quickly gathered everything, made for Malaca. Antoninus describes the road from this city to Gades, 145 miles long, through these towns: Sivel (Ptolemy's Molena, as it is commonly thought), Cilniana, Barbariana, Calpe-Carteia, Portus Albus, Mellaria (Beiar de Melena, or Beiar de la miel; others say Tarifa), Belo Claudia (Tarifa; by some, Vejer), Baesippo, Mergablum, Ad Herculem and Gades. Five miles from here, towards the rising sun and not far from the Mediterranean Sea, lies Velis Malaga, a town surrounded by very pleasant plains and fruitful hills, on which can be seen a citadel built long ago by the Africans. There are gathered raisins, both those commonly called Passa de Lexia and the blue-coloured ones called Passa de Sol. The rough ridges of the mountains here are so high that from their peaks one can conveniently see not only the Strait of Hercules but also the coasts of Barbary (as it is commonly called), the mountains, and even the African towns of Ceuta and Tangier, which lie at the mouth of the strait. The incredibly numerous villages are inhabited almost only by Moors who survived the last defeat. Professing the Christian faith, they keep by ancient custom their own dress and language. They plant the mountains with vines and fruit trees and adorn the neighbouring places with their labour so attractively that it is a delight to behold; they gather very rich fruit each year, which they sell to the inhabitants of this town. From them the foreign merchants buy it and, loading it onto cargo ships, export it to various parts of the whole world. On the seashore is a very large house called La Torre de Velis, in which various rooms are conveniently arranged. Into these are brought all the goods that the neighbouring territory supplies, and before they are shipped out they pay duty to the king. Almeria also lies on the coast: Abdaga [Ἀβδαγα] in Ptolemy, Audega [Ἀυδηγα] in Strabo, and the Great Harbour [μίγας λιμὴν] in Ptolemy, as Cuypers holds. It is thought to have been founded by the Thracians and to have taken its name from Abdera, the city of the Thracians, which, as is written, was founded by Diomedes' sister Abdera, who gave it her own name. Alhama, Aptigis [Ἀ(ψ)τιγις] in Ptolemy, Artigi in Pliny, who surnames its people Iulienses, is a town seven miles from Granada, founded by the Moors, as the histories relate, in a most pleasant setting;

units.la: nisimo: nitlimo: ab Natura varijs locupletatum doribus, & ob voluptatem ubertatemque Genio Gratijsque dicatum. Quidquid hic ab Deo Opt. Max. largissime conlocatum superant infinitis modis uberrimi Thermarum Fontes ; quibus meritissimo jure princeps inter Hispaniæ miracula locus. Aquæ illis tam illimes, limpidæ & perspicuæ, ut vel exiguus in fundo Numulus perfacile agnosci queat. Moderati sunt Caloris, quem nudum hominis corpus fert commodissime: Grati Saporis, quæque potæ varijs corporum Morbis curandis efficacissimæ. Multis inde votis expetuntur; adeunturque undique, Martio præcipue Septembrique Mensibus, quibus maxime salutares. Juxta est Domus ampla Hospites ex varijs Hispaniæ locis accurrentes suspiciens; non Equis solum ipsorum & jumentis omnem commoditatem; sed ipsis etiam Cubicula, Lectos, quidquid denique necessarium liberaliter præstans. Prope Opidum præcipites arduorum Montium rupes visuntur; inque earum una Crucis conspicitur Signum, quod quænam Mortalium Ars, quæque Industria in Dorso Montis, quum non modo ascensu difficile, sed plane inaccéssum sit ejus fastigium, collocarit, prorsus ignoratur. Ex his Montibus Rivulus gravi murmure delabitur, qui ex nivalis haud procul Granata Montibus tanto frigore promanat, ut nomen inde fuerit sortitus. Dicitur enim El Riofrio, Rivulus frigidus. Thermarum muros adluit; caldam Thermarum aquam absorbtam secum abripiens. Quæ Antequera vulgo Anticaria est Antonino; Singilia dicitur Plinio, cui cognominis ibidem est Fluvius Singulis. Opidum ab Mauris constructum, situ montoso & inæquali. Castrum habet in Montis Vertice amplum & bene munitum, cui nomen Alcassalia, peramœna Regum Granatensium, plurimum olim, sedes. Portæ omnes sunt ferreæ. Seruantur ibi hodieque multa bellica Maurorum Instrumenta, Loricæ, Spicula, Gladij, Scuta ex pelle ferroque adsabre confecta, squamosa item & ossea Instrumenta, quibus anteriorem sinistri brachij partem communiunt, nedum Sagittas sæpius in hostem conrorquent, recurrentes Arcuum nervi Manicarum plicis impediantur. Videntur & oblongæ Maurorum hastæ: Sagittæ, hamato, quod acutum valde, ferro præmunitæ; Arcus ex nobilissimo confecti Ligno, quod ob subtilitatem humoris extensum mira facilitate in priorem redit situm. Arci adhabitant, Loci amœnitate capti Aerisque puritate adductí. Nobiles: Planiciem Agricolæ incolunt, magnum facientes quæstum partim ex Agris, partim ex opera Salaria. Nam in vicinis opido Montibus plurima sunt Loca, Salinis naturæ beneficio oportuna: ubi passim incredibili abundantia candidi Salis grumos est conspicere, quod non Ignis adminiculo, sed Solis ardore concoquitur. Æstivis enim Mensibus tam fontana, quam pluvialis Aqua in his montibus conleċta vehementi Solis ardore concrescit, ac tandem excoquitur: unde tantam Salis copiam Adcolæ conficiunt; ut magnam partem huic Hispaniæ tractui sufficiat. Fiunt hic illa suspiciendæ Capacitatis Vasa fictilia, quæ Ventriosa quis non inepte dixerit, ad condenda & adservanda Cibaria, & cujuscunque generis Liquores, Aquam, Vinum, Oleum, Cappares, Olivas, & id genus alia: Vulgus Tenaiæ nuncupat. Iova situs tam amœnus est, tamque elegans, ut universæ Granatæ audiat Hortus, tanta exultus diligentia, ut in eum Ops, Magna Rerum omnium Mater, plenum efficacium Herbarum Fructuumque optimorum cornu larga manu ecfudisse videatur. Fervent etiam hoc loco Venationes, eo quod ob miram Pabuli abundantiam passim Leporum & Cuniculorum greges in patentibus Campis, Pascuis, atque Nemoribus Venantium oculis obversentur: quibus insidiæ struuntur vel Canum sagacitate, vel solertia Mustellarum, quas in specus & occultiores Terræ recessus immittunt ad Cuniculos è Cubilibus suis exturbandos, exturbatosque capiundos. Septenilium, vulgo Settenil Granatæ opidum in Monte, positione prorsus mirabili: pleraque Incolarum Damicilia habens subterranea, in cavernosis excisa rupibus. Solum quale in montibus frequens, asperum & lapidosum, Aratri impatiens; sed pecoris, varij generis, dives. Quæ haud procul Malaca, vulgo Ronda nominatur, Plinio Arunda, Ptolemæo Ἀρούνδα: quæ Guadix nunc, Ἀxxi Ptolemeo est, Accitana Colonia Plinio: quæ Veria, Ptolemæo Βάρια dicitur, Barea Plinio: quæ Ὀsia, καλίχνδα Ptolemæo appellatur: quæ denique Almunecar hodie, Ælenola creditur Plinio, Ammiano, & Antonino vocata, μαίνοβα in Bastulorum regione ad Ibericum mare Ptolemæo; μαίνοβα Straboni: corrigendus videtur Stephanus, apud quem legitur, Μαινοβεωγα. Μαινόβωρα πόλις μαγνῆτῶν. Menoba etiam Fluvi meminit Plinius hoc tractu, quem navigabilem esse perhibet.
units.tr: enriched by nature with various gifts, and dedicated to pleasure and fertility, to the genius and the Graces. Whatever the best and greatest God has most lavishly placed here, the very abundant springs of the hot baths surpass in countless ways; for this reason the place rightly holds first place among the wonders of Spain. Their waters are so clear, limpid and transparent that even a small coin lying at the bottom can easily be recognised. They are of moderate heat, which the bare human body bears most comfortably; they have a pleasant taste, and when drunk they are very effective in curing various bodily diseases. For this reason they are sought after by many who make vows, and people come from everywhere, especially in the months of March and September, when they are most healthful. Nearby is a large house that welcomes guests arriving from various parts of Spain, providing generously not only every convenience for their horses and beasts of burden, but also rooms and beds for the guests themselves, and in short whatever is necessary. Near the town are seen steep cliffs of high mountains; on one of them a sign of the cross is visible. What human art or industry set it on the back of the mountain, whose summit is not only hard to climb but quite inaccessible, is entirely unknown. From these mountains a stream flows down with a loud murmur; it rises from the snowy mountains not far from Granada with such cold that it has taken its name from this. It is called El Riofrio, the cold river. It washes the walls of the baths, carrying away with it the warm water of the baths that it has absorbed. The town commonly called Antequera is Anticaria in Antoninus; Pliny calls it Singilia, and there is a river of the same name, Singulis, there. It is a town built by the Moors, on a hilly and uneven site. It has on the top of the mountain a large and well-fortified citadel called Alcassalia, a very pleasant residence which in former times was the chief seat of the kings of Granada. All its gates are of iron. There are still preserved there many Moorish weapons of war: breastplates, javelins, swords, and shields made of hide and iron, carefully crafted; likewise scaly and bony pieces of armour with which they protect the front part of the left arm, so that they can often shoot arrows at the enemy without being hindered by the folds of their sleeves when the bowstrings spring back. There are also to be seen long Moorish spears, and arrows armed with a barbed iron point, very sharp; and bows made of most noble wood, which, because of its fine elasticity, returns to its former shape with wonderful ease when bent. The nobles live in the citadel, captivated by the pleasantness of the place and drawn by the purity of the air. The farmers inhabit the plain, making a large profit partly from the fields and partly from the working of salt. For in the mountains near the town there are many places suited by nature's kindness to salt-works, where everywhere one can see clumps of white salt in incredible abundance, which is refined not by the aid of fire but by the heat of the sun. For in the summer months, the water both from springs and from rain collected in these mountains thickens under the strong heat of the sun and is finally dried out; from this the inhabitants make such a quantity of salt that it suffices for a large part of this region of Spain. Here are made those earthenware vessels of wonderful capacity, which one might not inappropriately call Ventriosa (big-bellied), for storing and keeping foodstuffs and liquids of every kind: water, wine, oil, capers, olives and other such things. The common people call them Tenaiæ. Iova has so pleasant and so elegant a site that the whole of Granada calls it Hortus, the garden, so adorned with care that Ops, the great Mother of all things, seems to have poured out from her horn, with a lavish hand, a full supply of effective herbs and the finest fruits. Hunting also flourishes here, because, owing to the wonderful abundance of pasture, flocks of hares and rabbits are everywhere in sight of the hunters in the open plains, pastures and groves. Snares are set for them, either by the keenness of dogs or by the cleverness of ferrets, which they send into burrows and more hidden recesses of the earth to drive the rabbits out of their holes and, once driven out, catch them. Septenilium, commonly called Settenil, is a town of Granada on a mountain of quite remarkable position. Most of its inhabitants have their dwellings underground, cut into hollow rocks. The soil, like most on the mountains, is rough and stony and unfit for the plough, but rich in pasture for animals of various kinds. The town near Malaga, commonly called Ronda, is Arunda in Pliny and Arunda [Ἀρούνδα] in Ptolemy. The town now called Guadix is Acci [Ἀxxi] in Ptolemy and the colony of Accia in Pliny. The town called Veria is Baria [Βάρια] in Ptolemy and Barea in Pliny. The town called Osca [Ὀσια] in Ptolemy and Calicinda [καλίχνδα]. Finally, what is today Almunecar is believed to be Ælenola of Pliny, Ammianus and Antoninus; in Ptolemy, in the region of the Bastuli on the Iberian sea, it is Maenoba [μαίνοβα]; in Strabo it is Maenoba [μαίνοβα]. Stephanus seems to need correction, in whom is read Maenobe-ga [Μαινοβεωγα] and Maenobora, a city of the Magnetes [Μαινόβωρα πόλις μαγνῆτῶν]. Pliny also mentions the river Menoba in this district, which he says is navigable.

units.la: De Ortu & Initio Regni Regumque Granatæ legendi cum alij, tum Rodericus Sanctius Parte 1. de Rebus Hispan.cap.xv.Bellum autem Granatense,Regniqúe expugnationem delinearunt Petrus Sanctèramus Siculus Civis Messanus,Ferninandus Pulgarius Hispanicè, cujus Historiam in Latinum convertit sermonem Antonius Nebrissensis, qui & ipse lib.1.Dec.11;Petrus Martyr Protonotarius; Gonsalus Ajora Cordubensis, Regius Historicus, Alphonsus Palentinus, Tristanus Silvius, Karolus Verardus, L. Marineus Siculus de Rebus Hispaniæ libro xx. & alij.
units.tr: On the origin and beginning of the kingdom of Granada and its kings, others have written, and Rodericus Sanctius in Part 1 of his De Rebus Hispaniae, chapter 15. The war of Granada and the conquest of the kingdom have been described by Petrus Sanctermus, a Sicilian and citizen of Messina; Ferdinandus Pulgarius in Spanish, whose history Antonius Nebrissensis turned into Latin, and who himself wrote in book 1 of his Decades; Petrus Martyr, protonotary; Gonsalus Ajora of Cordoba, royal historian; Alphonsus Palentinus; Tristanus Silvius; Karolus Verardus; L. Marineus Siculus, in book 20 of his De Rebus Hispaniae; and others.

units.la: CAP. XXIV.
units.tr: Chapter XXIV.

units.la: Andaluzia.
units.tr: Andalusia.

units.la: ANDALVZIA ad Ortum habet Granatam, ad Septentrionem Castellam Novam, ad Occasum Pacensi Silvensique Dioecesibus & Ana Flumine terminatur, ad Meridiem Atlanticum spectat Mare. Nomen adepta dictaque quondam Vandalia putatur ab Vandalis, Germaniæ populis, quos olim ad hæc usque Loca devenisse, multi memoriæ produnt, & nos alibi diximus: Videndi præter alios Rodericus Sanctius parte 1. Hispaniæ cap. vii, Antonius Nebrissensis in Decadum Prolegomenis, Ioannes Vasæus Hispaniæ Chronico cap.viii. Sic igitur, ut nonnulli nomen penitus rimatis placet, Andaluzia appellatur quasi Wendenhrys, Vandalorum domus. Marius Aretius Andaluziam vocatam auguratur, quasi ante Lusitaniam, mutatis nonnihil litteris. Regio est, quæ insigni rerum omnium fertilitate luxuriat, cunctas universi Terrarum Orbis Provincias eo nomine facile superans.
units.tr: ANDALUSIA has Granada to the east, New Castile to the north, and is bounded to the west by the dioceses of Badajoz and Silves and the river Ana (Guadiana). To the south it faces the Atlantic Sea. It was once called Vandalia, and it is thought to have taken that name from the Vandals, a German people who, many writers record, once reached these parts, as we have said elsewhere. On this, see besides others Rodericus Sanctius, Part 1 of his History of Spain, ch. vii; Antonius Nebrissensis in the Prolegomena to his Decades; and Johannes Vasaeus in his Chronicle of Spain, ch. viii. Thus, as some who have searched the name thoroughly prefer, it is called Andaluzia, as if it were Wendenhrys, "the house of the Vandals." Marius Aretius conjectures that it was called Andaluzia, as if "before Lusitania," with the letters changed somewhat. It is a region that flourishes with a remarkable fertility of all things, easily surpassing on this account all the provinces of the whole world.

units.la: Tenuisse quondam hæc Loca existimantur Cunei, Κυνῆτοι Appiano in Ibericis; quorum urbs eidem Κυνηςοριςὶς; Straboni lib. iii Κονιτοςὶς; ubi hodie Chucena ad Fluvium, cui nomen Guadiamar; alijs ubi Niebla inter fluvios Luxiam & Vetum, quorum hic Rio Tinto vel Rio d'Azeche hodie, olim etiam Iberus; ille Rio Odiel. Celti, Κέλτοι Straboni ad Bætim Fluvium. Herodotus eos locat extra Cippos Herculis; Cynesis, de quibus mox, finitimos. Corrupti sunt Celti, opidoque misti apud Plinium lib. iii: sic enim legitur: Opida Hispalensis Conventus Celtiavana, Caniama, Acua Lipa cognomine Illa Italica; Emendandum Celti, Ava. Τεγδάλοι simpliciter (nam tria erant illorum genera) sic dicti; à quibus, Augusto Imperante, Ταρτήσσις habitabatur, Strabone tèste; cui ea circa ostium Bætis Fluminis delineatur: Calpe contiguam facit idem Strabo ex Eratosthene; & Erythiam Insulam Fortunatam etiam Tartessidem vocatam scribit. Eo referendum Silij illud libro xvi belli Pœnici; Nam repeto Herculeas Erythræa ad littora Gades.
units.tr: It is thought that the Cunei once held these places: Cunetes [Κυνῆτοι] in Appian's Iberica; their city Cynetoriscis [Κυνηςοριςὶς] in Strabo, book iii; Conitosis [Κονιτοςὶς] there too. Today this is Chucena, on the river called Guadiamar. Others place it where Niebla is, between the rivers Luxia and Vetus, of which the former is today the Rio Tinto or Rio d'Azeche, and formerly also the Iberus, and the latter is the Rio Odiel. The Celti [Κέλτοι] in Strabo are by the river Baetis. Herodotus places them beyond the Pillars of Hercules, and the Cynesii, of whom more shortly, as their neighbours. The name Celti is corrupted and mixed up with towns in Pliny, book iii. For thus it is read: "The towns of the Hispalensis conventus: Celtiavana, Caniama, Acua Lipa, surnamed Illa Italica." Celti should be emended to Ava. The Tartesii [Τεγδάλοι], simply so called (for there were three kinds of them), are the people from whom Tartessus was inhabited under the emperor Augustus, according to Strabo's testimony. Tartessus is placed by him near the mouth of the river Baetis. Strabo, following Eratosthenes, makes Calpe adjacent to it, and he writes that Erythia, the Fortunate Island, was also called Tartessis. To this belongs that line of Silius in book xvi of the Punic War: "For I seek again the Erythraean shores of Hercules, Gades."

units.la: Tartessiacum Tractum Campos Arganthonios vocari solitos notat Iosephus Scaliger in Ausonium, ab Arganthonio Regulo, quem ibi regnasse Veterum historiæ testantur. Hodie los Campos de Tarif. In hac Hispaniæ parte ad Bætim Fluvium fuit Locus, qui Ianus Augustus dicebatur; unde ad Oceanum usque Viam stravit Tiberius Imperator. Loquitur Inscriptio, quæ Cordubæ:
units.tr: Joseph Scaliger, in his notes on Ausonius, observes that the Tartessian district was commonly called the Arganthonian Fields, after King Arganthonius, whom the histories of the ancients attest reigned there. Today it is called los Campos de Tarif. In this part of Spain, by the river Baetis, there was a place called Janus Augustus; from there Emperor Tiberius built a road all the way to the Ocean. The inscription at Cordoba speaks:

units.la: TI. CÆSAR. DIVI. AVGVSTI. F DIVI. IVLI. NEPOS. AVGVSTVS PONTYF. MAX. VI. COS V. IMP. TRIB. POTEST. XXXVII AB. IANO. AVGVSTO. QVI. EST AD. BÆTEM. VSQVE. AD OCEANVM LXIII
units.tr: Tiberius Caesar, son of the divine Augustus, grandson of the divine Julius, Augustus, Pontifex Maximus, consul for the sixth time, hailed imperator for the fifth time, holding tribunician power for the thirty-seventh time: from Janus Augustus, which is by the Baetis, as far as the Ocean, 63 [miles].

units.la: Metropolis est, quæ Hispalis Plinio; Ἱσπαλις, Ptolemæo; Ἰσπαλον Philostrato; Hispal κατ' ἀποκοπὴν Silio Italico lib. iii Belli Pœnici:
units.tr: This is the metropolis, which Pliny calls Hispalis; Ptolemy calls it Hispalis [Ἱσπαλις]; Philostratus, Hispalon [Ἰσπαλον]; and Silius Italicus, in book iii of the Punic War, Hispal, by shortening:

units.la: Et celebre Oceano atque alternis æstibus Hispal.
units.tr: "And Hispal, famous for the Ocean and its alternating tides."

units.la: Spalis (unde Spalense Concilium) Graciano in Decretis. Hodie Sevilla; quod nomen antiquius, quam putatur; quum hoc loco Tartesiæ Urbs Ἱσπαλις ponatur Stephano; pro qua hodie Sivilla, quemadmodum Salmantica pro Ἀλμάντικα Polybij, vel Ἑλμαντικὴ Stephano; pro Exitania, Sexitania & similibus. Hispalis etiam apud Plinium legitur Colonia Romulensis. Hispalis Etymon sic indicat Arias Montanus, scribens ad Abrahamum Ortelium: Hispalis, inquit, nomen Phœnicum est ex Spila vel Spala deflexum, quod planitiem sive viventem regionem significat, qualis ejus Territorium conspicitur. A Græcis vero addita est Adspiratio. Arabes autem, quod P litteram non habent, ob idque pronunciare nequeunt, fere ad nativam vocem referentes, Sbilla dixerunt: deinde Christianorum vulgus Sevilla, ut nunc, appellavit. Audiamus & Ælium Antonium Nebrissensem in Prolegomenis, qui, quum dixisset hanc urbem Romulam dictam, Hæc à Pœnis, addit, deinde Ispilia, & à barbaris postea inversis litteris prioribus, & P in B mutata, Sibilia dicta, nunc Sevilla nominatur. Alij, inter quos Franciscus Tarapha, ad Hispalim, Herculis Libyci filium, nomen conditionemque referunt. Quidam ab Hispano Herculis Nepote exstructam & denominatam censent. Ridere, ut in multis, Isidorum; qui lib. Originum xv. cap. i. quum ab Iulio Cæsare conditam, exque ipsius & Romæ Urbis vocabulo Iuliam Romulam notasset appellatam, à Palis suffixis in loco palustri sic dictam memorat. Io. Gerundensis Episcopus Paralipom. Hispan. lib. xii, non improbans Isidori Etymon adscribit, videri vocatam Hispalim à Palude, quæ maxima Urbem circumdat. Urbs ad Bætim Situ amœnissimo excellens, Ambitu magna, Forma fere rotunda, Visu pulcra, Templis celebris. Ædium pulcherrimarum frequentia nitidissime culta, Plateis Vicisque insignis, Hortis Fontibusque Hilaris, Mœnibus Turribusque valida, Propugnaculis tuta, Campis jucunda, Frugibus abundans, Oliveris felix, Civibus plena, Mercatorum commerciis dives, Mechanicis Artibus nobilis, Academia (in qua, præter Avicennam & alios, floruit Leander, qui sua industria Hermigildum & Richardum Gothorum Reges ab Arriana Hæresi ad Religionem Catholicam adduxit) & Studijs liberalibus inlustris, Opulentia sua plerisque Hispaniæ Civitatibus anteponenda: Ostio Oceani (cuius vere perhibetur Regina) navigabili Fluvio, ligneo Ponte, quem parva Navigia catenis compactum sustinent, (vulgo Puente de Triana) delectabilis. Carmen, quod in Vulgatis Ausonij Exemplaribus inter Urbium Encomia Emeritæ adscribitur, Codices cum primitus editi, tum calamo exarati Hispali tribuunt; verbis hoc modo conceptis:
units.tr: Spalis (whence the Council of Seville, Spalense Concilium) in Gratian's Decretum. Today it is Sevilla. This name is older than is thought, since Stephanus places the city Hispalis [Ἱσπαλις] in Tartessis, and for it today is Sivilla, just as Salmantica is used for Almantica [Ἀλμάντικα] in Polybius, or Elmantike [Ἑλμαντικὴ] in Stephanus, and for Exitania, Sexitania and similar forms. Hispalis is also read in Pliny as the Colonia Romulensis. Arias Montanus gives the etymology of Hispalis in a letter to Abraham Ortelius: "Hispalis," he says, "is a Phoenician name, derived from Spila or Spala, which means a plain or a fertile region, such as its territory appears to be. But the Greeks added an aspirate. The Arabs, however, since they have no letter P and so cannot pronounce it, reproducing the native word as closely as they could, said Sbilla; then the common people of the Christians called it Sevilla, as it is now." Let us also hear Aelius Antonius Nebrissensis in his Prolegomena, who, after saying that this city was called Romula, adds: "This name is from the Phoenicians; then Ispilia, and afterwards, by the barbarians, with the earlier letters reversed and P changed to B, it was called Sibilia, and now it is named Sevilla." Others, among whom is Franciscus Tarapha, derive the name and origin of Hispalis from Hispal, son of Libyan Hercules. Some think it was built and named by Hispanus, a grandson of Hercules. Isidore is laughable here, as in many things. In book xv, chapter i, of his Origines, although he noted that it was founded by Julius Caesar and called Julia Romula from his own name and that of the city of Rome, he records that it was so called from the stakes (palis) driven in at a marshy spot. John, bishop of Gerona, in book xii of his Paralipomena of Spanish history, does not reject Isidore's etymology, but ascribes the name Hispalis to the marsh (palus) which surrounds the city on a large scale. The city, set on the Baetis in a most pleasant situation, is large in circuit, roughly round in shape, fine to look upon, and famous for its churches. It is richly adorned by the number of very handsome buildings, notable for its squares and streets, cheerful with gardens and fountains, strong with walls and towers, safe with bulwarks, pleasant with its fields, abundant in crops, blessed with olives, full of citizens, rich in the trade of merchants, distinguished by its skilled crafts, illustrious for its academy (in which, besides Avicenna and others, flourished Leander, who by his diligence brought the Gothic kings Hermenegild and Reccared from the Arian heresy to the Catholic religion) and for its liberal studies. Its wealth ranks it above most of the cities of Spain. It is pleasing for its navigable river, which flows to the mouth of the Ocean (of which it is rightly said to be the queen), and for its wooden bridge, which small boats hold up by chains fastened together (commonly called the Puente de Triana). The poem which in the common editions of Ausonius is ascribed among the Encomia of Emerita, both the manuscripts first printed and those written by hand, attribute to Hispalis, with these words so composed:

units.la: HISPALIS:
units.tr: HISPALIS:

units.la: Iure mihi post has memorabere, nomen Iberum, Hispal, aequoreus quam præterlabitur amnis: Submittit cui tota suos Hispania fasces: Corduba non, non arce potens tibi Tarraco certant, Quaque sinu pelagi jactat se Bracara dives. Et sane Hispali magis, quam Emeritae conveniunt Ausoniana illa. Probat, praeter alia, Argumentum illud validissimum, quod Hispal Iberum Hispanumque sit nomen; Emerita autem Latinum. Caetera vide apud Eliam Vinetum doctissimum Ausonij Interpretem. Portas habet Hispalis xii, quibus haec vulgo nomina, Puenta del Arcenal, ii de Triana, iii de Golis, iv de S. Iuan, v de la Almenilla, vi de Macarena, vii de Cordoba, viii del Sol, ix del Osurio, x de Carmona, xi de la Carne, xii de Geretz. Suburbia primae Classis illa, quae vulgo El Tablado & Triano: hoc a tribus circiter Civium millibus habitari dicitur; in quo ad Pontis Caput Palatium superbit, Inquisitioni (unde La S. Inquisitione) sacrum: in illo infinita nuper, praecipue anno cIↄ Iↄ LXV sunt eruta, hodieque eruuntur, ex terra venerandae Antiquitatis Monimenta, Tymbi, lapideae ac vitreae Lampades, Urnae, Numismata, idque genus alia. Inter Templa sane primas tenet illud, quod D. Mariae consecratum; quo nullum habet Christianus Orbis excellentius, si quis operis amplitudinem spectet & majestatem, Turrimque summae altitudinis, editissimo operosissimoque fastigio admirabilem: unde in universam Urbem CampOsque latissime laetissimeque circumjacentes jucundissimus est prospectus. Cochleam intus habet, per quam Eques commode adscendere potest. Qua fere summa est, ambitur ab hac Inscriptione, TVRRIS FORTISSIMA NOMEN DOMINI, PROVERB. XVIII. In supremo Apice Fidei est Statua aerea magnitudine hominem referens, versatilis Ventorum Index. Nihil hic dicam de Arcis regiae ornamentis vere regijs; de sumtuosis Ducum, Comitum, illustriumque Procerum Palatijs, deque alijs cum publicis, tum privatis Aedificijs. In vicino Urbi Agro Domus amplissima visitur, El Matadero nuncupata; in qua, optima Politiae ratione, mactantur Oves, Boves, aliaque Animantia; quorum Carnes Hispali Civibus mox divenduntur. In patentissimo vero Campo juxta hanc Domum jucundissimum spectaculum praebet Taurorum, quos robustissimos ibi saginant, Capitis Pectorisque robore praestantes. In hos, spectaculum edituri, Molossos Magnosque exstimulant Canes, quibus satis alioquin per se feroces, truces ac torvos, prius quam eos mactent, efferate solent. Illi in Canes magna rabie insilientes ignem naribus spirant, terram pedibus feriunt, in altum spargunt arenam, frontes adversarijs obserunt, tantoque adoriuntur impetu; ut eos Cornibus exceptos in aerem alte proijciant, inque cornuum cuspides rursum delabentes exspectent. Est & ad Hispalim Aquae ductus incredibilibus impensis opere fornicato ab Mauris exstructus; qui excavato viae dimidiati Miliaris spatio jucundam Incolis Aquationem praebet, unde quamplurimi Fontes ad Civium necessitates diriuantur. Mirabile dictu quanto itinere, sex nimirum milliarium, per caecos terrae meatus a Carmona opido scaturientes Fontes in hunc Aquaeductum deducantur: unde Los Cannos de Carmona Hispani nuncupant. Haud procul Hispali vasta jacent convulsae Urbis atque Theatri rudera: Locus Hispanis Sevilla la Vieja audit. Putant Viri Magni eam hic fuisse Urbem, quae Italica Ptolemaeo, Antonino, alijs. Nummum laudat Abrahamus Ortelius Tiberij Caesaris in cujus aversa parte haec leguntur: DIVI. AVG. MVNIC. ITALIC. PERM. Onuphrius inter Colonias Romanas numerat ex Agellij lib. xvi, cap. xiii. apud quem D. Hadrianus (qui, ut & Traianus, hinc ortus) in oratione, quam de Italicensibus in Senatu habuit, peritissime disseruit; mirarique se ostendit, quod & ipsi Italicenses, & quaedam item alia Municipia antiqua, in quibus Vticenses numerat, quum suis moribus legibusque uti possent, in Ius Colonarum mutari gestiverint. Ejus Ager Italicesia dicitur Stephano. In vetusto Exemplari Historiae Lucae, Tydensis Episcopi, in Limitatione, quae circumfertur, Dioecesium Hispaniarum Provinciarum haec habentur: Inveni in Chronicis, quod Italica e[st] Hispalis Antiqua, unde populata fuit haec Hispalis, quae nunc est. Falsum. Hispalis enim cum Italica facile antiquitatis nomine certat. Pagus sane, qui Vetus Hispalis cognominatur, non immerito censetur Italica, quum & in limitatione Agrorum ab Ferdinando Rege, qui eam Mauris extorsit cum aliis infinitis, facta, nomen Talca retineat. Temere credidit Petrus Crinitus, ab hac Italica genus cognomenque duxisse Silium Italicum. Dici enim debuisset Italicensis, uti docet Surita. Ierenna famosus est prope Hispalim locus ob mirabilem Saxorum in circuitu dispositionem tanta copia in terram defixorum, quasi caelesti pluvia huc essent delapsa. Terraemotu illud putatur factum; quo multa aedificia Hispali, Cordubae, inque vicinis locis frequenter corruerunt. Emporium porro est Hispalis omnium Europae ropæ Vrbium florentissimum, & amplissimum Mercium Indicarum, quæ ex Occidente advehuntur, Receptaculum: quoque ad illud Negociationis culmen ascendit, ut Privilegium fuerit consequutum, ne quæ Naves in Indiam, quod Aprili mense fieri solitum, solvant, nisi quæ mercibus in hujus Vrbis Portu oneratæ,quæque Machinis & Tormentis bellicis, Commeatu, Militeque,alijsque ad tantam navigationem necessarijs, serenissimi Hispaniarum Regis nomine, ibidem instructæ: quæ ex India Auro, Argento, preciosissimisque Thesauris, quos anteacta Secula non noverunt, constipatæ mensibus Augusto & Septembri quotannis feliciter recurrentes necesse itidem habent ad eiusdem Vrbis litus adpellere, Mercesque ibi primo exponere. In eum finem magnifica ibi est multoque adparatu nobilis Domus, cui ab Indicis Negocijs, geri tractarique ibi solitis, nomen impositum. La Casa de la Contratacion de las Indias; Gubernatorem habens & xii Consules, quorum consilio auctoritateque omnia ibi administrantur. Hispalis Divitijs adeo pollet, ut sola Regi suo, cujus Nomini Numinique devotissima est, sesquimilionem Aureorum in singulos annos obsequij & vectigalium ergo, libentissime reddat; quantum multi Principes ex integris Regnis corradere vix possunt. Tam multa de hac Vrbe præclara commemorari possent, ut natum sit inde & tritum vetustate Proverbium, Qui no ha visto Sevilla, no ha visto Maravilla. Cum alijs felicis ingenij alumnis gaudet,tum Benedicto Aria Montano, nobilissimo & summo Theologo, plurimarum Linguarum cognitione stupendo. Testantur id Opera ab ipso edita,quæ summam ejus admirationem apud omnes excitant:inter quæ primas merito sibi vindicat Veteris ac Novi Testamenti ad Græcam, Hebraicam,Chaldaicam & Syriacam Linguam translatio: deinde Commentariorum opus in xii Prophetas, & in reliquos Majores Paraphrasis; Liber Generationis & Regenerationis Adam sive de Historia Generis humani; Opus de Optimo Imperio, sive in Librum Iosuæ Commentarium: alia præterea. Primo ab Hispali Lapide Veteris Castri sunt ruinæ incredibili magnitudine, in Colle ad Bætim fluvium: nominantur vulgo S. Iuan del Forutche. Ex Ruderibus erutisque Antiquitatum titulis patet ab Gothis quondam constructum. Hispali Nemus adjacet ad xxx milliaria expansum, Oleis consitum. Ab hac urbe tria procedunt apud Antoninum Itinera: i Cordubam, ii Italicam, iii Emeritam.
units.tr: You will rightly be remembered after these, Iberian name, Hispal, past which the sea-born river flows; to whom all Spain submits its fasces. Cordoba does not contend with you, nor Tarragona, mighty in its citadel, nor rich Braga, which boasts of itself in the bosom of the sea. And indeed that Ausonian verse suits Hispali better than Emerita. Among other things, it proves the very strong argument that Hispal is an Iberian and Spanish name, whereas Emerita is Latin. For the rest, see Elias Vinetus, the most learned interpreter of Ausonius. Hispalis has twelve gates, commonly called: (1) Puenta del Arcenal; (2) de Triana; (3) de Golis; (4) de S. Iuan; (5) de la Almenilla; (6) de Macarena; (7) de Cordoba; (8) del Sol; (9) del Osurio; (10) de Carmona; (11) de la Carne; (12) de Geretz. The suburbs of the first class are those commonly called El Tablado and Triano. This district is said to be inhabited by about three thousand citizens. At the head of the bridge stands a palace, sacred to the Inquisition (hence La S. Inquisitione), which lords it over the place. In it, recently, and especially in the year 1565, countless monuments of venerable antiquity have been dug out of the earth, and they are still being dug out today: tombs, lamps of stone and glass, urns, coins, and other things of that kind. Among the churches, the first place is certainly held by the one consecrated to the Blessed Virgin Mary. No church in the Christian world is more outstanding than it, if one considers the vastness and majesty of the building, and its tower of great height, admirable for its very lofty and elaborate roof. From it there is a most delightful view over the whole city and the fields lying widely around. Inside it has a spiral stair, by which a horseman can conveniently ascend. Near its top it is encircled by this inscription: THE NAME OF THE LORD IS A VERY STRONG TOWER, PROV. 18. On the highest point is a bronze statue of Fides, the size of a man, a weathervane that turns with the winds. I will say nothing here of the truly royal ornaments of the royal citadel, nor of the sumptuous palaces of dukes, counts and illustrious nobles, nor of the other public and private buildings. Near the city, in the fields, there is a very large house called El Matadero, in which, by an excellent system of public management, sheep, oxen and other animals are slaughtered, and their meat is soon sold to the citizens of Hispalis. In the wide field next to this house there is a most pleasing spectacle of bulls, which they fatten there, outstanding for the strength of head and chest. To set on these, for the sake of the show, they goad on Molossian and large dogs, which otherwise are fierce enough, savage and grim, and which they usually make even more wild before they slaughter them. The bulls, leaping at the dogs with great fury, breathe fire from their nostrils, strike the ground with their feet, throw up sand on high, present their foreheads to their opponents, and attack with such force that, having caught the dogs on their horns, they fling them high into the air and wait for them to fall back onto the points of their horns. There is also an aqueduct to Hispalis, built by the Moors at incredible expense with arches; over a stretch of half a mile it has been hollowed out to give the inhabitants a pleasant supply of water, from which very many fountains are channelled to meet the needs of the citizens. It is remarkable to tell over what a distance, namely six miles, the fountains that spring from the town of Carmona are led through hidden channels under the earth into this aqueduct; the Spanish call them Los Cannos de Carmona. Not far from Hispalis lie the vast ruins of a city and theatre thrown down: the place is called Sevilla la Vieja by the Spanish. Great men think that this was the city which Ptolemy, Antoninus and others call Italica. Abraham Ortelius cites a coin of Tiberius Caesar, on the reverse of which these words are read: DIVI. AVG. MVNIC. ITALIC. PERM. Onuphrius counts it among the Roman colonies, from Aulus Gellius book 16, chapter 13, where the Emperor Hadrian (who, like Trajan, came from here) argued very skilfully in a speech he delivered in the Senate about the people of Italica; and he showed his surprise that the people of Italica themselves, and certain other ancient municipalities, among which he counts the people of Utica, although they could use their own customs and laws, were eager to be changed into the law of colonies. Stephanus says that its territory is called Italicesia. In an old copy of the History of Luke, bishop of Tuy, in the limitation of the dioceses of the Spanish provinces which is circulated, the following is found: "I have found in the chronicles that Italica is old Hispalis, from which this Hispalis, which is now, was peopled." This is false. For Hispalis can easily compete with Italica in antiquity. The village which is called Vetus Hispalis is rightly regarded as Italica, since in the survey of lands made by King Ferdinand, who wrested it from the Moors along with countless others, it keeps the name Talca. Peter Crinitus rashly believed that Silius Italicus took his race and surname from this Italica. For he ought to have been called Italicensis, as Surita teaches. Ierenna is a famous place near Hispalis, because of the remarkable arrangement of stones around it, such a quantity of them fixed in the ground as if they had fallen here by a heavenly rain. It is thought to have been caused by an earthquake, by which many buildings in Hispalis, Cordoba and the neighbouring places have often collapsed. Hispalis, moreover, is the most flourishing emporium of all the cities of Europe, and the most vast receptacle of Indian wares which are brought from the West. It has risen to such a height of commerce that it obtained a privilege that no ships may set sail for the Indies, which is usually done in the month of April, unless they have been loaded with merchandise in the port of this city, and have there been equipped, in the name of the most serene King of Spain, with machines and military engines, provisions, soldiers, and other things necessary for so great a voyage; and these ships, laden with gold, silver and most precious treasures from India, which past ages did not know, returning happily each year in the months of August and September, must likewise land on the shore of this same city and first unload their goods there. To this end there is a magnificent and very splendidly appointed house there, named after the Indian business usually conducted and managed there: La Casa de la Contratacion de las Indias, having a governor and twelve consuls, by whose counsel and authority everything there is administered. Hispalis is so powerful in riches that it alone most willingly pays to its king, to whose name and majesty it is most devoted, a million and a half gold pieces each year as a tribute and tax; what many princes can scarcely gather from entire kingdoms. Many illustrious things could be recorded about this city, so that the proverb, worn by age, has arisen from it: He who has not seen Seville has not seen a marvel. It rejoices in other alumni of a happy talent, and especially in Benedictus Arias Montanus, a most noble and eminent theologian, astonishing for his knowledge of very many languages. His works, published by himself, bear witness to this and arouse the greatest admiration in everyone. Among them he rightly claims first place for his translation of the Old and New Testaments into the Greek, Hebrew, Chaldee and Syriac languages; then a work of commentaries on the twelve Prophets and a paraphrase on the remaining greater ones; the book Generation and Regeneration of Adam, or on the History of the Human Race; the work On the Best Empire, or a commentary on the Book of Joshua; and others besides. First, from Hispalis, the ruins of an old castle of incredible size stand on a hill by the river Baetis, commonly called S. Iuan del Forutche. From the ruins and inscriptions of antiquities dug out, it is clear that it was once built by the Goths. A grove of olive trees, spread over thirty miles, borders Hispalis. Three roads proceed from this city according to Antoninus: (1) to Cordoba; (2) to Italica; (3) to Emerita.

units.la: Metropoli visa, reliquarum Vrbium nonnullas indicabo, Ordinis incuriosior; sic tamen, ut quasque Metropoli suæ proximas primo loco. Offert se quinta ab Hispali leuca Palatium vel Palantia, quod vulgo Palacios, sic dictum ab Arce perantiqua quæ lateri habet adhærentem. Via situm, quæ ad S. Lucæ Fanum Fretumque Gaditanum ducit, cum ex Agricultura victitat satisque floret, tum ex frequentia Viatorum, qui hac Nebrissam contendunt, Viam depressiorem tenentes, qua Paludes & Æstuaria Fluminis (Marisma nominant Hispani) ad quinque milliaria late se extendunt, & hiemali tempore ex Bæti flumine Itinera tam sunt uliginosa, tamque invia; ut hac commodus non pateat transitus, sed altior sit tenenda via Alcantaram & Caberam versus: vice autem versa æstate tam densis obsita sepultraq; pulveribus, ut transitum fere denegent; sed, quemadmodum in mari navigantibus, opus sit Indice Magnetico, ne quis in maximo Solis ardore, via consueta aberrans siti conficiatur. Mirum enim non est invenire hic subinde Viatores Solis æstu sitiq; enecatos. Hinc iter hac facturi de Vino sibi providenr, coriaceas Lagenas Equorum Ephippijs adpendere soliti: Borateias lingua patria vocantes. Nulla enim in tanto quinq; magnorum Milliarium spatio inveniuntur Hospitia: quû totus ille tractus ob Aquarum abundantiam Hiemę,ob intolerabilem Calorem Æstate sit inhabitabilis,& proinde incultus horridusq;; ne vna quidem Arbore occurrente, sub cujus umbra refocillare se virésque debilitatas & amissas recuperare quis queat. Alcantara, Hispanis Alcantarilla, Pons est in Palentiæ quidem Paludibus, sed ad latus siniistrum, Meridiem versus à Flumine Bæti aliquantulum distans & paullo editiore loco. Structuræ magnificentia opus esse Romanum ostendit. Vtroque in latere Majoris Turris Peristylia, Bases & Capita Columnarum apparent, quæ hic ex viridi Iaspide posita erant, nunc in templum Hispalense ad Altaris ornatum translatæ. Hic Pons ad superandam Paludis difficultatem constructus, ab L. Marineo Siculo cum Segoviensi celebratur, lib. i. de Rebus Hispanicis, capite de Regni Fluminibus. Est enim altitudine opere & artificio mirabilis. Altera ex parte Mesquita est vetus Maurorum Delubrum, nunc
units.tr: Having seen the metropolis, I will point out some of the other cities, in a rather careless order; yet so that each is placed first next to its own metropolis. Five leagues from Hispalis there presents itself Palatium or Palantia, commonly Palacios, so called from a very ancient citadel which stands attached to its side. It lies on the road that leads to the shrine of St. Luke and the Strait of Cadiz; it lives both from agriculture, in which it flourishes enough, and from the number of travellers who make for Nebrissa by this road, keeping to the lower way, where marshes and estuaries of the river (which the Spanish call Marisma) extend five miles wide; and in winter the roads from the river Baetis are so muddy and so impassable that no convenient crossing is open by this way, but the higher road must be kept towards Alcantara and Cabera. In summer, on the other hand, the roads are so thickly covered with dust that they almost deny passage; but, as with sailors on the sea, a magnetic compass is needed, lest anyone, wandering from the usual way in the greatest heat of the sun, be worn out by thirst. It is not surprising, therefore, to find travellers here from time to time killed by the heat of the sun and by thirst. Hence those who are about to make the journey provide themselves with wine, being accustomed to hang leather flasks from the saddles of their horses, which they call Borateias in their native tongue. For in so great a stretch of five large miles no inns are found; and that whole tract, because of the abundance of water in winter and the intolerable heat in summer, is uninhabitable, and therefore uncultivated and rough, with not even one tree to be met with, under whose shade anyone might refresh himself and recover his weakened and lost strength. Alcantara, called Alcantarilla by the Spanish, is a bridge in the marshes of Palantia indeed, but on the left side, a little distant from the river Baetis towards the south, and on a slightly higher spot. The magnificence of its construction shows it to be a Roman work. On either side of the greater tower can be seen the peristyles, bases and capitals of columns, which were here placed of green jasper, and are now transferred to the church of Hispalis for the decoration of the altar. This bridge, built to overcome the difficulty of the marsh, is celebrated by Lucius Marineus Siculus, together with Segovia, in book 1 of his On the Spanish Affairs, in the chapter on the rivers of the kingdom. For it is wonderful in height, work and craftsmanship. On the other side is a Mosque, an old shrine of the Moors, now
