units.la: Alcantarilla. nunc pietati Christianæ dicatum semperque clausum: ex altera Venta, id est Hospitium; qualia per totam Hispaniam multa conspiciuntur. Pontem transgresslo ad primum lapidem offerunt se Cabeca: opidulum in Montium, qui in Meridiem Magnam versus se extendunt, aditu situm. Vrbem quondam fuisse magnam, Rudera loquuntur & Mœniorum Vestigia. Quia vero Cabecas idem quod Capita sonat, Opidani vulgare hoc jactare sunt soliti, sibique laudi ducere: Non se haze nadà nel Consejo del Rey sensa Cabecas: quod interpretantur, Regis consilium sine Capitibus, id est prudenti judicio, cui sedes solet esse in cerebro, numquam coire. Cabecis versus Libonotum ad tertiam Leucam succedit Opidum. quod vulgo Lebrixa; Νεβρίξα Ptolemæo. Plinius Veneriam cognominat. Situm fuit olim inter Bætis Æstuaria, hodie octo passuum millibus ab Flumine, oblimato sinisteriore Alveo (ut lib. i dixi, cap. v i) distat. Conditor perhibetur Liber Pater. Silius ab Satyris cultum canit, propter ipsum nomen. Νεβρίς enim Cervina Pellis, qua Bacchantes Sacerdotes induti Libero sacrificabant. Silij verba lib. iii sunt hæc: At Nebrissa Dionyseis consita Thyrsis, Quam Satyri coluere leves, redimitaque Sacra Nebride, & Hortano Manas nocturna Lyæo.
units.tr: Alcantarilla. Now dedicated to Christian piety and always kept closed. On the other side is a Venta, that is, an inn; many of these can be seen all over Spain. Crossing the bridge, at the first milestone you come to Cabeca, a little town situated at the entrance to the mountains that stretch out toward the Great South. That it was once a large city is declared by its ruins and the traces of its walls. Because Cabecas sounds the same as Capita (heads), the townspeople were accustomed to repeat a common saying and to take pride in it: Nothing is done in the King's council without Cabecas, which they explain as the King's council without heads, that is, prudent judgement, whose seat is usually in the brain, never comes together. Toward the south-west, a third of a league beyond Cabecas, lies the town commonly called Lebrixa, Νεβρίξα [Nebrixa] for Ptolemy. Pliny surnames it Veneria. It once stood between the estuaries of the Baetis, but today it is eight miles from the river, the left-hand channel having silted up (as I said in book 1, chapter 6). It is said to have been founded by Liber Pater. Silius sings that it was tended by Satyrs, on account of the very name: νεβρίς [nebris] being a deerskin, in which the Bacchic priests, dressed in it, sacrificed to Liber. The words of Silius in book 3 are these: But Nebrissa, planted with Dionysian thyrsi, which the nimble Satyrs tended, and the sacred Nebris wreathed, and the Manades of the night with the Lyaeus of the garden.

units.la: Opidulum est peramœnum & pulcrum cum Arce perveteri, Agro undique beatissimo cinctum. Quocumque egressus te vertas, versus Meridiem præsertim Ortumque patentes te excipiunt Campi, Prata Floribus læta, Arva frugibus onusta, Vineta & maxime frequentia Oliveta. Cive nobilitatum est Ælio Antonio, Hispaniæ totius Ornamento; qui, ex Grammatico & Rhetore Historiographus factus Regius, Rerum ab Ferdinando Hispaniarum Rege gestarum Decadas duas, magna cum laude, conscripsit. Quæ Carmona vulgo, Καρμών Straboni est; Carmo Antonino, ut & Auctori de bello Alexandrino, apud quem tamen alio loco corrupte Carbona, vel, ut in aliis legitur Codicibus, Carniona; ex quo Narbonem nonnulli temere fecerunt. Χαρμούια Ptolemæo, parum fortean emendate. Incolæ Plinio Carmonenses, Cæsarique lib. ii de bello Civili, qui longe fortissimam totius Provinciæ Civitatem ipsorum appellat. Nummum habet Surita, vetustissimæ notæ, qui in una parte Veri effigiem præfert; in aversa vero facie sculptum gerit Opidi nomen, CARMO, inter duas Spicas, fertilissimi Agri ad idem opidum Symbola. Marchena hodie, Colonia quondam, inquit Onuphrius ex antiqua basi, Marcia. Conditam putant quidam ab M. Marcello, vel L. Marcio, qui Cn. Scipione apud Vrsaonem mortuo, Romanorum ductavit in Hispania Copias. Situm est hoc Opidum in Colliculo quodam, ubique planicies spectante. Suburbium est opido majus, ad Solis Occasum, qua Hispalim (unde novem milliaribus dirimitur) est iter. In eo fons est è regione Xenodochij, magnam, quæque Civibus omnibus sufficiat, Aquarum copiam eructans. Notatu illud dignum censui, quod Ager hujus Opidi, quamvis rerum omnium, præsertim Olivarum feracissimus, omnino tamen Fontibus, Rivulis, Aquæque ductibus careat; ita ut Agricolæ sæpenumero Aquarum laborent penuria, quæ Messem facit rariorem. Est ibidem hoc ævo nostro Ducum Arcobrigæ Sedes gentilitia; qui è Pontiorum nobilissimo stemmate orti Marchionatum Gaditanum cum Hispaniarum Rege commutarunt; atque hoc suum Municipium longo temporum intervallo ita exornarunt, ut cum vicinis opidis de Civium frequentia, Aedificiorum pulcritudine, Messiumque abundantia audeat concertare. L. Marineus Siculus opinatur eam esse, quæ Cæsari Plinioque Ategua, Ατεγύα Dioni. Ategua tamen vestigia haud procul ab Alcala Regali indicat Navagierus, fontemque ibidem nomen quodammodo servare notat; vocari enim Fuente de Teivela. Ategua Morali est Tebala Vieja, qui eam quoque Teguam nuncupari addit. Tebe nunc appellari memoriæ prodit Io. Mariana, distareque ab Corduba XVI lapide. Sunt & Andaluziæ Opida Lora ad dextram Bætis ripam: Axalita vetustis lapidibus, teste Clusio; Flavium Axalitanum Ambrosio Morali ex antiqua item Inscriptione: inter Hispalim est & Cordubam. Moron olim, ut scribit Clusius, Arucci; notantibus Plinio, Antonino, & prisco Lapide. Offuna Οψώνα Appiano in Ibericis, Οψσών Straboni; Vrso Plinio, cui & Genua (forte Gemina) Vrbanorum; Vrsaon in antiquis hujus loci Inscriptionibus, uti tradit Navagierus; Vrsao Belli Hispaniensis Scriptori, qui antiquissimum esse hoc Opidum, & maximi aliquando fuisse momenti
units.tr: The little town is very pleasant and fair, with a very old citadel, and is surrounded on every side by most fertile countryside. Wherever you turn as you go out, especially toward the south and the east, fields open before you: meadows bright with flowers, arable land heavy with crops, vineyards, and above all very numerous olive groves. It is made famous by Aelius Antonius, the ornament of all Spain, who, from a grammarian and rhetorician became royal historiographer, and wrote with great praise two decades of the deeds of Ferdinand, King of Spain. The town, commonly called Carmona, is Karmon [Καρμών] to Strabo; Carmo to Antoninus, and to the author of the Alexandrine War, in whose work it is elsewhere wrongly given as Carbona, or, as some manuscripts read, Carniona, from which some have rashly made Narbo. Charmouia [Χαρμούια] to Ptolemy, perhaps not very correctly emended. Its inhabitants are Carmonenses in Pliny, and in Caesar's second book of the Civil War, who calls it by far the strongest city of the whole province. Surita has a coin of very ancient mark which on one side bears the likeness of Verus; on the reverse it bears the name of the town, CARMO, between two ears of corn, a symbol of the very fertile land around this town. Today it is Marchena, formerly a colony; according to Onuphrius, from an ancient base, it was Marcia. Some think it was founded by M. Marcellus or L. Marcius, who led the Roman forces in Spain after Gnaeus Scipio died near Ursao. This town lies on a little hill that looks out over a plain on every side. Its suburb is larger than the town, to the west, where the road to Seville runs, from which it is nine miles distant. In it, opposite the hospice, is a fountain pouring out a great abundance of water, enough for all the citizens. I thought this worth noting: the land of this town, though most productive of all things, especially olives, nevertheless lacks springs, streams and water channels altogether, so that the farmers often suffer from lack of water, which makes the harvest scarcer. In our own age the hereditary seat of the Dukes of Arcobriga is here; they, sprung from the most noble stock of the Ponces, exchanged the Marquisate of Cádiz with the King of Spain, and over a long period have so adorned this their municipality that it can rival the neighbouring towns in the number of its citizens, the beauty of its buildings and the abundance of its harvests. L. Marineus Siculus thinks this is the town which Caesar and Pliny call Ategua, and which Dio calls Ategya [Ατεγύα]. Navagerus, however, shows the remains of Ategua not far from Alcala Regal, and notes that a spring there in some way keeps the name, for it is called Fuente de Teivela. Moral says that Ategua is Tebala Vieja, and adds that it is also called Tegua. Juan de Mariana records that it is now called Tebe, and that it is sixteen miles from Cordoba. There are also towns in Andalusia: Lora on the right bank of the Baetis; Axalita, according to Clusius, from ancient stones; Flavium Axalitanum according to Ambrosio Moral from an ancient inscription likewise; it lies between Seville and Cordoba. Moron was formerly, as Clusius writes, Arucci, as Pliny, Antoninus and an old stone inscription show. Offuna [Οψώνα] in Appian's Iberian history, Opsson [Οψσών] in Strabo; Urso in Pliny, to whom also belong Genua (perhaps Gemina) Urbanorum; Ursaon in the ancient inscriptions of this place, as Navagerus relates; Ursao in the writer of the Spanish War, who says that this town is very ancient and was at one time of the greatest importance.

units.la: {a} Nebrifa vulgo Lebrixa menti his docet verbis: Cæsar Gadibus rursum ad Hispalim revertit. Fabius Maximus, qui ab eo relictus erat ad oppugnandum Præsidium, tandem Urbem cepit: ac deinde Urfaonem profisiuntur, quod Opidum magna munitione tenebatur, natura firmissimum. Aqua, præterquam in Opido ipso, nusquam reperiebatur propius millia passuum certo, nec habebant ligna vel materies ad oppugnandum. Ita necessario deducebantur nostri, ut à Munda, quam proxime ceperant, Materiem illo deportarent. Apud eundem & alio loco legimus hodie vitiose Saonem & Verfaonenses, pro Vrsaone & Vrsaonensibus. Conveniunt autem Hirtij verba cum hodierno situ. A Munda Vrsaonem usque unius dei est iter: Opidum Aquam nullam habet conterminam; Arborum genus similiter nullum; præter Olivarū copiam; quas proculdubio Pœni, Romanis Hispaniisq; ad terræ cultum proclivores, post immanē illam Gothorum Provinciæq; totius Cladem: ibidem plantarunt. Inventa commemorantur ibi Fragmenta quædam testacea, quæ sequentes litteras præferebant: OFF.PATR. VRS. Interpretantur nonnulli Officium Patrum Vrsaonis, vel Officinam Patritiorum Vrsaonis: fieri addentes in hac Regione Vasa & Dolia multa fictilia; eo quod Gleba his talibus singendis sit aptissima. Est autem nostro hoc ævo Ducatus Caput, Sedesq; primaria Gironum Familiæ; quæ, relicto Vrenia Comitum titulo, Ducum Cosuna anno clɔ Iɔ LXII, Rege Philippo adnuente, vindicare sibi cœpit. Historiam hujus Stirpis contexuit Hieronymus Gudiel. Academiam hic Principes erexerunt anno clɔ Iɔ XLIX; in qua omnes fere scientiæ docentur. Fœia ad Singulim fluvium, hodie Xenil vel Chenil, Ptolemæo cluit Ἀσύγις: quod Astigi vocetur in antiquis Inscriptionibus docet Clusius: Augusta Firma cognominatur à Plinio. Dictum Astygi, ut quidam fabulantur ab Aster Memnonis auriga. Hujus opidi Divitiæ & negotiatio potissimum in Lanæ mercatura consistit, ob incredibilem Ovium hoc loco copiam. Pontem habet ad Latus Orientale ex Lapide vivo fornicato. Iuxta Supplicij est locus; El Roillo appellatus. Quod opidum non adeo magnum, hodie tredecim ab Hispali leucis vitatur, inter eandem Hispalim & Cordubam medio fere itinere, ad dexteram Bætis oram, Peña Flor, Ptolemæi putatur Ἰῶνχλα μεγάλη, in mediterraneis Turdulorum; Lipa cognomine Isa ica Plinij, qui Hispalensi Conventui attribuit. Decimo hinc Miliari ad ejusdem Fluvij ripam est Corduba, Κορδούβη Ptolemæo, Cordova vulgo: Plinius Coloniam Patriciam tradit cognominatam; quod etiam ex antiquis Marmoribus probat Moralis. Nummum item æreum Augusti Imperatoris vidisse se scribit Abrahamus Ortelius, in quo legebatur COLONIA PATRICIA. Μαρκίλλοι κτίσμα ἐ δέξῃ καὶ δωσάμει, inquit Strabo lib. iii. Hanc C. Iulius Cæsar scribit in Ephemeridibus & Provinciæ suæ caput, & de Populo Romano bene semper fuisse meritam. Corduba tamquam Cor Bætis dicitur Ioanni Gerundensi Episcopo, lib. i Paralipomen. cap. de Fluminibus. Alumnos habuit rei militaris gloria, doctrinæque studijs præcellentes. Suos olim habuit Reges, qui finem acceperunt in Humeia quodam, circa annum clɔ iii. Beata hodie est Corduba, præter alia multa bona, fertilissimis Agris, Hortis amœnissimis, Aquis salubberrimis. Solum Corduba vocat aureum Silius Italicus lib. iii.
units.tr: {a} Antonio de Nebrija, commonly called Lebrixa, teaches as follows: "Caesar returned from Gades again to Seville. Fabius Maximus, whom he had left behind to attack the garrison, at last took the city; and then they set out for Ursao, which was held by a great fortification, very strong by nature. Except in the town itself, water could nowhere be found nearer than a certain number of miles, nor did they have wood or material for the assault. So our men were forced to bring over material from Munda, which they had recently taken." In the same author, and elsewhere, we read today, wrongly, Saonem and Verfaonenses for Ursaone and Ursaonenses. Hirtius's words agree with the present site. From Munda to Ursao is a single day's journey. The town has no water nearby, and likewise no kind of tree except a quantity of olives, which without doubt the Carthaginians, who were more inclined than the Romans and Spaniards to cultivate the land, planted there after that dreadful destruction of the Goths and of the whole province. There are mentioned as found there some pieces of pottery bearing these letters: OFF.PATR. VRS. Some interpret them as Officium Patrum Ursaonis, or Officina Patritiorum Ursaonis (the workshop of the patricians of Ursao), adding that many earthen vessels and jars are made in this region, because the clay is most suitable for moulding such things. In our own age it is the capital of the Duchy and the chief seat of the family of the Girones, who, having abandoned the title of Counts of Urenia, began in 1562, with King Philip's consent, to claim the title of Dukes of Cosuna. Hieronymus Gudiel has written the history of this line. Here the princes founded an academy in 1549, in which nearly all the sciences are taught. Fooia on the river Singulis, today the Xenil or Chenil, is Asygis [Ἀσύγις] to Ptolemy; that it was called Astigi in ancient inscriptions Clusius shows; Pliny surnames it Augusta Firma. It is said to have been named Astygi, as some fable, after Aster, the charioteer of Memnon. The wealth and trade of this town consist chiefly in the wool trade, because of the incredible number of sheep here. It has a bridge on its eastern side, made of vaulted living rock. Near it is a place of execution, called El Roillo. This town, not very large, today is thirteen leagues from Seville, midway between Seville and Cordoba, on the right bank of the Baetis, Peña Flor. It is thought to be Ptolemy's Ionchla megale [Ἰῶνχλα μεγάλη], in the inland country of the Turduli; Lipa, with the surname Isa ica in Pliny, who assigns it to the jurisdiction of Seville. Ten miles from here, on the bank of the same river, is Corduba, Kordoube [Κορδούβη] to Ptolemy, commonly Cordova. Pliny reports that it was surnamed Colonia Patricia, which Moral also proves from ancient marbles. Abraham Ortelius writes that he saw a bronze coin of the Emperor Augustus on which was read COLONIA PATRICIA. Strabo, book iii, says: "It was founded by Marcillus [Μαρκίλλοι κτίσμα]..." Gaius Julius Caesar writes of it in his Commentaries as the capital of his province, and says it always deserved well of the Roman people. Corduba is called, as it were, Cor Baetis (the heart of the Baetis) by John of Gerona, bishop, in book i of his Paralipomena, chapter on rivers. It has had sons who excelled in the glory of war and in the pursuit of learning. Once it had its own kings, who met their end at a certain Humeia, about the year 300. Today Cordoba is blessed, besides many other goods, with very fertile fields, most pleasant gardens and very healthy waters. Silius Italicus in book iii calls Cordoba golden.

units.la: Nec decus aurifera cessavit Corduba terra.
units.tr: Nor has Corduba ceased to bear its glory in its gold-bearing land.

units.la: Ab hac Urbe tria describit Antoninus Itinera; Duo Castulonem (Castona la veia) Tertium Malacam (Malaga) Prius, quod Castulonem, per Millia passuum procedens xc xix, Urbes transit Calpurniaanam (Carpio nunc) Vrgaonem (Argione) & Itturgi (Aldea el rio) Posterius, per millia passuum lxviii, Urbes permeat Fporam (Montero) & Vciense. Tertium, quod Malacam ducit ccxci est millium passuum, currit; per Tugiam, Fraxinum, Hellaram, Acci (Guadix) Aibam Vrci, (forte quod Virgi alijs, Vera vulgo) Turaniam, Murgi (Murga) Seviranum (Motrel) Cariclum, Menobam, Malacam. Illud non immerito quis miretur, T. Livium in descriptione Belli Civilis, inquit Ioannes Vasæus in Hispaniæ Chronico, ubi de Episcopatibus Hispaniæ, quum multam Bæticarum Urbium mentionem faciat, tamen Corduba non meminisse. Quinque leucis ab Corduba versus Meridiem Mons est Maior, vulgo Monte Mator: Οὐλία existimatur Ptolemæi, Turdulorum in Hispania Bætica Urbs: Vlia Antonini: Vlla vitiose est apud Auctorem Belli tam Alexandrini, quam Hispaniensis. Villanovano Vlla hodie Veia nominatur. In Opido certe Monte-Maiore elegantissima vetustorum Lapidum monimenta visuntur, quæ satis docent eo loci Ruinas Vlia jacere. Nummum habere se restatur Hieronymus Surita, in quo turpissima Viri effigies cusa cernitur, supra Lunæ crescentis Astrum, & ante os Spica line Inscriptione: ex adversa facie Olearum ramusculi sunt expressi, cum Urbis nomine VLIA. Decem ab Corduba Miliaribus Mons Aureus est Montoro vocatur vulgo: Epora creditur Antonini. Male apud Ptolemaeum Ἐ͂βυρα pro Ἐ͂μερα, quum illa sit non Baeticae, sed Lusitaniae: pejus autem Ripepora in vulgatis Plinij Codicibus, ubi Foederatorum cognominatur. Eporensis Municipij, Pontifisq; ab eo excitati, mentionem facit Inscriptio, quam ibidem enotatam CL.V. Iusto Lipsio communicavit Nobilis. V. Augerius Busbequius; Ea sic habet:
units.tr: From this city Antoninus describes three itineraries. Two run to Castulo (Castona la veia), and the third to Malaca (Malaga). The first, which goes to Castulo over 199 miles, passes through the towns Calpurniana (Carpio now), Vrgao (Argione) and Ituirgi (Aldea el rio). The second, over 68 miles, passes through Epora (Montero) and Vciense. The third, which leads to Malaca and runs 291 miles, goes through Tugia, Fraxinum, Hellara, Acci (Guadix), Aiba, Urci (perhaps the Virgi of others, Vera in common usage), Turania, Murgi (Murga), Severanum (Motrel), Cariclum, Menoba, Malaca. One may not unreasonably wonder at this, says Juan Vasco in his Chronicle of Spain, where he discusses the bishoprics of Spain: although Livy in his account of the civil war mentions many of the towns of Baetica, he nonetheless makes no mention of Corduba. Five leagues south of Corduba is Mons Maior, commonly called Monte Mayor. It is thought to be the Oulia of Ptolemy [Οὐλία], a town of the Turduli in Hispania Baetica; it is Ulia in Antoninus, and Ulla in the writers of the Alexandrian and Spanish wars, where the form is faulty. Today Villanueva is called Ulla, or Veia. In the town of Monte Mayor there are certainly very elegant monuments of ancient stones, which sufficiently show that the ruins of Ulia lie there. Hieronymus Surita states that he possesses a coin on which is stamped a most unsightly image of a man, above the crescent of the moon, and before the face an ear of grain without inscription; on the reverse are sprigs of olive, with the name of the town, ULIA. Ten miles from Corduba is Mons Aureus, commonly called Montoro, believed to be the Epora of Antoninus. Ptolemy wrongly gives Ἐβυρα [Ebyra] for Ἐμερα [Emera], since that place belongs not to Baetica but to Lusitania; worse still is Ripepora in the common editions of Pliny, where it is surnamed Foederatorum. An inscription, which the noble V. Augerius Busbequius communicated to the most illustrious Justus Lipsius after copying it on the spot, mentions the municipality of Epora and the bridge built by its bishop. It reads thus:

units.la: Hispalim recurro, hincque per Palatium, Alcantarillae Pontem, Opidaq; Cabeccas & Nebrissam, Lucifery peto Fanum. Sic Latini meo judicio nominarunt, quod Strabo libro III Φωσφόρου ἱερὸν interpretatur; quodque appellatum etiam addit Αυχιμδοβιαω, Lucem Dubiam: hodie est S. Lucar de Barrameda. Haud procul hinc quarta fere Leuca versus Vulturnum, Opidum est, quod Hispanis Xeres de la Frontera dicitur, quasi Hispaniae ex hac ora vel Initium vel Terminus. Hoc Navagierus in Itinerario putat esse, quod Asta Livio lib.xxviii, Auctori de bello Hispaniensi, Plinio lib. III (qui Regiam cognominat) & aliis: Ἀστα Ptolemaeo & Straboni, qui cum Nebrissa ad Æstuaria Bætis collocat: Hasta Antonino per adspirationem in libris tam Editis, quam Manu-scriptis. Auctor etiâ Commentarij Hispaniensis memorat A. Baebium, C. Flavium, & A. Trebellium Equites Romanos Astenses; qui argento prope tecti ad Caesarem transfugerunt. Astam tamen Moralis scribit adhuc nomen retinere, vel locum illum esse, circa Guadeleten Amnem, qui vulgo Masa de Asta. Abrahamus Ortelius haud multum abest, quin submersam putet cum insula Tartesso in Baetis ostio. Praestantissimos Hispaniae totius Equos & maxime pernices Ager hujus Opidi profert; Genettas vulgus nuncupat; eos Nobiles industria singulari docent, eorumque cursu in Hippodromis oblectantur, dum Equestres instituunt pugnas, in quibus Arundinibus & Cannis, Hastarum loco se mutuo exercent, eum ad modum, quo Mauri Hastas torquere & in hostes jacere solent. Eos Ludos Juegos de Cannas patria lingua nominant. Centum stadijs à Baetis ostio distat Chipiona opidum, quod non dubito, quin Καπίων πύργος sit Straboni lib.III, Capionis Turris, ... Nam, ut idem addit, quum ejectus ab amne Limus vadosum reddat profundum, & latentibus sub Aqua saxis locus ipse promineat, conspicuo aliquo opus habebat signo. Ad Ostium Lethes fluminis, quod hodie Guadelete, vel Arabice Bedalac, Opidum est, cui nomen Portus S. Mariae, vulgo El puerto de S. Maria: Μενεδίων Λιμὴν Ptolemaeo & Straboni. Lethen transgresis occurrit cum aliis Medina Sidonia; quam Ἀνυδὸρ Ptolemaei censet Clusius. Meridionaliora versus Fretum petentibus offert se Conilium, non ignobile Hispaniae opidum, sex Leucis distans ab Gadium Urbe: inlustrissimo S. Lucae, qui & Medinae Sidoniae. Duci parens; Diuitiaeque praecipuas habens in captura variorum Piscium, potissimum vero Thynnorum, qua de re alibi plenius. Conilium habetur ab Georgio Austriaco apud Abrahamum Ortelium Καρπία Ptolemaei, Καθαία Stephani; Carteia Livio, qui lib. xxviii situm ejus hoc modo delineat: Dum haec ad Belin fluvium gerentur, Laelius interim Freto in Oceanum evectus ad Carteiam Classe accessit. Urbs ea in ora Oceani sita est, ubi primum è faucibus angustis panditur Mare. Ταρτησσὸς etiam Graecis legitur appellata, ut Strabo, Plinius & Pomponius testantur: Ταρτήσιον ὄλβιον ἄστυ est apud Homerum: Καρπησος vitiose fortean dicitur Appiano Alexandrino. Tartessò nomen dedisse volunt Flumen Ταρτησσὸν, quod postea Bætis, ut cap. vii dixi. Hinc Regio Ταρτησσὶς Eratostheni, Artemidoro, & aliis. De Tartessò sunt haec Anacreontis: Ἐ’γὼ τ᾽ αὖ ἔτ᾽ Ἀμαλθίης βυλοίμην κιεροῖς, ἔτ᾽ ἐπὶ Πευκονωδὶν καὶ ἐκάτην Ταρτησσᾶ Βασιλεῦον.
units.tr: I return to Hispalis, and from there, by Palatium, the bridge of Alcantarilla, and the towns of Cabeças and Nebrissa, I make for the Temple of Lucifer. The Latins named it so, in my judgement, because Strabo in book III translates it as the temple of Phosphorus [Φωσφόρου ἱερὸν]; and he adds that it was also called Αυχιμδοβιαω [Auchimdobiaō], that is, Doubtful Light. Today it is S. Lucar de Barrameda. Not far from here, about four leagues towards the south-east wind, is a town which the Spanish call Xerez de la Frontera, as if it were the beginning or the end of Spain on this coast. Navagero in his Itinerary thinks this is Asta, which Livy in book XXVIII, the author of the Spanish war, Pliny in book III (who surnames it Regia), and others call by that name. Strabo and Ptolemy write it Ἀστα [Asta], and Strabo places it with Nebrissa at the estuaries of the Baetis. Antoninus writes Hasta with an aspirate, in both printed and manuscript books. The author of the Spanish commentary also mentions A. Baebius, C. Flavius and A. Trebellius, Roman knights of Asta, who deserted to Caesar with almost all their silver. Moralis writes that Asta still keeps its name, or that the place is Masa de Asta, near the river Guadalete, as it is commonly called. Abraham Ortelius is not far from thinking that it was submerged along with the island of Tartessus at the mouth of the Baetis. The land of this town produces the most excellent and swiftest horses of all Spain; the common people call them Genettas. The nobles train them with remarkable skill and take pleasure in their running in the hippodromes, while they stage equestrian battles, in which they practise against each other with reeds and canes in place of spears, in the manner in which the Moors are accustomed to hurl spears and cast them at enemies. In their native tongue they call these games Juegos de Cannas. A hundred stadia from the mouth of the Baetis lies the town of Chipiona, which I do not doubt is the Καπίων πύργος [Kapiōn pyrgos] of Strabo in book III, that is, the Tower of Capion, ... For, as the same author adds, since the mud carried down by the river makes the shallow water deep, and the rocks hidden under the water project from the place, it needed some conspicuous sign. At the mouth of the river Lethe, which today is the Guadalete, or in Arabic Bedalac, is a town called Portus S. Mariae, commonly El puerto de S. Maria; it is the Μενεδίων Λιμὴν [Menedion Limēn] of Ptolemy and Strabo. Crossing the Lethe one comes to Medina Sidonia, which Clusius thinks is the Ἀνυδὸρ [Anydor] of Ptolemy. Heading farther south towards the Strait, there presents itself Conil, no mean town of Spain, six leagues from the city of Gades, most illustrious for the Lucas of Sidonia, who is also the parent of the Duke of Medina Sidonia; it has especially rich resources in the catching of various fish, above all the tunny, about which more fully elsewhere. Conil is considered by Georg Austriacus (in Abraham Ortelius) to be the Καρπία [Karpia] of Ptolemy, and the Καθαία [Kathaia] of Stephanus; it is Carteia in Livy, who in book XXVIII describes its position in this way: While these things were going on at the river Belis, Laelius meanwhile, having been carried through the Strait into the Ocean with his fleet, approached Carteia. That city lies on the shore of the Ocean, where the sea first spreads out from narrow jaws. It is also read in the Greeks as Ταρτησσὸς [Tartessos], as Strabo, Pliny and Pomponius bear witness; Ταρτήσιον ὄλβιον ἄστυ [Tartesion olbion astu], the wealthy city of Tartessus, is in Homer. Appian of Alexandria perhaps wrongly calls it Καρπησος [Karpēsos]. Some hold that the river Ταρτησσὸν [Tartessos], which afterwards was called the Baetis, as I said in chapter VII, gave Tartessus its name. Hence the region Ταρτησσὶς [Tartessis] in Eratosthenes, Artemidorus and others. Of Tartessus are these lines of Anacreon: "Would that I might again be at the temples of Amalthea, and again at Peucon and at the goddess of Tartessus, the queen" [Ἐ’γὼ τ᾽ αὖ ἔτ᾽ Ἀμαλθίης βυλοίμην κιεροῖς, ἔτ᾽ ἐπὶ Πευκονωδὶν καὶ ἐκάτην Ταρτησσᾶ Βασιλεῦον].

units.la: Silius lib. iii belli Poenici separare videtur Carteiam à Tartesso: Argantoniacos armat Carteia Nepotes: Rex Proavis fuit humani ditissimus aevi, Ter denos decies emensus belliger annos. Armat Tartessos stabulanti conscia Phoebo.
units.tr: Silius, in book III of the Punic War, seems to distinguish Carteia from Tartessos: "Carteia arms the Argantonian descendants; their ancestor was the richest king of the human age, a warrior who had lived through thirty decades of years. Tartessos arms [its people], conscious of Phoebus who keeps them."

units.la: Carteia non semel meminit M. Tullius cum aliis locis, tum in Epistolis ad Atticum, eamque ab Corduba abesse M.P.CLXX, perhibet Auctor Commentarij Hispaniensis: cujus, ut & Livij, quae paullo ante laudavi, verba si sint vera, satis arguunt, non bene Clusium adferere Carteiam hodie esse Carthagenam; quod videret hanc ab illa non prorsus abludere. Tariffam, quam Carteiam quidam opinantur, ex Tartesso corruptam si quis dixerit, non admodum pugnabo. Non procul inde Vegelium est, vulgo Vegel; opidum exiguum quidem, sed situ opereque clarum; Colli quem latissima undique planicies cingit, impositum: adeo ut inde circumquaque prospectus pateat, quo usque oculorum acies extendere se potest, tam in laetam laxamque planiciem locaq; compascua, versus Solis exortum; quam in Africae Montes & oram circa Meridiem: nec non in vastum & tumultuosum Oceanum versus Septemtrionem & Occidentem. Ejus Incolis Piscatus abunde ad vitam commode transigendam suppeditat. Hinc in Caurum iter flectentes obviam habent Mundam. Sic nominant Oppidum Plinius, alijque Latini Scriptores, quod hodie vulgo Monda. Putant tamen alij antiquam Mundam esse, quae hodie Ronda Veia: Mondam autem, cujus antea memini, duobus inde Milliaribus exstructam fuisse ab Arabibus, prisco retento nomine, uti mos illis. Videndus Didacus Mendosius de Bello ultimo Granatensi. Ioannes Gerundensis Episcopus lib. i & ix Paralip. Hispaniae procul hinc amotam Mundam, eandem scribit esse cum Coimbra Portugalliae Opido. De Conflictu porro ad Mundam inter C.Iulium Caesarem & Cn. Pompei Magni Liberos Cn. Sextumque, consulendi Plutarchus in Caesare, Appianus lib. ii Bellorum Civil. Auctor Commentarij de Bello Hispaniensi, Strabo lib. iii, Suetonius in Caesare cap. xxxvi & in Octaviano Augusto cap. xciv, Valer. Maximus lib. vii. cap. vi, & alij. Lucanus lib. i: Vitima funesta concurrent praelia Munda.
units.tr: Marcus Tullius mentions Carteia more than once, both in other places and in his Letters to Atticus, and the author of the Spanish Commentary states that it is 170 Roman miles from Corduba. If the words of this author, and of Livy, which I quoted a little earlier, are true, they sufficiently prove that Clusius was wrong to say that Carteia is today Carthagena, since it is plain that the one is not very different from the other. I shall not argue strongly if someone says that Tarifa, which some think is Carteia, has been corrupted from Tartessos. Not far from there is Vegelium, commonly Vegel, a small town, but famous for its site and its works, set on a hill surrounded on every side by a very wide plain, so that from it there is an open view on every side as far as the eye can reach: towards the east, over the broad and pleasant plain and pasture lands; towards the south, over the mountains and coast of Africa; and towards the north and west, over the vast and turbulent Ocean. Its inhabitants have plenty of fish, enough to live on comfortably. From here, turning towards the north-west, one meets Munda. Pliny and other Latin writers so name the town, which is commonly today Monda. Others, however, think that ancient Munda is what is today Ronda Vieja, and that Monda, which I mentioned before, was built two miles from there by the Arabs, keeping the old name, as is their custom. See Diego Mendoza on the last war of Granada. John Gerundensis, Bishop, in books I and IX of his Paralipomena, writes that Munda, which is far from here, is the same as Coimbra, a town of Portugal. Concerning the battle at Munda between Gaius Julius Caesar and the sons of Gnaeus Pompey the Great, Gnaeus and Sextus, consult Plutarch in his Life of Caesar, Appian in book II of the Civil Wars, the author of the Spanish Commentary, Strabo in book III, Suetonius in Caesar chapter 36 and in Augustus chapter 94, Valerius Maximus book VII chapter 6, and others. Lucan, book I: "The last deadly battles will clash at Munda."

units.la: Silius Ital. lib. iii Belli Poenici: Et munda Emathios Italiae paritura labores.
units.tr: Silius Italicus, book 3 of the Punica: "And Munda, which was to bring the Emathian toils upon Italy."

XII. | Pons, quo hodieque Insula Continenti jungitur, vulgo Puente de Suaço. | Carulam, M.P.XXIIII. | Alcolea. Portu Gaditan. M.P.XIIII. | Puerto Real, Baia de Cadiz. | Ilipam, M.P.XVIII. | Peña Flor. Hastam, M.P.XVI. | Asta hodieque, vel Masa de Asta: locus circa Guadeleten amnem. Vide supra. | Oftipponem, M.P.XIV. | Haec loca ita perierunt, ut ne vestigia quidem supersint. Vgiam, M.P.XXVII. | Cabeças, aut circiter. | Barbam, M.P.XX. | Oripponem, M.P.XXIV. | Inter Hispalim & Palatium, ubi multa hic ibi rudera. | Antiquaria, M.P.XXIV. | Monte-Maiore putatur, sed non admodum convenit Itinerario. Hispalim, M.P.IX. | Sevile, | Angellas, M.P.XXIII. | Bafilipponem, M.P.XXI. | Cantillana, ni fallor. | Ipagrum, M.P.XX. | | | Vliam, M.P.X. | | | Cordubam, M.P.XVIII. |
units.tr: The route that the Antonine Itinerary marks out from Gades to Corduba takes in the inland places of Andalusia by the river Baetis: Itin. Anto. | Modern names | Itin. Anto. | Modern names. Ad Pontem, 12 M.P. | The bridge by which the island is still joined to the mainland, commonly called Puente de Suaço. | Carulam, 24 M.P. | Alcolea. Portu Gaditan., 14 M.P. | Puerto Real, the Bay of Cadiz. | Ilipam, 18 M.P. | Peña Flor. Hastam, 16 M.P. | Asta to this day, or the Masa de Asta: a place near the river Guadelete. See above. | Oftipponem, 14 M.P. | These places have so completely disappeared that not even traces of them remain. Vgiam, 27 M.P. | Cabeças, or thereabouts. | Barbam, 20 M.P. | Oripponem, 24 M.P. | Between Hispalis and Palatium, where there are many ruins here and there. Antiquaria, 24 M.P. | Thought to be Monte-Mayor, but this does not agree well with the Itinerary. Hispalim, 9 M.P. | Seville. Angellas, 23 M.P. | Bafilipponem, 21 M.P. | Cantillana, if I am not mistaken. Ipagrum, 20 M.P. | | | Vliam, 10 M.P. | | | Cordubam, 18 M.P.

units.la: Estremadura.
units.tr: Estremadura.

units.la: ESTREMADURA extendere se scribitur ab Villa Regali ad Badaios sua longitudine; latitudine vero ab Mariano Monte, qui hodie Sierra Morena, ad Tagum fluvium. Adjacet illi ad Occasum Portugallia; ad Septemtrionem Castella Nova: ad Ortum Granata: Meridionale latus adluit Oceanus. Hujus Provinciae Campis nihil habet Hispania per hiemem magis apricum: quo fit, ut eo tempore Animalium greges ex Septemtrionalioribus locis in hanc conducantur. Æstate omnia nimis-quam ibi fervent, eamque ob caussam rarius habitatur.
units.tr: Estremadura is said to extend in length from Villa Regal to Badajoz, and in breadth from the Mariano Mountains, which today are the Sierra Morena, to the river Tagus. Portugal adjoins it to the west, New Castile to the north, and Granada to the east; the ocean washes its southern side. Spain has nothing sunnier in winter than the plains of this province, so in that season herds of animals are brought here from the more northern regions. In summer everything there nearly burns, and for that reason it is inhabited less often.

units.la: Totus autem hic Tractus Beturia legitur appellata apud Plinium, Livium, A. Hirtium (in cujus libris Bethuria scribitur) & alios. Beturia Sisaponensis Regio tribuitur à Plinio libro xxxiii, cap.vii, ubi de Minio agit. Vide quae notavi capite hujus Libri iii. Beturiam hodie Petroche ex Petrarum frequentia magna ex parte nominari, memoriae prodit Sepulveda ad F. Pincianum in Epist. Clar. Vir.
units.tr: This whole tract is read as called Beturia by Pliny, Livy, A. Hirtius (in whose books it is written Bethuria) and others. Beturia Sisaponensis Regio is assigned by Pliny, book 33, chapter 7, where he treats of minium. See what I noted in chapter 3 of this book. Sepulveda, in his commentary on F. Pincianus in the Epistles of Distinguished Men, records that Beturia is today called Petroche, largely from the abundance of rocks (petrae).

units.la: Fixisse quondam his locis suas sedes traduntur Celtici, quos partim Baeticam, partim Lusitaniam coluisse notat Ptolemaeus: Strabo Κελτὰς vocat: Celti per totam Hispaniam hic ubi frequentiores. Colarni Plinio, quorum Opidum Ptolemaeus nominat Κολάρνον. Turduli Veteres & Novi apud Plinium & Melam: De Turdulis simpliciter sic dictis (erant enim triplices) consulendum caput praecedens. Vettones, quorum mentio apud Plinium, Livium, & Caesarem. Fuerunt & cognomines his, ubi hodie Legio, ut capite xviii notavi.
units.tr: The Celtici are said to have once fixed their seats in these places. Ptolemy notes that they inhabited partly Baetica and partly Lusitania; Strabo calls them Keltai [Κελτὰς]. Celti are found throughout all Spain, here where they are more numerous. The Colarni are named by Pliny, and Ptolemy names their town Kolarnon [Κολάρνον]. The Turduli Veteres & Novi, Old and New, are mentioned by Pliny and Mela. Concerning the Turduli simply so called (for there were three kinds), consult the preceding chapter. The Vettones are mentioned by Pliny, Livy and Caesar. There were also namesakes of these where Legio is today, as I noted in chapter 18.

units.la: Visuntur in hac Hispaniae parte inter alia, Badaios, quae, ut docet in sua Chorographia, Lusitanice edita, Caspar Varrerius, adsentientibus illi magnis Viris, Pax Plinio (apud quem lib. v. cap.xxxii, Pacensis etiam Colonia, & alibi Pacensis Conventus) Παξαυγῆσα Straboni, ut quidem concepta legitur haec vox in MS. qui in Monasterio Regali Escuriali servatur, quemadmodum apud Ortelium testatur Iacobus Delgadus Pacensis: in Vulgatis est Πεζαυγῆα. Mauris olim Bavaugus, deinde Badavos, ab antiquo nomine Pacis Augustae. Villanovanus, Tarapha & Antonius Resendius in Epistola ad Ioannem Vasaeum adnotant Pacem Plinij, vel Πασωυγῆσαν Ptolemaei eamdem esse cum Pace Julia ejusdem Ptolemaei & Antonini: contra sentiunt Io. Mariana, Vasaeus & Clusius hanc non aliam censentes, quam quae hodie Beja vel Bexa; tempore Maurorum Pacca, ut tradit ex antiquo Chronico, cujus copiam sibi factam notat ab Resendio, quem nominavi, Vasaeus. Accedit, quod Clusius scribat in ipsa Beja multas etiamnum Inscriptiones exstare; Pacis Iulia facientes mentionem. Est ibidem Merida; olim, ut volunt Varrerius & Villanovanus, Ἡ μέριτα Prolemæo; Emerita Antonino; Augusta Emerita Plinio & Pomponio Melæ; Αὐγύστα Ἡ μέριτα Straboni. Exstant complures Nummi, in quibus priore quidem facie Effigies Augusti, Coronam radiatam capite gestantis, cum hac Inscriptione, DIVVS AVGVSTVS PATER; altera vero, Porta Vrbis, cui geminæ sunt additæ Turres, adsculpto Vrbis nomine AVGVSTA EMERITA. Quæ Emerita Antiquis, Taraphæ censetur Medina del Rio Seco: sed neminem habet Suffragatorem. Dio lib. liii & ex eo Isidorus lib. xv. Etymologiarum, memoriæ produnt Augustum Cæsarem, Cantabris, Asturibus, Lusitanisq; subactis, Veteranos in Hispania dimisisse; hancque Vrbem condidisse, Augustam Emeritam, ab Augusti Principis & ipsorum Emeritorum Nominibus nuncupatam. Coloniam factam docent Nummi Augusti, quos in Thesauro laudat Hubertus Goltzius. Testatur idem Prudentius in Dactylico de Virgine Eulalia, Christi Martyre:
units.tr: Among other places in this part of Spain are Badajoz, which, as Caspar Varrerius teaches in his Chorography, published in Portuguese, with the agreement of great men, is Pliny's Pax (where in book 5, chapter 32, there is also the colony Pacensis, and elsewhere the Pacensis Conventus), and Strabo's Paxaugēsa [Παξαυγῆσα], as this word is read in a manuscript kept in the royal monastery of the Escorial, as Jacobus Delgadus of Pax testifies in Ortelius; in the printed editions it is Pezaugēa [Πεζαυγῆα]. Formerly the Moors called it Bavaugus, then Badavos, from the ancient name Pax Augusta. Villanovanus, Tarapha and Antonius Resendius, in their letter to Joannes Vasaeus, note that Pliny's Pax or Ptolemy's Pasōugēsan [Πασωυγῆσαν] is the same as the Pax Julia of the same Ptolemy and of Antoninus. On the contrary, Juan de Mariana, Vasaeus and Clusius think it is none other than what is today Beja or Bexa, called Pacca in the time of the Moors, as Vasaeus relates from an ancient chronicle, a copy of which, he notes, was made available to him by Resendius, whom I named. Add that Clusius writes that many inscriptions still exist in Beja itself, mentioning Pax Julia. There is also Merida: formerly, as Varrerius and Villanovanus think, Hē Merita [Ἡ μέριτα] for Ptolemy; Emerita for Antoninus; Augusta Emerita for Pliny and Pomponius Mela; Augusta Hē Merita [Αὐγύστα Ἡ μέριτα] for Strabo. Several coins survive. On one side is the effigy of Augustus wearing a radiate crown, with this inscription: DIVVS AVGVSTVS PATER. On the other is the gate of a city with twin towers added, and the name of the city engraved: AVGVSTA EMERITA. Tarapha thinks that the ancient Emerita is Medina del Rio Seco, but he has no supporter. Dio, book 53, and from him Isidore, book 15 of the Etymologies, record that Augustus Caesar, after subduing the Cantabrians, Asturians and Lusitanians, discharged veterans in Spain, and founded this city, named Augusta Emerita after the Emperor Augustus and the Emeriti themselves. Coins of Augustus, which Hubert Goltzius cites in his Thesaurus, show that it was made a colony. The same Prudentius testifies in his Dactylics on the virgin Eulalia, a martyr of Christ:

units.la: Nunc locus Emerita est tumulo
units.tr: Now Emerita is a place on a hill,

units.la: Clara Colonia Vettonia:
units.tr: the famous colony of Vettonia,

units.la: Quam memorabilis amnis Anas
units.tr: which the notable river Anas

units.la: Præterit, & viridante rapax
units.tr: flows past, and with its swirling,

units.la: Gurgite mœnia pulcra lavat.
units.tr: greedy current washes its fair walls.

units.la: Vbi Vettonia, Vettonum, de quibus paullo ante, regio. Hyginus Augusti Libertus auctor est, D. Augustum in Beturiæ Emerita jugera quadringinta dedisse. Emeritenses juris Italici fuisse notat Paulus I. C. lib. ii. de Censibus, cujus verba exstant in Pandectis l. ult. Tit. de Censibus. Ab hac Vrbe Gades usque viam superiorum Consulum tempore inchoatam, multisque locis intermissam perduxit Octavianus Augustus, loquente, quod ibi videre est, Veteri Marmore, his verbis concepto:
units.tr: Here Vettonia is the region of the Vettones, mentioned a little before. Hyginus, a freedman of Augustus, is the authority that the Emperor Augustus gave four hundred jugera in Beturian Emerita. Paulus the jurist, book 2 On the Census, notes that the Emeritenses had Italian right; his words are in the Pandects, last law, title On the Census. From this city to Gades, the road begun in the time of the former consuls and interrupted in many places was carried through by Octavian Augustus, as can be seen from an old marble with these words:

units.la: IMP. CÆS. DIVI. F. AVGVSTVS, PONT. MAX. COS. XI. TRIBVNIC. POTEST. X, IMP. VIII ORBE. MARI. ET. TERRA. PACATO. TEMPLO IANI. CLVSO. ET. REF. P. R. OPTIMIS. LEGIBVS ET. SANCTISSIMIS. INSTITVTIS. REFORMATA VIAM. SVPERIOR. COS. TEMPORE. INCHOATAM ET. MVLTIS. LOCIS. INTERMISSAM. PRO. DIGNITATE IMPERI. P. R. LATIOREM. LONGIOREMQVE GADEIS. VSQ. PERDVXIT
units.tr: The Emperor Caesar, son of the divine (Julius), Augustus, Pontifex Maximus, consul for the eleventh time, holding tribunician power for the tenth time, imperator for the eighth time, the world having been pacified by sea and land, the temple of Janus closed, and the state restored by the best laws and most holy institutions, has carried through to Gades the road begun in the time of the former consuls and interrupted in many places, made wider and longer to suit the dignity of the Roman people.

units.la: Ad hanc item Vrbem à Cappara (quæ Capara Ptolemæo & Antonino; cujusque Cives Caperenses Plinio; hodie Caparra) Viam restituisse Vespasianum Imperatorem probat Columna, quæ Tarraconæ posita:
units.tr: That Vespasian also restored the road to this city from Capara (which is Capara for Ptolemy and Antoninus, whose citizens are the Caperenses for Pliny; today Caparra) is proved by a column set up at Tarragona:

units.la: IMP. CÆSAR. VESPASIANVS. AVG PONT. MAX. TRIB. POT. II IMP. VII. COS. III. DES. IIII P. P VIAM. A. CAPPARA. AD. EMERITAM. AVG VSQ. IMPENSA. SVA. RESTITVIT.
units.tr: The Emperor Caesar Vespasian Augustus, Pontifex Maximus, holding tribunician power for the second time, imperator for the seventh time, consul for the third time, designated consul for the fourth time, Father of his Country, restored the road from Capara to Augusta Emerita at his own expense.

units.la: Coccum Emeritense commendat Plinius lib. ix. Nat. histor. cap.xli. Carmen illud Ausonij, Vrbes cantantis, Emerita in Vulgatis libris inscriptum, Manuscriptos Codices Hispali tribuere docui capite præcedente. Vrbs porro hæc olim amplissima, Pontequeque Romani Operis longissimo nobilis, Opidulum est hodie, nihil habens memorabile præter ruinas & dolenda antiquitatis suæ Vestigia. Frequentia fuerunt inter Emeritenses & Cæsaraugustanos olim commercia, docentibus id tribus itineribus, quæ ab Antonino Emerita Cæsaraugustam delineantur; per Contosoliam, per Lacipeam, perque Locum, cui nomen ad Sorores. Fuit ibidem & Vrbs Turdetanorum, quæ Νερτόβριγα Prolemæo & Appiano, ex cujus ruderibus magna, uti apud Abrahamum Ortelium censet Arias Montanus, Opida ædificata, Frexenal, Fuentes, Bodenal, & Higuera. Addit Montanus ruinas Nertobriga immensas hodieque conspici tribus passuum millibus à Frexenal, ubi ipse natus; Locumque ab Adcolis Valeram nominari.
units.tr: Pliny praises the scarlet dye of Emerita (Coccum Emeritense) in book 9 of his Natural History, chapter 41. I showed in the preceding chapter that the manuscripts ascribe to Hispalis that poem of Ausonius, Vrbes cantantis, which in the printed books is inscribed Emerita. This city, once very large and famous for its long Roman bridge, is now a small town with nothing memorable except its ruins and the sad traces of its antiquity. There were frequent commercial dealings between the Emeritans and the Caesaraugustans in former times, as three routes laid out by Antoninus from Emerita to Caesaraugusta show: through Contosolia, through Lacipea, and through a place called ad Sorores. There was also a town of the Turdetani there, which is Nertobriga for Ptolemy and Appian. From its ruins, as Arias Montanus thinks (cited by Abraham Ortelius), many towns were built: Frexenal, Fuentes, Bodenal and Higuera. Montanus adds that the huge ruins of Nertobriga can still be seen today three miles from Frexenal, where he himself was born, and that the locals call the place Valera.

units.la: CAP. XXVI. Portugallia.
units.tr: CAP. XXVI. Portugal.

units.la: PORTVGALLIA hodie, si Terrae latitudinem ab Meridie Septemtrionem versus spectemus, major est, quam Vetus Lusitania; sin ab Occasu in Ortum, Longitudinem, Minor. Lusitania olim ad Boream terminabatur Durio Flumine, & alio minore, quod hodie Thormis, in ripa dextra Urbem gestans Salamanticam; ductaque ad faciendum Limitem Orientalem ab hujus fonte per Solerium montem Saltumque Manlianum ad Anam (ubi Castra quondam Vicelliana) Linea; Anæque porro progressu per Emeritam Augustam ad Mare. Consulendi de his Lusitaniæ Finibus cum alij, tum prisci Geographi, cum primis Plinius lib. IIII. cap. XXI, & Ptolemæus. Paullo sequiores Lusitaniæ terminos tribuit Strabo lib. III; versus Austrum quidem, Tagum; ab Occasu vero & Septemtrione, Oceanum; ad Ortum denique, Carpetanos, Vettones, Vaccæos & Callaicos. Sic, quidquid ad sinistram Tagi ripam Oceanum usque includunt Lusitaniæ alij, excludit Strabo, quidquid ultra Durium ad Oceanum adimunt alij, adcenset eidem Lusitaniæ Strabo. Huic Suffragari videtur lib. II, cap. VI. Pomponius Mela, Lusitania, inquiens, Oceano tantummodo objecta est; sed Latere ad Septemtrionem, Fonte ad Occasum. Idem tamen Strabo alibi, ubi de Bætica, suo tempore Durio terminatam fuisse Lusitaniam ait; hinc ad Artos, quæ hodie Gallecia, aliquando Lusitaniam quoque dictam. Portugallia vero hoc ævo versus Boream excurrit supra Confluentes Minium Aviamque ad opidum usque Ribadaniam, in Aviæ ripa positam; qua parte Galeciam spectat; ductaque hinc in ortum Linea ad Mirandam usque ad Durium collocatam; inde vero Meridiem versus recto fere progressu facto ad ostia Anæ Fluvij; quo latere Castellæ, Extremadurae & Andaluziæ est confinalis: ad Notum & Occidentem Atlanticum respicit Oceanum, adeo ut ambitus ejus censeatur esse Ioccexxc miliarium. Lusitania (quæ Λυσιτανία Ptolemæo & aliis; Appiano autem Alexandrino Λυσιτανία) nomen impositum tradunt M. Varro & Plinius, ab Luso Liberi Filio, Lysaque cum eo bacchante: Lusitaniam enim dici, tamquam Lusi regionem, quum Ταρία nihil aliud quam Regio. Marcianus putat Lusitaniam appellari ab Fluvio cognomine. An Tagum, qui mediam secabat Lusitaniam, an vero Anam designet, qui Orientale radebat latus, ipsis Incolis quærendum relinquo. Sunt certe alij, qui ab Ana sic nominatam censent, quasi apud eumdem Amnem Liber-Pater ac Lysas bacchantes simul luserint. Videndus Plinius III. cap. II. Portugalliam quidam sic nuncupatam volunt à Portu Gallorum. Andreas Refcendius, cujus sententiam fequuntur alij Docti, Portugallia appellationem manasse notat à Portu Cale, quod Opidulum Durij Fluminis ostio adpositum Piscationis gratia frequentari quondam solitum: unde tanta hominum multitudo confluxit, ut in Civitatem opulentissimam evaserit, & Portogalo (quasi Portus Cale) nominari coeperit; inde vero totum Regnum nomen postea obtinuisse. Alij Portugalliam appellari opinantur, tamquam Portum Galeciæ, ab Opido Portu, de quo antea dixi; quod Durio adlocatum ob summam opportunitatem ingressum dabat in totam olim Galeciam; cujus nomen longe lateque quondam se extendebat; quod alibi à me notatum. In tres fere partes secant hanc Regionem duo Fluvij, Tagus & Durius. Pars quæ ad sinisteriora Tagi (unde Transf. Tagana) versus Meridiem rarius habitatur, Montibus plurimum obsita & sterilis: quæ ad dexteriora Durij (Καλλαικα olim Straboni, hodie Antre Douro & Minho, Latinis quibusdam Scriptoribus Interamnis) vicinæ ibi Galeciæ non est dissimilis; Incola magis, quam Opibus abundans: quæ inter utramque ad dextram Tagi ripam, Castellas æmulatur, imo superat; ccccl xx circiter opidis arcibusque dives. De Regionis hujus fertilitate & optima Aëris temperie commemorat quædam Athenæus lib. viii. cap. 1.
units.tr: Portugal today, if we measure the breadth of the land from south to north, is larger than old Lusitania; but if we measure its length from west to east, it is smaller. Lusitania was formerly bounded on the north by the river Durius and by another smaller river, which is now called the Tormes, carrying the city of Salamanca on its right bank. Its eastern boundary was drawn from the source of this river through the Solerian mountain and the Manlian pass to the Anas (where the camp of Vicellia once stood), and from there along the course of the Anas through Augusta Emerita to the sea. On these boundaries of Lusitania both others and the ancient geographers should be consulted, above all Pliny, book 4, chapter 21, and Ptolemy. Strabo, book 3, assigns somewhat later limits to Lusitania: to the south, the Tagus; to the west and north, the Ocean; and to the east, the Carpetani, Vettones, Vaccaei and Callaici. Thus whatever others include in Lusitania as far as the Ocean on the left bank of the Tagus, Strabo excludes; and whatever others take away beyond the Durius to the Ocean, Strabo adds to the same Lusitania. Pomponius Mela, book 2, chapter 6, seems to support this view: "Lusitania," he says, "is bordered by the Ocean only; but its side lies to the north, its source to the west." Yet Strabo elsewhere, when speaking of Baetica, says that in his own time Lusitania was bounded by the Durius, and that from there to the Artabri, which is now Galicia, it was also sometimes called Lusitania. In this age, however, Portugallia extends northward above the confluence of the Minius and the Avia, as far as the town of Ribadavia, which lies on the bank of the Avia, on the side where it faces Galicia. From there a line is drawn eastward to Miranda, which is situated on the Durius; and from there the boundary runs almost straight to the south, to the mouths of the river Anas, on the side where it borders Castile, Estremadura and Andalusia. It faces the south and the western Atlantic Ocean, so that its circuit is reckoned at 1,500 miles. Lusitania (which is Λυσιτανία to Ptolemy and others, and Λυσιτανία to Appian of Alexandria) is said by M. Varro and Pliny to have received its name from Lusus, a son of Liber, and the Lysae raging with him in Bacchic frenzy. For Lusitania is said to be the region of Lusus, since Lusi [Ταρία] means nothing other than region. Marcian thinks that Lusitania was named after a river of the same name. Whether it is the Tagus, which cut through the middle of Lusitania, or the Anas, which bordered its eastern side, I leave for the inhabitants themselves to determine. There are certainly others who think it was named from the Anas, as if Liber-Pater and the raving Lysae had played together by the same river. Plinius, book 3, chapter 2, should be consulted. Some want Portugallia to be so called from the Portus Gallorum. Andreas Resendius, whose opinion other learned men follow, notes that the name Portugallia derives from Portus Cale, a small town placed at the mouth of the river Durius, which was once often frequented for fishing; from it such a crowd of people flocked together that it grew into a very wealthy city, and began to be called Portugalo (as if Portus Cale); and afterwards the whole kingdom took its name from it. Others think that Portugallia is so called as the Portum Galeciae, from the town of Porto, which I mentioned earlier; situated on the Durius, it gave, because of its great convenience, an entrance into all of Galicia, the name of which once extended far and wide; I have noted this elsewhere. Two rivers, the Tagus and the Durius, divide this region into roughly three parts. The part which lies to the left of the Tagus (whence Transf. Tagana) towards the south is inhabited more sparsely, is very much beset with mountains, and is barren. The part near the right of the Durius (Καλλαικα [Callaica] to Strabo of old, now Entre Douro e Minho, and by some Latin writers Interamnis) is not unlike the neighbouring Galicia; it is more abundant in people than in wealth. The region lying between these two, on the right bank of the Tagus, rivals and indeed surpasses Castile, being rich in about 250 towns and fortresses. Athenaeus, book 8, chapter 1, relates some things about the fertility of this region and the excellent temperature of its air.

units.la: Totum illud, quod hodie Portugallia adscribitur, tenuerunt olim, extra Veterem quidem Lusitaniam, versus Boream, præter Nemetatos Ptolemæi, & Origenos Plinij (quorum latiorem explicationem brevitati consulens omitto) Populi qui Gravij Plinio; quosque Pomponius Mela, inemendate forsitan, Grovios vocat: Gravios, quasi Grajos nuncupatos canit Silius Italicus lib. iii;
units.tr: All that is today ascribed to Portugal was held in former times, beyond old Lusitania toward the north, by the Nemetati of Ptolemy and the Origeni of Pliny (whose fuller explanation I omit, to keep this brief), and by the people whom Pliny calls Gravii, and whom Pomponius Mela, perhaps wrongly, calls Grovii. Silius Italicus, in book 3, sings that the Gravios were named as if they were Grajos (Greeks):

units.la: Et quos nunc Gravios violato nomine Graium Oeneæ miseræ Domus, Aetolaque Tydæ.
units.tr: And those whom they now call Gravii, their name corrupted from Graii, of the wretched house of Oeneus, and of Aetolian Tydeus.

units.la: Idem Silius lib. 1 Populos hosce locat ad Lethen, Hispaniæ Fluvium; qua de re cap. vii: Bracari Plinio; Βρακαροι Appiano: Βρακαιοι (forte an Βρακαιοι) Ptolemæo & Straboni: In ipsa vero Lusitania, Bellitani Plinio, Βελιταυοι Stephano; & alij. De Rebus contra Lusitanos, eorumque Ducem Viriatum ab s. p. q. r. gestis, anno ab v.c. 1001 multisque sequentibus, legendi Appianus in Ibericis, Epitomæ Livianæ, Eutropius lib. iv, Florus lib. ii. cap. xvii, Orosius lib. v. cap. iv, Velleius Paterculus lib. i, Strabo lib. iii, Obsequens cap. lxxvii, Silius Italicus lib. iii, Valerius Maximus lib. vi, Cicero lib. i. Officiorum, & alij. Lusitanos fortissimos, sed Latrocinijs infames; Agros minime colere; esse insidiandi indagandique peritos, celeres, leves & versatiles; Butyrum eis Olei usum supplevisse; Vasis uti solitos cereis; Coriacijs usos fuisse nauigijs vsque ad Brutum, postea vero Magnas habuisse Onerarias Naves, maximo numero, liquet ex Strabone; fidem ijs etiam faciente Sidonio Apollinari in Panegyrico, quem Majorano inscripsit. Apud Lusitanos Carbasa quoque primum reperta fuisse, notat Plinius. Scribit item Strabo Lusitanos Marti Caprum immolare, præterea Captivos & Equos futura ex Captivorum Extis prædicere, quin & ritu Græcorum hecatombas instituere, item gymnica exercere Certamina solitos.
units.tr: Silius places these peoples in book 1 near the Lethe, a river of Spain; on this matter see chapter vii. Pliny calls them Bracari; Appian Βρακαροι; Ptolemy and Strabo Βρακαιοι (perhaps rather Βρακαιοι). Within Lusitania itself, Pliny calls them Bellitani, and Stephanus Βελιταυοι; and others too. On the deeds done by the Senate and People of Rome against the Lusitanians and their leader Viriathus, in the year 1001 from the founding of the city and in many following years, one should read Appian in his Iberian history, the Livian epitomes, Eutropius book 4, Florus book 2, chapter 17, Orosius book 5, chapter 4, Velleius Paterculus book 1, Strabo book 3, Obsequens chapter 77, Silius Italicus book 3, Valerius Maximus book 6, Cicero, On Duties book 1, and others. The Lusitanians were very brave but infamous for brigandage; they hardly cultivated the fields; they were skilled at ambushing and tracking, swift, light and versatile. Butter served them in place of oil. They were accustomed to use vessels of wax. They used boats covered with hides until the time of Brutus, but afterwards they had large merchant ships in great numbers, as is clear from Strabo; Sidonius Apollinaris also bears witness to this in his Panegyric, which he dedicated to Majorian. Pliny notes that sailcloth of linen was first discovered among the Lusitanians. Strabo also writes that the Lusitanians sacrificed a goat to Mars, and foretold the future from the entrails of captives and of horses; and in the Greek manner they also instituted hecatombs and were accustomed to hold gymnic contests.

units.la: Portugalliæ Metropolis est Olisippo, ut ea dicitur in antiquis & probatæ fidei M. Terentij Varronis ii rerum rusticarum, Plinij, Antonini & Pomponij Melæ Exemplaribus. In Vulgatis enim nunc Olissipo, nunc Olysippo, item Vlysippo, aliisque modis scribitur: Ὀλισσὼν Straboni; Ὀυισσὼν Stephano: Hodie Lisbona, vel, ut Incolæ proferunt, Lisboa. Vrbis nomen ab Vlysse (quod ex Myrliani verbis conatur facere Strabo, & sequutus eum Isidorus lib. xv, cap. 1) dirivare, absurdissimum; quum is extra Fretum Herculeum numquam navigarit. Præit nonnihil ad verum Etymon Ptolemæus, apud quem divisim & vitiosa legitur ὀλίσ ιππων. Olisippo enim, meo quidem judicio, quasi ὀλίσ ιππων; quo innuitur totum illum Hispaniæ tractum, ubi antiquis Lusitania, tamquam Equorum quoddam fuisse Stabulum, ob incredibilem Equarum ijs in locis fœcunditatem; quæ tanta fuit, ut eas Favonio flanti obversas certo tempore solitas concipere, fabulata fuerit Antiquitas: qua de re dictum à me abunde hujus libri cap. iii. Apud Plinium etiam Felicitas Iulia nuncupatur. Emporium est, reliquis Orbis Terrarum nobilissimis concensendum; Divitijs supra modum adfluens; Mercium peregrinarum, quæ ex Asia, Africa, Americaque adferuntur, Promptuarium celebre: Situs ad Tagi fere Ostium amœnissimi commodissimique: amplum, quodque sua magnitudine Montes quinque, totidemque Valles (nam olim multo erat minus, unumque tantum, ut quidam tradunt, Collem occupabat) complectitur. Ex parte, qua mari adluitur, Portis distinguitur xxii: qua Continentem respicit, xvi: Turribus per Murorum gyrum lxxvii munitur. Ambitus septem passuum millibus designatur. Templa, quae Graecis Parochiae, xxv numerantur: praeter haec plurima sunt quae Monachis, Anachoretis, Vestalibusque sunt attributa. Eripuit eam Maurorum faucibus rex Alphonsus anno clocxlvii. Prolixior esset in hac Urbe delineanda, nisi eam peculiari libello descripsisset plene Damianus à Goes Eques Lusitanus. Antoninus in Itinerario quatuor Olisippone Itinera ducit; tria quidem Emeritam, per Equilonam (Couna hodie est) per Attium Praetorium, per Hierabrigam; quartum autem Bracaram Augustam per eandem Hierabrigam: quorum intermedia loca, quod praeter duo vel tria ad certam hodie stationem referri nequeant, hic non recensebo. Olisipponem, ut Matrem agnoscunt & venerantur Transtaganae: Ebora; sic nominatur Plinio, Antonino, Pomponio Melae; Ἐβορα autem Ptolemaeo; quae vulgo hodieque Evora. Ebora meminerunt veteres lapides; inter quos ex Andreae Resendii Monumentis ille satis cognitus, xii ab Urbe Milliario, via Salaciensi, cum hac Inscriptione: IMP. CAES. MAXIMIANO. PIO. FELICI. AVG. EBORA. M. P. XII. Liberalitas Julia cognominatur Plinio lib. iii, cap. xxii, ad differentiam aliorum Hispaniae Opidorum, quae Ebora dicebantur. Academiam habet Ebora, ab Henrico Cardinale Lusitaniae, ejusdemque Civitatis Praesule, nuper institutam. De ea Iacobus Payva, Quodsi Academiarum, inquit, gloria magis litterarum & virtutum splendore, quam Antiquitate constat; haec certe paullo ante constituta cum antiquissimis & toto orbe celeberrimis jure certare poterit. Satis enim illa praefert specimen Integritatis, Prudentiae, Pietatis, Fidei & Religionis, quibus mirum in modum excellit Henricus Princeps clarissimus; qui illam egregie fundatam, mirifice auctam, omnibus necessariis rebus munitam, nobis & posteritati exaedificavit. Begia, vulgo Beja, vel Bexa: olim, uti censent Io. Mariana, Clusius, Vasaeus, & Caspar Varrerius in Chorographia Lusitanicae edita, Pax Julia, Antonino: Παξ Ἰουλία, Ptolemaeo. Addit Vasaeus eam Maurorum adhuc tempore Paccam fuisse appellatam. De ea dixi nonnihil cap. xxvi. Setubal, olim, ut opinatur Clusius, Salacia; quae tamen Varrerio Moralique putatur Alcasar de sal in Algerbiae regione. Clusio ut subscribam, faciunt Veteres Scriptores. Pomponius; In Sacro Promontorio, inquit, Lacobriga: & in Magno Ebora, statimque subdit: Sinus intersunt, & est in proximo Salacia, in altero Olisippo & Tagi ostium. Plinius post Olisipponem à Tago Salaciam recenseт; cognominatam Urbem Imperatoriam. Ptolemaeo ab Occasu juxta Oceanum in Turdetanis Lusitaniae Σαλαξια. Consulendum & Antonini Itinerarium. Urbi nomen inditum videtur ab Salacia; quam Oceani Sororem Terraeque Filiam confinxerunt Antiqui. Almada; Ptolemaeo Καιν-Βρίξ; Antonino Caetobriga: Iacobus tamen Delgadus scribit hodie vulgo Troiam vocari. Cis Tagum haud procul Olisippone Aquilonem versus Cascale Opidum est situm, ubi Naves Onerariae, jactis Anchoris, Ventum Aestumque maris, ut flumen ascendant, operiuntur: Portum habet vadosum & amfractuosum. Propius ad Urbem accedenti Bethleem occurrit, Opidulum, Templum habens Divae Virgini dicatum, sumtuque incredibili exstructum: Emanuelis Lusitaniae Regis Monimentum, quod, dum viveret, sibi ipse designavit. Magna tamen Operi accessio facta ab Ioanne iii Emanuelis Filio; quod indicat inscriptum Arcui Tetrastichon; litteris bellalibus: Vasta moles sacrum divina in litore Matri Rex posuit, Regum maximus, Emmanuel: Auxit opus haeres Regni & pietatis; uterque Structura certant Religione pares.
units.tr: The metropolis of Portugal is Olisippo, so called in the old and trustworthy copies of M. Terentius Varro's Rerum rusticarum book 2, and of Pliny, Antoninus and Pomponius Mela. In the common printed editions it is written now Olissipo, now Olysippo, also Ulysippo, and in other ways; Ὀλισσών in Strabo, Ὀυισσών in Stephanus. Today it is Lisbona, or, as the inhabitants pronounce it, Lisboa. That the city's name derives from Ulysses (which Strabo tries to make out of the words of Myrlianus, and Isidore, book 15, chapter 1, following him) is most absurd, since Ulysses never sailed beyond the Pillars of Hercules. Ptolemy comes somewhat closer to the true etymology, in whom it is read divided and corruptly as ὀλίσ ιππων. For Olisippo, in my judgement, is as it were ὀλίσ ιππων [olis hippon], by which is meant that the whole tract of Spain where ancient Lusitania lay was, as it were, a certain stable of horses, because of the incredible fertility of the mares in those parts; this was so great that antiquity fabled that they, turned toward the west wind at a certain season, were accustomed to conceive. I have spoken about this at length in chapter 3 of this book. Pliny also calls it Felicitas Iulia. It is a trading city, the most noble of all the cities of the world, overflowing with riches beyond measure, a famous storehouse of foreign goods brought from Asia, Africa and America. Its site, almost at the mouth of the Tagus, is most pleasant and convenient. It is large, and by its size embraces five hills and as many valleys (for formerly it was much smaller and occupied only one hill, as some relate). On the side washed by the sea it has 22 gates; on the side facing the mainland, 16; and it is defended by 77 towers around the circuit of its walls. Its circumference is reckoned at seven miles. The churches, which the Greeks call parishes, number 25; besides these there are very many assigned to monks, anchorites and vestals. King Alphonsus snatched it from the jaws of the Moors in the year 1147. The description of this city would be more lengthy, had not Damian à Goes, a Portuguese knight, described it fully in a separate little book. Antoninus, in his Itinerary, lays out four routes from Olisippo: three to Emerita, one by Equilona (today Couna), one by Attium Praetorium, and one by Hierabriga; and a fourth to Bracara Augusta by the same Hierabriga. I shall not list the intermediate places here, since, apart from two or three, they cannot today be referred to a definite station. The people beyond the Tagus acknowledge Olisippo as their mother. Next comes Ebora, so named by Pliny, Antoninus and Pomponius Mela, and Ἐβορα by Ptolemy; it is commonly called Evora today. Ancient stones mention Ebora; among them the one well known from the monuments of Andreas Resendius, twelve miles from the city on the Salacian road, bears an inscription to the emperor Maximian Pius Felix Augustus, with the name of Ebora and the distance of twelve miles. Pliny, book 3, chapter 22, calls it Liberalitas Julia, to distinguish it from other Spanish towns that were called Ebora. Ebora has an academy, recently founded by Henry, Cardinal of Portugal and bishop of this city. Of it Jacobus Payva says: "If the glory of academies rests more on the splendour of letters and virtues than on antiquity, then this one, founded only a little while ago, will be able to compete rightly with the most ancient and most celebrated in the whole world. For it already shows enough of a pattern of integrity, prudence, piety, faith and religion, in which the most illustrious prince Henry excels in a remarkable way; he founded it splendidly, enlarged it wonderfully, furnished it with all necessary things, and built it for us and for posterity." Beja, commonly called Beja or Bexa, was formerly, as Juan de Mariana, Clusius, Vasaeus and Caspar Varrerius in their published Chorography of Lusitania think, Pax Julia to Antoninus, and Παξ Ἰουλία to Ptolemy. Vasaeus adds that in the time of the Moors it was still called Pacca. I said something about it in chapter xxvi. Setubal, formerly, as Clusius thinks, was Salacia; but Varrerius and Moralis think it is Alcacer do Sal in the region of Algarve. To agree with Clusius, the ancient writers support him. Pomponius says: "On the Sacred Promontory is Lacobriga, and on the Great one Ebora," and at once adds: "Bays lie between, and nearby is Salacia; on the other side Olisippo and the mouth of the Tagus." Pliny, after Olisippo, lists Salacia from the Tagus, surnamed the Imperial City. Ptolemy places Σαλαξια [Salaxia] to the west, near the Ocean, among the Turdetani of Lusitania. The Itinerary of Antoninus should also be consulted. The city seems to have been named after Salacia, whom the ancients imagined as the sister of Ocean and daughter of Earth. Almada: Ptolemy has Καιν-Βρίξ [Kain-Brix], Antoninus Caetobriga; James Delgado, however, writes that today it is commonly called Troia. On this side of the Tagus, not far from Olisippo toward the north, lies the town of Cascale, where merchant ships, having cast anchor, wait for the wind and the tide to carry them up the river; its harbour is shallow and winding. Approaching the city more closely, one meets Bethleem, a little town with a temple dedicated to the Virgin Mother of God, built at incredible expense. It is the monument of King Emmanuel of Lusitania, which he himself designed while he was alive. However, a great addition to the work was made by John III, son of Emmanuel; the four-line verse inscribed on the arch shows this, in handsome lettering: "The king, greatest of kings, Emmanuel, raised this vast pile of stone on the shore for the divine Mother; the heir of the kingdom and of piety increased the work; both vie in building with equal devotion."

units.la: Sunt ibidem Leiria, Tomar, Guarda; non ignobilia, neque obscuri nominis Opida. Propē Leiriam urbs fuit quae Plinio dicitur Colippo; cujus ruinas S. Sebastiani vocari ab Sacello proximo Varrerius in suo Itinerario, Lusitanica lingua scripto, memoriae prodit. Haud procul Tomare visitur Cetce, quam quibusdam fretus conjecturis idem Varrerius arbitratur esse Celium Antonini. Alanqueram ad Fluvium Tagum supra Olisipponem, Patriam suam Damianus Goesius, sic dictam putat tamquam Alankerke, Alanorum Fanum; ingeniose, &, non dubito, quin vere: Haec olim Ierabrica Antonino, uti censent Resendius apud Vasaeum, Varrerius, cujus saepe memini, & Ambrosius Moralis. Incolæ apud Plinium corrupte Axaltritenses, pro Hierabrigensibus. Hierabriga enim in melioribus Antonini Codicibus dicitur. Inter Mondam & Durium fluvios Conimbrica est: sic Plinius & Antoninus Opidum vocant, quod notante Emanule Enriquo Lusitano hodieque Coimbra: Phlegonti Tralliano Κοιμβεργεια nominatur. Olim caput fuit Regni Portugalliæ: hodie Academia, quam nuper instituit Ioannes II Portugalliæ Rex; & Aquæductu, quem maximo sumtu perfecit anno cIↄ IↄLxxii. Rex Sebastianus, celebris. Viseum, vulgo Viseo; Visensis Civitas in Conciliorum Opere: Ptolemæo, ut Villanovanus existimat, Βίσσεος; quod tamen ab Viseo multis parasangis distare, docet Varrerius in sua Chorographia: Viseum, Vicum Aquarium Antonini esse, non satis caute scribit Andreas Bacchius in suo de Balneis opere. Quod opidum hodie Ponte Vouga, Plinio putatur Vacca; Orosio libro quinto, cap. iv, vitiose Baccia; ubi scribit eam à Q. Fabio Serviliano deditione receptam. Lameca quæ vulgo Lamego, meminit Concilium Toletanum III: Lamecum etiam ab Latinis nuncupari notat Emanuel Enriquus Lusitanus. Inter Durium denique & Minium Braga superbit: sic hodie dicitur, quæ Βεγκαρ Αυγυστα Ptolemæo, Braccara Augusta Antonino, Augusta Bracarum Plinio; unde Bracari populi, de quibus paullo ante. Ab Gallis Bracatis conditam fama refert, anno ante Christum natum ccxc. Augusta cognomen addiderunt Romani Victores. Tam olim celebris, ut Conventus hic fuerit ex septem Citerioris Hispaniæ unus, unde Vrbes xxiv, auctore Plinio, jus petere consueverant; undeque ab Antonino quatuor Itinera Militaria in Asturias describuntur; Primum per Salaciam, Secundum per Aquas Celenias, Tertium per Salanianam, Quartum denique per Limiam. Ausonius hanc urbem tali nobilitat Elogio:
units.tr: There are also Leiria, Tomar and Guarda, towns that are not ignoble and not of obscure name. Near Leiria was a city that Pliny calls Colippo. Varrerius, in his Itinerary written in the Portuguese language, records that its ruins are called those of S. Sebastian, from a nearby chapel. Not far from Tomar is seen Cetce, which Varrerius, relying on certain conjectures, thinks is the Celium of Antoninus. Alanquer, on the river Tagus above Lisbon, his own homeland, Damianus Goesius thinks was so called as if it were Alankerke, the shrine of the Alani. He suggests this cleverly, and I do not doubt that it is true. This town was formerly Ierabrica in Antoninus, as Resendius (cited by Vasaeus), Varrerius, whom I often mention, and Ambrosius Moralis think. In Pliny the inhabitants are corruptly called Axaltritenses, for Hierabrigenses, since Hierabriga is the name in the better manuscripts of Antoninus. Between the rivers Mondego and Douro lies Conimbrica. Pliny and Antoninus call the town this, and it is today Coimbra, as the Lusitanian Emanuel Enriquez notes. Phlegon of Tralles calls it Κοιμβεργεια [Koimbergeia]. It was once the capital of the kingdom of Portugal. Today it has an Academy, which John II, King of Portugal, recently founded, and an aqueduct, which he completed at very great expense in 1572. King Sebastian, famous. Viseum, commonly Viseu, is the "city of Viseu" in the work of the Councils. In Ptolemy, as Villanovanus thinks, it is Βίσσεος [Bisseos]. Varrerius, in his Chorography, teaches that it is, however, many parasangs from Viseu. Andreas Bacchius, in his work on baths, writes not cautiously enough that Viseum is the Vicus Aquarius of Antoninus. The town that today is Ponte Vouga is thought by Pliny to be Vacca; in Orosius, book 5, chapter 4, it is wrongly called Baccia, where he writes that it was received by Q. Fabius Servilianus on surrender. Lameca, which is commonly Lamego, is mentioned by the Third Council of Toledo. Emanuel Enriquez the Lusitanian notes that it is also called Lamecum by Latin writers. Finally, between the Douro and the Minho, Braga holds its head high. It is so called today, and is Βεγκαρ Αυγυστα [Bengar Augusta] in Ptolemy, Braccara Augusta in Antoninus, and Augusta Bracarum in Pliny. From it come the Bracari people, of whom I spoke a little earlier. Report says it was founded by the Gauls called Bracati in the year 290 before the birth of Christ. The Roman victors added the surname Augusta. It was once so famous that this assize district was one of the seven of Hither Spain, and from it, according to Pliny, twenty-four cities were accustomed to seek law. From Antoninus, four military roads to the Asturias are described from it: the first through Salacia, the second through the Aquae Celenias, the third through Salaniana, and the fourth finally through Limia. Ausonius ennobles this city with this eulogy:

units.la: Quaeque sinu pelagi jactat se Bracara dives.
units.tr: "And Braga, rich, which boasts itself in the bosom of the sea."

units.la: Ad quem locum Vinetus: O quam dudum, inquit, sedes est, ubi Troia fuit. Everterunt & hanc cum Eme ita Barbari. Parva urbs, in magna illius Bracarae suburbio exstructa; ad cujus partem, eam quae Orientem respicit, effodiuntur subinde Veteris Urbis insignes ruinae. Sita est ad Alestcn fluvium; cujus fontes in Spino monte quatuor ab Vrbe milliaribus distant: Vallem amœnissimam Vrbi adjacentem irrigat: multis hortis, pomariis, pratis & viridariis excultam: Vrbem adluit, atque in Avum majoris famæ fluvium prope antiquum opidum Villam Comitis influit. Quidam falso Sethen vocant. Extra Portam, quæ de Sancto dicitur, D. Annæ Ædicula est, quam xii Columnæ ab Romanis variis quondam in locis erectæ, Litteris incisæ, ornant atque cingunt. Ad Meridionalem Vrbis partem Silva est Primattali, Perdicum ac Leporum abundantia celebris; in cujus fere medio Fons est amœnissimus. Hinc versus Occidentem progredienti locus se offert, quo Vrbis Arx Romanorum tempore fuisse creditur. Haud procul inde S. Sebastiani est ædicula, ubi Forum Romanorum fuisse perhibetur. Totius Hispaniæ Primatum antiquissimo jure sibi vindicat: qua de re cum Toletana Sede vetus ei Lis est & Contentio, cujus meminit Honorius iii p. m. in Cap. Coram. De in integrum restitutione: quæ tamen iis ab ejusdem Pontificis tempore ad nostram usque ætatem adhuc altum silet. Archiepiscopo Civitas pleno jure paret, sive spiritualem spectes Iurisdictionem, sive temporalem: multo quondam frequentior, nunc Incolarum numerat duo circiter millia. Conventus porro Bracaraugusiani, de quo paullo ante, meminit Inscriptio, quæ ibi hodieque in ædicula Laurentij cujusdam Bracarensis Archiepiscopi legitur: ISIDI. AVG. SACRVM LVCRETIA. FIDA. SACERDOS, PERP ROM. ET. AVG CONVENTVS. BRACARAVG. V. D Addam & duos Lapides in honorem duorum Civium Bracaraugustanorum positos, qui Tarraconę servantur: Q. IONTIO. Q. F. | M. VLTIO. C. F. QVIR. SEVERO | QVIR. REBVRRO BRAC. AVG | EX. BRACARAVG OMNIBVS. HONORIB | OMNIBVS. H. IN IN. RE. P. SVA. FVNCTO | RE. P. SVA. FVNC FLAM. P. H. C | FLAM. P. H. C P. H. C | P. H. C
units.tr: On this passage Vinetus says: "Oh, how long ago it became the seat where Troy once was! The barbarians overthrew this town too, along with Eme, in the same way. It is a small town, built in the suburb of that great Braga, and on the side facing east, remarkable ruins of the old city are constantly being dug up." It lies on the river Alestcn, whose sources are on Mount Spino, four miles from the city. It waters a most pleasant valley adjoining the city, cultivated with many gardens, orchards, meadows and groves. It washes the city and flows into the Avus, a river of greater fame, near the old town Villa Comitis. Some falsely call it Sethen. Outside the gate called "de Sancto" is a little shrine of St Anne, adorned and surrounded by twelve columns, inscribed with letters, which the Romans erected at various times and places. On the southern side of the city is the Primattali forest, famous for its abundance of partridges and hares; roughly in its middle is a most pleasant spring. Going westward from here, one comes to a place which is believed to have been the citadel of the city in Roman times. Not far from there is a little shrine of St Sebastian, where the Roman forum is said to have been. The city claims the primacy of all Spain by a most ancient right, and on this matter it has long had a dispute and contention with the See of Toledo. Honorius III mentions this in the chapter Coram, On Restitution in Integrum, but the matter has kept a deep silence from that Pope's time down to our own age. The city obeys the Archbishop with full right, whether one regards his spiritual or his temporal jurisdiction. It was once much more crowded, and now it has about two thousand inhabitants. Further, the assize of Braga Augusta, of which I spoke a little earlier, is recorded in an inscription that is still read today in the little shrine of a certain Laurentius, Archbishop of Braga: "To Isis Augusta, sacred. Lucretia Fida, priestess, in perpetuity, for the Roman people and Augustus; the assize of Braga Augusta." I will also add two stones set up in honour of two citizens of Braga Augusta, which are kept at Tarragona. To Q. Iontius, son of Quintus, and M. Ultius, son of Gaius, of the tribe Quirina, Severus and Reburrus, of Braga Augusta, who held all the honours of their own state and were priests of the province at their own expense.

units.la: Quod porro Ca'em Antonino, nunc Gaia censetur: quod Φόρῳ Λιμικὰν Ptolemæo, hodie Lima: quod κλιούσσσ eidem, hoc ævo putatur Bergança. Sex milliaribus à Bracara Augusta versus Euronorum locus est, qui Sita ia Incolis nominatur, habitatore carens, ubi olim Cinninia fuisse perhibetur, nobilis Lusitaniæ Vrbs.
