De ea sic Valerius lib. vi, cap. iv, quod Grauiter Dictis Factisque inscriptum: Cujus (egerat de M. Bruto) mentio mihi subiit, quod adversus D. Brutum in Hispania graviter dictum est, referre. Nam quum se ei tota pene Lusitania dedidisset, ac sola gentis ejus urbs Cinninia (sic enim perscriptum in exaratis manu Codicibus, non Cinniana) perinde acriter arma retineret, tentata redemptione propemodum uno ore Legatis Bruti respondit: Ferrum jam à Majoribus, quo Vrbem tuerentur, non Aurum, quo Libertatem ab Imperatore avaro emerent, relictum. Ad Tammagum flumen Vicus est, non ultimi tamen nominis; Chaves vulgo appellatus: olim Aquiflavia, nobilis Lusitaniæ Civitas: cujus aliorumque novem Opidorum Incolæ Imperatori Vespasiano, ejusque Filiis Tito & Domitiano, Columnam posuerunt, cum, quæ sequitur, Inscriptione: IMP. CAES. VESP. AVG. PONT MAX. TRIB. POT. X. IMP. XX. P.P. IX IMP. VESP. CAES. AVG. F. PONT. TRIB POT. VIII. IMP. XIIII. COS. VI C. CALPETANO. RANTIO. QVIRINAL VAL. FESTO. LEG. AVG. PR. PR D. CORNELIO. MARCIANO. LEG. AVG L. ARVNTIO. MAXIMO. PROC. AVG LEG. VII. GEM. FEL CIVITATES. X AQVIFLAVIENSES. AOBRIGENS BIBALI. CELERNI. EQVAESI INTERAMICI. LIMICI. AEBISOC QVARQVERNI. TAMAGANI
units.tr: What Antoninus calls Ca'em is now thought to be Gaia. What Ptolemy calls Forum Limicum is today Lima. What the same author calls Klioussa is thought in this age to be Bergança. Six miles from Braga Augusta, toward the Euronii, is a place which the inhabitants call Sita, without any inhabitant, where Cinninia, a noble city of Lusitania, is said to have stood. Valerius writes of it in book 6, chapter 4, which is headed "Things Said and Done with Weight": "The mention of Marcus Brutus brought to mind something said with great weight against Decimus Brutus in Spain, which I should report. For when almost all of Lusitania had surrendered to him, and the city of that people alone, Cinninia (so it is written in hand-copied manuscripts, not Cinniana), kept its arms just as fiercely, and when a ransom was tried, it answered the envoys of Brutus almost with one voice: that iron had been left to them by their ancestors, with which to defend their city, not gold, with which to buy their liberty from a greedy commander." Near the Tamagus river is a village, not of the least name, commonly called Chaves. Formerly it was Aquiflavia, a noble city of Lusitania. Its inhabitants, together with those of nine other towns, set up a column to the Emperor Vespasian and to his sons Titus and Domitian, with the inscription that follows: "The Emperor Caesar Vespasian Augustus, Pontifex Maximus, holding tribunician power for the tenth time, acclaimed Imperator twentieth time, Father of the Fatherland, ninth acclamation as Imperator; and Vespasian Caesar, son of Augustus, Pontifex, tribunician power eighth time, Imperator fourteenth time, consul six times. In the consulship of Calpetanus Rantius Quirinalis and Valerius Festus, legate of Augustus with propraetorian power; in the time of Cornelius Marcianus, legate of Augustus, and Lucius Arruntius Maximus, procurator of Augustus, the Legion VII Gemina Felix. The ten states: the people of Aquiflavia, of Aobriga, Bibali, Celerni, Equaesi, Interamici, Limici, Aebisoc, Querquerni, Tamagani."

units.la: Pro Aobrigens, alij legunt Aobrigens. Bibali, Ptolemæo Βίβαλοι: Vibalis Plinio. Coelerni, κοιλέρνοι Ptolemæo: Celerini Plinio. De Equaesis nihil habeo. Interamici fortean in alia Inscriptione Interamnienses. Limicorum Φόρῳ, id est Forum, antea indicatus ex Ptolemæo. In voce Aebisoc erratum ab Sculptore, si quidem servatus fuerit, uti paret, ordo Alphabeticus: fortean exprimere oportebat Lebisoc, id est Lebisocenses; quorum urbs Αἰβίσσα Ptolemæo; Libisosa Antonino, Libisofona cognomine Foraugustana; hodie Lezuza. Quarquerni, Plinio Querquerni, κυαρκύριοι Ptolemæo, Querquenna, non sine menda, Antonino. A Tamaganis denique Tammagus hodie Fluvius, Tamuga vulgo: cui Pons impositus conspicitur insignis, multam præ se ferens majestatem; in quo sequens legitur Titulus: IMP. CAES. NERVAE TRAIANO. AVG. GER DACICO. PONT. MAX TRIB. POT. COS. V.P.P AQVIFLAVIENSES PONTEM. LAPIDEVM DE. SVO. P. C Portugalliæ Regnum primum circa annum cIo c initium habuit. Ad id enim usque tempus sub Hispaniæ nomine censebatur. Legendus omnino præter alios Ioannes Barrus cap. i. Asiaticarum Decadum. Primum Regum Lusitanorum Progenitorem Fasti commemorant Henricum Ducem Lotharingiæ, Comitem Limburgium, Virum Animo Magnum, Manuque promtum: qui, Laribus in Hispaniam translatis, Tyresiam duxit Alphonsi vi Castellæ Legionisque Regis Filiam, accepta in dotem ea Galeciæ Lusitaniæque parte, quæ nunc Portugallia dicitur; quam non ita pridem ipsemet sua virtute ex Saracenorum & Maurorum servitute vindicarat. Defuncto circa annum cIo cxii Patri successit Alphonsus i, qui Portugalliæ se ducem appellans, Regis titulum ab exercitu accepit anno clo cxxxix, victoriam consequutus in Agro Orichiensi contra Ismarium, & alios quatuor Saracenorum Maurorumque Reges; quinque Scutorum Insignia facti monimentum posteris relinquens. Successerunt huic recta fere linea Sanctius, Alphonsus ii, Sanctius ii, Alphonsus, iii, Dionysius, qui primus Algarbiorum Regis titulum usurpare cœpit, Alphonsus iv, Petrus, Ferdinandus, Ioannes, Eduardus, Alphonsus, v Africanus cognomine, Ioannes ii, Emanuel, Ioannes iii, Henricus primo Cardinalis, & Antonius: quo, quod Nothus diceretur, pulso, ut proximus heres Regnum occupavit Philippus ii Hispaniarum Rex, Emanuelis per Isabellam primogenitam Nepos; cujus hodie Filius Philippus iii feliciter Hispaniæ, quanta quanta est, imperat. De Portugalliæ Regibus, eorumque ortu & Genealogia, rebusque gestis, adeundi Rodericus Toletanus lib. vii. de Rebus Hispaniæ, cap. v, Rodericus Sanctius Hist. Hispan. parte i cap. xiv, Lucius Marineus Siculus lib. vii de Rebus Hispaniæ, in fine, & alij.
units.tr: For "Aobrigens," some read "Aobrigens." Bibali is Βίβαλοι [Bibaloi] in Ptolemy, Vibalis in Pliny. Coelerni is κοιλέρνοι [koilernoi] in Ptolemy, Celerini in Pliny. I have nothing to say about the Equaesi. The Interamici are perhaps the Interamnienses of another inscription. The Limici are the Forum Limicum, already indicated from Ptolemy. In the word Aebisoc there is an error by the engraver, if the alphabetical order, as it appears to be, has been kept. Perhaps it ought to be Lebisoc, that is, the Lebisocenses, whose city is Αἰβίσσα [Aibissa] in Ptolemy, Libisosa in Antoninus, and Libisofona with the surname Foraugustana; today it is Lezuza. The Querquerni are Querquerni in Pliny, κυαρκύριοι [kyarkyrioi] in Ptolemy, and in Antoninus, not without a flaw, Querquenna. Finally, from the Tamagani comes the Tammagus, today a river, commonly Tamuga. Over it a bridge is seen, remarkable and bearing a great air of majesty, on which the following title is read: "To the Emperor Caesar Nerva Trajan Augustus, conqueror of Germany and Dacia, Pontifex Maximus, holding tribunician power, consul for the fifth time, Father of the Fatherland: the people of Aquiflavia, at their own cost, built this stone bridge." The kingdom of Portugal first began about the year 1100 after Christ. Until that time it was counted under the name of Spain. Among others, John Barros, chapter 1 of his Asian Decades, should certainly be read. The Annals record as the first progenitor of the Portuguese kings Henry, Duke of Lorraine, Count of Limburg, a man great in spirit and ready with his hand. He moved his household into Spain and married Teresa, daughter of Alphonso VI, King of Castile and León, receiving as her dowry that part of Galicia and Lusitania which is now called Portugal. He had himself won it not long before by his own valour from the slavery of the Saracens and Moors. He died about the year 1112, and was succeeded by his son Alphonso I, who, calling himself Duke of Portugal, received the title of King from his army in the year 1139, having won a victory in the district of Orichia over Ismarius and four other kings of the Saracens and Moors. He left to posterity a monument of the deed in five shields as insignia. In an almost direct line there succeeded him Sancho, Alphonso II, Sancho II, Alphonso III, Denis, who first began to use the title of King of the Algarves, Alphonso IV, Peter, Ferdinand, John, Edward, Alphonso V, surnamed the African, John II, Emanuel, John III, Henry, first a Cardinal, and Anthony. When Anthony, who was called the bastard, had been driven out, Philip II, King of Spain, grandson of Emanuel through his eldest daughter Isabella, seized the kingdom as the nearest heir. His son Philip III now reigns happily over Spain, such as it is. For the kings of Portugal, their origin and genealogy, and their deeds, one should consult Rodericus Toletanus, book 7, On the Affairs of Spain, chapter 5; Rodericus Sanctius, History of Spain, part 1, chapter 14; Lucius Marineus Siculus, book 7, On the Affairs of Spain, at the end; and others.

units.la: CAP. XXVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVII.

units.la: Algarbia.
units.tr: Algarve.

units.la: LINEA, cujus initium ab Ana fluvio inter amnes, qui vulgo Vataon & Careivas, finis autem ad Opidulum Odesciza; id est ab Oriente versus Occidentem protracta, separat Algarbiæ regnum ab ipsa Portugallia; omnium Hispaniæ Regnorum minimum & ignobilissimum. Comportantur eo ex variis Hispaniæ partibus secundo Anæ decursu Vina omnis generis, Sicca, Bastarda, Romana, & ejus classis alia; quæ porro navibus impositæ in Galliam, Inferiorem Germaniam, alioque avehuntur.
units.tr: The LINE, which begins at the River Ana between the streams commonly called Vataon and Careivas and ends at the little town Odesciza, running from east to west, separates the kingdom of Algarve from Portugal proper. It is the smallest and least noble of all the kingdoms of Spain. From various parts of Spain, wines of every kind are brought there along the course of the Ana: sack, bastard, Roman, and other sorts. These are then loaded onto ships and carried to Gaul, Lower Germany and elsewhere.

units.la: Locasse quondam sua hic Domicilia notant Geographi Veteres, præter Cynetas, quos omnium Europæ ultimos versus Occasum facit Herodotus, & apud quos Anam effluere scribit Avienus; & Ostidamnios, quos ad ipsum Promontorium Calbium Europæ extremum locat Strabo: etiam Turdetanos; qui Turdetani Ptolemæo; quousque cum Turdulis Veteribus, de quibus cap. xxv, quidam confundunt: Strabo quosdam inter Turdulos & Turdetanos distinguere scribit; sed nullam distinctionem suo tempore adparere. Eorum Regio Turdetania Artemidoro apud Stephanum; cui & Τάρτοι & Τυρτεταυοι sunt noti. Quædam in Turdetanorum laudem dicta sunt à me cap. viii, ubi de Veterum Hispanorum lingua ex Strabone, qui duobus locis lib. iii illos mirum in modum commendat ab Sapientia, Litterarumque studiis; addens apud eos servari venerandæ antiquitatis Volumina, Poëmata, Legesque versibus ante sex annorum millia conscriptas: Augusti autem principatu, Latinos prope tactos, propriæ memoriam linguæ habuisse fere nullam; inque Romanos penitus ritus fuisse transformatos.
units.tr: The ancient geographers note that peoples once had their homes here: besides the Cynetes, whom Herodotus places furthest west of all the peoples of Europe, and among whom Avienus writes that the Ana flows out; and the Ostidamnii, whom Strabo places at the Cape Calbium, the farthest point of Europe; also the Turdetani. Ptolemy calls them Turdetani, though some confuse them with the old Turduli, of whom I shall speak in chapter 25. Strabo writes that some distinguish between the Turduli and the Turdetani, but that no such distinction appears in his own time. Their region is Turdetania, according to Artemidorus in Stephanus, who also knows them as Tartoi and Turtetauoi [Τάρτοι, Τυρτεταυοι]. I have said some things in praise of the Turdetani in chapter 8, where I dealt with the language of the ancient Spaniards, drawing on Strabo. In two places in book 3 he commends them remarkably for their wisdom and their devotion to literary studies, adding that among them were preserved volumes of venerable antiquity, poems and laws composed in verse six thousand years earlier. But in the reign of Augustus, having been nearly touched by Latin influence, they had almost no memory of their own language, and had been thoroughly transformed into Roman customs.

units.la: Opida habet Baisam Ptolemæo. Plinio, Antonino & Pomponio Melæ; quæ hodie Tavila, ut Coquus opinatur. Offonobam Plinio & Antonino; quorum ille Lusitaniam cognominati; Ὀαρέναβα est Ptolemæo; putaturque quæ nunc Silvis. Fuit etiam ibidem ad Sacrum Promontorium Vrbs Lacobriga Pomponio; cujus etiam nunc ruinæ ruderaque visuntur prope Lagos opidum maritimum, in Vico, qui Lusitanica Lingua Lagoa vocatur, uti scribit Vasæus: Ejus Incolæ Ἀαγγοβριγες Plutarcho, Sertorium depingenti.
units.tr: Ptolemy gives the town Baisa; Pliny, Antoninus and Pomponius Mela also mention it, and it is today Tavila, as Coquus thinks. Pliny and Antoninus give Offonoba; Pliny calls it surnamed Lusitanian, while in Ptolemy it is Oarenaba [Ὀαρέναβα]; and it is thought to be what is now Silves. Also at the Sacred Promontory there was the city Lacobriga, according to Pomponius; its ruins and rubble are still to be seen near Lagos, a seaside town, in a village which in the Portuguese language is called Lagoa, as Vasaeus writes. Its inhabitants are the Lacobrigenses, called Ἀαγγοβριγες [Ἀαγγοβριγες] by Plutarch in his account of Sertorius.

units.la: Algarbia, Comitatus initio in dotem ab Alphonso x, Legionis Rege, ut prisci referunt Annales, datus fuit Alphonso iii Portugalliæ Regi, quum filiam ipsius Beatricem, quam ex Pellice genuerat, uxorem duceret. Natus ex eo Conjugio Dionysius, qui primus Algarbiorum Regis titulum usurpare cœpit.
units.tr: Algarve, originally a county, was given as a dowry, as the old annals report, by Alphonso X, king of Leon, to Alphonso III, king of Portugal, when he married Beatrice, Alphonso X's daughter, whom he had by a concubine. From this marriage was born Dionysius, who was the first to take up the title of King of the Algarves.

units.la: Sed de Hispania quæ dicta sunt hactenus, sufficiant. Nefas sit autem non adscribere, Coronidis quasi loco, præclarum hominis Galli de Hispania Testimonium; quo quidquid in ejus laudem & commendationem hucusque à me Variorum indicio prolatum, tamquam per ἀναχιφαλαίωσιν succincte nervoseque repetitur. Gallus, cujus memini, Latinus est Pacatus, qui Panegyricum doctissimum scripsit Theodosio Imperatori, Hispano. In eo sic inter alia loquitur: Iam profecto constabit, eum Principem declaratum, qui & ab omnibus legi debuerit, & ex omnibus. Nam primum tibi mater Hispania est; Terris omnibus Terra felicior: cui excolenda atque adeo distanda impensius, quam ceteris Gentibus supremus ille Fabricator Rerum indulsit, qua nec Austrinis obnoxia æstibus, nec Arctoos subjecta frigoribus, media fovetur Axis utriusque temperie: qua hinc Pyrenæis Montibus, illinc Oceani æstibus, inde Tyrrheni Maris litoribus coronata, Natura solertis ingenii, velut alter Orbis includitur. Adde tot egregias Civitates; adde culta incultaque omnia, vel Fructibus plena, vel Gregibus; adde auriferorum opes Fluminum; adde radiantium Metalla Gemmarum. Scio Fabulas Poëtarum, auribus mulciendis repertas, aliqua nonnullis gentibus attribuisse miracula, quæ dum sint vera, sint singula; nec jam excutio veritatem. Sint (ut scribitur) Gargara proventu lata Tritici; Menavia memoretur Armento; Campania censeatur Monte Gaurano; Lydia prædicetur Amne Pactolo: dum Hispania uni quidquid laudatur, adsurgat. Hæc durissimos Milites, Hæc expertissimos Duces, Hæc facundissimos Oratores, Hæc clarissimos Vates parit: Hæc Iudicum Mater, Hæc Principum est: Hæc Traianum illum, Hæc deinceps Hadrianum misit Imperio: Huic Te debes Imperium. Cedat his Terra Cretensis, parvi Iovis gloriata cunabulis & geminis Delos reptata Numinibus; & alumno Hercule nobiles Thebæ. Fidem constare nescimus anditis, Deum dedit Hispania, quem vidimus.
units.tr: But let what has been said of Spain so far suffice. Yet it would be wrong not to add, as a kind of crown, the splendid testimony of a Gaul concerning Spain, in which everything I have so far brought forward from various authors in its praise and commendation is briefly and forcefully repeated, as a recapitulation [ἀναχιφαλαίωσιν]. The Gaul I mean is the Latin writer Pacatus, who wrote a most learned panegyric to the Emperor Theodosius, himself a Spaniard. In it he speaks, among other things, as follows: "Now it will certainly be established that he is proclaimed a prince who ought to be read by all and read from all. For first of all Spain is your mother, a land happier than all other lands, which the supreme Maker of things has been more generous in cultivating and adorning than other peoples. It is not exposed to the scorching of the south nor subject to the cold of the north; it is warmed by the middle temperature of the heavens. Here it is crowned by the Pyrenean mountains on one side, by the tides of the Ocean on another, and by the shores of the Tyrrhenian Sea on a third, and it is enclosed, like a second world, with the gifts of a clever nature. Add so many distinguished cities; add all things cultivated and uncultivated, some full of crops, some of flocks; add the wealth of its gold-bearing rivers; add the metals of its shining gems. I know that the fables of the poets, devised to soothe the ears, have assigned some marvels to some peoples, and that, though they may be true individually, I do not now examine their truth. Let Gargara be said to be broad with its harvest of wheat, let Menavia be remembered for its herds, let Campania be reckoned by Mount Gaurus, let Lydia be praised for the river Pactolus; yet Spain alone rises above all of these praises. This land bears the hardest soldiers, this the most expert generals, this the most eloquent orators, this the most famous poets; this is the mother of judges, this of princes. This sent that Trajan, and afterwards Hadrian, to the empire. To this land you owe your empire. Let the land of Crete yield to these, boasting of the cradle of little Jove, and Delos, which was tossed about by two divinities, and Thebes, noble for its foster-son Hercules. We do not know how to make the hearers believe it, but Spain has given us a God, whom we have seen."

units.la: PAVLLI G.F.P.N. MERVLÆ COSMOGRAPHIÆ PARTIS II, LIBER III. DE GALLIA.
units.tr: Paulli G.F.P.N. Merulae Cosmographiae, Part II, Book III: On Gaul.

units.la: CAP. I. Gallia unde dicta, variaque ejus Nomina.
units.tr: Chapter I. Whence Gallia takes its name, and its various names.

units.la: ISPANIAM, qua potui fide, perlustravi: Pyrenæos transgresso Gallia se offert. Hanc, qua fere illam Methodo, percurram; Generalia priore loco indicaturus, inde Specialia. In Generalibus duo describam, Nomen ipsum & Res. Quod ad Nomen, id est Etymon variasq; Appellationes: Partem Europæ, quæ hoc tempore Francia, dictam olim multi memoriæ produnt Γαλατίαν, ab Γάλα, Lac Latinis sonante, quod lacteos, id est albi coloris homines producat: Montibus (hoc enim addunt) nimium Solis ardorem inde excludentibus. Videndus Isidorus lib. xiv Origin. cap. iv. 10 Diodorus nomen natum scribit ab Galata Herculis filia. Alij alia tradunt.
units.tr: I have travelled through Spain as faithfully as I could, and on crossing the Pyrenees Gaul presents itself. I shall go through it by roughly the same method, first setting out the general matters and then the particular. Under the general matters I shall describe two things: the name itself and the thing named. As to the name, that is, its etymology and its various appellations: the part of Europe which is now called France was, many records say, formerly called Galatia, from Γάλα, which means milk in Latin, because it produces milky people, that is, people of white complexion, the mountains (for they add this) shutting out the excessive heat of the sun. See Isidore, Origines, book xiv, ch. iv. 10. Diodorus writes that the name came from Galata, daughter of Hercules. Others hand down other accounts.

units.la: Κελτογαλατία Ptolemæo nominatur lib. ii, ceterisque Græcis.
units.tr: Ptolemy in book ii, and the other Greeks, call it Celtogalatia [Κελτογαλατία].

units.la: Ab Γαλατία Gallia putatur formata: quam tamen vocem alij aliunde derivant. Hæc talia non tanti, ut Lectorem multis morentur. Certe Gallia appellatio Latinis Scriptoribus olim fuit latissima, ut deinceps, præsertim ubi Distributio aperienda, plenius discemus.
units.tr: Gallia is thought to have been formed from Galatia [Γαλατία], though others derive this word from elsewhere. Such matters are not of such weight that they should hold up the reader at length. Certainly the appellation Gallia was once the broadest of all among Latin writers, as we shall learn more fully later on, especially when the division of the land is to be explained.

units.la: Scribit etiam Strabo lib. iii. Ἰβηρίαν antiquitus creditam quidquid esset extra Rodanum & Isthmum, qui ab Gallicis coarctatur finibus. Hebraeis [illegible, ~5 letters] vocari scribunt & Gulielmus Postellus & Arias Montanus Commentario in Abdiam Prophetam.
units.tr: Strabo, in book iii, writes that formerly everything beyond the Rhône and the Isthmus, which is bounded by the Gallic territories, was believed to be Iberia. Gulielmus Postellus and Arias Montanus, in his commentary on the prophet Obadiah, write that it is called [illegible, about five letters] by the Hebrews.

units.la: Francia nuncupatur hodie ab Francis, Germaniae ad Rhenum Populis; qui vi Regionem hanc & armata manu occuparunt: Vulgo Le Royaulme de France.
units.tr: Francia is today named after the Franks, a people of Germany by the Rhine, who seized this region by force of arms. In the vernacular it is Le Royaulme de France.

units.la: Gallos Graeci Celtas universim & Galatas vocarunt: auctoribus Appiano Alexandrino & Strabone lib. iv. Geograph. De Celtis lege, quae disserui libri i cap. iv. Qui nunc ab Graecis Galatae nominantur, inquit Iosephus lib. Antiquitatum i, olim dicti fuerunt Gomerita.
units.tr: The Greeks called the Gauls Celts in general and Galatians, on the authority of Appian of Alexandria and of Strabo, book iv of the Geography. On the Celts, read what I discussed in book i, ch. iv. What the Greeks now call Galatians, says Josephus in book i of the Antiquities, were formerly called Gomerites.

units.la: Veterum, cum primis autem Timagenis Graeci scriptoris, sententias super prima Gallorum origine satis multis commemorat Ammianus lib. xv: Ambigentes, inquit, super origine prima Gallorum Scriptores veteres, notitiam reliquere negocij semiplenam: sed postea Timagenes & diligentia Graecus & lingua (Timagenem hunc Plutarchus de Fluviis Syrum vocat; & pleraque de Callisthene Galaticorum scriptore tumultie indicat: meminit ejus & Strabo lib. iv.) quae diu sunt ignorata, collegit ex multiplicibus libris: cujus fidem sequuti, obscuritate dimota, eadem distincte docebimus & aperte. Aborigines primos in his Regionibus quidam visos esse firmarunt, Celtas nomine Regis amabilis, & Matris ejus vocabulo, Galatas dictos: ita enim Gallos sermo Graecus appellat. Alij Dorienses, antiquiorem sequutos Herculem, Oceani locos inhabitasse confines. * Drasidae memorant revera fuisse Populi partem indigenam: sed alios quoque ab Insulis extimis confluxisse & tractibus Transf-Rhenanis, crebritate bellorum & alluvione fervidi maris sedibus suis expulsos. Ajunt quidam paucos post excidium Troiae fugitantes Graecos ubique dispersos loca haec occupasse tunc vacua. Regionum autem Incolae id magis omnibus adseverant (quod etiam nos legimus in monimentis eorum incisum) Amphitruonis filium Herculem ad Geryonis & Tauristi saevorum Tyrannorum perniciem festinasse, quorum alter Hispanias, alter Gallias infestabat; superatisque ambobus coisse cum generosis feminis, suscepisseque Liberos plures; & eos Partes, quibus imperitabant, suis nominibus appellasse, & quae alia sequuntur: quibus omnibus refutandis tempus non teram. Difficultates Originum facile diffiniri possunt ex cap. xiiii libri iii Partis i.
units.tr: Ammianus, in book xv, records a number of opinions of the ancient writers on the first origin of the Gauls, especially those of the Greek writer Timagenes. The ancient writers, he says, being uncertain about the first origin of the Gauls, left an account of the matter that was only half complete; but afterwards Timagenes, a Greek both diligent and eloquent (Plutarch calls this Timagenes a Syrian, and in many places points out that he was following Callisthenes, the writer of Galatica; Strabo too mentions him in book iv), gathered from many books what had long been unknown. Following his reliability, with the obscurity removed, we shall teach the same things distinctly and plainly. Some have affirmed that the Aborigines were the first to be seen in these regions, and that they were called Celts, after the name of a beloved king, and Galatians after the name of his mother; for the Greek language calls the Gauls thus. Others say that the Dorians, following the earlier Hercules, inhabited the neighbouring parts of the Ocean. The Drasidae record that the indigenous part of the people was indeed there, but that others also flowed in from the outermost islands and the regions across the Rhine, driven from their seats by the frequency of wars and the flooding of the seething sea. Some say that a few Greeks, fleeing after the destruction of Troy, were scattered everywhere and occupied these places, which were then empty. The inhabitants of the regions, however, maintain above all else (which we also read carved in their monuments) that Hercules, son of Amphitryon, hastened to destroy Geryon and Tauristes, cruel tyrants, one of whom infested Spain and the other Gaul; and that, having overcome both, he lay with noble women and had many children, and called the parts over which they ruled by their own names, and other things that follow. I shall not waste time refuting all these things. The difficulties about the origins can easily be settled from ch. xiiii of book iii of Part i.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAP. II.

units.la: Galliae Fines, Longitudo, Latitudo, Circuitus.
units.tr: The Borders, Length, Breadth and Circuit of Gaul.

units.la: NOMEN brevibus exposui: succedunt Res, quas illustrabo cum in ipsa Regione, tum in Incolis. Ibi Adjuncta quaeram & Partes. Adiuncta mihi Quantitas & Qualitas. Quantitatem explicabo in Finibus, Longitudine, Latitudine, Circuituque. Quod ad Fines: Regni, quod Francia nunc dicitur, ad Septemtrionem, qua quidem Germaniam Inferiorem respicit, Limes statui solet inducta ab Caletibus in Argentoratensium usque Agros Linea; quae ab sinistra relinquit Artesios, Hannonios, Leuceburgenses & alios; ad dextram Picardos & Lotharingos: qua vero Angliae jacet obversa, vastus aestuosusque Oceanus, cui ab Vetere Britannia cognomen Britannici: Ad occidentem idem eam pulsat, ingenti facto in Aquitaniam Sinu, Oceanus. Ad Meridiem, qua quidem Hispaniae adhaeret, Pyrenaeos habet Montes; qua vero apertior, liberiorque & sui quasi fit juris, placidiore, nempe mediterraneo, terminatur Mari, quod ab ipsa Gallicum. Ad Ortum denique Alpibus separatur ab Italis, Iura ab Helvetijs, Rheno ab Germanis. Huc pertinent Ammiani Marcellini verba lib. xv Rerum gestarum: Hanc Galliarum plagam ob suggestus Montium arduos & horrore nivali semper obductos, Orbis residui Incolis antehac pene ignotam, nisi qua Littoribus est vicina, munimina claudunt undique natura velut arte circumdata. Et a Latere quidem Australi Tyrrheno adluitur & Gallico Mari: qua caeleste suscipit Plaustrum, a feris gentibus Fluentis distinguitur Rheni: ubi Occidentalis subjecta est Sideri, Oceano & altitudine Pyrenaei: unde ad Solis Ortus attollitur, aggeribus cedit Alpium Cottiarum, &c. Veteres singularum Antiquae Galliae Partium Fines fideliore digito erunt indicandi; ubi Galliarum Divisionem signabo.
units.tr: I have explained the name briefly. Next come the things, which I will illustrate both in the region itself and in its inhabitants. There I will look at its attributes and parts. The attributes for me are quantity and quality. I will explain quantity under borders, length, breadth and circuit. As to the borders: on the north, where it faces Lower Germany, the boundary of the kingdom now called France is usually drawn as a line running from Calais to the fields of Strasbourg. This line leaves the Artois, the Hainaulters, the people of Liège and others on the left, and the Picards and Lorrainers on the right. Where it lies facing England, there is the vast, stormy ocean, which from Old Britain has the name British. On the west the same ocean beats against it, forming a huge bay in Aquitaine. On the south, where it adjoins Spain, it has the Pyrenees; where it is more open and freer, and as it were its own master, it is bounded by the gentler, inland sea, which is called the Gallic Sea after France itself. On the east it is separated from the Italians by the Alps, from the Swiss by the Jura, and from the Germans by the Rhine. To this belong the words of Ammianus Marcellinus in book 15 of his Deeds: This region of Gaul, because of the steep heights of the mountains, always covered with snowy chill, was almost unknown to the inhabitants of the rest of the world before now, except where it lies near the shores; nature closes it off on every side with defences, as if they were built by art. On the south it is washed by the Tyrrhenian and the Gallic Sea; where it receives the heavenly Wagon, it is divided from the wild peoples by the flowing Rhine; where the west lies beneath the star, it is bounded by the Ocean and the height of the Pyrenees; from there it rises toward the rising of the sun, and yields to the ramparts of the Cottian Alps, etc. The borders of the individual parts of Ancient Gaul will have to be pointed out by a more trustworthy finger, when I set out the division of Gaul.

units.la: Galliae vel Franciae (nam voces has ἀδιαφόρως usurpabo) Longitudo, si ab Occasu recta in Ortum; ab Insula, inquam, Iuris Francici Heyssant, olim Sena, extremo Britanniae, quae in Galliis, Littori oppolita, usque ad Rheni ripam consideretur, Milliarium Gallicorum est paullo amplius ccc: sin, ut alij mensurandam censent Longitudinem, ab Cauro vel Argeste in Vulturnum vel Euronotum, id est, ab Insula Normanniæ, Aldernaij, quæ Veteribus Ebodia, Niceam usque, supra trecenta, numerantur triginta, quantum fere terrarum inter Parisios jacet & Romam.
units.tr: The length of Gaul, or France (for I shall use these words indifferently [ἀδιαφόρως]), if measured in a straight line from west to east, from the island of Heyssant in the territory of the French crown, formerly Sena, at the far end of Britain (which, lying opposite the coast in Gaul, is considered as far as the bank of the Rhine), is a little more than 300 Gallic miles. But if, as others think the length should be measured, from the north-west or west-north-west to the south-east or east-south-east, that is, from the island of Normandy, Aldernaij, which the ancients called Ebodia, to Nice, more than 330 miles are counted, about as much land as lies between Paris and Rome.

units.la: Latitudo ab Meridionalissimis ad Mare Mediterraneum Littoribus ad Caletensium usque urbem Milliarium fere est ccxxcv; quantum Itineris Parisios inter & Venetias.
units.tr: The breadth, from the most southern shores on the Mediterranean to the city of Calais, is about 225 miles, as far as the journey between Paris and Venice.

units.la: Circuitus ab Calcetibus per maritima Littora, Pyrenæum, Maris Mediterranei Oras, Alpes, Istram, Rhenum, Lineamque ex Argentoratensium Agris Caletes versus ductam deprehenditur supra mille viginti milliarium. Suetonius in Julij Cæsaris vita cap. xxv tradit, in Circuitu patere ad bis & tricies centum millia p. ssuum: comprehendens præter Helvetiam & alia, totum illud, quod in Vetere Belgica hodie ad Rhenum usque Inferiori Germaniæ adcensetur. Suetonij locum ad verbum pene expressit Eutropius libro Hist. Romanæ vi.
units.tr: The circuit, from Calais along the sea coasts, the Pyrenees, the shores of the Mediterranean, the Alps, Istria and the Rhine, and along the line drawn from the fields of Strasbourg back to Calais, is found to be more than 1,020 miles. Suetonius, in the life of Julius Caesar, chapter 25, states that in circuit it extends to two hundred and thirty thousand paces, taking in, besides Helvetia and other places, the whole of what is today reckoned in Ancient Belgium as far as the Rhine and Lower Germany. Eutropius, in book 6 of his Roman History, expressed Suetonius's passage almost word for word.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: Galliæ Clima, Qualitas.
units.tr: The Climate and Quality of Gaul.

units.la: EA igitur est Quantitas: sequitur jam nunc Qualitas; cujus causa plurimum Clima. Subjacet parti quidem Quinti Gallia, Totis autem Sexto Septimoque Climatibus, Parti quoque Octavi: inter Gradus Latitudinis xli & iii, Longitudinis autem xx & xxxviii. Maximus dies æstatis in Australi Parallelo, qui distat ab Æquatore Gradibus xlii, horarum est xv: in Borcali, qui ab Æquinoctiali Gradibus dirimitur ii, Horarum est xvi.
units.tr: This, then, is its extent. Now comes its quality, which depends chiefly on the climate. Gaul lies partly under the fifth clime, wholly under the sixth and seventh, and partly under the eighth, between latitudes 41 and 43 and longitudes 20 and 38. The longest summer day, on the southern parallel, which is 42 degrees from the equator, is 15 hours. On the northern parallel, which is separated from the equinoctial line by 2 degrees, it is 16 hours.

units.la: Licet universim Ventis obnoxia sit plurimum Septemtrionalibus (Circium, Venitum ex Gallia Terra flantem, Parti, quæ Narbonensis appellatur, præcipue infestum docet Plinius lib. ii cap. xlvii. innuuntque præter Lucanum de bello Pharsalico, Senecca lib. iv. Quæst. Natur. & Agellius lib. ii. noct. Attic cap. xxii) propter Aëris tamen salubritatem & temperiem optimis Europæ Regionibus adcensenda. Constitutione felicissimam facit Claudianus; Saluberrimam dicit Cæsar lib. iii bell. Civil. fertilissimam hominum Genitricem non obscure docent Cæsar de bello Gallico lib. ii, Strabo, ubi de Arvernis, Ammianus Marcellinus lib. xxi, & Vegetius lib. i. de re milit. cap. i, alijque.
units.tr: Although, taken as a whole, the country is much exposed to the north winds, (Pliny, book 2, chapter 47, shows that the Circius, a wind blowing from the Gallic land and especially hostile to the part called Narbonensis; and Seneca, Natural Questions book 4, and Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights book 2, chapter 22, also refer to it, besides Lucan in the Pharsalia), it must nevertheless be counted among the best regions of Europe for the healthiness and mildness of its air. Claudian calls it most fortunate in its situation; Caesar, in the third book of the Civil War, calls it most healthy; and Caesar in the Gallic War book 2, Strabo in his account of the Arverni, Ammianus Marcellinus book 21, and Vegetius, On Military Affairs book 1, chapter 1, and others, plainly show that it is the most fertile mother of men.

units.la: Ager magnam partem est planus: amœnos hic ibi habens colles, interque eos Valles jucundissimas: sua cum has, tum illos fœcunditate admirabiles.
units.tr: The land is for the most part flat, with pleasant hills here and there, and very agreeable valleys between them, admirable both for their fertility and for their charm.

units.la: Arva bene culta Triticum aliasque Segetes luxurie magna producunt. Multum fert Gallia Frumenti, uti docet Strabo lib. iv, Milij, Glandis; & omnigenum alit Pecus. Nihil in ea otiosum, nisi qua Paludes aut Silvæ obstant. Frumenti abundantem scribit Trebellius in Balista: quod idem verum facit M. Tullius in oratione pro M. Fonteio, ubi tradit magnum Frumenti numerum ab Romanis hinc avehi. Docent & Cæsar lib. iii. belli Gallici, & Dio lib. xxxix, Romanos misisse Legatos Frumenti petendi gratia ad populos Galliæ Venetos. Frumentum autem Gallicum omnium levissimum esse ex his generibus, quæ Romam invehuntur, testis est Plinius; apud quem leguntur & Aquitani uti Panico. Felices Gallias pinguibus glebis, & commodas proventibus fructuarijs; plerasque Vitibus Arbustisque consitas, omnique ad usum Animantium fœtu beatissimas describit in Polyhistore Solinus. Pomponius Mela eadem de re sic loquitur: Terra est Frumenti præcipue & Pabuli ferax, & amœna Lucis immanibus: quidquid ex satis frigoris impatiens est, Ager nec ubique alit, & noxio genere Animalium minime frequens.
units.tr: Well-tilled fields produce wheat and other crops in great abundance. Gaul bears much grain, as Strabo shows in book 4, and millet and acorns, and it feeds every kind of livestock. Nothing in it lies idle, except where marshes or forests stand in the way. Trebellius, in his Life of Balista, writes that it has an abundance of grain; Marcus Tullius, in his speech for Marcus Fonteius, makes the same true point, where he records that a great quantity of grain is carried from here by the Romans. Caesar, in book 3 of the Gallic War, and Dio, in book 39, show that the Romans sent envoys to the Veneti of Gaul to ask for grain. Pliny is witness that Gallic wheat is the lightest of all the kinds imported into Rome, and in his work the Aquitanians are also mentioned as using millet. Solinus, in his Polyhistor, describes the Gauls as fortunate for their rich soil and fitting yields of fruit, mostly planted with vines and orchards, and most blessed with produce for the use of living creatures. Pomponius Mela speaks on the same subject in this way: The land is especially fertile in grain and fodder, and pleasant with huge groves; whatever cannot bear the cold, the field does not nourish everywhere, and it is not very full of harmful kinds of animals.

units.la: Quod ad Arbores aliaque id genus: Abietem laudatissimam in Iura & Vogeso Montibus; Betulam, & ex ea Bitumen Incolas facere, indicat Plinius. Triumphi Gallici adparatum ex Citro comparasse Cæsarem, Velleius Paterculus auctor est: ut vero simile sit & Citro abundare solitam olim Galliam. Habuit & magna copia (ut Cæsar testatur) Taxum, Arborem venenatam. Eam Dioscorides Narbone tam præsentis esse veneni tradit; ut, si qui dormiant sub ea, aut in ejus umbra subsideant, sideant, lædantur & sæpenumero moriantur. Vasa Viatoria ex ea Vinis, inquit Plinius lib. xv i. cap. x, in Gallia facta, mortifera fuisse compertum est. Taxo se exanimasse Cattiuulcum Eburonum Regem memoriæ prodit Cæsar. Scribit etiam ex Artemidoro diligens auctor Strabo, Arborem in Gallia nasci, Fico similimam; Fructum autem Corno similem gignere; inde Pharetras fabricari; Arborem eandem incisam lethalem succum effundere ad inungendas Sagittas utilem. De Ficubus audiamus Iulianum oculatum testem, cujus in Misopogono verba Latine sic sonant: Hiems est ibi placidissima propter calorem, ut ajunt; Oceani ac fortasse quidam tenuis aër illinc diffunditur; videtur autem maritima aqua dulci esse calidior. Sive igitur ob hanc caussam, sive aliam mihi ignotam, ita se res habet. Hiems ejus terræ Incolis est mitior; præterea Vites optimæ illic nascuntur; quin etiam Ficus multi jam arte quadam extulerunt, quum eas per hiemem calamis Tritici, tamquam Vestimentis, contegerent & aliis hujusmodi rebus, quæ Cæli injurias ab Arboribus averruncare solent. Sed paullo distinctius hæc Strabo, cujus sæpe memini, libro iv: H' Ναρβωνίς ἄπεσι, ὥσπερ ἡ Ἰταλία, τὰς αὐτὰς ἐκφέρει καρπούς. Παρῆν δ' ὅτι τὰς Ἄρκτος καὶ τὸ Κεμμένον ὄρος ἡ μὲν ἐλαιόφυτος ἐ συνοφόρος ἐκλείπει· τἄλλα δὲ φύεται, καὶ ἡ Ἀμπελῶς δὲ πεζίαν ἡ ῥᾳδίως πλεσφορεῖ. Frigore sane, quia sub Septemtrionibus, ut habet Cæsar lib. i belli Gall. Frugum maturitatem nonnihil retardari, certum est. Qua de causa huc referendum quod Varro de R. R. i. scribit, In Gallia, inquiens, Transalpina ad Rhenum aliquot Regiones sunt, ubi nec Vitis, nec Olea, nec Poma nascerentur, nisi Agros stercorarent candida fossoria Creta. Marca hæc dicitur Plinio. Septemtrionaliorem igitur Galliam designant Claudianus, qui Nive eam ferocem dicit; Lucianus, qui Glaciem Gallicam memorat, de Histor. scribenda; Petronius, apud quem Adagium, Gallica Nive frigidior; Diodorus, qui Glaciem Gallicam tam immensam fatetur, ut Flumina congelata sint pervia non tantum paucis, sed totis Exercitibus, cum Curribus; M. denique Tullius, cujus in Provinciis Consularibus hæc legitur Exclamatio, vera an falsa? Quid ipsis locis asperius? quid incultius Opidis? quid Nationibus immanius? quid Oceano longius invenīri potest?
units.tr: As for trees and the like: Pliny reports that the fir is most praised in the Jura and Vosges mountains, and that the inhabitants make pitch from birch. Velleius Paterculus says that Caesar got the material for his Gallic triumph from citron wood; and indeed it is likely that Gaul was once accustomed to have plenty of citron. It also had (as Caesar testifies) a great quantity of yew, a poisonous tree. Dioscorides says that at Narbo it is so strongly poisonous that if anyone sleeps under it, or sits down in its shade, he is harmed and often dies. Drinking vessels made of it for wine in Gaul, says Pliny, book 16, chapter 10, have been found to be deadly. Caesar records that Cativolcus, king of the Eburones, killed himself with yew. The careful writer Strabo also writes, following Artemidorus, that in Gaul there grows a tree very like the fig, which bears a fruit like the cornel; from it quivers are made; and when the same tree is cut, it gives off a deadly juice, useful for smearing arrows. Let us hear Julian, an eyewitness, about figs; his words in the Misopogon sound in Latin thus: The winter there is very mild because of the heat, as they say; some thin air is perhaps spread from the ocean, and sea water seems to be warmer than fresh. Whether for this reason, or some other that is unknown to me, things are so. The winter of that land is milder for its inhabitants; moreover, the best vines grow there; indeed, many have already brought fig trees to fruit by a certain art, when they covered them in winter with wheat stalks, as with clothing, and with other such things that usually ward off the harm of the sky from trees. But Strabo, whom I have often mentioned, says these things more clearly in book 4: Narbonensis bears the same fruits as Italy. It should be noted that beyond the Arctic and the Cemmenus mountain the olive does not bear fruit; other things grow there, and the vine bears fruit easily [Ἡ Ναρβωνίς ἄπεσι, ὥσπερ ἡ Ἰταλία, τὰς αὐτὰς ἐκφέρει καρπούς. Παρῆν δ' ὅτι τὰς Ἄρκτος καὶ τὸ Κεμμένον ὄρος ἡ μὲν ἐλαιόφυτος ἐ συνοφόρος ἐκλείπει· τἄλλα δὲ φύεται, καὶ ἡ Ἀμπελῶς δὲ πεζίαν ἡ ῥᾳδίως πλεσφορεῖ]. It is certain that because the country lies under the north, the ripening of crops is somewhat delayed by the cold, as Caesar says in book 1 of the Gallic War. For this reason what Varro writes in On Agriculture book 1 should be referred here: In Transalpine Gaul, he says, there are several regions by the Rhine where neither vine, nor olive, nor fruit trees would grow, unless they manured the fields with white digging clay. Pliny says this district is called the Marca. Therefore Claudian, who calls Gaul fierce with snow, Lucian, who mentions Gallic ice in his work On How to Write History, Petronius, in whom there is the saying colder than Gallic snow, and Diodorus, who admits that the Gallic ice is so vast that rivers frozen over are passable not only by a few people but by whole armies, with carts, all describe a more northern Gaul. Finally, Marcus Tullius, in his speech On the Consular Provinces, has this exclamation, which is read there, true or false? What is rougher than the places themselves? What is more uncultivated than the towns? What is more savage than the peoples? What further than the ocean can be found?

units.la: Eliconem Helvetium Fabrum ex Italia primum in Galliam tulisse Ficum siccam & Uvam, Oleum ac Vinum, adnotavit Plinius. Inde Vini postea adeo ferax, ut hinc Vindemias condere Italos conquueratur quodammodo Columella; & Viennam Vinum, quod Picatum nominabant, Romam, ubi in pretio, mittere solitam referat v Convival. Plutarchus Quid ergo velint Vopiscus & Eusebius, dum Probum Imperatorem tradant Gallis permisisse, ut Vites haberent, docti Viri nondum capiunt. Putant quidam ad Probi usque tempora in Braccata Gallia sive Provincia tantum, non in ceteris Gallis, Vitem fuisse. Quod qui verum esse poterit, quum Plinius, multo ante Probi principatum Biturica Vitis, Vinique Arverni faciat mentionem? Diodorus sua ætate adfirmat in Gallia Comata Vinum nasci nullum solere. Cæsar lib. iv belli Gall. Suevos Germaniæ Nerviis Galliæ temperantia pares efficit. Vinum, inquit, ad se omnino importari non sinunt; quod ea re ad laborem ferendum remollescere hominess atque effeminari arbitrarentur. Hodie Vina Galliæ non unius generis; alia aliis locis colligunt generosiora, eaque partim suis Britannis, Normannis, Picardis, partim Continalibus Germanis, Belgis, Anglis, aliisque, quibus Vvarum maturitatem negare solet Aëris frigiditas, subvehunt.
units.tr: Pliny notes that Helico, a Helvetian smith, was the first to bring dried figs and grapes, oil and wine from Italy into Gaul. Afterwards its wine production became so great that the Italians, as Columella somewhat complains, stored their vintages from here; and Athenaeus, in book 5 of the Deipnosophists, reports that Vienna used to send to Rome its wine, which they called Picatum, and that it was valued there. What Vopiscus and Eusebius mean when they state that the Emperor Probus allowed the Gauls to have vines, learned men do not yet grasp. Some think that until the time of Probus there were vines only in Braccata Gaul or the Province, and not in the other parts of Gaul. How can this be true, since Pliny, long before the reign of Probus, mentions Bituriga vines and Arvernian wine? Diodorus asserts that in his own time wine was usually not produced at all in Comata Gaul. Caesar, in book 4 of the Gallic War, sets the Suevi of Germany on a par with the Nervii of Gaul in self-restraint: They do not allow wine to be imported to them at all, because they thought that men were softened and made effeminate by it for enduring labour. Today the wines of Gaul are not all of one kind; different places produce finer wines in different areas, and these are brought partly to its own Britons, Normans and Picards, and partly to the Germans, Belgians, English and others on the Continent, to whom the coldness of the air is accustomed to deny the ripening of grapes.

units.la: Vacinia purpurea hic provenire, habeque tingendi causa ad Servitiorum vestes, notat Plinius; ijsdem Coccum, Conchylium ac Tyrium tribuens, quibus Vestes tingere consueverunt. Nardum ad Theriacam conficiundam ex Gallia peti, Galenus testatur. Lini quoque sationem Galliæ dat idem Plinius (inde Linificium apud Strabonem lib. iv) ex quo Vela faciunt; quamvis Pellibus pro Velis uti Venetos Armoricæ Populos prodiderit Cæsar. Franci certe hodieque Linum apud se natum Cannabemque mittunt cum alio, tum in Hispaniam adparandis Funibus, Navibusque instruendis.
units.tr: Pliny notes that purple murex grows here, and that it is used for dyeing the clothes of slaves; he attributes to the same region the kermes, the shellfish and the Tyrian purple, with which they were accustomed to dye garments. Galen testifies that nard for making theriac is sought from Gaul. The same Pliny also gives Gaul the sowing of flax (hence the linen-making mentioned by Strabo in book 4), from which they make sails; although Caesar reports that the Veneti of the Armorican peoples used skins instead of sails. The Franks, at any rate, still today send flax grown among them, and hemp too, into Spain, both for preparing ropes and for equipping ships.

units.la: Auri quoque & Argenti apud Gallos esse Metalla, atque eorum præstantiora in Cemmeno Monte; Auri etiam Fodinas omnium esse excellentissimas apud Tarbellos; & Ferri Metalla apud Petrocorios & Biturigas Cubos, Strabo auctor est. Aurum apud Celtas quondam erui, scribit Athenæus. Auriferum Tarnem, Aquitaniæ fluvium, vocat Ausonius. Diodorus libro v plures in Gallis Fluvios auriferos dicit: unde apud Procopium legimus Gallos Aurcum nummum è nativo solo cudere,
units.tr: Strabo says that the Gauls also have mines of gold and silver, and that the finest of them are on the Cemmenus mountain; that the gold mines of the Tarbelli are the most excellent of all; and that the iron mines are among the Petrocorii and the Bituriges Cubi. Athenaeus writes that gold was once dug up among the Celts. Ausonius calls the Tarnes, a river of Aquitaine, gold-bearing. Diodorus in book 5 speaks of several gold-bearing rivers in Gaul; whence in Procopius we read that the Gauls struck gold coins from native soil,

units.la: Vinis,
units.tr: Wines,

units.la: Herbis,
units.tr: Herbs,

units.la: Metallis, dere, eumque non Romanorum Imperatorum, ut ceteri solent, imagine, sed sua impressa. Horum Pecuniam memorat Cassiodorus lib. vii Variar. cap. xxxvii. Merito igitur Gallia dives, Manilio; opibus florens, Dioni; Galli dites, Iosepho; auro locupletes in Oraculis Sibyllinis. Et quamvis Argento carere scripserit Diodorus; è Pyrenæis tamen Montibus, quum Silva casu accensa conflagraret, liquatum Argentum hic, ut & in Hispanijs profluxisse narrat Athenæus. Apud Ruthenos & Gabalos quoque describit Argenti Metalla Strabo. Ærarias item Secturas apud hos multis in locis esse, Cæsar est testis: Amethystum in Gallia, & Corallium circa Stoechadas Insulas reperiri, Plinius: Electrum apud Celtas in flumine quodam inveniri, Dion Prusæus.
units.tr: Metals, to strike it, and bearing not the image of the Roman emperors, as the others commonly do, but its own. Cassiodorus records their coinage in Variae, book 7, chapter 37. Rightly, then, Gaul is called rich by Manilius, flourishing in wealth by Dio, Gauls wealthy by Josephus, and abounding in gold in the Sibylline Oracles. And although Diodorus wrote that Gaul lacks silver, nevertheless, from the Pyrenean mountains, when a forest was accidentally set on fire and burned, silver was melted out here, just as Athenaeus relates that it also flowed in Spain. Strabo also describes silver mines among the Ruthenians and Gabali. Caesar is witness that there are bronze quarries among these people in many places. Pliny says amethyst is found in Gaul, and coral around the Stoechades islands. Dio of Prusa says electrum is found among the Celts in a certain river.

units.la: Ager, qui aliunde non occupatus omnis generis nutrit Armenta: quæ faciunt, ut Carnis, Lactis, Butyri, Caseii, Lanæ, Rerumque aliarum abundet copia. Pecuaria statuit divitem Sidonius in Panegyrico Majorani. Asinos non habere scribit in Admirandis Aristoteles: hodie secus se res habet. Equas fama nobilitatas commemorat Trebellius in D. Claudio. Canes hujus gentis numerosos laudant, præter Ovidium, Oppianum, Gratium Poetas, etiam Pollux Grammaticus & Euphrada Orator. Lupum Cervarium ex Gallia spectasse se in Cn. Pompei Magni Arena dicit Plinius. Sues altitudine, robore & celeritate præstantes, à quibus, qui non adsueverit, non minus, quam à Lupo periculi, commemorat Strabo. Hinc optimas pernas Gallos habere, recte scripsit Athenæus: earumque tantam scribit idem Strabo copiam, ut non solum Romæ, sed & plerisque Italiæ locis sufficiant. Sic Varro lib. ii de re rustica cap. iv: Quotannis è Gallia apportantur Romam pernæ, Tomacinæ, Petasones. Videndus & Plinius. Lepores permagnos hic esse ex ejusdem Varronis de Ling. Lat. libris discimus: apud quem quoque Gallicanæ Lanæ memoria; quam asperam indicat Strabo. Onocrotalum Avem hic versus Septemtrionem ad Oceanum celebrat Plinius: cui & Salmo hic fluviatilis, atque in Oceano Physeter marinum Animal, ingentis columnæ modo se attollens; altior navium velis Diluviem quamdam eructans. Nereides quoque, item Elephantos & Arietes Marinos hic idem agnoscit Plinius. In Arari flumine, ut habet ex Callisthene Strobæus, nascitur magnus quidam Piscis, Clupea nominatus ab Incolis: qui crescente Luna, albus; decrescente eadem, nigrescit; & Corpore nimium aucto à proprijs Spinis interimitur. In hujus Piscis capite Lapis perhibetur reperiri, similis grani salis, qui optime facit ad quartanas, sinistro lateri Corporis adligatus, decrescente Luna. Clopias nominatur Michaeli Glycæ Annalium parte i. ex Anastasio; Scolopidon, Plutarcho. Ranarum fœcundam numerositatem tantam narrat ex Varrone Plinius, ut ea civitatem pulsaverit. De Fossilibus porro Piscibus hæc apud Pomponium Melam lib. ii extremo, ubi de Gallia Narbonensi lego: Salsula fons non dulcibus, sed salsioribus, quam marina sunt, aquis defluens (in Gallia Narbonensi) Juxta Campus minuta arundine gracilique perviridis, ceterum stagno subeunte suspensus. Id manifestat media pars ejus, quæ absciissa proximis velut insula natat; pellitque se atque attrahi patitur; quin & ex ijs, quæ ad imum perfossa sunt, suffusum mare ostenditur. Unde Graiis nostrisque etiam Auctoribus, verine ignorantia an prudentibus etiam mendacij libidine, visum est tradere posteris, in ea regione Piscem è terra erui, qui, ubi ex alto hucusque penetrasset, per ea foramina ictu captantium interfectus extrahitur. Per Graios Auctores, quorum fidem elevat Pomponius, designari videntur Strabo & Athenæus: quorum ille lib. vi. tradit circa Rusinonem fluvium Lacum esse propinquum, ac paulo supra mare locum aquosum, plenum Salinarum, huncque Fossiles habere Mugiles sive Cestreos: ubi enim duos aut tres pedes foderis, inmisso in aquam limosam Tridente, configi solere justæ magnitudinis: alii autem limo, sicut Anguillas: hic autem lib. viii. ex Polybij lib. xxxiv, juxta Pyrenæos montes Narbonam usque Campos esse notat, per quos Iliberis & Rus-cino fluvij decurrunt: in ijs Fossiles, quos vocant, Pisces reperiri: ejus namque loci solum tenue esse, & subnascente multo gramine, herbosum: sub eo vero, quum ad duos tresve cubitos arenosa sit terra, Aquam inveniri, quæ à fluminibus aberravit: in ea Pisces sub terram discurrere per rivos ipsos pabuli causa; quod autem radicibus graminis delectentur, subterraneis piscibus universam illam oram repleri, quos egesta humo capiunt Incolæ. Fortean huc referendum, quod in Admirandis memoriæ mandat Aristoteles; in finibus Massilien-sium, sium, circa Ligusticum, Lacum esse, qui ebulliens effususque piscium multitudinem immensam, veri fidem superantem, eijciat, &c.
units.tr: Land that, not being occupied by anyone else, feeds herds of every kind, so that there is an abundance of meat, milk, butter, cheese, wool and other goods. Sidonius, in his Panegyric on Majorian, describes the country as rich in livestock. Aristotle, in the Admirable Things, writes that they have no donkeys; today things are otherwise. Trebellius, in his life of the deified Claudius, mentions mares made famous by their reputation. Besides the poets Ovid, Oppian and Gratius, the grammarian Pollux and the orator Euphrades also praise the numerous dogs of this people. Pliny says that he saw a Gallic wolfhound in the arena of Gnaeus Pompey the Great. Strabo mentions pigs excelling in height, strength and speed, and that anyone not accustomed to them is in no less danger from them than from a wolf. Hence Athenaeus rightly wrote that the Gauls have excellent hams, and the same Strabo writes that they have such a quantity of them that they supply not only Rome but most places in Italy. So Varro, in book 2 of On Agriculture, chapter 4: "Every year hams are brought to Rome from Gaul: Tomacine and Petasones." Pliny should also be consulted. From the books of the same Varro On the Latin Language we learn that there are very large hares here; in the same work there is mention of Gallic wool, which Strabo says is rough. Pliny praises the bustard here, toward the north by the ocean, and also the river trout here, and in the ocean the sperm whale, a marine animal that raises itself like a huge column, higher than the sails of ships, belching out a kind of deluge. Pliny likewise recognizes here Nereids, elephants and sea rams. In the river Arar, as Stobaeus has it from Callisthenes, there is a large fish that the inhabitants call clupea, which is white when the moon is waxing and turns black when it wanes, and which, when its body has grown too large, is killed by its own spines. A stone is said to be found in the head of this fish, like a grain of salt, which works very well against quartan fevers when tied to the left side of the body while the moon is waning. Michael Glycas, in part 1 of his Annals, from Anastasius, calls it clopias; Plutarch calls it scolopidon. Pliny, following Varro, relates such a prolific multitude of frogs that they drove a city out. Concerning fish found in the ground, Pomponius Mela writes in the last part of book 2, where I read about Narbonese Gaul: A salty spring flows out, with waters saltier than sea water (in Narbonese Gaul). Near it is a plain, bright green with fine, slender reeds, yet floating on a pool beneath. This is shown by its middle part, which, cut off from the nearby ground, floats like an island; it pushes itself and allows itself to be drawn along; and from the places that have been dug through to the bottom, the spreading sea is revealed. Hence Greek and also our authors, whether from ignorance of the truth or from a love of lying even among the wise, have thought fit to hand down to posterity that in that region a fish is dug out of the earth, which, having penetrated thus far from the deep, is taken out through those holes, killed by the blows of those who catch it. By the Greek authors, whose credibility Pomponius undermines, Strabo and Athenaeus seem to be meant. Strabo, in book 6, relates that near the river Rusino there is a lake, and a watery place a little above the sea, full of salt pits, and that this place has mullets, or Cestreus, in the ground: for when you dig two or three feet and thrust a trident into the muddy water, fish of a fair size are usually pierced; others, from the mud, like eels. Athenaeus, in book 8, drawing on book 34 of Polybius, notes that near the Pyrenees, as far as the plains of Narbo, through which the rivers Iliberis and Ruscino run, there are fish, which they call fossil, found in them: for the soil of that place is thin and, with much grass growing beneath, is grassy; but below it, when the sandy earth reaches two or three cubits, water is found, which has strayed from the rivers; in this water fish run under the earth through the channels themselves for the sake of food; and because they delight in the roots of the grass, the whole shore is filled with underground fish, which the inhabitants catch by digging out the soil. Perhaps this is to be referred to what Aristotle records in the Admirable Things: that in the territory of the Massilians, near Liguria, there is a lake which, bubbling up and overflowing, casts out an immense multitude of fish, beyond belief, and so on.

units.la: CAP. IV.
units.tr: Chapter IV.

units.la: Galliæ Montes.
units.tr: The Mountains of Gaul.

units.la: ADIVNCTA absolvi: succeduht Partes, cum Terra, tum Aqua: ibi Montes, Promontoria, Silvæ; hic autem Sinus, Portus, Flumina, & id genus alia. Quod ad Montes, Gallia alijs, quam alijs, locis est montosior. Eminent hic Delphinatus, Provincia, Sabaudia, & Burgundia. Andegavensis Ager suos etiam habet Montes, qui in Britannorum Pictonumque fines late se insinuant. Montes Galliæ cum primis celebrant Veteres Scriptores Cebennam, Vogesum, Juram.
units.tr: Having finished with the adjoining matters, we come to the parts of the land and of the water: there are mountains, headlands and forests; here are bays, harbours, rivers and the like. As for mountains, Gaul is more mountainous in some places than in others. The most prominent are Dauphiné, Provence, Savoy and Burgundy. The region of Anjou has its own mountains too, which extend widely into the territories of the Britons and the Poitevins. The ancient writers chiefly celebrate the mountains of Gaul under the names Cebenna, Vogesus, Jura.

units.la: Cebenna Mons est, qui, ut Cæsar scribit; Arvernos (ceulx d'Auverne) ab Helviis (ceulx de Vivaretz) distinguit. Gebennam Plinius; Gebennas, Lucanus & Ausonius nominant; Gebennicos Pomponius Mela. Vera genuinaque scriptura est, ut Scaliger suis ad me litteris monet, Cebenna, per C. Dici enim hodie Montaignes de Cebenes & Cevenes: ut rectius Κεμμένοι Ptolemæo & Straboni, Cebenna Latinis quibusdam dicantur. Non mirum autem multa Montium nomina utroque numero usurpata reperiri: quum unus Mons in multa plurimum adsurgat juga, & in plura quasi membra diffundatur; adeo ut qui vere unus, multi Montes esse videantur. Cebenna Vineto, Nozoreno, Villanovano Montaignes d'Auvergne nominantur. Horum Montium pars hodie Tarara, teste Guilielmo Budæo lib. iv. de Asse, qui Lugdunum euntibus est superandus. In vertice Sedes visitur Petræ incisa, cui Mercatores imponunt eos, qui Mercatum Lugdunensem numquam frequentarunt. Vulgo La Chere de la Verité vocatur. Iurare namque coguntur Veritatem, Lugduni fuerint umquam, nec ne; eoque nomine nonnihil, quo Genio simul indulgeant, polliceri.
units.tr: Cebenna is a mountain which, as Caesar writes, separates the Arverni (ceulx d'Auverne) from the Helvii (ceulx de Vivaretz). Pliny calls it Gebenna; Lucan and Ausonius call it Gebennas; Pomponius Mela calls it Gebennicos. The true and genuine spelling, as Scaliger advises me in his letters, is Cebenna, with a C. For today it is called Montaignes de Cebenes & Cevenes; and so, more correctly, some Latin writers call it Cebenna, as Ptolemy and Strabo call it Κεμμένοι. It is no wonder that many mountain names are found in both numbers, since one mountain rises into many ridges and spreads out into several limbs, so that what is truly one appears to be many mountains. Parts of this Cebenna are named Montaignes d'Auvergne by Vineto, Nozorenus and Villanovanus. Part of these mountains today is called Tarara, according to Guillaume Budé, book 4 of De Asse; it must be crossed by those going to Lyon. On the summit there is a seat cut in rock, on which merchants set those who have never frequented the Lyon fair. It is commonly called La Chere de la Verité. For they are compelled to swear to the Truth whether they have ever been in Lyon or not, and in that way, by promising something, they indulge their own inclination.

units.la: Vogesus Galliæ Mons Cæsari lib. de bello Gallico iv, Lucano lib. i. Plinio, & alijs. Vocetus vel Vocetius corrupte dicitur apud Tacitum lib. i. Historiarum & alibi, ut jam ab doctis viris notatum. Alpium nomine à Strabone describitur lib. iv. Hodie Mont de Faucilles, alijsque nomenclaturis incigetatur. Separat Burgundiam Alsatiamque ab Lotharingia. Provomit Mosam, ut etiam testatur Cæsar, & infinitos alios fluvios, quorum plerique Rhenum petunt. Pars, unde Mosella profluit, Mratzet appellatur, quod habere se tradit Ortelius ex Libello MS. Magni Gruberi, in quo Rhenum describit: addens, Tractum hunc Essaye Gallice, & Auff der Stap nuncupari in Chorographica Lotharingiæ Tabula, jussu & impensis Ducis ab Joanne Scyllio accurate delineata; nihilque ibi, eodem Scyllio teste, præter Asarum herbam provenire. Gignit Vogesus in Valle Leberia Argentum purum; sed, ut notat Munsterus, non ita multum.
units.tr: Vogesus, a mountain of Gaul, is mentioned by Caesar in book 4 of the Gallic War, by Lucan in book 1, by Pliny and by others. It is corruptly called Vocetus or Vocetius in Tacitus, book 1 of the Histories and elsewhere, as learned men have already noted. Strabo describes it under the name of the Alps, book 4. Today it is called the Mont de Faucilles, and it is given other names in other maps. It separates Burgundy and Alsace from Lorraine. It sends forth the Meuse, as Caesar also attests, and countless other rivers, most of which seek the Rhine. The part from which the Moselle flows is called Mratzet, as Ortelius reports from a manuscript booklet of Magnus Gruber, in which he describes the Rhine; adding that this tract is called Essaye in French and Auff der Stap in the chorographical map of Lorraine, carefully drawn by Johannes Scyllius at the command and expense of the Duke; and that, by the same Scyllius's testimony, nothing grows there except the herb asarum. Vosges produces pure silver in the valley of Lebertal, but, as Münster notes, not very much.

units.la: Iura Galliæ dicam Mons, an Germaniæ? Olim fere totus Galliæ; quum Helvetia Belgicæ adcenseretur: hodie magna etiam parte Germaniæ. Initium ejus statui solet in finibus Basiliensium, juxta Rhenum, e regione Waldzhuti. Altus est, multisque & ingentibus subnixus saxis. Meminerunt ejus Cæsar, Plinius, alij. Ptolemæo Iuragoris est: Straboni Iuqoio& & Ioges. Ævo nostro Accolis Incolisque pro ratione Locorum alijs atque alijs vocatur nominibus. Haud procul Arce Hasburgensi prope Brugim (Opidulum est sic dictum Idiomate Germanico à Ponte, qui hic super Arolam ex uno Arcu) Botzberg audit; uti, quum trajicerem, me docuerunt qui inhabitant, à Pago Botzen, qui cum multis alijs Pedi Montis adlocatus. Hanc Iuræ portionem Vocetum vel Vocetium esse Cornelij Taciti censent Sebastianus Munsterus, Ægidius Schudus, Wolffgangus Lazius, Christianus Vrstisius, & alij. Abrahamus tamen Ortelius apud Tacitum Vogesum, de quo ante, legendum esse minime dubitat. Est eadem hac Montis parte Vallis ingens, cui nomen Frikthal, à Pago cognomine. Occurrunt & aliæ hic ibi Valles, ut obiter hoc dicam, Lauffen-thal, & S. Innerfthal, & similes: quarum tamen nulla Montem per transversum penetrat. Vbicumque volueris trajicere, opus est alta scansione. Inter Ararim rim porro & Farspurgum hic Mons appellatur Schaffmat, quod Latinis Ovinum sonat Pratum. Inter opidum Olten & Humburgensem Præfecturam dicitur Nider-Haurvenstein, Inferior sestus Lapis: Per Saxa enim factum est iter. Inter Walnburgum & Balstallium Ober-Hauvrenstein vocatur, Superior sestus Lapis; ubi currus onusti grandibus funibus per Montis declivitatem demittuntur. Occasum versus procedendo Wasser-sal nuncupatur, id est Aqua ruina. Vlterius eundo Iurten ab Sabaudis, prisco fere nomine, appellatur. Brachium, quod se extendit Basileam versus, uno ab Vrbe milliario juxta Byrsam fluvium, Blourren dicitur: crescitque non parum in altitudine & asperitate, quousque Delspergum veneris, ubi rursus in planiciem diducitur. Vlterius, versus Bellele Monasterium Gallicum procedendo, rursum crescit; ad deinde iterum evanescit spacio unius milliarij: hinc iterum saxosum horrendumque Montis jugum ab Oriente in Occasum extenditur; quod pervium fecisse scribitur Julius Cæsar, perforato in portæ formam saxo. Portam hanc nominant alij Pierre-port, Petra portam; alij Pierre-pertus, Petram pertusam. Descriptam vere accurateque ab Sebastiano Munstero, ipse, qui eam aliquando transgressus, testor. Inscriptionem supra Portam satis claram deprehendi, nisi quod primæ vocis litteræ reliquis magis sint extritæ:
units.tr: Is the Jura to be called a mountain of Gaul or of Germany? Formerly it was almost wholly of Gaul, when Helvetia was counted as part of Belgica; today it belongs to Germany for a large part. Its beginning is usually placed in the territory of Basel, beside the Rhine, opposite Waldshut. It is high and rests upon many huge rocks. Caesar, Pliny and others make mention of it. In Ptolemy it is Iuragoris; in Strabo Iuqoio& and Ioges. In our age, the neighbours and inhabitants call it by different names according to the places. Not far from the castle of Habsburg, near Brugg (a small town so called in German, from the bridge which here crosses the Aare on a single arch), it is called Botzberg, as the inhabitants told me when I was crossing, from the village Botzen, which lies at the foot of the mountain along with many others. Sebastian Münster, Egidius Tschudi, Wolfgang Lazius, Christian Wurstisen and others think that this part of the Jura is the Vocetum or Vocetium of Cornelius Tacitus. Abraham Ortelius, however, has no doubt that in Tacitus we should read Vogesum, which I mentioned before. In this same part of the mountain there is a huge valley called Frikthal, from the village of the same name. Other valleys occur here and there, to mention this in passing, Laufenthal, S. Innerfthal, and similar ones; yet none of them penetrates the mountain right across. Wherever you wish to cross, a steep climb is needed. Between the Aare and Farspurg this mountain is called Schafmatt, which in Latin means Ovine Meadow. Between the town of Olten and the prefecture of Homburg it is called Nider-Haurvenstein, Lower Sestus Rock, for the road was made through rocks. Between Waldenburg and Balstal it is called Ober-Hauvrenstein, Upper Sestus Rock, where laden carts are lowered down the slope of the mountain on heavy ropes. Proceeding westward it is called Wassersal, that is, Water Ruin. Going further it is called Iurten by the Savoyards, an almost ancient name. The arm which extends towards Basel, one mile from the city beside the river Birs, is called Blauen; it grows not a little in height and roughness until you come to Delsberg, where it again spreads out into a plain. Further on, proceeding towards the French monastery of Bellelay, it rises again, and then vanishes again within the space of one mile; from here a rocky and dreadful ridge of the mountain stretches again from east to west. It is written that Julius Caesar made this passable by piercing the rock in the shape of a gate. Some call this gate Pierre-Pertuis, the Pierced Rock; others Pierre-pertus, the Pierced Stone. I myself, who once passed through it, testify that Sebastian Münster has described it truly and accurately. I made out the inscription above the gate quite clearly, except that the letters of the first word are more worn than the rest:

units.la: N.·.·.·.ANGVSTI VIA DVCTA PER ARDVA MONTIS FECIT ITER PETRAM SCINDENS IN MARGINE FONTIS
units.tr: N.·.·.·.A narrow way, led through the steep mountain, made a path, cutting the rock at the edge of the spring.

units.la: An Antiquitatem sapiat, non disputabo. Per Fontem intelligit Poëta Byrsam amnem, qui ibi ex Petra magna Aquarum vi erumpit. Procutrit inde Iura versus Libonotum inter Helvetios Sabaudosque, quos ad Vulturnum respicit, & Burgundos, quos ad Caurum relinquit (unde & apud Cæsarem lib.1 duobus locis Iura Sequanos ab Helvetijs dividit) secus varios Lacus, quorum præcipuus Lemannus; ubi longe lateque Mons S. Claudy nuncupatus ad Rodanum tandem terminatur.
units.tr: Whether it smacks of antiquity I will not dispute. By the Fountain the poet means the river Byrsa, which there bursts forth from a great rock with the force of its waters. From there the Jura runs on towards the south-west, dividing the Helvetii and the Savoyards, whom it faces toward the south-east, from the Burgundians, whom it leaves toward the north-west (whence also in Caesar, book 1, it divides the Sequani from the Helvetii in two places), past various lakes, of which the chief is Lake Lemannus; there, far and wide, the range called Mons S. Claudy finally ends at the Rhone.

units.la: De alijs, qui ad Gallias etiam nonnihil spectant, De Pyreneo, inquam, dixi lib.11, ubi Hispaniam delineavi: deque Alpitus differam libro sequenti; ubi Italiam percurrendum mihi erit.
units.tr: Of the others, which also bear somewhat on Gaul, I said in book 11, where I described Spain, the Pyrenees, I mean; and I will defer the Alpitus to the following book, where I shall have to traverse Italy.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAP. V.

units.la: Galliæ Promontoria.
units.tr: The Promontories of Gaul.

units.la: INTER Promontoria, quæ Montibus adcensui, nobilissimum est illud, quod ultra omnem Galliam in Occidentem excurrit. Ptolemæo Rêcaor; hodie, ut Villanovanus adnotat, S. Mathieu; vel, ut Gerardus Mercator, Le Four.
units.tr: Among the promontories that I have added to the mountains, the most famous is the one that juts furthest west beyond all of Gaul. Ptolemy calls it Rêcaor; today, as Villanovanus notes, it is S. Mathieu; or, as Gerardus Mercator has it, Le Four.

units.la: Supra Gobæum versus Septemtrionem Γιαον est eidem Ptolemæo, è conspectu Cantij, Albionis Promontorij. Blanckenest putatur Becano, Stapulas Meicro.
units.tr: North of Gobaeum, in the same Ptolemy, is Γιαον [Γιαον], looking out from Cantium, the promontory of Albion. Becanus thinks it is Blanckenest; Meicro thinks it is Stapulas.

units.la: Succedunt Gobæo versus Meridiem apud eumdem Ptolemæum Πηχτόνιον; Vornoc Mercatori; Talmond Clufio; sic dictum Adcolis, quasi Talon du Monde:
units.tr: South of Gobaeum, in the same Ptolemy, follows Πηχτόνιον [Πηχτόνιον]; for Mercator it is Vornoc; for Cluvius it is Talmond, so called by the locals as if it were Talon du Monde:

units.la: Σαντωαῶν Ptolemæo; Blaie hodieque, ut putat Villanovanus; vel, ut Mercator Maluason.
units.tr: Σαντωαῶν [Σαντωαῶν] in Ptolemy; it is still Blaie today, as Villanovanus thinks; or, as Mercator has it, Maluason.

units.la: Κυριακὸν ἄκρον Ptolemæo; Josepho Scaligero in Aufonianis Caput Boiatum hodie, sed lingua Vasconum Cap de Butz; Mercatori est Sellac, Vincto Gordan, Belleforestio S. Maria.
units.tr: Κυριακὸν ἄκρον [Κυριακὸν ἄκρον] in Ptolemy. Joseph Scaliger, in his Ausonian notes, calls it Caput Boiatum today, but in the Basque language Cap de Butz. For Mercator it is Sellac, for Vinctus Gordan, and for Belleforest S. Maria.

units.la: Ad Mare Mediterraneum Κιθαρίστης est Ptolemæo, Citharistes Plinio & Pomponio Melæ, Citarifta Antonino: Circelli Nautis, notante Mario Nigro; alijs Cabo de S. Sigo, quibusdam Cabo Bacro Belleforestio Cap de Gercel.
units.tr: On the Mediterranean sea, Κιθαρίστης [Κιθαρίστης] is Ptolemy's name for it; Citharistes in Pliny and Pomponius Mela, Citarifta in Antoninus. Sailors call it Circelli, as Mario Nigro notes. Others call it Cabo de S. Sigo, and some Cabo Bacro; Belleforest calls it Cap de Gercel.

units.la: Nominatur ibidem in Galliæ Narbonensis ora maritima & Σήτιον Ptolemæo, Setium Antonino, Σίγιον Straboni, corruptius, nisi hoc sit Cabo de S. Sigo, de quo paulo ante. Setium certe hodie Cap de Cete, scribente Clufio.
units.tr: In the same passage, on the maritime coast of Narbonese Gaul, Ptolemy also names Σήτιον [Σήτιον]; Antoninus has Setium, and Strabo Σίγιον [Σίγιον], a more corrupt form, unless this is the same as Cabo de S. Sigo, mentioned a little above. Setium is certainly today Cap de Cete, according to Cluvius.

units.la: Est & non incelebre Promontorium, quod Nautis Cap de la Hague, cui Insula objacet Ebodia. Sic appellat Paulus Diaconus lib.1.cap.vi. Longobardicorum; quam Franci nunc nominant Aldernay vel Ornay, de qua suo loco.
units.tr: There is also a promontory of some note, which sailors call Cap de la Hague, and off which lies the island Ebodia. Paul the Deacon calls it thus in book 1, chapter 6 of the History of the Lombards. The Franks now name it Aldernay or Ornay, which I will discuss in its place.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CAP. VI.

units.la: Gallia Silvæ.
units.tr: The Forests of Gaul.

units.la: SILVÆ Gallijs sunt frequentes, non tamen, ut alijs in regionibus, magnæ, non densæ, non ita dumis horridæ. Apud Cenomannos variæ sunt, Les Forests de Versay, Longoulnay, Persi, Sille, Charnay, Audain, Maine, Concise: apud Britannos Inferiores, de Bosilblanc, de Toriant, de Guierche: apud Pictonas, Les Forests de Mouliere, Dyne, Brosse, Ligne, & aliæ: apud Biturigies Silva Roberti cum alijs vitiatur: apud Andegavos, Lourfaie & Marson. Totus Bononiensium Ager una quasi obsessus est Silva, cujus partes, Les Bois de Surene, Celles, Hardelot, Dalles, Bompsin. Apud Veromanduos haud procul Perona Nemora sunt Recteigne & Boubau: Apud Picardos Bois de Baine, de Beaulieu, de la Fere, de Conssy. Nec suis caret Silvis Lotharingia; Warnedwalde, Le Banbois, Bois de Mandon, de Heyde, de S. Benoyt, de la Forge, Mortaigne, Lofcyne. In Burgundijs multæ sunt Silvulæ, quarum nunc non occurrunt nomina. Alias præterea, quæ passim per Gallias hic ibi sparsæ.
units.tr: The forests of Gaul are numerous, yet not, as in other regions, large or dense, nor so bristling with thickets. Among the Cenomanni there are various ones: Les Forests de Versay, Longoulnay, Persi, Sille, Charnay, Audain, Maine, Concise; among the Lower Britons: de Bosilblanc, de Toriant, de Guierche; among the Pictones: Les Forests de Mouliere, Dyne, Brosse, Ligne, and others; among the Bituriges the Silva Roberti is corrupted along with others; among the Andegavi, Lourfaie and Marson. The whole territory of the Bononienses is, as it were, beset by a single forest, whose parts are Les Bois de Surene, Celles, Hardelot, Dalles, Bompsin. Among the Veromandui, not far from Péronne, are the woods Recteigne and Boubau: among the Picards Bois de Baine, de Beaulieu, de la Fere, de Conssy. Nor is Lorraine without its forests: Warnedwalde, Le Banbois, Bois de Mandon, de Heyde, de S. Benoyt, de la Forge, Mortaigne, Lofcyne. In Burgundy there are many small woods, whose names are not now found. Besides these there are others scattered here and there throughout Gaul.

units.la: Arduenna, hodie potissima parte est in Inferiore Germania, ideoque ibi describenda. Gallicam vocat Claudianus; & Silvam Galliæ maximam Cæsar lib. vi. de bello Gallico, quod olim esset in Gallia Belgica.
units.tr: The Arduenna, today for the most part lies in Lower Germany, and so is to be described there. Claudian calls it Gallica, and Caesar, in book 6 of the Gallic War, calls it the greatest forest of Gaul, since it was once in Belgic Gaul.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: Gallia Sinus.
units.tr: The Gulfs of Gaul.

units.la: SINUS Gallijs sunt insignes; cum ad Oceanum, tum ad Mare Mediterraneum. Ad Oceanum est cum primis ille, qui Aquitanicus Æthico, Orosio; Tabulæ Peutingerianæ. Tarbellicus Ancon elegantissime apud Lucanum vocatur: Et ripas Atyri, quem littore curvo Molliter admissum claudit Tarbellicus Ancon.
units.tr: The gulfs of Gaul are notable, both on the Ocean and on the Mediterranean. On the Ocean the most important is the one that Aquitanicus in Aethicus and Orosius, and the Peutinger Tables, call Tarbellicus Ancon, which Lucan elegantly names: "and the banks of the Atyrus, which the Tarbellic Ancon receives and encloses where the shore curves gently." Joseph Scaliger, a most noble man, advises that this is how it must be read, not as it is printed today: "and the banks of the Satyrus, where the Tarbellic sea receives the gently curving shore," which makes no sense.

units.la: Ita enim omnino legendum monet Nobilissimus Vir Iosephus Scaliger; non, ut hodie: & ripas Satyri, qua littore curvo Molliter amissum claudit Tarbellicus æquor. nullo sensu. De hoc Sinu Strabo lib. iv Geographic. Male vertunt Interpretes: Sinum hunc habent Tarbelli. Dicendum enim fuerat: Habent vero & Sinum Tarbelli: ne Sinum Gallicum, de quo paulo ante verba fecerat Strabo, tribuere videatur Tarbellis: Gallicumque, qui ad Mare Mediterraneum, cum Tarbellico vel Aquitanico, qui ad Oceanum, confundere.
units.tr: On this gulf Strabo writes in Book 4 of his Geography. The translators render him badly: "The Tarbelli have this gulf." They should have rendered it: "The Tarbelli also have a gulf," so that he does not seem to assign the Gallic Gulf, which Strabo had discussed just before, to the Tarbelli, and so confuse the gulf on the Mediterranean, the Gallic one, with the Tarbellic or Aquitanian one, which lies on the Ocean.

units.la: Sinus etiam ad idem Mare sunt non ignobiles, in quorum intimis recessibus locata videmus opida, Diepam, Constantiam, & alia.
units.tr: There are also gulfs on the same sea that are not unknown. In their innermost recesses we see towns located, such as Diepa, Constantia and others.
