units.la: Ad Mare Mediterraneum Gallicus (γαλατικὸς) Sinus est duplex, Major, & Minor, Major ea Maris Mediterranei pars appellatur, ubi se in illud effundit Rodanus. Angulus Gallicus M. Porcio Catoni in Oratione de Consulatu; qua forma paulo ante Aquitanicus Sinus Lucano dicebatur Tarbellicus Ancon, voce Græca: Gallicus Sinus κατ' ἑσπέραν Livio lib. xxvi. & xxx, Iustino lib. xliii, & alijs. Minor apud eumdem Strabonem scribitur ad Promontorium Montis Pyrenæi, quod Aphrodisium appellatum dixi lib. ii, cap. v. Hic Salsus vocatur Pomponio Melæ. Littus, quod huic Sinui objacet, Phociacum videtur nominari in Inscriptione, quam præcedentis libri capite vii posui. Circa Massiliam & Emporias interpretatur Antonius Augustinus Dialogo iii de Nummis antiquis. Videndus & Silius Italicus lib. i, iii, & iiii Belli Pœnici.
units.tr: On the Mediterranean the Gallic [γαλατικὸς] Gulf is double, Major and Minor. Major is the name of the part of the Mediterranean into which the Rhône empties itself. Marcus Porcius Cato calls it the Gallic corner in his speech on the consulship. By a Greek term, Lucan had earlier called the Aquitanian gulf, in the same form, the Tarbellic Ancon. Livy in Books 26 and 30, Justin in Book 43, and others call it the Gallic Gulf toward the west [κατ' ἑσπέραν]. Minor is written about by the same Strabo as lying at the promontory of the Pyrenees, which I said in Book 2, chapter 5, was called Aphrodisium. Here it is called the Salsus by Pomponius Mela. The shore that faces this gulf seems to be named Phociacum in the inscription that I set out in chapter 7 of the previous book. Antonius Augustinus explains the gulf near Massilia and Emporiae in Dialogue 3 on ancient coins. Silius Italicus, in Books 1, 3 and 4 of the Punic War, should also be consulted.

units.la: Gamblacitanum etiam Sinum ponit ad Galliam Narbonensem Antoninus.
units.tr: Antoninus also places a Gamblacitanus gulf off Gallia Narbonensis.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CAP. VIII.

units.la: Galliarum Port- us.
units.tr: The Ports of Gaul

units.la: PORTVS, ut hodie, de quibus plene Lucas Aurigarius Charta v & quatuor sequentibus, sic olim habuit Gallia celeberrimos. Nam quæ non ad mare Gallicum opida vocarunt Antiqui, si modo quid commodi haberent situs, Portus? Principem obtinent locum Staliocanus, Vindana, Brivates, & alij quidam Veteribus nominati.
units.tr: Gaul once had, just as it does today, very famous ports, which Lucas Aurigarius treats fully in Chart 5 and the four following. For what towns did the ancients call ports on the Gallic Sea, if they had any advantage of position? The chief place is held by Staliocanus, Vindana, Brivates, and certain others named by the ancients.

units.la: Qui Ptolemæo, alijs S. Paul de Lyon in Britannia existimatur, Rosco aliis; quibus ut subscribam, facit, quod posterior priore multo sit fidior & commodior, quamvis enim oppositam habeat Insulam, cui cognomen vulgo De Bas, facilem tamen & tutum septemque altum hodie ulnas, utrimque præbet Navibus ingressum. Priori, cui ab D. Paullo nomen, minax objacet Taurus (Insula est, vulgo Le Taurean) qui circumpositas habet rupes innumeras & latentes & eminentes; a quibus magnum Nautis male providis creari solet periculum.
units.tr: The port that Ptolemy names is thought by others to be St Paul de Léon in Britain; I incline to Rosco, as others do. My reason is that the latter is much more trustworthy and convenient than the former. Although it has an island opposite, which is commonly called De Bas, it offers entry to ships on either side, the channel being easy and safe and seven fathoms deep today. The former port, which takes its name from St Paul, is threatened by the Taurus (an island, commonly called Le Taurean), which has around it countless rocks, both hidden and projecting; a great danger is usually created by these for sailors who are poorly prepared.

units.la: Haud procul inde in eadem Britannia versus Meridiem post flexum Promontorij Gobæi, de quo ante dixi, Vindana occurrit Portus; Ptolemæo. Fensliers hodie, vel Conquest. Iovio male Brest.
units.tr: Not far from there, in the same Britain, towards the south after the bend of the promontory of Gobaeus, which I mentioned earlier, there lies the port of Vindana, according to Ptolemy. Today it is Fensliers, or Conquest. Jovius wrongly gives it as Brest.

units.la: Adscribit hinc Portum nominatus à me sæpe Ptolemæus. Nomen hodie fere retinet, Brest.
units.tr: From here Ptolemy, whom I have often named, lists a port. Today it nearly keeps the name, Brest.

units.la: Sequitur apud eundem Ptolemæum Portus: Luffon vel Luxon hodie. Secor & Brivates corrupte leguntur in Tabula Peutingeriana, mistim in una voce Gesocribate.
units.tr: Next in Ptolemy's list is the port of Luffon, or today Luxon. Secor and Brivates are read corruptly in the Tabula Peutingeriana, run together in one word, Gesocribate.

units.la: Hinc Santonum, Portus Ptolemæo scribitur; hodie La Rochelle, ut arbitratur Villanovanus.
units.tr: From here the port of the Santones is written by Ptolemy; today it is La Rochelle, as Villanovanus thinks.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: Fluvij Galliæ celebriores.
units.tr: The more famous rivers of Gaul.

units.la: LÆTATVR Gallia Fluminibus, quæ magna, quæ parva, innumeris. De ijs in genere Strabo lib. iv: ... Hujus Fluviorum crebritatis caussam indicat Seneca libro Natur. Quæstion. iii: At contra, ait, constat Germaniam Galliamque, & proxime ab his Italiam abundare rivis & Fluminibus; quia Cælo humido utuntur, & ne æstas quidem Imbribus caret. Nominat simul Fluvios non paucos Ausonius Eidyllio iii, ubi de Mosella. Non tibi se Liger anteferet, non Axona præceps, Matrona non, Gallis, Belgisque interfusa finest Santonico refluus non ipse Carantonus æstu Amnis, & auriferum postponet Gallia Tarnem; Insanumque ruens per saxa rotantia late In mare purpureum, Domina tamen ante Mosella Numine adorato, Tarbellius ibit Asturnus. Et paullo post: Te Druna, te sparsis incerta Druentia ripis, Alpinique colent fluvij, duplicemque per urbem Qui meat, & dextra Rodanus dat nomina ripa; Te Stagnis ego cærulcis, magnumque sonoris Amnibus, æquorea te commendabo Garumna.
units.tr: Gaul rejoices in its rivers, great and small, past counting. On these in general, Strabo, book 4: ... The cause of this abundance of rivers is given by Seneca, Natural Questions, book 3: On the other hand, he says, it is established that Germany and Gaul, and next to them Italy, abound in streams and rivers, because they have a humid climate, and even summer is not free of rain. Ausonius, in Idyll 3, where he speaks of the Moselle, also names not a few rivers: "Neither will the Liger put himself before you, nor the headlong Axona, nor the Matrona, which flows between the Gauls and the Belgians; nor the Carantonus, itself a river that ebbs with the tide of the Santones; and Gaul will not set the gold-bearing Tarnes before you; and the Asturnus of the Tarbelli will go, though the mad river that rushes through the rocks and rolls widely into the purple sea, the Mosella, is the lady, her divinity adored. And a little later: Druna, and Druentia, uncertain in its scattered banks, and the Alpine rivers will worship you, and the one that flows through the double city, and the Rhône that gives its name to the right bank; you, Garumna, I will commend to the blue pools and the sea-like waters of the resounding streams."

units.la: Sic Tibullus lib. 1. Elegia v 11: Testis Arar, Rodanufque celer, magnusque Garumna Carnuti & Flavi caerula lympha Liger.
units.tr: So Tibullus, book 1, elegy 5, line 11: "Witness the Arar and the swift Rhône, and the great Garumna, and for the Carnutes and the Flavi, the blue water of the Liger."

units.la: Sic denique Sidonius Apollinaris in Panegyrico, quem dixit Cæsari Iulio Val. Maiorano Augusto: iflum jam Gallia laudat Quodque per Europam est rigidis hunc abluit undis Renus, Arar Rodanus, Mosa, Matrona, Sequana, Ledus, Clitis, Elaris, Atax, Vacalis, Ligerimque bipenni Excisum per frusta bibit, &c.
units.tr: Finally, so Sidonius Apollinaris in the Panegyric that he delivered to Caesar Julius Valerius Majorianus Augustus: Gaul now praises that river, and the Rhine, which bathes that through Europe with its stiff waters, the Arar, Rhône, Mosa, Matrona, Sequana, Ledus, Clitis, Elaris, Atax, Vacalis, and drinks the Liger, cut into pieces by the axe, etc.

units.la: 10 Ordine turbatiore præferuntur hæc ab Vulgatis Libris.
units.tr: 10 In a more confused order, these are put forward by the common books.

units.la: Primum autem inter Fluvios agmen ducunt Sequana, Ligeris, Garumna, Rodanus.
units.tr: The first place in the line of rivers is taken by the Sequana, Liger, Garumna, Rhône.

units.la: Qui Sequana Latinis, Σηκουάνα dicitur Ptolemæo, Σηκουανὸς Straboni, Σηκόαν@ Stephano, Siban Beniamino, Seyne vulgo. Oritur in Burgundiæ Ducatu, in Alsceti Regione paulo amplius Leuca versus Septemtrionem à Burgo, qui S. Sequano sacer: duobus rivulis, quos inter Pagi jacent Billy & Perriere. Lustratis sectisq; cum alijs, tum Lutetia Parisiorum, cui nobilissimam facit Insulā Romomagoque, Mare Britannicum vel Normannicum ostio satis lato irrumpit. Æstuarium ibi satis est navigantibus periculosum; ideoque provide magnaque solicitudine adeundum. Normannis vulgo vocatur La Bare. Sequana enim Mare ingressus repente contra Fluviorum cæterorum naturam refluit, horrendo sonitu ascendens ad hastæ longioris altitudinem. Inexspectata solent hic negligentibus & incuriosis oriri discrimina. De ortu Sequanæ sic Strabo lib. iv: Ἀλλὰ δ᾽ ἐστὶν ὁμοίως ἐν τοῖς Ἀλπεσι τὰς πηγὰς ἔχων, Σηκουανὸς ὄνομα. Ἡ δὲ τὸν Ὠκεανὸν, ... Alpium appellatio Straboni, ut & alijs, solet esse latissima. Stephanus Sequanam Massiliensium vocat Fluvium. Massilienses olim per Gallias late dominabantur. Currens Sequana fluvios suscipit varios, in quis nobiliores cæteris, Antiquis etiam noti, Matrona, Esia, Axona. Matrona (vulgo Marne) ingens Flumen, neque ipso minus Sequana, cum quo Celtas (Gallos Romani vocabant κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν) à Belgis dividebat, ut Cæsar, Aufonius (cujus versus ante positi) & Ammianus tradunt. Nascitur in Vogeso Monte, paulo supra Lingonum urbem (Langres) versus Euronotum.
units.tr: The Sequana is called in Latin; Ptolemy calls it Σηκουάνα, Strabo Σηκουανός, Stephanus Σηκόαν@; the Siban to Benjamin; the Seyne commonly. It rises in the Duchy of Burgundy, in the region of Alsace a little more than a league north of the town of Bourg, which is sacred to Saint Sequanus, between two little streams, between which lie the villages of Billy and Perriere. Having washed and cut through, among others, the Lutetia of the Parisians, which it makes most noble by its island, and Rouen, it bursts into the British or Norman Sea through a mouth sufficiently wide. The estuary there is quite dangerous for sailors, and must therefore be approached with foresight and great care. Among the Normans it is commonly called La Bare. For the Sequana, having entered the sea, suddenly flows back, against the nature of other rivers, rising with a dreadful roar to the height of a long spear. Dangers that are unexpected often arise here for the careless and the incautious. On the source of the Sequana Strabo says, book 4: "But it likewise has its sources in the Alps, and is called Sequanus [Ἀλλὰ δ᾽ ἐστὶν ὁμοίως ἐν τοῖς Ἀλπεσι τὰς πηγὰς ἔχων, Σηκουανὸς ὄνομα. Ἡ δὲ τὸν Ὠκεανὸν, ...]." The name "Alps" in Strabo, as in others, is usually taken very broadly. Stephanus calls the Sequana a river of the Massilians. The Massilians once ruled widely over the Gauls. The flowing Sequana takes in various rivers, among which the more noteworthy, and known even to the ancients, are the Matrona, Esia, Axona. Matrona (commonly Marne) is a huge river, no less than the Sequana itself, along with which it divided the Celts (whom the Romans called Gauls, by preeminence) from the Belgians, as Caesar, Ausonius (whose verses are quoted above) and Ammianus report. It rises on Mount Vosges, a little above the town of the Lingones (Langres), toward the south-southeast.

units.la: 30 Visis post Lingones multis Vrbibus Opidisque, quorum præcipua Iani-Villa, S.Desiderij Fanum, Catalaunum, Hahyum, Dormantium, Arx Theodorici, Meldæque; acceptis item in sinum suum aliquot minorum gentium Amnibus, qui vulgo Saule, Bloise, Ourq, & Trefme, Sequanæ convolvitur leuca supra Parisios ad Pontem Charentonii.
units.tr: 30 After many towns and strongholds, of which the chief are Jans-Villa, the shrine of Saint Desiderius, Châlons, Hahy, Dormans, the castle of Theodoric, and Meaux, have been seen after the Lingones, and after it has also taken into its bosom some streams of smaller peoples, which are commonly called Saule, Bloise, Ourq, and Trême, the Sequana winds about a league above Paris, at the bridge of Charenton.

units.la: Esia (AEsiam alij cribunt) initiū capit duodecima supra Guisam leuca versus Orientem, haud procul pago Orgny. Meminit Vibius Sequester. Vulgo Oyse vel Aise. Picardiam percurrit. Veneratus Guisam, Feram, Compendium, Pontem S. Maxentij, aliaque opida, paulo infra Pontem cognominem (Pont-Oyse vulgo) ad Posliacum Sequanæ se miscet: raptis secum cum alijs, tum supra Compendium Axona, qui vulgo Ayne, Aisne vel Esne. Axona Cæsari Fluvius Galliæ Belgicæ in extremis Remorum finibus. Fons ejus hodie apud Barrenses, supra Clarum-Montem (Clermont) ad pagum Souilly. In Axonæ transitu Germanos ab insequentibus Gallis magnum olim accepisse incommodum, memoriæ prodit Cæsar lib. ii belli Gallici. Ejus Adcolæ Axones fortean apud Lucanum lib. i.
units.tr: The Esia (some write AEsia) takes its beginning twelve leagues east of Guise, not far from the village of Orgny. Vibius Sequester mentions it. Commonly Oise or Aise. It runs through Picardy. Having passed Guise, Ferè, Compiègne, the bridge of Saint-Maxence, and other towns, a little below the bridge of the same name (commonly Pont-Oise) it mingles with the Sequana at Pontoise, having taken with it, among others, the Axona above Compiègne, which is commonly called Ayne, Aisne, or Esne. The Axona is, for Caesar, a river of Belgic Gaul on the farthest borders of the Remi. Its source today is near the people of Barres, above Clermont, at the village of Souilly. Caesar, book 2 of the Gallic War, records that the Germans once suffered a great disadvantage in crossing the Axona, when the Gauls pursued them. The inhabitants of the Axona are perhaps the Axones in Lucan, book 1.

units.la: Ligerim secundo loco nominavi, ab Cæsare alijsq; nobilitatum: Αἴγφ@ (vel, ut in alijs Codicibus melius, Αἴγερις) & Λύγηξ Straboni lib. iv & Ptolemæo: Hodie Loire & Leire. Caput ejus in Pago Velauno: Locus vulgo La Fonte de Leire. Strabo: Ἐπιῤῥῖθι δ᾽ ὁ Λύγηξ ... Amplior est reliquis, ut merito Pater Galliæ Fluviorum audiat: aquæ limpidissimæ. Facto inter varios Populos (Celtas ab Aquitanis olim ex Strabonis notatione dividebat) procursu, exonerat se in Oceanum Occidentale, inter Nannetes & Pictones, Strabone etiam scribente: ὁ δὲ Λύγηξ μεταξὺ Πικτόνων τε ἢ Ναμνίτων ἐκβάλλει: ostio quatuor fere Leucas amplo, Pulvillis aliquot infecto: interius ad duas cum semi leucas Rupes sunt, quibus à Porcis cognomen. Ingentes & Navigiorum patientes excipit Fluvios non paucos, Elaver, Carim, Vigennam, Meduanam, & alios. Elaver apud Cæsarem lib. vii. belli Gallici, qui Sidonio Apollinari Panegyrico ad Majoranum Flaris (apud quem tamen alij Elaver legendum putant) Allier vulgo. Nascitur ex Cemmenis montibus supra opidum Clarum-montem,prope Gergoviam: Ligeri æmulus, neque magnitudine cedens,& magis pisculentus. Fluvium hunc inlustrat Gabriel Simeonius in Dialogo suo Pio & Speculativo: sic enim Titulus habet. Caris apud Gregorium Turonensem; Cher hodie. Vigenna, cujus mentio apud Fortunatum, Gregorium Turonensem & Hugonem Floriacensem, hodie Vienne, Viane & Vignane. Meduana meminit ex emendatione Turnebi Lucanus lib. 1. belli Pharsal.
units.tr: I named the Liger second, as it has been made famous by Caesar and others: Αἴγφ@ (or, as in other manuscripts, better, Αἴγερις) and Λύγηξ in Strabo, book 4, and in Ptolemy. Today the Loire and Leire. Its head is in the district of the Velauni, at the place commonly called La Fonte de Leire. Strabo: "And the Lygx flows near ... It is larger than the rest, so that it is rightly called the Father of the Rivers of Gaul: its waters are very clear." After running through various peoples (in Strabo's account it divided the Celts from the Aquitanians of old), it empties into the Western Ocean between the Nannetes and the Pictones, as Strabo also writes: "the Lygx discharges between the Pictones and the Namnetes [ὁ δὲ Λύγηξ μεταξὺ Πικτόνων τε ἢ Ναμνίτων ἐκβάλλει]." Its mouth is about four leagues wide, and is stained by some sandbanks; further inland, at about two and a half leagues, there are rocks, from which it has the surname "of the Pigs." Having taken in a number of rivers, the Elaver, Carim, Vigennam, Meduanam, and others, it receives great ships and accepts navigation. The Elaver is in Caesar, book 7 of the Gallic War. In Sidonius Apollinaris's Panegyric to Majorian it is Flaris (though others think Elaver should be read there), commonly the Allier. It rises from the Cevennes mountains above the town of Clermont, near Gergovia: a rival of the Liger, not inferior in size, and more full of fish. Gabriel Simeoni illustrates this river in his dialogue, which is titled Pious and Speculative. The Caris is in Gregory of Tours; today the Cher. The Vigenna, which is mentioned in Fortunatus, Gregory of Tours and Hugh of Fleury, is today the Vienne, Viane and Vignane. The Meduana is mentioned by Lucan, book 1 of the Pharsalia, in Turnebus's emendation:

units.la: In ripis Meduana tuis marcere perofsus.
units.tr: Wasting away on the banks of your Meduana, weary.

units.la: Alij Medualla legunt; Theodorus Canterus lib. 111. Novar. Lect. Meditana. Medunam sane & Medunam Galliæ fluvium etiam nominant Regino & Turonensis: hodie Mayne. Andegavensium Vrbem adluit. Longum esset omnes persequi Fluvios,quos Ligeris suscipit cum ipse, tum aliorum devectione.
units.tr: Others read Medualla; Theodorus Canterus, book 3 of Novae Lectiones, reads Meditana. Regino and the Turonensis indeed also name the river of Gaul Medunam and Medunam; today the Mayenne. It washes the city of the Andegavians. It would be long to pursue all the rivers that the Liger takes in, both from its own course and by the carrying of others.

units.la: Garumna sequitur, Cæsari Gallos ab Aquitanis disjungens: Straboni lib. 1 v Ῥαυνᾶς; Ptolemæo Ῥαρωία, Garonna Frontino; quod nomen integrum hodieque retinet a capite ad Blaviam Castrum, ubi Lingua Romana incipit. Nam inde pro Garonna dicitur Geronde & Gironde. Sillabam enim Ga, primam in vocibus, Galli (quod me monuit magnus Scaliger) mutant in Gi. Exempla dabuntur in sequentibus. Gerunnam etiam vocat Guilielmus Brito in sua Philippeide:
units.tr: The Garumna follows, separating the Gauls from the Aquitanians, as Caesar says. In Strabo, book 4, it is Ῥαυνᾶς; in Ptolemy Ῥαρωία; Frontinus calls it Garonna. This name it still keeps entire from its head to the castle of Blaye, where the Romance language begins. For from there on it is called Geronde and Gironde. For the Gauls (as the great Scaliger reminded me) change the syllable Ga, the first in words, into Gi. Examples will be given in what follows. William the Breton also calls it Gerunna in his Philippeid:

units.la: Quum post retrofluum pelago crescente Gerunnam.
units.tr: When, after the backward flow, the Gerunna swells with the rising sea.

units.la: Oritur ex Pyrenæis, haud procul opido, quod vulgo Cadalup. De eo diligentissime Pomponius Mela lib. 111: Garumna ex Pyrenæo monte delapsus, nisi cum hiberno imbre aut solutis nivibus intumuit, diu vadosus & vix navigabilis fertur: at ubi obvium Oceani exæstuantis accessibus adauctus est, ijsdemq; retro remeantibus suas illusq; aquas agit, aliquantum plenior, & quanto magis procedit, eo latior fit, ad postremum magns Freti (manet & nunc eadem facies) similis, nec majora tantum navigia tolerat, verum etiam more Pelagi sævientis exsurgens jactat navigantes, atrociter utiq;, si alio Ventus, alio Vnda præcipitat. Et quæ alia sequuntur de Antro Insula, ad Garumnæ ostium sita. Non absimilia de eo tradit Claudianus in Rufinum lib. 11:
units.tr: It rises from the Pyrenees, not far from the town commonly called Cadalup. Pomponius Mela, book 3, describes it most carefully: "The Garumna, descending from the Pyrenean mountain, unless it swells with winter rain or melting snows, is held to be shallow for a long way and scarcely navigable; but where it is met by the approaches of the swelling Ocean, and increased by them, as they flow back again, it carries its own waters and theirs, becoming rather fuller, and the further it advances, the wider it grows, until at last it is like a great strait (the same appearance remains even now), and it bears not only larger ships but, after the manner of a raging sea, rises up and tosses about the sailors, savagely indeed, if the wind drives the one way and the wave the other." And the other things that follow about the island of Antrum, which lies at the mouth of the Garumna. Claudian in his book 2 against Rufinus hands down things not much unlike this:

units.la: Quousque rigat retro pernicior unda Garumna, Oceani pleno quoties impellitur æstu.
units.tr: "How far the swifter Garonne flows back, whenever it is driven by the full tide of the Ocean."

units.la: Sic Sidonius Apollinaris Carmine xxiii, cui titulus Burgus Pontij Leontij:
units.tr: So Sidonius Apollinaris in Carmen xxiii, which is entitled Burgus of Pontius Leontius:

units.la: At quum submotus lunaribus incrementis, Ipse Garumna suos in dorsa recolligit æstus, Præcipiti fluctu raptim redit, atque videturIn fontem jam non refluus, sed desluus ire. Tum recipit laticem, quanuis minor ille, minoréStagnantii de fratre suum, turgescit & ipseOceano, propriasque facit sibi littora ripas.
units.tr: "But when the Garonne, pushed back by the increase of the moon, gathers its tides back upon its own ridges, it rushes back with a headlong flood, and it seems no longer to flow back but to run down into its own source. Then it receives the water of its brother Stagnantius, though that stream is smaller, and it swells up itself against the Ocean, and makes for itself shores and banks of its own."

units.la: Et hinc Fluenta refluentia tribuit eidem Garumnæ Sidonius idem lib vIII, epist. xII. Hodie perlustratis cum alijs, tum Tolosa & Burdigala, Mari se miscet Aquitanico, duarum fere Leucarum ostio; quod intrantibus occurrunt Scopuli, quibus ab Asellis cognomen. Septemtrionalior Nautis Belgis Noorder-Esel, Australior, Suyder-Esel, Φάρον vel præaltam sustinens Turrim, quæ vulgo Le Tour Cordan. Excipit navigeros Fluvios Tarnim, Egercium, Oldum, Duranium & alios. Tarnus Plinio lib. 1 v. cap. x ix, Ausonio in Mosella (qui Auriferum nominat) Sidonioque in Propemptico ad Libellum (cui Citus dicitur) celebratus: Lo Tarn vulgo, ut censent Josephus Scaliger & Vinetus; Gallicè loquentibus Le Tar: Errat Navagierus, qui Dordonam esse arbitratur. Egirtius Fortunato lib. 1. Egirsius Sidonio; Vasconibus hodie Gers-Oldus sive Olites Arvernatibus & Montanis Cadurcis Ooldt, vel cum articulo l'Old, l'Oolt, l'Ould; alijs corruptius Loth. Duranius Ausonio & Sidonio Apollinari in Burgo Leontij: Dordonia apud Gregorium Turonensem & priscos Monachos in rebus ab Karolo Magno gestis: Hodie La Dordogne, & alibi Dordonne. Vnus ex præcipuis non solum Aquitaniæ, sed etiam totius Galliæ Fluminibus, Garumnæ nec æstus nec aluei magnitudine cedens. De Dordonia sic Aimoinus lib. 1. cap. v. Histor. sub finem: Dordonia qui ex monte, qui Dor dicitur, & est in finibus Arvernorum, duobus scaturiens fontibus, quorum uni nomen est Dor, alteri Donia; qui haud procul Monte ipso conjunguntur, in Garumnam influit: ad opidum Burgum (hodie Bourg) quod Sidonius decantat: cui Duranius ibidem muscosus curvata saburra. Quum autem Ῥαυνᾶς scribatur Straboni τέλει ποταμοῖς αὐξηθᾶς: intelligendi sunt Tarnus, Oldus & Duranius.
units.tr: And from this Sidonius, in Book viii, Letter xii, gives the same Garonne the name flowing-back streams. Today, having traversed both other places and Toulouse and Bordeaux, it mixes with the Aquitanian Sea at a mouth about two leagues wide. Entering it, sailors meet rocks which are called by the name Asellae: the more northern, which the Belgian sailors call Noorder-Esel, and the more southern, Suyder-Esel, support a very high tower, [Φάρον] or lighthouse, which commonly is called Le Tour Cordan. There receive the navigable rivers Tarnis, Egercius, Oldus, Duranius and others. Tarnus is celebrated by Pliny in Book iv, chapter xix, by Ausonius in the Mosella (where he names it the Gold-bearing), and by Sidonius in the Propemptikon to his little book (which is called Citus). It is commonly Lo Tarn, as Joseph Scaliger and Vinetus think; in French Le Tar. Navagerius is wrong in thinking it is the Dordogne. Egirtius in Fortunatus Book i; Egirsius in Sidonius; to the Vascones today Gers-Oldus or Olites; to the Arverni and the Cadurci of the mountains Ooldt, or with the article l'Old, l'Oolt, l'Ould; to others, more corruptly, Loth. Duranius in Ausonius and in Sidonius Apollinaris in the Burgus of Leontius; Dordonia in Gregory of Tours and the old monks in the deeds of Charlemagne; today La Dordogne, and elsewhere Dordonne. It is one of the chief rivers not only of Aquitaine but of all Gaul, yielding to the Garonne neither in the force of its tides nor in the size of its bed. Aimoin, in Book i, chapter v, near the end of his History, speaks of the Dordonia thus: "The Dordonia, which rises from a mountain called Dor, and lies within the borders of the Arverni, gushing from two springs, one of which is named Dor and the other Donia, which join not far from the mountain itself, flows into the Garonne." It flows past the town of Burgus (today Bourg), which Sidonius celebrates, and of which Duranius, in the same poem, speaks as mossy with its curved sediment. Since Strabo writes that the Rhaunas, [Ῥαυνᾶς], is increased by the final rivers, [τέλει ποταμοῖς αὐξηθᾶς], we must understand the Tarnus, the Oldus and the Duranius.

units.la: Vltimum Rodano dedi locum. Fluvius hic Scriptoribus omnibus & Græcis, quibus Ῥοδανὸς, & Latinis notissimus. In universum Gallis nuncupatur Le Rosne: sed Indigenis Lo Ros: Eridanum nominant Oppianus in Halieuticis lib. iv & Philostratus in Vitis Sophistarum. Plinius ab Roda, Rodiorum in illo tractu Colonia, nomen impositum scribit. Sic D. Hieronymus in Epistolam ad Galatas, de Lugduno: Oppidum Rodani Coloni Rodiorum locauerunt, unde amnis Rodanus nomen accepit. Germaniæ fluvium videtur agnoscere Pomponius Mela lib. iii, cap. iii, forte quod Fons illi apud Germanos potius, quam Gallos: idem enim lib. ii, cap. v distinctis verbis inter Galliæ Flumina describit: putant tamen alij Renum pro Rodano priore loco reponendum. Oritur haud procul Danubij, Reni, Arolæ, Ticini aliorumque fontibus, prope montem, qui vulgo Briga. Lacum Lemannum apud Pagum Novam-Villam (Neuf-Ville) ingressus, servato fere colore (quem ipse, qui Lacum sæpissime navigavi & familiarissime etiam cum periculo meo novi, viridiorem animaduerti, aquam autem Fluvij limpidam pellucidamque, quum quæ ipsius erat Lacus crassior esset, & ab terrena fæce impurior, coloríque cinerei permeat, & ad Genevensium oppidum egressus, rapido cursu pergens in mare Mediterraneum erumpit: septem ostijs, ut scribit Apollonius in Argonauticis: quinq;, ut Diodorus, Timæus apud Strabonem, & Sex. Avienus; tribus ut Artemidorus apud eundem Strabone, Plinius & Ammianus; duobus, ut Polybius eodem Strabone teste, & Ptolemæus; pluribus, ut prudenter libique, ne mendacij argui posset, cavens Livius: hodie quinque, & plura numerant nominantque Adcolæ, Gras Neuf, Gras d'Orgon, Gras Paulet, Gras Grant, Gras d'Enfer, Gras de Pajon: quorum postremum, quod versus Massiliam sit, Massaleoticum appellat Plinius, Μασσαλιωτικὸν Polybius, qui hoc Primum vocat, quod ad Gradus Marcellino & Antonino; à quo cæteris etiam Ostijs Gradus nomen inditum. Rodani Ortum Cursumque sic describit Strabo lib. v: Φέρεται δ' ἀνω τῶν πόλεων ἕτι (Ῥοδανὸς) πολὺς καὶ σφοδρός. Rodanum, Ararim & Isaram) Φερόμενος πρὸς Ἄρκτον, εἶτα πρὸς Δύσιν.
units.tr: I have given the last place to the Rhone. This river is very well known to all writers, both Greek, to whom it is Rhodanus [Ῥοδανὸς], and Latin. In general the French call it Le Rosne, but the natives Lo Ros. Oppian in Book iv of the Halieutica, and Philostratus in the Lives of the Sophists, call it Eridanus. Pliny writes that it took its name from Roda, a colony of the Rhodians in that district. So Saint Jerome, in his letter to the Galatians, speaking of Lyons: "The Rhodian colonists founded a town on the Rhone, whence the river Rhodanus received its name." Pomponius Mela, in Book iii, chapter iii, seems to acknowledge it as a river of Germany, perhaps because its source is among the Germans rather than the Gauls; for in Book ii, chapter v, he describes it in express words among the rivers of Gaul. Others, however, think that the Rhine should be put in place of the Rhone in the earlier passage. It rises not far from the sources of the Danube, the Rhine, the Arola, the Ticino and others, near the mountain commonly called Briga. After entering the Lake Geneva at the village called Neuf-Ville, it keeps almost its colour, and, as I myself, who have very often sailed on the lake and come to know it very intimately, even at my own risk, have noticed, it is greener; but the river's water is clear and transparent, and it runs through the lake's thicker water, which is more impure from earthly dregs, and keeps its ash-grey colour. Then, going out past the town of Geneva, it rushes on with a swift course and bursts into the Mediterranean through seven mouths, as Apollonius writes in the Argonautica; five, as Diodorus, Timaeus in Strabo, and Sextus Avienus say; three, as Artemidorus in the same Strabo, Pliny and Ammianus say; two, as Polybius, again on the testimony of Strabo, and Ptolemy say; more than these, as Livy, cautiously and prudently, avoiding being charged with falsehood, says. Today the neighbouring inhabitants count and name five, and more: Gras Neuf, Gras d'Orgon, Gras Paulet, Gras Grant, Gras d'Enfer, Gras de Pajon. The last of these, because it lies towards Marseilles, Pliny calls the Massaliotic mouth, and Polybius [Μασσαλιωτικὸν], who calls this the First, because it is at the Steps according to Marcellinus and Antoninus; and from this one the other mouths too were given the name Steps. Strabo, in Book iv, describes the origin and course of the Rhone thus: [Φέρεται δ' ἀνω τῶν πόλεων ἕτι (Ῥοδανὸς) πολὺς καὶ σφοδρός. Rodanum, Ararim & Isaram] Φερόμενος πρὸς Ἄρκτον, εἶτα πρὸς Δύσιν. That is, the Rhone, carried above the cities, is still large and violent, flowing towards the north and then towards the west.

units.la: Quia vero ab Alpibus profluit Rodanus, existimandum est Strabonem prima hæc à me laudata ad hunc modum scripsisse: Φέρεται δ' ἀπὸ τῶν Ἄλπεων, &c. Pro μεγάλης mallem etiam Ἀεμάνης. Exitum autem apud Strabonem hic, non exiens Latinis, sed exitum quærens. Innuit enim Rodanum undæ suæ colorem seruare, non quidem Lacu jam egressum, nam de eo nullum dubium: sed in ipso Lacu, dum eum percurrit, & exitum quærit. Videndus omnino Plinius lib. ii, nat. histor. cap. cIII. Pomponius Mela lib. ii: Rodanus non longe ab Istri Renique fontibus surgit: deinde Lemanno Lacu acceptus tenet impetum, seque per medium (inclinat magis ad Septemtrionale latus) integer (seruato fere colore) agens quantus venit, egreditur. Inde contra in Occidentem ablatus aliquamdiu Gallias dirimit. Post cursu in Meridiem abducto, hac intrat; accessuque aliorum Amnium jam grandis & subinde grandior inter Volcas & Cauaras emittitur. Clarius Ammianus Marcellinus lib. xv: cujus totus de hoc Fluvio locus dignus, qui adscribatur: A Pæninis Alpibus effusiore copia fontium (tres aliquando mihi ab Adcolis monstrati) Rodanus fluens, & proclini impetu ad planiora digrediens, proprio agmine ripas occultat, & Paludi sese ingurgitat nomine Lemanno; eamque intermeans nusquam Aquis miscetur externis, sed alrinseces summitates Vndæ præterlabens segniores (ipse perfecte vidi supra Lofannam, Fluvio ex liquefacta nive pluvijsque continuis supra modum aucto, violentiusque Lacum perrumpente) queritans exitus (ἐξιὼν Strabo, paulo ante) viam sibi impetu veloci (adeo ut, Lacu nondum plene relicto, Hydromylarum Tympana Genevensium circumagat) molitur. Vnde sine jactura rerum per densa Paludium fertur & Sequanos, longeque progressus Vtennensem latere sinistro perstringit, dextro Lugdunensem: & emensus spatia fluctuosa Ararim, quem Sauconnam (de eo paulo post) appellant inter Germaniam primam fluentem, suum in nomen adscitu: qui locus exordium est Galliarum. (excludebatur enim antiquis Galliarum limitibus ea, quæ Narbonensis & Provincia Romanorum dicebatur) Exinde non millenis passibus, seu Leucis itinera metiuntur: ubi auctus Rodanus Aquis advenis locupletior, vehit grandissimas naves, Ventorum flatu jaclari. Iactari sæpius adsuetas: finitusque inter Valles, quas ei natura præscripsit, spumeus (hac voce notatur impetus erumpentis) Gallico mari concorporatur per patulum Sinum, ab Arelate octavodecimo ferme lapide disparatum. Sed ne quid dissimulem; de Rodano, colorem suum servante; quæ dixi, negare videtur doctissimus Isaacus Casaubonus ad lib. iv. Strabonis Geograph. scribens, quum id diligenter observaret, vidisse se Rem non esse tam miram, quam videri volunt Veteres: se autem hoc magis mirari, quod in Arva ipse deprehendit. Is est, inquit, Fluvius, qui Rodanum ingreditur c circiter passus emensum, postquam è Lacu Genevensi exiit. Tanta autem est ejus Fluvii, seu verius Torrentis, vehementia, tantaque rapiditas, ut Rodani alveum ingressus, multos fluat passus ante, quam ei miscatur: ita ut duo Flumina juncta quidem, sed nullo modo mixta eodem labantur alveo: quin non raro contingit, ut nivalis li juefactis auctus ille Fluviolus Rodani cursum impediat, qui tum cogitur ad Lacum regredi, ut vere dicere illud possis, ἀνω ποταμῶν χωρῆσι παγαί. Id maxima cum omnium admiratione contigit famoso anno clɔ Iɔ LXXII. adeo ut Pistrina Genevensia, Rodano inter Lacum & Arva confluentem imposita, horarum aliquot spatio contrario motu moverentur, ac molerent. Porro quod paullo ante Ammianus ait de Navibus, Ventorum flatu jactari sæpius adsuetis, confirmat Ambrosius libro Hexaemeron secundo: Rodanus, inquit, rapido concitus cursu Tyrrheni aquoris (latius hoc nomen hic accipitur, quam apud alios Scriptores) freta findit: in quo non mediocre fertur Navigantium periculum, dum inter se Maris Fluctus & Amnis Fluenta decertant. Sed hæc talia Fluminibus omnibus, quibus violentiores in mare sunt Eruptiones, solent esse communia; præcipue si alio Venti, alio Aquæ præcipitent, quemadmodum paulo ante ex Pomponio audivimus de Garumna. Ab Rodano autem Rodanenses Regiones Irenæo lib. i. cap. ix. & Epiphanio lib. i. Tom. iii, hæref. xxxiii; item Rodanusia, Lugdunum. apud Sidonium Apollinarem lib. i. Epist. v. Rodani-potor denique Lugdunensis, Horatio lib. ii. Od. ult. Excipit præter Araram, de quo dixi, Rodanus Ararim, Isaram, Drunam, Druentiam, aliosque; & ad dexteram ripam Nardonem cum aliis. Araris Latinis, qui Ἄραρ Straboni, Ptolemæo & Sidonio carmine v. Hodie Saone vel Sone; quod nomen, quam putatur, est antiquius. Ammianus lib. xv; Ararim, quem Sauconnam appellant: melius fortean Saonam: & Ammiano multo prior Polybius, apud quem est Σαόρας, pro quo inaudie legendum Σαόνας. Oritur haud longe ab Fontibus Mosæ Mosellæque: Rodano non minor, anteaquam in illum reponatur, quod fit apud Lugdunum, ut in Urbis hujus explicatione videbimus. De Arare Strabo lib. iv: Ῥᾶ δὲ κᾶ ὁ Ἄραρ ἐκ τῶν Ἀλπέων (Vogesum designat Alpium appellatione, ut & alias indicavi) ἐςίζων Σηκοανὰς τε καὶ Αἰδουίας ἡ Λιγυκασίας. Φαλαβὼν δ᾽ ὑψηλὸν τὸν Δῆν ἐκ τῶν αὐτῶν ὄρων Φερεωδρον πλωτόν, ἐπικρατίσας τῷ ὀνόματι, ἡ γενόμενον ἐξ ἀμφοῖν Ἄραρ, συμμίσγει τῷ Ῥοδανῷ. De Araris cum Rodano concursu Venantius Fortunatus, Libro & Poemate v i, ut quidem ex MS. sui Codicis vestigijs legit amicissimus mihi Petrus Scriverius:
units.tr: Since, however, the Rhone flows from the Alps, we must suppose that Strabo wrote the first words I have quoted in this way: [Φέρεται δ' ἀπὸ τῶν Ἄλπεων, &c.]. I would prefer also [Ἀεμάνης] for [μεγάλης]. Here, in Strabo, exitum is not going out, as the Latins would say, but seeking an outlet. For he hints that the Rhone keeps the colour of its water not when it has already left the lake, for about that there is no doubt, but while it is still in the lake itself, as it crosses it and seeks an outlet. Pliny, Book ii of the Natural History, chapter ciii, should be consulted in full. Pomponius Mela, Book ii: "The Rhone rises not far from the sources of the Danube and the Rhine. Then, received by the Lake Leman, it holds back its force, and it passes through the middle of the lake (it inclines more to the northern side), whole, keeping almost its colour, and it goes out as large as it came in. Then, carried back to the west, it divides the Gauls for a while. Afterwards, led off to the south, it enters here, and, with other rivers joining it, now great and ever greater, it is discharged between the Volcae and the Cavari." Ammianus Marcellinus, Book xv, speaks more clearly. The whole of his passage on this river is worth quoting: "The Rhone, flowing from the Pennine Alps with a copious outpouring of springs (three of which were once shown to me by the inhabitants), and descending with a steep rush into the flatter country, hides its banks with its own onrush, and pours itself into a marsh called the Lemannus. Passing through it, it nowhere mingles with foreign waters, but slides past the upper surface of the water, which is more sluggish (I myself saw this clearly above Lausanne, when the river, swollen beyond measure by melted snow and continual rains, broke more violently into the lake), seeking an outlet, and it works out a swift way for itself with its force (so that, though it has not yet quite left the lake, it turns the water-mill wheels of the Genevans). Thence, without loss of its goods, it is carried through the dense marshes, past the Sequani, and, having gone far, it grazes the Vtennensis on the left side and the Lugdunensis on the right. Having traversed wave-tossed spaces, it takes the Arar, which the people call the Saucona (of this I shall speak a little later), flowing within Germania Prima, and adds it to its own name. This place is the beginning of Gaul (for the district called Narbonensis and the Province of the Romans was excluded from the ancient limits of Gaul). From there they measure their journeys not by thousands of paces, but by leagues. Here the Rhone, enriched by the waters of strangers, grows and carries very large ships, which are accustomed to be tossed by the blowing of the winds," and so on, until, bounded between the valleys which nature has prescribed for it, it flows foaming (this word marks the force of its bursting out) into the Gallic sea through a wide gulf, about eighteen miles from Arles. But, lest I conceal anything: the most learned Isaac Casaubon, writing on Book iv of Strabo's Geography, seems to deny what I have said about the Rhone keeping its colour. While carefully observing this, he says he saw that the thing is not as marvellous as the ancients wish us to believe, and that he himself wonders the more at what he discovered in the fields. "That is the river," he says, "which enters the Rhone after about a hundred paces, after it has come out of the Lake of Geneva. The violence and rapidity of this river, or rather torrent, are so great that, having entered the bed of the Rhone, it flows for many paces before it mixes with it; so that the two rivers, joined indeed but in no way mixed, flow in one bed. Indeed it not infrequently happens that this little stream, swollen by melted snow, impedes the course of the Rhone, which is then forced back to the lake, so that you could truly say of it, the springs flow back against the rivers." This happened to the great astonishment of all in the notable year 1572: the Genevan mills, placed on the Rhone where it flows together with the lake and the fields, were turned and ground for some hours with a contrary motion. Moreover, what Ammianus said a little before about ships, that they are often tossed by the blowing of the winds, is confirmed by Ambrose in Book ii of the Hexaemeron: "The Rhone," he says, "driven by a rapid course, cleaves the straits of the Tyrrhenian water (this name is taken here more broadly than by other writers), and there is said to be no small danger to sailors, while the waves of the sea and the streams of the river contend with each other." But such things are common to all rivers whose discharges into the sea are more violent, especially when the winds blow one way and the waters another, as we heard a little before from Pomponius about the Garonne. From the Rhone come the Rhodanenses regions in Irenaeus, Book i, chapter ix, and Epiphanius, Book i, tome iii, heresy xxxiii; likewise Rhodanusia, Lyons, in Sidonius Apollinaris, Book i, Letter v; and finally the Rhone-drinker of Lyons in Horace, Book ii, last Ode. Besides the Arar, of which I have spoken, the Rhone receives the Isara, Drona, Druentia and others, and on its right bank the Nardo with others. The Arar is the name the Latins use, which Strabo, Ptolemy and Sidonius in Carmen v call Araris. Today it is the Saône or Sone; a name which, as is thought, is older than the others. Ammianus, Book xv: "the Arar, which they call Saucona", better perhaps Saona; and much earlier than Ammianus, Polybius, in whom is Σαόρας, for which without doubt we should read Σαόνας. It rises not far from the sources of the Meuse and the Moselle; it is not smaller than the Rhone before it is poured into it, which happens at Lyons, as we shall see in the explanation of that city. On the Arar, Strabo in Book iv writes: [Ῥᾶ δὲ κᾶ ὁ Ἄραρ ἐκ τῶν Ἀλπέων (Vogesum designat Alpium appellatione, ut & alias indicavi) ἐςίζων Σηκοανὰς τε καὶ Αἰδουίας ἡ Λιγυκασίας. Φαλαβὼν δ᾽ ὑψηλὸν τὸν Δῆν ἐκ τῶν αὐτῶν ὄρων Φερεωδρον πλωτόν, ἐπικρατίσας τῷ ὀνόματι, ἡ γενόμενον ἐξ ἀμφοῖν Ἄραρ, συμμίσγει τῷ Ῥοδανῷ.] On the meeting of the Arar with the Rhone, Venantius Fortunatus, in Book vi, Poem v, as my most dear friend Peter Scriverius reads it from the traces of his manuscript codex:

units.la: Excipit hinc Narbo, qua litora plana remordens
units.tr: From here Narbo follows, where the gentle Arar, nibbling at the flat shores,

units.la: Mitis Arar Rodanas molliter intrat aquas.
units.tr: Enters the waters of the Rhone softly.

units.la: Quod autem Araris Rodano se jungat, putarunt Veteres nomen eum invenisse ἀπὸ τὸ ἡμιόδες, quum ante Brigulus vocaretur. Plutarchus in libello de Fluminibus: Ἄραρ ποταμὸς ἐςι τῆς Κελτικῆς, τὴν προσηγορίαν εὐληφῶς παρὰ τὸ ἡμιόλιος τῷ Ῥοδανῷ. καταφέρεται γὰρ εἰς τὸν τὸν κατὰ τὴν χώραν τῶν Ἀλλοβρίγων. Ἐκαλεῖτο δὲ πρότερον Βρίγυλλ. Ab hoc Fluvio Araricorum Nautarum Corpus vel Collegium. Mentio in Urna oblonga, parieti cuidam immissa Romæ in capite Pontis S. Bartholemæi, in Insula Tiberina: D. M. S. C. SEN. ... O. REGVLIANO. EQ. R. DIFFVS OLEARIO. EX. BÆTICA. CVRATORI. EIVSDEM CORPORIS. NEGOT. VINARIO. LVGDVN INCANABIS. CONSISTEN. CVRATORI. ET. PATRONO. EIVSD. CORPORIS. NAVTÆ. ARARICO PATRONO. EIVSD. CORPORIS. PATRONO. ... VIR LVGDVNI. CONSISTENTIVM. L. SILENIVS. REGINVS AVG. ET. VLATTIA. METRODORA. FILI. EIVSDEM PONENDVM. CVRAVERVNT. PROCVRANTE. DIONYSIO. ET. BELLICIANO. ET. Q. ... Araricum etiam Nautam nominant aliæ Inscriptiones, quas alia flagitant loca. unam hic adponam, quæ Lugduni in Domo Prioris S. Hirenei: D. M. ET MEMORIÆ ÆTERNÆ C. LIBERTI. DECIMANI CIVI. VIENNENS. NAVT ARARICO. HONORAT. VTRICVLARIO. LVGDVNI. CONSISTENTI PATRONA. MARCIAN. CONIVGI CARISSIMO. QVI. CVM. EA. VIXIT ANNIS. XV. SINE. VLLA. ANIMI LÆSIONE. PONENDVM. CVRAVIT ET. SVB. ASCIA. DEDICAVIT
units.tr: That Araris joins itself to the Rhone, the ancients thought, gave it its name from the Greek word ἡμιόλιος [hēmiolios], though it was earlier called Brigulus. Plutarch, in his little book on rivers: "The Arar is a river of Celtica, which has taken its name from the Greek hēmiolios, because it flows into the Rhone. For it empties into the Rhone in the territory of the Allobroges. It was formerly called Brigullos." [Ἄραρ ποταμός ἐστι τῆς Κελτικῆς, τὴν προσηγορίαν εἰληχὼς παρὰ τὸ ἡμιόλιος τῷ Ῥοδανῷ. καταφέρεται γὰρ εἰς τὸν Ῥοδανὸν κατὰ τὴν χώραν τῶν Ἀλλοβρίγων. Ἐκαλεῖτο δὲ πρότερον Βρίγυλλος.] From this river is named the Corporation or Guild of the Arar Boatmen. It is mentioned on an oblong urn set into a wall at Rome, at the head of the Bridge of St Bartholomew on the Tiber Island: To the Spirits of the Dead. ... Oleary of Baetica, curator of the same corporation, wine merchant of Lyon, curator and patron of the same corporation, patron of the boatmen of the Arar, patron of the same corporation ... a man of the Lyon corporation of the Consistentes, L. Silenius Reginus, Augustal, and Ulattia Metrodora, his daughter, had this set up; the work was carried out under Dionysius and Bellicianus and Q. ... Other inscriptions also name the Araricus boatman, and other places demand them. I will add one here, which is at Lyon in the house of the Prior of St Irenaeus: To the Spirits of the Dead and to eternal memory of C. Libertus Decimanus, citizen of Vienne, boatman of the Arar, honoured, bargeman of the Lyon corporation of the Consistentes; his patroness Marcia, to her dearest husband, who lived with her fifteen years without any injury to their affection, had this set up and dedicated it under the axe.

units.la: Araricus item Bibitor, id est, Lugdunensis, legitur apud Sidonium Apollinarem lib. I Epistola VIII. Araria denique Lugdunum ab eodem fluvio nuncupatur in Historia Lupi Lugdunensis Archiepiscopi. Arar tanta fluit lenitate, ut oculis in utram partem eat, judicari nequeat: unde apud Poëtas Araris tardior, & lentus Arar. Plinius lib. III. cap. IV de Rodano: Segnemque deferens Ararim, nec minorem ipso Torrentem Isaram & Druentiam. Isaram ecce, qui Ἰσαρᾶς Straboni, Ἴσαρ Ptolemaeo, hodie Isere. Rodano comparat Plinius: Maximus igitur merito Planco Imperatori dictus, qui de eo sic scribit ad M. Tullium: Itaque in Isara, Flumine maximo, quod in finibus est Allobrogum, ponte uno die facto, exercitum ad quartum Eidus Maii traduxi. Extat Epistola inter eas, quas ad Familiares scripsit Cicero lib. X. num. XV: legendæ & quæ sequuntur ejusdem Planci num. XVIII & XXI. Qui Druna Ausonio in Mosella (versibus supra recitatis) hodie Droma est, vel Drosne, uti censet Josephus Scaliger, ex Alpibus descendens, seque Rodano miscens infra Valentiam: Vincto ad Ausonium Druna parvus est hujus nominis Fluvius, ex agro Lemovicensi per Engulismensem & Petrogoricum veniens in Lilam; amnem Duranio se conjungentem ante Liburniam Urbem, à Burdigala quinque leucis distantem. Qui Druentia Plinio, Sidonio Apollinari; Cassiodoro alijs; Δρυέντια Straboni; Δρυέντιος Ptolemaeo; hodie Durance nominatur: de quo non possum non adscribere locum Livii ex lib. XXI, ubi de Annibale; Ad Druentiam flumen, inquit, pervenit. Is & ipse Alpinus amnis, longe omnium Gallia fluminum difficillimus transitu est. Nam quum Aquæ vim vehat ingentem, non tamen Navium patiens est: quia nullis coercitus ripis, pluribus simul, neque ijsdem alveis fluens, nova semper vada, novosque gurgites faciens (& ob eadem pediti quoque incerta via est) ad hæc saxa glareosa volvens, nihil stabilis nec tuti ingredienti præbet. Sed hæc de Fluminibus in præsentia sufficiant.
units.tr: Araricus, likewise Bibitor, that is, of Lyon, is found in Sidonius Apollinaris, book I, letter VIII. Finally, Araria is what Lyon is called from the same river in the History of Lupus, Archbishop of Lyon. The Arar flows with such gentleness that it cannot be judged in which direction it goes by the eye; hence in the poets, Araris tardior, and lentus Arar. Pliny, book III, chapter IV, on the Rhone: Bearing along the sluggish Arar, and the Isara and Druentia, not smaller than it. Note the Isara, which is Ἰσαρᾶς [Isaras] in Strabo, Ἴσαρ [Isar] in Ptolemy, and today the Isère. Pliny compares it with the Rhone: Maximus, rightly so called by the Emperor Plancus, who writes of it thus to M. Tullius: So on the Isara, a very large river which lies in the territory of the Allobroges, having made a bridge in one day, I led the army across on the fourth day before the Ides of May. The letter exists among those which Cicero wrote to his friends, book X, no. XV; the following letters of the same Plancus, nos. XVIII and XXI, should also be read. The Druna of Ausonius in the Mosella (verses quoted above), today the Droma or Drosne, as Joseph Scaliger thinks, descends from the Alps and mingles with the Rhone below Valence. Ausonius's Druna is a small river of this name, coming from the territory of the Lemovices through Angoulême and Périgueux into the Lile, and joining the Dordogne before the city of Libourne, five leagues from Bordeaux. The Druentia of Pliny, Sidonius Apollinaris, Cassiodorus and others, Δρυέντια [Druentia] in Strabo, Δρυέντιος [Druentios] in Ptolemy, today called the Durance. On this I cannot refrain from quoting Livy, book XXI, where he speaks of Hannibal: "He came to the river Druentia," he says, "which is also an Alpine stream, the most difficult of all the rivers of Gaul to cross. For although it carries a huge volume of water, it is not fit for boats, since, not confined by any banks, it flows in several channels at once, and not in the same beds, always making new shallows and new whirlpools; and for the same reason the way is uncertain even for infantry. Rolling over gravelly rocks, it offers nothing stable or safe to those entering it." But let these remarks on rivers suffice for the present.

units.la: CAP. X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: Lacus, Fontes.
units.tr: Lakes, Springs.

units.la: Svis etiam non carer Gallia Lacubus. Inter eos principis loci, qui Latinis Lemanus; plerisque Galliæ Lacus habitus: Straboni MS. lib. IV. Λίμνη Λεμάνη: Ptolemaeo in Narbonensi Galliæ descriptione Λίμνη Λιμέη: Hodie ab opidis ripæ adsitis, pars quidem Occidentalior Lac de Geneve, Orientalior autem Lac de Losanne; Germanis universim Genferse. Apud Antoninum in Itinerario Lausonius, in quibusdam Exemplaribus Lausinius. In Tabula Peutingeriana lego Lacui suprascriptum Lacum Losonne, inscriptum vero Lacus Losanete; vitiose, nisi sic ævum Theodosij Imperatoris enunciarit. Orientem versus recipit in se Rodanum; de quo ante dixi; ex adverso ad Occidentem est Geneva Allobrogum urbs: Latera utrimque vestiuntur aliquot opidis: quorum tamen nobiliora sunt, quæ ad ripam sedent Septemtrionalem, primas inter ea sibi vindicante Lausanna. Habet illud hic Lacus proprium & peculiare, quod flante nullo in superficie vento, facile idque admodum subito turbetur, sæpe non sine navigantium periculo, motus ab interiore aliquo, quique in imo Lacus fundo latere perhibetur, Vento: Adcolis La Vaudase vocatur. De hoc Lacu Lucanus lib. I. belli Pharsalici:
units.tr: Gaul is not without lakes either. The chief of them is the one called Lemanus by the Latins. Most have regarded it as the lake of Gaul. Strabo, in the manuscript of book IV, has Λίμνη Λεμάνη. Ptolemy, in his description of Narbonese Gaul, has Λίμνη Λιμέη. Today, from the towns on its shores, the western part is called Lac de Geneve and the eastern part Lac de Losanne. The Germans generally call it the Genfersee. In Antoninus's Itinerary it is Lausonius, and in some copies Lausinius. In the Peutinger Table I read, written above the lake, Lacum Losonne, and inscribed below it Lacus Losanete. This is faulty, unless the table reflects the age of the emperor Theodosius. Towards the east the lake receives the Rhone, which I have discussed earlier. Opposite, to the west, lies the city of Geneva, capital of the Allobroges. Both shores are dressed with several towns, of which the more notable are those on the northern bank, Lausanne claiming first place among them. This lake has a peculiar property of its own: when there is no wind on the surface, it is easily and quite suddenly disturbed, often not without danger to sailors, by a movement from some interior source, which is said to lie at the bottom of the lake. The local people call it La Vaudase, the Vaudaise wind. Lucan speaks of this lake in book I of the Pharsalia:

units.la: Deferuere cavo tentoria fixa Lemano:
units.tr: The tents fixed on the hollow Lemanus were struck down.

units.la: Cc 3 Cavum Cavum vocat propter ripas, quibus inclusus jacet, utrimque eminentiores. Notandum porro quod de eodem scribit Auctor Librorum de bello Gallico, quicumque sit: A Lacu Lemano, inquiens lib. 1. qui in flumen Rodanum influit, ad montem Iuram, &c. An verum illud? Res ipsa sequius loquitur. Rodanus Lacum influit, non Lacus Rodanum. Auctorem non capio, nisi legatur unica mutata littera, quem (ex qui in) flumen Rodanum influit. Turbavit vox Rodanum eos, qui non intellexerunt flumen Rodanum nominandi casu junctim ibi dici, quemadmodum Flumen Renum apud alios, & similia; ut ab Criticis nostris nuper plene probatum. Conjecturam hanc non enervat Ausonius, qui in Narbonis Elogio Lemanum Rodani genitorem appellat: Sic enim loquitur, non quod Rodanum generet Lacus; nam multo supra Lacum ex Alpibus hoc Flumen oritur; sed quod Rodanus Lacu egressus fiat quasi auctior, ejusque aliquantam auferat cum suis Aquarum vim, ut tumidior pleniorque procedat. Lemano Lacu Gebennicisque Montibus Gallia quondam in duo latera fuit divisa, inquit Pomponius Mela lib. II. Vetustissimi variorum Auctorum Codices N. in Lemano geminant. Magnum Lacum inter Massiliam & Orientalissimum Rodani Ostium collocant Veteres: Αιμνοθάλασσα dicitur Straboni lib. IV; Τ' αἰρεκται δὲ, inquit, τῶν ἐκβολῶν τῆς Ρόδανος, Λιμνοθάλασσα· καλεῖται δὲ σωματίμνδ ὀχεῖα και δ' ἔχει παράπτολλα, καὶ ἄλλως ἐνοψεῖ. Astromela est apud Plinium, cujus verba ex vetusto exemplari Toletano sic legenda & cum viris doctis distinguenda: Sunt Auctores & Heracleam oppidum in Ostio Rodani fuisse. Ultra, Fossa ex Rodano C. Marii opere & nomine, insigne Stagnum Astromela, oppidum Maritima Araticorum. Lacum hunc Stagni nomine designat etiam Pomponius Mela lib. II: Inter Massiliam & Rodanum Maritima Araticorum Stagno adsidet: Fossa Mariana partem ejus amnis navigabilis alveo effundit. Fossam porro Marianam, cujus mentionem faciunt Plinius & Mela, ut etiam Antoninus in Itinerario, Ταφρεῖ appellat Plutarchus, Διώρυχα Strabo; Ptolemaeus Latinum retinet nomen, φόσας vocans: Fossae hujus memoriam tuetur hodieque Pagus in Campo Lapideo, de quo suo loco, Fos vulgo audiens. Quarta ab opido Arverniae Bello miliaris parte Mons est, inque eo Lacus late se extendens: tam altus, ut fundo existimetur carere. Nulla in eum, quod quidem intuentium oculis parere potest, influit Aqua. Si quis quid in eum projiciat, Tonitrua dicitur mox auditurus, Fulgetra visurus, Pluviam & Grandinem habiturus. Haud procul inde Crypta est, cujus os rotundum, vulgo Creux de Soulcis; & Abyssus, cujus profunditas explorari nequit: & huic si quis injecto lapide aurem admoveat, Murmur perceptur auribus perhibetur ingens & mirabilem Strepitum, Tonitruo ex remotioribus venienti locis non absonum. Aestivis mensibus etiamtí nihil injiciatur, Strepitus tamen in Cavitatibus intelligitur. Putantur inesse Venti, inter se quasi belligerantes. Quae de Lacu duorum Corvorum apud Santonas, ad oram Oceani Gallici scribit Artemidorus, fabulosa censet Strabo lib. IV. Abitacini vel Avitaci, cui ab Avito nomen, Lacus in Arvernia apud Claromontem tam graphica est apud Sidonium lib. II Epist. II reique conveniens Descriptio, ut hodie primum delineata videatur, qua dexter, qua laevus. Videndi idem Sidonius in Epigrammate de Balneis, Praeses Fauchetius Gallicarum Antiquitatum lib. II. cap. XIV, & Papirius Matsonius Annalium lib. I. in Childerico. De Rubrefo Lacu legendus Pomponius Mela lib. II. cap. quo Gallia Narbonensis depingitur: Plinius Rubrensem nominat. Αἰμνη Ναρβωνιτις Straboni est & Stephano.
units.tr: Cc 3 He calls it hollow (cavum) because it lies enclosed between banks which rise higher on both sides. It is also worth noting what the author of the books on the Gallic War, whoever he was, writes about the same lake. In book I he says: from Lake Lemanus, which flows into the river Rhone, to the mountain Jura, and so on. Is that true? The facts themselves speak otherwise: the Rhone flows into the lake, not the lake into the Rhone. I cannot make sense of the author unless one letter is changed, so that qui in becomes quem, and it reads quem (for qui in) flumen Rhodanum influit, which the lake flows into the river Rhone. The word Rhodanum has confused those who did not realise that a river's name in the accusative is joined in this way, just as flumen Renum appears in other authors, and similar cases, as our critics have recently shown fully. Ausonius does not weaken this conjecture; in his Elogy on Narbo he calls the Lemanus the parent of the Rhone. He does not mean that the lake generates the Rhone, for the river rises far above the lake in the Alps, but that the Rhone, on leaving the lake, becomes as it were larger, and takes up some of its waters, so that it flows on fuller and more swollen. Pomponius Mela, book II, says that Gaul was once divided into two sides by the Lake Lemanus and the Gebennic mountains. The oldest manuscripts of various authors have a double reading in Lemano. The ancients place the Great Lake between Massilia and the most easterly mouth of the Rhone. Strabo, book IV, calls it Limnothalassa [Λιμνοθάλασσα]. Strabo's words, as read in the Greek, are: "The mouths of the Rhone form a lagoon, which is called Limnothalassa and has many islands and is otherwise unimportant." Astromela occurs in Pliny, whose words should be read and punctuated, as learned men agree, according to the old Toledo copy: There are authorities who say that there was also a town Heraclea at the mouth of the Rhone. Further on, a ditch from the Rhone, the work and name of Gaius Marius, and the notable pool Astromela, a town of the Maritime Aratici. Pomponius Mela, book II, also names this lake by the name Stagnum: Between Massilia and the Rhone, on the coast, the Maritime Aratici lie beside the pool. The Marian ditch drains part of it into the navigable channel of the river. The ditch, Fossa Mariana, which Pliny and Mela mention, as does Antoninus in his Itinerary, Plutarch calls taphrei [Ταφρεῖ], Strabo diorygha [Διώρυχα]. Ptolemy keeps the Latin name, calling it fosas [φόσας]. The memory of this ditch is still kept by a village in the Stony Plain, which I shall discuss in its place, commonly called Fos. A quarter of a mile from the town of Arvernia, Bellum, there is a mountain, and on it a lake spreading widely, so deep that it is thought to have no bottom. No water flows into it that eyes can see. If anyone throws something into it, it is said that he will shortly hear thunder, see lightning, and have rain and hail. Not far from there is a crypt, with a round opening, commonly called Creux de Soulcis, and an abyss whose depth cannot be explored. If anyone puts his ear to it after throwing in a stone, he is said to hear a great murmur and a wonderful noise, not unlike thunder coming from distant places. Even in the summer months, when nothing is thrown in, a noise is heard in the hollows. It is thought that winds are inside, fighting as it were with one another. What Artemidorus writes about the Lake of the Two Ravens among the Santones, on the coast of the Gallic Ocean, Strabo, book IV, considers fabulous. The lake called Abitacini or Avitaci, named after Avitus, at Clermont in Auvergne, is described by Sidonius, book II, letter II, so vividly and so accurately that it seems to have been drawn today, showing what is on the right and what on the left. Sidonius also treats of it in his epigram on the baths. See also the President Fauchet, Gallic Antiquities, book II, chapter XIV, and Papirius Masson, Annals, book I, on Childeric. On the Red Lake one should read Pomponius Mela, book II, chapter in which Narbonese Gaul is described. Pliny calls it Rubrensis. The Aemne Narbonitis [Αἰμνη Ναρβωνιτις] is in Strabo and Stephanus.

units.la: Fontes jam enumerare nimis esset operosum: ijs certe, Sacris & Vaporantibus, scatere Galliam notat Solinus. Paucos indicabo, quos suae comitantur Virtutes, suaque Miracula. In Narbonensi Provincia Fontem esse scribit Plinius, qui Orge vulgo; in eo Herbas nasci tanto opere expetitas bubus, ut mersis capitibus totis eas quaeritent. Apud eundem Plinium & haec leguntur: Tungri Galliae Civitas Fontem habet insignem, plurimis bullis stillantem, ferruginei saporis; quod ipsum non nisi in fine potus intelligitur. Purgat hic Corpora, Tertianas Febres discutit, Calculorumque vitia. Eadem aqua igne admoto turbida fit, ac postremo rubescit. In Delphinatu haud procul Gratianopoli Fons est admirandus, qui absque intermissione flammas evomit, ipsaque, quidquid admovetur, correptum statim consumit. Similis est in Epiro, de quo Augustinus in libris de Civitate Dei. Haud procul Encolismensium Civitate Scaturigo, vel Abyssus potius, monstratur admiranda: vulgo Tounre dicitur: Charentam rentam (qui Latinioribus Canentelus) fluvium, in quem se exonerat, latitudine superat. Fundus reperiri non posse perhibetur: nec aliquis certo statuere potest, unde Fonti, cui tanta Aquarum copia, origo. Ad Vrbem Limaniæ Claromontium Fluvius vulgo Tiretaine Pontem habet, cujus lapides ex Aqua Fontis proximi mirum quantum induruerint. Fons, qui Aquam hanc provomit, trecentorum passuum intervallo ab Fluvio distat, eumque versus labens, lapideam hanc induit & nanciscitur duritiem & firmitatem; ut pons etiam inde fuerit constructus; triginta longus ulnas, sex crassus, octo latus. Illud etiam fidem videtur superare, Fontis aquam in Pratis, per quæ Pontem versus se præcipitat, lapidescere. Ponti nomen est, 10 quod & Aquæ, Saulse. Ibidem ex Colle quodam Bitumen valde nigrum tenaxque, quo Incolæ Oves signant, Fontis instar fluit. Indicium indubie, Territorium hic esse pingue, inque intimis terræ visceribus latere Metalla, liquorem bituminosum extrudentia. Bitumen guttatim emanat; Copiam adfert continuitas: hiberno tempore frigus impedit, quo minus dissolvatur & fluat. Haud procul ab Monte, quem Vulgus de Cosne indigetat, locus est, qui Cherron dicitur; ibique Fons, maximis æstatis caloribus congelari contra naturam solitus; hibernis vero mensibus liquefit, tantumque recuperat calorem, ut fumos & exhalationes, tamquam Fornax, emittat. In Aquitania Australi quarta Leucæ ab Aquis Tarbellicis vulgo Aqs, Antrum est, La Grottesque dictum: in eo tres Tymbi sunt, qui per se Aqua Plenilunio implentur;20 decrescente vero Luna, nec Aquæ quidem guttam retinent. In Andegavensi Regio-ne, ne hoc præteream, haud procul Samuro Varaus pagus est, inque eo Rivulus, qui bis die fluit, bisque stagnat.
units.tr: To list the springs would now be too laborious. Solinus notes that Gaul abounds in them, both sacred and hot. I shall point out a few, which are accompanied by their own virtues and marvels. Pliny writes that in the province of Narbonne there is a spring, commonly called Orge, in which grass grows that is so eagerly sought by oxen that they put their heads entirely under the water to look for it. In the same Pliny we also read this: The Tungri, a state of Gaul, have a remarkable spring, which drips with many bubbles and has an iron taste, which is only noticed at the end of drinking. It cleanses the body, cures tertian fevers and disorders of the kidneys. When fire is put to this same water, it becomes muddy and finally reddens. In Dauphiné, not far from Grenoble, there is a remarkable spring which without interruption throws out flames, and consumes at once whatever is brought near it. There is a similar one in Epirus, of which Augustine speaks in the books On the City of God. Not far from the city of the Engolisme people a spring, or rather an abyss, is shown; it is commonly called Tounre. It is wider than the river Charente (in Latin writers Canentelus) into which it discharges itself. It is said that no bottom can be found, and no one can say for certain where the spring, which has so great an abundance of water, has its source. At the town of Limagne, Clermont, the river commonly called Tiretaine has a bridge, whose stones have hardened to a remarkable degree from the water of a nearby spring. The spring which pours out this water is at a distance of three hundred paces from the river, and as it flows towards it, it takes on and acquires such hardness and firmness of stone that a bridge was built from it, thirty ells long, six thick and eight wide. It also seems to surpass belief that the water of the spring turns to stone in the meadows through which it rushes down towards the bridge. The name of the bridge is Saulse, as is that of the water. In the same place, from a certain hill, a very black and tenacious bitumen flows like a spring, with which the inhabitants mark their sheep. This is undoubtedly a sign that the territory here is rich and that metals lie in the inner depths of the earth, expelling a bituminous liquid. The bitumen flows out in drops; its continuity gives an abundant supply. In winter the cold prevents it from melting and flowing. Not far from the mountain which the common people call de Cosne, there is a place called Cherron, and there a spring which, in the greatest heat of summer, is accustomed to freeze, contrary to nature; but in the winter months it melts and recovers so much heat that it sends out smoke and vapours like a furnace. In southern Aquitaine, four leagues from the Tarbellian waters, commonly called Aqs, there is a cave called La Grottesque. In it are three cisterns, which fill of themselves with water at full moon, but when the moon wanes they do not retain even a drop of water. In the region of Anjou, not to pass this over, not far from the Samur, there is the village of Varaus, and in it a little stream which flows twice a day and twice stagnates.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI.

units.la: Gallorum Genius; Mores item circa Res Sacras.
units.tr: The Genius of the Gauls; their customs also in matters of religion.

units.la: 30 SIc se habet universim ipsa Regio: videndum jam de Incolis. Eorum historiam cum fructu explicaturum me censeo, si de Ipsorum; qui olim hodieque, Genio præfatus, doceam, qui in Rebus Sacris & Profanis, cum publice domi militiæque, tum privatim, Mores; quæ quondam, quæ item nunc temporis Lingua: omnia paucis & summatim; Virorum Magnorum insistens vestigiis, quos in plerisque colligendis totos aliquando fuisse constat.
units.tr: 30 Thus stands the region itself. Now we must look at its inhabitants. I judge that I shall explain their history with profit if I first speak of their character, which both in the past and today, and then teach their customs, both in sacred and secular matters, at home and in war, in public and in private, and their language, once and now. I shall do all this briefly and in summary, following the footsteps of great men, who are known to have devoted whole lifetimes to gathering most of these things.

units.la: Gallos Corpora plusquam humana habere, memoriæ prodit Iornandes; Corpora mirifica specie & magnitudine, Hirtius; celsioris staturæ, Ammianus: procera, Livius. Scribit Cæsar lib. II. de Bello Gallico, Gallis ob magnitudinem corporum suorum Brevitatem Romanam contemtui fuisse. Oblongo Corpore, Molles, Albosque facit eos Strabo. Ad Albedinem sane referenda sunt illa Petronij ad Gyr40 tonem verba: Increta facies, ut Cives Gallia suos putet: respicientis, non ad consuetudinem aliquam increta ndi vultus, quam Gallis fuisse nonnulli, nulla freti auctoritate, perhibent; sed ad Artificium, quo multi apud Gallos utebantur ad ementiendum imitandumque Albedinem, quam ipsa Natura Gallis ultro concesserat: unde & Lactea Colla tribuuntur ipsis à Poeta Latino: Aurea Cæsaries illis, atque aurea Vestis, Virgatis lucent sagulis: tum lactea Colla Auro innectuntur.
units.tr: Jornandes records that the Gauls had bodies more than human; Hirtius, that they had bodies of wonderful appearance and size; Ammianus, that they were taller than others; Livy, that they were tall. Caesar writes in Book II of the Gallic War that the Gauls were looked down upon by the Romans because of the size of their bodies and the shortness of Roman stature. Strabo calls them long-bodied, soft, and white. To whiteness must be referred those words of Petronius about Gyrton: A face so painted that Gaul would take her for one of its own citizens. He is speaking not of some custom of painting the face, which some say the Gauls had without any reliable authority, but of the artifice by which many among the Gauls pretended to a whiteness, and imitated it, which Nature herself had freely granted to the Gauls. Hence the Latin poet also assigns them milk-white necks: golden hair is theirs, and golden clothing shines in striped cloaks; and milk-white necks are bound with gold.

units.la: Comam Gallos nutrire (unde & Comata Galliæ nomen) Clemens Alexandrinus post Strabonem est auctor. Scribit etiam Agathias, solenne esse Francorum Regi50 bus numquam tonderi, sed à pueris intonsos manere, Cæsariemque eis decentet in humeros propendere, & anteriorem comam è fronte discriminatam in utrumque latus deflectere. Comas hasce promissas & rutilas facit Livius lib. xxxvIII, ubi de Gallis plura. Comam habere rufam natura Gallos, studio tamen hunc colorem augere, inquit Diodorus. Ejus hæc lib.v.sunt verba: [illegible, ~40 letters] Calcis ablutione lavare Capillos adsidue, & à fronte ad verticem tendonesque retrahere notat: quod videmus hodieque plerosque in Gallia factitare, prorsus ut, quod subjicit idem Diodorus, vere ijs conveniat, possitque dici, τὰς ἀσέσεως αὐτῶν Φαίνεσθαι Σατύροις καὶ Πᾶσιν ἐοικέναι; Adspectum eorum simillimum videri Satyris & Panibus; &, quod sequitur, Capillos facere crassiores, ut nihil differant ab Equorum jubis. Et hinc forte an, Gallia Crine ferox, Claudiano. Rutilandis Capillis, ait Plinius, Gallorum inventum Sapo est, ex Sevo & Cinere: ita ut Flavum Verticem Claudianus, Aureamque Caesariem his adscribat, ut paullo ante audivimus, Virgilius. Congruenter admodum Ammianus Gallos Candidos & Rutilos vocat, à crine scilicet & Cute. Barbam promissam gerere omnes memoriae prodit Livius. Distinguit Diodorus, Barbam scribens quosdam radere, quosdam nutrire parce; Nobiles genas quidem radere, barbam vero promittere, ut operiant corpora; eo accidere, ut, quum edant, repleatur cibo; quum vero bibant, veluti per Canalem Potus videatur inferri. Operam dare, ne obesi fiant, neve prominentiorem Ventrem habeant; & si quis adulescens praescriptam Cingulo mensuram excedat, eum multari, tradit Strabo.
units.tr: That the Gauls grew their hair long (whence also the name Comata Gallia, long-haired Gaul), Clement of Alexandria, following Strabo, is the authority. Agathias also writes that it was the custom for the kings of the Franks never to be shorn but to remain unshorn from boyhood, their long hair falling becomingly over their shoulders, and the front hair parted from the forehead and turned down to either side. Livy, in Book 38, where he says more about the Gauls, calls these locks flowing and reddish. Diodorus says that the Gauls are naturally red-haired, but by effort they increase this colour. These are his words in Book 5: [illegible passage, about forty letters]. He notes that they constantly wash their hair with a lye of lime and draw it back from the forehead to the crown, which we see most of them still doing in Gaul today, so that what Diodorus adds fits them exactly and can be said of them: their appearance seems to resemble Satyrs and Pans [ὄψεις αὐτῶν φαίνεσθαι Σατύροις καὶ Πᾶσιν ἐοικέναι]; and what follows: they make their hair thicker, so that it differs in no way from horses' manes. Perhaps from this comes Claudian's Gaul fierce with hair. Pliny says that the invention of the Gauls for dyeing hair was soap made of tallow and ash; and so Claudian ascribes to them a flaxen crown and golden locks, as Virgil, whom we heard a little earlier, does too. Ammianus very aptly calls the Gauls white and ruddy, clearly from their hair and skin. Livy records that all of them wore their beards long. Diodorus distinguishes: writing that some shave their beards, others let them grow sparingly; the nobles shave their cheeks but let their beards grow to cover their bodies; as a result, when they eat, they are filled with food, and when they drink, the drink seems to be poured in through a channel. Strabo reports that they take care not to grow fat or to have a bulging belly, and that if any young man exceeds the measure prescribed by his belt, he is punished.

units.la: Acutos Ingenio, & ab Doctrina minime alienos esse, testantur iidem Diodorus & Strabo. Commendat illorum in bonis litteris studia non uno loco Symmachus: M. Porcius Cato Originum lib. II apud Charisium Sosipatrum, Pleraque Gallia, inquit, duas res induστriosissime persequitur, rem militarem & argute loqui; ne neseiamus Veteres Gallos inter alias gentes Eloquentiae gloriam reportasse. Et hinc Iuvenalis: Gallia Causidicos docuit facunda Britannos.
units.tr: Diodorus and Strabo both testify that they are sharp of wit and by no means alien to learning. Symmachus commends their zeal for good letters in more than one place. Marcus Porcius Cato, in Book 2 of the Origines, as quoted by Charisius Sosipater, says: Most of Gaul, he says, pursues two things most diligently, warfare and speaking shrewdly. Let us not forget that the ancient Gauls won the glory of eloquence among other peoples. And hence Juvenal: Gaul, rich in eloquence, taught the Britons to plead cases.

units.la: D. Hieronymus Rustico Monacho: Ac post studia Galliarum, quae vel florentissima sunt: paullo post: Vbertas Gallici nitorque sermonis. Idem ad Paullinum: S. Hilarius Gallicano cothurno attollitur. Et Prooemio Epist. II ad Galatas: Et quod nunc Oratorum fertiles sunt. Adversus Vigilantium: Sola Gallia monstra non habuit, sed Viris semper fortissimis & eloquentissimis abundavit. Symmachus lib. VIII epist. LXVIII: Nisi forte Gallia tua deduxit Helicon: lib. IX. epist. LXXXIII, Gallicana facundiae haustus requiro: & paullo post: Quidquid in me est, quod scio quam sit exiguum, Caelo tuo debeo: notandum illud. Rutilius Itinerario I. Facundus Iuvenis Gallorum nuper ab arvis, Missus Romani discere jura fori.
units.tr: Saint Jerome, to the monk Rusticus: And after the studies of Gaul, which are indeed most flourishing; a little later: The abundance and brilliance of Gallic style. The same, to Paulinus: Saint Hilary is raised up on the Gallic buskin. And in the preface to Letter II to the Galatians: And because they are now fertile in orators. In Against Vigilantius: Gaul alone has not had monsters, but has always abounded in the bravest and most eloquent men. Symmachus, Book 8, letter 68: Unless perhaps your Gaul has drawn Helicon down; Book 9, letter 83: I seek a draught of Gallic eloquence; and a little after: Whatever is in me, however small I know it to be, I owe to your sky. That passage should be noted. Rutilius, Itinerary I: An eloquent young man lately from the fields of Gaul, sent to learn the law of the Roman forum.

units.la: Imitatione porro Hieronymi, Gallicanum Cothurnum dixit Hicmarus in S. Remigij historia. Ingenium simplex, nullaque devinctum malignitate (egregia haec Veterum Gallorum laus) tribuit illis Strabo. Pronunciat de iis oculatus Testis Iulianus, Quod adulari nesciant; sed libere ac simpliciter cum omnibus aequabiliqe jure vivere: Venerem Nuptiarum Deam & Bacchum laetitiae datorem Conjugij Prolisque, & Vini, quamtum cuique libeat, potandi gratia, tantum novisse. Quae his aliisque talibus advorsantia nonnulli protulerunt, ut Convicia, & tamquam ab maligna mente manuque profecta, sunt exaudienda. Nam quis non videt, lectis Veterum Scriptorum de Gallorum Indole monimentis, factaque cum Genio, qui ijsdem hodieque est, commissione, falsum esse quod tradit Servius, Gallos pigrioris esse Ingenij; quod Iulius Firmicus, stolidos; quod Iulianus, quasi sui oblitus, stupidos, & rusticitatem amantes; quod Polybius, Doctrinae & Artibus operam non dare; quod idem cum Diodoro, Athenaeo, & Clemente Alexandrino, infidos esse, crapulaeque & Ebrietati deditos; quod Livius Polybiusque, molles esse & effeminatos; quod Mela, Auri avidos, superbos, superstitiosos; quod Solinus, Vaniloquos; quod denique pecuniae insatiabiles esse, Plutarchus in Pyrrho. Fatendum nihilominus multa Gallis instillata aliorum populorum commercio. Nemo Gallos, ait Florus lib. III, cap. x, tantum feroces dixerit, fraudibus agunt. Avidos Iurgiorum docet Ammianus lib. xv. Reprehendit etiam Diodorus in Gallis quamdam Linguae intemperantiam, Sermone notans uti eos brevi & subobscuro; multa ex animo dubia loqui, plurima ad jactantiam in suam laudem dicere, & ad ceterorum contemtum: minaces esse ac Detractores, opinioneque inflatos. Iactantia illa ab Strabone etiam est animadversa. Atque ea Gallica Ostentatio est, quae ab Caesare lib. VII. nominatur, & multis reliquorum Librorum exemplis adprobatur. Talis est libro I. Helvetij Diviconis elatio, dum Helvetiorum virtutem extollit, Romanae Cladis memoriam objicit, Caesaremque, minitando, admonet, ne committat, ut is locus, ubi Romani constitissent, ex calamitate Populi Romani internecione exercitus nomen caperet aut memoriam prodéret.
units.tr: Imitating Jerome, Hincmar in his history of Saint Remigius called it the Gallican buskin. Strabo ascribes to them a simple nature, not bound by any malice (an excellent praise of the ancient Gauls). Julian, an eyewitness, pronounces about them that they do not know how to flatter, but live frankly and simply with all people on equal terms; that they know Venus only as the goddess of marriage, and Bacchus only as the giver of joy in wedlock and offspring, and wine only for drinking as much as each likes. Whatever some have brought forward against these and similar views, as insults, and as if they came from a malicious mind and hand, should be disregarded. For who does not see, once the records of the ancient writers on the character of the Gauls have been read and compared with the Genius that the Gauls still have today, that what Servius says is false, that the Gauls are of a more sluggish nature; that Julius Firmicus calls them stupid; that Julian, as if forgetful of himself, calls them dull and lovers of rusticity; that Polybius says they do not devote themselves to learning and the arts; that the same Polybius, along with Diodorus, Athenaeus, and Clement of Alexandria, says they are faithless and given to drunkenness and gluttony; that Livy and Polybius say they are soft and effeminate; that Mela says they are greedy for gold, proud, and superstitious; that Solinus says they are babblers; and finally that they are insatiable for money, as Plutarch says in his Life of Pyrrhus. Yet it must be admitted that many faults were instilled into the Gauls by their dealings with other peoples. No one, says Florus in Book 3, chapter 10, would call the Gauls only fierce; they act by deceit. Ammianus, in Book 15, shows them eager for quarrels. Diodorus also finds in the Gauls a certain intemperance of speech, noting that they use a brief and somewhat obscure style; that they often speak doubtfully from their feelings, and say most things boastfully in their own praise and to the contempt of others; that they are threatening and slanderous, and puffed up with opinion.
