Strabo too noticed this boastfulness. This is the Gallic ostentation mentioned by Caesar in Book 7, and it is confirmed by many examples from the other books. Such is in Book 1 the boasting of Diviciacus the Helvetian, when he extols the valour of the Helvetii, reminds them of the memory of the Roman defeat, and warns Caesar, with threats, not to allow that place, where the Romans had halted, to gain its name and memory from the ruin of the Roman people and the destruction of their army.

units.la: quod ad Ingenium. ret. Sic Vercingetorix in concione jactat se unum Consilium totius Galliæ effecturum, cujus consensui ne Orbis quidem terrarum posset obsistere.
units.tr: As to their character: thus Vercingetorix boasts in an assembly that he alone will achieve one plan for all of Gaul, to which not even the whole world could oppose its consent.

units.la: Quod ad Veterum Gallorum Religionem, Cultumque in Rebus sacris servari solitum, flocci faciendus est M. Tullius oratione pro M. Fonteio scribens, Gallos minime ullâ Religione moveri. Audiendus potius Livius; qui, etsi in ceteris satis huic genti iniquus, negligentem tamen haudquaquam Religionis adfirmat; & Cæsar lib. vii belli Gall. cui penitus cognita hæc natio, dicit, eam admodum deditam Religionibus. Idem Cæsar: Deum maxime Mercurium colunt: hujus sunt plurima simulacra; hunc omnium inventorum Artium ferunt; hunc Viarum atque Itinerum Ducem; hunc ad Quæstum pecuniæ Mercaturasque habere vim maximam arbitrantur. Post hunc Apollinem, & Martem, & Jovem, & Minervam: de his eamdem fere, quam reliquæ Gentes, habent opinionem: Apollinem Morbos depellere; Minervam Operum atque Artificiorum initia tradere: Jovem Imperium Cælestium tenere: Martem belli gerere. Celtas Jovem colere attestatur Max. Tyrius; cujus signum altissima Quercus. De Mercurio Plinius lib. xxxiv, cap. vii: Omnem amplitudinem Statuarum vicit ætate nostra Xenodorus, Mercurio facto in Civitate Gallię Arvernis per annos decem H-S CCCC mansprætio. Dianam, eamque Ephesiam templum habuisse apud Massilienses, Strabo testis est: & apud Gallo-Græcos Dianam cultam, Polyænus lib. viii. & Plutarchus de Virtutibus Mulierum commemorant. Sed & aliam coluisse Gallos Dianam, Arduennæ cognomine, probat antiquum Marmor via Decia Salaria ad Septem Balneas repertum, at Marcilianum translatum, ut habet ex P. Ligorio Iulius Iacobonius in Appendice ad Bapt. Fonteii Commentaria de Prisca Gallorum gente: DIS. MANIBVS Q. CAESIVS. Q. F. CLAVD ATILIANVS. SACERDOS DEANAE. ARDVINNAE FECIT. SIBI. ET. SVIS. HAERED IN. FR. P. XII. IN. AGR. P. XV IIII. ID. OCT IMP. CAES. FLAVIO. DOMITIANO. VIII ET. C. VALERIO. MESSALINO. COS
units.tr: As to the religion of the ancient Gauls and the worship customarily kept in sacred matters, Marcus Tullius, writing in his speech for Marcus Fonteius, deserves no attention: The Gauls are not moved by any religion at all. Livy should rather be heard, who, although in other matters rather hostile to this people, asserts that they were by no means negligent of religion; and Caesar, Book 7 of the Gallic War, who knew this nation thoroughly, says that they were very devoted to religions. The same Caesar: They worship Mercury above all gods; there are very many images of him; they say he is the inventor of all the arts, the guide of roads and journeys, and they think he has the greatest power over gain of money and trade. After him they worship Apollo, Mars, Jupiter, and Minerva; about these they hold much the same opinion as other nations: that Apollo drives away diseases; Minerva teaches the beginnings of works and crafts; Jupiter holds the rule of the heavens; Mars directs war. Maximus of Tyre attests that the Celts worship Jupiter, whose image is a very tall oak. Concerning Mercury, Pliny, Book 34, chapter 7: In our age Xenodorus surpassed every statue in size: a Mercury made for the Arverni, a Gallic state, at a price of four hundred thousand sesterces over ten years. That the Massiliots had a temple of Diana, and of Ephesian Diana, Strabo is witness; and that Diana was worshipped among the Gallo-Greeks, Polyaenus in Book 8 and Plutarch in his work on the virtues of women record. But that the Gauls also worshipped another Diana, with the surname Arduenna, is shown by an ancient marble found on the Via Decia Salaria at Septem Balneae, and transferred to Marciliano, as Julius Iacobonius, in his appendix to the commentaries of Baptista Fonteius on the ancient Gallic people, reports from Pirro Ligorio. The inscription reads: To the spirits of the dead. Quintus Caesius Atilianus, son of Quintus, of the Claudian tribe, priest of the goddess Arduinna, made this for himself and his own, and for his heirs. Twelve feet in front, fifteen feet deep. On the fourth day before the Ides of October, in the consulship of the Emperor Caesar Flavius Domitian for the eighth time and Gaius Valerius Messalinus.

units.la: In Arduenna silva hanc maxime locum habuisse, cultamque fuisse, vero est simile. Esum sive Hesum, Teutatem, & Taranem Deos habuisse Gallos, Lactantius, Lucanus & Minutius Felix referunt: sed Martem, Mercurium, Jovem, hos plerique docti interpretantur. Belenus Gallorum Deus est apud Ausonium, qui Βελῆς apud Herodianum in Maximinis; idem fortean cum Tibiene Tertulliani in Apologetico, nisi vulgati Codices sint vitiosi, & ex membranis reducendus ibi sit Belenus. Hic, qui Græcis alisque Apollo, putatur fuisse: videndus Pet. Pitheus Adversf. Subsf. lib. L cap. iii. Colebatur & apud Gallos Abellio: de quo hæc monimenta extare notat in Convenis Nemopopulanii Vir Nobilis. Iosephus Scaliger ad Ausoni lib. i. cap. ix: DEO ABELLIO NI MINICIA IVSTA V. S. L. M.
units.tr: It is likely that this was the chief place of worship in the Arduenna forest and was cultivated there. Lactantius, Lucan and Minucius Felix report that the Gauls had the gods Esus or Hesus, Teutates and Taranis, but learned writers mostly identify them with Mars, Mercury and Jupiter. Belenus is a god of the Gauls according to Ausonius, who is the Belēs [Βελῆς] of Herodian in his Maximini. He may be the same as the Tibiene of Tertullian in the Apologeticus, unless the common copies are faulty and Belenus should be restored there from the manuscripts. He is thought to be what the Greeks and others call Apollo; see Pierre Pithou, Adversaria Subseciva, book 1, chapter 3. Abellio was also worshipped among the Gauls. A noble man notes that inscriptions about him survive at Nemausus: Iosephus Scaliger, on Ausonius book 1, chapter 9: "To the god Abellio, Ninminicia Justa fulfilled her vow willingly and deservedly." ## Likewise

units.la: Item
ABELLIONI. DEO. TAVRINVS BONE. CONI. SEVSIM
units.tr: To the god Abellio, Taurinus, son of Bonus Conus, [dedicated this]. ## Likewise

units.la: Item
ABELLIONI. CISONTEM. CISSONBONNIS. FIL V. S. L. M
units.tr: To Abellio, Cisontem, son of Cissonbonnus, willingly and deservedly fulfilled his vow.

units.la: Herculem etiam Ogmii nomine coluisse Gallos, auctor est Lucianus in Hercule Gallico. An Serapin etiam Deum (eumdem forte cum Plutone) colucrint, fere est, ut colligatur ex Ammiano Marcellino, cujus ex lib. xvi hæc sunt verba: Latus dextrum Serapio agebat, etiam tum adulta lanuginis juvenis, efficacia præcurrens ætatem, Mederici fratris Chonodomari (hoc fuit tum Alemannorum Regis nomen) filius, hominis, quoad vixerat, perfidissimi: ideo sic appellatus, quod pater ejus diu obsidatum pignore tentus in Gallia, d. Eufque Graeca quaedam arcana, hunc filium suum Aganerichum genitali vocabulo dictitatam ad Serapionis translulit nomen.
units.tr: The Gauls are said by Lucian, in his Hercules Gallicus, to have worshipped Hercules under the name of Ogmius. It is almost certain, as may be gathered from Ammianus Marcellinus, that they also worshipped Serapis (perhaps the same as Pluto). The words of Ammianus, book 16, are these: On the right wing marched Serapio, a youth whose down was only just growing, yet who went before his years in vigour, the son of Mederich, brother of Chonodomarius (this was then the name of the king of the Alemanni), a man most treacherous for as long as he lived. He was so called because his father, long held as a hostage in Gaul, had transferred to Serapis the name of a certain Greek mystery, and gave this son of his, whom he called Agenerich by his birth name, the name of Serapis.

units.la: Galli Veteres Deos suos in dextram conversi adorabant, Athenaeo scribente. Sic Plinius libri xxviii, cap. 11: In adorando dextram ad oculum referimus, totumque Corpus circumagimus; quod in laevum fecisse Gallia religiosum credunt.
units.tr: The ancient Gauls, as Athenaeus writes, worshipped their gods turning to the right. So Pliny, book 28, chapter 11: In adoring we bring the right hand to the eye and turn the whole body round; the Gauls are thought to have done this to the left, as a religious act.

units.la: Diis Homicidio aliisque rebus sacrificabant, Marti imprimis, teste Caesare, qui ita: Hunc, quum proelio dimicare constituerint, ea, quae bello ceperunt, plerumque devovent quae superaverint: Animalia capta immolant, reliquasque res in unum locum conferunt: multis in Civitatibus harum rerum exstructos tumulos locis consecratis conspicari licet: neque saepe accidit, ut, neglecta quisquam Religione, aut Capta apud se occultare, aut possita tollere auderet; gravissimumque et rei Supplicium cum Cruciatu constitutum est. Eadem fere apud Diodorum Siculum: Offerunt, inquit, in Deorum sacris, Templisque plurimum Aurt Dis obiatum spargunt; neque Incolarum quisquam propter Religionem audet contingere. Pergit Caesar: Qui sunt adflicti gravioribus morbis, quique in proeliis periculisque versantur, aut pro Victimis homines immolant, aut se immolaturos vovent: Administrisque ad ea Sacrificia Druidibus utuntur: quod pro Vita hominis, nisi vita hominis reddatur, non posse Deorum Immortalium Numen placari arbitrantur: publiceque ejus generis habent instituta Sacrificia. Aliy immani magnitudine Simulacra habent: quorum contexta Vimimbus membra vivis hominibus complent; quibus succensis circumventi flamma examinantur homines. Supplicia eorum, qui in furto aut latrocinio, aut aliqua noxa sunt comprehensi, grata Diis immortalibus esse arbitrantur: sed quum ejus generis copia defecit, etiam ad Innocentium supplicia descendunt. Eadem, sed paullo sequius, apud Strabonem: Quosdam in sacris Sagittis configebant, aut in Crucem agebant, ac Feras Colosso exstructo, desiso ligno, Pecudes & alterius generis bestias ac homines comburebant. Diodorus eadem de re, Noxios, inquit, quinquennio servatos, fustibus caesos, Diis sacrificant, cumque aliis primitus super ingentes pyras immolant. Mercurio quoque Gallos humanas hostias caedere, Minutius Felix auctor est. Major atas, inquit Tertullianus in Apologetico, Mercurio profecatur. Adeo ut satius fuisset, quemadmodum scribit Plutarchus de Superstitione, Galatis, si nullam omnino habuissent notionem Deorum: quam Deos esse existimarent, qui hominum Mactatorum cruore mulcentur, maxime solenne hoc Sacrificium & Victimam putantes. Solinus quoque hunc detestabilem morem non ad honorem, sed potius ad injuriam religionis facere existimat. Quamvis autem has hominum immolationes vetitas sub Tiberio Caesare probat Plinius: ad sua tamen usque tempora (quae sunt Constantini Magni) perduraße, deplorat Eusebius lib. iv. Praeparat.
units.tr: They sacrificed human beings and other things to the gods, above all to Mars, as Caesar testifies, who says: When they have resolved to fight a battle, they usually vow to the god whatever they have taken in war. After the victory they sacrifice the living creatures they have captured and gather the rest of the spoils into one place. In many states one may see mounds of such things piled up in consecrated places. It seldom happens that anyone, disregarding religion, dares to hide spoils he has taken or to remove what has been deposited, and the most severe punishment, with torture, is set for this. Diodorus says almost the same thing: They offer, he says, in the sacred rites and temples of the gods, and they sprinkle much of the spoils on the altars; no one of the inhabitants dares touch them because of religion. Caesar continues: Those who are afflicted with more serious diseases, or who are in battles and dangers, either sacrifice men as victims or vow that they will do so. For these sacrifices they use Druids as ministers, because they think the power of the immortal gods cannot be appeased unless a man's life is given for a man's life. They also have public sacrifices of this kind. Others have images of immense size, whose limbs, woven of twigs, they fill with living men; when these are set on fire, the men are killed by the flames. They think that the punishments of those caught in theft, robbery or some crime are pleasing to the immortal gods; but when a supply of such men fails, they even descend to punishing the innocent. Strabo says much the same, though a little differently: They shot some through with arrows in their sacred rites, or put others to death on a cross, and burned wild beasts, cattle and men in a great wicker figure. Diodorus on the same subject: They sacrifice criminals kept for five years, after beating them with clubs, and they first offer them on great pyres along with other victims. Minucius Felix is the authority that the Gauls also slaughtered human victims for Mercury. Tertullian in the Apologeticus says: They performed the greatest sacrifice to Mercury. So it would have been better for the Galatians, as Plutarch writes in his book on superstition, to have no notion of the gods at all, than to think that gods who are placated by the blood of slaughtered men are gods, and to regard this as the most solemn sacrifice and victim. Solinus also thinks this detestable custom was done not to honour religion but rather to injure it. Although Pliny shows that these human sacrifices were forbidden under the emperor Tiberius, Eusebius, in book 4 of the Praeparatio, laments that they lasted down to his own times, that is, those of Constantine the Great.

units.la: Hic autem hominum apud Gallos usus non in Sacrificiis solum fuit, verum etiam in Divinationibus. Ἀνθρωπον, inquit Strabo, καταςφάζειν παίσαντες εἰς τὸν μαχαίραν, ἐμαντεύοντο ἐκ τῆς σφαδασμῶν: Gallos notat, hominis Sacris devoti tergum ense ferire solitos, exque ejus palpitatione ariolari. Scribit etiam Diodorus, Gallos, quum de rebus magnis consultant, mirabilem incredibilemque habere consuetudinem; hominem enim immolantes ferire ense super Septum transversum: quo decidente, cum ex casu, tum ex membrorum dilaceratione, exque sanguinis fluxu novisse futura. Apud fortium Virorum Busta, Oraculorum captandorum caussa abnoctare solere, scriptum reliquit Tertullianus de Anima. Verbenaca herba hos etiam sortiri, & Responsa praecini, commemoratur à Plinio. Apud Spartianum in Pescennio legō, apud Gallos Sacra quaedam esse, quae castissimis decernebantur.
units.tr: This practice of human sacrifice among the Gauls was not confined to sacrifices but extended also to divination. Strabo says: After striking a man with a sword they divined from the convulsions [of his body] [ἄνθρωπον καταςφάξαντες εἰς τὸν μαχαίραν, ἐμαντεύοντο ἐκ τῆς σφαδασμῶν]: he means that the Gauls were accustomed to strike with a sword the back of a man devoted to sacrifice, and to foretell from his twitching. Diodorus also writes that when the Gauls consult about great matters they have a remarkable and incredible custom: they strike a man, offered in sacrifice, with a sword above a transverse beam, and when he falls they know the future from the manner of his fall, from the laceration of his limbs and from the flow of his blood. Tertullian, in his book on the soul, wrote that they were accustomed to spend the night among the tombs of brave men in order to seek oracles. Pliny records that they also drew lots with vervain and chanted responses. In Spartianus, in the life of Pescennius, I read that among the Gauls there were certain sacred rites which were restricted to the most chaste.

units.la: Nullum autem Gallis Veteribus Sacrificium erat sine Druide, inquit Diodorus. Druidarum Etymon Goropius Becanus ex Germanico Fonte petit. Druis enim illi lib. 1. Gallicorum, quasi Trow-Wis, & Britannorum Dialecto Truvis: à qua voce si tollatur littera Ƿ Latinis ignota, primaque, quae Tenuis, commutetur in Mediam, confectim erit Druis, Veri sapiens, Verum alijs monstrans, ostendensque, & cui sit fidendum, & qui cum Conjugii copula contrahenda; ita ut is, qui hoc sibi nomen sumit, sese omnis Veritatis & Fidei cum erga Deum, tum erga homines profiteatur Doctorem: unde & Sapientiae Magistros facit eos Pomponius. Certe Druin, vel Trutin, antiqua Germanorum lingua Deus, quasi Fidelis, ut videre est in Otfridi Euangelio Typis excuso. Apud Camdenum quoque in Britanniae Descriptione
units.tr: Among the ancient Gauls, says Diodorus, no sacrifice was performed without a Druid. Goropius Becanus derives the word Druid from the German source. For in the first book of the Gallic [writings] the Druids are called, as it were, Trow-Wis, and in the dialect of the Britons Truvis. If the letter Ƿ, unknown to Latin, is removed from this word, and the first letter, which is a tenuis, is changed into a media, it will at once become Druis, a wise man of truth, who shows the truth to others and shows whom one ought to trust, and who is to be joined in the bond of marriage. Thus the one who takes this name professes himself a teacher of all truth and faith, both towards God and towards men. For this reason Pomponius also calls them masters of wisdom. Certainly Druin or Trutin, in the ancient German language, means God, as if "faithful", as can be seen in the printed edition of Otfrid's Gospel book. Also in Camden's description of Britain.

units.la: Albricus quidam scribit Dry Saxonibus Magum vocari; ut non immerito Magos etiam nominet Druidas Plinius. Nomen enim ab Quercu ipsis non esse inditum, idem Plinius satis fatetur, dum addit, ab Quercu eos posse Graeca interpretatione appellatos videri. Nam qui possent ab Graeca voce Δρῦς denominati esse, quum ipsorum Disciplinam repertam scribant Caesar & Tacitus xiv Annal. in Britannia, ubi nulla umquam, nisi Fabulis quis locum censeat dandum, Graecorum fuit Colonia?Germanicae vero Linguae in Britannia usum fuisse, docent iidem Tacitus & Caesar: quorum hic ex Belgica (in qua eodem auctore Germani Cis-Renani) Colonos in hanc Insulam transfiisse, ibidemque remansisse, scriptum reliquit: Ille Caledoniam (Insulae hujus magnam partem) habitantibus Germanicam Originem tribuit. Nominantur hi Sacerdotes varie. Druidae, prima, ut Grammatice loquar, inflexione, apud Lucanum lib. i. belli Pharsal. & Autonium in Attio Rhetore, Professore; ut & Δρυΐδαι apud Strabonem, Diogenem Laertium & Sudam: Druides autem tertia, apud Caesarem de bello Gallico & M. Tullium de Divinatione. Sic enim ibi legit Nizolius; ubi Druidae in aliis sunt exemplaribus. Est autem hoc vocabulum inter ea, quae Veteres Librarij varie corruperunt. Driudae namque & Driadae frequentius, quam Druidae, in antiquis Codicibus occurrunt. Synonyma Druidarum fuerunt, uti censet Pitheus, Bardi, Vates, Eubages, Semnothei, Saronides: alij diversos hos ab Druidibus statuunt; quod innuere videtur Lucanus: Vos quoque qui fortes animas, belloque peremptas Laudibus in longum Vates demittitis aevum: Plurima securi fudistis carmina Bardi; Et vos Barbaricos ritus, moremque sinistrum Sacrorum Druidae positis repetistis ab armis.
units.tr: Albricus writes that Dry is called Magus by the Saxons, and so Pliny not unreasonably also calls the Druids Magi. That the name was not given them from the oak, Pliny himself sufficiently admits, when he adds that they could be called, by a Greek interpretation, after the oak. For how could they have been named from the Greek word δρῦς, when Caesar and Tacitus (Annals, book 14) write that their discipline was found in Britain, where, unless one thinks fit to give a place to fables, there was never any Greek colony? That the German language was used in Britain, Tacitus and Caesar both teach. Caesar wrote that colonists came into this island from Belgica (in which, by the same author, the Germans lived on the near side of the Rhine) and remained there; Tacitus attributes German origin to the inhabitants of Caledonia, which is a large part of this island. These priests are named in various ways. Druidae, in the first declension, as I speak grammatically, is found in Lucan, book 1 of the Pharsalia, and in Ausonius in his Attius Rhetor, Professor; so also Δρυΐδαι in Strabo, Diogenes Laertius and Suidas. Druides, in the third declension, is found in Caesar's De Bello Gallico and in Cicero's De Divinatione. For so Nizolius reads it there, where other copies have Druidae. This word is among those that the ancient scribes corrupted in various ways, for Driudae and Driadae occur more often than Druidae in the old manuscripts. Synonyms of the Druids were, as Pithou thinks, Bards, Vates, Eubages, Semnothei and Saronides. Others hold that these were distinct from the Druids, which Lucan seems to imply: "You also, bards, who hand down with lasting praise brave souls slain in war; you have sung many poems without care; and you, Druids, have brought back to us the barbarous rites and the grim custom of sacrifices, after the arms were laid down."

units.la: Bardi, Βάρδοι, Poetae sunt, testibus Athenaeo atque Strabone; & hymnos laudesque Clarorum Virorum cantant: sunt μελῶν ποιηταί apud Diodorum, qui cum Organis veluti cum Lyra cantant, hos laudantes, alios vituperantes. Festus quoque Pompeius hos Virorum fortium laudes canere scribit, & Gallice Bardum Cantorem significare. De ijsdem Marcellinus: Bardi quidam fortia Virorum inlustrium facta heroicis composita versibus cum dulcibus Lyrae modulis cantitarunt. Posidonius apud Athenaeum: τὰ δὲ ἀκεσμένα αὐτῶν ἱστορίαι οἱ καλούμενοι Βάρδοι: Ποιηταὶ δὲ ἐπὶ τυχχάνειν μετὰ φδῆς ἐπαίνους λέγοντες. οὐάτες, Vates, sunt apud Strabonem, qui sacrificare eos, & naturam rerum contemplari scribit: Eubages sunt apud Marcellinum, ibique scrutantes summa & sublimia Naturae pandere conantur: Σεμνόθεοι apud Laertium & Sudam: Σαρωνίδες apud Diodorum. Magos non semel Druidas nominat Plinius; Φιλοσόφους Lucianus in Hercule Ogmio. Erant enim Druidae vel Druides in Gallia, qui in Graecia Philosophi, apud Persas Magi, apud Indos Gymnosophistae, Chaldaei apud Assyrios, ut scribit Diogenes. De iis autem nusquam plura, quam in sexto Iulij Caesaris (vel quicumque Auctor sit habendus) Commentario de bello Gallico; ubi quum eorum hominum, qui aliquo essent numero & honore in Gallia suis temporibus, genera duo esse dixisset, alterum Druidarum, alterum Equitum, de Druidis subjicit, quod Rebus Divinis interessent: Sacrificia publica ac privata procurarent, Religiones interpretarentur. Ad hos, inquit idem, magnus Adolescentium numerus, Disciplinae causa concurrebat: magnoque hi erant apud eos honore. Nam fere de omnibus Controversijs publicis privatisque constituebant, & si quod admissum esset facinus, si caedes facta, si de hereditate, de finibus controversia esset, idem decernebant: praemia poenasque constituebant. Si quis aut privatus aut publicus eorum Decreto non stetisset, Sacrificiis interdicebant: quae poena apud eos erat gravissima. Quibus ita esset interdictum, in numero impiorum & sceleratorum habebantur. Ijs omnes decedebant, aditum sermonemque defugiebant, ne quid ex contagione incommodi acciperent; neque ijs petentibus Ius reddebatur, neque honos ullus communicabatur. His omnibus Druidis praerat unus, qui summam inter eos habebat auctoritatem. Hoc mortuo, si quis ex reliquis excellebat dignitate, succedebat: aut si essent plures pares, suffragio Druidarum adlegebatur. nonnumquam etiam armis de Principatu contendebatur.
units.tr: Bardi, Βάρδοι, are poets, according to Athenaeus and Strabo, and they sing hymns and praises of famous men. In Diodorus they are makers of songs [μελῶν ποιηταί], who sing with organs as well as with the lyre, some praising and others condemning. Festus Pompeius also writes that they sing the praises of brave men, and that in Gallic bardus means a singer. Marcellinus says of the same men: Certain bards sang the brave deeds of illustrious men, composed in heroic verses, with the sweet modulations of the lyre. Posidonius, quoted in Athenaeus, says: The so-called Bards are the narrators of their deeds [τὰ δὲ ἀκεσμένα αὐτῶν ἱστορίαι οἱ καλούμενοι Βάρδοι]; they are poets who recite praises to the accompaniment of song [Ποιηταὶ δὲ ... μετὰ φδῆς ἐπαίνους λέγοντες]. The Vates in Strabo are those who, he writes, offer sacrifices and contemplate the nature of things. The Eubages in Marcellinus are those who, searching out the highest and most sublime things, try to unfold the secrets of Nature. The Semnotheoi appear in Laertius and Suidas [Σεμνόθεοι], and the Saronides in Diodorus [Σαρωνίδες]. Pliny names the Druids Magi more than once, and Lucian in Hercules Ogmios calls them philosophers [Φιλοσόφους]. For the Druids, or Druides, were in Gaul what in Greece are philosophers, among the Persians Magi, among the Indians Gymnosophists, and among the Assyrians Chaldeans, as Diogenes writes. Nowhere is more said of them than in the sixth book of Julius Caesar's Commentary on the Gallic War (or whoever the author is held to be). There, after saying that there were two classes of men in Gaul in his time who had some number and honour, the Druids and the Knights, he goes on to the Druids: they took part in divine worship, managed public and private sacrifices, and interpreted religious matters. To these, he says, a great number of young men flocked for instruction, and they held great honour among the people. For they settled almost all public and private disputes; if a crime had been committed, if there had been a murder, or if there was a dispute about an inheritance or boundaries, they decided these too, and they fixed rewards and penalties. If any person, private or public, did not abide by their decision, they barred him from the sacrifices, which was the most severe penalty among them. Those so barred were counted among the impious and wicked. All people went away from them and avoided their approach and conversation, lest they catch some harm from the contagion; no justice was done to them when they sought it, and no honour was granted to them. Over all these Druids presided one man, who had the highest authority among them. When he died, whoever among the rest excelled in dignity succeeded him; or if several were equal, he was chosen by the vote of the Druids, and sometimes they even contested the leadership by arms.

units.la: Addit praeterea Caesar, quod Druidae certo anni tempore in Finibus Carnutum, Regione totius Galliae media, considere fuerint soliti, in loco consecrato: quo omnes undique, qui Controversias habebant, convenirebant, eorumque Decretis & Iudicijs parebant. Designare videtur Caesar Opidum illud, quod ab Carnutum Metropoli octavo distat lapide, vulgo Dreux, nomen retinens Druidarum. Gabriel Simeonius in Cæsare suo Renovato scribit, se in hujus Tractus saltibus vidisse horum Druidum antiqua Palatij vestigia. Druidæ, ut scribit idem Cæsar, à Bello abesse consueverant, neque Tributa una cum reliquis pendebant, Militiæ vacationem omniumque rerum immunitatem habebant. Tantis excitatis præmiis & sua sponte multi in disciplinam conveniebant & à parentibus propinquisque mittebantur. Magnum ibi numerum versuum edisebant, neque fas esse existimabant ea litteris mandare; quum in reliquis fere rebus publicis privatisque rationibus, Græcis litteris uterentur. Vnum ex his, quæ præcipiebant in specu aut abditis saltibus, ut meminit etiam Pomponius Mela libro III de situ Orbis, in Vulgus effluxit: videlicet æternas esse Animas, easque post certum tempus, quod addit Diodorus Siculus libro V, in alia corpora migrare. De animarum immortalitate ex Druidarum sententia scribunt etiam alij Ammianus Marcellinus: Druidæ ingenijs celsiores, ut auctoritas Pythagoræ decrevit, sodalitiis adstricti consortijs, quæstionibus occultarum rerum altarumque erecti sunt; ac despectantes humana, pronunciarunt Animas esse immortales. Strabo lib. IV. sic Latine sonat: Druidæ praeter rerum Naturæ Philosophiam etiam de Moribus disputant. De horum justitia summa est omnium opinio: ita & publica ijs & privata judicia committuntur, & aliquando Cansis bellorum disceptandis jam ante congressuros compescerunt. Maxime Iudicia de Cæde ijs commissa sunt: quumque horum multum est proventus, Agrorum quoque fertilitatem consequi putant. Cum hi, tum alij, Animam interitus expertem statuunt, & Mundum; tamen aliquando Ignem & Aquam superatura. Lucanus lib. I Belli Pharsalici:
units.tr: Caesar further adds that the Druids were accustomed to meet at a certain time of year in the territory of the Carnutes, which is the middle region of all Gaul, in a consecrated place. There all who had disputes gathered from every side, and they obeyed the decrees and judgments of the Druids. Caesar seems to point to the town which lies eight miles from the Carnutes' capital and is commonly called Dreux, keeping the name of the Druids. Gabriel Simeoni, in his Renewed Caesar, writes that he saw in the woods of this district the ancient palace ruins of these Druids. The Druids, as Caesar also writes, were accustomed to stay away from war; they did not pay tribute along with the others, they were exempt from military service and had immunity from all duties. With such great rewards offered, many came of their own accord to join the discipline, and they were sent by their parents and relatives. There they learned by heart a great number of verses, and they did not think it right to commit these to writing, although in almost all other public and private business they used Greek letters. One of the things they taught in caves or hidden woods, as Pomponius Mela also mentions in book III of his De situ orbis, became known among the common people: namely, that souls are eternal and, after a certain time, as Diodorus Siculus adds in book V, pass into other bodies. Other writers also speak of the immortality of the soul according to the Druids' opinion. Ammianus Marcellinus says: The Druids, raised above others in intellect, as the authority of Pythagoras decreed, bound together by fellowship in associations, were devoted to the investigation of hidden and lofty matters; and looking down on human affairs, they declared that souls are immortal. Strabo, book IV, runs thus in Latin: The Druids discuss morals as well as the philosophy of natural things. Everyone holds the highest opinion of their justice; public and private judgments are entrusted to them, and sometimes they restrain those about to go to war over the causes of the war. Judgments about murder are especially committed to them; and since there is a great abundance of these, they think they also bring about the fertility of the fields. These men, and others too, hold that the soul is free from destruction, and the world likewise; yet at some time fire and water will prevail. Lucan, book I of the Pharsalia:

units.la: Solis nosse Deos & Cæli Numina VobisAut solis nescire datum; nemora alta remotisIncolitis Lucis, Vobis auctoribus UmbraNon tacitas Erebi sedes, Ditisque profundiPallida regna petunt.
units.tr: To you alone it was granted to know the gods and the powers of heaven, or alone not to know them. You dwell in deep groves far from the light, and by your teaching the shades do not seek the silent abodes of Erebus or the pale kingdoms of deep Dis.

units.la: Multa insuper de Sideribus eorumque motu, de Mundo ac terrarum magnitudine, de Deorum immortalium vi ac potestate disputabant (ut notat cum aliis Cæsar) Druidæ, & juventuti tradebant. Hinc Divitiacus ille Eduus, quum ex Druidis unus esset, Naturæ rationem, quam Φυσιολογίαν Græci appellant, notam esse sibi profitebatur, & partim Augurijs, partim Conjectura, quæ essent futura, dicebat, ut scribit Cicero. Galli omnes, auctoribus Druidis, se ab Dite Patre, Inferorum Deo prognatos prædicabant; ob eamque causam, ut Cæsar memoriæ prodit, spatia omnis temporis non numero dierum, sed noctium, diffiniebant. & Dies Natales, Mensiumque ac Annorum initia sic observabant, ut Noctem Dies subsequeretur. Unde Elias Vinetus Commentario ad Ausonij Professores, manasse autumat; ut, quod Latini hodie, hoc die, Gallo-Romani anuit dicant, hac nocte.
units.tr: The Druids also taught the young many things about the stars and their motion, about the world and the size of the lands, and about the power and might of the immortal gods, as Caesar also observes. Hence that Divitiacus of the Aedui, who was one of the Druids, professed that he knew the nature of things, which the Greeks call physiologia, and, partly by augury and partly by conjecture, foretold what would happen, as Cicero writes. All the Gauls, on the authority of the Druids, claimed to be descended from Dis Pater, the god of the underworld; and for this reason, as Caesar records, they measured all periods of time not by the number of days but by nights. They also observed birthdays and the beginnings of months and years in such a way that the day followed the night. From this, Elias Vinetus, in his commentary on Ausonius' Professores, thinks it derives that, where Latins today say hodie, "on this day," the Gallo-Romans say anuit, "on this night."

units.la: Druidicam Magiam multis locis Naturalis Historiæ celebrat Plinius: sed in extremo lib. XVI ad hunc modum de Visco disputat: Non est omittenda, inquit, ea in re & Galliarum admiratio. Nihil habent Druidæ (ita suos appellant Magos) Viscum & Arborem, in qua gignatur, si modo sit Robur, sacratius. Iam per se Roboris nun cuignt Lucos, nec ulla Sacra sine ea fronde conficiunt, ut inde appellati quoque interpretatione Græca possint Druidæ videri. Enimvero quidquid adnascatur illis, e cælo missum putant, signumque esse electa ab ipso Deo Arboris. Est autem id rarum admodum inventu, & repertum magna religione petitur, & ante omnia sexta Luna: quæ principia Mensium Annorumque his facit & Sæculi post tricesimum annum: quia jam virium abunde habeat, nec sit sui dimidia. Omnia sanantem appellantes suo vocabulo, Sacrificijs Epulisque rite sub Arbore præparatis, duo admovent candidis coloris Tauros, quorum Cornua tunc primum vinciantur. Sacerdos candida Veste cultus Arborem scandit: Falce aurea demetit. Candido id excipitur sago. Tum deinde victimas immolant; precantes, ut suum donum Deus prosperum faciat his, quibus dederit. Fæcunditatem, eo poto, dari cuique animali steriti, arbitrantur, contraque Venena omnia esse remedio. Tanta gentium in rebus frivolis plerumque religio. Legitur & apud Dionem Prusæum, Celtas habere Druidas, Divinationis studiosos & sapientiæ; sine ijs nihil licitum esse Regibus facere, aut consulere: ita ut, si quis rem penitius examinet, illi regnent, Reges autem Sententiæ sint Ministri & Servi, licet in Thronis aureis sedeant, magnaque domos habitent, & sumptuose conviventur. Ad Druidarum autem Magiam respicere Virgilium lib. VI. Æneidos, ubi agit de Aureo Ramo, Viscoque & alijs, censet Petrus Crinitus lib. VI. cap. x; & apud eum Domitius Veronensis.
units.tr: Pliny treats of Druidic magic in many places in his Natural History, but at the end of book XVI he discusses mistletoe in this way: Nor is the admiration of the Gauls in this matter to be passed over, he says. The Druids (for so they call their magicians) have nothing more sacred than mistletoe and the tree on which it grows, provided that tree is an oak. They choose oak groves for their own sake, and perform no sacred rite without its leaves, so that the Druids may even be named from it in Greek. Whatever grows on them they think is sent from heaven, and a sign that the god himself has chosen that tree. It is very rarely found, and when it is found it is sought with great religious ceremony, and above all on the sixth day of the moon, which for them makes the beginnings of months and years, and of the thirty-year age, since by then it has enough strength and is not yet half spent. Calling it by a name meaning "healer of all," they prepare sacrifices and feasts under the tree, and they bring up two white bulls, whose horns are bound for the first time. The priest, dressed in a white robe, climbs the tree and cuts the mistletoe with a golden sickle; it is caught in a white cloak. Then they sacrifice the victims, praying that God may make his gift prosperous for those to whom he has given it. They believe that a barren animal, once it has drunk this, will become fertile, and that it is a remedy against all poisons. Such is the great religious feeling of the peoples about trivial things. It is also read in Dio of Prusa that the Celts have Druids, students of divination and of wisdom; without them nothing may lawfully be done or asked of kings. So that, if one examines the matter more closely, they rule, while the kings are their ministers and servants, even though they sit on golden thrones and live in great houses and feast sumptuously. Petrus Crinitus, book VI, chapter x, and after him Domitius Veronensis, think that Virgil in book VI of the Aeneid*, where he treats of the golden bough and mistletoe and other things, looks back to the magic of the Druids.

units.la: Erant etiam inter Druidas Feminæ, quæ eamdem cum Viris Sapientiam profitebantur. Earum frequens mentio apud Augustæ Historiæ Scriptores.
units.tr: There were also women among the Druids, who professed the same wisdom as the men. Writers of the Augustan History often mention them.

units.la: Sunt qui illud Au Gui l'an neuf, quod hactenus quotannis pridie Kalendas Ianuarij vulgo publice cantari in Gallia solet, ab Druidis manasse autumant, ex hoc forte Ovidij,
units.tr: Some authors claim that the custom Au Gui l'an neuf, which in France is still commonly sung publicly on the day before the Kalends of January, came down from the Druids, perhaps from this line of Ovid:

units.la: Ad Viscum Druidæ, Druidæ cantare solebant:
units.tr: To the Mistletoe the Druids, the Druids used to sing:

units.la: Solitos enim aiunt Druidas per suos Adolescentes Viscum suum cunctis mittere; eoque quasi munere bonum, tantum felicem & fortunatum omnibus Annum precari. Prolixe hac de re Goropius Becanus in Gallicis, Elias Vinctus in Ausonij Professores, Vigenereus ad Cæsaris Commentaria de Bello Gallico, & alij.
units.tr: For they say the Druids used to send their mistletoe around by their young men to everyone, and by this gift they prayed for a good, happy and fortunate year for all. Goropius Becanus in his Gallica, Elias Vinetus on Ausonius' Professores, Vigenère on Caesar's Commentaries on the Gallic War, and others, discuss this matter at length.

units.la: Druidarum porro Religionem apud Gallos dirae immanitatis Civibus interdixit Augustus, teste Suetonio in Claudij Principis Vita cap. xxxv; In Urbe item sustulit Tiberius, ut capiendus Plinius lib. iii. natur. hist. cap. 1; penitus abolere voluit in ipsa Gallia Claudius Imperator, eodem Suetonio notante in ejus vita capite, quod dixi, & Seneca in Menippæa Claudiana. Sed Claudius frustra fuit. Remansisse enim probat Tacitus sub Nerone lib. xiiii; Sub Alexandro Severo Ælius Lampridius: cujus hæc sunt: Mulier Druias eunti exclamavit Gallico sermone: Vadas nec Victoriam speres, nec militi tuo credas. Aurelianus quoque, si Vopisco fides, Druidas consuluit. Narrat ille, quodam tempore Aurelianum Gallicanas consuluisse Druidas, sciscitantem, utrum apud ejus posteros Imperium permaneret: tum illas respondisse: Nullius clarius in Rep. women, quam Claudy posteriorum futurum. Denique Mulier illa, quæ apud Tungros Diocletianum futurum Imperatorem, quum Aprum occidisset, prædixi, ex hoc genere fuit. Auctor idem Vopiscus in Numeriano. Plene tandem pulsos, scribunt Conradus Celtes, Irenicus, Althamerus, Aventinus, & alij, in Germaniam trans Rhenum habitatum venisse: indeque in hunc usque diem apud hos promanare Terriculamenti illud nocturni genus, quod Calceamentum Philosophicum appellant, Druttenfuß vulgo. Estque (quod communicatum sibi ab Ioachimo Camerario F. scribit Ortelius) figura Pentagona, olim Τγιεος, sive Bonæ Valitudinis symbolum. Hanc, inquit idem, Cunis ligneis incidunt, excitantes Pueros ea à nocturnis tutari lemuribus. Conradus Celtes describit quasdam lapideas antiquas imagines, ad radices Pinifseri Montis (Vichtelbe vulgo, in Vmbilico Germaniæ) in Cœnobio quodam à se visas, quas credit iconice horum Druidum referre formam. Frant sex numero, inquit, ad fores templi parietis infertæ, septem pedum singulæ, nudis pedibus, capita intecta, Græcanico pallio & cucullato, perniaque, barba ad inguina usque promissa, & circa naris fistulas bifurcata; in manibus Liber & Bacuus Diogenius; severa fronte, & trifidi supercilio; obstipo capite & figentes lumina terris.
units.tr: Augustus forbade the Druids' religion among the Gauls to citizens of savage cruelty, as Suetonius attests in the Life of the Emperor Claudius, chapter 35. Tiberius likewise suppressed it in the City, as Pliny, Natural History book 3, chapter 1, should be taken to show. The Emperor Claudius wished to abolish it completely in Gaul itself, as Suetonius notes in the same life, in the chapter I have mentioned, and Seneca in his Menippean Satire on Claudius. But Claudius failed. For Tacitus shows that they survived under Nero, book 14. Under Alexander Severus, Aelius Lampridius writes: A Druid woman shouted to him in the Gallic language as he went: Do not go, nor hope for victory, nor trust your soldier. Aurelian too, if we trust Vopiscus, consulted the Druids. He relates that at one time Aurelian asked the Gallic Druids whether his empire would remain with his descendants, and they replied: Nothing more famous in the state will there be than the name of Claudius's descendants. Finally, that woman who, when she had killed the boar, foretold that Diocletian would become emperor among the Tungri, was of this kind. The same author, Vopiscus, writes this in his life of Numerian. Conrad Celtis, Irenicus, Althamer, Aventinus and others write that, driven out completely, they came to live in Germany beyond the Rhine, and from there to this day among these people there spreads that kind of nocturnal bugbear which they call the Philosophical Shoe, commonly Druttenfuß. Its figure is pentagonal, once the symbol of Hygieia [ὑγίεια], or good health. As Ortelius writes, communicated to him by Joachim Camerarius the younger: They carve this on wooden cradles, to protect children from nocturnal ghosts. Conrad Celtis describes certain ancient stone images he saw in a certain monastery at the foot of the pine-clad mountain (commonly Fichtelberg, in the navel of Germany), which he believes represent the form of these Druids. There are six of them, he says, set into the wall beside the doors of the temple, each seven feet tall, with bare feet, uncovered heads, dressed in a Greek cloak with a hood, with calves and a beard reaching down to the groin, and forked around the nostrils; in their hands a book and a Diogenes staff; with stern brows and a forked eyebrow; heads bowed and eyes fixed on the ground.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CAP. XII.

units.la: Gallorum Veterum Mores circa Res publicas, Domi.
units.tr: The Customs of the Ancient Gauls concerning Public Affairs at Home.

units.la: Tales erant Veterum Gallorum in Rebus Sacris Mores: notantur & ab Antiquis Scriptoribus eorumdem Ritus in Profanis cum Domi, tum Militiæ.
units.tr: Such were the customs of the ancient Gauls in public affairs. Their rites are noted by ancient writers, both in civil matters at home and in military ones.

units.la: Quod ad prius Membrum, Gallos ad Concilium armatos venire solitos, prodit Livius lib. xxxi: In his (loquitur de Gallis) nova terribilisque species visa est, quod Armati (ita mos gentis erat) in Concilium venerunt.
units.tr: As to the first point, that the Gauls were accustomed to come armed to their assemblies, Livy in book xxxi reports: "In this (he is speaking of the Gauls) a new and frightening sight appeared, because they came armed into the council (such was the custom of the people)."

units.la: Tradit Plutarchus de Virtutibus Mulierum, Morem apud Gallos inolevisse, ut Pacis & Belli cum Feminis inirent Concilia, atque arbitrio earum hæc committerent. Scribit idem Polyænus lib. vii Strateg.
units.tr: Plutarch, in his work On the Virtues of Women, relates that a custom had taken hold among the Gauls that they held councils of peace and war with women and entrusted these matters to their judgment. Polyaenus writes the same in book vii of his Stratagems.

units.la: Addit Strabo lib. iv. id in Gallorum Concilijs (ἐν τῇς Συνεδρίοις) usitatum fuisse, si quis orantem (λέγοντα) interpellaret, progrediens Minister publicus distrito gladio, adjectisque minis, silentium imperabat; quod si non adquiesceret, idem iterum tertioque faciebat: denique de Sago Interpellatoris tantum amputabat, ut reliquum inutile redderetur.
units.tr: Strabo adds in book iv that it was usual in the Gallic assemblies (ἐν τοῖς Συνεδρίοις) that if anyone interrupted a speaker (λέγοντα), a public attendant would step forward with drawn sword, add threats, and command silence; if he did not comply, the attendant did the same a second and a third time; finally he cut off so much of the interrupter's cloak that what remained was useless. [ἐν τοῖς Συνεδρίοις; λέγοντα]

units.la: De ipsa porro re loquentem audiamus Cæsarem: Gallorum, inquit, subita & repentina Consilia: in Consiliis capiendis mobiles, & novis plerumque rebus student. Est autem hoc Gallica consuetudinis, ut & Viatores etiam invitos consistere cogant, & quod quisque eorum de quaque re audierit aut cognoverit, quærant: & Mercatores in Opidis Vulgus circumsistat, quibus ex regionibus veniant, quæsque res ibi cognoverint, pronunciare cogunt: & his rumoribus atque auditionibus permoti, de summis sæpe rebus consilia inicunt: quare è vestigio parum tere necesse est, quum incertis rumoribus serviant, & plerique ad voluntatem eorum fictâ respondeant. Eadem fere de Gallis scribuntur apud Polybium, Orosium, Trebellium & Vopiscum.
units.tr: Let us hear Caesar speaking of this very matter: "The Gauls' counsels are sudden and hasty; in taking decisions they are changeable and mostly eager for new things. It is, moreover, a Gallic custom that they force travellers even against their will to stop, and ask what each of them has heard or learned about any matter; and in the towns merchants are surrounded by the common crowd, and compelled to declare from what regions they come and what they have learned there; and moved by these rumours and reports, they often form plans on the most important affairs, which they must then regret, since they are at the mercy of uncertain rumours, and most people give answers made up to suit their wishes." Much the same things about the Gauls are written by Polybius, Orosius, Trebellius and Vopiscus.

units.la: De Celtis hoc Stobæi non negligendum: apud hos nempe gravius animadverti in eum, qui Peregrinum, quam qui Civem occiderit: huic enim Exilium, illi Mortem Pœnam statui.
units.tr: Stobaeus's remark about the Celts should not be overlooked: among them, a person who killed a foreigner was punished more severely than one who killed a citizen; for the former was condemned to exile, the latter to death.

units.la: Villas habebant nullis sepeas Mœnibus, ut scribit Polybius: Mœnibus cpidå includere, inquit Trogus, ab Massiliensibus didicere. Murorum structuram docet Cæsar lib. vii Belli Gallici.
units.tr: They had villages without walls, as Polybius writes. "To enclose towns with walls," says Trogus, "they learned from the Massilians." Caesar in book vii of his Gallic War teaches the construction of their walls.

units.la: Hoc etiam ad curam Rerum publicarum pertinere arbitror, quod notat idem Cæsar, Gallos, ubi major atque inlustrior res incideret, eam clamore per Agros Regionesque mira celeritate significare solitos; hinc alios deinde excipere, & proximis tradere.
units.tr: I think this also pertains to the care of public affairs, that Caesar notes that when a greater and more notable matter arose, the Gauls were accustomed to signal it with a shout through the fields and regions with remarkable speed; then others took it up in turn and passed it on to the neighbouring places.

units.la: Cap. XIII.
units.tr: Chapter XIII.

units.la: Gallorum Mores circa Res publicas, Militiæ.
units.tr: The Customs of the Gauls concerning Public Affairs: Military Matters.

units.la: QVOD ad Rem, qua Galli floruerunt, Militarem, ne nesciamus, quam in eam, ut hodieque, propenderint, quamque ipsorum in arma pronæ fuerint indoles, Colores videamus, quibus eos depingunt Veteres Scriptores.
units.tr: So that we are not ignorant of the military art in which the Gauls flourished, and of how strongly they inclined to it, as they still do today, and how prone their nature was to arms, let us look at the portraits the ancient writers draw of them.

units.la: Ælianus Gallos dicit omnium hominum ad subeunda pericula promptissimos M. Tullius & Eumenius, Immanes & barbaros: Immanissimos, Florus; Feroces, Lucanus & Trogus; Truces, Avienus & Seneca; Crudeles, Cassiodorus; Sanguineos, idem Lucanus; Duras & Retrogradas Mentes adsignat illis Lampridius: Gentium omnium inquietissimos ait Vopiscus; Iræ impotentes facit Livius. Crudelitatis Gallorum inter alia duo exstant Exempla: unum apud Trogum, qui memoriæ prodit, eos in bello prælioque contra Antigonum, dum hostiarum extis omnium interitus prædiceretur, non in timorem, sed in furorem versos, Conjuges & Liberos suos contrucidasse; auspicia belli à paricidio incipientes: alterum apud Florum, qui tradit, quosdam in bello captos, Catenas morsibus & ore tentasse, & effocandas invicem fauces præbuisse. Nisi quis hæc Libertatis amoris exempla potius vocitet. Hos enim Libertatis amantissimos semper fuisse, Orosius & Leo Imperator scriptum reliquere.
units.tr: Aelian says the Gauls were the readiest of all men to face danger. Cicero and Eumenius call them savage and barbarous; Florus calls them most savage; Lucan and Trogus, fierce; Avienus and Seneca, truculent; Cassiodorus, cruel; Lucan again, bloodthirsty. Lampridius ascribes to them hard and backward-looking minds; Vopiscus calls them the most restless of all peoples; Livy makes them unrestrained in anger. There survive two examples of Gallic cruelty. One is in Trogus, who records that when they fought against Antigonus, and the destruction of them all was being foretold from the entrails of the victims, they were turned not to fear but to frenzy, and slaughtered their own wives and children, beginning the omens of war with parricide. The other is in Florus, who relates that some men captured in war tried to bite through their chains with their mouths, and offered their throats to be strangled by one another. Unless someone would rather call these examples of love of liberty. Orosius and the Emperor Leo have written that the Gauls were always the greatest lovers of liberty.

units.la: Gallorum in Bellis Ferociam ad Thermopylas ostendit in Phocicis Pausanias. Quis hic non miretur Marium Victorinum Gallos scribentem semianimos, timidos & terga vertentes? quos contra Animosos facit Claudianus, quos Bellicosos & Armipotentes tradunt alij: quos Belli gloria ante Romanos fuisse commemorat Sallustius? An ita forte Victorinus interpretatur varia variorum Scriptorum de Gallis judicia? Cæsar certe, Ad bella suscipienda, inquit, ut alacer & promptus est animus, sic mollis ac minime resistens ad perferendas calamitates mens eorum est. Livius: Gallorum prima prælia plus quam Virorum; postrema minus quam Feminarum. Idem: Visu hoc cognitum est, si primum impetum, quem fervido ingenio & caca ira effundunt, sustinueris, sluunt sudore & lassitudine membra, labant arma, &c. Florus: Experimento deprehensum est, quippe sicut primus impetus eis major, quam virorum est; ita sequens minor quam feminarum: habent quiddam simile cum suis Nivibus: quæ mox, ut calucre pugna, statim in sudorem eunt, & levi motu quasi solæ laxantur. Dio: Galli ad quascumque res inexplebili cupiditate feruntur: ita neque audacia neque timoris modum servant; sed cum ab audacia in subitum metum, tum ab hoc in temerariam audaciam runnt. Aliter certe de Gallis Leo de Bellico apparatu, Galli, inquit, admodum infracto animo sunt in bello strenui. In magno opprobrio ignaviam & parvam retrocessionem ponunt, atque eam fugam esse existimant. Nam si quæ illi in medium adtulerunt, ita vera sint ut scribuntur; quæ causa quod Cicero, de Provinciis agens Consularibus, Gallium Romanis adeo timendam dixerit: quod Sallustius, Italiam omnem ab hac
units.tr: Pausanias shows the Gauls' ferocity in battle at Thermopylae, in the land of the Phocians. Who would not be amazed that Marius Victorinus writes of the Gauls as half-dead, timid, and turning their backs? Claudian, by contrast, makes them spirited; others report them as warlike and mighty in arms; Sallust mentions that they were famed for military glory before the Romans. Perhaps Victorinus interprets in this way the varied judgments of various writers about the Gauls? Caesar certainly says: As their spirit is eager and ready to undertake wars, so their mind is soft and hardly resistant in enduring misfortunes. Livy: The first battles of the Gauls are more than those of men; the last are less than those of women. The same: This has been learned by observation: if you withstand the first onslaught, which they pour out with fiery spirit and blind rage, their limbs run with sweat and exhaustion, their arms falter, and so on. Florus: Experience has shown that, just as their first attack is greater than that of men, so the following one is less than that of women. They have something similar to their snows, which as soon as they grow warm in battle at once turn to sweat and, with a light movement, as it were dissolve. Dio: The Gauls are carried towards whatever things with insatiable desire; thus they keep no measure either in boldness or in fear, but from boldness they rush into sudden fear, and from fear into reckless boldness. Leo writes quite differently of the Gauls in his account of military preparation: The Gauls, he says, are very vigorous in war, though of very broken spirit. They count cowardice and a slight retreat as a great disgrace, and think of that as flight. For if what they have brought forward is as true as it is written; for which reason Cicero, speaking in his consular provinces speech, said the Gaul was so much to be feared by the Romans; and Sallust that all Italy from this

units.la: Gallica consuetudinis ... Trogum ... ab hac gente contremuisse, adeo ut cum Gallis non de Gloria, sed de Salute certari fuerit solitum? Tantus Terror, inquit ex Trogo Iustinus lib. xxv. de Orientis Regibus, Gallici nominis & invicta Armorum felicitas erat, ut aliter neque Majestatem suam tutam, neque amissam recuperare se posse sine Gallica Virtute arbitrarentur. Solipater ex M. Terentij Varronis Originum lib. II scribit, ut antea dixi, Galliam duas res ingeniosissime persequi, Rem militarem & Argute loqui. Alia praetereo. Pauca solum, anteaquam ipsam Gallorum militiam explicem, insignis ipsorum Audaciae indicia notabo. Gallos Terramotum non timere, auctores sunt Aristoteles in Ethicis ad Nicomachum, & Plutarchus: verene an falso? Apud Strabonem legimus Gallos Alexandro Magno interroganti quid maxime timerent? Nihil esse, respondisse, nisi ne super ipsos Coelum rueret. Quod sequitur Æliani est, an non figmentum? Adeo ducunt, inquit, ignominiosum fugere, ut è corruentibus & collabantibus aedificiis saepe non effugiant, sed ne ardentibus quidem; ita ut incendio igneque circumventi pereant. Multi etiam inundantem Oceanum sustinent. Quidam etiam in fluctus ejus armati se conjiciunt, & eorum impetum excipiunt, protensis gladiis evaginatis & hastis vibratis: perinde ac si vel ferrere vel vulnerare possent. Ita nunc homines, qui Galliam habitant, sunt animati; ut haec talia, si non Stoliditati & Amentiae, certe Temeritati magnae censeantur adscribenda.
units.tr: Gallic custom ... Trogus ... that all Italy had trembled before this people, so that the contest with the Gauls was usually fought not for glory but for survival? Such great terror, says Justin, drawing on Trogus, in book 25, concerning the kings of the East, was caused by the Gallic name and the unconquered good fortune of their arms, that they judged they could neither keep their majesty safe nor recover what they had lost without Gallic valour. Solipater, from Marcus Terentius Varro's Origins, book II, writes, as I said before, that Gaul pursued two things most ingeniously: military affairs and clever speech. I pass over other things. I will only note, before I explain the Gallic military itself, a few clear signs of their boldness. Aristotle in the Nicomachean Ethics, and Plutarch, are authorities that the Gauls do not fear earthquakes. Is this true or false? In Strabo we read that when Alexander the Great asked the Gauls what they feared most, they replied that there was nothing, except that the sky might fall on them. What Aelian goes on to say: is it not a fiction? They think it so shameful to flee that they often do not escape from collapsing and crumbling buildings, nor even from burning ones, so that, surrounded by fire and flame, they perish. Many even withstand the flooding ocean. Some even throw themselves armed into its waves and meet its onslaught with swords drawn and spears brandished, as if they could strike or wound it. So the people who now inhabit Gaul are spirited; and such things, if not to be ascribed to stupidity and madness, must certainly be ascribed to great rashness.

units.la: Dilectus porro Imperatorum & Belli Ducum qui fuerit, Gallica Caesaris bella singulis annis ostendunt: Quod ad Privatos Milites; Ante Belli initium, inquit Caesar, armatum Concilium indicunt, quo lege communi omnes Pubere armati convenire coguntur, & qui ex iis novissimus venit, in conspectu multitudinis omnibus cruciatibus necatur. Eadem Galliae Consuetudo declaratur lib. VII, quum Vercingetorix Gallici belli Princeps electus Alexiae obsideretur. Consilium enim capit omnem Equitatum a se dimittere: discedentibus mandat, ut suam quisque eorum Civitatem adeat, omnesque qui per aetatem Arma ferre possunt ad bellum cogant: Galli tamen Concilio Principum decernunt, non omnes, qui Arma ferre possent, ut Vercingetorix statuerat, sed certum numerum cuique Civitati imperandum, ne tanta multitudine confusa, nec moderari, nec discernere suos, nec frumentationem habere possent. Hoc igitur Gallico Dilectu percipimus, quanta Militiae studia apud Gallos viguerint, quum Pueres omnes Arma ferre sint soliti. Ad militandum omnis aetas (inquit Ammianus Marcellinus lib. xv) aptissima, & pari pectoris robore Senex ad Procinctum ducitur, & Adultus, gelu duratis Artubus & labore assiduo, multa contemnentes & formidanda: nec eorum aliquando quisquam; ut in Italia, Munus Martium pertimescens pollicens sibi praecidit, quos jocaliter Murcos appellant. Cogebat igitur ad Militiam omnis Aetas; Adolescens, Vir, Senex. Vertiscus Remorum Praefectus, quamvis Equo propter Aetatem (ut legitur libro VIII) vix posset uti; tamen, consuetudine Gallorum, neque Aetatis excusatione in suscipienda Praefectura fuit usus, nec sine se dimicari voluit. Sic Parisino bello summa Imperii, ut est libro VII; traditur Camulogeno Aulerco, qui prope confectus aetate; tamen propter singularem scientiam rei militaris ad eum est honorem evocatus.
units.tr: As for the levy of soldiers by the commanders and leaders in war, Caesar's Gallic wars show it year by year. As for the private soldiers: Before the beginning of war, says Caesar, they summon an armed council, to which by common law all the men of military age are compelled to come armed; and whoever of them comes last is put to death in view of the crowd with every kind of torment. The same Gallic custom is described in book VII, when Vercingetorix, elected leader of the Gallic war, was besieged at Alesia. For he resolved to dismiss all his cavalry, and ordered them, when they left, to go each to his own state and to compel all who were of age to bear arms to join the war. The Gallic chiefs, however, decreed in their council that not all who could bear arms, as Vercingetorix had ordered, but a fixed number should be demanded from each state, lest, with so great a multitude in confusion, they could neither control nor distinguish their own men, nor provide grain. From this Gallic levy, then, we learn how greatly the zeal for war flourished among the Gauls, since all their boys were accustomed to bear arms. Every age, says Ammianus Marcellinus, book XV, is most fit for fighting; and the old man is led into the fray with the same strength of heart as the adult, their limbs hardened by cold and constant toil, despising many things that are to be feared. Nor did any of them ever, as in Italy, fear the gift of Mars and cut off the thumbs they promised themselves, which they jestingly call murci. So every age was compelled to military service: youth, man, and old man. Vertiscus, prefect of the Remi, though by reason of his age (as is read in book VIII) he could scarcely use a horse, nevertheless, by Gallic custom, neither used his age as an excuse in taking up the prefecture nor wished to fight without himself. So too in the Parisian war the supreme command, as is told in book VII, was handed to Camulogenus of the Aulerci, who was nearly worn out with age, yet was called to that honour on account of his singular knowledge of military affairs.

units.la: Quod ad Commeatum: Veteres Gallos militantes maximam rei Frumentariae rationem habuisse, ut ea ipsis suppeteret, hostibus autem deficeret, paret ex innumeris apud Auctorem de Bello Gallico Exemplis: inter quae illustria sunt illa, quibus docemur Vercingetorigem omnem aliquoties adhibuisse curam, ut Caesaris vires Frumentationum Pabulationumque inopia frangerentur, Vicis Opidisque quoquo versum incensis.
units.tr: As for provisions: that the ancient Gauls, when campaigning, took the greatest care of supply, so that it was plentiful for themselves but lacking for their enemies, is clear from countless examples in the author of the Gallic War. Among them are the notable ones which teach us that Vercingetorix repeatedly took every care that Caesar's forces should be broken by lack of grain and fodder, with villages and towns burned on every side.

units.la: Armatura vero Gallica Romanae dissimilis fuit, ut ex VII belli Gallici libro intelligi poterit, de Eduis Caesari militantibus, qui Gallicis Armis Romanos vehementer perterruerunt. Quaenam autem fuerint haec Gallorum Arma, variorum Scriptorum, Graecorum Latinorumque, indicio videamus.
units.tr: The Gallic armour, moreover, was unlike the Roman, as may be understood from book VII of the Gallic War, concerning the Aedui who fought for Caesar and who greatly terrified the Romans with Gallic arms. Let us see, however, from the testimony of various writers, Greek and Latin, what these Gallic arms were.

units.la: Gladij Gallis erant graves, Polybio; praelongi, Livio; sine Mucronibus, iisdem notantibus: ad hoc tantum utiles, ut, quemadmodum apud Strabonem est videre, desuper in hostem impingerentur: unde —— Aite consurgit in Ensem,
units.tr: Gallic swords were heavy, according to Polybius; very long, according to Livy; without points, as the same authors note; useful only in this way: as can be seen in Strabo, they were brought down upon the enemy from above; whence the line "and he rises up against the sword" [...].

units.la: Apud Vergilium, Censore Servio. His impetentes Capita hostium abscindebant: interim male erant fabricati & ex molli ferro, ut habet Polyaenus lib. VIII: quare de iisdem sic ex Polybio Sudas: Ita sunt parati, ut primo impetu unam plagam inferant: deinde statim flatim ita curvantur & inflectuntur in longitudinem & latitudinem, ut nisi spatium recedendi & pede corrigendi fuerit datum, celeriter alter ictus illorum sit irritus. Spathas vocat Diodorus, ænæaque catena à dextero latere pendentes. Verba ejus ex lib. v. operæprecium est audire: Ἀντὶ δὲ ἡ ξίφος Σπάθας ἰχυρὰ μαχαίρας, σιδηρᾶς ἢ χαλκαᾶς ἀλύσεων ἐξηρτημένους, ᾗ ἀπὸ τῆς δεξιᾶς λαγόνα ἀπηρτημένας. Sic Strabo lib. v. Μάχαιρα μαχαίρα, παρηρτημένη ἀπὸ τῆς δεξιοῦ πλευροῦ. μάχαιρα etiam Gallicus ensis dicitur & laudatur Polluci. De Spathis porro, id est gladus majoribus, & Semispathis, hoc est minoribus, legendi præter Tacitum & alios, Vegetius lib. ii de Re militari cap. xv & alibi, & Isidorus lib. xviii Etymol. cap. vi.
units.tr: In Virgil, as Servius comments. Attacking with these, they cut off the enemies' heads. Meanwhile they were badly made and of soft iron, as Polyaenus says in book VIII. Hence Suidas, quoting Polybius, says of the same: They are so prepared that with the first onset they deliver a single blow; then at once they are bent and curved lengthwise and breadthwise, so that unless room is given to withdraw and set the foot straight, a second blow from them is quickly ineffective. Diodorus calls them spathae, and says they hung from the right side by iron or bronze chains: "Instead of swords they had large spathai, hanging by iron or bronze chains from the right side" [Ἀντὶ δὲ ἡ ξίφος Σπάθας ἰχυρὰ μαχαίρας, σιδηρᾶς ἢ χαλκαᾶς ἀλύσεων ἐξηρτημένους, ᾗ ἀπὸ τῆς δεξιᾶς λαγόνα ἀπηρτημένας]. It is worth hearing his words from book V. So Strabo, book V: "a machaira hanging from the right side" [Μάχαιρα μαχαίρα, παρηρτημένη ἀπὸ τῆς δεξιοῦ πλευροῦ]. The machaira is also called a Gallic sword by Pollux, and praised there. Concerning spathae, that is the larger swords, and semispathae, that is the smaller, one should read, besides Tacitus and others, Vegetius, book II, On Military Affairs, chapter XV and elsewhere, and Isidore, Etymologies, book XVIII, chapter VI.

units.la: Scuta Gallis erant longa (inquit Livius; Θυρεὸς μαχαῖος Straboni) ceterum ad amplitudinem Corporum parum lata, & ea ipsa plana. Diodorus Θυρεὸς αἱρόμενος vocat, adjuratum viri facta, & ad hominis altitudinem adsurgentia.
units.tr: Scuta were long among the Gauls (says Livy; Straboni thyreos makhaios [Θυρεὸς μαχαῖος]), but since they were narrow for the size of their bodies, and flat. Diodorus calls them thyreos aeiromenos [Θυρεὸς αἱρόμενος], adorned with the work of men, and rising to the height of a man.

units.la: Gesa, quædam Gallorum Tela Nonius habet ex Varrone, ubi hæc Qui gladiis cinctì sive Scuto cum binis Gesis essent. De his quoque Virgilius: — Duo quisque Alpina coruscant
units.tr: Nonius, citing Varro, mentions the gesa, a kind of Gallic javelin, where the words are: Those who were girded with swords or with a shield and two gesae. Virgil also speaks of these: each man brandishes two Alpine spears. ## The gesa, carried in the hand.

units.la: Gesa manu.

Hastas Viriles interpretatur ad hunc locum Servius, & addit, Viros fortes Gesas ab Gallis vocari. Cæsar etiam tertio belli Gallici Gesa (vel, ut alij scribendum putant, Gasa, unde Gasati fortean, de quibus paullo post) Gallis tribuit.
units.tr: Servius, on this passage, explains hastae viriles and adds that the Gauls called brave men gesae. Caesar too, in the third book of the Gallic War, attributes the gesa (or gasa, as others think it should be written, whence perhaps gasati, of whom a little later) to the Gauls.

units.la: Lanceas Veteres Gallos, appellasse τὰς λόγχας (ut hodieque faciunt, cum Belgis) auctor est Diodorus, προσάλμενοι, inquit, τὰς λόγχας, ἃς ἐπαίνει Λαγχίας καλῶν πηχυαίας τῷ μήκει ἢ σιδήρῳ, καὶ ἐν μείζων τὸ ὀπλισμα ἰχύος: Ferrum cubitali longitudine, latitudine duorum palmorum habuisse notat. Λόγχας ἔχ' λόγον tribuit Gallis Strabo lib. iv. Videndum, an non huc pertineant hæc Eustathij verba: Ἀγγῶν, πόδος δὲ γατῶν Φεγγυνᾶ, ἐπὶ λίαν μακρᾶς Φασι, ἐπὶ μεγάλῳ, ἡ τὸ πλάσιον σιδηρῷ πεπείχιται.
units.tr: Diodorus is the authority that the ancient Gauls called lances lonchai [τὰς λόγχας], as the Belgians still do today. He says they took up the lances, which he calls lanchiai, a cubit in length with an iron head, and that their armour was the greater for it: he notes that the iron was a cubit long and two palms wide. Strabo in book iv attributes the logchai to the Gauls. It may be asked whether these words of Eustathius do not bear on this: they say the spear is very long and is tipped with a large piece of iron [Ἀγγῶν... σιδηρῷ πεπείχιται, obscure].

units.la: Materis etiam Gallis tribuitur ab antiquis Scriptoribus. Sisenna Historiar. lib. iii. apud Nonium in Lancea: Galli Materilus, Suevus Lanceis configuntur. Idem lib. iv. Alij Materibus aut Lanceis tamen medium perturbant agmen. Auctor ad Herennium lib. iv. Ut si quis Macedones appellaret hoc modo: non tam cito Sarissa Græcia potiti sunt: aut idem Gallos significans, dicat; Nec tam facile ex Italia Materis Transalpina depulsa est. Cæsaris, Livij, Agellij locos ab aliis adnotatos prætereo. Illud jam animadverterunt docti viri, Vocem hanc apud Strabonem lib. iv. esse corruptam: Μαγέας mala... emendandum enim, Μάνεας vel Μάτεας. Nam Epitome habet Μαλεας: Cæsar Mataras.
units.tr: The ancient writers also attribute the materes to the Gauls. Sisenna, in book iii of his Histories, cited by Nonius under lancea: The Gauls, the Suevi, are armed with materes and lances. The same, book iv: Others with materes or lances nevertheless disturb the middle of the column. The author of the Ad Herennium, book iv: As if someone were to call the Macedonians thus: "the Sarissa did not so quickly gain possession of Greece"; or, meaning the Gauls, said: "nor was the Transalpine materes so easily driven out of Italy." I pass over the passages of Caesar, Livy and Gellius that others have noted. Learned men have already observed that this word in Strabo, book iv, is corrupted: Mageas [Μαγέας] is wrong, for it should be emended to Maneas or Mateas [Μάνεας, Μάτεας]. The Epitome has Maleas [Μαλεας], and Caesar has mataras.

units.la: Galea ærea paullo eminentiore caput apud Diodorum Galli muniunt; in qua aut Cornua impressa essent, aut Avium vel Quadrupedum effigies sculptæ. Hinc apud Suetonium cap. xxiv in Cæsaris vita, legimus Legionem, ab eodem Cæsare bello Gallico ex Transalpinis conscriptam, vocabulo Gallico Alaudam fuisse appellatam: quod Militum hujus Novæ Legionis Galeæ Alaudæ Avis effigie vel cristis essent ornatæ; vel quod, ut alij volunt, Milites Galeis uterentur, ei Apici simillimis, qui in Alaudæ capite. Alauda autem Avis appellatio Gallica est, Galeritam sive Cassitam significans, apud Plinium lib. xi. nat. hist. cap. xxxvii & Marcellum Empiricum, cap. xxix, hominem Gallicæ Linguæ Veteris non imperitum.
units.tr: Diodorus says the Gauls protected the head with a bronze helmet rising to a slight peak; on it were either horns in relief, or sculpted figures of birds or quadrupeds. Hence in Suetonius, chapter xxiv, in the life of Caesar, we read that a legion which Caesar himself raised from the Transalpine peoples during the Gallic War was called by the Gallic name Alauda, because the helmets of this new legion's soldiers were decorated with the figure of a bird, or with crests; or, as others prefer, because the soldiers wore helmets very like the crest on the head of the alauda. The name alauda for a bird is Gallic, signifying the crested lark or the cassita, as in Pliny, Natural History book xi, chapter xxxvii, and in Marcellus Empiricus, chapter xxix, a man not unskilled in the old Gallic tongue.

units.la: Gallis etiam Arcu & Funda in usu fuit, ait Strabo: qui addit Fustem (χεῖρος ξύλον) apud eos esse, qui manu, non Amento (ἐκ χειρὸς, οὐκ ἐξ ἀγκύλης) jactus Sagitta longius ferit; quo præcipue in Aucupijs Avium uti consuerunt.
units.tr: Strabo says the Gauls also used the bow and the sling. He adds that among them there is a fustis (cheiros xylon [χεῖρος ξύλον]) which throws an arrow farther when it is cast by hand, not by a thong (ek cheiros, ouk ex agkyles [ἐκ χειρὸς, οὐκ ἐξ ἀγκύλης]); they especially used this in bird-catching.

units.la: Certa ac fide digna res est (ut auctor idem est) in Gallia nasci Arborem Fico similem, quæque fructum ferat capiti Columnæ Corinthiacæ respondentem: ea autem secta, Lethalem liquorem emitti ad usus Sagittarum. Sagittarios vero magno in usu Gallis fuisse, Cæsar lib. vii plane confirmat, quum de Vercingetorige loquitur, Sagittarios omnes, ait, quorum erat permagnus numerus in Gallia, conquiri & ad se mitti jubet.
units.tr: It is a certain and trustworthy fact (the same author says) that in Gaul there grows a tree like a fig, bearing fruit that corresponds to the capital of a Corinthian column; when this is cut, a deadly liquid flows out, used for arrows. That the sagittarii were in great use among the Gauls, Caesar in book vii clearly confirms, when speaking of Vercingetorix: He orders all the archers, he says, of whom there was a very great number in Gaul, to be sought out and sent to him.

units.la: Circum Collum Aureos Torques gestare (Lactea Colla Auro innectuntur, apud Virgil.) ac circa Brachia ac Manus Brachialia; & qui honores gerunt Vestes Tinctas atque aurovariegatas, docent Polybius, Strabo & Diodorus. Corallio adornabant Gladios & Scuta, ut refert Plinius. Thoraces ferreos etiam quidam ornabant Auro, teste Diodoro.
units.tr: They wore golden torques around the neck (Lactea colla auro innectuntur, in Virgil) and bracelets around the arms and hands; and those who held office wore dyed and gold-embroidered garments, as Polybius, Strabo and Diodorus teach. They adorned their swords and shields with coral, as Pliny reports. Some also decorated their iron breastplates with gold, according to Diodorus.

units.la: Plerique Galli super Vmbilicum nudi pugnare consueverant, ut in pugna Cannenti Livius ait, de quo etiam praelio Polybius idem tradit. Terribilis, inquit, erat nudorum hominum praecedentium & aspectus & incessus, robore nempe & specie praestantium. Sic in Gallograecia Livius ait, Gallos nudos dimicasse; ideoque eminus Romanis Pilis confixos occubuisse.
units.tr: Most Gauls used to fight naked above the navel, as Livy says of the battle at Cannae, and Polybius also records of that battle. Terrible, he says, was the sight and the advance of the naked men in front, men surpassing in strength and appearance. So too in Gallograecia, Livy says the Gauls fought naked, and therefore, pierced by Roman javelins from a distance, they fell.

units.la: Galli primas suae Militiae partes Equitibus dederunt; belliqué administrandi principes, ut ait Caesar, lib. vi, fecerunt. Hoc tamen de omnibus Galliae Civitatibus non temere est affirmandum. Treviri longe plurimum totius Galliae Equitatu valuere, ut est lib. v: Sontiates, ut est iii, eadem militia plurimum potuere: At Nervii plus Peditatu, ut est iii. Si genus universum spectetur, Equitatus Gallicus Militiae Gallicae praecipua gloria fuit: & Caesar bellis Civilibus isto praecipue Equitatu est usus; feliciter, ut constat ex iis, quae gesta contra Afranium & Petreium Cn. Pompei Legatos in Hispania, & in Africa deinde contra belli Civilis reliquias. Hinc illa vox Ciceronis quinta Philippica: Est enim opinio, ait, decreturum aliquem M. Antonio illam ultimam Galliam, quam Plancus obtinet: quid hoc est aliud, quam ad Bellum Civile Hosti Arma largiri; primum nervos Belli, Pecuniam infinitam, qua nunc eget; deinde Equitatum, quantum velit? Equites autem scribit Caesar, multis Carris magnisque impedimentis solere venire. Figis & Curribus dimicare hos, etiam Livius & Pomponius tradunt; Essedis Strabo. Ex his Curribus obvium hostem jaculo primum appetebant: tum, relicto curru, Pedites Enlibus certabant, ut affirmat Diodorus. Hinc Gallicum Axem vitandum monet Iuvenalis Satyra viii.
units.tr: The Gauls gave the chief part of their military service to the cavalry, and they made the leaders in conducting war, as Caesar says in book vi. Yet this should not be rashly affirmed of all the states of Gaul. The Treveri were by far the most powerful in cavalry of all Gaul, as in book v; the Sontiates, as in book iii, were also very strong in the same arm; but the Nervii were stronger in infantry, as in book iii. If the nation as a whole is considered, the Gallic cavalry was the chief glory of Gallic warfare; and Caesar in the civil wars used this cavalry especially, with success, as is evident from what was done against Afranius and Petreius, the legates of Pompey in Spain, and afterwards in Africa against the remnants of the civil war. Hence that saying of Cicero in the fifth Philippic: For there is an opinion, he says, that someone will hand over to Mark Antony that last Gaul which Plancus holds: what else is this than to give arms to the enemy for civil war; first the sinews of war, unlimited money, which he now needs; then as much cavalry as he wishes? Caesar writes that the cavalry usually came with many wagons and large baggage trains. Livy and Pomponius also report that they fought from chariots and carts; Strabo, from essedae. From these chariots they first attacked the enemy who met them with a javelin; then, leaving the chariot, the foot soldiers fought on foot, as Diodorus affirms. Hence Juvenal in satire viii warns us to avoid the Gallic axle:

units.la: Horrida vitanda est Hispania, Gallicus Axis.
units.tr: The bristling Spain is to be avoided, the Gallic axle.

units.la: Pertinet huc Manilij illud lib. iv. Astronomic.
units.tr: To this belongs that line of Manilius in book iv of the Astronomica:

units.la: Gallia pratentis, Hispania maxima bellis.
units.tr: Gaul for its cavalry, Spain for its great wars.

units.la: Pratenta (quas Ammianus & alij Praeturas vocant) à praetendendo, Equites, ut quidam volunt, Exploratores.
units.tr: The pratentae (which Ammianus and others call praeturae) are named from praetendere; they were, as some think, scouts [Exploratores].

units.la: Galli, ut etiam Celtiberi pluresque Barbaricae nationes, Catervis utebantur in praelio, in quibus erant sena millia Armatorum. Docet Vegetius lib. ii. cap. ii de Re Militari.
units.tr: The Gauls, like the Celtiberians and several other barbarian nations, used catervae in battle, each of which had six thousand armed men. Vegetius teaches this in book ii, chapter ii, On Military Affairs.

units.la: Gallos maximos exercitus educere solitos, testantur Caesar de bello Gallico libri ii initio, Ammianus Marcellinus lib. xxi & Strabo de Arvernis. Addam hic obiter, eosdem Legatis Romanorum ad se missis, autos fuisse respondere; Se in Armis jus ferre, omnia Virorum fortium esse, ut scribit Livius lib. v. ab V. C.
units.tr: Caesar in the first book of the Gallic War at its beginning, Ammianus Marcellinus in book xxi, and Strabo on the Arverni, attest that the Gauls were accustomed to lead very large armies. I may add in passing that when Roman legates were sent to them, they replied that they decided right by arms, and all things belonged to brave men, as Livy writes in book v, from the foundation of the city.

units.la: Secum etiam in bello ducebant (si fides apud Athenaeum Posidonio) Parasitos; à quibus Laudes ipsorum cum Cantu praedicari volebant. Diodorus sane idem confirmat.
units.tr: They also took with them into war (if we trust Posidonius as cited by Athenaeus) parasites, by whom they wished their praises to be proclaimed with song. Diodorus certainly confirms the same.

units.la: Castrorum, ut infinitis locis ex Caesaris Ephemeridibus discimus, fabrica, sive locum, sive munitionem consideremus, parum habuit artis. Vallis eligebatur, cujus Fossa & Vallum, Terra videlicet ac Coelum essent. Gallorum enim consuetudo fuit (ut est viii libro) relictis locis superioribus, ad ripas fluminis Castra demittere. Si quando diligentia major esset, Carri Rhedaeque tantum pro Vallo objiciebantur. Tandem quae Romanos facere cognoverant, imitari coeperunt.
