Exemplum in Nervijs libro v, adeo ut Caesar etiam Turres bellicas ab Gallis institutas, Testudines, Munitionesque fuerit miratus.
units.tr: As we learn from countless passages in Caesar's commentaries, their skill in making camps, whether in choosing a site or in fortifying it, was slight. A valley was chosen, whose ditch and rampart would be, namely, earth and sky. For the custom of the Gauls was (as in book viii) to leave the higher ground and pitch their camps on the banks of a river. If ever they showed greater care, only wagons and carts were set up in place of a rampart. At last they began to imitate what they had seen the Romans do. An example is among the Nervii, in book v; so much so that Caesar even marvelled at the siege towers, the tortoises and the fortifications which the Gauls had devised.

units.la: Praelium ineuntes horrendum edebant Cantum, Vlulatum, Clamores; Tripudiabant; Scuta in patrium quemdam morem quatiebant; Armorum suorum crepitu tantum eliciebant sonum, ut circumstantia omnia loca, quemadmodum memoriae produnt Polybius & Livius, vocem emittere viderentur. Vocem, ait Diodorus, Galli gravem habent atque asperam; sed & Tubas habent suo more barbaras, & quae asperum sonum reddant. Et totus hic Gallicus Tumultus frequenter à Livio, sed inimice & contumeliose, ut de Gallis loqui fere solet, notatus est. Galli, ait lib. v. ab V. C. truci Cantu, Clamoribusque variis, horrendo cuncta compleverant sono. Et ibidem: Mox Vlulatus Cantusque dissonos, vagantibus circa moenia turmatim Gallis, audiebant. Idem lib. xxxiv. Galli cum variis Vlulatibus Cantuq. moris sui quatientes Scuta supra capita, vibrantesq. dextris Tela. Libro xlviii de Gallis in Asia: Ad hoc tantus ineuntium praelium & Vlulatus & Tripudia, & Quatientium Scuta in patrium quemdam morem, horrendus Armorum Crepitus, omnia de industria composita ad Terrorem. Tumultum hunc aliquoties etiam attingit Caesar, sed levius, lib. v, vii & alibi.
units.tr: Joining battle, they raised a dreadful chant, howling and shouts; they danced; they shook their shields in a certain native manner; by the clash of their arms they produced such a sound that, as Polybius and Livy record, all the surrounding places seemed to give back a voice. The Gauls, says Diodorus, have a voice that is deep and harsh; and they have trumpets of their own barbarous kind, which give a rough sound. And this whole Gallic uproar is often noted by Livy, but unfriendly and insulting, as he usually speaks of the Gauls. The Gauls, he says in book v from the foundation of the city, had filled everything with a savage chant and various shouts, with a dreadful noise. And in the same place: Soon they heard howling and discordant song, as the Gauls wandered in troops around the walls. The same in book xxxiv: The Gauls, with various howlings and their own kind of song, shaking their shields over their heads and brandishing weapons in their right hands. In book xlviii, on the Gauls in Asia: Besides this, the onset of those joining battle was so great, with howling and dancing, and the shaking of shields in a certain native manner, and the dreadful crash of arms, all things deliberately arranged to inspire terror. Caesar too touches on this uproar several times, though more lightly, in books v, vii and elsewhere.

units.la: {a}Qualis autem in Gallis fuit prœliorum Virtus? Virium certe confidentia prorsus ingens. Galli, ut est apud Auctorem de Bello Africano, homines aperti minimeque infidi, per Virtutem, non per Dolum dimicare consueverunt. Hinc Divico Helvetius sic legitur loquutus ad Cæsarem, qui Tigurinos, Galliæ tunc Populos, circumvenerat, Se ita à Patribus Majoribusque suis didicisse, ut magis Virtute, quam Dolo contenderent, aut Insidiis niterentur. Et militaris hujus Virtutis singularia multis locis apud Cæsarem exempla sunt: de Helvetiis lib. 1; de Belgis & Nervijs lib. 11. de aliis alibi: de Gallis item universim, Cæsari ad Mundam militantibus, apud Auctorem Belli Hisp.
units.tr: But what was the courage of the Gauls in battle? Their confidence in their own strength was certainly enormous. The Gauls, as the author of the African War says, are an open people, least treacherous, and they have customarily fought by valour, not by trickery. Hence Divico the Helvetian is recorded as speaking thus to Caesar, who had surrounded the Tigurini, then a people of Gaul: He had learned from his fathers and ancestors to contend more by valour than by deceit, or to rely on ambushes. There are particular examples of this military valour in many places in Caesar: concerning the Helvetii in book 1; concerning the Belgae and the Nervii in book 2; concerning others elsewhere. Likewise, concerning the Gauls in general, who served under Caesar at Munda, see the author of the Spanish War.

units.la: Quod ad Acici instructionem & Ordinem: Quum ex pluribus Civitatibus Exercitus conflatus esset, Milites generatim distributi in Civitates & Pagos erant, separatimque singularum Civitatum copiæ collocabantur. Docet passim Cæsar. De horum Equestris Pugnæ constitutione, quam Trimarcam, ut infra dicam, appellabant, legendus Pausanias in Phocicis. De Soldurus etiam, ut Cæsar eos vocat (Athenæo Siloduni nominantur) consulendum Caput, quod sequitur, xv.
units.tr: As for the arrangement and order of their battle line: when the army was made up of several states, the soldiers were generally distributed by states and cantons, and the forces of each state were stationed separately. Caesar teaches this throughout. On the organisation of their cavalry fighting, which they called the trimarcus, as I shall say below, read Pausanias in the Phocica. Concerning the soldurii, as Caesar calls them (Athenaeus names them the Siloduni), consult the following chapter, the fifteenth.

units.la: Victoriam de hostibus consecuti, Dis Captivos immolabant, ut ex Sopatro credit Athenæus. A pugna redeuntes, ut scribit Strabo, Capita hostium de Collis Equorum suspendunt: ταῖς κεφαλαῖς τ' ὠλεμίων ait ἐξαπλεν ἐκ τ' αὐχένων τῶν ἵππων) & spectaculi gratia ante portas Opidorum adfigunt. Diodorus: τῶν δ' ἐπιτῶν πολεμίων τὰς κεφαλὰς ἀφαιρῶνται ἐκ τῶν αὐχένων τ' ἵππων. Livius lib. x: Nec ante ad Cosf. qui jam haud procul à Clusio aberant, famem ejus clades perlatam, quam in conspectu fuerint Gallorum Equites, pictoris ut Equorum suspensa gestantes Capita & Lanceis infixa, evantesque meris suis Carmine. Consuetudinis autem adfigendi Portis opidorum Hostium cæsorum capita, Vestigium manet hodieque per Galliias, & alibi, in Nobilium ædibus. Nam & his temporibus Galliæ Nobiles suis Foribus adfixa habent Ferarum Capita, quæ vel ipsi vel majores ipsorum occiderint. Scribit & Diodorus, Gallos Nobilium, acie cæsorum, Capita Aromatibus uncta in Thecis condere summa diligentia; ostendentes ea hospitibus; nulloque pretio vel parentibus vel aliis reddentes. Tradit Livius, hos Postumii Corporis spolia Caputq: præcisum ovantes in Templo, quod sanctissimum est apud eos intulisse. Purgato inde Capite, ut mos ijs est, Calvam Auro cælavisse, idque Sacrum Vas iis fuisse, quo Solennibus libarent, Poculumque Sacerdotibus fuisse ac tempoн Antistibus: unde hæc apud Silium; At Celtæ vacui Capitis circumdare gaudent Ossa (nefas) Auro: & Mensis ea Pocula servant.
units.tr: Having won the victory over their enemies, they sacrificed the captives to the gods, as Athenaeus believes on the authority of Sopater. Returning from battle, as Strabo writes, they hang the heads of the enemy from the necks of their horses [ταῖς κεφαλαῖς τ' ὠλεμίων ... ἐκ τ' αὐχένων τῶν ἵππων] and fix them before the gates of the towns as a spectacle. Diodorus: they cut off the heads of the slain enemy and hang them from the necks of the horses [τῶν δ' ἐπιτῶν πολεμίων τὰς κεφαλὰς ἀφαιρῶνται ἐκ τῶν αὐχένων τ' ἵππων]. Livy, book 10: "Nor did news of their disaster reach the consuls, who were already not far from Clusium, before the Gallic horsemen came into view, carrying on their horses the heads of the painted enemy hung up and fixed on lances, and shouting out their triumphant songs." The custom of fixing the heads of slain enemies to the gates of towns survives to this day in Gaul and elsewhere, in the houses of the nobles. For even in our own times the Gallic nobles have the heads of wild beasts fixed to their doors, which they or their ancestors killed. Diodorus also writes that the Gauls take the heads of their nobles slain in battle, anointed with aromatic spices, and store them in chests with the greatest care, showing them to guests, and they will not give them back for any price, to parents or to anyone else. Livy relates that these people brought the spoils of the body of Postumius and his head, cut off, into the temple which is most holy among them, exulting. After the head was cleaned, as is their custom, they overlaid the skull with gold, and it was a sacred vessel to them, from which they poured libations at solemn feasts, and a cup for their priests and chief men. Hence these lines in Silius: "But the Celts delight to surround the bones of an emptied skull with gold (sacrilege!), and they keep those cups for their tables."

units.la: Eosdem Gallos, ut concludam, Prædæ Partem Diis consecrare solitos, testis est Cæsar lib. vi. de bello Gallico.
units.tr: That the same Gauls were accustomed to consecrate a part of their booty to the gods, as I conclude, is witnessed by Caesar, book 6 of the Gallic War.

units.la: CAP. XIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV.

units.la: Gallorum Mores circa Res Privatas.
units.tr: The Customs of the Gauls concerning Private Property

units.la: Sic se habebant Publice Gallorum Mores: quod ad Privatiores, audivimus jam ante in omni Gallia, qui in aliquo sunt numero atque honore, genera esse duo: alterum Druidum, alterum Equitum: hos, quum est usus, atque aliquod Bellum incidit, omnes in eo versari, atque ut quisque eorum est genere copiisque amplissimus, ita plurimos circa se Ambactos Clientesque habere: illos Rebus Divinis interesse, Sacra publica & privata procurare, Religiones interpretari, &c. Pergens Cæsar, plebem notat Servorum haberi loco; in hos ea omnia esse jura, quæ Dominis in Servos.
units.tr: Such were the public customs of the Gauls. As for private persons, we have already heard that throughout all Gaul there were two classes of those who held any rank or honour: the Druids and the Knights. When there was need and some war broke out, all of them took part in it, and each man, in proportion to his birth and wealth, kept as many retainers and clients around him as he could. The Druids attended to divine matters, managed public and private sacrifices, and interpreted religious questions. Caesar goes on to note that the common people were held in the position of slaves, and that all the rights a master has over his slaves belonged to these men over the commons.

units.la: Liberos suos, ut idem scribit, nisi quam adoleverint, ut munus Militia sustinere possint, palam ad se redire non patiuntur: Filiumque in pueritia ætate in publico in conspectu Patris adsistere turpe ducunt.
units.tr: According to the same writer, they did not allow their children to come into their presence in public until they had grown up enough to bear the duties of military service. They considered it shameful for a son in boyhood to stand in his father's sight in public.

units.la: Viri quantas pecunias, eodem memorante, ab Uxoribus Dotis nomine acceperint, tantas ex suis Bonis æstimatione facta, cum Dotibus communicant: hujus omnis Pecunia conjunctim ratio habetur, fructusque servantur. Uter eorum vita superarit, ad eum pars utriusque cum fructibus superiorum temporum pervenit. Viri in Uxores. sic uti in Liberos, Vitæ Necisque habent Potestatem. Gallorum mulieres speciosas, magnitudine & robore Viris similes, facit Diodorus; fœcundas & bonas educatrices; sive, ut Strabo, pariendo educandoque felices. Has cum Liberis una lavantes in Balnea Ollas cum pulte detulisse, tradit Plutarchus viii. Convival.
units.tr: As the same writer relates, husbands received from their wives, as dowry, sums of money. An equal amount was assessed from the husband's own goods and placed together with the dowry. The whole of this money was accounted for jointly, and its income was kept. Whichever of the pair outlived the other received the share of both, together with the income of earlier times. Husbands held power of life and death over their wives just as they did over their children. Diodorus describes the Gallic women as beautiful, similar to the men in size and strength, fertile, and good at bringing up children, or, as Strabo says, happy in bearing and raising them. Plutarch, in the eighth book of the Table-Talk, reports that these women, bathing together with their children, brought pots of porridge into the baths.

units.la: Fuit & Gallis usitata more reliquarũ Gentium Servitus. Plerique,ait Cæsar lib. vi, quum aut ære alieno, aut magnitudine Tributorum, aut injuria Potentiorum premuntur, sese in Servitutem dicant Nobilibus; in hos eadem omnino sunt jura, quæ Dominis in Servos. Tractabantur tamen humanius liberaliusque, quam apud Romanos. Domini namq; Galli suos obæratos, atque, ut Cæsar voce Gallica appellat, Ambactos, honoris quodam loco circum se habebant, eorumq; opera in bellis utebantur. Huc spectare videtur illud Diodori, memoriæ mandatis, Gallos Custodes Corporis ex liberis hominibus Pauperes eligere solitos,qui & pro Aurugis in pugna serviant,& ferant scutum.
units.tr: The Gauls also had slavery, as is common among other nations. Caesar, in the sixth book, says: "Most of them, when they are oppressed by debt, or by the size of tributes, or by the wrongs of the powerful, bind themselves in servitude to the nobles; the nobles have over these exactly the same rights that masters have over slaves." Yet they were treated more humanely and liberally than among the Romans. For the Gallic lords kept their indebted men, whom Caesar calls by the Gallic word Ambacti, about them as a kind of honourable retinue, and used their services in wars. Diodorus's remark, which has been recorded in memory, seems to refer to this: that the Gauls were accustomed to choose as the bodyguards of their persons poor men from the free-born, who both served as attendants in battle and carried shields.

units.la: Domicilia, teste Cæsare, plerumque in Silvis, aut circa Flumina, æstus vitandi causa; eaque ex scandulis robustis aut stramentis, Vitruvio; e tabula & Cratibus rotunda testudinumque instar construere, magno impositio fastigio, tradit Strabo; stipula vero tegere, Plinius. Horum lanuas numquam claudebant, nisi fallat apud Stobæum Nicolaus. Hypocaustorum usum habuisse, documento est historiola Iuliani Imper. in Misopogone.
units.tr: According to Caesar, their dwellings were mostly in the woods or near rivers, to avoid the heat. Vitruvius says they were built of sturdy shingles or straw; Strabo reports that they were built of boards and wicker in a round shape like tortoise shells, with a high roof placed on top; Pliny says they were covered with straw. Nicolaus, in Stobaeus, says that they never shut their doors, unless he is mistaken. That they had the use of hypocausts (heated rooms) is shown by the short account of the Emperor Julian in the Misopogon.

units.la: Quod ad Vestitum, Saga ferebant, notante Strabone; eaque densa ex Lana texebant, Lanas (λαίνας, χλαίνας malunt alij, vide cap. xv) vocantes. Hujusmodi Saga scribit Plinius lib. viii. cap. xlviii Scutulis dividere Gallos instituisse. Quæ Plinio Scutulæ, Diodoro sunt σκυτάλια. Ait enim Gallos Sagula (βαβδωτα) gestare, σκυταλίσις πολυαντοι και πυκνας διαμυσμα, quadris & maculis quibusdam reticulate distincta. Nihil aliud intelligunt illi per Scutulas & πλαδία, ut in Conjecturis ad Varronem indicat Nobilissimus Vir Iosephus Scaliger, quam quas Galli hodie vocant Laufangias, quasi Laurangias, ab Lauri folio, quod habet Rhombi figuram.
units.tr: As for clothing, they wore a sagum, Strabo notes, and wove it thickly from wool, calling these garments lanae (others prefer lainai or chlainai; see chapter 15). Pliny, in book 8, chapter 48, writes that the Gauls had the custom of dividing these cloaks into scutulae. Diodorus calls what Pliny calls scutulae by the Greek name skytalia. For he says that the Gauls wear sagula [babdota], "many-coloured and closely patterned" [skytalisis polyantoi kai puknas diamysma], marked with squares and certain checks. The most distinguished man Joseph Scaliger, in his Conjectures on Varro, shows that they understand nothing else by scutulae and plagia than what the Gauls today call laufangiae, as if laurangiae, from the leaf of the laurel, because it has the figure of a rhombus.

units.la: Scutulatum igitur Sagum, reticulate distinctum, ac propterea Virgatum Virgilio: Virgatis lucent Sagulis.
units.tr: Thus the sagum that is scutulatum, checked in pattern, and for this reason called virgatum by Virgil: "They shine in striped sagula."

units.la: non purpureum, ut opinatur Servius. De Versicolore Sagulo etiam Cornelius Tacitus in Historia Augusta, de Cæcina loquens: Ornatum ipsius Municipia & Colonia in superbiam trahebant, quod versicolore Sagulo, Braccas tegmen barbarum indutus, Togatos adloqueretur. Bracis porro (quæ, quod Gallorum essent, Tegmen barbarum paulo ante Tacito) utebantur Galli circum extentis, ἀναξυρίδας περιτεταμένας, ut loquitur Strabo, vel lavis, ut Lucanus. Bracam Gallicam esse vocem indicat Diodorus: χρῶνται δὲ ἀναξυρίσιν, ὡς ἐκεῖνοι βρίκας καλοῦσιν. Bracarum,ut & Sagorum mentionem facit antiquissimus Poeta Lucilius Sat. xi. Conventus polcer! Braca, Saga, fulgere Torques Manlii.
units.tr: It is not purpureum, as Servius thinks. Cornelius Tacitus, in the Historia Augusta, speaking of Caecina, also mentions a many-coloured cloak: the municipal towns and colonies took pride in his dress, because he, wearing a many-coloured cloak and the breeches, a barbarian garment, addressed the men in togas. The Gauls used bracae (which, because they belonged to the Gauls, Tacitus had just called a barbarian garment), wearing them circum extentis, "stretched tight," as Strabo puts it (anaxyrides peritetamenas), or laxis, "loose," as Lucan says. Diodorus shows that braca is a Gallic word: "They wear anaxyrides, which those people call bricas." The very ancient poet Lucilius also mentions the bracae and the sagi in Satire 11: "A splendid assembly! Braca, saga, and the torques of Manlius shine."

units.la: Sic legendum, non Magni. Torques enim Manlii jocose dicit: quod T. Manlius, Torque Gallo detracto, Torquatus cognomen meruerit, primusque in suam familiam induxerit. Loco Tunicarum apud eundem Strabonem Vestem habent Galli Fissilem manicatam (χιτῶνας χιτωνάτας, de quibus etiam Agellius lib. vii cap. xii.) usque ad pudenda & nates demissam. Eam innuere videtur Martialis lib. i. Dimidiasque nates Gallica Palla tegit.
units.tr: One should read it thus, not Magni. For Lucilius jokingly speaks of the torque of Manlius: because Titus Manlius, having stripped the torque from a Gaul, earned the surname Torquatus and was the first to bring it into his family. In place of tunics, the Gauls, according to the same Strabo, wear a split (or slit) sleeved garment (chitones chitonatai, of which Aulus Gellius also speaks in book 7, chapter 12), let down as far as the private parts and buttocks. Martial in book 1 seems to refer to this when he says: "A Gallic cloak covers my half-buttocks."

units.la: Manet hodieque forma in illo Vestis genere, quod vulgo nobis Pallatrock, vel contracte Palt-rock. Eandem designat Aristoteles lib. vii Politic. ubi dicit Gallos breve tegumento vestiri. Idem Martialis etiam Gallorum Vestis, Bardocucullí Santonici meminit. Aliud Vestimenti genus describit Plinius: Lana, inquit, per se coacta Vestem faciunt; & si addatur Acetum, etiam ferro resistit; Gallorum, ut arbitror, Inventum.
units.tr: The form of that kind of garment remains even today, which we commonly call the pallatrock, or in shortened form palt-rock. Aristotle, in book 7 of the Politics, describes the same, where he says that the Gauls clothe themselves in a short covering. Martial also mentions the bardocucullus, a Gallic garment of the Santones. Pliny describes another kind of garment: "Wool pressed together by itself makes a garment; and if vinegar is added, it resists even iron. This is, I think, a discovery of the Gauls."

units.la: Annulis dicit uti in Digitis, nihil distinguens Diodorus; in medio tantum, Plinius natur. hist. lib. xxxiii cap. i.
units.tr: Diodorus says that they wear rings on their fingers, without distinguishing which; Pliny, in Natural History book 33, chapter 1, says they wore them only on the middle finger.

units.la: Fictilia porro in usu habebant, ut apud eumdem Diodorum legimus: densa ac floribus distincta. Coenabant sedendo omnes, non in sedibus, sed in Solo, super stratis Luporum aut Canum Pellibus (in Toris apud Strabonem, ἐν σιβάσι.) Ministrabant eis Pueri Iuniores, ætate tenera. Iuxta eos Ignes ficbant, ipsque adpositæ visebantur Ollæ, & Verua Carnibus plena; maxime suillis, tam recentibus quam salitis; sed & omnis generis Carnibus: plerumque vero Cibus erat cum Lacte, ut scribit Strabo. Audiamus hic Athenæum ex Posidonio, sic fere Latine sonantem: Celta fœno substrato Libationes propinant super ligneis mensis, à terra parum exstantibus. Panis & is pancus (Panem hunc Fermento leviorem eos facere, adnotat Plinius. Cibus est. Caro multa elixa in aqua vel super prunis aut in Ferubus assa: hanc Leonum modo; Gallos Edacitatis arguit Hieronymus adversus Vigilantium) ambalus manibus Arms integros tollunt, morsuque dilaniant; &, si quid ægrius divellatur, exiguo id cultello præcidunt. Adponunt in Convivys Pisces, qui Finitys adcolunt, Interiorisque & Exterioris maris historibus; & eos cum Sale, Aceto & Cymino (quod etiam Potioni injiciunt) assos. Convivia plures si adcœnam conveniant; in orbem considunt: In medio Præstantissimus sedes est, ejus nimirum, qui bellica dexteritate, vel nobilitate generis, vel divitiis cæteros antecellit. Qui sunt à Poculis Potum ferunt in vasis Ollæ similibus, aut fictilibus aut argenteis. Ex eadem materia sunt & Patinæ, quibus advehunt Cibaria; æneæ tamen aliquibus: nonnullis Patinarum loco, Canistra ligneaque Vitilibus contexta. Locupletes vinum bibunt ex Italia petitum, vel Massiliensium regione, & id merum, interdum Aquæ paululum affundentes: Διξκεραμα nuncupant. Sorbillant autem paulatim, ex eodem poculo, frequentius potissantes. Pocula dextra sinistraque manu puer circumfert. Hactenus ille. Sed & fruge madida Potum ad Ebrietatem fecisse, Plinius est auctor lib. xxii. cap. ult. Ex Hordeo Potum, quem Zythum appellabant, fecisse; & alium ex aqua, in qua favum Mellis laverint, Diodorus tradit. De Gallis hæc Ammianus lib. xv: Vini avidum genus, adfectans ad Vini similitudinem multiplices potus: & inter eos homines quidam, obtusis obtutate continua sensibus (quam Furoris voluntariam speciem Catoniana sententia dixerit) raptantur discursibus vagis; ut verum illud videatur, quod aut defendens Fontetum Tullius, Galli post hac diutius esse porcos; quod illi Venenum esse arbitrabantur. Humanis etiam Carnibus vesci, memorat Diodorus: ex uno fortean actu. Nam fecisse hoc eos ad Thermopylas, patet ex Pausania. De Scordiscis Gallis nihilominus legimus apud Sex. Rufum, eos ex Captivorum Capitum ossibus sanguinem aliquando bibisse humanum.
units.tr: Next, they used earthenware, as we read in the same Diodorus: thick and decorated with flower patterns. They all dined sitting, not on seats, but on the ground, on beds of wolf or dog skins (on couches, according to Strabo, en sibasi). Young boys of tender age waited on them. Fires were lit beside them, and pots were seen placed near the fires, and spits full of meat, chiefly pork, both fresh and salted, but also meat of every kind. Most often their food was with milk, as Strabo writes. Let us hear here Athenaeus, from Posidonius, which in Latin runs more or less thus: The Celts, with hay spread beneath, offer libations over wooden tables raised a little from the earth. Bread, and that a sort of pancus (Pliny notes that they make this bread lighter than with leaven; it is food), much boiled meat in water or roasted over embers or on spits, which they eat like lions; Jerome, against Vigilantius, charges the Gauls with gluttony. They take up whole pieces with their hands, and tear them with their teeth, and if something is harder to pull apart, they cut it off with a small knife. At their banquets they serve fish, which live on the coasts and in the waters of the inner and outer sea, and these they roast with salt, vinegar and cumin (which they also put into their drink). If several people gather for dinner, they sit in a circle. In the middle is the seat of the most distinguished man, namely the one who surpasses the others in warlike skill, noble birth, or riches. Those who serve the drinks carry the drink in vessels like pots, either earthenware or silver. Dishes for carrying the food are made of the same material, though for some they are bronze; for some, instead of dishes, there are baskets and wicker trays woven of wicker. The wealthy drink wine brought from Italy, or from the region of Massilia, and it is neat, sometimes with a little water poured in; they call it dixekerama. They sip it slowly from the same cup, drinking more often as they are thirsty. A boy carries the cups around, in the right hand and the left. Thus far Athenaeus. Pliny, in book 22, last chapter, also states that they made a drink to intoxication from moist grain. Diodorus records that they made a drink from barley, which they called zythos, and another from water in which they had washed honeycomb. Ammianus, in book 15, says of the Gauls: "A people greedy for wine, who seek many kinds of drinks in imitation of wine; and among them some men, their senses blunted by continual stupor (which Catonian opinion called a voluntary kind of madness), are carried off in wandering rushes," so that the saying of Tullius, defending Fonteius, seems true: "the Gauls later drank more than pigs," because they believed that to be poison. Diodorus also records that they ate human flesh, perhaps from a single act. For that they did this at Thermopylae is clear from Pausanias. Concerning the Scordisci, Gauls as well, we read in Sextus Rufus that they once drank human blood from the bones of captives' skulls.

units.la: Hospites etiam ad Epulas vocabant; &, qui essent, quaque causa venissent, post Cœnam rogabant, scribente Diodoro.
units.tr: They also invited guests to their feasts, and after dinner they asked who each one was and why he had come, as Diodorus writes.

units.la: Consueverant quoque, sumto Cibo, ad Verborum, prout Casus inferebat, concertationem surgentes, ex provocatione certare inuicem, nulla habita Vitæ cura; idque hoc modo, ut refert apud Athenæum Posidonius: Armati se invicem ad umbratilem pugnam provocant, summasque tantum manus ac gladiorum cuspides conferunt, mutuo parcentes; nonnunquam ad usque vulnera res procedit, ac tum irritati, nisi qui adsunt eos dirimant, ac inhibeant, ad mortem usque pugnantur. Priscis quoque temporibus mos apud illos fuit; ut, adpositis pecudum aribus, Femur sumeret strenuissimus; & si quis alius idsibi vindicaret, ad alterius interitum usque gladys pugnarent. Aureum Argentumve in Theatro accipiunt, aut Doliorum Vini certum numerum: & ubi jurejurando pollicitis sunt id se perpessuros, cujus causa dona acceperunt, Munera que accepta intimis & carissimis amicis dispertiri sunt; supinos se diffundunt, & in scutis jacent; adstante, qui gladio jugulum fodiat, & exsindat.
units.tr: After eating, they would rise to dispute over words, as the occasion prompted, and challenge one another to fight, paying no regard to their lives. Posidonius reports this in Athenaeus: armed men challenge each other to a sham fight, merely bringing their hands and the points of their swords together and sparing one another. Sometimes the contest goes on to wounds, and then, provoked, they fight to the death unless bystanders separate and restrain them. In earlier times there was also a custom among them: when animal shoulders were set out, the bravest man would take the thigh, and if anyone else claimed it for himself, they would fight with swords until one of them died. They receive gold or silver in the theatre, or a set number of casks of wine, and when they have sworn an oath that they will endure whatever they received the gifts for, the gifts received are shared out among their closest and dearest friends. They then lay themselves down on their backs and lie on their shields, while a man stands by with a sword to stab and cut through their throats.

units.la: In terra super strato gramine dormiunt, apud Polybium; in Ferarum autem pellibus, apud Diodorum.
units.tr: They sleep on the ground on a bed of grass, according to Polybius; but according to Diodorus, they sleep on the skins of wild beasts.

units.la: Adiuctos nare Gallos, dicit Ammianus Marcellinus lib.xxv in Iovians historia. Iumentis delectari eosdem, Cæsar est auctor in Ephemeridibus Belli Gallici.
units.tr: Ammianus Marcellinus, in book 25 of his history of Jovian, says that the Gauls were fond of the sound of... rather, that the Gauls were addicted to swimming; and Caesar is the authority that they took pleasure in beasts of burden.

units.la: In Venationibus Sagittis uti solere venenatis, apud Cornelium Celsum lego. De ijsdem ex Plinio habet Agellius; Gallos in Venatibus tingere Elleboro Sagittas, quod his icta examinata fera tenuiores ad epulas fiant: sed propter Elleboro contagium Vulnera ex Sagittis facta, circumtidere latius dicuntur. Plinius quoque Limeum herbam nominat, qua Sagittas suas in Venatu tinguat medicamento, quod Venenum Cervarium vocant. Aristoteles in Admirandis tradit, apud Celtas Venenum reperiri quod Toxicum ipsi appellant; tanta celeritate interficiens necantque, ut Venatores Celtæ, quum Cervum jaculo perculerint, festinato adcurrant, Carnemque vulneratam exsecent; ne, Veneno promeante, Animal putrefiat, alimentoque inutile reddatur. Ex Taxo Arbore hoc fieri, videtur innuere Plinius; ubi docet Taxica Venena appellata, quæ nunc Toxica dicimus, quibus Sagittæ tingantur. De Venenatis Sagittis plura me dicere memini eapite hujus libri xii.
units.tr: I read in Cornelius Celsus that they were accustomed to use poisoned arrows in hunting. Agellius has the same from Pliny: the Gauls, when hunting, dipped their arrows in hellebore, so that the game struck by them would be bled and made more tender for the feast; but, because of the contagion of the hellebore, the wounds made by the arrows are said to spread wider. Pliny also names the herb limeum, with which they dipped their arrows in a medicine for hunting, which they call deer poison. Aristotle in his Marvellous Stories reports that among the Celts there is a poison that they themselves call toxicum, which kills and destroys so quickly that Celtic hunters, when they have struck a stag with a javelin, hurry to run up and cut out the wounded flesh, so that the animal does not rot as the poison spreads and become useless as food. Pliny seems to hint that this comes from the yew tree; where he teaches that the poisons with which arrows were dipped were called taxica, which we now call toxica. I recall saying more about poisoned arrows in chapter 12 of this book.

units.la: Funera sunt Gallis magnifica & sumptuosa, inquit Cæsar; omniaque, quæ vivis cordi fuisse arbitrantur, in ignem inferunt, etiam Animalia: ac paulo supra hanc memoriam Servi & Clientes, tes, quos ab iis dilectos esse constabat, Iustis Funebribus confectis, una cremabantur. Sic Mela: Cum Mortuis cremant ac defodiunt apta viventibus olim: Negociorum ratio etiam & exactio Crediti differebatur ad Inferos. Erantque, qui se in Rogis suorum, velut una victuri, libenter immitterent. Diodorus: In defunctorum pyram Epistolas scriptas quidam conjiciunt, tamquam eas mortui sint lecturi. Increvit enim apud eos Pythagorae sententia, qua dixit, Animas hominum esse immortales (consule, quae dixi cap. xi) rursus eas, defunctis Corporibus, post certum tempus in alia Corpora reversuras. Valerius Maximus lib. II cap. I. Mos Vetus Gallorum occurrit; quos memoria proditum est, Pecunias mutuas, quae his apud Inferos redderentur, dare solitos: sed Philosophiam Foeneratoriam idem hanc vocat. Non mirum autem Gallos Veteres Pythagorae sententiam fuisse amplexos; si verum, quod apud Clementem Alexandrinum prodit quidam Alexander, Pythagoram nempe Galliae adisse. Apud Virorum porro Fortium Busta abnoctare Gallos, indeque Oracula captare solitos, scribit ex Nicandro Tertullianus.
units.tr: The funerals of the Gauls are magnificent and lavish, says Caesar; and they throw into the fire everything they thought dear to the living, even animals; and a little earlier than this memory, slaves and clients whom it was known they had loved were cremated together with them once the funeral rites were completed. So Mela: They cremate and bury with the dead things once suited to the living; the reckoning of business and the collecting of debts were postponed until the next world. And there were those who gladly threw themselves onto the pyres of their kinsmen, as if they would live on together with them. Diodorus: Some throw letters written onto the pyre of the dead, as if the dead were going to read them. For the saying of Pythagoras took hold among them, that the souls of men are immortal (see what I said in chapter 11), and that after a certain time they will return, once the bodies have died, into other bodies. Valerius Maximus, book 2, chapter 1: An old custom of the Gauls comes to mind; they are recorded as having been accustomed to give loans of money, which would be repaid to them in the world below; but this same author calls it a Philosophy of Usury. It is no wonder that the ancient Gauls embraced the opinion of Pythagoras, if what Clement of Alexandria reports on the authority of a certain Alexander is true, namely that Pythagoras went to Gaul. Tertullian writes, on the authority of Nicander, that the Gauls were accustomed to spend the night among the tombs of brave men and to seek oracles there.

units.la: CAP. XV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XV.

units.la: Gallorum, cum qui olim, tum qui hodie, Lingua.
units.tr: The Language of the Gauls, both of old and of today.

units.la: MORES in Rebus Sacris & Profanis cum publice, domi militiaeque, tum privatim, depinxi: promiseram additurum me de Lingua, qualis olim; qualis hodie.
units.tr: I have described the customs of the Gauls in sacred and secular matters, both public and private, at home and in war. I promised to add something about their language, what it was in former times and what it is today.

units.la: De Veterum Gallorum Lingua, quo certi quid statuatur, notandum in primis quod Caesar scribit lib. I. de Bello Gallico, totam Galliam in tris divisam partis; earumque Unam incolere Aquitanos; Aliam, qui ipsorum lingua Celtae, Romana Galli appellantur; Tertiam Belgas: eos omnes Lingua, Institutis, Legibus inter se differre. Quod in Lingua discrimen illud fuerit, an in Dialectis solum, an in tota Lingua, ut ea alia fuerit Aquitanis, alia Celtis, alia Belgis, nemo adhuc, quod ego quidem sciam, diffinite aperuit. Nam in re tam obscura tamque ab aevo nostro remota, quis certi quid & explorati statuerit? Si quis Conjecturis potest esse locus, Ego infimi in Rep. litteraria subsellij Senator sic censeo: Unum antiquissimis temporibus per totam Galliam fuisse Idioma, id nimirum, quo hodieque Britanni, Celticae ad Oceanum populi, quoque Coloni ab Gallis in adversam Insulam missi, sed ab Angelis, Germaniae gentibus, in Montana & Occidentaliora Loca compulsi, utuntur. Certe quod una eademque Gallis Britannisque Insularis (sic eos appello ad differentiam aliorum, qui in ipsis erant Gallijs ad mare, ubi & ipsorum Civitates Armoricae) Lingua fuerit, innuit satis clare Caesar; scribens moris fuisse, ut Galli, qui Druidum disciplinam diligentius cognoscere vellent; in adversam Britanniam ad Druidas proficiscerentur. Quum autem Druides libris non uterentur, sed omnia viva explicarent voce; consentaneum est, Gallos eodem, quo Britanni, usos in docendo fuisse sermone. Suffragatur Cornelius Tacitus; disertius, quod volo, adfirmans: Britannorum, inquit, & Gallorum (ille suo tempore Celtas Gallos praecipue intellegit) sermo haud multum diversus. Concedunt in hanc sententiam, quamvis ad antiquissimam illam Linguam non restringant, Beatus Rhenanus, Conradus Gesnerus, Franciscus Hotomannus, Petrus Ramus, Petrus Daniel, & alij; omniumque validissime Vir Optimus Gulielmus Cambdenus, qui in sua Britannia rem totam cum Argumentis variis illustrat, tum adducta in medium ingenti ex Grammaticorum aliorumque Scriptorum scrinijs copia Vocum, quae Gallis Britannisque deprehenduntur esse communes. Illa igitur, judicio meo, Galliae fuit antiquissima & peculiaris, congenitaque Populis, qui post Linguarum Confusionem primi Gallias occuparunt.
units.tr: As for the language of the ancient Gauls, to establish anything certain we must first note what Caesar writes in Book I of his Gallic War: all Gaul is divided into three parts, of which the Aquitani inhabit one, those who in their own tongue are called Celts and in ours Gauls another, and the Belgians the third. All of these differ from one another in language, institutions and laws. What this difference in language was, whether it lay only in dialects or in the whole language, so that Aquitanian was one thing, Celtic another and Belgian a third, no one yet, so far as I know, has clearly explained. For in a matter so obscure and so remote from our age, who could establish anything certain and proven? If conjecture has any place here, I, a senator of the lowest bench in the republic of letters, give this opinion: in the most ancient times there was one language throughout all Gaul, the same one that the Britons still use today, the Celtic peoples by the ocean, and also the colonists sent from Gaul to the opposite island, who were driven by the Angles, a German people, into the mountainous and more western regions. Certainly Caesar makes it clear enough that the Gauls and the Insular Britons (I so call them to distinguish them from the others who lived on the Gallic coast by the sea, where their Armorican states were) had one and the same language. He writes that it was the custom for Gauls who wished to learn the discipline of the Druids more carefully to go over to Britain to the Druids. Since the Druids did not use books but expounded everything by the living voice, it is consistent that the Gauls used the same speech as the Britons in teaching. Cornelius Tacitus supports this, asserting what I want more plainly: "The speech of the Britons and the Gauls (by which in his time he chiefly means the Celtic Gauls) is not much different." In this opinion agree, though they do not confine it to that most ancient language, Beatus Rhenanus, Conrad Gesner, François Hotman, Peter Ramus, Pierre Daniel and others; and most powerfully of all the excellent man William Camden, who in his Britannia illustrates the whole matter both with various arguments and with the great store of words, drawn from the chests of grammarians and other writers, which are found to be common to the Gauls and the Britons. That language, then, in my judgement, was the most ancient and peculiar to Gaul, and innate to the peoples who first occupied Gaul after the confusion of tongues.

units.la: Sed quum Gallis confinales essent versus Occasum quidem & Africum ad Pyrenaeos Hispani, versus Ortum autem & Septemtrionem ad Rhenum Germani, quumque inter conterminos facile lapsu temporis Commercia fiant Linguarum; factum est, ut paulatim extremis utrimque Gallis Vicinorum Idiomata fuerint communicata; Aquitanis quidem Hispanicum, Belgis autem Germanicum; Celtis Antiquum illud, de quo dixi, salvum & incorruptum conservantibus. Sic Caesar. tres Gallis esse coeperunt Linguæ. Cæsar lib. 1: Gallia est omnis divisa in partes tres: quarum unam incolunt Belgæ, aliam Aquitani, tertiam, qui ipsorum Lingua Celtæ, nostra Galli appellantur. Hi omnes Lingua, Institutis, Legibus inter se differunt. Differre ait omnes Linguæ. Putavi aliquando statuendas esse duas Linguas, unam quidem Aquitanorum; alteram vero Celtarum Belgarumque, sed Dialectis aliquot suis distinctam; abijsse ratus in Toto ab Celtis Belgisque Aquitanos; Celtas autem & Belgas Totum habuisse commune, sed varie inflexum & mutatum: at vero quum Cæsar Omnes nominat, Tres fuisse non difficulter tandem sum adductus.
units.tr: But since the Spanish were neighbours to the Gauls on the west and south-west towards the Pyrenees, and the Germans on the east and north towards the Rhine, and since with neighbouring peoples exchanges of language easily arise as time passes, it came about that gradually the neighbouring idioms were passed on to the outermost Gauls on each side: to the Aquitani the Spanish, to the Belgians the German; while the Celts preserved that ancient language of which I have spoken, safe and uncorrupted. So Caesar: "Gaul is all divided into three parts, of which the Belgians inhabit one, the Aquitani another, and the third are those who in their own tongue are called Celts and in ours Gauls. These all differ from one another in language, institutions and laws." He says that all differ in language. I once thought that two languages should be posited, one of the Aquitani and another of the Celts and Belgians, though divided into several dialects of their own, supposing that the Aquitani departed entirely from the Celts and Belgians, and that the Celts and Belgians had everything in common, but variously inflected and changed. But since Caesar names "all," I was not hard pressed to conclude at last that there were three.

units.la: Quum porro Aquitaniam Cæsar Oceano, Pyrenæis Montibus & Garumna Fluvio, angustioribus multo, quam sequentes Scriptores, Limitibus includat; Aquitanisque versus Africum & Occasum proxime confinales occurrant Cantabri: nulla video rationem, quur dici non possit, Aquitanos tunc temporis ea ferme usos Lingua, quam hodieque non pauci intra districtos ab Cæsare Limites communem habent cum Conregionalibus, Cantabris inquam Hispaniæ populis, antiquissimam sane & toti quondam Hispaniæ communem, ut antea docui. Illud autem eo majore adfirmare sum ausus adseveratione, quod legam apud Strabonem initio libri IV. & iterum fere circa medium, Aquitanos non modo Lingua, sed etiam corporis habitu ab natione Gallica permutatos, Hispanis magis quam Gallis fuisse similes: Τὰς Ἀκουιτανὰς, τελέως ἐξημαγμένας, ἀ τῇ γλώττῃ μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῖς σώμασιν, ἰσφρεῖς Ἴβηροι μᾶλλον, ἢ Γαλάται. Ἐξημαγμένας, inquit, differentes: innuens Aquitanos Vicinorum & mores induisse, & Linguam adsumsisse; quum antea nihil in his ab Celtis Belgisque, Fratribus quasi suis, differrent. Sic postea idem Strabo: καὶ τὰ τῶν σωμάτων καταστάσεις καὶ κατὰ τὴν γλῶτταν, ἰοίκασι δὲ μᾶλλον Ἴβηροι. Nihil puto esse clarius magisque perspicuum. Et auxit per Aquitaniam mirum in modum Linguæ Cantabricæ usus, postquam Ludovicus Karoli Magni filius Vasconcs, ferocissimos Hispaniæ populos, cum ab Majoribus, tum à se debellatos, una cum Idiomate suo Colonos eo deduxisset.
units.tr: Furthermore, since Caesar encloses Aquitania within boundaries far narrower than those of later writers, by the ocean, the Pyrenean mountains and the river Garonne, and since the Cantabrians, the nearest neighbours of the Aquitani towards the south-west, lie close by, I see no reason why it cannot be said that the Aquitani at that time used almost the same language which, even today, not a few within the limits set by Caesar share with their fellow regionals, I mean the Cantabrian peoples of Spain, a language certainly very ancient and once common to all Spain, as I taught earlier. I have dared to assert this with all the greater confidence because I read in Strabo at the beginning of Book IV, and again almost in the middle, that the Aquitani were changed from the Gallic nation not only in language but also in bodily appearance, and were more like the Spaniards than the Gauls: "The Aquitani, thoroughly civilised, differing from the Gauls not only in language but also in their bodies, are more like the Iberians than the Gauls. [Τὰς Ἀκουιτανὰς, τελέως ἐξημαγμένας, ἀ τῇ γλώττῃ μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῖς σώμασιν, ἰσφρεῖς Ἴβηροι μᾶλλον, ἢ Γαλάται. Ἐξημαγμένας]," he says, "differing," implying that the Aquitani had taken on the customs of their neighbours and adopted their language, whereas before there was nothing in them differing from the Celts and Belgians, their brothers as it were. So Strabo again later: "and in the constitution of their bodies and in their language they resemble the Iberians more. [καὶ τὰ τῶν σωμάτων καταστάσεις καὶ κατὰ τὴν γλῶτταν, ἰοίκασι δὲ μᾶλλον Ἴβηροι.]" I think nothing could be clearer or more evident. The use of the Cantabrian language also increased wonderfully throughout Aquitania after Louis, son of Charlemagne, had transplanted the Vascones, the fiercest peoples of Spain, subdued both by their ancestors and by himself, there as colonists together with their idiom.

units.la: Celtæ, qui inter Aquitanos & Belgas medij, quum vicinas non haberent aliorum Idiomatum Nationes, nulla difficultate suum illud, quod antiquissimum, totique Galliæ primo fuerat commune & proprium, retinuerunt. Quemadmodum autem Celtæ, tertia Gallorum portio, κατ' ἐξοχὴν Galli leguntur appellati, ut præter alios diserte notat Cæsar lib. 1. de bello Gallico: sic etiam Celticum Sermonem sæpe Gallicum priorum Imperatorum principatu reperio dictum, cum alibi, tum apud Lampridium in Alexandro Severo, ubi de Druide: Mulier Druias eunte exclamavit Gallico sermone: Vadas, nec Victoriam speres, nec militi tuo credas. Priorum Imperatorum principatu, addidi. Nam postea Gallicus Sermo videtur habitus Novus ille, qui ex Latino conflatus, longe diversus ab Celtico: adeo ut sensim aliud fuerit Gallice loqui, aliud Celtice. Sulpicius Severus Dialogo 1. cap ult. Tu vero (inquit Postumianus) vel Celtice, aut si mavis Gallice loquere, dummodo jam Martinum loquaris. Factum inde, ut tunc etiam in gratiam Romanorum Celticus sermo præ Gallico isto vilescit, æstimatusque fuerit horridior & incultior. Pacatus in Panegyrico Theodosij: Non esse fastidio rudem hunc & incultum Transalpini Sermonis horrorem. Irenæus in Præfatione libri 1. adversus Hæreses: Non autem exquires à nobis, qui apud Celtas commoramur, & in barbarum Sermonem plerumque avocamur, Orationis artem, quam non didicimus, &c. Hinc apud Sidonium Apollinarem Sermonis Celtici squama. Sic enim ille lib. III Epistola III ad Hecdicium: Misso isthic ob gratiam pueritiæ tuæ undique gentium confluxisse studia litterarum, tuaque Persona quondam debitum, quod Sermoni squamam (impoliatiam & horrorem) depositura Nobilitas, nunc Oratorio stilo, nunc etiam Camænalibus modis imbuebatur. Illud in te affectum principaliter universitatis accendit, quod quos olim Latinos fieri exegeras, deinceps esse Barbaros vetuisti.
units.tr: The Celts, who were in the middle between the Aquitani and the Belgians, since they had no neighbouring nations speaking other idioms, retained without any difficulty that ancient tongue which had first been common and proper to all Gaul. But just as the Celts, the third portion of the Gauls, are read to have been called "Gauls par excellence" [κατ' ἐξοχὴν Galli], as Caesar expressly notes among others in Book I of the Gallic War, so too I find the Celtic speech often called "Gallic" under the rule of the earlier emperors, both elsewhere and in Lampridius, in the life of Alexander Severus, where he speaks of a Druid: "A Druid woman, as he went, cried out in the Gallic tongue: Go, you shall not hope for victory, nor trust your soldier." I have added "under the rule of the earlier emperors," for afterwards that new "Gallic speech," formed from Latin, seems to have been regarded as something quite different from the "Celtic," so that gradually it was one thing to speak Gallic and another to speak Celtic. Sulpicius Severus, in the first Dialogue, last chapter: "But you, said Postumianus, speak either Celtic, or if you prefer Gallic, provided only you now speak of Martin." Hence it came about that then, too, out of favour to the Romans, the Celtic speech was held cheap in comparison with that Gallic, and was judged rougher and less cultivated. Pacatus in his Panegyric to Theodosius: "It is not distasteful to me, this rough and uncultivated harshness of the Transalpine speech." Irenaeus in the preface to Book I Against Heresies: "You will not seek from us, who dwell among the Celts and are for the most part drawn away into barbarous speech, the art of oratory, which we have not learned, etc." Hence in Sidonius Apollinaris: "the scale of the Celtic speech." For thus he writes in Book III, Letter III, to Hecdicius: "Since, for the favour of your boyhood, the studies of letters have flowed in from every quarter of the world, and your person was once owed to the nobility, which was about to lay aside the scale (roughness and harshness) of its speech, it was now imbued with the oratorical style, now even with the measures of the Muses. That universal affection has kindled chiefly in you, that you have forbidden those whom you had once required to become Latins to be thereafter barbarians."

units.la: Belgarum Sedes Cæsar ab Sequana Matronaque Fluviis ad Rhenum usque producit; trans Rhenum Germanos agere notat, cumque ijs Belgas adsidue bellum gerere. Quis hinc non colliget, participatam fuisse cum Belgis Galliæ Populis, Septemtrionalissimis primo, post autem sensim cum Ulterioribus versus Meridiem, postremo etiam ad Sequanam usque Matronamque, Germanorum Linguâ? Et hinc est quod D. Hieronymus notet in Alia Minore Galatas, ad quos scripsit D. Paulus, quiqué ab Gallis, præcipue Belgis, orti, i. tempore fuisse bilingues; & præter
units.tr: Caesar extends the seats of the Belgians from the Seine and the Marne to the Rhine; he notes that the Germans dwell beyond the Rhine and that the Belgians constantly wage war with them. Who from this would not conclude that the German language was shared with the peoples of Gaul who were Belgians, at first the most northerly, and afterwards gradually also with those further towards the south, and at last even as far as the Seine and the Marne? And hence it is that St Jerome notes that in Asia Minor the Galatians, to whom St Paul wrote, and who were sprung from the Gauls, especially the Belgians, were at that time bilingual; and besides...

units.la: Lingua Vetus Aquitanica eadem cum Cantabrica.
units.tr: The old Aquitanian language was the same as the Cantabrian.

units.la: Lingua Vetus Celtica eadem cum Britannica.
units.tr: The old Celtic language was the same as the British.

units.la: Lingua Vetus Belgica eadem cum Germanica [?]. praeter Sermonem Graecum, quo omnis tum Oriens loquebatur, propriam Linguam, eamdem pene cum Treviris, habuisse. Quis autem nescit Trevirorum Linguam eamdem fere cum Germanica fuisse? Quin Galli apud Iulium Caesarem referunt Belgas ab Germanis ortos, & Rhenum antiquitus traductos propter loci fertilitatem ibi consedisse; Gallosque, qui ea loca incolebant, expulisse. Innuit etiam hoc Ammianus Marcellinus, ubi Gallos ex tractibus Transrhenanis oriundos commemorat; Gallorum appellatione Belgas praecipue exaudiens.
units.tr: The old Belgic language was the same as the German [?]. Besides Greek, the common speech of the whole East at that time, they had their own language, almost the same as that of the Treveri. Yet who does not know that the language of the Treveri was nearly the same as German? Indeed the Gauls, in Julius Caesar, report that the Belgae were descended from the Germans, had crossed the Rhine in ancient times, and settled there because of the fertility of the land, and had driven out the Gauls who lived in those regions. Ammianus Marcellinus also hints at this, where he mentions the Gauls as coming from the lands beyond the Rhine, understanding the Belgae especially under the name of Gauls.

units.la: Sic igitur tres fuerunt tempore Caesaris tribus Galliae Populis Linguae; Aquitanis Cantabrica, Celtis Britannica, Belgis autem Germanica: quarum posterem calluisse, vel intellexisse saltem, priores autem, & Celticam potius quam Aquitanicam, ignorasse, sed longinqua quatuordecim annorum consuetudine addidicisse, intelligendus est apud Caesarem lib. 1. Ariovistus Germanorum Princeps.
units.tr: So in Caesar's time there were three languages of the three peoples of Gaul: the Aquitanians spoke Cantabrian, the Celts British, and the Belgae German. One should understand from Caesar, book 1, that Ariovistus, prince of the Germans, knew the last of these, or at least understood it, while the first two, and the Celtic rather than the Aquitanian, he did not know, but had learned them through a long custom of fourteen years.

units.la: Ab hac Linguarum Gallicarum Triga manavit, quod Vocum, quas Grammatici Latini aliique Scriptores Gallicas absque ulla distinctione laudant, nonnullae deprehendantur hodieque Aquitanicae quidem in Cantabrica, Celticae in Britannica, Belgicae vero in Germanica: omnes tamen sine discrimine Gallicae dictae, quod Aquitani, Celtae, Belgaeque Galliae essent populi.
units.tr: From this triad of Gallic languages came the fact that of the words which the Latin grammarians and other writers praise indiscriminately as Gallic, some are found even today: those of Aquitanian origin in Cantabrian, the Celtic in British, and the Belgic indeed in German. Yet all were called Gallic without distinction, because the Aquitanians, Celts and Belgae were peoples of Gaul.

units.la: De Aquitanicis nihil dicam, quod Cantabricum Idioma mihi parum notum. Faciant hoc alij, feliciter; quibus hanc ingredi arenam animus. Possent cum fructu voluptatesque Vasconis Galli, Cantabris Hispaniae populis confinales, eorumque nunc etiam temporis utentes Lingua, quemadmodum ex iis, quae mox sequentur, Lectoribus plenissime parebit.
units.tr: I will say nothing about the Aquitanian, since the Cantabrian idiom is little known to me. Let others do so, happily, whose spirit leads them to enter this arena. The Gauls bordering the Cantabrians, the peoples of Spain, could do so with profit and pleasure, using the language of the Vascones and the Cantabrians even now, as will fully appear to the readers from what follows.

units.la: Antiquorum Celtarum in Gallijs vocabula, cum Idiomate Britannico hoc etiam tempore consonantia, sunt, indicio CL. V. Gulielmi Cambdeni, haec fere: Divona, Deorum Fons Lingua Celtica, Ausonio sic canenti: Divona, Celtarum Lingua, Fons addite Divis.
units.tr: The words of the ancient Celts in Gaul, which still agree with the British idiom today, are, on the testimony of the most distinguished William Camden, roughly these: Divona, meaning "fountain of the gods" in the Celtic language, as Ausonius sings: Divona, the Celtic word, add "Fountain" for the Divi.

units.la: Divv Britannis, Deus; Fons Vonan; ex quibus Divonan. Scribit Nobilis. Vir Josephus Scaliger Ausonian. Lect. lib. 1. cap. xxiii, pro Divona Veteres libros habere Duionam, & hoc videri magis Gallicum; non enim à Divis dici: nam eo etiam nomine Civitatem Cadurcorum nominari & apud Ptolemaeum legi Δυίωνα. Frustra est Elias Vinetus ad Ausonium, qui censet Divonam Fontis nomen derivatum à Divis vel Diis, Latino vocabulo; addens etiam Celtarum Linguam Ausonio hic dici Romanam & Latinam, qua tunc Celtae utebantur. Iovem, qui ab Tonitru Romanis olim Tonans cognominatus, sub Taranis nomine cultum ab Gallis fuisse memoriae produnt non pauci: Iam vero Taran Britannis nihil aliud, quam Tonare. Gallos Mercurium, qui Itinerum dux habitus, sub Teutatis nomine coluisse, alibi dictum est: Britannis Divi-taith Itineris Deum sonat. Galli, inquit Polybius, milites conductitios Gessatas sua Lingua nominarunt: Servos conductitios Gneissin Britanni nunc vocant. Galli, quos Brennus in Graeciam duxit, Equestris Pugnae institutionem, quae ex tribus constabat Equis, patria voce, inquit Pausanias, Trimarcam nominarunt: Equus Marca Britannis Veteribusque Germanis. Scribit idem Pausanias Gallos Scuta patria Thireos vocasse; quae hodie etiam Britanni Tarian nominant: Θυρεὸς Scutum Graecis postea usurpatum. Covinus apud Melam Vehiculi Falcati genus, quo Britanni & Galli in praelijs utebantur: Kerrain Britannis hodieque in Vehiculo vehere. Circius vox Gallica apud Agellium Phavorino Philosopho, Ventus saevissimus à turbine ejus & vertigine: Cyrch Britannis Impetus & Violentia. Alpibus Peninis, quas apud Caesarem summas volunt Alpes, nomen inditum scribit Livius non ab Annibale Poeno; sed ab eo, quem summo sacratum vertice Penninum montani Galli nuncuparunt: Pen summitates Montium etiamnum Britannis vocantur, unde Pen-mon maur, Pendle, & Pennigent, Montes apud Britannos Insulanos edictissimi nomen invenerunt. Civitates Galliae, quae Oceanum attingunt, Aremoricas Gallorum consuetudine appellari, scribit Caesar: Britannis, quorum hae erant in Gallia Celtica Civitates, Ar-mor, ad Mare, vel supra Mare sonat. Bardocucullus Bardorum Gallicorum vestis, ut antea dixi ex Martiale: Britannis Cucul pallium. Galliae, inquit Plinius, suum genus Farris dedere, quod illi Brance vocant, apud nos Sandalum nidiitissimi generis: apud Britannos item candidissimi grani Far Guinenth-vrane nominatur; & in Norfolcia apud Anglos Branke.
units.tr: Div in British means God; fons is von or vonan, whence Divonan. The noble man Joseph Scaliger, in his Ausonian Lectures, book 1, chapter 23, writes that the old books have Duiona instead of Divona, and that this seems more Gallic; for it is not so called from the Divi. For the city of the Cadurci also bears this name, and in Ptolemy one reads Δυίωνα. Elias Vinetus, on Ausonius, is wrong, who thinks that the name of the fountain Divona is derived from the Latin word Divis or Diis, adding also that the Celtic language here is called by Ausonius Roman and Latin, which the Celts then used. Not a few authors record that Jupiter, who was called Tonans by the Romans from thunder, was worshipped by the Gauls under the name Taranis. Now Taran in British means nothing else than "to thunder". That the Gauls worshipped Mercury, who was regarded as the leader of journeys, under the name Teutates, has been said elsewhere; in British Divi-taith means "god of the journey". The Gauls, says Polybius, named their hired soldiers Gessatae in their own language; the British now call hired servants Gneissin. The Gauls whom Brennus led into Greece, says Pausanias, called the training of cavalry combat, which consisted of three horses, Trimarcia in their native tongue; marc means horse among the British and the ancient Germans. The same Pausanias writes that the Gauls called their shields thireos in their language, which the British still call tarian today; the Greek θυρεός was afterwards adopted for shield. Covinus in Mela is a kind of scythed chariot, which the British and Gauls used in battles; the British still say kerrain for carrying in a chariot. Circius is a Gallic word in Aulus Gellius, according to the philosopher Favorinus, a most violent wind from its whirling and eddying; cyrch in British means attack and violence. Livy writes that the Alpine pass Penninus, which Caesar says were the highest Alps, took its name not from the Carthaginian Hannibal, but from the god whom the mountain Gauls called Penninus, worshipped on the summit: pen, the tops of mountains, are still called by the British, whence Penmaenmawr, Pendle, and Pennigent, mountains among the British islanders, have found their most famous names. Caesar writes that the states of Gaul which touch the Ocean are called Armoricae in the custom of the Gauls; for the British, whose these states were in Celtic Gaul, ar-mor means by the sea or above the sea. Bardocucullus, a garment of the Gallic bards, as I said before from Martial: in British cucul means cloak. Gaul, says Pliny, produced its own kind of spelt, which they call brance; among us sandalum, of a very fine kind; among the British likewise the spelt of the whitest grain is called guinenth-vrane; and in Norfolk among the English branke.

units.la: Quæ Græcis Πεμπεδύλα à quinque Foliis, Pempedulan Gallis dicta docet Apuleius: Britannis Pempt quinque; Deslen folium. Petor Gallis quatuor, scilicet Festo; unde Petoritum Gallicum Vehiculum à quatuor rotis: Pedar Britannis quatuor. Gauna Gallis apud Isidorum, quod inter lignaria Instrumenta, Caustrum Latinis: Gwif Britannis. Betulla Plinio Gallica Arbor; Britannis, quibus latissime provenit. Bedu. Tripetia Gallis Sellula cripes apud Sulpitium Severum: Britannis Trabet; Inferioribus Germanicis Dry-voet, Taxea Gallis, Isidoro scribente; Lardum: Britannis idem hodie Terr. Zythum vel ζύθος Gallis apud Diodorum Siculum Potionis genus: Britannis hodie, aliisque Gallia populis Ayder. Cervisia item Gallis potus apud Plinium lib. xxii cap. xxv ex aqua frugibusque confectus. Hordeo, Avena, aliis: Keirch Britannis avena, ex qua Potum illi multis in locis conficiunt. Alijs, quæ apud Cambdenum recensendis supersedeo. Ex pauculis enim his constare quodammodo arbitror. Veteres Celtas Lingua usos, quam hodieque loquuntur Britanni, tam in Gallia Armorica, quam in adversa Insula: quum superiores aliaque multas laudent Latini Græcique Scriptores Gallicas voces, quæ, Celticæ proprie, nunc etiam in Britannico deprehenduntur esse Idiomate.
units.tr: The Gauls called what the Greeks call Pempedula, from five leaves, pempedulan, as Apuleius teaches. In British pempt is five and deslen is leaf. Petor, in Gaulish, means four, whence petoritum, a Gallic vehicle with four wheels; pedar in British means four. Gauna in Gaulish, according to Isidore, is among the wooden implements, a caustrum in Latin; gwif in British. Betulla, the birch, is a Gallic tree according to Pliny; in British bedu, where it grows most widely. Tripetia, a little stool with three feet, is cripes in Gaulish according to Sulpicius Severus; in British trabet; among the lower Germans dry-voet. Taxea in Gaulish, as Isidore writes, is lard; the British today also say terr. Zythum or ζύθος is a kind of drink in Gaulish according to Diodorus Siculus; today among the British and the other peoples of Gaul it is ayder. Cervisia, likewise a Gallic drink, according to Pliny book 22 chapter 25, is made from water and grain, from barley, oats, and other things; keirch in British is oats, from which they make drink in many places. I pass over others, which Camden lists. For I think that the matter stands to some extent on these few. The ancient Celts used the language which the Britons speak today, both in Armorican Gaul and in the opposite island, since the Latin and Greek writers, as I have said, praise many Gallic words which, being properly Celtic, are found even now in the British idiom.

units.la: Ut Aquitani Celtæ, sic Celtis succedunt Belgæ, loco tertio numerari censeriquæ inter Galliarum Populos soliti. Horum voces apud Antiquos Scriptores Germanis hodieque utitatæ, hæc cum aliis leguntur: Soldury Gallis apud Cæsarem Devoti homines: Soldenar (qui & Soudenter, Soldaet, Soudaet) hodie Inferioribus Germanis, Miles ærarius, qui alicui devotus Principi vel Reip. stipendia facit: Et quæ non natio Vocem hanc arripuit? Francis est Soldat, Italis Soldato, Hispanis Seldado. Anglis Souldier, Britannis Sowdiwr; Σιλοδωοι apud Athenæum lib. v i Ἀνσιοσοφιϛ. qui Græce ὁχωλμαιοι. Bulgæ Gallis, auctore Festo, Sacculi scortei: Inferioribus cæterisque Germanis Balgh, Scorteum, Pellis, Cutis, Venter, Stomachus: Italis etiam Bulge; Anglis Bealy & Belly: Francis item hodie Bulgete, Rusci sunt scortei. Galba Gallis præpinguis apud Suetonium in Galba cap. iii: Germanis Inferioribus Kaif homo obesus; Britannis Gaunus, prægrandis. Becco Gallis apud Suetonium Avis Rostrum: Germanis Inferioribus Bec; Britannis Pic. Rheda Gallorum vocabulum, inquit Quintilianus, ejusdem est significationis, cujus Caruca vel Currus Latinis: Rede antiquis Belgis, hodieque etiam Saxonibus & Sicambris συναξοχικὸς, Suffiamen, quo in descensu vel procursu nimio Rotæ currimum solent retineri. Essedum etiam Gallorum Vehiculum apud Belgas primo repertum, ut innuit Virgilius lib. iii Georgic. Belgica vel molli melius feret Esseda collo.
units.tr: As the Aquitanians were Celts, so the Belgae succeed the Celts, who were customarily counted among the peoples of Gaul in the third place. Words of theirs, used among the ancient writers and still used by the Germans today, are read along with others: soldury in Gaulish in Caesar means devoted men; soldenar (also soudenter, soldaet, soudaet), among the lower Germans today, a mercenary soldier who serves for pay a devoted prince or commonwealth. And what nation has not seized this word? It is soldat to the French, soldato to the Italians, soldado to the Spaniards, souldier to the English, sowdiwr to the Britons; Σιλοδωοι in Athenaeus book 6 (who in Greek are ὁχωλμαιοι). Bulgae, according to Festus, are leather bags in Gaulish; among the lower Germans and other Germans balgh: leather, skin, hide, belly, stomach; also bulge to the Italians; bealy and belly to the English; likewise today bulgete to the French; the Russians have scortei, leather. Galba in Gaulish, a very fat man, in Suetonius in Galba chapter 3; among the lower Germans kaif, an obese man; among the British gaunus, very large. Becco in Gaulish, a bird's beak, in Suetonius; among the lower Germans bec; among the British pic. Rheda, a Gallic word, says Quintilian, has the same meaning as caruca or currus in Latin; rede among the ancient Belgae and today also among the Saxons and Sicambri is the brake (the device by which the wheels of a carriage are held back on a steep descent or when running too fast). Essedum also was a Gallic vehicle, first found among the Belgae, as Virgil hints in Georgics book 3: "The Belgic chariots would bear the essedum better on a soft neck."

units.la: Persius de Cæsonia Caligulæ Principis Conjuge, Satyra vi, Essedaque, ingentesque locat Cæsonia Renos.
units.tr: Persius, on Caesonia, the wife of the emperor Caligula, Satire 6: "And Caesonia sets out chariots and great Germans."

units.la: Per Esseda Gallos, per Renos intelligit Germanos; quos in ordinem digerit Cæsonia in futurum Mariti triumphum. Essedi vel Essedia frequens mentio apud alios Scriptores.
units.tr: By essedae he means the Gauls, by reni the Germans, whom Caesonia arranges in line for her husband's future triumph. Frequent mention of essedum or essedia is made by other writers.

units.la: Eporedicas Galli apud Plinium lib. iii nat. hist. cap. xvii bonos Equorum Domitores vocant. Latent in corruptione voce mihi, Opper-Ryders; Primi Equestris militiæ, Magistri Equitum. Braca, à qua Bracata Galli, Gallorum Vestis, quæ, ut docet Diodorus, Græcis ἀναξυρίδες; Suetonius in Cæsare cap. xxc: Et illa vulgo canebantur: Gallos Cæsar in Triumphum duxit, idem in Curia Galli Bracas depositurunt, Latum Clavum sumiserunt:
units.tr: The Gauls, in Pliny natural history book 3 chapter 17, call the Eporedicae "good breakers of horses." Hidden in the corrupted word, to me it seems, is Opper-Ryders: the first masters of cavalry, the commanders of horsemen. Braca, from which the Gauls are called Bracati, a Gallic garment, which, as Diodorus teaches, the Greeks call ἀναξυρίδες [anaxyrides]; Suetonius in Caesar chapter 80: "And those verses were commonly sung: Caesar led the Gauls into triumph; in the Senate the Gauls put off their breeches and put on the broad stripe." (Ut the verses ran.)

units.la: Sic Flavius Vopiscus in Divo Aureliano: Inter hæc fuit Tetricum Chlamyde coccinea, Tunica galbina, Bracis Gallicis ornatus, adjuncto sibi Filio, quem Imperatorem in Gallia nuncupaverat: Mentio etiam apud Lampridium in Alexandro Severo, & alios: A Bracæ Bracati, id est Galli milites apud Ammianum Marcellinum lib. xvi, quorum etiam Virtus commendatur ab eodem, libro sequenti. Braca autem Broeke Inferioribus Germanis, Subligaculum, Fœmoralia: Brats etiam Britannis Veltes squalidæ & laceræ. Servius ad illud Virgilij viii Æneidos: duo quisque Alpina cornscant Gæsa manu, Scutis protecti Corpora longis,
units.tr: Thus Flavius Vopiscus, in his life of the deified Aurelian: Meanwhile Tetricus was dressed in a scarlet cloak and a yellow tunic, adorned with Gallic breeches, with his son attached to him, whom he had named Emperor in Gaul. There is also mention of them in Lampridius, in his life of Alexander Severus, and in others. Bracæ, that is, Bracati, Gallic soldiers, appear in Ammianus Marcellinus, book xvi, whose courage he also commends in the following book. Braca, however, is Broeke to the Lower Germans, meaning an undergarment or breeches; and Brats to the Britons means filthy and ragged clothing. Servius, on that line of Virgil's eighth book of the Aeneid, each of them brandishes two Alpine spears in his hand, and they protect their bodies with long shields,

units.la: Hasias, inquit, Viriles. Nam etiam Viros Fortes Galli Gæsos vocant. Vox in Inferiore Germania Bellis renata civilibus, pervolgataque & uni parti adversæ ab altera nuper per indita. Non abludit Geffatarum vox, de qua in Celticis. Diodorus auctor est Veteres Gallos Lanceas appellasse τὰς λόγχας: Vide quæ dixi cap. xii: Lancia Germanis Inferioribus; à quibus hodie etiam Francis Lance; Italis Lancia, Hispanis Lança, Anglis Launce. Ambactus Gallis apud Cæsarem Cliens; apud Ennium, ut testatur Glossarium, ἀμβάκτης: Ambachtsman Inferioribus Germanis Opifex, Manuarius mercede conductus. Delirat in hac voce Paullus Diaconus ex Festo. Benna, inquit Festus, lingua Gallica genus vehiculi: Penne Inferioribus Germanis Cista, Corbis, Arca; item Vehiculum Vimineum quadratum, duabus rotis volubile. Sparus Gallis apud Festum in Rumex teli genus: Sparre, Germanis Inferioribus Sudes.
units.tr: says: Hasias means Viriles, manly men. For the Gauls also call brave men Gæsi. The word was revived in Lower Germany in the civil wars, and it has become common, and was recently applied by one side to the opposing party. The word Geffatae, which I discuss under the Celtic words, is not far from this. Diodorus states that the ancient Gauls called lances Lanceae [τὰς λόγχας]. See what I said in chapter xii. Lancia is the word in Lower German, from which today the Franks say Lance; the Italians Lancia, the Spanish Lança, the English Launce. Ambactus in Caesar is a Gallic word for a client; in Ennius, as the Glossary attests, it is ἀμβάκτης [ambaktes]. Ambachtsman in Lower German means a craftsman, a manual labourer hired for wages. Paulus Diaconus raves about this word on the basis of Festus. Benna, says Festus, is a kind of vehicle in the Gallic language. Penne in Lower German means a chest, basket or box; also a square wicker vehicle that runs on two wheels. Sparus, in Festus, is a Gallic word for a kind of spear, the Rumex; Sparre in Lower German means a stake.

units.la: Servius rursus ad illud Virgilii xi Æneidos:
units.tr: Servius again, on that line of Virgil's eleventh book of the Aeneid:

units.la: Direptumque ab Equo dextra complectitur hostem.
units.tr: And with his right hand he seizes the enemy torn from the horse.

units.la: Hoc de Historia tractum est, inquit. Nam C. Julius Cæsar, quum dimicaret in Gallia & ab Hoste raptus, Equo ejus portaretur armatus, occurrit de Hostibus, qui eum noscet & insultans ait, Cecos Cæsar, quod Gallorum Lingua Dimitte significat; & ita factum est, ut dimitteretur. Legendum arbitror Set-af, vel ut quidam pronunciant Set-of, quod Germanis Inferioribus hodie depone, dimitte. In Servio Petri Danielis, qui nuper prodiit, legebatur non Cecos Cæsar; sed geminate, Cæsar Cæsar: in quibus, ante-capta vetere germanaque C. Litteræ ante vocales omnes indifferenter Pronunciatione, nonnihil etiam ex eadem Belgica Lingua, ingeniose potius quam vere, divinabam; sed quum satisfacere meo hic judicio nequirem, pronunciare tandem sum coactus, corrupta esse illa & deplorata apud Servium; neque de illis quidquam certi posse diffiniri. Strabo lib. iv, ἀφ' ἧς, inquit de Lana Gallorum alpera, τῆς δασέως σύγκεξφαίνεσθαι, ὡς Λάινας καλοῦσιν: ex ea densa Saga texunt, quas Lanas vocant: Reponend. χλαῖνας: Inferioribus Germanis Kleen. Lena testibus Varrone & Festo, Vestis Lanca, quæ super cetera Vestimenta imponebatur; Nonio Vestis est militaris; Ciceroni de Claris Oratoribus, Sacerdotalis, qua Flamines utebantur, quum Sacrificia facerent: Meminerunt Virgil. lib iv Æneid. & Juvenalis Sat. v. Sed aliud Latinorum Lena, meo judicio, aliud Gallorum, apud Strabonem χλαῖνα: quam tamen putam putam esse vult Græcam Isaacus Casaubonus, Vir doctissimus; dictam ᾱ ᾱ χλαίνην: χλαῖνα enim, ut & Lænam, littera una truncatam, ἱμάτιον fuisse ποχίς & χλαίνην: addens Festum quoque auctorem esse, quosdam existimasse, Lenam Græce quam χλαινίω dicunt, esse appellatam; quosdam tamen Tusce. Varro lib. iv. de LL. Operimentorum genera indicans, inter Peregrina, eaque Gallica, recensCet etiam Sagum: Quibus operiebantur, inquit, Operimenta & Pallia, Opercula dixerunt: In his multa peregrina, ut Sagum Reno Galli quid gannacumma ejus sagum & Amphimalon Græca. Corruptissima sic restituit Vir Magnus: ut Sagum, Reno, Gallica; Gaunacum majus sagum & Amph. Græca; Scio quidem Sagum apud alios etiam, ut cap. xii. notavi, vocem Gallicam centeri; sed scripserat forte vel scribere debuerat Varro de Operimentis agens, Sargum: Sargie Inferioribus Germanis hodie Lodix, Stragulum Cubiculare. Planarati Gallis apud Plinium lib. xviii nat. hist. cap. xviii, genus Aratri Rotulis instructi: Vox corrupta, quæ aliis atque aliis modis concepta legitur in exaratis manu Codicibus: eorum proxime ab vera & genuina scriptura absunt, qui Plummarat præferunt: Plinius enim vel scripserat vel scribere debuerat Ploeg-rat, quod hodie Inferioribus Germanis Aratri Rota; Superioribus Pflug-rat: Ridendi merito, qui vocem apud Plinium parum intellectam in Planetas commutandam opinantur, ut Planetas se prorsus & parum fixo judicio ostenderent. Marga Gallis Britannisque, scribente eodem Plinio, lib. xvii natur. hist. cap. vi, Terræ adeps vel Medulla; Marghel vel Merghel Inferioribus Germanis Superioribusque Creta fossilis, Terra candida Cretæ instar, stercorandis Agris serviens; Britannis Anglisque Marle; Francis Marne: Inde Marghelen ijsdem Germanis Marga stercorare agrum. Laudat & Plinius ejusdem libri cap. vii Britannorum Glisfhro-Margam, genus Terræ candidæ, Cretam fullonicam pingui terra mistam, Pabuli quam Frugum fertilitatem: quæ Gluysmarle Britannis hodie dici potest; Gluys enim illis splendidum. Morini Belgicæ populi, Paludum adcolæ: Moer & Moerland Inferioribus Germanis Palus bituminosa, Locus palustris & uliginosus. Dunum Vetere Gallorum Lingua Collis sive Mons, Clitophonte apud Plutarchum docente; unde Opida in Dunum terminata, quæ per Gallias plurima, omnia fere in Collibus & Locis editis reperiuntur sua: Duynen Inferioribus Germanis fabulosi & arenarij Montes, Oceano, ut in Hollandia Flandriaque videre est, objecti: Græcis etiam Sinus Cumuli Arenarum, qui vel in Litoribus vel in Ripis sunt, inquit, Hieronymus in cap. Iesaiahæ ix: Sic Hesychius; Οἶνος εἰ σαφὴς ἡ τὰ ἔσχατα ἡ Ψάμμος. Homerus Iliad. α.
units.tr: This is taken from history, he says. For Gaius Julius Caesar, when he was fighting in Gaul and was carried off by the enemy, was being borne away on horseback, armed, when he met one of the enemy who knew him and, mocking him, said, "Cecos Caesar," which in the Gallic language means "Let go." And so it happened that he was let go. I think it should be read Set-af, or, as some pronounce it, Set-of, which in Lower German today means put down, let go. In the Servius of Pierre Daniel, which appeared recently, the reading was not Cecos Caesar but a doubled Caesar Caesar. In these forms, since the letter C before all vowels is pronounced in the old and genuine way, I guessed somewhat, ingeniously rather than truly, at a form from the same Belgic language; but since I could not satisfy my own judgment on this, I was at last forced to conclude that the text in Servius is corrupt and hopeless, and nothing certain can be determined about it. Strabo, book iv, says of the coarse wool of the Gauls, from which, as he puts it, they weave a thick cloak which they call Lanae [ἀφ' ἧς ... ὡς Λάινας καλοῦσιν]. It should be restored to chlainas [χλαῖνας]. In Lower German it is Kleen. According to Varro and Festus, Lena is a woollen garment, which was put on over the other clothes. In Nonius it is a military garment; in Cicero's On Famous Orators it is a priestly garment worn by the flamens when they performed sacrifices. Virgil, book iv of the Aeneid, and Juvenal, satire v, mention it. But in my judgment the Latin lena is one thing and the Gallic chlaina in Strabo is another, although Isaac Casaubon, a most learned man, wishes to regard this as Greek, derived from χλαίνη [chlainē]; for chlaina, like lena, having lost one letter, was a garment [ἱμάτιον] of the kind called pochis and chlaina. He adds that Festus also says some thought lena was called in Greek what they call chlainion, though some said it was Tuscan. Varro, book iv of On the Latin Language, listing the kinds of coverings, among the foreign ones, and these Gallic, also enumerates sagum: They used coverings and cloaks, which they called opercula, he says; among these many are foreign, such as the Gallic sagum, Reno, and the gaunacum, a larger sagum, and the Greek amphimalon. The great man has restored this very corrupt passage thus: such as sagum, Reno, Gallic; gaunacum, a larger sagum, and amphimalon, Greek. I know indeed that other writers too, as I noted in chapter xii, present sagum as a Gallic word; but perhaps Varro, treating of coverings, wrote, or ought to have written, sargum. In Lower German today it is Sargie, a bed-covering or bedspread. Planarati, a Gallic word in Pliny, book xviii of the Natural History, chapter xviii, is a kind of plough fitted with wheels. It is a corrupt word, read in different forms in manuscripts. Those who prefer Plummarat come closest to the true and genuine reading. Pliny either wrote, or ought to have written, Ploeg-rat, which today in Lower German means the wheel of a plough, and in Upper German Pflug-rat. Those are rightly laughed at who think the word, little understood in Pliny, should be changed to Planetas, so that the planets appear quite unsteady and without firm judgment. Marga, according to the same Pliny, book xvii of the Natural History, chapter vi, is among the Gauls and Britons the fat or marrow of the earth. Marghel or Merghel in Lower and Upper German is a fossil chalk, a white earth like chalk, used for manuring fields; in English Marle; in French Marne. From this, the same Germans say Marghelen, to manure a field with marl. Pliny, in chapter vii of the same book, also cites the British Glisfhro-Marga, a kind of white earth, a fuller's chalk mixed with rich soil, fertile for fodder rather than for crops; in British today it can be called Gluysmarle, since gluys means shining to them. The Morini were a Belgic people living by the marshes; Moer and Moerland in Lower German mean a bituminous swamp, a marshy and boggy place. Dunum, in the ancient Gallic language, means a hill or mountain, as Clitophon teaches in Plutarch; hence the many towns in Gaul ending in -dunum, nearly all of which are found on hills and raised places. Duynen in Lower German means sandy and sandhill mountains, lying open to the ocean, as can be seen in Holland and Flanders. Among the Greeks also sinus, heaps of sand which lie either on the shores or the banks, as Jerome says on chapter ix of Isaiah. So Hesychius: Oinos, if clear, or the extremities, or sand [Οἶνος εἰ σαφὴς ἡ τὰ ἔσχατα ἡ Ψάμμος]. Homer, Iliad alpha:

units.la: ——σὺν δὲ Σῖνα ψαλάσσης.
