units.tr: —— together with the sea-sand [σὺν δὲ Σῖνα ψαλάσσης].

units.la: Cetera Celtarum Belgarumque Veterum Vocabula, quibus hodieque utuntur vel Britanni, quorum beneficio Celticum Idioma salvum permanet; vel Inferiores Germani, apud quos Belgicum illud tempore Iulij Cæsaris (quamvis paullo horridius, quam nunc) utitatum, parum abest, servatur integrum; quorumve saltem apud eosdem evidentissima exstant vestigia; ne commemorandis omnibus Lectori taedium pariam, silentio praetereo. Gallicæ item Sturpium, quæ apud Dioscoridem, Herbarumque, quæ in Marcell. Empirici libris occurrunt, Nomenclaturæ, alijs, an Aquitanicæ sint, an Celticæ, an denique Belgicæ, discutiendum relinquo.
units.tr: I pass over in silence the remaining words of the ancient Celts and Belgians, which the Britons still use today, through whose help the Celtic language remains intact, or which the Lower Germans, among whom the Belgic language in the time of Julius Caesar was in use (though a little rougher than now), have preserved nearly complete, or at least the very evident traces of which survive among them. I do not want to weary the reader by listing them all. Likewise I leave it to be discussed whether the Gallic sturpia which occur in Dioscorides, and the herbal names which occur in the books of Marcellus Empiricus, and the other names, are Aquitanian, or Celtic, or finally Belgic.

units.la: Quæ igitur antiquissimis temporibus una fuerit Gallis Lingua; quæ item tres simul, quum bellum contra eos gereret Cæsar, habemus. Sic discrepantes inter se variæ Doctorum Virorum de Vetere Gallorum, tempore Iulij Cæsaris, Lingua sententias haud difficile erit conciliare. Quidam putant, in quorum numero primas ducit Beatus Rhenanus, proprium quoddam Idioma Gallis exstitisse, nihil praeterea addentes: nonnulli disputant hodiernam Britannorum in Gallia Armorica Linguam Veterum Gallorum fuisse: Pauci Cantabricam attulerunt: Plures affirmant Germanicam; & eam præcipue, qua hodie ad Rhenum utuntur Treviri & Confinales, olim etiam Galliæ populi: Omnesque suffragia sua validis firmare nituntur rationibus. Omnes sane Veritati consentaneæ: modo Primi se patiantur adduci ad Cantabricum Idioma, quod omnium in Gallijs antiquissimum stetit: reliqui Cæsaris tempora respicientes: Secundi quidem Sententias suas restringant ad Celtas Gallos: Tertij ad Aquitanos; Quarti ad Belgas.
units.tr: What, then, was the single language of the Gauls in the most ancient times, and what three languages there were together when Caesar waged war against them, we have. Thus the differing opinions of learned men about the language of the ancient Gauls in the time of Julius Caesar will not be hard to reconcile. Some think, and among these Beatus Rhenanus leads the way, that the Gauls had a language of their own, adding nothing more. Some argue that the modern language of the Britons in Armorican Gaul was the language of the ancient Gauls. Few have brought forward the Cantabrian. Many affirm it was German, and especially that which the Treveri and their neighbours on the Rhine use today, and which the peoples of Gaul also once used. All of them strive to confirm their views with strong arguments. All are indeed consistent with truth, provided the first group allow themselves to be led to the Cantabrian idiom, which was the most ancient of all in Gaul, and the others look to the time of Caesar. The second group should restrict their views to the Celtic Gauls, the third to the Aquitanians, the fourth to the Belgians.

units.la: Quidam (inter quos primi Ægidius Schudus & Henricus Glareanus) volunt Suitensium, qui hodie Helvetiorum Sedes occupant, Sermonem esse Veterum Gallorum: at vero satis constat, ut suo loco dicetur. Suitenses hosce non esse Indigenas Gallos; quum Veteres illi Helvetij, ab Cæsare in suos Montes reclusi, postea à Quadis, (ut Eutropius ait) & Quadi ipsi tandem ab Alemannis fuerint profligati; Alemanni denique Vitis Saxonibus Agrum Helvetium, qui toties jam Dominum mutarat, cesserint; à quibus Suitenses tamquam Vitenses, quæ Beati Rhenani mens est, sunt nominati. Alij igitur quondam Helvetij, alij hodie Suitenses. Helvetij fortissimi erant Galliæ Populi; Suitenses Saxonum sunt proles. Quæ fuerit Veterum Helvetiorum Lingua, quum antiquæ Belgicæ fuerint populi, ex præcedentibus non potest non liquere. Quum autem audiamus Suitensium hodie Linguam isti haud absimilem esse, quæ per Inferiorem sonat Germaniam, quæque Belgis olim, inter quos erant Helvetij, fuit propria: facile Schudus & Glareanus, quiique ipsis suffragantur, verum dixerint, si Veteres Belgas, non autem Celtas etiam & Aquitanos, id est omnes universim & sine discrimine Gallos, velint usos Idiomate, qui hodie familiaris Suitensibus, quos Germanice loqui scimus. Belgas autem Germanicum Idioma sensim adsumsisse, antea probavi.
units.tr: Some (among whom the first are Egidius Schudus and Henricus Glareanus) want the speech of the Swiss, who now occupy the seats of the Helvetii, to be the speech of the ancient Gauls. But it is quite clear, as will be said in its place, that these Swiss are not native Gauls, since those ancient Helvetii, shut up by Caesar in their mountains, were afterwards overcome by the Quadi (as Eutropius says), and the Quadi themselves were at last routed by the Alemanni; and the Alemanni, finally, yielded the Helvetian land, which had already changed masters so often, to the Saxons, from whom the Swiss were named as the Saxons' people, the Vitenses, as Beatus Rhenanus thinks. So some were the Helvetii of old, others the Swiss today. The Helvetii were the bravest of the peoples of Gaul; the Swiss are the offspring of the Saxons. What the language of the ancient Helvetii was, since they were a Belgic people, cannot fail to be clear from what has gone before. But since we hear that the modern language of the Swiss is not unlike that spoken in Lower Germany, which was once the native tongue of the Belgians, among whom were the Helvetii, Schudus and Glareanus, and those who support them, may easily have said what is true, if they mean the Belgians only, and not the Celts and Aquitanians as well, that is, all the Gauls universally and without distinction, used the idiom which is now familiar to the Swiss, whom we know speak German. I have already shown that the Belgians gradually adopted the German idiom.

units.la: Iam Veteres Gallos Græce fuisse loquutos, probare conantur Ioachimus Perionius in Dialogis, quibus Gallicæ Græcæque Linguæ docet Cognationem, Ioannes Picardus in Celto-pædia, & alij. Argumentum sententiæ suæ firmandæ præcipuum in medium hoc adferunt: Quod Cæsar lib. vi Belli Gallici memoriæ prodat, Druides in publicis privatisque Rationibus extra suas Disciplinas (quas nefas existimabant litteris mandari) Græcis Characteribus uti solitos. Sed non sequitur: Druides uti fuerunt soliti Græcis litteris; ergo Græce sunt loquuti: & loquuti fuerint Græce Druides, qui Philosophi erant Gallorum & Sapientiæ Magistri; non inferendum statim Gallos omnes Græce fuisse loquutos. Imo habuerint cum Druidibus multi alij, non solum Galliarum Primores, verum etiam è Vulgo plurimi, Græcæ Linguæ cognitionem: an inde efficietur Græcam, non aliam, Gallis fuisse Linguam? Sic Germani Inferiores Franci esse-mus; quia plerique bilingues non solum Germanice, sed etiam Francice vel Gallo-Romanè loquimur; sed Germanice ab natura, Francice ab arte. Gallos, propriam habentes Linguam & naturalem maternamque ut vocant, φιλόπλωες reddiderat Massilia, Phocensium Colonia, clarissima Gallię Narbonensis ad Mare Mediterraneum Civitas; ὥστε καὶ τὰ συμβόλαια ἐπῆρξι χαράξι, inquit Strabo lib. iv, ut Contractus etiam & Pacta Conventa Graeco conciperent sermone. Et inde hodieque tam frequens est in Gallo-Romano Idiomate Hellenismus, cui probando singularium Libellum edidit vir doctus, cujus nomen jam non occurrit. Eodem modo evertitur aliud, quod quidam proferunt, Argumentum, ex Caesaris lib. i. de Bello Gallico, Tabulas in Castris Helvetiorum (qui, ut dixi, Galliae Veteris erant Populi) Graecis Litteris exaratas, fuisse inventas. Non negatur: At vero non inde stabilitur, Tabulas illas Graeco sermone fuisse conceptas. Aliud est Graecis litteris quid concipere; aliud Graeca Lingua. Sic Thalmud Chaldaicum Hebraeo constaret Sermone, quod Hebraicis Characteribus sit excusum. Hoc addam, esse Viros Doctos, qui putent Characteres illos, quibus Graeci utuntur, non vere Graecos esse, sed Gallicos; & ex Gallia in Graeciam, non ex Graecia in Galliam fuisse advectos; ideoque Caesarem eos appellare debuisse Gallicos, non Graecos; Graecos tamen dixisse, quum sciret Graecos iis tunc uti, ignoraret autem Graecos ab Gallis accepisse. Certe ipsorum Graecorum testimonio Characteres isti α. β. γ. & reliqui, non vere Graeci sunt, sed Barbari. Legimus enim apud Varronem lib. vii. de Lingua Latina, quum Crates Graecus Quaestionem Grammaticam in Graecia agitaret, quaereretque quur non diceretur Alpha Alphatos; Graecos alios Grammaticos respondisse, Haec non sunt Vocabula Nostra, sed penitus Barbara. Audimus hic ipsorum Graecorum Consessionem, non has ipsorum esse Litteras. Confitetur etiam in Magico Aristoteles, Philosophiam ab Celtarum Semnotheis initium cepisse, & Galliam denique Graeciae fuisse Magistram. Sed ego haec talia in medio malo relinquere, quam certi quid, quod opinione difficilius & non extra odium, diffinire. Quod prae manibus, Veteres nimirum Gallos Graecam habuisse, ut quidam volunt, propriam & maternam, ut ita loquar, congenitamque Linguam, paucissimis est enervandum.
units.tr: Joachim Périon in his Dialogues, which set out the kinship of the French and Greek languages, John Picard in his Celtopaedia, and others try to prove that the ancient Gauls once spoke Greek. The main argument they bring forward is that Caesar, in Book 6 of his Gallic War, records that the Druids, in public and private accounts outside their teachings (which they thought it wrong to commit to writing), were accustomed to use Greek letters. But it does not follow that because the Druids were in the habit of using Greek letters, they spoke Greek, and that the Druids, who were the philosophers and teachers of wisdom among the Gauls, spoke Greek, so that all the Gauls must at once be said to have spoken Greek. Indeed, many others besides the Druids had a knowledge of the Greek language, not only the chief men of Gaul but also very many of the common people. Will it be concluded from this that the language of the Gauls was Greek and no other? In the same way we Lower Germans would be French, since most of us are bilingual and speak not only German but also French or Gallo-Roman; but we speak German by nature and French by training. Massilia, the colony of the Phocaeans and the most famous city of Narbonese Gaul on the Mediterranean, made the Gauls, who had their own native and, as they say, mother tongue, "fond of seafaring" [φιλόπλοες]. So Strabo, in Book 4, says that "even their contracts and agreements were drawn up in Greek speech" [ὥστε καὶ τὰ συμβόλαια ἐπῆρξι χαράξι]. And so even today there is a very frequent Greek element in the Gallo-Roman idiom, a fact which a learned man, whose name no longer comes to mind, published a separate little book to prove. In the same way another argument, which some put forward, is overturned: from Caesar's Book 1 on the Gallic War, that tablets written in Greek letters were found in the camp of the Helvetii (who, as I have said, were peoples of ancient Gaul). It is not denied; but it does not follow from this that those tablets were composed in the Greek language. It is one thing to write something in Greek letters, another to write in the Greek language. Thus the Chaldaic Talmud is not in the Hebrew language, although it is printed in Hebrew characters. I will add this: there are learned men who think that those letters which the Greeks use are not truly Greek but Gallic, and were brought from Gaul into Greece, not from Greece into Gaul; and that therefore Caesar ought to have called them Gallic rather than Greek. Yet he called them Greek, since he knew that the Greeks then used them, but did not know that the Greeks had received them from the Gauls. Certainly, by the testimony of the Greeks themselves, those characters alpha, beta, gamma and the rest are not truly Greek but barbarian. For we read in Varro, Book 7 on the Latin language, that when Crates the Greek was debating a grammatical question in Greece and asked why Alpha was not said in the genitive as Alphatos, the other Greek grammarians answered: "These are not our words, but utterly barbarous." Here we hear the confession of the Greeks themselves, that these letters are not theirs. Aristotle also admits in his Magicus that philosophy took its beginning from the Semnothei of the Celts, and that Gaul was finally the teacher of Greece. But I prefer to leave these matters in the middle, rather than define something certain that is more difficult than opinion and not free from controversy. What is before us, namely that the ancient Gauls had Greek as their own and mother tongue, as some want, and as I may say, their native language, must be refuted in very few words.

units.la: C. Julius Caesar, ut scribitur lib. v. ad Q. Ciceronem, apud Nervios obsessum, Graecam dedit per Equitem Gallum, magnis praemiis persuasum, Epistolam; ne Consilia ipsius litteris commissa ab Gallis, intercepta Fortean Epistola, cognoscerentur: quod quur fecisset, si Eques ille Gallus, si Galli omnes Graece novissent? Et numquid hinc satis paret, Graecam Linguam Gallis non fuisse, certe Caesaris tempore, tam, ut nonnulli volunt, familiarem? Et qui in Asia Minore Galatae fuissent Bilingues, quod antea notavi ex D. Hieronymo, si Gallica (quam propriam habebant a Progenitoribus Gallis, eoque secum translatam) eadem fuisset cum Graeca, cujus usus erat in ea, quam occuparant, Regione? Quum etiam Varro scribat Massilienses Trilingues fuisse, loquutosque Latine, Graece, Gallice; Graece quidem ab natura, Latine Gallicèque ab arte: quis non videt Gallicam aliam ab Graeca fuisse? Et vero quae Cognatio cum Graeca Lingua Vocibus est Gallicis, quas ex Veteribus paullo ante laudavi Grammaticis? Nihil est, quod quis dicat Druidum nomen Graecae esse originis, innuente Plinio; & inde parere Gallicam Linguam non aliam ab Graecae fuisse: Nam Plinius ita loquitur, Videri voce usus, ut nihil adfirmet: Alioquin ex Vetere Gallica Lingua petendum esse Druidarum Etymon, alibi a me dictum.
units.tr: Gaius Julius Caesar, as is written in Book 5 to Quintus Cicero, when he was besieged among the Nervii, gave a letter in Greek to a Gallic horseman, who was persuaded by great rewards, so that his plans entrusted to the letter should not be known to the Gauls, in case the letter was intercepted. Why would he have done this if that Gallic horseman, if all the Gauls, had known Greek? And does it not follow plainly from this that Greek was not the language of the Gauls, at least in Caesar's time, however familiar it was, as some want? And if the Galatians in Asia Minor were bilingual, as I noted earlier from St Jerome, would their Gallic speech (which they had as their own from their Gallic ancestors and had carried with them there) have been the same as Greek, whose use prevailed in the region they had occupied? Since Varro also writes that the people of Massilia were trilingual and spoke Latin, Greek and Gallic, Greek by nature, Latin and Gallic by training: who does not see that Gallic was different from Greek? And indeed, what kinship with the Greek language do the Gallic words have, which I praised a little earlier from the ancient grammarians? There is nothing in the claim that someone makes that the name of the Druids is of Greek origin, relying on Pliny, and that from this it follows that the Gallic language was no different from Greek. For Pliny speaks thus: he seems to have used the word without affirming anything. Otherwise the etymology of Druids must be sought from the ancient Gallic language, as I have said elsewhere.

units.la: Tales igitur tempore Julij Caesaris erant Linguae tribus Gallijs: quae, in Provinciam ab Romanis redactae, propriam coactę fuerunt Linguas dedisceree, Romanęque loqui; positis ibidem passim Romanis non solum Legibus, verum etiam Legionibus. Forum autem Romanum Militiaque Romana Veterum Gallorum Linguas non aboleverunt quidem, sed intra multo angustiores coegerunt Limites. Sic Lingua Aquitanica, quam dixi fuisse Cantabricam, compulsa est ab sinistra Garumnae ripa versus Pyrenęos, adeo ut hodie initium sit Cantabrismo ab Suburbicariis partibus Bajonæ, Lapurdensium. Celtica, quę eadem fuit cum hodierna Britannica, in extremam Galliam abiit, quę Armorica olim, hodie Bretaigne. Belgica, quam docui fuisse Germanicam, exturbata Partibus iis, ubi hodie bona Normanniæ pars, tota Picardia, Hannonia, Artesia, magnęque Flandriæ, Brabantiæ, Limburgi, Leuceburgi, Leodiensis Tractus portione, tandem Septemtrionaliora antiquarum Sedum petiit; quum antea latius multo, quam reliquę, dominaretur; ipsiusque Celticę penitiora
units.tr: Such, therefore, were the languages of the three peoples of Gaul at the time of Julius Caesar. These, when Gaul was reduced into a province by the Romans, were compelled to unlearn their own languages and to speak Latin; and Roman laws, and indeed Roman legions, were placed everywhere there. Roman law and Roman military service did not indeed abolish the languages of the ancient Gauls, but confined them within much narrower limits. Thus the Aquitanian language, which I said was Cantabrian, was pushed from the left bank of the Garonne towards the Pyrenees, so that today Basque begins in the suburban parts of Bayonne, among the Lapurdenses. The Celtic language, which is the same as the modern British, withdrew into the furthest part of Gaul, which was once Armorica and is today Brittany. The Belgic language, which I showed to have been German, was driven out of those parts where today a large part of Normandy, all of Picardy, Hainault, Artois and a portion of great Flanders, Brabant, Limburg, Liège and the district of Luxembourg lie; and at last it sought the more northern seats of the ancient peoples, although before it had ruled much more widely than the others, and had already penetrated the inner parts of Celtic territory.

units.la: Veterū Gal. lix Linguarum Sedes ubi hodie.
units.tr: Seats of the languages of the ancient Gauls, where they are today.

units.la: Aquitanica.
units.tr: Aquitanian.

units.la: Celtica.
units.tr: Celtic.

units.la: Belgica. jam fuisset ingressa, adeo ut pellere eam & exstirpare tam feliciter nequierint Victores, ut non multæ Voces ibi remanserint, quæ hodieque Gallis in usu, augenribus earumdem numerum cum Burgundionibus, qui ex Superiore, tum Francis Sicambris, qui postea, pulsis Romanis, ex Inferiore Germania (ad Rhenum enim habitabant, ubi nunc Gelri & ipsis Conregionales) in Galliam irruperunt. Nam quis ignorat Linguæ Germanorum, Inferiorum præcipue, quodammodo peritus, voces esse Germanicas, quibus hodie Franci utuntur, innumeras, quæ ad Latinam Linguam ab Romanis invectam referri nequeunt, Radicesque omnino habent in Germanica? Pauculas tantum, docendi gratia, dabo: omnes enim colligere hoc opus, hic labor esset:
units.tr: Belgic. had already entered, so that the victors could not drive it out and root it out so successfully that many words did not remain there, which are still in use among the French today; and they increased their number with the Burgundians, who came from Upper Germany, and with the Frankish Sicambri, who afterwards, when the Romans were driven out, rushed into Gaul from Lower Germany (for they lived by the Rhine, where the Gelderlanders and their neighbours now are). For who does not know that the words of the Germans, especially of the Lower Germans, which the Franks use today, are countless, and cannot be traced back to the Latin language brought in by the Romans, and have their roots entirely in German? I will give only a few, for the sake of teaching; for to collect them all would be too great a labour here:

units.la: NOMINA.
units.tr: NAMES.
