units.la: Ab ipsdem Francis manarunt etiam Voces, Nominaque, quæ in Magus, Mundus, Ritus, Manus, Baldus, Artus & aliis modis terminantur; passim hodie per Gallias nota & usurpata, ut suis locis patebit. Et ob latissima hæc linguæ Belgicæ, id est Germanicæ, pomeria, amplissimumque ejus etiam per Celticam usum, dicendi sunt Druides optime sibi suisque rebus consuluisse, quod ab Ti. Claudio Imperatore pulsi ex Gallijs, ut memoriæ proditur, in Germaniam trans Rhenum, tamquam ad Gentem cognatam sibi & ejusdem quasi sermonis, quamvis non omnes tunc temporis, migrarint.
units.tr: From these same Franks there also came words and names that end in Magus, Mundus, Ritus, Manus, Baldus, Artus and other such endings; they are widely known and used throughout Gaul today, as will be shown in their places. And because the wide bounds of the Belgic, that is, the German, language, and its very extensive use among the Celts as well, the Druids must be said to have looked very well to themselves and their affairs. When they were driven out of Gaul by the Emperor Tiberius Claudius, as is recorded, they migrated across the Rhine into Germany, as to a kindred people who shared, as it were, the same speech, although not all of them went at that time.

units.la: Romana autem Lingua cum reliquis mista, quam initio scabra fuerit, aspera & inculta, docebunt facile Iusjuranda illa, quæ apud Nithardum Historiographum (filius hic fuit Angilberti, Karoli autem Magni Imperatoris ex Bertha filia Nepos) Historiæ de Dissensionibus Filiorum Ludovici Pii, lib. iii, præstant cum Ludovicus Rex, tum Subditi ejus. Verba Nithardi sic se habent: Quoniam Karolus quaedam Romana Lingua peroraffet, Ludovicus, quoniam major natu erat, prior hæc deinde se servaturum testatus est: Pro Dom amur & pro Xpian poblo & nostro commun salvament dist di en avant in quant des savir & podir me dunat si salvarai eo cist meon fradre Karlo & in adjudha & in cadhuna cosa si cum om per dreit son fradra salvar dist ino quid il mi altre si fazer & abludher nul plaid numquam prindrai qui meon vol cist meon fradre Karle in damno sit. Quod quum Ludovicus explesset, Karolus Tenditia lingua sic hac eadem verba est testatus: In Godes minna indwrthes rpannes folches und unser bedhero gealtnisse son thesemo dage fram ... so mir Got gewuzz et indi madh furgibit so bald ibtis an minan bruher scal inti utha zernug sosso maduo indinut luberem in nothe in nut bungnege gango themma willon imo ce scadhen uuerhen. Sacramentem autem, quod utrorumque populus, propriaque lingua testatus est, Romana lingua sic habet: Si Ludouuigs sagramer quo son fradre Karlo jurat conservat, & Karlus meos sendra de suo part si los tanir, si io returnar non lint pois ne io ne neuliciu eo returnar int pois in nulla ajudha contra Lodhuuig nun li iver. Tendisca antem lingua: Oba Karl then eid then er sineno buodher Ludhuuige gesuoz geleisit, indi Ludhuuig min herro then er imo gesuoz forbuhdhit, ob ih ina nef armuendenne mag/ noh ih/ noh thero/ noh hein thenihes iruuenden mag uuodhar Karle imo ce follus tine uuirdhit. Quibus peractis, Lodhunicus Reno tenus per Spiram, & Karolus juxta Wafagum per Vuizzumburg Warmaciam iter direxit. Sed hodie Lingua Gallo-Romana vel Francica (loquor de ea praecipue, quae in mediterranea Galliae inter Sequanam & Ligerim auditur) tam est pura, tam tersa, tantumque proximis annis ab variorum Ingeniorum cura & industria cultum ornatumque induit; ut felicitate sua & elegantia jam gravida laboret: cum aliis gentibus, tum Inferioribus Germanis tantis experta votis, ut major fere passim ipsius, quam Vernaculae Domesticeque sit usus.
units.tr: That the Roman language, mixed with the others, was at first rough, harsh and uncultivated, the oaths that Nithard the historian (he was the son of Angilbert and grandson, through his daughter Bertha, of the Emperor Charlemagne) records in the third book of his History of the Dissensions of the Sons of Louis the Pious will easily show, when both King Louis and his subjects swore them. Nithard's words run as follows: Since Charles had spoken certain things in the Roman language, Louis, as the elder, then declared that he would keep these first: "For the love of God and for the Christian people and our common salvation, from this day forward, so far as God grants me knowledge and power, I will protect this my brother Charles, both in aid and in every matter, as one rightly should protect his brother, provided he does likewise for me; and I will never make any agreement with Lothar that by my will would be to this my brother Charles's harm." When Louis had finished, Charles, in the Tudesque tongue, likewise swore these same words: "In God's love, and for the Christian people's and our common salvation, from this day, so far as God gives me knowledge and power, I will keep this my brother, and in each matter I will help him, as one rightly should help his brother, provided he does likewise for me; and I will make no agreement with Lothar which by my will would be to this my brother Louis's harm." The oath the peoples of each swore in their own tongue, the Roman language has as follows: "If Louis keeps the oath which he swears to his brother Charles, and Charles my lord, on his part, breaks it, if I cannot turn him from it, neither I nor any whom I can turn will give him any aid against Louis." In the Tudesque tongue: "If Charles keeps the oath which he swore to his brother Louis, and Louis my lord, on his part, breaks it, if I cannot turn him from it, neither I nor any whom I can turn will give him any aid against Charles." When these things were done, Louis led his army along the Rhine as far as Speyer, and Charles through Vosges, by Wissembourg, toward Worms. But today the Gallo-Roman or French language (I speak chiefly of that which is heard in the inland part of Gaul between the Seine and the Loire) is so pure, so polished, and in recent years has been so cultivated and adorned by the care and industry of many gifted men, that it labours, already rich, in its good fortune and elegance; so much so that other peoples, and the Lower Germans too, have so greatly desired it that its use is now nearly everywhere greater than that of their own native and domestic tongue.

units.la: Quod restat, quo modo Francorum universim Linguae se hodie habeant, quotque ejus species, malim, Lector, discas ex Litteris ad me Magni Scaligeri, quam aliunde. Quis enim de iis differere posset solidius? Post multa alia, In regno Franciae varia Lingua Romanensis, inquit, Idiomata sunt. Romanensis Linguae tres Propagines alibi (consulendum caput VIII Libri I hujus Partis II) ferimus, Italicum Idiotismum, Hispanicum, Gallicanum: qui Idiotismi a Latina matrice tamquam traduces producti. Romanensis igitur Idiotismus Galliae in duo summa fastigia diducitur, in Francicum & Tectosagicum, sive Provinciale. Francicus Idiotismus vulgo dicitur Langue d'Oui, alter Langue d'Oc; hoc est, Lingua, qua pro Nae aut Ita dicunt Oui aut Oc. Francicus Idiotismus est, quo Aulici & Literati utuntur, quae est hodie omnium Romanensium Linguarum excultissima, elegantissima & suavissima; & cum qua neque Italica, neque Hispanica contendere possent. Sed quia nulla est tam emendata Dialectus, cui non adiaceant Παραdiaspofai; Francici Idiotismi duae praecipue sunt Διασπορα, Walonismus & Pictonismus. Walanismo utuntur omnes Belgae, qui non Teutonizant. Itaque latissime patet, initio sumto a Leodiensibus, & desinens in finibus fere Parisiorum. Sed, ut fit, in illis nationibus, ut alia aliis depravatius loquuntur; ita alia aliis minus intelliguntur a Parisiensibus. Nam Leodiensem Rusticum, mere Materna Lingua loquentem, vix intelligat Parisiensis Opifex; quamquam eadem fere verba sunt, sed Inflexio alia, item Pronunciatio faciunt, ut alia lingua videatur, quum tamen eadem Verba sunt, his, quae diximus tantum discrepantia. Pictonismus incipit a Flumine Vigenna in finibus Turonensium; definit circiter fines Burgi Opidi in Dioecesi Burdigalensi. Inter has duas Διασποράς, & alias item longe moderatiores consistit verus & emendatus Francismus; quamquam periti negant, illam Puritatem in vulgo esse, sed in illis tantum, qui Negocia graviora tractant, & aut in Aula versantur, aut Causas agunt apud Tribunalia Regni. Idiotismus Tectosagicus latissime patet. Ejus duae sunt summae differentiae: altera continetur in Vetere Aquitania Caesaris, hoc est intra Garumnam, Pyrenaeos & Oceanum Aquitanicum. Hic Idiotismus proprie dicitur Vasconismus, multum a reliqua Parte Tectosagici Idiotismi discrepans; adeo ut neque Commercium quotidianum, neque Vicinitas, neque Flumina Pontibus juncta illam differentiam tollere potuerint. (De Vasconismo vel Novempopulanorum Lingua etiam consulenda moneo, quae idem Scaliger scribit Ausonius. Lect. lib. II. cap. VII.) Reliquae partis, quae citra Garumnam in usu est, etiam multa sunt Differentia: in quibus Lemovicismus & Petrocorismus a reliquis Idiomatibus valde alienus est. Denique in Tota Europa non invenies in tantis angustiis Finium tot Discrepantias Dialectorum. Atque haec est Romanensis Idiomatis Gallicani summa Divisio. Nam omnis Francorum Veterum ditio, hoc est Gallia, Finibus Romanorum circumscripta Reno, Oceano, Pyrenaeis, Alpibus & mari Mediterraneo, jamdudum, quum Francorum Opes vigerent, in duas partes divisa fuit in Franciam Tiotiscam vel Tioscam, id est Teutonicam & Franciam Romanam. Francia Romana incipit a Finibus Flandrorum: cujus meminit Luitprandus: Quumque, inquit, Burgundiorum Regna transiens Franciam, quam Romanam dicunt, ingredi vellet. Nimirum Franciam Romanam vocat, quae Romanensi Lingua loquitur, ut distingueret ab ea, quae Tiotisimo seu Teutonismo utitur, quae Flandros, Brabantos, Hollandos, Treveros, Colonienses, & alios Ripenses Germanos continet. Rursus praeter Romanensem Linguam duae sunt in Regno Franciae, quae nullam Cognationem, neque inter se neque cum Romanensi habent, Aremoricus Britonismus & Cantabrica Dialectus, quam Basculorum Linguam vocant. Britonismus Aremoricus est idem, cum eo, qui in Cornuballia Angliae in usu est. Nam Aremorici & Anglicani sine interventu interpretis inter se negociantur, & alter alterum intelligit; quamquam Propagines Aremoricæ à Matrice Anglicana multum degenerare iamdudum cœperint. In tribus Diœcesibus Aremoricanis, Curosopitensi, Leonensi & Trecoriensi nulla alia Lingua in usu est, præter Britonismum: In Nannetensi, Venetensi, & Briocensi utraque Dialectus locum habet, Romanismus & Britonismus. Cantabrismus incipit à Suburbicariis Partibus Baionæ Lapurdensium, & itinere sex aut septem dierum in intima Montana Hispaniæ extenditur. Galli omnes, qui ea Lingua utuntur, vocant Bascos, vel Basculos. Hispani Regionem, in qua illa Dialectus locum habet, generali nomine Bascuença vocant. Nihil barbari, aut stridoris, aut anhelitus habet. Lenissima est & suavissima: estque sine dubio vetustissima, & ante tempora Romanorum illis Finibus in usu erat. Hactenus de Francorum suorum Linguis Vir Nobilissimus, quo in his talibus nemo solertior: omnium in huiusmodi Palæstris industriam longe superans. Linguæ nunc Francicæ Specimen adscribam Puræ, quam dixi, & emendatæ.
units.tr: As to what remains, how the languages of the French in general now stand, and how many kinds of it there are, I would rather, Reader, learn this from the letters of the great Scaliger to me than from elsewhere; for who could discourse on these matters more solidly? Among many other things he writes: In the kingdom of France there are various Romance idioms. We bring forward three offshoots of the Romance language elsewhere (see chapter VIII of Book I of this Part II): the Italian idiom, the Spanish, and the Gallic; these idioms are derived from the Latin mother as offshoots. So the Romance idiom of Gaul divides into two main branches, the French and the Tectosagic, or Provençal. The French idiom is commonly called Langue d'Oui, the other Langue d'Oc; that is, the language in which they say oui or oc for yes. The French idiom is that used by courtiers and men of letters, and it is today the most cultivated, most elegant and sweetest of all the Romance languages, and neither Italian nor Spanish could rival it. But since there is no dialect so correct that it has no neighbouring parádiaspora, there are two chief diaspora of the French idiom: Walloon and Picard. All Belgians who do not speak German use Walloon. It extends very widely, beginning with the people of Liège and ending almost at the borders of the Parisians. But, as happens, among these peoples some speak more corruptly than others, and so some are less understood by the Parisians than others. For the Parisian craftsman can scarcely understand a Liège peasant who speaks purely his mother tongue; the words are almost the same, but the inflection and pronunciation make it seem another language, though the words are the same and differ only in the ways we have described. Picard begins at the river Vienne in the territory of the Tourangeaux and ends roughly at the boundaries of the town of Bourg in the diocese of Bordeaux. Between these two diaspora and others much more moderate lies the true and correct French; though the experts deny that this purity is found among the common people, but only among those who handle weightier affairs, and who either live at court or plead causes before the courts of the realm. The Tectosagic idiom extends very widely. It has two main differences: one is found in old Aquitaine of Caesar, that is, between the Garonne, the Pyrenees and the Aquitanian Ocean. This idiom is properly called Gascon, differing greatly from the rest of the Tectosagic idiom; so much so that neither daily commerce, nor neighbourhood, nor rivers spanned by bridges have been able to remove that difference. (On the Gascon or language of the Novempopulani I also advise consulting what the same Scaliger writes in his Ausonius, Lectures, book II, chapter VII.) Of the rest of the part spoken on this side of the Garonne there are also many differences; among these the Limousin and the Périgord dialects differ greatly from the other idioms. Finally, in all Europe you will not find so many differences of dialect within such narrow borders. And this is the chief division of the Gallic Romance idiom. For all the ancient territory of the French, that is, Gaul, bounded by the Romans' frontiers, the Rhine, the Ocean, the Pyrenees, the Alps and the Mediterranean, was long ago, when the power of the Franks flourished, divided into two parts: the Tiotisk or Tiois France, that is, the Teutonic, and the Romance France. Romance France begins at the borders of Flanders, as Liutprand records: And when he wished, he says, passing through the kingdoms of the Burgundians, to enter France, which they call Romance. Clearly he calls it Romance France because it speaks the Romance language, to distinguish it from that which uses Tiotisk or Teutonic, which includes the Flemings, Brabanters, Hollanders, Trevirans, Cologners and the other Rhineland Germans. Moreover, besides the Romance language there are two others in the kingdom of France which have no kinship either with each other or with Romance: the Armorican Breton and the Cantabrian dialect, which they call the language of the Basques. Armorican Breton is the same as that spoken in Cornwall in England. For the Armoricans and the English deal with each other without an interpreter, and each understands the other; though the Armorican offshoots have long since begun to degenerate greatly from the English mother. In the three Armorican dioceses of Cornouaille, Léon and Tréguier no other language is in use except Breton; in Nantes, Vannes and Saint-Brieuc both dialects are found, Romance and Breton. Cantabrian begins at the suburban parts of Bayonne among the Lapurdenses, and extends over a six or seven days' journey into the inner mountains of Spain. All the French who use this language call them Basques, or Basculi. The Spanish call the region in which that dialect is found, by the general name Vascuence. It has nothing barbarous, harsh or breathless; it is very gentle and sweet, and is without doubt most ancient, and was in use in those regions before the time of the Romans. So far concerning the languages of the French, from that most noble man, who in such matters is no more skilful than anyone, surpassing by far the diligence of all in such contests. Now I will add a specimen of the French language, of the pure and correct kind I have mentioned.

units.la: Psalmus Regis Prophetaque Davidis VI.
units.tr: The Sixth Psalm of King and Prophet David

units.la: SEIGNEVR, ne me repren point en ton ire, & ne me chastie point en ta fureur.
units.tr: O LORD, rebuke me not in thine anger, neither chasten me in thy hot displeasure.

units.la: Seigneur, ayc merci de moi, car c'est faict de moy: gueri moy Seigneur, car mes os sont estonnez.
units.tr: Have mercy upon me, O LORD, for I am weak; heal me, O LORD, for my bones are troubled. (The French here follows the sense: it is all over with me.)

units.la: MonAme aussi est grandement troublee. mais toy Seigneur, jusques à quand?
units.tr: My soul also is greatly troubled: but thou, O LORD, how long?

units.la: Seigneur retourne toy, & delivre mon Ame, & me sauve pour l'amour de ta bonté.
units.tr: Turn thee, O LORD, deliver my soul, and save me for thy goodness' sake.

units.la: Car il n'est faict nulle mention de toy en la mort, qui est ce qui te louera au sepulcre?
units.tr: For in death no one makes mention of thee; who will praise thee in the grave?

units.la: I'ay ahanné en mon gemissement: je baigne ma couche toutes les nuicts, & trempe mon lict de mes larmes.
units.tr: I have laboured in my groaning: every night I soak my bed, and drench my couch with my tears.

units.la: Mon œil est esbloui de despit; & est envielli entre tous ceux qui me travaillent.
units.tr: My eye is dazed with grief, and grown old among all who trouble me.

units.la: Retirez vous de moy vous tous ouvriers d'iniquité: Car le Seigneur ha-ouy la voix de mon pleur.
units.tr: Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity, for the LORD has heard the voice of my weeping.

units.la: Le Seigneur ha-ouy ma priere : le Seigneur recevra mon oraison.
units.tr: The LORD has heard my prayer; the LORD will receive my petition.

units.la: Tous mes ennemis seront confuz & troublez grandement: ilz s'en retourneront & seront confuz en un moment.
units.tr: All my enemies shall be confounded and greatly troubled; they shall turn back and be put to shame in a moment.

units.la: Domine ne in furore tuo arguas me, neque in ira tua corripias me.
units.tr: O LORD, rebuke me not in thy fury, neither chasten me in thine anger.

units.la: Miserere mei Domine, quoniam infirmus sum; sana me Domine, nam ossa mea sunt conturbata.
units.tr: Have mercy upon me, O LORD, for I am weak; heal me, O LORD, for my bones are troubled.

units.la: Et anima mea turbata est valde. sed tu Domine usquequo?
units.tr: My soul also is greatly troubled; but thou, O LORD, how long?

units.la: Convertere Domine, & eripe Animam meam, salvum me fac propter misericordiam tuam.
units.tr: Turn, O LORD, deliver my soul; save me for thy mercy's sake.

units.la: Quoniam non est in morte, qui memor sit tui: in Inferno autem quis confitebitur tibi?
units.tr: For in death there is none that remembers thee; and in hell who shall confess to thee?

units.la: Laboravi in gemitu meo, lavabo per singulas noctes lectum meum, lacrymis meis stratum meum rigabo.
units.tr: I am weary with my groaning; every night I wash my bed, and water my couch with my tears.

units.la: Turbatus est à furore oculus meus, inveteravi inter omnes inimicos meos.
units.tr: My eye is troubled with indignation, and has grown old among all my enemies.

units.la: Discedite à me omnes qui operamini iniquitatem: quoniam exaudivit Dominus vocem fletus mei.
units.tr: Depart from me, all you that work iniquity; for the LORD has heard the voice of my weeping.

units.la: Exaudivit Dominus deprecationem meam: Dominus Orationem meam suscepit.
units.tr: The LORD has heard my supplication; the LORD has received my prayer.

units.la: Erubescant & conturbentur vehementer omnes inimici mei; convertantur & erubescant valde velociter.
units.tr: Let all my enemies be ashamed and sore troubled; let them be turned back and be greatly ashamed, suddenly.

units.la: Oratio Dominica.
units.tr: The Lord's Prayer

units.la: NOstre Pere, qui es cieux, Ton Nom soit sanctifié: Ton Regne advienne: Ta volonté soit faicte en la Terre comme au Ciel. Donne nous aujourd'huy nostre pain quotidien. Pardonne nous nos Offenses; comme nous pardonnons à ceux, qui nous ont offensez. Et ne nous induy point en Tentation; mais delivre nous du Mal. Amen.
units.tr: Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name; thy kingdom come; thy will be done in earth as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread. Forgive us our offences, as we forgive those who have offended us. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. Amen.

units.la: PATER Nostep, qui es in Cœlis, Sanctificetur Nomen tuum. Veniat regnum tuum. Fiat voluntas tua in Terra, quemadmodum in Cœlo. Da nobis hodie nostrum Panem quotidianum. Remitte nobis Debita nostra, sicut nos remittimus nostris Debitoribus. Et ne nos inducas in Tentationem: sed libera nos à malo. Amen.
units.tr: Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done on earth, as in heaven. Give us today our daily bread. Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. Amen.

units.la: Si jam singularum Romanensis Linguæ Dialectorum, quarum antea facta mentio, Walonismi, Pictonismi, Vasconismi, Lemovicismi, & Petrocorismi specimina hic, aliisque locis aliarum, essent adscribenda; in immensum senum excresceret Volumen. Temperandum. Quum vero monuerim Britonismum & Cambrobritannicum, in Gallijs etiam usurpatos, ab Francica Romanensi Lingua prorsus esse alienos, nihilque cum ea habere commune; meum institutum suo quasi jure postulat, ut Utriusque Exemplar adponam. Prioris quidem in Oratione Dominica quemadmodum aliorum solet, & Symbolo Apostolico, ut ea mihi ab Nobilissimo Viro Iosepho Scaligero sunt communicata: Posterioris autem in Symbolo, quod idem mihi transmisit Scaliger, solus quum Oratio istius Idiomatis Dominica locum acceperit lib. II cap. VIII, ubi de Cantabrica apud Hispanos Lingua. Hoc obiter dicendum, me Orationem quoque Dominicam adscripturum istius Britonismi, cujus usus hodie apud Cambrobritannos vel Cymbræcos in Anglia: ut, quod hodie inter utrumque discrimen, ex commissione Lector cognoscat:
units.tr: If I were to set out specimens of each of the dialects of the Romance language mentioned earlier (Walloon, Picard, Gascon, Limousin and Périgord), and those of other regions here and elsewhere, the volume would swell beyond all measure. I must restrain myself. But since I have pointed out that Breton and Cambro-British, which are also used in Gaul, are wholly foreign to the Romance French language and have nothing in common with it, my plan requires, as if by its own right, that I append an example of each. Of the former, I will add the Lord's Prayer, as is customary with the others, and the Apostles' Creed, both sent to me by the most noble Joseph Scaliger. Of the latter, I will give the Creed, which Scaliger likewise sent me, since the Lord's Prayer of that language alone has already found a place in Book II, chapter VIII, where I treat of the Cantabrian language among the Spaniards. I should say in passing that I will also add the Lord's Prayer in this Breton dialect, whose use today is among the Cambro-Britons, or Welsh, in England, so that the reader may by comparison learn the present difference between the two:

units.la: Oratio Dominica,
units.tr: The Lord's Prayer,

units.la: HOs tad pehudij fu en efaou, Da hanon bezet sanctificet. Devet aornomp da rouantelaez. Da eol bezet graet en donar, eual maz ean en euf. Ro dimp bryzion hon bara pemdezuec. Pardon dimp hon pechedou, eual sua pardonomp da nep pegant ezomp offanczet. Ha nas dilaes-quet a hanomp en temptation; beguen hon dilor dyouz drouc. Rac dit ez aparebant an rouantelaez an gloar, hac an galbout da bizauyquen, Amen.
units.tr: Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done on earth as in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread. Forgive us our sins, as we forgive those who have sinned against us. Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. For thine is the kingdom, and the glory, and the power, for ever. Amen.

units.la: EIN tâd yr hvvn ydvvyt yn y nefoedd, Sanctéiddier 'dy envv. Deled dy deyrnas. Bydded dy evvyllys ar yddaiar, megis yn y nefoedd. Dyro i ni heddyvv ein bara beunyddiol. A maddeu di i ni ein dyledion, fel y maddeuom ninnau i'n dyled-vvyr. Ac nac arvvain ni i brofedigaeth; eithr gvvaret ni rhag drvvg. Canys eiddott ti yvv'r deyrnas, a'r nerth, a'r gogoni amt yn oes oesoedd, Amen.
units.tr: Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done on earth, as in heaven. Give us today our daily bread. And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever and ever. Amen.

units.la: PATER nofter, qui es in Calu, Sanctificetur nomen tuum. Veniat regnum tuum. Fiat voluntas tua in terra, quemadmodum in Cælo. Da nobis hodie panem nostrum quotidianum. Remitte nobis debita nostra, sicut nos remittimus debitoribus nostris. Et ne nos inducas in tentationem: sed libera nos à malo. Quia tuum est regnum, & potentia, & gloria, in secula, Amen.
units.tr: Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven. Give us today our daily bread. Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever. Amen.

units.la: In Aremorici exempla non pauca audimus, quæ ab Romanensi Francorum Idiomate sunt mutuata; in Cambrobritannici autem, quæ ab Anglicano: adeo nulla fere est (quod semel dicendum sæpe parebit) Lingua, quæ non ab vicinis & confinalibus, mutui Commercij beneficio & ope sibi quærat auctum & incrementum. Docet idipsum Symbolum Apostolicum, quo utuntur Britones Aremorici;
units.tr: In the Armorican examples we find not a few that have been borrowed from the Romance French idiom, and in the Cambro-British, those borrowed from English. So there is almost no language (as will often appear, once said) that does not seek growth and increase for itself from its neighbours and borderers, by the benefit and help of mutual commerce. The Apostles' Creed itself shows the same, which the Armorican Britons use;

units.la: Symbolum Apostolicum.
units.tr: The Apostles' Creed.

units.la: BRITANNICE apud Aremoricos.
units.tr: In the Breton language, among the Armoricans.

units.la: MEA cret en doue ad tad hollgalloudec, Crouer an euf, hac an douar: hac e Iesu Christ e map unic hou aoutro: Pchuny son conceuet dre an sperct glan: ha ganet eux an guerches Mary en deueux, gonzauet dydan Pócz Pilat, crucifiet, marou, ha sebelyet: so bezet disquennet dan yfernou: an trede deiz ez eou dazforchet a marou: hac ez eou pignet en efaou: hac asezet en tu de hou da doue an tad hollgalloudec. A hanc e deuhy da barn an beou, hac an marou. Mea cret en sperct glan; en ylys universal; communion an sent; Remission an pechedou; dazsotchen an quyc; hac an buhez aeternal.
units.tr: I believe in God the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth; and in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord; who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died and was buried; he descended into hell; on the third day he rose again from the dead; he ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of God the Father almighty; from there he will come to judge the living and the dead. I believe in the Holy Spirit; in the universal Church; the communion of saints; the forgiveness of sins; the resurrection of the flesh; and eternal life.

units.la: CREDO in Deum patrem omnipotentem, (creatorem cæli & terræ; Et in Iesum Christum, Filium ejus unicum, Dominum nostrum: Qui conceptus est de Spiritu Sancto: natus ex Maria Virgine; Passus sub Pontio Pilato, crucifixus, mortuus & sepultus: Descendit ad Inferos: tertia die resurrexit à mortuis: ascendit in Cælum: Sedet ad dextram Dei Patris omnipotentis: Et inde venturus ad judicandum vivos & mortuos. Credo in Spiritum Sanctum, Ecclesiam universalem; Communionem Sanctorum, Remissionem Peccatorum; carnis resurrectionem: Et vitam æternam.
units.tr: I believe in God the Father almighty, creator of heaven and earth; and in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord: who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died and was buried; he descended into hell; the third day he rose again from the dead; he ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of God the Father almighty; from there he will come to judge the living and the dead. I believe in the Holy Spirit, the universal Church, the communion of saints, the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the flesh, and eternal life.

units.la: Sequitur iam Cantabrismi.
units.tr: Now follows the Cantabrian version.

units.la: Symbolum Apostolicum.
units.tr: The Apostles' Creed.

units.la: CANTABRICE.
units.tr: In Cantabrian.

units.la: SINHESTEN dut Iainco Aita bothere gucitaco cervaren, eta lurraren creaçalea baithan. Eta Iesus Christ haren seme bakoitz gure Iauna baithan: cein concebiru içan baita Spiritu sainduaganic: Sortu Maria virginaganic: Pontio Pilateren az pian passionatu, crucifiatu, hil eta ohortze: Iautsi içan da iffernetuara: Hereneco egunean resuscitatu icanda hiletaric: Igan içan da ceruëtera: Iarria da Iainco Aita bothere-gucitacoaren escuinean: Handic ethorteco da vicien eta hilen iugeatzera.
units.tr: I believe in God the Father almighty, Creator of heaven and earth. And in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord: who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died and was buried. He descended into hell; on the third day he rose again from the dead; he ascended into heaven; he sits at the right hand of God the Father almighty; from thence he shall come to judge the living and the dead.

units.la: CREDO in Deum patrem omnipotentem, Creatorem (caeli & Terræ. Et in Iesum Christum Filium ejus unicum, Dominum nostrum: qui conceptus est de Spiritu Sancto: Natus ex Maria Virgine: Passus sub Pontio Pilato, crucifixus, mortuus & sepultus: Descendit ad inferos: tertia die resurrexit ex mortuis: ascendit in cœlum: sedet ad dexteram Dei Patris omnipotentis: Inde venturus ad judicandum vivos & mortuos.
units.tr: I believe in God the Father almighty, Creator of heaven and earth. And in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord: who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, dead and buried. He descended into hell; the third day he rose again from the dead; he ascended into heaven; he sits at the right hand of God the Father almighty; from thence he shall come to judge the living and the dead.

units.la: Sinheften dut Spiritu Saindua baithan: Sinheften dut Elica saindu Catholicoa: Sainduen communionea: Bekatuén barkamendua; Haraguiaren resurrectionea; Vicitze eternala. Amen.
units.tr: I believe in the Holy Spirit; I believe the holy Catholic Church; the communion of saints; the forgiveness of sins; the resurrection of the flesh; life everlasting. Amen.

units.la: CREDO in Spiritum Sanctum: Credo Sanctam Ecclesiam Catholicam; Sanctorum communionem; Remissionem Peccatorum; Carnis resurrectionem; Vitam aeternam. Amen.
units.tr: I believe in the Holy Spirit: I believe the holy Catholic Church; the communion of saints; the forgiveness of sins; the resurrection of the flesh; eternal life. Amen.

units.la: Et hic, qui Francicam novit Linguam, multas ejus audit Voces ad Cantabrismum inflexas.
units.tr: And here, anyone who knows the French language hears many of its words bent into Cantabrian forms.

units.la: CAP. XVI.
units.tr: Chapter 16.

units.la: Gubernatio Galliarum Prisca tam in Sacris, quam Profanis.
units.tr: The government of the Gauls, ancient, both in sacred and in secular matters.

units.la: SED de Moribus Linguisque Gallorum hactenus; flagitat ordo, ut Gubernationem, cum quae olim in rebus & Sacris & Profanis fuerit, tum quae hodie est utrimque, explicemus.
units.tr: But so much for the customs and languages of the Gauls; the order of the work now requires that we explain their government, both that which once existed in affairs both sacred and secular, and that which exists today on both fronts.

units.la: Fuit Galliae, saltem Comatae, quum in eam C. Iulius Caesar veniret, Respublica, genere ipso Timocratica, Romanae Libertatis multis partibus simillima. Caesar lib. vi. de Bello Gallico, duo Magistratus apud Veteres Gallos genera proponit; alterum Divinis, alterum Humanis & Civilibus Rebus praepositum. Divinis praefecti erant Druides, de quibus abunde cap. xi; ubi, praeeunte verba Caesare, didicimus eos Sacrificijs peragundis, Controversijs audiundis decidendisque, Artibus denique & Scientijs publice explicandis illustrandisque praefuisse, hasque ob res maxima ijs statuta fuisse Praemia, Privilegia, & quasi Minervalia, ingentemque eisdem ab omnibus honorem haberi solitum.
units.tr: When Gaius Julius Caesar came into Gaul, at least into Gallia Comata, there was a commonwealth there, timocratic in kind and very like Roman liberty in many respects. In book VI of his Gallic War, Caesar sets out two kinds of magistrates among the ancient Gauls: one set over divine affairs, the other over human and civil affairs. Over divine affairs were the Druids, of whom I shall say more in chapter XI. There, following Caesar's words, we learned that they presided over the performance of sacrifices, the hearing and settling of disputes, and finally the public teaching and cultivation of the arts and sciences. For these services very great rewards, privileges, and what were like scholarship payments were established for them, and all were accustomed to show them great honour.

units.la: In Druidibus igitur prius erat Magistratus veteris Gallicae Reip. membrum: secundum Principum genus, secundumque Reip. gradus erat in Equitibus; unde belli gerendi Principes a Populo pro ipsius arbitrio commodoque deligebantur; ac, si contra facerent, abdicare cogebantur. Caesar, qui saepe hic laudandus, lib. vi; In Gallia, inquit, non solum in omnibus Civitatibus, atque in omnibus Pagis Partibusque, sed pene etiam in singulis Domibus Factiones sunt, earumque Factionum Principes sunt, qui summam auctoritatem eorum judicio habere existimantur, quorum ad arbitrium judiciumque Summa omnium rerum Consiliorumque redeat. Id ejus rei causa antiquitus institutum videtur, ne quis ex Plebe contra Potentiorem auxilij egeret. Suos enim quisque opprimi & circumveniri non patitur; neque, aliter si faciat, ullam inter suos habet auctoritatem: hac eadem ratio est in summa totius Gallia. Sic Caesar: qui satis clare docet Statum Reip. Veterum Gallorum Timocraticum fuisse.
units.tr: Among the Druids, then, the magistracy was the first part of the ancient Gallic commonwealth. The second rank of the princely class, and the second grade of the commonwealth, was that of the knights. From them the leaders in war were chosen by the people according to its own judgement and advantage; and if they acted contrary to this, they were forced to stand down. Caesar, whom I often praise here, says in book VI: "In Gaul, not only in all the states and in all the districts and divisions, but almost in every single household too, there are factions, and the leaders of these factions are thought to hold the highest authority in their judgement, and the decision and judgement of these men determine the sum of all affairs and plans. This seems to have been instituted long ago for this reason: that no one of the common people should lack help against a more powerful man. For each man does not allow his own people to be oppressed and circumvented; and if he did otherwise, he would have no authority among his own. The same reasoning holds for all of Gaul as a whole." Thus Caesar, who teaches clearly enough that the state of the ancient Gauls was timocratic.

units.la: Iterum Caesar: Tanta Galliae libertas fuit, ut in singulis Civitatibus, singulis etiam Pagis, ac pene etiam Domibus suae Factiones essent; tam libera nempe Suffragiorum ac studiorum cuique potestas erat, ut vel infimis libere ac sine ullo metu Sententiae dicendae Suffragyque ferendi facultas esset. Electores igitur Magistratuum Gallicorum tales erant: unde intelligimus etiam Plebis in Rep. permagnam fuisse auctoritatem; quum Populi suffragijs Magistratus instituerentur. Singularis autem, an multiplex Principatus hic esset, quove temporeditinitus, Caesar non addit: aperit utrumque Strabo lib. ix: Α'ξιοποιητικὰ ... Strabonis haec illustriora faciunt Exempla, cum Commune totius Galliae, quod de lecto Vercingetorige deferibitur ab Caesare lib. vii, tum Singularia, quae suis a me ponentur locis, de Massiliensibus, origine tamen Graecis; item de Belgis, Aremoricis Civitatibus in Celtica, & Aquitanis: specialius denique de Heduis, Arvernis, Senonibus, Parisijs, Carnutibus, Remis, Suessionibus, Bellovacis, Nervijs, Atrebatibus, Eburonibus, Morinis, Treviris & Sontiatibus.
units.tr: Caesar again: "Gaul enjoyed such liberty that in each state, in each district, and almost in each household there were factions of their own; the power of voting and of pursuing one's inclinations was so free that even the lowest could give an opinion and cast a vote freely and without any fear." The electors of Gallic magistrates were therefore of this sort, and from this we understand that the common people also had very great authority in the commonwealth, since magistrates were appointed by the votes of the people. Whether this principate was held by one man or by several, or for what term it was limited, Caesar does not add. Strabo, in book IX, makes both clear: [Α'ξιοποιητικὰ ...]. Strabo's account is made clearer by examples: the common (leadership) of all Gaul, which Caesar describes in book VII as chosen for Vercingetorix; and particular examples, which I shall set out in their places, concerning the Massiliots, who were however of Greek origin; likewise concerning the Belgians, the Armorican states among the Celts, and the Aquitanians; and finally, more particularly, concerning the Aedui, Arverni, Senones, Parisii, Carnutes, Remi, Suessiones, Bellovaci, Nervii, Atrebates, Eburones, Morini, Treveri and Sontiates.

units.la: Hoc ad Veterum Gallorum laudem magnopere pertinet, quod Puerorum Imperia ferre non possent, & Principes requirerent constantes. Probat prius Trebellius Pollio in Vita Postumi 11 Triginta Tyrannorum: Hic vir, in Bello fortissimus, in Pace constantissimus, in omni Vita gravis; usque adeo, ut Saloninum filium suum eidem Gallieno in Gallia positum crederet, quasi custodi Vita. Vitæ & Morum & Artium Imperialium Institutori. Sed, quamtum plerique adferunt (quod ejus non convenit moribus) positea fidem fregit & occiso Salonino, sumpsit Imperium: ut autem verius plerique tradiderunt, quum Galli vehementissime Gallienum odissent, Puerum autem apud se imperare ferre non possent, eum, qui commissum regebat Imperium, Imperatorem appellarunt, missisque militibus Adolescentem interfecerunt. Utrumque autem Flavius Vopiscus in Caro: Ut dicitur quidem, ait, sæpe dixisse se miserum, quod Carinum ad Gallias Principem misteret; neque illa atas esset Numeriani, ut illi Gallicanum, quod maxime constantem Principem quærit, crederetur Imperium. Ad continuandam autem Gallorum Veterum Timocratiam, de Equitibus, quorum antea memini, sic pergit Cæsar: Atque Equites, quum est ipsus atque aliquod bellum incidit, omnes in bello versantur, atque eorum ut quisque est genere copiisque amplissimus, ita plurimos circum se Ambactos Clientesque habet: hanc unam gratiam potentiamque noverunt. Ambacti, ut antea dixi, obærati erant, ideoque in servitutem Equitibus ipsis addicti. Clientibus autem, ut est libro VII, nefas erat vel in extrema fortuna deserere Patronos. Sed de Timocratico Veteris Galliæ Magistratio Principatuque latis: quem cum Toti, tum singulis Partibus saluum stetisse docent Historiæ, donec in potestatem Romanorum Galli (de iis loquor hic, qui Romanis erant Trans-Alpini,) fuerunt redacti: quod his quasi gradibus factum.
units.tr: This redounds greatly to the praise of the ancient Gauls, that they could not bear the commands of boys and required steady princes. Trebellius Pollio shows this first, in the Life of Postumus among the Thirty Tyrants: "This man was most brave in war, most steady in peace, and grave in his whole life; so much so that he thought his son Saloninus, placed in Gaul under Gallienus himself, was a guardian of life, the teacher of life, manners and imperial arts. But, as most writers report (which did not accord with his character), he later broke faith and, Saloninus having been killed, took the empire. Yet, as most have truly handed down, when the Gauls most vehemently hated Gallienus, and could not bear a boy ruling over them, they called the man who held the entrusted empire emperor, and sent soldiers who killed the young man." Flavius Vopiscus also says both things in the Life of Carus: "It is said, he tells us, that he often said he was wretched, because he sent Carinus as prince to the Gauls; nor was Numerian's age such that the Gallic empire, which seeks a most steady prince, could be entrusted to him." To continue the timocracy of the ancient Gauls, Caesar continues about the knights, whom I mentioned before: "And the knights, whenever a war breaks out, are all engaged in it; and each has as many clients and dependants around him as he is most distinguished in birth and resources. They know only this one kind of favour and power." The ambacti, as I said before, were men in debt, and so had been handed over into servitude to the knights themselves. As for the clients, as is said in book VII, it was wrong to desert their patrons even in the worst fortune. But enough about the timocratic magistracy and principate of ancient Gaul. History shows that it stood safe both in the whole and in its separate parts, until the Gauls (I speak here of those who were Transalpine and under the Romans) were brought into the power of the Romans; and this was done by a sort of steps.

units.la: M. Plautio Hypsæo & M. Fulvio Flacco Coss. ab v. c. CCXXVIII primum cum Gallis trans Alpes dimicatum est. Auctores belli fuerunt Salyes, quum Massiliensium, Sociorum Populi Romani, fines invaderent. Salybus accesserunt Arverni, Ruteni & Allobroges; quibus quadriennij spatio subactis Bellum finitum est, quod a Principe facile populo Allobrogicum est appellatum. Res deinde adversus eosdem prospere, Bituito etiam Hostium rege capto, gesserunt Imperatores Romani, M. Fulvius Flaccus anno Iocxxix, C. Sextius Calvinus anno Iocxxx, & seq. Cn. Domitius Ahenobarbus anno Iocxxxii. & Q. Fabius Maximus, qui postea Allobrogicus dictus est, anno Iocxxxiii; de quorum rebus gestis & triumphis legendi Florus lib. III. histor. Romanæ, cap. II, & in Epitom. LX, Strabo lib. IV. Orosius lib. V. cap. XVI, Plinius lib. VII. nat. hist. cap. XXV, Appianus in Celtico, Velleius Paterculus vol. II, Ammianus Marcellinus lib. XV, Cæsar lib. I. de Bello Gallic. Eutropius lib. V, Iustinus lib. XXXVII, & alij. Sic eo bello Gallia Narbonensis in Provinciæ formam fuit redacta, atque, ut quotannis in eam Prætores mitterentur, institutum. Videndus Auctor I. 2. D. de orig. juris; legendaque Critognati Arverni apud Cæsarem Oratio lib. VII, qui de hac Narbonensi Gallia sic inter alia: Quod si ea, quæ in longinquis Regionibus geruntur, ignoratis; respicite finitimam Galliam, quæ in Provinciam redacta, Iure & Legibus commutatis, securibus subjecta, perpetua premitur servitute. Post Allobrogicum aliquot Romani Duces de ipsdem Gallis, & præsertim Alpinis, tumultuantibus & victis triumpharunt. Postremo eam C. Marius ab impetu Cimbrorum Teutonorumque (qui ex veteri Germania, cujus erant, ut alibi doceo, Populi, in extremas ad Oceanum Belgicæ Galliæ, ubi nunc Flandria, terras quondam transgressi, indeque facta in pen itiorem Galliam irruptione, adjunctis sibi Ambronibus & Tigurinis, Gallicis Nationibus, per Narbonensem Provinciam & Alpes Cottias Italiam occupare, Romanumque Imperium concutere statuerant: quia de re Plutarch. in Mario, & alij quarto Consulatu, anno ab v. c. DCLII egregie defendit; atque, Cimbris, reliquisque, cum alibi, tum ad Aquas Sextias cæsis, pacem & quietem ejus conservavit. C. Pontinius Allobroges etiam tumultuantes compescuit, deque ijs triumphavit anno v. c. 1ocxcix. Quam postremo Provinciam quum Cæsar L. Calpurnio Pisone & A. Gabinio Coss. anno ab v. c. 1ocxcv obtinuisset, elferis & fortissimis Gentibus variè lacessitis, novem annis, quibus in Imperio fuit, omnem Galliam, quæ à Saltu Pyrenæo, Alpibus, & monte Gebenna, fluminibusque Reno & Rodano continetur, patetque circuitu ad bis & tricies centum millia passuum, præter socias ac bene meritas Civitates, in Provinciæ formam redegit; eique in singulos annos Stipendij nomen imposuit. De quibus omnibus plenè ipse Cæsar, sive qui alius Auctor habendus, in Ephemeridum libris VII. Suetonius & Plutarchus in ejus Vita variis locis, Florus lib. III. cap. X. & Epitom. CIII & seqq. Appianus in Celtico, Lucanus lib. I belli Pharsalici, Eutropius, Orosius, & alij. Paucis, quæ dixi, Velleius: Gallias, inquit, quit, primum Domitio & Fabio nepoti Paulli, qui Allobrogicus appellatus est. intrat as cum exercitu, magna mox clade nostra saepe & adfectavimus & amisimus: sed fulgentissimum C. Caesaris opus in his conspicitur: quippe ejus ductu auspiciisque infracta pene, idem, quod totus Terrarum orbis, ignavum conferunt Stipendium. Ammianus Marcellinus lib. xv. Ha Regiones, praecipue quae confines Italicis, paullatim levius odere sub Imperium venire Romanum: primo tentata per Fulvium, deinde praelis parvis quassata per Sextium; ad ultimum per Fabium Maximum domita, cui negocij plenus effectus, asperiore Allobrogum gente devicta, hoc indidit cognomentum. Nam omnes Gallias, nisi quae Paludibus inviae fuere, ut Sallustio docetur auctore, post Decennalis Belli mutuas clades Caesar Societati nostrae foederibus junxit aeternis. Rufus denique, Geterum Caesar, ait, cum decem Legionibus Gallias per annos novem subegit; cum Gallis (Germanis legendum) ultra Renum positis conflixit: ad Alpibus Britanniam usque transfivit; decimo anno Gallias & Britannias tributarias fecit.
units.tr: In the consulship of Marcus Plautius Hypsaeus and Marcus Fulvius Flaccus, in the year of the city 228, there was first fighting with the Gauls beyond the Alps. The Salyes were the originators of the war, since they invaded the territory of the Massiliots, allies of the Roman people. The Arverni, Ruteni and Allobroges joined the Salyes; when these were subdued over a period of four years, the war was ended, and from its leader it was easily called the Allobrogic War. Afterwards the Roman commanders waged successful campaigns against the same peoples, even capturing Bituitus, king of the enemy: Marcus Fulvius Flaccus in the year 629, Gaius Sextius Calvinus in the year 630 and following, Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus in the year 632, and Quintus Fabius Maximus, who was afterwards called Allobrogicus, in the year 633. Concerning their deeds and triumphs, one should read Florus, Roman History book III, chapter II, and in the Epitome LX; Strabo book IV; Orosius book V, chapter XVI; Pliny, Natural History book VII, chapter XXV; Appian in Celtica; Velleius Paterculus, volume II; Ammianus Marcellinus book XV; Caesar, Gallic War book I; Eutropius book V; Justin book XXXVII; and others. Thus in that war Gallia Narbonensis was reduced into the form of a province, and it was established that praetors be sent to it every year. See the author Digest 1.2, De origine iuris; and one should read the speech of Critognatus the Arvernian in Caesar, book VII, who says among other things about this Narbonese Gaul: "But if you are ignorant of what is done in distant regions, look to neighbouring Gaul, which has been reduced into a province, its law and rights changed, subjected to the axes, and pressed under perpetual servitude." After the Allobrogic War several Roman commanders triumphed over the same Gauls, especially the Alpine peoples, who rose in revolt and were defeated. Finally Gaius Marius saved it from the attack of the Cimbri and Teutons (who, having migrated from old Germany, of which they were peoples, as I teach elsewhere, had once crossed to the farthest lands of Belgic Gaul by the ocean, where Flanders now is; and from there, after a raid into the inner Gaul, joined to themselves the Ambrones and Tigurini, Gallic nations, and had resolved to occupy Italy through the Narbonese province and the Cottian Alps and shake the Roman empire). Plutarch, in his Life of Marius, and others, treat this matter excellently; in his fourth consulship, in the year of the city 652, Marius, having destroyed the Cimbri and the rest, both elsewhere and at Aquae Sextiae, preserved the peace and quiet of that province. Gaius Pontinius also checked the Allobroges when they rose, and triumphed over them in the year of the city 699. When Caesar had finally held this province with Lucius Calpurnius Piso and Aulus Gabinius as consuls, in the year of the city 695, he reduced into the form of a province all of Gaul, which is bounded by the Pyrenean ridge, the Alps, the Cevennes mountains, and the rivers Rhine and Rhône, and which stretches in circuit to three hundred and twenty thousand paces, apart from the allied and well-deserving states, though he was variously harassed by fierce and brave peoples during the nine years in which he held command; and he imposed upon them the name of tribute, to be paid each year. Caesar himself fully describes all these matters, or whatever other author is to be trusted, in seven books of his Commentaries; Suetonius and Plutarch in his Life at various places; Florus book III, chapter X, and Epitome CIII and following; Appian in Celtica; Lucan, book I of the Pharsalia; Eutropius, Orosius, and others. Briefly, what I have said, Velleius says: "Gaul, he says, first attempted and then lost by our side with great disaster, when Domitius and Fabius, grandson of Paullus, who was called Allobrogicus, entered it with an army; but the most splendid work of Gaius Caesar is seen in these matters: for under his leadership and auspices it was almost wholly subdued, and it pays the same tribute as the whole orbit of the lands." Ammianus Marcellinus, book XV: "These regions, especially those bordering on Italy, little by little, though with reluctance, came under Roman rule: first attempted by Fulvius, then shaken by small battles by Sextius; at last subdued by Fabius Maximus, who, having achieved his task fully, after conquering the fiercer Allobroges, gave himself this surname. For Caesar joined all the Gauls, except those which were unreachable because of marshes, as is taught by Sallust as authority, to our alliance by eternal treaties, after the mutual disasters of the ten years' war." Finally Rufus: "Caesar, he says, subdued Gaul with ten legions over nine years; he fought with the Gauls (read Germans) who were placed beyond the Rhine; he crossed as far as Britain by the Alps; in the tenth year he made Gaul and Britain tributary."

units.la: Manserunt sub Romanorum Imperio Galliae ad principatum usque Honorij: quo tempore natus exitio Imperij Romani Stilico, ut Filio suo Rerum omnium gubernacula compararet, cum alia patravit scelera, tum Vandalos, Sucvos, Alanos & Burgundiones, ut Gallias invaderent, solicitavit. Qui quum ingenti multitudine, Arcadio vi & Probo Coss, anno Christi cccc vi, Reno trajecto, pridie Kalendas Ianuarij Gallias Crosco Duce ingressi essent, omnia ferro, flammis, vi & rapinis subverterunt; Episcopos plurimos, aliosque Sacerdotes obtruncarunt, nihilque reliquerunt, quod non impietate sua defoedarint. Dum haec ibi gerebantur, Halatrichus Gothorum Rex, ab Expeditione Hunnica reversus, Gallias Vandalorum ceterorumque furori expositas ab Imperatore Honorio obtinuit: verum iniuriis atque impotentia Stiliconis exstimulatus, Gallijs insuperhabitis, Italiam omnem, Urbe capta, vastavit.
units.tr: Gaul remained under Roman rule until the reign of Honorius. At that time Stilicho, born for the ruin of the Roman Empire, wanting to secure the reins of all government for his own son, committed many crimes, and among them he incited the Vandals, Suevi, Alani and Burgundians to invade Gaul. When they, in great numbers, in the consulship of Arcadius and Probus, in the year of Christ 406, had crossed the Rhine and on 31 December entered Gaul under their leader Crocus, they overturned everything with fire, sword, violence and plunder. They cut down very many bishops and other priests, and left nothing which they did not defile by their impiety. While these things were happening there, Halatrichus, king of the Goths, returning from his Hunnic expedition, obtained from the Emperor Honorius the Gauls that had been exposed to the rage of the Vandals and the others. But, goaded by the wrongs and arrogance of Stilicho, he disregarded Gaul and, after capturing the city, laid waste all of Italy.

units.la: Hujus Successor Athaulphus, Gallicanam Militiam aggressus, Vandalos & Suevos magnis praelijs superatos ex Gallijs emovit: qui per Pyrenaeos montes in Hispaniam migrantes, eam omnem armis obtinuerunt, ut lib. ii. dixi. Post Athaulphum Vise-Gothorum Rex in Gallijs fuit Sigericus: Hunc sequutus est Vallia; qui, Pace cum Honorio Imperatore facta, Gallias omnes Romanis restituit; Aquitania tantum, in qua Gothi habitarent, perpetuoque contra Vandalos aliosque, qui nuperrime in Hispaniam irruperant, communes hostes, excubarent, obtenta: ubi, lecta in Urbe primaria suo Principatui Sede, Successores habuit multos, Tolosae Reges nominatos; ut postea in Languedociae delineatione plenius indicabo.
units.tr: His successor Athaulphus attacked the Gallic army and, defeating the Vandals and Suevi in great battles, drove them out of Gaul. They migrated over the Pyrenees into Spain and held all of it by arms, as I said in book 2. After Athaulphus, the king of the Visigoths in Gaul was Sigericus. He was followed by Vallia, who, after making peace with the Emperor Honorius, restored all of Gaul to the Romans, except Aquitaine, where the Goths were to live and keep watch, as common enemies against the Vandals and others who had lately burst into Spain. There, having chosen the chief city of Toulouse as the seat of his rule, he had many successors, called the Kings of Toulouse, as I will show more fully later in the description of Languedoc.

units.la: Rebus porro Galliarum ita compositis, haud multo post Hunni, Atila Duce, qui Occidentis Imperium adfectabat, Gallias hostiliter ingressi, omnia indignissimis modis protriverunt. Missus Galliarum praesidio Aetius, adjuvantibus Theodorico Vise-Gothorum & Meroveo Francorum Regibus, Atilam memorabili praelio in Campis Catalaunicis vicit; eoque fugato, Gallias omnes liberavit.
units.tr: Once the affairs of Gaul had been settled in this way, not long afterwards the Huns, under their leader Attila, who aspired to the empire of the West, entered Gaul as enemies and trampled everything in the most shameful ways. Aetius was sent to command the garrison of Gaul, and with the help of Theodoric, king of the Visigoths, and Meroveus, king of the Franks, he defeated Attila in a memorable battle on the Catalaunian Plains. With him put to flight, he freed all of Gaul.

units.la: Non longo post tempore Aetius Patricius, cujus Virtute Occidentis Imperium hactenus conservatum fuerat, ab Valentiniano Imperatore occisus est, cum cujus morte etiam Imperium concidit. Nam ejus caede cognita, Barbari, qui Virtutem ipsius veriti intra suos fines quieverant, undique excitari coeperunt. Hunni, reparatis viribus, Italiam invaserunt; Franci, Sugambrorum ad Renum proles, & Burgundiones Gallias, quae Renum versus sunt; Gothi eas Galliarum partes, quae Aquitaniae propinquae erant, occuparunt: atque ita Romanorum brevi in Gallijs defecit Imperium. Mortuo Valentiniano, quum Imperij Romani dignitas ita periisset, ut omnia in Barbarorum potestate & ditione jam essent, Gothi & Franci cum Burgundionibus bello inter se decertare coeperunt. Gothi ab Francis ex Gallia profligati Hispanias occuparunt: Vandali, qui ab Gothis ex Hispania exturbati in Africam transierant, Karthagine capta, totam Provinciam Romanis eripuerunt: Franci & Burgundiones Gallias in deditionem redactas diviserunt; ut Burgundiones propinquas Reno Regiones tenerent, Franci vero interiorem Galliam. Omnes tandem Gallias ijdem pacifice obtinuerunt sub Rege Hlodoveo, qui primus omnium totius Galliae Monarcha est factus, primusque Christi nomen professus, ea, quibus in hodiernum usque diem Francorum Reges utuntur, Trium Liliorum Insignia, coelitus, ut volunt, accepta usurpavit. Regnasse post cum scribuntur Successione nunc directa, nunc collaterali, Childericus, Hlotairus i, Cherebertus, Childericus II, Hlotarius II, Dagobertus Magnus, Hlodoveus II, Hlotarius III, Childericus III. Theodoricus I, Hlodoveus III, Childebertus II, Dagobertus II, Hlotarius IV, Chilpericus I, Theodoricus II, Chilpericus II. Hic anno Regni XI, Christi vero 1 0 C C L I, auctoritate & jussu Zachariæ Pontificis, cui Pipinus vituperabilem & probrosam Regis vitam, tranmisso libello, depinxerat, Regni lure privatus ad Monachatum est coactus. In locum ejus factus est Accusator ipsius Pipinus Karoli Martelli F. Pipini N. Brevis cognomine, ex Præfecto & Majore-Domus. Hunc sequuti commemorantur Karolus Magnus, Ludovicus Pius, Karolus Calvus, Ludovicus III Balbus, Ludovicus IV & Karolomannus, Karolus Crassus, Odo, Karolus Simplex, Rudolphus Burgundio, Lotharius V, & Ludovicus V, ultimus ex Karoli Magni posteritate; quo veneno necato, habenæ Regni translatæ sunt ad Hugonem Capetum, Primum Gallum, Comitem Parisiensem, Ducemque Francorum & Burgundiæ titulo-tenus. Capeto successerunt Robertus Pius, Henricus I, Philippus I, Ludovicus VI Crassus, Ludovicus VII Iunior, Philippus II Adeodatus Augustus, Ludovicus VIII, Divus Ludovicus IX, Philippus III, Philippus IV Pulcher, Ludovicus X Hutinus, Philippus V Longus, Karolus IV Pulcher: cui sine prole mascula defuncto suffectus est Philippus VI Valesius, Karoli Valesiorum Comitis I filius. Sequuti hunc Ioannes Valesius, Karolus V Sapiens; Karolus VI Benenatus. Karolus VII, Ludovicus XI, Karolus VIII Gibbosus, Ludovicus XII Karoli Aureliani F. Franciscus Valesius I Karoli Comitis Angolismensis F. Henricus II Valesius, Franciscus II, Karolus IX, Henricus III: cui Iacobitæ Monachi manu obtruncato legitimus pronunciatus est Successor Henricus IV Borbonius, Antonij Borbonij Ducis Vindocinensis F. Rex Navarræ: cujus hi sunt nuperi Majores:
units.tr: Not long afterwards, Aetius the Patrician, by whose valour the Western Empire had until then been preserved, was killed by the Emperor Valentinian, and with his death the Empire also fell. For when news of his slaughter spread, the barbarians, who had kept quiet within their own borders out of fear of his valour, began to be stirred up on all sides. The Huns, with their strength restored, invaded Italy; the Franks, a offspring of the Sugambri by the Rhine, and the Burgundians seized the parts of Gaul that lie towards the Rhine; the Goths occupied those parts of Gaul that were near Aquitaine. And so in a short time the Roman rule in Gaul came to an end. After Valentinian died, and the dignity of the Roman Empire had perished in this way, so that everything was now in the power and dominion of the barbarians, the Goths and Franks began to fight against each other, along with the Burgundians. The Goths, driven out of Gaul by the Franks, occupied Spain. The Vandals, who had been driven from Spain by the Goths and had crossed into Africa, after capturing Carthage tore the whole province away from the Romans. The Franks and Burgundians divided among themselves the Gauls that had been reduced to surrender, so that the Burgundians held the regions near the Rhine and the Franks the interior of Gaul. In the end the same peoples held all of Gaul peacefully under King Hlodoveus, who was the first of all to be made sole monarch of the whole of Gaul, and the first to profess the name of Christ. He adopted the arms of the three lilies, which the kings of the Franks use to this day, said to have been received from heaven. After him, the following are recorded as reigning, in direct or collateral succession: Childericus, Hlotairus I, Cherebertus, Childericus II, Hlotarius II, Dagobertus the Great, Hlodoveus II, Hlotarius III, Childericus III; Theodoricus I, Hlodoveus III, Childebertus II, Dagobertus II, Hlotarius IV, Chilpericus I, Theodoricus II, Chilpericus II. In the eleventh year of his reign, in the year of Christ 751, he was, by the authority and order of Pope Zacharias, to whom Pipinus had written a libel depicting the king's shameful and disgraceful life, forced to become a monk, stripped of the right to rule. In his place was made Pipinus, the accuser himself, called Pipin the Short, son of Charles Martel, grandson of Pipin, formerly prefect and mayor of the palace. After him are recorded Charles the Great, Louis the Pious, Charles the Bald, Louis III the Stammerer, Louis IV and Carloman, Charles the Fat, Odo, Charles the Simple, Rudolph of Burgundy, Lothair V, and Louis V, the last of the posterity of Charles the Great. After he was killed by poison, the reins of the kingdom passed to Hugh Capet, the first Frenchman, count of Paris and duke of the Franks, with the title of Burgundy. Capet was succeeded by Robert the Pious, Henry I, Philip I, Louis VI the Fat, Louis VII the Younger, Philip II Augustus, Louis VIII, Saint Louis IX, Philip III, Philip IV the Fair, Louis X Hutin, Philip V the Tall, Charles IV the Fair; on his death without a male heir, Philip VI of Valois, son of Charles, count of Valois, succeeded. After him came John of Valois, Charles V the Wise, and Charles VI the Beloved. Then Charles VII, Louis XI, Charles VIII the Hunchback, Louis XII, son of Charles of Orléans; Francis I of Valois, son of Charles, count of Angoulême; Henry II of Valois, Francis II, Charles IX, Henry III. When he was struck down by the hand of a Jacobin friar, Henry IV of Bourbon, son of Antoine de Bourbon, duke of Vendôme, king of Navarre, was declared the lawful successor. These are his recent ancestors:

units.la: HENRICI IV GALLIARVM REGIS POTENTISSIMI MAIORES NVPERI.
units.tr: THE RECENT ANCESTORS OF HENRY IV, MOST POWERFUL KING OF THE FRENCH.
