units.la: HENRICVS GALLIARVM REX CHRISTIANISSIMVS.
units.tr: Henry, Most Christian King of the French.

units.la: CAP. XVII.
units.tr: CAP. XVII.

units.la: Hodierna Galliarum in Politicis Gubernatio.
units.tr: The Present Government of France in Political Affairs

units.la: PRISCAM Galliarum Gubernationem cum in Sacris, tum in Profanis delineavi, Regesque variarum Stirpium ad eum deduxi, qui Francis nostra tempestate summo praeest Imperio: pertexenda jam porro succedit Hodierni in Politicis Ecclesiasticisque Rebus Principatus Historia.
units.tr: I have set out the ancient government of France, both in sacred and in secular matters, and traced the kings of its various dynasties down to him who now presides over the French empire in our own time. I now proceed to continue with the history of the present principate in political and ecclesiastical affairs.

units.la: Status Galliarum, qui quondam, ut dixi, Timocraticus, hodie Monarchicus est: locusque ibi Regiae, quae vetustissima divinissimaque Aristoteli censetur, Gubernationi. Rex nascitur, non suffragijs designatur, Sexus Masculini, volente id, ut quidam perhibent, Lege Salica. Ego scio Legem agere de Privato Patrimonio tantum; nec de Feudis, sed de Allodijs, ut Practici loquimur. Regem ita amant, ita colunt, ita venerantur Subditi, ut nihil supra. Penes eundem Rerum omnium est arbitrium. Ius habet & auctoritatem Bellum Hostibus inferendi, Pacemque cum ijs sanciendi; Foedera cum aliis Principibus Rebusque publicis pangendi; Tributa imperandi; Magistratus creandi; Leges Constitutionesque faciundi; Privilegia dandi; aliaque infinita pro suo nutu agundi: adeo ut quidquid lubet, ei fere liceat; & quidquid dicit, instar sit Legis, modo Aequo Bonoque non repugnet: eo semper laudabilior aestimatus, Suisque carior habitus; quo in Statuum, id est sui Regni Praesulum, Nobilium, Civitatumque, Comitia propensior, inque suggesta ab ijs salutaria omnibus Consilia pronior. De Rege Galliarum duo memoranda tradit Villanovanus: Prius, In Ecclesia Remensi Vas esse, Chrismate perenni redundans, ad Regis unctionem, tempore Hlodovaei v Francorum Principis, coelitus demissum: Alterum, quod Rex ipse solo contactu strumas sive scrofulas curet.
units.tr: The state of France, which was once, as I said, timocratic, is now monarchical. Here the royal office, which is considered the most ancient and most divine of all by Aristotle, holds the place of government. The king is born to his position; he is not chosen by vote, and only males succeed, which some say is required by the Salic Law. I know that the Salic Law deals only with private inheritance, not with fiefs, but with allodial lands, as the lawyers say. Subjects love, cherish and venerate their king as much as they can. In him rests the decision over all matters. He has the right and the authority to make war on enemies and to make peace with them; to form alliances with other princes and states; to impose taxes; to appoint magistrates; to make laws and ordinances; to grant privileges; and to do countless other things at his pleasure. So much so that almost anything he wishes is permitted to him, and whatever he says has the force of law, provided it is not opposed to what is fair and good. He is esteemed all the more praiseworthy and held the dearer by his people the more readily he attends the assemblies of the estates, that is, of the prelates, nobles and cities of his realm, and the more willingly he takes up the wholesome counsels offered him by them all. Villanovanus relates two notable things about the king of France: first, that in the church of Reims there is a vessel, overflowing with perpetual chrism, sent down from heaven for the anointing of the king in the time of Clovis, prince of the Franks; second, that the king himself cures scrofula or king's evil by touch alone.

units.la: Primus Princepsque Familiae Regis Francorum is, qui Proximus ipsi, Necessarius futurusque Heres. Vocatur ille Delphinus: cujus appellationis haec traditur origo. Humbertus Delphinatium Princeps, ex Filij, quem habebat unicum, morte dolorem tantum conceperat, ut saepius Monasticae Vitae cogitaret Profectionem. Quum autem accideret, ut ab Sabaudis bello premeretur, viribus impar, Suis consultum properans, omni Dominatu Philippo cessit; ea Lege, ut Regis Proximus Heres Delphinus vocaretur. Alij aliter rem narrant. Curiosius inquirere non mei instituti. Paucula addam ad cap. xxxiix. Videndi Paulus Aemilius, Nicolaus Gillius, alij. Delphini cognomine primus fuit census Karolus v.
units.tr: The first prince of the royal family of the Franks is he who is next to the king, who will necessarily be his heir. He is called Delphinus, the Dauphin, and the origin of this title is given as follows. Humbert, prince of the Dauphiné, having only one son, was so grieved by his death that he often thought of leaving for the monastic life. When it happened that he was hard pressed in war by the Savoyards, being too weak for them, he hastened to provide for his subjects and surrendered all his dominion to Philip, on the condition that the king's next heir should be called Delphinus. Others tell the story differently, but it is not my purpose to inquire too closely into it. I will add a few words at chapter 39. Those who wish to see more may consult Paulus Aemilius, Nicolaus Gillius and others. The first to bear the title Delphinus was Charles V.

units.la: Inter Regis porro Ministros primum facile locum tuetur Magnus Chamberlanus (Le grand Chambellan) qui praecipuam Cubiculi Regij curam custodiamque habet. Munus ejus, Regi praesto esse, Sanctiorique Cubiculo praeesse, nec non Concilijs publicis cum Alijs Proceribus interesse. Summum Cubicularium vel Cubiculo Praefectum Latine, vel Admissionalem cum Imperio declinante, quis dixerit.
units.tr: Among the king's ministers, the first place is rightly held by the Magnus Chamberlanus (Le grand Chambellan), who has the chief care and guardianship of the royal bedchamber. His office is to attend the king, to preside over the most private chamber, and also to take part in public councils with the other nobles. One might call him in Latin Summum Cubicularium or Cubiculo Praefectum, or, in the decline of the empire, Admissionalem.

units.la: Magnus Magister (Le grand Maistre) quotannis cum Principe Instrumentum Ministerij Aulici describit; maximam habens auctoritatem in Ministros Aulicos, ipsosque etiam Oeconomos.
units.tr: The Magnus Magister (Le grand Maistre) draws up each year with the prince the instrument of the court office, and has the greatest authority over the court officials, and even over the stewards themselves.

units.la: Magnus Scutarius (Le grand Escuyer) Regi equum adscensuro, vel ex eo descensuro manum praebet auxiliatricem: Ensem illi Balteumque Liliatos praeferens. Eiusdem curae incumbit ex Ludovici xi instituto, Curiores Veredarios per Stathmos & Mansiones collocare.
units.tr: The Magnus Scutarius (Le grand Escuyer) offers the king a helping hand when he is about to mount or dismount his horse, carrying before him his sword and his belt decorated with lilies. It is also his task, from the institution of Louis XI, to station the royal couriers at the posting stations and lodgings.

units.la: Magnus Venator (Le grand Veneur) Venatorum cujuscumque generis turmis est Praefectus.
units.tr: The Magnus Venator (Le grand Veneur) is the commander of the companies of huntsmen of every kind.

units.la: Sunt item; Praepositus Hospitij, Magistri Hospitij, Nobiles Servientes, Centum Nobiles, & alij; quibus omnibus suae sunt decretae in Familia Regis provinciae.
units.tr: There are also the Praepositus Hospitij, the Magistri Hospitij, the Nobiles Servientes, the Centum Nobiles, and others; to each of these have been assigned their own duties in the royal household.

units.la: Statum Politicum Varij constituunt. Francorum Regibus vel adhuc Pueris, vel in longinquas Regiones Expeditionesque proficiscentibus, vel mente captis, vel denique in Hostium adductis potestatem, adhiberi solet Rector, qui Regens vulgo; omnia Regis nomine administrans.
units.tr: Various writers set out the political condition. When the kings of the Franks were either still children, or setting out on distant expeditions, or out of their minds, or finally held captive by enemies, a ruler was usually appointed, commonly called the Regens, to administer everything in the king's name.

units.la: Magister Equitum fuit olim in Francia, quem primariæ Nobilitatis, rerumque usu & explorata fide præstantem eligebat sibi Rex; ut cura solutus quieti se daret: Magister Aulæ & Major-Domus vel Palatij etiam appellari solitus. Hic quicquid ad Regni Gubernationem pertinebat, pro suo arbitrio, Regis tamen nomine, gerebat. Tales primis temporibus fuerunt Ebroinus, Metellus, Pipinus. Nomen Regibus lapsu temporis invisum & odiosum, legalare, sustulit Ludovicus x i, cavirque, ne in posterum ullus Magister diceretur Equitum. Instituto Vetere renovato Magistrum Equitum creavit Ioannem Borbonij Ducem Carolus v iii. Ornavit eodem honore Franciscus i Karolum Borbonium; eoque ad Cæsaris partes transgressio, Annam Mommorancium.
units.tr: In France there was once the Magister Equitum, whom the king chose for himself from the foremost nobility, one distinguished for his experience in affairs and his proven loyalty, so that he might be freed from care and give himself to rest. He was also commonly called the Magister Aulae and Major-Domus or Palatii. He managed, at his own discretion though in the king's name, everything that pertained to the government of the realm. Such men in the early period were Ebroin, Metellus and Pepin. As time passed, the name became hateful and odious to the kings; Louis XI abolished it by law, and provided that no one should in future be called Magister Equitum. Charles VIII restored the ancient institution and appointed John, Duke of Bourbon, as Magister Equitum. Francis I bestowed the same honour on Charles of Bourbon, and afterwards, when he went over to the emperor's side, on Anne de Montmorency.

units.la: Duodecim-Virorum Collegium Karoli Magni est institutum. Alij ab ovo Trojano repetunt. Pares (Les Pairs de France) dicti, quod proxima secundum Regem & velut pari essent dignitate. His solis sacrandi Reges jus est, & in Regni possessionem mittendi. Horum tex vulgo Laici; reliqui dicuntur Ecclesiastici, vel Clerici.
units.tr: The college of the Twelve Peers was established by Charles the Great. Others trace it back to the Trojan egg. They are called Pares (Les Pairs de France) because they stood next to the king and were, as it were, of equal dignity. Only these have the right to consecrate kings and to install them in possession of the realm. Of these, the peers are commonly called laymen; the rest are called ecclesiastics or clerics.

units.la: PARES FRANCIÆ
units.tr: PARES FRANCIÆ

units.la: Laici, | Ecclesiastici, Duces: | Comites: | Duces: | Comites: Burgundus, | Flander, | Remensis, Archiepisc. | Catalaunensis, Normannus, | Campanus, | Laudunensis, Episc. | Noviomagensis, Episc. Aquitanus. | Tolosas. | Lingonensis. | Belovacensis.
units.tr: Lay peers and ecclesiastical peers. Dukes: Burgundy, Flanders. Counts: Rheims, the Archbishop; Châlons; Normandy; Champagne; Laon, the Bishop; Noyon, the Bishop; Aquitaine; Toulouse; Langres; Beauvais.

units.la: Remensis, qui inter Ecclesiasticos Primus, Reges inungendi sunt partes. Laici esse delierunt: adjectis Imperio Francico ipsorum Principatibus. Flandriam, post captum ad Ticinum Regem Franciscum, Karolus v Imperator Francorum Limonni & Provocationibus, quæ ad Curiam Parisiensem deferebantur, exeunt. In Remensibus nihilominus Sacris peragundis ab Rege diliguntur, qui ipsorum Ducum Comitumque vices subeant.
units.tr: Remensis, the Archbishop of Rheims, who is first among the ecclesiastical peers, has the duty of anointing the kings. The lay peers have ceased to hold their offices, since their principalities have been added to the French empire. After King Francis was captured at Ticino, Charles V, Emperor, took Flanders, and the appeals and provocations that used to be brought before the Parisian court went out of use. Nevertheless, at Rheims the king appoints men to perform the sacred rites in place of the dukes and counts.

units.la: Sunt & Quatuor-Viri, Tribuni seu Præfecti Militum, ad quos post Equitum Magistrum Rei Militaris summa refertur. Mareschali nominantur, quasi Equorum Præfecti. Maer antiqua voce Equus; Schalck Minister, vel Artis sue peritus. Ineptum cum Ioanne Aventino putare, Maerschalckes dici, quasi Marofa, id est, Majores in Sala vel Aula.
units.tr: There are also the Quatuor-Viri, the tribunes or prefects of the soldiers, to whom the chief command of the military is referred after the Master of the Horse. They are called Mareschali, as if they were prefects of the horses. Maer is an old word for Equus (horse); Schalck Minister means a servant, or one Artis sue peritus (skilled in his craft). It is foolish to think, with Johannes Aventinus, that they are called Maerschalckes, as if from Marofa, that is, Majores in Sala vel Aula (the greater ones in the hall or court).

units.la: Hamiralus (Ammir, Arabibus Rex seu Imperator; ἀλς, Mare Græcis) Maris Præfectus, Thalassiarchus. Huic totius Belli maritimi concreditur provincia; Portuumque, Triremium & Navalium procuratio; totius denique Rei Maritimæ dispensatio. Decimam habet Prædæ Manubiarumque partem. Unus plerumque Munus hoc obit. Leguntur etiam plures uno tempore fuisse; Vnus, qui Aquitanicus Alter, qui Britannico; Tertius, qui Francico præfuit Mari.
units.tr: The Hamiralus (Ammir; among the Arabs a king or emperor; ἀλς, Mare, for the Greeks) is the prefect of the sea, a thalassiarch. To him is entrusted the whole province of naval warfare, the management of harbours, triremes and naval stores, and in short the oversight of all maritime affairs. He has a tenth part of the booty and spoils. Usually one man holds this office. It is recorded that several have held it at the same time: one for the Aquitanian sea, another for the British, a third who presided over the French sea.

units.la: Equites Ordinis (Chevaliers de l'Ordre) D. Michaelis instituit Ludovicus x i anno Christi cio ccccLxix Kalendis Augusti. Fuit initio Cohors xxxvi Procerum. Gestant quotidie Conchyliatum Torquem ducentorum Aureorum; quem alteri donare, vendere, oppignerare nefas. Fratres se mutuo appellant. Sui sunt Ordini Cancellarius, Thesaurarius, Caduceator, Scriba. Quibus cognomen ab S. Spiritu Parentem agnoscunt Henricum ii, temputque nativitatis suæ referunt ad Kalendas Ianuarias anni cio io Lxxix; ipsdem fere utentes Legibus & Cerimoniis. Collegijs hisce simile jam instituerat Ioannes Rex, cui qui nomen dederant Stellam in Penula vel Pileo gestabant, & Sodales dicebantur Nobilis Domus Divi Odoeni.
units.tr: The Equites Ordinis (Chevaliers de l'Ordre) of St Michael were instituted by Louis XI on 1 August 1469. At first it was a company of thirty-six nobles. They wear daily a purple collar worth two hundred gold pieces, which it is wrong to give to another, sell or pawn. They call one another brothers. The order has its own chancellor, treasurer, herald and secretary. They take their name from the S. Spiritu (Holy Spirit) and acknowledge as their founder Henry III, and they date the beginning of their order to 1 January 1579. They use almost the same laws and ceremonies. King John had already set up a society like these, whose members wore a star on their cloak or cap, and were called the Sodales (companions) of the Nobilis Domus Divi Odoeni (Noble House of St Ouen).

units.la: Locum-Tenentes (Lieutenants) Regis vocantur, per quos, tanquam Legatos, Bella gerere; quosque locis in potestatem redactis, ut sint Pro-Rege Victoque in officio contineant, imponere consueverunt.
units.tr: The Locum-Tenentes (Lieutenants) Regis are called, through whom, as legates, wars are waged. Kings have usually appointed them to places brought under their power, so that they might act as deputies of the king and keep the conquered in obedience.

units.la: Cubernatores (Gouverneurs) Regionum sunt, qui, occupato variis negotijs Rege, in Regni limitibus ad ipsius custodiam excubant.
units.tr: The Cubernatores (Gouverneurs) Regionum (governors of the regions) are those who, when the king is occupied with various affairs, keep watch on the boundaries of the kingdom for his protection.

units.la: Magnum
units.tr: Grand.

units.la: Magnus Artillaria Magister (grand Maistre de l'Artillerie) is, qui æneis Tormentis præfectus; cujusque curæ & fidei Machinæ Bellicæ, quæque ad eas pertinent, in prælio & alibi committuntur. Armamentarij Tribunos vel Rei Machinariæ Præfectos Latine quis dixerit.
units.tr: The Magnus Artillaria Magister (grand Maistre de l'Artillerie) is the one placed in charge of the bronze cannon; to his care and trust are committed the war machines and whatever pertains to them, in battle and elsewhere. How one might say Armamentarij Tribunos or Rei Machinariae Praefectos in Latin, I do not know.

units.la: Heraldi (Heraults, voce Germanica Her-aut, vel Her-out, quasi Senex in armis, Veteranus) per quos Bella indicuntur vel finiuntur: Caduceatores & Feciales (quibus præerat Pater-Patratus) Latinis. Nomen sortiuntur ab Regionibus, quibus adscripti, veluti Normannia, Aquitania, aliis.
units.tr: The Heraldi (Heraults, from the German word Her-aut, or Her-out, as if an old man in arms, a veteran) are those through whom wars are declared or ended. In Latin they are the Caduceatores & Feciales (over whom presided the Pater-Patratus). They take their names from the regions to which they are attached, such as Normandy, Aquitaine and others.

units.la: Atque hi Magistratus sunt Militares: Togati me vocant.
units.tr: These are the military offices. The men in gowns claim me as their own.

units.la: Concilium Secretum vel Privatum (Le Conseil Privé) quod & Strictum (Esstroict) constat Agnatis Necessariisque Principis Proceribus, Antistitibus, Cardinalibus, cum Cancellario & Iurisperitis. In eo tractari solet quidquid ad publicum Regni Statum Rerumque Summam.
units.tr: The Concilium Secretum or Privatum (Le Conseil Privé), which is also called the Strictum (Esstroict), consists of the king's kinsmen and close nobles, bishops and cardinals, together with the chancellor and jurists. In it are usually discussed whatever concerns the public state of the kingdom and the highest affairs of the realm.

units.la: Cancellarius (Le Chancelier) is audit, quem Rex in Rebus omnibus ad Rempubl. pertinentibus, veluti Apollinem quendam, consulit. Regis oculus est Aurisque. Ejus partes sunt operam dare diligenter, ne quod Edictum, Rescriptum, Decretum contra Ius vel Remp. ab aliquo impetretur: quod si præsenserit, transversa linea circumducere vel conscindere. Hoc Cancellare vulgo vocatur. Signum sanctius, quod Principis gestat imaginem, quoque Diplomata magni ponderis & momenti signantur, servat.
units.tr: The Cancellarius (Le Chancelier) is the one whom the king consults on all matters that pertain to the commonwealth, as if he were a kind of Apollo. He is the king's eye and ear. His duty is to take care that no edict, rescript or decree is obtained from anyone contrary to law or the public good; and if he perceives such a thing, he is to draw a line through it or tear it up. This is commonly called Cancellare (to cancel). He keeps the more sacred seal, which bears the prince's image, and with which documents of great weight and importance are sealed.

units.la: Magistri Requestarum (Maistres des Requestes) qui octo sunt numero, jus habent in Magno Principis Concilio, in Curia Centenaria, in omnibus denique Curiis, quibus ultima Causarum disceptatio comperit, honestissimo loco sedendi, sententiamque secundum Præsides dicendi. Præcipuæ autem ipsorum partes sunt Principi præsto esse è Cubiculo prodeunti, Postulationibusque Supplicum vacaturo. Latinis nuncupantur A Libellis, Sacrorum Scriniorum Magistri, aliisque modis, ut videre est apud Declinantis Imperij Scriptores.
units.tr: The Magistri Requestarum (Maistres des Requestes), who are eight in number, have the right, in the great council of the prince, in the Hundred Court, and in all courts where the final hearing of causes takes place, to sit in a most honourable place and to give their opinion after the presidents. Their chief duty is to be present with the prince when he comes out from his chamber, and to attend to the petitions of suppliants. In Latin they are called A Libellis (masters of petitions), Sacrorum Scriniorum Magistri (masters of the sacred archives), and by other titles, as may be seen among the writers of the declining empire.

units.la: Est & Concilium, quod vulgo Financiarum (Conseil des Finances) vocant; universi Regij Regnique Thesauri curam habens. In eo Intendentes sunt, ut nominant, Secretarij, Quæstoresque Ærarij.
units.tr: There is also a council which people commonly call the Financiarum (Conseil des Finances), having charge of the whole royal treasury and the wealth of the kingdom. In it are the Intendentes, as they are called, secretaries and treasury quaestors.

units.la: Iam quod ad Parlamenta: initio ipsi Francorum Reges, ut Subditorum sibi animos conciliarent, jus dicere solebant, orbosque parentibus Liberos, Viduas & Tenuiores à Potentiorum injuria liberare. His postea ab iurisdictione abstinentibus, statuit Pipinus Proceres, qui dijudicandis Controversijs convenirent, nullo certo vel tempore vel loco. Hinc crescente Causarum multitudine, bina Parlamenta (quibus nomen ab Francica voce Parler; huic autem ἀπὸ τῶ ἀγγελλειν) haberi cœpta, singulis annis. Postremo ab Rege Philippo Pulcro, vel, ut alij scribunt, Huttrino, ejus filio, Curia, quæ vaga fuerat & incerti loci, Lutetiæ Parisiorum Domicilium accepit. Parlamentum Parisiense in varias Classes vel Decurias, quas indicant Vincentius Lupanus libris de Magistratibus Francorum, ex quo pleraque huc transtulimus, & Ioannes Aubanus, est distributum. Quum autem Parisiensis Curia, longe propagatis Imperij Finibus, Causis dijudicandis non sufficeret, alia accesserunt Parlamenta: Tolosinum, Gratianopolitanum, Burdigalense ab Karolo VII. instituta; Aquense, Divionense, & Rotomagense ab Ludovico XII; Redonense denique in Britonibus Aremoricis memoria nostra ab Henrico II. Burdigalense autem Gratianopolitano postposui. Quum enim per Populares Factionis Anglicæ rebellassent Burdigalenses, receptæ iterum armis à Karolo Urbe, Privilegijs suis sunt multati & Tribunali; atque à Decuria Senatus Parisiensis tam diu recti sunt, donec Ludovicus XI iterum Tribunal restituit. Hinc factum, ut Senatus Burdigalensis, qui antea Gratianopolitanum tempore antecedebat, nunc posterior fit, & quartus in ordine Supremorum Senatuum Galliæ. De quo forte quædam specialiora cap. XXXIV. Cognoscunt singula de Causis & Civilibus & Criminalibus; & quidquid ab ijs diffinitum, servandum est, eique standum. Parisiensis amplissima est, ut jam innui, Iurisdictio. Appellant eo Picardia, Francia speciali bus sumta, Belsia, Campania; Agri item vel Pagi-Lugdunenses, Biturigum, Borboniorum, Pictonum; nec non, cum Inculismenslbus & Alnisiensibus, tota Alvernia. Idem quoque parium Franciæ est Parlamentum, cujus ipsi sunt Consiliarij. Constabat enim antiquitus ex LXXVII Senatoribus & XII Paribus Franciæ, quos dixi; ut omnino Centumviralis esset Regni Senatus. Apud hoc igitur solum Pares convenire, Caussam dicere, &, si opus, condemnari consueverunt. Illud etiam Parisiense præ cæteris habet, quod in id ipsi nonnumquam Reges, quoties magni quid, quod vel Belli vel Pacis spectat negocia decernere est animus, introire sint soliti. Hodie, ut & hoc addam, Pactiones Regum & quidquid omnino ad Regni constitutionem pertinet, in eo recitatur, Actisque Publicis, quorum hujus Parlamenti Senatus custodiam habet; quo magis ratum fiet, inscribitur. Iam Supremis Tolosani Parlamenti Decretis adquiescunt Languedokium, Cadurcium, Rutenium; item in Vasconia Armaniacenses, Bigerrones, & Convenæ. Ab Gratianopolitano summa petit Iura Delphinatus. Burdigalensi subsunt Lemovicum, Petrocorium, Guienna; & in Vasconia Albrebreti Ducatus, Agennensisque Senescballia. Aquensis paret Provincia; Divionensi Burgundiæ Ducatus; Rotomagensi Normannia; Redonensi denique Britannia. Atque hi sunt octo Amplissimi Senatus Franciæ: quibus, quum iure Successorio capesseret Regni Sceptrum Christianissimus Henricus Navarræ Rex, adiecit Senatus Supremus Benearnensis. Institutum autem fuerat hoc Tribunal in Castro Palo, ab Henrico Navarrææorum Rege Henrici IV. Avo Materno. In Civitate etiam Mediomatricum Magistratus ab Rege missus Senatui Urbis præsidet: ut hic quasi sit decimum Franciæ Tribunal. Habent, præter Præsides & Senatores, suos Parlamenta Procuratores Generales & Advocatos Regios.
units.tr: As for the Parlamenta: at first the Frankish kings themselves used to administer justice, in order to win the minds of their subjects, and to free orphans from their parents' loss, and widows and the poorer sort from injury by the powerful. Later, when they abstained from this jurisdiction, Pepin appointed nobles to meet and decide controversies, at no fixed time or place. Then, as the number of cases grew, two Parlamenta began to be held each year, named from the Frankish word Parler (to speak), and this in turn from [ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀγγέλλειν] (from announcing). Finally, under King Philip the Fair, or, as others write, Hutrin, his son, the court, which had been wandering and of uncertain place, received Paris as its seat. The Parlamentum Parisiense was divided into various classes or decuries, as indicated by Vincentius Lupanus in his books on the magistrates of the French, from whom I have taken much of what I have said here, and by Johannes Aubanus. Since the Parisian court, with the boundaries of the empire greatly extended, was not enough to decide the cases, other parlements were added: the Tolosinum, Gratianopolitanum, Burdigalense, established by Charles VII; the Aquense, Divionense, & Rotomagense by Louis XII; and finally the Redonense among the Armorican Bretons in our own memory, by Henry II. I have placed the Burdigalense after the Gratianopolitano. For when the people of Bordeaux rebelled through the popular faction of the English, the city was retaken by Charles with arms, and its privileges and tribunal were taken away; and it was placed beneath the Parisian senate until Louis XI restored the tribunal. Hence it happened that the Senate of Bordeaux, which had previously ranked before the Grenoble one, now comes after it and is the fourth in order among the supreme senates of France. I may perhaps say more about this in chapter XXXIV. The courts judge each case, both civil and criminal, and whatever they decide must be observed and abided by. The Parisiensis has, as I have already hinted, the widest jurisdiction. To it appeal Picardy, taken from France proper, Brie, Champagne; likewise the Lyonnais, the districts of Bourges, Bourbonnais and Poitou; and also, together with the Inculisma and Alnisian regions, the whole of Auvergne. The Parlement of the peers of France is the same court, and its members are its councillors. For in ancient times it consisted of seventy-seven senators and the twelve peers of France I have mentioned, so that it was in effect a hundred-man senate of the realm. Here alone the peers were accustomed to meet, to plead cases and, if need be, to pass sentence. The Parisian court also has this distinction above the rest: kings were often wont to enter it whenever they wished to decide some great matter concerning war or peace. Today, to add this too, the agreements of kings and whatever pertains to the constitution of the kingdom are read out there and recorded among the public acts, the custody of which belongs to the senate of this parlement, so that they may be more firmly established. The Languedoc, Quercy and Rouergue abide by the supreme decrees of the Tolosani Parlement; likewise in Gascony the people of Armagnac, Bigorre and Comminges. The Gratianopolitano seeks the chief law of Dauphiné. The Burdigalensi is subject to Limousin, Périgord and Guienne; and in Gascony the Duchy of Albret and the seneschalship of Agen. The Aquensis governs Provence; the Divionensi the Duchy of Burgundy; the Rotomagensi Normandy; and finally the Redonensi Brittany. These are the eight most ample senates of France. To them, when the most Christian Henry, King of Navarre, took up the sceptre of the kingdom by right of succession, the Supreme Senate of Benearnensis (Béarn) was added. This tribunal had been established in the castle of Pau by Henry, king of Navarre, grandfather of Henry IV on his mother's side. In the city of Metz also, a magistrate sent by the king presides over the city's senate, so that this may be regarded as a tenth tribunal of France. Besides their presidents and senators, the parlements have their own Procuratores Generales (attorneys general) and royal advocates.

units.la: Hodiernus in Ecclesiasticis Galliarum Status.
units.tr: The Present State of the Church in France.

units.la: TALIS igitur hodie Galliæ Status est militiæ domique: sequitur qui in Ecclesiasticis. Christianam Religionem ipsos Apostolos in Galliam intulisse perhibent Regni Annales, præcipue Paulum & Philippum. Lucam quoque Euangelistam in Gallijs docuisse auctor est Epiphanius. D. item Clemens Episcopos se in Galliam ex D. Petri mandatu missurum scribit ad Iacobum Fratrem Domini, Epistola 1, contra Iudæos. Inlatam semel diligenter propagasse, multorumque sensim animis instilasse traduntur Crescens, Martialis, Dionysius Areopagita, Eleutherius, Aphrodisius, Rusticus, & alij: adeo ut Tertullianus profiteatur suo tempore ab diversis Galliarum Nationibus Christum fuisse cultum. Totum tandem Regnum ad Christi Fidem conversum est circa annum CCCCXCV, hac occasione: Bellum adversus Alemannos gerebat Rex Hlodoveus. Quum jam instructa utrimque acie ad Tolbiacum (Vicus est in finibus Agrippinensium, Zulpich hodie) manus conferrentur, Rex suos inclinare videns, molemque praesagiens Calamitatum, oculis in cœlum sublatis, Christi (quem sæpe inculcarat jam Christiana Coniux, Crothildis Burgunda) auxilio invocato, pollicitus se Sacra ejus, quæ respuerat, cum suis suscepturum, Victoriam præclaram reportavit: adeo ut Alemanni, amisso Rege suo, pacem Supplices petere fuerint coacti. Hlodoveus domum reversus iterum ab Vxore exstimulatus; & quod caput erat, Christianæ Fidei documentis ab S. Vedasto imbutus, Remos profectus, Aqua salutifera Fontis cum tribus hominum millibus est ablutus ab S. Remigio, Remensi Antistite, his tunc in Sacro opere verbis utente: Mitis depone colla Sicamber: adora quod incendisti, incende quod adorasti. Consulendi Cassiodorus lib. 11. Variarum, ubi Theodorici Amali Regis Italiæ litteræ, quibus Rex Regi Victoriam gratulatur, Sigebertus; Hermannus Contractus Manuscriptus, nam Vulgata Exemplaria hic in vitio; Gregorius Turonensis lib. 11. cap. xxx. & seq. Aimoinus lib. 1. cap. xv, & seq. Thomas 11. libr. de reg. princ. cap. ult. Hincmarus, Remorum Episcopus; Frodoardus in Vita S. Remigij; Otto Frisingensis lib. IV. cap. xxxii; & Rerum Francicarum Scriptores qui non? Ab eo tempore Francorum gens Christiana: in quam quod & quantum jus competat Romano Pontifici, curiose hic non disputabo: fecerunt hoc alij, in quorum messem falcem ego non immittam. Alienum enim istud ab instituto Geographico. Illud tantum hoc loco dicam, esse sub Ditione Christianissimi Francorum Regis Diœcefes c x v i, inque ijs Archiepiscopatus x i v, Episcopatus autem c c i i: quos non possum distinctius, quam per octo Parlamenta, Tribunaliaq; duo, quæ adcreverunt, Bencarnense & Metense, quibus singuli subsunt, enumerare, ex præscripto Magni Scaligeri, quem omnium scio hac in re versatissimum, cujusque ea de re prolixam apud me servo Epistolam: in qua quæcunque Præsulatuum designationi leguntur admissa, quæ ad quorumdam Franciæ Locorum declarationem pertinent, ad suas postea referam classes.
units.tr: SUCH, then, is the present condition of France in war and at home. Next comes its condition in ecclesiastical matters. The annals of the kingdom report that the Apostles themselves brought the Christian religion into Gaul, chiefly Paul and Philip. Epiphanius asserts that Luke the Evangelist also taught in Gaul. Clement likewise writes, in his first Epistle against the Jews, that he would send bishops into Gaul by the command of St. Peter, addressed to James the brother of the Lord. Crescens, Martial, Dionysius the Areopagite, Eleutherius, Aphrodisius, Rusticus and others are said to have carefully spread the faith once it had been introduced, and gradually instilled it into the minds of many. So much so that Tertullian declares that in his time Christ was worshipped by various nations of Gaul. The whole kingdom was finally converted to the faith of Christ around the year 495, on this occasion. King Clovis was waging war against the Alemanni. When the armies on both sides had been drawn up at Tolbiacum (a village in the territory of the Agrippinenses, today Zulpich) and were joining battle, the king, seeing his men giving way and foreseeing a great disaster, lifted his eyes to heaven and invoked the help of Christ (whom his Christian wife, Clotilde the Burgundian, had often urged upon him). He promised that he would embrace with his people the sacred rites he had rejected, and he won a famous victory. As a result the Alemanni, having lost their king, were forced to beg for peace as suppliants. Clovis returned home, again prompted by his wife, and, what mattered most, instructed in the teachings of the Christian faith by St. Vedastus. He went to Reims and was washed with the saving water of the font, with three thousand of his men, by St. Remigius, bishop of Reims, who then used these words in the sacred rite: Meek bow your necks, Sicambrian: worship what you burned, burn what you worshipped. On these matters consult Cassiodorus, book 11 of the Variae, where there is a letter of Theodoric the Amal, king of Italy, congratulating the king on his victory; Sigebert; Hermann Contractus in manuscript, for the printed editions are faulty here; Gregory of Tours, book 11, chapter 30 and following; Aimoin, book 1, chapter 15 and following; Thomas, book 11 of De regimine principum, last chapter; Hincmar, bishop of Reims; Flodoard in the Life of St. Remigius; Otto of Freising, book 4, chapter 32; and the writers of French history, who does not? From that time the French nation has been Christian. What right and how much of a right belongs to the Roman Pontiff over it I will not discuss in detail here. Others have done this, and I will not put my sickle into their harvest, for that matter is foreign to the purpose of a geographical work. I will say only this here: under the dominion of the most Christian King of the French there are 116 dioceses, among them 14 archbishoprics and 202 bishoprics. I cannot list these more precisely than by the eight parliaments and the two additional tribunals, Bayonne and Metz, to which they are each subject, following the plan of the great Scaliger, whom I know to be the most versed of all in this matter, and whose lengthy letter on the subject I keep with me. Whatever I find in that letter about the designation of the prelacies, admitted as valid, and relating to the identification of certain places in France, I will later refer to their proper classes.

units.la: De Abbatibus, aliisque Sacrorum Antistitibus, quorum numerum inire, quod ingenue fateor, non possum: nihil hic dicam: faciant hoc, quibus haec talia explorationa.
units.tr: Concerning abbots and the other holders of sacred office, whose number I frankly confess I cannot work out, I will say nothing here. Let those do it to whom such investigations are familiar.

units.la: Quum vero tanta, ut audivimus, Praesulum per Gallias ab multis jam seculis absque intermissione fuerit copia, eosque Pietate, Probitate, Doctrina plurimum praecellentes esse oportear; non est, quod quis magnopere miretur, Regnum hoc abundasse plerumque Viris, qui cum alijs commisi primam in Rep. literaria semper laudem obtinuerunt: ad quorum Senatum indies magis & magis augendum maximi momenti fuerunt, quae quondam floruerunt, quaeque nunc florent, Academiae. De Augustoduno sic scribit Tacitus lib. iii Annalium: Apud Aeduos major moles exorta, quanto Civitas opulentior, & comprimendi procul praesidium. Augustodunum, caput gentis, armatis cohortibus, Sacrevir occupaverat, & nobilissimam Galliarum subolem, liberalibus studiis ibi operatam, ut eo pignore Parentes Propinquosque eorum adjungeret. Innuit eam Urbem jam tunc, post Massiliam, de qua alibi, Musarum fuisse hospitium, & speciem quamdam Academiae. Hanc Bagaudicae cujusdam rebellionis, ut Eumenius loquitur, latrocinio eversam, morteque Rectoris conlapsam restituit Constantius Imp. Constantini Magni pater; misso eo, qui Praefectum ageret, Eloquentiamque ibi profiteretur, Eumenio, cujus memini, Rhetore: qui Provinciam ingressus peculiarem habuit Orationem pro Scholis instaurandis ad V. P. Praesidem Galliae, quae exstat. Imperator Rescriptum suum his verbis ad Eumenium orditur: Merentur & Galli nostri, ut eorum Liberis, quorum vita in Augustodunensium opido ingenuis Artibus erudiretur; & ipsi Adolescentes, qui hiemi consensu meum suscepere comitatum, ut eorum indoli consulere cupiamus: ubi male quidam & contra Veterem Editionem, Augustocliviensium; ab Gallis alio transferre gloriam hanc volentes. Restauratio autem illa tanti fuit fructus, ut non multo post Constantius ab Donatistis in Africa rogatus, ut ipsis Iudices daret ex Gallijs, qui suam & Catholicorum Causam cognoscerent, Maternum ex Agrippinensi Colonia, Rheticum autem Augustoduno evocarit. Paullatim tamen rursum intercidit. Non defuerunt interim Gallijs celebres alijs locis Scholae. Docet Ausonij liber de Professoribus Burdigalensibus, Tolosanis, Narbonensibus, &c. Admirari soleo Cathedram apud Burdigalenses Ti. Victoris Minervij, de qua inter alia sic canit Poëta: Asserat usque licet Fabium Calagurris alumnum: Non sit Burdigale dum Cathedra inferior. Mille foro dedit hic Iuvenes: bis mille Senatus Adjecit numero, purpureisque togis. Me quoque, &c.
units.tr: Since, as we have heard, there has been for many centuries through the Gauls an unbroken abundance of prelates, who ought to excel greatly in piety, uprightness and learning, it is no wonder that this kingdom has generally abounded in men who, among others, have always won the highest praise in the literary republic. Those universities which once flourished, and which now flourish, were of the greatest importance in continually increasing their senate. Tacitus writes thus of Autun in the third book of the Annals: "Among the Aedui a greater disturbance arose, as their state was more wealthy, and the garrison to suppress it was far off. Sacrovir had seized Augustodunum, the capital of the nation, with armed cohorts, and he had put the most noble youth of Gaul, who were engaged there in liberal studies, under his control, so that by this pledge he might bind their parents and kinsmen to himself." He hints that this city, after Marseille, of which I speak elsewhere, was already then a home of the Muses and a kind of image of an academy. This city, overthrown by the brigandage of a certain Bagaudic rebellion, as Eumenius puts it, and collapsed through the death of its ruler, was restored by Constantius, father of Constantine the Great, who sent thither as governor, and to profess eloquence there, the rhetor Eumenius whom I have mentioned. On entering the province, he delivered a special oration for the restoration of the schools, addressed to the Vicar, the governor of Gaul, which survives. The Emperor opens his rescript to Eumenius with these words: "Our Gauls also deserve that the children whose lives are to be educated in the liberal arts in the town of the Augustodunenses, and those young men who with consent have taken up my service, should be cared for by us in their talents." Where some, wrongly and against the old edition, read "Augustoclivienses," wishing to transfer this glory from Autun to another Gallic town. That restoration bore such fruit that, not long after, when Constantius was asked by the Donatists in Africa to give them judges from Gaul to examine their cause and that of the Catholics, he summoned Maternus from Cologne and Rhetikus from Autun. Yet it gradually fell again. Meanwhile there were not lacking other famous schools in various places in Gaul. Ausonius' book on the professors of Bordeaux, Toulouse, Narbonne, and so on, bears witness to this. I am accustomed to wonder at the chair at Bordeaux of Tiberius Victorius Minervius, of which the poet sings among other things thus: "Let Calahorra claim Fabius as her pupil as long as she likes; Bordeaux will not have an inferior chair while she has this one. He has given a thousand young men to the forum; he has added twice a thousand to the senate's number, and to the purple togas. Me also, etc."

units.la: 40 Exstat etiam in Codice Theodosiano, Tit. de Professorib. & Medic. Imperatoris Gratiani Rescriptum ad Antonium, Praefectum Praetorio Galliarum, jubentis; ut in singulis Galliae Metropolibus excitarentur alerenturque studia Litterarum, egregiique ijs Professores praficerentur; decretis liberalissime Honorarijs. Tandem Carolus Magnus conversus cum ad Ius Francorum in ordinem redigendum, Legumque Libros conscribendos (nam antiqua Romanorum lura per Langobardos aliosque Imperij Hostes obliterata fere & sepulta jacebant) tum ad excolenda aliarum Artium & Scientiarum studia, earumque Professores debite colendos: circa annum 1occ1xxi, ex Alcuini Praeceptoris sui, Venerabilisque Bedae discipuli, consilio, Academiam Parisijs erexisse fertur, ad ejus, quae Romae jam erat, archetypum, ut scribunt Cardinalis Sabarella & Petrus Anchoran. I C. Clement. de Magist. Ex Parisiensi, velut uberrimo quodam Sapientiae fonte, plurimae per varias Europae Regiones, praesertim Germaniam & Galliam, sunt derivatae. Gallicas sane has (ne cujus dignitati violato ordine, detraham) numero: Andegavensem, Avenionensem, Aurelianensem, Bituricensem, Burdigalensem; Cadomensem, Cadurcensem, Dolanam, Lugdunensem, Massiliensem omnium antiquissimam, ab Graecis ortam, Montispessulanam, Nannetensem, Nimecensem, Pictavitensem, Remensem & Tolosanam. Ex his omnibus tamquam ex multis Equis Trojanis, qui docti Viri, Theologi, Iurisconsulti, Medici, Alij fuerint progressi, suis videbimus locis. Nam uno cos ductu enumerare si conarer, maximum mihi quidem conciliarem laborem, Lecturis vero tædium. Nobilitas sane Gallica (quæ frequentissima est) hodie tam pertinaci diligentia, ut hoc universim dicam, tamque adliduo labore Meliorum Litterarum Studia persequitur, adeoque in omni Disciplinarum Artiumque genere excellit, ut nusquam terrarum magis. Videre ibi est summo loco natos illustribusque ortos familiis noctes diesque inhærere Chartis, & numquam non Musarum Sacris operari. Novi cum stupore, qui de quacumque re in medium prolata expeditissime poterant, methodo admiranda, ex tempore & absque ulla præmeditatione per horas aliquot differere.
units.tr: 40 There also survives in the Theodosian Code, title on professors and physicians, a rescript of the Emperor Gratian to Antonius, Praetorian Prefect of Gaul, ordering that the study of letters be established and maintained in each metropolis of Gaul, and that distinguished professors be set over them, with most generous honoraria decreed. Finally, Charlemagne, turning to reduce the law of the Franks to order and to write down the books of law (for the ancient laws of the Romans had been almost obliterated and lay buried through the Lombards and other enemies of the empire), and also to cultivate the studies of the other arts and sciences and to honour their professors as they deserve, is said to have established an academy at Paris around the year 781, on the counsel of Alcuin, his teacher, and a pupil of the venerable Bede, as a model of the one that already existed at Rome, as Cardinal Sabarella and Pierre d'Ancharano, in the Clementines on teachers, write. From the Parisian academy, as from a most abundant fountain of wisdom, many others have been derived through the various regions of Europe, especially Germany and France. I shall enumerate the Gallic ones (lest, by disturbing the order, I detract from anyone's dignity): Angers, Avignon, Orléans, Bourges, Bordeaux, Caen, Cahors, Dole, Lyon, Marseille, the oldest of all, which arose among the Greeks, Montpellier, Nantes, Nîmes, Poitiers, Reims and Toulouse. From all these, as from many Trojan horses, the learned men, theologians, jurists, physicians and others who have emerged we shall see in their places. For if I tried to list them in one sweep, I would earn for myself the greatest labour, but for the readers only tedium. Indeed the Gallic nobility (which is very numerous) pursues the studies of the better letters today with such persistent diligence, and with such constant labour, to put it generally, and it excels in every kind of discipline and art so much that nowhere on earth more so. There one may see men born of the highest rank and descended from illustrious families cleaving to their papers night and day, and never failing to labour at the rites of the Muses. I have seen with amazement men who could most readily speak on any subject put before them, with admirable method, extemporaneously and without any premeditation, for several hours at a stretch.

units.la: CAP. XIX.
units.tr: CAP. XIX.

units.la: Varia Galliarum Distributiones.
units.tr: Various Divisions of Gaul.

units.la: GENERALIA finivi: vocant me Specialia; quæ parebunt in singulis Galliarum partibus: quæ quot sint (de Principibus loquor) & quo modo inter se connectantur, Divisione est aperiendum.
units.tr: I have finished the General matters; the Specific matters call me on: these will follow in the individual parts of Gaul. How many they are (I am speaking of the Princes) and how they are connected with one another must be set out by division.

units.la: Galli Veteres ita suas Sedes promovisse leguntur, ut non solum in Italia ad Rubiconem usque Fluvium, verum etiam in Asia Minore eas fixerint. Hanc ob causam Gallia dividunda videbatur in Asiaticam & Europæam; hæc autem in Cisalpinam & Transalpinam. Sed quum Asiatica illa proprie pertineat ad Asiam Minorem, quæ quarta mei Operis parte explicatur sub Gallatia vel Gallo-Græcia appellatione; & Cisalpina omnino sit illa Italiæ portio, quæ hodie Lombardia: de Transalpina solum, quæ Oceano, Pyrenæis Montibus, Mari Mediterraneo, Alpibusque cingitur, statui hoc loco agere. Transalpinam appello quasi Romæ positus: alioqui quæ Græcis Latinisque Scriptoribus Transalpina, Γαλατία ἡ ἐντὸς τῶν Ἄλπεων, Gallis vere est Cisalpina: contra quæ illis Cisalpina, ἡ ἐκτὸς τῶν Ἄλπεων, his Transalpina censetur.
units.tr: The ancient Gauls are said to have extended their seats so far that they settled not only in Italy as far as the river Rubicon, but also in Asia Minor. For this reason Gaul seemed to need dividing into Asiatic and European, and the European part into Cisalpine and Transalpine. But since that Asiatic part properly belongs to Asia Minor, which in the fourth part of my work is explained under the name Galatia or Gallo-Graecia, and the Cisalpine part is entirely that portion of Italy which is today Lombardy, I have decided to treat here only of the Transalpine region, which is bounded by the Ocean, the Pyrenees, the Mediterranean Sea and the Alps. I call it Transalpine as if one were placed at Rome; otherwise what Greek and Latin writers call Transalpine, [Γαλατία ἡ ἐντὸς τῶν Ἄλπεων], is truly Cisalpine for the Gauls, and conversely what for those writers is Cisalpine, [ἡ ἐκτὸς τῶν Ἄλπεων], is for the Gauls Transalpine.

units.la: Transalpina igitur per Gebennam & Iuram Montes, ut volunt Plinius & Solinus; vel per Lemannum Lacum, Rodanum Fluvium, Montesque Gebennicos, uti censent Mela, Eutropius & Suetonius, dividitur in Bracatam & Comatam.
units.tr: Transalpine Gaul is therefore divided into Bracata and Comata either by the Gebenna and Jura mountains, as Pliny and Solinus hold, or by Lake Geneva, the river Rhone and the Cevennes mountains, as Mela, Eutropius and Suetonius think.

units.la: Bracata ad Meridiem Mare Gallicum vel Tuscum Pelagus attingens, magis culta & magis consita, inquit idem Mela, ideoque cultior; sic vocabatur ab Vestis genere, cujus in ea erat usus, ut alibi dicitur. Appellata fuit & hæc, in dextra præcipue Rodani ripa, Narbonensis, testibus, præter alios, Plinio lib. 11 & Pomponio Mela, qui lib. 11 hanc describit, ut ceteras lib. 111; Καλλιαλλιατία Ναρβωνησία Ptolemæo: ab Narbone, quam Tectosagum urbem idem Ptolemæus, Decumanorum Coloniam facit Plinius, de qua suo loco: in sinistra vero Provincia κατ' ἐξοχὴν dicebatur: hodieque nomen id servans. Hæc Bracata citius ceteris, nec sane difficile, facta est Provincia à Populo Romano: congruebant mores; & Massilia, Studiorum sedes, sua, id est, Græca mollitie propinquum Agrum ab feritate & Armorum amore ad mansuetius Vitæ genus avocaverat: aliæ duriorís cæli, tum & origine & Armorum exercitio Germanis persimiles, adusque C. Iulij Cæsaris Dictatoris tempora liberæ manserunt: mox volentibus Fatis ab illo deviætæ, qui non multo post Romam ipsam vicit. Bracatam describit hoc modo Strabo lib. iv: Ταύτης δὲ τὴ χώρα ... τὸ Κελτικὸν Ἐπιοδονίας ... & quæ ibi alia. Sic Ausonius: Insinuant qua se Sequanis Allobroges oris; Excluduntque Italos Alpina cacumina fines; Qua Pyrenæis vicibus dirimuntur Iberi; Qua rapitur præceps Rodanus, genitore Lemanno, Interiusque premunt Aquitanica rura Cebenna,
units.tr: Bracata, reaching to the Gallic or Tuscan Sea in the south, is more cultivated and more full of settlements, says the same Mela, and therefore more civilised; it was so called from the kind of trousers (bracae) whose use was customary there, as is said elsewhere. This region was also called Narbonensis, especially on the right bank of the Rhone, as attested, among others, by Pliny in book 11 and by Pomponius Mela, who in book 11 describes it as he describes the others in book 3. Ptolemy calls it Καλλιαλλιατία Ναρβωνησία; it takes its name from Narbo, which Ptolemy makes a city of the Tectosages and Pliny makes a colony of the Decumani, about which more in its place. On the left bank it was called Province par excellence, a name it keeps even today. This Bracata became a province of the Roman people sooner than the other regions, and not at all with difficulty: the customs agreed, and Massilia, the seat of learning, had by its own Greek refinement drawn the neighbouring land away from its savagery and love of arms to a gentler way of life. The others, of harsher climate and, in origin and in the practice of arms, very like the Germans, remained free until the time of Gaius Julius Caesar the Dictator, and were then conquered by him, who soon after also conquered Rome itself, the fates willing it. Strabo in book 4 describes Bracata in this way: "Of this land ... the Celtic part ... of Aquitania ..." and what follows there. So Ausonius: "Where the Allobroges insinuate themselves into the shores of the Sequani; where the Alpine peaks shut off Italy's borders; where the Iberians are divided by the Pyrenean turns; where the headlong Rhone is carried, with Lemannus its father; and where the Cevennes press down on the Aquitanian fields within," and as far as the Tectosages, originally called Belgae: all of it was Narbo.

units.la: Ffque Vsque in Tentosagos, primaevo nomine Belgae: Totum Narbo fuit.
units.tr: Even as far as the Tectosages, originally called Belgae; all of it was Narbo.

units.la: Belgis hinc amotis, scribo Belcas: sic appellat Ausonius, quos alii Volcas, Graeci οὐόλκας; ut suo loco videbimus. Bracati nescio an Semibarbari Gallorum sint intelligendi, quos Civitate donatos Suetonius scribit cap. LXXVI C. Caesarem in Curiam Romanam recepisse, Senatoresque fecisse. Fere est, ut mihi videatur. Bracati enim politiores mores, ut suos Romani volebant, plurimum inducrant. Bracatorum Pueros nominat Iuvenalis Sat. VIII. Narbonensem porro Provinciam etiam Septimaniam lego appellatam apud Imperii labentis & lapsi jam scriptores: vel a Septimanis Militibus: nam Narbo Colonia Septimanorum; vel ab Septem Provinciis, quarum Conventus ex Constitutione Imp. I. Constantini Arelate (ut cap. XXXIIX plenius dicam) agebantur. Erant Ex Viennensis, utraque Narbonensis, utraque Aquitania, Novem-populania, & Alpes Maritimae. Septimaniam autem vocant Sidonius Apollinaris lib. III. epist. I; Gregorius Turonensis lib. VIII cap. XXVIII & XXX; item lib. IX cap. VII; Vuardus ad XI Kalend. Aprilis: Eginarthus in Vita Karoli Magni; Aimoinus Monachus lib. IV. cap. XXXIV. Ionas Aurelianensis lib. I. & alij.
units.tr: Having put the Belgae aside here, I write Belcae; Ausonius calls them so, while others call them Volcae, Greek Οὐόλκαι, as we shall see in its place. I do not know whether the Bracati should be understood as the half-barbarian Gauls, whom Suetonius writes that Caesar admitted to Roman citizenship in chapter 76 and made senators; it seems to me that they might be. For the Bracati had largely adopted the more civilised customs which the Romans wished their own people to have. Juvenal in Satire 8 names the boys of the Bracati. Further, I read that the Province of Narbonensis was also called Septimania by the writers of the declining and fallen Empire, either from the Seventh Legion soldiers, since Narbo was the Colony of the Seventh, or from the Seven Provinces, whose assemblies were held at Arles by the constitution of the Emperor Constantine I (as I shall say more fully in chapter 38). These were: Vienne, both Narbonensis, both Aquitania, the Nine Peoples, and the Maritime Alps. They call it Septimania: Sidonius Apollinaris in book 3, letter 1; Gregory of Tours in book 8, chapters 28 and 30, and also book 9, chapter 7; Vuardus at 11 Kalends of April; Eginhard in the Life of Charlemagne; Aimoin the monk in book 4, chapter 34; Jonas of Orléans in book 1, and others.

units.la: Comata, quae Septemtrionem versus in Oceanum inclinabat, nominabatur ab alendi comas studio. Lucanus de Bello Pharsalico:
units.tr: Comata, which inclines northward toward the Ocean, was named from the custom of nourishing long hair.

units.la: Crinibus effusis toti pralate Comatae.
units.tr: Lucan in the Pharsalia: "With hair flowing loose, all of long-haired Gaul ..."

units.la: Fines Comatae Galliae & Provinciae Narbonensis indicat incertus quidam Scriptor; nondum editus, quem ad me misit, anno CIO IOXCIX mense Septembri, Vir cum nobilissimus, tum humanissimus & doctissimus Marcus Velserus, Patricius & IIVIR Augustanus, sua manu exscriptum ex Codice Membranco, quo Notitia Utriusque Imperii, Itinerarium Antonini, & quaedam alia, quae conjungi plerumque solent, continebantur. Verba A'ναγρά istius haec sunt: Gallia Comata cum Insulis Britannicis finitur, ab Oriente Flumine Rheno; ab Occidente Pyrenaeo; a Septemtrione Oceano Maris; a Meridie Rhodano & Montibus Cebennicis: Longitudine mil. pass. IO CCCC XXVIII, Latitudine CCCLXIII: juxta Plinium Secundum in Quarto lib. o in Longitudinem IO CCCCXX, in Latitudinem CCCVIII. Provincia Narbonensis finitur ab Oriente Alpibus, ab Occidente Saltu Pyrenaeo, a Septemtrione Fimbus Viennensium & Montibus Cebennicis: a Meridie Mari Gallico. Longitudo Mill. pass. CCCXXXIV. Latitudo CLXXXVIII, iuxta Plinium Secundum. In eodem Longitudinem Provinciae Narbonensis CCCLXX passuum Agrippa tradidit: Latitudinem CCCXLVIII. De Comata porro tantum exaudiendi sunt illi, qui ante Augusti tempora de Imperii Romani Provinciis scripserunt. Hi enim in Divisione Galliarum Bracatam numquam comprehendere consueverunt: adeo ut quoties apud eos Galliarum occurrat mentio, semper fere excipienda sit Bracata vel Narbonensis, si res gestae ante Augusti principatum memorantur. Primus Latinorum (sunt enim quibus triplex Galliae distributio in Aquitanos, Celtas & Belgas, antiquissimorum Graecorum esse videtur) C. Caesar, ut Galliās armorum arbitrio subegit, ita etiam suo illas divisit in Belgas ab Reno ad Matronam usque; hinc ad Garumnam in Celtas; quod reliquum est inter Garumnam, Pyrenaeos & Mare in Aquitanos, relicta extra Divisionem Bracata. De triplici hac Divisione consulendi ipse Caesar lib. I. belli Gallici, Strabo libri I. initio, Ptolemaeus, Plinius lib. IV. nat. historiae, Pomponius Mela lib. III Geographiae, Ammianus Marcellinus lib. XV & alij. Tres hasce Galliae Provincias designat, nisi fallor, Inscriptio, quae in Gallia Lugduni in Domo contigua Templo S. Cosmi. S E R V I L I O M · A R C I A N O A R · V E R N O C. S E R V I L I I D O M I T I. F I L I O S A C E R D O T I. A D T E M P L V M. R O M A E E T. A V G V S T O R V M T R E S. P R O V I N C I A E G A L L I A E Nominantur & in aliis Marmoribus; quæ brevitati studens, prætereo. De Singulis seorsim etiam aliquid dicam. Aquitanicam nonnulli dictam volunt ab Aquis, quibus abundare fertur; alij ab Opido, Aquis, Aqs dirivant. Aquitanos non modo lingua, sed etiam legibus & institutis ab ceteris Gallis differre, Hispaniisque similiores esse, quam Gallis, antea dixi ex Cæsare & Strabone. De Aquitanis scribit idem Ammianus lib. xv, quod de Bracatis alij. Aquitani, inquit, ad quorum littora, ut proxima placidaque, Merces adventitiæ convehuntur, Moribus ad mollitiem lapsis, facile in Dicionem venere Romanam. Laudant Aquitaniam cum alij, tum Salvianus lib. vii. Nemini dubium est, ait, Aquitanos ac Novem-populos medullam fere omnium Galliarum & uber totius Fœcunditatis habuisse, nec solum Fœcunditatis; sed, quæ præponi interdum Fœcunditati solet, Iocunditatis, Voluptatis, Pulcritudinis: illic omnis admodum Regio, aut intertexta Vineis, aut florulenta Pratis, aut distincta Culturis, aut consita Pomis, aut amœnata Lucis, aut irrigata Fontibus, aut interfusa Luminibus, aut crinita Messibus fuit: ut vere Possessores ac Domini Terræ illius, non tam Soli ipsius portionem, quam Paradisi imaginem possedisse videantur: sed (omissis aliis Aquitaniæ Populis) Burdigala & Arverni excellunt. Aquitanorum Remp. aliquo modo suis coloribus depingit Cæsar lib. iii. de bello Gallico, Tum Aquitani Legatos, inquit, quoque verbum mittere, conjurare, obsides inter se dare, Copias parare cæperunt: à Cantabris finitimis auxilia accersuntur; Duces vero hi deliguntur, qui una cum Q. Sertorio omnes annos fuerant, summamque scientiam rei militaris habere existimabantur.
units.tr: An unknown writer, whose work is still unpublished, indicates the boundaries of Comata Gaul and of the Province of Narbonensis. He sent it to me in September of 1599, copied by his own hand from a parchment codex, which also contained the Notitia of Both Empires, the Itinerary of Antoninus and certain other things usually joined with them. The man was as noble as he was kind and learned, Marcus Velserus, patrician and duumvir of Augsburg. The words of this writer, [Ἀναγραφή], are these: Gallia Comata is bounded together with the British Islands: on the east by the river Rhine; on the west by the Pyrenees; on the north by the Ocean; on the south by the Rhone and the Cevennes mountains. Its length is 10,428 miles and its breadth 363, according to Pliny the Elder in book 4, whose figures are 10,420 in length and 308 in breadth. The Province of Narbonensis is bounded on the east by the Alps, on the west by the Pyrenean pass, on the north by the Fimbi of the Viennese and the Cevennes mountains, and on the south by the Gallic Sea. Its length is 334 miles and its breadth 188, according to Pliny the Elder. Agrippa gave the length of the same Province of Narbonensis as 370 paces and its breadth as 348. Only those should be heard concerning Comata who wrote about the provinces of the Roman Empire before the time of Augustus. For they were accustomed never to include Bracata in their division of Gaul, so that whenever Gaul is mentioned in their works, Bracata or Narbonensis must almost always be understood, if the deeds recorded belong to the time before the principate of Augustus. The first of the Latin writers (for there are some who think the threefold division of Gaul into Aquitani, Celtae and Belgae belongs to the most ancient Greeks) was Gaius Caesar, who, as he subdued the Gauls by force of arms, so also divided them by his own judgment: into the Belgae, from the Rhine to the Marne; from there to the Garonne, the Celtae; and what remains between the Garonne, the Pyrenees and the sea, the Aquitani, with Bracata left outside the division. On this threefold division consult Caesar himself in book 1 of the Gallic War, Strabo at the beginning of book 1, Ptolemy, Pliny in book 4 of the Natural History, Pomponius Mela in book 3 of the Geography, Ammianus Marcellinus in book 15, and others. The inscription, which is found at Lyon in a house adjoining the Temple of St. Cosmas, seems to me to designate these three provinces of Gaul: "To Servilius Marcianus, son of Servilius Domitius, priest of the temple of Rome and of Augustus, of the Three Gauls Provinces," and the same names occur in other marbles, which I pass over, aiming at brevity. I shall also say something about each of them separately. Some want Aquitania to be named from the Waters, of which it is said to have abundance; others derive it from the town Aquae, Aqs. I have said before, following Caesar and Strabo, that the Aquitani differ from the other Gauls not only in language but also in laws and institutions, and are more like the Spaniards than the Gauls. Ammianus in book 15 says of the Aquitani what others say of the Bracati: "The Aquitani, on whose shores, as they are nearby and calm, foreign goods are carried; with their customs having slipped into softness, they easily came under Roman rule." Many praise Aquitania, and Salvianus in book 7 among them: "No one doubts," he says, "that the Aquitani and the Nine Peoples had almost the marrow of all the Gauls and the rich fruitfulness of the whole, and not only fruitfulness, but also what is sometimes preferred to fruitfulness: pleasure, delight and beauty. There almost the whole region was either interwoven with vineyards, or flowery with meadows, or divided by cultivation, or planted with orchards, or made pleasant with groves, or watered with springs, or spread with lights, or crowned with harvests; so that its true possessors and masters seem to have possessed not so much a portion of the soil as an image of Paradise. But, leaving aside the other peoples of Aquitania, Burdigala and the Arverni excel." Caesar in book 3 of the Gallic War paints the state of the Aquitani in its own colours: "Then the Aquitani began to send envoys and to conspire with one another, to give hostages to each other, and to prepare forces; auxiliaries were summoned from the neighbouring Cantabrians; and the leaders chosen were those who had served with Quintus Sertorius and were thought to have the greatest knowledge of military affairs."

units.la: Celtica, κελτικὴ Græcis, ab Celtis: à quibus universos Gallos ab Græcis Celtas appellatos opinantur Strabo lib. iv. Qui Græcis Celtæ, Romanis speciatim Galli vocabantur, scribente Cæsare lib. i. ex quo Ammianus lib. xv. Temporibus prisciis, quum latèrent hæ partes, ut barbaræ, tripartita fuisse creduntur, in Celtas (eosdem Gallos) divisæ, & Aquitanos & Belgas, Lingua Institutis, Legibusque discrepantes. Et Gallos quidem, qui sunt Celtæ, ab Aquitanis Garumna disterminat flumen, &c. Celtas describit Silius Italicus lib. viii: Quin etiam ingenio fluxi, sed prima feroces Vaniloquum, Celtæ, genus, ac mutabile mentis, Repetere domos, mærebant cæde sine ulla (Insolitum sibi) bella geri, siccasque cruore Inter tela sui Maveris bebescere dextras.
units.tr: Celtica [κελτικὴ] in Greek, from the Celts. Strabo, book 4, thinks that the Greeks called all the Gauls Celts on this account. Those whom the Greeks called Celts the Romans called Gauls in particular, as Caesar writes in book 1. From this, Ammianus, book 15: "In early times, when these regions lay hidden and were considered barbarous, they are believed to have been divided into three parts: the Celts (the same as the Gauls), the Aquitanians and the Belgians, differing in language, institutions and laws. And the Gauls, who are Celts, are separated from the Aquitanians by the river Garonne," and so on. Silius Italicus, book 8, describes the Celts: "Moreover, the Celts, a people light of mind yet fierce at first, and changeable in temper, were lamenting that they must return home, since wars were being waged without bloodshed, which was unusual for them, and that their right hands, dry of blood, were growing dull amid the weapons of their own Mars."

units.la: Celtarum Amphyctionatum in exemplo Aremoricarum Civitatum, quæ nobilissimam Celticæ constituebant partem: proponit Cæsar lib. iii. in Venetorum, Olismiorum, Nannetum, Diablintum, Curiosolitorum, Unellorum, & aliorum conjuratione, quæ incidit in Bellum Veneticum: Celeriter, inquit, missis Legatis per suos Principes inter se conjurant; Nihil nisi communi consilio acturos, eundemque omnis Fortunæ exitum esse laturos; reliquasque Civitates solicitant, ut in ea Libertate, quam à Majoribus acceperant, permanere, quam Romanorum servitutem perferre maluit.
units.tr: Caesar, in book 3, sets out an example of the amphictyony of the Celts in the Armorican states, which formed the noblest part of Celtica. He describes the conspiracy of the Veneti, Osismii, Namnetes, Diablintes, Curiosolites, Unelli and others, which led to the Venetian war: "They quickly sent envoys through their chief men and bound themselves together, resolving to act only by common counsel and to share whatever fate came to them. They also urged the remaining states to remain in that liberty which they had received from their ancestors, rather than endure Roman slavery."

units.la: Belgica nomen dedisse creditur Belgis Civitas. Isidorus lib. xiiii. Etymologic. cap. iv. Belgis autem Civitas est Gallia, à qua Belgica Provincia dicta est. Sic Stephanus Byzantius: Βελγικὴ, αἱτ, ἡ χώρα, ὡς Βαυτικὴ. Ἔστι δὲ ἡ Βελγικὴ, ἡ χώρα. Hanc Urbem Vulgus interpretatur Bruay. Abrahamus Ortelius in operoso Geographiæ Thesauro audet ex ea facere Veltfig vel Veltfick (Pagus est Flandriæ, ab Gandavo plus minus tribus distans milliaribus) propter, inquit, non tantum majorem fori adlusionem, sed & propter Loci antiquitatem, quam ostendunt ruinarum sub terra multa hactenus vestigia: unde singulis diebus fere omne genus veteris Supellectilis, ut Simulacra, Numismata, Vasculæ, & alia, eruuntur. Veltfick tamen nonnulli interpretantur Ciceronis Castra. de qua re alibi. Belgas omnium Gallorum fortissimos scribit Cæsar lib. i. Sic Ammianus lib. xv: Horum omnium apud Veteres Belgæ dicebantur esse fortissimi. Strabo lib. iv: Τούτων δὲ τὰς Βελγας ... Publicum Belgarum Concilium delineat Cæsar lib. iii; eo contra Cæsarem publice pro Galliæ totius libertate conjuratum, & ad Galbam Suessionum regem propter justitiam prudentiamque, summam totius Belli omnium voluntate fuisse delatam: atque ad ipsum Bellum de suo numero contulisse Armatorum millia, Bellovacos sexaginta, Suessiones quinquaginta, totidem Nervios, Atrebates quindecim, Ambianos decem, Morinos viginti quinque, Menapios septem. Caletos decem, Velocasses & Veromandu̅s totidem, Aduaticos nouemdecim; Condrusos, Eburones, Cerefos, Pæmanos, qui uno nomine Germani appellabantur, quadraginta.
units.tr: It is believed that the city of the Belgae gave the name to Belgica. Isidore, Etymologiae book 14, chapter 4: "The Belgae are a state of Gaul, from which the province of Belgica takes its name." So too Stephanus of Byzantium: "Belgica is the region, as Bautica is." This town the common people call Bruay. Abraham Ortelius, in his laborious Thesaurus Geographiae, ventures to make it Veltfig or Veltfick (a village of Flanders, some three miles from Ghent), "not only because of the greater resemblance to the market, but also because of the antiquity of the place, which the many traces of ruins under the ground have shown until now; from which almost every day all kinds of old household goods, such as statues, coins, small vessels and other things, are dug up." Some, however, translate Veltfick as Ciceronis Castra; but of this matter elsewhere. Caesar writes that the Belgae were the bravest of all the Gauls, book 1. So Ammianus, book 15: "Of all these, the Belgae were said by the ancients to be the bravest." Strabo, book 4: "Of these, the Belgae..." [Τούτων δὲ τὰς Βελγας]. Caesar, book 3, describes the public council of the Belgae, in which, against Caesar, a conspiracy was made publicly for the liberty of all Gaul; and the supreme command of the whole war was, by the will of all, conferred on Galba, king of the Suessiones, for his justice and prudence. For the war itself they contributed from their own number armed men: the Bellovaci sixty thousand, the Suessiones fifty thousand, the Nervii as many, the Atrebates fifteen thousand, the Ambiani ten thousand, the Morini twenty-five thousand, the Menapii seven thousand, the Caleti ten thousand, the Velocasses and Veromandui as many, the Aduatuci nineteen thousand; the Condrusi, Eburones, Caeroesi and Paemani, who were called Germans by a single name, forty thousand.

units.la: Quum autem Aquitania tertia Comata pars, facta cum alterutra, vel Celtica vel Belgica commissione, nimis videretur exigua, ἐπέδη, inquit Strabo lib. iv, μικρὰ μέρος ὧν η ποιῦν, loquens de Aquitania) C. Cæsar Octavianus Augustus Distributionem illam non solum castigavit, sed etiam in nova Galliarum Divisione instituenda, Bracatam est complexus; quidquid intra Alpes, Mare Mediterraneum, Oceanum & Renum continetur, uno Galliarum nomine comprehendens. Sic universa Gallia partita est in Narbonensem, quæ & Bracata, Aquitanicam, Celtica vel Lugdunensem, & Belgicam. Hanc divisionem sequuti sunt Strabo, Plinius, Ptolemæus, Mela, & alij.
units.tr: Since Aquitania, the third part of Comata Gaul, made together with one or the other, either Celtica or Belgica, seemed too small, Strabo, book 4, says (speaking of Aquitania): "[ἐπέδη] it is a small part of the whole" [μικρὰ μέρος ὧν η ποιῦν]. Gaius Caesar Octavianus Augustus not only found fault with that division, but also, in arranging the new division of Gaul, embraced Bracata, comprehending everything contained within the Alps, the Mediterranean Sea, the Ocean and the Rhine under the single name of Gaul. Thus all Gaul was divided into Narbonensis, which is also Bracata, Aquitanica, Celtica or Lugdunensis, and Belgica. Strabo, Pliny, Ptolemy, Mela and others followed this division.

units.la: Galliarum itaque Distributiones per varios gradus ad subscriptum deduxi χῆμα.
units.tr: I have therefore reduced the divisions of Gaul, through various stages, to the form set out below [σχῆμα].

units.la: In utraque autem Transalpinæ Galliæ Partitione, tam quæ ante Augusti fuit Principatum, quam quæ sub eodem cœpit, non idem ab Geographis tribuuntur Partibus Fines. Helvetios tamen Cæsar quidem jungit Celticæ, quæ illi versus Ortum dilatatur ad Renum usque: Plinius autem & Ptolemæus collocant in Belgica, quam illi versus Euronotum producunt ad Pœninas usque Alpes. Iam vero Belgicam Cæsar ab Reno ad Matronam, Plinius ab Scaldi ad Sequanam extendunt: sed hic Vogesum transcendit, ut comprehendat Helvetios; ille intra eundem montem se continet, ut eosdem Populos hinc excludat, Celticæ jam adcensitos. Terminus denique inter Celtas & Aquitanos Garumna est Cæsari & Pomponio Melæ; Ligeris autem Straboni & Ptolemæo ex Augusti instituto.
units.tr: In both divisions of Transalpine Gaul, both the one that was before the principate of Augustus and the one that began under him, the geographers do not assign the same boundaries to the regions. Caesar, indeed, joins the Helvetii to Celtica, which extends eastward to the Rhine; but Pliny and Ptolemy place them in Belgica, which they extend southward to the Pennine Alps. Further, Caesar extends Belgica from the Rhine to the Marne, Pliny from the Scheldt to the Seine; but the latter crosses the Vosges, so as to include the Helvetii, while the former keeps within the same mountain so as to exclude these peoples, who were by then already assigned to Celtica. Finally, the boundary between the Celts and the Aquitanians is the Garonne for Caesar and Pomponius Mela, but the Loire for Strabo and Ptolemy, following the arrangement of Augustus.

units.la: Sequentibus porro temporibus, ut commodius Gallia gubernaretur, quidquid intra Fines, quos jam indicavi, situm, in decem & septem Provincias ab Augusto Cæsare est distributum: quæ in Notitia Provinciarum Romanarum Imperij Occidentalis (cujus Auctor existimatur Marianus Scotus) sic recensentur.
units.tr: In later times, moreover, so that Gaul might be governed more conveniently, all that lay within the boundaries I have already indicated was divided by Augustus Caesar into seventeen provinces. These are listed thus in the Notitia of the Roman provinces of the Western Empire (whose author is thought to be Marianus Scotus).

units.la: Edita sunt hæc paulo sequiore ordine ab Antonio Schoonhovio cum Eutropij historia Romana, & Andrea Schotto cum Antonini Itinerario. Adjecerunt autem illi Galliarum Provinciarum Civitates ex B. Isidori Breviculo seu Canonibus, ut etiam censet Petrus Pithoeus lib. ii. Adversf. Subiec. cap. i: quæ quum depravatæ admodum circumferantur, ex Veteribus Codicibus emendatas, liberalitate Magni Scaligeri, adjecta etiam Interpretatione, proponam. Sciat autem Lector, quidquid discrepat ab Excusis, esse id ab scripta lectione.
units.tr: These provinces were published in a slightly later order by Antonius Schoonhovius, together with Eutropius's Roman history, and by Andreas Schott, together with Antoninus's Itinerary. Those editors also added the cities of the Gallic provinces, taken from the Breviculus or Canons of St Isidore, as Petrus Pithoeus also thinks (Adversaria, book 2, chapter 1). Since these lists circulate in a badly corrupted state, I shall set them out emended from old manuscripts, through the generosity of Joseph Scaliger, with a translation added. The reader should know that wherever this differs from the printed editions, the difference comes from the manuscript reading.

units.la: Notitiam hanc Provinciarum Galliæ in Membranis etiam mihi monstravit in Bibliotheca, quam habet instructissimam cum ab Impressis, tum MSS. Libris V. CL. Bonaventura Vulcanius, Græcæ Linguæ in Academia Batavorum Professor, Collega mihi amicissimus. In ea (nec & hæc indicta mihi abeant) ad Lugdunensem II post Civitatum Abrincantum, additur Civitas Ebroicorum, cui recentiore manu innotatum Evancorum: non dubito, quin qui libellum exaravit, scribere voluerit Eburonum, Eborum vel Hburovicum. Nam & his in Lugdunensi II sedes erant, ut cap. xxx dicam. Hodie L'Evesché d'Eureux. Sequebatur mox in ipsdem Membranis Civitas Salarum, id est, Saiorum: quod monco, non probo. Ad Germaniam II. Civitatis Tungrorum subiicitur Civitas Nova, I. Leodium. In fine Viennensis I notatur etiam Civitas Massiliensium, quæ aliis deest. 20
units.tr: I was shown this list of the provinces of Gaul in manuscript as well, in the library which our most learned Bonaventura Vulcanius, Professor of Greek in the Academy of the Dutch, a most friendly colleague of mine, possesses in great abundance, both of printed and manuscript books. In it (and let these things not pass unremarked by me), after the city of the Abrincatui, in Lugdunensis II, the city of the Ebroici is added, to which, in a more recent hand, is noted "of the Evancii". I do not doubt that the writer of the little book meant to write Eburonum, Eborum or Eburovicum. For they also had their seat in Lugdunensis II, as I shall say in chapter 30. Today it is the bishopric of Évreux. Next in the same manuscript comes the city of the Salarum, that is, of the Saii: which I suggest, but do not prove. In Germania II, after the city of the Tungri, the city Nova is added, that is, Liège. At the end of Vienna I, the city of the Massilienses is also noted, which is missing in others. 20

units.la: Ammianus Marcellinus lib. xv confuse quæ in Notitia Provinciarum, & non satis plene commemorat: At nunc numerantur Provincia per omnem ambitum Galiarum: SECUNDA GERMANIA, Prima ab Occidentali exordiens cardine, Agrippina & Tungris munita, Civitatibus amplis & copiosis. Dein PRIMA GERMANIA; ubi, præter alia Munitipia, Magontiacum est, & Vangiones, & Nemetes, & Argentoratus, barbaricis Cladibus nota. Post hæs BELGICA PRIMA, Mediomatricas pertendens, & Treveros, Domicilium Principum clarum. Huic adnexa est SECUNDA BELGICA; quæ Ambiani sunt, Vrbs inter alias eminens, Catallauni & Remi. Apud SEQVANOS (designat MAXIMAM SEQVANORVM, quæ & LVGDVNENSIS QVINTA) Vesuntios vidimus, & Raurices, alys pottores Gpidis multis. LVGDVNENSEM PRIMAM Lugdunum ornat, & Cabalitiones, & Senones (pertinent hi apud alios ad LVGDVNENSEM QVARTAM) & Bituriges (commemorantur ijs, qui in AQVITANIA PRIMA) & mœnium-Augustoduni magnitudo vetusta. SECVNDAM enim LVGDVNENSEM Rotomagi, & Turini Mediolanum (legendum Turoni & Cenomani: qui duo Populi ab alijs concenseentur LVGDVNENSI TERTIÆ) ostendunt: & Trecassini (Trecasses alij describunt in LVGDVNENSI QVARTA.) ALPES GRAIÆ & PENINÆ (notat Provinciam VIENNENSEM QVINTAM) exceptis obscurioribus, habent & Aventicum (hæc tamen Vrbs ab alijs ponitur in LVGDVNENSI QVINTA) desertam quidem Civitatem, sed non ignobilem quondam, ut ædificia semiruta nunc quoque demonstrant. Ha Provinciæ Vrbesque sunt splendida Galliarum. In Aquitania, quæ Pyrenæos Montes, & cum parte specie Oceani, quæ pertinet ad Hispanos, prima Provincia est AQVITANICA (universum sumta pro PRIMA, SECVNDA, TERTIA: nam Vox Prima apud Ammianum non ordinis esse videtur, sed dignitatis: Prima, præcipua est Aquitanica, si cum alijs 30 Aquitania Regionibus, ut Novempopulonia & Narbonensi committatur) amplitudine Civitatum admodum culta: emissis a.ys multis, Burdegala & Arverni (in AQVITANIA PRIMA) excellunt, & Santones & Pictavi (uterque Populus in AQVITANIA SECVNDA.) NOVEM POPVLOS (NOVEMPOPVLANIA eadem cum AQVITANIA TERTIA & VIENNENSI OCTAVA) Auscitanorum commendant & Vasates. In NARBONENSI (eadem cum VIENNENSI SECVNDA) clusa est Narbona & Tolosa, quæ principatum Vrbium tenent. VIENNENSIS (PRIMAM significat) Civitatum exsultat decore multarum, quibus potiores sunt Vienna ipsa, & Arelate, & Valentia: quibus Massilia jungitur, cujus societate & viribus in discriminibus arduis fultam aliquoties legimus Romam. His prope Salluvij sunt, & Nicaea, & Antipolis, Insulaeque Stœchades. Nominat ordinis incuriosior Lugdunensem Primam, Lugdunensem Secundam, Maximam Sequanorum (quae eadem cum Lugdunensi Quinta) Belgicam Primam, Belgicam Secundam, Germaniam Primam, Germaniam Secundam, Viennensem Primam, Narbonensem (eamdem cum Viennensi Secunda) Alpes Graias & Peninas (quae in Viennensi Quinta) Aquitanicas Primam & Secundam, Novempopulaniam denique, vel Aquitaniam Tertiam: nullam faciens mentionem, ad plenum xvii Provinciarum numerum constituendum, Lugdunensis Tertiae & Quartae: nullam item Viennensis Tertiae & Quartae.
units.tr: Ammianus Marcellinus, book 15, mixes things up and mentions them not quite fully, in the list of provinces: "But now the provinces are counted through the whole circuit of the Gauls: SECOND GERMANY, beginning from the western hinge, fortified by Agrippina and the Tungri, with large and populous cities. Then FIRST GERMANY, where, besides other municipalities, there is Mainz, and the Vangiones, and the Nemetes, and Strasbourg, known for barbarian disasters. After these, FIRST BELGIUM, stretching to the Mediomatrici, and the Treveri, a famous home of princes. Joined to it is SECOND BELGIUM, in which are Amiens, a city outstanding among the others, the Catalauni and the Remi.
