Among the SEQUANI (he means the MAXIMA SEQUANORUM, which is also LUGDUNENSIS V) we have seen Besançon, and Augst, and other towns rich in many ornaments. LUGDUNENSIS I is adorned by Lyon, and the Cabalitiones, and the Senones (these belong, according to others, to LUGDUNENSIS IV) and the Bituriges (they are mentioned among those in AQUITANIA I) and the ancient greatness of the walls of Autun. For SECOND LUGDUNENSIS, Rouen and the Turones and Mediolanum (read Turones and Cenomani: which two peoples are reckoned by others among LUGDUNENSIS III) show it: and the Trecasses (other writers describe the Trecasses in LUGDUNENSIS IV). The GRAIAN and PENNINE ALPS (he means the Province of VIENNA V), apart from the more obscure places, have also Avenches (though this city is placed by others in LUGDUNENSIS V), a city indeed deserted, but once not ignoble, as half-ruined buildings still show today. These are the splendid provinces and cities of the Gauls. In Aquitaine, which lies beyond the Pyrenean mountains, and along with part of the ocean which belongs to the Spaniards, the first province is AQUITANICA (taken as a whole for FIRST, SECOND, THIRD: for the word 'first' in Ammianus seems to refer not to order but to dignity: 'first' means that Aquitania is the chief, if it is joined with the other Aquitanian regions, such as Novempopulonia and Narbonensis) very cultivated for the size of its cities: with many peoples sent forth, Bordeaux and the Arverni (in AQUITANIA I) excel, and the Santones and the Pictavi (each people in AQUITANIA II). They commend the NINE PEOPLES (NOVEMPOPULANIA, the same as AQUITANIA III and VIENNA VIII) of the Auscii and the Vasates. In NARBONENSIS (the same as VIENNA II) Narbonne and Toulouse are enclosed, and they hold the chief place among the cities. VIENNENSIS (meaning PRIMA) exults in the splendour of many cities, of which the more important are Vienne itself, and Arles, and Valence: to which Marseilles is joined, whose alliance and forces we read have several times supported Rome in grave dangers. Near these are the Salluvii, and Nice, and Antibes, and the Stoechad islands. The less careful of the order names Lugdunensis Prima, Lugdunensis Secunda, Maxima Sequanorum (which is the same as Lugdunensis Quinta), Belgica Prima, Belgica Secunda, Germania Prima, Germania Secunda, Viennensis Prima, Narbonensis (the same as Viennensis Secunda), the Graian and Pennine Alps (which are in Viennensis Quinta), Aquitanica Prima and Secunda, and finally Novempopulania or Aquitania Tertia: making no mention, in order to fill out the full number of seventeen provinces, of Lugdunensis Tertia and Quarta: and likewise none of Viennensis Tertia and Quarta.

units.la: Hæ igitur Septemdecim sunt Provinciæ, in quas Augustus Cæsar Gallias divisit, & in quibus Constantinus Magnus varia Officia & Magistratus constituit; ut in Notitia Provinciarum Imperij Romani plenius est videre. De Primis nonnihil addam. Constantinus, de quo dixi, instituti quatuor Præfectus Prætorio, duobus in Oriente, totidem in Occidente; alterum Occidentis in Urbe Roma, alterum in Urbe Treverensi collocavit, qui Præfectus Prætorio Galliarum vocatus fuit: & quia per occupationes Imperij in illis Urbibus perpetuo haerere ipsis non licebat, Vicarij aliquot eis sunt attributi, qui eadem potestate Provincijs Ius redderent. Præfecto igitur Prætorij Galliarum tres Vicarij dati. Primo Sedes designata Treveris, Secundo Lugduni, Tertio Viennae. Ideoque ut horum Vicariorum magna erat auctoritas, ita Urbium quoque, in quibus Sedem habebant, maxima claritas. Treverensi Vicario parebant Prima & Secunda Germania, & Belgica, & tota Britannia Insula: Lugdunensi quatuor Lugdunensis cum Maxima Sequanorum: Viennensi Prima & Secunda Narbonensis & Aquitania, Alpes Graiae & Poenina, Alpes Maritimae, Novempopulania. Totum illud, quod unius Vicarij Iurisdictioni subjacebat, Latini quo modo designarint, non constat: sed Græci Ἐξαρχίαν, Διοίκησιν, Πατρίδα vocabant.
units.tr: These, then, are the seventeen provinces into which Augustus Caesar divided the Gauls, and in which Constantine the Great established various offices and magistracies; as may be seen more fully in the Notitia of the Provinces of the Roman Empire. I shall add something about the first. Constantine, of whom I have spoken, established four Praetorian Prefects, two in the East, as many in the West; he placed one of the West in the city of Rome, and the other in the city of Trier, and he who was called Praetorian Prefect of the Gauls was in that city. And since, because of the upheavals of the empire, it was not always allowed for them to remain in those cities, several Vicars were assigned to them, who by the same power rendered justice to the provinces. Three Vicars were therefore given to the Praetorian Prefect of the Gauls. The first had his seat appointed at Trier, the second at Lyon, the third at Vienne. Hence, as the authority of these Vicars was great, so too was the high renown of the cities in which they had their seats. To the Vicar of Trier were subject the First and Second Germany, and Belgica, and the whole island of Britain: to the Vicar of Lyon, the four Lugdunenses together with the Maxima Sequanorum: to the Vicar of Vienne, the First and Second Narbonensis and Aquitania, the Graian and Pennine Alps, the Maritime Alps, Novempopulania. How the Latins designated the whole that lay under the jurisdiction of one Vicar is not certain: but the Greeks called it Exarchy [Ἐξαρχίαν], Dioecesis [Διοίκησιν], Patria [Πατρίδα].

units.la: Sequens ætas, quum jam Romanorum Imperium ad exitium vergeret, sensimque suis partibus variorum Populorum incursibus miserum in modum truncaretur, varie Galliæ distribuit. Quum enim Gothi Francique omnia occupassent, alia ibi coeperunt esse Gothorum, alia Francorum, alia Romanorum Gallorumque Indigenarum, quorum, quod à priorum nutu & arbitrio penderent, inferior pejorque erat conditio. Præcipue ex Fœdere inter Constantium Comitem & Walliam Gothorum Regem, quod incidit in annum Christi cccccxvi, quo cos. erant Theodosius Iunior Augustus vii, & Iunius Quartus Palladius. Consulendi Prosper, Cassiodorus, Iornandes in histor. Gothor. cap. xxxii, Paullus Diaconus lib. iv, Isidorus in Chronico Gothorum. De Limite etiam inter Gothos & Romanos multa legere est apud Sidonium Apollinarem, cum primis lib. i. epist. vii, lib. iii. epist. i, lib. vii. epist. vi, lib. viii. epist. iii. Anno cccclxi Childerico iv Francorum Rege Regia dignitate ob Luxum, cui deditus erat, & Tributa, quibus Populum vexabat, exuto; habenisque Ægidio Romano Magistro Militum, qui pro Romanis apud Suessones sedebat, magno animorum consensu traditis; expacto maxima Lugdunensis Galliæ pars Romanis, Narbonensis & omnis Aquitania Gothis: quidquid ab Rheno ad Ligerim Merovæi cessit. Videndi Vigebertus, Trithemius, Otto Frisingensis lib. iv. cap. xxxii, Gregorius Turonensis lib. ii. cap. xii & alij.
units.tr: A later age, when the Roman empire was already tending to ruin and was gradually being cut to pieces in a wretched manner on its own parts by the incursions of various peoples, divided Gaul in various ways. For when the Goths and the Franks had occupied everything, some parts began to belong to the Goths, some to the Franks, some to the Romans and the native Gauls, whose condition was lower and worse, because it depended on the nod and will of the former. This was especially so by the covenant between Constantius the Count and Walia, king of the Goths, which fell in the year of Christ 416, when Theodosius the Younger, Augustus for the seventh time, and Junius Quartus Palladius, were consuls. Consult Prosper, Cassiodorus, Jordanes in the History of the Goths, chapter 32, Paulus Diaconus book 4, Isidore in the Chronicle of the Goths. Much about the boundary between the Goths and the Romans may also be read in Sidonius Apollinaris, especially book 1 letter 7, book 3 letter 1, book 7 letter 6, book 8 letter 3. In the year 461, Childeric IV, king of the Franks, was stripped of royal dignity on account of the luxury to which he was devoted and the tributes with which he burdened the people; and the reins were handed over, with great agreement of minds, to Aegidius, the Roman Master of the Soldiers, who sat for the Romans at Soissons; and thus the greatest part of Gallia Lugdunensis was assigned to the Romans, Narbonensis and all Aquitania to the Goths, and whatever lay from the Rhine to the Loire fell to the Merovingians. See Vigebert, Trithemius, Otto of Freising book 4 chapter 32, Gregory of Tours book 2 chapter 12, and others.

units.la: Tempore Iustiniani Galliarum Regna leguntur sex, Parisiorum, Mediomatricum, Aurelianorum, Suessonum, Burgundorum, Aquitanorum. Adeundi Venantius Fortunatus, Paulus Diaconus, Gregorius Turonensis, Sigebertus, Regino, Ado Viennensis reliquique Francici Scriptores.
units.tr: In the time of Justinian the kingdoms of Gaul are said to be six: the Parisians, the Mediomatrici, the Aurelians, the Suessones, the Burgundians, and the Aquitanians. On this, see Venantius Fortunatus, Paulus Diaconus, Gregory of Tours, Sigebert, Regino, Ado of Vienne, and the other Frankish writers.

units.la: Post Karoli Magni Principatum illa Divisio, quamquam antea non prorsus ignota, obtinuit; ut alia diceretur Austrasia, id est Orientalis; alia Vvestria (corrupte enim quibusdam scribitur Neustria) id est Occidentalis: ut iidem Scriptores testantur.
units.tr: After the reign of Charlemagne this division, though not entirely unknown before, prevailed, so that one part was called Austrasia, that is, the Eastern, and the other Vvestria (for some write it wrongly as Neustria), that is, the Western. The same writers attest this.

units.la: Sic igitur Regnorum vices multa, ut vidimus, in Antiquis Divisionibus immutarunt: sed (ut in litteris suis ad me Nobilissimus Vir Iosephus Scaliger, de sua Gallia) Status Ecclesiasticus tam in Oriente quam in Occidente ejus integra Vestigia hactenus retinuit. Nam Civitates, quae Provincijs nomina fecerunt, Μητροπόλεις vocant, & si in eis sedes fuerit Vicarij, quem Ἐξαρχον dicebant, eas non solum Μητροπόλεις, Ἐξαρχοι πόλεις, sed & Ἐξαρχίας, & Πατριαρχίας nominant; & Præsules earum Ἐξάρχας & Πατριάρχας. reliquos μητροπολίτας ᾗ Ἀρχιεπισκόπους, qui sub se tantum Ἐπισκόπους habent: Nam οἱ Ἐξάρχαι sub se, præter Ἐπισκόπους, etiam μητροπολίτας habent: μητροπολίται vero tantum ἐπισκόπους. In Ecclesia Latina Archiepiscoporum & nomen & jus manet, & Iurisdictio Canonica in suos Episcopos Suffraganeos: sed Ἐξαρχᾶν nulla vestigia exstant: nisi forte quædam umbra ejus fuerit, quod Metropolita sive Archiepiscopus Viennensis Primatem Primatum sese appellat. Eo enim ostendit sub se Primates habuisse, qui sub eo essent, Narbonensem Primatem Provinciæ, Bituricensem Primatem Aquitaniæ. Aliter quo modo, aut quo jure, Primas Primatum diceretur, nisi ratione Diœcesios Vicarij Viennensis Præf. Præt. Prætorio, qui septem Provincias sub se habebat, in quibus Prima Narbonensis & Prima Aquitania? Quod vero Lugdunensis Primatem se vocari gaudeat, numerum est, & illi ex beneficio Romani Pontificis indultum: neque tamen adeo novum est. Nam Guilhelmus Brito in sua Philippeide ita canit:
units.tr: Thus, as we have seen, the changes of kingdoms have altered much in the old divisions; but (as the most noble Joseph Scaliger wrote to me in his letters concerning his own Gaul) the ecclesiastical order, both in the East and in the West, has kept its whole traces up to now. For the cities that gave their names to provinces are called metropolises [Μητροπόλεις], and if the seat of a vicar, whom they called exarch [Ἐξαρχον], was in them, they are named not only metropolises but exarchal cities [Ἐξαρχοι πόλεις], and exarchates [Ἐξαρχίας] and patriarchates [Πατριαρχίας]; and their bishops are called exarchs [Ἐξάρχας] and patriarchs [Πατριάρχας]. The rest are metropolitans or archbishops [μητροπολίτας ᾗ Ἀρχιεπισκόπους], who have only bishops under them. For the exarchs have under them, besides bishops, also metropolitans [μητροπολίτας], while metropolitans have only bishops [ἐπισκόπους]. In the Latin Church the name and right of archbishops remain, and canonical jurisdiction over their suffragan bishops; but no traces of the exarchs survive, unless perhaps some shadow of them is that the metropolitan or archbishop of Vienne calls himself the Primate of Primates. For by this he shows that he had primates under him, who were subject to him, the Primate of the province of Narbonne and the Primate of Aquitaine. Otherwise, how or by what right would he be called Primate of Primates, except by reason of the diocese of the Vicar of the Praetorian Prefect of Vienne, who had seven provinces under him, among which were the First Narbonensis and the First Aquitania? As for the Archbishop of Lyon rejoicing to be called Primate, this is a matter of honour, and was granted to him by favour of the Roman Pontiff; yet it is not so very new. For Guillaume le Breton sings thus in his Philippeid:

units.la: Et Lugdunensis, quo Gallia tota solebat,Ut fama est, Primate regi.
units.tr: And Lyon, by whose primate, as fame has it, all Gaul used to be ruled.

units.la: At Primas Primatum antea dici jure non potuit, quia nullam Primam Provinciam sub se habebat. Viennensis Primas quidem Primatum vocari vult, sed Caullam tam ille, quam omnis Ecclesia ignorat. Quapropter Divisio Galliarum per Diœceses Ecclesiasticas & Episcopatus, ut omnium antiquissima, ita certissima nobis sequenda erat, neque ulla melior erat quærenda, si integræ illæ Ἐξαρχίαι adhuc finibus Regni Francorum continerentur, ut olim sub Karolo Magno, & ejus filio & Nepotibus: sed quia ex illo amplissimo Imperio multæ Provinciæ detractæ sunt, alia nobis Tributio instituenda. Galliæ igitur sive Franciæ Imperium octo Tribunalibus temperatur, quæ ius reddunt Provincijs suis, à quibus Provocatio non est, quorumque & Majestas augustissima est & Auctoritas sacrosancta. Parlamenta Galli Idiomate suo vocant, ut prolixius docui capite xvii. Non possum meliorem Partitionis rationem inire, quam si in octo hæc Parlamenta omne Francorum Regnum dividam, & ea in Provincias suas. Provincias quidem novi, quot Galliæ Reges adipiscitur, tot fere Mutationes, Nomina & Regimina subire; eam ob causam non ignorans consultius esse ut à Parlamentis Divisio procederet porro per Diœceses & Episcopatus, quum etiam illa proxime accedat ad priscam Imperij Romani notitiam: sed quia Geographis in more positum, ut quæ suis temporibus obtinent in Regnorum Regionumque terminis, ea quam fidelissime fieri potest, indicent & proponant, religio mihi ab recepta tam multis probataque hactenus consuetudine discedere. Quamobrem talem ego docendi, Galliasque commode cumque structu explicandi gratia, Distributionem excogitavi.
units.tr: But the primate could not rightly be called Primate of Primates before, because he had no First Province under him. The Primate of Vienne wishes to be called Primate of Primates, but that title is unknown to Caulla, and to the whole Church as well. Therefore the division of Gaul by ecclesiastical dioceses and bishoprics, as the most ancient of all, is also the most certain for us to follow, and no better one should be sought, if those whole exarchates were still contained within the borders of the kingdom of the Franks, as once under Charlemagne and his son and grandsons. But since many provinces have been taken away from that vast empire, another arrangement must be devised by us. The realm of Gaul, or France, is therefore governed by eight courts, which administer justice to their provinces, from which there is no appeal, and whose majesty is most august and whose authority sacrosanct. The French call them parlements in their own idiom, as I explained more fully in chapter xvii. I cannot devise a better plan of division than to divide the whole kingdom of the Franks into these eight parlements, and their provinces into them. I know that the provinces, as many as the kings of Gaul have acquired, have undergone almost as many changes of names and governments; for that reason, not ignoring that it is more prudent for the division to proceed further by dioceses and bishoprics, since that also comes closest to the ancient knowledge of the Roman Empire, yet because it is the custom of geographers to show and set out, as faithfully as possible, the boundaries of kingdoms and regions as they stand in their own times, I have thought it a duty not to depart from a custom so widely received and so long approved. Therefore I have devised such a distribution for the sake of teaching, and for explaining Gaul conveniently in whatever order.

units.la: Galliarum hodierna distributio.
units.tr: The present division of Gaul.

units.la: Provinciæ quæ in Galliarum delineatione ab Geographis hodie solent exponi, aliæ Francorum sunt Regis, vel Regi subjectæ; aliæ extra Francorum Ditionem. Quæ prioris generis optime meoque Instituto convenientissime, divido in sua Parlamenta, quæ, ut dixi, octo sunt numero: Unum quidem Principale; reliqua Accessoria. Principale est Parisiense, omnium Primum, & olim unicum solumque Parlamenti Parisiensis Sedes Præsidiales, ut multæ (nam latissime ejus se extendit iurisdictio) sic variæ admodum sunt, in variis constitutæ Provincijs. Ligeris facit alias Septemtrionales, alias Meridionales. Quod ad Priores in Vetere quidem Belgica, hodie est Picardia La Picardie, in Celtica vero versus Occidentem Francia, La France, strictius sumta (cujus tamen etiam nonnulla incidunt in Belgicam) & Brisia, La Beausse: versus ortum Campania, La Champagne, & Lugdunensis tractus, Pais de Lionnois. Quod ad Meridionales, posside bat eas olim ex Veterum delineatione, cum Narbonensi, Aquitanica. Dicebatur autem Aquitania in dextra Garumnæ ripa, partim Prima, ubi hodie cis Vigennam Bituricum, Berry, & Borbonium, Bourbonnois; ultra vero Pictonium Poitou, Ageraque & Incultensis Angoulesme, & Alnistensis, Le Pais d'Aulnis: partim Secunda, ubi nunc Arvernia, Auvergne. Accessoria Parlamenta sunt, quæ Principale illud quasi circumeunt, versus Occidentem ad Ligeris dextram Rotomagense, sub quo Normannia, La Normandie: & Redonense cui subest Britannia, La Bretagne: ad sinistram Burdigalense & Tolosinum, quorum quodque sua extendit jura nunc integre & separatim; nunc vero multum in aliquot adsignatas sibi Veteris Aquitaniæ Narbonensisque Galliæ Ditiones.
units.tr: The provinces that geographers nowadays usually set out in their description of Gaul are partly under the King of the Franks or subject to the King, and partly outside the dominion of the Franks. I divide those of the first kind, which suit my plan best and most conveniently, into their parlements, which, as I said, are eight in number: one principal and the rest subordinate. The principal one is the Parisian, the first of all, and formerly the sole seat of the Parisian parlement. Its presidial seats, as many as they are (for its jurisdiction extends very widely), are also very varied, being situated in various provinces. On the side of the Loire, some lie in the north and some in the south. As for the northern ones, in old Belgica there is today Picardy (La Picardie); in Celtic Gaul, towards the west, France (La France), taken more narrowly (though some parts of it also fall within Belgica), and Brie (La Beausse); towards the east Champagne (La Champagne), and the Lyonnais district (Pais de Lionnois). As for the southern ones, formerly, according to the old delineation, they held Narbonensis and Aquitania. Aquitania was said to lie on the right bank of the Garonne, partly the First, where today, on this side of the Vienne, are Bourges (Berry) and Bourbon (Bourbonnois); but beyond the Vienne are Poitou (Poitou), Angoumois (Angoulesme), and Aunis (Le Pais d'Aulnis); partly the Second, where now is Auvergne (Auvergne). The subordinate parlements are those that surround that principal one as it were, towards the west on the right of the Loire: the Rouen parlement, under which lies Normandy (La Normandie), and the Rennes parlement, under which lies Brittany (La Bretagne); on the left, the Bordeaux and Toulouse parlements, each of which extends its jurisdiction now wholly and separately, and now largely into some territories assigned to them from old Aquitania and Narbonensis Gaul.

units.la: Integre quidem Burdigalensi subiiciunt LEMOVICIVM, Limoges, PETROCORIVM, Perigord, GVIENNA, La Guienne; Tolosano autem CADVRCIVM, Quercy, RVTENIVM, Rouargue, LANGVEDOXIVM, Languedoc: Multum vero utrique VASCONIA, La Gascogne: quemadmodum plenius ex sequentibus patebit. Iam versus Orientem ad Mare Gallicum, Parlamentum est Aquensi, cuius iurisdictioni obtemperat PROVINCIA, La Provence; in Mediterraneis Gratianopolitanum, ab cuius nutu pendet DELPHINATVS, Le Dauphiné & Dyensonensi, quod in iure Summo dicundo agnoscit DVCATVS BVRGVNDIÆ, La Duché de Bourgogne. Hactenus quæ Regis. Extra Ditionem Francorum, in Francia tamen, suos habent etiam Dominatus alii Principes, & Ecclesiastici & Politici. Pontificis enim Romani est COMITATVS AVENIONENSIS, Avignon; Politicorum alii sunt Ducatus, ut SABAVDIA, Savoye, & LOTHARINGIA, Lorraine; alii sunt Principatus, ut BEARNIA, Bearn, & ARAVSIO, Aurange; alii Comitatus, ut BVRGVNDIA, La Comté de Bourgogne & CAROLESIVM, Charolois. Has Regiones si fideliter ordine a me indicato perambulato, Lectores spero ita iudicaturos, me nullam non partem, vel obiter, attigisse: plerasque Vrbes adiisse; &, si non omnia, praecipua saltem de singulis dixisse. Illud obiter hic monendum duxi, Appianum testari Gallicarum Gentium numerum, fuisse Tetragonicam · Πόλις ἐπὶ ἐκ ἔτεσι ... xeoriae. Minor est numerus in Templo, quod ab omnibus communi consilio Gallis Augusto Lugduni exstructum: de quo Strabo lib. iv. ... Vnde tanta in numero Gentium Galliæ discrepantia? Appianum existimo Gentes universim designare totius Galliæ; eas fuisse circiter quadringentas: Aram autem Lugdunensem eas tantum habuisse, a quibus illa in Augusti honorem fuit posita, sexaginta scilicet.
units.tr: Wholly, indeed, the Bordeaux parlement holds under it LEMOVICES, Limoges, PETROCORII, Périgord, and GUIENNE, La Guienne; the Toulouse parlement holds CADURCI, Quercy, RUTENI, Rouergue, and LANGUEDOC, Languedoc. Largely both hold GASCONY, La Gascogne, as will appear more fully from what follows. Now towards the east, on the Gallic Sea, is the Aix parlement (Aquensi), to whose jurisdiction the province of PROVENCE, La Provence, submits. In the inland part is the Grenoble parlement (Gratianopolitanum), at whose nod the DAUPHINÉ depends, Le Dauphiné, and the Dijon parlement (Dyensonensi), which acknowledges the DUCHY OF BURGUNDY, La Duché de Bourgogne, as its supreme court of law. So far the regions of the King. Outside the dominion of the Franks, yet in France, other princes, both ecclesiastical and secular, also have their own dominions. For the COUNTY OF AVIGNON, Avignon, belongs to the Roman Pontiff; among the secular lords some hold duchies, such as SAVOY, Savoye, and LORRAINE, Lorraine; others hold principalities, such as BEARN, Bearn, and ORANGE, Aurange; others hold counties, such as BURGUNDY, La Comté de Bourgogne, and CHAROLAIS, Charolois. I hope that readers, if they travel faithfully through these regions in the order I have indicated, will judge that I have touched upon every part, though sometimes only in passing; that I have visited most of the cities; and that, if not everything, at least the chief things have been said about each. I think it worth noting here in passing that Appian testifies to the number of the Gallic nations as ... [Πόλις ἐπὶ ἐκ ἔτεσι ... xeoriae]. The number is smaller in the temple, which was built at Lyon by Augusto for all the Gauls by common counsel, of which Strabo speaks in book iv ... [Strabo lib. iv]. Whence such a discrepancy in the number of nations in Gaul? I think that Appian means in general all the nations of the whole of Gaul, and that these were about four hundred; but the Lyon altar had only those nations from which it was set up in honour of Augustus, namely sixty.

units.la: Qui porro, quam ego vel in superioribus attuli, vel in sequentibus sum allaturus, plura, vel saltem mea pluribus fusiusque explicata, petat: consulat moneo, quod quidem ad universæ Galliæ delineationem, præter alios, Robertum Cœnalem, qui integro volumine Gallias descripsit. Gilbertum Cognatum Nozorenum, Ioannem Marium, Chassanæum lib. xii de Gloria mundi, Guilielmum Postellum in libello Vniversitatis, Sebastianum Munsterum, Franciscum Belleforestium, Andream Thevetum, Abrahamum Ortelium & Gerardum Mercatorem; quorum ille xvi, hic xii Chartis Galliam depingit: quod autem ad Gallorum Mores, Reliquæ ab illis gestas, adeat Lector ex Antiquis C. Iulij Cæsaris Libros vii de Bello Gallico, ipsque addictum ab A. Hirtio viii, Appiani Alexandrini Celticum, sive de Bello Gallico, & alios, quos variis supra locis laudavi; ex Recentioribus, medijque ævi, Scriptores illos Annalium & Historiæ Francorum, quos maximo Reip. litterariæ bono nuper edidit P. Pithœus IC: his addat Hunibaldi libros xviii, in quibus tamen multa fabulosa & commentitia, sermoque plane barbarus; Gregorij Turonensis Episcopi libros x; Aimoini Monachi Floriacensis Cœnobij Libros de Regibus Francorum v; item Ioannem Tritemium, Froissardum, quoque cum supplevit, Enguerranum, Robertum Gaguinum, Philippum Comineum, Nicolaum Gillium, Paulum Æmilium, Ioannem Ferronium, Ioannem Tilium, Henricum Leonardum, Hermannum Coleatium Capellam, qui scripsit de bellis in Italia gestis inter Karolum V & Franciscum Galliarum Regem. De Gallorum Imperio & Philosophia libros vii scripsit elegantes & eruditos Stephanus Forcatulus IC. Alios alijs, quibus otium curiosus hæc talia consectandi, adponendos nominaris à me relinquo.
units.tr: Whoever seeks more than I have brought forward above or shall bring forward below, or my points explained more fully and at greater length, let him consult, I advise, for the delineation of all Gaul, besides others, Robert Cenalis, who described Gaul in a whole volume; Gilbert Cognatus of Nozeroy; John Marius; Chassanée, book xii of his De gloria mundi; Guillaume Postel in his little book on the University; Sebastian Münster; François de Belleforest; André Thevet; Abraham Ortelius and Gerard Mercator, of whom the former portrays Gaul on sixteen maps and the latter on twelve. As for the manners of the Gauls and the other things done by them, let the reader consult, among the ancients, the seven books of Julius Caesar's De bello Gallico, with the eighth added by Aulus Hirtius; Appian of Alexandria's Celtica, or On the Gallic War; and others that I have praised in various places above. Among the more recent writers, and those of the middle ages, let him consult those writers of the Annals and History of the Franks whom Pithou, the jurist, lately edited for the great benefit of the literary republic. To these let him add the eighteen books of Hunibald, in which, however, there is much that is fabulous and made up, and the language is plainly barbarous; the ten books of Gregory of Tours, bishop; the five books on the Kings of the Franks by Aimoin, monk of the monastery of Fleury; likewise John Trithemius, Froissart, with the continuation of Enguerrand, Robert Gaguin, Philippe de Commynes, Nicole Gilles, Paulus Aemilius, John Ferron, John Tillet, Henri Léonard, and Hermann Coleatius Capella, who wrote on the wars waged in Italy between Charles V and Francis, King of the Gauls. Stephen Forcadel, jurist, wrote seven elegant and learned books on the empire and philosophy of the Gauls. I leave it to others to name further authors for the curious reader who has leisure to pursue such matters.

units.la: Ad specialiora Galliarum pergo. Occurrit in mea Distributione primo loco Picardia.
units.tr: I now go on to more particular matters concerning Gaul. In my division, the first place is occupied by Picardy.

units.la: Gallicarum Gentium numerum, fuisse Romanorum Lugdunensium.
units.tr: The number of the Gallic nations, [according to] the Lugdunensian Romans.

units.la: Scriptores Rerum Gallicarum.
units.tr: Writers on the affairs of Gaul.

units.la: Picar- dia.
units.tr: Picar- dy.

units.la: Picardia.
units.tr: Picardy.

units.la: PICARDIÆ Nomen quamvis non magnæ antiquitatis, nulla tamen ejus certa potest reddi ratio. Alij aliam augurantur: Inter eos Robertus Cenalis, Episcopus Abrincantensis, vel, ut alij, Arboriensis, Picardos dicit vere esse Gallos; se nihilominus ignorare, nam à Begardis hæreticis (quos constat Ludovici Bavari Imperatoris tempore, circa annum clo cccxiv, quasdam Inferioris Germaniæ Urbes coluisse) nomen hoc sint mutuati. Belleforestius Picardos antea fuisse vocatos scribit, quam Becardi in rerum essent natura, quamque ulla istius Sectæ audiretur mentio. Sunt qui appellatos censent Picardos: quod ab his ortus primo usus Lancearum, quæ vulgo Picques nuncupantur. Ego rem in medio relinquo.
units.tr: The name of Picardy, though not of great antiquity, cannot be given any certain explanation. Others have conjectured differently. Among them, Robert Cenalis, Bishop of Abrincae (or, as others have it, of Arboria), says that the Picards are truly Gauls, but that he nevertheless does not know where the name came from, since they borrowed it from the Beghards, heretics (who, it is well established, occupied some cities of Lower Germany in the time of the Emperor Louis of Bavaria, about the year 1314). Belleforest writes that the Picards were called so before the Beghards existed in nature, and before any mention of that sect was heard. Some think that the Picards were so named because they first used the lances commonly called pikes. I leave the matter open.

units.la: Hujus Regionis, quæ quondam in Antiqua Belgica (ea præcipuè, quæ Secunda posteriori ævo) appellatio latius olim patuit: complexa Artesiam Flandriæque partem ad Lisam usque Amnem: alijs multo etiam ulterius tendentibus ad Scaldim usque & Renum Fluvios. Hodie Picardiam, ut crasse diffiniam, ad Occasum respicit, cum nonnulla Normanniæ portione, Oceanus Britannicus: ad Septemtrionem istæ Veteris Belgicæ jacent Regiones, quæ hodie Artesia & Hannonia: ad Ortum Leuceburgum & Lotharingia sunt porrectæ: ad Meridiem denique Campania, isque nobilissimi Regni Tractus, qui specialiore notione Francia vocatur, occurrunt.
units.tr: The name of this region, which in ancient times, in Belgica (especially the part called Second Belgica in later times), once extended more widely, took in Artois and part of Flanders as far as the river Lys, while others extended it even further, as far as the rivers Scheldt and Rhine. Today, to define it roughly, Picardy faces west, together with part of Normandy and the British Ocean; to the north lie those regions of Old Belgica that are today Artois and Hainaut; to the east stretch Liège and Lorraine; and to the south lies Champagne, that most noble tract of the kingdom which in a narrower sense is called France.

units.la: Regio est fertilissima, Hortreumque Parisiorum, atque adeo plenæque Franciæ. Vino caret, ignava potius Incolarum socordia, quam vel Cœli vel Soli injuria.
units.tr: It is a very fertile region, and a match for the Parisian and indeed the whole of France in abundance. It lacks wine, a fault due to the idleness of its inhabitants rather than to any injury from the sky or the sun.

units.la: Picardiam habitarunt olim Ambiani, Suessiones, Veromandui, Essui, Oromansaci, Morini, & alij fortean. Ambianorum Sedes, ubi hodie opulentissima Urbs Ambianum, vulgo Amiens: Eorum frequens apud antiquos Scriptores mentio, Cæsarem, Plinium, alios. Ἀμβιανοὶ Ptolemæo, & Straboni. Cæsar Ambianos Morinis jungit, quorum fines Nervy attingebant: Strabo Ambianos Morinis facit propinquos, & Suessiones: Ptolemæus post Bellovacos in Gallia Belgica statuit Ambianos. Suessiones, vel, ut alij scribunt Suessiones, sæpe apud Cæsarem (qui & Eleutheros, Liberos, prænominat lib. vii quemadmodum & Cadurcos, de quibus cap. xxxv) memorantur. Σuεσιῶνες apud Strabonem: ubi Isaacus Casaubonus legit Ζυεσρᾶνς: Ptolemæo ᵾⁱⁱσρονς, repono Ζυίσρονς. Hodie Souessons. Apud Suessones ætate memoriaque Cæsaris Rex Diuiciacus, totius Galliæ potentissimus, fuit; qui cum magnæ partis harum Regionum, tum etiam Britanniæ Imperium obtinuit: Deinde Galba successit. Et cujusmodi Regnum hoc fuerit, hinc intelligi potest, quod Suessones Remorum Fratres Consanguineique eodem jure ijsdemque legibus uterentur, unum Imperium, unumque Magistratum cum illis haberent. Suessonum latissimi feracissimiqúe fuerunt Agri, & Opida duodecim; quorum unicum ab Cæsare nominatur Noviodunum, quod ipse post Belgarum discessum ex itinere oppugnare conatus, propter latitudinem Fossæ, murique altitudinem, paucis licet defendentibus, expugnare non potuit.
units.tr: Formerly the Ambiani, Suessiones, Veromandui, Essui, Oromansaci, Morini, and perhaps others, inhabited Picardy. The seat of the Ambiani was where the very wealthy city of Amiens (commonly Amiens) now stands. They are often mentioned in ancient writers: Caesar, Pliny and others. Ptolemy and Strabo call them Ambianoi (Ἀμβιανοὶ). Caesar joins the Ambiani to the Morini, whose borders the Nervii touched; Strabo makes the Ambiani neighbours of the Morini and the Suessiones; Ptolemy places the Ambiani in Belgic Gaul after the Bellovaci. The Suessiones, or as others write the Suessiones, are often mentioned by Caesar (who in book 7 also calls them Eleuthri, the Free, just as he does the Cadurci, of whom in chapter 35). Strabo has Suessiones (Σuεσιῶνες), where Isaac Casaubon reads Ζυεσρᾶνς; Ptolemy has Ζυίσρονς, which I restore. Today they are Soissons. In Caesar's time and within living memory, the king of the Suessiones was Diviciacus, the most powerful man in all Gaul, who held rule over a great part of these regions and also over Britain. Afterwards Galba succeeded him. What kind of kingdom this was can be understood from the fact that the Suessiones, brothers and kinsmen of the Remi, used the same law and the same laws, and had one government and one magistracy with them. The fields of the Suessiones were very broad and fertile, and they had twelve towns. Of these only one is named by Caesar, Noviodunum, which he himself, after the departure of the Belgae, tried to storm on his march; but because of the width of its ditch and the height of its wall, he could not take it, though few defended it.

units.la: Veromandui Cæsari (qui in libris de bello Gallico de ijs multa) Plinioque Galliæ Belgicæ Populi: qui Ῥωμάνδιοι Ptolemæo, & in nonnullis Exemplaribus Ῥομάνδυς pro Οὐερομάνδις, inquit Surita; Veromandui Epitomæ Liviana libri CIV, item Lapidi antiquo, qui, ceste apud Abrahamum Ortelium Iacobo Carondiletio, Cancellario Leodiensi, in Pago Hannoniæ, qui vulgo Affaures prope Bavacum. Effuos Cæsar nominat: Eorum Sedes ubi hodie illa Picardiæ portio, quæ Tirascha, quali, ut Bovillus cum aliis opinatur, Terra Effluorum. Alij Effuos ponunt ubi nunc Retelois: alij ubi Bessin, prope Baiocasses, Baieux: Diuæus Comitatum de Eu putat. Hubertus Leodius tradit eos Athuum Hannoniæ Vrbem occupare: sic quot Capita, tot Sententiæ inceriores nos relinquunt, Oromansaci, juncti Pago, inquit Plinius, quæ Gessoriacus appellatur: fuisse censentur, ubi hac tempestate Comitatus Guinersis. Morini Virgilio, Cæsari, Plinio, aliisque noti; Ptoleæo & Straboni Μέρμοι: olim, ubi nunc in ruinis jacet Teroana, quæ in Notitia, ut alibi vidimus, Civitas Morinorum, id est Ponticum. Morinorum meminit Lapis, qui in Gelria, dimidiato ab Vrbe Neomagensi Miliario, repertus.
units.tr: The Veromandui are mentioned by Caesar (who says much about them in his books on the Gallic War) and by Pliny as a people of Belgic Gaul. Ptolemy calls them Rhomandioi (Ῥωμάνδιοι), and in some copies Rhomandys instead of Veromandoi (Οὐερομάνδις), says Surita. The Veromandui appear in the Epitome of Livy, book 104, and also in an ancient stone, which Abraham Ortelius received from Jacob Carondelet, chancellor of Liège, found in a district of Hainaut commonly called Affaures near Bavay. Caesar names the Essui; their seat was where that part of Picardy now stands which is called Tirasche, which Bovillus, with others, thinks is the land of the Essui. Others place the Essui where Retelois is now, others where Bessin is near Bayeux (Baiocasses); Divaeus thinks of the county of Eu. Hubert Lisdeus relates that they occupied Athus, a town of Hainaut. Thus so many heads, so many opinions, and these leave us uncertain. The Oromansaci, joined to the district which Pliny says is called Gesoriacus, are thought to have lived where the county of Guines now is. The Morini are known to Virgil, Caesar, Pliny and others; Ptolemy and Strabo call them Mermoi (Μέρμοι). Formerly they lived where Thérouanne now lies in ruins, which in the Notitia, as we have seen elsewhere, is the city of the Morini, that is, Pontic. A stone found in Guelders, half a mile from the city of Nijmegen, also mentions the Morini.

units.la: MINERVAE CVR. LADAE T. FVNICIVS. C. NIALIS. II. VIR. C. LON. MORINO RVM. SAGRIDS ROMAE. ET. AVG OB. HONOREM P. V. A. M. D. V. L
units.tr: To Minerva, the ward of Lada: Titus Funicius Nialis, duumvir, Gaius Lon(gus?) of the Morini, a priest in Rome and of Augustus, in honour of his... (dedicated) ... willingly and deservedly.

units.la: Vadicasses sunt apud Plinium; qui Οὐδικάσιοι Ptolemæo: quondam, ubi nunc Noion, Noviomagus Antonino inter Suessones & Ambianos; Νουιόμαγο Vadicassium Ptolemæo. Alij sunt Vadicasses ab Baiocassibus; de quibus in Normannia: nam temere quidam confundunt.
units.tr: The Vadicasses are mentioned by Pliny; Ptolemy calls them Oudikasioi (Οὐδικάσιοι). They once lived where Noyon now is, Noviomagus in Antoninus, between the Suessiones and the Ambiani; Ptolemy has Nouiomago (Νουιόμαγο) of the Vadicasses. Others distinguish the Vadicasses from the Baiocasses, about whom see under Normandy, for some people carelessly confuse them.

units.la: Picardia porro in tris dividitur partes, Veram, Inferiorem, Superiorem. De postrema nihil hoc libro dicam. Occupatur enim Tota fere ab ijs Regionibus, quæ in Inseriore Germania, interque Septemdecim Provincias principem obtinent locum; de quibus libro v.
units.tr: Picardy is further divided into three parts: True Picardy, Lower Picardy, and Upper Picardy. I shall say nothing in this book about the last. For almost all of it is occupied by those regions which lie in Lower Germany and hold the leading place among the seventeen provinces, about which in book 5.

units.la: Vera (La vraye Picardie) cœpto Parisijs itinere, superatisque Bellovacorum Agris, initium est ad Crepacorium. Comprehendit Vicedamias (Communibus utar Vocabulis, ut melius intelligat) Ambianum, Corbiensem & Pequignyam: Comitatus Veromandorum & Retelorum; Ducatum Tiraschensem.
units.tr: True Picardy (La vraye Picardie), beginning from the road from Paris and passing the fields of the Bellovaci, extends to Crépy. It comprises the Vidamate (I shall use common terms so that it may be better understood) of Amiens, Corbie and Péquigny; the counties of the Veromandi and of Rethel; and the Duchy of Thiérache.

units.la: Ambiana (Visdamie d'Amiens) nomen dedit Amlianum, vulgo Amiens: olim uti censent V. N. Iosephus Scaliger, Petrus Divæus, Goropius Becanus, Iosias Simlerus, & alij, Samarobriva. Sigebertus etiam Ambianum idem facit cum Sommonobria; sic ille scripsit pro Samarobriva. Alij, quum Samarobrivam & Ambianos duo diversa se dicerent legere opida apud Antoninum, in eam ierunt sententiam, ut arbitrarentur Samarobriva memoriam hodieque servari in opido, quod ad Somonam (vel, ut alij scribunt, Suminam) Brayum nominatur. Sed potuit eadem urbs & Samarobriva vocari & Ambiani, quod horum Populorum ea esset caput. Itinera Antonini, quæ utriusque faciunt mentionem, alibi videbimus: Prius quidem, quod ad Picardiam proprie pertineat, ad finem hujus capitis, alterum, quod multas simul Galliæ Regiones complectatur, ad Libri finem. Samarobrivæ meminerunt, præter posteriores ævi Scriptores, aliquoties Cæsar lib. v de Bello Gallico & Cicero lib. vii. Epist. ad Trebatium; ut falsum sit, quod superioribus adscribit Sigebertus, Urbem hanc ab Antonino Pio Imperatore fuisse conditam. Majorem habet vetustatem. Ptolemæo appellatur Σαμαροβριγα. Quidam Antonini Codices Samarabrivam, alij Samarabrigam præferunt. Brigam antiqua Hispanorum Lingua, & Briam Thracio sermone, Urbem nuncupari alias dixi. Nonnulli Somonobrigam scribunt à Ponte (Belgice Brug) quo Somona fluvius traijciebatur. Ambianum certe Urbs est ad Somonam, qui eam hic ibi findit (unde quidam Ambianum putant dictum ab Imperatore Gratiano, quod Aquis ambiatur) municipioribus Galliarum & ab natura & ab hominum industria merito connumeranda; Fossis pulcris præaltisque vallata; Clavis ea parte Regni. Templum habet speciosissimum. Incolæ multis clarent Privilegijs; inter ea, quod cum ab exterorum militum Præsidijs, tum ab subsidijs sint immunes. Probitate sane Fidelitateq; sunt insignes. Fabulantur quidam ab Alexandri Magni Militibus conditum. Ambiano tribuit Antonini Itinerarium Legionem xxiii, Episcopos ejus Belleforestius recenset lxiii; inter eos autem ultimum Ioannem Crequium.
units.tr: The Vidamate of Amiens (Visdamie d'Amiens) gave its name to Amiens, commonly Amiens, which, as V. N. Joseph Scaliger, Peter Divaeus, Goropius Becanus, Josias Simler and others think, was formerly Samarobriva. Sigebert also makes Ambianum the same as Sommonobria; so he wrote for Samarobriva. Others, since they read that Samarobriva and Ambiani were two different towns in Antoninus, came to the view that the memory of Samarobriva survives even today in the town called Bray on the Somme (or as others write, Somme). But the same city could be called both Samarobriva and Ambiani, since it was the chief town of these peoples. The itineraries of Antoninus, which mention both, we shall see elsewhere: the first, which belongs properly to Picardy, at the end of this chapter, and the second, which covers many regions of Gaul at once, at the end of the book. Besides later writers, Caesar in book 5 of the Gallic War and Cicero in book 7 of his letters to Trebatius mention Samarobriva several times; so what Sigebert ascribes to earlier writers, that this city was founded by the emperor Antoninus Pius, is false. It is much older. Ptolemy calls it Samarobriga (Σαμαροβριγα). Some manuscripts of Antoninus have Samarabriva, others Samarabriga. I have said elsewhere that briga in the ancient Spanish language, and bria in the Thracian, mean town. Some write Somonobriga, from the bridge (in Dutch Brug) over which the river Somme was crossed. Amiens is certainly a town on the Somme, which cuts through it here and there (whence some think Ambianum was named after the emperor Gratian, because it is surrounded by waters), and it must rightly be counted among the towns of Gaul both for its natural position and for the industry of its people. It is enclosed by fine, very deep ditches; it is a key to the kingdom in that part. It has a very splendid temple. Its inhabitants are distinguished by many privileges, among them that they are exempt both from garrisons of foreign soldiers and from subsidies. They are notable for their honesty and loyalty. Some fables say it was founded by soldiers of Alexander the Great. The Antonine Itinerary assigns the Twenty-third Legion to Amiens; Belleforest lists sixty-three of its bishops, the last of whom is John of Crequy.

units.la: Corbiensis ab Corbia, quod Opidum est ad Somonam; quo loco fluvius, cui adjacet, Somonam ingreditur: Clavis itidem, qua parte jacet, Franciæ. Carminiaca forte Antonini, inter Samarobrivam, Ambiens & Caesaromagum, Roye, ni fallor.
units.tr: Corbie takes its name from Corbia, a town on the Somme, at the point where the river to which it lies adjacent enters the Somme. It is likewise a key to France in the part where it lies. Carminiaca of Antoninus, between Samarobriva, Ambiens and Caesaromagus, is perhaps Roye, unless I am mistaken.

units.la: Pequignia denique à Pequigmo, vulgo Pequigny. Opidum est sic dictum, si vulgo fides, à Pignone, Alexandri Magni Milite. Historiographis nobilitatum, quod ibi Gulielmus Normanniæ Dux, cui cognomen erat Longa-Spatha, positis insidijs fuerit obtruncatus per factionem Balduini Comitis Cameracensis, qui cum pacis inundæ prætextu eo loci pellexerat. Testantur Normanniæ Annales. Memoriæ etiam produnt Francicarum rerum Scriptores Anglos, postquam prælio jam essent victi, superstites omnes ibidem fuisse occisos, qui nomen Pequigny literis omnibus pronunciare nequibant, Pequenij loco Pequigny proferentes.
units.tr: Péquigny, finally, is named from Pequigmum, commonly Péquigny. It is a town, so called, if popular belief is to be trusted, from Pignon, a soldier of Alexander the Great. It was made famous to the historians because William, duke of Normandy, whose surname was Longsword, was there ambushed and slain by the treachery of Baldwin, count of Cambrai, who had lured him to that place under the pretext of a truce. The annals of Normandy bear witness to this. Writers on French affairs also record that the English, after they had already been defeated in battle, were all killed there as survivors, since they could not pronounce the name Péquigny in all its letters, and said Pequenij instead of Péquigny.

units.la: Veromandui de quibus antea dixi, hodie vulgo Vermandois, retento, si qui alij Galliæ populi, prisco Nomine. Picardiæ pars, aliquando Comitatus titulo celebris. Inter Comites primum invenio Hugonem, Henrici I Francorum Regis filium, Philippi Regis fratrem: qui cum alijs Proceribus Bello Sacro, quod in Palæstina, Duce Godefredo Bilionæo, anno cIↄ xcix gestum, interfuisse legitur. Successerunt huic duo Rudolphi Filius & Nepos; quorum hoc sine Liberis defuncto, Comitatus ad Regnum est devolutus. Wandali, facta in Gallias cum Burgundionibus irruptione, Provinciam hanc miserum in modum adflixerunt. Comprehendere vero sub se Comitatum hunc signant Franciæ Geographi Suessonum, Laudunensium, Tartenorum Ditiones; Urbes item Noviomagum & Fanum S. Quintini.
units.tr: The Veromandui, of whom I spoke earlier, are today commonly called Vermandois, keeping their old name, as do some other peoples of Gaul. It is part of Picardy and was once famous under the title of a county. The first count I find among them is Hugh, son of Henry I, King of the Franks, and brother of King Philip. He is read to have taken part, with other nobles, in the Holy War fought in Palestine under Duke Godfrey of Bouillon in the year 1099. He was succeeded by two men named Rudolph, father and son. When the latter died without children, the county passed to the crown. The Vandals, making an invasion into Gaul together with the Burgundians, afflicted this province in a wretched way. The French geographers include under this county the domains of the Suessones, the Laudunenses and the Tartenes, and likewise the towns of Noyon and Saint-Quentin.

units.la: Suessones, quorum antea memini, hodie vulgo Soueffones, vel, ut alij pronunciant, Soiffonnois. Suessonum Vrbs, quae hodie Soiffon, Arce praedita; Suessones gentis voce, apud Antoninum, qui Legionem ei xxv attribuit; Σuεσιωνες Straboni; Αυγυστα Σuεσσονων (sic enim emendandum, pro Ουεσσωνων) Ptolemaeo; Civitas Suessonum in Dignitatum libello dicitur. Eripuit hanc Vrbem Syagrio, Gilonis Romani Praetoris filio Hlodovaeus: quo defuncto, Filij decus illi Regiae Civitatis, quo Caesaris tempore claruerat, reddiderunt. Postea Comitatus Titulo fuit insignis. Karolus Ludovici Principis Condaei filius Comes audit Suessonum. Episcopatus est, cujus Belleforestius Praesules numerat nominatque lxxix; ultimum Matthiam Parisinum.
units.tr: The Suessones, whom I mentioned before, are today commonly called Soueffones, or, as others pronounce it, Soiffonnois. The city of the Suessones, today Soissons, is fortified with a citadel. The name of the people Suessones appears in Antoninus, who assigns to them a legion of 25; Strabo has Σουεσιωνες [Suesiones]; Ptolemy has Αυγυστα Σουεσσονων [Augusta of the Suessones] (which must be so corrected, instead of Ουεσσωνων); the Civitas Suessonum is named in the Notitia Dignitatum. Louis took this city from Syagrius, son of Gilo the Roman governor. When he died, his sons restored to the royal city the honour it had enjoyed in Caesar's time. Afterwards it became distinguished by the title of a county. Charles, son of Prince Louis of Condé, is called count of the Suessones. There is a bishopric, whose prelates Belleforest counts and names as 79, the last being Matthias of Paris.

units.la: Laudunensium Ager, Laonnois, dictus ab Lauduno: cujus meminit Vita Karoli Magni, quodque inemendatius forte apud Antoninum Alauna, quod denique plenius effert suis ad me Litteris Magnus Scaliger, Laudunum Clavatum: hodie Laon. Conditam vult hanc Vrbem Papirius Massonius ab Matrobio Praetore. Situs ipsi in Colle. Invasit eam Karolus Lotharingiae Dux, Ludovici Regis Francorum, Stirpis Karolinae ultimi, Patruus; quum se jure Successionis videret privatum ab Hugone Capeto. Praesules se Duces & Pares Franciae scribunt. Eorum Syllabus apud Belleforestium, cui lxxxiii recensentur, eorumque postremus Joannes Burserius.
units.tr: The territory of the Laudunenses, the Laonnois, takes its name from Laudunum. The Life of Charlemagne mentions it, and Antoninus perhaps less accurately has Alauna, which Magnus Scaliger, in his letters to me, more fully gives as Laudunum Clavatum; today it is Laon. Papirius Masson holds that this city was founded by Matrobius, a praetor. It stands on a hill. Charles, Duke of Lorraine, the uncle of King Louis of the Franks, the last of the Carolingian line, seized it, since he saw himself deprived of the right of succession by Hugh Capet. The prelates write themselves as dukes and peers of France. Their list in Belleforest, in which 83 are enumerated, ends with John Bourseur.

units.la: Tartenorum, vernacule Tartenois, Metropolis est Fera, vulgo La Fere: Vrbs egregie munita, situque commodissimo, ad Oysam Servamque confluentes; Arcem habens satis validam.
units.tr: The Tartenorum, in the vernacular the Tartenois, has as its metropolis Fère, commonly La Fère: a city excellently fortified and most conveniently situated, where the Oise and the Serre meet, and it has a fairly strong citadel.

units.la: Quae nunc Vrbs Noion, Antonino Noviomagus nuncupatur, inter Suessonas & Ambianos, ut antea dixi, eam collocanti, Decimamque octavam Legionem illi tribuenti. Noviomagus Vadicassium est Ptolemaeo. Vulgo Ecclesiasticorum Noviomum vocatur per compendium; ut Trefies pro Trinasses. Falluntur, qui eamdem faciunt cum Noviodvno. Quatuor quidem Noviodunua nominantur ab variis Scriptoribus, sed eorum nullum commune quid habet cum Noviomago, de quo agimus. Vir N. Iosephus Scaliger suis ad me Litteris, Se Nugatoribus hac in re, etiam jurantibus, crediturum negat. Vrbs est, Antiquitatis suae notas non paucas praeferens. Episcopalis Sedes: cujus Praesules Comites se Noviomagienses & Franciae Pares scribunt. Catalogus eorum apud Belleforestium, qui postremum edit Joannem Hangestum, Senlisij Dynastae filium.
units.tr: The city now called Noyon, named Noviomagus by Antoninus, which I placed earlier between the Suessones and the Ambiani, and to which he assigns the eighteenth legion. Noviomagus is Vadicassium in Ptolemy. Among churchmen it is commonly called Noviomum by contraction, as Trefies is used for Trinasses. Those are mistaken who identify it with Noviodunum. There are four places called Noviodunum by various writers, but none of them has anything in common with Noviomagus, the subject of our discussion. Mr. Joseph Scaliger, in his letters to me, says that he will not believe those trifling writers even when they swear to it. It is a town bearing not a few marks of its antiquity. It is an episcopal see, whose prelates write themselves as counts of Noyon and peers of France. Their catalogue in Belleforest ends with John of Hangest, son of the lord of Senlis.

units.la: Fano S. Quintini, quod Comitum Veromanduorum aliquando Domicilium & Regiunculae caput, nomen a Quintino, qui Martyrium ibi passus. Olim Augusta Veromanduorum. Sic etiam dicitur in Vita S. Quintini. Robertus tamen Coenalis scribit hanc Augustam omnino dirutam, ejusque hodie nihil restare praeter Coenobium, quod vulgo Vermand-Abbaye. Quidquid sit, Fanum S. Quintini, Arce nunc potens, multa sustinuit Damna, Calamitatesque Bello inter Philippum Hispaniarum & Henricum Galliarum Reges: quæ plenius à me explicata in Historia Rerum per Belgicam nuperis hisce Tumultibus gestarum.
units.tr: Fanum S. Quintini, which was at one time the residence of the counts of the Veromandui and the capital of a little kingdom, takes its name from Quentin, who suffered martyrdom there. Formerly it was Augusta Veromanduorum, and it is so called in the Life of St Quentin. Robert Cenalis, however, writes that this Augusta was utterly destroyed and that nothing of it survives today except a monastery, commonly called Vermand-Abbaye. Whatever the case, Fanum S. Quintini, now powerful with a citadel, has suffered many losses and calamities in the war between Philip of Spain and Henry, King of the French. I have explained these more fully in my History of the events in the Low Countries during the recent disturbances.

units.la: Hæc de Veromanduis: Retelorum (vulgo Reteloïs) ditio sita est inter Hannonios, Lotharingos & Barros. Metropolis Retestum.
units.tr: So much for the Veromandui. The territory of the Retelori (commonly Retelois) lies between the Hainaulters, the Lorrainers and the Barrois. Its metropolis is Rethel.

units.la: Tirasche (La Tirasche) de qua ante nonnihil, primaria Vrbs est Guisa: Arce superbiens; Propugnaculum contra Leuceburgenses: Vetus Patrimonium Fratrum Primogeniti Lotharingiæ Ducis. Ducum Guisæ proximorum hoc lego Stemma:
units.tr: Tirasche (La Thiérache), of which I said something a little earlier, has as its chief town Guise, proud of its citadel and a bulwark against the men of Luxembourg, the old patrimony of the younger brothers of the Duke of Lorraine. I read the following genealogy of the nearest Dukes of Guise:

units.la: CLAVDIVS Lotharingius, Dux Guisæ & Aumaliæ.
units.tr: CLAUDE of Lorraine, Duke of Guise and Aumale.

units.la: FRANCISCVS, Dux Guisiæ obiit xii Kal. Mart. MDLXXIII, in Obsidione Autelianensi. HENRICVS, Dux Guisiæ natus xviii Kal. Ianuar. MDXLVIII, in Comitiis Blesensibus. LVDOVICVS Cardinalis Lotharingiæ: exitus cum Fratre eodem tempore, isidem Comitiis, in conspectu Regis. CAROLVS Dux Mayennæ. MARIA, defuncto Primo Marito Duce Longevillano, cum suo inde Iacobi V Scotiæ Regis. MARIA Stuarda Scotiæ Regina, supplicio affecta xviii Feb. Mart. MDLXXXVII. CLAVDIVS Dux Aumalius.
units.tr: FRANCIS, Duke of Guise, died 18 February 1573, at the siege of Orléans. HENRY, Duke of Guise, born 15 December 1548, at the Estates of Blois. LOUIS, Cardinal of Lorraine: he died at the same time as his brother, at the same Estates, in the sight of the King. CHARLES, Duke of Mayenne. MARY, after the death of her first husband, the Duke of Longueville, married James V, King of Scotland. MARY Stuart, Queen of Scotland, executed 18 February 1587. CLAUDE, Duke of Aumale.

units.la: Sic se habet Vera Picardia: Inferiori (La Basse) variæ sunt partes: Sanctterra, Pontium, Bolonefinum, Gunæum, Oyum.
units.tr: Thus True Picardy stands. Lower Picardy (La Basse) has various parts: Santerre, Ponthieu, Boulonnais, Guînes, Oye.

units.la: Sanctterra, Santerre, concluditur inter Montem S. Desiderij, Peronam & Roiam: Frumenti varioramque Fructuum valde ferax. Monti S. Desiderij, vulgo Mondidier, unde sit nomen, notum est. Perona, bellicis cladibus sæpe fatigata. Clavis ibi Franciæ, Arce potens. Hic Heribertus Veromanduorum Comes Captiuum detinuit Karolum Simplicem, Galliarum Regem. Late Papirius Massonus rerum Francicarum lib. x, & alij. Roia, opidum non contemnendum, Arce, ut fere omnia limitaneis his locis, validum: Cæsaromagus, nisi fallor, Antonino & Itinerariæ Tabulæ: Cæsaromagi etiam in Bellovacis meminit Ptolemæus. Alij Rodrinam esse volunt: quæ mihi Romorantin, ut suo dicam loco. Est ibidem Nella, Propugnaculum, ut multa alia; hac parte Regni, Arce munitum, ad Fontem fere Ingonis Fluvij; qui, exiguo cursu confecto, mox inter Ronyam & Voiennam in Somonam se exonerat. Nella Clararum Virorum genitrix. Eius Dynastæ Marchiones adfinitate iuncti leguntur Familiæ Ceurtenæ, quæ originem traxit ab Regibus Franciæ.
units.tr: Santerre is bounded between Montdidier, Péronne and Roye, and is very fertile in grain and various other crops. Montdidier, from Mons Sancti Desiderii, commonly Mondidier, is well known and gives its name to the district. Péronne, often worn down by the calamities of war, is the key of France and powerful with a citadel. Here Heribert, Count of the Veromandui, held Charles the Simple, King of the Gauls, captive. Papirius Masson treats this at length in book 10 of his Frankish history, and others do too. Roye, a town not to be despised, is strong with a citadel, as nearly all places on this frontier are. If I am not mistaken, it is Caesaromagus, in Antoninus and the Itinerary tables; Ptolemy also mentions Caesaromagus among the Bellovaci. Others want it to be Rodrina, which I will discuss in its own place as Romorantin. There too is Nesle, a bulwark, like many others, fortified on this side of the kingdom, almost at the source of the river Ingon, which, after a short course, empties itself into the Somme between the Ronne and the Voyenne. Nesle was the birthplace of famous men. Its lords, the marquesses, are read to have been connected by marriage with the family of Coucy, which traced its origin from the Kings of France.

units.la: Pontium, vernacule Ponthieu, Comitatus est, cui nomen creditur datum à Pontium, qui passim ibi, multitudine. Est enim Regio inter Somonam & Authyam fluvios: Paludibus plena: quæque Stagnis suis, ut ipse deprehendi, multis in locis invia. Cogitandum aliis relinquo, an non Nomen huius opinione quorundam verustius. Ego hoc Tractu apud Antoninum invenio Pontes cum Legione xxiv. inter Ambianos & Gelloriacum. In Notitia item Romanarum Dignitatum scribitur Civitas Morinorum, id est Ponticum. Comitatus fulget dignitate. Meminerunt Annales Guilelmi huius Provinciæ Comitis, qui vixit tempore Lotharij Francorum Regis. Anglici iuris factus est, quum Eduardus I Angliæ Rex uxorem duceret Eleonoram, Ferdinandi Castellæ Regis Filiam ex Ioanna Coniuge, quæ Filia erat Simonis Pontium Comitis. Anglo plenius solidiusque adquisitum fuit Ius per Pacem inter Lo-nuem & Eduardum factam anno MCCLX. Non multo post Incolæ, instigante Guidone S. Pauli Comite, Præsidiarios, quos Rex Eduardus ibi reliquerat, exturbarunt; Regisque Francorum Karolo V se dediderunt. Sic nobilissimus Comitatus Franconiæ cessit, post annos cxii, quam ipsum Dotis nomine Rex Eduardus I accepisset. Primarium Comitatus opidum Abbatis-Villa, Abbeville vulgo: non antiquum valde uti nomen indicat: Bailliuatus titulo insignitum. Opida habet & alia non magni nominis, Crotoyam, Ruam, Treportum, Fanum S. Richiery. Cressiacum, Cressi, Vicus est, Gallorum clade memorabilis, de qua Papirius Massonus lib. iv Annalium. Comprehendere autem notatur sub se hic Comitatus duos alios Monstroliensem & S. Pauli, utrumque nomen à principibus Vrbibus, quæ vulgo Monstreuil & S. Pol. Montreuil quibusdam quasi
units.tr: Ponthieu, in the vernacular Ponthieu, is a county, which is believed to have received its name from the Pontes, who were numerous there everywhere. It is a region between the rivers Somme and Authie, full of marshes and, as I myself have found, in many places impassable because of its pools. I leave it to others to consider whether this name is not older than that opinion. I find in Antoninus, in this tract between the Ambiani and Gesoriacum, the Pontes with the twenty-fourth legion. Likewise in the Notitia of Roman Dignities the Civitas Morinorum is written, that is, Ponticum. The county shines with dignity. The annals mention William, count of this province, who lived in the time of Lothair, King of the Franks. It came under English law when Edward I, King of England, married Eleanor, daughter of Ferdinand, King of Castile, by his wife Joan, who was the daughter of Simon, Count of Ponthieu. The English acquired the right more fully and securely through the peace made between Louis and Edward in the year 1260. Not long afterwards the inhabitants, at the urging of Guy, Count of St Pol, drove out the garrison that King Edward had left there, and surrendered themselves to Charles V, King of the French. So this most noble county of Ponthieu passed away, 112 years after King Edward I had received it as a dowry. The chief town of the county is Abbeville, commonly so called: not very old, as its name indicates, and distinguished by the title of a bailiwick. It also has other towns of no great name: Crotoy, Rue, Le Tréport, Saint-Riquier. Crécy, Cressi, is a village memorable for the defeat of the French, of which Papirius Masson writes in book 4 of his Annals. This county is, however, said to include two other counties, that of Montreuil and that of Saint-Pol, each named from its principal towns, which are commonly called Montreuil and Saint-Pol, as if Mont-Royal, though others derive them from Monstrum, supposedly because it had a residence there.

units.la: cuius Metro-polis Abbatis-Villa. quique com-plectitur duos alios comitatus. Monstrolien-sem, Monstreuil. & Fani S. Pauli, S. Pol. quasi Mont-Royal; aliis ab Monstro, quod eo loci domicilium habuisse fingitur. Comites S. Paulli. Progenitorem memorant ex Stirpe Leuceburgica Walleramum Leuceburgium, Lignij Comitem, germanum Henrici vii Romanorum Imperatoris fratrem. Vltimam ejus Stemmatis lego Mariam Leuceburgicam, Petri Filiam, Fani D. Paulli ac Lignij Comitem, Anhiani Dominam; Vxorem prius Iacobi Sangij Ramondi Vaussiique Comitis; inde vero Francisci Comitis Vendomij; Matrem ex illo Filiae, quae nupsit Henrico Nassavio; ex hoc autem Karoli Primi Vendomiae Ducis.
units.tr: whose metropolis is Abbeville. It also includes two other counties, that of Montreuil (Monstreuil) and that of Saint-Pol (S. Pol), as if Mont-Royal; others derive it from Monstrum, which is supposed to have had a residence there. The Counts of St Paul. They name as their ancestor, from the Luxembourg line, Waleran of Luxembourg, Count of Ligny, brother of Henry VII, Emperor of the Romans. I read the last of his lineage as Mary of Luxembourg, daughter of Peter, Count of St Paul and Ligny, Lady of Anhiam; first wife of James de Sancy, Count of Ramonde and Vaussi; then of Francis, Count of Vendôme; mother by the latter of a daughter who married Henry of Nassau, and by the former of Charles I, Duke of Vendôme.

units.la: Bolonia, vel ut alij, Bononia Comitatus (Comté de Boulogne) satis est amplus. Initium illi ab Montibus S. Ingelberti: procurritque ad Fluvium Cancham, quae ejus Longitudo et Latitudo ad Lucum usque Tournohensem porrigitur. Totus Tractus arenosus est, ejus generis arenae, quam Vrentem vocant: unde & nonnulli Bo'oniam censent derivatam a Bouiller; quod ridere soleo. Nomen Comitatui a Bolonia Opido, quod in Superius hodie & Inferius divisum. Illud altiore situm loco, Burgus tantum, anteaquam ab Anglis obsidione premeretur:
units.tr: Bolonia, or as others call it, Bononia, the County of Boulogne (Comté de Boulogne), is quite large. It begins at the Mountains of St. Ingelbert and runs to the river Canche, and its length and breadth extend as far as the grove of Tournehem. The whole tract is sandy, of the kind of sand they call vrente, and so some think Bononia takes its name from bouiller, a derivation I am accustomed to laugh at. The county takes its name from the town of Bolonia, which today is divided into Upper and Lower. The upper town, set on higher ground, was then only a borough, before it was besieged by the English. ## The Caletenses and the Bononienses.

units.la: Caletenses & Bononienses.

Hoc autem planiora occupans Mare adluit. Alterum ab altero passibus distat centum, aut circiter. Bononiam etiam nominant hac Galliarum parte, praeter Ammianum lib. xx, Olympiodorus & Sozomenus. Scripsit ille Historiam Honorij Senioris, Theodosij & Honorij Iunioris, inque scrinijs adhuc & Armarijs Bibliothecarum delitescit. Loquens autem de Constantino Tyranno, Τὰς Βρεττανίας ἱάσας, ait, μεγίστην ἀμα τῆς ἀνῆ ἀῆ Βονωνίαν, πλὴν ἐτω καλῳμένην, ὥσπερ Γαλατίας, καὶ πρῶτον ἐν τῆς τῶν Γαλατῶν ἔθνος κεκμήλε. Emendandus hinc, cujus memini, Sozomenus, qui libro ix loquens eadem de re, μεγιστῶς δὲ Κωνσταντῖνον, inquit, ἐπὶ Βρετανίας ἐπὶ Βυθονίας (leg. Bononiae) πλὴν τῆς Γαλατίας, ὥσπερ Γαλατῶν κεκμήλε, ὥσπερ ἀγρῶν τὰς ἐπὶ Γαλάτας καὶ Ἀχαιτάνοις φορμὰς. Bononiense opidum habet quoque Panegyricus Incerti Auctoris Imperatori Constantino dictus. Civitas Bononiensium est in Notitia Provinciarum inter Belgicae Secundae Civitates. Hodie Francorum Vulgo Boulongne; Flandris, reliquisque Inferioris Germaniae Populis, propius ad Veterem appellationem accedentibus, Reunen. Antiquissimis temporibus, uti censent V. N. Iosephus Scaliger suis ad me Litteris (nam ad Ausonium Gessoire opidum hoc tractu nomen retinere docet) Papirius Massonius, Lelandus, Abrahamus Ortelius, & alij, Gesforiacum. Differte Tabula Peutingeriana, quam cum maximo Reip. litterariae bono nuper editam a se mihi liberaliter transmisit Vir Nobilis. Marcus Velserus Patritius & II-Vir Augustanus: Gessogiaco, Quod nunc Bonomia; Civitas Ecolismensium. l'Evesché d'Engoulesme. Civitas Sanctonum. l'Evesché de Saintes. Civitas Pictavorum, vel Pectavorum. l'Evesché de Poitiers. Civitas Petrogoriorum. l'Evesché de Perigueux. Civitas Convenas. l'Evesché de Comminges. Civitas Consarannorum, vel Consorannorum. l'Evesché de Couserans. Civitas Boatum, id est, Borus. Le Pais de Buchs. Civitas Benearnensium, id est, Benaanus. Le Pais de Bearn.
units.tr: The lower town, which occupies the flatter ground, is washed by the sea. The two are about a hundred paces apart, or thereabouts. In this part of Gaul they also call it Bononia: besides Ammianus in book 20, there are Olympiodorus and Sozomen. Ammianus wrote a history of Honorius the Elder and of Theodosius and Honorius the Younger, which still lies hidden in chests and in the cupboards of libraries. Speaking of the tyrant Constantine, who had subdued Britain, he says that the greatest city, Bononia (called thus, as Gaul is), was the first to be taken by the Gallic nations [Τὰς Βρεττανίας ἰάσας ... μεγίστην ἅμα τῆς Ἀρελάτου ... Βονωνίαν, πλὴν οὕτω καλουμένην, ὥσπερ Γαλατίας, καὶ πρῶτον ἐν τοῖς τῶν Γαλατῶν ἔθνεσι κατεσχέθη]. Sozomen, whom I recall, should be corrected here, for in book 9, speaking of the same matter, he says that Constantine, after Britain, went to Bononia (read Bononiae), except Gaul, as the Gauls and the Franks were then called [μεγίστως δὲ Κωνσταντῖνον ... ἐπὶ Βρεττανίας ἐπὶ Βυθονίας (leg. Βονωνίας) πλὴν τῆς Γαλατίας, ὥσπερ Γαλατῶν κεκλημένης, ὥσπερ ἀγρῶν τὰς ἐπὶ Γαλάτας καὶ Ἀχαιτάνοις φορμάς]. The Panegyric of an unknown author, delivered to the Emperor Constantine, also has the town of Bononiense. The Civitas Bononiensium is listed in the Notitia Provinciarum among the cities of Belgica Secunda. Today the French call it Boulogne, while the Flemings and the other peoples of Lower Germany, who come closer to the old name, call it Reunen. In the most ancient times, as the most learned Joseph Scaliger tells me in his letters (for he teaches that in Ausonius the town of this district keeps the name Gessoire), Papirius Massonius, Leland, Abraham Ortelius and others hold it was Gesforiacum. The Peutinger Table, which has lately been published, to the great benefit of the republic of letters, was generously sent to me by a noble man, Marcus Velserus, patrician and duumvir of Augsburg, and it differs from them: Gessogiaco, which is now Bononia; the city of the Ecolismenses, the bishopric of Angoulême; the city of the Santones, the bishopric of Saintes; the city of the Pictavi or Pectavi, the bishopric of Poitiers; the city of the Petrocorii, the bishopric of Périgueux; the city of the Convenae, the bishopric of Comminges; the city of the Consarani or Consorani, the bishopric of Couserans; the city of the Boatae, that is, Bordeaux, the country of Buch; the city of the Benearnenses, that is, Benearnum, the country of Béarn.

units.la: PROVINCIA AQVITANIA TERTIA NOVEMPOPVLANA octava Viennensis.
units.tr: PROVINCE OF THIRD AQUITAINE, NOVEMPOPULANIA, EIGHTH VIENNENSIS.

units.la: METROPOLIS. Civitas Auscio-rum. l'Archevesché d'Auch. Civitas Aquensium. l'Evesché d'Aqs. Civitas Lactoratium, vel Lastoracium. l'Evesché de Laitoure. Civitas Aturensium. l'Evesché d'Aire. Civitas Valatica. l'Evesché de Bazats. Civitas Tarba, vel Castrum Begorra. l'Evesché de Tarbe, de Bigorre, Civitas Eloronensium. l'Evesché d'Oloron en Bearn. Civitas Iluturium. La Ville & Pais d'Eusse en Gascogne.
units.tr: METROPOLIS. The city of the Auscii: the archbishopric of Auch. The city of the Aquenses: the bishopric of Aqs. The city of the Lactorates, or Lastoracium: the bishopric of Laitoure. The city of the Aturenses: the bishopric of Aire. The city of Valatica: the bishopric of Bazats. The city of Tarba, or Castrum Begorra: the bishopric of Tarbe, in Bigorre. The city of the Eloronenses: the bishopric of Oloron in Bearn. The city of Iluturium: the town and country of Eusse in Gascony.

units.la: Notitiam hanc Provinciarum Galliæ in Membranis etiam mihi monstravit in Bibliotheca, quam habet instructissimam cum ab Impressis, tum MSS. Libris V. CL. Bonaventura Vulcanius, Græcæ Linguæ in Academia Batavorum Professor, Collega mihi amicissimus. In ea (ne & hæc indicta mihi abeant) ad Lugdunensem II post Civitatum Abrincantum, additur Civitas Ebroricorum, cui recentiore manu innotatum Evancorum: non dubito, quin qui libellum exaravit, scribere voluerit Eburonum, Eborum vel Eburovicum. Nam & his in Lugdunensi II sedes erant, ut cap. xxx dicam. Hodie L'Evesché d'Eureux. Sequebatur mox in ijsdem Membranis Civitas Salarum, id est, Saiorum: quod moneo, non probo. Ad Germaniam II. Civitatis Tungrorum subiicitur Civitas Nova, 1. Leodium. In fine Viennensis 1 notatur etiam Civitas Massiliensium, quæ aliis deest.
units.tr: This list of the provinces of Gaul was also shown to me in a manuscript on parchment in the library, which is very well stocked with both printed and manuscript books, by the most distinguished Bonaventura Vulcanius, professor of Greek at the Academy of the Batavians, my most friendly colleague. In it (so that these things too may not pass unmentioned), after the city of the Abrincates, there is added the city of the Ebroici, to which a later hand has added in the margin "of the Evanci." I do not doubt that the writer of the little book meant to write Eburonum, Eborum or Eburovicum, for these also had their seats in Lugdunensis II, as I shall say in chapter 30. Today it is the bishopric of Evreux. Next in the same manuscript follows the city of the Salarum, that is, of the Saii: which I note but do not endorse. To Germania II, after the city of the Tungri, is subjoined the city of Nova, that is, Liège (Leodium). At the end of Viennensis I is also noted the city of the Massilienses, which others lack.

units.la: Ammianus Marcellinus lib. xv confuse quæ in Notitia Provinciarum, & non satis plene commemorat: At nunc numerantur Provinciæ per omnem ambitum Galliarum: SECUNDA GERMANIA, Prima ab Occidentali exordiens cardine, Agrippina & Tungris munita, Civitatibus amplis & copiosis. Dein PRIMA GERMANIA; ubi, præter alia Municipia, Magontiacum est, & Vangiones, & Nemetes, & Argentoratus, barbaricu Cladibus nota. Post hæc BELGICA PRIMA, Mediomatricos prætendens, & Treveros, Domicilium Principum clarum. Huic adnexa est SECUNDA BELGICA; quæ Ambiani sunt, Urbs inter alias eminens, Catellauni & Remi. Apud SEQVANOS (designat maximam Sequanorum, quæ & Lugdunensis quinta) Vesuntios vidimus, & Rauricos, alys pestores Cipidis multis. LVGDVNENSEM PRIMAM Lugdunum ornat, & Cabillones, & Senones (pertinent hi apud alios ad Lugdunensem quartam) & Bituriges (commemorantur ijs, qui in AQVITANIA PRIMA) & mœnium Augustodunum magnitudo vetusta. SECVNDAM enim Lugdunensem Rotomagi, & Turini Mediolanum (legendum Turoni & Cenomani: qui duo Populi ab alys concensentur Lugdunensi tertiæ) ostendunt: & Trecassini (Trecasses alij describunt in Lugdunensi quarta.) ALPES GRAIÆ & PENINÆ (notat Provinciam VIENNENSEM QVINTAM) exceptis obscurioribus, habent & Aventicum (hæc tamen Urbs ab alijs ponitur in Lugdunensi quinta) desertam quidem Civitatem, sed non ignobilem quondam, ut ædificia semiruta nunc quoque demonstrant. Hæ Provinciæ Urbesque sunt splendidæ Galliarum. In Aquitania, quæ Pyrenæos Montes, & eam partem Siceas Oceani, quæ pertinet ad Hispanos, prima Provincia est AQVITANICA (universum sumta pro PRIMA, SECVNDA, TERTIA: nam Vox Prima apud Ammianum non ordinis esse videtur, sed dignitatis: Prima, præcipua est Aquitanica, si cum aliis Aquitania Regionibus, ut Novempopulonia & Narbonensi committatur) amplitudine Civitatum admodum culta: emissis ayus multiis, Burdegala & Arverni (in AQVITANIA PRIMA) excellunt, & Santones & Pictavi (utrque Populus in AQVITANIA SECVNDA.) NOVEM POPVLOS (NOVEMPOPVLANIA eadem cum AQVITANIA TERTIA & VIENNENSI OCTAVA) Auscii commendant & Vasates. In NARBONENSI (eadem cum VIENNENSI SECUNDA) clusa est Narbona & Tolosa, quæ principatum Vrbium tenent. VIENNENSIS (PRIMAM significat) Civitatum
units.tr: Ammianus Marcellinus, book 15, mentions confusedly and not very fully the things that are in the Notitia of the Provinces: "But now the provinces are enumerated through the whole circuit of the Gauls. SECOND GERMANY, beginning from the western hinge, fortified by Agrippina and the Tungri, with ample and populous cities. Then FIRST GERMANY, where, besides other towns, there is Mogontiacum, and the Vangiones, and the Nemetes, and Argentoratum, known for barbarian slaughters. After these FIRST BELGIUM, extending to the Mediomatrici and the Treveri, a famous home of princes. Joined to this is SECOND BELGIUM, in which are the Ambiani, a city outstanding among the others, and the Catelauni and the Remi. Among the SEQUANI (he means the greater Sequani, who are also Lugdunensis Quinta) we have seen Vesontio, and the Raurici, and many other cities. LUGDUNENSIS PRIMA is adorned by Lugdunum, and the Cabillones, and the Senones (others assign these to Lugdunensis Quarta), and the Bituriges (mentioned among those in AQUITANIA PRIMA), and the ancient greatness of the walled city of Augustodunum. For SECUNDA Lugdunensis is shown by Rotomagus, and Turones and Mediolanum (read Turoni and Cenomani: two peoples which others reckon to Lugdunensis Tertia), and the Trecassini (others describe the Trecasses in Lugdunensis Quarta). The ALPES GRAIAE and PENINAE (he means the province VIENNENSIS QUINTA), leaving aside the more obscure places, also have Aventicum (though others place this city in Lugdunensis Quinta), a city indeed deserted, but once not undistinguished, as its half-ruined buildings still show today. These provinces and cities are the splendours of Gaul. In Aquitania, which is bounded by the Pyrenees and by that part of the Ocean coast which belongs to the Spaniards, the first province is AQUITANICA (taken generally for PRIMA, SECUNDA and TERTIA; for the word prima in Ammianus seems to denote not order but rank: prima, that is, chief, is Aquitanica, when it is compared with the other Aquitanian regions, such as Novempopulonia and Narbonensis), very cultivated for the size of its cities. With many others sent out, Burdigala and the Arverni (in AQUITANIA PRIMA) excel, and the Santones and the Pictavi (both peoples in AQUITANIA SECUNDA). The NOVEM POPULI (NOVEMPOPULANIA, the same as AQUITANIA TERTIA and VIENNENSIS OCTAVA) are commended by the Ausci and the Vasates. In NARBONENSIS (the same as VIENNENSIS SECUNDA) are enclosed Narbo and Tolosa, which hold the chief place among the cities. VIENNENSIS (signifying PRIMA) ..."

units.la: Ammiani Locus de xvii Galliæ Provinciis discussus. Civitatum exsultat decore multarum, quibus potiores sunt Vienna ipsa, & Arelate, & Valentia: quibus Massilia jungitur, cujus societate & viribus in discriminibus arduis fultam aliquoties leginus Romam. His prope Sallluvij sunt, & Nicaea, & Antipolis, Insulaeque Stœchades. Nominat ordinis inculiosior Lugdunensem Primam, Lugdunensem Secundam, Maximam Sequanorum (quae eadem cum Lugdunensi Quinta) Belgicam Primam, Belgicam Secundam, Germaniam Primam, Germaniam Secundam, Viennensem Primam, Narbonensem (eamdem cum Viennensi Secunda) Alpes Graias & Peninas (quae in Viennensi Quinta) Aquitanicas Primam & Secundam, Novempopulaniam denique, vel Aquitaniam Tertiam: nullam faciens mentionem, ad plenum xvii Provinciarum numerum constituendum, Lugdunensis Tertia & Quarta; nullam item Viennensis Tertia & Quarta.
units.tr: It boasts the beauty of many cities, of which the most important are Vienna itself, and Arelate, and Valentia; to these is joined Massilia, whose alliance and strength we read have several times supported Rome in dire straits. Near these are the Salluvii, and Nicaea, and Antipolis, and the Stoechades islands. He names, in a less exact order, Lugdunensis Prima, Lugdunensis Secunda, Maxima Sequanorum (the same as Lugdunensis Quinta), Belgica Prima, Belgica Secunda, Germania Prima, Germania Secunda, Viennensis Prima, Narbonensis (the same as Viennensis Secunda), the Alpes Graiae and Poeninae (which are in Viennensis Quinta), Aquitanica Prima and Secunda, and finally Novempopulania, or Aquitania Tertia, making no mention of Lugdunensis Tertia and Quarta, in order to make up the full number of seventeen provinces; likewise none of Viennensis Tertia and Quarta.

units.la: Hæ igitur Septemdecim sunt Provinciæ, in quas Augustus Cæsar Gallias divisit, & in quibus Constantinus Magnus varia Officia & Magistratus constituit; ut in Notitia Provinciarum Imperij Romani plenius est videre. De Primis nonnihil addam. Constantinus, de quo dixi, instituit quatuor Præfectis Prætorio, duobus in Oriente, totidem in Occidente; alterum Occidentis in Urbe Roma, alterum in Urbe Treverensi collocavit, qui Præfectus Prætorio Galliarum vocatus fuit: & quia per occupationes Imperij in illis Urbibus perpetuo hærere ipsis non licebat, Vicarij aliquot eis sunt attributi, qui eadem potestate Provincijs Ius redderent. Præfecto igitur Prætorij Galliarum tres Vicarij dati. Primo Sedes designata Treveris, Secundo Lugduni, Tertio Viennæ. Itaque ut horum Vicariorum magna erat auctoritas, ita Urbium quoque, in quibus Sedem habebant, maxima claritas. Treverensi Vicario parebant Prima & Secunda Germania, & Belgica, & tota Britannia Insula: Lugdunensi quatuor Lugdunenses cum Maxima Sequanorum: Viennensi Prima & Secunda Narbonensis & Aquitania, Alpes Graiæ & Pœninæ, Alpes Maritimæ, Novempopulania. Totum illud, quod unius Vicarij Iurisdictioni subjacebat, Latini quo modo designarint, non constat: sed Græci Ἐξαρχίας, Διοίκησιν, Πατριάς vocabant.
units.tr: These, then, are the seventeen provinces into which Augustus Caesar divided the Gauls, and among which Constantine the Great established various offices and magistracies, as is more fully seen in the Notitia of the Provinces of the Roman Empire. I will add something about the chief of them. Constantine, of whom I have spoken, appointed four Praetorian Prefects, two in the East and as many in the West. He placed one of the Western ones in the city of Rome, and the other in the city of Trier, and this one was called the Praetorian Prefect of Gaul. And because, owing to the upheavals of the empire, they could not always remain in those cities, some vicars were assigned to them, who with the same power dispensed justice to the provinces.
