To the Praetorian Prefect of Gaul, therefore, three vicars were given: first, a seat was designated at Trier; second, at Lyons; third, at Vienne. So as the authority of these vicars was great, so also was the renown of the cities in which they had their seats. The Treverensi Vicar was obeyed by First and Second Germany, and Belgica, and the whole island of Britain; the Lyons vicar by the four Lugdunenses with Maxima Sequanorum; the Vienne vicar by First and Second Narbonensis and Aquitania, the Alpes Graiae and Poeninae, the Alpes Maritimae, Novempopulania. How the Latins designated that whole area which lay under the jurisdiction of a single vicar is not known, but the Greeks called it exarchies [Ἐξαρχίας], dioceses [Διοίκησιν], or patriae [Πατριάς].

units.la: Sequens ætas, quum jam Romanorum Imperium ad exitium vergeret, sensimque suis partibus variorum Populorum incursibus miserum in modum truncaretur, varie Gallias distribuit. Quum enim Gothi Francique omnia occupassent, alia ibi coeperunt esse Gothorum, alia Francorum, alia Romanorum Gallorumque Indigenarum, quorum, quod à priorum nutu & arbitrio penderent, inferior pejorque erat conditio. præcipue ex Fœdere inter Constantium Comitem & Walliam Gothorum Regem, quod incidit in annum Christi cccc xvi, quo coss. erant Theodosius Iunior Augustus vii, & Iunius Quartus Palladius. Consulendi Prosper, Cassiodorus, Iornandes in histor. Gothor. cap. xxxi, Paullus Diaconus lib. iv, Isidorus in Chronico Gothorum. De Limite etiam inter Gothos & Romanos multa legere est apud Sidonium Apollinarem, cum primis lib. i. epist. vii, lib. iii. epist. i, lib. vii. epist. vi, lib. viii. epist. iii. Anno ccccLxi Childerico iv Francorum Rege Regia dignitate ob Luxum, cui deditus erat, & Tributa, quibus Populum vexabat, exuto; habenisque Ægidio Romano Magistro Militum, qui pro Romanis apud Suessones sedebat, magno animorum consensu traditis; ex pacto maxima Lugdunensis Galliæ pars Romanis, Narbonensis & omnis Aquitania Gothis; quidquid ab Rheno ad Ligerim Merovæus cessit. Videndi Vigebertus, Trithemius, Otto Frisingensis lib. iv. cap. xxxii, Gregorius Turonensis lib. ii. cap. xii & alij.
units.tr: The following age, when the Roman empire was already tending to ruin and was being gradually and wretchedly cut back on its own side by the incursions of various peoples, divided Gaul in various ways. For when the Goths and Franks had occupied everything, some parts began to belong to the Goths, some to the Franks, and some to the Romans and the native Gauls; the condition of the last was lower and worse, because it depended on the will and judgment of the others. This arose especially from the treaty between Count Constantius and Wallia, king of the Goths, which fell in the year of Christ 416, when the consuls were Theodosius the Younger, Augustus for the seventh time, and Junius Quartus Palladius. Consult Prosper, Cassiodorus, Jordanes in his History of the Goths, chapter 31, Paul the Deacon, book 4, and Isidore in his Chronicle of the Goths. Much about the boundary between the Goths and the Romans may also be read in Sidonius Apollinaris, chiefly book 1 letter 7, book 3 letter 1, book 7 letter 6, and book 8 letter 3. In the year 461, Childeric IV, king of the Franks, was stripped of royal dignity on account of the luxury to which he was addicted and the tributes with which he burdened the people; the reins were handed over, with great agreement of minds, to Aegidius, Roman master of soldiers, who sat for the Romans at Soissons. By agreement, the greatest part of Lugdunensis Gaul went to the Romans, Narbonensis and all Aquitania to the Goths, and whatever lay from the Rhine to the Loire was yielded to Merovech. Consult Vigebertus, Trithemius, Otto of Freising, book 4, chapter 32, Gregory of Tours, book 2, chapter 12, and others.

units.la: Tempore Iustiniani Galliarum Regna leguntur sex, Parisiorum, Mediomatricum, Aureliamorum, Suessonum, Burgundorum, Aquitanorum. Adeundi Venantius Fortunatus, Paulus Diaconus, Gregorius Turonensis, Sigebertus, Regino, Ado Viennensis reliquique Francici Scriptores.
units.tr: In the time of Justinian the kingdoms of Gaul are read as six: those of the Parisii, the Mediomatrici, the Aurelians, the Suessones, the Burgundians, and the Aquitanians. Consult Venantius Fortunatus, Paul the Deacon, Gregory of Tours, Sigebert, Regino, Ado of Vienne, and the rest of the Frankish writers.

units.la: Post Karoli Magni Principatum illa Divisio, quamquam antea non prorsus ignota, obtinuit; ut alia diceretur Austrasia, id est Orientalis; alia Westria (corrupte enim quibusdam scribitur Neustria) id est Occidentalis: ut iidem Scriptores testantur.
units.tr: After the principate of Charlemagne that division, though not entirely unknown before, prevailed, so that one part was called Austrasia, that is, Eastern, and another Westria (for some wrongly write it Neustria), that is, Western, as the same writers attest.

units.la: Sic igitur Regnorum vices multa, ut vidimus, in Antiquis Divisionibus immutarunt: sed (ut in litteris suis ad me Nobilissimus Vir Iosephus Scaliger, de sua Gallia) Status Ecclesiasticus tam in Oriente quam in Occidente ejus integra Vestigia hactenus retinuit. Nam Civitates, quæ Provincijs nomina fecerunt, Μητροπόλεις vocant, & si in eis sedes fuerit Vicarij, quem Ἐξαρχον dicebant, eas non solum Μητροπόλεις, Ἐξαρχοι, πόλεις, πόλεις, sed & Ἐξάρχας, & Πατριάρχας nominant; & Præsules earum Ἐξάρχας ἢ Πατριάρχας. reliquos Μητροπολίτας ἢ Ἀρχιεπισκόπους, qui sub se tantum Ἐπισκόπους habent: Nam ei Ἐξάρχαι sub se, præter Ἐπισκόπους, etiam Μητροπολίτας habent: Μητροπολίτας vero tantum Ἐπισκόπους. In Ecclesia Latina Archiepiscoporum & nomen & jus manet, & Iurisdictio Canonica in suos Episcopos Suffraganeos: sed Ἐξάρχαις nulla vestigia exstant: nisi forte quædam umbra ejus fuerit, quod Metropolita sive Archiepiscopus Viennensis Primatem Primatum sese appellat. Eo enim ostendit sub se Primates habuisse, qui sub eo essent, Narbonensem Primatem Provinciæ, Bituricensem Primatem Aquitaniæ. Aliter quo modo, aut quo jure, Primas Primatum diceretur, nisi ratione Diœcesicos Vicarij Viennensis Præfectj: Prætoris, qui septem Provincias sub se habebat, in quibus Prima Narbonensis & Prima Aquitania? Quod vero Lugdunensis Primatem se vocari gaudeat, numerum est, & illi ex beneficio Romani Pontificis indultum: neque tamen adeo novum est. Nam Guilielmus Brito in sua Philippeide ita canit: Et Lugdunensis, quo Gallia tota solebat, Vt fama est, Primate regi.
units.tr: So, as we have seen, the changes of kingdoms have altered many things in the ancient divisions. But, as the most noble Joseph Scaliger wrote to me in his letter about his own France, the ecclesiastical order has kept its original traces intact so far, in the East as in the West. For the cities that gave their names to provinces are called metropolises [Μητροπόλεις]. If a vicar, whom they called an exarch [Ἐξαρχος], had his seat in one of them, they name these cities not only metropolises, exarchs [Ἐξαρχοι], and cities [πόλεις], but also exarchates [Ἐξάρχας] and patriarchates [Πατριάρχας]. Their prelates are called exarchs or patriarchs, and the rest are called metropolitans or archbishops [Μητροπολίτας ἢ Ἀρχιεπισκόπους], who have only bishops under them. For exarchs have under them, besides bishops, also metropolitans, while metropolitans have only bishops. In the Latin Church the name and the right of archbishops remain, together with canonical jurisdiction over their suffragan bishops. But no traces of exarchs survive, unless perhaps some shadow of them is found in the fact that the metropolitan or archbishop of Vienne calls himself "Primate of Primates." That title shows that he had primates under him, who were subject to him: the Primate of Narbonne for the province, and the Primate of Bourges for Aquitaine. Otherwise, how or by what right would he be called Primate of Primates, unless by reason of the diocesan vicar, the Prefect of Vienne, the praetor who had seven provinces under him, among them the First Narbonensis and the First Aquitaine? That the Archbishop of Lyon rejoices to be called Primate, however, is a matter of ambition, and the title was granted to him by favour of the Roman Pontiff; nor is it so new. For William the Breton sings in his Philippeid: "And Lyon, where all Gaul was once wont, as the story goes, to be ruled by a primate." [Lugdunensis … Primate]

units.la: At Primas Primatum antea dici jure non potuit, quia nullam Primam Provinciam sub se habebat. Viennensis Primas quidem Primatum vocari vult, sed Caullam tam ille, quam omnis Ecclesia ignorat. Quapropter Divisio Galliarum per Diœceses Ecclesiasticas & Episcopatus, ut omnium antiquissima, ita certissima nobis sequenda erat, neque ulla melior erat quærenda, si integræ illæ Ἐξάρχαι adhuc finibus Regni Francorum continerentur, ut olim sub Karolo Magno, & ejus Filio & Nepotibus: sed quia ex illo amplissimo Imperio multæ Provinciæ detractæ sunt, alia nobis Tributio instituenda. Galliæ igitur sive Franciæ Imperium octo Tribunalibus temperatur, quæ ius reddunt Provinciis suis, à quibus Provocatio non est, quorumque & Majestas augustissima est & Auctoritas sacrosancta. Parlamenta Galli Idiomate suo vocant, ut prolixius docui capite xvii. Non possum meliorem Partitionis rationem inire, quam si in octo hæc Parlamenta omne Francorum Regnum dividam, & ea in Provincias suas. Provincias quidem novi, quot Gallia Reges adipiscitur, tot fere Mutationes, Nomina & Regimina subire; eam ob causam non ignorans consultius esse ut à Parlamentis Divisio procederet porro per Diœceses & Episcopatus, quum etiam illa proxime accedat ad priscam Imperij Romani notitiam: sed quia Geographis in more positum, ut quæ suis temporibus obtinent in Regnorum Regionumque terminis, ea quam fidelissime fieri potest, indicent & proponant, religio mihi ab recepta tam multis probataque hactenus consuetudine decedere. Quamobrem talem ego docendi, Galliasque commode cumque structu explicandi gratia, Distributionem excogitavi.
units.tr: But a primate could not rightly be called Primate of Primates before, because he had no First Province under him. The Primate of Vienne does indeed want to be called Primate of Primates, but neither he nor any church knows of Caulla. For this reason the division of Gaul by ecclesiastical dioceses and bishoprics, as the most ancient, is also the most certain, and it was the one we ought to follow; no better one should be sought. If those entire exarchates were still contained within the borders of the kingdom of the Franks, as once under Charlemagne and his son and grandsons, we could keep it. But since many provinces have been cut away from that vast empire, another arrangement must be set up for us. Therefore the empire of Gaul, or France, is governed by eight tribunals, which dispense justice to their provinces, from which there is no appeal, and whose majesty is most august and whose authority is sacrosanct. The French call them parlements in their own language, as I explained at more length in chapter xvii. I cannot devise a better plan of division than to divide the whole kingdom of the Franks into these eight parlements and to treat each in its provinces. I know that the provinces of Gaul change their names, rulers, and governments almost as often as its kings change. For that reason, aware that it is more prudent for the division to proceed by dioceses and bishoprics, since this comes closest to the ancient knowledge of the Roman Empire, I still feel bound not to depart from a custom so widely received and so long approved, namely that geographers show, as faithfully as possible, what holds within the boundaries of kingdoms and regions in their own times. So I have devised this arrangement for teaching, and for explaining Gaul in a convenient order.

units.la: Provinciæ quæ in Galliarum delineatione ab Geographis hodie solent exponi, aliæ Francorum sunt Regis, vel Regi subiectæ; aliæ extra Francorum Ditionem. Quæ prioris generis optime mecumque Instituto convenientissime, divido in sua Parlamenta, quæ, ut dixi, octo sunt numero: Unum quidem Principale; reliqua Accessoria. Principale est Parisiense, omnium Primum, & olim unicum solumque, Parlamenti Parisiensis Sedes Præsidiales, ut multæ (nam latissime ejus se extendit iurisdictio) sic variæ admodum sunt, in variis constitutæ Provinciis. Eas Ligeris facit alias Septemtrionales, alias Meridionales. Quod ad Priores in Vetere quidem Belgica, hodie est Picardia La Picardie; in Celtica vero versus Occidentem Francia, La France, strictius sumta (cujus tamen etiam nonnulla incidunt in Belgicam & Blesia, La Beauce: versus ortum Campania, La Champaigne, & Lugdunensis tractus, Pais de Lionnois. Quod ad Meridionales, possidebat eas olim ex Veterum delineatione, cum Narbonensi, Aquitanica. Dicebatur autem Aquitania in dextra Garumnæ ripa, partim Prima, ubi hodie cis Vigennam Biturices, Berry, & Borbonium, Bourbonnois; ultra vero Pictonum Poitou, Agerque & Inculisensis Angoulesme, & Alnisiensis, Le Pais d'Aulnis: partim Secunda, ubi nunc Arvernia, Auvergne. Accessoria Parlamenta sunt, quæ Principale illud quasi circumeunt, versus Occidentem ad Ligeris dextram Rothomagense, sub quo Normannia, La Normandie: & Redonense cui subest Britannia, La Bretagne: ad sinistram Burdigalense & Tolosinum, quorum quodque sua extendit jura nunc integre & separatim; nunc vero mistim in aliquot adsignatas sibi Veteris Aquitaniæ Narbonensisque Galliæ Ditiones. Integre quidem Burdigalensi subsunt Lemovicivm, Limosin, Petrocorivm, Perigort, Gvienna, La Guienne; Tolosano autem Cadurcivm, Querci, Rvtenivm, Rouargue, Langvedokivm, Languedoc: Mistim vero utrique Vasconia, La Gascoigne: quemadmodum plenius ex sequentibus patebit. Iam versus Orientem ad Mare Gallicum, Parlamentum est Aquensis, cujus iurisdictioni obtemperat Provincia, La Provence; in Mediterraneis Gratianopolitanum, ab cujus nutu pendet Delphinatus, Le Dauphiné & Dinionense, quod in iure Summo dicundo agnoscit Ducatus Burgundiæ, La Duché de Bourgongne. Hactenus quæ Regis. Extra Dirionem Francorum, in Francia tamen, suos habent etiam Dominatus alij Principes, & Ecclesiastici & Politici. Pontificis enim Romani est Comitatvs Avenionensis, Avignon; Politicorum alij sunt Ducatus, ut Sabaudia, Savoye, & Lotharingia, Lorraine; alij sunt Principatus, ut Bearnia, Bearn, & Aravsio, Aurange; alij Comitatus, ut Burgundia, La Conté de Bourgongne & Carolesivm, Charolois. Has Regiones si fideliter ordine a me indicato perambularo, Lectores spero ita judicaturos, me nullam non partem, vel obiter, attigisse: plerasque Vrbes adijisse; &, si non omnia, præcipua saltem de singulis dixisse. Illud obiter hic monendum duxi, Appianum testari Galliarum εἴη fuisse Τετραγωνία· Πόλις ὑπὲρ ἐκ-ξοσίας. Minor est numerus in Templo, quod ab omnibus communi consilio Gallis Augusto Lugduni exstructum: de quo Strabo lib. iv. τὸ, τε ἱερὸν τὸ ἀναδέχθεν τῶν πάντων κοινῆ τῶν Γαλατῶν Καίσαρι τῷ Σεβαστῷ. μετὰ ταύτης ἱδρυται τῆς πόλεως, ὅτι τῇ συμ-βολῇ τῶν πολεμῶν. Ἐι δὲ ἔωμεν ἀχρόλογ ὅπιγραφῶ ἔχων τῶν Ἐθνῶν ἐξ τὸν ἀριθμόν. Vnde tanta in numero Gentium Galliæ discrepantia? Appianum existimo Gentes universim designare totius Galliæ; eas fuisse circiter quadringentas: Aram autem Lugdunensem eas tantum habuisse, à quibus illa in Augusti honorem fuit posita, sexaginta scilicet. Qui porro, quam ego vel in superioribus attuli, vel in sequentibus sum allatus, plura, vel saltem mea pluribus fusiusque explicata, petat: consulat moneo, quod quidem ad universæ Galliæ delineationem, præter alios, Robertum Cœnalem, qui integro volumine Galliias descripsit, Gilbertum Cognatum Nozorenum, Ioannem Marium, Chassanæum lib. xii de Gloria mundi, Guilielmum Postellum in libello Vniversitatis, Sebastianum Munsterum, Franciscum Belleforestium, Andream Thevetum, Abrahamum Ortelium & Gerardum Mercatorem; quorum ille xvi, hic xii Chartis Galliam depingit: quod autem ad Gallorum Mores, Resque ab illis gestas, adeat Lector ex Antiquis C. Iuli Cæsaris Libros vii de Bello Gallico, ijsque additum ab A. Hirtio viii, Appiani Alexandrini Celticum, sive de Bello Gallico, & alios, quos variis supra locis laudavi; ex Recentioribus, medijque ævi, Scriptores illos Annalium & Historiæ Francorum, quos maximo Reip. litterariæ bono nuper edidit P. Pithœus IC: his addat Hunibaldi libros xviii, in quibus tamen multa fabulosa & commentitia, sermoque plane barbarus; Gregorij Turonensis Episcopi libros x; Aimoini Monachi Floriacensis Cœnobij Libros de Regibus Francorum v; item Ioannem Tritemium, Froissardum, quique eum supplevit, Enguerranum, Robertum Gaguinum, Philippum Cominæum, Nicolaum Gillium, Paulum Æmilium, Ioannem Ferronium Ioannem Tilium, Henricum Leonardum, Hermannum Comitem, Nicolaum Vignerium, Guilielmum Paradinum, Papirium Massonium, Galeatium Capellam, qui scripsit de bellis in Italia gestis inter Karolum V & Franciscum Galliarum Regem. De Gallorum Imperio & Philosophia libros vii scripsit elegantes & eruditos Stephanus Forcatulus IC. Alios alijs, quibus otium curiosius hæc talia consectandi, adponendos nominaris à me relinquo
units.tr: The provinces that geographers today usually set out in their description of Gaul are some belonging to the King of the Franks or subject to him, and others outside the dominion of the Franks. I divide those of the first kind, which suit my plan best and most conveniently, into their parlements, which, as I said, are eight in number. One is principal, and the rest are subordinate. The principal one is the Parisian, first of all and once the only one, whose presidial seats are various, as its jurisdiction extends very widely, and it is established in many different provinces. The Loire divides them into northern and southern. The northern ones lie, in Old Belgica, in what is now Picardy, La Picardie; in Celtica, to the west, in France, La France, taken more narrowly (though some of it also falls into Belgica and into Blésois, La Beauce); to the east lie Champagne, La Champaigne, and the district of Lyon, Pais de Lionnois. The southern ones, according to the old description of the ancients, once held Aquitaine along with Narbonensis Gaul. Aquitaine was said to lie on the right bank of the Garonne. Part of it was the First Aquitaine, where now lie, on this side of the Vienne, Bourges, Berry, and Bourbon, Bourbonnois; beyond the Vienne lie the Poitevins, Poitou, the territory of Angoulême, Angoulesme, and Aulnis, Le Pais d'Aulnis. Part was the Second Aquitaine, where Auvergne, Auvergne, now is. The subordinate parlements are those that roughly encircle the principal one. To the west, on the right bank of the Loire, lies the Rouen parlement, under which is Normandy, La Normandie; and the Rennes parlement, under which is Brittany, La Bretagne. On the left bank lie the Bordeaux and Toulouse parlements, each of which extends its jurisdiction now wholly and separately, and now mixed together over several districts of Old Aquitaine and Narbonensis Gaul assigned to them. Wholly under Bordeaux are the Limousin, Limosin, Périgord, Perigort, and Guienne, La Guienne; under Toulouse are Quercy, Querci, Rouergue, Rouargue, and Languedoc, Languedoc; but both share Gascony, La Gascoigne, as will be clearer from what follows. Now to the east, on the Gallic Sea, is the Aix parlement, to whose jurisdiction the province of Provence, La Provence, submits; inland is Grenoble, Gratianopolitanum, on whose authority Dauphiné, Le Dauphiné, depends, and Dijon, Dinionense, which in the highest court of justice acknowledges the Duchy of Burgundy, La Duché de Bourgongne. So far, the regions of the King. Outside the dominion of the Franks, yet still in France, other princes also hold lordships, both ecclesiastical and secular. The County of Avignon, Avignon, belongs to the Roman Pontiff. Among the secular lords, some hold duchies, such as Savoy, Savoye, and Lorraine, Lorraine; others hold principalities, such as Béarn, Bearn, and Orange, Aurange; others hold counties, such as Burgundy, La Conté de Bourgongne, and Charolais, Charolois. If I have faithfully traversed these regions in the order I have indicated, I hope readers will judge that I have touched on almost every part, if only in passing; that I have visited most of the cities; and that, if not everything, at least the chief things about each have been said. I thought it worth noting here in passing that Appian testifies that Gaul's shape was a quadrilateral, a city beyond ... [the Greek is corrupt and cannot be fully recovered]. The number in the temple is smaller, the one that was built at Lyon by all the Gauls together in common to Augustus. Of it Strabo, book iv, says that the temple was founded in this city by all the Gauls together for Caesar Augustus, as a sign of the wars ... [the Greek is corrupt]. Why, then, such a discrepancy in the number of Gallic peoples? I think Appian means the peoples of all Gaul in general, which were about four hundred; but the altar at Lyon had only those from which it was set up in honour of Augustus, namely sixty. As for anyone who wants more than I have brought forward here or will bring forward below, or wants my points explained at greater length, I advise him to consult, besides others, Robert Cénalis, who described Gaul in a whole volume; Gilbert Cognatus of Nozeroy; John Marius; Chassanaeus, book xii, On the Glory of the World; William Postel in his little book On the University; Sebastian Münster; François de Belleforest; André Thevet; Abraham Ortelius; and Gerard Mercator, of whom the first depicts Gaul on sixteen charts and the second on twelve. As for the customs of the Gauls and the deeds they performed, the reader may consult, among the ancients, the seven books of Julius Caesar's Gallic War, with the eighth added by Aulus Hirtius, Appian of Alexandria's Celtic Affairs, or On the Gallic War, and others I have cited in various places above. Among the more recent writers of the Middle Ages, there are those annals and histories of the Franks that P. Pithou, a jurist, recently edited for the great good of the literary commonwealth. To these he may add the eighteen books of Hunibald, though in them there is much that is fabulous and invented, and the style is plainly barbarous; the ten books of Gregory of Tours, bishop; the five books on the Kings of the Franks by Aimoin, monk of the monastery of Fleury; likewise John Trithemius, Froissart and his continuator Enguerrand, Robert Gaguin, Philippe de Commynes, Nicolas Gilles, Paulus Aemilius, John Ferron, John Tillet, Henry Léonard, Hermann Comes, Nicolas Vignier, William Paradin, Papirius Masson, and Galeazzo Capella, who wrote about the wars waged in Italy between Charles V and Francis, King of the French. Stephen Forcadel, a jurist, wrote seven elegant and learned books on the empire and philosophy of the Gauls. I leave to others, to whom leisure for pursuing such things more carefully is given, the task of naming further authors to be added to these.

units.la: Ad specialiora Galliarum pergo. Occurrit in mea Distributione primo loco
units.tr: I now turn to the more specific parts of Gaul. In my division, the first to come up is

units.la: Picardia.
units.tr: Picardy.

units.la: PICARDIÆ Nomen quamvis non magnæ antiquitatis, nulla tamen ejus certa potest reddi ratio. Alij aliam augurantur: Inter eos Robertus Cenalis, Episcopus Abrincantensis, vel, ut alij, Arboriensis, Picardos dicit vere esse Gallos; se nihilominus ignorare, num à Begardis hæreticis (quos constat Ludovici Bavari Imperatoris tempore, circa annum clo cccxiv, quasdam Inferioris Germaniæ Vrbes coluisse) nomen hoc sint mutuati. Belleforestius Picardos antea fuisse vocatos scribit, quam Becardi in rerum essent natura, quamque ulla istius Sectæ audiretur mentio. Sunt qui appellatos censent Picardos: quod ab his ortus primo usus Lancearum, quæ vulgo Picques nuncupantur. Ego rem in medio relinquo.
units.tr: The name Picardy is not very ancient, and no certain explanation of it can be given. Others guess differently. Among them, Robert Cenalis, bishop of Avranches (or, as others say, of Arbois), says that the Picards are truly Gauls, but he admits he does not know whether they took the name from the heretical Beghards, who are known to have occupied some cities of Lower Germany in the time of the emperor Louis of Bavaria, around the year 1314. Belleforest writes that the Picards were so called before the Becards existed in nature, and before any mention of that sect was heard. Some think the people were called Picards because the use of lances, commonly called picques, first arose among them. I leave the matter open.

units.la: Hujus Regionis, quæ quondam in Antiqua Belgica (ea præcipue, quæ Secunda posteriori ævo) appellatio latius olim patuit: complexa Artesiam Flandriæque partem ad Lisam usque Amnem: alijs multo etiam ulterius tendentibus ad Scaldim usque & Renum Fluvios. Hodie Picardiam, ut crasse diffiniam, ad Occasum respicit, cum nonnulla Normanniæ portione, Oceanus Britannicus: ad Septemtrionem istæ Veteris Belgicæ jacent Regiones, quæ hodie Artesia & Hannonia: ad Ortum Leuceburgum & Lotharingia sunt porrectæ: ad Meridiem denique Campania, isque nobilissimi Regni Tractus, qui specialiore notione Francia vocatur, occurrunt.
units.tr: This region, which in ancient times, in the Belgica of old (especially the part later called the Second), once extended its name more widely, took in Artois and part of Flanders as far as the river Lys, while others extended it even further, as far as the rivers Scheldt and Rhine. Today Picardy, to define it roughly, faces west, with part of Normandy and the British Ocean. To the north lie the regions of old Belgica that today are Artois and Hainault; to the east stretch Luxembourg and Lorraine; and to the south lies Champagne, that most noble part of the kingdom which in the narrower sense is called France.

units.la: Regio est fertilissima, Horreumque Parisiorum, atque adeo pleraque Franciæ. Vino caret, ignava potius Incolarum socordia, quam vel Cœli vel Soli injuria.
units.tr: It is a very fertile region, and the granary of Paris and indeed of much of France. It lacks wine, a fault due to the laziness of its inhabitants rather than to any harm from the climate or the sun.

units.la: Picardiam habitarunt olim Ambiani, Suessones, Veromandui, Effui, Oromansaci, Morini, & alij fortean. Ambianorum Sedes, ubi hodie opulentissima Vrbs Ambianum, vulgo Amiens: Eorum frequens apud antiquos Scriptores mentio, Cæsarem, Plinium, alios. Ἀμβιανοὶ Ptolemæo, & Straboni. Cæsar Ambianos Morinis jungit, quorum fines Nervij attingebant: Strabo Ambianos Morinis facit propinquos, & Suessiones: Ptolemæus post Bellovacos in Gallia Belgica statuit Ambianos. Suessiones, vel, ut alij scribunt Suessiones, sæpe apud Cæsarem (qui & Eleutheros, Liberos, prænominat lib. vii quemadmodum & Cadurcos. de quibus cap. xxxv) memorantur. Σουεσσιῶνες apud Strabonem: ubi Isaacus Casaubonus legit Σuiorῶνς: Ptolemæo ῾Ιστορυς, repono Σuiorυς. Hodie Souessons. Apud Suessones ætate memoriaque Cæsaris Rex Diviciacus, totius Galliæ potentissimus, fuit; qui cum magnæ partis harum Regionum, tum etiam Britanniæ Imperium obtinuit: Deinde Galba successit. Et cujusmodi Regnum hoc fuerit, hinc intelligi potest, quod Suessones Remorum Fratres Consanguineique eodem jure ijsdemque legibus uterentur, unum Imperium, unumque Magistratum cum illis haberent. Suessonum latissimi ferœcissimiqúe fuerunt Agri, & Opida duodecim; quorum unicum ab Cæsare nominatur Noviodunum, quod ipse post Belgarum discessum ex itinere oppugnare conatus, propter latitudinem Fossæ, murique altitudinem, paucis licet defendentibus, expugnare non potuit. Veromandui Cæsari (qui in libris de bello Gallico de ijs multa) Plinioque Galliæ Belgicæ Populi: qui Ὁυερομάνδυι Ptolemæo, & in nonnullis Exemplaribus Ὁυερομάνδυς pro Ουερομάνδις, inquit Surita; Veromandui Epitomæ Livianæ libri c i v, item Lapidi antiquo, qui, teste apud Abrahamum Ortelium Iacobo Carondiletio, Cancellario Leodiensi, in Pago Hannoniæ, qui vulgo Arfaures prope Bavacum. Effuos Cæsar nominat: Eorum Sedes ubi hodie illa Picardiæ portio, quæ Tirascha, quasi, ut Bovillus cum aliis opinatur, Terra Effuorum. Alij Effuos ponunt ubi nunc Retelois: alij ubi Bessin, prope Baiocasses, Bayeux: Divæus Comitatum de Eu putat. Hubertus Leodius tradit eos Aëthum Hannoniæ Vrbem occupare: sic quot Capita, tot Sententiæ inceptiores nos relinquunt, Oromansaci, junctii Pago, inquit Plinius, quæ Gessoriacus appellatur: fuisse censentur, ubi hac tempestate Comitatus Guinersis. Morini Virgilio, Cæsari, Plinio, aliisque noti; Ptolemæo & Straboni Μέροι: olim, ubi nunc in ruinis jacet Teroana, quæ in Notitia, ut alibi vidimus, Civitas Morinorum, id est Pontificum. Morinorum meminit Lapis, qui in Gelria, dimidiato ab Vrbe Neomagensi Miliario, repertus. MINERVAE CVR. LADAE T. PVNICIVS. C NIALIS. II. VIR. CLON. MORINO RVM. SACRDS ROMAE. ET. AVG OB. HONOREM V. V. A. M. D. V. L
units.tr: The Ambiani, Suessones, Veromandui, Effui, Oromansaci, Morini, and perhaps others, once inhabited Picardy. The seat of the Ambiani is where the very wealthy city of Amiens (commonly Amiens) stands today. They are often mentioned by ancient writers such as Caesar, Pliny, and others. Ptolemy and Strabo call them Ambiani [Ἀμβιανοί]. Caesar joins the Ambiani to the Morini, whose borders the Nervii reached; Strabo places the Ambiani near the Morini and the Suessiones; Ptolemy puts the Ambiani after the Bellovaci in Belgic Gaul. The Suessiones, or as others write, Suessiones, are often mentioned in Caesar (who also calls them Eleutheri, the Free, in book 7, just as he does the Cadurci, of whom in chapter 35). In Strabo they are Σουεσσιῶνες [Suessiones], where Isaac Casaubon reads Σουϊόνες; in Ptolemy, ῾Ιστορυς, which I would restore to Σουϊόνες. Today the place is Soissons. In Caesar's time and memory, Diviciacus, the most powerful king in all Gaul, ruled among the Suessiones; he held power over a large part of these regions and also over Britain. Galba succeeded him. What kind of kingdom this was can be understood from the fact that the Suessiones, who were brothers and kinsmen of the Remi, used the same law and the same laws, and had one government and one magistracy with them. The fields of the Suessiones were very broad and very fertile, and they had twelve towns. Only one is named by Caesar, Noviodunum, which he himself tried to storm on the march after the Belgae had withdrawn. Because of the width of its ditch and the height of its wall, he could not take it, though few defended it. The Veromandui are a people of Belgic Gaul, mentioned by Caesar (who speaks much of them in his books on the Gallic War) and by Pliny. Ptolemy calls them Οὐερομάνδυι [Veromanduoi], and in some copies Οὐερομάνδυς for Οὐερομάνδις, says Surita. They are called Veromandui in the Epitome of Livy, book 104, and also on an ancient stone which, according to Abraham Ortelius, was reported to James Carondelet, chancellor of Liège, in a district of Hainault commonly called Arfaures, near Bavay. Caesar names the Effui; their seat is where that part of Picardy now stands which is called Tirasche, as if, as Bovillus with others thinks, it were the land of the Effui. Others place the Effui where Retelois is now; others where Bessin is, near Baiocasses (Bayeux); Divaeus thinks of the County of Eu. Hubert Leodius reports that they occupied Aëthum, a city of Hainault. Thus as many heads, so many opinions, which are rather too rash for us to settle. The Oromansaci, joined to a district which Pliny says is called Gessoriacus, are thought to have been where the County of Guines now is. The Morini are known to Virgil, Caesar, Pliny, and others; Ptolemy and Strabo call them Μέροι [Meroi]. Formerly they lived where Thérouanne now lies in ruins, which in the Notitia, as I have seen elsewhere, is the city of the Morini, that is, of the Pontifices. The Morini are also mentioned in an inscription found in Gelderland, half a mile from the city of Nijmegen: "To Minerva, sacred to Lada, T. Punicius, son of C., duumvir of the Morini, priest of Rome and of Augustus, for his honour, gladly and deservedly fulfilled his vow."

units.la: Vadicasses sunt apud Plinium, qui Οὐδικάσιοι Ptolemæo: quondam, ubi nunc Noion, Noviomagus Antonino inter Suessones & Ambianos; Νευιόμαγος Vadicassium Ptolemæo. Alij sunt Vadicasses ab Baiocassibus; de quibus in Normannia: nam temere quidam confundunt.
units.tr: The Vadicasses are in Pliny, and are Οὐδικάσιοι [Oudikasioi] in Ptolemy. They once lived where Noyon now is, and Antoninus calls it Noviomagus, between the Suessiones and the Ambiani; Ptolemy calls Noviomagus of the Vadicasses Νευιόμαγος [Neuiomagos]. Others are the Vadicasses who are distinct from the Baiocasses, of whom I speak in Normandy; for some carelessly confuse them.

units.la: Picardia porro in tris dividitur partes, Veram, Inferiorem, Superiorem. De postrema nihil hoc libro dicam. Occupatur enim Tota fere ab ijs Regionibus, quæ in Inseriore Germania, interque Septemdecim Provincias principem obtinent locum; de quibus libro v.
units.tr: Moreover, Picardy is divided into three parts: True Picardy, Lower Picardy, and Upper Picardy. I shall say nothing in this book about the last. For almost all of it is occupied by those regions which lie in Lower Germany and hold the chief place among the Seventeen Provinces, of which I shall speak in book 5.

units.la: Vera (La vraye Picardie) cœpto Parisijs itinere, superatisque Bellovacorum Agris, initium est ad Crepacorium. Comprehendit Vuedamias (Communibus utar Vocabulis, ut melius intelligat) Ambianum, Corbiensem & Pequignyam: Comitatus Veromanduorum & Retelorum; Ducatum Tiraschensem.
units.tr: True Picardy (La vraye Picardie), with the road from Paris taken and the lands of the Bellovaci passed, begins at Crépy. It includes the Vidamies (I shall use common terms so that it may be better understood): Amiens, Corbie, and Péquigny; the County of the Veromandui and of the Retelois; and the Duchy of Thérache.

units.la: Ambiana (Visdamie d'Amiens) nomen dedit Amlianum, vulgo Amiens: olim uti censent V. N. Josephus Scaliger, Petrus Divæus, Goropius Becanus, Josias Simlerus, & alij, Samarobriva. Sigebertus etiam Ambianum idem facit cum Sommonobria; sic ille scripsit pro Samarobriva. Alij, quum Samarobrivam & Ambianos duo diversa se dicerent legere opida apud Antoninum, in eam ierunt sententiam, ut arbitrarentur Samarobriva memoriam hodieque servari in opido, quod ad Somonam (vel, ut alij scribunt, Suminam) Brayum nominatur. Sed potuit eadem urbs & Samarobriva vocari & Ambiani, quod horum Populorum ea esset caput. Itinera Antonini, quæ utriusque faciunt mentionem, alibi videbimus: Prius quidem, quod ad Picardiam proprie pertineat, ad finem hujus capitis, alterum, quod multas simul Galliæ Regiones complectatur, ad Libri finem. Samarobrivæ meminerunt, præter posteriores ævi Scriptores, aliquoties Cæsar lib. v de Bello Gallico & Cicero lib. v i i. Epist. ad Trebatium; ut falsum sit, quod superioribus adscribit Sigebertus, Vrbem hanc ab Antonino Pio Imperatore fuisse conditam. Majorem habet vetustatem. Ptolemæo appellatur Σαμαροβριγα. Quidam Antonini Codices Samarabrivam, alij Samarabrigam præferunt. Brigam antiqua Hispanorum Lingua, & Briam Thracio sermone, Vrbem nuncupari alias dixi. Nonnulli Somo-nobrigam scribunt à Ponte (Belgice Brug) quo Somona fluvius traijciebatur. Ambianum certe Vrbs est ad Somonam, qui eam hic ibi findit; unde quidam Ambianum putant dictum ab Imperatore Gratiano, quod Aquis ambiatur) munitionibus Galliarum & ab natura & ab hominum industria merito connumeranda; Fossis pulcris præaltisque vallata; Clavis ea parte Regni. Templum habet spectiosissimum. Incolæ multis clarent Privilegijs; inter ea, quod cum ab exterorum militum Præsidijs, tum ab subsidijs sint immunes. Probitate sane Fidelitateq; sunt insignes. Fabulantur quidam ab Alexandri Magni Militibus conditum. Ambiano tribuit Antonini Itinerarium Legionem xxiii. Episcopos ejus Bellesforestius recenset lxiii; inter eos autem ultimum Ioannem Crequium.
units.tr: The Vidamy of Amiens (Visdamie d'Amiens) gave its name to Amiens, commonly called Amiens. Long ago, as V. N. Joseph Scaliger, Peter Divaeus, Goropius Becanus, Josias Simler, and others think, it was Samarobriva. Sigebert also makes Ambianum the same as Sommonobria; so he wrote for Samarobriva. Others, since they read that Samarobriva and Ambiani are two different towns in Antoninus, came to the view that Samarobriva is still remembered in the town called Brai on the Somme (or, as others write, the Somme). But the same city could be called both Samarobriva and Ambiani, since it was the capital of these peoples. The itineraries of Antoninus that mention both will be seen elsewhere: the first, which properly concerns Picardy, at the end of this chapter, and the second, which covers many regions of Gaul at once, at the end of the book. Samarobriva is mentioned, apart from later writers, several times by Caesar in book 5 of the Gallic War, and by Cicero in book 7 of the Letters to Trebatius. So it is false what Sigebert ascribes to the earlier writers, that this city was founded by the emperor Antoninus Pius. It is much older. Ptolemy calls it Σαμαροβριγα [Samarobriga]. Some manuscripts of Antoninus prefer Samarabrivam, others Samarabrigam. I have said elsewhere that Brigam in the old Spanish language and Briam in the Thracian tongue mean a town. Some write Somo-nobrigam, from the bridge (in Flemish Brug) over which the river Somme was crossed. Amiens is certainly a town on the Somme, which cuts through it here; hence some think Ambianum was named after the emperor Gratian, because it is surrounded by waters. It is rightly counted among the fortresses of Gaul, both by nature and by human effort, protected by fine and very deep ditches, and it is the key to the kingdom on that side. It has a most splendid church. Its inhabitants are distinguished by many privileges, among them that they are exempt both from garrisons of foreign soldiers and from subsidies. They are indeed remarkable for their honesty and loyalty. Some tell the fable that it was founded by the soldiers of Alexander the Great. The itinerary of Antoninus assigns the Legionem XXIII to Amiens. Bellforest lists sixty-three of its bishops, the last of whom is John Crequi.

units.la: Corbiensis ab Corbia, quod Opidum est ad Somonam; quo loco fluvius, cui adjacet, Somonam ingreditur: Clavis itidem, qua parte jacet, Franciæ. Carmesiaca forte Antonini, inter Samarobrivam, Ambiens & Cæsaromagum, Roye, ni fallor.
units.tr: Corbie takes its name from Corbia, a town on the Somme, where the river to which it lies adjacent flows into the Somme. It is likewise a key of France on the side where it lies. Carmesiaca is perhaps the place in Antoninus between Samarobriva, Ambiens and Cæsaromagum, now Roye, unless I am mistaken.

units.la: Pequigny denique à Pequigmo, vulgo Pequigny. Opidum est sic dictum, si vulgo fides, à Pignone, Alexandri Magni Milite. Historiographis nobilitatum, quod ibi Gulielmus Nortmanniæ Dux, cui cognomen erat Longa-Spatha, positis insidijs fuerit obtruncatus per factionem Balduini Comitis Cameracensis, qui cum pacis incundæ prætextu eo loci pellexerat. Testantur Nortmanniæ Annales. Memoriæ etiam produnt Francicarum rerum Scriptores Anglos, postquam prælio jam essent victi, superstites omnes ibidem fuisse occisos, qui nomen Pequigny literis omnibus pronunciare nequibant, Pequenij loco Pequigny proferentes.
units.tr: Finally, Péquigny is named from Pequigmo, commonly Pequigny. It is a town so called, if common belief is to be trusted, from Pignone, a soldier of Alexander the Great. It is made famous in the historians because there William, duke of Normandy, whose surname was Longa-Spatha (Longsword), was ambushed and cut down by the faction of Baldwin, count of Cambrai, who had lured him to that place under the pretext of a pleasant peace. The Annals of Normandy bear witness to this. Writers on French affairs also record that the English, after they had already been defeated in battle, were all killed there, since they could not pronounce the name Pequigny with all its letters, and said Pequenij instead of Pequigny.

units.la: Veromandui de quibus antea dixi, hodie vulgo Vermandois, retento, si qui alij Galliæ populi, prisco Nomine. Picardiæ pars, aliquando Comitatus titulo celebris. Inter Comites primum invenio Hugonem, Henrici 1 Francorum Regis filium, Philippi Regis fratrem: qui cum alijs Proceribus Bello Sacro, quod in Palæstina, Duce Godefredo Bilionæo, anno c l o x c i x gestum, interfuisse legitur. Successerunt huic duo Rudolphi Filius & Nepos; quorum hoc sine Liberis defuncto, Comitatus ad Regnum est devolutus. Wandali, facta in Gallias cum Burgundionibus irruptione, Provinciam hanc miserum in modum adflixerunt. Comprehendere vero sub se Comitatum hunc signant Franciæ Geographi Suessonum, Laudunensium, Tartenorum Ditiones; Vrbes item Noviomagum & Fanum S. Quintini.
units.tr: The Veromandui, of whom I spoke earlier, are today commonly called the Vermandois, keeping the ancient name as some other peoples of Gaul do. It is part of Picardy and was once famous under the title of county. Among the counts, the first I find is Hugh, son of Henry I, King of the Franks and brother of King Philip. He is read to have taken part with other nobles in the Holy War, which was waged in Palestine under Duke Godfrey of Bouillon in the year 1099. Two Rudolphs succeeded him, son and grandson. When the latter died without children, the county passed to the crown. After the Vandals made their incursion into Gaul together with the Burgundians, they afflicted this province in a wretched manner. The geographers of France include under this county the lordships of the Soissonnais, the Laonnois and the Tartenois, and also the towns of Noyon and Saint-Quentin.

units.la: Suessones, quorum antea memini, hodie vulgo Soueßones, vel, ut alij pronunciant, Soissonnois. Suessonum Vrbs, quæ hodie Soisson, Arce prædita; Suessones gentis voce, apud Antoninum, qui Legionem ei xxv attribuit; Σουεσσιῶνες Straboni; Αὐγῦσα Σουεσσόνων (sic enim emendandum, pro Ουεσσονῶν) Ptolemæo; Civitas Suessonum in Dignitatum libello dicitur. Eripuit hanc Vrbem Stagrio, Gilonis Romani Prætoris filio Hlodovæus: quo defuncto, Fil. decus illi Regiæ Civitatis, quo Cæsaris tempore claruerat, reddiderunt. Postea Comitatus Titulo fuit insignis. Karolus Ludovici Principis Condæi filius Comes audit Suessonum. Episcopatus est, cujus Belleforestius Præsules numerat nominatque lxxix; ultimum Matthiam Parisinum.
units.tr: The Suessones, whom I mentioned before, are today commonly called the Soissonnais, or, as others pronounce it, Soueßones. The city of the Suessones is today Soissons, which has a citadel. The name of the people appears as "Suessones" in Antoninus, who assigns them legion xxv; as Σουεσσιῶνες in Strabo; and as Αὐγῦσα Σουεσσόνων in Ptolemy (which must be emended to Ουεσσονῶν); and the city is called "Civitas Suessonum" in the Notitia Dignitatum. Clovis took this city from Stagrius, son of Gilo, the Roman prefect. After Clovis's death his sons restored to it the honour of a royal city, which it had enjoyed in Caesar's time. Afterwards it was distinguished by the title of county. Charles, son of Louis, Prince of Condé, is called Count of Soissons. There is a bishopric, whose prelates Belleforest counts and names as 79; the last of them was Matthias of Paris.

units.la: Laudunensium Ager, Laonnois, dictus ab Lauduno: cujus meminit Vita Karoli Magni, quodque inemendatius forte apud Antoninum Alauna, quod denique plenius effert ad me Litteris Magnus Scaliger, Laudunum Clavatum: hodie Laon. Conditam vult hanc Vrbem Papirius Massonius ab Matrobio Prætore. Situs ipsi in Colle. Invasit eam Karolus Lotharingiæ Dux, Ludovici Regis Francorum, Stirpis Karolinæ ultimi, Patruus; quum se jure Successionis videret privatum ab Hugone Capeto. Præsules se Duces & Pares Franciæ scribunt. Eorum Syllabus apud Belleforestium, cui lxxxiii recensentur, eorumque postremus Ioannes Burseius.
units.tr: The territory of the Laudunenses, the Laonnois, takes its name from Laon. It is mentioned in the Life of Charlemagne, and in Antoninus, perhaps less correctly, as Alauna. Magnus Scaliger, in a letter to me, gives the fuller form Laudunum Clavatum. Today it is Laon. Papirius Masson holds that this city was founded by the praetor Matrobius. Its site is on a hill. Charles, Duke of Lorraine, uncle of King Louis of the Franks, the last of the Carolingian line, seized it, when he saw himself deprived of the right of succession by Hugh Capet. The prelates write themselves Dukes and Peers of France. Their list in Belleforest enumerates 83, and the last of them is John Bourseius.

units.la: Tartenorum, vernacule Tartenois, Metropolis est Fera, vulgo La Fere: Vrbs egregie munita, situque commodissimo, ad Oysam Servamque confluentes; Arcem habens satis validam.
units.tr: The Tartenois, in the vernacular the Tartenois, has as its metropolis La Fère, commonly called La Fère. It is a town remarkably fortified and of most convenient position, at the confluence of the Oise and the Serre, and it has a fairly strong citadel.

units.la: Quæ nunc Vrbs Noion, Antonino Noviomagus nuncupatur, inter Suessonas & Ambianos, ut antea dixi, eam collocanti, Decimamque octavam Legionem illi tribuenti. Νοβιόμαγος Vadicassium est Ptolemæo. Vulgo Ecclesiasticorum Noviomum vocatur per compendium; ut Tresses pro Tricasses. Falluntur, qui eamdem faciunt cum Novioduno. Quatuor quidem Novioduna nominantur ab variis Scriptoribus, sed eorum nullum commune quid habet cum Noviomago, de quo agimus. Vir N. Iosephus Scaliger suis ad me Litteris, Se Nugatoribus hac in re, etiam juran-tibus, creditur em negat. Vrbs est, Antiquitatis suæ notas non paucas præferens. Episcopalis Sedes; cujus Præsules Comites se Noviomagienses & Franciæ Pares scribunt. Catalogus eorum apud Belleforestium, qui postremum edit Ioannes Hangestium, Senlisij Dynastæ filium.
units.tr: The city now called Noyon, named Noviomagus by Antoninus, is placed, as I said before, between the Suessones and the Ambiani, and Antoninus assigns it the eighteenth legion. Noviomagus is Vadicassium in Ptolemy. Among churchmen it is commonly called Noviomum, by contraction, as Tresses is for Tricasses. Those are mistaken who identify it with Noviodunum. Four places are named Noviodunum by various writers, but none of them has anything in common with Noviomagus, which is our subject. Mr. Joseph Scaliger, in his letters to me, says that in this matter he does not trust the triflers, even when they swear to it. It is a town bearing not a few marks of its antiquity. It is an episcopal see, whose prelates style themselves Counts of Noyon and Peers of France. Their catalogue is in Belleforest, who names last John of Hangest, son of the lord of Senlis.

units.la: Fano S. Quintini, quod Comitum Veromanduorum aliquando Domicilium & Regiunculæ caput, nomen à Quintino, qui Martyrium ibi passus. Olim Augusta Veromanduorum. Sic etiam differte dicitur in Vita S. Quintini. Robertus tamen Cœnalis scribit hanc Augustam omnino dirutam, ejusque hodie nihil restare præter Cœnobium, quod vulgo Vermand-Abbaye. Quidquid sit, Fanum S. Quintini, Arce nunc potens, multa sustinuit Damna, Calamitatesque Bello inter Philippum Hispaniarum & Henricum Galliarum Reges: quæ plenius à me explicata in Historia Rerum per Belgicam nuperis hisce Tumultibus gestarum.
units.tr: Saint-Quentin, which was at one time the residence of the counts of the Veromandui and the capital of a little kingdom, takes its name from Quentin, who suffered martyrdom there. Formerly it was Augusta Veromanduorum. It is called by a different name in the Life of St Quentin. Robert Cénalis, however, writes that this Augusta was utterly destroyed, and that nothing of it remains today except the monastery, commonly called Vermand-Abbaye. Whatever the case, Saint-Quentin, now strong with its citadel, suffered many losses and calamities in the war between Philip, King of Spain, and Henry, King of France. I have explained these more fully in my History of the events in the Netherlands during the recent disturbances.

units.la: Hæc de Veromanduis: Retelorum (vulgo Retelois) ditio sita est inter Hannonios, Lotharingos & Barros. Metropolis Retelium.
units.tr: So much for the Veromandui. The territory of the Rethelois (in the vernacular, Rethelois) lies between the Hainaulters, the Lorrainers and the Barrois. Its metropolis is Rethel.

units.la: Tirasiche (La Tirasiche) de qua ante nonnihil, primaria Vrbs est Guisa: Arce superbiens; Propugnaculum contra Leuceburgenses: Vetus Patrimonium Fratrum Primogeniti Lotharingiæ Ducis. Ducum Guisæ proximorum hoc lego Stemma:
units.tr: The Thiérache (La Thiérache), of which I spoke a little earlier, has as its chief town Guise, which prides itself on its citadel. It is a bulwark against the men of Liège (Leuceburgenses), and was the old patrimony of the younger brothers of the Duke of Lorraine. I read the following pedigree of the nearest Dukes of Guise:

units.la: CLAVDIVS Lotharingius, Dux Guisæ & Aumaliæ.
units.tr: Claude of Lorraine, Duke of Guise and Aumale.

units.la: FRANCISCVS, Dux Guisæ obiit xii Kal. Mart. MDLXIIII; in Obsidione Aureliaensi. | MARIA, defuncto Priore Marito Duce Longevillano, coniux inde Iacobi V Scotiæ Regis. | CLAVDIVS Dux Aumalius. HENRICVS, Dux Guisæ: cæsus xviii Kal. Ianuar. MDLXXXVIII in Comitiis Blesensibus. | LVDOVICVS Cardinalis Lotharingiæ: cæsus cum Fratre eodem tempore, ipsdem Comitiis, in conspectu Regis. | CAROLVS Dux Mayennæ. | MARIA Stuarda Scotiæ Regina; supplicio adfecta xii Kal. Mart. MDLXXXVII. FRANCISCVS Dux Iamvillæ.
units.tr: Francis, Duke of Guise, died 12 Kal. March 1564, at the siege of Orléans. | MARY, after the death of her first husband, the Duke of Longueville, then wife of James V, King of Scots. | CLAUDE, Duke of Aumale. HENRY, Duke of Guise, slain 18 Kal. January 1588 at the Estates of Blois. | LOUIS, Cardinal of Lorraine, slain with his brother at the same time and at the same Estates, in the sight of the King. | CHARLES, Duke of Mayenne. | MARY Stuart, Queen of Scots, executed 12 Kal. March 1587. FRANCIS, Duke of Joinville.

units.la: Sic se habet Vera Picardia: Inferiori (La Basse) variæ sunt partes: Sanctterra, Pontium, Bolonesium, Guynæum, Oyum.
units.tr: Thus Picardy Proper is arranged. Lower Picardy (La Basse) has several parts: Santerre, Ponthieu, the Boulonnais, Guînes and Oye.

units.la: Sanctterra, Santerre, concluditur inter Montem S. Desiderii, Peronam & Roiam: Frumenti variorumque Fructuum valde ferax. Monti S. Desiderii, vulgo Mondidier, unde sit nomen, notum est. Perona, bellicis cladibus sæpe fatigata. Clavis ibi Franciæ, Arce potens. Hic Heribertus Veromanduorum Comes Captiuum detinuit Karolum Simplicem, Galliarum Regem. Late Papirius Massonius rerum Francicarum lib. x, & alij. Roiis, opidum non contemnendum, Arce, ut fere omnia limitaneis his locis, validum: Cæsaromagus, nisi fallor, Antonino & Itinerariæ Tabulæ: Cæsaromagi etiam in Bellovacis meminit Ptolemæus. Alij Rodrinam esse volunt: quæ mihi Romorantin, ut suo dicam loco. Est ibidem Nella, Propugnaculum, ut multa alia; hac parte Regni, Arce munitum, ad Fontem fere Ingonis Fluvij; qui, exiguo cursu confecto, mox inter Rouyam & Voiennam in Somonam se exonerat. Nella Clarorum Virorum genitrix. Ejus Dynastæ Marchiones adfinitate juncti leguntur Familiæ Ceurtenæ, quæ originem traxit ab Regibus Franciæ.
units.tr: Santerre, bounded by Montdidier, Péronne and Roye, is very fertile in wheat and other crops of various kinds. Montdidier, commonly called Mondidier, is well known, and the district takes its name from it. Péronne, often worn down by the disasters of war, is the key of France there and is powerful with its citadel. Here Herbert, Count of Vermandois, held Charles the Simple, King of France, captive. Papirius Masson treats this at length in book x of his Frankish history, as do others. Roye is a town not to be despised, fortified with a citadel as nearly all places in these border regions are. It is Caesaromagus, unless I am mistaken, in Antoninus and the Itinerary tables; Ptolemy also mentions Caesaromagus in the territory of the Bellovaci. Others want it to be Rodrina, which to me is Romorantin, as I shall say in its place. There is also Nesle, a bulwark like many others in this part of the kingdom, fortified with a citadel, near the source of the river Ingon. After a short course, the Ingon discharges itself into the Somme between Roye and Voyenne. Nesle is the birthplace of famous men. Its lords, the Marquises, are read to have been united by marriage to the family of Courtenay, which drew its origin from the kings of France.

units.la: Pontium, vernacule Ponthieu, Comitatus est, cui nomen creditur datum à Pontium, qui passim ibi, multitudine. Est enim Regio inter Somonam & Authyam fluvios; Paludibus plena: quæque Stagnis suis, ut ipse deprehendi, multis in locis invia. Cogitandum aliis relinquo, an non Nomen hujus opinione quorundam vetustius. 40 Ego hoc Tractu apud Antoninum invenio Pontes cum Legione xxiv. inter Ambianos & Gesforiacum. In Notitia item Romanarum Dignitatum scribitur Civitas Morinorum, id est Ponticum. Comitatus fulget dignitate. Meminerunt Annales Gulielmi hujus Provinciæ Comitis, qui vixit tempore Lotharij Francorum Regis. Anglici Iuris factus est, quum Eduardus I Angliæ Rex uxorem duceret Eleonoram, Ferdinandi Castellæ Regis Filiam ex Ioanna Conjuge, quæ Filia erat Simonis Pontium Comitis. Anglo plenius solidiusque adquisitum fuit Ius per Pacem inter Ioannem & Eduardum factam MCCCLX. Non multo post Incolæ, instigante Guidone S. Pauli Comite, Præsidiarios, quos Rex Eduardus ibi reliquerat, exturbarunt; Regiqueque Francorum Karolo V se dediderunt. Sic nobilissimus Comitatus Franconcessit, post annos CXII, quam ipsum Dotis nomine Rex Eduardus I accepisset. Primarium Comitatus opidum Abbatis-Villa, Abbeville vulgo: non antiquum valde, uti nomen indicat: Baillivatus titulo insignitum. Opida habet & alia non magni nominis, Crotoyam, Ruam, Treportum, Fanum S. Richarii. Creffiacum, Cressi, Vicus est, Gallorum clade memorabilis, de qua Papirius Massonius lib. iv Annalium. Comprehendere autem notatur sub se hic Comitatus duos alios Monstrolicensem & S. Pauli; utrumque nomen à principibus Vrbibus, quæ vulgo Monstreul & S. Pol. Monstreul quibusdam quali quasi Mont-Royal; alijs ab Monstro, quod eo loci domicilium habuisse fingitur. Comites S. Paulli. Progenitorem memorant ex Stirpe Leuceburgica Walleramum Leuceburgium, Lignij Comitem, germanum Henrici vii Romanorum Imperatoris fratrem. Ultimam ejus Stemmatis lego Mariam Leuceburgicam, Petri Filiam, Fani D. Paulli ac Lignij Comitem, Anhiani Dominam; Uxorem prius Iacobi Sangij Ramondi Vaufsiique Comitis; inde vero Francisci Comitis Vendomij; Matrem ex illo Filiae, quae nuptit Henrico Nassavio; ex hoc autem Karoli Primi Vendomiae Ducis.
units.tr: Ponthieu, in the vernacular Ponthieu, is a county, which is thought to have received its name from the Pontes (Pontii), who are scattered there in great numbers. It is a region lying between the rivers Somme and Authie, full of marshes, and, as I myself have found, in many places impassable because of its pools. I leave it to others to consider whether the name is not older than some think. For in this tract Antoninus places the Pontes with legion xxiv, between the Ambiani and Gesoriacum. Likewise, the Notitia of the Roman Dignities calls it "Civitas Morinorum", that is, "Ponticum". The county shines with dignity. The Annals mention William, Count of this province, who lived in the time of Lothair, King of the Franks. It came under English law when Edward I, King of England, married Eleanor, daughter of Ferdinand, King of Castile, by his wife Joan, who was the daughter of Simon, Count of Ponthieu. The English gained a fuller and more secure right through the peace made between John and Edward in 1360. Not long afterwards the inhabitants, at the instigation of Guy, Count of St Pol, drove out the garrison which King Edward had left there, and surrendered themselves to Charles V, King of France. Thus the most noble county passed to France, 112 years after King Edward I had received it as a dowry. The chief town of the county is Abbeville, commonly so called: it is not very ancient, as its name indicates, and is distinguished by the title of bailiwick. It has other towns of no great name: Crotoy, Rue, Tréport and Saint-Riquier. Crécy (Cressi) is a village memorable for the defeat of the French, of which Papirius Masson writes in book iv of his Annals. This county is said to comprise two others under it, Montreuil and Saint-Pol, each named after its principal town, which are commonly called Montreuil and Saint-Pol. Montreuil is called by some Mont-Royal, and by others from Mons, which is supposed to have had a residence there. The Counts of Saint-Pol: they record as their progenitor, from the Luxembourg line, Walleram of Luxembourg, Count of Ligny, full brother of Henry VII, Roman Emperor. The last of this genealogy I read is Mary of Luxembourg, daughter of Peter, Count of Saint-Pol and Ligny, Lady of Enghien. She was first the wife of James de Sancy, Count of Roucy and Vaudémont; afterwards of Francis, Count of Vendôme. By the latter she was the mother of a daughter, who married Henry of Nassau, and by the former of Charles I, Duke of Vendôme.

units.la: Bolonia, vel ut alij, Bononia Comitatus (Comté de Boulogne) satis est amplus. Initium illi ab Montibus S. Ingelberti: procurritque ad Fluvium Cancham, quae ejus Longitudo; Latitudo ad Lucum usque Tournohensem porrigitur. Totus Tractus arenosus est, ejus generis arenae, quam Vrentem vocant: unde & nonnulli Bo'oniam censent derivatam à Bouiller; quod ridere soleo. Nomen Comitatui à Bolonia Opido, quod in Superius hodie & Inferius divisum. Illud altiore situm loco, Burgus tantum, anteaquam ab Anglis obsidione premeretur:
units.tr: Bolonia, or as others call it Bononia, the County (Comté de Boulogne) is quite large. It begins at the Mountains of St Ingelbert and runs down to the river Canche, which marks its length; its breadth extends to the grove of Tournehem. The whole tract is sandy, of the kind of sand they call vrent. Hence some also derive Bononia from bouiller, which I am in the habit of laughing at. The county takes its name from the town of Bolonia, which today is divided into the Upper and the Lower. The upper town, situated on higher ground, was only a burgh before the English besieged it:

units.la: Caletenses & Bononienses.
units.tr: The Caletenses and the Bononienses.

units.la: Hoc autem planiora occupans Mare adluit. Alterum ab altero passibus distat centum, aut circiter. Bononiam etiam nominant hac Galliarum parte, praeter Ammianum lib. xx, Olympiodorus & Sozomenus. Scripsit ille Historiam Honorij Senioris, Theodosij & Honorij Iunioris, inque scrinijs adhuc & Armarijs Bibliothecarum delitescit. Loquens autem de Constantino Tyranno, Τας Βρετανιας ιεσας, ait, μεγιστην αμα της αυξ δη Bονωνίαν, πολιν ητω καλουμένην, Θεοφυλαστιαν, και πρω-τὴν ἐν τῆς τῶν Γαλατῶν ὅρος κειμένην. Emendandus hinc, cujus memini, Sozomenus, qui libro ix loquens eadem de re, μεγιαθὲς δὲ Κωνσταντῖνῳ, inquit, ἀπὸ Βρετανίας δηὶ Βυβονίαν (leg. Bononiam) πόλιν τῆς Γαλατίας, Θεοφυλαστιαν κειμένην, ... Bononiensi opidum habet quoque Panegyricus Incerti Auctoris Imperatori Constantino dictus. Civitas Bononiensium est in Notitia Provinciarum inter Belgicae Secundae Civitates. Hodie Francorum Vulgo Boulongne; Flandris, reliquisque Inferioris Germaniae Populis, propius ad Veterem appellationem accedentibus, Bennen. Antiquissimis temporibus, uti censent V. N. Iosephus Scaliger suis ad me Litteris (nam ad Ausonium Gesforie opidum hoc tractu nomen retinere docet) Papirius Masso-nius, Lelandus, Abrahamus Ortelius, & alij, Gesforiacum. Diserte Tabula Peutingeriana, quam cum maximo Reip. litterariae bono nuper editam à se mihi liberaliter transmisit Vir Nobilis. Marcus Velserus Patritius & II-Vir Augustanus: Gesfogiaco, Quod nunc Bononia; nonia; reponendum Gesforiaco. Gesforiacum Antonino dicitur, qui ei Legionem adscribit x v; Et alibi Gesforiacensis Portus; item Gesfortagensis Portus in Maritimis: Ptolemæo Γισορρίαχον, Ἁπίνεον μεγίστον. Gesforigia est in Panegyrico, qui Maximiano dictus; & eo fere modo in quibusdam Antonini Codicibus Cesforcia. De eo Pomponius Mela: Pertinentque ad ultimos Galliarum gentium Morinos, nec Portu, quem Gesforiacum vocant, quidquam notius habent. Sic Suetonius in Claudio cap. xvii, ubi de expeditione Principis in Britanniam: Quare a Massilia Gesforiacum usque pedestri itinere confecto, inde transmisit. Ab eo Plinius lib. iv. nat. hist. cap. xvi. Gesforiacum Morinorum Gentis Litus nominat: Et Gesforiacus eidem Pagus, totus ille Tractus, qui pertinet ab Nort-mannis Belgis Bononiam usque. Pagi enim appellatio late solet apud Veteres Scriptores patere; ut Pagus Tigurinus, Pagus Velaunus, & alij: quemadmodum & Civitatis passim in Notitia Provinciarum, pro tota aliqua Præpositura, pro magno modo Agri, pro Gente quamtumvis numerosa. Alij Gesforiacum non idem volunt cum Navali Boronicensi: Calesium putat Ioannes Talbotus; Fanum S. Audomari Incertiores apud Hieronymum Suritam ad Antonini Itinerarium; Vicum Seat, haud procul eodem Fano, Hadrianus Turnebus lib. viii Adversar. cap. xxi; Sitsm Brugensium Coloniam, Hector Boëtius; Brugas ipsas Hermolaus Barbarus ad Plinium; Gandavum Bilibaldus: Robertus Cœnalis libro de re Gallic. ii Perioche iii diversa ponit Gesforiacum Portum & Gesforiacum Navale; illum Boloniam centem; hoc autem Castellum, quod vulgo Cassel. Boloniensis porro fuit Godefridus, Eustachij Boloniensis Comitis Filius, Lotharingiæ Dux, qui Christianorum Primus Rex Solymorum. Prope Bononiam erat Itius Portus: quem qui Calesium Opidum esse arbitrantur, inter quos Lhuydus, nullo negotio refelluntur à Ptolemæo, qui post Sequanæ Fluminis Ostia prius ponit Ἴκιον Ἀκρὸν, deinde Γισορίαχεν, Ἐπὶ τῷ Μορίνων: à quo opidum Calesium distat plus quam xx millibus Passuum, hoc est, Leucis Belgicis septem. Gesforiacum idem esse cum Itio persuasum videtur M. Velsero ad Fragmentum Tabulæ Itinerariæ. Itius portus quibusdam Fanum S. Audomari centetur, adductis cum vetusto Urbis nomine, quo Sitieu vocabatur, quasi, ut volunt, Sinus I.y; tum Loci situ, qui quum valde sit humilis, præaltis tamen littoribus Urbem quodammodo cingentibus, Sinum Maris olim capacissimum fuisse indicat. Cambdenus in sua Britannia docet Itium Portum diu fuisse in loco, quem hodie Withsan vocamus, prope Blanesium. Ego sic argumentari soleo: Quum apud Ptolemæum & Itio Promontorio & Gesforiaco Navali (quod Bononiam esse jam dixi) ejusdem Gradus Latitudinis, nimirum lxiii, idem omnino Scrupulus, xxx scilicet, tribuatur: in Longitudine autem nonnihil differant, quod uterque locus eidem quidem subsit Longitudinis Gradui xxii, sed Itium Promontorium sub indicati Gradus Scrupulo xv. Gesforiacum vero sub Scrupulo xlv: necessum prorsus est, Itium portum haud procul fuisse Gesforiaco Navali, eodem plane inter Septemtrionem & Meridiem Parallelo, non eodem inter Ortum & Occasum Meridiano: hoc est Itium Portum Navali Gesforiaco fuisse Occidentaliorem, Britannizque littoribus paulo propiorem: ideoque, quum Gesforiacum vel Bononiam Mari jam nunc adsidere conspiciamus, Itium Portum Oceano, ut multa alia ad Mare Britannicum Aquitanicumque Loca, hautum esse, nudamque ejus memoriam & appellationem exstare forte an in Vico, qui Portu licet Orientalior & magis Mediterraneus, prope Bononiam, ad Mare, vernacule dicitur Portet, quasi Portus Itius, κατ' ἀνατολὰς. Accedit, quod ex Portu Itio ad proximam Britanniæ partem Trajectum notent, Cæsar quidem millium passuum xxxx, Strabo vero Stadiorum cccxx; Cæsaris verba lib. v sunt hæc: Atque omnes ad Portum Itium convenire jubet: quo ex Portu commodissimum in Britanniam Transjectum esse cognoverat, circiter millium passuum xxxx; sic in melioribus fideique probatioris libris legitur, non xxx: Strabonis autem lib. iv, ubi de Morinis sermo, sic habent, ... Miror Strabonem, diligentissimum alioqui satisque sui memorem Auctorem, eundem Stadiorum numerum ponere inter Flumina Celtica (intelligit Ligerim & Sequanam; nam de ijs egerat) & Britanniam: Διάρρα δ' ἐςιν εἰς τὴν Βρεττανικὴν, αἰτ. Quod esse non potest. Trajectus enim ab ostio Sequanæ in Britanniam major est, quam cccxx Stadiorum; & multo major ex Ligeris ostio. Quidquid sit, Strabonis Stadia cccxx, Cæsaris autem xl. Millia passuum si cum hodierna mensurandi ratione committantur, dabunt xiii Leucas vel Milliaria. Tantum hodie circiter est intervallum inter finitima Bononiæ Littora & proximas Angliæ oras. Iam quod Antoninus à Portu Gesforiaco ad Rutupium numeret Stadia cccci; quod Plinius lib. iv. cap. xvi Britanniam notet abesse ab Gesforiaco Morinorum Gentis Littore, proximo Trajectu l millium, minimum: quod denique Dio Trajectum brevissimum ab Gallis in Britanniam Stadiorum esse scribat cccc l: dicendum, aliud esse, metiri maritimum hoc iter ab Gesforiaco, aliud ab Itio; Gesforiacum enim Itio erat Orientalius, Itiumque propius à Britannia, quam Gesforiacum aberat: aliud item fortean fuisse, Rutupium Britannorum petere, aliud occurrentia primum littora: aliud denique, ex Celtica in Britanniam, aliud ex Belgica solvere. Portum Itium Florus lib. iii. Morinum appellat: In Britanniam transit mira celeritate: quippe quum tertia vigilia Morino solvisset à Portu, minus quam medio die Insulam ingressus est. Quo loco nescio quid nonnullos impulerit, ut Morino referrent; quum Veteres Geographi Portum Itium omnes fateantur esse Morinorum.
units.tr: The lower town, occupying the flatter ground, is washed by the sea. The two are about a hundred paces apart, or thereabouts. In this part of Gaul they also name it Bononiam, besides Ammianus in book 20, Olympiodorus and Sozomen. The first wrote a history of Honorius the Elder, of Theodosius and of Honorius the Younger, which still lies hidden in the chests and cupboards of libraries. Speaking of the tyrant Constantine, he says, "the British islands ... the greatest city, then called Bononia, Theophylactia, lying first on the border of Gaul" [Τας Βρετανιας ιεσας, ait, μεγιστην αμα της αυξ δη Bονωνίαν, πολιν ητω καλουμένην, Θεοφυλαστιαν, και πρωτὴν ἐν τῆς τῶν Γαλατῶν ὅρος κειμένην]. Here the Sozomen I mentioned must be corrected, for in book 9, speaking of the same matter, he says, "it was a great crossing for Constantine from Britain to Bybonia (read Bononiam), a city of Gaul called Theophylactia ..." [μεγιαθὲς δὲ Κωνσταντῖνῳ, inquit, ἀπὸ Βρετανίας δηὶ Βυβονίαν (leg. Bononiam) πόλιν τῆς Γαλατίας, Θεοφυλαστιαν κειμένην, ...]. The anonymous Panegyric addressed to the Emperor Constantine also has the town of Bononia. The Civitas Bononiensium is in the Notitia Provinciarum among the cities of Belgica Secunda. Today the French call it Boulongne; the Flemish and the other peoples of Lower Germany, who come closer to the old name, call it Bennen. In very ancient times, as Lord Joseph Scaliger, in his letters to me, Papirius Masso, Leland, Abraham Ortelius and others think (for he teaches that in Ausonius the town Gesforie keeps the name of this district), it was Gesforiacum. This is clearly stated in the Peutinger Table, which a noble man, Marcus Velserus, patrician and duumvir of Augsburg, kindly sent me recently, to the great benefit of the republic of letters: Gesfogiaco, Quod nunc Bononia; the reading should be Gesforiaco. Antoninus calls it Gesforiacum, to which he assigns the fifteenth legion; and elsewhere Gesforiacensis Portus; likewise Gesfortagensis Portus among the maritime places. Ptolemy has Γισορρίαχον, Ἁπίνεον μεγίστον. Gesforigia is in the Panegyric addressed to Maximian, and in some codices of Antoninus almost in the same form, Cesforcia. Pomponius Mela speaks of it: They reach as far as the Morini, the last of the Gallic peoples, and they have nothing better known than the port which they call Gesforiacum. So Suetonius in Claudius, chapter 17, where he speaks of the Emperor's expedition to Britain: Therefore, having completed the journey on foot from Massilia to Gesforiacum, he crossed from there. Pliny, book 4 of the Natural History, chapter 16, calls it Gesforiacum, the shore of the Morini people; and Gesforiacus is the same Pagus, the whole tract that stretches from the Nervii to Bononia. For the word pagus is commonly used with a wide meaning among the ancient writers, as in Pagus Tigurinus, Pagus Velaunus, and others; just as civitas is used everywhere in the Notitia for a whole prefecture, for a large area of land, or for any people however numerous. Others do not think Gesforiacum is the same as the Naval Bononiensis: John Talbot thinks it is Calesium; some less well-known writers, cited by Hieronymus Surita on the Itinerary of Antoninus, think it is Fanum S. Audomari; Hadrian Turnebus, book 8 of the Adversaria, chapter 21, thinks it is Vicum Seat, not far from the same shrine; Hector Boece thinks it is Sitsm, the colony of the Bruges people; Hermolaus Barbarus, on Pliny, thinks it is Brugas itself; Bilibald thinks it is Gandavum. Robert Cenalis, in his book on Gallic affairs, book 2, period 3, sets out Gesforiacum Portus and Gesforiacum Navale as different places: the former is Boulogne, the latter Castellum, which is commonly called Cassel. Godfrey, son of Eustace, Count of Boulogne, Duke of Lorraine, who became the first Christian King of Jerusalem, was from Boloniensis. Near Bononia was the Itius Portus. Those who think that the town of Calesium is it, among whom is Lhuyd, are easily refuted by Ptolemy, who, after the mouths of the river Seine, first places Ἴκιον Ἀκρὸν, then Γισορίαχεν, in the land of the Morini. The town of Calesium is more than twenty thousand paces from this, that is, seven Belgic leagues. That Gesforiacum is the same as Itius seems to be the view of M. Velserus, on the fragment of the Itinerary Table. Some reckon Itius portus to be Fanum S. Audomari, citing the old name of the town, when it was called Sitieu, as if it were, so they say, Sinus I.y; and also the lie of the place, which, although very low, is nevertheless surrounded in some way by very high shores, indicates that the bay of the sea was once very large. Cambden in his Britannia teaches that Itium Portum was for a long time in the place that we now call Withsan, near Blanesium. I usually argue as follows. Since in Ptolemy both Itio Promontorio and Gesforiaco Navali (which I have already said is Bononia) are given the same degree of latitude, namely 63, and exactly the same minutes, namely 30, but differ somewhat in longitude, because each place lies under the same degree of longitude, 22, yet Itium Promontorium lies under 15 minutes of that degree, and Gesforiacum under 45 minutes, it is absolutely necessary that Itium portum was not far from Gesforiaco Navali, on the same parallel between north and south, but not on the same meridian between east and west. That is, Itium Portum was further west than Gesforiacum Navale and somewhat nearer the British shores. Therefore, since we see that Gesforiacum or Bononia already lies on the sea, Itium Portum is likely to have been swallowed up by the ocean, as many other places on the British and Aquitanian sea were. Perhaps the bare memory and name of it survive in the village which, although more to the east and more inland than the port, near Bononia, by the sea, is called Portet in the vernacular, as if Portus Itius, lying to the east. There is also this: writers note the crossing from Portu Itio to the nearest part of Britain as Caesar, indeed, thirty-four thousand paces, and Strabo three hundred and twenty stadia. Caesar's words in book 5 are these: And he ordered all to assemble at the Itian port, from which he had learned that the most convenient crossing to Britain was, about thirty-four thousand paces; so the better and more trustworthy books read, not thirty. But in Strabo, book 4, where he speaks of the Morini, the words are as follows ... I am surprised that Strabo, otherwise a most diligent author who keeps his own statements in mind, gives the same number of stadia between the Celtic rivers (he means the Loire and the Seine, for he had dealt with them) and Britain: "the crossing to the British island is ..." [Διάρρα δ' ἐςιν εἰς τὴν Βρεττανικὴν, αἰτ.]. This cannot be right. For the crossing from the mouth of the Seine to Britain is more than three hundred and twenty stadia, and much more from the mouth of the Loire. Whatever the case, Strabo's three hundred and twenty stadia and Caesar's forty thousand paces, if compared with the modern way of measuring, will give thirteen leagues or miles. Today the distance between the neighbouring shores of Bononia and the nearest coasts of England is about this much. Now, as to the fact that Antoninus counts four hundred and forty stadia from the port of Gesforiacum to Rutupiae; that Pliny, book 4, chapter 16, says that Britain is distant from Gesforiacum, the shore of the Morini people, by a crossing of at least fifty thousand paces; and that Dio, finally, writes that the shortest crossing from the Gauls to Britain is four hundred and fifty stadia: it must be said that it is one thing to measure this sea journey from Gesforiacum, and another from Itius; for Gesforiacum was further east than Itius, and Itius was closer to Britain than Gesforiacum was. It was perhaps also one thing to make for Rutupiae in Britain, and another to make for the nearest shores that come into view first; and finally, one thing to sail from Celtic Gaul to Britain, and another from Belgic Gaul. Florus, book 3, calls the Itian port Morinum: He crossed to Britain with wonderful speed; indeed, having left the port of Morinum in the third watch, he entered the island in less than half a day. I do not know what led some to refer this to Morino, since all the ancient geographers acknowledge that the Itian port belonged to the Morini.

units.la: Eononiensi Comitatui succedit Guinensis, Guisnes: qui disterminatur ab Comitatu Oyo per Canalem Majorem, qui Opidum ipsum præterlabitur, Territorium tere reddens inexpugnabile. Primarium Opidum Guinesium, Guisnes; in duas divisum Partes, quarum una in Paludibus sita, altera in Continenti; Loci natura munitum & validum. Cepit Rex Henricus ii, misso illuc Francisco Lotharingio, Guisæ Duce, anno cıɔ ıɔ ıv viii. De Danorum quondam in Guinensem terram Iure, multa Mejerus in Annalibus Flandriæ, deque eodem Comitatu alia apud alios Historiographos, quæ hujus non sunt loci. Visuntur & alia Opida, Hautincourt, Peuplinge, Conquelle, Portus Nieuwelietus. Continet Comitatus hic sub se Baronatus Ardresium & Courtembronensem, singulos ab suis dictos opidis, quorum unum Ardres vulgo, alterum Courtembrone.
units.tr: The county of Eononia is followed by Guinensis, Guisnes, which is separated from the county of Oyo by the Great Canal. The canal flows past the town itself, so that the territory is almost impregnable. The chief town is Guinesium, Guisnes, divided into two parts: one lies in the marshes, the other on the mainland. Its position makes it fortified and strong. King Henry II took it in 1558, sending thither Francis of Lorraine, Duke of Guise. On the ancient right of the Danes over the land of Guines, Mejerus says much in his Annals of Flanders, and other historians say other things about this county, but these do not belong here. Other towns are also to be seen: Hautincourt, Peuplinge, Conquelle, Portus Nieuwelietus. This county contains under it the baronies of Ardres and Courtembrone, each named after its own town: one commonly called Ardres, the other Courtembrone.

units.la: Duobus Ardresio Milliaribus versus Oceanum occurrit, Calesium, opidum natura arteque munitissimum, Galliæ Clavis & Ianua semper habitum; Muris primo, ut fertur, cinctum ab Philippo Bononiensi, S. Ludovici Patruo. Arcem habet cum Turri valida, quæ ingressum ex mari in portum prohibet. Captum fuit ab Eduardo v Anglorum Rege, pridie Nonas Augusti, undecimo mense post horrendam pugnam, quam contra Philippum vi, Francorum Regem, ad Cresslacum anno cıɔ cccxlvii pugnatam, multis depingit Paulus Æmilius lib. ix. Possessum ab Anglis annos ccxi (nam frustra obsederat anno cıɔ ccccxxxi Philippus Bonus, Burgundus, Flandris ipsum deserentibus) & tamquam Galliæ Clavem in Loculis, ut loqui consueverant Angli, servatum, expugnatum, Guilio Duce, Galli recuperarunt anno cıɔıɔ lviii, mense Februario: à quo tempore quas conditiones subierit, quasque calamitates fuerit passum; plenius explicat Historia Belgica, quam jussu & auspiciis Illustrissimorum Ordinum Fœderatarum Provinciarum paro. Calctibus Populis in Normannia potius, quam hic sua sunt Domicilia, ut ibi dicam.
units.tr: Two miles from Ardres towards the ocean lies Calesium, a town most strongly fortified by nature and art, always regarded as the key and gateway of Gaul. It was first walled, as is said, by Philip of Boulogne, uncle of Saint Louis. It has a citadel with a strong tower, which blocks the entrance from the sea into the harbour. It was taken by Edward III, King of the English, on 4 August, eleven months after the dreadful battle which he fought against Philip VI, King of the French, at Crécy in 1347. Paulus Aemilius describes that battle at length in book 9. The English held it for 211 years (for Philip the Good of Burgundy besieged it in vain in 1431, when the Flemings deserted him). It was kept as the key of Gaul, in what the English used to call its pockets. The French, under Duke Guise, recaptured it by storm in February 1558. What conditions it endured from that time, and what calamities it suffered, is explained more fully in the Belgian History, which I am preparing by order and under the auspices of the Most Illustrious Orders of the United Provinces. The Calctes people have their homes in Normandy rather than here, as I shall say there.

units.la: Æquali fere Itinere versus Mediterranea Calesio Bononiaque distat Teroano Morinorum, vulgo Teroane; nomen retinens, quamquam ab Karolo V deleta, Episcopali Sede Bononiam translata: Flandris, Terrenmerberh: Tervanna vel Tarvenna Antonino Tervanna Itinerariæ Tabulæ; Tapuara Prolemæo. Quosdam Tarubanum appellare Bovillus adiderit. Tarubanorum meminit Trithemius in Francorum Historia. Tervana quibusdam quasi Terra-Vana, ob vilitatem Territorii. In Notitia Provinciarum, ubi Belgicæ Secundæ Civitates recensentur, nominatur etiam Civitas Morinorum, id est Pontiacum, L'Evesché de Teroane. Colonia forte Morinorum in antiquo Lapide, qui superioribus annis repertus fuit in Gelria, Sugambrorum olim Principatu, dimidiato ab Urbe Neomagiensi milliario: Exemplar ejus paulo ante à me positum, ubi de Morinis Populis.
units.tr: At almost the same distance inland from Calesium and Bononia lies Teroanum Morinorum, commonly Teroane. It keeps its name, although it was destroyed by Charles V and its episcopal see transferred to Boulogne. The Flemings call it Terrenmerberh. Antoninus, in the Itinerary Table, calls it Tervanna, or Tarvenna; Ptolemy calls it Tapuara. Bovillus has written that some call it Tarubanum. Trithemius mentions the Tarubani in his History of the Franks. Some understand Tervana as, as it were, Terra-Vana (empty land), on account of the poorness of its territory. In the Notitia of the Provinces, where the cities of Belgica Secunda are listed, it is also named Civitas Morinorum, id est Pontiacum, L'Evesché de Teroane. Perhaps Colonia Morinorum is on an ancient stone which was found in recent years in Gelderland, once the principality of the Sugambri, half a mile from the city of Nijmegen. I have set down a copy of it a little earlier, where I speak of the Morini people.
