units.la: Ditio porro Oyana, Terra de Oye, porrigere se scribitur Duynkerkam usque, Flandriæ Opidum. Sunt ibi præter Oyam, alia quædam Opida, sed ignobiliora.
units.tr: The district of Oyana, Terra de Oye, is said to extend as far as Dunkirk, a town of Flanders. There are, besides Oya, certain other towns there, but less well known.

units.la: Ut Picardiæ finem imponam, pertinet eo Iter, quod Antoninus ab Teroana describit Durocortorum: Illud cum Itineraria Peutingeri Tabula, vulgatisque nunc temporis Locorum appellationibus collatum hoc se habet modo:

units.tr: The itineraries of Antoninus, which pertain to Picardy.

units.la: πόλεις, sed & Ε᾽ξαρχίας, & Πατριαρχίας nominant; & Præsules earum Ε᾽ξάρχας ἡ Πατριάρχας. reliquos μητροπολίτας ἡ Αρχιεπισκόπους, qui sub se tantum Ε᾽πισκόπους habent: Nam οἱ Ε᾽ξαρχοι sub se, præter Ε᾽πισκόπους, etiam μητροπολίτας habent: μητροπολίτας vero tantum Ε᾽πισκόπους. In Ecclesia Latina Archiepiscoporum & nomen & jus manet, & Iurisdictio Canonica in suos Episcopos Suffraganeos: sed Ε᾽ξαρχῶν nulla vestigia exstant: nisi forte quædam umbra ejus fuerit, quod Metropolita sive Archiepiscopus Viennensis Primatem Primatum sese appellat. Eo enim ostendit sub se Primates habuisse, qui sub eo essent, Narbonensem Primatem Provinciæ, Bituricensem Primatem Aquitaniæ. Aliter quo modo, aut quo jure, Primas Primatum diceretur, nisi ratione Diœcesios Vicarij Viennensis Præf. Præt. Prætorio, qui septem Provincias sub se habebat, in quibus Prima Narbonensis & Prima Aquitania? Quod vero Lugdunensis Primatem se vocari gaudeat, nuperum est, & illi ex beneficio Romani Pontificis indultum: neque tamen adeo novum est. Nam Guilielmus Brito in sua Philippeide ita canit: Et Lugdunensis, quo Gallia tota solebat, Ut fama est, Primate regi.
units.tr: …cities, but they also call them exarchates [Ε᾽ξαρχίας] and patriarchates [Πατριαρχίας], and their presidents exarchs [Ε᾽ξάρχας] or patriarchs [Πατριάρχας]. The rest they call metropolitans [μητροπολίτας] or archbishops [Αρχιεπισκόπους], who have only bishops under them. For the exarchs have under them, besides bishops, also metropolitans, while metropolitans have only bishops. In the Latin Church the name and right of archbishops remain, and canonical jurisdiction over their suffragan bishops. But no traces of the exarchs survive, unless perhaps some shadow of them is found in the fact that the metropolitan or archbishop of Vienne calls himself Primate of Primates. By this he shows that he had primates under him, who were subject to him: the Primate of Narbonne for the province, the Primate of Bourges for Aquitaine. Otherwise, by what method or what right would he be called Primate of Primates, unless by reason of the diocese of the Vicar of the Praetorian Prefect of Vienne, who had seven provinces under him, among which were First Narbonensis and First Aquitaine? As for the Archbishop of Lyon rejoicing to be called Primate, this is recent, and granted to him by the favour of the Roman Pontiff. Yet it is not so very new. For William the Breton sings in his Philippeid: "And Lyon, where all Gaul used, as report has it, to be ruled by a primate."

units.la: At Primas Primatum antea dici jure non potuit, quia nullam Primam Provinciam sub se habebat. Viennensis Primas quidem Primatum vocari vult, sed Caussam tam ille, quam omnis Ecclesia ignorat. Quapropter Divisio Galliarum per Diœceses Ecclesiasticas & Episcopatus, ut omnium antiquissima, ita certissima nobis sequenda erat, neque ulla melior erat quærenda, si integræ illæ Ε᾽ξαρχίαι adhuc finibus Regni Francorum continerentur, ut olim sub Karolo Magno, & ejus Filio & Nepotibus: sed quia ex illo amplissimo Imperio multæ Provinciæ detractæ sunt, alia nobis Tributio instituenda. Galliæ igitur sive Franciæ Imperium octo Tribunalibus temperatur, quæ Ius reddunt Provinciis suis, à quibus Provocatio non est, quorumque & Majestas augustissima est & Auctoritas sacrosancta. Parlamenta Galli Idiomate suo vocant, ut prolixius docui capite xvii. Non possum meliorem Partitionis rationem inire, quam si in octo hæc Parlamenta omne Francorum Regnum dividam, & ea in Provincias suas. Provincias quidem novi, quot Galliæ Reges adipiscitur, tot fere Mutationes, Nomina & Regimina subire; eam ob causam non ignorans consultius esse ut à Parlamentis Divisio procederet porro per Diœceses & Episcopatus, quum etiam illa proxime accedat ad priscam Imperij Romani notitiam: sed quia Geographis in more positum, ut quæ suis temporibus obtineant in Regnorum Regionumque terminis, ea quam fidelissime fieri potest, indicent & proponant, religio mihi ab recepta tam multis probataque hactenus consuetudine discedere. Quamobrem talem ego docendi, Galliasque commode cumque structu explicandi gratia, Distributionem excogitavi.
units.tr: But the title Primas Primatum could not rightly have been used before, because the archbishop had no First Province under him. The Primate of Vienne wishes to be called Primate of Primates, but the cause of this is unknown to him, as to the whole Church. Therefore the division of Gaul by ecclesiastical dioceses and bishoprics, as the most ancient of all, is also the most certain, and must be followed by us. Nor should a better one be sought, if those whole exarchates still lay within the borders of the kingdom of the Franks, as once under Charlemagne and his son and grandsons. But since many provinces have been taken away from that vast empire, another arrangement must be set up for us. Therefore the empire of Gaul, or France, is governed by eight tribunals, which dispense justice to their provinces, from which there is no appeal, and whose majesty is most august and whose authority sacrosanct. The French call these Parlamenta in their own language, as I explained more fully in chapter 17. I cannot find a better plan of division than to divide the whole kingdom of the Franks into these eight Parlamenta, and these into their provinces. I know that the provinces, with almost every change of king in Gaul, undergo changes of name and government. For this reason, not unaware that it is more prudent for the division to proceed further by dioceses and bishoprics, since this too comes closest to the ancient notion of the Roman Empire, yet because it is the practice of geographers to set out, as faithfully as possible, the boundaries of kingdoms and regions as they hold them in their own times, I thought it wrong for me to depart from a method so widely received and so long approved. Therefore I have devised such a division, for the sake of teaching and of explaining Gaul in a convenient order.

units.la: Provinciæ quæ in Galliarum delineatione ab Geographis hodie solent exponi, aliæ Francorum sunt Regis, vel Regi subjectæ; aliæ extra Francorum Ditionem. Quæ prioris generis optime meoque Instituto convenientissime divido in sua Parlamenta, quæ, ut dixi, octo sunt numero: Unum quidem Principale; reliqua Accessoria. Principale est Parisiense, omnium Primum, & olim unicum solumque Parlamenti Parisiensis Sedes Præsidiales, ut multæ (nam latissime ejus se extendit Iurisdictio) sic variæ admodum sunt, in variis constitutæ Provinciis. Eas Ligeris facit alias Septemtrionales, alias Meridionales. Quod ad Priores in Vetere quidem Belgica, hodie est Picardia La Picardie; in Celtica vero versus Occidentem Francia, La France, stricius sumta (cujus tamen etiam nonnulla incidunt in Belgicam) & Bel-sia, La Beausse: versus ortum Campania, La Campagne, & Lugdunensis tractus, Pais de Lionnois. Quod ad Meridionales, possidebat eas olim ex Veterum delineatione, cum Narbonensi, Aquitanica. Dicebatur autem Aquitania in dextra Garumnæ ripa, partim Prima, ubi hodie cis Vigennam Bituricum, Berry, & Borbonivm, Bourbonnois; ultra vero Pictonivm Poitou, Agerque & Incvlisensis Angoulesme, & Alnisiensis, Le Pais d'Aulnis: partim Secunda, ubi nunc Arvernia, Auvergne. Accessoria Parlamenta sunt, quæ Principale illud quasi circumeunt, versus Occidentem ad Ligeris dextram Rotomagense, sub quo Normannia, La Normandie; & Redonense cui subest Britannia, La Bretagne: ad sinistram Burdigalense & Tolosanum, quorum quodque sua extendit jura nunc integre & separatim; nunc vero mistim in aliquot adsignatas sibi Veteris Aquitaniæ Narbonensisque Galliæ Ditiones.
units.tr: The provinces which geographers today usually set out in the outline of Gaul are partly those of the King of the French, or subject to him, and partly outside the dominion of the French. I divide those of the first kind, which best and most conveniently suit my plan, into their Parlamenta, which, as I have said, are eight in number: one principal and the rest subordinate. The principal is Parisiense, first of all, and once the only seat of the Parliament, its presidential seat. Its jurisdiction extends very widely, and so its provinces are many and very various. The Loire divides them into northern and southern. Of the northern, in old Belgica, today is Picardy, La Picardie; in Celtic Gaul, towards the west, is France, La France, taken more narrowly (though some parts of it also fall into Belgica), and the Beauce, La Beausse; towards the east is Champagne, La Campagne, and the district of Lyon, Pais de Lionnois. Of the southern, according to the ancient map, it formerly held these, along with Narbonensis, Aquitania. Aquitania was called, on the right bank of the Garonne, partly First, where today on this side of the Vienne are Bourges, Berry, and Bourbon, Bourbonnois; beyond the Vienne are Poitou, Poitou, the territory of Angoulême, Angoulesme, and Aulnis, Le Pais d'Aulnis; partly Second, where now is Auvergne, Auvergne. The subordinate Parliaments are those which almost surround that principal one: towards the west, on the right of the Loire, Rotomagense, under which lies Normandy, La Normandie; and Rennes, to which Brittany, La Bretagne, is subject; on the left, Burdigalense and Tolosanum, each of which extends its jurisdiction now wholly and separately, and now mixed in some districts assigned to it from old Aquitania and Narbonensian Gaul.

units.la: Integre quidem Burdigalensi subsunt LEMOVICIVM, Limosin, PETROCORIVM, Perigort, GVIENNA, La Guienne; Tolosano autem CADVRCIVM, Querci, RVTENIVM, Rouargue, LANGVEDOKIVM, Languedoc: Mistim vero utrique VASCONIA, La Gascoigne: quemadmodum plenius ex sequentibus parebit. Iam versus Orientem ad Mare Gallicum, Parlamentum est Aquense, cujus Iurisdictioni obtemperat PROVINCIA, La Provence; in Mediterraneis Gratianopolitanum, ab cujus nutu pendet DELPHINATVS, Le Dauphiné & Divionense, quod in Iure Summo dicundo agnoscit DVCATVS BVRGVNDIÆ, La Duché de Bourgogne. Hactenus quæ Regis. Extra Ditionem Francorum, in Francia tamen, suos habent etiam Dominatus alij Principes, & Ecclesiastici & Politici. Pontificis enim Romani est COMITATVS AVENIONENSIS, Avignon; Politicorum alij sunt Ducatus, ut SABAVDIA, Savoye, & LOTHARINGIA, Lorraine; alij sunt Principatus, ut BENEARNIA, Bearn, & ARAVSIO, Aurange; alij Comitatus, ut BVRGVNDIA, La Conté de Bourgogne & CAROLESIVM, Charolois. Has Regiones si fideliter ordine à me indicato perambularo, Lectores spero ita judicaturos, me nullam non partem, vel obiter, attigisse: pleraque Vrbes adijise; &, si non omnia, præcipua saltem de singulis dixisse. Illud obiter hic monendum duxi, Appianum testari Galliarum E? fuisse Τετραχεσία · Πόλις ὑπὸ ἐκ-ιοσίας. Minor est numerus in Templo, quod ab omnibus communi consilio Gallis Augusto Lugduni exstructum: de quo Strabo lib. iv. Τὰ, τε ... Vnde tanta in numero Gentium Galliæ discrepantia? Appianum existimo Gentes universum designare totius Galliæ; eas fuisse circiter quadringentas: Aram autem Lugdunensem eas tantum habuisse, à quibus illa in Augusti honorem fuit posita, sexaginta scilicet.
units.tr: Indeed, LEMOVICIVM (Limousin), PETROCORIVM (Périgord) and GVIENNA (Guienne) are wholly subject to the Parlement of Bordeaux, and CADVRCIVM (Quercy), RVTENIVM (Rouergue) and LANGVEDOKIVM (Languedoc) to the Parlement of Toulouse. VASCONIA (Gascony) is shared between the two, as will appear more fully from what follows. Towards the east, on the Mediterranean Sea, lies the Parlement of Aix, whose jurisdiction is obeyed by PROVINCIA (Provence). In the interior is the Parlement of Grenoble, on whose authority DELPHINATVS (Dauphiné) depends, and the Parlement of Dijon, which acknowledges the DVCATVS BVRGVNDIÆ (Duchy of Burgundy) as its highest court of appeal. So far the regions of the King. Outside the dominion of the French, yet within France, other princes also have their lordships, both ecclesiastical and secular. The County of Avignon (Avignon) belongs to the Roman Pontiff. Among the secular lordships, some are duchies, such as SABAVDIA (Savoy) and LOTHARINGIA (Lorraine); some are principalities, such as BENEARNIA (Béarn) and ARAVSIO (Orange); others are counties, such as BVRGVNDIA (Franche-Comté) and CAROLESIVM (Charolais). If I have faithfully traversed these regions in the order I have indicated, I hope readers will judge that I have touched upon almost every part, at least in passing, have visited most of the cities and, if not all, have said at least what is most important about each. Here I thought it worth noting in passing that Appian testifies that Gaul had [Τετρακόσια ἔθνη], four hundred nations, and [πόλεις ὑπὸ ἑξήκοντα], under sixty cities. There is a smaller number in the Temple which all the Gauls, by common counsel, built at Lyon in honour of Augustus, concerning which Strabo, book iv, [Τὰ, τε ...]. Whence comes so great a discrepancy in the number of Gallic peoples? I think Appian means by "nations" all the peoples of the whole of Gaul, which were about four hundred; but the altar at Lyon included only those by whom it was set up in honour of Augustus, namely sixty.

units.la: Qui porro, quam ego vel in superioribus attuli, vel in sequentibus sum allaturus, plura, vel saltem mea pluribus fusiusque explicata, petat: consulat moneo, quod quidem ad universæ Galliæ delineationem, præter alios, Robertum Cœnalem, qui integro volumine Gallias descripsit, Gilbertum Cognatum Nozorenum, Ioannem Marium, Chassanæum lib. xii de Gloria mundi, Guilelmum Postellum in libello Vniversitatis, Sebastianum Munsterum, Franciscum Belleforestium, Andream Thevetum, Abrahamum Ortelium & Gerardum Mercatorem; quorum ille xvi, hic xii Chartis Galliam depingit: quod autem ad Gallorum Mores, Resque ab illis gestas, adeat Lector ex Antiquis C. Iulij Cæsaris Libros vii de Bello Gallico, ijsque additum ab A. Hirtio viii, Appiani Alexandrini Celticum, sive de Bello Gallico, & alios, quos variis supra locis laudavi; ex Recentioribus, medijque ævi, Scriptores illos Annalium & Historiæ Francorum, quos maximo Reip. literariæ bono nuper edidit P. Pithoeus IC: his addat Hunibaldi libros xviii, in quibus tamen multa fabulosa & commentitia, sermoque plane barbarus; Gregorij Turonensis Episcopi libros x; Aimoini Monachi Floriacensis Coenobij Libros de Regibus Francorum v; item Ioannem Tritemium, Froissardum, quique cum supplevit, Enguerranum, Robertum Gaguinum, Philippum Comineum, Nicolaum Gillium, Paulum Æmilium, Ioannem Ferronium Ioannem Tilium, Henricum Leonardum, Hermannum Comitem, Nicolaum Vignerium, Guilelmum Paradinum, Papirium Massonium, Galeatium Capellam, qui scripsit de bellis in Italia gestis inter Karolum V & Franciscum Galliarum Regem. De Gallorum Imperio & Philosophia libros vii scripsit elegantes & eruditos Stephanus Forcatulus IC. Alios alijs, quibus otium curiolius hæc talia consectandi, adponendos nominaris à me relinquo
units.tr: Whoever seeks more on the matters I have mentioned above or will mention below, or my points explained at greater length and more fully, let him consult, as I advise. For the general description of all Gaul, besides others, there are Robert Cœnalis, who described Gaul in a whole volume; Gilbert Cognatus of Nozeroy; Jean Marius; Chassanæus, book xii, On the Glory of the World; Guillaume Postel in his little book on the University; Sebastian Münster; François de Belleforest; André Thevet; Abraham Ortelius and Gerard Mercator, of whom the former depicts Gaul on sixteen maps and the latter on twelve. As for the customs of the Gauls and the deeds they performed, the reader may consult, among the ancients, the seven books of Gaius Julius Caesar On the Gallic War, with the eighth book added by Aulus Hirtius, the Celtic history or On the Gallic War of Appian of Alexandria, and others which I have cited at various places above; among the more recent writers of the Middle Ages, those writers of the Annals and History of the Franks whom Pithou, the jurist, lately published for the great benefit of the republic of letters. To these he may add the eighteen books of Hunibald, in which, however, there is much that is fabulous and invented, and the language is plainly barbarous; the ten books of Gregory, Bishop of Tours; the five books On the Kings of the Franks by Aimoin, monk of the monastery of Fleury; likewise Johannes Trithemius, Froissart, and whoever completed him, Enguerrand, Robert Gaguin, Philippe de Commynes, Nicolas Gilles, Paolo Emilio, Jean de Ferron, Jean Tillet, Henri Léonard, Hermann Comes, Nicolas Vignier, Guillaume Paradin, Papire Masson, Galeazzo Capella, who wrote on the wars waged in Italy between Charles V and Francis, King of the French. Stephanus Forcatulus, jurist, wrote seven elegant and learned books on the empire and philosophy of the Gauls. Others I leave to be named by those who have leisure to pursue such matters more diligently.

units.tr: I now proceed to the more particular regions of Gaul. In my arrangement the first to present itself is

units.la: Picardia.

units.la: PICARDIÆ Nomen quamvis non magnæ antiquitatis, nulla tamen ejus certa potest reddi ratio. Alij aliam augurantur: Inter eos Robertus Cenalis, Episcopus Abrincantensis, vel, ut alij, Arboricensis, Picardos dicit vere esse Gallos; se nihilominus ignorare, num à Begardis hæreticis (quos constat Ludovici Bavari Imperatoris tempore, circa annum clo cccxiv, quasdam Inferioris Germaniæ Vrbes coluisse) nomen hoc sint mutuati. Belleforestius Picardos antea fuisse vocatos scribit, quam Becardi in rerum essent natura, quamque ulla istius Sectæ audiretur mentio. Sunt qui appellatos censent Picardos: quod ab his ortus primo usus Lancearum, quæ vulgo Picques nuncupantur. Ego rem in medio relinquo.
units.tr: The name Picardy is not very old, and no certain account of it can be given. Others have guessed differently. Among them, Robert Cenalis, Bishop of Avranches (or, as others say, of Arboricium), says that the Picards are truly Gauls, though he admits he does not know whether they took the name from the heretical Beghards (who, it is established, held some cities of Lower Germany in the time of the Emperor Louis of Bavaria, about the year 1314). Belleforest writes that the people were called Picards before the Becards existed in the world, and before any mention of that sect was heard. Some think the Picards were so named because they first used the lances commonly called picques. I leave the matter open.

units.la: Hujus Regionis, quæ quondam in Antiqua Belgica (ea præcipuè, quæ Secunda posteriori ævo) appellatio latius olim patuit; complexa Artesiam Flandriæque partem ad Lisam usque Amnem: alijs multo etiam ulterius tendentibus ad Scaldim usque & Renum Fluvios. Hodie Picardiam, ut crasse diffiniam, ad Occasum respicit, cum nonnulla Normanniæ portione, Oceanus Britannicus: ad Septemtrionem istæ Veteris Belgicæ jacent Regiones, quæ hodie Artesia & Hannonia: ad Ortum Leuceburgum & Lotharingia sunt porrectæ: ad Meridiem denique Campania, isque nobilissimi Regni Tractus, qui specialiore notione Francia vocatur, occurrunt.
units.tr: The name of this region once extended quite widely over what was formerly Belgic Gaul, especially the part that in later times was called Secunda. It took in Artois and part of Flanders as far as the river Lys, and others extend it much further, to the rivers Scheldt and Rhine. Roughly speaking, Picardy today faces west, with part of Normandy and the British Ocean. To the north lie those regions of Old Belgica that are today Artois and Hainault. To the east it stretches toward Luxembourg and Lorraine. To the south lies Champagne, and that most noble tract of the kingdom which in the narrower sense is called France.

units.la: Regio est fertilissima, Hortreumque Parisiorum, atque adeo pleraque Franciæ. Vino caret, ignava potius Incolarum socordia, quam vel Cœli vel Soli injuria.
units.tr: The region is very fertile, as is the territory of the Parisians, and indeed most of France. It lacks wine, a fault that is due to the laziness of the inhabitants rather than to any unkindness of the climate or the sun.

units.la: Picardiam habitarunt olim Ambiani, Suessones, Veromandui, Effui, Oromansaci, Atorini, & alij fortean. Ambianorum Sedes, ubi hodie opulentissima Vrbs Ambianum, vulgo Amiens: Eorum frequens apud antiquos Scriptores mentio, Cæsarem, Plinium, alios. Ἀμβιανοὶ Ptolemæo, & Straboni. Cæsar Ambianos Morinis jungit, quorum fines Nervy attingebant: Strabo Ambianos Morinis facit propinquos, & Suessiones: Ptolemæus post Bellovacos in Gallia Belgica statuit Ambianos. Suessiones, vel, ut alij scribunt Suessiones, sæpe apud Cæsarem (qui & Eleutheros, Liberos, prænominat lib. vii quemadmodum & Cadurcos. de quibus cap. xxxv) memorantur. Σuessiones apud StraboStrabonem: ubi Isaacus Casaubonus legit Σντοράσις: Ptolemaeo Νίσροντς, repono Σντσροντς. Hodie Souessons. Apud Suessones aetate memoriaque Caesaris Rex Diuiciacus, totius Galliae potentissimus, fuit; qui cum magnae partis harum Regionum, tum etiam Britanniae Imperium obtinuit: Deinde Galba successit. Et cuiusmodi Regnum hoc fuerit, hinc intelligi potest, quod Suessones Remorum Fratres Consanguineique eodem jure ijsdemque legibus uterentur, unum Imperium, unumque Magistratum cum illis haberent. Suessonum latissimi feracissimiqúe fuerunt Agri, & Oppida duodecim; quorum unicum ab Caesare nominatur Noviodunum, quod ipse post Belgarum discessum ex itinere oppugnare conatus, propter latitudinem Fossae, murique altitudinem, paucis licet defendentibus, expugnare non potuit.
units.tr: The following peoples are said to have once lived in Picardy: the Ambiani, Suessones, Veromandui, Effui, Oromansaci, Atrebates, and perhaps others. The seat of the Ambiani was where the very rich city of Amiens stands today. They are often mentioned by ancient writers, such as Caesar and Pliny, and others. Ptolemy and Strabo call them [Ἀμβιανοί]. Caesar joins the Ambiani to the Morini, whose borders reached the Nervii. Strabo makes the Ambiani neighbours of the Morini and the Suessiones. Ptolemy places the Ambiani in Belgic Gaul after the Bellovaci. The Suessiones (or, as others write, the Suessiones) are often mentioned in Caesar, who also calls the Eleutheri, that is the free people, as he does the Cadurci (see chapter 35). In Strabo they are [Σουεσσίονες], where Isaac Casaubon reads [Σντοράσις]; in Ptolemy [Νίσροντς], which I would replace with [Σντσροντς]. Today they are Soissons. In the time and memory of Caesar, King Diviciacus, the most powerful man in all Gaul, ruled among the Suessiones. He held dominion over a large part of these regions and also over Britain. Galba succeeded him. What kind of kingdom this was can be understood from the fact that the Suessiones, brothers and kinsmen of the Remi, used the same law and the same laws, and shared one government and one magistracy with them. The fields of the Suessiones were very wide and fertile, and they had twelve towns. Caesar names only one of them, Noviodunum, which he tried to storm on his march after the departure of the Belgae. Because of the width of its ditch and the height of its wall, he could not take it, though it was defended by few men.

units.la: Veromandui Caesari (qui in libris de bello Gallico de ijs multa) Plinioque Galliae Belgicae Populi: qui Ϝομάρδιοι Ptolemaeo, & in nonnullis Exemplaribus Ϝομάρδυες pro Ουεϱομάρδυς, inquit Surita; Veromandui Epitomae Liviane libri cxv, item Lapidi antiquo, qui, teste apud Abrahamum Ortelium Iacobo Carondiletio, Cancellario Leodiensi, in Pago Hannoniae, qui vulgo Arfaures prope Bavacum. Effuos Caesar nominat: Eorum Sedes ubi hodie illa Picardiae portio, quae Tirascha, quasi, ut Bovillus cum aliis opinatur, Terra Effluorum. Alij Effuos ponunt ubi nunc Retelois: alij ubi Bessia, prope Baiocasses, Bateux: Divaeus Comitatum de Eu putat. Hubertus Leodius tradit eos Ahbum Hannoniae Vrbem occupare: sic quot Capita, tot Sententiae inceriores nos relinquunt, Oromansaci, junctii Pago, inquit Plinius, qui Gessoriacum appellatur: fuisse censentur, ubi hac tempestate Comitatus Guinersis. Morini Virgilio, Caesari, Plinio, aliisque noti; Ptolemaeo & Straboni Μέροι: olim, ubi nunc in ruinis jacet Teroana, quae in Notitia, ut alibi vidimus, Civitas Morinorum, id est Pontìcum. Morinorum meminit Lapis, qui in Gelria, dimidiato ab Vrbe Neomagensi Miliario, repertus.
units.tr: The Veromandui are mentioned by Caesar (who writes much about them in his books on the Gallic War) and by Pliny among the peoples of Belgic Gaul. Ptolemy calls them [Ϝομάρδιοι], and in some copies [Ϝομάρδυες], for which Surita reads [Οὐεϱομάρδυς]. The Veromandui appear in the 115th book of Livy's Epitome, and also on an ancient stone. According to Abraham Ortelius, who had it from Jacques Carondelet, Chancellor of Liège, the stone was found in a district of Hainault, commonly called Arfaures, near Bavay. Caesar names the Effui. Their seat was where that part of Picardy now called Tirascha lies, as if it were, as Bovillus thinks with others, the "land of the Effui". Others place the Effui where Retelois is now, others where Bessin lies near the Baiocasses, at Bateux. Divaeus thinks of the County of Eu. Hubert Leodius reports that they occupied the town of Aubi in Hainault. So many heads, so many uncertain opinions leave us in doubt. The Oromansaci, joined to a district, says Pliny, which is called Gesoriacum, are thought to have lived where the County of Guines is at present. The Morini are known to Virgil, Caesar, Pliny and others; Ptolemy and Strabo call them [Μέροι]. Long ago they lived where Thérouanne now lies in ruins, which in the Notitia, as we have seen elsewhere, is the city of the Morini, that is, of the Pontiaci. A stone found in Gelderland, half a mile from the city of Nijmegen, also mentions the Morini.

units.la: MINERVAE CVR. LADAE T. PVNICIVS. NIALIS. II. VIR. LON. MORINO RVM. SAGRIDS ROMAE. ET. AVG OB. HONOREM V. V. A. M. O. V. L
units.tr: To Minerva. Titus Punicius Nialis, duumvir of the Morini, [set this up] at Rome, and [in honour of] Augustus, V.V.A.M.O.V.L.

units.la: Vadicasses sunt apud Plinium; qui Οὐδικάσιοι Ptolemaeo: quondam, ubi nunc Noion, Noviomagus Antonino inter Suessones & Ambianos; Νουιόμαγος Vadicassium Ptolemaeo. Alij sunt Vadicasses ab Baiocassibus; de quibus in Normannia: nam temere quidam confundunt.
units.tr: The Vadicasses are mentioned by Pliny; Ptolemy calls them the Οὐδικάσιοι [Oudikasioi]. Their town was once where Noyon now stands, Noviomagus in Antoninus, between the Suessones and the Ambiani; Ptolemy gives Νουιόμαγος [Nouiomagos] as the town of the Vadicasses. Others distinguish the Vadicasses from the Baiocasses, whom we shall discuss in Normandy; some people carelessly confuse the two.

units.la: Picardia porro in tris dividitur partes, Veram, Inferiorem, Superiorem. De postrema nihil hoc libro dicam. Occupatur enim Tota fere ab ijs Regionibus, quae in Inseriore Germania, interque Septemdecim Provincias principem obtinent locum; de quibus libro v.
units.tr: Picardy is further divided into three parts: Vera, Inferior and Superior. I shall say nothing in this book about the last, since it is occupied almost entirely by those regions which hold the leading place in Lower Germany among the Seventeen Provinces; I shall treat them in Book 5.

units.la: Vera (La vraye Picardie) coepto Parisijs itinere, superatisque Bellovacorum Agris, initium est ad Crepacorium. Comprehendit Vuedamiae (Communibus utar Vocabulis, ut melius intelligat) Ambianam, Corbiensem & Pequignyam: Comitatus Veromandunorum & Retelorum; Ducatum Tiraschensem.
units.tr: True Picardy (La vraye Picardie), beginning from the road from Paris and passing the lands of the Bellovaci, extends to Crépy. It includes (I shall use the common names so that it may be better understood) Vermandois, comprising Amiens, Corbie and Péquigny; the county of the Veromandui and Rethel; and the duchy of Thiérache.

units.la: Ambiana (Visdamie d'Amiens) nomen dedit Amlianum, vulgo Amiens: olim uti censent V. N. Iofephus Scaliger, Petrus Divaeus, Goropius Becanus, Iofias Simlesrus, & alij, Samarobriva. Sigebertus etiam Ambianum idem facit cum Sommonobria; sic ille scripsit pro Samarobriva. Alij, quum Samarobrivam & Ambianos duo diversa se dicerent legere opida apud Antoninum, in eam ierunt sententiam, ut arbitrarentur Samarobrivae memoriam hodieque servari in opido, quod ad Somonam (vel, ut alij scribunt, Suminam) Brayum nominatur. Sed potuit eadem urbs & Samarobriva vocari & Ambiani, quod horum Populorum ea esset caput. Itinera Antonini, quae utriusque faciunt mentionem, alibi videbimus: Prius quidem, quod ad Picardiam proprie pertineat, ad finem hujus capitis, alterum, quod multas simul Galliæ Regiones complectatur, ad Libri finem. Samarobrivæ meminerunt, præter posterioris ævi Scriptores, aliquoties Cæsar lib. v de Bello Gallico & Cicero lib. v i i. Epist. ad Trebatium; ut falsum sit, quod superioribus adscribit Sigebertus, Urbem hanc ab Antonino Pio Imperatore fuisse conditam. Majorem habet vetustatem. Ptolemæo appellatur Σαμαροβριγα. Quidam Antonini Codices Samarabrivam, alij Samarabrigam præferunt. Brigam antiqua Hispanorum Lingua, & Briam Thracio sermone, Urbem nuncupari alias dixi. Nonnulli Somenobrigam scribunt à Ponte (Belgice Brug) quo Somona fluvius traijciebatur. Ambianum certe Urbs est ad Somonam, qui eam hic ibi findit, unde quidam Ambianum putant dictum ab Imperatore Gratiano, quod Aquis ambiatur, munitionibus Galliarum & ab natura & ab hominum industria merito connumeranda; Fossis pulcris præaltisque vallata; Clavis ea parte Regni. Templum habet speciosissimum. Incolæ multis clarent Privilegijs; inter ea, quod cum ab exterorum militum Præsidijs, tum ab subsidijs sint immunes. Probitate sane Fidelitateq; sunt insignes. Fabulantur quidam ab Alexandri Magni Militibus conditum. Ambiano tribuit Antonini Itinerarium Legionem XXIII, Episcopos ejus Belleforestius recenset LXIII; inter eos autem ultimum Ioannem Crequium.
units.tr: Amiénois (Visdamie d'Amiens) took its name from Amiens, commonly called Amiens. Some, such as the learned Joseph Scaliger, Pierre Divaeus, Goropius Becanus, Josias Simler and others, think that the town was formerly Samarobriva. Sigebert also identifies Ambianum with Sommonobria, writing that name for Samarobriva. Others, since they read in Antoninus two different towns, Samarobriva and Ambiani, have taken the view that the memory of Samarobriva survives today in the town called Breteuil on the Somme (or, as others write, the Somme). But the same town could have been called both Samarobriva and Ambiani, since it was the chief town of this people. Antoninus's itineraries, which mention both, we shall examine elsewhere: the first, which belongs properly to Picardy, at the end of this chapter, and the second, which covers many regions of Gaul at once, at the end of the book. Apart from later writers, Caesar mentions Samarobriva several times in Book 5 of the Gallic War, and Cicero in Letter 7 of Book 16 to Trebatius. So Sigebert's claim, mentioned above, that this city was founded by the emperor Antoninus Pius is false: it is much older. Ptolemy calls it Σαμαροβριγα [Samarobriga]. Some manuscripts of Antoninus read Samarabriva, others Samarabriga. I have said elsewhere that Briga in the ancient Spanish language, and Bria in the Thracian, meant a town. Some write Somenobriga, from the bridge (in Dutch Brug) by which the Somme was crossed. Ambianum is certainly a town on the Somme, which cuts through it here; hence some think it was called Ambianum by the emperor Gratian, because it is surrounded by waters (Aquis ambiatur). It is rightly counted among the fortresses of Gaul, strong both by nature and by human industry; it is walled with fine, very deep ditches, and it is the key to the kingdom in that part. It has a most splendid church. Its inhabitants are distinguished by many privileges, among them that they are exempt from garrisons of foreign soldiers and from subsidies. They are certainly noted for their honesty and loyalty. Some fable that it was founded by soldiers of Alexander the Great. Antoninus's Itinerary assigns the Twenty-third Legion to Amiens. Belleforest lists sixty-three bishops of it, the last of whom was John Crequy.

units.la: Corbiensis ab Corbia, quod Opidum est ad Somonam; quo loco fluvius, cui adjacet, Somonam ingreditur: Clavis itidem, qua parte jacet, Franciæ. Carmiliaca forte Antonini, inter Samarobrivam, Amiens & Caesaromagum, Roye, ni fallor.
units.tr: Corbie takes its name from Corbia, a town on the Somme, where the river to which it lies adjacent flows into the Somme. It is likewise the key to France in the part where it lies. Carmiliaca is perhaps, unless I am mistaken, the place in Antoninus between Samarobriva, Amiens, and Caesaromagus, Roye.

units.la: Pequignya denique à Pequignyo, vulgo Pequigny. Opidum est sic dictum, si vulgo fides, à Pignone,- Alexandri Magni Milite. Historiographis nobilitatum, quod ibi Gulielmus Nortmanniæ Dux, cui cognomen erat Longa-Spatha, positis insidijs fuerit obtruncatus per factionem Balduini Comitis Cameracensis, qui cum pacisineundæ prætextu eo loci pellexerat. Testantur Nortmanniæ Annales. Memoriæ etiam produnt Francicarum rerum Scriptores Anglos, postquam prælio jam essent victi, superstites omnes ibidem fuisse occisos, qui nomen Pequigny literis omnibus pronunciare nequibant, Pequeny loco Pequigny proferentes.
units.tr: Péquigny, finally, takes its name from Pequigny, commonly Pequigny. It is a town so called, if popular belief is to be trusted, from Pignon, a soldier of Alexander the Great. It is made famous in the historians because William, duke of Normandy, who had the surname Longsword, was there cut down by a plot of Baldwin, count of Cambrai, who had enticed him there under pretext of making peace. The Annals of Normandy bear witness to this. The writers of French history also record that the English, after they had already been defeated in battle, were all killed on the spot, since they could not pronounce the name Pequigny with all its letters, and said Pequeny instead of Pequigny.

units.la: Veromandui de quibus antea dixi, hodie vulgo Vermandois, retento, si qui alij Galliæ populi, prisco Nomine. Picardiæ pars, aliquando Comitatus titulo celebris. Inter Comites primum invenio Hugonem, Henrici I Francorum Regis filium, Philippi Regis fratrem: qui cum alijs Proceribus Bello Sacro, quod in Palæstina, Duce Godefredo Bilionæo, anno c I ɔ x c i x gestum, interfuisse legitur. Successerunt huic duo Rudolphi Filius & Nepos; quorum hoc sine Liberis defuncto, Comitatus ad Regnum est devolutus. Wandali, facta in Gallias cum Burgundionibus irruptione, Provinciam hanc miserum in modum afflixerunt. Comprehendere vero sub se Comitatum hunc signant Franciæ Geographi Suessonum, Laudunensium, Tarterorum Ditiones; Urbes item Noviomagum & Fanum S. Quintini. Suessones, quorum antea memini, hodie vulgo Souessones, vel, ut alij pronunciant, Soissonnois. Suessonum Vrbs, quæ hodie Soisson, Arce prædita; Suessones gentis voce, apud Antoninum, qui Legionem ei xxv attribuit; Συεσιωνες Straboni; Αυγυστα Συεσσονων (sic enim emendandum, pro Ουεσσονων) Ptolemæo; Civitas Suessonum in Dignitatum libello dicitur. Eripuit hanc Vrbem Siagrio, Gilonis Romani Prætoris filio Hlodovæus: quo defuncto, Filij decus illi Regiæ Civitatis, quo Cæsaris tempore claruerat, reddiderunt. Postea Comitatus Titulo fuit insignis. Karolus Ludovici Principis Condæi filius Comes audit Suessonum. Episcopatus est, cujus Belleforestius Præsules numerat nominatque lxxix; ultimum Matthiam Parisinum.
units.tr: The Veromandui, of whom I spoke earlier, are today commonly called Vermandois, keeping, as with other peoples of Gaul, their ancient name. It is a part of Picardy, once famous under the title of a county. Among the counts, the first I find is Hugh, son of Henry I, king of the Franks, and brother of King Philip; he is read to have taken part, with other nobles, in the Holy War fought in Palestine under Duke Godfrey of Bouillon in the year 1099. He was succeeded by two Rudolphs, son and grandson; when the latter died without children, the county passed to the crown. The Vandals, when they made their invasion of Gaul along with the Burgundians, afflicted this province in a wretched manner. The French geographers indeed include within it the domains of the Suessones, Laudunenses and Tarterani, and likewise the towns of Noyon and Saint-Quentin. The Suessones, whom I mentioned earlier, are today commonly called Soissonnais, or, as others pronounce it, Soissonnois. The town of the Suessones, now Soissons, has a citadel; in Antoninus, which assigns it the Twenty-fifth Legion, the name is the people's name, Suessones; Strabo gives Συεσιωνες [Suesiones]; Ptolemy gives Αυγυστα Συεσσονων [Augusta Suessonon] (which must be emended in that way, in place of Ουεσσονων); the Notitia Dignitatum calls it the city of the Suessones. Clovis took this town from Syagrius, son of Egidius, the Roman governor; when he died, his sons restored to it the honour of a royal city that it had enjoyed in the time of Caesar. Afterwards it was distinguished by the title of a county. Charles, son of Prince Louis of Condé, is styled count of Soissons. It is a bishopric; Belleforest counts and names seventy-nine of its prelates, the last being Matthias of Paris.

units.la: Laudunensium Ager, Laonnois, dictus ab Lauduno: cujus meminit Vita Karoli Magni, quodque inemendatius forte apud Antoninum Alauna, quod denique plenius effert suis ad me Litteris Magnus Scaliger, Laudunum Clavatum: hodie Laon. Conditam vult hanc Vrbem Papirius Massonius ab Matrobio Prætore. Situs ipsi in Colle. Invasit eam Karolus Lotharingiæ Dux, Ludovici Regis Francorum, Stirpis Karolinæ ultimi, Patruus; quum se jure Successionis videret privatum ab Hugone Capeto. Præsules se Duces & Pares Franciæ scribunt. Eorum Syllabus apud Belleforestium, cui lxxiii recensentur, eorumque postremus Ioannes Burserius.
units.tr: The land of the Laudunenses, Laonnois, takes its name from Laudunum. Its mention occurs in the Life of Charlemagne; Antoninus perhaps gives the less accurate form Alauna; Joseph Scaliger, in a letter to me, gives the fuller form, Laudunum Clavatum. Today it is Laon. Papirius Masson holds that this town was founded by a governor named Matrobius. It stands on a hill. Charles, duke of Lorraine, uncle of King Louis of the Franks, the last of the Carolingian line, seized it, since he saw himself deprived of the right of succession by Hugh Capet. Its bishops style themselves dukes and peers of France. Their list in Belleforest, where seventy-three are recorded, ends with John Bourser.

units.la: Tartenorum, vernacule Tartenois, Metropolis est Fera, vulgo La Fere: Vrbs egregie munita, situque commodissimo, ad Oysam Servamque confluentes; Arcem habens satis validam.
units.tr: The metropolis of the Tarterani, in the vernacular Tartenois, is Fère, commonly La Fère: a town excellently fortified, with a very convenient site, where the Oise and the Serre meet, and with a fairly strong citadel.

units.la: Quæ nunc Vrbs Noion, Antonino Noviomagus nuncupatur, inter Suessonas & Ambianos, ut antea dixi, eam collocanti, Decimamque octavam Legionem illi tribuenti. Noviomagus Vadicassium est Ptolemæo. Vulgo Ecclesiasticorum Noviomum vocatur per compendium; ut Treffes pro Tricasses. Falluntur, qui eamdem faciunt cum Novioduno. Quatuor quidem Novioduna nominantur ab variis Scriptoribus, sed eorum nullum commune quid habet cum Noviomago, de quo agimus. Vir N. Iosephus Scaliger suis ad me Litteris, Se Nugatoribus hac in re, etiam jurantibus, creditus negat. Vrbs est, Antiquitatis suæ notas non paucas præferens. Episcopalis Sedes; cujus Præsules Comites se Noviomagienses & Franciæ Pares scribunt. Catalogus eorum apud Belleforestium, qui postremum edit Ioannem Hangestum, Senlisij Dynastæ filium.
units.tr: The town now called Noyon is named in Antoninus Noviomagus; I have said above that it lies between the Suessones and the Ambiani, and Antoninus assigns it the Eighteenth Legion. Noviomagus is the Vadicassian town in Ptolemy. Commonly, among churchmen, it is called Noviomum for short, as Tréfles is for Tricasses. Those are mistaken who identify it with Noviodunum. Four places are indeed named Noviodunum by various writers, but none of them has anything in common with Noviomagus, which is our subject. Joseph Scaliger, in a letter to me, denies that it is the same, even though some trifling writers insist on it under oath. It is a town which preserves not a few marks of its antiquity. It is an episcopal see; its prelates style themselves counts of Noyon and peers of France. Their list in Belleforest ends with John Hangest, son of the lord of Senlis.

units.la: Fano S. Quintini, quod Comitum Veromanduorum aliquando Domicilium & Regiunculæ caput, nomen à Quintino, qui Martyrium ibi passus. Olim Augusta Veromanduorum. Sic etiam dicitur in Vita S. Quintini. Robertus tamen Cœnalis scribit hanc Augustam omnino diruram, ejusque hodie nihil restare præter Cœnobium, quod vulgo Vermand-Abbaye. Quidquid sit, Fanum S. Quintini, Arce nunc potens, multa sustinuit Damna, Calamitatesque Bello inter Philippum Hispaniarum & Henricum Galliarum Reges: quæ plenius à me explicata in Historia Rerum per Belgicam nuperis hisce Tumultibus gestarum.
units.tr: Saint-Quentin, which was at one time the residence of the counts of the Veromandui and the capital of a small region, takes its name from Quentin, who suffered martyrdom there. Formerly it was Augusta Veromanduorum, as it is also called in the Life of Saint Quentin. Robert Cénalis, however, writes that this Augusta was utterly destroyed, and that nothing of it remains today except the abbey, commonly called Vermand-Abbaye. Whatever the case, Saint-Quentin, now powerful with its citadel, suffered many losses and calamities in the war between Philip, king of Spain, and Henry, king of France; I have explained these more fully in my History of the events of the recent troubles in the Low Countries.

units.la: Hæc de Veromanduis: Retelorum (vulgo Retelois) ditio sita est inter Hannonios, Lotharingos & Barros. Metropolis Retelium.
units.tr: These are the lands of the Veromandui: the district of Rethel (commonly Retelois) lies between the Hainaulters, the Lorrainers and the Barrois. Its metropolis is Rethel.

units.la: Tiraschæ (La Tirasche) de qua ante nonnihil, primaria Vrbs est Guisa: Arce superbiens; Propugnaculum contra Leuceburgenses: Vetus Patrimonium Fratrum Primogeniti Lotharingiæ Ducis. Ducum Guisæ proximorum hoc lego Stemma:
units.tr: Tirasche (La Tirasche), of which I said something a little earlier, has as its chief town Guise, proud of its citadel and a bulwark against the men of Luxembourg. It is the old patrimony of the younger brothers of the Duke of Lorraine. I read the following genealogy of the nearest Dukes of Guise:

units.la: CLAVDIVS Lotharingius, Dux Guisæ & Aumaliæ.
units.tr: CLAUDIUS of Lorraine, Duke of Guise and Aumale.

units.la: FRANCISCVS, Dux Guisæ obiit xii Kal. Mart. MDLXIIII in Obsidione Aureliapensi. HENRICVS, Dux Guisæ: cæsus xviii Kal. Ianuar. MDLXXXVIII in Comitiis Blesensibus. FRANCISCVS Dux Iamvillæ. LVDOVICVS Cardinalis Lotharingiæ: cæsus cum Fratre eodem tempore, ipsidem Comitiis, in conspectu Regis. CAROLVS Dux Mayennæ. MARIA, defuncto Priore Marito Duce Longevillano, coniux inde Iacobi V Scotiæ Regis. MARIA Stuarda Scotiæ Regina; suppleto adfecta xii Kal. Mart. MDLXVII. CLAVDIVS Dux Aumalius.
units.tr: FRANCIS, Duke of Guise, died 12 Kal. March 1564 at the siege of Orléans. HENRY, Duke of Guise, slain 18 Kal. January 1588 at the Estates of Blois. FRANCIS, Duke of Joinville. LOUIS, Cardinal of Lorraine, slain together with his brother at the same Estates, in the sight of the King. CHARLES, Duke of Mayenne. MARY, whose first husband, the Duke of Longueville, had died, became the wife of James V, King of Scots. MARY Stuart, Queen of Scots, put to death by the axe, 12 Kal. March 1567. CLAUDE, Duke of Aumale.

units.la: Sic se habet Vera Picardia: Inferiori (La Basse) variæ sunt partes: Sanctterra, Pontium, Bolonesium, Guynæum, Oyum.
units.tr: Thus stands True Picardy: Lower Picardy (La Basse), which has several parts: Santerre, Ponthieu, Boulonnais, Guînes, Oye.

units.la: Sanctterra, Sancterre, concluditur inter Montem S. Desiderÿ, Peronam & Roiam: Frumenti variorumque Fructuum valde ferax. Monti S. Desiderÿ, vulgo Mondidier, unde sit nomen, notum est. Perona, bellicis cladibus saepe fatigata. Clavis ibi Franciæ, Arce potens. Hic Heribertus Veromanduorum Comes Captiuum deriuuit Karolum Simplicem, Galliarum Regem. Late Papirius Masson rerum Francicarum lib. x, & alij. Roia, opidum non contemnendum, Arce, ut fere omnia limitaneis his locis, validum: Cæsaromagus, nisi fallor, Antonino & Itinerariæ Tabulæ: Cæsaromagi etiam in Bellovacis meminit Ptolemæus. Alij Rodrinam esse volunt: quæ mihi Romorantin, ut suo dicam loco. Est ibidem Nella, Propugnaculum, ut multa alia; hac parte Regni, Arce munitum, ad Fontem fere Ingonis Fluvij; qui, exiguo cursu confecto, mox inter Ronyam & Voiennam in Somonam se exonerat. Nella Clarorum Virorum genitrix. Ejus Dynastæ Marchiones adfinitate iuncti leguntur Familiæ Ceurtenæ, quæ originem traxit ab Regibus Franciæ.
units.tr: Santerre, Sancterre, is bounded between Montdidier, Péronne and Roye, and is very rich in grain and various other crops. Montdidier, commonly Mondidier, from which it takes its name, is well known. Péronne, often worn down by the calamities of war, a key of France, strong with its citadel. Here Heribert, Count of the Veromandui, captured Charles the Simple, King of the French; Papirius Masson tells this at length in book x of his Histories of the French, and others too. Roye, a town not to be despised, strong with its citadel, as nearly all the places on these frontier lines are: Caesaromagus, unless I am mistaken, in Antoninus and in the Itinerary Tables; Ptolemy also mentions Caesaromagus in the land of the Bellovaci. Others want it to be Rodrina, which to me is Romorantin, as I shall say in its place. There is also Nesle, a stronghold, as are many others in this part of the kingdom, fortified with a citadel, near the source of the river Ingon, which, after a short course, soon discharges itself into the Somme between Roye and Ham. Nesle is the mother of famous men. Its lords, the marquises, are read to have been joined by marriage to the family of Courtenay, which drew its origin from the Kings of France.

units.la: Pontium, vernacule Ponthieu, Comitatus est, cui nomen creditur datum à Pontium, qui passim ibi, multitudine. Est enim Regio inter Somonam & Authyam fluvios: Paludibus plena: quæque Stagnis suis, ut ipse deprehendi, multis in locis invia. Cogitandum aliis relinquo, an non Nomen huius opinione quorundam vetustius. Ego hoc Tractu apud Antoninum invenio Pontes cum Legione xxiv. inter Ambianos & Gesforiacum. In Notitia item Romanarum Dignitatum scribitur Civitas Morinorum, id est Ponticum. Comitatus fulget dignitate. Meminerunt Annales Guilelmi huius Provinciæ Comitis, qui vixit tempore Lotharij Francorum Regis. Anglici Iuris factus est, quum Eduardus i Angliæ Rex uxorem duceret Eleonoram, Ferdinandi Castellæ Regis Filiam ex Ioanna Conjuge, quæ Filia erat Simonis Pontium Comitis. Anglo plenius solidiusque adquisitum fuit Ius per Pacem inter Ioannem & Eduardum factam MCCLX. Non multo post Incolæ, instigante Guidone S. Pauli Comite, Præsidiarios, quos Rex Eduardus ibi reliquerat, exturbarunt; Regiqueque Francorum Karolo V se dediderunt. Sic nobilissimus Comitatus Franco cessit, post annos cxii, quam ipsum Doris nomine Rex Eduardus i accepisset. Primarium Comitatus opidum Abbatis-Villa, Abbeville vulgo: non antiquum valde, uti nomen indicat: Baillivatus titulo insignitum. Opida habet & alia non magni nominis, Crotoyam, Ruam, Treportum, Fanum S. Richiery. Cressiacum, Cressy, Vicus est, Gallorum clade memorabilis, de qua Papirius Masson lib. iv Annalium. Comprehendere autem notatur sub se hic Comitatus duos alios Monstrolien-sem & S. Pauli; utrumque nomen à principibus Vrbibus, quæ vulgo Monstreul & S. Pol. Montreul quibusdam quasi Mont-Royal; alijs ab Monstro, quod eo loci domicilium habuisse fingitur. Comites S. Paulli. Progenitorem memorant ex Stirpe Leuceburgica Walleramum Leuceburgium, Lignij Comitem, germanum Henrici VII Romanorum Imperatoris fratrem. Ultimam ejus Stemmatis lego Mariam Leuceburgicam, Petri Filiam, Fani D. Pauli ac Lignij Comitem, Anhiani Dominam; Vxorem prius Iacobi Sangij Ramondi Vaufsiique Comitis; inde vero Francisci Comitis Vendomij; Matrem ex illo Filiae, quae nuptit Henrico Nassavio; ex hoc autem Karoli Primi Vendomiae Ducis.
units.tr: Ponthieu, in the vernacular Ponthieu, is a county, which is believed to have been named from the Pontes, who were numerous there everywhere. For the region lies between the rivers Somme and Authie; it is full of marshes, and, as I myself have found, in many places impassable because of its pools. I leave it to others to consider whether the name is not older than this opinion of some. I find in Antoninus that the Pontes, with the Legion xxiv, lay along this route between the Ambiani and Gesoriacum. Likewise the Notitia of the Roman Dignities writes Civitas Morinorum, that is, Ponticum. The county shines with dignity. The Annals mention Guillaume, Count of this province, who lived in the time of Lothair, King of the Franks. It became subject to the English law when King Edward I of England married Eleanor, daughter of Ferdinand, King of Castile, by his wife Joan, who was the daughter of Simon of Ponthieu, Count. The English acquired the right more fully and firmly through the peace made between John and Edward in 1260. Not long afterwards the inhabitants, at the instigation of Guy, Count of St Pol, drove out the garrison which King Edward had left there, and surrendered themselves to Charles V, King of the French. So this most noble county passed to the French, after 112 years since King Edward I had received it through Doris. The chief town of the county is Abbeville, commonly Abbatis-Villa, not very old, as its name indicates, and distinguished by the title of a bailiwick. It has other towns of no great name: Crotoy, Rue, Tréport, Saint-Riquier. Cressy, Cressiacum, is a village memorable for the defeat of the French, of which Papirius Masson writes in book iv of his Annals. This county is said to include two others under it, Montreuil and St Pol; each name comes from its principal town, which is commonly called Monstreul and S. Pol, Montreul; some say, as it were, Mont-Royal; others from Monstrum, which is supposed to have had a dwelling in that place. The Counts of St Pol: they record as their progenitor from the Luxembourg line Walram of Luxembourg, Count of Ligny, brother of Henry VII, Emperor of the Romans. I read that the last of his line was Mary of Luxembourg, daughter of Peter, Count of St Pol and Ligny, Lady of Enghien; first wife of James of Saint-Pol, Count of Ramerupt and Vaudémont; then of Francis, Count of Vendôme; mother by the latter of a daughter who married Henry of Nassau, and by the former of Charles I, Duke of Vendôme.

units.la: Bolonia, vel ut alij, Bononia Comitatus (Comté de Boulogne) satis est amplus. Initium illi ab Montibus S. Ingelberti; procurritque ad Fluvium Cancham, quae ejus Longitudo & Latitudo ad Lucum usque Tournohensem porrigitur. Totus Tractus arenosus est, ejus generis arenae, quam Vrentem vocant: unde & nonnulli Fo'oniam censent derivatam à Bouiller; quod ridere soleo. Nomen Comitatui à Bolonia Opido, quod in Superius hodie & Inferius divisum. Illud aliotiore situm loco, Burgus tantum, anteaquam ab Anglis obsidione premeretur:
units.tr: Boulogne, or as others call it Bononia, the county (Comté de Boulogne) is fairly large. It begins at the Mountains of St Ingelbert and runs down to the river Canche; its length and breadth extend as far as the wood of Tournehem. The whole tract is sandy, of the kind of sand that they call Vrentem; hence some hold that Fo'oniam was derived from Bouiller, which I am wont to laugh at. The county takes its name from the town Bolonia, which today is divided into Upper and Lower. The former lies in a higher place and was only a village before it was pressed by an English siege:

units.la: Caletenses & Bononienses.
units.tr: The Caletenses and the Bononienses.

units.la: Hoc autem planiora occupans Mare adluit. Alterum ab altero passibus distat centum, aut circiter. Bononiam etiam nominant hac Galliarum parte, praeter Ammianum lib. xx, Olympiodorus & Sozomenus. Scripsit ille Historiam Honorij Senioris, Theodosij & Honorij Iunioris, inque serinijs adhuc & Armarijs Bibliothecarum delitescit. Loquens autem de Constantino Tyranno, Τας Βρεττανιας ιδιας, ait, μεγιστην αμα της ουδ' δε Βονωνιας, πλιν γε καλυμμενων, ὠφελιαλασιαν, και πρωτων εν τοις των Γαλατων ἐρους κειμενων. Emendandus hinc, cujus memini, Sozomenus, qui libro ix loquens eadem de re, μεγιωθης δε Κωνσταντιου, inquit, και Βριτανιας δε Βονωνιας (leg. Βονωνιας) πλιν της Γαλατιας, ωδε φιλοσοφων κειμενων, ωδεμπαζεσθαι τας ωδε Γαλατας και Αλεσσανεις φορμωτας. Bononiense opidum habet quoque Panegyricus Incerti Auctoris Imperatori Constantino dictus. Civitas Bononiensium est in Notitia Provinciarum inter Belgicae Secundae Civitates. Hodie Francorum Vulgo Boulongne; Flandris, reliquisque Inferioris Germaniae Populis, propius ad Veterem appellationem accedentibus, Beunen. Antiquissimis temporibus, uti censent V. N. Iosephus Scaliger suis ad me Litteris (nam ad Ausonium Gesforie opidum hoc tractu nomen retinere docet) Papirius Masonius, Lelandus, Abrahamus Ortelius, & alij, Gesforiacum. Diserte Tabula Peutingeriana, quam cum maxime Reip. litterariae bono nuper editam à se mihi liberaliter transmisit Vir Nobilis. Marcus Velserus Patricius & II-Vir Augustanus: Gesfogiaco, Quod nunc Bononia; nonia; reponendum Gesforiaco. Gesforiacum Antonino dicitur, qui ei Legionem adscribit x v; Et alibi Gesforiacensis Portus; item Gesfortagensis Portus in Maritimis: Ptolemæo Γεσσοριάκων, Γεσσορίακον μοζίναν. Gesforigia est in Panegyrico, qui Maximiano dictus; & eo fere modo in quibusdam Antonini Codicibus Ceforicu. De eo Pomponius Mela: Pertinentque ad ultimos Galliarum gentium Morinos, nec Portu, quem Gesforiacum vocant, quidquam eorum habent. Sic Suetonius in Claudio cap. xvii, ubi de expeditione Principis in Britanniam: Quare a Massilia Gesforiacum usque pedestri itinere confecto, inde transmisit. Ab eo Plinius lib. iv. nat. hist. cap. xvi. Gesforiacum Morinorum Gentis Littus nominat: Et Gesforiacus eidem Pagus, totus ille Tractus, qui pertinet ab Nore-mannis Belgis Bononiam usque. Pagi enim appellatio late solet apud Veteres Scriptores patere, ut Pagus Tigurinus, Pagus Velaunus, & alij; quemadmodum & Civitatis passim in Notitia Provinciarum, pro tota aliqua Præpositura, pro magno modo Agri, pro Gente quamcumvis numerosa. Alij Gelloriacum non idem volunt cum Navali Fononiensi: Calesium putat Ioannes Talbotus; Fanum S. Audomari Incertiores apud Hieronymum Suritam ad Antonini Itinerarium; Vicum Scas, haud procul eodem Fano, Hadrianus Turnebus lib. viii Adversar. cap. xxi; Sirium Brugensium Coloniam, Hector Boëtius; Brugæ ipsas Hermolaus Barbarus ad Plinium; Gandavum Bilibaldus: Robertus Cœnalis libro de re Gallic. ii Periochæ iii diversa ponit Gesforiacum Portum & Gesforiacum Navale; illum Ecomanam centum; hoc autem Castellum, quod vulgo Calsel. Boloniensis porro fuit Godefridus, Eustathii Boloniensis Comitis Filius, Lotharingiæ Dux, qui Christianorum Primus Rex Solymorum. Prope Bononiam erat Itius Portus: quem qui Calesium Opidum esse arbitrantur, inter quos Lhuydus, nullo negotio refelluntur à Ptolemæo, qui post Sequanæ Fluminis Ostia prius ponit Ἰτίου Λ κρὸν, deinde Γεσοριάκων, Ἐπίσεσσ Μορίνων: a quo opidum Calesium distat plus quam xx millibus Passuum, hoc est, Leucis Belgicis septem. Gesforiacum idem esse cum Itio persuasum videtur M. Veltero ad Fragmentum Tabulæ Itinerariæ. Itius portus quibusdam Fanum S. Audomari censetur, adouctis cum vetusto Vrbis nomine, quo Sitien vocabatur, quasi, ut volunt, Sinus I. y; tum Loci situ, qui quum valde sit humilis, præaltis tamen littoribus Vrbem quodammodo cingentibus, Sinum Maris olim capacissimum fuisse indicat. Cambdenus in tua Britannia docet Itium Portum diu fuisse in loco, quem hodie Withsan vocamus [prope Blanesium. Ego sic argumentari soleo: Quum apud Ptolemæum & Itio Promontorio & Gesforiaco Navali (quod Bononiam esse jam dixi) ejusdem Gradus Latitudinis, nimirum lxiii, idem omnino Scrupulus, xxx scilicet, tribuatur: in Longitudine autem nonnihil differant, quod utrque locus eidem quidem subsit Longitudinis Gradui xxii, sed Itium Promontorium sub indicati Gradus Scrupulo xv. Gesforiacum vero sub Scrupulo xlv: necessum prorsus est, Itium portum haud procul fuisse a Gesforiaco Navali, eodem plane inter Septemtrionem & Meridiem Parallelo, non eodem inter Ortum & Occasum Meridiano: hoc est Itium Portum Navali esse aut fuisse Occidentaliorem, Britanniæque littoribus paulo propiorem: idcoque, quum Gesforiacum vel Bononiam Mari jam nunc adlidere conspiciamus, Itium Portum Oceano, ut multa alia ad Mare Britannicum Aquitanicumque Loca, haustum esse, nudamque ejus memoriam & appellationem exstare fortean in Vico, qui Portu licet Orientalior & magis Mediterraneus, prope Bononiam, ad Mare, vernacule dicitur Portet, quasi Portus Itius, κατ' ἐοποτικὸν. Accedit, quod ex Portu Itio ad proximam Britanniæ partem Trajectum notent, Cæsar quidem millium passuum xxxx, Strabo vero Stadiorum cccxx; Cæsaris verba lib. v sunt hæc: Atque omnes ad Portum Itium convenire jubet: quo ex Portu commodissimum in Britanniam Transpectum esse cognoverat, circiter millium passuum xxxx; sic in melioribus fideique probationis libris legitur, non xxx: Strabonis autem lib. iv, ubi de Morinis termo, sic habent, Ναυ-ς εἰς ἴσι καὶ τὸ Ἴτιον, ᾧ ἐκρέησαν Ναυσαφμῳ Καισαρ ὁ Θεὸς, Διαιρῶν εἰς τὴν Νῆσον. Νυκτὸς δ᾽ αὐτὸν ἐκ ἑτέρου καὶ τὴν ὑστερίαν κατὰ ὀμιαντος ὁμοίαν ἄραι, τῶν καὶ ἑπεροι ἐκ ἑτέρου τὴν Δαλμα. Miror Strabonem, diligentissimum aliàs-que latiqué sui memorem Auctorem, eundem Stadiorum numerum ponere inter Flumina Celtica (intelligit Ligerim & Sequanam; nam de iis egerat) & Britanniam: Διαππα δ᾽ ἐσιν εἰς τὴν Βρεττανικὴν, καὶ ἐν τῶν πολιμῶν τ Κελτικῆς ἑκοσι ἡ τῶν φάδιον. Quod esse non potest. Trajectus enim ab ostio Sequanæ in Britanniam major est, quam cccxx Stadiorum; & multo major ex Ligeris
units.tr: The sea, occupying these lower-lying lands, washes over them. The one place is about a hundred paces, or thereabouts, from the other. In this part of Gaul they also call it Bononia, as do Olympiodorus and Sozomen, besides Ammianus in book xx. Ammianus wrote the history of Honorius the Elder, of Theodosius and of Honorius the Younger, and it still lies hidden in libraries and archives. Speaking of the tyrant Constantine, he says: "Τας Βρεττανιας ιδιας, making the greatest of the British lands, along with that of Bononia, which was then called so, and the first of those lying in the territory of the Gauls, [μεγιστην αμα της ουδ' δε Βονωνιας, πλιν γε καλυμμενων, ὠφελιαλασιαν, και πρωτων εν τοις των Γαλατων ἐρους κειμενων]." Hence Sozomen, whom I remember, must be corrected on this point. Speaking of the same matter in book ix, he says: "making Constantius, and the British lands at Bononia (read Βονωνιας), then part of Gaul, lying there..." [μεγιωθης δε Κωνσταντιου, και Βριτανιας δε Βονωνιας (leg. Βονωνιας) πλιν της Γαλατιας, ωδε φιλοσοφων κειμενων, ωδεμπαζεσθαι τας ωδε Γαλατας και Αλεσσανεις φορμωτας]. The anonymous Panegyric addressed to the Emperor Constantine also has Bononiense opidum. The Civitas Bononiensium is among the cities of Belgica Secunda in the Notitia of the Provinces. Today the French call it Boulongne, while the Flemings and other peoples of Lower Germany, who keep closer to the old name, call it Beunen. In the most ancient times, as V. N. Joseph Scaliger thinks in his letters to me (for he teaches that in Ausonius this town in this region retains the name Gesforie), as do Papirius Masso, Leland, Abraham Ortelius and others, it was Gesforiacum. Clearly so does the Peutinger Table, which the noble man Marcus Velserus, patrician and duumvir of Augsburg, kindly sent to me, having recently edited it for the great benefit of the literary republic: Gesfogiaco, Quod nunc Bononia; this should be read as Gesforiaco. Antoninus calls it Gesforiacum, and ascribes to it the Fifteenth Legion; and elsewhere Gesforiacensis Portus; likewise Gesfortagensis Portus among the maritime places. Ptolemy has Γεσσοριάκων and Γεσσορίακον μοζίναν. Gesforigia is in the Panegyric addressed to Maximian, and in some codices of Antoninus almost in the same form, Ceforicu. Of it Pomponius Mela says: "The Morini, the furthest of the peoples of Gaul, extend to it, and none of them have anything beyond the harbour which they call Gesforiacum." So Suetonius in Claudius chapter 17, where he speaks of the Emperor's expedition to Britain: "Therefore, having completed the journey on foot from Massilia to Gesforiacum, he crossed from there." Pliny, book iv of the Natural History, chapter 16, calls it Gesforiacum, the shore of the Morini people. The same Pliny calls Gesforiacus a Pagus, that whole district which extends from the Belgic Nervii to Bononia. For the term Pagus is commonly used broadly by the ancient writers, as in Pagus Tigurinus, Pagus Velaunus, and others; just as Civitas is used throughout the Notitia for a whole praepositura, for a large part of territory, or for any populous people. Others do not think that Gelloriacum is the same as the Fononiensis naval station. John Talbot thinks it is Calesium; some less well-known writers, in Hieronymus Surita's edition of the Antonine Itinerary, think it is the Fanum S. Audomari; Hadrianus Turnebus, book viii of the Adversaria, chapter 21, thinks it is Vicum Scas, not far from the same shrine; Hector Boëtius thinks it is Sirium Brugensium Coloniam; Hermolaus Barbarus, on Pliny, thinks it is Brugae itself; Bilibald thinks it is Gandavum. Robert Cenalis, in book ii of his work on Gallic affairs, period iii, sets down as different places Gesforiacum Portum and Gesforiacum Navale: the former a hundred Ecomana, the latter the Castellum which is commonly called Calsel. Godfrey of Boulogne, son of Eustace, Count of Boulogne, was further Duke of Lorraine, who was the first Christian King of Jerusalem. Near Bononia was the Itius Portus. Those who think that the town of Calesium is this, among whom is Lhuyd, are refuted without difficulty by Ptolemy, who, after the mouths of the river Seine, first places the Ἰτίου Λ κρὸν, then Γεσοριάκων, and the Ἐπίσεσσ of the Morini; from which the town of Calesium is more than twenty thousand paces distant, that is, seven Belgic leagues. That Gesforiacum is the same as Itius seems to be the view of M. Velser, on the fragment of the Itinerary Table. Some judge that Itius Portus is the Fanum S. Audomari, supported by the old name of the town, by which it was called Sitien, as if, they say, from Sinus I. y; and by the position of the place, which, though very low, is nevertheless surrounded by very high shores, indicating that the bay of the sea was once very capacious. Camden, in his Britannia, teaches that Itius Portus was for a long time in the place which we now call Withsan [near Blanesium]. I am accustomed to argue thus: since in Ptolemy both the Itium Promontorium and the Gesforiacum Navale (which I have already said is Bononia) are assigned the same degree of latitude, namely 63, and exactly the same minutes, namely 30; but they differ somewhat in longitude, since both places lie under the same degree of longitude, 22, but the Itium Promontorium lies under 15 minutes of that degree, and Gesforiacum under 45 minutes. It must be that the Itium Portus was not far from Gesforiacum Navale, plainly on the same parallel between north and south, but not on the same meridian between east and west: that is, the Itium Portus was or is more western than the Navale, and somewhat nearer to the shores of Britain. Therefore, since we see that Gesforiacum or Bononia already beats upon the sea, the Itius Portus was perhaps swallowed by the Ocean, as were many other places on the British and Aquitanian seas; and its bare memory and name perhaps survive in the village which, though more eastern and more inland than the port, lies near Bononia by the sea, and is called in the vernacular Portet, as if Portus Itius, by a Greek-style usage. Moreover, writers note a crossing from the Portus Itius to the nearest part of Britain: Caesar indeed gives forty thousand Roman paces, Strabo three hundred and twenty stadia. Caesar's words in book v are these: "And he orders all to assemble at the Portus Itius, from which port he had learned that the crossing to Britain was most convenient, about forty thousand paces." So it is read in the better and more trustworthy books, not thirty. But in Strabo's book iv, where he speaks of the Morini, the text reads: "Ναυ-ς εἰς ἴσι καὶ τὸ Ἴτιον, ᾧ ἐκρέησαν Ναυσαφμῳ Καισαρ ὁ Θεὸς, Διαιρῶν εἰς τὴν Νῆσον..." I am surprised that Strabo, otherwise a most diligent and widely learned author, sets the same number of stadia between the Celtic rivers (he means the Loire and the Seine, for he had treated of them) and Britain: "The crossing to Britain is three hundred and twenty stadia from the mouths of the Celtic rivers..." This cannot be. For the crossing from the mouth of the Seine to Britain is greater than three hundred and twenty stadia, and much greater from the Loire.

units.la: Itium Portus, vbi locorum geris ostio. Quidquid fit, Strabonis Stadia cccxx, Cæsaris autem xl. Millia passuum si cum hodierna mensurandi ratione committantur, dabunt xiii Leucas vel Milliaria. Tantum hodie circiter est intervallum inter finitima Bononiæ Littora & proximas Angliæ oras. Iam quod Antoninus à Portu Gessoriaco ad Rutupium numeret Stadia cccci; quod Plinius lib. iv. cap. xvi Britanniam notet abesse ab Gessoriaco Morinorum Gentis Littore, proximo Trajectu i millium, minimum: quod denique Dio Trajectum brevissimum ab Gallijs in Britanniam Stadiorum esse scribat cccci: dicendum, aliud esse, metiri maritimum hoc iter ab Gessoriaco, aliud ab Itio; Gessoriacum enim Itio erat Orientalius, Itiumq; propius à Britannia, quam Gessoriacum aberat: aliud item fortean fuisse, Rutupium Britanniarum petere, aliud occurrentia primum littora: aliud denique, ex Celtica in Britanniam, aliud ex Belgica solvere. Portum Itium Florus lib. iii. Morinum appellat: In Britanniam transit mira celeritate: quippe quum tertia vigilia Morino solvisset à Portu, minus quam medio die Iusuam ingressus est. Quo loco nescio quid nonnullos impulerit, ut Morino referiberent; quum Veteres Geographi Portum Itium omnes fateantur esse Morinorum.
units.tr: Itius Portus, where the mouth of the river lies among the places. Whatever the case, Strabo's three hundred and twenty stadia and Caesar's forty miles (millia passuum), if they are compared with the present method of measuring, will give thirteen leagues or miles. Today the distance between the nearby shores of Boulogne and the nearest coasts of England is about that much. As to Antoninus, who counts four hundred stadia from the Portus Gessoriacus to Richborough; Pliny, book iv, chapter 16, who notes that Britain is distant from Gessoriacum, the shore of the Morini people, by the shortest crossing of one thousand paces at the least; and finally Dio, who writes that the shortest crossing from the Gauls to Britain is four hundred stadia: it must be said that it is one thing to measure this sea journey from Gessoriacum, and another from Itius. For Gessoriacum was further east than Itius, and Itius was closer to Britain than Gessoriacum was. It is also perhaps one thing to make for Richborough in Britain, another to make for the first shores that come into view; and one thing to sail from the Celtic coast to Britain, another from the Belgic. Florus, book iii, calls the Portus Itius Morinum: "He crossed to Britain with remarkable speed; for having set out from the port at Morinum in the third watch, he entered Ituna before midday." I do not know what has moved some to refer this to Morinum, since all the ancient geographers agree that the Portus Itius belonged to the Morini.

units.la: Bononiensi Comitatui succedit Guinensis, Guisnes: qui disterminatur ab Comitatu Ojo per Canalem Majorem, qui Opidum ipsum præterlabitur, Territorium fere reddens inexpugnabile. Primarium Opidum Guinefium, Guisnes; in duas divisum Partes, quarum una in Paludibus sita, altera in Continenti; Loci natura munitum & validum. Cepit Rex Henricus ii, misso illuc Francisco Lotharingio, Guisæ Duce, anno cio io lviii. De Danorum quomdam in Guinensem terram Iure, multa Mejerus in Annalibus Flandriæ, deque eodem Comitatu alia apud alios Historiographos, quæ hujus non sunt loci. Visuntur & alia Opida, Hautincourt, Peuplinge, Conquelle, Portus Nieuwlietum. Continet Comitatus hic sub se Baronatus Ardresium & Courtembronensem, singulos ab suis dictos opidis, quorum unum Ardres vulgo, alterum Courtembrone.
units.tr: The County of Boulogne is followed by Guînes (Guisnes), which is separated from the County of Oye by the Great Canal. The canal flows past the town itself, so that the territory is almost impregnable. The chief town is Guînes (Guisnes), divided into two parts, one lying in the marshes and the other on the mainland; its position makes it strong and well defended. King Henry II took it in 1558, after sending Francis of Lorraine, Duke of Guise, there. Meyer, in his Annals of Flanders, writes much about the right of the Danes to the land of Guînes, and other historians say other things about the same county, but these are not the place for them. Other towns are also to be seen: Hautincourt, Peuplinge, Conquelle, and the port of Nieuwlietum. This county contains under it the baronies of Ardres and Courtembronne, each named after its own town, one commonly called Ardres and the other Courtembrone.

units.la: Duobus Ardresio Milliaribus versus Oceanum occurrit, Calesium, opidum natura arteque munitissimum, Galliæ Clavis & ianua semper habitum; Muris primo, ut fertur, cinctum ab Philippo Bononiensi, S. Ludovici Patruo. Arcem habet cum Turri valida, quæ ingressum ex mari in portum prohibet. Captum fuit ab Eduardo v Anglorum Rege, pridie Nonas Augusti, undecimo mense post horrendam pugnam, quam contra Philippum vi, Francorum Regem, ad Cressiacum anno cio cccxlvii pugnatam, multis depingit Paulus Æmilius lib. ix. Possessum ab Anglis annos ccxi (nam frustra obsederat anno cio ccccxxxi Philippus Bonus Burgundus, Flandris ipsum deferentibus) & tamquam Galliæ Clavem in Loculis, ut loqui consueverant Angli, servatum, expugnatum, Guilio Duce, Galli recuperarunt anno cio io lviii, mense Februario: à quo tempore quas conditiones subierit, qualesque calamitates suerit passum; plenius explicat Historia Belgica, quam jussu & auspiciis Illustrissimorum Ordinum Fœderatarum Provinciarum paro. Caletibus Populis in Normannia potius, quam hic sua sunt Domicilia, ut ibi dicam.
units.tr: Two miles from Ardres towards the ocean lies Calais, a town most strongly fortified by nature and by art, always regarded as the key and gate of France. It was first walled, as is said, by Philip of Boulogne, uncle of St Louis. It has a citadel with a strong tower, which blocks entry from the sea into the harbour. Edward III, King of the English, took it on the day before the Nones of August, eleven months after the dreadful battle fought against Philip VI, King of the French, at Crécy in 1347, which Paulus Aemilius describes at length in book 9. The English held it for 211 years (Philip the Good of Burgundy besieged it in vain in 1431, though the Flemings had offered it to him). The English kept it as the key of France in their "little chests", as they used to say, until Duke Guise and the French recovered it in February 1558. What conditions it passed through from that time, and what calamities it suffered, is explained more fully in the Belgian History which I am preparing by order and under the auspices of the Most Illustrious Orders of the United Provinces. The Caletes live in Normandy rather than here, as I shall say there.

units.la: Æquali fere Itinere versus Mediterranea Calesio Bononiaque distat Teroano Morinorum, vulgo Teroane; nomen retinens, quamquam ab Karolo V delcta, Episcopali Sede Bononiam translata: Flandris, Terrenneberh: Tervanna vel Tarvenna Antonino; Tervanna Itinerariæ Tabulæ; Tapuaiva Prolemæo. Quosdam Tarubarum appellare Bovillus adserit. Tarubanorum meminit Trithemius in Francorum Historia. Tervana quibusdam .quasi Terra-Vana, ob vilitatem Territorij. In Notitia Provinciarum, ubi Belgicæ Secundæ Civitates recensentur, nominatur etiam Civitas Morinorum, id est Pontificum, L'Evefché de Teroane. Coloma forte Morinorum in antiquo Lapide, qui superioribus annis repertus fuit in Gelria, Sugambrorum olim Principatu, dimidiato ab Vrbe Neomagiensi milliario: Exemplar ejus paulo ante à me politum, ubi de Morinis Populis.
units.tr: Almost the same distance inland from Calais and Boulogne lies Thérouanne of the Morini, commonly called Teroane. It keeps its name, although Charles V destroyed it and its episcopal see was transferred to Boulogne. In Flemish it is Terrenneberh; Antoninus calls it Tervanna or Tarvenna; the Itinerary Tables give Tervanna; Ptolemy gives Tapuaiva. Bovillus asserts that some call it Tarubarum, and Trithemius mentions Tarubanorum in his History of the Franks. Some explain Tervana as, as it were, "Terra-Vana" (empty land), on account of the poverty of the territory. In the Notitia of the Provinces, where the cities of Belgica Secunda are listed, the "Civitas Morinorum", that is "of the Bishops", is also named: L'Evêché de Teroane. Perhaps Coloma of the Morini is named on an ancient stone which was found in recent years in Gelderland, formerly under the Sugambri, half a mile from the city of Nijmegen. I lately had a copy of it polished, where it speaks of the Morini peoples.

units.la: Ditio porro Oyana, Terra de Oye, porrigere se scribitur Duynkerkam usque, Flandriæ Opidum. Sunt ibi præter Oyam, alia quædam Opida, sed ignobiliora.
units.tr: The district of Oye (Terra de Oye) is said to extend as far as Dunkirk, a town of Flanders. There are some other towns there besides Oye, but they are less well known.

units.la: Vt Picardiæ finem imponam, pertinet eo Iter, quod Antoninus ab Teroana describit Durocortorum: Illud cum Itineraria Peutingeri Tabula, vulgatisque nunc temporis Locorum appellationibus conlatum hoc se habet modo:
units.tr: To finish Picardy, the route which Antoninus describes from Teroana to Durocortorum belongs here. Collated with the Peutinger Table and with the place names now in use, it stands as follows:

units.la: BELGICAM, cui varias Picardiæ Partes tribui, quà potui fide, diligentia, brevitateque percurri: succedit in mea distributione Vetus Celtica, cui versus Occidentem dedi Franciam & Belsiam; versus Ortum vero, Campaniam & Lugdunensem Tractum.
units.tr: I have run through the Belgic region, to which I have assigned various parts of Picardy, as faithfully, carefully and briefly as I could. In my arrangement, Old Celtica follows. To its west I have assigned France and Belsia, and to its east Champagne and the Lyonnais tract.

units.la: FRANCIÆ nomen hoc capite locoque Limitibus, quàm alibi, angustioribus circumscribitur; & toti alioquin Regno proprium, pro Parte tantum ejus (quam sequentia docebunt) hic accipitur.
units.tr: In this chapter and place the name France is confined within narrower limits than elsewhere. Although it is in general proper to the whole kingdom, here it is taken only for a part of it, as the following pages will show.

units.la: Coluerunt hanc Galliæ Partem olim cum aliis Bellovaci & Parisij. Bellovaci sæpe nominantur apud Cæsarem & Plinium. Straboni, Βελλόακοι; Ptolemæo, Βελλάκοι: Mediæ ætatis Chronographis Gregorio Turonensi, Adoni Viennensi, Reginoni, Aimoino, & aliis, Belgivaci; Notitiæ Provinciarum Civitas Bellovacorum: Hodie Beauvoisin, L'Evesché de Beauvais. Testatur Cæsar, Bellovacos inter Belgas plurimum & virtute, & auctoritate, & hominum numero valuisse. Scribit etiam Auctor Libri VIII de Bello Gallico, Bellovacos belli gloria Gallos omnes Belgasque superasse. De ijsdem Strabo lib. IV: Αὐτῶν δὲ τῶν Βελγῶν Βελλοάκοι ἀρίστοι φασί. μεγάλοι δὲ τῆτες Συσσίονας. Bellovacorum Remp. aliquo modo depingit Cæsar; quum docet, eos Principes suos ex se diligere solitos; ut, inter cæteros, Corbeum illum; qui, licet Civium suorum exercitu deleto, nulla tamen calamitate victus adduci potuit, ut excederet prælio, aut silvas peteret, aut, licet Romanis invitantibus, sese dederet; quin fortissime præliando compluresque vulnerando cogeret elatos iracundia Victores in se tela conjicere. Senatus item Bellovacorum memoratur ab Cæsare, & Plebis auctoritas: unde illa fuit ad Cæsarem Bellovaci Senatus excusatio, Numquam Senatum in Civitate tantum vivo Corbeo, quantum imperitam Plebem potuisse. Parisiorum, qui Populi ad Sequanam (ubi hodie Lutetia, vulgo Paris) frequens passim apud Latinos mentio, præcipue Cæsarem, qui initio libri VI confines eos facit Senonibus, Civatemque Patrum memoria conjunxisse. Παρίσιοι Straboni & Ptolemæo: Civitas Parisiorum in Notitia Provinciarum. Parisiorum Prælium pro Libertate Patriæ, communi variarum Civitatum Concilio, susceptum, Ducemque belli Camulogenum, propter sciemtiam rei militaris electum, legimus lib. Ephemerid. belli Gallici v 11. Parisios quidam dictos autumant vel in Paridis Trojani memoriam, vel à Parrhasijs Asiaticis, Herculis Comitibus, vel ab Iside πρὸς Ἰσιδος, hoc est, prope Templum Isidu: cujus Statuam scribunt nonnulli ad D.Germani Pratensis paucis ante annis adhuc fuisse (Idolum S. Germani vocatum) sed anno cıɔ ıɔ xıv sublatæ Crucem rubram ab Episcopo Melodunensi substitutam. Fuerunt & in his Galliæ locis Silvanectes, quorum Civitas nominatur in Notitia Provinciarum sub Belgica 111 L'Evesché de Senlis. Silvanectes fortean in vitio cubant apud Plinium libro iv capite xviii. Nam ubi leguntur Vibanectes Liberi, reponendi sunt, ni fallor, Silvanectes Liberi. Nec minus arbitror recte apud Ptolemæum vocantur Οὐβάνεκτοι.
units.tr: In former times the Bellovaci and the Parisii, among others, inhabited this part of Gaul. The Bellovaci are often named by Caesar and Pliny. Strabo calls them [Βελλόακοι]; Ptolemy [Βελλάκοι]. Medieval chroniclers such as Gregory of Tours, Ado of Vienne, Regino, Aimoin and others call them Belgivaci. The Notitia of the Provinces calls them the Civitas Bellovacorum. Today they are the Beauvoisin, the Evêché de Beauvais. Caesar testifies that the Bellovaci were the most powerful of the Belgae in courage, influence and number of men. The author of Book VIII of the Gallic War also writes that the Bellovaci surpassed all the Gauls and Belgae in the glory of war. Strabo, in Book IV, says of the same people: "Among the Belgae themselves, the Bellovaci are said to be the best; the Suessiones are also described as great" [Αὐτῶν δὲ τῶν Βελγῶν Βελλοάκοι ἀρίστοι φασί. μεγάλοι δὲ τῆτες Συσσίονας].
