Caesar in some measure describes the constitution of the Bellovaci state, when he teaches that they were accustomed to choose their chiefs from among themselves. Among the rest was that famous Corbeus, who, though his fellow citizens' army had been destroyed, could not be persuaded by any disaster to leave the battle, to seek the woods, or, although the Romans invited him, to surrender. On the contrary, fighting most bravely and wounding many, he so provoked the victors in their rage that they hurled their weapons at him. Caesar also mentions the senate of the Bellovaci and the authority of the common people. Hence came the excuse the Bellovaci senate offered to Caesar: "The senate in the state had never had as much power while Corbeus lived as the untrained common people had." The Parisii, a people on the Seine (where Lutetia, commonly called Paris, now stands), are frequently mentioned in Latin writers, especially Caesar, who at the beginning of Book VI makes them neighbours of the Senones and says they had joined that state in ancient memory. Strabo and Ptolemy call them [Παρίσιοι]. The Notitia of the Provinces has the Civitas Parisiorum. We read in the Ephemerides of the Gallic War, Book VII, that the Parisii undertook a battle for the liberty of their country, in a common council of several states, and chose Camulogenus as leader of the war because of his skill in military affairs. Some hold that the Parisii were named either in memory of Paris of Troy, or from the Asiatic Parrhasii, companions of Hercules, or from Isis [πρὸς Ἰσιδος], that is, near the temple of Isis. Some write that a statue of her was still standing a few years ago at Saint-Germain-des-Prés (called the Idol of St Germanus), but that in the year 1514 it was removed, and a red cross put in its place by the Bishop of Melun. There were also in these parts of Gaul the Silvanectes, whose civitas is named in the Notitia of the Provinces under Belgica III; today it is the Evêché de Senlis. The Silvanectes perhaps lie corrupted in Pliny, Book IV, chapter 18. For where the text reads Vibanectes Liberi, I think, unless I am mistaken, it should be restored to Silvanectes Liberi. And I think they are rightly called [Οὐβάνεκτοι] in Ptolemy as well.

units.la: Francia autem, de qua hic ago, comprehendere sub se scribitur hodie Præfecturam & Comitatum (vel ut alij, Vicecomitatum) Parisiensem, Ducatum Valesium, Ditionesque Hurepensium & Gastinensium.
units.tr: The France of which I am speaking is today said to comprise the Prefecture and County (or, as others say, the Viscounty) of Paris, the Duchy of Valois, and the districts of the Hurepois and the Gâtinais.

units.la: Præfectura Parisiensis. La Prevosté & Comté de Paris, in quatuor dividitur Ditiones, Parisium, Goellam, Insulam Franciæ, Vexinum Francicum
units.tr: The Prefecture of Paris, the Prévôté et Comté de Paris, is divided into four districts: the Parisis, the Goële, the Île de France, and the Vexin français.

units.la: Parisiam appello, quod vulgo Le Parisis. Complectebatur olim quidquid erat hinc à Porta Parisiensi, de qua paulo post, usque ad Pontem Æsiæ (Pontoise) inde vero Clayam usque, versus Brienses. Nomen fere periit, nisi quod ejus etiamnum memoria servetur cum in quibusdam Pagis, Louvres, Cormeilles, Efiona, & aliis, qui Parisij, (en Parisis) cognominantur: tum in Nummis, qui vulgo Solidi Denarique Parisij, Sols & Deniers Parisis, & quibusdam Parlamenti Parisiensis Taxationibus. Quin etiam sunt qui Portæ, quam nunc Lutetiam incolentes Parisiensem vocant, non aliunde nomen esse censent, quam quod ea in Parisium, de quo mihi sermo, duceret. Parisij hujus Urbs, totiusque nunc Galliæ Metropolis est Lutetia. Sic Cæsari nominatur: Λουτεκία, Ptolemæo; Λουτία, Iuliano: Lutetia, Castellum Parisiorum Marcellino, digitum proculdubio intendenti in Ædificium antiquissimum, quod hodieque ibi cum stupore visitur: Parisium Zosimo lib. iii, qui Germaniæ facit Urbem, quod Franci Sugambri Germaniæ Populi hunc præcipue Tractum quomdam obtinuerint. Nuperis istis Lutetia Parisius; non tam barbare, ut quidam hodie putant. Sic dicebatur Santonum Mediolanum, Augusta Vindelicum; item apud Frontinum libro de Coloniis, Colonia Tarquinius, Colonia Gravisci, Colonia Vejus. Hodie Paris, Vulgo, ab ipsis hujus Agri Populis: quod passim per Galliias accidit, ut Urbes, antiquis Nominibus rejectis & obliteratis, augustiores ipsarum Gentium appellationes adsumserint. Lutetia quibusdam à Luto, propter Paludes vicinas, quarum apud Cæsarem lib. vii est mentio: earum hodieque, ut ferunt, memoriam servante Foro Primario, quod Marche-Palus dictum, quasi Forum Paludosum: alijs ab Gypsi fodinis proximis, quasi Λουτεκία, quod fere tota crustario constet opere. Civitatem Iuly Boëtius lib. de Disciplin. Schol. nominat, quod is multa fortean illic ædificarit. Lutetia multo quondam fuit, quam hodie, minor: in Insula tantum, quam ambit Sequana. Describit eam genuine Iulianus Cæsar in Oratione, cui Titulus Ἀντεχωρίς ἢ Μισοπώγων. ubi inter alia: Ἐτύγχανον ἐγὼ χειμάζων &c. Faciunt etiam nonnihil quæ scribit Cæsar lib. vi: Dum haec apud Cæsarem geruntur, Labienus eo supplemento, quod nuper ex Italia venerat, relictio Agendici, ut esset impedimentis præsidio, cum iv Legionibus Lutetiam præficiebatur. Id est Oppidum Parisiorum, positum in Insula Sequana fluminis. Et paulo post: Exercitum transduxit, & secundo Flumine ad Lutetiam iter facere capit. Hostes, re cognita ab ys, qui à Meloduno profugerant, Lutetiam incendunt, Pontesque ejus Opidi reficiendi jubent: ipsi profecti Palude in ripa Sequana e regione Lutetiæ, contra Labieni castra considunt. Sic Strabo lib. i v: Περὶ δὲ τὴν Σηκουάνας πόλεμον ... Ammianus: Matrona & Sequana Amnes magnitudinis gemina, fluentes per Lugdunensem post circumclausum ambitu insulari Parisiorum Castellum, Lutetiam nomine, confociatim meant, meantesque protinus prope Castra consistentia funduntur in Marne. Ex quibus omnibus paret, quam tenue tantæ Urbi fuerit initium. Tantilla Insula adcrescencrescentem indies hominum multitudinem paullatim capere non fuit potis. Ductis in utramque Continentem quasi Colonijs, additisque Locis Suburbanis, ita sensim, productis varie Pomerijs, excrevit, ut jam totius Galliæ sit maxima. In tres nunc secatur Partes: quarum Major, eaque ad Ripam Fluminis dextram, humilior est, ad Ortum & Septemtrionem vergens, Villa vulgo dicitur, La Ville: Minor ad sinistram versus Austrum & Occidentem loco altiore, & qui per colliculos suos nonnihil adsurgit, Universitas vocatur, L'Université: Media est Insula, quam Civitatem, antiqua appellatione, La Cité, nuncupant; Fluvio undique cincta; Pontibus, duobus quidem Minori, tribus vero Majori juncta. Villa speciem præbet Lunæ διχοτμεως; hinc Sequana, illinc Mœnibus, Vallis, Fossilisque in Hemicycli figuram circumdata. Portas habet septem, D. Antonij, Templa, D. Martini, D. Dionysij, Montis Martyrum, S. Honorij, Nozam: Suburbia quinque; Templa, D. Martini, S. Dionysij, Montis Martyrum, S. Honorij. Hujus Vetera Mœnia pro incremento ratione contractiora fuere. Ad Arcis Luparia caput orta, D. Eustachij Templum, Hospitaliaque DD. Jacobi & Juliani complectebantur; juxta Sacellum Braccorum ad D. Catharinæ Vallis Scholarium adlurgebant; D. Antonij Portam continebant; hinc ad Monasterium, quod Ave Maria vulgo, Sequanæ vicinum, desinebant. Successerunt Nova, quibus Suburbia etiam inclusa fuere, Vallo atque Fossis, ex Sequana irriguis, munita; Vetustiis illis vel dejectis soloque æquatis, vel in Privatarum ædium usum conversis. Civitas quatuor parvulis Insulis superioribus ordine & in linea sitis, tamquam obicibus contra vim Fluminis defenditur; primum, ut dixi, propter situs commoditatem habitata; Ligneisque Pontibus adiri solita: totius Urbis veluti Cor, propter Episcopale Regiumque Palatium. Portas habuisse olim videtur quatuor ad totidem Pontium capita: Castelli Majoris seu Parisiensis, Superiorem quidem ad Pontem Virginis, Inferiorem autem sive Inferni Portam ad Pontem Trapezitarum, Castelli Minoris ad Pontem Parvum, Quartam denique ad D. Michaelis. Pontes habet tamquam Alas, dextras quidem D. Virginis, Trapezitarum, Monasterium, qui Villam respiciunt; Sinistras autem, Pontem Parvum & D. Michaelis, quibus in Universitatem tenditur. D. Virginis & Parvus lapidei sunt; ceteri lignis & sublicis impositi. Lapideorum sane Major, qui D. Virginis sacratus, olim longitudinem habebat LXX passuum, latitudinem XVIII; Ordines XVII (ordo quivis XXX Lignis constabat) Ædes utrimque lateritias, pari magnitudine & altitudine, LX impositas gerens. LXXX post anno sub Ludovico XII, quum mole sua corruisset, refectus est summo artificio sex Arcubus lapideis; Domibus LXVIII æqualibus superstructis, Pavimentoque Lapidibus strato, ut Pontem esse multi nesciant. Pons Parvus restauratus est sub Karolo VI, ex ludaorum multis. S. Michaelis ædificatus ab Hugone Aubrioto, Præfecto Parisiensi, sub Karolo VI, quum anno MCCCXLVII Navium impetu convulsus corruisset, non multo post refectus est, æqualibus Domibus lateritijs hinc inde ornatus. Est & hodie Pons inter Arcem Lupariam & Augustinensium Cœnobium Sextus; cujus fundamentum posuit Henricus III Franciæ Rex, Pridie Kalend. Junij MCCCLXXVIII. In eo absolvendo adhuc sedulo laboratur. Civitas autem hæc Muris olim fuit cincta, qui inferiore parte Palatium & Domum Regiam adhuc circumdant; reliquis dejectis. Universitas quamdam Galeri speciem exhibere videtur, quo Caput tantæ Urbis tegatur quasi, & ornetur. Porta illi septem, D. Victoris, D. Marcelli, D. Jacobi, S. Michaelis, S. Germani, Buffia & Nella. Suburbia quinque, S. Germani, S. Michaelis, D. Jacobi, D. Marcelli; D. Victoris. Hæc Lutetiæ pars Mœnibus etiam, ut Villa, est cincta, sed Fossis propter Loci situm siccis. Longum esset enumerare quæ in tribus hisce Partibus occurrunt, deque ijs adferri possunt, Singularia. Brevis ero, & in Brevitate, spero, non obscurus. Episcopus Parisiensis Spiritualibus præest. Episcopi numerantur CVII; quorum ultimum novi Petrum Gondium. Urbs Regi paret, habens peculiarem quamdam Iurisdictionem. Suburbiis idem Ius cum Urbe concessit Karolus V Francorum Monarcha anno MCCCLXXIV. Academia Rectoris unius arbitratu regitur, Magistratu trimestri. Philippus I Galliæ Rex anno MCXC Efthevinus (Viros Consulares) Urbi dedit; locoque Insignium Navem Lilijs aureis ornatam. Civibus Parisiensibus Iura Nobilitatis largitus est Karolus V, cujus memini, anno MCCCLXXI. Templa numeravi LXII universum: inter ea augustissimum, Cathedrale D. Virginis; quod, jactis
units.tr: I call the Parisis what is commonly called Le Parisis. Formerly it included everything from the Paris Gate (of which I will speak shortly) on this side as far as the bridge of Aisne (Pontoise), and from there as far as Clay, toward the people of Brie. The name has nearly disappeared, except that its memory is still kept in certain villages, Louvres, Cormeilles, Essonne and others, which are surnamed Parisis (en Parisis), and in the coins commonly called the sous and deniers parisis, and in certain fees fixed by the Parliament of Paris. Indeed, there are some who think that the gate which the present inhabitants of Lutetia call the Porte Parisienne gets its name from nothing else than that it led into the Parisis that concerns me here. The city of these Parisii, and now the metropolis of all France, is Lutetia. Caesar so names it; Ptolemy calls it [Λουτεκία]; Julian [Λουτία]; Marcellinus calls it Lutetia, the castle of the Parisii, no doubt pointing at the very ancient building that is still visited there today with wonder. Zosimus in Book III, who makes it a city of Germany, because the Franks, a German people, the Sugambri, held this particular tract. Lutetia Parisius is a recent name, and not so barbarous as some today think. Thus Saintes was called Mediolanum of the Santones, and Augsburg Augusta Vindelicorum. Likewise in Frontinus' book on colonies: Colonia Tarquinii, Colonia Graviscae, Colonia Veii. Today it is commonly called Paris, from the people of this land themselves. This happens everywhere in Gaul: cities, with their old names rejected and forgotten, have taken the more august names of their peoples. Some derive Lutetia from luto (mud), on account of the neighbouring marshes, which Caesar mentions in Book VII; the main market, which is still said to keep their memory, is called the Marché-Palu, as if it were Forum Paludosum. Others derive it from the nearby gypsum quarries, as if [Λουτεκία], because it is almost wholly built of plaster. Boethius in his book on the discipline of schools names the City of Julius, perhaps because Julius built many things there. Lutetia was once much smaller than it is today: only on the island that the Seine surrounds. Julian Caesar describes it exactly in his oration entitled Misopogon, where, among other things: "I happened to be spending the winter..." [Ἐτύγχανον ἐγὼ χειμάζων] etc. What Caesar writes in Book VI also contributes something: "While these things were going on with Caesar, Labienus, with the reinforcement that had recently come from Italy, was left at Agedincum to guard the baggage, and with four legions was sent ahead to Lutetia. This is the town of the Parisii, placed on an island of the river Seine." And a little later: "He led the army across and began to march toward Lutetia by the downstream current. The enemy, learning of it from those who had fled from Melodunum, set fire to Lutetia and ordered its bridges to be repaired. They themselves, having set out from the marsh, camped on the bank of the Seine opposite Lutetia, facing Labienus' camp." So too Strabo in Book IV: "Concerning the war with the Sequani..." [Περὶ δὲ τὴν Σηκουάνας πόλεμον ...]. Ammianus: "The Matrona and the Sequana, two rivers of equal size, flowing through the Lugdunensis, enclose the island castle of the Parisii, called Lutetia, and flow together, and, passing close by the standing camps, pour themselves into the Marne." From all these things it is clear how slender the beginning of so great a city was. That tiny island could not hold the human multitude increasing day by day, so it gradually spread out, as colonies were, as it were, sent into each bank, and suburbs were added; the walls were variously extended, and it grew until it is now the largest in all France. It is now divided into three parts. The larger, on the right bank of the river, is lower, and slopes to the east and north; it is commonly called the Ville, La Ville. The smaller, on the left, toward the south and west, rises on a higher site and somewhat climbs up on its little hills; it is called the Université, L'Université. In the middle is the island, which by its ancient name they call the Cité, La Cité, surrounded on all sides by the river, joined to the banks by two bridges on the smaller side and three on the larger. The Ville presents the shape of a half-moon, bounded on one side by the Seine, on the other by walls, a ditch, and a rampart in the form of a semicircle. It has seven gates: St Antony, the Temple, St Martin, St Dionysius, Montmartre, St Honoré, and Nesle; and five suburbs: the Temple, St Martin, St Dionysius, Montmartre, and St Honoré. Its old walls were narrower in proportion to its growth. Beginning at the head of the Luparia Citadel, they enclosed the church of St Eustace and the hospitals of Sts James and Julian; near the chapel of the Braques they rose up to St Catherine's valley of the Scholars; they contained the Gate of St Antony; and from there they ended near the monastery which is commonly called Ave Maria, close to the Seine. New walls followed, which also enclosed the suburbs, fortified with a rampart and ditches watered from the Seine; the old ones were either pulled down and levelled with the ground, or turned to the use of private houses. The Cité is protected against the force of the river by four small islands lying above it in order and in a line, as if they were barriers. It was inhabited first, as I said, because of its convenient position, and was usually approached by wooden bridges. It is like the heart of the whole city, because of the episcopal and royal palace. It seems formerly to have had four gates to as many bridge-heads: that of the Greater Castle, or Parisiensis, the upper one at the Bridge of the Virgin, and the lower, or Infernal Gate, at the Bridge of the Money-changers; that of the Lesser Castle at the Little Bridge; and finally the fourth at St Michael's. It has bridges like wings: on the right the Bridge of the Virgin, that of the Money-changers, and the Monastery bridge, which face the Ville; on the left the Little Bridge and St Michael's, by which one goes to the Université. The Virgin's bridge and the Little Bridge are of stone; the others are built on piles and timber. Of the stone bridges, the larger, dedicated to the Virgin, once had a length of 70 paces and a breadth of 18; it had 17 arches (each arch consisted of 30 beams), and it bore on each side houses of brick of equal size and height, sixty in all. Eighty years after that, under Louis XII, when it had fallen down under its own weight, it was rebuilt with the greatest skill with six stone arches, with sixty-eight equal houses built upon it and a pavement laid with stone, so that many do not know it is a bridge. The Little Bridge was restored under Charles VI from the fines of many Jews. St Michael's was built by Hugh Aubriot, provost of Paris, under Charles VI; when it collapsed in the year 1347 from the assault of ships, it was rebuilt not long after, adorned on either side with houses of brick of equal size. There is also today a bridge between the Luparia Citadel and the Augustinian monastery, the Sixth; Henry III, King of France, laid its foundation on 21 May 1578, and work on finishing it is still being diligently pursued. This Cité* was once surrounded by walls, which in their lower part still enclose the palace and the royal house; the rest have been pulled down. The Université seems to present a kind of helmet, as if to cover and adorn the head of so great a city. It has seven gates: St Victor, St Marcel, St James, St Michael, St Germanus, Buffia and Nella; and five suburbs: St Germanus, St Michael, St James, St Marcel, and St Victor. This part of Lutetia is enclosed by walls too, like the Ville, but its ditches are dry because of the site. It would be long to list what occurs in these three parts and what singular things can be said of them. I shall be brief, and I hope not obscure in my brevity. The Bishop of Paris presides over spiritual matters. Its bishops are counted as 107; the last of whom I knew was Peter Gondi. The city obeys the King, and has a special jurisdiction of its own. Charles V, monarch of the French, granted the same right to the suburbs as to the city in 1374. The Academy is governed by the arbitrary power of a single Rector, with a magistracy for three months. In 1190 Philip I, King of France, gave the city its échevins (consular men), and in place of the arms a ship adorned with golden lilies. Charles V, whom I recall, granted the rights of nobility to the citizens of Paris in the year 1371. I have counted 62 churches in all, among which the most august is the Cathedral of the Virgin, whose foundations were laid by Philip Augustus in the year 1191, under Maurice, Bishop of Paris, and which was seriously begun to be built in February 1307, under John, Master Mason, in the reign of Lord Louis. It is the chief of the miracles of France. It is supported by 120 columns. Its length is 184 paces, its breadth 60, its height 100. The choir…

units.la: ab Philippo Augusto anno cIↄ cxci, sub Mauricio Parisiorum Episcopo, fundamentis, serio ædificari cœptum anno cIↄ cccvii, mense Februario, Ioanne Kalenti Latomo, regnante D. Ludovico; ex Galliæ Miraculis præcipuum. Columnis cxx sustinetur. Longitudo Pasluum clxxxiv; Latitudo lx; Altitudo c. Chorus Lapide cinctus; Historijs ex Veteri Novoque Testamento insculptis, quas anno cIↄ ccccı absolutas, loquitur Inscriptio. In Ambitu habet Sacella xlv, ferreis Clathris munita. Universim Portæ xı. In Fronte tres biforæ, Statuis xxviii Regum insignes. Ad latera Turres visuntur, seu Moles verus Campanariæ, altitudine xxxiv Cubitorum. Campana Maxima, cui ab Maria Virgine cognomen, viginti Viros flagitat pulsanda; Sonitus sereno cœlo per septem Leucas auditur. Sacella Parisijs non pauca, xiii circiter: inter quæ primi censendum loci, quod in Palatio Regio Sanctum audit, ab D. Ludovico exstructum; omnium Cismontanorum audacissimum; nam Sacellum Sacello fornicato incumbit, nullis Columnis medijs, sed lateralibus tantum subfultum: Porta Inferior veram D. Virginis imaginem; Superior Iesu Christi fertur exhibere. Servantur ibi (sic perhibent Curiones) Corona Spinea, Toga Purpurea, Arundo, Spongia, Sudarium, Mappaque Cœnæ ultimæ: quæ omnia à Balduino Imperatore Constantinopolitano Venetis oppignerata, Gallus redemta ibi reposuit. Cœnobia plurima (xxiv, si recte numerum memini) & ampla: Templariorum sane circuitum notavi spaciosissimum, Vrbis instar: Templarijs anno cIↄ cccix è medio sublatis, Bona Hospitalarijs S. Iohannis fuerunt adsignata. Est & Canobium Filiarum Dei prope Portam S. Dionysij, quæ Damnatis ad supplicium ducendis tres Panis bolos cum Vino porrigere solitæ. D. Victoris Cœnobium Canonicorum Regularium S. Augustini ab Ludovico Crasso cIↄ cxiii, victoria de Perduellionibus parta, ædificatum: sub Francisco i magnifice reparatum. Templum DD. Petri & Pauli ab Hlodoveo ædificatum est, anno ccccxcix, hortatu Genovefæ, quæ ibi sepulta, anno Ioxxi. Canonicorum Secularium prius, post ab Ludovico Crasso Regularium est factum. Turris anno cIↄ ccccxxciii fulmine conflagravit. S. Germani Fratersis Carolinum Benedictinorum; ab Childeberto ii in honorem S. Vincentij exstructum; post, sepulto illic D. Germano Episcopo Parisiensi, nomen ejus induit. Opulentia nulli Cœnobio cedit; Privilegijs & Iurisdictione liberrimum: Muris claudltur. Forum habet annuum. Collegia adii innumera; Publica xx; Privata ex amplissimorum hominum beneficio xxx. Omnium pulcherrimum Navarræum, ab Ioanna Navarræa, Philippi Pulcri Conjuge, exstructum. Sorbonna Collegium instituit Robertus de Sorbona, Theologus, D. Ludovico Regi familiaris. Bernardinorum Collegium & Templum, à Benedicto xii P. M. excitatum, auxit Guilielmus Cardinalis Tolosanus & Bibliotheca, & xv i Studiosorum, qui Theologiæ darent operam, stipendijs. Officina Mechanica in suas quasi Regiones sunt distributæ, certisque locis adsignatæ: Membranariorum sunt ad Pontem D. Michaëlis; Fullonum, prope S. Ioannem Grevensem: Monetariorum, prope Lupariam Arcem; ubi Mola Monetaria Sequanæ sublicis impositæ: Aliorum, alibi. Apud Celestinos Officina est Regia Tormentorum ancorum. Plateæ sunt supra cccc, inter quas facile principes: Viliæ quidem, Pivorum Antonij, Martini, Dionysij, Honorij, Templi Veteris & Novi, Montis Martyrum, Lupariæ ad ripam Sequanæ: Vniversitatis, Sanctorum Victoris, Marcelli, Iacobi, Germani, & aliæ; Civitatis denique, præter Pontes ipsos, Via hinc ad Cathedralem, inde Palatium. Iam Domus Parisienses, cum Publicæ, tum Privatæ, universim anno cIↄ Iↄ xlix ad x millia sunt numeratæ; exceptis Collegijs, Templis, Cœnobijs, ijsque, quæ in Suburbijs. Eminent inter reliquas Domus Regia vicina Palatio, Nella, Flandra, Artesia, Aureliaenensis, Albretia, Lotharinga, Nivernensis, Alençonia, Seronum, Remensis, Lugdunensis, Fescampia, Bellovacensis, Rotomagensis, Biturensis, Heurefia, Sabauda, Claromontia, Cabillonensis, Bavaria, Burgunda, Regina, S. Pauli, & aliæ. Palatium Thermarum propè D. Mathurini quidam ab C. Iulio Cæsare conditum volunt. Cœnaculum illic est fornicatum, cui Hortus cum Arboribus imminet. Nomen habere creditur ab Thermis Iuliani Apostatæ. Aquis ex Pago vicino Gentillio eo deductis. Domus Publica Parisiensium, anno cIↄ Iↄ xxxiii cœpta ab fundamentis exstrui, sub Francisco i. Quid vero dicam de Arcibus? Majus Castellum ab Iulio Cæsare ædificatum ajunt: magis credo ab Iuliano Cæsare, qui aliquamdiu hic habitavit. Prima Parisiorum Porta fuisse fertur: Vulgo Le grand Chastelet. Castellum Parvum, Le petit Chastelet, refectum legitur sub Karolo vi, contra nocturnas Studiosorum grassationes. Arx Bastilia, La Bastille, excitari coepit sumtibus regijs, anno cıə ccc lxix, sub Karolo v Rege, per Hugonem Aubriotum Praefectum Parisiensem, qui post haereses nomine in perpetuos Carceres fuit relegatus. Turnellensem, Lupiriam, Divisque Germani Layensis fieri fecit Karolus v, cujus paullo ante memini: Lupariam Franciscus i. ampliare coepit; absolvitque Henricus ii anno cıə ıə lviii. Quid de Turribus? Turrim Arcis Lupariae editissimam Franciscus i, ut Arca Regiae major fieret, demolitus est. Turris in Coemiterio Innocentium aedificata creditur initio contra Latrocinia, quum vicina omnia Loca silvestria essent & parum tuta. Turris Billia Pulvere Tormentario plena, fulmine tacta, adiita Templa Monasteriaque Celestinorum, S. Paulli, Gervasij, Victoris, Marcelli, maximis adfecit damnis anno cıə ıə xxxviii. Quid de Xenodochys, Nosocomijs, Ptochodochys, & Orphanotrophys? Domum in villa ccc Caeorum, ab Saracenis excaecatorum, D. Ludovicus condidit. Alia praetereo. Quot Urbis Areae (inter quas primas obtinent Grevensis, Templaria, Lupara) Foraque, ut Mauberti & aliorum; tot & plura Supplicium sunt Loca, Malefactis plectendis destinata; quorum Cadavera post in Montem Falconium extra Portam D. Martini transferuntur. Restauravit Petrus Remigius, Thesaurarius & Regni Gubernator sub Karolo Pulcro; Reusque sub Philippo Valesio factus Repetundarum ibidem est suspensus. Inter Sepulcreta, prima censere solco, SS. Innocentium & S. Ioannis Grevensis: illud amplissimum est, muris ab Philippo Augusto circumdatum, Sepulcrorum numero & Sceleris admirandum; Cadavera novem dierum spatio absumi ajunt. Sepulcra vero, praesertim Regum, Principum, Ducum, Comitum, Nobiliumque utriusque sexus quot in hac Urbe vidi? Eorum plena est enumeratio apud Aegidium Corrozetium, cujus extat accuratum de Parisiensis Urbis antiquitate opus. Variorum etiam (liceat enim haec speciatim commemorare) quorum praeclara Ingenij monimenta cum admiratione leguntur, quorumque fama jam volitat docta per ora virum, Cineres variis hic locis reverenter adservantur: Petri Lombardi, in S. Marcelli Suburbio: Roberti Cenalis Episcopi Abrincantensis, Viri doctissimi, ad D. Paullum; ubi & Nicolai Gillij Secretarij Regij & Historici Gallorum; Petri Berchovi Prioris, qui fecit quinque Opera solennia, Dictionarium, Reductorium, Breviatorium, Descriptionem Mundi, & Translationem cujusdam Libri Latini in Gallicum, ad D. Eligij; Petri Comestoris, Hugonis Richardi & Adae de S. Victore, ad D. Victoris; Aegidij de Roma, Archiepiscopi Bituricensis, Philosophi summi, & Philippi Commines Historiographi, apud Augustinianos; Roberti Gagunni, Ioannis de Sacrobosco, Francisci Baldaini I. C. ad D. Maturinum; Paulli Aemilij Veronensis, Historiographi, ad Cathedralem Cosmae Guymier, qui Glossas scripsit ad Pragmaticam Sanctionem, in Coemiterio Innocentum, Gulielmi Budaei apud Maturinos; Ioannis Ravisij Textoris in Sacello Collegij Navarrae; Claudij Espencaei Theologi, in Templo S. Cosmae; Christophori Thuanni & Petri Sigonii, Praesidum, ad D. Andreae Artium; Aliorum alibi. Fontes gustavi publicos supra xvi; inter quos admiratus sum, qui Innocentum dictus, quique in S. Martini Coenobio, Statuas etiam stupui variis locis Regum omnium in Palatio Regio; Karoli Magni in Templo S. Marcelli, Philippi Valesij in Primario; ubi & D. Christophori Gigantea, anno cıə ccce xiii ab Antonio d'Effars, Equite erecta. Est ibi & effigies Petri Cugneri, juxta Chorum in angulo ad altare Beatae Mariae. Fabulantur per ludibrium positam, quum Bona Ecclesiastica nomine regio in Fiscum trahere conaretur, sub Philippo Valesio; sed frustra. Bibliothecas inspexi varias, publicas quidem, cum primis Regiae Majestatis, & S. Victoris: privatorum autem infinitas, praecipue, cl. Puteani, Pithoeorum, Nicolai Fabri, Barnabae Brissonij, & aliorum; omnes optimis rarissimisque cum editis, tum Manu-scriptis refertas libris. Quot porro Parisiensis Urbs Seditionibus agitata, quot Incendiis deformata, quot Inundationibus vastata, quotque Hostium Incursionibus fuerit concussa & laniata, copiose notant Francorum Annales. Haec de Una Urbe sufficiant. Qui plura desiderat, adeat Aegidium Corrozetium, cujus antea memini, & Iacobum Capellum, qui de Luteria singulares scripserunt Libellos. Extat & Carmen Eustachij à Cnobbeldorf Prutteni. Franciscus Belleforestius omnium accuratissime Luteciam delineavit.
units.tr: Begun in earnest on the foundations laid by Philip Augustus in 1191, under Maurice, Bishop of Paris, and built in earnest from February 1307, with John Kalenti as master mason in the reign of Lord Louis, it is the most distinguished of the marvels of France. It is supported by 120 columns. Its length is 184 paces, its breadth 60, its height 100. The choir is enclosed in stone; the inscription states that the scenes from the Old and New Testaments carved on it were finished in 1401. In the precinct it has 45 chapels, protected by iron grilles. In all there are 11 doors. On the front are three double-arched windows, notable for 28 statues of kings. At the sides are towers, or rather the true bell-tower mass, 34 cubits high. The largest bell, which takes its name from the Virgin Mary, needs twenty men to ring it; on a clear day its sound carries seven leagues. In Paris there are not a few chapels, about 13. Among them the first place is to be given to the one in the royal palace called Holy (Sainte-Chapelle), built by Lord Louis, the boldest of all the chapels on this side of the Alps; for one vaulted chapel rests upon another, supported not by central columns but only by side supports. The lower door is said to display a true image of the Virgin, the upper one an image of Jesus Christ. There are kept there (so the guides assert) the Crown of Thorns, the purple robe, the reed, the sponge, the napkin and the tablecloth of the Last Supper; all of which were pledged to the Venetians by Baldwin, Emperor of Constantinople, and were redeemed by a Frenchman and placed there. Monasteries are very many (24, if I remember the number correctly) and large. I noted that the enclosure of the Templars was very spacious, like a city; after the Templars were suppressed in 1309, their goods were assigned to the Knights Hospitallers of St John. There is also the convent of the Daughters of God near the Gate of St Denis, which used to offer three loaves of bread and wine to those condemned to be led to execution. The convent of Regular Canons of St Augustine of St Victor, built by Louis the Fat in 1113 after a victory over rebels, was magnificently restored under Francis I. The church of Saints Peter and Paul was built by Clovis in 499, at the urging of Genevieve, who was buried there in 1021. It was first a house of secular canons, and afterwards was made into one of regular canons by Louis the Fat. The tower was destroyed by lightning in 1493. The Benedictine monastery of St Germain, built by Childebert II in honour of St Vincent, and afterwards, when Bishop Germain of Paris was buried there, took his name. In wealth it yields to no monastery; it is very free in its privileges and jurisdiction, and is enclosed by walls. It has an annual fair. I visited countless colleges: 20 public and 30 private, founded by the generosity of very distinguished men. The most beautiful of all is the Navarre college, built by Joan of Navarre, wife of Philip the Fair. The Sorbonne college was founded by Robert de Sorbon, a theologian and familiar of King Louis. The college and church of the Bernardines, raised by Pope Benedict XII, was enlarged by Cardinal William of Toulouse, and also its library and the stipends for 16 students who were to devote themselves to theology. The mechanical workshops are distributed, as it were, into their own districts and assigned to fixed places: those of the parchment makers are at the bridge of St Michael; the fullers' near St John en Grève; the moneyers' near the Louvre fortress, where the money mill is set on piles in the Seine; the others elsewhere. At the Celestines is the royal workshop of artillery and anchors. There are more than 400 squares, of which the chief are easily these: the streets of the Pivots, of Antony, Martin, Denis, Honoré, of the Old and New Temple, of Mount of Martyrs, of the Louvre on the bank of the Seine; the streets of the University, of St Victor, Marcel, James, Germain, and others; and finally the city streets, apart from the bridges themselves, the road from here to the cathedral and from there to the palace. In 1549 the houses of Paris, both public and private, were counted at about 10,000 in all, not including the colleges, churches, monasteries, and those in the suburbs. Among the other houses the following stand out: the royal house next to the palace, and those of Nevers, Flanders, Artois, Orléans, Albret, Lorraine, Nivernais, Alençon, Sérant, Reims, Lyon, Fécamp, Beauvais, Rouen, Bourges, Heurefia, Savoy, Clermont, Chalon, Bavaria, Burgundy, the Queen's, St Paul's, and others. Some think the Palace of the Baths near St Mathurin was founded by Gaius Julius Caesar. There is a vaulted room there, overlooked by a garden with trees. It is believed to have its name from the baths of Julian the Apostate, with water brought from the nearby village of Gentilly. The public house of the Parisians, begun from the foundations in 1533, was built under Francis I. But what shall I say of the citadels? They say the Grand Châtelet was built by Julius Caesar; I rather believe it was by Julian Caesar, who lived here for some time. It is said to have been the first gate of Paris. Commonly called Le grand Chastelet; the Petit Châtelet, Castellum Parvum, is read to have been rebuilt under Charles VI against the nightly raids of students. The fortress of the Bastille, La Bastille, began to be erected at royal expense in 1369, under King Charles V, by Hugues Aubriot, provost of Paris, who after being convicted of heresy was banished to perpetual imprisonment. Charles V, whom I mentioned a little earlier, had the Tournelle, the Louvre and Divisque Germani Layensis made: Francis I began to enlarge the Louvre, and Henry II completed it in 1558. What of the towers? Francis I demolished the very high Tower of the Louvre fortress so that the royal chest might be made larger. The Tower in the cemetery of the Innocents is believed to have been built at first against robbers, since all the surrounding places were wooded and not very safe. The Tower of Billy, full of gunpowder, struck by lightning, damaged the nearby churches and monasteries of the Celestines, St Paul, Gervais, Victor and Marcel with great losses in 1538. What of the Xenodochia, Nosocomia, Ptochodochia, and Orphanotrophia? King Louis founded a house in the village of the 300 blind men, who had been blinded by the Saracens. I pass over other things. Of the city's squares (of which the Grève, the Templars', and the Louvre hold the first place), and markets, such as that of Aubert and others, there are as many and more places of punishment, destined for the punishment of wrongdoers; their corpses are afterwards carried to Montfaucon, outside the Gate of St Martin. Peter Remi, treasurer and governor of the kingdom under Charles the Fair, restored it; and Reus, made a collector of extortions under Philip of Valois, was hanged there. Among the cemeteries I am accustomed to rank first the Holy Innocents and St John en Grève: the former is the largest, surrounded by walls by Philip Augustus, admirable for the number of graves and for its wickedness; they say corpses are consumed there within nine days. But the tombs, especially of kings, princes, dukes, counts and nobles of both sexes, how many have I seen in this city? A full list of them is found in Gilles Corrozet, whose accurate work on the antiquity of the city of Paris exists. Also the ashes of various men, whose famous monuments of genius are read with admiration, and whose learned fame now flies on the lips of men, are reverently kept in various places here (for let me mention these individually): of Peter Lombard, in the suburb of St Marcel; of Robert Cenalis, bishop of Avranches, a most learned man, at St Paul; where also are Nicolas Gilles, royal secretary and historian of the French; Peter Berchorius, prior, who wrote five solemn works, a Dictionary, a Reductorium, a Breviary, a Description of the World, and a translation of a certain Latin book into French, at St Éloi; Peter Comestor, Hugh Richard and Adam of St Victor, at St Victor; Giles of Rome, archbishop of Bourges, a supreme philosopher, and Philippe de Commynes, historian, among the Augustinians; Robert Gaguin, John of Sacrobosco, François Baudouin, jurist, at St Martin; Paulus Aemilius of Verona, historian, at the cathedral; Cosmas Guymier, who wrote glosses on the Pragmatic Sanction, in the cemetery of the Innocents; Guillaume Budé among the Mathurins; John Ravisius Textor in the chapel of the Navarre college; Claude d'Espencé, theologian, in the church of St Cosmas; Christophe de Thou and Pierre Sigonius, presidents, at St Andrew des Arts; and others elsewhere. I have tasted more than sixteen public fountains; among them I admired the one called of the Innocents, and the one in the monastery of St Martin. I was also astonished by the statues of all the kings in various places in the royal palace; of Charlemagne in the church of St Marcel, of Philip of Valois in the principal church; where also is the giant St Christopher, erected in 1413 by Antoine d'Effiat, knight. There too is the effigy of Peter Cugnier, beside the choir in the corner at the altar of the Blessed Mary. They tell a joke that it was placed there as a mockery when, under Philip of Valois, the ecclesiastical goods were to be drawn into the treasury in the king's name; but in vain. I visited various libraries, public ones indeed, especially those of the King's Majesty and of St Victor; but of private ones countless, above all those of the most distinguished Pithou, Pithou, Nicolas Fabri, Barnabé Brisson, and others; all full of books, both printed and manuscript, of the very best and rarest kind. How often the city of Paris was troubled by seditions, how often disfigured by fires, how often laid waste by floods, and how often shaken and torn by incursions of enemies, the French annals note fully. These things may suffice about this one city. He who desires more, let him consult Gilles Corrozet, whom I mentioned before, and Jacques Cappel, who wrote separate little books about Lutetia. There is also a poem by Eustachius à Cnobbeldorf of Prussia. François de Belleforest drew the most accurate outline of Lutetia of all.

units.la: {a} Torres. vit. Anteaquam ad alia pergam, cum pace fiat Lectoris, ut pauculis, quæ cap. xviii. de Academia Parisiensi à me notata sunt, paucissima hic addam. Institutam dixi ab Karolo Magno, Romanorum Imperatore, incitantibus eo Magnanimum Principem quatuor Venerabilis Bedæ discipulis Alcuino, Rabano, Claudio, Ioanne Scoto. Quatuor firmissimis nititur Columnis, Facultatibus, inquam, Theologiæ, Iuris Canonici, Medicinæ, Artium. Tribus, quas nominavi primo loco, singulis præsidet Decanus, duoque inserviunt Cursores, quos Pedellos vulgo dicimus. Toti Corpori præest Rector, ab Artium Facultate, singulis Trimestribus legi solitus, Festis Solennibus, i mense Decembri, Nativitatis Christi; ii Martio, Divæ Virginis; iii Iunio, S. Ioannis Baptistæ; iv Octobri, Divi Dionysij. Quatuor sunt Cancellarij, duo quidem Baccalaureorum, ut vocant; Tertius, Ecclesiæ Divæ Virginis Parisiensis; Quartus, S. Genovefæ. Sunt & Sex Advocati: Quatuor quidem, cum duobus Procuratoribus in Parlamento; Duo vero, cum uno Procuratore in Castello. Nihil hic dicam de Librariis, aliisque id genus Academiæ Ministris; singularum item Nationum Nuncijs & Tabellarijs, qui omnes magnis fruuntur Privilegiis. Ex quatuor autem constat Academia Nationibus, ut sequens indicat Synopsis:
units.tr: {a} Torres. vit. Before I go on to other matters, with the reader's leave I will add here a very few things, the fewest possible, to what I noted about the Academy of Paris in chapter 18. I said it was founded by Charlemagne, Emperor of the Romans, who was prompted to it by that great prince's four pupils of the venerable Bede: Alcuin, Rabanus, Claudius, and John Scotus. It rests on four most firm pillars: the Faculties of Theology, Canon Law, Medicine, and Arts. Over each of the first three I have named, a Dean presides, and two beadles, whom we commonly call pedels, serve them. The whole body is headed by the Rector, chosen by the Faculty of Arts, who used to be elected every three months on the solemn feasts: (i) in December, on the feast of Christ's Nativity; (ii) in March, on the feast of the Virgin; (iii) in June, on the feast of St John the Baptist; (iv) in October, on the feast of St Dionysius. There are four Chancellors: two of the bachelors, as they are called; the third of the church of the Virgin at Paris; the fourth of St Genevieve. There are also six Advocates: four, with two Procurators, in the Parlement; two, with one Procurator, in the Châtelet. I will say nothing here about the booksellers and other such servants of the Academy, nor about the messengers and couriers of each nation, who all enjoy great privileges. The Academy consists of four Nations, as the following synopsis shows:

units.la: Synopsis: Quatuor Parisiensis Academiæ sunt Nationes: In ipsa quidem Gallia, PARISIENSIS, REMENSIS, BITURICENSIS, SENONENSIS, TVRONENSIS; PICARDICA; NORMANNICA; Extra Galliæ limites, ALEMANNICA; Tertia comprehendens Angliam, Scotiam, Hiberniam.
units.tr: Synopsis: The four nations of the Paris Academy are: in France itself, PARISIAN, REMIGIAN (Rheims), BITURIGAN (Bourges), SENONIAN (Sens), TURONIAN (Tours); PICARD; NORMAN; outside the bounds of France, GERMAN; and the third, comprising England, Scotland, and Ireland.

units.la: Haud procul Parisijs Pons Charentonus est, vulgo, Le Pont Charenton, non ignobilis vicus, ubi Matrona Sequanæ miscetur. Auditur hic ηχω τεσσαρακοντάκις Φωνᾶ, quæ terdecies humanam reddit Vocem; quæque, quod admirationE dignum maiore, quadrisillabum integre & perfecte, quater quinquiesve retonat.
units.tr: Not far from Paris is Pons Charentonus, commonly Le Pont Charenton, a village of no little note, where the Marne (Matrona) mingles with the Seine. Here one hears an echo, ηχω τεσσαρακοντάκις Φωνᾶ [echo forty times voice], which returns the human voice thirteen times; and what is more worthy of wonder, it repeats a four-syllable word completely and perfectly four or five times over.

units.la: Hæc de Parisio: sequitur Goella, ut quam minime potest, discedam ab Vulgato nomine, La Goelle. Huic etiam antiqui perierunt Limites. Manet ejus tantum memoria quibusdam in locis, ab Goella cognominatis. Est ibi Comitatus Dam-Martinensis, La Comté de Dam-Martin, ab insigni quondam Opido, Dam-Martino, quod nunc in Vici formam est redactum, in Colliculo collocatum.
units.tr: So much for Paris. Next comes the Goella, so that I may depart as little as possible from the common name, La Goelle. Its old boundaries have also perished. Only the memory of it remains in certain places named after the Goella. There is there the County of Dam-Martin, La Comté de Dam-Martin, named after the once famous town of Dam-Martin, which has now been reduced to the form of a village and lies on a little hill.

units.la: Insula Franciæ, L'Isle de France (quam tertio loco sub Præfectura Parisiensi posui) ex ipsorum Gallorum distinctione comprehendit quidquid Terrarum est ab Fano S. Dionysij Pessiacum usque & Montmorancium; atque universim quidquid inter Sinus Gyrosque jacet Sequanæ, hinc Picardiam, inde Normanniam versus. Alij alios ipsi Fines statuunt. Ego in his non statui pugnare. Mutationi enim hæc talia ex arbitrio Regum Principumque nutu perquam obnoxia. San Dionysianum, quod vulgo Saint Denys en France, non alia re nobilitari solet, quam Fano superbissimo, cui initium tenue satis ab Dagoberto Francorum rege. Auxit mirum in modum anno clocxli aut circiter, Suggerus Abbas, ut ipse in suartestatur Historia. Servari memorantur ibi Corpora SS. Dionysij, Francorum Apostoli, Eleutherij, & Rustici; item Dionysij, Corinthiorum Episcopi (cujus Historia Ecclesiastica subinde meminit) Hippolyti, & aliorum. Vidi hic aliquando, præter alia Singularia, grande Monceriotis Cornu, sex-semis pedum: Labrum vel Solium ex Jaspide, rotei coloris: quo usum ferunt in Balneis Regem Dagobertum: Crucem aueam: Lychnum pensilem ex argento, quem pro accepto S Eugenij corpore obtulit Philippus Hispaniarum Rex; anno cIↄ IↄLXV. Servantur in Thesauro S. Dionysij, quæ ad Regem pertinent Ornamenta, Diadema, Sceptrum, & alia; quæ quoties quis Rex consecrandus, Remos solenniter deportantur. Longitudo hujus Templi ccexc pedum; Latitudo c; Altitudo lxxx ad interiorem Fornicem. Nam Tectum altius multo exturgit. Turres habet duas excelsas, quadrata forma, inque iis Campanas ex puro ære. Sunt etiam Valuæ æreæ, auro obductæ. Locus hic a multis jam annis destinatus Regum aliorumque Principum Sepulcris. Sitos ibi notavi quamplurimos. Sunt illic, præter Dagobertum Cœnobij Conditorem, in Choro versus Meridiem, ut Nomina loquuntur: Ludovicus, Rex, Filius Dagoberti; Karolus Martellus, Rex; Pipinus Rex, Pater Karoli Magni; Berta Regina, Uxor Pipini Regis; Kallomanus Rex, Filius Ludovici Balbi; Ludovicus Rex, Filius Ludovici Balbi. Visuntur ibidem paullo inferiore loco tres Effigies ex Alabastrite Lapide, cippis nigri Marmoris impositæ, quæ perhibentur (nam carent Inscriptionibus) Philippi Regis, S. Ludovici Filij; Isabella Aragonia, ipsius Conjugis; Philippique Pulcri, ipsorum Filij. In Choro versus Septemtrionem leguntur Kallomanus Rex, Filius Pipini; Hirmintrudis Regina, Uxor Karoli Magni; Constantia Regina II (adscriptis his verbis, Venit de Hispania) Odo, Rex; Hugo Capet, Rex; Robertus, Rex; Constantia, Uxor Roberti; Henricus, Rex, Filius Roberti; Ludovicus Gressus, Rex; Philippus Rex, Filius Ludovici Grossi. Ad Latus Summi Altaris Septemtrionale tres testantur Effigies Titulique, Philippum Longum, cum corde Joanne, ipsius conjugis; & Karolum cum Joanna Uxore, Franciæ Navarræque Reges, Philippi Pulcri Filios; Philippum Valesium, Joannemque ejus filium. Ad Latus fere Matutini, ut vocant, Altaris Septemtrionale Sepulcrum est & Effigies Marmorea Ludovici Hutini, ejusque Filij Joannis, & Filiæ Joannæ, Navarrarorum Reginæ. Haud procul inde Statua est Karoli VIII in genua procumbentis, cum Epitaphio non indocto. In medio Choro, ubi Monachi cantare soliti, Sepulcrum spectatur Karoli Calui Regis & Imperatoris. Post Altare Matutinum Sepulcra sunt (quorum tamen exigua adparent vestigia) Philippi Augusti: qui Conquestor cognominatus, Ludovici VIII, Ludovici Sancti, cujus Corpus postea fuit elevatum. Ante Primum Altare positam legi, Margaretam, S. Ludovici Conjugem. Conditos item in Choro memorant Monachi, licet indicia desint, Hlotarium III, Theodoricum II, Hlotarium penultimum Stirpis Karolinæ, & Alphonsum Comitem Pictavienstem, S. Ludovici Fratrem. Isti igitur in Choro: extra eundem, versus Meridiem quidem in Sacello Karoli V, sitos didici ipsum Karolum V Joannis Filium, cum Conjuge Joanna Borbonia Petri Filia; Karolum VI, Karoli V Filium, cum Isabella Conjuge, Stephani Bavariæ Ducis, Comitis Palatini, Filia; Karolum VII, Karoli VI Filium, cum uxore Maria Regis Siciliæ Filia: præter hos. Bertrandum de Guesclin, Longæ-Villæ Comitem, Franciæ Constabulum; Ludovicum Sancerranum, Franciæ IV-Virum; moxque Connestablium, fratrem germanum Comitis Sancerrazi; Arnaldum Guillenium, Barbazanis Dynastam, Karoli v ii Regis consiliarium; Karolum denique Delphinum Viennensem, Karoli v i Francorum Regis Filium. Visitur haud procul inde magnificum Francisci i, Magni cognomine, ejusque Conjugis Claudia Britanna, Ludovici xii Filiæ, Mausoleum; ipsorumque Liberorum, Francisci Delphini, Britanniæ Ducis, Karoli Ducis Aurelianensis, & Karlotta Filiæ; adiculptis, præter omnium effigies, Bellorum, Victoriarum, Rerumque ab eodem gestarum monimentis. Ad Septemtrionem in variis Sacellis conspiciuntur Busta, in Blancæ quidem Sacrario, Maria Blancaeque, Karoli iv Franciæ Navarræque Regis Filiarum; Ludovici Abrincantensis, Stamparum Comitis, Paris Franciæ; Ioanna d'Eu, Stamparum item Comitis, Athenari mque Ducis, Rudolphi Comitis Filiæ: in S. Hippolyti, Blanca, Francorum Reginæ, Philippi Navarræorum Regis Filiæ, cum Joanna Filia: in S. denique Martini, Alphonsi comitis Euensis, Ioannis Bainensis, Hierosolymarum Regis & Imperatoris Constantinopolitani Filij. In ipso Templo, qua Septemtrio est, visitur Monumentum ex Alabastrite, Ludovici xii, ejusque Conjugis Anna Britanna. In Novo Sacello, quod rotunda forma se extendit ad Septemtrionem in Cœmiterium, magnifice positi leguntur Henricus ii; ejusque Filii, Franciscus ii, Karolusque ix: Franciæ Reges. Hæc de San-Diorysiaco: Poissiacum, Poissy, oppidum non ignobile. Arx ibi Regibus quondam in deliciis. Eo Reginas se conferre solitas, anteaquam D. Germani Arx esset, lego, Partum edituras. Ibidem Regum Liberi educabantur, ut postea Blaesis & Ambaxiæ. Rex Ludovicus ix Poissiacensem se cognominabat, quod Poissiaci esset baptizatus. Celebre ibi Nobilium Virginum est cœnobium; Inter Poissiacum & Lutetiam Fanum est D. Germano consecratum, quod vulgo S. Germain en Laye: Opidum nonnullius antiquitatis. Arcis fundamenta iecit, vel saltem, ut quidam volunt, Arcem restauravit Karolus v Francorum Rex. Restituit etiam Franciscus i, Venationibus addictior. Superat omnes Regias Domos; Aeris saluberrimi. Nullius censetur Diœcesios. Silva adjacet caedua, Quercubus consita; quæ vulgo Le Fois de Trabisson. In ejus angulo, qui opidum ipsum respicit, Mensa Lapidea mihi monstrata prægrandis, ad quam Proditio fertur concepta; quæ qualis fuerit & à quibus facta, malo ab alijs explicari, quam in re satis dubia & incerta errare. Quod quidam narrant Silvæ ramos, si in Sequanam projiciantur, statim, Lapidum instar, fundum petere, non ego sum expertus: ideoq; nihil temere volo adserere. Mommorancium vernacule dicitur Mommorenci. Mommorancorum Domus admirandæ censetur ab Francis antiquitatis. Ex ea namq; fuisse memorant, quem omnium Gallorum Primum ad Fidem Christianam convertit S. Dionysius: eamque ob causam Mommorancies inter Barones Equestrisq; Dignitatis Viros semper primos duxisse ordines ferunt. Summam in Everardo Mommorancio Fidelitatem expertus est Hugo Capetus. Ejus Filius fuit Ioannes, cui recta Linea successerunt Bouchardus, Gualtherus, Bouchardus ii. Matheus cognomine Magnus, Connestabilis Franciæ. Huic duo fuerunt Filij, Matheus ii & Guido. Matheus duas habuit Filias, Ioannam, quæ nupsit Thibaldo Barrensi Comiti, & Emmam Godefridi Guyerchæ & Provinciæ Domini Conjugem. Guidoni ex secunda Vxore (Prima enim fuerat Philippa Vitrensis, Andreæ Vitreæ filia, cum qua in Dorem acceperat Dynastiam Vitream) duo fuerant Filij, Matheus Mari Præfectus, postea vero Connestabilis, & Bouchardus: à quibus Familia hæc nobilissima est propagata, non per Franciam solum longe lateque, verum etiam in Inferiore Germania, in Comitibus Hornanis.
units.tr: The Island of France, L'Isle de France (which I placed third under the Prefecture of Paris), according to the Gauls' own division, comprises all the land from the fanum of St Denis to Poissy and Montmorency; and generally all that lies within the bends and windings of the Seine, toward Picardy on one side and Normandy on the other. Others fix its boundaries differently; I do not intend to quarrel over these, since such things are very liable to change at the will and nod of kings and princes. Saint-Denis, commonly Saint Denys en France, is famous for nothing so much as its very proud abbey, which had a quite humble beginning under Dagobert, king of the Franks. In about the year 775 Abbot Suger greatly enlarged it, as he himself attests in his history. The bodies of the saints Dionysius, apostle of the Franks, Eleutherius, and Rusticus are said to be preserved there; also Dionysius, bishop of Corinth (whose ecclesiastical history mentions him from time to time), Hippolytus, and others. Here once, among other curiosities, I saw a great horn of a Monceriot, six and a half feet long; a basin or throne of jasper of a reddish colour, which they say King Dagobert used in his baths; a golden cross; a hanging lamp of silver, which Philip, King of the Spains, offered in return for the body of St Eugenius that he received, in the year 1665. In the treasury of St Denis are kept the royal ornaments that belong to the king: the diadem, the sceptre, and others, which are solemnly carried to Rheims whenever a king is to be consecrated. The length of this church is 250 feet; its breadth 100; its height 80 to the inner vault, for the roof rises much higher. It has two tall towers, square in form, with bells of pure bronze. There are also bronze doors covered with gold. This place has for many years been set aside for the tombs of kings and other princes, and I noted very many buried there. Besides Dagobert, founder of the monastery, there lie in the choir toward the south, as their names tell: Louis, king, son of Dagobert; Charles Martel, king; Pepin, king, father of Charlemagne; Bertha, queen, wife of King Pepin; Carloman, king, son of Louis the Stammerer; Louis, king, son of Louis the Stammerer. Somewhat lower down are three effigies of alabaster set on pedestals of black marble, which are said (for they have no inscriptions) to be of Philip, king, son of St Louis; Isabella of Aragon, his wife; and Philip the Fair, their son. In the choir toward the north may be read: Carloman, king, son of Pepin; Hirmintrudis, queen, wife of Charlemagne; Constantia, second queen (with these words added, She came from Spain); Odo, king; Hugh Capet, king; Robert, king; Constance, wife of Robert; Henry, king, son of Robert; Louis the Fat, king; Philip, king, son of Louis the Fat. At the north side of the high altar are three effigies with inscriptions attesting Philip the Tall, with his heart; Joan, his wife; and Charles with Joan, his wife, kings of France and Navarre, sons of Philip the Fair; and Philip of Valois and his son John. Near the north side of the so-called Matins altar is the tomb and marble effigy of Louis Hutin, of his son John, and of his daughter Joan, queen of the Navarrese. Not far from there stands a statue of Charles VIII kneeling, with an epitaph not unlearned. In the middle of the choir, where the monks were accustomed to sing, is seen the tomb of Charles the Bald, king and emperor. Behind the Matins altar are tombs (though only faint traces of them appear) of Philip Augustus, who was surnamed the Conqueror, of Louis VIII, and of Louis the Saint, whose body was afterwards raised up. In front of the first altar I read the name of Margaret, wife of St Louis. The monks also report that the following are buried in the choir, though there are no traces of them: Lothar III, Theodoric II, Lothar, the second-last of the Carolingian line, and Alphonse, count of Poitiers, brother of St Louis. These are in the choir; outside it, toward the south, in the chapel of Charles V, I learned that the following lie buried: Charles V, son of John, with his wife Joan of Bourbon, daughter of Peter; Charles VI, son of Charles V, with his wife Isabella, daughter of Stephen, Duke of Bavaria, count palatine; Charles VII, son of Charles VI, with his wife Mary, daughter of the king of Sicily; besides these, Bertrand du Guesclin, count of Longueville, constable of France; Louis of Sancerre, fourth man of France, and soon afterwards constable, full brother of the count of Sancerre; Arnold Guillen, lord of Barbazan, councillor of King Charles VII; and finally Charles, Dauphin of Vienne, son of Charles VI, king of the Franks. Not far from there is seen the magnificent mausoleum of Francis I, surnamed the Great, and of his wife Claude of Brittany, daughter of Louis XII; and of their children, Francis the Dauphin, Duke of Brittany, Charles, Duke of Orléans, and Charlotte, daughter; with, besides the effigies of all of them, monuments of the wars, victories, and deeds done by him. On the north side, in various chapels, are seen tombs: in the sacristy of Blanche, those of Mary and Blanche, daughters of Charles IV, king of France and Navarre; of Louis of Abrincates, count of Stampes, peer of France; of Joan of Eu, likewise countess of Stampes, duchess of Athens, daughter of Count Rudolph; in the chapel of St Hippolytus, that of Blanche, queen of the Franks, daughter of Philip, king of Navarre, with her daughter Joan; and finally, in the chapel of St Martin, that of Alphonse, count of Eu, son of John of Bain, king of Jerusalem and emperor of Constantinople. In the church itself, on the north side, is seen a monument of alabaster to Louis XII and his wife Anne of Brittany. In the new chapel, which extends in a round form to the north toward the cemetery, lie magnificently placed Henry II, and his sons Francis II and Charles IX, kings of France. So much for Saint-Denis. Poissy, Poissy, a town of no little note; there was once a citadel there, a favourite of the kings. I read that queens used to go there to give birth before the citadel of St Germain existed. There the children of the kings were brought up, as later at Blois and Amboise. King Louis IX used to call himself "of Poissy", because he had been baptized at Poissy. There is a famous convent of noble virgins there. Between Poissy and Paris is the shrine dedicated to St Germanus, commonly St Germain en Laye, a town of some antiquity. Charles V, king of France, laid the foundations of the castle, or at least, as some think, restored the castle; Francis I also restored it, being more given to hunting. It surpasses all the royal houses, and its air is most wholesome. It is not counted in any diocese. Adjoining it is a coppice of oaks, which is commonly called Le Fois de Trabisson. In its corner facing the town I was shown a very large stone table, where the treachery is said to have been devised; how it was and by whom it was done, I prefer to leave to others to explain rather than go wrong in a matter so doubtful and uncertain. That some say that branches of this wood, if thrown into the Seine, at once sink to the bottom like stones, I have not tested myself; therefore I do not wish to assert it rashly. Montmorency is called in the vernacular Mommorenci. The house of the Montmorencys is thought by the French to be of remarkable antiquity. For they relate that from it came he whom St Dionysius converted to the Christian faith, the first of all the Gauls; and for this reason they say the Montmorencys have always held the first rank among the barons and men of knightly dignity. Hugh Capet experienced the greatest loyalty from Everard of Montmorency. His son was John, to whom in direct line succeeded Burchard, Walter, Burchard II; Matthew, surnamed the Great, constable of France. He had two sons, Matthew II and Guy. Matthew had two daughters, Joan, who married Theobald, count of Bar, and Emma, wife of Godfrey, lord of Guyerche and Provence. To Guy, by his second wife (for his first had been Philippa of Vitry, daughter of Andrew of Vitry, with whom he had received the lordship of Vitry as dowry), two sons were born: Matthew, prefect of Marly, afterwards constable, and Burchard. From them this most noble family has spread, not only far and wide through France, but also into Lower Germany, among the counts of Hornes.

units.la: Insula succedit Vexinum Francicum, Vexin, vel, ut alij, Valxin Le François. Continet quidquid est ab Aelia Fluuio Claromontem usque, versus Picardiam. Periit & hujus memoria, nisi quod quodammodo servetur, ut Actuarij quidam mihi narrarunt, in antiquis quibusdam Chartis & Monimentis.
units.tr: Insula follows Vexinum Francicum, Vexin, or, as others call it, Valxin Le François. It takes in everything from the river Aelia as far as Clermont, towards Picardy. Its memory has also perished, except that it is somehow preserved, as certain record-keepers have told me, in some old charters and documents.

units.la: Hactenus de Praefectura Parisiensi, quatuorque ejus Ditionibus, Parisio, Goella, Insula Franciæ, & Vexino Francico: Alteram Franciæ, strictius sumtæ, partem statui, cum ipsis Regni Geographis, Valesium, quod vulgo Le Pais de Valois. Nomen habere putatur ab amoenissimis, quibus hæc ditio superbit, Vallibus. Alij aliunde derivant. Comitatus olim, hodie Ducatus. Primus Valesiorum, ut & Alençonij, Comes dictus fuit Karolus Philippi iii, Franciæ Regis Filius, Philippi Pulcri Frater: à quo per Philippum v i Filium Regium Valesiorum Stemma in Gallijs fuit propagatum. gatum. Extendit se Ducatus Valesius in Picardiam usque. Primarium Opidum (praeter Cresspiacum, Cressy) Silvanectum est, Francis Senlis. Dictum Latinis quidam augurantur, quod Silvae nectatur. Meminit Notitia Provinciarum Galliae in Belgica 11, ubi Civitas Silvanectum, hodie L'Euesché de Senlis. Opidum est antiquum, praeter Episcopatum, Praefectura & Baillivatu nobile. Episcopos numerat Fr. Bellcforestius LXXIV, postremum nominans Renatum Roulierum. Ditavit Silvanectensis Praefectura Valesium Ducatum Dynastijs, quae vulgo audiunt Pierrefons, Bethisi; & Verberie, comprehensis opidis quae nunc Angy, Le Pont S. Maxence (Paludibus hoc cinctum est, Limitemque statuit Franciae & Picardiae) Pongoing, Brenonville, &c.
units.tr: So far on the Prefecture of Paris and its four districts, Parisio, Goella, Insula Franciæ, and Vexino Francico. I set down the other part of France, taken in a stricter sense, with the geographers of the kingdom themselves, as Valesium, which is commonly called Le Pais de Valois. It is thought to take its name from the most pleasant valleys in which this district takes pride. Others derive it from elsewhere. It was once a county and is now a duchy. The first Count of Valois, as also of Alençon, was Karolus, son of Philip III, King of France, and brother of Philip the Fair. From him, through Philippus VI, a royal son, the line of the Valois was propagated in France. The Duchy of Valois extends as far as Picardy. Its chief town, apart from Crépy (Cressy), is Senlis, Silvanectum in Latin, Senlis in French. Some conjecture that it was called in Latin Silvanectum because it is bound by woods. The Notitia of the Provinces of Gaul mentions in Belgica II the city of Silvanectum, today the Bishopric of Senlis. The town is ancient, and famous for its bishopric, its prefecture, and its bailiwick. Fr. Bellforest counts 74 bishops, naming Renatus Roulier as the last. The Prefecture of Senlis enriched the Duchy of Valois with lordships, commonly called Pierrefonds, Bethisy, and Verberie, together with the towns now called Angy, Le Pont-Sainte-Maxence (it is surrounded by marshes, and marks the boundary of France and Picardy), Pont-Saint-Ouen, Brenonville, and others.

units.la: Complectitur eadem Praefectura Compendium, Compiegne; Sedem olim Principum; Karolopolin alijs appellatum, ab Karolo Calvo, qui Pomeria ejus scribitur produxisse & munijsse. Eundem Karolum Comitia Statuum Regni Francici, Conciliumque Nationale Praesulum Ecclesiae Gallicanae in hoc opido celebratae, loquuntur Historiae. Transgressis Compendium occurrunt statim Picardiae Populi, Suessiones & Laudunenses. Sub Compendio sunt Magny, Thorette, Creil. Haud procul Creil Stagnum visitur unius semis Leucae; Munimentum item in Monte, quod ab Iulio Caesare fertur conditum. Continet quoque Silvanectum Pontis Aesie (Pontoise, vulgo: Pontesium nominat Ivo epistola cv) Baillivatum, Praefecturam & Vicecomitatum; cui parent Ville-neuve le Roy & L'Isle Adam. Si Pontesium non sit, quae Antonino Brivaisara, Itinerariae autem Tabulae corruptius Brivfura; fuit certe in agro Ponteslij suburbicario.
units.tr: The same Prefecture includes Compiègne (Compendium), once the seat of princes, called Karolopolis by others, after Charles the Bald, who is written to have extended and fortified its walls. Histories speak of the assemblies of the estates of the Frankish kingdom and of the national council of the prelates of the Gallican Church, held in this town under the same Charles. Crossing beyond Compiègne, one comes at once upon the peoples of Picardy, the Soissonnais and the Laonnais. Under Compiègne lie Magny, Thorette, and Creil. Not far from Creil can be seen a pool half a league across, and likewise a fortification on a hill, which is said to have been built by Julius Caesar. The Silvanectine district also includes the bailiwick, prefecture and viscounty of Pontoise (Pontesium, as Ivo names it in letter cv), to which Villeneuve-le-Roi and L'Isle-Adam owe obedience. If Pontoise is not the place which Antonine calls Brivaisara, and which the Itinerary Tables corruptly give as Brivfura, it was certainly in the country around Pontoise.

units.la: Scribit ad Antonini Itinerarium Hieronymus Surita, summo consensu in omnibus Exemplaribus esse Brivanisare; in Blandinianae autem Bibliothecae Codice ita distinctum esse, ut Briva videatur Opidum esse, cognomento Isara Fluminis. Isara tamen hic nullus, sed in Gallia Narbonensi; ut fere, nisi Veteres obclamarent Membranae, reponere auderem Briva-Aesiae; vel saltem in Brivaisare nullum agnoscerem fluvium. Briva simpliciter est apud Gregorium Turonensem Episcopum, qui lib. VII magno incendio Basilicam B. Martini apud Brivum Vicum ab imminente hoste conflagratam fuisse perhibet; & Avitum ad Brivatensem Vicum mortuum delatum. Meminit idem Brivatensis Diaecesis. Ad rem. Ponte-Aesia superato, se offert Normannia.
units.tr: Hieronymus Surita, writing on Antonine's Itinerary, says that in all copies the reading is, with complete agreement, Brivanisare; but in the codex of the Blandinian library it is so divided that Briva appears to be the town, with the surname of the river Isara. There is no Isara here, however, but in Narbonese Gaul; so I would dare to restore Briva-Aesiae, unless the old manuscripts cried out against it, or at least I would not recognise any river in Brivaisare. Briva occurs simply in Gregory of Tours, bishop, who in book VII reports that in a great fire the basilica of St Martin at Briva Vicus was burned by an enemy closing in; and that Avitus was carried dead to the village of Briva. The same author mentions the diocese of Briva. To the point: with Pontoise passed, Normandy presents itself.

units.la: Silvanectensis insuper Praefecturae Ius agnoscit Comitatus Belmontius ad Aesiam, La Comte de Beaumont sur Oyse. antiqua Praefectura, cui subsunt Persing & Metu. Comitatus Belmontius Dominos agnoscit proprios, Principes regiae stirpis Vendomensis. Ad hoc opidum ultra Aesiam initium capit Bellovacensis Ditio. Bellum hunc Montem fere est, ut opiner esse Angustomagum Antonini, quodque corrupte apud Ptolemaeum Ratomagus. Videtur & quibusdam esse opidum, quod ab Caesare describitur lib. II. Belli Gall. egregie natura munitum, ex omnibus in circuitu partibus altissimas habens rupes & despectus; Aditum autem una ex parte, leviter adclivem. Sub Silvanectensi denique Praefectura, simulque sub Valesio Ducatu est Comitatus Belovacensis, Comte de Beauvais, Beauvoisin. De Belovaci antea dixi.
units.tr: The county of Beaumont-sur-Oise (La Comte de Beaumont sur Oyse), an ancient prefecture to which Persing and Metz are subject, also acknowledges the right of the Silvanectine prefecture. The county of Beaumont acknowledges its own lords, princes of the royal stock of Vendôme. Beyond the Oise, at this town, the district of Beauvais begins. I think that this Bellum Mons is nearly the Angustomagus of Antonine, and what is corruptly given in Ptolemy as Ratomagus. It also seems to some to be the town described by Caesar in book II of the Gallic War, excellently fortified by nature, having on all sides very high rocks and precipices, with access on one side only, a gentle slope. Finally, under the Silvanectine prefecture, and at the same time under the Duchy of Valois, lies the county of Beauvais (Comte de Beauvais, Beauvoisin). I have spoken of Beauvais before.

units.la: Agricolae huius Territorij tempore Ioannis Regis Seditionem moverunt, quae vulgo dicebatur Iaquerie. Petebantur ea praecipue Nobiles, quorum non pauci leguntur trucidati. Compescuit tandem Karolus Delphinus Franciae. Metropolim habet Belovacum: sic nominem opidum, quod vulgo Beauvais. Apud Caesarem, ut Nob. Vir Iosephus Scaliger ad me scribit, Bratuspantium, addens sub Caesaribus transnominatum Caesaromagum. Bratuspantium tamen, ne quid dissimulem, Karolo Bovillo Pagus hodie putatur Granviller, vel Grattepance: alijs Clermont en Beauvoisin; Vigenereo Beaumont ad Aesiam. Bratuspantij memoria servatur in Vita S. Guiberti; item in Historia Ansfridi Episcopi Ultrajectensis apud Sigebertum.
units.tr: The farmers of this territory stirred up a sedition in the time of King John, which was commonly called the Jacquerie. It was aimed chiefly at the nobles, of whom not a few are read to have been butchered. Charles the Dauphin of France at last put it down. Its metropolis is Beauvais, which I name as the town commonly called Beauvais. In Caesar, as the noble Joseph Scaliger writes to me, it is Bratuspantium, adding that under the Caesars it was renamed Caesaromagus. Lest I conceal anything, however, Bratuspantium is today thought by Charles Bovillus to be the village of Granviller or Grattepanche; by others, Clermont-en-Beauvaisis; by Vigenère, Beaumont on the Oise. The memory of Bratuspantium is preserved in the Life of St Guibert, and likewise in the history of Ansfrid, Bishop of Utrecht, in Sigebert.

units.la: Est autem Belovacum Vrbs situ amoenissimo, adsitos habens hinc Montes fertiles non adeo excelsos; inde Agros excipiendae Sementi commodos. Nec desunt vina. Incolis, praesertim Foeminis, magna sunt Privilegia, ab Ludovico XI Francorum Rege ipsis concessa, anno CIↃ CCCCLXXII; quod Karolum Burgundiae Ducem obsidionem solvere, reque infecta abire coegerint. Episcopi Belovacenses Comites se scribunt & Pares Franciae. Numerat eos Bellcforestius LXXXIV; eorumque ultimum Karolum Borbonium. Haud procul Belovaco est Clariomontium, & Clermont; Comitatus, jure Apannagij ab Rege Ludovico IX (qui Sanctus cognominatus) datus Roberto Filio. Hujus Filius Ludouicus cognomine Magnus, Comes Claromontanus 11, ab Philippo VI Valesio Francorum Rege Primus Borbonij Dux fuit factus, anno cIↄ ccc xxix; à quo deinceps Borboniorum Stemma productum. Opidum est Arce munitum.
units.tr: Beauvais is a city of most pleasant situation, with fertile hills not very high close by on one side, and on the other fields suitable for sowing. Nor is wine lacking. The inhabitants, especially the women, have great privileges, granted to them by Louis XI, King of the Franks, in the year 1472, because they forced Charles, Duke of Burgundy, to abandon the siege and leave with nothing achieved. The Bishops of Beauvais style themselves counts and peers of France. Bellforest counts them as 84, the last of whom was Charles of Bourbon. Not far from Beauvais lies Clermont, and the county of Clermont (Clariomontium), given by King Louis IX, surnamed the Saint, to his son Robert by right of appanage. Robert's son, Louis, surnamed the Great, Count of Clermont, was made by Philip VI of Valois, King of the Franks, the first Duke of Bourbon, in the year 1327; from him the line of the Bourbons was afterwards descended. The town is protected by a citadel.

units.la: Hæc de Valesio: sequitur tertia Franciæ Pars Heurepense Territorium, Heure pois. Initium capit ad Sequanam, sub Ponte Parisienti, qui Parvus cognominatur; secusque eundem fluvium procurrit Corbolium, Melodunum, & Moretum, ubi Verina Amne, qui in Lonium se exonerat, sejungitur ab Gastinensium Agro. Adhæret Brientibus, ubi respicit Fanum, cui cognomen ab S. Columba Grandi apud Senones. Continet autem Vicecomitatum & Baillivatum Melodunensem. Metropolis est Melodunum. Nomen hoc perperam apud Cæsarem bis est infultum; pro quo Veteres omnes scripti Codices Commentariorum de Bello Gallico habent Metropedunum. Verum quidem est Melodunum & Metrofedum unum idemque oppidum esse: sed Melodunum posterius est. Antiquum nomen corruptum videtur apud Antoninum, ubi legitur Methedum: reponere autem Metrofedum. Sic in Tabula Peutingeri Itineraria Metegio scriptum est pro Metrofedo. In aliis Antonini libris exstat Medetum & Medletum. Melodunense Castrum apud Gregorium Turonensem est lib. x. Hodie Melun, in Insula Sequanæ, instar Lutetiæ Parisiorum. Unde Fabula nata: Melodunum olim Ijs nomen habuisse; indeque Urbem, quæ totius nunc Galliæ Metropolis, cui idem in Insula erat situs, appellatam fuisse, quod Par-Ijs esset. Credant, qui velint, non Ego. Hoc addam, alios pro Metrofedo legere Iofedum, idque Corbolium interpretari; quibus bonam mentem precatur suis ad me litteris Scaliger. Melodunum Arce validum. Quod Opidum bonis piscibus, præcipue Cancris suavissimus, nobilitatum & celebre, nunc Corbeil vulgo, Corbeium nominatur in Vita S. Petri Tarentasij. Habet & hoc, cum multis aliis, Arcem. Fons Belle-Aquæ, vernacule Fontaine-Belle-eau; Secessus Regum amœnissimus quietique aptissimus: vere Palatium: Domicilium olim S. Ludovici, post Philippi, postremo Francisci Valesij. Multa ibi Singularia.
units.tr: So much for Valois. Next comes the third part of France, the territory of Heurepense, Heure pois. It begins at the Seine, below the bridge of Paris called the Little Bridge, and along the same river run Corbolium, Melodunum, and Moretum, where the river Verina, which discharges into the Loing, separates it from the country of Gâtinais. It borders on Brie, where it faces the sanctuary whose surname from St Columba is "the Great", near Sens. It contains the viscounty and bailiwick of Melodunum. Its metropolis is Melodunum. This name has been wrongly mangled twice in Caesar, where all the old manuscripts of the Commentaries on the Gallic War have Metropedunum instead. It is true that Melodunum and Metrofedum are one and the same town, but Melodunum is the later name. The ancient name seems to be corrupted in Antonine, where Methedum is read; but one should restore Metrofedum. So in the Peutinger Table Metegio is written for Metrofedo. In other books of Antonine there appear Medetum and Medletum. The Melodunense Castrum occurs in Gregory of Tours, book X. Today it is Melun, on an island of the Seine, like Lutetia of the Parisians. Hence a fable arose: that Melodunum once had the name Ijs, and that the city which is now the metropolis of all France, which had the same kind of site on an island, was called Par-Ijs from that. Let those believe it who wish; I do not. I will add this: others read Iofedum for Metrofedo and interpret it as Corbolium; for these Scaliger prays good sense in his letters to me. Melodunum is strong with a citadel. This town, famed and noted for its good fish, especially the most delicious crayfish, is now commonly called Corbeil, and is named Corbeium in the Life of St Peter of Tarentaise. It also has a citadel, like many other towns. The Fons Belle-Aquæ, in the vernacular Fontaine-Belle-eau, is a most pleasant retreat of kings, most suited to quiet: truly a palace, once the home of St Louis, afterwards of Philip, and lastly of Francis of Valois. There are many singular things there.

units.la: Quartum in Francia locum dedi Gastinensium Ditioni; vulgo Gastinois; quæ ab Heurepensi separatur Verina fluvio. Comprehendit sub se Ducatus Stampensem & Nemurcensem, Comitatumque Rupif-Fortis, & alios. Stampæ, Estampes vulgo; Opidum medio inter Lutetiam Parisiorum & Genabum Aurelianensium itinere, ad Iunnam Fluvium: Cammarorum, qui delicatissimi, parentem largum, ad Corbolium in Sequanam se exonerantem. Stamparum meminerunt Aimoinus & Gregorius Turonensis. Stampensis Pagus est apud Nithardum de Dissensionibus Filiorum Ludovici Pij lib. 1. Stampense etiam Comitium nominatur apud Ivonem. Ducatus (qui olim Comitatus fuit) claret dignitate. Vide quæ dicam cap. xli, ubi de Comitibus Nivernensibus. Nemursium Nemours opidum ad Lonium Flumen, quod paullo infra Moretum Sequanæ concurrit. Inter Ducatus Franciæ etiam non postremi loci. Vixit nuper Philippus Sabanaus, Nemursij Dux; cujus Filia Ioanna secundo loco nupsit Nicolao Lotharingo, Duci Mercuerrio, Marchioni Nomenei, & Vandalimontis Comiti. Rupes Fortis, Roche-fort Gallo-Romanis dicta, Comitatus gaudet titulo. Loco parum esse, aut nihil antiquitatis, ipsum loquitur nomen: nisi Transnominationum frequentia sit passim admittenda. In Gastinensium quoque Ditione cum Millio & Moreto (quod Limes Gastinenses inter & Heurepenses) utroque Arce præditio, aliisque opidis, est Montargium, quasi Mons-Argi, ut quidam ratiocinantur; quod in circuitu adspectus ejus procul extendatur. Incendio vastatum circa annum cIↄ Iↄ xvIII, postea renovatum fuit. Arcem & hoc habet, in qua depicta visitur Historia Canis Venatici, qui heri sui mortem vindicavit; occiso eo, qui necem illi attulerat.
units.tr: We have given the fourth place in France to the Gâtinais district, commonly Gastinois, which is separated from Hurepoix by the river Verina. It comprises under it the Duchies of Étampes and Nemours, the County of Rochefort, and others. Stampæ, commonly Estampes, is a town midway on the road between Paris and Orléans, on the river Juine, famed for its crayfish, which are most delicate, and for its great parent river, which discharges at Corbeil into the Seine. Aimoin and Gregory of Tours mention Stamparum. The Stampensis Pagus occurs in Nithard, in his book on the Dissensions of the Sons of Louis the Pious, book I. Stampense Comitium is also the name in Ivo. The duchy, which was once a county, shines with dignity. See what I will say in chapter XLI, where I discuss the Counts of Nevers. Nemursium, Nemours, is a town on the river Loing, which joins the Seine a little below Moret. It is among the duchies of France not of the least rank. Recently lived Philip Sabanaus, Duke of Nemours, whose daughter Joan married, as her second husband, Nicholas of Lorraine, Duke of Mercœur, Marquis of Nomeny and Count of Vaudémont. Rupes Fortis, called Roche-fort by the Gallo-Romans, the county enjoys as a title. That the place is of little or no antiquity the name itself declares, unless the frequency of renaming is to be admitted everywhere. In the district of Gâtinais too, with Millio and Moreto (which is the boundary between the Gâtinais and the Heurepense), both provided with citadels, and with other towns, is Montargium, as if Mons-Argi, as some reason; because its prospect extends far around it. It was devastated by fire around the year 1518, and afterwards rebuilt. It too has a citadel, in which is painted the story of the hunting dog that avenged the death of his master, the man who had caused the death being killed.

units.la: BELSIA, quæ in nostra Veteris Celticæ Distributione secundo se offert loco, vulgari voce La Beausse dicta, Regio est, quæ siccitate Aquarumque laborat penuria; fertilis nihilominus, & frumenti valde ferax. Meminit ejus Venantius Fortunatus Poeta.
units.tr: BELSIA, which in our division of Old Celtic Gaul appears in second place and is called La Beausse in the vernacular, is a region that suffers from dryness and a lack of water. Nevertheless it is fertile and very productive of grain. The poet Venantius Fortunatus mentions it.

units.la: Coluerunt olim quidquid Belsiæ nunc nomine censetur, Carnutes, Aurelianenses, Andicavi, Cenomani, & Turones. Carnutes ab Cæsare celebrantur: Καρνῶτες Ptolemæo; Carnuta, Plinio, qui eos Fœderatos cognominat; Carnuti Tibullo: Civitas Carnotum Notitiæ Provinciarum Galliæ in Lugdunensi Quarta; Hodie L'Evesché de Chartes, Le Pais Chartrain. Tempore Cæsaris erat in Carnutibus, summo loco natus, Tasgetius; cujus Maiores in sua Civitate Regnum obtinuerant.
