Huic Cæsar, ut ipse scribit, pro ipsius virtute atque insigni in se benevolentia, quod in omnibus bellis singulari ejus opera fuisset visus, Maiorum locum & dignitatem restituerat. Quum vero tertium jam annum regnaret, Inimici palam, multis ex Civitate Auctoribus, interfecerunt. Habebant nempe tunc etiam Veterum Gallorum Civitates suos Brutos. Carnutum frequens mentio apud Antiquos Scriptores. In iis Locum fuisse annuis Druidum Comitiis dicatum, alibi à me est dictum. Carnutes dictos quidam arbitrantur ab Græca voce Κάρυον, quæ Nucem significat, ob ingentem Nucum copiam, quam ea Regio producit. Aurelianenses sunt apud Paullum Diaconum lib. v. de Gestis Longobardorum cap. 11: ubi male nonnulli absque disjunctiva particula legunt, Venientes de Cenomannicorum Aurelianensium Regione Franci: quasi Cenomanni cognominati fuissent Aurelianenses: quod falsum. Sunt enim diversi Populi. Civitas Aurelianorum in Notitia Provinciarum Galliæ, in Lugdunensi Quarta & in Præfatione Concilij Aurelianensis 1. Le Duché & Evesché d'Orleans. Qui Andicavi, Andicavi vel Andecavi Tacito, Ptolemæo Ἀνδηκαυοι vocantur: in Vulgatis exemplaribus vitiose leguntur Ἀνδηκαῶν. Andegavi Plinio nominantur; apud quem in Editis quibusdam Andegavenses. Civitas Andegavorum Notitiæ in Lugdunensi Tertia. Andes apud Cæsarem, quorum Ducem Dumnacum ab eodem Cæsare victum, scribit lib. viii Hirtius. Vulgo Duché d'Anjou, L'Evesché d'Angiers, Angevins. Cenomani Galliæ Populi celebrantur Cæsari, Ptolemæo, & aliis: Civitas Cenomanorum Notitiæ, in Lugd. Tertia. Pais de Maine, L'Evesché de Mans. Aulerci (Præienomen putatur
units.tr: The peoples who once inhabited whatever is now called Belsia were the Carnutes, the Aurelianenses, the Andicavi, the Cenomani and the Turones. The Carnutes are celebrated by Caesar; Ptolemy calls them Karnotes [Καρνῶτες]; Pliny calls them Carnuta, and gives them the surname Federates; Tibullus has Carnuti; the Civitas Carnotum appears in the Notitia of the Provinces of Gaul, in Lugdunensis Quarta; today they are L'Evesché de Chartes, Le Pais Chartrain. In Caesar's time there was among the Carnutes a man of the highest rank, Tasgetius, whose ancestors had held royal power in their state. Caesar writes that, because of his valour and his remarkable goodwill toward himself, since he had seemed in all the wars to have served with singular effort, he restored him to his ancestors' place and dignity. But when Tasgetius had already reigned for a third year, enemies killed him openly, with many of the citizens as authors of the deed. The ancient Gallic states then also had their Bruti. The Carnutes are often mentioned by ancient writers. I have said elsewhere that a place among them was dedicated to the annual assembly of the Druids. Some think the Carnutes were named from the Greek word Κάρυον, which means nut, because of the great abundance of nuts this region produces. The Aurelianenses are found in Paul the Deacon, History of the Lombards book 5, chapter 11, where some wrongly read the passage without a disjunctive particle: "Franks coming from the region of the Cenomannian Aurelianenses", as if the Cenomani had been called Aurelianenses. That is false, for they are different peoples. The Civitas Aurelianorum appears in the Notitia of the Provinces of Gaul, in Lugdunensis Quarta, and in the preface to the First Council of Orléans; today Le Duché & Evesché d'Orleans. The Andicavi, called Andicavi or Andecavi by Tacitus and Ἀνδηκαυοι by Ptolemy (in the common texts wrongly read as Ἀνδηκαῶν), are named Andegavi by Pliny, though in some printed editions of Pliny they are Andegavenses. The Civitas Andegavorum appears in the Notitia in Lugdunensis Tertia. Caesar has the Andes, whose leader Dumnacus was defeated by Caesar himself, as Hirtius writes in book 8. Today they are the Duché d'Anjou, L'Evesché d'Angiers, the Angevins. The Cenomani, a people of Gaul, are celebrated by Caesar, Ptolemy and others; the Civitas Cenomanorum appears in the Notitia, in Lugdunensis Tertia; today Pais de Maine, L'Evesché de Mans.

units.la: Ii tur fuisse aliquot Antiquæ Galliæ Populis) Cenomanos habet Plinius. Cenomanorum in Italiam inruptiones commemorantur apud varios Historiographos, Polybium, Livium, Iustinum. Hinc in Italia Trans-Padana, ut suo videbimus loco, Κενομανοὶ Ptolemæo; Cenomanni, Plinio: Hinc item Κενομανοὶ apud Strabonem supra Venetos, Carnis vicinī: Hinc denique, quod suis Sedibus parum essent contenti, Cenomannos locat Plinius lib. iii. cap. xix in Gallia Narbonensi, in Volcis. Turones apud Cæsarem & Tacitum, qui Τυρῶνες Ptolemæo lib. ii. cap. viii Tabula iii Europæ: Sic enim ibi legendum pro Τυρώνες: Civitas Turonorum Notitiæ in Lugdunensi Tertia: La Duché de Touraine, L'Archevêché de Tours.
units.tr: Ii tur fuisse aliquot Antiquæ Galliæ Populis) Pliny has the Cenomani. Incursions of the Cenomani into Italy are recorded by various historians, Polybius, Livy and Justin. Hence, in Transpadane Italy, as we shall see in its place, Ptolemy has Κενομανοὶ, and Pliny the Cenomanni. Hence also Strabo has Κενομανοὶ above the Veneti, neighbours of the Carni. Finally, because they were not content enough with their own seats, Pliny places the Cenomanni in Narbonese Gaul, among the Volcae, in book 3, chapter 19. The Turones appear in Caesar and Tacitus, and are Τυρῶνες in Ptolemy, book 2, chapter 8, table 3 of Europe; for so it should be read there instead of Τυρώνες. The Civitas Turonorum appears in the Notitia in Lugdunensis Tertia; today La Duché de Touraine, L'Archevêché de Tours.

units.la: Belsia porro triplex est, Superior, Media, Inferior.
units.tr: Belsia, moreover, is threefold: Superior, Media and Inferior.

units.la: Superior, La Haulte Beaulse, initium capit ab Vico, qui vulgo Ablys indigetatur, petens porro Carnutum Agros & ulteriora. Concensentur illi Carnutum Regio, Ducatus Andegavensis, Comitatus Perchensis. Carnutum Territorium (quod Galliæ totius, ut notat Cæsar, medium, & quasi Centrum) vulgo Le Pays Chartrain, adhæret hinc Perchensi Comitatui, inde Ducatui Aurelianensi. Castrensis Pagus dicitur Nithardo, de Dissensionibus Filiorum Ludovici Pii lib. i. Carnuticum Solum nulli reliquæ Galliæ parti fertilitate vel amœnitate cedit omni genere Frumenti, Pecoris, Fructuum abundans; Vino non deficitum. Primarium Opidum Carnutum audit. Sic nominat Rotinus, quod Ptolemæo Αὐτρεμον appellatur; quodque nunc temporis Chartres. Vetus apud Onuphrium Panuinium Lapis Coloniam fuisse testatur. Opidum hodie non postremi loci; situm partim in planicie, partim in Colle; frequentibus Ædificijs refertum; Mœnibus firmis cinctum; Aggeribus Fossisque circumvallatum; Incolarum divitijs pollens. Perluit ad Collis pedem Fluvius, Pistrinis versandis commodus, qui è Perchensibus ortus, hucque eivium industria derivatus apud Luparias (Louviers) paullo supra Rotomagum in majores Sequanæ undas influit. Summum Templum Mariæ Virgini est consecratum, in cujus Crypta Puteus ostenditur, Sanctorum Fortium dictus: in quem, quum Carnutes Christo nomen primitus dedissent, magnus Christianorum numerus ab Quirino Galliæ Proconsule dicitur præcipitatus. Adservari fertur hic etiam ingenti pietate Subuucula Divæ Virginis. Portas habet opidum viii: quarum sex patent; reliquas Bella clauserunt Civilia; quibus anno cıɔ ıɔ lxvii fuit obsessum oppugnatumque, sed virtute Ligneri fortiter defensum. Loquitur Carmen, quod ad Mœniorum partem, quæ Hostium Machinis prostrata, post fuit restituta, Lapidi incisum legi: Dum Nova Religio Studia in contraria cacas Gallorum Mentes agit, & Bello omnia miscet, Carnutum premitur magna obsidione: globisque Machina sulphureis oppugnat Mœnia, quæ nunc Sarta & tecta vides: Salva incolumisque remansit Vrbs, Duce Ligneriio; Populi curaque fidelis Atque manu parva numerosum reppulit agmen. Quam pro Rege suo Patriaque Arisque Focisque Sit pulcrum pugnare atque Hasta cedere numquam; Exemplo hoc discant Nati seriqe Nepotes.
units.tr: Superior, La Haulte Beaulse, begins at the village commonly called Ablys, and reaches onward into the fields of the Carnutes and beyond. To it belong the Region of the Carnutes, the Duchy of Anjou and the County of Perche. The Territory of the Carnutes (which, as Caesar notes, is the middle of all Gaul and almost its centre) is called in the vernacular Le Pays Chartrain; it borders the County of Perche on one side and the Duchy of Orléans on the other. Nithard, in his work on the Dissensions of the Sons of Louis the Pious, book 1, calls it the Castrensis Pagus. The soil of the Carnutes yields to no other part of Gaul in fertility or pleasantness; it abounds in every kind of grain, livestock and fruit, and there is no lack of wine. Their chief town is called Carnutum. Rotinus names it thus; Ptolemy calls it Αὐτρεμον; and today it is Chartres. An ancient stone in Onuphrius Panvinius testifies that it was a colony. The town today is of no small rank; it is situated partly on a plain and partly on a hill, is full of frequent buildings, is enclosed by strong walls, is surrounded by embankments and ditches, and is rich in the wealth of its inhabitants. A river washes the foot of the hill, suitable for turning mills; it rises in the country of Perche, and is led hither by the industry of the citizens, and flows past Louviers (Louviers), a little above Rouen, into the greater waters of the Seine. The chief temple is consecrated to the Virgin Mary; in its crypt is shown a well called that of the Sancti Fortes, into which, when the Carnutes had first embraced the name of Christ, a great number of Christians is said to have been thrown by Quirinus, the proconsul of Gaul. Here too, it is said, is preserved with great devotion a undergarment of the divine Virgin. The town has eight gates, of which six stand open; the others were closed by the civil wars, during which in the year 1567 it was besieged and attacked, but bravely defended through the valour of Ligneris. A poem is carved on a stone, which can be read on the part of the walls that was thrown down by the enemy's engines and later restored: "While the New Religion drives the minds of the Gauls to its opposing studies, and throws everything into war, Chartres is pressed by a great siege, and with sulphurous balls its engines assault the walls, which you now see whole and intact. The city remained safe and unharmed under the leadership of Ligneris; the faithful care of the people and a small hand drove back the numerous host. How beautiful it is to fight for one's king, country, altars and hearths, and never to yield the spear! Let children and later grandchildren learn from this example."

units.la: Dies, quo ab Obsidione repulsi Hostes, Festis est adscriptus. Suos olim habuit Comites. Eorum, ni fallor. Progenitor Otho: cuius Pater Theobaldus Senior; Rollonis Normanni Adgnatus, Comes Bletensis Carnutum armis adquisicrat. Otho quosdam habuit Successores: Filios Theobaldum ii ἀπαιδα, & Stephanum; Nepotem ex Posteriore Theobaldum iii, & Pronepotem Theobaldum iiii, Inprolem: post quem nihil amplius de Carnutensibus Comitibus ego quidem invenio. Carnutum Territorio solitus est adscensi Comitatus Druidensis; nec non, ut quibusdam placet, Montfortius. Druidensis, La Comté de Dreux, ortum habet ab Roberto, Ludovici vi Crassi Francorum Regis Filio. Successit huic Robertus ii Iunior, cuius Filiorum maximus natu Petrus conditor fuit Britanniæ Principum: secundus, Robertus iii Comites Druidenses continuavit per Filium Joannem i, Nepotem Robertum iv; Pronepotem Joannem iii; Abnepotemque Robertum v, Joannem iii & Petrum, ἀπαιδας mortuos: quibus Soror Joanna succedens, nuptit primo Ludovico Thoarensi, inde autem Gawino Beaufardo; Maritisque caussam dedit Novos quasi Comites Druidenses condendi, quorum tamen haud magna est apud Historiographos memoria. Opidum hoc, quod vernacule Dreux, Druidum quondam sedes creditum; ad Fluvium, qui Fbrus, Eureux vulgo. Montfortius Comitatus, La Comté de Montfort, non minus, quam superior, nobilis. Inter alios obtinuisse legitur cum Roberto IV, de quo paullo ante, Dreusii Comes; Uxore ducta Beatrice, Ioannis Comitis Montfortii Filia & Herede. Montfortium opidum, medio fere inter Druidum urbem & Lutetiam itinere.
units.tr: The day on which the enemy was driven back from the siege has been assigned to the feasts. The Carnutes once had their own counts. Of these, unless I am mistaken, the progenitor was Otho; his father was Theobald the Elder, a kinsman of Rollo the Norman, who had acquired the County of Blois by arms, together with the Carnutes. Otho had some successors: his sons Theobald II, childless [ἄπαιδα], and Stephen; from the latter's line, a grandson Theobald III, and a great-grandson Theobald IV, who had no offspring. After him I, at least, find nothing more about the Counts of Chartres. To the territory of the Carnutes there used to be added the County of Dreux, and, as some think, Montfort. The Druidensis, La Comté de Dreux, took its origin from Robert, son of Louis VI the Fat, King of the Franks. Robert II the Younger succeeded him; the eldest of his sons, Peter, became the founder of the Princes of Brittany; the second, Robert III, continued the Counts of Dreux through his son John I, his grandson Robert IV, his great-grandson John III, and his great-great-grandson Robert V, while John III and Peter died childless. Their sister Joanna succeeded them; she was first married to Louis of Thouars, and then to Gawain of Beaufort, and by her husbands she gave occasion for new Counts of Dreux to be created, though there is not much memory of them among the historians. This town, which in the vernacular is Dreux, was once believed to have been a seat of the Druids; it lies by the river that is called Eure in the vernacular. The County of Montfort, La Comté de Montfort, is no less noble than the one above. It is recorded that among others it was held together with Robert IV, of whom a little earlier, Count of Dreux, by Robert's wife Beatrice, daughter and heiress of John, Count of Montfort. The town of Montfort lies almost midway along the road between the city of Dreux and Paris.

units.la: Hæc de Carnutum Regione: sequitur Ducatus Andegavensis, La Duché d'Anjou, incipiens ab Vico Choufay; finem autem accipiens inter Moncontour & Herrant, ubi initium Pictavensis Territorij, quod illi ab Meridie; versus Orientem Confinia sunt Turonensium & Vindocinotum; ad Septemtrionem Comitatus, qui vulgo Maine & Laval: ad Occidentem denique Britanniam attingit. In ea Provincia plus quam xi sunt Flumina, multa Stagna, magnus Lacuum numerus, Rivuli non pauci: sunt & Vivaria Paludesque, Fontes item infiniti. Regio fertilis & montosa. Colles ibi Vitibus passim consiti; Valles Silvis Saltibusque viridantes; læta Prata; Eryceta gratissimum Pecori Pabulum præstantia. Vina hic alba, notæ nobilissimæ, vulgo Vins d'Anjou. In nonnullis hujus Provinciæ locis illud genus Lapidis cæruleum & fissile effoditur, quo Templorum ubique Ædiumque tecta contra cœli injurias muniuntur. Ardoises vernacule vocantur. Suos olim habuerunt Andes Regulos & Duces, quorum Dumnacum ab Cæsare victum scribit octavo libro Hirtius. Postea cum aliis Galliarum populis in Francorum venerunt ditionem. Rex Chilpericus, occiso Comite Paullo, Andegavensem Urbem obtinuit; suisque eam Posteris reliquit, Franciæ Regibus: quorum Karolus Calvus Superiorem quidem Provinciæ partem Torquato (alij aliter vocant) dedit, reservato sibi supremo in eam jure; Inseriorem autem Fudoni Parisiorum Comiti, cujus ex fratre Ruperto Comite Andegavensi, Duceque Celticæ Nepos, Hugo Magnus eam largitus est Fulconi, Torquati ex Ingelgero Filio Nepoti. Fulconi ordine successerunt Fulco II; Gotefridus, vulgo dictus Grisgonella: Fulco III; Gotefredus II; Fulco IV; Fulco V: qui Hierosolymorum Rex fuit, post Balduinum, cujus Filiam ipse viduus duxerat uxorem; Gotefredus denique VI Barbatus, cui sociata fuit Machthildis, Henrici I Angliæ Regis F. Hujus Filij, Henricus quidem Rex fuit Angliæ, ejus nominis II; Anduum vero Comites Gotefredus VI & Guilelmus: quos quum paricidiali bello victos terris suis pepulisset Frater Rex, Filios natu majores in Angliæ Regno, Gotefredum autem VIII in Comitatu Andegavensi Successores habuit. Gotefridi Filio Arturo Comiti, Britanniæque per Matrem Duci, bellum movit Patruus Ioannes Angliæ Rex. Fecerat jam Arturus Homagium, vt loquuntur, & Fidem Principatus sui nomine promiserat Francorum Regi Philippo Augusto: à quo instigatus quum Pictones Regi Patruo ereptum properaret, cum exercitu Ligerim jam transgressus, ab eo ex improviso superveniente captus, Rotomagum est abductus, ibique non multo post occisus. Id non ferendum rata Arturi Mater, Constantia Conani Britanniæ Principis Filia & Heres, Regem Ioannem Paricidij accusavit apud Franciæ Regem, quem dixi; quumque vocatus non litteret, Paricidij damnatus est sententia Pariuum Franciæ; ejusque Provinciæ, quas in Galliis habebat, Fisco Regis sunt adjudicatæ: quam sententiam ipse Rex exsequens Andegavenses sibi deditione subjecit, Regique Francorum Ludovico Filio Nominis ejus VIII reliquit. Huic successit Filius Ludovicus IX, Sanctus cognominatus, qui Provinciam hanc Karolo Fratri, Apennagij jure, concessit. Hunc sequutus Karolus II, qui Clementiam Filiam locans Karolo Valesio Provinciam hanc Dotis nomine largitus est. Huic successerunt Franciæ Reges, Philippus Valesius Filius, & ex eo Nepos Ioannes, qui nobilissimam hanc Regni portionem Ducatus titulo, anno cIↄ cccI, decoratam Filio Ludovico Apennagij jure dedit. Hunc secuti sunt descendente linea Ludovicus II, & Ludovicus III, quo sine Herede mortuo Principatum adiit Renatus Frater. Hic, defunctis Liberis, Heredem dixit sui Fratris Filium Karolum (alij Fratrem fuisse volunt) qui Heredem scriptit Ludovicum XI. Regem. Et sic Coronæ Franciæ sunt adnexus, eique unitus mansit; nisi quod Franciscus I eundem jus Matri Aloisiæ Sabaudæ in usumfructum 20 tradiderit. Rex Karolus IX cum jure Apennagij tribuit Henrico Fratri, qui deinde Poloniæ & Franciæ Rex. Metropolis Ducatus Andegavum est; Andegavenfis Civitas Paullo Diacono; vulgo Angiers. Ptolemæo dicitur Ἀλίωμαγος Andecavarum, sic enim legendum antea monui. In utraque Meduana, Maine, Ponte strati lapideo, ripa est magnifice exstructa. Insignis ibi Politia. Episcopali fulget dignitate: Senescallatu etiam & Bailliivatu, Sedeque superbiens Præsidiali. Academiam habet celebrem, ab Ludovico II Andegavensium Duce, anno cIↄ cccxxcix institutam, & nuperrime ab Henrico Valesio Andium Duce, Karoli IX Fratre, restauratam; evocato, qui Ius ibi profiteretur, Francisco Balduino, qui hac de re legendus ad l. Si pacto. C. de Pactis. Extra Vrbem vetustæ monstrantur Ruinæ, quæ vulgo Grohan dicuntur, Nomine ab Romano non abludente. Hic quondam Theatrum ab Romanis exstructum fuisse perhibetur. Apparent multæ Parietinarum Murorumque reliquiæ. Effodiuntur & infinita probæ notæ Numismata. Habet hic Ducatus multa insignia Opida, alia aliis majora. Pauca, ut vernacule sonant, dabo: Samur ad Ligerim cum Arce: Academiam, quam apud Regem Magni Viri moliuntur, brevi habiturum; Montreneau, Bauge, Beau-fort, Briffac, Monstreul-Belay, Malevrier, Chantonceau, Vibers, Duretail, La Flesche, Chafleau-Gontier, Segre.
units.tr: Such is the account of the Region of the Carnutes. Next comes the Duchy of Anjou, La Duché d'Anjou, beginning at the village of Choufay. It ends between Moncontour and Herrant, where the territory of Poitou begins, lying to the south. To the east its borders are those of the Tourangeaux and Vendôme; to the north lies the county commonly called Maine and Laval; and to the west it reaches Brittany. In this province there are more than eleven rivers, many pools, a large number of lakes and not a few streams. There are also fishponds and marshes, and countless springs. The region is fertile and mountainous. Hills are planted everywhere with vines; valleys are green with woods and thickets; the meadows are pleasant; the heaths provide very good pasture for flocks. Here are white wines of the highest renown, commonly called Vins d'Anjou. In some parts of this province that kind of stone is dug up which is blue and splits easily, and with it the roofs of temples and buildings everywhere are protected against the injuries of the sky. In the vernacular these are called Ardoises. The Andes once had their own kings and dukes, of whom Hirtius writes in the eighth book that Dumnacus was defeated by Caesar. Afterwards they came, along with the other peoples of Gaul, under the rule of the Franks. King Chilpericus, after killing Count Paullus, took the city of Angers and left it to his posterity, the kings of France. Of these, Karolus Calvus gave the upper part of the province to Torquatus (others call him differently), reserving to himself supreme right over it. The lower part he gave to Fudo, Count of Paris, whose nephew, through his brother Rupert, Count of Anjou and Duke of Celtica, Hugo Magnus granted it to Fulco, grandson of Torquatus through his son Ingelgerus. The successors of Fulco in order were: Fulco II; Gotefridus, commonly called Grisgonella; Fulco III; Gotefredus II; Fulco IV; Fulco V, who was King of Jerusalem after Balduinus, whose daughter he himself, now a widower, had married; and finally Gotefredus VI Barbatus, joined in marriage to Machthildis, daughter of Henry I, King of England. Of their sons, Henricus indeed became King of England, the second of that name; but the Counts of Anjou, Gotefredus VI and Guilelmus, whom their brother the King, after defeating them in a war against a father, drove from their lands, had as successors their elder sons in the Kingdom of England, and Gotefredus VIII in the County of Anjou. King John of England, the uncle, made war on Arturus, son of Gotefridus, Count and, through his mother, Duke of Brittany. Arturus had already done homage, as they say, and had promised fealty for his principality to Philippus Augustus, King of the Franks. Urged on by him, when he hurried to seize Poitou from his uncle the King, he had already crossed the Loire with an army, but he was captured by John, who came upon him unexpectedly, and was led off to Rouen, where he was killed not long afterwards. His mother Constantia, daughter and heiress of Conan, Prince of Brittany, thought this intolerable and accused King John of parricide before the King of France mentioned above. When he did not appear after being summoned, he was condemned by the sentence of the peers of France for parricide, and the provinces he held in Gaul were adjudged to the royal treasury. King Philip himself carried out this sentence, subjecting the Angevins to himself by their surrender, and left them to Ludovicus, King of the Franks, son of Philip, the eighth of that name. His son Ludovicus IX, surnamed Sanctus, succeeded him, and granted this province to his brother Karolus by right of appanage. He was followed by Karolus II, who, giving his daughter Clementia in marriage to Karolo Valesio, granted this province to him as her dowry. To him succeeded the Kings of France: Philippus Valesius, his son, and from him his grandson Ioannes, who in the year 1351 adorned this most noble part of the kingdom with the title of duchy and gave it to his son Ludovicus by right of appanage. The line then descended through Ludovicus II and Ludovicus III, and when the latter died without heir, his brother Renatus took possession of the principality. He, when his own children had died, named as heir his brother's son Karolus (others want him to have been a brother), who named Ludovicus XI, King, as his heir. And so it was joined to the crown of France and remained united with it, except that Franciscus I handed over the same right in usufruct to his mother Aloisia Sabauda. King Karolus IX granted it, with the right of appanage, to his brother Henricus, who afterwards became King of Poland and of France. The metropolis of the duchy is Andegavum, the city of the Andegavenses (Paul the Deacon's name), commonly Angiers. Ptolemy calls it Aliomagus of the Andecavi; as I noted earlier, it must be read thus. On both banks of the Meduana, Maine, which is crossed by a bridge of stone, the riverbank has been splendidly built up. The city is distinguished in its government. It shines with an episcopal dignity, and it also has a seneschalship and a bailiwick, and it is proud of its seat of the presidial court. It has a famous academy, founded by Ludovicus II, Duke of the Andegavenses, in the year 1389, and very recently restored by Henricus Valesius, Duke of Anjou, brother of Karolus IX; to teach law there, Franciscus Balduinus was summoned, whom one should read on this matter at the law "Si pacto", C. de Pactis. Outside the city are shown ancient ruins, commonly called Grohan, a name not far from the Roman one. Here, it is said, a theatre once built by the Romans stood. Many remains of walls and ruins are visible, and countless coins of good quality are dug up. This duchy has many notable towns, some larger than others. I will give a few, as they are called in the vernacular: Samur on the Loire with its castle, which will soon have an academy, which great men are preparing with the King; Montreneau, Bauge, Beaufort, Briffac, Montreul-Belay, Malevrier, Chantonceau, Vibers, Duretail, La Flesche, Chasteau-Gontier, Segre.

units.la: Andegavensibus, Turonensibus, Normannis & Perchensibus contiguus est Comitatus Cenomanensis, vulgo Comté de Maine. Provincia, quæ tribus præcipue Fluviis irrigatur Meduana (Maienne,) Ledo (Loir) & Sartra. Ornatus illi multus ab Silvis 40 Saltibusque accedit. Tota Regio superioribus annis in duas quasi abijt Partes. Civitas Cenomanensis, Le Mans, Ditioni addita est Regis Franciæ; Vrbs autem Mania, Maine, cum Marchionatu, nunc in Ducatus decus erecto, Guisiæ gentis agnoscit Dominium. Novi Karolum Ducem Menium, sive Maienna, Francisci Ducis Guisiæ Filium, Henrici Ducis Fratrem. Opidum Primarium ad Sartram Fluvium, quod vulgo Le Mans. Nobilissimus Vir Iosephus Scaliger suis ad Me litteris putat esse οὐνδιω Ptolemæi, Aulerciorum Cenomanorum Caput, de quo ante dixi. Ab initio Sedes Bailliivatus; post Henricum II Præsidialis fuit facta: ad quam variorum Opidorum appellationes devolvuntur. Hanc Provinciam, sub Aquitania comprehensam, aliquando parvisse lego Ducibus Aquitanis, donec inter Reges Franciæ 50 Ludovicum IX & Angliæ Henricum III pactum fuit, ut Anglus Aquitania, quam ab Septemtrione Carantonus Fluvius, ab Meridie Pyrenæi Montes terminarent, contentus, in perpetuum cederet Normannia Terrisque Cenomanorum & Andegavensium; eique numerarentur CIↄ Iↄ aureorum millia. Rex Franciæ Ioannes Andium & Cenomanorum Comitatum Ludovico Filio Secundo-genito dedit. Donationis Diploma anni cIↄ ccc IX in Scrinio Regis adhuc visitur. Ludovici Stemma est tale:
units.tr: Adjoining the Andegavenses, the Turonenses, the Normans and the Perchenses is the Cenomanensian County, commonly Comté de Maine. It is a province watered chiefly by three rivers, the Meduana (Mayenne), Ledo (Loir) and Sartra. It is adorned with many woods and thickets. The whole region in recent years has been divided, as it were, into two parts. The city of the Cenomani, Le Mans, has been added to the dominion of the King of France; but the city of Mania, Maine, together with the marquisate, now raised to the honour of a duchy, acknowledges the lordship of the house of Guise. I know Karolus, Duke of Menium or Maienna, son of Francis, Duke of Guise, and brother of Henry, Duke of Guise. The chief town is on the river Sartra, commonly called Le Mans. The most noble man Joseph Scaliger writes to me that it is the οὐνδιω of Ptolemy, the capital of the Aulerci Cenomani, of whom I spoke before. In the beginning it was the seat of a bailiwick; afterwards under Henry II it was made a presidial seat, to which the appeals of various towns are referred. I read that this province, included under Aquitaine, once obeyed the dukes of Aquitaine, until between Ludovicus IX, King of France, and Henricus III, King of England, an agreement was made that the Englishman, content with Aquitaine, which the river Charente on the north and the Pyrenean mountains on the south bound, would cede in perpetuity Normandy and the lands of the Cenomani and the Andegavenses; and that 1,000,000 gold pieces would be counted to him. King John of France gave the county of Anjou and Maine to his second son Ludovicus. The charter of the donation of the year 1309 is still seen in the King's archive. The coat of arms of Ludovicus is as follows:

units.la: cuius Metropolis Andegavum, Angiers.
units.tr: whose metropolis is Angers.

units.la: cum Comitatus Cenomanensis, Comté de Maine.
units.tr: with the County of Maine, Comté de Maine.

units.la: cuius Partes Civitas Cenomanensis, Le Mans, Vrbs Mania, Maine.
units.tr: whose parts are the city of Le Mans, and the city of Mans in Maine.

units.la: Alia opida, Samur, &c. LVDOVICVS I Valesius, Dux Andegavensis, Cenomanorum Comes; ab Ioanna I Neapolis Regina adoptatus, & Rex Hierosolymorum, Siciliae Neapolisque designatus. Obiit anno MCCCCXIV, mense Septembris. LVDOVICVS II Dux Andegavensis, Cenomanorum Comes; Rex Hierosolymorum & Siciliae. Obiit anno MCCCCXVII. LVDOVICVS III Dux Andium & Cenomanorum Comes, ab Ioanna II Neapolis Regina adoptatus in Regem Siciliae. Ducem Calabriae, Comitemque Provinciae. Sine liberis defunctus est anno MCCCCXXXIV. RENATVS Dux Andegavensis, Comes Cenomanorum, Dux Calabriae & Barri, Comes Provinciae & Guisiae; ab Ludovico Fratre Germano, consensu Ioannae II Heres institutus. Mortuus est anno MCCCCLXX. CAROLVS, cui Renatus Frater, mortuo Filio Ioanne, Nepoteque Nicolao, reliquit iura Regni Neapolitani, Comitatus Provinciae & Cenomanorum. Hic Ludovicum XI sustum Rerum Haeredem instituit. IOANNES Calabriae Dux, &c. Huic Pater superstes fuit. Defunctus enim anno MCCCC LXX. IOLANTA nupta Friderico Vadimontano Obiit anno MCCCC LXXIII. NICOLAUS Calabriae Dux. Marchio Pontensis, &c. Ante Avum Renatum mortuus anno MCCCC LXXIII. RENATUS praeteritus ab Avo Renato. Obiit anno MDVIII.
units.tr: Other towns: Saumur, etc. LUDOVICUS I of Valois, Duke of Anjou, Count of the Cenomani, adopted by Joanna I, Queen of Naples, and designated King of Jerusalem, Sicily and Naples. He died in the year 1414, in September. LUDOVICUS II, Duke of Anjou, Count of the Cenomani; King of Jerusalem and Sicily. He died in the year 1417. LUDOVICUS III, Duke of Anjou and Count of the Cenomani, adopted by Joanna II, Queen of Naples, as King of Sicily, Duke of Calabria and Count of Provence. He died without children in the year 1434. RENATUS, Duke of Anjou, Count of the Cenomani, Duke of Calabria and Bar, Count of Provence and Guise; instituted heir by Louis, his full brother, with the consent of Joanna II. He died in the year 1470. CHARLES, to whom his brother Renatus, after his son John had died and his grandson Nicholas, left the rights to the Kingdom of Naples and the counties of Provence and Maine. He named Louis XI, the just, heir of his affairs. JOHN, Duke of Calabria, etc. His father outlived him, for he died in the year 1470. YOLANDA, married to Frederick of Vaudémont, died in the year 1473. NICHOLAS, Duke of Calabria, Marquis of Pont, etc. He died before his grandfather René, in the year 1473. RENATUS, passed over by his grandfather René. He died in the year 1508.

units.la: Sequitur postremo loco cum Superiore Belsia explicandus Comitatus Perchensis, Comté du Perche. Dividitur hic in duas Partes, quarum una Inferior dicitur, vulgo Le Perche Gouet; Castellania Carnutensi Territorio quasi inclusa; Primarium habens opidum, quod Nogent le Rotron vernacule: Altera Superior est, quae proprie Comitatum constituit. Opidum cum aliis habet Mortanium, Mortaigne; ubi Sedes Baillivi Perchensis. Terminatur, qua Normannos respicit, in Vernuelio, Vernueil; qua Cenomanos, in Memerfio, Memers.
units.tr: Last of all, to be explained along with the Upper Beauce, comes the County of Perche, Comté du Perche. It is divided into two parts. One is called the Lower, commonly Le Perche Gouet, lying almost enclosed within the territory of Chartres, and its chief town is Nogent le Rotron in the vernacular. The other, the Upper, properly constitutes the county. Its towns include Mortanium, Mortaigne, where the seat of the Bailli of Perche is. It is bounded, on the side facing the Normans, by Vernuelio, Vernueil, and on the side facing the Cenomani, by Memerfio, Memers.

units.la: Illa de Superiore Belsia, ejusque Partibus: succedit ordine Medis, cui tribui solitum quidquid est, inde quidem ad utramque Ligeris ripam ab Ratomago, Romorantin vernacule, quod opidum ad Saudram est Fluvium, qui Grandis cognominatur, Vendomium usque: hinc autem in dextra ejusdem Ligeris ripa quidquid Castelloduno (Chasteau-dun) porrigitur Blesas & ad Turonensium usque Agros. Vocatur haec Belsiae Pars Vindocina, Vendosmoise; quod finem ibi capiat versus Septemtrionem. Reliquas fertilitate sua Belsias superat. Comprehendit partim Comitatus Blesensem, Dunensem & Tonnerrensem; partim Ducatus Vindocinensem & Turonensem. Comitatui Blesensis (La Comté de Blois; Pagus Blesensis forte Nithardo) nomen dedit Opidum antiquum Blesense. Blesenses Gregorio Turonensi noti circa annum MLX. Castri Blesensis ad Montis cujusdam, quem Liger praeterfluit, latus in Agiulphi Vita fit mentio. Certe Castrum hodieque est in Rupe elegante situm, ab Opido versus Occasum separatum; Sedem Palatiumque Regibus praebens: unde prospectus cum in Urbem ipsam, tum in vicinos Agros. Regalis Civitas vulgo vocari solita, quod & amoenissimus saepe Regum Secessus, & educandis Ipsorum Principumque aliorum Liberis consecrata. Salubberrimi enim Aeris est: gratissimi Soli: Agri amoenissimi, Vitibus pulcherrimis consiti, omnique Frumentorum genere, fructiferisque Arboribus luxuriantis. Fontes habet dulcissimos, Rivulosque dulcissimi ob sinuosos amfractus Murmuris. Templa habet duo: unum in Arce S.Salvatori dicatum; à Comitibus, quique ipsis successerunt Regibus, amplissimis dotatum Reditibus: Alterum in ipsa Urbe, D. Iacobo sacrum. In Priore Sepulcra spectantur, summi Artificij, Comitum Blesensium Ludovici & Guidonis; item Ioannis Albaniae Ducis, aliorumque complurium. Visunda se praebent apud Blesenses admiranda Aquaeductuum vestigia, tanti spatij, tantae altitudinis, ut tribus Equitibus junctim incedentibus facile transitum concedant. Romanorum esse Opera vero simile est. Cives & Incolae comes admodum sunt, faciles & humani; munditiei & splendoris in Victu, Potu, Amictuque studiosissimi; in quorum denique ore purissima quasi habitat Francicae Linguae Proprietas. Secundo ab hac Urbe Lapide conlapsae Aedificiorum ruinae monstrantur. Locum Orcheze vulgo nominant. Orchestra pars apud Veteres Romanos Theatri. Nihil adfirmo. Adcolae C. Iulij Caesaris Horreum fuisse volunt. Inter Primos Blosij Comites invenio Theobaldum, cognomine Seniorem, Gedonis F. Rollonis Roberti, Primi Normanniae Ducis, adgnatum. Filium hic habuit Othonem (alijs Fudo dicitur) qui auctis cum Patris, tum sua Virtute Principatibus, Comes fuit Campaniae, Blosij, Briae, Turonum & Carnutum. Liberos procreavit Theobaldum II & Stephanum, qui Fratri sine prole mortuo successit. Hoc ex Adela Gulielmi Conquæstoris Angliæ Regis Filia geniti, cum alijs, Theobaldus III & Stephanus: quorum Prioris Filius Patri cognominis, quum inprolis vita defungeretur, amplissimas hæreditates reliquit sui Patrui Stephani, qui Angliæ Regnum adeptus fuerat, Posteris: inter quos legitur Ludovicus, Henrici II Comitis Campaniæ, Briæque Filius, Henrici Largi N. Stephani Regis Pronepos, Comes fuisse Blesensis; donatus insuper ob egregia ad Constantinopolin facinora, Romaniæ Ducatu. Ἀ mortuo successit, post Theobaldum etiam improlem, Margareta Sororis Vxor primo Othonis Burgundiæ Comitis, secundo Gualtheri Avennaris Dynastæ: quo nata Maria Avennæ Domina, Comes Carnutum & Blosij, quæ nupsit Hugoni Castilionæo, Comiti Fani S. Pauli: Post eam nihil de hoc Comitatu certi tradunt Historiographi. Comitatus Dunensis, La Comté de Dunois principem habet Vrbem Castrodunum, Chasteau-dun. . Opidum est cum Arce ad Loiram (vulgo Loir, qui alius ab Ligeri; in quem ad Andegavensium Vrbem se effundit) conditum in eminentiore Rupe, ad quam haud facilis patet accessus, ne ad Septemtriones quidem, qua parte Regio latissime se oculis pandit. Recte Castrodunum, quod Castrum vel Propugnaculum in Duno sit exstructum. Dunum alias docui Gallorum Veterum Idiomate Colem vel Rupem sonare. Turri munitum est amplissima. Majus aliquando fuisse testantur in Suburbijs hic ibi augusta Ædificiorum Rudera. Templi Primarij, D. Magdalenæ sacri, conditor fertur Karolus Magnus. Suburbia habet quatuor, ipsa Vrbe majora, Ædibus, quam ipsa Vrbs, splendidioribus, Templisque duodecim decorata. Vrbis, superioribus bellis horrendum in modum vastatæ, magnam partem restaurarunt Cives, qui ut sibi studium illud perpetuandi animum esse declararent, in Vrbis Insignibus utuntur tribus Semilunulis cum Inscriptione in ΕΚΦΕΙΑ, EXSTINCTA REVIVISCO. De Comitatu Tonnorierfi, Comté de Tonnoire nihil in præsentia mihi est quod scribam; destitutus ab ijs auctoribus, qui eum potuerunt diffinivisse. Ducatus, olim Comitatus, Vindocinensis, Duché de Vendosme, initium capit à Baugenciaco, Limite inter duas Belsias, quæ cognominantur Solonia & Vindocina: fines longe lateque extendens, ad Santonas usque, ut quidam volunt. Dictus ab Vindocino Opido: sic Venantius Fortunatus appellat, quod vulgo Vendosme. Ptolemæo forte Ουνδικον (sic enim legendum) est Aulerciorum Cenomanorum, in Gallia Lugdunensi vrbs. Nihil hic adfirmo. Nam Ουνδικον illud, certius fortean, est opidum, quod hodie Le Mans; quæ Magni Scaligeri sententia, ut antea monui. Vindocinum Arcem habet vetustam & ejus ævi, quo Gallias invaserunt Franci. Vindocini Comites originem ducunt ex Borboniorum Stemmate. Primum Comitem lego Ludovicum Borbonium, Ioannis Marcæ Clermontijq; Comitis F. Successerunt huic recta linea Filius Ioannes, Francisus Nepos, & Karolus Pronepos, quem Primum Vindocini Ducem creavit Franciscus I Galliarum Rex. Filium Karolus habuit Antonium, Vindocini Ducem, Franciæ Parem, & per Ioannam Albretam Conjugem, Navarrorum Regem, quo natus Henricus Borbonius, Galliæ ejus nominis IV, Navarrææque Monarcha potentissimus, Bearnij Princeps, Dux Vindocini, &c. Turonensis Ducatus, Duché de Touraine, incipit tribus supra Ambaciensem Vrbem Miliaribus, versus Blesas; terminatur in Vicis, qui vulgo La Chapelle Blanche, in Spiritualibus agnoscens Episcopum Andegavensem, & Chousi. Hi enim Limites statuunt inter Turonenses & Andegavenses. Incredibilem Regionis Amœnitatem amœniorem facit placidissima suave-spirantis Aëris constitutio; adeo ut totius Galliæ Hortus atque Pomarium vocetur. Vini Frumentique ferax est: Nemora habet Venationi commoda. Metropolis Ducatus est Caesarodunum Turonum; quod Ptolemæo Καισαρόδουνον Turoniorum; hos enim Turupiis exturbatis apud Nobilissimum Geographum substituendos antea monui: Turonem vocat Sidonius Apollinaris; Turonicam Gregorius Turonensis: Vernacule Tours. Iactant Incolæ Conditorem Vrbis Turnum, ejusque audent monstrare Sepulcrum. Martinopolin etiam ab D. Martino nominat Mathæus Vindocinensis in sua Tobiæ Historia. Vrbs opibus & Ædificiorum præstantia nobilis. Vicinus illi ad Orientem Ligeris, cujus beneficio multæ ex Oceano Merces Incolis subvehuntur: ad Meridiem & Occidentem Idra fluit. Mercatura & Lanificio claret. Populus ibi sincerus, Regi suo fidelis & obsequens. Archiepiscopalis est Sedes, cui Antistites præfuerunt multi, doctrina {a}arina sanctitateque præstantes: inter eos etiam D. Martinus, de quo tres extant Libri Sulpitij Severi. Suffraganei sunt huic Sedi omnes fere Episcopi Britannorum, Cenomanorum & Andium. Vrbs Turonum ab initio Coronæ Francicæ fuit inserta. Primus Ludovicus III post factas Danorum & Normannorum in Galliam irruptiones, eam transtulit in Ingelgerum Comitem Andegavensem; quo hostiles Barbarorum impetus copijs suis validius repelleret, & Ligeris oram commodius propugnaret. In Campestribus & Territorio Turonij memorabili pugna aliquot Saracenorum millia (quadringenta fuisse narrant) sunt cæsa, obtruncato etiam Rege ab Karolo Martello, anno 10 CCXXV, ut Beda notat. Mirum est Rusticos ejus rei, tamquam nuperæ, memoriam conservare. Locus dicitur S. Martinus Bellus. Minorum gentium hujus Ducatus opida sunt Ambocia, Langersum, Chinonum, & alia. Ambociam, Vicum Ambocienfem vocat Gregorius Turonensis; hodie Amboise: opidum ad Ligerim loco tam amœno situm, ut cum omnibus alijs hujus Regi certare audeat; ut mirum non sit, Reges ibi sæpe degere solitos. Langersum, Langers opidum non ignobile, paulo supra confluentes Ligerim & Indrum versus Orientem. Chinonum, Chinon, Opidum Arce præditum, Francorum Regibus olim in delicijs, præsertim Karolo VII, quo tempore Æmuli non alio illum dignabantur titulo, quam Regis Biturigum. Territorium habet fertile & amœnum. Ab hoc Opido grandes mitium capiunt versus Pictones Leutæ. Visitur haud procul hinc Pons, qui vulgo de la Nonnain. Arcus sunt lapidei ad medium procurrentes milliare. Insula Bouchardi, L'Isle Bouchard, ad Vigennam est Fluvium, quo circumdatur, instar olim Lutetiæ. Caudi, Caude, situm habet, ubi Vigenna cum Ligeri concurrit. Castellum, Chastillon, opidum Regale ad Indrum Fluvium. Lochum, Loche, ibidem est opidum firme munitum. In Crypta Arcis repertum olim Corpus Viri, staturæ raræ: Ossa loquuntur hominem fuisse octo Pedum: inventus narratur insidens grandi Lapidi, Capite in ambas Manus inclinato. Asayum duplex, unum ad Indrum, quod Asay le Bruffe; alterum ad Carim (Cher) Asay le Ferron. Mons Richardi, Mont-Richard, opidum in amœna planitie situm, rupibus silvisque (quæ vulgo Les Forests de Mont-Richard) cinctum. In Suburbanis Domus sunt Subterraneæ, superque eas Horti & Vineta. Paulmiam, Arx, Vicecomitatus titulo gaudet, sita loco edito. Vivarium adjacet, duorum fere milliarium, muro cinctum. Dominum ejus novi Renatum Voyerum, Turonensis Ditionis Baillivum, Caput sine controversia in eo tractu Nobilitatis, Regis Cubicularium, Conchyliatique Ordinis Equitem. Lodonum, Lodon vel Loudon, Pictavien si Ditioni ab nonnullis adscribi solitum: Olim Privatis paruit, nunc Sedes Tribunalis Regij est. Sunt qui Iuliodunum vocant, nescio quo antiquo Scriptore.
units.tr: That was the Upper Beauce and its parts. Next in order comes the Middle Beauce, to which is usually assigned whatever lies on both banks of the Loire from Ratomago, Romorantin, a town on the river Saudram, which is surnamed the Grande, as far as Vendôme; and, on the right bank of the same Loire, whatever stretches from Chasteau-dun to Blois and as far as the fields of the Tourangeaux. This part of Beauce is called Vindocina, Vendosmoise, because it ends there towards the north. It surpasses the other Beauces in fertility. It comprises partly the counties of Blesensis, Dunensis and Tonnerrensis, and partly the duchies of Vendôme and Touraine. The County of Blois, Comitatui Blesensis (La Comté de Blois; perhaps the Pagus Blesensis of Nithard), took its name from the ancient town of Blesense. The Blesenses were known to Gregory of Tours around the year 560. Mention is made in the Life of Agiulf of the Castri Blesensis on the side of a hill which the Loire flows past. Certainly the castle still stands today on an elegant rock, separated from the town to the west, providing a seat and palace for kings, and thence a view both over the city itself and the neighbouring fields. It is commonly called the Regalis Civitas, the Royal City, because it is both a most pleasant retreat often chosen by kings and consecrated to the education of their own children and those of other princes. Its air is very healthy, its soil very agreeable, and its fields most lovely, planted with fine vines and abounding in every kind of grain and fruit tree. It has very sweet springs, and streams whose murmur is sweet because of their winding course. It has two churches: one in the citadel, dedicated to St Saviour, richly endowed with revenues by the counts and by the kings who succeeded them; the other in the town itself, sacred to St James. In the former can be seen tombs of great artistry, of the counts of Blois Ludovici & Guidonis, likewise of Ioannis, Duke of Albany, and of many others. Among the people of Blois there are admirable remains of aqueducts, of such extent and height that they readily allow passage to three horsemen riding abreast. It is likely that these are the work of the Romans. The citizens and inhabitants are very courteous, affable and humane, most devoted to cleanliness and splendour in food, drink and dress; in their mouths, as it were, the purest propriety of the French language dwells. Second from this city, the collapsed stone ruins of buildings are pointed out. The people call the place Orcheze. The Orchestra was a part of the Roman theatre among the ancients. I assert nothing. The neighbours want it to have been a granary of Julius Caesar. Among the first counts of Blois I find Theobaldum, surnamed the Seniorem, son of Gedo and kinsman of Rollo Robert, first Duke of Normandy. He had a son Othonem (alijs Fudo dicitur), who, with the principalities of his father and his own virtue increased, was Count of Champagne, Blois, Brie, Tours and Chartres. He begot Theobaldum II and Stephanum, who succeeded his brother when he died without issue. Born of Adela, daughter of William the Conqueror, King of England, were the others, Theobaldus III and Stephanus. The son of the former, who bore his father's name, died without children and left the ample inheritances of his uncle Stephen, who had obtained the kingdom of England, to his posterity. Among these is read Ludovicus, son of Henry II, Count of Champagne and Brie, grandson of Henry the Liberal, great-grandson of King Stephen, who was Count of Blois. Moreover, for his outstanding exploits at Constantinople he was granted the Duchy of Romania. After him, Ἀ (Ad) the succession passed, since Theobald also died without issue, to Margareta, his sister's wife, first of Otto, Count of Burgundy, then of Gualtherus, lord of Avesnes. From her was born Maria, Lady of Avesnes, Countess of Chartres and Blois, who married Hugh of Châtillon, Count of Saint-Pol. After her, the historians hand down nothing certain about this county. The Comitatus Dunensis, La Comté de Dunois, has as its chief town Castrodunum, Chasteau-dun. The town, with its citadel, lies on the Loir (commonly Loir, a different river from the Loire, into which it pours at the town of Angers), on a high rock to which access is not easy, not even from the north, where the region spreads out widely to the eye. Rightly is it called Castrodunum, because the castle or bulwark was built on the Dunum. I have shown elsewhere that Dunum in the idiom of the ancient Gauls means a hill or rock. It is fortified with a very large tower. Traces of ruins of splendid buildings here and there in the suburbs testify that it was once larger. The founder of the chief church, sacred to St Magdalen, is said to be Charlemagne. It has four suburbs, larger than the town itself, with buildings more splendid than the town, and adorned with twelve churches. The town, dreadfully devastated in the recent wars, was largely restored by its citizens, who, to declare their determination to perpetuate that effort, use in the town's arms three crescents with the inscription ΕΚΦΕΙΑ [ekpheia], EXSTINCTA REVIVISCO, "Extinguished, I revive". Concerning the Comitatu Tonnorierfi, Comté de Tonnoire, I have at present nothing to write, having been left without those authors who could have defined it. The Ducatus, once a county, Vindocinensis, Duché de Vendosme, begins at Baugency, the boundary between the two Beauces called Solonia and Vindocina, extending its limits far and wide, as far as the Santones, as some wish. It is named from the town Vindocino; so Venantius Fortunatus calls it, commonly Vendosme. In Ptolemy it is perhaps Ουνδικον (for so it should be read), a town of the Aulerci Cenomani in Gallia Lugdunensis. I assert nothing here. For that Ουνδικον, more certainly perhaps, is the town which today is Le Mans; this is the opinion of the great Scaliger, as I said before. Vindocinum has an ancient citadel, of the age when the Franks invaded Gaul. The Counts of Vendôme derive their origin from the stemma of the Bourbons. The first count I read of is Ludovicum Borbonium, son of John Marcus and Count of Clermont. In direct line he was succeeded by his son Ioannes, his grandson Franciscus, and his great-grandson Karolus, whom Francis I, King of France, first created Duke of Vendôme. Karolus had a son Antonium, Duke of Vendôme, Peer of France, who through Joan of Albret, his wife, became King of Navarre. From him was born Henricus Borbonius, Henry IV of France of that name, most powerful monarch of France and Navarre, Prince of Béarn, Duke of Vendôme, etc. The Turonensis Ducatus, Duché de Touraine, begins three miles above the town of Amboise, towards Blois, and ends at the villages commonly called La Chapelle Blanche, which in spiritual matters acknowledges the Bishop of Angers, and Chousi. For these are the limits set between the people of Tours and of Angers. The very placid and gently breathing constitution of the air makes the incredible pleasantness of the region even more pleasant, so that it is called the Hortus and Pomarium of the whole of France. It is fertile in wine and grain, and has woods suitable for hunting. The metropolis of the duchy is Caesarodunum Turonum, which in Ptolemy is Καισαρόδουνον of the Turonians; for I said earlier that the Turones, driven out of the Turupii, must be substituted, according to that most noble geographer. Sidonius Apollinaris calls it Turonem, Gregory of Tours Turonicam; in the vernacular it is Tours. The inhabitants boast that the founder of the town was Turnus, and they dare to show his tomb. Matthew of Vendôme in his History of Tobias also calls it Martinopolin after St Martin. The town is noted for its wealth and the excellence of its buildings. To its east lies the Loire, by whose favour many goods from the ocean are carried up for the inhabitants; to the south and west flows the Indre. It is famous for trade and wool-making. The people there are sincere, loyal and obedient to their king. It is an archiepiscopal see, over which many bishops have presided, distinguished for learning and holiness; among them is also St Martin, about whom three books by Sulpicius Severus survive. Almost all the bishops of the Britons, the Cenomani and the Andes are suffragans of this see. The town of Tours was from the beginning incorporated into the French crown. Louis III, after the invasions of the Danes and Normans into Gaul, transferred it to Ingelger, Count of Anjou, so that he might more strongly repel the hostile assaults of the barbarians with his forces and more conveniently defend the bank of the Loire. In the plains and territory of Tours, in a memorable battle, several thousand Saracens (they say four hundred thousand) were slain, and their king too was cut down, by Charles Martel, in the year 732, as Bede notes. It is strange that the country people keep the memory of this event as if it were recent. The place is called S. Martinus Bellus. The lesser towns of this duchy are Ambocia, Langersum, Chinonum, and others. Gregory of Tours calls Ambociam Vicum Ambocienfem; today it is Amboise, a town on the Loire situated in so pleasant a place that it dares to compete with all the others of this region, so that it is no wonder that kings were accustomed often to stay there. Langersum, Langeais, is a not undistinguished town, a little above the confluence of the Loire and the Indre, towards the east. Chinonum, Chinon, is a town endowed with a citadel, once a delight of the kings of the Franks, especially of Charles VII, at a time when his rivals did not deign to address him by any other title than King of Bourges. It has fertile and pleasant territory. From this town large lakes extend towards the Poitevin marshes. Not far from here can be seen a bridge, commonly called de la Nonnain, whose stone arches project into the middle of a mile. Insula Bouchardi, L'Isle-Bouchard, lies by the river Vienne, which surrounds it, as Paris was once surrounded by the Seine. Caudi, Chouzé, is situated where the Vienne joins the Loire. Castellum, Châtillon, is a royal town on the Indre river. Lochum, Loches, is a town strongly fortified in the same place. In the crypt of the citadel there was once found the body of a man of rare stature; the bones show that he was eight feet tall. He is reported to have been found sitting on a large stone, with his head bowed to both hands. There are two places called Asayum: one on the Indre, called Asay le Bruffe; the other on the Cher, Asay le Ferron. Mons Richardi, Montrichard, is a town situated on a pleasant plain, surrounded by rocks and woods (commonly Les Forests de Mont-Richard). In the suburbs there are underground houses, and above them gardens and vineyards. Paulmiam, a citadel that enjoys the title of viscounty, is set on a raised place. Adjacent to it is a game park of nearly two miles, enclosed by a wall. Its present lord is Renatus Voyerus, bailiff of the Tours district, undoubtedly the chief of the nobility in that tract, the king's chamberlain and knight of the Order of the Shell. Lodonum, Loudun or Loudon, which some have been accustomed to assign to the district of Poitou, was formerly under private lords; now it is the seat of a royal tribunal. Some call it Iuliodunum, on the authority of I know not what ancient writer.

units.la: Belsia mihi restat Inferior percurrenda, quæ vulgo Basse Beaussé. Ea Campestris omnino est & plana; Frumenti valde ferax, totius Galliæ, ut Sicilia quondam Latij, horreum: Porrecta inter Episcopatus Aurelianensem & Carnutensem ab opido Stampensi procurrit, versus Orientem quidem ad Senones usque, versus Meridiem ad Pontem Aurelianensem. Comprehendit Ducatum Aurelianensem, Ditionesq. vel Territoria Lorriacum & Solemium. Ducatui, Duché d'Orleans, nomen ab Vrbe Primaria ad Ligerim sita, quæ Genabum Cæsari lib.VII, & Hirtio lib.IX; quod qui negant, habent oppositæ omnia veri vestigia & multa argumenta. Nam quo nomine vocandi sunt, inquit suis ad me litteris Scaliger, qui Gram Opidum ad eumdem Fluvium esse putant: inter eos autem Paradinus & Vigenereus. Clare Aimoinus lib.I. cap.v. Genabum, ubi nunc Aurelianis. Vrsini & Manutij Codices apud Cæsarem habent Genabin. Cenabum est apud Antoninum; Κήναβον apud Ptolemæum: an in prima syllaba vitiose? Vitiosius, & contra fidem etiam historiæ, apud Orosium lib.VI cap.XI Cenapum. Γλώσσ. Ρόμα. Straboni lib.IV. Aureliani sis Vrbs legitur apud Sidonium lib. VIII. Epist.XV ad Prosperum Papam, & Gregorium Turonensem lib.V. Historiæ cap. XXXIII, & Aimoinum lib.I. cap.V. Aureliana Civitas apud Iordanem de Rebus Geticis. Aurelianus simpliciter nulla inflexione Aimoino paulo ante, Idacio, Bedæ XV Kalend. Decembr. Vluardo VII Eid. Sept. & alijs. Herricus Poëta ad Karolum: Obvius advenienis Vrbem, cui Genabus olim Nomen erat, noto quod deinde recessit ab usu, Diversumque illi nunc Aurelianis habetur. Aurelia item Turonensi lib. i. cap. vii Histor. & in Historia S. Galli & S. Aniani. Unde transnominata? ab Aureliano Imperatore, nisi fallit Otho Frisingensis lib. iiii. cap. xli. Ridendi qui ab Aurelia Cæsaris Matre, qui item ab Auro dirivant. Tempore Cæsaris hæc Vrbs Carnutibus adcensebatur: præclara hodie, ipsq; Franciæ connumeranda, quæ primi nominis. Aëre gaudet puro atque salubri. Qua Septemtrionem spectat, paulo editiore est loco; unde Templum S. Crucis magnificum, sed non ita pridem cum aliis omnibus, quod dolendum sane, diruțum, advenientibus augustæ se ostentabat. Multum ejus prolata sunt Pomeria ab ea parte, qua itur in Burgundiam. Visuntur etiam nunc antiqua Mœnia post ædem S. Stephani: monstratur & ibi Porta magni ævi, quæ hodie Porta Vetus Burgundiæ dicitur; 10 & quidquid Ædificiorum ultra est ad recentiorem usque Portam, Nova vocatur Civitas. Mœnia adluit Ligeris, Ponte stratus per Mediam Insulam lapideo, in quo Monimenta videre est, Ioanna Darcia Virgini, quæ sub Karolo vi obsessam ab Anglis Vrbem anno cIↄ cccc xxviii scribitur liberasse, erecta. Libellum integrum ea de re composuit Ioan. Ludovicus Micquellus Aurelianensis ad Karolum Lotharingum Cardinalem. In perpetuam Liberationis memoriam Cives, cujuscumque generis, quotannis die viii mensis Mai, Supplicationibus publice decretis, gratulabundi Civitatem obeuntes ad Pontem procedunt; ibique ad Crucem, ubi inhibitus perhibetur Anglorum irruentium impetus, re divina peracta, in Vrbem redeunt. Appellatur κατ' ἐξοχὴν vernacule La Feste de la Ville. Ad Pontis Caput Suburbanum est egregium, quod Portereau vulgo. Forum Primarium Eflappe audit, quod ibi Vina stabulentur, alio exportanda. Suppliciorum locus Martroy, ab Martyrum, ut volunt, memoria, nominatur. Academiam habet inter alias Galliæ celebrem; quæ anno cIↄ ccc xii ab Philippo Pulcro instituta, Iurisprudentiæ cum primis est conservatrix. Ex ea quot Viri Docti olim prodierint, hodieque prodeant, longum esset commemorare. Silentio certe non prætereundus Bertrandus Burdigalensis Archiepiscopus, qui postea P. M. creatus Clemens v fuit dictus. Ibi docentes audivi anno cIↄ Iↄ lxxxiii & seqq. Ioannem Robertum & Guilielmum Forncrium; hunc certe, Virum cum in sua Palæstra versatissimum, tum facundissimum, atque etiam meliorum litterarum doctissimum; quod edita ab eo testantur Opera. Lingua Franco-Romana hic tam pura, ut Gallis omnibus sit Aurelianismus, Vocibus quibusdam emotis, qui Græcis quondam Atticismus. Ejus elegantiæ Virgines mirum in modum dant operam, itaque in ea excellunt, ut Pindarum exprimere se glorientur, quod Pindarisser appellant. Vrbs Episcopatus titulo superbit. Inter Primos illos & Sanctiores Præsules primus facile fuit Anianus, qui ob Vitæ sanctitatem Sanctorum adscriptus est numero, Divusque Tutelaris Vrbi lectus. exstat ejus Vita. Legendi de eo Sidonius Apollinaris lib. viii. Epist. xv. Gregor. Turon. lib. ii. cap. vii. Hist. Petrus Equilinus libro viii, cap. xlviii, Beda xv Kalend. Decembr. Martyr. Roman. Reges hic quoque aliquot inauguratos fuisse, ut Remis, loquuntur Historiæ. Ager illi undique rerum omnium fertilissimus: Vinorum ferax, quæ 40 nobilissima in alias Europæ partes magna copia evehuntur, nomen ab Vrbe consequuta. Olim hæc, ut Galliarum reliquæ, proprios & indigenas habuisse videtur Principes: postea cum cæteris paruit Romanis; quibus vel ejectis vel pacto digressis, Francorum Reges, qui eam Regni titulo decorarunt, cœpit agnoscere. Primus ejus Rex fertur Clodomirus; cui cum prole mortuo Clotarius frater successit, qui item totius Galliæ Imperium, Fratribus omnibus exstinctis, est adeptus. Ita semper Coronæ mansit connexa usque ad Valesiorum tempora. Ioannes Rex à Patre Philippo jussus eam Ducatus titulo ac perpetuo quasi Regni Feudo, Fratri Philippo Comiti Valesio contulit. Ab eo tempore Ducatus appellationem retinuit. Philippo sine Prole masculà defuncto, secundo ad Regnum Francicum redit. Cautum postremo, ut semper Aurelianensis Ducatus Secundo Regis Filio, quemadmodum Primo Delphinatus, cederet. Quondam ab Attila Hunnorum Rege, qui se Dei Flagellum nominabat, obsessa, & paulum aberat capta legitur; sed liberata rursum partim strenua Civium pugnantium industria, partim adcurrentibus cum auxilio validaque Militum manu Actio Patricio, Merovæo Francorum & Theodorico Gothorum Regibus, qui Hunnos fugarunt, & ab Vrbe discedere, relictis spoliis, compulerunt. Consulendi Aimoinus lib. i. cap. vi, & seq. Petrus Equilinus lib. x. cap. LXXI, Sigebertus ad annum CCCC LIII, Gregorius Turonensis lib. II, cap. VII, Iornandes cap. XXXVII, qui tamen ab Historia nonnihil recedit: & alij ejus ævi. Aniani Merita & Orationes magni hic ponderis fuisse, notant Sidonius Apollin. lib. VIII. Epist. XVI, Idacius in Chron. MS, Auctor Historiæ S. Aniani, cum Gregorio Turonensi & Aimoino, quorum jam memini. Addam hic quod fidem excedere videtur. Memorant Cives, duos olim captivos fuisse apud Turcas Viros Christianos: de quibus quum Supplicium esset sumendum, pridie firmissimis Arcis fuisse inclusos: eos autem, quum nocte, cui Supplicij dies inluceret, majorem in modum se commendassent Reliquijs S. Crucis, quas in Aurelianensi Urbe servari fama erat, una cum Arcis ex tam longinqua Regione Aurelham fuisse per Aerem transportatos, intraque ædem positos S. Crucis: Mox, pultantibus nullo movente Campanis, factoque ab Civibus concursu, Arcas ante Altare fuisse inventas; apertis, Captivos, qui apud Turcas adhuc esse se, quaeque ad Supplicium spectabant jam parata, putabant, prodijsse; re cognita, vovisse se oblaturos singulis annis Canales duas, magnitudine qua Arcæ fuerant, Cera plenas. Quidquid sit hujus miraculi in medio relinquo. Ipse certe fieri Oblationem hanc vidi, pridie S. Crucis, secunda Mai; atque adeo ab coactis Heredibus, hujusmodi Voti, Majorum facto, damnatis. Multa de hac Urbe apud Franciscum Belleforestium. Leo Trepautius, Senator Aurelianensis, peculiarem de Patria sua scriptit Libellum. Nostro tempore bello Civili miserum in modum jactata est.
units.tr: Belsia remains for me to survey: the Inferior part, commonly called Basse Beaussé. This region is entirely flat and open country, and so fertile in grain that it was once to all of Gaul what Sicily was to Latium, its granary. Stretching between the bishoprics of Orléans and Chartres, it runs from the town of Étampes eastward as far as the Senones and southward to the Bridge of Orléans. It includes the Duchy of Orléans, and the territories or lordships of Lorris and Sully. The Duchy, Duché d'Orléans, takes its name from the chief city on the Loire, which Genabum Caesar mentions in Book VII, and Hirtius in Book VIII. Those who deny this have no lack of evidence and many arguments on their side. Scaliger, in his letter to me, asks by what name those are to be called who think the town of Gien lies on the same river. Among them are Paradin and Vigenère. Aimoin clearly says in Book I, chapter 5, "Genabum, where Orléans now stands." The Ursinus and Manutius manuscripts of Caesar read Genabin. Cenabum is found in Antoninus, and Κήναβον [Kēnabon] in Ptolemy. Is the first syllable wrongly written there? More wrongly, and even against the testimony of history, Orosius, Book VI, chapter 11, has Cenapum. The Glossary of Rome has it too. In Strabo, Book IV, the city is called Aurelian. The name Aureliani appears in Sidonius, Book VIII, Letter 15, to Pope Prosper; in Gregory of Tours, Book V, chapter 33 of his History; and in Aimoin, Book I, chapter 5. Jordanes, in his De rebus Geticis, has Aureliana Civitas. Without inflection, Aurelianus appears in Aimoin shortly before, in Idatius, in Bede (15 Kalends of December), in Wandalbert (7 Ides of September), and elsewhere. The poet Herric, addressing Charles, writes: "Meeting you as you approached the city, which was once called Genabus, a name that has since fallen out of use, and which is now called differently, Aurelianis." Aurelia likewise appears in Gregory of Tours, Book I, chapter 7 of his History, and in the histories of St Gall and St Anian. Whence the change of name? From the emperor Aurelian, unless Otto of Freising, Book IV, chapter 41, is mistaken. Those who derive it from Aurelia, mother of Caesar, or from aurum, gold, are to be laughed at. In Caesar's time this city belonged to the Carnutes. Today it is distinguished and must be counted among the foremost cities of France itself. It enjoys a pure and wholesome air. On the side facing north it stands on slightly higher ground, and there the magnificent church of the Holy Cross used to show itself to arriving visitors, a splendid sight until not long ago, when, sadly, it was razed along with all the others. Its walls were pushed out considerably on the side toward Burgundy. Even now the ancient ramparts can be seen behind the church of St Stephen, and there is pointed out a gate of great age, today called the Old Gate of Burgundy*; and whatever buildings lie beyond it, up to the newer gate, are called the New City. The Loire washes the walls. A bridge of stone crosses through the middle island, and on it stands a monument erected to Joan of Arc, the Virgin who, under Charles VI, is recorded as having freed the city, then besieged by the English, in the year 1428. Jean-Louis Micquel of Orléans wrote a whole little book on this matter, addressed to Charles, Cardinal of Lorraine. In perpetual memory of this deliverance, the citizens of every rank, each year on the 8th day of May, by public decree, go in procession with thanksgiving, come out of the city to the bridge, and there, at the cross where the assault of the attacking English is said to have been halted, after the sacred rites are performed, return into the city. This is called, par excellence [κατ' ἐξοχὴν], in the vernacular, La Feste de la Ville. At the head of the bridge, on the suburban side, lies the fine suburb commonly called Portereau. The main marketplace is called Eflappe, because wine is stored there before being exported elsewhere. The place of execution is Martroy, named, as some say, after the memory of the martyrs. The city has a university, celebrated among the others in France, founded in the year 1312 by Philip the Fair, which above all preserves the study of law. To list how many learned men have come from it in the past and still come from it today would take too long. Surely not to be passed over in silence is Bertrand, archbishop of Bordeaux, who was later made supreme pontiff and called Clement V. I heard lecturers there in the year 1583 and following: John Robert and William Fornier. Fornier, a man as highly practised in his own arena as he was eloquent, and also most learned in better literature, as his published works attest. The Franco-Roman language here is so pure that Aurelianism is, for all Frenchmen, what Atticism once was for the Greeks, provided certain words are removed. The young women here take remarkable pains over this elegance, and excel in it to such a degree that they boast of imitating Pindar, which they call Pindarisser. The city prides itself on its episcopal title. Among its first and holiest prelates the first was easily Anianus, who, because of the holiness of his life, was counted among the saints and is read of as the divine patron of the city. His life survives. For him one should read Sidonius Apollinaris, Book VIII, Letter 15; Gregory of Tours, Book II, chapter 7 of his History; Peter Equilinus, Book VIII, chapter 48; Bede, 15 Kalends of December; and the Roman Martyrology. The histories also state that several kings were anointed here, as at Reims. The land around is everywhere most fertile in all things, rich in wines, which, the noblest of their kind, are exported in great quantity to other parts of Europe, and it takes its name from the city. Formerly this region, like the rest of Gaul, seems to have had its own native princes; afterwards it submitted with the others to the Romans. When they were either expelled or departed under a treaty, it began to acknowledge the kings of the Franks, who adorned it with the title of kingdom. Its first king is said to have been Clodomir, after whose death, with his children, his brother Clotaire succeeded, who likewise obtained the rule of all Gaul when all his brothers had died. Thus it remained always joined to the Crown, up to the times of the Valois. King John, ordered by his father Philip, gave it, with the title of duchy and as a kind of perpetual fief of the kingdom, to his brother Philip, Count of Valois. From that time it kept the name of duchy. When Philip died without male issue, it returned to the Frankish kingdom for the second time. Finally it was provided that the Duchy of Orléans should pass, as the first son of the king holds Dauphiné, to the king's second son. Once it was besieged by Attila, king of the Huns, who called himself the Scourge of God, and it is read that it was almost taken; but it was freed again, partly by the vigorous efforts of the citizens who fought, partly by Aetius the patrician, along with Merovech, king of the Franks, and Theodoric, king of the Goths, who came to its aid with a strong force of soldiers, put the Huns to flight, and compelled them to leave the city, abandoning their plunder. For this consult Aimoin, Book I, chapter 6 and following; Peter Equilinus, Book X, chapter 71; Sigebert under the year 453; Gregory of Tours, Book II, chapter 7; Jordanes, chapter 37, who nevertheless departs somewhat from history; and other writers of that age. That the merits and prayers of Anianus were of great weight here is noted by Sidonius Apollinaris, Book VIII, Letter 16; Idatius in his unpublished Chronicle; the author of the History of St Anian; and Gregory of Tours and Aimoin, whom I have already mentioned. I will add here something that seems to go beyond belief. The citizens report that once two Christian men were captives among the Turks; when their execution was to be carried out, they had been shut up the day before in a very strongly fortified castle. But on the night when the day of their execution was to dawn, they commended themselves most earnestly to the relics of the Holy Cross, which were said to be kept in the city of Orléans. Then the castle, together with them, was carried through the air from so distant a region to Orléans and placed inside the church of the Holy Cross. Soon, without anyone moving them, the bells began to ring, and a crowd of citizens gathered. The castle was found standing before the altar. When it was opened, the captives came out, thinking they were still among the Turks and that the preparations for their execution were ready; when the matter became known, the citizens vowed that they would offer every year two candles, as large as the castle had been, full of wax. Whatever the truth of this miracle, I leave it undecided. I myself certainly saw this offering made, on the day before the feast of the Holy Cross, on the second of May; and so, by the act of their ancestors, the heirs, though unwillingly, are bound by this kind of vow. Much about this city is found in Francois de Belleforest. Leo Trepautius, a senator of Orléans, wrote a separate little book about his homeland. In our own time it was wretchedly tossed about by civil war.

units.la: Territorium Lorriacum, Pais de Lorris dicitur ab Lorriaco. Opido quondam non ignobili. In Castellania Lorriaci primo factæ sunt Consuetudines, quibus hodieque utuntur Aurelianenses.
units.tr: The Territory of Lorris, called in French the Pays de Lorris, takes its name from Lorris, once a town of some note. In the Castellany of Lorris the customs were first drawn up, which the people of Orléans still use today.

units.la: Solonia, Solongne, restat delineanda; pars Inferioris Belsiæ, comprehendens quidquid est trans Ligerim ab Aurelianensi Urbe ad Ambocienses usque; & hinc porrigens se versus Orientem per adjacentia Cari Fluvio loca. Duplex est: Superior, ubi Agri Siliginei, Ericeta, Silvæ. Inferior multis Rivulis Patcuisque ornata; arenosior, & non ita pinguis. Præcipua Urbs, quæ vulgo Romorantin. Antiquam esse docent Ruderā. Rodrina forte in Notitia M. S. Incolæ, ne nimium discedant ab Vulgata appellatione, Romam Antiquam suum opidum audent dicere. Castellum Novum, Chasteau-neuf opidum Castro validum. Multa hic quondam Viridaria, Prætoriaque exhilarandis animis consecrata; Melfensium Principum hodie Dominium. Aubinium, Aubigny, Sedes quondam Regalis, quam ibi erexerat Ludovicus XI. Clariacum, cujus mentio in Vita S. Liphardi, hodie Nostre Dame de Clery; Opidum Peregrinationibus Religionis caufla nobile. Iargolium, vernacule Iargeau nominatur.
units.tr: Sologne (Solonia, in French Solongne) remains to be described. It is part of Lower Berry, comprising all the land beyond the Loire from the city of Orléans as far as Amboise, and extending eastward through the districts adjoining the river Cher. It is of two kinds: the Upper, where there are fields of rye, heaths and woods; and the Lower, adorned with many streams and marshes, sandier and not so rich. Its principal town is what is commonly called Romorantin; ruins show that it is ancient. Perhaps it is the Rodrina of the unpublished Notitia; lest they stray too far from the common name, the inhabitants venture to call their town Romorantin, "Old Rome." Châteauneuf, a town strong with its castle, is in the hands of the Princes of Melfi today; here there were once many pleasure gardens and halls dedicated to the cheering of minds. Aubigny (Aubinium) was once a royal seat, which Louis XI had built there. Clery (Clariacum), whose mention occurs in the Life of Saint Liphardus, is today Notre-Dame de Clery, a town renowned for religious pilgrimages. Jargeau, in the vernacular Jargeau, is its name.

units.la: Cap. XXIII.
units.tr: Chapter 23.

units.la: Campania.
units.tr: Champagne.

units.la: CAMPANIÆ, quæ tertium in Celtica mea locum occupat (Comté de Champagne) nomen, quemadmodum Italicæ, à Camporum latitudine longitudineque, ut notat Gregorius Turonensis lib. IX. Hist. cap. XIV, & libro de Gloria Confessor. cap. LXVII. Est enim Campestris admodum & plana, Sementique apta. Qui illi Circundant eam undique Brienfium, Burgundionum, Karolesiorum & Lotharingorum Ditiones atque Territoria. Cælum ibi serenum; Aer temperatus; Flumina magna, salubria, piscosa: Populus industrius, suisque commodis & rei faciendæ invigilans: Nobilitas frequens & generosa: Civitates lautæ: Pagi Incolis referti: Agri passim Frumento, Vino, omnique Pecorum genere abundant: necque desunt Silvæ, opimas quæ præbent Venationes, jucundaque Aucupia.
units.tr: CHAMPAGNE, which holds third place in my Gaul (Comté de Champagne), takes its name, as the Italian Campania does, from the breadth and length of its plains, as Gregory of Tours notes in Book 9 of his History, ch. 14, and in the book On the Glory of the Confessors, ch. 67. It is indeed very open and flat, and suited to sowing. It is bordered on every side by the lands and territories of the Brienne, Burgundian, Charolais and Lorraine lords. The sky there is clear, the air mild, the rivers large, wholesome and full of fish. The people are industrious and attentive to their own advantage and to making a living. The nobility is numerous and well born. The towns are elegant, the villages full of inhabitants. The fields everywhere abound in wheat, wine and every kind of livestock, and there are no lack of woods that offer rich hunting and pleasant fowling.

units.la: Sedes hic olim habuerunt suas Tricasses, Lingones, Remi, Catalauni, Melda, Senones, & fortean alij, quorum memoria jam obliterata. Tricasses nominantur in memorie notæ Plinij libris; qui Τρικασσιοι Ptolemæo, Tricassini Ammiano, Panegyricis quibusdam & Antiquo Lapidi; Tricæ Herico in Vita S. Germani, Trecs Vulgo Ecclesiastico per compendium; Civitas Trecassium in Notitia Lugdunensi IV. Hodie ubi Troie en Champaigne. Lingones Cæsari, Plinio, aliisque sunt qui Αὶγονες Ptolemæo: mæo: mæo: Fœderatos idem Plinius indigetat: Civitatem Lingonum habet Notitia Provinciarum in Lugdunensi i. Exstat Cohortis ii. Ling. Eq. memoria in elegante Inscriptione, quæ visitur in Piceno vel Marchia Anconitana, in opido, quod olim Forum Sempronij, vulgo Foßambrone: Hodie La Duché, Pairie & Euesché de Langres. Lingonum sæpe meminit Martialis, obliquè eos subinde perstringens. Occurrunt crebro apud eundem Lana, Saga, Tomenta, & Bardocuculli Lingonum. Remi apud Cæsarem & Plinium, qui Ῥήμοι apud Ptolemæum & Strabonem: Fœderatos Plinius nominat: Civitas Remorum Notitiæ Provinciarum in Lugdunensi ii: Duché, Pairie & Archevesché de Reims. Remorum fines Romanorum tempore latissimi fuere; Sequanis, Mediomatricibus, Treviris, Veromanduis, Suessionibus conregionales. Cæsare Gallias administrante post Heduos secundum Dignitatis locum obtinebant. Nominat ipsorum Senatum idem Cæsar, & civitatis Principem atque Præfectum Vertiscum, de quo in Ephemeridibus Belli Gallici multa. Catalaunos, præeuntibus Membranis; scribendos monent Viri docti, qui in Vulgatis Ammiani Marcellini libris Cathelauni. Sic etiam nominantur in exaratis calamo codicibus Eutropij, qui Tetricum notat ab Aureliano superatum apud Catalaunos. Catalaunorum Civitas; Notitiæ Provinciarum Galliæ in Lugdunensi ii, L'Euesché de Chaalon. Ad hos Catalauni pertinent Campi, in quibus prælio magno superatus ab Romanis, Gothis & Francis, Ducibus Actio Patricio, Theodorico & Merovæo, Hunnorum Rex Attila, anno ab V. C. cıɔ cc iii. Imper. Cæsare Fl. Marciano P. F. Augusto & Clodio Adelphio V. C. Romæ Coss. ab Christo nato cccci, cæsis utrimque clxii millibus, exceptis xc millibus Gepidarum & Francorum, qui paulo ante occubuerant. Legendi Sidonius Apollinar. Carm. vii, Cassiodorus lib. iii Variar. Epist. i & alibi, Paulus Diaconus lib. v, Isiodor. in Chronic. Iornandes de Rebus Goth. cap. xxxvi, & seqq. Gregorius Turonensis variis locis, Aimoinus lib. i, cap. vi, Sigebertus in Chronic. Otto Frisingensis lib. iv, cap. xxvi, Freculphus Lexoviensis lib. v, cap. xiv, Tom. ii, Idacius M. S. Sabellicus Ennead. viii, lib. i, Gaguinus lib. i, & alij. Delineat hos Campos, locumque Pugnæ Iornandes, cap. xxxvi: Convenitur itaque in Campos Catalaunicos, qui & Mauricij nominantur, c. Leugas, ut Galli vocant, in longum tenentes, & lxx in latum: cap. xxxviii; Erat autem positio loci declivi tumore, in modum collis excrescens. Et in fine cap. Fit ergo de loci opportunitate certamen. Attila suos dirigit, qui cacumen montis invaderent, sed à Thorismundo & Aetio præventus est, qui elutiati collis excelsa ut conscenderent, superiores effecti sunt, venientesque Hunnos Montis berrificio facile turbavere. Indicat ibi Iornandes hos Campos etiam Mauricios fuisse nominatos: Sic quoque vocat Callimachus Experiens; Mauriacos autem Freculphus: Mauriacus Campus est apud Gregorium Turonensem lib. ii, cap. vii; Mauriacum & Mauriacensis Campania apud Idacium; unde & Mauriacensis Pugna in Legibus Burgundionum. Alij Catalaunos Campos Tolosæ proximos locant, cumque Catalanis, qui ibi, confundunt. Male. Numquam enim eo progressus Attila. Sunt qui sic dictos volunt ab Catalico, quod in Montanis Arverniæ situm, cujusque mentio in Historia MS. S. Ægidij. Certe qui posterioris sententiæ non invalida habent argumenta: Loci Naturam, ab Iornande Paulouque Diacono descriptum, mire concinere: esse in planicie Catalaunensi Collem; in ejus apice Crucem fixam, quæ vulgo Croix des Batailles: in eadem planicie Vicos esse quibus cognomen de Catalaco; inter alios vetustissimum, qui in Panchartis de Veterrimo Campo vocatur; alterum, qui Entilliacum Catalaunensis, quem ab Attila nomen sumsisse sibi persuadent doctiores Indigenæ: Rivulum item præterlabi, qui planiciem in xII Aquitanicas Leucas protensam intersecat; Rivulum autem in Campis Catalaunicis fluxisse, tradere Paulum Diaconum lib. iv: &, quod omnium validissimum argumentum, Tractum dici Mauriacum, vulgo Prevosté de Mauriac ab Mauriaco Urbe, quam huic planiciei adjacentem olim in his Montanis præcipuam fuisse loquitur Historia Autremonij, quæ adhuc in Membranis. Sed pugnat cum his, & quæ alia in medium adferri possunt, obstatque considerata penitratius Attilæ Expeditio. Eum quidem Pannonijs egressum in Belgicam primum per Germaniam venisse, certo est certius. Affirmant omnes, quos paulo ante laudavi. Sequutum mox Metensis Urbis excidium, Gregorio Turonensi teste lib. ii, cap. vi: Hinc Treuirorum direptio, quæ apud Aimoinum lib. i, cap. vi: mox Tricassium obsidio, de qua Sidonius Apollin. lib. viii, Epist. xv: ad extremum Aurelianis irruptio, nec direptio, cujus ibidem meminit Sidonius.
