Iam si verum, quod unanimi consensu traditur, Attilam fractum, exque confinalibus Ligeri locis, cum ab alijs, tum ab Actio (qui inde Ligeris liberator Sidonio lib. vii, Epist. xii) pulsum & fugatum, evestigio ad Belgas se contulisse: qui esse poterit, ut in montana Arverniæ, centum ab Aurelianensi Urbe Leucis dissita, præcipitem se dederit; præcipue quum tam magnis copijs tamque multis impedimentis onerato trajiciendi essent Ligeris, Alanio, & Elaver; peragranda item invia, confragosa, aspera & dura loca. Si Ligerim numquam (quod omnino verum est) Attila transgressus fuerit, fallit falliturque Paradinus, qui Lugdunum ab eo eversum, ab Majorano autem Augusto restitutum scribit: labuntur item, qui ulteriora Lugduno versus Meridiem loca, Vasatum, Nemausensium, aliorumque, Attilæ ignes & furores senisse, memoriæ produnt. Fuerunt igitur in Belgica Campi Catalaunici, sic dicti à Catalauno, de quo post. Designat eos, inque Belgica notat non obscure Sidonius Apollinaris Carmine vii:
units.tr: The Tricasses, Lingones, Remi, Catalauni, Melda, Senones, and perhaps others, once had their seats here, though the memory of some of them has now faded. The Tricasses are named in Pliny's books, and as Τρικασσιοι [Trikassioi] by Ptolemy, as Tricassini by Ammianus, in certain Panegyrics and an ancient inscription. Heric, in the Life of St Germanus, calls them Tricae, and common ecclesiastical usage shortens the name to Trecs. The Notitia of Lugdunensis IV has Civitas Trecassium. Today it is Troyes in Champagne. The Lingones are named by Caesar, Pliny and others, and by Ptolemy as Αἰγονες [Aigones]. Pliny also calls them Foederati. The Notitia of the Provinces, in Lugdunensis I, has Civitas Lingonum. An elegant inscription, which can be seen in Picenum or the March of Ancona, in the town formerly called Forum Sempronii and now commonly Fossombrone, records the memory of the Second Cohort of the Lingones, mounted. Today they are La Duché, Pairie & Euesché de Langres, the Duchy, Peerage and Bishopric of Langres. Martial often mentions the Lingones, sometimes glancing at them obliquely. The same author frequently mentions Lana, Saga, Tomenta, and the Bardocuculli Lingonum, the Lingonian woollens, cloaks and hooded garments. The Remi appear in Caesar and Pliny, and as Ῥήμοι [Rhemoi] in Ptolemy and Strabo. Pliny names them Foederati. The Notitia of the Provinces, in Lugdunensis II, has Civitas Remorum. Today it is Duché, Pairie & Archevesché de Reims, the Duchy, Peerage and Archbishopric of Reims. In Roman times the territory of the Remi was very extensive, bordering the Sequani, Mediomatrici, Treveri, Veromandui and Suessiones. While Caesar governed Gaul, they held the second place in rank after the Aedui. Caesar names their senate and their chief magistrate and prefect, Vertiscus, about whom there is much in the Commentaries on the Gallic War. The learned advise that the Catalauni should be written so, following the manuscripts, whereas in the printed books of Ammianus Marcellinus it appears as Cathelauni. They are named in the same way in handwritten copies of Eutropius, who records that Tetricus was overcome by Aurelian near the Catalauni. The Notitia of the Provinces of Gaul, in Lugdunensis II, has Catalaunorum Civitas; today it is L'Euesché de Chaalon, the Bishopric of Châlons. To the Catalauni belong the Campi, the Plains, where Attila, King of the Huns, was overcome in a great battle by the Romans, Goths and Franks, led by Aetius the patrician, Theodoric and Merovech. This was in the year 1203 from the founding of the city, in the reign of the emperor Caesar Flavius Marcianus Pius Felix Augustus, when Clodius Adelphius, of consular rank, and Marcianus were consuls at Rome, and in the year 451 after the birth of Christ. On both sides 162,000 were slain, not counting 90,000 Gepids and Franks who had fallen shortly before. The following should be read: Sidonius Apollinaris, Carm. vii; Cassiodorus, book iii of the Variae, letter i and elsewhere; Paulus Diaconus, book v; Isidore, in the Chronicle; Jordanes, On the Origin and Deeds of the Goths, chapter xxxvi and following; Gregory of Tours in various places; Aimoinus, book i, chapter vi; Sigebert, in the Chronicle; Otto of Freising, book iv, chapter xxvi; Frechulf of Lisieux, book v, chapter xiv, vol. ii; Idatius, manuscript; Sabellicus, Ennead viii, book i; Gaguin, book i; and others. Jordanes describes these Plains and the place of battle in chapter xxxvi: So they came to the Catalaunian Plains, which are also called Mauriacian, extending a hundred leagues in length, as the Gauls call them, and seventy in breadth. In chapter xxxviii: Now the position of the place was a sloping rise, swelling up in the manner of a hill. And near the end of the chapter: The contest therefore turned on the advantage of the ground. Attila directed his men to seize the summit of the mountain, but he was anticipated by Thorismund and Aetius, who climbed the high parts of the hill and so got the upper hand, and by the advantage of the mountain they easily threw into confusion the Huns as they came up. Here Jordanes indicates that these Plains were also named Mauriacian. Callimachus Experiens also calls them so, and Frechulf speaks of the Mauriaci. The Mauriacus Campus is in Gregory of Tours, book ii, chapter vii. Mauriacum and the Mauriacensis Campania are in Idatius, whence also the Mauriacensis Pugna in the Laws of the Burgundians. Others place the Catalaunian Plains near Toulouse and confuse them with the Catalans who live there. This is wrong, for Attila never advanced that far. Some want them named from Catalacum, a place situated in the mountains of Auvergne, which is mentioned in the manuscript history of St Giles. Certainly those who hold the latter opinion have no weak arguments. The nature of the place, as described by Jordanes and Paulus Diaconus, agrees remarkably: there is a hill in the Catalaunian plain, with a cross fixed on its summit, commonly called the Croix des Batailles. In the same plain there are villages bearing the surname de Catalaco, among them the most ancient, called in the Panchartes de Veterrimo Campo, and another, Entilliacum Catalaunensis, which learned natives persuade themselves took its name from Attila. A stream also flows past, cutting across the plain, which stretches twelve Aquitanian leagues. Paulus Diaconus, book iv, relates that a stream flowed in the Catalaunian Plains. And the most powerful argument of all: the district is called Mauriacum, commonly the Prevosté de Mauriac, after the city of Mauriac, which the history of Autun, still in manuscript, says was formerly the principal city in these mountains, adjoining this plain. But this and other arguments that can be brought forward conflict with the Expedition of Attila, considered more closely. That he came first from Pannonia into Belgica through Germany is more than certain. All the authors I cited a little earlier affirm it. Soon afterwards came the destruction of the city of Metz, according to Gregory of Tours, book ii, chapter vi; then the plundering of Trier, recorded by Aimoinus, book i, chapter vi; then the siege of Troyes, of which Sidonius Apollinaris speaks, book viii, letter xv; and finally the irruption into Orléans, though not its plundering, which Sidonius also mentions there. Now if it is true, as is handed down by unanimous consent, that Attila was broken and driven out of the places bordering the Loire, both by others and by Aetius (who for that reason is called liberator of the Loire by Sidonius, book vii, letter xii), and that he at once withdrew to the Belgians, how could it be that he threw himself headlong into the mountains of Auvergne, a hundred leagues from the city of Orléans? Especially since, burdened with such great forces and so many baggage trains, he would have had to cross the Loire, the Allier and the Elaver, and to traverse pathless, rugged, rough and hard country. If Attila never crossed the Loire, which is entirely true, then Paradin is mistaken and misled, for he writes that Lyon was overthrown by him and restored by the emperor Majorian. Those also go astray who report that the places beyond Lyon towards the south, Vasatum, Nemausus and others, felt the fires and fury of Attila. So the Catalaunian Plains were in Belgica, and were so called from Catalaunus, of whom more later. Sidonius Apollinaris, in his poem vii, points them out and clearly locates them in Belgica:

units.la: Et jam territiis diffuderat Attila turmis
units.tr: Et jam territis diffuderat Attila turmis

units.la: In Campos se Belga tuos.
units.tr: In Campos se Belga tuos.

units.la: Ipse, quum potissimam Camporum Catalaunicorum partem aliquando peragrarem; Pugnæ locum attentius inspectum deprehendi prorsus convenire cum ijs, quæ ab Iornande, &, qui eum exscribit, Paulo Diacono memorantur. Certe Planicies est maxima, neque eo solum prælio memorabilis. Ammianus Marcellinus lib. xxvii; Et maturato, inquit, itinere omen prope Catalaunos invenit, ad congrediundum promptissimum; &, vallo oportune metato, suisque pro temporis copia cibo recreatis & somno, primo Aurora exortu in aperta planicie composuit aciem, &c. qua de re consulendi etiam Panegyricus Flavicnsium Constantino dictus, & Eutropius in Aureliano. Sed de his satis: ad Veteres, qui superant, Campaniæ Incolas pergo. Melda Cæsari & Plinio, qui eos Liberos cognominat, noti: Μηλδοι Straboni; Μηλδαι Ptolemæo; Melds antiquo Lapidi. Meldos Strabo imprudenter cum Lexovijs ταρωκιαιοι facit, qui sunt in ipso Galliæ meditullio; ubi nunc ad Matronam amnem Meaulx opidum. Senones Cæsari, Plinio, & alijs celebrati: Σένονες Ptolemæo, qui eos in Gallia Lugdunensi describit. Civitas Senonum Notitiæ Provinciarum Galliæ in Lugdunensi iv: Alij, credo, sunt Senones Straboni Nervijs vicini, versus Occasum, de quibus in Normannia. Prioribus, ut mage notis, adscribendas censeo horrendas in Italiam Incursiones: unde & ibi ab Strabone circa Flaminiam, à Polybio in Piceno, ab Suda in Albanorum terra Senones describuntur: de quibus in Italia fuisse. Atrocissimum sane Romanis bellum moverunt anno V. C. cccLxiv Galli Senones, quod ab iis Bellum Senonum Gallicum dicebatur. Dux erat Brennus, Gallorum Regulus. Post pugnam Alliensem (a qua dies Alliensis in Romanorum Fastis) Urbem ingressi, caesis obvijs, omnibusque incendio foedè vastatis, Capitolium, in quod Romana juventus confugerat, obsederunt multos menses; tandemque facta cum Obsessis Pace, Aurique quantitatem stipulati, contra fidem ab M. Furio Camillo Dictatore, Urbem cum copijs conjectis ingressi, partim obtruncati sunt, partim in fugam acti. Quæ omnia suis coloribus plenè delineant Livius lib. v, Florus lib. i, cap. xiii, Eutropius lib. i, Plutarchus in Camillo & Probl. xxiv, Auctor de VV. Illustr. cap. xxiii, Augustinus lib. ii. de Civitate Dei cap. xxii, & lib. iii, cap. xvii, Ovidius lib. vi, Fastor. Orosius lib. ii, cap. xix, Valerius Maximus lib. i, cap. v, in pr. & multi alij Scriptores. Senones scribit Verrius Flaccus apud Festum: ideo appellari, quia novi venerunt ex Trans-Alpina Gallia quasi Kaiνοs, littera immutata. xaiνos enim Græcè, Latinè Novus dicitur. Hæc talia ridere soleo.
units.tr: When I myself was once walking through the greater part of the Catalaunian Plains, I found on careful inspection that the site of the battle corresponds exactly with what is recorded by Jordanes, and by Paulus Diaconus, who copies him. The plain is certainly very large, and it is not remarkable for that battle alone. Ammianus Marcellinus, book xxvii: And having hastened his march, he found an omen near the Catalauni, most ready for battle; and, a rampart being opportunely marked out, and his men refreshed with food and sleep according to the supply of the time, at the first rising of the dawn he drew up his line in the open plain, and so on. On this matter one should also consult the Panegyric of the Flavians spoken to Constantine, and Eutropius in Aurelian. But enough of these matters. I now turn to the ancient inhabitants of Champagne who survive. The Melda are known from Caesar and Pliny, who surnames them Liberi; Strabo has Μηλδοι [Meldoi], Ptolemy Μηλδαι [Meldai], and an ancient inscription Melds. Strabo carelessly places the Meldi together with the Lexovii, who are in the very middle of Gaul, where the town of Meaux now stands on the river Marne. The Senones are celebrated by Caesar, Pliny and others: Σένονες [Senones] in Ptolemy, who describes them in Lugdunensis Gaul. The Notitia of the Provinces of Gaul, in Lugdunensis IV, has Civitas Senonum. There are other Senones, I believe, in Strabo, neighbours of the Nervii towards the west, of whom I shall speak in relation to Normandy. I think the terrible invasions of Italy should be attributed to the better-known ones. Hence Strabo describes the Senones around Flaminia, Polybius in Picenum, and Suidas in the land of the Albani, and it was these who were in Italy. Indeed the Gallic Senones waged a most savage war against the Romans in the year of the city 364. It was called the Gallic War of the Senones. Their leader was Brennus, a chief of the Gauls. After the battle of the Allia, from which the day of the Allia takes its name in the Roman calendar, they entered the city, slaughtered those they met, and foully laid waste everything with fire. They besieged the Capitol, where the Roman youth had taken refuge, for many months. At length a peace was made with the besieged, and they demanded a quantity of gold; but contrary to their pledge, the city was entered by Marcus Furius Camillus, the dictator, with his troops assembled, and some of the Gauls were cut down and others put to flight. All these events are fully depicted in their own colours by Livy, book v; Florus, book i, chapter xiii; Eutropius, book i; Plutarch in Camillus and Problems xxiv; the author On Illustrious Men, chapter xxiii; Augustine, City of God, book ii, chapter xxii, and book iii, chapter xvii; Ovid, Fasti, book vi; Orosius, book ii, chapter xix; Valerius Maximus, book i, chapter v, at the beginning; and many other writers. Verrius Flaccus, in Festus, writes that the Senones were so called because they came as newcomers (novi) from Transalpine Gaul, as if from the Greek καινός [kainos], with the letter changed. For καινός in Greek means novus in Latin. I am accustomed to laugh at such things.

units.la: Inter primos Comitum Campaniæ, ut & Briæ, Blosij, Turonum & Carnutum Progenitores, Geriomem lego Normannum, qui Rollonem, de quo alibi, in eam Franciæ partem, quæ nunc Normannia, est comitatus; ejusque in rectâ linea Successores Theobaldum, Fudonem, Stephanum, Theobaldum ii: cujus Filium Theobaldum iii sine liberis defunctum sequutus est Patruelis Henricus Largus cognomine, Filius Stephani Angliæ Regis, qui Theobaldi ii erat Frater. Henricus Filium habuit cognominem, Campaniæ & reliquarum Ditionum Comitem. Eo improlè mortuo, Comitatum invasit Frater Theobaldus, qui se Comitem Palatinum Campaniæ scriptis; Rex Navarræ morte Avi materni factus, Comitatum in Domum regiam intulit: Successorem, ut fertur (nam ego hujus generis timidius scribo) nactus tam in Comitatu Campaniæ, quam in Navarræ Regno Henricum, cujus filia Joanna, Philippo Pulcro Francorum Regi nupta, Campaniam reliquasque Provincias Coronæ univit: à qua numquam deinceps separatæ.
units.tr: Among the first Counts of Champagne, as also of Brie, Blois, Tours and Chartres, I read of Geriom the Norman, who was count of that part of France which is now Normandy, the one Rollo, of whom I write elsewhere, held. His direct successors were Theobald, Fulk, Stephen and Theobald II. Theobald III, Theobald's son, died without children, and was succeeded by his cousin Henry, surnamed the Large, son of Stephen, King of England, who was the brother of Theobald II. Henry had a son of the same name, Count of Champagne and of his other domains. When this son died childless, his brother Theobald seized the county and styled himself Count Palatine of Champagne. On the death of his maternal grandfather he became King of Navarre and brought the county into the royal house. As successor, so it is reported (for I write about this kind of thing rather timidly), he found in both the county of Champagne and the kingdom of Navarre Henry, whose daughter Joan, married to Philip the Fair, King of the French, united Champagne and the other provinces to the Crown, and they were never separated from it again.

units.la: Campania porrò, quam paulo ante sum ingressus, explicari solet hodie, cum Per Se, tum per Conjacentes ipsi Principatus. Per Se, propriéque consideranda duplex est, Inferior & Superior. Inferiores adcententur Trecassium, Ditionesque, quæ vulgò Ivigny, Bassigny, Vallage.
units.tr: Champagne, which I have just entered, is commonly described today both in itself and through the principalities lying next to it. Considered in itself and properly, it is twofold: Lower and Upper. The Lower part includes Troyes and the domains commonly called Ivigny, Bassigny and Vallage.

units.la: Trecassium nominatur ab ævi posterioris Scriptoribus, quæ hodie Troie, Urbs ad Sequanam. Trecasis Antonino, qui Legionem ibi ponit xxii; Trecassa Ammiano lib. xvi; Trecassa Bedæ, Trecassinum Nithardo lib. i. de Dissensionibus Filiorum Ludovici Pij, &c. Trecæ Sigeberto, Aimoino Monacho, Gregorio Turonensi; Augusta Trecarum Herico lib. iii. Vitæ S. Germani. Nobilissimus Vir Iosephus Scaliger suis ad me Literis monet Veteribus Augustobonam Trecassium appellatam. Augustobonam habet etiam alio itinere Antoninus, apud quem jam dixi esse Trecasses. Quum tamen Augustobona Antonini uno quidem itinere fere incidat in eum locum; ubi Trecasis alia est via; dicendum hanc Urbem duplex habuisse, quod sæpe fiebat, nomen; vel Transnominationem sensim fuisse factam: quod si verum, certum est, quod vitiosè legatur apud Ptolemæum Αὐγουστόβονα. In Itineraria Tabula Peutingeriana scribitur Aug. Bona. Qui Campania quondam erant, ab hac Urbe sæpe se Trecarum dicebant Comites. Episcopalis nunc Sedes, cujus Præsules habet Bellesorestius xxciii. In eorum fuit numero Lupus ille conclamatissimus, quem ab suis Virtutibus laudat passim Sidonius Apollinaris lib. vi Epist. i. iv. & i. ,item lib. ix Epist. xi, ad ipsum scriptis: & lib. viii Epist. xiv, quæ ad Principium Papam Carmine quoque xvi. Videndi & Paulus Diaconus in Marciano, Beda lib. i. Historiæ cap. xvii, Eucherius de Eremi laudibus, Constantius Presbyter in Vita S. Germani lib. i cap. xix, & seqq. Vetus Historia S. Lupi. Urbs ad Sequanam (qui Charianus hic magno est usui & commodo) in plano sita est, fertilis mercaturaque dedita: Arce potens.
units.tr: Troyes is called by writers of a later age what is today Troie, a city on the Seine. Antoninus calls it Trecasis, where he places Legion XXII; Ammianus, book 16, Trecassa; Bede, Trecassa; Nithard, book 1 of the Dissensions of the Sons of Louis the Pious, Trecassinum; Sigebert, Aimoin the monk and Gregory of Tours, Trecae; Heiric, book 3 of the Life of St Germanus, Augusta Trecarum. The most noble man Joseph Scaliger, in a letter to me, reminds me that in ancient times it was called Augustobona Trecassium. Antoninus also has Augustobona by another route, and I have said that Trecasis is on it. Yet since Antoninus's Augustobona falls on one route roughly at the place where Trecasis lies on another, I must say that this city had a double name, as often happened, or that the name was gradually changed. If that is so, it is certain that Αὐγουστόβονα in Ptolemy is misread. In the Peutinger Table it is written Aug. Bona. Those who were once Counts of Champagne often called themselves Counts of Troyes from this city. It is now an episcopal see, whose prelates Belleforest counts as 93. Among them was that most celebrated Lupus, whom Sidonius Apollinaris praises everywhere for his virtues, in book 6, letters 1, 4 and 1, and likewise in book 9, letter 11, written to him, and book 8, letter 14, which he also addressed to Pope Principius in verse, poem 16. Paulus Diaconus in Marcian, Bede in book 1 of his History, chapter 17, Eucherius in On the Praises of the Desert, and Constantius the Presbyter in the Life of St Germanus, book 1, chapter 19 and following, are also worth seeing, as is the old History of St Lupus. The city on the Seine (where Charianus is of great use and convenience here) lies on a plain, is fertile and given to trade, and is strong in its citadel.

units.la: Ivigny Comitatus Campaniam separat a Burgundia; adhærens Senonibus. Oppidum Primarium Ivigny, Iurisdictionem agnoscens Ballivatus Trecensis.
units.tr: The county of Ivigny separates Champagne from Burgundy and adjoins the Senones. Its chief town is Ivigny, which acknowledges the jurisdiction of the bailiwick of Troyes.

units.la: Bassigny sic nominatur, quod potiorem constituat Inferioris Campaniæ partem. Bas Francis Infra. Cincta Fluminibus Marrona & Mosa, exiguaque Moselle portione, Aquis magis irrigatur, quam hujus Ditionis reliqua. Metropolim habet, cui ab Calab Calvo Monte (qui notus Ivoni Epist. cv.) nomen: Chaumont en [?] vulgo; Bailli-vatus titulo claram; Arce antiqua, quae in Rupe sita beneque munita, superbientem: Turris ad Occidentem vernacule Domon & La haulte fucille. Tribui solent illi (praeter Andomatunum Lingonum, Vulgo Langres; de quo postea) Montigny, Goeffy, Nogent le Roy, Monteclar, Andelot, Bisnay, Choiseul, Visnorry, Clesmont; omnia opida non invalida, pleraque Arcibus firmata.
units.tr: Bassigny is so named because it makes up the main part of Lower Champagne; "bas" in French means "lower". Enclosed by the rivers Marne and Meuse and a small portion of the Moselle, it is watered more by its waters than the rest of this domain. It has a metropolis, whose name comes from Calvus Mons (known from Ivo, letter 105), commonly called Chaumont en [?]. It is famous for the title of its bailiwick, and has an ancient citadel set on a well-fortified rock, which lifts itself proudly. To the west is a tower, called in the vernacular "Domon" and "La haulte fucille". Besides Andomatunum of the Lingones (commonly Langres, which I shall discuss later), the following are usually assigned to it: Montigny, Goeffy, Nogent le Roy, Monteclar, Andelot, Bisnay, Choiseul, Visnorry and Clesmont. All are towns of some strength, most of them secured by citadels.

units.la: Vallense Territorium, Vallage vulgo, nomen gerere creditur ab Vallibus, quas habet pulcras admodum & fertiles: Partensibus hinc contiguum, inde Barrentibus. Opida primi facile loci Vasseium, Vassy, ad Blottam, Ditionis Guisiae. Profectus eo Franciscus, Dux Guisius, anno cIↄ Iↄ LXII Vasseianam illam Stragem, ab Gallis Historiographis nobilitatam, in eos, qui Reformatam profitebantur Religionem, edidit Kalendis Martij, multis concisis. Haud procul inde genus Terrae inventitur, ex qua Bolus fit Armenius. Fanum S. Desiderij, S. Defer, vel Didier; quod expugnatum ab Karolo V Imperatore, pace facta, Gallis fuit restitutum; Arcem habet: Lani-Villa, Iamville, quod ab Iano fabulantur dictum, Familiae Guisiae Apanagium, ut vocant; alijs IamtVille scribitur. Vititur ibi Tumulus Claudij Ducis Guisiae, superba stupendaq; structura, Baronia quondam, cognominata La Fontaine de Blanche Roche; instituta ab Fulfiatho Comite Bononio & Bilionaeo; cui tres fuerunt Filij: Gotefredus Baronae, post Avunculi sui Gotefredi Strumosi excessum, Dux Lotharingiae, primusque ex Christianis Rex Hierosymorum; Balduinus, Remorum & Cameraci Praesul; Gulielmus, LaniVilla Baro; de cujus Filij Gotefredi Successoribus & Posteris nihil invenio. Principatus titulo clarere coepit tempore Henrici 11. In praesentia Dux Iani-Villae Francus est, Henrici Ducis Guisij, qui Blesis in cubiculo confectus; Regis mandantis Henrici III, anno cIↄ Iↄ XXXIX decimooctavo Kalendis Ianuarij pugionibus est consossus, Filius & Heres unicus. Ab eo dependent Baronatus, qui vulgo Sully, aliaeque Arces & Pagi. Sunt & in Vallensi Ditione Montirandelium, Abbatia insigne; Dontierant, Le Chasteau aux forges, Efclaron, & alia. Arsi ad Albam Fluvium Burgum est; Antonino Artiaca, ubi Legio XII ab ipso ponitur.
units.tr: The Vallense territory, commonly called Vallage, is believed to take its name from the valleys, which it has in great beauty and fertility. It is contiguous with the Partenses on one side and the Barrenses on the other. The towns of the first rank are Vasseium, Vassy, on the Blaise, in the domain of Guise. Francis, Duke of Guise, going there in the year 1562, carried out on 1 March that massacre at Vassy, made famous by French historians, against those who professed the Reformed religion, and many were cut down. Not far from there is found a kind of earth from which Armenian bole is made. There is the shrine of St Desiderius, St Dizier or Didier, which, stormed by Emperor Charles V, was restored to the French after peace was made; it has a citadel. Lanivilla, Joinville, which they fable was named after Janus, is the apanage of the family of Guise, as they call it; others write it Jamville. There stands the tomb of Claude, Duke of Guise, a proud and astonishing structure. It was once a barony, surnamed La Fontaine de Blanche Roche, founded by Fulk, Count of Boulogne and Bouillon. He had three sons: Godfrey of Bouillon, who after the death of his uncle Godfrey the Hunchback became Duke of Lorraine, and the first of the Christians to be King of Jerusalem; Baldwin, archbishop of Reims and Cambrai; and William, baron of Joinville. Of Godfrey's successors and descendants I find nothing. It began to be distinguished by the title of principality in the time of Henry II. At present the Duke of Joinville is Francis, son and sole heir of Henry, Duke of Guise, who was stabbed with daggers at Blois in the king's chamber on 23 December 1588, on the orders of King Henry III. From him depend the baronies commonly called Sully, and other citadels and villages. In the Vallense domain there are also Montier-en-Der, a famous abbey; Dommartin, Le Chasteau aux Forges, Esclaron, and others. At Arsi on the River Aube there is a town, which Antoninus calls Artiaca, where he places Legion XII.

units.la: Haec de Inferiore Campania: succedit Superior, quae vere Territorium Parensie, Le Pais de Perrois: Nomen illi a Burgo, qui vulgo Perte ad Matronam; quondam, ut perhibent, quam nunc, nobiliore. Meminit Pagi Patensis Nithardus lib. 1. Dissent. Liberorum Ludovici Pij; nisi Pagus Partensis ibi tota Partensium sit Ditio. Regio est fertilissima; abundans Frugibus, Lignis, Cannabi. Metropolis illi Virodunum, Vi-try, ad Saltum Matronamque concurrentes; quod ab Legione Romana Vilt ice putatur nuncupatum. Sedes hic Baillivi, cujus Iurisdictio ad xxxv & amplius milia in quadratum se extendit. Continentur sub eo Argillers, Lisaincourt, Louvement, & alia Opida.
units.tr: So much for Lower Champagne. Upper Champagne follows, which is properly the territory of the Partenses, the Pays de Perrois. It takes its name from the town commonly called Perte on the Marne, which was once, as they say, more noble than it is now. Nithard, in book 1 of the Dissensions of the Sons of Louis the Pious, mentions the Pagus Patensis, unless the Pagus Partensis there is the whole domain of the Partenses. The region is very fertile, abounding in crops, timber and hemp. Its metropolis is Virodunum, Vitry, where the Marne and the Matrona meet; it is thought to have been named from the Roman Legion Vitrix. The seat of the bailiff is here, whose jurisdiction extends over thirty-five thousand and more square miles. Under him are Argillers, Lisaincourt, Louvement and other towns.

units.la: Sic Campania quodammodo sit inlustrata per se: Conjacentia designo Ducatus quidem Remensem & Lingonensem: Comitatus autem Catalaunensem, Ligniensem & Mottensem, sui juris, Campanaeque non subjectos.
units.tr: So Champagne is in a sense made illustrious in itself. The neighbouring territories I single out are the Duchy of Reims and the Duchy of Langres, and the counties of Châlons, Ligny and Mottensis, which have their own rights and are not subject to Champagne.

units.la: Remensis Ducatus (Duché, Pairie & Archeuesché de Reims) nomen ab Urbe, quae Veteribus Durocortorum (ut in Melioribus Antonini Codicibus & Itineraria Peutingeri Tabula dicitur) hodie Reims. Ἀνδροκόσσορον, Ptolemaeo; Ἀνδρακόρτεγα, Strabon; Δεροκορτεω, Stephano; Durocortum Remorum, Caesari, apud quem in quibusdam libris Datocortorum: Antoninus illi Legionem adscribit xviii. Vrbs est inclusa, & ut ita dicam, incorporata Campaniae, sui tamen juris; unde in antiquis Chartis quasi cognominatur Reims lez Champaigne. Archiepiscopum habet, qui Dux Primusque Par Franciae. Praesules numerat Belleforestus LXXX: quorum ultimus Karolus, Cardinalis Lotharingiae. Hic Galliarum Reges Oleo caelitus, ut scribunt, missio, inaugurari solent. Portae nomina adhuc retinent Veterum Deorum Martis & Bacchi, Dearumque Cereris & Veneris. Haud procul Urbe locus est, qui vulgo Le Fort de Cæsar.
units.tr: The Duchy of Reims (Duché, Pairie and Archbishopric of Reims) takes its name from the city which the ancients called Durocortorum (as it is named in the better manuscripts of Antoninus and in the Peutinger Table), and today is Reims. Ptolemy calls it Androkossoron [Ἀνδροκόσσορον], Strabo Andrakortega [Ἀνδρακόρτεγα], Stephanus Derokorteo [Δεροκορτεω]; Caesar calls it Durocortum Remorum, though in some books Datocortorum. Antoninus assigns Legion XVIII to it. The city is enclosed within Champagne and, so to speak, incorporated into it, yet it has its own rights; hence in old charters it is called "Reims lez Champaigne". It has an archbishop, who is Duke and first peer of France. Belleforest counts eighty prelates, the last of whom was Charles, Cardinal of Lorraine. Here the Kings of France are usually anointed with oil, which, as they write, was sent from heaven. The gates still keep the names of the old gods Mars and Bacchus, and of the goddesses Ceres and Venus. Not far from the city is a place commonly called Le Fort de César.

units.la: Lingonensis Ducatus (Duché, Pairie & Euesché de Langres) Vrbem habet, quae quondam Andomatunum Lingonum, vulgo Langres. Ἀνδομάτουνον, Ὀλεμαχος; Antemantunum vitiose apud Antoninum; paulo inclius Andematunum in Itineraria Peutingeri Tabula: Tacito Lingonum Vrbs; Gregorio Turonensi, Vrbs Lingonica. Episcopalis est, cujus Antistites Duces sunt & Pares Franciae. Inter Vetustatis monimenta, quae illic visuntur, non postremi est loci Triumphalis Arcus, in ipsis Moenibus excita-
units.tr: The Duchy of Langres (Duché, Pairie and Bishopric of Langres) has a city which was once Andomatunum of the Lingones, commonly Langres. Ptolemy calls it Andomatunon [Ἀνδομάτουνον], Olemachus; Antoninus, with a corruption, Antemantunum; the Peutinger Table, a little more correctly, Andematunum; Tacitus calls it the city of the Lingones, and Gregory of Tours the Lingonian city. It is an episcopal see whose bishops are dukes and peers of France. Among the monuments of antiquity to be seen there, not the least is the triumphal arch raised on the very walls itself

units.la: Ex Caesari Commentariis. excitatus: Geta nici exercitus cæsi haud dubie Trophæum: qui quum pugnandi copiam Cæsari Constantino pene puero fecisset, pro ipsis Mœnibus, & spectante Lingonum Vrbe, obtritus est; sexaginta hominum millibus eo prælio desideratis. Ejus pugnæ pluribus locis exstant etiamnum testimonia, Leonum, Equorum, Virorumque Statuæ, Via regia, quæ ad Sequanos pertinet. Vidend. Guilielm. Paradinus de Antiquo Statu Burgundiæ.
units.tr: From Caesar's Commentaries. The arch was undoubtedly raised as a trophy for the army of Geta that was cut down there. When the young Caesar Constantine gave him the chance to fight, he was crushed in front of the walls, in full view of the city of the Lingones, with sixty thousand men lost in that battle. Evidence of the battle still survives in several places: statues of lions, horses and men, and the royal road, which leads to the Sequani. See William Paradin, On the Ancient State of Burgundy.

units.la: Comitatus Catalaunensis (Evesché, Comté & Pairie de Chalon) nomen impositum ab Vrbe Catalauno: Cathetaunnum posterioris ævi Scriptores vocant, quæ Chalon hodie, cognomine en Champagne. Morboniam istos, quibus Chalon à Campis Longis. Episcopalis Civitas, cujus Præsul Comes est & Par Franciæ. Vrbs ad Matronam placni situs, excelsis decorata Turribus, Pyramidum instar exsurgentibus: Frumento Pannisque lineis Mercaturam exercens.
units.tr: The county of Châlons (the bishopric, county and peerage of Châlons) takes its name from the city of Catalaunum, which later writers call Cathetaunnum and which is today Châlons, surnamed "en Champagne". Some derive it from Campi Longi, "long fields", which is why Châlons is called "à Campis Longis". It is an episcopal city whose prelate is both count and peer of France. The city lies on the Marne, adorned with lofty towers that rise like pyramids, and it trades in grain and linen cloth.

units.la: Ligniensis Comitatus (Comté de Ligny) opidum est Lignium, insignis vetustatis, ad Saltum Fluvium. Abbatia hic in Vertice Montis ad latus Opidi Orientale, cum Fonte admirandæ pulcritudinis.
units.tr: The county of Ligny (Comté de Ligny) has the town of Lignium, of notable antiquity, on the river Saltus. Here there is an abbey on the top of a hill, on the eastern side of the town, with a spring of wonderful beauty.

units.la: De Mottensi (Comté de la Motte) præter nomen, nihil adhuc ad me perlatum. Parum comperta scribere, prorsus à me sit alienum.
units.tr: Beyond its name, nothing about Mottensis (the county of La Motte) has yet come to my attention. To write about things so little known is quite foreign to my purpose.

units.la: Cum Campania solet explicari Brienfium (Brionenses appellantur Nithardo lib. 1. de Dissensionib. Filiorum Ludovici Pij) Tractus, Heurepentibus contiguus, La Brye, antiquus Comitatus, de quo quædam cap. xxxi. De Nomine varie disputant. Abri Francis Umbraps inter alia notat & Opacitatem, locumque, quo Venti non perflant. Quum autem omnia hic valde sint opaca, fructiferisque consita arboribus; nusquam non, si vel Pluviæ ingruant subitæ, vel nimius Solis ardor adurat, umbrosa se obserunt Loca, quorum beneficio vel Incolæ, vel Viatores gratam auram capere, seque inopacare, quod Francis Se mettre à l'abri, consueverunt. Alii ab Sicambris, quos hic volunt habitasse, παρ' ἀφαιρεσιν derivant; quod longe petitum & contra Historiarum fidem. Ridicula quorumdam Etyma prætereo. Initium illi ad Cretelium Pagum, haud procul Ponte Charantonio, ubi Matrona Sequanæ commiscetur: quorum ille Campanos fere, hic Gastinenses à Brienfibus separat. Nam quidquid ferme inter duo hæc Flumina est, ad Burgundiæ utique Ducatum, Brienfibus adscribi solet. Manet nomen in Opido, quod vulgo Brye vel Bray Comte Robert, sic dictum à Comite Roberto, Brienfium quondam Principe, cui hic erat Domicilium. Brienfium Vrbes Castellum Theodorici, Chasteau Thierry, Latinum (Medorum vel Meldarum, Provinfium & aliæ. Latinum, Λάτινον Meldarum Vrbs, ad Matronam Fluvium, Ptolemæo nota: Meldarum Civitas Notitiæ Provinciarum: Hodie Meaux; Præfectura, Vicecomitatus, Sedesque Ballivatus de Nogent. Forum, instar Arcis, vidi Matronæ cinctum alveo; Pars una Brienfium est, altera Valesiorum: Episcopatus item, cujus Præsules apud Bellesforestium ci, ultimus Ludovicus Bresius. Provinsium, Provins, Opidum ab Rosis suave-olentibus, Conditis & Dulciarijs celebre. Quædam hic Antiquitatum Rudera.
units.tr: The region of Brie, which adjoins Hurepoix and is an ancient county (of which something is said in chapter 31), is commonly explained together with Champagne. The Brienses are named by Nithard, book 1, On the Dissensions of the Sons of Louis the Pious. Opinions on the name vary. The French Abri among other things means shelter, and also shade, a place where the winds do not blow. Since everything here is very shady and planted with fruit trees, wherever sudden rain or the heat of the sun is severe, shady places offer themselves, where inhabitants or travellers can enjoy a pleasant breeze and shelter themselves, which the French call se mettre à l'abri. Others derive the name from the Sicambri, whom they think lived here, by aphaeresis [παρ' ἀφαίρεσιν]; this is far-fetched and contrary to the evidence of the histories. I pass over the ridiculous etymologies of some. The region begins at the pagus of Crételle, not far from the bridge of Charenton, where the Marne joins the Seine. The one separates the Campanians from the Brienses, the other the Gastinenses. For whatever lies between these two rivers is generally assigned to the Duchy of Burgundy, to the Brienses. The name survives in the town commonly called Brye or Bray Comte Robert, so named after Count Robert, once prince of the Brienses, who had his home there. The towns of Brie are Castellum Theodorici (Château-Thierry), Latinum (of the Medi or Meldi), Provinsium and others. Latinum [Λάτινον] is a city of the Meldi on the Marne, known to Ptolemy; the Notitia of the Provinces calls it the city of the Meldi. Today it is Meaux, a prefecture, a viscounty and the seat of the bailiwick of Nogent. I have seen its forum, which is like a citadel, surrounded by the Marne; one part belongs to Brie, the other to Valois. It is also a bishopric, whose prelates are listed by Bellforest, the last being Louis Bresius. Provinsium, Provins, is a town famous for fragrant roses, preserves and confections. There are some remains of antiquity here.

units.la: Adcenseatur item huic Tractui Archiepiscopatus Senonensis, L'Archevesché de Sens, cum Opido Pontio. Senonum Vrbs olim Agendicum, vulgo Sens: ad Icaunam, qui vernacule Tonne. Meminit Cæsar. Ἀγέδικον Ptolemæo; Agredicum, & aliis modis, vitiose apud Antoninum; Agetincum Itinerariæ Tabulæ. Ad Portam Ædificium est, cui nomen Carcer Cæsaris: Extra Vrbem quædam sunt Antiquitatum Monimenta. Stultos vocat suis ad me litteris V. N. Iosephus Scaliger, quibus Agendicum censetur Provins. Inter eos Marlianus. Vigenereo videtur Milly en Gastinois.
units.tr: The archbishopric of Sens (L'Archevêché de Sens), with the town of Pont, should also be included in this region. The city of Sens, formerly Agendicum, lies on the Yonne, which in the vernacular is the Tonne. Caesar mentions it. Ptolemy has Agedikon [Ἀγέδικον]; Antoninus has it corrupted in various ways, such as Agredicum; the Itinerary Table has Agetincum. Near the gate there is a building called Caesar's Prison. Outside the city there are some monuments of antiquity. In his letters to me, the most noble Joseph Scaliger calls fools those who think Agendicum is Provins; among them is Marlianus. Vigenère seems to identify it with Milly en Gâtinais.

units.la: CAP. XXIV. Lugdunensis Tractus.
units.tr: CHAP. XXIV. The Lugdunensis Region.

units.la: LVGDVNENSIVM CIVITATI, vt in Notitia Prouinciarum dicitur, L'Archeuefché de Lion, (Le Pais & Seneschaucée de Lionnois) postremum in Veteri mea Celtica locum occupanti, Limites scribuntur ad Septemtrionem Bressia; ad Orientem Sabaudia: qua Meridiem spectat, Delphinatus est cum Languedokia, qua Occidentem, Forenses jacent & Arverni.
units.tr: The city of the LUGDUNENSES, as it is called in the Notitia of the Provinces, the Archbishopric of Lyons (the Country and Seneschalsy of Lyonnais), which occupies the last place in my old Celtica, has as its boundaries: to the north, Bresse; to the east, Savoy; to the south, the Dauphiné together with Languedoc; to the west, the Foréziens and the Arverni lie.

units.la: Sua hic olim habuerunt Domicilia Segusiani. Sic dicuntur Plinio, Veterique Inscriptioni, qui Σεγυσιανοὶ Ptolemæo, Σαυγοσιανοὶ Straboni: (alio apud eumdem loco vitiosè Έργυσιανοὶ nominantur) Secusiani, vel, ut alij scribunt, Sebusiani Cæsari, Secusiani Antiquo Lapidi, si fides Hermolao Barbaro: Hodie Le Pais & Seneschaucée de Lionneis, vti censet V. N. Josephus Scaliger: Nam, inquit suis ad me Litteris, Lugdunum est in Segusianis, vt illud alterum in Convenis ad Garumnam. Sed & totus Pagus Forensis, qui hodie Le Pais de Fores dicitur, continetur in Segusianis, & vetus Inscriptio exstat in Opido Furs, in qua mentio est Fori Segusianorum. Nam à Foro Forenses dicti, & ipsum Opidum Furs. Segusianos Bresse vertit Villanovanus; Foresiens P. Saniulianus; Lionnois Abrahamus Ortelius: Sebusianos Brixiam & Bungiacum putat Philibertus Pingonius; Pais de Bresse & Bressantz Pinetus & Vigenereus; eam Sabaudiæ partem, quæ hodie Burgo Presso Scudus: Sebasianos Bugey facit magnum Dalechampij Herbarium: Secusianos denique Belliecenses, vulgo Bellay, censet Marhanus. An vero Segusiani, Secusiani, & Sebusiani varij sint Populi, disquirendum alijs relinquo. Segnsianos Plinius vocat Liberos: Secusiani Cæsari Aeduorum dicuntur Clientes, & extra Prouinciam Primi.
units.tr: The Segusiani once had their homes here. They are so called by Pliny and in an ancient inscription; Ptolemy calls them Σεγυσιανοί [Segysianoi] and Strabo Σαυγοσιανοί [Saugosianoi] (in another passage of the same author they are wrongly named Έργυσιανοί [Ergysianoi]). Caesar calls them Secusiani or, as others write, Sebusiani; an ancient stone has Secusiani, if we trust Hermolaus Barbarus. Today it is the Country and Seneschalsy of Lyonnais, as Josephus Scaliger, of venerable memory, thinks. For, he says in his letter to me, Lugdunum is in the Segusiani, just as that other Lugdunum is among the Convenae by the Garonne. But also the whole Forez district, which today is called the Pays de Forez, is contained in the Segusiani, and an ancient inscription survives in the town of Feurs which mentions the Forum of the Segusiani. For the Foresiens are named from the Forum, and the town itself is Feurs. Villanovanus renders Segusiani as Bresse; P. Saniulianus as Foresiens; Abraham Ortelius as Lionnois. Philibert Pingon thinks the Sebusiani are Brixia and Bungiacum; Pinet and Vigenère, the Pays de Bresse and Bressantz; Scudus, that part of Savoy which today is called Burgo Presso. The great Dalechamps' Herbarium makes them Sebasiani, the Bugey. Finally, Marhan holds the Secusiani to be the Belliecenses, commonly Bellay. Whether Segusiani, Secusiani and Sebusiani are different peoples I leave to others to inquire. Pliny calls the Segnsiani Liberi; Caesar says the Secusiani were clients of the Aedui and lay outside the Province, the first ones.

units.la: Caput hujus Tractus ad confluentem Ararim cum Rodano (κατὰ τὸ συμβολὴ τῆ τε Άραρ῾ ποταμῶ καὶ τῆ Ρ῾οδανῷ, inquit Strabo lib. iv.) Lugdunum est. Sic amplifsimam, ornatissimam, florentissimam Vrbem nominant Tacitus, Plinius, Antoninus; & qui Latinorum Scriptorum non? Λούγδουνον Straboni, Ptolemæo, alijsque Græcis: Λούγδυνα Stephano. Notat Dio Λουγάδουνον prius, postea Λούγδουνον appellatum: Lugdunum sane in Antiquis ejus loci Lapidibus non semel animadverti: Testantur idem alij de Numismatibus. Plutarchi libellus de Montibus & Fluminibus in voce Araris tradit Civitatem Λούγδολον vocari; Montem autem, cui insidet, Λούγδουνον: Historiam adducens de Nomine, deque Origine fabulosam, Rationesque prorsus frivolas & ridendas. Vetus nomen hodie, sed contractius, servat. Ludunt enim, qui in vulgata appellatione Lion, Leonem Gallicum quærunt. Paradinus in sua Lugdunensi HistoHistoria, quam Gallice edidit, docet ab Livio & Plutarcho Insulam vocatam; inque veteribus Inscriptionibus Civitatem Sequanorum dici. Memorat idem ab Sidonio lib. i. epist. v. Rodanusiam, Ararium item cognominari in Historia S. Lupi, Præsulis Lugdunensis: ab Fluminibus eam, ut cap. ix. scripsi, interfluentibus. Ornamentum Provinciarum audit apud Plinium in Epistolis: Nobilissima Gregorio Turonensi, ex eo, quod Martyrum sanguine fuerit inlustrata. Fuisse dicuntur xviii millia; eorumque laniena facta, Antonino Vero Imperatore, quo loco nunc Athenatense visitur Templum. Consulenda Historia Ecclesiastica. Nomen derivant quidam ab Lugere, quod illi proprium fuit post fatale Incendium, de quo post: nonnulli ab Lucere, quod in Monte, tamquam Specula, longe lateque luceret: alii ab Lugdo Celtarum Rege. Maccis & Bucconibus sua linquenda. Vetus Itinerarium à Burdigala Hierosolymas usque, quod Pithæo debemus, in fine Lugdunum Desideratum Montem interpretatur, Idiomate proculdubio Veterum Gallorum: cujus penitiora scrutati, sunt qui diducunt ab Voce Luck, quæ hodieque Gallis Belgis, Germaniæque Inferioris Populis pro Fortuna in usu, ut Lugdunum fuerit, Fortuna quasi dicatus Mons. Ericus Monachus lib. iv. de Vita S. Germani in Lugduno dictionem Lucht, quæ Gallorum Belgarum Lingua Lucem sonat, agnoscere videtur: Lugduno celebrant Gallorum famine nomen Impositum quondam, quod sit Mons Lucidus.
units.tr: The chief town of this region is Lugdunum, at the confluence of the river Arar with the Rhône (κατὰ τὸ συμβολὴ τῆ τε Ἄραρ῾ ποταμῶ καὶ τῆ Ῥοδανῷ [kata to symbole te te Arar potamo kai te Rhodano], says Strabo, book iv). Tacitus, Pliny and Antoninus call it a most large, most splendid and most flourishing city; and what Latin writer does not? Strabo, Ptolemy and the other Greeks write Λούγδουνον [Loudoun]; Stephanus writes Λούγδυνα [Loudyna]. Dio notes that it was first called Λουγάδουνον [Lougadoun] and afterwards Λούγδουνον. Lugdunum has certainly been observed more than once on the ancient stones of that place, and other authors bear witness to it from coins. The little book of Plutarch on Mountains and Rivers, under the word Araris, says that the town is called Λούγδολον [Loudolon] but the mountain on which it sits Λούγδουνον; it gives a fabulous story about the name and its origin, and reasons that are altogether frivolous and laughable. Today the town keeps the old name, though in a shorter form. For those who look for a Lion or the Gallic Lion in the common name are playing with words. Paradin, in his Lyons history, which he published in French, teaches that it was called an Island by Livy and Plutarch, and that in ancient inscriptions it is called the Civitas of the Sequani. The same writer records from Sidonius, book i, letter v, that it was also surnamed Rhodanusia and likewise Ararica, in the history of St Lupus, bishop of Lyons; from the rivers flowing around it, as I wrote in chapter ix. Pliny in his Letters calls it the Ornament of the Provinces. Gregory of Tours calls it most noble, because it was made illustrious by the blood of martyrs. It is said there were eighteen thousand of them, and that they were slaughtered in the reign of the emperor Verus Antoninus, in the place where the church of Athenatense is now seen. The ecclesiastical history should be consulted. Some derive the name from lugere, to mourn, which was proper to it after the fatal fire, of which more below; some from lucere, to shine, because on the mountain, as on a lookout, it shone far and wide; others from Lugdo, king of the Celts. The Maccae and Bucconae must leave their own claims. The ancient itinerary from Bordeaux as far as Jerusalem, which we owe to Pithou, at the end renders Lugdunum as Desired Mountain, in the idiom without doubt of the ancient Gauls. Those who have searched its deeper meaning derive it from the word Luck, which even today is in use among the Gallic and Belgic peoples and the peoples of Lower Germany for Fortune, so that Lugdunum would be a mountain dedicated, as it were, to Fortune. Eric the Monk, in book iv of the Life of St Germanus, seems to recognise in Lyons the word Lucht, which in the language of the Belgic Gauls means light: he says that the name was once given to the place by the Gallic people, because it is a Bright Mountain.

units.la: Dunum sane antiquis Callis Montem esse, dixi cap. xv. Montis Lugdunensis etiam meminit Petrus Arvernus Cluniacensis Abbas lib. iv Epist. ii: At postquam de Vivarensium colle ad Lugdunensium Montem divina Dispositio te transtulit. Sic Seneca in Ludo Claudii: Vidi duobus imminens Fluvius Iugum.
units.tr: It is certainly true that Dunum meant mountain to the ancient Gauls, as I said in chapter xv. Peter the Venerable of Cluny, abbot, also mentions the Mountain of Lyons in book iv, letter ii: But after divine Disposition transferred you from the hill of the Vivarienses to the Mountain of the Lugdunenses. So Seneca in the Ludus de Claudio: I saw a river overhanging the two peaks.

units.la: Montem hunc Adcolis cratiliorem causlari Aërem innuit apud Sidonium lib. i. Epist. viii Candidianus: Nebulas ergo mihi meorum Lugdunensium exprobras, & diem quæreris nobis matutina caligine obstructum vix meridiano fervore reserari? Et tu ista hæc mihi Cesenatis furni potius, quam Cupidi Verna deblateras? Sic etiam apud Strabonem Αὐγοῦστος ... Quis Urbis conditor, incertum. Amplificavit & ex Monte, qui primo habitatus, in planiora loca Pomerium produxit L. Munatius Plancus: Colonia in eam Augusti principatu ducta; anno Urbis MDCCXI. Testatur Inscriptio, quæ Cajetæ in Neapolitanorum Agris reperta dicitur:
units.tr: Sidonius, book i, letter viii, hints that the air on this hill is thicker for its inhabitants. Candidianus says: Do you therefore reproach me with the mists of my Lyonnais, and complain that the day, shut in by morning fog, can scarcely be opened up by the midday heat? And do you chatter these things to me, you slave of the Cesenas oven rather than of Cupid? So also in Strabo, Αὐγοῦστος [Augoustos] ... Who the founder of the city was is uncertain. L. Munatius Plancus enlarged it, and extended its pomerium from the mountain, where it was first settled, down into the flatter ground. It was made a colony under the principate of Augustus, in the year of the City 711. An inscription found, it is said, at Gaeta in the territory of Naples bears witness to this:

units.la: L. MVNATIVS. L. F. L. N. L. PRON PLANCVS. COS. IMP. ITER. VII. VIR EPVLON. TRIVMPH. EX. ROETIS. AEDEM. SATVRNI FECIT. DE. MANVBIS. AGROS. DIVISIT. IN. ITALIA BENEVENTI. IN. GALLIA. COLONIAS. DEDVXIT LVGDVNVM. ET. RAVRICVM
units.tr: L. Munatius, son of Lucius, grandson of Lucius, great-grandson of Lucius, of the tribe Pronia, Plancus, consul, imperator, for the second time, septemvir of the sacred banquets, triumphed over the Raetians. He built the temple of Saturn. From the spoils he divided lands. In Italy he led colonies to Beneventum; in Gaul, to Lugdunum and Raurica.

units.la: Coloniam etiam nominant Tacitus lib. i Historiar. & Plinius lib. iv cap. xviii natur. histor. In vetere quadam Inscriptione lego COL. AVG. LVG. Ab eo tempore semper cum primis Galliarum Urbibus censeri solita, dignaque habita, quæ cum Vicinis Inmunitate gauderet. Nam Sequsianos Liberos vocat Plinius lib. iv cap. xviii, & Lugdunenses Gallos cum Viennensibus Iuris Italici facit Paulus IC. lib. i. Digestor. Tit. xv. cap. ult. Digna item, ex qua totius Galliæ Itinera ab Agrippa distinguerentur; cui Ius Monetæ cudendæ tribueretur; in qua Gallorum omnium Tributa & Vectigalia colligerentur. Digna denique, ubi Templum ad Confluentes Ararim & Rodanum ab omnibus Galliæ Civitatibus in honorem Augusti cum formidanda illa ineptis Scriptoribus Ara exstrueretur. De Templo sane Strabo lib. iv: Τότε ἱερὸν τὸ σεβαστὸν ... Ex huius Templi ruinis, inquit Paradinus de Antiquo Burgundiæ Statu, concreta est illa Summi Templi structura: quod Ioannis Burgundiæ quondam Regis Opus dicitur, ut ex antiquis marmorum ruderibus Saxorumque Inscriptionibus conjicere licet. Ara variis Scriptoribus nota. Augusto dedicatam, Iulo Antonio Africano & Q. Fabio Maximo Coss. anno ab V. C. MDCCXLIV, memoriæ prodit Suetonius in Claudio cap. ii. Sic ad ea tempora Epitoma Livij lib. cxxxvii. Ara Caesaris ad confluentem Araris & Rodani dedicata. Ad eam vivente adhuc Augusto, ut scribit Dio sub finem lib. liv, Ludi celebrabantur; addens eos sua quoque ætate permansisse. Caligulam Certamen ibi quoque instituisse Græcæ Latinæque facundiæ, scribit idem Suetonius in ejus vita cap. xx. Quo certamine, inquit pergens, ferunt Victoribus præmia Victos contulisse, eorumdem & Laudes componere coactos; eos autem, qui maxime displicuissent, Scripta sua spongia linguaque delere jussos, nisi ferulis objurgari, aut Flumine proximo mergi maluissent. Respicit eo Iuvenalis: Palleat ut nudis pressit qui calcibus anguem: Aut Lugdunensem Rhetor dicturus ad Aram.
units.tr: Colonia is also what Tacitus (Histories, book 1) and Pliny (Natural History, book 4, chapter 18) call it. In an old inscription I read COL. AVG. LVG. From that time it was always counted among the chief cities of Gaul and considered worthy of that rank, since it enjoyed immunity together with its neighbours. For Pliny (book 4, chapter 18) calls the Sequsiani "free," and the jurist Paulus (Digest, book 1, title 15, last chapter) places the Lugdunenses Gauls on the same footing as the Viennenses in respect of Italian law. It was also worthy to be the city from which Agrippa measured all the roads of Gaul, to which the right of coining money was granted, and in which the tributes and taxes of all the Gauls were collected. Finally, it was worthy of having, at the confluence of the Arar and the Rhône, a Temple to Augustus built by all the states of Gaul, together with that Altar which the foolish writers have so dreaded. Strabo, in book 4, speaks clearly of the Temple: "Then the temple of Augustus ..." [Τότε ἱερὸν τὸ σεβαστὸν ...]. From the ruins of this Temple, says Paradin in his work on the ancient state of Burgundy, "that great structure of the Summit was put together," which, as one may gather from old fragments of marble and inscribed stones, "is said to be the work of John, once king of Burgundy." The Altar is known to various writers. That it was dedicated to Augustus in the consulship of Julus Antonius and Quintus Fabius Maximus, in the year 744 from the founding of the City, Suetonius records in Claudius, chapter 2. Likewise the Epitome of Livy, book 137, says: "The altar of Caesar was dedicated at the confluence of the Arar and the Rhône." Games were celebrated there while Augustus was still alive, as Dio writes near the end of book 54, adding that they continued in his own time. The same Suetonius, in the life of Caligula, chapter 20, writes that Caligula also instituted there a contest of Greek and Latin eloquence. "In that contest," he goes on, "they say the victors gave prizes to the vanquished, and the vanquished were forced to compose panegyrics on them; those whose work had displeased most were ordered to erase their writings with a sponge or with their tongue, unless they preferred to be beaten with rods or drowned in the nearby river." Juvenal alludes to this: "Let him turn pale who with bare heels trod on a snake, or the rhetorician who is about to speak at the Altar of Lyons."

units.la: De hac Ara Strabo; ἐν δὲ βωμὸς ἀξιόλογος Σεβαστῷ ἔχων τὸν ἱερέα ἐξ ἀρχῆς, καὶ εἰκόνες τῶν ἱκανῶν μία, καὶ ἀλλ᾽ μέγας. Hujus Ara Sacerdotem edit Inscriptio, quæ in ipsa Urbe ad Murum Templi vetustissimi Divi Petri.
units.tr: Of this Altar Strabo says: "And in it is a notable altar to Augustus, which has had a priest from the beginning, and one statue of ..., and another large one" [ἐν δὲ βωμὸς ἀξιόλογος Σεβαστῷ ἔχων τὸν ἱερέα ἐξ ἀρχῆς, καὶ εἰκόνες τῶν ἱκανῶν μία, καὶ ἀλλ᾽ μέγας]. An inscription which is in the City itself, at the wall of the most ancient Temple of the divine Peter, sets out this Altar's Priest.

units.la: IOVI. O. M.
units.tr: TO JUPITER, BEST AND GREATEST

units.la: Q. ADGINNIVS. VRBICI FIL. MARTINVS. SEQ. SACERDOS. ROMÆ. ET. AVG. AD. ARAM. AD. CONFLVENTES ARARIS. ET. RHODANI FLAMEN. II. VIR. IN. CIVITATE SEQVANORVM
units.tr: Q. Adginnius Martinus, son of Urbicus, Sequanian, priest of Rome and of Augustus at the altar at the confluence of the Arar and the Rhone, flamen, duumvir in the state of the Sequani.

units.la: Quid jam dicam de reliquis, quas ibi & nunc est legere, Inscriptionibus? Superat omnes Tabula ærea, quæ Claudii Imperatoris Orationem continet super Civitate Gallis danda. Legitur cum apud alios, tum accuratissime descripta apud Iustum Lipsium, & in Commentario ad xi Annalium Tacit, & in Auctario, quod Vir Magnus adposuit Thesauro Inscriptionum Martini Smetii. Priscam ejus Magnificentiam testantur passim Templorum, Arcuum Triumphalium, Aquaeductuum, & alia Antiquitatis Monimenta. Fori Veneris memoriam servari ajunt in Forviere. Ab ea Urbe nobilissima Galliæ Pars in quinque distincta quondam est Lugdunenses i, ii, iii, iv, v; uti in Notitia Provinciarum Galliæ, de qua supra, est videre. Igne Fatali miserandum in modum suo tempore exustam conqueritur, Clademque inde acceptam deplorat epistola ad Lucilium xci i Seneca. Accidit centesimo anno ab Colonia deducta, eodem Seneca observante. Solatium isti calamitati adhibitum ab Nerone, septimo post Incendium anno. Legendus Tacitus lib.xvi Annal. Quum ejus Moenibus se continuisset Albini exercitus, ab Imperatore Severo obsessa, brevi post capta, direpta, iterumque incensa fuit: uti refert Herodianus lib. iii. Lugdunum Philippus Pulcher Francorum Rex Pontificis jussu Ditioni suæ adjecit, scribente in Annalibus Papirio Massonio. Urbem hanc magna cum voluptate conspexi superioribus annis amœno commodoque sitam loco; natura fere inexpugnabilem: ab una parte duobus munitam Collibus, ipsque fructiferis, ab altera totidem beatam Fluviis, Arari, Rodanoque: Templorum Ædificiorumque, cum publicorum, tum privatorum magnificentia superbientem; opibus & mercatura supra modum florentem: ut celeberrimum facile sit hodie totius Galliæ Emporium, Regnique Cor & Clavis instar, qua Aditus recluduntur in Italiam, Germaniam, aliasque Provincias: confluentibus eo ad publicas Nundinas solenniter, & ex conditio quasi, quater singulis annis undique variarum Gentium Mercatoribus. Regnante Karolo ix, quum tota arderet Bellis Civilibus Gallia, Arcem futuris Motibus averruncandis, invita satis, accepit. Sedes est cum Archiepiscopalis, cujus Præsules Belleforestius recensetcii, quique, ut antea dixi, Primates se gerunt Cleri Gallicani; tum Præsidiales & antiquus Senescallatus, cui subsunt Territoria Lugdunense, Forense, Matisconense & Bellolocense; quæ postea nonnihil mutata. Ecclesiam Lugdunensem Bernardus Abbas Clarevallensis hoc celebrat Elogio: Inter Ecclesias Galliæ constat præfectio Lugdunensem anteire, sicut dignitate Sedis, sic honestis Studiis & laudabilibus Institutis. Ubi enim aeque viguit Disciplina Censura? Morum Gravitas? Maturitas Consiliorum? Auctoritatis Pondus? Antiquitatis Insigne? Præsertim in Officiis Ecclesiasticis haud facile umquam visa est repentinis Novitatibus adquiescere, nec se aliquando juvenili passa est decolorari Levitate. Lugdunensis Episcopus fuit aliquando Irenæus, Græcus Scriptor; cujus exstant Libri v contra impias Veterum Hæreticorum opiniones. De Antiquitate & Origine Urbis Lugdunensis Virisque ejusdem inlustribus, cum Episcopis, tum aliis (inter quos L. Plotius Gallus, qui primus Rhetoricam Romæ professus est, teste Suetonio, & à quo cum Q. Fratre Latine primum se doctum refert M. Cicero, plene scripsit Symphorianus Champerius Lugdunensis Medicus. Adeundus & Guhelmus Paradinus de Statu Antiquæ Burgundiæ.
units.tr: What more shall I say about the other inscriptions that can still be read there? The bronze tablet containing the speech of the Emperor Claudius on granting citizenship to the Gauls surpasses them all. It has been read in other writers, and it is copied most accurately by Justus Lipsius, in his commentary on the eleventh book of Tacitus's Annals, and in the supplement that the great man added to the Inscriptions Thesaurus of Martin Smetius. Its former magnificence is attested everywhere by the temples, triumphal arches, aqueducts, and other monuments of antiquity. They say the memory of the Forum of Venus survives in Forviere. From that most noble city, a part of Gaul was once divided into five, the Lugdunenses I, II, III, IV, V, as can be seen in the Notitia of the Provinces of Gaul mentioned above. Seneca, in his letter 91 to Lucilius, laments that the city was burned in a dreadful way in his time, and he bewails the disaster that befell it. It happened in the hundredth year after its founding as a colony, as Seneca also notes. Comfort was offered for that calamity by Nero, seven years after the fire. Tacitus, book 16 of the Annals, should be read. When the army of Albinus had shut itself up within its walls, it was besieged by the Emperor Severus, and soon after it was taken, plundered, and burned again, as Herodian reports in book 3. Philip the Fair, King of the Franks, added Lyons to his dominion by the Pope's command, as Papirius Masso writes in his Annals. I saw this city with great pleasure in recent years: it is set in a pleasant and convenient place, and is almost impregnable by nature. On one side it is protected by two hills, which are themselves fruitful, and on the other it is blessed by two rivers, the Arar and the Rhone. It takes pride in the magnificence of its temples and buildings, both public and private, and it flourishes in wealth and trade beyond measure. So it is easily today the most famous market of all Gaul, like the heart and key of the kingdom, through which the way opens into Italy, Germany, and other provinces. Merchants of various nations gather there from everywhere for the public fairs, solemnly and as if by agreement, four times a year. In the reign of Charles IX, when all Gaul was burning with civil wars, it received, though quite unwillingly, a citadel to ward off future disturbances. It is the seat of an archbishopric, whose prelates Belleforest lists, and who, as I said before, claim the rank of primates of the Gallican clergy. It also has a presidial court and an ancient seneschalship, under which lie the territories of Lyons, Forez, Mâcon, and Bellley, though these have since been somewhat changed. Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, praises the Church of Lyons in this eulogy: "It is agreed that the Church of Lyons goes before the other churches of Gaul in precedence, as in the dignity of its see, so in honourable studies and praiseworthy institutions. For where has discipline and censure flourished equally? Gravity of manners, maturity of counsels, weight of authority, distinction of antiquity? Especially in ecclesiastical offices it has seldom been seen to yield to sudden novelties, nor has it ever allowed itself to be stained by youthful levity." Irenaeus, a Greek writer, was once bishop of Lyons; his five books against the impious opinions of the ancient heretics survive. Symphorien Champier, a physician of Lyons, has written fully on the antiquity and origin of the city of Lyons and its distinguished men, both bishops and others, among whom is Lucius Plotius Gallus, who first taught rhetoric at Rome, according to Suetonius, and from whom Marcus Cicero says he first learned Latin, along with his brother Quintus. Guillaume Paradin, On the State of Ancient Burgundy, should also be consulted.

units.la: CAP. XXV. Bituricensis Tractus.
units.tr: CHAP. XXV. The Bourges Tract.

units.la: REGIONES, quæ in Belgia Celticaque Veteri Iurisdictionem nunc agnoscunt Parlamenti Parisiensis, perlustravi: succedunt quæ ejusdem sunt conditionis in Aquitania; in Prima quidem Bituricum, Forbonium, Pictonium, Agerque & Inculismensis & Almisiensis; Secunda vero Auvernia.
units.tr: I have gone through the regions which in the old division of Belgica and Celtica now acknowledge the jurisdiction of the Parlement of Paris. Next come those of the same condition in Aquitaine: in the First, Bourges, Forbonium, Poitou, and the lands of Angoulême and Aulnis; in the Second, Auvergne.

units.la: BITVRICVM vel BITVRICENSIS DVCATVS, Duché de Berry, cum aliis, tum Pecore abundat, quod ab Incolis per universam distrahitur Galliam. Infinitus hic Opidorum, Burgorum, Pagorum, Saltuum, Montium, Pratorum, Pascuorum, Rivulorum, Fontium, Vinetorum numerus. Ab Septemtrione Soloniam Inferioris Belliæ partem, à qua Caris fluentis disterminatur; ad Orientem Hurepenses, Nivernenses, & Borbonios respicit, constituente hic Limitem Rivulo, cui nomen La Faye: qua Meridies est, Lemovices habitant, ubi Creuse fluit; qua Occidens, Pictones & Turones, à quibus Fluviolo, qui Clery vulgo, separatur.
units.tr: The Duchy of BOURGES, or of the Bituriges, Duché de Berry, abounds in livestock as well as other things, which the inhabitants sell throughout all Gaul. The number of towns, villages, hamlets, woods, mountains, meadows, pastures, streams, springs, and vineyards here is endless. On the north it borders the part of Lower Berry called Sologne, from which it is separated by the river Cher; on the east it faces the people of Herry, Nevers, and Bourbon, the boundary here being a stream called the Faye; on the south live the Lemovices, where the Creuse flows; on the west are the Poitevins and the Tourangeaux, from whom it is separated by a small river commonly called the Cléry.

units.la: Domicilium hic olim fuit Biturigibus, quos Κέλτας scribunt cognominatos Strabo, Ptolemæus, alij. Biturriges enim Galliæ Populi, duplices erant, cognomentis distincti, Biturriges Cubi, quorum Metropolis Avaricum, Primæ Aquitaniæ; Biturriges Vibisci, aut Vivisci, quis, ut postea dicam, primaria Vrbs Burdigala, Secundæ Aquitaniæ. Vtraque Civitas libera sub Romanis, teste Plinio. Civitas Bituricum vel Biturigorum Notitiæ Provinciarum, in Aquitania Prima vel Sexta Viennensi. De Gentis appellatione multa Ioannes Calamæus (Chaumeau) qui Biturigum Historiam sex libris complexus est. Esse apud hos Populos magnas Ferrarias testantur Cæsar lib. VII & Strabo lib. IV. Sic Rutilius lib. I:
units.tr: This land was once the home of the Bituriges, whom Strabo and Ptolemy and others call Celts. For the Bituriges were two peoples of Gaul, distinguished by surnames: the Bituriges Cubi, whose metropolis was Avaricum, in First Aquitaine; and the Bituriges Vibisci, or Vivisci, whose chief city, as I will say later, was Bordeaux, in Second Aquitaine. Both states were free under the Romans, according to Pliny. The state of the Bituriges in the Notitia of the Provinces lies in First or Sixth Aquitaine, Vienne. Jean Chaumeau, who wrote a history of the Bituriges in six books, says much about the name of the people. Caesar in book 7 and Strabo in book 4 attest that there were great iron-works among these peoples. So Rutilius, book 1:

units.la: Non Biturix largo potior Stricta Camino.
units.tr: Non Biturix largo potior Stricta Camino.

units.la: Metropolim habet Avaricum: sic Cæsar, sic Antoninus, sic alij, qui paullo humaniores, vocant Vrbem, quæ nunc vernacule Bourges. Stultos dicit in suis ad me literis Iosephus Scaliger, qui esse putat (inter eos video Marlianum & Petrum Sanlulianum) opidulum Bituricensis Diœceleos nomine Vierzon, vel, ut quibusdam scribitur, bitur, Viarons. Biturigæ, Ammiano lib. xv sub finem, Gregorio Turonensi lib. r. cap. xxxv & lib. vi. cap. xxxi. Bedæ xviii Kalend. Febr. & v Eid. Nov. Vfuardo iv Eid. Ianuar. xiii Kal. Iunij, iv Eid. Oct. & v Eid. Nov. Biturica eidem Gregorio Turonensi lib. ii. cap. xviii; Biturica, Sidonio Apollinari lib. vii epist. v; Biturigæ Vrbs eidem Turonensi non semel: Biturica Civitas Bedæ dicitur iiii Nonas Iulij & Vfuardo ibidem. Auaricum quidam volunt dictum ab Fura flumine, quo adluitur. Locatam hanc Vrbem aliquando ipse notavi in Agro perquam amœno; qui non modo Frumentorum omnium & Leguminum, verum etiam Vinorum præstantissimorum, Pecorum, Piscium, Volucrum, & quorumcumque Fructuum feracissimus. Quatuor beata est Rivulis, qui vulgo Aufren, & Aurette ab una; Ture & Molon ab altera fluentes parte. Quis condiderit, ut pleraque alia Opida, incertum est. Veteris paullo sequior, quam Hodiernæ, Vrbis tunc situs. Ad Paludes scilicet vergebat, cujus etiam nunc cum admiratione visuntur Muri, propemodum integri, solidissima materia, ut passim Veterum Romanorum Opera, constructi: initium capiunt ab Turri, quam Magnam vocant, pergentes per medium D. Stephani Templum, Plateam D. Ioannis Campestris, Portamque Gordianam usque ad Novam, cui olim ab S. Andrea nomen: inde per Plateam Amphitheatri, vulgo des Arenes, se ad Portam Turonensem extendunt; hinc autem, porrecto ambitu versus Portam D. Paulli, paullatim Turrim, quam dixi, repetunt. Postea prolatis variè Pomeriis ita fuit hæc Vrbs amplificata ab Karolo Magno & aliis; ut jamnunc cum maximis & munitissimis Galliæ Civitatibus contendat; Formam habens oblongam, amplissimam & spaciosissimam. Munita est octoginta editis crassisque Turribus. Inter eas principem tuetur locum, quam antea Magnam dixi appellatam, La grosse Tour, ab insolita crassitudine, Minoribus undique Turribus Muroque & Fossis profundissimis, Philippo II Augusto Galliarum Rege circa annum cIↄcxc. curante, cincta: Forma est rotunda, magnæ altitudinis. Aliam omnino similem fuisse ajunt, sed dirutam; à binis Turribus Biturigibus nomen inditum fabulantes. Et laudat antiqui Grammatici Carmen Calamæus: Turribus à binis, inde vocor Biturii.
units.tr: Its metropolis is Avaricum, so called by Caesar, by Antoninus, and by others who are a little more refined; the city is now called in the vernacular Bourges. Joseph Scaliger, in his letters to me, calls foolish those who think (among them I see Marliani and Pierre Sanlulien) that the small town in the diocese of Bourges named Vierzon, or, as some write it, Viarons, is the place. The Bituriges appear in Ammianus book 15 near the end, in Gregory of Tours book 1 chapter 35 and book 6 chapter 31, and in Bede on 18 Kalends of February and 5 Ides of November; Usuard on 4 Ides of January, 13 Kalends of June, 4 Ides of October, and 5 Ides of November. Biturica appears in the same Gregory of Tours, book 2 chapter 18; Biturica in Sidonius Apollinaris, book 7 letter 5; the city of the Bituriges in the same Turonensian many times; Biturica Civitas is called so by Bede on 4 Nones of July, and by Usuard in the same place. Some hold that Avaricum is named from the river Fura, by which it is washed. I myself once noted that this city is situated in a very pleasant country, which is most fertile not only in all grain and pulse but also in the finest wines, livestock, fish, birds, and every kind of fruit. It is blessed by four streams, which flow commonly called the Auron and Aurette on one side, and the Yèvre and Moulon on the other. Who founded it, like many other towns, is uncertain. The site of the old city was then somewhat further from the present one. It inclined toward the marshes, and its walls can still be seen with wonder, nearly intact, built of the most solid material, like most works of the ancient Romans. They begin at the tower called the Great Tower, and run through the middle of the church of St. Stephen, the Place St. John of the Fields, and the Gordian Gate as far as the New Gate, once named after St. Andrew; from there through the Place of the Amphitheatre, commonly called des Arenes, they extend to the Turonian Gate; and from there, stretching around toward the Gate of St. Paul, they gradually return to the tower I mentioned. Later, with boundaries variously extended, this city was enlarged by Charlemagne and others, so that now it can compete with the largest and most strongly fortified cities of Gaul. It has an oblong form, very ample and spacious. It is defended by eighty high and thick towers. Among them the chief place is held by the one I said was called the Great Tower, La grosse Tour, from its unusual thickness; it is surrounded on all sides by smaller towers, a wall, and very deep ditches, under the care of Philip II Augustus, King of France, about the year 1190. It is round in shape and of great height. They say another, entirely similar, once stood there but was destroyed, and they make up a tale that the Bituriges took their name from two towers. Calamaeus also quotes an old grammarian's verse: "From two towers, hence I am called Bituria."

units.la: Hæc talia patior aliis persuasa magis, quam mihi. Septem habet Vrbs Suburbia, totidemque Portas, præter Minores aliquot, quæ hac ibi flagitanti sunt factæ Necessitate. Ingruente ab hostibus metu, quatuor tantum patent; Burbonia, S. Privati, S. Sulpicy & Aronia. Septemdecim sunt Ecclesiæ, quas Collegiatas vulgo vocant: Septemdecim Parochiæ: Quatuor Mendicantium Ordines: duæ Virorum Abbatiæ; una S. Sulpicy, potens & dives, extramuranea; altera intra Vrbem D. Ambrosii, valdeetiam dotata: tres Mulierum; prima Nunnade vulgo, in honorem D. Virginis; altera D. Laurentij; tertia Sororum Mendicantium D. Clarae. Artes hic florent Mechanicæ, cum primis Textrinum; & ab ea, Mercatura Pannaria. Annuas habet Nundinas valde celebres, D. Laurentii, D. Lazari, D. Martini, S. Vfini, & alias. Extructum ibi non ita pridem fuit à pio Magistratu Ptochodochium, Pauperibus aliisque Adflictis alendis consecratum. inter splendida Ædificia, quorum magnus semper hic fuit numerus, primum agmen ducit Domus Iacobi Cordi, qui vixit tempore Karoli vii, superba & sumtuosa; Dominos, quum ibi essem, agnoscens Alba-Spinæos. Sunt & Ædes Almanorum, qui quondam Regiæ Gazæ præfuerunt, antequam Nundinæ, quæ ibi maximo Peregrinorum concursu celebrari solitæ, Lugdunum transferrentur anno cIↄ ccccxcvii. Hæc Vrbs Archiepiscopali fulget Sede, cujus Præsules numerat nominatque Bellefortestius xcvii; postremum Antonium Vallatum Parisiensem. Sua floret Academia, cui nulla per totam Galliam par; Doctissimorum Virorum genitrix & Emporium. Viget in ea maxime Iurisprudentia, quam ibi professi sunt Professores excellentissimi, Andreas Alciatus, Eguinarius Baro, Petrus Rebuffus, Franciscus Duarenus, Franciscus Balduinus, Antonius Contius, Hugo Donellus, & alij; meo vero tempore Iacobus Cujacius, Vir omni laude superior. Infinita monstrantur Avarici cum intra, tum extra Muros Veterum Ædificiorum elaborati operis & materiæ præstantis Rudera: multa & quotidie eruuntur, præsertim ex Fossa Arenarum, uti vocant; ubi quondam Amphitheatrum. Vrbem maximæ non semel Calamitates afflixerunt. Quinquies & amplius expugnata ab hostibus, fere funditus diruta fuit, incendioque abluta; sed magnificentius semper restaurata. Recepisse se in eam scribitur Karolus vii, pressus prestius ab hostibus, bello Anglico: nominatus ab Adversarijs, quod ea una & sola ipsi superesse videretur, Rex Biturigum. Prope Bituriges inter Vicos Solange & Nohant, locum monstrant Incolæ, quo Veromanduorum Castra sua posuerat contra Cæsarem, qui oppidum obsidione cinxerat, ut cum inde moveret.
units.tr: I suffer these things, though they are more convinced of them than I am. The city has seven Suburbs and as many Gates, besides some smaller ones that were made here because of the pressing need of the moment. With fear of the enemy looming, only four stand open: Burbonia, S. Privati, S. Sulpicy and Aronia. There are seventeen Churches, which people commonly call Collegiate; seventeen Parishes; four Orders of Mendicants; two Abbeys of men, one of S. Sulpicius, powerful and rich, outside the walls, and the other within the city, of S. Ambrose, also very well endowed; and three for women: the first, commonly called the Nunnery, in honour of the Blessed Virgin; the second of S. Laurence; and the third of the Mendicant Sisters of S. Clare. The mechanical arts flourish here, above all weaving, and from it the cloth trade. It has yearly fairs, very well attended: those of S. Laurence, S. Lazarus, S. Martin, S. Ursinus and others. Not long ago a Poorhouse, dedicated to feeding the poor and other afflicted people, was built here by the pious magistrate. Among the splendid buildings, of which there has always been a large number here, the first place is held by the House of Jacques Cœur, who lived in the time of Charles VII, proud and sumptuous; when I was there, its owners were the Alba-Spinaei. There are also the Houses of the Almains, who once presided over the royal treasury, before the fairs, which used to be held here with a very great concourse of foreigners, were transferred to Lyons in the year 1497. This city shines with an archiepiscopal See, whose prelates Bellefortest counts and names, ninety-seven, the last being Antonius Vallatus of Paris. Its Academy flourishes, to which no other in all France is equal; a mother of most learned men and a marketplace of them. Law thrives in it above all, taught there by most excellent professors: Andreas Alciatus, Eguinarius Baro, Petrus Rebuffus, Franciscus Duarenus, Franciscus Balduinus, Antonius Contius, Hugo Donellus and others; in my own time Jacobus Cujacius, a man above all praise. Countless ruins of old buildings, of elaborate workmanship and fine material, can be seen both inside and outside the walls, and many things are dug up every day, especially from the Ditch of the Sands, as they call it, where there once stood the amphitheatre. The city has been struck by terrible disasters more than once. Taken by enemies five times and more, it was almost utterly razed and burnt out, yet it was always restored more splendidly. It is recorded that Charles VII took refuge here, hard pressed by the enemy in the English war, and that his opponents called him, because this city alone seemed to remain to him, King of the Bituriges. Near Bourges, between the villages of Solange and Nohant, the inhabitants point out the place where the Veromandui pitched their camp against Caesar, who had surrounded the town with siege, from which he was to move.

units.la: Est autem Avatici summum totius Ducatus Tribunal, cui præsidet Monarcha Biturigum, qui vulgo Le Bailli de Berry. Ad hunc devolvuntur omnes Appellationes cum à Prætore Urbano, tum ab omnibus finitimorum aliorumque Territorij Bituricensis locorum Magistratibus. Habet autem Præfectus Bituricensis sub se Metropolim ipsam Avaricum & v Dioeceses, quas vulgatis nominibus exprimam, ne mea translatione obscurentur, Tissendun, Dun le Roy, Vierzon, Mehun, Concressault.
units.tr: The highest court of the whole duchy is at Bourges, presided over by the Bailiff of Berry, who is commonly called Le Bailli de Berry. To him all appeals are referred, both from the Urban Praetor and from the magistrates of all the neighbouring places and of the other localities of the Bourges territory. The Bourges governor has under him the metropolis itself, Bourges, and five dioceses, which I shall name in their common vernacular forms, so that they are not obscured by my translation: Tissendun, Dun le Roy, Vierzon, Mehun, Concressault.

units.la: Metropoli, de qua abunde dictum, adcententur Comitatus Sancerre & S. Aignan; Baronia Montfaucon; Castellaniæ, ut loquuntur, fere xl. Sancerram quidam arbitrantur dictam ab Cerere, quæ ibi culta perhibetur; tamquam Sacrum vel Sacellum Cereris. Doctiores Latine scribentes huiusmodi Etymologiam averlati Xantoiorum vocant. Comitatus gaudet titulo, qui anno MCCCXV permutatus cum Peterborough. Rogerius namque Præsul Belovacensis Eudoni Campaniæ Comiti pro Comitatu Beaujolais tradidisse legitur in Historia Sancerrarum. Arctissimam sustinuit Sancerra Obsidionem anno MCCCLXXIII: Famem passa tam sævam, ut post devoratos avide Canes, Feles, Equos, Glires, Mures, Talpas; post consumpta Cornua, Corium, Pergamenas, & similia, ne excrementis quidem Carnibusque humanis fuerit parcitum. Parent ipsi Castellaniæ sive Municipalia Magisteria, Sancergues, Bearfu, Chapelle d'Angillon, Le Chastel de Boncard, Ivonges, Tarenay, Verdigny, Menesme, Charentonnay, Bue, & aliæ.
units.tr: To the metropolis, of which I have spoken at length, are attached the county of Sancerre and S. Aignan, the barony of Montfaucon, and about forty castellanies, as they call them. Some think Sancerre was named from Ceres, who is said to have been worshipped there, as if it were the sacred place or shrine of Ceres. Scholars writing in Latin, rejecting this etymology, call it Xantoiorum. The county enjoys a title which, in the year 1315, was exchanged for Peterborough; for it is read in the History of the Sancerres that Roger, bishop of Beauvais, handed over to Eudes, count of Champagne, the county of Beaujolais in exchange.
