Sancerre endured a most close siege in the year 1373: it suffered such savage famine that, after they had greedily devoured dogs, cats, horses, dormice, mice and moles, and had used up horn, leather, parchment and the like, not even excrement or human flesh was spared. The castellanies, or municipal magistracies, obeying it are Sancergues, Bearfu, Chapelle d'Angillon, Le Chastel de Boncard, Ivonges, Tarenay, Verdigny, Menesme, Charentonnay, Bue, and others.

units.la: S. Aignan nomen habet ab S. Aniano Episcopo, de quo antea dixi ex Sidonio, Idacio, aliis.
units.tr: S. Aignan has its name from S. Anianus, bishop, of whom I spoke earlier, drawing on Sidonius, Idacius and others.

units.la: Baronia Montfaucon, Latine sonans Montem Falconis, complectitur Dominia Baugy & Gron: item La Fane, Lyuron, Coin, Villabon, Senry, Marcilly, Marnay, Farges, Anor, Saigny, Percigny, Cru, Lassay, Bouboson, Nuisement, Villiers, Compoy.
units.tr: The barony of Montfaucon, which in Latin means Mons Falconis, comprises the lordships of Baugy and Gron; likewise La Fane, Lyuron, Coin, Villabon, Senry, Marcilly, Marnay, Farges, Anor, Saigny, Percigny, Cru, Lassay, Bouboson, Nuisement, Villiers, Compoy.

units.la: Castellaniæ denique nominantur: Ays d'Angillon, Sury en Vaux, S. Soulange, S. Palais, La Salle du Roy, Bueil, Quantilly, Lomorigny, Franche-Ville, La Chapelle, Nançay, Drye, Leureux (Leprosus Vicus Gregorio Turonensi; oppidum probe Muris cinctum) Beaulieu, Brecy, Bengy, S. Ficurant, Neufuy sur Barangeon (vel, ut nonnullis scribitur, Berenton; quidam putant esse Noviodunum Biturigum, cujus meminit Cæsar lib. vii. de Bello Gallico) Morthennier, Marmaignes, Manlranches, S. Vrsin, Tilly, Bouiers, Vatan (Arcem habet) S. Satur, Lury (antiquum cum Arce Oppidum, cuius iurisdictioni etiam, quæ se extendit ad Carum usque Fluvium, alia subjacent Oppida) Ilfreches, Mandpas, Ville-neufue, S. Crapaix, Assilly, Iussy le Chaudrier, La Corne, Les Chatizes, Vaunrilles, Les Cloyes, Bouge.
units.tr: Finally, the castellanies are named: Ays d'Angillon, Sury en Vaux, S. Soulange, S. Palais, La Salle du Roy, Bueil, Quantilly, Lomorigny, Franche-Ville, La Chapelle, Nançay, Drye, Leureux (Leprosus Vicus in Gregory of Tours, a town well walled in), Beaulieu, Brecy, Bengy, S. Ficurant, Neufuy sur Barangeon (or, as some write, Berenton; some think it is Noviodunum of the Bituriges, which Caesar mentions in book vii of the Gallic War), Morthennier, Marmaignes, Manlranches, S. Ursin, Tilly, Bouiers, Vatan (it has a citadel), S. Satur, Lury (an old town with a citadel, to whose jurisdiction other towns also are subject, which extends as far as the river Cher), Ilfreches, Mandpas, Ville-neufue, S. Crapaix, Assilly, Iussy le Chaudrier, La Corne, Les Chatizes, Vaunrilles, Les Cloyes, Bouge.

units.la: Hæc de ipsa Metropoli latissimaque ejus Iurisdictione: succedunt explicandæ paucis reliquæ Dioeceses. Tissendon Regia Civitas & Ballivatus, qui sub se habet Baronias aliquot, & Castellanias supra xx. Baronias quidem, Chay eau-roux, Castellum Rufum tonat Latinis: oppidum insigni Arce ornatum: in Comitatus decus ab Karolo ix Francorum Rege erectum, ut Baroni gratificaretur Aumontio, cujus Filius natu maximus Comitem se gessit Primum Castelli Rufi. Is antea Deroux audiebat Efflabonne. Sequuntur inde Cernay, cui Arx, S. Sezerc, Lyneres, cui adnexa est Castellania Rizay; Argenton, in qua Rancennes Senescallus & Serrignet Præfectura. Argentomagus autem hoc putatur Antonini & Itinerariæ Tabulæ. Oppidum est cum Arce, cui Turres decem; Maiores septem, tres Minores, quarum una dicitur Hesaclv, in qua Tauri effigies, cui insculpta Cæsaris illa, VENI, VIDI, VICI. Dominos agnoscit Montpenserios. Antiquitates, quæ quotidie ex Terræ Visceribus exturbantur, vetustum esse loquuntur. Castellaniæ vero numerantur Bouffac, Chasteau Meillant, Marcul, Neuffy S. Sepulcre, Rully, Pauday, Massay, Caho s, Ieroufe, Chasseliet, Massenure, Augurande, S. Chartier, le Pallecteau, Temmeres, Moche Fully, Vouliou, la Ferte, Nohant, Ville Dieu; Chastre, Castra Latine, oppidum validissimum, firmis cinctum Muris, Turresque habens fortes, Fossas profundas, Arcemque insignem: nunc Comiti subest Castri-Rufi: Charoux denique, Oppidum inter Avaricum & Yllodunum, quod ex multis indicijs satis paret antiquum esse. Hæc de Niffoudunensi Diœcesi tertio loco nominavi Dunum Regium, vernacule Dun le Roy. Dunum quid sit, alibi dictum. Hujus Tribunalis iurisdictio late etiam se extendit. Subsunt illi Castellaniæ præter alias, Pradictl Callant, Baronia; Chasteau-neuf, ad Carim, S. Julian.
units.tr: So much for the metropolis itself and its very wide jurisdiction. The remaining dioceses must now be explained briefly. Tissendon is a royal city and bailiwick, which has under it several baronies and more than twenty castellanies. Among the baronies are Chay eau-roux, which in Latin is Castellum Rufum: a town adorned with a notable citadel, raised to the dignity of a county by Charles IX, King of the French, to do a favour to the baron Aumont, whose eldest son took the title of First Count of Castelli Rufi. Previously it was called Deroux and was heard as Efflabonne. Next follow Cernay, which has a citadel; S. Sezerc, Lyneres, to which the castellany of Rizay is joined; Argenton, in which Rancennes is the seneschal's seat and Serrignet the prefecture. Argenton is thought to be the Argentomagus of the Antonine Itinerary and the Tables. It is a town with a citadel, which has ten towers: seven greater and three lesser, one of which is called Hesaclv, on which is the image of a bull, with that inscription of Caesar's, VENI, VIDI, VICI, carved on it. It acknowledges the lords of Montpensier as its masters. The antiquities which are dug out of the bowels of the earth every day show that it is ancient. The castellanies that belong to it are Bouffac, Chasteau Meillant, Marcul, Neuffy S. Sepulcre, Rully, Pauday, Massay, Caho s, Ieroufe, Chasseliet, Massenure, Augurande, S. Chartier, le Pallecteau, Temmeres, Moche Fully, Vouliou, la Ferte, Nohant, Ville Dieu; Chastre, which in Latin is Castra, a very strong town, enclosed by firm walls, with sturdy towers, deep ditches and a notable citadel; now it is subject to the Count of Castrum Rufum; and finally Charoux, a town between Bourges and Yzeure, which by many signs clearly appears to be ancient. These are the things I have named concerning the diocese of Nieffoudunensis. Third, I have named Dunum Regium, in the vernacular Dun le Roy. What Dunum means has been said elsewhere. The jurisdiction of this tribunal also extends widely. Under it are, besides others, the castellanies Pradictl Callant, a barony; Chasteau-neuf, on the Cher; and S. Julian.

units.la: Sequitur Vierzon, Civitas Regia & Diœcesis; sub se habens Dominia, Champre, Motte d'Aify, Saragosse, Brisay, Mery.
units.tr: Next comes Vierzon, a royal city and diocese, having under it the lordships Champre, Motte d'Aify, Saragosse, Brisay, Mery.

units.la: Succedit inde Mehun, Mihodunum vel Mitidunum apud Aimoinum: Mediolanium Antonini quibusdam, nescio quâ bene. Ius dicit Castellanijs Loue & Forcy, aliisque forteau.
units.tr: Next is Mehun, called Mihodunum or Mitidunum by Aimoin, and Mediolanium by some of the Antonine writers, I know not on what good grounds. It exercises jurisdiction over the castellanies of Loue and Forcy, and others of less note.

units.la: Postremo positus loco Concressault, vel, ut alij scribunt, Concoursault. Latine nonnullis redditur Concordia Saltus. Burgus est Habitatore frequens. Arcem habet situ opere inexpugnabilem. Subsunt ejus iurisdictioni Vailly, Clemon, Beau-jeu.
units.tr: Lastly, situated in place is Concressault, or, as others write, Concoursault. Some render it in Latin as Concordia Saltus. It is a town thick with inhabitants. It has a citadel, impregnable by its position and workmanship. Under its jurisdiction are Vailly, Clemon, Beau-jeu.

units.la: Principatum apud Francos Hugone Capeto tenente, Biturigibus præerat nomine regio Gotefredus. Ab eo originem traxisse perhibetur Harpinus is, qui ab Rege Henrico I emit Comitatum Biturigum. Hic non multo post accingens se ad expeditionem Palæstinæ cum aliis Principibus, eundem Coronæ unendum vendidit Philippo I.
units.tr: When Hugh Capet held the principality among the Franks, Gotefredus presided over the Bituriges with royal authority. From him Harpinus is said to have derived his origin, the man who bought the county of the Bituriges from King Henry I. Not long afterwards, preparing for the expedition to Palestine with the other princes, he sold it to the Crown to be united with it, to Philip I.

units.la: Aliquot post annis Apannagii jure Comitatum, in Ducatus dignitatem tunc evectum, obtinuit à Patre Ioanne Valesio Francorum Rege Ioannes Valesius: quo sine Prole mascula mortuo, Ducatus ad Regnum redit. Assignatus est postea Ioanni Karoli VI, qui numerosa prole gravatus erat, Filio. Hic, quum ααα obiisset, successorem reliquit Karolum Fratrem, qui Rex Francorum inauguratus Sponsalibus, quæ inter Henricum Angliæ Regem & Katharinam iptius Germanam contracta jam ante fuerant, insuperhabitis, quum ei major Regni pars ab Anglis esset erepta, per ludibrium Biturigum Rex fuit appellatus. Patri Karolo subrogatus est Karolus, Ludovici XI Francorum Regis Frater. Post eum Margareta, Regis Francisci Soror, nupta primo Karolo Alençonio Duci, deinde Henrico Albretano Navarrae Regi, Ducatum Biturigum ab Fratre in Vlum-fructum accepisse scribitur. Margareta denique, eiusdem Francisci Regis Filia, Biturigses accepisse traditur ab Fratre Henrico II, quum nuberet Emanuel Philiberto Allobrogum Principi.
units.tr: Some years later, by right of an appanage, Ioannes Valesius obtained the County, by then raised to the dignity of a Duchy, from his father, John of Valois, King of the Franks. When he died without a male heir, the Duchy returned to the Crown. It was afterwards assigned to John, son of Charles VI, who was burdened with a large family. When he died, he left as successor his brother Charles, who was crowned King of the Franks. Since the marriage agreement made earlier between Henry, King of England, and Catherine, his sister, was disregarded, and most of the kingdom had been seized by the English, he was mockingly called King of Bourges. His father Charles was succeeded by Charles, brother of Louis XI. After him, Margaret, sister of King Francis, is written to have received the Duchy of Berry from her brother in usufruct, first when she married Charles, Duke of Alençon, and then Henry of Albret, King of Navarre. Finally, Margaret, daughter of the same King Francis, is said to have received the Berry lands from her brother Henry II when she married Emanuel Philibert, Prince of the Allobroges.

units.la: CAP. XXVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVI.

units.la: Borbonius Tractus.
units.tr: The Bourbonnais District.

units.la: BORBONII, Le Pais & Duché de Bourbonnois, qua Corus est Occidensque, Bituriges & Lemovices habent conterminos; qua Septemtrio, Nivernenses: ad Orientem Burgundi fere jacent, ad Meridiem sunt Lugdunenses.
units.tr: BOURBONNAIS: Le Pais & Duché de Bourbonnois has the Bituriges and the Lemovices as its neighbours to the west and north-west; the Nivernais lie to the north; the Burgundians lie roughly to the east, and the Lyonnais to the south.

units.la: Putantur hic olim suæ fuisse Sedes Populis, quos Ædui adtributos, nominat Cæsar lib. I. de bello Gallico; quorumque Opidum Gergovia dicit lib. VII; ubi etiam Boie, Boiorum proculdubio Opidi, ne mentio. Segusianos quoque totum Pagum Forensem, qui hodie Le Pais de Forez, habitasse antea monui, quum de Lugdunensi agerem Territorio; addam nonnihil paullo post.
units.tr: This district is thought to have once been the seat of those peoples whom Caesar, in book I of the Gallic War, names as attached to the Aedui. In book VII he mentions their town Gergovia, and there is also mention of Boie, which was without doubt a town of the Boii. I have already noted that the Segusiani also inhabited the whole Forez district, which today is Le Pais de Forez, when I was dealing with the territory of Lyon. I will add something a little later.

units.la: Totum hoc Territorium, ut multa alia Conregionalia, Aquitaniæ quondam Regibus parusse scribitur. Postea suos habuit Proceres, qui ab non postremæ dignationis Opido Borbony audiebant. Eorum postremus legitur Archbaldus, cui unica fuit Filia & Heres Agnes. Hæc nupta Ioanni Burgundiæ Duci, Beatrici Filiæ, quam ex eo susceperat, quum cum Roberto, Ludovici IX Filio, clocaret, Borbonium Dominium in dotem dedit, cavens ut nomen Vxoris, id est Borboniæ Gentis (hic enim illud ad Posteros studebat transmittere) gereret. Quod factum. Robertus igitur Ludovici IX, qui in Sanctorum relatus numerum, Filius Borboniorum porro fuit Progenitor. Filius enim illi fuit Ludovicus Magnus cognomine, quem Philippus VI Valesius primum Borbonij Ducem fecit anno c13 cccxxx ix, aut circiter. Hunc sequuti sunt recta linea Petrus I (cujus Frater Iacobus Marchiæ Vendomæque Comites produxit) Ludovicus II, Ioannes, Ioannes I, Karolus & Ioannes II. Huic, licet Trigamo, inproli tamen defuncto, successit Petrus II; cujus Filia Hereseque Susanna, nubens Karolo Borbonio, Mompensierio Comiti (Gilberti Borboni Filio, Ludovici Nepoti, Ioannis I, de quo dixi, Ducis Borboni, Comitis etiam Mompensierij & Arverniæ Delphini, Pronepoti) Maritum suis nuptijs Borboni fecit Ducem. Hic ille Karolus, qui Franciæ Comestabilis, facta ab suo Principe Francisco I Galliarum Rege defectione, ad Karoli V Imperatoris Partes transgressus, Romam ejus auspicijs oppugnans, plumbeaque glande anno cIↄ IↄXXVII pridie Nonas Mai trajectus, Victoriæ suæ caruit fructu. Post Susanna Conjugis obitum, Rege Eo bonum sibi vindicante, Vendomæ Duces Arma sibi nudumque Titulum Cognationis jure retinuerunt; de quibus alio loco.
units.tr: This whole territory, like many other neighbouring regions, is said to have once belonged to the kings of Aquitaine. Afterwards it had its own lords, who took their title from the town of Bourbon, a place of no small standing. The last of them is read to be Archbaldus, whose only daughter and heir was Agnes. She married John, Duke of Burgundy, and by him she had a daughter, Beatrice. When this daughter was to marry Robertus, son of Louis IX, Agnes gave the lordship of Bourbon to her as dowry, on condition that the bride bear the name of her husband's house, that is, the name of the Bourbon family, for she was eager to pass that name on to posterity. This was done. So Robertus, son of Louis IX, who was counted among the saints, became the progenitor of the Bourbons. His son was Ludovicus Magnus, whom Philip VI of Valois first made Duke of Bourbon in the year 1339, or thereabouts. In direct line he was followed by Petrus I (whose brother Iacobus founded the counts of La Marche and Vendôme), Ludovicus II, Ioannes, Ioannes I, Karolus and Ioannes II. He was succeeded by Petrus II, who, although married three times, died without issue. Petrus's daughter and heir Susanna married Karolo Borbonio, Count of Montpensier, the son of Gilbert of Bourbon, grandson of Ludovici, and great-grandson of Ioannis I, of whom I have spoken, Duke of Bourbon and also Count of Montpensier and Dauphin of Auvergne. By this marriage she made him Duke of Bourbon. This is that Karolus who was Constable of France. He broke with his prince, Francis I, King of France, went over to the side of the Emperor Charles V, and attacked Rome under his leadership. He was struck by a leaden ball on 6 May 1527, and so he lost the fruit of his victory. After the death of his wife Susanna, King Eo bonum claimed the estates for himself. The Dukes of Vendôme kept the arms and the bare title of kinship by right; of them I shall speak in another place.

units.la: Borbonium porro Tractus hodie Geographis Franciæ duplex describitur, Inferior & Superior.
units.tr: The district of Bourbonnais is now described by French geographers as twofold, Inferior and Superior.

units.la: Inferior comprehendit Urbes ipsas, duosque Comitatus. Quod ad Urbes, Metropolis totius Ducatus censetur Moulinum, oppidum ad Flumen, quod Cæsari Elaver, hodie Allier, ut alibi docui: Antiqua Ducum Sedes; post autem Domus Deliciarum, amœnissimusque Regum Franciæ Secessus. Sunt qui putant Gergobinam Cæsaris esse; sed vide quæ dicam cap. sequenti: Arce superbit Molinum perquam elegante: cui Hortus conjacet nitidissimus, Aureorum etiam Citreorumque Pomorum ferax. In quodam Arcis Xysto videre est Ducum Borboniorum ad vivum effigies, eorumque Genealogiam. Augustissimum quoque hic conspexi Fontem. Reliquæ Urbes Opidaque sunt Borbonium, Borbon, antiquitate clarum; dignumque quondam habitum, quod nomen daret Provinciæ; Boia, quorundam judicio, Cæsaris lib. VII. Arcem habet validissimam & Thermas: L'Archimont; Montmeraut; Cosne, cognominatum ex Bourbonnois ad Ligerim, Arce præditum, Territorio suo, quod Pecori pascendo idoneum, reliqua superans, Montluison; S. Porcin, cujus Ager præstantia producit Vina, (de hujus tamen jure disceptatur: quidam enim Arvernia adscribunt) Cusset; Chantelle; Charroux; Vernueil, Vinis suis celebre; Varennes ad Flaverem Opidum clarum; Gaunat Arverniæ conterminum; Le Mont aux Moines; Sonnigny le Comté ou aux Moines; La Palisse, insigni superbiens Arce; Erisson; Sancings; S. Pierre le Moustier; Aimes le Chasteau, sic cognominatum ab Arce; S. Amand; & alia. Hæc de Urbibus opidisque: Comitatus sunt duo, qui vulgo Beau-jolois & Forest. Prior Bello-Iolesius complectitur quidquid est inter Ligerim & Ararim, situs Orientem versus inter Forenses & Burgundos: Antiquum Borboniorum Patrimonium. Urbs primaria vernacule dicitur Beau-jeu. Alter nomen habet non ab Silvis Saltibusque, ut quidem vox videtur sonare; sed ab Fori nomine, de quo mox. Forenses, sic enim Populos nominem, versus Septemtrionem Borbonensibus germanis suis objacent; ad Occidentem Arvernis; qua Meridiem spectant, Lugdunenses habent confinales; qua Orientem, Bello-Iolesios. Præfuerunt quondam Comites, ex quorum etiam stirpe prognati Bello Iolesii Proceres. Celebratur Francorum Historiographis Comes quidam Lugdunensis, Forcellii, ut cum vulgo loquar, & Bello-Iolesii, cui tres fuerunt Filij, Arthaudus Comes Lugdunensis, Stephanus Foresii, Emfridus Bello-Iolesii. Quum ita Comitatus Foresii & Bello-Iolesii longo tempore fuissent distracti, coaluerunt rursum morte Guicardi, Comitis Bello-Iolesii qui tempore Philippi II Francorum Regis cum honore Comitem Strabuli egerat. Ipsius enim Soror Isabella Bello Iolesii Comes, matrimonio collocata est Reginaldo, Foresii Comiti, qui procreatus erat stirpe Arthaudi, de quo dictum; ut ipsa ex prosapia Stephani, qui Arthaudo, ut paullo ante scriptum, erat Frater. Eo autem Conjugio editi leguntur Guido, cui hereditate obvenit Comitatus Foresii; & Ludovicus, cui Dominium obtigit Bello-Iolesij. Post eos nihil traditur certi. Rex Galliarum Henricus III, antequam ad Monarchiam veniret Franciæ, una cum Ducatu Andegavensi Apannagij jure possedit Ducatus Borbonii & Arvernia, Comitatumque Foresii. Primarium Forensium Opidum Roana, ad Ligerim, qui Ponte ibi stratus: Regiæ versus Lugdunenses Viæ imminet, Arcem habens. Secundum facile tuetur locum Forum Segusiavorum: Sic olim nuncupabatur, quod nunc vulgo Feurs: Φόρῳ Σιγυσιαυῶν Ptolemæo: Forum Segusiavarum corrupte Tabulæ Itinerariæ. Extat in hoc Opido Vetus Inscriptio, mentionem faciens antiquæ Appellationis: NVMINI. AVG DEO. SILVANO FABRI. TIGNVAL QVI. FORO. SEGVS CONSISTVNT D. S. P. P. Ab hoc igitur Foro Pagus Forensis, vulgo Le Pais de Forest, corrupte; quum' dicendum potius esset, de Fores. Hoc Opidum hodieque locus est Commercij totius Provinciæ. Reliqua sunt Mombrisonium, Sedem Baillivo præstans: Fanum S. Stephani, S. Estienne de Furan, Officina Armorum & Cannarum ferrearum, quæ inde per omnes Galliæ ditiones exportantur: Artem suggesserunt Incolis cum Aquæ commoditas, quæ Ferrum egregie temperat, tum Carbones, qui ibi eruuntur: Fanum S. Galmari, S. Galmier, in cujus Suburbanis Fons est aluminosus, qui vulgo Font-Foule: Fanum S. Germani, S. Germain Laval, generosissimi Vini ferax: Fanum D. Boveti, S. Bovet le Chastel, in quo fabricantur optimæ notæ Forcipes: Fanum D. Remberti, S. Rembert, primo Ligeris Ponte famosum. Alia prætereo.
units.tr: The Inferior part comprises the towns themselves and two counties. As for the towns, Moulins, a town on the river which Caesar calls Elaver and which is today the Allier, as I have shown elsewhere, is regarded as the metropolis of the whole duchy. It was the ancient seat of the dukes and afterwards the house of delights and the most pleasant retreat of the kings of France. Some think it is the Gergobina of Caesar, but see what I say in the following chapter. Moulins takes pride in a very elegant castle, beside which lies a most spruce garden, rich also in golden apples and citrons. On a certain terrace of the castle one may see lifelike portraits of the Bourbon dukes and their genealogy. I also saw a most splendid fountain here. The other towns and small towns are Bourbonium and Bourbon, famous for antiquity and once thought worthy to give its name to the province; Boia, in the judgement of some, is Caesar's town of book VII. It has a very strong castle and baths. Then come L'Archimont, Montmeraut, and Cosne, called ex Bourbonnois because it lies on the Loire; it has a castle, and its territory, suited to pasturing flocks, surpasses the rest. Next are Montluison, S. Porcin, whose fields produce wines of distinction (though its ownership is disputed, since some assign it to Auvergne), Cusset, Chantelle, Charroux, Vernueil, famous for its wines, Varennes, a notable town on the Allier, Gaunat, bordering Auvergne, Le Mont aux Moines, Sonnigny le Comté or aux Moines, La Palisse, proud of its notable castle, Erisson, Sancings, S. Pierre le Moustier, Aimes le Chasteau, so called from its castle, S. Amand, and others. So much for the towns. There are two counties, commonly called Beau-jolois and Forest. The former, Bello-Iolesius, takes in everything between the Loire and the Arar, lying to the east between the men of Forez and the Burgundians. It was the ancient patrimony of the Bourbons. Its chief town is called Beau-jeu in the vernacular. The other county takes its name not from forests and woods, as the word may seem to suggest, but from the name of Forum, which I shall discuss shortly. The Forenses, for so I name the people, lie to the north, next to their Bourbonnais kinsmen; to the west they border the Auvergnats; to the south their neighbours are the Lyonnais, and to the east the Bello-Iolesii. Formerly they were ruled by counts, and from the same line sprang the lords of Beaujolais. Among the French historians is celebrated a certain count of Lyon, of Forez (to speak as the common people do), and of Beaujolais, who had three sons: Arthaudus, Count of Lyon; Stephanus, of Forez; and Emfridus, of Beaujolais. Since the counties of Forez and Beaujolais had been separated for a long time, they were reunited on the death of Guicardus, Count of Beaujolais, who had held the rank of Count of Stralbul with honour in the time of Philip II, King of France. His sister Isabella, Countess of Beaujolais, was married to Reginaldus, Count of Forez, who was descended from the line of Arthaud, mentioned above, while she herself came from the family of Stephen, who, as stated a little earlier, was Arthaud's brother. Two children of this marriage are recorded: Guido, who inherited the county of Forez, and Ludovicus, who received the lordship of Beaujolais. After them nothing certain is handed down. King Henry III of France, before he came to the throne of France, held as an appanage, together with the Duchy of Anjou, the duchies of Bourbon and Auvergne and the county of Forez. The chief town of the Forezians is Roanne, on the Loire, which has a bridge built there; it overlooks the royal road towards Lyon and has a castle. The second town, which occupies an easily defended site, is Forum Segusiavorum. It was formerly called so, and is now commonly called Feurs; Ptolemy gives it as Φόρῳ Σιγυσιαυῶν [Phoro Sigysiauon], and the Antonine Itinerary, through a corruption, gives Forum Segusiavarum. In this town there is an old inscription mentioning the former name: "To the godhead of the Emperor, to the god Silvanus, the smiths of Tignval, who are at the Forum of the Segusiavi, have dedicated this at their own expense." From this forum comes the Pagus Forensis, commonly and corruptly called Le Pais de Forest, when it should rather be called de Fores. This town is still today the centre of trade for the whole province. The remaining places are Mombrisonium, which has the seat of the bailiff; Fanum S. Stephani, S. Estienne de Furan, a workshop of arms and iron cannon, which are exported from there to all the lands of France. Its craft was suggested to the inhabitants by the water, which tempers iron excellently, and by the coal dug out there. Fanum S. Galmari, S. Galmier, has in its suburbs an aluminous spring, commonly called Font-Foule. Fanum S. Germani, S. Germain Laval, produces very fine wine. Fanum D. Boveti, S. Bovet le Chastel, is where excellent pincers are made. Fanum D. Remberti, S. Rembert, is famous for the first bridge over the Loire. I pass over the others.

units.la: Sic se habet Inferior Borbonij Tractus: Superior proprio vocabulo dicitur Le Pais de Cambraille; Inferiore montosior.
units.tr: Thus stands the Inferior part of the Bourbonnais district. The Superior part is called in its own name Le Pais de Cambraille; it is more mountainous than the Inferior.

units.la: CAP. XXVII.
units.tr: CAP. XXVII.

units.la: Pictonius Tractus.
units.tr: The Poitou Region.

units.la: PICTONIVM vel PICTAVIA, Poitou, Regio est Frugum, Pecoriscque, Lanæ, Linique feracissima; Vino Frumentoque dives; Piscium abundans; Avium Ferarumque magnam habens copiam: comprehendens mille ducentas Parœcias, sub tribus Episcopatibus, Pictavien-si, Maleacensi, Luxonensi: in Primi quidem Diœcesi Abbatiæ numerantur xxvii; in Secundi, iv; in Tertij, x. Agricolæ nonnihil habent peculiaris Linguæ; quibus qui parum fidit, sapere perhibent. Hominum genus, quod, Feras prohibitum, Lites venatur, contentiosum, & in simpulo fluctus excitare gnarum. Vrbani dissimilis plane genij & ingenij, faciles, benefici, liberales, candidi, fucos & impostu-ras detestantes, Eruditionis & Eruditorum, qui hic non pauci, amantes. Nobilitas provida, strenua, audentior. Spectat versus Meridiem hæc Regio Ecolismenses & Sanctones; ad Occidentem habet Oceanum; qua Septemtrio est, Britannos respicit & Andegavenses; reliqua Turones, Bituricenses, & Lemovices claudunt.
units.tr: Poitou, or PICTAVIA, is a region exceedingly rich in grain, livestock, wool and flax; abounding in wine and corn; well supplied with fish, and with a great abundance of birds and game. It comprises 1,200 parishes under three bishoprics: Poitiers, Maillezais and Luçon. In the diocese of the first there are 27 abbeys; in that of the second, 4; in that of the third, 10. The farmers have a somewhat peculiar language, and those who trust it little are said to be wise. The people, who, forbidden to hunt wild beasts, hunt quarrels, are contentious and skilled at stirring up a storm in a teacup. The townsfolk are quite different in character and disposition: easy-going, kind, generous, open, hating flattery and deceit, and fond of learning and of scholars, of whom there are not a few here. The nobility is prudent, vigorous and rather bold. Towards the south this region is bounded by Angoulême and Saintes; to the west it has the ocean; to the north it faces Brittany and Angers; the remaining sides are closed by Tours, Bourges and Limoges.

units.la: Veteres Incolæ fuerunt Pictones, ut Cæsar, Strabo, & Plinius nominant: Ptolemæo scribuntur Pictavi sunt Ammiano Marcellino. Pictonicam Regionem appellat Ausonius: Civitatem Pictavorum vel Pectavonum Notitia Provinciarum in Aquitania ii, vel vii Viennensi. Hodie Le Pais de Poictou. Sunt qui Pictones à Pictis Britanniæ Populis ortos dictosque fabulantur. Consulendi plenius Ioannis Boucheti Annales Aquitanici, Belleforestius, Thevetus & alij. Peculiarem de hac Regione gione scripsit libellum Ioannes de la Haye, Gallico Idiomate. Pictonibus Populos Agesinates jungam cum Plinio. Horum verisimile est memoriam adhuc superesse in Pago Aigounois, haud procul Fano S. Maxentii, quod Opidum ad Severum Fluvium. Toto coelo errant, qui Aginnates cum Agesinatibus confundunt: quum inter utrosque minimum inter quinque dierum sit interjectum. Videndus Iosephus Scaliger Ausonianar. Lection. lib. II. cap. x.
units.tr: The ancient inhabitants were the Pictones, as Caesar, Strabo and Pliny call them; Ptolemy writes Pictavi, and Ammianus Marcellinus likewise. Ausonius calls it the Pictonic Region; the Notitia of the Provinces lists the City of the Pictavi or Pectavones in Aquitaine II, or in Vienne VII. Today it is Le Pais de Poictou. There are those who fable that the Pictones were descended from the Picts, a people of Britain, and so named. For a fuller account, consult the Aquitanian Annals of Jean Bouchet, Belleforest, Thevet and others. Jean de la Haye wrote a separate little book on this region in the French language. I shall join to the Pictones the Agesinates mentioned by Pliny. It is probable that their memory still survives in the district of Aigounois, not far from the town of Saint-Maixent, which lies on the river Sèvre. They are wholly mistaken who confuse the Aginnates with the Agesinates, since between the two there lies a distance of about five days' journey. See Joseph Scaliger, Ausonian Lections, book II, chapter x.

units.la: Regni Titulo decorata legitur hæc Provincia ab Gothis; quos hinc, ut tota Aquitania, exegit Francorum Rex Clodovæus. Imperator Ludovicus Pius Aquitaniæ Regnum Filio Pipino dedit; cujus Filios Pipinum & Karolum quum Karolus Calvus, ipsorum Patruus, Aquitania dejectos Monasteriis inclusisset, ipse Principatum invasit, donoque Consanguineo suo Arnulpho dedit: sed, abrogato Regni Titulo, Ducatus honore insignitum. Arnulpho succesllerunt ordine Guilelmus Fortis; Eblo I, & II; Guilelmus II, & III; Guido; Guilelmus IV & V; huius unica Filia & Heres Eleonora collocata fuit Ludovico VII, Francorum Regi: à quo propter Adulterij & Proditionis suspicionem repudiatam duxit Henricus Normanniæ Dux, qui defuncto Stephano Angliæ Regi successit. Henricum tam in Angliæ Regno, quam in Dotalibus paternisque in Francia Ditionibus, sequuti sunt ipsius Filij Richardus & Ioannes. Quum autem Arthurus Filius Godefredi (qui Regis Ioannis major natu fuerat) praeferendum se Ioanni diceret, persuasus ab Francorum Rege Philippo Augusto, ut Pictones Patruo Ioanni eriperet, rem viribus adgressus, ab Ioanne, qui ex improviso supervenerat, fusis copijs, captus est, Rotomagumque raptus temeritatis suæ poenas dedit. Eam ob causam Ioannes Rex ab Constantia Arthuri Matre apud Philippum Regem Paricidij accusatus, damnatus fuit; ejusque bona Philippo, tamquam Feudorum Domino, sunt adjudicata, cum alia, tum Pictavia: quam mox Successor ipsius Ludovicus VIII Alphonso Filio concessit: quo Inproli defuncto, in potestatem Regis Philippi III venit, penesque ipsius Posteros mansit, donec, regnante Philippo Valesio, ab Eduardo III Anglorum Rege fuerit recuperata, retentaque plenius cum tota Aquitania per sancitam inter eumdem & Ioannem Francorum Regem Pacem. Factum mox ex Aquitaniæ Ducatu Principatum Rex Eduardus Filio concessit; qui quum Aquitanis gravissimum imperasset Tributum, magnam partem amisit, defectione ab ijs facta ad Karolum V Francorum Regem: cuius Filius Karolus VII Anglos tota Aquitania, anno cIↄ cccclIII exturbavit, Filioque Regi Ludovico XI reliquit. Hic eam Fratri largitus est Karolo; quo mortuo, rursus Rex Ludovicus receptam ad Regem Karolum VIII Filiam transmisit: à quo tempore Aquitania, cujus non ignobilis portio Pictavium, deinceps in potestate permansit Regum Francia.
units.tr: This province is recorded as having been adorned with the title of a kingdom under the Goths, whom King Clovis of the Franks drove out from here, as from all Aquitaine. The Emperor Louis the Pious gave the kingdom of Aquitaine to his son Pepin; when Charles the Bald, their uncle, had shut up Pepin's sons Pepin and Charles in monasteries, having deposed them from Aquitaine, he himself seized the principality and gave it to his kinsman Arnulf; but, the title of kingdom being abolished, it was invested with the honour of a duchy. Arnulf was succeeded in order by William the Strong; Eudes I and II; William II and III; Guy; William IV and V. The only daughter and heiress of the last, Eleanor, was married to Louis VII, King of the Franks; but he repudiated her on suspicion of adultery and treason, and she then married Henry, Duke of Normandy, who after the death of Stephen succeeded as King of England. Henry was followed, both in the kingdom of England and in the dominions in France which came to him by dowry and from his father, by his sons Richard and John. When Arthur, son of Geoffrey (who had been older than King John), claimed that he should be preferred to John, and was persuaded by King Philip Augustus of the Franks to wrest Poitou from his uncle John, he attacked the matter by force; but John, who came upon him unexpectedly, routed his forces, and Arthur was captured and carried off to Rouen, where he paid the penalty of his rashness. For this reason King John was accused of parricide before King Philip by Constance, Arthur's mother, and was condemned; and his goods were adjudged to Philip, as lord of the fiefs, together with other lands and among them Poitou. His successor Louis VIII soon granted it to his son Alphonse; when he died without issue, it came into the power of King Philip III and remained with his descendants until, in the reign of Philip of Valois, it was recovered by Edward III, King of the English, and retained, together with all Aquitaine, by the peace concluded between him and John, King of the Franks. Shortly afterwards King Edward granted the principality, made out of the duchy of Aquitaine, to his son; but when he had imposed a very heavy tribute on the Aquitanians, he lost a large part of it through their defection to Charles V, King of the Franks. His son Charles VII drove the English out of all Aquitaine in the year 1453, and left it to his son King Louis XI. He bestowed it on his brother Charles; when he died, King Louis again took it back and transferred it to King Charles VIII. From that time Aquitaine, of which Poitou is no small part, has remained in the power of the Kings of France.

units.la: De varij generis Principatibus, qui Pictonio concenseri soliti, quæ habeo adscribam, si prius de Metropoli & regia ejus Civitate nonnihil dixero. Ea est Pictavia. Sic Latini nunc vocant, quæ Αὐγουστόριτον Prolemæo, Augustoritum Antonino. Pictaviam Urbem appellat Gregorius Turonensis. Urbs amoenissimo sita est loco, clivoso tamen; nisi quod una parte, quam Tranchæam patrio vocabulo dicunt, in planiciem abeat; latissimi, si quæ in Gallijs alia, ambitus; sed cujus ingens portio ab Habitatoribus vacua; Pratis, Vineis, alijsque agrestibus Operibus occupata: reliqua excellentibus Ædificiorum structuris veneranda. Adluit latus illud Clanus Fluvius, Aqua latis copiosa manans; Insulasque diducto Alveo efficiens, aliquot inde versus Septentrionem miliaribus Vingennæ commiscetur. Visuntur ibi præter Arcem Validam, Palatium Gallicni; vasta Amphitheatri rudera, vulgo Les Arenes, nota voce; Aquaeductuum Fornices, quos Arceaux de Parigne Vulgus dicit: Romanorum hoc loco Imperij vestigia. Primarium Templum D. Petro est consecratum. Claram reddit hanc Urbem Episcopalis Sedes; cujus Bellesorestius Praesules commemorat XCIII; eorum postremum nominans, Karolum Defiursium. Praefuit inter alios D. Hilarius Antistes, invictum se gerens Arrianis Antagonistam; à quo Regionem hanc ad Christianam Religionem conversam tradunt Ecclesiastici Scriptores. Academiam habet Horentissimam, cui alter post Parisiensem locus solet tribui. Instituit Karolus VII Francorum Rex, anno cIↄ cccc xxxi. Rebuffus in Authentic. Habita. C. Ne Filius pro Patre, vehementer improbat, quod ibi Studiosis homines vilissimi turpissimique graves saepe injurias inferre permittantur, contra salubberrimam piissimi Imperatoris ratoris Constitutionem. Docuit aliquando Augustoriti Grammaticam Ammonius Anastasius Burdigalensis, ut notat Ausonius Carm. de Professoribus xi. Magnas sustinuerunt aliquoties Incolae Calamitates ab Anglorum aliorumque Incursionibus. Medio circiter ab Vrbe miliari, itinere, quod Avaricum Biturigum ducit, in Via Regia ingens spectatur Saxum, forma quadratum, quinque lapidibus fulcitum, unde vulgo La Pierre Levée. De eo Distichon hoc extat:
units.tr: I shall add what I have concerning the various kinds of principalities which are usually reckoned under Poitou, if first I have said something about its metropolis and royal city. This is Poitiers. Thus the Latins now call it; it is the place which Ptolemy calls Augustoritum and Antoninus Augustoritum. Gregory of Tours calls it the City of Poitiers. The city lies in a most pleasant spot, though sloping; except that on one side, which the natives call Tranchée, it runs out into a plain. Its circuit is very wide, as wide as any in France; but a great part of it is empty of inhabitants, occupied by meadows, vineyards and other rustic works; the rest is venerable for the excellent structures of its buildings. The river Clain washes that side, a stream flowing with abundant water; it forms islands by spreading its channel, and some miles to the north it joins the Vienne. There are seen there, besides the strong citadel, the palace of Gallienus; the vast ruins of an amphitheatre, commonly called Les Arènes, a well-known name; the arches of the aqueducts, which the common people call Arceaux de Parigne: these are traces of Roman rule in this place. The chief church is consecrated to St Peter. The episcopal see makes this city famous; Belleforest records 93 of its prelates, naming the last of them Charles de Dursius. Among the others, St Hilary presided, a bishop who showed himself an unconquered opponent of the Arians; the ecclesiastical writers relate that this region was converted to the Christian religion through him. It has a most flourishing academy, which is usually counted second after that of Paris. Charles VII, King of the Franks, founded it in the year 1431. Rebuffus, on the Authentica Habita, Ne filius pro patre, strongly disapproves that there students are often permitted to inflict serious injuries on the most worthless and vile men, contrary to the most wholesome constitution of that most pious emperor. Ammonius Anastasius of Bordeaux once taught grammar at Augustoritum, as Ausonius notes in his poem on the professors, xi. The inhabitants have several times suffered great calamities from the incursions of the English and others. About a mile from the city, on the road which leads to Bourges, on the royal highway, there is seen a huge stone, square in shape, supported by five stones, which is commonly called La Pierre Levée. About it this couplet exists:

units.la: Hic Lapis ingentem superat gravitate ColossumPonderis, & grandi Sidera Male petit.
units.tr: This stone surpasses the huge Colossus in weight of its mass, and with its great bulk it seeks out the stars.

units.la: Viatores plerumque sua insculpunt Nomina. Inscriptos legi cum aliis Obertum Gifanium Buranum, Gerardum Mercatorem, Abrahamum Ortelium, Philippum Gallaeum, Georgium Braun Colonien-sem, Gerardum Hovenaglium. Curia Pictavien-sis regitur manu Praesidis & duorum Vicariorum, quorum unus Civiles, alter Criminales cognoscit causas. Ad hanc multorum hujus Provinciae Opidorum Tribunalia pertinent: ut praeter Pictaviam ipsam, de qua dixi, sunt: Niort cum Arce: hic amplissimi Pictonum Merkatus ter anno: Fontenay le Comte, Arce item praeditum; Moenia hujus Opidi praeterfluit Rivulus Vendaeus (Vendee) qui subinde adeo excrescit, ut totum Fontenaei Territorium vicinaque Loca inundet: Lusignan, ubi Castrum antiquum, quod vulgo Melusine (sunt & alia loca ab hac denominata Vouvant & Mauzevant, quae sit Melusine) Montmorillon La basse Marché; Dorat; S. Maxent, & alia fortean: quibus additum Sivray erectum in Senechallatus dignitatem, Arce potens.
units.tr: Travellers for the most part carve their names on it. Among the names I have read inscribed there were Obert Giffen of Bruges, Gerard Mercator, Abraham Ortelius, Philip Gallaeus, Georg Braun of Cologne, and Gerard Hovenagel. The court of Poitiers is governed by the hand of a president and two vice-governors, one of whom hears civil cases and the other criminal cases. To this court the tribunals of many towns of this province belong; besides Poitiers itself, of which I have spoken, they are: Niort, with its citadel: here is the very large market of the Poitevins, held three times a year; Fontenay-le-Comte, likewise furnished with a citadel; past its walls flows the little stream Vendée, which at times swells so much that it floods the whole territory of Fontenay and the neighbouring places; Lusignan, where there is an ancient castle, commonly called Mélusine (there are also other places named from her, Vouvant and Mauzevant, which is said to be Mélusine's); Montmorillon, La Basse-Marche; Dorat; Saint-Maixent, and perhaps others: to these is added Civray, raised to the dignity of a seneschalship, powerful with its citadel.

units.la: Est autem, ut eam nunc partem adgrediar, sub Pictonio Principatus Titulo ornata (praeter Talmontem, Talmont: sic dictum quasi Talon du Monde, Calcaneus Mundi, ut quidam volunt) Rupes super Ionnam, Roche sur-Ion. Familiae regalis Borboniae. Noverunt Avi nostri Ludovicum Borbonium, Ioannis Vendomae Comitis F. Rupis ad Ionnam Principem, Comitem Mompensierium, ejusque Filium Karolum. Ducatus dignitate claret Castellum Heraldi, Chatelherault, ad Vingennam. Vicecomitatus sunt Tonars ad Touium Fluvium, Brosse, Bricieres, Roche-Chouart. Baronatus Dominiique honore insignita sunt Opida non pauca, quae turbato, ut in oculos veniunt & mentem, ordine ponam: Mainlers, ubi Piscatio Salmonum, Alosarum, quae Clupeae aliis, Balaenarum & Asellorum praecipue; qui arefacti Ventoque & Frigore indurati in varias Regiones solent exportari: Partenay; S. Maxent; Melle; Chizay; Chauvigny; Luffac; Bressuyre, Charron; Chasleneraye; S. Mesmin; S. Gillis; Chasteaumur; Les Sables d'Aulonne; S. Hermine; Montaigu, Opidum cum Arce, Salinis nobile; Mirebeau; La Motte; S. Beraye; Vouvant; S. Hilaire; Mortemer; Luzay; S. Savin; l'Isle Jourdain; S. Benoist du Sault; Bourg-neuf; Mereuil, Mervant; Brigo; Vouvert, Ville-faignaix, & alia.
units.tr: Now, to take up that part, it is adorned with the title of the principality of Poitou (besides Talmont, so called as if Talon du Monde, the heel of the world, as some wish) La Roche-sur-Yon, of the royal house of Bourbon. Our grandfathers knew Louis of Bourbon, prince of La Roche-sur-Yon, son of John, Count of Vendôme, and Count of Montpensier, and his son Charles. The dignity of a duchy is conspicuous in Châtellerault, Chastelherault, on the Vienne. There are viscountcies at Thouars on the river Thouet, Brosse, Bricquebec, and Roche-Chouart. Not a few towns, honoured with the title of barony and lordship, which I shall set out in a disordered sequence as they come to eye and mind: Mauléon, where fishing takes place for salmon, shad, which others call herring, and especially whales and dogfish; which, dried and hardened by wind and cold, are usually exported to various regions: Parthenay; Saint-Maixent; Melle; Chizé; Chauvigny; Lussac; Bressuire, Charroux; Chasseneuil; Saint-Maixme; Saint-Gilles; Châteaumur; Les Sables-d'Olonne; Sainte-Hermine; Montaigu, a town with a citadel, noted for its salt-works; Mirebeau; La Motte; Saint-Béray; Vouvant; Saint-Hilaire; Mortemer; Luçay; Saint-Savin; L'Isle-Jourdain; Saint-Benoist-du-Sault; Bourgneuf; Mareuil, Mervent; Brigueil; Vouvray, Villefagnan, and others.

units.la: Silentio non est praetereundus hic Pagus Dovaus, vulgo Dowe; paucis ab hinc annis celebrari coeptus vel ob Amphitheatrum, quod ipsi adjacet, seminativum; manu quidem & arte humana factum, sed ita, ut videri posset a natura. Totum enim excisum & cavatum est in Monte, sine ulla externa Materiatione Calcis, Lapidis, Ligni. Montis ipsius & Amphitheatri plenissima est delineatio, ex fide Levini Kersmakeri, Consulis quondam Zirickzaei, Zelandiaeque primis hujus belli Motibus Gubernatoris, apud Iustum Lipsium libello de Amphitheatris, quae extra Romam cap. vi. qui Pagum Dovaum addit aliquid amplius olim fuisse, cum ex eo non pagani Operis argumento, tum ex Viae antiquae publicaeque reliquiis, quae ex pago eodem pertinuit ad Pontem Caesarianum, vulgo Pont du Sey: cujus Viae Pars adhuc variis locis conspicitur, Pars autem maxima corrupta est, Lapidibus in aedificia varie absumtis aut avectis. Sed & Incolas scribit Antiquitatem aliquam jactare, Druidesque apud se tedes habuisse. Pagum autem Ptolemaei Daveonam fuisse suspicatur ex claro Nominis, quod nunc praefert, argumento, exque Situ, qui ab ipsa Ptolemaei collocatione non abscedit. Vide tamen quae dicam cap. xxxv. ubi de Cadurcibus.
units.tr: This place must not pass without mention: the Pagus Dovaus, commonly called Dowe. It has begun to be celebrated in the last few years, partly because of the amphitheatre that lies next to it, which is half-natural: it was indeed made by human hand and skill, but in such a way that it could seem to be the work of nature. For the whole of it has been cut and hollowed out of the mountain, without any external building material of lime, stone or wood. A very full drawing of the mountain itself and of the amphitheatre is available, on the authority of Lieven Kersmaker, once consul of Zierikzee and governor of Zeeland at the first stirrings of this war, in Justus Lipsius's book on amphitheatres outside Rome, chapter 6. Lipsius thinks that the Pagus Dovaus was formerly something larger, both from the evidence of the work, which is not rural, and from the remains of an ancient public road which ran from this district to the Caesarian Bridge, commonly called the Pont du Sey. Parts of this road can still be seen in various places, but most of it has been destroyed, its stones having been variously used up or carried off for buildings. Lipsius also writes that the inhabitants boast of some antiquity and that the Druids had temples among them. He suspects that the Pagus of Ptolemy was Daveona, from the clear evidence of the name it now bears, and from its site, which does not differ from Ptolemy's placement of it. See, however, what I shall say in chapter 35, where I treat of the Cadurci.

units.la: Fuisse & in Pictonibus Limonum, colligitur ex Antonini Itinere, quod Burdigala ducitur Augustodunum: Λιμωνον Ptolemaeo; In Tabula Itineraria scribitur Lemonum. Illud magni Viri putant idem esse transnominatione quadam, cum Augustoritô, Poictiers. Ego nihil ausus sum hic affirmare. Limoni mentio in Commentario Gallico A. Hirtij ter; ubi tamen quidam Libri Lemovicum contra fidem & auctoritatem Manuscriptorium Codicum praeferunt.
units.tr: That Limonum was also among the Pictones is gathered from the Antonine Itinerary, which runs from Burdigala to Augustodunum; Ptolemy has it as Λιμωνον [Limōnon], and the Table of Roads writes it as Lemonum. Great men think that it is the same place under another name, Augustoritum, that is, Poitiers. I have not dared to assert this here myself. The mention of Limonum occurs three times in Aulus Hirtius's Gallic Commentary; there, however, some books have Lemovicum, contrary to the faith and authority of the manuscript codices.

units.la: CAP. XXVIII. Inculisménsis Ager.
units.tr: CHAP. XXVIII. The District of Angoulême.

units.la: INCVLISMENSIS AGER, qui vulgo Engoulefme ad Septemtrionem Pictonibus est conterminus; ad Orientem Santonibus; ad Meridiem Burdigalensibus & Petrocorijs, ad Orientem denique Lemovicibus. Longitudo ejus ab Ortu in Occasum xxiv est milliarium: Latitudo ab Meridie in Septemtrionem, xvi. Fertilis Vini optimi, Frugum, Cannabis. Silvam habet, quæ Bacona, cvo io i jugerum. Familiæ hic Antiquitate inlustres & Factis. Litteræ magni pretij. Qui Metropolin ceteraque colunt Opida, præstantes sunt ingenio, excellentiarum, candidi pectoris, Mercaturæ dediti, Opibus affluentes; in novis rebus, quod cum Vicinis reliquisque adeo Francis habent commune, se supra modum oblectantes. Qui ruri degunt, bardi sunt & rudes, Laborumque patientissimi. Universum vero ad Arma apti, feroces in hostem, impavidi nihilque timentes.
units.tr: THE DISTRICT OF ANGOULÊME, commonly called Engoulefme, borders on the Pictones to the north, on the Santones to the east, on the Burdigalenses and Petrocorii to the south, and finally on the Lemovices to the east. Its length from east to west is 24 miles, and its breadth from south to north is 16. It is fertile in very good wine, in grain and in hemp. It has a forest called Bacona, of cvo io i jugera. Its families are distinguished by antiquity and by deeds, and its literature is of great worth. Those who inhabit the capital and the other towns are gifted in mind, excellent, of an upright heart, devoted to trade and abounding in wealth. In novelties, which they share with their neighbours and with the rest of the Franks, they delight themselves beyond measure. Those who live in the country are rough and unpolished, and most patient of toil. In general they are fit for arms, fierce against the enemy, fearless and afraid of nothing.

units.la: Ecolismenses appellat Veteres hujus Agri Incolas Notitia Provinciarum Galliæ; qui in aliis Codicibus Inculismenses. Nam in quibus Etolismenses vocantur; improbioris sunt notæ: pro quibus qui substituunt vel Lemovicenses vel Helvienses, sunt frustra. Hodie les Engoulmois nominantur.
units.tr: The Notitia of the Provinces of Gaul calls the ancient inhabitants of this district the Ecolismenses; in other manuscripts they are Inculismenses. The readings Etolismenses are of less reliable authority, and those who substitute either Lemovicenses or Helvienses do so to no purpose. Today they are called les Engoulmois.

units.la: Ecclesmensium vel Inculismensium Metropolis Inculisma; quæ apud Ausonium Epistola xi ad Tetradium, pro Librorum diversitate, varie legitur, Ichnusa vitiosissime; Inculisna vel Iculisna ferendo modo; Iculisma vere germaneque, & ex Poëtæ ipsius mente, Ecoicsma & Ecolisma in Antiquis ipsorum monumentis, Ecolesina mendose in Sigeberti Chronicis ad annum 1019, ut quidem ea sunt edita ab Henrico Stephano Lutetiæ. Engolisma Gregorio Turonensi in Vita S. Eparchii. Equosilina alijs, ejusdem Vitam scribentibus; male. Vrbs Equolenensis corrupte pro Ecolismensis apud eundem Gregorium Turonensem in Confessoribus extremis. Hodie Engoulesme. Est autem Vrbs Antiquitate insignis. In Veterum Mœnium, quæ quod olim fuit Suburbium ab Vrbe dividebant, fundamentis reperta sunt superioribus annis, quum muniretur, signa certa & vestigia pervetustæ Vrbis. Sita est in Colle, qui Flumini Carantono imminet, Agro devio & ab Regiis Viis remotiore, quod etiam indicat Ausonius: Iculisma quum te abscónderet; Et invidebam devio ac solo loco Opus Camœnarum tegi.
units.tr: The metropolis of the Ecclesmenses or Inculismenses is Inculisma. In Ausonius, Epistle xi to Tetradius, the name is read variously according to the diversity of the books: Ichnusa, most corruptly; Inculisna or Iculisna, in the common way of reading; Iculisma, which is true and genuine and, in the mind of the poet himself, Ecoicsma and Ecolisma in their own ancient monuments; Ecolesina, wrongly, in the Chronicles of Sigebert at the year 1019, as they were published by Henri Estienne at Paris. Engolisma in Gregory of Tours, in the Life of St Eparchius. Equosilina in others who wrote his Life, wrongly. Urbs Equolenensis, corruptly for Ecolismensis, in the same Gregory of Tours, in the Confessors at the end. Today it is Engoulesme. The city is famous for its antiquity. In recent years, when it was being fortified, sure signs and traces of a very ancient city were found in the foundations of the old walls, which divided the city from what was once its suburb. It stands on a hill that overhangs the river Charente, in a secluded region somewhat remote from the royal roads, as Ausonius also indicates: When Iculisma hid you, and I grudged that the work of the Muses should be concealed in a secluded and solitary place.

units.la: Commentarium fecit de Engulisma Antiquitate Elias Vinetus, quem Pictavis edidit Enguilbertus Marnefius. Scripsit item de Engulisma sua, Engulismensiumque Comitibus Librum Franciscus Corlicus, Regius Engulisma Procurator. Perfantæ colunt Engulismenses & pro magno habent Numine Ausonium quemdam; quem suorum Episcoporum fuisse primum, & ab Santonibus Engulismam accersitum dicitant: qui an idem sit cum Ausonio Poeta Burdigalensi, dubitant adhuc docti Viri. Certe Ausonius Agrum habuit apud Santones, ut innuit in Epistolis ad Axium, Paullum & Tetradium, ubi Senex non illubenter commorabatur. Quin quibus temporibus Engulismenses Ausonium suum volunt vixisse, ea non male quadrant cum Ausonij Poetæ seculo.
units.tr: Elias Vinetus wrote a commentary on the antiquity of Engulisma, which Enguilbert Marnef published at Poitiers. Francis Corlieu, royal procurator of Engulisma, likewise wrote a book on Engulisma itself and on the counts of the Engulismenses. The Engulismenses worship a certain Ausonius and regard him as a great divinity. They say he was the first of their bishops, and that he was summoned from the Santones to Engulisma; learned men still doubt whether he is the same as the poet Ausonius of Burdigala. Certainly Ausonius had an estate among the Santones, as he hints in his Epistles to Axius, Paullus and Tetradius, where the old man lingered not unwillingly. Indeed, the times in which the Engulismenses want their Ausonius to have lived fit reasonably well with the age of the poet Ausonius.

units.la: Minorum gentium apud Inculismenses Opida sunt, quæ vulgo; Marton, ad Fluvium Bandiatum, quod Secundo genitis Rupistocaldæ gentis adsignari solitum; Chasteau-neuf; Blaisac; Chabannes; Confollant, Ruffec; Aigres; Gourville; La Roche-foucault, Opidum cum Arce, Comitatus Titulo clarum; Mareuil, Lanzac, Villebois, quæ illustri Familiæ Mareuli sunt in patrimonio: Momberon & Boutevilla Mommeranciorum sunt Dynastarum.
units.tr: The lesser places among the Inculismenses are these, as they are commonly called: Marton, on the river Bandiat, which used to be assigned to the second-born of the Rupistocalda family; Chasteau-neuf; Blaisac; Chabannes; Confollant; Ruffec; Aigres; Gourville; La Roche-foucault, a town with a citadel, famous for its countship title; Mareuil, Lanzac, Villebois, which belong to the illustrious family of Mareuil as its patrimony; Momberon and Boutevilla belong to the dynasts of Mommeranci.

units.la: Visuntur in hac Provincia multi Burgi passim, Arces & Castella. Varsay non magnus est Vicus, ad octo circiter millia passuum supra Inculismam, in sinistra Carantoni ripa. Hic anno cIↄ Iↄ xli Agricultor quidam Scrobem in Agro suo serendæ Arbori faciens, terramque altius versans, Arcam plumbeam invenit, oblonga forma; lapideo Sepulcro sic impositam, ut illud media nullibi contingeret, sed undique la-teribus abesset plus tertia pedis parte, sic, ut Pixides solent, opera. Operculum enim, ut illas, extremis oris replicatis & ad tres digitos demissis, ipsam obtegebat: accedentibus quatuor Cingulis ferreis, tres latis digitos, unum crassis. Operculo sublato, in conspectum venit Corpus humanum; quod, accepto Aere, statim in Cineres abiit: Ossibus solum manentibus, quae mediocri statura situm ibi hominem loquebantur. Excussis omnibus, reperta fuit & Bractea, & purissimo auro, parva, perquam tenuis, longior quam latior, Semiducatum pendens. In ea expressae erant Vocales Graecae septem, totidem repetitae mutato ordine versibus, hoc modo: A E H I O T Ω Ω T O I H E A E H I O T Ω A T O I H E A Ω H I O T Ω A E O I H E A Ω T I O E Ω A E H
units.tr: Many villages, citadels and castles are found scattered throughout this province. Varsay is not a large village, about eight miles above Inculisma, on the left bank of the Charente. Here, in the year 1541, a farmer digging a pit in his field to plant a tree, and turning the soil deeper, found a leaden chest of oblong shape. It had been placed on a stone sepulchre in such a way that it touched the sepulchre nowhere in the middle, but was everywhere more than a third of a foot away from its sides. It was made like pyxides usually are. For its lid, like theirs, had its outer edges folded back and let down three fingers' breadth, covering the chest itself. Four iron bands were attached, three broad fingers wide and one thick. When the lid was lifted, a human body came into view, which, as soon as it received air, turned to ashes, only the bones remaining, which showed that a man of medium stature had lain there. When everything had been sifted, there was found a gold bracteate, of purest gold, small, very thin, longer than it was broad, weighing half a ducat. On it were engraved seven Greek vowels, each repeated in lines with the order changed, in this way: A E H I O T Ω Ω T O I H E A E H I O T Ω A T O I H E A Ω H I O T Ω A E O I H E A Ω T I O E Ω A E H

units.la: Quae Arcana, si quidem talia sint, quid sibi velint, divinent Pythagorei, & quibus, quam mihi, plus ocij.
units.tr: If these are indeed mysteries of that kind, let the Pythagoreans guess what they mean, and those who have more leisure than I do.

units.la: Karolus v Francorum Rex cognomine Sapiens, Inculisimensium Comitatum Anglis ereptum Filio Ludovico dedit: cui ad Regnum evecto successit Filius Ioannes; huic vero Karolus, Regum Franciae, qui nunc Rerum potiuntur, Progenitor. Hujus Filius Franciscus. ex Comite Inculisimensium, Rex factus, quum Comitatum Ducatus Titulo auxillet, eum Matri dedit: qua defuncta Titulum Ducis gessit Filius ejus Karolus; coque sine Liberis mortuo, Ducatus Coronae Franciae fuit unitus, donec Karolus Henrici II. Fe enim consequutus, moxque Rex factus, eum dedit Henrico Fratri, qui postea Rex Poloniae & Franciae.
units.tr: Charles V, King of the Franks, called the Wise, gave the county of Inculisimensis, which had been wrested from the English, to his son Louis. When Louis was raised to the kingdom, his son John succeeded him; and from John came Charles, the progenitor of the kings of France who now hold power. His son was Francis, who, made king from being count of Inculisimensis, gave the county, which he had raised to the title of duchy, to his mother. When she died, her son Charles bore the title of duke; and when he died without children, the duchy was united to the crown of France, until Charles, son of Henry II, succeeded to it, and soon became king, and gave it to his brother Henry, who afterwards became King of Poland and of France.

units.la: Inculisimensi Almisiensem obiter jungam Agrum, hodie vulgo Le Pais d'Aulnis. Nomen factum quidam putant ab Francorum Rege, quem Anglos bello persequentem dixisse ferunt, Se suis rebus satis superque prospicere, modo singulis diebus hostibus unam solum Agri Vlnam (quae Gallo-Romanis Aulne) ademtam suo Principatui adjiceret. Ego icio Aunedonnacum, hodie Aulnay, ab Antonino haud procul Mediolano Santonum collocari, & Anedonacum vitiosius in Itineraria Tabula legi. Cogitandum censeo. Certe Pagi Almisiensis appellatione vetera Monimenta intelligunt Territorium Rupellae & adcentebatur Senescballiae Santonum. Sed ex quo Rupella, excusso Anglorum jugo, dedidit se Regi Franciae, Pagus Almisiensis in privatam cessit Praefecturam, eltque ab Santonio seclusus, neque ulli Curiae potest subditus esse praeterquam Parisiensi. Id enim inter Capita ipsorum continetur Privilegiorum. Almiensis Pagi Angolismensis meminit Historia de Revelatione Capitis S. Ioannis, quae cum D. Cypriano excusa.
units.tr: I shall briefly add to Inculisimensis the district Almisiensis, today commonly called Le Pais d'Aulnis. Some think the name came from a king of the Franks, who is said to have declared, while waging war on the English, that he had more than enough provision for his own affairs, provided that each day he might add to his principality one ell (in Gallo-Roman aulne) of land taken from the enemy. I think Aunedonnacum, today Aulnay, not far from Mediolanum, was located by Antoninus among the Santones, and that Anedonacum is read more carelessly in the Itinerary Table. This needs thought. Certainly ancient records understand by the name Pagus Almisiensis the territory of La Rochelle, which was also attached to the seneschalsy of the Santones. But since La Rochelle, having thrown off the English yoke, surrendered itself to the King of France, the Pagus Almisiensis passed into a private prefecture, and was cut off from Saintonge, and can be subject to no court except the Parisian. For this is contained among the chapters of their privileges. The Almiensis Pagus Angolismensis is mentioned in the history of the Revelation of the Head of St John, which was published together with that of Cyprian.

units.la: CAP. XXIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIX.

units.la: Arvernia.
units.tr: Arvernia.

units.la: FRANCIAE Provincias, quae nunc in Prima Veterum Aquitania sunt, indicavi: succedit, quae in Secunda est, ARVERNIA, Le Pais & Duché d'Auvergne. Situs illi in locis partim planis, partim montosis. Vicinos habent Arverni ad Orientem Forenses & Lugdunenses; ad Meridiem, Languedokios; ad Occidentem, Cadurces, Petrocorios & Lemovices: Septemtrionem versus, Bituricenses & Borbonios. Arverniam qui posset universim elegantius fideliusq. depingere, quam verbis C. Solli Apollinaris Sidonii, Arvernorum Episcopi, qui de ea sic scribit lib. iv. Epist. xxi ad Asprum suum: Taceo Territorij peculiarem fecunditatem, taceo illud aequor Agrorum, in quo sine periculo quaestuosae fluctuant in Segetibus Vndae, quod industrius quisque quo plus frequentat, hoc minus naufragat: Viatoribus molle, fructuosum Aratoribus, Venatoribus voluptuosum: quod Montium cingunt dorsa Pascuis, latera Vinetis, terrena Villa, saxosa Castellu,
units.tr: I have described the provinces of France that now make up Aquitania Prima. Next comes Arvernia, which belongs to Aquitania Secunda: the country and duchy of Auvergne (Le Pais & Duché d'Auvergne). Its situation is partly on level ground and partly in mountains. The Arverni have as neighbours the Forenses and Lugdunenses to the east, the Languedocians to the south, the Cadurci, Petrocorii and Lemovices to the west, and the Bituriges and Bourbonnais to the north. Who could describe Arvernia as a whole more elegantly and faithfully than Gaius Sollius Apollinaris Sidonius, bishop of the Arverni, who writes of it thus in book 4, letter 21, to his friend Asper: "I say nothing of the peculiar fertility of the territory, nothing of that plain of fields where the profitable waves of the grain roll without danger, so that the more diligently anyone sails over it, the less he suffers shipwreck. It is soft for travellers, fruitful for ploughmen, pleasant for hunters. The backs of the mountains are girdled with pastures, their sides with vineyards, their levels with farmsteads, their rocky places with castles, their shady parts with woods, their open parts with tillage, their hollows with springs, their steep places with rivers."

units.la: L1 3 Castellis, opaca Lustris, aperta Culturis, concava Fontibus, abrupta Fluminibus. quod denique ejusmodi est, ut semel visum Advenis multis Patriæ oblivionem sæpe persuadeat. Egregie Theodoricus Gothorum Rex apud Gregorium Turonensem lib. iii. cap. ix & xi; his verbis Milites animans: Ad Advernos me sequemini, & ego vos inducam in Patriam, ubi Aurum & Argentum accipiatis, quantum vestra poterit desiderare cupiditas; de qua Pecora, de qua Mancipia, de qua Vestimenta in abundantiam adsumatis. Petrus Pictaviensis: Hunc Cluniace tibi Tellus Arvernica misit, Quo nihil uberius Gallia nostra tenet.
units.tr: "Finally, the country is such that, once seen, it often persuades many newcomers to forget their homeland." Theodoric, king of the Goths, encouraged his soldiers in these words, as reported by Gregory of Tours in book 3, chapters 9 and 11: "Follow me to the Arverni, and I will lead you into a country where you may take as much gold and silver as your greed can desire; where you may take up herds, slaves and clothing in abundance." Peter of Poitiers: "The land of Auvergne has sent you to Cluny; our Gaul holds nothing more abundant than it."

units.la: Arvernorum nomen valde celebre cum apud alios, tum apud Cæsarem in libris de Bello Gallico: Ἀρπέρος, Ptolemæo & aliis; Ἀρβέρνοι, Plutarcho; Ἀρέπρος, vitiose Stephano; Civitas Arvernorum, Notitiæ Provinciarum Galliæ in Aquitania i vel vi Viennensi. Arvernorum Resp. prima quondam Galliæ Respublica fuit. Erant enim olim Galliæ totius (ut Cæsar scribit lib. i.) Factiones duæ: alterius principatum tenebant Ædui, alterius Arverni. Horum autem potiorem potentioremque fuisse Factionem, docet Strabo lib. iv, quum eorum principatum ad Narbonensium Massiliensiumque Fines, Pyrenæos Montes, Oceanum & Rhenum extendit. Ostendunt etiam id duo cruenta Gallorum, Bituito Arverno Duce, contra Romanos prælia; de quibus ibidem Strabo, Livius lib. lxi, & alij: alterum contra Domitium ad Sulgæ & Rodani; alterum adversus Fabium ad Tisiaræ ejusdemque Rodani confluentem commissa. Victos tunc Gallos, aut certe Romanæ Provinciæ Finibus repulsos Senatus Romanus (ut idem Cæsar tradit) liberos esse, suisque Legibus uti voluit: quinetiam, quo liberior esset Gallia, Vituitum ipsum Arvernorum Regem, ut Livius appellat, quum Romam Satisfactionis causa venisset, Albæ custodiendum censuit; decrevitque, ut Congentiatus ejus Filius comprehensus Romam mitteretur. Postea Celtillus Vercingetorigis Pater, licet Principatum totius Galliæ obtinuisset, Bello quippe aliquo; attamen eam ob causam, quod Regnum adpeteret, ut est libro vii, ab Civitate interfectus est. Vercingetorix autem ipse suorum quorundam Factione Rex Arvernorum salutatus est, & videtur eodem libro ab Gallis omnibus Rex appellari? verum ab iisdem Prodirionis insimulatur, & ad eos, tamquam superioris auctoritatis Iudices Caullam dicit: nec denique Filio Regni Cupiditas fortunatior fuit, quam Patri. Regibus igitur exactis, Arvernorum Civitas libera permansit ad Cæsaris usque tempora. Plinius etiam sua ætate lib. iii natur. histor. cap. xix Liberos vocat Arvernos. Nec solum Liberi, ut multi in Gallijs alij, fuerunt; verum etiam, ut Ædui, Romanorum Fratres. Lucanus lib. i. Arverni Latio sese auši dicere Fratres, Sanguine ab Iliaco.
units.tr: The name of the Arverni is very famous, both among other writers and in Caesar's books on the Gallic War. It is written Ἀρπέρος [Arpheros] by Ptolemy and others, Ἀρβέρνοι [Arbernoi] by Plutarch, and Ἀρέπρος [Areprhos], wrongly, by Stephanus. The civitas Arvernorum appears in the Notitia of the provinces of Gaul under Aquitania I or Vienne VI. The Arvernian commonwealth was once the first republic of Gaul. For, as Caesar writes in book 1, all of Gaul was once divided into two factions: the Aedui held the leadership of one, the Arverni of the other. That the Arvernian faction was the more important and powerful is shown by Strabo in book 4, who extends its dominion to the borders of the Narbonese and Massiliots, the Pyrenees, the ocean and the Rhine. Two bloody battles of the Gauls against the Romans, under the leader Bituitus Arvernus, also show this; Strabo, Livy in book 61 and others describe them. One was fought against Domitius at the Sulga and the Rhone, the other against Fabius at the confluence of the Tisiara and the same Rhone. The Roman Senate, after the Gauls were defeated or driven back beyond the borders of the Roman province, wanted them to be free and to use their own laws (as Caesar himself relates). Indeed, to make Gaul freer still, when Vituitus, whom Livy calls king of the Arverni, came to Rome to make satisfaction, the Senate decided he should be kept in custody at Alba, and that his son Congentiatus should be seized and sent to Rome. Later, Celtillus, the father of Vercingetorix, although he had obtained the leadership of all Gaul in some war, was killed by his own state for aspiring to kingship, as is told in book 7. Vercingetorix himself was hailed king of the Arverni by the faction of some of his people, and in the same book he seems to be called king by all the Gauls; yet by these same people he was accused of treason, and he refers to them, as judges of higher authority, at Gergovia. In the end, the desire for kingship was no more fortunate for the son than for the father. So, with the kings expelled, the Arvernian state remained free down to the time of Caesar. Pliny too, in his own day, in book 3 of his Natural History, chapter 19, calls the Arverni free. And they were not merely free, as were many other peoples in Gaul; they were also, like the Aedui, brothers of the Romans. Lucan, book 1: "The Arverni, who claim to be brothers of the Latins and to trace their blood from Ilium."

units.la: Lucani hæc transcripsit Sidonius Apollinaris in suam ad Græcum Episcopum Massiliensem Epistolam, quæ extat lib. vii ordine vii: Arvernorum, proh dolor, Servitus, qui (si Prisca replicarentur) audebant se quondam Fratres Latio dicere, & Sanguine ab Iliaco Populos computare: si Recentia memorabuntur, y sunt, qui viribus propriis Hostium publicorum arma remorati sunt. Sic Petrus Pictavensis in Panegyrico Petri Venerabilis: Hunc Latiæ Gentes, Regum de stirpe potentes Arverni Populi progenuere Ducem.
units.tr: Sidonius Apollinaris transcribed these words of Lucan in his letter to Graecus, bishop of Marseilles, which is in book 7, letter 7: "Alas, the servitude of the Arverni, who (if old deeds were recalled) dared once to call themselves brothers of the Latins and to reckon their peoples from the blood of Ilium! If recent deeds are recounted, there are some who by their own strength held back the arms of the public enemies." So Peter of Poitiers, in his panegyric on Peter the Venerable: "The peoples of Latium, powerful in the line of kings, the Arvernian people produced this leader."

units.la: Sidonius Carmine vii: Est mihi quæ Latio se sanguine tollit alumnam Tellus clara Urbis, cui non dedit optima quondam Rerum Opifex Natura parem, &c.
units.tr: Sidonius, in poem 7: "I have a land that raises itself in Latin blood as a foster-child, the famous land of the city, to which the best Maker of all things, Nature, has never given an equal," etc.

units.la: Videndus & Aimoinus libro v, cap. xlix.
units.tr: Aimoin, book 5, chapter 49, should also be consulted.

units.la: Arvernium porro hodie duplex est, Superius vel Montanum; & Inferius, quod planum. Superius, Le haut Pais d'Auvergne, & Arvernia κατ' ἐξοχὴν. Primariam habet Urbem Fanum S. Flori, Saint Flour, in edita Rupe sitam; Vicum olim, cui nomen Mons planus: Prioratu quondam, hodie Episcopatu, qui ex Claromontensi delibatus, claram. Præsules numerat xix Belloforestius; eorum postremum nominans Antonium Levium. Reliqua Opida vulgo dicuntur Orillæ Latinis Aureliacus (Sedes antiqua Baillivatus, cujus iurisdictioni subsunt præter Opidum & Primariam Urbem, de qua dixi, Carlatum, Muratum; Pagique, qui vernacule, Saillères, Mauriac, S. Martin, & alij) Billons, Le Puy, &c. Territorium quoque & Baillivatus Beaucaire. Prope Pongibautum Opidulum Pagus est Roia, in quo Argenti ferax Fodina.
units.tr: Arvernia today is in fact twofold: the Upper, or Mountainous, and the Lower, which is level. Upper Auvergne, Le haut Pais d'Auvergne, is Arvernia in the strict sense. Its chief city is Fanum S. Flori, Saint-Flour, set on a high rock; it was once a village called Mons planus, and it had a priory and is now a bishopric, which was carved out of the diocese of Clermont. Belleforest counts nineteen bishops, naming as the last Antonius Levius. The other towns are commonly called Orillae, in Latin Aureliacus (the ancient seat of a bailiwick, under whose jurisdiction lie, besides the town and the chief city I have mentioned, Carlat, Murat, and the parishes which in the vernacular are called Saillères, Mauriac, S. Martin and others), Billons, Le Puy, and so on. There is also the territory and bailiwick of Beaucaire. Near Pongibautum, a small town, is the village of Roia, where there is a silver mine rich in ore.

units.la: Inferius vel Planum Arvernium, le bas Pais d'Arvergne, Alimaniam, l'Alimaigne, proprie dictam lego; eamque vocem quosdam ab Alimonia, nonnullos à pingui limosoque Solo derivare. Potius est, ut sic vocata censeatur ab Amne, qui hodie Lamone & Lymone, quemque Elaver Fluvius ingens in se recipit. Parum laboro. Lemanem Arvernam nuncupat forte Gregorius Turonensis lib. iv. cap. ix. Historiae: Dicere enim erat solitus Rex: Velim unquam Arvernam Lemanem, quae tanta jocunditatis gratia refulgere dicitur, oculis cernere. Limaniam hanc putant quidem designari Angulis appellatione apud Sidonium Apollinarem lib. iv. Epist. 1, & lib. vii Epist. 11, in Carmine denique, quod insertum ejusdem Libri Epistolae xvii. Longitudo à Ponte Veteris Brivatae Ganatum usque (aliis procurrit ulterius) circiter leucarum est viginti; Latitudo ab Monte, qui vulgo Poy de Dome (hic totius Galliae altissimis solet adnumerari; Simplicium judicio Medicorum feracissimus, in summo culmine multa Rudera testantur Arcem ibi fuisse, vel quid aliud: Poy, Arvernica Lingua, locus excelsus & montosus) ad Opidum Tiert vel Croppiere, fere octo. Regio opima est & fertilissimae Civitatibus amplissimis, Vicis, Villis, Praetorijs magnificis exculta, Vinis praestantissimis, Frugibus, Melle, Pecudibus, Lana, Croco, Piscuis, Nemoribus, Fluminibus, Fontibus, Lacubus, Balneis, aliisque Naturae Donis supra modum referta. Metropolis illi Clarimontium, Clermont vulgo: Sidonio ejus Urbis Episcopo Arvernum Opidum lib. vi. Epist. xii, & lib. vii. Epist v. Eidem Sidonio Arvernum forte Municipiolum lib. iii Epist. 1. & lib. vii Epist. 11. Iornandi Arverna Civitas & Urbs Arvernas, qui eam occupatam memorat ab Erico Vitigothorum Rege. Αυγασιμαρον Prolemaeo, ut suis ad me litteris censet Scaliger. Νεμαωσιν, quam Strabo lib. iv Arvernorum dicit Caput, Ligeri adpositam notans, cujusque meminit Lucanus lib 1, non eamdem esse, ut quidam opinantur, cum hac Urbe, ipse clamat Situs. Urbem hanc olim etiam Propugnaculis undique circumseptam & munitissimam fuisse docet Gregorius Turonensis de Vita Patrum & de S. Quintiano: Ecce Muri Civitatis illius fortissimi sunt, eamque Propugnacula ingentia vallant. Propugnaculorum etiam ipsius meminit Sidonius lib. v. Epist. xii, & lib. vii Epist. 1. Terror quondam Gothorum, à quibus saepe obsessa tandemque post Calamitates multas ad Deditionem coacta. Passim Sidonius, praesertim lib. vii. Epist. vii. Cinctam Ego hanc Urbem vidi anno cIↄ Iↄ LXXXV Colliculis fertilissimis, ex quibus magnus Rivulorum & Fontium profluit numerus, qui Hortos & Loca Incolarum Delicus consecrata irrigant. Arce superbit, & Episcopalis est Sedes. Inter Praesules fuit etiam C. Sollius Sidonius Apollinaris, quem saepe laudavi. Hic Ecclesiae Arvernae se immerito praepositum conqueritur lib. iii Epist. 1, quod & de eo testatur Gregorius Turonensis lib. ii cap. xxi: Vnice autem laudo & amplector Sidonij modestiam, qui se immerito Arvernae Ecclesiae praepositum esse conqueritur. Eleganter & ipse Sidonius lib. v Epist. iii: Ego autem infelicis Conscientiae mole depressus vi febrium nuper extremum Salutis accessi, utpote cui indignissimo tanta Professionis pondus impactum est, qui miser ante compulsus docere, quam discere, & ante praesumens Bonum praedicare, quam facere, tamquam sterilis Arbor, quum non habeam Opera pro Pomis, spargo verba pro Foliis. Sunt & aliae Inserioris Arvernias Urbes & Opida: in quis principis loci Rionium, Rion, Arcem habens; Sedes Senescballi Inferioris Arverniae, cui cum ipsa Metropoli subsunt & Opida, & Vici, Opidorum Privilegiis gaudentes. Succedunt Montferrantum, Arce praeditum, ut & Tfoira & Brionda. Sequuntur inde Cambraillia; Mons Acutus, Mont-aigu ad Iovum Fluvium, qui prope Mariganum miscetur cum Flavere; Aqua persa, Aiguepersé; Vichium, Bilhonum, Anzona, Fanum S. Germani, Lambonum, Eusbreula, Sanpourfainum, & alia. Fuit in hac Arverniae parte semileuca ab Augustonemeto quondam Urbs celebris Gergovia: cujus adhuc quaedam superstant vestigia in edito loco cum veteri appellatione, Gergoie enim audit. Gergovia rerumque ad Opidum illud gestarum mentionem saepe facit Auctor Commentariorum de Bello-Gallico, in cujus quibusdam libris etiam legitur Gergobia: item quodam loco Gergobina, sed vitiose. Nam Gergobinam aliud esse ab Gergovia Opidum, nondum mihi possum persuadere, Gergoviam quidem Strabo Arvernis, Gergobinam autem Caesar Bois tribuit: at nihil refert. Illud enim saepe fieri animadvertimus in Populis Confinalibus, ut Opida nunc his, nunc illis adscribantur. Τεργοβια dicitur Straboni; Τεργοβυη, Polyaenos Rep-
units.tr: Lower Arvernia, or level Arvernia, I read as le bas Pais d'Arvergne, properly called Alimania, l'Alimaigne. Some derive this word from alimonia (sustenance), others from the rich and muddy soil. It is more likely that it takes its name from the river which is today the Lamone or Lymone, into which the great river Elaver flows. I do not labour the point. Gregory of Tours, book 4, chapter 9 of his History, perhaps names it Lemanem Arvernam: "For the king used to say: I would like one day to see with my own eyes the Arvernian Leman, which is said to shine with such charm of delight." Some think this Limania is indicated by the name Angulis in Sidonius Apollinaris, book 4, letter 1, and book 7, letter 11, and in the poem inserted in letter 17 of the same book. Its length, from the bridge of Old Brioude to Ganat (and in some places it extends further), is about twenty leagues; its breadth, from the mountain commonly called Puy de Dôme (which is usually counted among the highest in all of Gaul, and which, in the judgement of the simple people and of physicians, is the most fertile; many ruins on its summit bear witness that a citadel or something else once stood there; Puy, in the Arvernian language, means "a lofty and mountainous place") to the town of Tiert or Croppière, is nearly eight leagues. The region is rich and very fertile, cultivated with very large cities, villages, farmsteads and magnificent manors, and filled beyond measure with excellent wines, crops, honey, livestock, wool, saffron, fish, woods, rivers, springs, lakes, baths and other gifts of nature. Its metropolis is Clarimontium, Clermont in the vernacular. Sidonius, bishop of that city, calls it Arvernum oppidum in book 6, letter 12, and book 7, letter 5. To the same Sidonius, Arvernum, perhaps a small municipal town, appears in book 3, letter 1, and book 7, letter 11. Jordanes calls it Arverna civitas and urbs Arvernas, and records that it was seized by Eric, king of the Visigoths. Ptolemy has Αὐγασιμαρον [Augasimaron], as Scaliger thinks in his letter to me. The place Strabo in book 4 calls Νεμαωσος [Nemaosos], the capital of the Arverni, lying on the Loire, and which Lucan mentions in book 1, is not, as some think, the same as this city; the very site proves it. Gregory of Tours, in his book on the Lives of the Fathers and on St Quintian, shows that this city was once also surrounded on every side by bulwarks and very well fortified: "Behold, the walls of that city are very strong, and huge bulwarks surround it." Sidonius too mentions its bulwarks, in book 5, letter 12, and book 7, letter 1. It was once the terror of the Goths, by whom it was often besieged and at last, after many calamities, forced to surrender. Sidonius speaks of it often, especially in book 7, letter 7.
