I myself saw this city, girt with very fertile little hills, from which flows a great number of streams and springs that water the gardens and the places consecrated to the pleasure of its inhabitants, in the year 1585. It is proud of its citadel, and it is an episcopal see. Among its bishops was Gaius Sollius Sidonius Apollinaris, whom I have often praised. He complains in book 3, letter 1, that he was unworthily set over the Church of the Arverni; Gregory of Tours also bears witness to this in book 2, chapter 21: "I particularly praise and embrace the modesty of Sidonius, who complains that he was unworthily placed over the Arvernian Church." Sidonius himself says it elegantly in book 5, letter 3: "But I, crushed by the weight of an unhappy conscience, have lately come near to death's end through six fevers, since such a great burden of profession was laid upon me, who, though unworthy, was before compelled to teach rather than to learn, and presumed to preach good before doing it; like a barren tree, since I have no works for fruit, I scatter words for leaves." There are also other towns and villages of Lower Arvernia. Of these, the chief place is Rion, which has a citadel and is the seat of the seneschal of Lower Auvergne; under it, together with the metropolis itself, lie both towns and villages, the latter enjoying the privileges of towns. Next come Montferrand, which has a citadel, and likewise Tfoira and Brionde. After these follow Cambrailles; Mons Acutus, Mont-aigu, on the river Iovus, which near Mariganum mingles with the Flavere; Aqua persa, Aiguepersé; Vichy, Billom, Anzon, Saint-Germain, Lamboune, Eusbreule, Sanpourçain, and others. In this part of Auvergne, half a league from Augustonemetum, there once stood the famous city of Gergovia, of which some traces still survive on a high place under the old name, for it is still called Gergoie. The author of the Commentaries on the Gallic War often mentions Gergovia and the events that took place at that town; in some books of his the name is also read as Gergobia, and in one passage as Gergobina, but wrongly. For I cannot yet persuade myself that Gergobina is a different town from Gergovia; Strabo assigns Gergovia to the Arverni, while Caesar assigns Gergobina to the Boii. But it makes no difference, for we notice that this often happens with neighbouring peoples, so that towns are sometimes ascribed to one and sometimes to the other. Strabo calls it Τεργοβια [Tergobia], and Polyaenus Τεργοβυη [Tergobyē].

units.la: Inferior, cuius propinquue, ... Unde dicta.
units.tr: Lower Auvergne, whose neighbourhood ... Whence the name.

units.la: Longitudo. Latitudo.
units.tr: Length. Breadth.

units.la: Qualitas.
units.tr: Quality.

units.la: Metropolis (Clarimontium, olim Arvernum).
units.tr: Metropolis (Clarimontium, formerly Arvernum).

units.la: Alia opida.
units.tr: Other towns.

units.la: Ejus Episcopi, inter quos Sidonius Apollinaris.
units.tr: Its bishops, among whom Sidonius Apollinaris.

units.la: Gergovia. no; Ῥαγγοβυια, Dioni. Apud Cæsarem Gergovia in altissimo posita legitur Monte, omnes aditus habens difficiles; apud Strabonem, ἐφ' ὑψηλᾶς ὄρος. Sidonius in Panegyrico Aviti: Quosvis vincis equo: testis mihi Cæsaris esto Hic nimium Fortuna parens, quum Colle repulsus Gergovia, Castris miles vix restitit ipsis.
units.tr: Gergovia. No; in Dio it is Rhangobyia [Ῥαγγοβυια]. In Caesar, Gergovia is said to lie on a very high mountain, with all approaches difficult; in Strabo, it is on a high mountain [ἐφ' ὑψηλᾶς ὄρος]. Sidonius, in his Panegyric on Avitus: You surpass all others on horseback; be my witness, Caesar's own. Here Fortune, too much a parent, when repulsed from the hill at Gergovia, the soldier scarcely held out even in the camp itself.

units.la: Notat idem Opidum & Sidonius lib. iii. Epist. iii: Subducta est tota protinus acies in superciliun Collis abrupti, quæ quum prius adplicata esset oppugnationi, te viso non est explicata congressui. Castellum vocat Orosius lib. vii cap. xi. Quo loco quondam fuit Gergovia, hodieque difficta passim visuntur Rudera, Lateres, & coagmentati Cæmentorum acervi.
units.tr: Sidonius, book iii, letter iii, also marks the same town: The whole line was at once drawn back to the brow of a steep hill, which, when it had previously been applied to the assault, was not deployed for battle when you were seen. Castellum is what Orosius calls it, book vii, chapter xi. Where Gergovia once stood, broken ruins, bricks and heaps of cemented masonry are still seen everywhere today.

units.la: Non ignobiles hodie sunt Arvernia Vici, qui vulgo Volvic & Marsac. Pagi Violvascensis (ut quidem in melioribus Libris legitur) meminit Sidonius lib. ii. Epist. xiv. Marsac ipsi Violvico adhinis & contiguus; olim, eodem Sidonio, scribente, Martialis, propter hiberna Legionum Iulianarum. Martiacus Villa nominatur in Pancharta Nigra S. Martini Turonensis M. S. Eeluacus ad calciamenta Fratrum cum omnibus sibi pertinentibus, pro qua subdole decepti Martiacum Villam in Pago Arvernensi in concambium Fratres dederunt. Non procul erat ab Urbe Ricomagensi, cujus mentio apud Gregorium Turonensem lib. i. de Gloria Martyrum, & Vico qui Mousiacus eidem Turonensi de Gloria Confessorum cap. xxi, qui vulgo Mousac.
units.tr: Not unknown today are the Arvernian villages commonly called Volvic & Marsac. Sidonius, book ii, letter xiv, mentions the Pagi Violvascensis (as it is read in the better books). Marsac lies next to and adjoining Violvico itself; formerly, as Sidonius writes, it was Martialis, because of the winter quarters of the Julian legions. The Martiacus Villa is named in the Black Pancharta of St Martin of Tours (manuscript): Eeluacus, for the shoes of the brothers with all that belongs to them, for which the brothers, cunningly deceived, gave Martiacus Villa in the Arvernian pagus in exchange. Not far away was the city of Ricomagus, mentioned by Gregory of Tours in book i of De Gloria Martyrum, and the village of Mousiacus, mentioned by the same Gregory in De Gloria Confessorum, chapter xxi, commonly called Mousac.

units.la: De Comitibus qui Arvernia præfuerunt alij multa scribunt, sed intricata, incerta, quæque haud magnæ apud me, quamvis meliora non habentem, sunt fidei.
units.tr: Other writers have much to say about the counts who governed Auvergne, but their accounts are confused and uncertain, and, though I have no better ones, I do not place great trust in them.

units.la: Addam hic Coronidis loco Comites & Duces Arcis Mompenserii, quæ in hac Regione sita.
units.tr: By way of a coronis I shall add here the counts and dukes of the citadel of Montpensier, which lies in this region.

units.la: Genealogical tree of the Counts and Dukes of Montpensier and Bourbon, printed below the text, lines as in the diagram: Ioannes Valesius, Ioannis Francorum Regis Filius, Biturigum & Arvernia Dux; Uxorem habuit secundo loco Ioannam, Iohannis III Boloniæ Arvernizque Comitis Filiam & Hæredem. Ex eo Conjugio nati: Ioannes Montpenserii Comes, Inprolis; Maria Bituricensis, quæ Fratri successit in Ducatum Arvernia & Comitatum Mompenserium: Uxor Ioannis I. Borbon. Ducis; Anna Bituricensis nupta Amadeo Comiti Sabaudiæ; eoque mortuo, Bernardo Comiti Armeniaco. Karolus I Borbon. Dux V.; Ludovicus Borbonius, Comes Mompenserius: Duxit primo Ioannam Beraldi Iunioris Delphini Arvernia Filiam iterum: inde Gabrielem Turensem, ex qua suscepit; Ioannes Abbas Cluniacensis. Gilbertus Borbonius, Comes Mompenserii & Arvernia, Uxor illi Eleonora Gonzaga Friderici Marchionis Mantuani F.; Gabriela Uxor Ludovici Tremoulliani; Karolotta, Uxor Wolfhardi Baralliani Comitis Suscanensis. Ludovicus Borbonius, mortuus in regno Neapolit.; Franciscus Borbonius, Castelli Heraldini Dux; Gyrus Borbonius, Comes Mompenserii, Dux Borbonionum VIII, Comestabilis Franciæ; Ludovica Borbonia, Successit Fratri in Comitatu. Nuptæ primum Andreæ Caluignano, postea Ludovico Borbonio, Ioannis Vindocinensis F. Rupis ad Ioannam Principi; Renata Borbonia Antonii Ducis Lotharingiæ comitis. Ludovicus Borbonius, Dux Mompenserius Primus: Coniux ipsi Iacoba Longovicana; Karolus Borbonius Rupis ad Ioannam Principem; Susanna Borbonia nupta Ruisselio Dynastæ. Franciscus Borbonius, Dux Mompenserii Secundus, Delphinus Arvernia. Vixit illi in Coniugio ... Heredes de Melietes; Filiæ aliquot. Henricus Borbonius, Princeps Dombensis.
units.tr: Genealogical tree of the Counts and Dukes of Montpensier and Bourbon (printed below the text, with the lines as in the diagram): John of Valois, son of John, King of France, Duke of Berry and Auvergne; he married, in second place, Joanna, daughter and heiress of John III, Count of Boulogne and Auvergne. Children of this marriage: John, Count of Montpensier, without issue; Mary of Berry, who succeeded her brother in the duchy of Auvergne and the county of Montpensier, wife of John I, Duke of Bourbon; Anne of Berry, married to Amadeus, Count of Savoy, and after his death to Bernard, Count of Armagnac. Charles I, Duke of Bourbon, the fifth; Louis of Bourbon, Count of Montpensier, who first married Joanna, daughter of Béraud III, Dauphin of Auvergne, and secondly Gabrielle of Turenne, by whom he had issue; John, Abbot of Cluny. Gilbert of Bourbon, Count of Montpensier and Auvergne, whose wife was Eleonora Gonzaga, daughter of Frederick, Marquess of Mantua; Gabrielle, wife of Louis de La Trémoille; Charlotte, wife of Wolfhard, Count of Suze. Louis of Bourbon, who died in the kingdom of Naples; Francis of Bourbon, Duke of Châtellerault; Gyrus of Bourbon, Count of Montpensier, eighth Duke of Bourbon, Constable of France; Louise of Bourbon, who succeeded her brother in the county, first married to Andrea Caluignano, then to Louis of Bourbon, son of John of Vendôme, of Roche-sur-Yon, to the Princess Joanna; Renée of Bourbon, wife of Antoine, Duke of Lorraine and Count. Louis of Bourbon, the first Duke of Montpensier, whose wife was Jacqueline of Longwy; Charles of Bourbon, of Roche-sur-Yon, to the Princess Joanna; Susanna of Bourbon, married to the lord Rousselet. Francis of Bourbon, the second Duke of Montpensier, Dauphin of Auvergne; he lived in marriage with ... Heirs of Mélites; several daughters. Henry of Bourbon, Prince of Dombes.

units.la: CAPVT XXX.
units.tr: CAPVT XXX.

units.la: Normannia.
units.tr: Normandy.

units.la: AMPLISSIMAM Parlamenti Parisiensis Iurisdictionem, quæ per Belgicam, Celticam Aquitaniamque Galliarum Regiones agnoscunt, diligenter, speculo, percurri, fideliterque notavi: succedunt in mea Distributione, quæ reliquis subsunt Parlamentis, Principale, quod hactenus præ manibus fuit, quasi circumeuntibus. Initium ijs statuit mea Methodus versus Occidentem ad Ligeris dextram in Normannia, quæ sub Rotomagensi est Tribunali; inde in Britanniam, quæ Redonensi paret, transitura.
units.tr: Having carefully examined, with the help of a map, and faithfully noted the very wide jurisdiction of the Parliament of Paris, which covers the regions of Belgica, Celtica and Aquitania in Gaul, my Distribution now turns to the Parliaments that are subordinate to it. I am leaving the principal one, which I have so far kept before me as I went around them. My method begins with those lying to the west, on the right bank of the Loire, in Normandy, which is under the court of Rouen. From there it will pass into Brittany, which belongs to the court of Rennes.

units.la: NORMANNIÆ nomen à Populis Septemtrionalibus. Nort, enim, Idiomate Germanico, Septemtrionalis Orbis terrarum plaga; Man, Vir: Normannia, Terra Franciæ, Viris eo ab Septemtrionaliore vel Arctoo orbe ex Dania Norvegiaque profectis ad habitandum data. Notæ sunt Normannorum in Germaniam Galliamque Excursiones. Omnium atrocissima fuit; quæ facta Rollone Duce in pleraque Galliarum littoralia, & inde porro in Loca mediterranea & penitissima: de qua in Præfatione quadam Meldensis Synodi, quæ anno Christi Redemtoris 911, Karoli Regis anno VI celebrata est: Quia divinas Iussiones non est sequuta Obedientia, dedit Dominus ab Aquilone, unde juxta Prophetam pandetur Malum, dignos Meritis nostris Apostolos, crudeles videlicet & inmanissimos Christianitatis Persequutores, qui Parisios usque venientes, quod jussit Dominus, monstraverunt. Eo tempore ad tantam tandem redactus est necessitatem Karolus Simplex Francorum Rex, ut Rolloni, ad Christianam Pietatem invitato, Filiam Gillam dederit Uxorem, totamque Dotis nomine West-richam (quæ vulgo corrupte Neustria) &c, qui super Ligerim, Britannos. Successorum ejus hæc legitur series:
units.tr: The name Normandy comes from the Northern peoples. For Nort, in the German idiom, means the northern region of the world, and man means man. Normandy, a land of France, was given to men who had come from the more northern or Arctic region, from Denmark and Norway, to live there. The raids of the Normans into Germany and Gaul are well known. The most savage of them was made under Duke Rollo against most of the coastal parts of Gaul, and then further inland into the most remote places. Of it a certain preface to the Synod of Meaux, held in the year of Christ the Redeemer 911, in the sixth year of King Charles, speaks: Because obedience did not follow the divine commands, the Lord sent from the north, whence, according to the Prophet, evil is poured out, apostles worthy of our merits, namely cruel and most savage persecutors of Christianity, who came as far as Paris and showed what the Lord had commanded. At that time Charles the Simple, King of the Franks, was at last reduced to such necessity that he gave his daughter Gilla as wife to Rollo, who had been invited to Christian piety, and granted him, as her dowry, West-richa (commonly and wrongly called Neustria), &c., the country beyond the Loire, the Britons. The following is the list of his successors:

units.la: NORMANNIÆ Ducum Stemma 1 ex Normannis.
units.tr: Genealogy of the Dukes of Normandy, I, from the Normans.

units.la: Rollo Normannus. Christianus factus cum Gente sua, ab Karolo Simplice Francorum Rege Neustriam (West-Richam proprie, id est Occidentalis Franciæ Regnum) incolendam obtinuit, circa annum 911. Primusque factus est Dux Normanniæ. Uxorem habuit priore loco Pupam, Berengarii Comitis Bellinensis & Bajocacensis F. Guilelmi Successoris. Matrem; qua repudiata duxit Ægidiam (vulgo Gilla audiebat) Karoli Simplicis F. inprolem. Obiit 933.
units.tr: Rollo the Norman. Having become a Christian with his people, he obtained from Charles the Simple, King of the Franks, Neustria (properly West-Richa, that is, the kingdom of Western France) to inhabit, around the year 911. He was the first to become Duke of Normandy. He first had as wife Poppa, mother of William Longsword, daughter of Berengar, Count of Bayeux and Bessin. Having repudiated her, he married Ægidia (commonly called Gilla), daughter of Charles the Simple, by whom he had issue. He died in 933.

units.la: Guilelmus, cognomine Longa-Spatha, Rollonis ex priore Conjuge F. Dux Normanniæ II. Rudolpho Francorum Regi Fidem omnem pollicitus totaque sonatus scribitur Britannia, Uxor illi Sphotta Herberti Comitis Suvanensis filia. Ab Arnolpho Flandriæ Comite occisus Rotomagum delatus est & sepultus, anno 942.
units.tr: William, surnamed Longsword, son of Rollo by his first wife, was the second Duke of Normandy. He promised complete fidelity to Rudolph, King of the Franks, and is said to have been sent over all Brittany. His wife was Sphotta, daughter of Herbert, Count of Vermandois. He was killed by Arnulf, Count of Flanders, and was carried to Rouen and buried, in the year 942.

units.la: Richardus Intrepidus, Dux Normanniæ III obiit 10 CCCCXXC, Sepultus Fescampi. Vxorem habuit Annam (alijs Agnes dictam) Hugonis Magni Filiam, inprolem, qua mortua duxit Gonroram Danam, ex qua nati:
units.tr: Richard the Fearless, third Duke of Normandy, died in 10 CCCCXXC, and was buried at Fécamp. He had as wife Anna (also called Agnes), daughter of Hugh the Great, by whom he had issue. When she died he married Gonnora, a Dane, by whom he had children:

units.la: Richardus II, Dux Normanniæ IV. obiit CIↃ XXVI, Sepultus Fescampi apud Patrem. Vxores habuit duas: Iuditham Comitis Britanniæ Sororem, & Paullam, Gunnoram Regis Daniæ & Norvegiæ Filiam. Nati ex
units.tr: Richard II, Duke of Normandy, the fourth of that name, died in 1126 and was buried at Fécamp beside his father. He had two wives: Judith, sister of the Count of Brittany, and Paulla, Gunnora, daughter of the King of Denmark and Norway. Children born of

units.la: Robertus Comes Ebu-roicensis. Vxor, ex qua duos suscepera liberos, mortua, Archiepiscopus factus Rotomagensis XLIII.
units.tr: Robert, Count of Eu. His wife, by whom he had two children, died; he was made Archbishop of Rouen, the forty-third.

units.la: Maugerius Archiepiscopus Rotomagensis XLIV, post Fratrem.
units.tr: Maugerius, Archbishop of Rouen, the forty-fourth, after his brother.

units.la: Richardus III, Dux Normanniæ V. A Fratre veneno sublatus scribitur. Vxorem non duxit. Liberos aliquot eius illegitimi.
units.tr: Richard III, fifth Duke of Normandy. It is written that he was poisoned by his brother. He took no wife. Some of his children were illegitimate.

units.la: Robertus, Liberalis cognomine, Dux Normanniæ VI post Fratrem. Obiit in Peregrinatione Hierosolymitana, Sepultus Niceæ, anno CIↃ XXXV. Natus illi ex Concubina.
units.tr: Robert, surnamed the Liberal, sixth Duke of Normandy after his brother. He died on pilgrimage to Jerusalem, was buried at Nicaea in 1035. He had a son by a concubine.

units.la: Gulielmus Nothus, Natalibus à Patre ante Peregrinationem Hierosolymitanam restitutus, Dux Normanniæ VII, Conquestor cognominatus, quod Angliæ Regnum ab Eduardo Cognato ipsi legatum testamento, conquisierit; ibique Armorum vi subjecerit. Mortuus est anno CIↃ XCVII, Sepultus Cadomi in Aede S. Stephani.
units.tr: William the Bastard, restored to legitimate status by his father before the pilgrimage to Jerusalem, became the seventh Duke of Normandy. He was surnamed the Conqueror because he gained the kingdom of England, which his cousin Edward had left to him by will, and subdued it by force of arms. He died in 1097 and was buried at Caen in the church of St Stephen.

units.la: Robertus II, Normanniæ Dux VIII. Bello Parisiensi se contaminavit, primo contra Patrem, deinde in Fratrem. Obiit in Carcere CIↃ CXXIV in Anglia.
units.tr: Robert II, eighth Duke of Normandy. He stained himself in the war at Paris, first against his father and then against his brother. He died in prison in England in 1124.

units.la: Richardus Puer obiit.
units.tr: Richard the Boy died.

units.la: Gulielmus Rufus Patri successit in Angliæ Regno, Avarus Tyrannus.
units.tr: William Rufus succeeded his father in the kingdom of England, a greedy tyrant.

units.la: Henricus I Beau-clerc Fratri Gulielmo successit in Angliæ Regno, Dux Normanniæ X.
units.tr: Henry I Beauclerc succeeded his brother William in the kingdom of England; he was the tenth Duke of Normandy.

units.la: Filiæ VI inter quas Alicia (alias Adela) quæ nupsit Stephano Comiti Bolonien-si.
units.tr: Six daughters, among whom Alice (also called Adela), who married Stephen, Count of Boulogne.

units.la: Stephanus Bolonien-sis Comes post Henricum I Avunculum, Regnum Angliæ tenuit.
units.tr: Stephen, Count of Boulogne, after his uncle Henry I, held the kingdom of England.

units.la: Gulielmus Dux Normanniæ II. Obiit CIↃ CXXVIII absque prolis.
units.tr: William, second Duke of Normandy of that name. He died without issue in 1128.

units.la: Henricus II. Hic cum Stephano Comite Bolonien-si bella varia gessit. Pax tandem facta, ut Stephanus, quoad vixeret, Angliæ dominium... Vxorem duxit Eleonoram, unicam Filiam & Heredem Gulielmi Aquitanorum Ducis, ab Ludovico VII Francorum Rege repudiatam.
units.tr: Henry II. He waged various wars with Stephen, Count of Boulogne. Peace was at last made, on terms that Stephen should keep the dominion of England for as long as he lived. He married Eleanor, the only daughter and heir of William, Duke of the Aquitanians, who had been repudiated by Louis VII, King of the Franks.

units.la: Henricus III Normanniæ Dux XIII, Fratris Donatione. Vxor Margareta Ludovici Filii Francorum Regis F. Inprolis. Sepultus Rotomagi CIↃ CXCII.
units.tr: Henry III, thirteenth Duke of Normandy, by his brother's gift. He married Margaret, daughter of Louis, son of the King of the Franks, and had no children. He was buried at Rouen in 1192.

units.la: Richardus I, Cor Leonis, Rex Angliæ post Patrem, & Dux Normanniæ post Fratrem XIV. Vxor Berengaria Gatiæ Regis Navarræ F. obiit CIↃ CC Annos.
units.tr: Richard I, Lionheart, King of England after his father and, after his brother, the fourteenth Duke of Normandy. His wife was Berengaria, daughter of Garcia, King of Navarre. He died in 1200.

units.la: Gaufredus Vxor Constantia unica Filia & Heres Conani Britanniæ Comitis: Ex qua natus ille præter Eleonoram.
units.tr: Geoffrey. His wife Constance, the only daughter and heir of Conan, Count of Brittany. By her he had, besides Eleanor, a son.

units.la: Joannes Richardo successit in Angliæ Regnum & Normanniæ Principatum, Dux X. Obiit anno CIↃ CCCXVI.
units.tr: John succeeded Richard in the kingdom of England and the principality of Normandy, the tenth Duke. He died in 1316.

units.la: Henricus III Angliæ Rex: de quo supra.
units.tr: Henry III, King of England: concerning whom see above.

units.la: Arthurus Dux Britanniæ. Hic Patruo Joanni bellum movens Andegavos, Cenomanos & Turones eripuit, & ab eodem lu, cerevinem capt. Rotomagumque tractus, occisus est.
units.tr: Arthur, Duke of Brittany. Making war on his uncle John, he seized Angers, Le Mans and Tours, and was taken prisoner by the same man at Lucerne(?). Brought to Rouen, he was killed.

units.la: NORMANNIÆ DUCUM Stemma II ex Francis.
units.tr: Stemma II of the Dukes of Normandy, from the French.

units.la: Philippus Augustus, Francorum Rex, Dux Normanniæ, post Arturi cædem, XVI.
units.tr: Philip Augustus, King of the Franks, Duke of Normandy, after the killing of Arthur: 16th.

units.la: Ludovicus VIII Francorum Monarcha, Dux, post Patrem, Normanniæ XVII.
units.tr: Louis VIII, King and Duke of the French, after his father, of Normandy: 17th.

units.la: Ludovicus IX. Sanctus, Francorum Rex, Dux Normanniæ XVIII, cum quo Henricus III Angliæ Rex Ioannis F. patus est, ut Anglus in perpetuum Normanniæ, Andegavensiumque & Cenomanorum Ditionibus coderet.
units.tr: Louis IX the Saint, King of the Franks, Duke of Normandy: 18th. With him Henry III, King of England and son of John, agreed to give up Normandy, and the lordships of Anjou and Maine, forever, as an Englishman.

units.la: Philippus III Audax Francorum Rex, Dux Normanniæ XIX.
units.tr: Philip III the Bold, King of the Franks, Duke of Normandy: 19th.

units.la: Philippus IV Pulcher Francorum Rex, Dux Normanniæ XX. Carolus Valesius Primus Valesiorum & Alenconis Comes. Ludovicus Hutinus Rex Francia, Dux Norm. xxi. Philippus v Longus Rex Francia, Dux Norm. xxii. Carolus Calvus Rex Francia, Dux Norm. xxiii. Philippus Valesius, post Carolum Pulchrum, Franciae Rex. Dux Normanniae xxiv. Joannes ex Patris Donatione Dux Normanniae xxv, Rex Franciae. Contra hunc bellum gessit Eduardus Angliae Rex pro Normannia. Carolus ex Donatione Patris Dux Normanniae xxvi, Rex Franciae post Patris mortem. Carolus Rex Franciae & Dux Normanniae xxvii. Huic Rex Angliae Henricus v Normanniam eripuit; sed postea interventu Matrimonii inter eumdem Henricum & Katharinam Caroli F. cautum fuit, ut, dum Rex Carolus viveret, Henricus Franciae Regnum gubernaret, post Regis Caroli mortem ipse id obtineret, & si prior moreretur, ejus Filio natu maximo, ex Katharina genito, id cederet: Carolo Delphino Viennensi, Regis Caroli Filio, Hostis patriae judicato, quod Joannem Burgundiae Ducem sub specie Colloquii evocatum Monasterioli (vulgo Montereau au faux Yonne) occidi curasset. Carolus, nulla habita ratione Sponsaliorum inter sororem Katharinam & Henricum Angliae Regem, post Patris mortem Franciae Monarcham se fecit. Rex Biturigum per iudibrium vocatus ab Anglis, quibus Normanniam eripuit, totaque Francia profligavit. Dux Normanniae xxviii. Ludovicus Valesius, Franciae Rex, Normanniae Dux xxix. Carolus, Normanniae Dux, Fratris beneficio, xxx: qua tamen mox privatus est, accepta ejus loco Aquitania. Ab eo tempore Normannia in Franciae Regum potestate manet, nec Regiorum Filiorum alicui data est.
units.tr: Philip IV the Fair, King of the Franks, Duke of Normandy: 20th. Charles of Valois, first of the Valois and Count of Alençon. Louis the Quarrelsome, King of France, Duke of Normandy: 21st. Philip V the Long, King of France, Duke of Normandy: 22nd. Charles the Bald, King of France, Duke of Normandy: 23rd. Philip of Valois, after Charles the Fair, King of France, Duke of Normandy: 24th. John, Duke of Normandy by his father's gift: 25th, and King of France. Edward, King of England, waged war against him over Normandy. Charles, Duke of Normandy by his father's gift: 26th, and King of France after his father's death. Charles, King of France and Duke of Normandy: 27th. Henry V, King of England, took Normandy from him. Afterwards, however, by means of a marriage arranged between this Henry and Catherine, daughter of Charles, it was provided that while King Charles lived Henry should govern the kingdom of France; after King Charles's death he himself should obtain it; and if he died first, it should pass to his eldest son born of Catherine. Charles the Dauphin of Vienne, son of King Charles, was judged an enemy of the country, because he had arranged for John, Duke of Burgundy, to be called to a meeting under the pretence of a conference at Montereau (commonly Montereau-faut-Yonne) and killed there. Charles, paying no regard to the betrothal between his sister Catherine and Henry, King of England, made himself King of France after his father's death. The King of Bourges, a title given him in mockery by the English, from whom he took Normandy, crushed all France. Duke of Normandy: 28th. Louis Valois, King of France, Duke of Normandy: 29th. Charles, Duke of Normandy, by his brother's favour: 30th. He was soon deprived of it, however, Aquitaine being received in its place. From that time Normandy has remained in the power of the kings of France, and it has not been given to any of the royal sons.

units.la: Normanniam porro sic describit Robertus Gaguinus lib. vii: Est Normannia una Metropoli & sex Urbibus, quatuorque & nonaginta munitissimis oppidis, atque Arcibus potens, plerisque Vicis frequens ad Civitatum speciem exstructis, quam sexto vix die expeditus perstranseat: Piscium & Pecorum ferax, Frumenti uberrima; Pomorum atque Pirorum tam passim conserta, ut hinc Potum Gens sibi adfatim exprimat, & ad Exteros copiose Fructus exportet. Lanificy Plebs studiosa & bibax etiam Pomacy, quod Siceram vocant. Gens omnis suapte natura callida; nullis exteris Legibus obnoxia: Moribus suis & Consuetudine, quam pertinacissime tuetur, vivit: Doli quidem & Litis adprime gnara: quo fit, ut cum illa Societatem aut Negocium sortiri Exteri reformident, alioqui Doctrinae & Religioni dedita: Bello insuper idonea & fortis, cuius egregia in Exteros Gesta plurima referuntur. Ego sane, nobilissimum Franciae Regnum peragrans, nusquam maiorem vel Soli fertilitatem, vel Urbium Pagorumque vidi copiam. Quid? quod exercendae Mercaturae non solum Mare habeat Normannia oportunissimum: verum etiam Incolas ingeniosos, cautos, deceptu difficiles, adsabiles, humanos, Lucro intentiores; quin & facundos Litterisque addictos, animi insuper contra hostes praesentissimi. Nobilium ibidem ingens numerus.
units.tr: Robert Gaguin, book 7, describes Normandy in this way: Normandy has one metropolis and six cities, and ninety-four very strongly fortified towns, and is strong in citadels, and abounds in many villages built up like cities, which a man hardly travelling quickly could cross in six days. It is rich in fish and cattle, and very fertile in grain. Its apple and pear trees are so widely planted that the people draw drink from them in plenty and export abundant fruit to foreigners. The common people are devoted to weaving, and are fond of drink, and also of cider, which they call sicera. The whole nation is by its nature shrewd; it is subject to no foreign laws, but lives by its own customs, which it defends most stubbornly. It is very knowledgeable in trickery and lawsuits, so that foreigners shrink from entering partnership or business with it. Otherwise it is devoted to learning and religion; moreover it is fit for war and brave, and many of its notable exploits against foreigners are recorded. For my part, travelling through the most noble kingdom of France, I have nowhere seen greater fertility of soil, or a greater abundance of cities and villages. What more? Normandy has not only a most convenient sea for carrying on trade, but also clever, cautious inhabitants, hard to deceive, affable, humane, and more intent on profit; moreover they are eloquent and devoted to letters, and very ready in spirit against enemies. There is a huge number of nobles there.

units.la: Nobilissimam autem Galliae Partem, hodie Normannia nomenclatura notam, coluerunt quondam Venellocasses, Baiocasses, Abrincanti, Auleroi Eburovices, Sai, Sesquini, Constantienses, Lexovii, Caletes, & Nervii. De Primis illud praemonendum duxi: Tres Populos, Venellocasses, Baiocasses & Vadicasses in antiquorum Historiographorum Libris nunc mirum in modum confundi, nunc nimisquam vitiose scribi. Illud satis constat varia ab iis Loca fuisse habitata: Venellocasses & Baiocasses ad Normanniam nunc pertinent, Vadicasses ad Picardiam: ut quum eam Franciae Regionem perambularem, docui. Venellocasses (sic enim scribendi, ex Variorum Auctorum commissione, Doctorumque Virorum, cum primis Josephi Scaligeri, suis ad me litteris, judicio) dicuntur Ptolemaeo, pro quibus leui fortean mutatione reponendi Ουενελλοκασσοι: Velocasses apud Caesarem lib. ii (in aliis libris legitur Verocasses) syllaba mutilati, pro Venellocasses; Velocasses tamen Caesaris Scaliger scribi vitiose censet pro Baiocassibus. Olim Venellocasses, ubi nunc Civitas Rotomagensium, ut in Notitia Provinciarum Galliae sub Lugdunensi ii legitur, l'Archevesché de Rouen. Rotomagum enim Ptolemaeus Venellocassium statuit Urbem. Cogitandum alijs relinquo, an veteris Venellocassium appellationis memoria non sit reliqua in ijs Normanniae Populis, qui vulgo nunc Veulquessins ad Sequanam (alij Vergassins, quibusdam contractius Vulxin) quorum primarium Opidum Gisortium vocatur. Certe ejus mentis esse video Hadrianum Turnebum lib. ix. Adversariorum. cap. viii, Petrum Divaeum, Abrahamum Ortelium, Robertum Coenalem, & alios. Deviat Marlianus, qui ex Velocassibus Caesaris facit Cassel Opidum Flandriae, in cacumine Montis situm. Iam ab Venellocassibus alij omnino erant Baiocasses. Ausonius de Professoribus Carmine 1v de Attio Patera, ex emendatione Petri Pithei lib. 1 Adversarior. cap. iii: Tu Baiocassis stirpe Druidarum satus. Baiocassini Gregorio Turonensi lib. v. cap. xxvi: Civitas Baiocassium Notitiæ Provinciarum in Lugdunensi ii, Le Baillage & Evesché de Baieux en Normandie. Vitiose Pellocassi apud Cæsarem lib. vii. Vellocasses apud Plinium lib. iv cap. xviii. Velocasses apud Orosium lib. vi. cap. vii. A Baiocassibus Prædia Baiocassina in Lugdunensi ii, Sidonio lib. iv Epist. ad Lucontium, quæ ordine xviii. Sic Baiocassini Saxones, Gregorio Turonensi lib. v. cap. xxvi & lib. x. cap. ix: Baiocassinus Pontifex, eidem lib. ix. capite xiii, Baiocassinus Civis, eidem lib. ii de Vita S. Martini cap. liiii Baiocassinus Incola, eidem lib. iv. cap. xxii.
units.tr: The most noble part of Gaul, now known by the name Normandy, was once inhabited by the Venellocasses, Baiocasses, Abrincanti, Auleroi, Eburovices, Sai, Sesquini, Constantienses, Lexovii, Caletes and Nervii. About the first of these I think this should be noted beforehand: the three peoples Venellocasses, Baiocasses and Vadicasses are in the books of the ancient historians now confused in a remarkable way, and now written very wrongly. It is quite certain that they inhabited different places: Venellocasses and Baiocasses now belong to Normandy, Vadicasses to Picardy, as I showed when I travelled through that region of France. Venellocasses (for so it should be written, by the agreed judgment of various authors and learned men, above all Joseph Scaliger, in his letters to me) are called by Ptolemy, for which Ουενελλοκασσοι should perhaps be restored with a slight change. Velocasses in Caesar, book ii (in other books it is read Verocasses) is Venellocasses with a syllable cut off; yet Scaliger judges that Velocasses in Caesar is wrongly written for Baiocassibus. Formerly the Venellocasses lived where the Civitas Rotomagensium now is, as is read in the Notitia Provinciarum Galliae under Lugdunensis II: l'Archevesché de Rouen. For Ptolemy makes Rotomagum the city of the Venellocassii. I leave it to others to consider whether the memory of the old name Venellocassium survives among those Normandy peoples who are now commonly called Veulquessins on the Seine (others Vergassins, and some more shortly Vulxin), whose chief town is called Gisortium. Certainly I see that Hadrianus Turnebus (book ix of the Adversaria, chapter 8), Petrus Divaeus, Abraham Ortelius, Robertus Coenalis and others are of this mind. Marlianus goes astray, who from Caesar's Velocassibus makes Cassel, a town of Flanders, set on a mountain top. Now others were entirely different from the Venellocassibus: they were the Baiocasses. Ausonius, in his poem on the Professors, poem 4, on Attius Patera, as corrected by Petrus Pithoeus (Adversaria, book 1, chapter 3): Thou, sprung from the stock of the Baiocasses' Druids. Baiocassini. Gregory of Tours, book v, chapter 26: Civitas Baiocassium. Notitia Provinciarum, Lugdunensis II: Le Baillage & Evesché de Baieux en Normandie. Wrongly Pellocassi in Caesar, book vii. Vellocasses in Pliny, book iv, chapter 18. Velocasses in Orosius, book vi, chapter 7. Prædia Baiocassina, from the Baiocasses, in Lugdunensis II; Sidonius, book iv, letter to Lucontius, which is number 18 in order. So Baiocassini Saxones, Gregory of Tours, book v, chapter 26, and book x, chapter 9; Baiocassinus Pontifex, the same author, book ix, chapter 13; Baiocassinus Civis, the same author, book ii, on the Life of St Martin, chapter 54; Baiocassinus Incola, the same author, book iv, chapter 22.

units.la: Abrincanti, ut in Antiquo Notitiæ exemplari legitur, Plinio lib. iv. cap. xiiii. Abrincatui; Ἀβρίγκαρτοι Ptolemæo: Civitas Abrincantorum, Notitiæ Provinciarum in Lugdunensi ii. In Bonaventuræ Vulcanij Membranis, quarum antea memini, Civitas Abrincantum: Vulgo, L'Evesché d'Avranches. Aulerci Eburovices, apud Cæsarem lib. vii, & Plinium lib. iv nat. hist. cap. xviii. Male enim in Vulgaris legitur: apud illum quidem, Aulercis, Eburonibus, interjecta etiam distinctione, quasi duo essent Populi; apud hunc vero, Aulerci, qui cognominantur Eburones. Ptolemæo Αὐλέρκιοι Ἐβουρῶνες: Ebores vel Ebures Ausonio, Epistola ad Paullum de Ostreis Nobilibus: L'Evesché d'Evreux en Normandie, ut censent Scaliger ad me scribens, Orontius, Vigenereus, Vinetus, & alij; quorum tamen nonnulli Aulercos ab Eburovicibus separant, contra Veterum Scriptorum, præcipue Plinij & Ptolemæi, mentem: Ego alibi docui Aulercorum sive prænomen, sive cognomen sit habendum, aliquot Veteris Galliæ Populis fuisse commune. Eburovices autem sunt, quos cap. xix dixi vitiose notari in MS. Codice Bonaventuræ Vulcanij Ebroreos, hoc modo, Civitas Ebroreorum. Scribendum enim fuerat Civitas Eburonum, Eburum, vel Eburovicum. Hoc addam, Aulercorum, de quibus hic ago, Vrbem Mediolanum nominari apud Antoninum, Itinere, quod Rotomago ducit Lutetiam, pro quo in Itineraria Tabula vitiose, Mediolano Autercorum. Sai nusquam noti, quam in Notitia Provinciarum Galliæ, ubi in Lugdunensi ii Saiorum Civitas, hodie L'Evesché de Sés vel Sais: Sagiensis Episcopi mentio apud Ivonem in Epistolis, item in Concilio Aurelianensi, Vitis denique S. Ansiberti, & S. Oportunæ, non semel. Sefuni apud Cæsarem forte an, ubi hodie Vicus, qui vulgo La Sezai: alijs Civitas Episcopalis Provinciæ Turonensis, quæ vernacule Exisfins. Constantienses nominat eadem Provinciarum Notitia, ubi in Lugdunensi ii. Civitas Constantiensium, L'Evesché de Contances. Lexovij vel Lexobij Cæsari lib. iii. Plinioque lib iv. c. xviii. qui Ἀξοβίοι Straboni lib. iv; Ἀξουίοι Ptolemæo, & in quibusdam Codicibus Ἀξοβίοι: Civitas Lexoviorum Notitiæ Provinciarum in Lugdunensi ii; L'Evesché & Pais de Lisieux en Normandie. Caletes Cæsari, qui Caleti Orosio lib. iv. cap. xi (nam in quibusdam Exemplaribus mendose scribuntur Saletes) Καλῖτοι Straboni, μίχρι τῆς ἐκβολῆς τῦ Ση40 ιχάνα πεταμῶ pertingere eos ajenti: apud eundem alio ejusdem libri loco prave, Τα- δῖτοι nominantur, unde in Britanniam diurno brevior notatur Cursus: Καλῆται sunt Ptolemæo. Galleti corrupte apud Plinium lib. iv. cap. xviii, qui emendare Caleti apud eumdem lib. xiii. cap. ii. Hodie, Le Baillage de Caus en Normandie, ex sententia Scaligeri, Turnebi, Divæi, aliorum: ubi nescio, an Opidum Cailly memoriam etiam servet Caletum. Errant enim, qui ex similitudine nominis Morinorum Opidum, quod Anglis eripuerunt anno cio 10 lvin Franci, Calesium vulgo, esse arbitrantur. Vero similius, eo ab Caletibus Coloniam una cum appellatione aliquando ductam. Videntur & in hoc Galliæ angulo fuisse Nervij. Liber Notitiæ Imperij Occidentis Nervicanum Tractum & Limitem habet circa Armoricam. Legitur enim ibi: Sub Dispositione Viri Spectabilis Ducis Tractus Armoricani & Nervicani. Et paullo post: 50 Extenditur tamen Tractus Armoricani & Nervicani Limitis per Provincias quinque: Per Aquitanicam Primam & Secundam, Senoniam, Secundam Lugdunensem & Tertiam. Divus etiam Paullinus Nervici meminit Litoris ad Victricium, Præsulem Rotomagensem. Olim, ubi nunc pars Normandiæ, quæ vulgo Bessin, aut circiter. Quæ de Nervijs Ptolemæi ad Normanniam adferunt nonnulli, non magnum hic habent locum. Nam si bene examinentur, pertinent illi cum ijs, quorum meminerunt Cæsar, Tacitus, Plinius, alij, ad Inferiorem Germaniam.
units.tr: Abrincanti, as is read in the old copy of the Notitia, and in Pliny, book iv, chapter 14, Abrincatui; Ptolemy [Ἀβρίγκαρτοι]: Civitas Abrincantorum, Notitia Provinciarum, Lugdunensis II. In the parchments of Bonaventura Vulcanius, which I mentioned before, Civitas Abrincantum. Commonly L'Evesché d'Avranches. Aulerci Eburovices, in Caesar, book vii, and Pliny, book iv, Natural History, chapter 18. For in the common text it is wrongly read: in Caesar Aulercis, Eburonibus, with a punctuation mark inserted, as if they were two peoples; in Pliny Aulerci, qui cognominantur Eburones. Ptolemy [Αὐλέρκιοι Ἐβουρῶνες]. Ebores or Ebures in Ausonius, Epistle to Paulus on noble oysters. L'Evesché d'Evreux en Normandie, as Scaliger, writing to me, Orontius, Vigenerius, Vinetus and others think; yet some of them separate the Aulerci from the Eburovices, against the mind of the ancient writers, especially Pliny and Ptolemy. I have shown elsewhere that Aulerci, whether it is taken as a first name or a surname, was shared by several peoples of ancient Gaul. The Eburovices are those whom I said in chapter 19 were wrongly noted in the manuscript codex of Bonaventura Vulcanius as Ebroreos, in this form: Civitas Ebroreorum. For it should have been Civitas Eburonum, Eburum or Eburovicum. I will add this: the Aulerci of whom I am speaking here are said in Antoninus' Itinerary, the route that leads from Rotomagus to Lutetia, to have the city Mediolanum, for which the Itinerary map wrongly has Mediolano Autercorum. The Sai are nowhere known except in the Notitia Provinciarum Galliae, where under Lugdunensis II there is the Saiorum Civitas, today L'Evesché de Sés or Sais. The bishop of Sées is mentioned in Ivo's letters, likewise in the Council of Orléans, and in the Lives of St Ansbert and St Opportuna, more than once. Sesuni in Caesar, perhaps, where today there is a village commonly called La Sezai; others take it as a bishopric city of the Province of Tours, called in the vernacular Exisfins. The same Notitia Provinciarum names the Constantienses, under Lugdunensis II: Civitas Constantiensium, L'Evesché de Contances. Lexovii or Lexobii in Caesar, book iii, and Pliny, book iv, chapter 18, who [Ἀξοβίοι] in Strabo, book iv; [Ἀξουίοι] in Ptolemy, and in some codices [Ἀξοβίοι]: Civitas Lexoviorum in the Notitia Provinciarum, Lugdunensis II; L'Evesché & Pais de Lisieux en Normandie. The Caletes: Caesar, who writes Caleti; Orosius, book iv, chapter 11 (for in some copies they are wrongly written Saletes); Strabo [Καλῖτοι], saying that they reach as far as the mouth of the river Seine [μέχρι τῆς ἐκβολῆς τοῦ Σηκουάνα ποταμοῦ]. In another passage of the same book, wrongly, they are named [Ταδῖτοι], whence the shorter daily crossing to Britain is noted. Ptolemy has [Καλῆται]. Galleti corruptly in Pliny, book iv, chapter 18, who is emended to Caleti in the same author, book xiii, chapter 2. Today Le Baillage de Caus en Normandie, according to Scaliger, Turnebus, Divaeus and others; I do not know whether the town of Cailly preserves the memory of Caletum. For they err who, from the similarity of name, think that the town of the Morini, which the French wrested from the English in 1558, and which is commonly called Calesium, is the same. It is more likely that the colony was once founded by the Caletes together with its name. The Nervii also seem to have been in this corner of Gaul. The Notitia Imperii Occidentis has the Nervican Tract and Limes around Armorica. For there it is read: Under the command of the distinguished man, the Duke of the Armorican and Nervican Tracts. And a little after: The Tract of the Armorican and Nervican Limes nonetheless extends through five provinces: through Aquitania First and Second, Senonia, Lugdunensis Second and Third. The divine Paulinus also mentions the Nervican shore near Victricius, bishop of Rouen. Formerly, where now is the part of Normandy commonly called Bessin, or thereabouts. What some bring forward about the Nervii of Ptolemy in relation to Normandy has little weight here. For if they are carefully examined, they belong with those whom Caesar, Tacitus, Pliny and others mention, in Lower Germany.

units.la: In explicanda porro, qualis hodie, Normannia, cum Dignitatum Sedes expendam, tum Partes Maiores. Dignitates ibi partim Ecclesiasticæ, partim Politicæ. Ecclesiasticas appello Archiepiscopatum, &c, qui sub eo, sex Episcopatus.
units.tr: In explaining what Normandy is like today, I shall consider both its seats of dignity and its major parts. Its dignities are partly ecclesiastical and partly civil. By ecclesiastical dignities I mean the archbishopric and so on, under which there are six bishoprics.

units.la: Archiepiscopatus Sedes est Vrbs, quæ Latinis Rotomagum, vulgo Rouen: Ptolemæo, ut ad me scribens sentit Vir Nobilissimus Iosephus Scaliger, Γωπμαγος Ἀντιλοxωσιων: Alijs alia mens est. Rotomagum apud Antoninum inter Iuliobonam & Lutetiam: Rotumagus vitiose in Itineraria Tabula. Ammianus Caput facit Galliæ Lugdunensis Secunda. Dictam hanc Vrbem fabulantur ab Romo nescio quo Rege; quidam ab Roto Idolo; nonnulli, similem meo iudicio insanientes insaniam, ab rubicundo Lapidum, ex quibus Pons extructus, colore: Alij aliunde. Qui Germanice callemus, non ignoramus vocem Magus Vrbem significare; unde & Magen, qui ejusdem Vrbis, maxime vero qui Cognationis inter se vinculo iuncti. Fluviis adsidet ad Sitas; Meridiem quidem Sequana, maximarum Navium (unde ingens Mercaturæ commoditas) capaci: ad Orientem Minoribus Rubeco & Aubetta: qua Septemtrio est, latissimos Pratorum habet Campos, Montesque præcelsos. Sequana Ponte stratus est ingeniosi artificij structuraque, si quid in Gallijs aliud, admirabilis; lapide quadrato, validis columnis, pulcris Arcubus, qui tredecim numero; altitudinis latitudinisque insignis. Per eum rari permittuntur onustis Curribus Carrucisq; transitus. Magno namque constat reparatio, si quid forte destructum vel ruptum. Vehiculis Sequanam transportandis præsto semper jacent duo Pontones, longi satis latique. Aeten Navibus onerandis exonerandisque commodam habet. Vrbs ad eundem Sequanam, interposito Ponte bipartitam: Inferiori ab Navibus nomen, Le Quay des Nariies; Superiori ab Franciæ Metropoli, Le Quay de Paris.
units.tr: The seat of the archbishopric is the city that the Latins call Rotomagum and the common people call Rouen. Ptolemy calls it Γωπμαγος Ἀντιλοxωσιων [Rotomagus of the Lexovii], as the most noble Joseph Scaliger tells me in a letter. Others have other opinions. In Antoninus, Rotomagum lies between Juliobona and Lutetia; in the Itinerary Table it is wrongly written Rotumagus. Ammianus makes it the capital of Gallia Lugdunensis Secunda. People fable that this city was named after a king called Romus, some after the idol Roto, and some, raving in a madness that I judge to be much like the others, after the reddish colour of the stones from which its bridge was built. Others give other derivations. Since we know German, we are aware that the word Magus means "city"; whence also Magen, the people of the same city, and especially those bound together by ties of kinship. The city sits on rivers, by its situation. To the south is the Seine, which can take the largest ships (hence its great commercial convenience); to the east are the smaller rivers Robec and Aubette. Where the north lies, it has very broad meadows and very high hills. The Seine is spanned by a bridge of ingenious design and construction, admirable if anything in Gaul is: it is of square stone, with sturdy columns and fine arches, thirteen in number, and remarkable for its height and breadth. Carts and wagons loaded with goods are rarely allowed to cross it, for repairs cost a great deal if anything is destroyed or broken. Two pontoons, long and wide enough, always lie ready for carrying vehicles across the Seine. The Aeten has a convenient place for loading and unloading ships. The city is divided into two parts by the same Seine and the bridge: the lower part takes its name from the ships, Le Quay des Nariies, and the upper part from the metropolis of France, Le Quay de Paris.

units.la: Primarium Templum, quod D. Virgini sacrum, artis absolutissimæ, tres habet Turres; quarum quæ media S. Romani, Rotomagiensium Archiepiscopi vocitatur: Secundæ nomen inditum Butyraceæ; ædificatam enim ferunt stipibus è populo corrogatis ad obtinendum quadragenarij ieiunij tempore Butyri usum. Ejus Canonici egregijs ab Francorum Regibus donati sunt Privilegijs, cum alijs, tum quod singulis annis Ascensionis Christi die vinculis eximere possint Hominem aliquem facinorosum, Damnationi proximum, certoque supplicio jamjam destinandum. Peragi Negocium illud variis Cerimonijs, Capsulamque magni pretij, qua D. Romani ossa Cineresque continerī dicebantur, Reum humeris portare vidi, non sine stupore, anno MDXXXVII. Ritus ejus caulam narrabant mihi Cives, liberatam aliquando ab Serpentis cujusdam incursu Vrbem; D. Romani precibus, Latronis autem ope; quam quod postea in Ecclesiastica Rotomagensium historia multis perscriptam viderim, meis his non adponam. In Turri Butyracea Campanam spectavi, cuius pondus Librarum triginta sex millium, Lingua septingentas decem pendente. Nomen illi Georgius Ambosius, ab Archiepiscopo, qui anno MDCI Civitati donavit. Latitudo decem est pedum; Altitudo totidem, comprehensis Ansis. Circuitus triginta sex est pedum, continens hos versus: Ipsa ego sum, quamvis sonitu veneranda Tonanti, Prima est Auctori gloria danda meo. Namque ter & denis cum ternis millibus aris Obtulit hac vero dona dicata DXO Scilicet Ambosius, qui sancta Georgius arma, Cunctaque Francigenis tractat habenda viris. Rotomagum tanto felix Antistite gaudet, Quum sit cardinei gloria summa Chori.
units.tr: The main church, sacred to the Blessed Virgin and of the most perfect workmanship, has three towers. The middle one is called the tower of S. Romanus, archbishop of Rouen. The second has the name Butyracea (the Butter Tower), for they say it was built from alms collected from the people so that butter could be used during the forty days of fasting. Its canons were given excellent privileges by the kings of France, among them that once a year, on the day of Christ's Ascension, they may release from chains a criminal who is near condemnation and about to be put to certain death. I saw that business carried out with various ceremonies, and I saw the prisoner carry on his shoulders a casket of great value, in which the bones and ashes of S. Romanus were said to be kept, not without astonishment, in the year 1537. The citizens told me the reason for this rite: once the city was delivered from the attack of a certain serpent, through the prayers of S. Romanus and the help of a thief. I shall not add this to my account, since I have seen it written at length in the ecclesiastical history of Rouen. In the Butter Tower I saw the bell, weighing thirty-six thousand pounds, with a tongue of seven hundred and ten pounds hanging from it. It is called Georgius Ambosius, after the archbishop who gave it to the city in the year 1601. Its width is ten feet, its height as much, including the handles. Its circumference is thirty-six feet, and it bears these verses: I am she, who am to be revered for the sound I make for the Thunderer; the first glory is to be given to my maker. For he offered these gifts, dedicated to me, three and thirty thousand times three hundred, and five hundred and forty; namely Ambosius, who as Saint George handles arms and all things to be held by the men of France. Rouen rejoices, happy in so great a prelate, since he is the highest glory of the cardinal's choir.

units.la: Vas omnium, quæ in Gallijs, vastissimum. Festum Rotomagi celebratur xii Augusti anniversarium, in memoriam exactorum cum Vrbe, tum tota Francia Anglorum. Res incidit in annum MCCCC XLIX. Est ibi, præter alia splendida variorum Principum Nobiliumque Familiarum Palatia, S. Ouenuy Cœnobium, ab Hlothario Rege conditum, loco situm totius Vrbis pulcherrimo; cui jucundissimus ad Orientem prospectus, Hortique mirum in modum amoeni. Hic Reges Galliæ, quoties Rotomagum veniunt, plerumque excipiuntur. Sedes porro hæc Vrbs non solum Archiepiscoporum Normanniæ, quos XXCI recensēt Belleforestius, postremum nominans Karolum Cardinalem Borbonium: verum etiam Parlamenti, quod per Donuculium, Normanniam eamdem institutum antea dixi ab Ludovico xii, circa annum cIↄ cccc xlix. Incendia quatuordecim numerantur horrenda, quibus nunc hic, nunc ibi potissimæ Vrbis partes fuerunt disjectæ & subversæ, annis ıo cccxlii, cIↄ cxviii, biennioque post, cIↄ cxxvi, cIↄ clxxiii, cIↄ cxciiii, cIↄ cciii & sequenti, cIↄ ccx, succedenteque, cIↄ ccxx, & octennio post, cIↄ ccxliii, & cIↄ ıo xiiii.
units.tr: A vessel, the largest of all in Gaul. An annual festival is celebrated at Rouen on 12 August, in memory of the English being driven out both from the city and from all France. The event fell in the year 1449. Among other splendid palaces of various princes and noble families, there is the abbey of S. Ouen, founded by King Lothar and set in the most beautiful place in the whole city; it has a most pleasant view to the east and gardens wonderfully delightful. The kings of France are usually received here whenever they come to Rouen. This city is the seat not only of the archbishops of Normandy, whom Belleforest counts as ninety-one (XXCI), naming Charles Cardinal of Bourbon last, but also of the Parliament, which I said earlier was established for Normandy through Donuculius by Louis XII, around the year 1449. Fourteen dreadful fires are recorded, by which now here and now there the chief parts of the city were burnt and destroyed, in the years 1342, 1118, two years later 1126, 1173, 1194, 1203 and the following year, 1210, the next after that, 1220, and eight years later 1243, and 1314.

units.la: Hæc de Vrbe Archiepiscopali: Episcopales sunt, quæ vulgo, Aurenches, Eureux, Baieux, Sais, Contances, Lisieux. Aurenches, Latinis olim Ingena Abrincantorum: Ῥύῳα Ἀ Ptolemæo: Abrincanta Vrbs Armorica est in libro Notitiarum. Abrincantinam Villam nominat Sigebertus, quæ vocatur Landa Aronis. Cohors i. Ingenuorum, quæ in antiqua Inscriptione visitur Florani, in Agro Veronensi, nescio an huc pertineat: quod moneo, quum in ea sententia videam doctissimum Virum Abraham Ortelium. Ea sane sic habet:
units.tr: So much for the archiepiscopal city. The episcopal sees are those commonly called Avranches, Evreux, Bayeux, Sees, Coutances and Lisieux. Avranches, called Ingena Abrincantorum by the Latins of old, is Ῥύῳα Ἀ in Ptolemy [Rhyoa A]; Abrincanta is an Armorican city in the book of the Notitiae. Sigebert names the Abrincantine villa, which is called Landa Aronis. I do not know whether the First Cohort of Ingenui, which is seen in an ancient inscription of Floranus in the territory of Verona, belongs here. I mention it because I see that the most learned Abraham Ortelius holds this opinion. The inscription indeed reads as follows:

units.la: Abrincantenses Præsules nominat Belleforestius xlv; ultimum L. Sitierum Parisiensem. Abrincanta Vrbs fere mœnia pulsat Mare, quod Montem D. Michaelis circundat. Eureux, olim, ut videre est apud Ptolemæum Mediolanum (μεδιόλανιον) Aulercorum Eburovicum, quod suis ad me litteris monet Nobilis. Vir Iosephus Scaliger: Mediolanum Aulercorum, Antonino. Episcoporum Nomenclaturam nullus adhuc vidi. In huius Vrbis Territorio sunt opida Vernon, Aigle, Passey, Tullieres, Ingles, Canches, Bertueil, Rugles, Bruin, Hermenville. Baieux, Baiocensis Vrbs in vita S. Vegoris ejus Episcopi apud Surium. Baiocas in Catalogo Metropolcan, & Vsuardo pridie Eid. Septembris, Kalendisque Novembris; necnon Aimoino lib. v. cap. xliii. Sic Notitia Imperij: Sub dispositione V. Spectabilis Ducis Moguntiacensis; Præfectus Latorum, Batavorum, & Gentilium Suevorum Baiocas & Constantia Lugdunensis Secunda. Vrbs Arce prædita adsidet Auræ Fluvio, qui haud procul Estrehaino in abismum se condit. Templum ibi visendum cum insigni Horologio. Qui quoque Præsules Ecclesiæ præfuerint, nondum didici. An altera Retomagus Ptolemæi, videant peritiores. Res parum certa formulam veterem mihi exprimit, N. L. Adeat præter alios Lectorem Eliam Vinctum ad Professores Ausonij, Carmine iv. Sais, Ses, vel Seez (varie enim scribitur) Sagium legi Latinis appellari, sed apud quem non occurrit in præsentia Scriptorem. Saiorum Civitas in Notitia Provinciarum non tam opidum, quam totus eorum Pagus & Ditio. Multa huic parent opida, & fere totum Alençoniense Territorium, Parsque Regionis, quæ vulgo La Perche. De Episcopis nihil habeo certi. Opidi, quod Arce præditum, pars una Regni est, sub judicium cadens Magistratus Regii, cui Sedes est Falaisæ, altera Ducatus Alençonij. Contances, vel, origini suæ convenientius, Constances, Constantina Castra Ammiano; Flavia Constantia in Libro Notit. Opinantur nonnulli Ῥοκιάτωον Venelorum esse apud Ptolemæum, quod Caracotinum Antonini, Crouciaconnum Peutingeri Tabulæ: cui sanius & emendatius, nondum capio. Opidum hodie nullis muris, nullo vallo cinctum: Arcem tamen habens. Magna & multa ibi Antiquitatis vestigia. Pontem egregium hic construxerunt Proceres, quibus cognomen Les Pulsneaux, super Rivum, qui Bafart vulgo. Episcopos numerat Belleforestius lxxii, ultimumque nominat Arturum Cossaum, Marescalli Brisaccii Filium. Lisieux opido quod olim Nomen, quosque & quot ad hoc usque tempus habuerit Antistites, mihi non est compertum: Hodie Levovium Latine scribentibus nuncupatur.
units.tr: Belleforest lists forty-five bishops of Avranches (Abrincantenses Præsules), the last being L. Sitierus of Paris. The city of Avranches is nearly struck by the sea, which surrounds the Mount of St Michael. Évreux, formerly Mediolanum (Μεδιόλανιον) of the Aulerci Eburovices, as seen in Ptolemy; a distinguished man writes this to me in his letter, and Joseph Scaliger says: Mediolanum of the Aulerci, in Antoninus. I have not yet seen a list of its bishops. In the territory of this city lie the towns of Vernon, Aigle, Passey, Tullières, Ingles, Canches, Bertheuil, Rugles, Bruyère and Hermenville. Bayeux, the city of the Bayeux diocese, appears in the life of St Vigor, its bishop, in Surius; it is called Baiocas in the Metropolitan catalogue and in Usuard on the day before the Ides of September and on the Kalends of November, and likewise in Aimoin, book 5, chapter 43. So the Notitia Imperii says: under the authority of the Spectabilis Duke of Mainz, the Prefect of the Lati, Batavi and Gentile Suevi at Bayeux and Coutances, Lugdunensis Secunda. The city, provided with a citadel, sits on the river Aure, which hides itself in a chasm not far from Estrehain. There is a church to be seen there with a notable clock. I have not learned who were the bishops of the Church there. Whether the other Retomagus of Ptolemy is meant, let the more skilled judge; the matter is uncertain and only recalls an old formula to me: N. L. The reader may consult, among others, Elias Vinetus on the professors of Ausonius, Carmen iv. Sais, Ses or Seez (for it is variously written) is said by the Latins to be called Sagium, but I do not at present find an author who says so. The Civitas Saiorum in the Notitia Provinciarum is less a town than the whole district and dominion of the Saii. Many towns obey it, and nearly the whole territory of Alençon, and part of the region commonly called La Perche. I have nothing certain about its bishops. The town, which is provided with a citadel, is partly under the royal jurisdiction, whose seat is at Falaise, and partly belongs to the Duchy of Alençon. Coutances, or, more fittingly to its origin, Constances (Constantina Castra in Ammianus; Flavia Constantia in the book of the Notitia). Some think that Rokiatōn of the Venelli in Ptolemy is the same, which is Caracotinum in Antoninus and Crouciaconnum in the Peutinger Tables; I do not yet grasp what is more sound and more correct. The town today is surrounded by no walls or rampart, though it has a citadel. There are many great traces of antiquity there. The nobles called Les Pulsneaux built a fine bridge here, over the stream commonly called the Bafart. Belleforest counts seventy-two bishops and names the last as Arthur Cossé, son of Marshal Brissac. Of the town of Lisieux, what name it once had, and who and how many bishops it had up to this time, I have not learned. Today it is called Levovium by those who write in Latin.

units.la: Haec de Dignitatibus, quae Maiores per Normanniam, Ecclesiasticis: sequuntur Politicae in Ducatibus, & Comitatibus: nam minorum gentium praeteribo, ne sim prolixior. Ducatus sunt tres Alençon, Aumale, Longue-Ville. Alençonium ad Sartram Fluvium, qui apud Andegavenses in Ligerim provolvitur, Comitatus olim titulo fuit celebre. Primus Valesiorum & Alençonii Comes legitur Karolus, Philippi III Franciae Regis Filius. Hic tres habuit Conjuges; Clementiam, Karoli II Regis Apuliae; Katharinam, Philippi Filiam, Balduini I Imperatoris Byzantini Neptem: Mechtildem Guidonis Castilionaei, Comitis S. Pauli Filiam. Ex alio autem utriusque sexus nati: ex postrema Ludovico: quo sine liberis mortuo, Comitatus ad Karolum II, Fratrem Consanguineum, quem ex prima Conjuge Karolus Valesius procrearat, est devolutus. Karolo successit Filius Karolus III, quo in Archiepiscopum Lugdunensem lecto, Comes v factus est frater Petrus, Pater Joannis, quem primum Alençonii Ducem inauguravit Karolus VI, Rex Franciae: Hunc recta linea sunt sequuti Joannes II, Dux II; Renatus Dux Alençonii III, & Comes Perchae; Karolus denique IV, Dux IV: quo sine Liberis non multo post Pugnam Ticinensem exstincto, Ducatus ad Franciscum I Francorum Regem redit. Renatum rursus Ducatus nomen in Herculē Andegavensi, qui postea Francisci nomen adsumlit. Hic improlis anno MD XXXIII mortuus Ducatum Regno restituit.
units.tr: These are the ecclesiastical and greater dignities through Normandy; the political ones follow, in the duchies and counties, for I shall pass over the lesser peoples so as not to be too long. There are three duchies: Alençon, Aumale, Longueville. Alençon, on the river Sarthe, which flows through the Andegavi into the Loire, was once famous under the title of county. The first Count of Valois and Alençon is read to be Charles, son of Philip III, King of France. He had three wives: Clemence, daughter of Charles II, King of Apulia; Catherine, daughter of Philip, granddaughter of Baldwin I, Emperor of Byzantium; and Mechtild, daughter of Guy of Châtillon, Count of St Pol. He had children of both sexes by another wife; by the last, Louis, who died without children, and the county passed to Charles II, his full brother, whom Charles of Valois had begotten by his first wife. Charles was succeeded by his son Charles III, and when he was elected Archbishop of Lyon, his brother Peter, the father of John, became Count. King Charles VI of France invested John, whom he first made Duke of Alençon. The following in direct line were John II, Duke II; René, Duke of Alençon, III, and Count of Perche; and finally Charles IV, Duke IV; who died without children not long after the battle of Pavia, and the duchy returned to King Francis I of France. The title of duke came back to René in Hercules of Anjou, who afterwards took the name Francis. He died without children in 1533 and restored the duchy to the crown.

units.la: In hoc Oppido Baillivatus Normanniae est praecipuus. Quod ad Aumalae Ducatum, legitur ab Antonio, Comite Vadimontio, ducta Maria, Filia & Heres Joannis Harcuriae & Aumalae Comitis. Ex eo Conjugio natus, cum Margareta (quae Antonio Croviaco, Porciae Comiti, in dotem attulit Airichotum & Birbecam Brabantiae opida) Fridericus, Comes Vadimontius & Aumalius. Hic, ducta Iola Renati Andegavensis Regis Siciliae Filia, Lotharingiae Ducatum Herede vacuum ad veterem Sirpem Bihonaeam reduxit: Successorem nactus Filium Renatum, Lotharingiae Ducem, Comitemque Vadimontium & Aumalium: cui quum plures essent Liberi, Antonius tertiogenitus Dux fuit Calabriae, Lotharingiae, Barri; Marchio Montisfumopontis, Comes Provinciae, Vadimontis & Afpromontis: Claudius, septimo loco natus, Dux Guiliae & Aumaliae: Comitatu jam in Ducatus dignitatem erecto: Ludovicus, qui Liberorum nonus, Vadalamontis Comes: Franciscus denique postremus, Lambesci & Orgonis Comes. Claudio duo fuerunt Filii, Franciscus, Dux Guisius; & Claudius, Dux Aumalius. Filia vero Maria, quae, priore Conjuge Longovillano Duce mortuo, nupsit Iacobo V. Regi Scotiae, mater ex eo Mariae Stuardae, Scotiae Reginae. Claudius, de quo dixi, unicam habuit Filiam & Heredem Katharinam, quae nupsit Nicolao Comiti Vadimontio suo Agnato. De Longovillano Ducatu nihil, quam quod obiter paulo ante dictum habeo.
units.tr: In this town is the chief bailiwick of Normandy. As for the Duchy of Aumale, it is read that Antony, Count of Vaudémont, married Mary, daughter and heir of John of Harcourt, Count of Aumale. From this marriage was born Frederick, Count of Vaudémont and Aumale, who, with Margaret (who brought the towns of Aerschot and Herbais in Brabant as dowry to Antony of Croy, Count of Porcien), was the father of Frederick. He married Yolande, daughter of René of Anjou, King of Sicily, and brought the vacant Duchy of Lorraine back to the old house of Bar. He had as successor his son René, Duke of Lorraine, and Count of Vaudémont and Aumale. Since he had several children, Antony, the third-born, became Duke of Calabria, Lorraine and Bar, Marquis of Mont-Fumoy, Count of Provence, Vaudémont and Aspremont. Claude, born seventh, was Duke of Guise and Aumale, the county having now been raised to a duchy. Louis, the ninth of the children, was Count of Vaudemont; Francis, last of all, was Count of Lambesc and Orgon. Claude had two sons, Francis, Duke of Guise; and Claude, Duke of Aumale. His daughter Mary, who, after the death of her first husband, the Duke of Longueville, married James V, King of Scotland, was the mother of Mary Stuart, Queen of Scots. Claude, of whom I spoke, had one daughter and heir, Catherine, who married Nicholas, Count of Vaudémont, her kinsman. Of the Duchy of Longueville I have nothing except what I have said in passing a little earlier.

units.la: Haec de Ducatibus: Comitatus sunt Eu, Harcourt, Eureux, Tancarville, Malemvrier, Mortain, Mongommery, Thorigny, Gisors. Fuisum Comitatum (cujus pars est in Francia, sic speciatim dicta) translatum lego in Comitum Nivernensium & Stamparum Familiam, quum Philippus, Philippi Valesii, Burgundiae Ducis, Filius, Comes Neversii, Rethelii, & Stamparum, Conjugem duceret Bonam Philippi Artesii, Comitis Eusii Filiam. Vide quae plenius dicturus cap. xxxix, ubi de Comitibus Nivernensibus. Harcuria Comitatus, una cum Aumalio ad Vadimontios Comites pervenit, Conjugio inter Antonium Vadimontium Comitem & Mariam Filiam Heredemque Joannis Harcuriae & Aumaliae Comitis Filiam, de quo antea. De Ebroicensi, Tancarvillano, Malevrensi, Mortanio & Gisortio (de ipso opido post dicam) Comitatibus nihil jam explorati occurrit. Praestat enim nihil adferre, quam parum cognita. Mongommerianum Comitatum nobilitavit supra modum non ita pridem Gabriel Lorgius, Comes Mongommerius, Princeps magnanimus, cujus res fortiter gestae Supplicium-que inciderunt in annum MDXXXIV. Thorigniym obtinuit nuper Jacobus Mathignonus, cujus contra Mongommerium gesta in Francorum Historiis legantur ad annum, cujus meminimi. Oppidum est ruinis & Porticuum, quae dives fuisse loquuntur, ruderibus deformatum. Sedes Baillivatus. Addam hic nonnihil de Regno, quod vulgo Yvetot, Royaulme d'Yvetot, exiguis finibus circumscriptum, haud procul Urbe Rotomagenti, in ea Normanniae parte, quae vernacule Caux. Regni Titulus natus fertur sub Hlotario I, Francorum Regei qui Vici Dominum obtruncarat, ipso Parasceues die. Damnatus enim rex scribitur Romani Pontificis sententia, ut Cæ-si heredibus tantum in suam Dynastiam juris, præter Regium Titulum, concederet, quamtum Regibus deinceps in totum Franciæ competeret Regnum.
units.tr: These are the duchies; the counties are Eu, Harcourt, Évreux, Tancarville, Malemvrier, Mortain, Montgommery, Thorigny, Gisors. I read that the County of Eu (part of which lies in France and is so called specifically) passed to the family of the Counts of Nevers and Étampes, when Philip, son of Philip of Valois, Duke of Burgundy, Count of Nevers, Rethel and Étampes, married Bonne of Artois, daughter of the Count of Eu. See what I shall say more fully in chapter 39, where I speak of the Counts of Nevers. The county of Harcourt, together with Aumale, came to the Counts of Vaudémont through the marriage of Antony, Count of Vaudémont, and Mary, daughter and heir of John of Harcourt, Count of Aumale, which I mentioned above. Concerning the counties of Évreux, Tancarville, Malevrier, Mortain and Gisors (I shall speak of the town of Gisors later) nothing certain has come to hand now; it is better to say nothing than to say so little that is known. The County of Montgommery was made greatly famous, not long ago, by Gabriel Lorges, Count of Montgommery, a magnanimous prince, whose brave deeds and execution fell in the year 1574. Thorigny was lately held by Jacques Matignon, whose exploits against Montgommery are read in the histories of France up to the year I mentioned. The town is disfigured by ruins and the rubble of porticoes which are said to have been rich. It is the seat of a bailiwick. I shall add here something about the Kingdom commonly called Yvetot, the Royaume d'Yvetot, enclosed within narrow bounds, not far from the city of Rouen, in that part of Normandy which in the vernacular is Caux. The title of the kingdom is said to have arisen under Lothair I, King of the Franks, who had slain the lord of the village on Good Friday itself. For the king is recorded to have been condemned by the sentence of the Roman Pontiff, so that he should grant to the heirs of Caesar only the right to his own dynasty, besides the royal title, as much as belonged to the kings thereafter over the whole kingdom of France.

units.la: Sic se habent per Normanniam Dignitates & Ecclesiasticæ & Politicæ: succedit explicatio Partium Majorum. Normannia quibusdam statuitur Duplex Superior & Inferior.
units.tr: Thus stand the ecclesiastical and political dignities throughout Normandy; there follows an explanation of its greater parts. Normandy is by some divided into two, Upper and Lower.

units.la: Superior, La Haulte Normandie, continet (præter Ducatus, Comitatusque præscriptos) illam Regionis portionem, quæ vulgo Vesquecin, aliis Vulx & Vulxin cognomine Le Normand. Vrbs primaria Gisortum, Gisors vulgo; quam Metropolin agnoscunt, quæ notis nominibus Estrepaigny, Escouys la grande, Forest de Lyhonis, S. Clair sur Astre, Les deux Andelys, Chasteau Gaillard.
units.tr: Upper Normandy, La Haute Normandie, contains (besides the duchies and counties listed) that portion of the region which is commonly called Vexin, by others Vulx and Vulxin, with the surname Le Normand. Its chief town is Gisortum, commonly Gisors, which they acknowledge as its metropolis; and it has the well-known places Étrépagny, Écouis la Grande, Forêt de Lyons, St Clair sur Epte, Les Deux Andelys, Château Gaillard.

units.la: Inferior, La Basse Normandie, in Minores distrahitur Partes, quæ vernacule, Caulx, Bessin, Constantin. Caulx, Caletum quis Latine dixerit. Veterum Caletum, ut antea dixi, Sedes. Faciem habet Peninsulæ, quæ Sequana minoribusque aliquot Fluviis & Oceano fere jacet inclusa. Extendit se Treportum usque & Fanum S. Valerij, quod prope Abbatis-Villam & opidum Eusium. Promontorium habet, quod Francis Capo de Caulx; vel Le Grosnez du Caulx; quod ex Sequana petentibus Angliam est præternavigandum. Metropolis Diepa, cui nomen ab Fluvio perlabente. Cives maximam sibi famam pepererunt suis in Orbem remotiorem Navigationibus. 10
units.tr: Lower Normandy, La Basse Normandie, is divided into smaller parts, which in the vernacular are called Caux, Bessin, Cotentin. Caux is what one would call Caletum in Latin. As I said before, it was the seat of the ancient Caleti. It has the shape of a peninsula, lying almost enclosed by the Seine, some smaller rivers and the ocean. It extends as far as Tréport and the church of St Valery, which is near Abbeville and the town of Eu. It has a headland which the French call Cap de Caux or Le Grosnez du Caux, which those sailing from the Seine to England must pass. The metropolis is Dieppe, named after the river that flows through it. Its citizens have won great fame for their voyages to more distant parts of the world.

units.la: Minorum gentium Opida sunt Harfleu ad dextram Sequanæ ripam, quasi Arcus, ut quidam conjiciunt, Finctus Maris: Honfleu ad ejusdem sinistram, cum Arce: insignis Portus: Ptolemæo, ut nonnulli censent, Iulioboua, ut & Antonino, & Itinerariæ Tabulæ, in qua vitiose Iuliobona. Meminit & Iuliobona Sigebertus, qui dicit eam ab Iulio Cæsare conditam & nominatam, destructa Vrbe Calcta. Iuliobona Hadriano Turnebo Villebon putatur: Havre de grace, Portus Gratiæ Latinis sonat, opidum, quod Piratis terrori; Francici Regni ea parte Clavis & Ianua; Condidit contra Anglorum irruptiones Franciscus I; Ejus incunabula inciderunt in annum MDIX: Caudebec ad ripam Sequanæ dexteram: Fescamp quasi, ut quidam augurantur, Fisci Campus; Abbatiam habet celebrem, ubi Mausolæum Normanniæ Ducum; Sepultos ibi scio Richardum I & Richardum II Intrepidum, Patrem & Filium, Tertium & Quartum Normanniæ Duces. Bessin habet præter Baiocensem Vrbem, de qua paullo ante, Cadomum, vulgo Caen, opidum ad Fluvium, qui Ολνα Ptolemæo, Aufne & Orne vernacule vocatur; Arce præditum, Baillivatus sede nobilitatum, Academia celebre, quam instituit Henricus V Angliæ Rex anno MCCCCXVIII; Antiqua igitur, sed ob Viciniores ignobiliore; Sunt qui nuncupatum volunt, quasi Car, id est Cæsaris, Domum; Insignis ibi Architecturæ Curiam est videre. Cadomum sequuntur: Falaisse, opidum ad Antam Fluvium: Formam Navis refert; Arcem habens, quæ Puppis quasi vicem subit; Ambitur Fossis profundissimis, duobusque cingitur Stagnis; Patria Guilelmi Conquæstoris, cujus in Ducum Catalogo feci mentionem; Superioribus annis, quum forte Terra foderetur, inventa fuit magna vis Nummorum Æreorum, quibus & nomen & imago C. Iulij Cæsaris erant insculpta: In Suburbanis opidi locis Sacellum est Divæ Virgini dicatum, cui cognomen La Cambray, ubi Mercatus, maximis propositis Immunitatibus, celebratur singulis annis famosissimus; Hyesmes, Oximum Surio in vita S. Oportunæ; Arce præditum. Vire, opidum ad Fluvium cognominem, qui innumeras versat Molas, subigendis eluendisque pannis, quorum magnus hic Mercatus: Alortain, opidum cum Arce ad Auram Fluvium; Reliquiæ hic servantur S. Guilielmi; in Primario Templo Canonici Sacra celebrant ritu Parisiensi; Majoribus Festis Regius Adparitor nomine Regis se sistit, nudum manu tenens, donec Sacrum peractum, Ensem; nec aliud, quam hunc Ensem in publicis Supplicationibus gestant Signum. Constantia complectitur (præter Constantiensem urbem; Baroniam Honyvec, & Regnum Yvetot) opida Valloignes, cujus Incolæ Litibus addictiores, Arce nobile, ut & quæ sequuntur pleraque: Cherbourg, quasi Cæsaris Burgum; exstructum enim ab Cæsare creditur; Postremum fuit eorum, quæ Karolus Rex Anglis cripuit: S. Lo, opidum ad Viram Fluvium, anno MCCCCLXXXIV ab Comite Mongommerio captum, moxque ab Matignone Regis nomine recuperatum: Quarentan, Portum Maris: S. Saulveur; S. Hermont,
units.tr: The towns of the lesser districts are Harfleur on the right bank of the Seine, named, as some guess, from Arcus, or Finctus Maris; Honfleur on the left bank, with a castle, a notable harbour, which some think is Iulioboua in Ptolemy, as also in Antoninus and in the Itinerary Table, where it is wrongly written Iuliobona. Iuliobona is also mentioned by Sigebert, who says it was founded and named by Julius Caesar after the town of Calcta was destroyed. Hadrian Turnebus thinks Iuliobona is Villebon. Havre de Grâce, which in Latin means Port of Grace, is a town that terrifies pirates and is the key and gateway of the kingdom of France in that part. Francis I founded it against the English invasions; its beginnings fall in the year 1519. Caudebec lies on the right bank of the Seine. Fécamp, as some surmise, from Fisci Campus (the Field of the Treasury); it has a famous abbey, where the mausoleum of the Dukes of Normandy is. I know that Richard I and Richard II the Fearless, father and son, third and fourth Dukes of Normandy, are buried there. Bessin has, besides the city of Bayeux, of which I spoke a little earlier, Cadomum, commonly Caen, a town on the river which Ptolemy calls Olna and which is called in the vernacular Aufne and Orne. It has a castle and is made noble by the seat of a bailiwick. It has a celebrated academy, which Henry V, King of England, founded in the year 1418. It is therefore old, but less noted because of its nearer neighbours. Some want its name to be taken as Car, that is Caesar's, Domum (house). There one may see a remarkable court of architecture. After Caen come: Falaise, a town on the river Ante. It resembles the shape of a ship, having a castle which takes the place of the stern; it is surrounded by very deep ditches and enclosed by two pools. It was the homeland of William the Conqueror, of whom I made mention in the catalogue of Dukes. In recent years, when the ground was dug up by chance, a great quantity of bronze coins was found, bearing the name and image of Gaius Julius Caesar. In the suburbs of the town there is a chapel dedicated to the Blessed Virgin, which has the surname La Cambray, where a market, with very great exemptions offered, is held every year and is very famous. Hyesmes, Oximum in Surius's life of St Opportuna; it has a castle. Vire, a town on the river of the same name, which turns countless mills for fulling and washing cloths, of which there is a great market here. Alortain, a town with a castle on the river Aure; the relics of St William are kept here. In the principal church the canons celebrate the sacred rites according to the Paris use; on the greater feasts the royal officer presents himself in the king's name, holding a bare sword in his hand until the sacred service is finished; and they carry only this sword in public processions as their sign. Constantia comprises (besides the city of Coutances, the barony of Hambye and the kingdom of Yvetot) the towns Valognes, whose inhabitants are rather inclined to lawsuits, and which, like most of those that follow, is noted for its castle; Cherbourg, as if Caesar's Burg, for it is believed to have been built by Caesar. It was the last of those things which King Charles snatched from the English. St Lô, a town on the river Vire, taken in the year 1484 by Count Montgommery, and soon recovered for the king by Matignon. Quarentan, a harbour on the sea; St Sauveur; S. Hermont,

units.la: Quarentan, & alia. S. Hermont, S. Gilles. In eodem hoc Tractu Ville-Dieu, Commendatariam, ut nota utar voce, habet Rodiensem.
units.tr: Quarentan, and others. S. Hermont, S. Gilles. In this same district is Ville-Dieu, which has a commandery of Rhodes, to use the familiar term.

units.tr: The part of the route which Antoninus Augustus, since he is the author of the Itinerary that circulates under his name, leads from Carocotinum to Augustobona belongs to Normandy. I shall not hesitate to set down the comparison with the Peutinger Table. Itinerary of Antoninus | Peutinger Table | Modern names. From Carocotinum to Augustobona, 153 Roman miles; Ptolemy's Chrochiaton [χροχιάτων]. | Crouciaconnum, XXI. Wrongly; read Cruciatono. What if it is Cruciacordo? | Crevecoeur. Iuliobona, 10 Roman miles. | Luliobona, XVIII. To be corrected to Iuliobona. | Honfleur. Lotum, 6 Roman miles. | ........ | Pontaudemer. Latomagum, 13 Roman miles. | Rattumagus, VIII. To be restored as Brivalsara. | Pontoise. Lutetia, 18 Roman miles. | Luteci, XVII. | Paris.
