units.la: BRitannia, vulgo La Duché de Bretaigne, nomen habet à Britannis Populis, de quibus paullo post dicam. Ad Orientem Nortmannos habet, Cenomanos & Andegavenses confinales; ad Meridiem Pictones: reliqua Latera claudit Mare Britannicum. Provinciarum Galliæ ad Oceanum est ultima; in altum ultra reliquas omnes procurrens, Peninsulæ instar. Vere Plinius lib. iiii. natur. Histor. cap. xviii: Sed Peninsulam spectatiorem excurrentem in Oceanum à fine Osismiorum, circuitu 10 cxxv. M. Pass. cervice in latitudinem cxxv M. Non inconcinne igitur Cornu Galliæ vocatur in Veteris Historiæ Francorum libellulo. Ejus verba paullo post dabo. Solex ferreæ speciem referre dicitur, cujus exterior pars subrotunda Mare: interior vero, quæ concava, respicit Mediterranea. Longitudo ejus sex dierum est itineris, trium autem Latitudo. Regio est amœnissima & fertilissima. Pratis abundat & Erycetis, ex quibus gratum Pecori Pabulum. Mare ibi Commercijs aptissimum: unde Sal extrahunt Adcolæ, quod ab Sole induratum Conregionalibus vendunt. Venas Fodinasque habet Britannia Argenti, Ferri, Plumbi. Incolæ non omnes eadem animi alacritate; non omnes eadem comitate: plerique tamen cauti Lucrique cupidi; gravissima Negocia ad Pocula tractare soliti. Bilingues. Quum enim novem habeat Episcopatus, ut antea monui; in Briocensi, Nannetensi & Venetensi absque discrimine utuntur Francica Lingua & Britonismo; in Leonensi, Tricoriensi & Curosopitensi, solo Britonismo, in Machlovien-si denique, Dolensi & Redonensi Gallica tantum.
units.tr: Britannia, commonly called La Duché de Bretaigne, takes its name from the Britanni, a people of whom I shall speak a little later. To the east it has the Normans, and the Cenomani and Andegavi as neighbours; to the south the Pictones; the British Sea bounds its other sides. It is the last of the provinces of Gaul on the Ocean, jutting out into the deep beyond all the rest, like a peninsula. Pliny rightly says in Book 4 of his Natural History, chapter 18: But the more conspicuous peninsula runs out into the Ocean from the boundary of the Osismii, with a circuit of 125 miles, and a neck 125 miles across. So it is not inappropriately called the Horn of Gaul in the little old History of the Franks. I shall give its words a little later. It is said to resemble an iron sole, whose outer part, rounded, faces the sea, while the inner part, which is hollow, faces the inland regions. Its length is six days' journey, but its breadth three. It is a most pleasant and fertile region, abounding in meadows and heaths, which provide welcome pasture for cattle. The sea there is most suitable for trade, and from it the local inhabitants extract salt, which they sell, hardened by the sun, to their neighbours. Britannia has veins and mines of silver, iron and lead. The inhabitants are not all equally lively in spirit, nor all equally courteous; yet most of them are cautious and eager for gain, and they are accustomed to conduct the most serious business over their cups. They are bilingual. For since it has nine bishoprics, as I said before: in the dioceses of Saint-Brieuc (Briocensis), Nantes (Nannetensis) and Vannes (Venetensis) they use indiscriminately both French and Breton; in Léon (Leonensis), Tréguier (Tricoriensis) and Cornouaille (Curosopitensis) only Breton; and finally in Saint-Malo (Machlovien­sis), Dol (Dolensis) and Rennes (Redonensis) only French.

units.la: Olim Armorica (cuius vocis latiorem fuisse notionem innuit Plinius lib. iiii. nat. Hist. cap. xvii.) fuit appellata; præcipue, qua ad Mare vergit, ubi nunc Inferior est Britannia. Ar-Mor enim veteribus Britannis nihil aliud, quam ad Mare, vel supra Mare, ut etiam docet cum Ioanne Lelando doctissimus Vir Gulielmus Cambdenus.
units.tr: In former times it was called Armorica (a word whose wider meaning Pliny hints at in Book 4 of his Natural History, chapter 17), especially the part that borders on the sea, where Lower Britain now lies. For Ar-Mor meant nothing else to the ancient Britons than by the sea or above the sea, as the most learned Englishman William Camden also teaches, together with John Leland.

units.la: Armoricas Civitates Oceanum attingentes celebrat Cæsar lib. vii, earumque in numero ponit Curiosolites, Redones, Ambibaros, Cadetes, Osismios. Lemovices, Venetos & Vinellos. Easdem in ultimis Galliæ finibus positas Oceanoque conjunctas ait A. Hirtius, sive quis alius, qui septem Ephemeridum de Bello Gallico Libris Octavum adjecit. De iisdem, earumque pro Libertate sua in Romanos Conjuratione multa memorantur lib. iii. Belli Gallici. Aremoricus Lar apud Ausonium in Versibus, qui à Monosyllabis cœpti in ijsdem finiuntur, Viridomarus Gallorum Dux, de quo Tertia Opima Spolia retulit M. Claudius Marcellus Consul. Druides Gentis Armorica nominantur ab eodem Ausonio Carmine x de Grammaticis Latinis Burdigalensibus. Aremoricum quinque syllabarum est & aliis apud eumdem Poëtam locis; ut in Technopægnio versu lxxxiii, & Epistola ad Paulum de Ostreis versu xxxv, item apud Plinium lib. iv, & Sidonium in Panegyrico, qui Avito Augusto dictus: apud alios, ut Cæsarem & Eutropium est Tetrasyllabum Armoricum, Armorica Letavia quondam etiam vocata, si fides Pontico Virunnio: hodie sane antiquo Britannorum Idiomate Llydaw dicitur, ut scribit Humfredus in suo Britannicæ Descriptionis fragmento. Illud etiam hoc loco monendum duxi, totum Britanniæ Normanniæque, ut & ex adverso ipsius Insulæ Britanniæ, Littus longe lateque Saxonicum in Libro Notitiarum vocari ab Saxonibus, Piraticam ibi exercere solitis. Eo spectant hi Sidonij Apollinaris Versus in Panegyrico, quem Avito Augusto Socero dixit: Quin & Aremoricus Pyratam Saxona Tractus Sperabat, cui pelle Salum sulcare Britannum Ludus, & adsuto glaucum Mare findere Lembo.
units.tr: Caesar, in Book 7, celebrates the Armorican States that reach the Ocean, and among them he lists the Curiosolitae, Redones, Ambibari, Cadetes, Osismii, Lemovices, Veneti and Unelli. A. Hirtius, or whoever else added an eighth book to the seven books of the Journal of the Gallic War, says that the same peoples were situated at the furthest borders of Gaul and joined to the Ocean. Much is recorded about them, and about their conspiracy against the Romans for the sake of their liberty, in Book 3 of the Gallic War. Aremoricus Lar appears in Ausonius, in verses that begin and end with monosyllables; Viridomarus, the Gallic leader from whom Marcus Claudius Marcellus, as consul, won the third spoils of honour; Druids of the Armorican people are named by the same Ausonius in his tenth poem, on the Latin grammarians of Bordeaux. Aremoricum has five syllables, as in other places in the same poet, such as the Technopaegnion, verse 83, and the letter to Paulus about oysters, verse 35; likewise in Pliny Book 4, and in Sidonius in the Panegyric addressed to the emperor Avitus. In others, such as Caesar and Eutropius, Armoricum is a four-syllable word. Armorica was once also called Letavia, if we trust Ponticus Virunnius; today it is indeed called Llydaw in the ancient idiom of the Britons, as Humphrey writes in his fragment of a Description of Britain. I think it also worth noting here that the whole coast of Britain and Normandy, as well as the opposite shore of the island of Britain itself, is called far and wide the Saxon Shore in the Book of Notices, after the Saxons, who were accustomed to practise piracy there. To this refer those verses of Sidonius Apollinaris in the Panegyric he delivered to Avitus his father-in-law: Moreover, the Armorican tract hoped for a Saxon pirate, for whom it was a game to plough the sea with a hide-covered boat and to cleave the grey sea with a patched hull.

units.la: Quanta autem immanitate per hæc littora grassati fuerint Saxones, docet idem Sidonius lib. viii. Epist. v i. ad Nammatium: Sed ecce dum jam Epistolam, quæ diu garrit, claudere optarem, subditus à Santonis nuncius, cum quo dum tui obtentu aliquid horarum sermocinanter extraximus, constanter adseveravit, nuper vos Classicum in Classe cecinisse, atque inter officia nunc Nauta, modo Stelitis, littoribus Oceani curvis inerrare contra Saxonum pandos Myoparones, quorum quot Remiges videris, totidem te cernere putes Archipiratas; ita simul omnes imperant, parent, docent, discunt latrocinari. Unde nunc etiam ut quamplurimum caveas, causa successit maxima monendi. Hostis est omnis Hostle truculentior. Improvisus adgreditur, provisus elabitur, sternit objectos, sternit incautos; si sequatur, intercipit, si fugiat, evadis. Ad hoc, exercent illos Naufragia, non terrent. Est eis quedam cum discriminibus Pelagi non notitia solum, sed familiaritas. Nam quoniam ipsa, si qua tempestas est, hunc secures efficit occupandos; hunc prospici vetat occupaturos in medio Fluctuum Scopulorumque confragosorum ipse superveniens lassi periclitantur. Præterea, priusquam, de continentis in patriam vela laxantes, hostico mordaces anchoras vado vellant, mos est remeaturis decimum quemque captorum per æquales & cruciarias pœnas, plus ob hoc tristi, quod superstitioso ritu, necare; superque collectam turbam perituram Mortis iniquitatem Sortis æquitate dispergere. Talibus se ligant Votis, Victimis solvunt: & per hujusmodi non tam Sacrificia, quam Sacrilegia polluti, religiosum putant Cædis infausta perpetratores de Capite capitis o magis exigere Tormenta, quam Pretia. De Saxonibus plura erunt dicenda in mea Germania. Certe crebriores Saxonum infestantium depræda ntiumque Superventus pepererunt tandem huic Tractui Præfecturas Præsidiaque Militum Grannonæ, Blaviæ, Marcis, quorum in Imperij Notitia fit mentio. Inde item nati Vicarij, Comites, Duces Britanniarum, qui Tractum Britannicum sub sua haberent Dispositione: ut legere est in eadem Notitia, & apud Constantium in vita S. Germani, nec non apud Gildam Sapientem de Excidio Britannico.
units.tr: How great the savagery was with which the Saxons raided these shores, Sidonius also shows in Book 8, Letter 6, to Namatius: But see, while I was about to close this letter, which has chattered on for a long time, a messenger came to me from Saintes, and while for your sake we spent some hours in conversation with him, he firmly asserted that you had lately sounded the trumpet of war at sea, and that now, among your duties, you sailors wander about the curving shores of the Ocean, now near the Stelitae, against the crooked Saxon pirate-ships; and as many rowers as you see, you would think you see as many arch-pirates; so all at once they command, obey, teach and learn to plunder. Hence there is now the greatest reason to warn you to be as careful as possible. The enemy is more savage than any enemy. He attacks unforeseen, he escapes when seen; he strikes down those who stand in his way, he strikes down the unwary; if you follow, he cuts you off; if you flee, you escape. Besides, shipwrecks train them rather than terrify them. They have not merely an acquaintance but a familiarity with the perils of the sea. For whatever storm there is, it makes them more secure in their seizures; and when they are menaced by the approach of those who would seize them, the shoals and jagged rocks of the waves in the midst of which they are beset, ready to suffer shipwreck, prevent them from being seen. Moreover, before they weigh the biting anchors from the shallows of the enemy coast, and set sail from the mainland for their homeland, it is their custom, when returning, to kill every tenth captive by equal and cruel tortures; the more sadly because they do this by a superstitious rite, and scatter the injustice of death over the gathered crowd by a fair lot, which is destined to perish. By such vows they bind themselves, by victims they fulfil them; and polluted by such acts, which are less sacrifices than sacrileges, they think the perpetrators of this ill-omened slaughter are more bound to exact torments from the head of the captive than payment. More will be said about the Saxons in my Germany. Certainly the frequent raids of the Saxons who harassed the coast, and their sudden onsets, finally brought about the establishment in this tract of prefectures and garrisons of soldiers at Grannona, Blavia and Marcae, which are mentioned in the Notitia of the Empire. From these also arose the vicars, counts and dukes of the Britains, who held the British tract under their control; as one may read in the same Notitia, and in Constantius in the Life of St Germanus, and also in Gildas the Wise, On the Ruin of Britain.

units.la: Rediit postremo toti huic Provinciæ Nomen antiquum, Britanniaque cœpit iterum audire; Britannis eo ex adversa Insula ab Anglo-Saxonibus, Pictis, Scotisque circa annum cccc l contra fidem compulsis. Fragmentum Historiæ Francicæ, quod cum aliis edidit ex sua Bibliotheca non ita pridem P. Pithœus I. C. Iuxta quos (loquitur de Normannis) habitationem habent Britanni, qui pulsi à Britannica Insula dudum à Saxonibus, eamdem Regionem, quam modo incolunt, sibi vindicantes, appellavere à sua gente Britanniam, quæ prius Cornu Gallia dicebatur. Aliorum hac de re testimonia præteréo. Reduisse autem dixi. Sciendum enim Britannos Insulanos sic in Galliam ex Insula tunc temporis transgressos; ut olim Britanni Galli ex Celtica in adversam Insulam Colonias ducturi transierant. Britanni namque Insulani Britannorum Celtarum antiquissimi sunt censendi Coloni. Plenius hoc explicabo Parte Operis mei postrema; ubi de Insulis, Reginaque Insularum omnium Anglia. Britannos sane (ut ad Veterum Incolarum sensim devenieam indicium) in hac maritima Galliarum parte Populos habet Plinius lib. iiii. natur. Histor. cap. xviii; eosque diversis verbis super Ligerim sitas notat. Sidonius Apollinaris lib. i. Epistola vii ad Vincentium Britones sunt hi Dionysio Afro: Britanniciani in Libro Notitiarum; Brit-anes vel Brittones cum apud Iuvenalem in Satyris
units.tr: Finally the old name returned to this whole province, and Britannia began again to be heard; for around the year 450 the Britons were driven, against their will, from the opposite island by the Anglo-Saxons, Picts and Scots. A fragment of Frankish history, which Pithou, a lawyer, published not long ago from his own library together with other pieces, says: Near them (he speaks of the Normans) the Britons have their dwelling, who, long ago driven from the British island by the Saxons, claimed for themselves the same region which they now inhabit, and from their own people called it Britannia, which was previously called the Horn of Gaul. I pass over other testimonies on this matter. But I said that they returned. For it must be noted that the insular Britons thus crossed over from the island into Gaul at that time, just as the Gallic Britons had once crossed from Celtic territory to the opposite island, intending to lead colonies there. For the insular Britons are rightly considered the colonists of the most ancient Celtic Britons. I shall explain this more fully in the last part of my work, where I speak of the islands, and of England, the queen of all the islands. Pliny, in Book 4 of his Natural History, chapter 18, does indeed place Britons in this maritime part of Gaul (so that we may gradually come to the evidence concerning the ancient inhabitants), and he designates them with various words as dwelling beyond the Loire. Sidonius Apollinaris, in Book 1, Letter 7 to Vincentius, names these as Britons; Dionysius Afer names them Britons; in the Book of Notices they are Britanniciani; and Britanes or Brittones, as in Juvenal in the Satires.

units.la: Qua nec terribiles Cimbri, nec Britones umquam;
units.tr: Where neither the terrible Cimbri nor the Britons ever came;

units.la: Ausonium Epigrammate cvii, de quodam Silvio Bono, qui erat Brito: & in antiquo Lapide, qui visitur Romæ in Pariete Porticus S. Mariæ Rotundæ: tum apud ætatis mediæ Scriptores, Iornandem, Freculphum, Bedam & alios: Brettons hodie vulgo. Ab his Britannis tota hæc Regio Britannia Cis-Marina & Minor ad differentiam Insulane, quæ Minor & Trans-Marina, vocatur apud Sigebertum & alios. Ab isidem Letus dicitur Britannicum, quod Eginarthus describit. Pergo ad reliquos Veteres hujus Ditionis Incolas. Sunt illi, Redones, Nannetes, Curiosolitæ, Venetii, Osismii, Diablintes, Ambibari, Venelii, Ambiliates, Biducesij, Lemovices, & alij. Redones apud Cæsarem lib. iii, qui Ῥηδονες Ptolemæo; Redonica Regio Gregorio Turonensi; Civitas Redonum in Notitia Provinciarum in Lugdunensi iii; L'Evesché de Rennes. In hujus Diœcesis Agro Abbatia est, quæ Redon vulgo Populi memoriam plane adhuc servat. Nannetes vel Namnetes (varie enim pro Codicum diversitate scribuntur) Cæsari lib. iii; Ναμνίται Strabonı lib. iv; Ναμνίται Ptolemæo vitiose. Civitas Namnetum Notitiæ Provinciarum in Lugdunensi iii: L'Evesché de Nantes. Curiosolitæ apud Cæsarem Coriosopitenses esse plerisque placet, inquit in Geographico Alphabeto Raimundus Marlianus. Notitia Provinciarum in Lugdunensi iii Civitatem habet Curosopitorum, ut quidem legitur in optimis Codicibus: in Bonaventuræ Vulcanij, amicissimi mei Collegæ, Membranis est Civitas Crisopotum: L'Evesché de Cornoüaille. Venetii, Reliquæ ab iis contra Cæsarem gestæ in ipsius Ephemeridibus satis sunt nobiles. Οὐένετοι Strabonı, qui & ipsorum navale cum Cæsare prælium celebrat lib. iv. Mirum autem Vulgares Strabonis Editiones Venetos Belgis adscribere, his verbis: μετὰ δὲ τὰ Λεχθὲντα ἔθνη, τὰ λοιπὰ Βελγῶν ἐστὶ ἔθνη τῶν παροικούντων, ἀν Οὐένετοι μὲν &c. Venetii non Belgicæ, sed Celticæ sunt Populi; unde legendum pro Βελγῶν apud Strabonem censeo Κελτῶν. In Notitiæ Provinciarum Lugdunensi, cujus sæpe memini, iii Civitas scribitur Ciantium, id est, Venetorum: L'Evesché de Vennes ou Vannes. Venetos hosce putat Strabo Venetiarum in Adriatico Sinu esse auctores. Osismii Plinio lib. iv. cap. xviii. & Pomponio Melæ: Οσισμιοι Strabonı & Ptolemæo; qui Osismii in Commentario de Bello Gallico, corruptius. Civitas Osismiorum in Notitia Provinciarum. Τιμίας apud Strabonem nominat Pytheas, ledeaque illis tribuit in Promontorio quodam, ἀκρωτήριον ἱκανὸν, porrecto satis. Sunt qui eos locant, ubi hodie Tricoriensium Urbs, vulgo Trignier, vel Landrigniér. Diablintes (sic enim, ut censent Iosephus Scaliger, Fulvius Ursinus, & alij, non Iablintres, ex Membranis scribendi) apud Cæsarem, qui Diablinti Plinio; Διαβλίντες vero Ptolemæo, minus bene. Notitia Provinciarum, Civitas Diablintum, id est Carifes: quid hoc sit, non adsequor. Diablintes olim, ut quibusdam videtur, ubi nunc Leondoul. Goropius Becanus in suis Advaticis eos longe ex Britannia removet, exque iis facit Pagum Brabantiæ, qui vulgo Linter, ad Flumen Getam; quem non mihi animus hic refellere. In S. Domnoli, Cenomanorum Episcopi, Vita hæc leguntur: Villa Tridenta sita in Condita Diablintica: quæ quid sibi velint, nondum capio. Ambibaros Cæsaris existimat fuisse Vigenereus, ubi nunc Ambie, prope Montem S. Michaelis: Qui Οὐινελοι, Venelii, Ptolemæo; Venellis, Plinio; Vinelli sunt in Commentarijs belli Gallici; Οὐισσίοι, Dioni inemendatius. Constituuntur a plerisque ubi hodie Laval oppidum, Comitatus titulo clarum. Ambilitates (quidam Codices Ambialites præferunt) apud Cæsarem; hodie, voce parum abludente, Lambalois. Alij putant habitasse, ubi nunc Nortmanniæ Vicus Amblie, haud procul Baiocassibus. Qui Βιδουκισιοι Ptolemæo interpretantur nonnulli Briocenses, S. Brieu. Lemovices, alij apud Cæsarem ab Lemovicibus Aquitaniæ, Leonenses (S. Paul. de Leon) esse censentur. Ego in his, ut in multis aliis, nihil temere adfirmo. Leguntur & in hoc Tractu, apud Ptolemæum quidem Ἀρβιοι, apud Cæsarem autem Cadetes; de quorum Prioribus nihil habeo certi quod dicam: Posteriores explodit Fulvius Ursinus; Caletes, de quibus in Normannia, substituens. Cadetes tamen audent nonnulli interpretari Castellum Briantum, vulgo Chasteau Briant, quod in Superiore Britannia paret Monmorancijs.
units.tr: Ausonius, in Epigram 107, speaks of a certain Silvius Bonus, who was a Briton. The name also occurs on an ancient stone that can be seen at Rome, on the wall of the portico of S. Maria Rotunda; and among medieval writers, in Jordanes, Freculphus, Bede and others. Today it is commonly Brettons. From these Britons the whole region is called Britannia Cis-Marina and Minor, to distinguish it from the island, which Sigebert and others call Minor and Trans-Marina. From the same people the Letus is called Britannicum, as Eginhard describes. I now turn to the other ancient inhabitants of this district. They are the Redones, Nannetes, Curiosolitae, Venetii, Osismii, Diablintes, Ambibari, Venelii, Ambiliates, Biducesii, Lemovices, and others. The Redones appear in Caesar, book 3, and as Ῥηδονες [Rhēdones] in Ptolemy; the Redonica Regio in Gregory of Tours; the Civitas Redonum in the Notitia Provinciarum, Lugdunensis III; now the Évêché de Rennes. In the territory of this diocese there is an abbey, which still keeps the memory of the people, being called Redon in common speech. The Nannetes, or Namnetes (for they are written variously according to the differences among the manuscripts), appear in Caesar, book 3; as Ναμνίται [Namnitai] in Strabo, book 4; and as Ναμνίται in Ptolemy, wrongly. The Civitas Namnetum is in the Notitia Provinciarum, Lugdunensis III; now the Évêché de Nantes. Most people think that the Curiosolitae of Caesar are the Coriosopitenses, says Raimundus Marlianus in his Geographical Alphabet. The Notitia Provinciarum, Lugdunensis III, has a Civitas Curosopitorum, as is read in the best manuscripts; in the manuscripts of my very dear colleague Bonaventura Vulcanius there is a Civitas Crisopotum; now the Évêché de Cornouaille. The Venetii: the remaining actions taken against Caesar by them are famous enough in his own Commentaries. Strabo has Οὐένετοι [Ouenetoi], and he also describes their naval battle with Caesar, book 4. It is strange, however, that the common editions of Strabo assign the Veneti to the Belgians, in these words: "after the peoples named, the remaining peoples are of the Belgae who dwell nearby, of whom the Ouenetoi..." etc. The Veneti are not a Belgian but a Celtic people; so I think that in Strabo we should read Κελτῶν [Keltōn] for Βελγῶν [Belgōn]. In the Notitia Provinciarum, Lugdunensis III, which I have often mentioned, a civitas is written as Ciantium, that is, of the Veneti; now the Évêché de Vennes or Vannes. Strabo thinks these Veneti were the founders of the Venetians in the Adriatic gulf. The Osismii are in Pliny, book 4, chapter 18, and in Pomponius Mela; Strabo and Ptolemy have Οσισμιοι [Osismioi]; in the Commentary on the Gallic War they are called Osismii, in a more corrupt form. There is a Civitas Osismiorum in the Notitia Provinciarum. Pytheas names the Timiae [Τιμίας] and assigns them a cape, ἀκρωτήριον ἱκανὸν [akrōtērion hikanon], a fairly long promontory. Some place them where the city of the Tricorienses is today, commonly called Trégunc or Landrigniér. The Diablintes (for so, as Joseph Scaliger, Fulvius Ursinus and others think, not Iablintres, is the correct spelling according to the manuscripts) are in Caesar, who calls them Diablinti, and in Pliny; but in Ptolemy they are Διαβλίντες [Diablintes], less accurately. The Notitia Provinciarum has Civitas Diablintum, that is, Carifes; what this means I do not understand. The Diablintes were once, as some think, where Laval now is. Goropius Becanus in his Origines Antwerpianae removes them far from Britain and makes them a district of Brabant, commonly called Linter, on the river Geta; I do not intend to refute him here. In the Life of S. Domnolus, bishop of the Cenomani, these words are read: "the estate of Tridenta, situated in the district of the Diablintes." What these words mean I still do not grasp. Vigenère thinks the Ambibari of Caesar were where Ambie now is, near Mont Saint-Michel. The Οὐινελοι [Ouinelloi] of Ptolemy, the Venelli of Pliny, are the Vinelli in the Commentaries on the Gallic War; Οὐισσίοι [Ouissioi] in Dio, less correctly. Most place them where the town of Laval now is, famous for its title as a county. The Ambiliates (some manuscripts prefer Ambialites) are in Caesar; today, with a scarcely different name, the Lamballois. Others think they lived where the village of Amblie in Normandy now is, not far from Bayeux. Some interpret the Βιδουκισιοι [Biducisioi] of Ptolemy as the people of Briec, S. Brieuc. The Lemovices: others in Caesar are thought to be the Lemovices of Aquitaine, the Leonenses (S. Pol de Léon). I do not affirm anything rashly on these matters, as on many others. In this district there are also, in Ptolemy, the Ἀρβιοι [Arbioi], and in Caesar the Cadetes; I have nothing certain to say about the former. The latter Fulvius Ursinus rejects, substituting the Caletes, who were in Normandy. Some, however, dare to interpret Cadetes as Château-Briant, commonly Chasteau Briant, which belongs to the Montmorencys in Upper Brittany.

units.la: Britannia hodie duplex est: Superior & Inferior. Superior. La Haulte Bretaigne, pars Orientalior ab Inferiore separatur Linea, ex Vico ducta, qui (inter Guingantum, & Briocense Opidum) vulgo dicitur Chasteau-Andron, cujusque Incolarum pars Britannice, pars Francice loquuntur: porrectaque porro inter Quintinum & Corlayum versus extremitatem Sinus Venetensis ad Flumen usque Vilanium; sic tamen, ut Fanum S. Ioannis, S. Jean, in Inferiore relinquatur Britannia. Metropolis est Vrbs Nannetica. Sic Gregorius Turonensis indigetar, quæ vulgo Nantes. Ptolemæo Κοσδαυσοι Ναννετυμ, ut censent Iosephus Scaliger suis ad me Litteris, Cognatus, & alij. Secus videtur Abrahamo Ortelio, qui Corbilonem Strabonis ex Polybio hoc loco mavult collocare. Sedes fuit olim Britanniæ Ducum; Comitatus habens Titulum, Ducisque Primogenito adscribi solita: ad Ligerim duosque alios Fluviolos sita loco peropportuno, haud procul mari. Episcopalis Statio, ut & quatuor quæ sequuntur. Vrbs Redonica nuncupatur Gregorio Turonensi, quæ vernacule Renes. Κορδατς Redonum Ptolemæo; Condate, Antonino & Itinerariæ Peutingeri Tabulæ, ut censent Iosephus Scaliger, Villanovanus, & alij. Dolum, Opidum nunc, olim Arx: vulgo Dol vel Doul. Dolenfis Vici, Biturigum terminii, meminit Gregorius Turonensis in vita S. Lusoris, qui apud eumdem lib. ii. Historiar. poni videtur in Britannia. Addit Cœnalis Neodunum etiam quondam appellatum: Νεοδυνσον Ptolemæus habet Aulirciorum Diablintarum. Præsules Dolenses, ut alibi a me dictum, jus habent Pallij, eamque ob causam locum inter Archiepiscopos. Fanum Brioecense, vulgo S. Brieu, opidum non ignobile. Rupes ibi excelsa tutam præbet Navibus Stationem: in ea Arx Vrbi protegendæ excitata. Fanum S. Machlovij, vernacule S. Malo. Alesum esse putatur in Libro Notitiarum, Nervicani Littoris. Aletham Vrbem Galliæ maritimam, quam Rinctus Fluvius adluit, haud procul Aaronis Insula, describit Surius ex Gemblacensi in S. Machlovij, Primi hujus opidi Præsulis, Vita. Patria Iacobi Cartieri, insignis Navarchæ, qui auspiciis Regis Francisci I. Canadam invenit, aliasque Terras in Mari, quod Septemtrionem versus est, litas. In hujus Diœcesi Abbatiæ sunt opulentæ, Belli-Locu, Montis-fortis, Preaux. Dinan, opidum pulchritudinis eximiæ, in deliciis aliquando Britanniæ Ducibus. Riculx ad Vilanium Flumen. Nescio an apud Ptolemæum sit Δαμόριγον: quod tamen Cœnali & Villanovano Venetensis est Vrbs. Vannes vulgo, in Inferiore Britannia: Dariortum vitiose scribitur in Itineraria Peutingeri Tabula. Chasteau-Briant, opidum Arce præditum, Limitaneum inter Britannos Armoricos & Andegavenses; Proceribus parens Mommorancijs. Lamballum, Lamballe vulgo; à quo Ditio Lamballoia; Sedes olim fortean Ambiliatum, ut antea dixi. Officinæ hic Membranarum, quæ Chartæ Pergamenæ nominantur. Vitray, opidum, quod inter & Vicum, qui vulgo Croisille, rivulus est, qui Britannos ab Cenomanis hic sejungit: quin & ea parte, haud procul Herucio Burgo, Vimus visitur, eumdem statuens terminum. Sunt & Britanniæ Superioris alia opida Lugon, ubi Arces visuntur insignis Antiquitatis; S. Aulbin de Cermier, in cujus Territorio committum scribitur Prælium, quod in Francorum Historijs La Bataille S. Aulbin: Item Mont-contour, Plerel, Iocelin, Malestroit, Pontigny, S. Iulian; Encenis denique, extremum versus Pictones, sub quo comprehendi solent Diuones, quæ vulgo Chiffonneii, Raiz, & alix.
units.tr: Brittany today is twofold: Upper and Lower. Upper Brittany, La Haute Bretagne: its eastern part is separated from the lower by a line drawn from the village which (between Guingamp and the town of Bréhat) is commonly called Château-Andron, whose inhabitants speak partly Breton and partly French; and this line runs on between Quintin and Corlay towards the end of the Gulf of Vannes, as far as the river Vilaine; yet in such a way that the shrine of S. John, S. Jean, is left in Lower Brittany. The metropolis is the city of Nannetica. So Gregory of Tours calls it, and it is commonly Nantes. In Ptolemy it is Κοσδαυσοι Ναννετυμ [Kosdausoi Nannetum], which Joseph Scaliger, in his letters to me, and others think is a kindred name. Abraham Ortelius thinks otherwise, preferring to place Strabo's Corbilo here, from Polybius. It was formerly the seat of the Dukes of Brittany; it has a county title, which was usually given to the duke's firstborn; it lies on the Loire and two other small rivers, in a very suitable spot not far from the sea. It is an episcopal see, as are the four that follow. The city of Redonica is called so by Gregory of Tours, which in the vernacular is Rennes. Κορδατς [Kordats] of the Redones in Ptolemy; Condate in Antoninus and in the Peutinger Table, as Joseph Scaliger, Villanovanus and others think. Dolum, now a town, formerly a fortress: commonly Dol or Doul. Gregory of Tours mentions the Dolenses vicus, a boundary of the Bituriges, in the Life of S. Lusorius, who in the second book of his Histories seems to be placed in Brittany. Cenalis adds that it was once also called Neodunum; Ptolemy has Νεοδυνσον [Neodunson] of the Aulercii Diablintes. The bishops of Dol, as I have said elsewhere, have the right of the pallium, and for this reason a place among the archbishops. Fanum Brioecense, commonly S. Brieuc, a not ignoble town. A high cliff there provides a safe anchorage for ships; on it a citadel was raised to protect the city. Fanum S. Machlovii, in the vernacular S. Malo. Alesum is thought to be in the Book of Notitiae, of the Nervican shore. Surius, from Gembloux on the Life of S. Malo, the first bishop of this town, describes Aletham, a maritime city of Gaul, washed by the river Rance, not far from the island of Aaron. The birthplace of Jacques Cartier, the famous navigator, who under the auspices of King Francis I discovered Canada and other lands on the sea that lies to the north. In this diocese there are wealthy abbeys: Beaulieu, Montfort, Préaux. Dinan, a town of exceptional beauty, at one time a favourite of the Dukes of Brittany. Riculx on the river Vilaine. I do not know whether Δαμόριγον [Damorigon] in Ptolemy is this place, though Cenalis and Villanovanus take it to be the city of Vannes. Vannes in common speech, in Lower Brittany; Dariortum is wrongly written in the Peutinger Table. Château-Briant, a town with a citadel, on the border between the Armorican Britons and the Andegavi; it gave its name to the Montmorencys, the nobles. Lamballum, Lamballe in common speech, from which the district is called Lamballoia; perhaps formerly the seat of the Ambiliates, as I said before. Here are workshops for membranes, which are called parchment paper. Vitray, a town; between it and the village, commonly Croisille, there is a stream which here separates the Britons from the Cenomani; and indeed in that part, not far from the town of Hervé, the Vilaine is seen, marking the same boundary. There are also other towns of Upper Brittany: Lugon, where citadels of remarkable antiquity are seen; S. Aubin de Cormier, in whose territory the battle is written as having been fought, which in the histories of the French is La Bataille S. Aubin; likewise Montcontour, Plérel, Josselin, Malestroit, Pontivy, S. Julien; and finally Ancenis, at the extreme edge towards the Poitevins, under which are usually included the Diablintes, commonly Châteaufonneau, Rais, and others.

units.la: Inferior, La Basse Bretaigne, porrigit se ab communibus cum Superiore Limitibus in Occidentem versus Oceanum, qui tria ejus Latera late pulsat. Vrbes in ea & opida celebriora: Venetis ab Cæsare lib. iii de Bello Gallico cum primis nobilitata, Venetorum Metropolis & Caput facile Armoricarum: Vannes hodie. Arcem habet, quæ vulgo L'Hermine, Palatium quondam Ducum Britanniæ. Adhuc quæro, an Arci ab Insignibus, an vero his ab Arce nomen & ratio. Argutantur hic nonnulli. Insignia certe, quorum nunc in Britannia usus, Caudæ sunt Mustellarum, quæ vulgo Hermelina, in Area candida. S. Paulli Fanum, S. Paul de Leon, Ptolemæi putatur esse Σταλιονας. Portus: de quo antea dixi. In Latinis Ptolemæi exemplaribus Salocanus legitur, vitiose, quod videre nolens Cœnalis Portui nomen inditum scribit ab Sale conficiendo. In hujus Diœcesi Abbatiæ sunt: Gerber des Religieux, S. Mathurin du sin de terre, S. Marie de Gerler. Triconense Opidum, vulgo Triguier, Landtriguier, insignem habens Portum. Blabia in Libro Notitiarum Armoricani vel Nervicani opidum dicitur, quod nostro tempore Blavet, ad Maris Sinum, in quem committi se infundunt hinc inde duo Fluvij; quorum qui Vulturnum versus, opido est cognominis; qui Caurum spectat, Ella vocatur. Portum, omnium hac Franciæ parte princi-
units.tr: Inferior, La Basse Bretaigne, extends from the boundaries it shares with Superior westward to the ocean, which beats hard against its three sides. Its more famous cities and towns are these. Venetis, which Caesar in Book 3 of the Gallic War makes especially famous, was the metropolis and chief city of the Veneti, easily the leading city of the Armoricae; today it is Vannes. It has a citadel, commonly called L'Hermine, once the palace of the Dukes of Brittany. I still ask whether the citadel takes its name from the insignia, or the insignia from the citadel. Some people argue about this here. The insignia now used in Brittany are certainly the tails of Hermelina (ermines), that is, of weasels, set on a white field. S. Paulli Fanum (S. Paul de Leon) is thought to be Ptolemy's Σταλιονας [Stalionas]. The port I spoke of earlier is Salocanus in the Latin copies of Ptolemy, which is a mistake; someone who did not want to see it wrote that the name was given to the port of Cœnalis from Sale, salt, because salt was made there. In this diocese there are the abbeys of Gerber des Religieux, S. Mathurin du sin de terre, and S. Marie de Gerler. The town of Triconense, commonly Triguier or Landtriguier, has a notable port. Blabia is called a town in the Book of Notices of the Armoricans or Nervicans; in our time it is Blavet, on the bay of the sea into which two rivers flow from either side. The one that faces south-east gives its name to the town; the one that faces north-west is called Ella.

units.la: {y} Nota: marginal notes are set in small type beside the text. principem, qui hodie Brest, Brest in Gallia Lugdunensi Ptolemaeo dici censet Iosephus Scaliger. Alias monui. Sunt qui hinc Britannia nomen derivant. Ego nec ajo, nec nego. Sunt & alia oppida, quae vulgo: Morlaix, commodissimus Anglis Portus; Guincamp, Dominos agnoscens Heredes antiquorum Comitum Stamparum, qui Domo Britannica sunt editi. Guincampi Dominum lego Petrum, Britanniae Ducem septimum, Ioannis v, Ducis quinti Filium. Dicam paulo post. Item, Q. imperiras, Conquerneaux, Quimpercorentin, S. Regnant des bois; & alia. Praeter Superiores Urbes & oppida, commodissimos etiam Portus praestant Aimerum, haud procul Venetia; Hanebontum, Pontscorot, ubi magna Ostrearum copia legitur.
units.tr: Joseph Scaliger thinks that the chief port of all in this part of France, which today is Brest, is the one Ptolemy calls Brest in Gallia Lugdunensis. I have noted this elsewhere. Some derive the name Britannia from it. I neither affirm nor deny. There are also other towns, commonly called Morlaix, a very convenient port for the English; Guincamp, which acknowledges as lords the heirs of the ancient Counts of Stampes, who were descended from the British house. I read the lord of Guincamp as Peter, the seventh Duke of Brittany, son of John V, the fifth Duke. I shall say more about this shortly. Likewise Q. imperiras, Conquerneaux, Quimpercorentin, S. Regnant des bois, and others. Besides the towns and cities named above, the most convenient ports are Aimerum, not far from Venetia; Hanebontum; and Pontscorot, where a great abundance of oysters is found.

units.la: Britannia, ut concludam, Comitatus olim titulo ornata, Ducatus dignitatem adsequuta est tempore Henrici II Angliae Regis, circa annum MCLXXXIX. Comitum Ducumque haec traditur series:
units.tr: To conclude about Brittany: it was once adorned with the title of a county, and attained the dignity of a duchy in the time of Henry II, King of England, around the year 1189. The following is handed down as the succession of its counts and dukes.

units.la: Comites Daciaeque Britanniae.
units.tr: The Counts and Dukes of Lower Brittany.

units.la: Isabella, tenerm etate exlinēta. Anna Britannica, deficiente Stirpe masculā. Dux Britanniæ v. Desponsata primum Richardo Vvalliæ Principi, Eduardi iv Regis Angliæ Filio, inde autem Maximiliano i, Cæsari Augusto, nuptā tandem Karolo viii, eoque mortuo, Ludovico xii Galliarum Regibus: sicque Ducatus Britanniæ Regno conexus fuit.
units.tr: Isabella, who died in tender infancy. Anne of Brittany, when the male line failed; she was Duchess of Brittany. She was first betrothed to Richard, Prince of Wales, son of Edward IV, King of England; then to Maximilian I, Caesar Augustus; at last she was married to Charles VIII, and after his death to Louis XII, Kings of the French. Thus the Duchy of Brittany was joined to the Kingdom.

units.la: Inlustres in Britannia Familiæ sunt Montfort Comitatus, Rohan Vicecomitatus, Pontbieuvra, Rieux, Rau, Blossac, Avaulgour, Clifson, Leon, Vitre, Foulgeres, Ancenis, Grello, & aliæ, quarum quædam ab ipsis Britanniæ Ducibus, ut ex ipsorum patet Genealogia, originem ducunt.
units.tr: The illustrious families in Brittany are the County of Montfort, the Viscounty of Rohan, Pontbieuvra, Rieux, Rau, Blossac, Avaulgour, Clifson, Leon, Vitre, Foulgeres, Ancenis, Grello, and others, some of which, as their genealogy shows, trace their origin to the Dukes of Brittany themselves.

units.la: CAP. XXXII.
units.tr: CAP. XXXII.

units.la: Lemovicium.
units.tr: Lemovicium.

units.la: Sequuntur inter Parlamenta, quæ Accesoria dixi, ad ripam Ligeris sinistram Burdigalense, & Tolosanum. Hæc duo coactus sui in Distributione mea conjungere, quod suprema iura exerceant Singula, nunc integre & separatim, nunc vero mistim in varias, quæ cuique sunt adsignatæ, Veteris Aquitaniæ Narbonensisque Galliæ Provincias. Integre, Burdigalensi quidem subsunt Lemovicium, Petrocorium, Guienna: Tolosano autem Cadurcium, Rutenium & Languedokum: Mistim, perque Partes & quasi Sectiones utrique obtemperat Vasconia. Singulas ordine expediam. Principis est hic loci Lemovicium.
units.tr: Next, among the Parlements that I called subordinate, on the left bank of the Loire, come Bordeaux and Toulouse. In my division I was forced to join these two, because each exercises supreme jurisdiction, sometimes wholly and separately, sometimes mixed, over the various provinces assigned to each, namely Old Aquitaine and Narbonese Gaul. Wholly, Bordeaux has under it Limoges, Périgord and Guyenne; under Toulouse are Cahors, Rodez and Languedoc. Mixed, and through parts and as it were sections, Gascony obeys both. I shall deal with each in order. Here the first is Limoges.

units.la: Lemovicio, Pais ou Comté de Limosin, ad Septemtrionem & Aquilonem adjacent Bituricenses; ad Ortum Borbonij; ad Meridiem & Vulturnum Arvernì; ad Africum & Occidentem Petrocorij: ad Caurum denique Pictones. Vlmus visitur, grandioris ætatis, inter Vicum, cui ab Nova Domo nomen, La Maison neuve, & Argentonium, Bituricense opidum, Septemtrionem versus, quæ quatuor Ditionum regit Fines, Bituricensium, Borboniorum, Arvernorum & Lemovicum; adeo ut aliquando quatuor horum Populorum Principes dicantur hic sermones inter se conseruisse, quique in suo Territorio. Terra non eiusdem ubique indolis: universim sterilior; producens tamen omnis generis fruges, cum primis Siliginem, Hordeum, Panicum; Castaneas item, Rapas, Vinum, sed ignobilius, quod tamen in Inferiore Lemovicio generosius. Incolæ Cibi Potusque sunt ἀπλῶς parcissimi, parvo contenti, Lautitiarumque osores; Panis tamen helluones, ut Proverbio locum dederint: Vini usum Pagi sere ignorant. Industrij sunt, ingeniosi, cauti catique, non præcipræcipites; egregie sibi suisque rebus consulentes. Vulgus tenax, domique sordidius: Nobilitas magnifica, altioris animi, liberalis. Ad provectissimam plerique perveniunt ætatem. Sunt qui in Familia sua vident Abnepotes. Dicuntur Cognati inter se, ne soluti quidem per Pontificem ab Iure communi, Matrimonia contrahere; Bonaque non partiri. Scribit Belleforestius vidisse se Familias, in quibus centum Cognatione per Nuptias juncti simul vivebant; ut Collegia quædam agnoscere quis posset.
units.tr: Limoges, the pays or county of Limousin: on the north and northeast it borders the Bituriges; on the east, the Bourbonnais; on the south and southeast, the Arverni; on the southwest and west, the Périgordins; and finally on the northwest, the Poitevins. There is an elm, of great age, between the village called La Maison Neuve and Argenton, a town of the Bituriges, toward the north, which marks the boundary of four jurisdictions: those of the Bituriges, the Bourbonnais, the Arverni and the Lemovices. So much so that the rulers of these four peoples are said at times to have held talks here with one another, each in his own territory. The land is not of the same character everywhere; on the whole it is rather barren, yet it produces every kind of crop, especially rye, barley and millet, also chestnuts, turnips and wine, though the wine is poor, although in Lower Limousin it is finer. The inhabitants are utterly frugal in food and drink, content with little, and haters of luxury; yet they are gluttons for bread, so that they have given cause for the proverb. The country folk are almost ignorant of the use of wine. They are industrious, clever, wary and cautious, not rash, and remarkably careful of themselves and their affairs. The common people are tight-fisted and rather squalid at home; the nobility is magnificent, high-minded and generous. Most of them reach a very advanced age; some see great-great-grandchildren in their family. They are said to be so closely related to one another that, even when released by the Pope from the common law, they do not contract marriages, nor do they divide their goods. Belleforest writes that he saw families in which a hundred kinsmen, joined by marriage, lived together at one time, so that one could recognise them as a sort of college.

units.la: Lemovices (sic enim Veteres Incolas nominat Plinius, qui Αιμοβικες Straboni; Ptolemæo Αιμονικες, forte Αιμοσικες, hodie Limosins; Notitiæ Provinciarum Galliæ Civitas Limovicum; aliis interim, quos Capite præcedente ex Cæsare laudavi, censendis) quidam Indigenas esse volunt & Aborigines; eorumque Conditorem faciunt Lemovicem, ab Gomoritis oriundum. Subjugarunt eos aliquando Gothi cum tota Aquitania. Scribuntur inde Franci, Gothis exturbatis, Lemovicibus dedisse Gubernatores. Leguntur & constituti ipsis Comites & Duces; hi quidem gerendo Bello, illi vero Iustitiæ administrandæ.
units.tr: The Lemovices (for so Pliny names the ancient inhabitants, whom Strabo calls Ailobikes [Αιμοβικες], Ptolemy Ailonikes [Αιμονικες], perhaps Aimosikes [Αιμοσικες], and who are today the Limousins; the Notitia of the Provinces of Gaul calls them the State of the Lemovices; and to be counted among others whom I cited from Caesar in the preceding chapter) are held by some to be natives and aborigines, and they make Lemovex, sprung from the Gomorites, their founder. At one time the Goths subdued them together with all Aquitaine. Then it is written that the Franks, after expelling the Goths, gave governors to the Lemovices. Counts and dukes are also read as having been appointed for them: the former for conducting war, the latter for administering justice.

units.la: Lemovicium plerique duplex statuunt, Superius & Inferius. Superius (proprie Limosin) Inferiore planius. Metropolin habet Lemovicum. Sic A. Hirtio vocari censent multi lib. viii. de Bello Gallico, quæ hodie Limoges. Limonum legit Fulvius Ursinus, fretus Veterum Codicum auctoritate. Ratiasum Ptolemæo dicitur in Gallia Aquitanica, ut ad me scribens arbitratur Iosephus Scaliger; consentiente ipsi Villanova-no. Ratiastum tamen Ratz esse putat Bertrandus, ob similitudinem nominis. Quidquid sit, Urbs est ad Vigennam, partim in Valle, partim in Monticuli sita fastigio Arce Murisque bene munita, ipsissima Diligentiæ Officina, Desidiæ Ergastulum. Castitas hic Feminis in pretio, & Misericordia. Episcopatus gaudet dignitate. Alia hic Opida, quæ vernacule La Souburraine, Le Buisson, Barat, Dorat, Confoulat, & cetera, brevitati studens prætereo. Inter ea Chassufio famam conciliant annuæ Pecudum Equorumque Nundinæ, D. Georgij Festo. Sunt & hic Abbatiæ; inter quas Grandimons, caput Ordinis Grandimontensis; item Fanum D. Leonardi, S. Lenard, magni nominis, inter Lemovicum & Felletinum. Familiæ hic illustres sunt, quæ vulgo Pierre-Buffiere, Chasteau-neuf, Carsie, quæ Vicecomitatus honore fulget, Roche-Chouart, cui inter antiquissimas Aquitaniæ locus; Maygnac, & alias.
units.tr: Most authorities hold that Limousin is twofold, Upper and Lower. Upper (properly Limousin) is flatter than the Lower. It has Limoges as its metropolis. Many think it is called Lemovicum in Book 8 of Hirtius's Gallic War, which is today Limoges. Fulvius Ursinus reads Limonum, relying on the authority of old manuscripts. By Ptolemy it is said to be Ratiasum in Aquitanian Gaul, as Joseph Scaliger, writing to me, thinks, with the agreement of Villanovanus. Bertrand, however, thinks that Ratiastum is Ratz, because of the similarity of the name. Whatever the case, the city lies on the Vienne, partly in a valley and partly on the summit of a little hill, well fortified with citadel and walls; it is the very workshop of diligence and the prison of idleness. Chastity and mercy are held in high esteem here among women. The bishopric enjoys dignity. Other towns here, which in the vernacular are called La Souterraine, Le Buisson, Barat, Dorat, Confolens and the rest, I pass over, aiming at brevity. Among them, Chasseneuil wins fame by its annual fairs of cattle and horses, held on the feast of St. George. There are also abbeys here; among them Grandmont, the head of the Order of Grandmont; likewise the shrine of St. Léonard, St. Lenard, of great renown, between Limoges and Felletin. The illustrious families here are those commonly called Pierre-Buffière, Châteauneuf, Carsie, which shines with the honour of a viscounty, Roche-Chouart, which has a place among the most ancient in Aquitaine, Maignac, and others.

units.la: Inferius Superiore montosius: dicitur proprie La Marche de Limosin; limitaneum Arvernis & Petrocorijs. Primaria ibi Urbs Tutela, Tulle; in aspero montosoque collocata Territorio: Sedes non Baillivatus solum, sed & Episcopatus novi, ex Monasterio deminuti, ut antea dixi de Lemovicensi. Tutelensem Latini nominant. Est ibidem Vsarcha, Vsarche, opidum non inamœnum, grati aeris, ad Flumen Vezeram: quod expugnari non posse Fama jactitat. Proverbium sane ferrur: Cui Vsarche est Domus, Arcem eam possidere in Lemovicum ditione. Non silent Virtutem Civium Historiæ, quibus narrantur Anglis, per totam Aquitaniam Triumphos agentibus, restitisse; suoque Principi Francorum Regi fideles summa constantia perstitisse. Briva, opidum in læta fertilique planicie situm, Silvis obsitum, Vinctis non destitutum. Sedes est Senefchalli. Quondam Ditionis fuisse perhibetur Petrocoriorum; sed, volente Karolo VI Francorum Rege, Lemovicibus accessisse. Sunt & alia: Treignacum, Donzenacum, Allassacum, Bellus-Locus, Meissacum, Vssetum, Belle-Montium. Nobilitant & hanc Limogiæ partem Nobiles Familiæ, Pampadeura, Aumontia, Roffignaca, San-Iala, & aliæ Infinitæ.
units.tr: Lower Limousin is more mountainous than the Upper; it is properly called La Marche de Limousin, and borders the Arverni and the Périgordins. The chief city there is Tulle, Tutela, set in a rough and mountainous territory; it is the seat not only of a bailiwick but also of a bishopric, newly diminished from the monastery, as I said earlier of Limoges. The Latins call it Tutelensis. In the same region is Uzerche, Usarcha, Usarche, a not unpleasant town of pleasant air, on the river Vézère, which rumour boasts cannot be taken by assault. There is indeed a proverb: Whoever has Uzerche as his home, let him hold that citadel in the dominion of Limousin. Nor do the histories remain silent about the courage of its citizens, who, when the English were triumphing through all Aquitaine, are said to have resisted them, and who remained most steadfastly faithful to their prince, the King of the Franks. Brive, a town set in a pleasant and fertile plain, covered with woods and not lacking vineyards, is the seat of a seneschal. It is said to have once belonged to the territory of the Périgordins, but, at the wish of Charles VI, King of the Franks, it was joined to the Limousins. There are others too: Treignac, Donzenac, Allassac, Beaulieu, Meyssac, Ussel, Beaumont. This part of Limousin is also ennobled by noble families: Pompadour, Aubusson, Rochefort, Saint-Yrieix, and countless others.

units.la: LEMOVICIO succedit in mea Methodo PETROCORIVM; Civitas Petragoriarum in Notitia Provinciarum Galliæ; vulgo Le Pais de Perigord. Conjacent illi, qua Septemtrio est, Lemovicium; qua Occidens, Santonia; ad Meridiem Vasconum gentes occurrunt; ad Ortum Cadurces & Arverni. Regio Lapidosa, Montosa, Silvosa; Castanearum valde ferax; Vinis beata, pro locorum genio varij generis: Aëre fruens sereno salubrique rarioribus obnoxia est Morbis: Herbariæ Rei studiosis commoditissima, quod Simplicium ad luxuriem sit fertilis: Argenti-fodinis abundat: Fontibus scatet, quorum non pauci deprehenduntur Medici, quod Venas permeent sulphureas.
units.tr: After Lemovicium, in my method, comes PETROCORIUM, the city of the Petragorians, listed in the Notitia of the provinces of Gaul, and today called Le Pais de Perigord. It is bounded on the north by Lemovicium, on the west by Santonia, on the south by the peoples of the Vascones, and on the east by the Cadurci and the Arverni. The region is stony, mountainous and wooded, and very fertile in chestnuts. It is blessed with wines of various kinds according to the nature of the locality. It enjoys a clear and healthy air and is subject to few diseases. It is very convenient for those who study herbs, since it abounds in simples. It is rich in silver mines and full of springs, many of which are found to be medicinal because they pass through veins of sulphur.

units.la: Incolæ (quos Petrocorios Cæsar, Petrogoros Plinius, Petrogorios Sidonius lib. vii. Epist. v 1, Vesunnicos ab Metropoli Vesunna idem lib. viii. Epist. x 1. appellat) sunt alacres, fani, longævi, paucis contenti, aptabiles, ad omnes honestas Actiones, Literas, Arma, Scientias Mechanicas nimis quam idonei. Nobilitas antiqua, facilis, humana, Progenitores adferens sibi Francos, qui primi Gallias irruperunt. Feminæ forma sunt præstantes; non luxui deditæ, modestæ probæque Matres-familias, omnem avorsantes Desidiam.
units.tr: The inhabitants (whom Caesar calls Petrocorii, Pliny Petrogoros, Sidonius Petrogorios in book 7, letter 5, and who are named Vesunnici after their metropolis Vesunna by the same author in book 8, letter 10) are lively, healthy and long-lived, content with little, adaptable, and very well suited to all honourable pursuits: letters, arms and the mechanical arts. Their nobility is ancient, affable and courteous, and they trace their ancestry to the Franks, who first broke into Gaul. The women are outstanding in beauty; they are not given to luxury, but are modest and upright mothers of families, shunning all idleness.

units.la: . Metropolis vulgo Perigeux, quæ Ptolemæo lib. ii. cap. vii. Οὐέσοννα Petrocorum; Vesuna Antonino; Vesonna Tabulæ Itinerariæ: Petrogoricum Aimoino: Latine scribentibus hodie Perigordum, & Perigurd. Vesuna etiam meminit Inscriptio, quæ ibi extat:
units.tr: Metropolis, commonly called Perigeux, which Ptolemy in book 2, chapter 7 calls Ouesonna of the Petrocorii [Οὐέσοννα], Vesuna in Antoninus, Vesonna in the Itinerary Table, Petrogoricum in Aimoin, and by Latin writers today Perigordum and Perigurd. An inscription still standing there also mentions Vesuna:

units.la: TVTELÆ AVG VESVNNÆ SECVNDVS SOTTID. S. D
units.tr: TUTELAE AUG. VESUNNAE SECUNDUS. SOTTID. S. D.

units.la: Vesuam sane quondam fuisse dictam, adeo verum est, ut quum Urbs in duo divisa sit hodie opida, Vetus & Novum; Illud nunc quoque temporis dicatur Vesuna priscâ voce, populariter Vesune; eamdem insuper appellationem etiam servante antiquissima ibi Turre, quæ satis integra conspicitur. Sita est autem in planicie, haud asperis levisque adlurgentibus undique circumdata Montibus, qui Vini generosissimi feraces. Ad partem Urbis Septemtrionalem vastæ visuntur Ruinæ Amphitheatri; vulgo Les Rolphies dicuntur. Vocant etiam La Cacarota, cum Accentu in ultima, qui numerum denotat Pluralem. Longitudo protenditur in Orgyias xxx; Latitudo fere in xx. Ejusdem operis est & structuræ, cujus Turris Vesuna. In Interioribus Cavæ monstrantur, quibus Ferae edendo Muneri includebantur. Haud procul Urbe Fontes sunt acidi, Alumen sapientes. Est autem Episcopalis hæc Urbs; quemadmodum & Sarlatum vulgo Sarlat, cujus Præsulatus Petrocoriensi est detractus, ut antea dixi. Bregeratum Tribunali superbit regio. Riberacum opidum, Vicecomitatus Titulo clarum. Nontronum Baronatus dignitate nobilitatum; Arcem habens inexpugnabilem. Lunellum in Rupe situm ad Duranium; cujus Dynastæ ex illustri gente Turonia. Bironium opidum limitaneum inter Petrocorios & Aginnenses. Brathommae opidulum, Abbatiam prædivitem; præter quam sunt & aliæ multæ: Marsacum Pagus, Fontem, qui Maris instar fluit & refluit: Rupes denique opidum, vulgo la Roche, Cryptam habet largam & speciosam, ex qua Terra ecfoditur subrubra, ejusdem coloris virtutisque, cujus Bolus, quam Armeniam Medici vocant. Haud procul opido, quod vulgo Atraumont, Crypta monstratur, quæ Incolis Le Cluzeau. Ingressi mira solent narrare: Protendi eam sub terra ad v aut vi milliaria; Aulas ibi esse pulcherrimas & Cubicula vermiculato strata lapide; Altaria item, & multis in locis Picturas; Vestigia quoque omnis generis Pecudum apparere: Fontes item & Fluvios inesse, eorum unum centum & amplius pedes largum rapide fluere, cavum admodum & profunditatis admirandæ, cum neminem audere transmittere, licet ultra longe lateque Terra pateat. Cryptam nemo subit, nisi pluribus concomitatus, magnoque Facium accensarum & Laternarum numero prælucente, cibisque coctis adsumptis. Cryptæ non aliud perhibetur Lumen, quam quod ex Aditu.
units.tr: That Vesua was indeed once its name is so certain that, although the city is now divided into two towns, Old and New, the former is still called Vesuna in the ancient tongue, popularly Vesune; and the most ancient tower there, which can still be seen in fairly good condition, keeps the same name. It lies on a plain, surrounded on all sides by hills, neither rough nor steep, which bear the most generous wines. On the northern side of the city can be seen the vast ruins of an amphitheatre, which are commonly called Les Rolphies. They also call it La Cacarota, with the accent on the last syllable, which marks the plural number. Its length extends to 30 orgyiae, its breadth to about 20. It is of the same construction and workmanship as the tower of Vesuna. Within are shown the cellars where wild beasts were penned in for the games. Not far from the city are acid springs, tasting of alum. This city is an episcopal see, as is Sarlat, commonly called Sarlat, whose bishopric was taken from Périgueux, as I said before. Bergerac prides itself on a royal court of justice. Ribérac is a town famed for its viscounty title. Nontron is ennobled by the dignity of a barony and has a fortress that cannot be taken. Lunel is set on a rock by the Dordogne; its lords come from the noble family of Turenne. Bironne is a border town between the Périgordins and the Agenais. Brantôme is a small town with a very rich abbey; besides this there are many others. Marsac is a village with a spring that ebbs and flows like the sea. Lastly, the town of Roche, commonly called La Roche, has a large and handsome cave, from which is dug a reddish earth of the same colour and virtue as bole, which the physicians call Armenian. Not far from the town commonly called Atramont is shown a cave, which the inhabitants call Le Cluzeau. Those who have entered it are wont to tell wonderful things: that it stretches underground for five or six miles; that there are most beautiful halls and chambers paved with variegated stone; altars likewise, and paintings in many places; that traces of every kind of cattle appear; and that springs and rivers flow within, one of which runs swiftly, more than a hundred feet wide, very deep and of marvellous depth, so that no one dares to cross it, though the land stretches far and wide beyond. No one enters the cave unless accompanied by several people, with a great number of lit torches and lanterns to light the way, and after taking cooked food. It is said that the cave has no other light than that which comes from the entrance.
