units.la: POST Petrocorium pandit mea Methodus Guiennam: GVIENNA depravatum nomen est ex Aquitania, ut res ipsa loquitur. Quis Aquitania quomdam, & tempore Cæsaris & sub Octaviano Augusto, fuerint Fines, dictum est supra Capite xix. Angustioribus determinari cœpit Limitibus, ex quo tempore Reges Angliæ, per Affinitatem cum Francorum Monarchis contractam, ejus fuerunt Domini. Quum Eduardus iii nomine, Aquitania Homagium, ut usitata notaque utar voce, faceret Regi Franciæ, has Præfecturas sive Senescballias nominatim comprehenditse legitur: citra Garumnam quidem Pictonum, amplissimam Regionem; Xantonium, Engolismenses, Lemovicum, Petrocorium, Agennenses, Cadurcium & Rutenenses; ultra vero Garumnam, totam Novem populaniam vel Vasconiam, præter Benearnum, quod absoluti semper fuit imperij. Itaque omnium illorum Tractuum nomine Rex, aut Primogenitus Angliæ (Prince des Galles dictus) fidem clientelarem pollicebantur Regi Franciæ: Comites autem Armaniacus, Bigorrensis, Foxensis, & alij faciebant ipsi Anglo Homagium, non Regi Franciæ. Hæc latissima, amplissima & prædivés Regio nomine Guienna censebatur usque ad Regnum Ludovici xi. Hic quum Fratri Karolo attributisset Ducatum Aquitaniæ, ipsiqúe quinque promisisset Senescballias, ex una Burdigalensi tres fecit, Burdigalensem, quæ unam tantum Diœcesin complectitur, Engdig. I m ipsam: Vasatensem; in qua duæ Diœceses, nempe Adurensis & ipsa Vasatensis: Tertiam Lapurdensem, in qua itidem duæ Diœceses, Aquæ Tarbellicæ & Lapurdensium Civitas sive Bayona; Quartam Senescballiam addens Xantonium. Ab eo tempore Aquitania vel Guienna vocari cœpit totum illud, quod quatuor tantum indicatas à me continet Senescballias. Sed Regum est mutare Terminos Provinciarum, non memoriam rerum. Nam Hactenus Nitobriges (seule d'Agennois) & omnes reliquæ Senescballiæ vocant se Aquitanos vel Guienenses; atque adeo Senescballus Burdigalensis dicitur Magnus Senescballus, non quidem, quod hodie talis sit (est enim minimus omnium) sed quod Burdigalensis Senescballia quinque olim Diœcesibus finiretur. Nam eo nomine Magnus, ut ie vera erat, olim appellatus, hodie, Ditione licet imminuta, nomen integrum retinet. Quin etiam quidquid ad Burdigalam solam pertinet, id non Burdigalense hodie nuncupatur sed Aquitanum vel Guiennense; & Curia Minor Burdigalæ, à qua Provocatio est ad Parlamentum, Curia Guienna & Iudices Guienna nominantur, non Burdigala. Hæc igitur Guienna, quæ hodie quatuor Senescballiis censetur, appellari jure merito potest Aquitania sive Guienna Ludovici ix. De Pictonio, quod in Feudo Aquitania sive Guienna comprehendit Eduardus iii, sciendum sæpe exclusum fuisse ex Aquitania, & sub Ludovico ix ejusdem finibus sæpe restitutum. Certe hodie non parva pars Pictonij dicunt se Guienna fes, ut olim erant revera. Guienna igitur Ludovici xi, quæ mihi hoc loco explicanda, versus Occidentem Sinu cognomine, impetuotis Oceani undis tumente clauditur; qua Meridies est, Montes adjacent Pyrenæi: ad Ortum, Languedokium, Cadurcium, Petrocorium, Lemovicium, alisque Regiones occurrunt; ad Septemtrionem Pictonium illi est continale. Regio est non unius passim genij: qua ad Pyrenæos vergit, quam reliqua Gallia, horrnator adiurgit, frigida & Vini interax; unde ἀσκῶλαν χωρα nominat Ausonius Epist. xv: versus Curianum Promontorium humilior est & paludosior, Inundationibusque frequenter obnoxia: in Mediterraneis cultior, variarum Rerum non prorsus parca est genitrix. Universim autem ob Locustarum Incursibus sæpenumero infestatur. Inter Burdigalam & Baionam Territorium est sterile: Landas vocant Indigenæ. Incolæ proceriores sunt reliquis Gallis; agilitate præstantes, corporis viribus pollentes; excelsi masculique Animi, liberales, hilares, subacti Ingeni; Libertatis amantes, Armorum tractandorum peritissimi. Sedes hic quondam habuerunt varij Populi, quos Aquitanos in genere Plinius vocat lib. iv. natur. hist. cap. xix; Garumnos paulo strictius, quod Garumnæ illorum multi essent adcolæ, nuncupat Cæsar lib. iii. Erant autem Tarbelli, Lapurdenses, Boi, Meduli, Bituriges Vibisci, Atrenses, Vasates, Santones. Tarbellorum nomen his locis latis satis Finibus distinitum fuisse constat. Quum enim eos Strabo lib. iv cum aliis collocet ad Pyrenen & Oceanum; Ptolemæus ii Geographicæ inter Pyrenæos ponit & Agrum Burdigalensem. Plinius in Aquitania Tarbellos Quatuor-Vignanorum cognomine celebrat. Tarbellorum memoria servari putatur hodie in Tarba, primario Bigerronum, alterius scilicet gentis, opido. Ab his Tarbella Pyrene Tibullo, ex emendatione Magni Scaligeri; Tarbellus Oceanus Ausonio in Parentalibus Carmine iv; & Tarbella Mater ibidem Carm. ii, quæ & Tarbellica eidem in Professorum Syllabo Carmine xviii: Tarbelins Fluvius Aturrus in extremo Mosella, qui per Tarbam Bigerronum, Aquas Augustas (quæ & Aquæ Tarbellicæ, hodie Acs, Tarbellorum Metropolis, ut suo loco dicam) & Baionam in Oceanum exit. Tarbellica Arma eidem Ausonio, Epistola xxiii ad Paullinum: Tarbellinus Æquor Lucano lib. i. In Tarbellis erant cum aliis Populis Lapurdenses, ut à Pyrenæis cum Ptolemæo ordiar. Horum fuisse totum illum Tractum Syrtium, quas Landes vocant, scribit ad me Iosephus Scaliger. Lapurdum etiam notum Libro Notitiarum Imperii in Provincia Novempopulana: Tribunus Cohortis Novempopulanæ Lapurdo. Sic enim legendum. Videndum & Exemplar Pactionis inter Guntramum & Childebertum Reges apud Gregorium Turonensem lib. ix. cap. xx. Hodie, Le Pais de Lapord: vel, ut aliis scribitur, Labord; aliis etiam contractius Lorda & Lourde. Lapurdensium Metropolis hodie Bayona, de qua suo loco: unde & Baionentis Episcopus, Lapurdensis dicitur in Veteribus Episcopi Chartis. Lapurdensium Locustarum meminit Sidonius lib. viii. Epist. xii, quæ ad Trigetium. Boy, qui memorantur Paullino, ad Ausonium scribenti Epist. i, Piscosque cognominanti à Picis Relinaque copia, ad ostia sunt hodieque Garumnæ Fluvii, Bates dicti, ut notat Vinetus, agrum colentes, qui vulgo Buchs. Eorum quoque mentio in Itinerario; quo ponuntur inter Loca, per quæ ab Aquis Tarbellicis Burdigalam est iter; sedecim millium passuum intervallo ab Urbe Burdigalensi: In Notitiæ Provinciarum Aquitania iii Novempopulania legitur Civitas Boatum, id est Borus, quæ nihil aliud, quam Le Pais de Buchs. Voiates pro Boates male apud Cæsarem. Coloni fortean Boy vel Boiates Boiorum, de quibus cap. xxvii. Apud Boios Sinum facit Oceanus, in quo Promontorium est, quod Caput berutum, vel, ut ipsorum lingua efferam, Cap de Buts appellatur. Ad eundem Sinum aliæ hodie nominantur nominis haud magni Gentes, quas omnes Baionam usque Boios quondam fuisse dictos, quin & Meduli ipsos Boiorum fuisse partem, facilis credo; quum verisimile sit Baionam, de qua post, à Boiis nomenclaturam habere. Nam & nunc Boiona quibusdam pronunciatur. Meduli sane, qui apud Ausonium leguntur, coluerunt quidquid Agri hodie jacet infra Burdigalam; inter mare Aquitanicum & Garumnam, Mari se miscentem; ——extremis Telluris in oris, Oceani finem juxta, Solemque cadentem,
units.tr: After Petrocorium, my method brings me to Guiennam. The name Guienna is a corruption of Aquitania, as the thing itself makes clear. What the boundaries of Aquitania were, in the time of Caesar and under Octavian Augustus, was said above in chapter xix. It began to be defined by narrower limits from the time when the kings of England, through a marriage alliance with the monarchs of France, became its lords. When Edward III did homage for Aquitania, to use the familiar and customary phrase, to the king of France, it is recorded that these provinces, or seneschalships, were named specifically: on this side of the Garonne, the very wide region of Poitou, along with Saintonge, Angoulême, Limousin, Petrocorium, Agen, Quercy and Rouergue; and beyond the Garonne, all of Novempopulania, or Gascony, except Béarn, which was always a sovereign domain. So the king of England, or his eldest son (called the Prince of Wales), pledged feudal fealty to the king of France for all those territories under one name. The counts of Armagnac, Bigorre and Foix, and others, did homage directly to the English king, not to the king of France. This widest, most ample and most fertile region was called by the name Guienna until the reign of Louis XI. When he granted the duchy of Aquitaniæ to his brother Charles and promised him five seneschalships, he made three out of the one of Burdigalensem: Bordeaux, which embraces only one diocese; Vasatensem, in which there are two dioceses, Aire and Bazas itself; and Lapurdensem, in which there are likewise two dioceses, Dax and the city of the Lapurdenses, or Bayonne. He added a fourth seneschalship, Saintonge. From that time Aquitania, or Guienna, began to be the name for the whole area that is contained in these four seneschalships I have listed. But it is for kings to change the boundaries of provinces, not to erase the memory of things. For until now the Nitobriges (the seule d'Agennois) and all the other seneschalships call themselves Aquitanians or Guiennese. Indeed the seneschal of Bordeaux is called the Magnus Senescballus, not because he is great today (in fact he is the smallest of all), but because the seneschalship of Bordeaux was once bounded by five dioceses. Under that name, Magnus, it was once called, as it was truly great; today, though its domain is diminished, it keeps the full name. Moreover, whatever pertains to Bordeaux alone is not today called Burdigalense but Aquitanum or Guiennense; and the Lesser Court of Bordeaux, from which appeal lies to the Parlement, is called the Curia Guienna and the Iudices Guienna, not Burdigala. This Guienna, therefore, which today is reckoned as four seneschalships, may rightly be called Aquitania, or Guienna of Louis IX. It should be noted concerning Poitou, which Edward III included in the fief of Aquitania or Guienna, that it was often excluded from Aquitania, and under Louis IX was often restored to its boundaries. Certainly today no small part of Poitou says it is Guienna, as once it really was. So the Guienna of Louis XI, which I must explain at this point, is enclosed to the west by the bay of the same name, swollen by the violent waves of the Ocean; to the south lie the Pyrenean mountains; to the east lie Languedoc, Quercy, Périgord, Limousin and other regions; to the north it is adjacent to Poitou. The region is not of one kind throughout. The part that slopes toward the Pyrenees is rougher and more rugged than the rest of Gaul, cold and without wine; for this reason Ausonius, in Epistle xv, calls it ἀσκῶλαν χωρα [the land of wineskins]. Near the Curian promontory the land is lower and marshier, and frequently exposed to floods; in the inland parts it is more cultivated and is not at all a poor mother of many kinds of produce. In general, however, it is often troubled by invasions of locusts. Between Bordeaux and Bayonne is barren country, which the natives call the Landes. The inhabitants are taller than the rest of the Gauls, excellent in agility, strong in bodily power, of lofty and manly spirit, generous, cheerful, quick of wit, lovers of liberty, and most skilled in handling arms. Various peoples once had their seats here: Pliny, in book iv of the Natural History, chapter xix, calls them Aquitanians in general; Caesar, in book iii, more narrowly calls them Garumnians, because many of them lived along the Garonne. The peoples were the Tarbelli, Lapurdenses, Boii, Meduli, Bituriges Vibisci, Atrenses, Vasates and Santones. It is established that the name of the Tarbelli was distinguished in these places by fairly wide boundaries. For when Strabo, in book iv, places them with others by the Pyrenees and the Ocean, and Ptolemy, in book ii of his Geography, places them among the Pyrenees and the territory of Bordeaux, Pliny celebrates the Tarbelli in Aquitania under the surname of the Four-Villagers. The memory of the Tarbelli is thought to survive today in Tarbes, the chief town of the Bigerrones, a different people. From them come Tarbella Pyrene in Tibullus, according to the emendation of Scaliger; Tarbellus Oceanus in Ausonius, in the Parentalia, poem iv; and Tarbella Mater in the same place, poem ii, which in the Syllabus of Professors, poem xviii, is also called Tarbellica. The Tarbellus Fluvius is the Adour, which at the far end of the Moselle flows past Tarbes of the Bigerrones, Aquae Augustae (also called Aquae Tarbellicae, today Dax, the metropolis of the Tarbelli, as I shall say in its place), and Bayonne, and empties into the Ocean. Tarbellica Arma is also Ausonius, in Epistle xxiii to Paulinus; Tarbellinus Aequor is in Lucan, book i. Among the Tarbelli, along with other peoples, were the Lapurdenses, to begin from the Pyrenees with Ptolemy. Josephus Scaliger writes to me that the whole tract of sandy country, which the French call the Landes, belonged to them. Lapurdum is also known from the Book of the Notitia of the Empire, in the province of Novempopulana: "Tribune of the Cohort of Novempopulana at Lapurdum." For so it should be read. The copy of the agreement between the kings Guntram and Childebert in Gregory of Tours, book ix, chapter xx, should also be consulted. Today it is Le Pais de Lapord, or, as others write it, Labord; others again in a more contracted form write Lorda and Lourde. The metropolis of the Lapurdenses today is Bayonne, of which more in its place; hence the bishop of Bayonne is called Lapurdensis in old episcopal charters. Sidonius, in book viii, Epistle xii, addressed to Trigetius, mentions the locusts of the Lapurdenses. The Boii, who are mentioned by Paulinus when he writes to Ausonius in Epistle i, and whom he surnames the Fishy ones from the abundance of pitch and resin, are at the mouths of the Garonne to this day; they are called Bates, as Vinetus notes, who cultivate the land, and are commonly called Buchs. They are also mentioned in the Itinerary, where they are listed among the places along the road from Aquae Tarbellicae to Bordeaux, at a distance of sixteen thousand paces from the city of Bordeaux. In the Notitia of the Provinces, in Aquitania iii or Novempopulana, there is mention of the Civitas Boatum, that is Borus, which is nothing other than Le Pais de Buchs. Voiates for Boates is an error in Caesar. Perhaps they were colonists of the Boy or Boiates Boiorum, of whom more in chapter xxvii. The Ocean forms a bay by the Boii, in which there is a promontory called the Caput berutum, or, to put it in their own language, Cap de Buts. Around the same bay, other peoples of no great name are today called by various names, and I readily believe that all of them, as far as Bayonne, were once called Boii, and that even the Meduli were a part of the Boii; for it is likely that Bayonne, of which more later, takes its name from the Boii. For even now some pronounce it Boiona. The Meduli, who are mentioned in Ausonius, certainly occupied all the land that today lies below Bordeaux, between the Aquitanian sea and the Garonne, which mingles with the sea: —at the far edges of the earth, near the end of the Ocean, and the setting sun,

units.la: uti canit Epistola v ad Theonem Medulinum Ausonius, cui ille non insicie Cultor Arenarum Vates appellatur. Est enim in Medulorum Angulo, ubi nunc Solacus Pagus, magna Arenæ vis, Cumulique, qui multis Pyrenes aut Alpium jugis magnitudine nihil cedant. Abundantem etiam Tractum Arboribus, quæ Picem & Relinam ferunt, innuit non obscure idem Ausonius hoc versu: Et tingit piceo lacrumosa Colonica fumo.
units.tr: as Ausonius sings in Epistle v to Theon the Medulian, and to whom he gives the name Cultor Arenarum Vates (the poet, cultivator of sands). For in the corner of the Meduli, where the village of Solac now lies, there is a great mass of sand and dunes, which in size are not inferior to many ridges of the Pyrenees or the Alps. The same Ausonius, in this line, clearly indicates that the region also abounds in trees that yield pitch and resin: Et tingit piceo lacrumosa Colonica fumo. [And the tearful Colonica is dyed with pitch smoke.]

units.la: Medulica Ostrea, cum Baianis certantia, celebrat idem Ausonius Epist. vii, quæ item ad Theonem; & Epist. xiii ad Paulum: Sed mihi pra cunctis distissima, qua Medulorum Educat Oceanus, qua Burdigalensia nomen Usque ad Cæsareas tulit admiratio mensas, Non laudata minus nostri quam gloria Vini.
units.tr: The Medulan oysters, which rival those of Baiae, are celebrated by the same Ausonius in Epistle 7, also addressed to Theon, and in Epistle 13 to Paulus: "But to me the most distinguished of all is the land that the Medulan ocean nurtures, the land whose name Burdigala has carried, through admiration, even to Caesar's tables, praised no less than the glory of our wine." And so on.

units.la: Et quæ sequuntur. Medulinus Notus ab Meduli spirans, apud eundem nominatur Epistola v, cujus antea facta mentio. Qui Meduli quondam, hodie Medoc appellantur. Bituriges in Gallis duplices leguntur, cognomentis distincti; vel Cubi, quorum Metropolis Avaricum Primæ Aquitaniæ, de quibus capite xxv: vel Vibisci aut Vivisci, Aquitaniæ Secundæ, de quibus hoc loco. Biturigas οὐβισονες Ptolemæo, θέντος vitiosius Straboni, qui innuit hos Bituriges Superiorum, Cuborum inquam, fuisse Colonos; Beturiges simpliciter Itinerariae Tabulae. Designat eosdem Lapis Burdigalensis, in quo haec sculpta: AVGVSTO. SACRVM ET. GENIO. CIVITATIS BIT. VIV
units.tr: Medulinus Notus, the south wind blowing from the Meduli, is named by the same author in Epistle 5, already mentioned. The Meduli, once so called, are today called Médoc. In Gaul there are two peoples called Bituriges, distinguished by surnames: the Cubi, whose metropolis Avaricum belonged to Prima Aquitania, on which see chapter 25; and the Vibisci or Vivisci of Aquitania Secunda, on which see this place. Ptolemy calls them Ουβισονες [Oubisones], and Strabo, less accurately, θέντος [thentos]. Strabo implies that these Bituriges, that is, the Cubi, were colonists of the Superiores. The Itinerary tables simply call them Beturiges. The same people are named on the stone of Bordeaux, on which is carved: "Sacred to Augustus and to the genius of the state of the Biturges Vivisci."

units.la: Exsulant apud Plinium lib. iv cap. xix. Lacuna enim locanda inter illa, Sefignani & cognomine Vibisci. Biturigis Vivisci meminit etiam ecfossus nuper ex fundamentis antiquorum Moenium Burdigalae Lapis, in quo sic fuisse scriptum Architectus, qui vidit, apud Vinetum adseverat: IVL. LVPVS. C BITVRIX. VR D. E. ANN. XXXI. FIL. EIVS. P. C.
units.tr: They are absent from Pliny, book 4, chapter 19, where a gap must be filled between those names and Sefignani and the surname Vibisci. A stone recently dug out of the foundations of the ancient walls of Bordeaux also mentions the Biturges Vivisci. The architect who saw it, reported by Vinetus, says it read thus: "Julius Lupus, citizen of the Biturix, aged thirty-one years; his son set this up."

units.la: Ibi Vr puto fuisse VB, ut sit triplex littera pro VIB. Canit Ausonius in Epilogo Moselle, se Vivisca ab origine ducere gentem:
units.tr: There I think VR was VB, so that it is a triple letter for VIB. In the Epilogue to the Moselle, Ausonius sings that he traces his race from the Vivisci by origin:

units.la: Vbi male quondam, Vivisca. Bituriges Vivisci Notitiae Provinciarum in Aquitania Secunda, Civitas Burdigalensium, L'Archevesché de Bourdeaux. Biturigum enim Vibiscorum Metropolis est apud Strabonem & Ptolemaeum Burdigala. Ardente nimis in Vibiscos amore abripi puto Burdigalenses, & inter eos Gab. Lurbeum IC, Civitatis Amplissimae Procuratorem & Syndicum (qui videndus ad calcem Burdigalensium Rerum Chronici, ab ipso non ita pridem editi) Inscriptionem hanc antiquo operis Statuae ad memoriam Vivisci nominis trahentes: D. M TARQVINIÆ. FASTI NAE. M. CALVENT SABINIANVS. VIV SIBI. ET. CONIVG.
units.tr: "Where once (alas) Vivisca..." The Bituriges Vivisci appear in the Notitia Provinciarum, in Aquitania Secunda, as the civitas of the Burdigalenses, the archbishopric of Bordeaux. For according to Strabo and Ptolemy, Burdigala is the metropolis of the Bituriges Vivisci. I think the Burdigalians are carried away by excessive love for the Vivisci, and among them Gabriel Lurbe, licentiate in law, procurator and syndic of the most distinguished city (who should be consulted at the end of the Burdigalian chronicle that he recently published). They draw this inscription, from an ancient statue, into the memory of the name Vivisci: "To the spirits of the dead. Tarquinia Fastina. Marcus Calventius Sabinianus, living, for himself and his wife."

units.la: VIV. enim ibi non Vivisci, sed, ut in infinitis aliis Marmoribus, Vivens. Ignoscent mihi, spero, optimi Cives. Non enim haec ego; ut Vivisorum (qui aliunde satis nobiles) memoriam obscurem, sed ut veram istius Sabiniani aperiam mentem & quasi scitum. Littorales fere habemus: repetito Pyrenaeo, inter Mediterraneos excellunt hic Aturenses, qui sua habuerunt Domicilia, ubi hodieque ipsorum Vrbs Aturensis; quae Idiomate Vasconico & depravate, Airensis, vulgo Aire, de qua post. Civitas Aturensium in Notitia Provinciarum, L'Evesché d'Aire. Aturenses dicti, ut Garumni, quod Aturi Fluminis, de quo alibi, essent Adcolae. Qui Vasates, ibidem, Ammiano Marcellino lib. xv, Sidonio lib. vii. Epist. v i, Ausonio in Epicedio de Vita sua, item in Epistol. xxxiv, & in Parentalibus; inemendate Οὐασάτες dicuntur Ptolemaeo, Vasfei Plinio lib. iv, cap. xix. Nomen Gentis manet in Vrbe Bafatz; quae, ut paulo post dicam, olim Cossio Vasatum. Sic enim saepe factum animadvertimus, ut Vrbibus, quae principem in aliqua Gente locum obtinebant, & Metropoles erant, rejectis & abolitis propriis appellationibus, Gentis suae vel totius Populi nomen induerint. Exempla sunt in Lutetia Parisiorum, Mediolano tam Santonum, quam Aulercorum Eburovicum, Avarico Biturigum, Vesuna Petrocoriorum, Ratiaste Lemovicum, Ingena Abrincantorum, & aliis. A Vasatibus Vasatica Reda apud Ausonium Epistola vii. ad Theonem. Et hi Vltra-Garumnani fere Veteres Guiennae nostrae Populi: cis Garumnam sunt Santones. Novit eos, cum aliis, Caesar lib. i. de Bello Gallico; in cuius nonnullis Codicibus eduntur Xantones: Santoni eidem lib. ii; item Santona lib. iii. de Bello Civili, nisi si mendum subsit. Σαιτονες Straboni: Σαιτωνς Ptolemaeo, pro Σαιτωνς, ut scribuntur Stephano. Santones Liberi tradit Plinius cap. xix, cujus meminì. Σαντονες Galeno, Santonicam herbam nomen inde sortiri scribenti. Saintonge vel Xantoigne hodie. Civitas Santonum in Notitia Provinciarum Galliæ, L'Evesché de Saintes. Ab Santonibus Oceanus Santonicus, Tibullo lib. i. Eleg. viii; Santonicum Salum, Ausonio Epistola xiii; Σαντονικὴ Κάμπος eidem Epistola xv; Santonicum Absinthium, Plinio; Santonica Herba, Columellæ lib. vi: Santonica Virga, Martiali lib. v. Epigr. xcvi, cui & Santonicus Rufus Epigr. ejusdem libri xc; Santonius Cuculus, Juvenali Satyra iii, qui Bardocucullus Martiali lib. xiv, de quo ante nonnihil à me dictum, cap. xii.
units.tr: Here VIV does not stand for Vivisci but, as in countless other marbles, for vivens, "living." I hope the best citizens will forgive me. I do not say this to obscure the memory of the Vivisci, who are noble enough elsewhere, but to reveal the true mind of that Sabinianus and, as it were, his decision. We have mostly coastal peoples. Beyond the Pyrenees, among the inland peoples, the Aturenses stand out; they had their homes where their city of Aturensis still is today, which in the Basque idiom and corruptly is Airensis, commonly Aire, on which more later. The civitas of the Aturenses is in the Notitia Provinciarum, the bishopric of Aire. They are called Aturenses, like the Garumni, because they were neighbours of the river Aturus, on which elsewhere. The Vasates are named in the same region by Ammianus Marcellinus, book 15, Sidonius, book 7, Epistle 6, Ausonius in the Epicedion on his own life, likewise in Epistle 34 and in the Parentalia. Ptolemy incorrectly calls them Οὐασάτες [Ouasates], and Pliny, book 4, chapter 19, calls them Vasfei. The name of the people survives in the town of Bazas, which, as I shall say a little later, was once Cossio Vasatum. For we often observe that cities which held the leading place among some people, and were metropolises, have rejected and abolished their own names and taken the name of their people or of the whole nation. Examples are Lutetia of the Parisii, Mediolanum of the Santones as well as of the Aulerci Eburovices, Avaricum of the Bituriges, Vesunna of the Petrocorii, Ratiaste of the Lemovices, Ingena of the Abrincatui, and others. The Vasatica Reda in Ausonius, Epistle 7 to Theon, comes from the Vasates. These beyond-Garonne peoples are nearly the old peoples of our Guienne; on this side of the Garonne are the Santones. Caesar, book 1 of the Gallic War, knows them along with others; in some manuscripts of that work they are printed Xantones. He names the Santoni in book 2 of the same work, and Santona in book 3 of the Civil War, unless there is a mistake. Strabo has Σαιτονες [Saitones], Ptolemy Σαιτωνς [Saitons], for Σαντονες, as Stephanus writes it. Pliny, chapter 19, of whom I have spoken, reports the Santones Liberi. Galen has Σαντονες [Santones], writing that the Santonic herb takes its name from them. Today it is Saintonge or Xantoigne. The civitas of the Santones is in the Notitia Provinciarum Galliae, the bishopric of Saintes. From the Santones come the Santonic Ocean in Tibullus, book 1, elegy 8; the Santonic sea in Ausonius, Epistle 13; the Santonic plain (Σαντονικὴ Κάμπος) in the same Epistle 15; Santonic wormwood in Pliny; the Santonic herb in Columella, book 6; the Santonic rod in Martial, book 5, epigram 96, along with Santonicus Rufus in epigram 90 of the same book; and the Santonian cuckoo in Juvenal, Satire 3, which is the bardocucullus of Martial, book 14, of which I said something earlier, in chapter 12.

units.la: De Antiquis Incolis hactenus: quum autem Guienna antea monuerim habere nunc temporis quatuor Senescliallias; Burdigalensem, Vasatensem, Lapurdensem & Xantonisam: primo loco explicandam se offert Burdigalensis; cujus Metropolis Burdigala. Urbs est in Aquitania (Καλλογαλλίας facit Sudas) Biturigum Vivisciorum nobilissima. Sic autem Latinis dicitur prioris ævi: Βορδιγαλα Græcis, Straboni, Ptolemæo, aliis: Burdegala Recentioribus, ut Ammiano, Eutropio, reliquis; Burdegalum Isidoro. Hodie Bourdeaux. Eam inter Metropoles Imperij Romani nominat Testamentum Karoli Magni. Quod ad Etymon; non hic adferam, quæ non meo solum judicio, incipit ad Epigr. xxxiii. Libri ix. Martialis Domitius Calderinus, Burdigalos nominatos esse quasi Burdigalos, id est stultos Gallos. Audiendus potius, quamquam sæpe etiam vanus, Isidorus, cujus Burdigalum, Biturigalum quamdam esse & ab Biturigibus Gallis conditam innuentis, ut vult Vinetus, hæc sunt lib. xv verba: Burdegalum appellatum ferunt, quod Bituriges Gallo- primum habuerit Colonos, quibus ante Cultoribus admpleta est. Sic lego ex Veterum Codicum auctoritate. In Vulgatis sunt Burgi Galli. Sita est in Garumnæ ripa, ad Pyrenæos pertinente vel Occidentem spectante: adversa ripa Collibus surgit amœnissimus, vario Arborum genere consitis, in primis Vitè. In iis Clivus est in Urbem & Meridiem obversus, perveetusto Cupressino Luco, qui nunc vix septem est jugerum; olim longe major fuit, cum primis visendus. Cupressus enim Arbor in Gallia satis est rara: quam ob rem hoc suo se Cupresseto valde jactant Burdigalenses. Quin jam inde antiquitus duravit hic mos usque ad nostra, inquit Vinetus, tempora; ut quicumque Vinum Burdigala asportaturi sunt, solvere ante non liceat, quam Cupressinum Ramum ab Magistratu acceperint; pro quo pendit quælibet Navis Drachmam unam & Drachmæ duas septimas partes. De Situ, ut eo redeam, sic Strabo lib. iv: Ἐ ... (loquitur de Aquitania) Ἐμπορεῖον Βορδιγαλα ... Innuit scilicet, quod verum est, hodieque cernitur, Burdigalam, ut notat Casaubonus, ad Garumnæ Ostia esse sitam, in quæ effundens se Oceanus, Lacum veluti quemdam efficit, qui eodem æstus patitur cum Oceano; quod, ipse Burdigalensis, Ausonius, Patriam suam docto carmine celebrans, etiam non obscure docet, ut ex sequentibus patebit. Nam Paludem significare Strabonem, quæ lapsu temporis purgamentis Urbis, arena, silice, aliisque injectis exsiccata, uti vult doctissimus Vinetus, non est verisimile. De Climate quali, & ex eo Soli Burdigalensis Qualitate, idem Poëta: Burdigala est natale Solum: Clementia Cœli Mitis, ubi & rigua larga Indulgentia Terra, Ver longum, Brumaque breves, Inga frondea subsunt.
units.tr: So much for the ancient inhabitants. Since I have noted earlier that Guienne now has four seneschalties, Bordeaux, Bazas, Lapurd and Xaintonge, the first to be explained is Bordeaux, whose metropolis is Burdigala. It is a city in Aquitaine (Sudas calls it "Kallogallias"), the most noble city of the Bituriges Vivisci. In earlier Latin it is so called: Βορδιγαλα [Bordigala] by the Greeks, Strabo, Ptolemy and others; Burdegala by later writers, such as Ammianus, Eutropius and the rest; Burdegalum by Isidore. Today it is Bourdeaux. The Testament of Charlemagne names it among the metropolises of the Roman Empire. As for its etymology, I shall not bring forward here the explanations which, in my judgment alone, begin at the thirty-third epigram of book 9 of Martial. Domitius Calderinus thinks that Burdigalos was named as if it were "Burdigalos," that is, foolish Gauls. Isidore, though often also vain, is rather to be heard. His words in book 15 suggest that Burdigalum is Biturigalum and was founded by the Gallic Bituriges, as Vinetus wishes: "They say it was called Burdegalum because the Gallic Bituriges first had colonists there, by whom it was filled with cultivators." I read it so on the authority of the old manuscripts; in the printed editions it reads Burgi Galli. It lies on the bank of the Garonne, toward the Pyrenees or facing west. On the opposite bank rises a most pleasant hill, planted with various kinds of trees, above all vines. Among them is a slope facing the city and the south, covered with a very ancient cypress grove, which now is barely seven acres; formerly it was much larger, and well worth seeing. For the cypress is quite a rare tree in Gaul, and for this reason the Burdigalians greatly boast of their cypress grove. Indeed, this custom has lasted from ancient times down to our own, says Vinetus: whoever is going to carry wine away from Bordeaux may not unload before receiving a cypress branch from the magistrate, for which each ship pays one drachma and two sevenths of a drachma. To return to its situation: Strabo, book 4 (speaking of Aquitaine), says that Bordigala is an emporium. He hints, truly, as can be seen even today, that Bordeaux, as Casaubon notes, lies at the mouths of the Garonne, into which the ocean pours and makes a kind of lake that suffers the same tides as the ocean. The Burdigalian Ausonius himself, celebrating his homeland in learned verse, also teaches this not obscurely, as will be clear from what follows. For it is not likely that Strabo means a marsh which, with the passage of time and the rubbish of the city, sand, flint and other things thrown in, was dried up, as the most learned Vinetus thinks. On the climate, and from it the quality of the soil of Bordeaux, the same poet says: "Burdigala is my native soil: the sky is mild in its clemency, and the land is watered and generous in its abundant indulgence; the spring is long, the winters brief, and leafy ingas grow beneath."

units.la: Idem, prima conditione, ut Roma, Quadratam fuisse canit his verbis: Quadrus Murorum species, sic Turribus altis Ardua, ut aërias intrent fastigia nubes. Distinctas interne vias murere, Domorum Dispositum & latas nomen servare Plateas, Tum respondentes directa in Computa Portas.
units.tr: The same poet sings that, in its first foundation, like Rome, it was square, in these words: "Square in the form of its walls, so high with towers that its lofty summits enter the airy clouds; within, it divides the city by streets, the arrangement of the houses, and keeps the name of broad squares; then gates face one another in straight lines."

units.la: Notat Vinetus, qui omnino legendus, Burdigalam Ausonij centum & quatuor fuisse jugerum: hodie multo majorem, quadringentorum & quinquaginta. Docent antiqua hodieque in media Urbe Mœnia. Pomerium Urbis productum est cum alias, tum vero præcipue circa annum cıɔ cccii. Videndum Gab. Lurbei Chronicon Rerum Burdigalensium. Est Burdigalæ inter alios Vicus non ignobilis, cui cognomen ab Lupis, quorum in Urbem incursus incidit in annum ıɔ xxcii. Sunt hodie ibi duæ insignes Ecclesiæ Collegiatæ, quarum una est Metropolitana; xii Paroiciæ; octo Cœnobia Monachorum; unum Sacrarum Virginum; & Collegium Societatis Iesu, quod institutum anno cIↄ Iↄ LXXIII, cura & liberalitate Fr. Baulonij Senatoris Burdigalensis. Palatium quod Gallieni vocant vel Gallena, ab Gallieno Augusto (facessant enim Fabulæ nomen videtur habere. Tristes sunt & tenues insignis quondam Amphitheatri Reliquiæ. Id circumdabant, ut notat oculatus testis Vinetus, Parietes sex: eratque Extimi, qui reliquos altitudine superabat, & Intimi omnium humillimi intervallum octoginta sex pedes, quantum quidem semiruta & jacentia Monimenta metiri licuit. Mediæ Arcæ Longitudo, quam excipiebant utrimq; Portæ singulæ, CCXXIV; Latitudo CXL pedes patebat; ut hæc Ovi figura construi mos erat. Extra Vrbem semper fuit, distabatque a proximo Mœnium Autonianæ Burdigalæ angulo passus minimum CCCC. Tutela, vel Palatium Tutelæ quod appellatur, & ipsum extra Quadratum erat Vrbem, sed propius Garumnam, & juxta Follam, qua Latus Vrbis Septemtriones spectans, muniebatur: tandem Pomerio ea parte prolato, in ipsa inclusum est Vrbe. Peristylium est quadrangulum orthogonium, longum pedes LXXXVII, latum LXII. Pilis (sic etiam Vulgus vocat) sive Columnis adsurgebat striatis octo in longitudine, & sex in latitudine: quæ fiebant in toto ambitu Columnæ quatuor & viginti. Earum adhuc steterunt decem & octo. Subest vero Camera antiquo artificio; in qua Vinum conditur. Templum fuisse patens quidam suspicantur, & ex ipso nominis vestigio Dei Tutelaris Fanum. Podium Paulini, vel Puy Paulin nomen habet à Pontio Paulino, Ausonij Discipulo, ex illustri Paulinorum & Leontiorum Familia, ad quem Sidonius Carmen de Burgo scriptit, cujus meminerunt DD. Ambrosius & Augustinus. Inde Domini de Candale, tamquam Possessores ejus Domus, primum inter Cives Burdigalenses locum sibi vindicant. Navale in media quondam Vrbe fuisse canit non solum Ausonius; Per mediumque Vrbis Fontani Fluminis alveum, Quem pater Oceanus refluo quum impleverit æstu, Adlabi totum spectabis classibus æquor:
units.tr: Vinetus, who is well worth reading in full, notes that Burdigala was once only 104 jugera in Ausonius's day, and is now much larger, 450. Ancient walls still stand in the middle of the city today. The city's pomerium was extended on several occasions, especially around the year 1302. See Gab. Lurbe's Chronicon Rerum Burdigalensium. Among other districts, Bordeaux has a not inconsiderable quarter named after the Lupi (wolves), whose incursion into the city fell in the year 1082. Today the city has two notable collegiate churches, one of them the metropolitan; twelve parishes; eight monasteries of monks; one convent of nuns; and the college of the Society of Jesus, founded in 1573 through the care and generosity of Fr. Baulon, a senator of Bordeaux. The building that people call the Palatium Gallieni or Gallena (for the name seems to derive from the fable of Gallienus Augustus) is merely the sad and meagre remains of a once-famous amphitheatre. As the eyewitness Vinetus observes, it was surrounded by six walls: the outermost was the highest of them all, and the innermost was the lowest of all. The interval between them measured eighty-six feet, as far as the half-ruined and fallen remains allowed it to be measured. The length of the central arena, which had a gate at each end, was 224 feet, and its width 140 feet, since this egg-shaped plan was the customary way of building such structures. It always lay outside the city, and it stood at least 400 paces from the nearest corner of the walls of Ausonian Burdigala. The Tutela, or what is called the Palatium Tutelae, also lay outside the square city, nearer the Garonne and beside the Folle, on the northern side of the city, which was fortified there; but when the pomerium was extended in that part, it was finally enclosed within the city. The peristyle is a rectangular, right-angled court, 87 feet long and 62 wide. It rose on fluted piers (which the common people also call columns), eight along the length and six along the breadth, so that there were twenty-four columns around the whole circuit. Eighteen of them still stand. Beneath it is a vault built with ancient skill, in which wine is stored. Some suspect that it was once an open temple, and they infer from a trace of the name that it was a shrine of the tutelary god. The Podium Paulini, or Puy Paulin, takes its name from Pontius Paulinus, a disciple of Ausonius, of the illustrious family of the Paulini and Leontii, to whom Sidonius addressed his poem on Burdigala. The Fathers Ambrose and Augustine also mention him. From this house, the lords of Candale, as its possessors, claim first place among the citizens of Bordeaux. That the Navale (naval dockyard) once lay in the middle of the city is sung not only by Ausonius: "Through the middle of the city, along the channel of the river Fontanus, which the father Ocean fills with his ebbing and flowing tide, you may see the whole sea covered with ships coming in."

units.la: verum etiam Poëta Anonymos Burdigalensis in Eucharistico; Tandem autem exacto longarum fine Viarum, Majorum in patriam, tectisque advectus avitis, Burdigalam veni: cujus speciosa Garumna Mœnibus Oceani refluas Maris invehit undas Navigeram per Portam: quæ Portum spaciosum Nunc etiam Muris speciosa includit in Vrbe.
units.tr: So too the anonymous poet of Bordeaux in his Eucharisticon: "At last, having come to the end of the long roads, I was brought to my ancestral country and ancestral houses, and I came to Burdigala. Here the beautiful Garonne, through the gate that carries ships, brings in the ebbing waves of the sea within its walls. And even now the beautiful city encloses within its walls a spacious harbour."

units.la: Sed ejus Navalis nullum nunc extat Vestigium: nisi in ostio Peugæ Fluvioli, ad cujus utrumque latus duæ stant Turres præaltæ, per quas olim Catena, quæ adhuc visitur, traducebatur, juxta Portam Vrbis, quæ vocatur du Caillau. Postea tamen Interstitium illud anno cIↄ Iↄ LXXXI est muratum. Hodie nullum Navigii genus Burdigalam ingreditur: sed omnibus Portus & Navale tutissimum & amplissimum est totus Garumna. De Divona autem, qui prorsum exhaustus hodie evanuit, idem Poëta sic canit: Quid memorem Pario contectum Marmore Fontem Euripi fervere Freto? quanta unda profundi? Quantus in Amne tumor? quanto ruit agmine præceps Margine contentus bissena per ostia Cursus, Innumeros Populi non unquam exhaustus ad usus?
units.tr: But no trace of that naval dockyard survives today, except at the mouth of the little river Peugue, on each side of which stand two very tall towers, through which a chain was once stretched across (it can still be seen), beside the city gate called du Caillau. Yet that gap was walled up in the year 1581. Today no kind of ship enters Bordeaux; but the whole Garonne serves as a harbour and a most secure and spacious dockyard for all. As for the Divona*, which has now been drained dry and has vanished altogether, the same poet sings: "Why should I mention the spring roofed with Parian marble, boiling like the Euripus' strait? How great is the wave of its depth, how great the swelling in the river, how headlong it rushes in a crowd, its course divided by twelve mouths, content with its margins, never exhausted for the countless uses of the people?"

units.la: Et paulo post: Salve, Fons ignote Ortu, sacer, alme, perennis, Vitrce, glauce, profunde, sonore, intimis, opace. Salve Vrbis Genius, medico potabilis hausta Divona, Celtarum Lingua Fons addite Divis: Non Aponus potu, vitrea non luce Nemausus Parior, æquoreo non plenior amne Timavus.
units.tr: And a little later: "Hail, unknown spring, sacred in origin, nourishing, everflowing, clear, blue-green, deep, sounding, hidden, dark! Hail, Divona, genius of the city, drinkable by the healing draught, spring added to the gods in the Celtic tongue: not Aponus with its drink, nor Nemausus with its glassy light, nor the Timavus, fuller with its sea-like river, is equal to you."

units.la: Aquæ Fontanæ Ductuum quorundam Rudera eruit extra Burdigalam Vinetus in Fontis ipsius explicatione. Quibus Patriam celebrat Ausonius, Insignem Baccho, Fluviisque, Virisque, Moribus, Ingeniisque hominum, Proceramque Senatu, canens: ijs adhuc maxime est nobilis. In Gallia nulla Regio Vino magis abundat, eoque generoso. Vulgo Vin de Grave dicitur. Grave, quod, quamvis Valco, non intellexit Belleforestius, per totam Galliam significat Arenam, ut me docuit Scaliger, & Terram Arenosam sive Saburretum. Solum autem Suburbanum, in quo praestantissimum illud Vinum nascitur, dicitur Grave, quia totum arenosum est: quod nec tacuit Strabo, qui illud viderat; ἐ’στι δ’ ἡ παρωκεανίτις, inquit, τῶν Ἀκυιτανῶν ἀμπελώνες ἡ ἀλλὰ ἐπὶ λεπτῆς, &c. Sunt & alia Vina, notae vix viloris, La Larmont, & de la Haftide. Adluit Burdigalam hodieque Garumna, Maris aestum sentiens plus 1 passuum mill. supra Urbem: latitudinem habet ad superiorem partem duorum millium pedum; ad inferiorem multo est latior. Minorum gentium Fluvios, inter quos Peuga & Divisa, praetereo. Ostrea Burdigalensis celebrat Ausonius sua illa nobili de diversarum Nationum Ostreis Centura. Scribit Sidonius Apollinaris lib. viii. epist. xii, Burdigalae quoque fuisse Ostrearum Vivaria. Ostreae haec Medulorum proprie Solacensis nunc vulgo nominant, ab Solaco, ultimorum Medulorum Vico. Rempublicam administrant, cum Senatus sui Principe, qui Maior dicitur, Magistratus, qui Iurati vulgo vocantur; olim Triceni numero, & viceni-quaterni; inde anno clɔ ccc lxxviii pro numero Regionum Urbis, Duodeni: hodie ex Constitutione Henrici ii, Seni biennes, redactis etiam ad eundem numerum Urbis Regionibus. His autem adjungitur Concilium xxx Civium ordinarie, in de rebus maximi momenti agundum, ccc. Majoris libere creandi jus Burdigalensibus concessit anno clɔ c lxxiiii Henricus Angliae Rex, Eleonorae, quam Ludovicus Francorum Monarcha repudiarat, Maritus. Lectus a Populo Primus Dominus de Monedes, Civis Burdigalensis. Ejusdem electio iterum Civium consensu ad Principem est translata in gratiam Eduardi, Henrici Angliae Regis Primogeniti, anno clɔ ccc lx. Nec hoc praetercundum, Eduardum Angliae Regem, Aquitaniae Principem, anno clɔ ccc lxxviii Rescripto suo prohibuisse, Ne quis Nobilis aut Miles generosus (hic enim verba habent) deinceps Iuratus foret: quod consensu Civium anno clɔ ccc xcii abrogavit Ioannes Dux Lancastriae, suam relinquens Suffragiorum Civibus Libertatem. Nec illud tacendum, Philippum Francorum Regem in Burdigalensium gratiam, utque eorum sibi animos devinciret, Rescripto suo, quod adhuc religiose in Aerario publico servatur, concessisse Collegio Majoris & Iuratorum Urbis omne Imperium & Iurisdictionem, non solum in Urbe & Suburbiis, sed etiam in Terris ultra primum Lapidem, sive Territorio, quod Banlieucam vocant, cum omnimoda potestate; sibi tantummodo Iure Imperii Supremi recepto, & Iurisdictione Civili, inter Extraneos exercenda per Praepositum Vmbrariae. Haec Constitutio vulgo Philippina vocatur. Hinc fit etiam hodie, ut in Supremi Imperii notam & tanti beneficii memoriam, etiamsi Praepositi Vmbrariae nulla sit Iurisdictio, & ab Senescallo exerceatur, Sententiam Capitalem ab Juratis latam & ab Senatu confirmatam, non prius exequi, & lege agere in damnatum liceat, quam Reus ante Castrum 40 Vmbrariae ductus sit, & ibi a Lictore ter nomen Praepositi Vmbrariae, etiam nemine respondente, proclamatum fuerit. Praeter quam quod jus habeat Senescballiae, de qua antea quaedam a me dicta, Burdigala, digna quoque fuit judicata, quae Domicilium daret Parlamento Regio, quod ibi ab Civibus anno clɔ ccc li, in Conventione post diuturnum Bellum cum Karolo vii Francorum Rege facta pactum, decennio post (nam Rebellio intervenerat: Vide quae Capite xvii obiter dixi) Ludovico xi jam regnante, habere coepit, Novembris xii; quo die juratum in Legibus more Senatus Parisiensis; statutumque, ut ab eo Parlamento Provinciae Burdigalensis, Fuscatensis, Agennensis, Condomiensis, Landarum, Armeniacensis, Cadurcensis, Lemovicensis, Petracoricensis, Angolisimensis, Santonensis & Rupellensis Iura peterent. Postea tamen Provinciae Armeniacensis, Angolisimensis, Rupellensis, & maxima pars Cadurcensis distractae sunt. Quum autem, septimo post Institutionem Primam anno, Rex Ludovicus Aquitaniam jure Apannagii, ut utitata utar voce, Legeque Fiduciae Karolo Fratri cesserat, Parlamentum, mutato loco, ad Pictones fuit translatum; sed mox anno clɔ ccc lxxii. Karolo mortuo, omnique Aquitania ab Ludovico Rege recepta, Kalendis Iunii solenniter, unde moverat, reductum, & non multo post ab Karolo Rege tribus Praesidibus decemque & octo Consiliariis, Edicto anni clɔ ccc xxxiii Decembr. iv, est compositum. Adjecit anno clɔ ɪɔ xix, mense Maio Francisco i novam Senatorum Decuriam, quæ Iudicijs Caussarum Criminalium præesset, quam Tornellum vocant. Tam insigni Prærogativa, ut & alijs multis Privilegijs, Burdigalenses ob motos à Plebe Tumultus, privavit anno cıɔ ıɔ xlviii Annas Mommorancius, Equitum Magister; accipereque coegit è Parisienti, Tolosano & Rotomagensi Senatu Iudices, qui Populo jus dicerent: quibus demum anno sequenti regredi jussis, amplissima Senatus Dignitas ab Henrico ii Civibus in gratiam receptis est restituta; quæ quum aliquamdiu de Antiquitate certaslet cum Divionenti, tandem ejusdem Regis Rescripto anno cıɔ ıɔ liii triumphavit. Domicilium autem Parlamenti est in Castro, Vmbraria cognominato, eam ob caussam, quod antiquitus undique Aquifolio & aliis Arboribus Vmbram facientibus circumdatum esset: nomen retinens, etiamsi, Vrbe aucta Incolis & Ædificiis, hodierno die Arbores desint. Habuit cum alijs Prætidem Nicolaum Foerium, cujus doctissimæ extant Lucubrationes. Obiit Burdigalæ, legata Senatui Bibliotheca, mense Maio, anno cıɔ ıɔ xxxviii; sepultus in Xenodochio publico, ab ipso Ædificus aucto & multis Redditibus locupletato. Sedes olim quidem Episcopalis, hodie Archiepiscopalis & Metropolitana fulgens dignitate. Primum Præsulem lego D. Gilbertum, circa Principatum Vespasiani Imperatoris. Meminerunt antiquissima Monimenta litis, quæ adhuc sub Iudice pendet, inter Archiepiscopos Burdigalensem & Bituricensem, de Primatu Aquitaniæ: quem Clemens v, antea Berrandus Gotthus dictus, exque Archiepiscopo Burdigalensi creatus anno cıɔ ccc v Pontifex Maximus, altero Pontificatus anno, Burdigalensi contra Bituricensem adiecit; idque optimo, inquit in suo Chronico Gab. Lurbeus, cujus antea memini, jure, quidquid dicat Majsonius; qui etiam hic consulendus. Archiepiscopi autem Burdigalenses, eorumque in perpetuum Successores, Consiliarij Senatus cum libero suffragio, mense Februario anni cıɔ ıɔ liv Principis Diplomate sunt declarati. De Suffraganeis ipsorum, ut & reliquorum, dictum antea. Anno ccc lxxxvii Concilium Burdigalense celebratum est, jussu Maximi Tyranni, cui D. Martinus, Turonensis Episcopus, præfuisse scribitur. In eo Priscillianitarum Hæresis damnata est, & Instantius Episcopatu dejectus. A sententia Synodi quum appellasset Priscillianus ad Maximum, quem dixi, Treviris Capite pœnas luit, & aliquot ejus Sectatores, inter quos fuit Euchrotia Burdigalensis, Nobilis Matrona, Vxor Delphidij Oratoris; cujus mortem ideo felicem vocat Ausonius, quod non viderit supplicium suæ Conjugis. Inter Episcopos quatuor Sanctorum numero memorantur adlecripti, Gilbertus, de quo dixi; Amandus i, cujus Reliquiæ Lutetiæ feruntur esse in Monasterio D. Germani Suburbani, Severinus & Amandus ii. Academia Burdigalensis ad instar Tolosanæ erecta est vii. Eidus Mai, cıɔ cccc xli, Rescripto Eugenii Summi Pontificis; comprobata vero, confirmata, Privilegiisque ornata variis, anno cıɔ cccc lxxii, ab Ludovico Francorum Rege. Gymnasium Aquitanicum vocatur. Docetur ibi omne genus Artium. Est antiquissima, si primam originem spectemus; ejusque numerat aliquot, nominatque Professores, qui Rhetoricam ibi magna cum laude fructuque docuerunt, Ausonius, Tiberium Vitlorem Minervium, Præceptorem suum: cujus Patrem Romæ etiam Rhetoricam florentissime professum, circa annum ccc lxix, tradit Eusebius: Latinum Alcimum Alethium: cujus etiam (ut & Delphidy, de quo post) mentio apud Eusebium ad annum ccc lxx, & Sidonium Apollinarem lib. v. Epist. x, & lib. viii, Epist. xi: Lucio-lum, Condiscipulum suum primo, Magistrum hunc, postremo autem in Docendi Munere Collegam: Attium Pateram: Attium Tironem Delphidium, quem Hieronymus, se Adolescentulo, omnes Gallos Prosa Versuque suo inlustrasse Ingenio, scribit in Epistola ad Hedibram; cujus abundantiam laudat Sidonius Apollinaris lib. v, Epist. x: quem denique Ammianus Marcellinus Oratorem dicit acerrimum, initio lib. xviii: Alethium Minervium Filium. Grammaticos deinde Latino quidem Leontio Beato subjungit Græcos quosdam; rursus Latinos, Jucundum Leontij fratrem, Macrinum, Concordem, Phœbitium, Ammonium Anastasium, Herculanum Thalassium & Cutarium Seculum Syracusanum, Grammaticum Græcum: quibus deinde addit Censorinum Atticum Acræcium, Rhetorem: & Nepotianum Grammaticum, eumdemque Rhetorem. Prodierunt & ex hac Burdigalensi Schola, qui alibi docuerunt, Ammonius Anastasius, Grammaticus, qui Augustoriti Pictonum; Aemilius Magnus Arborius, Exsuperius & Sedatus Rhetores, qui Tolosæ: Dynamius, qui in Hispania, Ilerdæ. Plerorum tamen Reliquiæ & Ἀσὶμα, morte obita, Burdigalam sunt translata, ut non obscure variis locis innuit Poeta. Sedato sane magnum habuerunt Concives honorem, qui non solum Ossa ejus in Municipium suum transtulerunt, sed & Imagine hominem honorarunt. Loco enim, qui hodie Podium Paulini vocatur, saxea Imago locata fuit, Capillo & Barba crispa, Librum manu tenens, cum hac Inscriptione:
units.tr: Vinetus, in his explanation of the fountain itself, has dug up the remains of certain aqueducts outside Bordeaux. Ausonius, who sings its praises, celebrates the homeland in these lines: renowned for Bacchus, for its rivers and its men, for their character and talents, and for its senate of nobles, and it is still especially famous for these things. No region in France abounds more in wine, and wine of such quality. It is commonly called Vin de Grave. Grave, which Belleforest did not understand, though it is Vallensian, means throughout all of France sand, as Scaliger taught me, and sandy ground or gravel. The suburban soil where that outstanding wine grows is called Grave because it is all sandy. Strabo, who had seen it, did not pass this over either: "The coastal part of Aquitania," he says, "has vineyards, but on thin soil," and so on [ἔστι δ' ἡ παρωκεανῖτις τῶν Ἀκυιτανῶν ἀμπελῶνες ἀλλὰ ἐπὶ λεπτῆς, κτλ.]. There are also other wines, scarcely of note, La Larmont and de la Haftide. The Garonne still washes Bordeaux today; it feels the tide of the sea more than 1 mile above the city. Its width at the upper part is two thousand feet, and at the lower part it is much wider. I pass over the rivers of the lesser peoples, among which are the Peuga and the Divisa. Ausonius celebrates the Bordeaux oysters in his famous poem on the oysters of various nations. Sidonius Apollinaris writes in book 8, letter 12, that there were also oyster beds at Bordeaux. The Medulians now commonly call these Ostreae Solacensis, properly, after Solac, the most remote village of the Medulians. They govern the commonwealth with the prince of their senate, who is called the Maior, and with magistrates, who are commonly called Iurati. Formerly there were thirty-six of them, and then in the year 1378, according to the number of districts of the city, twelve. Today, by the constitution of Henry II, there are six, serving two-year terms, the city's districts also having been reduced to the same number. To these is added a council of thirty citizens, ordinarily, and three hundred for matters of the greatest importance. Henry, King of England, granted the people of Bordeaux the right to elect their Maior freely in the year 1174. He was the husband of Eleanor, whom Louis, the French monarch, had repudiated. The first lord de Monedes, a citizen of Bordeaux, was chosen by the people. His election was again transferred to the prince, with the consent of the citizens, in favour of Edward, the firstborn son of Henry, King of England, in the year 1360. This must not be passed over either: Edward, King of England and Prince of Aquitaine, by a rescript of 1378 forbade that "no noble or well-born knight" (for these are the words) "should henceforth be a Iuratus." The citizens by common consent abrogated this in 1392, when John, Duke of Lancaster, left the citizens the freedom of their votes. Nor should it be passed over in silence that Philip, King of the French, for the favour of the Bordelais and to bind their minds to himself, granted by his rescript, which is still kept scrupulously in the public treasury, to the college of the Maior and the Iurati of the city all power and jurisdiction, not only in the city and its suburbs but also in the lands beyond the first milestone, or the territory which they call the Banlieue, with full authority. He reserved for himself only the right of supreme empire and civil jurisdiction over foreigners, to be exercised through the Provost of the Umbrary. This constitution is commonly called the Philippina. Hence it happens even today that, as a mark of supreme authority and in memory of so great a benefit, even though the Provost of the Umbrary has no jurisdiction and it is exercised by the seneschal, a capital sentence pronounced by the Iurati and confirmed by the senate may not be carried out, nor may the condemned man be dealt with by law, until the accused has been led before the castle of the Umbrary, and there the lictor has proclaimed the name of the Provost of the Umbrary three times, even though no one answers. Besides this right of the Senescballia, of which I have said something earlier, Bordeaux was also judged worthy to be the seat of the royal Parlement. This the citizens obtained by agreement in 1450, after a long war with Charles VII, King of the French. Ten years later (for a rebellion had intervened; see what I said in passing in chapter 17), with Louis XI already reigning, it began to sit on 12 November, the day on which it took the oath according to the laws of the Parisian senate. It was decreed that the provinces of Bordeaux, Fuscatensis, Agennensis, Condomiensis, Landarum, Armeniacensis, Cadurcensis, Lemovicensis, Petracoricensis, Angolisimensis, Santonensis and Rupellensis should seek justice from that parliament. Later, however, the provinces of Armeniacensis, Angolisimensis, Rupellensis, and the greater part of Cadurcensis were separated off. When, in the seventh year after its first establishment, King Louis had ceded Aquitaine to his brother Charles by right of appanage (to use that word), and by the law of trust, the parliament was transferred to a different place, to the Pictones. But soon after, in 1472, when Charles was dead and all of Aquitaine had been recovered by King Louis, it was solemnly brought back on the Kalends of June to the place from which it had moved. Not long afterwards it was reconstituted by King Charles with three presidents and eighteen councillors, by an edict of 4 December 1433. In May 1519 he added to it, for Francis I, a new decury of senators, which would preside over criminal trials, and which they call the Tornellum. Annas Montmorency, Master of the Horse, deprived the Bordelais of this distinguished prerogative, along with many other privileges, in 1548, because of tumults stirred up by the common people. He compelled them to take judges from the Parisian, Toulouse and Rouen senates, to pronounce justice to the people. When these were finally ordered to return home the following year, Henry II, having received the citizens back into favour, restored the very ample dignity of the senate. This dignity had contended for some time over antiquity with the senate of Dijon, but at last, by a rescript of the same king in 1553, it prevailed. The seat of the parliament is in the castle called the Umbraria, for the reason that in ancient times it was surrounded on all sides by holly and other trees that cast shade. It keeps the name, even though, with the city enlarged in inhabitants and buildings, the trees are gone today. It had among its presidents Nicolaus Foerius, whose very learned writings survive. He died at Bordeaux, leaving his library to the senate, in May 1538, and was buried in the public hospital, which he himself had enlarged and enriched with many revenues. It was once an episcopal see, and today it shines with the dignity of an archbishopric and metropolitan. I read that the first bishop was St. Gilbert, in the time of the principate of the emperor Vespasian. The most ancient records mention the lawsuit, still pending before a judge, between the archbishops of Bordeaux and Bourges concerning the primacy of Aquitaine. Clement V, formerly called Bertrand de Got, who had been made pope from the archbishopric of Bordeaux in the year 1305, in the second year of his pontificate added it to Bordeaux against Bourges; "and rightly," says Gabriel Lurbeus, whom I mentioned earlier, "whatever Majsonius may say," who is also to be consulted here. The archbishops of Bordeaux, and their successors in perpetuity, were declared by a diploma of the prince, in February 1554, to be councillors of the senate with a free vote. Of their suffragans, and of the others, I have spoken above. In the year 387 the Council of Bordeaux was held, by order of the tyrant Maximus, at which St. Martin, Bishop of Tours, is written to have presided. In it the heresy of the Priscillianists was condemned, and Instantius was deposed from his bishopric. When Priscillian had appealed from the sentence of the synod to Maximus, whom I mentioned, he paid the penalty with his head at Trier, and some of his followers did likewise, among whom was Euchrotia of Bordeaux, a noblewoman, the wife of Delphidius the orator. Ausonius calls her death happy because she did not live to see the punishment of her husband. Among the bishops, four are remembered as having been enrolled in the number of the saints: Gilbert, of whom I have spoken; Amandus I, whose relics are said to be at Paris in the monastery of St. Germain in the suburbs; Severinus; and Amandus II. The Academy of Bordeaux was founded on the model of Toulouse on 7 May 1441, by a rescript of Pope Eugene; it was approved, confirmed and adorned with various privileges in 1472 by Louis, King of the French. It is called the Gymnasium of Aquitaine. Every kind of art is taught there. It is very ancient, if we look at its first origin, and Ausonius lists and names a number of professors who taught rhetoric there with great distinction and profit: Tiberius Vitlorius Minervius, his own teacher, whose father, Eusebius tells us, also taught rhetoric most brilliantly at Rome around the year 369; Latinus Alcimus Alethius, whose mention is also found in Eusebius under the year 370, and in Sidonius Apollinaris, book 5, letter 10, and book 8, letter 11; Lucio-lus, his fellow pupil at first, and later this teacher, and finally his colleague in the office of teaching; Attius Patera; Attius Tiro Delphidius, whom Jerome writes, in his letter to Hedibia, had illustrated all the Gauls in prose and verse by his talent when he himself was a young man; his abundance is praised by Sidonius Apollinaris, book 5, letter 10; and finally Ammianus Marcellinus calls him a most sharp orator, at the beginning of book 18; Alethius Minervius, son. Next, among the grammarians, he adds to the Latin Leontius Beatus certain Greeks; then again Latins: Jucundus, brother of Leontius, Macrinus, Concordius, Phoebitius, Ammonius Anastasius, Herculanus Thalassius, and Cutarius Seculus of Syracuse, a Greek grammarian. To these he then adds Censorinus Atticus Acraecius, a rhetorician, and Nepotianus, a grammarian who was also a rhetorician. From this Bordeaux school there also came forth those who taught elsewhere: Ammonius Anastasius, grammarian, who taught at Augustoritum of the Pictones; Aemilius Magnus Arborius, Exsuperius and Sedatus, rhetoricians, who taught at Toulouse; Dynamius, who taught in Spain, at Lérida. Yet the remains of most of them, when they died, were brought back to Bordeaux, as the poet hints in various places. The citizens certainly held Sedatus in great honour: they not only transferred his bones to their own town but also honoured the man with an image. For in the place which is now called the Podium Paulini, a stone statue was set up, with curly hair and beard, holding a book in its hand, with this inscription:
