units.la: Quin & ipse Ausonius ibidem Professorem egit, quemadmodum ipse de se scribit in Carmine xxv. de Professoribus Burdigalensibus, in Protreptico ad Nepotem, & in Semigræca ad Paulium Axium Epistola. Scholæ Burdigalensi proximis annis præfuerunt, ibique cum maxima laude docuerunt Math. Corderius, Antonius Govea-nus, Ioannes Costanus, Georgius Buchananus, Nicolaus Gruchius, Guilelmus Guerentœus, Ia. Tevius, & Elias Vinetus, qui, postquam Collegio Aquitanico per xxv. annos cum summa gloria præfuisset, tandem post multas vigilias & indefessos labores ibidem mortuus est xiv Mai, anno clo lo xxcvii. Impetrarunt Burdigalenses ab Karolo ix anno clo lo lxv. Ius Nundinarum, quæ ad instar Lugdunensium libere, mensibus Martio & Octobri, per xv dies haberi solitæ. Res à Burdigalensibus gestas commemorare non Cosmographi est, sed Historiographi: Hoc obiter dicam, Tetricum unum ex xxx Tyrannis, sub Galieno ex Præside Provinciæ factum hic esse Imperatorem; Purpuramque, quod Crimen erat lætæ Majestatis, sumsisse. Ferro Igneque cum ab aliis feris Gentibus, tum ab Vandalis, Gothis, Saracenis & Normannis sæpe vastata, decorem illum amisit & elegantiam, quam ejus Vijs Plateisque tribuit Ausonius.
units.tr: Ausonius himself also taught here as Professor, as he writes of himself in his poem xxv on the Professors of Bordeaux, in the Protreptikos to his grandson, and in the Semigraeca, his letter to Paulus Axius. In recent years Math. Corderius, Antonius Govea-nus, Ioannes Costanus, Georgius Buchananus, Nicolaus Gruchius, Guilelmus Guerentœus, Ia. Tevius, and Elias Vinetus have headed the Bordeaux school and taught there with the greatest distinction. Vinetus, after he had presided over the Collège d'Aquitaine for twenty-five years with great renown, died there at last, worn out by many night watches and tireless labours, on 14 May 1597. In 1565 the people of Bordeaux obtained from Charles IX the right of fairs, which, after the manner of Lyon, were to be held freely in March and October for fifteen days, as was customary. To recount the deeds of the Bordelais is the business of the historian, not the cosmographer. I will only note in passing that Tetricus, one of the Thirty Tyrants under Gallienus, was made emperor here, having been governor of the province, and that he assumed the purple, which was a crime of treason. The city, repeatedly laid waste with fire and sword by barbarian peoples, and especially by the Vandals, Goths, Saracens and Normans, lost that beauty and elegance which Ausonius ascribed to its streets and squares.

units.la: De ipsa Urbe portiora, ni fallor, dixi: illud addam, anno clo ccc lxxix Societatem arctam initam fuisse inter Urbes Burdigalam & Burgum; ut Burdigala quasi Princeps præesset Burgo, ceterisque Provinciæ Oppidis: Inde autem servatum fuisse usque ad extremum Anglici Imperii diem; ut, urgente Bello, Maior & Iurati Burdigalenses ex Civium numero aliquos seligerent, futuros Urbibus Castrisque Provinciæ Burdigalensis Præfectos. Hæc causa fuit, quod opida Blavia, Burgus, Libumia, Fanum S. Æmiliani, Castellum, Cadillacum, Fanumque S. Macarij, Filiola dictæ fuerint Civitatis Burdigalensis. De Prioribus nonnihil addam.
units.tr: I have, I think, said the more important things about the city itself. I will add that in the year 379 a close alliance was made between the cities Bordeaux and Bourg, so that Bordeaux as it were presided over Bourg and the other towns of the province. This arrangement was kept up until the last day of English rule: when war pressed, the mayor and jurats of Bordeaux chose some of their citizens to be future governors of the towns and castles of the Bordeaux province. This is the reason why the towns Blaye, Bourg, Libourne, Saint-Émilion, Castillon, Cadillac, Saint-Macaire, and Fronsac were called towns of the city of Bordeaux. I will say something further about the first of these.

units.la: Blavia, quæ vulgo Blaie, munitissimum est opidum, ad dexteram, quæque Santonos spectat, Garumnæ Ripam, xii leucis ab ejus ostio, vii à Burdigala, ab Santonis xv. Meminerunt ejus, præter Gregorium Turonensem de Gloria Confessorum & Aimoinum Floriacensem in Rebus Karoli Martelli, etiam Ausonius Epistola xii ad Paulum, Militarem appellans. In posteriore Tabulæ Peutingerianæ Editione Blavium quoque nuncupari video, quum in prioribus Schidis Blaantum vel Blanutum legi, Viri Docti indignentur. Blavium est Turpino in Vita Karoli: Blabia Notitiæ Imperij Romani, adsignato illi Præfecto Militum Carronensium. Sane pergit esse, quod olim fuit, Blavia; vix quadraginta Iugera obtinens Soli, Custodes Vigilesque habet perpetuos, qui nocte dieque non modo Locum illum custodiant diligenter, verum etiam ex ea Specula, quid toto late fiat Garumna, sursum deorsumque, studiose observent: & si qua forte hostilis Classis præterire conetur, prohibeant inde illi naviter Tormentis, quamtum per Fluminis liceat latitudinem, quæ illic duum millium & ducentorum est passuum: ut vere Ausonio sit Militaris, vereque etiam Castrum dicatur Gregorio Aimoinoque; quorum ille Romanum Blavienfem laudat inter Confessores, Ausonio Poetæ & Martino Turonensi Episcopo coætaneum, quem Sigebertus mortem obiisse notat anno cccxxcv; cuiusque Sepulcrum Blavienfi Castello contiguum, ut idem Gregorius loquitur, & Basilicam, in qua sepultum fuisse Regem Charibertum Ado Viennensis scribit, Civilia Bella solo nuper æquarunt. Incolæ volunt Rolandum Palatinum, Præfectum sub Karolo Magno Littoris Britannici, apud se natum, suum fuisse Comitem, apud se denique tumulatum in Ecclesia D. Romani; Ense adposito, quem Durandal vocitant, Cornuque ipsius ad pedes Tumuli; quod tamen postea in Ecclesiam D. Severini Burdigalam digalam perhibetur translatum. De hoc Rolando, aniles circumferuntur Fabulæ.
units.tr: Blaye, commonly called Blaie, is a very strongly fortified town on the right bank of the Garonne, facing the Saintonge side, twelve leagues from its mouth, seven from Bordeaux and fifteen from Saintes. Besides Gregory of Tours in his book on the Glory of the Confessors and Aimoin of Fleury in his History of Charles Martel, Ausonius too mentions it, in letter xii to Paulus, calling it Militaris. I see that in the later edition of the Peutinger Table it is also called Blavium, whereas in the earlier copies it is read as Blaantum or Blanutum, which learned men find outrageous. Turpin in his Life of Charlemagne has Blavium; the Notitia of the Roman Empire has Blabia, with a prefect of the Carronensian soldiers assigned to it. It still remains what it once was, a Blavia: it holds barely forty acres of soil, and it has constant guards and watchmen who, night and day, not only diligently guard the place but also keenly watch from that lookout what is happening up and down the Garonne across its whole breadth. If some hostile fleet tries to slip past, they forbid it, with artillery, as far as the river's width allows, which there is two thousand two hundred paces. So it is truly Militaris for Ausonius, and truly called a castrum by Gregory and Aimoin. Gregory praises the Roman Blavian among the Confessors; he was a contemporary of the poet Ausonius and of Martin, bishop of Tours, and Sigebert notes that he died in the year 395. Ado of Vienne writes that his tomb was next to the Blavian castle, as Gregory also says, and that the basilica in which King Charibert was buried was lately levelled to the ground in the civil wars. The inhabitants want Roland the Paladin, prefect under Charlemagne of the British coast, to have been born among them, to have been their count, and finally to have been buried among them in the church of St. Romanus, with his sword laid beside him, which they call Durendal, and his horn at the foot of the tomb; yet it is said that this was afterwards transferred to the church of St. Severinus at Bordeaux. Old wives' tales circulate about this Roland.

units.la: Burgus, Ebromagum videtur Antiquis appellatum, si emendate scriptum (nam in quibusdam Codicibus legitur Ebromagnus, sed perperam proculdubio) Paullino Epistola v ad Severum Sulpicium Fratrem. In Iambis Ausonij ad Paullinum Hebromanum paret appellatum, ubi Vinetus testatur se & Hebromagium, item utramque vocem sine adspiratione in Libris scriptis reperisse. Erat autem hoc oppidum Pontii Leontii Paulini. Probat non obscure Ausonius Epist. xx ii, quæ ad ipsum scripta: Is nunc adusque vectus Ebromagum tuam, Sedem locavit mercibus.
units.tr: Bourg seems to have been called Ebromagum by the ancients, if the reading is correct (for some manuscripts read Ebromagnus, but undoubtedly wrongly), in Paulinus's letter v to his brother Severus Sulpicius. In Ausonius's Iambics to Paulinus it is called Hebromanum, where Vinetus testifies that he has found both Hebromagium and the same word without the aspirate in written books. This town belonged to Pontius Leontius Paulinus. Ausonius makes this plain in letter xxii, written to him: "He has now been carried as far as your Ebromagum and has placed his goods there as a store."

units.la: Et alibi: Qui apud Ebromagum conditis Mercibus, quas per agros diversos coemit, concessō ab hominibus tuis ususque hospitio. Quum igitur in modum Castrorum, ut scribit Scaliger lib. ii. Auson. Lect. cap. ix, Horreis publicis & Turribus postea esset amplificatum ab eodem Pontio Leontio Burgus vocatum fuit: ita enim eo tempore oportuna Bello & munita Annonæ copia Castra vocabant. In hunc Burgum Carmen Panegyricum extat Sidonij Apollinaris, qui ab Munitione Horreorum & Propugnaculorum sic vocatum fuisse manifesto canit his versibus: Cernere jam videor, quæ sint tibi Burge futura. Dicere sic: namque Domus de Flumine surgunt, Pendentesque sedent per Propugnacula Tiema, &c.
units.tr: And elsewhere: "You who have stored your wares at Ebromagum, which you bought up across various fields, with the use of lodging granted by your people." Since it was then enlarged by the same Pontius Leontius, with public granaries and towers, in the manner of a camp, as Scaliger writes in book ii of his Lectiones on Ausonius, chapter ix, it was called Bourg (Burgus), for in that age a store of provisions suited to war and fortified was called a camp. There is a panegyric poem on this Bourg by Sidonius Apollinaris, who sings plainly in these verses that it was so called from the fortifying of its granaries and bulwarks: "I seem already to see what you, Burgus, are to become. Speak thus: for houses rise from the river, and sit hanging on the bulwarks, and so on."

units.la: Elias tamen Vinetus Ebromagum agnoscit in Vico, qui intra Blaviam, vulgo Embran, vel Bran nuncupatur, quatuor leucis à Burgo. Liburnis ad Confluentes Duranij & Liliæ frequenter Parlamenti Burdigalensis legitur fuisse Sedes, grassante in Metropolitanos Peste. Oppidum Novum. Nam qui mentionem faciat, non est antiquior Froissardo. Conditum lego circa Philippi Pulcri Francorum Regis tempora; Eduardi Angliæ Regis & Aquitaniæ Ducis auspiciis, qui suo Diplomate (Exscriptum est Gallo Romano Idiomate apud Vinetum ad Epistolam Ausonij vi) anni cıɔ cc-xxxix jus Collegij & Civitatis Liburniam habitantibus est largitus: ut credibile putetur Muris Liburnia factis, Condatenses Vicinos in novum oppidum commigrasse: licque Liburnia ortum & incrementum Condati Portui fuisse decrementum & interitum. Hodieque enim paullum supra Liburniam, secundum Dordoniam, Paludes sunt & Pascua Condatis nomine, quo locus Portus olim fuit & Vicus; manentibus nunc solis priscarum Follarum Reliquiis. De Porta testatur Ausonius Epistola vi: Vnus à Domnotoni te littore perferet ustum Condatem ad Portum, si modo deproperes.
units.tr: Yet Elias Vinetus identifies Ebromagum with a village within Blaye, commonly called Embran or Bran, four leagues from Bourg. At the confluence of the Dordogne and the Lidoire, Libourne is frequently read as the seat of the Parlement of Bordeaux, when plague was raging among the metropolitans. It is a new town. For no one who mentions it is older than Froissart. I read that it was founded around the time of Philip the Fair, King of the French, under the auspices of Edward, King of England and Duke of Aquitaine, who by his charter (it is copied in Gallo-Roman idiom in Vinetus's notes on Ausonius's letter vi) granted in the year 1289 the right of a college and a city to the inhabitants of Libourne. It is therefore thought credible that, once walls were built at Libourne, the people of Condat, their neighbours, migrated into the new town; and thus the rise and growth of Libourne was the decline and ruin of Condat Port. For even today, a little above Libourne, along the Dordogne, there are marshes and pastures called by the name of Condat, where the port and village once stood, with only the remains of the old walls left now. Ausonius bears witness to the port in letter vi: "One boat will carry you from the shore of Domnotonus to the burnt port of Condat, if only you hurry."

units.la: De Vico Paullinus Epistola i ad Ausonium: In Condatino diceris degere Vico.
units.tr: Paulinus, in letter i to Ausonius, speaks of the village: "You are said to dwell in the village of Condat."

units.la: Est & Condate in Itineraria Tabula. Et post Ausonij Paullinique tempora annis plus nongentis Eduardus i Angliæ Rex, Aquitaniæ Dux Condatis morabatur. Ejus exstant duorum Diplomatum exempla: in quorum priore est; Datum & actum apud Condatum prope Liburniam, anno millesimo ducentesimo, octogesimo nono. In altero, Datum apud Condat. prope Liburniam, secundo die Iunij, anno Regni nostri decimoseptimo. Liburnenses porro, ut ad eos redeam, quum anno cıɔ ıɔ xliv contra Civitatis Burdigalensis auctoritatem obtinuissent à Principe Ius & Sedem Senescalliæ, justi sunt ejusdem Edicto ab Senatu comprobato vii Iulij moribus antiquis vivere, & Ius ab Senescallo Burdigalensi petere.
units.tr: There is also Condate in the Itinerary Table. And more than nine hundred years after the times of Ausonius and Paulinus, Edward I, King of England and Duke of Aquitaine, stayed at Condat. Copies of two of his charters survive. In the first it reads: "Given and done at Condat, near Libourne, in the year one thousand two hundred and eighty-nine." In the second: "Given at Condat, near Libourne, on the second day of June, in the seventeenth year of our reign." The people of Libourne, to return to them, having in the year 1344 obtained against the authority of the city of Bordeaux the right and seat of the seneschalsy from the prince, were ordered by his edict, approved by the Senate on 7 July, to live by their ancient customs and to seek justice from the seneschal of Bordeaux.

units.la: Sunt autem & in Burdigalensi Senescallia Territoria, quæ vulgo Terra inter duo Maria, Medocum, Buchsium & Fronsaca. Terra inter duo Maria, vulgo Le Pais entre deux Mers, pinguissimus est Tractus inter Garumnam & Duranium, ingentes Fluvios, qui propter magnitudinem vocantur Maria ab Incolis. Huic adscribi solent Opida cum aliis, Parlamento Burdigalensi subjectis, Fanum S. Macary & Liburnia, de quibus paullo ante dixi. Medocum Medulorum Domicilium, vulgo Le Pais de Medoc. Huic tribui consuevit quidquid Agri inter Burdigalam est, Oceanum & Garumnam in eum influentem. Ager Meduliacus nihil fere est, quam Arena: circa Paludes valde depressus; Aquarum Inundationibus supra modum obnoxius, ut mirum non sit Littus Medulicum indies atteri, & ab Oceano Medulos sensim sepeliri & obrui. Sic ibi periit Curianum Promontorium, de quo alibi, cujus memoria servari videtur in Scopulo, Cordan vulgo, qui in Medulico Oceano non procul vel potius in ipso Garumnæ ostio, Φάρος sustinens vel Turrim præaltam, & à proximo Medulorum quinque circiter passuum millibus distans angulo, cujus olim partem fuisse non est dubitandum. Sic ibidem perit Ναυσμαγ, Vrbs Ptolemæo Biturigum Vibiscorum: Novioregum fortean Antonino; cujus Rudera, retrocedentibus Fluctibus, subinde conspici narrantur, inter Arenas. Erat Burdigalensibus versus Cautum, sub eodem cum Santonis Meridiano sita, & æque ad Occasum vergens; sed australior, quam illa, unius Partis dimidio, ut omnino collocata fuisse videatur ad Ostium Garumnæ, ubi fere nunc Solacus, Vicus nobilis infra Burdigalam ad octoginta fere passuum millia. Sic denique ex eiusdem Loci adverso, in Littore Santonico perierunt vel Opida vel Vici, quod summa quædam docent Ædificia, in Arenaceis Montibus apud Arvertinos apparentia. Sunt sane sui Rebus omnibus, etiam maximis, Ortus: sui Interitus. Abundat porro Medulorum Ager Arboribus, quæ Picem & Resinam ferunt. An Tædam habeant, inquit ad Ausonii Epist. v. Vinctus, mihi non est compertum; sed hoc scio, illos Tædas vocare (hoc ipso vocabulo Latino Vulgus utitur) quas faciunt ex Arboribus, Resinam Picemque ferentibus. Filæ namque ardent propter ingenitum illum Succum, tamquam Faces Candelæque, quas ex Canabino filo, cera, sevoque obducto facere solemus. Carroco, Vibisco Idiomate, Medulicus est Piscis apud Ausonium Epistola v, quem fere est ut Vinctus putet Acipenserem esse, qui Medulis, Boys, aliisque Aquitaniæ Populis Creac, Burdigalensibus cum adjectione Creac de Buch à Bois dicitur. Nominat ibidem Ausonius & alios Medulorum Belorumque Pisces: qui hodieque iis in locis & Burdigalæ noti. Pauliacus, cujus meminit Ausonius Epist. v i ad Theonem, hodieque Vicus est nobilis, nomen adhuc retinens Pauliac, apud eosdem Medulos in sinistra Garumnæ ripa, novem Leucis à Burdigala, ut vulgus illic metitur itinera. Fuit non procul Pauliaco in Medulis, in eadem Garumnæ ripa, etiam Parus Domnotinum (alij alio modo scribunt) cujus mentio apud Ausonium Epist. v i, non uno loco. Vestigium videtur manere in Vico, qui Domnessam hodie, Pauliaco minor & obscurior, Burdigalæque propior. Natus hic erat Theon Poeta: quem, alioquin Amicum, Ausonius eadem Epistola nimia exagitat Libertate, Stuporem Medulum Vibisco Sale supra modum perfricans. Inde Theon Domnotinus, indeque Domnotina Domus eidem Ausonio gens & familia Theonis. Medoco conregionale est Buchsium vel Buzium, Boiorum vel Boatum, de quibus alibi, Sedes: vernacule Le Pais de Buchs, Principatus Titulo clarum. Dynasta vulgo Capeal (Capitalis, Princeps, Dominus) de Buchi, id est Buziorum seu Buorum, nominatur; estque sub Dominio illustris Candalarum Comitum Familiæ, quæ Gastonem Capitalem Buziorum, Arcembaldi Filium, Progenitorem suum agnoscens, Navarræ Pannoniæque Regibus etiam Affinitate juncta fuisse, Præsulesque & Præfectos Aquitaniæ dedite legitur. Bos autem supra Medulos sunt, secundum Oceani Aquitanici litus. Ipsorum Ager, infelicissimum Solum, non alius fere generis, quam Medulorum; Arcnis (quarum cultorem facit suum Theonem fuisse nimis Ausonius Epistola vj) obductus, Frugibus infæcundus, præter Secali & Milio: Arboribus Resinam Picemque ferentibus abundat, cujus utrumque speciei magna vis Burdigalam singulis Veneris diebus Carris advehitur. De ipsa Gente, ut & de aliis, alibi a me dictum, ubi Boiorum etiam mentio mihi facta sinus. Exit in hunc Leria, Vicinæ Gentis Fluvius, in Vasatensi Agro ortus; qui Ponte, Cymba nonnumquam Vado transitur apud Vicum Montes: qua via brevissima Baionam Burdigala tolet iri. Qui Leria li non est, quem Ptolemæus lib. 11 nominat Sigmanem, cujusque ostium constituit inter Aturri Baionam, & Garumnæ Burdigalam præterfluentis Ostia, totus ille Sigmas cum suo nomine prorsus disparuit. Nulla namque alia est aqua, quam Leria inter Garumnam & Aturrum in Oceanum influentes, quæ Fluvii nomine digna videatur. Fronsiaca, Le Pais de Fronsac, Marchionatus Dignitate celebris est. Nomen illi ab Opido Castroque Fronsiaco, cujus ad Confluentem cum Duranio Lilam fundamenta posuit Karolus Magnus, quum Hunoldum Aquitaniæ Ducem bello peritum profligaret.
units.tr: There are also in the Senescalsy of Bordeaux districts commonly called Terra inter duo Maria, Le Pais entre deux Mers, and Medocum, Buchsium and Fronsaca. The Terra inter duo Maria is the most fertile tract, lying between the Garonne and the Dordogne, great rivers which the inhabitants call Maria ("seas") on account of their size. To it are usually assigned the towns under the Parlement of Bordeaux, along with the others, namely Fanum S. Macary and Liburnia, of which I spoke a little while ago. Medocum is the home of the Medulli, commonly Le Pais de Medoc. To it is assigned whatever land lies between Bordeaux, the Ocean and the Garonne flowing into it. The Ager Meduliacus is almost nothing but sand, very low-lying around the marshes and excessively exposed to floods of water, so that it is no wonder the Medulican shore is worn away daily and the Medulli are gradually buried and overwhelmed by the Ocean. In this way the Curianum Promontorium, of which I speak elsewhere, has perished; its memory seems to survive in a rock called Cordan, which lies not far off in the Medulican Ocean, or rather at the very mouth of the Garonne, bearing a Pharos (Φάρος), or a very high tower, and is about five thousand paces from the nearest corner of the Medulli. There is no doubt that it once formed part of that promontory. In the same place has perished Nausmag (Ναυσμαγ), a city which Ptolemy assigns to the Vibisci of the Bituriges; perhaps it is the Novioregum of Antoninus, whose ruins are said to be seen from time to time among the sands when the waves recede. It lay on the Bordeaux side towards the Cautes, under the same meridian as the Santones and likewise inclined to the west, but a half-part further south, so that it seems to have been situated at the mouth of the Garonne, where now stands Solacus, a noted village about eighty miles below Bordeaux. Finally, in the opposite region on the Santonic shore, towns or villages have likewise perished, as certain large buildings appearing on the sandy hills among the Arvertini indicate. Indeed all things, even the greatest, have their origin and their ruin. Moreover the territory of the Medulli abounds in trees which yield pitch and resin. Whether they have pine-torches, as Vinctus says on Ausonius' Epistle v, I have not discovered; but this I know, that they call "torches" (the very Latin word the common people use) those they make from trees yielding resin and pitch. For these burn because of that inborn juice, like torches and candles, which we usually make from hemp thread coated with wax and tallow. Carroco, in the Vibiscan language, is the Medulican fish mentioned by Ausonius in Epistle v, which Vinctus almost thinks is the sturgeon; among the Medulli, the Boys and other peoples of Aquitaine it is called Creac, and at Bordeaux, with the addition Creac de Buch, it is called from the Bois. Ausonius there names also other fish of the Medulli and Belli, which are known to this day in those places and at Bordeaux. Pauliacus, which Ausonius mentions in Epistle vi to Theon, is still a noted village, keeping the name Pauliac, among the same Medulli on the left bank of the Garonne, nine leagues from Bordeaux, as the common people there measure their journeys. Not far from Pauliacus among the Medulli, on the same bank of the Garonne, there was also Parus Domnotinum (others write it differently), which Ausonius mentions in Epistle vi in more than one place. A trace of it seems to remain in the village now called Domnessam, smaller and less known than Pauliac, and nearer to Bordeaux. Here was born the poet Theon, whom Ausonius, though he was his friend, in the same epistle attacks with excessive freedom, rubbing the dullard Medulli thoroughly with Vibiscan salt. Hence Theon was called Domnotinus, and the family and clan of Theon the Domnotina Domus of Ausonius. Neighbouring Medocum is Buchsium or Buzium, the seat of the Boiorum or Boatum, of which I speak elsewhere; in the vernacular Le Pais de Buchs, renowned for its title of principality. Its lord is called in the vulgar tongue the Capeal (Capitalis, Prince, Lord) de Buchi, that is, of the Buzii or Buorum; and he is under the rule of the illustrious family of the Counts of Candale, who acknowledge Gaston, the Capital of the Buzii and son of Arcembald, as their progenitor, and are read to have been connected by marriage with the kings of Navarre and Pannonia, and to have given bishops and prefects to Aquitaine. Beyond the Medulli, along the shore of the Aquitanian Ocean, lie the Boi. Their land, a most unfortunate soil not very different in kind from that of the Medulli, is covered with sand (Ausonius, in Epistle vi, makes Theon too much its tiller), is barren of crops except rye and millet, and abounds in trees yielding resin and pitch, of which great quantities of both kinds are carted to Bordeaux every Friday. I have spoken of this people, as of others, elsewhere, where I also mentioned the Boiorum gulf. Into this flows the Leria, the river of the neighbouring people, rising in the territory of Vasates; it is crossed by a bridge, sometimes by a boat, sometimes by a ford, at the village of Montes, by which very short route they say the journey from Bayonne to Bordeaux is made. The Leria is not the river which Ptolemy in book II calls the Sigmanes, and with whose mouth, placed between the mouths of the Adour at Bayonne and the Garonne flowing past Bordeaux, that whole Sigmas has utterly disappeared together with its name. For there is no other water between the Garonne and the Adour flowing into the Ocean that seems worthy of the name of river. Fronsiaca, Le Pais de Fronsac, is famous for the dignity of a marquisate. It takes its name from the town and castle of Fronsiacum, at whose confluence with the Dordogne Charlemagne laid the foundations of Libourne when he was defeating Hunold, Duke of Aquitaine, a warrior skilled in war.

units.la: Hæc de Burdigalensi Senescballia: sequitur Vasatensis, La Senescbaussée de Bazadois, vicinos habens alios Guiennæ Vasconiæque Populos. Ager hic ibi Frugum, Vini, Fructuum, Pecorumque fertilis: plerusque alioquin fabulosus, & Arenis fluens; quemadmodum eum describit Pontius Paullinus: Quique superba tua contemnis moenia Roma Consuli, arenosas non dedignare Vasatas.
units.tr: So much for the Senescalsy of Bordeaux. Next comes the Senescalsy of Vasatensis, La Senescbaussée de Bazadois, having as neighbours the other peoples of Guienne and Gascony. Its land is fertile in crops, wine, fruit and livestock, though otherwise for the most part barren and flowing with sand, just as Pontius Paulinus describes it: "You who scorn with contempt the proud walls of your Rome, do not disdain sandy Vasatae."

units.la: Item Sidonius Apollinaris lib. viii. Epistola xii ad Trigettium: Tantum te Vasatium Civitas non Cespitis impesita, sed Pulveri, tantum Syrticus Ager, ac vagum Solum, & volatiles Ventis alternantibus Arena sibi possident: ut te magnis flagitatum precibus, parvis separatum spatiis, multis exspectatum diebus attrahere Burdigalam non Potestates, non Amicitia, non optimata Vivarii Ostrea queant? an temporibus hibernis Vsarum te dubia suspendunt. Et quia solet Bigerricus turbo mobilium Aggerum Indicia confundere, quoddam vetere in Itinere terreno naufragium. Non potuit melius Solum Vasaticum describi. Quin & hodie totus ille Tractus Vasatium usque ad Flumen Aturrum patria Lingua vocant Incolae Landas, ut & alibi notavi, hoc est, deserta & inculta Loca. Hoc enim, inquit ad Ausonium Scaliger, propter arenosam Solis naturam, Arenosum Solum Syrtes vocabant temporibus Ausonianis, & Sidonius Agrum Syrticum dixit in verbis a me prolatis. Duas habet Dioeceses; Vasatensem & Aturensem. In Priore Metropolis est, quae olim Cossio Vassatum. Sic nominat Ausonius in Parentalibus, Carmine xxiv: Κοσσιον Ουασατεια Ptolemaeo: Vide quae supra dixi, ubi de Populis: Alijs Κασσιον scribitur; Civitas Vasatas, Itinerario, quod Burdigala ducit Hierosolymas; Vasatum Civitas Sidonio, ut jam audivimus, & Gregorio Turonensi lib. vi cap. xxi, cui & Vasatensis Vrbs eodem libro, cap. xvi, & lib. i. de Miraculis cap. xii & xiii. Vasate simpliciter Pontio Paullino in Eucharist. & Ammiano Marcellino: Basas pro Vasas Vasconice B pro V. Nam Galli Vasas vocant. Parvum opidum xx. fere jugerum, unius diei itinere à Burdigala: duorum, ab Aquis Tarbellicis. Inspecta curiosius Moenia antiquum esse loquuntur, & certare posse cum jam nominatis.
units.tr: Likewise Sidonius Apollinaris, book VIII, Epistle XII to Trygetius: "So much does the city of the Vasates hold you, not laid upon turf but upon dust, so much do the Syrtic field, the wandering soil and the sands blown about by the alternating winds possess it for themselves, that you, entreated with great prayers, separated by short distances, awaited for many days, cannot be drawn to Bordeaux by powers, by friendship, or by the choice oysters of Vivarium. Or do the doubtful Landes of the Usca hold you suspended in the winter season? And because the Bigerrian whirlwind is wont to confuse the signs of the moving mounds, some shipwreck happened on the old land-journey." The Vasatian soil could not have been described better. Indeed even today the inhabitants call that whole tract of the Vasates, as far as the river Adour, Landas in their native tongue, as I have noted elsewhere, that is, deserted and uncultivated places. For, says Scaliger on Ausonius, "because of the sandy nature of the soil, in Ausonian times they called sandy ground Syrtes, and Sidonius spoke of the Syrtic field in the words I have quoted."

units.la: Aturensis, Aturensium vel Atyrensium Civitas in libello Provinciarum, ab Flumine Atyro vel Aturro nomen retinet, sed depravatione Vasconica. Vocatur enim Atrensium Civitas vulgo Aire. Consulendae Iosephi Scaligeri Lectiones Ausonianae lib. ii. cap. vii. Senescalchalli Vasatensis Iurisdictio cis & ultra Garumnam vires exercet. Ad dextram sunt Fanum Basilia, Regula, ubi Arx valida, Monsignur, S. Ferme, Castel Muron, Geronde, Sauveterre, & Pagi non pauci ad Duranium usque: ad sinistram vero, Mont de Marsan, Castes, Geloux, & nonnulla alia.
units.tr: The Aturensis, Aturensium or Atyrensium Civitas in the list of Provinces keeps its name from the river Atyro or Aturro, but in a Basque corruption. It is called the Atrensium Civitas and commonly Aire. See Joseph Scaliger's Ausonian Lectures, book ii, chapter vii. The jurisdiction of the seneschal of Bazas extends on both sides of the Garonne. On the right are Fanum Basilia, Regula, where there is a strong citadel, Monsignur, S. Ferme, Castel Muron, Geronde, Sauveterre, and not a few villages as far as the Duranius. On the left are Mont de Marsan, Castes, Geloux, and some others.

units.la: Vasatensem Seneschalliam sequitur Lapurdensis. Lapurdenses Populi, ubi quondam fuerint, alibi notavi. Eorum Sedes Lapurdum, ut quibusdam placet, appellatur Notitiae Imperii, Pactionique inter Gunthramum & Childebertum Reges initae, cujus Exemplar notavi apud Gregorium Turonensem lib. i x. cap. x x. Hodie vulgo, Le Pais de Lapord, vel ut alij Labord; etiam Lorda & Lourda. Duas habet Dioeceses, Bayonam & Aquas Tarbellicas.
units.tr: The seneschalsy of Bazas is followed by Lapurdensis. Where the Lapurdenses peoples once lived, I have noted elsewhere. Their seat, Lapurdum, as some prefer, is named in the Notitia of the Empire and in the agreement made between the kings Gunthram and Childebert, a copy of which I noted in Gregory of Tours, book ix, chapter 20. Today it is commonly called Le Pais de Lapord, or by others Labord; also Lorda and Lourda. It has two dioceses, Bayonne and Aquas Tarbellicas.

units.la: Baiona vulgo Bayonne: Antiquis Baiona Lapurdensium in Tarbellis. Vrbs perantiqua, ut veterum Murorum indicat fabrica, in Radice sedens Pyrenaei, inque ripa Aturi, (qui mox cum Gravia maritimis ibi se miscet undis) Hispaniam spectante, quatuor fere millibus passuum ab Oceano. A Fois, ut antea obiter monui, nomen habere videtur. Primum enim non omnibus Baionam, sed nonnullis Botonam fuisse perhibent. Egregie est munita: quae, quum Anglorum jugum abjecisset, se in Karoli vii Francorum Regis fidem tradidit. Ejus Iurisdictio protenditur ultra Flumen Iron, usque ad Fanum D. Ioannis, cui cognomen de Luz, quod Franciae Regnum ab Hispania sejungit. Gubernatorem habet seu Provinciae Praefectum. Singulare est Baionae, quod Vrbem nemo ingrediatur Armatus, nisi Rex ipse, quique Regij Sanguinis: reliqui, cujuscumque dignitatis & loci, sua ad Inferiorem Vrbis partem Arma coguntur relinquere. Episcopali fulget dignitate. Episcopus Baionensis etiam Lapurdensis dicitur in Veteribus Episcopii Chartis. Aqua Tarbellica Antonino, quae Tarbella Ausonio; Tarbellorum aliis: Civitas Tarbella Vibio Sequestro: Aqua Augusta, Ἀκουαι Ἀυγουστα, Ptolemaeo lib. ii; Aquae simpliciter Itinerariae Tabulae: Hodie Aqs: & Aquensium Civitas Notitiae Provinciarum in Aquitania: L'Evesché d'Aqs. Erant, qui vel Tarbam Bigerronum vel Baionam esse volunt: nimisque argutantur, qui Ptolemaei Ἀκουων centent. Videndus omnino Iosephus Scaliger lib. i Ausonian. Lectio cap. vi, plene solideque probans, Aquensem hanc Aquas esse Tarbellicas, non aliam; non, quod maxime conatur evertere, Tarbam Bigerronum. Distat hoc opidum ab Oceano, extremum Pyrenæum adluente, non plus dici unius itinere. Parvum sed munitissimum; Vetustatem in Mœnibus non exiguam ostentans. Balneis nobilitatum. In medio Fons illi calidus, perpetuo fervens; Aquas (a quibus primum Loco nomen; accedentibus mox cum ab Gente, tum ab nescio quo Augusto, cognominibus) multas in propinquum Aturrum emittens. Habet quidem totus hic Tractus propius Pyrenæum multos alios Fontes Calidos, magis celebres hoc tempore, quod Valetudini conducere magis deprehendantur: verum Aquensem olim celeberrimum fuisse, argumento sunt vetusta Solia marmorea, quæ in Margine adhuc exstant. Cives Gregorio Turonensi & aliis Aquenses vocantur. Paullini Mater, quæ Aquensis vel ex Aquis Augustis erat, Stirpis Aquitanæ dicitur Ausonio in Parentalibus Carmine xxiv. Quo tempore Guienna parebat Anglis, Vrbs Nobilium dicta scribitur, quod ab xii Nobilibus regeretur, quorum unusquisque in ea Turrim habebebat suæ Genti cognominem.
units.tr: Baiona, commonly Bayonne; to the ancients Baiona Lapurdensium in Tarbellis. It is a very ancient city, as the construction of its old walls shows, sitting at the foot of the Pyrenees and on the bank of the Adour (which soon mingles there with the sea waters together with the Gave), facing Spain, about four miles from the ocean. It seems to have its name from Fois, as I noted earlier in passing. For they say that at first it was called not Baiona by everyone, but Botona by some. It is excellently fortified. When it had cast off the English yoke, it surrendered itself to the good faith of Charles VII, king of the Franks. Its jurisdiction extends beyond the river Iron, as far as the church of St John, which bears the surname de Luz, which separates the kingdom of France from Spain. It has a governor, or prefect of the province. It is remarkable at Bayonne that no one enters the city armed except the king himself and those of royal blood; all others, of whatever rank or place, are compelled to leave their arms at the lower part of the city. It shines with episcopal dignity. The bishop of Bayonne is also called the bishop of Lapurdum in the old charters of the bishopric. Aqua Tarbellica in Antoninus, which Ausonius calls Tarbella, and of the Tarbelli in others; Civitas Tarbella in Vibius Sequester; Aqua Augusta, Ἀκουαι Ἀυγουστα [Akouai Augousta] in Ptolemy, book ii; simply Aquae in the Itinerary Tables. Today Aqs, and the Aquensium Civitas of the Notitia of the Provinces in Aquitaine; L'Evesché d'Aqs. Some want it to be either Tarba of the Bigerrones or Baiona, and those who think it is Ptolemy's Ἀκουων [Akouōn] argue too subtly. Joseph Scaliger, book i of the Ausonian Lectures, chapter vi, must certainly be consulted; he proves fully and solidly that this Aquensis Aquas is the Tarbellicas, and no other, and not, as he especially tries to refute, Tarba of the Bigerrones. This town is not more than one day's journey from the ocean, which washes the far end of the Pyrenees. It is small but very well fortified, showing no little antiquity in its walls. It is famous for its baths. In the middle is a hot spring that boils constantly; it sends out many waters into the nearby Adour (from which the place first got its name, and afterwards surnames from the people and from some Augustus I know not whom). Indeed, this whole district nearer the Pyrenees has many other hot springs, more celebrated nowadays because they are found more useful for health; but that Aquensis was once very famous is shown by the ancient marble seats, which still stand on the edge. Gregory of Tours and others call the citizens Aquenses. The mother of Paulinus, who was Aquensis or ex Aquis Augustis, is called by Ausonius, in the Parentalia poem xxiv, of the Stirps Aquitana. At the time when Guienne obeyed the English, the city is written of as Urbs Nobilium, because it was governed by twelve nobles, each of whom had in it a tower named after his own family.

units.la: Quarta superat describenda Guiennæ Senescballia, Santonia, cujus Veteres Incolas alibi indicavi Santones. Habet ad Septemtrionem Pictones, ad Orientem Eduilmenses & Petrocorios; ad Meridiem Garumnam, ad Occidentem Oceanum. Olim latiores Santonibus fuisse Terminos, non obscure colligitur ex Auctore Ephemeridum de Bello Gallico; qui scribit eos non longe ab Tolosatium Finibus abesse; illiisque, in magno illo contra Cæsarem Bello, Concilium Principum Gallorum xii millia hominum imperasse, quum octo tantum millia Pictonibus, Lemovicibus decem fuerint imperata. Vulgo Le Pais de Saintonge. Metropolis vernacule Saintes, terminatione pluralis ut reliqua fere, quæ Gallis in S desinunt; cuius Classis sunt Paris, Reims, & similia. Non dubium, quin Mediolanum sit Xantonum vel Santonum: Mediolanum Santonum, Antonino, Itinere à Burdigala Augustodunum; Mediolanum Santon, corrupte in Itineraria Tabula: Mediolanum Straboni & Ptolemæo: Mediolanum Stephano. Quid ni? Antiquitatem testantur varia. Primo multæ priscorum Mœnium adhuc manentes hic ibi particulæ: Deinde nobiles extra Muruia versus Occidentem Amphitheatri, Petrocoriensi quam Burdigalensi similioris, Reliquiæ: Tertio in Ponte Carantoni, Urbem præterfluentus, antiquæ Structuræ cum Inscriptione duplici Arcus: Postrema non exigua, qua Mediolano Iter Angenacum ducit, Aquæductus Rudera. Urbs etiam Santonum appellatur Ausonio Epistola xxiii, & Lucano, ni fallor, lib. i. Santones item eidem Ausonio Epistola xiv; & xviii; ut & forte Tacito lib. v Histor. Augusti Sidonioque Apollinari lib. viii. Epist. vi. Ab hoc Mediolano nomen ei fuisse impositum, quod Galli, ut testatur Livius, in Agro Insubrum condiderunt, per est vero simile, ne dicam, ut Calaubono adsentiar, certum. Hujus Urbis Agrum si diligentius inspexisset Strabo, pro arenoso & sterili, præpinguem Frugumque omnium feracissimum dixisset. De Saxonum in Santonum Solum Incursionibus, legendus Sidonius lib. viii. Epist. vi. Episcopalis est Civitas, cujus Præsules Belletoretius numerat lxiii; postremum nominans Tristanum Bisetum. Mediolanum, vel, ut quidam Latine scribentes vocant, Santoniam sequitur Rupella, vernacule La Rochelle. Urbs non antiqua, ab Franciæ Regibus exstructa ob Portus commoditatem. Est enim ibi fidissima Navium Statio. Viribus humanis inexpugnabilis creditur. Nulli sane cedit. Meridionale fere Latus insignis Oceani Sinus; adversum Paludes Locaque Vlignosa (quæ conficiendo Sali non inidonea, Salantes vulgo dicuntur) munivit: reliqua Muri, Foveæ, Turres, validaque Propugnacula, quibus omnibus sua sunt Cognomina, mirandum in modum firmant; ut Tormentis bellicis nullus fere sit ad eam aditus. Libera Civitas, quamque multis & magnis Immunitatibus atque Privilegiis ornarunt retro Principes; cum aliis, quæ rei Maritimæ faciunt promovendæ, tum quod Cives ex suo Corpore Maiorem Scabinosque legant, qui Urbis Politiæ præsint; quod nullam Peregrinorum gubernationem admittere cogantur; quod nullis Militum Præsidiis divexentur: quod denique Arcis ab suis Pomerijs arcendæ jus habeant: quorum pleraque consequuti anno cIↄ cccLxii, quum, exturbato Anglorum præsidio, se Francorum Regi Karolo v submitterent. Gravem obsidionem passi sunt anno cIↄ lxxiii ab Henrico Valesio Andegavensium Duce, qui Rex postea Poloniæ Franciæque, de qua nulli non Historiographi. Reliquæ Santonum Urbes & opida vulgo nominantur, S. Jean d'Angely, S. Ioannes de Angeria; Lorgairo, Archant, Pont Lonbleze, Lobletz, Talleboure, Iarnac, Barbesieux, arcipotens, Rupefocaldios agnoscens Dominos, Iosac, & alia. Bronage Vicus est, Belgis alijsque Salipetis notissimus.
units.tr: The fourth Seneschalsy of Guienne to be described is Santonia, whose ancient inhabitants, the Santones, I have indicated elsewhere. It has the Pictones to the north, the Eduilmenses and Petrocorii to the east, the Garonne to the south, and the ocean to the west. That the Santones' boundaries were once wider is clearly gathered from the author of the Ephemerides on the Gallic War, who writes that they were not far from the borders of the Tolosates; and that in that great war against Caesar the council of the leading Gauls levied twelve thousand men from them, whereas only eight thousand were levied from the Pictones and ten thousand from the Lemovices. Commonly Le Pais de Saintonge. The metropolis in the vernacular is Saintes, with the plural ending found in almost all the others that end in S in French, of which class are Paris, Reims, and similar names. There is no doubt that Mediolanum is Xantonum or Santonum: Mediolanum Santonum in Antoninus, on the road from Burdigala to Augustodunum; Mediolanum Santon, corrupted, in the Itinerary Table; Mediolanum in Strabo and Ptolemy; Mediolanum in Stephanus. Why not? Various things attest its antiquity. First, many remains of the ancient walls still stand here and there. Second, the remains of a noble amphitheatre to the west outside the walls, more like that of Petrocorii than that of Burdigala. Third, on the bridge of Charente, which flows past the city, there is an arch of old construction with a double inscription. Last, and no small thing, there are the ruins of an aqueduct along which the road from Mediolanum leads to Angeac. The city is also called Santonum by Ausonius in Epistle xxiii, and by Lucan, unless I am mistaken, in book i; the Santones likewise by the same Ausonius in Epistles xiv and xviii; and perhaps also by Tacitus in book v of the Histories, by the Augustan History, and by Sidonius Apollinaris in book viii, Epistle vi. That the name Mediolanum was given to it by the Gauls, who founded it in the land of the Insubres, as Livy testifies, is likely, not to say certain, though I do not agree with Casaubon on this. If Strabo had examined the territory of this city more carefully, he would not have called it sandy and barren, but very fat and most fertile in all crops. On the Saxon incursions into the land of the Santones, read Sidonius, book viii, Epistle vi. It is an episcopal city, whose prelates Belleforest counts as sixty-three, naming last Tristan Bisetus. Following Mediolanum, or Santonia, as some who write in Latin call it, comes Rupella, in the vernacular La Rochelle. It is not an ancient city, built by the kings of France on account of the convenience of its harbour, for there is a very safe station for ships there. It is believed to be impregnable to human forces, and certainly yields to none. Its south side is protected by a notable inlet of the ocean, and against the marshes and muddy places (which are not unsuitable for making salt, and are commonly called Salantes) by a wall; the remaining walls, ditches, towers and strong bulwarks, each with its own name, make it remarkably secure, so that there is almost no approach to it for siege engines. It is a free city, adorned by former princes with many great immunities and privileges, both those that promote maritime affairs and the fact that the citizens elect from their own body a mayor and aldermen to preside over the government of the city; that they are not compelled to admit any outside administration; that they are not harassed by any military garrisons; and finally that they have the right to keep off the citadel from their own boundaries. They obtained most of these in the year 1362, when, the English garrison having been driven out, they submitted themselves to Charles V, king of the Franks. They suffered a grievous siege in the year 1573 from Henry of Valois, Duke of Anjou, who afterwards became king of Poland and France, which all historians mention. The other cities and towns of the Santones are commonly named S. Jean d'Angely, S. Ioannes de Angeria; Lorgairo, Archant, Pont Lonbleze, Lobletz, Talleboure, Jarnac, Barbesieux, a powerful place, acknowledging the lords of Rochefoucauld, Jonzac, and others. Bronage is a village, very well known to the Belgians and other salt-makers.

units.la: CAP. XXXV.
units.tr: CHAP. XXXV.

units.la: Cadurcium.
units.tr: Cadurcium.

units.la: DE Tribus Provincijs, quæ Integre Burdigalensi parent Parlamento, verba feci; succedunt quæ Tolosano Cadurcium, Rutenium, Languedokium.
units.tr: I have dealt with the three provinces that wholly obey the Parlement of Bordeaux. Next come those that belong to Toulouse: Cadurcium, Rutenium, Languedokium.

units.la: CADVRCIVM cingunt Petrocorij, Nitiobriges, Ruteni, Arverni & Lemovices. Regio est montibus innexa. Vulgo Querci; vel, ut alijs pronunciatur, Crecy.
units.tr: The Petrocorii, Nitiobriges, Ruteni, Arverni and Lemovices surround Cadurcium. It is a region bound by mountains. Commonly it is called Querci, or, as others pronounce it, Crecy.

units.la: Habitarunt olim Cadurci, quos, præter Plinium lib. iv cap. xix (an & lib. xviii cap. 1? nondum liquet) cum infinitis alijs Galliæ Populis, celebrat Cæsar lib. vii, cui & Eleutheri, Ἐλεύθεροι, id est, Liberi cognominantur. Sic enim vocem illam scribens accipio: non adsentiens novos inde fabricantibus Populos. Sic apud eundem Cæsarem post paucula verba Suessones Eleutheri prænominantur, ut dixi cap. xx. Ita alij multi apud Plinium Populi vocantur Liberi.
units.tr: The Cadurci once inhabited this region. Besides Pliny (book 4, chapter 19; whether also book 18, chapter 1, is not yet clear), they are mentioned along with countless other peoples of Gaul by Caesar in book 7, and they are also surnamed Eleutheri, Ἐλεύθεροι, that is, Free. For this is how I understand that word as written there, not agreeing with those who thereby invent new peoples. Thus in the same Caesar, a few words later, the Suessones are given the prefix Eleutheri, as I said in chapter 20. In the same way many other peoples in Pliny are called Liberi.

units.la: Duas habet Diœceses, Doveonam Cadurcorum & Montalbanum. Δυήονα Ptolemæo nota; pro qua Ducona vitiose Interpretibus. Cahors vulgo, ad Lothum Fluvium. Divona dicitur quibusdam doctis Viris. Certe, quocumque modo scribenda, Cadurcorum esse Metropolin censent Iosephus Scaliger suis ad me Litteris, Vinetus ad Ausonium, & alij. Iustus Lipsius, ne quid celem, in aureo de Amphitheatris Libello, Doveonam arbitratur esse Pagum, qui vulgo Dore, plus minus diei mediæ itinere distantem ab Ligeri, parte ea, qua ab Andegavis in Pictones fit iter. Consule quæ dixi cap. xxvii. Adsonat quidem Pagi nomen: sed sic Doveona non posset esse ex mente Ptolemæi Cadurcorum Metropolis, quæ ab eo loco plus lx leucis dirimitur. Aliud addo. Cum Doveona Ptolemæi, si quidem vulgo Cahors, non potest idem esse, quod putant magni viri, Aunedonacum Antonini, vel Aucdonacum Tabulæ Peutingerianæ, in Itinere, quod Burdigala ducit Augustodunum. Inter enim Aunedonacum ibi & Mediolanium Santonum millia passuum scribuntur xvii inter Doveonam autem & Mediolanium, id est inter opida, quæ vernacule Cahors & Santes, xl circiter sunt leucæ, quæ constituunt centum, & quæ excurrunt, passuum millia. Accedit & illud, quod Cadurcorum Metropolis tanto intervallo vergat Ortum versus, ut in iter illud Burdigala Augustodunum incidere non possit. Ego igitur censeo, Aunedonacum esse opidum illud, quod vulgo Aulnay, Mediolanio Santonum distans versus Septemtrionem paullo amplius sex leucis. Quædam obiter dixi in fine cap. xxviii. Cadurcorum autem Metropolin designat Ausonius libro Professorum, Carmine xviii, de Exsuperio Tolosæ Rhetore: Decedens placidos mores, tranquillaque Vita Tempora pradivesfinistis Sede Cadurca,
units.tr: It has two dioceses, Doveona of the Cadurci and Montauban. Doveona is known to Ptolemy as Δυήονα [Dyēona]; translators have wrongly rendered it Ducona. Today it is Cahors, on the river Lot. Some learned men call it Divona. Whatever the right spelling, Joseph Scaliger, in his letters to me, Vinetus on Ausonius, and others hold that it was the metropolis of the Cadurci. To be honest, Justus Lipsius, in his golden little book on amphitheatres, thinks that Doveona was a district, commonly called Dore, about half a day's journey from the Loire, on the side where the road runs from Angers into Poitou. See what I said in chapter 27. The name of the district is similar, but Doveona could not, on Ptolemy's reckoning, be the metropolis of the Cadurci, since that place lies more than sixty leagues from that spot. I add another point. If Ptolemy's Doveona, which is today Cahors, cannot be the same as what great men think is Aunedonacum in Antoninus, or Aucdonacum in the Peutinger Table, on the road that leads from Bordeaux to Autun. For between Aunedonacum there and Mediolanum of the Santones the distance is written as 17 miles; but between Doveona and Mediolanum, that is, between the towns now called Cahors and Saintes, there are about 40 leagues, which make 100 and more miles. Moreover, the metropolis of the Cadurci lies so far to the east that it cannot fall on that road from Bordeaux to Autun. I therefore think that Aunedonacum is the town now called Aulnay, a little more than six leagues north of Mediolanum of the Santones. I touched on some of these points in passing at the end of chapter 28. The metropolis of the Cadurci is indicated by Ausonius in his book of Professors, poem 18, on Exsuperius the rhetor of Toulouse: Leaving behind gentle manners and a peaceful life, in the rich seat of Cadurca.

units.la: Altera Diœcesis Montalbanum est, hodie Montaulban, S. Theodard de Montaulban. Vrbs, Arcem habens, ad Tarnum Fluvium, stratum hic Ponte, cujus pars media Languedokiæ est Ditionis. Sunt & alia Opida, quæ vulgo Burelle, Nazareth, Soullac, Gourdan, Martel, & alia.
units.tr: The other diocese is Montalbanum, today Montauban, and St Theodard of Montauban. It is a city with a citadel, on the river Tarn, spanned here by a bridge, the middle part of which belongs to the jurisdiction of Languedoc. There are also other towns, commonly called Burelle, Nazareth, Soullac, Gourdan, Martel, and others.

units.la: Fuit prope Opidum Martellum in Finibus Cadurcorum, ut Auctor quoque notat lib. viii. de Bello Gallico, Vxellodunum, nomen retinens: Vocatur & Vffoldun, & Le Puech d'Vfoldun, id est Podium Vxelloduni, quod in editissimo & valde prærupto loco situm. Horrendum est adspectu Præcipitium. Multæ sunt ibi Reliquiæ Vetustatis venerandæ. Quotidie ab Arantibus Numismata Romana effodiuntur. Vix reperias Rusticum, qui de Loco interrogatus non statim respondeat Castrum Vxellodunum illud ab Cæsare magnis Operibus fuisse oppugnatum Auctor, quem dixi, sic inter alia: Flumen infimam Vallem dividebat, qua pene totum montem cingebat, in quo positum erat præruptum undique Vxellodunum. Hoc avertere loci natura prohibebat. Sic enim imis radicibus Montis ferebatur, ut nullam in partem, depressis fossis, derivari posset. Flumen, cujus nomen tacet auctor, est quod vulgo Dordonia. Idem paullo post: Sub ipsum ipsum Opidi murum magnus Fons prorumpebat, ab ea parte, qua fere pedum trecentorum intervallo Flaminis circuitu vacabat. Hoc Fonte prohiberi posse Opidanos quum optarent reliqui, Cæsar unus videret, non sine magno periculo, èregione ejus. Vineas agere adversus Montem & Ageres struere cœpit, magno cum labore, & continua dimicatione. Fontem hunc, cujus usum Obsellis interclusisse scribuntur hic Romani, hodieque ostendunt Adcolæ. Si uspiam Scriptores hujus ævi in notandis veterum locorum appellationibus hariolati sunt, hic vero unus est locus; de quo melius fuisset illos tacuisse.
units.tr: Near the town of Martel, in the territory of the Cadurci, there was (as the author of the Gallic War also notes in book 8) Uxellodunum, keeping its name. It is also called Uffoldun, and Le Puech d'Uffoldun, that is, Podium Uxelloduni, the hill of Uxellodunum, which lies on a very high and steeply broken spot. The precipice is dreadful to look at. There are many remains of venerable antiquity there. Every day the farmers dig up Roman coins. You can hardly find a countryman who, when asked about the place, does not at once reply that this is the castle Uxellodunum, which Caesar attacked with great works. The author I mentioned says, among other things: "A river divided the lowest valley, which almost wholly encircled the mountain on which steep Uxellodunum stood on every side. Nature of the place prevented its diversion, for it flowed so at the foot of the mountain that it could not be turned into any other channel by digging trenches. The river, whose name the author does not mention, is what is commonly called the Dordogne." The same author, a little later: "Right beneath the town wall a great spring burst forth, on the side where, for about three hundred feet, the ground was clear by the circuit of the flank. When the rest of the townsmen wished that this spring could be cut off, Caesar alone saw how it might be done, though not without great danger, from its opposite side. He began to drive forward siege sheds against the hill and to build mounds, with great labour and continual fighting." This spring, whose use the Romans are said to have cut off from the besieged, the locals still point out today. If any writers of this age have guessed at the names of ancient places, here is one case in which they would have done better to keep silent.

units.la: Rutenium.
units.tr: Rutenium.

units.la: CADVRCIO versus Ortum conjacet RVTENIVM; reliqua claudunt Languedokij, Arverni, aliique Conregionales Populi. Vulgo Rouargois, La Senefchaussée de Rouargne.
units.tr: Cadurcio lies to the east, and Ruthenium lies to the north; the remaining sides are bounded by Languedoc, the Arverni, and other neighbouring peoples. Commonly called Rouargois, La Sénéchaussée de Rouergue.

units.la: Sedes olim Rutenorum. Ruteni in Itineraria Tabula, apud Sidonium lib. vii. Epist. vi, Plinium lib. iv. cap. xix, item lib. iii cap iv (nisi alij sint à Prioribus) & Cæsarem lib. i. & vii variis locis, ubi & Rutheni scribuntur, qui Parmeni Ptolemæo.
units.tr: The former seat of the Ruteni. The Ruteni are named in the Itinerary Table, in Sidonius book vii, letter vi, in Pliny book iv, chapter xix, likewise book iii, chapter iv (unless these are others from the earlier writers), and in Caesar book i and book vii in various places, where they are also written Rutheni; they correspond to Parmenius of Ptolemy.

units.la: Senefchallia Rutenensis duas complectitur Dioeceses, cum Vabris, Segodunum Rutenorum; Σεγόδουνον Ptolemæo, vulgo Rodas; Rutena apud Turonensem: Vrbs, quæ multa ab Gothis, Francis, Saracenis passa, tandem in Francorum venit ditionem. Gregor. Turonensis lib. ii. Histor. cap. xxxvi & seq. & de Vita Patrum cap. iii. Sunt & alia Opida: Ville Franche de Rouargne, Gordon, Estanges, Espeiron.
units.tr: The Seneschalsy of Rouergue comprises two dioceses, together with Vabres. Segodunum of the Ruteni, Σεγόδουνον in Ptolemy, commonly Rodez; Rutena in Gregory of Tours: a city which, having suffered much at the hands of the Goths, the Franks and the Saracens, at last came under the rule of the Franks (Gregory of Tours, book ii of the Histories, chapter xxxvi and following, and On the Life of the Fathers, chapter iii). There are also other towns: Villefranche de Rouergue, Gordon, Estaing, Espeyron.

units.la: CAPVT XXXVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXVII.

units.la: Languedokium.
units.tr: Languedoc.

units.la: RESTAT in Tolosani Parlamenti Iurisdictione Major Superioribus, Cadurcio Rutenioque, Portio, LANGVEDOKIVM.
units.tr: There remains, within the jurisdiction of the Parlement of Toulouse, the greater province of Languedoc, with Quercy and Rouergue and Périgord, which I shall describe later.

units.la: Provinciæ nomen; quod Incolæ, reliquis Gallis pro Ya vel Ita Latinorum, Oui proferentibus: Oc dicant. Quum capite xv Romanensem Galliæ Idiotismum, ex litteris Nobilissimi Viri Iosephi Scaligeri, in duo summa diducerem fastigia, Francium, & Tectosagicum sive Provinciale: Francici duas feci Species, quæ vulgo
units.tr: This is the name of the province. The inhabitants say Oc where other Gauls say Oui, as the Latins say Ya or Ita. In chapter 15, when I divided the Romance idiom of Gaul into two main branches, on the authority of the most noble Joseph Scaliger, namely Francium and Tectosagicum or Provinciale, I made two species of the French branch, which are commonly called Langue d'Oui and Langue d'Oc.

units.la: Oo Langue d'Oui, & Langue d'Oc. In Posteriore plene est Provinciæ Nomenclatura: ut Regio quasi sit, quæ huic Linguæ dicata & consecrata. Nugantur, qui aliam quærunt Appellationis rationem; inter quos maxime, qui Gothos hic somniant, Languedokum scribentes nominari, quasi Langothiam, id est, Terram Gothicam: quo nihil dici potest absurdius. Morboniam tales. Stupiditas ipsa non posset stupidius. Scimus ex Sidonij lib. iii. Epist. ad Avitum, Gregorio Turonensi lib. viii, cap. xxx & aliis locis, Gothos olim hic habitasse; sed Provinciam ab iis dictam, sanus nemo credet. Quum vero Lingua Oc latissime pateret, Regio, quæ delineanda nobis præ manibus, hoc nomine præcipue notata est, quod Sedes ibi esset Regiminis Linguæ Oc. Nam Regnum Franciæ ante ducentos annos in duo summa Regimina dividebatur; in Linguam Oui, cujus caput Lutetia; & Linguam Oc, cujus caput alternis erat nunc Tolosa, nunc Mompelius. Franci hoc Regimen vocabant etiam Gubernamentum Linguæ Torte: ita nominantes Linguam Oc, quam illi putant esse Distortam, Suam vero Rectam. Habent Linguam Oc loquentes ad Occidentem Vasconnes, interfluente Garumna; ad Caurum, Cadurces: ad Septemtrionem, Arvernos & Forenses, ad Orientem, Delphinates & Provinciales, sic, ut totus Rodanus sit Languedokiæ Ditionis, & sub Parlamento Tolosano; Meridionale denique Latus partim pulsat Mare Mediterraneum, quod Gallicum ibi audit; partim Montes claudunt Pyrenæi: quem Tractum sic finit Strabo lib. iv: Ἐντὸς δὲ τῶν ἄκρων, ἐν ᾗ ἐστι τὰ Πορτμίω Τρόπαια, ἔχει Ἰδηρίας ἐσχάτων. Ἐν δὲ ... Ἐκ Νεμαύσου δὲ ... Regio est nobilissima. Scriptoribusque Romanis cum primis celebrata: quæ causa, quod Veteres ejus Incolæ multo nominentur numerosiores, quam reliquarum Galliæ partium. Eos, anteaquam, quo modo sic nunc habeat Regio, doceam, animus est recensere paucis, non servato curiosius ordine.
units.tr: The name of the province is fully explained by the second of these, so that the region seems to be the one dedicated and consecrated to this language. Those who look for another derivation talk nonsense, and above all those who dream here of the Goths, writing that it is named Languedoc as if it were Langothia, that is, the land of the Goths. Nothing can be more absurd than this. Such people are mad; stupidity itself could not be more stupid. We know from Sidonius, Letters book 3 to Avitus, from Gregory of Tours book 8, chapter 30, and from other places, that the Goths once lived here, but no sane person will believe that the province was named after them. Since the language Oc was spoken very widely, the region we now have before us was marked especially by this name, because the seat of the government of the language Oc was there. For about two hundred years before, the kingdom of France was divided into two main governments: the language Oui, whose capital was Lutetia, and the language Oc, whose capital was alternately Toulouse and Montpellier. The French called this government the government of the Langue Torte, thus naming the language Oc as distorted, which they think it is, while their own was right. Those who speak the language Oc are the Vascones to the west, along the river Garonne; the Cadurci to the north-west; to the north the Arverni and the Forenses; to the east the Dauphinois and the Provençals. So the whole Rhône belongs to the jurisdiction of Languedoc and under the Parlement of Toulouse. Finally, the southern side is washed in part by the Mediterranean, which is called the Gallic Sea there, and in part closed off by the Pyrenees. Strabo, book 4, marks the limits of this tract thus: Ἐντὸς δὲ τῶν ἄκρων, ἐν ᾗ ἐστι τὰ Πορτμίω Τρόπαια, ἔχει Ἰδηρίας ἐσχάτων [Within the headlands, where the trophies of Pompey are, it has the furthest parts of Iberia]. Ἐν δὲ ... Ἐκ Νεμαύσου δὲ ... [And ... From Nemausus ...]. It is a very noble region, and celebrated above all by the Roman writers. The reason is that its ancient inhabitants are named as much more numerous than those of the other parts of Gaul. I intend to review these briefly, without following a very careful order, before I teach how the region now stands.

units.la: Sedes igitur hic suas olim habuisse leguntur Volca & Arecomici & Tectosages, Septimani, Decumani, Atacini, Tolosates, Gabali, Albigenses, Velauni, Consoranni, Helvij, Nemausenses, Aletenses, Beterienses, Agathenses, Lutevani, Magalonenses, Sontiates. Volcarum Nomen in primis hic magnum, quod varie scribi reperio. Nam qui Volcæ Cæsari, Livio, Plinio, Stilio, Melæ, alijs, Οὐόλκαι autem Straboni & Ptolemæo: in quibusdam Cæsaris Codicibus Volgæ dicuntur; Dionysio Halicarnassæo Οὐάλκαι: Belca Ausonio in Tolosæ Urbis Delineatione. Quod ad Volgas, magnam scimus cognationem inter γ & κ, Græcorum litteras: Dionysij Οὐάλκας, in morbo cubare censeo, restituendosque saltem Οὐάλκας. In Belcis Ausonij varie laboratur: Versus in postrema Editione sic habet: Vsque ad Tentosagos primaevo nomine Belgas;
units.tr: Here, then, the following are read as having once had their seats: the Volcae, the Arecomici and the Tectosages, the Septimani, the Decumani, the Atacini, the Tolosates, the Gabali, the Albigenses, the Velauni, the Consoranni, the Helvii, the Nemausenses, the Aletenses, the Beterienses, the Agathenses, the Lutevani, the Magalonenses, the Sontiates. The name of the Volcae is first and foremost here, and I find it written in various ways. Those who are called Volcae by Caesar, Livy, Pliny, Silius, Mela and others are called Οὐόλκαι [Ouolkai] by Strabo and Ptolemy. In some manuscripts of Caesar they are called Volgae; Dionysius of Halicarnassus has Οὐάλκαι [Oualkai]; Ausonius in his description of the city of Toulouse has Belca. As for Volgae, we know there is a strong kinship between the Greek letters γ and κ; I think the Οὐάλκας [Oualkas] of Dionysius is sick and should at least be restored to Οὐάλκας [Oualkas]. The reading of Belcae in Ausonius is confused. In the latest edition the verse reads thus: Vsque ad Tentosagos primaevo nomine Belgas;

units.la: Testatur doctissimus Vir Elias Vinetus in quibusdam Exemplaribus esse, Panaque nomina Belgas;
units.tr: The most learned man Elias Vinetus testifies that some copies have Panaque nomina Belgas;

units.la: In aliis autem, Paganaque nomina Belgas: Emendat Beatus Rhenanus lib. i. rerum Germ. Germanaque nomina Belgas. Legerat enim lib. ii. Ephemerid. Belli Gallici, Cæsarem ab Remis didicisse, plerosque Belgas ab Germanis ortos, Renumque antiquitus traductos propter loci fertilitatem ibi consedisse: Gallos autem, qui ea loca incolebant, expulisse. Ingeniose quidem, ut multa alia: sed quid conjectura illa ad Tectosages, Galliæque Narbonensis Fines, quos ibi regit Ausonius? Iosephus Scaliger lib. i. Ausonianar. Lect. cap. xxiii legit, Paganaque nomina Belcas; & quid Pagana sint nomina, quidque Pagi, docte explicat. Non improbæ nihilominus notæ censendi sunt illi Codices, qui præferunt, Primaevo nomine Belcas. Nam Belcæ, si quidem ita scripserit Ausonius, homo Gallus, forte ex genuina Incolarum pronunciatione, idem omnino sunt cum reliquorum Volcis: quorum nomen hodie in ore Vulgi nusquam agnoscitur, nisi quis velit in Belgarum (modo Belcæ Ausonio sint, ut dixi, qui ceteris Volcæ servari, quæ nunc vernacule ea Galliæ Narbonensis vel Languedokij pars, ut notat Vinetus, cujus princeps est Nemausus. Recte autem Ausonius Teutosagos, qui Tectosages alijs, primaevo nomine Belcas, canit: iudicans eos Belcas vel Volcas prænominatos. Volca enim duplices erant, Arecomici & Tectosages. Qui Arecomici Cæsari & Plinio: Ἀρεκόμικοι scribuntur Ptolemaeo,
units.tr: while others have Paganaque nomina Belgas: Beatus Rhenanus, book 1 of his Rerum Germanicarum, emends it to Germanaque nomina Belgas. He had read in book 2 of the Ephemerides of the Gallic War that Caesar learned from the Remi that most of the Belgae were descended from the Germans, and had been brought across the Rhine on account of the fertility of the place, and had settled there, driving out the Gauls who lived in those parts. This is clever, as are many of his ideas, but what has that conjecture to do with the Tectosages and the limits of Gallia Narbonensis, which Ausonius describes here? Joseph Scaliger, book 1 of his Ausonian Readings, chapter 23, reads Paganaque nomina Belcas, and learnedly explains what pagana names are, and what pagi are. Nevertheless, those manuscripts which give Primaevo nomine Belcas must be regarded as not unsound. For Belcae, if Ausonius really wrote that, a Gaul, perhaps from the genuine pronunciation of the inhabitants, are altogether the same as the rest of the Volcae, whose name is nowhere recognised today on the lips of the common people, unless someone wishes to keep it in the Belgae (provided, as I said, that the Belcae of Ausonius are the Volcae of the others). In the vernacular, this part of Gallia Narbonensis or Languedoc, of which Nemausus is the chief city, is called ... as Vinetus notes. Ausonius rightly sings of the Teutosagi, whom others call Tectosages, as Belcas by their earliest name, judging that they were named in advance Belcae or Volcae. For the Volcae were of two kinds, the Arecomici and the Tectosages. The Arecomici are so named by Caesar and Pliny; Ptolemy writes Ἀρεκόμικοι [Arekomikoi],

units.la: Fines, mæro, Ἆγκομικοὶ, & non semel Ἆγκομικοὶ Straboni lib. iv, qui eos maximum incolere spatium scribit, cuique Ἆγκομικοὶ ipsorum ἡ Ναρβών. Hi olim, ubi nunc, ut suis ad me Litteris monet Nobilissimus Vir Iosephus Scaliger, Nemausus, Vzetenses, Magalonenses, & Bitterrae. Civitates Nemausensium, Magalonensium, & Beterrensium, item Castrum Vzetense ponit Notitia Provinciarum in Viennensi 11; hodie, Les Evesches de Nimes, Montpeliers, Beziers & Fesz. Qui Tectosages Plinio lib. v, Pomponio, Melx lib. ii, Τεκτοσάγες Straboni; Tectosagi vocantur eidem Plinio lib. iii, Livio lib. xxxviii, nec non Iustino, ex lib. xxxii Trogi Pompei, cujus Majorum hic fuit Patria, ut ipse ait lib. xliii. VOLCÆ TECTOSAGI. Teutosagi autem, ut jam vidimus, Autonio. Τεκτοσάγες est apud Stephanum, ut Ἆγκομικοὶ, ἎσΦαξ: quibus subscribit, Τεκτοσάγες, Ἐ͂ν⊗· Γαλατικόν. Εὐρεῖν Τεκτοσάγες & Ἐ͂νᾶ. καὶ Τεκτοσάγαι, &c. Inepte faciunt, qui apud Caesarem lib. vii. de Bello Gallico, & lib. i. de Bello Civili, distinctionem inter Volcas & Arecomicos ponunt: ineptius, qui Copulam apud Ptolemaeum interjiciunt, cum inter Volcas & Tectosages, tum inter Volcas & Arecomicos; ineptissime, qui in ejusdem Caesaris Ephemeridum vii legunt Cadurcosque ad Fines Volcarum Arecomicorumque depopulabundos misit, contra Membranarum fidem & auctoritatem, in quis, Arecomicorum depopulabundos. Non enim duo, sed unus Populus, cum Volcae Arecomici, tum Volcae Tectosages. Tectosages autem Arecomicis fuerunt celebriores, à quibus Colonias in Asiam, Pannoniam, Germaniamque ductas, scribunt Caesar, Livius, Iustinus, Strabo, Florus, alii; apud quos de antiqua Gentis virtute, Rebusque praeclare gestis, multa. Tectosages apud Plinium tenent eam Galliae partem, quae est inter Pyrenaeos & Cebennam: Pomponius Principem Tectosagum Urbem Tolosam appellat; Iustinus antiquam Tectosagorum Patriam: apud Ptolemaeum Tectosagum Urbes, praesertim Mediterraneae, nominantur Illiberis, Ruscino, Tolosa Colonia, Cessero, Carcaso, Bestiva, Narbo Colonia. Tectosages igitur quondam, ubi nunc praecipue Carcasso & Tolosa: quae mens, ut aliis, sic etiam Iosepho Scaligero. Ex quibus omnibus liquet, Volcae habitasse ad alteram tantum Rodani ripam; licet in utraque eos constituat Livius lib. xxi. Arecomicorum pars fuerunt Septumani, Galliae Narbonensis Populi apud Plinium lib. iii. cap. iv, & Melam lib. ii. cap. v, qui eorum Urbem faciunt Biterrae, & Biteram: Bitteras & Biteras lego in Libris melioribus. De ea post. Septumanorum etiam mentio in Imperii Notitia. Eorum Regio Septumania, Sidonio lib. iii, Epist. i, Eginartho in Vita Karoli Magni, Gregorio Turonensi lib. viii. cap. xxviii, & xxx, item lib. ix. cap. vii, Aimoino lib. iv. cap. xxciv, Vuardo xi. Kal. April. Ionae Aurelianensi lib. i, Petro Atverno Cluniacensi cap. i, & aliis. Nomen proculdubio ab vii. Legionis Mulitibus, quibus sua ibi fuerunt Praesidia. Meminit, ni fallor, Inscriptio, quam Dianij in Hispania extare scribit ex Apiano Martinus Smetius:
units.tr: and Strabo, book 4, more than once writes Ἀγκομικοὶ [Ankomikoi], who says they inhabited a very large territory, whose chief city was Narbo, Ναρβών [Narbon]. Formerly these people lived where now, as the most noble Joseph Scaliger tells me in his letters, the cities of Nîmes, Uzès, Maguelone and Béziers are. The Notitia of the Provinces, in the Viennese province, lists the cities of the Nemausenses, Magalonenses and Beterrenses, and also the castle of Uzès; today they are the bishoprics of Nîmes, Montpellier, Béziers and Agde. The Tectosages are called so by Pliny, book 5, by Pomponius, by Mela, book 2, and by Strabo as Τεκτοσάγες [Tektosages]; they are called Tectosagi by the same Pliny, book 3, by Livy, book 38, and also by Justin, from book 32 of Trogus Pompeius, whose ancestors came from this place, as he himself says in book 43. VOLCAE TECTOSAGI. Teutosagi, as we have already seen, is the name used by Ausonius. Τεκτοσάγες [Tektosages] is in Stephanus, as are Ἀγκομικοὶ [Ankomikoi] and ἄσφαξ [asphax]; to these he adds Τεκτοσάγες [Tektosages], ... Galatian. Εὐρεῖν Τεκτοσάγες & Ἐ͂νᾶ [Heurein Tektosages kai Ena], and Τεκτοσάγαι [Tektosagai], etc. They act foolishly who set a distinction between the Volcae and the Arecomici in Caesar, book 7 of the Gallic War and book 1 of the Civil War. Even more foolishly act those who insert a conjunction in Ptolemy, both between the Volcae and the Tectosages and between the Volcae and the Arecomici. Most foolish of all are those who read in the seventh book of the same Caesar's Ephemerides, He sent the Cadurci to ravage the borders of the Volcae and the Arecomici, against the testimony and authority of the manuscripts, in which it reads Arecomicorum depopulabundos. For it was not two peoples but one, the Volcae Arecomici as well as the Volcae Tectosages. The Tectosages, however, were more celebrated than the Arecomici; Caesar, Livy, Justin, Strabo, Florus and others write that colonies were led from them into Asia, Pannonia and Germany, and in their writings there is much about the ancient valour of the people and their gloriously achieved deeds. In Pliny the Tectosages hold that part of Gaul which lies between the Pyrenees and the Cevennes. Pomponius calls the city of Toulouse the chief city of the Tectosages; Justin calls it the ancient homeland of the Tectosages. In Ptolemy the cities of the Tectosages, especially the inland ones, are named Illiberis, Ruscino, Tolosa Colonia, Cessero, Carcaso, Bestiva, Narbo Colonia. So the Tectosages once lived where now especially Carcassonne and Toulouse are; this is the opinion of Joseph Scaliger as well as of others. From all of these it is clear that the Volcae lived only on one bank of the Rhône, although Livy, book 21, places them on both banks. The Septimani, peoples of Gallia Narbonensis, were part of the Arecomici, according to Pliny, book 3, chapter 4, and Mela, book 2, chapter 5. They make Béziers, Biterrae or Biterae, their city; I read Bitteras and Biteras in the better books. I shall say more about it later. The Septimani are also mentioned in the Notitia of the Empire. Their region is called Septimania by Sidonius, book 3, letter 1; by Einhard in the Life of Charlemagne; by Gregory of Tours, book 8, chapters 28 and 30, and also book 9, chapter 7; by Aimoin, book 4, chapter 94; by Vuard, 11 Kalends of April; by Jonas of Orléans, book 1; by Peter the Venerable of Cluny, chapter 1; and by others. The name undoubtedly comes from the soldiers of the Seventh Legion, who had their garrisons there. I think the inscription which Martin Smetius writes, taken from Appian, exists at Denia in Spain, mentions this:

units.la: D. M. Q. MONEIO VERECVNDO NARBONENSI VET. LEG. VII. GEM. PIA. ÆLIA VALENTINA MARITO BENEMERENTI
units.tr: To the spirits of the departed: Quintus Moneius Verecundus of Narbo, veteran of the Seventh Legion Gemina Pia. Aelia Valentina to her deserving husband.

units.la: Haud procul Septumanis erant Decumani; in quis, Plinio Pomponioque Auctoribus, erat Narbo Marcius. Decumanos accipio, Decimae Legionis Veteranos: Civitas Narbonensium, Notitiae Provinciarum in Viennensi ii, L'Archevesché de Narbone. Per Narbonem exit in Mare Internum Atax Fluvius, in Saltu Pyrenaeo ortus. Ab Atace Atacini Populi, eidem Pomponio. Atacinorum Urbs erat Atax, ubi natus P. Ille Terentius Varro, Atacinus inde cognominatus, qui scripsit Argonauticôn lib. i v, Epigrammata, Bellum Sequanicum, quod citat Priscianus lib. x, & alia. Videndi Plinius lib. i. & Eusebius in Chronicis. Tolosates apud Caesarem lib. i. & vii, Tolosani vero Plinio, qui sine, notius, quam ut à me dicatur. Civitas Tolosatium, Notitiae Provinciarum, L'Archevesché de Tolose, Metropolis eorum Tolosa, de qua post. Gabals apud Cafarem lib. vii sunt, qui Gabales Plinio, Γαβαλες Straboni; Ptolemæo corrupte Ταβαλλοι. Gabali hodie Le Pais de Gevaudan. Vicus Ɔ Mitmates Gabalorum vel Gabalitanorum, ut nominatur Sidonio lib. vii. Foɔ. vi. hodie Mende de Gevaudan. Nam Syllabam Ga primam in Vocibus Galli mutant in Gi: Gabalitanum Gevaudan, Gabalon, Gibei, Garumna, Gironda. Marlianus dicit fuisse quondam Provinciæ Bituricensis, nunc vero Provinciæ Arelatensis. Certe & nunc quoque Provinciæ, ut me monet Scaliger, Bituricensis. Mimatensis enim Episcopatus Tribunalis est vel Parlamenti Tolosani, sub Metropoli Bituricensi. Inter Gabalos & Provinciam Arelatensem,
units.tr: Not far from the Septumani were the Decumani; among them, according to Pliny and Pomponius, was Narbo Martius. I take the Decumani to be veterans of the Tenth Legion. The state of the Narbonenses, in the Notitia Provinciarum under Vienna ii; the Archbishopric of Narbonne. Through Narbo the river Atax flows into the Inner Sea, rising in the Pyrenean forest. From it comes the Atacini people, according to the same Pomponius. The town of the Atacini was Atax, where Publius Terentius Varro was born, surnamed Atacinus from it, who wrote the Argonautica in book iv, Epigrams, the Sequanian War, which Priscian cites in book x, and other works. See Pliny book i and Eusebius in the Chronicle. The Tolosates appear in Caesar books i and vii, and the Tolosani in Pliny, a form too familiar to need explanation from me. The state of the Tolosates, in the Notitia Provinciarum, the Archbishopric of Toulouse, whose metropolis is Toulouse, of which more later. The Gabali in Caesar book vii are the people whom Pliny calls Gabales and Strabo Γαβαλες [Gabales]; Ptolemy wrongly gives Ταβαλλοι [Tabalsoi]. The Gabali today are the Pays de Gevaudan. The village of the Gabali, or Gabalitani, as Sidonius calls it in book vii, letter vi, is today Mende in Gevaudan. The Gauls change the first syllable Ga into Gi in words such as Gevaudan (from Gabalitanum), Gibei (from Gabalon), Garonne (Garumna) and Gironde. Marlianus says it once belonged to the province of Bourges, now to the province of Arles. Certainly even now it belongs to the province of Bourges, as Scaliger tells me. The bishopric of Mende is a tribunal or parlement of Toulouse, under the metropolitan see of Bourges. Between the Gabali and the province of Arles,

units.la: Longa procul longè Via dividit iniuria terris.
units.tr: Far apart, the long road divides the lands with cruel wrong.

units.la: Gabalitæ Cæsi memimt Plinius lib. xi. nat. Hist. cap. xii. Albigenses in Aquitania ad Flumen Tarnum, hodie Albigeois: Albigensium Civitas in Notitia Provinciarum. L'Evesque de Albi. De Albigensibus Hæreticis alij. Vide quæ infra dicam de Helvis. Velaunni Plinio lib. iv. cap. xix (corrupte enim vulgo Venami sunt, qui Velaunni Cæsari lib. vii in cujus antiquis Codicibus Velavi, Οὐελαύνοι Ptolemæo, Οὐελαύνοι Strabonis lib. iv, ad cujus scripturam proxime accedit hodierna appellatio, qua Languedocii Tractus vocatur Velay, vel Velave. Civitas Velaunorum Notitiæ Provinciarum Galliæ in Aquitania vel vi Viennensi, Le Pais de Velay, ut notant Iosephus Scaliger, Ioannes Poldus, Belleforestius, & alij. Martyrologia scribentibus Pagus Velaunus; doctus, quam ipsi opinabantur, pro tota Præfectura Velaunorum. Pagus enim Latinus Veteribus, non tam Vicus, quam magnus modus Agri, Gensque una cuamtumus numerota, ut alibi noto. Ab hujusmodi latiore Pagi notione Gallis vox manavit Pais, numquam ꝛ ante Vocalem pronunciare solitis, quemadmodum & in Pèrga, Piayes & alijs, quæ prætereo. Quæ Civitas Confluentium in Vulgatis Notitiæ Provinciarum est Exemplaribus; Confuarum vel Confarannorum in Antiquis scribitur: L'Evesche de Conserans: Confuaranı vocantur Plinio lib. iii. cap. iv: Soranni Tertean Gregorio Turonensi. Qui Helvi apud Cæsarem lib. vii. de Bello Gallico, duobus locis, & initio fere lib. i. de Bello Civili, Helvi apud Plinium, Ελουι apud Strabonem: Ptolemæo putantur esse Ελαυαιοι; Albenses, in Notitia Provinciarum Galliæ, ubi sub Viennensi Prima, Civitas Albensium, nunc Vivario: L'Evesche de Viviers. Sic in Scriptis legitur Codicibus. Nam mepta est, quæ in Vulgatis libris est, Scriptura, Civitas Albensium, hoc est Belisio. Habitarunt olim, ut suis ad me literis monet Scaliger, ut item sentire video Dalechampium; ut denique satis ex Notitia Provinciarum paret, Helvi Agrum, qui vulgo nunc Vivarais nuncupatur. Helvei Cæsaris omnes (inter quos Orontius, Belleforestius, Poldus, Canalis) hactenus interpretati sunt Albigenses, Albigeois; eorumque Urbem, Albi. At Albigenses sunt in Aquitania, ad Fluvium Tarnum; Albenses autem vel Elvy ad Rodanum. Cæsar lib. vii trans Rodanum esse dicit extra Provinciam Romanam, proximos Arvernis & Cebennis Montibus. De Alba Helviorum Plinij, & Alba Augusta Ptolemæi, hodie Aubenas, paullo post, ubi de Vivariensi Oppido, Vivariensis Diœcesis, id est Albensium, vel Helviorum nunc Metropoli. Nominantur & in Notitia Provinciarum, cujus iam iam memini, Nemausenses, Metenses, Petrucorij & Agathenses; quorum omnium Domicilia nunc etiam notissima, ubi hodie Episcopatus de Nîmes, d'Alet, de Béziers, d'Agde. Adduntur & alij: Lutevani, qui & Foro-Neronensis Plinio; quondam, ubi nunc Lutevensis Episcopatus. L'Evesche de Lodeve, vel, ut alij scribunt, Ledeve: Castrum Luteva Notitiæ Provinciarum in Viennensi ii. Magalonenses ab Insula Magalone, ubi prius Sedes fuit Episcopalis, quæ nunc in Monte Pessulo. Demum adhuc gerit Insula cum Templo, in medijs Stagnis. Civitas Magalonensium in Notitia Provinc. L'Evesche de Magalone, ou Montpelier. Sontiates apud Cæsarem lib. iii. interpretantur nonnulli: Lavedani (Lavedan) Incolas. In quibusdam Libris Sociates scribuntur. Fulvius Ursinus ex Orosio M. S. legit Sociates: Sontiates sunt apud Plinium; Σωντιατες apud Athenæum lib. iv.
