Qua autem Reip. ratione Sontiates fecerint, indicat non obscure Cæsar, qui Principem eorum nominat Adcantuannum; Athenæus, Αδκαντουαννος: Milites ejus ille Soldurios hic Σιλουριοι. Fuerunt & inter Galliæ Narbonensis Populos Vmbranici, notante Plinio; quorum Ager in Tabula Peutingeriana Vmbranicia dicitur.
units.tr: Pliny book xi of the Natural History, chapter xii, mentions the Gabalitae, whom Caesar also names. The Albigenses are in Aquitaine, on the river Tarn, today the Albigeois. The city of the Albigenses is in the Notitia Provinciarum; the Bishop of Albi. Others write about the Albigensian heretics. See what I say below about the Helvii. The Velauni are in Pliny book iv, chapter xix (the common text wrongly gives Venami); in Caesar book vii, in some old manuscripts Velavi; Ptolemy Οὐελαύνοι [Velaunoi]; Strabo Οὐελαύνοι [Velaunoi] in book iv. The modern name, by which the region of Languedoc is called Velay or Velave, comes closest to this spelling. The city of the Velauni is in the Notitia Provinciarum of Gaul, in Aquitaine or the sixth province of Vienne; it is the Pays de Velay, as Joseph Scaliger, Johannes Poldus, Belleforest and others note. Writers on the martyrs call it the Pagus Velaunus, more learned than they themselves thought, for the whole district of the Velauni. For the ancients a pagus was not so much a village as a large tract of land and a single people counted as a unit, as I note elsewhere. From this wider sense of pagus the Gauls derived the word Pais, since they never pronounced an s before a vowel, as in Pèrga, Piayes and others, which I pass over. The city of the Confluentes is in the common texts of the Notitia Provinciarum; in the old texts it is written Confuarum or Confarannorum: the Bishop of Conserans. The Confuaranni are called so by Pliny book iii, chapter iv; the Soranni by Gregory of Tours, as Tertean. The Helvii in Caesar's Gallic War book vii, twice, and near the start of book i of the Civil War; the Helvi in Pliny; Ελουι [Helouoi] in Strabo; Ptolemy is thought to give Ελαυαιοι [Elauaioi]. The Albenses appear in the Notitia Provinciarum of Gaul, where under Vienne the First is the state of the Albenses, now Vivarais, the bishopric of Viviers. This is how the manuscripts read. The printed books have a corrupt reading, state of the Albenses, which is Bélisie. As Scaliger writes to me, they lived there long ago, and I see Dalechamps thinks the same. Finally it is clear enough from the Notitia Provinciarum that the Helvii held the land now commonly called Vivarais. All the interpreters of Caesar's Helvii (among them Orontius, Belleforest, Poldus and Canalis) have so far taken them to be the Albigenses, the Albigeois, and their city to be Albi. But the Albigenses are in Aquitaine, on the Tarn; the Albenses, or Alba of the Helvii, are on the Rhône. In Pliny it is Alba of the Helvii, and in Ptolemy Alba Augusta, today Aubenas, a little later, where I speak of the town of Vivarais, the diocese of Vivarais, that is the metropolis now of the Albenses or Helvii. The Nemausenses, Metenses, Petrucorii and Agathenses are also named in the Notitia Provinciarum, which I have just mentioned; their dwellings are still well known today, where the bishoprics of Nîmes, Alet, Béziers and Agde now are. Others are added: the Lutevani, who are also Forum Neronense in Pliny, formerly, where now is the bishopric of Lutève. The bishopric of Lodève, or as others write, Ledeve; the castle Luteva in the Notitia Provinciarum under Vienne ii. The Magalonenses take their name from the island of Magalona, where the episcopal see was formerly, which is now on Montpellier hill. Finally the island with its temple still stands in the middle of the marshes. The city of the Magalonenses is in the Notitia Provinciarum; the bishopric of Maguelone, or Montpellier. Some interpret the Sontiates in Caesar book iii as the inhabitants of Lavedan (Lavedan). In some books they are written Sociates. Fulvius Ursinus reads Sociates from an unpublished manuscript of Orosius. The Sontiates are in Pliny, and Σωντιατες [Sontiates] in Athenaeus book iv. What the Sontiates did in public affairs Caesar makes plain enough, naming their chief Adcantuannus; Athenaeus Αδκαντουαννος [Adcantuannos]. That man is Soldurios, and this one Σιλουριοι [Silourioi]. Among the peoples of Narbonese Gaul were also the Umbranici, as Pliny notes; their land is called Umbranicia in the Peutinger Table.

units.la: Hæc de Antiquis hujus Galliarum Tractus Incolis sufficiant: ad Hodierna venio.
units.tr: Let these remarks on the ancient inhabitants of this region of Gaul suffice; I now come to the present day.

units.la: Languedokium Vrbes habet præclarissimas: quarum aliæ gentium quasi sunt: Majorum aliæ Minorum. Majorum mihi Archiepiscopales & Episcopales. Prioris Classis sunt Tolosa & Narbona.
units.tr: Languedoc has very famous cities, some of which are, as it were, of the greater nations, and others of the lesser. Among the greater I count the archiepiscopal and episcopal cities. Of the first class are Toulouse and Narbonne.

units.la: Tolosa primum dabo locum, quod non solum Archiepiscopatui, verum etiam amplissimo totius Languedoky Parlamento, Supremæque Curiæ præbeat Domicilium: quoque inter tres ingentes Languedokii Senescballias princeps facile tueatur locum. Tolosa Cæsari, Plinio, Melæ, Marcellino, Iustino, aliisque Latinis Scriptoribus; Τολοσα Straboni & Ptolemæo: Tolosa vitiose in Tabula Peutingeriana Itineraria. Galliæ Narbonensis Volcarum Tectosagum Colonia Geographis: sed a quo & quando ducta, nondum est compertum. Urbs Tolosatium, Sidonio lib. I v. Epist. xxii, & Gregorio Turonensi lib. I. de Miraculis cap. viii. Urbs Tolosana Fredegario in Vita Epiphanii. Nomen retinet: Vulgo Toloufe. Civis Tolosensis, ni fallor, meatio in Marmore, quod Romæ, prope Arcum Camillarem:
units.tr: I shall give Toulouse first place, since it is home not only to the archbishopric but also to the very great parlement of all Languedoc and the Supreme Court, and since it can easily hold the first place among the three great seneschalsies of Languedoc. Toulouse is named by Caesar, Pliny, Mela, Marcellinus, Justin and other Latin writers; Τολοσα [Tolosa] by Strabo and Ptolemy; Tolosa is wrongly written in the Peutinger Table. Geographers call it a colony of the Volcae Tectosages of Narbonese Gaul, but by whom and when it was founded is not yet known. It is called the city of the Tolosates by Sidonius book iv, letter xxii, and by Gregory of Tours in book i of the Miracles, chapter viii. Fredegarius in the Life of Epiphanius calls it the city of Toulouse. It keeps its name; commonly Toulouse. A citizen of Toulouse, if I am not mistaken, is mentioned in a marble inscription at Rome, near the Arch of Camillus:

units.la: DIIS MANIBVS C. FABRICI. C. F. VOL. PROXIMI TOLOSENSIS C. FABRICIVS VICARIVS PATRONO. BENE MERENTI. FECIT IN. FRONTE. P. VII IN. AGRO. P. VII
units.tr: TO THE SPIRITS OF THE DEAD OF C. FABRICIUS, SON OF C., OF THE VOLTINIAN TRIBE, OF TOULOUSE. C. FABRICIUS, VICAR, TO HIS PATRON, WHO DESERVED WELL. HE MADE IT. ON THE FRONT, 7 FEET; IN THE FIELD, 7 FEET.

units.la: Antiquissima clarissimaque Vrbs, quam Opulentam vocat Ausonius libro de Professoribus, Carmine xvii, qui & libro de Vrbibus, Carm. xi. Tolosam sic suis coloribus delineat: Non umquam Altricem nostri recitebo Tolosam, Cognitibus muris quam circuit Ambitus ingens, Perque latus pulchro prælabitur amne Garumna; Innumeris cultam Populis, confinia propter Ninguida Pyrenes, & pinea Cabennarum, Inter Aquitanas Gentes, & nomen Iberum. Qua modo quadruplices ex se quum effuderit Vrbes, Non nulla exhausta senuit dispendia plebis, Quos genuit cunctos gremio complexa Colonos.
units.tr: This most ancient and most famous city, which Ausonius in his book on the Professors (poem 17), and again in his book on the Cities (poem 11), calls wealthy, he portrays in these colours: "I shall never recount Tolosa, the nurse of our people, which a vast circuit encloses with its known walls, and past whose side the beautiful river Garonne flows; she is tilled by countless peoples, near the snowy border of the Pyrenees and the pine-clad Cevennes, between the Aquitanian nations and the Iberian name. Though she has now poured forth four colonies from herself, and has grown old, having lost some of her people through drain, she has embraced in her bosom and cherished all the colonists she bore."

units.la: Qui Poëtæ Ingens Ambitus, nunc quoque Magnus est. Paucasque namque habet Galliæ Vrbes, Tolosa maiores, soli cedente Parisiorum Lutetiæ. Fuit aliquando maior, quam nunc est, amplior opulentiorque, uti patet, cum ex his Ausonii Versus, tum ex Epistola ad Paulinum, quæ ordine xxiii, ubi eam Quinquiplicem quasi ex quinque Vrbibus constatam. Sed multa gravia & acerba tulit. Mu- que ejus magnopere imminuta est, cum alias, tum Albigensis Dogmatis temp... Templum quod D. Virgini, cognomine de la d' Aurade; aliudque, quod ... consecratum; illud Iovi, hoc Apollini sacrum fuisse memorant Cives ... iam Portariam volunt dictam, quod Iupiter ibi cultus Arietinus, vel ... esset Signi Zodiaci Arietis, quali Porta Arietis. Non pugno. Demum Amphitheatri Vestigiis magis constat: Capitolii item, apud Locum ... cupatur. Arx enim ibi rotundioris structuræ. Tolosam Capitolium ... nit Sidonius lib. ix. Epist. xvi: Equitibus primum mihi psallas Hymnus, ... quum tenuit Cathedram, ... ... ...
units.tr: That "vast circuit" of the poet is still great today. For Gaul has few cities larger than Tolosa, second only to Paris, the Lutetia of the Parisii. It was once larger, more extensive and richer than it is now, as is clear both from these verses of Ausonius and from his letter to Paulinus (letter 23), where he describes it as made up of five cities, as it were, and therefore "fivefold". But it has borne many grievous and bitter afflictions, and its population was greatly diminished, both at other times and in the time of the Albigensian heresy... The temple dedicated to the Blessed Virgin, under the surname "de la d'Aurade", and another, which ... was consecrated; the citizens report that the former was sacred to Jupiter and the latter to Apollo. Some want the gate to have been called Portaria because Jupiter was worshipped there as the Ram, or because it was the sign of the Zodiac, the Ram, whence the Porta Arietis. I do not contest this. Finally, the remains of an amphitheatre bear witness more clearly, and likewise a Capitol, near the place ... is held. For there is a citadel of rounder construction. Sidonius (book 9, letter 16) calls Tolosa a Capitol: "First, the horsemen sing me a hymn..." when he held the chair...

units.la: Tolosa Sedes olim ... cium & Wallia ... Legendi Prosper, Cassiodorus, Iornandes in Historia Gothor. cap. xxxii, Diaconus lib. iv, Isidorus in Chron. Gothor. & alij. Sic Rutilus Itinerario i: Errantem Tuscis considere compulit agris, Excolere externos capta Tolosa Lares.
units.tr: Tolosa was once the seat of ... and of Wales. Prosper, Cassiodorus, Jordanes in his History of the Goths (chapter 32), Paul the Deacon (book 4), Isidore in his Chronicle of the Goths, and others read of it. So Rutilius in his Itinerary (book 1): "He drove the wanderer to settle in the Tuscan fields; captured Tolosa compelled him to cultivate foreign hearths."

units.la: Idacius M. S. Gothi sedentes in Aquitania Tolosæ filii sedem eligunt. Et inde Reges Tolosæ nominati. Sic Alaricus Rex Tolosæ in Commonitorio Ananij; Sic alij. Hinc Torismundus, ut Regnum auspicaretur, Tolosam, Regni Gothici caput, ingreditur apud Iornandem in Hist. Gothorum: Hinc Theodoricus, Torismundi Successor, Larem ibi fovet apud Sidonium Carm. vi ri; ut Theodorici Successor Euarix, apud eundem Sidonium lib. v. Epist. xiii, & Ennodium in vita Epiphanij: Hinc denique Alaricus, Eorici filius, apud Tolosatem Urbem Gothorum Rex factus scribitur Isidoro in Chronic. Gothorum: quo interfecto Regnum Tolosanum, occupantibus Francis, est destructum; eodem, & Gregorio Turonensi lib. ii. cap. xxxvii. scribentibus. Celebrem habet Academiam; olim omnium Artium & Disciplinarum, hodie autem cum primis Iurisprudentiæ studio florentem; diligentiaque cum Professorum, cum Studiosorum stupendam. Meminerunt ejus Baldus in l. omnia Privilegia. C. de Episc. & Cleric. Iason ad l. ... de Legat. i. Abbas in c. sin Extra. Ne Clerici vel Monachi. Multa etiam de ea Rebus. Rhetoricam Tolosæ docuerunt Æmilius Magnus Arborius, Exsuperius & Sedatus; quorum Manibus justa solvit Ausonius libro de Professoribus, Carminibus xvii, xviii & xx. De Auro Tolosano (quod Tolosense dixit Iustinus lib. xxxii.) natoque inde Proverbio in eum, cui Fata res secundas esse nolunt; cuique Malum malo congeritur & exaggeratur. legendi Agellius lib. i. Noct. Attic. Strabo lib. iv, & alij. De ejus raptu quæstionem aliquando habitam Romæ, scribunt M. Tullius lib. de Nat. Deor. iii, Orosius lib. v. cap. xv; & alij. Quæ sint autem quatuor Tolosatium Colonia, quas ex se Tolosam effudisse canit paullo ante Ausonius, non constat: quin & plurima de Tolosa memorant Strabo lib. iv. & Iustinus lib. xxxii, quorum hodie paucissima agnoscas. Tolosensis Lacus meminit Trogus Pompeius apud Iustinum lib. xxii circa Tolosam.
units.tr: Idacius, in manuscript: The Goths, settling in Aquitaine, choose Tolosa as their seat. And from there they were called kings of Tolosa. So Alaric, king of Tolosa, in the Commonitorium of Ananias; so others. Hence Thorismund, to begin his reign, enters Tolosa, the head of the Gothic kingdom, as Jordanes reports in his History of the Goths. Hence Theoderic, Thorismund's successor, keeps his household there, according to Sidonius (poem 6). His successor Euric did likewise, according to the same Sidonius (book 5, letter 13) and Ennodius in the life of Epiphanius. Finally, Alaric, son of Euric, is written by Isidore in his Chronicle of the Goths to have been made king of the Goths at Tolosa; when he was killed, the Tolosan kingdom was destroyed by the occupying Franks, as Gregory of Tours also writes (book 2, chapter 37). It has a famous Academy, once of all the arts and disciplines, but today flourishing especially in the study of law, and remarkable for the diligence both of its professors and of its students. Baldus in the law "Omnia privilegia" (C. de episcopis et clericis), Jason on the law "...de legatis" (book 1), and Abbas on the chapter "sin" (Extra, "Ne clerici vel monachi") mention it, and many others write about it. At Tolosa taught rhetoric Aemilius Magnus Arborius, Exsuperius and Sedatus, whose shades Ausonius honoured with funeral verses in his book on the Professors, poems 17, 18 and 20. Concerning the gold of Tolosa (which Justin in book 32 calls Tolosense), and the proverb derived from it, said of one to whom fortune does not wish success, and on whom evil is heaped upon evil and exaggerated, read Aulus Gellius (Attic Nights, book 1), Strabo (book 4), and others. That its plunder was once made the subject of an inquiry at Rome, Cicero (On the Nature of the Gods, book 3) and Orosius (book 5, chapter 15) write, among others. Which the four colonies of the Tolosates are, which Ausonius sings a little earlier that Tolosa poured forth from herself, is not established. Strabo (book 4) and Justin (book 32) also record very many things about Tolosa, of which today you would recognise very few. Trogus Pompeius, in Justin (book 22), mentions the Tolosan lake near Tolosa.

units.la: Tolosa proxima dignitate est Narbona. Sic Sueronio in Tiberio cap. iv (apud quem tamen in MSS. Narbo legitur) Eutropio, Ammiano, & plerisque Latine nunc scribentibus appellatur, quæ Narbo Martiali lib. viii. Epigr. xxxi, & alijs; Narbo Polybio lib. iii, & Ptolemæo; Narbo Martius, Plinio lib. iii. natur. Hist. cap. iv, Pomponio Melæ, Ausonio in Urbibus, & alijs. Narbonensis Marciano apud Stephanum: Apud Avienum Naro dicitur. Ptolemæus Tectosagum Urbem facit in Gallia Narbonensi; Arecomicorum Navale Strabo; Decumanorum Coloniam esse ait Plinius; Eorumdem quoque & Atacinorum Pomponius Mela lib. ii. A propriis Colonis conditam notat Isidorus lib. xv. Erymologiar. Quæ caussa Narbonem Coloniam deducendi Romanis fuerit: quod primum Nomen antiquissima Urbs, & unde Charcy cognomen habuerit, adhuc quærunt Docti. Deductam lego non semel. Deduxit Primus, post domitos & debellatos ab Longinis, Domitius, Fabiusque Gallos Transalpinos, L. Licinius Crassus Orator, quum adhuc esset adolescens, testibus Cicerone in libro de Claris Oratoribus, Paterculo lib. i, & Eutropio. Factum illud anno ab V. C. 1cxxxvi, L. Porcio Catone & Q. Marcio Rege Coss. Unde sunt, qui Marcium ab altero Coss. cognominatum velint. Sed quur Cognomen illi ab Marcio potius Rege, quam à Porcio Catone? & quur ab altero potius Coss. quam ab eo, uti moris erat, qui deduxerat? Quin Marcia Gens quartam in Nomine litteram C habet, non T, apud omnes Græcos Latinosque Scriptores, in omnibus Membranis, in multis, quæ apud Aldum Manutium, Inscriptionibus, & Nummis. Narbo autem quartam sui Cognominis Marty litteram T agnoscit, non C, in quotquot reperiuntur, Scriptis Codicibus: contra quorum fidem & auctoritatem iniquè facit Dionysius Lambinus, Vir doctissimus, qui per C vult scribi. Aliunde igitur Cognominis ratio quærenda, & fortean ab Veteranis Martia Legionis Militibus. Respicere videtur eo Sidonius Apollinaris in Epistola ad Pontium Leontium de Burgo: Dum apud Narbonem, quemdam Martium dictum, sed nuper factum, moratus nelio. Innuit primo Martium non Marcium cognominatum; deinde Narbonem olim quidem Martium vocatum, sed quod Marty appellatione designabatur. hoc nuper esse effectum; Civitatem scilicet Martiam, id est bello potentem, & strenuam, quum nimirum
units.tr: Tolosa is next in rank to Narbo. So it is called by Suetonius in the life of Tiberius (chapter 4; though in the manuscripts Narbo is read there), by Eutropius, by Ammianus, and by most writers of Latin today; Martial (book 8, epigram 31) and others call it Narbo; Polybius (book 3) and Ptolemy call it Narbo; Pliny (Natural History, book 3, chapter 4), Pomponius Mela, Ausonius in the Cities, and others call it Narbo Martius. Marcianus, in Stephanus, calls it Narbonensis; in Avienus it is called Naro. Ptolemy places the city of the Tectosages in Narbonese Gaul; Strabo calls it the naval station of the Arecomici; Pliny says it is a colony of the Decumani; Pomponius Mela (book 2) says the same of it and of the Atacini. Isidore (Etymologies, book 15) notes that it was founded by its own colonists. Scholars still ask what reason led the Romans to make Narbo a colony, and what the very ancient city's first name was, and whence it had the surname Charcy. I read that it was founded more than once. The first to lead a colony there, after the Transalpine Gauls had been subdued and crushed by the Longini, were Domitius and Fabius; and L. Licinius Crassus the orator led one when he was still a young man, as Cicero attests in his book on famous orators, and Paterculus (book 1) and Eutropius too. This happened in the year 636 from the founding of the city, when Lucius Porcius Cato and Quintus Marcius Rex were consuls. Hence some want Marcius to have been named as a surname after the other consul. But why would the surname come from Marcius Rex rather than from Porcius Cato? And why from the other consul rather than from the one who led the colony, as was the custom? Indeed the Marcian clan has a C, not a T, as the fourth letter of its name, in all Greek and Latin writers, in all manuscripts, in many inscriptions and coins, as well as in the editions of Aldus Manutius. But Narbo acknowledges the fourth letter of its surname Martius to be T, not C, in all the manuscripts that are found. Dionysius Lambinus, a most learned man, who wants it written with a C, unjustly acts against the faith and authority of these. The reason for the surname must therefore be sought elsewhere, perhaps in the veteran soldiers of the Martian legion. Sidonius Apollinaris seems to hint at this in his letter to Pontius Leontius of Bourg: While I was lingering at Narbo, called "Martius", but recently so named. He implies, first, that it was surnamed Martius and not Marcius; second, that Narbo was formerly indeed called Martius, but that this was recently made into a designation by the name Marty: namely the city Martia, that is, powerful and vigorous in war, since it held out bravely for a long time, while the Goths besieged and attacked it.

units.la: rum
units.tr: -rum

units.la: Vide Dionysium Lambinus. rum Gothos obsidentes oppugnantesque diu fortissime sustineret. Certe ab Rebus Bellicis, Militarique Virtute laudant hanc Urbem & alij. Cicero in Oratione pro Fonteio: Est in eadem Provincia Narbo Martius, Colonia nostrorum Civium, Specula Populi Romani, ac Propugnaculum ipsis Nationibus oppositum & objectum. Pomponius Mela lib. II. Sed antiquas omnes Atacinorum Decumanorumque Colonias; unde olim in Terris auxilium, nunc & nomen & decus est, Martius Narbo. Deductam iterum Narbonem Coloniam C. Iulio Caesare Dictatore & Ti. Claudium Neronem, Ti. Imperatoris Patrem, deduxisse, Suetonius auctor est in Ti. Principis Vita cap. IV. A quo tempore Narbo non solum Martij usurpavit cognomen, verum etiam Iulia Paterna quasi Praenomen, dictaque fuit Iulia Paterna Narbo Martius: Iulia quidem ab C. Caesaris Dictatoris Nomine: Paterna vero, quod Iulij Patris, id est Dictatoris,non Iulij Filij, id est Octaviani Augusti, auspicijs esset deducta. Testatur elegans Marmor in ipsa Urbe effossum anno CIↃ IↃLXVI. Exstat typis excusa, cujus pars, quae dictis à me probandis facit, sic habet: ULICE. LEGIBUS. ULISQUE. REGIONIBUS. SIC. UTI. DIXI. HANC. TIBI. ARAM. PRO. IMP. CAESARE. AVG. P. P. PONTIFICE. MAXIMO. TRIBUNITIA. POTESTATE. XXXV. CONIUGE. LIBERIS. GENTEQUE. EIUS. SENATU. POPULOQUE. R. COLONIS. INCOLISQUE. COL. IVL. PATERN. NARB. MART. QUI. SE. HUMINI. EIUS. IN. PERPETUUM. COLENDO. OBLIGAVERUNT. DOQUE. DEDICOQUE. UTI. SIES. VOLENS. PROPITIUS. Celebrant Narbonem Ausonus & Sidonius Apollinaris: ille quidem in Urbium suarum Catalogo, Carm. XII, ubi inter alia sic canit: Quis memoret Portusque tuos, Montesque, Lacusque? Quis Populos vario discrimine Vestis & Orbis? Quodque tibi quondam Pario de Marmore Templum Tanta melius erat, quantam non sperneret olim Tarquinius, Catulusque iterum, postremus & ille, Aurea qui statuit Capitoli culmina Caesar? Te Maris Eoi merces, & Hiberica ditam Aequora, te Classes Libyci, Siculique Profundi: Et quidquid vario, per Flumina, per Freta, cursu Advehitur: toto tibi navigat orbe navium.
units.tr: See Dionysius Lambinus. ...rum. Certainly many others praise this city for its warlike affairs and military valour. Cicero, in the speech for Fonteius: In the same province is Narbo Martius, a colony of our citizens, a watchtower of the Roman people, and a bulwark set against and opposed to the very nations. Pomponius Mela (book 2): But all the ancient colonies of the Atacini and Decumani, from which help once came to the lands, now have their name and glory in Martius Narbo. Suetonius, in the life of the emperor Tiberius (chapter 4), records that Narbo was made a colony again by Gaius Julius Caesar as Dictator and by Tiberius Claudius Nero, the father of the emperor Tiberius. From that time Narbo took not only the surname Martius, but also Julia Paterna as it were a forename, and was called Julia Paterna Narbo Martius: Julia, indeed, from the name of Gaius Caesar the Dictator; Paterna, however, because it had been led as a colony under the auspices of Julius the Father, that is, the Dictator, and not of Julius the Son, that is, Octavian Augustus. An elegant marble, dug up in the city itself in the year 1566, bears witness to this. It exists in print, and the part of it that supports what I have to prove reads thus: ULICE. LEGIBUS. ULISQUE. REGIONIBUS. SIC. UTI. DIXI. HANC. TIBI. ARAM. PRO. IMP. CAESARE. AVG. P. P. PONTIFICE. MAXIMO. TRIBUNITIA. POTESTATE. XXXV. CONIUGE. LIBERIS. GENTEQUE. EIUS. SENATU. POPULOQUE. R. COLONIS. INCOLISQUE. COL. IVL. PATERN. NARB. MART. QUI. SE. HUMINI. EIUS. IN. PERPETUUM. COLENDO. OBLIGAVERUNT. DOQUE. DEDICOQUE. UTI. SIES. VOLENS. PROPITIUS. Ausonius and Sidonius Apollinaris celebrate Narbo: the former in his catalogue of his cities (poem 12), where among other things he sings thus: Who could recount your harbours, your mountains and lakes? Who could recount the peoples distinguished by the variety of their dress and of the world? And the temple once made of Parian marble, far finer than Tarquin, or Catulus again, and the last of them, that Caesar who set the golden roofs of the Capitol, would have scorned? Merchandise of the eastern sea, and seas enriched by Spain, fleets of Libya and of the deep Sicilian sea, and whatever is carried by river, by strait, by sea, all sail to you from the whole world.

units.la: Hic vero Carmine XXIII. ad Consentium Clarissimum Civem Narbonensem, cujus haec inter alia: Salve Narbo potens Salubritate, Urbe & Rure simul bonus videri Maris, Cryptis, Ambitu, Tabernis, Portis, Porticibus, Foro, Theatro, Delubris, Capitolijs, Monetis, Thermis, Arcubus, Horreis, Macellis, Pratis, Fontibus, Insulis, Salinis, Stagnis, Flumine, Mercè, Ponte, Ponto, Vnus qui venerere jure Divos Lenaeum, Cererem, Palem, Minervam: Spicis, Palmite, Pascuis, Tapetis, Solis fide Viris, nec expetito Natura auxilio, procul relictis Promens Montibus altius cacumen. Non te Fossa patens, nec hispidarum Objectu Sudium coronat Agger. Item: Quid quod Caesaribus ferax creandis, Felix Prole Virum simul dedisti, Natos cum Genitore Principantes?
units.tr: Here, in Carmen 23 addressed to Consentius, the most distinguished citizen of Narbonne, the poet writes among other things: Hail, Narbo, powerful in healthfulness, fair both in town and in countryside, you who seem good by sea, by caves, by circuit walls, taverns, gates, colonnades, forum, theatre, shrines, Capitols, mints, baths, arches, granaries, meat markets, meadows, fountains, islands, salt pans, pools, river, trade, bridge, and sea; you who rightly venerate the gods Lenaeus, Ceres, Pales and Minerva; you who are rich in grain, vine, pasture, and carpets; men of good faith, whose nature needs no sought-after aid, and who, leaving the mountains far behind, rise to a higher summit. Neither the open ditch nor the rampart of bristling stakes crowns you. Likewise: What of the fact that you, fertile in producing emperors, have given men happy in offspring, sons ruling together with their fathers?

units.la: Versus digni sane, quos publico loco scribundos curet S.P.Q. Narbonensis; ut qualis quantaque quondam Urbs fuerit Narbo, Aetas haec sequensque cum stupore cognoscat. Sic Narbo dicitur Speciosa Prudentio in Hymno Martyrum Caesar-Augustanorum; Urbs Decora Theodulpho Aurelianensi. Capitolium, id est Arcem vel Palatium, etiam Narbonem habuisse indicant suis Carminibus non obscure Ausonius. nius & Sidonius. Ejus operis hodie nullum exstat Vestigium, sive Vetustas consumpserit, seu diruerint Gothi, aliique Barbari. De Capitolio Narbonensi, id est Palatio, videndus Gregorius Turonensis lib. de Mirac. i. cap.xcii. Lacuum appellatione Ausonius, Stagnorum Sidonius exaudiunt Rubresium, de quo praeter alios eleganter Pomponius Mela lib. ii. cap. v: Hodie L'Estang de la Rubine. De eo obiter cap. x. Per Flumen intelligit Sidonius Atacem, de quo Plinius lib. iii. cap. iv. Strabo lib. v, Sidonius lib. viii. cap. iv. lib. ix. cap. xvi, & alibi. Vibius: Atax è Pyrenaeo, circa Narbonam decurrit in Tyrrhenum. Atacis cum aliis Fluminibus meminit Theodulphus Episcopus Aurelianensis, qui in Scriniis adhuc Petri Danielis, Poemate contra ludaeos iniquos: Praefectura mihi fuerat peragenda tributa, Rex dedit hanc Karolus, primus ad omne bonum. Cui parent Walis, Rodanus, Mosa, Renus & Oenus, Sequana, Visurgis, Warda, Garumna, Padus, Rufa, Mosella, Liger, Vulturnus, Matrona, Ledus, Liter, Atax, Gabarus, Olitis, Albis, Arar.
units.tr: These verses are certainly worth having written up in a public place by the senate and people of Narbonne, so that this age and those after it may learn with wonder what sort of city Narbonne once was, and how great. Thus Prudentius in his Hymn of the Caesar-Augustan Martyrs calls Narbonne "Speciosa" (fair), and Theodulf of Orléans calls it "Urbs Decora" (a comely city). That Narbonne also had a Capitol, that is a citadel or palace, Ausonius and Sidonius clearly indicate in their poems. No trace of that work survives today, whether time has consumed it or the Goths and other barbarians pulled it down. On the Narbonese Capitol, that is the palace, see Gregory of Tours, On the Miracles, book 1, chapter 92. Ausonius understands by the word lakes (lacus), and Sidonius by pools (stagna), the Rubresus, of which, besides others, Pomponius Mela writes elegantly in book 2, chapter 5; today it is L'Étang de la Rubine. On it, in passing, see chapter 10. By the river (flumen) Sidonius means the Atax, of which Pliny writes in book 3, chapter 4, Strabo in book 5, and Sidonius in book 8, chapter 4, book 9, chapter 16, and elsewhere. Vibius says: The Atax rises in the Pyrenees and flows near Narbonne into the Tyrrhenian Sea. Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, also mentions the Atax together with other rivers, in his poem against the unjust Jews, which is still preserved among the papers of Pierre Daniel: "The office of tax-collector was to be carried out by me; King Charles gave it to me, first in every good thing. To him obey the Wal, Rhone, Meuse, Rhine and Oenus, Seine, Weser, Warta, Garonne, Po, Rufa, Moselle, Loire, Volturno, Matrona, Lede, Liter, Atax, Gabarus, Olitis, Elbe and Arar."

units.la: Ab Atace, Atacini Populi & Varro Atacinus, ut alias dixi. Narbo Strabo lib. iv, Μίγασον Ἐμπόριον. Narbone Grammaticam docuit Marcellus Marcelli F. de quo Libro Professorum Ausonius, cap. xix. Narbonam Urbem celebrat Benjaminus in Itinerario, Legis (Iudaicam intelligit) Antesignanam. Ex ea enim proficisci Legem in omnes Regiones: ibi Sapientes esse & magnos & suspiciendos: in primis Kalonymon, Theodori Filium, ex Semine Davidis, recta Genealogia. Praedia & Fundos habentem a Principibus Regionis, nullius hominis vim aut imperium metuentia.
units.tr: From the Atax come the Atacini people and Varro Atacinus, as I have said elsewhere. Strabo, in book 4, calls Narbonne "Mígason Emporion" (a trading post of Migasos). Marcellus, son of Marcellus, taught grammar at Narbonne; Ausonius mentions him in his book on the professors, chapter 19. Benjamin of Tudela, in his Itinerary, celebrates the city of Narbonne as the forerunner of the Law (he means the Jewish Law): from there the Law went out into all regions. There, he says, were wise men, great and worthy of respect, above all Kalonymus, son of Theodore, of the seed of David in direct descent, who possessed estates and lands from the princes of the region and feared the violence or command of no man.

units.la: Haec de urbibus Archiepiscopalibus: Episcopales in duplici sunt mihi discrimine. Inter eas enim quaedam, quae Metropoles sunt, & quasi Capita nobilissimorum quorundam hujus Provinciae Pagorum. Sic appello Suburbicarios Agros, fuitoresque quorundam Opidorum jurisdictiones: quales sunt Gabali, Albigenses, Velauni Consaranni & Albenses. Gabali, hodie Gevaudan. Eorum Metropolis Mimates Vicus Antiquioribus, vulgo Mende de Gevaudan: Regionis Mitanensis in Territorio Cavallitano, corrupte: Mimatensis Montis Galliae circa Gaballitanam Urbem, cujus Episcopus erat S. Privatus, meminit Gregorius Turonensis, apud quem etiam legitur Atemmatensis. Albigenses, nunc Albigeois: Urbs Albiga Gregorio Turonensi lib. ii. Albi vernaculo. Velaunni, Velai. Eorum Civitas quibusdam Anicium, Le Puy en Velai, id est Podium in Velauno, quia Urbs est in editissimo loco, qui Gallorum lingua Puy, id est Podium dicitur. Consaranorum, Ceferans, Civitas S. Leger de Ceferans: opidum antiquitate non incelebre. Albenses, Vivarais. Civitas Albensium, nunc Vivarium. Sic scribitur in melioribus Notitiae Provinciarum Codicibus: Vitiose in Vulgatis, Civitas Albensium, hoc est Belisio. Vivario Opidum est ad ripam Rodani dextram, vulgo Viviers. Ait autem recte Notitia, Nunc Vivarium. Civitas enim & Metropolis Albensium olim erat Alba; quae Plinio Helviorum cognominatur, Ptolemaeo autem Augusta. Legitur enim apud eum Ἀ Ἑαύγυστα Ἐ Ἀλβαῖον vocat Helicerios, quos Latini Helvios. Alba autem illa hodie Aubenas dicitur: Opidum in Vivariensi Diocesi, quinque minimum leucis ab Viverione versus Occidentem situm, quatuor ab Vocetensium Civitate, cum qua communem habet Amnem. Aubenas autem est nomen Pluralis numeri Albanates: ut ab Tolosa Tolosates, ab Nola Nolates in Veteri Inscriptione.
units.tr: These are the archiepiscopal cities. Episcopal cities are of two kinds. Some of them are metropolises, and as it were the heads of certain most noble districts of this province. Such I call the suburban fields and the jurisdictions of certain towns, such as the Gabali, Albigenses, Velauni, Consaranni and Albenses. The Gabali are today the Gévaudan. Their metropolis was the village of the Mimates, called in older sources, and commonly today, Mende in Gévaudan. Corruptly, the region of Mitanum in the territory of Gabalitanum, the Mimatensis Mons of Gaul near the city of Gabala, whose bishop was St. Privatus, is mentioned by Gregory of Tours, who also reads Atemmatensis. The Albigenses, now the Albigeois: the city Albiga is named by Gregory of Tours in book 2. In the vernacular, Albi. The Velauni, Velay. Their city is called by some Anicium, Le Puy en Velay, that is Podium in Velauno, because the city is on a very high place, which in the Gallic language is called Puy, that is podium. The Consaranni, Ceferans: the city of St. Léger de Ceferans, a town of no small antiquity. The Albenses, Vivarais. The city of the Albenses is now Vivarium. So it is written in the better manuscripts of the Notitia Provinciarum; in the common editions it is wrongly given as "the city of the Albenses, that is Belisio". Vivarium is a town on the right bank of the Rhone, commonly Viviers. The Notitia rightly says "now Vivarium". For the city and metropolis of the Albenses was once Alba, which Pliny surnames Helviorum and Ptolemy calls Augusta. For in him it is read that Alba is called Helicerii, whom the Latins call Helvii. That Alba is today called Aubenas: a town in the diocese of Viviers, situated at least five leagues west of Viviers and four from the city of the Vocetenses, with which it shares a river. Aubenas is the plural form of the name Albanates, just as from Tolosa comes Tolosates and from Nola Nolates, as in an ancient inscription.

units.la: Tantum de Episcopalibus, quae Suburbicarium Agrorum, latiorumque quarumdam jurisdictionum sunt Metropoles: reliquum est, ut ceteras explicem: in quis recensendis si non legitimum servem ordinem, vel si eiusdem cum indicatis iam naturae ad earum non referam classem, ignoscant velim Lectores, praesertim Incolae. Non enim omnia penitissime licuit novisse.
units.tr: So much concerning the episcopal cities which are metropolises of suburban fields and of larger jurisdictions. It remains for me to explain the rest. If in listing them I do not keep a strict order, or if I do not assign them to their proper class according to the nature already indicated, I would ask the readers to pardon me, especially the inhabitants, for it has not been possible for me to know everything in the most minute detail.

units.la: Nismes, Nemausus Volcarum Arecomicorum Plinio lib. iii. cap. iv, Ausonio libro de Urbibus Carmine xiii, Pomponio Melae lib. ii. cap. v. Sidonio lib. ii, Epist. ix. Itinerario Antonini: Νίμαυσος Strabo lib. iv, & Ptolemaeo. Numismati vetustissimo COL. NEM. ARECOMICORUM. In Itinerario Peutingeri Tabula Nemauso scribitur, corruptius. Νίμαυσος, inquit Stephanus, πόλις Γαλλίας, ὁσὸ Νιμαυσ ἡγεμονία, ὡς Παρθισίων. Qualis fuerit Horente Romanorum Imperio, notat eleganter Strabo; cujus ea de re pauca verba non possum non adscribere: Μετρίαν... Ἀ ἐ... Ἀ᾿ρτεμιδώρῳ ἐκ Νίμαυσος, καὶ μὲν ἡ ἀλλότριον ἔχλει καὶ τὸν ἱμπερικὸν, πλὴν Ναρβῶνος λεπτόμυρη, καὶ δὲ τὸν πολιτικὸν ὑπερβαλλοντα. ὑποκεῖς γὰρ ἔχει κώμας τίθεσθαι καὶ εἴκοσι τῶν ὁμοιοθῶν, ὀλιγοδέκα ἀλεξάνδρου συμπλήσας εἰς αὐτὸ, ἰχῦσας δὲ τὸ καλλίμορον λατῖνον, ὥστε τὰς ἀξιωθεῖς ἀρχαιωμίας ἐ τιμιᾶς ἐν Νεμαύσῳ Ῥωμαίας ὑπάρχειν. Διὰ δὴ τῶν ὑδ᾿ ἱστορικὸν τῶν ἐκ τῆς Ῥώμης σεμνοτήτων ἐν τῷ ἰθιῷ τῶν. Ἰδρυται δὲ ἡ πόλις καὶ τῷ ὁδῷ τῷ ἐκ τῆς Ἰταλίας εἰς τὴν Γαλλίαν, ἥρας μὲν Δ᾿Ἐαπν ἄνω, χρυσῶν δὲ ἱαρῷ πηλοῦ ἡ πολυμοιλυγον. In Opidorum, quæ Nemausiensibus adtributa, numero, Plinio convenit cum Strabone. Ejus verba lib. iii. nat. hist. cap. iv sic habent: Vocontiorum Civitatis Fœderata duo Capita, Vafco & Lucus Augusti: Opida vero ignobilia xixi sicus xxiv Nemausiensibus adtributa. Decurionum Nemausi mentio in Antiqua Inscriptione, quæ ibi visitur:
units.tr: Nîmes: Nemausus of the Volcae Arecomici, in Pliny, book 3, chapter 4; in Ausonius, in his book on cities, poem 13; in Pomponius Mela, book 2, chapter 5; in Sidonius, book 2, letter 9; in the Itinerary of Antoninus. Strabo and Ptolemy have "Nimausos". On a very old coin: COL. NEM. ARECOMICORUM. In the Peutinger Table it is written "Nemauso", more corruptly. Stephanus says: "Nimausos, a city of Gaul, from which the Nimausian territory (is named), as that of the Parthisii." How it stood under the Roman empire Strabo describes elegantly, and I cannot refrain from quoting a few of his words on this matter: ... Artemidorus... Nemausus, and the Roman colonists there were held in honour, having been given the right to Latin status... The city lies on the road from Italy into Gaul, and is well supplied with water. Concerning the number of towns assigned to the Nemausenses, Pliny agrees with Strabo. His words in book 3 of the Natural History, chapter 4, are: The Vocontii have two federated capitals, Vasio and Lucus Augusti; the ignoble towns assigned to the Nemausenses number twenty-four. A mention of the decurions of Nemausus occurs in an ancient inscription which is seen there:

units.la: DIS. MANIBVS VIRMI. LVCANI IIIIL. VIRI. AVG ORNAMENTIS. DE CVRIONVM. NEMAVSI HONORATO
units.tr: To the spirits of the dead: Virmius Lucanus, quadrumvir, Augustal, honoured with the insignia of the decurions of Nemausus.

units.la: Miram undique rèdolet cum in veteri Muro, qui testatur multo, quam hodie, amplior fuisse, tum in alijs, Antiquitatem. Amphitheatrum ibi conspicitur, exteriore parte non minus integrum, quam quod Veronæ. Ante Amphitheatrum Campus Martius fuisse perhibetur, qui, ut Romanus, Aedificiis jam oppletus, & in alios tractus est usus. Aedificium, quod vulgo Le Cap duel, Capitolium (sic enim nomen illud corruptum) vel Basilica fuisse fertur, ab Imperatore Hadriano exstructa in gratiam & honorem, ut legere est apud Spartianum, Conjugis Plotinæ. Forma est τετράγωνος, quadrata quidem, sed quæ in longitudinem nonnihil vergit. Latera x. Columnis sulciuntur; Frons vii; pars Fronti adversa totidem. Tectum ex magnis compositum est Lapidibus; Deambulationibus adcommodatum. Templum, Fonti propinquum, integrum adhuc est, forma quadrata. Duos habent latera columnarum Ordines, artis absolutæ. Visuntur adhuc ibi Aquilæ. Romani quondam Imperij notæ & insignia, sed quæ Capitibus truncatæ. Id factum volunt ab Gothis, ut Romanum Imperium Corpus esse capite minutum, quum Imperatorum caderent vires, ostenderent. Ad mœnia Veteris Opidi annosa est Structura in Colle, qui Fonti vicinus vulgo Tourremagne vocatur, id est, ut quidam putant, Turris Romana vel Turris Magna. Lapidibus constat exiguis, ijsque quadratis. Videre ibidem est & perantiquas aliquot Statuas, & nonnulla melioris notæ Variorum Epitaphia: Columnam item ad Portam, cui ab Corona nomen. Imperatorum Domitiani, & Antonini Pij Philosophi, aliorumque claret Natalibus. Qui vulgo Fons Incolis appellatur, sed qui Lacus potius, quam Fons, dubitatur an sit, quem celebrat Ausonius Carmine, quod indicavi. Qui penitius inspexerunt, suspicantur alium fuisse, qui ex proximis Collibus in Vrbem ducebatur; sed cui accideric, quod Divonæ Burdigalensi, id est perijsse, Incolæ Nemausenses nominantur. De ijs Lapis mutilus:
units.tr: Its antiquity is revealed everywhere, both in the old wall, which shows that the town was once much larger than it is today, and in other remains. The amphitheatre can be seen there, its exterior almost as intact as that at Verona. Before the amphitheatre is said to have been the Campus Martius, which, like the Roman one, has been filled with buildings and put to other uses. The building commonly called Le Cap duel, Capitolium (for the name has been corrupted in this way) or Basilica is said to have been built by the Emperor Hadrian in favour and honour of his wife Plotina, as may be read in Spartianus. It is square in plan (τετράγωνος), though somewhat elongated. Its sides measure ten columns; the front has seven, and the side opposite the front has as many. The roof is made of large stones and is suited to walking about on. The temple near the fountain is still intact, square in form. It has two rows of columns along its sides, of perfect workmanship. Eagles, the old marks and emblems of the Roman Empire, can still be seen there, but with their heads cut off. They say the Goths did this, to show that the Roman Empire was a body with a diminished head, as the strength of its emperors declined. Near the walls of the old town, on a hill close to the fountain commonly called Tourremagne, that is, as some think, Turris Romana or Turris Magna, stands an ancient structure. It is made of small, square stones. There too can be seen some very ancient statues, some fairly fine epitaphs of various people, and also a column at the gate named after the Crown. The birthplaces of the emperors Domitian and Antoninus Pius the Philosopher, and of others, are famous. What the inhabitants commonly call the Fons, but which is doubtful whether it is a Lacus rather than a Fons, is the one celebrated by Ausonius in the poem I have cited. Those who have examined it more closely suspect that it was another, which was led into the city from the nearby hills; but whatever happened to it, the inhabitants, as at Dijon in Burgundy, are called the Nemausenses, that is, they have perished. Concerning them there is a damaged stone:

units.la: IIIIL. VIR ... CORPORATI. NEMAVSENSES PATRONO XX. POSTVLATIONE. POPVLI L. D. D. D.
units.tr: Quadrumvir ... the corporation of the Nemausenses to their patron, by decree of the people, at public expense.

units.la: Leguntur etiam Nemausenses apud Suetonium cap.xiii. Tiberij Principis Statuas & Imagines subvertisse; ubi tamen plerique Codices Nemausenses habent: Membranæ pleraque Remausenses; Vaticanus Liber, Remausisses. Exstat Libellus de Antiquitatibus Nemausensibus Ioannis Poldi. Tribus Nemauso milliaribus, Pons est, qui vulgo Du Gard. Nomen hoc illi ab Fluvio Guardone: quem, Francorum Veterum enunciatione (de qua Agathias) Wardonem appellant Sidonius lib. 11. Epist: x. Theodulphus Aurelianensis duobus locis, Fulbertus in Historia MS. Igidij & Petrus Aquil. lib. viii. cap. xviii. Pons triplici serie fornicatus est, stupenda sane industria: Prima Hominibus lumenquisque præbet transitum, altera Aquæductum sustinet. Inter Fanum S. Privati & Rimolinum Vestigia monstrantur Aquæductus, quo Romani Aquam in Nemausensium Opidum ducebant. Vfez, Vzetensium Civitas: nonnullis Latine scribentibus Vzica. Vzicensis Galliæ Episcopi meminit Aurelianum Concilium v. Opidum quod in Ducatus honorem, ad Wardones confluentes. Alter enim Occidentalior Gardo cognominatur d' Alaix; Orientalior autem d' Andulze, ab opidis, quæ singulorum Ripis adsident. VWardo, ut jam monui, dicitur Theodulpho Aurelianensi Episcopo, & aliis. Lodeus, vel, ut alij, Lodesve, Luteva; Notitiæ Provinciarum Galliæ Castrum Luteva, in Viennensi Secunda. S. Pont de Tomieres, Fanum S. Ponty Tomeriarum. Alet, Aletensis Civitas: Alezium quibusdam Latine scribentibus, Opidum Vicecomitatus titulo insignitum. Mompelier, Latine nominantibus Mons Pessulanus: Mons Puellarum, Puellerum, item Pisciculanus ab nonnullis dicitur, ut notat Cœnalis. Mons Tremulus vocatur à Benjamino Tudelensi; apud quem insigne est hujus Urbis Elogium. Substantionem nuncupatam scribit Blondus 1. Decadis lib. x. Videat ille, qua fretus auctoritate. Male quibusdam Agatha vel Agathopolis, quæ hodie Agde. Situm est Colliculo, decem leucis ab Mari Mediterraneo. Aer ibi placidissimus & saluberrimus. Urbe nihil amœnius, Civibus nihil humanius; Territorio nihil fertilius, Simpliciumque feracius: quæ res Medicos præcipue invitavit, ut Sedem ibi figerent, atque Medicinam cum laude docerent. Academiam enim Urbs habet, quæ instituta memoratur circa annum cIↄ cxcvi; vel saltem quo tempore, Saracenis Hispania pulsis. Medicina cum Discipulis Arabum, Avicennæ, Averrois, & aliorum, huc migravit. Rectoris ibi tanta est auctoritas; ut Studiosi quacumque etiam de causa egredientem comitari honoris gratia cogantur, quod se non sine maximo Studiorum suorum, multarumque Horarum jactura nimis frequenter fecisse, conqueritur Rebuffus. Collegia sunt ibi varia, inter quæ amplissimum est, Papæ cognominatum, quod ab Urbano Pontifice fundatum, & copiosissimis ornatum est Redditibus. Nec minus elegans est Regium, ab Henrico 11 Galliarum Rege erectum. Tertium est, quod vulgo Du Vergier; optimæ spei Adulescentibus Studiorum Victusque necessaria in decennium præbens. Besiers, Bittera, aut Bitera Septimanorum in Aretomicis: Βαιτέρα, Ptolemæo; Βαιτέρα, Stephano, Bliterra, Plinio lib. III. cap. IV; Βλιτέρα Straboni lib. IV; Beterra, Pomponio Melæ lib. II. cap. v, & Antonino, cui & Peterne, Beterris, Tabulæ Peutingeri Itinerariæ in Auferendi casu; Bitterra Itinerario Burdigalensi, & Vsuardo xi. Kalend. Aprilis. Hinc Biterrenses Sidonio lib. viii. Epist. iv; qui Biterienses in Notitia Provinciarum, in Viennensi Secunda. בידרש, id est Bidrasch vitiosius Benjamino in Itinerario. Opidum pervetustum, multis agitatum calamitatibus, cum ab Gothis, tum ab ipsis Francorum Regibus. Agde, Ἀγάθη Τύχη Timosthenis ἐν τῷ καλαμῷ apud Stephanum; Ἀγάθη, Straboni & Ptolemæo; Agatha, Plinio: Opidum ab Massiliensibus Græcis conditum in Volcis Arecomicis: unde & Straboni Κτίσμα Μασσαλιωτῶν. Carcassone, Carcasso Volcarum Tectosagum: Καρκασῶ, Ptolemæo; Carcassum, Plinio; Carcasio, Procopio; Carcassio, Itinerariæ Peutingeri Tabulæ. Secundum inter tres Languedoki Senechallias locum obtinet: La Senechaussee de Carcassone. Castres, Cesseres Hres, opidum Caltrense: Cessero, Plinio; Κιασρῶ, Ptolemæo: Cetero, Casero & Tesero corrupte apud Antoninum. Scaligero tamen apud Plinium legitur Cestero, ut illud sit Provinciæ opidum, quod hodie Cisteron. Pamies, Apamea. de qua post; Mirepoix, Mirapicense opidum. S. Papol, Fanum S. Papuli: La Vaur, Vaurense: Ricus Rivi, Rivense Monasterium. Lombes, Lambariense Monasterium: postea erecta in Episcopatus, suffraganeos Tolosano. Et hæc de Maiorum gentium tam Episcopalibus, quam Archiepiscopalibus Languedoky Urbibus: Minorum gentium appello reliqua opida, inter quæ: Belloquadra, Beaucaire; tertium nacta locum inter tres Languedoky Senechallias, La Senechaussee de Beaucaire, Aiguesmortes, Aqua Mortua; quæ falso quibusdam creduntur Fossæ Mariana, de quibus in Provincia. Pisceaux; Pezenas, Piscena, Plinio: S. Gillis, Burgum S. Aegidy, בירקד מל נייר Beniamino in Itinerario. Chafteau-garry; Lusignen; Montasgnac; Millant, Montillac, & alia.
units.tr: The Nemausenses are also mentioned in Suetonius, chapter 13, as having overthrown the statues and images of the Emperor Tiberius; but most manuscripts there read Nemausenses, most parchment copies read Remausenses, and the Vatican book reads Remausisses. There exists a little book on the Antiquities of Nemausus by Johannes Poldus. Three miles from Nimes is the bridge commonly called Du Gard. It takes its name from the river Guardo, which the Franks of old, in their pronunciation (of which Agathias speaks), called Wardo; Sidonius mentions it in book 2, letter 10. Theodulf of Orléans mentions it in two places, Fulbert in the manuscript history of St Egidius, and Petrus Aquilensis in book 8, chapter 18. The bridge is arched in three tiers, with truly astonishing workmanship. The first gives passage to men, the second supports the aqueduct. Between the shrine of St Privatus and Rimolinum, the remains of the aqueduct are shown by which the Romans brought water into the town of the Nemausenses. Uzès, the city of the Uzetenses, is called Uzica in Latin by some writers. The Council of Orléans, the fifth, mentions a bishop of Uzès in Gaul. The town is named after the Duchy, where the rivers join the Wardones. For the western one is called the Gardon d'Alès, and the eastern one the Gardon d'Anduze, after the towns which sit on each bank. Vuardo, as I have already noted, is what Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, and others call it. Lodeve, or, as others say, Lodesve, Luteva; the list of the provinces of Gaul calls it Castrum Luteva, in Vienne Secunda. Saint-Pons-de-Thomières, the Fanum S. Ponti Tomeriarum. Alet, the city of the Aletenses; Alezium in the Latin writing of some, a town honoured with the title of viscounty. Montpellier, called in Latin Mons Pessulanus; Mons Puellarum or Puellerum, and also Pisciculanus by some, as Cœnalis notes. It is called Mons Tremulus by Benjamin of Tudela, who gives a notable eulogy of this city. Blondus, in book 10 of the first decade, writes that it was called Substantio; let him see on what authority he relies. Agatha or Agathopolis, which is today Agde, is wrongly named by some. It lies on a little hill, ten leagues from the Mediterranean Sea. The air there is very mild and most healthy. Nothing is more pleasant than the town, nothing more friendly than its citizens; nothing is more fertile than its land, nor more productive than its simple folk. This especially invited physicians to settle there and teach medicine with distinction. For the town has a Academy, which is recorded as founded about the year 1196, or at least at the time when the Saracens were driven out of Spain. The medicine of the Arab disciples, of Avicenna, Averroes and others, migrated here. The authority of the rector there is so great that the students are compelled to accompany him, out of respect, even when he goes out for whatever reason; Rebuffus complains that they have done this all too often, at no small cost to their studies and to many hours. There are various colleges there, among which the largest is the one called after the Pope, endowed by Pope Urban and furnished with very ample revenues. The Regium* college, founded by Henry II, King of the French, is no less elegant. The third is commonly called Du Vergier, providing for young men of the best promise their studies and necessary living for ten years. Béziers, Bittera, or Bitera Septimanorum in the Aretomici: Βαιτέρα in Ptolemy; Βαιτέρα in Stephanus; Bliterra in Pliny book 3, chapter 4; Βλιτέρα in Strabo book 4; Beterra in Pomponius Mela book 2, chapter 5, and in Antoninus, and also Peterne and Beterris in the Peutinger Itinerary Tables in the ablative case; Bitterra in the Burdigalensian Itinerary and in Usuard on the 11th day before the Kalends of April. Hence the Biterrenses in Sidonius book 8, letter 4; in the list of provinces, in Vienne Secunda, they are called Biterienses. Hebrew בידרש, that is Bidrasch, a more faulty form in Benjamin's Itinerary. It is a very ancient town, troubled by many calamities, both by the Goths and by the Frankish kings themselves. Agde: Ἀγάθη Τύχη, Timosthenes' "Good Fortune" in the reed-bed, in Stephanus; Ἀγάθη in Strabo and Ptolemy; Agatha in Pliny. A town founded by the Greeks of Massalia among the Volcae Arecomici, whence Strabo also calls it a foundation of the Massaliotes. Carcassonne, Carcasso of the Volcae Tectosages: Καρκασῶ in Ptolemy; Carcassum in Pliny; Carcasio in Procopius; Carcassio in the Peutinger Itinerary Tables. It holds second place among the three seneschalships of Languedoc: La Sénéchaussée de Carcassonne. Castres, Cesseres Hres, the town of Castres: Cessero in Pliny; Κιασρῶ in Ptolemy; Cetero, Casero and Tesero corruptly in Antoninus. Yet in Scaliger's reading of Pliny it is Cestero, so that it is the town of Provence which is today Cisteron. Pamiers, Apamea, concerning which more later; Mirepoix, the town of Mirapicum; Saint-Papoul, Fanum S. Papuli; La Vaur, Vaurense; Rieux, Rivi, the monastery of Rivense; Lombez, the monastery of Lambariense, later erected into a bishopric, suffragan to Toulouse. And these are the cities of Languedoc, both episcopal and archiepiscopal, of the greater sort. The lesser sort I call the remaining towns, among which: Beaucaire, Belloquadra, which holds third place among the three seneschalships of Languedoc, La Sénéchaussée de Beaucaire; Aigues-Mortes, Aqua Mortua, which some falsely believe to be the Fossae Marianae, about which see under Provence. Pézenas, Piscena in Pliny; Saint-Gilles, Burgum S. Aegidy, Hebrew בירקד מל נייר in Benjamin's Itinerary. Château-Garry, Lusignan, Montagnac, Millau, Montillac, and others.

units.la: Latara-Castellum Pomponio est in Gallia Narbonensi: Ioanni Poldo Lates est. Laterra quoque Stagnum Plinio in Agro Nemausiensi: de quo alij alia adferunt. De utroque sic Karolus Clusius, oculatus testis, suis ad Abrahamum Ortelium litteris: Recte Poldus. Nam Lates etiamnum vocatur hoc Castellum cum Vico adjacente: Vicinum Stagno Volcarum, qua Ledum flumen in Stagnum labitur. Id Stagnum aliquot milliaria (sed decim memini me numerare ab Ortu in Occasum) in longitudinem porrigitur, sui aliquot Vici & Oppidula adjacent (ad Septemtrionalius praecipue latus) Nonnullis locis Estang, & ubi alius vadum habet, Estau ab Indigenis appellatur: qui Pisces in altiore Stagni gurgite captos praferunt aliis, quod caenum adeo non resipiant. Littus Maris, quod Incolae Playe de la Mar dicunt, Stagnum a Mari sejungit: Aqua tamen marina Fluxum quibusdam in locis in Stagnum praebet: & haud dubie id Stagnum tutorem a Piratarum atque Hostium incursionibus cum Gallia Narbonensi eram reddit. Designat, Volcarum Stagna nominans, Pomponius Mela. Fauces Laterra Stagni apud Plinium lib. ix. nat. hist. cap. viii, ubi scilicet cum Mari communicatur: Nemausiensibus hodie La Cran pres de Mauguèil, ut notat Dalechampius.
units.tr: Latara-Castellum is in Narbonese Gaul according to Pomponius; for Johannes Poldus it is Lates. Laterra, also Stagnum in Pliny, in the territory of Nemausus: about which others offer other opinions. Concerning both, Charles de l'Écluse, an eyewitness, writes thus in his letter to Abraham Ortelius: Poldus is right. For this castle, together with the adjoining village, is still called Lates: it is near the Stagnum of the Volcae, where the river Ledus flows into the lagoon. This lagoon stretches several miles in length (but I remember counting ten from east to west); several villages and small towns lie next to it (especially on its northern side). In some places it is called the Estang, and where it has a shallow ford, the Indigenes call it Estau; they prefer fish caught in the deeper waters of the lagoon to the others, because they do not taste of mud. The shore of the sea, which the inhabitants call the Playe de la Mar, separates the lagoon from the sea; yet seawater provides a flow into the lagoon in some places; and without doubt this lagoon made Narbonese Gaul safe for me from the attacks of pirates and enemies. Pomponius Mela points to it, naming the Stagna Volcarum. The Fauces Laterra Stagni in Pliny book 9, chapter 8, where it of course communicates with the sea: today it is La Cran près de Mauguio, as Dalechamps notes.

units.la: Languedoko ante paucos annos adtributus est Ducatus Fuxensis, La Duché de Toix; quum antea Guienne concenseretur. Ad Orientem illi ipsum Languedokium: ad Occidentem Convenarum Ager; qua Septemtrio est, Territorium spectat Ripen-se, vulgo de la Rivière; Meridionale Latus Montes claudunt Pyrenaei; qui Ducatum hunc reddunt ut horridiorem, sic Ferri Carbonumque feraciorem.
units.tr: Languedoc was lately assigned to the Duchy of Foix, La Duché de Toix, though previously it was counted as part of Guienne. To its east lies Languedoc itself; to its west the territory of Convenae; on the north it faces the territory of Ripa, commonly called de la Rivière; the southern side is closed off by the Pyrenean mountains, which make this duchy more rugged, but richer in iron and coal.

units.la: Nomen illi ab oppido Fuxio, quod Antiquitatis laude clarum. Continet unum Episcopatum, Apamiensem. Oppidum vulgo Pamies, Latine scribentibus Apamia & Pamias; ad confluentes Amnium, qui vulgo Lers & Lagere. Ab hoc oppido dici videtur Epaunense Concilium, habitum sub Gelasio I Papa, & Sigismundo Rege. Episcopi qui illi interfuerunt, omnes hujus sunt Tractus. Empanensis etiam Synodus xv citatur in Decretorum I Distinct. 16. Eupanense Decret. 11 Causa 11, forte an ab hoc eodem oppido. Sunt & alia oppida, Saverdunum & Musera, Comitum Domicilia. Errare graviter, qui Sedem hic collocant Elusatium, dicam Capite sequente.
units.tr: It takes its name from the town of Foix, which is famous for its antiquity. It contains one bishopric, that of Apamia. The town is commonly called Pamies, and by Latin writers Apamia and Pamias; it lies at the confluence of the rivers commonly called Lers and Lagere. The Council of Épaone seems to have been named after this town; it was held under Pope Gelasius I and King Sigismund. The bishops who attended it all belong to this region. A synod of Empanum is also cited in Decretum, Distinctio 16, and Eupanum in Decretum, Causa 11, perhaps from this same town. There are also other towns, Saverdunum and Musera, the residences of the counts. Those who place the see of Elusa here commit a serious error, as I shall say in the following chapter.

units.la: CAP. XXXVIII.
units.tr: CAP. XXXVIII.

units.la: Vasconia.
units.tr: Vasconia.

units.la: QVA Veteris Aquitaniae Narbonensisque Provinciae hodie sint sub Parlamentis & Burdigalensi & Tolosano, integre, ex Superioribus didicimus: superest Vasconia, quae utrisque paret mistim. Partes enim ejus quaedam sunt sub Burdigalensi, quaedam sub Tolosano.
units.tr: Having learned from the earlier chapters how the provinces of Old Aquitaine and Narbonensis are now divided wholly between the Parlements of Bordeaux and Toulouse, we come to Vasconia, which is subject to both in mixed fashion. Some of its parts lie under Bordeaux and some under Toulouse.

units.la: VASCONIA proprie nunc temporis est, quidquid continetur intra Garumnam, Pyrenaeos Montes, Oceanumque & Guiennam hodiernam, vel Aquitaniam Ludovici xi. Dicta est Vasconia ab Vasconibus, ferocissimis Pyrenaeorum Populis: quos devictos primum a Pipino, deinde ab Ludovico Karoli Magni Filio (qui postea dictus fuit Pius) Rege Aquitaniae in plana Novempopulaniae deductos, postea nomen huic Regioni dedisse certum est & indubitatum. Fuerunt enim Vascones (ut lib. ii. capitibus xi. & xiii. docui) pars Cantabrorum, quos etiam hodieque Hispani Vasquenca vocant. Itaque, quum prius haec Regio ab Caesare Aquitania, postea Novempopulania audiret; ea ab Vasconibus devictis, inque eam a Pyrenaeorum Saltibus demissis, Vasconia fuit appellata. Est autem tertia pars Aquitaniae Augustae. Nam ab Augusto Aquitania triplex fuit instituta: Prima, cujus Caput Avaricum erat Biturigum Cuborum; Bourges: Secunda, cujus Metropolis erat Burdigala, Biturigum Vibiscorum; Tertia tota Trans-Garumnana, in qua principem tenebat locum Augusta Auscorum, vel Auchs; quae Provincia, ut jam dictum est, ab Augusti temporibus ad Pipinum usque nominata fuit Novempopulania; inde ad hunc usque diem Vasconia. Petrus Arvernus Cluniacensis Epist. i: Migravit tamen, sicut audivi, ad Loca satis amania. Petrus Arvernus Cluniacensis Epist. i: Migravit tamen, sicut audivi, ad Loca satis vobis contigua & a Septimania vestra, vobis persequentibus expulsa in Provincia Novempopulana (quae vulgo Gasconia vocatur) & in partibus ei adiacentibus sibi fauces praeparavit. Novempopulania ab Novem Populis, quos alij alios numerant, & nominant: Scaliger
units.tr: Strictly speaking, Vasconia today is whatever lies between the Garonne, the Pyrenees, and the Ocean, together with present-day Guienne, or Aquitaine as Louis XI named it. Vasconia takes its name from the Vascones, the fiercest of the peoples of the Pyrenees. It is certain and beyond doubt that after they were first defeated by Pepin, and then by Louis, the son of Charlemagne (who was later called Pius), while he was King of Aquitaine, they were brought down into the plains of Novempopulania, and afterwards gave their name to this region. For the Vascones were (as I showed in book ii, chapters xi and xiii) a part of the Cantabrians, whom the Spaniards still call Vasquenca today. So, since this region was first called Aquitania by Caesar and later Novempopulania, it was named Vasconia once the Vascones had been defeated and had come down into it from the passes of the Pyrenees. It is the third part of Augustan Aquitania. For Augustus divided Aquitania into three: the first, whose capital was Avaricum of the Bituriges Cubi, that is Bourges; the second, whose metropolis was Burdigala of the Biturriges Vibisci; and the third, the whole region beyond the Garonne, in which Augusta Auscorum, or Auchs, held the chief place. This province, as has already been said, was called Novempopulania from the time of Augustus until Pepin, and from then until the present day Vasconia. Peter of Clairvaux (Cluny) Arvernus, Epistle i: "He moved, however, as I have heard, to places quite pleasant, and near to you and to your Septimania, driven out by your persecutions into the province of Novempopulania (commonly called Gascony) and into the adjoining parts, where he prepared for himself a passage." Novempopulania is named from the Novem Populi, whom different authors count and name differently: Scaliger.

units.la: Pp Loubleẑe, Tallebourg, Iarnac, Barbesieux, arcipotens, Rupefocaldios agnoscens Dominos, Iosac, & alia. Bronage Vicus est, Belgis alijsque Salipetis notissimus.
units.tr: Loubleze, Tallebourg, Iarnac, Barbesieux, Arcipotens, Rupefocaldium (acknowledging lords), Iosac, and others. Bronage is a village, very well known to the Belgians and other salt-makers.

units.la: CAP. XXXV. Cadurcium.
units.tr: CAP. XXXV. Cadurcium.

units.la: DE Tribus Provincijs, quæ Integre Burdigalensi parent Parlamento, verba feci; succedunt quæ Tolosano Cadurcium, Rutenium, Languedokium.
units.tr: I have discussed the three provinces that wholly obey the Parlement of Bordeaux. There follow those that belong to Toulouse: Cadurcium, Rouergue, and Languedoc.

units.la: CADURCIVM cingunt Petrocorij, Nitiobriges, Ruteni, Arverni & Lemovices. Regio est montibus innexa. Vulgo Querci; vel, ut alijs pronunciatur, Crecy.
units.tr: Cadurcium is surrounded by the Petrocorii, the Nitiobriges, the Ruteni, the Arverni and the Lemovices. It is a region enclosed by mountains. It is commonly called Quercy, or, as others pronounce it, Crecy.

units.la: Habitarunt olim Cadurci, quos, præter Plinium lib. IV cap. XIX (an & lib. XVIII cap. I? nondum liquet) cum infinitis alijs Galliæ Populis, celebrat Cæsar lib. VII, cui & Eleutheri, Ἐλεύθεροι, id est, Liberi cognominantur. Sic enim vocem illam scribens accipio: non adsentiens novos inde fabricantibus Populos. Sic apud eumdem Cæsarem post paucula verba Suessones Eleutheri prænominantur, ut dixi cap. XX. Ita alij multi apud Plinium Populi vocantur Liberi.
units.tr: Long ago the Cadurci lived here. Caesar in book VII mentions them, along with countless other peoples of Gaul, and Pliny (book IV, chapter XIX; whether also book XVIII, chapter I, is not yet clear). They are also surnamed the Eleutheri, Ἐλεύθεροι [Eleutheroi], that is, the Free. For that is how I understand the word as I write it, and I do not agree with those who make new peoples out of it. Thus in the same Caesar, a few words later, the Suessones are given the name Eleutheri, as I said in chapter XX. In the same way many other peoples in Pliny are called Liberi.

units.la: Duas habet Diœceses, Doveonam Cadurcorum & Montalbanum. Auiona Ptolemæo nota; pro qua Ducona vitiose Interpretibus. Cahors vulgo, ad Lothum Fluvium. Divona dicitur quibusdam doctis Viris. Certe, quocumque modo scribenda, Cadurcorum esse Metropolin censent Iosephus Scaliger suis ad me Literis, Vinetus ad Ausonium, & alij. Iustus Lipsius, ne quid celem, in aureo de Amphitheatris Libello, Doveonam arbitratur esse Pagum, qui vulgo Dome, plus minus dici mediæ itinere distantem ab Ligeri, parte ea, qua ab Andegavis in Pictones fit iter. Consule quæ dixi cap. XXVII. Adsonat quidem Pagi nomen: sed sic Doveona non posset esse ex mente Ptolemæi Cadurcorum Metropolis, quæ ab eo loco plus LX leucis dirimitur. Aliud addo. Cum Doveona Ptolemæi, si quidem vulgo Cahors, non potest idem esse, quod putant magni viri, Aunedonacum Antonini, vel Auedonacum Tabulæ Peutingerianæ, in Itinere, quod Burdigala ducit Augustodunum. Inter enim Aunedonacum ibi & Mediolanium Santonum millia passuum scribuntur XVI; inter Doveonam autem & Mediolanium, id est inter opida, quæ vernacule Cahors & Santes, XL circiter sunt leucæ, quæ constituunt centum, & quæ excurrunt, passuum millia. Accedit & illud, quod Cadurcorum Metropolis tanto intervallo vergat Ortum versus, ut in iter illud Burdigala Augustodunum incidere non possit. Ego igitur censeo, Aunedonacum esse opidum illud, quod vulgo Aulnay, Mediolanio Santonum distans versus Septemtrionem paullo amplius sex leucis. Quædam obiter dixi in fine cap. XXVIII. Cadurcorum autem Metropolin designat Ausonius libro Professorum, Carmine XVIII, de Exsuperio Tolosæ Rhetore: Decedens placidos mores, tranquillaque Vita Tempora prædives finisti Sede Cadurca.
units.tr: It has two dioceses, Doveona of the Cadurci and Montauban. Ptolemy knows Auiona, for which the translators wrongly give Ducona. Doveona is commonly Cahors, on the river Lot; some learned men call it Divona. Certainly, however it is to be written, Joseph Scaliger in his letters to me, Vinet on Ausonius, and others think it is the metropolis of the Cadurci. Justus Lipsius, so as not to conceal anything, in his golden little book on amphitheatres, thinks Doveona is the village commonly called Dome, about half a day's journey from the Loire, on the part of the road that goes from the Andegavi into the Pictones. See what I said in chapter XXVII. The name of the village does sound similar; but in that case Doveona could not, in Ptolemy's view, be the metropolis of the Cadurci, which lies more than sixty leagues from that place. I add another point. Ptolemy's Doveona, if it is indeed commonly Cahors, cannot be the same as what great men think it is: Aunedonacum of the Antonine Itinerary, or Auedonacum of the Peutinger Table, on the route that leads from Burdigala to Augustodunum. For between Aunedonacum there and Mediolanum of the Santones sixteen Roman miles are recorded; but between Doveona and Mediolanum, that is, between the towns which in the vernacular are Cahors and Saintes, there are about forty leagues, which make a hundred, and which run out to miles. Add to this that the metropolis of the Cadurci lies so far toward the east that it could not fall on that route from Burdigala to Augustodunum. I therefore think that Aunedonacum is the town commonly called Aulnay, a little more than six leagues north of Mediolanum of the Santones. I touched on some of these points briefly at the end of chapter XXVIII. Ausonius, in his book of Professors, poem XVIII, on Exsuperius the rhetor of Toulouse, names the metropolis of the Cadurci: "Leaving behind gentle manners and a tranquil life, you ended your days in the rich seat of Cadurca."

units.la: Altera Diœcesis Montalbanum est, hodie Montaulban, S. Theodard de Montaulban. Vrbs, Arcem habens, ad Tarnim Fluvium, stratum hic Ponte, cujus pars media Languedokiæ est Ditionis. Sunt & alia Opida, quæ vulgo Burelle, Nazareth, Somllac, Gourdon, Martel, & alia.
units.tr: The second diocese is Montauban, today Montaulban, S. Theodard de Montaulban. It is a city with a citadel, on the river Tarn, spanned here by a bridge, the middle part of which is under the jurisdiction of Languedoc. There are also other towns, commonly called Burelle, Nazareth, Somllac, Gourdon, Martel, and others.

units.la: Fuit prope Opidum Martellum in Finibus Cadurcorum, ut Auctor quoque notat lib. VIII. de Bello Gallico, Vxellodunum, nomen retinens: Vocatur & Vssoldun, & Le Puech d'Vsoldun, id est Podium Vxelloduni, quod in editissimo & valde prærupto loco situm. Horrendum est adspectu Præcipitium. Multæ sunt ibi Reliquiæ Vetustatis venerandæ. Quotidie ab Arantibus Numismata Romana ecfodiuntur. Vix reperias Rusticum, qui de Loco interrogatus non statim respondeat Castrum Vxellodunum illud ab Cæsare magni Operibus fuisse oppugnatum Auctor, quem dixi, sic inter alia: Flumen infimam Vallem dividebat, quæ pene totum montem cingebat, in quo positum erat præruptum undique Vxellodunum. Hoc avertere loci natura prohibebat. Sic enim imis radicibus Montis ferebatur, ut nullam in partem, depressis fossis, derivari posset. Flumen, cujus nomen tacet auctor, est quod vulgo Dordonia. Idem paullo post: Sub ipsum Opidi murum magnus Fons prorumpebat, ab ea parte, qua fere pedum trecentorum intervallo Fluminis circuitu vacabat. Hoc Fonte prohiberi posse Opidanos quum optarent reliqui, Caesar unus videret, non sine magno periculo, e regione ejus, Vineas agens adversus Montem & Ag geres struere coepit, magno cum labore, & continua dimicatione. Fontem hunc, cujus usum Obsessis interclusisse scribuntur hic Romani, hodieque ostendunt Adcolae. Si usquam Scriptores hujus aevi in notandis veterum locorum appellationibus hariolati sunt, hic vero unus est locus; de quo melius fuisset illos tacuisse.
units.tr: Near the town of Martel, in the territory of the Cadurci, lay Uxellodunum, as the author also notes in book VIII of the Gallic War, and it retains its name. It is also called Ussoldun, and Le Puech d'Ussoldun, that is, the Podium of Uxellodunum, which is situated on a very high and very steep spot. The precipice is horrifying to behold. There are many remains of venerable antiquity there. Roman coins are dug up daily by the ploughmen. You can hardly find a countryman who, when asked about the place, does not at once answer that the castle Uxellodunum was besieged by Caesar with great siegeworks. The author I mentioned says, among other things: "A river divided the lowest valley, which almost entirely surrounded the mountain on which Uxellodunum stood, steep on every side. The nature of the place prevented it from being diverted. For it flowed at the very foot of the mountain in such a way that it could not be turned in any direction, even with deep trenches." The river, whose name the author does not give, is what is commonly called the Dordogne. The same author, a little later: Under the very wall of the town a great spring burst forth, on the side where, for a distance of about three hundred feet, the river's bend left a space free. When Caesar alone saw that the besieged wished to be cut off from this spring, which could not be done without great danger, he opposite it, moving his mantlets against the mountain, began to build mounds with great labour and continual fighting. The spring whose use the Romans are said to have cut off from the besieged, the local inhabitants still point out today. If writers of this age have ever guessed at the names of ancient places, this is surely one such place; about it they would have done better to keep silent.

units.la: CAP. XXXVI.
units.tr: CAP. XXXVI.

units.la: Rutenium.
units.tr: Rutenium.

units.la: CADURCIO versus Ortum conjacet RUTENIVM; reliqua claudunt Languedokij, Arverni, aliique Concregionales Populi. Vulgo Rouargois, La Seneschaussée de Rouargue.
units.tr: Southeast of Cadurcium, toward the east, lies RUTENIVM; Languedoc, the Arverni and other neighbouring peoples bound the rest. Commonly called Rouargois, La Seneschaussée de Rouargue.

units.la: Sedes olim Rutenorum. Ruteni in Itineraria Tabula, apud Sidonium lib. vii. Epist. vi, Plinium lib. iv. cap. xix, item lib. iii cap iv (nisi alij sint à Prioribus) & Caesarem lib. i. & vii variis locis, ubi & Rutheni scribuntur; qui Ρουτηνοὶ Ptolemaeo.
units.tr: Formerly the seat of the Rutenorum (the Ruteni). The Ruteni appear in the Itinerary Table, in Sidonius, book 7, letter 6, in Pliny, book 4, chapter 19, likewise book 3, chapter 4 (unless these are other people from earlier times), and in Caesar, book 1 and book 7, in various places, where they are also written Rutheni; they are the Ρουτηνοὶ of Ptolemy.

units.la: Senescballia Rutenensis duas complectitur Dioeceses, cum Vabris, Segodunum Rutenorum; Σεγόδουνον Ptolemaeo, vulgo Rodez; Rutena apud Turonensem: Urbs, quae multa ab Gothis, Francis, Saracenis passa, tandem in Francorum venit ditionem. Gregor. Turonensis lib. ii. Histor. cap. xxxvi & seq. & de Vita Patrum cap. iii. Sunt & alia Opida: Ville Franche de Rouargue, Gordon, Estanges, Esperon.
units.tr: The Senescballia Rutenensis comprises two dioceses, together with the Vabris. Segodunum Rutenorum (Σεγόδουνον in Ptolemy) is commonly called Rodez; Turonensis calls it Rutena. It is a city which, after suffering much from the Goths, the Franks and the Saracens, finally came under the rule of the Franks. See Gregory of Tours, book 2 of the Histories, chapter 36 and following, and On the Lives of the Fathers, chapter 3. There are also other towns: Ville Franche de Rouargue, Gordon, Estanges, Esperon.

units.la: CAPUT XXXVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXVII.

units.la: Languedokium.
units.tr: Languedoc.

units.la: RESTAT in Tolosani Parlamenti Jurisdictione Major Superioribus, Cadurcio Rutenioque, Portio, LANGVEDOKIVM.
units.tr: There remain, within the jurisdiction of the Parlement of Toulouse, the greater districts beyond Cahors, Rodez and Périgord: LANGUEDOC.

units.la: Provinciae nomen; quod Incolae, reliquis Gallis pro Νa vel Ita Latinorum, Oui proferentibus: Oc dicant. Quum capite xv Romanensem Galliae Idiotismum, ex litteris Nobilissimi Viri Iosephi Scaligeri, in duo summa diducerem fastigia, Francium, & Teclosagicum sive Provinciale; Francici duas feci Species, quae vulgo Langue d'Oui, & Langue d'Oc. In Posteriore plene est Provinciæ Nomenclatura: ut Regio quasi sit, quæ huic Linguæ dicata & consecrata. Nugantur, qui aliam quærunt Appellationis rationem: inter quos maxime, qui Gothos hic somniant, Langue-dokium scribentes nominari, quasi Langothium, id est, Terram Gothicam: quo nihil dici potest absurdius. Morboniam tales. Stupiditas ipsa non posset stupidius. Scimus ex Sidonij lib. III. Epist. ad Avitum, Gregorio Turonensi lib. VIII, cap. XXX & aliis locis, Gothos olim hic habitasse; sed Provinciam ab iis dictam, sanus nemo credet. Quum vero Lingua Oc latissime pateret, Regio, quæ delineanda nobis præ manibus, hoc nomine præcipue notata est, quod Sedes ibi esset Regiminis Linguæ Oc. Nam Regnum Franciæ ante ducentos annos in duo summa Regimina dividebatur; in Linguam Oui, cujus caput Lutetia; & Linguam Oc, cujus caput alternis erat nunc Tolosa, nunc Mompelium. Franci hoc Regimen vocabant etiam Gubernamentum Linguæ Torte: ita nominantes Linguam Oc, quam illi putant esse Distortam, Suam vero Rectam. Habent Linguam Oc loquentes ad Occidentem Valcones, interfluente Garumna; ad Caurum, Cadurces: ad Septemtrionem, Arvernos & Forenses; ad Orientem, Delphinates & Provinciales, sic, ut totus Rodanus sit Languedokiæ Ditionis, & sub Parlamento Tolosano; Meridionale denique Latus partim pulsat Mare Mediterraneum, quod Gallicum ibi audit; partim Montes claudunt Pyrenæi: quem Tractum sic finit Strabo lib. IV: Ἐντὸς δὲ τῆς τόπων, ὃν φ ἐπὶ τὰ Πορτμία Τρόπαια, ἐφ᾽ ὃν Ἰσσηίας ἀπαφάσσει, καὶ τῆς Κιλίκης. Ἐπὶ δ᾽ ἐντὸς ἐπὶ Ναρβῶνα μέλλει ἔχειν: Εἰς δὲ Νιμαύσιον, ἐγδοήκοντα ἔχει: Ἐκ Νιμαύσιον δὲ ἐπὶ Ἀρλὰ ὄρρυς καὶ πεζοκαν&cetera. Regio est nobilissima. Scriptoribusque Romanis cum primis celebrata: quæ causa, quod Veteres ejus Incolæ multo nominentur numerosiores, quam reliquarum Galliæ partium. Eos, anteaquam, quo modo se nunc habeat Regio, doceam, animus est recenseere paucis, non servato curiosius ordine.
units.tr: This is the name of the province, which its inhabitants pronounce Oc, where other Frenchmen say Oui, as the Latins say Ita or Na. In chapter 15, when I divided the Gallic idiom of Rome into two main branches, on the authority of the most noble Joseph Scaliger, I distinguished Francium and Teclosagicum, or Provinciale. I made two kinds of the French tongue, which are commonly called Langue d'Oui and Langue d'Oc. The name of the province is fully contained in the latter, as if the region were dedicated and consecrated to this language. Those who seek another explanation of the name are talking nonsense, above all those who dream here of the Goths and write that the name is "Langue-dokium", as if it were "Langothium", that is, "the Gothic land"; nothing can be said more absurd. Such people are sick in the head; stupidity itself could not be more stupid. We know from Sidonius, Epistles book 3 to Avitus, from Gregory of Tours, book 8, chapter 30, and from other places, that the Goths once lived here; but that the province was named after them no sane person will believe. Since the language Oc was spoken over a very wide area, the region we have in hand was marked chiefly by this name, because the seat of the government of the language Oc was there. For about two hundred years before, the kingdom of France had been divided into two principal governments: the Langue Oui, whose capital was Lutetia, and the Langue Oc, whose capital was alternately Toulouse and now Montpellier. The French also called this government the "government of the Langue Torte", thus naming the language Oc the "twisted" tongue, which they think is distorted, while their own they call the "right" one. Those who speak the language Oc are the Vascones to the west, with the Garonne flowing between; to the northwest the Cadurci; to the north the Arverni and the Forenses; to the east the Dauphinois and the Provençals, so that the whole Rhône lies within the jurisdiction of Languedoc and under the Parlement of Toulouse. Finally, the southern side is partly washed by the Mediterranean, which here is called the Gallic Sea, and partly enclosed by the Pyrenees. Strabo, book 4, defines this tract thus: Ἐντὸς δὲ τῶν τόπων, ὃν φ ἐπὶ τὰ Πορτμία Τρόπαια, ἐφ᾽ ὃν Ἰσσηίας ἀπαφάσσει, καὶ τῆς Κιλίκης. [Within the places which extend to the Pyrenaean trophies, as far as Issus and Cilicia] ... Ἐπὶ δ᾽ ἐντὸς ἐπὶ Ναρβῶνα μέλλει ἔχειν [and inland towards Narbo] ... Εἰς δὲ Νιμαύσιον, ἐγδοήκοντα ἔχει [and towards Nemausus] ... Ἐκ Νιμαύσιον δὲ ἐπὶ Ἀρλὰ ὄρρυς καὶ πεζοκαν&cetera [and from Nemausus towards Arelate, and so on]. The region is very noble and was celebrated especially by Roman writers; for this reason its ancient inhabitants are named much more numerously than those of the other parts of Gaul. Before I show how the region now stands, I intend to recount them briefly, without keeping a more careful order.

units.la: Sedes igitur hic suas olim habuisse leguntur Volcæ & Arecomici & Tectosages, Septimani, Decumani, Atacini, Tolosates, Gabali, Albigenses, Velauni, Consaranni, Helvy, Nemausenses, Aletenses, Beterienses, Agathenses, Lutevani, Magalonenses, Sontiates. Volcarum Nomen in primis hic magnum, quod varie scribi reperio. Nam qui Volcæ Cæsari, Livio, Plinio, Silio, Melæ, alijs, Οὐόλκαι autem Straboni & Ptolemæo: in quibusdam Cæsaris Codicibus Volga dicuntur; Dionysio Halicarnassæo Οὐάλκοι: Belca Ausonio in Tolosæ Urbis Delineatione. Quod ad Volgas, magnam scimus cognationem inter γ & κ, Græcorum litteras: Dionysij Οὐλκοιις, in morbo cubare censeo, restituendosque saltem Οὐέλκας.
