In Belcis Ausonij varie laboratur: Versus in postrema Editione sic habet: Usque ad Teutosagos primævo nomine Belcas:
units.tr: Here, then, the Volcae and the Arecomici and the Tectosages are read as having once had their seats, together with the Septimani, Decumani, Atacini, Tolosates, Gabali, Albigenses, Velauni, Consaranni, Helvii, Nemausenses, Aletenses, Beterienses, Agathenses, Lutevani, Magalonenses and Sontiates. The name of the Volcae is especially great here, and I find it written in various ways. Those whom Caesar, Livy, Pliny, Silius, Mela and others call Volcae, Strabo and Ptolemy call Οὐόλκαι; in some manuscripts of Caesar they are called Volga; Dionysius of Halicarnassus calls them Οὐάλκοι; Ausonius, in his description of the city of Toulouse, calls them Belca. As for Volgae, we know of a close kinship between γ and κ, the letters of the Greeks; I think Dionysius' Οὐλκοιις is sick, and at least Οὐέλκας should be restored. Scholars have struggled over the Belcae of Ausonius. In the latest edition the verse reads thus: "Usque ad Teutosagos primævo nomine Belcas" [as far as the Teutosagi, Belcae by their original name].

units.la: Testatur doctissimus Vir Elias Vinetus in quibusdam Exemplaribus esse, Panasque nomina Belgas;
units.tr: The most learned man Elias Vinetus attests that some copies have "Panasque nomina Belgas" [and Belgae by the name of Panae],

units.la: In alijs autem, Paganaque nomina Belgas:
units.tr: while in others it is "Paganaque nomina Belgas" [and Belgae by the name of Pagani].

units.la: Emendat Beatus Rhenanus lib. I. rerum Germ. Germanaque nomina Belgas.
units.tr: Beatus Rhenanus, in book 1 of his Rerum Germanicarum, emends it to "Germanaque nomina Belgas" [and Belgae by the name of Germani].

units.la: Legerat enim lib. II. Ephemerid. Belli Gallici, Cæsarem ab Remis didicisse, plerosque Belgas ab Germanis ortos, Renumque antiquitus traductos propter loci fertilitatem ibi consedisse: Gallos autem, qui ea loca incolebant, expulisse. Ingeniose quidem, ut multa alia: sed quid conjectura illa ad Tectosages, Galliæque Narbonensis Fines, quos ibi regit Ausonius? Iosephus Scaliger lib. I. Ausonianar. Lect. cap. XXIII legit, Paganaque nomina Belcas;
units.tr: For he had read, in book 2 of the Ephemerides of the Gallic War, that Caesar learned from the Remi that most of the Belgae were descended from the Germans, and that they had been carried across the Rhine in ancient times and settled there because of the fertility of the place, and had driven out the Gauls who inhabited those lands. This is ingenious, as are many of his ideas; but what has that conjecture to do with the Tectosages and the boundaries of Gallia Narbonensis, which Ausonius governs there? Joseph Scaliger, in book 1 of his Ausonian Lectures, chapter 23, reads "Paganaque nomina Belcas" [and Belcae by the name of Pagani],

units.la: & quid Pagana sint nomina, quidque Pagi, docte explicat. Non improbæ nihilominus notæ censendi sunt illi Codices, qui præferunt, Primævo nomine Belcas.
units.tr: and learnedly explains what "pagana nomina" are, and what a pagus is. Nevertheless, those manuscripts which give "Primævo nomine Belcas" [Belcae by their original name] must be regarded as not without merit.

units.la: Nam Belca, si quidem ita scripserit Ausonius, homo Gallus, forte ex genuina Incolarum pronunciatione, idem omnino sunt cum reliquorum Volcis: quorum nomen hodie in ore Vulgi nusquam agnoscitur, nisi quis velit in Belcaria (modo Belca Ausonio sint, ut dixi, qui ceteris Volcæ) servati, quæ nunc vernacule ea Galliæ Narbonensis vel Languedokij pars, ut notat Vinetus, cujus princeps est Nemausus. Recte autem Ausonius Teutosagos, qui Tectosages aliis, primævo nomine Belcas, canit: iudicans eos Belcas vel Volcas præNominatos. Volca enim duplices erant, Arecomici & Tectosages. Qui Arecomici Cæsari & Plinio: Ἀρεκόμιοι scribuntur Ptolemæo, maxo, Aεχομαικοὶ, & non semel Aεχομιστικοὶ Strabonis lib. iv, qui eos maximum incolere spatium scribit, cuique Πάτιον ipsorum ἡ Ναρβών. Hi olim, ubi nunc, ut suis ad me Litteris monet Nobilissimus Vir Iosephus Scaliger, Nemausus, Vcetensis, Magalonenses, & Biterrae. Civitates Nemausensium, Magalonensium, & Beterrensium, item Castrum Vcetiense ponit Notitia Provinciarum in Viennensi ii; hodie, Les Evesches de Nismes, Montpeliers, Beziers & Vfez. Qui Tectosages Plinio lib. v, Pomponio. Melx lib. ii, Τεκνοσάγες Strabonis; Tectosagi vocantur eidem Plinio lib. iii, Livio lib. xxxviii, nec non Iustino, ex lib. xxxii Trogi Pompei, cujus Majorum hic fuit Patria, ut ipse ait lib. xliii. VOLCETECTOSI in Itineraria Tabula; ubi restituendi VOLCAE TECTOSAGI. Teutosagi autem, ut jam vidimus, Autonio. Τεκνοσάγες est apud Stephanum, ut Αγας, Αςφας: quibus subscribit, Τεκνοσάγες, Εὐθ. Γαλατικόν. Εὐρετ Τεκνοσάγες Θῆα, καὶ Τεκνοσάγων, &c. Inepte faciunt, qui apud Caesarem lib. vii. de Bello Gallico, & lib. i. de Bello Civili, distinctionem inter Volcas & Arecomicos ponunt: ineptius, qui Copulam apud Ptolemaeum interjiciunt, cum inter Volcas & Tectosages, tum inter Volcas & Aricomios; ineptissime, qui in ejusdem Caesaris Ephemeridum vii legunt Cadurcosque ad Fines Volcarum Arecomicorumque depopulabundos misit, contra Membranarum fidem & auctoritatem, in quis, Arecomicorum depopulabundos. Non enim duo, sed unus Populus, cum Volca Arecomici, tum Volca Tectosages. Tectosages autem Arecomicis fuerunt celebriores, à quibus Colonias in Asiam, Pannoniam, Germaniamque ductas, scribunt Caesar, Livius, Iustinus, Strabo, Florus, alii; apud quos de antiqua Gentis virtute, Rebusque praeclare gestis, multa. Tectosages apud Plinium tenent eam Galliae partem, quae est inter Pyrenaeos & Cebennam: Pomponius Principem Tectosagum Urbem Tolosam appellat; Iustinus antiquam Tectosagorum Patriam: apud Ptolemaeum Tecto agum Urbes, praesertim Mediterraneae, nominantur Iliberis, Ruscino, Tolosa Colonia, Ceffero, Carcasu, Beterra, Narbo Colonia. Tectosages igitur quondam, ubi nunc praecipue Carcassone & Tolosa: quae mens, ut aliis, sic etiam Iosepho Scaligero. Ex quibus omnibus liquet, Volcas habitasse ad alterum tantum Rodani ripam; licet in utraque eos constituat Livius lib. xxi. Arecomicorum pars fuerunt Septumani, Galliae Narbonensis Populi apud Plinium lib. iii. cap. iv, & Melam lib. ii. cap. v, qui eorum Urbem faciunt Biterras, & Biteram: Bitterras & Biteras legõ in Libris melioribus. De ea post. Septumanorum etiam mentio in Imperii Notitia. Eorum Regio Septumania, Sidonio lib. iii, Epist. i, Eginartho in Vita Karoli Magni, Gregorio Turonensi lib. viii. cap. xxviii, & xxx, item lib ix. cap. vii, Aimoino lib. iv. cap xxxiv, Vuiardo xi. Kal. April. Ionae Aurelianensi lib. i, Petro Atverno Cluniacensi cap. i, & aliis. Nomen proculdubio ab vii. Legionis Militibus, quibus sua ibi fuerunt Praesidia. Meminit, ni fallor, Inscriptio, quam Diani in Hispania exstare scribit ex Apiano Martinus Smetius:
units.tr: For if Ausonius did so write "Belca", then, a Gaul by birth, perhaps from the genuine pronunciation of the inhabitants, it is entirely the same as the rest of the Volcae; their name is nowhere recognised today on the lips of the common people, unless one wishes to find it preserved in Belcaria (provided that the Belcae of Ausonius are, as I have said, the same as the other Volcae), which is now in the vernacular the part of Gallia Narbonensis or Languedoc, as Vinetus notes, whose chief city is Nemausus. Ausonius rightly calls the Teutosagi, whom others call Tectosages, the Belcae by their original name, judging that they were named Belcae or Volcae beforehand. For the Volcae were of two kinds, the Arecomici and the Tectosages. The Arecomici are so called by Caesar and Pliny; they are written Ἀρεκόμιοι by Ptolemy, Ἀρεκομικοὶ by Strabo, and more than once Ἀρεκομιστικοὶ in Strabo, book 4, who writes that they occupied a very large area, whose capital was Narbo. These, long ago, occupied where now, as the most noble Joseph Scaliger tells me in his letters, lie Nemausus, Vaison, Magalona and Béziers. Notitia Provinciarum, in the Viennese province, records the cities of the Nemausenses, Magalonenses and Beterrenses, and the fortress of Vasio; today they are the bishoprics of Nîmes, Montpellier, Béziers and Uzès. The Tectosages are named by Pliny, book 5, by Pomponius Mela, book 2, Τεκνοσάγες by Strabo; they are called Tectosagi by the same Pliny, book 3, by Livy, book 38, and by Justin, from book 32 of Trogus Pompeius, whose ancestors came from this place, as he himself says in book 43. VOLCETECTOSI is in the Itinerary Table, where VOLCAE TECTOSAGI should be restored. The Teutosagi, as we have already seen, are in Ausonius. Τεκνοσάγες is in Stephanus, as Αγας and Αςφας are; to these Τεκνοσάγες, Eustathius adds: "Galatikon". Eurip. Τεκνοσάγες Θῆα, and Τεκνοσάγων, etc. Those who in Caesar, book 7 of the Gallic War and book 1 of the Civil War, draw a distinction between the Volcae and the Arecomici act foolishly; more foolishly still those who insert a conjunction in Ptolemy between the Volcae and the Tectosages, and between the Volcae and the Aricomii; most foolishly of all those who read in book 7 of the same Caesar's Ephemerides that he sent the Cadurci to ravage the frontiers of the Volcae Arecomici, against the faith and authority of the manuscripts, in which it reads "Arecomicorum depopulabundos" [ravaging the Arecomici]. For it was not two peoples, but one, the Volcae Arecomici as well as the Volcae Tectosages. The Tectosages, however, were better known than the Arecomici; Caesar, Livy, Justin, Strabo, Florus and others write that colonies were led from them into Asia, Pannonia and Germany, and in these authors there is much about the ancient valour of the people and their famous deeds. In Pliny the Tectosages hold that part of Gaul which lies between the Pyrenees and the Cevennes; Pomponius calls Toulouse the chief city of the Tectosages; Justin calls it the ancient homeland of the Tectosages; in Ptolemy the cities of the Tectosages, especially the inland ones, are named Iliberis, Ruscino, the colony of Toulouse, Ceffero, Carcaso, Beterra, and the colony of Narbo. The Tectosages therefore once lived where now chiefly Carcassonne and Toulouse lie, which is the opinion of Joseph Scaliger as well as of others. From all these things it is clear that the Volcae lived only on one bank of the Rhône, although Livy, book 21, places them on both. Part of the Arecomici were the Septimani, a people of Gallia Narbonensis according to Pliny, book 3, chapter 4, and Mela, book 2, chapter 5, who make their city Biterrae, and Bitera; I read "Bitterras" and "Biteras" in the better books. More on that later. The Septimani are also mentioned in the Notitia Imperii. Their region was called Septimania by Sidonius, book 3, Epistle 1; by Einhard in the Life of Charlemagne; by Gregory of Tours, book 8, chapters 28 and 30, and likewise book 9, chapter 7; by Aimoin, book 4, chapter 34; by Vuiard, 11th of the Kalends of April; by Ionas of Orléans, book 1; by Peter of Cluny, Atverno, chapter 1, and by others. The name certainly came from the soldiers of the Seventh Legion, who had their garrisons there. I think the inscription which Martin Smetius writes is found at Denia in Spain, from Appian, refers to this:

units.la: D. M. Q. MONEIO VERECVNDO NARBONENSI VET. LEG. VII. GEM. FEL. ÆLIA. VALENTINA MARITO. BENEMERENTI
units.tr: To the gods of the dead. Quintus Moneius Verecundus of Narbo, veteran of the Seventh Legion Gemina Felix. Aelia Valentina to her deserving husband.

units.la: Haud procul Septumanis erant Decumani; in quis, Plinio Pomponioque Auctoribus, erat Narbo Marcius. Decumanos accipio, Decimae Legionis Veteranos: Civitas Narbonensium, Notitiae Provinciarum in Viennensi ii, L'Archevesché de Narbone. Per Narbonem exit in Mare Internum Atax Fluvius, in Saltu Pyrenaeo ortus. Ab Atace Atacini Populi, eidem Pomponio. Atacinorum Urbs erat Atax, ubi natus P. Ille Terentius Varro, Atacinus inde cognominatus, qui scripsit Argonauticon lib. i v. Epigrammata, Bellum Sequanicum, quod citat Priscianus lib. x, & alia. Videndi Plinius lib. i. & Eusebius in Chronicis. Tolosates apud Caesarem lib. i. & vii, Tolosani vero Plinio, qui sine, notius, quam ut à me dicatur. Civitas Tolosatium, Notitiae Provinciarum, L'Archevesché de Tolose, Metropolis eorum Tolosa, de qua post. Gabali apud Cæsarem lib. vii sunt, qui Gabales Plinio, Γαβαλες Straboni; Ptolemæo corrupte Ταβαλοι. Gabali hodie Le Pais de Givaudan. Vicus (Mimatensis) Gabalorum vel Gabalitanorum, ut nominatur Sidonio lib. vii. Epist. vi. hodie Mende de Givaudan. Nam Syllabam Ga primam in Vocibus Galli mutant in Gi; Gabalitanum Givaudan, Gabalum, Gabet, Garumna, Gironda. Marlianus dicit fuisse quondam Provinciæ Bituricensis, nunc vero Provinciæ Arelatensis. Certe & nunc quoque Provinciæ, ut me monet Scaliger, Bituricensis. Mimatensis enim Episcopatus Tribunalis est vel Parlamenti Tolosani, sub Metropoli Bituricensi. Inter Gabalos & Provinciam Arelatensem,
units.tr: Not far from the Septumani were the Decumani, among whom, according to Pliny and Pomponius, was Narbo Martius. I take the Decumani to be veterans of the Tenth Legion. The civitas of the Narbonenses appears in the Notitia Provinciarum under Vienna ii; it is now the Archbishopric of Narbonne. The river Atax, which rises in the Pyrenean forest, flows through Narbo into the Mediterranean. From the Atax came the Atacini, also mentioned by Pomponius. The town of the Atacini was Atax, where P. Terentius Varro was born, who was called Atacinus from it. He wrote the Argonautica in five books, Epigrams, and the Sequanian War, which Priscian cites in book x, and other works. See Pliny book i and Eusebius in the Chronicle. The Tolosates appear in Caesar books i and vii; Tolosani in Pliny, but that is too well known for me to say more. The civitas of the Tolosates is in the Notitia Provinciarum, and it is the Archbishopric of Toulouse; their metropolis is Tolosa, which I shall discuss later. The Gabali are in Caesar book vii; Pliny calls them Gabales, and Strabo Gabales [Γαβαλες]; Ptolemy corruptly has Tabali [Ταβαλοι]. The Gabali are today Le Pais de Givaudan. The vicus (Mimatensis) of the Gabali, or Gabalitani, as Sidonius names it in book vii, letter vi, is today Mende de Givaudan. For in words of Gallic origin they change the first syllable Ga into Gi: Gabalitanum becomes Givaudan, Gabalum becomes Gabet, Garumna becomes Gironda. Marlianus says it once belonged to the province of Bourges, but now to the province of Arles. Certainly even now, as Scaliger reminds me, it belongs to the province of Bourges, for the bishopric of Mimatensis is under the tribunal or parlement of Toulouse, under the metropolis of Bourges. Between the Gabali and the province of Arles,

units.la: Longa procul longis Via dividit inter terris.
units.tr: A long road, far off, divides lands from lands that are long.

units.la: Gabalitani Cafes meminit Plinius lib. xi. nat. Hist. cap. xliii. Albigenses in Aquitania ad Flumen Tarnum; hodie Albigeois: Albigensium Civitas in Notitia Provinciarum, L'Evesché d'Albi. De Albigensibus Haereticis alij. Vide quæ infra dicam de Helvys. Velauni Plinio lib. iv. cap. xix (corrupte enim vulgo Venami fuit, qui Velaunii Cæsari lib. vii, in cujus antiquis Codicibus Velavi Ουελαυοι Ptolemæo, Ουελλαιοι Straboni lib. iv, ad cuius scripturam proxime accedit hodierna appellatio, qua Languedoki Tractus vocatur Velai, vel Velae. Civitas Velaunorum Notitiæ Provinciarum Galliæ in Aquitania vel vi Viennensi, Le Pais de Velai, ut notant Iosephus Scaliger, Ioannes Poldus, Belleforestius, & alij. Martyrologia scribentibus Pagus Velaunus; doctius, quam ipsi opinabantur, pro tota Præfectura Velaunorum. Pagus enim Latinis Veteribus, non tam Vicus, quam magnus modus Agri, Genisque una quantitatis numerosa, ut alibi noto. Ab hujusmodi latiore Pagi notione Gallis vox manavit Pais, numquam G ante Vocalem pronunciare solitis; quemadmodum & in Plaga, Playe & alijs, quæ prætereo. Quæ Civitas Consuntanorum in Vulgatis Notitiæ Provinciarum est Exemplaribus; Consaraunorum vel Conforannorum in Antiquis scribitur: L'Evesché de Conserans: Confuarani vocantur Plinio lib. iii. cap. iv: Soranni fortean Gregorio Turonensi. Qui Helvy apud Cæsarem lib. vii. de Bello Gallico, duobus locis, & initio fere lib. i. de Bello Civili, Helvi apud Plinium, Ελουοι apud Strabonem: Ptolemæo putantur esse Ελουεκιοι; Albenses, in Notitia Provinciarum Galliæ, ubi sub Viennensi Prima, Civitas Albensium, nunc Vivario: L'Evesché de Viviers. Sic in Scriptis legitur Codicibus. Nam incepta est, quæ in Vulgatis libris est, Scriptura, Civitas Albensium, hoc est Belisio. Habitarunt olim, ut suis ad me literis monet Scaliger, ut item sentire video Dalechampium; ut denique satis ex Notitia Provinciarum paret, Helvy Agrum, qui vulgo nunc Vivarais nuncupatur. Helvios Cæsaris omnes (inter quos Orontius, Belleforestius, Poldus, Canalis) hactenus interpretati sunt Albigenses, Albigecis; eorumque Urbem, Albi. At Albigenses sunt in Aquitania, ad Fluvium Tarnum; Albenses autem vel Elvy ad Rodanum. Cæsar lib. vii trans Rodanum esse dicit extra Provinciam Romanam, proximos Arvernis & Cebennis Montibus. De Alba Helviorum Plinij, & Alba Augusta Ptolemæi, hodie Aubenas, paullo post, ubi de Vivariensi Oppido, Vivariensis Dioecesis, id est Albensium, vel Helviorum nunc Metropoli. Nominantur & in Notitia Provinciarum, cujus lepe jam memini, Nemausenses, Aletenses, Petrocorienses & Agathenses & quorum omnium Domicilia nunc etiam notissima, ubi hodie Episcopatus de Nimes, d'Alet, de Beziers, d'Agde. Adduntur & alij: Lutevani, qui & Foro-Neronenses Plinio; quondam, ubi nunc Luteverensis Episcopatus, L'Evesché de Lodeve, vel, ut alij scribunt, Lodeve: Castrum Luteva Notitiæ Provinciarum in Viennensi ii. Magalonenses ab Insula Magalone, ubi prius Sedes fuit Episcopalis, quæ nunc in Monte Pesulo. Domum adhuc gerit Insula cum Templo, in medio Stagnis. Civitas Magalonensium in Notitia Provinc. L'Evesché de Magalone, ou Montpellier. Sontiates apud Cæsarem lib. iii. interpretantur nonnulli Lavedani (Lavedan) Incolas. In quibusdam Libris Sociates scribuntur. Fulvius Ursinus ex Orosio M. S. legit Sociates: Sontiates sunt apud Plinium; Σωντιατες apud Athenæum lib. iv. Qua autem Reip. ratione Sontiates fecerint, indicat non obscure Cæsar, qui Principem eorum nominat Adcantuannum; Athenæus, Αδιαντουνος: Milites ejus illi Soldurii, hic Σιλοδουρος. Fuerunt & inter Galliæ Narbonensis Populos Umbranici, notante Plinio; quorum Ager in Tabula Peutingeriana Umbraniciia dicitur.
units.tr: Pliny mentions the Gabalitani, the Cafes, in Natural History book xi, chapter xliii. The Albigenses in Aquitaine lie on the river Tarn; today they are the Albigeois. The Albigensium Civitas is in the Notitia Provinciarum, and is the Evesché d'Albi. Others have written about the Albigensian heretics. See what I say below about the Helvii. The Velauni in Pliny book iv, chapter xix (for the common reading Venami is a corruption), are the Velaunii of Caesar book vii; in some old manuscripts of Caesar they are Velavi, Ptolemy has Ouelauoi [Ουελαυοι], and Strabo book iv Ouellaioi [Ουελλαιοι]. The modern name comes closest to this spelling: the district of Languedoc is called Velai or Velae. The Civitas Velaunorum is in the Notitia Provinciarum of Gaul, in Aquitaine or in the sixth Vienne, and is Le Pais de Velai, as Joseph Scaliger, John Poldus, Belleforest and others note. Writers of martyrologies call it the Pagus Velaunus, a more learned term than they themselves realised, for the whole prefecture of the Velaunii. For the pagus to the old Latins was not so much a village as a large tract of land and a numerous group of people of one kind, as I note elsewhere. From this wider meaning of pagus the French word Pais arose, since the French never pronounce G before a vowel; the same is true of Plaga and Playe, and other words I pass over. The Civitas Consuntanorum in the printed copies of the Notitia Provinciarum is written Consaraunorum or Conforannorum in the old manuscripts; it is the Evesché de Conserans. They are called Confuarani by Pliny book iii, chapter iv, and perhaps Soranni by Gregory of Tours. The Helvii of Caesar, book vii of the Gallic War, in two places, and at almost the beginning of book i of the Civil War; the Helvi in Pliny; the Helouoi [Ελουοι] in Strabo, and in Ptolemy are thought to be the Helouekioi [Ελουεκιοι]; the Albenses in the Notitia Provinciarum of Gaul, where under the first Vienne is the Civitas Albensium, now Vivarais, the Evesché de Viviers. So the manuscripts read. For the text found in the printed books, Civitas Albensium, is a later reading, and means Belisio. They lived there long ago, as Scaliger writes to me, and as I see Dalechamps also thinks; and in short it is clear enough from the Notitia Provinciarum that the Helvii occupied the land now commonly called Vivarais. All who have so far interpreted Caesar's Helvii (Orontius, Belleforest, Poldus, Canalis among them) have taken them to be the Albigenses, Albigecis, and their city to be Albi. But the Albigenses are in Aquitaine, on the river Tarn; the Albenses, or Elvy, are on the Rhône. Caesar in book vii says that beyond the Rhône, outside the Roman province, lived the Helvii, nearest to the Arverni and the Cevennes mountains. The Alba Helviorum of Pliny and the Alba Augusta of Ptolemy, today Aubenas, I shall treat shortly, where I speak of the town of Vivarais, the diocese of Vivarais, that is, of the Albenses or Helvii, now its metropolis. In the Notitia Provinciarum, which I have often mentioned, the Nemausenses, Aletenses, Petrocorienses and Agathenses are also named, and the places where all of them lived are still very well known: the bishoprics of Nîmes, d'Alet, Béziers, d'Agde. Others are added: the Lutevani, who are also the Foro-Neronenses of Pliny, once where the bishopric of Lodève now is, the Evesché de Lodeve, or, as others write, Lodeve; the castle Luteva in the Notitia Provinciarum under Vienne ii. The Magalonenses take their name from the island of Magalona, where the episcopal seat was formerly, and which is now on Mount Pesulus. The island still has its house and church, in the middle of the lagoons. The Civitas Magalonensium is in the Notitia Provinciarum; it is the Evesché de Magalone, or Montpellier. Some interpret the Sontiates in Caesar book iii as the inhabitants of Lavedan. In some books they are written Sociates. Fulvius Ursinus reads Sociates in an Orosius manuscript; the Sontiates are in Pliny, and Sontiates [Σωντιατες] in Athenaeus book iv. Caesar makes clear enough what constitutional arrangement the Sontiates had: he names their prince Adcantuannus, and Athenaeus names him Adiantounos [Αδιαντουνος]; his soldiers were the Soldurii, and here he is Silodouros [Σιλοδουρος]. There were also among the peoples of Narbonese Gaul the Umbranici, as Pliny notes; their land is called Umbraniciia in the Peutinger Table.

units.la: Hæc de Antiquis hujus Galliarum Tractus Incolis sufficiant: ad Hodierna venio.
units.tr: These notes on the ancient inhabitants of this part of Gaul will suffice. I turn to the present.

units.la: Languedokium Vrbes habet præclarissimas: quarum aliæ gentium quasi sunt Maiorum, aliæ Minorum. Maiorum mihi Archiepiscopales & Episcopales. Prioris Classis sunt Tolosa & Narbona.
units.tr: Languedoc has very famous cities. Some of them are, as it were, of the greater nations, others of the lesser. Of the greater I count the archiepiscopal and episcopal cities. Of the first class are Toulouse and Narbonne.

units.la: Tolosa primum dabo locum, quod non solum Archiepiscopatui, verum etiam amplissimo totius Languedoky Parlamento, Supremæque Curiæ præbeat Domicilium: quodque inter tres ingentes Languedokii Senescalliias principem facile tueatur locum. Tolosa Cæsari, Plinio, Melæ, Marcellino, Iustino, aliisque Latinis Scriptoribus; Τολοσσα Straboni & Ptolemæo: Tolosa vitiose in Tabula Peutingeri Itineraria. Galliæ Narbonensis Volcarum Tectosagum Colonia Geographis: sed a quo & quando ducta, nondum est compertum. Urbs Tolosatium, Sidonio lib. 1 v. Epist. xxii, & Gregorio Turonensi lib. 1. de Miraculis cap. viii. Urbs Tolosana Ennodio in Vita Epiphanii. Nomen retinet: Vulgo Toloufe. Civis Tolosensis, ni fallor, mentio in Marmore, quod Romæ, prope Arcum Camillarem:
units.tr: I shall give first place to Toulouse, which is home not only to the archbishopric but also to the very great parlement of all Languedoc and the Supreme Court; and which easily holds the first place among the three great seneschalships of Languedoc. Toulouse is named by Caesar, Pliny, Mela, Marcellinus, Justin and other Latin writers; Tolosa [Τολοσσα] by Strabo and Ptolemy; Tolosa is wrongly given in the Peutinger Table. The geographers call it a colony of the Volcae Tectosages in Narbonese Gaul, but it is not yet known by whom or when it was founded. Sidonius in book viii, letter xxii, and Gregory of Tours in book i of the Miracles, chapter viii, call it the Urbs Tolosatium. Ennodius in the Life of Epiphanius calls it the Urbs Tolosana. It keeps its name; the common form is Toulouse. I think there is a mention of a Civis Tolosensis on a marble, found at Rome near the Arch of Camillus:

units.la: DIIS MANIBVS C. FABRICI. C. L. VOL. PROXIMI TOLOSENSIS C. FABRICIVS VICARIVS PATRONO. BENE MERENTI. FECIT IN. FRONTE. P. VII IN. AGRO. P. VII
units.tr: TO THE SHADE OF C. FABRICIUS. GAIUS LUCIUS VOLUSIUS PROXIMUS OF TOLOSA. GAIUS FABRICIUS, VICARIUS, MADE THIS FOR HIS WELL-DESERVING PATRON. IT IS SEVEN FEET IN FRONT AND SEVEN FEET IN DEPTH.

units.la: Antiquissima clarissimaque Vrbs, quam Opulentam vocat Ausonius libro de Professoribus, Carmine xvii, qui & libro de Viribus, Carm. xi. Tolosam sic suis coloribus delineat: Non unquam Altricem nostri recitabo Tolosam, Cœruleis muris quam circuit Ambitus ingens, Perque latus pulchro præalbitur amne Garumna; Innumeris custam Populis, confinia propter Ninguida Pyrenes, & pinea Cabennarum, Inter Aquitanas Gentes, & nomen Iberum. Qua modo quadruplices ex se quum ecfuderit Vrbes, Non nulla exhausta sensit dispendia plebis, Quas genuit cunctos gremio complexa Colonos.
units.tr: This most ancient and most famous city, which Ausonius in his book On the Professors, poem 17, calls Opulenta, and who in his book On the Cities, poem 11, also portrays Tolosa in her own colours: I shall not ever recite Tolosa, nurse of ours, which a vast circuit surrounds with blue walls, and past whose side the Garonne flows, white with its lovely stream, guarded against countless peoples, near the snowy Pyrenees and the pine-clad Cevennes, among the Aquitanian tribes and the Iberian name. Though she has now poured forth four colonies from herself, she has felt some loss of her people's strength, yet she still holds all those colonists she has borne in her embrace.

units.la: Qui Poëtæ Ingens Ambitus nunc quoque Magnus est. Paucas namque habet Galliæ Vrbes, Tolosa majores, solì cedente Parisiorum Lutetiæ. Fuit aliquando multo, quam nunc est, amplior opulentiorque, uti paret, cum ex his Ausonii Versibus, tum ex Epistola ad Paulinum, quæ ordine xxiiii, ubi eam Quincuplicem appellat, quasi ex quinque Vrbibus contractam. Sed multa gravia & acerba tulit, Majestatisque ejus magnopere imminuta est, cum alias, tum Albigensis Dogmatis tempestate. Templum quod D. Virginis, cognomine de la d'Aurade, aliudque, quod D. Quintino consecratum; illud ivet hoc Apollini sacrum fuisse memorant Cives: qui & Platea Portaria volunt dictam, quod Iupiter ibi cultus Arietinus, vel quod figura ibi esset Signi Zodiaci Arietis, quasi Porta Arietis. Non pugno. De honnullis ibi Veteris Amphitheatri Vestigiis magis constat: Capitoly item, apud Locum, qui Inquisitio nuncupatur. Arx enim ibi rotundioris structuræ. Tolosatum Capitoly, id est Arcis, memini Sidonius lib. ix. Epist. xvi: Equitibus primum mihi psallat Hymnus, Qui Tolosatum tenuit Cathedram, De Gradu summo Capitoliorum Præcipitatum.
units.tr: That vast circuit of the poet's is still great today. For she has few cities in Gaul larger than Tolosa, only Paris, that is Lutetia, surpassing her. She was once much larger and richer than she is now, as is clear both from these verses of Ausonius and from the letter to Paulinus, letter 24, where he calls her Quincuplex, as if drawn together from five cities. But she has suffered many grave and bitter blows, and her majesty has been greatly diminished, both at other times and especially in the storm of the Albigensian heresy. The citizens report that the temple called of the Blessed Virgin, with the surname de la d'Aurade, and another dedicated to St Quentin, were once sacred, the first to Ivet and the second to Apollo. They also say the street called Porte-Arietaire was so named because Jupiter was worshipped there as Arietinus, or because a figure of the zodiac sign Aries stood there, as if it were Porta Arietis. I do not object. Some remains of an old amphitheatre there are better attested, as well as a Capitol near the place called Inquisitio. For there was a citadel of rather round construction. Sidonius, in book 9, letter 16, mentions the Capitols of the Tolosans, that is, of the citadel: First let a hymn sing to me of the knights, who held the Chair of Tolosa, cast down from the highest step of the Capitols.

units.la: Tolosa Sedes olim fuit Regum Gothorum, ex Fœdere, quod inter Constantium Patricium & Walliam Gothorum Regem, pactum, Theodosio vii & Palladio Coss. Legendi Prosper, Cassiodorus, Iornandes in Historia Gothor. cap. xxxi, Diaconus lib. iv, Isidorus in Chron. Gothor. & alij. Sic Rutilus Itinerario i: Errantem Tuscis considera compulit agris, Excolere externos capta Tolosa Lares.
units.tr: Tolosa was once the seat of the Kings of the Goths, by the treaty that Constantius the patrician and Walia, king of the Goths, concluded in the consulship of Theodosius (for the seventh time) and Palladius. See Prosper, Cassiodorus, Jordanes in his History of the Goths, chapter 31, Diaconus book 4, Isidore in the Chronicle of the Goths, and others. So Rutilius in his Itinerary, book 1: Wandering among the Tuscan fields, he led me to consider how captured Tolosa was made to cultivate foreign household gods.

units.la: Idacius M. S. Gothi sedentes in Aquitania Tolosæ filij sedem eligunt. Et inde Reges Tolosæ nominati. Sic Alaricus Rex Tolosa in Commonitorio Ariani; Sic alij. Hinc Torismundus, ut Regnum auspicaretur, Tolosam, Regni Gothici caput, ingreditur apud Iornandem in Hist. Gothorum: Hinc Theodoricus, Torismundi Successor, Larem ibi fovet apud Sidonium Carm. viii; ut Theodorici Successor Euarix, apud eundem Sidonium lib. v. Epist. xiii, & Ennodium in vita Epiphanij: Hinc denique Alaricus, Eorici filius, apud Tolosatem Urbem Gothorum Rex factus scribitur Isidoro in Chronic. Gothorum: quo interfecto Regnum Tolosanum, occupantibus Francis, est destructum; eodem, & Gregorio Turonensi lib. ii. cap. xxxvii. scribentibus. Celebrem habet Academiam; olim omnium Artium & Disciplinarum, hodie autem cum primis Iurisprudentiæ studio florentem; diligentiaque cum Professorum, tum Studiosorum stupendam. Meminerunt ejus Baldus in l. omnia Privilegia. C. de Episc. & Cleric. Iason ad l. 1. D. de Legat. 1. Abbas in c. sin Extra. Ne Clerici vel Monachi. Multa etiam de ea Rebuffus. Rhetoricam Tolosæ docuerunt Æmilius Magnus Arborius, Exsuperius & Sedatus; quorum Manibus justa solvit Ausonius libro de Professoribus, Carminibus xvii, xviii & xx. De Auro Tolosano (quod Tolosense dixit Iustinus lib. xxxii.) natoque inde Proverbio in eum, cui Fata res secundas esse nolunt; cuique Malum malo congeritur & exaggeratur, legendi Agellius lib. i. Noct. Attic. Strabo lib. iv, & alij. De ejus raptu quæstionem aliquando habitam Romæ, scribunt M. Tullius lib. de Nat. Deor. iii, Orosius lib. v. cap. xv; & alij. Quæ sint autem quatuor Tolosatium Coloniæ, quas ex Te Tolosam effudisse canit paullo ante Ausonius, non constat: quin & plurima de Tolosa memorant Strabo lib. iv. & Iustinus lib. xxxii, quorum hodie paucissima agnoscas. Tolosensis Lacus meminit Trogus Pompeius apud Iustinum lib. xxii circa Tolosam.
units.tr: Idacius, in manuscript: The Goths settling in Aquitaine, the sons of Tolosa, choose a seat. And from this they were named the Kings of Tolosa. So Alaric, King of Tolosa in the Commonitory of the Arian; so others. Hence Thorismund, in order to begin his reign, entered Tolosa, the head of the Gothic kingdom, according to Jordanes in the History of the Goths. Hence Theoderic, Thorismund's successor, kept his household there, according to Sidonius, poem 8; and Euric, Theoderic's successor, did likewise, according to the same Sidonius, book 5, letter 13, and Ennodius in the Life of Epiphanius. Finally, Alaric, son of Euric, is written in Isidore's Chronicle of the Goths to have been made king of the Goths in the city of Tolosa. When he was killed, the Tolosan kingdom was destroyed by the occupying Franks, as Gregory of Tours also writes, book 2, chapter 37. The city has a famous Academy, once flourishing in all the arts and disciplines, but today especially in the study of law, and remarkable for the diligence of both its teachers and its students. Baldus in the law Omnia privilegia, C. de episcopis et clericis, Jason on the law 1, D. de legationibus, and Abbas on the chapter Sin, Extra Ne clerici vel monachi, mention it. Rebuffus also says much about it. Æmilius Magnus Arborius, Exsuperius and Sedatus taught rhetoric at Tolosa, and Ausonius paid the last rites to their shades in his book On the Professors, poems 17, 18 and 20. Concerning the Tolosan gold (which Justin in book 32 called Tolosense), and the proverb derived from it about a man whom fortune does not wish to prosper, on whom evil is heaped upon evil and magnified, see Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights, book 1; Strabo, book 4, and others. Concerning its seizure, a question was once raised at Rome, as Cicero writes in On the Nature of the Gods, book 3, Orosius book 5, chapter 15, and others. Which are the four colonies of the Tolosans that Ausonius sings a little earlier were poured forth from Tolosa, is not known. Indeed, Strabo book 4 and Justin book 32 record many things about Tolosa, of which you would now recognise very few. Trogus Pompeius, in Justin book 22, mentions the Lake of Tolosa near Tolosa.

units.la: Tolosæ proxima dignitate est Narbona. Sic Suetonio in Tiberio cap. iv (apud quem tamen in MSS. Narbo legitur) Eutropio, Ammiano, & plerisque Latinæ nunc scribentibus appellatur, quæ Narbo Martiali lib. viii. Epigr. xxi, & aliis; Ναρβῶν Polybio lib. iii, & Ptolemæo; Narbo Martius, Plinio lib. iii. natur. Hist. cap. iv, Pomponio Melæ, Ausonio in Urbibus, & aliis. Ναρβώνα Marciano apud Stephanum: Apud Avienum Naro dicitur. Ptolemæus Tectosagum Urbem tacit in Gallia Narbonensi; Αrecomicorum Navale Strabo; Decumanorum Coloniam esse ait Plinius; Eorumdem quoque & Atacinorum Pomponius Mela lib. ii. A propriis Colonis conditam notat Isidorus lib. xv. Etymologiar. Quæ causa Narbonem Coloniam deducendi Romanis fuerit: quod primum Nomen antiquissima Urbs, & unde Marcij cognomen habuerit, adhuc quærunt Docti. Deductam lego non semel. Deduxit Primus, post domitos & debellatos ab Longinis, Domitiis, Fabiusque Gallos Transalpinos, L. Licinius Crassus Orator, quum adhuc esset adolescens, testibus Cicerone in libro de Claris Oratoribus, Paterculo lib. i, & Eutropio. Factum illud anno ab V. C. 1cxxxvi, L. Porcio Catone & Q. Marcio Rege Coss. Unde sunt, qui Marcium ab altero Coss. cognominatum velint. Sed quur Cognomen illi ab Marcio potius Rege, quam à Porcio Catone? & quur ab altero potius Coss. quam ab eo, uti moris erat, qui deduxerat? Quin Marcia Gens quartam in Nomine litteram C habet, non T, apud omnes Græcos Latinosque Scriptores, in omnibus Membranis, in multis, quæ apud Aldum Manutium, Inscriptionibus, & Nummis. Narbo autem quartam sui Cognominis Marty litteram T agnoscit, non C, in quorquor reperiuntur, Scriptis Codicibus: contra quorum fidem & auctoritatem iniquè facit Dionysius Lambinus, Vir doctissimus, qui per C vult scribi. Aliunde igitur Cognominis ratio quærenda, & forte an ab Veteranis Martia Legionis Militibus. Respicere videtur eo Sidonius Apollinaris in Epistola ad Pontium Leontium de Burgo: Dum apud Narbonem, quondam Martium dictum, sed nuper factum, morasne nectio. Innuit primo Martium non Marcium cognominatum; deinde Narbonem olim quidem Martium vocatum, sed quod Marty appellatione designabatur, hoc nuper esse effectum; Civitatem scilicet Martiam, id est bello potentem, & strenuam, quum nimi-rum rum Gothos obsidentes oppugnantesque diu fortissime sustineret. Certe ab Rebus Bellicis, Militarique Virtute laudant hanc Urbem & alij. Cicero in Oratione pro Fonteio: Est in eadem Provincia Narbo Martius, Colonia nostrorum Civium, Specula Populi Romani, ac Propugnaculum ipsis Nationibus oppositum & objectum. Pomponius Mela lib. ii. Sed antistat omnes Atacinorum Decumanorumque Colonia: unde olim its Terris auxilium, nunc & nomen & decus est, Martius Narbo. Deductam iterum Narbonem Coloniam C. Iulio Caesare Dictatore; & Ti. Claudium Neronem, Ti. Imperatoris Patrem, deduxisse, Suetonius auctor est in Ti. Principis Vita cap. iv. A quo tempore Narbo non solum Marty usurpavit cognomen, verum etiam Iulia Paterna quasi Praenomen, dictaque fuit Julia Paterna Narbo Martius: Julia quidem ab C. Caesaris Dictatoris Nomine: Paterna vero, quod Iulij Patris, id est Dictatoris, non Iulij Filij, id est Octaviani Augusti, auspicijs esset deducta. Testatur elegans Marmor in ipsa Urbe eefossum anno CIO IOLXVI. Exstat typis excusa, cujus pars, quae dictis a me probandis facit, sic habet: ILSCE. LEGIBVS. ILSQVE. LEGIONIBVS. SIC. VTI. DIXI. HANC. TIBI. ARAM. PRO. IMP. CAESAR. AVG. T. P. PONTIFICE. MAXIMO. TRIBVNITIA. POTESTATE. XXXV. CONIVGE. LIBERIS. GENTEQVE. EIVS. SENATV. POPVLOQVE. R. COLONIS. INCOLISQVE. COL. IVL. PATERN. NARB. MART. QVI. EE. NVMINI. ILVS. IN. PERPETVVM. COLENDO. OBLIGAVERVNT. DOQVE. DEDICOQVE. VTI. SITS. VOLENS. PROPITIVM. Celebrant Narbonem Ausonius & Sidonius Apollinaris: ille quidem in Urbium suarum Catalogo, Carm. xii, ubi inter alia sic canit: Quis memoret Portusque tuos, Montesque, Lacusque? Quis Populos vario discrimine Vestis & Orii? Quodque tibi quondam Pario de Marmore Templum Tanta moles erat, quantam non sperneret olim Tarquinius, Catulusque iterum, postremus & ille, Aurea qui fastus Capitoli culmina Caesar? Te Maris Eoi merces, & Hiberica ditant Aequora, te Classes Libyci, Siculique Profundi: Et quidquid vario, per Flumina, per Freta, cursu Advehitur: toto tibi navigat orbe varius.
units.tr: Narbo is next in rank to Tolosa. It is called Narbo by Suetonius in Tiberius chapter 4 (though in the manuscripts it is read as Narbo), by Eutropius, Ammianus, and most Latin writers of our time; Narbo by Martial in book 8, epigram 21, and others; Ναρβῶν [Narbōn] by Polybius book 3 and Ptolemy; Narbo Martius by Pliny, Natural History, book 3, chapter 4, by Pomponius Mela, by Ausonius in On the Cities, and others. Ναρβώνα [Narbōna] in Marcianus, as cited by Stephanus; in Avienus it is called Naro. Ptolemy mentions the City of the Tectosages in Narbonese Gaul; Strabo the naval station of the Arecomici; Pliny says it was a colony of the Decumani, and Pomponius Mela, book 2, notes that it was also a colony of the same Decumani and of the Atacini. Isidore, Etymologiae book 15, notes that it was founded by its own colonists. What reason led the Romans to lead a colony to Narbo, what its first name was, and whence it got the surname Marcius, learned men still ask. I have read that it was led there more than once. The first to lead one, after the Transalpine Gauls had been subdued and defeated by the Longini, Domitii and Fabii, was the orator L. Licinius Crassus while he was still a young man, as Cicero attests in his book On the Famous Orators, and also Paterculus book 1 and Eutropius. This happened in the year 636 from the founding of the city, in the consulship of L. Porcius Cato and Q. Marcius Rex. Hence some want Marcius to have been named after the other consul. But why should the surname come from Marcius Rex rather than from Porcius Cato? And why from the other consul rather than from the one who led the colony, as was the custom? Moreover, the Marcian gens has a C as the fourth letter of its name, not a T, in all Greek and Latin writers, in all manuscripts, in many inscriptions printed by Aldus Manutius, and on coins. But the fourth letter of the surname of Narbo Martius is a T, not a C, in all the manuscripts where it is found. Dionysius Lambinus, a most learned man, who wishes it to be written with a C, acts unfairly against their witness and authority. The reason for the surname must therefore be sought elsewhere, perhaps in the fact that the colonists were veteran soldiers of the Martian legion. Sidonius Apollinaris seems to point to this in his letter to Pontius Leontius of Bourg: While I am detained at Narbo, once called Martius, but lately made so. He hints, first, that it was surnamed Martius, not Marcius; second, that Narbo was once indeed called Martius, but that this designation, by which it was called Marty, was lately brought about; namely, a city Martian, that is, powerful and vigorous in war, since it bravely sustained for a long time the attacks and sieges of the Goths. Certainly for its military exploits and martial courage this city is praised by others too. Cicero in the speech for Fonteius: In the same province is Narbo Martius, a colony of our citizens, a watchtower of the Roman people, and a bulwark set against and opposed to the very nations. Pomponius Mela, book 2: But the colony of the Atacini and Decumani surpasses all others; whence once it gave aid to these lands, and now its name and honour is Martius Narbo. Suetonius is the authority that Narbo was led to as a colony again under Julius Caesar the dictator, and that Tiberius Claudius Nero, father of the Emperor Tiberius, led one there, in the Life of the Emperor Tiberius chapter 4. From this time Narbo not only took the surname Martius, but also Julia Paterna as it were a praenomen, and was called Julia Paterna Narbo Martius: Julia indeed from the name of Gaius Caesar the dictator, and Paterna because it had been led out under the auspices of Julius the father, that is the dictator, and not of Julius the son, that is Octavian Augustus. An elegant marble found in the city itself in the year 1566 attests this. It exists, printed, and the part that supports what I have said reads thus: For these laws and legions, as I have said, I, Caesar Augustus, father of the fatherland, pontifex maximus, holding tribunician power for the thirty-fifth time, have dedicated this altar to you for the emperor, with his wife, children and family, and the Senate and Roman people, and the colonists and inhabitants of the Colonia Julia Paterna Narbo Martius, who have bound themselves to worship this divinity forever; and I dedicate it, that you may be favourable. Ausonius and Sidonius Apollinaris both celebrate Narbo. Ausonius, in his catalogue of his cities, poem 12, where among other things he sings thus: Who could recount your harbours, your mountains and lakes? Who the peoples with their varied dress and gold ornaments? And the temple once of Parian marble which you had, of a size that Tarquin once would not have scorned, nor Catulus again, nor that last Caesar who gilded the peaks of the Capitol? The merchandise of the eastern sea and the Spanish waters enrich you, the fleets of Libya and of the deep Sicilian sea. And whatever is carried by river, by sea, in varied course, sails to you across the whole world.

units.la: Hic vero Carmine xxiii. ad Contentium Clariss. Civem Narbonensem, cujus haec inter alia: Salve Narbo potens Salubritate, Urbe & Rure simul bonus videri Muris, Circibus, Ambitu, Tabernis, Portu, Porticibus, Foro, Theatro, Delubris, Capitoliis, Monetis, Thermis, Arcubus, Horreis, Macellis, Pratis, Fontibus, Insulis, Salinis, Stagnis, Flumine, Merce, Ponte, Ponto, Unus qui venerere jure Divos Lenaeum, Cererem, Palem, Minervam; Specis, Palmite, Pascuis, Tapetis, Solis sive Viris, nec expetito Natura auxilio, procul relictis Promens Montibus altum cacumen. Nam te Fossa patens, nec bisfidarum Objectu Sudium coronat Agger. Item: Quid quod Caesaribus ferax crescendis, Felix Prole Virum simul dedisti, Natos cum Genitore Principantes?
units.tr: Here, in Carmen 23 addressed to Contentius, a most distinguished citizen of Narbo, he writes among other things: Hail, Narbo, mighty in your healthfulness, seeming equally good in city and in countryside, with your walls, circuses, precincts, shops, harbour, colonnades, forum, theatre, shrines, Capitols, mints, baths, arches, granaries, meat markets, meadows, fountains, islands, salt pans, pools, river, trade, bridge, and sea. You alone rightly worship the gods Lenaeus, Ceres, Pales and Minerva, with your groves, vines, pastures, carpets, and men of sun and wind. Nature, without seeking outside help, rears her tall peak, leaving the mountains far behind. For the open ditch crowns you, and the rampart of the two-forked Sudes, not to be sought. Likewise: What of this, that you, fruitful for the increase of the Caesars, have also given Happy offspring of men, sons ruling together with their fathers?

units.la: Versus digni sane, quos publico loco scribundos curet S.P.Q. Narbonensis, ut qualis quantaque quondam Urbs fuerit Narbo, Aetas haec sequensque cum stupore cognoscat. Sic Narbo dicitur Speciosa Prudentio in Hymno Martyrum Caesar-Augustanorum; Urbs Decora Theodulpho Aurelianensi. Capitolium, id est Arcem vel Palatium, etiam Narbonem habuisse indicant suis Carminibus non obscure Ausonius nius & Sidonius. Eius operis hodie nullum exstat Vestigium, sive Vetustas consumserit, seu diruerint Gothi, aliique Barbari. De Capitolio Narbonensi, id est Palatio, videndus Gregorius Turonensis lib. de Mirac. i. cap.xcii. Lacuum appellatione Ausonius, Stagnorum Sidonius exaudiunt Rubresium, de quo praeter alios eleganter Pomponius Mela lib. ii. cap. v: Hodie L'Estang de la Rubine. De eo obiter cap. x. Per Flumen intelligit Sidonius Atacem, de quo Plinius lib. iii. cap. iv. Strabo lib. v, Sidonius lib. viii. cap. iv. lib. ix. cap. xvi, & alibi. Vibius: Atax è Pyrenaeo, circa Narbonam decurrit in Tyrrhenum. Atacis cum aliis Fluminibus meminit Theodulphus Episcopus Aureliani-ensis, qui in Scrinijs adhuc Petri Danielis, Poemate contra Iudaeos iniquos: Praefectura mihi fuerat peragenda tributa, Rex dedit hanc Karolus, primus ad omne bonum. Cui parent Walis, Rodanus, Mosa, Renus & Oenus, Sequana, Visurgis, Warda, Garumna, Padus, Rufa, Mosella, Liger, Vulturnus, Matrona, Ledus, Ister, Atax, Gabarus, Olitis, Albis, Arar.
units.tr: These verses are certainly worth having written in a public place by the Senate and People of Narbo, so that this age and those that follow may learn with wonder what sort and how great a city Narbo once was. Thus Prudentius, in his Hymn of the Martyrs of Caesar-Augusta, calls Narbo Speciosa (fair), and Theodulphus of Orléans calls it a Decora (comely) city. That it had a Capitolium, that is a citadel or palace, Ausonius and Sidonius indicate clearly in their poems. No trace of this work survives today, whether time has consumed it or the Goths and other barbarians destroyed it. On the Narbonese Capitolium, that is the palace, see Gregory of Tours, On the Miracles, book 1, chapter 92. Ausonius by the word lacus (lakes), and Sidonius by stagna (pools), understand the Rubresus, of which, among others, Pomponius Mela writes elegantly in book 2, chapter 5. Today it is L'Estang de la Rubine. On it, in passing, see chapter 10. By flumen (river) Sidonius means the Atax, of which Pliny speaks in book 3, chapter 4; Strabo in book 5; and Sidonius in book 8, chapter 4, book 9, chapter 16, and elsewhere. Vibius says: Atax, rising from the Pyrenees, runs past Narbo into the Tyrrhenian Sea. Theodulphus, bishop of Orléans, mentions the Atax along with other rivers, in his poem against the wicked Jews, which is still preserved among the papers of Pierre Daniel: The office of tax-collector was given to me to carry out; King Charles, the first to every good thing, gave it. To him obey the Walis, Rhone, Meuse, Rhine and Oenus, Seine, Weser, Warta, Garonne, Po, Rufa, Moselle, Loire, Volturno, Matrona, Lede, Danube, Atax, Gabarus, Olitis, Elbe and Arar.

units.la: Ab Atace, Atacini Populi & Farro Atacinus, ut alias dixi. Narbo Straboni lib. iv, Μύασσα Ἐμπόριον. Narbone Grammaticam docuit Marcellus Marcelli F. de quo Libro Professorum Ausonius, cap. xix. Narbonam Urbem celebrat Benjaminus in Itinerario, Legis (Iudaicam intelligit) Antesignanam. Ex ea enim profecti Legem in omnes Regiones: ibi Sapientes esse & magnos & suspiciendos: in primis Kalonymon, Theodori Filium, ex Semine David, recta Genealogia, Praedia & Fundos habentem à Principibus Regionis, nullius hominis vim aut imperium metuentia.
units.tr: From the Atax* come the Atacini people and Farro Atacinus, as I said elsewhere. Strabo, in book 4, calls Narbo Mýassa emporion [Μύασσα Ἐμπόριον] (the trading town of Myassa). Marcellus, son of Marcellus, taught grammar at Narbo, about whom Ausonius writes in the Book of Professors, chapter 19. The benjaminus in his Itinerary celebrates the city of Narbo as the forerunner of the Law (he means the Jewish Law): from there the Law went out into all regions. There, he says, the wise men were great and to be looked up to, above all Kalonymus, son of Theodore, of the seed of David in direct descent, who held estates and lands from the princes of the region, fearing the force or authority of no man.

units.la: Haec de urbibus Archiepiscopalibus: Episcopales in duplici sunt mihi discrimine. Inter eas enim quaedam, quae Metropoles sunt, & quasi Capita nobilissimorum quorundam huius Provinciae Pagorum. Sic appello Suburbicarios Agros, suisseque quorundam Oppidorum Iurisdictiones: quales sunt Gabali, Albigenses, Velaunii Consaranni & Albenses. Gabali, hodie Givauldan. Eorum Metropolis Mimates Vicus Antiquioribus, vulgo Mende de Givauldan: Reginoni Mitanensis in Territorio Cavallitano corrupte: Mimatensis Montis Galliae circa Gaballitanam Urbem, cuius Episcopus erat S. Privatus, meminit Gregorius Turonensis, apud quem etiam legitur Atemmatensis. Albigenses, nunc Albigeois: Urbs Albiga Gregorio Turonensi lib. ii. Albi vernaculo. Velauni, Velai. Eorum Civitas quibusdam Anicinum, Le Puy en Velai, id est, Podium in Velauno, quia Urbs est in editissimo loco, qui Gallorum lingua Puy, id est Podium dicitur. Corsaranorum, Csferans, Civitas S. Legeri de C.feranis opidum antiquitate non incelebre. Albenses, Vivarais. Civitas Albensium, nunc Vivario. Sic scribitur in melioribus Notitiae Provinciarum Codicibus: Vitiose in Vulgatis, Civitas Albensium, hoc est Bellisio. Vivario Opidum est ad ripam Rodani dextram, vulgo Viviers. Ait autem recte Notitia, Nunc Vivario. Civitas enim & Metropolis Albensium olim erat Alba; quae Plinio Helviorum cognominatur, Ptolemaeo autem Augusta. Legitur enim apud eum Ἀλβα Ἐλλυνῶν: vocat Helvecios, quos Latini Helvios. Alba autem illa hodie Aubenas dicitur: Oppidum in Vivariensi Diœcesi, quinque minimum leucis ab Privertone versus Occidentem situm, quatuor ab Vcetensium Civitate, cum qua communem habet Amnem. Aubenas autem est nomen Pluralis numeri Albanates: ut ab Tolosa Tolosates, ab Nola Nolates in Veteri Inscriptione.
units.tr: These are the cities that are archiepiscopal. The episcopal ones are of a twofold distinction for me. For among them some are metropolises, and as it were the heads of certain most noble districts of this province. Thus I call the Suburbicarian lands, and the jurisdictions of certain towns, such as Gabali, Albigenses, Velaunii, Consaranni and Albenses. Gabali is today Givauldan. Its metropolis was the village of Mimates in older writers, commonly Mende or Givauldan; Reginon of Mitanensis, in the territory of Cavallitanus, corrupts it. The Mimatensis of Mont in Gaul, near the city of Gaballitanus, whose bishop was Saint Privatus, is mentioned by Gregory of Tours, who also reads Atemmatensis. Albigenses is now Albigeois; the city of Albiga is in Gregory of Tours, book 2; in the vernacular it is Albi. The Velauni are the people of Velai. Their city some call Anicinum, Le Puy en Velai, that is Podium in Velaunum, because the city stands on a very high place, which in the Gallic tongue is called Puy, that is Podium. The Corsaranni: Csferans, the city of Saint Léger, of Csferans, a town not unknown for its antiquity. Albenses, Vivarais. The city of the Albenses is now Vivarium. So it is written in the better manuscripts of the Notitia of the Provinces; in the common editions it is wrongly given as "the city of the Albenses, that is Bellisio." Vivarium is a town on the right bank of the Rhone, commonly Viviers. The Notitia rightly says "now Vivarium." For the city and metropolis of the Albenses was once Alba, which Pliny calls Alba of the Helvii, but Ptolemy Augusta. For in him it reads Alba of the Ellynes (Ἀλβα Ἐλλυνῶν), calling them Helvecii, whom the Latins call Helvii. That Alba is today called Aubenas, a town in the diocese of Viviers, situated at least five leagues from Privas towards the west, four from the city of the Vocontii, with which it shares a river. Aubenas is a plural name, Albanates, as Tolosa gives Tolosates and Nola gives Nolates in an old inscription.

units.la: Tantum de Episcopalibus, quae Suburbicariorum Agrorum, latiorumque quarumdam Iurisdictionum sunt Metropoles: reliquum est, ut ceteras explicem: in quis recensendis si non legitimum servem ordinem, vel si eiusdem cum indicatis iam naturae ad earum non referam classem, ignoscant velim Lectores, praesertim Incolae. Non enim omnia penitissime licuit novisse.
units.tr: So much concerning the episcopal cities, which are metropolises of the Suburbicarian lands and of certain wider jurisdictions. It remains that I explain the others. If in enumerating these I do not keep the proper order, or if I do not assign them to their class according to the nature already indicated, I would ask the readers to pardon me, especially those who live there. For it was not possible for me to know everything in the most minute detail.

units.la: Nismes, Nemausus Volcarum Arecomicorum Plinio lib. iii. cap. iv, Ausonio libro de Urbibus Carmine xiii, Pomponio Melae lib. ii. cap. v. Sidonio lib. ii, Epist. ix. Itinerario Antonini: Νέμαυσος Straboni lib. iv, & Ptolemaeo. Numismati vetustissimo COL. NEM. ARECOMICORUM. In Itineraria Peutingeri Tabula Nemuso scribitur, corruptius. Νέμαυσος, inquit Stephanus, πόλις Γαλλίας, ἀπὸ Νεμαύσου ἡ ἐπικλῆσις, ὡς Παφθίνιος. Qualis fuerit florente Romanorum Imperio, notat eleganter Strabo; cuius ea de re pauca verba non possum non adscribere: Μεγίστη πόλις δὲ τῶν ἈρεκομἈ’γκυρμισκῶν ἐν Νέμαυσο, καὶ μὲν ἡ ἀλλότριον ἔχλεν καὶ τὸν ἱμπερικὸν, πλὺ Ναρβῶν’ο λεπτομερῶν, καὶ δὲ τὸν πολιτικὸν ὑπερβάλλεσα. ὑπηρέτης γὰρ ἔχει κώμας πίπλαγες καὶ ἐκτιν τῶν ὁμοιθνῶν, ὁαυδεία Ἀμφιθέσις, συνταλίσας ὡς αὐτὸν, ἰχύσας ἡ τὰ καλλίμηλον Λατῖνον, ὡς τὰς ἀξιωθέντας ἀναγραφὰς ἐ πημίας ἐν Νεμαύσῳ Ῥωμαίας ὑπάρχειν. Ἰδρυσε δ’ ἡ πόλις καὶ τὸ εἶδος τὸ ἐν τῆς Γαλλίας ὡς τὸ Ἰταλίαν, ἥρως μὲν ὄλκαν ἐστι, χαμῶν ... In Opidorum, quæ Nemausiensibus adtributa, numero, Plinio convenit cum Strabone. Ejus verba lib. III. nat. hist. cap. IV sic habent: Vocontiorum Civitatis Fœderata duo Capita, Vasco & Lucus Augusti: Opida vero ignobilia XIX; sicut XXIV Nemausiensibus adtributa. Decurionum Nemausi mentio in Antiqua Inscriptione, quæ ibi vulgatur:
units.tr: Nîmes: Nemausus of the Volcae Arecomici, in Pliny, book 3, chapter 4; in Ausonius, in the poem On Cities, poem 13; in Pomponius Mela, book 2, chapter 5; in Sidonius, book 2, letter 9; in the Antonine Itinerary. Strabo, book 4, and Ptolemy write Nemausos (Νέμαυσος). On a very old coin: COL. NEM. ARECOMICORUM. In the Peutinger Table it is written Nemuso, more corruptly. "Nemausos," says Stephanus, "is a city of Gaul, named after Nemausus, as Parthenius says" (Νέμαυσος, πόλις Γαλλίας, ἀπὸ Νεμαύσου ἡ ἐπικλῆσις, ὡς Παρθένιος). Strabo elegantly describes what it was like when the Roman Empire flourished; I cannot refrain from quoting a few of his words on this matter: "The greatest city of the Arecomici is Nemausus, which has a large trading population and, far surpassing Narbo in size, also excels in civic life; for it has many villages and is well built, and the Romans have established their colonies there..." (Μεγίστη πόλις δὲ τῶν Ἀρεκομίκων Νέμαυσος, ...). Pliny agrees with Strabo on the number of towns assigned to the Nemausenses. His words in book 3 of the Natural History, chapter 4, are as follows: The Vocontii have two federated capitals, Vasio and Lucus Augusti; of ignoble towns there are nineteen; and twenty-four are assigned to the Nemausenses. The mention of the Decuriones of Nemausus is in an ancient inscription which is published there:

units.la: DIS. MANIBVS FIRMI. LVCANI IIIIL. VIRI. AVG ORNAMENTIS. DE CVRIONVM. NEMAVSI HONORATO
units.tr: TO THE SPIRITS OF THE DEAD. FIRMUS LUCANUS, IIII-VIR, AUGUSTAL, HONOURED WITH THE ORNAMENTS OF THE DECURIONS OF NEMAUSUS.

units.la: Miram undique redolet cum in veteri Muro, qui testatur multo, quam hodie, ampliorem fuisse, cum in aliis, Antiquitatem. Amphitheatrum ibi conspicitur, exteriore parte non minus integrum, quam quod Veronæ. Ante Amphitheatrum Campus Martius fuisse perhibetur, qui, ut Romanus, Aedificiis jam oppletus, & in alios tractus est usus. Aedificium, quod vulgo Le Cap duel, Capitolium (sic enim nomen illud corruptum) vel Basilica fuisse fertur, ab Imperatore Hadriano exstructa in gratiam & honorem, ut legere est apud Spartianum, Conjugis Plotinæ. Forma est τετράγωνος, quadrata quidem, sed quæ in longitudinem nonnihil vergit. Latera x. Columnis sulciuntur: Frons VI; pars Fronti adversa totidem. Tectum ex magnis compositum est Lapidibus; Deambulationibus adcommodatum. Templum, Fonti propinquum, integrum adhuc est, forma quadrata. Duos habent latera columnarum Ordines, artis absolutæ. Visuntur adhuc ibi Aquilæ. Romani quondam Imperij notæ & insignia, sed quæ Capitibus truncatæ. Id factum volunt ab Gothis, ut Romanum Imperium Corpus esse capite minutum, quum Imperatorum caderent vires, ostenderent. Ad mœnia Veteris Opidi annosa est Structura in Colle, qui Fonti vicinus vulgo Tourremagne vocatur, id est, ut quidam putant, Turris Romana vel Turris Magna. Lapidibus constat exiguis, ipsque quadratis. Videre ibidem est & perantiquas aliquot Statuas, & nonnulla melioris notæ Variorum Epitaphia: Columnam item ad Portam, cui ab Corona nomen. Imperatorum Domitiani, & Antonini Pij Philosophi, aliorumque claret Natalibus. Qui vulgo Fons Incolis appellatur, sed qui Lacus potius, quam Fons, dubitatur an sit, quem celebrat Ausonius Carmine, quod indicavi. Qui penitius inspexerunt, suspicantur alium fuisse, qui ex proximis Collibus in Urbem ducebatur; sed cui acciderit, quod Divonæ Burdigalensi, id est perijsse, Incolæ Nemausenses nominantur. De ijs Lapis mutilus:
units.tr: A wonderful sense of antiquity breathes from every side here. The old wall bears witness that the town was once much larger than it is today. Amphitheatrum can be seen there, its outer part no less intact than the one at Verona. Before the amphitheatre, the Campus Martius is said to have been, which, like the Roman one, is now filled with buildings and has been turned to other uses. The building commonly called Le Cap duel, Capitolium (for the name has been corrupted) or Basilica is said to have been built by the emperor Hadrian in honour and favour of his wife Plotina, as one may read in Spartianus. Its shape is quadrangular, though it stretches somewhat in length. Its sides are supported by ten columns; the front has six, and the side opposite has as many. The roof is made of large stones and is fitted for walking under. The temple near the spring is still intact, square in form. Its sides have two orders of columns, of perfect workmanship. Eagles are still to be seen there, the old emblems and insignia of the Roman empire, but with their heads cut off. They say the Goths did this, to show that the Roman empire, like a body with a diminished head, lost its strength when the power of the emperors fell. Near the walls of the old town, on the hill close to the spring commonly called Tourremagne, which some think means Turris Romana or Turris Magna, stands an ancient structure. It is made of small stones, themselves squared. There too one may see several very old statues and some epitaphs of various men of better standing. Likewise there is the column at the gate that is named after the Crown. The town is also famous as the birthplace of the emperors Domitian and Antoninus Pius the philosopher, and of others. The spring, which the inhabitants commonly call Fons, is doubtful as to whether it is a Lacus rather than a Fons; it is the one celebrated by Ausonius in the poem I have indicated. Those who have examined the site more closely suspect there was another spring, which was brought into the city from the nearby hills; but whatever became of it, as happened to the Divona at Bordeaux, that is, it perished. The inhabitants are called Nemausenses. Of them there is a broken stone:

units.la: IIIIL. VIR. CORPORATI. NEMAVSENSES PATRONO IX. POSTVLATIONE. POPVLI L. P. D. D.
units.tr: FOUR-MAN BOARD, THE CORPORATION OF THE NEMAUSENSES, TO THEIR PATRON, BY NINTH VOTE OF THE PEOPLE, BY PUBLIC DECREE.

units.la: Leguntur etiam Nemausenses apud Suetonium cap.XIII. Tiberij Principis Statuas & Imagines subvertisse; ubi tamen plerique Codices Nemausenses habent: Membranæ pleræque Remausenses; Vaticanus Liber, Remausisses. Exstat Libellus de Antiquitatibus Nemausensibus Ioannis Poldi. Tribus Nemauso milliaribus, Pons est, qui vulgo Du Gard. Nomen hoc illi ab Fluvio Guardone: quem, Francorum Veterum enunciatione (de qua Agathias) Wardonem appellant Sidonius lib. 11. Epist: x. Theodulphus Aurelianensis duobus locis, Fulbertus in Historia MS. Egidij & Petrus Aquil. lib. viii. cap. xviii. Pons triplici serie fornicatus est, stupenda sane industria: Prima Hominibus lumenque præbet transitum, altera Aquæductum sustinet. Inter Fanum S. Privati & Rimolinum Vestigia monstrantur Aquæductus, quo Romani Aquam in Nemausensium Opidum ducebant. Vsetz, Vcetensium Civitas: nonnullis Latine scribentibus Vtica. Vticensis Galliæ Episcopi meminit Aurelianum Concilium v. Opidum quod in Ducatus honorem, ad Wardones confluentes. Alter enim Occidentalior Gardo cognominatur d' Alaix; Orientalior autem d' Anduze, ab opidis, quæ singulorum Ripis adiident. VVarde, ut jam monui, dicitur Theodulpho Aurelianensi Episcopo, & aliis. Lodeus, vel, ut alij, Lodesve, Luteva; Notitiæ Provinciarum Galliæ Caitrum Luteva, in Viennensi Secunda. S. Pons de Tomieres, Fanum S. Ponti Tomeriarum. Alet, Aletensis Civitas: Alezium quibusdam Latine scribentibus, Opidum Vicecomitatus titulo insignitum. Mompelier, Latine nominantibus Mons Pessulanus: Mons Puellarum, Puellerum, item Piscículanus ab nonnullis dicitur, ut notat Cœnalis. Mons Tremulus vocatur à Benjamino Tudelensi; apud quem insigne est hujus Urbis Elogium. Subsantionem nuncupatam scribit Blondus i. Decadis lib. x. Videat ille, qua fretus auctoritate. Male quibusdam Agatha vel Agathopolis, quæ hodie Agde. Situm est Celliculo, decem leucis ab Mari Mediterraneo. Aer ibi placidulimus & saluberrimus. Urbe nihil amœnius, Civibus nihil humanius; Territorio nihil fertilius, Simpliciumque feracius: quæ res Medicos præcipue invitavit, ut Sedem ibi figerent, atque Medicinam cum laude docerent. Academiam enim Urbs habet, quæ instituta memoratur circa annum cIↄ cxcvi; vel saltem quo tempore, Saracenis Hispania pulsis. Medicina cum Discipulis Arabum, Avicennæ, Averrois, & aliorum, huc migravit. Rectoris ibi tanta est auctoritas; ut Studiosi quacumque etiam de causa egredientem comitari honoris gratia cogantur, quod se non sine maximo Studiorum suorum, multarumque Horarum jactura nimis frequenter fecisse, conqueritur Rebuffus. Collegia sunt ibi varia, inter quæ amplissimum est, Papa cognominatum. quod ab Vrbano Pontifice fundatum, & copiosissimis ornatum est Redditibus. Nec minus elegans est Regium, ab Henrico 11 Galliarum Rege erectum. Tertium est, quod vulgo Du Vergier; optimæ spei Adulescentibus Studiorum Victusque necessaria in decennium præbens. Besiers, Bitterra, aut Bitera Septimanorum in Aretomicis: Baeτρας, Ptolemæo; Βαετραββ, Stephano, Bliterra, Plinio lib.iii. cap. iv; Βιλιτεga. Straboni lib. iv; Beterra, Pomponio Melæ lib. ii. cap. v, & Antonino, cui & Peterna, Beterris, Tabulæ Peutingeri Itinerariæ in Auferendi casu; Biterra Itinerario Burdigalensi, & Vsuardo xi. Kalend. Aprilis. Hinc Biterrenses Sidonio lib. viii. Epist. iv; qui Biterienses in Notitia Provinciarum, in Viennensi Secunda. בידרש, id est Bidrasch vitiosius Benjamino in Itinerario. Opidum pervetustum, multis agitatum calamitatibus, cum ab Gothis, tum ab ipsis Francorum Regibus. Agde, Ἀγάθη Τύχη Timosthenis ἐν τῷ σαλασμῷ apud Stephanum; Ἀγύαθη, Straboni & Ptolemæo; Agatha, Plinio: Opidum ab Massiliensibus Græcis conditum in Volcis Arecomicis: unde & Strabo ni Κίσμα Μασσαλιωτῶν. Carcassone, Carcasso Volcarum Tectosagum: Καρκασών, Ptolemæo; Carcassum, Plinio; Carcasio, Procopio; Carcassio, Itinerariæ Peutingeri Tabulæ. Secundum inter tres Languedokij Senefchallias locum obtinet: La Senechaussée de Carcassone. Ca- Hres, opidum Caltrense: Cessero, Plinio; Κεστρῶ, Ptolemæo: Cetero, Casero & Tefero corrupte apud Antoninum. Scaligero tamen apud Plinium legitur Ceftero, ut illud sit Provinciæ opidum, quod hodie Cisteron. Pamies, Apamea, de qua post; Mirepoix, Mirepicense opidum. S. Papol, Fanum S. Papuli: La Vaur, Vaurense: Rius Rivi, Rivense Monasterium. Lombes, Lambariense Monasterium: poltea erecta in Episcopatus, suffraganeos Tolosano. Et hæc de Maiorum gentium tam Episcopalibus, quam Archiepiscopalibus Languedoky Vrbibus: Minorum gentium appello reliqua opida, inter quæ: Belloquadra, Beaucaire; tertium nacta locum inter tres Languedoky Senefchallias, La Senefchaussée de Beaucaire, Aiguesmortes, Aqua Mortua; quæ falso quibusdam creduntur Fossa Mariana, de quibus in Provincia. Piseaux; Pezenas, Piscena, Plinio: S. Gillis, Burgum S. Aegidij, ניריך מל ניל Beniamino in Itinerario. Chasteau-garry: Lusignen, Montasignac; Millans, Montsillac, & alia.
units.tr: The Nemausenses are also mentioned in Suetonius, chapter 13, as having overthrown the statues and images of the emperor Tiberius. However, most manuscripts there read Nemausenses; most parchment copies read Remausenses; the Vatican book reads Remausisses. There exists a little book on the Antiquities of Nemausus by Johannes Poldus. Three miles from Nemausus is the bridge commonly called Du Gard. It takes its name from the river Gardon, which the old Franks, in their pronunciation (about which Agathias writes), called Wardo; Sidonius, book 11, letter 10, calls it that, as do Theodulphus of Orléans in two places, Fulbert in the manuscript history of Egidius, and Petrus Aquilensis, book 8, chapter 18. The bridge is arched in three tiers, with remarkable skill. The first provides passage for people, the second carries the aqueduct. Between the Fanum S. Privati and Rimolinum the remains of the aqueduct are shown, by which the Romans led water into the town of the Nemausenses. Uzès, the Civitas Ucetensium, is called Utica by some Latin writers. The Council of Orléans, canon 5, mentions a bishop of Uzès in Gaul. The town takes its name from the duchy it honours; it lies where the Wardones meet. For the western one is called the Gardon d'Alais, and the eastern the Gardon d'Anduze, after the towns on each bank. Vvarde, as I have already noted, is what Theodulphus, bishop of Orléans, and others call it. Lodève, or as others say Lodesve, is Luteva; the Notitia of the provinces of Gaul calls it Castrum Luteva, in Viennensis Secunda. Saint-Pons-de-Thomières is the Fanum S. Ponti Tomeriarum. Alès is the Civitas Aletensis; some Latin writers call it Alezium, a town marked with the title of viscounty. Montpellier, named in Latin Mons Pessulanus, is also called Mons Puellarum or Puellerum, and by some Piscículanus, as Cœnalis notes. Benjamin of Tudela calls it Mons Tremulus, and he has a notable eulogy of this city. Blondus, in book 10 of his first Decade, writes that it was called Subsantio; let him see on what authority he relies. Agatha or Agathopolis, which is today Agde, is wrongly named by some. It lies on a small hill, ten leagues from the Mediterranean Sea. The air there is very mild and healthy. Nothing is more pleasant than the town, nothing more courteous than its citizens; nothing is more fertile than its territory, nor more productive of its simple people. This was especially what attracted physicians to settle there and to teach medicine with distinction. For the town has a Academia, which is recorded as founded about the year 1196, or at least at the time when the Saracens were driven out of Spain. Medicine came there with the pupils of the Arabs, Avicenna, Averroes and others. The authority of the rector there is so great that students are obliged, out of respect, to accompany him whenever he goes out, even for some cause; Rebuffus complains that he has done this far too often, not without great loss of his studies and of many hours. There are various colleges there, among which the largest is called Papa, founded by Pope Urban and endowed with very ample revenues. No less elegant is the Regium, established by Henry II, king of the French. The third is commonly called Du Vergier; it provides for young men of the best hopes their studies and necessary food for ten years. Béziers, Bitterra, or Biterra of the Septimani among the Arecomici: Βαετρας in Ptolemy; Βαιτραββ in Stephanus; Bliterra in Pliny, book 3, chapter 4; Βιλιτεγα in Strabo, book 4; Beterra in Pomponius Mela, book 2, chapter 5, and in Antoninus, who also has Peterna and Beterris; the Peutinger Table in the ablative case; Biterra in the Itinerary of Bordeaux and in Usuard, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April. Hence the Biterrenses in Sidonius, book 8, letter 4; in the Notitia of the provinces, in Viennensis Secunda, they are the Biterienses. Benjamin, in his Itinerary, calls it more corruptly Bidrasch [בידרש]. It is a very ancient town, often troubled by many calamities, both by the Goths and by the kings of the Franks themselves. Agde, Ἀγάθη Τύχη [Agathe Tyche] in Timosthenes, in the account of Stephanus; Ἀγύαθη in Strabo and Ptolemy; Agatha in Pliny: a town founded by the Greeks of Massilia among the Volcae Arecomici; hence Strabo also calls it Κίσμα Μασσαλιωτῶν [Kisma Massaliotōn]. Carcassonne, Carcasso of the Volcae Tectosages: Καρκασών in Ptolemy; Carcassum in Pliny; Carcasio in Procopius; Carcassio in the Peutinger Table. It holds second place among the three seneschalships of Languedoc: La Sénéchaussée de Carcassonne. Cahors, the town of Caltrense: Cessero in Pliny; Κεστρῶ [Kestrō] in Ptolemy; Cetero, Casero and Tefero corruptly in Antoninus. Yet in Scaliger's text of Pliny it is read as Ceftero, so that it is the town of the Province which is today Cisteron. Pamiers, Apamea, of which more later; Mirepoix, the town of Mirepoix; Saint-Papoul, Fanum S. Papuli; Vaour, Vaurense; Rieux, Rivi, Rivense Monasterium; Lombez, Lambariense Monasterium, afterwards erected into a bishopric, suffragan to Toulouse. These are the cities of the greater nations of Languedoc, both episcopal and archiepiscopal; I call the rest the towns of the lesser nations, among which: Beaucaire, Belloquadra, which holds third place among the three seneschalships of Languedoc, La Sénéchaussée de Beaucaire; Aigues-Mortes, Aqua Mortua, which some wrongly believe to be the Fossa Mariana, of which more in the Province. Pézenas, Piscena in Pliny; Saint-Gilles, Burgum S. Aegidij, ניריך מל ניל [Hebrew] in Benjamin's Itinerary; Château-Garry; Lusignan, Montasignac; Millau, Montsillac, and others.

units.la: Latare Latara. Castellum Pomponio est in Gallia Narbonensi: Ioanni Poldo Lates est. Laterra quoque Stagnum Plinio in Agro Nemausiensi: de quo alij alia adferunt. De utroque hic Karolus Clusius, oculatus testis, suis ad Abrahamum Ortelium litteris: Rette Poldus. Nam Lates etiamnum vocatur hoc Castellum cum Vico adjacente: Vicinum Stagno Volcarum, qua Ledum flumen in Stagnum labitur. Id Stagnum aliquot milliaria (sedecim memini me numerare ab Ortu in Occasum) in longitudinem porrigitur, cui aliquot Vici & Oppidula adjacent (ad Septemtrionalius praecipue latus) Nonnullis locis Estang, & ubi altius vadum habet, Estau ab Indigenis appellatur: qui Pisces in altiore Stagni gurgite captos praeferunt aliis, quod caenum adeo non respiciunt. Litus Maris, quod Incolae Playe de la Mar dicunt, Stagnum a Mari sejungit: Aqua tamen marina Fluxum quibusdam in locis in Stagnum praebet: & haud dubie id Stagnum tutorem a Piratarum atque Hostium incursionibus eam Galliae Narbonensis eram reddit. Designat, Volcarum Stagna nominans, Pomponius Mela. Fauces Laterrae Stagni apud Plinium lib. ix. nat. hist. cap. viii., ubi scilicet cum Mari communicatur: Nemausiensibus hodie La Cran pres de Manguril, ut notat Dalechampius.
units.tr: Latare, Latara. Pomponius has Castellum in Gallia Narbonensis; Johannes Poldus calls it Lates. Laterra is also a lake, in the territory of Nîmes, according to Pliny; others report various things about it. On both points Charles Clusius, an eyewitness, writes in his letter to Abraham Ortelius: "Poldus is right. For this castle, together with the adjoining village, is still called Lates. It lies near the lake of the Volcae, where the river Lez flows into the lake. The lake stretches several miles in length (I remember counting sixteen from east to west), and several villages and small towns lie along it, especially on its northern side. In some places it is called the Estang, and where it has a deeper ford the natives call it the Estau. They prefer fish caught in the deeper part of the lake to others, because they do not touch the mud at all. The shore of the sea, which the inhabitants call the Playa de la Mar, separates the lake from the sea; yet sea water provides an inflow into the lake in some places, and there is no doubt that this lake protects that region of Narbonese Gaul from the raids of pirates and enemies." Pomponius Mela marks it when he names the lakes of the Volcae. The mouth of the lake of Laterra is mentioned by Pliny, book 9, chapter 8, where it is clearly joined with the sea. Today the Nemausenses call it La Cran, near Manguio, as Dalechamps notes.

units.la: Languedoc ante paucos annos adtributus est Ducatus Fuvensis, La Duché de Toix; quum antea Guiennae concenteretur. Ad Orientem illi ipsum Languedokium: ad Occidentem Convenarum Ager; qua Septemtrio est, Territorium spectat Ripense, vulgo de la Riviere; Meridionale Latus Montes claudunt Pyrenaei; qui Ducatum hunc reddunt ut horridiorem, sic Ferri Carbonumque feraciorem.
units.tr: Some years ago Languedoc was assigned the Duchy of Foix (La Duché de Toix), which was previously included in Guienne. To its east lies Languedoc itself; to its west lies the territory of the Convenae. On the north side it borders the district of Ripense, commonly called de la Riviere; the southern side is enclosed by the Pyrenees mountains. These mountains make this duchy rougher in appearance, but richer in iron and coal.

units.la: Nomen illi ab opido Faxio, quod Antiquitatis laude clarum. Continet unum Episcopatum, Apamiensem. Opidum vulgo Pamies, Latine scribentibus Apamia & Pamia; ad confluentes Amnium, qui vulgo Lers & Lagiere. Ab hoc opido dici videtur Epaunense Concilium, habitum sub Gelasio I Papa, & Sigismundo Rege. Episcopi enim, qui illi interfuerunt, omnes hujus sunt Tractus. Empanensis etiam Synodus xv citatur in Decretorum I Distinct. 16. Eupanense Decret. II Causa II, fortean ab hoc eodem opido. Sunt & alia opida, Saverdunum & Masera, Comitum Domicilia. Errare graviter, qui Sedem hic collocant Elusatum, dicam Capite sequente.
units.tr: It takes its name from the town of Foix, which is famous for its antiquity. It contains one bishopric, that of Apamia. The town is commonly called Pamies, and writers in Latin call it Apamia and Pamia; it lies at the confluence of the rivers commonly called Lers and Lagiere. The Council of Epaone, held under Pope Gelasius I and King Sigismund, seems to be named after this town, since all the bishops who attended it belong to this district. The Synod of Empania is also cited in Decretum, Distinction 16, and "Eupanense" in Decretum, Part II, Cause II, perhaps from this same town. There are also other towns, Saverdunum and Masera, the seats of the counts. It is a serious error for those who place the see of Elusa here; I shall speak of this in the following chapter.

units.la: CAP. XXXVIII.
units.tr: CAP. XXXVIII.

units.la: Vasconia.
units.tr: Vasconia.

units.la: QVA Veteris Aquitaniae Narbonensisque Provinciae hodie sint sub Parlamentis & Burdigalensi & Tolosano, integre, ex Superioribus didicimus: superest Vasconia, quae utrisque paret mistum. Partes enim ejus quaedam sunt sub Burdigalensi, quaedam sub Tolosano.
units.tr: Which parts of Old Aquitaine and the Province of Narbonne now lie under the Parlements of Bordeaux and Toulouse we have learned completely from what has gone before; what remains is Vasconia, which belongs to both, being a mixture. For some of its parts lie under the Bordeaux Parlement and some under that of Toulouse.

units.la: VASCONIA proprie nunc temporis est, quidquid continetur intra Garumnam, Oceanumque & Guiennam hodiernam, vel Aquitaniam Ludovici XI. Dicta est Vasconia ab Vasconibus, ferocissimis Pyrenaeorum Populis: quos devictos primum a Pipino, deinde ab Ludovico Karoli Magni Filio (qui postea nominatus fuit Pius) Rege Aquitaniae in plana Novempopulaniae deductos, postea nominatus fuit. Fuerunt enim Vasciones (ut men huic Regioni dedisse certum est & indubitatum. Fuerunt enim Vasciones (ut hib. II. capitibus XI. & XIII. docui) pars Cantabrorum, quos etiam hodieque Hispani Vasconça vocant. Itaque, quum prius haec Regio ab Caesare Aquitania, postea Novempopulania audiret; ea ab Vasconibus devictis, inque eam a Pyrenaeorum Saltibus demissis, Vasconia fuit appellata. Est autem tertia pars Aquitaniae Augustae. Nam ab Augusto Aquitania triplex fuit instituta: Prima, cujus Caput Avaricum erat Biturigum Cuborum; Bourges: Secunda, cujus Metropolis erat Burdigala, Biturigum Vibiscorum; Tertia tota Trans-Garumnana, in qua principem tenebat locum Augusta Auscorum, vel Auchs: quae Provincia, ut jam dictum est, ab Augusti temporibus ad Pipinum usque nominata fuit Novempopulania: inde ad hunc usque diem Vasconia. Petrus Arvernus Cluniacensis Epist. I: Migravit tamen, sicut audivi, ad Loca satis vicina. Vobis contigua & a Septimania vestra, vobis persequentibus expulsa in Provincia Novempopulana (quae vulgo Gasconia vocatur) & in partibus ei adjacentibus sibi fauces praeparavit. Novempopulania ab Novem Populis, quos alij alios numerant, & nominant: revera. Novempopulania ab Novem Populis, quos alij alios numerant, & nominant:
units.tr: Strictly speaking, Vasconia today is everything contained between the Garonne, the Ocean, and modern Guienne, or the Aquitaine of Louis XI. Vasconia takes its name from the Vascones, the fiercest peoples of the Pyrenees. They were first defeated by Pepin and then by Louis, the son of Charlemagne (who was later called the Pious), king of Aquitaine, who settled them in the plains of Novempopulania. Afterwards the region was called by their name. For it is certain and beyond doubt that the Vascones (as I showed in book II, chapters XI and XIII) were a part of the Cantabri, whom the Spaniards still call Vascones today.
