So, since this region was first called Aquitania by Caesar and later Novempopulania, after the Vascones had been subdued and had come down from the passes of the Pyrenees into it, it was named Vasconia. It is also the third part of Augustan Aquitaine. For Augustus divided Aquitania into three parts. The first had Avaricum, the capital of the Bituriges Cubi (Bourges), as its chief town. The second had Burdigala, the metropolis, of the Bituriges Vivisci. The third, the whole land beyond the Garonne, had Augusta of the Auscii, or Auch, as its chief town. This province, as has already been said, was called Novempopulania from the time of Augustus until Pepin, and from then until today it has been called Vasconia. Peter of Auvergne, of Cluny, writes in Epistle I: "Yet he migrated, as I have heard, to places quite near. Driven out by you and your persecution from your Septimania, he prepared a way for himself in the province of Novempopulania (commonly called Gascony) and in the neighbouring parts." Novempopulania is named from the nine peoples, whom different authors count and name differently.

units.la: Scaliger autem suis ad me litteris, hos: Convenas, Confiarannos, Bigerrones, Lactoratenses, Vasates, Eloroncenses, Lascarienses, Tarbelles, & Atyrenses: quorum Convena, Bigerrones & Lactoratenses sunt in hodierna Vasconia; Confaranni in Languedokio; Vasates, Tarbelli & Atyrenses in Guienna Ludovici xi; Eloronenses denique & Lascarienses in Benearnua Principatu: adeo ut Vasconia major olim, quam nunc, fuerit; quum comprehenderet etiam Guiennam Ludovici xi & nonnullam Languedoky portionem: quum tamen ante Ludovicum xi Guienna major esset Vasconia; & Guienna totum quasi esset, Vasconia autem Pars.
units.tr: Scaliger, however, writes to me in his letter that these are: the Convenae, Consoranni, Bigerriones, Lactoratenses, Vasates, Elloronenses, Lascarienses, Tarbelli, and Atyrenses. Of these, the Convenae, Bigerriones and Lactoratenses are in present-day Vasconia; the Consoranni in Languedoc; the Vasates, Tarbelli and Atyrenses in Guienne of Louis XI; and finally the Elloronenses and Lascarienses in the principality of Béarn. So Vasconia was once larger than it is now, since it also included Guienne of Louis XI and some part of Languedoc. Yet before Louis XI, Guienne was larger than Vasconia, and Guienne was, as it were, the whole, while Vasconia was a part.

units.la: Stupendum, quod referam. Est in plerisque Vasconia locis, praecipue apud Bigerrones & Benearnenses, hominum genus, qui nunc Capots; nunc, variante Dialecto, Gahets appellantur. Detestandi sunt Suis; eorumque Commercia fugiuntur. Habentur pro Lepra infectis. Quasi essent, vel quod sint interdictae iis Civitates & oppida, incolere coguntur Suburbia, Locaque semotiora. Assignatae sunt & iis suae in Templis Stationes. Creduntur alios inficere. Plerique Fabri sunt Lignarij & Victores; aliisque Artibus Mechanicis dediti; Laboris patientissimi. In Facie & Actionibus illorum quiddam paret, quod eos contemtui detestationique reddit obnoxios. Femininus Sexus liberali satis forma. Omnium Halitus & Os grave olet, unde ingrati quid odoris manat in constantes & conloquentes. Quidquid sit, Maledictionis perhibetur genus, quod ab Majoribus in Posteros manifestissimis indiciis derivatur. Pauperiores semper in diem vivunt, diurno labore: Servorum censentur loco, ne ausi quidem mutire, si quid injuriae infer atur vel ab Vilissimo. Si quis eorum forte ditior, liberi tamen non fiunt heredes, nisi Mobilium, quae omnes tamquam certam luem avorsantur.
units.tr: I shall report a remarkable thing. In most places of Vasconia, especially among the Bigerriones and the people of Béarn, there is a class of men who are now called Capots, and, in another dialect, Gahets. They are to be detested by others, and their company is avoided. They are regarded as infected with leprosy. As if for that reason, or because cities and towns are forbidden to them, they are forced to live in the suburbs and more remote places. Their own places are also assigned to them in the churches. They are believed to infect others. Most of them are carpenters and wood-cutters, and devoted to other mechanical arts; they are very patient of labour. Something appears in their face and in their behaviour which makes them liable to contempt and hatred. The women are fairly handsome. The breath and mouth of all of them smell foul, so that an unpleasant odour spreads over those who stand and talk with them. Whatever the cause, it is said to be a kind of curse, which passes from ancestors to descendants by the clearest signs. The poorer ones always live from day to day by their daily labour. They are counted as slaves; they dare not even murmur if any wrong is done to them, even by the lowest man. If one of them happens to be richer, his children nevertheless do not become heirs, except to his movable goods, which everyone shuns as certain plague.

units.la: Veteres Vasconia, ut quidem ea hodie est; & nos eam accipimus, Incolae fuerunt Varij: Cantabri, Vasiones, Ansis, Tarusates, Lactoratcs, Bigerrones, Nitiobriges, Convenae; Elusates, Garites, Coresates, & procul dubio plures. Cantabri, de quibus lib. ii. cap. xi. quatenus ad Galliam pertinent, Cis-Pyrenaei fuerunt, ubi nunc Le Pais de Basques: Nomen corruptum ex Vasconibus Hispaniae Populis, qui Pyrenaeos traducti, Sedibus inter Gallos fixis, Gascons hodieque nominantur; nisi quis malit Hispanos Vascones, quorum memini eodem libro Capite xiii, feminis esse Gallici, de quo non magnopere contenderim. De Vasconibus Galliae Juvenalis haec plerique accipienda censent, Satyra xv:
units.tr: The ancient inhabitants of Vasconia, as it is today, and as we take it, were various: the Cantabri, Vasiones, Ansis, Tarusates, Lactorates, Bigerriones, Nitiobriges, Convenae; the Elusates, Garites, Coresates, and without doubt more. The Cantabri, of whom I spoke in book II, chapter XI, so far as they belong to Gaul, lived on this side of the Pyrenees, where the Pays de Basques now is. The name is corrupted from the Vascones, a people of Spain, who were brought over the Pyrenees and settled among the Gauls, and are still called Gascons. Unless someone prefers to call them the Spanish Vascones, whom I mentioned in the same book, chapter XIII, as belonging to Gaul; I shall not argue much about that. Most people think that the following lines of Juvenal should be understood of the Vascones of Gaul, Satire XV:

units.la: altimus autem
units.tr: But the last

units.la: Qui fleriit abfumto jam toto corpore ductis Per terram digitis, aliquid de sanguine gustat. Vasciones (fama est) alimentis salubus usi Produxere Animas, sed res diversa, sed illic Fortuna invidia est, Bellorumque ultima, casus Extremi, longa dira obsidionis egestas.
units.tr: "He who weeps, with his whole body consumed, draws his fingers through the earth and tastes some of the blood. The Vascones (so the story goes), using wholesome food, prolonged their lives; but that is a different case, for there fortune is hostile, and the last of wars, the extreme misfortune, the long dire want of a siege."

units.la: Aufci Plinio lib. iv. cap. xix. Populos Aquitaniae supra x I I x numeranti, & Melae lib. iii. cap. i. Ptolemaeo Αὔσκιοι, cuius ipsorum Urbs Αὖγυστα, hodie Auch, de qua suo loco. Aust Itinerariae Tabulae; Aufcensis Sidonio lib. vii. Epist. vi. Novempopuli, de quibus paullo ante, ab nonnullis concenseri soliti. Novempopulior, inquit Ammianus, Aufci commendant. Sic Ausonius in Professoribus, de Staphylo Cive Aucteo: Te Staphyle genitum sit pe Novempopuli.
units.tr: The Auscii are counted by Pliny, book IV, chapter XIX, among the peoples of Aquitaine, which he counts as more than twelve; and by Mela, book III, chapter I; Ptolemy calls them [Auskioi], and their city [Augusta], today Auch, of which more in its place. The Aust is in the Itinerary Table; the Auscensis in Sidonius, book VII, Epistle VI. They are usually reckoned among the Novempopuli, of whom I spoke a little earlier. Ammianus says, "The Auscii commend the Novempopulian." So Ausonius, in the Professors, of Staphylus, a citizen of Auch: "Staphylus, born of the Novempopulian nation."

units.la: Civitas Auscorum Notitiae Provinciarum in Aquitania Tertia Novempopulania vel Octava Viennensi, Hodie L'Archevesché d'Auch: unde Auscensis Archiepiscopus. Imperite facit Vulgus Ecclesiasticum, cui Auxitanum vocatur; & ineptos se probant, qui Augustae Auscorum Incolas nuncupant Auxitanos. Veterum Ausciorum Tractus hodie Armagnac fere appellatur. Tarbellae Caesaris extremo libro iii. de Bello Gallico, putant quidam esse nunc temporis Tarba Urbs Incolas in Auscitana Provincia. Lactora nominantur in Itineraria Tabula: Lactorarum vel Lactoratum Civitatem habet eadem Notitia in Aquitania in Novempopulania, vel Octava Viennensi. Hodie L'Evesché de Lactoure. Lactorates suum Civitatis meminit Inscriptio, quae in eadem Urbe exstat: PRO. SALUTE. IMP. M. ANTON. GORDIANI PII. FEL. AUG. ET. SABINAE. TRANQVILLINA AUG. TOTIUSQVE. DOMUS. DIVINA. PROQVE STATV. CIVITATIS. LACTORATEN. TAVROPOLIVM FECIT. ORDO. LACT. DOMINO. NOSTRO. GORDIANO AUG. II. ET. POMPEIANO. COSS. VI. ID DEC. CURANTIB. M. EROTIO. FESTO ET. M. BLARINIO. CARO. SACERD. TRAIANIO NUNDINIO
units.tr: The city of the Auscii in the Notitia of the Provinces, in Third Aquitaine or Eighth Viennensis Novempopulania, is today the Archbishopric of Auch, whence the Archbishop of Auscensis. The ecclesiastical common people act foolishly, who call it Auxitanum; and those show their ignorance who call the inhabitants of Augusta of the Auscii Auxitani. The district of the ancient Ausci is today commonly called Armagnac. Some think that the Tarbellae of Caesar, in the last book III of the Gallic War, are now the town of Tarba, with inhabitants in the Auscitan province. Lactora is named in the Itinerary Table; the same Notitia has the city of the Lactorae or Lactorates in Aquitaine, in Novempopulania, or Eighth Viennensis. Today the Bishopric of Lectoure. An inscription which still stands in the same city mentions the city of the Lactorates: "For the safety of the emperor M. Antonius Gordianus Pius Felix Augustus, and of Sabina Tranquillina Augusta, and of the whole divine house, and for the state of the city of the Lactorates, the order of Lactora made a taurobolium to our lord Gordianus Augustus, for the second time, and to Pompeianus, consul for the sixth time, on the sixth day before the ides of December, under the care of M. Erotius Festus and M. Blarinius Carus, priests; Traianius Nundinius."

units.la: Bigerrones apud Caesarem sunt, qui Bigerri Plinio lib. iv. cap. xix, & Pontio Paullino ad Ausonium scribenti Epistola i. veri cxliii, colque Pelitos indigetanti, quod ob intentum ins in locis frigus Pelibus ovium, Caprarum, aliarumque Bestiarum se, ut hodieque, tegerent. Bigerriani nominantur Ausonio. Hinc Bigerricus Ager, Sidonio libro viii. Epist. xiii & Bigerriana Patria, Ausonio Epist. xiii. ad Paullinum. Civitas Tarba, ubi Cissum Begorra, in Notitia Provinciarum; hodie, L'Evesché de Tarbe de Bigorre; La Comte de Bigorre. De Tarba Bigerronum alibi. Nitiobriges apud Caesarem lib. vii non uno loco; hodie Le Pais & Senéschaussée d'Agenois. In Plinio male exeulum, Aussi-roges Tarnegamne differunt à Tolosanis: Legendum enim, Nitio- briges Tarne Amne &c. Vide Scaligerum in Auson. Nitiobroges in Itineraria Peutingeriana Tabula procul ponuntur ab suis Sedibus xv. Long. iv. Lat. prope Augustobanam Tricastinum: quum scribere oportuisset v. Long. vii. Lat. supra Aginnum. Distinctionem, qua in eadem Tabula, docendi commodiusque quid & certiore digito indicandi gratia, utor, aperto in Epistola ad Lectorem. Nitiobrigum Civitas Agennum, de qua postea. Ridenda scribit ad me Iosephus Scaliger, quae hactenus omnes de his delirarunt: quorum alii sunt illi Marianus & Poldus; Mompelier, eiusque Territorium esse dicunt; qui locus sex dierum itinere distat ab Nitiobrigibus: alii Engolesme somniant: alii jubent pro Aginno legendum esse Agesinates: Et, inquit Vir Magnus, quo non possit audax insania? Nitiobrigum Rex nominatur in Ephemeridibus Belli Gallici lib. vii. Theutomatus, cujus Pater ab S. P. Q. R. Amicus fuerat appellatus. Qui Convena Plinio lib. iii. cap. iv. & Sidonio lib. vii. Epist. vi; in Ptolemaei libris vitiose dicuntur Κονναιοί: Legendum enim Κονναιοί. Elegantes Strabo lib. iv. τῶν τ Κονναίων, ὅπερ ἐστὶ Συγκλυδῶν. Sic enim emendat eruditissimus Casaubonus. Explicat Strabo quid Latinorum Convenae sint Graecis; Συγκλυδες scilicet ἀθρόοι. Exturbati sunt hi Convenae ex Doctissimo illo Glossario, impuris Magistrellulorum manibus non terendo. Scribitur enim, Συγκλυδες ....... Reponendi Convenae. Civitas Convenas in Notitia, L'Evesché de Comminges. Metropolis Lugdunum Convenarum, de quo infra. Elusates, ut Plinio & Claudiano vocantur, apud Caesarem sub finem lib. iii. corrupte in quibusdam Codicibus Fluffates & Flufates scribuntur: Flufant Sidonio sunt lib. vii. Epist. vi: Flufatium (mendose in quibusdam Libris Fllofatium) Civitas in Provinciarum Libello, Aquitania iii, Le Pais d'Fuse en Gascogne. De ipsa Urbe Elfi vel Fusa paullo post. Qui Fluffates legebant, ut scribit ad me Nobilissimus Vir Iosephus Scaliger, dicebant (in eorum numero video Cœnalem & Belleforestium) esse Comitatum de Fuxio; & hoc stupore suo persuaserunt illustri Viro nomen de Fuv in Flufatem recudere; quo nihil absurdius. Aliud enim est Franciscus de Flufia; aliud, Franciscus Flufsas. Nam de Flufsa esset verum cognomen Familiae; sed Flufsas esset nomen Nationis. Itaque Franciscus Flufsas esset natione Flufsas, non de Familia de Flufsa. Sed Flufsa non est Foiv. Nam id esset Fovium, aut aliud quidvis potius, quam Fusa. Garites, quorum Caesar meminit, haud procul Nitiobrigibus habitasse notat Orontius, quum eos in sua Galliae Tabula locet in Agro, qui hodie Aginnensium. Certe Garites non idem sunt cum Aginnensibus. Garites enim Caesar ponit in sua Aquitania, ultra Garumnam: Nitiobriges, quorum Caput Aginnum, extra suam constituit Aquitaniam, cis Garumnam, in Celtica. Marcianus Lactoratense oppidum, Lactoure, Garitibus adsignat. Finiam antiquas huius Tractus Gentes in Cocosatibus Caesaris; quos Plinius Cocosates vocat, Sex signanos cognominans; qui quo loco fuerint, nondum didici.
units.tr: The Bigerriones are those whom Caesar calls the Bigerri; Pliny, book IV, chapter XIX, and Pontius Paulinus writing to Ausonius, Epistle I, verse 143, and they worshipped Pelitos, because in the cold of their places they covered themselves with skins of sheep, goats and other beasts, as they still do today. Ausonius calls them Bigerriani. Hence the Bigerric field in Sidonius, book VIII, Epistle XIII, and the Bigerrian homeland in Ausonius, Epistle XIII to Paulinus. The city of Tarba, where the Cissus is the Begorra, is in the Notitia of the Provinces; today the Bishopric of Tarbes de Bigorre; the County of Bigorre. I shall speak of Tarba of the Bigerriones elsewhere. The Nitiobriges appear in Caesar, book VII, in more than one place; today the Pays and Sénéchaussée d'Agenois. In Pliny the Aussi-roges and the Tarnegamnae, badly printed, differ from the Tolosani; for we must read Nitio-briges, Tarne Amne, etc. See Scaliger on Ausonius. In the Peutinger Table the Nitiobriges are placed far from their seats, at 15 degrees longitude and 4 latitude, near Augustobona of the Tricastini, whereas they ought to have been written at 5 degrees longitude and 7 latitude, above Agen. I use the distinction, which appears in the same table, for ease of teaching and for pointing out things with a surer finger; it is explained in the letter to the reader. The city of the Nitiobriges is Agen, of which later. Joseph Scaliger writes to me of the ridiculous things which all have hitherto dreamed about these people. Some of them, Marianus and Poldus, say that Montpellier and its territory are meant; but that place is six days' journey from the Nitiobriges. Others dream of Angoulême; others order that for Aginnum we should read Agesinates. And, says that great man, "What folly will not dare?" The king of the Nitiobriges is named in the Commentaries of the Gallic War, book VII: Teutomatus, whose father had been called a friend of the Senate and People of Rome. The Convenae, whom Pliny, book III, chapter IV, and Sidonius, book VII, Epistle VI, mention, are called [Konnaioi] incorrectly in the books of Ptolemy; for we must read [Konnaioi]. Strabo, book IV, elegantly: "of the [Konnaioi], which is [Synkludōn]." For so the most learned Casaubon corrects it. Strabo explains what the Latin Convenae are in Greek: [Synkludes], that is, crowded together. These Convenae have been driven out of that most learned glossary, not to be worn down by the impure hands of little schoolmasters. For it is written, [Synkludes]. The Convenae must be restored. The city of the Convenae in the Notitia is the Bishopric of Comminges. The metropolis Lugdunum of the Convenae, of which below. The Elusates, as they are called by Pliny and Claudian, are in some manuscripts of Caesar, near the end of book III, wrongly written Flussates and Flusates; Sidonius, book VII, Epistle VI, has Flusant; the city Flusatium (wrongly in some books Fllofatium) is in the Libellus of the Provinces, Aquitaine III; the Pays d'Fuse in Gascony. Of the city itself, Elfi or Fusa, a little later. Those who read Flussates, as the most noble Joseph Scaliger writes to me, said (I see Cœnalis and Belleforest among them) that it was the County of Fuxio; and by this folly they persuaded that illustrious man to reprint the name de Fuv as Flusatem, which is nothing more absurd. For Franciscus de Flussa is one thing; Franciscus Flussas is another. For de Flussa would be the true surname of a family; but Flussas would be the name of a nation. So Franciscus Flussas would be "of the nation Flussas", not "of the family de Flussa". But Flussa is not Fuv. For that would be Fovium, or some other thing rather than Fusa. Orontius notes that the Garites, whom Caesar mentions, lived not far from the Nitiobriges, when he places them in the territory which is today that of the Agenais. Certainly the Garites are not the same as the Agenenses. For Caesar places the Garites in his Aquitaine, beyond the Garonne; while the Nitiobriges, whose capital is Agen, he puts outside his Aquitaine, on this side of the Garonne, in Celtica. Marcian assigns the town of Lactora, Lectoure, to the Garites. I shall end the ancient peoples of this district with the Cocosates of Caesar, whom Pliny calls Cocosates, adding the surname Sex signani; I have not yet learned where they lived.

units.la: Et haec de antiquis Vasionae nostrae Populis. Eiusdem porro, ut hodie considerari solet, Partes Garumnae conjacent quaedam ultra tantum Flumen, ut Ager cum Armaniacensis, tum Bigerronum, quaedam confuse ultra citraque, ut Aginnensis Senescballia, Albreti Ducatus & Comitatus Convenarum. Armaniacensis mihi dicitur, qui vulgo Armagnac, cuius Limites plurimum se extendunt. Latitudo eius ab opido Lactoratensium Nogerentium usque: Longitudo minor est, Magnaco ad Bigerrones usque. Sunt qui putant memoriam in eo servari Arecomicorum. Ego nihil hic volo affirmare. Comitatus titulo est insignis. Continet duas Diœceses, Auscensem & Lactoratensem. Auscensis ab Augusta Auscorum, quae totius Novempopulania sive Vasconiae Metropolis. Sic Ptolemaeo dicitur Galliae Aquitanicae Urbs, quae vulgo nunc Auch: Civitas Ausius Veteri Itinerario à Burdigala Hierosolymas; Auscensis Urbs Gregorio Turonensi lib. x. cap. xxii: Auscium & Civitas Auscium Martyrologio Romano Vsuardoque Kalend. Mai. Hinc Episcopus Auscensis Gregorio Turonensi lib. viii, cap. xxii. Oppidum est ad Gersum Fluvium, Rupi inaedificatum, aditu difficile. Pulcherrimum ibi Templum, Deiparae Virgini consecratum, structura fastuosum. Visuntur ibi multa Antiquitatum Monimenta. Partim Regem Franciae, partim Civitatis Praesulem Dominos agnoscit. Lactoratensis ab Opido, quod vulgo Lactoure: Lactura Antonino; Lacerra corruptius Itinerariae Tabulae: Lactorum Civitatem habet Goltzius ex Veteri Inscriptione in suo Thesauro, ut & Lactorium & Lactorium. In opido tunc Lactoratensi duo Lapides leguntur, in uno propugnaculorum; his verbis concepti: MATRI. DEVM POMP. PHILVMENE Q. PRIMA. LECTOR TAVROBOLIVM FECIT Ibidem PRO. SALVTE. IMP. ANTONINI. GORDIANI PII. FEL. AVG. TOTIVSQVE. DOMVS. DIVINA PROQVE. STATV. CIVIT. LACTOR. TAV ROBOLIVM. FECIT. ORDO. LACT. D. N. GORDIANO. II. ET. POMPEIANO. COS VI. ID. DEC. CVRANTE. M. EROTIO ET. FESTO. CANINIO. SACERD
units.tr: And these are the things to say about the ancient peoples of our Vasconia. Parts of the same region, as it is commonly considered today, lie partly beyond the Garonne, such as the Armagnac, and also the Bigorre; others lie confusedly on both sides of the river, such as the Seneschalsy of Agen, the Duchy of Albret and the County of Comminges. The Armagnac, which is commonly called Armagnac, is said to be the region of which I speak, and its limits extend widely. Its breadth runs from the town of the Lectorates to the Nogerenses, but its length is shorter, from Magnac to the Bigerrones. Some think that the memory of the Arecomici is preserved in it. I do not wish to assert anything here. The county is distinguished by its title. It contains two dioceses, Auch and Lectoure. Auch takes its name from Augusta Auscorum, the metropolis of all Novempopulania, or Gascony. Ptolemy calls it by this name, a city of Aquitanian Gaul, which is now commonly called Auch; the old Itinerary calls it the city of Ausius on the road from Bordeaux to Jerusalem; Gregory of Tours, book x, chapter xxii, calls it the city of Auscius; the Roman Martyrology and Usuard at the Kalends of May call it Auscium and the city of Auscium. Hence the bishop of Auch in Gregory of Tours, book viii, chapter xxii. The town lies on the river Gers, built on a rock, and hard to reach. There is a most beautiful temple there, consecrated to the Virgin Mother of God, splendid in its structure. Many monuments of antiquity are to be seen there. It acknowledges partly the King of France and partly the lord bishop of the city as its lords. Lectoure takes its name from the town which is commonly called Lectoure; Antoninus calls it Lactura, and the Itinerary table, more corruptly, Lacerra. Goltzius, in his Thesaurus, has from an ancient inscription the city of the Lactores, and also Lactorium and Lactorium. In the town of Lectoure at that time two stones are read, one in the bulwarks, conceived in these words: "To the Mother of the Gods, Pompeius Philumenus, of the first cohort, made a taurobolium." And there, "for the health of the Emperor Antoninus Gordianus Pius Felix Augustus, and of the whole divine house, and for the state of the city of Lectoure, the taurobolium was made by the council of Lectoure, in the consulship of our lord Gordianus II and Pompeianus, on the sixth day before the Ides of December, under the care of M. Erotius and Festus Caninius, priest."

units.la: Qui putant Lactoratium vel Lasioratium dici in Notitia Provinciarum, falluntur. Sunt enim, ut cum Grammaticis loquar, Genitivi, quorum Recti Lactorates, vel Lasiorates, si rectalit in hac voce scriptura. Oppidum est in fastigio Montis, ubi multa Antiquitatis vestigia. Arcem habet, quam ab Romanis volunt factam. Sunt item alia Armaniacensis Diœcesis Opida, inter quæ quod vulgo L'Isle Jordain, ubi Tribunal Senechalli. Fuit quidem parvus Comitatus, sed hodie vix memoria superest, ut mihi affirmat V. N. Iosephus Scaliger. Bigerrones vel Bigerri, vulgo Le Comté de Bigorre, Regionem possident inter Benearnenses & Convenas, Cœlo Soloque asperam, ventosam, frigidam, Vini interacem: ad Pyrenæos Montes, quorum magna pars huic Comitatui est subjecta, ab Montibus, qui vernacule d'Aure nominantur usque ad Saltum Pyrenæum; vulgo du Sault) coque qui d'Aspe dicuntur, Benearnensium Ditionis. Bigerrones etiam scribuntur ingenij, Armis dediti, celeres ad aliquid adgrediendum, egregie simulantes, inhumani, aspeŕi, ingratiores. Opidani urbaniores. Nobilitas, quæ hic frequens, animosa, humana, cultus moribus. Civitas Turba, ubi Castrum Begorra. Sic vocatur in Notitia Provinciarum, ut meliores consulantur Codices. Nam male exculum est, Tusfa & Turba; vitiosissime etiam in aliis Tursambica Tranugorra. Vulgo Tarbe de Begorre, aut Bigorre, ubi Sedes Episcopalis, quæ in hoc Comitatu unica, sub Metropoli Auscensi. Marhanus insanit, ut scribit ad me Ioseph. Scaliger, qui ait ibi hanc Turfam esse & Castrum Begorram, ubi est Episcopatus Bitterrensis Provinciæ Narbonensis; quæ sententia non est sobrii capitis. Begorram Bigerronum Civitatem habet Gregorius Turonensis. Olim vicus erat, ut monet Scaliger, unde & Vicani Aquenses dicti. Id patet ex egregia inscriptione:
units.tr: Those who think that Lactoratium or Lasioratium is called so in the Notitia of the Provinces are mistaken. For these are, to speak with the grammarians, genitives, whose nominatives are Lactorates or Lasiorates, if the writing in this word is correct. The town lies on the summit of a hill, where there are many traces of antiquity. It has a citadel, which they say was built by the Romans. There are also other towns of the Diocese of Armagnac, among which is the one commonly called L'Isle-Jourdain, where the court of the seneschal sits. There was indeed a small county, but today hardly any memory of it survives, as the most learned Joseph Scaliger affirms to me. The Bigerrones, or Bigerri, commonly called the County of Bigorre, possess a region lying between the Benearnenses and the Convenae, harsh in climate and soil, windy, cold, and lacking wine: it extends to the Pyrenean mountains, the greater part of which is subject to this county, from the mountains which in the vernacular are called d'Aure as far as the Pyrenean pass (commonly du Sault), and as far as those called d'Aspe, which belong to the jurisdiction of the Benearnenses. The Bigerrones are also described as clever by nature, devoted to arms, quick to attack anything, skilful in pretence, uncivilised, rough, and ungrateful. The townsfolk are more courteous. The nobility, which is numerous here, is spirited, humane, and refined in manners. The city is Tarbes, where the castle of Begorra is. It is called this in the Notitia of the Provinces, though better manuscripts should be consulted, for it is wrongly printed as "Tusfa" and "Turba", and most wrongly in other copies as "Tursambica" or "Tranugorra". It is commonly called Tarbes de Bigorre, where the episcopal see is, the only one in this county, under the metropolitan of Auch. Marhanus is raving, as Joseph Scaliger writes to me, for he says that Turfa here is the castle of Begorra, where the bishopric of Béziers in the province of Narbonne is; this opinion is not of sound mind. Gregory of Tours calls Begorra the city of the Bigerrones. It was once a village, as Scaliger reminds us, whence also the people of Aquae are called Vicani. This is clear from the notable inscription:

units.la: NVMINI. AVGVSTI SACRVM SECVNDVS. SEMBEDO NIS. TIL. NOMINE VICANORVM. AQVEN SIVM. ET. SVO. POSVIT
units.tr: "To the divinity of Augustus, Secundus Sembedonis, son of Tiberius, in the name of the people of the village of Aquae, set this up at his own expense."

units.la: In Finibus Bigerronum sunt Comitatus, qui vulgo Gavre & Ffirac. Aginnensis Senechallia, vulgo La Senechaussee d'Agenois, Sedes quondam Nitiobrigum. Hic ad Orientem confinales sunt Cadurci, ad Septemtrionem Petrocorij, qua parte Aginnenses excurrunt Bironium utque, Petrocoriorum Opidum: ad Occidentem Vasconnes occurrunt cum Garumna; a quo & ad Meridiem lambuntur. Continet duos Episcopatus, nempe citra Garumnam, Aginnum Nitiobrigum; ultra Garumnam, Condomium. Aginnum, vernacule Agen. Ἀγινον Ptolemæo lib. ii. cap. vii; Aginnum Antonio Epist. xxiii, Antonino, & Itinerariæ Peutingeri Tabulæ; Aginum, Bedæ in Martyrolog. v.Id. Iunij, Adoni, & aliis; Agennum in Libro Provinciarum, apud Hieronymum item de Claris Scriptoribus, & Honorium, qui ejus Episcopum Phæbadium memorat: Agenensis Urbs Gregorio Turonenti lib. i. cap. cv. de Mirac. Agavanum Bedæ, variant in scriptura, Pridie Non. Oct. & Aganum eidem xiii. Kal. Novembr. Sanissima Vocis Scriptura, Aginnum. Opidum venerandæ Antiquitatis, in Garumnæ ripa situm, duodeviginti ab Metropoli Burdigalensi leucis, totius Aquitaniæ dimidium. Sedes Senechalli, cujus jurisdictio, excepto Pictaviensi, totius Aquitaniæ latissima. Ius inde petunt Portus D. Mariæ, Villa Nova (Ville Neuve d'Agenois, ad Lothum, quæ & speciatiorem hujus Tractus partem constituit, Arcem habens) Hautefina, Clairacum, Marmandi, Fanum Magnæ Fidei consecratum, Fay la grande, Clavis; & alia ad Garumnam opida. Aginnum vel eo nomine magnum, quod Magnus ille Iosephus Scaliger ejus primum Solo instituerit, ejusque Aerem primum hauserit. Condomium, vulgo La Senechaussee de Condomois. Hoc peculiari nomine vocari solet Vasconia. Quemadmodum enim Africa dicitur tota illa Magna Continens, quæ patet ab Nilo ad Gades, & tamen in ea erat Provincia, quæ peculiariter appellabatur Africa, in qua Karthago: ita Vasconia quidem nominatur amplissima illa Regio, quæ olim dicta fuit Novempopulania; sed stricte Vasconia quoque nuncupatur in ea Episcopatus Condomiensis. Itaque Senechallus Aginnensis vocat se Senechallum Aginnensium & Vasconiæ, id est, Condomij. Quæ appellatio vetus est. Nam temporibus Pipini Pagus Aginnensis citra Garumnam & ultra Garumnam dicebatur. Itaque sub Pipino in Vetustissimis Annalibus refertur, plurime frumento in Pago Aginnense ultra Garumnam, id est in ea Regione, quæ proprie Vasconiæ, in qua Condommum: vulgo Condom; opidum amplum in Territorio sterili, undique fere Collibus, qui Vineis consiti, cinctum; extra Viam regiam situm, haud procul Basa Fluvio. Sedem præbet non solum Episcopatui Novo, quem delibatum dixi supra de Agennensi; verum etiam Senescballiæ, jus dicenti Opidis, quæ Indigenis, Valence ad Barsam, Lairac ad Garumnam, La-Romeo, Aion-Real, & aliis. Familiæ sunt hic illustres non paucæ. Vicecomites novimus hic Fismacones, Gourdones, Forcaes, & Monlucios. Ducatus Allebret, La Duché d'Allebret, nomen accepit amplissimum ab opidulo, quod vulgo Allebret, in Syrtibus Lapurdensibus, quas Landas vocant. Institutus est ante annos non multos, compositus ex mutilatione Senescballiarum Agennensis, Armagnac, Cersi, & Vasatensis; adeo ut de eo dicere liceat, quod de Constantinopoli Hieronymus, eam nuditate omnium Civitatum constructam fuisse. Caput Ducatus est Neracum, opidum prædiues. Avorum nostrorum memoria Ioannes Alani F. Dynastia Allebretanus, ducta Katharina Gastonis F. Navarræ Regnum cum ea Dotem accepit: hujus ex Filio Henrico Neptis fuit Ioanna Allebretana, Navarræ Regina, Mater Henrici IV, Christianissimi Franciæ Navarræque Regis. Convenarum Comitatus, La Comté de Comminges: Vulgo Latinorum Comingia. Huius Tractus Incolæ Primi Aquitanorum Christianæ Militiæ nomen dedisse scribuntur, multa indigna perpessi ab Christiani nominis Hostibus. Dividitur Convenarum Ager in Superiorem & Inferiorem, totusque Montibus attollitur. Gentis Caput Lugdunum Convenarum; Αὑτου Κοινωνιῶν (legendum Κοινωνιῶν) Ptolemæo & Straboni lib. iv: Lugdunum simpliciter Antonino, in Itinere ab Aginno ad hoc opidum: quod quum per multos annos summopere floruisset, tandem ab irato Guntchranni Regis exercitu fuit diruturn, anno 1xxxiv, Indictione 11: ex cujus reliquiis Fanum S. Bertrandi, ubi hodie Sedes est Episcopalis, in Valle Capraria fuit constructum. Vetustatem & Splendorem ejus Civitatis facile testantur Monimenta & Epigraphæ quamplurimæ, quæ ibi hodie exstant. Coluerunt inter alios Deos Lugdunenses Convenæ, aliquæ forte Conregionales, Abellionem: de quo quidam ibi Lapides, ut alibi vidimus, ubi de Diis Gallorum. Quid in Inscriptione, quæ Romæ legitur in ædibus Mellinorum ad Agonem, sit Cavem Aquitaniæ, alij videant. Ea sic habet: D. M. VALERIÆ. IVSTINÆ NATA CONVENA AQVITANIA VIXIT. ANNOS. XXI IVN. VALERIANVS MIL. COH. III. PR T. FELICIS. CONI. B. M. T.
units.tr: On the borders of the Bigerrones are the counties which are commonly called Gavre and Firac. The Seneschalsy of Agen, commonly called the Seneschalsy of Agenais, was formerly the seat of the Nitiobriges. Here on the east are the Cadurci as neighbours, on the north the Petrocorii, where the people of Agen extend to Bironium, a town of the Petrocorii; on the west the Vasconnes meet them along the Garonne, by which also they are washed on the south. It contains two bishoprics, namely on this side of the Garonne Agen, the city of the Nitiobriges; beyond the Garonne Condom. Agen, in the vernacular Agen: Ptolemy, book ii, chapter vii, gives it as Aginnon [Ἀγινον]; Antoninus, in Epistle xxiii, the Antonine Itinerary and the Peutinger Table give Aginnum; Bede in the Martyrology at the fifth of the Ides of June, and Adon and others give Aginum; the Book of Provinces gives Agennum, and so does Jerome in his book on illustrious writers, and Honorius, who mentions its bishop Phoebadius; Gregory of Tours, book i, chapter cv, On Miracles, calls it the city of Agenum. Bede's Agavanum varies in writing, on the day before the Nones of October, and the same author's Aganum on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November. The most sound reading is Aginnum. A town of venerable antiquity, situated on the bank of the Garonne, eighteen leagues from the metropolis of Bordeaux, and half of all Aquitaine. It is the seat of the seneschal, whose jurisdiction, except that of Poitiers, is the widest of all Aquitaine. From here seek justice the Port of St Mary, Villeneuve d'Agenais (on the Lot, which also constitutes a more specific part of this region, having a citadel), Hautefage, Clairac, Marmande, the shrine consecrated to Our Lady of Great Faith, Fargues, Clérac, and other towns on the Garonne. Agen is great also for this reason: that the great Joseph Scaliger first set foot on its soil, and first drew its air. Condom, commonly the Seneschalsy of Condomois. This region is usually called by this special name, Vasconia. For just as Africa is the name of that whole great continent which stretches from the Nile to Cadiz, and yet within it there was a province specifically called Africa, in which Carthage lay, so Vasconia is indeed the name of that very wide region which was once called Novempopulania; but strictly speaking Vasconia is also the name of the Diocese of Condom within it. Thus the seneschal of Agen calls himself seneschal of the Agenais and of Vasconia, that is, of Condom. This appellation is old. For in the times of Pepin the district was called Agen on both sides of the Garonne. So under Pepin in the most ancient annals it is recorded that much grain was (sent) to the district of Agen beyond the Garonne, that is, to that region which is properly Vasconia, in which Condom lies: commonly Condom, a large town in a barren territory, surrounded almost everywhere by hills planted with vines, situated off the royal road, not far from the river Baïse. It provides a seat not only for the new bishopric, which I said above was taken from that of Agen, but also for the seneschalsy, whose judge serves the towns which the natives call Valence-sur-Baïse, Lectoure-sur-Garonne, La Romieu, Aiguillon, and others. Not a few illustrious families are found here. We know the viscounts here as Fismacones, Gourdons, Forcès, and Montluc. The Duchy of Albret, La Duché d'Albret, has taken its very wide name from a little town which is commonly called Albret, in the Landes of Lapurdum, which they call Landes. It was established not many years ago, put together from the mutilation of the seneschalsies of Agen, Armagnac, Quercy, and Vasatensis; so that one may say of it what Jerome said of Constantinople, that it was built from the nakedness of all cities. The capital of the duchy is Nérac, a wealthy town. In the memory of our grandfathers, John of Albret, son of Alain, a lord, married Catherine, daughter of Gaston, and with her received the kingdom of Navarre as dowry; from his son Henry was born the granddaughter, Joan of Albret, Queen of Navarre, mother of Henry IV, most Christian King of France and Navarre. The County of Comminges, La Comté de Comminges, is commonly called by the Latins Comingia. The inhabitants of this region are written to have first given their name to the Christian soldiery of the Aquitanians, having suffered many unworthy things from the enemies of the Christian name. The territory of the Convenae is divided into Upper and Lower, and the whole of it is raised up by mountains. The capital of the people is Lugdunum of the Convenae; Ptolemy and Strabo, book iv, give it as Koinonion [Κοινωνιῶν] (the reading should be Κοινωνιῶν); Antoninus simply gives Lugdunum, on the road from Agen to this town. Since it had flourished greatly for many years, it was at last to be destroyed by the angry army of King Guntram, in the year 584, indiction 11; from its remains the shrine of St Bertrand, where the episcopal see is today, was built in the Valley of Capraria. The antiquity and splendour of that city are easily attested by the many monuments and inscriptions which still exist there today. Among other gods the Lugdunensian Convenae worshipped, perhaps some fellow-regional ones, Abellio: concerning whom there are certain stones there, as we have seen elsewhere, where we speak of the gods of the Gauls. What is meant in the inscription which is read at Rome in the house of the Mellini near the Agonalian gate, "Aquitaine's Cave", let others see. It reads thus: "To the spirits of the dead: Valeria Justina, a native of the Convenae in Aquitaine, lived twenty-one years. Junius Valerianus, soldier of the third cohort of the praetorian guard, of the century of Felix, erected this to his well-deserving wife."

units.la: Vasconia priusquam egrediar, addam tria verba de Elusatium Agro, qui vulgo Le Pais d'Eufe en Gascoigne. Ejus Metropolis Elusa. Sic dicitur Ammiano Marcellino lib. xv, & Itinerario, quod Burdigala ducit Hierosolymas; quæ Paulino Epistola ad Severum vi. Elusa. Ammiani verba, quod corruptiora, adscribam: In Narbonensi Elusa, & Narbo, & Tolosa, & principatum urbium tenent: Viennensis Civitatum exsultat decore multarum: quibus potiores sunt Vienna ipsa & Arelate & Valentia, quibus Massilia jungitur. Pro Elusa vulgati Codices habebant Clusa. Hinc Elusana Plebs apud Sulpitium Severum Historiæ Sacræ lib. ii. Fuisse videtur olim Episcopatus. Laban Elusensis Episcopus nominatur Gregorio Turonensi lib. viii. cap. xxii.
units.tr: Before I leave Vasconia, I will add a few words about the district of the Elusates, commonly called Le Pais d'Eufe en Gascoigne. Its metropolis is Elusa. It is so called by Ammianus Marcellinus, book xv, and by the Itinerary which runs from Burdigala to Jerusalem; and by Paulinus in his letter to Severus, number vi, Elusa. I will set down Ammianus's words, which are rather corrupt: In Narbonensis, Elusa, Narbo and Tolosa hold the leading place among the cities; the Viennese province boasts the beauty of many cities, among which Vienna itself, Arelate and Valentia are the most important, to which Massilia is joined. In place of Elusa the common manuscripts had Clusa. Hence the Elusana Plebs in Sulpicius Severus, Sacred History, book ii. It seems to have once been a bishopric: Laban, Bishop of Elusa, is named by Gregory of Tours, book viii, chapter xxii.

units.la: CAP. XXXIX.
units.tr: CAP. XXXIX.

units.la: Provincia.
units.tr: Provincia.

units.la: PROVINCIAS Parlamentis subjectas Accessoriis, Parisienseque illud ad Occidentem Meridiemque quasi circumeuntibus, quanta fieri potuit industria perlustravi: sequuntur jamnunc Regiones, quae reliquis parent Tribunalibus, Orientalior ejusdem Parisiensis Latera velut claudentibus. Ea sunt Aquensis, Gratianopolitanum, Divionense. Aquensis Iurisdictioni obtemperat Provincia.
units.tr: I have surveyed, with all the diligence I could, the provinces subject to the Parlements and their dependencies, going round the Parisian region toward the west and south. Now follow the regions which obey the other courts and close in the eastern flank of that same Parisian region. These are Aix, Grenoble and Dijon. Aix is under the jurisdiction of the province.

units.la: Unde & qua occasione PROVINCIAE nomen inditum praestantissimo huic Galliarum Tractui, etiam ultra Rodanum ad Garumnam usque, petendum est ex Capite huius libri XVI; ubi omnia Romanorum contra Veteres Gallos Bella paucis commemorantur. Narbonensis enim Gallia ab Romanis in Provincia formam multis ante Christum natum annis redacta, hodieque illud impositae quondam conditionis nomen mordicus in exigua sui portione, in qua Massilia & Aquae Sextiae, retinet, quasi & ut ostenderet se Primam, non quidem ordine, sed dignitate inter omnes Imperii Romani fuisse Provincias. Est enim totus ille Narbonensis Ager pars totius Franciae praestantissima. Paucis Plinius lib. III. cap. IV, Agrorum cultu; Virorum Morumque dignatione, amplitudine opum nulli Provinciarum post ferenda, breviterque Italia verius, quam Provincia. Provincia sane, de qua mihi sermo, praeter Segetes, Fructus profert, non solicita cultura, nobilissimos. Vvarum Passarum Ficuumque tanta hic Copia, ut potiori Europae sufficiat. Ros Marinus, Myrtus, Iuniperi Baccae, aliaque id genus larga hic manu ab Natura proveniunt. Castaneae nusquam majores. Mala Citria, Cydonia, Granata; item Crocus, Oryza, similiaque pleno ibidem cornu funduntur. Vites generosissima dant Vina. Solum denique passim gratum, ferax, benignum: Coelum mite, clemens, & valde purgatum. Conjacet Provincia ad Septemtrionem Delphinatus, Montium interpositu Velaxorum, qui vulgo Velaye, intercursuque magnam partem Druentij Fluminis; Orientale ejus Latus claudunt & Alpes, & Varus Fluvius, cujus sinistrae Ripae adsidet Nicaea, Italiae hic principium; qua Meridies est, ab Gallico pulsatur Mari: Occidentalis illi Limes partim Araufiorum Principatus & Avenionensis vel Venissae Comitatus, hujus quondam Partes. Francorumque Ditionis, nunc autem aliorum Principum; partim Rodanus, integer, Lugduno Arelatem usque, ad Languedokij Parlamenti Iurisdictiones, ut antea dixi, spectans. nius & Sidonius. Ejus operis hodie nullum exstat Vestigium, sive Vetustas consumserit, seu diruerint Gothi, aliique Barbari. De Capitolio Narbonensi, id est Palatio, videndus Gregorius Turonensis lib. de Mirac. i. cap.xcii. Lacuum appellatione Ausonius, Stagnorum Sidonius exaudiunt Rubresium, de quo praeter alios eleganter Pomponius Mela lib. ii. cap. v: Hodie L'Estang de la Rubine. De eo obiter cap. x. Per Flumen intelligit Sidonius Atacem, de quo Plinius lib. iii. cap. iv. Strabo lib. v, Sidonius lib. viii. cap. iv. lib. ix. cap. xvi, & alibi. Vibius: Atax e Pyrenaeo, circa Narbonam decurrit in Tyrrhenum. Atacis cum aliis Fluminibus meminit Theodulphus Episcopus Aurelianensis, qui in Scrinijs adhuc Petri Danielis, Poemate contra Iudaeos iniquos: Praefectura mihi fuerat peragenda tributa, Rex dedit hanc Karolus, primus ad omne bonum. Cui parent Walis, Rodanus, Mosa, Renus & Oenus, Sequana, Visurgis, Warda, Garumna, Padus, Rufa, Mosella, Liger, Vulturnus, Matrona, Ledus, Iiter, Atax, Gabarus, Olitis, Albis, Arar.
units.tr: Where, and on what occasion, this most distinguished part of Gaul, stretching from the Rhone as far as the Garonne, received the name Province, must be sought in Chapter 16 of this book, where all the Roman wars against the ancient Gauls are briefly recalled. For Narbonese Gaul was reduced by the Romans into a Province many years before the birth of Christ, and even today it clings stubbornly to the name of that former status in a small part of itself, in which Massilia and Aquae Sextiae lie. It seems to have wished to show that it was first among all the provinces of the Roman Empire, if not in order, then in dignity. For that whole Narbonese territory is the most excellent part of all France. Pliny, briefly, in Book 3, chapter 4: "In the cultivation of its fields, in the worth of its men and customs, and in the abundance of its wealth, it is second to no province, and is more truly Italy than a province." Indeed the Province of which I speak, apart from grain, produces fruits of the finest kind without anxious cultivation. Here the supply of raisins, figs and dried grapes is so great that it could supply the best part of Europe. Rosemary, myrtle, juniper berries and other things of that kind are lavishly produced here by nature. Chestnuts are nowhere larger. Citrons, quinces and pomegranates; likewise saffron and rice, and similar things, pour out here from a full horn of plenty. The vines yield the finest wines. The soil is everywhere pleasant, fertile and kindly; the sky is mild, gentle and very clear. The Province lies to the north of Dauphiné, with the Velaye mountains lying between, which the common people call the Vellaves, and the course of the river Durance covering much of the way. Its eastern side is enclosed by the Alps and by the river Var, on whose left bank Nice sits, the beginning of Italy here. Toward the south it is struck by the Gallic Sea. Its western boundary is partly the principality of Orange and the county of Avignon or Venaissin, which were formerly part of the Frankish dominion, but now belong to other princes; and partly the Rhone, which, entire, from Lyon as far as Arles, belongs to the jurisdiction of the Parlement of Languedoc, as I said before. Of that work no trace survives today, whether antiquity has consumed it or the Goths and other barbarians destroyed it. On the Capitol of Narbonne, that is, the palace, see Gregory of Tours, On the Miracles, book 1, chapter 92. By the name lakes Ausonius, and by pools Sidonius, understand the Rubresus, concerning which Pomponius Mela, among others, writes elegantly in book 2, chapter 5: today L'Estang de la Rubine. On it, in passing, see chapter 10. By the river Sidonius means the Aude, concerning which Pliny, book 3, chapter 4; Strabo, book 5; Sidonius, book 8, chapter 4, book 9, chapter 16, and elsewhere. Vibius: "The Atax rises in the Pyrenees and runs near Narbonne into the Tyrrhenian Sea." Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, who is still preserved among the papers of Pierre Daniel, mentions the Atax along with other rivers, in his poem against the wicked Jews: "The charge of collecting tribute was given to me; King Charles, first in every good thing, gave me this office. To him obey the Waal, the Rhone, the Meuse, the Rhine and the Oen, the Seine, the Weser, the Warta, the Garonne, the Po, the Rufa, the Moselle, the Loire, the Volturno, the Matrona, the Lede, the Iiter, the Atax, the Gabarus, the Olitis, the Elbe and the Arar."

units.la: Ab Atace, Atacini Populi & Varro Atacinus, ut alias dixi. Narbo Straboni lib. iv, Μίναρον Ε΄μπορίον. Narbone Grammaticam docuit Marcellus Marcelli F. de quo Libro Professorum Ausonius, cap. xix. Narbonam Urbem celebrat Benjaminus in Itinerario, Legis (Iudaicam intelligit) Antesignanam. Ex ea enim proficisci Legem in omnes Regiones: ibi Sapientes esse & magnos & suspiciendos: in primis Kalonymon, Theodori Filium, ex Semine David, recta Genealogia. Praedia & Fundos habentem a Principibus Regionis, nullius hominis vim aut imperum metuentia.
units.tr: From the Atax come the Atacini people and Varro Atacinus, as I said elsewhere. Strabo, book 4, calls Narbo a trading town: [Μίναρον ἐμπόριον]. Marcellus, son of Marcellus, who taught grammar at Narbonne, is praised by Ausonius in the book of Professors, chapter 19. Benjamin, in his Itinerary, celebrates the city of Narbonne as the forerunner of the Law (he means the Jewish Law), for from there the Law went out into all regions. There, he says, were wise men, great and to be admired, above all Kalonymos, son of Theodore, of the seed of David in direct descent, who possessed estates and farms and, being held by the princes of the region, feared the force or authority of no man.

units.la: Haec de urbibus Archiepiscopalibus: Episcopales in duplici sunt mihi discrimine. Inter eas enim quaedam, quae Metropoles sunt, & quasi Capita nobilissimorum quorundam hujus Provinciae Pagorum. Sic appello Suburbicarios Agros, fuioresque quorundam Oppidorum Iurisdictiones: quales sunt Gabali, Albigenses, Velauni Conscaranni & Albenses. Gabali, hodie Givaudan. Eorum Metropolis Mimates Vicus Antiquioribus, vulgo Mende de Givaudan: Reginoni Mitanensis in Territorio Cavallitano, corrupte: Mimatensis Montis Galliae circa Gaballitanam Urbem, cujus Episcopus erat S. Privatus, meminit Gregorius Turonensis, apud quem etiam legitur Memmatensis. Albigenses, nunc Albigeois: Urbs Albiga Gregorio Turonensi lib. ii. Albi vernacule. Velauni, Velai. Eorum Civitas quibusdam Anicium, Le Puy en Velai, id est, Podium in Velauno, quia Urbs est in editissimo loco, qui Gallorum lingua Puy, id est Podium dicitur. Conscarannorum, Ceferans, Civitas S. Legier de C. ferans opidum antiquitate non incelebre. Albenses, Vivarais. Civitas Albensium, nunc Vivario. Sic scribitur in melioribus Notitiae Provinciarum Codicibus: Vitiose in Vulgatis, Civitas Albensium, hoc est Bebsio. Vivario Oppidum est ad ripam Rodani dextram, vulgo Viviers. Ait autem recte Notitia, Nunc Vivario. Civitas enim & Metropolis Albensium olim erat Alba; quae Plinio Helviorum cognominatur, Ptolemaeo autem Augusta. Legitur enim apud eum Α΄ζουγουστα Ε΄λικιῶν: vocat Helvecios, quos Latini Helvios. Alba autem illa hodie Aubenas dicitur; Oppidum in Vivariensi Diœcesi, quinque minimum leucis ab Viverione versus Occidentem situm, quatuor ab Vcetensium Civitate, cum qua communem habet Amnem. Aubenas autem est nomen Pluralis numeri Albanates: ut ab Tolosa Tolosates, ab Nola Nolates in Veteri Inscriptione.
units.tr: So much for the archiepiscopal cities. The episcopal cities I must divide into two classes. For among them are some which are metropolises, and as it were the heads of certain most noble districts of this province. I call these the suburban fields and the jurisdictions of certain towns, such as: Gabali, Albigenses, Velauni, Conscaranni and Albenses. Gabali is today Givaudan. Its metropolis, Mimates Vicus in older writers, is commonly called Mende of Givaudan. Regino writes Mitanensis in the territory of Gévaudan, corruptly; the Mimatensis of Mount, a Gallic town near the city of Gabali, whose bishop was St Privatus, is mentioned by Gregory of Tours, who also has the reading Memmatensis. Albigenses, now Albigeois: the city Albiga in Gregory of Tours, book 2; in the vernacular Albi. Velauni, Velai. Their city is called by some Anicium, Le Puy en Velai, that is, Podium in Velauno, because the town stands on a very high place, which in the Gallic tongue is called Puy, that is, Podium. Conscarannorum, Ceferans: the city of St Légier de Ceferans, a town not unknown for its antiquity. Albenses, Vivarais: the city of the Albenses, now Vivario. So it is written in the better manuscripts of the Notitia of the Provinces; in the printed editions it is wrongly given as Civitas Albensium, that is, Bebsio. Vivario is a town on the right bank of the Rhone, commonly Viviers. The Notitia rightly says now Vivario. For the city and metropolis of the Albenses was once Alba, which Pliny calls Alba of the Helvii, and Ptolemy Augusta. For in him we read [Ἀουγουστα Ἑλικιῶν], calling them Helvecii, whom the Latins call Helvii. That Alba is today called Aubenas, a town in the diocese of Viviers, lying at least five leagues to the west of Viviers, and four from the city of the Vocontii, with which it shares a river. Aubenas is a name in the plural number, Albanates, as from Tolosa comes Tolosates, and from Nola Nolates in an ancient inscription.

units.la: Tantum de Episcopalibus, quae Suburbicarium Agrorum, latiorumque quarundam Iurisdictionum sunt Metropoles: reliquum est, ut ceteras explicem: in quis recensendis si non legitimum servem ordinem, vel si ejusdem cum indicatis iam naturae ad earum non referam classem, ignoscant velim Lectores, praesertim Incolae. Non enim omnia penitissime licuit novisse.
units.tr: So much for the episcopal cities which are metropolises of the suburban fields and of certain wider jurisdictions. It remains for me to explain the rest. In enumerating these, if I do not keep a proper order, or if I do not refer some to the same class as those already indicated, I would ask my readers to pardon me, especially those who live there. For it was not possible for me to know everything in the most exact detail.

units.la: Nïsmes, Nemausus Volcarum Arecomicorum Plinio lib. iii. cap. iv, Ausonio libro de Urbibus Carmine xiii, Pomponio Melae lib. ii. cap. v. Sidonio lib. ii, Epist. ix. Itinerario Antonini: Νέμαυσος Straboni lib. iv, & Ptolemaeo. Numismati vetustissimo COL. NEM. ARECOMICORUM. In Itineraria Peutingeri Tabula Nemuso scribitur, corruptius. Νέμαυσος, inquit Stephanus, πόλις Γαλλίας, ἡ Νέμαυσα Ηεγ-αλειδὸς, ὡς Παρθίνος. Qualis fuerit florente Romanorum Imperio, notat eleganter Strabo; cujus ea de re pauca verba non possum non adscribere: Μεγίστολις δὴ τῶν Α΄ζυγἈ᾽ςκομιςκῶν ἐκ Νἡμαυσ͏ῶ, καὶ μὲν ἡ ἀλλότριον ἔχλεν καὶ τὸν ἱμπεριὸν, μᾶλλον Ναρβῶν͏ῶ λεγομένη, καὶ δὲ τὸν μάλιστα ὑπερβάλλειν. ὑπαίως γὰρ ἔχοι κώμας πίπαρας καὶ ἐκάτερα τῶν ὀμοιθῶν, ξύαδεζία ἀρὲ φύσις, συμπλέσας εἰς αὐτὴν, ἰχύσας ἡ τὴ καλέμενον Λα-τῖνον, ὡς τὰς ἀξιωθέντας ἀρξεγραμμένας ἐ πιμιῶν ὁ Νημαύσω Ῥωμαίας ὑπάρχειν. Διὰ δὲ τὴν μὲν ἐν τὰς παράγματα τῶν ἐν τῆς Ῥώμης σεμνῶν εἰς τὸ ἰδίον τῶν. Ἱδρυτα δὲ ἡ πόλις καὶ τῷ ὁδῷ τῷ ἐν τῆς Ἰταλίας εἰς τὸ Ἰταλίαν, ἴπρως μὲν ὄλαν ἴσως, χθαῶν͏ῶ δὲ ἡ ἰαρ͏ῶ πολλῶν ἡ πομοκλυσιν. In Opidorum, quæ Nemausicnsibus adtributa, numero, Plinio convenit cum Strabone. Ejus verba lib. iii. nat. hist. cap. iv sic habent: Vocontiorum Civitatis Fœderata duo Capita, Vasco & Lucus Augusti: Opida vero ignobilia xix; sicut xxiv Nemausiensibus adtributa. Decurionum Nemausi mentio in Antiqua Inscriptione, quæ ibi visitur:
units.tr: Nîmes, Nemausus of the Volcae Arecomici: in Pliny, book 3, chapter 4; Ausonius in his poem on cities, poem 13; Pomponius Mela, book 2, chapter 5; Sidonius, book 2, letter 9; in the Itinerary of Antoninus; [Νέμαυσος] in Strabo, book 4, and in Ptolemy. On a very ancient coin: COL. NEM. ARECOMICORUM. In the Tabula Peutingeriana it is written Nemuso, more corruptly. [Νέμαυσος], says Stephanus, a city of Gaul, [ἡ Νέμαυσα], the Nemausa of ... Of what kind it was in the flourishing time of the Roman Empire, Strabo notes elegantly; I cannot refrain from transcribing a few of his words on this matter: "Nemausus is the greatest city of the Arecomici, and it is much more Roman than any other, and it is more like Narbonne, and in some respects surpasses it. For it has suburbs, and both sides of the roads, and a great many fine buildings, and the most Roman of all the cities here..." In the number of towns assigned to the Nemausenses, Pliny agrees with Strabo. His words in book 3 of the Natural History, chapter 4, read thus: "The Vocontii have two federated capitals, Vasio and Lucus Augusti; but nineteen insignificant towns, and twenty-four assigned to the Nemausenses." A mention of the Decurions of Nemausus occurs in an ancient inscription which is seen there:

units.la: DIS. MANIBVS FIRMI. LVCANI IIIIL. VIRI. AVG. ORNAMENTIS. DE CVRIONVM. NEMAVSI HONORATO
units.tr: TO THE SPIRITS OF THE DEAD: FIRMUS LUCANUS, IIII-VIR AUGUSTAL, HONOURED WITH THE ORNAMENTS OF THE DECURIONS OF NEMAUSUS

units.la: Miram undique redolet cum in veteri Muro, qui testatur multo, quam hodie, ampliorem fuisse, tum in aliis, Antiquitatem. Amphitheatrum ibi conspicitur, exteriore parte non minus integrum, quam quod Veronæ. Ante Amphitheatrum Campus Martius fuisse perhibetur, qui, ut Romanus, Aedificiis jam oppletus, & in alios tractus est usus. Aedificium, quod vulgo Le Cap duel, Capitolium (sic enim nomen illud corruptum) vel Basilica fuisse fertur, ab Imperatore Hadriano exstructa in gratiam & honorem, ut legere est apud Spartianum, Conjugis Plotinæ. Forma est τετράγωνος, quadrata quidem, sed quæ in longitudinem nonnihil vergit. Latera x. Columnis sulciuntur: Frons vi; pars Fronti adversa totidem. Tectum ex magnis compositum est Lapidibus; Deambulationibus adcommodatum. Templum, Fonti propinquum, integrum adhuc est, forma quadrata. Duos habent latera columnarum Ordines, artis absolutæ. Visuntur adhuc ibi Aquilæ. Romani quondam Imperij notæ & insignia, sed quæ Capitibus truncatæ. Id factum volunt ab Gothis, ut Romanum Imperium Corpus esse capite minutum, quum Imperatorum caderent vires, ostenderent. Ad mœnia Veteris Opidi annosa est Structura in Colle, qui Fonti vicinus vulgo Torremagne vocatur, id est, ut quidam putant, Turris Romana vel Turris Magna. Lapidibus constat exiguis, ipsque quadratis. Videre ibidem est & perantiquas aliquot Statuas, & nonnulla melioris notæ Variorum Epitaphia: Columnam item ad Portam, cui ab Corona nomen. Imperatorum Domitiani, & Antonini Pij Philosophi, aliorumque claret Natalibus. Qui vulgo Fons Incolis appellatur, sed qui Lacus potius, quam Fons, dubitatur an sit, quem celebrat Ausonius Carmine, quod indicavi. Qui penitius inspexerunt, suspicantur alium fuisse, qui ex proximis Collibus in Vrbem ducebatur; sed cui accideric, quod Divonæ Burdigalensi, id est perijsse. Incolæ Nemausenses nominantur. De ijs Lapis mutilus:
units.tr: The place smells of antiquity on every side, both in the old wall, which shows that the city was once much larger than it is today, and in other remains. The Amphitheatre can be seen there, its outer face no less intact than that at Verona. Before the Amphitheatre there is said to have been a Campus Martius, which, like the Roman one, is now filled with buildings and has been put to other uses. The building commonly called Le Cap duel, Capitolium (for that is how the name has been corrupted), or Basilica, is said to have been built by the Emperor Hadrian in favour and honour of his wife Plotina, as one may read in Spartianus. Its plan is square (τετράγωνος), though it stretches somewhat in length. Its sides measure ten columns, and the front has six columns, with the same number on the opposite front. The roof is made of large stones and is suited to walking about. The temple near the spring is still intact, of square plan. Its sides have two orders of columns, of perfect workmanship. Eagles can still be seen there, the marks and insignia of the old Roman empire, but with their heads broken off. They think the Goths did this, to show that the Roman empire, like a body with its head cut off, lost its strength when the power of the emperors fell. Near the walls of the old town, on a hill close to the spring commonly called Torremagne, which some think means Turris Romana or Turris Magna, there is an ancient structure. It is made of small stones, themselves squared. In the same place one can see several very old statues and some inscriptions of various persons of better quality. There is also a column at the gate named after the Crown, and it is famous as the birthplace of the emperors Domitian and Antoninus Pius, the philosopher, and others. The place the inhabitants call the Fons, but it is doubtful whether it is a Lacus rather than a Fons, the one which Ausonius celebrates in the poem I have cited. Those who have examined it more closely suspect that there was another, which was led into the city from the nearby hills; but what happened to it, as happened to the Divona at Bordeaux, is not known, that is, it has perished. The inhabitants are called the Nemausenses. There is a mutilated stone about them:

units.la: IIIIL. VIR. ... CORPORATI. NEMAVSENSES PATRONO EX. POSTVLATIONE. POPVLI L. D. D. D.
units.tr: IIII-VIR ... THE CORPORATION OF THE NEMAUSENSES TO THEIR PATRON, BY DECREE OF THE PEOPLE. BY PUBLIC DECREE, AT PUBLIC EXPENSE.

units.la: Leguntur etiam Nemausenses apud Suetonium cap.xiii. Tiberij Principis Statuas & Imagines subvertisse; ubi tamen plerique Codices Nemausenses habent: Membranæ pleræque Remansenses; Vaticanus Liber, Remansisses. Exstat Libellus de Antiquitatibus Nemausensibus Ioannis Poldi. Tribus Nemauso milliaribus, Pons est, qui vulgo
units.tr: The Nemausenses are also mentioned by Suetonius, chapter 13, as having overthrown the statues and images of the emperor Tiberius. However, most manuscripts read Nemausenses; most parchment copies read Remansenses, and the Vatican book reads Remansisses. There is a little book on the Antiquitatibus Nemausensibus by Johannes Poldus. Three miles from Nemausus is the bridge commonly called

units.la: Note: marginal notes are rendered in the notes section below. vulgo Du Gard. Nomen hoc illi ab Fluvio Guardone: quem, Francorum Veterum enunciatione (de qua Agathias) Wardonem appellant Sidonius lib. 11. Epist: x. Theodulphus Aurelianensis duobus locis, Fulbertus in Historia MS. Egidij & Petrus Aquil. lib. viii. cap. xviii. Pons triplici serie fornicatus est, stupenda sane industria: Prima Hominibus lumenteisque præbet transitum, altera Aquæductum sustinet. Inter Fanum S. Privati & Rimolinum Vestigia monstrantur Aquæductus, quo Romani Aquam in Nemautensium Opidum ducebant. Vfetz, Vcetensium Civitas: nonnullis Latine scribentibus Vtica. Vticensis Galliæ Episcopi meminit Aurelianum Concilium v. Opidum quod in Ducatus honorem, ad Wardones confluentes. Alter enim Occidentalior Gardo cognominatur d' Alaix; Orientalior autem d' Anduze, ab opidis, quæ singulorum Ripis adhident. VVardo, ut jam monui, dicitur Theodulpho Aurelianensi Episcopo, & aliis. Lodeuc, vel, ut alij, Lodesve, Luteva; Notitiæ Provinciarum Galliæ Castrum Luteva, in Viennensi Secunda. S. Pont de Tomieres, Fanum S. Pontij Tomeriarum. Alet, Aletensis Civitas; Alezium quibusdam Latine scribentibus, Opidum Vicecomitatus titulo insignitum. Mompelier, Latine nominantibus Mons Pessulanus: Mons Puellarum, Puellerum, item Pisciculanum ab nonnullis dicitur, ut notat Cœnalis. Mons Tremulus vocatur à Benjamino Tudelensi; apud quem insigne est hujus Vrbis Elogium. Subsistentiam nuncupatam scribit Blondus 1. Decadis lib. x. Videat ille, qua fretus auctoritate. Male quibusdam Agatha vel Agathopolis, quæ hodie Agde. Situm est Celliculo, decem leucis ab Mari Mediterraneo. Aer ibi placidissimus & salubberrimus. Vrbe nihil amoenius, Civibus nihil humanius; Territorio nihil fertilius, Simplicumque feracius: quæ res Medicos præcipue invitavit, ut Sedem ibi figerent, atque Medicinam cum laude docerent. Academiam enim Vrbs habet, quæ instituta memoratur circa annum cıɔ cxcvı; vel saltem quo tempore, Saracenis Hispania pulsis. Medicina cum Discipulis Arabum, Avicennæ, Averrois, & aliorum, huc migravit. Rectoris ibi tanta est auctoritas; ut Studiosi quacumque etiam de causa egredientem comitari honoris gratia cogantur, quod se non sine maximo Studiorum suorum, multarumque Horarum jactura nimis frequenter fecisse, conqueritur Rebuffus. Collegia sunt ibi varia, inter quæ amplissimum est. Papa cognominatum. quod ab Vrbano Pontifice fundatum, & copiosissimis ornatum est Redditibus. Nec minus elegans est Regium, ab Henrico II Galliarum Rege erectum. Tertium est, quod vulgo Du Vergier; optimæ spei Adulescentibus Studiorum Victusque necessaria in decennium præbens. Befiers, Bitterra, aut Bitera Septimanorum in Arecomicis: Βαιτερα, Ptolemæo; Βαιτιτερρα, Stephano, Biterra, Plinio lib. iii. cap. iv: Βιλιτερρα. Straboni lib. iv; Beterra, Pomponio Melæ lib. ii. cap. v, & Antonino, cui & Peterna; Beterrii, Tabulæ Peutingeri Itinerariæ in Auferendi casu; Biterra Itinerario Burdigalensi, & Vfuardo xi. Kalend. Aprilis. Hinc Biterrenses Sidonio lib. viii. Epist. iv; qui Biterienses in Notitia Provinciarum, in Viennensi Secunda. בידרש, id est Bidrasch vitiosius Benjamino in Itinerario. Opidum pervetustum, multis agitatum calamitatibus, cum ab Gothis, tum ab ipsis Francorum Regibus. Agde, Αγαθη Τυχη Timosthenī ἐν τῷ σαλασσῳ apud Stephanum; Αγαθη, Straboni & Ptolemæo; Agatha, Plinio. Opidum ab Massiliensibus Græcis conditum in Volcis Arecomicis: unde & Strabonī Κνισμα Μασσαλιωτων. Carcassone, Carcassio Volcarum Tectosagum: Καρκασσων, Ptolemæo: Carcassum, Plinio; Carcasio, Procopio: Carcassio, Itinerariæ Peutingeri Tabulæ. Secundum inter tres Languedokij Senefchallias locum obtinet: La Senefchauffée de Carcassone. Castrum, Cessero, Cessero, Opidum Castrense: Cessero, Plinio; Κεσσηρα, Ptolemæo: Cetero, Casero & Tesero corrupte apud Antoninum. Scaligero tamen apud Plinium legitur Cesteo, ut illud sit Provinciæ opidum, quod hodie Cisteron. Pamies, Apamea, de qua post; Mirepoix, Mirapicense opidum. S. Papol. Fanum S. Papuli: La Vaur, Vaurense: Ricus Rivi, Rivense Monasterium. Lombes, Lambariense Monasterium: poltea erecta in Episcopatus, suffraganeos Tolosano. Et hæc de Maiorum gentium tam Episcopalibus, quam Archiepiscopalibus Languedoky Urbibus: Minorum gentium appello reliqua opida, inter quæ: Belloquadra, Beaucaire; tertium nacta locum inter tres Languedoky Senefchallias, La Senefchaussée de Beaucaire, Aiguesmortes, Aqua Mortua: quæ talso quibusdam creduntur Fossæ Mariana, de quibus in Provincia. Piseaux; Pezenas, Piscena, Plinio: S. Gillis, Burgum S. Aegidy, נירקיד בל ניל Beniamino in Itinerario. Chasteau-garry; Lusignen; Montaisgnac; Millaut, Montillac, & alia.
units.tr: Du Gard. The name comes from the river Guardo, which the Franks of old, in their pronunciation (about which Agathias writes), called Wardo, as Sidonius says in Book 2, Letter 10. Theodulphus of Orléans mentions it in two places, Fulbert in his manuscript history of St Giles, and Petrus Aquilensis in Book 8, chapter 18. The bridge is arched in three tiers, a truly astonishing piece of work. The first tier gives passage to men and beasts, and the second carries the aqueduct. Between the shrine of St Privatus and Rimolinum the remains of the Aquæductus by which the Romans led water into the town of the Nemausenses can still be seen. Vfetz, the city of the Vcetenses; by some Latin writers called Vtica. The bishop of Gaul named Vticensis is mentioned at the Council of Orléans, Canon 5. The town, which in honour of the duchy meets the Wardones (the two rivers join). For the more westerly branch is called the Gardo of d' Alaix; the more easterly is called d' Anduze, after the towns which sit on each bank. VVardo, as I have already said, is what Theodulphus, bishop of Orléans, and others call it. Lodeuc, or, as others say, Lodesve, Luteva. The Notitia of the Provinces of Gaul has Castrum Luteva, in Vienne's Second Province. S. Pont de Tomieres, the shrine of St Pontius of the Tomeriae. Alet, the city of Aletensis; Alezium to some Latin writers, a town distinguished by the title of viscounty. Mompelier, which Latin writers call Mons Pessulanus; Mons Puellarum, Puellerum, and also Pisciculanum by some, as Cœnalis notes. It is called Mons Tremulus by Benjamin of Tudela, who gives a famous eulogy of this city. Blondus writes in Book 10 of the first Decade that it was called Subsistentiam; let him see on what authority he relies. Agatha or Agathopolis, which is today Agde, is wrongly given by some. It lies ten leagues from the Mediterranean Sea, on a little hill. The air there is very calm and most healthful. Nothing is more pleasant than the city, nothing more humane than its citizens; nothing is more fertile than the countryside, nor more productive than the simple folk. These things especially attracted physicians, who settled there and taught medicine with credit. The city has an Academia, which is recorded as founded about the year 1196, or at least at the time when the Saracens were driven out of Spain. Medicine, together with the disciples of the Arabs, Avicenna, Averroes and others, migrated here. The authority of the rector is so great that students are compelled, even for whatever cause, to accompany him as he goes out, as a mark of honour; Rebuffus complains that they do this all too often, to the great loss of their studies and of many hours. There are various colleges, of which the largest is called Papa, because it was founded by Pope Urban and endowed with very ample revenues. No less elegant is the Regium, erected by Henry II, King of the French. A third is the one commonly called Du Vergier, which supports young men of excellent promise with the necessities of study and living for ten years. Befiers, Bitterra, or Bitera of the Septimani among the Arecomici: Baiterra [Βαιτερα] in Ptolemy; Baititerra [Βαιτιτερρα] in Stephanus; Biterra in Pliny, Book 3, chapter 4; Bilitera [Βιλιτερρα] in Strabo, Book 4; Beterra in Pomponius Mela, Book 2, chapter 5, and in Antoninus, where also Peterna; Beterrii in the Peutinger Table in the ablative case; Biterra in the Bordeaux Itinerary and in Ufuardus, 11 Kalends of April. From this come the Biterrenses in Sidonius, Book 8, Letter 4; and the Biterienses in the Notitia of the Provinces, in Vienne's Second Province. Bidrasch [בידרש], more corruptly, in Benjamin's Itinerary. An ancient town, troubled by many calamities, both from the Goths and from the kings of the Franks themselves. Agde, Agathe Tyche of Timosthenes in the sea [Αγαθη Τυχη Timosthenī ἐν τῷ σαλασσῳ] in Stephanus; Agathe [Αγαθη] in Strabo and Ptolemy; Agatha in Pliny. A town founded by the Greeks of Massilia among the Volcae Arecomici; hence Strabo also calls it a colony of the Massiliots [Κνισμα Μασσαλιωτων]. Carcassone, Carcassio of the Volcae Tectosages: Carcasson [Καρκασσων] in Ptolemy; Carcassum in Pliny; Carcasio in Procopius; Carcassio in the Peutinger Table of the Itinerary. It holds second place among the three seneschalships of Languedoc: La Senefchauffée de Carcassone. Castrum, Cessero, Cessero, a fortified town: Cessero in Pliny; Kessera [Κεσσηρα] in Ptolemy; Cetero, Casero and Tesero are corruptions in Antoninus. Yet in Scaliger's Pliny the reading is Cesteo, so that it is the town of the Province which is today Cisteron. Pamies, Apamea, of which more later; Mirepoix, the town of Mirapicense. S. Papol, the shrine of S. Papulus; La Vaur, Vaurense; Ricus Rivi, the monastery of Rivense. Lombes, the monastery of Lambariense, later erected into a bishopric, suffragan to Toulouse. These are the cities of Languedoc, both bishoprics and archbishoprics, of the greater sort; I call the remaining towns those of the lesser sort, among which: Belloquadra, Beaucaire, which has gained third place among the three seneschalships of Languedoc, La Senefchaussée de Beaucaire; Aiguesmortes, Aqua Mortua, which some falsely believe to be the Fossæ Mariana, of which more in the account of Provence; Piseaux; Pezenas, Piscena in Pliny; S. Gillis, the town of St Giles, [Hebrew transcription, garbled, as printed] in Benjamin's Itinerary; Chasteau-garry; Lusignen; Montaisgnac; Millaut, Montillac, and others.

units.la: Latara Castellum Pomponio est in Gallia Narbonensi: Ioanni Poldo Lates est. Laterra quoque Stagnum Plinio in Agro Nemaufiensi: de quo alij alia adferunt. De utroque sic Karolus Clusius, oculatus testis, suis ad Abrahamum Ortelium litteris: Recte Poldus. Nam Lates etiamnum vocatur hoc Castellum cum Vico adjacente: Vicinum Stagno Volcarum, qua Ledum flumen in Stagnum labitur. Id Stagnum aliquot milliaria (secedecim memini me numerare ab Ortu in Occasum) in longitudinem porrigitur, cui aliquot Vici & Opidula adjacent (ad Septemtrionalis praecipue latus) Nonnullis locis Estang, & ubi altius vadum habet, Estau ab Indigenis appellatur: qui Pisces in altiore Stagni gurgite captos praeferunt aliis, quod caenum adeo non respiraat. Littus Maris, quod Incolae Playe de la Mar dicunt, Stagnum a Mari sejungit: Aqua tamen marina Fluxum quibusdam in locis in Stagnum praebet: & haud dubie ad Stagnum tutiorem a Piratarum atque Hostium incursionibus eam Galliae Narbonensis oram reddit. Designat, Volcarum Stagna nominans, Pomponius Mela. Fauces Laterra Stagni apud Plinium lib. ix. nat. hist. cap. viii., ubi scilicet cum Mari communicatur: Nemaufiensibus hodie La Cran pres de Mangueil, ut notat Dalechampius.
units.tr: Latara is a castle in Gallia Narbonensis, according to Pomponius; Johannes Poldus calls it Lates. Laterra is also the Stagnum of Pliny in the territory of Nemausus, about which others say other things. Karolus Clusius, an eyewitness, writes of both in his letter to Abraham Ortelius: Poldus is right. For this castle, together with the neighbouring village, is still called Lates: it lies near the lake of the Volcae, where the river Ledus flows into the lake. This lake stretches several miles in length (I remember counting sixteen from east to west), and several villages and small towns lie beside it, especially on its northern side. In some places it is called the Estang, and where it has a deeper ford the natives call it the Estau. They prefer the fish caught in the deeper waters of the lake to the others, because the mud there does not smell. The shore of the sea, which the inhabitants call the Playe de la Mar, separates the lake from the sea; yet in some places sea water gives the lake a flow, and no doubt this makes that coast of Gallia Narbonensis safer for the lake against the raids of pirates and enemies. Pomponius Mela marks it when he names the Volcarum Stagna. The Fauces Laterra Stagni in Pliny, Book 9, Natural History, chapter 8, is where it communicates with the sea; today the Nemausenses call it La Cran pres de Mangueil, as Dalechamps notes.

units.la: Languedoria ante paucos annos adtributus est Ducatui Fuvensis, La Duché de Foix; quum antea Guiennae concenseretur. Ad Orientem illi ipsum Languedokium: ad Occidentem Convenarum Ager; qua Septemtrio est, Territorium ipectat Ripense, vulgo de la Riviere; Meridionale Latus Montes claudunt Pyrenaei; qui Ducatum hunc reddunt ut horridiorem, sic Ferri Carbonumque feraciorem.
units.tr: Languedoc was a few years ago assigned to the Duchy of Foix, La Duché de Foix, although formerly it was counted in Guienne. To its east lies Languedoc itself; to its west the territory of the Convenae; on its north side borders the territory of Rieux, commonly called de la Rivière; the Pyrenees close off its southern side. These mountains make this duchy more rugged, but also richer in iron and coal.

units.la: Nomen illi ab opido Fuxio, quod Antiquitatis laude clarum. Continet unum Episcopatum, Apamiensem. Opidum vulgo Pamies, Latine scribentibus Apamia & Pamia ad confluentes Amnium, qui vulgo Lers & Lagiere. Ab hoc opido dici videtur Epaunense Concilium, habitum sub Gelasio I Papa, & Sigismundo Rege. Episcopi enim, qui illi interfuerunt, omnes hujus sunt Tractus. Empanensis etiam Synodus xv citatur in Decretorum I Distinct. 16. Eupanense Decret. II Causa II. fortean ab hoc eodem opido. Sunt & alia opida, Saverdunum & Masera, Comitum Domicilia. Errare graviter, qui Sedem hic collocant Elusatium, dicam Capite sequente.
units.tr: It takes its name from the town of Foix, which is famous for its antiquity. It contains one bishopric, that of Apamia. The town, commonly called Pamiers, is written in Latin Apamia or Pamia; it lies at the confluence of the rivers commonly called the Lers and the Lagiere. The Council of Epaunum, held under Pope Gelasius I and King Sigismund, seems to have been named from this town, for all the bishops who attended it belong to this district. The Synod of Empanum is also cited as the fifteenth in Decretum I, Distinctio 16, and Eupanum in Decretum II, Causa II, perhaps from this same town. There are also other towns, Saverdunum and Masera, the seats of the counts. Those who place the see of Elusa here are gravely mistaken, as I will say in the following chapter.
