units.la: QVA Veteris Aquitaniae Narbonensisque Provinciae hodie sint sub Parlamentis & Burdigalensi & Tolosano, integre, ex Superioribus didicimus: superest Vasconia, quae utrisque paret mistim. Partes enim ejus quaedam sunt sub Burdigalensi, quaedam sub Tolosano.
units.tr: From the earlier chapters we have learned completely how the lands of Old Aquitaine and the province of Narbonne are today divided between the parlements of Bordeaux and Toulouse. What remains is Vasconia, which obeys both in a mixed way. Some of its parts lie under Bordeaux and some under Toulouse.

units.la: VASCONIA proprie nunc temporis est, quidquid continetur intra Garumnam, Pyrenaeos Montes, Oceanumque & Guiennam hodiernam, vel Aquitaniam Ludovici XI. Dicta est Vasconia ab Vasconibus, ferocissimis Pyrenaeorum Populis: quos devictos primum a Pipino, deinde ab Ludovico Karoli Magni Filio (qui postea dictus fuit Pius) Rege Aquitaniae in plana Novempopulaniae deductos, postea nomen huic Regioni dedisse certum est & indubitatum. Fuerunt enim Vasciones (ut lib. II. capitibus XI. & XIII. docui) pars Cantabrorum, quos etiam hodieque Hispani Vascuenças vocant. Itaque, quum prius haec Regio a Caesare Aquitania, postea Novempopulania audiret; ea ab Vasconibus devictis, inque eam a Pyrenaeorum Saltibus demissis, Vasconia fuit appellata. Est autem tertia pars Aquitaniae Augustae. Nam ab Augusto Aquitania triplex fuit instituta: Prima, cujus Caput Avaricum erat Biturigum Cubrorum; Bourges: Secunda, cujus Metropolis erat Burdigala, Bituriigum Vibiscorum; Tertia tota Trans-Garumnana, in qua principem tenebat locum Augusta Auscorum, vel Auchi: quae Provincia, ut jam dictum est, ab Augusti temporibus ad Pipinum usque nominata fuit Novempopulania: inde ad hunc usque diem Vasconia. Petrus Arvernus Cluniacensis Epist. I: Migravit tamen, sicut audivi, ad Loca satis vobis contigua & a Septimania vestra, vobis persequentibus expulsa in Provincia Novempopulana (quae vulgo Gasconia vocatur) & in partibus ei adiacentibus sibi foveas praeparavit. Novempopulania ab Novem Populis, quos alij alios numerant, & nominant:
units.tr: Properly speaking, Vasconia today is whatever is contained between the Garonne, the Pyrenees and the Ocean, together with present-day Guienne, or the Aquitaine of Louis XI. It is named from the Vascones, the fiercest peoples of the Pyrenees. It is certain and beyond doubt that they were first conquered by Pepin and then by Louis, son of Charlemagne (who was later called Pius), king of Aquitaine. They were led down into the plains of Novempopulania, and afterwards they gave their name to this region. The Vasciones (as I showed in book II, chapters XI and XIII) were a part of the Cantabrians, whom the Spaniards still call the Vascuenças. So, since this region was first called Aquitania by Caesar and afterwards Novempopulania, it came to be called Vasconia, after the Vascones had been conquered and had been sent down into it from the passes of the Pyrenees. It is the third part of Augustan Aquitaine. For under Augustus Aquitaine was divided into three. The first, whose capital was Avaricum of the Bituriges Cubi, is Bourges. The second, whose metropolis was Burdigala of the Bituriges Vivisci, is Bordeaux. The third comprised all the land beyond the Garonne, in which Augusta of the Ausci, or Auch, held the chief place. As has already been said, this province was called Novempopulania from the time of Augustus until Pepin, and from then until today it has been called Vasconia. Peter of Auvergne, of Cluny, in Letter I: "He migrated, as I have heard, to places quite close to you and to your Septimania, driven out by your persecution, into the province of Novempopulania (which is commonly called Gascony), and he prepared pits for himself in the adjacent parts." Novempopulania is named from the Nine Peoples, whom different writers count and name differently.

units.la: Scaliger autem suis ad me litteris, hos: Convenas, Consuarannos, Bigerrones, Lactoratenses, Vasates, Eloronenses, Lascarienses, Tarbellos, & Atyrenses: quorum Convenæ, Bigerrones & Lactoratenses sunt in hodierna Vasconia; Consaranni in Languedokio; Vasates, Tarbelli & Atyrenses in Guienna Ludovici xi; Eloronenses denique & Lascarienses in Benearnia Principatu: adeo ut Vasconia major olim, quam nunc, fuerit: quum comprehenderet etiam Guiennam Ludovici xi & nonnullam Languedoky portionem: quum tamen ante Ludovicum xi Guienna major esset Vasconia; & Guienna totum quasi esset, Vasconia autem Pars.
units.tr: Scaliger, however, in his letter to me, names these: the Convenae, Consuarranni, Bigerrones, Lactoratenses, Vasates, Eloronenses, Lascarienses, Tarbelli and Atyrenses. Of these, the Convenae, Bigerrones and Lactoratenses are in present-day Vasconia; the Consuarranni are in Languedoc; the Vasates, Tarbelli and Atyrenses are in Guienne of Louis XI; and the Eloronenses and Lascarienses are in the principality of Béarn. So Vasconia was once larger than it is now, since it also included Guienne of Louis XI and some part of Languedoc. Yet before Louis XI, Guienne was larger than Vasconia: Guienne was, as it were, the whole, and Vasconia a part.

units.la: Stupendum, quod referam. Est in plerisque Vasconiæ locis, præcipue apud Bigerrones & Benearnenses, hominum genus, qui nunc Capots: nunc, variante Dialecto, Gabets appellantur. Detestandi sunt Suis; eorumque Commercia fugiuntur. Habentur pro Lepra infectis. Quasi essent, vel quod sint interdictæ iis Civitates & opida, incolere coguntur Suburbia, Locaque semotiora. Adsignatæ sunt & iis suæ in Templis Stationes. Creduntur alios inficere. Plerique Fabri sunt Lignarij & Victores: aliisque Artibus Mechanicis dediti; Laboris patientissimi. In Facie & Actionibus illorum quiddam paret, quod eos contemtui detestationique reddit obnoxios. Femininus Sexus liberali satis forma. Omnium Halitus & Os grave olet, unde ingrati quid odoris manat in constantes & conloquentes. Quidquid sit, Maledictionis perhibetur genus, quod ab Majoribus in Posteros manifestissimis indiciis derivatur. Pauperiores semper in diem vivunt, diurno labore: Servorum censentur loco, ne ausi quidem mutire, si quid injuriæ inferatur vel ab Vilissimo. Si quis eorum forte ditior, liberi tamen non fiunt heredes, nisi Mobilium, quæ omnes tamquam certam luem avorsantur.
units.tr: Here is a remarkable thing to report. In most places of Vasconia, especially among the Bigerrones and the Béarnais, there is a race of people now called Capots and, with the dialect varying, Gabets. They are detested like swine, and their company is avoided. They are regarded as infected with leprosy. Since cities and towns are closed to them, or as if they were, they are forced to live in the suburbs and more remote places. Even in the churches they are assigned places of their own. They are believed to infect others. Most of them are carpenters and woodcutters, and are given to other mechanical crafts; they are very patient of labour. Something in their faces and conduct makes them liable to scorn and loathing. The women are fairly handsome. The breath and mouth of all of them smell foul, so that an unpleasant odour spreads over those who stand and talk with them. Whatever the cause, it is said to be a kind of curse, which passes from ancestors to descendants by the clearest signs. The poorer ones always live from day to day by daily labour, and are counted in the place of slaves; they do not dare even to murmur if any wrong is done to them, even by the most worthless man. If one of them happens to be richer, still they do not become free heirs, except to movables, which all of them shun as a certain plague.

units.la: Veteres Vasconia, ut quidem ea hodie est; & nos eam accipimus, Incolæ fuerunt Varij: Cantabri, Vasiones, Anses, Tarusates, Lactorates, Bigerrones, Nitiobriges, Convenæ; Elusates, Garites, Cocosates, & proculdubio plures. Cantabri, de quibus lib. ii. cap. xi. quatenus ad Galliam pertinent, Cis-Pyrenæi fuerunt, ubi nunc Le Pais de Basques: Nomen corruptum ex Vasconibus Hispaniæ Populis, qui Pyrenæos traducti, Sedibus inter Gallos fixis, Gascons hodieque nominantur: nisi quis malit Hispania Vasciones, quorum memini eodem libro Capite xiii, feminis esse Gallici, de quo non magnopere contenderim. De Vasconibus Gallia Iuvenalis hæc plerique accipienda censent, Satyra xv:
units.tr: The ancient inhabitants of Vasconia, as it is today, and as we understand it, were various: the Cantabri, Vasiones, Anses, Tarusates, Lactorates, Bigerrones, Nitiobriges, Convenae, Elusates, Garites, Cocosates, and doubtless more. The Cantabri, of whom I spoke in book II, chapter XI, so far as they belong to Gaul, lived on this side of the Pyrenees, where now is Le Pays de Basques. The name is corrupted from the Vascones, a people of Spain, who, carried across the Pyrenees and settled among the Gauls, are still called Gascons today. Unless someone prefers that the Vasciones, whom I mentioned in the same book, chapter XIII, were Spanish, I would not greatly dispute it. Most people think that the following lines of Juvenal, Satire XV, should be understood of the Vascones of Gaul:

units.tr: He who, his whole body now consumed, licks blood from the ground with his fingers. The Vasciones (so the story goes), having used wholesome food,

units.tr: prolonged their lives. But the case is different; there Fortune is envious, and there is the last of wars, the extreme of misfortune, the long and dreadful want of a siege.

units.la: Ausci Plinio lib. iv, cap. xix, Populos Aquitaniæ supra xiiix numeranti, & Melæ lib. iii. cap. i: Ptolemæo Αὔσκιοι, cum ipsorum Vrbs Αὔσκυσε, hodie Auch, de qua suo loco. Aust Itinerariæ Tabulæ: Ausciensis Sidonio lib. vii. Epist. vi. Novempopuli, de quibus paulo ante, ab nonnullis concenseri solitis. Novempopulos, inquit Ammianus, Ausci commendant. Sic Ausonius in Professoribus, de Staphylio Cive Aucto:
units.tr: The Ausci are in Pliny, book IV, chapter XIX, who counts the peoples of Aquitaine as more than thirteen, and in Mela, book III, chapter I. In Ptolemy they are the Αὔσκιοι [Auskioi], whose city Αὔσκυσε [Auskyse] is today Auch, of which more in its place. They are the Ausci of the Itinerary Table, and the Ausciensis of Sidonius, book VII, letter VI. The Novempopuli, of whom a little before, are often counted together with them. "The Ausci," says Ammianus, "commend the Novempopuli." So Ausonius, in the Professors, of Staphylius, a citizen of Auch:

units.la: Te Staphyli genitum sterpe Novempopulis.
units.tr: "You, Staphylius, born of the Novempopulan stock."

units.la: Civitas Ausciorum Notitiæ Provinciarum in Aquitania Tertia Novempopulania vel Octava Viennensi, Hodie L'Archevêsché d'Auch, unde Auscitensis Archiepiscopus. Imperite facit Vulgus Ecclesiasticum, cum Auxitanus vocatur; & ineptos te probant, qui Augusta Ausorum Incolas nuncupant Auxitanos. Veterum Ausiorum Tractus hodie Armagnac fere appellatur. Tarbelli Cæsaris extremo libro iii. de Bello Gallico, putant quidam esse nunc temporis Tarsa Vrbs Incolas in Aquitania Provincia. Lactora alias nominantur in Itineraria Tabula: Lactorates vel Lactoratum Civitatem habet eadem Notitia in Aquitania in Novempopulania, vel Octava Viennensi. Hodie L'Evêsché de Lactoure. Lactorate sium Civitatis meminit Inscriptio, quæ in eadem Vrbe extat: PRO. SALVTE. IMP. M. ANTON. GORDIANI PII. FEL. AVG. ET. SABINÆ. TRANQVILLINÆ AVG. TOTIVSQVE. DOMVS. DIVINÆ. PROQVE STATV. CIVITATIS. LACTORATEN. TAVROPOLIVM FECIT. ORDO. LACT. DOMINO. NOSTRO. GORDIANO AVG. II. ET. POMPEIANO. COS. II. ID DEC. CVRANTIB. M. EROTIO. FESTO ET. M. ELARINIO. CARO. SACERD. TRAIANIO NVNDINIO
units.tr: The city of the Ausci is in the Notitia of the Provinces, in Aquitaine Third, Novempopulania, or the Eighth Viennensis. Today it is the archbishopric of Auch, whence the Archbishop of Auch. The common churchmen unskilfully call it Auxitanus, and those who call the inhabitants of Augusta of the Ausci Auxitani show themselves ignorant. The region of the ancient Ausci is now commonly called Armagnac. Some think that the Tarbelli of Caesar, at the end of book III of the Gallic War, are today the town of Tarsa in the province of Aquitaine. Lactora is named otherwise in the Itinerary Table. The Notitia has the Lactorates, or the city of Lactoratum, in Aquitaine, in Novempopulania or the Eighth Viennensis. Today it is the bishopric of Lactoure. An inscription still extant in the same city mentions the state of the Lactoratensian city: "For the safety of the emperor Marcus Antonius Gordianus Pius Felix Augustus, and of Sabina Tranquillina Augusta, and of the whole divine house, and for the welfare of the city of the Lactoratenses, the order of Lactora made a taurobolium to our lord Gordian Augustus for the second time, and to Pompeianus, consul for the second time, on the Ides of December, under the care of M. Erotius Festus and M. Elarinius Carus, priests; Traianius Nundinius."

units.la: Bigerrones apud Cæsarem sunt, qui Bigerri Plinio lib. iv. cap. xix, & Pontio Paullino ad Ausonium scribenti Epistola i. versu cviii, colque Pelliti indigetanti, quod ob intentum ius in locis frigus Pelibus ovium, Caprarum, aliarumque Bestiarum sic, ut hodieque, tegerent. Bigerrani nominantur Ausonio. Hinc Bigerricus Ager, Sidonio libro viii. I pist xii; & B.gerrana Patria, Ausonio Epist.xiiii. ad Paullinum. Civitas Tarba, ubi Cæsium Begorra, in Notitia Provinciarum: hodie, L'Evesché de Tarbe de Bigorre; La Comte de Bigorre De Tarba Bigerronum alibi. Nitiobriges apud Cæsarem lib. vii non uno loco; hodie Le Pais & Senechaussée d'Agenois. In Plinio male excusum, Auto roges Tarnegamne diserati à Tolosis: Legendum enim, Nitiobriges Tarnæ Amne &c. Vide Scaligerum in Auson. Nitiobroges in Itineraria Peutingeri Tabula procul ponuntur ab suis Sedibus xv. Long. iv. Lat. prope Augustobanam Tru atlium; quum scribere oportuisset v. Long.vii. Lat. supra Aginnum. Distinctionem, qua in eadem Tabula, docendi commodiusque quid & certiore digito indicandi gratia, utor, aperio in Epistola ad Lectorem. Nitiobrigum Civitas Agennum, de qua postea. Ridenda scribit ad me Iosephus Scaliger, quæ hactenus omnes de his delirarunt; quorum alii sunt illi Marlianus & Poldus. Mompelier, cuiusq; Territorium esse dicunt; qui locus sex dierum itinere distat ab Nitiobrigibus: alii Engolismæ nominant; alii jubent pro Aginno legendum esse Aegisinates: Et, inquit Vir Magnus, quo non p o cpit audax infinita? Nitiobrigum Rex nominatur in Ephemeridibus Belli Gallici lib. vii. Theutomatus, cujus Pater ab S. P. Q. R. Amicus fuerat appellatus. Qui Convenæ Plinio lib.iii. cap.iv, & Sidonio lib. vii. Epist. vi; in Ptolemæi libris vitiose dicuntur Κονανοὶ: Legendum enim Κονανοὶ. Eleganter Strabo lib. iv. τῶν τ Κονανῶν, ἐπὶ ἰσὶ Συγκλυδῶν. Sic enim emendat eruditissimus Casaubonus. Explicat Strabo quid Latinorum Convenæ sint Græcis: Συγκλυδες scilicet ἀδρωτεῖ. Exturbati sunt hi Convenæ ex Doctissimo illo Glossario, impuris Magistrellulorum manibus non terendo. Scribitur enim, Συγκλυδες ....... Reponendi Convenæ. Civitas Convenæ in Notitia, L'Evesché de Comminges. Metropolis Lugdunum Convenarum, de quo infra. Elusates, ut Plinio & Claudiano vocantur, apud Cæsarem sub finem lib. iii. corrupte in quibusdam Codicibus Fluffates & Flufiates scribuntur: Elufani Sidonio sunt lib. vii. Epist. vi: Elufatium (mendose in quibusdam Libris Illofatscum) Civitas in Provinciarum Libello, Aquitania iii, Le Pau d'Eufe en Gascogne. De ipsa Vrbe Elfi vel Fusa paullo post. Qui Fluffates legebant, ut scribit ad me Nobilissimus Vir Iosephus Scaliger, dicebant (in eorum numero video Cœnalem & Belleforestium) esse Comitatum de Fuxo; & hoc stupore suo persuaserunt illustri Viro nomen de Foix in Flusfatem recudere; quo nihil absurdius. Aliud enim est Franciscus de Fluffa; aliud, Franciscus Fluffas. Nam de Fluffa esset verum cognomen Familiae; sed Fluffas esset nomen Nationis. Itaque Franciscus Fluffas esset natione Fluffas, non de Familia de Fluffa. Sed Fluffa non est Foix. Nam id esset Foxium, aut aliud quidvis potius, quam Fusca Gartes, quorum Cæsar meminit, haud procul Nitiobrigibus habitasse notat Orontius, quum eos in sua Galliæ Tabula locet in Agro, qui hodie Aginnensium. Certe Garites non idem sunt cum Aginnensibus. Garites enim Cæsar ponit in sua Aquitania, ultra Garumnam: Nitiobriges, quorum Caput Aginnum, extra suam constituit Aquitaniam, cis Garumnam, in Celtica. Marcianus Lactoratense oppidum, Lactoure, Garitibus adsignat. Finiam antiquas huius Tractus Gentes in Cocosatibus Cæsaris; quos Plinius Cocosates vocat, Sex-signanos cognominans; qui quo loco fuerint, nondum didici.
units.tr: The Bigerriones are in Caesar, and are the Bigerri of Pliny, book IV, chapter XIX, and of Pontius Paulinus writing to Ausonius, letter I, verse 108, who call them the Pelliti, because on account of the sharp cold of their country they covered themselves with the skins of sheep, goats and other beasts, as they still do today. Ausonius names them Bigerrani. Hence the Bigerrican field in Sidonius, book VIII, letter XII, and the Bigerrane homeland in Ausonius, letter XIV to Paulinus. The city of Tarba, where Caesium Begorra is, is in the Notitia of the Provinces; today it is the bishopric of Tarbes de Bigorre, and the County of Bigorre. Elsewhere it is called Tarba of the Bigerriones. The Nitiobriges are in Caesar, book VII, in many places; today they are Le Pays and Sénéchaussée d'Agenois. In Pliny the text is badly printed, "Auto roges Tarnegamne diserati à Tolosis"; one should read it as referring to the Nitiobriges by the river Tarn, and so on. See Scaliger on Ausonius. The Nitiobroges are placed in the Peutinger Table far from their seats, at 15 degrees of longitude and 4 of latitude, near Augustobona Tricastinorum, whereas they should have been written at 5 degrees of longitude and 7 of latitude, above Aginnum. I explain the distinction used in that same table, which I employ for the sake of teaching and of pointing out things more clearly and with a more certain finger, in the letter to the reader. The city of the Nitiobriges is Agennum, of which later. Joseph Scaliger writes to me that all who have talked about these people until now have raved absurdly, and laughable things they are. Among them are Marlianus and Poldus, who say that Montpellier and its territory belonged to them, though that place is six days' journey from the Nitiobriges; others name Angoulême; others order that for Aginnum we should read Aegisinates. "And," says that great man, "what does audacity not attempt, when it is unlimited?" The king of the Nitiobriges is named in the Commentaries of the Gallic War, book VII, as Teutomatus, whose father had been called a friend by the Senate and People of Rome. The Convenae, in Pliny, book III, chapter IV, and in Sidonius, book VII, letter VI, are wrongly called Κονανοὶ [Konanoi] in the books of Ptolemy; one should read Κονανοὶ [Konanoi] ... Strabo, book IV, elegantly: "τῶν Κονανῶν, ἐπὶ ἰσὶ Συγκλυδῶν" ["of the Konanoi, who are the Synklydoi"]. So the most learned Casaubon emends it. Strabo explains what the Convenae of the Latins are to the Greeks: the Synklydes, that is, "washed-up" people. These Convenae were thrown out of that most learned glossary by the impure hands of little schoolmasters, who should not be allowed to mangle it. For it is written "Συγκλυδες" ... The Convenae must be restored. The city of the Convenae is in the Notitia; today it is the bishopric of Comminges. Its metropolis is Lugdunum of the Convenae, of which below. The Elusates, as they are called in Pliny and Claudian, are written in some manuscripts of Caesar, near the end of book III, corruptly as Fluffates and Flufiates. In Sidonius, book VII, letter VI, they are the Elufani. The city Elusatium (wrongly in some books Illofatscum) is in the Provincial Libellus, Aquitaine III; it is Le Pau d'Eufe en Gascogne. Of the city itself, Elusa or Fusa, a little later. Those who read Fluffates, as Joseph Scaliger writes to me, said (among them I see Cœnalis and Belleforest) that it was the County of Foix; and by this absurdity they persuaded that illustrious man to reprint the name "de Foix" as "Flusfatem," nothing more absurd. For "Franciscus de Fluffa" is one thing, and "Franciscus Fluffas" another. "De Fluffa" would be the true surname of a family, but "Fluffas" would be the name of a nation. So "Franciscus Fluffas" would be "of the nation Fluffas," not "of the family de Fluffa." But Fluffa is not Foix; for that would be Foxium, or anything else rather than Fusca. The Garites, whom Caesar mentions, dwelt not far from the Nitiobriges, as Orontius notes, when he places them in his map of Gaul in the district which today belongs to the Agenais. Certainly the Garites are not the same as the Aginnenses. For Caesar places the Garites in his Aquitaine, beyond the Garonne; he places the Nitiobriges, whose head is Aginnum, outside his Aquitaine, on this side of the Garonne, in Celtica. Marcianus assigns the town of Lactora, Lactoure, to the Garites. I shall end the ancient peoples of this tract with the Cocosates of Caesar, whom Pliny calls Cocosates, adding the surname Sexsignani. Where they were I have not yet learned.

units.la: Et haec de antiquis Vasconum nostræ Populis. Eiusdem porro, ut hodie considerari solet, Partes Garumnæ conjacent quædam ultra tantum Flumen, ut Ager cum Armaniacensi, tum Bigerronum, quædam confuse ultra citraque, ut Aginnensi Senescallia, Albreti Ducatus & Comitatus Convenarum. Armaniacensis mihi dicitur, qui vulgo Armagnac, cuius Limites plurimum se extendunt. Latitudo eius ab opido Lactoratensium Nogerentium usque: Longitudo minor est, Magnaco ad Bigerrones usque. Sunt qui putant memoriam in eo servari Arecomicorum. Ego nihil hic volo affirmare. Comitatus titulo est insignis. Continet duas Diœceses, Auscensem & Lactoratensem. Auscensis ab Angusta Auscorum, quae totius Novempopulania sive Vasconiae Metropolis. Sic Ptolemæo dicitur Galliæ Aquitanicæ Vrbs, quæ vulgo nunc Auch: Civitas Auscium Veteri Itinerario à Burdigala Hierosolymas; Auscensis Vrbs Gregorio Turonensi lib. x. cap. xxii: Auscium & Civitas Auscium Martyrologio Romano Vsuardoque Kalend. Mai. Hinc Episcopus Auscensis Gregorio Turonensi lib. viii, cap. xxii. Oppidum est ad Gersum Fluvium, Rupi inædificatum, aditu difficile. Pulcherrimum ibi Templum, Deiparæ Virgini consecratum, structura fastuosum. Visuntur ibi multa Antiquitatum Monimenta. Partim Regem Franciæ, partim Civitatis Præsulem Dominos agnoscit. Lactoratensis ab Opido, quod vulgo Lactoure: Lactura Antonino; Lacerra corruptius Itinerariæ Tabulæ: Lactorum Civitatem habet Goltzius ex Veteri Inscriptione in suo Thesauro, ut & Lactorium & Lactorum. In opido tunc Lactoratensi duo Lapides leguntur, in uno propugnaculorum; his verbis concepti: MATRI. DEVM POMP. PHILVMENE Q. PRIMA. LECTOR TAVROBOLIVM FECIT Ibidem PRO. SALVTE. IMP. ANTONINI. GORDIANI PII. FEL. AVG. TOTIVSQVE. DOMVS. DIVINÆ PROQVE. STATV. CIVIT. LACTOR. TAV ROBOLIVM. FECIT. ORDO. LACT. D. N. GORDIANO. II. ET. POMPEIANO. COS VI. ID. DEC. CVRANTIB. M. EROTIO ET. FESTO. CANINIO. SACERD
units.tr: These are the ancient peoples of our Vasconia. Of the same region, as is usually considered today, some parts lie beyond the Garonne only: the Ager with the Armaniacensi territory, and the Bigerronum territory. Others lie confusedly on both sides of the river, such as the Aginnensi Senescallia, Albreti Ducatus (the seneschalsy of Agen and the duchy of Albret) and the Comitatus Convenarum (the county of Comminges). I am told that the Armaniacensis is what is commonly called Armagnac, and its limits extend widely. Its breadth runs from the town of Lectoure to Nogaro; its length is less, from Magnac to the Bigerrones. Some think the memory of the Arecomici is preserved in it, but I do not wish to affirm anything here. The county is distinguished by its title. It contains two dioceses, Auscensem (Auch) and Lactoratensem (Lectoure). The Auscensis diocese takes its name from Angusta Auscorum, which is the metropolis of all Novempopulania, or Gascony. Ptolemy calls it a city of Aquitanian Gaul, and it is now commonly called Auch: Civitas Auscium in the old Itinerary from Bordeaux to Jerusalem; Auscensis Vrbs in Gregory of Tours, book 10, chapter 22; Auscium and Civitas Auscium in the Roman Martyrology and in Usuard, under 1 May. Hence the Episcopus Auscensis in Gregory of Tours, book 8, chapter 22. It is a town on the river Gers, built on a rock and hard to approach. There is a very beautiful temple there, dedicated to the Virgin Mother of God, splendid in its structure. Many monuments of antiquity are to be seen there. The town acknowledges the King of France in part and the bishop of the city in part as its lords. The Lactoratensis diocese takes its name from the town now commonly called Lactoure: Lactura in Antoninus; Lacerra is a more corrupt form in the Itinerary Table. Goltzius, in his Thesaurus, has Lactorum Civitatem from an ancient inscription, as well as Lactorium and Lactorum. In the town of Lectoure at that time two stones are read. On one, on a bastion, the following words are inscribed: "To the Mother of the gods. Pompeia Philumene; Q. Prima, reader, made the taurobolium." And there, on the other: "For the health of the Emperor Antoninus Gordianus Pius Felix Augustus and of his whole divine house, and for the welfare of the city of Lactora, the taurobolium was made by the order of Lactora, in the consulship of our lord Gordianus II and Pompeianus, on the sixth day before the Ides of December, under the curators M. Erotius and Festus Caninius, priest..."

units.la: Qui putant Lactoratium vel Lasioratium dici in Notitia Provinciarum, falluntur. Sunt enim, ut cum Grammaticis loquar, Genitivi, quorum Recti Lactorates, vel Lastorates, si rectâ in hac voce scriptura. Oppidum est in fastigio Montis, ubi multa Antiquitatis vestigia. Arcem habet, quam ab Romanis volunt factam. Sunt item alia Armaniacensis Dioecesis Opida, inter quae quod vulgo L'Isle Jordain, ubi Tribunal Senescalli. Fuit quidem parvus Comitatus, sed hodie vix memoria superest, ut mihi affirmat V. N. Iosephus Scaliger. Bigerrones vel Bigerri, vulgo Le Comté de Bigorre, Regionem possident inter Benearnenses & Convenas, Coelo Soloque asperam, ventosam, frigidam, Vini interacem: ad Pyrenaeos Montes, quorum magna pars huic Comitatui est subjecta, ab Montibus, qui vernacule d'Aure nominantur usque ad Saltum Pyrenaeum; vulgo du Saule) colque qui d'Aspe dicuntur, Benearnensium Ditionis. Bigerriones clati scribuntur ingenii, Armisediti, celeres ad aliquid adgrediundum, egregie simulantes, inhumani, aspeni, ingratiores. Opidani urbaniores. Nobilitas, quae hic frequens, animosa, humana, cultus moribus. Civitas Turba, ubi Castrum Begorra. Sic vocatur in Notitia Provinciarum, ut minores consulantur Codices. Nam male excusum est, Tursa & Turba; vitiosissime etiam in aliis Tursambua Tranugorra. Vulgo Turbe de Begorre, aut Bigorre, ubi Sedes Episcopalis, quae in hoc Comitatu unica, sub Metropoli Auscensi. Marlianus infamat, ut scribit ad me Ioseph. Scaliger, qui ait ibi hanc Tursam esse & Castrum Begorram, ubi est Episcopatus Bitterensis Provinciae Narbonensis; quae sententia non est sobrii capitis. Begorram Bigerronum Civitatem habet Gregorius Turonensis. Olim vicus erat, ut monet Scaliger, unde & Vicus Aquensis dicti. Id patet ex egregia Inscriptione: NVMINI. AVGVSTI SACRVM SECVNDVS. SEMBEDO NIS. FIL. NOMINE VICANORVM. AQVEN SIVM. ET. SVO. POSVIT
units.tr: Those who think Lactoratium or Lasioratium is named in the Notitia of the Provinces are mistaken. For these are, to speak with the grammarians, genitives, whose nominatives are Lactorates or Lastorates, if the spelling of this word is right. The town lies on the summit of a mountain, where there are many traces of antiquity. It has a citadel, which they say was built by the Romans. There are also other towns in the diocese of Armagnac, among them what is commonly called L'Isle-Jourdain, where the tribunal of the seneschal sits. There was indeed a small county there, but today hardly any memory of it survives, as my venerable friend Joseph Scaliger assures me. The Bigerrones or Bigerri, commonly called the County of Bigorre, hold a region between the Benearnenses and the Convenae, harsh in climate and soil, windy, cold, and short of wine. It reaches to the Pyrenees, a large part of whose mountains is subject to this county, from the mountains called in the vernacular d'Aure as far as the Pyrenean pass (commonly du Saule), and also the mountains called d'Aspe, which belong to the lordship of the Benearnenses. The Bigerriones are described as proud in spirit, quick to take up any undertaking, skilled at dissimulation, unkind, rough, and ungrateful. The townspeople are more courteous. The nobility here is numerous, spirited, humane, and refined in manners. The city is Turba, where the castle of Begorra stands. It is so called in the Notitia of the Provinces, so that the smaller codices may be consulted; for it is badly printed as Tursa and Turba, and even more faultily as Tursambua or Tranugorra in other editions. It is commonly called Turbe de Begorre, or Bigorre, where the episcopal see is, the only one in this county, under the metropolis of Auch. Marlianus is wrong, as Joseph Scaliger writes to me, when he says that Tursa is here and that the castle of Begorra is where the bishopric of Béziers in the province of Narbonne is; that opinion is not that of a sober mind. Gregory of Tours calls Begorra the city of the Bigerrones. In former times it was a village, as Scaliger points out, whence it was also called the village of Aquae. This is clear from a fine inscription: "Sacred to the divinity of Augustus. Secundus, son of Sembedo, in the name of the villagers of Aquae and in his own name, set this up."

units.la: In Finibus Bigerronum sunt Comitatus, qui vulgo Gaure & Fflrac. Agennensis Senescalsia, vulgo La Senescaussée d'Agenois, Sedes quondam Nitiobrigum. His ad Orientem continales sunt Cadurci, ad Septemtrionem Petrocorii, qua parte Agennensis excurrunt Bironium usque, Petrocoriorum Opidum: ad Occidentem Vasconnes occurrunt cum Garumna; a quo & ad Meridiem lambuntur. Continet duos Episcopatus, nempe citra Garumnam, Aginnum Nitiobrigum; ultra Garumnam, Condomium. Aginnum, vernacule Agen. Aginnum Ptolemaeo lib. ii. cap. vii; Aginnum Antonio Epist. xxiii, Antonino, & Itinerariae Peutingeri Tabulae; Aginnum, Bedae in Martyrolog. v. Eid. Iunij, Adoni, & aliis Agennum in Libro Provinciarum apud Hieronymum item de Claris Scriptoribus, & Honorium, qui ejus Episcopum Phoebadium memorat: Agennensis Urbs Gregorio Turonensi lib. i. cap. cv. de Mirac. Agzinum Bedae, varianti in scriptura, Pridie Non. Oct. & Agaunum eidem xiii. Kal. Novembr. Sanctissima Vocis Scriptura, Aginnum. Opidum venerandae Antiquitatis, in Garumnae ripa situm, duodeviginti ab Metropoli Burdigalensi leucis, totius Aquitaniae ditissimum. Sedes Senescalli, cujus iurisdictio, excepto Pictavienii, totius Aquitaniae latissima. Ius inde petunt Portus D. Mariae, Villa Nova (Ville Neuve d'Agenois, ad Lothum, quae & speciatim hujus Tractus partem constituit, Arcem habens) Hautefaya, Clairacum, Marmanda, Fanum Magnae Fidei consecratum, Fay la grande, Clavis; & alia ad Garumnam opida. Aginnum vel eo nomine magnum, quod Magnus ille Iosephus Scaliger ejus primum Solo instituerit, ejusque Aerem primum hauserit. Condomium, vulgo La Senescaussée de Condomois. Hoc peculiari nomine vocari solet Vasconia. Quemadmodum enim Africa dicitur tota illa Magna Continens, quae patet ab Nilo ad Gades, & tamen in ea erat Provincia, quae peculiariter appellabatur Africa, in qua Karthago: ita Vasconia quidem nominatur amplissima illa Regio, quae olim dicta fuit Novempopulania; sed stricte Vasconia quoque nuncupatur in ea Episcopatus Condomiensis. Itaque Senescallus Aginnensis vocat se Senescallum Aginnensium & Vasconia, id est, Condomy. Quae appellatio vetus est. Nam temporibus Pipini Pagus Aginnensis citra Garumnam & ultra Garumnam dicebatur. Itaque sub Pipino in Vetustissimis Annalibus refertur, pluisse frumento in Pago Aginnense ultra Garumnam, id est in ea Regione, quae proprie Vasconia, in qua Condomum: vulgo Condom; opidum amplum in Territorio sterili, undique fere Collibus, qui Vineis consiti, cinctum; extra Viam regiam situm, haud procul Baisa Fluvio. Sedem præbet non solum Episcopatui Novo, quem delibatum dixi supra de Aginnensi; verum etiam Senefchallix, jus dicenti Opidis, quæ Indigenis, Valence ad Eusim, Lairac ad Garumnam, La-Romeo, Aton-Real, & aliis. Familiæ sunt hic illustres non paucæ. Vicecomites novimus hic Fifmaconos, Gourdonos, Forcaos, & Monluctos. Ducatus Allebret, La Duché d'Allebret, nomen accepit amplissimum ab opidulo, quod vulgo Allebret, in Syrtibus Lapurdensibus, quas Landas vocant. Institutus est ante annos non multos, compositus ex mutilatione Senefchalliarum Aginnensis, Armaniacensi, & Vasatensis; adeo ut de eo dicere liceat, quod de Constantinopoli Hieronymus, eam nuditate omnium Civitatum constructam fuisse. Caput Ducatus est Neracum, oppidum præclarum. Avorum nostrorum memoria Ioannes Alani F. Dynastia Allebretanus, ducta Katharina Gastonis F. Navarræ Regnum cum ea Dotem accepit: hujus ex Filio Henrico Neptis fuit Isaanna Allebretana, Navarræ Regina, Mater Henrici iv, Christianissimi Franciæ Navarræque Regis. Convenarum Comitatus, La Comté de Comminges: Vulgo Latinorum Cominghia. Huius Tractus Incolæ Primi Aquitanorum Christianæ Militiæ nomen dedisse scribuntur, multa indigna perpessi ab Christiani nominis Hostibus. Dividitur Convenarum Ager in Superiorem & Inferiorem, totusque Montibus attollitur. Gentis Caput Lugdunum Convenarum; Ἀργεντοράτα Κονβεναῶν (legendum Κονυεναῶν) Ptolemæo & Strabonı lib. iv; Lugdunum simpliciter Antonino, in Itinere ab Aginno ad hoc opidum: quod quum per multos annos summopere floruisset, tandem ab irato Guntchrahni Regis exercitu fuit diruturn, anno 1ƆLXXXIV, Indictione 11: ex cujus reliquiis Fanum S. Bertrandi, ubi hodie Sedes est Episcopalis, in Valle Capraria fuit constructum. Vetustatem & Splendorem ejus Civitatis facile testantur Monimenta & Epigraphæ quamplurimæ, quæ ibi hodie exstant. Coluerunt inter alios Deos Lugdunenses Convenæ, aliique forte Conregionales, Abelionem: de quo quidam ibi Lapides, ut alibi vidimus, ubi de Diis Gallorum. Quid in Inscriptione, quæ Romæ legitur in ædibus Mellinorum ad Agonem, sit Convena Aquitania, alij videant. Ea sic habet: D. M. VALERIÆ. IVSTINÆ NATA CONVENA AQVITANIA VIXIT. ANNOS. XXI IVN. VALERIANVS MIL. COH. III. PR 7. FELICIS. CONS. P. M. F.
units.tr: Within the borders of the Bigerrones are the counties commonly called Gaure and Fezensac. The seneschalsy of Agen, commonly the Senescaussée d'Agenois, was once the seat of the Nitiobriges. Adjoining it to the east are the Cadurci; to the north the Petrocorii, where the Agen territory runs out as far as Bironium, a town of the Petrocorii; to the west the Vasconnes meet it at the Garonne, by which it is also washed to the south. It contains two bishoprics: on this side of the Garonne, Agen, the town of the Nitiobriges; beyond the Garonne, Condom. Agen, in the vernacular Agen. Ptolemy calls it Aginnum, book 2, chapter 7; Antonine in Epistle 23 calls it Aginnum, as do Antoninus and the Itinerary Table of Peutinger; Bede in his Martyrology under 5 June, and Adon, call it Aginnum, and in the Book of Provinces, in Jerome's De viris illustribus, and in Honorius, who names its bishop Phoebadius, it is Agennum. Gregory of Tours, book 1, chapter 105, On Miracles, calls it the city of Agenna. Bede has the variant spelling Agzinum on the day before the Nones of October, and Agaunum on the same author's 13th day before the Kalends of November. The most sacred form of the name is Aginnum. It is a town of venerable antiquity, situated on the bank of the Garonne, eighteen leagues from the metropolis of Bordeaux, the richest of all Aquitaine. It is the seat of the seneschal, whose jurisdiction, apart from Poitiers, is the widest in all Aquitaine. Those who seek justice there include Port-Sainte-Marie, Villeneuve (Ville Neuve d'Agenois, on the Lot, which also forms a particular part of this district and has a citadel), Hautefage, Clairac, Marmande, the shrine of Our Lady of Great Faith, Fayl-la-Grande, Clairac, and other towns along the Garonne. Agen is great even for this reason, that the great Joseph Scaliger first established its soil and first breathed its air. Condom, commonly the Senescaussée de Condomois. This is the particular name by which Vasconia is usually called. For just as Africa is the name of the whole great continent that stretches from the Nile to Cadiz, and yet within it there was a province specially called Africa, in which Carthage lay, so Vasconia is the name of that very wide region which was formerly called Novempopulania; but strictly speaking Vasconia is also the name given to the bishopric of Condom within it. And so the seneschal of Agen calls himself seneschal of the Agenais and of Vasconia, that is, of Condom. This designation is old. For in the times of Pepin the district was called Agen on both sides of the Garonne. Hence in the very ancient Annals under Pepin it is recorded that it rained wheat in the district of Agen beyond the Garonne, that is, in that region which is properly Vasconia, in which Condom lies. Condom, commonly Condom, is a large town in a barren territory, surrounded almost everywhere by hills planted with vines; it lies off the royal highway, not far from the river Baïse. It is the seat not only of the new bishopric, which I said above was carved out of the Agen diocese, but also of the seneschalsy, which administers justice for the towns that the natives call Valence-sur-Baïse, Lectoure on the Garonne, La Romieu, Aton-Réal, and others. There are not a few illustrious families here. We know of the viscounts of Fimarcon, Gourdon, Forcas, and Montluc. The duchy of Albret, La Duché d'Allebret, has taken its very wide name from a small town, commonly called Albret, in the Lapurdensian marshes, which they call the Landes. It was established not many years ago, put together from the mutilation of the seneschalsies of Agen, Armagnac, and Vasatensis, so that one may say of it what Jerome said of Constantinople, that it was built from the nakedness of all the cities. The capital of the duchy is Nérac, a famous town. In the memory of our grandfathers, John of Albret, son of Alan, lord of Albret, having married Catherine, daughter of Gaston, received the kingdom of Navarre as her dowry. Of his son Henry, Isabella of Albret, queen of Navarre, was the granddaughter, mother of Henry IV, most Christian king of France and Navarre. The county of Comminges, La Comté de Comminges, is in Latin called Cominghia by the vulgar. The inhabitants of this district are said to have first given the name of Christian Militia to the Aquitanians, having suffered many indignities from the enemies of the Christian name. The Convenae territory is divided into Upper and Lower, and the whole of it is raised up by mountains. The capital of the people is Lugdunum Convenarum, which Ptolemy and Strabo, book 4, call Argentorate of the Convenae (the reading should be Convenae). Antoninus simply calls it Lugdunum, on the route from Agen to this town. Though for many years it had flourished greatly, it was finally to be destroyed by the angry army of King Guntram in the year 585, Indiction 11. From its remains the shrine of St Bertrand was built in the Valley of the Goats, where the episcopal see is today. The antiquity and splendour of this city are easily attested by the many monuments and inscriptions that still survive there. Among other gods, the Convenae of Lyon, and perhaps other neighbours, worshipped Abellio, concerning whom there are certain stones there, as we have seen elsewhere, where we treat of the gods of the Gauls. What the inscription read at Rome in the house of the Mellini near the Agonalia means by "Convena Aquitania", let others consider. It reads as follows: "To the gods of the dead. Valeria Justina, born a Convenan of Aquitaine, lived 21 years. June. Valerianus, soldier of the third cohort of the praetorians, to his well-deserving wife, in the consulship of Felix and Consul, set this up."

units.la: Vasconiæ priusquam egrediar, addam tria verba de Elusatium Agro, qui vulgo Le Pais d'Eufe en Gascoigne. Ejus Metropolis Elusa. Sic dicitur Ammiano Marcellino lib. xv, & Itinerario, quod Burdigala ducit Hierosolymas; quæ Paullino Epistola ad Severum vi. Elusa. Ammiani verba, quod corruptiora, adscribam: In Narbonensi Elusa, & Narbo, & Tolosa, & principatum urbium tenent: Viennensis Civitatum exsultat decore multarum: quibus potiores sunt Vienna ipsa & Arelate & Valentia, quibus Massilia jungitur. Pro Elusa vulgati Codices habebant Clusa. Hinc Elusana Plebs apud Sulpitium Severum Historiæ Sacræ lib. ii. Fuisse videtur olim Episcopatus. Labau Elusensis Episcopus nominatur Gregorio Turonensi lib. viii. cap. xxii.
units.tr: Before I leave Vasconia, I will add a few words about the Elusatium Agro, commonly called Le Pais d'Eufe en Gascoigne. Its metropolis is Elusa. So Ammianus Marcellinus calls it in book xv, and so does the Itinerary that runs from Burdigala to Jerusalem; Paulinus also names it in his Letter to Severus 6, Elusa. I will transcribe Ammianus's words, though they are rather corrupt: In Narbonensi Elusa, & Narbo, & Tolosa, & principatum urbium tenent: Viennensis Civitatum exsultat decore multarum: quibus potiores sunt Vienna ipsa & Arelate & Valentia, quibus Massilia jungitur. The printed editions, however, read Clusa where the manuscripts have Elusa. Hence the Elusana Plebs in Sulpicius Severus, Sacred History book ii. It seems to have been an episcopal see once: Labau Elusensis Episcopus is named by Gregory of Tours, book viii, chapter 22.

units.la: CAP. XXXIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXIX.

units.la: Provincia.
units.tr: Provence.

units.la: PROVINCIAS Parlamentis subjectas Accessorijs, Parisiensequae illud ad Occidentem Meridiemque quasi circumeuntibus, quanta fieri potuit industria perlustravi: sequuntur jamnunc Regiones, quae reliquis parent Tribunalibus, Orientaliora ejusdem Parisiensis Latera velut claudentibus. Ea sunt Aquense, Gratianopolitanum, Diniensis. Aquensis Iurisdictioni obtemperat Provincia.
units.tr: I have traveled through the PROVINCES subject to the Parlements, along with their dependencies, as diligently as I could, going round the Parisian region toward the west and south. Now follow the regions that obey the remaining courts, lying along the more eastern flank of that same Parisian region. They are the Aix, Grenoble, and Digne regions. Aix submits to the jurisdiction of Provence.

units.la: Vnde & qua occasione Provinciae nomen inditum praestantissimo huic Galliarum Tractui, etiam ultra Rodanum ad Garumnam usque, petendum est ex Capite huius libri xvi; ubi omnia Romanorum contra Veteres Gallos Bella paucis commemorantur. Narbonensis enim Gallia ab Romanis in Provincia formam multis ante Christum natum annis redacta, hodieque illud impositae quondam conditionis nomen mordicus in exigua sui portione, in qua Massilia & Aqua Sextia, retinet, κατ' ἐξοχὴν quasi & αὐτονομαστικῶς, utque ostenderet se Primam, non quidem ordine, sed dignitate inter omnes Imperij Romani fuisse Provincias. Est enim totus ille Narbonensis Ager pars totius Franciae praestantissima. Paucis Plinius lib. iii. cap. iv, Agrorum cultu; Virorum Morumque dignatione, amplitudine opum nulls Provinciarum post ferenda, breviterque Italia verius, quam Provincia. Provincia sane, de qua mihi sermo, praeter Segetes, Fructus profert, non solicita cultura, nobilissimos. Vvarum Passarum Ficuumque tanta hic Copia, ut potiori Europae sufficiat. Ros. Marinus, Myrtus, Iuniperi Baccae, aliaque id genus larga hic manu ab Natura proveniunt. Castaneae nusquam majores. Mala Citria, Cydonia, Granata: item Crocus, Oryza, similiaque pleno ibidem cornu funduntur. Vites generosissima dant Vina. Solum denique passim gratum, ferax, benignum: Coelum mite, clemens, & valde purgatum. Conjacet Provincia ad Septemtrionem Delphinatus, Montium interpositu Velaxorum, qui vulgo Velaye, intercursuque magnam partem Druentij Fluminis; Orientale ejus Latus claudunt & Alpes, & Varus Fluvius, cujus sinistrae Ripae adsidet Nicaea, Italiae hic principium; qua Meridies est, ab Gallico pultatur Mari: Occidentalis illi Limes partim Araufiorum Principatus & Avenionensis vel Venissae Comitatus, hujus quondam Partes. Francorumque Ditionis, nunc autem aliorum Principum; partim Rodanus, integer, Lugduno Arelatem usque, ad Languedokij Parlamenti Iurisdictiones, ut antea dixi, spectans.
units.tr: Where and by what occasion the name Provence was given to this outstanding tract of Gaul, reaching beyond the Rhône as far as the Garonne, must be sought in chapter 16 of this book, where all the Roman wars against the ancient Gauls are briefly recounted. For Narbonensis Gaul, reduced by the Romans into the form of a province many years before Christ's birth, still holds fast, in a small part of itself where Marseille and Aquae Sextiae lie, to the name of that former condition, kat' exochēn [κατ' ἐξοχὴν], as it were, and autonomastikōs [αὐτονομαστικῶς], so that it showed itself to be the first of all the provinces of the Roman Empire, not in rank but in dignity. For that whole Narbonese territory is the most excellent part of all France. Pliny, briefly, in book 3, chapter 4: for the cultivation of its fields, for the dignity of its men and customs, and for the abundance of its wealth, it is to be placed before no other province, and it is more truly to be called Italy than a province. The Province of which I am speaking, indeed, yields, besides grain, very noble fruits without anxious cultivation: here there is such a supply of raisins, figs, and dates that it suffices for the greater part of Europe. Rosemary, myrtle, juniper berries, and other things of this kind are produced here by nature with a generous hand. Chestnuts are nowhere larger. Citrons, quinces, and pomegranates, and likewise saffron, rice, and similar things, are poured out here from a full horn of plenty. The vines give the most excellent wines. The soil everywhere is pleasant, fertile, and kindly; the sky is mild, gentle, and very clear. The Province lies to the north adjoining Dauphiné, with the Vaucluse mountains, commonly called Velaye, lying between, and for a great part the River Durance running through. Its eastern side is bounded by the Alps and the River Var, on whose left bank sits Nice, the beginning of Italy here. On the south it is struck by the Gallic sea. Its western boundary is partly the principality of Orange and the county of Avignon or Venaissin, which were once parts of this province but are now under the rule of the French or of other princes, and partly the Rhône, wholly from Lyon to Arles, belonging, as I said before, to the jurisdictions of the Parlement of Languedoc.

units.la: Habitarunt hic olim Sahi, Aquenses, Arelatenses, Sextani, Sentij, Ebrodunty, Dinienses, Vesdiantiij, Sanicienses, Nerufij, Vencienses, Vulgientes, Aptenses, Reienses, Octavani, Commoni, Foro-Iulienses, Segeflorij, Albici, Oxuby, Desiates, &c alij.
units.tr: The following once lived here: the Salyi, Aquenses, Arelatenses, Sextani, Sentii, Ebrodunti, Dinienses, Vesdiantii, Sanicienses, Nerusii, Vencienses, Vulgientes, Aptenses, Reienses, Octavani, Commoni, Forojulienses, Segeflorii, Albici, Oxubii, Desiates, and others.

units.la: Salyos primo potiuntur loco. Salyes sunt Plinio; Σάλυες Straboni, Αἴγυες olim, id est Ligures vocatos addenti, eorumque Regionem Αἰγυσικὴν: unde & Posteriores Κελτολύγυες, Gallo-Ligures, nominarunt, ut distinguerent ab Liguribus Italiæ Populis. Ligures enim Sedes suas habuerunt longe lateque in his Galliæ oris, etiam ultra Rodanum. Σάλυκες dicuntur Ptolemæo: Salyas appellat Livius Epitome Libri lxi; Salluvies Fasti Triumphales & Ammianus Marcellinus. Olim, ubi nunc Archiepiscopatus Aquensis, quæ Civitas Aquensium in Notitia Provinciarum Galliæ, Vienenenti iii, & Arelatensis, quæ & Civitas Arelatensium; Les Archevesches d'Air & d'Arles. Certè Domicilium ipsorum non obscurè notat Strabo lib. iv, ubi scribit Sextium, redactis in potestatem Salyas, non longe ab Massilia suæ nominis ædificasse oppidum: de quo postea. Et de Salyas idem paullo post: Ἀμὰ δ' ἡτὶ τῶν Σαλύων ἐρὶ τὴ ἔπὶ ἀπὸ Ἀρτόν ... Habitasse eos satis ample, docet idem his verbis: ... Ptolemæus Salyum opida inter alia nominat Arelatum & Aquas Sextias. Pagum Provinciæ, qui Soles vulgo, Veteris Appellationis vestigium servare censet Dalechampius. Ab his Salyis Frames Salo, legemque Sanicam, nomen habere putat Guilelmus Bellaius Langius apud Paradinum de antiquo Statu Burgundiæ. Mihi alia mens est, ut doceo in Germania. Inter Salyos habitasse Sextanos constat ex Plinio lib. iii, Pomponiusque lib. ii. qui Arelatem ijs adsignant: Sextani dicti, quod Milites essent vi. Legionis Veterani. De ijs Vetus Inscriptio, quæ Romæ eruta anno MDXLII:
units.tr: The Salyes hold the first place. The Salyes are called by Pliny, and by Strabo Salyes [Σάλυες], though he adds that they were formerly called Aigyes [Αἴγυες], that is Ligures, and that their region was Aigysikē [Αἰγυσικὴν]. Hence later writers also called them Keltolygyes [Κελτολύγυες], Gallo-Ligures, to distinguish them from the Ligures, the peoples of Italy. For the Ligures had their seats far and wide along these shores of Gaul, even beyond the Rhône. Ptolemy calls them Salykes [Σάλυκες]; Livy in the Epitome of book 61 calls them Salyas; the Triumphal Fasti and Ammianus Marcellinus call them Salluvies. Formerly, where the archbishopric of Aix now is, there was the City of the Aquenses in the Notitia of the Provinces of Gaul, Vienne, chapter 3, and the Arelatensis, which is also the City of the Arelatenses; Les Archevesches d'Air & d'Arles. Certainly Strabo, book 4, clearly indicates their home, where he writes that Sextius, having reduced the Salyas to his power, built a town bearing his own name not far from Marseille; more on this later. And Strabo says of the Salyas, a little later: [Ἀμὰ δ' ἡτὶ τῶν Σαλύων ἐρὶ τὴ ἔπὶ ἀπὸ Ἀρτόν ...] ... That they lived quite widely, the same author shows in these words: [...]. Ptolemy names among other towns of the Salyum, Arelatum and Aquae Sextiae. Dalechampius thinks that the district of the Province, which is commonly called Soles, preserves a trace of the old name. Guillaume Bellaius Langius, cited by Paradin in his work on the ancient state of Burgundy, thinks that the Frames Salo and the Sanic law take their name from these Salyi. My own view is different, as I show in my work on Germany. That the Sextani lived among the Salyes is established from Pliny, book 3, and Pomponius, book 2, who assign Arles to them: they were called Sextani because they were veterans of the Sixth Legion. Concerning them there is an ancient inscription, which was dug up at Rome in the year 1542:

units.la: DIVAE FAVSTINAE AVG SEXTANI ARELATENSES
units.tr: THE SEXTANI OF ARELATE, UNDER DIVA FAUSTINA AUGUSTA

units.la: Sentij, Σίννοι Ptolemæo; Ebrodunty videntur esse Plinio lib. iii. cap. iv. Nam utrumque Civitatem ijs tribuit Diniam. Civitas Dinienfium Notitiæ Provinciarum in Viennensi iv & Alpibus Maritimis. Plinius auctor est Galbam imperatorem Narbonensi Provinciæ adjecisse ex Inalpinis Gentibus Ebrodunites. Vesdiantij, Οὐεσδιάντιοι, Ptolemæo; Vediuntij, Plinio. Eorum Metropolis Sanitium, Senas hodie: Notitiæ Civitas Sanicienfium, L'Evesché de Senas. Nerufij Plinio in Alpibus Maritimis, ubi hodie Ventium, S. Paul de Vences: Notitiæ Civitas Vencienfium, L'Evesché de S. Paul de Vences. Vulgientes Plinio, Aptam Iuliam ijs Metropolim tribuenti, sunt, qui Vulcientes in Fastis Triumphalibus, ab Verrio Flacco concinnatis. Civitas Aptensium Notitiæ Provinciarum in Viennensi iii, L'Evesché d'Apt, ubi male Athenfium. Civitas Reiensium, legitur in eadem Notitia, L'evesché de Riés: Regenses Galliæ Narbonensis Populis connumerat Sidonius lib. vi. Epist. ad Papam Patientem; apud quem reponendi Reienses. Reis Apollinaris, quod in Itineraria legitur Tabula, Long. xxii. Lat. viii. huc videtur pertinere, nihil tamen certi diffinio. Octavani Plinio in melioribus Codicibus, qui Octaviani in Vulgatis, quinque Octavani Pomponio Melæ, ijdem forte cum Commonis Ptolemæi. Forum Iuly, quod Octavanorum Coloniam facit Mela, apud Ptolemæum Commonis tribuitur, apud Plinium autem Pacensis & Classica vocatur. Est & in Augusti Nummo apud Goltzium, COL. IVL. OCTAV. Civitas Forojulienfium est in Notitia Provinciarum sub Viennensi iii. Meminit ejusdem Lapis, qui Nemausi in Horto Ioannis Poldi, Antiquitatum Nemausensium descriptoris:
units.tr: The Sentii, called Σίννοι by Ptolemy, are probably the Ebrodunty of Pliny, Book 3, chapter 4, for he assigns both of these to the Dinia. The Dinienses (the city of the Dinienfium) appear in the Notitia Provinciarum under the Viennese province, iv, and under the Maritime Alps. Pliny records that the emperor Galba added to the Province of Narbonne the Ebrodunites from the Inalpine peoples. The Vesdiantii (Vesdiantij), Οὐεσδιάντιοι in Ptolemy, are the Vediuntii of Pliny. Their metropolis was Sanitium, today Senas. The Notitia calls it the Civitas Sanicienfium, now L'Evesché de Senas. The Nerusii are mentioned by Pliny in the Maritime Alps, where Ventium (today S. Paul de Vences) now stands. The Notitia calls it the Civitas Vencienfium, now L'Evesché de S. Paul de Vences. The Vulgientes of Pliny, who give Apta Julia as their metropolis, are the Vulcientes of the Triumphal Fasti compiled by Verrius Flaccus. The Civitas Aptensium of the Notitia Provinciarum, under the Viennese province iii, is now L'Evesché d'Apt, where the manuscript wrongly reads Athenfium. The Civitas Reiensium is read in the same Notitia; it is now L'evesché de Riés. Sidonius, in Book 6 of his letters, to Pope Patiens, counts the Regenses among the peoples of Gallia Narbonensis, and there Reienses should be restored. Reis Apollinaris, which is read in the Itinerary Table (long. 22, lat. 8), seems to belong here, though I define nothing certain. The Octavani of Pliny (in the better manuscripts; the printed editions have Octaviani) and the five Octavani of Pomponius Mela are perhaps the same as the Commones of Ptolemy. The Forum Iulii, which Mela makes the colony of the Octavanorum, is assigned by Ptolemy to the Commones, while Pliny calls it Pacensis and Classica. There is also a coin of Augustus in Goltzius reading COL. IVL. OCTAV. The Notitia Provinciarum under the Viennese iii has the Civitas Forojuliensium. The same is recorded by an inscription that was in the garden of Johannes Poldus at Nîmes, the describer of the antiquities of Nemausus:

units.la: Hodie L'Evesché de Feriuls. Segestorica notat melioris notæ Notitia Provinciarum, sub Viennensi, quam dixi. III. eorum mentionem faciens Civitatis, quæ hodie L'Evesché de Sisteron. Segestory corrupte nominantur Seteri in Itineraria Tabula, VII. Lat. XXV. Long. ut mihi quidem videtur. Certe si non illi, qui tandem sint Selters, nescio. Albicos Populos, Montes supra Massiliam incolentes habet Cæsar lib. I. Bell. Civil. Putant nonnulli eosdem esse cum Albensibus, de quibus in Languedokio. Sunt sane non alij, quam qui nunc Ἀλβίκες, nunc Ἀλβίκωνοι apud Strabonem, eos post Salyas collocantem. Ὀξύβιοι Strabani lib. IV. & Quadrato Ῥωμαικῆς χιλιαρχίας ἐν βίβλ. apud Stephanum, qui Oxiby Plinio: Onelæ Comitatum esse vult Pingonius: Oberrois Dalechampius. Ab his Ὀξυβίων Αἰμιλίων apud Strabonem legitur eodem libro; unde patet Oxubios littorales fuisse populos, ad Mare Mediterraneum Gallicum. Qui Decuates Plinio Melaque, censet Plinetus habitasse loca illa, ubi nunc Comitatus Raigni; Cœnalis, ubi Draguinien, Pingonius, ubi Marri: Ego nihil habeo certi. Sunt autem hi, Δεκιάτες, Strabono; Δεκυάτοι, Ptolemæo; Δεκιᾶται denique, Stephano. Legunturque præter alios apud Plinium lib. III. cap. IV. Tafaedunitans & Canonicenses: fabricati fortean ex Tarasconensibus, quorum Caput & Metropolis ad Rodanum Tarascon, de qua postea. Reliquos incertioris positionis Populos prætereo; quales inter alios apud Ptolemæum Ἀνατίλι, item in Notitia Provinciarum Galliæ sub Viennensi III. Rigomagenses, Solinienses, & Cemelevenses. Nam nihil est mihi de iis explorati. Ex Solinienisibus Senez facit Cœnalis: Cemelevenensibus Vrbs forte Κεμελιῶν Ptolemæo; Cemelson, Plinio; Cemenelum, Antonino: Cenez eidem Cœnali, sed dubitanti; Monte Camelione apud Leandrum.
units.tr: Today it is the L'Evesché de Feriuls. The better Notitia Provinciarum, under the Viennese province I have mentioned, makes iii mention of them as the Segestorica civitas, which today is the L'Evesché de Sisteron. They are wrongly named Segestory. In the Itinerary Table they are called Seteri (vii; lat. 25; long. as far as I can judge). Certainly, if they are not those who are now Selters, I do not know who they are. Caesar, in Book 1 of the Civil War, has the Albicī, peoples dwelling in the mountains above Massilia. Some think they are the same as the Albenses of whom I speak in Languedoc. They are indeed none other than those whom Strabo calls Ἀλβίκες and Ἀλβίκωνοι, placing them after the Salyes. The Oxybii are in Strabo, Book 4, and in Quadratus's Roman Chiliarchy, in a book quoted by Stephanus, who has Ὀξύβιοι; Pliny has Oxybii. Pingonius wants the Onelae to be a county, and Dalechamps the Oberrois. From them Strabo, in the same book, mentions the Ὀξυβίων Αἰμιλίων, so it is clear that the Oxubii were coastal peoples on the Gallic Mediterranean. Plinetus thinks the Decuates of Pliny and Mela lived where the county of Raigni now is; Cœnalis places them where Draguinien is, and Pingonius where Marri is. I have nothing certain. They are called Δεκιάτες by Strabo, Δεκυάτοι by Ptolemy, and finally Δεκιᾶται by Stephanus. Among others, Pliny, Book 3, chapter 4, names the Tafaedunitans and the Canonicenses, perhaps fabricated from the Tarasconenses, whose head and metropolis on the Rhone is Tarascon, about which I will speak later. I pass over the other peoples of uncertain location, such as, among others, the Ἀνατίλι in Ptolemy, and in the Notitia Provinciarum of Gaul under the Viennese iii the Rigomagenses, Solinienses and Cemelevenses. About these I have nothing established. Cœnalis makes Senez from the Solinienses. The Cemelevenses may be a city, Κεμελιῶν in Ptolemy, Cemelson in Pliny, Cemenelum in Antoninus. Cœnalis, though doubtfully, makes it Cenez, and Leandro has Monte Camelione.

units.la: Anteaquam ad hodiernam Provinciæ explicationem veniam, nonnihil dicendum mihi de Campis Lapideis, qui in hac Galliæ parte inter Massiliam & Orientalissimum Rodani Ostium. Herculis Præliorum memoriam servare eos dicit Plinius; ex eo, quod Herculem hic dimicantem contra Albiona & Bergionem Neptuni Filios, quum Tela ei defecissent, ab invocato Iove adjutum Imbre Lapidum ferunt. Credas pluisse, adeo multi & passim & late jacent. Huic Fabulæ adsentiuntur quoque Pomponius Mela, Iulius Solinus, & Marcianus; quibus Strabonis sententia plane præponenda, qua certius nihil dari dicique possit. Is enim hoc modo Campum hunc depingit lib. IV: Μέγας ξύ γὰρ ἡ Μεσαλίας ἡμῖν τῆ ἐκβολῶν τῶ Ῥοδανοῦ Πεδίον ἰστί, ἡ ψηλάτης διήκει εἰς ἱκανὴν ἐυθίας: ποιῶν δὲ τὸν Αἰμιλίτειον, κυκλοπεὶς τὸ ἄχθμα. καλοῦντ δὲ Αἰ-θῶδες. Μεσὸν γὰρ ἰστὶ λίθων χαροπληθῶν, ... Vitatur hodieque hic Campus, vocaturque Les Craux inter Arelate & Massiliam; suntque in eo Opida quædam & Vici.
units.tr: Before I come to the present description of the Province, I must say something about the Stony Plains (Campi Lapidei) in this part of Gaul, between Massilia and the most easterly mouth of the Rhone. Pliny says they preserve the memory of Hercules' battles, because there, as they tell it, Hercules, fighting against Albion and Bergion, the sons of Neptune, when his weapons had failed him, was helped by Jupiter, whom he had invoked, with a shower of stones. You would think it had rained them, so many lie everywhere and far and wide. Pomponius Mela, Julius Solinus and Martianus also agree with this fable; but Strabo's opinion, than which nothing more certain can be given or said, must be placed far above theirs. He describes this plain in Book 4 in this way: "For between Massalia and the mouth of the Rhone there is a great plain, which stretches in a straight line for a considerable distance; it is called the Aemilian, and is round-shaped... and is called Aethodes. For in the middle of it lie stones of a rough, cheerless kind..." This plain is still visited today, and is called Les Craux, between Arles and Marseille; and there are some towns and villages in it. [Μέγας γὰρ ἐστι Μεσσαλίας ἡμῖν τῆς ἐκβολῶν τοῦ Ῥοδανοῦ πεδίον, ἡ ψηλάτης διήκει εἰς ἱκανὴν εὐθείας· ποιῶν δὲ τὸν Αἰμιλίτειον, κυκλοπεὶς τὸ ἄχθμα. καλοῦντ δὲ Αἰ-θῶδες. Μεσὸν γὰρ ἐστὶ λίθων χαροπληθῶν, ...]

units.la: Sunt porro in Provincia sub Parlamento Aquensi, præter multa minorum gentium Opida, Vrbes, duæ quidem Archiepiscopatus, undecim autem Episcopatus dignitate nobiles. Archiepiscopales sunt Aquæ Sextiæ & Arelatæ.
units.tr: Furthermore, in the Province under the Parlement of Aix, apart from many towns and villages of lesser peoples, there are two cities of archiepiscopal rank and eleven of episcopal dignity. The archiepiscopal sees are Aquae Sextiae and Arelate.

units.la: Aquæ Sextiæ, Colonia, Latinis, Paterculo, Solino, aliisque dicuntur; quæ Τὰ ἔατα Σέξτια, Καλωνία, Ptolemæo: Σεξτιλία est apud Plutarchum in Vita C. Marii: Aquæ Sextiæ Itinerariæ Tabulæ. Coloniam Iuliam Aquas vocat Lapis qui hodie Lugduni ad D. Benedicti: COL. IVL. AQVIS. ET COL. IVI. F. AREL
units.tr: Aquae Sextiae, called Colonia by the Latins (Paterculus, Solinus and others), is what Ptolemy calls Τὰ ἔατα Σέξτια, Καλωνία. Σεξτιλία is found in Plutarch's Life of C. Marius, and Aquae Sextiae in the Itinerary Tables. An inscription which is today at Lyon by St Benedict's calls it the Colonia Julia Aquae: COL. IVL. AQVIS. ET COL. IVI. F. AREL

units.la: Item alius ad ipsas Aquas: F. SEXTIVS. FLORVS IIIIII. VIR. AVG. COL. IVL AQVIS. ET. COL. AREL VALERIÆ. SPVRIÆ. FLASSINÆ VXORI. PIENTISS SEX. VALERIO. PROCVLO. ET. SVIS
units.tr: Another, at the Aquae themselves: F. SEXTIUS FLORUS, IIIIII VIR. AUG., OF THE COLONY OF JULIA AQUIS AND OF THE COLONY OF ARELATE VALERIA, TO HIS MOST DEVOTED WIFE SPURIA FLASSINA, AND TO SEX. VALERIUS PROCULUS AND HIS FAMILY.

units.la: Plinius nominat Coloniam Iuliam Angustam Aquas Sextias Monimentum, quod in Agro Arelatensi hodie reperiri notat ad Ausonium lib. 1. cap. xxx, Vir Nobilissimus Iosephus Scaliger: M. FRONTONI. EVPOR IIIIII. VIR. AVG. COL. IVLIA AVG. AQVIS. SEXTIS. NAVICVLAR MAR. AREL. CVRAT. EIVSD. CORP PATRONO. NAVTAR. DRVENTI CORVM. ET. VTRICLARIORVM CORP. ERNAGINENSVM IVLIA. NICE. VXOR CONIVGI. KARISSIMO
units.tr: Pliny names the Colonia Julia Augusta Aquae Sextiae the Monument, which Joseph Scaliger, a most noble man, notes can today be found in the territory of Arles, in his note on Ausonius, Book 1, chapter 30: M. FRONTO EUPOR, IIIIII VIR. AUG., OF THE COLONY JULIA AUGUSTA AQUIS SEXTIIS, CURATOR OF THE BOATMEN OF THE SEA AT ARELATE, OF THE SAME BODY, PATRON OF THE BOATMEN, OF THE DRUENTI AND OF THE UTRICULARII, OF THE BODY OF THE ERNAGINENSES. JULIA NICE, HIS WIFE, TO HER DEAREST HUSBAND.

units.la: Colonia item Iulia Aquæ Sextiæ, Legio xxv vocatur in antiqua Inscriptione, Nummoque Vespasiani; si fides Huberti Goltzii Thesauro. Aquæ quidem, quod Aquarum ibi Caldarum Balnea; unde & hodie Aix: Sextia ab C. Sextio Calvino cos. anno ab V. C. 1cxxx. Hic enim, victa Salyorum Gente, Coloniam Aquas Sextias condidit, eo consilio, ut Romanum illic collocaret præsidium; quo Barbaros ex iis reprimeret Itineribus, quæ ex Massilia ducunt in Italiam, quum Massiliensibus, illis coercendis, non suppeterent vires. Legendus Livius lib. lxi ab V.C. Paucis Strabo lib. iv: Σέξτιος γαρ ὁ καλούμενος τὰς Σάλυας, ὁ πλὴν ἀπὸ τὰς Μασσαλίας, κτίσας ... [illegible, ~12 letters]. Iulia Augusta vero ab C. Iulio Cæsare Augusto, qui eam Colonis auxit, deductis eo Legionis xxv. Veteranis. Parlamenti Provincialis Sedes, quod inde Aquense. Partim ad Aquas Sextias, partim in Italia, in Campo Raudino, vicit Cimbros Teutonosque Germaniæ Populos, quique ipsis se junxerant, Tigurinos Ambronesque, Gallicas Nationes, C. Marius. D. Hieronymus ad Gerontiam: Gens Teutonum, inquit, ex ultimis Germaniæ profectā Littoribus omnem Galliam inundavit, sepiusque caeis Romanis exercitibus, apud Aquas Sextias, Mario pugnante, superata est. Nota est Historia. Alias locis etiam hac de re nonnulla. Arelas simpliciter Orosio & Ausonio lib. de Urbibus in Epigraphe & ipso Carmine vii: Arelatum, eidem Ausonio in eodem Carmine, & aliis; Arelate, Cæsari, Plinio, Suetonio in Ti. Principis Vita, Pomponio Melæ, & aliis; Ἀρελάτη denique Strabon: quæ Ἀρελάται, Salyorum Colonia, Ptolemæo lib. ii. cap. x; & Arelate, Sextanorum, Plinio lib. iii. nat. Hist. cap. iiii. & Calliodoro. Ut Coloniæ meminerunt Lapides paullo ante ad Aquas Sextias à me positi. Salyorum quidem, ab antiquissimis Galliæ Populis, de quibus ante: Sextanorum vero, ab Legione vi, cui hic sua fuerunt Stativa, quorum etiam initio huius Capitis meminit. Hodie Arles, plurali voce. Thelinen olim nuncupatam ab Græcis eam incolentibus, memoriæ prodit Festus Avienus: Arelatum illic Civitas attollitur,Theline vocata sub priore seculoGraio incolente.
units.tr: The Colonia Julia Aquae Sextiae is also called Legio XXV in an ancient inscription and on a coin of Vespasian, if one trusts the Thesaurus of Hubert Goltzius. It is called Aquae, because of the warm baths of waters there; hence also today Aix. It is called Sextia after C. Sextius Calvinus, consul in the year 630 from the founding of the City. For he, having defeated the Salyan people, founded the colony of Aquae Sextiae, with the purpose of stationing a Roman garrison there, to restrain the barbarians from those roads which lead from Massilia into Italy, since the Massilians lacked the strength to restrain them. Livy, Book 61, from the founding of the City, should be read. Strabo, Book 4, says briefly: "For Sextius, called the founder of the Salyes, apart from Massilia, founded..." [illegible, about twelve letters]. It is called Julia Augusta from C. Julius Caesar Augustus, who enlarged it with colonists, after the veterans of the twenty-fifth legion were settled there. It is the seat of the Provincial Parlement, and so it is called Aquense. Partly at Aquae Sextiae and partly in Italy, on the Raudine Plain, C. Marius conquered the Cimbri and Teutones, German peoples, and the Tigurini and Ambrones, Gallic nations, who had joined them. St Jerome, to Gerontia: "The race of the Teutones," he says, "coming from the furthest shores of Germany, flooded all Gaul, and, having often defeated Roman armies, was at last overcome at Aquae Sextiae, Marius fighting." The story is well known. I have said something about this matter in other places. Orosius and Ausonius in his book on cities call it simply Arelas, in the epigraph and in the poem itself, Book 7; Ausonius in the same poem, and others, call it Arelatum; Pliny, Suetonius in the Life of the Emperor Tiberius, Pomponius Mela and others call it Arelate; and finally Strabo calls it Ἀρελάτη. Ptolemy, Book 2, chapter 10, calls the Salyan colony Ἀρελάται, and Pliny, Natural History Book 3, chapter 4, and Calliodorus call it Arelate of the Sextani. The inscriptions I have placed a little earlier at Aquae Sextiae mention this colony. It was of the Salyes, the most ancient people of Gaul, which I mentioned before; and of the Sextani, from the sixth legion, whose winter quarters were here, which he also mentioned at the beginning of this chapter. Today it is Arles, in the plural. Festus Avienus records that the Greeks who inhabited it once called it Thelinen: "There rises the city of Arelatum, called Theline by the Greeks who lived there in the earlier age."

units.la: Mamilliaria cognominatur, quam ob causam nescitur, in Inscriptione pulcherrima, quæ ibidem in Columna legitur, teste V. N. Iosepho Scaligero, in ædibus honestissimæ Matronæ Vallensis: SALVIS. DD. NN THEODOSIO. ET VALENTINIANO P. F. V. AC. TRIVM SEMPER. AVG. XV CONS. VIR. INL AVXILIARIS. PRAE PRAETO. GALLIA DE. ARELATE. MA MILIARIA. PONI. S M. P. I
units.tr: Mamilliaria is the name given to it, though the reason is not known. It appears in a very fine inscription, which is read on a column in the house of a most honourable matron of Vaison, as reported by my kinsman Joseph Scaliger: "For the safety of our lords Theodosius and Valentinian, perpetual Augusti, in the fifteenth consulship... Vir Inlustris, auxiliary praetorian prefect of Gaul, of Arles, set up the Mamilliaria column."

units.la: Constantina ut diceretur, ibique Septem Provinciarum, Viennensis, utriusque Narbonensis, utriusque Aquitaniæ, Novempopulaniæ, & Alpium Maritimarum, Conventus ageretur: sanxit Fl. Constantinus Imperator: cujus egregiam ea de re Constitutionem videre est apud Scaligerum lib. I. Ausonianarum Lectionum, cap. xxiv. Gallulam Romam vocat Ausonius, Carmine, cujus memini, quod esset celeberrimum & oportunissimum Emporium; quodque Romanorum Colonia, ab Ti. Claudio Nerone, Ti Principis Patre, deducta, teste Suetonio, Romam Genitricem suam in multis æmularetur & exprimere conaretur, indeque parva quædam videretur Roma. Urbs ad Rodanum sita. Eo pertinet Philostrati illud in Vita Favorini Galli Arelatensis: Ἐω μὲν γὰρ τῶν ἰσοτιμῶν Γαλατῶν ἀπὸ, Ἀρελάτη πόλις, ἡ ἐν Ἐδανῷ πο-λεμῷ ὤυσεν. Vbi nemo non videt legendum, Ῥοδανῷ pro Ἐδανῷ. Sic Strabo lib. iv: Πρὸς δὲ τῇ Ῥοδανῷ πόλις ἐστὶ καὶ Ἐμπορεῖον ἡ μικρὸν, Ἀρέλατη. Simpliciter utrumque: Hic, πρὸς Ῥοδανῷ: ille, ἀπὸ Ῥοδανῷ. Ad Sinistram autem ripam hodie. Itineraria Tabula collocat ad dextram, ubi hodie Languedokium. Antoninus etiam in Itinerario Maritimo ab Urbe Arelatum usque, in fine: A Grado, inquit, per Fluvium Rodanum Arelatum M. P. xxx. Non male; si Rodani Brachia, ut tunc se diducebant, considerentur. Ausonius Arelatum Rodani Fluentis interscindi, notat. Carmen ejus, ut semel hic ponam, sic habet: Pande, duplex Arelate, tuos blanda hospita Portus Gallula Roma Arelas: quam Narbo Martius, & quam Adcolit Alpinis opulenta Vienna Colonis. Præcipitis Rodani sic intercisa fluentis, Vt mediam facit us navalis Ponte Platcam: Per quem Romani commercia suscipis orbis, Nec cohibes: Populosque alios & Mœnia datas: Gallia quæ fructur, gremioque Aquitania lato.
units.tr: It was to be called Constantina, and it was there that the assize of the seven provinces (Vienne, both Narbonensis, both Aquitaniae, Novempopulania and the Maritime Alps) was to be held. Emperor Flavius Constantine decreed this, and his excellent constitution on the matter may be seen in Scaliger, Ausonian Lectures, book 1, chapter 24. Ausonius calls it Gallula Roma, in a poem I have mentioned, because it was a most famous and convenient market; and because it was a colony of the Romans, founded by Tiberius Claudius Nero, father of the emperor Tiberius, as Suetonius reports, it strove to imitate its mother Rome in many things and to reproduce her, so that it seemed a little Rome. It is a city on the Rhone. To this belongs the passage of Philostratus in the Life of Favorinus of Gaul of Arles: "Ἐω μὲν γὰρ τῶν ἰσοτιμῶν Γαλατῶν ἀπὸ, Ἀρελάτη πόλις, ἡ ἐν Ἐδανῷ πολεμῷ ὤυσεν." Everyone can see that Rhodanos must be read for Edanos. So Strabo, book 4: "Πρὸς δὲ τῇ Ῥοδανῷ πόλις ἐστὶ καὶ Ἐμπορεῖον ἡ μικρὸν, Ἀρέλατη." Both say the same thing: the one has "beside the Rhone", the other "from the Rhone". Today it lies on the left bank; the Itinerary Table places it on the right, where Languedoc is today. Antoninus also, in the Maritime Itinerary, at the end of the route from the city to Arles: "From Grado," he says, "by the river Rhone to Arles, 30 miles." This is not wrong, if the branches of the Rhone are considered as they then divided. Ausonius notes that Arles is cut through by the flowing of the Rhone. His poem, which I shall quote once here, runs thus: "Open up, double Arles, your welcoming harbour, little Rome of Gaul, Arles: which Martian Narbo, and rich Vienne, home of the Alpine colonists, both attend. Thus, divided by the swift currents of the Rhone, you make a naval bridge across the middle, through which you receive and do not check the trade of the Roman world; and you give your walls and peoples to others: Gaul, which enjoys you, and Aquitaine in its broad lap."

units.la: Arelas hic, item in extremo Mosella & Epistola xxiii ad Paullinum, Duplex, quod in duas partes ab Rodano secaretur. Quin & Pontis in Rodano, præter Ausonium, meminit etiam Cassiodorus in Epistola quadam ad Senatum Urbis Romæ lib. viii, Epistola x: Arelate est Civitas supra undas Rodani constituta: quæ in Orientis prospectum, tabulatum Pontem, per nuncupatum Fluminis dorsi, transmittit. Hunc & Hostibus capere, Nostris defendere, necessarium fuit. Hodie, mutata ibi rerum facie, Simplex est, rota in ripa Rodani, quæ Italiam respicit, potita: septa undique Paludibus, in quibus præferoces aluntur Boves. Putatur hinc major fuisse, creduntque magni Viri partem Urbis olim florentissimæ alteram ab Gothis excisam. Videndi obiter Iornandes in Histor. Goth. Cassiodorus lib. iii, Epist. xxxiv, Prosper in Chronicis ad Theodosij xi & Valentiniani Consulatum, apud quem vitiose legitur Archillem, pro Arelas; ut & apud Paulum Diaconum in Theodosio Iuniore. Consulendi item Sidonius lib. vii. Epist. xii, Isidorus in Chronico Gothor. Sigebertus in Chron. ad annum cccclxxi. Forum Arelatense, &c, quæ ibi erant, Statuas Columnasque numerat idem Sidonius lib.i. Epist. xi. Emporium autem fuisse satis constat ex Ausonio, cujus Verius paulo ante laudavi: unde & Strabo, Ἐμπορεῖον ἀ μικρόν. Audiendus hic Fl. Constantinus Imp. ad Agricolam Præfectum Prætorio Galliarum: Tanta est Loci opportunitas, tanta est copia Commerciorum, tanta illic frequentia commeantium, ut quidquid usquam nascitur, illic commodius distrahatur. Neque enim ulla Provincia fructus sui facultate latatur, ut non nisi hac propria Arelatensis Soli credatur esse fecunditas. Quidquid enim dives Oriens, quidquid odoratus Arabs, quidquid delicatus Assyrius, quod Africa fertilis, quod speciosa Hispania, 10 quod fecunda Gallia potest habere præclarum, ita illi exhibetur adfatim, quasi ibi nascantur omnia, quæ ubique constat esse magnifica. Iam vero de cursu Rhodani & Turons recursu, necesse est, ut vicinum faciant & pene conterminum; vel quod ille prætereffluit, vel ille quod circuit. Quum ergo huic servias Civitatis quidquid habet Terra præcipuum: ad hanc vel Navi, vel Vehiculo, Terra, Mari, Flumine deferatur, quidquid singulis nascitur. &c. Cæsar bello contra Massi-liensis suum ibi habuisse legitur Navale. Amphitheatrum Arelate esse ajunt, sed parum integrum: vulgo Les Arenes. Quod nonnulli augurentur Arelatem fuisse nuncupatam, tamquam Aram Latam (adeundus, præterea hos, Gulielmus Paradinus de Antiquo Statu Burgundiæ) quod item non pauci scribant, extra Urbem loco, qui vulgo La Roquette, super duas Columnas Aram fuisse prægrandem & exlecrandam, Cæsari Augusto dicatam; inque ea duos juvenes huic Sacrificio destinatos, 20 publicisque sumtibus in eum finem saginatos, immolari quotannis statio die solitos; quod denique quidam velint Canalem ex Rodano deductum Camargue dici, tamquam Campum Marij; mera sunt otiosorum & ignavorum hominum somnia, puraque delirantium figmenta. In Collegio, quod in Urbis summitate, duæ visuntur Columna; quas, Romanorum procul dubio, Herculis esse persuasum habet Vulgus. Grata olim Regibus Burgundiorum Sedes fuisse legitur, cum apud alios, tum apud Procopium Græcum, qui à Burgundionibus occupatam fuisse, principatu Iustiniani Augusti, scriptum reliquit, quum tamen prius constet fuisse. Sic Ligurinus Poëta: Quaque caput Regni, Sedesque fuisse vetustis Fertur Arelatum, priscorum Curia Regum.
units.tr: Here Arelas, likewise at the end of the Mosella and in Epistle 23 to Paulinus, is called Duplex, because the Rhone divides it into two parts. Besides Ausonius, Cassiodorus also mentions the bridge on the Rhone, in a letter to the Senate of the city of Rome, book 8, letter 10: "Arelate is a city set above the waters of the Rhone, which sends across to the view of the East a bridge of planks, through what is called the back of the river. It was necessary to take this from the enemy and to defend it for ourselves. Today, the face of things having changed there, it is a single [bridge], and the wheel-shaped [structure] has taken possession of the bank of the Rhone which faces Italy, surrounded on all sides by marshes, in which very fierce oxen are reared. It is thought that it was larger before, and great men believe that the other part of the once most flourishing city was destroyed by the Goths." See also, in passing, Jordanes in the History of the Goths; Cassiodorus, book 3, letter 34; Prosper in the Chronicles, for the consulship of Theodosius (11) and Valentinian, where Archillem is wrongly read for Arelas, as also in Paulus Diaconus, on Theodosius the Younger. Consult likewise Sidonius, book 7, letter 12; Isidore in the Chronicle of the Goths; Sigebert in the Chronicle for the year 471. The same Sidonius, book 1, letter 11, counts the Forum Arelatense and what was there, the statues and columns. That it was a Emporium, a market, is sufficiently clear from Ausonius, whose verses I quoted a little earlier; hence also Strabo calls it "a small market". Here we should hear Flavius Constantine the Emperor, writing to Agricola, Praetorian Prefect of Gaul: "The location is so favourable, the supply of trade so great, the crowd of those coming and going so dense there, that whatever is produced anywhere is sold there more conveniently. For no province is so pleased with the abundance of its produce that the fertility of the soil of Arles is not thought to surpass it. For whatever the rich East, whatever the fragrant Arab, whatever the luxurious Assyrian, whatever fertile Africa, whatever beautiful Spain, whatever fruitful Gaul can have that is splendid, is brought to it in abundance, as if all those things which are known to be magnificent everywhere were born there. Moreover, since the course of the Rhone and its return from the Tyrrhenian Sea make it near and almost neighbouring, whether because the one flows past it or the other goes around it, since therefore whatever the earth has that is most outstanding serves this city, let whatever each place produces be carried to it by ship, by cart, by land, by sea or by river." etc. We read that Caesar had a naval yard there in his war against the Massilians. They say there is an amphitheatre at Arles, but a rather incomplete one, commonly called Les Arenes. Some guess that Arles was so named as Ara Lata (one should also consult, on this, Guillaume Paradin, On the Ancient State of Burgundy). Likewise, not a few write that outside the city, in a place commonly called La Roquette, there was a very large and accursed altar, dedicated to Caesar Augustus, upon two columns; and that two young men destined for this sacrifice, fattened at public expense for that purpose, were accustomed to be slaughtered on it every year on the station day. Finally, some want the canal drawn from the Rhone to be called the Camargue, as if it were the Field of Marius. These are mere dreams of idle and lazy men, and pure fictions of madmen. In the college, which stands on the top of the city, two columns are seen; the common people are persuaded that these are without doubt of the Romans, or of Hercules.
