It is read that the seat was once pleasing to the kings of the Burgundians, both in other writers and in the Greek Procopius, who left it written that it was occupied by the Burgundians in the reign of the Emperor Justinian, though it is established that it was so earlier. So the poet Ligurinus: "And the place which is said to have been the head of the kingdom and the seat of the old kings is Arles, the court of the ancient kings."

units.la: Et paullo post: Nomen apud Veteres Regni, Titulumque gerebat: Cujus Arelatum Sedes.
units.tr: And a little later: "It bore among the ancients the name and title of the kingdom, of which Arles was the seat."

units.la: Postea Comitum Provincialium fuit Domicilium. Primus ibi Episcopum egisse scribitur D. Trophimus, Pauli Apostoli Discipulus, anno Imperij Neronis secundo in Gallias ab eo destinatus: ex cujus fontibus, ut Zosimus Pontifex Maximus scribit, universa Gallia Fidei rivulos accepit. Arce potens hodie, Honorato Hilarioque, Præsulibus quondam suis, est clara. 40
units.tr: Afterwards it was the home of the Provincial Counts. Saint Trophimus, a disciple of the Apostle Paul, is written to have been the first bishop there, sent into Gaul by him in the second year of the emperor Nero; from whose springs, as Zosimus, Pontifex Maximus, writes, the whole of Gaul received the streams of the faith. Today it is powerful in its citadel, and famous for Honoratus and Hilary, once its own prelates.

units.la: Et hæc de Archiepiscopalibus Provincia Civitatibus: Episcopales sunt undecim, in quis, quod absque aliarum fiat indignatione & præjudicio, primas dabo Massilia. Massiliam Latini omnes, Græcique nominant nonnulli: quæ Μασσαλία Straboni lib. iv, Stephano, Veteribusque Nummis: Μασσαλία Ptolemæo; Marseille vulgo: Græcorum cognominatur in Itineraria Tabula; quin & Suburbicarius ipsorum Ager ibidem Gracia dicitur. Nam Phocaensium Græcorum in Asia Minore est Colonia. Μασσαλία, inquit Stephanus, ἄστυ Φωκαίων: κτίσμα Φωκαίων. Pomponius lib. ii: Hæc à Phocais orundā, & olim inter asperas posita, nunc ut pacatu, ita dissimillimis tamen vicina Gentibus. Mirum quam facile & tunc Sedem alienam ceperit, & adhuc morem summa tenere. Condita Olympiade xlv, scribente Solino, cap. viii; tempore Tarquinij Regis, ut notat Iustinus lib. xliii, qui totam Iuventutis Phocaensis, Pertinacem Servitutem fugientis, Navigationem, ejusque Cautelam & Effecta pluribus commemorat. Consulendi & Agellius lib. x. Noct. Att. Ammianus lib. xv, Agathias, & alij. Hinc Phocæus, id est Massiliensis, Iuventus Lucano, in libris de Bello Pharsalico; Phocais in dubiis ausa est servare Iuventus Non Græca levitate fidem.
units.tr: And this is said of the archiepiscopal cities of the province. There are eleven episcopal cities; among them, so that no offence or prejudice is done to the others, I shall give the first place to Massilia. All Latin writers, and some Greeks, call it Massilia; in Strabo, book 4, Stephanus, and ancient coins it is Μασσαλία, in Ptolemy Μασσαλία; commonly it is Marseille. In the Itinerary Table it is called of the Greeks; indeed its suburban territory there is called Gracia. For it is a colony of the Phocaean Greeks in Asia Minor. "Μασσαλία," says Stephanus, "city of the Phocaeans, founded by the Phocaeans." Pomponius, book 2: "This was founded by Phocaeans and was once placed among rough peoples, now as peaceful, yet very unlike the neighbouring nations. It is remarkable how easily it took up a foreign seat and still keeps the custom of the highest rank." It was founded in the forty-fifth Olympiad, as Solinus writes, chapter 8; in the time of King Tarquin, as Justin notes in book 43, who recounts at length the whole youth of Phocaea, fleeing stubborn servitude, their voyage, its caution and its results. Consult also Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights, book 10; Ammianus, book 15; Agathias, and others. Hence Lucan, in his books on the Pharsalian war, speaks of "the Phocaean, that is the Massilian, youth": "The Phocaean youth dared to keep faith in doubtful times, not with Greek fickleness."

units.la: Hinc Phocaica, id est Massiliensis, ora, Silio lib. iv de Bello Pœnico, Scipio Phocaicis sese referebat ab oris: Hinc denique Phocaicum Litus circa Massiliam & Emporias, de quo alibi. A Phocaea scilicet, quæ Φωκαια, Ptolomæo Æolidis Stephano Ioniæ oppidum; Phocis Pomponio & Lucano lib v. Hinc enim in has oras profecti Massiliæ Conditores. Plutarchus in Solone conditam scribit a Proto, qui Protis aliis dicitur. Unde autem dicta Massilia, paucis indicat ex Timæo Stephanus: Τιμαιος δε Ὀ ... Situm petrolo in loco, ostia Rodani Amnis, in remoto Sinu, velut in Angulo Maris, aut ex Trogo Iustinus. De Situ hæc Cæsar lib. ii. Bell. Civil. Massilia fere ex tribus oppidi partibus navi alluitur; reliqua quarta est, quæ aditum habet a terra: huius quoque partis ea, quæ ad arcem, pertinet, locus natura & valle antiquissima munitatione & difficilem habet expugnationem Et addit Strabo, De Portu isto Dionysius: ἀθα π χαῖα Μασσιλίη τεῖχυσεν, ἐπ' ἀφέρη ἐχμεν ἔχεια.
units.tr: Hence Phocaica, that is, Massiliensis ora ("the Massiliot shore"): Silius, book 4 of the Punic War, has "Scipio was returning from the Phocaean shores." Finally, hence the Phocaicum Litus ("Phocaean coast") around Massilia and Emporiae, which I discuss elsewhere. It is named after Phocaea, which in Greek is Φωκαια, a town of Aeolis according to Ptolemy and a town of Ionia according to Stephanus. Pomponius and Lucan (book 5) call it Phocis. From there, indeed, those who went to these shores founded Massilia. Plutarch, in his Life of Solon, writes that it was founded by Protos, who is called Protis by others. Stephanus briefly indicates, from Timaeus, why it was named Massilia: Timaeus says [Τιμαιος δε Ὀ ...]. It lies on a rocky site at the mouth of the river Rhone, in a remote bay, as if in a corner of the sea, according to Justin, following Trogus. Caesar, in book 2 of the Civil War, describes its situation: "Massilia is washed by the sea on nearly three sides of the town; the fourth part is the only one that has access by land. Of this part, the section that belongs to the citadel has a position and an ancient fortification by nature and by its valley which make it difficult to storm." Strabo adds this, and Dionysius writes about this harbour: [ἀθα π χαῖα Μασσιλίη τεῖχυσεν, ἐπ' ἀφέρη ἐχμεν ἔχεια].

units.la: Nomen Portus fuit ut Eustathius notat Λακυδῶν. Hinc apud Melam ex veteribus libris legendum: Et Lacidon Massiliensium Portus & in eo ipsa Massilia. Pergit Strabo: Τετράχισμεν δὲ καλῶς ἡ πόλις συμπλεκει, μέγαλῶ ἰχνου ἀξιόλογον. Ἐν δὲ τῇ ἀκρᾳ τὸ Ἐφεσιον ἱερὸν, καὶ τὸ τῆς Δελφινίας Ἀπόλλωνος ἱερόν. Rempublicam porro Massiliensium tantopere laudat M. Tullius; ut, audiente Populo Romano, dicere auderet in Defensione Fontei, Civitatis illius Disciplinam atque Gravitatem non solum Græcia, sed pene cunctis Gentibus anteponendam. Ejus (ut plene scribit Strabo) Sexcenti erant Senatores, quos Τιμούχος vocabant, quique totam vitam isthoc honore potiebantur: ex eo numero Quindecimviri quotidianis Litibus dirimendis legebantur. Atque ij nimirum sunt Sexcenti Massiliensium, & Quindecim-Primi, quos libro belli civilis i apellat Cæsar. Sexcentorum etiam meminit Valerius Maximus lib. ii. cap vi Ex Quindecim-viris autem Tres-viros optabant, in quibus auctoritas esset summa Τιμουχος. nemo creabatur qui Liberos non haberet, quive à tertia usque progenie ac stirpe civis non esset. Massiliensium igitur Respublica Ἀριστοκρατία (hæc Strabonis est vox) administrabatur Aristoteles πολιτεία. lib v. & viii. eos Ὀλιγαρχίαν usos testatur. Oliarchicum sane fuit, genere, ut audivimus, non virtute, Reip Principes fieri. Eorum leges Ionici generis, inquit Strabo, publice sunt propositæ. Instituta Reip. Massiliensium paucis recensem Iustinus lib xliii Consuevisse scilicet, ab condita fere urbe festis diebus portas claudere, vigilias agere, stationem in muris observare, peregrinos recognoscere curas habere: ac veluti bellum habeant, sic Urbem pacis temporibus custodire? adeo illic bene instituta non temporum necessitate, sed recte faciendi consuetudine servari. Alia de Manumissionibus Spectaculis Validis mendicantibus, Suppliciis, Funeribus Sepulchris & hospitiorum jure leguntur apud Valerium, capite quod indicavi. Consonabant optimis institutis Sanctissimi publice privatimque Mores. Τῆς δὲ λιτότητος, inquit Strabo lib. iv, τ βίου καὶ τ σωφροσύνης τ Μασσαλιωτῶν οὐχ ἱλαχιστον ἀνῆς θεῖν τοῦτο πιμήμενον. ἡ γὰρ μιμησις ... Massiliam Tacitus ait locum græca comitate & provinciali parsimonia mistum & bene compositum. Sed isti morum integritati multum ademit unum, quo se infamare soliti Massilienses, vitium Notum est proverbium Πλεῖν ... Massiliam naviges, de quo Athenæus lib. xii, Suidas & alij Credebantur enim Γωνακωνιτῶν. Hinc Massilienses Mores Plauto in Casina, molles impudici, effœminati: Huc illa Clementis Alexandrini ix, Recog. referenda. Apud Gallos, inquit, Lex prisca constituit nuptum tradi publice pueros, nec opprobrium ex hoc aliquod duci, innuere videtur eadem Diodorus scribens, Gallos licet habeant speciosas fœminas, ad Mares tamen esse proniores: Strabo item, ubi memorat, apud Gallos turpe non judicari, si adolescentes ætatis flore abuterentur. Tradit & Athenæus lib xiii Gallos super pellibus sæpius cum duobus catamitis concumbere. Hæc enim talia non de Gallis veteribus generatim, sed de Massiliensibus Græca mollitia fractis exaudienda censent Magni viri. Sidonius aperte carmine xxii: Et te Massiliensium per hortos Sacri Stipitis Arbiter colonum Hellespontiaco parem Priapo &c. Infamibus Massilienses Moribus adscribam quæ notat ad illud Virgilij, Auri sacra fames,
units.tr: The name of the harbour was, as Eustathius notes, Lacydon [Λακυδῶν]. Hence in Mela we should read, from the old books: Et Lacidon Massiliensium Portus & in eo ipsa Massilia. Strabo continues: the city is well joined together and has a notable circuit [Τετράχισμεν δὲ καλῶς ἡ πόλις συμπλεκει, μέγαλῶ ἰχνου ἀξιόλογον]. On the headland stands the temple of Ephesian Artemis and the temple of Delphinian Apollo [Ἐν δὲ τῇ ἀκρᾳ τὸ Ἐφεσιον ἱερὸν, καὶ τὸ τῆς Δελφινίας Ἀπόλλωνος ἱερόν]. Marcus Tullius praises the constitution of the Massiliots so highly that, speaking before the Roman people in his defence of Fonteius, he dared to say: Civitatis illius Disciplinam atque Gravitatem non solum Græcia, sed pene cunctis Gentibus anteponendam. As Strabo fully describes, its senate had six hundred members, called Timouchoi [Τιμούχος], who held this honour for their whole lives. From this number the Fifteen were chosen to settle daily disputes. These, no doubt, are the Sexcenti Massiliensium and the Quindecim-Primi whom Caesar calls by that name in book 1 of the Civil War. Valerius Maximus, book 2, chapter 6, also mentions the Six Hundred. From the Fifteen they chose the Three, who held the highest authority [Τιμουχος]. No one was created who did not have children, or who was not a citizen from the third generation and stock onward. The republic of the Massiliots was therefore governed as an aristocracy (this is Strabo's word) [Ἀριστοκρατία], though Aristotle, in books 5 and 8, says they used an oligarchy [Ὀλιγαρχίαν]. It was indeed an oligarchy, for, as we have heard, the leaders of the state were made by birth, not by virtue. Strabo says that their laws of the Ionian kind were published openly. Justin, book 43, briefly reviews the institutions of the Massiliot state: from almost the founding of the city they were accustomed on festival days to shut the gates, keep night watches, maintain guard on the walls, take care to examine foreigners, and guard the city in times of peace as if they were at war. So well-established institutions were kept not by the necessity of the times but by the custom of doing right. Other matters concerning manumissions, shows, the healthy and the beggars, punishments, funerals, tombs and the law of hospitality are read in Valerius, in the chapter I have indicated. Their public and private morals matched their excellent institutions. Strabo, book 4, says: "Of the simplicity of life and the sobriety of the Massiliots, this is no small example, that it is praised" [Τῆς δὲ λιτότητος ... τ Μασσαλιωτῶν οὐχ ἱλαχιστον ἀνῆς θεῖν τοῦτο πιμήμενον]. Tacitus says Massilia was a place mixing Greek courtesy with provincial thrift, and well ordered. But one thing took much from that integrity of morals: the Massiliots were accustomed to be disgraced by it, a notorious vice. There is the proverb [Πλεῖν ... Massiliam naviges], about which Athenaeus, book 12, Suidas and others write. For they were believed to be Gonaconitae [Γωνακωνιτῶν]. Hence Plautus, in the Casina, uses Massilienses Mores for soft, shameless, effeminate ways. The passage of Clement of Alexandria, Recognitions book 9, should be referred to here: "Among the Gauls," he says, "an ancient law established that boys be publicly given in marriage, and no disgrace was thought to attach to this." Diodorus seems to imply the same when he writes that the Gauls, though they have handsome women, are nonetheless more inclined to males. Strabo likewise notes that among the Gauls it was not considered shameful if young men in the flower of their age were abused. Athenaeus, book 13, also reports that the Gauls often lay with two catamites on animal skins. Great men judge that these things should not be understood of the ancient Gauls in general, but of the Massiliots, corrupted by Greek softness. Sidonius plainly says in poem 22: "And you, arbiter of the sacred pillar among the gardens of the Massiliots, a farmer equal to the Hellespontine Priapus, etc." I shall attribute to the infamous morals of the Massiliots what Servius notes on Virgil's line, Auri sacra fames:

units.la: Servius, id est, inquit, execrabiles, ut Sacræ panduntur Portæ. Tractus est autem Sermo ex more Gallorum. Nam Massilienses quoties pestilentia laborabant, unus si ex pauperibus offerebat, alendus anno integro publice & purgatiōnibus Civis. Hic post eiusdem numerum Virtutem & Vestibus sacris, circumducebatur per totam Civitatem cum exsecrationibus, ut in ipsum reciderent mala totius Civitatis, & sic præcipitabatur, &c. Agathias sua ætate Massiliam iam ex Græca Civitate iam barbaram notat factam: Nam patrio priscoque vivendi more rejecto, Imperantium Institutis usam fuisse. Massilienses porro Bella, Reliquæ contra Ligures, Gallos, Karthaginienses, aliosque Conregionales & Remotiores Populos gestas; item Victorias earundem, Triumphos, Tropæa & Exuvias; Fœdera denique cum Romanis, Hispanis, alioque, commemorant Strabo lib. iv, Justinus lib. xliii, & alij. Quin Fratres appellatos fuisse Romanorum, patet ex Panegyrico, qui Constantino & Maximiano dictus; Cujus, inquit, Civitatis antiqua Nobilitas & quondam fraterno Populi Romani nomine gloriata.
units.tr: Servius says: "That is, accursed, as sacrae panduntur portae. The expression is taken from the custom of the Gauls. For whenever the Massiliots were troubled by pestilence, one of the poor offered himself, to be fed at public expense for a whole year, and to be purified. After the year was over, he was led around the whole city, clad in sacred garments, with curses, so that the evils of the whole city might fall upon him; and then he was thrown down a cliff," and so on. In his own age Agathias notes that Massilia had already ceased to be a Greek city and had become barbarian. For, having rejected its ancestral and ancient way of living, it had adopted the institutions of its rulers. Strabo, book 4, Justin, book 43, and others record the wars the Massiliots waged against the Ligurians, the Gauls, the Carthaginians and other neighbouring and more distant peoples, and likewise their victories, triumphs, trophies and spoils, and finally their treaties with the Romans, the Spaniards and others. Indeed, that they were called brothers of the Romans is clear from the Panegyric delivered to Constantine and Maximian: "The ancient nobility of that city, which once took pride in the brotherly name of the Roman people."

units.la: Certe in magno erant Romanis honore. Princeps Rhodiorum Legationis, Oratione in Senatu Romæ habita, de iis apud Livium lib. xxxvii, sic loquitur: Massilienses, anos, si natura insita, velut ingenio terra usci posset, jam pridem efferassent tot inhumanas circumfusas Gentes, in eo honore, in ea merito dignitate audimus apud vos esse, ac si medium uni tantum Gratiæ incorerent.
units.tr: Certainly they were held in great honour by the Romans. The leader of the Rhodian embassy, in a speech given in the Senate at Rome, speaks of them in Livy, book 37, in these words: "If the Massiliots could, by their nature, as if by their own genius, have tamed the many inhuman peoples around them, we hear that they are held in such honour and esteem by you, as if they had been brought up in the lap of your favour alone."

units.la: Non enim sonum modo Linguæ Vestitumque & Habitum, sed ante omnes Mores & Leges Ingenium suscerunt, integrumque à contagione Incolarum servarunt. Colonias ex hac Urbe ductas non paucas indicant idem Scriptores. Iustinus: Qui periculo propulsando in tantum extenuerunt, ut victis Hostibus in captivis Agris multas Colonias constituerent.
units.tr: For they took on not only the sound of the language, clothing and dress, but above all the morals and laws and character, and they kept themselves untouched by the contagion of the inhabitants. The same writers indicate that not a few colonies were led out from this city. Justin: "Who, in repelling danger, so reduced the enemy that, having defeated them, they founded many colonies on the captured lands."

units.la: Quos autem Ritus servare fuerint soliti in Coloniis deducendis, sic notat Strabo: Ἐντὶ ζῶις Ἀπολλωνιαῖς Ἀρτεμιδος ... (loquitur de Aristarcha) ... Ephesiæ Sacra, more patrio, tradidisse; &, ut Græcanicis Ritibus immolarent, jussisse. Colonias enumerat variis locis idem Strabo; in iis Aphrodisium Pyrenæorum Promontorium, Agatham, Antipolin, Nicæam: & alia, quæ ipsa nomina satis arguunt. Concussa supra modum fuit ejus Felicitas anno i. Belli Civilis inter Cn. Pompeium Magnum & C. Iulium Cæsarem, cujus in eam Victoria fuit talis, tamque moderata, ut pro Nomine & Vetustate potius, quam pro Meritis salva ipsi sua relicta fuerit Libertas. Legendi, præter Cæsarem ipsum, Strabo lib.v,& Lucanus lib. iii. de Bello Civili: Ab Gothis postea captam, posteriores ævi scribunt Auctores. Iornandes in Histor. Gothor. Et quomodo Euricus Rex Visegothorum Romani Regni vacillationem cernens, Arelatum & Massiliam propria subdidit Ditioni. Isidorus in Chronic. Era 1 ii: In Galliis autem regressus, Arelatum & Massiliam Urbes capit, suoque Regno utramque subjecit. Sigebertus in Chronic. ad annum ccccLxxi, Arelatum & Massiliam Galliarum Urbes invasit.
units.tr: Strabo notes what rites they were accustomed to keep when founding colonies: "... (he speaks of Aristarchus) ... that he had handed over the sacred rites of Ephesian Artemis according to the ancestral custom, and ordered that they sacrifice according to Greek rites" [Ἐντὶ ζῶις Ἀπολλωνιαῖς Ἀρτεμιδος ...]. Strabo lists colonies in various places; among them are Aphrodisium, a promontory of the Pyrenees, Agatha, Antipolis, Nicaea, and others, whose very names are sufficient proof. Its prosperity was shaken beyond measure in the first year of the civil war between Gnaeus Pompey the Great and Gaius Julius Caesar. Caesar's victory over it was of such a kind, and so moderate, that its liberty was left intact for it, in consideration of its name and antiquity rather than its deserts. Besides Caesar himself, one should read Strabo, book 5, and Lucan, book 3, of the Civil War. Later writers say that it was afterwards captured by the Goths. Jordanes, in his History of the Goths: "And when Euric, king of the Visigoths, saw the Roman kingdom wavering, he brought Arles and Marseille under his own dominion." Isidore in his Chronicle, era 1 ii: In Galliis autem regressus, Arelatum & Massiliam Urbes capit, suoque Regno utramque subjecit. Sigebert in his Chronicle, at the year 471: Arelatum & Massiliam Galliarum Urbes invasit.

units.la: Mercatus hic olim fuit, ut memoriæ prodit Strabo lib. iv, bonarum Artium & Disciplinarum celeberrimus. Eo, tanquam ad alteras Athenas, Romani, Galli, Hispani, omnesque, quibus licebat Philosophiæ Græcæque Linguæ gratia se conferebant. Tentatur Tacitus in Vita Agricolæ Soceri, cum parvulum sedem ac Magistram Studiorum habuisse Massiliam; Locum, ut antea etiam monui, Græca Comitate & Provinciali Parsimonia mistum benequecompositum. Hæc Eumenidis, qui tam accurate quæsivit de Nilo; Hæc Pythea quem tam studiose insectatur Strabo: Hæc aliorum, quorum, Scripta intercidernt, fuit, Patria. Hic verisimile est Philosophiam didicisse Favorinum Arelatensem. Hæc Gallos omnes ita φιλολογίας reddebat, ut ἐκ ζῶν συμβόλαια ἐπιστολῶν γεγράφειν, ut Contractus omnes Græco Idiomate conficerent, & in omnibus publicis privatisque Rationibus Græcis Litteris uterentur, Strabone Teste. Inde Tabulæ in Helvetiorum Castris repertæ Græco Charactere conscriptæ, ad Cæsarem perlatæ, ut in Ephemeridibus Belli Gallici est legere. Hinc hodieque tam frequens in Gallo-Romano sermone Hellenismus. Alia prætereo: Nam plura à me alibi notata. Habuisse Massilienses Navalia & Armamentarium, copiam item Navium, Armorum, Machinarum, quibus & contra Barbaros se tuebantur & Romanorum societatem sibi compararunt, tradit idem Strabo: qui & Territorium ipsorum celebrat, Ἐλαιοφόρον ... Vinum Vinum Mafsiliensis esse Athenaeus esse κὰὶ ἐν, sed ὀλίγον, ἐ πᾶχὺ καὶ σαχαρῶδες. Ostrea Massiliensia laudat Antonius Epist. xiii; eadem fere cum ipsis, quae Strabo magna copia repetiri scribit in Rodani ostiis Lacteres apud Massilienses fieri, qui projecti in aquam natant, ut ait Vitruvius. Incolas Trilingues fuisse, ut qui Graece, Latine, Gallicėque loquerentur, refert ex Varrone D. Hieronymus. Digna igitur maximis Elogiis Massilia, cum quod tantae Antonitatis, tum quod hodieque situ opereque sit pulcher potens, Regnique suo fidelissima; quod item suorum Incolarum industria per Asiam, Africam, atque remotissimas Regiones longe lateque negotietur. Theatrale & nunc fere servat formam; sed ita, ut in Septemtrione Cornu portio sit Civitatis Austrahore Collis, in quo Monumenta, quae vulgo Le Fort de Notre Dame de la Garde, & de S. Nicolas, adjacente Colli domo cubernatoris cum Armamenta in Interutrumque Cornu Portus est; cum praecedent insulae, vulgo Les Pommeres, in quarum una Stationem navium habuit D. Iunius Brutus, quam Urbs ab Caesare, cujus ille erat Legatus, esset obsessa. Vitatur ibi hoc tempore Arx, quae vernacule Le Chateau Fit. Urbe per Portam Franciscam egresso ad sinistram se offerunt magna Aqueductum Rudera, quae ad ipsum Opidum jungantur Memimento, quod inter eamdem Franciscam & Aquensem Portas, Magnum cognomine. Episcopos hic numerant ab D. Lazaro, quem Christus ab morte suscitavit. Eum bonis facibusque exeuntem, saeviente Persecutione, quae Stephanum absultarat, cum sororibus Maria Magdalena & Martha in has oras venisse, Christique fidem nuncupasse, narrant Massilienses. Quin & caput ejus monstrant in Primario templo: quod incolis La Mattre, ad urbis Moenia, versus Mare. Haec de Massilia: reliquae urbes Episcopales sunt: Dune: Dunes Plinio in Ebroduntius; Aima Prolemaeo in tentus. Graeci, Gratiolae, Glandeve, Glannatae, Viris Doctis Latine scribentibus, Glannatena Civitas, Notitiae Provinciarum Galliae in Viennensi iv: in aliis libris est Glanatina, in quibusdam Glanaticona. Glandeves sic Episcopi meminit concilium Aurelianum vi. Falluntur, qui Glanum Plinii, Pomponii & Antonini cum Glannate confundunt. Glanum enim Antoninus ponit inter Cabellionem & Arelatum: at quam procul inde Glannate? Quid Glanum hodie, ignoratur. Senas, Σανίσσος, Veldantiorum opidum in Alpibus Maritimis, Ptolemaeo. S. Paul de Vences, οὐντιον, Nerutiorum Opidum in Alpibus Maritimis, Ptolemaeo, οὐνλια, Dioni lib. xxxvii. Apt. Apta Julia Vulgentium Plinio, Arva Julia & Abtenulia corrupte apud Antoninum: Nam in melioribus est apta Julia: ut & in Itineraria Tabula. Aptensis Episcopatus memineruntconcilium Aurelianense, & alia. Ries, Reins Notitiae Provinciarum Galliae, in qua sub Viennensi iii sic legitur, Civitas Reiensium, id est Reias. In Tabula Itineraria, ut paullo ante dixi, scriptum est, Reis Apollinaris; quod nondum liquet. Fersus Forum Julii Planco Imperatori Epistola ad M. Tullium, addenti abesse ab Foro Voconii xx. M.P. Tabula Itineraria inter Forum Voconii & Forum Julii notat xvii. M.P. Φέρωμ Ἰουλίου, Commonorum urbs Ptolemaeo; col. ivl octav. in Augusti Nummo apud Hubertum Goltzium: Forum Julium Clavanorum Colonia, quae Pacensis appellatur & Classica, Plinio lib. iii. cap. iv. τὰ Ναυτὰ θόμεσ ἐκ καίουχον ἐξ ἰάω, inquit Strabo lib. iv: Et hodie Portus est marinus. Cesserum, Segeslera apud Antoninum & in itineraria tabula: Cettero inquit suis ad me litteris Iosephus Scaliger, Plinio; apud quem tamen excusum est Cessero. Sed mihi semper Plinian Cessero eadem censeri solet cum ea, quae Ksarιo apud Ptolemaeum, Tolosae & Carcassonm connumerata, quae hodie in Languedokio Castres, ut ibi monui. Plinius enim Ceferonem locat inter Opida Volcarum Tectosagum, qui ad dextram Rodani ripam. Tolon, Telonum Doctis Latine scribentibus: Telo Martius, Antonino, Opidum in interiore Maris recessu, novem Leucis Massilia.
units.tr: This city was once a famous market and a most celebrated seat of the liberal arts and disciplines, as Strabo records in book 4. To it, as to a second Athens, came Romans, Gauls, Spaniards, and everyone else who could afford it, for the sake of philosophy and the Greek language. Tacitus, in the Life of his father-in-law Agricola, says that Massilia was a small seat and a teacher of studies, a place that, as I have also said before, combined Greek refinement with provincial thrift and was well ordered. This was the homeland of Eumenides, who investigated the Nile so carefully, and of Pytheas, whom Strabo attacks so eagerly, and of others whose writings have perished. It is likely that Favorinus of Arles learned philosophy here. The city so devoted all the Gauls to Greek learning that they drew up their contracts in writing from living speech (ἐκ τῶν ζῶν συμβολαίων [ek tōn zōn symbolaiōn]) and used Greek letters in all public and private accounts, as Strabo attests. Hence the tablets found in the camps of the Helvetii, written in Greek characters and brought to Caesar, as one can read in the Commentaries on the Gallic War. Hence, even today, Hellenisms are so frequent in the Gallo-Roman speech. I pass over other matters, since I have noted many of them elsewhere. The same Strabo reports that the Massilians had docks and an arsenal, and a supply of ships, arms and engines, with which they defended themselves against the barbarians and secured the alliance of the Romans. He also praises their territory as olive-bearing (Ἐλαιοφόρον [Elaiophoron]). Athenaeus says that the wine of Massilia is also good, but in small quantity, and not strong and sugary (καλὸν ... ὀλίγον [kalon ... oligon]). Antonius, in Epistle 13, praises the oysters of Massilia. Strabo writes that the same kind of creatures, which he says are gathered in great numbers at the mouths of the Rhône, are called lacteres by the Massilians; they are cast into the water and float, as Vitruvius says. Jerome, citing Varro, reports that the inhabitants were trilingual, speaking Greek, Latin and Gallic. Massilia therefore deserves the highest praise, both for its great antiquity and because even today it is beautiful, powerful and most faithful to its king by its situation and its fortifications; likewise, through the industry of its citizens, it trades far and wide throughout Asia, Africa and the most remote regions. It still nearly keeps the shape of a theatre, but in such a way that on the northern horn of the city there is a part of the town, and on the southern hill stand the monuments commonly called the fort of Notre Dame de la Garde and of Saint Nicholas, with the governor's house beside the hill. On either horn of the city is a harbour, and in front of them lie islands, commonly called Les Pommeres, on one of which Decimus Junius Brutus had his naval station when the city was besieged by Caesar, whose legate he was. Today the citadel, which is vernacularly called Le Château If, is seen there. Leaving the city by the Porta Franciscana, on the left there appear the great ruins of an aqueduct, which connect to the town itself; note that it lies between the Porta Franciscana and the Porta Aquensis, and is called the Great. Here they count bishops from Saint Lazarus, whom Christ raised from the dead. The Massilians relate that he, having fled from his property during the persecution that had raged against Stephen, came to these shores with his sisters Mary Magdalene and Martha, and professed faith in Christ. Indeed they show his head in the principal church, which the inhabitants call La Major, near the city walls towards the sea. So much for Massilia. The other cities with bishoprics are these: Digne (Dunes, in Pliny; Dinia, in Ptolemy's Digne; Ebrodunum). Glandève (Glannatena civitas, in the Notitia of the Provinces of Gaul under Vienne, as learned writers write in Latin; in other books it is Glanatina, and in some Glanaticona). The Council of Orléans (vi) also mentions a bishop of Glandève. Those who confuse Glanum of Pliny, Pomponius and Antoninus with Glannate are mistaken, for Antoninus places Glanum between Cabellio and Arelate; but how far from there is Glannate? What Glanum is today is unknown. Senez (Sanisson, a town of the Vediantii in the Maritime Alps, according to Ptolemy). Saint-Paul-de-Vence (Vintium, a town of the Nerusii in the Maritime Alps, according to Ptolemy; Ounelia, according to Dio, book 37). Apt (Apta Julia of the Vulgientes in Pliny; Arva Julia and Abtenulia, corruptly in Antoninus, for the better manuscripts have Apta Julia, as also in the Itinerary Table). The bishopric of Apt is mentioned by the Council of Orléans and others. Riez (Reii, in the Notitia of the Provinces of Gaul, where under Vienne iii it is read thus: the civitas of the Reienses, that is, Reia). In the Itinerary Table, as I said a little earlier, it is written Reis Apollinaris, which is still unclear. Fréjus (Forum Julii; a letter of Plancus, the emperor, to Cicero, adds that it is twenty miles from Forum Voconii; the Itinerary Table notes seventeen miles between Forum Voconii and Forum Julii). Pheroum Iulii (Commonorum urbs, according to Ptolemy; Col. Iul. Octav. on a coin of Augustus in Hubert Goltzius; Forum Julium, colony of the Clavenni, which is called Pacensis and Classica, in Pliny, book 3, chapter 4). Strabo, book 4, says that there the harbour was built by the ... and it is still a sea port today. Furthermore, Segesteria in Antoninus and in the Itinerary Table; Josephus Scaliger writes to me in his letters that in Pliny it is Cettero, though it has been printed as Cessero there. But to me the Plinian Cessero is always thought to be the same as the Ksarion of Ptolemy, numbered among the Tolosates and Carcassonne, which today is Castres in Languedoc, as I have noted there. For Pliny places Ceferon among the towns of the Volcae Tectosages, who live on the right bank of the Rhône. Toulon (Telonum, to learned writers writing in Latin; Telo Martius, in Antoninus, a town in the inner recess of the sea, nine leagues from Massilia).

units.la: Haec de Episcopalibus: sunt alia non minoris nominis & antiquitatis opida: Antibes; Ἀντίπολις, Deciatorum opidum Ptolemaeo; Opidum Latinum, Antipolis, Plinio: Tacitus Antipolim Narbonensis Galliae Municipium appellat. Colonian vocat Nummus Titi imperatoris: Meminit Ἀντίπολις, & Strabo, scribens inter eam & Olbiam constructum esse Forum Julium. Olbia tanc, quae & Ptolemaeo Melaque nota, Teres vel Hieres hodie centetur ad Mare, tribus fere leucis Telono. Contra Opidum jacent nobilissimae insulae, quae Ptolemaeo Σαμχαδὲς, Ἀνγυσίδες Stephano & Apollonio lib. iv. De ius lib. ultimo. Hodie, Opido cognominies, Les Isles dicuntur de Teres, vel vio. Sedem præbet non solum Episcopatui Novo, quem delibatum dixi supra de Aginnensi; verum etiam Senefchalliæ, jus dicenti Opidis, quæ Indigenis, Valence ad Rufam, Lairac ad Garumnam, La-Romeo, Alon-Real, & aliis. Familiæ sunt hic illustres non paucæ. Vicecomites novimus hic Efmaconos, Gourdonos, Forcaos, & Monlucios. Ducatus Allebret, La Duché d'Allebret, nomen accepit amplissimum ab opidulo, quod vulgo Allebret, in Syrtibus Lapurdensibus, quas Landas vocant. Institutus est ante annos non multos, compositus ex mutilatione Senefchalliarum Aginnensis, Armaniacensi, & Vasatensis; adeo ut de eo dicere liceat, quod de Constantinopoli Hieronymus, eam nuditate omnium Civitatum constructam fuisse. Caput Ducatus est Neracum, opidum prædiues. Avorum nostrorum memoria Ioannes Alani F. Dynasta Allebretanus, ducta Katharina Gastonis F. Navarræ Regnum cum ea Dotem accepit: hujus ex Filio Henrico Neptis fuit Ioanna Allebretana, Navarræ Regina, Mater Henrici IV, Christianissimi Franciæ Navarræque Regis. Convenarum Comitatus, La Comté de Comminges: Vulgo Latinorum Cominogia. Huius Tractus Incolæ Primi Aquitanorum Christianæ Militiæ nomen dedisse scribuntur, multa indigna perpessi ab Christiani nominis Hostibus. Dividitur Convenarum Ager in Superiorem & Inferiorem, totusque Montibus attollitur. Gentis Caput Lugdunum Convenarum; Ἀσγού Κεντεων (legendum Κονβεων) Ptolemæo & Straboни lib. iv; Lugdunum simpliciter Antonino, in Itinere ab Aginno ad hoc opidum: quod quum per multos annos summopere floruisset, tandem ab irato Guntchranni Regis exercitu fuit diruetum, anno 1ɔʟxxxıv, Indictione 11: ex cujus reliquiis Fanum S. Bertrandi, ubi hodie Sedes est Episcopalis, in Valle Capraria fuit constructum. Vetustatem & Splendorem ejus Civitatis facile testantur Monumenta & Epigraphæ quamplurimæ, quæ ibi hodie exstant. Coluerunt inter alios Deos Lugdunenses Convenæ, aliique forte Concregionales, Abelionem: de quo quidam ibi Lapides, ut alibi vidimus, ubi de Diis Gallorum. Quid in Inscriptione, quæ Romæ legitur in ædibus Mellinorum ad Agonem, sit Covena Aquitania, alij videant. Ea sic habet:
units.tr: These are the episcopal cities; there are others of no less renown and antiquity: Antibes (Antipolis, in Greek Ἀντίπολις [Antipolis]; Deciatorum oppidum, in Ptolemy; Oppidum Latinum, Antipolis, in Pliny). Tacitus calls Antipolis a municipium of Narbonese Gaul. A coin of the emperor Titus calls it a colony. Strabo also mentions Antipolis, writing that Forum Julium was founded between it and Olbia. Olbia, which is also known to Ptolemy as Melaque, is today thought to be Hyères, almost three leagues from Toulon on the sea. Opposite the town lie the most noble islands, which Ptolemy calls Stoechades, Stephanus and Apollonius (book 4) call Ankysides, and in the last book of Dio ... Today, named after the town, they are called the Îles d'Hyères. The town provides a seat not only for the new bishopric I mentioned above, of Agen, but also for the seneschalty that administers justice in the towns, which the natives call Valence-sur-Baïse, Lauzerte on the Garonne, La Romieu, Alan-Réal and others. There are not a few illustrious families here. We know of the viscounts Esmaconus, Gourdon, Forcas and Montluc. The Duchy of Albret (La Duché d'Albret) took its very ample name from a small town, commonly called Albret, in the Lapurdensian sandbanks, which they call the Landes. It was established not many years ago, put together from the mutilation of the seneschalties of Agenais, Armagnac and Vasatensis; so that one may say of it what Jerome said of Constantinople, that it was built from the nakedness of all the cities. The capital of the duchy is Nérac, a wealthy town. In the memory of our grandfathers, John, son of Alan, lord of Albret, having married Catherine, daughter of Gaston, received the kingdom of Navarre as her dowry. From his son Henry, his granddaughter was Joan of Albret, Queen of Navarre, mother of Henry IV, most Christian King of France and Navarre. The County of the Convenae (La Comté de Comminges), in the Latin of the vulgar, Cominogia. It is written that the first inhabitants of this district gave the name of the Christian militia to the Aquitanians, having suffered many unworthy things from the enemies of the Christian name. The territory of the Convenae is divided into Upper and Lower, and the whole is raised by mountains. The head of the people is Lugdunum of the Convenae (Ἀσγού Κεντεων [Asgou Kenteōn], to be read Κονβεων [Konbeōn], in Ptolemy and Strabo, book 4); Antoninus simply calls it Lugdunum, on the road from Agen to this town. Although it had flourished greatly for many years, it was at last destroyed by the angry army of King Guntram in the year 585, indiction 11; from its remains the Fanum of Saint Bertrand, where the episcopal see is today, was built in the Valley of Capraria. The antiquity and splendour of this city are easily attested by the very many monuments and inscriptions that still exist there today. Among other gods the Lugdunenses and Convenae, and perhaps other neighbouring peoples, worshipped Abellio, about whom certain stones are found there, as we have seen elsewhere, where we discuss the gods of the Gauls. Others may consider what is meant by "Covena Aquitania" in the inscription that is read in Rome in the house of the Mellini at the Agonalis; it reads thus:

units.la: { } D. M. VALERIÆ IVSTINÆ NATA CONVENA AQVITANIA VIXIT ANNOS XXI IVN. VALERIANVS MIL. COH. III. PR. 7. FELICIS. CONI. F. M. F.
units.tr: To the divine Manes. Valeria Justina, a native of Convena in Aquitaine, lived 21 years, June. Valerianus, soldier of the third cohort, praetorian, of the century of Felix, son of Conius, set this up. M. F.

units.la: Vasconis priusquam egrediar, addam tria verba de Elusatium Agro, qui vulgo Le Pais d'Eufe en Gascoigne. Ejus Metropolis Elusa. Sic dicitur Ammiano Marcellino lib. xv, & Itinerario, quod Burdigala ducit Hierosolymas; quæ Paulino Epistola ad Severum vi. Elusso. Ammiani verba, quod corruptiora, adscribam: In Narbonensi Elusa, & Narbo, & Tolosa, & principatum urbium tenent: Viennensis Civitatum exsultat decore multarum: quibus potiores sunt Vienna ipsa & Arelate & Valentia, quibus Massilia jungitur. Pro Elusa vulgati Codices habebant Clusa. Hinc Elusana Plebs apud Sulpitium Severum Historiæ Sacræ lib. II. Fuisse videtur olim Episcopatus. Laban Elusensis Episcopus nominatur Gregorio Turonensi lib. viii. cap. xxii.
units.tr: Before I leave the Vascones, I will add a few words about the territory of the Elusates, which is commonly called Le Pais d'Eufe en Gascoigne. Its metropolis is Elusa. So Ammianus Marcellinus calls it in book 15, and so does the Itinerary that runs from Burdigala to Jerusalem; in Paulinus's letter to Severus, number 6, it is Elusso. I will quote Ammianus's words, which are rather corrupt: In Narbonensi Elusa, & Narbo, & Tolosa, & principatum urbium tenent: Viennensis Civitatum exsultat decore multarum: quibus potiores sunt Vienna ipsa & Arelate & Valentia, quibus Massilia jungitur. In place of Elusa, the printed codices had Clusa. Hence the Elusana plebs in Sulpicius Severus, Sacred History book II. It seems there was once a bishopric there: Laban Elusensis Episcopus is named by Gregory of Tours, book 8, chapter 22.

units.la: CAP. XXXIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXIX.

units.la: Provincia.
units.tr: Provence.

units.la: PROVINCIAS Parlamentis subjectas Accessorijs, Parisiensequeque illud ad Occidentem Meridiemque quasi circumeuntibus, quanta fieri potuit industria perlustravi: sequuntur jamnunc Regiones, quae reliquis parent Tribunalibus, Orientaliora ejusdem Parisiensis Latera velut claudentibus. Ea sunt Aquensis, Gratianopolitanum, Divionense. Aquensis Iurisdictioni obtemperat Provincia.
units.tr: I have gone through the PROVINCES subject to the Parlements, as far as diligence allowed, circling round the Parisian region to the west and south. Now follow the regions that obey the other courts, lying along the eastern flank of the Parisian region. These are Aix, Grenoble and Dijon. Provence falls under the jurisdiction of Aix.

units.la: Vnde & qua occasione Provinciæ nomen inditum praestantissimo huic Galliarum Tractui, etiam ultra Rodanum ad Garumnam usque, petendum est ex Capite huius libri xvi; ubi omnia Romanorum contra Veteres Gallos Bella paucis commemorantur. Narbonensis enim Gallia ab Romanis in Provincia formam multis ante Christum natum annis redacta, hodieque illud impositæ quondam conditionis nomen mordicus in exigua sui portione, in qua Massilia & Aquæ Sextiæ, retinet, κατ' ἐξοχὴν quasi & αὐτονομαςικὼς, utque ostenderet se Primam, non quidem ordine, sed dignitate inter omnes Imperij Romani fuisse Provincias. Est enim totus ille Narbonensis Ager pars totius Franciæ praestantissima. Paucis Plinius lib. iii. cap. iv, Agrorum cultu; Virorum Morumque dignatione, amplitudine opum nulli Provinciarum post ferenda, breviterque Italia verius, quam Provincia. Provincia sane, de qua mihi sermo, praeter Segetes, Fructus profert, non solicita cultura, nobilissimos. Vvarum Passarum Ficuumque tanta hic Copia, ut potiori Europæ sufficiat. Ros. Marinus, Myrtus, Iuniperi Baccæ, aliaque id genus larga hic manu ab Natura proveniunt. Castaneæ nusquam majores. Mala Citria, Cydonia, Granata; item Crocus, Oryza, similiaque pleno ibidem cornu funduntur. Vites generosissima dant Vina. Solum denique passim gratum, ferax, benignum: Cœlum mite, clemens, & valde purgatum. Conjacet Provincia ad Septemtrionem Delphinatus, Montium interpositu Velaxorum, qui vulgo Velaye, intercursuque magnam partem Druentij Fluminis; Orientale ejus Latus claudunt & Alpes, & Varus Fluvius, cujus sinistræ Ripæ adsidet Nicæa, Italiæ hic principium; qua Meridies est, ab Gallico pulsatur Mari: Occidentalis illi Limes partim Araufiorum Principatus & Avenionensis vel Venissæ Comitatus, hujus quondam Partes. Francorumque Ditionis, nunc autem aliorum Principum; partim Rodanus, integer, Lugduno Arelatem usque, ad Languedokij Parlamenti Iurisdictiones, ut antea dixi, spectans.
units.tr: Where and on what occasion the name Province was given to this outstanding region of Gaul, which extends beyond the Rhône as far as the Garonne, must be sought in chapter xvi of this book, where all the Roman wars against the ancient Gauls are briefly recounted. Narbonese Gaul, reduced to the form of a Province by the Romans many years before the birth of Christ, still keeps stubbornly, in a small part of itself where Marseilles and Aix lie, the name of its former status, as if it were the Province par excellence (κατ' ἐξοχήν) and by its very name (αὐτονομαστικῶς), so as to show that it was the first of all the provinces of the Roman Empire, not in rank but in dignity. For that whole Narbonese territory is the most outstanding part of all France. Pliny says briefly (book iii, chapter iv): for the cultivation of its fields, for the worth of its men and manners, and for the abundance of its wealth, it is second to no province, and it is, in short, more truly Italy than a province. Province indeed, the land I am speaking of, yields, besides grain and fruit, very noble produce without anxious cultivation. There is such an abundance of raisins, figs and olives here that it would suffice for the greater part of Europe. Rosemary, myrtle, juniper berries and other things of that kind are produced here by nature with a generous hand. Chestnuts are nowhere larger. Citrons, quinces and pomegranates, as well as saffron, rice and similar things, pour forth here in full horn of plenty. The vines give very fine wines. The soil is everywhere pleasant, fertile and kindly, and the sky is mild, gentle and very clear. Province lies to the north of Dauphiné, separated by the Vaucluse mountains, which the common people call the Velaye, and by the course of a large part of the river Durance. Its eastern side is bounded by the Alps and by the river Var, on whose left bank stands Nice, the beginning of Italy here. Where it faces south it is beaten by the Gallic sea. Its western boundary is partly the principality of Orange and the county of Avignon or Venaissin, once parts of this province, which belonged to the Franks but now to other princes, and partly the Rhône, which, whole, from Lyon as far as Arles, belongs, as I said before, to the jurisdiction of the Parlement of Languedoc.

units.la: Habitarunt hic olim Salii, Aquenses, Arelatenses, Sextani, Sentij, Ebroduntij, Dinienses, Vesdiantij, Sanicienses, Nerufij, Vencienses, Vulgientes, Aptenses, Reienses, Octavani, Commoni, Foro-Iulienses, Segeflorij, Albici, Oxnbij, Deciates, & alij.
units.tr: Once there lived here the Salii, Aquenses, Arelatenses, Sextani, Sentii, Ebrodunti, Dinienses, Vesdiantii, Sanicienses, Nerusii, Vencienses, Vulgientes, Aptenses, Reienses, Octavani, Commoni, Forojulienses, Segeflorii, Albici, Oxybii, Deciates, and others.

units.la: Salyos primo posui loco. Sallyi sunt Plinio: Σαλυες Straboni, Αιγυαε olim, id est Ligures vocatos addenti, eorumque Regionem Αιγυστικὴν: unde & Posteriores Κελτολιγυας, Gallo-Ligures, nominarunt, ut distinguerent ab Liguribus Italiæ Populis. Ligures enim Sedes suas habuerunt longe lateque in his Galliæ oris, etiam ultra Rodanum. Σαλυκες dicuntur Ptolemæo: Salyos appellat Livius Epitome Libri lxi; Salluvies Fasti Triumphales & Ammianus Marcellinus. Olim, ubi nunc Archiepiscopatus Aquensis, quæ Civitas Aquensium in Notitia Provinciarum Galliæ, Viennensi iii, & Arelatensis, quæ & Civitas Arelatensium; Les Archevesches d'Aix & d'Arles. Certe Domicilium ipsorum non obscure notat Strabo lib. iv, ubi scribit Sextium, redactus in potestatem Salyas, non longe ab Massilia sui nominis ædificasse oppidum; de quo postea. Et de Salyis idem paullo post: Ἀμα δ' ἡ̓τε τῶν Σαλύων ἐξῆνε ἐπὶ τὰς Αρελατ ... Habitasse eos satis ample, docet idem his verbis: ... Ptolemæus Salyum opida inter alia nominat Arelatum & Aquas Sextias. Pagum Provinciæ, qui Soltes vulgo, Veteris Appellationis vestigium servare censet Dalechampius. Ab his Salyis Francos Salios, legemque Salicam, nomen habere putat Gulielmus Bellaius Langius apud Paradinum de antiquo Statu Burgundiæ. Mihi alia mens est, ut docco in Germania. Inter Salyos habitasse Sextanos constat ex Plinio lib. iii, Pomponioque lib. ii. qui Arelatem ijs adjungunt: Sextani dicti, quod Milites essent vi. Legionis Veterani. De ijs Vetus Inscriptio, quæ Romæ eruta anno MDLXII:
units.tr: I have placed the Salyi first. The Sallyi are in Pliny; Σαλυες [Salyes] in Strabo; they were once also called Αιγυες, that is, Ligures, as he adds, and their region was called Αἰγυστική [Aigystike]. Hence later writers also called them Κελτολιγυες [Keltoligyes], Gallo-Ligures, to distinguish them from the Ligurians of Italy. For the Ligures had their seats far and wide along these shores of Gaul, even beyond the Rhône. Ptolemy calls them Σαλυκες [Salykes]; Livy in the Epitome of book lxi calls them Salyos; the Triumphal Fasti and Ammianus Marcellinus call them Salluvies. Formerly, where the archbishopric of Aix now is, was the City of the Aquenses in the Notitia of the Provinces of Gaul, Vienne iii, and the Arelatensis, which is also the City of the Arelatenses; Les Archevesches d'Aix & d'Arles. Certainly Strabo, book iv, clearly marks their dwelling, where he writes that Sextius, having reduced the Salyes to his power, built a town bearing his name not far from Marseilles, about which more later. And of the Salyes the same author says a little later: Ἅμα δ' ἡ τε τῶν Σαλύων ἐξῆνε ἐπὶ τὰς Ἀρελατ ... [Hama d' hē te tōn Salyōn exēne epi tas Arelat ...]. That they lived quite extensively, the same author shows in these words: ... Ptolemy names among the Salyan towns, besides others, Arelatum and Aquae Sextiae. The district of the Province which is commonly called Soltes, Dalechampius thinks, preserves a trace of the old name. Gulielmus Bellaius Langius, quoted by Paradin in his work on the ancient state of Burgundy, thinks that the Frankish Salii and the Salic law take their name from these Salyes. My own view is different, as I show in my work on Germany. That the Sextani lived among the Salyes is clear from Pliny, book iii, and from Pomponius, book ii, who join them to Arles: they were called Sextani because they were veterans of the sixth Legion. An ancient inscription concerning them, dug up at Rome in the year 1562:

units.la: DIVAE FAVSTINAE AVG SEXTANI ARELATENSE- S
units.tr: To the deified Faustina Augusta: the Sextani of Arelate

units.la: Sentij, Σέντις Ptolemæo; Ebroduntij videntur esse Plinio lib. iii. cap. iv. Nam utrumque Civitatem ijs tribuit Diniam. Civitas Dinienfium Notitiæ Provinciarum in Viennensi iv & Alpibus Maritimis. Plinius auctor est Galbam imperatorem Narbonensi Provinciæ adjecisse ex Inalpinis Gentibus Ebrodunties. Vesdiantij, Οὐεσδιάντοι, Ptolemæo; Vedantij, Plinio. Eorum Metropolis Sanitium, Senas hodie: Notitiæ Civitas Sanicienfium, L'Evesché de Senás. Nerufij Plinio in Alpibus Maritimis, ubi hodie Ventium, S. Paul de Vences: Notitiæ Civitas Vencienfium, l'Evesché de S. Paul de Vences. Vulgientes Plinio. Aptam Iuliam ijs Metropolim tribuenti, sunt, qui Vulcientes in Fastis Triumphalibus, ab Verrio Flacco concinnatis. Civitas Aptenfium Notitiæ Provinciarum in Viennensi iii, L'Evesché d'Apt, ubi male Athenfium. Civitas Reienfium, legitur in eadem Notitia, L'evesché de Riés: Regenses Galliæ Narbonensis Populis connumerat Sidonius lib. vi. Epist. ad Papam Patientem: apud quem reponendi Reienses. Reis Apollinaris, quod in Itineraria legitur Tabula, Long. xxii. Lat. viii. huc videtur pertinere, nihil tamen certi affirmo. Octavani Plinio in melioribus Codicibus, qui Octaviani in Vulgatis, quique Octoviani Pomponio Melæ, ijdem forte cum Commonis Ptolemæi. Forum Iulij, quod Octavanorum Coloniam facit Mela, apud Ptolemæum Commonis tribuitur, apud Plinium autem Pacensis & Classica vocatur. Est & in Augusti Nummo apud Goltzium, COL. IVL. OCTAV. Civitas Forojulienfium est in Notitia Provinciarum sub Viennensi iii. Meminit ejusdem Lapis, qui Nemausi in Horto Ioannis Poldi, Antiquitatum Nemausensium descriptoris:
units.tr: Sentii, Σέντις in Ptolemy; Ebroduntii seem to be in Pliny book 3, chapter 4. For he assigns to both of them the city of Dinia. The city of the Diniensians is in the Notitia Provinciarum under Vienne, section iv, and the Maritime Alps. Pliny reports that the emperor Galba added the Ebrodunties from the Inalpine peoples to the province of Narbonne. Vesdiantii, Οὐεσδιάντοι in Ptolemy; Vedantii in Pliny. Their metropolis was Sanitium, today Senas: in the Notitia, the city of the Sanicienses, the bishopric of Senas. Nerusii in Pliny, in the Maritime Alps, where today is Ventium, S. Paul de Vences: in the Notitia, the city of the Vencienses, the bishopric of S. Paul de Vences. Vulgientes in Pliny. Those who make Apta Julia their metropolis are those who read Vulcientes in the Triumphal Fasti compiled by Verrius Flaccus. The city of the Aptenses is in the Notitia Provinciarum under Vienne, section iii, the bishopric of Apt, where it is wrongly given as Athenses. The city of the Reienses is read in the same Notitia, the bishopric of Riez: Sidonius, book 6, letter to Pope Patiens, counts the Regenses among the peoples of Gallia Narbonensis, where Reienses should be restored. Reis Apollinaris, which is read in the Itinerary Table, long. 22, lat. 8, seems to belong here, though I affirm nothing certain. The Octavani of Pliny in the better manuscripts, the Octaviani in the printed editions, and the Octoviani of Pomponius Mela, are perhaps the same as the Commones of Ptolemy. The Forum Julii, which Mela makes the colony of the Octavani, is assigned by Ptolemy to the Commones, while Pliny calls it Pacensis and Classica. There is also a coin of Augustus in Goltzius with COL. IVL. OCTAV. The city of the Forojulienses is in the Notitia Provinciarum under Vienne, section iii. The same name is found on an inscription that is in the garden of Johannes Polus in Nîmes, the describer of the antiquities of Nemausus:

units.la: Q. SOLONIO. Q. F. VOL SEVERINO EX V. DECVRIIS. EQVO PVBLICO ℨ LVPERCO IIII. VIR. AB. AERAR. PONTIFIC. FLAMINI. PROVINCIÆ NARBONENSIS. TRIB. MILITVM. LEG. VIII. AVG. CIVITAS. FOROIVLIENSIVM PATRONO
units.tr: To Quintus Solonius Severinus, son of Quintus, of the Voltinian tribe, from the five decuries, public horseman, Luperc, quattuorvir with judicial power, pontiff, flamen of the province of Narbonne, military tribune of Legio VIII Augusta: the colony of the Forojulienses to its patron.

units.la: Hodie L'Evesché de Feriuls. Segestorites notat melioris notæ Notitia Provinciarum, sub Viennensi, quam dixi. III. eorum mentionem faciens Civitatis, quæ hodie L'Evesché de Sisteron. Segestory corrupte nominantur Seltei in Itineraria Tabula, VII. Lat. XXV. Long. ut mihi quidem videtur. Certe si non illi, qui tandem sint Selters, nescio. Albicos Populos, Montes supra Massiliam incolentes habet Cæsar lib. I. Bell. Civil. Putant nonnulli eosdem esse cum Albensibus, de quibus in Languedokio. Sunt sane non alij, quam qui nunc Ἀλβιεϛ, nunc Ἀλβιϛιϛοι apud Strabonem, eos post Salyas collocantem. Ὀξύβιοι Straboni lib. IV. & Quadrato apud Stephanum, qui Oxiby Plinio: Onelie Comitatum esse vult Pingonius; Oberrois Dalechampius. Ab his Ὀξυβίων Ἀμφὶ apud Strabonem legitur eodem libro; unde patet Oxubios littorales fuisse populos, ad Mare Mediterraneum Gallicum. Qui Deciates Plinio Melaque, censet Plinetus habitasse Loca illa, ubi nunc Comitatus Raigni; Cœnalis, ubi Draguinien, Pingonius, ubi Marri: Ego nihil habeo certi. Sunt autem hi, Δεκιάτες, Straboni; Δεκιάτοι, Ptolemæo; Δεκίαι denique, Stephano. Leguntur & præter alios apud Plinium lib. III. cap. IV. Tarasconenses & Cononenses: fabricati fortean ex Tarasconensibus, quorum Caput & Metropolis ad Rodanum Tarascon, de qua postea. Reliquos incertioris positionis Populos prætereo; quales inter alios apud Ptolemæum Ναντᾶλοι, item in Notitia Provinciarum Galliæ sub Viennensi III. Rigomagenses, Sollinienses, & Cemelevenses. Nam nihil est mihi de iis exploratî. Ex Solliniensibus Senez facit Cœnalis: Cemelevensibus Urbs forte Κεμελενόν Ptolemæo; Cemelion, Plinio; Cemenelum, Antonino; Cenez eidem Cœnali, sed dubitanti; Monte Camelione apud Leandrum.
units.tr: Today it is the bishopric of Fréjus. The better-known Notitia of the Provinces, under Vienne, which I mentioned, names Segestorites when it mentions the third of these cities, which today is the bishopric of Sisteron; they are corruptly called Segestory. In the Itinerary Table, the Seltei are at 7 lat., 25 long., as it seems to me. Certainly, if they are not those people, I do not know who the Selters are. Caesar, book 1 of the Civil War, has the Albici, a people living in the mountains above Marseille. Some think they are the same as the Albenses, who are discussed in Languedoc. They are certainly none other than those who are called Ἀλβιεϛ, or Ἀλβιϛιϛοι, in Strabo, who places them after the Salyi. The Oxybii of Strabo book 4 and of Quadratus in Stephanus, who are Oxiby in Pliny: Pingonius wants Onelie to be the county; Dalechamps says Oberrois. From these, the Ὀξυβίων Ἀμφὶ is read in Strabo in the same book; whence it is clear that the Oxubii were coastal people on the Gallic Mediterranean. Plinius thinks the Deciates of Pliny and Mela lived in the places where the county of Raigni now is; Cœnalis, where Draguignan is; Pingonius, where Marri is. I have nothing certain. They are Δεκιάτες in Strabo, Δεκιάτοι in Ptolemy, and finally Δεκίαι in Stephanus. Among others, the Tarasconenses and the Cononenses are also read in Pliny book 3, chapter 4: perhaps the latter were invented from the Tarasconenses, whose head and metropolis on the Rhône is Tarascon, which I will discuss later. I pass over the other peoples of uncertain position, such as, among others in Ptolemy, the Ναντᾶλοι, and likewise in the Notitia of the Provinces of Gaul under Vienne, section iii, the Rigomagenses, Sollinienses and Cemelevenses. For I have nothing certain about them. Cœnalis makes Senez from the Solliniensibus. The Cemelevenses may be the city Κεμελενόν in Ptolemy; Cemelion in Pliny; Cemenelum in Antoninus; Cenez to the same Cœnalis, though he is doubtful; Monte Camelione in Leandro.

units.la: Anteaquam ad hodiernam Provinciæ explicationem veniam, nonnihil dicendum mihi de Campis Lapideis, qui in hac Galliæ parte inter Massiliam & Orientalissimum Rodani Ostium. Herculis Præliorum memoriam servare eos dicit Plinius; ex eo, quod Herculem hic dimicantem contra Albiona & Bergionem Neptuni Filios, quum Tela ei defecissent, ab invocato Iove adjutum Imbre Lapidum ferunt. Credas plu isse, adeo multi & passim & late jacent. Huic Fabulæ adsentiuntur quoque Pomponius Mela, Julius Solinus, & Marcianus; quibus Strabonis sententia plane præponenda, qua certius nihil dari dicique possit. Is enim hoc modo Campum hunc depingit lib. IV: [Greek text illegible, ~40 letters] ... [Greek text illegible] ... Describit hunc eumdem Campum, quamvis non nominet, & Ventum infestantem Diodorus lib. V. Vilitur hodieque hic Campus, vocaturque Las Craux inter Arelate & Massiliam; suntque in eo Opida quædam & Vici.
units.tr: Before I come to the present description of the Province, I must say something about the Stony Plains (Campi Lapidei), which lie in this part of Gaul between Marseille and the most easterly mouth of the Rhône. Pliny says they keep the memory of Hercules' battles. For they say that when Hercules fought here against Albion and Bergion, sons of Neptune, and his weapons had run out, he was helped by Jupiter, whom he invoked, with a shower of stones. You would believe it rained, so many stones lie here, everywhere and far and wide. Pomponius Mela, Julius Solinus and Martianus also agree with this fable; but Strabo's opinion must clearly be preferred to them, for nothing more certain can be given or said. For he describes this plain in this way in book 4: [Greek text illegible, about 40 letters] ... [Greek text illegible] ... Diodorus, book 5, describes this same plain, though he does not name it, and the wind that troubles it. This plain is still inhabited today and is called Las Crau, between Arles and Marseille; and there are some towns and villages in it.

units.la: Sunt porro in Provincia sub Parlamento Aquensi, præter multa minorum gentium Opida, Vrbes, duæ quidem Archiepiscopatus, undecim autem Episcopatus dignitate nobiles. Archiepiscopales sunt Aquæ Sextiæ & Arelata.
units.tr: Furthermore, in the Province under the Parlement of Aix, apart from many towns of lesser peoples, there are two cities of archiepiscopal rank and eleven of episcopal dignity. The archiepiscopal sees are Aix and Arles.

units.la: Aquæ Sextiæ, Colonia, Latinis, Paterculo, Solino, aliisque dicuntur; quæ Γάτα Σίξνια, Κολωνία, Ptolemæo: Σιξηπλία est apud Plutarchum in Vita C. Marii: Aquæ Sextiæ Itinerariæ Tabulæ. Coloniam Iuliam Aquas vocat Lapis qui hodie Lugduni ad D. Benedicti: COL. IVL. AQVIS. ET COL. IVV. P. AREL
units.tr: Aquae Sextiae, called Colonia by Latin writers such as Paterculus and Solinus and others, which in Ptolemy is Γάτα Σίξνια or Κολωνία. Σιξηπλία is in Plutarch's Life of Marius. Aquae Sextiae in the Itinerary Table. An inscription which is today at Lyon by St Benedict calls it the Colonia Julia Aquis: COL. IVL. AQVIS. ET COL. IVV. P. AREL.

units.la: Item alius ad ipsas Aquas: P. SEXTIVS. FLORVS IIIIII. VIR. AVG. COL. IVL AQVIS. ET. COL. AREL VALERIÆ. SPVRIÆ. FLASSINÆ VXORI. PIENTISS SEX. VALERIO. PROCVLO. ET. SVIS
units.tr: Another, at the Waters themselves: To P. Sextius Florus, sevir of Augustus, of the colony Julia Aquis and of the colony Arelate Valeria; to his most devoted wife Spuria Flassina, and to Sextus Valerius Proculus and his people.

units.la: Plinius nominat Coloniam Iuliam Angustam Aquas Sextias Monimentum, quod in Agro Arelatensi hodie repertum notat ad Ausonium lib. 1. cap. xxx, Vir Nobilissimus Iosephus Scaliger: M. FRONTONI. EVPOR IIIIII. VIR. AVG. COL. IVLIA AVG. AQVIS. SEXTIS. NAVICVLAR MAR. AREL. CVRAT. EIVSD. CORP PATRONO. NAVTAR. DRVENTI CORVM. ET. VTRICLARIORVM CORP. ERNAGINENSVM IVLIA. NICE. VXOR CONIVGI. KARISSIMO
units.tr: Pliny names the colony Julia Augusta Aquae Sextiae. The monument found today in the territory of Arles, which Joseph Scaliger, a most noble man, notes on Ausonius book 1, chapter 30: To M. Fronto Euporus, sevir of Augustus, of the colony Julia Augusta Aquis Sextiis, curator of the sea-shipping guild of Arles, patron of the guild of the boatmen of the Drventi and of the utricularii, of the Ernaginenses. Julia Nice, his wife, to her dearest husband.

units.la: Colonia item Iulia Aquæ Sextiæ, Legio xxv vocatur in antiqua Inscriptione, Numismoque Vespasiani; si fides Huberti Goltzij Thesauro. Aquæ quidem, quod Aquarum ibi Calidarum Balnea; unde & hodie Aix: Sextiæ ab C. Sextio Calvino cos. anno ab V. C. 1 DCXXX. Hic enim, victa Salyorum Gente, Coloniam Aquas Sextias condidit, eo consilio, ut Romanum illic collocaret præsidium; quo Barbaros ex iis reprimeret Littoribus, quæ ex Massilia ducunt in Italiam, quum Massiliensibus, illis coercendis, non suppeterent vires. Legendus Livius lib. lxi. ab V.C. Paucis Strabo lib. iv: Σιξηπ... Itaque ... Ἀρελᾶτε, &c. Iuliæ Arelate vero ab C. Iulio Cæsare Augusto, qui eam Colonis auxit, deductis eo Legionis xxv Veteranis. Parlamenti Provincialis Sedes, quod inde Aquense. Partim ad Aquas Sextias, partim in Italia, in Campo Raudino, vicit Cimbros Teutonosque Germaniæ Populos, quique ipsis se junxerant, Tigurinos Ambronesque, Gallicas Nationes, C. Marius D. Hieronymus ad Gerontiam: Gens Teutonum, inquit, ex ultimis Germaniæ profectus Littoribus omnem Galliam inundavit, sepiusque cæsis Romanis exercitibus, apud Aquas Sextias, Mario pugnante, superata est. Nota est Historia. Aliis locis etiam hac de re nonnulla. Arelas simpliciter Orosio & Ausonio lib. de Vrbibus in Epigraphe & ipso Carmine vii: Arelatum, eidem Ausonio in eodem Carmine, & alius: Arelate, Cæsari, Plinio, Suetonio in Ti. Principis Vita, Pomponio Melæ, & alius; Ἀρελάτη denique Strabon: quæ Ἀρελάτη, Salyorum Colonia, Prolemæo lib. 11. cap. xi; & Arelate, Sextanorum, Plinio lib. iii. nat. Hist. cap. iiii. & Cassiodoro. Ut Colonie meminerunt Lapides paullo ante ad Aquas Sextias à me positi. Salyorum quidem, ab antiquissimis Galliæ populis, de quibus ante: Sextanorum vero, ab Legione vi, cui hic sua fuerunt Stativa, quorum etiam initio huius Capitis meminit. Hodie Arles, plurali voce. Thelinen olim nuncupatam ab Græcis eam incolentibus, memoriæ prodit Festus Avienus: Arelatum illic Civitas attollitur,Theline vocata sub priore seculoGraio incolente.
units.tr: The colony Julia Aquae Sextiae is also called Legio XXV in an ancient inscription and on a coin of Vespasian, if one trusts Hubert Goltzius's Thesaurus. It was called Aquae because of the hot baths there, whence today it is Aix; Sextiae from C. Sextius Calvinus, consul in the year 630 from the founding of the city. For he, after the nation of the Salyi was defeated, founded the colony Aquae Sextiae, with the purpose of stationing a Roman garrison there, to restrain the barbarians from those shores which lead from Marseille into Italy, since the Massilians did not have the strength to restrain them. Livy, book 61, from the founding of the city, should be read; briefly Strabo, book 4: Σιξηπ... Thus ... Arelate, etc. Julia Arelate, however, was named by C. Julius Caesar Augustus, who enlarged it with colonists, veterans of Legio XXV being led there. It is the seat of the Provincial Parlement, and from this the name Aquense comes. Partly near Aquae Sextiae and partly in Italy, on the Raudine Plain, he defeated the Cimbri and Teutons, German peoples, and the Tigurini and Ambrones, Gallic nations, who had joined them: C. Marius. St Jerome to Gerontia: "The race of the Teutons," he says, "coming from the furthest shores of Germany, flooded all Gaul, and, after the Roman armies had often been cut down, was overcome near Aquae Sextiae by Marius fighting." The story is well known. Some other matters about this are touched on in other places. Orosius and Ausonius in the book on cities call it simply Arelas, in the title and in the poem itself, number vii; the same Ausonius in the same poem, and another writer, Arelate; Caesar, Pliny, Suetonius in the Life of the Emperor Tiberius, Pomponius Mela and another, and finally Strabo, Ἀρελάτη. This Ἀρελάτη was a colony of the Salyi in Ptolemy, book 2, chapter 11; and Arelate, of the Sextani, in Pliny, Natural History book 3, chapter 4, and in Cassiodorus. The inscriptions I placed a little earlier at Aquae Sextiae mention the colonies: of the Salyi, the most ancient peoples of Gaul, of whom I spoke before; and of the Sextani, from Legio VI, whose winter quarters were here, of whom he also mentions at the beginning of this chapter. Today it is Arles, in the plural. Festus Avienus records that the Greeks who lived there formerly called it Thelinen: "There rises the city of Arelatum, called Theline in earlier times when Greeks lived there."

units.la: Mamilliaris cognominatur, quam ob causam nescitur, in Inscriptione pulcherrima, quae ibidem in Columna legitur, teste V. N. Iosepho Scaligero, in aedibus honestissimae Matronae Vallensis: SALVIS. DD. NN THEODOSIO. ET VALENTINIANO P. F. V. AC. TRIVM SEMPER. AVG. XV CONS. VIR. INL AUXILIARIS. PRAE PRAETO. GALLIA DE. ARELATE. MA MILIARIA. PONI. S M. P. I
units.tr: Mamilliaris is the cognomen, for what reason is not known, in a very fine inscription that is read on a column in the house of the most honourable matron of Vaison, as reported by my honoured kinsman Joseph Scaliger: "For the safety of our lords Theodosius and Valentinian, the perpetual Augusti, consuls for the fifteenth time (Pii Felices Victores ac Triumphatores semper Augusti), Vir Inlustris Auxiliaris, praetorian prefect of Gaul, set up this milestone at Arles, [marked] 1 mile." (Here the abbreviations are as printed on the stone.)

units.la: Constantina ut diceretur, ibique Septem Provinciarum, Viennensis, utriusque Narbonensis, utriusque Aquitaniae, Novempopulaniae, & Alpium Maritimarum, Conventus ageretur; sanxit Fl. Constantinus Imperator: cujus egregiam ea de re Constitutionem videre est apud Scaligerum lib. i. Ausonianarum Lectionum, cap. xxiv. Gallulam Romam vocat Ausonius, Carmine, cujus memini, quod esset celeberrimum & oportunissimum Emporium; quodque Romanorum Colonia, ab Ti. Claudio Nerone, Ti Principis Patre, deducta, teste Suetonio, Romam Genitricem suam in multis aemularetur & exprimere conaretur, indeque parva quaedam videretur Roma. Urbs ad Rodanum sita. Eo pertinet Philostrati illud in Vita Favorini Galli Arelatensis: ὧν μὴ γὰρ τῶν ἰσοτιμῶν Γαλατῶν ἐστὶν, Ἀρελάτη πόλις, ἡ ἐπ' Ἐρόδανῳ ᾠκισται. Ubi nemo non videt legendum, Ῥοδανῷ pro Ἐρόδανῳ. Sic Strabo lib. iv: Πρὸς δὲ τῷ Ῥοδανῷ πόλις ἐπὶ τῇ ἐμπορίῳ ἡ μικρὰ, Ἀρελάτη. Simpliciter uterque: Hic, πρὸς Ῥοδανῷ: ille, ἐπὶ Ῥοδανῷ. Ad Sinistram autem ripam hodie. Itineraria Tabula collocat ad dextram, ubi hodie Languedokium. Antoninus etiam in Itinerario Maritimo ab Urbe Arelatum usque, in fine; A Gradu, inquit, per Flurium Rodanum Arelatum M. P. xxx. Non male; si Rodani Brachia, ut tunc se diducebant, consideren-tur. Ausonius Arelatum Rodani Fluentis interscindi, notat. Carmen ejus, ut semel hic ponam, sic habet: Pande, duplex Arelate, tuas blanda hospita Portus Gallula Roma Arelas: quam Narbo Maritima, & quam Adcolis Alpinis opulenta Viennat omnis, Praecipitis Rodani sic interciso fluentis, Ut medium faciens navali Ponte Platcam: Per quem Romani commercia suscipiunt orbis, Nec cohibes: Popu osque aras & Manua datas: Gallia quae fruitur, gremioque Aquitania lato.
units.tr: Constantina, so that it might be called that, and so that the assizes of the seven provinces (Vienne, both Narbonese provinces, both Aquitaines, Novempopulania and the Maritime Alps) might be held there, was decreed by the Emperor Flavius Constantine. His splendid constitution on this matter can be seen in Scaliger, Ausonian Lectures, book 1, chapter 24. Ausonius calls it Little Rome in a poem I recall, because it was a very famous and very convenient trading place, and because it was a Roman colony, founded by Tiberius Claudius Nero, the father of the Emperor Tiberius, as Suetonius reports; it imitated its mother Rome in many things and tried to copy her, so that it seemed a little Rome. It is a city set on the Rhone. To this belongs the passage in Philostratus's Life of Favorinus of Arles: "For Arelate, the city founded on the Rhone, is not one of the Gauls of equal rights" [ὧν μὴ γὰρ τῶν ἰσοτιμῶν Γαλατῶν ἐστὶν, Ἀρελάτη πόλις, ἡ ἐπ' Ἐρόδανῳ ᾠκισται.]. Here everyone sees that we must read Ῥοδανῷ for Ἐρόδανῳ. Strabo, book 4, says likewise: "Near the Rhone is a small city, a trading place, Arelate" [Πρὸς δὲ τῷ Ῥοδανῷ πόλις ἐπὶ τῇ ἐμπορίῳ ἡ μικρὰ, Ἀρελάτη.]. Both are simple: the one says "near the Rhone" (πρὸς Ῥοδανῷ), the other "on the Rhone" (ἐπὶ Ῥοδανῷ). Today it lies on the left bank. The Antonine Itinerary places it on the right bank, where Languedoc now is. Antoninus too, in the Maritime Itinerary, at the end of the route from the City to Arelate, says: "From Gradus, by the river Rhone, to Arelate, 30 miles." This is not wrong, if one considers the arms of the Rhone as they then divided. Ausonius notes that Arelate is cut through by the streams of the Rhone. His poem, which I shall quote once here, runs thus: "Speak out, double Arelate, you pleasant hostess of the port, little Rome of Gaul: you whom Maritime Narbo, and Vienne rich in its Alpine neighbours, envy, as the headlong waters of the Rhone are cut so as to make a middle island by a boat bridge..." (the poem continues in the same vein about the trade you receive from the world, and about the peoples and the Gallic and Aquitanian lands that enjoy your broad lap).

units.la: Arelas hic, item in extremo Mosella & Epistola xxiii ad Paullinum, Duplex, quod in duas partes ab Rodano secaretur. Quin & Pontis in Rodano, praeter Ausonium, meminit etiam Cassiodorus in Epistola quadam ad Senatum Urbis Romae lib. viii, Epistola x: Arelate est Civitas supra undas Rodani constituta: quae in Oriente profectum, tabulatum Pontem, per nuncupatis Finmenis dorsa, transmittit. Hunc & Hostibus capere, Nostris defendere, necessarium fuit. Hodie, mutata ibi rerum facie, Simplex est, tota in ripa Rodani, quae Italiam respicit, polita: septa undique Paludibus, in quibus praeferoces aluntur Boves. Putatur hinc major fuisse, creduntque magni Viri partem Urbis olim florentissimae alteram ab Gothis excisam. Videndi obiter Iornandes in Histor. Goth. Cassiodorus lib. iii, Epist. xxxiv, Prosper in Chronicis ad Theodosij xi & Valentiniani Consulatum, apud quem vitiose legitur Archilius, pro Arelas; ut & apud Paulum Diaconum in Theodosio Iuniore. Consulendi item Sidonius
units.tr: Ausonius calls Arelas here, and in the Mosella and in Letter 23 to Paulinus, Duplex, because it was divided into two parts by the Rhone. Indeed, besides Ausonius, Cassiodorus also mentions a bridge over the Rhone there, in a letter to the Senate of the City of Rome, book 8, letter 10: "Arelate is a city set above the waters of the Rhone; it carries a bridge of planks across the backs of the rivers, which were called by a name [from the Eastern side]. It was necessary to hold this both against enemies and to defend it for ourselves." Today, with the face of things changed there, it is a single town, built entirely on the bank of the Rhone that faces Italy, and surrounded on all sides by marshes, in which very fierce oxen are kept. It is thought that it was once larger, and great men believe that the other part of that once most flourishing city was destroyed by the Goths. On this see in passing Jordanes in the History of the Goths, Cassiodorus book 3, letter 34, Prosper in the Chronicle at the consulship of Theodosius (11th) and Valentinian, where it is wrongly read Archilius for Arelas, as also in Paulus Diaconus in the life of Theodosius the Younger. Consult likewise Sidonius

units.la: donius
units.tr: donius

units.la: Hinc denique Massiliorum Littus circa Massiliam & Emporias, de quo alibi. A Phocaea scilicet, quae Φωκαια, Ptolomaeo Aeolidis Stephano Ioniae oppidum; Phocis Pomponio & Lucano lib. v. Hinc enim in has oras profecti Massiliae Conditores. Plutarchus in Solone conditam scribit a Proto, qui Protis alias dicitur. Unde autem dicta Μασσαλια, paucis indicat ex Timaeo Stephanus: Τιμαιος δε Φησιν, οτι στρογγυλον ευουσιρης την ιδιαν αλλην, πελτοειδη μασσαν το δογυλον χρωμα. Μασσα γαρ η οικουμενη Αιολεις απ' εκεινου της Λιγυς εν τη Μασσα ανεμασσον. Situm petrolo in loco, οδι χωρα πετρωδες, indicat Strabo: prope ostia Rodani Amnis, in remoto Sinu, velut in Angulo Maris, aut ex Trogo lustinus. De Situ sic Caesar lib. II. Bell. Civil. Massilia fere ex tribus oppidi partibus portu naturali alitur; reliqua quarta est, quae aditum habet a terra: huius unoque latus parte ea, quae ad arcem pertinet, loci natura & valle altissima munita longam & difficilem habet expugnationem. Et addit Strabo, Τιμοκρατικος δε αυτης ο Αιολιος Ιλαγυρικα, βλαπτον προς την Νεμι. De Portu isto Dionysius: ἠδὲ ἡ γαῖα Μασσαλίη τεῖχος ἔχει, ὅπι προφέρων ἔρχηνι ἔχεις.
units.tr: Hence, finally, the Shore of the Massilians round Marseille and Emporiae, of which I shall speak elsewhere. Of course it comes from Phocaea, which is Φωκαια, a town of Aeolis according to Ptolemy and of Ionia according to Stephanus; Pomponius and Lucan, book 5, call it Phocis. For the founders of Marseille set out from there to these shores. Plutarch in his Solon writes that it was founded by Protis, who is also called Protes. How the name Μασσαλια arose, Stephanus briefly indicates from Timaeus: "Timaeus says that the land was round, with a different colour, like a kneaded cake, a dark colour; for the Aeolians called a kneaded mass 'massa'; from that Liguria was kneaded into Massa." [Τιμαιος δε Φησιν, οτι στρογγυλον ευουσιρης την ιδιαν αλλην, πελτοειδη μασσαν το δογυλον χρωμα. Μασσα γαρ η οικουμενη Αιολεις απ' εκεινου της Λιγυς εν τη Μασσα ανεμασσον.] Strabo indicates its rocky site: near the mouths of the river Rhone, in a remote bay, as if in a corner of the sea; or, as Justin says from Trogus. Caesar, book 2 of the Civil War, describes the site thus: "Massilia is nourished for the most part on three sides by a natural harbour; the remaining fourth part, which has access from the land, is protected on one side by the nature of the place and a very deep valley, which is part of the citadel, and it has a long and difficult siege." Strabo adds that its aristocratic (oligarchic) government... (the text is corrupt here) and it is harmful to the Nemesian... On this harbour Dionysius says: "The land of Massalia has a wall where the harbour projects" [ἠδὲ ἡ γαῖα Μασσαλίη τεῖχος ἔχει, ὅπι προφέρων ἔρχηνι ἔχεις.].

units.la: Nomen Portus fuit ut Eustathius notat Λακυων. Hinc apud Melam ex veteribus libris legendum: Et Lacidon Massiliensium Portus & in eo ipsi Massilia. Pergit Strabo: Τεταγμενα δε καλως η πολις συμμαχια, μιχθ. ιχνος αξιολογον. εν δε τη ακρα το Εφεσιον ιερον, την και το τε Διαφαν Αλλιαν ιερον. Rempublicam porro Massiliensium tantopere laudat M. Tullius; ut, audiente Populo Romano, dicere auderet in Defensione Fontei, Civitatis illius Disciplinam atque Gravitatem non solum Graciae, sed pene cunctis Gentibus anteponendam. Ejus (ut plene scribit Strabo) Sexcenti erant Senatores, quos Τιμουχοι vocabant, quique totam vitam ist hoc honore potiebantur: ex eo numero Quindecimviri quotidianis Litibus dirimendis legebantur. Atque ij nimirum sunt Sexcenti Massiliensium, & Quindecim-Primi, quos libro belli civilis I apellat Caesar. Sexcentorum etiam meminit Valerius Maximus lib. II. cap VI. Ex Quindecim-viris autem Trecentos optabant, in quibus auctoritas esset summa Τιμηχω. nemo creabatur qui Liberos non haberet, quive a tertia usque progenie ac stirpe civis non esset. Massiliensium igitur Respublica Αριστοκρατικη (haec Strabonis est vox) administrabatur Aristoteles πολιτικα. lib. v. & viii. eos Ολιγαρχιαν usos restatur. Oligarchicum sane fuit, genere, ut audivimus, non virtute, Reip Principes fieri. Eorum leges Ionici genii, Ιανιοι inquit Strabo, publice sunt propositae. Institutiones Reip. Massiliensium paucis recenset lustinus lib. XLIII Consuevisse scilicet, ab condita fere urbe festis diebus portas claudere, vigilias agere, stationem in muris observare, peregrinos recognoscere curas habere: ac veluti bellum habeant, si Urbem pacis temporibus custodire? adeoillic bene instituta non temporum necessitate, sed recte faciendi consuetudine servari. Alia de Manumissionibus Spectaculis Validis mendicantibus, Supplicis, Funeribus Sepulchris & hospitiorum jure leguntur apud Valerium, capite quod indicavi. Consonabant optimis institutis Sanctissimi publice privatimque Mores. Τες δε λιτοτης, inquit Strabo lib. IV, τ βιου και ο σωφροσυνης τ Μασσαλιωτων σεμ ιλαχιστην αυτης δεην τουτο πεπαιδευον. η γαρ μιγιστη περιτ αυτοις ιση ιναιτιν χρυσον, η ιση εις νεον, η νεον εις χρυσον κομιζουσι: αλιον δε ουκ εχεται. Massiliam Tacitus ait locum graeca comitate & provinciali parsimonia multum & bene compositum. Sed isti morum integritati multum ademit unum, quo se infamare soliti Massilienses, vitium Notum est proverbium Παλαιος εις Μασσαλιαν navigeas, de quo Athenaeus lib. XII, Suidas & alij Credebantur enim Γυναικομανεις Hinc Massilienses Mores Plauto in Cafina, molles impudici, effoeminati: Huc illa Clementis Alexandrini IX, Recog. referenda. Apud Gallos, inquit, Lex prisca constituit nuptum tradi publice pueros, nec opprobrium ex hoc aliquod duci, innuere videtur eadem Diodorus scriptens, Gallos licet habeant speciosas foeminas, ad Mares tamen esse proniores: Strabo item, ubi memorat, apud Gallos turpe non judicari, si adolescentes aetatis flore abuterentur. Tradit & Athenaeus lib. XIII Gallos super pellibus saepius cum duobus catamitis concumbere. Haec enim talia non de Gallis veteribus generatim, sed de Massiliensibus Graeca mollitia fractis exaudienda censent Magni viri. Sidonius aperte carmine XXII: Et te Massiliensium per hortos Sacri Stupitus Arbiter colonum Hellespontiaco parem Priapo &c. Infamibus Massiliensium Moribus adiciebam quæ notat ad illud Virgilij, Auri sacra fames,
units.tr: The name Port was, as Eustathius notes, Λακυων. Hence in Mela, from old books, we should read: "And the Lacidon, the port of the Massilians, and in it Massilia itself." Strabo goes on: "The city is well arranged in alliance, mixed... and on the headland is the temple of Ephesian (Artemis), and the temple of Diaphanes Allia." Marcus Tullius praises the state of the Massilians so highly that, with the Roman people listening, he dared to say in the defence of Fonteius: "The discipline and dignity of that city is to be preferred not only to Greece, but almost to all nations." (As Strabo fully writes) it had six hundred senators, whom they called Timuchi, who held power for their whole lives by this honour; from this number the Fifteen were chosen to settle daily disputes. These are surely the Six Hundred of the Massilians and the Fifteen-Firsts, whom Caesar names in book 1 of the Civil War. Valerius Maximus, book 2, chapter 6, also mentions the Six Hundred. Of the Fifteen, three hundred were chosen, in whom the highest authority (Timuchi) lay; no one was created who did not have children, or who was not a citizen from the third generation and stock. So the Massilian commonwealth was governed aristocratically (this is Strabo's word), and Aristotle in his Politics, books 5 and 8, says they used oligarchy.
