It was indeed oligarchic, for, as we have heard, the rulers of the state were made by birth, not by virtue. Their laws, of the Ionian kind (Ἰανιοι, says Strabo), were published publicly. Justin, book 43, briefly lists the institutions of the Massilian state: from almost the founding of the city they were accustomed on festival days to close the gates, to keep watches, to observe guard on the walls, and to take care to examine strangers; as if they had war, if they guarded the city in peacetime; so well were the institutions maintained, not by the necessity of the times, but by the custom of doing right. Other matters concerning manumissions, shows, strong and beggarly suppliants, funerals, tombs and the right of hospitality are read in Valerius, in the chapter I have indicated. The most holy morals, public and private, agreed with these excellent institutions. "The frugality of life and the temperance of the Massilians," says Strabo, book 4, "taught this to need the least possible; for their greatest dowries are carried either from gold to iron, or from iron to gold; and they have no other." Tacitus says Massilia was a place very well arranged with Greek courtesy and provincial thrift. But one thing took much from its integrity of morals, a vice by which the Massilians were wont to disgrace themselves; it is a well-known proverb, "You sail to Massilia" (Παλαιος εις Μασσαλιαν navigeas), about which Athenaeus, book 12, Suidas and others write. For they were believed to be women-mad (Γυναικομανεις). Hence Plautus in the Casina calls the Massilian manners soft, shameless, effeminate. To this passage of Clement of Alexandria, Recognitions 9, should be referred: "Among the Gauls," he says, "ancient law established that boys be publicly handed over in marriage, and no disgrace was thought to arise from this," which the same Diodorus seems to hint at when writing that the Gauls, although they have beautiful women, are nevertheless more inclined to males. Strabo likewise, where he mentions that among the Gauls it was not judged shameful if men abused young people in the flower of their age. Athenaeus, book 13, also reports that the Gauls often lay with two catamites upon skins. Great men think these things should be understood not of the ancient Gauls generally, but of the Massilians, broken by Greek softness. Sidonius plainly, in poem 22: "And you, the Stupid Arbiter of the Massilian gardens, a colonist equal to Hellespontine Priapus, etc." I would add to the infamous Massilian morals what Servius notes on that line of Virgil, Accursed hunger for gold: that is, says he, execrable, as in "the sacred gates are opened." This was a custom of the Gauls. For whenever the Massilians were troubled by pestilence, one of their poor people offered himself, to be fed at public expense for a whole year, and to be a citizen of the ministers. He, by a ceremony, with a sacred verbena and clothing...

units.la: Servius, id est, inquit, exsecrabilis, ut Sacra pandantur Portæ. Tradius est autem Sermo ex more Gallorum. Nam Massilienses quoties pestilentia laborabant, unus sui ex pauperibus offerebat, alendus anno integro publice & pastoribus Civis. Hic per ceremoniam Verbenam & Vestitus sacris, circumducebatur per totam Civitatem cum Exsecrationibus, ut in ipsum residerent mala totius Civitatis, & sic præcipitabatur, &c. Agathias lua ætate Massilia iam ex Græca Civitate jam barbaram notat factam: Nam patrio prisceque vivendi more rejecto, Imperantium Institutis usam fuisse. Massiliensium porro Bella, Reliquæque contra Ligures, Gallos, Karthaginienses, aliosque Contegionales & Remotiores Populos gestas; item Victorias earundem, Triumphos, Trophæa & Exuvias; Fœderaque denique cum Romanis, Hispanis, aliisque, commemorant Strabo lib. iv, Iustinus lib. xliii, & alij. Quin Fratres appellatos fuisse Romanorum, patet ex Panegyrico, qui Constantino & Maximiano dictus: Cujus, inquit, Civitatis antiqua Nobilitas & quonam fraterno Populi Romani nomine gloriata. Certe in magno erant Romanis honore. Princeps Rodiorum Legationis, Oratione in Senatu Romæ habita, de iis apud Livium lib. xxxvii, sic loquitur: Massilienses, quos, si natura injuria, velut ingens terra usui posset, jam pridem efferant tot inhumanæ circumfusæ Gentes, in eo honore, in ea merito dignitate audimus apud vos esse, ac si medium umbrinum Græciæ incolerent. Non enim sonum modo Linguæ Vestitumque & Habitum, sed ante omnia Mores & Leges Ingentium sacerum, integrumque à contagione Incolarum servarunt. Colonias ex hac Urbe ductas non paucas indicant idem Scriptores. Iustinus: Qui perniciola propulsando ita tantum extenuerunt, ut victis Hostibus in captivi Agris multas Colonias constituerent.
units.tr: Servius, that is, he says, accursed, as in "Let the sacred gates be opened." But the account is a tradition from the custom of the Gauls. For whenever the Massilians were afflicted by pestilence, one of their poor people offered himself, to be maintained at public expense for a whole year and fed with pure food. Then, in a ceremony, he was dressed in sacred vestments and wreaths and led about the whole city amid curses, so that the evils of the entire community would settle upon him; and so he was thrown down from the city, and so on. Agathias notes that in his own time Massilia, once a Greek city, had become barbarian, for having cast off its ancestral and ancient way of life, it had adopted the institutions of its rulers. Strabo, book 4, and Justin, book 43, and others record the wars the Massilians waged against the Ligurians, the Gauls, the Carthaginians and other neighbouring and more distant peoples; likewise their victories, triumphs, trophies and spoils; and finally the treaties they made with the Romans, the Spaniards and others. That the Massilians were called "brothers" of the Romans is clear from the Panegyric delivered to Constantine and Maximian: "Of this city," it says, "the ancient nobility and the fraternal name of the Roman people." Certainly they were held in great honour by the Romans. The leader of the Rhodian embassy, in a speech given in the Senate at Rome, speaks of them thus in Livy, book 37: "The Massilians, whom, if nature had permitted, all these inhuman tribes surrounding them would long ago have devoured as a rich land for their use, we hear are held by you in such honour and such dignity of merit, as if they lived in the shade of Greece. For they have preserved not only the sound of their language, their dress and bearing, but above all the customs and laws of their ancestors, and have kept themselves untainted by contact with the surrounding inhabitants." The same writers point out that not a few colonies were led out from this city. Justin: "They so reduced the power of their enemies by repelling their attacks that, having defeated them, they founded many colonies in the conquered fields."

units.la: Quos autem Ritus servare fuerint soliti in Colonijs deducendis, sic notat Strabo: Ἐν τοῖς ἐν Ἀσίᾳ πόλεσι παρὰ ἔθος τοῦ ὑπερφυοῦς ... (loquitur de Aristarcha) καὶ τὰ ἄλλα νόμιμα φυλάσσειν ἐν αὐτῷ, ὥσπερ ἐν τῇ Μητροπόλει ἐνέμεισθαι. Et paulo post scribit Massilienses Colonijs abductis Dianæ Ephesiæ Sacra, more patrio, tradidisse; &, ut Græcanicis Ritibus immolarent, jussisse. Colonias enumerat variis locis idem Strabo; in iis Aphrodisium Pyrenæorum Promontorium, Agatham, Antipolim, Nicæam: & alia, quæ ipsa nomina satis arguunt. Concussa supra modum fuit ejus Felicitas anno i. Belli Civilis inter Cn. Pompeium Magnum & C. Iulium Cæsarem, cujus in eam Victoria fuit talis, tamque moderata, ut pro Nomine & Vetustate potius, quam pro Meritis salva ipsi sua relicta fuerit Libertas. Legendi, præter Cæsarem ipsum, Strabo lib. v, & Lucanus lib. iii. de Bello Civili: Ab Gothis postea captam, posteriori ævi scribunt Auctores. Iornandes in Histor. Gothor. Et quomodo Euricus Rex Visi Gothorum Romani Regni vacillationem cernens, Arelatum & Massiliam propria subdidit Ditioni. Isidorus in Chronic. Era 1111: In Gallias autem regressus, Arelatum & Massiliam Urbes cepit, suoque Regno utramque subjecit. Sigebertus in Chronic. ad annum CCCCLXXI, Arelatum & Massiliam Galliarum Urbes invasit.
units.tr: What rites they were accustomed to observe in founding colonies is noted thus by Strabo: "In the cities of Asia, contrary to the custom of ... (he is speaking of Aristarcha) ... and to keep the other customs among them, just as they were observed in the mother city" [Ἐν τοῖς ἐν Ἀσίᾳ πόλεσι παρὰ ἔθος τοῦ ὑπερφυοῦς ... καὶ τὰ ἄλλα νόμιμα φυλάσσειν ἐν αὐτῷ, ὥσπερ ἐν τῇ Μητροπόλει ἐνέμεισθαι]. And a little later he writes that the Massilians, when they led out colonies, handed over the sacred rites of Diana of Ephesus according to their ancestral custom, and ordered that they should sacrifice in the Greek manner. The same Strabo lists colonies in various places, among them Aphrodisium, a promontory of the Pyrenees, Agatha, Antipolis, Nicaea, and others, whose very names sufficiently show their origin. Their prosperity was shaken beyond measure in the first year of the civil war between Gnaeus Pompey the Great and Gaius Julius Caesar; Caesar's victory over them was of such a kind and so moderate that, on account of its name and antiquity rather than its merits, their liberty was left to them intact. Besides Caesar himself, read Strabo, book 5, and Lucan, book 3, of the Civil War. Later writers record that it was afterwards captured by the Goths. Jordanes in the History of the Goths: "And when King Euric of the Visigoths saw the tottering of the Roman kingdom, he subjected Arles and Marseilles to his own rule." Isidore in the Chronicle, year 1111: "But returning to Gaul, he took the cities of Arles and Marseilles, and subjected both to his kingdom." Sigebert in the Chronicle, at the year 471: "He invaded Arles and Marseilles, cities of Gaul."

units.la: Mercatus hic olim fuit, ut memoriæ prodit Strabo lib. iv, bonarum Artium & Disciplinarum celeberrimus. Eo, tamquam ad alteras Athenas, Romani, Galli, Hispani, omnesque, quibus licebat Philosophiæ Græceque Linguæ gratia se conferebant. Testatur Tacitus in Vita Agricolæ Soceri, eum parvulum sedem ac Magistram Studiorum habuisse Massiliam: Locum, ut antea etiam monui, Græca Comitate & Provinciali Parsimonia multum henequeecompositum. Hæc Eumenidis, qui tam accurate quæsivit de Nilo; Hæc Pythia quem tam studiose insectatur Strabo; Hæc aliorum, quorum Scripta intercidurunt, fuit, Patria. Hic verisimile est Philosophiam didicisse Favorinum Arelatensem. Hæc Gallos omnes ita φιλολόγους reddebat, ὥστε ἐκ τῶν συμβολαίων ... ut Contractus omnes Græco Idiomate conficerent, & in omnibus publicis privatisque Rationibus Græcis Litteris uterentur, Strabone Teste. Inde Tabulæ in Helvetiorum Castris reperte Græco Characterere conscriptæ, ad Cæsarem perlatæ, ut in Ephemeridibus Belli Gallici est legere. Hinc hodieque tam frequens in Gallo-Romano sermone Hellenismus. Alia præterco: Nam plura à me alibi notata. Habuisse Massilienses Navalia & Armamentarium, copiam item Navium, Armorum, Machinarum, quibus & contra Barbaros se tuebantur & Romanorum societatem sibi compararunt, tradit idem Strabo: qui & Territorium ipsorum celebrat, Ἐ'λαίοφυον ... κατάμπλον. Vinum Massilieense ait Athenaeus esse καλὸν, sed ἐλίγον, ἐ παχὺ καὶ ταχυδὲς. Oss. ea Massiliensis laudat Antonius Epist. c. 11; eadem fere cum iis, quae Strabo magna copia reperiri scribit in Rhodani ostiis Lateres apud Massilienses fieri, qui projecti in aquam natant, ut ait Vitruvius. Incolas Trilingues fuisse, ut qui Graece, Latine, Gallicèque loquerentur, refert ex Varrone D. Hieronymus. Digna igitur maximis elogiis Massilia, cum quod tantae antiquitatis, tum quod hodieque situ opereque sic praeporens, Regique suo fidelissima; quod item suorum incolarum industria per Asiam, Africam, aliaque remotissimas regiones longe lateque negotietur. Theatrales & nunc fere servat formam; sed ita, ut in Septemtrione Cornu petitor sit Civitasam Australiore Collis, in quo Monumenta, quae vulgo Le Fort de Notre Dame de la Garde, & de S. Nicolas, adjacente Colli domo gubernatoris cum Armamentis. Inter utrumque Cornu Portus est; cui praejacent insulae, vulgo Les Pomegues, in quarum una Stationem navium habuit D. Junius Brutus, quum Urbs ab Caesare, cujus ille erat Legatus, esset obsessa. Visitur ibi hoc tempore Arx, quae vernacule Le Chasteau Fit. Urbe per Portam Franciscam egresso ad sinistram se offerunt multa Antiquitatis Rudera, quae ad ipsum Oppidum junguntur Monumento, quod inter eamdem Franciscam & Aquensem Portas, Magnum cognomine. Episcopus sues numerant ab D. Lazaro, quem Christus ab morte suscitavit. Eum bonis sedibusque exutum, saeviente persecutione, quae Stephanum abstulerat, cum sororibus Maria Magdalena & Martha in has oras venisse, Christique fidem nuncinasse, narrant Massilienses. Quin & caput ejus monstrant in Primario templo: quod incolis La Mayeur, adurius Moenia, versus Mare. Haec de Massilia: reliquae urbes Episcopales sunt: Dune; Diuna Plinio in Ebroduntius; Dinia Prolen aro in tentus. Gratia, Graviae ortidum, Glandeve, Glanatte Viris Doctis Latine scribentibus, Glannatena Civitas, Notitiae Provinciarum Galliae in Viennensi iv; in aliis libris est Glanatina, in quibusdam Glannatena. Glandeteensis Episcopi meminit concilium Aurelianum vi. Falluntur, qui Glanum Plinii, Pomponii & Antonini cum Glannate confundunt. Glanum enim Antoninus ponit inter Cabellionem & Arelatum: at quam procul inde Glannate? Quid Glanum hodie, ignoratur. Senas, Σανίας, Veldantiorum oppidum in Alpibus Maritimis, Ptolemaeo. S. Paul de Vences, οὐντιον, Nerulinorum Oppidum in Alpibus Maritimis, Ptolemaeo, οὐσία, Dioni lib. xxxvii. Apt. Apta Iulia Vulgientium Plinio, Arta Iulia & Abtejulia corrupte apud Antoninum: Nam in melioribus est apta Iulia: ut & in Itineraria Tabula. Aptensis Episcopatus meminerunt concilium Aurelianense, & alia. Reis, Reims Notitiae Provinciarum Galliae, in qua sub Viennensi iii sic legitur, Civitas Reiensium, id est Reims. In Tabula Itineraria, ut paullo ante dixi, scriptum est, Reis Apollinaris; quod nondum liquet. Feriuli Forum Iulii Planco Imperatori Epistola ad M. Tullium, addenti abesse ab Foro Voconii xx. m.p. Tabula Itineraria inter Forum Voconii & Forum Iulii notat xvii. m.p. Φερ ... Ιουλιος, Commonorum urbs Ptolemaeo; col. ivl octav. in Augusti Numno apud Hubertum Goltzium: Forum Iulium Clavanorum Colonia, quae Paerensis appellatur & Glaucia, Plinio lib. iii. cap. iv. τὸ Ναυσαβματ & Καίσαρος & Σεβαστὸ ο καλεισι Φερον Ιουλιον inquit Strabo lib. iv: Et hodie Portus est marinus. Cessero, Segustero apud Antoninum & in itineraria tabula: Cessero inquit luis ad me litteris Iosephus Scaliger, Plinio: apud quem tamen excusum est Cessero. Sed mihi semper Pliniana Cessero eadem centeri solet cum ea, quae Κεστεύ apud Ptolemaeum, Tolosae & Carcassonum connumerata, quae hodie in Languedokio Castres, ut ibi monui. Plinius enim Cesseronem locat inter Opida Volcarum Tectosagum, qui ad dextram Rodani ripam. Tolon, Telonum Doctis Latine scribentibus: Telo Martius, Antonino, Opidum in interiore Maris recessu, novem Leucis Massilia.
units.tr: It was once a market, as Strabo, book 4, records, very famous for the good arts and disciplines. To it, as to a second Athens, came Romans, Gauls, Spaniards, and all who were permitted, for the sake of philosophy and the Greek language. Tacitus, in the Life of his father-in-law Agricola, testifies that Massilia was for him, as a boy, the seat and teacher of his studies: "a place, as I have already said, much blended with Greek courtesy and provincial frugality." This was the homeland of Eumenes, who inquired so carefully about the Nile, of Pytheas, whom Strabo so eagerly pursues, and of others whose writings have perished. Here it is likely that Favorinus of Arles learned philosophy. This city made all the Gauls so devoted to learning [φιλολόγους] that, as Strabo testifies, they drew up all their contracts [ὥστε ἐκ τῶν συμβολαίων ...] in the Greek idiom and used Greek letters in all public and private accounts. Hence the tablets found in the camps of the Helvetians, written in Greek characters and brought to Caesar, as one may read in the Commentaries on the Gallic War. Hence to this day Hellenism is so frequent in the Gallo-Roman speech. I pass over other matters, since I have noted many of them elsewhere. The same Strabo relates that the Massilians had docks and an arsenal, and likewise a supply of ships, arms and engines, with which they defended themselves against the barbarians and secured the alliance of the Romans; and he praises their territory as "olive-bearing ... fertile" [Ἐλαιόφυον ... κατάμπλον]. Athenaeus says the Massilian wine is "good [καλὸν], but small in quantity, not thick and quick" [ἐλίγον, ἐ παχὺ καὶ ταχυδές]. Antonius Musa, in Epistle 11, praises this wine, and in nearly the same terms Strabo writes that in great quantity at the mouths of the Rhône bricks are made by the Massilians, which, thrown into the water, float, as Vitruvius says. Saint Jerome, citing Varro, reports that the inhabitants were trilingual, since they spoke Greek, Latin and Gallic. Massilia is therefore worthy of the highest praise, both for its great antiquity and because even today it flourishes in its situation and its works, most faithful to its king, and because by the industry of its inhabitants it carries on trade far and wide through Asia, Africa and other very remote regions. Even now it nearly keeps the form of a theatre, but in such a way that on the northern horn is the city, and on the southern hill is a fortress, called in common speech Le Fort de Notre Dame de la Garde and of St Nicholas, with the governor's house and arsenal adjoining the hill. Between the two horns lies the harbour, in front of which lie islands, commonly called Les Pomègues, on one of which Decimus Junius Brutus had his naval station when the city was besieged by Caesar, whose legate he was. There is now to be seen a citadel, called in the vernacular Le Château d'If. Leaving the city by the Porte Française, on the left there present themselves many remains of antiquity, joined to the town itself, and a monument which lies between the Porte Française and the Porte d'Aix, called by the surname "the Great." The bishops count from St Lazarus, whom Christ raised from the dead. The people of Marseilles relate that he, stripped of his goods and home, during the persecution that had carried off Stephen, came to these shores with his sisters Mary Magdalene and Martha, and preached the faith of Christ. Indeed they show his head in the principal church, which the inhabitants call La Major; it lies by the walls, towards the sea. So much for Massilia. The other episcopal cities are: Digne, which Pliny calls Dinia; Embrun, which in the Latin writers is Ebrodunum; Gap, Vence, Glandève, which learned writers in Latin call Glannatena or Glanatte, the city of Glannatena; the Notitia of the Provinces of Gaul, under Vienne, number 4, has Glanatina in some books and Glannatena in others. The Council of Orléans, canon 6, mentions the bishop of Glandève. They are mistaken who confuse Pliny's, Pomponius's and Antoninus's Glanum with Glannate. For Antoninus places Glanum between Cavaillon and Arles; but how far from there is Glannate? What Glanum is today is unknown. Senas [Σανίας], a town of the Vedantii in the Maritime Alps, according to Ptolemy. St Paul de Vence [οὐντιον], a town of the Nerulini in the Maritime Alps, according to Ptolemy; [οὐσία], according to Dio, book 37. Apt: Apta Julia, of the Vulgientes according to Pliny; Arta Julia and Abtejulia are corruptions in Antoninus, for in the better manuscripts it is Apta Julia, as also in the Itinerary Table. The bishopric of Apt is mentioned by the Council of Orléans and others. Reis, Reims: the Notitia of the Provinces of Gaul, under Vienne number 3, reads thus: the city of the Reiensi, that is, Reims. In the Itinerary Table, as I said a little before, it is written "Reis Apollinaris," which is not yet clear. Fréjus: Forum Julii. Plancus, in a letter to Cicero, adds that it is 20 Roman miles from Forum Voconii; the Itinerary Table puts 17 miles between Forum Voconii and Forum Julii. Φερ ... Ιουλιος [Pher ... Ioulios] is the city of the Commoni according to Ptolemy; Col. Iul. Octav., on a coin of Augustus in Hubert Goltzius: Forum Julium, colony of the Clavani, which is called Paerensis and Glaucia, in Pliny, book 3, chapter 4. Strabo, book 4, says: "[that which the Massilians call] Nausabmat, and Caesar's and Sebastos, which they call Pheron Ioulion." And it is still a marine port today. Cessero, Segustero in Antoninus and in the Itinerary Table: Joseph Scaliger wrote to me that Cessero is in Pliny, though in the printed edition it is Cessero. But to me the Plinian Cessero always seems to be the same as the Κεστεύ in Ptolemy, numbered among the cities of Toulouse and Carcassonne, which today in Languedoc is Castres, as I have noted there. For Pliny places Cesseron among the towns of the Volcae Tectosages, who lived on the right bank of the Rhône. Toulon: Telonum for learned writers in Latin; Telo Martius in Antoninus, a town in the inner recess of the sea, nine leagues from Massilia.

units.la: Haec de Episcopalibus: sunt alia non minoris nominis & antiquitatis opida: Antibes; Ἀντίπολις, Deciatorum oppidum Ptolemaeo; Oppidum Latinum, Antipolis, Plinio: Tacitus Antipolim Narbonensis Galliae Municipium appellat. Coloniam vocat Nummus Titi imperatoris: Meminit Ἀντίπολις, & Strabo, scribens inter eam & Olbiam constructum esse Forum Iulium. Olbia Iane, quae & Ptolemaeo Melaeque nota, Teres vel Hieres hodie censetur ad Mare, tribus fere leucis Telono. Contra Opidum jacent nobilissimae insulae, quae Ptolemaeo Σπηκάδες, Αιγυσίδες Stephano & Apollonio lib. iv. De us lib. ultimo. Hodie, Opido cognominus, Les Isles dicuntur de Teres, vel
units.tr: These are the bishoprics. There are other towns of no less name and antiquity: Antibes, which Ptolemy calls Antipolis [Ἀντίπολις] and the town of the Deciates; Antipolis, which Pliny calls the Latin town. Tacitus calls Antipolis a municipium of Narbonese Gaul, and the coin of the emperor Titus calls it a colony. Strabo also mentions Antipolis [Ἀντίπολις], writing that Forum Iulium was founded between it and Olbia. Olbia, known also to Ptolemy and Mela, is today thought to be Toulon or Hyères on the coast, about three leagues from Telo. Opposite the town lie the very famous islands, which Ptolemy calls the Spekades [Σπηκάδες] and Stephanus and Apollonius the Aigyside [Αιγυσίδες], in book 4 and in the last book of De us. Today they are called, from the town of the same name, the Îles d'Hyères.

units.la: Oliva Lateres. Incolae Lateres. Tirinees Telin. Hieres, Olbia. Alia Urbes & Opida. Telon, Telo Martius. Segustero. Cessero. Feriuli Forum. Reis, Reims. vel Hieres. Coralium ibi colligitur optimum, & quo non aliud præstantius in Mari Ligustico. S. Maximin, Tecoata videtur Antonino in Itinerario; sex grandioribus leucis Massilia, versus Boream. Tarascon, Ταραςκων Straboni; Ταρασκων Ptolemæo; ad sinisteriorem Rodani ripam; cuius dexteriore opposita visitur Bellouadra, vulgo Beaucarre, Fluvio tantum intercurrente: unde vsitatum illud Gallis; Entre Beaucarre & Tarascon, Ne repaci. Brebis ne Oisón, Non plus qu'entre Tain & Tournon. Nam & hæc apud Valentinos utrimque ad Rodanum. Comitatus dignitate fulgens Opida, Sault, S. Cesàris, & alia. Iam quas hodie habeant appellationes ignoro Opida, quæ apud Antoninum & in Itineraria Tabula scribuntur, Alaunium & Catoluca, quæ Catuiacia, Tabulæ Itinerariæ. Vtrumque certe locatur inter Segusteronem & Aptam Iuliam. Neque certiora habeo de Glano & Ernagino, quæ quondam inter Cabellionem & Arelate. Glanum Plinio, Pomponio, Antonino; Γλανὸν Ptolemæo in Salyis: quod Itinerariæ Tabulæ Glanum. Falluntur, ut alibi moneo, qui Glanum idem faciunt cum Glannate, hodie Glandeve. Et Ernaginum, quod Ἐρναγινον Ptolemæo, Ernagina Itinerariæ Tabulæ; οὐγερνον Straboni esse videtur; apud quem MS. Codicibus ουγερνον legi notat Casaubonus: Vgernum nominat Gregorius Turonensis. Ernaginensium memoria in antiquo extat Lapide, quem paullo ante posui, ubi de Aquis Sextis. Præter Massiliam, Telonum, Olbiam, Forum Iulium & Antipolin, alia quoque ab Veteribus opida nominantur Provinciæ huius Mari adposita. Ea animus est ordine enumerare ex Parte Itinerarij Maritimi, quod sub Antonini nomine circumfertur, collata cum alijs:
units.tr: Oliva, Lateres. The inhabitants are the Lateres. Tirinees, Telin. Hyères, Olbia. Other cities and towns: Toulon, Telo Martius; Segustero; Cessero; Forum of the Feriuli; Reis, Reims; or Hieres. Coral is gathered there, the best, and none is finer in the Ligurian Sea. S. Maximin, Tecoata seems to be the place in Antoninus' Itinerary, six longer leagues from Massilia, towards the north. Tarascon, Ταραςκων in Strabo, Ταρασκων in Ptolemy, lies on the left bank of the Rhône, and opposite its right bank is seen Bellouadra, commonly Beaucarre, with only the river running between them. Hence the common Gallic saying: Entre Beaucarre & Tarascon, Ne repaci. Brebis ne Oisón, Non plus qu'entre Tain & Tournon. For these places, among the Valentinians, also lie on both sides of the Rhône. Towns that shine with the rank of a county: Sault, S. Cesàris, and others. As for the names they now bear, I do not know the towns that are written in Antoninus and in the Itinerary Table, Alaunium and Catoluca, which is Catuiacia in the Itinerary Table. Both are certainly placed between Segusteron and Apta Julia. Nor do I have more certain information about Glano and Ernagino, which once lay between Cabellio and Arelate. Glanum in Pliny and Pomponius and Antoninus; Γλανὸν in Ptolemy among the Salyes, which the Itinerary Table calls Glanum. Those who take Glanum to be the same as Glannate, today Glandeve, are mistaken, as I note elsewhere. And Ernaginum, which is Ἐρναγινον in Ptolemy, Ernagina in the Itinerary Table, seems to be οὐγερνον in Strabo; Casaubon notes that in the manuscripts of Strabo ουγερνον is read. Gregory of Tours names it Vgernum. The memory of the Ernaginensium survives in an ancient stone, which I set out a little earlier, where I spoke of Aquae Sextiae. Besides Massilia, Telo, Olbia, Forum Iulium and Antipolis, the ancients also name other towns of this province lying on the sea. It is my intention to list them in order, from the part of the Maritime Itinerary that is circulated under the name of Antoninus, compared with other sources:

units.la: Pars Itinerarij Maritimi apud Antoninum, ad Provinciam, pertinens.
units.tr: Part of the Maritime Itinerary in Antoninus, pertaining to the Province.

units.la: A Nicia Antipolim. Port. M.P.XVI. | Antibe, suo loco. Ab Antipoli Lero & Lerina Insula. M.P.XI. | Les Isles de S. Margarete & de S. Honorat. A Lerone & Lerina Forum Iulij. Port. M.P. XXIV. | Feriuls. Alibi dixi. A Foro Iulio Sinus Sambracitanus. Plag. M.P.XXV. | Goulfe de Grimault. A Sina Sambracitano Heraclia Caccabaria, Portus, M.P.XVI. Ab Heraclia Caccabaria, Alconis, M.P.XII. Ab Alconi Pompeianas Portus. M.P.XXX. A Pompeianis Telonem Martium Port. M.P.XV. A Telone Martio Taurentum. Port. Vbi sit, ignoro. A Taurento Carsicim. Portus. M.P.XVIII. | Memoria loci servatur ad Promontorium Cerchiech. A Carsici Citharista Portus. M.P.XVIII. | Κιθαριστὰς Ptolemæo: Citharista Plinio & Melæ. Hodie alijs alia Promontoria inter se vicina, Cape de S. Sigo, Circelli, S. Bacro. A Citharista Portus Aemines. Posit. M.P.VI. | In alijs Exemplaribus Mines, item Heminæs. A Portu Aeminis Immadras. Posit. M.P.XII | Forte ubi hodie Maire. Varie legitur apud Antoninum. Ab Immadris Massiliam Graecorum. Port. M.P.XII. | Marseille. A Massilia Graecorum Incarum. Posit. M.P.XII. | Incidit fere in locum, qui hodie ad Sinum Massalioticum, Carri. Ab Incaro Dilum. Posit M.P.VIII. A Dilis Fossæ Marianæ. Portus. M.P.XX. | Nomen servare videtur opidum Fos, in Campis Lapideis.
units.tr: From Nicaea to Antipolis, a port, 16 Roman miles. | Antibes, in its place. From Antipolis to Lero and the island Lerina, 11 miles. | The Îles de Sainte-Marguerite and de Saint-Honorat. From Lero and Lerina to Forum Iulium, a port, 24 miles. | Fréjus. I have spoken of it elsewhere. From Forum Iulium to the Sambracitan Gulf, a bay, 25 miles. | Golfe de Grimaud. From the Sambracitan Gulf to Heraclea Caccabaria, a port, 16 miles. From Heraclea Caccabaria to Alconis, 12 miles. From Alconis to the Pompeian ports, 30 miles. From the Pompeians to Telo Martius, a port, 15 miles. From Telo Martius to Taurentum, a port, 12 miles. | Taurenta, a castle of the Massiliots, in Caesar; Ταυρεντον in Strabo, Ptolemy and Stephanus. Cenalis, Albenas, Massonius and others think it is the town that is today Toulon; but that it cannot be so is clear here from Antoninus, who puts Telo first. Where it lay I do not know. From Taurentum to Carsicum, a port, 18 miles. | The memory of the place is preserved at the promontory of Cerchiech. From Carsici to Citharista, a port, 18 miles. | Κιθαριστὰς in Ptolemy; Citharista in Pliny and Mela. Today different promontories lie close together: Cap de Sainte-Sigo, Cirgelli, Saint-Bacro. From Citharista to the port of Aemines, a fortified place, 6 miles. | In other copies Mines, likewise Hemines. From the port of Aemines to Immadrae, 12 miles. | Perhaps where Maire is today. It is read variously in Antoninus. From Immadrae to Massilia Graecorum, a port, 12 miles. | Marseille. From Massilia Graecorum to Incarus, a fortified place, 12 miles. | It falls roughly at the place that today, on the Massaliot Gulf, is Carry. From Incarus to Dilum, a fortified place, 8 miles. From Dilis to the Marian ditches, a port, 20 miles. | The town of Fos, in the Stony Plains, seems to keep the name.

units.la: De Antiquissimis porro Provincia Comitibus pauca inveniuntur. Tempore Ludovici VIII, Francorum Regis, lego in vetustissimis Annalibus fuisse Raimundum Berengarium Provinciae Comitem ejusque Filiam unicam & Heredem Beatricem, Uxorem fuisse ductam ab Karolo Andium & Cenomanorum Comite, ejusdem Ludovici Regis Filio, qui hoc Matrimonio Provinciae Comitatum est adeptus. Successit huic Karolus, Claudius cognomine, Princeps Salernitanus, & Rex Neapolis. Hunc sequutus est Filius Robertus, Dux Calabriae, & Rex Neapolitanus. Robertum Avum excepit Ioanna (cujus Pater Karolus, Calabriae Dux, jam vitam cum morte commutarat) testamento cum Regina Neapolis, tum Provincia Comes facta. Haec Ludovicum Andegavensem, Ioannis Francorum Regis Filium, quem explendo in Adversarios odio adoptarat, Successorem & in aliis Principatibus, & in eodem Comitatu reliquit. Post Ludovicum Comes factus est Filius ejus Ludovicus II; quem sequutus Ludovicus III Filius, quum etiam ab Ioanna II. Neapolis Regina in Regem Siciliae, Calabriaeque Ducem esset adoptatus, in prolis Successorem habuit in suis Principatibus, ex consensu ejusdem Ioannae II, Renatum Andegavensem, Fratrem. Hic quum Regni Neapolitani Provinciaque Comitatus jura resignare nollet Renato Lotharingiae Duci, ex Filia Iolanta Nepoti, ea transscripsisse memoratur in Karolum Fratrem Cenomanorum Comitem: qui Filio Karolo orbatus Ludovicum XI, Francorum Regem, omnium Bonorum Haeredem instituisse scribitur. Alii suprema id Renati voluntate factum volunt; non absque gravissima justissimaque Renati Lotharingici expostulatione.
units.tr: Little is found about the earliest counts of Provence. In the time of Louis VIII, King of the Franks, I read in very old annals that Raimund Berengar was Count of Provence, and that his only daughter and heir, Beatrice, was married to Charles, Count of Anjou and Maine, son of the same King Louis; by this marriage he obtained the county of Provence. He was succeeded by Charles, surnamed Claudius, Prince of Salerno and King of Naples. He was followed by his son Robert, Duke of Calabria and King of Naples. Robert's grandchild Joan (whose father Charles, Duke of Calabria, had already died) succeeded him, and by his will was made Countess of Provence along with the Queen of Naples. She left this county, and her other principalities, to Louis of Anjou, son of John, King of the Franks, whom in her hatred of her enemies she had adopted. After Louis, his son Louis II became count. He was followed by his son Louis III; and since he too had been adopted by Queen Joan II of Naples as King of Sicily and Duke of Calabria, he had as successor in his principalities, with the consent of the same Joan II, his brother René of Anjou. When René would not surrender the rights to the kingdom of Naples and the county of Provence, he is recorded to have transferred them to Charles, his brother, Count of Maine, to Renée's nephew René, Duke of Lorraine, son of his daughter Yolande. Charles, bereaved of his son Charles, is written to have made Louis XI, King of the Franks, heir to all his goods. Others hold that this was done by René's last will, not without a most grave and most just protest by René of Lorraine.

units.la: CAP. XL.
units.tr: CHAPTER XL.

units.la: Sic se habet Provincia, quae Aquensi paret Parlamento: sequitur Delphinatus, qui Gratianopolitano.
units.tr: Such is the Province that is subject to the Parlement of Aix. Next comes Dauphiné, which is subject to Grenoble.

units.la: Delphinatus ad Meridiem adhaeret Provinciae; ad Septentrionem Territorium, quod vulgo Bresse, interfluente Rodano: qua Occidens est, Venetiae se pandit Comitatus; qua Oriens, Conregionalia iacent Pedemontium & Sabaudia. Nomen illi volunt ab Castello Delphini, quod vernacule Chasteau Dolphin. Regio est non eiusdem ubique geniī: ferax plerisque locis variarum rerum; nonnullis etiam sterilior praecipue qua vestita Montibus; qui crebri hic sunt distincti Cognominibus. Incolae magni sunt Libertatis aestimatores: Fan Deo, tuoque Sanguini acceptam ferunt: Militiae contra Hostem feroces; domi peragundis inter se Negociis satis industrii, ab Vicinis astu facile superantur. Agri olim bardi sunt, stupidi, crassaeque naris: Nobiles, quique Vires habitant, humani, nihil prae se ferunt Fastus, procul ab omni Arrogantia: Moribus, citra Gravitatis detrimentum, amoenis; alacris ingenii; Scientiarum omnium, maxime vero Matheleos, mirum quam capaces; studiosissimi rerum Naturalium indagatores.
units.tr: Dauphiné borders on Provence to the south and on the territory commonly called Bresse to the north, with the Rhône flowing between. On the west it stretches out to the County of Venaissin, and on the east lie the neighbouring regions of Piedmont and Savoy. Some hold that its name comes from the Castle of the Dauphin, which in the vernacular is called Chasteau Dolphin. The region is not of the same character everywhere. In many places it is fertile in various products, but in some places it is rather barren, especially where it is covered by mountains, which here are numerous and distinguished by their own names. The inhabitants greatly value liberty; they attribute it to God and to their own blood. They are fierce in war against the enemy, and sufficiently industrious in carrying on their affairs among themselves at home, though they are easily outdone in cunning by their neighbours. The fields were formerly rough and stupid, with broad noses. The nobles, and those who inhabit the cities, are courteous and show no pride, far from all arrogance. Their manners are pleasant without loss of dignity, and their wit is lively. They are wonderfully capable of all the sciences, and especially of mathematics, and they are most eager investigators of natural things.

units.la: Floruerunt hic olim praeter Allobroges (de quibus Delphinatus etiam olim Incolis, in Sabaudia mea) Viennenses; Caturiges, Ebroduncenses, Segalauni, Valentini, Vocontii, Dcnses, Gratianopolitani, Tricastini, Vapincenses, Brannovii. Vienne sium Civitas nominatur in Notitia Provinciarum Galliae; Hodie L'Archevesché de Vienne: Viennensium Colonia, quae hodie Vienna, nominatur in Oratione Claudii, de qua post. Caturiges Plinio Caesarique dicuntur, qui Καθύρεγες Strabonii & Ptolemaeo. Eorum Nomen manere putatur hodieque in oppido, quod ad Druentiam Chorges audit, haud procul Ebrduno, quod Caturigum Metropolis Viris doctis contentur. Ebrodunensium certe Civitas Notitiae Provinciarum in Viennensi iv, hodie L'Archevesché d'Ambrun. Dicam plenius paullo post. Vide & praecedente Capite quae scripsi de Ebrodunensibus, qui iidem videntur cum Ebrodunensibus: an non & cum Ambivaritis, Eduorum Clientibus, apud Caesarem lib. vii? Segalauni, Σεγαλαυνοι Ptolemaeo, qui forte Plinio Segellauni, restituendi, ni fallor; apud Iustinum lib. xiii, in locum Segobrigiorum: hodie, Pais de Valentinois. Valentia enim apud Ptolemaeum Segalaunorum est Metropolis, non autem Cavarum, ut est apud Plinium. Valentinorum Civitas Notitiae Provinciarum in Viennensi i, L'Evesché de Valence. Voconti Caesari, Tacito, Melx;
units.tr: Formerly there flourished here, besides the Allobroges (of whom I have also spoken in my account of Savoy, under the inhabitants of Dauphiné), the Viennenses, Caturiges, Ebroduncenses, Segalauni, Valentini, Vocontii, Deenses, Gratianopolitani, Tricastini, Vapincenses and Brannovii. The city of the Viennenses is named in the Notitia of the Provinces of Gaul; today it is the Archbishopric of Vienne. The colony of the Viennenses, which today is called Vienna, is named in the speech of Claudius, which I shall discuss later. The Caturiges are called by Pliny and Caesar, and Καθύρεγες by Strabo and Ptolemy. Their name is thought to survive to this day in the town on the Durance called Chorges, not far from Embrun, which learned men maintain was the metropolis of the Caturiges. The city of the Ebrodunenses certainly appears in the Notitia of the Provinces, in the Viennese region, as number iv; today it is the Archbishopric of Embrun. I shall say more about this a little later. See also what I wrote in the previous chapter about the Ebrodunenses, who seem to be the same people as the Ebrodunenses. Are they not also the same as the Ambivareti, clients of the Aedui, in Caesar, book vii? The Segalauni, Σεγαλαυνοι in Ptolemy, who perhaps in Pliny are the Segellauni, should, unless I am mistaken, be restored in Justin, book xiii, in place of the Segobrigii. Today it is the Pays de Valentinois. For in Ptolemy Valentia is the metropolis of the Segalauni, not of the Cavari, as it is in Pliny. The city of the Valentini in the Notitia of the Provinces, in the Viennese region, is number i; today it is the Bishopric of Valence. The Vocontii are named by Caesar, Tacitus and Mela; Strabo has οὐεσόντιοι; Ptolemy has Ouerdes, corruptly. The Vecuni in Justin, book xliii, should be restored in place of the Vesii, the manuscript written by hand supporting this. Pliny calls them a people. They are mentioned in the Roman Fasti, together with the neighbouring Ligurians and Salluvii, in a passage of Verrius Flaccus. Today it is the Pays de Die as far as Vaison. For, as Joseph Scaliger, my revered friend, pointed out to me in a letter, the Augusta of the Diatonici is read in the inscriptions; the city of the Deenses in the Notitia of the Provinces is Vence de Die. There, too, is the city of the Gratianopolitani, the Bishopric of Grenoble. The Tricastini are named by Livy and Pliny, who call their metropolis Augusta Tricastinorum. Ptolemy calls their city ἡ Ἀγκυονα, as the better manuscripts have it, for in the others it is Νεμαυσος. Ammianus, book xv, reads Tricastini, and Ape Castra is the better reading. The Notitia of the Provinces, in the Viennese region, names the city of the Tricastini; today it is the Bishopric of Saint-Paul-Trois-Châteaux, in the Tricastin. The same Notitia also has the city of the Vapincenses in the Viennese region; today it is the Bishopric of Gap, in the Gapençois. I do not know whether the Brannovii, whom Caesar, book vii, makes clients of the Aedui along with the others, should also be referred here. The town that is commonly called Briançon is added.

units.la: { } Delphinatus ad Meridiem adhaeret Provinciae. lx; οὐεσόντιοι, Straboni; qui ⸀ Ouerdes corrupte Ptolemaeo. Vecuni apud Iustinum lib. xliii. reponendi, exturbatis Vesii, suffragante Manu exarato Codice. Plinius Vocatur Gentem vocat. Triumphantur in Fastis Romanorum, ab Verrio Flacco concinn. ius, cum vicinis Liguribus Salluviisque. Hodie Le Pais de Die jusques à Vaifon. Nam, uti notavit uus ad me literis V. N. Iosephus Scaliger, Augusta Diatonorum legitur in Inscriptionibus Civitas Deensium in Notitia Provinciarum, Ventche de Die. Ibidem Civitas Gratianopolitanorum, L'Eveche de Grenoble Trecastini Livio & Plinio qui eorum. Metropolin vocat Augustam Treviorum Ptolemaeo cui Civitas ipsorum ἡ Ἀγκυονα, ut quidem meliores habent Codices. Nam in aliis Νεμαυσος, legitur Tricastini, inquit Ammianus lib. xv. Ape Castra melius. Notitiae Provinciarum in Viennensi Civitas Tricastinorum: Hodie l'Eveche S. Aventi de Tricastin. Habet & eadem Notitia in Viennensi Civitatem Vapincensium, L'Eveche de Gap, le Pais de Gapençois. Nescio an huc etiam referendi Brannovii, quos cum aliis Eduorum Clientes facit Caesar lib. vii. Adiunat Urbs, quae vulgo Briançon.
units.tr: Delphinatus ad Meridiem adhaeret Provinciae. The Vocontii are named by Strabo... Ptolemy corruptly has Ouerdes. The Vecuni in Justin, book xliii... The Vesii are to be displaced, as the hand-written codex supports. Pliny calls the people... They are mentioned in the Fasti of the Romans, a passage of Verrius Flaccus, together with the neighbouring Ligurians and Salluvii. Today it is the Pays de Die as far as Vaison. For, as Joseph Scaliger wrote to me, Augusta Diatonorum is read in the inscriptions. The city of the Deenses in the Notitia is Vence de Die. There too is the city of the Gratianopolitani, the Bishopric of Grenoble. The Tricastini are named by Livy and Pliny, who call their metropolis Augusta Treviorum... in Ptolemy, whose city is ἡ Ἀγκυονα, as the better manuscripts have it. In others it is Νεμαυσος. Ammianus, book xv, reads Tricastini; Ape Castra is better. The Notitia in the Viennese region names the city of the Tricastini; today it is the Bishopric of Saint-Paul-Trois-Châteaux. The same Notitia also has the city of the Vapincenses in the Viennese region; today it is the Bishopric of Gap, the Gapençois.

units.la: Haec de Antiquis Delphinatus nostri Populis; venio ad Urbes, quarum duae Archiepiscopales, quinque Episcopales, reliquae minorum gentium. Archiepiscopales sunt Vienna & Ebrodunum.
units.tr: These things are said concerning the ancient peoples of our Dauphiné. I come now to the cities, of which two are archiepiscopal, five episcopal, and the rest of lesser rank. The archiepiscopal cities are Vienne and Embrun.

units.la: Vienna (cui nomen fertur ab Venerio Asio Exsule, qui hiemato exstruxisse dicitur: quod quis non rideat?) Caesari lib. vi. belli Gallici, Tacito, aliisque Auctoribus, interpretationibus item passim notissima: Civitas Allobrogum Metropolis, Straboni lib. iv. eorundem Urbs mediterranea, Ptolemaeo, Βιέννα, Stephano: Gratissima Colonia in Oratione Claudii, quae Lugduni exstat, aere Tabulae incisa: Vulgo Vienne, Vetus nomen retinens Iuris quondam Italici, inquit Paullus IC. Tit. D. de Censibus. Ad decimum sextum lapidem abesse Lugduno, testatur in Ludo Mortis Claudii Imperat. Seneca. Sita ad Rodanum, Ἀδέννα ἐπὶ τῷ Ῥοδανῷ, inquit de ea Strabo. Alpiam dixit Rutilius Epist. xxiii. Sic & Carmine iv Parentali.
units.tr: Vienne (whose name is said to come from Venerius Asius, an exile, who is reported to have built it while wintering there; who would not laugh at this?) is well known throughout from Caesar, book vi of the Gallic War, from Tacitus and other authors, and also from interpreters. It was the metropolis of the Allobroges, according to Strabo, book iv; the city of the same people in the interior, according to Ptolemy, Βιέννα, according to Stephanus. It is the most pleasing colony in the speech of Claudius, which survives at Lyon, engraved on bronze tablet. Today it is called Vienne, keeping the old name of its former Italian right, as the jurist Paulus says, Digest, title On the Census. Seneca, in the Satire on the Death of the Emperor Claudius, testifies that it is sixteen miles from Lyon. Strabo says of it: "Vienna is situated on the Rhône." Rutilius, Epistle xxiii, called it Alpia, and so also in the fourth Parental Poem.

units.la: quaque potentes Aedues, Alpino cuaque Vienna iugo.
units.tr: "and wherever the mighty Aedui are, and Vienna on its Alpine ridge."

units.la: Hinc apud eundem Libro de Urbibus, Carmine vii:
units.tr: Hence, in the same author, in the book on Cities, poem vii:

units.la: Alpinis opulenta Vienna Colonis.
units.tr: Vienna, rich in its Alpine colonists.

units.la: Senatoriam aliquando appellatam notat Paradinus, de antiquo Statu Burgundiae, quo Auctore, mihi nondum constat: & sic eam nominat Papirius Massonius in Annalibus. Non Archiepiscopatus solum honorata Titulo; verum etiam in Ducatus hodie dignitatem evecta: Duché de Viennois. Episcopus Primus perhibetur fuisse Crescens, D. Pauli Discipulus. Eiusdem Urbis Antistes fuisse scribitur Mamertus; qui Cladem Urbi imminentem deprecatus fertur indictis, quas & ad Posteros transfinit, Supplicationibus. De Vetere inter Lugdunenses Viennensesque ob principatum discordia, mutuoque odio, legendus Cornelius Tacitus lib. i. Historiarum. Memorat Suetonius, Vitellio Imperatori, Vienna pro Tribunali Iura reddenti. Galinaceum supra humerum, ac deinde in Capite adstitisse; nec fefellisse coniecturam eorum, qui Augurio non aliud portendi praedixerant, quam venturum in alicuius Gallicani Hominis potestatem: si quidem ab Antonio, primo Adversarium Partium Duce, oppressus, cui Tolosae nato cognomen in pueritia Pero fuerat: id valet Gallinacei rostrum. Vienna Calamitatem magnam passa est ab Rodani exundantis impetu, anno cIↄ Iↄ xliii. In gratiam porro Turnonii Vini generosissimi non abs re videtur addendum: quod Plinius de eo iam olim prodidit: Iam inventa, inquit, Vitis, per se in Vino Puram respiciens, Vienneñsem Agrum nobilitans, Arverno, Sequanorumque & Helvetiorum generibus non pridem illustrata. Pontii Pilati Fabulam; famosum illud Specus, quod Nebulis perpetuo obumbratur: Pyramidesque, quas monstrant in Vineis ad Urbem Incolae, exsulantis ibi Domum fuisse perhibentes, alii majore praeconio celebrent: Nam mihi non magnae haec talia solent esse fidei. Ebrodunum, Ἐβρόδουνον Ptolemaeo, Caturigum vel Alpium Maritimarum, Ἐμβρόδουνον κώμη, Straboni; Ebrodunum, Antonino; Eburnum, vitiose, Tabulae Itinerariae: Vernacule Ambrun. Aliud est Ebrodunum in Finibus Helvetiorum, Iverdum. In Notitia Imperii legitur: Sub Duce Magontiacensi Praefectus Classis Barcariorum Ebredunensi Sapandia. Unde nomen Ebrodune, solicite non quaeram. Quid Dunum alibi à me dictum. Montibus cingitur, qui Vini, Fructuum, Simpliciumque innumerorum feraces. Suis parcere Præsulibus, eosque Principes ie dicere, legos multis magnisque donatos ab Regibus Francia Privilegiis; inter quæ abi lata luitio Administratio, Ius cudendæ Monetæ, aliaque id genus Regalia. Metropolis est Pagi, qui vulgo imbrunois.
units.tr: Paradin notes that it was once called Senatoria, in his work on the ancient state of Burgundy, though I am not yet sure of his authority. Papirius Massonius calls it by the same name in his Annals. It is honoured not only with the title of archbishopric but has also been raised today to the dignity of a duchy, the Duché de Viennois. The first bishop is said to have been Crescens, a disciple of St Paul. Mamertus is recorded as bishop of the same city. He is said to have averted the disaster threatening the city by proclaiming supplications, which he also handed down to posterity. On the ancient rivalry between the people of Lyon and those of Vienne, over precedence, and their mutual hatred, the reader should consult Cornelius Tacitus, Histories book 1. Suetonius reports that when Vitellius the emperor was dispensing justice from the tribunal at Vienne, a rooster stood first on his shoulder and then on his head. The conjecture of those who had foretold from this omion only that it portended something would come under the power of some Gaul was not wrong. For he was overthrown by Antonius, the first leader of the opposing party, who had been born at Toulouse and in boyhood bore the nickname Pero, which means a rooster's beak. Vienne suffered great calamity from the violent flood of the Rhône in the year 1543. In favour of Tournon's most excellent wine, it seems worth adding what Pliny long ago reported of it: "Now the vine has been discovered," he says, "which, pure in itself, looks toward wine, ennobling the territory of Vienne, lately made famous by the Arverni and by the Sequani and Helvetii." As for the story of Pontius Pilate, that notorious cave always shrouded in mist, and the pyramids which the inhabitants point out in the vineyards near the city, claiming that Pilate lived there in exile, others celebrate these with greater acclaim. I myself do not usually put much faith in such things. Ebrodunum, Ἐβρόδουνον in Ptolemy, of the Caturiges or of the Maritime Alps, Ἐμβρόδουνον, a village according to Strabo; Ebrodunum in Antoninus; Eburnum, wrongly, in the Itinerary Table; in the vernacular, Ambrun. There is another Ebrodunum in the territory of the Helvetii, Yverdon. In the Notitia Imperii one reads: under the Duke of Mainz, the prefect of the fleet of the Barcarii at Ebrodunum, Sapandia. I shall not anxiously inquire where the name Ebrodunum comes from. As for Dunum, I have spoken of it elsewhere. It is girt by mountains, fertile in wine, fruit and countless simples. Its bishops are accustomed to be called princes, and I have read that they were endowed by the kings of France with many great privileges, among which are the administration of justice, the right to mint coin, and other regalia of that kind. It is the metropolis of the district commonly called the Embrunais.

units.la: Episcopales Vrbes sunt quinque: Valentia, Dea, Gratianopolis, Augusta, Vapincum. Valentia, Antonino Οὐαλεντία, Ptolemæo, Segalaunorum Vrbs, non autem Calarum, ut est apud Plinium: Valentina Vrbs, Sidonio lib. vi. Epist. xii. & Prospero in Chronico; Civitas Valentia, Itinerario Burdigalensi, Valentina Civitas, Pontificio Papæ ad Episcopos Galliæ: Nobilissima Galliarum Civitas, eidem Prospero: Vulgo Valence; Ducatus titulo gaudens. Metropolis Territorii, quod Indigenæ Valentinois, Duché de Valentinois. Audiens semper Romanorum Imperio, circa annum cccxv occupata legitur ab Gothis; inde a Burgundionibus; passa etiam obsidionem anno 15 lxxvi ab Langbardis, frustra. Visuntur ibi Singularia quædam. In Monasterio Iacobitarum, Effigies Gigantis Buardi, xv Cubitos proceri; eiusque Ossa. Extra Vrbem, in Aedis D. Petri Ruderibus, Antrum sub Rodani Fluenta productum: Alia præterea. De invento extra Portam Divi Felicis Vineis Corpore Iuslina, cum quibusdam Ornamentis, alij legendi: Nam ego parum hic certus. Dea Vocontiorum, Antonino, in melioribus Libris; in aliis Dea Vocontiorum: Augusta D. à Vocontiorum, in antiquis Inscriptionibus, ut suis ad me Literis testatur V. N. Iosephus Scaliger. Deas Caistrum forte an Gregorio Turonensi lib. iii. Dies vulgo; Metropolis Agri, qui vernacule, Pais de Diois. Gratianopolis olim Cularo vocabatur. In Epistola Planci ad Ciceronem, quæ incipit, Numquam me hercle, in fine ita editum vulgo: Octavo Idus Iunias, Civarone in Finibus Allobrogum ubi legendum, Cularone. In Notitia Imperii ita excusum est, In Provincia Gallia Riparensi, Tribunus Cohortis Primæ Flaviæ Vapaudræ Calarone; ubi reponendum, Culasee, aut Cularone. Et quum non sit dubium, quin & Ptolemæus Vrbis tam præclaræ, Priscisque etiam celebratæ, fecerit mentionem; fere est, ut putem nomen apud eum periisse. Legitur hodie lib. ii. cap. x. quo Galliæ Narbonensis Situs delineatur, Ἀκουσίων, Latinis Interpretibus, imperitius huiusmodi Voces, quasi pluralis essent numeri, vertentibus, Acusiorum Colonia, quum simpliciter scribenda fuisset Acusio. Sed reponendum ibi, meo quidem iudicio, antiquum illud Vrbis Nomen Κυλαρὼν, Cularo. Ab Curalone porro Culaxonenses Muri in Antiquis Inscriptionibus: quarum una quidem in Vrbis Porta visitur, quæ ad Meridiem pertinet, Romana dicta; altera vero in Porta, qua Viennam itur, queque ad Septemtriones vergit. Post, ampliata fortean ab Imperatore Gratiano, Gratianopolis fuit appellata: Eo nomine nota Augustino lib. xxi. De Civitate Dei, cap. vii, Sidonio Apollinari lib. iii. Epistol. xiv, Gregorio Turonensi lib. iv. cap. xliv. Paullo Diacono lib. iii. de Gestis Langbardor. cap. viii. Civitas Gratianopolitana, Isidoro. Vulgo Grainople. Sedes amplissimi Senatus Delfinatensis, Isarsi, cujus sæpe meminit Plancus, adsita: ad Pedem Montis, qui vulgo Chalemont. Qua fuerit olim forma, monstrant antiqui Muri Portæque. Mœnia ab Francisco I Galliarum Rege cœpta, quum absoluta fuerint, Vrbem fere facient quadratam. Ad Septemtrionem inter ipsam Vrbem & elegans Suburbium, cui ab D. Laurentio cognomen, fluit Isara, Ponte stratus, omnium pulcherrimo. Ad Meridiem præter labitur Draeus, Torrens valde vehemens, Agros non raro limosis deformans Inundationibus, nulloque volens valensque Aggere coerceri. Territorium vel potius Ager Suburbicarius vocatur Graisivouidan ab Vulgo Delfinatium, & à quibusdam contracte Grivauldan, voce corrupta ex Gratianopolitano. Haud procul Vrbe, qua Septemtrio est, Fodina sunt, ex quibus Lapides in Civitatis usum eruuntur. Primo ab Vrbe Lapide Vicus est, qui vulgo Parisct: ibi Turris visitur, quæ Incolis La Tour S. Venin. Appellationis caufiam intelligo, quod quale quale Venenatum Animal in eam inlatum evestigio enecetur. Ab nemine interim mortalium habitatur. Augusta Tricastinorum, Plinio lib. iv. cap. iii. Tricastina Vrbs, Sidonio lib. vi. Epist. xii: Τυλλομαγυ forte Ptolemæo, apud quem in Vulgatis legitur Νοιμαγυ. Hodie, ut censet V. N. Iosephus Scaliger, S. Antoni de Tricastin. Alij aliud fabricant huic Augusta opidum. Ioannes Poldus Avmargues, vel Trois Chasteaux; Cœnalis. S. Paul; Similerus Tricuci. Augusta putatur Antonini: sed situs non patitur. Vapingum Antonino, vel quemadmodum in quibusdam Libris legitur Vapincum, ut & in Itineraria Tabula; Vapinquum pinarum Aimoino: Cap hodie. Caput Agri, qui vernacule Gapençois montibus obsiti. Iptum Opidum, ut hodie, hic & olim celebre. Nam Antoninus Iter Vapincum designat ducitque Mediolano) ad pedem est situm Montis excelsi, qui Adcolis Le Col S. Dom: Sedes siallivatus.
units.tr: The episcopal cities are five: Valentia, Dea, Gratianopolis, Augusta, Vapincum. Valentia, Οὐαλεντία in Antoninus, is a city of the Segalauni, not Calaris as in Pliny; the city of Valentia in Sidonius, book 6, letter 12, and in Prosper's Chronicle; the city Valentia in the Bordeaux Itinerary; the Valentinian city in a papal letter to the bishops of Gaul; the most noble city of Gaul in the same Prosper. In the vernacular, Valence. It enjoys the title of a duchy, and is the metropolis of the territory which the natives call Valentinois, Duché de Valentinois. It is recorded as always subject to the Roman empire until about the year 315, when it was taken by the Goths, and then by the Burgundians. It also endured a siege by the Lombards in the year 576, to no purpose. Certain singular things are to be seen there. In the monastery of the Jacobites is the effigy of the giant Buardus, fifteen cubits tall, and his bones. Outside the city, among the ruins of the church of St Peter, is a cave extending beneath the streams of the Rhône; there are other things besides. Concerning what was found outside the Gate of St Felix in the vineyards, a body of Iuslina with certain ornaments, others may read; for I am not very certain of it. Dea of the Vocontii, in Antoninus in the better books; in others Dea Vocontiorum: Augusta of the Vocontii, in ancient inscriptions, as Joseph Scaliger, my most learned friend, attests in his letters to me. Deas Caistrum, perhaps in Gregory of Tours, book 3, commonly Dies; the metropolis of the district which in the vernacular is called Pais de Diois. Gratianopolis was formerly called Cularo. In Plancus's letter to Cicero, which begins "Never, by Hercules," the end is printed commonly as: On the eighth day before the Ides of June, at Civaro in the territory of the Allobroges, where one should read Cularone. In the Notitia Imperii it is printed thus: In the province of Gallia Riparensis, the tribune of the First Flavian Cohort of Vapaudra at Calaro, where Culasee or Cularone should be restored. And since there is no doubt that Ptolemy too made mention of so famous a city, celebrated even in ancient times, I think it likely that the name has perished in his text. It is read today in book 2, chapter 10, where the situation of Gallia Narbonensis is described, as Ἀκουσίων, which Latin translators, less skilfully, rendered as if such words were plural, the colony of the Acusii, whereas it should simply have been written Acusio. But there, in my judgement, the ancient name of the city, Κυλαρὼν [Kylarōn], should be restored: Cularo. From Curalo come the Culaxonenses walls in ancient inscriptions. One of these is seen at the city gate that faces south, called Romana, and another at the gate by which one goes to Vienne, which faces north. Afterwards, perhaps enlarged by the Emperor Gratian, it was called Gratianopolis, a name known from Augustine, City of God, book 21, chapter 7; Sidonius Apollinaris, book 3, letter 14; Gregory of Tours, book 4, chapter 44; Paul the Deacon, History of the Lombards, book 3, chapter 8; and the city of Gratianopolis in Isidore. In the vernacular, Grenoble. It is the seat of the most ample Senate of Dauphiné, Isarsi, often mentioned by Plancus, and lies at the foot of the mountain which in the vernacular is called Chalemont. Its former shape is shown by the ancient walls and gates. The walls begun by Francis I, king of the French, when completed will make the city almost square. Between the city itself and its elegant suburb, which takes its name from St Laurence, flows the Isère, spanned by a bridge, the most beautiful of all. To the south flows the Drac, a very violent torrent, which often disfigures the fields with muddy floods, and which, wishing to be restrained by no embankment, cannot be checked by any. The suburban territory, or rather district, is called by the Dauphinois in the vernacular Graisivaudan, and by some, in a shortened form, Grivauldan, a corrupted word from Gratianopolitanus. Not far from the city, to the north, there are quarries from which stone is dug for the city's use. Nearest to the city is a village called Parisct in the vernacular; there is a tower there, called La Tour S. Venin by the inhabitants. I understand the reason for the name: whatever poisonous creature is brought into it is killed on the spot. Meanwhile no mortal lives there. Augusta of the Tricastini, in Pliny book 4, chapter 3; the Tricastinian city, in Sidonius book 6, letter 12. Perhaps Τυλλομαγυ in Ptolemy, where the printed texts read Νοιμαγυ. Today, as Joseph Scaliger, my most learned friend, thinks, it is S. Antoine de Tricastin. Others invent a different town for this Augusta: John Pold makes it Aymargues or Trois Châteaux; Cenalis, St Paul; Similerus, Tricuci. Augusta is thought to be in Antoninus, but the situation does not allow it. Vapingum in Antoninus, or as some books read, Vapincum, as also in the Itinerary Table; Vapinquum in Aimoin: today Gap. It is the head of the district which in the vernacular is called Gapençois, dotted with mountains. This town, as today, was also famous in former times. For Antoninus designates the road to Vapincum, leading from Milan, and it is situated at the foot of a high mountain, which the locals call Le Col S. Dom. It is the seat of a bailiwick.

units.la: Praeter Pagos illos Suburbicarios, quos jam nominavi, Viennois, Ambrunnois, Vallentinois, Diois, Graisivaudan, & Gapençois: sunt & alij quidam, qui vernacule, Les Pais de Trieves, des Baronnies, & Briançonnois. Primi primarium opidum est Mens; Secundi, Bays; Tertij Briançon, Brigantio Antonino & Itinerariae Tabulae, nεμμοτ Strabonis & Ptolemaeo, Brigantium, de quibus alibi, Urbs; Virgantia Ammiano, cuius, de Via Alpium Cottiarum loquentis, verba sunt haec: Unde declive quidem ster, sed expeditius ad sine Castellum Virgantiam patet. Haud procul Brigantio Rupes est in formam Portae pertusa, cui insculpta leguntur: D. CAESARI. AVGVSTO. DEDICATA. SALVTATE EAM: quae mihi non sapiunt Antiquitatem. Factam perhibent ab C. Iulio Caesare, ut ea in Gallias penetraret. Comitatus Titulo nobilia sunt Champsaur & Kel Iilon, quod Vosgis omnino Antonini. Alia multa habet Delfinatus minorum gentium opida: quae, cum Superioribus, Francorum Geographi trium faciunt genera. Fluvijs adsident; Rodano quidem, cum Vienna & Valentia, Montmartum & Tricastinum; quorum hoc Proceribus paret Tournonentibus: Illarae vero, praeter Grasmopolin, item Mon-Melianum & Romanum, opida Arcipotentia; hoc etiam dives admodum, insignem habens Pontem, Romanos, ut multi centent testans tua Nomenclatura Conditores; vel eos saltem, qui Romani Nominis studiosi, sic dixisse volunt. In Montanis, praeter Ebrodunum, Diam, Vapincum, Brigantium & Bucium, quorum jam memini sunt, quae Francico Idiomate; Talart, Alamontis Antonino; apud quem & Alapuntis & Alabuntis, item Alalontis: Alarante est in Itineraria Tabula hoc loco, bis, nullo alio opido interjecto. Charges, Caturigum Sedes, ut antea monui; Caturiae & Caturigae Antonino, ni fallor: Catoriscomagus Itinerariae Tabulae, in qua sequitur Icododurum inter Caturigas & Vapincum. Chastran roux, Laminarum hic Fons, quae Scandulae solent dici, Ardoises Francis. S. Crespin: nisi hoc Rame sit Antonini, & Rama Itinerariae Tabulae; certe haud procul inde fuit. Montana item sunt Vayne, Sarre, Le Bayz, S. Euphemiae, Vanxerre, Corp, La Meutre, Men, Visible, magna hic Marmoris & Alabastritae copia; Ours; Effilles, Delfinatus Clavis, quibusdam Ocelum Caesaris, Ouelu Strabonis: Chapeau-Doifin, unde nomen putant impositum Provinciae; Guillestre, Scyne, Meulon, Chastillon, Montbrun, Romuillanette, Vraiz; S. Clement, Pagus interiori Montis Recessui, quod mirandum, inaedificatus. In planioribus porro locis, praeter Augustam Tricastinorum & Rofilionem sunt: Quirien, Cremieu, La Forpliere, Bourgoing, La Tour du Pin, Le Pont Beauvoisin, cujus pars media Sabaudiae est, La Cotte S. André, S. Donat, Macelan, Villeneuve, S. Marcelin, Tulous, Lamben, Modian, Moretel, S. Vallier, Beau repaire, Beaupas, Murat, Nerion, Len, cui fertile Territorium, Ten, ubi praestantia Vina: Chasteau-d'Imble, Aleffan, Montelier, Beaumont, Laurenel, Cres, Sallions, locus Monaulis Litiuique nobilitatus, Verane, S. Paul, Arzallon.
units.tr: Besides those suburban districts which I have already named, Viennois, Ambrunois, Valentinois, Diois, Graisivaudan and Gapençois, there are some others which in the vernacular are called Les Pays de Trièves, des Baronnies and Briançonnois. The chief town of the first is Mens; of the second, Bays; of the third, Briançon, Brigantio in Antoninus and the Itinerary Table, Νεμμοτ in Strabo, Brigantium in Ptolemy, about which I shall speak elsewhere. Virgantia in Ammianus, whose words, speaking of the road through the Cottian Alps, are these: "From there the way down is indeed steep, but leads more quickly to the castle of Virgantia." Not far from Brigantio is a rock pierced in the form of a gate, on which the following is read carved: TO THE EMPEROR CAESAR AUGUSTUS, DEDICATED FOR HIS SAFETY, which does not smack of antiquity to me. They say it was made by Gaius Julius Caesar, so that he might penetrate into Gaul. Champsaur and Quiel are noted for their titles of county, which is entirely the Vosegus of Antoninus. Dauphiné has many other towns of lesser peoples, which, together with the greater ones, French geographers make into three classes. They lie on rivers: on the Rhône, with Vienne and Valence, Montmeyran and Tournon, of which the last is subject to the lords of Tournon; on the Isère, besides Grenoble, also Mont-Mélian and Romans, very powerful towns; this last is also very rich, having a remarkable bridge, and it is said by many, and its name testifies, to have been founded by the Romans, or at least by those who are fond of the Roman name and want it to be so. In the mountains, besides Embrun, Die, Vapincum, Briançon and Buis, of which I have already spoken, there are those which in French idiom are called: Talard, Alamontis in Antoninus, where also are Alapuntis and Alabuntis, likewise Alalontis; Alarante is in the Itinerary Table in this place, twice, with no other town between. Chorges, the seat of the Caturiges, as I said before; Caturiae and Caturigae in Antoninus, unless I am mistaken; Catoriscomagus in the Itinerary Table, where Icododurum follows between Caturiges and Vapincum. Châtelarour, here the source of the Laminarum, which are usually called Scandulae, Ardoises in French. St Crespin; unless this Rame is the Antoninus Rama of the Itinerary Table, it is certainly not far from there. Also mountain places are Vayne, Sarre, Le Bayz, St Euphémie, Vanxerre, Corps, La Meutte, Mens, Vizille, where there is a great abundance of marble and alabaster; Ours; Effilles; the Key of Dauphiné, which some call the Eye of Caesar and Strabo calls Ouelu; Chapeau-Dauphin, from which some think the name was given to the province; Guillestre, Saint-Sein, Meolon, Châtillon, Montbrun, Romuillanette, Vraiz; St Clément, a village built in the innermost recess of the mountain, which is remarkable. In the lower places, besides Augusta of the Tricastini and Rosillon, there are: Quirieu, Crémieu, La Forteresse, Bourgoin, La Tour-du-Pin, Le Pont-de-Beauvoisin, of which the middle part belongs to Savoy, La Côte-Saint-André, St Donat, Macelan, Villeneuve, St Marcellin, Tullins, Lamben, Moirans, Moretel, St Vallier, Beaurepaire, Beaupas, Murat, Nerion, Lens, to which belongs a fertile territory, Ten, where there are excellent wines; Châteaud'Imbert, Aleffan, Montelier, Beaumont, Laurenel, Crest, Saillans, a place made famous by the Monaulis and Liviu, Veynes, St Paul, Arzallon.

units.la: Inter postremos Delfinatium Principes legitur Guido, qui bellum cum Sabaudo gerens acie periit. Memineruntplene Francici posterioris aevi Scriptores: inter quos nonnulli incredibile quid de Guidone narrant. Improli successit Frater Humbertus, qui circa annum cIↄ cccxl dolore ardens amissi Filij, quem unicum habebat, nolensque ut nobilissima Provincia post obitum ipsius haereditaria Divisione in partes discerperetur, Coenobio Dominicanorum se sacraturus, Principatum Ioanni Francorum Regi addixit, ea lege, ut semper Primogenitus Franciae Delfinus esset. Quod factum: sicque primus Delfinus fuit Karolus ejusdem Ioannis Filius. Dixi nonnihil supra cap. xvii. Humbertus sane Monachum egit Parisiis in Iacobitarum Coenobio; ubi eius Sepulcrum visitur cum hoc Elogio: Cy gist le Pere & tres-illustre Seigneur Humbert jadis Dauphin de Viennois: puis laissant sa Principaute fut faict frere de nostre Ordre, & Prieur de ce Convent de Paris, & en sin Patriarche d'Alexandrie & perpetuel Administrateur de l'Archevesche de Reims, & principal Bienfaicteur de ce nostre Convent. Il mourut l'an de grace, mil trois cens cinquante cinq.
units.tr: Among the last Dauphins of Dauphiné we read of Guy, who waged war against the Savoyard and died in battle. French writers of the later period have recorded him at length, and some of them tell incredible things about Guy. Humbert, Guy's brother, succeeded him, and in about the year 1340, burning with grief at the loss of his only son and unwilling that this most noble province should be torn into pieces by hereditary division after his death, he resolved to consecrate himself to a Dominican house. He handed the principality over to John, King of the French, on the condition that the eldest son of the French kings should always be Dauphin. This was done, and so Charles, son of the same John, became the first Dauphin. I mentioned this briefly above in chapter 17. Humbert indeed lived as a monk in Paris, in the convent of the Jacobins, where his tomb may be seen with this inscription: Here lies the Father and most illustrious lord Humbert, formerly Dauphin of Vienne; then, having left his principality, he became a brother of our Order and Prior of this convent of Paris, and finally Patriarch of Alexandria and perpetual administrator of the archdiocese of Reims, and principal benefactor of this our convent. He died in the year of grace 1355.

units.tr: So much for Dauphiné, following the plan of this method. Next comes the Duchy of Burgundy, which falls under the jurisdiction of the Parlement of Dijon.

units.tr: The Duchy of Burgundy; Duché de Bourgogne; Burgundia ducatus.

units.la: BVRGVNDIÆ Nomen à Burgundionibus; qui Germaniæ Populi, ex Vandalorum orti sanguine. dictique à Burgo, ut suo dicam loco. ab Almannis (in horum enim Agris violenter in Capellatio, ubi hodie Palatini Comitis Ditio, confederant) exturbati, sub Theodosio Arcadij Filio, Iuniore, expulsis late Sequanis Eduisque, Edulfque, hanc Veteris Galliæ partem cum Nuithonibus (quorum Tacitus meminit) occuparunt. Legendum cum alijs. Mamertini Panegyricon. Eleganter Orosius lib. vii. cap. xxxii: de Burgundionibus: Galliæ hodieque testes sunt, in quibus præclara pacis fine consistunt, quamvis providentia DEI omnes Christiani modi facti Catholica fide, non ipsi quoque Gentis, quibus obedirent, receptis, blandè, mansuetè, innocenterque vixerunt; non quasi cum subjectis Gallis, sed vere cum Fratribus Christianis. Petrus Sancto-Julianus Burgundiæ Etymen ab Loco quodam ducit, qui vulgò Burg-Ogne in Agro Lingonensi. Burgundiones Romanis, quorum virtute non semel fuerant profligati, facta cum iis Pace, suppetias tulerunt adversus Chunnos in Campis Catalaunicis. Imperium illis fuit olim vastum. Partem enim Vallis Pœninæ, Sedunos, Allobroges, Lugdunum item, Viennam & alias Civitates Burgundiæ complectebatur, uti multis Francorum commemorant Annales. Gregorius Turonensis. lib. ii cap. ix. In his Thoringorum Partibus, id est ad Meridionalem plagam habitabant Romani, usque Ligerim Fluvium; ultra Ligerim vero Gothi dominabantur; Burgundiones quoque Arvernorum fidem sequentes, habitabant trans Rodanum, qui adjacet Civitati Lugdunensi. Et Ligurinus Poeta, scite Regni quondam Fines indicans: sic canit: Hæc adeo Tellus a Sedibus usque illis, Qua Rhætica suos vicino Flumine Muros Admovet, & Rhenum vententem læva salutat: Innumerosque tenens Populos, hinc Gallica Rura Mordet, & hinc rigidis Populosa Rupibus Alpis Arctatur, tractæque maris protenditur usque, Qua rapidus primas Rodanus maris influit undas. Quæque Caput Regni, Sedesque fuisse vetustis Fertur Arelatum præsorum Curia Regum. Teque sibi tangens aquo Provincia fine. Nomen apud Veteres Regni, titulumque gerebat, Cujus Arelatum Sedes, & Finis ab illa Parte ferebatur, donec suprema voluntas Regis Radulphi, Regnum accedere nostris Iussit, & antiqui detraxit nomen honoris; Vt iam non Regnum, sed sit bona portio Regni,
units.tr: The name Burgundy comes from the Burgundians, a people of Germanic stock, sprung from the blood of the Vandals, and named from a fortress (Burgus), as I shall say in its place. Driven out by the Alemanni (for they had settled violently in their lands, in Capellatio, where the territory of the Count Palatine now lies), under Theodosius the Younger, son of Arcadius, and with the Sequani and Aedui driven out far and wide, they seized this part of Old Gaul together with the Nuithones, whom Tacitus mentions. (The reading is to be corrected with the others; see the Panegyric of Mamertinus.) Orosius, book 7, chapter 32, speaks elegantly of the Burgundians: The Gauls to this day are witnesses, in whose regions they live in splendid peace; although by the providence of God they all became Christians and received the Catholic faith, they lived kindly, gently and harmlessly, not as with subjects of the Gauls, but truly as with Christian brothers, even though they had received as their rulers men of another nation. Petrus Sanctius Julianus derives the etymology of Burgundy from a certain place, commonly called Burg-Ogne, in the territory of Langres. The Burgundians, whose strength had more than once defeated the Romans, made peace with them and gave them aid against the Huns on the Catalaunian Plains. Their empire was once vast. For it included part of the Valais, the Sedunians, the Allobroges, Lyons also, Vienne and other cities of Burgundy, as many annals of the Franks record. Gregory of Tours, book 2, chapter 9: In these parts of the Thoringi, that is, in the southern region, the Romans lived as far as the river Loire; beyond the Loire the Goths ruled; the Burgundians also, who followed the faith of the Arverni, lived across the Rhône, which lies next to the city of Lyons. And the poet Ligurinus, indicating the old boundaries of the kingdom neatly, sings thus: This land, from those seats as far as where Rhaetia brings its walls near the neighbouring river, and greets the Rhine flowing on the left; holding countless peoples, here it bites the Gallic fields, and here the Alps, populous with their rigid cliffs, are pressed in, and it stretches out to the sea, where the swift Rhône pours its first waves into the sea. And Arles, which is said to have been the head of the kingdom and the seat of the ancient court of kings, and the province touching you with its near boundary. In the old days it bore the name and title of the kingdom, whose seat was Arles and whose boundary on that side was said to lie, until the last will of King Rudolph ordered the kingdom to be joined to ours and took away the name of its ancient honour; so that it is no longer a kingdom, but a good portion of the kingdom.

units.la: Aliorum Testimonia prætereo. Dissensiones itidem erant immortales fere cum Gothis, qui late tunc temporis per Gallias imperabant. Notat hoc Sidonius Epistola ad Felicem, de Arvernis loquens lib. iii. Epist. iv: Oppidum siquidem nostrum, quasi quondam sui Limitis obicem, circumfusarum nobis gentium arma terrificant. Sic æmulatorum sibi in medio positi populorum lacrymabilis præda, suspectis Burgundionibus, proximi Gothi, nec impugnantium ira, nec propugnantium careamus invidia. Idem lib. i. Epist. vii. ad Vincentium de Arvando Præfectorio, Læsæ Majestatis Reo, Litteras interceptas scribit, quibus ille Theoderico Gothorum Regi suadebat, cum Burgundionibus jure Gentium Gallias dividi debere. Fracta tandem est tanta ipsorum Felicitas ab Francis Sugambris; qui, facta post ipsos in Galliam irruptione, non solum Romanos potenter eiecerunt, verum etiam viribus Burgundionum armorum vi supra modum imminutis, potentiam eorum angustioribus concluserunt terminis. Consulendi, præter Francorum Annales, Agathias, cui Burgundiones appellantur, & alij. Olim Regnum, cujus Sedes, nunc, ut alibi doceo, & proxime ex Ligurino indicavi, Arelate, nunc Arelia fuisse legitur. Regum in Gallia primus nominatur Francis Scriptoribus Gundiachus Hirpis, utrumque notant, Gothicæ. Ceto ab Attila, cum multis aliis, in Campis Catalaunicis superstites fuerunt quatuor Filij, Gundebaldus, Gundegisilus, Hilperichus & Godomarius; quos scribunt ab excelsu Patris Burgundionibus simul imperasse. Ditionem in Tetrarchias partita. Sed quum rara sit Fratrum Concordia, orta inter eos simultate, Gundebaldus & Gundegisillus, ictu fædere, in Hilpericum & Godomarium arma movent, signisque conlatis utrumque obtruncant, Filijs ipsorum securi perculsis. Filiæ erant Hilperico duæ: earum altera Corona detonsa Monasterio includitur; altera Hrothildis, forma & indole regia, in Aula Patrui educatur Gundebaldi: quo in Italiam profecto, ibique rebus gerendis occupatione, Conjux ab Hlodovzeo Francorum Rege petita, eique mox solenniter data, Maritum paucis post nuptias diebus ad Patrem ulciscendum, Regnumque recuperandum exstimulavit. Belli inter ipsos finis fuit: quod Gundegisilo occiso, Gundeta.dus, facta indignissimis conditionibus Deditione, universæ Burgundiæ Rex, Francorum quasi patientia & beneficio, manserit: cui defuncto successit cum Gundemaro Fratre Sigismundus. Hunc quum Hlodomirus, Aurelianensium Princeps, bello victum captumque in altissimum puteum præcipitem cum Vxore Liberisque provolvisset; Gundemarus, Hlodomiro debellato, ab Hlotario Suessonum, & Hhuldeberto Parisiensium Regibus Heorhildis instigatione, Augustoduni obsessus est, urbeque capta jugulatus. Sic Regnum Burgundionum ad Francos devolutum, datum est, Theodorico, Hlodovei Filiorum natu maximo. Hic Burgundiam Theodoberto Filio reliquit, qui Successorem habuit Theobaldum. Eum sine Liberis defunctum sequutus est Hlothavius, Galliæ totius Monarcha, a quo tempore Burgundia penes Francorum Reges mansit. Regnum hoc circa annum CIO XXXIV, bipartitum in Ducatum & Comitatum abiit: quorum ille, versus Occidentem, Burgundia Inferior & Regia: hic, ad Orientem, Superior & Imperatoria. De ducatu hoc Capite mihi agitur: De Comitatu postea dicetur.
units.tr: I pass over the testimonies of others. There were likewise almost unending disputes with the Goths, who at that time ruled widely through the Gauls. Sidonius notes this in his letter to Felix, speaking of the Arverni, book 3, letter 4: Our town, as if it were once the bar of its own boundary, is terrified by the arms of the peoples surrounding us. Thus, placed in the middle of rival peoples, a tearful prey, with the Burgundians under suspicion, the neighbouring Goths, we lack neither the anger of our attackers nor the envy of our defenders. The same writer, book 1, letter 7, to Vincentius about Arvandus, the prefect, accused of treason, writes that letters were intercepted in which Arvandus urged Theodoric, king of the Goths, that the Gauls ought to be divided with the Burgundians by the law of nations. That great prosperity of theirs was at length broken by the Salian Franks, who, after making an invasion into Gaul behind them, not only powerfully drove out the Romans but also, the strength of the Burgundians' arms being diminished beyond measure, confined their power within narrower limits. Besides the annals of the Franks, Agathias, who calls them Burgundians, and others should be consulted. It is read that formerly there was a kingdom whose seat, as I show elsewhere, and as I have just indicated from Ligurinus, was Arles, and now Arelia. The first king of the Gauls named by the Frankish writers is Gundiachus of the Hirpi; both names are Gothic. After Attila had slain many others in the Catalaunian Plains, four sons survived: Gundebald, Gundegisil, Hilperic and Godomar; they are written to have ruled the Burgundians together after their father's death, having divided the dominion into tetrarchies. But since concord among brothers is rare, a quarrel arose among them, and Gundebald and Gundegisil, by breaking their treaty, took up arms against Hilperic and Godomar, and joining their standards, they cut down both, their sons having been struck down by the axe. Hilperic had two daughters: one of them, her hair shorn, was shut up in a convent, Corona; the other, Chrothild, of royal form and character, was brought up in the court of her uncle Gundebald. When he went to Italy and was occupied there with affairs of state, his wife, sought from Clovis, king of the Franks, and soon solemnly given to him, urged her husband, a few days after the wedding, to avenge the father and recover the kingdom. The end of the war between them came when Gundegisil was killed, and Gundebald, having made surrender on most unworthy terms, remained king of all Burgundy, by the patience and favour, as it were, of the Franks. When he died, Sigismund succeeded him, together with his brother Gundemar.
