When Chlodomir, prince of Orléans, had defeated and captured Sigismund in war and thrown him headlong with his wife and children into a very deep well, Gundemar, after Chlodomir was overcome, was besieged at Autun by the kings Chlothar of Soissons and Childebert of Paris, at the instigation of Chrothild, and when the city was taken he was throttled. So the kingdom of the Burgundians fell to the Franks and was given to Theodoric, the eldest of the sons of Clovis. He left Burgundy to his son Theodebert, whose successor was Theobald. When he died without children, Chlothar, monarch of all Gaul, succeeded him, and from that time Burgundy remained in the hands of the kings of the Franks. About the year 534 this kingdom was divided into a duchy and a county: the former, towards the west, became Lower Burgundy and Royal; the latter, towards the east, Upper Burgundy and Imperial. This chapter deals with the duchy; the county will be discussed later.

units.la: Ducatum cingunt, qua Oriens est Rodano interfluente Sabaudia & Burgundiæ Comitatus; qua Meridies, Lugdunense Territorium: ad Occasum laetissimi Nivernensium Borboniorumque occurrunt Agri; ad Septemtrionem Campania te offert. Controversiæ vero de jure in amplissimum Burgundiæ Ducatum, quæ parum superioribus annis inter varios Principes, partim autem anno CIO IOLV, & ab Imperatore Karolo, Hispaniæ Rege, &c. & Henrico Galliarum Monarcha, quum de Pace inter ipsos suscienda per Legatos frustra laboraretur, fuerunt magnis clamoribus motæ, à me plene explicantur libro Historiæ Belgicæ vi. Vide quædam huc pertinentia capite XLVII.
units.tr: The Duchy is bounded on the east, where the Rhône flows through, by Savoy and the County of Burgundy; on the south by the territory of Lyons; on the west the very fertile fields of the Nivernais and the Bourbonnais meet it; and on the north Champagne presents itself to you. But the disputes over right to the very large Duchy of Burgundy, which in recent years were stirred up with great outcry among various princes, partly in the year 1477 and by the Emperor Charles, king of Spain, etc., and by Henry, monarch of the Gauls, when peace between them was being vainly sought through envoys, are fully explained by me in book 6 of my History of Belgium. See certain matters pertaining to this in chapter 47.

units.la: Floruerunt olim ante Burgundionum ijs in locis principatum, Edui. Sic in melioribus Cæsaris, Livij, Taciti, Plinij, Pomponij, & aliorum Scriptorum Latinorum, Codicibus scribuntur; qui Straboни Ε'δυοι Ptolemæo Αίδυοι, Aedui vetustis Marmoribus vocantur; Aeduus Ausonio Parentalibus, Carmine iv: Qua Lugdunensis Provincia, quaque potentes Aeduus, Alpino quaque Vienna jugo.
units.tr: Long before the Burgundians, the Aedui were the leading people in these places. So they are written in the better manuscripts of Caesar, Livy, Tacitus, Pliny, Pomponius and other Latin writers; they are called Aedui in old inscriptions; Strabo writes them [Ἑδυοι] and Ptolemy [Αἰδυοι]; Ausonius, in the Parentalia, poem 4, calls them Aeduus: where the Lugdunensian province lies, and where Vienne, powerful with its Alpine heights, lies.

units.la: Ab Aeduibus Aeduicum Stemma eodem Carmine dicitur Ausonio, & Aeduicus Pater ibidem Carmine ii, & Libro Professorum Carmine xviii: Male enim in Vulgatis, priore loco Aeducii, posteriore Aedui legitur. Testatur Cæsar non semel, Eduos ab Senatu Romano Fratres Consanguineosque fuisse aliquoties nominatos. Leguntur eadem apud Ciceronem lib. vii. Epist. x. & ad Attic. lib. i. Epist. xvi, Tacitum lib. ii. Plutarchum in Cæsare. Sic Strabo lib. iv: οἱ δὲ Ἑδυοι ἐκ συγγενοῦς Ῥωμαίων ἀνεμάζοντο, καὶ πρῶτοι τῶν Ἑαυτῶν ἀφιστάμενοι πρὸς τὸν Φιλίαν καὶ συμμαχίαν. Auctor Panegyrici, qui Flaviensium nomine Constantino Augusto dictus: Quenam, inquit, igitur gens toto orbe terrarum in amore Nominis Romani Heduis se postulet anteponi? qui primi omnium inter illas immanes & barbaras Galliæ Gentes plurimum Senatus consultis Fratres Populi Romani appellati sunt: & quum à ceteris Rodano ad Rhenum usque populis ne Pax quidem posset nisi suspecta sperari, soli & Consanguinitatis nomine gloriati sunt. Et derivarunt Edui Amicitiam illam Romanorum in Successores suos Burgundiones. Ammianus lib. xxviii: Prima, quod iam inde temporibus profecto sololem esse Romanam Burgundii sciunt. Edui, Cæsare bellum Gallicum administrante, clarissimi Gallorum fuerunt. His Vergobretus (sic dictus, ut nonnullis placet, tamquam Verg-oberste, Supremus Exsequutor) regia potestate per Sacerdotes certo loco, certoque tempore, ex diversis familiis quotannis creabatur; cui extra fines excedere non licebat. Sic enim libro i. Cæsar de Eduis: Convocatis eorum Principibus, quorum magnam copiam in Castris habebat, in his Diviciaco & Liscio, qui summo Magistratui praefuerat, quem Vergobretum Edui appellant, qui creatur annuus, & vita necisque habet potestatem. Cetera sunt lib. vii, & Senatus & Populus Eduus, propter hunc Magistratum seditione commotus, discribitur, ad eamque Seditionem sedandam Cæsar evocatur. Eduorum Clientes apud Cæsarem nominantur praeter Segusianos, Ambivaritos & Brannonios, de quibus alibi, etiam Aulerci Brannovices, quos Morinae interpretantur nonnulli. Fuerunt &, ubi hodie Burgundia, Mandubij, quorum mentio apud Cæsarem: Mandubii sunt Straboni lib. iv, qui eorum Opidum appellat Α'λεσια: in quibusdam Codicibus scribuntur [illegible, ~3 letters] opidumque [illegible, ~3 letters]. Eam ab Hercule conditam, [illegible, ~10 letters] [illegible, ~6 letters] ... fuisse nuncupatam scribit lib. v. Diodorus. Alesia, quae aliis per ξ Alexia scribitur contra Membranarum auctoritatem, meminerunt Caesar, Dio (apud quem male is Σαλσσιαν pro is Ἀλεσίαν) Plutarchus in Caesare, Velleius Paterculus lib. 11, Orosius lib. vi. cap. xii, & alij. Describit his verbis Caesar lib. vii: Ipsum erat Oppidum in Colle summo, admodum edito loco, ut nisi obsidione, expugnari non posse videretur: cuius collis radices duo, duas ex partibus, Flumina subluebant: ante id Oppidum Planities circiter mille passuum III in longitudinem patebat; reliquis ex omnibus partibus Colles, mediocri intervallo ipsum pari altitudine circumjacebant, Oppidum cingebant. Sub muro, quae pars Collis ad Orientem spectabat, hunc omnem locum Copiae Gallorum compleverant &c. Expressit Cæsaris illa Strabo: [Greek], inquit: [Greek]. Hodie tantæ Urbis vix superstant Rudera. Nomen umbra servatur in Pago, Alize, ad radicem Montis, qui vulgo Ansoi, haud procul Flavigny, secundo ab Semuro, de quo post, lapide. Sæviorem fere, quam Alexia fortunam subire coacta quondam fuit, hic in locis Bibracte, Bibracte Strabonis oppidum Eduorum, quum res ipsorum florerent, longe maximum & copiosissimum: Beinam nunc esse putant Orontius & Vigenereus, Angustodunum Petrus Sancto Iulianus; Alij aliud. Marianus scribit Bibracten nomen retinere: & notat Ortelius habere se ab Ioanne Macario, Beuvet hodie vocari, quatuor miliaribus distare ab Augustoduno, versus Septentrionem, & paullulum ad Occidentem; sed locum esse desertum, Vepribus & Dumis obsitum. Bibracten Cæsar lib. i. tanquam in principem Eduæ Nationis Urbem, Frumenti ab Eduis impetrandi causa, contendere statuerat: eo (ut est septimo libro) quum Litavicus receptus esset, quia oppidum apud Eduos maximæ auctoritatis erat, Convictolitanes Magistratus magnaque pars Senatus ad eum convenit: eo Galliæ Obsides, interfectis Noviodunj Cæsaris Custodibus deducti sunt: eo totius Galliæ Concilium adversus Cæsarem indictum est; eo denique Cæsar, tandem receptis Eduis, hiematum secessit.
units.tr: From the Aedui, the Aeduan lineage is named by Ausonius in the same poem, and Aeducus Pater in poem 2 there, and in the Book of Professors, poem 18. For in the common editions the first is wrongly read as Aeducii and the second as Aedui. Caesar testifies more than once that the Aedui were often named by the Roman Senate as brothers and kinsmen. The same is read in Cicero, book 7, letter 10, and to Atticus, book 1, letter 16; Tacitus, book 2; and Plutarch in his Life of Caesar. So Strabo, book 4: the Aedui were reckoned kinsmen of the Romans, and were the first of their neighbours to break away and attach themselves to friendship and alliance [οἱ δὲ Ἑδυοι ἐκ συγγενοῦς Ῥωμαίων ἀνεμάζοντο, καὶ πρῶτοι τῶν Ἑαυτῶν ἀφιστάμενοι πρὸς τὸν Φιλίαν καὶ συμμαχίαν]. The author of the Panegyric, who was addressed to Constantine Augustus in the name of the Flavians, says: What nation, then, in all the world, in its love of the Roman name, can claim to be placed before the Aedui? They, first of all among those savage and barbarous peoples of Gaul, were called brothers of the Roman people by many decrees of the Senate; and when from the Rhône to the Rhine peace could hardly be hoped for from the other peoples except under suspicion, they alone boasted of the name of kinship. And the Aedui drew that friendship of the Romans down to their successors, the Burgundians. Ammianus, book 28: First, because they know that from those times the Burgundians were indeed the allies of the Romans. The Aedui, when Caesar was conducting the Gallic war, were the most famous of the Gauls. Among them the Vergobret (so called, as some like to think, as if Verg-oberste, the chief executor) was created every year by the priests, by royal power, at a fixed place and fixed time, from different families; he was not allowed to leave the boundaries. For in book 1 Caesar says of the Aedui: when he had called together their chiefs, of whom he had a great number in his camp, among them Diviciacus and Liscus, who had presided over the highest magistracy, which the Aedui call Vergobret, who is created annually and has power of life and death. The rest is in book 7: the Senate and People of the Aedui, stirred to sedition over this magistracy, are divided, and to quell that sedition Caesar is summoned. Clients of the Aedui are named by Caesar besides the Segusiani, Ambivareti and Brannovii, of whom elsewhere; also the Aulerci Brannovices, whom some interpret as the Morini. There were also, where Burgundy now is, the Mandubii, mentioned by Caesar. The Mandubii are mentioned by Strabo, book 4, who calls their town Alesia [Ἀλεσία]; in some manuscripts it is written [illegible] and the town [illegible]. Diodorus, book 5, writes that it was founded by Hercules [illegible] and was called [illegible]. Alesia, which is written by others with an x, Alexia, against the authority of the manuscripts, is mentioned by Caesar, Dio (in whom Salassian is wrongly read for Alesian), Plutarch in his Life of Caesar, Velleius Paterculus, book 2, Orosius, book 6, chapter 12, and others. Caesar describes it in book 7 in these words: The town itself stood on a very high hill, in a place so steep that it seemed it could not be taken except by siege. Two rivers washed the roots of this hill, one on each side. In front of the town a plain stretched about three thousand paces in length; on all other sides, hills of equal height surrounded the town at a moderate distance. Under the wall, on the side of the hill which faced east, all that place had been filled by the forces of the Gauls. Strabo expressed Caesar's words thus: [Greek text not legible]. Today scarcely the ruins of so great a city survive. The name survives as a shadow in the district called Alize, at the foot of the mountain which is commonly called Ansoi, not far from Flavigny, second from Semur, of which more later, by a stone. Bibracte, the town of the Aedui named by Strabo, once was compelled to undergo a fortune almost crueler than that of Alesia, here in these places; when their affairs were flourishing it was by far the largest and most populous. Orontius and Vigenerius think it is now Beine, Petrus Sanctius Julianus Autun; others other things. Marianus writes that Bibracte keeps its name; and Ortelius notes that he has it from John Macarius that it is now called Beuvet, four miles distant from Autun, towards the north and a little to the west; but the place is deserted, overgrown with brambles and thorns. Caesar, in book 1, had resolved to hasten to Bibracte, as the chief city of the Aeduan nation, to obtain grain from the Aedui; there (as is said in book 7), when Litavicus had been received, because the town had the greatest authority among the Aedui, the magistrates Convictolitavis and a large part of the Senate came together to him; there the hostages of Gaul were brought, after Caesar's guards at Noviodunum had been killed; there the council of all Gaul was summoned against Caesar; and finally there Caesar, having at last received the Aedui, withdrew to winter.

units.la: Metropolis Ducatus Divio, Divio Castrum in Martyrologiis Vetustissimis, si probata sit scriptura (nam alij alio modo legendum censent) Gregorio Divionum, si proba fit scriptura (nam alij alio modo legendum censent) Gregorio Turonensi lib. iii, qui Urbem non inleganter delineat. Vulgo Dyon, Divionis Conditor habetur vulgo, mihi potius Restaurator, Pomeriique Productor, Aurelianus Imperator. Nomen ab Divis, quis plurimus ibi fuit cultus, impositum putatur. Hæc Urbe nihil in Burgundia pulcrius. Sita est in planitie amœnissima, duobus Fluminibus Suzione & Ofcara (Suson & L'Ouche vernacule) utrimque Muros adluentibus: Ille quidem periculosissimis Exundationibus Urbem infestare consuevit; hic piculentus admodum alueo fluit quietiore, Rerum multarum usum subministrare solitus. Muri ad iustam propugnandi magnitudinem in altum sunt educti; Turribus Propugnaculisque, quæ nuper exstructa, muniti. Sub Cœnobio D. Benigni, quod ab Gregorio conditum Lingonensium Episcopo, vastum ostenditur Specus, Cryptas Cisternasque habens, in quo Benignus Vir sanctus vinctus fuisse traditur, quum Populum ad Christum traduceret. Dæmonum adhuc Sacris operantem. Iustitiæ ibi est Tribunal & Parlamenti Sedes; unde, veluti ex Sinu, Patriæ Iura petuntur. Qui in Maiorem huius Oppidi legitur, non tam Honorem, quam Onus suscipere, vel invitus & renitens, cogitur. Iusque-jurandum præstare in Templo D. Virginis, præeunte verba Procuratore Regio, se Regi fidelem futurum, defensurumque sua Civitati Iura, Libertates, & Privilegia, adversus quoscumque, Regem etiam, quoties flagitat necessitas. Gregorius Turonensis memoriæ prodit, Hilarium quemdam, Senatorem Divionensem, adeo uxorem adamasse: ut quum defuncta inferretur Tumulo ipsius, qui retro multis annis obierat, avida iam dextra fuerit eius Cadaver arctissime complexus. In vicinis Urbi Montibus optima crescunt Vina. Haud procul Urbe versus Meridiem duo visuntur Colles; in quorum uno Arx Talentum, natura loci arteque & perpetuis limitaneorum Militum excubiis ad stuporem valida; in Altero situm est Castellum, cui ab Fontibus nomen cum Pago cognomine, Bernardi, qui Caput ordinis Clarevallensis, Patria.
units.tr: The metropolis of the Duchy is Dijon (Divio). In the oldest martyrologies it appears as Divio Castrum, and Gregory of Turs, book 3, who describes the city not inelegantly, gives it as Divionum, if that reading is accepted (others read it in other ways). It is commonly held that Aurelian the Emperor was its founder, but to me he seems rather its restorer and the extender of its pomerium. The name is thought to come from the Divi (the gods), whose worship was most widespread there. Nothing in Burgundy is finer than this city. It lies in a most pleasant plain, and two rivers, the Suzon and the Ouche (Suson and L'Ouche in the vernacular), wash its walls on either side. The former is accustomed to threaten the city with most dangerous floods; the latter, though very troublesome, flows in a quieter channel and usually supplies many useful things. The walls have been raised to a height adequate for defence, and the city is fortified with towers and bulwarks recently built. Beneath the monastery of St Benignus, which was founded by Gregory, bishop of Langres, a vast cave (Specus) is shown, with crypts and cisterns. Benignus, a holy man, is said to have been bound there while he was leading the people to Christ, who were still performing the rites of demons. There is the seat of justice and of the Parliament, from which, as from a bosom, the laws of the homeland are sought. Whoever is chosen as Mayor of this town is compelled to undertake not so much an honour as a burden, even if unwilling and resisting. He must take an oath in the church of the Blessed Virgin, the royal prosecutor dictating the words, that he will be faithful to the King and will defend his city's rights, liberties and privileges against anyone, even the King, whenever necessity demands. Gregory of Turs records that a certain Hilarius, a senator of Dijon, so loved his wife that when her body was carried to his tomb (he himself had died many years before), his hand, already eager, embraced her corpse most tightly. On the mountains near the city excellent wines grow. Not far from the city, to the south, two hills are seen. On one stands the citadel of Talent, strong enough to astonish by the nature of the site, by art, and by the constant watch of border soldiers. On the other lies a castle, which takes its name from Fontaines, together with the village that bears the surname of Bernard, the head of the Clairvaux order, who was born there.

units.la: Episcopales porro Ducatus huius Urbes sunt Augustodunum & Cabillinum; sua utrumque suspiciendum Antiquitate.
units.tr: The episcopal cities of this duchy are Autun and Chalon, and each of them is to be regarded with respect for its antiquity.

units.la: Priori nomen Augustoduni natum ab Augusto (Octaviano, an quo alio, non valde laborandum: nam qui ab Auge, Apollinis Conjuge, derivant, Fabulas mihi narrant: qui diruturn Bello, quod Cæsar contra Gallias gessit, restauravit. Eo enim tempore aliud habebat Nomen: quod autem, mihi nondum satis liquet. Eduenses (cujus præclara frequentique est apud Cæsarem mentio) appellatam fuisse variis Argumentis probare conatur in sua Burgundia Petrus Sancto-Iulianus, apud Cabillenses Canonicorum Decurio: Cujus sententiæ nondum ego adduci possum ut subscribam. Eduum olim fuisse nominatam colligit ex Cæsare Aimoinus lib. 1. cap. v Augustidunum, inquit, quam Iulius Eduam nominat. Cæsaris verba, in quæ digitum intendit Aimoinus, lib. v. de Bello Gallico sunt hæc; Hæc à compluribus ad Cæsarem deferebantur: quæ re cognita, Cæsar, quod tantum Civitati Eduæ dignitatis tribuebat, certiorem atque deterrendum quibusque rebus posset, &c. Licet Ego semper tuerum arbitratus Eduam Civitatem ab Cæsare dici, non Opidum aliquod, sed, more docte scribentium, totum Eduorum Imperium & Nomen: tamen, quum apud Aimoinum etiam paullo ante laudata à me verba, legatur, Edua, qua Augustidunus, quumque Andochium, quem pallium reliqui omnes AugustodunI notant, Edua Martyrio coronatum scribat Petrus Venerabilis lib. 1. cap. de Basilicis; quum denique nonnihil juvare videatur & Sidonius lib. v. Epist. xviii, & Notitia Provinciarum Galliæ, ubi sub Lugdunensi 1. scribitur, Civitas Eduorum, hoc est Augustodunum: facile dabo, ut antiquissimis temporibus Edua, ab ipsa gente, quod Caput ejus esset, fuerit dicta; diruta autem Bello, quod inter Cæsarem Gallosque magnis viribus patratum, & ab Augusto, forte an Octaviano, restaurata, Augustodunum, tamquam Augusti Collis, transnominatione quadam, quod sæpe fieri solitum, cœperit audire. Ab Augusto dixi restauratum. Qui enim ab Augusto non solum dictum, sed & conditum volunt, graviter meo judicio falluntur, planeque refelluntur ab Ammiano Marcellino, qui lib. xv. maximam Augustoduni Antiquitatem Iuliani tempore ostendit: Cæsar, inquit, quum in ea Urbe (Viennam intelligit) Hiemem ageret, inter ceteros, qui quotidie disseminabantur, Rumores, intellexit, in Augustodunenses Muros, qui magnum complecterentur spatium, & Vetustate nimia exesi corruptique essent, à Barbaris subsitas fieri Impressiones. Idem lib. xvi; Compertum Augustoduni Civitatis antiqua Muros spatiosi quidem ambitus, sed carte vetustatis intrahdo, Parlarorum impetu repentino infiri. Nimiam Murorum Urbis vetustatem diierte prædicat: quæ certe non fuisset, si ab Augusto condita, dictaque, in Iuliani usque tempus tantum steterit. Neque enim ab ejus Conditione plus tum quadringentis annis exactum esse poterat: quod tempus si nimiam Ædificio Vetustatem conciliare quis dicat, ridendum se præbebit. Esto igitur, dum certius nomen occurrit, ut ante Augustum, & Cæsaris tempore, dicta fuerit hæc Urbs Edua; post Augusti vero principatum Augustodunum, qua appellatione nota cum aliis, tum Antonino, qui Legionem ibi locat xxii. & Itinerariæ Peutingeri Tabulæ, in qua notatur Aug. Dunum. Nomen hodie retinet, contractus: Autun enim scribitur, diciturque. Pergo. Aureliianum etiam videtur appellatum. Quos enim Martyres Andochium, Thyrsum & Felicem apud Aurelianum Martyrii coronam accepisse tradit Petrus Equilinus lib. viii. cap. cxvi; eos Augustoduni mactatos signant Martyrologium Romanum, Beda, Vsuardus & Ado; Andochium autem Eduæ Petrus Venerabilis, ut antea dixi. Hinc Appendix in Gregor. Turon. cap. lxxxix initio: Aurelianus in Burgundia Regnum venit: & Aimoinus lib. iv. cap. xxxix, Aurelianus, Caput Regni Burgundiæ: quemadmodum etiam antea Tacitus lib. v. Augustodunum nominarat Caput Gentis. Aurelianum autem forte ab Aureliano Imperatore, qui Gallias peragravit, ut scribunt Vopiscus & Victor in ejus Vita, quæque Eduam (quæ iterum paullo ante, circa Gallieni tempora, magnas fuerat Calamitates passa) restituit, ut indicat Gregorius Turonensis lib. iii. Hist. cap. xix. Putat Paradinus etiam nuncupatam fuisse Flaviam Eduorum, ex Panegyrico, quem Rhetor Gallus dixit Fl. Constantino Imperatori, Claudii Filio, ab ipsius Principis prænomine. Sed secus videtur Magnis Viris, qui Flavia memoriam conservari censent in Vico non ignobili, qui Incolis Flavigni vocatur, ut postea dicam. Adfirum est Augustodunum Radicibus Montium, qui vulgo Iereoltons de Cine, ad Fluvium Arroulium. Vrbs rudibus adhuc Mundi initiis amplissima & populosissima: hodie Ædificiis supra modum vacua; & diu quondam in Gallis Rerum potita, Populoque Romano Foederata, in ordinem quasi & ad Inferiorum fere eiusdem conditionem est redacta. Superbis hodie nihilominus coruscat Templis, quorum maximum est Nazarú, Sedes Episcoporum, quos Bellef orestius numerat lxxxv, ultimum nominans Karolum Attelonsium. Alia Templa, Xenodochia, Coenobia, Collegiaque, ne sim prolixior, silentio praetereo. Non enim mihi animus, omnia persequi & colligere. Est etiam, inquit Paradinus, Radons, pridem Urbis Episcopi, monasticum Septum, miraeque magnitudinis Sepulchrum, ibique Tebandrion, cuius Gregorius Turonensium Episcopus meminit. Multa vivuntur Augustodunensium cum intra, tum extra Urbem Antiquitatum Monumenta, quae paucis ita commemorat Paradinus de Antiquo Statu Burgundiae: Ad Septemtrionalem afflictam non procul a fluentis Aroti Fanum Proserpinae & Pluonis tutelatum, ubi Argures, Aeteri, Arupices, Genethliaci de Futuris pronunciabant: cuius Fani adhuc vetusta quaedam Turris extat, quae dicitur ad Urbis Portam, vulgo Genethoyez. Ego Structurae formam intuitus, quum dicerem vulgo dici scribique La Ianitoye, centeo vel Iani Templum fuisse, vel Ianum: Iani Veteribus Aedificia erant quadriformia & perviaequales Romae per omnes Regiones fuisse notat P. Victor. Pergit Paradinus: In Urbe insuper media fuisse Martis Templum contendunt. Est enim Urbis pars, forma rotundiore & ovali, ab reliqua suis quasi Portis Moenibusque secluda, quae Gallica voce corruptius Marchault, quasi, ut quidam volunt, Martis Campus. Tum etiam in Plaga, quae ad Orientem pertinet, Collis est Phthelia, in quo Cupidinis eadem struxerant Idoli: nec ab eo procul erant Speluncae & Fornices Veneris, Sacrorum Diversoria. In eo Cosmio in Vepreto est Cucubarus, Iamque rotatum a Cunio Eburneo (si fides habenda Recentioribus) qui illic impudens Deo, impudentissima victima caedebatur. Est enim Axis Adulteriis Lenociniisque e famis. Visuntur & magnae ruinae Theatri eo loci, ubi sacra olim scaturigo fuit ad Murorum antiquorum fundamenta, ubi Fons limpidissimus. In superiore etiam Urbis parte erat Capitolium, cuius tantum restat Nomen. Deinde Ita Fraxinea erat Apollinis Templum, quod haud absurde in editissima Urbis parte exaedificatum censeatur, nempe quod Arcem Acropolinque Ingenii Apollo teneat. Caninus praeterea Fanum in quo Anubis Simulacrum canino capite celebrabatur, ad Occidentalem plagam, ubi convicti furti Anubi mactabantur. Erat rursus Rochi Dei Delubrum. Hunc in Deorum Allonon agnoscunt Poetae: cuius Auspiciis ab Iduis permulta gerebantur. Porro sunt ruinae Statuarum, Columnarum, Aquaeductuum, Pyramidum, Theatrorum, Arcuum, atque alia innumera Vetustatis opera. Effodiuntur insuper annis prope singulis antiquorum Numismatum Fasciculae auri atque argenti, cuiusmodi quamplurima Mangarius meus, ditissimus apud Eduos, superioribus annis corrasit. Scribunt etiam quidam Augustodunum Senatum fuisse Druidum, Locumque ei dicatum ab Druidibus vulgato sermone Mont-Druide vocari: praeterea mille ab Urbe passibus ad Occidentem Montem esse editissimum, cui ab Iove cognomen; ubi in hanc usque diem Familia illustris floret Mont-Ioviorum. Et quis, haec omnia si vera, non videt Urbem hanc Urbis (Romae) Simulam esse voluisse? & quis miretur Augusta quondam appellatione non contentam, ad Augustiorum adspirasse. Canit aetatis mediae Poeta Hericus lib. I. Vitae S. Germani;
units.tr: The former, Autun, took its name from Augustus (whether Octavian or someone else, we need not labour greatly over this). Those who derive it from Auge, the wife of Apollo, tell me fables. It was restored after the destruction caused by the war Caesar waged against the Gauls, but at that time it had another name, which I am not yet fully clear about. Peter of Saint-Julien, a canon-dean at Chalon, tries by various arguments to prove in his Burgundy that it was called Eduenses (a name that Caesar mentions often and with distinction), and I cannot yet be brought to agree with his opinion. Aimoin, book 1, chapter 5, gathers that it was formerly called Eduum from Caesar: "Augustidunum," he says, "which Julius calls Eduam." The words of Caesar, at which Aimoin points his finger, are in book 5 of the Gallic War: "These things were reported to Caesar by many, and when he learned of them, since he gave such dignity to the state of the Aedui, he took care to inform and deter them by whatever means he could," and so on. I have always thought that Caesar means by Edua the state of the Aedui, not some town, but, as learned writers usually do, the whole empire and name of the Aedui. Yet in Aimoin the words I quoted a little earlier are read, "Edua, which is Augustidunum." Peter the Venerable, book 1, on basilicas, writes that Andochius, whom all others call the Augustodunian martyr, was crowned with martyrdom at Edua. Finally, Sidonius, book 5, letter 18, and the Notitia Provinciarum Galliae, where under Lugdunensis I it is written "the state of the Aedui, that is Augustodunum," seem somewhat to help this view. So I readily grant that in very ancient times it was called Edua by the people themselves, because it was their chief town; but when it had been destroyed in the great war between Caesar and the Gauls, and restored by Augustus, perhaps Octavian, it began to be called Augustodunum (as if Augustus's hill) by a sort of renaming, which was often done. I said it was restored by Augustus; for those who hold that it was not only named but also founded by Augustus, in my judgement are gravely mistaken, and are plainly refuted by Ammianus Marcellinus, who in book 15 shows the great antiquity of Autun in Julian's time: "Caesar," he says, "while he was spending the winter in that city (he means Vienne), heard among the other rumours that were spread daily that the walls of Augustodunum, which enclose a large space and were eaten away by excessive age and decay, were being breached by the barbarians." The same author, book 16: "It was discovered that the ancient walls of the city of Augustodunum, indeed of wide circuit but weakened by the great age of their structure, were broken by the sudden attack of the Parisians." He plainly proclaims the excessive age of the city's walls, and these could not have been so old had the city been founded and named by Augustus and stood only until Julian's time. For it could not have been more than four hundred years since its foundation; if anyone says that such a period gives the building excessive age, he will make himself a laughing stock. Let it stand, then, until a more certain name turns up: that before Augustus, and in Caesar's time, this city was called Edua, and after the principate of Augustus Augustodunum. This name is recorded, among others, by Antoninus, who places the Twenty-second Legion there, and by the Peutinger Table, where it is marked Aug. Dunum. It keeps the name today in a contracted form, for it is written and pronounced Autun. I proceed. It also seems to have been called Aurelianum. For Peter Equilinus, book 8, chapter 116, says that the martyrs Andochius, Thyrsus and Felix received the crown of martyrdom at Aurelianum; the Roman Martyrology, Bede, Usuard and Ado mark them as put to death at Augustodunum; and Peter the Venerable, as I said before, places Andochius at Edua. Hence the Appendix to Gregory of Turs, chapter 89 at the start: "Aurelian came into the kingdom of Burgundy," and Aimoin, book 4, chapter 39: "Aurelian, the capital of the kingdom of Burgundy," just as Tacitus, in book 5, had earlier called Augustodunum "the capital of the people." But Aurelianum is perhaps named after the Emperor Aurelian, who travelled through Gaul, as Vopiscus and Victor write in his life, and who restored Edua, which had suffered great calamities a little before, around the time of Gallienus, as Gregory of Turs indicates in book 3 of his History, chapter 19. Paradin thinks it was also called Flavia Eduorum, from the panegyric that a Gallic rhetor delivered to the Emperor Flavius Constantine, son of Claudius, from the Prince's first name. But it seems otherwise to great men, who think the memory of Flavia is preserved in a village of no little note, which the inhabitants call Flavigny, as I will say later. Autun lies at the foot of the mountains, which the people call Jereoltons de Cine, by the river Arroux. In the rude first beginnings of the world it was a very large and populous city; today it is strangely empty of buildings. Long ago it held power over the Gauls for a time, and was allied to the Roman people, but it has been reduced almost to the same condition as the lesser towns. Nevertheless it still gleams with proud temples, the greatest of which is the church of Saint Nazarius, the seat of bishops, whom Bellefores counts as eighty-five, naming the last as Charles of Attelon. I will pass over in silence the other temples, hospices, monasteries and colleges, so as not to be too long; for I have no wish to pursue and gather up everything. Paradin also says there is Radon, once the seat of the city's bishops, a monastic enclosure and a tomb of remarkable size, and there is Tebandrion, which Gregory, bishop of Turs, mentions. Many monuments of antiquity of the Augustodunenses survive, both within and outside the city, which Paradin briefly describes in his account of the ancient state of Burgundy: "Not far from the river Arroux, to the north, was a temple of Proserpina and Pluto, guarded by the Argurians, Aeterians, Arupices and Genethliaci, who used to pronounce about future things. An old tower of this temple still stands, which is said to be near the city gate and is commonly called Genethoyez." Looking at the form of the structure, I think that when it is commonly called and written La Ianitoye it was either a temple of Janus or Janus himself; Victor notes that the ancients had buildings with four faces, and that these were in all regions of Rome. Paradin continues: "They also maintain that in the middle of the city there was a temple of Mars. For there is a part of the city of rounder and oval shape, cut off from the rest as if by its own gates and walls, which in the French tongue is corruptly called Marchault, as if, as some wish, Campus Martis." Then also, on the eastern side, there is a hill, Phthelia, where they had set up an idol of Cupid; nor far from it were caves and vaults of Venus, lodgings for sacred rites. In that Cosmium in Vepretum is Cucubarus, and an ivory Cunius (if recent writers are to be believed), who was sacrificed there to the shameless god as a most shameless victim, for it is an axis of adulteries and pimping. Also to be seen are the large ruins of a theatre in the place where a sacred spring once welled up beside the foundations of the old walls, where there is a crystal-clear fountain. In the upper part of the city was also the Capitol, of which only the name remains. Then there was the temple of Apollo at Fraxinea, which is reasonably thought to have been built on the highest part of the city, because Apollo holds the citadel and the acropolis of the intellect. Besides this there was the temple of Anubis, where Anubis was worshipped with a dog's head, on the western side, where thieves caught were sacrificed to Anubis. There was also a shrine of the god Rochus; the poets acknowledge him among the gods of Allon, under whose auspices very many things were done by the Idui. Moreover there are ruins of statues, columns, aqueducts, pyramids, theatres, arches, and countless other works of antiquity. Almost every year bundles of ancient gold and silver coins are dug up, of which my friend Mangarius, the richest man among the Aedui, has collected a great many in recent years. Some also write that Autun was the senate of the Druids, and that the place dedicated to them is called in common speech Mont-Druide. Further, a thousand paces from the city to the west there is a very high mountain, which has the surname of Jupiter, where to this day the illustrious family of Mont-Ioviorum flourishes. And who, if all this is true, does not see that this city wished to be a likeness of the city of Rome? And who would wonder that it aspired to the name Augustior, since it was once not content with the name Augusta? The medieval poet Heric sings of it in book 1 of the Life of St Germanus.

units.la: Celtica Roma dein voluit caput vocari.
units.tr: Then Celtic Rome wished to be called the capital.

units.la: In hac Urbe Magnentius, natione Gallus, post Constantem in Galliis fraude occisum Purpuram Imperialem induit. Magistratum habuerunt olim Vergobretum, de quo dixi paullo ante: Vulgus hodie, ut notat idem Paradinus, antiqui Nominis vestigia retinens, Vieg, appellat. Augustodunum olim Hospitium Musarum, & Bonarum Artium Sedes; ubi, ut Tacitus scribit lib. III. Annalium, nobilissima Galliarum Soboles Liberalibus Studiis operabatur. In Scholis Augustodunensium restaurandis occupatur tota Oratio Eumenij Rhetoris, quae inter Panegyricos legitur: ubi celebratissimi Gymnasij famam Beatus Rhenanus, mutata contra Veterem Editionem Scriptura, transferre voluit ad Augusto Civium. Restituit suam Augustoduno gloriam, adductis in medium paucis Panegyristae verbis, V. Cl. Iustus Lipsius ad Taciti lib. III Annalium; Civitatem iflam & olim Fraterno Populi Romani Nomine gloriatam; ubi ille: Quae Galliae, inquit, Fratres Populi Romani praeter Eduos, quorum haec Urbs Caput?
units.tr: In this city Magnentius, a Gaul by birth, put on the imperial purple after Constans had been treacherously killed in Gaul. They once had a magistrate called Vergobretus, of whom I spoke a little earlier. The common people today, as the same Paradin notes, still keep a trace of the ancient name and call him Vieg. Augustodunum was once the home of the Muses and the seat of the good arts, where, as Tacitus writes in Book III of the Annals, the noblest offspring of Gaul studied the liberal arts. The whole oration of the rhetor Eumenius, which is read among the Panegyrics, is devoted to restoring the schools of Augustodunum. There the learned Beatus Rhenanus, changing the wording against the old edition, wished to transfer the fame of that famous school to Augusto Civium. Justus Lipsius, most learned man, restored Augustodunum's glory by bringing forward a few words of the panegyrist, in his note on Tacitus Annals III: that city, once also proud of the brotherly name of the Roman people. Then he says: Which of the Gallic peoples, he says, are the brothers of the Roman people, apart from the Aedui, whose head is this city?

units.la: Haec de Augustoduno: sequitur Caballinum vel Caballionum Eduorum; vulgo Chalon sur Saone: ita scribi debet, ut me monuit Magnus Scaliger, Gallice, non Chaalion. Nam hoc est, inquit, Catalaunum, de quo alibi. Cabillo appellatur Bedae, Vuardo & Adoni; Cabellio, Antonini Itinerario, ubi Legio illi tributitur XIII, & Pomponio Melx, Cabillo Itinerariæ Tabulæ; Καβυλλινον Straboni ἐπὶ τῇ Αἰγέφ, lib. iv; Cabillonum, Ammiano lib. xv, D. Ambrosio Epist xxvii sub finem, & Gregorio Turonensi lib. x.cap. xi. Cabilonum Catari lib. vii. de bello Gallico; Cabillenum, Sidonio Apollinari lib. iv. Epist. xv; Cabillidunum in Notitia Imperij, ubi: In Provincia Lugdunensi Prima Præf. Ettu Civitas Aruricæ, Cabillodano. Cabillonense Castrum, in Notitia Provinciarum Galliæ sub Lugdunensi Prima. Καβιλλῶν Κολωνια Ptolemæo. Quis condiderit, non constat. Displicet Fabula de tribus Herobus, eorumque Toi quibus; in Gynæceo nata. Sita est ad dextram Araris ripam; Agri uberrimi, Cœliqueque salubberrimi Eximie felix, convehenditque secundo Arari Mercimonijs idonea; unde ab Cæsare Commeatu parando, Exercituique, qui sæpe in plures distractus erat partes, distribuendo dilecta. Testatur hoc ipse sub finem lib. vii, Profligato, inquiens, ad Alexiam Gallicorum Exercitu, Cæsar T Labienum cum duabus Legionibus & Equitatu in Sequanos prosi: si iubet. Huc M. Sempronium Fustium adtribuit. Q. Tullium Ciceronem & P. Sulpitium Cabilloni & Matisconæ in I duo ad Ararim, res Frumentarias ei ad sustentandum ca. Ipse Ibi & hiemare constituit. Majorem olim fuisse loquuntur antiqua Rudera. Rerum apud Francos potiente Hlodovæo, Concilium hic habitum legitur ab Christianis Antistitibus. Regiam hic Sedem habuit Guntchramnus Hilotharij I. Filius, Chereberti Francorum Regis Frater, Aureliaensium Princeps, qui eam supra modum variis Ædificijs ornavit; in S. Marcelli Cœnobio ibi conditus. Evertit contra, cum quatuor Suburbijs, Hotharius, Ludovici Pij Augusti Filius, quum in Italiam Solum vertere cogeretur: Augusto Patre ex Cœnobio ad Regni gubernacula ab Optimatibus retracto; idque e dio Anselmi Cabilonensium Comitis: quem, Procerum nomine, in Hlotherium potius, quam apud Hlothairium orationem habuisse ferunt. Primarium Templum, consecratum olim sub nomine D. Stephani, hodie D. Vincentio, quod ejus ibi Reliquiæ ab Hluldeberto I. conditæ, est dicatum. Est & Templum D. Georgij: quod, quo tempore Urbs ab Hlothario vi stata, nullis Incendij facibus aut Tormentis unquam dejici potuisse memoratur. Binis ornata quondam fuit Nundinis: utrisque ad totum mensem durantibus, alterisque Francofordia, alteris ab Augusto mense nuncupatis: quæ tamen, Urbe suis Cladibus fere sepulta, primo quidem Genevam, quæ tunc etiam Regni Burgundici erat, postea vero Lugdunum, ubi nunc quoque habentur, sunt translatæ. Retinet tamen Cabilonum, quas Nundinarum beneficio solitum habere, Immunitates. Vsurpat enim Cabilonensis Magistratus Nundinarum & Mercatuum: Magistri nomen: & quo anni tempore Nundinæ habentur, nemo Cabilonij Adparitor vel Regius, vel alius, quemquam potest jure sistere, vel in ejus bona manus injicere. Comitatus olim fuit, quem anteaquam Burgundia Duces sui Iuris fecissent, acceptum circa annum cIↄ CCLVI ab Ioanne Cabilonensi Comite, Stephani Comitis Burgundiæ & Salinarum Principis Filio, Episcopus erat præcipuus Urbis Dominus & Patronus: Editaque promulgabantur sub Nominibus & Episcopi & Comitis. Hodie Civitas pro dimidia tantum parte Episcopi est; pro altera Regis, ut Burgundiæ Ducis. In duas enim divisa Iurisdictiones habet & Curiam Iudicium: Ten. Castelli, quæ Regia est; & Episcopi Collegiumque Canonicorum Cathedralium, in qua Episcopalis Nomarcha jus dicit. Subjecta quondam Matisconensium Nomarchiæ, nunc quoque Mensura Vini Matisconensi utitur. Cabilonensium Familia secundum Principes longe fuit clarissima, cujus Parens Gulielmus ille Magnus fertur, cui ab Venatorio Cornu erat cognomen. Quæ gesserint, non mei est instituti commemorare. De Ioanne Cabilonensi, qui Arausiorum Principatum iuæ Genti quæsivit, postea dicendi erit locus. Hæc de Metropoli, Urbibusque Episcopalibus: sequuntur nonnulla Ducatus hujus minorum gentium Opida. Inter C. Vallinum & Matisconem, medio fere itinere opidum est, quod vulgo Tornus, Tinnertium Spartiano in Vita Severi Imperatoris, & Antonino, qui Legionem xiii. vocat. Solo situm est fertilissimo; ab Arari undique cinctum. Colles in Agro Suburbicario Vini generosissimi feraces. Quidam in tres divisum olim fuisse partes perhibent: qua de re nihil habeo certi. Spectatur ibi Abbatia loco editiore; quæ, nisi Templi Turres eminerent, Arx potius, quam Monasterium videretur. Ordinis est S. Benedicti; Caput multorum, ut vulgata utar voce, Prioratuum, qui non solum in locis Congregationalibus, verum etiam in Delfinatu, Arvernia, Pictonio, Britannia, & alibi. Ab utraque etiam Urbe Matisconensi & Cabillonensi itineris spatio prope æquali distat Cuseiïum, Regiæ Ditionis opidum, ut Paradinus centet, Sequsianorum, Sequsiumque Ammiano dictum. Contendere nolo. Situm ad radices luræ Montis, multis hodie licet ruinis deformarum, miram tamen præ se ferens antiquitatem. Ab Oriente Montes habet, ut idem Paradinus scribit, excelsos, Amnesque perennes, qui limpidas & potu suaves edunt Aquas: unde Fons saluberrimus ex Topho & vasta Rupe in opidum longe perrigitur per ligneos tubos. Montes initio leviter adclives generosum Vinum proferunt; qua se altius tollunt, denliore saltu horrent, in quo omnis generis Feræ latabuntur; magnus etiam illic Vrsorum concursus, qui maturas uvas deglubunt avidissime. Qui rem Herbariam Medicamque curant, eo advolare solent, atque illinc non vulgatas Herbas legere. Nascitur enim illic Elleborum, aliæque Simplices, ut loquuntur, Herbræ ac Stirpes. Accedunt & Boli Armenæ Fodinæ, Argentique Venæ. Ab Occasu planicies se in Sinum laxissimum pandit; Agri optimi uberisque, qui Frugum omnium Fructuumqi haud parce subministrat annonam. Laccum etiam piscosum habet ad primum Lapidem, ex Rivis undique concurrentibus. Opidum ipsum Structuris non ita conspicuus exultum est: sed incendio ruinisque lacerum, ut tantum Vrbis Cadaver agnoscas. Cives rei Rusticæ, quam Negotiationum studiosiores. Tertia fera leuca ab Vrbe Cabillonensi versus Septemtrionem est Pelna, vulgo Beaulne, ad Amnem, Adcolis Rouseize dictum. Sunt qui volunt Bibracten esse Cæsaris & Strabonis. Alij, ut alibi dico, alia mens est. Situm est hoc opidum loco uliginoso; & quod, ut scribit Paradinus, nullo pene negocio, nulloque ab Hostibus diserimine, posset Lacum Verbi ad primum Lapidem offundere, quo hostes ab se submoveat. Vrbs tota valido Mœnium sepimento circumdata Propugnacula habet, quibus omnium Tormentorum vim queat excipere. In ea insigne Monimentum Pietatis, impensis Raulini Burgundiæ olim Archigrammatei ædificatum est, Xenodochium, quod Nosotrophij Prochotrophijque vice sit. Totius Galliæ est amplissimum; Regum Palatio, quam Pauperum Hospitio similius. Arcem ibi extruxit Ludovicus xii Francorum Monarcha. Belnensis Ager pinguis est, & optimæ notæ: Vites habet toto Terrarum orbe nominatissimas, & Vino non vulgari nobilissimas. In eodem Agro visitur Cistertium ab Cisternis, Odonis Ducis opus stupendum in vastissimo Nemore, exstructum anno cIↄ xcv iii. Ejus Cœnobiarchiam agnoscunt supra mille octoginta Virorum Cœnobia; ac totidem prope Velatarum, ejusdem instituti, quod hinc Cistertiense dicitur. Semurium, quod vernacule Semur, situm est in medirullio Territorij quod vulgo Auxois terminati ab Oriente quidem Divionensi Agro, ab Occidente Nivernensi; qua Meridies est, Augustodunensi; qua denique Septemtrio, Altiliodorensi Semurium in tres dividitur Partes, ita Murris separatas, ut lingulæ sint opidi instar. Prima, quæ præcipua frequentiusque habitata, Bargi nomen habet; quæ in medio, Le Dounon dicitur: Tertiæ Nomen ab Arce inditum. Inter Divionem & Belnam itinere medio Nuithonium est, vulgo Nuit: quod conditum putatur ab Nuithonibus, quos Burgundionum partem fuisse testis est Nuithlandia quæ in Maxima Sequanorum Minor Burgundia dicitur. Hoc opidum semper Gladiorum opificio fuit celeberrimum. Nuithonum meminit Tacitus de Moribus Germanorum. Quod Opidum hodie Avalon, apud Antoninum Haallon, ubi Legio xvi dicitur; Abulium in Itineraria Peutingeri Tabula. De prodigiola Abaltonis Arcis expugnatione legendi Burgundionum Annales. Quod Sanlicu vernacule, Sidotocum est Antonino, qui Legionem illi tribuit xviii: Sidotocum corruptius Itinerariæ Tabulæ. Quod Flavigni, selquileuca Semurio versus Orientem, Flavio Eduorum cenetur olim dictum. De eo Rhetor Gallus in Panegyrico ad Constantinum: Si Flavia Eduorum Sacer Imperator commovere se funditus, atque huc venire potuisset, tota profecto coram de tuis in se maximis pulcherrimisque Beneficiis una voce io ineretur, tibique Restitutori suo, imo, ut verum fatear, Conditori in ea potissimum Civitate gratias ageret: cuius tamquam similem facere cœpisti. Sed, quoniam non potest, gesta, quæ natura non patitur; Clamoresque suos, quibus quotidie laudes tuas tollis in cœlum, qui exaudiri a te non possunt; tamen interjecta longinquitate, id quod fieri decebat, gaudiorum patriæ meæ nuncium sponte suscepi, ut essem tamen non privatus Studii litterarum, sed publica Gratulationis orator Sunt & alia Burgundiæ opida Burgiqve, quis delineandis brevitati studens, supersedeo: ut sunt Ausone, Arcem habens, Clavis Ducatus Orientalior,
units.tr: So much for Augustodunum*. Next comes Caballinum, or Caballionum of the Aedui, commonly Chalon sur Saône. It should be written that way, as Magnus Scaliger advised me, in the French form, not Chaalion, for, he says, this is Catalaunum, about which I shall speak elsewhere. It is called Cabillo by Bede, Vuard and Ado; Cabellio in the Itinerary of Antoninus, where Legion XIII is assigned to it; and by Pomponius Mela, Cabillo in the Itinerary Table; Kabyllinon [Καβυλλινον] in Strabo, book IV; Cabillonum in Ammianus, book XV, in St Ambrose, Epistle 27 near the end, and in Gregory of Tours, book X, chapter 11; Cabilonum in Caesar's Gallic War, book VII; Cabillenum in Sidonius Apollinaris, book IV, Epistle 15; Cabillidunum in the Notitia Imperii, where it says: In the Province of Lugdunensis Prima, the Civitas of the Aruricae, Cabillodunum; and Cabillonense Castrum in the Notitia of the Provinces of Gaul under Lugdunensis Prima. Ptolemy has Kabillon Kolonia [Καβιλλῶν Κολωνια]. Who founded it is not known. I dislike the fable about the three Herobi and their wives, born in the women's quarters. It lies on the right bank of the Arar. It is exceptionally fortunate, with very rich fields and a most healthy air, and it is well suited to carry goods down the Arar, which is why Caesar chose it for getting supplies ready and distributing them to the army, which was often split into several parts. Caesar himself attests this near the end of Book VII: After the Gallic army was defeated at Alesia, Caesar sent T. Labienus with two legions and the cavalry into the land of the Sequani. He assigned M. Sempronius Rutilus to winter... Q. Tullius Cicero and P. Sulpicius to Cabillonum and Matisco on the Arar, to provide grain for their support. He himself decided to winter there. Ancient ruins show that it was once larger. When Hlodovech held power among the Franks, a council of Christian bishops is recorded as having been held here. Guntchramnus, son of Lothair I and brother of Charibert, king of the Franks, prince of Orléans, had his royal seat here and adorned it beyond measure with various buildings; he was buried here in the monastery of St Marcel. On the other hand, Hotharius, son of the emperor Louis the Pious, overthrew it together with four suburbs, when he was forced to go into exile in Italy. His father, the emperor, had been dragged out of his monastery back to the government of the realm by the nobles, and this was on the advice of Anselm, count of Chalon, who, speaking on behalf of the nobles, is said to have addressed Lothair rather than spoken before him. The principal church, once consecrated under the name of St Stephen and now dedicated to St Vincent, is dedicated to him, since his relics were placed there by Hildebert I. There is also the church of St George, which, at the time the city was taken by force by Lothair, is recorded as having been impossible to destroy by any firebrands or engines. The city was once adorned with two fairs, each lasting a whole month, one called Frankfurt and the other named from August. Yet when the city was almost buried under its disasters, these were moved, first to Geneva, which then also belonged to the kingdom of Burgundy, and later to Lyon, where they are still held. Nevertheless Chalon keeps the privileges it used to have from the fairs. For the magistrate of Chalon claims the name and rights of master of the fairs and markets; and during the time of year when the fairs are held, no bailiff of Chalon, royal or otherwise, may lawfully summon anyone or lay hands on his goods. It was once a county, which, before the dukes of Burgundy made it their own, was received about the year 1256 from John, count of Chalon, son of Stephen, count of Burgundy and prince of Salins. The bishop was the chief lord and patron of the city, and edicts were issued in the names of both bishop and count. Today the city belongs half to the bishop and half to the king, as duke of Burgundy. For it is divided into two jurisdictions and has two courts of justice: the castle, which is royal, and the bishop and the college of cathedral canons, where the episcopal nomarch gives judgment. Once subject to the nomarchy of Mâcon, it still uses the Mâcon measure for wine. The family of the lords of Chalon was by far the most famous after the princes, and its ancestor is said to be that William called "the Great", who had the surname from his hunting horn. What they achieved is not my concern to recount. About John of Chalon, who sought the principality of Orange for his own family, there will be an occasion to speak later. So much for the metropolis and the episcopal cities; there follow some of the lesser towns of this duchy. Between Chalon and Mâcon, about halfway along the road, lies a town which is commonly called Tornus, Tinnertium in Spartianus's Life of the Emperor Severus, and which Antoninus calls the town of Legion XIII. It lies on very fertile soil, surrounded on all sides by the Arar. The hills in the suburban territory bear very fine wine. Some say it was once divided into three parts, but I have nothing certain on this. There is an abbey there on a higher site, which, were it not for the towers of its church rising above it, would look more like a citadel than a monastery. It belongs to the Order of St Benedict and is the head, to use the common term, of many priories, which lie not only in the Congregation's places but also in Dauphiné, Auvergne, Poitou, Brittany and elsewhere. Equally distant from both Mâcon and Chalon, by almost the same length of journey, is Cuiseaux, a town in the royal domain, which Paradin thinks is the Sequsiani, called Sequsium by Ammianus. I do not wish to argue the point. It lies at the foot of the Jura mountains, and although today it is much disfigured by ruins, it still shows a remarkable antiquity. To the east it has high mountains, as Paradin also writes, and perennial streams which produce clear and pleasant drinking water; from them a most healthy spring, flowing from a rock of tufa and a huge crag, is carried far into the town through wooden pipes. The hills at first gently rising produce noble wine; where they rise higher they become rougher with thicker woodland, in which wild beasts of every kind delight. There is also a great gathering of bears there, which most eagerly strip the ripe grapes. Those who study herbs and medicines often flock there and gather uncommon herbs from it, for there grows hellebore and other so-called simple herbs and plants. There are also mines of Armenian bole and veins of silver. To the west the plain opens into a very wide bay, of the finest and richest fields, which supply grain and all kinds of fruit in plenty. It also has a fish-filled lake at the first milestone, fed by streams flowing in from every side. The town itself is not very notable for its buildings, but is so torn by fire and ruins that you would recognise only the corpse of a city. Its citizens are more devoted to farming than to trade. Three leagues from Chalon, to the north, is Pelna, commonly Beaune, on a river which the locals call the Rouseize. Some want Bibracte to be this place, of Caesar and Strabo; others, as I say elsewhere, think otherwise. This town lies on marshy ground, and, as Paradin writes, could with almost no effort and no danger from enemies flood the lake at the first milestone, to keep the enemy away. The whole city is surrounded by a strong wall with bastions, able to withstand the force of all artillery. In it stands a remarkable monument of piety, built at the expense of Raulin, once chancellor of Burgundy: a hospice, which serves as both hospital and almshouse. It is the largest in all of France, and looks more like a royal palace than a poorhouse. King Louis XII of France built a citadel here. The country around Beaune is rich and of the best quality; it has vines most famous throughout the world, and it produces wine of no common nobility. In the same district is seen Cîteaux, from its cisterns, a stupendous work of Duke Odo in a very vast forest, built in the year 1098. The abbey of this place is the head of more than 1,080 monasteries of men, and nearly as many of women of the same rule, which for this reason is called Cistercian. Semur, commonly called Semur, lies in the middle of the territory commonly called Auxois, bounded on the east by the territory of Dijon, on the west by Nevers, on the south by Autun, and on the north by Auxerre. Semur is divided into three parts, separated by walls in such a way that they look like the tongues of the town. The first, which is the chief and most densely inhabited, is called Bargi; the middle one is called Le Dounon; the third takes its name from the castle. Halfway along the road between Dijon and Beaune is Nuits, commonly Nuit, which is thought to have been founded by the Nuithones, whom the land of Nuithonia, called in the greatest Sequanian region Lesser Burgundy, shows to have been part of the Burgundians. This town has always been very famous for sword-making. Tacitus mentions the Nuithones in his Germania. The town which today is Avallon, called Haallon by Antoninus, where Legion XVI is placed, and Abulium in the Peutinger Table. For the astonishing capture of the citadel of Abaltonis, read the Annals of the Burgundians. That which is called Sanlieu in the vernacular, Sidotocum to Antoninus, who assigns Legion XVIII to it, is Sidotocum in a corrupted form in the Itinerary Table. Flavigny, two leagues east of Semur, is thought to have once been called Flavium of the Aedui. Of it a Gallic rhetor says in his Panegyric to Constantine: If the holy emperor could have moved himself from the foundations and come here, the whole town would surely have cried out with one voice in gratitude for your very great and most beautiful benefits towards it, and would have thanked you, its restorer, or rather, to speak the truth, its founder, especially in this city, of which you have begun to make a copy. But since it cannot do what nature does not allow, and cannot be heard by you with its shouts, with which it daily raises your praises to heaven, nevertheless, the distance intervening, I have willingly taken on the task, which ought to be done, of announcing the joys of my homeland, so that I might be not a private man of literary study, but a public orator of congratulation. There are also other towns and places of Burgundy, whose description I pass over, being intent on brevity, such as Auxonne, which has a citadel and is the key of the more eastern part of the duchy,

units.la: Cuseiïum ... Alia. talior, Arari Mu nia lambente; Noicrs, Rovieres, Letone, Memi ard, Cla ll n, S. Seigne Abbatiam habet: haud procul hinc Sequane Fons; Seatgne, Cre aut, Vlteau, Verdum, Arnay, Seure; Tonnerre, Tronoderum, Antenno.
units.tr: Cuseiïum ... Other [places]. Orientalior [Ausone?], washed by the Arar (Saône); Noiers, Rouvres, Létone, Mémillard, Clamecy, Saint-Seine (it has an abbey); not far from here is the Source of the Seine; Saint-Seine, Crée(?), Vitteaux, Verdun, Arnay, Semur; Tonnerre, Tronoderum, Antenno.

units.la: Burgundiæ Ducatui confenseri solent: hæ tres Vrbes Episcopales, quæ tamen Parlamenti Parisiensis iurisdictionem agnoscunt: vernacule nominantur Nevers, Aufferre, Mafon. Primum dignitate guadet & honore Ducatus, cuius Titulo, Duché de Nivernois, late patens tribus qui navigeri, Fluvius irrigatur, Icauna, Fluvere, Ligeri. Incolæ Pastioni. Reique Pecuariæ sunt dediti. Frumentum producit Ager patrum, Vini tere nihil. Præter Ferri, Venas etiam habet Argenti, circa Fanum D. Leonardi. Carbonum Lapideorum, qui haud procul Decita opido effodiuntur, magnus ibi usus. Numerantur ibi xiii. Opida clausa, quorum Nivernum est Metropolis, iurisdictionem exercens in xxx ut vocant, Castellani is. Noviodunum Dunum namque, quod Vetere Gallorum Lingua Montaulun, occurrit à Cæsari notum, cuius lib. vii hæc de eo sunt verba: Noviodunum erat Oppidum Eduorum, ad ripas Ligeris opportuno loco positum: & quæ multa sequuntur. Nevidunum Florianeni vocatur. Ne quis amplius ambigat, Vrbem Ligeri adpositam, quæ Nevers vulgo, esse Noviodunum Cæsaris; ditterte addita Gentis voce, Noviodunum Nivernensium dicitur in quadam Notitia Provinciarum Galliæ, quæ penes Magnum IC. Iacobum Cujacium fuit, quod suis ad me Litteris testatur V. N. Iosephus Scaliger; addens multis conjecturis iam antea sibi exploratum fuisse Noviodunum illud Eduis proximum Civitatem esse Nivernensium, eaque ejus Opidi investigatione multos multa nugatos esse: Alia duo Opida hoc nomine Cæsarem meminerare, sed sibi ignota. Nam Nugatoribus etiam jurantibus se non credere. Accedit & Aimoinus Historiæ suæ initio; Noviodunum, quam hodie Nivernis esse putant, inquiens. Antonino Nivernium vocatur in Itinere, quod Augustoduno ducitur Lutetiam Parisiorum; ubi in quibusdam Codicibus Nevernum legitur; in aliis Nivernum & Nevirnum. In Itineraria Tabula Long. xii, Lat. v. Ebirrei mutile. Opidum est omni ex parte moenibus cinctum firmissimis, Turribusque amplissimis, & Fossis profundissimis probe munitum. Qua Meridies est, Moenia Ligeris lambit, Pontem habens, pulcerrime quadrato Lapide constructum, viginti Arcuum. Nivernis, unde vernaculum opido Nomen, ab Ortu circumfluens, duobus acceptis Ponticulis, mox in Ligerim se exonerat. Ab Septemtrionem & Occasum Fontes sunt, ex quibus etiam Aquæ in Urbis Fossas deduci possunt. Arcem habet & Palatium Principum Nivernensium, juxta Primariam Ecclesiam, quæ D. Cyro sacra, cuique Episcoporum adhæret. Nihil, aut certe parum, Suburbiorum; quod secus in aliis Galliæ opidis: & hinc Nivernum munitius, minusque Insidiis obnoxium. Infra opidum dimidij fere milliaris itinere; nobilissimus Arvernorum Fluvius Elaver, vulgo Allier, Ligeri commiscetur: Locus Conslans ab Confluentibus dicitur. Inter præcipua Ducatus Nivernensis Opida sunt Dezisa; De ise apud Antoninum, ut quidem in melioribus Libris legitur in Itinere, quod Burdigala ducitur Augustodunum; Nam in aliis Dececida, Deciade & Decide exaratum est; Decetia vero dicitur alio Itinere, quod Augustoduno pergit Lutetiam, Degena, mendose in Itineraria Tabula: Clameeynum, Donzyum, Molinium, Angilbertsum, Corbignium, Fanum D. Leonardi, Luzinum, Premecyum, & alia. Comitatus olim, hodie Ducatus floret titulo. Memoratur in Annalibus Franciæ Philippus Nivernij, Rhetelli & Estampij Comes, Philippi Valesij Burgundiæ Ducis Filius; qui cum Fratre in pugna Azincurtiana cecidit: Successores nactus filios; in Nivernensi quidem & Rhetellano Comitatu Karolum; in Stampano autem Ioannem, qui, Fratre sine Liberis defuncto, reliquosque quoque Principatus est adeptus. Hic ex tribus Conjugibus plures quidem suscepit Liberos: sed, præmortuis ceteris, unam tantum Filiam habuit superstitem Karolam: cujus Ioanni Albretano, Orivallæ apud Britones Regulo, nuptæ, Comitatuque Nivernensi a Patre donatæ, Filia fuit Maria Albretana, uxor Karoli Clivensis. Ioannis II Clivia Ducis Filij; qui Primus Nivernij Dux legitur. Huic Filius fuit Franciscus II Dux, cui ex Margareta Borbonia, Karoli I Ducis Vendocinensis Filia, Liberi fuerunt Franciscus, Dux III. Nivernij. Comes Eusij, qui nulla Prole relicta periit Pugna Drentiana, anno MDLXIII; Iacobus, Ille Marchio, Dux Nivernij IV, qui etiam obiit: Henricus, Nivernij Dux V, qui item, ut Fratres, improlis est defunctus; quibus omnibus sufficeta est Soror ror Hemi.a, Dux Niverlij vi; quæ Vxor facta Ludovico Gonzagæ Marchioni Mantua-no, Principatum Nivernensem Dotis nomine ad eum attulit. Ex eo Conjugio natus Karolus Gonzaga Clevensis, Dux Niverlij vii, &c. quem utilissime peregrinantem, & Magnorum Principum, anteaquam propriis Gubernaculis tenendis se admonveant, exemplo, noscendis penitissime variorum Populorum Rerumque publicarum Moribus & Institutis invigilantem, vidi, salutavi, convenii, quum hæc scriberem, Lugduni Batavorum, anno cIↄ Ic cII, die Mensis Mai viii.
units.tr: These are usually reckoned as belonging to the Duchy of Burgundy. These three are episcopal cities which nevertheless acknowledge the jurisdiction of the Parlement of Paris; in the vernacular they are called Nevers, Auxerre, Mâcon. The first, Nevers, enjoys the dignity and honour of a duchy, whose title, Duché de Nivernois, extends widely and is watered by three navigable rivers, the Icauna, the Fluvere and the Liger. Its inhabitants are devoted to pasturage and livestock. The fields produce grain, but no wine at all. Besides iron, it also has veins of silver, near the church of Saint Leonard. Quarries of coal, dug up not far from the town of Decize, are of great use there. There are thirteen walled towns, of which Nivernum is the metropolis, exercising jurisdiction over thirty so-called castellanies. Noviodunum Dunum, which in the old Gallic language is Montaulun, occurs as a place known from Caesar, of whom in book vii these are the words about it: Noviodunum was a town of the Aedui, placed at a convenient spot on the banks of the Liger, and much that follows. Nevidunum is called by Florianenus. Lest anyone should doubt any further that the town on the Loire, which is commonly called Nevers, is Caesar's Noviodunum: with the addition of the name of the people, it is called Noviodunum Nivernensium in a certain list of the provinces of Gaul, which was in the possession of the great jurist Jacques Cujas, as Joseph Scaliger, a most learned man, attests in his letter to me; adding that by many conjectures he had long ago established that that Noviodunum, near the Aedui, is the city of the Nivernesi, and that many had talked a great deal of nonsense in their search for that town. Caesar mentions two other towns of this name, but they are unknown to him; for he does not believe the triflers even when they swear. Aimoin also agrees, at the beginning of his history, saying: Noviodunum, which today they think is Nevers. In Antoninus it is called Nivernium in the itinerary which leads from Augustodunum to Lutetia of the Parisii; where in some manuscripts it is read as Nevernum, in others as Nivernum and Nevirnum. In the Itinerary Table, longitude 12, latitude 5; Ebirrei is a mistake. The town is on every side surrounded by very strong walls, large towers and very deep ditches, and well fortified. On the south side it is washed by the walls of the Loire, with a bridge of twenty arches, very finely built of square stone. The Nivernis, from which the town takes its vernacular name, flows round it on the east, and after receiving two small bridges, soon empties into the Loire. To the north and west are springs, from which water can also be led into the town's ditches. It has a citadel and the palace of the Princes of Nevers, beside the principal church, which is consecrated to Saint Cyrus, and belongs to the bishop. There are few or practically no suburbs, unlike in other towns of Gaul; and hence Nivernum is better fortified and less exposed to ambushes. About half a mile's journey below the town, the most famous river of the Arverni, the Elaver, commonly called the Allier, joins the Loire; the place is called Conslans from the Confluentes. Among the chief towns of the Duchy of Nevers are Dezisa; De ise in Antoninus, as is read in the better books, in the itinerary which leads from Burdigala to Augustodunum; for in others it is written as Dececida, Deciade and Decide; but Decetia is the name in another itinerary, which goes from Augustodunum to Lutetia; Degena is a mistake in the Itinerary Table; Clameeynum, Donzyum, Molinium, Angilbertsum, Corbignium, Fanum D. Leonardi, Luzinum, Premecyum, and others. The county, once, now flourishes with the title of duchy. In the annals of France is mentioned Philippus, Count of Nevers, Rethel and Eu, son of Philip of Valois, Duke of Burgundy; who fell with his brother in the battle of Agincourt. He had sons as successors: in the county of Nevers and Rethel, Karolus; in the county of Eu, however, Ioannes, who, when his brother died without children, also obtained the rest of the principality. He indeed had many children by his three wives, but, the others having died before him, he had only one daughter surviving, Karola; she was married to Jean d'Albret, a chieftain of Orval among the Bretons, and was given the county of Nevers by her father; her daughter was Maria Albretana, wife of Charles of Cleves, son of Duke John II of Cleves; who is read as the first Duke of Nevers. His son was Franciscus II, Duke, by Margaret of Bourbon, daughter of Charles I, Duke of Vendôme; their children were Franciscus, third Duke of Nevers, Count of Eu, who died without issue in the battle of Dreux in the year 1563; Iacobus, that Marquis, fourth Duke of Nevers, who also died; Henricus, fifth Duke of Nevers, who likewise died childless, like his brothers; and after all of them the sister, Hemi.a, sixth Duke of Nevers, succeeded; she, having become the wife of Ludovico Gonzaga, Marquis of Mantua, brought the principality of Nevers to him as her dowry. From this marriage was born Karolus Gonzaga Clevensis, seventh Duke of Nevers, etc., whom, as he travels most profitably, and is an example of great princes before they are instructed to take the reins of government, as he diligently studies the customs and institutions of various peoples and states most thoroughly, I saw, greeted and met, while I was writing these things at Leiden, in the year 1602, on the 8th day of May.

units.la: Antissiodorum sequitur: Antisiodorum Antonino, Legionem hic locanti xxii: ubi male quidam Antisiodorum & Antesiodorum, per N litteram, contra Veterum Codicum fidem & auctoritatem. Autodorum. Ammiano lib. xvi. Corruptum huius Urbis Nomen video in Itineraria Peutingeri Tabula, in qua sic scriptum, Autisio. Duro: emendandum Autissiodoro, iunctim. Civitas Autissiodorum in Notitia Provinciarum Galliæ, sub Lugdunensi iv; Auxerre d'Auxerre. Territorium huius Urbis, quod vulgo Le Pais d'Auxerrois, Vino cognomine est nobilitatum. Cum Antisiodoro Antonini, eadem facit Guilhelmus Paradinus Vellaudunum Cæsaris, & Avegnov Ptolemæi; Avegnov & Antisiodorum idem etiam esse scribit Hericus Benedictinus lib. i. Vitæ S. Germani. Vellaudonum Vigenercus docet potius constitui debere, ubi hodie Chasteau-Landon. Ego adhuc hæreo.
units.tr: Antissiodorum follows: Antoninus places it here as Antisiodorum, where he locates the twenty-second Legion; where some wrongly write Antisiodorum and Antesiodorum, with an N, against the faith and authority of the old manuscripts. Autodorum, in Ammianus book xvi. I see the name of this city corrupted in the Peutinger Table, where it is written thus: Autisio. Duro; it should be emended to Autissiodoro, as one word. The city Autissiodorum in the list of provinces of Gaul, under Lugdunensis iv; Auxerre in French. The territory of this city, commonly called Le Pais d'Auxerrois, has been made famous by its wine, which gives it its name. Guillaume Paradin identifies Caesar's Vellaudunum with the Antisiodorum of Antoninus, and Ptolemy's Avegnov; Heric the Benedictine, in book i of the Life of Saint Germanus, also writes that Avegnov and Antisiodorum are the same. Vigenère teaches that Vellaudonum should rather be located where Châteauneuf-Landon is today. I am still undecided.

units.la: Urbs, quæ hodie Mascon, Cæsari dicitur Matisco: Matisco Itinerariæ Tabulæ; Matisconensis Castrum, Notitiæ Provinciarum Galliæ, & Antonino, qui Legionem ibi ponit x; Mastico in Veteri quodam Diplomate, ut notat Philippus Bugnonius, qui huius Urbis Historiam concinnavit. Machaonem Villam puto dici Paulo Diacono in Longobardicis; Matisina est Gregorio Turonensi, & aliis. Caballino, si situm quis Culeumque & Artes respiciat, similissima. Porrecta jacet ad Ararim, qui Ponte insigni stratus, recto longoque ad Orientem tractu; reliquis Lateribus in Arcus speciem se formantibus. Inter Sacras Aedes, quarum Cathedralis S. Vincentio est consecrata, pulcherrimum fuit Dominicanorum Cœnobium, quo loco ante Comitum erat Palatium, ab S. Ludovico exstructum; vastatum cum reliquis omnibus publicis Ædificiis annis cIↄ Iↄ lxii, & cIↄ Iↄ lxvii, ab iis, qui Reformatam Religionem se profiteri ajebant. Hic primum celebrari cœpit ab Christianis Dies Dominica, ut videre est ex Guntchranni Aurelianensium Regis Edicto, quod in Synodo ibi celebrata promulgatum. Exstat apud Paradinum de Antiquo Statu Burgundiæ. Comitatus Titulo clarui: quem Francorum Rex Ludovicus ix emit ab Ioanne, eiusque Conjuge, Comitibus Matisconensibus. Tragœdiam de Guilelmo, Matisconensi Comite, quem, quod Cluniacenses Monachos indignis modis tractaverit, ex Convivio ab Ignoto raptum fama loquitur vulgatissima, aliunde petat Lector: eique, quod per me licet, idem habeat.
units.tr: The town which today is Mâcon is called by Caesar Matisco: Matisco in the Itinerary Table; Matisconensis Castrum in the list of provinces of Gaul, and in Antoninus, who places there the tenth Legion; Mastico in an old charter, as Philippe Bugnon notes, who compiled the history of this town. I think Machaonem Villam is what Paul the Deacon means in his Lombard history; Matisina is the form in Gregory of Tours and others. In situation, if one considers the sheltered position and the crafts, it is very like Cabellino. It lies stretched out along the Saône, which is spanned by a notable bridge running straight and long toward the east, with the other sides curving into the shape of arches. Among the sacred buildings, of which the cathedral is dedicated to Saint Vincent, the most splendid was the Dominican monastery, which was built by Saint Louis on the site where the palace of the counts once stood; it was devastated, along with all the other public buildings, in the years 1562 and 1567, by those who professed to be of the Reformed religion. Here the Lord's Day was first observed by Christians, as may be seen from the edict of Guntram, king of the Aurelianenses, which was promulgated in a synod held here. It is found in Paradin's On the Ancient State of Burgundy. The town is famous for its title of county: King Louis IX of France bought it from John and his wife, the Counts of Mâcon. The tragedy about William, Count of Mâcon, whom, as common report tells, a stranger snatched from a banquet because he had treated the monks of Cluny in unworthy ways, the reader may seek elsewhere; and may he have, so far as I am able to grant it, the same [satisfaction].

units.la: CAP. XLII.
units.tr: CAP. XLII.

units.la: Avenionensis Comitatus.
units.tr: The County of Avignon.

units.la: Hæc de Galliarum Provinciis, quæ sub octo Parlamentis Francorum hodie sunt Regis, eique subjectæ: ordo flagitat, ut quæ ab Francorum ditione separatæ sunt, indicemus, quæque aliorum Principum, vel Ecclesiasticorum, ut Pontificis Romani vel Politicorum.
units.tr: So much for the provinces of France which today belong to the King and are subject to him under the eight Parlements of France. Order requires me now to note those which have been separated from the French dominion, and those which belong to other princes, whether ecclesiastical, such as the Roman Pontiff, or secular.

units.la: Pontificis Romani est Comitatus Avenionensis, qui & Venissa: Vulgo, Le Comte de Venissy: cui ad Occidentem, interposito Rodano, Languedokij; ad Meridiem, interfluente Druentia, Provinciales: ad Ortum, idemque ad Septentrionem denique Delphinates. Varios habuit Dominos, cum primis, amissa Libertate, Romanos: ut reliqua Narbonensis Gallia, cuius hæc Comitatus erat pars. Romanis pulsis, successerunt Gothi: his profligatis, Burgundiones: quibus in contractiores fines coactis, Franci. Horum Rex Karolus Calvus cum dedit Boson, qui se Regem Arelatensem dixit. Regno Arelatensi potitus Imperator Otho, Comitatum etiam hunc occupavit: quæ causa, quod adhuc loca ibi non pauca Camerae Imperialis Iurisdictionem agnoscant. Pervenit inde hæc Civitas in Ditionem Comitum Provinciæ. Karolus, Ludovici ix Frater, ducta in uxorem Beatrice, Raimundi Provinciae Comitis Filia, Comitatum est consequutus. Idem postea Regna Neapolitanum & Siciliæ subegit; in quibus, ut & in Provincia Comitatu, ipsius successerunt Posteri, inter quos fuit Ioanna I, Karoli Calabriæ Ducis Filia; quæ nobilissimum Comitatum dedit Pontifici Clementi VI, ad compensationem Tributi. Romanæ Sedi per multos annos non soluti, nomine Regni Neapolitani, cuius Beneficiarium Dominum se dicit Pontifex Maximus, à quo Terra Papæ vocatur: cuique aliquando per XXX annos Sedem præbuit hujus Comitatus Metropolis Avenio. Irrigatur ab Rodano, Druentia & Sorga, Fluvio Petrarchæ decantatissimo.
units.tr: The County of Avignon, also called Venissa, and in the vernacular Le Comte de Venissy, belongs to the Roman Pontiff. To the west, across the Rhône, lies Languedoc; to the south, Provence, with the Durance flowing between; to the east and also to the north, the Dauphiné. It has had various lords: first the Romans, after it lost its liberty, as did the rest of Narbonese Gaul, of which this county was a part. When the Romans were driven out, the Goths succeeded them; when the Goths were overthrown, the Burgundians; and when the Burgundians were forced into narrower bounds, the Franks. Charles the Bald, King of the Franks, gave it to Boso, who called himself King of Arles. When the Emperor Otto gained possession of the kingdom of Arles, he also seized this county; this is why a number of places there still acknowledge the jurisdiction of the Imperial Chamber. From there the city passed into the power of the Counts of Provence. Charles, brother of Louis IX, obtained the county by marrying Beatrice, daughter of Raymond, Count of Provence. Afterwards he also subdued the kingdoms of Naples and Sicily, and in these, as in the county of Provence, his descendants succeeded him, among them Joanna I, daughter of Charles, Duke of Calabria. She gave this most noble county to Pope Clement VI as compensation for a tribute. The tribute, under the name of the kingdom of Naples, had not been paid to the Roman See for many years; the supreme Pontiff declares himself the beneficiary lord of that kingdom, and for this reason the land is called Terra Papæ. For thirty years at one time its metropolis, Avignon, provided the seat of this county. It is watered by the Rhône, the Durance and the Sorgue, the river so celebrated by Petrarch.

units.la: Habitarunt hic olim Cavares, Memini, & alij. Cavares Plinio; qui Cavara, Pomponio Melæ; Καύαροι, Ptolemæo: Κυάροι, Straboni. Servari videtur eorum memoria in toto illo Tractu, qui ad Rodanum ab Urbe Valentia Avenionem usque Gavoiz indigetatur. Memini Plinio lib. III. cap. IV. & lib. XVIII. cap. VIII, ubi quidam Codices Memini; Μέμμοι, Ptolemæo. Dalechampius Memosque, vel Mormas interpretatur, oppidum antiquum, Rodano adsitum; alij, Mure, prope Grattanopolin. De Voconti, quorum hic etiam Sedes fuerunt, dixi cap. XI; de Allobrogibus, quis hic quoque latum fuit aliquando Nomen & Imperium, postea dicturus.
units.tr: The Cavares, the Memini and others once lived here. The Cavares are so called by Pliny; Cavara by Pomponius Mela; Kauaroi [Καύαροι] by Ptolemy; Kuaroi [Κυάροι] by Strabo. Their memory seems to survive in the whole tract that runs along the Rhône from the city of Valence to Avignon and is called Gavoiz. The Memini appear in Pliny, book III, chapter IV, and book XVIII, chapter VIII, where some manuscripts read Memini; Memmoi [Μέμμοι] in Ptolemy. Dalechamps interprets it as Memosque or Mormas, an ancient town beside the Rhône; others take it as Mure, near Grenoble. I spoke of the Voconti, whose seats were also here, in chapter XI; I shall speak later of the Allobroges, whose name and rule once extended here too.

units.la: Habet hic Comitatus quatuor Diœceses: unum Archiepiscopatum, Avenionem; tres Episcopatus, Avenioni suffragantes; Carpentoractensium, Cavallicorum, Carpentoractensi, Cavaillon, Vaison. Omnes olim in Viennensi, ut indicat Notitia Provinciarum Galliæ, in qua Civitas Avenniorum, L'Archevêché d'Avignon: Civitas Carpentoractensium, Cavallicorum, & Vasionensium: Les Evêchez de Carpentras, Cavaillon & Vaison.
units.tr: This county has four dioceses: one archbishopric, Avignon, and three bishoprics subject to Avignon: Carpentoractensium, Cavallicorum, Carpentras, Cavaillon and Vaison. All of these once belonged to Vienne, as the Notitia Provinciarum Galliæ shows, where we read Civitas Avenniorum, the Archbishopric of Avignon; Civitas Carpentoractensium, Cavallicorum, and Vasionensium: the bishoprics of Carpentras, Cavaillon and Vaison.

units.la: Avenio, Avenio, Cavarum, Plinio lib. III. cap. IV, Melæ lib. II. cap. V. & Ptolemæo; Αὐενιὼν simpliciter Straboni lib. IV; & Avenio, Vibio Sequestro de Fluminibus: Cassiodoro lib. III. Variar. Epist. XXXVIII. ad Wandilium, & Veteri Itinerario Burdigala Hierosolymas: Avinio, Gregorio Turonensi lib. VII, cap. XXXVI; Avennio eidem lib. II. cap. XXXII, & Itinerariæ Peutingeri Tabulæ. Avenionem, Sidonio Apollinari lib. VI. Epist. XIII; Avennica Urbs, eidem Turonensi lib. VII. cap. X. & lib. X. cap. XIII. Qodie Avignon. Avennici Muri nominantur apud Turonensem lib. VI. cap. I. Sita est in sinistra Rodani ripa, Arce potens. Agri gaudet bonitate; Pannorum Byssiqué tinctura; Papyraceis item Molis nomen merita. Pontem hic habet Rodanus. Is cum Fluvio, quod notandum, totus Regis est Francix; non Papæ, præter modicam particulam, Portæ Urbis propiorem. Hanc Urbem Septenarius numerus, omnium perfectissimus, reddit laudabilem. Septies enim ibi, & hæc quidem septies inter se septenario numero repetita, visuntur præcipua urbis Ornamenta: Septem Palatia; totidem Parochia Xenodochia, Monasteria Fœminarum, Collegia, CanvænConventus, Porta. Cathedralis Ecclesia D. Virgini est sacra. Carthusianorum ibi est Coenobium, quo nullum in Gallis celebrius. Academia claret; florentissima, quum Romani Pontifices ibi morabantur. Huic Paulus Cassianensis, multum attulit splendoris, ut ipsius ad Ius Civile Commentaria, quae Praelectiones Avinionenses dicuntur, ostendunt. Docuit ibidem inter alios Andreas Alciatus. Inter Palatia est, cui nomen Brusie, in quo Pontificem quemdam insignis Crudelitatis Facinus perpetrasse Fama loquitur.
