units.tr: Avenio, Avenio, Cavarum, in Pliny, book III, chapter IV, in Mela, book II, chapter V, and in Ptolemy; Aueniōn [Αὐενιὼν] simply in Strabo, book IV; and Avenio in Vibius Sequester's work on rivers; in Cassiodorus, Variae, book III, letter XXXVIII, to Wandilius; and in the old Itinerary from Bordeaux to Jerusalem. Avinio in Gregory of Tours, book VII, chapter XXXVI; Avennio in the same author, book II, chapter XXXII, and in the Peutinger Table. Avenionem in Sidonius Apollinaris, book VI, letter XIII; Avennica Urbs in the same Gregory of Tours, book VII, chapter X, and book X, chapter XIII. Today Avignon. The Avennici Muri are named in Gregory of Tours, book VI, chapter I. It lies on the left bank of the Rhône, strong with its citadel. It enjoys fertile land, and is famed for dyeing cloth and silk, and also for its paper mills. The Rhône has a bridge here. This bridge, together with the river, and this is worth noting, belongs wholly to the King of France, not to the Pope, except for a small part nearer the city gate. The number seven, the most perfect of all, makes this city praiseworthy, for seven of its chief ornaments are found here, and these too are repeated seven times over in the septenary: Seven Palaces; as many parish churches, hospitals, convents of women, colleges, convents of men, and gates. The cathedral church is dedicated to the Blessed Virgin. There is a Carthusian monastery here, none more famous in France. The academy flourished greatly while the Roman Pontiffs dwelt here. Paulus Cassianensis added much splendour to it, as his commentaries on civil law, called the Praelectiones Avinionenses, show. Among others, Andreas Alciatus taught here. Among the palaces is one called Brusie, in which, report says, a certain Pope committed a deed of notable cruelty.

units.la: Carpentoracte Plinio est oppidum, quod hodie Carpentras. In Notitia Provinciarum scribitur, Civitas Carpentoracteusis, nunc Vindarjica, ubi alias legitur Vindisia.
units.tr: Carpentoracte in Pliny is a town, today Carpentras. In the Notitia Provinciarum it is written Civitas Carpentoracteusis, nunc Vindarjica, where elsewhere Vindisia is read.

units.la: Cabalio, Dodis. Latine scribentibus; Cabellio, Plinio & Antonino in Itinere, quod Mediolano per Alpes Cottias Arelatum ducitur. Itineraria Tabula hic Cabalinè legitur: Καβελλίων πόλις Μασσαλίας, Stephano de Urbibus ex Artemidoro: Καβέλλιον, Ptolemaeo; ubi quidam inepte vertunt, quasi pluralis esset, Cabelliorum Colonia: Καβαλλικῶν, Straboni: Hodie Cavaillon de Comtat. Cabellonensis Portus meminit Panegyricus Constantino dictus.
units.tr: Cabalio, Dodis. Among Latin writers it is Cabellio in Pliny and in the Antonine Itinerary, the route that runs from Milan through the Cottian Alps to Arles. The Tabula Itineraria reads Cabalinè here. Stephanus of Byzantium, citing Artemidorus, has Cabellion, a city of Massalia [Καβελλίων πόλις Μασσαλίας]; Ptolemy has Cabellion [Καβέλλιον]; Strabo has Kabalikon [Καβαλλικῶν]. Some translators foolishly render the name as if it were plural, Cabelliorum Colonia, the colony of the Cabellii. Today it is Cavaillon de Comtat. The Panegyric dedicated to Constantine mentions the Cabellonensis Portus.

units.la: Vasio Vocontiorum Pomponio Melae lib. II. cap. V. Οὐάσιον Οὐοκοντίων, Ptolemaeo lib. II. cap. X. (apud quem male Interpretes Vasiorum Civitatem vertunt) quae simpliciter Vasio dicitur Plinio lib. III. cap. IV. apud quem in nonnullis Exemplaribus mendose Vaso: Vasio Civitas, Concilio Arelatensi II; Vasionensis Civitas, Beda, & Vuardo XV. Kalend. Mart. Vasionense oppidum, Sidonio lib. V. Epist. VII. ad Apollinarem & lib. VII. Epist. ad Fontelum IV; Civitas Vasensium in Catalog. Metropol. Civitas Valensis. Can. I. Concilii Valensis; Vicus Valensis, initio Concilii Valensis II. Hodie, Vaison. Vasionis meminit Inscriptio, quae Romae in Aede D. Pudentianae:
units.tr: Vasio Vocontiorum in Pomponius Mela, book II, chapter V; Ouasion Ouokontiōn [Οὐάσιον Οὐοκοντίων] in Ptolemy, book II, chapter X (where the translators wrongly render it as Vasiorum Civitatem); it is simply called Vasio in Pliny, book III, chapter IV, where in some copies it is wrongly given as Vaso. Vasio Civitas in the Second Council of Arles; Vasionensis Civitas in Bede, and in Usuard on 15 Kalends of March; Vasionense oppidum in Sidonius, book V, letter VII, to Apollinaris, and book VII, letter IV, to Fonteius; Civitas Vasensium in the Catalogue of Metropolitans; Civitas Valensis in canon I of the Council of Valence; Vicus Valensis at the beginning of the Second Council of Valence. Today Vaison. An inscription at Rome, in the church of St Pudentiana, mentions Vasionis:

units.la: C. ACILIO. C. F. VOL. MARTIALI VASIONE. VETER. EX. COH. XII. PR. MILITAVIT. ANNIS XVII. VIXIT. AN NIS. LV. M. I. Q. DOMITIVS. ADIVTOR HERES. CONSORTI. SVO. BENE. MER FECIT. ET. SIBI
units.tr: C. ACILIUS C. F. VOL. MARTIALIS, VASIONE, VETERAN OF COHORT XII PRAETORIAN, SERVED SEVENTEEN YEARS, LIVED FIFTY-FIVE YEARS. M. I. Q. DOMITIUS ADIUTOR, HIS HEIR, MADE THIS FOR HIS WELL-DESERVING COMRADE AND FOR HIMSELF.

units.la: Alia minorum gentium oppida praetereo. Fuit olim haud procul Avenione ad Confluentem cum Rodano Sorgem (sic hodie dicitur, qui Straboni Σούλγης: Vindelicum, Floro, ab oppido conjacente) Urbs potens, quae Vindelicum Floro: Vindalium Epitomae I. vitae libri LXI, & Orosio lib. V. cap. XIII. Οὐινδαλιῶν, Straboni lib. IV. apud quem V. N. legi hus Scaliger emendat Οὐινδαλιῶν. Intercidisse monet idem, ejusque loco hodie clie Pontem Trullia; Trullium Nautas Rodanicos vocare Trasennam, quae in utramque Fluminis ripam extenditur qua Pontonibus trajicitur Rodanus; eamque positam esse propter Fluvii rapiditatem, ne ab ejus impetu Pontenes, vel potius traiectoria Navigia abripiantur. Paradinus Vindalium fuisse notat, ubi hodie Pons Sulga. Ioannes Poldus in Nemausiensium Historia scribit putare se Vindalium fuisse in Provincia circa locum, quem vulgo S. Remy vocant; ibi exstare hactenus Mausoleum, Arcum Triumphalem, & Statuas subjugatorum Gallorum. Ad haec porro oppidum magnam de Gallis Victoriam consequutus est Cn. Domitius Ahenobarbus. Docent Strabo, Florus, aliique. Praeter Sulgam nominantur Straboni & alij duo Fluvij, Κουλγος & Οὐάλγον; de quibus idem Scaliger consulendus.
units.tr: I pass over the other towns of the lesser peoples. Long ago, not far from Avignon, at the confluence of the Rhône with the Sorgis (as it is called today; Strabo's Σούλγης; Florus's Vindelicum, from the town lying nearby), there was a powerful city, which Florus calls Vindelicum, the Epitome of Book LXI of Livy calls Vindalium, and Orosius in Book V, chapter XIII, calls Οὐινδαλιῶν [Vindalion], as in Strabo Book IV, where Scaliger emends the reading V. N. to Οὐινδαλιῶν. The same writer notes that it has perished, and that in its place today there is the bridge called Pont Trullia; the Rhône boatmen call the Trullium the Trasenna, which stretches across both banks of the river, where the Rhône is crossed by pontoons; and he says it was placed there because of the swiftness of the river, lest the pontoons, or rather the ferry boats, be swept away by its force. Paradin notes that Vindalium was where today stands Pons Sulga. John Pold, in his History of the Nemausenses, writes that he believes Vindalium was in the Province near the place commonly called St. Remy; there, he says, a mausoleum, a triumphal arch and statues of the subjugated Gauls are still standing. Moreover, Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus gained a great victory over the Gauls at this town. Strabo, Florus and others record this. Besides the Sulga, Strabo and others name two more rivers, Κουλγος [Koulgos] and Οὐάλγον [Oualgon]; on these Scaliger too should be consulted.

units.la: Inter Avenionem & Aquas Sextias Vallis Clausa est, quae vulgo Vaucluse: quo conferre se solitus scribitur Francifcus Petrarcha, Philosophicis Meditationibus operam daturus. Vallis est amoenissima: Rupibus, unde Fontes manant limpidissimi, cincta.
units.tr: Between Avignon and Aix there is the Vallis Clausa, commonly called Vaucluse, to which Francis Petrarch is written to have been accustomed to withdraw, intending to devote himself to philosophical meditations. The valley is most pleasant, surrounded by cliffs from which the clearest springs flow.

units.la: CAP. XLIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XLIII.

units.la: Sabaudiæ.
units.tr: Savoy.

units.la: PONTIFICIS igitur Romani in Franciæ Regno hodie est Avenionensis vel Venessæ Comitatus: sunt & suæ Politicis quibusdam Principibus ibidem Partes; quæ in triplici sunt differentia. Aliæ enim Ducatus, aliæ Principatus, aliæ denique Comitatus clarent titulo & dignitate. Ducatus sunt Sabaudia & Lotharingia; vulgo, Les Duchez de Savoye & Lorraine.
units.tr: Within the Kingdom of France, the Roman Pontiff today holds the County of Avignon and Venaissin. There are also some other territories there that belong to certain princes, and these differ in three ranks. Some are distinguished by the title and dignity of duchies, some of principalities, and others of counties. The duchies are Savoy and Lorraine, in the vernacular Les Duchez de Savoye & Lorraine.

units.la: SABAVDIA unde nomen impositum, varij varie quæruntur. Quidam à Sabatiis Vadis derivant. Sabatium Vadum Plinio Ligurix Vrbs, quæ Sablatia Pomponio Melæ; Σαβαταῖα, Ptolemæo: Σαββατων ὀυάδα Straboni, ut libro sequenti videbimus. Alijs Sabandia dicitur, quasi Sabbatorum, quos Sabandienses scribit Volaterranus, Auwe, id est, Ager, Pratum, Locus Pascuus. Quibusdam quasi Saul-Voie, Via per Silices, Dumosaque & aspera quondam Loca. Nonnullis nec quos omittam, quasi Saulve Voie, Salva Via; quamex mala Latronibusq: obiectâ fecisse fingitur nescio quis ab ijs, qui Fabulis Lectores distinere solent. Sabaudia certe non semel in Libro Notitiarum nominatur inter Galliæ Narbonensis Provincias. Meminerunt ejusdem, nunc Sabaudiam, nunc variante scriptura Sapaudiam nominantes, & medij ævi Scriptores. Conjacent Sabaudia, quæ quidem Septemtrio est, Burgundiæ Comitatus, turbationibus Limitibus; & Helvetia, Lemanno Lacu interposito: quæ Ortus, Valesia Pedemontiumque, finibus non multo certioribus: nisi quod Montes intercurrant editissimi: ad Meridiem & Occasum Delfinatus se offerunt cum nonnulla Rodani portione, Sabaudos separantis ab Burgundiæ Ducatus Incolis. Aer Sabaudia purus est. Regio valdequam montosa: ad Septemtrionem altissima Iuræ, quem alibi descripsi, Iuga respicit: in Veragris Pœninæ Alpes exsurgunt; in Salassis, Graiæ; in Medullis, Cottiæ; de quibus omnibus libro sequenti. Quod ad Valles & Campestria Loca, Solum amœnum latis & fœcundum, præcipue versus Septemtrionem, secundum Lemanni Lacus Tractum; ubi Vinum gignit generosum, quod Ripalium vocatur ab Lacus Ripa. Pascua Animantibus omne genus enutriendis optima; cum alibi, tum qua Mons Minor S. Bernardi attolitur. Irrigant Sabaudiam Fluvij, præter Ararim & Isaram, de quibus suo loco dixi, Doria, Arva, Danius, alij.
units.tr: Various writers give various accounts of where the name Savoy comes from. Some derive it from Sabatia Vada. Pliny calls the Ligurian city Sabatium Vadum, Pomponius Mela calls it Sablatia, Ptolemy calls it Σαβαταῖα [Sabataia], and Strabo calls it Σαββατων ὀυάδα [Sabbaton ouada], as we shall see in the following book. Others say it is called Sabandia, as if from the Sabbati, whom Volaterranus calls the Sabandienses, and from Auwe, that is, field, meadow, pasture land. Some take it as Saul-Voie, a way through stones, thickets and rough places once found there. Some others, whom I will not bother to name, take it as Saulve Voie, a safe way, since it was supposedly made safe from bad men and robbers by someone, a story told by those who usually keep readers occupied with fables. Sabaudia is certainly named more than once in the Notitia among the provinces of Narbonese Gaul. Medieval writers also mention it, sometimes writing Sabaudiam and sometimes, with a variant spelling, Sapaudiam. Sabaudia lies to the north of the County of Burgundy, with boundaries that are disputed, and of Helvetia, with Lake Geneva lying between them. To the east, Valais and Piedmont border it, with boundaries that are not much more certain, except that very high mountains run between. To the south and west, Dauphiné comes into view, with part of the Rhône separating the people of Savoy from the inhabitants of the Duchy of Burgundy. The air of Savoy is pure. The region is very mountainous. To the north it faces the very high ridges of the Jura, which I have described elsewhere. In the territory of the Veragri the Pennine Alps rise, in that of the Salassi the Graian Alps, and in that of the Medulli the Cottian Alps, all of which I will discuss in the following book. As for the valleys and plains, the soil is pleasant, broad and fertile, especially to the north along the shore of Lake Geneva, where it yields a noble wine called Ripalium from the shore of the lake. The pastures are excellent for raising every kind of animal, both here and where Mount Little St Bernard rises. Rivers water Savoy, besides the Arar and Isara, which I have discussed in their place, and the Doria, Arva, Danius and others.

units.la: Sedes hic quondam habuerunt suas cum Allobrogibus (quis quasi in reliquos principatus, vel quorum nomen reliquis fortean commune erat) Centrones, Nantuates, Garoceli, Medulli, Veragri, Salassi, & alij. Allobroges Latinis omnibus, ut Sallustio, Cæsari, vio, Plinio, alijs. Ἀλλόβρογες etiam vocant Charax, teste Stephano, & Strabo lib. iv. qui Ἀλλοβρηγες, v pro o Apoliodoro apud eumdem Stephanum, Prolemæo lib. ii, apud quem tamen in multis Exemplaribus Ἀλλοβρηγες; Ἀλλεβρυγες Polybio apud eumdem Stephanum, Dioni, aliisque Græcis. Ie eorum Frymo antiquus Interpres ad Iuvenalis Satyram viii: Allobroga Galli sunt. Ideo autem dicti Allobrogæ, quoniam Broga Galli Agrum dicunt, Alia autem aliud. Dicti igitur quia ex alio loco fuerant transfati. Quid Brige Germanis, sæpe dixi; ea nimirum voce, transposita Canina, ut hic Ferg, hodieque multa ipsorum Oppida terminari. Nogas de Allobrogum Etymo huc non conferam Annij Viterbiensis, ad xviii Assyriorum Regem supposititij Berosi. Allobrogas Sabaudos interpretatur Scudus; Delfinates Marhanus, Poldus & Rhenanus. Non male. Latum enim & potens fuit olim Allobrogum nomen iis in locis, ubi hodie Sabaudia, Delfinatus, & Regiones Confinales. ἐ ἡ-ἀυ ατα ταν ταλαντον, Apollodoro apud Stephanum. Livius Gentem notat multa Gallica Gente opibus aut fama inferiorem: Hannibalemque, quum per ea loca Italiam peteret, jam tum inter duos Principes Fratres, de Allobrogum Regno ambigentes, Arbitrum factum, Imperium Majori natu Brancoaderiuile. Ptolemæus Vienuam Allobrogum facit Metropolim: Cæsar lib. i. extremam Allobrogum, proximamque Helvetiorum Finibus Genevam dicit. Multa contra eos gesta memorantur in Historiis Romanis. Legendi Strabo lib. iv, Cæsar in Commentarijs Belli Gallici, Dio lib. xxxvii, Sallustius in Conjuratione Catilinaria, Plutarchus in Vitis, Appianus in Celtico, Velleius lib. ii, Epitomæ Liviana lib. lxi, Orosius lib. v. cap. xvi, Plinius lib. vii, Iustinus lib. xxxvii, Eutropius lib. v. & alij. Triumphavit de iis, eorumque Rege Bituito Q. Fabius Maximus: inde Allobrogicus cognominatus, ut idem testantur; vel Allobrox, ut Pædianus; vel, ut in antiquo Lapide, qui Romæ, exprellum est, Allobrogenimus. Horatio in Epodis Carmine ad Populum Romanum, quo commiteratur Resp. propter Bella civilia, Novis Reliquis infidelis Allobrox nominatur; ubi Vetus Commentator, Allobroges sunt Galli rufi & Sequanis dicti, incolentes illum Tractum Alpium, qui est a Visontio in Germaniam, qui vehementer res novas adsciscunt, unde & Dumbus sub raro fidem servant, habentque flavum præcipue Capillitium. Ad alios huius Regionis Populos venio. Qui Centrones Cæsari lib. i. Belli Gallici, Strabon, & Antonino, Grajarum Alpium Populi; habitasse eos censent Marhianus, Vigenereus, Scudus & alij, ubi hodie Tarantaise. Legitur in Notitia Provinciarum Galliæ sub Viennensi v, Civitas Centronum, hoc est Tarantasia, L'Archevesche de Tarentaise. Male nonnulli apud Cæsarem legendum arbitrantur Centrones. In multis Plinij Exemplaribus Antiatones scribuntur pro Centronibus. Nantuates Plinio & Cæsari lib. iv. apud quem, mitio lib. iii. vitiose Antuates) qui Νανταται Strabom. Eos alijs atque alijs locis recentiores ponunt Scriptores. Marhianus locat ad Lacum Acronium; ubi hodie Constantienses, Ægidius Schudus scribit Tractum eorum, hodie De Zeeuwe & Vitzlandt (Nuithlandia, ab Nuithonibus Germanice: Gallice vero, Le Pais de Vaud dici. Paradinus Nantuatium Regionem & Nomen exstare hodieque notat in Opidulo, quod etiamnum Nantua, haud procul Chamberiaco. Adferibam huc, quæ ad me suis litteris Vir Nobilis. Iosephus Scaliger: Ne credas, inquit de Nantuatibus, esse Monasterium loco nomine in Sabaudia, ut quidam non satis Capitatum volunt. Sunt ij, in quibus Pagus Ocloduru est, id est Sanctus Maurficus: cujus rei fidem faciunt Monumenta Passionis Legionis Thebæorum, in quibus Ocloduri est mentio: Ocloduorum autem à Cæsare in Nantuatibus, Veragris proxime, collocatur. Quidam legunt Antuates. Sed qui Nantuates ad Lacum Acronium constituunt, & Constantienses esse dicunt, non minus desipiunt, quam qui Monasterium illud Benedictorum interpretantur. Hæc ille. Garoceli apud Cæsarem lib. i. de Bello Gall. putantur esse Raimundo Marhiano, ubi hodie Mons Cinefius, vel Cinerum; Mont-Cenu vulgo: Vigenerens Vallem iis tribuit, cui cognomen Mortenne. Vicini superioribus fuerunt Medulli, quorum meminit Vitruvius lib. viii. Philander & Barbarus eos Vallis Celera habitatores faciunt; Dalechampius, Miollantij & Tarantasia. μεδύλοι apud Strabonem & Ptolemæum altissimis insident Montibus. Iofias Simlerus Vallem Marianam, de qua ante, iis adsignat. Veragrorum, qui cum alijs apud Cæsarem lib. iii, quosque Varagros vocat Plinus, ditio, Wallisserlands Guilelmo Paradino dicitur: Pais du Gavot, Acgidio Scudo: Chablasii Ducatus, Pingonio, Montes S. Bernardi & Friga, Raimundo Marliano, Caput Gentis statuenti Vicum; ubi Ablacia S. Mauritij. Hoc certum, Nantuatibus, de quibus paullo ante, Veragri fuisse confinales. Apud Cæsarem Nantuates, Veragri, & Seduni ab Finibus Allobrogum & Lacu Lemano Flumineque Rodano ad summas Alpes pertinent. Salassij, Σαλασσοι apud Ptolemæum, olim fuisse putantur, ubi hodie Augstall, ut Germani vocant; vel, ut Itali, Val d'Aosta. Salassos à Polybio Λάρις dici notat Gaudentius Merula. De Salassiis plura dicendum in Italia. Civitatis etiam Genevensium fit mentio in Notitia Provinciarum sub Viennensi Prima; L'Evesche de Geneve. Fuerunt profecto dubio & alij Regionis, quæ nunc Sabaudia, Incolæ, quorum vel memoria periit, vel Sedes sunt incertiores. De Segusianis, qui huc etiam aliquo modo pertinebant, dictum in Lugdunensi: de Catuurigibus, in Delphinatu de Lepontiis dicam in Rhetia; de Sedunis, in Vallesia: de Latobrigis, in Helvetia. Sabbatos etiam Populos hodie Sabaudienses esse scribit Volateranus; quorum ego apud Veteres nullam reperio mentionem.
units.tr: Once the Allobroges (who perhaps gave their name to the other principalities, or whose name was perhaps shared in common by the others) had their seats here, together with the Centrones, Nantuates, Garoceli, Medulli, Veragri, Salassi and others. Latin writers, such as Sallust, Caesar, Livy and Pliny, all write Allobroges. Charax, as Stephanus reports, calls them Ἀλλόβρογες [Allobroges], and Strabo in book iv writes Ἀλλοβρηγες [Allobreges], with υ used for ο, as Apollodorus does in the same Stephanus. Ptolemy in book ii writes Ἀλλοβρηγες [Allobreges], though in many manuscripts it is Ἀλλοβρηγες; Polybius, as cited by the same Stephanus, Dio and other Greeks write Ἀλλεβρυγες [Allebryges]. Frymo, an ancient interpreter of Juvenal's eighth satire, says: "The Allobroges are Gauls. They were called Allobroges because the Gauls call a field broga, and other peoples call it something else. They were called so because they had been transferred from another place." I have often said that Brige means the same in German, and in that word, with its letters transposed in the Celtic manner, Ferg, which is still the ending of many of their towns today. I will not here bring together the etymology of the Allobroges given by Annius of Viterbo in his notes on the spurious Berosus, the Assyrian king. Scudus interprets Allobroges as Savoyards; Marhanus, Poldus and Rhenanus take them as Dauphinois. Not badly. For the name of the Allobroges was once wide and powerful in those places where Savoy, Dauphiné and the neighbouring regions lie today. (so Apollodorus reports in Stephanus, concerning a talent.) Livy uses the word of a people somewhat inferior in resources or reputation to the other Gallic peoples; and when Hannibal was making for Italy through those parts, he was already chosen as arbiter between two brothers, princes, who disputed the kingdom of the Allobroges; the greater of them was given the rule. Ptolemy makes Vienna of the Allobroges the metropolis, while Caesar in book i calls Geneva the furthest town of the Allobroges, nearest the borders of the Helvetii. Many deeds against them are recorded in Roman histories. Read Strabo in book iv, Caesar in his Commentaries on the Gallic War, Dio in book xxxvii, Sallust in the Catilinarian Conspiracy, Plutarch in the Lives, Appian in the Celtic history, Velleius in book ii, the Livian Epitome in book lxi, Orosius in book v, chapter xvi, Pliny in book vii, Justin in book xxxvii, Eutropius in book v, and others. Q. Fabius Maximus triumphed over them and their king Bituitus, and for this he was surnamed Allobrogicus, as the same authors testify, or Allobrox, as Pedianus has it, or, as on an ancient stone at Rome, Allobrogenicus. In the Epodes, in his poem to the Roman People, in which he bewails the state of the republic because of the civil wars, Horace calls the Allobrox faithless to the new kings. There the old commentator says: "The Allobroges are Gauls with red hair, called Sequani, who inhabit that region of the Alps which runs from Besançon into Germany. They are very eager for revolution, and so they rarely keep faith with the Romans, and they have mostly yellow hair." I turn now to other peoples of this region. The Centrones, mentioned by Caesar in book i of the Gallic War, and by Strabo and Antoninus, were a people of the Graian Alps. Marhanus, Vigenerus, Scudus and others think they lived where Tarentaise is today. In the Notitia of the provinces of Gaul, under the first Viennese province, there is a Civitas Centronum, that is, Tarantasia, the Archbishopric of Tarentaise. Some wrongly think that Centrones should be read in Caesar. In many copies of Pliny they are written Antiatones instead of Centrones. The Nantuates are mentioned by Pliny and by Caesar in book iv (in book iii, in the text of Caesar, the faulty reading is Antuates), and by Strabo as Νανταται [Nantatai]. Later writers place them in various other spots. Marhanus locates them by Lake Acronium, where Constance is today. Gilles Schudé writes that their district is today called De Zeeuwe & Vitzlandt (Nuithlandia, from the Nuithones in German, but in French Le Pays de Vaud). Paradin notes that the region and name of the Nantuates still survive in a small town, still called Nantua, not far from Chambéry. I will add here what the noble man Joseph Scaliger wrote to me in his letter: "Do not believe," he says of the Nantuates, "that there is a monastery of that name in Savoy, as some who have not thought the matter through very carefully want. There are the people in whose district Ocloduru is, that is St Maurice, a fact confirmed by the records of the Passion of the Theban Legion, in which Ocloduru is mentioned. Caesar places the Ocloduri among the Nantuates, next to the Veragri. Some read Antuates. But those who place the Nantuates by Lake Acronium and say they are the Constantienses are no less foolish than those who take that Benedictine monastery as meaning them." So far Scaliger. The Garoceli in Caesar, book i of the Gallic War, are thought by Raimundus Marhanus to be where Mont-Cenis, or Cinerum, is today, commonly called Mont-Cenu. Vigenerus gives them a valley which bears the name Mortenne. Neighbours to the above were the Medulli, whom Vitruvius mentions in book viii. Philander and Barbarus make them inhabitants of the Vallis Celera; Dalechamps makes them the people of Miollans and Tarentaise. The μεδύλοι [medyloi] in Strabo and Ptolemy inhabit the highest mountains. Josias Simler assigns to them the Vallem Marianam, of which I spoke before. The district of the Veragri, who are mentioned with the others in Caesar, book iii, and whom Pliny calls Varagri, is called Wallisserlands by Guillaume Paradin, Pays du Gavot by Gilles Schudé, the Duchy of Chablais by Pingonius, and the Mountains of St Bernard and Frigus by Raimundus Marhanus, who makes their chief settlement the village where the Abbey of St Maurice is. It is certain that the Veragri bordered the Nantuates, of whom I spoke a little while ago. In Caesar the Nantuates, Veragri and Seduni stretch from the borders of the Allobroges and from Lake Geneva and the river Rhône up to the highest Alps. The Salassi, Σαλασσοι [Salassoi] in Ptolemy, are thought to have lived where Augstall is today, as the Germans call it, or, as the Italians do, Val d'Aosta. Gaudentius Merula notes that Polybius calls the Salassi Λάρις [Laris]. More will have to be said about the Salassi in Italy. A town of the Genevenses is also mentioned in the Notitia under the first Viennese province: L'Evêché de Genève. Certainly there were also other inhabitants of the region that is now Savoy, whose memory has perished, or whose seats are less certain. I will speak of the Segusiani, who also belonged here in some way, in the account of Lyonnais; of the Catuurigi in Dauphiné; of the Lepontii in Rhaetia; of the Seduni in Valais; of the Latobrigi in Helvetia. Volaterranus writes that the Sabbati, whom he calls Sabaudienses, are today the people of Savoy; but I find no mention of them among the ancient writers.

units.la: Totus hic Tractus, ubi hodie Sabaudia, Delphinatus, aliæque Conreglonales Provinciæ, Regni titulo quondam superbierunt, quemadmodum patet ex Livij lib. xxi, ubi Hannibal Arbiter lectus legitur ab duobus Fratribus, qui de Allobrogum Regno inter se digladiabantur. Regni pars, de qua agimus, Sabaudia, varios inde Dominos Principesque nacta, hoc tempore Imperium, agnoscit Ducem; quibus ante quingentos annos contractiores fuerunt Limites. Tunc enim Mauriennæ tantum Comites dicebantur: quorum Primus legitur Bertholdus, qui patrium Solum vertere coactus in eam Burgundiæ Transiuraniæ partem abijsse scribitur, quæ inter Allobroges Comitatus Mauriennæ appellatur; rebusque pro Imperio bene feliciterque gestis eumdem obtinuisse Comitatum; quem Filius ejus Humbertus 1. Iure Beneficiario, ab Henrico 111 Imperatore plenius acceptum transmisit ad Filium Amedeum 1. & Humbertum 11. Nepotem; qui successione Adelheidæ, Humberti 1 Conjugis, Marchionis quoque fuerunt Segusiani; Tarantasia etiam Ditionibus suis adjecta. Humberti 11 Filius fuit Amedeus 11, Primus Sabaudiæ Comes, Marchio Taurinorum & Segusianorum. Eum recta linea sequuti sunt Humbertus 111, Thomas, qui Pedemontanum Principatum bello sibi adquisivit; Amedeus 111, qui Vallis Augustæ Petram & Chablasij Dittionem, hæredibus masculis vacuas, occupavit; & Bonifacius: cui improli defuncto successerunt Patrui, Petrus, qui Principatum suum supra modum auxit, expugnatis plerisque ad Lacum Lemanum Oppidis; & Philippus, Archiepiscopus antea Lugdunensis, qui spe prolis orbatus potiorem Hereditatis Partem transmisit ad Fratris Thomæ Filium Amedeum v, cui Magni erat cognomen. Exceperunt hunc Filij Eduardus, Hærede carens masculo & Amedeus v: post quem Sabaudorum Rebus, descendente serie, præfuerunt Amedeus vi, Ordinis Equestris Annunciatorij institutor: Amedeus vii; Amedeus viii, quem Primum Sabaudiæ Ducem creavit Sigismundus Imperator, anno cIↄ ccccxvi, quemque post voluntariam Principatuum suorum in Filium Ludovicum transcriptionem, Monachum jam factum, Concilij Basiliensis Patres Pontificem Maximum contra Eugenium iv consecrarunt, sub Felicis v. appellatione. Dignitatem tamen illam nono post anno concessit Nicolao v, solo Cardinalatus honore contentus. Obiit cIↄ ccccclii Ripali; ad Lacum Lemanum. Amedei porro viii Stemma tale legitur: Amedeus viii, Dux Sabaudiæ Primus: de cuius Abdicatione, Pontificatuque alij plura. Ludovicus, Dux Sabaudiæ Secundus, defunctus anno cIↄ cccc lxiii. Uxor Anna Ioannis Cypri Regis F. Alij utriusque sexus Liberi. Amedeus ix, Dux Sabaudiæ iii, Divus Paracque cognominatus: Obiit cIↄ cccc lxxv. Uxor tota Caroli vii Valesij, Galliarum Regis, F. Ludovicus Rex Cypri. Duxerat enim Karolatam. Ioannis Regis Filium unicum & Heredem. Philippus Bresse. Bengrati Comes, & Erdlix Dominus: Adgnatis mortuis Dux Sabaudiæ vii in humanis esse desiit Chambenaci anno cIↄ cccc xcviii. Uxores illi fuerunt. Alij multi utriusque sexus. Philibertus Dux Sabaudiæ ivobiit cIↄ ccccxcv. Karolus, Dux Sabaudiæ v. Veneno periit cIↄ ccccxxc ix Uxor Blanca Guilelmi Marchionis Montisferrati F. Alij Liberi. Margareta Karoli i Ducis Borbonij F. Ex qua nati. Claudia Ioannis Bonifacij Ducis Dominus Filia. Ex qua procreati.
units.tr: This whole region, where Savoy, Dauphiné and the other neighbouring provinces now lie, once took pride in the title of kingdom, as is clear from Livy book 21, where Hannibal is read of as chosen arbiter by two brothers who were fighting each other for the kingdom of the Allobroges. The part of the kingdom under discussion, Savoy, has since come under various lords and princes and now acknowledges a Duke as its ruler, with an empire. Five hundred years ago its boundaries were narrower, for then the rulers were called only counts of Maurienne. The first of these we read of is Berthold, who, forced to leave his native soil, is said to have gone to that part of Transjurane Burgundy which among the Allobroges is called the County of Maurienne; by serving the Empire well and successfully he obtained that county. His son Humbert I received it more fully by feudal right from the Emperor Henry III and passed it on to his son Amadeus I and to his grandson Humbert II. Through the succession of Adelheid, wife of Humbert I, they also became marquises of Segusia, and Tarentaise was added to their lands. The son of Humbert II was Amadeus II, the first Count of Savoy, marquis of Turin and Segusia. In direct line followed Humbert III; Thomas, who won the Piedmontese principality for himself by war; Amadeus III, who seized the Aosta Valley's rock and the lordship of Chablais, which had no male heirs; and Boniface. When he died childless, he was succeeded by his uncles: Peter, who greatly enlarged his principality by capturing most of the towns on Lake Geneva; and Philip, formerly archbishop of Lyons, who, deprived of hope of offspring, passed the greater part of the inheritance to the son of his brother Thomas, Amadeus V, who bore the surname the Great. After him came his sons Edward, who had no male heir, and Amadeus V... After him, in descending order, ruled the affairs of Savoy: Amadeus VI, founder of the Order of the Annunciation; Amadeus VII; and Amadeus VIII, whom the Emperor Sigismund created first Duke of Savoy in the year 1416, and who, after voluntarily transferring his principalities to his son Louis, having now become a monk, was consecrated supreme pontiff by the Fathers of the Council of Basel against Eugenius IV, under the name of Felix V. Nevertheless, nine years later he gave up that dignity to Nicholas V, content with the honour of the cardinalate alone. He died at Ripaille, by Lake Geneva, in the year 1451. The family tree of Amadeus VIII reads thus: Amadeus VIII, first Duke of Savoy, concerning whose abdication and papacy others say more. Louis, second Duke of Savoy, died in the year 1463. Wife Anne, daughter of John, King of Cyprus. Other children of both sexes. Amadeus IX, third Duke of Savoy, surnamed the Blessed. Died in the year 1475. Wife Yolande entirely, daughter of Charles VII of Valois, King of France. Louis, King of Cyprus, had married Charlotte, the only son and heir of King John. Philip of Bresse, count of Bugey and lord of Ehrlich: with the male relatives dead, he became Duke of Savoy VII and ceased to be among the living at Chambéry in the year 1498. He had wives, and many other children of both sexes. Philibert, Duke of Savoy IV, died in 1495. Charles, Duke of Savoy V, perished by poison in 1489. Wife Blanche, daughter of William, Marquis of Montferrat. Other children. Margaret, daughter of Charles I, Duke of Bourbon. Children born of her. Claudia, daughter of John Boniface, lord of the duchy. Children born of her.

units.la: Karolus II, Dux Sabaudiae VI. Mortuus sexennis anno MCCCCXCVI.
units.tr: Charles II, Duke of Savoy VI. He died at the age of six, in the year 1496.

units.la: Metropolis Sabaudiae Chamberiacum, vulgo Chamberi, quod Camerinum Antiquis appellatum fuisse notat in sua Sabaudia Paradinus. Auctoritatem adducenti fidem dabo. Putat Pinetus Veteribus vocatum Forum Vocony, cujus meminerunt Plinius lib.III. cap.IV. & Antoninus in Itinerario. Atqui fieri hoc non posse, satis inde constat, quod Forum Vocony utrumque numeretur inter ea Oppida, quae hodie ad Mare fere Mediterraneum in Provincia. Et ibidem etiam Forum Voconij locat, haud procul litore Maris Gallici, Tabula Peutingeri Itineraria, inter Forum Julij, hodie Fresul, & Mataronem. Vide Caput xxxix. Frustra quoque est in Chorographia Lusitanica Varrerius, qui ex Foro Vocony, Forum facit Voconty, quasi illud Vocontiorum, de quibus ego in Delfinatu, fuisset Metropolis, quum primaria Gentis ejus Urbs Augusta Dia Vocontiorum, hodie Die. Chamberiacum etiam Coenali & Castilionio censetur Civaro, cujus meminit Cicero in Epistolis: sed Cularonem, quae hodie Grațianopolis, restituendam ibi, ante monui. Chamberiacum porro, Arce praeditum. Domicilium praebet plurimum Sabaudiae Ducibus, qui Sedem hic signarunt Iustitiae, Supremoque Provinciae Tribunali, quod Parlamentum vulgo.
units.tr: The metropolis of Savoy is Chambéry, commonly Chamberi, which Paradin in his Savoy notes was called Camerinum by the ancients. I will give credit to the authority he cites. Pinet thinks that it was called by the ancients Forum Vocony, which Pliny mentions in book 3, chapter 4, and Antoninus in the Itinerary. But that this cannot be so is quite clear from the fact that Forum Vocony is counted among those towns which today lie almost on the Mediterranean coast in Provence. And the Peutinger Table likewise places Forum Voconii, not far from the shore of the Gallic sea, between Forum Julii, today Fréjus, and Matarona. See chapter 39. Varrerius too is wrong in the Lusitanian Chorography, when he makes Forum Vocony into Voconty, as if that had been the metropolis of the Vocontii, whom I discuss in Dauphiné, whose chief city was Augusta Dia Vocontiorum, today Die. Chambéry is also identified by Cenalis and Castilionius with Civaro, which Cicero mentions in his letters; but I have already pointed out earlier that Cularo, today Grenoble, should be restored there. Chambéry, moreover, is a town with a citadel. It provides a residence for most of the Dukes of Savoy, who established here the seat of justice and the supreme tribunal of the province, commonly called the Parlement.

units.la: Cum Sabaudia tamquam Partes ejus explicantur Comitatus Genevensis, Mauriennensis, Tarantasius, Marchionatus Susa, & aliquot Dominia Ditio denique Bressanensis. De singulis pauca.
units.tr: Savoy, with its parts explained, includes the County of Geneva, Maurienne, Tarentaise, the Marquisate of Susa, and finally some lordships, the Lordship of Bresse. A few words on each.

units.la: Comitatus Genevensis nomen ab Geneva, cujus media corripienda, ut in Elusa, quod non solum Helveticus Germanismus ostendit, qui Genff vocat, sed docent etiam ipsi Rustici Suburbicarij & reliqui Sabaudi, qui Zeneuam accentu in prima enunciant. Sed Gallorum proprium est, mediam correptam producere, ut in publique, facile, & id genus aliis; quae Latine corripitur. Et, hodierna fere Adcolarum pronunciatione, Cenava dicitur Antonino in Regio Exemplari, in Itinere, quod ducitur Mediolano per Alpes Graias Argentoratum: In reliquis Codicibus non habetur. Urbs est mirae antiquitatis. Meminit Caesar lib.1. Belli Gallici Pontis ad Genevam super Rodanum Fluvium siti, & ab ipso refcisi: Muriqe, hic ab Lacu Lemano ad Montem Iuram ducti per millia Passuum decem & novem; in altitudinem pedum sexdecim. Et Muri & Pontis non obscura vidi vestigia. Quod apud reliquos, Strabonem, Plinium, Ptolemaeum, aliosque nulla Urbs tam praeclarae sit memoria, summopere mirari soleo. Sita hodie est ad Lacum Lemanum; bipartita in duabus Rodani ripis, conjuncta Ligneo Ponte; cui, per interiectam Insulam firmiori, utrimque Domus impositae: Major Meridiem est versus, Minor ad Septemtrionem. In Insulae extremitate, qua Oriens, Specula cernitur, quam quidam ab Caesare volunt factam. Ego haereo. In Majore Templum est, praeter alia, Primarium, D. Petro consecratum: olim, ut Inscriptiones, quas hic aliquando vidi, docent, Apollinis. In Minore Aedes est S. Gervasij a quo & tota illa Urbis Pars habet denominationem. De antiquo hujus Urbis statu, Controversiisque pro ejus Principatu inter Episcopos & Sabaudiae Comites Ducesque, consulenda, quae cum aliis scribit, ad Sebastianum Munsterum Franciscus Bonivardus. In Libertatem se vindicavit circa annum MDXXXV, teste Tabula, quae publice ibi posita ad Curiam. Cum Bernatibus Helvetiae Populis Ius Civitatis pactum firmavit anno MDXXXVI. postea aliquoties renovatum. Quas ob causas quoties Insidijs impetiti; quantisque proximis annis fuerint adfecti confecticque cladibus; memoriæ produnt Scriptores non pauci.
units.tr: The name of the County of Geneva comes from Geneva, whose middle syllable is short, as in Elusa. This is shown not only by the Helvetic Germans, who call it Genff, but also by the country people of the suburbs and the other Savoyards, who pronounce Zeneva with the stress on the first syllable. But it is peculiar to the French to make the middle syllable long, as in publique, facile and others of that kind, which in Latin is short. And, in the present-day pronunciation of the inhabitants, it is called Cenava in the royal copy of Antoninus, in the itinerary that runs from Milan through the Graian Alps to Strasbourg; it is not found in the other manuscripts. It is a city of remarkable antiquity. Caesar, in book 1 of the Gallic War, mentions a bridge at Geneva, set over the river Rhône, and its being broken down by himself; and a wall, extending from Lake Geneva to Mount Jura for nineteen thousand paces, sixteen feet high. I have seen the clear traces of the wall and the bridge. I often wonder greatly that no other writer, Strabo, Pliny, Ptolemy or the rest, has any memory of so famous a city. It today lies by Lake Geneva, divided into two parts on the two banks of the Rhône and joined by a wooden bridge; on an island between them, made firmer, houses are built on each side: the greater lies towards the south, the lesser towards the north. At the eastern end of the island there is a watch-tower, which some think was built by Caesar. I hesitate. In the greater part is the principal church, dedicated to St Peter, formerly, as inscriptions I once saw here show, to Apollo. In the lesser part is the church of St Gervase, from whom that whole part of the city takes its name. Concerning the ancient state of this city, and the disputes over its principality between the bishops and the counts and dukes of Savoy, one should consult what Francis Bonivard writes, along with others, to Sebastian Münster. It asserted its liberty around the year 1535, as a tablet publicly placed there at the Town Hall attests. It made a treaty of citizenship with the Bernese, a Swiss people, in 1536, which was renewed several times afterwards. For these reasons it has been attacked by ambushes many times; and as to the great disasters it has suffered and inflicted in recent years, many writers record them.

units.la: Mauriananensis, vulgo La Mortenne, expansus est ad Archum Fluvium, ubi Fanum S. Ioannis, cui inde Cognomen. Dicitur enim S. Ioan de Morienne. Opidum non ignobile, Arce superbiens; ubi sepultus Humbertus I, qui Mauriananensem Comitatum, nunc Sabaudiæ Ducatum, iure beneficiario ab Henrico III Imperatore acceperat. Mortem obiit anno cIↄ XI VIII. Conjacet Patri Filius, Amedæus I, Cauda cognomine. Mauriananensis Episcopi meminit Concilium Matisconense I.
units.tr: Maurienne, commonly La Maurienne, stretches to the river Arc, where there is the shrine of St John, from which it has its surname; for it is called St Jean de Maurienne. It is a not unimportant town, proud of its citadel, where Humbert I is buried, who had received the County of Maurienne, now the Duchy of Savoy, by feudal right from the Emperor Henry III. He died in the year 1103. His son, Amadeus I, surnamed Tail, lies beside his father. The Council of Mâcon I mentions a bishop of Maurienne.

units.la: Tarantasius, vernacule Tarentaise, conclusus fere spectatur inter Montes Alpinos, Fluviosque Archum, & Aram, Archo ie ad Chamezium miscentem. Appellationem habet ab Urbe Tarantasia; quæ hodie scribente Scudo, Moniter Incolis; Germanis autem Munster in Taratasen; ut censet Iolias Simlerus: Mustertum est Latine scribentibus. Sepultus ibi in Basilica Humbertus II, Mauriananensis vel Moriennæ Comes, & Segusianorum Marchio, qui Ditioni suæ Tarantasiam bello domitam adjecit. Obiit circa annum cIↄ CIX. Legitur hæc Urbs apud Antoninum, variante scriptura, Tarentasis, & Darantasia; posteriore modo etiam in Itineraria Tabula. In Notitia Provinciarum Galliæ sub Viennensi v Alpium Graiarum Peninatum est Civitas Centronum, hoc est Tarantasia; L'Archeveché de Tarantaise.
units.tr: Tarentaise, in the vernacular Tarentaise, is seen to be shut in almost entirely between the Alpine mountains and the rivers Isère and Arc, which mingles with the Isère near the Chamoise. It takes its name from the city of Tarentasia, which today, according to Scudo, is called Moûtiers by its inhabitants; the Germans call it Münster in Tarantasen, as Josias Simler thinks; those who write in Latin use Mustertum. Buried there in the basilica is Humbert II, count of Maurienne or Morienne and marquis of the Segusians, who added Tarentaise, conquered in war, to his lordship. He died around the year 1109. This city is found in Antoninus, with variant spellings, Tarentasis and Darantasia; the latter form also in the Peutinger Table. In the Notitia of the Provinces of Gaul, under Vienne, in the Graian Alps and Pennine, there is the civitas Centronum, that is Tarentasia; today the Archbishopric of Tarentaise.

units.la: Marchionatus Susæ ab Opido Susa, haud procul Fonte Doriæ Fluvij, qui infra Turinum in Padum se exonerat. Censent viri docti Susam in Graiis Alpibus Σεγύσιον Ptolemæo dici; Segusionem, Plinio, Ammiano, Antonino, Tabulæque Itinerariæ. Notat Ammianus lib. xv. Cottiarum Alpium Segusionem opidum initium esse. Dicit idem Cottij Regulí Sepulcrum Segusione esse, Mœnibus proximum. Pertinet huc Nazarius in Panegyrica Oratione, quæ Constantino dicata: Differamus, inquit, parumper Italicas Expeditiones, quibus Segusiensium Civitatem, quæ superatis Alpibus Italiæ Claustrum objicit, quum vi & virtute velut Ianuam Belli refregissent, inde per obiectas acies, per exercitus obvios, usque ad Romana Mœnia inoffensus Victoriarum impetus percurrit. Alij Susam adscribunt Pedemontanæ Regioni: quod mihi non displicet.
units.tr: The Marquisate of Susa, named from the town Susa, not far from the source of the river Dora, which discharges into the Po below Turin. Learned men think that Susa is called Σεγύσιον [Segysion] by Ptolemy in the Graian Alps, and Segusio by Pliny, Ammianus, Antoninus and the Tabula Itineraria. Ammianus, book xv, notes that the town Segusio is the beginning of the Cottian Alps. The same writer says that the tomb of the Cottian king is at Segusio, next to the walls. Nazarius belongs here, in his Panegyric dedicated to Constantine: "Let us put off for a little while the Italian campaigns, in which, having broken by force and valour the city of the Segusians, which bars the gate of Italy beyond the Alps, as it were the gate of war, the unchecked rush of victories then ran on through the lines set before them and the armies they met, all the way to the Roman walls." Others assign Susa to the Piedmontese region, which does not displease me.

units.la: Addam nonnihil de Dominiis. Foßigni prope Lacum est Lemanum. In eo esse ferunt (Ego incertior sum) Ripaliam, Ripam ἀλὸς (ludere liceat: nam Lacus Lemanus Adcolis quibusdam Mare audit, & sane sæpe Maris instar sævit) Ripaille vulgo. Locus est non inamœnus; vel eo nomine celebris, quod ibi Amedæus VIII, Dux Sabaudiæ Primus, facta Principatuum suorum abdicatione, Monachum fuerit professus: & in Pontificem Maximum ab Concilij Basiliensis Patribus postulatus contra Eugenium IV, consecratusque IX Kalendas Septembris, anno cIↄ CCCC XL, & Felix vocatus, aliquamdiu egerit: constrictus sibi suisque, operis Sumtusque non magni, Ædificijs, quæ superesse vidi ipse anno cIↄ Iↄ XXXV. Mortuus ibi est anno cIↄ CCCC LII mense Ianuario; quum triennio ante dignitatem Pontificiam Nicolao, pacis causa, concessisset, solo Cardinalatus honore contentus. Foßignij Domini Filia Eleonora nuptiæ legitur Petro Comiti Sabaudia Sexto. Maria item Amedæi IV, Comitis Sabaudia VIII ex Brabantina Filia, locata perhibetur huius Ditionis Dynastæ. De reliquis nihil habeo. Chablaßij Principatum, qui Foßinio versus Orientem, Chablais vulgo, adquisiße, suisque Dominijs adjecisse memoratur Amedæus III; quum legitimi heredes masculi jam defecissent. Adcensent illi quidam Tonomum, Fruanum, Gringaunum, & alia; quæ, ut non satis comperta, timidius scribo. De Dominio, quod vulgo Val d'Ossa, dicendum erit commodiore loco in Italia, ubi de Pedemontio. De reliquis Dynastiis Vaulx, Geü, Dombe, & si quæ aliæ, silere malo, quam parum explorata meis his adscribere.
units.tr: I will add something about the lordships. Fossigny lies near Lake Geneva. In it is said to be (I am less certain) Ripaille, "Ripa halos" [Ῥιπὰ ἁλός] (let me make a little play on words, for some locals call Lake Geneva Mare, the sea, and indeed it often rages like the sea). The place is not unpleasant, and it is famous chiefly for this: there Amedæus VIII, the first Duke of Savoy, after renouncing his principalities, professed himself a monk. He was sought as Supreme Pontiff by the fathers of the Council of Basel against Eugenius IV, was consecrated on 9 Kalends of September in the year 1440, and was called Felix; for some time he lived there, confined to himself and his own, in buildings of no great cost or expense, which I myself saw still standing in the year 1635. He died there in January 1452, three years after he had yielded the papal dignity to Nicholas for the sake of peace, content with the honour of the cardinalate alone. Eleonora, daughter of the lord of Fossigny, is said to have been married to Peter, Count of Savoy, the sixth. Likewise Maria, daughter of Amedæus IV, Count of Savoy VIII, by his Brabantine wife, is said to have been given in marriage to a lord of this domain. I have nothing on the rest. Amedæus III is recorded to have acquired the principality of Chablais, which lies east of Fossigny and is commonly called Chablais, and to have added it to his own dominions, since the legitimate male heirs had by then died out. Some add to these Tonon, Fruanum, Gringaunum and others; these, since they are not sufficiently established, I write about rather timidly. The domain commonly called Val d'Ossa will have to be discussed in a more convenient place in Italy, where I treat of Piedmont. Of the other lordships, Vaulx, Geü, Dombe, and any others, I prefer to keep silent rather than attribute to my work things too little explored.

units.la: Sunt & alia Sabaudiæ Opida: Aiguebelle ab Aquis bellis, ad Fluvium, qui haud procul inde Archo se jungit; Mont-belual, Pellay, Nici ad Lacum cognominem, Montmelian; Insilles, supra Segusionem, Ὀρσιὰ Ptolemæo, qui Cottiis Alpibus (male in Vulgatis Scutiis) Leontiorum abscribit, quibus quæ superant curiosioribus adponenda relinquo. Vide interim huc Partem Itinerarij Antonini, quæ infra cap. XLVII.
units.tr: There are also other towns of Savoy: Aiguebelle, from the Aquae Bellae, on the river that joins the Arc not far from there; Montbel-ual, Pellay, Nici on the lake of the same name, Montmélian; Insilles, above Segusio, which Ptolemy calls Orsia, and assigns to the Cottian Alps (wrongly given as Scutiis in the printed editions) and to the Leontii. What else remains I leave to more curious readers to add. Meanwhile see here the part of the Antonine Itinerary, which is given below in chapter XLVII.

units.la: Concenseri solet Sabaudia Regio Breßanensis, vulgo Païs de Bresse inter Ararim & Rodanum Fluvios, intercurrente fere Dænio: Segusianorum olim Sedes, ut quidam censent. Opidum ibi Bourg en Bresse, quod male quidam putant Forum Segusianorum. Vide quæ dixi cap. xxvi. In hac Regione sunt Comitatus Varax, Montreuil, Pont de Vaulx, Vaulx, Basgey, Ulricus Basgai Comes & Bressiae Dominus Filiam reliquit unicam & Heredem Sibyllam, quam quum Uxorem duxisset Amedaeus IV, Sabaudiae Comes VIII. Comitatum Basgeensem, totamque Bressiam sibi fecit Ditionis.
units.tr: Savoy is usually counted to include the Bresse region, commonly Pays de Bresse, lying between the rivers Saône and Rhône, with the Dain flowing through almost its whole length; it was once, as some think, the seat of the Segusiani. There is a town there, Bourg-en-Bresse, which some wrongly think is Forum Segusianorum. See what I said in chapter xxvi. In this region are the counties of Varax, Montreuil, Pont-de-Vaux, Vaux, Bagé. Ulric of Bagé, Count and lord of Bresse, left a single daughter and heiress, Sibylla, whom Amadeus IV, Count of Savoy VIII, took as his wife; and so he made the county of Bagé and all of Bresse part of his own domain.

units.la: CAPUT XLIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XLIV.

units.la: Lotharingia.
units.tr: Lorraine.

units.la: SABAVDIAM in mea Partitione sequitur Lotaringia Ducatus. LOTHARINGIA, ut quidem Latine scribentes vocant, dicta ab Lotario, Ludovici Imperatoris; Francorumque Regis vel Filio, vel Nepote. Parum refert. Ludovico sane Pio quatuor fuerunt Filii; qui, moto paricidiali in Parentem Bello, eoque apud Suessiones in Monasterium detruso, omnes ejus Principatus inter se diviserunt constituntque Terrarchia, Proceribus Imperii intervenientibus; Res eo deducta est, ut Lotarius Primogenitus Imperii Titulo, cum Italia, Narbonensi Gallia, iisque Ditionibus, quae mox Lotaringia appellatione innotuerunt, frueretur: Ludovicus, Germaniam Karolus, Franciam ab Mosa ad Oceanum: Pipinus denique, vel ex eo Filius cognominis, Aquitaniam possideret. Lotario Filius fuit, praeter Ludovicum in Imperio Successorem, Lotarius Lotaringiae Rex. Quae igitur initio Lotar-ryk, vel Lot-reych Germanis, id est, Lotharii Regnum; Latina, eaque depravatiore Terminatione postea Lotaringia coepit audire: Loraine Incolis, reliquisque Francis, quasi Lot.regne, concisis litteris. Memoriae produnt Rerum Francicarum Scriptores, Lotaringia quondam ampliores fuisse Limites, Austrasiamque olim nuncupatam vel Austriam, Oost-reych (quum ex adverso esset Westrasia vel Westria, Westreych; corrupte etiam Neustria, Occidentale Regnum) divisam in Superiorem & Inferiorem; contentamque inter Renum, Scaldim, Mosamque Flumina inferiorem hodie varia nomina obtinere, diversisque subesse Principibus; Superiorem, quae & Mosellanica & Tullingia cognominabatur, exceptis aliquot ejus Portionibus, sub unius nunc esse Imperio, & Quorum Totius Partem antiquo nomine florere: adeo ut Lotaringia hodie conjaceant ad Orientem quidem Alsatia, & quae speciaiiore notione Westrasia: ab Meridie vero Burgundia: qua Occidens est, Campaniam habeat; qua Septemtrio Arduenna Silva terminetur (occurrentibus mox Leuceburgis, Trevirensibus, aliisque Populis ibi Conregionalibus) quae olim etiam Lotaringia Partes fuerunt nobilissimae. Lotaringia haec nostra, licet altissimis innexa Montibus Silvisque densissimis, externae tamen opis non indiget, per se ferax Frumenti & Vini: Animalia producit varia: Stagna habet piscosa: Salinas Thermasque que insignes: Metalla generat varij generis, Argentum, Æs, Ferrum, Stannum, Plumbum: Nec Gemmæ desunt; quarum ad Vogeli radices lucrosa est Pilcano. Reperiuntur & Lapides, quos ab cæruleo colore Lazulos nominant Incolæ, magnum inde Lucrum facientes. Et & Materia, qua Specula & Vitrinæ fabricantur: qualis in reliquis Europæ Provincijs non invenitur. Nascuntur insuper hic miræ magnitudinis Calcidoniæ, ita ut e fructis permagni Calices concinantur. Equos procreat Lotharia generosissimos, Neapolitanis Turcicisque tubinde non impares. Fluminibus insignitur celeberrimis Moe, Mosella, Sarave, Vol-ta, Motana, Murta, Sella, Nida, & aliis. De Moela ad Inferiorem Germaniam. Reliqui ad hunc Ducatum propinquo fer inent: Mosa quidem & Sarave potiore parte: ceteri fere integri. Oritur Mosella in Mon e Vogelo, haud procul Araris fontibus, paullo supra Vicum, qui vulgo Bässan; lapsusque ab Vulturno ad Caurum, perlustratis Opidis, quæ vernacule L'estraje, Remiremont, Efinal, Charmes, Faron, flexoque ab Oriente in Occidentem cursu, recta pe it Tullium, Urbem Episcopalem: unde in Orientem resurgens, Finardum usque versus Aquisgranum tendens visisque Mediomatricibus, Treviriensibus, aliisque Populis, Confluentium, cui ab renomen, Reno confluit. Germanis Mosel: Gallis Moselle, o Βεζηγγ& phiam ab Rhenano & aliis Ptolemæo dicti lib. ii. cap. ix. Ioannes tamen Heroldus o Βεζηγ apud Ptolemæum non Fluvium esse notat, sed designari Tractum cum ad Renum, qui nunc temporis Ober-Rhingaw appellatur: Clemens etiam Trelaus Mosellanus citatur, ut scribit Abrahamus Ortelius, quemdam ad Mosellam Tractum Obrimi, nomen hactenus retinere. Mosellam singulari doctoque Carmine celebrat Ausonius Eidyll. iii. ab Aquæ limpiditate, Navigandique facilitate: Villis Arenisque, quibus utraque Ripa decoratur, Piscibus Capitone, Salari, Redone, Vmbra, Barbi, Salmone, Mustella, Perca, Tinca, Alburno, Alausa, Gobio, & Siluro, quibus abundat; Humimbus denique in ipsum decurrentibus, Pronæ, Nemesa, Sura, Gelöi, Frubio, Le-sura, Drahon, Sarmora, Saravo, Aisonia. Mosellam & Ararim, facta inter utrumque Fossa, connectere, Imperatore Domitio Nerone, adgressus est L. Vetus; ut Copiæ ex Italia per Mare, dein Rodano & Arare subvectæ per eam Fossam, mox Fluvio Mosella in Renum, exin in Oceanum decurrerent; sublatisque itinerum difficultatibus, navigabilia inter se Occidentis Septemtrionisque litora fierent, uti scribit Cornelius Tacitus lib. xiii. Saravus, haud procul Salmentibus ortus, Fluviorum omnium, qui in Mosellam exeunt, est maximus; Navigiorum patiens, & aliorum Amnium, quos in se recipit, clarus Lustratis Urbibus Opidisque, quæ vulgo Sar-Fure, Feneitrange, Sar-Werden, Sar-Alben, Guemund, Sar-Pruck, Waldeburg, SarBrug, & aliis, tandem sub Moenia Augustæ Trevirorum Mosellam convenit, non longe à Kentherbruk. Meminit ejus Ausonius in Mosella. Nomen hodie retinet. Sar enim Adelus audit Sarra etiam Veteribus dictus, docente Inscriptione, quæ Treviros translata ex opido ad eum Fluvium sito, quod hoc tempore vocatur SarPruck, hoc est Sarræ-Pons.
units.tr: After Savoy, in my division, comes the Duchy of Lorraine. LOTHARINGIA, as Latin writers call it, takes its name from Lothar, son or perhaps grandson of the Emperor Louis and of a King of the Franks. The point matters little. Louis the Pious had four sons who, after a parricidal war against their father, which ended with his confinement in a monastery at Soissons, divided all his principality among themselves and set up separate kingdoms, with the nobles of the Empire acting as intermediaries. The outcome was that Lothar, the eldest, kept the imperial title together with Italy, Narbonese Gaul, and those territories that soon became known by the name Lotharingia. Louis got Germany, Charles got France from the Meuse to the Ocean, and Pepin, or a son of the same name, held Aquitaine. Besides Louis, who succeeded in the Empire, Lothar had a son, Lothar, King of Lotharingia. The region was therefore first called by the Germans Lotharryk or Lotharreych, that is, the kingdom of Lothar. In Latin, and later in a more corrupt ending, it came to be called Lotharingia, and among its inhabitants and the other Franks it was called Loraine, as if it were "Lot-regne," with the letters run together. The writers of Frankish history record that Lotharingia once had wider boundaries, and that Austrasia, once also called Austria (Oostreych), was divided, over against which lay Westrasia or Westria (Westreych; corruptly also Neustria, the Western Kingdom), into an Upper and a Lower part. The part lying between the rivers Rhine, Scheldt and Meuse, which is the Lower part, today bears various names and is subject to different princes. The Upper part, also called Mosellan and Tullian, now lies under a single rule, apart from some portions of it, and every part of the whole still flourishes under its ancient name. Thus Lotharingia today borders: to the east, Alsace, and what in a narrower sense is called Westrasia; to the south, Burgundy; to the west, it has Champagne; to the north it is bounded by the Ardennes forest, where the Leuci of Luxembourg, the Trevirans and other peoples of the same region soon meet. These parts were once also among the most noble parts of Lotharingia. This our Lotharingia, though it is enclosed by very high mountains and very dense forests, needs no outside help, being by itself fertile in grain and wine. It produces various animals; it has fish-filled ponds; it has famous salt-works and hot springs; it yields metals of various kinds: silver, copper, iron, tin, lead. Nor are gems lacking; at the foot of the Vosges, the Pilcano yields a profitable harvest of them. There are also stones which the inhabitants call lazuli from their blue colour, and from which they make great profit. There is also the material from which mirrors and glass vessels are made, such as is not found in the other provinces of Europe. Moreover, here are born chalcedonies of extraordinary size, so that very large cups are fashioned from single pieces. Lotharingia breeds very noble horses, sometimes not inferior to Neapolitan or Turkish ones. It is marked by very famous rivers: the Moselle, Mosella, Sarave, Volta, Motana, Murta, Sella, Nida, and others. The Moselle flows into Lower Germany. The rest mostly lie close to this Duchy: the Meuse and the Saar for the greater part, the others almost entirely. The Moselle rises in the Vosges, not far from the sources of the Arar, a little above the village commonly called Bässan. It flows from south to north, passing the towns called in the vernacular L'estraje, Remiremont, Epinal, Charmes, Pharon; its course then bends from east to west, and it heads straight for Toul, the episcopal city. From there it rises again eastward, reaching towards Finard and Aachen, and after passing the Mediomatrici, the Trevirans and other peoples, it joins the Rhine at Confluentes, from which the town takes its name. To the Germans it is Mosel, to the French Moselle, [Βεζηγγ] and it is called by Ptolemy and others in book ii, chapter ix. However, John Herold notes that the Bezinge [Βεζηγγ] in Ptolemy is not a river but denotes a district near the Rhine, now called Ober-Rheingau. Clemens Trelaus of Moselle is also cited, as Abraham Ortelius writes, as saying that a certain district by the Moselle, called Obrimus, has so far retained the name. Ausonius celebrates the Moselle in a unique and learned poem, Idyll iii, for the clearness of its water and the ease of navigation; for the villas and sands that adorn both banks; and for the fish with which it abounds: the capito, salar, redo, umbra, barbus, salmon, mustela, perch, tench, alburnus, alausa, gobio and silurus. Lastly, it is fed by streams flowing into it: Prona, Nemesa, Sura, Gelöi, Frubio, Lesura, Drahon, Sarmora, Savara and Aisonia. L. Vetus undertook, in the reign of the Emperor Domitian Nero, to connect the Moselle and the Arar by digging a ditch between them, so that supplies brought from Italy by sea, then by the Rhone and the Arar, would pass through that ditch and then down the Moselle into the Rhine, and from there into the Ocean; and, the difficulties of transport being removed, the shores of the West and North would become navigable for one another, as Cornelius Tacitus writes in book xiii. The Saravus, rising not far from the Salmentes, is the greatest of all the rivers that flow into the Moselle; it is suitable for ships and famous for the other streams it receives. Passing through the towns and villages commonly called Sar-Fure, Feneitrange, Sar-Werden, Sar-Alben, Guemund, Sar-Pruck, Waldeburg, Sar-Brug and others, it finally joins the Moselle beneath the walls of Augusta Trevirorum, not far from Kentherbruk. Ausonius also mentions it in the Mosella. It still keeps its name: the Saar is called Adelus, and the Ancients called it Sarra as well, as an inscription shows, which was moved to Trier from the town on that river now called Sar-Pruck, that is, Sarra-Bridge.

units.la: CÆS. RO. EXTER. IMP. P. P. S. C. AVG. TREVI. INGR. ESSVM. M. CASTRA. SARRÆ. FLV. PRO. MIL. CVSTODIA. RIEN. POTITVS. EST
units.tr: For Caesar, Emperor, Father of the Fatherland, Augustus: the Trevirans, having entered Essum, the camp on the river Sarra, for the protection of the soldiers, took possession of nothing.

units.la: Volta Fluvius est Margaritiferus, qui ad Vicum Charmeni Mosellam ingreditur. Mortans ad Pagum cognominem Murtæ miscetur. Murta vel Meutsa, multis in se receptis Amnibus, Mosellam loco plano inter Prata paullatim accedit; & longo tractu, æquali quasi cursu, comitatur, relicta inter utrumque alveum exigua admodum terra, donec tandem paullum supra Condeium Arcem, quæ à dextris in rupe est Pago sibi cognomini impendens, facto cum Mosellæ Alveo Angulo acutissimo, ejus & Aquis miscetur. Iungit se eidem ad Mediomatricum Urbem Sella, initium quasi capiens ex Lindero Lacu, qui Sale dives & Piscatura. Duplex denique Nida (Orientalior enim Germanicus, Occidentalior Gallicus dicitur) facto ad Pagum Northenium concursu, duobus infra Bossonf-Villam (Abbatiæ nomen est) milliaribus in Saravum exoneratur.
units.tr: The Volta is a pearl-bearing river, which enters the Moselle at the village of Charmeni. The Mortans mingles with the Murta at the village of the same name. The Murta, or Meutsa, having received many streams into itself, gradually approaches the Moselle across a level meadow, and for a long stretch accompanies it, as if running on an even course, leaving only a very narrow strip of land between the two channels, until at last, a little above Condé, the castle which stands on a rock on the right and overhangs the village of the same name, it meets the waters of the Moselle at a very sharp angle, forming a junction with its channel. The Sella joins the Moselle near the city of the Mediomatrici, taking its beginning, as it were, from Lake Lindre, which is rich in salt and fish. Lastly, the double Nied (the eastern one is called German, the western one French) meets at the village of Nornich, and two miles below Bossendorf (the name of an abbey) it discharges into the Saar.
