units.la: Habitarunt olim Lotaringiam, quæ nobis præ manibus, Mediomatrices & Leuci. Mediomatrices Cæsari lib. iv, Tacito, Plinio; Mediomatrices Straboni & Ptolemæo; Mediomatrices etiam Cæsari lib. vii. quorum Metropolis Divodurum, hodie Metz appellatur. Civitas Mediomatricum, hoc est, Metis, Notitiæ Provinciarum sub Belgica i; L'Evesché de Metz, Le Pais Messin. Leuci Cæsari lib. i, Lucano lib. i. & Plinio Liberos cognominantur, Ptolemæo, qui Metropolin ipsorum facit. Sic in Notitia Provinciarum sub Belgica i, Civitas Leucorum, hoc est Tullo, L'Evesché de Toul. Sunt etiam qui Tulingos Cæsaris ad Lotaringiam referunt.
units.tr: The peoples who once inhabited the Lotharingia that lies before us were the Mediomatrici and the Leuci. The Mediomatrici are named by Caesar in book iv, by Tacitus and Pliny; the Mediomatrici by Strabo and Ptolemy; and the Mediomatrici again by Caesar in book vii. Their metropolis, Divodurum, is today called Metz. The "Civitas Mediomatricum," that is Metis, appears in the Notitia of the Provinces under Belgica i; it is the Bishopric of Metz, the Pays Messin. The Leuci, called Liberi by Pliny, are named by Caesar in book i, by Lucan in book i, and by Ptolemy, who makes their metropolis. So in the Notitia of the Provinces under Belgica i, "Civitas Leucorum," that is Toul, the Bishopric of Toul. There are also those who refer Caesar's Tulingi to Lotharingia.

units.la: Decorata fuit olim Lotaringia Regni titulo, ut patet ex Francicorum Scriptorum Monimentis. Reges pauci admodum, & vix duo tresve, memorantur. Statim enim Karolus Calvus, post Fratruelis Lotarii excessum, ipsius Diitiones invasit, suisque adjecit Principatibus. Non multo post ad Ducatus dignitatem est redacta. Primi Duces sparsi per Historias & Variorum Scripta. Proximos produxit Stirps Bilhonæa, ex qua natos cum Antiquioribus legimus Comites Vadimontios, Ducum, qui hodie Lotaringiæ Guisæq. præsunt, Progenitores. Eorum hoc statui solet Stemma:
units.tr: Lotharingia was once adorned with the title of a kingdom, as is clear from the records of the Frankish writers. Very few kings are mentioned, and scarcely two or three. For soon Charles the Bald, after the death of his cousin Lothar, seized its territories and added them to his own principalities. Not long after, it was reduced to the rank of a duchy. The first dukes are scattered through the histories and the writings of various authors. The nearest of them were produced by the house of Bilhon, from which we read that the Counts of Vaudémont, the ancestors of the Dukes who now rule Lotharingia and Guise, were born, as were some of the older ones. Their lineage is usually set out thus:

units.la: Antonius Comes Vadimontius Uxor Maria, Filia & Heres Ioannis. Hæreditas & Aumalæ Comitis, & Mariæ Ducis Aurelia-nensis.
units.tr: Antoine, Count of Vaudémont, wife Marie, daughter and heir of Jean, Count of Aumale, and of Marie, Duchess of Orléans.

units.la: Fridericus Comes Vadimontius Hæreditas tota. Renati Andegavensis Regis Sicilæ Filia, Lotaringia Ducatum Heredes vacuum ad Veterem Stirpem bilhoneam revocant.
units.tr: Frederick, Count of Vaudémont: his whole inheritance, the daughter of René of Anjou, King of Sicily. The heirs recall the vacant duchy of Lorraine to the old stock.

units.la: Renatus Dux Lotaringiæ & Comes Vadimontius. Hic ab Karolo Burgundo magna cum periculo in urbe & Ducatu quoque pulsus cum ope Helvetiorum, Alsatiam ad Nanceium, recuperavit. Primæ Coniugis, Isabellæ Comitis Filiæ, denuo repudiata. Philippam duxit. Adolphi Egmondani Ducis Geldriæ Filiam. Obiit anno MCCCCLXXVIII.
units.tr: René, Duke of Lorraine and Count of Vaudémont. Driven from the city and the duchy by Charles the Bold, at great risk, he recovered Alsace and Nancy with the help of the Swiss. His first wife, daughter of Count Isabella, was repudiated again, and he married Philippa, daughter of Adolf of Egmont, Duke of Guelders. He died in 1478.

units.la: Antonius Calabriæ, Lotaringiæ, Barri Dux, Montis-tum-mopontis Marchio, Vadimontii & Alpismontis Comes, Princeps tetra telaris fumnaque cum gloria genus clarissimus. Natus MCCCCXIX. in pr. die Novembris, obiit MCCCCLXVIII. Kalendas Quintilis anno MCCCCXIIII. Uxores Renata Borboni, Gilberti Ducis Montipensis Filia.
units.tr: Antoine, Duke of Calabria, of Lorraine, of Bar, Marquis of Pont-à-Mousson, Count of Vaudémont and of Aumale, a prince of most illustrious lineage, renowned for his great glory. Born on 1 November 1419, he died on 1 July 1470. His wife was Renée of Bourbon, daughter of Gilbert, Duke of Montpensier.

units.la: Franciscus Dux Calabriæ, Lotaringiæ, Barri, Gelriæ, Montissanimo punctus Marchio, & Obiit MCCCCXII. quarto Iduum Quintil. Uxor Claudia Dunensis.
units.tr: Francis, Duke of Calabria, of Lorraine, of Bar, of Guelders, Marquis of Mons, died on the fourth day before the Ides of July 1632. His wife was Claude of Dunois.

units.la: Nicolaus Lotharingiæ, Dux Mediomatris, Marchio Nomeny, & Multa Italiæ tributa Coniugibus Princeps, inter eas Ludovicam, Henrici III. Franciae regis Coniugem.
units.tr: Nicholas, Duke of Lorraine and of the Mediomatrici, Marquis of Nomeny, a prince with many Italian territories by his marriages; among his wives was Louise, wife of Henry III, King of France.

units.la: Karolus, Calabriæ, Lotaringiæ, Barri, Gelriæ Dux, Montissanimopontis Marchio, & Uxor Claudia Valesia, Henrici II. Galliarum Regis Filia.
units.tr: Charles, Duke of Calabria, of Lorraine, of Bar, of Guelders, Marquis of Pont-à-Mousson; his wife was Claude of Valois, daughter of Henry II, King of the French.

units.la: Henricus Calabriæ, Lotaringiæ & Dux, Montistuæmonpontis Marchio, & Karolus Calabriæ, Lotaringiæ Principepus Mediomatricum.
units.tr: Henry, Duke of Calabria and of Lorraine, Marquis of Pont-à-Mousson; and Charles, Prince of Calabria and of Lorraine, of the Mediomatrici.

units.la: De Lotaringia Ducum Stemmatibus, Rebusque gestis Volumen satis magnum edidit Franciscus Roseus.
units.tr: Franciscus Roseus has published a fairly large volume on the genealogies and deeds of the Dukes of Lorraine.

units.la: Metropolis Lotaringiæ est Nanceium, vulgo Nancy: Oppidum non amplum, sed situ pulcro commodoque, loco plano, forma quadrata, magnifico Lotaringicorum Ducum Palatio nobile. Adjacet illi Aedes D. Georgii, in qua Monumentum visebatur Karoli Audacis, Burgundiæ Ducis, ab Helvetiis & Lotaringis Nonis Ianuarij anno MCCCCLXXVII. acie caesi: cuius reliquias, Karoli V. Imperatoris, ipsius Proneepotis jussu, anno MDXXI. mense Octobri inde Leuceburgum solenniter transtulit Boisotus, Ordinis Aurei Velleris Praeco, Brugas hinc mox, Mariæ Hungariæ Reginæ mandatu, transportandas. Sunt in eadem D. Georgii Aede aliquot Lotaringicorum Ducum Tumuli, qui Inscriptionibus carent; ut & in aliis Templis.
units.tr: The metropolis of Lorraine is Nancy, commonly called Nancy: a town not large, but pleasant and conveniently situated, on level ground, square in plan, and notable for the magnificent palace of the Dukes of Lorraine. Next to it is the church of St George, in which was seen the monument of Charles the Bold, Duke of Burgundy, who was cut down in battle by the Swiss and the Lorrainers on 5 January 1477. In October 1521, by the command of his great-great-grandson, Emperor Charles V, Boisot, herald of the Order of the Golden Fleece, solemnly transferred his remains from there to Luxembourg, and soon afterwards they were carried on to Bruges by order of Queen Mary of Hungary. In the same church of St George lie several tombs of the Dukes of Lorraine which have no inscriptions, as also in other churches.

units.la: Nam certum Sepulturæ Locum non habent. Posteriorum Ducum pars potior ad D. Francisci Ædem (quæ ad alterum Palatij latus) sita est. Spectare ibi est superbum Renati, qui Victoria potitus est contra Karolum Burgundiæ Ducem, Monumentum. Conditi jacent ibidem Dux Antonius, ejusque Filius Franciscus, Karolique Ducis Vxor Claudia Valesia, Henrici II. Galliarum Regis Filia. Namcen Moenia lambit Musa, qui tribus inde milliaribus paullo supra Arcem Candei Mosellam intrat. Armamentarium habet Nancetum, Machinis bellicis omnis generis instructissimum. Putant Petrus Divæus aliique Nanceium hodie esse, quod Nasium Ptolemæo, Nasium Antonino in Itinere, quod Durocortoro ducit Divodurum. Sed si quis penitius Itineris illius rationem consideret, ejusque ductum & stilia diligenter sequatur: facile deprehendet Antonini Nasium incidere non posse in locum illum, ubi hodie Nanceium: adeo ut Nasium illud sit, non quod nunc Nanceium dicimus, sed Pagus XII. inde milliaribus distinctus non procul ab Mosa in Barroducana Provincia, qui vulgo Nay dictus, unde Nasiensis in Lapide, qui eccfossus ibi: FABRICIVS MACIENSIS CVRATORIBVS ET MINIS TRIS IVVENTIDIO FIRMO ET ATEVLA SOLLI F. HVIVS FANI FACIENDI. Certe Nasium illud amplissimam aliquando Vrbem fuisse, satis paret ex Ruderibus: quod etiam tentatur apud Ortelium Clemens Trelæus Mosellanus. Iter Antonini, quo Nasij fit mentio, collatum cum Itineraria Tabula & hodierna nomenclatura, sic se habet:
units.tr: For they have no certain place of burial. The greater part of the later Dukes lie at the church of St Francis, which is on the other side of the palace. There one may see the proud monument of René, who gained the victory over Charles, Duke of Burgundy. Buried there lie Duke Antoine and his son Francis, and Claude of Valois, wife of Duke Charles, daughter of Henry II, King of the French. The Moselle washes the walls of Nancy, and from there, about three miles off, it flows past the castle of Condé, a little above. Nancy has an arsenal, most fully equipped with war engines of every kind. Pierre Divès and others think that Nancy is today the Nasium of Ptolemy and the Nasium of Antoninus' Itinerary, which leads from Durocortorum to Divodurum. But if anyone considers the course of that Itinerary more closely, and follows its route and distances carefully, he will easily see that Antoninus' Nasium cannot lie at the place where Nancy now stands. So that Nasium is not what we now call Nancy, but a village twelve miles from there, not far from the Meuse, in the province of Bar, commonly called Nay; hence the inscription found there, Nasiensis: FABRICIUS MACIENSIS, TO THE CURATORS AND MINISTERS, TRIBUNE, JUVENTIDIUS FIRMUS AND ATEULA SOLLI DAUGHTER, FOR THE BUILDING OF THIS TEMPLE. Certainly that Nasium was at one time a very large city, as the ruins make plain; Clement Trelaeus of the Moselle also attempts this, in Ortelius. The Itinerary of Antoninus, in which Nasium is mentioned, compared with the Peutinger Table and present-day names, stands thus:

units.la: Antonini Itinerar. | Tabula Peutingeriana | Vulgata Nomencl.
units.tr: Antonine Itinerary | Peutinger Table | Modern names

units.la: Durocortoro Divodurum usque Millia Pass. LXXXVII. sic: | Durocortoro, XIX. | De Reims à Metz, Lienes 30. Fanum Minervæ, M.P.XIIII. | Tanomia, Legendum Fano Min. id est Minervæ | ubi hodie Basones, aut circiter. Arielam, M.P.XVI. | ...... | ubi Bony vel Memehoule. Caturigas, M.P.IX. | Caturices, IX. | Clermont forte. Nasium, M.P.IX. | Nasie, Leg. Nasio, .. | Nas. Tullum, M.P.XVI. | Tullio, Leg. Tullo, X. | Toul. Scarpona, M.P.X. | Scarponna, XIIII. | Sarpaigne, ad Mosellam. Divodurum, M.P.XII. | Divo. Durimedio. Matricorum. Scrib. Divoduro Mediomatricum. | Metz.
units.tr: From Durocortorum to Divodurum, eighty-seven Roman miles, thus: | Durocortoro, XIX. | From Reims to Metz, leagues 30. Fanum Minervae, 14 miles | Tanomia, read Fano Min., that is, Minervae | where Basones is today, or near it. Ariela, 16 miles | ...... | where Bony or Memehoule is. Caturigas, 9 miles | Caturices, IX. | perhaps Clermont. Nasium, 9 miles | Nasie, read Nasio | Nas. Tullum, 16 miles | Tullio, read Tullo, X. | Toul. Scarpona, 10 miles | Scarponna, XIIII. | Sarpaigne, on the Moselle. Divodurum, 12 miles | Divo. Durimedio. Matricorum, write Divoduro Mediomatricum. | Metz.

units.la: Scarponæ, quæ in Itinerariis nominatur, meminit etiam Ammianus lib. XXVII. Retinet hodie Veterem Appellationem Vicus Sarpaigne, ubi multa Antiquitatis Rudera visuntur. De iis non possum, quin adscribam Petri Divæi verba ex ipsius Itinerario: Hic, inquit, paullo viterius ad eamdem Mosellæ ripam Vicus est exiguus Sarpaigne, de cujus Antiquitate multa Incolæ referebant. Oppidum olim amplum fuisse à Sarpignæ quadam Regina (non abhunt hæc ab Fabulis) denominatum, quæ & in eo Regiam habuerit. Oitendunt in eius rei testimonium Ruinas quasdam Murorum, ubi Thermas quondam fuisse volebant: Nos quæ eorum figura fuisset, non valebamus conjicere: tantum subdubitabamus, num Castrorum inservissent Munitioni, quum eorum magnæ sit crassitudo, & Foraminæ in eis cernantur adhuc rotunda & angusta, quasi ad ejaculanda Missilia. Hic & Numismata antiqua erant: & Hospes, ad quem diverteramus, nobis dedit aureum Nummum C. Cæsaris Caligulæ, quem se ibidem reperisse affirmabat. Exstat in Pariete Domus cuiusdam rustica antiquum Marmor, in quo Regina illius Imaginem esse volunt. Est manu omnino artifice sculpta Imago mulieebris, longioribus induta Vestibus, Equæ insidens, quam Pullus videtur lactare; ipsa vero Calathum, aut simile quidpiam gestiat, in quo Pomorum figuram, ficubus haud absimilitum videbamur dignoscere. Suspicari sane est ex hac Scalptura Locum hunc alicujus olim nomine fuisse, sed de hoc, ut & de alijs quamplurimis desiderantur Historiæ: Fabellarum vero inanium apud profanum Vulgus nullum esse modum, nemins non Exploratum existimamus.
units.tr: Scarpona, which is named in the Itineraries, is also mentioned by Ammianus, book 27. The village of Sarpaigne still keeps the old name, and many remains of antiquity are seen there. About these I cannot help adding the words of Pierre Divès from his own Itinerary: "Here," he says, "a little further on, on the same bank of the Moselle, is the small village of Sarpaigne, about whose antiquity the inhabitants told many things. It is said that the town was once large, named after a certain queen of Sarpaigne (which is not far from fable), who also had a palace there. In evidence of this they show some ruins of walls, where they said there were once baths. We could not conjecture what shape they had; we only doubted whether they served for the defence of a camp, since their thickness is great, and round, narrow openings can still be seen in them, as if for hurling missiles. Here there were also ancient coins, and our host, at whose house we lodged, gave us a gold coin of Caligula Caesar, which he said he had found there. In the wall of a certain country house there is an ancient marble, in which they wish the queen's image to be. It is a female figure, sculpted by a thoroughly skilled hand, dressed in long garments, sitting on a mare, which seems to suckle a foal; she herself holds a basket or something similar, in which I seemed to make out the shape of fruits, hardly unlike figs." It is certainly reasonable to suspect from this sculpture that the place once bore someone's name, but, as with very many other things, the history of it is lacking; as for the vain fables of the common people, everyone knows there is no limit to them."

units.la: Haud procul Nanceio Locum vidi, ubi obtruncatus Karolus Burgundus, ad Rivulum quemdam, quem quum, cæsis jam copiis, fugiens pararet transilire effuso Equo, miserè fuit ab Insequentibus confoslus. Testatur rem gestam Crux Lapidea °cum Inscriptione Gallica in ærea Lamina, cujus Exscriptum est apud Divæum in Itinerario Belgico. Paullo altius, ubi Prælium id commissum volunt, Sacellum mihi monstratum est à Burgundionibus cognominatum, cum adjuncto Cœmeterio & Tabula ærea, in qua Gallici Verisus memoriam atrocissimi Prælij conservant. Prope Nanceium ad Montium Radices Pagus est Marche-Ville, cujus Incolas perfidia aliquando in suum Ducem (eum Historiæ Fridericum II appellant) notatos ferunt, atque ea de causa, quotiescumque cum reliquis Principibus domesticis epulari contingit, Panem eis invērium apponi consuevisse. Exstant ibidem Rudera rotundæ Turris, in qua Dux, quem diximus, ex Venatione subductus ad triennium detentus memoratur.
units.tr: Not far from Nancy I saw the place where Charles the Burgundian was cut down, at a certain little stream, which, as his troops were already slaughtered and he was fleeing and trying to leap across on a foaming horse, he was wretchedly trampled by his pursuers. The event is attested by a stone cross with a French inscription on a bronze plate, of which a copy is found in Divès' Belgian Itinerary. A little higher up, where they say that battle was fought, I was shown a chapel called by the Burgundians (Burgundionibus), with an attached cemetery and a bronze tablet, on which French verses preserve the memory of that most savage battle. Near Nancy, at the foot of the hills, is the village of Marche-Ville, whose inhabitants, they say, were once branded for treachery against their duke (whom the histories call Frederick II), and for that reason, whenever it happens that the princes dine with their household, they were accustomed to be served bread made of bran. There are still the ruins of a round tower there, in which the duke I mentioned is recorded to have been held for three years, after being led away from a hunt.

units.la: Nanceium dignitate sequitur Fanum S. Nicolai, vulgo S. Nicolas, duobus inde distans versus Orientem milliaribus, ad Murtam Fluvium, Loco plano & fertili. Templum non magnæ est antiquitatis, sed vastæ molis, editæque structuræ. Columnæ, quæ totum Fastigium sustinent, tantæ sunt cum gracilitate, tum altitudinis, ut tanto oneri ferendo vix judicentur pares. Turres habet duas, in quarum una Karoli Lotaringici Cardinalis, qui idem Metensis erat Episcopus, cuique hæc pasrebat Ecclesia sub Prioratus, ut loquuntur, titulo, in summo Culmine Symbolum: obeliscus seliciter cum Hedera circumplicata, & Inscriptione, TE STANTE VIREo. Asseruari ferrur in hac Ede ex D. Nicolai, Myræ Episcopi, quæ urbs erat Lyciæ, ex eadem Lycia, Pataria Vrbe, oriundi, Manu Articulus unus inclusus Auro, Gemmis multis interstincto: unde hujus primum loci nata Religio; qui advenarum frequentia in eam excrevit amplitudinem, ut jam non Pagum, sed Urbem, & quidem totius Lotaringiæ cultissimam, quas posset dicere, si muro clauderetur: ea est Ædificiorum venustate, aptâ Viarum dispositione, Incolarum multitudine, ut nihil requiri queat: sed ob Mercaturam præcipue, & omnis generis opificia commendaturi Mercatores habens perquam opulentos, Vicinis suis dinores.
units.tr: After Nancy in rank comes Fanum S. Nicolai, commonly S. Nicolas, two miles to the east, on the river Meurthe, in a level and fertile place. The church is not of great antiquity, but is of vast bulk and elegant construction. The columns which support the whole roof are so slender and yet so tall that they hardly seem equal to bearing so great a load. It has two towers, in one of which, on the topmost ridge, is an obelisk entwined with ivy and with the inscription TE STANTE VIREO, which is the emblem of Charles of Lorraine, Cardinal and Bishop of Metz, to whom this church belonged under the title of a priory, as they say. It is reported that in this church there is kept one finger of St Nicholas, bishop of Myra, a city of Lycia, enclosed in gold and studded with many gems; he was a native of the same Lycia, of the city of Patara. From this, the religion of this place first arose; from the crowds of strangers it grew to such a size that it is no longer a village but a city, and indeed the most cultivated in all of Lorraine, which one could call a town if it were walled. It is so well supplied with fine buildings, a suitable arrangement of streets and a multitude of inhabitants that nothing more can be asked; but it is especially notable for trade, and it has very wealthy merchants, who surpass their neighbours in all kinds of manufactures.

units.la: Alia minorum gentium Opida, ne Lectori tædium pariam, præterēo. Uno distat milliari Nanceio Fraust, tribus, Ormes; paullo amplius, Bayen & Lunevillæ; quatuor, Le Font à Monson & Gerbeviller; quinque, Charmes; sex, Chaltenoy, Morhanges & Vaucoleur; paullo plus, Maxen soubs Bresse septem, Dompaire, Deneuvre, Hodon Chasteau; octo, Ramberville, Raon, Bellemont, Neuff-Chasteau, Mugstat, Marchain-Ville: novem, Epinal, Bruyeres, Darney; decem, Ormont, Valdersing, Beaumans: tredecim, Vaigny: quatuordecim, L'Estraye.
units.tr: I pass over the other towns of the lesser districts so as not to weary the reader. One mile from Nancy lies Fraust; three miles, Ormes; a little further, Bayen and Lunéville; four miles, Le Font à Monson and Gerbéviller; five, Charmes; six, Chaltenoy, Morhanges and Vaucouleurs; a little more, Maxen sous Bresse; seven, Dompaire, Deneuvre, Hodon Chasteau; eight, Ramberville, Raon, Bellemont, Neufchâteau, Mugstat, Marchainville; nine, Épinal, Bruyères, Darney; ten, Ormont, Valdersing, Beaumont; thirteen, Vaigny; fourteen, L'Estraye.

units.la: Comitatus titulo & dignitate clarent: quæ vernacule Vaudemont, quinque Nan- ceio milliaribus. Chaligny ad dextram Mosellæ, Leuca semi Nanceio. Amance septem milliaribus ab Mediomatricum Urbe versus Meridiem; Almentia Latine scribentibus: Scrinium olim & antiqua Lotaringiæ Cancellaria, testantibus Archivis ab Rosiero prolatis. Richecourt haud procul Lacu, qui vulgo La Garde Lac, unde Amnis profluit, qui inter Fanum S. Nicolai & opidum Rosieres Murtæ misceretur. Remiremont ad sinistram Mosellæ, Insulam ibi facientis, in Lotaringiæ Meridionalissimis: Rumaticum Castellum habet hic Aimoinus Monachus; Adromarici corrupte legitur apud Reginonem, pro Ad Romarics, divitiis; Remelsberg Germanice nominatur Spigelio ad Bartholini Austriad. Spectantur haud procul inde Valles, quæ vulgo L'Estraye & Vagny. La Mothe ad amnem situm est, qui mox in Mosam se exonerat. Vsitur ibi Territorium, cui nomen Le Sanctoy. Sunt & Comitatus quidam Imperij Salmensis, Kirchinganus & Blanckoburgius. Blanckenberg, Gallis Blanc-mont, oppidum est non magnum, sed pulcrum & amœnum. Spectatur ibi Castrum Vetus, spaciosum & magnificum, cui Palatium Novum Ducis, venusta structura insigne, est conjunctum. Incolæ Agriculturæ dant operam.
units.tr: The counties are distinguished by their title and dignity: the one called Vaudémont in the vernacular, five miles from Nancy; Chaligny on the right bank of the Moselle, half a league from Nancy; Amance, seven miles south of the city of the Mediomatrici; Almentia to those who write in Latin, formerly the chest and old chancery of Lorraine, as the archives produced by Rosier attest. Richecourt lies not far from the lake commonly called La Garde Lac, from which the river flows that mingles with the Murthe between the church of St Nicholas and the town of Rosières. Remiremont lies on the left bank of the Moselle, which forms an island there, in the most southerly part of Lorraine; here Aimoinus the monk mentions Rumaticum Castellum. Adromarici is read corruptly in Regino for Ad Romarici, meaning "to the riches". Remelsberg is called in German by Spiegel in his notes on Bartholin's Austrias. Nearby are seen the valleys commonly called L'Estraye and Vagny. La Mothe lies on a river which soon empties into the Meuse. There is a district there called Le Sanctoy. There are also some counties of the Empire of Salm, Kirchheim and Blankenburg. Blanckenberg, in French Blanc-mont, is a town, not large but pleasant and attractive. There is seen there an old castle, spacious and magnificent, to which the new palace of the Duke, notable for its elegant structure, is joined. The inhabitants devote themselves to agriculture.

units.la: Nomeny Baronatus est ad dextram Sellæ Fluvii, tribus milliaribus ab Urbe Mediomatricum, Meridiem versus.
units.tr: Nomeny is a barony on the right bank of the river Seille, three miles south of the city of the Mediomatrici.

units.la: Dominia sunt: Marsal ad Sellæ sinistram, haud procul Lacu Lindero, in quo Insula cum Opido Techemsul. Remerevilleo tribus Nanceio milliaribus. S. Bellemont, totidem Mora. Rambert-Ville ad dextram Mortanæ, haud procul Fonte, ubi Silva Mortanensis. Rosieres ad Murtam, prope Fanum D. Nicolai, duobus Nanceio milliaribus. Homburg grandiore Leuca ab opido Sarbruck, ad Amnem, qui mox Saravo concurrit. Mariemont ab Monte, cui opidum impolitum, uno ab Lindero Lacu milliari, meridiem versus. Sandaceurt medio fere itinere inter Vaudimontem & Mottam, in Agro, qui vulgo Sanctey.
units.tr: The lordships are: Marsal on the left bank of the Seille, not far from Lake Lindre, in which lies an island with the town of Techemsul; Remerevile, three miles from Nancy; S. Bellemont, as many from Mora; Rambertvillers on the right bank of the Mortagne, not far from the spring where the Forest of Mortagne is; Rosières on the Murthe, near the church of St Nicholas, two miles from Nancy; Homburg, a greater league from the town of Saarbrücken, on a river which soon joins the Saar; Mariemont, from the mountain, an unpolished town one mile south of Lake Lindre; Sandaucourt, about halfway between Vaudémont and Mothe, in the country commonly called Sanctey.

units.la: Mediomatricum Urbem, quæ cum Tullo aliisque Imperialis olim erat, in suam potestatem redegit Galliarum Monarcha, Henricus II. Præsidet Urbis Senatui missus ab Rege Magistratus. Tribunal autem Mediomatricis Urbis tres habet Episcopatus, sub Metropoli Trevirensi: Metensem, Tulensem, Verdunensem, sic ab Locis nuncupatos, in quis suæ singulis Sedes.
units.tr: The city of the Mediomatrici, which with Toul and others was formerly imperial, was brought under its own rule by Henry II, King of the French. A magistrate sent by the King presides over the city senate. The tribunal of the city of the Mediomatrici has three bishoprics under the metropolitan of Trier: Metz, Toul and Verdun, so named from their places, each of which has its own see.

units.la: Quæ vulgo Metz, & posterioris ævi Scriptoribus Mete, Gregorio autem Turonensi & aliis Urbs Metensis; Divodurum Mediomatricum Antiquitus appellatum. Itineraria Tabula: Divo, Durimedio. Matricorum; Lege, Divoduro Mediomatricorum, ut antea monui. Simpliciter Ἀπεδύρον Ptolemæo; Divodurum Tacito lib. IV & Antonino, qui eo varia ducit Itinera. Variorum Nugas de recentis Nominis ratione non libet adscribere. Sedes olim fuit Regni Lotaringiæ Lumprandus: Metensem Urbem, quæ potentissima in Regno Lotarij claret. De ea eleganter Petrus Divæus in Itinerario: Metensis Urbs in ampla sita est Planitie, quam Mosella in varios divisus alveos irrigat, & pars quidem eius muro ad Lævam lambit, pars & eodem subit, ut Civium usibus inserviat, atque sic divisum fluit ad inferiorem usque eorum ambitum, ubi recepto Sella, altero Flumine, qui dextram Urbis partem adiit, in unum denuo alveum colligitur. Sed Situ imprimis ipsius Urbis delectabamur: quum enim Agrum late circumjacentem planum habeat, ejus tamen Area paullum prominet, ut in eo Veterum rationem in condendis Urbibus agnoscas. Ad Summum siquidem Templum multis gradibus ascenditur: juxta quod Forum Rerum Venalium altiorem totius Area partem occupat, & ab eo undique versus Muros paullatim descendit, præcipuo tantum in una parte Clivo, ubi Vias duas Lapidibus stratas sic dispositas viaeas, ut altera per alterius domorum culmina excurrat. Templum D. Stephani nomen tenet, qui Civitatis est Patronus, pulcherrimum vero opus, si quod aliud toto hoc Itinere vidimus, & sua mole spectabile; quodque raro accidit, omni ex parte consummatum. Dicebatur, in eo fuisse Crucifixi ligneam Imaginem, totam Laminis aureis superinductam. Vidimus Labrum Porphyreticum rubes Coloris, magna capacitatis, Pedes x. longitudine excedens, in quo Lustrales Aquas adservant. Sunt & alia in hac eadem Urbe sumtuosa Templa, & multa erant in eius Suburbiis, inter quæ D. Arnolphi Basilica, Imp. Ludovici Pij Augusti, Karoli Filij & Filiarum aliquot Pipini Regis sepultura celebris. Omnia hæc absumpsit Belli rabies, sta-ut Suburbia ne Vestigium quidem nunc superfit, neque ultra Muros quidquam præter Campestria videas. De Bello Nupero consulendus Historiæ meæ Belgicæ Liber V. Cives Mediomatrices nominantur in Inscriptione, quæ extat Moguntiæ ad S. Albanum: D. M PRIMVLÆ. COMITILLÆ QVÆ. VIXIT. ANNIS. XX CIVES. MEDIOMATRIC A. MATERNIVS. NEMAVSVS STRATOR. COS. ET LVCIVS. LVCINVS. MENSOR. ÆRVMENTI. NVMER.
units.tr: The city which is called Metz in the vernacular, and Mete by writers of later times, but the city of the Metenses by Gregory of Tours and others, was formerly called Divodurum Mediomatricum. The Itinerary table has Divo, Durimedio; read Divoduro Mediomatricorum, as I noted earlier. Ptolemy simply has Apedyron; Tacitus in book IV and Antoninus, who runs several routes through it, have Divodurum. I do not care to record the trifles of various writers about the origin of the more recent name. Lumprandus was once the seat of the kingdom of Lorraine: he calls Metz "the most powerful city in the kingdom of Lothar". On it Pierre Divé writes elegantly in his Itinerary: The city of Metz lies on a broad plain, which the Moselle waters, divided into several channels; part of it licks the wall on the left, and part passes under it, so as to serve the citizens' needs, and thus divided it flows to the lower part of their circuit, where, having received the Seille, another river which reaches the right part of the city, it is gathered again into a single channel. But I was especially delighted by the site of the city itself: although it has a plain spreading widely around it, its own ground rises a little, so that in it you may recognise the method of the ancients in founding cities. For the great temple is reached by many steps; beside it the market for goods occupies the higher part of the whole area, and from there it gradually slopes down on every side towards the walls, with a steep slope only on one side, where two streets paved with stones are so arranged that one runs over the rooftops of the other's houses. The church bears the name of St Stephen, the patron of the city; it is a most beautiful work, if we have seen any other on this whole journey, and impressive in its size; and what rarely happens, it is finished in every part. It was said that in it there was a wooden image of the crucified Christ, entirely covered with gold plates. We saw a porphyry basin of deep red colour, of great capacity, exceeding ten feet in length, in which they keep the lustral waters. There are also other sumptuous churches in this same city, and there were many in its suburbs, among which the basilica of St Arnulf, the famous burial place of the Emperor Louis the Pious, Augustus, of his son Charles and of several daughters of King Pepin. The rage of war has destroyed all these, so that not even a trace of the suburbs now remains, and beyond the walls you see nothing but open country. Concerning the recent war, consult book V of my Belgian History. The citizens of the Mediomatrici are named in an inscription which stands at Mainz at St Alban's: "To the spirits of the dead: to Primula Comitilla, who lived twenty years. The citizens of the Mediomatrici: Maternius Nemausus, consular courier, and Lucius Lucinus, surveyor of the Aerumentine numerus."

units.la: Haud procul Metus, prope Pagum Iovy, in Mosella antiqui Aquæductus sunt Vestigia. De iis sic Divæus in Itinerario: In hoc Itinere Pagus est Iovy vulgo dictus inter Montium radices & Mosellam, ubi quantacumque est inter Montes utrosque, qui Ripas ambiunt, distantia, Aqua-ductum antiquitus fuisse, indicant eiusdem, quæ adhuc exstant; reliquiæ, Arcuum adhuc restant multi, sintque ex albo Lapide, in Laterum formam dissecto; & nonnulli quoque eiusdem operis in adversa ripa cernuntur. Incolæ affirmabant in eodem loco Fontem hodieque esse, quamvis hos Arcus (joints infecta) Ponti inservisse putantes, & ab hoc Pago in Montis ipsius juge minores alios Arcus fuisse dicebant, qui versus Urbem Metensem quæ uno hinc distat Miliari, excurrisse viderentur. Altitudo juxta Ripam Pedum est circiter LX: Unde conjicere est, quanta totius Operis moles fuerit, quantaque altitudo Arcuum, qui in ipso erant Fluminis alveo, quorum hodie mihi superesset. Referebant ydem Incolæ, superiosuperiorem Arcuum Partem planam omnino esse, cemento rubeo coloris induetam; & in eius medio Domunculam non ita multis adhuc annis adhuc fuisse, ab utraque parte patentem, quam nos partem Tecti fuisse, quae Tubum tegeret, suspicabamur.
units.tr: Not far from Metz, near the village of Jouy, on the Moselle, are the remains of an ancient aqueduct. Divé writes of them thus in his Itinerary: On this journey there is a village commonly called Jouy, between the foot of the mountains and the Moselle; wherever the distance between the two mountains that border the banks is as great as it is, the remains that still stand show that there was once an aqueduct; there are still many arches, made of white stone cut into the shape of bricks, and some of the same work can also be seen on the opposite bank. The inhabitants affirmed that the spring is still there at the same place, although they thought these arches had served as a bridge; and they said that from this village along the ridge of the mountain itself there were other smaller arches, which seemed to run towards the city of Metz, which is one mile from here. The height near the bank is about sixty feet; from which one may conjecture how great the mass of the whole work was, and how high the arches were that stood in the very bed of the river, of which none now remain to me. The same inhabitants reported that the upper part of the arches was entirely flat, covered with red cement; and that in its middle there was a little house, open on both sides, not many years ago, which we supposed was part of a roof covering the conduit.

units.la: Quae Toul vernacule, Tullum olim; Tullum, Leucorum opidum, Ptolemaeo: Tulligo Antonino, Itinere a Durocortoro Divodurum, & alibi: Tullium Itinerariae Tabulae.
units.tr: The place which in the vernacular is Toul, formerly Tullum: Tullum, a town of the Leuci, in Ptolemy; Tulligo in Antoninus, in the route from Durocortorum to Divodurum, and elsewhere; Tullium in the Itinerary table.

units.la: Quae denique Verdun, Latinis vocatur hodie Virdunum & Verdunum: Verdunum Antonino dicitur. Civitas Verdunensium in Notitia Provinciarum sub Belgica I. L'Evesche de Verdun. Leguntur autem tres Urbes, quas commemoravi, Comitatus etiam titulo & dignitate insignes. Postremi sane Ambianum diligentissime notarum reperi in vetustissima quadam Charta. Non gravabor ipsissima adscribere Verba. Contin. ea: Lector ad Sermonis, si quae est, scabritiem, crebraque quarundam Vocum Repetitiones. Ea sic se habet: Circuitus Comitatus Verdunensis Incipit enim a Leone Montis Falconis, & usque ad Pertusam Petram tendit. De Pertusa Petra usque ad Subtriam Villam, & inde usque ad Villam de Falley. Deinde usque ad Longmon, ubi Crima cadit in Caram lucium; & sicut Crima, sursum deurrit usque ad Naram, quae usque ad Ertezum tendit, & usque ad Banmadum, ubi cadit in Ornam. Et in longitudine superius usque ad Fontem, apud Ayoncourtem; & inde usque ad Quercum Sadei; & inde sulmontioni ad Fontem Lupimontis, & hinc ad Meaborn Fontem. Deinde Pertusadura; deinde usque Confancia, ubi cadit in Mosam Fluvium: deinde usque Warnoncourtem per Nuclearios iuxta Bussey & Warnoncourt: & deinde contra Vallem iuxta Longam Campum, recta Via ad Herisiam: & inde usque ad Fontem apud Sarindum ad Fontes es. Exhinc usque ad summam Asina & postea usque ad Vlmos. & inde usque ad locum, ubi Gronna fluit in Asinam: & inde per descensum Asinae iuxta Vitsnam: Et usque Viennam per Ferrieres, & per Momblaterullam, & per Contecourt per Castrum iuxta Quarnayum, & inde per Superiorem Partem Villae, quae dicitur Cuche; & inde recta via usque ad Iemas & inde usque ad Spanulphivillam: Et inde recta via usque ad Montem Falconis: & usque ad Leucem, a quo primum coepimus.
units.tr: Lastly, Verdun, which in Latin is today called Virdunum and Verdunum; Verdunum is the name used by Antoninus. The state of the Verdunenses is listed in the Notitia Provinciarum under Belgica I. L'Evesche de Verdun. Now the three cities I have mentioned are read of, and the counties too are distinguished by title and rank. Finally, I found Ambianum very carefully noted in a certain very old charter. I shall not hesitate to copy the very words. The content is as follows; the reader will forgive the roughness of the style and the frequent repetition of certain words: "The boundary of the county of Verdun begins at the Lion of Montfaucon and runs to the Pertuis Stone. From the Pertuis Stone to the village of Subtria, and from there to the village of Falley. Then to Longmont, where the Crima falls into the Caram Lucium; and as the Crima runs upward to the Nara, which extends to Ertezum, and to Banmad, where it falls into the Orne. And along its length upward to the spring at Ayoncourt; and from there to the Oak of Sadei; and from there to the spring of Lupimont, and from here to the spring of Meaborn. Then Pertusadura; then as far as Confancia, where it falls into the river Meuse; then to Warnoncourt through the Nuclearii near Bussey and Warnoncourt; and then opposite the valley near Longa Campus, by a straight road to Herisia; and from there to the spring at Sarindum, to the springs. From there to the top of the Asina, and afterwards to the Elms; and from there to the place where the Gronna flows into the Asina; and from there down the course of the Asina near Vitsna; and to Vienna through Ferrières, and through Momblaterulla, and through Contecourt past the castle near Quarnayum, and from there through the upper part of the village called Cuche; and from there by a straight road to Iemas, and from there to Spanulphivilla; and from there by a straight road to Montfaucon; and to the Leuca from which we first began."

units.la: Cum Lotharingia porro solet explicari Territorium Barrense, vulgo Le Barrois, quod extendit se ad Novum usque Castellum, Neuf Chastel. Metropolis illi Bar le Duc, sic cognominata ad differentiam aliarum, quae Bar sur Seyne, & Bar sur Aube. Minorum gentium Opida sunt La Motte, Ligny, Arq, & alia multa; ad Mosam se offerunt Commercy & Vaucouleur, quae partim Franciae, partim Barri.
units.tr: Next, Lorraine is commonly explained to include the Barrois, commonly called Le Barrois, which extends as far as Neufchâteau (Novum Castellum). Its metropolis is Bar-le-Duc, so named to distinguish it from the others, Bar-sur-Seine and Bar-sur-Aube. The towns of the lesser districts are La Motte, Ligny, Arques, and many others; on the Meuse lie Commercy and Vaucouleurs, which belong partly to France and partly to the Barrois.

units.la: CAPUT XLV.
units.tr: CAPUT XLV.

units.la: Benearnia.
units.tr: Benearnia.

units.la: HAEc de Ducatibus, Francorum potestate exemtis; sequuntur Principatus Benearnensis & Araufionensis.
units.tr: These are the duchies that were exempt from French rule. There follow the principalities of Béarn and Orange.

units.la: BENEARNENSIS, vulgo Pearn, semper separatus fuit ab Francorum Dictione, eodemque, quo Regnum ipsum, habitus jure, id est, optimo maximo: sed adeo ut Regno Franciae, quum Christianissimus Henricus, Navarrae Rex, Regni Franciae capeleret Sceptrum, iure Successorio. Unde Nomen nobilissimo Principatui, varie disputant Novi Scriptores; inque eo eruendo incredibile, quantum se torquent, ne dicam ineptiant. Memoriae produnt quidam Benearnum, tempore Regis Hlodovei, subditam fuisse Francis, inque dotem datam Galiswindae Brunechildis Reginae, quae Sigeberto nupta erat, Sorori; sub nomine Benearno. Nonnulli denominatos putant Benearnenses a Biarmis Septemtrionalibus Populis, quos, cum Gothus, aliisque, Hispaniam petentes ijs in locis sedes fixisse volunt. Sunt qui scribunt originem traxisse a Bernatibus, Helvetiae nunc Populis; ijsque Regionem ab Karolo Martello dono fuisse datam. Alij alia adferunt: quam vera, prudentiores judicent. Scimus nos Benearni (de quo postea, mentionem heri apud Antoninum in Itinere, quod ad illud opidum ducit Caesar-Augusta ex Hispania Citeriore. Legitur etiam in Notitia Provinciarum Galliae sub Aquitania Tertia Novempopulania, Civitas Benearnensium, id est Benaanum. A Benearno si quis Totii Tractui nomen inditum censeat, fortean non errarit: sed Benearnum unde dictum, nescire me fateor. Sita est Benearnia ad radices Pyrenæorum Montium, inter Bigerronum, Baionensium, aliorumque Contnalium Populorum Territoria & Agros: in duas divisa Partes; quarum una, Montibus obsita, Eloronum habet Opidum; altera, ab Vallibus Locisque planioribus occupata, Lascariensem Civitatem, Regioni cum in Montibus, tum in Planicie, mirandus est genius & stupenda indoles: vix Opidum ibi, vix Pagus, cui non aliquid singulare. Potior Pars Millo, Lino, Canabi (quarum rerum maximam Incolæ exercent Mercaturam) abundat: Frumento etiam hic ibi beata: Pascuis valde dives, Pecoreque: unde incredibilis Butyri Caseique copia: Capris supra modum scatet; quæ hic nullo labore nutriuntur in Rupibus, & Ericetis, citra Fructuum teneriorumque Arborum perniciem & detrimentum. Nec Vina desunt. Generosum valde, nulliqúe Francico bonitate sua cedens, producit Territorium, quod vulgo Iurancon. Balnea habet passim Thermasque, omnium, quæ in Europa, præstantissimas. De Aquis Benearnensibus Plinius lib. xxi. nat. hist. cap. xi: Emicant, inquit, benigne, passimque in plurimis terris alibi frigida, alibi calida, alibi tuntta, sicut in Tarbellis, Aquitanica Gente, & in Pyrenaeis Montibus, tenui intervallo discernente: Ad quæ Nobilis. Vir Iosephus Scaliger: Qui Aquas Benearnensis Saltus in Pyrenaeis viderunt & biberunt, non dubitabunt Plinium de illis sensisse. Incolæ elatos habent animos: strenui sunt & fortes; Armorum periti candidi proculque ab omni fuco; adfabiles & ad omnem humanitatem propensissimi; cauti interim subtilesque lingua sua cloquentes: Libertatis amantes, Magnis gaudent Immunitatibus & Privilegiis. Ad Doctrinas eos varias capessendum non ineptos docent Magni Viri, qui inde oriundi. Omnes Nobilitatem affectant: qui reipsa nobiles, contendunt magis, ut bene fortiterque agant, quam ut splendide molliterque vestiantur. Inter ipsos primum obtinent locum illustres Familiæ, quas ex Cantabris ajunt ortas, Grammontia & Lussea. Baronatus clarent dignitate Mirens, Iadre, Monens, S. Celombe, Ffganalabagne, Coderch, Navailes, Castelnau, Maseres, Luz, Suz, & aliæ.
units.tr: Béarn, commonly called Pearn, was always separate from the rule of the French. It was held under the same law as the kingdom itself, that is, the best and greatest law. But this was so only until Henry the most Christian King, King of Navarre, took up the scepter of the kingdom of France by right of succession, and so was united to the kingdom of France. Recent writers dispute variously where the name of this noble principality comes from, and they twist themselves in incredible knots over it, not to say talk nonsense. Some report that Béarn was subject to the Franks in the time of King Clovis and was given as a dowry to Galswintha, sister of Brunhilda the queen, who was married to Sigebert, under the name Béarn. Some think the people of Béarn were named after the Northern Biarmi, whom they say the Goths and others, on their way to Spain, settled in those places. Some write that the name came from the Bernates, now a people of Switzerland, and that the region was given to them as a gift by Charles Martel. Others bring other explanations; the wiser sort may judge which is true. We know that Benearnum (of which more later) is mentioned in Antoninus's Itinerary, the road that leads from Caesar-Augusta in Hispania Citerior to that town. It is also read in the Notitia of the Provinces of Gaul, under Aquitania Tertia, Novempopulania, the civitas of the Benearnenses, that is, Benaanum. If anyone thinks the name Béarn was given to the whole tract from the town, he may perhaps not be wrong; but I confess I do not know where the name Benearnum itself came from. Benearnia lies at the foot of the Pyrenees, between the territories and fields of the Bigerrones, the Bayonnese, and other neighbouring peoples. It is divided into two parts: one, covered with mountains, has the town of Oloron; the other, occupied by valleys and flatter places, has the city of Lescar. The character and natural disposition of the region, both in the mountains and on the plain, is remarkable and astonishing: there is hardly a town or village that does not have something singular about it. The greater part abounds in millet, flax and hemp (the inhabitants carry on a very large trade in these goods). Here the land is also rich in wheat; it is very well supplied with pasture and cattle, whence there is an incredible abundance of butter and cheese. It swarms beyond measure with goats, which are kept here without any labour on the rocks and heaths, without harm or loss to the fruit and to young trees. Nor is wine lacking. The territory called commonly Jurançon produces a very fine wine, which yields to no French wine in quality. It has baths and hot springs everywhere, among the most excellent in all Europe. Pliny, in book 21 of the Natural History, chapter 11, writes of the waters of Béarn: "They spring up kindly and in many lands everywhere, some cold, some warm, some lukewarm, as in the Tarbelli, a people of Aquitaine, and in the Pyrenees, separated by a short interval." On these words the noble man Joseph Scaliger remarks: "Those who have seen and drunk the waters of the Béarnese wood in the Pyrenees will not doubt that Pliny thought of them." The inhabitants have lofty spirits; they are vigorous and brave, skilled in arms, candid and far from all deceit; affable and most inclined to every kind of courtesy; yet cautious and subtle, eloquent in their own tongue. They love liberty and enjoy great immunities and privileges. Great men born there teach that they are not unfit to take up various studies. All aspire to nobility; those who are noble in fact strive more to act bravely and well than to dress splendidly and softly. Among themselves the first place is held by the illustrious families, which they say came from the Cantabri, Grammont and Lusse. The baronies that are distinguished in rank are Mirepoix, Ladre, Montaner, Sainte-Colombe, Ferrière-Labastide, Coderc, Navailles, Castelnau, Maserès, Luz, Soule, and others.

units.la: Sedes hic olim suæ fuerunt Benearnensibus, Eloronensibus & aliis. Civitatem Benearnensium nominat Notitia Provinciarum sub Aquitania tertia Novempopulania, vel Octava Viennensi; hodie Le Pais de Bearn. Scribitur ibidem & Civitas Eloronensis nunc, L'Evesché d'Oleron en Bearn. Precianos etiam, quos cum aliis Aquitaniae Populis recensset Cæsar, nonnulli, ut Vigenereus habet, in suis ad Cæsarem Adnotationibus, esse volunt, ubi hodie Bearn; alij, ubi Precins; quidam, quo loco Baiona.
units.tr: Here the Benearnenses, Oloronenses and others once had their seats. The Notitia of the Provinces, under Aquitania Tertia, Novempopulania, or the Eighth Viennensis, names the civitas Benearnensium; today it is Le Pais de Bearn. The same work also writes the civitas Eloronensis, now L'Evesché d'Oleron en Bearn. Some, as Vigenère has it in his notes on Caesar, hold that the Precianos, whom Caesar counts among the other peoples of Aquitaine, were where Béarn is today; others, where Precins is; some, at the place where Bayonne is.

units.la: Principum Benearnensium series hæc traditur: Gaston Guilelmi Moncada, Hispani Filius, Benearnensium Princeps primus: Uxore ducta Martha, Filia & Heredee unica Equitis Bigerronum Comitis Ilia, Bigerronum Comitatum Dotalibus suis adquisivit. Duos sacrum illi Filios. Margareta nupta Rogerio Bernardo, Comiti Foxensi, Rogerii Bernardi & Margaritae Narbonensis Filio. Hanc Patri succedenti Principatum, Dominiumque & Domos Benearnensis, Bigorra & Foxij conjunxit ... contracta Comiti Armagnacensi. Gaston II Princeps Benearniae III, Comes Foxi, & Bigorrae. Uxor Joanna Lauretana Francia, Ludovicensis Comitis Filia. | Brunisse, Comitis Ellae Comitis Petrocoriorum. | Constantia Comitis Ant. Levyi. Mitepolis Dynastae. | Joanna, Petro Aragonio in matrimonium data. Gaston III, Princeps Benearniae IV uxorem habuit Eleonoram Comagenensem, Comitis Convenarum Filiam. | Rogerius Bernardus, Moncada Dynastia, Vicecomes Castelloboni, vel Castelbaani. Gaston IV Princeps Benearniae V, laudatus plurimum ab Froissardo. Uxor illi Agnes, Caroli Navarrae Regis Soror. Gaston, quem Pater suis manibus interfecit. Mattheum, Vicecomes Castelloboni, Gastonis IV Successor, Princeps Benearniae VI. Uxor Joanna Aragonia, &c. | Joanna defuncta Masculis, Fratri Mathaei successit, Princeps Benearniae VII. Uxor Antonio Beaumont, Capitalis Buchii. Joannes, Princeps Benearniae VIII, Comes Foxi & Bigorrae, Moncadae Dominus. Duos habuit Uxores, Mariam Navarrae, ... Joannem Albretanum. | Gaston Capitalis Buchius, Francisci Nomine immicus, Candaleorum Comitum Progenitor, Uxor Joanna, Philippi Arielci Filia. | Archambaudus Nouilleri Dynastia. | Petrus Episcopus Ebicensis, postea Cardinalis & Legatus, qui Collegium Tolosae erexit. Gaston V, Princeps Benearniae VIII, Comes Foxi, &c. Uxor Eleonora, Joannis Navarrae Regis Filia: quae vidua, post Patrem excessum, Retinuit potuit. Gaston VI, Princeps Benearniae X, Comes Foxi, Bigorrae Vicina, &c. Obiit ante Patrem, Idemque Regnum Navarrae non accepit. Uxor illi Magdalena Caroli VII Galliarum Regis Filia. | Joannes Foxius, Vicecomes Narbonensis, Uxor Maria, Caroli Valesii, Ducis Andegavensis Filia. | Alii utrumque lexus. Franciscus Joannes, Rex Navarrae XXIV, A iis Eleonorae Successor, Princeps Benearniae X, Comes Foxi, &c. Obiit 1483. Sepultus in Lascarensi oppido. | Catharina Regina Navarrae XXV, Princeps Benearniae XIII, Comes Foxi, &c. Nupta Joanni Alani Magni Filio Dynastae Albretano, eique Regnum in dotem attulit. Is, sumtis contra Ludovicum XII, pro Ludovico XII, Francorum Rege, Armis, ab eo proscriptus universam Navarram Ditionem amisit, occupatam ab Ferdinando Catholico, Hispaniarum Regi. | Gaston, Comes Foxi, Dux Nemuri, Acie cecidit contra Iulium II, Pontificem Maximum. Uxor Maria Caroli I Ducis Borbonii Filia, Imperatrix. | Germana, nupta Ferdinando Regi Aragoniae, inde Ferdinando Regi Calabriae. Henricus Albretanus, Rex Navarrae XXVI, Princeps Benearniae XIII, Comes Foxi, &c. Obiit 1517. Uxor Margareta Valesia, Caroli Alenconii Vidua. | Carolus extinctus ad Neapolim, extra matrimonium. | Filii aliquot. Joanna Albretana Regina Navarrae XXVII, Princeps Benearniae XIIII, Comes Foxi, &c. Desponsata Guilelmo Clivio Duci, nuptiis Pontificis Maximi dispensatione Antonio Borbonio, Vendomae Duci, qui socero successit in Regno. Obiit Parisiis 1572, ætatis suae XLIII, diebus aliquot ante Filii nuptias. Henricus Borbonius, Galliarum Monarcha (Successor Henrici III) Navarrae Rex XXVIII, Princeps Benearniae XV, Comes Foxi, &c. | Catharina.
units.tr: The following series of the Princes of Béarn is handed down: Gaston, son of Guilelmus Moncada, a Spaniard, the first Prince of Béarn. Having married Martha, the only daughter and heiress of the knight Ilia, Count of Bigorre, he acquired the county of Bigorre by her dowry. He had two sons. Margaret, married to Roger Bernard, Count of Foix, son of Roger Bernard and Margaret of Narbonne. She, succeeding her father, joined the principality, the dominion and the houses of Béarn, Bigorre and Foix ... married to the Count of Armagnac. Gaston II, Prince of Béarn III, Count of Foix and Bigorre. Wife Joanna of Laurete, daughter of Louis, Count of France. | Brunissa, of the Count of Ella, Count of Périgord. | Constance, of Count Anthony Levis, lord of Mirepoix. | Joanna, given in marriage to Peter of Aragon. Gaston III, Prince of Béarn IV, had as wife Eleanor of Comminges, daughter of the Count of Convenes. | Roger Bernard, lord of Moncada, Viscount of Castelbon, or Castelbaano. Gaston IV, Prince of Béarn V, very much praised by Froissart. His wife was Agnes, sister of Charles, King of Navarre. Gaston, whom his father killed with his own hands. Matthew, Viscount of Castelbon, successor of Gaston IV, Prince of Béarn VI. Wife Joanna of Aragon, etc. | Joanna, who died without male heirs, succeeded the brother of Matthew, Prince of Béarn VII. Wife to Anthony of Beaumont, captain of Buch. John, Prince of Béarn VIII, Count of Foix and Bigorre, lord of Moncada. He had two wives, Mary of Navarre, ... John of Albret. | Gaston, captain of Buch, an enemy of the name of Francis, progenitor of the Counts of Candale; wife Joanna, daughter of Philip of Arielci. | Archambaud, lord of Nouilleres. | Peter, Bishop of Ebicium, afterwards Cardinal and Legate, who founded the college at Toulouse. Gaston V, Prince of Béarn VIII, Count of Foix, etc. Wife Eleanor, daughter of John, King of Navarre; she, a widow after her father's death, was able to retain ... Gaston VI, Prince of Béarn X, Count of Foix, neighbour of Bigorre, etc. He died before his father, and did not receive the kingdom of Navarre. His wife Magdalen, daughter of Charles VII, King of the French. | John of Foix, Viscount of Narbonne, wife Mary, daughter of Charles of Valois, Duke of Angoulême. | Others of both sexes. Francis John, King of Navarre XXIV, successor of Eleanor by them, Prince of Béarn X, Count of Foix, etc. He died in 1483, buried in the town of Lescar. | Catherine, Queen of Navarre XXV, Princess of Béarn XIII, Countess of Foix, etc. Married to John of Albret, son of Alain the Great, lord of Albret, to whom she brought the kingdom as dowry. He, taking up arms against Louis XII, King of the French, was proscribed by him and lost all his dominion of Navarre, which was occupied by Ferdinand the Catholic, King of Spain. | Gaston, Count of Foix, Duke of Nemours, fell in battle against Julius II, the Supreme Pontiff. Wife Mary, daughter of Charles I, Duke of Bourbon, Empress. | Germaine, married to Ferdinand, King of Aragon, then to Ferdinand, King of Calabria. Henry of Albret, King of Navarre XXVI, Prince of Béarn XIII, Count of Foix, etc. Died 1517. Wife Margaret of Valois, widow of Charles of Alençon. | Charles, died at Naples, outside marriage. | Several sons. Joanna of Albret, Queen of Navarre XXVII, Princess of Béarn XIV, Countess of Foix, etc. Betrothed to William, Duke of Cleves; with the Supreme Pontiff's dispensation married to Anthony of Bourbon, Duke of Vendôme, who succeeded his father-in-law in the kingdom. She died at Paris in 1572, aged 43, a few days before her son's marriage. Henry of Bourbon, Monarch of the French (successor of Henry III), King of Navarre XXVIII, Prince of Béarn XV, Count of Foix, etc. | Catherine.

units.la: Metropolis porro Benearniae est Castrum Palum: sic Docti, Latine scribentes, vocant, quod vulgo Pau. Sedes hic Principum: fastuosumque Ædificium ab Henrico Albretano Navarrae Rege, Christianissimi Regis Henrici IV Avo Materno, extructum. Tribunal ibidem Benearnense, ab eodem Henrico institutum, & Curia totius Principatus suprema, ubi Controversiæ omnes dijudicantur secundum Regionis Leges & Consuetudines.
units.tr: The metropolis of Béarn is Castrum Palum, as learned writers who write in Latin call it, or Pau as the common people say. It is the seat of the princes, and a splendid building erected by Henry of Albret, King of Navarre, maternal grandfather of Henry IV, the Most Christian King. Here too is the Béarn tribunal, established by the same Henry, the supreme court of the whole principality, where all disputes are decided according to the laws and customs of the region.

units.la: Sub eo Tribunali Episcopatus sunt duo, Auscorum Metropoli suffraganei, Lascariensi & Oloronensis. Lascariensis dictus ab Opido, quod Indigenis Lescar, Domicilium quondam Principum, qui postea Castrum-Palum ei praetulerunt. In Lascariensi Civitate sepultus est Franciscus Phoebus, Princeps Benearniæ xı, qui Eleonorae Aviae in Regno Navarrae fuit Successor. Oloronensis appellatus ab eo, quod vernacule oleron, in fastigio positum Montis: Iluro vocatur apud Antoninum Itinere, quod Cæsar Augusta ducit Benearnum, ubi quidam Codices Nurone, corruptius, pro Ilurone. Olorensis Episcopi meminit Concilium Aurelianum v, fortean pro Oloronensi. Olarionenses Lepusculi sunt apud Sidonium Apollinarem lib. viii Epist. vi. Oleronum hoc Αυγδυνὸν esse Convenarum apud Ptolemaeum censet Villanovanus: sed Lugdunum illud in ruinis jacere, exque eius reliquiis Fanum S. Bertrandi esse exstructum, docui cap. xxxviii: ubi de Vasconia.
units.tr: Under this tribunal there are two bishoprics, suffragans of the metropolitan see of Auch: Lascariensis & Oloronensis. Lascariensis is named from the town which the natives call Lescar, once the residence of the princes, who afterwards preferred Castrum-Palum to it. Francis Phoebus, Prince of Béarn, who succeeded his grandmother Eleanor in the kingdom of Navarre, was buried in the city of Lascariensis. Oloronensis is named from the fact that, in the vernacular, oleron means a place set on the summit of a mountain. Antoninus in his Itinerary, the road that leads from Caesaraugusta to Benearnum, calls it Iluro; some manuscripts read the more corrupt Nurone for Ilurone. The Council of Orléans (the fifth) mentions a bishop of Olorum, perhaps meaning Oloron. The Olarionenses are hares in Sidonius Apollinaris, Book 8, Letter 6. Villanovanus thinks that Oleronum is the Augdunum [Αυγδυνὸν] of the Convenae in Ptolemy; but I have shown, in chapter 38, where I speak of Gascony, that that Lugdunum lies in ruins, and that the shrine of St Bertrand was built from its remains.

units.la: Sunt & alia minorum gentium Opida Orthes, ad Fluvium Gaven, antiqua Comitatum Foxij, Benearniæque Principum Sedes. Benearnum (unde Principatui nomen, ut antea monui) Antonino dici, idque certissimum esse, notat ad Ausonium V. Nobilissimum Iosephus Scaliger lib. ii. cap. vii. Fenearni mentio apud Gregorium Turonensem lib. ix: De Civitatibus, inquit, hoc est, Burdegala, Lemovica, Cadurco, Renarno & Begorra, quas Gaulesuindam, Germanam Domina Brunichildis, tam in Dote, quam in Morgonegiba, hoc est matutinali dono in Franciam venientem, certum est adquisisse, & quæ sequuntur. Morlaas, Officina A. A. A. F. F. quondam consecrata. Navarrins (unde Navarra nomen videtur natum) Opidum ad Pyrenæorum Pedem, probe munitum, iussu mandatuque cum aliorum, tum Henrici I Navarrae Regis. Serrance in Monte situm est, Galliae versus Hispanias postremum. Sabaulada Abbatia est.
units.tr: There are also other towns of lesser peoples: Orthes, on the river Gave, an ancient seat of the county of Foix and of the princes of Béarn. That Benearnum (from which the principality takes its name, as I said earlier) is called so by Antoninus, and that this is quite certain, Joseph Scaliger notes in his commentary on Ausonius, Book 5, and most nobly in Book 2, chapter 7. There is mention of Fenearnum in Gregory of Tours, Book 9: De Civitatibus, he says, that is, Bordeaux, Limoges, Cahors, Renarnum and Begorra, which it is certain Gaelsuinda, the sister of Lady Brunichild, acquired, both in her dowry and in the morning gift (morgengabe) she brought into France, and what follows. Morlaas, once the workshop of A. A. A. F. F. Navarrins (from which the name Navarre seems to have arisen), a town at the foot of the Pyrenees, well fortified, by command and order of both others and of Henry I, King of Navarre. Serrance lies on a mountain, the last place in Gaul on the way to Spain. Sabaulada is an abbey.

units.la: CAPUT XLVI
units.tr: CHAPTER XLVI

units.la: Araufio.
units.tr: Arausio.

units.la: ARAVSICENSI PRINCIPATVI nomen ab Metropoli Aransione, cujus meminerunt Veteres Scriptores, uti paullo post videbimus. Vulgo La Principauté d'Orange. Innexus undique jacet Avenionensi Comitatui; fluente illi ad Occidentaliora Rodano: forma fere semilunari, exurgentibus utrimque versus Septemtrionem Cornibus. Terra variarum Rerum ferax, fluminibus irrigatur, quæ vulgo Maine, Sorgue, Ouenze, & aliis, cum Rodano se miscentibus.
units.tr: THE PRINCIPALITY OF ARAUSIO takes its name from its metropolis Aransio, which ancient writers mention, as we shall see shortly. Commonly it is called La Principauté d'Orange. It lies enclosed on all sides by the County of Avignon, with the Rhône flowing past it to the west. Its shape is nearly semilunar, with horns rising toward the north on either side. The land is fertile in many things and is watered by rivers, commonly called Maine, Sorgue, Ouenze, and others, which mingle with the Rhône.

units.la: Habitarunt hic olim & Cavares Populi, de quibus cap. xlii; Nam latius Cavarum nomen accipitur quibusdam Geographis, præcipue Straboni: & Araufici, quorum Civitas, id est Ager vel Pagus, nominatur in Notitia Provinciarum sub Viennensi Prima, L'Evesché d'Aurange.
units.tr: The Cavares peoples also lived here formerly, of whom see chapter 42. For some geographers, especially Strabo, the name Cavarum is taken more broadly. The Araufici, whose civitas (that is, district or territory) is named in the Notitia Provinciarum under Vienne Prima, are L'Evesché d'Aurange.

units.la: Metropolis Francis dicitur Aurange vel Orange: Indigenis Aurage; Vulgo Latinorum incepto Arausio & Auraica; Doctioribus Arausio Cavarum; Ἀραυσίων Ptolemaeo, apud quem vitiosius in quibusdam Libris Ἀραυσίων: Arausio apud Plinium lib. iii. cap. iv & Pomponium Melam lib. ii: qui Secundanorum cognominant. Sic in Antiquo Lapide legitur: COL. ARAVSIO SECVNDANORVM. COH. XXXII. VOLVNT. Arausio Civitas Veteri Itinerario, quod Burdigala ducit Hierosolymas: Arausica Civitas Concilij Arausicani ii Canone i, Vluardo xvi Kalendas Novembr. Bedæ & Adoni vi Kalend. Iunij, Sigeberto de Viris Illustrib. cap. lxxiii. Arausionensi Vrbs Sidonio lib. vi. Epist. xii. Arausio Episcopatu claret & Academia, quamvis non admodum nobili. Magna ibi Antiquitatum Vestigia, cum aliarum, tum Theatri & Arcus Triumphalis in Porta, per quam in Lugdunensium Agros patet iter. Arcui Equestres Pugnæ spectantur insculptæ, Spectatores mirum in modum delectantes. Sunt & minoris rei opida Martignan, Cap de Rouffe, Courthezon, Caussans, S. André de Ramieres, Prabion, & alia. Darbou cum nonnullo Territorio extra formam semilunarem jacet; Occidentaliori obvorsum Cornui.
units.tr: The metropolis is called in French Aurange or Orange, by its inhabitants Aurage, and in common Latin usage from the beginning Arausio and Auraica; by the more learned Arausio Cavarum. Ptolemy calls it Arausion [Ἀραυσίων], which in some books is written more faultily as Arausion [Ἀραυσίων]. Arausio appears in Pliny, book 3, chapter 4, and in Pomponius Mela, book 2, who give it the surname of the Secundani. So an ancient stone reads: COL. ARAVSIO SECVNDANORVM. COH. XXXII. VOLVNT. (the colony of Arausio of the Secundani; the thirty-second cohort of volunteers). The old Itinerary, which leads from Burdigala to Jerusalem, calls it Arausio Civitas; the first canon of the Council of Orange calls it Arausica Civitas; Usuard (16 days before the Kalends of November), Bede and Ado (6 days before the Kalends of June), and Sigebert in De Viris Illustribus, chapter 73, do likewise. Sidonius, book 6, letter 12, calls it Arausionensi Vrbs. Arausio is distinguished by its episcopal see and its academy, though the latter is not very noble. There are many traces of antiquity there, both of other buildings and of the theatre and of the triumphal arch at the gate through which the road leads into the fields of the Lugdunenses. On the arch are carved equestrian battle scenes, which delight the onlookers greatly. There are also smaller towns, Martignan, Cap de Rouffe, Courthezon, Caussans, S. André de Ramieres, Prabion, and others. Darbou, with some territory, lies outside the semilunar shape, turned toward the western horn.

units.la: Habet hic Principatus hodie Proprium Dynastam ex Gente Illustrissima Nassavia. fawin. Nuperi Arausionis Principes cum ex Cabillonensi, tum ex Nassavio Stemmate orti sic se habent:
units.tr: Today this principality has its own lord from the most illustrious house of Nassau. The recent princes of Orange, descended both from the Chalon and from the Nassau pedigree, stand thus:

units.la: Stemma Cabillonense:
units.tr: Chalon pedigree:

units.la: Ioannes Cabillonensis, Ludovici Pauci unicus heres, ducta Maria Baufia, Reinoldi Bauffi Arausionum Principis Filia & Heres, Primogenitus familiae tantum ... Ludovicus Cabillonensis, Arausionum Princeps, Uxores illi fuerunt Ioanna Henrici ultimi Comitis Mompelgardi Filia, & Eleonora Armagnaca Pater ea. Mompelgardensis. Armagnaca. Gulielmus Cabillonensis, Arausionum Princeps, cui Uxor fuit Katharina Sorori Francisci Comitis Burgundiae. Ioannes Cabillonensis, Arausionum Princeps, Uxores eius, I Ioanna Caroli Ducis Borbonij Filia, Bertha i ei Philiberta, Antonij Leuceburgij Filia, Charnij Comes, ex qua nati. Ludovicus Cabillonensis, qui cum Katerina Burgundo bello contra Helvetios periit. Hugonis Cabillonensis, Carolo Burgundo bello contra Helvetios periit. Obiit anno 1534. Ioannes Cabillonensis Arausionum Princeps, Parens Ioannis, Petri, Nicolai Pedrinae ... Obiit anno 1523, aetatis XXVIII. Claudia Cabillonensis, Arausionum Princeps, omnium Fortunatum Fratris Heres, Nupta Henrico Nassavio. Renatus Nassavius Arausionum Princeps.
units.tr: John of Chalon, sole heir of Louis Pauc, married Maria of Baux, daughter and heir of Raimbaut of Baux, Prince of Orange; the eldest of the family only ... Louis of Chalon, Prince of Orange, whose wives were Joanna, daughter of Henry, the last Count of Montbéliard, and Eleanor of Armagnac, the father of that Montbéliard and Armagnac line. William of Chalon, Prince of Orange, whose wife was Catherine, sister of Francis, Count of Burgundy. John of Chalon, Prince of Orange, whose wives were, first, Joanna, daughter of Charles, Duke of Bourbon; second, Bertha; third, Philiberta, daughter of Antoine de Luxembourg, Count of Charny; from whom were born ... Louis of Chalon, who perished with Charles the Bold in the war against the Swiss. Hugh of Chalon, who perished in the war against the Swiss. He died in 1534. John of Chalon, Prince of Orange, father of John, Peter, Nicholas (Pedrina) ... He died in 1523, aged 28. Claudia of Chalon, Princess of Orange, heir of her brother Fortunatus, all of whose property she inherited, married Henry of Nassau. René of Nassau, Prince of Orange.

units.la: Stemma Nassavium.
units.tr: Nassau pedigree.

units.la: Ioannes Iunior Comes Nassavius, Dillenburgi, Viandae, Bredae, &c. Dominus. Uxor Elisabetha, Henrici Landgravii Hassiae, & Annae Comitatus Catzenelnbogensis Heredis Filia. Henricus Comes Nassavius, Dillenburgensis, Bergensis, Ludovicus, Engelbertus, Ioannes, Vilhelmus, Ottonis, &c. Obiit anno 1562. Uxor illi Claudia, Ioanna Cabillonensis, Principis Arausionum, Filia. Gulielmus Senior, Dives cognominatur, Comes Nassavius, Catzenelnbogensis, &c. Obiit anno 1559. Duas habuit Uxores: I Valpurgim Egmontanam, Petri, et Iulianam, Bothonis Comitis Stolbergensis Filiam, matrem ex ipso factam ut Liberorum, in quis Primogenitus. Renatus Comes Nassavius & Catzenelnbogensis, Viandae & Ducatus Domnus, Eques Auream Vellerum, ab Philiberto Arausionis adoptatus & Arausionum Princeps nominatus. Obiit in Gallia anno 1544. Gulielmus Arausionum Princeps, Comes Nassavius, &c. Heros rebus praeclare domi militiaque gestis nobilissimus. Obiit consulis ab summo Stolbergensi Delphis anno 1584, quarto Idus Iunii Quatuor ordine duxit Uxores quarum I Annae, Mariannae Egmondanae, Comitis Buraei, Filiae & Heredis, ex quibus natus. Maria Nassavia, Philippo Comitis Hohenloi Coniux. Katerina Gustava Nassavia, Arausionum Princeps, Comes Burae, Helleni, &c. Dominus.
units.tr: John the Younger, Count of Nassau, lord of Dillenburg, Vianden, Breda, etc. His wife was Elizabeth, daughter of Henry, Landgrave of Hesse, and of Anna, heiress of the County of Katzenelnbogen. Henry, Count of Nassau, of Dillenburg and Berg; Louis, Engelbert, John, William, Otto, etc. He died in 1562. His wife was Claudia, daughter of John of Chalon, Prince of Orange. William the Elder, called the Rich, Count of Nassau, Katzenelnbogen, etc. He died in 1559. He had two wives: first, Walpurga of Egmont, daughter of Peter; second, Juliana, daughter of Botho, Count of Stolberg, by whom he had children, of whom the eldest was the first. René, Count of Nassau and Katzenelnbogen, lord of Vianden and of the Duchy, knight of the Golden Fleece, adopted by Philibert of Orange and named Prince of Orange. He died in France in 1544. William, Prince of Orange, Count of Nassau, etc., most noble hero, renowned for deeds done at home and in war. He died at Delft in 1584, on the fourth of the Ides of June, by a wound from an assassin of the Stolberg... He married four wives in succession; the first was Anna, Mariana of Egmont, daughter and heiress of the Count of Buren, by whom he had children. Maria of Nassau, wife of Philip, Count of Hohenlohe. Catherine Gustava of Nassau, Princess of Orange, Countess of Buren, Hellen, etc., lady.

units.la: TANTVM de Principatibus, qui licet in Francia, Francorum tamen Imperium non agnoscunt: explicandi succedunt eiusdem generis Comitatus, Burgundia & XXX Olim.
units.tr: So much for the principalities which, although they lie in France, do not acknowledge the rule of the Franks. There follow the counties of the same kind: Burgundy and Thirty Olim.

units.la: Unde Nomen Burgundiae, dictum cap. XLI, ubi docui Regnum olim circa annum cIↃ xxxv bipartitum abiisse in Ducatum & Comitatum: quorum ille versus Occidentem, Burgundia Inferior & Regia: hic, ad Orientem, Inferior & Imperialis:
units.tr: The name Burgundy was explained in chapter XLI, where I showed that the kingdom, about the year 1035, was divided into a duchy and a county. The duchy lay to the west and was called Lower and Royal Burgundy; the county lay to the east and was called Lower and Imperial.

units.la: BVRGVNDIAE COMITATVS Francis audit Franche Comté, id est, Liber Comitatus. Provincia namque plane sub suo est Comite; ab omnibus, ut aiunt, Tributis & Exactionibus libera. Feudum est Imperij, sub protectione Bernensium Helvetiorum. Conregionales illi sunt ad Septemtrionem Lotaringa Superiorque Germania; ad Occidentem Burgundiae Ducatus; qua Oriens est, occurrunt Helvetij; qua Meridies, Allobroges & Segusiani. Longitudo xc, latitudo lx est milliarium. Regio Silvis, Montibus, Vallibus gratissima vicissitudine spectatur variata: uberis Agri, qui Pecori alendo, faciendae Sementi, Arboribus serendis, Vinetis Vini laudatissimi sustollendis commodissimus. Variis generis videre est ibi Animalia magnaque lumentorum & Pecudum copiam. Gravellenses Equos Gradarios, Caque itidem tractus ferocissimos probant omnes. Summa est ubique Tritici, Siligi-
units.tr: The County of Burgundy is called in French Franche Comté, that is, Free County. The province is entirely under its own count and, as they say, free of all tributes and exactions. It is a fief of the Empire, under the protection of the Bernese Swiss. Its neighbours are: to the north, Lorraine and Upper Germany; to the west, the Duchy of Burgundy; to the east, the Swiss; to the south, the Allobroges and the Segusiani. It is ninety miles long and sixty miles broad. The region, full of woods, mountains and valleys, presents a most pleasing variety of scenery. Its fields are fertile and very suitable for feeding cattle, for sowing grain, for planting trees, and for raising vineyards of most praised wine. Many kinds of animals are to be seen there, and a great store of draught animals and livestock. Everyone commends the horses of Gray for their pace, and likewise the very spirited breed of that district. Wheat, rye, ...
