units.la: Siliginis, Hordei, Avenæ Fabarum, Milij, aliorumque Leguminum fertilitas. Arborum haud minor fœcunditas. Ager pascuum, præterim qua umbilicus est & Regionis meditullium, Colles habet præstantissimorum, primaque nobilitatis Vinorum feraces. Prætereunt reliquis bonita e, quæ colliguntur ad Arbosium, Vadam, Grimonium Arcem, Pontebrium, Losthanum, Castrum Karois, Villephanum, Gyum, Mo cllum: quorum quædam, cum primis Arbosium natus in suo Territorio suam etiam Nomenclaturam communicant. Quod prope Gyum natentur cum Optimis consuevit certare; vehi solitum in Germaniam, non quidem publicitus distrahendum, sed distribuendum Magnatibus: Apud Arbosiano & Vadanos Vata Vinaria sunt adeo magna, ut Domos altitudine videantur æquare. Prope Regiam Veterum Burgundiæ Regum, quæ Accolis hodie Chambrette au Roy, ex Terra Gypsum, Materiam Calci similem, effodiunt. Fruitur ibidem & in Dolano Agro in Magnatum sepulturas Marmor candidi coloris, quod Alabastrites Græcis appellatur: & aliud nigerrimum, maculis purpureis variatum. Quatuor fere milliaribus Bitontione versus Aquilonem Antrum est in Monte, quod hieme fervet, æstate vero frigore riget. Flumina scindunt eam beantque plurimum non pauca, Arar, Dubis, Longononus, Danus, Lucus, alij. De Arari dictum alibi. Dubis totus ad hunc Comitatum pertinet. Δαβις Ptolemæo vocatur: Apud Iulianum Imperatorem Epistola ad Maximum Philosophum non sine Mendi suspicione Δαυβις dicitur. Alduabus est Cæsari, si proba sit conjectura Fulvii Ursini. In aliis Codicibus Alduasdubus & Aldnasdiatis vitiose legitur Vulgo Doux: Oritur ex Monte Iura paullo supra Pagum amoenissimum, quinque instar opidi, Motam. Mirari licet, quod Paradinus scribat Dubis Fontem esse haud procul ab Arari. Dubis porro, corpto ab Meridie in Septemtrionem curtu, per Pontium Lacum lapsus, nonnullis Amfractibus prætergressus Pontarlum, Mortuam & Vafrum, Fanum petit S. Hippolyti: unde in Occidentem flexus, ad Pagum Chasteiot versus Africum tendens, Vesuntionemque permeans, & facta ad Dolam Insula, post multas ambages receptoque Fluvios prope Virdunum Arari committitur. Totus etiam Burgundiæ Superioris est Longonus, vulgo Lougnon, qui in Lotaringia Finibus ortus, variis Opidis Pagisque lustratis, paullo supra Auxonam in Ararim se fundit. Danum evomit ex sinuoso recessu Mons arduus, Syrodo, grandi & celeberrimo Pago, incumbens, hoc modo: Postquam descenderis, est Antrum profundi Præcipitij, & intus Fons imperscrutabilis profunditatis, latitudine fortitan decem passuum. Huic Rupes horrendæ imminent; quæ contemplantibus horrorem plane incutiunt: ac per Gurgitem altissimum tanta Aquarum copia ebullit, ut stagnum in ipso ortu (dictum incredibile) Flumen Navigis, si ab rupes & saxi, per quæ devolvitur, liceret, satis capax esset. Incolis hoc Flumen Dain vocatur. Fluvios in se recipit varios: cum aliis prope Fontem, Senam, Amnem fama & natura ingentem. tem, ex Fonf. Sena Pago, qui immensus multisque constans Villis, ab eo denominatus, exorientem, & laxola convalle per Planeas & Sienum vicos labentem iuxta Burgum opidum. Et ficalis ix auctus Fluminibus decimens ac praeterlabens per Superioris Burgundiae meridionalem partem, in Rodanum imbus Lugduno versus Orientem miliaribus invehitur: unde Dani nomen in posterioribus Rodani sunt qui arbitrantur latere. Pisces habet Danus grantissimi saporis, praeter alios Troclam & Auratam. Lupus vel Lupa, vulgo Loue, altissimus, lautissimus, rapacissimus Burgundiae Fluvius, multa habet Piscium genera, inter quos numerantur Alosa, Barbatulus, Anguilla, & Aurata. Gritur paulo supra Villephanum in Ovino pago, & non procul ab Dola cum Dubide in Ararim aquis properantibus devolvitur. Lacus habet hic Burgundia ingentes & mirabiles: inter eos non postremi loci, cui ab Foraminibus nomen mirum Naturae ludentis opus. Super enim Aqua et Limus, qui aeco durescit, ut Continens videatur: super quo tamen Equites Currutq. iecure non ambulant, sed soli Pedites. Is caelo pluvioso & nebuloso non emergit, nisi Serenitas sit futura. tunc per Foramina brevi tempore auctus totam Columbanem Planiciem rigat. Et Mons celsus ab Oriente immmer, unde crebri Fontes in illum diffluunt. Inter Nozeiethum porro & Ripariam alius est Lacus in Bonvalli, Lupis, Parcis, & aliis Piscibus abundans, qui septimo quoque anno in aliquot hebdomadas fugitivos & delitescens, iterum emergit. Quae res in Miraculum exit, Fidemque vincit. Tractus huius Comitatus Australior Lacubus scatet: Videre ibi est, qui vernacule Maisteux Maior Minorque: Narlay, profunditatis vix credendae; Vernoy, duo Chambiers, Frogesy, Ronchault & alii. Thermae quoque cum magna Calidarum Aquarum copia ad Luxovium opidum scaturiunt.
units.tr: Barley, oats, beans, millet and other pulses are everywhere abundant, and the trees are no less fruitful. The pasture land, especially where the centre and heart of the region lies, has hills bearing the finest and most prized wines. The other good products are gathered at Arbois, Vadans, the castle of Grimont, Pontbrillant, Lons-le-Saunier, Château-Chalon, Villefrancon, Gy and Mouchard. Of these, some, Arbois above all, share their name with their own territory. The wine grown near Gy is commonly thought to rival the best; it used to be carried into Germany, not to be sold publicly, but to be distributed among the great men. At Arbois and Vadans the wine vats are so large that they seem to equal the houses in height. Near the old royal palace of the Burgundian kings, which the locals now call Chambrette au Roy, they dig up gypsum from the earth, a material similar to lime. In the same place, and in the Dole country, marble of white colour is used for the tombs of the great, which is called alabaster by the Greeks; and another very black marble, streaked with purple spots. About four miles north of Besançon there is a cave in a mountain which is warm in winter and cold in summer. The rivers cut through the region and water it in many places: the Arar (Saône), Doubs, Longeau, Dan, Loue and others. I have spoken of the Arar elsewhere. The Dubis (Doubs) belongs wholly to this county. Ptolemy calls it Δαβις; in Julian the Emperor's letter to the philosopher Maximus, not without suspicion of error, it is called Δαυβις. Caesar's Alduabus is it, if Fulvio Orsini's conjecture is sound. In other manuscripts it is wrongly read as Alduasdubus and Aldnasdiatis; it is commonly called Doux. It rises from the Jura mountain a little above the very pleasant village of Mota, which is like a small town. It is surprising that Paradin writes that the Doubs is a spring not far from the Arar. The Doubs then, starting in the south and running northward in a curved course, flows through Pontarlier, passes by several windings Mortuau and Vaufrey, and heads for the shrine of St Hippolytus; from there it bends to the west, runs towards the south-west past the village of Chasteiot, passes through Besançon, and after forming an island at Dole, after many twists and turns, and taking in other rivers, joins the Arar near Verdun. The Longeau (Lougnon) also belongs wholly to Upper Burgundy; it rises on the borders of Lorraine, passes through various towns and villages, and empties into the Arar a little above Auxonne. The Dan bursts forth from a winding recess beneath the steep mountain that overhangs the great and famous village of Syrod, in this way: after you have descended, there is a cave of deep precipice, and within it a spring of unfathomable depth, perhaps ten paces wide. Dreadful rocks hang over it, which strike horror into those who look upon them; and through a very deep whirlpool such a great volume of water boils up that, at its very source (an incredible thing to say), the pool would be large enough for boats, if the rocks and stones over which it rushes allowed it. The inhabitants call this river the Dain. It receives various rivers into itself: with others near its source, the Seine, a river great in fame and nature; from the spring of the Seine, the village of that name, which is vast and made up of many farms and takes its name from it, rising, and flowing through a narrow valley past the villages of Planes and Sienne, next to the town of Bourg. And, increased by nine rivers, the Dan, flowing past through the southern part of Upper Burgundy, is carried into the Rhône a few miles east of Lyon; whence some think the name Dan remains in the latter part of Rhône. The Dan has very tasty fish, besides others, the trout and the gilt-head. The Loue (Lupus or Lupa), the highest, most abundant and most rapacious river of Burgundy, has many kinds of fish, among which are counted the shad, the barbel, the eel and the gilt-head. It rises a little above Villefrancon in the village of Ovans, and not far from Dole it is carried with the Doubs into the Arar, its waters rushing down. Here Burgundy has huge and marvellous lakes; among them not the least is the one called Les Foraminibus, a wonderful work of playful nature. For over the water there is a mud which hardens in the air so that it seems solid ground; yet horsemen and carts do not cross it, only foot-soldiers. In rainy and cloudy weather it does not appear, unless clear weather is about to come; then, swelled for a short time through the holes, it waters the whole plain of Colombe. And a high mountain rises to the east, from which many springs flow down into it. Between Nozeroy and Ripaille there is another lake in Bonvaux, abounding in pike, perch and other fish, which every seventh year hides itself and lies concealed for some weeks, and then emerges again. This thing turns into a wonder and surpasses belief. The southern part of this county abounds in lakes. There are to be seen those which are called in the vernacular Maisteux, greater and lesser; Narlay, of depth scarcely credible; Vernoy; the two Chambiers, Frasne, Ronchaux and others. Hot springs also gush forth with a great supply of hot water at the town of Luxeuil.

units.la: Floruerunt longe latequae his locis olim Sequani. Sic Caesar lib. 1, & alibi, Cicero in Epist. ad Atticum, Ammianus Marcellinus lib. xv, Sidonius lib. 1. Epist. xi, aliique nominant; qui Σηκουανοί Strabo lib. iv; Σηκανοί, Ptolemaeo, Σηκοανοί, Dioni Coccelo. Hodie Le Pais de Besancon & Franche Comte: quae Maxima Sequanorum apud Sex. Rufum. Scribit Caesar lib. 1 Montem Iuram Sequanorum Fines ab Helvetiis dividere. Sequanicum, Provinciam appellat Notitia Imperii Occidentis. Civitas Sequanorum universim pro tota Ditione, in Inscriptione, quam Lugduni exscriptam posui cap. xxiv. Dumnorigem gratia & largitione apud sequanos plurimum potuisse, notat Caesar lib. 1. item eodem lib. & vi Ariovistum in Germanorum Regem a Sequanis contra Eduos evocatum, tertiam partem Agri Sequani, qui esset optimus totius Galliae, occupasse. Alia praetereo. De iis Strabo lib. iv. Περὶ δὲ τῆς Ἀγρ. Σηκουανοί, διαφορὰ καὶ τῆς Ῥωμαίοις ἐν πολλῇ γεγονήσεως τῆς Εὐρώπης, & quae ibi alia. Sequanos etiam ultra Iuram versus Euronotum habitasse, innuit Entropius lib. vi. Helvetii, inquit, qui nunc Sequani appellantur. Sequanus, Σηκουανός, nominatur in Inscriptione, quae Lugduni legitur in Templo vetustissimo D. Petri, ad Basin Columnae, quae ad sinistram est Arae Maximae: Q. FVLIO. SEVERINO SEQVANO. OMNIB HONORIBVS. IN TER. SVOS FVNCTO &c.
units.tr: The Sequani, who once lived in these places, flourished far and wide. So Caesar in book 1 and elsewhere, Cicero in his letter to Atticus, Ammianus Marcellinus in book 15, Sidonius in book 1, letter 11, and others name them; Strabo in book 4 calls them Σηκουανοί, Ptolemy Σηκανοί, Dio Σηκοανοί. Today they are the region of Besançon and the Franche-Comté, which Sextus Rufus calls Maxima Sequanorum. Caesar in book 1 writes that the Jura mountain divides the lands of the Sequani from the Helvetii. The Notitia of the Western Empire calls it the Province of the Sequani. The Civitas Sequanorum is used generally for the whole territory in the inscription which I have copied at Lyon, in chapter XXIV. Caesar in book 1 notes that Dumnorix had great influence among the Sequani through favour and largesse; likewise in the same book and in book 6 he notes that Ariovistus, called in by the Sequani against the Aedui and made king of the Germans, seized a third part of the land of the Sequani, which was the best in all Gaul. I pass over other matters. Strabo in book 4 treats of them, and what else is there. That the Sequani also lived beyond the Jura toward the south-east is hinted by Eutropius in book 6: "The Helvetii," he says, "who are now called Sequani." A Sequanus, Σηκουανός, is named in the inscription that is read at Lyon in the very old church of St Peter, at the base of the column to the left of the Great Altar: Q. FULVIUS SEVERINUS THE SEQUANIAN, WHO HELD ALL OFFICES AMONG HIS PEOPLE, etc.

units.la: De Antiquis huius Burgundiae Comitibus, Stirpis etiam Imperatoriae Fancicaeque, multi multa memoriae produnt. Nuperorum hoc est Stemma: Nam certum Sepulturæ Locum non habent. Posteriorum Ducum pars potior ad D. Francisci Ædem (quæ ad alterum Palatij latus) sita est. Spectare ibi est superbum Renati, qui Victoria potitus est contra Karolum Burgundiæ Ducem, Monimentum. Conditi jacent ibidem Dux Antonius, cujusque Filius Franciscus, Karolique Ducis Vxor Claudia Valesia, Henrici II. Galliarum Regis Filia. Nancei Moenia lambit Mosa, qui tribus inde miliaribus paullo supra Arcem Candei Mosellam intrat. Armamentarium habet Nanceium. Machinis bellicis omnis generis instructissimum. Putant Petrus Divæus aliique Nanceium hodie esse, quod Nanceum Ptolemæo, Nasium Antonino in Itinere, quod Durocortoro ducit Divodurum. Sed si quis penitius itineris illius rationem consideret, ejusque ductum & stila I deliter sequatur: facile deprehendet Antonini Nasium incidere non posse in locum illum, ubi hodie Nanceium: adeo ut Nasium illud sit, non quod nunc Nanceium dicimus, sed Pagus XII. inde miliaribus dissitus non procul ab Mosa in Barroducana Provincia, qui vulgo Nas dictus, unde Nasiensis in Lapide, qui effossus ibi: FABRICIVS NACIENSIS CVRATORIBVS ET MINIS TRIS IVVENTIDIO FIRMO ET ATEV-LA SOLLI F. HVIVS FANI FACIENDI. Certe Nasium illud amplissimam aliquando Vrbem fuisse, satis patet ex Ruderibus: quod etiam testatur apud Ortelium Clemens Trelæus Mosellanus. Iter Antonini, quo Nasij fit mentio, collatum cum Itineraria Tabula & hodierna nomenclatura, sic se habet:
units.tr: Many writers have recorded much about the ancient counts of this Burgundy, who were of imperial and Frankish stock. This is the genealogy of the more recent ones, since they have no certain place of burial. Most of the later dukes lie in the church of St Francis, which stands on one side of the palace. There one can see the proud monument of René, who gained the victory over Charles, Duke of Burgundy. Buried there lie Duke Antoine, his son François, and Claude de Valois, wife of Duke Charles, daughter of Henri II, King of France. The Moselle is a river that washes the walls of Nancy, and it enters the Moselle at Charmes, three miles above the citadel of Nancy. Nancy has an arsenal, very well equipped with war machines of every kind. Pierre Davis and others think that Nancy today is the Nasium of Antonine's itinerary, which Ptolemy calls Nanceum, on the road from Durocortorum to Divodurum. But if anyone considers that itinerary more closely and follows its course and distances carefully, he will easily see that Antonine's Nasium cannot lie where Nancy now is. It must therefore be not what we now call Nancy, but a village twelve miles from there, not far from the Meuse in the province of Bar, commonly called Nas. From there comes the Nasiensis of the inscription found there: "Fabricius of Nasium, to the curators and ministers, Juventidius Firmus and Atevla, son of Solus, for the building of this temple." It is clear enough from the ruins that Nasium was once a very large city, and Clement Trelaeus of Moselle also attests this in Ortelius. The itinerary of Antonine, in which Nasium is mentioned, compared with the Peutinger Table and modern names, stands as follows:

units.tr: Antonine's Itinerary | Peutinger Table | Modern names. From Durocortorum to Divodurum, eighty-seven miles, thus: Durocortorum, nineteen. From Reims to Metz, thirty leagues. Fanum Minervae, fourteen miles: Tanomia, where Buones is today, or near it; read Fano Minervae, that is, Minerva's temple, Ariola, sixteen miles: ..., where Bony or Menehoult is. Caturigas, nine miles: Caturices, nine: perhaps Clermont. Nasium, nine miles: Nasie, read Nasio: Nas. Tullum, sixteen miles: Tullio, read Tullo, ten: Toul. Scarpona, ten miles: Scarponna, fourteen: Sarpaigne, on the Moselle. Divodurum, twelve miles: Divo; Durimedio Matricorum, write Divoduro Mediomatricum: Metz.

units.la: Scarponæ, quæ in Itinerariis nominatur, meminit etiam Ammianus lib. xxvii. Retinet hodie Veterem Appellationem Vicus Sarpaigne, ubi multa Antiquitatis Rudera visuntur. De iis non potuimus, quin adscribam Petri Divæi verba ex ipsius Itinerario: Hic, inquit, paullo viterius ad eandem Mosellæ ripam Vicus est exiguus Sarpaigne, de cujus Antiquitate multa Incolæ referebant. Oppidum olim amplum fuisse à Sarpigna quadam Regina (non abhunt hæc ab Fabulis) denominatum, quæ & in eo Regiam habuerat. Ostendunt in eius rei testimonium Ruinas quasdam Murorum, ubi Thermae quondam fuisse volebant: Nos quæ eorum figura fuisset, non valebamus conjicere: tantum subdubitabamus, num Castrorum inservissent Munitioni, quum eorum magna sit crassitudo, & Foramina in eis cernantur adhuc rotunda & angusta, quasi ad ejaculanda Missilia. Hic & Numismata antiqua erant: & Hospes, ad quem diverteramus, nobis dedit aureum Nummum C. Cæsaris Caligulæ, quem se ibidem reperisse adfirmabat. Extat in Parte Domus cuiusdam rustica anti-qua Marmor, in quo Regina illius Imaginem esse volunt. Est manu omnino artifice Ipsa vero Calathum, aut simile quid quidam gestat, in quo Pomorum figuram, ficubus haud absimilium videbamur dignoscere. Suspicari sane est ex hac Sculptura Locum hunc alicuius olim nomen fuisse, sed de hoc, ut & de aliis quamplurimis desiderantur Historia: Fabellarum vero inanium apud profanum Vulgus nullum esse modum, nemins non Exploratum existimamus.
units.tr: Ammianus, book 27, also mentions Scarpona, which is named in the itineraries. The village of Sarpaigne still keeps the old name, and many remains of antiquity can be seen there. We cannot pass these by without quoting the words of Pierre Davis from his own itinerary: "Here, a little further along the same bank of the Moselle, is a small village, Sarpaigne, about whose antiquity the inhabitants told many things. It is said that the town was once large and was named after a certain queen Sarpigna (these things are not far from fables), who also had a palace there. As evidence of this they show some ruins of walls, where they claimed there were once baths. We could not guess what their shape had been; we only doubted whether they had served as a fortification, since the walls are very thick and round, narrow openings can still be seen in them, as if for hurling missiles. Here there were also ancient coins, and our host, at whose house we lodged, gave us a gold coin of Gaius Caesar Caligula, which he said he had found there. In part of a certain old country house there is a marble slab on which they say is the image of the queen. It is certainly done by a skilled hand. She herself carries a basket or something similar, in which we seemed to make out a shape of fruits, not unlike figs. It is certainly reasonable to suspect from this carving that this place once had the name of someone, but of this, as of very many other things, history is lacking. As for the empty fables among the common people, we think no one is unaware that they have no limit."

units.la: Haud procul Nanceio Locum vidi, ubi obtruncatus Karolus Burgundus, ad Rivulum vulum quemdam, quem quum, cæsis jam copiis, fugiens pararet transfilire effusò Equo, miserè sunt ab intequentibus confossus. Testatur rem gestam Crux Lapidea cum Inscriptione Gallica in ærea Lamina, cujus Exscriptum est apud Divaeum in Itinerario Belgico. Paullo altius, ubi Prælium id commissum volunt, Sacellum mihi monstratum est à Burgundionibus cognominatum, cum adjuncto Cœmiterio & Tabula ærea, in qua Gallici Vgrius memoriam atrocissimi Prælij conservant. Prope Nanceium ad Montium Radices Pagus est Marche-Ville, cujus Incolas perfidia aliquando in suum Ducem (cum Historiæ Fridericum ii appellant) notatos ferunt, atque ea de causa, quoniamcumque cum reliquis Principibus domesticis epulari contingit, Panem eis inverium apponi consuevisse. Exstant ibidem Rudera rotundæ Turris, in qua Dux, quem dixi, ex Venatione subductus ad triennium detentus memoratur.
units.tr: Not far from Nancy I saw the place where Charles the Burgundian was cut down. He was killed by the pursuers, who pierced him wretchedly, when, his forces already destroyed, he was fleeing and tried to leap across a small stream with his horse at full gallop. A stone cross with an inscription in French on a bronze plate records the deed; a copy of it is in Davis's Belgian itinerary. A little higher up, where they say that battle was fought, I was shown a chapel which the Burgundians call by that name, with an attached cemetery and a bronze tablet, on which the Gauls of Vogue preserve the memory of the most savage battle. Near Nancy, at the foot of the hills, is the village of Marche-Ville, whose inhabitants, they say, were once marked for their treachery against their duke (whom the histories call Frederick II). For this reason, whenever it happened that they dined with the other princes of the house, they were accustomed to be served unleavened bread. There remain on the spot the ruins of a round tower, in which the duke I mentioned is recorded to have been held for three years after being taken from a hunt.

units.la: Nanceium dignitate sequitur Fanum S. Nicolai, vulgo S. Nicolas, duobus inde distans versus Orientem milliaribus, ad Murtam Fluvium, Loco plano & fertili. Templum non magnæ est antiquitatis, sed vastæ molis, editaque structuræ. Columnæ, quæ totum Fastigium sustinent, tantæ sunt cum gracilitatis, tum altitudinis, ut tanto oneri ferendo vix judicentur pares. Turres habet duas, in quarum una Karoli Lotaringici Cardinalis, qui idem Metensis erat Episcopus, cuique hæc parebat Ecclesia sub Prioratus, ut loquuntur, titulo, in summo Culmine Symbolum: obeliscus felicet cum Hedera circumplicata, & Inscriptione, TE STANTE VIREBO. Adiervari fertur in hac Ede ex D. Nicolai, Myræ Episcopi, quæ urbs erat Lyciæ, ex eadem Lycia, Patara Urbe, oriundi, Manu Articulus unus inclusus Auro, Gemmis multis interlitus: unde hujus primum loci nata Religio: qui advenarum frequentia in eam excrevit amplitudinem, ut jam non Pagum, sed Urbem, & quidem totius Lotaringiæ cultissimam, quam posset dicere, si muro clauderetur: ea est Ædificiorum venustate, aptâ Viarum dispositione, Incolarum multitudine, ut nihil requiri queat: sed ob Mercaturam præcipue, & omnis generis opificia commendaturi Mercatores habens perquam opulentos, Vicinis suis ditiores.
units.tr: After Nancy in rank comes the church of St Nicholas, commonly called St Nicolas, two miles east of it, by the river Murte, in a flat and fertile place. The church is not of great antiquity, but it is vast in bulk and lofty in construction. The columns which support the whole roof are so slender and so tall that they hardly seem equal to bearing so great a weight. It has two towers. In the top of one of them, at the summit, is the device of Charles, Cardinal of Lorraine, who was also Bishop of Metz, and to whom this church was subject under the title, as they say, of a priory: an obelisk, namely, with ivy twining around it, and the inscription "STANDING, I SHALL FLOURISH." It is said that in this church is kept one finger of St Nicholas, bishop of Myra, a city of Lycia, who was born in the same Lycia, in the city of Patara. It is enclosed in gold and inlaid with many gems. From this, the religion of this place first arose; and from the crowds of strangers it grew to such a size that it is now not a village but a city, and indeed the most cultivated in all of Lorraine, which one could call a city even if it were not walled. It is so complete in the elegance of its buildings, the suitable arrangement of its streets, and the number of its inhabitants that nothing more could be asked. It is distinguished above all by its trade and by merchants who deal in goods of every kind; it has very wealthy merchants, richer than their neighbours.

units.la: Alia minorum gentium Opida, ne Lectori tædium pariam, prætereo. Uno dis- stat milliari Nanceio Fruarti tribus. Ormes: paullo amplius, Bayon & Lunevillé; quatuor, Le Pont à Monsun & Gerbeviller; quinque, Charmes, sex, Chatlenoy, Morhanges & Vaucoleur; paullo plus, Maxen soubs Brefve septem, Dompaire, Denewvre, Hodon Chasteau: octo, Ramberville, Raon, Vellemont, Neuff-Chastean, Mugstat, Marchain-Ville: novem, Espinal, Brusseres, Darney; decem, Ormont, Valderfing, Beaurains: tredecim, Vaigny: quatuordecim, L'Ffraye.
units.tr: I pass over the other towns of lesser peoples, so as not to weary the reader. One mile from Nancy is Fruarti; three, Ormes; a little more, Bayon and Lunéville; four, Le Pont à Mousson and Gerbéviller; five, Charmes; six, Châtenoy, Morhange and Vaucouleurs; a little more, MAxen sous Brèves; seven, Dompaire, Denèvre and Hodon Château; eight, Ramberviller, Raon, Vellemont, Neufchâteau, Mirecourt and Marchainville; nine, Épinal, Bruyères and Darney; ten, Ormont, Valderfing and Beaurains; thirteen, Vaigny; fourteen, L'Effraye.

units.la: Comi atus titulo & dignitate clarent; quæ vernacule Vaudemont, quinque Nanceio milliaribus. Chaligny ad dextram Mosellæ, Leuca semi Nanceio. Amance septem milliaribus ab Mediomatricum Urbe versus Meridiem; Almentia Latine scribendis; Scrinium olim & antiqua Lotaringiæ Cancellaria, testantibus Archivis ab Roseiro prolatis. Richecourt haud procul Lacu, qui vulgo La Garde Lac, unde Amnis profluit, qui inter Fanum S. Nicolai & opidum Rosieres Murtæ miscetur. Remiremont ad sinistram Mosellæ, Insulam ibi facientis, in Lotaringiæ Meridionalissimis: Rumaricum Castellum habet hic Aimoinus Monachus; Adromarici corrupte legitur apud Reginonem, pro Ad Romarici, divitum; Rimelsberg Germanice nominatur Spigelio ad Bartholini Austriad. Spectantur haud procul inde Valles, quæ vulgo L'Ffraye & Vagny. La Mothe ad amnem situm est, qui mox in Mosam se exonerat. Visitur ibi Territorium, cui nomen Le Sanctoy. Sunt & Comitatus quidam Imperii Salmensis, Kirchinganus & Blanckenburgius. Blanckenberg, Gallis Blanc-mont, opidum est non magnum, sed pulcrum & amœnum. Spectatur ibi Castrum Vetus, spaciosum & magnificum, cui Palatium Novum Ducis, venusta structura insigne, est conjunctum. Incolæ Agriculturæ dant operam.
units.tr: Counties shine with their titles and dignity: Vaudémont, which in the vernacular is called that, five miles from Nancy; Chaligny, on the right bank of the Moselle, half a league from Nancy; Amance, seven miles from the city of Metz to the south. Almentia, as it is written in Latin, was once the chest and the old chancery of Lorraine, as the archives brought forth by Roseiro attest. Richecourt lies not far from the lake commonly called La Garde Lac, from which flows a stream that mixes with the Murte between the church of St Nicholas and the town of Rosières. Remiremont lies on the left bank of the Moselle, forming an island there, in the most southern parts of Lorraine. Aimoin the monk mentions the castle of Rumaricum here; in Regino it is wrongly read as Adromarici for Ad Romarici, of the rich. In German it is named Rimelsberg, as Spiegel notes in Bartholin's Austrias. Valleys are seen not far from there, commonly called L'Effraye and Vagny. La Mothe is situated on a river which soon discharges into the Meuse. There one can see a territory called Le Sanctoy. There are also some counties of the Empire: Salm, Kirchheim and Blankenburg. Blankenberg, in French Blanc-Mont, is a town not large, but fine and pleasant. There is to be seen an old castle, spacious and magnificent, to which is joined the new palace of the duke, notable for its graceful construction. The inhabitants devote themselves to agriculture.

units.la: Nomeny Baronatus est ad dextram Sellæ Fluvii, tribus milliaribus ab Urbe Mediomatricum, Meridiem versus.
units.tr: Nomeny is a barony on the right bank of the Seille river, three miles south of the city of Metz (Mediomatrici).

units.la: Dominia sunt: Marsal ad Sellæ sinistram, haud procul Lacu Lindero, in quo Insula cum Opido Techemsul. Remerevillé tribus Nanceio milliaribus. S. Bellemont, totidem Mota. Rambert-Ville ad dextram Mortanæ, haud procul Fonte, ubi Silva Mortanensis. Rosieres ad Murtam, prope Fanum D. Nicolai, duobus Nanceio milliaribus. Homburg grandiore Leuca ab opido Sarbruck, ad Amnem, qui mox Saravo concurrit. Mariemont ab Monte, cui opidum impositum, uno ab Lindeto Lacu milliari, meridiem versus. Sandaconst medio fere itinere inter Vaudimontem & Mottam, in Agro, qui vulgo Sanctoy.
units.tr: The lordships are these: Marsal, on the left bank of the Seille, not far from Lake Lindre, in which lies an island with the town of Techemsul. Remerevillé, three miles from Nancy. S. Bellemont, the same distance from Mota. Rambertvillers on the right bank of the Mortagne, not far from the spring where the Forest of Mortagne lies. Rosières on the Meurthe, near the church of St Nicholas, two miles from Nancy. Homburg, a greater league from the town of Sarrebruck, on the river that soon joins the Saar. Mariemont, from the hill on which the town is set, one mile from Lake Lindre to the south. Sandaucourt, about halfway between Vaudémont and Mothe, in the district commonly called Sanctoy.

units.la: Mediomatricum Urbem, quæ cum Tullo aliisque Imperialis olim erat, in suam potestatem redegit Galliarum Monarcha, Henricus II. Præsidet Urbis Senatui missus ab Rege Magistratus. Tribunal autem Mediomatricis Urbis tres habet Episcopatus, sub Metropoli Trevirensi: Metensem, Tullensem, Virdunensem, sic ab Locis nuncupatos, in quis suæ singulis Sedes.
units.tr: The king of France, Henry II, brought the city of Metz (Mediomatricum), which once belonged to the Empire along with Toul and other places, under his own power. A magistrate sent by the king presides over the city council. The see of the city of Metz, however, has three bishoprics under the metropolitan of Trier: Metz, Toul and Verdun, so called from their places, each with its own seat.

units.la: Quæ vulgo Metz, & posterioris ævi Scriptoribus Metæ, Gregorio autem Turonensi & aliis Urbs Metensis; Divodurum Mediomatricum Antiquissimum appellatum. Itineraria Tabula: Divo, Durimedio. Matricorum; Lege, Divoduro Mediomatricorum, ut antea monui. Simpliciter Ἀπέδωρον Ptolemæo; Divodurum Tacito lib. IV & Antonino, qui eo varia ducit Itinera. Variorum Nugas de recentis Nominis ratione non libet adscribere. Sedes olim fuit Regni Lotaringiæ. Lumprandus: Metensem Urbem, quæ potentissima in Regno Lotarij erat. De ea eleganter Petrus Divæus in Itinerario: Metensis Urbs in amplissima est Planitie, quam Mosella in varios divisus alveos irrigat, & pars quidem eius muros ad lævam lambit, pars & eosdem subit, ut Civium usibus inserviat, atque sic divisum fluit ad inferiorem usque eorum ambitum, ubi recepto Sella, altero Flumine, qui de dextra Urbis partem adluit, in unum denuo alveum colligitur. Sed Situ imprimis ipsius Urbis delectabamur: quum enim Agrum late circumjacentem planum habeat, ejus tamen Area paullum prominet, ut in eo Veterum rationem in condendis Urbibus agnoscas. Ad Summum siquidem Templum multis gradibus ascenditur: juxta quod Forum Rerum Venalium alterem totius Area partem occupat, & ab eo undique versus Muros paullatim descendit, præcipito tantum in una parte Clivo, ubi Vias duas Lapidibus stratas sic dispositas videas, ut altera per alterius domorum culmina excurrat. Templum D. Stephani nomen tenet, qui Civitatis est Patronus, pulcherrimum vero opus, si quod aliud toto hoc Itinere vidimus, & sua mole spectabile; quodque raro accidit, omni ex parte consummatum. Dicebatur, in eo fuisse Crucifixi ligneam Imaginem, totam Laminis aureis superinductam. Vidimus Labrum Porphyreticum rubei Coloris, magna capacitatis, Pedes x. longitudine excedens, in quo Lustrales Aquas asservant. Sunt & alia in hac eadem Urbe fumtuosa Templa, & multa erant in eius Suburbis, inter quæ D. Arnolphi Basilica, Imp. Ludovici Pij Augusti, Karoli Filij & Filiarum aliquot Pipini Regis sepultura celebris. Omnia hæc absumsit Belli rabies, stant Suburbia nec vestigium quidem nunc superest, neque ultra Aruros quidquam prater Campestria videas. De Bello Nupero consulendus Historiæ meæ Belgicæ Liber v. Cives Mediomatrices nominantur in Inscriptione, quæ extat Moguntiæ ad S. Albanum: D. M PRIMVLÆ. COMITILLÆ QVÆ. VIXIT. ANNIS. XX CIVES. MEDIOMATRIC A. MATERNIVS. NEMAVSVS. STRATOR. COS. ET LVCIVS. LVCINVS. MENSOR. FRVMENTI. NVMER.
units.tr: The city now commonly called Metz, by writers of later times Metae, and by Gregory of Tours and others the city of the Mediomatrici, was called Divodurum Mediomatricum by the most ancient writers. The Itinerary table has Divo and Durimedio; read Divoduro Mediomatricorum, as I noted before. Ptolemy simply gives Apedoron; Tacitus, book IV, and Antoninus, who leads several roads through it, give Divodurum. I do not care to set down the trifles of various writers about the reason for the recent name. It was once the seat of the kingdom of Lorraine. Lumprandus calls the city of Metz, which was the most powerful in the kingdom of Lothar. Petrus Divaeus writes elegantly about it in his Itinerary: The city of Metz lies on a very wide plain, which the Moselle waters, divided into several channels. Part of it laps the walls on the left, and part even passes under them, to serve the citizens' needs; and so divided it flows on to the lower end of their circuit, where, having taken in the Seille, another river which washes the part of the city on the right, it is gathered again into a single channel. But I was especially delighted by the site of the city itself: although it has a level plain spreading wide around it, its area rises a little, so that in it you may recognise the method of the ancients in founding cities. For the chief temple is reached by many steps; beside it the cattle market occupies the other part of the whole area, and from there it descends gradually on all sides toward the walls, with a steep slope on one side only, where you see two roads paved with stones, so arranged that one runs over the roofs of the other's houses. The temple bears the name of St Stephen, patron of the city, a most beautiful work, if we saw any other on this whole journey, and impressive in its bulk; and, which is rare, finished in every part. It was said that in it there was a wooden image of the Crucified, wholly covered with gold plates. We saw a basin of red porphyry, of great capacity, more than ten feet long, in which they keep the water for purification. There are also other sumptuous churches in this same city, and many were in its suburbs, among which the basilica of St Arnulf, the burial place of the emperor Louis the Pious, of Charles his son, and of several daughters of King Pepin, was famous. The rage of war has destroyed all these; the suburbs stand no longer, and not even a trace of them remains now, nor can you see anything beyond the ploughed fields and plains. On the recent war, consult the fifth book of my Belgian History. The citizens of Metz are named in the inscription which is at Mainz at St Alban's: To the spirit of the dead, to Primula Comitilla, who lived twenty years; the citizens of Metz, Maternius Nemausus, stratorcos, and Lucius Lucinus, measurer of grain, numerarius.

units.la: Haud procul Metus, prope Pagum Iovy, in Mosella antiqui Aquæductus sunt Vestigia. De iis sic Divæus in Itinerario: In hoc Itinere Pagus est Iovy vulgo dictus inter Montium radices & Mosellam, ubi quantacumque est inter Montes utrosque, qui Ripas ambiunt, distantia, Aqua-ductuum antiquitus fuisse, judicant eiusdem, quæ adhuc exstant, reliquiæ, Arcuum adhuc restant multi, sintque ex albo Lapide, in Laterum formam dissecto; & nonnulli quoque eiusdem operis in adversa ripa cernuntur. Incolæ affirmabant in eodem loco Fontem hodieque esse, quamvis hos Arcus (solita infectia) Ponti inservisse putantes, & ab hoc Pago in Montis ipsius jugo minores alios Arcus fuisse dicebant, qui versus Urbem Metensem quæ uno hinc distat Milliari, excurrisse viderentur. Altitudo juxta Ripam Pedum est circiter 1 x: Unde conjicere est, quanta totius Operis moles fuerit, quantaque altitudo Arcuum, quis in ipso erant Fluminis alveo, quorum hodie nihil superest. Referebant ydem Incolæ, superiosuperiorem Arcuum Partem planam omnino esse, cemento rubei coloris inductam; & in eius medio Domunculam non ita multis adhinc annis adhuc fuisse, ab utraque parte patentem, quam nos partem Tecti fuisse, quae Tubum tegeret, suspicabamur.
units.tr: Not far from Metz, near the village of Jouy, on the Moselle, are the remains of an ancient aqueduct. Divaeus writes of them thus in his Itinerary: On this journey is the village commonly called Jouy, between the roots of the hills and the Moselle; where, however great the distance between the two hills that border the banks, the remains of aqueducts of the same kind, which still exist, show that they were built in ancient times. Many arches still remain, made of white stone cut into the shape of bricks, and some of the same work can be seen on the opposite bank. The inhabitants affirmed that a spring still exists in the same place, though they thought these arches (as is customary with such stories) served a bridge; and from this village they said that other, smaller arches ran along the ridge of the hill itself toward the city of Metz, which is one mile from here, and seemed to extend that way. The height beside the bank is about eleven feet; hence one may conjecture how great the bulk of the whole work was, and how high the arches were that stood in the very bed of the river, of which nothing survives today. The same inhabitants reported that the upper part of the arches was entirely flat, covered with cement of red colour; and that in its middle, not many years ago, there was still a little house, open on each side, which we suspected was part of a roof covering the conduit.

units.la: Quae Toul vernacule, Tullum olim; Τύλλιον, Leucorum opidum, Ptolemaeo: Tubum Antonino, Itinere à Durocortoro Divodurum, & alibi: Tullum Itinerariae Tabulae.
units.tr: What is now called Toul in the vernacular, formerly Tullum; Tullion, the town of the Leuci, according to Ptolemy; Tubum according to Antoninus, in the itinerary from Durocortorum to Divodurum, and elsewhere; Tullum in the Itinerary table.

units.la: Quae denique Verdun, Latinis vocatur hodie Virdunum & Verdunum: Verodunum Antonino dicitur. Civitas Verdonensium in Notitia Provinciarum sub Belgica 1. L'Evesche de Verdun. Leguntur autem tres Urbes, quas commemoravi, Comitatus etiam titulo & dignitate insignes. Potuerunt tunc Ambitum diligentissime notarum reperi in vetustissima quadam Charta. Non gravabor ipsissima adscribere Verba. Conferat Lector ad Sermonis, si quae est, scabritiem, crebraque quorundam Vocum Repetitiones. Ita sic habet: Circuitus Comitatus Verdunensis incipit enim à Leone Menij Falconis, & usque ad Pertusam Petram tendit. De Pertusa Petra usque ad Subtrianam Villam, & inde usque ad Villam de Faller. Deinde usque ad Longmon, ubi Crima cadit in Caram Luvinum; & sicut Crima, sursum decurrit usque ad Aa fiam, quae usque ad Ertezum tendit, & usque ad Baninadum, ubi cadit in Ornam. Et in longitudine superius usque ad Fontem, apud Ayoncourtem; & inde usque ad Quercum Saldei; & inde Sulmiotoni ad Fontem Lupimontis, deinde ad Meabori Fontem. Deinde Ferrifundura; deinde usque Confuncta, ubi cadit in Mosam Fluvium: deinde usque Warnoncourtem per Nuclearios iuxta Boffry & Warnoncourt: & deinde contra Vallem iuxta Longam Campum, recta Via ad Herisiam: & inde usque ad Fontem apud Sarindum ad Fontes. Exhinc usque ad summam Asinam, & postea usque ad Vimos, & inde usque ad locum, ubi Gronea fuit in Asinam: & inde per descensum Asinae iuxta Vitsnam: Et usque Viennam per Ferrieres, & per Momblarvillam, & per Concecourt ter Castrum iuxta Quarnasium, & inde per Superiorem Partem Villa, quae dicitur Chebe; & inde recta via usque ad Lemas & inde usque ad Ipannulphivillam: Et inde recta via usque ad Montem Falconis: & usque ad Lrenem, à quo primum cepimus.
units.tr: What is finally called Verdun, is today called in Latin Virdunum and Verdunum; Antoninus calls it Verodunum. The city of the Verdunenses is listed in the Notitia Provinciarum under Belgica I: L'Evêché de Verdun. The three cities I have mentioned are read of as well, distinguished by the title and dignity of a county. They could then find the boundary most carefully noted in a very old charter. I shall not hesitate to copy the very words, that the reader may compare them with the roughness of the style, if there is any, and the frequent repetition of certain words. It reads thus: The circuit of the county of Verdun begins at Leo of Menij Falconis and stretches to the Pertusa Petra. From Pertusa Petra to the village of Subtriana, and from there to the village of Faller. Then to Longmon, where the Crima falls into the Caram Luvinum; and as the Crima runs upward to Aafiam, which stretches to Ertezum, and to Baninadum, where it falls into the Orne. And, lengthwise, upward to the spring at Ayoncourt; and from there to the oak of Saldei; and from there to Sulmiotoni, to the spring of Lupimontis, then to the spring of Meabor. Then Ferrifundura; then as far as Confuncta, where it falls into the river Meuse; then as far as Warnoncourt through the Nuclearii, by Boffry and Warnoncourt; and then opposite the valley by Longcamp, the straight way to Herisia; and from there to the spring at Sarindum at the springs. From there to the high Asina, and afterwards to Vimos, and from there to the place where Gronea was on the Asina; and from there down the course of the Asina by Vitsna; and as far as Vienna, through Ferrières and through Momblarville, and through Concecourt, thrice by the castle near Quarnasium, and from there through the upper part of the village called Chebe; and from there by a straight way to Lemas, and from there to Ipannulphivilla; and from there by a straight way to Mons Falconis; and to Lren, from which we first began.

units.la: Cum Lotharingia porro solet explicari Territorium Barrense, vulgo Le Barrois, quod extendit se ad Novum usque Castellum, Neuf Chastel. Metropolis illi Bar le Duc, sic cognominata ad differentiam aliarum, quae Bar sur Seyne, & Bar sur Aube. Minorum gentium Opida sunt La Motte, Ligny, Arg, & alia multa; ad Mosam se offerunt Commercy & Vaucouleur, quae partim Franciae, partim Barri.
units.tr: Next to Lorraine is commonly explained the territory of Bar, commonly called Le Barrois, which extends as far as Neufchâteau. Its metropolis is Bar-le-Duc, so named to distinguish it from the others, Bar-sur-Seine and Bar-sur-Aube. The smaller towns are La Motte, Ligny, Arg, and many others; on the Meuse lie Commercy and Vaucouleurs, which belong partly to France and partly to Bar.

units.la: CAPUT XLV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XLV.

units.la: Benearnia.
units.tr: Béarn.

units.la: HAEc de Ducatibus, Francorum potestate exemtis; sequuntur Principatus Benearnensis & Aranfionensis. BENEARNENSIS, vulgo Bearn, semper separatus fuit ab Francorum Ditione, eodemque, quo Regnum ipsum, habitus jure, id est, optimo maximo: sed adcrevit quasi Regno Franciae, quum Christianissimus Henricus, Navarrae Rex, Regni Franeici caperet Sceptrum, iure Successorio. Unde Nomen nobilissimo Principatui, varie disputant Novi Scriptores; inque eo eruendo incredibile, quantum se torqueant, ne dicam ineptiant. Memoriae produnt quidam Benearnam, tempore Regis Hlodovei, subditam fuisse Francis, inque dotem datam Gailsvindae Brunechildis Reginae, quae Sigeberto nupta erat, Sorori; sub nomine Benarm. Nonnulli denominatos putant Benearnenses à Biarinis Septemtrionalibus Populis, quos, cum Gothis, aliisque, Hispaniam petentes ijs in locis sedes fixisse volunt. Sunt qui scribunt originem traxisse à Bernatibus, Helvetiae nunc Populis; ipsaque Regionem ab Karolo Martello dono fuisse datam. Alij alia adferunt: quam vera, prudentiores judicent. Scimus nos Benearni (de quo postea, mentionem fieri apud Antoninum in Itinere, quod ad illud opidum ducit Caesar-Augusta ex Hispania Citeriore. Legitur etiam in Notitia Provinciarum Galliae sub Aquitania Tertia Novempopulania, Civitas Benearnensium, id est Benearnus. A Benearno si quis Toti Tractui nomen inditum censeat, fortean non errarit: sed Benearnum unde dictum, nescire me fateor. Sita est Benearnia ad radices Pyrenæorum Montium, inter Bigerronum, Baionensium, aliorumque Contrialium Populorum Territoria & Agros: in duas divisa Partes; quarum una, Montibus oblita, Eloronum habet Opidum; altera, ab Vallibus Locisque planioribus occupata, Lascarienfem Civitatem, Regioni cum in Montibus, tum in Planicie, mirandus est genius & stupenda indoles: vix Opidum ibi, vix Pagus, cui non aliquid singulare. Potior Pars Millo, Lino, Canabi (quarum rerum maximam Incolæ exercent Mercaturam) abundat: Frumento etiam hic ibi beata: Pascuis valde dives, Pecoreque: unde incredibilis Butyri Caseique copia: Capris supra modum scatet; quæ hic nullo labore nutriuntur in Rupibus, & Ericetis, citra Fructuum teneriorumque Arborum perniciem & detrimentum. Nec Vina desunt. Generosum valde, nullique Francico bonitate sua cedens, producit Territorium, quod vulgo Iurancon. Balnea habet passim Thermasque, omnium, quæ in Europa, præstantissimas. De Aquis Benearnensibus Plinius lib. xxi. nat. hist. cap. xi: Emicant, inquit, benigne, passimque in plurimis terris alibi frigida, alibi calida, alibi tepida, sicut in Tarbellis, Aquitanica Gente, & in Pyrenais Montibus, tenui intervallo discernente: Ad quæ Nobilis. Vir Iosephus Scaliger: Qui Aquas Benearnensis Saltus in Pyrenais viderunt & biberunt, non dubitabunt Plinium de illis sensisse. Incolæ elatos habent animos: strenui sunt & fortes; Armorum periti, candidi proculque ab omni suco; adfabiles & ad omnem humanitatem propensissimi; cauti interim subtileque lingua sua eloquentes: Libertatis amantes, Magnis gaudent Immunitatibus & Privilegiis. Ad Doctrinas eos varias capessendum non ineptos docent Magni Viri, qui inde oriundi. Omnes Nobilitatem adfectant: qui reipsa nobiles, contendunt magis, ut bene fortiterque agant, quam ut splendide molliterque vestiantur. Inter ipsos primum obtinent locum illustres Familiæ, quas ex Cantabris ajunt ortas, Grammontia & Luffea. Baronatus clarent dignitate Mirens, Iadre, Monens, S. Celombe, Fsganalabagne, Coderch, Navailles, Castelnau, Maseres, Luz, Suz, & aliæ.
units.tr: So much for the duchies that are exempt from the power of the French. Next come the principalities of Béarn and Aranjuez. Béarn, commonly called Bearn, was always separate from the rule of the French, and it held the same right as the kingdom itself, that is, the best and greatest right. But it was added, as it were, to the kingdom of France when the most Christian Henry, King of Navarre, took up the scepter of the kingdom of France by right of succession. Recent writers dispute variously about the origin of the name of this most noble principality, and in searching for it they twist themselves into knots, not to say that they talk nonsense. Some record that Béarn, in the time of King Hlodovech, was subject to the Franks and was given as a dowry to Gailsvinda, the sister of Queen Brunhild, who was married to Sigebert, under the name Benarm. Some think the people of Béarn were named after the Biarini, a northern people, whom they hold, along with the Goths and others, to have fixed their seats in those places when they were making for Spain. Some write that the name derives from the Bernates, now a people of Switzerland, and that the region itself was given as a gift by Charles Martel. Others bring forward other views; let wiser men judge which is true. We ourselves know that Benearnum (about which more later) is mentioned by Antoninus in his Itinerary, the road that leads from Caesar-Augusta in Hither Spain to that town. It is also read in the Notitia Provinciarum Galliae, under Aquitania Tertia Novempopulana, the city of the Benearnenses, that is, Benearnus. If anyone thinks that the whole tract took its name from Benearnum, he may perhaps not be wrong; but I confess I do not know whence Benearnum itself got its name. Béarn lies at the foot of the Pyrenees, between the territories and fields of the Bigerri, the Baiona and the other coastal peoples. It is divided into two parts: one, covered with mountains, has the town of Oloron; the other, occupied by valleys and more level places, has the city of Lascar. The character and natural gifts of the region, both in the mountains and on the plain, are remarkable: there is hardly a town or village that does not have something special. The greater part abounds in millet, flax and hemp, of which the inhabitants carry on a great trade. Here the land is also rich in wheat; it is very well supplied with pasture and livestock, so that there is an incredible abundance of butter and cheese. It swarms with goats beyond measure, which are fed here without any labor on the rocks and heaths, without harm or loss to the fruit and young trees. Nor is wine lacking. The territory, commonly called Jurançon, produces a very fine wine, which yields to no French wine in quality. It has baths and hot springs everywhere, the most outstanding of all in Europe. Concerning the Waters of Béarn, Pliny in book 21 of the Natural History, chapter 11: They gush out agreeably, he says, and in most lands elsewhere some are cold, some hot, some lukewarm, as among the Tarbelli, a people of Aquitaine, and in the Pyrenean mountains, separated by a short distance. To which the noble man Joseph Scaliger adds: Those who have seen and drunk the waters of the Benearnese woodland in the Pyrenees will not doubt that Pliny had them in mind. The inhabitants have lofty spirits; they are vigorous and brave, skilled in arms, open and entirely free of guile; they are affable and most inclined to every courtesy, yet at the same time cautious and eloquent in their subtle speech. They love liberty and enjoy great immunities and privileges. Great men born there show that these people are not unfit to take up various branches of learning. All of them aspire to nobility, and those who are truly noble strive more to act well and bravely than to dress splendidly and softly. Among themselves the first place is held by the illustrious families, which are said to have come from the Cantabri, Grammont and Luffea. The baronies that shine in dignity are Mirens, Iadre, Monens, Saint-Colombe, Fsganalabagne, Coderch, Navailles, Castelnau, Maseres, Luz, Suz, and others.

units.la: Sedes hic olim suæ fuerunt Benearnensibus, Eloronensibus & aliis. Civitatem Benearnensium nominat Notitia Provinciarum sub Aquitania tertia Novempopulania, vel Octava Viennensi; hodie Le Pais de Bearn. Scribitur ibidem & Civitas Eloronensis nunc, L'Evesché d'Oleron en Bearn. Precianos etiam, quos cum aliis Aquitaniæ Populis recensel Cæsar, nonnulli, ut Vigenereus habet, in suis ad Cæsarem Adnotationibus esse volunt, ubi hodie Bearn; alij, ubi Precins quidam, quo loco Bayona.
units.tr: The seats here were once those of the Benearnenses, Eloronenses and others. The Notitia Provinciarum, under Aquitania Tertia Novempopulana, or Eighth Viennensis, names the city of the Benearnenses; today it is Le Pais de Béarn. There it is also written city of the Eloronenses, now L'Evêché d'Oloron en Béarn. Some, as Vigenère has it in his notes on Caesar, wish the Preciani, whom Caesar counts among the other peoples of Aquitaine, to be where Béarn is today; others place them where a certain Precins is, which is at the site of Bayonne.

units.la: Principum Benearnensium series hæc traditur:
units.tr: The following succession of the princes of Béarn is handed down:

units.la: Veteres Lacolæ, Benearnenses, Eloronenses, Tarbelli. Gaston Guilhelmi Moncadae Hispani Filius, Benearnensium Princeps primus. Uxore ducta Martha, Filia & Heredc un ca Vicecomitum Bigorritanum Comitis Filia, Bigerronum Comitatum Dominiis suis adquisivit. Duas foeerunt illa Filias. Margareta nupta Rogerio Bernardo, Comiti Foxensi, Rogerii Bernardi & Mengardis Narbonensis Filio. Hanc Patri successit Principe ..., Dominumque & Dominos Bearnie, Bigorra & Foxi conjunxit. ... conjugata Comiti Armagnacensi. Gaston II Princeps Benearnensis III, Comes Foxensis & Bigorra. Uxor Joanna Lodoici Franci, Ebroicensis Comitis Filia. Dionisia, Comiti Filia Comitis Fezensacensium. Constantia Comitis Antonii Levysi Mitegonis Dynastae. Joanna, Petro Aragonio in matrimonium data. Gaston III, Princeps Benearnensis IV. Uxorem habuit Leonoram Comingensem, Comitis Convenarum Filiam. Rogerius Bernardus, Moncadae Dynasta, Vicecomes Castelloboni, vel Castelbonni. Gaston IV Princeps Benearnensis V. laudatus plurimam ob Proditionem. Uxor Agnes, Karoli Navarrae Regis Soror. Marcus, Vicecomes Castelloboni, Gastonis IV Successor, Princeps Benearnensis VI. Uxor Joanna Aragonia. Marcia deficientibus Masculis, Fratri Markus successit. Princeps Benearnensis VII. Uxor Azcumbaldi, Capitalis Buchisij. Gaston, quem Pater suis manibus interfecit. Joanna, Princeps Benearnensis VIII Comes Foxij & Bigorrae, Moncadae Dominus. Uxor Maria Navarrae, ab Agnete nominatur, & Joannam Albretanam. Gaston Captalis Buchisius, Francici Nominis Inimicus, Candalecorum Comitatus Progenitor. Uxor Joanna, Philippi Atrebi Filia. Archambaudus Nosleij Dynasta. Petrus Episcopus Elicatensis, postea Cardinalis, & Legatus, qui Collegium Fori Tolosae esse, redditusque dotavit.
units.tr: The ancient Lacoli, Benearnenses, Eloronenses, Tarbelli. Gaston, son of Guilhelm of Moncada, a Spaniard, the first Prince of Béarn. Having married Martha, the only daughter and heiress of the Viscount of Bigorre, a count's daughter, he acquired the County of Bigorre for his lordships. They had two daughters. Margaret, married to Roger Bernard, Count of Foix, son of Roger Bernard and Mengarde of Narbonne. She was succeeded by her father, the Prince ..., and he joined the lordship and lordships of Béarn, Bigorre and Foix. ... married to the Count of Armagnac. Gaston II, the third Prince of Béarn, Count of Foix and Bigorre. His wife Joan, daughter of Louis of France, Count of Évreux. Dionisia, daughter of a count, daughter of the Count of Fezensac. Constance, of Count Antoine Levis of Mirepoix, lord. Joan, given in marriage to Peter of Aragon. Gaston III, the fourth Prince of Béarn. He had as wife Leonor of Comminges, daughter of the Count of the Convenae. Roger Bernard, lord of Moncada, Viscount of Castelbó or Castelbonne. Gaston IV, the fifth Prince of Béarn, much praised for his great treachery. His wife Agnes, sister of Charles, King of Navarre. Mark, Viscount of Castelbó, successor of Gaston IV, the sixth Prince of Béarn. His wife Joan of Aragon. Marcia, the males failing, Mark's brother succeeded. The seventh Prince of Béarn. His wife of Azcumbaldus, chief of Buchis. Gaston, whom his father killed with his own hands. Joan, the eighth Prince of Béarn, Count of Foix and Bigorre, lord of Moncada. His wife Maria of Navarre, named by Agnes, and Joan of Albret. Gaston, Captal of Buch, an enemy of the French name, ancestor of the counts of Candale. His wife Joan, daughter of Philip of Artois. Archambaud, lord of Noailles. Peter, Bishop of Élicante, later Cardinal and Legate, who endowed the college of Foix at Toulouse and its revenues.

units.la: Gaston V, Princeps Benearnensis VIII, Comes Foxij, &c. Uxor Eleonora, Joannis Navarrae Regis Filia: quae vidua, post Patris Excessum, Regnum est potita. Gaston VI, Princeps Benearnensis X, Comes Foxij Bigorrae Viennae, &c. Obiit ante Patrem, Regnum Navarrae non accepit. Uxorem Magdalenam Caroli VII Galliarum Regis Filiam. Joannes Foxius, Vicecomes Narbonensis, Uxor Maria, Karoli Valesij, Ducis Aurelianensis Filia. Alii, utrumque lexus. Franciscus Foxius, Rex Navarrae XXIV, Aze Eleonorae Successit, Princeps Benearnensis X, Comes Foxij, &c. Obiit 1517, sepultus in Lascarbanis oppido. Katharina Regina Navarrae XXV, Princeps Benearnensis VIII, Comes Foxij, &c. Nuptae Joanni Alani Magni Filio Dynastae Albretano, eique Regnum in dotem attulit. Gallo, Comes Foxij, Dux Nemausi. Acie cecidit contra Iulium II, Pontificem Maximum. Uxor Maria Caroli I Ducis Borbonii Filia, Imprudens. Germana, nupta Ferdinando Regi Aragoniae, inde Ferdinando Regi Calabriae. Henricus Albretanus, Rex Navarrae XXVI, Princeps Benearnensis XIII, Comes Foxij, &c. Obiit 1518. Uxor Margareta Valesia, Karoli Eduliminensium Comitis Filia, Francisci I Regis Franciae Soror, Karoli Alenconij Vidua. Karolus crinitus ad Neapolim, extra matrimonium. Filiae aliquot. Joanna Albretana Regina Navarrae XXVII, Princeps Benearnensis XIIII, Comes Foxij, &c. Desponsata Gulielmo Clivie Duci, nupsit ex Pontificis Maximi dispensatione Antonio Borbonio, Vendomae Duci, qui Socero successit in Regno. Obiit alia Parisiis 1572. Henricus Borbonius Galliarum Monarcha (Successor Henrici III) Navarrae Rex XXVIII, Princeps Benearnensis XV, Comes Foxij, &c. Katharina.
units.tr: Gaston V, the eighth Prince of Béarn, Count of Foix, etc. His wife Eleanor, daughter of John, King of Navarre; she, being a widow after her father's death, took possession of the kingdom. Gaston VI, the tenth Prince of Béarn, Count of Foix, Bigorre, Vienne, etc. He died before his father and did not receive the kingdom of Navarre. He married Magdalen, daughter of Charles VII, King of the French. Joan of Foix, Viscount of Narbonne, wife Maria, daughter of Charles of Valois, Duke of Orléans. Others, of both sexes. Francis of Foix, the twenty-fourth King of Navarre, succeeded his mother Eleanor, the tenth Prince of Béarn, Count of Foix, etc. He died in 1517 and was buried in the town of Lescar. Catherine, the twenty-fifth Queen of Navarre, eighth Prince of Béarn, Count of Foix, etc. She married Joan of Albret, son of the great John of Alain, lord of Albret, and brought him the kingdom as her dowry. Gaston, Count of Foix, Duke of Nemours. He fell in battle against Julius II, the Supreme Pontiff. His wife Maria, daughter of Charles I, Duke of Bourbon, imprudent. Germaine, married to Ferdinand, King of Aragon, afterwards to Ferdinand, King of Calabria. Henry of Albret, the twenty-sixth King of Navarre, thirteenth Prince of Béarn, Count of Foix, etc. He died in 1518. His wife Margaret of Valois, daughter of Charles, Count of Angoulême, sister of Francis I, King of France, widow of Charles of Alençon. Charles the Bearded, at Naples, outside of marriage. Several daughters. Joan of Albret, the twenty-seventh Queen of Navarre, fourteenth Princess of Béarn, Countess of Foix, etc. Betrothed to William, Duke of Cleves, she married, by dispensation of the Supreme Pontiff, Antoine of Bourbon, Duke of Vendôme, who succeeded his father-in-law in the kingdom. The other died at Paris in 1572. Henry of Bourbon, Monarch of the French (successor of Henry III), the twenty-eighth King of Navarre, fifteenth Prince of Béarn, Count of Foix, etc. Catherine.

units.la: Metropolis porro Benearnia est Castrum Palum: sic Docti, Latine scribentes, vocant, quod vulgo Pau. Sedes hic Principum: fastuosumque Aedificium ab Henrico Albretano Navarrae Rege, Christianissimi Regis Henrici IV Avo Materno, extructum. Tribunal ibidem Benearnense, ab eodem Henrico institutum, & Curia totius Principatus suprema, ubi Controversiae omnes dijudicantur secundum Regionis Leges & Consuetudines. fawin. Nuperi Arausiones Principes cum ex Cabillonensi, tum ex Nassavica Stemmate orti ita se habent:
units.tr: The metropolis of Béarn is further the castle of Pau: so learned men writing in Latin call it, which in the vernacular is Pau. Here is the seat of the princes, and a magnificent building erected by Henry of Albret, King of Navarre, maternal grandfather of the most Christian King Henry IV. There is also the Tribunal of Béarn, instituted by the same Henry, and the supreme court of the whole principality, where all controversies are decided according to the laws and customs of the region. The recent princes of Orange, sprung both from the Chabillon and the Nassau stemma, stand thus:

units.la: Stemma Cabillonense:
units.tr: Cabillon pedigree:

units.la: Joannes Cabillonensis Ludovici Patris unicus heres, duxit Mariam Baudiam, Reinoldi Baudi Arausiorum Principis Filiam & Heredem. Primus sua familia factus est Aurasiensium Principes.
units.tr: John of Cabillon, the only heir of his father Louis, married Maria Baux, daughter and heiress of Raimond de Baux, Prince of Orange. He was the first of his family to become Prince of Orange.

units.la: Ludovicus Cabillonensis, Aurasicum Princeps. Uxorem illi fecerunt Joannam Henrici ultimi Comitis Mompelgardi Filiam, & Eleonoram Armagnaci Patre ex.
units.tr: Louis of Cabillon, Prince of Orange. He was given as his wife Joanna, daughter of Henry, the last Count of Montbéliard, and Eleanor, daughter of the Count of Armagnac.

units.la: Gulielmus Cabillonensis, Aurasicum Princeps, cui Uxor fuit Katharina, Soror Francisci Ducis Britanniae.
units.tr: William of Cabillon, Prince of Orange, whose wife was Katharina, sister of Francis, Duke of Brittany.

units.la: Ludovicus Cabillonensis, qui cum Karolo Burgundo bello contra Helvetios periit.
units.tr: Louis of Cabillon, who died in the war against the Swiss alongside Charles the Bold.

units.la: Hugo Cabillonensis, Chountau-guanus & Dulcia Domina. Obiit anno MCCCXLV.
units.tr: Hugh of Cabillon, Count of Chountau-guanus and Lady of Dulcia. He died in the year 1345.

units.la: Joannes Cabillonensis, Aurasicum Princeps, Uxores eius, 1 Joanna, Karoli Ducis Barbarici Filia, Hedwigis et Elisabetha, Antonii Leuchtenburgi Filia. Charus Comes, ex qua nati:
units.tr: John of Cabillon, Prince of Orange. His wives: (1) Joanna, daughter of Charles, Duke of Bar; (2) Hedwig and Elizabeth, daughter of Anton of Leuchtenberg. Dear Count, by whom were born:

units.la: Philippus Cabillonensis, Aurasicum Princeps, Uxor eius Neapolitana, Portis Florentinus, anno MCDXLIII, stabilis ut vixit.
units.tr: Philip of Cabillon, Prince of Orange. His wife was a Neapolitan, Portia of Florence. He died in the year 1543, as steadfast as he had lived.

units.la: Claudia Cabillonensis, Aurasicum Princeps, omnium Fortunatarum Fratris Heres. Nupta Henrico Nassavio.
units.tr: Claudia of Cabillon, Prince of Orange, heir of all the property of her fortunate brother. She was married to Henry of Nassau.

units.la: Renatus Nassavius Aurasicum Princeps.
units.tr: René of Nassau, Prince of Orange.

units.la: Stemma Nassavium.
units.tr: Nassau pedigree.

units.la: Joannes Junior Comes Nassavius, Dillenburgi, Vianda, Breda, &c. Dominus. Uxor Elisabetha, Henrici Landgravii Hassiae, & Annae Comitatus Catzenelnbogensis Heredis Filia.
units.tr: John the Younger, Count of Nassau, lord of Dillenburg, Vianden, Breda, etc. His wife was Elizabeth, daughter of Henry, Landgrave of Hesse, and of Anna, heiress of the County of Katzenelnbogen.

units.la: Henricus Comes Nassavius, Dillenburgensis Dominus, Hispaniae Aurei Velleris Eques, Heres Cabillonensis. Obiit anno MDXXIII. Uxor Claudia, Joannis Cabillonensis Filia.
units.tr: Henry, Count of Nassau, lord of Dillenburg, Knight of the Golden Fleece of Spain, heir of Cabillon. He died in the year 1523. His wife was Claudia, daughter of John of Cabillon.

units.la: Renatus Comes Nassavius & Catzenelnbogensis, Vianda & Dillenburgi Dominus, Hispaniae Aurei Velleris Eques adoptatus, & Aurasicum Princeps nominatus. Obiit anno MDLXI, Labore Quinquelibus; Gulielmo Patruele heredem instituto. Uxor Anna Lothoringa, quae postea nupsit Philippo Croiensi.
units.tr: René, Count of Nassau and Katzenelnbogen, lord of Vianden and Dillenburg, adopted Knight of the Golden Fleece of Spain, and named Prince of Orange. He died in the year 1561, at Labore Quinquelibus, having named as his heir his cousin William. His wife was Anna of Lorraine, who afterwards married Philip of Croÿ.

units.la: Gulielmus Senior, Dives cognomine, Comes Nassavius, Catzenelnbogensis, &c. Obiit anno MDLXXIV. Duas habuit Uxores, V Valburgim Egmontanam, Perillem, & Juliannam, Bothonis Comitis Stolbergensis Filiam, matrem ex ipso factam illi Liberorum, in quis Primogenitus.
units.tr: William the Elder, called the Rich, Count of Nassau, Katzenelnbogen, etc. He died in the year 1574. He had two wives: (1) Walburga of Egmont, daughter of Perille; and (2) Juliana, daughter of Count Bothos of Stolberg, who bore him children, among whom the firstborn.

units.la: Gulielmus Aurasicum Princeps, Comes Nassavius, &c. Heres rebus praeclare domi militiaeque gestis nobilissimus. Obiit confectus ab Sulumillo Sicario de plus anno MDLXII, quarto kalendas Junii. Quatuor ordine duxit Uxores; quarum I Anna Maximiliani Egmondani, Comitis Buranii Filia & Heredem, ex qua nati.
units.tr: William, Prince of Orange, Count of Nassau, etc. The heir, most noble in his distinguished deeds at home and in war. He was killed, worn down by the assassin Sulumillus, in the year 1562 (more than one year), on the fourth day before the Kalends of June. He married four wives in succession; of the first, Anna, daughter and heiress of Maximilian of Egmont, Count of Buren, by whom were born children.

units.la: Maria Nassavia, Philippi Comitis Hohenloi Conjux. Adrianus Guilielmus Nassavius Aurasicum Princeps, Comes Buranus, Hollandiae &c. Dominus.
units.tr: Maria of Nassau, wife of Philip, Count of Hohenlohe. Adrian William of Nassau, Prince of Orange, Count of Buren, lord of Holland, etc.

units.la: CAP. XLVII.
units.tr: CHAP. XLVII.

units.la: Burgundiae Comitatus.
units.tr: The County of Burgundy.

units.la: TANTVM de Principatibus, qui licet in Francia, Francorum tamen Imperium non agnoscunt: explicandi succedunt eiusdem generis Comitatus, Burgundiae & Aquitanicum.
units.tr: So much for the principalities which, although they lie in France, do not acknowledge the rule of the Franks. Next I shall describe the counties of the same kind, Burgundy and Aquitanicum.

units.la: Unde Nomen Burgundiae, dictum cap. XLI, ubi docui Regnum olim circa annum cIↄ xxxiv bipartitum abiisse in Ducatum & Comitatum: quorum ille versus Occidentem, Burgundia Inferior & Regia: hic, ad Orientem, Inferior & Imperialis:
units.tr: Hence the name of Burgundy, mentioned in chapter 41, where I showed that the kingdom, divided in two around the year 934, passed into a duchy and a county. Of these, the duchy lies to the west and is Lower and Royal Burgundy; the county lies to the east and is Lower and Imperial.

units.la: BVRGVNDIAE COMITATVS Francis audit Franche Comté, id est, Liber Comitatus. Provincia namque plane sub suo est Comite; ab omnibus, ut aiunt, Tributis & Exactionibus libera. Feudum est Imperii, sub protectione Bernensium Helveriorum. Conregionales illi sunt ad Septemtrionem Lotaringa Superiorque Germania: ad Occidentem Burgundiae Ducatus; qua Oriens est, occurrunt Helvetij; qua Meridies, Allobroges & Segusiani. Longitudo xc, latitudo lx est milliarium. Regio Silvis, Montibus, Vallibus gratissima vicissitudine spectatur variata: uberis Agri, qui Pecori alendo; faciendae Sementi, Arboribus serendis, Vinetis Vini laudatissimi sustollendis commodissimus. Varii generis videre est ibi Animalia magnamque iumentorum & Pecudum copiam. Granvellenses Equos Gradarios, Canesque eiusdem tractus ferocissimos probant omnes. Summa est ubique Tritici, Siligi-
units.tr: The County of Burgundy is called Franche-Comté by the French, that is, the Free County. The province is entirely under its own count and, as they say, free from all tributes and exactions. It is an Imperial fief, under the protection of the Bernese Helvetians. Its neighbouring regions are Lorraine and Upper Germany to the north, the Duchy of Burgundy to the west, the Helvetii where it faces east, and the Allobroges and Segusiani to the south. Its length is 90 miles and its breadth 60. The region, with its forests, mountains and valleys, presents a most pleasing variety of scenery. Its fields are rich and very well suited to pasturing livestock, sowing grain, planting trees and raising vineyards that yield the most praised wine. Many kinds of animals are to be seen there, and a great abundance of draught animals and cattle. Everyone commends the horses of Granvelle for their pacing, and the very fierce dogs of this district. Everywhere there is the greatest fertility of wheat, rye

units.la: Tt Siliginis, Hordei, Avenæ Fabarum, Milii, aliorumque Leguminum fertilitas. Arborum haud minor fecunditas. Ager patium, præterim qua umbilicus est & Regionis meditullium. Colles habet præstantissimorum, primaque nobilitatis Vinorum feraces. Præterunter reliquis bonita e, quæ colliguntur ad Arlosiam, Fadam, Grimoniam Aream, Postetinum, Lothanum, Casseum Karoit, Villephonum, Gyum, Mo clium: quorum quadam, cum primis Irbosium natus in suo Territorio suam etiam Nomenclaturam communicant. Quod prope Gyum nascitur cum Optimis consuevit certare; vehi solitum in Germaniam, non quidem publicitus distrahendum, sed distribuendum Magnatibus: Apud Arlosiam & Fadanos Vasa Vinaria sunt adeo magna, ut Domos altitudine videtur æquare. Prope Regiam Veterum Burgundiæ Regum, quæ Accolis hodie Chambrette an Roy, ex Terra Gypsum, Materiam Calci similem, effodiunt. Eruitur ibidem & in Dolano Agro in Magnatum sepulturas Marmor candidi coloris, quod Λαβασεύτης Græcis appellatur: & aliud nigerrimum, maculis purpureis variatum. Quatuor fere milliaribus Bitontione versus Aquilonem Antrum est in Monte, quod hiemè fervet, æstate vero frigore riget. Flumina scindunt eam beantque plurimum non pauca, Arar, Dubis, Longnonius, Danum, Lupus, alij. De Arari dictum alibi. Dubis totus ad hunc Comitatum pertinet. Δαύβις Prolemæo vocatur: Apud Iulianum Imperatorem Epistola ad Maximum Philosophum non sine Mendi suspicione Δαυσβις dicitur. Aldubis est Cætari, si proba sit conjectura Fulvii Ursini. In aliis Codicibus Aldusdubis & Aidnasilis vitiose legitur Vulgo Doux: Oritur ex Monte Iura paullo supra Pagum amœnissimum, quinque instar opidi, Motam. Miror tamen, quod Paradinus scribat Dubis Fontem esse haud procul ab Arari. Dubis porro, corpto ab Meridie in Septemtrionem curtu, per Pontium Lacum lapsus, nonnullis Amfractibus prætergressus Pontarlum, Mortuam & Vafrum, Fanum petit S. Hippolyti: unde in Occidentem flexus, ad Pagum Chasteiot versus Africum tendens, Velumnonemque permeans & facta ad Dolam Insula, post multas ambages receptoque Fluvios prope Virdunum Arari commiscetur. Totus etiam Burgundiæ Superioris est Longuenus, vulgo Longnon, qui in Lotaringiæ Finibus ortus, variis Opidis Pagisque lustratis, paullo supra Auxonam in Ararim se fundit. Danum evomit ex sinuoso recessu Montis ardui, Syrofo, grandi & celeberrimo Pago, incumbens, hoc modo: Postquam descenderis, est Antrum profundi Præcipitij, & intus Fons imperscrutabilis profunditatis latitudine fortitan decem passuum. Huic Rupes horrendæ imminent; quæ contemplantibus horrorem plane incutiunt: ac per Gurgitem altissimum tanta Aquarum copia ebullit, ut fluvium in ipso ortu (dictum incredibile) Flumen Navigijs, si ob rupes & saxa, per quæ devolvitur, liceret, satis capax esset. Incolis hoc Flumen Dain vocatur. Fluvios in se recipit varios: cum alijs prope Fontem, Senam, Amnem fama & natura ingenium.
units.tr: rye, barley, oats, beans, millet and other pulses. The fruitfulness of the trees is no less. The land is open, especially where the navel and the middle of the region lie. It has hills that bear the finest wines, which rank first in renown. Among the other good places are those gathered around Arlosia, Fada, Grimonia Area, Postetinum, Lothanum, Casseum Karoit, Villephonum, Gyum and Moclium. Some of these, especially Irbosium, which is born in its own territory, also share their own name. The wine that grows near Gyum has customarily competed with the best; it was usually carried into Germany, not to be sold publicly but to be distributed among the great men. At Arlosia and Fada the wine vats are so large that they seem to equal the houses in height. Near the old royal palace of the kings of Burgundy, which the locals today call Chambrette an Roy, they dig up gypsum from the earth, a material similar to lime. In the same place, and in the Dole district, marble of a white colour is dug up for the tombs of the great men; the Greeks call it labasseutes [Λαβασεύτης]. There is also a very black marble variegated with purple spots. About four miles north of Bitonsione there is a cave in a mountain that boils in winter and freezes in summer. Many rivers cut through this land and water it: the Arar, Dubis, Longnonius, Danum, Lupus and others. The Arar has been discussed elsewhere. The Dubis belongs entirely to this county. Ptolemy calls it Dauvis [Δαύβις]; in the letter of the Emperor Julian to the philosopher Maximus it is called Dausbis [Δαυσβις], though not without suspicion of error. If Fulvio Orsini's conjecture is sound, it is the Aldubis of Caesar. In other manuscripts it is read wrongly as Aldusdubis and Aidnasilis; commonly it is called the Doux. It rises from Mount Jura a little above the very pleasant village of Motam, which is like a small town. I am surprised, however, that Paradin writes that the Dubis is a spring not far from the Arar. The Dubis then runs from south to north in a short course, glides through the Pontium Lake, passes Pontarlier, Morteau and Vaufrey with several windings, and makes for the shrine of St Hippolytus. From there it turns westward and, heading southwest toward the village of Chasteiot, passes Velumno. After making an island at Dole, and after many twists, it receives the other streams and mingles with the Arar near Verdun. The Longuenus, commonly called the Longnon, belongs entirely to Upper Burgundy. It rises on the borders of Lorraine, flows past various towns and villages, and pours itself into the Arar a little above Auxonne. The Danum pours forth from a winding recess of a steep mountain, overhanging Syrof, a large and very famous village, in this manner: after you have descended, there is a cave of deep precipice, and inside it a spring of unfathomable depth, perhaps ten paces across. Frightful cliffs overhang it, which plainly strike horror into those who gaze upon them. Through a very deep whirlpool such a quantity of water bubbles up that the river, at its very source (an incredible thing to say), would be large enough for navigation, if the rocks and stones over which it tumbles allowed it. The locals call this river the Dain. It receives various streams into itself; with others, near the spring, the Seine, a river in name and nature as in character.
