units.la: Sena. tem, ex Fons-Sequanæ Pago, qui immensus multisque constans Villis, ab eo denominatus, exorientem, & saxosa convalle per Planeas & Sienum vicos labentem iuxta Burgum oppidum. Et sicalis ix auctus Fluminibus decurrens ac praeterlabens per Superioris Burgundiæ meridionalem partem, in Rodanum tribus Lugduno versus Orientem miliaribus invehitur: unde Dani nomen in posterioribus Rodani sunt qui arbitrantur latere. Pisces habet Danus gratissimi saporis, præter alios Troctam & Auratam. Lupus vel Lupa, vulgo Loue, altissimus, lautissimus, rapacissimus Burgundiæ Fluvius, multa habet Piscium genera, inter quos numerantur Alosa, Barbatulus, Anguilla, & Aurata. Gritur paulo supra Villephanum in Ovino pago, & non procul ab Dola cum Dubide in Aratim aquis properantibus devolvitur. Lacus habet hæc Burgundia ingentes & mirabiles: inter eos non postremi loci, cui ab Voraginibus nomen, mirum Naturæ ludentis opus. Super enim Aqua et Limus, qui aeco durescit, ut Continens videatur; super quo tamen Equites Currusq. tecure non ambulant, sed soli Pedites. Is coelo pluvioso & nebuloso non emergit, nisi Serenitas sit futura, tunc per Foramina brevi tempore auctus totam Columbinam Planitiem rigat. Fi Mons celsus ab Oriente imminet, unde crebri Fontes in illum diffluunt. Inter Nozeretum porro & Ripariam alius est Lacus in Bonvalli, Lupis, Parcis, & aliis Piscibus abundans, qui septimo quoque anno in aliquot hebdomadas sufflugiens & delitescens, rerum emergit. Quæ res in Miraculum exit, Fidemque vincit. Tractus huius Comitatus Aultralior Lacubus scatet: Videre ibi est, qui vernacule Mai.teux Major Minorque; Nartay, profunditatis vix credendæ; Vernoy, duo Chambiux, Frogeray, Ronchault & alij. Thermæ quoque cum magna Calidarum Aquarum copia ad Luxovium oppidum scaturiunt.
units.tr: The Seine. It comes from the village of Fonts-Sequanae, which is vast and made up of many villages, named after it. It rises and flows through a rocky valley past the villages of Planeas and Sienum, next to the town of Burgum. Increased by nine rivers as it runs on, and flowing past the southern part of Upper Burgundy, it is carried into the Rhône three miles east of Lyon. For this reason some think the name Danum lives on in the later name Rhodanus. The Danum has fish of a most pleasant flavour, among them the trout and the gilthead. The Lupus, or Lupa, commonly called the Loue, is the highest, richest and most rapacious river of Burgundy. It has many kinds of fish, among which are counted the shad, the barbel, the eel and the gilthead. It rises a little above Villefans in the village of Ovin, and not far from Dole it is carried with the Dubis into the waters of the Arar, which hurry on. This Burgundy has huge and marvellous lakes. Among them, not the least is one named after the Voragines, a marvellous work of playful nature. For upon it there is water and mud which hardens into what looks like solid ground, yet upon it horsemen and carriages do not walk safely, only foot soldiers. In rainy and cloudy weather it does not rise, unless fair weather is about to come; then through holes it swells for a short time and waters the whole Columbine plain. A high mountain overhangs it from the east, from which many springs flow down into it. Between Nozeret and Riparia there is another lake, in Bonvallis, abounding in pike, perch and other fish, which every seventh year sinks and lies hidden for some weeks, and then rises again. This thing becomes a wonder and surpasses belief. The part of this county toward the south is full of lakes: there one can see those called in the vernacular Maiteux, Major and Minor; the Nartay, of depth scarcely to be believed; the Vernoy; the two Chambiux, Frogeray, Ronchault and others. Hot springs also gush forth with a great abundance of warm waters at the town of Luxeuil.

units.la: Floruerunt longe lateque his locis olim Sequani. Sic Cæsar lib. 1, & alibi, Cicero in Epist. ad Atticum, Ammianus Marcellinus lib. xv, Sidonius lib. 1. Epist. xi, aliique nominant; qui Σηκανοὶ Straboni libro iv; Σηκανοὶ, Ptolemæo, Σηκανοὶ, Dioni Cocceio. Hodie Le Pais de Besançon & Franche Comte, quæ Maxima Sequanorum apud Sex. Rufum. Scribit Cæsar lib. 1 Montem Iuram Sequanorum Fines ab Helvetiis dividere. Sequanum, Provinciam appellat Notitia Imperij Occidentis. Civitas Sequanorum universim pro tota Ditione, in Inscriptione, quam Lugduni exscriptam posui cap. xxiv. Dumnorigem gratia & largitione apud Sequanos plurimum potuisse, notat Cæsar lib. 1. item eodem lib. & vi Ariovistum in Germanorum Regem ab sequanis contra Eduos evocatum, tertiam partem Agri Sequani, qui esset optimus totius Galliæ, occupasse. Alia praetereo. De iis Strabo lib. iv. πέρι δὲ ἡ Ἀρ... Σηκανοὶ, διαφόροι κ... Sequanos etiam ultra Iuram versus Euronotum habitasse, innuit Entropius lib. vi. Helvetii, inquit, qui nunc Sequani appellantur. Sequanus, τὸ ἐθνικὸν, nominatur in Inscriptione, quæ Lugduni legitur in Templo vetustissimo D. Petri, ad Basin Columnæ, quæ ad sinistram est Aræ Maximæ: Q. PVLIO. SEVERINO SEQVANO. OMNIB HONORIBVS. IN TER. SVOS FVNCTO &c.
units.tr: The Sequani flourished long ago far and wide in these places. So Caesar in book 1 and elsewhere, Cicero in his letter to Atticus, Ammianus Marcellinus in book 15, Sidonius in book 1, letter 11, and others name them. Strabo in book 4 calls them Sēkanoi [Σηκανοὶ]; Ptolemy and Dio Cocceianus likewise. Today it is called Le Pais de Besançon and Franche-Comté, which Sextus Rufus calls the Greater Sequania. Caesar in book 1 writes that the Jura mountains divide the territory of the Sequani from the Helvetii. The Notitia of the Western Empire calls it the Province of the Sequani. The inscription, which I copied at Lyon and set down in chapter 24, uses "the state of the Sequani" to mean the whole domain. Caesar in book 1 notes that Dumnorix had very great influence among the Sequani through favour and generosity; also in the same book and in book 6 he notes that Ariovistus, summoned by the Sequani against the Aedui as king of the Germans, seized a third part of the territory of the Sequani, which was the best in all Gaul. I pass over other matters. Strabo in book 4 speaks of these people. Entropius in book 6 hints that the Sequani also lived beyond the Jura toward the south-east: "The Helvetii," he says, "who are now called the Sequani." The adjective Sequanus [τὸ ἐθνικὸν] is named in the inscription read in the ancient temple of St Peter at Lyon, at the base of the column on the left of the Great Altar: "To Quintus Pulius Severinus, a Sequanian, who held all offices among his own people," and so on.

units.la: De Antiquis huius Burgundiæ Comitibus, Stirpis etiam Imperatoriæ Fanciceque, multi multa memoriae produnt. Nuperorum hoc est Stemma:
units.tr: Many writers have recorded much about the ancient counts of this Burgundy, and also about its imperial and French lineage. This is the genealogy of more recent times:

units.la: Philippus v Cognomine Longus Francorum Rex. Vxor Ioanna Orbona, vel Otonis Burgundiæ Comitis, Fil. & Heres: Ioanna Comes Burgundiæ defuncta Othone, Avo materno & Roberto Aumaulo Ducis cum Otho (alij Eudo) Dux Burgundiæ, qui hoc Comitatu Ducatum Comitatumque continuavit. Philippus Burgundus ante Patrem mortuus. Philippus, Dux Comesque Burgundiæ, Avi Othonis Successor. Impuberis obiit. Maria uxor Philippo, Nepoti, vel Iohanne Ioanna successam, Comitatum ad ea est Burgundia. Nam Ducatum dedit filio suo Philippo, qui Avi cognominatus Francorum Rex Iohannes. Duces Brabantiæ Filia & Heres. Margarete Mararetta Mavaos, unica Pottii Heredi, Dux Brabantiæ &c. Comes Flandriæ, Superioris Burgundiæ, &c. Ioannes Cognomento Intrepidus. Philippus Bonus. units.tr: Philip V, surnamed the Tall, King of the Franks. Wife: Joan the Orphan, daughter and heir of Otto, Count of Burgundy. Joan, Countess of Burgundy, was widowed by Otto, her maternal grandfather, and Robert, Duke of Aumale. Otto (others say Eudo), Duke of Burgundy, who continued the duchy and county through this county. Philip of Burgundy died before his father. Philip, Duke and Count of Burgundy, successor to his grandfather Otto. He died without issue while still a minor. Mary, wife of Philip, grandson, or Joan, succeeded by Joan; by this means Burgundy came to the county. For she gave the duchy to her son Philip, who was surnamed John, King of the Franks, after his grandfather. She was married to Louis of Nevers, Count of Flanders. Louis the Male, Count of Flanders, Nevers and Rethel, and after his mother's death, Joseph of Bra... Wife Margaret, daughter and heiress of John III, Duke of Brabant. Margaret, Mararetta Mavaos, sole heiress of Pottius, Duke of Brabant, etc. Count of Flanders, of Upper Burgundy, etc. John, surnamed the Fearless. Philip the Good. Charles the Bold. Mary, married to Maximilian of Austria. Philip of Austria. Charles V, Emperor, etc. Philip, King of Spain, Philip, Monarch of Spain.

units.tr: As for the political state of this Free County: whenever the provincial assemblies are to be held, three estates convene, summoned in the name of the Count by the Prince of Orange, the Lord of Nozeret and Arlay. These are the nobles, the clergy and the towns. We owe this list of them to Gilbert Nozereno. Counts of the Upper Diocese: Montbéliard, Roche and Varax, Montrichard, Thoiray and Vaulgrenant, Vergy, Rey, Lisle-en-Noz; abbots: Cherlieu (Croissant), La Charité, Bizaine, Cornelieu, Tulley, Clairefontaine, Luxeuil, Belleranche, Grace-Dieu, Charlieu, Trois-Rois; priors: Vaucluse, Lanthenans, Cusance, Marteret, Jussey, Port-sur-Saône, Montreuil-sur-Sagone, Saint-Marcel; canons: Calemostier, and others in other places; towns: Gray, Vesoul, Montboisson, Jussey, Pesmes, Port-sur-Saône, Cromary, Mont-Justin, Faucogney; lords: Aumont and Saint-Loup, Saint-Martin, Taulans, Villeneuve, Rupt, Montgeveille, Châtillon and Rellevye, Conflandey, Mentaillon, Vellefaux, Dicey, Igny and Chemilly, d'Oiselet, Cicon, Trefves, Rainconnières, Cossebrune, Sombernon, Vallefaux, Bermont, d'Avilly, Mugnay, Vereur, Touraize, Citey, Provenchères, Grandmont, Velle, Cheurelous, Voisey, Dampierre, Fretey, Benta, Matay, Notrende, Tromarcy, Millesey, Maillerancourt, Myon, Bennenge, Villeroi-le-Lot, Cierlé, Betoncourt, Montaillotte, d'Amondans and de Fresne, Chaviré, Mortot, Mont-Saint-Léger, Cuvry, Montereau, Sorans and Lambry; and very many others. The Lower Counts are Ruffey and Saint-Aubin; baron, Chevreaux; abbots: Saint-Fugeau, Beaume, Baume, Mont-Sainte-Marie, Mont-Benoît, Beleen, Rauffières; priors: Mainneau, Vaucluse, Bonlieu, Mente, Lonsle-Saunier, Arbois, Mote, Syrod, Val-sur-Poligny, Mortau; canons of Saint-Maurice, Saint-Anatole, Saint-Michel, Salins; of Arbois, Poligny, Nozeret, and of other towns and places, others; towns: Salins, Aalois, Poligny, Pontarlier, Nozeret, Château-Charles, Montmorot, Orgelet. Lords: Conjonc and Andelot, Courtiaux and Le Pin, Saint-Amour, Argent, Laubespin, Pompet, Saint-Sorlin, Dannemarie and Tramecey, Bofia, Crête, Fétigny, Chambéry-Montaigu, Vercel, Rosay, Narigne, Beaufort, Nancy, L'Auge, Courtavon, Vertamboz, Largilla, Moiron, L'Esloille, Chasnée, Arfeuille, Coges, Bar, and Jousseaux, d'Augé-Muyre, Charrin, Charlin, Chaumes, Bretterières, Fontenay, Cogne, Chaux, Mantuet, Vadans, Villette, Les Arbois, Aiglepierre, Châteauvillain, Saint-Julien. Deserines, Verges, Chay, Champagne, Beaumont-le-Chemin, Villeneuve-Eleze, Orgelet, Châtes. The governor of the citadel of Joux, or Mont-Jura, Vincelle, Vinsneaux, and many others. Diocese of Dole: the lord of Givrey; Longepierre, and Rahon, Clerval; abbots: Billon, Saint-Vincent, Saint-Paul of Besançon, Acey; priors: Loye, Lanval, Damparis, Jouhe, Montrottier, Mote-sur-Hautepierre, Faye, Moutier-en-Seugne; canons of Dole, of Besançon, and others in other places; towns: Dole, Quingey, Ornans, Loye, Rochefort, Vercel; lords: Vaudrey, Rainans, Ruy, Montfort, Montrichard, Fertans, Maillot, Bermont, Cléron, Verchamps, Doffans, Port, Château-Rouillant, d'Abbans and Marchaux, Reculot, Chantrans, Mont-Grosfain, Mutigny, Chassey, Pareisey, Choisey, Saint-Ligier; Faye, Parrel, Chemin, Rahon, Champdivers, and Rasiveres, Rainchecourt, Vaisitre, Montrambert, Salins, Goussans, Chaverey, Ancier, and others. The nobility of this county, as we see from this, is very numerous. There are four families, however, which are recorded as tracing their origin from the kings and princes of Burgundy, or as having allied themselves with them by marriage: the De Vienne, to whom the epithet of Nobility is given; the De Vergy, to whom the title of Valiant is given; the De Chalon, who hold the name of Wealthy Lord and the title of the Principality of Orange; the De Neufchâtel, who are distinguished by their fiefs.

units.la: Quum autem Comitatus in tres, ut iam vidimus, Diœceses & Præfecturas, quæ Baillivatus vulgo, iuri facilius dicundo, divisa sit; Dolanam, Superiorem, Inferiorem:
units.tr: Since the county, as we have already seen, is divided into three dioceses and prefectures, which are commonly called bailiwicks, to make the administering of justice easier: Dole, Upper and Lower.

units.la: Primæ Sedes est Dola: Secundæ, Vesulij; Tertiæ, Polichnij: Singulis suæ sunt Vrbes, Opida, Pagi; quibus,cum Comitibus, Abbatibus, Prioribus, Canonicis Dominisque, ad Comitia Provincialia veniendi, ibique Sessionis & Suffragij ius est. Eorum, quæ principis loci paucis indicabo, postea alia quædam adscripturus.
units.tr: The seat of the first is Dole; of the second, Vesoul; of the third, Poligny. Each has its own cities, market towns and villages; to these, together with the counts, abbots, priors, canons and lords, belongs the right of coming to the provincial assembly, and there of sitting and voting. I shall briefly indicate the most notable of these, and afterwards add some others.

units.la: Dolana Dioecesi adcententur Dola, Quingeium, Ornatum, Rupes fortis, Vercellæ, Lona, Dola, Arce potens, totius Comitatus est Metropolis, reliquarumque Vrbium celeberrima: ad Dubim sita Fluvium, qui in duo hic brachia finditur. Putant quidam Ptolemæo esse Δώαφιον, lib. II. cap. IX, Sequanorum Vrbs. Nihil ibi earum rerum, quæ ad Civitatis splendorem faciunt, desideratur. Forum hic vidi reg. ntissimum & spaciotum; forma quadrata, longitudine tamen Latitudinem nonnihil superante. In parte Occidentali Prætorium est, cum Carceribus. Primarium Templum, quod pulcherrimum & admirandi operis, Deiparæ Virgini est sacratum. Academiam habet Dola veterem quidem, sed quæ circa annum cIↄ cccclxxxiv, sopitis bellis, tertio florere cœpit. In collegio Hieronymiano bibliotheca servatur multorum Auctorum & optimorum Codicum. Sedes hic Supremi Senatus, quo ab Inferioribus Comitatus Tribunalibus, absque ulteriore Provocatione, appellatur. Expugnatam vi ab Ambosio, perniciosoque Incendio funditus fere, anno cIↄ cccclxxix mense Maio, delectam. Pij Cives tensim restituerunt; Pontibusque variis, Mœnibus validissimis, stupendis Propugnaculis, magnificis Templis, & sumtuosissimis Ædificiis ornarunt. Quingium, vulgo Quingey, vetustissimum est oppidum in Lupiæ ripa situm: ab Ambosio solo adæquatum, nunc utcumque restauratum. Ornatum, Ornans, inter excelsissimos Montes, interfluente Lupa, piscoso Fluvio, positum: Nicolai Perrenoti Granvellani, Supremi Rerum Status Consiliarij & Sigillorum Cæsariæ Majestatis Custodis, ortu & natalibus nobile. Vrba, ni fallor, Antonini, in Itinere, quod ducitur Mediolano per Alpes Graias Argentoratum. Vide infra. Rupes-Fortis, Roche-Fort. Oppidulum, deditione captum, postquam aliquamdiu obsessum fuisset, ab Ambosio, anno cIↄ cccc lxxix. Mar xvii. Vercellarum oppidum Mœnia habet ruinis deformia. Lona, Pagus est amplissimus. Ad Superiorem Comitatus Dioecesin pertinent Graeum, Vesulium, Monf-Tolonis, Iussicum, Portus ad Sarnam, Cromarium, Monf-Iustini, Falconeum. Graeum, Gray, Vrbs præcipuis, quæ in Burgundiæ Comitatu connumeranda. Mœnia ipsa amœnissima situs in Araris ripa; Plateis, Fontibus, Templis, aliisque Ædificijs cum publicis tum privatis, superba. Terra Suburbia; Dives opum varianum, & nullius indiga cultus. Ad alteram Araris ripam patentes habet Campos, omnium rerum copia fœcundissimos; naturali Locorum Vbertate, grata Fructuum Varietate, mira Pascuorum Felicitate Convicinis antecellentes. Vesulium, Vesoul, ad Amnem locatum, qui haud procul inde Arari miscetur. Validissima habet Mœnia, Ædes luculenter exstructas, Solum valde vitiferum. Incendio vastatum est horrendo circa annum cIↄ Iↄ xxxiii. Monf-Tolonis, vel, ut alij contractius, Mombesium, Montbeliard, in dextra Lugoni Fluminis ripa conditum. Iussicum, Jussey, ad Continia Comitatus versus Septemtrionem, Fluvio adsitum, qui Ararim hic ingreditur. Portus super Sarnam, quibusdam Latine scribentibus Portuzona, Port sur Saone, secundum Araris Ripam positum. Cromarium, Cromary; Monf Iustini, Mont-justin; Falconeum, Faulcongney; suis singula sunt nobilitata bonis & Dotibus. Inferioris Comitatus Præfecturæ sunt Salina, Arbesium, Polschnium, Pontarlium, Nozeretum, Castrum Karoli, Mommoretum, Orgelotum. Salina, amplissima Civitas, toto terrarum Orbe celebris; ab salsis denominata Fontibus, Salequè inde igne densari solito: qui candore præstans in finitimas Regiones exportatus maximum huius Comitatus est Vectigal. Vrbs supra modum firmissimo Muro, celsissimisque Turribus munita; magnificis altisque Ædibus ornata. Per magnam angustamque Vallem inter horrendos altitudine Montes, Vinum tamen fundentes apricis in locis præstantissimum, extensæ adjacent Arces, Brachiorum instar, duæ; quarum quæ Austrialor in Rupe edita, Bracon vulgo dicitur; quæ ex adverso, ejusdem situs, Belin. Vallem ipsam olim Seodingam appellatam docet D. Anatolij historia. Fertiles quidem habet Agros, sed qui ob Loca concava montiumque asperitatem cultu difficiliores alioquin. Te 3
units.tr: To the Dole diocese belong Dole, Quingey, Ornans, Rochefort, Vercel, Lons. Dole, a city strong in its citadel, is the metropolis of the whole county and the most celebrated of the other towns, set on the Doubs river, which here splits into two arms. Some think it is Ptolemy's Δώαφιον [Dōaphion], a city of the Sequani, in book II, chapter IX. Nothing is lacking there of those things that add to a city's splendour. Here I have seen a very regular and spacious forum, square in shape, though somewhat longer than it is wide. On the western side is the praetorium, with its prisons. The chief temple, which is very beautiful and of wonderful workmanship, is dedicated to the Virgin Mother of God. Dole has an academy, old indeed, but which, after the wars were quieted, began to flourish again about the year 1584. In the Jesuit college a library of many authors and excellent manuscripts is kept. Here sits the Supreme Senate, to which appeals are made from the lower courts of the county without further recourse. It was taken by storm by Ambrosius, and nearly destroyed by a deadly fire, in May 1479. Its pious citizens gradually restored it, and adorned it with various bridges, very strong walls, remarkable bulwarks, magnificent temples and most sumptuous buildings. Quingey, commonly Quingey, is a very ancient town situated on the bank of the Loue; levelled to the ground by Ambrosius, it has now been restored after a fashion. Ornans, set among very high mountains, with the Lison, a fish-filled river, flowing through it, is noble by the birth and descent of Nicolas Perrenot de Granvelle, Councillor of the Supreme State Affairs and Keeper of the Seals of His Imperial Majesty. Vrba, unless I am mistaken, is the Antonine itinerary's town on the road that runs from Milan through the Graian Alps to Strasbourg. See below. Rupes-Fortis, Rochefort: a small town, taken by surrender after it had been besieged for some time, by Ambrosius, in the year 1479, March 17. The town of Vercellae has walls disfigured by ruins. Lona is a very large village. To the Upper Diocese of the county belong Gray, Vesoul, Montfort, Jussey, Port-sur-Saône, Cromary, Mont-Justin, Faucogney. Gray, the chief city, which is to be reckoned among the towns of the County of Burgundy. Its walls, set on the bank of the Saône, are very pleasant; it is distinguished by its squares, fountains, temples and other buildings, both public and private. Its suburbs are on the land; rich in wealth of various kinds, and needing no cultivation. On the other bank of the Saône it has open plains, most fertile in every kind of produce; surpassing its neighbours in the natural richness of the place, the pleasing variety of its fruits, and the remarkable abundance of its pastures. Vesoul, set by a river which joins the Saône not far from there. It has very strong walls, well-built houses, and a soil very rich in vines. It was devastated by a dreadful fire about the year 1533. Montfort, or, as others say more briefly, Mombelgard, Montbéliard, founded on the right bank of the river Lizaine. Jussey, on the boundary of the county towards the north, beside the river that enters the Saône here. Port-sur-Saône, by some writing in Latin Portus-Zona, Port-sur-Saône, situated on the bank of the Saône. Cromary, Cromary; Mont-Justin, Mont-Justin; Faucogney, Faucogney; each of these is distinguished by its own goods and endowments. The prefectures of the Lower County are Salins, Arbois, Poligny, Pontarlier, Nozeret, Château-Charles, Montmorot, Orgelet. Salins, a very large city, famous throughout the whole world; named from its salt springs, and from which salt is usually made by fire; which, excelling in whiteness and exported to the neighbouring regions, is the greatest revenue of this county. The city is fortified beyond measure with a very strong wall and very lofty towers; it is adorned with magnificent and high houses. Through a great and narrow valley, between frightful high mountains yet producing a most excellent wine in sunny places, two extended citadels lie adjacent, like arms; of these, the one on the southern rock, commonly called Bracon, and the one opposite, of the same situation, Belin. The history of Saint Anatole shows that the valley itself was formerly called Seodinga. It has fertile fields, indeed, but which, owing to the hollow places and the roughness of the mountains, are otherwise more difficult to cultivate.

units.la: Fontibus omnia puris
units.tr: Fountains everywhere, pure ones,

units.la: Hic sunt irrigua, & Rivi de Rupe cadentes,
units.tr: Here are the well-watered places, and streams falling down from the rock,

units.la: Prata per & Campos labuntur Murmure dulci.
units.tr: Gliding through meadows and fields with a sweet murmur.

units.la: Vrbem Forcia Fluvius rapidior perfluit: Molis, quæ ibi non paucæ, versandis aptus. Princeps Templum D. Anatolio dicatum est: reliqua sunt DD. Mauritii & Michaelis. Parochiæ sunt quatuor: D. Anatoly, Mauritij, Ioannis Baptistæ, Virginis Mariæ. Pauperum Xenodochia tria, duo quidem in Vrbe, Monte-Aurti & D. Bernardi; tertium Brachionis, in Rupe Occidentem versus. Arbosium, Arborosa Ammiano lib. xvi, Arboise; peramœno situm loco, omnium Rerum copia, imprimis optimo & in multâ ætatem durante Vino, quod inde Vin d'Arboise, florens & celebre. Undique sunt Montes; adspectu Fontium, Vinetorum, Arborum copia suavissimi. Arbosium creditur dictum, quod Arboribus conditum. Fructibus enim sic referta est hæc Vallis, ut Pomarium tota videri possit. Polichnium; vulgo Poligny: Vox creditur Græcæ Originis. Πολιχνιον tamen Platoni lib. 11. de Rep. aliisque, quod Latinis Oppidulum. Munitum est Mœnibus Turribusque pulcherrimis. Præter Arcem, cui nomen Grimonia, Forum habet angustissimum, Plateasque rectas & nitidas; quibus emundandis Rivuli sunt, miræ jucunditatis. Pontarium, Pontarlier, oppidum in ima duorum Montium planicie positum, secundum Dubidis ripam. Haud procul inde Arx est lura, munitissima & inexpugnabilis in Colle summo, loco admodum edito collocata, adeoque difficili adscensu & arduo, ut humanis viribus cessura vix videatur. Ad hanc multæ Helvetiorum copiæ Avorum nostrorum memoria sunt contritæ. Nozerethum, Nozereth, Oppidum est triangularis formæ, Loci natura (eminentiori enim impositum est colli) Ædificiorum splendore, Civium humanitate eximium. Emporium totius Burgundiæ celeberrimum. Non admodum amplum angusta quadam angustia quamvis amplissimas Burgundiæ Civitates superat. Nucillum antea dictum notat Gilbertus Cognatus, ab Nuciðus, quarum magnus ibi proventus; Nomen autem mutatum esse ab Ludovico Cabillonensi, ejus appellationis 1: Eum enim Hierosolymis in Burgundiam reversum, oppidum restauratum Nazarethum ab Galileæ Urbe vocasse: inde vero corruptum vulgo, mutatis litteris, Nozerethum esse nominatum. In australiore Oppidi Parte Arx est Principis (quam Plumbeam vocant, eo quod Plumbo sit intecta) amplissima, quadrata, communi cum Urbe Muro inclusa; Turribus octo præcelsis, præcipitibus Fossis, Machinis omne genus bellicis valida. Iucundus ob Loci amœnitatem, salubritatemque, & Venationis copiam, Arausiorum Principum ante funesta bella Recessus. Natus hic magnus Heros Philibertus Cabillonensis, Arausiorum Princeps. Nundinarum Ius huic oppido quater anno; statim post Pentecosten, Initio Novembris & Februarij, Primaque Quadragesimæ septimana. Festum porro D. Antonii (cui primarium Templum est dedicatum) ejus est generis, ut veteri ethnicoque ritu undique ingens confluat hominum multitudo, cum ob D. Antonium, tum ob elegantissimarum Puellarum Conventum, quo nullus in Burgundia celebratior. Is dies in locis, Ludis, Tripudijs, Convivisque peragitur. Castrum Karoli, Castel Chalon, oppidum ab Karolo Magno, ut volunt Incolæ, nuncupatum, situ validum, Monasterio celebre, in quod Nobilium tantum Filiæ Virgines recipiuntur. Monsmoretum, Mommoret, oppidum in Monte non arduo, vicinum Lonsaino, vulgo Lonlesaunier, à quo gloriæ suæ detrimentum est passum. Orgeletum, Orgelet, Opidum Mercimoniis florens. Incolæ Lanificium exercent. Pars altera cum Arce in edito est loco: altera plano, ad radices collis. Ager sterilior, rupibus saxisque asper: de cuius Incolis dici solitum, Ipsos habere Campos sine Graminibus; Fluvios sine Piscibus; Montes sine Nemoribus.
units.tr: The river Forcia flows through the town, rather swift. There are not a few mills, suited to turning. The chief temple is dedicated to St Anatolius; the others are to Saints Maurice and Michael. There are four parishes: St Anatolius, St Maurice, St John the Baptist, and the Virgin Mary. There are three almshouses for the poor, two in the town, Mont-Aurti and St Bernard's, and a third at Brachion, on the rock to the west. Arbosium, called Arborosa by Ammianus in book 16, is Arboise: a place of pleasant situation, with every abundance of things, and above all an excellent wine, which lasts for many years, and is therefore called Vin d'Arboise, flourishing and famous. There are mountains on every side; the sight of its springs, vineyards and abundance of trees is most delightful. Arbosium is thought to have been named from being full of trees (arbores), for this valley is so filled with fruit that the whole of it can look like an orchard. Polichnium, commonly Poligny: the name is thought to be of Greek origin. Yet Plato in book 11 of the Republic and others use πολιχνιον [polichnion] for what the Latins call a oppidulum, a little town. It is fortified with walls and very handsome towers. Besides the citadel, called Grimonia, it has a very narrow market place and straight, bright streets, which are cleaned by streams of wonderful pleasantness. Pontarium, Pontarlier, a town set on the lowest level plain between two mountains, beside the bank of the Doubs. Not far from there is the citadel of Iura, very strongly fortified and impregnable, on a high hill, placed in a very lofty spot, and so steep and hard to climb that it hardly seems likely to yield to human strength. Many Swiss forces were destroyed against it within the memory of our grandfathers. Nozerethum, Nozeret, is a town of triangular shape, distinguished by the nature of its site (for it is set on a rather high hill), the splendour of its buildings, and the courtesy of its citizens. It is the most famous trading centre of all Burgundy. It is not very large, but in a certain narrowness it surpasses the most spacious cities of Burgundy. Gilbert Cognatus notes that it was formerly called Nucillum, from nuces (nuts), of which there is a great yield there; but that the name was changed by Louis of Chalon, of that family name: for he, returning to Burgundy from Jerusalem, restored the town and named it Nazareth after the city of Galilee; and then, the name being corrupted in common usage by changing letters, it came to be called Nozeret. In the southern part of the town is the prince's citadel (which they call the Leaden, because it is roofed with lead), very large, square, enclosed with the town wall; strong with eight very high towers, steep ditches, and every kind of war machine. Because of the pleasantness and healthiness of its site and its abundance of game, it was the pleasant retreat of the Princes of Orange before their disastrous wars. Here was born the great hero Philibert of Chalon, Prince of Orange. This town has the right to hold markets four times a year: immediately after Pentecost, at the beginning of November and February, and in the first week of Lent. The feast of St Anthony (to whom the chief church is dedicated) is of such a kind that from everywhere a huge crowd comes together in the old pagan manner, both on account of St Anthony and for the gathering of the most elegant girls, of which there is none more famous in Burgundy. That day is spent in games, dances and feasts. Castrum Karoli, Castel Chalon, a town named, as the inhabitants say, after Charlemagne, strong in its situation, famous for its monastery, into which only the daughters of nobles are received as virgins. Monsmoretum, Mommoret, a town on a not steep mountain, near Lons-le-Saunier, commonly Lonlesaunier, from which it suffered loss of its glory. Orgeletum, Orgelet, a town flourishing in trade. The inhabitants practise wool-working. One part, with the citadel, is on a high place; the other is on flat ground at the foot of the hill. The land is rather barren, rough with rocks and stones; of its inhabitants it is customary to say that they have fields without grass, rivers without fish, and mountains without woods.

units.la: Quas, distinctione quadam, indicavi hactenus Urbes, quæque oppida, Sessionis inComitijs Publicis, Suffragiisque jure sunt donata: sequuntur quædam, ordine turbatiore, quæ non tantæ dignationis. Iunia, vulgo Iongne, oppidum antiquissimum, in excelso & prærupto colle ad Sabaudiæ Limites positum: Nivibus Silvisque opacis gravatum. Hic lura transitur; hic Vectigal exigitur Rerum, quæ alio exportantur; Hujus Suburbia ad Occidentem dicuntur Hospitalia: quod nomen etiam proximo Pago est indicum. Ussierum, Ussier, opidum Arcem habet, cum quatuor vicis, quorum Incolæ Lepórum sunt & Facetiarum Patres: Burgundis reliquis ipsorum Dicta Factaque ridicula sæpe fallendo tempori recitantibus. Mortua ingens, sed sine Mœnibus, opi-bus, opibus, opidum; sic nuncupatum, quod cum Vicis Prædisque suis in caussam mortici- næ Pollestionis ceciderit. S. Hippolyts Fanum, S. Ippolyte, Montibus undique natura, velut arte, cinctum. Incolæ hujus Tractus ceteris Burgundis corporis magnitudine sunt procreriores, belloq; magis valent. Hippolytum, Patricium Romanum, ferunt Iuvenem ea loca protectum, odio feminei generis Dianæ Studijs se totum addixisse, despecto Veneris Numine; Christianum inde factum Martyrij gloriam metuisse. Burgum uno milliari distans Nozeretho, Opidum est edito in loco. Ibi, si utpiam, placidissime fluit Danus. Semidirutum est, prostratis ab Ambosio Mœnibus. Hoc solum putatur in Burgundia antiquum servare nomen. Clara-Vallis, Clervaulx, Opidum ad Dani fluenta situm, cujus Incolæ Lanificio Pannisque texendis dant operam. Claudianum, vel Fanum S. Claudij, S. Clande, nomen habere perhibetur ab D. Claudio, Salmensium progenie orto, Archiepiscopo Bisontino, cujus ibi reliquias monstrant Sacriculi. Cœnobium exstruxisse scribitur Chilpertus Burgundiæ Rex. Ibi Sepulturas vidi aliquot Regum. Incolæ, factis ex variorum generum Lignis, præcipue Buxo, Vasis, Cochlearibus, Fistulis, Tubis, Precatorijs Sphærulis vel Pilulis, aliisque quamplurimis Instrumentis & varia admodum Supellectile, magnum faciunt quæstum; vendentes hæc talia, & non sine Mendicitatis infamia, expertus Ioquor, obtrudentes ijs, qui eo religionis causa superstitiose undique concurrunt. Turmaya Lanarijs abundat; tenues habet Muros & circumquaque Aedificijs contiguos & impeditos, ut nullus in liberum ambitum pateat transitus: id quod fiuminis Opidis est commune. Campignola, opidum est undique natura circumvallatum, ab Dano irrigatum. Monetum, Monnet, Opidulum antiquum, summo in Monte, ruinosum & vetustate pene collapsum. Mirebellum, Mirebeau, opidum in Pagum per belli furias redactum, Arcis parte superstite. Non aliud tota Burgundia ruinas ostentat æque memorabiles. Sorlinum, Sorlin, in Monte positum, quem Danus adluit. Arcem habet, cui precium decusque conciliat Vetustas: Castellana, opidum in excelsa rupe locatum, sine Mœnibus. Antiquitatem loquuntur Rudera, Templique pars superstites. Nunc Vicus est. Arx ab Hortis occupatur. Balma, Baume, opidum natura munitum; undique, nisi qua ad Castrum Karoli itur, altissimis, veluti Muro, circumvallatum, rupibus, ex quibus Cella flumen prorumpit. Clarum est antiquo & omnium maximo Monasterio Ordinis Cluniacensis, cujus fundamenta jecit Bonno, Chilperici Burgundiæ Regis Filius: Vetustate conlapsum restituit Gulielmus Poupetus, Loci Anniftes. Celera Incendijs, parum abest, prostratæ: Arcem habentes etiam semidirutam. Arlaum, Arley, antiquum & nobile: Sedes olim Burgundiæ Ducum, qui postea Nozeretum migrarunt. Pars una in Montis planicie, Arci adjacens, Burgus vocatur; altera in Cellæ ripa est posita. Rufacum, Ruffey, amœnum opidum, lætissima habens rura. Bleterum, Bleterrans, in Planicie situm: Mœnibus, Turribus, Arce egregie munitum, Cella Muros obeunte. Ager suburbicarius Tritici feracissimus, unde nomen opido volunt quidam impositum, sicque dictum, quasi Frumenti, quod Ble Francis, Terram. Totum fere incendio periit anno cIↄ IↄXIX Kalendis Iulij. Lonsalinum, vernacule Lyon vel Lon le Saunier, opidum est cum primis elegans, in plano situm, Emporium celeberrimum, quodque omnem vicinorum Montium, Moreti & Acuti gloriam ad se transduxit. Ante annos aliquot ter incendio fortuito est corruptum. Plateas habet amplas & rectas: Domos magnificas grandia Suburbia. Laurentianum, S. Laurens de la Roche, exiguum quidem est, sed miram referens Antiquitatem. San-Iulianum, S. Julian, ab Iuliano Antiochiensi Martyre volunt dictum, medio est fere itinere inter Burgum Segusianorum & Orgeletum. Mons Floridus, Mont-fleur, in excelso & munito natura loco: Vallem habens fœcundam admodum & amœnam. Chevanne, Chavannes, opidum annosum & ruinis deformatum. Amurcum, S Amour, Mercatoribus insigne, potens & amplum satis. Montronis, Montron, opidi, Bisantio duobus distantis miliaribus, naturam, situm, commoda nemo non miratur. Turres habet & Domos excelsis in rupibus exstructas. Claravallis, Clervaux & Lila, Lille, ripensia Dubidis opida; quorum prius incendio miserabili conflagravit anno cIↄ Iↄ XXXXIII. Luxovium, Luxoul, præter Thermas, Cœnobio, quod Chilpericus Burgundionum Rex construxit, est insigne. Mentio ejus apud Aimoinum, & in Vita S. Galli Abbatis & Confessoris. Rubimons, Rougemont, opidum olim opulentum nunc
units.tr: The cities I have so far indicated, with a certain distinction, and the towns which have been given a seat and a vote in the public assemblies, are followed by certain places, in a rather disordered sequence, which are not of such dignity. Iunia, commonly Jougne, a very ancient town, placed on a high and steep hill at the border of Savoy, weighed down by snow and dark woods. Here the Jura is crossed; here a toll is levied on goods exported elsewhere. Its suburbs to the west are called Hospitalia, a name which also indicates the nearby village. Ussierum, Ussier, a town with a citadel, and four villages, whose inhabitants are fathers of jests and witticisms, often beguiling the time by reciting their own funny sayings and deeds to the rest of the Burgundians. Mortua, a huge but unwalled town, rich in resources; so called because, together with its villages and estates, it fell into the cause of a deadly plague. St Hippolyte's shrine, St Hippolyte, surrounded on all sides by mountains, as if by art as well as nature. The inhabitants of this district are larger in bodily size than the other Burgundians, and more vigorous in war. They say that Hippolytus, a Roman patrician, a young man protected in these places, hating the female sex, devoted himself wholly to the studies of Diana, scorning the divinity of Venus; and that he was thereupon made a Christian and feared the glory of martyrdom. Burgum, a town a mile from Nozeret, is set on a high place. There, if anywhere, the Doubs flows most peacefully. It is half in ruins, its walls razed by Ambrose. This alone is thought to keep its ancient name in Burgundy. Clara-Vallis, Clervaux, a town set by the streams of the Doubs, whose inhabitants devote themselves to wool-making and weaving cloth. Claudianum, or the shrine of St Claude, St Claude, is said to have its name from St Claude, born of the Salmes family, Archbishop of Besançon, whose relics the sacristans show there. Chilperic, King of Burgundy, is written to have built the monastery. There I have seen the tombs of several kings. The inhabitants, making objects from various kinds of wood, especially box, such as vessels, spoons, pipes, trumpets, prayer beads or little balls, and many other instruments and a quite varied household stock, make a great profit; selling these things, and not without the infamy of beggary, as I speak from experience, and foisting them on those who flock superstitiously from everywhere to the place for religion's sake. Turmaya abounds in wool-workers; it has thin walls, and buildings contiguous and crowded all round, so that no open passage lies through the enclosure; which is common to nearly all the towns of this sort. Campignola is a town surrounded on every side by nature's fortification, watered by the Doubs. Monetum, Monnet, an old little town on a high mountain, ruinous and almost collapsed with age. Mirebellum, Mirebeau, a town reduced to a village by the fury of war, with a part of its citadel surviving. No other place in all Burgundy shows ruins equally noteworthy. Sorlinum, Sorlin, set on a mountain which the Doubs washes. It has a citadel, to which antiquity gives its worth and dignity. Castellana, a town placed on a high rock, without walls. Its remains and surviving parts of a temple speak of its antiquity. Now it is a village; the citadel is taken over by gardens. Balma, Baume, a town fortified by nature; enclosed on all sides, except where the road goes to Castrum Karoli, by very high rocks, as if by a wall, from which the river Cella bursts forth. It is famous for the ancient and greatest monastery of the Cluniac Order, whose foundations were laid by Bonno, son of Chilperic, King of Burgundy; fallen into ruin with age, it was restored by William Poupet, Abbot of the place. Celera, almost razed by fires, still having a half-ruined citadel. Arlaum, Arlay, an ancient and noble place: formerly the seat of the Dukes of Burgundy, who afterwards moved to Nozeret. One part lies on a mountain plain next to the citadel, and is called the Burgus; the other is set on the bank of the Cella. Rufacum, Ruffey, a pleasant town with very cheerful countryside. Bleterum, Bleterrans, situated on a plain, excellently fortified with walls, towers and a citadel, with the Cella flowing past the walls. The suburban land is most fertile in wheat, whence some think the town got its name, as if from frumentum, grain, which the Franks call ble, land. It was almost entirely destroyed by fire on 1 July 1519. Lonsalinum, in the vernacular Lyon or Lons-le-Saunier, is a town among the most elegant, set on a plain, a very famous trading centre, which has drawn to itself all the glory of the neighbouring mountains, Moreti and Acuti. Some years ago it was thrice ruined by accidental fire. It has wide and straight streets, and splendid houses and large suburbs. Laurentianum, St Laurent de la Roche, is indeed small, but shows remarkable antiquity. San-Iulianum, St Julien, is said to be named from Julian, the martyr of Antioch; it lies about halfway between the town of the Segusians and Orgelet. Mons Floridus, Montfleur, in a high place, naturally fortified: it has a very fertile and pleasant valley. Chevanne, Chavannes, an old town disfigured by ruins. Amurcum, St Amour, notable for its merchants, powerful and large enough. Montronis, Montron, two miles from Besançon: no one fails to admire its situation, its position and its advantages. It has towers, and houses built on high rocks. Claravallis, Clervaux, and Lila, Lille, towns on the bank of the Doubs; of which the former was burned in a miserable fire in the year 1543. Luxovium, Luxeuil, apart from its baths, is notable for the monastery which Chilperic, King of the Burgundians, built. It is mentioned by Aimoin, and in the Life of St Gall, Abbot and Confessor.

units.la: T t 4 nunc in ruinis fere jacens. Eo quotannis Georgii Festo totius Burgundiæ Nobiles conveniunt, denique illum sacris Ritibus magnaque lætitia prosequuntur. Institutum id traditur circa annum {ǝ} cccLxx. Gyum, Gys, opidum adjitum Amni, qui ad Graum, Grey, in Araris se exonerat. De Gensis Agri Vino antea dixi. Iuxtilla, Iontille, amplum & vetus opidum, Mœnibus semino nutantibus.
units.tr: now lying almost in ruins. Every year on the feast of St George, the nobles of all Burgundy gather there and honour him with sacred rites and great rejoicing. This custom is said to have been instituted around the year 370. Gyum, Gys, a town on the river Amnis, which discharges into the Graus, Grey, and so into the Arar. I have already spoken of the wine of the Gensis region. Iuxtilla, Iontille, a large and ancient town, with walls that are half collapsed.

units.la: Sunt & Pagi Famæ celebritate conspicui. Mota, La Motte, instar opidi, Dubidis fonte superbiens. Rupes Ioannis, Roche Ioan, Conditoris nomen servat. Fraxinum, Frane, opidi speciem refert, ab Fraxini copia dictum. Fons-Senæ, Pagus immensus, sic appellatus, quod in eo Fons fit Fluvio Senæ, qui validus jam ibi xxvii. Rotis, partim ad Molas, partim ad Serras, circumagendis. Versum, Vers, Pagus fere quimoliari distat Nozeretho, ad Angelonem Fluvium, in quo Arx est omnium nobilissima cum Vivario nemoroso, Mœnibus undique septo, includens Damas, Cervos Lepores, Cuniculos, aliaque id genus Animalia. Vicina est Arx Monrivallis in Monte excelso, scatebris Fontium, qui ex Vertice prorumpunt, inclyto. Cortena, Pagus Amplissimus ad Occidentem subjectus Arci, quæ vulgo Saegan, minor olim, quam est hodie, ut veteres docent Muri. Castellionum, Chastillon. Pagus cum Arce cognomine, integra, vicinis diruts, & munitissima. Rolandus Mons, Mont Roland Pagus haud procul Dola, appellationem scribitur traxisse ab Rolando, Karoli Magni ex Sorore Nepote; de cujus Fortitudine bellicaque Virtute alii multa. Lotharingum. S. Lotharii, Pagus opidi instar in fœcundissimo viticeroque Monte conspicuus, satis dispertus, sed elegantissimis Ædificiis plenus. In Fano monstratur Tumulus D. Lothari Sepulcrum. Salisilum, vulgo Sanibre ab alto Fonte, qui eo loci quondam fuit, denominatum. Dornon, Vicus haud procul Salinus, Gallorum clade, Superiorumque Burgundionum victoria nobilitatus.
units.tr: There are also villages that are well known for their renown. Mota, La Motte, is like a town and takes pride in the source of the Dubis. Rupes Ioannis, Roche-Jean, keeps the name of its founder. Fraxinum, Frane, presents the appearance of a town and is named from its abundance of ash trees. Fons-Senae, an immense village, so called because the source of the river Seine rises in it; there the river, already strong, turns twenty-seven wheels, some for mills and some for saws. Versum, Vers, a village nearly five miles from Nozeret, on the river Angelon, in which stands the most noble castle, with a wooded game park walled in on all sides, enclosing fallow deer, stags, hares, rabbits and other such animals. Near it is the castle of Monrivallis, famous on a high mountain for the springs of water that burst forth from its summit. Cortena, a very large village lying to the west below the castle, which is commonly called Saegan; as the old walls show, it was once smaller than it is today. Castellionum, Chastillon: a village with a castle of the same name, intact, while its neighbours are destroyed, and very strongly fortified. Rolandus Mons, Mont Roland, a village not far from Dole, is recorded as having taken its name from Roland, nephew of Charlemagne through his sister; many others tell much about his strength and martial valour. Lotharingum, S. Lotharii: a village like a town, conspicuous on a very fertile, vine-clad hill; it is fairly spread out but full of very elegant buildings. In the church is shown a mound, the tomb of St Lothar. Salisilum, commonly Sanibre, named from the deep spring that once rose there. Dornon, a village not far from Salins, made famous by the defeat of the Gauls and the victory of the Upper Burgundians.

units.la: Videamus & nonnullas hujus Burgundiæ Arces. Tribus ab opido Nozeretho versus Meridiem milliaribus Arx est cum Pago cognomine, Calx, La Chaux, celebris natura (nam in admodum arduo situm est Monte) & Manu munitissima. Afna, Arx illustris, opidi instar, omnium celeberrima, natura loci valida, in Colle saxoso, qui in infinitam exsurgit altitudinem: aditu difficilis: Vallibus circumdatus omni ex parte, quarum profunditatem visu quis comprehendere nequit. Inde uno Lapidis intervallo est Monf Major, pervetus Arx in excelso Monte, Speculæ instar spectandam se præbens multo splendore multis utrinque Burgundiæ opidis. Inter Lantrentianum & Montem Acutum Arx etiam fuit fere inexpugnabilis; quæ quod Viarum obsessores reciperet, & Exsulibus esset Asylum, Burgundionum Armis subversa fertur. Alias prætereo.
units.tr: Let us also look at some of the castles of this Burgundy. Three miles south of the town of Nozeret there is a castle with the village of the same name, Calx, La Chaux, famous for its natural setting (for it stands on a very steep mountain) and most strongly fortified by human effort. Afna, an illustrious castle, like a town and the most celebrated of all; strong by the nature of its site, on a rocky hill that rises to an immense height; difficult of access, and surrounded on every side by valleys whose depth no one can take in with the eye. One stone's throw from there is Mont Major, a very ancient castle on a high mountain, which presents itself to be viewed like a watchtower, with great splendour to many towns of Burgundy on every side. Between Lantrentianum and Montem Acutum there was also a castle that was almost impregnable; because it harboured the highway robbers who preyed on travellers and was a refuge for exiles, it is said to have been overthrown by the arms of the Burgundians. I pass over the others.

units.la: Ad Vesontionem venio, quæ in Comitatus Burgundiæ Vmbilico, Libera, Imperialis, Metropolitana. Vesontio Cæsari, & Itinerariæ Tabulæ: Vesontio, Antonino: Vesuntium Ammiano lib. xvi; & Οὐεσοντιον Ptolemæo, quam Βησοντιον vocat Iulianus Imper. in Epistolis, & idem Ammianus lib. xx. Besantionem: Hodie Besançon. In Notitia Provinciarum sub Lugdunensi v legitur Civitas Crispolinorum, hoc est Vesuntio: Hodie L'Archevesché de Besançon. Scribit Paradinus Chrysopolin quoque appellatam, & putat Ortelius sic vocari in Vita S. Petri Archiepiscopi Tarentasii: & sic etiam nominat Ligurinus Poeta, qui Frederici Ahenobarbi Imperatoris Vitam Resque ab eo gestas descripsit. Vesontii quoque sunt apud Ammianum lib. xv. Apud Sequanos Vesontios vidimus. Legitur in aliis Codicibus Bisontios. Maximam Sequanorum nominat Cæsar lib. 1, qui antiquum ejus Situm sic depingit: Natura loci sic munitus, ut magnam ad ducendum bellum daret facultatem: propterea quod Flumen Aldubis, ut circino circumductum, pene totum opidum cingit: reliquum spatium, quod non est amplius pedum 100, qua Flumen intermittit, Mons continet magna altitudine ita, ut Radices eius Montis ex utraque parte ripæ fluminis contingant. Hunc Murus circumdatus Arcem efficit & cum opido coniungit. Eundem Situm hodieque fere retinet, præterquam quod Fluvius eam nunc magna ex parte intersecet; accepto Ponte; ut Pars Occidentalior post tempora Iulii Cæsaris adcrevisse videatur. Muri, cujus meminit Cæsar, & Dubi Fluvio utroq; ex latere claudi adfirmat, etiam hodie ingentes conspiciuntur Reliquiæ ad D. Stephani montem. Initium illi à Porta Scilla, vulgo Taillée, quæ est cupes ferro insuper excavata: Finis autem ad Portam Mali Passus, vulgo Maupas; Sunt qui adserant Plateam, vulgo Ronchaux, Dubis olim alveum fuisse: item se: item Turrim S. Quintini Veteris Vrbis fuisse Portam: idem affirmant de Porta Nigra. Inter publica ibi Aedificia fuisse ferunt olim Pantheon: Campum Martium, ad Meridionalem Vrbis partem, Moenibus hodie contiguum: Campum Minervae, &>c alia. Vrbs hoc tempore magnifica ad insultus Hostium sustinendos & propulsandos cum natura, Dubiis beneficiorum validissimis Propugnaculis mirum in modum munita; silvosis, interfluisque Montibus egregie cincta; Piscium Fructuumque delicatissimorum adfluentia valde dives. Frumentorum autem ubertate tam beata, ut, quemadmodum olim universae Italiae Sicilia, sic totius Burgundiae Granarium suburbicarius Vesontionis Ager semper fuerit habitus. Intra Moenia sunt Horti spaciosi, Vineta, Viridaria, apriquae Studiis & Meditationibus Recessus. Archiepiscopatus dignitate clara est. Praefuisse Primus scribitur S. Anthidius, missus ab Irenaeo Lugdunensi Episcopo. Suffraganei leguntur in Accepti Papae Tabulis, Episcopi Basileensis, Lausanensis & Lausicensis; traditurque ibidem pro Archiepiscopatu Bisontino, si contigerit vacare, Apostolicae Sedi, seu pro Reserva, ut vocant, aut pro Annata, aut pro Provisione cum Florenos numerari.
units.tr: I come now to Besançon, which lies at the navel of the county of Burgundy; it is a free, imperial and metropolitan city. Vesontio in Caesar and in the Itinerary Table; Vesontio in Antoninus; Vesuntium in Ammianus, book 16; and Οὐεσοντιον [Ouesontion] in Ptolemy, which the emperor Julian calls Βησοντιον [Besontion] in his letters; and the same Ammianus, book 20, has Besantion. Today it is Besançon. In the Notitia of the Provinces, under Lugdunensis V, is read the civitas Crispolinorum, that is, Vesontio. Today it is the archbishopric of Besançon. Paradin writes that it was also called Chrysopolis, and Ortelius thinks it is so called in the Life of St Peter, archbishop of Tarentaise; the poet Ligurinus, who described the life and deeds of the emperor Frederick Barbarossa, also calls it so. Vesontii also occurs in Ammianus, book 15: "We saw Vesontio among the Sequani." In other manuscripts it is read as Bisontios. Caesar, book 1, names it the chief town of the Sequani and describes its ancient site thus: the nature of the place so fortifies it that it offers a great facility for conducting war, because the river Dubis, as if drawn with a compass, surrounds almost the whole town; the remaining space, which is not more than 100 feet, where the river does not run, is filled by a mountain of great height, so that the roots of that mountain touch the river bank on each side. A wall encircling this mountain makes a citadel and joins it to the town. Today it keeps almost the same site, except that the river now cuts through it for the greater part, a bridge having been built; so that the western part seems to have grown since the time of Julius Caesar. Remains of the wall that Caesar mentions, and which, it is affirmed, closed the town on both sides by the Dubis, can still be seen in great extent near the mount of St Stephen. It begins at the Porta Scilla, commonly Taillée, which is a cleft hollowed out of the rock with iron, and ends at the Porta Mali Passus, commonly Maupas. Some assert that the Plateam, commonly Ronchaux, was once the channel of the Dubis; likewise that the tower of St Quentin was the gate of the old city, and they say the same of the Porta Nigra. They report that among the public buildings there was once the Pantheon, and the Campus Martius on the southern side of the city, now contiguous to the walls, and the Campus Minervae, etc. The city at present is magnificent; with its natural setting, and with the help of the Dubis and the most powerful bulwarks, it is wonderfully fortified against the assaults of enemies, and it is excellently girt by wooded and intervening mountains. It is very rich in abundance of fish and most delicate fruits. It is so blessed with the richness of grain that, as Sicily once was to all of Italy, so the suburban fields of Besançon have always been regarded as the granary of all Burgundy. Within the walls are spacious gardens, vineyards, pleasure grounds, and sunny retreats for study and meditation. The archbishopric is distinguished in dignity. The first to preside is written to have been S. Anthidius, sent by Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons. The suffragans listed in the papal register of accepted fees are the bishops of Basel, Lausanne and Lausitz; and it is stated there that, for the archbishopric of Besançon, should it happen to fall vacant, florins are to be paid to the Apostolic See, either as reservation, as they call it, or as annates, or as provision.

units.la: ET haec de Burgundia restat paucis explicandus KAROLESII Comitatus, vulgo Charolois. Nomen illi ab Opido, quod vulgo Charrolles. Situs est inter Fluvios Ligerim & Ararim. Ad Septemtrionem conregionales illi sunt Burgundiae Ducatus Inocolae; ad Occidentem Borbonenses & Forenses: qua Meridies est, Bello-Iolecij occurrunt & Lugdunenses; qua Oriens, Bresliani se offerunt.
units.tr: It remains to say a few words about the County of Charolais (Karolesium Comitatus), commonly called Charolois, and about the town from which it takes its name, commonly called Charrolles. It lies between the rivers Loire and Saône. To the north are the inhabitants of the Duchy of Burgundy, who share the region; to the west are the people of Bourbonnais and Forez; to the south meet the Beaujolais and the people of Lyon; to the east lie the Bressans.

units.la: Habitasse quondam videntur populi, quos Caesar & Livius Ambarros appellant.
units.tr: The people whom Caesar and Livy call the Ambarri seem once to have inhabited this area.

units.la: Insigniri solet huius Comitatus titulo, Patre Superstite, Filius Burgundiae Ducis Primus natu quod observatum videmus in Karolo Audace, quamdiu in vivis erat Pater, Philippo Bono; isque eo nomine in Belgicis Francicisque Historiis nusquam non occurrit, Comte de Charrolois. Idem factum in Karolo, qui postea Romanorum fuit Imperator, vivo patre Philippo.
units.tr: This county is customarily given as a title to the eldest son of the Duke of Burgundy while his father is still living. We see this observed in Charles the Bold, who was called Count of Charolais, a title he bore in Belgian and French histories everywhere, while his father Philip the Good was alive. The same was done with Charles, who later became Emperor of the Romans, while his father Philip was living.

units.la: De hoc Comitatu, cui iure competeret, magna fuit inter Reges Philippum Hispaniarum, & Henricum II Galliarum, Lis & Controversia; quum post atrocissima Bella & funestas Belgarum Francorumque calamitates, per Legatos solidae perpetuaeque Paci sanciendae, & Nuptiis inter Philippum atque Isabellam, Henrici Filiam, contrahendis in Arce Cambresia sedula navaretur opera. Sed vicisse tandem Rationes & Argumenta eorum, qui Partes Philippi agebant; Comitatumque, qui ab Henrico Rege detentus fuerat, Philippo ex integro fuisse restitutum, plane docco in Historia Belgica ad annum MDLIX. Ab eo tempore, uti prius, Provocationes eius Iuridicae Dolam ad Parlamentum sive Senatum Regis, uti supremi eius Domini, rursus coepcrunt devolvi, ibique silti. Rex interim Franciae est Dominus Feudatarius.
units.tr: Over this county, to which of right it belonged, there was a great dispute and controversy between the kings Philip of Spain and Henry II of France. This was pursued by envoys at Cambrai, where the Peace of Cateau-Cambrésis was being carefully negotiated, and where a marriage was arranged between Philip and Isabella, the daughter of Henry, after the most savage wars and deadly calamities of the Belgians and the French. But in the end the arguments and reasons of those who supported Philip prevailed, and the county, which King Henry had held, was wholly restored to Philip in 1559, as is clearly shown in the Belgian History. From that time, as before, appeals from it were again referred to the Parliament or Senate of Dole, as to the King's supreme court, and there they fell silent. Meanwhile the King of France remains its feudal lord.

units.tr: Here are explained matters concerning Spain in general and in its particulars. Its name, with its etymology and both of its appellations, chapter 1. Its quantity, which consists in its boundaries, its circuit and its shape, chapter 2. Its quality, which is considered both in itself and in the advantages that arise from its quality, chapter 3. Its limits and mountains, chapter 4. Promontories, chapter 5. Waters, such as gulfs and harbours, chapter 6. Rivers, lakes, marshes, springs, etc., chapter 7. Its inhabitants, in whom are considered their stock and character, with their language in passing, chapter 8. Government by the political state, chapter 9. The ecclesiastical state, chapter 10. Then particularly. For Spain, by the division of the ancients, is double: the northern part, beyond the Pyrenees, chapter 11; Cantabria, chapter 12; on this side of the mountains, Cingam and Navarre, chapter 13; Aragon, chapter 14; Cetana, Gargan and Cantabria, chapter 15; African [...] here, or on this side of the Tagus, in two banks: Hesperia, the West, chapter 16; the East, Baetica, Lusitania, chapter 17; the region [...] on the left, Callaica Vetus, chapter 19, New, chapter 20; beyond the Tagus, Valencia, chapter 21, Murcia, chapter 22.

units.la: De Gallia agitur in Genere. Hic exponuntur hæc. Nomen, ubi de Etymo variisque Galliæ Appellationibus cap. i. Res quoad Regionis: Adiacentia Quantitas, quæ consistit in Finibus, Longitudine, Latitudine, Circuitu cap. ii. Qualitas, quæ conspicua est in Cautis, ut in Climate cap. iii. Partes, eaque Terra, Talia. Montes cap. iv; Flumina cap. v; Silvæ cap. vi. Aqua, Qualitates: Sinus cap. vii; Fontes cap. viii; Lacus cap. ix; Lacus Fontes &c cap. x. Incolæ in quibus Adiacentia pertinent. Recepta, ut tunc: Mores Hos prefatos de eorum Instituto, consideratis circa Rempublicam Sacras cap. xi; Publicas Domi. cap. xii; Mores cap. xiii; Privatas cap. xiv, xv. Lingua, cap. xv Occupata. Gubernatio: Fidei, tam in Sacris quam Profanis cap. xvi Hodierna: Politica cap. xvii; Ecclesiastica cap. xviii Antiquis Temporibus, cap. xix Spe cie. Hic de Dittri butione ut ferentur, quæ in Ca. Ho die. Ære nostro Provinciæ quæ in Gallia tum Dehi nationum ab Ut[?] migra phi ii licet explicari, alia. Franconi tum Regni Ac Regi subiecta Has communicatas de tum in sua Parlamentaria quæ tecto numero quorum. Principalis, quæ est fere Parisiensis, eum in Parlamentis Italiæ fere ut multo Provincia quæ Lit, quæ in Gallia facit alias. Accessoria & Principalia quæ circumeunt veritas. Septentrionales ubi a Mari Oceano Vetustam Septentrionem & Frigoriam, quæ Oceanus Occidentalis. Meridionales, Vbi ex eo tumulo Veterum demi nuncupata cum Narbonensi Aquitania, quæ tota in Gallia Ac Ligeris ut ad Germanias & Pyrenæos montes Duce. Prima ubi tunc in Vigenna Ripa: Dextra: Ilirur tum cap. xxv; Sinistra: Protensum cap. xxvii; Ager Ioan. &c. cap. xxviii. Secunda, ubi hodie in Durantes finitur cap. xxix. Occidentem seu Ligeris: Dextram: Rutenensis, tub. Nurrarensis cap. xxx; Aquitaniæ Pyrenæ cap. xxxi. Sinistra, Pictavia & Lemanum quæ tota lata invariata Aquitanica Narbonensi Itiquæ Pyrenæi, sunt enim. Integre fab: Bordeaux cap. xxxii; Ultra Garumna cap. xxxiii; Inter Pirenæos cap. xxxiv. Inter ipsum Pictavia: Minor cap. xxxv; Maior cap. xxxvi. Orientem: Ultra Druentiam tum cap. xxxvii; citra Druentiam cap. xxxviii. Ab Francorum Dimone tenuerit ab ipso & Ioan. Principum: Ecclesiasticorum Pontificis Romanum cap. xxxix; Potitorum, quorum ad fuit: Ducatus, ut Principatus, ut Comitatus, ut cap. xl.
units.tr: Gaul is treated in general. Here the following are set out. Its name, with its etymology and the various appellations of Gaul, chapter 1. Its condition as to the region: its neighbours; its quantity, which consists in its boundaries, length, breadth and circuit, chapter 2. Its quality, which is evident in its climate, chapter 3. Its parts and its land, and such things. Mountains, chapter 4; rivers, chapter 5; forests, chapter 6. Water and its qualities: gulfs, chapter 7; springs, chapter 8; lakes, chapter 9; lakes, springs, etc., chapter 10. Inhabitants, in whom their neighbours belong. The accepted matters, as then: their customs, with their institutions considered in relation to the commonwealth, sacred matters, chapter 11; public matters at home, chapter 12; customs, chapter 13; private matters, chapters 14 and 15. Language, chapter 15, occupied. Government: of faith, both in sacred and in profane affairs, chapter 16; the present day: political, chapter 17; ecclesiastical, chapter 18. In ancient times, chapter 19. The kind. Here on the distribution as it is reported, which in the present day, in our age, the provinces which in Gaul [...] of the nations, can be explained, others. The Franks, and the kingdom, and the king subject. These shared in their parliamentary [...] by a fixed number, of whom. The principal, which is nearly Parisian, in the parliaments of Italy, nearly as much; the province which [...] which in Gaul makes others. Accessory and principal matters which surround the truth. The northern, where from the Ocean Sea, the ancient north and the cold, which is the Western Ocean. The southern, where from that ancient mound of the ancients, called Narbonne, Aquitaine, which is all in Gaul, and the Loire, as far as the Germanies and the Pyrenean mountains, the leader. The first, where now on the Vienne bank: on the right, Ilirur, chapter 25; on the left, Protensum, chapter 27; the field of John, etc., chapter 28. The second, where today it ends in the Durance, chapter 29. Toward the west, or the Loire: on the right, Rutenensis, [...] Nurrarensis, chapter 30; Aquitaine, the Pyrenees, chapter 31. On the left, Poitou and Le Mans, which are all broad and unchanged, Aquitanian, Narbonensian, the Pyrenean, for they are. Entirely: Bordeaux, chapter 32; beyond the Garonne, chapter 33; between the Pyrenees, chapter 34. Between Poitou itself: the Lesser, chapter 35; the Greater, chapter 36. Toward the east: beyond the Durance, chapter 37; on this side of the Durance, chapter 38. From the Frankish [...] he held from him and from John, the princes: the ecclesiastical, of the Roman Pontiff, chapter 39; the possessors, to whom belonged: duchies, principalities, counties, chapter 40.

units.la: FINIS
units.tr: THE END

units.la: PAVLLI G.F.P.N. MERVLÆ, COSMOGRAPHIÆ PARTIS II. LIBER IV. DE ITALIA. CAPVT I.
units.tr: PAVLLI G.F.P.N. MERVLÆ, COSMOGRAPHIÆ PARTIS II. LIBER IV. DE ITALIA. CAPVT I.

units.la: Italia Nomen unde, & varia eius Nomina sive Cognomina.
units.tr: Whence the name Italy comes, and its various names or surnames.

units.la: Ic olim habuerunt se, sicque hodie sese habent, & universim & speciatim, Gallia: jamnunc Alpibus, de quibus mox dicam, per impervia fere itinera, difficiles & flexuosas vias, immensos & inexplicabiles, expertus loquor, amfractus, superatis, laboriosisque devoratis molestijs, ITALIAM ingredior; Italiam, Regionem Diis Sacram, inquit Plinius lib. iii. natur. histor. cap. xx. totius Europæ beatissimam, optimamque, omnium prope Terrarum Alumnam, Rerum Dominam, Principem Gentium, Mundi Reginam.
units.tr: Things once stood, and still stand today both in general and in particular, as Gaul does. I speak from experience: having now made my way through the Alps, which I will describe shortly, by almost impassable routes, difficult and winding roads, vast and intricate passes, and after overcoming many twists and laborious troubles, I enter ITALY. Italy, a region sacred to the gods, says Pliny in book 3 of his Natural History, chapter 20: the most blessed and best part of all Europe, the nurse of nearly all lands, the mistress of things, the leader of nations, the queen of the world.

units.la: Varias habuit olim Appelationes: quæ quibus fuerint priores, quamque late sese extenderint, anxie non quæram. Id enim ab alijs huius ævi præstitum; licet confuse admodum, incertisque indicijs. Dionysij Halicarnass. Scriptoris diligentissimi, sequar ordinem, qui lib. i. Roman. Antiquit. Regionem hanc nobilissimam Indigenas vocasse scribit Saturniam: Græcos vero Hesperiam, Ausoniam, Oenotriam; Herculis denique tempore dici cœpisse Italiam. Σαngvία igitur, ut inde ordiar, inquit Stephanus in Vrbium Nomenclatore, ἡ Ιταλία περὶ τὴν εκαλεῖτο. Vnde autem Iustinus ex Trogo, agens de Saturno Rege, Itaque, concludit, Italia Regis nomine Saturnia appellata est. Notat idem Macrobius lib. 1. Saturnal. cap. VII. Saturnia, ait Festus lib. XVII. Italia, & Mons, qui nunc est Capitolinus, Saturnius appellabatur, quod in tutela Saturni esse existimatur. &c Isidorus lib. XIII Etymol. cap. IV: Italia o tm a Graecis populis occupata Magna Graecia appellata est: deinde ab Regis nomine Saturnia, mox & Latium. Crediderim ego Saturnia appellationem non ad totam pertinuisse Regionem, quae post Italia sed tantum ad eius partem, quae & Latium. Latinis enim Latium, quae Tuscis vicinis Saturnia: illud ab Latende; hoc ab Aramaea voce לט, quae Latere, occultare se & abscondere notat. Varro lib. IV de LL. ubi de Tarpeio: Hunc antea in Montem Saturnium appellatum prodiderunt, & ab eo late Saturniam Terram, ut etiam Ennius appellat: ubi pro late reponendum esse Latium, olim monui in meo ad Poetae Annales Commentario. Antequam autem Saturnia fuerit haec Regio dicta, nomen illi fuisse videtur Camesene, ab Camese Indigena, cum quo (ut apud Macrobium Higinus, Protarchum Trallianum sequutus, tradidit) Ianus Regionem (Latium mihi) partim sapa potentia possidebat, ita ut Regio (ad sinistram Tiberis ripam) Camesene, oppidum Ianiculum (ad dexteram Tiberis oram) vocitaretur. Addit deinde, post ad Ianum solum Regnum suisse redactum: quae quum, inquit, Saturnum classe pervectum excepisset hospitio, & ab eo edoctus peritiam ruris, ferum illum & rudem ante f uges cognitas victum in metus redegisset, regni cum societate muneravit. Ianus mox Ianiculum opidum Nomen retinuisse, Regionem autem, depositta priore, appellationem sumsisse Saturnia; duos vero Reges concorditer regnasse, vicinaque opida opera communi condidisse; indeque apud Maronem legi:
units.tr: It has had various names in the past. I will not anxiously inquire which of them came first, or how widely each extended. Other writers of this age have already done that, though very confusedly and on uncertain evidence. I will follow the order of Dionysius of Halicarnassus, a most diligent writer, who in book 1 of his Roman Antiquities writes that the native inhabitants called this most noble region Saturnia; the Greeks called it Hesperia, Ausonia and Oenotria; and finally, in the time of Hercules, it began to be called Italia. To begin there, Stephanus, in his Dictionary of Cities, says that Italy was formerly called [Σατυρνία?] ... Justin, drawing on Trogus and speaking of King Saturn, concludes: "Therefore Italy was called Saturnia from the name of its king." Macrobius, book 1 of the Saturnalia, chapter 7, notes the same. Festus, book 17, says: "Saturnia" is Italy, and the hill that is now the Capitoline was called Saturnian, because it is thought to be under the protection of Saturn. Isidore, Etymologies book 13, chapter 4: "Italy, once occupied by the Greek peoples, was called Magna Graecia; then from the name of its king it was called Saturnia, and soon Latium." I would believe that the name Saturnia did not apply to the whole region that was afterwards called Italy, but only to that part which was also called Latium. For the Latins called their land Latium, and the Tuscans, their neighbours, called it Saturnia. The former name comes from latere (to lie hidden); the latter from the Aramaic word [לט], which means to lie hidden and conceal oneself. Varro, book 4 of On the Latin Language, speaking of the Tarpeian rock, says: "They have handed down that this hill was formerly called Saturnian, and that from it the land was widely called Saturnia, as Ennius also calls it." In that passage, I have previously argued in my commentary on the Annals of the poet that late should be read as Latium. Before this region was called Saturnia, it seems to have been called Camesene, after the native Camese. Higinus, following Protarchus of Tralles, as Macrobius reports, relates that Janus held part of the region (Latium, in my view) with a considerable power, so that the district on the left bank of the Tiber was called Camesene and the town of Janiculum, on the right bank, was so named. He adds that afterwards the kingdom was reduced to Janus alone: "When Saturn, he says, arrived by ship, Janus received him as a guest, and having been taught by him the skill of farming, he brought that wild and rude people, once unacquainted with civilization, under the sway of law, and rewarded him with a share of his kingdom." Afterwards Janus kept the name of the town Janiculum, while the region, dropping its former name, took the name Saturnia; the two kings reigned in harmony and jointly founded the neighbouring towns. Hence in Virgil we read:

units.la: Ianiculum huic, illi fuerat Saturnia Nomen.
units.tr: Janiculum was the name of the one, and Saturnia of the other.

units.la: Hesperiam (Ἑσπερίαν) nominasse Hesperum, ab Atlante Fratre in exsilium acturn, inque haec Loca delatum, scribit ad Virgilium Servius. Quidam Hesperiam dictam esse notant hanc Regionem ab Graecis, quod Occasui subiecta, ipsiusque Occidentalior esset. Scribunt alij Hesperias antiquitus fuisse duas: unam, quae post Hispania; alteram, quae Italia; hanc quidem Magnam audiisse Hesperiam, ab Hespero Atlantis Fratre: eum enim nomen vel suum, vel Regionis, unde pulsus fuerat, indidisse: illam autem, addito cognomine, Vltimam appellari solitam, ab Hespero, occidentali Stella. De Italia iane loquitur Virgilius lib. I. Aen.
units.tr: Servius, on Virgil, writes that Hesperus (Ἑσπερίαν) gave the name Hesperia to this region; Hesperus was a brother of Atlas, driven into exile and brought to these places. Some note that Hesperia was so called by the Greeks because it lies under the setting sun and is more western than they are. Others write that there were formerly two Hesperiae: one, which is now Hispania; the other, which is Italia. The latter was called Magna Hesperia after Hesperus, the brother of Atlas, who gave it either his own name or the name of the region from which he had been driven; while the former, with an added surname, was usually called Ultima, from Hesperus, the western star. Virgil, book 1 of the Aeneid, certainly speaks of Italy:

units.la: Est locus, Hesperiam Graij cognomine dicunt.
units.tr: There is a place which the Greeks call by the name Hesperia.

units.la: De Hispania Horatius lib. 1. Carminum.
units.tr: Horace, book 1 of the Odes, speaks of Hispania:

units.la: Qui nunc Hesperia vitior ab Vltima.
units.tr: Who now is more hostile than the farthest Hesperia.

units.la: Ausoniam, inquit Festus lib. I, appellavit Ausoni Vlysis & Calypsus Filius (de Ausone apud alios alia leguntur) eam primo Partem Italiae, in qua sunt Vrbes Beneventum & Cales: deinde paullatim tota quoque Italia, quae Apennino finitur, dicta est Ausonia ab eodem Duce, a quo etiam conditam fuisse Auruncam Vrbem ferunt. Videndus & Paullus Diaconus lib. II. Histor. Langbard. cap. XXIII. Ad priorem sententiam accedunt fere Dion Cocceius, Ioannes Tzetza, & Iacius in Lycophronem, qui scribunt Αὐσονίαν solam dici solitam Auruncorum (Αὐρυγκῶν) Terram, inter Campanos & Volscos, iuxta mare sitam. Ad posteriorem inclinat Stephanus de Vrbibus, Αὔσων, ait, ὁ Ιταλός: Et paullo post Αὐσονία, ἡ χώρα.
units.tr: Festus, book 1, says that Ausonia was named after Ausonus, the son of Ulysses and Calypso (other writers tell different things about Ausonus). At first it was the name of the part of Italy in which the cities of Beneventum and Cales lie; then gradually the whole of Italy, bounded by the Apennines, was called Ausonia after the same leader, by whom they also say the city of Aurunca was founded. Paul the Deacon, book 2 of the History of the Lombards, chapter 23, should also be consulted. Dion Cocceius, John Tzetzes and Iacius on Lycophron nearly agree with the former opinion; they write that Αὐσονίαν was the usual name only for the land of the Aurunci (Αὐρυγκῶν), lying by the sea between the Campanians and the Volsci. Stephanus in his work On Cities leans toward the latter view: "Ausonus," he says, "is the Italian" [Αὔσων, ὁ Ιταλός]. And a little later: "Ausonia is the country" [Αὐσονία, ἡ χώρα].

units.la: Oenotria, Οἰνωτρία, quur dicta fuerit, ingens, & quasi Reip. salus hic laboraret, inter Auctores fuit pugna. Ab Oenotro Arcade, Lycaonis Filio, qui primus, transfretato Sinu Ionio, Italiam incoluit, ita appellatam scribit Dionysius Halicarnass. Suffragatur Pausanias, Oenotrum tradens in Arcadicis, Filiorum Lycaonis natu minimum, ab Nyctimo Fratre Pecuniis Virisque impetratis, in Italiam traiecisse, eumque Primum omnium ex Graecia Coloniam navigio deportasse, imo nec Barbarum quidem ullum ante Oenotrum, alienam Terram invasisse. Antiochus etiam Syracusanus apud eundem Dionysium lib. 1. Oenotrum, Lycaonis Filium, Ducem Arcadum, Ionico Sinu transmisso, in Calabriam adpulisse, ibique in ora maritima Colonias posuisse memorat. Varro Oenotrum, Latinorum Regem, nomen creasse Regioni existimat. Servius ab Vino optimo natam Oenotriam appellationem adnotat, quod οἶνον Graeci Vinum vocent. Oenotriam pro Italia habet, Sidonius Apollinaris: inde autem Oenotria Virgilio lib. 1. Strictiores Oenotria Terminos indicat Strabo lib. VI, ante hunc Aristoteles, uti docent ponenda mox iptius verba. Sabinorum Terram propriè Oenotriam fuisse dictam tenbit Servius ad vii Aeneid.
units.tr: Why Oenotria [Οἰνωτρία] was so called, a name by which the great and, as it were, the safety of the state was at stake, has been a matter of dispute among the writers. Dionysius of Halicarnassus writes that it was named after Oenotrus the Arcadian, son of Lycaon, who first settled in Italy after crossing the Ionian Sea. Pausanias supports this, saying in his Arcadica that Oenotrus, the youngest of Lycaon's sons, obtained money and men from his brother Nyctimus and crossed over to Italy; that he was the first of all from Greece to bring a colony by ship; and indeed that before Oenotrus no barbarian had invaded a foreign land. Antiochus of Syracuse, in the same Dionysius book 1, reports that Oenotrus, son of Lycaon and leader of the Arcadians, sailed across the Ionian Sea, landed in Calabria, and founded colonies on its coast. Varro thinks that Oenotrus, king of the Latins, gave his name to the region. Servius notes that the name Oenotria came from the best wine, since the Greeks call wine οἶνον. Sidonius Apollinaris uses Oenotria for Italia, and from this Virgil in book 1 [uses it]. Strabo, book 6, indicates narrower limits for Oenotria; before him Aristotle did so, as the words of the latter, which I will shortly set out, show. Servius, on Aeneid 7, holds that the land of the Sabines was properly called Oenotria.

units.la: Italiæ nomen acceptum ab Italo, quem Oenotriæ Regem facit Aristoteles. Fins hæc sunt: Φασὶ γὰρ οἱ λόγιοι τὴν καλουμένην Βασιλέα τῶν Οἰνωτρῶν, ἀπὸ τοῦ Ἰταλοῦ ... Polybius etiam lib. i. & Antiochus Xenophanes apud Dionysium Halic. tacitum Regionis Regem; Arcadum autem Regulum, in has oras profectum, Timaeus lib. vi. Memoriæ prodit idem Halicarnass. Italus, Siculorum Regem fuisse & Isidorum lib. xiiii cap. iv. & Paullum Diaconum Autor. Langbard. lib. ii. cap. xxiiij primum, cum Agriculturæ, tum Legum in his locis Auctorem, Regionem sic ab se vocasse. Regem Italum simpliciter agnoscit Festus. Hyginus Italum Ducem ex Penelope & Telegono natum hic commemorat. Alii alio abeunt. Timæus, inquit Agellius lib. xi Noct. Attic. cap. i. in Historiis, quas oratione Græca de rebus P. p. Rom. compulsi, & M. Varro in Antiquitatibus Rerum humanarum, Terram Italiam de Graeco Vocabulo appellatam scripserunt: quorum Graeci a vetere lingua Italiae vocitati sunt, quorum in Italia magna copia fuit; hincque in ea Terra gregis pascuaque multa fuisse. Festus lib. ix: Italia dicta, quod magnos Italos, hoc est Bovesbaculas. Paullus Diaconus lib. i. Langbard. Hist. Sive ob hanc Italia dicitur, quia magni in ea Boves, hoc est Italorum nomen. Timaeus etiam fabulatur appellari ab Italo Bove, uno ex armento Geryonis, qui abactus ab Hercule Siculi Freti angustias tranaverat, Tyrrhena Lingua Italum Taurum dicente. Sic Hellanicus Lesbius apud eundem Dionysium, quoniam optimos Boves gignat ea Regio, eiusdem Vocabuli occasione nuncupatam censet Italiam. Italia quoque quondam dicta, ut fides Hellanico, apud eundem Dionysium Halic. lib. i. Antiq. Rom.
units.tr: The name Italia was taken from Italus, whom Aristotle makes the king of the Oenotrians. His words are these: "For the learned say that the so-called king of the Oenotrians was named after Italus..." Polybius, in book 1, and Antiochus Xenophanes, as reported by Dionysius of Halicarnassus, also mention a king of the region; Timaeus, in book 6, records that an Arcadian chieftain went to these shores. The same Halicarnassian reports that Italus was king of the Sicilians; Isidore, book 14, chapter 4, and Paul the Deacon, History of the Lombards, book 2, chapter 24, say that he was the first author both of agriculture and of laws in these places, and that he named the region after himself. Festus simply recognises a king Italus. Hyginus mentions here Italus, a leader born of Penelope and Telegonus. Others take other views. "Timaeus," says Aulus Gellius, book 11 of the Attic Nights, chapter 1, "and Marcus Varro in his Antiquities of Human Affairs, wrote in histories, which I compiled in Greek on the affairs of the Roman people, that the land of Italy was named from a Greek word. The Greeks were called by the old language of Italy, of whom there were great numbers in Italy, and hence there were many herds and pastures in that land." Festus, book 9: "Italy is so called because of the great Italoi, that is, ox-staves." Paul the Deacon, book 1 of the History of the Lombards: or Italy is so called because there are great oxen in it, that is, the name of the Italians. Timaeus also fancifully says that it was named after Italus the Bull, one of the herd of Geryon, which, driven off by Hercules, had crossed the straits of the Sicilian strait, the Tyrrhenian language calling it Italus Taurus. So Hellanicus of Lesbos, in the same Dionysius, thinks that, because that region produces the finest oxen, it was named Italia on the occasion of the same word. Italia was also once called, according to Hellanicus, as reported in the same Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 1 of the Roman Antiquities.

units.la: Quod Αρχαῖα etiam primo appellata, aut, ut aliis scribitur, Μάργητα ab Margetum gente, quos Dionysius Halicarnass. lib. i.
