Μεργῆτας vocat ex Antiocho Syracusano, docent Antiquorum Scriptorum Monimenta. Dicitur Morges Italo successisse, a quo Morgetes dicti, qui prius Oenotri. Porro & Morgetes & Siculos ex Italia in Siciliam traiecisse, etiam ex Thucydide & Diodoro Siculo est notum.
units.tr: Its earliest name, the author says, was Archaea [Αρχαῖα], or, as others write, Margeta [Μάργητα], after the Margetes people, whom Dionysius of Halicarnassus in book 1 calls Mergetae [Μεργῆτας], following Antiochus of Syracuse. The records of ancient writers show this. Morges is said to have succeeded Italus, and from him the Morgetes were named, who were formerly the Oenotrians. That both the Morgetes and the Sicels crossed from Italy into Sicily is also known from Thucydides and Diodorus Siculus.

units.la: Alii alias veteres Italiæ appellationes in medium adferunt, sed quæ non tam Tuscis, quam Partibus conveniant: quod etiam de Superiorum nonnullis aliquo modo dici potest. Tyrrheni, Tuscia, proprie Tusci, inter Macram & Tiberim fluvios. Cona, χωνία vel χων, Lucanæ pars: Hesperia apud Stephanum Pars tantum, ut & infra videbimus: Antiochus autem, eodem scribente, τὴν Ἰταλίαν Φησὶ καλεῖσθαι Ἡσπερίαν, ἐπὶ Οἰνωτρίαν. Maiorem Graeciam, quam quidam ex Festo antiquis Appellationibus adnominant, certum est fuisse Orientaliorem Italiæ partem.
units.tr: Others bring forward other ancient names for Italy, but these fit not so much the Tuscans as particular regions, which may also be said in some way of some of the names listed above. Tyrrheni and Tuscia (properly the Tuscans) lay between the rivers Macra and Tiber. Cona, χωνία or χων, was part of Lucania. Hesperia, according to Stephanus, was only a part, as we shall also see below. Antiochus, however, in the same writer, says that Italy is called Hesperia after Oenotria [τὴν Ἰταλίαν φησὶ καλεῖσθαι Ἑσπερίαν, ἐπὶ Οἰνωτρίαν]. Magna Graecia, which some add among the ancient names on the authority of Festus, was certainly the more eastern part of Italy.

units.la: Quod reliquat Ianiculum ab Iano fuisse nuncupatam Italiam, quum Ianiculum tantum fuerit opidum: Oegygiam ab Oegyge, qui & Ianus: Saturnia, ab Sale & Vimbrona; Aperuam, id est Taurinam, ab Apis Deorum Italiæ ultimo: Palensanam denique, nescio unde: probent ex suppositivis Berosi, Catonis, Myrsili Lesbii, Q. Fabij Pictoris fragmentis cum Annio Viterbiensi Monacho alii, quibus plus temporis, quique maiorem consuevervunt Edem adhibere Commentis Oraculorum & Nugis.
units.tr: As for the claim that Italy was named after Janus, from Ianiculum, when Ianiculum was only a town: Oegygia is named after Oegyges, who is also Janus; Saturnia after Sal and Vimbrona; Aperua, that is Taurina, after Apis, the last of the gods of Italy; and Palensana, I know not from where. Others, with the Viterbo monk Annius, support these views from the spurious fragments of Berosus, Cato, Myrsilus of Lesbos and Q. Fabius Pictor, men who had more time and were accustomed to give more weight to the inventions of oracles and trifles.

units.la: Quidquid sit; venerandum Italia Nomen, sive ab animo fuerit, & quæ a me indicatæ Appellationes Cognomina tantum, quod facile credo, sint habenda: sive, posthabitis aliis Nomenclaturis, postea fuerit natum: semper sane mansit; hodieque manet apud omnes fere populos, omnibus propemodum litteris בתים (vide supra part. i. lib. iii, cap. iv) vocari Hebraïs, tradit in Appendice Biblica Arias Montanus. משך Mafech, vel Mosoch videntur appellare lxx. Interpretes cap. lxiii. lxi. Vivoka Slavonice dicitur.
units.tr: Whatever the case, the venerable name Italia, whether it came from an original meaning, so that the appellations I have mentioned are only surnames, as I readily believe, or whether it arose later after the other names had been set aside, has certainly always remained. Even today it survives among almost all peoples, and the Hebrews call it by nearly all its letters בתים [Bethim] (see above, part 1, book 3, chapter 4), as Arias Montanus relates in the Biblical Appendix. The Seventy translators seem to call it Mafech or Mosoch, in chapters 63 and 61. The Slavs call it Vivoka.

units.la: Antiquissimos porro Italiæ Incolas & Cultores, quique in eam successu temporis vel habitandi, vel prædandi causa inundarunt, recensent Dionysius Halicarnass. lib. i. Livius lib. i, Iustinus ex Trogi lib. xx, Solinus in Polyhist. Ioannes Iovianus Pontanus lib. vi Histor. Leander Albertus in Italiæ Prolegomenis, & alii, Aborigines, Aurunci, Pelasgos, Lycaones, Oenotros, Morgetes, Ausones, Arcades, Tretanos, nos, Venetos, Ligures, Ardeates, Rutulos, Siculos, Iapyges, Lacedæmonios, aliosque Græci generis: item Gallos, Pænos, Herulos, Gothos, Hunnos, Hungaros, Ciepidas, Turingos, Avares, Langobardos, Saracenos, Cimbros, Teutones, Francos, Vasiones, Helvetios, Germanos, Hispanos, & quos non? quorum quidam vel sedes ibi suas fixerunt, hodieque habent, præclaris conditis Civitatibus: vel, Populationibus peractis, ad sua sunt reversi. Ptolemæus xliv enumerat Veteris Italiæ Populos; quos non commemorabo, quum de iis plene infequentibus.
units.tr: Next, the most ancient inhabitants and cultivators of Italy, and those who in the course of time flooded into it either to settle or to plunder, are listed by Dionysius of Halicarnassus in book 1, Livy in book 1, Justin from Trogus book 20, Solinus in the Polyhistor, Giovanni Gioviano Pontano in book 6 of his Histories, Leander Alberti in the Prolegomena to Italy, and others: Aborigines, Aurunci, Pelasgi, Lycaones, Oenotrians, Morgetes, Ausonians, Arcadians, Tretani, ourselves, Veneti, Ligurians, Ardeates, Rutuli, Sicels, Iapygians, Lacedaemonians, and others of Greek stock; likewise Gauls, Carthaginians, Heruli, Goths, Huns, Hungarians, Gepids, Thuringians, Avars, Lombards, Saracens, Cimbri, Teutons, Franks, Vasiones, Helvetians, Germans, Spaniards, and who not? Some of these fixed their seats there and still hold them, having founded famous cities; others, after their plundering, returned home. Ptolemy lists the peoples of Old Italy in book 3; I shall not recount them here, since I will deal with them fully in what follows.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: Italiæ Quantitas, quæ patet in Finibus, Longitudine, Latitudine, Circuitu, & similibus: Italiæ Dorjum, Um- bilicus, Figura.
units.tr: The extent of Italy, as shown by its boundaries, length, breadth, circuit and the like; the spine, the navel and the shape of Italy.

units.la: TANTVM de Nomine Regionis Nobilissimæ, eiusque Cognominibus: sequitur Res ipsa in eiusdem vel Adiunctis, vel Partibus. Adiuncta sunt Quantitas & Qualitas. Illa consistit in Finibus, Longitudine, Latitudine, & id genus aliis.
units.tr: So much for the name of this most noble region and its surnames. The thing itself follows, in its attributes or parts. The attributes are its extent and quality. Extent consists in its boundaries, its length, its breadth and similar matters.

units.la: Peninsulam χερσόνησον faciunt Italiam Strabo libro secundo sextoque & Ptolemæus, quam Natura Mari Supero, Infero, Ionio munivit lateribus tribus: quarto autem vallavit Alpibus. Nam Occasum Caurumque versus adsuæ sunt Italiæ Alpes, quæ suis apud Veteres cognominibus distinctæ fuerunt, Maritimæ, Cottiæ, Graiæ, Rheticæque ad Arsiam usque flumen; Septemtrionem respiciens Pannas habet Iuliasque: succedente mox, qua Aquilo est. Mari Hadriatico ab animo Recessu usque ad Sinum Ionium, qui ad Orientem Vulturnumque illi obvertus. Qua denique longe lateque spectat Austrum, Africum Zephyrumque ab Mari pulsantur Mediterraneo, quod ad eas oras Tyrrhenum audit & Ligusticum: faciente etiam partem Australem Hadriatico, qua Tota connectuntur Partes, Forum Iulij & Histria. Hos Italiæ Terminos agnoscunt, unanimique propemodum consensu, si bene verba perpenduntur, statuunt Polybius, Thucydides, Strabo, Dionysius Halicarnassensis, Ptolemæus, Dionysius Afer, Plinius, Orosius, Pomponius Mela, Solinus, Auctor incertus de Mensura Orbis Terræ, quem mihi transmisit sua manu descriptum Vir Nobilissimus Marcus Velserus, Reip. Augustanæ II Viri omnesque, qui accuratiores, Novitij, Natalis Comes lib. Hiltor xxiv, Leander Albertus initio, & alij.
units.tr: Strabo in books 2 and 6, and Ptolemy, make Italy a peninsula (chersonesos [χερσόνησον]). Nature has protected it on three sides by the Upper Sea, the Lower Sea and the Ionian Sea, and on the fourth it is walled off by the Alps. To the west and north-west the Alps run along its edge; among the ancients these were distinguished by their own names: the Maritime, Cottian, Graian and Rhaetian Alps, as far as the river Arsia. Facing north, Italy has the Pannonian and Julian Alps, and next to them, where the north wind blows, the Alps follow on. From the innermost recess of the Adriatic Sea as far as the Ionian Gulf, which faces east and the Vulturnus wind, is its boundary. Finally, the part that looks far and wide toward the south, and is struck by the south-west and west winds, is bounded by the Mediterranean, which along those shores is called the Tyrrhenian and Ligurian Sea. The southern part also borders on the Adriatic, where the regions of Forum Iulii and Istria join the whole. Polybius, Thucydides, Strabo, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Ptolemy, Dionysius Afer, Pliny, Orosius, Pomponius Mela, Solinus, the unknown author of the On the Measurement of the Earth, whose copy written out by his own hand was sent to me by the most noble Marcus Welser, one of the two magistrates of Augsburg, and all who have been more careful, the newer writers, Natalis Comes in book 24 of his history, Leander Alberti at the beginning, and others, acknowledge these boundaries of Italy. If their words are weighed carefully, they lay them down with almost unanimous agreement.

units.la: Italia, Finibus indicatis inclusæ, Longitudo ab Augusta Prætoria Regium usque est, uti scribunt Strabo lib. v, Plinius lib. iii. cap. x, aliisque locis, Solinus in Polyhist. P. Rutilius Claudius Numatianus, Auc. orque, quem dixi, de Mensura Orbis Terræ, serram tamen inter se nonnihil reciprocantes, decies centenorum & viginti millium passuum; extendens se, ut Strabo indicat lib. vi, ἀπὸ Ἀρκτων, τὸ πλάτος: Latitudo varia; Maxima quidem quadringentorum decem millium, inter Varum Arsiamque fluvios; Media, centum triginta tenum, circa Urbem Romam, ab Ostio Aterni amnis usque ad Tiberis in Tyrrhenum Pelagus eruptionem; Minima, non amplius quadraginta millium, inter Portum Magnæ Græciæ, quem Annibalis Castra nominant, & Hipponiatem vel Vibonensem Sinum. Ego, Dimensione curiosius facta, Longitudinem eius ab Augusta Prætoria ad Brutium usque Promontorium vel Leucopetram deprehendi cccxlv plus minus Miliariorum: Latitudinem, qua, ut paullo ante accipiundam monui, Maxima, ccccl xxv, qua Media, cxxx: qua denique Minima, lxxii: ubi in duplex exit cornu, multo est minor. Minima illa, quam quidam ponunt inter Sinum Vibonensem & Scylaceum vel Portum, qui ab Annibalis Castris denominatus, non totius est Italiæ, sed alterius ipsius versus Meridionalior cornu: ubi Aristoteles, cuius ante laudavi verba, ponit ἰσθμιας ἡμέρας. Adfirmant Incolæ & Locorum gnari, Italiam, ubi Isthmus inter Sinus Sanctæuphemianum, qui olim Hipponiates vel Vibonentis, Aristoteli autem Λαμπτικός, & Scylaceum maximas facit eiusdem Cornu angustias. Intervallum habere Continentis, xv, aut ad summum xx Miliariorum. In eduitissimo ipsius Isthmi fastigio amoenissima sunt Prata, Agrique culti, cum Silva crassissimarum & praecelsarum Ilicum, unde utrumque Mare Tyrrhenum & Hadriaticum conspicitur, tamquam haud magnis sejuncta spatiis.
units.tr: Italy, enclosed within the boundaries indicated, extends in length from Augusta Praetoria to Regium, as Strabo writes in book 5, Pliny in book 3 chapter 10 and elsewhere, Solinus in the Polyhistor, P. Rutilius Claudius Namatianus, and the author I have mentioned, on the Measurement of the Earth. They differ from one another somewhat, but the length is 1,120 miles (passuum). It stretches, as Strabo shows in book 6, "from the north" [ἀπὸ Ἀρκτων] in breadth. The breadth varies: the greatest is 410 miles, between the rivers Var and Arsia; the middle is 130 miles, around the city of Rome, from the mouth of the river Aternus to the outlet of the Tiber into the Tyrrhenian Sea; the least is not more than 40 miles, between the Harbour of Magna Graecia, which they call Hannibal's Camp, and the Gulf of Hipponium or Vibo. I, having made the measurement more carefully, have found its length from Augusta Praetoria to the Brutian Promontory or Leucopetra to be about 345 miles. Its breadth, which as I have just noted must be taken as the greatest, is 425; the middle is 130; and the least is 72, where it runs out into a double horn and is much narrower. That narrowest part, which some place between the Gulf of Vibo and Scylaceum or the harbour named after Hannibal's camp, belongs not to the whole of Italy but to the more southerly horn of it. There Aristotle, whose words I quoted earlier, places the "isthmus of a day" [ἰσθμιας ἡμέρας]. The inhabitants and those who know the places affirm that Italy, where the isthmus lies between the Gulf of Sant'Eufemia, which was formerly called Hipponiates or Vibonensis and by Aristotle Lamptikos, and Scylaceum, has the greatest narrowness of that horn. The land-bridge (intervallum continentis) is 15, or at most 20, miles. On the highest ridge of this isthmus there are very pleasant meadows and cultivated fields, with a forest of very thick and tall holm oaks, from where both the Tyrrhenian and the Adriatic Sea can be seen, as if separated by no great distance.

units.la: Circuitus & περίμετρα Italiae quibusdam apud Leandrum Albertum milliarior. cıɔ cıɔ cıɔ cıɔ ıɔ cccc; nonnullis cıɔ cıɔcıɔ cıɔ ıɔ ccxı. Castaldus colligit cıɔ cıɔ ıɔ l. Qui exactius sunt metiti, signant cıɔ cıɔ ccc; qui exactissime, non multo minus, cıɔ cıɔ ccc lx.
units.tr: The circuit and perimeter of Italy, according to some in Leander Alberti, is 4,450 miles; according to others 4,261. Castaldus reckons 2,100. Those who measured more exactly give 2,300; those who measured most exactly, not much less, 2,360.

units.la: Dorsum Italiae Mons est Apenninus, qui Spinae instar per mediam sensim incedens eam in duo secat latera; quorum unum Favonio, vel, ut quidam ejus Situm notant, 10 Africo; alterum Euro, vel Aquilone potius, est obversum.
units.tr: The spine of Italy is the Apennine mountain, which, like a backbone, runs gently through the middle and divides it into two sides: one faces the west (Favonius), or, as some note its position, the south-west (Africus); the other faces the east (Eurus), or rather the north (Aquilo).

units.la: Umbilicum M. Terentius Varro statuit in Agro Reatino Cutilia Lacum, in quo fluctuer Insula, teste Plinio lib. iii. Nat. histor. cap. xii. alii Lacum Velinum, qui non procul inde, Italiae medium tenere affirmant. Sive Cutiliensis, sive Velinus Lacus Regionis hujus Umbilicus sit censendus, Centrum sane sic depingit Virgilius lib. vii. Aeneidos: Est locus Italiae in medio sub Montibus altis, Nobilis, & fama multis memoratus in orbi, Amsancti Valles: densis hunc frondibus atrum Vrget utrinque latus Nemus: medioque fragosus Dat sonitum saxis & torto vortice Torrens. Hic Specus horrendum & saevi Spiracula Ditis Monstrantur, ruptoque ingens Acheronte vorago Pestiferas aperit fauces, quis condita Erinnys Invisum Numen terras caelumque levabat.
units.tr: Marcus Terentius Varro places the navel in the territory of Reate at the lake of Cutilia, in which there is a floating island, as Pliny says in book 3 of the Natural History, chapter 12. Others affirm that the lake Velinus, which is not far from there, holds the middle of Italy. Whether the lake Cutilia or the Velinus is to be regarded as the navel of this region, Virgil certainly portrays its centre thus in book 7 of the Aeneid: "There is a place in the middle of Italy, under high mountains, famous and renowned in many accounts throughout the world, the valleys of Amsanctus. On either side a dark wood presses in with dense foliage, and in the middle a roaring torrent gives a noise over rocks and with a twisting whirl. Here a horrible cave and the breathing holes of cruel Dis are shown, and a huge abyss, Acheron having burst open, opens its pestilent jaws, into which the Fury, hidden, lifted the hateful power from the lands and sky."

units.la: In quorum Versuum expositione parum fidi Donatus & Servius. Hic enim Cosmographos ait Italiae Medium prope Venosam designare, nimirum in Herpinis ad Apuliae Campaniaeque confinium, ubi sulphureae foetidaeque, quod Silvis umbrosis circumdentur, sunt Aquae; ideoque Viam & Aditum ad Inferos ibi in locis esse, dicit, quod ibi Victimae noxiarum aquarum teterrimo perimi foetore solent: Ille autem Locum hunc juxta Canosam ad flumen Calorem esse censet. Errat uterque. Nam quis lanus Italiae Umbilicum statuet in Apulia? Reclamat mensura. Quinimo nec Valles, nec Montes in Apulia reperiuntur illi, quos commemorat Virgilius. Plura dicam alio loco.
units.tr: Donatus and Servius are not very reliable in their explanation of these verses. For Donatus says that the cosmographers mark the middle of Italy near Venusia, namely in the Herpini, on the border of Apulia and Campania, where there are sulphurous and foul-smelling waters, surrounded by shady woods; and therefore he says that the way and entrance to the underworld is in those places, because victims of harmful waters are usually killed there by a most foul stench. Servius thinks that this place is near Canusium, on the river Calor. Both are wrong. For who would place the navel of Italy in Apulia? The measurement refutes it. Indeed, neither the valleys nor the mountains that Virgil mentions are found in Apulia. I will say more about this in another place.

units.la: Italiam Eustathius Hederae; Quercus adsimulant folio Plinius lib. iii. cap. v, Solinus in Polyhistore, & Rutilius Claudius Numatianus lib. i, ut procerritate multo sit amplior, quam Latitudine; in laevum se flectens cacumine, & Amazonicae figura definens Parma. Recentiores convenientissime Humano Cruri comparant; cujus Tibia vel Anticnemion Mari objacet Infero; Sura, Supero; Pes universum Ionio abluitur Pelago; Calcaneus Epirum spectat; Vola vel Concavitas Sinum facit Tarentinum; Carnosiores Partes Promontoria statuunt Zephyrium, Carcynum, & Bruttium; Digiti in Siciliam sunt conversi; Genu in Promontorio est Populonio; Coxendix & Femoris Superiora late contingunt Alpes.
units.tr: Italy Eustathius compares to an ivy leaf; Pliny in book 3 chapter 5, Solinus in the Polyhistor, and Rutilius Claudius Namatianus in book 1 compare it to an oak leaf, so that it is much wider in length than in breadth; bending to the left at its top, and defining itself in the shape of an Amazonian shield. More recent writers compare it most aptly to a human leg: its shin or front of the lower leg lies along the Lower Sea; the calf faces the Upper Sea; the whole foot is washed by the Ionian Sea; the heel faces Epirus; the hollow of the sole makes the Gulf of Taranto; the fleshier parts are the promontories of Zephyrium, Carcinum and Bruttium; the toes are turned toward Sicily; the knee is at the promontory of Populonium; the hip and the upper part of the thigh touch the Alps widely.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CAP. III.

units.la: Italiae Situs Caelestis.
units.tr: The Celestial Situation of Italy.

units.la: DE Quantitate dixi: succedit explicanda Qualitas, cujus causa potior solet esse Situs Coelestis. Plinius Italiam per Maria incedere, Caeli regione, si quis id diligenter exigat, inter Horam Sextam Primamque Brumalem, scribit. Nos illud Meridiem & Exortum Solis Hibernum dicere solemus. Hora enim Sexta Antiquis Meridies fuit. Ptolemaeus inter Septimum & Quartum Clima, gradu Longitudinis xv, Latitudinis plus vii collocat. Si quis hodie diligentissimam ineat Situs Caelestis rationem: secundum Longitudinem quidem Occidentalissimum xliii: secundam Latitudinem completi Gradus octo: Australissimum enim Parallelum distare ab Aequatore Grad. xxxviii, & Borealissimum xlvi; sicque occupare discet Italiam Quintum & Sextum Climata, omnesque Parallelos, qui sunt inter xI & xvI, in quo Terræ tractu contingit Varietas Diei Artificialis unius Horæ. Maior enim Dies Aestatis in Parallelo Australi Horarum est xIIII, cum tribus quintis; in Boreali vero Horarum xv cum Quintis totidem.
units.tr: I have spoken of its quantity; next comes its quality, whose chief cause is usually its celestial situation. Pliny writes that Italy runs through the seas in a region of the sky which, if anyone examines it carefully, lies between the sixth hour and the first hour of the winter day. We usually call this the south and the winter sunrise, for among the ancients the sixth hour was noon. Ptolemy places Italy between the seventh and fourth climates, at 15 degrees of longitude and a little more than 7 of latitude. If anyone today works out the celestial situation with the greatest care, he will find that for longitude the westernmost point is 43 degrees, and for latitude the full eight degrees: the southernmost parallel lies 38 degrees from the equator, and the northernmost 46 degrees. Thus Italy occupies the fifth and sixth climates, and all the parallels lying between 40 and 46 degrees, in which stretch of land the length of the artificial day varies by one hour. For the longest summer day on the southern parallel is 14 hours and three fifths, while on the northern it is 15 hours and as many fifths.

units.la: CAP. IIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: De Qualitate, quæ pendet plurimum ex Situ Cælesti, paretque in Commodis, quæ inde proveniunt.
units.tr: On the quality of the air, which depends chiefly on the celestial situation, and on the advantages that follow from it.

units.la: COELESTI Situ sic se habente, accedentibus etiam Apenninis Montibus, qui per mediam Italiæ porrecti Longitudinem, ab utroque Latere, præcipue, quo meridianos excipit Calores, Campos, Collesque relinquunt frugiferos: non magnopere mirandum est, tam moderatam omnium anni Partium in Italia esse Temperiem, tantamque rerum omnium fertilitatem: quæ tamen aliis, quam aliis, locis major. Vere Strabo lib. VI, præcipuas Italiæ Qualitates enumerans: Τέλος δὲ, τὸ πολλαχῆς εὐκρατότατον ... ἄερα τε καὶ κλίματα, ... Huc pertinet locus Plinij lib. xvii. cap. v: Idem (inquit, de Catone) Agrum optimum judicat ad radicem montium. Planitiæ in Meridiem excurrentes, quæ est totius Italiæ Situs: nimirum, ut illustrando Catoni nonnihil addam, ad Apenninī latus, qua, si Longitudo ejus (ut idem Cato non obscure innuit) ab Occidente in Orientem vergit, Auster est, vel, si ab Septemtrione in Meridiem, inquit Strabo, se extendit, qua Favonius; vel denique, si mediam ingrediundum viam ab Cauro in Vulturnum, qua Africus. Ad alterum Apenninī latus, Planitiæ in contrarias plagas excurrente, Italiæ Agri minus sunt fœcundi ob Frigorum Ventorumque Borealium impetum & violentiam. De Priore Latere exaudiendus præcipue Virgilius, quum inquit: Hic Ver adsiduum, atque alienis mensibus Æstas, Bis gravida Pecudes, bis Pomis utilis Arbos.
units.tr: With Italy's position in the heavens as it is, and with the Apennine mountains also running the whole length of the peninsula, leaving fertile plains and hills on either side (chiefly on the side that receives the warmth from the south), it is not very surprising that Italy has such a mild temperature in every part of the year and such fertility in all things, though this fertility is greater in some places than in others. Strabo, in Book VI, listing Italy's chief qualities, truly says: And finally, that it is for the most part most temperate ... air and climates [Τέλος δὲ, τὸ πολλαχῆς εὐκρατότατον ... ἄερα τε καὶ κλίματα]. To this belongs the passage of Pliny, Book XVII, chapter 5: Cato (he says) judges the best land to lie at the foot of the mountains, on plains running out to the south, which is the situation of all Italy. To make Cato's meaning a little clearer: on the flank of the Apennines, where the range runs (as Cato himself hints not obscurely) from west to east, the land faces the south wind; if it runs from north to south, as Strabo says, it faces the west wind (Favonius); and if one takes the middle course from the northwest to the southeast, it faces the southwest wind (Africus). On the other flank of the Apennines, where the plains run out in the opposite directions, the fields of Italy are less fruitful, because of the onslaught and violence of the cold north winds. For the advantages of the former side, Virgil should be heard above all, when he says: Here is perpetual spring, and summer in months not its own; twice in the year the flocks bear young, and twice the trees bear fruit.

units.la: Specialiora videamus. Incolarum Italiæ fuit semper, hodieque est ditissima. Sola, inquit Plinius lib. III natur. hist. sine externis ullis auxiliis, atque etiam tunc (annum designat, quo nunciato Gallico tumultu, Coss. Romæ erant L. Æmilius Papus & C. Attilius Regulus, qui ab V. CIƆXXIX) sine Transpadanis, Equitum LXXX milia, Peditum IOCC M. armavit. Quis Italus sit genius, quæque indoles, postea peculiari capite dicam. Quosdam autem Italiæ incolas CXXVI annos vitæ contingere, tradit idem Plinius lib. VII. cap. XLIX.
units.tr: Let us look at more particular matters. Italy has always been, and is still today, the richest in inhabitants. Pliny, in Book III of the Natural History, says that without any foreign help, and even then (he refers to the year when, on the news of the Gallic uprising, the consuls at Rome were L. Aemilius Papus and C. Attilius Regulus, which was the 529th year after the founding of the city) without the Transpadanes, it armed 80,000 horse and 1,200,000 foot. What sort of people the Italians are, and what their character is, I shall discuss later in a separate chapter. Pliny also reports, in Book VII, chapter 49, that some Italians reach the age of 126 years.

units.la: Nec recensendis variorum generum Animalibus tempus teram, magnam Boum (qui vetere lingua Græca Γάλαι dicebantur) copiam in Italia fuisse, Bucesque in ea Terrigeni pasciqueque solita compluria, docent apud Agellium lib. XI. Noct. Attic. cap. I. Timæus in Historijs, quas oratione Græca de Rebus Populi Rom. composuit, & M. Terentius Varro in Antiquit. Rer. Humanar. Lucana Armenta maxima & validissima olim ibidem fuisse, testatur Lucillius: Quem neque Lucanus orlandi montibus Tauri Ducere protelo validis cervicibus possent.
units.tr: Nor shall I waste time listing the various kinds of animals. Agellius, in Book XI, chapter 1 of the Attic Nights, shows that there was a great number of oxen in Italy (which in the old Greek language were called galai), and that many buffaloes, born in the country, were often pastured there. Timaeus, in his histories of the Roman people written in Greek, and Marcus Terentius Varro, in his Antiquities of Human Affairs, also attest to this. Lucilius bears witness that the Lucanian herds were once very large and very strong there: such as the Lucanians could not lead down from the mountains of Taurus with a yoke on their strong necks.

units.la: Nutrit Italia, præter alias Aves, Aquilas Vulturesque, carnivoras & rapaces Volucres, Historijs Romanorum Veterum etiam nobilitatas.
units.tr: Italy also feeds, besides other birds, eagles and vultures, carnivorous and predatory birds made famous even in the histories of the ancient Romans.

units.la: Ager, valde est temperatus, benignus, lætus, copiosus, ad Segetes aliaque omnia proferenda supra modum adcommodus, magnique suis Cultoribus quæstus, sumtus autem exigui. Rosellanus Ager in Umbria juxta Lacum Velinum tantæ fertilitatis fuisse scribitur, ut auctore Varrone, Cæsar Vopiscus, quum Cautam apud Censores ageret, Campos Rosea dixerit Italia Sumen esse, in quibus Pertice prædie relictas Gramen, una nocte, operiret. Videndi Plinius lib. XVII natur. Hist. & Servius ad VII Aeneidos addit: Quinetiam quantum per diem demtum esset, tantum per noctem crescebat, quod Virgilius ad suam provinciam transtulit dicens:
units.tr: The land is very temperate, kindly, pleasant and abundant, exceedingly well suited to producing grain and all other crops, and it brings great profit to its farmers at small expense. It is written that the Rosellan land in Umbria, beside Lake Velinus, was of such fertility that, according to Varro, when Caesar Vopiscus was conducting the census of Cautus before the censors, he called the plains of Italy rosy (Sumen), in which the grass grew back in one night on the pasture poles left behind. Pliny, in Book XVII of the Natural History, should be consulted, and Servius, on the Seventh book of the Aeneid, adds: Moreover, as much as was taken away during the day grew back during the night, which Virgil applied to his own province, saying:

units.la: Et quamtum longu carpent Armenta diebus,
units.tr: And as much as the herds crop in long days,

units.la: Exigua tantum gelidus ros nocte reponet,
units.tr: The cold dew will restore in a single short night.

units.la: Fimi usum, scribit eodem libro Plinius, ab Hercule divulgatum in Italia, quæ, addens, Regi suo Sterculio, Fauni Filio, ob hoc inventum immortalitatem tribuit. Ad Vitium optima fert, inquit Varro Italiæ dotes persequens: Ager Campanus, Frumentum; Falernus, Vinum; Cafinas, Oleum; Tusculanus, Ficum; Mel, Tarentinum; Piscem, Tiberis. Plinius, quum dixisset Tritici genera esse plura, Italicum, adiicibit, nullum equidem comparaverim candore ac pondere, quo maxime differnitur; Montanus modo comparetur Italia Agris externis, in quo principatum tenuit Baetica, deinde Syria, mox Africa. Addit idem paullo post, annis fere cxlv Sophoclem Poetam in fabula Tripolemo Italiam ante cuncta laudasse, ad verbum translata sententia:
units.tr: Pliny writes, in the same book, that the use of manure was spread in Italy by Hercules, who, he adds, in return gave immortality to his king, Sterculius, the son of Faunus, for this invention. Varro, following up on Italy's gifts, says: "It bears the best of vines": the Campanian land for wheat; Falernian for wine; Cales for oil; Tusculum for figs; Tarentum for honey; the Tiber for fish. Pliny, having said that there are several kinds of wheat, among them the Italian, adds: I certainly would not compare any with it for whiteness and weight, in which it is especially distinguished; only Montanus, among foreign lands, can be compared with Italy, where Baetica held first place, then Syria, and soon Africa. Pliny adds shortly afterward that about 145 years earlier the poet Sophocles, in his play Tripolemus, had praised Italy above all others, the sentence being translated word for word:

units.la: Et fortunatam Italiam Frumento carere candido.
units.tr: And fortunate Italy, which lacks no white wheat.

units.la: Quæ laus, inquit, peculiaris hodieque Italico est. Quo magis admiror Poëteros Græcorum nullam mentionem huius fecisse frumenti. Sed illam Italiæ benignitatem exhausit tandem Avaritia, adeo ut tandem vera e literis opinio eorum, qui tum illam Terram existimavere lasam, ut inquit nominatus sæpe Plinius, qui ex quorundam cœnatione, Latifundia, exclamat, perdidere Italiam, tam vero & Provincias, &c.
units.tr: This praise, he says, is still peculiar to Italy today. So much the more I wonder that the Greek poets made no mention of this wheat. But avarice at last exhausted that kindness of Italy, so that the true opinion of those who then judged that land to be worn out, as the aforementioned Pliny often says, came to pass. He cries out, from the dinner-table talk of certain men, that the great estates have ruined Italy, and indeed the provinces too, and so on.

units.la: Italiam porro peculiarem omnium Arborum Parentem videri posse, testatur idem Plinius libri xiv Proœmio. Vulgatas non commemorabo. Earum, quæ vulgo Aurantia, Citria vel Medica, Cydonia, aliaque id genus, incredibilis hic copia. Tota ora, ut ea nobis sit exemplo, quæ in Liguria ab D. Remi, atque etiam ulterius, ad Genuam pertinet, tot tamque nobilibus Arboribus, itemque Palmis summæ proceritatis, unde fructus admodum generosi odoriferique percipiuntur, ornata est, ut cum aspectu, tum odoratu sit pertucunda; Horti passim occurrentibus, ad recreandas tristes afflictasque hominum mentes, amœnissimis. Idem de mille aliis dici potest locis. Vivere in Italia Piperis arborem, docet laudatus paullo ante Plinius lib. xvi cap. xxxii, sterilesque autem ibi Palmas esse, lib. xiii, cap. iv. Oleam omnino non fuisse in Italia, Hispania atque Africa, L. Tarquinio Prisco regnante, scribit Fenestella apud eumdem Plinium lib. xv. cap. i: qui eodem libro cap. 11. Olea laudat Venafranum & Licinianum. Præstantissime autem ceteris Venafranum, declarat etiam Martialis hoc Distichon:
units.tr: Pliny, in the preface to Book XIV, also testifies that Italy may be seen as the special parent of all trees. I shall not mention the common ones. Of those commonly called oranges, citrons or Median apples, and quinces, and others of that kind, there is an incredible abundance here. The whole coast, as an example of this, from Liguria, from St. Remy and even further, reaches to Genoa, and is adorned with so many and such noble trees, and likewise with palms of great height, from which very fine and fragrant fruits are gathered, so that it is delightful both to the sight and to the smell; gardens everywhere, most pleasant for refreshing the sad and afflicted minds of men. The same may be said of a thousand other places. The laudable Pliny, a little before, in Book XVI, chapter 32, teaches that the pepper tree lives in Italy, and in Book XIII, chapter 4, that the palms there are barren. Fenestella, cited by the same Pliny in Book XV, chapter 1, writes that the olive was not found in Italy, Spain or Africa at all during the reign of Lucius Tarquinius Priscus; and in the same book, chapter 2, he praises the olive of Venafrum and Licinianum. Venafrum is by far the best of the rest, as Martial also declares in this couplet:

units.la: Hoc tibi Campani sudavit Baccia Venafri
units.tr: The Campanian berry of Venafrum sweated for you,

units.la: Unguentum quoties sumis, & ipsa olet.
units.tr: Whenever you use ointment, and it itself smells sweet.

units.la: Videndus & Horatius lib. ii. Carm. Od. vi. lib. ii Sat. iv. & viii. Oleæ hodie maxime fertet Terra Hydruntina, in qua tanta copia, ut cui Olearum his in locis ingentia nemora non sunt visa, incredibile plane videri possit. Ager Barianus in Apulia Peucetia Oleum, Vinum, Frumentum, Amygdalam, Gossypium aliosque fructus ubertate quadam & abundantia fundit incredibili. Unus Vallis Oneliæ Ager in Liguria tanto gaudet Olei proventu, ut quandoque duodeviginti, nonnumquam vicena millia reddat Vrnarum, quas Incolæ Barilas vocant. Nec Manna negavit Italia Natura. Prope Altomontium in Brutiis Manna colligitur, noctu rorans: præcipue quum Imbres diurnos liquidum purumque cælum noctis excipit. Legitur ex frondibus & Arborum quarumdam truncis. Eodem beata Munere Magna Græcia, quo loco Thurinorum nobis vestigia visuntur. Loca petis plura Lector? Servare se aiunt in Campania Amalphitani ollà D. Andreæ, ex iis peculiarem liquorem (Incolæ Manna vocant) exsudare adherentes, cumque voti causa peregrinantibus elargientes. Commemorantur similia ab Apulis Peucetiis de Mauri Episcopi, Sergii & Pantaleonis Equitum atque Martyrum reliquiis, apud Vigilias; de Nicolai Mireani Antistitis, ab Opidi Bariani Civibus; de Hippolyti denique Martyris Ossibus ab Tripaltinis apud Samnites.
units.tr: Horace, Odes Book II, ode 6, and Satires Book II, satires 4 and 8, should also be consulted. Today the land of Otranto bears olives most abundantly, in such quantity that to one who has not seen the vast groves of olives in these places it may seem quite incredible. The Barian land in Apulia Peucetia pours out oil, wine, wheat, almonds, cotton and other fruits with incredible richness and abundance. The single field of the Onelian valley in Liguria so rejoices in its yield of oil that sometimes it produces eighteen, sometimes twenty thousand jars, which the locals call barile. Nor has Italy's nature denied manna. Near Altomonte in the Bruttii, manna is collected; it drips at night, especially when clear, pure sky follows the daytime rains. It is gathered from the leaves and trunks of certain trees. Magna Graecia, where traces of the Thurii are seen, was blessed with the same gift. Do you, reader, seek more places? In Campania, the people of Amalfi say that St. Andrew's bone-box preserves a special liquid (which the locals call manna) that exudes and clings to it, and they distribute it to pilgrims travelling for vows. Similar things are recorded by the Peucetian Apulians about the relics of the Bishop Mauritius, of the knights and martyrs Sergius and Pantaleon, as described by Vigilius; about the relics of the bishop Nicholas of Myra, by the citizens of the town of Bari; and finally about the bones of the martyr Hippolytus, by the men of Tripalta among the Samnites.

units.la: Vitium principatum in tantum proprium esse & peculiarem Italia notat idem Plinius Proœmio, quod dixi, lib. xiv. ut vel hoc uno omnia gentium vicisse, quamquam odorifera, possint videri bona; quamquam ubique pubescentium odori nulla suavitas præfertur. Tellantur generosissima, quæ passim nascuntur, Vina, ab Antiquis Scriptoribus decantata. De iis universim Athenæus lib. i. Δωμαῖοι. Octoginta fere in toto orbe genera Vini nobilia, exque eo numero duas partes Italiæ esse memoriæ prodit Plinius lib. xiv. cap. xi. Idem ejusdem libri cap. vi. pleraque Italia Vina ad quatuor refert classes. Omnibus aliis præfert, ex alieno iudicio, Setinum, ab Setia Latii opido dictum.
units.tr: Pliny, in the preface to Book XIV which I have mentioned, notes that the vine holds such a primacy and is so special to Italy, that on this one point alone it may seem to have surpassed all the good things of the nations, although fragrant ones; although in every place the odour of the flowering plants is not held to be pleasant. The most noble wines, which grow everywhere, were praised by the ancient writers. Athenaeus, in Book I, The Romans, discusses them generally. Pliny, in Book XIV, chapter 11, reports that about eighty kinds of wine are famous throughout the whole world, and that two parts of that number belong to Italy. In chapter 6 of the same book he sorts most of the wines of Italy into four classes. Above all others he prefers, on the judgment of others, the Setinian, named after Setia, a town of Latium [Δωμαῖοι].

units.la: Vin. quæ
units.tr: Wines which

units.la: Primæ qui dem classis, Setinum. Diuus Augustus Setinum, inquit, praetulit cunctis, & fere sequuti principes, &c. Commendat etiam cum Strabone, (vide infra, ubi de Signino) Setina Vina Martialis: Pendula Pomtines quae spectat Setia Campos, Exigua vetulos misit ab Urbe Cados.
units.tr: Of the first class, Setinum. The divine Augustus preferred Setinum to all others, and the emperors who followed him nearly all did so, etc. Strabo also commends it (see below, where I discuss Signinum): Setine wines. Martial: Setia, which looks down on the Pomptine plains, sent its little Cados from the city to our aged wines.

units.la: Nascitur supra Forum Appij, Plinio; qui addit: Antea Caecubo erat generositas celeberrima in palustribus Populetis, Sinu Amyclano, quod tam intercidit & incuria Coloni Locique angustia, magis tamen Fossa Neronis &c. De Caecubo Athenaeus lib. 1. Εὐγλὴς δὲ καὶ ὁ Καικύνος, πλησίον, ὅπου δ' ἀκλεεστέραν δὲ μὴ ἴσχυρὰ ἐπὶ: sensum pungit ac ferit, vehemens est, vetustatem colligit post aliquam multos annos. Martialis: Caecuba Fundanis generosa coquuntur Amyclis; Vitis & in media nata palude viret.
units.tr: It grows above the Forum of Appius, says Pliny, who adds: Formerly Caecuban had the most famous quality, in the marshy Populetum near the Amyclan Gulf, but this has declined through the neglect of the farmer and the narrowness of the site, though more because of the Fossa Neronis, etc. Athenaeus, book 1, on Caecuban: Εὐγλὴς δὲ καὶ ὁ Καικύνος, πλησίον, ὅπου δ' ἀκλεεστέραν δὲ μὴ ἴσχυρὰ ἐπὶ. The sense is that it pricks and strikes the palate, it is strong, and it gathers age after many years. Martial: Caecuban wine is brewed by the noble people of Amyclae at Fundi, and the vine that grows in the middle of the marsh flourishes.

units.la: Meminit & Horatius lib. 1. Carm. Od. xxxvii, ubi monet ob Victoriam Actiacam Genio indulgendum esse: Venam quoque Caecubam nominans lib. 1. Ode xx: Caecubam, & prelo domitam Caleno Tu bibes Faunam: mea nec Falerna Temperant Vites, neque Formiani Pocula colles.
units.tr: Horace also mentions it in book 1 of the Odes, Ode 37, where he advises that the Genius be indulged because of the victory at Actium. Naming the Caecuban vintage again in book 1, Ode 20: You will drink Caecuban, pressed in the Calenian press, and Faunus; neither the Falernian vines nor the Formian hills temper my cups.

units.la: Tribuit secundum locum Plinius Falerno: Secunda Nobilitas Falerno Agro erat, & ex eo maxime Faustiano cura culturaque id collegerat. Exoleseit hoc quoque copia potius, quam bonitati fluentium. Et paullo post: Nec ulli in Vino maior austeritas; sed in Vinorum flamma accenditur. Tria eius genera Austerum, Dulce, Tenue. Quosdam ista distinguunt, Summis Collibus Gauranum gigni; mediis, Faustianum; imis, Falernum. Athenaeus Vini Falerni duas facit species: οὐχ ἓν δύο, inquiens, τῆ Φαλέρνῳ, ὁ αὐστηρὸς, καὶ ὁ γλυκάζων. Quod illis Austerum, Horatio Severum est lib. 1. Carminum Ode xxvii & Forte lib. ii. Satyr. iv. Qualitatem hanc indebat fortean Vetustas, quam optime ferebat. Vetulum dicitur Catullo Carmine xxvii, Macrobio in Saturnalib. & aliis. Temperabatur autem vel alio Vino, vel Melle. Falerni Austeritatem Vino Chio, quod lenius erat ac mitius, obtundi solitam innuit Horatius lib. 1. Satyr. x: —— at Sermo Lingua concinnus utraque Suavior, ut Chio nota si commissa Falerni est.
units.tr: Pliny gives Falernian second place: Falernian land held second rank in fame, and it had gained that reputation chiefly through the care and cultivation of the Faustian estate. This too has faded, through quantity rather than quality of the wine. And shortly after: No wine is more austere, yet the flame of wines is kindled in it. It has three kinds: austere, sweet, and thin. Some distinguish these by place: the Gauran grows on the highest hills, the Faustian on the middle slopes, the Falernian on the lowest. Athenaeus makes two kinds of Falernian wine, saying: not one but two Falernians, the austere and the sweet [οὐχ ἓν δύο τῆ Φαλέρνῳ, ὁ αὐστηρὸς, καὶ ὁ γλυκάζων]. What they call austere, Horace calls severe (book 1, Ode 27), and strong (book 2, Satire 4). Age probably softened this quality, which it bore very well. Catullo calls it old (Carmen 27); Macrobius in the Saturnalia and others do the same. It was tempered either by another wine or by honey. Horace hints that the austerity of Falernian was usually softened by Chian wine, which was gentler and milder, in book 1, Satire 10: but my speech is more pleasing, since both tongues are blended as Chian wine is blended with Falernian.

units.la: Eandem Austeritatem Veteres Melle lenire ac mitigare solitos, indicat idem Horatius lib. ii. Sat. iv: Ausidius Forti miscebat Mella Falerno.
units.tr: Horace, book 2, Satire 4, shows that the ancients were accustomed to soften and mitigate the same austerity with honey: Ausidius mixed honey with strong Falernian.

units.la: Et eodem libro Sat. ii: —— nisi Hymettia Mella Falerno Ne biberis diluta.——
units.tr: And in the same book, Satire 2: unless you drink Falernian diluted with Hymettian honey.

units.la: Respicit eo Virgilius lib. iv. Georgic. Dulcia Mella premes, nec tantum dulcia, quantum Et liquida, & durum Bacchi domitura saporem.
units.tr: Virgil has this in mind in book 4 of the Georgics: you will press sweet honey, not only sweet but also clear, to tame the harsh taste of Bacchus.

units.la: Vbi durus Bacchi Sapor, Vinum Falernum; quod Plinio & Athenaeo Austerum. Dulce, quod idem vocant, fieri solitum notat Athenaeus, ὅταν ἐκ τῶν ἡμερῶν ἐστιν ἀποδιδόμενον. Intima porro Nota Falerni apud Horat. lib. ii. Od. iii, Vinum signat Falernum, optimae notae, in intima Cella Vinaria, ut volunt Interpretes, recondi solitum. Liberalitatem in Falerno distribuendo Iulij Caesaris celebrat Plinius lib. xiv. cap. xv. apud quem & aliis locis Falerni est mentio, ut etiam apud Strabonem lib. v, & alios. Ad Tertiam veniunt apud Plinium palmam Vina Albana, Surrentina, Massica, Statana, Calena, Fundana, Veliternina, Privernatia, Signina, Albana, inquit, Vrbs vicina, ac rara in aevitero. Athenaeus lib. i, Γίνεται δὲ ἐκ τῶν Καμπανίας Κύμβω ὁ καλούμενος Ἀλβανὸς, μῆμος, ξύφος δοτ' ἐπὶ τῶν τόπων εἶναι. De Albano Horatius lib. ii. Sat. viii: Hic Herus, Albanum Maecenas, sive Falernum Te magis appositis delectat.
units.tr: Here the harsh taste of Bacchus is Falernian wine, which Pliny and Athenaeus call austere. Athenaeus notes that the sweet kind, which they also name, was usually produced when it is sold off after a few days [ὅταν ἐκ τῶν ἡμερῶν ἐστιν ἀποδιδόμενον]. The inner vintage of Falernian in Horace, book 2, Ode 3, means Falernian of the best quality, which, as the commentators think, was usually stored in the innermost wine cellar. Pliny praises Julius Caesar's generosity in distributing Falernian, book 14, chapter 15, where Falernian is also mentioned elsewhere, as it is in Strabo, book 5, and others. Pliny gives third place to the Alban, Surrentine, Massic, Statanian, Calenian, Fundanian, Veliternian, Privernatian and Signine wines: Alba, he says, is a neighbouring city, and rare in old age. Athenaeus, book 1: From the Campanian Cumae comes the so-called Albanum, a wine which is said to be found in those places. On Albanum, Horace, book 2, Satire 8: Here is my master Maecenas, who is more pleased by Albanum, or by Falernian, than by the wines served with food.

units.la: Albanum Vinum, si austerius, vetustate in dulcedinem: sin dulcius, in austeritatem transire, subindicat Plinius lib. xiv, cap. ii: qui descriptis Albanis haec subnectit: Item Surrentina in Vineis tantum nascentia, convalescentibus maxime probata, propter tenuitatem salubritatemque Tiberium Caesar dicebat consensisse Medicos, ut nobilitatem Surrentino darent, alioquin esse generosum Acetum: C. Caesar, qui successit illi, nobilem Vappam. Fuisse certe admodum laudata Surrentina declarat Martialis lib. xiv. Surrentina libi ? nec Murrhina picta, nec aurumSume, dabunt Calices hac tibi Vina suos.
units.tr: Pliny, book 14, chapter 2, suggests that Alban wine, if austere, turns to sweetness with age, but if sweeter, turns to austerity. After describing the Albans he adds: Likewise Surrentine, which grows only in the vineyards and is most highly approved when convalescents drink it, because of its thinness and healthfulness. Tiberius Caesar used to say that the physicians had agreed to give Surrentine the reputation of nobility, otherwise it would be a fine vinegar. Gaius Caesar, who succeeded him, called it noble vappa. That Surrentine was highly praised is clear from Martial, book 14: Surrentine, neither painted murrhine nor gold: take these, and these wines will give you their cups.

units.la: Eadem Vina memorat Strabo, ætate sua Romam deportari solita scribens Falerna, Setina, Calenaque, & cum iis certantia Surrentina; quod experientia vetustatem illa ferre comperta fuissent. Idem confirmat Higinus. Meminit Horatius lib. 11. Sat. 1111. Calicum, quos canit Martialis, nobilitate Surrentum celebratum auctor etiam est Plinius lib. xxxv. De ipsdem Martialis, quem dixi:
units.tr: Strabo mentions these same wines, writing that Falernian, Setine and Calenian were usually carried to Rome in his time, and that Surrentine competed with them, since experience had shown that it could bear age. Hyginus confirms this. Horace mentions it in book 2, Satire 3. The author also says that Surrentum was famed for the nobility of the Calices which Martial sings of; Pliny also says so in book 35. Of the same, Martial, whom I have quoted:

units.la: Ac ipse non vini Calices de pulvere natos,Sed Surrentina leve torcumaroia.
units.tr: And not cups made from the dust of wine, but a light Surrentine wine-cask...

units.la: Pergit Plinius: Certant Massica atque ex Monte Gaurano, Puteolos Baiasque prospectantia. Virg. lib. 11 Georgic.
units.tr: Pliny continues: Massic wine competes with the wine of Mount Gaurus, which looks out over Puteoli and Baiae. Virgil, book 2 of the Georgics:

units.la: Sed gravida fruges & Bacchi Massicus humorImp. evertere.
units.tr: But Massic, the moisture of Bacchus, has filled fruitful and heavy...

units.la: Lib. vii Æneidos.
units.tr: Book 7 of the Aeneid.

units.la: vertunt felicia Baccho Massica.
units.tr: They turn the Massic fields happy with Bacchus.

units.la: quemlocum exponens Servius, Massicum Campania Montem ait esse, Vini generosiferacem. Silius lib. vii. de Bello Pœn.
units.tr: Servius, explaining this passage, says that Massicum is a mountain of Campania, "generous and fertile of wine." Silius, Punic War book 7:

units.la: Vniferis late florebat Massicus Arvis,Miratus Nemora & florentes Sole Racemos.
units.tr: Far and wide the Massic fields flourished with their vine-bearing soil, marvelling at the groves and the clusters ripening in the sun.

units.la: Et paullo post:
units.tr: And a little later:

units.la: Massicus Vniferis addebat nomina glebis.
units.tr: The Massic land lent its name to the vine-bearing clods.

units.la: Item Horatius lib. 1. Carm. Oda 1:
units.tr: Likewise Horace, Odes book 1, ode 1:

units.la: Est qui nec Veteris pocula Massici, &c.
units.tr: There is one who does not refuse the cups of old Massic wine, etc.

units.la: Idem, Indolem Massicorum nonnullam indicans, lib. 11. Sat. iv:
units.tr: The same, indicating a certain character of Massic wines, in Satires book 2, satire 4:

units.la: Massica si cæno supponas Vina sereno,Nocturna, si quid crassi est, tenuabitur aura.
units.tr: If you mix Massic wine with cold water, the night air will thin whatever is heavy in it.

units.la: Massicum Athenæus austerum quidem esse notat sed Stomacho utile: ætate maturescebat, austeritatemque minuebat. De Statanis, quæ sequuntur, sic loquitur Plinius: Falerno contermina Statana ad principatus venere non dubie, palamque fecere, suaque cuiusque terris tempora esse, sicut rerum proventus occasusque. Statanum Vinum celebrat etiam Strabo lib. ix. Dictum videtur ab Statanis Paludibus Campaniæ, quarum meminit Statius lib. iii. Silvarum. Vide infra cap. xii. Prosequitur sua Vina Plinius: Iuncta hu prægeat foliebant Calena (sic dicta ab Caleno: De Caleno Athenæus; ὁ καλαιὸς τῶ Φαλέρνῳ & ςμαχύτης: meminit Horatius cum alibi; tum lib. 1. Od xx, & xxxi) & quæ in Vineis Arbusculisque nascuntur Fundana (Strabo quoque Vinum Fundanum & Cacubum valde commendat: laudat & his versibus Martialis:
units.tr: Athenaeus notes that Massic is indeed austere but useful for the stomach; it matured with age and lost its austerity. On the Statanian wines that follow, Pliny speaks thus: "Next to Falernian, the Statanian wines undoubtedly came to the fore and made it plain that each has its own season on its land, as with the yields and failures of crops." Strabo, book 9, also praises Statanian wine. It seems to be named from the Statanian marshes of Campania, which Statius mentions in Silvae book 3. See below, chapter 12. Pliny goes on to his own wines: "Calena, which used to be grown in combination with the others (so called from Calenus; Athenaeus speaks of Calenus, the Calaios of Falernian and its sharpness; Horace mentions it elsewhere, in Odes 1.20 and 1.31), and the Fundana, which grow in the vineyards and rows of vines" (Strabo also highly commends Fundanian and Caecuban wine; Martial praises it in these verses):

units.la: Hæc Fundana tulit felix Autumnus Opimi:Expressit Muisum Consul, & ipse bibit.)
units.tr: This Fundanian wine the fortunate autumn of Opimius produced; the consul pressed the must, and he himself drank it.

units.la: Ex alia vicinia Vibi Veliternina, Privernatisque. Nam quod Signia nascitur austeritate nimis continenda utile alvo, inter medicamina numeratur. Sic Strabo lib. v: Σηταῖα τῶν Σι- γνία Φιρακαλαῖα: ἢ ἀπὸ τῶν μολυνλῶν ἐνα; ἢ δὲ τὴν ἀλλήκωτήν νηλίας, τὴν Σίγνιον λεγόμενον.
units.tr: From another neighbourhood come the Viban, Veliternian and Privernatian wines. For the Signian wine, which is grown there, is too astringent but useful for the bowels, and is counted among the medicines. So Strabo, book 5: ... Read Σιγνιον (Signion). Priscian calls it so, and Martial:

units.la: Legendum Σιγνιον. Sic appellat Priscianus: sic Martialis:
units.tr: Signian wine

units.la: Potabis liquidum Signina moranti Ventrem:Ne nimium sistant, sit tibi parca sitis.
units.tr: You will drink clear Signian wine to stop the bowels; lest they stop too much, let your thirst be moderate.

units.la: Hinc Signia spumans inimico Musto legitur apud Silium lib. viii. Belli Pœnici. Quartum obtinent, Plinio teste, curriculum, beneficio D. Iulii, qui primus auctoritatem ijs tribuit, ut in ejus epistolis apparet, ad Superum Mare Pratutia, atque Ancone natascentia, & quæ à Palma una forte enata Palmesia appellantur. Pratutia à Pratutianis, Samnitium populis, nominata. Haud procul Ancone Sirolum est opidum, Vino nobile; quod hic Ancenitani nomine celebrat Plinius. De Palmesio non habeo quod dicam, nisi quod suspeca mihi sit scriptura, in Vina voce fortean Vea latente. De reliquis ita Plinius: In Mediterraneo vero Cesenatia ac Macenatiana. In Veronensi item Rhetica, Falernis tantum posthabita ab Virgilio. Vinum Rheticum Theodoricum Ostrogothorum Regem tertium Athesi & Hadriatico Mari, ac deinde iumentis Romam usque sibi adferri curavisse, refert Blondus. Id Cassiodorus Acinaticum nominans hoc modo describit, Colore esse rubens, Saporis regij ac optimi; cuius dulcedo mirifice cum quadam suavitate placeat: quamvis quam is autem ad latium densius crassiusque videatur instar carnis incoris vel marderda sa- tionis, tamen esse lucuaiissimum. Audiamus enarrantem cetera Plinium: Mox ab intimo sinu Maris Hadriana nominat & ... Albano Falernoque, faciundum monet ..., ponendumque ... Ab Ierso autem Lattenensia, Gratiliana, Statoniensia ab Graziliis & Statonia Etruriae opidis; de quibus suo loco.) Etruriae Falmam Lunae Habet, Ligurie Genus. Ligurum opida, quae vulgo Mons Ruber, Vuiveria, Manariola, Rivulique Maior, Gallis hodie Anglique sunt celeberrima, propter nobilitatem Vini, quod hinc eas in partes exportatur, Blondo telle. Admirationem profecto habet ingenium, ut notat Leander, qui in tam excelsis praeruptisque montium ingis, ad quae vix ipsae volucres accedere posse videantur, quaque tam perpetuas habent cautes, nulla ut terrae mica propemodum apparet, tanta quaeat esse copia Vitium, ut quum astate vestiuntur pampinis, Mutum hederaceo tegmine obductum teneant. Hinc tamen suavissima Vina, hinc nobilis ille succus percipitur. Adait Leander: De Plinio nomen satis nequeo, celebrata illi hac Vina non esse, nisi fonte cum Luminibus, quae laudari it quaque ... aguas gignuntur ... Est etiam in Liguria Tabia Castellum, Vinis Apianis inclutum, ambitu quidem exiguum, sed nomine celeberrimum et generis natalem fuisse, nec Malvatico Cretae, nec Cypro, nec ulli cum habeo, cum exotico Vino suavitate cedentis. Quae superant, ut recenter Plinius. Verum & omnium ... ab Au- sonio mari, non ea rum gloria, Tarentina & Serrinas, & Consensis genera, & Tempsae, ac Balista, Lacaniana ... Thuriniis. Omnium vero eorum maxime illustrata Mesalia potu & facile Lacanianae, non ... Gnumento masc. entia. His omnibus sua ab opidis vicinis, de quibus suo loco, erant nomina. Servitiana autem scripta censeo apud Plinium pro Vernitiana, vel saltem apud Antoninum in Itinere, quod Mediolano per Picenum & Campaniam ducit ad Columnam, id est Trajectum Siciliae, Vernacium potius arbitror pro Servitio quod opidum Samnium est, inter Aufidenam & Bovianum: quidam tamen pro Servino ibi retinuunt ex fidelissimis Antonini Exemplaribus Aesernianam. Quod Vinum Babia natum laudat Plinus; pro Babia legunt alij Badiam: quidam Barbiam. Certe Barmium Vinum habet etiam Athenaeus. Campania, aut Fiem Vinis molcens Plinius, nuper exivarit non iis Nominibus auctoritatem, sive cura, sive casa, ad quartum ab Neapoli lapidem Trebellis laudantur & ab Athenaeo lib. 1. juxta Capuam Caulinus, & in suo agro Trebulanis (Trebulam vel Tribulam habent Ptolemaeus & Plinius in Campania, pari, ut quidam putant, inter Capuam & Suessulam intervallo, quoque semper inter plebeia & Trifolium, ab Trifolino Monte, quem Neapoli vicinum memorat Galenus. Meminit Vitium Terfolini Agri Iuvenalis Satyr. iii: Te Trifo nus Ager fecunda Vitibus implet)
units.tr: Hence "Signia foaming with hostile must" is read in Silius, Punic War book 8. Fourth in the course, by Pliny's testimony, come the wines of Pratutia and those growing near Ancona, and those called Palmesian from a single palm tree that sprang up there. This was owed to the favour of the deified Julius, who first gave them authority, as appears in his letters. Pratutia is named after the Pratutians, a people of the Samnites. Not far from Ancona is the town of Sirolum, famous for its wine, which Pliny here celebrates under the name Ancenitan. About Palmesian I have nothing to say, except that the reading seems doubtful to me, the word Vina perhaps hiding Vea. Of the rest, Pliny says: "In the inland region, the Cesenatian and Macenatian wines; in the Veronese region likewise the Rhaetian, placed only after the Falernian, which Virgil preferred." Blondus reports that Theodoric, third king of the Ostrogoths, had Rhaetian wine brought to him by pack animals from the Adige and the Adriatic Sea all the way to Rome. Cassiodorus, calling it Acinatican, describes it thus: "It is red in colour, of royal and excellent flavour, and its sweetness pleases wonderfully with a certain charm; although it seems somewhat denser and thicker in the Latin manner, like the flesh of an ox or of a well-fed mullet, it is nonetheless most clear." Let us hear Pliny continue the rest: "Next, from the innermost bay of the Adriatic Sea..." he names ... and he advises that Albanian and Falernian be ... and placed ... "From Ierso come the Lattenensian, Gratilian and Statoniensian wines," from Gratilia and Statonia, towns of Etruria, of which in their place. "Etruria has Falma and Luna, Liguria has Genua." The towns of Liguria, commonly called Monte Rosso, Vivaria, Manariola and Rivulo Maggiore, are today most famous among the French and English for the nobility of their wine, which is exported from there to those regions, as Blondus tells. The ingenuity of the place is truly admirable, as Leander notes: among such lofty and steep mountain ridges, where scarcely the birds themselves seem able to approach, and where the cliffs are so unbroken that scarcely any earth is visible, there is so great an abundance of vines that when they are clothed in leaves in summer, they hold the rocks covered with an ivy-like mantle. Yet from here come the sweetest wines, and from here that noble juice is gathered. Leander adds: "I can hardly agree with Pliny that these wines are not celebrated, unless from a source with the lights which are praised..." are produced in the waters... There is also in Liguria the castle of Tabia, famous for Apian wines, small in circuit but most celebrated in name, and it was the birthplace of the sort which yields in sweetness neither to Cretan malmsey, nor to Cyprian, nor to any foreign wine. The rest, as Pliny recently said: "But indeed of all ... from the Ausonian sea, not their glory, the Tarentine and Serrinas, and the Consensian kinds, and Tempsa, and Balista, Lacanian ... Thurine. Of all of these, the most renowned for drinking is the Mesalian, and the Lacanian is easy..." All of these took their names from the neighbouring towns, of which in their place. I think Servitiana should be written in Pliny for Vernitiana, or at least in Antoninus' Itinerary, which runs from Milan through Picenum and Campania to Columna, that is, the crossing to Sicily. I rather think Vernacium stands for Servitium, a town of the Samnites between Aufidena and Bovianum; some, however, retain Servinum there, following the most faithful copies of Antoninus, and Aesernian. Pliny praises Babian wine as born there; others read Badia for Babia, and some Barbia. Athenaeus certainly also has Barmian wine. Pliny, who praises the wines of Campania, says: "Recently they have not been given authority by those names, whether by care or by chance, at the fourth milestone from Naples: the Trebellian wines are praised, and by Athenaeus in book 1; near Capua the Caulinian, and in its own field the Trebulan." (Ptolemy and Pliny have Trebula or Tribula in Campania, at an interval, as some think, between Capua and Suessula; then the ... Trifolinian, from Mount Trifolinus, which Galen mentions as near Naples. Juvenal in Satire 3 mentions the wine of the Trifolinian field: "The Trifolinian field fills you with its fruitful vines.")

units.la: gloriata. Nam Pompeiani summum x annorum incrementum est, nihil Senectla conferente. Dolore etiam capitum in sextam horam diei sequenti infesta deprehenduntur. Ut concludam varia Vinorum Nomina, hactenus a Plinio commemorata, circa annum ab V. C. ID CXXX, nondum, ut ipse docet lib. XIIII. cap. XIIII, in claritate erant. Itaque omnia tunc genita unum habebant Consulis L. Opimii nomen. De iis sic idem Plinius lib. XIIII. cap. II: Anno fuit omnium generum bonitas, L. Opimio Consule, quum C. Gracchus Tribunus, plebem seditionibus agitans, interemtus, ea Coeli Temperies fuit, quam Coeluram vocant, Solis opere, Natali Vibis ID CXXXIII. Durantque adhuc Vina ducentis fere annis, tam in spetiem redacta Mellis asperi. Sed de his alij: ego ad reliquas Italiae Dotes pergo; strictim eas indicaturus.
units.tr: ... for the Pompeian wine has a maximum of ten years' increase, nothing contributing by age. They also are found to be harmful to the head at the sixth hour of the following day. To conclude, the various names of wines, hitherto mentioned by Pliny, around the year 130 from the foundation of the city, were not yet in renown, as he himself teaches in book 14, chapter 14. Therefore all those then produced had only the name of the consul Lucius Opimius. Pliny himself says of them in book 14, chapter 2: "In the year of Lucius Opimius' consulship, when Gaius Gracchus, the tribune, was killed while stirring the people with sedition, there was an excellent quality of all kinds, and such a climate as they call Coelura, by the work of the sun, in the 133rd year of the city." And the wines still endure, almost two hundred years later, though reduced to the appearance of bitter honey. But others treat of these; I proceed to the remaining gifts of Italy, which I shall indicate briefly.

units.la: Herbarum omnis generis est fertilissima. Non gignere autem Musobalanes, Kiger, Amomum, Kinnamomi, Kemaron, Kladamomon, & alia multa, prodit memoriae Plinius lib. XIII. cap. II. Sed magna hic facta est mutatio.
units.tr: It is most fertile in herbs of every kind. Pliny in book 13, chapter 2, records that it does not produce musobalanes, kiger, amomum, cinnamon, kemaron, kladamomon, and many other things. But here a great change has occurred.

units.la: Quid vero de Metallis, Lapidibus, aliisque Muneribus dicam? Metallorum omnium fertilitate, ait Plinius lib. III. nat. histor. cap. XX. nullis cedit Terris; quod lib. XXXVII. cap. IV repetens, Italiae, inquit parcitum est (ab inquietandis ad exturbanda Metalla eius Viscoribus) Veteri Edicto Patrum: aliaque nulla fecundior Metallorum quoque erat Tellus. In Foro Iulio Hydra fluvius est, & haud procul inde Argenti-Vivi Fodina. In Agro Volaterrano nonnullis locis Terra est lutea, similis Auripigmento, foecundissima: quamobrem Incolae Regionis, quam possint illudiose iter hac vitant: odorem enim tam gravem exhalat, ut supervolantes Aves mortuae statim concidant. Magna Alumanis Aluminis copia ante aliquot annos reperta est apud Etruscos in Territorio Massæ. In Campania Felice Cuniculi sunt, ex quibus effoditur Sulphur; ibidem etiam Convallis est, ubi Alumen coquitur. In Agro quoque Volaterrano Marantioque Loca putida monstrantur, quorum graveolentiam & fœtorem, Sulphuris Nigri Metallum, quod hic invenitur, & haud procul paratis ad id officinis excoquitur, exhalare censendum est. Ab Volaterris amnem Cecinam versus, millia tria, Colles aliquot visuntur, ubi Officinæ Salarie. Apud Brutios mille passibus ab Altomontio Salis fodinæ sunt, in intima montis viscera excavatæ, longitudine quædam 10, quædam 110 passuum, aut amplius, unde Salem effodiunt. Circa Tibur Latomia occurrunt, ubi Lapis Tiburtinus cæditur, Plinio nominatus. In Agro Vicentino, haud procul Pago, qui vernacule Cosfozza, Loca sunt, in longis profunditique Specubus; ex quibus Lapis cædituir, non absimilis Tiburtino, quo antiqua Patavinorum & Vicentinorum Aedificia speciantur confecta. Gabinus Albanusque Lapis impervius est igni, ut docet Tacitus lib. xv. Annal. Sic Isidorus lib. xvi: Savinus (leg. Gabinus) Lapis fusilis addito Oleo etiam lucere fertur. Est & quidam viridis Lapis, vehementer igni resilliens. Gabiorum Lapidis meminit etiam Strabo: Ταβίαι μὲν, inquit, ἐν τῇ Περγάμῳ ἱδὲ κατὰ λαμπρὸν ἔχοντα, ὑπὸ ... Latomus Gabinus non alias Romanis fuisse utibiliores. In Breonia Istriæ, Lapis cædituir, qui ab Venetis aliisque Conregionalibus ad Ædificia magnifica expeti solitus. Sunt & Lapidicinæ in Istria, Ædificiis Venetorum cum publicis tum privatis struendis ornandisque non inutiles. In Pedemontana Regione propè Fontes Padi nobilia Marmora ex imis Terræ penetralibus eruuntur: Sunt item Marmorum Fodinæ in Valdamio Lombardiæ Vico. In Rovienii Istriæ Agro Marmor exciditur, quod Istrucum vocatum: maximi per totam Italiam precij. Apud Tuscos in Agris Montibusque Lunæ vicinis candidi ac varij Marmoris lucidi esse Lapomias, perhibet Strabo lib. vi ex quibus unico solidoque Lapide Tabulæ integræ, Columnæque cædi solebant immensæ: summa addit & hinc olim ea Marmora, quæ ad Opera nobilissima cum Romæ, tum aliis in partibus expetebantur; tam ob insignem lævorem, quam propter summam exportandi hinc facilitatem; quippe quia vicinæ Littori ipsæ Lapicidinæ opportunitatem maximam haberent Lapidum ad Naves deferendorum; quos ab Mari subvehendos excipiebat Tiberis. Columnæ hic etiamnum peringentes aliaque rudia Marmorum frustra cernuntur: quæ florentibus rei Romanæ temporibus excisa, dein autem, ea labente, derelicta nemo exportavit vel expolivit. Importantur nunc quidem adhuc ex his locis Marmora Pisas, Genuam, Florentiam, Romam, Bononiam & in Ulteriorem Galliam: sed hauquaquam, recte Leandro, ejus Magnitudinis eaque copia, ut olim solebant Romam, vigente illius Urbis imperio. Meminit horum Marmorum Plinius lib. xxx. cap. x, in Liguria Lapidum Album facile terra secari scribens, quem prius, lib. xxx, cap. v. Lunensi Marmor dixerat. Mentionem facit & horum Marmorum Iuvenalis, quum inquit:
units.tr: What shall I say of metals, stones and other gifts? "For its fertility in all metals," says Pliny in book 3 of the Natural History, chapter 20, "it yields to no lands"; repeating this in book 37, chapter 4, he says: "Italy was spared" (from having its veins disturbed for digging out metals) "by an ancient edict of the Fathers; no other land was more fertile in metals." In Friuli there is a river Hydra, and not far from it a quicksilver mine. In the territory of Volterra, in some places there is yellow earth, like orpiment, very fertile; for this reason the inhabitants of the region, who are able to avoid it, avoid the road, for it exhales so heavy an odour that birds flying over it die at once. A great quantity of alum was found some years ago among the Etruscans in the territory of Massa. In Campania Felix there are tunnels from which sulphur is dug; in the same place is a valley where alum is boiled. In the Volterran and Maremma district, foul places are shown, whose stench and fetor must be ascribed to the black sulphur metal found here, which is smelted in workshops prepared for it nearby. Three miles from Volterra towards the river Cecina, several hills are seen where there are salt works. Among the Bruttii, a thousand paces from Altomonte, there are salt mines, hollowed out in the innermost bowels of the mountain, some ten, some a hundred and ten paces or more in length, from which they dig out salt. Around Tibur there are quarries where the Tiburtine stone is cut, named by Pliny. In the territory of Vicenza, not far from the village called Cossozza in the vernacular, there are places with long and deep caves, from which stone is cut, not unlike the Tiburtine, from which the ancient buildings of the Paduans and Vicentines are seen to have been constructed. The Gabine and Alban stone is impervious to fire, as Tacitus teaches in Annals book 15. So Isidore, book 16: "The Savine (read Gabine) fusible stone is said to shine even with oil added." There is also a certain green stone that springs back vehemently from fire. Strabo also mentions the stone of the Gabii: "The Tabiae in Pergamum ... shining ..." The Gabine quarry was never more useful to the Romans. In Breonia of Istria stone is cut, which is customarily sought by the Venetians and other neighbouring peoples for magnificent buildings. There are also quarries in Istria, not useless for building and adorning the public and private buildings of the Venetians. In the Piedmontese region near the springs of the Po, noble marbles are dug out from the deepest recesses of the earth. There are likewise marble quarries in Valdamio, a village of Lombardy. In the territory of Rovigno in Istria marble is cut, called Istrian, of very great value throughout Italy. Among the Tuscans, in the fields and mountains near Luna, Strabo, book 6, reports that there are shining quarries of white and variegated marble, from which entire slabs and immense columns were usually cut from a single solid stone. He adds that from here in former times were taken those marbles that were sought for the most noble works both at Rome and in other parts, both for their remarkable smoothness and because of the great ease of exporting them from here; for the quarries lay near the shore and had the greatest convenience for loading stones onto ships, which the Tiber received to carry from the sea. Columns still rise here and rough pieces of marble are seen in vain; these were cut in the flourishing times of the Roman state, but afterwards, when that declined, were abandoned, and no one exported or polished them. Indeed marbles are still brought from these places to Pisa, Genoa, Florence, Rome, Bologna, and into farther Gaul, but by no means, as Leander rightly says, of such size and in such abundance as they once used to be carried to Rome, while that city's empire flourished. Pliny mentions these marbles in book 36, chapter 10, writing that in Liguria the white stone can easily be cut, which he had earlier called Lunensian marble in book 36, chapter 5. Juvenal also makes mention of these marbles when he says:

units.la: Procubuit veluti, qui Saxa Ligustica portat.
units.tr: He falls down, like one who carries Ligurian stones.

units.la: Sic Facius Vbertus Canico vi, lib. iii. E vedemmo Carrara, one la gente Trova il candido Marmo in tanta copia, Che assai n'haurebbe tutto l'Oriente.
units.tr: So Fazio degli Uberti, in Canto 6 of Book 3: "We saw Carrara, where the people find the white marble in such abundance that all the East would have enough of it."

units.la: Lescalia porro, Volaterranensis Agri Vicus, Alabastrites copia abundat. Eius duo hic genera, durum ac molle: prius è Terra cædituir, dictum Vitrinum; aliud supra Terram invenitur, & excoctum igne Gypsum fit. Ex primo nobilia fabricantur Opera; veluti illa, quæ maximus quidam Artifex Neapolitanus olim Organa fecit, Leoni x P. M. muneri destinata: quo fatis intercepto priusquam absolverentur, Friderico Gonzagæ, Primo Mantuæ Duci, donata fuere. Opus profecto, quod inter rara mirabiliaque nunc quæ ulpiam sint, censeri debeat. Ex Alabastrite Fistulæ Modulique tori. Apud Gravisicas Coralium in mari nascitur, retibus reduci solitum. In Brutijs propè Altomontium Montes sunt editissimi, numquam fere nivibus carentes, ubi Crystallus, magna copia, reperitur: etenim quum ea luga intentissimis frigoribus perpetuo rigeant, Aquæ vi Solis de Nive stillantes, quum sunt congelatæ, postea diuturnitate temporis in saxa durantur. Terria ab Volaterris lapide Castellum est, ubi mira effoditur Chalcitis abundantia. Haud procul inde Aquæ Rivulus occurrit; iuxta quem, per Convalles quasdam modicas & depressa loca incedendo, Porphyretes, ophites, Achates, Chalcedonios, aliosque id genus pretiosos Lapides, varij coloris, est invenire: quos plerumque curtius aquarum eruit. In Tuscia prope Libbianum Terra Nigra foditur, magnaque Chaturn, unde Sutorium fit Atramentum, copia. In agro Vejentino Lapidem inveniri nel idem memorat his verbis lib. xxx. cap. x. Plinius: Vesentana Itatica gemma est, in Veis reperta; nigriam materiam distinguente Limite albo. Ad radices Tynnorum Montium Coeruleum tingendae Purpurae reperiri constans est rumor. Eruuntur & in Agro Volaterrano, quae vulgo Lazzuum, Vitriolum, aliaque subterranea.
units.tr: Lescalia, a village in the territory of Volterra, abounds in alabaster. There are two kinds here, hard and soft. The first is cut from the earth and is called vitrinum. The other is found above ground, and when burned in the fire it becomes gypsum. Fine works are made from the first, such as the organs that a certain outstanding Neapolitan craftsman once made as a gift for Pope Leo X. Death overtook Leo before they were finished, and they were given to Federico Gonzaga, first Duke of Mantua. It is certainly a work that ought to be counted among the rare and wonderful things anywhere in the world today. Pipes and moulded columns are made from alabaster. Near Grosseto coral grows in the sea and is usually brought up in nets. In the Bruttian lands near Altomonte there are very high mountains, almost never free of snow, where crystal is found in great quantity. For those ridges are held in perpetual rigour by the most intense cold, and the water dripping from the snow under the force of the sun freezes, and afterwards, over a long lapse of time, hardens into rock. Terria, a castle made of stone, lies some distance from Volterra, where a remarkable abundance of chalcitis is dug up. Not far from there a small stream runs by. Along it, as one walks through certain small valleys and low-lying places, porphyry, ophite, agate, chalcedony and other precious stones of that kind, of various colours, may be found; the flowing water usually uncovers them. In Tuscany, near Libbiano, black earth is dug up, and a great quantity of chalcanthum, from which shoemakers' ink is made. In the territory of Veii Plinius, in book 30, chapter 10, reports that a stone is found, in these words: "The Vesentine Itatica is a gem, found at Veii; a dark material is marked by a white line." It is a established rumour that blue for dyeing purple is found at the foot of the Tynnus mountains. In the territory of Volterra are also dug up what the common people call lazzuolo, vitriol, and other subterranean things.

units.la: Infinita, ne prolixior fiam, praetereo. Complectitur pleraque duplici Encomio Plinius, quorum unum lib. iii cap. v: Nec ignoro ingrats ac signis animi existimari posse, merito, si breviter atque in transcursu ad hunc modum dicatur: Terra omnium Terrarum Alumna, eadem & Parens; Numine Deum electa, quae Caelum ipsum clarius faceret, sparsa congregans Imperia Ritusque mollires; & tot Populorum discordes ferasque Linguas Sermonis commercio contraheret ad Colloquia & Humanitatem Hominis daret, breviterque una cunctarum Gentium in toto orbe Patria fieret. Sed quid agam? Tanta Nobilitas omnium Locorum, quos qui attigerit, tanta rerum singularum Populorumque claritas tenet. Vobis Roma vel sola in ea & digna tanta fama cervice facies, quo tandem narrari debet opere? Qualiter Campania ora per se, felixque illa ac beata amoenitas? ut palam sit uno in loco gaudentis opus esse Naturae. Iam vero tota ea vista is ac perennis salubritatis Caeli temperies est, tam fertiles Campi, tam aprici Colles, tam innoxii Saltus, tam opaca Nemora, tam munifica Silvarum genera, tot Montium adflatus, tanta Frugum & Vitium Olearumque fertilitas, tam nobilia Pecori Vellera, tot optima Taurii colla, tot Lacus, tot Amnium, Fontiumque ubertas, totam eam perfundens, tot Maria, Portus, Gremiumque Terrarum commercio patensundique, & tamquam ad iuvandos Mortales ipsa avide in Maria procurrens. Neque Ingenia Ritusque ac Viros, & Linguam Manusque superat ut commemoro Gentes. Ipsi de ea indicavere Graeci genus in gloriam suam esse sissimum, quorum Partem ex ea appellando Graeciam Magnam, &c. Alterum, quo finem imponit nobilissimo suo Naturae operi, lib. xxxvii cap. xiii: In toto Orbe, & quacunque Caeli convexitas vergit, pulcherrima est omnium, Rebusque merito principatum Natura obtinens Italia, Rectrix Parensque Mundi altera, Virtus, Feminis, Ducibus, Militibus, Servitus, Artium praestantia, Ingeniorum claritatibus, tam Sitis ac salubritate Caeli atque temperie, Accessu cunctarum Gentium facili, Littoribus Portuosis, benigno Ventorum adflatu. Etenim contingit recurrentis Positio in partem utilissimam, & inter Ortus Occasusque mediam Aquarum copia, Nemorum salubritate, Montium articulis, Ferorum Animalium innocentia, Solis fertilitate, Pabuli ubertate. Quidquid est quo carere Vita non debeat, nusquam est praestantius: Fruges Vinum, Olea, Vellera, Lina, Vestes, Iuvenci. Ne Fanos quidem in trigariis praeferri ullos vernaculus animadverto. Metallis Auri, Argenti, Aeris, Ferri, quamdiu iubuit (malim lucuit. Nam postea vetitum id Senatusconsulto: vide Plinium lib. xxxiii. cap. iv. vel Libuit, scilicet Patribus, Senatuique Romano) exercere, nullis cessit. Et iis nunc in se gravida pro omni Dote varios Succos & Frugum Pomorumque Sapores fundit. Italiam etiam valde commendat Dionys. Halicarnass. lib. i. omnes eam Europae Regiones sua commoditate superare scribens & fertilitate. Non inelegans Italiae Encomium scripsit Baptista Mantuanus ad Philippum Beroaldum, inter alia haec canens: Tradidit Italiae sua munera quisque Deorum: Et fuit ad dandas ingeniosus ope. Iuppiter Imperium docuit, Sceptrumque tenere, Et premere aequali barbara colla iugo. Arma dedit Mavors, Galeas, Ensesque corusos, Et cava loricae Scuta ferenda sinu: Addidit & latos Humeros Cervicibus amplis, Aptaque Thoraci Pectora squamifere; Per Campos Equitum Turmas, & nautica Bella Per Fluvios docuit currere, perque Fretum. Fronte graves Italos Lingua Incessuque modestos Esse facit lento falcifer igne Deus. Barbaricam stimulat Rabies in bella cohortem: Itala Consilium, Non Furor, arma movet. Hic Deus Agrorum Cultus, Artemque serendae Vitis, & arboreas insinuavit opes. Cynthius ad Musas animos inflexit Apollo, Et Disciplina tradidit omne genus. Arma Venus Populis Urbes implevit & Agros, Silvestresque Casas, Arboreasque Domos: Ut sint, qui curent Urbana Negocia Cives: Qui ferat Arma Manu, qui colat Arva Boves. Foedera Mercurius docuit Leges que feras, Et dare Clamori Litigiisque modum. Luna Pudicitiam suadet, caelumine ruborem Ne furat ardescens & sine Lege Venus. Arma Ceres: docuit Frugei, quae somne tactu Decolor incurvo rusticum ense metit. Vina dedit Bacchus, & quae multa alia sequuntur.
units.tr: I pass over countless others, lest I make this too long.
