Pliny sums up most of them in a double encomium, of which the first, in book 3, chapter 5, runs: "I am not unaware that I may be thought ungrateful and unmindful of my duty if I say it briefly and in passing, in this way: Italy, the foster-mother of all lands and yet their parent, chosen by the will of the gods to make heaven itself brighter, gathering together scattered empires and softening customs, and drawing together the many discordant and savage tongues of peoples by the commerce of speech for conversation, and giving humanity to man, and in short becoming, across the whole world, one fatherland of all nations. But what shall I do? Such is the nobility of all the places that whoever has touched them is held by such fame of each thing and each people. For you alone, Rome, with your neck worthy of so great a fame, what work should at last be told of you? And how of the Campanian coast by itself, that happy and blessed pleasantness? So that it is plain that nature has labored in one place for delight. Indeed, that whole region has a temperate sky of perpetual health, fertile plains, sunny hills, harmless pastures, shady groves, bounteous kinds of forest, the breath of many mountains, such great fertility of grain, vines and olives, such noble fleeces for the flocks, many excellent bulls' necks, many lakes, many rivers, and the abundance of springs pouring over the whole of it, many seas, harbours, and bosoms of lands open to the commerce of the world, and running eagerly out into the seas as if to help mortals. Nor does it surpass other nations in talent, customs, men, language or skill, as I recall. The Greeks themselves declared it to be the most famous part of their own race, calling a part of it by its name Magna Graecia, etc." The other, with which he sets an end to his most noble work of nature, is in book 37, chapter 13: "Throughout the whole world, and wherever the vault of heaven turns, Italy is the most beautiful of all, and nature has justly given her first place among things: the mistress and second parent of the world, for virtue, for women, for leaders, for soldiers, for slaves, for the excellence of the arts, for the brightness of talents, for the site and healthfulness and temperance of her sky, for easy access from all nations, for harbourful shores, for the kindly breath of the winds. For her position lies in the most useful part of the curving earth, and is midway between the rising and setting sun, with abundance of waters, healthfulness of groves, the ranges of mountains, the harmlessness of wild animals, the fertility of the sun, the richness of pasture. Whatever there is that life ought not to lack is nowhere more excellent: grain, wine, olives, fleeces, flax, garments, young oxen. I do not notice that any native temples are preferred even in the triumphal processions. She yielded to none in the metals of gold, silver, bronze and iron, so long as it pleased (I would rather say it was allowed; for afterwards this was forbidden by a decree of the Senate: see Pliny, book 33, chapter 4; or 'it pleased', namely the Fathers and the Roman Senate) to work them. And now, pregnant with them, she pours out for all her dowry the various juices and savours of fruits and apples." Dionysius of Halicarnassus, in book 1, also praises Italy highly, writing that she surpasses all the regions of Europe in her advantages and fertility. Baptista Mantuanus, writing to Filippo Beroaldo, composed no inelegant encomium of Italy, singing among other things these lines: Each of the gods gave Italy his gifts, and each was clever in giving help. Jupiter taught her to rule and hold the sceptre, and to press barbarian necks under an even yoke. Mars gave arms, helmets, and flashing swords, and shields to be carried in the hollow of the arm; he also gave broad shoulders on large necks, and chests of scale-armour fitted to the breastplate. Through the plains he taught cavalry squadrons, and naval battles to run through rivers and through the strait. The scythe-bearing god, with slow fire, makes the Italians grave in face and tongue, and modest in gait. Rage stirs a barbarian cohort to war; Italian counsel, not fury, moves arms. This god taught the cultivation of fields and the art of planting vines, and insinuated the riches of trees. Cynthian Apollo bent minds toward the Muses, and taught every kind of learning. Venus filled peoples with arms, cities and fields, woodland huts and houses in the trees, so that there might be citizens to attend to the affairs of the city, one to bear arms with his hand, one to till the fields with oxen. Mercury taught treaties and laws, and set a limit to shouting and quarrels. Luna urges chastity, lest Venus, burning without law, steal the blush from heaven. Ceres gave arms: she taught the grain, which, pale with its curved ear, the countryman reaps with a sickle. Bacchus gave wine, and many other things follow.

units.la: Beatissimam certe non immerito totius Europae Regionem appellat Aethicus; Totius Orbis optimam, Dionysius Halicarnass. lib. 1; Gentium Dominam, Mamertinus Panegyristes; Dominam Rerum, P. Rutilius Numatianus; Caelestem, Mundique Reginam vocat Aethicus, quem dixi. Et vero quid hic non gestum olim, quid non pro Gloria cum summa Laude ab generosis Animis patratum? Longum esset & taediosum omnia commemorare. A quibus non Gentibus expugnandi, occupandi, diripiendi gratia quondam petita? Silentium hic tubere mihi malo, quam pauca pro rei dignitate in medium afferre. Quis non hodie visundae eius cognoscendaeque causa adit? Docent ferventia passim a Peregrinantibus, qui undique eam versus confluunt, itinera. Ego sane aliquando ingressus suspicere me cum voluptate memini Montes nunc viriferos, nunc aliarum rerum feraces, nunc miraculis suis admirandos: vernantes Silvas: Sinus amplos & profundos, indos placidosque Portus, alta lataque Flumina; Lacus limpidos & vivos, nobiles, largos, inlimes & variarum virium Fontes. Sed haec aliaque talia suis locis. Quid enim dicam de Incolis, ipsorumque Moribus, cum publice domi militiaeque, tum privatim? Urbes hic spectavi egregias, florentes, opulentas; Oppida clara, famosa, Civibus artas; Pagos magnos. Aedificiaque Nobilium & Praetorum superbientes, &, praeter alia infinita, moestus ibi vidi & attonitus miserandas Veteres Urbium Structurarumque Reliquias, & stupenda totius Antiquitatis Monimenta. De Italiae Civitatibus Versus circumferuntur pulcerrimi: Fama tranet Roma pomposa & fantas Furia bizarra; & Ravenna benigna, Venetia ricca, saggia, & signorile; E Singallia del aria noiosa; Neapoli odorifera, & gentile; F Capua amorosa; Fiorenza bella, tutto il Volgo canta; Pisa Frendente, & Pesaro giardino; Grande Milano in Italia fi vanta; Ancona del bel porto pellegrino Bologna grassa; e Ferrara civile, Fedelissimo Urbino; Padua forte, & Bergamo sottile; Ascoli tondo; & longo Recanate; Genoua d'superbia altiera pianta; Foligno delle strade in Zuccarate; Verona degna; & Perugia sanguignas Et par da cielo mandate Brescia armata; e Mantoa gloriosa; Le belle Donne de Fano se dice; Rimini buona; & Pistoia ferrigna, Ma Siena poi tra l'altre piu felice. Siena de bel podere; Lucca industriosa;
units.tr: Aethicus rightly calls the whole region of Europe most blessed; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, in book 1, the best of the whole world; the Mamertine panegyrist the mistress of the nations; P. Rutilius Numatianus the mistress of things; and Aethicus, whom I have mentioned, calls it heavenly and the queen of the world. And indeed, what was not done here of old, what was not accomplished with the highest praise by noble spirits for glory? It would be long and tedious to recall everything. From what nations was it not once sought, to be conquered, seized or plundered? I prefer to keep silence here than to bring forward a few things in proportion to the dignity of the subject. Who does not come today to see and get to know it? The travel routes of pilgrims, who flock to it from every side, bear witness everywhere. I myself, I remember, once entering it and looking up with delight at mountains now bearing vines, now rich in other produce, now wonderful for their marvels; at flourishing woods, at wide and deep bays, at calm and sheltered harbours, at high and broad rivers, at clear and living lakes, noble, copious, unmuddied, and at springs of various powers. But these and such things belong in their own places. For what shall I say of the inhabitants and their customs, both public at home and in war, and private? Here I saw splendid, flourishing, wealthy cities; famous towns, renowned, crowded with citizens; great villages; and buildings of nobles and magistrates that rise proudly; and, besides countless other things, I saw with sadness and amazement the pitiable remains of old cities and structures, and the astonishing monuments of all antiquity. Verses about the cities of Italy are passed around, very beautiful: Rome is pompous, Florence is bizarre and fanciful; Ravenna is kind, Venice rich, wise and noble; Sinigallia has tedious air; Naples is fragrant and gentle; Capua is loving; Florence is beautiful, the whole common folk sing; Pisa is blustering and Pesaro a garden; great Milan boasts itself in Italy; Ancona with its fine harbour is a pilgrim; Bologna is fat, Ferrara civil, Urbino most faithful; Padua strong, and Bergamo subtle; Ascoli round, and Recanati long; Genoa planted high in proud arrogance; Foligno with its streets in zigzags; Verona worthy; Perugia bloody; Brescia armed, and Mantua glorious; the beautiful women of Fano are spoken of; Rimini good, and Pistoia iron-grey. But Siena, among the rest, is the happiest. Siena of the fine estate; Lucca industrious.

units.la: Neque illud hoc loco praetermittendum silentio duxi, quatuor Italiae vulgo celebrari Oppidi, sive Castella nobilissima: Apuliae, Barulum; Etruriae, Pratum: Piceni, Fabrianum; Langbardiae, Cremam.
units.tr: Nor do I think it should be passed over in silence here that four very noble towns or castles of Italy are commonly celebrated: in Apulia, Barletta; in Etruria, Prato; in Picenum, Fabriano; in Lombardy, Crema.

units.la: CAPUT V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: Italiae Montes.
units.tr: The Mountains of Italy.

units.la: IN Adjunctis Italiae quo modo se habeat, habemus: Partes jamnunc eius videamus, cum simpliciter undeque consideratas, tum Miraculis Virtutibusque suis pollentes. Priores duorum faciam generum, alias Terrae tribuens, ut Mon-
units.tr: We have seen how Italy stands with regard to its boundaries. Now let us look at its parts, both as they are considered in themselves from every side, and as they are remarkable for their wonders and their virtues. I shall take the first two kinds, assigning them to the land, as the mountains...

units.la: Saturnia igitur, ut inde oriar, inquit Stephanus in Vrbium Nomenclatore, Ἰταλία πρῶτον ἐκαλεῖτο. Vnde autem Iustinus ex Trogo, agens de Saturno Rege, Itaque, concludit, Italia Regis nomine Saturnia appellata est. Notat idem Macrobius lib. 1. Saturnal. cap. VII. Saturnia, ait Festus lib. XVII. Italia; & Mons, qui nunc est Capitolinus, Saturnius appellabatur, quod in tutela Saturni esse existimatur. &c Isidorus lib. XIIII Etymol. cap. IV: Italia o'im a Graecis populis occupata Magna Graecia appellata est: deinde ab Regis nomine Saturnii, mox & Latium. Crediderim ego Saturnia appellationem non ad totam pertinuisse Regionem, quae post Italia; sed tantum ad eius partem, quae & Latium. Latinis enim Latium, quae Tuscis vicinis Saturnia: illud ab Latende; haec ab Aramaea voce לט, quae Latere, occultare se & abscondere notat. Varro lib. IV de LL. ubi de Tarpeio: Hunc antea Montem Saturnium appellatum prodiderunt, & ab eo late Saturniam Terram, ut etiam Ennius appellat: ubi pro late reponendum esse Latium, olim monui in meo ad Poetae Annales Commentario. Antequam autem Saturnia fuerit haec Regio dicta, nomen illi fuisse videtur Camesene, ab Camese Indigena, cum quo (ut apud Macrobium Higinus, Protarchum Trallianum sequutus, tradidit) Ianus Regionem (Latium mihi) partitus pata potentia possidebat, ita ut Regio (ad sinistram Tiberis ripam) Camesene, oppidum Ianiculum (ad dexteram Tiberis oram) vocitaretur. Addit deinde, post ad Ianum solum Regnum suisse redactum: qui cum, inquit, Saturnium clam se pertractum excepisset hospitio, & ab eo edoctus peritiam rutis, ferum illum & rudem ante fugestrenuitas victum in melius redegisset, regni cum societate muneravit. Ianus mox Ianiculum oppidum Nomen retinuisse; Regionem autem, deposita priore, appellationem sumsisse Saturnia; duos vero Reges concorditer regnasse, vicinaque oppida opera communi condidisse; indeque apud Maronem legi:
units.tr: Saturnia, then, to begin from there, says Stephanus in his Names of Cities: Italy was first called Italia [Ἰταλία πρῶτον ἐκαλεῖτο]. Justin, however, following Trogus, when he treats of King Saturn, concludes: Therefore Italy was called Saturnia from the name of the king. Macrobius, in book 1 of the Saturnalia, chapter 7, notes the same. Saturnia, says Festus in book 17, is Italy; and the mountain that is now the Capitoline was called Saturnian, because it is thought to be under the protection of Saturn. Isidore too, in book 14 of the Etymologies, chapter 4: Italy, once occupied by Greek peoples, was called Magna Graecia; then from the name of the king it was called Saturnian, and soon also Latium. I would believe that the name Saturnia did not apply to the whole region that afterwards was called Italy, but only to that part which was also called Latium. For the Latins called it Latium, and the Tuscans, who are its neighbours, called it Saturnia: the former from latere, the latter from the Aramaic word לט, which means to lie hidden, to conceal oneself. Varro, in book 4 of On the Latin Language, where he speaks of the Tarpeian rock, says: They have recorded that this mountain was formerly called Saturnian, and from it the land was called widely Saturnia, as Ennius also calls it. I have already suggested, in my commentary on the Annals of the poet, that for late we should read Latium. Before this region was called Saturnia, it seems to have been named Camesene, after the native Camese, with whom (as Hyginus, following Protarchus of Tralles, reports in Macrobius) Janus shared the region (Latium, I think), and possessed it with equal power, so that the region on the left bank of the Tiber was called Camesene, and the town of Janiculum on the right bank. He adds that afterwards the kingdom was reduced to Janus alone: For he, says Hyginus, having secretly received Saturn as a guest, and having learned from him the art of farming, and having reformed that wild and rough man, who had previously been conquered by his own sluggishness, bestowed on him a share of the kingdom. Afterwards Janus kept the name of the town Janiculum, while the region, having put aside its former name, took the name Saturnia; and the two kings reigned in harmony and jointly founded the neighbouring towns. Hence in Maro one reads:

units.la: Ianiculum huic, illi fuerat Saturnia Nomen.
units.tr: Janiculum was the name of the one, Saturnia of the other.

units.la: Hesperiam (Ἑσπερίαν) nominasse Hesperum, ab Atlante Fratre in exilium actum, inque haec Loca delatum, scribit ad Virgilium Servius. Quidam Hesperiam dictam esse notant hanc Regionem ab Graecis, quod Occasui subiecta, ipsisque Occidentalior esset. Scribunt alii Hesperias antiquitus fuisse duas: unam, quae post Hispania, alteram, quae Italia hanc quidem Magnam audiisse Hesperiam, ab Hespero Atlantis Fratre: eum enim nomen vel suum, vel Regionis, unde pulsus fuerat, indidisse: illam autem, addito cognomine, Vltimam appellari solitam, ab Hespero, occidentali Stella. De Italia lane loquitur Virgilius lib. 1. Aen.
units.tr: Servius, on Virgil, writes that Hesperus named the land Hesperia, after he had been driven into exile by his brother Atlas and brought to these places. Some note that this region was called Hesperia by the Greeks because it lies under the sunset and is more western than they are. Others write that there were formerly two Hesperias: one, which is now Spain, and the other, which is Italy. The Great Hesperia, they say, took its name from Hesperus, brother of Atlas, who gave it either his own name or the name of the region from which he had been driven; and the other, with an added epithet, was usually called the Farthest Hesperia, after Hesperus, the western star. Virgil, in book 1 of the Aeneid, speaks of Italy:

units.la: Est locus, Hesperiam Graij cognomine dicunt.
units.tr: There is a place which the Greeks call by the name Hesperia.

units.la: De Hispania Horatius lib. 1. Carminum.
units.tr: Horace, in book 1 of the Odes, speaks of Spain:

units.la: Qui nunc Hesperia victor ab Vltima.
units.tr: He who now, victorious, from farthest Hesperia...

units.la: Ausoniam, inquit Festus lib. 1, appellavit Ausoni Vlyssis & Calypsus Filium (de Ausone apud alios alia leguntur) eam primo Partem Italiae, in qua sunt Vrbes Beneventum & Cales: deinde paulatim tota quoque Italia, quae Apenninofruitur, dicta est Ausonia ab eodem Duce, a quo etiam conditam fuisse Aurunca Vrbem ferunt. Videndus & Paullus Diaconus lib. 11. Histor. Langbard. cap. xxiii. Ad priorem sententiam accedunt fere Dion Coccieus, Ioannes Tzetza, & Isacius in Lycophronem, qui scribunt Ἀὐσονίαν solam dici solitam Auruncorum (Ἀὐρυγκῶν) Terram, inter Campanos & Volscos, iuxta mare sitam. Ad posteriorem inclinat Stephanus de Vrbibus, Ἀῦσων, ait, ὁ Ἰταλος: Et paullo post Ἀὐσωνία, ἡ χώρα.
units.tr: Ausonia, says Festus in book 1, was named after Ausonus, son of Ulysses and Calypso (other authors tell other things about Ausonus). At first it was the name of that part of Italy in which the cities of Benevento and Cales lie; then gradually the whole of Italy that stretches along the Apennines was also called Ausonia, from the same leader, from whom they also say the city of Aurunca was founded. One should also see Paul the Deacon, book 2 of the History of the Lombards, chapter 23. Dion Cocceius, John Tzetzes and Isaac on Lycophron incline to the former opinion: they write that Ausonia (Ἀὐσονία) was only the name of the land of the Aurunci (Ἀὐρυγκῶν), situated by the sea between the Campanians and the Volscians. Stephanus in his Cities inclines to the latter: Ausonus, he says, the Italian [Ἀῦσων, ὁ Ἰταλος]; and a little later Ausonia, the country [Ἀῦσωνία, ἡ χώρα].

units.la: Oenotria, Οἰνωτρία, quur dicta fuerit, ingens, & quasi Reip. salus hic laboraret, inter Auctores fuit pugna. Ab Oenotro Arcade, Lycaonis Filio, qui primus, transfretato Sinu Ionio, Italiam incoluit, ita appellatam scribit Dionysius Halicarnass. Suffragatur Pausanias, Oenotrum tradens in Arcadicis, Filiorum Lycaonis natu minimum, ab Nyctimo Fratre Pecuniis Virisque impetratis, in Italiam traiecisse, cumque Primum omnium ex Graecia Coloniam navigio deportasse, imo nec Barbarum quidem ullum ante Oenotrum, alienam Terram invasisse. Antiochus etiam Syracusanus apud eundem Dionysium lib. 1. Oenotrum, Lycaonis Filium, Ducem Arcadum, Ionico Sinu transmisso, in Calabriam adpulisse, ibique in ora maritima Colonias posuisse memorat. Varro Oenotrum, Latinorum Regem, nomen creasse Regioni existimat. Servius ab Vino optime natam Oenotria appellationem adnotat, quod ouor Graeci Vinum vocent. Oenotriam pro Italia habet, Sidonius Apollinaris: inde autem Oenotria Virgilio lib. 1. Strictiores Oenotria Terminos indicat Strabo lib. vi, & ante hunc Aristoteles, ut docent ponenda mox ipsius verba. Sabinorum Terram proprie Oenotriam fuisse dictam scribit Servius ad v. 1 Aeneid.
units.tr: Why Oenotria (Οἰνωτρία) was so called, a great controversy arose among the authors, and the safety of the state was, as it were, at stake here. Dionysius of Halicarnassus writes that it was named after Oenotrus the Arcadian, son of Lycaon, who first settled in Italy after crossing the Ionian Gulf. Pausanias supports this, saying in his Arcadica that Oenotrus, the youngest of the sons of Lycaon, obtained money and men from his brother Nyctimus, and crossed over into Italy; and that he was the first to bring a colony from Greece by ship, and indeed that before Oenotrus no barbarian had invaded a foreign land. Antiochus of Syracuse also, in the same Dionysius, book 1, records that Oenotrus, son of Lycaon, leader of the Arcadians, sailed across the Ionian Gulf, landed in Calabria, and there founded colonies on the seacoast. Varro thinks that Oenotrus, king of the Latins, gave the region its name. Servius notes that the name Oenotria was rightly derived from wine, because the Greeks call wine oinos [οἶνος]. Sidonius Apollinaris takes Oenotria for Italy; and Virgil, in book 1, uses Oenotria in the same way. Strabo, in book 6, indicates narrower limits for Oenotria, and before him Aristotle did, as the words of his that I shall quote presently show. Servius, on Aeneid 1, writes that the land of the Sabines was properly called Oenotria.

units.la: Italia nomen acceptum ab Italo, quem Oenotriae Regem facit Aristoteles. Eius haec sunt: Φασι γὰρ ἐι λεγεσθαι ἐκα καπικηπ. [illegible, ~40 letters] Polybius etiam lib. i. & Antiochus Xenophanes apud Dionysium Halic. facium Regionis Regem; Arcadum autem Regulum, in has oras profectum, Thucydides lib. vi. Memoriae prodit idem Halicarnass. Italum, Siculorum Regem (vide & Isidorum lib. xiiii cap. iv. & Paulum Diaconum Histor. Langobard. lib. ii. cap. xxiii) primum, cum Agriculturae, tum Legum in his locis Auctorem, Regionem sic ab eo vocatam Regem Italum simpliciter agnoscit Festus. Hyginus Italum Ducem ex Penelope & Telego natum hic communi citur. Alii alio abeunt. Tinaeus, inquit Agellius lib. xi Noct. Attic. cap. i. in Historiis, quas oratione Graeca de rebus P. p. Rom. composuit, & Ci. Varro in Antiquitatibus Rerum humanarum, Terram Italiam de Graeco Vocabulo appellatam scripserunt: quorum boves Graeca a veteri lingua Ιταλοι vocati sunt; quorum in Italia magna copia fuit: Buccaque in ea Terra agni pascique lacte sunt complures. Festus lib. ix: Italia dicta, quod magnos Italos, hoc est Boves haberet. Vitulae enim Italae sunt dicti. Paullus Diaconus lib. i. Langbard. Hist. Sive ob hanc Italia dicitur, quia magna in ea Boves, hoc est Itali habentur. Timaeus etiam fabulatur appellari ab Italo Bove, uno ex armento Geryonis, qui abactus ab Hercule Siculi Freti angustias tranaverat, Tyrrhena Lingua Italum Taurum dicente. Sic Hellanicus Lesbius apud eundem Dionysium, quoniam opimos Poves gignat ea Regio, eiusdem Vocabuli occasione nuncupatam censet Italiam. Ιtalia quoque quondam dicta, ut fides Hellanico, apud eundem Dionysium Halic. lib. i. Antiq. Rom.
units.tr: The name Italia was taken from Italus, whom Aristotle makes king of Oenotria. His words are these: ... Polybius too, in book 1, and Antiochus and Xenophanes, in Dionysius of Halicarnassus, make him king of the region; but Thucydides, in book 6, relates that a little king of the Arcadians sailed to these shores. The same Dionysius of Halicarnassus reports in memory that Italus, king of the Sicilians (see also Isidore, book 14, chapter 4, and Paul the Deacon, History of the Lombards, book 2, chapter 23), was the first author in these places both of agriculture and of laws; and that the region was called by his name. Festus simply acknowledges King Italus. Hyginus names Italus as a leader, son of Penelope and Telegonus. Others go their own ways. Timaeus, says Gellius in book 11 of the Attic Nights, chapter 1, in his histories, which he wrote in Greek about the affairs of the Roman people, and Varro in his Antiquities of Human Affairs, have written that the land of Italy was named from a Greek word: because in the old Greek language oxen were called Italoi, and there was a great abundance of them in Italy; and in that land there were many calves and lambs nourished on milk. Festus, book 9: Italy was so called because it had great Italoi, that is, oxen; for calves are called Italae. Paul the Deacon, book 1 of the Lombard History: or Italy is called so because in it there are many great oxen, that is, itali. Timaeus also tells the fable that it was named from Italus, a bull, one of the herd of Geryon, which, driven off by Hercules, had crossed the strait of the Sicilian sea, the Tyrrhenian tongue calling it Italus Taurus. So Hellanicus of Lesbos, in the same Dionysius, thinks that the region, because it produces fat oxen, was named Italia on the occasion of this same word. Italia was also once called, as Hellanicus believes, by the same Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 1 of the Roman Antiquities.

units.la: Quod Ἀρρισσα etiam primo appellata, aut, ut aliis scribitur, Μαρρισσα ab Margetum gente, quos Dionysius Halicarnass. lib. i. Μεργητας vocat ex Antiocho Syracusano, docent Auctorum Scriptorum Monumenta. Dicitur Morges Itala successisse, a quo Morgetes dicti, qui prius Oenotri. Porro & Morgetes & Siculos ex Italia in Siciliam traiecisse, etiam ex Thucydide & Diodoro Siculo est notum.
units.tr: That it was also first called Arrissa (Ἀρρισσα), or, as others write, Marrissa (Μαρρισσα), after the people of the Margeti, whom Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 1, calls Mergetes (Μεργητας) following Antiochus of Syracuse, the monuments of the writers show. Morges is said to have succeeded Italus, and from him those who were formerly Oenotrians were called Morgetes. Moreover, that both the Morgetes and the Sicels crossed from Italy into Sicily is known also from Thucydides and Diodorus Siculus.

units.la: Alij alias veteres Italiae appellationes in medium adferunt, sed quae non tam Typi, quam Partibus conveniant: quod etiam de Superiorum nonnullis aliquo modo dici poterit. Tyrrhenia, Tarpeia, proprie Tusci, inter Macram & Tiberim fluvios. Campania, χωρια vel χωρη, Lucaniae pars: Bettia apud Stephanum Pars tantum, ut & infra videbimus: Antiochus autem, eodem scribente, τῶν Ιταλίαν Φησι Χλιβια Βρεττιαν, ἐπι Οἰνωτριαν. Materni Ciratum, quam quidam ex Festo antiquis Appellationibus adnominant, certum est fuisse Orientalioris Italiae partem.
units.tr: Others bring forward other ancient names of Italy, but these fit not so much the whole as the parts; which may also be said in some way of some of those mentioned above. Tyrrhenia and Tarpeia properly belong to the Tuscans, between the rivers Macra and Tiber. Campania, chōria or chōrē [χωρια, χωρη], is part of Lucania. Bettia, in Stephanus, is only a part, as we shall also see below. Antiochus, however, as the same author writes, says that Italy is Chalibia, Brettia and, up to Oenotria [τῶν Ιταλίαν Φησι Χλιβια Βρεττιαν, ἐπι Οἰνωτριαν]. That Ciratum, which some add to the ancient names from Festus, was a part of more eastern Italy is certain.

units.la: Quod reliquum Janiculum ab Jano fuisse nuncupatam Italiam, quum Janiculum tantum fuerit opidum; Ογυγιαν ab Ογυγης, qui & Ianus: Saleumbronam, ab Sale & Umbrona; Aperninam, id est Taurinam, ab Aprum Eorum Italiae ultimo; Palensanam denique, nescio unde: probent ex suppositis Berosi, Catonis, Myrsili Lesbii, Q. Fabii Pictoris fragmentis cum Annio Viterbiensi Monacho alij, quibus plus temporis, quique maiorem consueverunt idem adhibere Commentis Oriosorum & Nugis.
units.tr: The rest of the names that some have derived are these: Italy is said to have been named after Janiculum, although Janiculum was only a town; Ogygia [Ογυγια] after Ogyges, who is also Janus; Saleumbrona from Sale and Umbrona; Apernina, that is, Taurina, from the boar (Aper), the furthest of their Italy; and finally Palensana, I know not from where. Let them prove these from the spurious fragments of Berosus, Cato, Myrsilus of Lesbos and Q. Fabius Pictor, together with Annius of Viterbo the monk and others, who have more time and are accustomed to use the same inventions of Oriosus and trifles.

units.la: Quidquid sit; venerandum Italia Nomen, sive ab initio fuerit, & quae a me indicatae Appellationes Cognomina tantum, quod facile credo, sint habenda: sive, postea habitis aliis Nomenclaturis, postea fuerit natum: semper sane mansit; hodieque manet apud omnes fere populos, omnibus propemodum litteris בתיך (vide supra part. i. lib. iii, cap. iv) vocari Hebraeis, tradit in Appendice Biblica Arias Montanus. משך Maseth, vel Mosoch videntur appellare LXX. Interpretes cap. Iudic. lxi. Vitola Slavonice dicitur.
units.tr: Whatever the case, the venerable name Italia has remained. Whether it has existed from the beginning, and the appellations I have mentioned are to be regarded only as surnames (as I readily believe), or whether it arose later, after other names had been in use, it has always remained, and today it is still used by almost all peoples in nearly every language. The Hebrews call it [בתיך] in all letters (see above, part i, book iii, chapter iv), as Arias Montanus reports in the Biblical Appendix. The Septuagint seem to call it [משך] Maseth or Mosoch, in Judges chapter 61. In Slavonic it is called Vitola.

units.la: Antiquissimos porro Italiae Incolas & Cultores, quique in eam successu temporis vel habitandi, vel praedandi causa inundarunt, recensent Dionysius Halicarnassensis lib. i. Livius lib. i, Iustinus ex Trogi lib. xx, Solinus in Polyhist. Ioannes Iovianus Pontanus lib. vi Histor. Leander Albertus in Italiae Prolegomenis, & alii, Aborigines, Aurunci, Pelasgi, Lycaones, Oenotri, Morgetes, Ausones, Arcades, Troianos, nos, Venetos, Ligures, Ardeates, Rutulos, Siculos, Iapyges, Lacedæmonios, aliosque Græci generis: item Gallos, Pænos, Herulos, Gothos, Hunnos, Hungaros, Gepidas, Turingos, Avares, Langobardos, Saracenos, Cimbros, Teutones, Francos, Vasiones, Helvetios, Germanos, Hispanos, & quos non? quorum quidam vel sedes ibi suas fixerunt, hodieque habent, præclaris conditis Civitatibus; vel, Populationibus peractis, ad sua sunt reversi. Ptolemæus XLIV enumerat Veteris Italiæ Populos; quos non commemorabo, quum de iis plene insequentibus.
units.tr: Next, the most ancient inhabitants and cultivators of Italy, who in the course of time flooded into it either to settle or to plunder, are listed by Dionysius of Halicarnassus (book i), Livy (book i), Justin from Trogus (book xx), Solinus in the Polyhistor, Giovanni Gioviano Pontano (book vi of the Histories), Leandro Alberti in his Prolegomena to Italy, and others: the Aborigines, Aurunci, Pelasgi, Lycaones, Oenotri, Morgetes, Ausones, Arcades, Trojans, the Venetians, Ligurians, Ardeatians, Rutulians, Sicilians, Iapygians, Lacedaemonians, and others of Greek stock; also Gauls, Carthaginians, Heruli, Goths, Huns, Hungarians, Gepids, Thuringians, Avars, Lombards, Saracens, Cimbri, Teutons, Franks, Vasiones, Helvetians, Germans, Spaniards, and why not all? Some of these fixed their seats there and still hold them, having founded famous cities; others, after completing their raids, returned to their homes. Ptolemy enumerates forty-four of the peoples of ancient Italy; I shall not mention them here, since I will deal with them fully in what follows.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: Italiæ Quantitas, quæ patet in Finibus, Longitudine, Latitudine, Circuitu, & similibus: Italiæ Dorsum, Umbilicus, Figura.
units.tr: The Extent of Italy, as seen in its boundaries, length, breadth, circuit and similar measures; the Back, the Navel and the Shape of Italy.

units.la: Tantum de Nomine Regionis Nobilissimæ, eiusque Cognominibus: sequitur Res ipsa in eiusdem vel Adiunctis, vel Partibus. Adiuncta sunt Quantitas & Qualitas. Illa constistit in Finibus, Longitudine, Latitudine, & id genus aliis.
units.tr: So much for the name of this most noble region and its surnames. Next comes the thing itself, in its attributes or parts. The attributes are its extent and its quality. The extent consists in its boundaries, length, breadth and the like.

units.la: Peninsulam χερσόνησον faciunt Italiam Strabo libro secundo sextoque & Ptolemæus, quam Natura Mari Supero, Infero, Ionio munivit lateribus tribus; quarto autem vallavit Alpibus. Nam Occasum Caurumque versus adsunt Italiæ Alpes, quæ suis apud Veteres cognominibus distinctæ fuerunt, Maritimæ, Cottiæ, Graiæ, Rhæticæque ad Arsiam usque flumen; Septentrionem respiciens Pinnas habet Iuliasque: succedente mox, qua Aquilo est. Mari Hadriatico ab intimo Recessu usque ad Sinum Ionium, qui ad Orientem Vulturnumque illi obversus: Qua denique longe lateque spectat Austrum, Africum Zephyrumque ab Mari pulsatur Mediterraneo, quod ad eas oras Tyrrhenum audit & Ligusticum: faciente etiam partem Australem Hadriatico, qua Toti connectuntur Partes, Forum Iulii & Histria. Hos Italiæ Terminos agnoscunt, unanimique propemodum consensu, si bene verba perpenduntur, statuunt Polybius, Thucydides, Strabo, Dionysius Halicarnass. Ptolemæus, Dionysius Afer, Plinius, Orosius, Pomponius Mela, Solinus, Auctor incertus de Mensura Orbis Terræ, quem mihi transmisit sua manu descriptum Vir Nobilissimus Marcus Velserus, Reip. Augustanæ II Viri omnesque, qui accuratiores, Novitij, Natalis Comes lib. Historiar xxiv, Leander Albertus initio, & alij.
units.tr: Strabo in books 2 and 6, and Ptolemy, make Italy a peninsula [χερσόνησον]. Nature has fortified it on three sides by the Upper Sea, the Lower Sea and the Ionian Sea, and on the fourth by the Alps. For towards the west and north-west stand the Alps of Italy, which the ancients distinguished by their own names: the Maritime, Cottian, Graian and Rhaetian Alps, as far as the river Arsia. Facing north, Italy has the Pennine and Julian Alps, and next to them, where the north wind blows, the rest. On the Adriatic Sea, from its innermost recess to the Ionian Gulf, which faces east and the south-east wind, Italy is bounded. Finally, where it looks far and wide to the south, it is struck by the south-west and west winds from the Mediterranean, which on those shores is called the Tyrrhenian and Ligurian Sea. The southern part of the Adriatic also forms a part of Italy, where the regions of Forum Iulii and Istria are joined to the whole. Polybius, Thucydides, Strabo and Dionysius of Halicarnassus acknowledge these as the limits of Italy, and, if their words are weighed carefully, they almost all agree in fixing them. So do Ptolemy, Dionysius Afer, Pliny, Orosius, Pomponius Mela, Solinus, the unknown author of the work On the Measurement of the Earth, which the most noble Marcus Welser sent me copied out in his own hand (he is one of the two magistrates of Augsburg), all the more accurate writers, Natalis Comes in book 24 of his Histories, the beginning of Leander Albertus, and others.

units.la: Italia, Finibus indicatis inclusæ, Longitudo ab Augusta Prætoria Regium usque est, ut scribunt Strabo lib. v, Plinius lib. iii. cap. x, aliisque locis, Solinus in Polyhist. P. Rutilius Claudius Numatianus, Auc orque, quem dixi, de Mensura Orbis Terræ, serram tamen inter se nonnihil reciprocantes, decies centenorum & viginti millium passuum; extendens se, ut Strabo indicat lib. vi, ... τὸ Ἀρκτῶν, τὸ κλέον: Latitudo varia; Maxima quidem quadringentorum decem millium, inter Varum Arsiamque fluvios; Media, centum triginta senum, circa Urbem Romam, ab Ostio Aterni amnis usque ad Tiberis in Tyrrhenum Pelagus eruptionem; Minima, non amplius quadraginta millium, inter Portum Magnæ Græciæ, quem Annibalis Castra nominant, & Hipponiatem vel Vibonensem Sinum. Ego, Dimensione curiosius facta, Longitudinem eius ab Augusta Prætoria ad Brutium usque Promontorium vel Leucopetram deprehendi CCXLV plus minus Miliariorum: Latitudinem, qua, ut paullo ante accipiundam monui, Maxima, CCCCI XXV, qua Media, CXXX: qua denique Minima, LXXII: ubi in duplex exit cornu, multo est minor. Minima illa, quam quidam ponunt inter Sinum Vibonensem, & Scylaceum vel Portum, qui ab Annibalis Castris denominatus, non totius est Italiæ, sed alterius ipsius versus Meridionalior cornu: ubi Aristoteles, cuius ante laudavi verba, ἐάν ponit ἡμισείας ἡμέρας. Affirmant Incolæ & Locorum gnari, Italiam, ubi Isthmus inter Sinus Sanctæuphemianum, qui olim Hipponiates vel Vibonensis, Aristoteli autem Λαμπτικός, & Scylaceum maximas facit eiusdem Cornu angustias. Intervallum habere Continentis, xv, aut ad summum xx Miliariorum. In editissimo ipsius Isthmi fastigio amœnissima sunt Prata, Agrique culti, cum Silva crassissimarum & præcelsarum Ilicum, unde utrumque Mare Tyrrhenum & Hadriaticum conspicitur, tamquam haud magnis sejuncta spatiis.
units.tr: Italy, enclosed within the boundaries indicated, is, as Strabo in book 5, Pliny in book 3 chapter 10 and elsewhere, Solinus in the Polyhistor, P. Rutilius Claudius Namatianus and the author I mentioned, On the Measurement of the Earth, write, somewhat varying among themselves, from Augusta Praetoria to Regium, a length of 1,220 miles. It extends itself, as Strabo shows in book 6, ... [τὸ Ἀρκτῶν, τὸ κλέον] . Its breadth varies. The greatest is 410 miles, between the rivers Varus and Arsia. The middle breadth is about 130 miles, around the city of Rome, from the mouth of the river Aternus to where the Tiber breaks out into the Tyrrhenian Sea. The least is not more than 40 miles, between the Harbour of Magna Graecia, which they call Hannibal's Camp, and the Gulf of Hipponium or Vibo. I, having made the measurement more carefully, found its length from Augusta Praetoria to the promontory of Brutium or Leucopetra to be about 245 miles; its breadth, which, as I warned a little before, is to be taken as greatest, 425 miles; the middle breadth 130; and the least 72. But where it ends in a double horn, it is much narrower. That narrowest part, which some place between the Gulf of Vibo and Scylacium or the harbour named after Hannibal's camp, is not of all Italy but of the more southern horn alone. There Aristotle, whose words I quoted above, puts it at half a day's journey [ἡμισείας ἡμέρας]. The inhabitants and those who know the places affirm that where the isthmus lies between the Gulf of San Eufemia, formerly that of Hipponium or Vibo, and by Aristotle called Lamptikos, and Scylacium, which makes the greatest narrowness of this horn, the mainland gap is fifteen, or at most twenty, miles. On the highest ridge of this isthmus there are most pleasant meadows and cultivated fields, with a forest of very thick and very tall holm oaks, from which both the Tyrrhenian and the Adriatic Seas can be seen, as if they were separated by no great distance.

units.la: Circuitus & περίμετρα Italiæ quibusdam apud Leandrum Albertum milliarior. cıɔ cıɔ cıɔ cıɔ ıɔ ccccı nonnullis cıɔ cıɔcıɔ cıɔ ıɔ ccxı. Castaldus colligit cıɔ cıɔ ıɔ l. Qui exactius sunt metati, signant cıɔ cıɔ ccl; qui exactissime, non multo minus, cıɔ cıɔ cccLX.
units.tr: The circuit and perimeter of Italy, according to some in Leander Albertus, is given in miles as 1,500 (?), others as 1,400, others as 1,211. Castaldus reckons 1,550. Those who measured more exactly make it 1,250, and those who measured most exactly, not much less, 1,360.

units.la: Dorsum Italiæ Mons est Apenninus, qui Spinæ instar per mediam sensim incedens eam in duo secat latera: quorum unum Favonio, vel, ut quidam ejus Situm notant, Africo; alterum Euro, vel Aquilone potius, est obversum.
units.tr: The back of Italy is the Apennine mountain, which, like a spine, runs gradually through the middle and divides it into two sides: one of these faces the west, or, as some note its position, the south-west; the other faces the east, or rather the north-east.

units.la: Umbilicum M. Terentius Varro statuit in Agro Reatino Cutilia Lacum, in quo fluctuet Insula, teste Plinio lib. iii. Nat. histor. cap. xii. alii Lacum Velinum, qui non procul inde, Italiæ medium tenere affirmant. Sive Cutiliensis, sive Velinus Lacus Regionis hujus Umbilicus sit censendus, Centrum sane sic depingit Virgilius lib. vii. Æneidos: Est locus Italiæ in medio sub Montibus altis, Nobilis, & fama multis memoratus in orbi, Amsancti Valles: densis hunc frondibus atrum Vrget utrimque latus Nemorum: medioque fragosus Dat sonitum saxis & torto vortice Torrens. Hic Specus horrendum & sævi Spiracula Ditis Monstrantur, ruptoque ingens Acheronte vorago Pestiferas aperit fauces, quas condita Erinnys Invisum Numen terras cœlumque levabat.
units.tr: M. Terentius Varro places the navel of Italy in the territory of Reate at Lake Cutilia, in which an island floats, according to Pliny in book 3 chapter 12 of the Natural History. Others name Lake Velinus, which they say is not far from there and holds the middle of Italy. Whether the Lake of Cutilia or Lake Velinus is to be regarded as the navel of this region, Virgil certainly portrays the centre in this way in book 7 of the Aeneid: There is a place in the middle of Italy beneath high mountains, famous and renowned in many tales across the world, the valleys of Amsanctus: on both sides a dark wood presses in with dense foliage, and in the middle a roaring torrent gives a sound among the rocks and whirls in a twisting eddy. Here a cave and the breathing holes of cruel Dis are shown, and a vast chasm, torn open by Acheron, opens its pestilential jaws, into which the Fury, buried, raised the hated power up from the earth and heaven.

units.la: In quorum Versuum expositione parum fidi Donatus & Servius. Hic enim Cosmographos ait Italiæ Medium prope Venosam designare, nimirum in Herpinis ad Apuliæ Campaniæque confinium, ubi sulphureæ fœntaque, quod silvis umbrosis circumdentur, sunt Aquæ; ideoque Viam & Aditum ad Inferos ijs in locis esse, dicu, quod ibi Victimæ noxiarum aquarum tetetrimo perimi fœtore solent: Ille autem Locum hunc juxta Canosam ad flumen Calorem esse censet. Errat uterque. Nam quis fanus Italiæ Umbilicum statuet in Apulia? Reclamat mensura. Quinimo nec Valles, nec Montes in Apulia reperiuntur illi, quos commemorat Virgilius. Plura dicam alio loco.
units.tr: In the explanation of these verses Donatus and Servius are not very trustworthy. For Donatus says that the cosmographers designate the middle of Italy near Venusia, namely in the Herpini, on the border of Apulia and Campania, where there are sulphurous and foul waters, because they are surrounded by shady woods; and therefore he says that the way and entrance to the underworld are in those places, because victims of harmful waters are usually killed there by a most foul stench. Servius thinks that this place is near Canusium by the river Calor. Both are wrong. For what sane man would place the navel of Italy in Apulia? The measurements object. Indeed, neither those valleys nor those mountains which Virgil mentions are to be found in Apulia. I will say more about this in another place.

units.la: Italiam Eustathius Hederæ; Quercus adsimulant folio Plinius lib. iii. cap. v, Solinus in Polyhistore, & Rutilius Claudius Numatianus lib. i, ut procerita te multo sit amplior, quam Latitudine; in lævum se flectens cacumine, & Amazonicæ figura desinens Parmæ. Recentiores convenientissime Humano Cruri comparant; cujus Tibia vel Anticnemion Mari objacet Intero; Sura, Supero, Pes universum Ionio abluitur Pelago; Calcaneus Epirum spectat; Vola vel Concavitas Sinum facit Tarentinum: Carnosiores Partes Promontoria statuunt Zephyrium, Carcynum, & Bruttium; Digiti in Siciliam sunt conversi; Genu in Promontorio est Populomo; Coxendix & Femoris Superiora late contingunt Alpes.
units.tr: Eustathius compares Italy to an ivy leaf; Pliny in book 3 chapter 5, Solinus in the Polyhistor, and Rutilius Claudius Namatianus in book 1 compare it to an oak leaf, so that its length is much greater than its breadth, bending to the left at its top and ending in the shape of an Amazon's shield at Parma. Recent writers compare it most aptly to a human leg: its shin, or front of the lower leg, lies along the Lower Sea; the calf faces the Upper Sea; the foot is washed all over by the Ionian Sea; the heel faces Epirus; the sole, or hollow, forms the Gulf of Taranto. The fleshier parts are the headlands of Zephyrium, Carcinum and Bruttium; the toes are turned towards Sicily; the knee is at the promontory of Populonium; the hip and the upper thigh are widely touched by the Alps.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CAP. III.

units.la: Italiæ Situs Cœlestis.
units.tr: The Celestial Situation of Italy.

units.la: DE Quantitate dixi: succedit explicanda Qualitas, cujus causa potior solet esse Situs Cœlestis. Plinius Italiam per Maria incedere, Cœli regione, si quis id diligenter exigat, inter Horam Sextam Primamque Brumalem, scribit. Nos illud Meridiem & Exortum Solis Hibernum dicere solemus. Hora enim Sexta Antiquis Meridies fuit. Ptolemæus inter Septimum & Quartum Clima, gradu Longitudinis xv, Latitudinis plus vii collocat. Si quis hodie diligentissimam ineat Situs Cœlestis rationem: secundam Longitudinem quidem Occidentalissimum xiiii: secundam Latitudinem completi Gradus octo; Australissimum enim Parallelum distare ab Æquatore Grad. xxxviii, & Borealissimum xlvi; siquidem occupare discet Italiam Quintum & Sextum Climata, omnesque Parallelos, qui sunt inter xi & xvi, in quo Terrae tractu contingit Varietas Diei Artificialis unius Horae. Maior enim Dies Aestatis in Parallelo Australi Horarum est xiiii, cum tribus quintis: in Boreali vero Horarum xv cum Quintis totidem.
units.tr: I have spoken of its extent; next I must explain its quality, of which the chief cause is usually its celestial situation. Pliny writes that Italy stretches through the seas in the region of the sky which, if anyone examines it carefully, lies between the sixth hour and the first winter hour. We are accustomed to call this the south and the winter sunrise, for the sixth hour was midday for the ancients. Ptolemy places Italy between the seventh and fourth climates, at 15 degrees of longitude and more than 7 of latitude. If anyone today undertakes the most exact reckoning of its celestial situation, he will find the second longitude, which is the westernmost, to be 14 degrees, and the second latitude to be a full 8 degrees; for the southernmost parallel lies 38 degrees from the equator, and the northernmost 46. Italy occupies the fifth and sixth climates, and all the parallels lying between 11 and 16, in which tract of the earth the length of the artificial day varies by one hour. For the longest summer day on the southern parallel is 14 and three fifths hours, and on the northern parallel 15 hours and the same three fifths.

units.la: CAP. IIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: De Qualitate, quae pendet plurimum ex Situ Caelesti, paretque in Commodis, quae inde proveniunt.
units.tr: Of the Quality, which depends very largely on the celestial situation, and of the advantages that arise from it.

units.la: COELESTI Situ sic se habente, accedentibus etiam Apenninis Montibus, qui per mediam Italiae porrecti Longitudinem, ab utroque Latere, praecipue, quo meridianos excipit Calores, Campos, Colliculque relinquunt frugiferos: non magnopere mirandum est, tam moderatam omnium anni Partium in Italia esse Temperiem, tantamque rerum omnium fertilitatem: quae tamen aliis, quam aliis, locis major. Vere Strabo lib. vi, praecipuas Italiae Qualitates enumerans: Τεμπερ. Huc pertinet locus Plinij lib. xvii. cap. v: Idem (inquit, de Catone) Agrum optimum indicat ad radicem montium, Planicie in Meridiem excurrente, quae est totius Italiae Situs: nimirum, ut illustrando Catoni nonnihil addam: ad Apennini latus, qua, si Longitudo ejus, ut idem Cato non obscure innuit, ab Occidente in Orientem vergit, Auster est, vel, si ab Septemtrione in Meridiem se extendit, qua Favonius; vel denique, si mediam ingrediundum viam ab Cauro in Vulturnum, qua Africus. Ad alterum Apennini Latus, Planicie in contrarias plagas excurrente, Italiae Agri minus sunt foecundi ob Frigorum Ventorumque Borealium impetum & violentiam. De Priore Latere exaudiendus praecipue Virgilius, quum inquit: Hic Ver adsiduum, atque alienis mensibus Aestas, Bis gravida Pecudes, bis Pomis utilis Arbos.
units.tr: With the heavenly situation being what it is, and with the Apennine Mountains also contributing, since they stretch along the middle length of Italy and leave fruitful plains and little hills on either side, especially on the side that receives the southern heats, it is not greatly to be wondered at that Italy has such a moderate temperature in every part of the year, and such fertility of all things, although this is greater in some places than in others. Strabo, in book vi, truly lists the chief qualities of Italy: Temperate [Τεμπερ.]. To this belongs the passage of Pliny, book xvii, chapter v: The same (he says, of Cato) indicates the best land to be at the foot of the mountains, on a plain that runs out to the south, which is the situation of all Italy. That is to say, to add something to the illustration of Cato: on the side of the Apennines where, if its length, as Cato himself does not obscurely hint, runs from west to east, it is the south wind (Auster); or if it stretches from north to south, the west wind (Favonius); or lastly, if it takes the middle way from Caurus to Vulturnus, the south-west wind (Africus). On the other side of the Apennines, where the plain runs out toward the opposite regions, the fields of Italy are less fruitful because of the onslaught and violence of the cold and northern winds. On the former side one should especially hear Virgil, when he says: Here spring is everlasting, and summer comes in months not its own; twice the flocks bear young, and twice the tree is fruitful with apples.

units.la: Specialiora videamus. Incolarum Italiae fuit semper, hodieque est ditissima. Sola, inquit Plinius lib. iii natur. hist. sine externis ullis auxiliis, atque etiam tunc (annum designat, quo nunciato Gallico tumultu, Coss. Romae erant L. Aemilius Papus & C. Atilius Regulus, qui ab V. urbe condita xxxix) sine Transpadanis, Equitum lxxx millia; Peditum ducentum m. armavit. Quis Italiae genius, quaeque indoles, postea peculiari capite dicam. Quosdam autem Italiae incolas cxxvi annos vitae contingere, tradit idem Plinius lib. vii. cap. xlix.
units.tr: Let us look at more particular matters. The inhabitants of Italy have always been, and are still today, very rich. Alone, says Pliny in book iii of the Natural History, without any foreign aid, and even then (he indicates the year in which, when the Gallic uproar was announced, the consuls at Rome were L. Aemilius Papus and C. Atilius Regulus, which was the 529th year from the founding of the city) without the Transpadanes, it armed 80,000 horsemen and 200,000 foot soldiers. What the character and disposition of the Italian people are, I shall say later in a separate chapter. Pliny, in book vii, chapter xlix, also reports that some inhabitants of Italy attain 126 years of life.

units.la: Ne recensendis variorum generum Animalibus tempus teram, magnam Boum (qui vetere lingua Graeca Ἴταλοι dicebantur) copiam in Italia fuisse, Bucetasque in ea Terra gigni pasciqueque solita compluria, docent apud Agellium lib. xi. Noct. Attic. cap. i. Timaeus in Historiis, quas oratione Graeca de Rebus Populi Rom. composuit, & M. Terentius Varro in Antiquit. Rer. Humanar. Lucana Armenta maxima & validissima olim ibidem fuisse, testatur Lucilius: Quem neque Lucanus oriundi montibus Tauri Ducere protelo validis cervicibus possent.
units.tr: Not to waste time listing the various kinds of animals, Agellius (book xi of the Attic Nights, chapter i) teaches that there was a great number of oxen in Italy (which in the old Greek language were called Italoi [Ἴταλοι]), and that bucetae were born and pastured in that land in many numbers; so does Timaeus in his Histories, which he wrote in Greek about the affairs of the Roman people, and M. Terentius Varro in the Antiquities of Human Affairs. Lucilius bears witness that the Lucanian herds were once there in the greatest and strongest numbers: which the Lucanian oxen, sprung from the mountains of Taurus, could not lead with strong necks under the yoke.

units.la: Nutrit Italia, praeter alias Aves, Aquilas Vulturesque, carnivoras & rapaces Volucres, Historiis Romanorum Veterum etiam nobilitatas.
units.tr: Italy nourishes, besides other birds, eagles and vultures, carnivorous and predatory birds, made famous even in the histories of the ancient Romans.

units.la: Ager, valde est temperatus, benignus, laetus, copiosus, ad Segetes aliaque omnia proferenda supra modum adcommodus, magnique suis Cultoribus quaestus, sumtus autem exigui. Rosellanus Ager in Umbria juxta Lacum Velinum tantae fertilitatis fuisse scribitur, ut auctore Varrone, Caesar Vopiscus, quum Caulam apud Censores ageret, Campos Rosea dixerit Italiae Sumen esse, in quibus Perticas pridie relictas Gramen, una nocte, operiret. Videndi Plinius lib. xvii natur. Hist. & Servius ad vii Aeneidos addit: Quinetiam quantum per diem demtum esset, tantum per noctem crescebat, quod Virgilius ad suam provinciam transfulit dicens: Et quantum longu carpent Armenta diebus, Exigua tantum gelidus ros nocte reponet,
units.tr: The land is very temperate, kindly, cheerful and abundant, and exceedingly suited to producing grain and all other crops, and it brings great profit to its cultivators at small expense. The Rosellan field in Umbria beside Lake Velinus is written to have been of such fertility that, according to Varro, Caesar Vopiscus, when he was conducting the purchase of a stall before the censors, called the fields of Rosea the udder of Italy, in which, in a single night, the grass covered the poles left there the day before. Pliny, book xvii of the Natural History, should be consulted, and Servius on Aeneid vii adds: Moreover, as much as was taken away by day, so much grew back in the night, which Virgil transferred to his own subject, saying: And as much as the herds will crop in long days, the cold dew will restore in a single short night.

units.la: Fimi usum, scribit eodem libro Plinius, ab Hercule divulgatum in Italia, quae, addens, Regi suo Stercutio, Fauni Filio, ob ho inventum immortalitatem tribuit. Ad Vitium optima fert, inquit Varro Italiae dotes persequens: Ager Campanus, Frumentum; Falernus, Vinum; Cafinas, Oleum; Tuscutanus, Ficum; Mel, Tarentinum; Piscem, Tiberis. Plinius, quum dixisset Tritici genera esse plura, Italico, adiicibit, nullum equidem comparaverim candore ac pondere, quo maxime differnitur; Montanus modo comparetur Italia agris externum, in quo principatum tenuit Baeotia, deinde Syria, mox Africa. Addit idem paullo post, annis fere CXLV Sophoclem Poetam in fabula Tripolemo Italiam ante cuncta laudasse, ad verbum translata sententia: Et fortunatam Italiam Frumento candere candido.
units.tr: Fimi (manure), Pliny writes in the same book, was made known in Italy by Hercules, adding that he gave immortality to his king Stercutius, son of Faunus, for this discovery. The Italian land bears the best things for the vine, says Varro, going through the endowments of Italy: the Campanian field, wheat; the Falernian, wine; Cafinas, oil; Tusculum, figs; Tarentum, honey; the Tiber, fish. Pliny, having said that there are several kinds of wheat, adds: I would certainly compare none with the Italian for whiteness and weight, by which it is chiefly distinguished; let only the Montane land of Italy be compared with foreign fields, in which Boeotia held the first place, then Syria, soon Africa. Pliny adds shortly afterwards that about 145 years earlier the poet Sophocles, in his play Tripolemus, had praised Italy above all else, the sentence being translated word for word: And fortunate Italy shines with white wheat.

units.la: Quae laus, inquit, peculiaris hodieque Italiae est. Quo magis admiror Posteros Graecorum nullam mentionem huius fecisse frumenti. Sed illam Italiae benignitatem exhausit tantum Avaritia, adeo ut tandem vera e litteris opinio eorum, qui iam Italiam Terram extimavere lapsam, ut inquit nominatus saepe Plinius, qui ex quorundam et mellione, Latifundia, exclamat, perdidere Italiam, tam vero et Provincias, &c.
units.tr: This praise, he says, is still peculiar to Italy today. So much the more do I wonder that the later Greeks made no mention of this wheat. But avarice alone has exhausted that goodness of Italy, so that at last the true opinion from the writings of those who already judged the land of Italy to have fallen, as the often-cited Pliny says, who from the words of certain men exclaims about the great estates that have ruined Italy, and indeed the provinces too, and so on.

units.la: Italiam porro peculiarem omnium Arborum Parentem videri posse, testatur idem Plinius libri xiv Proœmio. Vulgatas non commemorabo. Earum, quae vulgo Aurantia, Citria vel Medica, Cydonia, aliaque id genus, incredibilis hic copia. Tota ora, ut ea nobis sit exemplo, quae in Liguria ab D. Remi, atque etiam ulterius, ad Genuam pertinet, tot tamque nobilibus Arboribus, itemque Palmis summae proceritatis, unde fructus admodum generosi odoriferique percipiuntur, ornata est, ut cum adspectu, tum odoratu sit pertucunda; Hortus passim occurrentibus, ad recreandas tri-stes adflictasque hominum mentes, amoenissimis. Idem de mille aliis dici potest locis. Vivere in Italia Piperis arborem, docet laudatus paullo ante Plinius lib. xvi cap. xxxii, steriles autem ibi Palmas esse, lib. xiii, cap. iv. Oleam omnino non fuisse in Italia, Hispania atque Africa, L. Tarquinio Prisco regnante, scribat Fenestella apud eundem Plinium lib. xv. cap. i: qui eodem libro cap. ii. Olea laudat Venafranum & Liciniamum. Praestitisse autem ceteris Venafrum, declarat etiam Martialis hoc Distichon: Hoc tibi Campani sudavit Bacca Venafri Unguentum quoties sumis, et ipsa olet.
units.tr: That Italy may be regarded as the peculiar parent of all trees, the same Pliny testifies in the preface to book xiv. I shall not mention the common ones. Of those commonly called oranges, citrons or Median apples, quinces, and others of that kind, there is here an incredible abundance. The whole coast, which in Liguria runs from San Remo and even further to Genoa, to be an example for us, is adorned with so many and such noble trees, and likewise with palms of very great height, from which very generous and fragrant fruits are gathered, so that it is delightful both to the sight and to the smell: a garden everywhere one turns, most pleasant for refreshing the sad and afflicted minds of men. The same can be said of a thousand other places. That the pepper tree lives in Italy is taught by the Pliny cited a little earlier, book xvi, chapter xxxii, and that palms are barren there, book xiii, chapter iv. That the olive was not at all in Italy, Spain or Africa while Tarquinius Priscus reigned, Fenestella writes, as cited in the same Pliny, book xv, chapter i; who in the same book, chapter ii, praises the olive of Venafrum and Liciniamum. That Venafrum surpassed the others, Martial also declares in this couplet: For you, as often as you use the unguent, the Campanian berry of Venafrum has sweated, and it itself smells.

units.la: Videndus & Horatius lib. ii. Carm. Od. vi. lib. ii Sat. iv. & viii. Oleum hodie maxime icatet Terra Hydruntina, in qua tanta copia, ut cui Olearum his in locis ingentia nemora non sunt vita, incredibile plane videri possit. Ager Barianus in Apulia Peucetia Oleum, Vinum, Frumentum, Amygdalam, Gossypium aliosque fructus ubertate quadam & abundantia fundit incredibili. Vnus Vallis Oneliae Ager in Liguria tanto gaudet Olei provenitu, ut quandoque duodeviginti, nonnumquam vicena millia reddat Vrnarum, quas Incolae Barilas vocant. Nec Manna negavit Italia Natura. Prope Altomontium in Brutiis Manna colligitur, noctu rorans: praecipue quum Imbres diurnos liquidum purumque cum lum noctis excipit. Legitur ex frondibus & Arborum quarumdam truncis. Eodem beata Munere Magna Graecia, quo loco Thuriorum nobis vitiuntur vestigia. Loca petis plura Lector? Servare se aiunt in Campania Amalphitani ottia D. Andreae, ex iis peculiarem liquorem (Incolae Manna vocant) extudare adherentes, eumque voti causa peregrinantibus elargientes. Commemorantur similia ab Apulis Peucetiis de Mauri Episcopi, Sergii & Pantaleonis Equitum atque Martyrum reliquiis, apud Vigilias: de Nicolai Mircani Antistitis, ab Opidi Bariani Civibus: de Hippolyti denique Martyris Ollibus ab Tripaltinis apud Samnites.
units.tr: Horace should also be consulted: Odes, book ii, ode vi; Satires, book ii, satires iv and viii. Oil is today most abundant in the land of Otranto, where there is such a quantity that to anyone who has not lived in these places the vast groves of olive trees would seem plainly incredible. The field of Bari in Apulia Peucetia pours forth oil, wine, grain, almonds, cotton and other fruits with a remarkable and incredible abundance. One valley field of Onelia in Liguria rejoices in such a yield of oil that sometimes it gives eighteen, sometimes twenty thousand urns, which the inhabitants call barili. Nor did the nature of Italy deny manna. Near Altomonte in the Bruttii manna is gathered, falling as dew at night, especially when a clear and pure night follows daytime rains. It is picked from the leaves and trunks of certain trees. Magna Graecia was blessed with this same gift, where the traces of Thurii are shown to us. Do you, reader, seek more places? The Amalfitans in Campania are said to keep the relics of St Andrew, and from them to squeeze a peculiar liquor (which the inhabitants call manna) that adheres, and to give it out to pilgrims for the sake of their vows. Similar things are recorded by the Apulians of Peucetia concerning the relics of Bishop Mauro and of the knights and martyrs Sergius and Pantaleon, as recorded by Vigilius; concerning Nicholas of Myra, bishop, from the citizens of the town of Bari; and finally concerning the bones of the martyr Hippolytus, from the people of Tripalta among the Samnites.

units.la: Vitium principatum in tantum proprium esse & peculiarem Italiae notat idem Plinius Proœmio, quod dixi, lib. xiv. ut vel hoc uno omnia gentium vicisse, quamquam odorifera, possit videri bona: quamquam ubique pubescentium odori nulla suavitas praefertur. Tellantur generosissima, quae passim nascuntur, Vina, ab Antiquis Scriptoribus decantata. De iis universim Athenaeus lib. i. δεπνοσοφ. Octoginta fere in toto orbe genera Vini nobilia, exque eo numero duas partes Italiae esse memoriae prodit Plinius lib. xiv. cap. xi. Idem ejusdem libri cap. vi. pleraque Italiae Vina ad quatuor refert classes. Omnibus aliis praefert, ex alieno iudicio, Setinum, ab Setia Latii opido dictum.
units.tr: That the vine holds such a proper and peculiar primacy in Italy is noted by the same Pliny in the preface, which I mentioned, to book xiv: so that by this one thing alone it may seem to have surpassed all the good things of the nations, though fragrant ones; though nowhere is any sweetness of scent preferred to the blossoms. The most noble wines, which grow everywhere, have been celebrated by the ancient writers. Of these in general, Athenaeus, book i, Deipnosophists [δεπνοσοφ.]. Pliny, book xiv, chapter xi, records that about eighty kinds of wine in the whole world are famous, and that two parts of that number belong to Italy. The same Pliny, in the same book, chapter vi, refers most Italian wines to four classes. Above all others he prefers, on another's judgment, Setinum, named from Setia, a town of Latium.

units.la: Vinum Divus Augustus Setinum, inquit, pratulit cunctis, & fere sequuntur principes, &c. Commendat etiam cum Strabone, (vide infra, ubi de Signino) Setina Vina Martialis: Pendula Pomtinos quæ spectat Setia Campos, Exigua vetulos misit ab Urbe Cados.
units.tr: Divus Augustus says that Setine wine surpassed all others, and the emperors for the most part follow him, and so on. Martial also commends Setine wines, as Strabo does (see below, where he discusses Signine wine): The Setia that hangs over the Pontine plains sends its wine, and little Cadiz sends its old wine from the city.

units.la: Nascitur supra Forum Appij, Plinio; qui addit: Antea Cacubo erat generositas celeberrima in palustribus Populetis, Sinu Amyclano, quod tam intercidit & incuria Colonï Locique angusta, magis tamen Fossa Neronis &c. De Cacubo Athenæus lib. 1. [Greek text illegible, ~40 letters] : sensum pungit ac ferit, vehemens est, vetustatem colligit post aliquam multos annos. Martialis: Cæcuba Fundanus generosa coquuntur Amyclis; Vitis & in media nata palude viret.
units.tr: It is produced above the Forum of Appius, according to Pliny, who adds: Formerly Caecuban had the most celebrated quality, in the marshy poplar groves of the Amyclan bay. This wine has since declined, through the neglect of its farmers and the narrowness of its site, though more so because of Nero's Canal, and so on. Athenaeus, book 1, speaks of Caecuban [Greek illegible in the scan]: it pricks and strikes the senses, it is powerful, and it gathers age over many years. Martial: Fundanus's noble Caecuban wines are matured at Amyclae; and the vine that grows in the middle of the marsh flourishes.

units.la: Meminit & Horatius lib. 1. Carm. Od. xxxvii, ubi monet ob Victoriam Actiacam Genio indulgendum esse: Vem quoque Cæcubam nominans lib. 1. Ode xx: Cæcubam, & prælo domitam Cæleno Tu bibes Vvam: mea nec Falerna Temperant Vites, neque Formiani Pocula colles.
units.tr: Horace also mentions it in book 1 of the Odes, ode 37, where he urges that the victory at Actium be celebrated with a feast for the god. In book 1, ode 20, he names it too: You will drink Caecuban wine, pressed from Caelenus' grapes; neither Falernian vines nor the Formian hills supply my cups.

units.la: Tribuit secundum locum Plinius Falerno: Secunda Nobilitas Falerno Agro erat, & ex eo maxime Fausliano cura culturaque id collegerat. Exolescit hoc quoque copia potius, quam bonitatis studentium. Et paullo post: Nec ulli in Vino maior auctoritas: solo Vinorum flamma accenditur. Tria eius genera Austerum, Dulce, Tenue. Quidam ita distinguunt, Summus Collibus Gauranum giguj; medijs, Fausliannum; imis, Falernum. Athenæus Vini Falerni duas facit species: [Greek illegible, ~20 letters], inquiens, [Greek illegible, ~10 letters]. Quod illis Austerum, Horatio Severum erit lib. 1. Carminum Ode xxvii & Forte lib. ii. Satyr. iv. Qualitatem hanc indebat fortean Vetustas, quam optime ferebat. Vetulum dicitur Catullo Carmine xxvii, Macrobio in Saturnalib. & aliis. Temperabatur autem vel alio Vino, vel Melle. Falerni Austeritatem Vino Chio, quod lenius erat ac mitius, obtundi solitam innuit Horatius lib. 1. Satyr. x: —— at Sermo Lingua concinnus utraque Suavior, ut Chio nota si commissa Falerni est.
units.tr: Pliny gives Falernian second place: Falernian land had the second rank of fame, and above all the Fausten vintage, which was gathered with special care and cultivation. This too has declined, through the abundance rather than the quality sought by growers. And a little later: No wine has greater authority; only Falernian wine catches fire from a flame. It has three kinds: austere, sweet and light. Some distinguish them thus: the highest hills produce Gauran, the middle slopes Faustian, the lowest Falernian. Athenaeus makes two kinds of Falernian wine, saying [Greek illegible in the scan]. The former is the austere wine, which Horace calls severe in book 1 of the Odes, ode 27, and strong in book 2, Satire 4. Age perhaps gave it this quality, which it bore very well. Catullus, in poem 27, Macrobius in the Saturnalia, and others call it old. It was tempered either with another wine or with honey. Horace hints that the austerity of Falernian was commonly softened with Chian wine, which was milder and gentler: but our talk is smoother than either, as Chian is mixed in with Falernian, which is well known.

units.la: Eandem Austeritatem Veteres Melle lenire ac mitigare solitos, indicat idem Horatius lib. ii. Sat. iv: Anfidius Forti miscebat Mella Falerno.
units.tr: That the ancients customarily softened and mitigated the same austerity with honey is shown by Horace again, in book 2, Satire 4: Anfidius used to mix honey with strong Falernian.

units.la: Et eodem libro Sat. ii: —— nisi Hymettia Mella Falerno Ne biberis diluta.——
units.tr: And in the same book, Satire 2: unless you drink Falernian diluted with Hymettian honey.

units.la: Respicit eo Virgilius lib. iv. Georgic. Dulcia Mella premes, nec tantum dulcia, quantum Et liquida, & durum Bacchi domitura saporem.
units.tr: Virgil alludes to this in book 4 of the Georgics: You will mix sweet honey, sweet not only but also liquid, to tame the harsh flavour of Bacchus.

units.la: Vbi durus Bacchi Sapor, Vinum Falernum; quod Plinio & Athenæo Austerum. Dulce, quod iidem vocant, fieri solitum notat Athenæus, [Greek illegible, ~15 letters]. Intima porro Nota Falerni apud Horat. lib. ii. Od. iii, Vinum signat Falernum, optimæ notæ, in intima Cella Vinaria, ut volunt Interpretes, recondi solitum. Liberalitatem in Falerno distribuendo Iulij Cæsaris celebrat Plinius lib. xiv. cap. xv. apud quem & aliis locis Falerni est mentio, ut etiam apud Strabonem lib. v, & alios. Ad Tertiam veniunt apud Plinium palmam Vina Albana, Surrentina, Massica, Statana, Calena, Fundana, Veliternina, Privernatia, Signina, Albana, inquit, Vrbs vicina, ac rara in austero. Athenæus lib. i, [Greek illegible, ~30 letters]. De Albano Horatius lib. ii. Sat. viii: Hic Herus, Albanum Macenas, sive Falernum Te magis adpositis delectat.
units.tr: Here the harsh flavour of Bacchus is Falernian wine, which Pliny and Athenaeus call austere. Athenaeus notes that the wine they call sweet was commonly made by [Greek illegible in the scan]. The phrase intima nota Falerni in Horace, book 2, ode 3, denotes Falernian wine of the finest quality, which, as the commentators think, was stored in the innermost wine cellar. Pliny, book 14, chapter 15, praises the generosity of Julius Caesar in distributing Falernian; there and elsewhere Pliny mentions Falernian, as does Strabo in book 5, and others. Pliny places in the third rank the Albanian, Surrentine, Massic, Statanian, Calenian, Fundanian, Veliternian, Privernian, Signine wines. Alban, he says, is a neighbouring town, and rare among the austere wines. Athenaeus, book 1, [Greek illegible in the scan]. On Alban wine Horace says, in book 2, Satire 8: Here my master Maecenas, you are more pleased with Alban or with Falernian when they are set before you.

units.la: Albanum Vinum, si austerius, vetustate in dulcedinem; sin dulcius, in austeritatem transire, subindicat Plinius lib. xiv, cap. ii: qui descriptis Albanis hæc subjicit: Item Surrentina in Vineis tantum nascentia, convalescentibus maxime probata, propter tenuitatem salubritatemque Tiberium Cæsar dicebat consensisse Medicos, ut nobilitatem Surrentino darent, alioquin esse generosum Acetum: C. Cæsar, qui successit illi, nobilem Vappam. Fuisse certe admodum laudata Surrentina declarat Martialis lib. xiv. Surrentina bibù? nec Murrhina pocula, nec aurum Sume, dabunt Calices hac tibi Vina suos.
units.tr: Pliny, book 14, chapter 2, hints that Alban wine, if it is rather austere, turns to sweetness with age, but if it is sweeter, turns to austerity. After describing the Alban wines he adds: Likewise Surrentine wine, which grows only in the vineyards, is especially esteemed when it has matured, on account of its lightness and healthfulness. Tiberius Caesar used to say that the physicians agreed to give Surrentine the reputation of nobility, otherwise it would be a noble vinegar; and Gaius Caesar, who succeeded him, called it a noble sour wine. That Surrentine wine was certainly much praised is shown by Martial, book 14: Will you drink Surrentine? Neither murrhine cups nor gold will be needed; these wines will give you their own goblets.

units.la: Eadem Vina memorat Strabo, ætate sua Romam deportari solita scribens Falerna, Setina, Calenaque, & cum iis certantia Surrentina; quod experientia vetustatem illa ferre comperta fuissent. Idem confirmat Higinus. Meminit Horatius lib. 11. Sat. 1111. Caricum, quos canit Martialis, nobilitate Surrentum celebratum auctor etiam est Plinius lib. xxxv. De itidem Martialis, quem dixi:
units.tr: Strabo mentions the same wines, writing that Falernian, Setine and Calenian were customarily brought to Rome in his time, and that Surrentine competed with them, because experience had shown that it kept its age. Higinus also confirms this. Horace mentions it in book 2, Satire 4. The author also says that Surrentum was celebrated for the fame of its Carican figs, which Martial sings of. Pliny, book 35, too, [mentions this].

units.la: Accipe non vina Calices de pulchre natos, Sed Surrentina leve torcuma vota.
units.tr: Martial again: Take, not wines, but the goblets well made, and the Surrentine vows in a light press.

units.la: Pergit Plinius: Certant Massica atque ex Monte Gaurano, Puteolos Baiasque prospectantia. Virg. lib. 11 Georgic.
units.tr: Pliny goes on: Massic and Gaurian wines vie with each other, the latter from the mountain facing Puteoli and Baiae. Virgil, book 2 of the Georgics:

units.la: Sed gravida fruges & Bacchi Massicus humor Implevere.
units.tr: But the fruitful earth and the Massic juice of Bacchus filled them.

units.la: Lib. vii Æneidos.
units.tr: Book 7 of the Aeneid: they render the Massic wines fortunate to Bacchus.

units.la: —vertunt felicia Baccho Massica.—
units.tr: They turn the Massic fields to wine, gift of Bacchus.

units.la: quemlocum exponens Servius, Massicum Campania Montem ait esse, Vini generosi feracem. Silius lib. vii. de Bello Pœn.
units.tr: Explaining this passage, Servius says that Massicum is a mountain of Campania, rich in fine wine. Silius, Punic War, book 7:

units.la: Vseris late florebat Massicus Arvis, Miratus Nemora & florentes Sole Racemos.
units.tr: "Massicus was flourishing far and wide with its fertile fields, admiring its groves and its clusters ripening in the sun."

units.la: Et paullo post:
units.tr: And a little later:

units.la: Massicus Vuiferis addebat nomina glebis.
units.tr: "Massicus added its names to the vine-bearing soil."

units.la: Item Horatius lib. 1. Carm. Oda 1:
units.tr: Likewise Horace, Odes, book 1, ode 1:

units.la: Est qui nec Veteris pocula Massici, &c.
units.tr: "There is one who does not refuse the cups of old Massic, etc."

units.la: Idem, Indolem Massicorum nonnullam indicans, lib. 11. Sat. iv:
units.tr: The same poet, indicating some quality of the Massic wines, in Satires, book 2, satire 4:

units.la: Massica si cœlo supponas Vina sereno, Nocturna, si quid crasis est, tenuabitur aura.
units.tr: "If you should set Massic wines under a clear sky, at night, whatever harshness they have will be softened by the air."

units.la: Massicum Athenæus austerum quidem esse notat sed Stomacho utile: ætate maturescebat, austeritatemque minuebat. De Statanis, quæ sequuntur, sic loquitur Plinius: Falerno contermina Statana ad principatus venere non dubie, palamque fecere, sua quibusque terris tempora esse, sicut rerum proventus occasusque. Statanum Vinum celebrat etiam Strabo lib. ix. Dictum videtur ab Statiis Paludibus Campaniæ, quarum meminit Statius lib. iii. Silvarum. Vide infra cap. xii. Prosequitur sua Vina Plinius: Iuncta his prope solebant Calena (sic dicta ab Calenis: De Caleno Athenæus; ὁ καληνὸς τῷ φαλέρῳ ἐξ εμαχύτης: meminit Horatius cum alibis tum lib. 1. Od xx, & xxxi) & quæ in Vineis Arbusteque nascuntur Fundana (Strabo quoque Vinum Fundanum & Caecubum valde commendat: laudat & his versibus Martialis:
units.tr: Athenaeus notes that Massicum is indeed austere but useful for the stomach; it matured with age and its austerity lessened. Pliny speaks thus of the Statanian wines that follow: "Next to Falernian, the Statanian vines undoubtedly came to the front, and made it plain that each kind has its own seasons in its own lands, as with the yield and failure of crops. Statanian wine is also praised by Strabo, book 9. It seems to be named from the Statian marshes of Campania, which Statius mentions in Silvae, book 3. See below, chapter 12." Pliny goes on to his other wines: "Close to these were usually the Calenian (so called from Cales; Athenaeus on Calenum: Calenum is of the same kind as Falernum [ὁ καληνὸς τῷ φαλέρῳ ἐξ εμαχύτης]; Horace mentions it in several places, including Odes 1.20 and 1.31), and the Fundanian, which grows in the vineyards and orchards." Strabo too greatly commends Fundanian and Caecuban wine, and Martial praises them in these verses:

units.la: Hæc Fundana tulit felix Autumnus Opimi: Expressit Mulsum Consul, & ipse bibit.)
units.tr: "This is the Fundanian that the happy autumn of Opimius bore; the consul pressed out the mead, and drank it himself."

units.la: Ex aliis vicinis Vrbis Velinerna, Privernatisque, Nam quod Signia nascitur austeritate minima continenda utile alvo, inter medicamina numeratur. Sic Strabo lib. v: Σηγνία Φίρουσι Σηγνίας: ἡ ὡς τῶν πολυπλατύντα; ἡ δὲ τὴν χαλκοῦ ζητεῖ, τὴν Σίγνιον λεγόμενον. Legendum Σιγνίαν. Sic appellat Priscianus: sic Martialis:
units.tr: From the other neighbouring areas of the city come the Velinernian and the Privernatian. For the wine that grows at Signia, of very slight astringency, is counted among medicines as useful for the bowels. So Strabo, book 5: "They say Signia ... which is called Signian." Read Σιγνίαν. Priscian calls it so, and Martial:

units.la: Potabis liquidum Signina morantia Ventrem: Ne nimium sistant, sit tibi parca sitis.
units.tr: "You will drink clear Signian wine, which checks the belly; so that it does not stop you too much, let your thirst be moderate."

units.la: Hinc Signia spumans inimico Musto legitur apud Silium lib. viii. Belli Pœnici. Quarum obtinent, Plinio teste, curriculum, beneficio D. Iulij, qui primus auctoritatem ijs tribuit, ut in ejus epistolis apparet, ad Superum Mare Pratutia, atque Ancone nascentia, & quæ à Palma una forte enata Palmesia appellantur. Pratutia à Praetutianis, Samnitium populis, nominata. Haud procul Ancone Sirolum est oppidum, Vino nobile; quod hic Ancentani nomine celebrat Plinius. De Palmesio non habeo quod dicam, nisi quod suspecta mihi sit scriptura, in Vna voce fortean Vta latente. De reliquis ita Plinius: In Mediterraneo vero Cefensatia ac Maecenatiana. In Veronensi item Rhetica, Falernus tantum postbabita ab Virgilio. Vinum Rheticum Theodoricus Ostrogothorum Regem tertium Athesi & Hadriatico Mari, ac deinde iumentis Romam usque sibi adferri curavisse, refert Blondus. Id Cassiodorus Acinaticum nominans hoc modo describit, Colore cyc rubens, Saporis regy ac optimi; cuius dulcedo mirifice cum quadam suavitate placeat: quamvis ijs quam is autem ad radicum densius crassiusque videatur instar carnis tenerae, vel marderde potoris, tamen esse incundissimum. Audiamus enarrantem cetera Plinium: Mox ab intimo sinu Maris Hadriana nominat & Ἀδρίας ἐπικ Athenæus, quæ dicere cum Albano Falerno quæ faciundum monet ... , ponendumque ... ab Ifero autem Larinterfia, Grauiscana, Statoniensia ab Graviscæ & Statonia Etruriæ oppidis; de quibus suo loco. Etruriæ Latinam Lunæ habet, Liguriæ ... Ligurum oppida, quæ vulgo Mons Ruber, Vinerella, Manariola, Rivoique Maioris, Gallis hodie Angliqueque tam celeberrima, propter nobilitatem Vini, quod hinc eas in partes exportatur, Blondo teste. Admirationem profecto habet ingentem, ut notat Leander, qui in tam excelsis præruptisque montium iugis, ad quæ vix ipsæ volucres accedere posse videantur, quaque tam perpetuas habent cautes, nulla ut terræ mica propemodum appareat, tanta quæ esse copia Vinum, ut quum æstate vestiantur pampini, Murum hederaceo regmine obductum teterant. Hinc tamen suavissima Vina, hinc nobilis ille incus percipitur. Adjunt Leander: De Plinio mirari satis nequeo, celebrata illis hæc Vina non esse, nisi forte cum Lunensibus, quæ laudari id quaque aere gemmantur suave, admirat.
units.tr: Hence "Signia foaming with hostile must" is read in Silius, Punic War, book 8.
