Pliny testifies that these wines ran their course with the favour of the deified Julius, who first gave them authority, as appears from his letters: wines from Pratutia and Ancona on the Upper Sea (the Adriatic), and those called Palmesian, from Palma, which perhaps grew up from a single palm tree. Pratutia is named from the Praetutians, a people of the Samnites. Not far from Ancona is the town of Sirolum, famous for its wine, which Pliny calls by the name Ancentanum. About Palmesian I have nothing to say, except that the reading seems doubtful to me, perhaps with "Vta" hidden in the one word. Of the rest Pliny says: "In the inland regions, Cefensatian and Maecenatian. In the Veronese district too, the Rhetian, which Virgil ranks only just behind Falernian." Blondus reports that Theodoric, third king of the Ostrogoths, had Rhetian wine brought to him by pack animals from the Adige and the Adriatic as far as Rome. Cassiodorus, calling it Acinatican, describes it in this way: its colour is reddish-black, its flavour rich and excellent, and its sweetness pleases wonderfully with a certain agreeableness; though nearer the roots it seems denser and thicker, like tender flesh or the marrow of a bird, yet it is most pleasant. Let us hear Pliny go on with the rest: "Next, from the innermost bay of the Adriatic Sea, he names the Adrianum and the Adrias [Ἀδρίας] ... Athenaeus; which, he advises, must be set beside the Albanian Falernian ... and from Ifer the Larinterfian, the Graviscan and the Statonian, from the towns of Graviscae and Statonia in Etruria, of which in their place." Etruria has the Latin wine of Luna; Liguria has ... the towns of the Ligurians, which are commonly called Mons Ruber, Vinerella, Manariola, Rivoi Maioris, now so celebrated among the French and English, on account of the nobility of the wine exported from there into those regions, according to Blondus. Leander notes that it is truly a great marvel that on such high and steep mountain ridges, where scarcely the birds themselves seem able to approach, and where the rocks are so continuous that hardly any speck of soil appears, there should be such an abundance of wine, so that when the vine-shoots are clothed in summer they cover the wall with an ivy-like canopy. Yet from here come the sweetest wines, and from here that famous ... is drawn. Leander adds: I can hardly wonder enough at Pliny, that these wines are not celebrated among them, unless perhaps he admires them along with the Lunensian wines, which are said to be praised for their sweetness as well as their bouquet.

units.la: Est etiam in Liguria Tabia Caficli in Vinis Aptiana laudatum ambitu quidem exiguum, sed nomine celeberrimum ob generis liberatem sueri, nec Malvatico Cretæ, nec Cyprio, nec ullo cum ha'ico, tum exotico Vino suavitate cedentis. Quæ superant, sic recenset Plinus: Verum & ostentarum Italiæ ab Aufido mari, non ea cum gloria, Faustina & Seruiliana, & Conjunctæ genita, & Tenefi, ac Patræ, Lauanæ quæ antecedentibus Tiburnis. Omnium vero eorum maxime illi sistata Messala potu & famæ Lagaricana, ne proeum Grumenio nuncentia. His omnibus sua ab oppidis vicinis, de quibus suo loco, erant nomina. Serviliana autem scripta centeo apud Plinium pro Servitana, vel saltem apud Antoninum in Itinere, quod Mediolano per Picenum & Campaniam ducit ad Columnam, id est Trajectam Siciliæ, Servitium potius arbitror pro Servitio quod opidum Sammitium est inter Aufidenam & Bovianum; quidam tamen pro Servitio ibi refutuum ex fidelissimis Antonini Exemplaribus Aeserniam. Quod Vinum Babia natum laudat Plinus: pro Babia legunt alii Barbam; quidam Barium. Certe Barium Vinum habet etiam Athenæus. Campania, aut Fitem Vinis molicus Plinus, nuper excitatus ut no is Nominibus auctoritatem, sive curæ, sive cæsa, ad quartum ab Neapoli lapide Trebelli: laudantur & ab Athenæo lib. 1; iuxta Capuam Caulinus, & in suo ago Trebulanum (Trebulum vel Trebulani habent Ptolemæus & Plinius in Campania, pati, ut quidam putant, inter Capuam & Suessulam intervallo: quod semper inter plebeii & Trifolinæ; ab Trifolino Monte, quem Neapoli vicinum memorat Galenus. Meminit Vitium Trifolini Agri Iuvenalis Satyr. iii: Te Trifolinus Ager fœcundo Vitibus implet
units.tr: In Liguria there is also the Tabian, of Caficlus, and among the wines the Aptian is praised, small in extent but very famous by name for the freedom of its quality, yielding in sweetness neither to the Mulvaticum of Crete, nor the Cyprian, nor to any other wine, whether native or foreign. As for the rest, Pliny enumerates them thus: "But also the wines of Italy from the Aufidus sea, not with that glory: the Faustian and the Servilian, the Conjuncta-born, Tenesian and Patrine, Lavanian, which come before the Tiburnian. Of all of these, the Messalan is greatest in strength and fame, and the Lagaricanian, which is not inferior to the Gromenian. All of these had their names from neighbouring towns, of which in their place." The Servilian is written in Pliny's text as Servitana, or at least in Antoninus' Itinerary, which leads from Mediolanum through Picenum and Campania to Columna, that is Trajecta of Sicily; I think it rather Servitium, a Samnite town between Aufidena and Bovianum; some, however, from the most faithful copies of Antoninus, read Aesernia instead of Servitium. Pliny praises the wine of Babia: others read Barba for Babia, some Barium. Certainly Athenaeus also has Barian wine.

units.la: gloriata. Nam Pompeianus summum x annorum incrementum est, nihil Senectæ conferente. Dolore etiam capitum in sexiam diem sequenti infesta deprehenduntur. Ut concludam varia Vinorum Nomina, hactenus à Plinio commemorata, circa annum ab V.C. 1cxxx, nondum, ut ipse docet lib. xiiii. cap. xiiii, in clamore erant. Itaque omnia tunc genita unum habebant Consulis L. Opimii nomen. De iis sic idem Plinius lib. xiiii. cap. ii: Anno fuit omnium generum bonitas, L. Opimio Consule, quum C. Gracchus Tribunus, plebem fœnantibus agitans, interemtus, ea Cæli Temperies fuisse, quam Coeluram vocant, Solis opere, Nata i Vinis 1 cxxxiiii. Durantque adhuc Vina ducentum fere annos, tam in spatium reducta Mellis asperi. Sed de his alij: ego ad reliquas Italiæ Dotes pergo; strictum eas indicaturus.
units.tr: gloried in. For the Pompeian ... has the greatest increase over ten years, with nothing added by age. Headaches are also found to trouble people on the sixth day after drinking. To conclude the varied names of wines hitherto mentioned by Pliny: around the year 630 from the founding of the city, as he himself teaches in book 14, chapter 14, they were not yet in common use. So all the wines produced then had only the one name of the consul L. Opimius. On these things the same Pliny writes, book 14, chapter 2: "There was a goodness of all kinds in the year when L. Opimius was consul, when C. Gracchus, the tribune who stirred up the common people, was killed; that weather of the sky which they call Coelura was from the sun's work, and the wines produced that year still last nearly two hundred years, having been reduced in volume to the sweetness of bitter honey." But I will leave these matters to others; I go on to the remaining endowments of Italy, which I shall indicate briefly.

units.la: Herbarum omnis generis est fertilissima. Non genere autem Μυρσίνη, Κέρας, Ἀμύγδαλα, Κυνάμωμα, Κύμινον, Κοδάμωμον, & alia multa, prodit memoriæ Plinius lib. xiii. cap. ii. Sed magna hic facta est mutatio.
units.tr: It is most fertile in herbs of every kind. Pliny, book 13, chapter 2, records, not of this kind, the myrtle [Μυρσίνη], the cherry [Κέρας], the almond [Ἀμύγδαλα], the cinnamon [Κυνάμωμα], the cumin [Κύμινον], the cardamom [Κοδάμωμον], and many other things. But here a great change has taken place.

units.la: Quid vero de Metallis, Lapidibus, aliisque Muneribus dicam? Metallorum omnium fertilitate, ait Plinius lib. iii. nat. histor. cap. xx. nullo cedit Terræ; quod lib. xxxii. cap. iv repetens, Italæ, inquit parcitum est (ab inquietandis ad exturbanda Metalla eius Viscembus) Veteri Edicto Patrum: alioqui nulla fœcundior Metallorum quam nunc erat Tellus. In Foro Iulio Hydra fluvius est, & haud procul inde Argenti-Vivi Fodina. In Agro Volaterrano nonnullis locis Terra est lutea, similis Auripigmento, fœcundissima: quamobrem Incolæ Regionis, quam possunt illudiole iter hac vitant: odorem enim tam gravem exhalat, ut supervolantes Aves mortuæ statim concidant. Magna Alumnus
units.tr: What shall I say of metals, stones, and other gifts? Pliny, Natural History, book 3, chapter 20, says that in fertility of all metals Italy yields to no land. Repeating this in book 32, chapter 4, he says: "Italy has been spared, by the old edict of the Fathers, from having its veins of metal disturbed and dug out; otherwise no land would have been more fruitful in metals than it now is." In the Forum Julium there is a river Hydra, and not far from it a quicksilver mine. In the Volterran territory, in some places the earth is yellow, like orpiment, and very fertile; for this reason the inhabitants of the region, wherever they can, avoid the road, since it gives off so heavy an odour that birds flying over fall dead at once. A great abundance of alum was discovered some years ago among the Etruscans, in the territory of Mafla. In Campania Felix there are tunnels from which sulphur is dug; there is also a valley where alum is boiled. In the Volterran territory too, and at Marantium, putrid places are pointed out, whose foul smell ... A great abundance of alum

units.la: Alumnus Aluminis copia ante aliquot annos reperta est apud Etruscos in Territorio Maflæ. In Campania Felice Cuniculi sunt, ex quibus effoditur Sulphur; ibidem etiam Convallis est, ubi Alumen coquitur. In Agro quoque Volaterrano Marantioque Loca putida monstrantur, quorum graveolentiam & foetorem, Sulphuris Nigri Metallum, quod hic invenitur, & haud procul paratis ad id officinis excoquitur, exhalare censendum est. Ab Volaterris amnem Cæcinam versus, millia tria, Colles aliquot visuntur, ubi Officinæ Salaria. Apud Brutios mille passibus ab Altomontio Salt fodinæ sunt, in intima montis viscera excavatæ, longitudine quadam 10, quadam 110 passuum, aut amplius, unde Salem effodiunt. Circa Tibur Latomia occurrunt, ubi Lapis Tiburtinus caeditur, Plinio nominatus. In Agro Vicentino, haud procul Pago, qui vernacule Costoza, Loca sunt, in longis profunditque Specubus: ex quibus Lapis caeditur, non absimilis Tiburtino, quo antiqua Patavinorum & Vicentinorum Aedificia speciantur confecta. Gabinus Albanusque Lapis impervius est igni, ut docet Tacitus lib. xv. Annal. Sic Isidorus lib. xvi: Savinus (leg. Gabinus) Lapis fusilis addito Oleo etiam incenditur. Est & quidam viridis Lapis, vehementer igni resistens. Gabiorum Lapidum meminit etiam Strabo: ... indicat Latomis Gabinus non alias Romanis fuisse utibiliores. In Breonia Istriae, Lapis caeditur, qui ab Venetis aliisque Conregionalibus ad Ædificia magnifica expeti solitus. Sunt & Lapidicinae in Istria, Ædificiis Venetorum cum publicis tum privatis struendis ornandisque non inutiles. In Pedemontana Regione prope Fontes Padi nobilia Marmora ex imis Terræ penetralibus eruuntur: Sunt item Marmorum Fodinæ in Valdamo Lombardiæ Vico. In Rovinensi Istriæ Agro Marmor excieditur, quod Istricum vocatum; maximi per totam Italiam precii. Apud Tuscos in Agris Montibusque Lunæ vicinis candidi ac varij Marmoris lucidi esse Latomias, perhibet Strabo lib. vi ex quibus unico solidoque Lapide Tabulæ integræ, Columnæque cædi solebant immensæ: summa addit & hinc olim ea Marmora, quæ ad Opera nobilissima cum Romæ, tum alijs in partibus expetebantur: tam ob insignem lævorem, quam propter summam exportandi hinc facilitatem; quippe quia vicinæ Littori ipsæ Lapicidinæ opportunitatem maximam haberent Lapidum ad Naves deferendorum; quos ab Mari subvehendos excipiebat Tiberis. Columnæ hic etiamnum peringentes aliaque rudia Marmorum frustra cernuntur: quæ florentibus rei Romanæ temporibus excisa, dein autem, ea labente, derelicta nemo exportavit vel expolivit. Importantur nunc quidem adhuc ex his locis Marmora Pisas, Genuam, Florentiam, Romam, Bononiam & in Ulteriorem Galliam: sed hauquaquam, retre Leandro, ejus Magnitudinis eaque copia, ut olim solebant Romam, vigente illius Urbis imperio. Meminit horum Marmorum Plinius lib. xxx. cap. x, in Liguria Lapidum Album facile terra secari scribens, quem prius, lib. xxx, cap. v. Lunense Marmor dixerat. Mentionem facit & horum Marmorum Iuvenalis, quum inquit:
units.tr: Some years ago a large quantity of alum was discovered among the Etruscans, in the territory of Massa. In Campania Felice there are tunnels from which sulphur is dug out, and nearby is a valley where alum is boiled. In the territory of Volterra and at Maranti, foul-smelling places are pointed out, whose stench and reek must be thought to come from the black sulphur metal found there, which is smelted in workshops set up close by. Three miles from Volterra towards the river Cecina there are some hills where the salt works are. Among the Bruttii, a thousand paces from Altomonte, are salt mines, hollowed out in the innermost parts of the mountain, some 10 or 110 paces long or more, from which they dig out salt. Around Tibur there are quarries where the Tiburtine stone, named by Pliny, is cut. In the territory of Vicenza, not far from the village that is called Costoza in the vernacular, there are long and deep caves from which a stone is cut, not unlike the Tiburtine, of which the ancient buildings of Padua and Vicenza are seen to be made. Gabine and Alban stone cannot be touched by fire, as Tacitus teaches in book 15 of the Annals. So too Isidore, book 16: "Savine (read Gabine) stone is fusible, and when oil is added it even catches fire." There is also a certain green stone, very resistant to fire. Strabo also mentions the Gabine stones: ... he points out that the quarries of Gabii were especially useful to the Romans. In Istrian Breonia a stone is cut, which the Venetians and other neighbouring peoples used to seek for magnificent buildings. There are also quarries in Istria, not useless for building and adorning the public and private buildings of the Venetians. In the Piedmontese region near the springs of the Po, noble marbles are dug out from the deepest recesses of the earth. There are likewise marble quarries in Valdamo, a village of Lombardy. In the territory of Rovigno in Istria marble is quarried, called Istrian, of the greatest value throughout Italy. Strabo, book 6, reports that among the Tuscans, in the fields and mountains near Luna, there are quarries of white and variegated shining marble, from which whole tablets and immense columns were usually cut from a single solid block. He adds that from here came those marbles once sought for the most splendid works, both at Rome and elsewhere, on account of their remarkable smoothness and the great ease of exporting them; for the quarries, lying near the shore, had the greatest convenience for loading the stones onto ships, which the Tiber received from the sea to carry them up. Columns and other rough blocks of marble still stand here in vain, which were cut in the flourishing days of the Roman state and then, when that state declined, were abandoned and no one exported or polished them. Even now marbles are still imported from these places to Pisa, Genoa, Florence, Rome, Bologna and into Further Gaul, but by no means in such quantity or size as they once were when they were sent to Rome while the power of that city flourished. Pliny, book 36, chapter 10, mentions these marbles, writing that in Liguria a white stone is easily cut from the earth, which he had earlier, in book 36, chapter 5, called Luna marble. Juvenal also mentions these marbles when he says:

units.la: Procubuit veluti, qui Saxa Ligustica portat.
units.tr: He fell down like a man who carries Ligurian stones.

units.la: Sic Facius Vbertus Cantico vi, lib. iii. E vedemmo Carrara, one la gente Trova il candido Marmo in tanta copia, Che assai n'haurebbe tutto l'Oriente.
units.tr: So Fazio degli Uberti, Canto 6, book 3: "We saw Carrara, where the people find white marble in such abundance that all the East would have enough of it."

units.la: Lescalia porro, Volaterranensis Agri Vicus, Alabastrite copia abundat. Eius duo hic genera, durum ac molle: prius è Terra caeditur, dictum Vitrinum; aliud supra Terram invenitur, & excoctum igne Gypsum fit. Ex primo nobilia fabricantur Opera; veluti illa, quæ maximus quidam Artifex Neapolitanus olim Organa fecit, Leoni x. P M. muneri destinata: quo fatis intercepto priusquam absolverentur, Friderico Gonzagæ, Primo Mantuæ Duci, donata fuere. Opus profecto, quod inter rara mirabiliaque nunc quæ uspiam sint, censeri debeat. Ex Alabastrite Fistulæ Modulique tori. Apud Gravisca Coralium in mari nascitur, retibus reduci solitum. In Brutijs prope Altomontium Montes sunt editissimi, numquam fere nivibus carentes, ubi Crystallus, magna copia, reperitur: etenim quum ea luga intentissimis frigoribus perpetuo rigeant, Aquæ vi Solis de Nive stillantes, quum sunt congelatæ, postea diuturnitate temporis in saxa durantur. Tertia ab Volaterris lapide Castellum est, ubi mira effodit Chalcitis abundantia. Haud procul inde Aquæ Rivulus occurrit; iuxta quem, per Convalles quasdam modicas & depressa loca incedendo, Porphyre-
units.tr: Furthermore, Lescalia, a village in the territory of Volterra, is rich in alabaster. It has two kinds here, hard and soft: the first is quarried from the earth and is called vitriform; the other is found above ground, and when burnt in the fire it becomes gypsum. From the first, noble works are made; such as those which a certain very great Neapolitan craftsman once made as organs, destined as a gift for Pope Leo X; when fate cut him off before they were finished, they were given to Frederick Gonzaga, first Duke of Mantua. Truly a work which ought to be counted among the rarest and most wonderful things anywhere. Pipes and turned mouldings are also made from alabaster. At Gravisca coral grows in the sea and is usually brought up with nets. Among the Bruttii, near Altomonte, there are very high mountains, almost never free of snow, where crystal is found in great quantity; for since those ridges are kept perpetually frozen by the most intense cold, the water dripping from the snow under the power of the sun, once it has frozen, is afterwards hardened into stone by the lapse of time. Three miles from Volterra there is a village where the chalcite is dug out in remarkable abundance. Not far from there a small stream of water meets one; along which, passing through some small valleys and low places, porphyry-

units.la: 885, Cynthius ad Musas animos inflexit Apollo, Et Disciplina tradidit omne genus.
units.tr: Cynthian Apollo turned the minds of the Muses, and handed down every kind of learning.

units.la: Arma Venus Populis Urbes implevit & Agros, Silvestresque Casas, Arborcasque Domos: Ut sint, qui curent Urbana Negotia Cives: Qui ferat Arma Manu, qui colat Arva Boves. Foedera Mercurius docuit Legesque severas, Et dare Clamori Litigiisque modum. Luna Pudicitiam suasit, castumque iuborem Ne furat ardescens & sine Lege Venus. Arma Cerer docuit Fruges, quae femine facto Decolor incurvo rusticus efie metit. Vina dedit Bacchus, & quae multa alia sequuntur.
units.tr: Venus filled the peoples' cities and fields with arms, and woodland huts and tree-built homes, so that there might be citizens to look after urban affairs, someone to bear arms in hand, someone to till the fields with oxen. Mercury taught treaties and stern laws, and set a limit to shouting and quarrels. The Moon persuaded chastity, lest a burning Venus without law steal the chaste labourer. Ceres taught the arts of grain, which the rustic reaps, now made into a pale, bent-over harvest. Bacchus gave wine, and many other things follow.

units.la: Beatissimam certe non immerito totius Europae Regionem appellat Aethicus; Totius Orbis optimam, Dionysius Halicarnass. lib. 1; Gentium Dominam, Mamertinus Panegyristes; Dominam Rerum, P. Rutilius Numatianus; Caelestem, Mundique Reginam vocat Aethicus, quem dixi. Et vero quid hic non gestum olim, quid non pro Gloria cum summa Laude ab generosis Animis patratum? Longum esset & taediosum omnia commemorare. A quibus non Gentibus expugnandi, occupandi, diripiendi gratia quondam petita? Silentium hic iubere mihi malo, quam pauca pro rei dignitate in medium adferre. Quis non hodie visundae eius cognoscendaeque causa adit? Docent ferventia passim a Peregrinantibus, qui undique eam versus confluunt, itinera. Ego sane aliquando ingressus suspicere me cum voluptate memini Montes nunc vituferos, nunc aliarum rerum feraces, nunc miraculis suis admirandos: vernantes Silvas: Sinus amplos & profundos; ndos placidosque Portus, alta lataque Flumina; Lacus limpidos & vivos; nobiles, largos, inlimes & variarum virium Fontes. Sed haec aliaque talia suis locis. Quid enim dicam de Incolis, ipsorumque Moribus, cum publice domi militiaeque, tum privatim? Urbes hic spectavi egregias, florentes, opulentas; Oppida clara, famosa, Civibus arcta; Pagos magnos, Aedificiaque Nobilium & Praetorum superbientes, &, praeter alia infinita, maestus ibi vidi & attonitus miserandas Veteres Urbium Structurarumque Reliquias, & stupenda totius Antiquitatis Monimenta. De Italiae Civitatibus Versus circumferuntur pulcherrimi: Fama tranus Roma pomposa & fanta; | Furli bizarro; & Ravenna benigna, Venetia ricca, faggia, & signorile; | E Sinigallia del ariano noriofa; Neapoli odorifera, & gentile: | E Capua amorofa; Fiorenza bella, tutto il Volgo canta; | Pisa Frendente; & Pesaro giardino; Grande Milano in Italia fi vanta; | Ancona del bel porto pellegrino Bologna grassa e Ferrara civile, | Fedelissimo Urbino; Padua forte, & Bergamo sottile; | Ascoli tondo; & longo Recanate; Genova di superbia altiera piantas; | Foligno delle strade in Zuccarate; Verona degna, & Perugia sanguigna; | Et par da cielo mandate Brescia l'armata; e Mantoa gloriosa; | Le belle Donne de Fano se dice; Rimini buona; & Pistoia ferrigna, | Ma Siena pos tra l'altre piu felice. Siena de bel podere: Lucca industriosa;
units.tr: Not undeservedly, Aethicus calls it the most blessed region of all Europe; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 1, calls it the best of the whole world; the Panegyricist Mamertinus calls it the lady of nations; P. Rutilius Namatianus calls it the mistress of affairs; Aethicus, whom I mentioned, calls it heavenly, the queen of the world. And indeed, what has not been done here in former times, what has not been accomplished for glory, with the highest praise, by noble spirits? It would be long and tedious to recall everything. From what peoples was it not once sought for the sake of conquest, occupation and plunder? I prefer here to bid silence rather than to bring forward a few things in proportion to the dignity of the subject. Who does not go there today for the sake of seeing and knowing it? Travellers, who flock to it from every side, write of their journeys everywhere in glowing terms. I myself, I remember, when I once entered it, looked up with delight at the mountains, now fertile with vines, now rich in other produce, now to be admired for their wonders; the flourishing woods; the wide and deep bays; the calm and gentle harbours; the high and broad rivers; the clear, living lakes; the noble, abundant springs of various powers. But these and such things belong in their own places. For what shall I say of the inhabitants and their customs, both public at home and in war, and private? Here I saw splendid, flourishing, wealthy cities; famous, celebrated towns, crowded with citizens; large villages, and buildings proud of their nobles and magistrates; and, besides countless other things, I saw with sorrow and astonishment the pitiable remains of ancient cities and structures, and the amazing monuments of all antiquity. Concerning the cities of Italy, beautiful verses are passed around: "Rome is famed as proud and grand; Forlì as brave; and Ravenna as kind; Venice rich, learned and noble; from Senigallia comes the fame of the Adriatic; Naples fragrant and gentle; and Capua amorous; Florence beautiful, the whole crowd sings; Pisa blooming, and Pesaro a garden; great Milan boasts in Italy; Ancona of the fine, unrivalled harbour; Bologna fat and Ferrara civil; most faithful Urbino; Padua strong, and Bergamo subtle; Ascoli round and Recanati long; Genoa planted in haughty pride; Foligno with its streets in zigzags; Verona worthy and Perugia bloody-minded; and Brescia, its army sent as if from heaven; and glorious Mantua; the fair ladies of Fano are spoken of; Rimini good, and Pistoia iron-hard; but Siena most fortunate of all. Siena of the fine estate; Lucca industrious."

units.la: Neque illud hoc loco praetermittendum silentio duxi, quatuor Italiae vulgo celebrati Oppida, sive Castella nobilissima: Apuliae, Barulum; Etruriae, Pratum: Piceni, Fabrianum; Langbardiae, Cremam.
units.tr: Nor have I thought it right to pass over in silence here four very famous towns, or rather most noble castles of Italy: Barulum in Apulia; Pratum in Etruria; Fabriano in Picenum; and Crema in Lombardy.

units.la: CAPUT V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: Italiae Montes.
units.tr: The Mountains of Italy.

units.la: IN Adjunctis Italia quo modo se habeat, habemus: Partes jamnunc eius videamus, cum simpliciter undeque consideratas, tum Miraculis Virtutibusque suis pollentes. Priores duorum faciam generum, alias Terrae tribuens, ut Mon-
units.tr: Having seen how Italy lies within its boundaries, let us now look at its parts, considered both in themselves and for their wonders and virtues. I shall divide them into two kinds, assigning some to the land and others to the waters. The land has mountains, promontories, valleys, plains, meadows, roads, woods, groves and forests; the waters have bays, harbours, rivers, lakes, marshes, pools, ditches and springs.

units.la: Xx tes, Promontoria, Valles, Campos, Prata, Vias, Silvas, Lucos, Nemora; Aquæ alias, ut Sinus, Portus, Flumina, Lacus, Paludes, Stagna, Fossas, Fontes. Aquas.
units.tr: Mountains, promontories, valleys, plains, meadows, roads, woods, groves and glades; and of the waters, bays, harbours, rivers, lakes, marshes, pools, ditches and springs.

units.la: Montes primum dabo. Inter eos principem obtinent locum Alpes, quas Galliæ quis (Celticos Montes) nominat Procopius lib. i. Rer. Gothicar.) an Germaniæ, vel Italiæ adscribat, parum refert: sunt certe Montes, qui Italiam hodie ab Gallia Germaniaque, procul tuo, tanquam nativo muro, separant. Alpes peculiari libello descripsit docte Iosias Simlerus, quem in compendium traham, adscriptis paucis, quæ illum fugerunt.
units.tr: I shall deal with the mountains first. Among them the Alps hold the chief place. Whether one assigns them to Gaul (which Procopius, in book 1 of his Gothic War, calls the Celtic Mountains), or to Germany or to Italy, matters little. They are certainly mountains which today separate Italy from Gaul and Germany, like a natural wall. Josias Simler has described the Alps learnedly in a separate little book, and I shall condense it, adding a few points that he missed.

units.la: Nomen Alpibus datum censet Festus ab Candore, Sabini enim Alpum dixere, inquit, quod postea Latini Album. Scribit ad Virg. Georgic. Iunius Philargyrius, altos Montes Gallorum Alpes vocari. Inuotus etiam clarius Alpium nomen vult esse Gallicum: Alpes, aic, proprie Montes sunt Gallia, de quibus Virgilius, Aerias Alpes: & dicendo Aerias, verbum expressit a verbo. Nam Gallorum lingua Alpes Montes alti vocantur. Hæ sunt enim, quæ Italiæ Murorum vicem exhibent. Agnoscit hodie nomen Alpium Idioma Germanicum: cui tamen non id, quod notat Iunius Philargyrius & Isidorus significat. Alp enim & Alpen Germanis Montes vocantur passim, in quibus fœnum non secatur, neque hibernos usus colligitur: sed in quos Boves aliaque Armenta pascendi tantum gratia mittuntur: ut zu Alp faren, nihil aliud sit, quam Armenta in pascua montana ducere, in quibus plerumque ad summum ternis mensibus æstivis agunt. Accedit, quod & nunc multis in locis hos Montes Alben Germani nuncupent.
units.tr: Festus thinks the Alps got their name from their whiteness: the Sabines, he says, called them Alpes, which the Latins later called Album (white). Junius Philargyrius, writing on Virgil's Georgics, says that the high mountains of the Gauls are called Alps. Another author holds even more clearly that the name Alps is Gallic: "Alps," he says, "are properly the mountains of Gaul, of which Virgil speaks as 'the airy Alps'; and by saying 'airy' he rendered the name in a word." For in the Gallic language the Alps are called high mountains. These are the ones which serve Italy as walls. The German language today also recognises the name Alps, but not in the sense given by Junius Philargyrius and Isidore. For Alp and Alpen are commonly used by the Germans of mountains where hay is not cut and winter fodder is not gathered, but to which oxen and other herds are sent only for grazing; so that "zu Alp faren" means nothing else than to drive herds to mountain pastures, where they usually stay at most three summer months. Moreover, many Germans even now call these mountains Alben in many places.

units.la: Notant Græci, & inter eos Stephanus, Veteres non tantum Ἄλπεις vel Ἄλπις, vel Ἄλπια ἐρπ dixisse, Ἀλπ̀ ἕ π, sed & Ἄλβια, Ἀλπ̀ ἕ β. Scribit etiam Strabo lib. iv, τὰ Ἄλπια olim vocata fuisse Ἄλβια, & apud Iapodes Montem, qui Alpium extremus est, Ἄλβιον dici, quod eousque Alpes se extendant: quum item Ligurum alii sint Ingauni, alii Intemelii; contentaneum fuisse, eorum Colonias maritimas, alteram Ἄλβιον Ὑγμιλιον, quasi Ἄλπιον; alteram concilius aliquanto Ἀλβιγγαύιον appellari. Ὀλβία sunt Phavorino; Σάλμει Lycophroni, ut sentit Interpres eius Iacius. Alpis singulari numero est apud Ovidium iii de Arte Amandi, Lucanum de Bello Pharsalico, Iuvenalem Sat. ix, Sidonium non uno loco, lib. v Epist. xvi, Carmine ii, ix & xvi; Priscianum lib. vii, Antoninum, & in Itineraria Tabula. Ἀλπ apud Dionysium Afrum.
units.tr: The Greeks note, and among them Stephanus, that the ancients said not only Ἄλπεις, Ἄλπις or Ἄλπια [Alpes, Alpis, Alpia], but also Ἄλβια and Ἄλβεις [Albia, Albeis]. Strabo, in book 4, writes that the Alpia were formerly called Albia, and that among the Iapodes the mountain which is the furthest extremity of the Alps is called Ἄλβιον [Albion], because the Alps extend that far. Likewise, since some of the Ligurians are Ingauni and others Intemelii, it is fitting that one of their maritime colonies should be called Ἄλβιον Ὑγμίλιον [Albion Hygmilion], as if Ἄλπιον, and another, somewhat further inland, Ἀλβιγγαύιον [Albingauion]. Ὀλβία [Olbia] occurs in Phavorinus, and Σάλμει [Salmei] in Lycophron, as his interpreter Iacius thinks. The singular Alpis is found in Ovid's Ars Amatoria book 3, in Lucan's Pharsalia, in Juvenal's Satire 9, in Sidonius in several places (Epistles book 5, letter 16; poems 2, 9 and 16), in Priscian book 7, in Antoninus, and in the Itinerary Table. Ἀλπ [Alp] occurs in Dionysius Afer.

units.la: Alpium Nomen Polybius, Strabo, Plinius. Ptolemæus, Herodianus, & alii, his solum Montibus tribuerunt, qui Italiam ab Gallia Germaniaque dividunt. Mela Alpes in Thraciam usque extendit. Meminerunt Tacitus & Sex. Rufus Alpium Pannoniarum. Certe, si quis rem bene expendar, Alpes ad Mare Ligusticum oriri per Allobrogas, Helvetios, Rhæatos, Vindelicos, Noricos, Carnos, Illurios, perpetuari fere videntur in Servium usque, ubi in duo scissa brachia, uno per Thraciam procurrentes ad Pontum Euxinum; altero per Macedoniam ad Actium Promontorium hinc tuntur. Et hæc est causa, quod alia ab aliis statuantur Alpium Longitudo, ut etiam Latitudo. Variorum, ut Cælii, Imaginis, Cornelii Nepotis & Livii sententias commemorat Plinius lib. iii. cap. xix, in morbo tamen ibi desperatione cubans. Consulendi & Polybius lib. ii. Strabo lib. iv, aliique. Hoc obiter sciendum Alpium nomine omnes fere Minores intelligi Montes, qui prope Alpes hinc inde surgunt: hinc Salyum Montes Alpes appellarunt Veteres, ut Polybius, qui lib. ii scribit, τῶν τῶν Ἄλπεων ... Μακεδονίας. Sic Strabo etiam lib. iv eorundem Salyum Montes Alpes nuncupat. Quin & Pyrenæi Montes Alpes dicti Ausonio ad Paulinum suum scribenti, Epistola xxv. Tristis, egens, deserta colat, tacitusque peregrret Alpinis connexa jugis.
units.tr: Polybius, Strabo and Pliny use the name Alps; Ptolemy, Herodian and others applied it only to those mountains which divide Italy from Gaul and Germany. Mela extends the Alps as far as Thrace. Tacitus and Sextus Rufus mention the Alps of Pannonia. Certainly, if one weighs the matter carefully, the Alps seem to rise by the Ligurian Sea, pass through the Allobroges, Helvetii, Raetians, Vindelici, Norici, Carni and Illyrians, and to continue almost to Servia, where they split into two arms: one runs through Thrace to the Black Sea, the other through Macedonia to Cape Actium. This is why different authorities set different lengths, and also different breadths, for the Alps. Pliny, in book 3, chapter 19, recalls the opinions of various writers, such as Caelius, Imago, Cornelius Nepos and Livy, though he himself is there lying sick in despair. Polybius, book 2, and Strabo, book 4, should also be consulted. It should be noted in passing that under the name of the Alps nearly all the lesser mountains rising near them on either side are understood. Hence the ancients called the mountains of the Salyes Alps, as Polybius does in book 2, where he writes of the Alps ... of Macedonia. Likewise Strabo, in book 4, calls the mountains of the same Salyes Alps. Indeed the Pyrenees too were called Alps by Ausonius, writing to his Paulinus in Epistle 25: "Let him, sad and needy, dwell in the deserts and wander in silence, among ridges joined in Alpine chains."

units.la: id est Montibus Pyrenæis. Sic eidem Epistola xxiii, ad eundem Paulinum: Nunc tibi trans Alpes & marmoream Pyrenen Cæsarea Augusta domus est.
units.tr: That is, the Pyrenean mountains. So in the same author's Epistle 23, to the same Paulinus: "Now beyond the Alps and the marble Pyrenees lies the house of Caesar Augusta for you."

units.la: Agellius item Alpinos Hispanos ex Catone dixit. Sic enim loquens de Catone scribit, Quum de Alpinis Hispanis scriberet, qui circa Iberum colunt, verba hæc posuit, &c. De Altitudine quoque Alpium serras reciprocari video. Affirmant plerique Alpes omnium Europæ Montium esse editissimas. Legendus Polybius apud Strabonem. Hoc certum, non parem ubique esse Altitudinem: qua incipiunt, humiliores sunt; qua finiuntur, mitescunt; intermediae plerisque locis altiores sunt. Solinus Vesulo Monti, unde Padus oritur, maximam tribuere videtur altitudinem, eumdum exsuperantissimum inter Alpium juga nominans. Alij Leponticas Alpes summas esse volunt, hoc argumento, quod inde in varias Orbis partes defluant Renus, Rodanus, Ticinus, Athesis, Vrsa, Arola, & alij. Quin & Rheti suas Alpes contendunt omnium esse altissimas.
units.tr: Gellius likewise called the Spanish people Alpini, following Cato. For, speaking of Cato, he writes: "When he was writing about the Spanish Alpini, who live around the Ebro, he put these words," and so on. I see that disputes also go back and forth about the height of the Alps. Most affirm that the Alps are the highest of all the mountains of Europe. Polybius should be read in Strabo. This much is certain: the height is not everywhere equal. Where they begin they are lower; where they end they subside; the middle parts are higher in most places. Solinus seems to give the greatest height to Mount Vesulus, where the Po rises, calling it the most eminent of the ridges of the Alps. Others want the Lepontine Alps to be the highest, on the argument that from there the Rhine, the Rhone, the Ticino, the Adige, the Ursa, the Arola and others flow down into different parts of the world. Indeed the Rhaetians too contend that their Alps are the highest of all.

units.la: Mentionem Alpium faciunt nulli non Auctores. Describunt graphice praeter alios Herodianus non uno loco, Silius Italicus lib. III Bellici Punici, Alciatus Commentarius ad Tacitum de Germania, Iosias Simleri peculiari, ut dixi, libello. Paucis dicam: Summa Alpium loca horrida tum expertus, & sterilia, nive inveterata & perpetua fere geluque rigentia. Media vidi pascua, & cultui apta: Radices Campoque ijs subiectos, praesertim versus Italiam, qua Calores Australiores ab ipsarum lateribus in planiora repercutiuntur, omnium rerum deprehendi fertilissimos.
units.tr: Every author mentions the Alps. Among others, Herodian describes them vividly in several places, as do Silius Italicus in book 3 of the Punic War, Alciati in his commentary on Tacitus' Germania, and Simler in his separate book, as I have said. To put it briefly: I have experienced that the highest places of the Alps are bristling and barren, with snow long-lying and almost perpetual, and stiff with frost. I saw middle pastures suited to cultivation. And at their foot, and in the plains beneath them, especially towards Italy, where the warmer southern heat is reflected from their flanks onto the flatter land, I found all kinds of produce most fertile.

units.la: Primum Alpes transisse cum armatis Copus memoriae produnt antiqui Scriptores Herculem; & ab eo nomen Graius Alpibus impositum: Secundum autem statuunt Hannibalem, Poenorum Ducem. Quae de Hercule scribuntur rejicit, & inter fabulas refert Livius, quae vero de Hannibale gravissimis refutat rationibus Polybius. Alpes multo ante Hannibalem, L. Tarquinio Prisco regnante, traducit Gallos, & Celtas & Cenomanos, cum exercitu, Livius. Quin censendum ipsam Locorum utrimque vicinam & humanam curiositatem, quae semper remotiora rimatur, haud dubie ante Tarquinij tempora Alpes pervias fecisse, jam tum scilicet, quum Gallia Italiaque cultae habitataeque essent. Narrat autem Polybius Itinera per Alpes in Italiam fuisse quatuor; unum per Ligures proxime Mare Tyrrhenum, alterum per Taurinos, quo usus fertur Hannibal; tertium per Salassos; quartum per Rhetos.
units.tr: Ancient writers record that Hercules was the first to cross the Alps with armed men, and that the Graian Alps were named after him. The second to do so, they say, was Hannibal, the Carthaginian general. Livy rejects what is written about Hercules and counts it among the fables, while Polybius refutes what is said of Hannibal with the weightiest arguments. Livy says that long before Hannibal, in the reign of Lucius Tarquinius Priscus, the Gauls, Celts and Cenomani led an army across the Alps. Indeed one must think that the close human curiosity of the peoples on either side, which always searches out what is more remote, undoubtedly made the Alps passable before Tarquin's time, since Gaul and Italy were already cultivated and inhabited by then. Polybius relates that there were four routes into Italy over the Alps: one through the Ligurians, close to the Tyrrhenian Sea; a second through the Taurini, which Hannibal is said to have used; a third through the Salassi; and a fourth through the Rhaetians.

units.la: Multa etiam Alpium Nomina in Veterum Monimentis occurrunt, quae indicant multas quoque Alpium Partes fuisse, per quas Itinera patuerunt. Commemorantur cum primis Maritimae, quae proximae sunt Mari Ligustico, inhabitatae ab Liguribus ut Dion scribit, Comatis, ideoque Ligurum, aut Ligusticae Alpes etiam nominatae. Meminerunt Dion, Tacitus, Ptolemaeus, Itineraria Tabula, alij. Ligustini Montes, Livio lib. XXXIV, Ligustici M. Terentio Varroni dicti. Addam Inscriptionem, quae ad San-Georgium, Delfinatus oppidum, visitur, in via Militari, Mediolanum ducente, prope Druentiam Amnem: Pio. Principi INVICTO RESTITVTORI ORBIS PROVIDENTISSIMO RETRO. PRINCIPVM OMNES FORTISSIMO NANIVS. RVF. KARVS. V. F. PROC. II PRAEFECTVS. ALPIVM. MARITIMAR DEVOTVS. NVMINI. MAIESTATIQ EIVS
units.tr: Many names of parts of the Alps also occur in ancient monuments, which show that there were many parts of the Alps through which routes lay open. Chief among them are the Maritime Alps, nearest the Ligurian Sea, inhabited by the Ligurians, who, as Dio writes, wore long hair (Comati), and therefore called also the Ligurian or Ligustic Alps. Dio, Tacitus, Ptolemy, the Itinerary Table and others mention them. The Ligustine Mountains are called Ligustici by Livy in book 34, and by Marcus Terentius Varro. I shall add an inscription, which is seen at San-Giorgio, a town of Dauphiné, on the military road leading to Milan, near the river Durance: "To Pius, the Prince, UNCONQUERED, most provident RESTORER OF THE WORLD ... Nanius Rufus Karus, procurator of the second class, prefect of the Maritime Alps, devoted to his divine power and majesty."

units.la: Ab his Principium Alpibus ponunt Veteres plerique: Recentiorum aliquibus ab Istria & Arsia fluvio, ubi Veteres finem faciebant, inchoare malentibus. Quum autem Alpes Maritima initio pertinerent partim ad Galliam Narbonensem, partim ad Italiam, Finium postea Rectores peculiarem statuerunt Provinciam, cuius Civitates recensentur in Notitia Provinciarum sub Viennensi IV in Alpibus (haec enim adduntur) Maritimi: Civitas Ebrodunensium. L'Archevesché d'Ambrun, Civitas Dinienfium. L'Evesché de Dine. Civitas Rigomagensium. Civitas Sollinicensium.
units.tr: Most of the ancients begin the Alps here. Some of the moderns prefer to begin them at the river Istria and the Arsia, where the ancients made the end. Since the Maritime Alps at first belonged partly to Gallia Narbonensis and partly to Italy, the later rulers of the provinces established a separate province, whose civitates are listed in the Notitia Provinciarum under Vienne, no. IV, "in the Alps" (for these words are added), "Maritimi": the civitas of the Ebrodunenses, now the Archbishopric of Embrun; the civitas of the Dinienses, now the Bishopric of Digne; the civitas of the Rigomagenses; the civitas of the Sollinicenses.

units.la: Civitas Sanicien sium, id est Sanici, L'Evefché de Senas.
units.tr: The city of the Sanicienses, that is, of Sanici. The Bishopric of Senas.

units.la: Civitas Glannatena. L'Evefché de Glandeves.
units.tr: The city of the Glannatenses. The Bishopric of Glandeves.

units.la: Civitas Cemeleventium.
units.tr: The city of the Cemelevenses.

units.la: Civitas Vencientium. L'Evefché de S. Paul de Vences.
units.tr: The city of the Vencienses. The Bishopric of St Paul de Vences.

units.la: De quibus omnibus plenius ego lib 111.cap.xxxix & sequenti. In Itinerario Antonini Iter describitur per Viam Aureliam ab Roma per Tuscia m & Alpes Maritimas, Arelatum usque. Maritimarum portio Acema, Mons apud Plinium, ex quo Amnis Varus profunditur, Galliam ab Italia distinguens. Vocatur hodie Monte Camelione. Augustinus enim Iustinianus Nebiæ Episcopus, qui Corticæ Descriptionem in Tabulam redegit, ut ipsemet inquit in Historia sua Genuensi, notat Varum hodie ex Monte Camelione oriri.
units.tr: I deal with all of these more fully in book III, chapters XXXIX and following. In Antoninus's Itinerary, a route is described along the Via Aurelia from Rome through Tuscany and the Maritime Alps as far as Arles. The part of the Maritime Alps called Acema is a mountain, according to Pliny, from which the river Var flows, marking the boundary between Gaul and Italy. Today it is called Monte Camelione. For Augustinus Iustinianus, Bishop of Nebbio, who drew up a map of Corsica, as he himself says in his Genoese history, notes that the Var today rises from Monte Camelione.

units.la: Maritimas Alpes sequuntur Cottiæ, sic dictæ, ut præter alios opinatur Paullus Diaconus de Gestis Langbardor. II, cap. XVI, ab Rege Cottio, de cuius contra Romanos gestis, ipsisque nominatis abeo Alpibus, legendi Suetonius in Nerone, Dio Cassius, Eutropius, Auctor de Viris Illustribus, Ammianus Marcellinus, qui Cottias elegantissime describit, & alij. Suetonio Cottiæ, Tacito Cottianæ appellantur: Κότιοι sunt Ptolemæo, apud quem male quidam Ἐξύλαι. Ammianus in summitate Cottiarum duos ponit Vertices; unum cognomine Martis, alterum Matronæ, cuius Vocabulum casus nobilis Feminæ dedit. Mirandum quum Regni Cottiani tot Auctores meminerint, autos fuisse nonnullos Alpes has Gothicas ab Gothis nominare: Erroris cautissam præbuerunt Librarij; quorum alij Cottias, alij Gothicas Alpes scripserunt. Iter per Alpes Cottias Mediolano ducit Arelatem Antoninus in Itinerario. Pars Cottiarum, lugumque nominatissimum, quod ex Pedemontio in Delphinatum euntibus est superandum, Mons est, qui Genebre dicitur: unde, nondum mihi liquet. Hac Hannibalem transisse putat in eius vita Acciaolus. Cremonis lugum vocat Alpium partem Livius, lib. XXI, qua transgressus creditur Hannibal. Ἀιοῦ & Ἀνίβα dicitur Appiano in Ibericis. Neque tamen hoc lugum duntaxat Cottias Alpes esse censendum est, sed alia quoque, quibus inter Maritimas & Graias Alpes in Galliam transitur. Ab Susa enim, de qua cap. XLIII lib. III, per Novaleciam & Ferreram ascenditur, Mons S. Dionysij, cuius summum La Polla vocatur; inde in Vallem Maurianensem, cuius eodem cap. XLIIII memini, vulgo Maurienne, descenditur Lunæ-burgum, ubi D. Dionysij Statua in Foro columnæ impositæ cernitur, & ab Gallis colitur: indeque Monti nomen impositum creditur. Quidam Cinesium, alij Cinerum Montem (Minorem, vernacule Mont Senis, appellant: Italice Strada Romana dicitur. Iter hodie usitatissimum ex Gallis Romam euntibus. Per hoc lugum scribunt quidam Karolum Magnum Exercitum direxisse contra Desiderium, Langbardorum Regem, in Italia tunc late dominantem. De Cinesio hoc non incommode exaudiri potest Iter illud, quod aperuisse se gloriatur apud Sallustium in Historiis Cn. Pompeius Magnus, cuius rei meminit etiam Appianus lib. I. de Bello Civili. Sunt & alia itinera inter Montem, qui vulgo Genebre & Alpes Maritimas, veluti per Valles Perosæ, Luserna, Angrogna, & Crucis, quarum Incolæ vulgo Christiani nominantur. Vesulus etiam Mons, cuius mentio apud Plinium & Solinum, ex quo Padus oritur, & ab altera parte paullo altiore iugo Druentia Minor, ad Alpes Cottianas pertinet; & Vetus adhuc nomen, Mont Vefo, dictus, retinet. Eundem Vesevum Virgilio dici II Georgic. innuit Servius ad eum Versum,
units.tr: The Maritime Alps are followed by the Cottian Alps, so called, as Paulus Diaconus thinks, among others, in his Deeds of the Lombards, book II, chapter XVI, after King Cottius. Readers wishing to learn about his wars against the Romans, and about the Alps named after him, should consult Suetonius in Nero, Dio Cassius, Eutropius, the author of On Illustrious Men, Ammianus Marcellinus, who describes the Cottian Alps most elegantly, and others. Suetonius calls them Cottiae, Tacitus Cottianae. Ptolemy's name for them is Κότιοι [Kotioi], though some wrongly write Ἐξύλαι [Exylai]. Ammianus places two peaks at the summit of the Cottian Alps: one named after Mars, the other after Matrona, whose name gave the title to a noble lady. It is remarkable that, although so many authors mention the kingdom of the Cottians, some have named these Alps the Gothic Alps after the Goths. Copyists were the most careful source of this error, since some wrote Cottias and others Gothicas Alpes. Antoninus, in his Itinerary, leads the route through the Cottian Alps from Milan to Arles. Part of the Cottian Alps, and the most famous pass, which must be crossed by those going from Piedmont into Dauphiné, is the mountain called Genèvre; why it is so called I do not yet know. Acciaiuoli thinks Hannibal crossed here in his life. Livy, book XXI, calls part of the Alps the Cremonis lugum, the pass by which Hannibal is believed to have crossed. Appian in the Iberian books calls it Αἰοῦ [Aiou] and Ἀννίβα [Hanniba]. Yet this pass should not be considered the only one of the Cottian Alps; there are others too, by which one passes into Gaul between the Maritime and Graian Alps. From Susa, which I discuss in book III, chapter XLIII, one climbs through Novalesa and Ferrera to Mont Saint-Denis, whose summit is called La Polla; from there one descends into the Maurienne valley, which I mentioned in the same chapter XLIIII, to Lunæburgum (Lanslebourg), where a statue of St Denis stands on a column in the square and is worshipped by the Gauls; and the mountain is believed to have taken its name from this. Some call it the Cinesian Mountain, others the Mount of Ashes; the lesser one, called in the vernacular Mont Cenis, is in Italian called the Strada Romana. It is the most frequently used route today for those going from Gaul to Rome. Some write that Charlemagne led his army through this pass against Desiderius, King of the Lombards, who then ruled widely in Italy. This route may not inappropriately be understood as the one that Gnaeus Pompey the Great boasted in Sallust's Histories that he had opened, a matter also mentioned by Appian in book I of the Civil Wars. There are also other routes between the mountain commonly called Genèvre and the Maritime Alps, such as through the valleys of Perosa, Luserna, Angrogna and Crucis, whose inhabitants are commonly called Christians. Mount Vesulus, mentioned by Pliny and Solinus, from which the Po rises, and a little further along, on a higher ridge, the Lesser Durance, also belong to the Cottian Alps, and it still keeps its old name, Mont Viso. Servius, on the line of Virgil in the second Georgic, suggests that the same mountain is called Vesevus:

units.la: Talem dives arat Capua & vicina Vesevo
units.tr: Such is the rich land that Capua ploughs, and the shores near Vesevus

units.la: Ora jugo:
units.tr: beneath its ridge.

units.la: Certum est, Vesevum Montem esse Campaniæ: ideoque Servium puto, vel vitio non carere; vel similitudine Vocis fallum & in animo habuisse Vesulum. Videndus hic lolias Simlerus Commentario de Alpibus, qui Vatorum, ut Spiegelij, Iovij, Aliati, Leandri Alberti, & Aventini de Cottiis Alpibus opiniones docte solideque refutat. Agathias & Procopius contra omnium Scriptorum Sententias statuunt etiam Alpes Cottias in Tuscia.
units.tr: It is certain that Vesevus is the mountain of Campania; so I think Servius is either at fault or, by a similarity of words, had Vesulus in mind. Here the learned Josias Simler, in his commentary on the Alps, should be consulted, who thoroughly and solidly refutes the opinions of various writers on the Cottian Alps, such as Spiegel, Giovio, Aliati, Leandro Alberti and Aventinus. Agathias and Procopius, against the views of all other writers, also place the Cottian Alps in Tuscany.

units.la: Post Cottias sunt Graiæ, positæ inter Centrones & Salassos. Plinius, Salassorum, inquit, Augusta Praetoria, iuxta geminas Alpium fauces, Graias atque Peninas. Hic Poenos, Graiis Herculem transisse memorant. Graiarum meminit Tacitus. Γραίαι Ptolemæo: Graius Mons appellatur Senecæ in Epistolis & Tacitus lib. IV Histor. Graias Salutis est apud Æmilium Probum in Vita Hannibalis. Describuntur apud Antoninum Itinera duo ab Vrbe Mediolanensi per Alpes Graias, unum quidem Viennam, alterum Argentoratum. Quod Viennam ducit exhibet etiam Itineraria Tabula, quæ medio fere itinere Mansionem notat In Alpe Graia. Notitia, cuius frequens a me facta est in Gallus mentio, inter Galliæ Provincias nominat quoque Viennensem Quintam Alpium Graiarum Pennarum; cuius Civitates Centronum, hoc est Tarantasia, Archevesché de Tarantaise & Vallensium, hoc est Octodurum, S. Maurice. In eadem Provincia ponitur ab Ammiano Aventicum. Caput quondam Helvetiorum Grais Alpibus Cæsarem, quum Bellum Civile spiraret, exercitum in Italiam duxisse, canit Petronius Arbiter, apud quem graphica Gratarum delineatio. Grata Alpes hodie sunt Mons S. Bernardi Minor, Monte Minori de S. Bernardo; Petit Bernard, ut affirmant probantque Iosias Simlerus. Ægidius Scudus, Ioannes Stumpfius, Leander Albertus, & alij: sic dictus ab Cænobio, quod D. Bernardo sacrum, quo loco Berginetrum ab Antonino locatur. Prope hoc lugum aliæ etiam sunt Alpes, quas Montem Cales & Cinisium Maiorem appellant: per utrasque ad Centrones itur, ab Taurinis, recto itinere, iuxta Sturam fluvium: de his dubitat Simlerus Graiisne an Cottius Alpibus adnumerari debeant. De Graiis Alpibus Errores Pauli Iovii, Raimundi Marliani, Cuspiniani refellit Iosias Simlerus, cuius ante memini.
units.tr: After the Cottian Alps come the Graian Alps, situated between the Centrones and the Salassi. Pliny says: "Augusta Praetoria of the Salassi, near the twin jaws of the Alps, the Graian and Pennine." Here men record that Hercules crossed the Graian Alps, as did the Carthaginians. Tacitus mentions the Graian Alps. Ptolemy calls them Γραῖαι [Graiai]; Seneca in his Letters and Tacitus in book IV of the Histories call the mountain the Graius Mons. The Graian Alps appear as Graias Salutis in Aemilius Probus's Life of Hannibal. Antoninus describes two routes from Milan through the Graian Alps: one to Vienne and the other to Strasbourg. The Itinerary Map, which also shows the route to Vienne, marks a stage almost midway, In Alpe Graia. The Notitia, which I have often cited in my discussion of the Gallic provinces, also names among the provinces of Gaul the Viennese Fifth of the Graian and Pennine Alps. Its cities are those of the Centrones, namely Tarantasia (Archbishopric of Tarentaise), and of the Vallenses, namely Octodurum, St-Maurice. Ammianus places Aventicum in the same province. Petronius Arbiter, in whom there is a vivid description of the Graian Alps, sings that Caesar, when civil war was brewing, led his army into Italy through the Graian Alps, the former capital of the Helvetii. Today the Graian Alps are the Little Mont St Bernard, Monte Minore di S. Bernardo, or Petit Bernard, as Josias Simler affirms and proves, together with Gilles Tschudi, Johannes Stumpf, Leandro Alberti and others. It is so called from the monastery dedicated to St Bernard, at the place which Antoninus locates as Bergintrum. Near this pass there are other Alps, which they call Mount Cales and Cinisium Maior; through both one goes to the Centrones by a direct route from Turin, beside the river Stura. Simler doubts whether these should be counted among the Graian or the Cottian Alps. Josias Simler refutes the errors about the Graian Alps of Paolo Giovio, Raimundo Marliani and Cuspinian, as I mentioned earlier.

units.la: Post Graias Pennarum Alpium succedit explicatio. Eas plerique Veterum dictas censent ab Hannibalis transitu, Pœnorum Ducis. Legendi Plinius in libris nat. histor. Ammianus Marcellinus lib. xv, Servius ad Æneidem Virgilianam. Livius lib. xxi a Pennino Deo nominatas innuit, quem in summo harum Alpium vertice Veragri colebant. Quidam Penninas appellatas arbitrantur, quasi Pinninas, ab celsi Cacuminis eminentia, quo ceteras Alpes superant. Pinna namque, Germanis Pinne, maxime quid elatum significat. Pennum, inquit Nonius ex Varrone, Antiqui dicebant Acutum. Penninas Alpes apud Salassos ostendunt Strabo & Plinius; & quum, supra Augustam Prætoriam duæ sint Viæ per Alpes, huc, quæ ad Orientem est, & ad Veragros ducit, Pennini nomen tribuuntur. Livius etiam, ubi Pennum sit, non obscure monstrat libro a me indicato, Veragros eius lugi Incolas nominans: ubi vero sint Veragri, alibi ex Cæsare patebit. Iter ab Mediolano per Alpes Penninas Magonti-acum ducit Antoninus, Summum ibi Pennınum edens. Pennınum Montem multi superioris & nostræ ætatis Scriptores Montem Iovis vocant. Vulgo, ut Ægidius Scudus, Iosias Simlerus, Stumpfius, Leander & alii docent, Mons S. Bernardi Maior dicitur; Monte Maiore de S. Bernardo, Grand Bernard, Groß S. Bernhardsberg. Pintzgewinterpretatur Lazius. Meridiem magis versus locant Pennınas Iovius & Alciatus; ille, ubi Mons Cinelius, hic ubi Druentia: sed utrumque refutat Simlerus. Vestigium antiqui nominis apud Salassos manet. Vallis enim, quæ Augusta Prætoria ad Pennınum ducit, Incolis Pelinna nuncupatur. Eam hodie Vallesiam Vallem opinatur esse Beatus Rhenanus: sed situs vix patitur. Per Pennınas has existimat Luitprandus Ticinensis Hannibalem in Italiam venisse, scribens Arnulphum Imperatorem ex Italia domum reversum per Hannibalis viam, quam Bardum dicunt & Montem Iovis. Scribit & Iovius apud Parrum Litteras Cotibus insculptas ostendi; monimentum Hannibalis, qui hac Alpes traiecerit. Est autem Bardum Vicus inter Eporediam & Augustam Salassorum, ubi Vallis arctissime coit, & fere clauditur: Germani vocant Im hart. Quum igitur hic Monimenta Hannibalis ostendantur, & gravissimi tamen Auctores Pœnum alia via transisse in Italiam tradant, ut antea docui, censendum est, totum eius Exercitum in plura agmina divisum pluribus locis traiecisse. Ptolemæus nonnullas alpes diversas à Pennino describit; eæque iuxta ipsius sententiam Rhetiam ab Italia separant, positæque sunt inter Rheticas Alpes & Octam Montem, ad fines Iuvavi flumine. Alpes illas Aventinus dictas ait a Pennone, Noricorum Rege: Alpes etiam Botas nominans, addensque ab eodem nuncupatum Pennınum Montem, unde oriuntur Athesis & Renus, quem vulgo Vennusticum dicunt. Describit autem Alpes illas his verbis: Vindelicia, quam nunc Rotariam nominamus, claudit ab Austro perpetuis Montium iugis, & hoc dorsum à Lyco ad Oenum pertinet. Quod amplius, si am fractus sequeris, centum & viginti millia passuum percurris. Quod si hinc quinquaginta demseris, reliquum est rectis itineris intervallum. Alpes à Ptolemæo Pennınæ nuncupantur, sicut celsissimæ undique præruptæ & abscissæ rupes. Cacumina perpetua nive. rive albicant, longe, late, ad quadragesimum & amplius lapidem à peritis discernuntur. Alpium, quas Aventinus describit, Summa Iuga ab nostris, inquit Simlerus, nominantur, de Arlberg oder Albeln; item Venustius Mons, Vinstermunts, atque inter Lycum & Oenum Montes ipsi longe procurrunt, & Vallem efficiunt, quae Intal a nostris vocatur. Hanc arbitratur idem Simlerus esse Peninam Vallem, quae regebatur à Prolegato Rhetiae & Vindelicia, ut habet Inscriptio, quae Florani visitur in agro Veronensi:
units.tr: After the Graian Alps comes the account of the Pennine Alps. Most of the ancients think they were so named after Hannibal's crossing, the Carthaginian general. Read Pliny in his Natural History, Ammianus Marcellinus book XV, and Servius on Virgil's Aeneid. Livy, book XXI, hints that they were named after the Pennine God, whom the Veragri worshipped on the highest peak of these Alps. Some think the Pennine Alps were so called as if they were Pinnine, from the towering height of the lofty peak by which they surpass the other Alps. For pinna, in German Pinne, signifies anything especially high. Nonius, quoting Varro, says: "The ancients called pennum the sharp point." Strabo and Pliny show the Pennine Alps among the Salassi; and since there are two roads through the Alps above Augusta Praetoria, the one that lies to the east and leads to the Veragri is given the name Pennine. Livy also clearly shows, in the book I have cited, where the Pennine peak is, naming the Veragri as the inhabitants of that ridge; where the Veragri themselves are will be made clear elsewhere from Caesar. Antoninus leads the route from Milan through the Pennine Alps to Mágontiacum, giving the summit Penninum there. Many writers of earlier and our own time call the Pennine Mountain the Mons Iovis. Commonly, as Gilles Tschudi, Josias Simler, Stumpf, Leandro and others teach, it is called the Great Mont St Bernard; Monte Maggiore di S. Bernardo, Grand Bernard, Groß S. Bernhardsberg. Lazius interprets it as Pintzgau. Giovio and Alciati place the Pennine Alps further toward the south: the former where Mount Cinelius is, the latter where the Durance is; but Simler refutes both. A trace of the ancient name remains among the Salassi. For the valley that leads from Augusta Praetoria to the Pennine Alps is called Pelinna by the inhabitants. Beatus Rhenanus thinks this is today the Valais, but its position hardly allows it. Luitprand of Pavia thinks Hannibal came into Italy through these Pennine Alps, writing that the Emperor Arnulf, returning home from Italy, went by Hannibal's route, which they call the Bardus and the Mons Iovis. Giovio also writes, citing Parrus, that letters carved in the rocks are shown there, a monument to Hannibal, who crossed these Alps. The Bardus is a village between Ivrea and Aosta, the town of the Salassi, where the valley narrows sharply and is almost closed off; the Germans call it Im Hart. Since monuments of Hannibal are shown here, and yet very weighty authors record that the Carthaginian crossed into Italy by another route, as I taught earlier, it must be held that his whole army, divided into several columns, crossed at several places. Ptolemy describes some Alps distinct from the Pennine; according to him these separate Rhaetia from Italy, and they lie between the Rhaetian Alps and Mount Octa, at the boundaries of the river Iuvavus. Aventinus says these Alps were named after Pennon, King of the Norici, and he calls them the Botae Alps, adding that the Pennine Mountain from which the Adige and the Rhine arise was named after the same man, which they commonly call Vennusticum. He describes these Alps in these words: "Vindelicia, which we now call Rotaria, is enclosed on the south by unbroken mountain ridges, and this spine extends from the Lycus to the Oenus. If you follow its bends, you will cover a hundred and twenty thousand paces more; if you take away fifty thousand from this, what remains is the straight distance of the journey. Ptolemy calls these the Pennine Alps, as they are very lofty, everywhere steep and sheer cliffs. Their summits gleam with perpetual snow, and are distinguished by experts from far, wide, and at forty miles and more." The highest ridges of the Alps that Aventinus describes are called by our people, says Simler, the Arlberg or Albeln; likewise the Venustian Mountain, the Vinstermunts; and between the Lycus and the Oenus the mountains themselves stretch far forward and form a valley, which our people call the Intal. Simler thinks this is the Pennine Valley, which was governed by the Propraetor of Rhaetia and Vindelicia, as the inscription says, which is seen at Verona's countryside near Florano:

units.la: Sequi videntur Alpes Summa, quarum meminit Caesar; scribens Nantuates, Veragros, Sedunosque ab finibus Allobrogum, Lacu Lemano & Flumine Rodano ad Summas Alpes pertinere. Glareanus Summas Alpes locat, ubi in omnes mundi plagas Flumina eximia evomuntur, & originem habent, qualia sunt Ticinus, Tosa & Madia, qui ad Meridiem; Rodanus, qui ad Occasum; Arola & Vrsa, qui ad Septemtrionem; Renus, qui duobus fontibus ad Ortum fluunt. Glareano suffragantur Scudus, Stumphus, Leander. Rhenanus Summarum Alpium appellatione designari putat Penninas, hoc est partem illarum hoc nomine donari. Alciatus Summas Alpes ait ab Caesare nominari, quae sunt inter Sedunos & Veragros, ubi nunc Octodurus est pagus: idem adfirmant Raimundus Marlianus, Iovius, Cuspinianus, aliique plures. Iofias Simlerus arbitratur nomen Summi apud Caesarem non poni, ut aliquae Alpes illo quasi proprio titulo discernantur ab reliquis Alpibus, sed esse nomen Appellativum, ut Grammatici vocant, & idem esse atque τὰ ἄκρα τῶν Ἀλπέων, vel Alpium Cacumina, ut Caesari dicuntur. Eum omnino vide. Ego Simlero subiicibo: eaque notione accipiendam censeo Antonini Alpem Summam in Itinere, quod Roma per Alpes Maritimas ducit Arelatum; uti etiam alibi vocantur Summus Peninus & Summus Pyrenaeus.
units.tr: The Summae Alpes seem to be the ones Caesar mentions, when he writes that the Nantuates, Veragri and Sedunni lie from the territory of the Allobroges, Lake Geneva and the river Rhone, up to the Summae Alpes. Glareanus places the Summae Alpes where great rivers well up and have their sources flowing out in every quarter of the world: the Ticinus, Tosa and Madia, which flow south; the Rhone, which flows west; the Arola and Ursa, which flow north; and the Rhine, which flows east from two sources. Scudus, Stumpf and Leander support Glareanus. Rhenanus thinks that the name Summae Alpes designates the Penninae, that is, that part of the Alps was given this name. Alciatus says that Caesar calls Summae Alpes those lying between the Sedunni and the Veragri, where the village of Octodurus now stands. Raimundus Marlianus, Jovius, Cuspinianus and many others affirm the same. Josias Simler holds that Summus is not used by Caesar as a proper title distinguishing some Alps from the rest, but is an appellative, as the grammarians call it, meaning the same as τὰ ἄκρα τῶν Ἀλπέων [the summits of the Alps], or the peaks of the Alps, as they are called by Caesar. You should see him in full. I add to Simler that I think the Alpes Summa in Antoninus's Itinerary, which runs from Rome through the Maritime Alps to Arelate, should be understood in this sense; in the same way, Summus Peninus and Summus Pyrenaeus are also so named elsewhere.

units.la: Lepontias Alpes, quarum Antiqui Scriptores meminerunt, esse, non est dubium, omnes Alpes ab Reni fontibus ad Rodani usque scaturiginem, ubi hodie Levantina Brennaeque Vallis, quae Palensa dicitur, Incolae, ad quos Grisaltus & Lucumonis Mons, Crispalt & Luckmanier altera parte pertinent. Certe vestigium adhuc ibi manet antiqui nominis. Vallis enim, per quam Ticinus delabitur, Levantina ab Italis, quasi dicas Lepontina, nominatur: Adcolae vocant Livner tal vel Leverntner tal. Mons altissimus, per quem ab Uranis Helvetiis in Italiam traicitur, Gothardi Mons dicitur. Consentiunt hic aetaris nostrae doctissimi viri. Iovius has Minores Lepontias vocat, ad differentiam Alpium, quibus ab Lario Lacu per Clavennam Curiam Rhaetorum iter, quas Lepontias Maiores nominat. Alciatus Lepontias statuit in Suitensibus, qua Claronam ex Bilitonis Castro recta tenditur.
units.tr: There is no doubt that the Lepontian Alps, which ancient writers mention, are all the Alps from the sources of the Rhine to the spring of the Rhone, where today the Levantine Valley and the Valley of Bregaglia (called Palensa) lie, with the inhabitants of Grisons, and Mount Lukmanier and the Crispalt pass on the other side. Certainly a trace of the ancient name still remains there. For the valley through which the Ticinus flows is called Levantina by the Italians, as if you said Lepontina; the locals call it Livner Tal or Leverntner Tal. The highest mountain, across which one passes from the Helvetian Uri into Italy, is called Mount Gotthard. The most learned men of our age agree on this. Jovius calls these the Lesser Lepontian Alps, to distinguish them from those Alps over which the road runs from Lake Como through Chiavenna to the Rhaetian Chur, which he calls the Greater Lepontian Alps. Alciatus places the Lepontian Alps among the Suitenses, where the road runs straight from the castle of Bilitio to Claro.

units.la: Alpes Rhetica me vocant. Ad Rhetos pertinent Alpes ab Como Veronam usque; Rheti enim, inquit Strabo, ad Italiam spectant supra Comum & Veronam, Iugorum Rhaeticorum mentio apud Tacitum & Plinium. Plurima autem sunt Rhaeticarum Alpium iuga. Adulas Mons principem inter eas tenet locum: Rhetis Calmen de Olcello, Germanis Der Vogel, ut Simlerus & Scudus notant; utque alii, Mons S. Bernardini, per quem ab Rhetis Bellinzonam itur. Ἀδούλα Straboni, qui Rhenum inde deducit, & Ptolemaeo. Bralium vocat Simplicitas vernacula, ut ait apud Simlerum Alciatus; qui, quod Strabonem corruptum censens pro Adula reponendum putat Adam, truitra est. Graias hodie appellari scribit Iovius in Lari Lacus descriptione. Adula Adule proximus est Speluga (celebris Vici est nomen) Mons: Rheti Calmen del Orso, Germani den Drschler und den Splüger- berg vocant. Rhetico Germaniæ Mons, inter altissimos à Pomponio Mela, lib. iii. numeratus: Scudus Prettigou- werberg appellat, qui in Helvetia est. De eo sic in Commentariis ad Taciti Germaniam Andreas Althamerus: Rhetico Mons apud Pomponium Melam est Iugum illud Rhetia Prima, inter fines Curiensium & Vallesianorum, Helvetiis imminens; cui adhærens Vallis vetustî nominis reliquias servat: Vulgo enim Braetigou (Viuum habens Ienatium) id est, Rhetorum Ager, Pagus, aut Vallis pro Rhetiacone appellatur. Puto insuper Pomponium Braetingaou ad Romanam Linguam figuram in Rhæticonem deflexisse. Dicitur præterea Vallis Montatum ab Comitibus de Sonnebergo, quibus paret. Hæc Althamerus, qui de variis Rhæticarum Alpium nominibus sic pergit: Ubi incipiunt, Grisones Graubündten/ Engedini, & Helvetica Montana, das Schwartzer gebürg/ zum Einsiedeln , id est, ad Anachoritas, Montes S. Bernhardi, S. Gothardi der Gothart , Sprulus, S. Nicolai, ubi desinunt, Tridentina Alpus das Trientisch gepürg , nuncupantur: ac juxta Adiolarum diversitatem diversa invenerunt vocabula. Varia per Rhæticas Alpes ducuntur Itinera apud Antoninum, de quibus in mea Rhætia.
units.tr: The Rhaetian Alps call me. The Alps from Como to Verona belong to the Rhaetians; for the Rhaetians, says Strabo, face Italy above Como and Verona. There is mention of the Rhaetian ridges in Tacitus and Pliny. Many ridges belong to the Rhaetian Alps. Mount Adula holds the chief place among them: the Rhaetians call it Calmen de Olcello, the Germans Der Vogel, as Simler and Scudus note; and others call it Mount St. Bernardino, across which one goes from the Rhaetians to Bellinzona. Strabo calls it Ἀδούλα [Adoula], and so does Ptolemy, who derives the Rhine from it. The local simple people call it Bralium, as Alciatus says, according to Simler; he thinks Strabo is corrupt and that Adam should be put in place of Adula, but he is wrong. Jovius, in his description of Lake Como, writes that it is now called Graias. Next to Adula is Mount Spluga (the name of a well-known village), which the Rhaetians call Calmen del Orso, and the Germans call den Drschler und den Splügerberg. The Rhetico mountain of Germany, counted by Pomponius Mela (book iii) among the highest, Scudus calls Prettigauwerberg, and it is in Helvetia. On it Andreas Althamer writes thus in his commentary on Tacitus's Germania: "The Rhetico mountain in Pomponius Mela is that ridge of Rhaetia Prima, between the territories of the Curians and the Vallesians, overhanging the Helvetians; the valley adjoining it preserves a remnant of the old name. For it is commonly called Braetigou (having a living Ienatium), that is, the land, district or valley of the Rhaetians, in place of Rhaetiacon. I suppose moreover that Pomponius bent the figure into Rhaeticon in the Roman language, from Braetingaou. Besides, the valley is called Montatum by the Counts of Sonneberg, whom it obeys." So Althamer. He goes on about the various names of the Rhaetian Alps thus: "Where they begin, the Grisons (Graubünden) and the Engadine, and the Helvetian mountains, called das Schwartzer Gebürg and Zum Einsiedeln, that is, to the anchorites, the mountains of St. Bernard, St. Gotthard (der Gothart), Spluga, and St. Nicholas, where they end, are called the Tridentine Alps (das Trientisch Gepürg). And according to the diversity of the Adiolae they have found diverse names." Various roads through the Rhaetian Alps are given in Antoninus, which I treat in my Rhaetia.

units.la: Postremo loco sunt (si quæ Alpes Italiam contingunt, consideremus) Iulia & Carnica. Iulys, quarum meminit Mela, nomen ab Iulio Cæsare videtur impositum. Nam, ut Sex. Rufus scribit, Iulio & Octaviano Imp. per has Alpes iter est factum. Iulien Incolis hodie & Adcolis; quin & Zelte vel Zulien lingua & pronunciatione Tusca, Z pro I consonante. Positæ sunt inter Rhæticas & Carnicas; Venetorum Ditionibus incumbentes; unde etiam Ammianus libro xxxi. Venetas ab Antiquis dictas notat. Tarvisiam quoque Montes sunt apud Plinium lib. iii. cap. xviii. ab Tarvisanorum agris appellati. Meminere Iuliarum Tacitus lib. xix. & D. Hieronymus in Epitaphio Nepotiani. Mentionem facere videtur Livius, ubi Gallos per Taurinos Saltus Iuliasque Alpes transcenedisse, duce Bellovesio, scribit; sed reponenda apud eum ex sententia Magnorum Virorum Iuvia. Iuliarum pars Taurus apud Melam, in Episcopatu Salisburgensi; ubi hodie multa loca Thaurn vocantur, uti sunt Kar̃n thaurn/ Krumleck thaurn/ Rhadstatter thaurn/ & alia. Rhenanus tamen pro Tauro Taunum legendum scribit apud Pomponium & Tacitum: Taunus etiam præfertur in Codice Taciti, qui Venetiis excusus anno MDXII. Ego nihil muto. Memini namque, quum anno MDXXIV. mense Novembri, redux ex Italia, comitatus V. CL. Petro Brederodio, Montem hunc transcenderem cum aliis, tum Hospitem, qui Cauponam in summo ibi vertice exercebat, lugum illud, quod Radstadio, Salisburgensis Præsulis oppido, imminet, litteris omnibus Radstatter- Thaurn appellare. Transcendi autem non sine summo Vitæ periculo. Exterioribus enim Artubus (ut obiter hoc dicam) immenso frigore adstrictis, quum Interioribus Visceribus, quæ contra ex operosiore adscensu supra modum æstuabant, refocillandis gelidissimum haustem, avidius quam par erat, Fontem, aliquamdiu pro conclamato jacum subito stratus; sed adfuit ope sua clementissimus Deus.
units.tr: Lastly (if we consider which Alps border on Italy), there are the Julian and Carnic Alps. The Julian Alps, which Mela mentions, seem to have taken their name from Julius Caesar. For, as Sex. Rufus writes, the Emperors Julius and Octavian crossed through these Alps. Today the inhabitants and neighbours call them Iulien; and also Zelte or Zulien in the Tuscan language and pronunciation, with Z for consonant I. They are placed between the Rhaetian and Carnic Alps, bordering on the territories of Venice; hence Ammianus too, in book xxxi, notes that the Venetae were called Venetas by the ancients. Plinius (book iii, chapter xviii) mentions the Montes Tarvisiae too, named from the fields of the Tarvisians. Tacitus (book xix) and St. Jerome in the Epitaph of Nepotianus mention the Iuliae. Livy seems to mention them where he writes that the Gauls crossed through the Taurinian pass and the Julian Alps under the leadership of Bellovesus; but according to the opinion of great men, the reading there should be Iuvia. A part of the Julian Alps is the Taurus, in Mela, in the bishopric of Salzburg, where many places are today called Thaurn, such as Karnthaurn, Krumleckthaurn, Radstatterthaurn and others. Rhenanus, however, writes that in Pomponius and Tacitus one should read Taunus instead of Taurus; Taunus is also preferred in the manuscript of Tacitus printed at Venice in 1512. I change nothing. For I remember that in November 1524, returning from Italy and accompanied by the most illustrious Peter Brederode, I crossed this mountain, along with others and with a host who kept an inn at the very summit there. All the people call the ridge that overhangs Radstadt, a town of the Archbishop of Salzburg, the Radstatter Thaurn. I crossed it not without the greatest danger to life. For my outer limbs (to say this in passing) were gripped by immense cold, while my inner organs, which on the contrary were overheated by the more laborious ascent, I was refreshing with a very cold drink, drinking more eagerly than was right; I was for a while thought dead, having suddenly collapsed. But the most merciful God was present with his help.

units.la: Carnica Alpibus finem ponunt, ceteris minus arduæ, quæque faciles superari possunt. Nomen ab Carnis, qui hodie Krainer. Earum portio Mons Ocra; Ὀκρα Straboni lib. iv. & vii. & Ptolemæo, Alpium pars humillima, qua ad Carnos itur. Itinera quædam per Alpes has describit Antoninus ab Aquileia in varias Norici Urbes: quæ dare explicareque alius est loci. Tam Iulia quam Carnica Alpes etiam Norica audiunt, quod Noricum Germaniæ, Armis adquisitæ, Regio ijs adjaceat.
units.tr: The Carnic Alps, less steep than the others and easily crossed, mark the end of the Alps. They take their name from the Carni, who today are the Krainer. Part of them is Mount Ocra; Ὀκρα [Ocra] in Strabo (books iv and vii) and Ptolemy, the lowest part of the Alps, by which one goes to the Carni. Antoninus describes certain roads through these Alps from Aquileia into the various cities of Noricum; to give and explain these belongs to another place. Both the Julian and the Carnic Alps are also called Noric, because Noricum, a region of Germany won by arms, lies next to them.

units.la: Iam quo loco dictæ fuerint Alpes Atreetiana, mihi nondum liquet. Earum mentio in antiqua Inscriptione, quæ sic habet:
units.tr: Now, where the Alpes Atreetiana were so called, is not yet clear to me. They are mentioned in an ancient inscription, which reads thus:

units.la: Carnica. Quarum portio Ocra. Norica. Atrianæ. Quarumque partes Tauri. Venetas et Venetiana.
units.tr: Carnic. Of which part Ocra. Noric. Atrianae. And of which parts Tauri. Venetae and Venetiana.

units.la: T. APPÆO T. F. VEL ALPINIO. SECVNDO PROC. AVGVST. XX HERED PROC. ALP. ATRECTIANAR
units.tr: T. Appaeus, son of Titus, or Alpinius Secundus, procurator of Augustus for twenty years, heir to the procurator of the Alpine Atrectiani

units.la: PRÆF. VEHICVL. SVB. PRÆF CLASS. PRÆT. RAVENN. PR ALÆ. I AVG. THRAC. TRIB. COHI ALIÆ. BRITTON. PRÆF COH. IIII. GALLOR. PATRON COLON. FLAMINI. DIVOR OMNIVM. AVGVRI II. VIR. QVINQ. BIS OB MERITA EIVS
units.tr: Prefect of the vehicles, deputy prefect of the fleet at Ravenna, prefect of the first Augustan Thracian ala, tribune of the cohort called Brittonum, prefect of the fourth cohort of Gauls, patron of the colony, flamen of all the deified emperors, augur, quinquennial duumvir twice, on account of his services.

units.la: Alpinas porro Gentes universim enumerat Inscriptio, quam ex Alpium Trophæo in Opus suum Naturalis Historiæ contulit Plinius lib. III. cap. XX. Initium eius hoc modo conceptum fuisse censendum est:
units.tr: The inscription that Pliny transferred into his Natural History, Book III, chapter 20, from the trophy of the Alps, enumerates the Alpine Peoples in general. We must suppose that its opening was worded as follows:

units.la: IMP. CAESARI. DIVI. F. AVGVSTO PONT. MAX. IMP. XIIII. TRIB. POT. XVII S. P. Q. R. QVOD. EIVS. DVCTV AVSPICIISQ GENTES. ALPINAE. OMNES, QVAE. A. MARI SVPERO. AD. INFERVM PERTINEBANT SVB IMPERIVM P. R. REDACTAE SVNT
units.tr: The Emperor Caesar, son of the deified Augustus, pontifex maximus, in his fourteenth year of imperium, in his seventeenth of tribunician power, the Senate and People of Rome, because under his leadership and auspices all the Alpine peoples, from the upper sea to the lower, were brought under the empire of the Roman people.

units.la: Sequebantur inde Gentes circiter quadraginta quinque: nam eas adsculptas fuisse, tatis patet ex subsequentibus Plinij verbis: licet alij sequnus sentiant, Inscriptionem ita ponentes, quasi non fuissent adiectæ. De singulis dicendum suis locis, cum in Italia, tum Germania: de nonnullis etiam dictum iam in Gallia libro superiore, de Nantuatibus, inquam. Medullis, Caturigibus, & aliis.
units.tr: After this came about forty-five peoples. That these were carved on the monument is clear from Pliny's following words, although others think otherwise, setting out the inscription as if nothing had been added. I shall discuss each in its place, both in Italy and in Germany. Some of them I have already discussed in the earlier book on Gaul, namely the Nantuates, Medulli, Caturiges and others.

units.la: Alpibus originem suam debent quatuor nobilissima Europæ Flumina, quæ innumeros pene Amnes secum in diversa Maria deferunt: Padus per Italiam in mare Hadriaticum defluens; Rhodanus per Galliam in Ligusticum; Rhenus, inter Germaniam & Galliam Fluitor, in Oceanum; postremus Danubius, (quem ex Alpibus oriri alibi dicam) longissimo curru Illyrici provincias emensus Euxinum intrat Pontum. Lacus habent infinitos, inter quos principis loci, qui in editissima Montis Cenisij planicie, ex vivis perennibusque purus scaturiris; in Campo summo, celsissimo, planissimo, cui nihil Montium vel Chivorum imminet.
