Nam non mirum est, alibi alios esse, ex nivibus pluviisque collectos. Fontes frigidos pariter & calidos, quibus Alpina Regio abundat, prætereo. In Alpibus, quæ perpetua rigent glacie, plurima pulcherrimaque Crystalla reperiuntur. Metallorum teraces esse, exploratum est: quur autem Fodinas Incolæ fieri nolint, docet Iohias Simlerus. Provenium ibidem scelcissime cum aliæ Arbores, tum Abietes, Pinastri, Piceæ: Abietes certe nonnunquam cxxx pedum invenirtur; commendari expetique solitæ non solum ob procertitatem, verum etiam ob Materiæ firmitatem. Non tantum Pascuas Herbas Pecoribus gratissimas, suppeditant (quid hic sit 3u Alpsfarcn/ alibi noto) sed & multa Plantarum genera, rara & non facile alibi obvia, passim ibi tele offerunt; partim ab Veteribus descripta, partim adhuc antiquo nomine, certaque descriptione destituta. Plerarum enumeratio est apud Conradum Gesnerum, Ioannem Fabricium, Benedictum Aretium & Iohiam Simlerum; apud quem & Animalium Alpinorum, Quadrupedumque & Avium est Catalogus diligenter concinnatus.
units.tr: To the Alps the four most noble rivers of Europe owe their origin; they carry with them almost countless streams into different seas: the Po, flowing through Italy into the Adriatic Sea; the Rhône through Gaul into the Ligurian Sea; the Rhine, a river running between Germany and Gaul, into the Ocean; and last, the Danube (which I shall say elsewhere rises in the Alps), which, after the longest course through the provinces of Illyricum, enters the Euxine Sea. The Alps have countless lakes, the chief of which, the one that gushes pure, perennial, living water on the very high plain of Mount Cenis, on the highest and flattest field, above which no mountain or peak rises. It is no wonder that others are elsewhere, gathered from snows and rains. I pass over the cold and warm springs with which the Alpine region abounds. In the Alps, which stay frozen in perpetual ice, very many and very beautiful crystals are found. That the Alps are full of metals is well known; why the inhabitants do not want mines dug is explained by Johann Simler. There grow there, most abundantly, both other trees and firs, pines and spruces; firs are certainly sometimes found 130 feet tall, and they have been commended and sought after not only for their height but also for the firmness of their timber. They supply not only pasture grasses most pleasing to cattle (what this is called in German, "Alpsfarcn", I note elsewhere), but also many kinds of plants, rare and not easily found elsewhere, which everywhere present themselves there in abundance; some have been described by the ancients, others still lack a certain description and retain their old name. A list of most of them is found in Conrad Gesner, Johann Fabricius, Benedict Aretius and Johann Simler; in Simler there is also a carefully compiled catalogue of Alpine animals, quadrupeds and birds.

units.la: Hæc de Alpibus quæ Italiam secundum Latitudinem ab Gallia Germaniaque separant: sequitur Apenninus, qui inter Superum Mare & Inferum excurrens, perpetuo ductu eamdem secundum Longitudinem secat in duo Latera. Sic dictus putatur, quod radices habeat sub Penino Hannibalis transitu: ejusque luga contingat media sua Latitudine: Nonnullis Apenninus, quasi à Poenis, quum, Hannibale Duce, in Italiam irrumperent, patefactus: Quidam ab Api, prisco Duce, qui totam Italiam devicit, dirivant. Apennina Ptolemaeo, & aliis; Apennon, Stephano. Scribit Polybius lib. iii. oriri hunc Montem paullo supra Inferum Mare ab Alpibus, moxque se magis ac magis ab illis disiungentem recto dorso in Superum Mare ferri, quasi ad Urbem Senam; inde rursus ad dextram se flectentem per mediam Italiam in Siculum Fretum discurrere. Notat Strabo lib. v, Montes Apennini, quum Arimini & Anconis loca contigerint, Iapygiae Latitudinem ab Mari ad Mare terminare: rursusque flexu totam Regionem in longum secare usque ad Picentes & Lucanos; nec multum ab Hadriatico distare Sinu; quum vero Lucanis adpropinquant ad alterum inclinari Mare: de hinc per Lucanos & Brutios tendere, seque ad Leucopetram, Agri Rhegini Promontorium, terminare. Apenninus Mons, inquit Plinius lib. iii. cap. v, Italiae amplissimus, perpetuo lugo ab Alpibus tendens ad Siculum Fretum. Ptolemaeus ait Apenninum ad Anconem in latus digredi, Hadriaticum Mare versus, idque pene contingere: ac deinde ad Garganum explicatum, hinc in meridiem conversum ad Leucopetram procurrere, Rhegioque Iulio finiri. Perpetuum sane Montis hujus lugum instar est Italiae Dorsi, quod elatum per mediam Regionem tensim incedens, tandem in duo Cornua diducitur, altero Siculum, altero Ionium Mare respiciens, ut Solinus & Mela tradiderunt. Lucanus lib. ii.
units.tr: So much for the Alps, which separate Italy by its breadth from Gaul and Germany. Next comes the Apennine, which runs between the Upper Sea and the Lower Sea and, in a continuous line, cuts the same land lengthwise into two sides. It is thought to be so named because its roots lie under Penninus, the passage of Hannibal, and its ridges touch the middle of its breadth. Some think the Apennine is named as if from the Carthaginians, since it was opened when they broke into Italy under Hannibal as leader; others derive it from Apis, an ancient leader who conquered all Italy. Ptolemy and others call it the Apennina; Stephanus, the Apennon. Polybius writes, in Book III, that this mountain rises a little above the Lower Sea from the Alps, and soon, separating itself more and more from them, runs with a straight ridge toward the Upper Sea, as far as the city of Siena; from there it turns again to the right and runs through the middle of Italy to the Strait of Sicily. Strabo, in Book V, notes that the Apennine mountains, when they reach the places of Rimini and Ancona, bound the breadth of Iapygia from sea to sea; then, bending again, they cut the whole region lengthwise as far as the Picentes and Lucani, and are not far from the Adriatic gulf; but when they approach the country of the Lucani they incline toward the other sea, and from there stretch through the Lucani and Bruttii and end at Leucopetra, the promontory of the Rhegian territory. "The Apennine mountain," says Pliny in Book III, chapter 5, "the greatest of Italy, stretching in one continuous ridge from the Alps to the Strait of Sicily." Ptolemy says that the Apennine branches off toward Ancona, toward the Adriatic Sea, and nearly touches it; then, extended as far as Garganus, it turns from there to the south and runs to Leucopetra, and ends at Julian Rhegium. The unbroken ridge of this mountain is truly like the back of Italy, which, raised up, runs gently through the middle of the region, and at last divides into two horns, one looking toward the Strait of Sicily, the other toward the Ionian Sea, as Solinus and Mela have handed down. Lucan, Book II:

units.la: Mons inter geminas medius se porrigit undas Inferni Superique Maris.
units.tr: "A mountain stretches out in the middle between the two twin waves, of the Lower Sea and the Upper Sea."

units.la: Longus porro dicitur Iuvenali Satyra i.
units.tr: It is called long by Juvenal in Satire I:

units.la: Sic, coelum longo subduximus Apennino.
units.tr: "Thus we have drawn the sky down by the long Apennine."

units.la: Longitudo Monti eadem, quae ipsi, quam secat, Italiae. Altitudo eadem fere, quae Alpibus. Silius Italicus:
units.tr: Its length is the same as that of Italy itself, which it cuts; its height is nearly the same as that of the Alps. Silius Italicus:

units.la: Alpibus aquatum tollens caput Apenninus.
units.tr: "The Apennine, lifting its head, watered, above the Alps."

units.la: Apenninus utrimque clarissima provomit in utrumque Mare Flumina: In Tyrrhenum quidem praeter eos, qui minorum gentium, Arnum, Tiberim, Liris, Vulturnum; in Hadriaticum autem Rubiconem, Tronto, Aternum, Aufidum, & alios.
units.tr: On both sides the Apennine pours out very famous rivers into both seas. Into the Tyrrhenian indeed, besides the smaller ones, the Arno, the Tiber, the Liris and the Volturnus; into the Adriatic the Rubicon, the Tronto, the Aterno, the Aufidus, and others.

units.la: Multos alios habet Italia Montes: vel qui Minores Apennini sunt Portiones & quaedam quasi Membra: vel quos idem, tanquam foecundus multorum Genitor, ex se hinc inde protendit; vel denique, quos haud procul ab se locatos radicibus eos suis contingens majestate quadam & superiore coniacentibus fastigio despicit. Eos, non omnes tamen, paucis indicabo, servato Regionum, in quis illi, ordine.
units.tr: Italy has many other mountains: some are parts and, as it were, limbs of the Apennine lesser ranges; others the same Apennine, like a fruitful father of many, stretches out from itself on this side and that; finally, others which, placed not far from it, touch it with their roots and look down from a certain majesty and superior height on those lying below. I shall point out these, though not all of them, briefly, in the order of the regions in which they lie.

units.la: Liguriae sunt Falista, Suimontium, Letus. Balista Livio lib. xli. Mons Liguriae: Valestra Leandro. Adjungit illi Livius non semel alterum, quem Suimontium vocat, qui & Suifmontium scribitur lib. xxxiiix: itidem Letum, cujus etiam mentio apud Valerium Maximum; Leandro L'Alpi del Peregrino.
units.tr: In Liguria there are the Falista, the Suimontium and the Letus. Livy, Book XLI, calls the Balista a mountain of Liguria; Leander, the Valestra. Livy also joins to it, more than once, another which he calls the Suimontium, also written Suifmontium, in Book XXXIIII; likewise the Letum, which is also mentioned by Valerius Maximus. Leander calls it L'Alpi del Peregrino.

units.la: Aemiliae praeter Zibium & Petram Pisoniam, Bardonis est Mons, qui nominatur apud Paullum Diaconum lib. v. & vi. Langbard. Histor. & Ottonem Frisingensem libro ii. de rebus gestis Friderici i. Pardonis scribitur, per P. Conrado à Lichtenau. Ab hac voce fluxit, quod non ignobilis Apennini pars in Saxonum Chronico (ut Reinechius tradit in suo de Familijs Syntagmate) dicatur das Parther Gebirge. Bardonis Apennini lugum Blondus esse conjicit inter Parmensem & Lucensem Agrum.
units.tr: In Emilia, besides the Zibium and the Petra Pisonia, there is the Bardo mountain, which is named by Paul the Deacon in Books V and VI of the Lombard History, and by Otto of Freising in Book II, on the deeds of Frederick I. Conrad of Lichtenau writes it Pardo. From this word it comes that a not unimportant part of the Apennine is called in the Saxon Chronicle (as Reinecke relates in his Syntagma on families) "das Parther Gebirge". Blondus conjectures that the ridge of the Bardo Apennine lies between the territory of Parma and that of Lucca.

units.la: Infubrorum cum Lucumone, Plontino, Iacere, Margotio & Brigantia (quae vulgaria & nota Collium Apennini Nomina) est, quem Sempronium Latini vocant; alij Scipionis: Sempronio, Italis: Simpler Vallesianis.
units.tr: Of the Infubri, with Lucumo, Plontinus, Iacer, Margotius and Brigantia (which are the common and well-known names of the hills of the Apennine), there is the one which the Latins call Sempronius, others Scipio's; the Italians call it Sempronio, the Valaisans Simpler.

units.la: Apud Cenomanos est Stella.
units.tr: Among the Cenomani there is the Stella.

units.la: Apud Venetos velin Marka Tarvisana cum Gemula & Vinda, Colles sunt Euganei, ab Euganeis, qui & Heneti, & postea Veneti, denominati; Lucano, Martiali, aliis Poetis decantati. Tarvisanos ibidem Montes habet Plinius lib. iii. cap. xviiii; ubi in Vulgatis Exemplaribus sunt Tanrisani. Est & Baldus, mons altissimus, Herbarum
units.tr: Among the Veneti, in the Marca Trevigiana, with Gemula and Vinda, there are the Euganean hills, named after the Euganei, who were also called Heneti and afterwards Veneti; they are celebrated by Lucan, Martial and other poets. Pliny, Book III, chapter 19, gives the Tarvisan mountains there; in the common texts they are called Tanrisani. There is also the Baldus, a very high mountain, abounding in a great supply of medicinal herbs; to fetch these for curing whatever diseases, herbalists have been accustomed to gather there from all parts of Europe.

units.la: {y} Vide Ptolemaeum. barum Medicinalium abundans copia; quibus ad sanandos quoscumque Morbos petendis Herbarij ex omnibus Europæ partibus eo confluere sunt solita.
units.tr: {y} See Ptolemy. ... abounding in medicinal herbs, to fetch which for curing whatever diseases, herbalists have been accustomed to gather there from all parts of Europe.

units.la: Apud Picenos præter Vitiorem & Furcas Pesc as Auximus est, ab Auximo, Picenorum Vrbe, & Cerus, unde cum Albula & Truento multi fluunt Amnes per Marrucinos, Præcutianos, Marsos.
units.tr: Among the Picentes, besides the Vitiorem and the Furcae Pescarenses, there is Auximum, named after Auximum, a city of the Picentes, and Cerus; from there, together with the Albula and the Truentum, many streams flow through the Marrucini, the Praecutiani and the Marsi.

units.la: In Etruria porro offerunt se cum alij, tum Cimimus, vel, ut alijs scribitur, Cyminus Livio Vibroque notus; nec non Virgilio lib.vii. Hi Soractis habent Arces Flaventaque Arva, Et Ciminj cum Monte Lacus, Lucosque Capenos;
units.tr: Elsewhere in Etruria there are other mountains, among them Cimimus, or, as others write it, Cyminus, known from Livy and Vibius. Virgil also mentions it in book 7: "Here are the citadels of Soracte and the golden fields, and the Ciminian mountain with its lake, and the Capenan groves."

units.la: Prope Viterbum est; vulgo, ut Leander notat, Monte Viterbo dictus: Soractes, Plinio lib. vii. Tuscia Mons apud Hirpos haud procul ab Via Flaminia, teste Servio: hodie, ut Leander aliique volunt, Monte di S. Silvestro, ab Romano Præsule, qui Constantini Principis iram veritus ibi aliquamdiu latitasse perhibetur. Erythræus Monte S. Trefio interpretatur. Notat ad Horatium Acron esse Apuliæ montem; Porphyrius, majore fide, Falisconum. Monstrat quasi digito Horatius amico suo Thaliarcho, sive in Agro suo Sabino, sive in Urbe Roma constitutus, quum inquit lib.1. Carminum, Ode ix. Vides, ut alta stet nive candidum Soracte.
units.tr: It lies near Viterbo and is commonly called, as Leander notes, Monte Viterbo. Soractes: Pliny, book 7, calls it "a Tuscan mountain near the Hirpi, not far from the Via Flaminia," according to Servius. Today, as Leander and others hold, it is Monte di S. Silvestro, named after a Roman prelate who is said to have hidden there for some time for fear of the anger of the emperor Constantine. Erythraeus identifies it with Monte S. Trefio. In his note on Horace, Acron says that it is a mountain of Apulia; Porphyrio, with greater authority, says that it belongs to the Falisci. Horace, when he writes in book 1 of the Odes, ode 9, "See how Soracte stands white with deep snow," seems to point it out with his finger to his friend Thaliarchus, whether the two were in his Sabine country or in the city of Rome.

units.la: Ad hunc Montem Hirpi, ut tradunt Veteres Scriptores, annuum faciebant sacrificium Apollini, idque operantes gesticulationibus religiosis exultabant, super ambustam lignorum struem, flammis parcentibus, ambulantes; & ob id perpetuo SC. Militiæ omniumque aliorum Munerum habebant vacationem. Hinc Virgilianus Aruns: Summe Deum Custos sancti Soractis Apollo, Quem primi colimus, cui pineus ardor acervo Pascitur, & medium freti pietate per ignem Cultores multa premimus vestigia prima.
units.tr: According to the ancient writers, the Hirpi used to offer an annual sacrifice to Apollo on this mountain. While performing it, they danced in religious gestures and walked over a heap of burning wood, with the flames sparing them; for this reason they had a perpetual exemption from military service and all other public duties. Hence Virgil's Arruns: "Highest god, Apollo, guardian of holy Soracte, whom we first worship, for whom the pine-wood heap burns and is fed, and we, trusting in our devotion, walk barefoot across the middle of the fire."

units.la: Eadem sunt apud Silium Italicum lib.v. Belli Pœnici, qui Soractis quoque meminit lib.vii. & viii. Strabo non Apollini, sed Dea Feroniæ Sacrum illud fieri solitum notat; Parcentes autem Flammas Varro non Pietati tribuit, sed Medicamento, quo Hirpi plantas tingebant. Fesculanos Montes habet etiam in Etruria Orosius, sic appellatos ab Fesculis, Tusciæ Urbe: Cortonenses ibidem sunt ad Septemtrionem Lacus Trasumeni, ab Cortona oppido.
units.tr: Silius Italicus has the same account in book 5 of the Punic War; he also mentions Soracte in books 7 and 8. Strabo notes that this sacrifice was customarily made not to Apollo but to the goddess Feronia. Varro does not attribute the sparing of the flames to devotion but to a medicine with which the Hirpi smeared their feet. Orosius also places the Fescennine mountains in Etruria, so called from Fescennia, a town of Tuscany. The Cortonenses are likewise there, north of Lake Trasimene, named after the town of Cortona.

units.la: In Latio, præter septem Urbis Romæ Montes, de quibus alibi, Albanus est, Scriptoribus omnibus, Græcis Latinisque, celeberrimus; ab Alba, cui imminet, dictus. Mons est præcelsus; longitudine se porrigens ad Artemisium; vertice perarduo & aspero, ut scribit Strabo. Fuit olim in eo Iovis Latialis Templum, ab L. Tarquinio Prisco, v Romanorum Rege, ædificari jussum, quo Latini aliique Fœderati quotannis ad Feriæ Latinas, accepturi Victerationem, conveniebant. Legendus omnino præter alios Dionysius Halic. lib. iv. Ejus Templi aliorumque Ædificiorum multa adhuc hodie ibi rudera. In hoc Monte, quum Romæ negaretur, ab Impp. triumphari solitum, memoriæ produnt Veteres Scriptores. Mons Cacubus in Sinum Caietanum usque porrigitur, ab Vini, quod ferat, generositate nominatissimus. Arboribus conteus est fructiferis multis. Vestinus Mons est Hygeno de Limitibus constituendis, circa Minturnas. Algidus xii. ab Vibe est lapide, uti numerat Eutropius lib. 1. ab Algido oppido, quod hodie Rocha del Papa. Obtelius in hoc monte Q. Minutius cos. liberatus legitur ab L. Quinctio Cincinnato Dictatore apud Rerum Romanarum Scriptores. Aventinum vocat Vibius Sequester Montem, in quo Præneste Civitas. Leprinus Mons, in quo Signia Coloniæ de eo Columella lib.x. Castilius Mons Tiburti apud eundem Vibium & Servium, qui cum Castelum vocari ait per corruptionem: hodie Castelli. Cerauvius etiam Montes Latij habet Halicarnassæus.
units.tr: In Latium, apart from the seven hills of the city of Rome, which are discussed elsewhere, the Alban mountain is most famous among all writers, Greek and Latin alike; it is named after Alba, which lies beneath it. It is a very lofty mountain, stretching out in length toward Artemisium, with a very steep and rugged summit, as Strabo writes. On it there once stood a temple of Jupiter Latiaris, which Tarquinius Priscus, the fifth king of the Romans, ordered to be built, and where the Latins and other allies used to gather every year for the Latin Festival, to receive their share of the sacrifice. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 4, among others, is well worth reading on this. Many ruins of that temple and of other buildings still survive there today. Ancient writers record that generals used to celebrate triumphs on this mountain when they were refused one at Rome. Mount Caecubus stretches down to the Gulf of Gaeta and is most famous for the excellence of the wine it produces; it is covered with many fruit trees. Vestinus is a mountain, according to Hyginus on fixing boundaries, near Minturnae. Algidus lies twelve miles from Veii, as Eutropius, book 1, counts it; from the town of Algidum, which today is Rocca del Papa. On this mountain, according to Roman historians, Q. Minucius, the consul, was rescued by the dictator L. Quinctius Cincinnatus. Vibius Sequester calls Aventinum a mountain on which the city of Praeneste stands. Leprinus is a mountain on which the colony of Signia stands, as Columella writes in book 10. Castilius is a mountain at Tibur, according to the same Vibius and Servius, who says it is called Castelum by corruption; today it is Castelli. Halicarnassus also mentions the Cerauvian mountains of Latium.

units.la: In Vmbria, quæ hodie Ducatus Spoletinus, præter Inginium, cujus meminit Strabo, Esubinum, Floridam, & alios; sunt, qui Ἠρασιδαι Halicarnassæo lib.i; Latinis forte Cormalis videtur Zonaras Καρίτας vocare. Crustumenses Montes ibidem, ex quibus Alba flumen præalto defluit alveo, ut Livius testatur. Fisicellum lugum illud Apennini Plinio dicitur, unde duobus erumpit Fontibus Nar Fluvius: hodie Monte Fiscello. Sequitur inde pars Apennini, quae Mons Victor, ubi Apenninus supra Castellum Arquatam altissimis cacuminibus effertur, ut adeo seipsum celsitudine videatur superare, id est, ut adhaerentia circumquaque juga cetera, quamquam editissima, longe vincat; ideoque & ex re nomen huic Culmini datum Mons Victor.
units.tr: In Umbria, which today is the Duchy of Spoleto, there are, besides Inginium, which Strabo mentions, Esubinum, Florida and others. Some call the Ἠρασιδαι [Erasidai] mountains, in book 1 of Halicarnassus; perhaps Zonaras calls them Καρίτας [Karitas], which the Latins perhaps call Cormalis. The Crustumine mountains are there too, from which the river Alba flows down in a very deep channel, as Livy attests. The ridge of the Apennines that Pliny calls Fisicellum is where the river Nar bursts out from two springs; today it is Monte Fiscello. Next follows that part of the Apennines which is called Mons Victor, where the Apennine rises above the town of Arquata with its very high peaks, so that it seems to surpass itself in height, that is, it far exceeds the other ridges that adjoin it on every side, though these are also very lofty; and so this summit has been given the name Mons Victor from the nature of the place.

units.la: Ad Campaniam Felicem pertinent Gaurus, Massicus, Falernus, alii. Gaurus prope Puteolos est. & Vulturnum fluvium, notantibus Juvenale, Servio, & Auctore de Viris Illustribus cap. xxvi; Strabone; Gaurani Montes Plinio in Nat. Histor. libris. Meminit praeter Livium, Ciceronem, Statium, Vibium, alios, aque Arnoldus Abbas in Slavorum historia. Gallicanus dicitur Plutarcho in Hannibale, unde Gallicanus Saltus Ciceroni pro L. Quinctio. Hodie Monte Gerro & Barbaro, uti censent, praeter Blondum & Leandrum, Fern. Lofredus, Franc. Lombard. & Scipio Mazella Neapolitanus, qui Libellum auxit Ioannis Elysii de Balneis. Ejus inter alia de hoc Monte sunt verba: Huius Montis pars Occidentalis Gaurus; Orientalis & Iuga eiusdem, Massicus; & Septentrionalis Falernus dicebatur. Quod ad Gaurum an is qui Γαύρος, apud Stobaeum de Morbis ex Heliodoro, Italiae Mons, cui ad laevum Regio nivosa, ubi Aqua cum odore, rum potu amarissima, qua Accolae medicandis oculis utuntur? Gauranam Nymphaeum locum nominat hoc tractu Symmachus lib. viii. epist. xxii. Massicum non semel celebrat Virgilius, cujus de eo locum lib. vii. exponens Servius Massicum Campaniae Montem Vini generosi feracem ait. De Mons Massicus antea dixi. Massicus hodie Monte Mirso: ejusdem Promontorium Monte Dracone, vel Mondragone, ab Arce cognomine, nunc appellari scribit Leander. Massici verum nomen Osinium esse arbitratur Servius ad x Aeneid. Massicum Montem, ut propinquum Vesevum, Sulfur exludare scribit lib. iiii. cap. vi. Plinius; ut mirum non sit, ex eo haud procul Turre Balneorum calidos Fontes prorumpere, ad plurima Morborum, ut Strabo notat, genera salubres. Per Massici juga exercitum ducit, ut Hannibalem Cunctatione frangeret, Q. Fabius Maximus apud Livium lib. xxii & alios. Quod ad Falernum, cum Plinius a Ponte Campano incipere ait, laeva petentibus urbanam Coloniam Sullanam, antea Capuae contributam. Protripus vocatur in Libello Lombardi de Balneis Puteolanis: & Postripus apud Ioannem Elysium. Falernos Montes Massicos dici notat Iunius Philargyrius: hodie Rocca di Mondagone. Ab eo Falernus Ager & Vina Falerna, de quibus alibi. Vesuvius Mons Tacito lib. iv. Plinio lib. iii. nat. hist. cap. v. Melae lib. ii. Floro lib. iii. hist. Rom. cap. xx. Vitruvio lib. ii. Architect. Cassiodoro, optimisque quibusque Scriptoribus nominatur; qui Vesevus Virgilio lib. ii. Georgic. & Suetonio in Tito cap. viii; Vesevus mss. Suetonij Codicibus; Vesbius Silio Italico lib. xii. Οὐεσούβιος Appiano lib. i. bell. Civilium, Βέσβιος Plutarcho, Galeno, Georgio Cedrenos Bebius Paullo Diacono lib. vi. Rer. Langbar. i. Vesevus Valerio Flacco, ut apud eum legit Ludovicus Carrio, quemadmodum & reponendum censet idem apud Statium & Martialem; Οὐεσούιον Diodoro lib. iv, qui cum quoque Phlegraeum vocat, ab ignium exaestuatione. Nominis Etymon ab Conflagratione tractum quidam putant: Nam Vesuvius olim Favillas fuisse dictus. Alii Lebinum initio vocatum ab Lesbiis advenis aiunt, ut Galenus libro v. de Curatione pro hic. Mavus appellatur Vibio Sequestro, emendante Simlero: nam antea Mavus ribebatur. Hodie Monte di Somma, ab Castello Somma, radicibus adhito; a quo & Summanus Latine scribentibus. Depingunt hunc Montem eleganter post Strabonem lib. v, Leander Alberrus in Campania & Laurentius Schraderus in Italiae Monimentis. Legenda etiam scitu digna de eo apud Cassiodorum lib. iiii. Variar. cap. i. Abesse ab Neapoli tradit Procopius lib. ii. Belli Gothici ferme lxx. stadiis, Urbemque ipsam & Aquilonem spectare; undique ab circumjectis Montibus divisum, circum radices Saltibus silvosum, uti etiam in summis cacuminibus: ibi enim invium horridumque esse: Medio ejus Voraginem esse profundam; eam in intima Terrae Viscera penetrare conjecturam esse, inde ignem & flammas prorumpere. Vesuvius Floro lib. i. cap. xvi, pulcherrimus omnium Aetnei ignis imitator. Silius Italicus lib. xii. Bell. Punici: Monstrantur Veseva Juga, atque in vertice summo Depasti flammis Scopuli, fractuisque ruina Mons circum, atque Aetna satis certantia Saxa. Conflagravit cum alias, tum sub Tito Imperatore, ut scribunt Suetonius cap.viii, Dio & Xiphilinus in Tito, Plinius Epist. ad Tacitum, Tertullianus Apologetico cap.xlviii, Minucius Felix Octavio, Orosius lib.vii cap.ix. Pacianus de Pœnitentia & Confess. Eleganter Martialis lib.i. Hic ejus pampineis viridis modo Vesevus umbris, Presse at hic madidos nobilis Vva lacus: Hæc Iuga quam Nysæ Colles plus Bacchus amavit, Hoc nuper Satyri monte dedere Choros; Hæc Veneris sedes, Lacedæmone gratior illis; Hic locus Herculeo Numine clarus erat: Cuncta iacent flammis & tristi mersa favilla, Nec Superi vellent hoc licuisse sivi.
units.tr: To Campania Felix belong Gaurus, Massicus, Falernus, and others. Gaurus lies near Puteoli. It is noted by Juvenal, Servius, the author of the book On Illustrious Men, chapter 26, and Strabo, and by Pliny in the books of his Natural History, where it is called the Gaurani Montes. Besides Livy, Cicero, Statius, Vibius and others, Arnoldus the Abbot also mentions it in his history of the Slavs. Plutarch in his Life of Hannibal calls it Gallicanus, whence Cicero's Gallicanus Saltus in the speech for L. Quinctius. Today it is, as Blondus and Leander as well as Fernando Lofredus, Francesco Lombardi and Scipio Mazella of Naples think, Monte Gerro and Barbaro; Mazella expanded the little book of Giovanni Elisio On Baths. Among other things, he says of this mountain: "The western part of this mountain was called Gaurus; the eastern and its ridges, Massicus; and the northern, Falernus." As to whether Gaurus is the mountain of Italy that is called Γαύρος [Gauros] in Stobaeus, On Diseases, from Heliodorus, with a snowy region on its left, where there is water with an odour, bitter to drink, which the inhabitants use for treating their eyes? Symmachus, book 8, letter 22, names the Gaurane Nymphaeum as a place in this district. Virgil celebrates Massicus more than once; explaining his passage in book 7, Servius calls Massicus a mountain of Campania rich in fine wine. I have already spoken of Mons Massicus. Today Massicus is Monte Mirso; Leander writes that its promontory is now called Monte Dracone or Mondragone, after the castle of that name. Junius Philargyrius notes that the true name of Massicus is thought to be Osinium, according to Servius on Aeneid 10. Pliny, book 3, chapter 6 of his Natural History, writes that Massicus, being near Vesuvius, gives off sulphur, so that it is no wonder that hot springs burst forth from it not far from the Tower of the Baths, which, as Strabo notes, are healthful for many kinds of disease. Through the ridges of Massicus Quintus Fabius Maximus led his army, so as to wear down Hannibal by delay, as told in Livy, book 22, and others. As for Falernus, Pliny says that it begins at the Campanian Bridge, on the left for those heading to the Sullan colony of the city, which was earlier added to Capua. It is called Protripus in Lombardi's little book on the baths of Puteoli, and Postripus by Giovanni Elisio. Junius Philargyrius notes that the Falernian mountains are called Massic; today it is the Rocca di Mondragone. From it come the Falernus Ager and the Falernian wines, which I discuss elsewhere. Vesuvius is the name of the mountain in Tacitus, book 4; Pliny, book 3, chapter 5, of his Natural History; Mela, book 2; Florus, book 3 of his Roman History, chapter 20; Vitruvius, book 2 of his Architecture; Cassiodorus, and in all the best writers. Virgil, book 2 of the Georgics, and Suetonius in his Life of Titus, chapter 8, write Vesevus; the manuscripts of Suetonius also have Vesevus; Silius Italicus, book 12, writes Vesbius. Appian in book 1 of the Civil Wars has Οὐεσούβιος [Ouesoubios], Plutarch, Galen and George the Cedrenus have Βέσβιος [Besbios], Paulus Diaconus in book 6 of the History of the Lombards, Bebius. Valerius Flaccus has Vesevus, as Ludovicus Carrio reads it in him, and the same scholar thinks it should also be restored in Statius and Martial. Diodorus, book 4, has Οὐεσούιον [Ouesouion], and he also calls it Phlegraeum, from the boiling up of its fires. Some think the etymology of the name comes from conflagration, for they say that Vesuvius was once called Favillae [ashes]. Others say that it was first called Lebinum by Lesbian settlers, as Galen says in book 5 of On Treatment, for this place. Vibius Sequester calls it Mavus, a reading Simler corrects, for earlier it was read Mavus as a mistake. Today it is Monte di Somma, from the castle of Somma at its foot, from which the Latin writers also derive Summanus. After Strabo, book 5, Leander Alberti in his Campania and Laurentius Schrader in his Monuments of Italy depict this mountain elegantly. Things worth knowing about it are also to be read in Cassiodorus, Variae, book 4, chapter 1. Procopius, book 2 of the Gothic War, says that it is about seventy stadia from Naples, and that it looks toward the city and the north; it is divided on all sides from the surrounding mountains; around its base it is wooded with thickets, as also on its highest peaks, for there it is pathless and rough; in its middle there is a deep chasm, which is thought to reach into the innermost bowels of the earth, and from it fire and flames burst forth. Florus, book 1, chapter 16, calls Vesuvius the most beautiful imitator of the fire of Aetna. Silius Italicus, book 12 of the Punic War: "The ridges of Vesevus are shown, and on its highest peak crags grazed by flames, and a mountain around with the crash of its shattered rocks, rivalling Aetna in its stones." It has burned on several occasions, and in particular under the emperor Titus, as Suetonius, chapter 8, Dio and Xiphilinus in Titus, Pliny in his letter to Tacitus, Tertullian in his Apology, chapter 48, Minucius Felix in Octavius, and Orosius, book 7, chapter 9, write. Pacianus, On Repentance and Confession, and Martial, book 1, elegantly: "Here Vesevus was lately green with vine-leaf shade, here the famous grape pressed its dripping vats. These slopes, which Bacchus loved more than the hills of Nysa, these were where the Satyrs lately danced their choruses on the mountain; this was Venus's seat, more pleasing to her than Lacedaemon; this place was famous for the power of Hercules. All lies in ruin, sunk in flames and grievous ash, and the gods above would not have wished this to be allowed."

units.la: Periit eo incendio Plinius Avunculus cum Salcio Bassο, quum ad causas eius explorandas propius, quam oportebat, processisset, teste Plinio Iuniore, Suetonio, Eusebioque de Temporibus. Vesuvium magnam emisisse vim flammarum anno cIↄ cccvi, Conradi Imperatoris temporibus, legimus in Bononiensium Annalibus. Patrum etiam nostrorum memoria circa annum cIↄ Iↄxxxviii horrendam fecisse eruptionem notat Sebastianus Munsterus lib.ii. Cosmograph. Tradit Livius lib.viii ad Vesuvii radices pugnam illam Romanorum T. Manlio Torquato, P. Decio Mure coss. cum Latinis parratam, quando se Decius pro salute exercitus devovit, & in medios hostes invectus periit. Parthenope Mons, hodie Posilipo, Roma Neapolim tendentibus occurrit; instar Promontorii in mare vergens. Cæsarem haud procul eo Piscinam habuisse scribit Columella, in qua Piscis sexaginta annos vixerit, cujus quoque mentionem facit Plinius lib.ix nat. hist. cap.iii Viam, qua Puteolis Neapolim itur, intersecat & præcludit; &c. ni perfossus esset, aut ambitu longissimo circumeundus foret, aut arduus jugorum abruptusque ejus Vertex superandus. Pertusus est ad passus plus minus mille, viaque patet lata pedes xii, totidemque alta; qua, sicut Strabo testatur, duo contraria Plaustra simul commeare & transire possunt. Speluncam appellat ipse; Seneca Cryptam Neapolitanam, ubi fortem Athletarum omnem se perpessum scribit ad Lucilium Epist. xviii; qui Carcerem longum & obscurum vocans, satis indicat Neronis temporibus nullas habuisse fenestras vel Aeris spiracula, præterquam in utrisque faucibus. Asserit tamen Strabo, per Montis Crepidinem olim fenestras plures variis locis ex alto lumen infudisse; quæ lapsu temporis sunt obturatæ; sicque diu manserunt, donec Alphonsus I Aragonum Rex, Provincia in potestatem redacta, Via Fauciibusque dilatatis perforari Montis Dorsum iusserit, duasque fieri Fenestras, quæ Lumen obliquum in mediam Speluncam ex adverso nunc infundunt. Ampliavit restauravitque id opus Petrus Toletanus; quum, Karoli V Imperatoris nomine, Regnum Neapolitanum administraret. Quis primus huius operis auctor fuerit, non admodum est certum. Fabulam de magicis Virgilii, Poëtæ Incantamentis insulto Vulgo relinquamus. Zenobius Acciaolus in Panegyrico quodam Urbis Neapolitanæ ejusque Civium, nonnullos ab L. Lucullo factum, alios a Basso dixisse tantum refert. Leander & alii Cocceium auctorem existimant, verbis Strabonis inhærentes, qui Cocceium cavam illam ac subterraneam viam a Cumis usque Baias; & alteram a Puteolis Neapolim fecisse tradit. Plura vide apud eumdem Leandrum in Campania, & Stephanum Vinandum Pighium in Herculæ Prodicio. Navaiλνr@ videtur quibusdam appellatus, tanquam ademptor Molestiarum & Laboris, quo ante Perfossionem Viatoribus superandus erat. Benedictus Falconius in sua Neapolitana Descriptione tradit Montem hunc Neapolim cingere; eumque nunc hæc nova habere nomina, S. Hermæ, Antoniano, vel Antignano, Conochia, & Cabo di Monte, quo Promontorium ipsum desinatur. Misenus formam Promontorii habet, minus viscieribus adeo perfossus, Cryptisque & ædificiis fornicatis ita excavatus, ut Fornicum Pilis prorsus incumbere & insidere videatur. Meminerunt eius Livius, Virgilius vi Æneid. Silius lib. viii, Tacitus lib.xiv & seqq. alique. Monte Miseno hodie. In Opicis eum describit Halicarnassæus. Vide Caput sequens de Promontoriis. Calena mons celsissimus propter altitudinem hic dictus, Templo D. Mariæ imminens, prope Tripergulana Balnea: ubi & Mons Christi, ita vocatus, quod imperitum Vulgus Christum ab Inferis ris cum Sanctorum Manibus revertentem isthac transiisse credat. Taburnus Mons altus. De eo Virgil. II Georgic.
units.tr: Pliny the Elder perished in that eruption, along with Bassus Salcius, when he went closer to the danger than he ought to have in order to investigate its causes; this is attested by Pliny the Younger, Suetonius, and Eusebius in his Chronicle. We read in the Annals of Bologna that Vesuvius threw out a great burst of flames in the year 1306, in the time of the Emperor Conrad. Sebastian Münster, in the second book of his Cosmography, notes that in the memory of our fathers, around the year 1538, it produced a dreadful eruption. Livy, in book 8, relates that the battle of the Romans against the Latins was fought at the foot of Vesuvius, in the consulship of T. Manlius Torquatus and P. Decius Mus, and that Decius, devoting himself for the safety of the army, charged into the midst of the enemy and died. Mount Parthenope, today Posillipo, meets those travelling from Rome to Naples, jutting out into the sea like a promontory. Columella writes that Caesar had a fishpond near there, in which a fish lived for sixty years; Pliny also mentions it in book 9 of his Natural History, chapter 3. The road that runs from Puteoli to Naples cuts across and blocks this hill; if it had not been pierced through, one would have had to go round by a very long detour, or climb over its steep, precipitous summit. It has been bored through for about a thousand paces, and the road is twelve feet wide and as high; through it, as Strabo attests, two carts travelling in opposite directions can pass at the same time. Seneca calls it a cave, and in his letter to Lucilius (Ep. 18) he writes that he endured all the toil of an athlete in the Neapolitan crypt, calling it a long, dark prison, which makes clear that in Nero's time it had no windows or air vents, except at its two mouths. Strabo nevertheless asserts that formerly several windows at various places in the mountain's flank let light in from above, but over time these were blocked up, and they remained so until Alfonso I, King of Aragon, having brought the province under his control, ordered the road and its mouths to be widened and the mountain's back to be pierced, so that two openings were made, which now pour in slanting light into the middle of the cave from opposite sides. Peter of Toledo enlarged and restored this work, while governing the Kingdom of Naples in the name of the Emperor Charles V. Who first began this work is not entirely certain. Let us leave aside the fable about the magic of Virgil the poet, which is an insult to the common people. Zenobius Acciaiuoli, in a certain panegyric of the city of Naples and its citizens, reports that some attribute it to Lucius Lucullus and others only to Bassus. Leander and others think Cocceius was the author, relying on the words of Strabo, who says that Cocceius made the hollow underground road from Cumae to Baiae, and another from Puteoli to Naples. More on this may be found in Leander's Campania and in Stefano Vinandi Pighius's Hercules Prodicius. It is thought by some to have been called [Navaiλνr@], as the remover of trouble and labour that travellers had to overcome before it was pierced. Benedetto Falconi, in his Neapolitan description, writes that this hill surrounds Naples, and that it now has these new names: S. Ermo, Antoniano or Antignano, Conocchia, and Capo di Monte, where the promontory itself ends. Misenum has the shape of a promontory, less hollowed out by tunnels, yet so excavated by crypts and vaulted buildings that it seems to rest and sit upon the piers of its arches. Livy, Virgil in book 6 of the Aeneid, Silius in book 8, Tacitus in book 14 and following, and others mention it. Today it is Monte Miseno. Halicarnassus describes it among the Opici. See the following chapter on promontories. Calena is a very lofty mountain, so called for its height, overhanging the Temple of St Mary, near the Tripergulan baths. Here also is Mount Christ, so called because the ignorant common people believe that Christ passed this way, returning from the underworld with the spirits of the saints. Taburnus is a high mountain. Virgil speaks of it in the second book of the Georgics:

units.la: Non signes lucent Terra, inviat ipsa a Baccho
units.tr: The lands do not lie idle, but Bacchus himself favours them

units.la: Conferre, atque oleo magnum vestire Taburnum:
units.tr: to be compared, and to clothe the great Taburnus with olive trees.

units.la: quem locum exponens Servius, Taburnum Campaniæ Montem Oleis abundantem scribit: Vibio Sequestro Samnitium est; Apuliæ Probo Grammatico & Pomponio Sabino. Concors Discordia. Omnium enim Fines aliquo modo premit. De eodem Virgilius lib. XII Æneidos:
units.tr: Explaining this passage, Servius writes that Taburnus is a mountain of Campania, abounding in olive trees; for Vibius Sequester it belongs to the Samnites, for Probus the grammarian and Pomponius Sabinus to Apulia. Concordant discord, for it presses on the borders of all of them in some way. Virgil again, in book 12 of the Aeneid:

units.la: At velut ingens Silva summoque Taburno.
units.tr: But as a huge forest, and high Taburnus.

units.la: 20 Sic Gratius Poëta, ——— Candens lava Talurni.
units.tr: 20 So too the poet Gratius: ——— the gleaming lava of Taburnus.

units.la: Hodie Tabor, Erythræo teste Tabu o autem Leandro. Tifata Livio lib. VII, XXIII, XXVI & XXXII, Velleioque Vol. II. Colles Campaniæ, Capuæ Urbi imminentes. Festus libro penultimo de Verb. sig. Tifata lo ua in ta Capuam. Apud Dionem lib. XLII Τυφαγλαια legit Robertus Stephanus. Silius lib. X II:
units.tr: Today it is Tabor; according to Erythraeus, but according to Leander Tabu. Tifata is mentioned by Livy in books 7, 23, 26 and 32, and by Velleius in volume 2. These are hills of Campania, overhanging the city of Capua. Festus, in the penultimate book of De verborum significatu, says: Tifata is a hill above Capua. Robert Estienne reads Τυφαγλαια in Dio, book 42. Silius, book 12:

units.la: T sita umbrisi ro generatum monte Calenum.
units.tr: Calenum born on the shady mountain

units.la: Hodie Monte di Capua. Habet & ut alij notant, hæc nova Nomina: Monte della Caserta, Mataloue, ab oppidis conjacentibus. Plinius editissimus est mons, ex Apennino oriens, in cujus declivitate supra Sarum Arca est oppidum, aliaque in ipso Monte. In Agro Puteolano Mons est Afruunus, altissimus, in cujus medio tanquam ingens quedam est Lacuna, milliariorum fere trium, circa supremam oram, lenique clivo descendens capacitatis in fundo modicæ. Formam habet Theatri arte facti, profunditatis stadij plus minus unius. Per imam aream Aquula fluit clarissima, ad quam exiguus est Lucus perbellus, & introitus una in parte patet angustus. Suum de eo judicium aperit in Campania sua Leander Albertus. Τεμφολ Galeno lib. I. de Antidotis, Mons est Neapolis. Hodie apud Fontem S. Martini monstratur. Nihil in eo nasci scribitur præter Tifum, unde nomen. Meminerunt Trifo tai ab eo Fini Athenæus, Martialis, Plinius. Vide cap. IV.
units.tr: Today it is Monte di Capua. As others also note, it has these new names too: Monte della Caserta, Matalone, taken from the neighbouring towns. Plinius: the most lofty mountain, rising from the Apennines, on whose slope above Sarno there is a town called Arca, and others on the mountain itself. In the territory of Puteoli there is a mountain called Afrunus, very high, in whose middle there is, as it were, a huge hollow, about three miles around at its upper rim, descending by a gentle slope to a rather modest floor. It has the shape of a theatre made by art, about one stadium deep. Through the bottom flows a very clear little stream, beside which there is a lovely small grove, and the entrance lies open on one side, narrow. Leander Albertus gives his own opinion of it in his Campania. Galen in book 1 of On Antidotes calls it [Τεμφολ] a mountain of Naples. Today it is shown near the Fountain of St Martin. It is written that nothing grows on it except Tifum, from which it takes its name. Athenaeus, Martial and Pliny mention Trifo tai, and from it Fini. See chapter 4.

units.la: In Samnitibus porro Montes adeo sunt excelsi, ut etiam ipsos Apenninos superent. Inter eos Mons Virginus, ob Divæ Mariæ Templum nominatissimum. Ab Apennino divisus est, itemque ab ceteris Montibus, quos solum radicibus contingit. Et tales etiam plures, ab Apennino ita separatos, tantæque altitudinis, qua etiam ipsa illius juga superent, Beneventanus Ager habet. Mavella amplitudinis vastissimæ, ascensu difficillimus, rupibus asperrimus. Cacumen perpetua nive tegitur; multa herbida habet Prata; plurimos effundit Fluvios; Silvis superbit immensis, Ferarum copia scatentibus, præcipue Ursorum; Rupibus etiam abruptis horret plurimis. Earum unam coluit Petrus Moronensis, postea Celestinus V. P. M. Auctor Sodalitatis Celestinorum, qui & Moronenses, & ab hoc Monte Maiellani cognominantur. Sunt & in Samnitibus lugæ Apennini quæ Montes Tremuli vocantur, unde Sabbatus oritur. Item Mons Mathesius, qui ab Apennino instar ramí longissimæ latissimeque per Mediterranea protenditur; totus horridus, asper, saxosus & inanis. Grumus ibidem Antiquis pars Apennini, quam hodie Crepacore vocant, ut inquit Scipio Mazella in historia Neapolitana.
units.tr: Further, the mountains in the land of the Samnites are so high that they even surpass the Apennines themselves. Among them is Mons Virginus, famous for the very renowned Temple of the Divine Mary. It is separated from the Apennines, and likewise from the other mountains, which it touches only at their roots. The territory of Benevento has several other such mountains, separated from the Apennines in this way and of such height that they even surpass its ridges. Mavella is of very vast extent, most difficult to climb, very rugged with cliffs. Its summit is covered with perpetual snow; it has many grassy meadows; it pours forth many rivers; it is proud of its immense forests, teeming with wild animals, especially bears; it also bristles with many steep cliffs. Peter of Morrone dwelt in one of these caves, later Pope Celestine V, founder of the Order of the Celestines, who are also called Morronenses, and from this mountain Maiellani. In the land of the Samnites there are also ridges of the Apennines called Montes Tremuli, from which the Sabbatus rises. Likewise there is Mount Mathesius, which extends from the Apennines like a very long and wide branch through the interior; it is entirely rugged, rough, stony and barren. Grumus there, a part of the Apennines in antiquity, which today they call Crepacore, as Scipio Mazella says in his Neapolitan history.

units.la: Sabinis tribuuntur haud procul Reate Tetricum & Severus. De Tetrico Virgilius lib. VII. Æneid.
units.tr: Near Reate, not far off, Tetricum and Severus are assigned to the Sabines. Of Tetricum Virgil speaks in book 7 of the Aeneid:

units.la: Qui Tetrica horrentes rupes:
units.tr: Who hold the bristling Tetrican crags:

units.la: quod Carmen exponens Servius, Montem hunc difficillimum in Sabinis ait esse: Poëtaque vocari Tetrum, id est asperum, uti homines tristes & difficiles Tetricos appellare solemus, id est asperos. Mentio ejus apud Silium lib. VIII.
units.tr: Explaining this verse, Servius says that this mountain is very difficult in the land of the Sabines, and that the poet calls it Tetrum, that is, rough, just as we are accustomed to call gloomy and difficult men Tetrici, that is, harsh. It is mentioned by Silius in book 8:

units.la: 50 Nursia & a Tetrica comitantur rupe cohortes.
units.tr: 50 Nursia and the cohorts that come from the Tetrican crag.

units.la: Tetrica Varroni de Re Rustica lib. II. Succedit Mons Severus, Virgilio etiam notus, quum addit,
units.tr: Tetrica is mentioned by Varro in book 2 of De re rustica. Next is Mons Severus, also known to Virgil, since he adds:

units.la: Montemque Severum.
units.tr: and Mount Severus.

units.la: ubi Servius hanc Montis esse propriam appellationem docet. Hodie Monte de S. Giovanni, Severo, Nero, ut notat Leander. Lucretilis etiam Mons in Sabinis, teste ex Festi Collectaneis Paullo Diacono. Horatius lib. I. Carm.
units.tr: where Servius teaches that this is the proper name of the mountain. Today it is Monte di S. Giovanni, Severo, Nero, as Leander notes. Lucretilis is also a mountain in the land of the Sabines, as Paulus the Deacon attests from the collections of Festus. Horace, book 1 of the Odes:

units.la: Velox amœnum sæpe Lucretilem
units.tr: Swift Faunus often exchanges the pleasant Lucretilis for Lycaeus

units.la: Mutat Lycæo Faunus, & igneam Defendit astatem capelüs I sunt mtis, pluuiosque uentos.
units.tr: and defends my goats from the fiery summer and from the rainy winds.

units.la: Iuxta Gabios cum describit Acron. Cortuu Mons Dionysio Halicarnassaeo ... per ... est in Græco Exemplari, qui hodie, ut Leander opinatur, Monte Cerno dicitur.
units.tr: Near Gabii, where Acron describes the mountain, which in the Greek copy of Dionysius of Halicarnassus is ... and which today, as Leander thinks, is called Monte Cerno.

units.la: Apud Apulos visitur cum aliis, qui Garganus Plinio, Pomponio Melæ, aliísque Παρπαροs Straboni; Παρπαροs Ptolemæo: Carcinum appellant Luithprandus Ticinensis & Sigebertus. Hodie Monte de S. Angelo. Meminerunt, præter Liuium, Virgilius xi Æneid. Horat. lib. 11. Odar. Lucanus lib. v, Silius lib. viii, & alij. Præcelsus valde est & adscensu difficillimo; Siluis quibusdam peranœnis consitus. Herbisque medicis & salutiferis scatens. Latere, quo Mare spectat, ut Strabo notat, Promontorium habet in exortum spatio cec stadiorum procurrens. Incipit ab Apennino, ex cuius radicibus lugum enascitur editissimum, latitudine P. M. duorum, longitudine viginti post quod ita paulatim Mons ipse absurgit, ut in summam altitudinem, vastitatem, amplitudinemque desinat. In mare tam longe protenditur, ut ambitu radicum, quas planicies excipit, ad ducenta P. M. contineat; quamquam Plinius spacium hoc cxxxiv esse prodiderit. Lacum habet cum aliis Varanum, cuius ambitus xxx Milliarium. De Promontorio Garganis alibi. Scribit Strabo Geographiæ libro vi in Agro Daunio (inemendati Codices Saunium habent) circa collem, ὠ ἐπεμα Δεῖον, duo exstitisse Fana; unum summo in vertice, Calchantis, cui oraculum consulentes Nigrum Arietem cædebant, ejusque pelli strata ' dormiebant; alterum ad Montis infimas radices Podalirij, c ab mari stadijs, ex quo riuulus ad omnes Pecudum Morbos salutaris promanabat. Leander aliquè locorum Apuliæ Daunię periti, Templa hæc Collemque Drium Agris Garganô Monti finitimis exstitisse arbitrantur.
units.tr: In Apulia, among others, there is the mountain that Pliny, Pomponius Mela and others call Garganus, and that Strabo calls Parparos [Πάρπαρος], Ptolemy also Parparos [Πάρπαρος]; Luitprand of Pavia and Sigebert call it Carcinum. Today it is Monte di Sant'Angelo. Besides Livy, Virgil in book xi of the Aeneid, Horace in book ii of the Odes, Lucan in book v, Silius in book viii, and others mention it. It is very lofty and very difficult to climb, and it is covered with pleasant woods and full of medicinal and healthful herbs. On its side facing the sea, as Strabo notes, it has a promontory running out to the east for a distance of sixty stadia. It begins at the Apennines, from whose roots rises a very high ridge, two miles broad and twenty miles long, after which the mountain itself rises so gradually that it ends in great height, vastness and breadth. It extends so far into the sea that the circuit of its base, which a plain receives, is about two hundred miles, although Pliny reported this distance as 134. Among other things it has a lake, Varano, whose circuit is thirty miles. I shall speak of the promontory Garganum elsewhere. Strabo, in book vi of his Geography, writes that in the Daunian land (the faulty manuscripts have Saunium) there were two shrines near a hill called Drion [Δεῖον]: one at the very top, of Calchas, whose consulters sacrificed a black ram and slept on its fleece spread out; the other at the lowest foot of the mountain, of Podalirius, six stadia from the sea, from which a little stream flowed out, healing all the diseases of cattle. Leander, who is skilled in the places of Daunian Apulia, thinks these temples and the hill Drium stood in the fields bordering on the mountain Garganus.

units.la: Apud Locros denique Epizephyrios Clibanus Mons est, cuius meminit Plinius, quemque Pinetus Monte Leone interpretatur: Barrius Vsardo, ponens in Calabria. Olibanum legendum suadet Celsus Cittadinus, vocars hodie scribens la Bolenti di Solano, estque in Apennini summitate inter Cosentiam & Rhegium. Est ibidem ε Ciuno, supercilium Locrorum Epizephyriorum, in quo Strabone telte, urbs Locri condita.
units.tr: Finally, among the Epizephyrian Locrians there is the mountain Clibanus, which Pliny mentions and which Pinetus interprets as Monte Leone; Barrius, placing it in Calabria, interprets it as Usardo. Celsus Cittadinus urges that it should be read Olibanus, writing that today it is called la Bolenti di Solano; it lies at the summit of the Apennines between Consentia and Rhegium. There is also at the same place the promontory Zephyrium [Ζεφύριον], the headland of the Epizephyrian Locrians, near which, as Strabo testifies, the city of Locri was founded.

units.la: CAPVT VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: Italiæ Promontoria, Cornua, Scopuli.
units.tr: Promontories, Horns and Reefs of Italy.

units.la: INDICATIS plerisque Italiæ Montibus, adscribam Promontoria. Eorum enarrationem ab Liguria ordiar: prosequuturus porro Italiæ versus Euronorum litora, totamque mox circumspatiaturus.
units.tr: Having indicated most of the mountains of Italy, I shall now add the promontories. I shall begin their description from Liguria, intending next to proceed along the coasts of Italy toward the Euronotus, and then soon to survey the whole circuit.

units.la: Ad Ligurian igitur pertinet quod hodie Merula Promontorium, ab Merula Fluvio, cuius Plinius meminit; hodie Capo delle Melle; aliudque quod ævo superiori Sumarium, hodie Caput Montis, vulgo Codemonte. Mons est saxosus, adscensuque perdifficilis, mare spectans, D. Fructuoso sacer, cui in eo Fanum augustum. Ex altis eius rupibus asperisque claræ præcipitant Aquæ, mox per angustas Fauces Mare petentes.
units.tr: To Liguria belongs the promontory now called Merula, from the river Merula, which Pliny mentions; today it is Capo delle Melle. There is also another, which in earlier times was called Sumarium and is now Caput Montis, commonly Codemonte. It is a rocky mountain, very difficult to climb, facing the sea and sacred to St Fructuosus, who has a noble shrine on it. From its high and rugged cliffs clear waters plunge down and then make their way to the sea through narrow gorges.

units.la: In Etruria Populonium est; Πoπλωνιον Straboni & Ptolemæo; nomen habens ab Vrbe Populonia, Maritima, hodie penitus excisa, neminiique habitata; vulgo Porto Baratto. Post Populonium statuo Cherronetum ingentem, seu Promontorium in Mare excurrens, quod Montem Argentarium vocant, cui uno in latere D. Stephani Opidum, altero Portus Herculis. Annius Montem Volcentarium appellandum contendit, ab Vrbe Etruscorum Volce, quam Antoninum & Catonem adscit memorare, quæque vicina ipsi fuit Promontorio; nec procul Roseto, ut Volaterranus perhibet, nunc propemodum exstincta tota. Voceque dicta, pro Volce. Addit Annius vocalem Vol, antiquissimum & priscum significare: Ce vero vel Cen, nihil aliud esse quam Aes, aut Argentum; hinc Montem Argentarium nunc pro Volce vocari, seu corcorruptione, seu interpretatione. De Monte Argentario Rutilius Numatianus lib. ii: Tenditur in medias Mons Argentarius Undas, Anfipitique ingo cauda rura premit: Transversoque Colles bis tenus millia ter effert, Circuitu Pontis ter duodena patet.
units.tr: In Etruria there is Populonium, called Πoπλωνιον by Strabo and Ptolemy, named after the city Populonia, a seaside town now completely destroyed and inhabited by no one; it is commonly called Porto Baratto. After Populonium I place the great headland, or promontory jutting out into the sea, which they call Montem Argentarium; on one side of it lies the town of St Stephen, on the other the harbour of Hercules. Annius insists that it should be called Montem Volcentarium, from the Etruscan city Volce, which Antoninus and Cato are cited as mentioning, and which lay near this promontory, not far from Roseto, as Volaterranus reports; it is now almost wholly extinct. He says it was called Voce, for Volce. Annius adds that the vowel Vol signifies something very ancient and primitive, while Ce or Cen means nothing else than bronze or silver; hence the promontory is now called Montem Argentarium instead of Volce, either through corruption or through reinterpretation. Rutilius Namatianus, in book ii, speaks of Monte Argentario: The Argentarian Mountain stretches out into the middle waves, and presses down the fields with its double-peaked tail: it lifts its ridges across to the hills for thirty miles, and its circuit by the bridge extends thirty-six.

units.la: Latii est, quod Circaeum Plinius & Pomponius Mela vocant Κιρκαῖον Strabo, Ptolemaeus, & Aristoteles in Admirandis. Hodie Monte Circello, uti censet Leander Albertus. Descriptio ejus est apud Theophrastum de Plantis lib. ix. cap. ix. Insulam olim fuisse, circumfluam immenso Mari, aevo autem senescente additam fuisse continenti, ait Solinus in Polyhistore. Sic Plinius: Circaei quondam Insula, immenso quidem Mari circumdata, si credtur Homero, at nunc planitie. An fabulosus hic Homerus? Sic videtur Procopio lib. i. rer. Gothic. quem vide. Strabo Montem Circaeum statuit ccxc stadiis ab Antio, Mari propinquum: ac partim eo, partim Paludibus Insulae modo, cinctum. Videndus & Servius ad Aeneid. Virgil. vi. Dionysius lib. iv. Circaeum locum oportunum ad Mare situm, Promontoriumque Tyrrheno imminens describit, ubi Circe, Solis Filia, dicitur habitasse; si fides Melae, Solino, Ovidio, aliis. Fuit in eo quondam opidum Sacellumque Circes, & Minervae Ara. Stratonis aetate Poculum ibi ostendebatur, quo bibisse dicebant Vlyssem. Mons efficacissimis Herbis abundasse scribitur; quarum vi Circen homines in bestias commutavisse ferunt. Circaeum Promontorium etiam Ptolemaeus deprigit, in quo Civitas parva Circaeum, Tarquinii Superbi Colonia, loco in Pomptinis Campis totius Latii maximis peropportuno, ut Halicarnassaeus & Livius prodiderunt. Refertus hodie hic Mons Robore, Lauro, Myrto, Stirpibusque variis, quae faciendis Medicamentis potentes & aptae. Promontorii hujus mentio videtur esse in Antiquo Lapide, Veneriisque vocari: PROMVNTORIVM VENERIS CIRCAEIENSIVM
units.tr: Belonging to Latium is the headland that Pliny and Pomponius Mela call Circaeum, and that Strabo, Ptolemy and Aristotle in the Admirabilia call Κιρκαῖον [Kirkaion]. Today it is Monte Circello, as Leander Albertus thinks. A description of it is found in Theophrastus, On Plants, book ix, chapter ix. Solinus, in his Polyhistor, says that it was once an island surrounded by the vast sea, but that as the ages wore on it was joined to the mainland. Pliny says: Circe's island once stood, surrounded indeed by the immense sea, if we believe Homer, but now it is a plain. Is this Homer a fabulist? So it seems to Procopius, in book i of his History of the Goths, which you may consult. Strabo places Mount Circaeum two hundred and ninety stadia from Antium, close to the sea, and partly surrounded, partly enclosed, by marshes in the manner of an island. Servius on the Aeneid of Virgil, book vi, should also be consulted. Dionysius, book iv, describes Circaeum as a suitable place lying by the sea, and a promontory overhanging the Tyrrhenian sea, where Circe, daughter of the Sun, is said to have lived, if we trust Mela, Solinus, Ovid and others. There was once a town there, and a shrine of Circe and an altar of Minerva. In the time of Strabo a cup was shown there, from which they said Ulysses drank. The mountain is said to have abounded in very powerful herbs, by whose virtue they say Circe changed men into beasts. Ptolemy also records a Circaean Promontory, on which lay the small town Circaeum, a colony of Tarquin the Proud, in a spot in the Pontine plains most suitable for the whole of Latium, as Halicarnassus and Livy have reported. Today this mountain is full of oak, laurel, myrtle, and various shrubs useful and effective for making medicines. A mention of this promontory seems to occur in an ancient inscription, where it is called Venus's: PROMVNTORIVM VENERIS CIRCAEIENSIVM.

units.la: Extare testatur in ipsius Montis superficie Angelus Breventanus, rei Antiquariae Romanae diligens indagator; putans numeris in Inscriptione indicari Loci istius ab Vrbe distantiam.
units.tr: Angelo Breventano, a diligent investigator of Roman antiquities, testifies that this inscription still exists on the surface of the mountain itself; he thinks that the numbers in the inscription indicate the distance of this place from the city.

units.la: Occurrunt mox in Campaniae Littoribus Promontoria Caieta, Massicum, Misenum, & Minervae. Primum sic dictum, ut Leander ex Strabone notat, Laconico vocabulo, ab Curvitate: Laconces enim Curva omnia καίαδα appellare solitos. Solinus tamen auctor, sic ab Aeneae Nutrice nominatum, quod etiam canit Virgilius lib. vii. Tu quoque Litoribus nostris Aeneia Nutrix Aeternam moriens famam Caieta dedisti.
units.tr: Next, on the coasts of Campania, the promontories Caieta, Massicum, Misenum and Minerva's come into view. The first was so called, as Leander notes from Strabo, by a Laconian word meaning curvature, for the Laconians were accustomed to call all curved things καίαδα [kaiadas]. Solinus, however, states that it was named after Aeneas's nurse, as Virgil also sings in book vii: You too, Caieta, nurse of Aeneas, by dying gave our shores an eternal fame.

units.la: Quem in locum Servius adnotat, aliis hanc Aeneae Nutricem, alios Creusae, alios Alcanii dicere: lectum tamen etiam in Philologis, hoc loco Classem Trojanorum casu concrematam; indeque Caietam ἀπὸ τοῦ καίειν dictam, quod accendere adureque Latinis significat. Visitur hodieque in altissimo hujus Promontorii Cacumine L. Munatii Planci Oratoris, Ciceronis Discipuli, Mausoleum marmoreum, sub Augusto Caesare exstructum, adhuc integrum, longe lateque prospectans in Mare. Turris Orlandina vulgo nunc vocatur, fabulosis involuta originibus. Describit docte & eleganter Franciscus Schottus IC. ab Corona Pighio, diligentissimo Antiquitatum Investigatore. Inscriptionem, quae ibidem in honorum Planci posita, vide Lib. v cap. de Rhetia. Massici Montis Promontorium Plinio in Campania Felice est: hodie Monte Dracone, ut cap. praecedente dixi. Misenum Promontorium celebratur à Ptolemaeo, Strabone, Solino, Plinio, Pomponio Mela, Antonino, Tacito, aliis. Nomen illi ab Miseno, Aeneae Tubicine & Remige, qui vel fato raptus vel immolatus ad Avernum, ut Servius tradit, hic sepultus creditur. Virgilius lib. vi Aeneidos: At pius Aeneas ingenti mole SepulcrumImponit, suaque Arma Viro, Remumque TubamqueMonte sub Aerio: qui nunc Misenus ab illoDicitur, aeternumque tenet per saecula Nomen.
units.tr: On this passage Servius notes that some call this nurse of Aeneas Creusa, others Alcanius; yet it is also read in the philologists that here the fleet of the Trojans was accidentally burned, and that Caieta was so named from καίειν [kaiein], which in Latin means to kindle and to burn. Even today, on the highest peak of this promontory, stands the marble mausoleum of L. Munatius Plancus, orator and pupil of Cicero, built under Augustus Caesar, still intact, looking far and wide over the sea. It is now commonly called the Turris Orlandina, and its origins are wrapped in fables. Francis Schott, doctor of law, learnedly and elegantly describes it, drawing on Pighius of Campen, a most diligent investigator of antiquities. For the inscription placed there in honour of Plancus, see book v, chapter on Rhaetia. The promontory of Mount Massicus lies in Campania Felix according to Pliny; today it is Monte Dragone, as I said in the preceding chapter. The promontory of Misenum is celebrated by Ptolemy, Strabo, Solinus, Pliny, Pomponius Mela, Antoninus, Tacitus and others. It took its name from Misenus, trumpeter and oarsman of Aeneas, who, whether snatched by fate or sacrificed at Avernus, as Servius relates, is believed to have been buried here. Virgil, in book vi of the Aeneid: But pious Aeneas raised a tomb with a huge mound, and set up his arms and oar and trumpet under the airy mountain, which is now called Misenus after him, and keeps that name eternally through the ages.

units.la: Festus: Misenum Promontorium ab Miseno Tubicine Aeneae ibi sepulto appellatum est. Canit Virgilius Aerium antea dictum: an quod propter meatus & concavitates Aerem patlum & Ventos admittat: Certe ut olim, ita nunc etiam Cryptis & Cavernis multis pertusus est & concavus; ita exhaustis magna ex parte Montis Visceribus, ut suo Cacumine pensilis esse videatur. Promontorium hoc infame naufragiis fuisse, patet ex Taciti lib. xv & Senecae Epist. lxxviii, de Alexandrinis Navibus naufragium ibi passis. Innuit idem Seneca, Minervam ibi cultam, & procellosæ loci Deæ libare solitos Nautas, periculo maris defunctos. Statius:
units.tr: Festus: The promontory of Misenum was named after Misenus, trumpeter of Aeneas, who was buried there. Virgil sings that it was formerly called Aerium, perhaps because, on account of its passages and hollows, it admits a thin air and winds. Certainly, as in former times, so now too it is pierced and hollowed by many caves and grottoes; so much of the mountain's interior has been hollowed out that it seems to hang suspended by its summit. That this promontory was notorious for shipwrecks is clear from Tacitus, book xv, and from Seneca, Letter lxxviii, concerning the Alexandrian ships that suffered shipwreck there. Seneca also hints that Minerva was worshipped there, and that sailors, having escaped the danger of the sea, were accustomed to make offerings to the goddess of that stormy place. Statius:

units.la: Prima salutavit Capreas & margine dextroSparsit Tyrrhena Mareotica Vina Minervae.
units.tr: First he greeted Capri, and along the right-hand shore he poured Tyrrhenian Mareotic wine to Minerva.

units.la: Canit autem non abs re Virgilius Æneam hic potuisse Miseni sui Arma, Remumque Tubamque, insinuans Montem celebrem perpetuo futurum propter Classem & bellicarum Navium Stationem, quam ibi juxta Misenum Augustus ad tutelam Maris Inferi tunc primum collocarat. Adcommodavit Stationem illam M. Vipsanius Agrippa, uti memorat Dio, bello Siculo contra Sex. Pompeium Praefectus Classis ab Augusto factus: atque in eo sinu Maris posuit, qui inter Misenum & Cumas collibus cinctus instar Lunæ corniculatæ incurvus & inflexus erat, loco nimirum capacissimo vel maximæ Classi oportuno, propter vicinos Maris Sinus triplices ab altero latere inter Baias & Puteolos ingruentes: Bajanum videlicet, Lucrinum, & Avernum Lacus, quædam Maris Ostia pulcre nuncupatos ab L. Floro. Legendi Tacitus lib. iv Annal. Suetonius in Octaviano cap. xlix, Vegetius lib. iv de Re militari, cap. xxxi. Classis Misenensis mentio in Antiquo Lapide, qui Romæ in hortis Cardinalis Carpensis: D. M MAGIA. IANVARIA. TATA. SVO BENEMERENTI. FECI C. ANTONIO. ANTARINO MILITI. EX. CLASSE. PRÆTORIA. MISENATIVM. VIX. ANN XL. MIL. ANN. XXIV.
units.tr: Virgil rightly says that Aeneas could have placed here the arms, oar and trumpet of his Misenus, implying that the mountain would be famous forever on account of the fleet and the station of warships, which Augustus first established near Misenum to guard the Lower Sea. M. Vipsanius Agrippa, appointed by Augustus prefect of the fleet in the Sicilian war against Sextus Pompeius, fitted out this station, as Dio relates; and he placed it in that bay of the sea which, enclosed by hills like a crescent moon, lay curved and bent between Misenum and Cumae. It was clearly a place most capacious and suitable even for the greatest fleet, because of the three neighbouring bays of the sea that press in on the other side between Baiae and Puteoli, namely the Bay of Baiae, the Lucrine, and Lake Avernus, which L. Florus nicely called the gateways of the sea. Read Tacitus, book iv of the Annals; Suetonius, in the life of Augustus, chapter xlix; and Vegetius, book iv, On Military Affairs, chapter xxxi. A mention of the Misenum fleet occurs in an ancient inscription in Rome, in the gardens of Cardinal Carpensis: TO THE DIVINE SPIRITS. MAGIA IANVARIA MADE THIS FOR HER WELL-DESERVING HUSBAND C. ANTONIVS ANTARINVS, SOLDIER OF THE PRAETORIAN FLEET AT MISENUM. HE LIVED 40 YEARS, SERVED 24 YEARS.

units.la: Adscribam & aliam, quæ Romæ itidem, in ædibus Laurentij Vellei: D. M T. FLAVI. VALENTIS. MIL CLASS. PR. MISIENIENSIS AGRADIESIS. VIX. ANN. XXVII MIL. ANN. VI
units.tr: I shall add another, likewise in Rome, in the house of Laurentius Vellei: TO THE DIVINE SPIRITS. OF T. FLAVIUS VALENS, SOLDIER OF THE PRAETORIAN FLEET AT MISENUM, OF THE AGRADIAN (?) CENTURY. HE LIVED 27 YEARS, SERVED 6 YEARS.

units.la: Minervæ Promontorium Livio lib. xlii. Vitruvio, Melaque dicitur; quod Ἀθηναῖον Straboni, aliis addenti Ἀθηνοῦσσον vocant: Strenuum appellat Sedem Plinius; ex quo Casaubonus Σεληναῖον apud Strabonem emendat. Eum vide. Campanellam lovius nominat: Capo de Campanella Scipio Mazella; ut & Monte de Massa, ab Urbe eidem imminente.
units.tr: Livy in book xlii, Vitruvius and Mela call it the Promontory of Minerva; Strabo calls it Ἀθηναῖον [Athenaion], and others Ἀθηνοῦσσον [Athenousson]. Pliny calls it the Strenuum Seat, from which Casaubon emends Σεληναῖον [Selenaion] in Strabo. See him. Iovius names it Campanella; Scipio Mazella calls it Capo de Campanella, as also Monte de Massa, from the city overhanging it.

units.la: Lucania Promontorio superbit Posidoniate, ab Urbe Posidonia, cujus in Lucania descriptio: hodie Caput Leucosium, Capo Leuco, ab Insula proxima vocant, ut ait Leander. Meminit ejus Strabo: ut & Pyxunti, quod nunc vulgo Caput Piscitanum, Capo di Piscita. Ulterius Palinurus; sic Virgilio, Horatio, Patereculo, Plinio, Melæ, aliisque dicitur, quod Dion, Strabo, Ptolemæus Παλίνουρον nuncupant. Promontorium est Paestanæ Sinus. Nomen à Palinuro, Classis Æneæ Præfecto, qui hic sepultus fertur, notante Servio ad vi. Æneidos Virgilij, multis Mortem ejus & sepulturam celebrantis. Niger Palinurus, Caltaldus Cabo Palinudo appellat.
units.tr: Lucania boasts the promontory of Posidoniate, named from the city Posidonia, whose description is in Lucania. Today it is called Caput Leucosium (Capo Leuco) after a nearby island, as Leander says. Strabo mentions it, and also Pyxus, now commonly called Caput Piscitanum (Capo di Piscita). Further on is Palinurus. Virgil, Horace, Paterculus, Pliny, Mela and others so call it, while Dion, Strabo and Ptolemy name it Παλίνουρον [Palinouron]. It is a promontory of the Gulf of Paestum. The name comes from Palinurus, prefect of Aeneas' fleet, who is said to have been buried here, as Servius notes on Virgil's Aeneid book vi, where many writers record his death and burial. Niger calls it Palinurus, and Caltaldus Cabo Palinudo.

units.la: Apud Brutios, præter Lampen, Linum est, Αυγ ακρα apud Lycophronem: quod hodie, ut opinatur Gabriel Barrius, Ferre. Scyllaeum, Σκυλλαιον vocant Strabo & Ptolemæus, quod Garofolo vernacule, ut Leander scribit, Vetus, ut Niger. Scopulus præcelsus, notante Strabone: exiguo terræ brachio, tamquam Peninsula, Continenti adhærens. Nomen ab Scylla, quod Saxum in mari prominens, sua summitate procul intuentibus speciem ostenait humanam. Haud procul est Cenæ, Promontorium Plinio notum, oppositum Peloro Siculo, intervallo Stadiorum xii, ut auctor est Plinius; vel xx, ut Thucydides lib. vi, veritati propior: Κανὸς Stephano; Σλωνὶς Polybio lib. i; Cenus legitur apud Hieronymum: hodie Seglio, Si rum ex Leandri; Coda di Volpe, ex Fazelli sententia. Ab Mediana abest apud eundem Leandrum Stadijs ccc. Leucopetra ab candore Saxi, Ciceroni lib. i. Philipp. & Itinerariæ Tabulæ; Λευκόπετρα Strabon lib. v, Ptolemæo, Appiano lib. v, & Thucydidi lib. vii. Promontorium Brutiorum Agri Rhegini. Vox Aibam Petram significat. Hodie Capo di Larme est Nigro, Ananiensi & Leandro: cui etiam, ut & Fazello Capo di Spartovento; Etymo ex vulgari lingua petito, quod huc ex Sicilia navi delatis, quoniam in mare superum veniunt, commutare vela necesse sit, alioque vento cursum instituere, si progredi velint. Ariuum hoc Promontorium videtur appellari Pomponio Melæ ab ipsis Populis: Italia Humerus, Plinio. Quod sequitur Herculeum dicitur, non ita magni momenti, quod in mare haud multum procurrat.
units.tr: Among the Bruttii, besides Lampa, there is Linum, called Αὖγ ἄκρα [Aug akra] by Lycophron, which today, as Gabriel Barrius thinks, is Ferre. Strabo and Ptolemy call Scyllaeum Σκύλλαιον [Skyllaion], which in the vernacular is Garofolo, as Leander writes, or Vetus, as Niger has it. It is a very high cliff, as Strabo notes, joined to the mainland by a narrow neck of land, like a peninsula. Its name comes from Scylla: the rock juts out into the sea, and from its summit it shows a human shape to those who look at it from afar. Not far off is Cenae, a promontory known to Pliny, opposite the Sicilian Pelorus, at a distance of twelve stadia according to Pliny, or twenty according to Thucydides in book vi, which is nearer the truth. Stephanus gives Κανός [Kanos], Polybius in book i gives Σλωνίς [Slonis], and Cenus is read in Jerome. Today it is Seglio, Sirum according to Leander, or Coda di Volpe according to Fazellus. From Mediana it is, according to the same Leander, 300 stadia distant. Leucopetra takes its name from the whiteness of the rock: Cicero in Philippics book i and the Itinerary tables call it so, as do Strabo in book v (Λευκόπετρα [Leukopetra]), Ptolemy, Appian in book v and Thucydides in book vii. It is a promontory of the Bruttii in the territory of Rhegium. The word means "white rock". Today it is Capo di Larme, according to Niger, Ananias and Leander; Leander, like Fazellus, also gives Capo di Spartovento. The etymology is drawn from the vernacular: ships that come here from Sicily, since they enter the upper sea, must change their sails and set their course by another wind if they wish to go on. This promontory seems to be called Ariuum by Pomponius Mela, after the peoples themselves; Pliny calls it the shoulder of Italy (Humerus). What follows is called Herculeum, of no great importance, since it does not project far into the sea.

units.la: Offert se mox in Magna Græcia, quod Zephyrium Plinio, Melæ, aliisque, Locrorum Promontorium; Ζεφύριον Straboни & Ptolemæo: hodie Capo di Burfano dicitur Leandro & Bonacciolo: Bruzzano, Scipioni Mazzellæ. Portus est opportunum, ad Ventos ab Occasu spirantes patente. Zephyrum scribitur, unde illi nomen. Inde est quod Καρκίνον Ptolemæo, Carcinum Plinio, qui longissimum Italiæ dicit. Veteres Plinij Codices Carcinium habere monet Hermolaus. Cocinthum sane, præter Polybium, nominat etiam Antoninus, hinc ad Scyllaceum P. M. xxii esse scribens. Hodie Capo di Stilo, uti censent Leander & Celsus Citradinus. Sequitur Scyllaceum, Scopulis & marinorum Æstuum cum ingenti fremitu reciprocatione periculosum; dictum ab Urbe, quam Coloniam eo duxerunt Athenienses, de qua alibi. Sic nominatum Servius ad Virg. lib. iii Æneidos aut ab Scylla, Nautis perinfesta. Scyllaceo succedit quod Lacinium Plinio & Pomponio Melæ: Λακίνιον Ptolemæo, Lacinium Itinerariæ Tabulæ, Tarina & Tecina corrupte Antonino, ni fallor. Hodie, ut sentit Leander, Capo delle Colonne ab exstantibus adhuc Columnis Templi Junonis Lacinie, quod olim ibi fuit. De eo cum alij, tum Livius lib. xxiv, xxix, xlii, Diodorus lib. xiii historicus. Appianus lib. xv, Servius ad iii Æneid. Σπέρυγγον appellari ab Lycophrone putat Gabr. Barrius: Cacumen vertunt VV. Nobiliss. Iosephus Scaliger & Theodorus Canterus. In habitatile scribitur olim hoc Promontorium Pythagoras Philosophus, ibique Scholam erexisse. Ruscium Thurinorum est Promontorium in Sinu Tarentino: dictum ab opido Rusciano, quod in eo visitur, nonnullo intervallo distans ab Mari. Videndi Procopius lib. iii de Bello Gothorum, & Agathias lib. iv.
units.tr: Next, in Magna Graecia, is Zephyrium, the promontory of the Locri in Pliny, Mela and others; Ζεφύριον [Zephyrion] in Strabo and Ptolemy. Today it is called Capo di Burfano by Leander and Bonacciolo, and Bruzzano by Scipio Mazzella. It is a suitable harbour, open to the winds blowing from the west. It is written Zephyrum, which is the source of its name. From it comes Ptolemy's Καρκίνον [Karkinon], Pliny's Carcinum, which he says is the longest point of Italy. Hermolaus notes that the old codices of Pliny have Carcinium. Besides Polybius, Antoninus also names Cocinthum, writing that it is twenty-two Roman miles from here to Scyllaceum. Today it is Capo di Stilo, as Leander and Celsus Citradinus think. Next comes Scyllaceum, dangerous because of its rocks and the reciprocating tides, which roar violently. It is named from the city, which the Athenians led there as a colony, of which I shall speak elsewhere. Servius, on Virgil's Aeneid book iii, says it was so named either from Scylla, which is very hostile to sailors. After Scyllaceum comes Lacinium, in Pliny and Pomponius Mela; Λακίνιον [Lakinion] in Ptolemy; Lacinium in the Itinerary tables; and Tarina and Tecina, corruptly, in Antoninus, unless I am mistaken. Today, as Leander thinks, it is Capo delle Colonne, from the columns still standing of the temple of Juno Lacinia that was once there. Both others and Livy (books xxiv, xxix and xlii), the historian Diodorus (book xiii), Appian (book xv) and Servius on the Aeneid book iii write about it. Gabriel Barrius thinks Lycophron calls it Σπέρυγγον [Sperygon], and the most noble Joseph Scaliger and Theodore Canter render it "Cacumen" (summit). It is written that the philosopher Pythagoras once lived on this promontory and set up a school there. Ruscium is a promontory of the Thurini in the Gulf of Taranto, named from the town of Rusciano, which is seen on it at some distance from the sea. See Procopius, On the Gothic War, book iii, and Agathias, book iv.

units.la: Iam Salentinorum Promontoria sunt Iapygium & Leuca Caput. Iapygium, Ἰαπύγιον Ptolemæo est, & Straboni Σκυλλαῖον, ὅτι καλοῦν ἀκρα γι' ἀπυγίαν. Plinio Acra Iapygia; quod Salentinum Sallustio; Σαλεντίνον, eidem Ptolemæo; Pomponio, Sale, nisi truncata sit vox. Unde nomen, notum. Ipsa enim Regio Iapygia & Salentina vocatur. Hodie Capo de S. Maria, ut scribit Leander: Mazzellæ S. Maria de Finibus Terræ a peraugusto, quod ibi Divæ Virgini sacratum, Fano. Olim ibi Templum erat Minervæ, ut scribit Strabo, cujus etiamnum certa superiant vestigia ad jactum lapidis ab D. Mariæ. Ab hac Minerva etiam Ἁλικαρνασσὸς Halicarnassæo videtur nuncupatum. Stalatum Indigenæ appellant, inquit Barrius. In Maria quam longissime procurrit, ut & Strabo Plinuisque notant, versus exortum hibernum, paullatim mox se convertens ad Lacinium, à quo abest 15 cc stadijs. Testatur Antonius Galateus Philologus & Medicus, qui de Situ Iapygiæ scripsit, se ex peritis Navigantibus audisse usque ad xi vel i millia passuum in mare protendi longa Apennini, quum hic ibi altius metirentur Mare. Caput Leuca nomen habet ab Leuca opido, quod hic fuit Strabonis ætate: hodie Capo Leucoso, vel Capo de Lenca. Scribit Sulpitius ad Lucani iv, distare ab Tarento 15 Stadijs, ab Hydrunto, cx; hunc Brundisium cccc(sic enim legendum) numerari.
units.tr: Now the promontories of the Salentini are Iapygium and Leuca Caput. Iapygium is Ἰαπύγιον [Iapygion] in Ptolemy, and in Strabo Σκυλλαῖον [Skyllaion], because they call it the promontory of Iapygia. Pliny calls it Acra Iapygia; Sallust calls it Salentinum; Ptolemy, Σαλεντῖνον [Salentinon]; Pomponius calls it Sale, unless the word is truncated. The origin of the name is well known, for the region itself is called Iapygia and Salentina. Today it is Capo de S. Maria, as Leander writes. Mazzella calls it S.
