Maria de Finibus Terrae, from the very famous shrine there, dedicated to the Virgin. Formerly there was a temple of Minerva here, as Strabo writes, and its sure traces still remain within a stone's throw of Santa Maria. From this Minerva the place also seems to have been called Ἁλικαρνασσός [Halikarnassos]. Barrius says the natives call it Stalatum. It juts out into the sea as far as possible, as Strabo and Pliny also note, turning gradually from the east-south-east towards Lacinium, from which it is 1500 stadia distant. Antonius Galateus, a philologist and physician who wrote on the situation of Iapygia, testifies that he heard from experienced sailors that the long spur of the Apennines extends into the sea for eleven or one thousand paces, since sailors here measure the sea as deeper. Caput Leuca takes its name from the town of Leuca, which existed here in Strabo's time. Today it is Capo Leucoso, or Capo de Lenca. Sulpitius, on Lucan book iv, writes that it is fifteen stadia from Taranto and 110 from Hydrus; he says Brundisium is reckoned at 400, for so the text should be read.

units.la: In Apulia Daunia Mons Garganus, de quo antea dixi, latere, quo mare spectat, Promontorium habet, in exortum spatio ccc Stadiorum procurrens, præceps & abruptum. Ptolemæus Promontorium Garganum discrimen Ionij Hadriaticiq; Sinus constituit: quod alij Brundisium.
units.tr: In Apulia Daunia, Mount Garganus, of which I have spoken before, has on the side facing the sea a promontory, steep and precipitous, running out to the east for 300 stadia. Ptolemy makes the Promontory Garganum the dividing line between the Ionian and Adriatic gulfs, while others make it Brundisium.

units.la: Cameram Picenì est Promontorium apud Plinium: quod hodie, ut Leander notat, Monte d'Ancona, nonnulis Monte Santo dici scribit Nonius Marcellus, recens Auctor, in sua Aigialogia; propter frequentes Eremitarum habitationes. Olim huc Veneris ædem fuisse canit Iuvenalis, ubi de Rhumbo ante id fanum capto munerique Domitiano Cæsari dato, sic inquit:
units.tr: The Camera of Picenum is a promontory in Pliny. Today, as Leander notes, it is Monte d'Ancona, which some say is called Monte Santo, as the recent author Nonius Marcellus writes in his Aigialogia, because of the frequent dwellings of hermits. Juvenal sings that a temple of Venus once stood here, where, speaking of the rumbus taken before that shrine and given as a gift to the emperor Domitian, he says:

units.la: 10 Ante domum Veneris, quam Dorica sustinet Ancon.
units.tr: 10 "Before the house of Venus, which Doric Ancona upholds."

units.la: Hodie Templum ibi D. Cyriaci. Loci tanta est altitudo, ut sereno cœlo prospectus pateat in Dalmatiam. Sunt ibi Græcæ Inscriptiones vetustæ, sed quæ ob nimiam Antiquitatem, arrosis lapidibus, legi nequeunt.
units.tr: Today there is a temple of St Cyriacus there. The height of the place is such that, with a clear sky, the view extends into Dalmatia. There are ancient Greek inscriptions there, but because of their great antiquity, the stones being worn away, they cannot be read.

units.la: Focaria Blondo Promontorium est Flaminiæ, quæ hodie Romanula, ad mare Hadriaticum. Id Leander dicit Incolis nunc nominari Monti di Pesaro, ab Urbe Pisauro. Vini Oleique suavissimi, ac Ficuum, aliorumque Fructuum mirificam generat copiam.
units.tr: Focaria, according to Blondus, is a promontory of Flaminia, which today is Romanula, on the Adriatic Sea. Leander says the inhabitants now call it Monti di Pesaro, after the city of Pisaurum. It produces a wonderful abundance of very sweet wine and oil, as well as figs and other fruits.

units.la: Habet & Istria quædam sua Promontoria, sed haud magni nominis, Veteribus incognita; Fanaticum, Cisanum, Comparu & Crucifixa; de quibus quod adferam, nihil habeo singulare.
units.tr: Istria too has some promontories of its own, but of no great name and unknown to the ancients: Fanaticum, Cisanum, Comparu and Crucifixa. I have nothing special to add about them.

units.la: Pertinent ad hoc Caput duo Italiæ Cornua, quæ nominantur à Plinio lib. iii. cap. v & Pomponio Mela lib. ii cap. iv. Nam & Sallustius vocat Promontoria in Fragmentis, Brutium nempe & Salentinum; ut & Paullus Diaconus lib. ii. Langbardic. cap. xvii & xxi: hoc Dextrum, illud Sinistrum appellans: Inter duo illa Cornua Frontem Italiæ statuunt Plinius, Solinus, Marcianus; in Sinu Tarentino.
units.tr: Belonging to this head are the two "Horns of Italy", named by Pliny (book iii, chapter v) and Pomponius Mela (book ii, chapter iv). Sallust, in the Fragments, also calls them promontories, namely the Bruttian and the Salentine; so does Paulus Diaconus (book ii of the Lombard History, chapters xvii and xxi), calling the one the Right Horn and the other the Left. Between those two horns Pliny, Solinus and Marcian place the "Brow of Italy", in the Gulf of Taranto.

units.la: Referam huc & nominationes Scopulos, Scyllam & quæ cum illa plurimum solet explicari, licet Siciliæ propior & propria, Charybdim. Scylla Plinio Scopulus in Freto Mamertino inter Siciliam & Italiam. Scyllam & Scyllæum vocat Strabo. Hodie Scylio nominari, auctor est Fazellus. Magna fuit in Scylla Poëtis fingendi materia. Virgilius lib. iii. Æneidos Helenum introducit, ejus formam Æneæ narrantem his verbis:
units.tr: I shall also mention here the rocks called Scylla, and what is usually explained along with it, though it lies nearer to Sicily and belongs to it: Charybdis. Pliny calls Scylla a rock in the Straits of Messina between Sicily and Italy. Strabo calls it Scylla and Scyllaeum. Fazellus reports that it is now called Scilio. Scylla was a great source of material for the poets' inventions. Virgil, in book iii of the Aeneid, introduces Helenus, who describes her form to Aeneas in these words:

units.la: 30 Prima hominis facies, & pulcro pectore Virgo Puberemus: postrema immani corpore Pristis, Delphinum caudas utero commissa luporum.
units.tr: 30 Her face is a human one, and she is a maiden with a lovely breast down to the groin; below, she is a monstrous fish-shaped body, with dolphins' tails joined to the belly of wolves.

units.la: Fictionis huius argumentum est, quod, ut antea monui, Scylla Saxum sit, in mari prominens summitate procul intuentibus, uti legere est apud Sallustium in Historiarum fragmentis, speciem offendens humanam, infra vero Scopulos plurimos invicem divisos habens; sub quibus cavernæ noti recessus, in quos irruentes inlisique fluctus undarum, ingenti sonitu Canum latratum, ejulatumque Luporum & aliorum Animalium voces edere ac imitari videntur: quapropter Poëtæ commenti sunt Scyllam à pube succinctam Canibus aliisque Feris esse. Virgilius in Bucolicis:
units.tr: The basis of this fiction is, as I said before, that Scylla is a rock jutting out into the sea, which is visible from afar, as can be read in Sallust's fragments of the Histories. It presents a human appearance, but below it has many rocks split apart from one another. Beneath them are caves and hollow recesses into which the waves rush and beat, and they seem to give out a great roar, to imitate the barking of dogs and the howling of wolves and other animals. For this reason the poets invented that Scylla was girt about the groin with dogs and other wild beasts. Virgil in the Bucolics:

units.la: 40 Quid loquar aut Scyllam? Nisi quam fama sequuta est, Candida succinctam latrantibus inguina monstris Ah timidos Nautas Canibus lacerasse marinis.
units.tr: 40 "What shall I say of Scylla? Except what report has followed: how she, with gleaming groin girt round with barking monsters, tore the timid sailors with sea-dogs."

units.la: Nec inelegantler Poëta Ovidius:
units.tr: The poet Ovid, not without wit, says:

units.la: 50 Altera Scylla tuo monstrum medicamine Circes; Pube premit rapidos inguinibusque Canes.
units.tr: 50 "The other Scylla, a monster from the drug of Circe; she surrounds the swift ones with dogs at her groin and loins."

units.la: Ad Siciliam Charybdis est, nominatissima Scriptoribus; Navigantibus admodum infesta. quod, aut vi ventorum, aut Æstu marino Fluctus propellente in Scopulos, quum eodem illi impetu reciprocant, ita vorticolis undis absorberi & obrui navigia solent. Syrtem vocat Iacius Tzerza. Galofaro appellatur hodie, Fazello & Arctio testibus. Laurentius Ananiensis scribit Cannatello nominari: Auctor est idem Sallustius Charybdim absorbere universa, quæque absorbuerit, ea circa Tauromenitanum minitanum litus egerere: ideoque plus semper discriminis in Charybdi, quam in Scylla, ponunt Scriptores Veteres; inter quos Homerus Odyss. M. qui periculum utriusque Scopuli describens, Circen facit Ulyssi suggerentem, ut ad Scyllam potius inflecteret cursum, quam ad Charybdin, propterea quod latius esset, [?]ex e Sociis desiderari, quam pariter omnes interire: Aut enim:
units.tr: Near Sicily is Charybdis, most famous among writers, and very dangerous to sailors. Whether by the force of the winds or by the sea's tide driving the waves against the rocks, when they flow back with the same force, ships are commonly swallowed up and overwhelmed by the whirling waves. Iacius Tzerza calls it Syrtis. It is now called Galofaro, according to Fazellus and Arctius. Laurentius Ananiensis writes that it is named Cannatello. The same Sallust is the authority that Charybdis swallows everything, and throws back up on the shore of Tauromenium whatever it has swallowed. Therefore the ancient writers always place more danger in Charybdis than in Scylla, among whom Homer, in Odyssey 12, describes the peril of each rock. He makes Circe advise Ulysses to steer his course toward Scylla rather than toward Charybdis, because it was better to lose some of his companions than for all to perish together. For he says:

units.la: — [?]μὴ σύγε κεῖθι τύχῃς ὅπῃ [?]ἰχθύοεσσιν,
units.tr: "Do not, you, happen to be there where [the fish-sea-monsters?]" [μὴ σύγε κεῖθι τύχῃς ὅπῃ ἰχθύοεσσιν]

units.la: [?]Οὐ γάρ κεν [?]ἡμεῖς ... [illegible, ~12 letters] κακά, ἀλλ᾽ ἰνοσίχθων,
units.tr: "For we could not [...] evils, but the earth-shaker [...]" [Οὐ γάρ κεν ἡμεῖς ... κακά, ἀλλ᾽ ἐνοσίχθων]

units.la: [illegible, ~30 letters]
units.tr: [illegible]

units.la: [illegible, ~30 letters]
units.tr: [illegible]

units.la: [illegible, ~30 letters]
units.tr: [illegible]

units.la: Notum est celebratum Graecis Adagium: τὸν Χαρυβδὶν ἐκφυγὼν, τῇ Σκύλλῃ πεσεῖται: cui consonat Latinus Versus:
units.tr: There is a well-known Greek saying: "Whoever escapes Charybdis will fall into Scylla" [τὸν Χαρυβδὶν ἐκφυγὼν, τῇ Σκύλλῃ πεσεῖται]; a Latin verse agrees with it:

units.la: Incidit in Scyllam, cupiens vitare Charybdim.
units.tr: "He falls into Scylla, wishing to avoid Charybdis."

units.la: De Scylla, deque Charybdi multa fabulantur Poetae. Videndi praeter alios Pausanias in Corinthiacis & Servius ad Virgilij Bucolica. Pergo. Taurianum Scopulum est in Brutiis apud Ptolemaeum, quem Tyrrhenum vocat Plinius. Pietra della Nave nominatur Ligorio: Nave simpliciter Barrio. Alios, qui hic ibi ad Italiae littora, praetereo.
units.tr: The poets tell many fables about Scylla and Charybdis. Besides others, Pausanias in the Corinthiaca and Servius on Virgil's Bucolics are to be consulted. I go on. The Taurian rock is in the land of the Bruttii, according to Ptolemy, which Pliny calls Tyrrhenian. Ligorio names it Pietra della Nave, and Barrio simply Nave. I pass over the others, here and there along the shores of Italy.

units.la: CAPUT VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: Italiae Valles, Campi, Agri, Prata, Via.
units.tr: The valleys, plains, fields, meadows and roads of Italy.

units.la: VT Italiam Montes horridiorem; sic amoeniorem faciunt eamdem, & animos spectantium incredibili explent gaudio Valles, Campi, Agri, aliaque id genus planiora loca, quae utrinque Apenninis adjacent, eorumque lateribus inclusa sunt & quasi vallata. Valles huiusmodi sunt innumerae. Praecipuas notabo, quae suis distinctae nominibus.
units.tr: Just as the mountains make Italy rather rugged, so the valleys, plains, fields and other flatter places of that kind make it more pleasant, filling the minds of onlookers with incredible delight. They lie on both sides of the Apennines, enclosed by its slopes and, as it were, walled in by them. Valleys of this kind are innumerable. I shall note the chief ones, which are distinguished by their own names.

units.la: Ligurum sunt Onelia, Pagis Vicisque multis nitens, quae Dianis quoque dicta ab Opido Diano: Porcifera ab Amne cognomine, quo perluitur, appellata; Villis sumptuosis superbiens: Rapallina peramoena plane, passimque Citris, Medicis, Limonibus, Oleis, aliisque fructiferis Arboribus ornata; Sinui adiacens Rapallinae.
units.tr: Among the Ligurians are Onelia, shining with many villages and hamlets, also called Dianis after the town of Diano; Porcifera, named after the river of the same name by which it is watered, proud of its sumptuous villas; Rapallina, very pleasant indeed and everywhere adorned with citrons, medlars, lemons, olives and other fruit trees; Rapallina lies next to the gulf.

units.la: Tuscorum sunt Mugelli Vallis, cui Mugellum opidum dedit nomen; & Arni, ab Arno fluvio dicta: hanc antea Paludes occupabant: sed, post tarum ibi quoddam ferro aperrum, exsiccata, totaque nunc exculta, consitaque nobilium hortorum est instar: Mentionem eius facit Livius, Hannibalis iter hac memorans, docensque Paludosam tunc fuisse: Poenorum Ducem ob Intemperiem vernam, humore nocturno paluströ coeno caput gravante, altero captum fuisse oculo; Elephante insuper, qui unicus supererat, quo altius ab Aquis exstaret, vectum, qua fluvius Arnus per eos dies solito magis inundarat; item in praealtis ac profundis Fluvij voraginibus hausisse pene fuisse Duces; maxime tamen omnium confecisse Vigilias, per quatriduum iam & tres noctes toleratas, quum omnia obtinentibus Aquis, nil, ubi in sicco tella sternerent corpora, poterat inveniri. Est ibidem Vallis Umbrosa, ubi Coenobium cognomine: Eo enim loco id Institutum Vitae, quod ab Umbrosa Valle cognominatur, primus est exortus Ioannes Gualbertus Florentinus, anno post Christum natum c1o lxx, item Piscina, ab fluvio Piscia, qui hac fluit, nuncupata.
units.tr: Among the Tuscans are the valley of Mugello, to which the town of Mugello gave its name, and Arni, named after the river Arno. Marshes formerly covered this area, but after a certain channel was cut there with iron tools, it was drained, and it is now wholly cultivated and planted, and resembles a noble garden. Livy mentions it, recounting Hannibal's route through here and showing that it was then marshy: the Carthaginian leader, because of the spring weather, had his head weighed down by the nocturnal damp and muddy swamp, and lost one eye; moreover, on the one elephant that remained, he was carried higher above the waters, since the Arno was flooding more than usual in those days; also, in the deep and steep whirlpools of the river, the leaders nearly drowned; most of all, however, the watches wore them out, endured now for four days and three nights, since the waters held everything and nowhere on dry ground could they lay down their bodies. In the same place is Vallis Umbrosa, where there is a convent of the same name; for in that place the religious order called after Vallombrosa first arose, through John Gualbert of Florence, in the year 1070 after the birth of Christ. Also Piscina, named after the river Piscia, which flows through it.

units.la: Umbrorum est Sabina, Vallis nitidissima, Farfaroque irrigata; cuius meminit Horatius lib. iii. Od. qui Villam ibi habebat amoenam:
units.tr: Among the Umbrians is Sabina, a very bright valley, watered by Farfa; Horace mentions it in Book 3 of the Odes, since he had a pleasant villa there:

units.la: Quae Valle permutem Sabina
units.tr: For which valley would I exchange

units.la: Diviticas operosiores?
units.tr: the Sabine, for riches more toilsome?

units.la: Sunt eorumdem Spoletina, ab Urbe Spoleto, iucunda sane planicies: Topina ab Topino Amne, ipsam percurrente: Cippa, seu D. Ioannis, ubi transmissio Tiberis: Angustiarum, quae admodum est saxosa altissimisque clausa rupibus: cuiusque in exitu quarto fere ab Interamnia lapide Olearum Silvae, Vitcs, aliaque Arborum genera.
units.tr: Of the same people are the Spoletine valleys, named after the city of Spoleto, a truly pleasant plain; Topina, from the river Topino, which runs through it; Cippa, or St John's, where the Tiber is crossed; the Angustiae, which is very rocky and enclosed by high cliffs, and at its exit, about four miles from Interamna, has groves of olives, vines and other kinds of trees.

units.la: Fuerunt etiam in Vmbria Amfanctti Valles, quarum Virgilius meminit Æneid. vii. Manet hodieque circa Velinum Lacum Vetus Nomen. Apertenim ibi in hodiernum usque diem Vulgo Nesincina appellatur, perperam pro Amfancto, quod undique Sanctum & fertilem significat. Vide quæ dixi cap. ii ubi de Italia Vmbriæ. Mentio etiam Vallis huius apud Ciceronem de Divinatione.
units.tr: There were also in Umbria the Amfanctine valleys, which Virgil mentions in Aeneid 7. The old name remains even today around Lake Velinus. For there, to this day, it is commonly called Nesincina, wrongly for Amfanctum, which means holy and fertile on every side. See what I said in chapter 2, where I spoke of Umbrian Italy. This valley is also mentioned by Cicero in his De Divinatione.

units.la: Apud Brutios Vallis est D. Martini, purissimarum Aquarum fontibus scatens.
units.tr: Among the Bruttians is the Valley of St Martin, teeming with springs of very pure water.

units.la: Peitanas Valles à Pæsto, Lucaniæ oppido, nominat Solinus.
units.tr: Solinus names the Peitanas valleys after Paestum, a town of Lucania.

units.la: Apud Samnites Vallis est amœna, quæ inter Apenninum & Cráthidem fluvium plurimum longitudine patens, in lacum haud valde, per transversum Fluminibus dispescitur quinque, multisque Torrentibus, qui ex Apennino in Crathidem feruntur.
units.tr: Among the Samnites is a pleasant valley, which stretches a great length between the Apennines and the river Crathis. Not far from the lake it is divided crosswise by five rivers and many torrents, which flow from the Apennines into the Crathis.

units.la: Apud Apulos Caudina est, quæ nunc Gardani dicta, teste Collenutio lib. vi. Hist. Reg. Cernuntur ibi antiquæ Vrbis Candy vestigia. Sunt & Furcæ Caudinæ, de quibus alibi.
units.tr: Among the Apulians is Caudina, now called Gardani, according to Collenuccio, Book 6 of the Histories of the Kings. Remains of the ancient city of Candy can be seen there. There are also the Caudine Forks, of which I shall speak elsewhere.

units.la: Est in Flaminia Anemonis Vallis (quæ Lamone Adcolis) ab Amne Anemone: supra Faventiam est: perpulcra Colonisque plena, cum opidulis aliquot Vicisque non inhonestis. Exercitum in ea Oddonis, Bracij Montonij filij, anno MCCCCXXIV concisum, ipso etiam Duce peremto, prodit memoriæ Blondus lib. xxii Histor.
units.tr: In Flaminia is the valley of Anemone (which the neighbours call Lamone), named after the river Anemone; it lies above Faenza, very beautiful and full of farms, with some small towns and not inglorious villages. Blondus, in Book 22 of his Histories, records that the army of Oddo, son of Braccio Montone, was cut to pieces in it in 1424, and the leader himself was killed.

units.la: In Æmilia vero Fanusci, ab opido Banisco; Rhenique, sic dicta, quod per eius Amnis ripam pandatur sinistram, amœnissima, ubertateque Frumenti & Vini nobilissimi, maxime Apiani Vulnerianique, ac Fructuum generis omnis copia valde fœcunda. Item Vesi supra Salutium inter duos Montes præcelsos: Vulgus Valionem Vesi nuncupat. Præcipitat per eam Amnis Bronda magno cum impetu. Circeola denique Valis, ubi olim Vlmus fuit formosa.
units.tr: In Aemilia are the valley of Fanusci, named after the town of Banisco, and the valley of the Rhine, so called because it spreads along the left bank of that river; it is very pleasant, very fertile in grain and most noble wine, especially the Apiane and Vulneriane, and abundant in every kind of fruit. Also Vesi, above Salutium, between two very lofty mountains; the common people call it Valion Vesi. The river Bronda plunges through it with great force. Finally, the Circeola valley, where once there was a beautiful elm.

units.la: Iam in Langbardia Transpadana, quod reliquis Italiæ partibus montosior, quantum pallim occurrit cerniturque cum voluptate Valtinum? Sunt ibi Tropia. Colonis haud infrequens: Solis, Ollij Fonte, ut quidam eum statuunt, irrigata: Camunia, cuius Incolæ Camuni Plinio, Καμουνοι Straboni, ut quidem emendandus; Καμουνοι Dioni; hodie Camunen teste Ægidio Schudo: Brembana ab Flumine, cuius in ripa est, id nominis tenens: D. Martini, Pontidam, Cesanum, Caurinum, Callotium, aliaque gestans opida: Mancana, cui initium apud D.Peregrinum ubi Villa D.Peregrini, ad D. Ioannem, Platiates & Roncolates: Telina, vulgo Veltulina pro Valle Telina; vel ut quidam volunt, Turrena seu Volturrena, à Patribus V. Turrenis Etruscis, qui huc avitis sedibus ab Gallis pulsi cum Rhæto commigrarunt, dicta: Malenga merito sic appellata, quum tota deserta præcelsis rupibus & abruptis horridisq; Montium, nulla prorsus Arbore vel herba virescentium, culminibus includitur. Clavenna, ab Clavenna iuxta Meiram miliar. ab Lario xvi, nobili opido dicta: Bregalia, prope Montem Perminem: Assina ab Assi Pago infra Comum, Bregantinis propinquæ Montibus: Plumbana ad ripam Ticini: Lugana, ab Lugano celebri & opulento opido: Morobia, quæ x M. P. Larium Lacum versus, rectaque ad Mullum pandit. Cluria ad Verbanum Lacum; ut & Travaltia; item haud procul inde Majoris & Minoris Consilii (Di Consiglio Maggiore & Minore) inter altissimos Montes modicæ: Mesauca ab Mesauco munita Arce ad amnem Muetij, montes inter celsissimos asperrimosque conclusa; unde Mesauci Populi Plinio lib. iii natur. histor. cap. xix: Caranga ad eumdem fluvium faucibus perangustis & difficilibus: Breunia à Breunio fluvio, pertinens Coriatum versus, P. M. xvi, Incolæ Plinio Brenni: Lepontina, sic ab Lepontiis Populis, de quibus suo loco dicta: de hac Valle nonnihil cap.v, ubi de Lepontiis Alpibus: Intratia, ab Intratia flumine nuncupata: Verciasca, ab Verciasco fluvio, angusta præcepsque: Dolia, ab Amne Dolia, qui ex Monte per eam Madiæ fluminis inlabitur, appellata. Pertinet usque ad Locarnum. Habet Vegnotium, Cordaucum, Conum, Sumanum, Suncum, Mogenum, Lavelerium, Brontalium, Marcionum, Broilum, Sornicum & Fulium. Caseria prope idem opidum Locarnum, ut & Antigoria, multo quam Caseria, latior planiorque: Obitur inde Lusernonia, Centumque Valles iuxta Canobium: Doneria ab Doneria amne, quem Atilo excipit. Veggetia ab fluvio Lamietia percurritur, ex præcelsis iugis in Madiam defluente. Est hæc Convallis in medio longarum faucium & asperrimarum rupium editissimo simo frigidissimoque situ: quam ob rem homines alit admodum agrestes, duros, ingenijs validissimis, ex quibus est genus illud rude, quod per universam Europam oberrans Caminis everrendis locat operam: Ronana opidis super bit Cerentino, Rusco, Caprino, Campo & Bugnatco: Domodoscellia ab opido cognomine, Arcem habente munitissimam: Ancialca ab eiusdem appellationis Amne, ubi via difficilis inter asperos horridosq; Montes ad Vallem Augustam ducit: E regione faucium Vallis Ancialcae, laeva, propter Atisonem Voconia cernitur, ad Montis radices, Muro septa cum Arce permunita. Vallis ibidem apparet Veconia, quam Agonum Veteribus appellatam tradit Aegidius Tschudus, ab Agonibus populis, quos commemorat Polybius: Seciasam Amnis Secia, nunc Senza percurritur; Verus ad laevam est Atisonis ripam: tum Montibus transitis ultra Atisonem Fagnana; porroque Maginiaca. Anquita Praetoria Valla admodum est longa; multisque pagis, inter collissima luga sitis, frequens. Excipit Eporediam. Tractus ibi omnis editissimis rupibus concluduntur, inter quas maximus est Campus, quem Veteres Bardum appellarunt; hodie Bart dicitur, optimis fructibus nobilisque Vino Apiano & aliis generibus fecundus. Medium Amnis interluit Duria Maior, ut etiam Strabo notat. Felina perperam vocatur pro Penina, quod ad Montem Peninum: Valli Vallis ad Flumius Cognominis fontem; Planicies amoena, Incolis Liverna dicitur ab Opido, quod habet. Liverna.
units.tr: Now in Transpadane Lombardy, which is more mountainous than the other parts of Italy, how much of the Valtellina appears and is seen with delight! There are the Tropia valleys, not infrequently settled by colonists, watered by the Sole and by the Ollio spring, as some hold. Camunia, whose inhabitants are the Camuni to Pliny, Καμουνοι to Strabo (as it should be emended), Καμουνοι to Dio, and today Camunen according to Egidius Schudus. Brembana, from the river on whose bank it lies, which keeps the name. St Martin's, containing Pontida, Cesano, Caurino, Callotio and other towns. Mancana, which begins at St Peregrine, where the villa of St Peregrine is, extending to St John, Platiates and Roncolates. Telina, commonly Veltulina for Valle Telina; or, as some prefer, Turrena or Volturrena, named after the Etruscan fathers V. Turreni, who, driven from their ancestral seats by the Gauls, migrated here with the Rhaetians. Malenga, rightly so called, since the whole of it is deserted, enclosed by lofty and sheer cliffs and the horrid summits of mountains, and no tree or herb grows there at all. Clavenna, named after the town of Clavenna, near the Mera, sixteen miles from Lake Como, a noble town. Bregalia, near Mount Permine. Assina, from the village of Assi below Como, near the Bregantine mountains. Plumbana, on the bank of the Ticino. Lugana, from the famous and wealthy town of Lugano. Morobia, which lies ten miles toward Lake Lario and runs straight to Mullo. Cluria by Lake Verbano, as also Travaltia; likewise, not far from there, the small Major and Minor Consilium (Di Consiglio Maggiore & Minore), among very high mountains. Mesauca, from Mesauco, a castle fortified on the river Muetius, enclosed between very lofty and rugged mountains; whence the Mesauci people of Pliny, Natural History, Book 3, ch. 19. Caranga, on the same river, with very narrow and difficult passes. Breunia, from the river Breunio, extending toward Coira for sixteen miles; its inhabitants are the Brenni of Pliny. Lepontina, so named from the Lepontii, of whom I shall speak in their place; of this valley something in chapter 5, where I discuss the Lepontine Alps. Intratia, named after the river Intratia. Verciasca, after the river Verciasco, narrow and steep. Dolia, named after the river Dolia, which flows down from the mountain through it into the river Maggia. It extends as far as Locarno. It contains Vegnotium, Cordaucum, Conum, Sumanum, Suncum, Mogenum, Lavelerium, Brontalium, Marcionum, Broilum, Sornicum and Fulium. Caseria, near the town of Locarno, and likewise Antigoria, which is much wider and flatter than Caseria. From there one comes to Lusernonia, and the hundred valleys near Canobio. Doneria, from the river Doneria, which the Atilo receives. Veggetia is traversed by the river Lamietia, which flows down from the high ridges into the Maggia. This valley lies in the midst of long and rough gorges and steep rocks, in a very high and very cold situation; for this reason it nourishes men who are very rustic, hardy, and of the strongest character, from whom comes that rough race which wanders through all Europe and hires itself out to sweep chimneys. Ronana lies above Cerentino, Rusco, Caprino, Campo and Bugnatco. Domodoscellia, named after the town of the same name, which has a very strong citadel. Ancialca, named after the river of the same name, where a difficult road leads through rough, horrid mountains to the Augusta valley. Opposite the gorges of the valley of Ancialca, on the left, near Atiso, Voconia can be seen, at the foot of the mountain, enclosed by a wall, with a very strongly fortified castle. The valley Veconia also appears there, which Egidius Tschudus says was called Agonum by the ancients, after the Agones, a people whom Polybius mentions. The river Secia, now called Senza, runs through Seciasa; Verus is on the left bank of the Atiso. Then, having crossed the mountains beyond the Atiso, comes Fagnana, and further on Maginiaca. The Aosta Praetoria valley is very long and populous, with many villages set among very steep ridges. It is followed by Ivrea. All the tracts there are enclosed by very high cliffs, and among them is the greatest plain, which the ancients called Bardum; today it is called Bard, fertile in excellent crops and in the noble Apiano wine and other kinds. The Dora Maior flows through its middle, as Strabo also notes. Felina is wrongly named for Penina, after Mount Peninus; Valli Vallis lies by the spring of the river of the same name. It is a pleasant plain, which the inhabitants call Liverna, after the town it has, Liverna.

units.la: Ad Venetiam pertinet Vallis Pelusella, ab opido Pelusio vocata. Guarinus tamen Policellam appellari dicit propter nitorem & pulcritudinem Pomorum, quae ferri tamquam politam, ut scribit Blondus.
units.tr: Belonging to Venetia is the Vallis Pelusella, so called from the town of Pelusium. Guarinus, however, says it is called Policella because of the brightness and beauty of its apples, which are carried as though polished, as Blondus writes.

units.la: Habet & suas Valles Forum Iulii Plitianam, Caporetinam, Ronconam vel Sontij, aliasque ignobiliores, angustas & confragosas.
units.tr: The Friulian territory also has its valleys: Plezzo, Caporetto, Ronchi (or Sontius), and others less noted, narrow and rugged.

units.la: Haec de Vallibus: quid iam commemorem Planicies illas, quae Camporum vel Agrorum appellatione Veteribus sunt notae: Planitiem quamdam (ut hanc in genere praescribam) amoenam pulcramque, Apennini montibus & Germanibus Alpibus inclusam, Padoque Flumine divitam, describit Polybius hac sententia: Tertio Italiae Lateri, quod Alpibus terminatur ab Meridiana Regione, versus Septemtrionem subiacent Campi extremi totius Italiae, totius Europae maximi & uberrimi. Horum etiam forma triquetra est: Apicem Trianguli faciat Apenninus atque Alpium copulatio non longe ab Mari Sardoo supra Massiliam. Latus, quo Septemtrionem spectat, Alpes, ut dixi, faciunt; quae ad duo millia & ducenta stadia protenduntur: Latus vero, quod ad Meridiem vergit, perficit Apenninus; hic ad tria millia & sexaginta stadia procurrit. Basis locum tenet litus ipsum Hadriae. Huius magnitudine est ab Sena urbe usque ad intimum eiusdem Maris Sinum: haec duorum millium & quingentorum Stadiorum spatio continentur. Ita omnis Camporum circuitus decem Stadiorum millibus clauditur. De Fertilitate haud facile dixerim, ita omnibus frugum generibus abundat. Sic fere Polybius; immensam illius plagae ubertatem, & Ingeniorum excellentiam sigillatim deinde commemorans,
units.tr: These are the valleys. Why should I now mention those plains which the ancients knew by the name of Campi or Agri? Polybius describes one plain (to set out its general character first), pleasant and beautiful, enclosed by the Apennine and the German Alps and rich in the Po river, in these words: On the third side of Italy, which is bounded by the Alps, facing south, there lie towards the north the furthest plains of all Italy, and the largest and richest of all Europe. Their shape is also triangular: the apex of the triangle is made by the Apennine and its junction with the Alps, not far from the Sardinian Sea above Massilia. The side facing north is formed by the Alps, as I said, which extend for about 2,200 stadia; the side that inclines to the south is completed by the Apennine, which runs for about 3,060 stadia. The base is the very shore of the Adriatic. Its length, from the city of Sena to the innermost bay of the same sea, is contained within a space of 2,500 stadia. Thus the whole circuit of the plains is enclosed by 100,000 stadia. I could hardly say enough about their fertility, so abundant are they in every kind of crop. So far Polybius. Then, recalling in detail the immense richness of that region and the excellence of its inhabitants,

units.la: Selonius Campus est in Latio, Agri Lanuvini; apud Ciceronem I. & II. de Divinatione, ubi apud focum Angues nundinari solent. Scribendus Solonius: dictus enim ab Solonio, Latij opido; cuius meminerunt Dionysius Halicarnass. lib. II, Livius lib. VIII, Plutarchus in Mario. Cicero II. ad Attic. epist. III. Pometini ibidem Campi, ab opido Pometia: quos omnium Latinorum maximos refert Halicarnassaeus.
units.tr: The Selonius Campus lies in Latium, in the territory of Lanuvium; Cicero mentions it in the first and second books of De Divinatione, where snakes are wont to trade by the hearth. It should be written Solonius, for it is named after Solonium, a town of Latium, which Dionysius of Halicarnassus mentions in book II, Livy in book VIII, and Plutarch in his life of Marius. Cicero, in book II of his letters to Atticus, letter III, speaks of the Pometini plains there, named after the town of Pometia; Halicarnassus reports these as the largest of all the Latin plains.

units.la: Sunt in Campania Campi, qui quondam Laborini, vel Laboria, ut videre est apud Plinium: à quibus hodie Campania ipsa Italis, ut censent Viri docti, Terra di Lavoro. Phlegraeum, eodem teste, lib. XVIII cap. XI. Graeci nominarunt. Campi Phlegraei Solfatara vulgo nuncupari. Vide plenius in mea Campania. Campus Cumanus Diodoro lib. IV. Maximam partem hodie Guadam dici tradit Lofredus in suo de Puteolis libello. Manet Laborinorum nomen multis post seculis; si, quae scribit Rasanus, sint vera. Affirmat enim se, quum aliquando Capuae esset, eruditos quosdam peritosque Vetustatis homines audivisse, qui tam Civium privatorum, quam ipsius Vibis Tabulas publicas trecentorum amplius annorum vidisse adseverabant, quibus Laborinorum Camporum circum Aversam fiebat mentio: unde, inquit, Terrae Laboris errore Vulgi corrupta defluxit appellatio. Finiuntur Laboria, inquit idem Plinius lib. xviii cap. xi, Via ab utroque latere Consularis, quæ à Puteolis & ab Cumis Capuam ducit. Idem lib. iii cap. v. Ibi (de Campania loquitur) Laborini Campi sternuntur & in delicias Alicæ politur Mellis. Et lib. xvii cap. iv; Stipula crassitudinem tantam in Laborino Campo notat, ut inde ex Ligni vice utantur. Describuntur ab Silio, Petronio, & Cornelio Severo. Fuit ibidem Stellatis Campus, Montibus & Fluminibus (verba sunt Livii lib. xxii) clausus: meminit idem lib. ix & x Stellatis Ager vocatur Suetonio in Cæsare. Santelicius ostendit cum hodie in Territorio Carmolo. Quod Mazzone vulgo dicatur, testis est Scipio Mazzella. De Campi Stellatis præstantia extat M. Tullii Testimonium in Oratione contra Rullum. Habet item Campania Agrum Falernum, de quo Plinius lib. xiv cap. vi: Falernus Ager à Ponte Campanus læva petentibus Urbanam Coloniam Sullanam, nuper Capuæ contributum, incipit. Et addit: Faustianus autem circiter quatuor milliaria ab Vico prope Cedias, qui Vicus à Sinuessa vi milliaria abest. Nec ulli in Vino maior auctoritas: Faustianum Agrum circa Cumas locat Athenæus, ubi Vinum eius describit.
units.tr: In Campania there are plains which were once called Laborini or Laboria, as may be seen in Pliny; from these, according to learned men, the Italians today call Campania itself Terra di Lavoro. Pliny, in the same passage, book XVIII chapter XI, says the Greeks named the Phlegraeum. The Campi Phlegraei are commonly called Solfatara. See more fully in my Campania. Diodorus, book IV, speaks of the Campus Cumanus. Lofredus, in his little book on Puteoli, reports that most of it is now called Guada. The name Laborini remained for many centuries afterwards, if what Rasanus writes is true. For he affirms that when he was once at Capua he heard certain learned men, skilled in antiquity, who asserted that they had seen public records more than three hundred years old, both of private citizens and of the city itself, in which mention was made of the Laborini Campi around Aversa; hence, he says, the name Terra di Lavoro came from the corruption of the name by the error of the common people. "The Laboria are bounded," says the same Pliny, book XVIII chapter XI, "on either side by the Consular Way, which leads from Puteoli and Cumae to Capua." The same author, book III chapter V, says (speaking of Campania): "There the Laborine plains are spread out, and the honey of Alica is refined for delight." And book XVII chapter IV: "Straw in the Laborine plain grows so thick that people use it in place of wood." They are described by Silius, Petronius and Cornelius Severus. There was also a Stellatis Campus there, enclosed by mountains and rivers (these are Livy's words, book XXII); Livy mentions it again in books IX and X, and Suetonius in his life of Caesar calls it the Stellatis Ager. Santelicius shows that it is today in the territory of Carmolo. That it is commonly called Mazzone, Scipio Mazzella is the witness. On the excellence of the Stellatine plain there is the testimony of Marcus Tullius in his speech against Rullus. Campania also has the Falernian territory, of which Pliny says in book XIV chapter VI: "The Falernian territory begins at the Campanian bridge, for those heading left towards the Colonia Urbana Sullana, lately added to Capua. And he adds: the Faustian territory is about four miles from the village near Cedias, which village is six miles from Sinuessa." Nor is there any greater authority on wine: Athenaeus places the Faustian territory near Cumae, where he describes its wine.

units.la: Visuntur in Langbardia Cispadana Campi, qui Livio lib. xi i Marri; Str. boni Mapoi (legebatur antea corrupte Naxpoi) Kaʼ‬μ: qui circa Mutinam & Parmam (ut Columella indicat lib. vii cap. ii) hodie Valle di Montirono, ut Leandro videtur, sic scribenti: A Finali suršum incedentis Paludes apparent multa, vastissimaque Mantironi Vallis: quæ ad dextram aggerem habet non latum quidem, sed qui longissime ab Ema Via usque in Padi fere ripam excurrat. Adcolæ Dorsum vocant, Frumenti ubertate mirabili copiosum. Vallis hæc ab occasu longo illo claditur tumulo, ab Mirandula, quæ superius inter Anstrum & Occasum sita est, millibus quinque distante. Nos hanc longe lateque patentem Planitiem, Italis Valem appellatam Campos esse Nacros putamus, quorum meminit Strabo lib. v, ubi quotannis Forum habere solitum ait. Eos autem hoc modo designat: Inter Placentiam, inquit, & Ariminum sunt Parma, Mutina, Bononia; harum medio exigua quædam tacent oppida, per quae iter est Romam, Acara, Regium Lepidi, Nacri Campi, Claterna, & quæ sequuntur. Quamquam autem Volaterranus lib. iv Commentar. Urbanor. hos Campos ibi esse censet, ubi nunc Carpi: Ego tamen, inquit Leander, exacte mecum hanc planitiem consideratam, Strabonisque verba inspectis, hos ipsos esse Nacros Campos arbitror: idque ut sentiam, eodem maxima Antiquitatis vestigia, nobilissimumque ædificiorum opere musivo, ut vocant, ornatorum, quæ hic vidimus, faciunt: ubi etiam indies Numismata varia, Pavimenta tesselata, vetustaque Vasa, Sepulcrorum antiquorum ruinæ cum insignibus Lapillis inveniuntur. Et paullo post: Patens hic Campi latissime, nullis plane Arboribus, herbam ferentes colore rubellam, sapore salsam, Adcolæ Porcellanam vocant, ovina Pastioni admodum expetitam: prætereaque Salem hic ex terra igne decocta, magno tamen artificio, conficiunt. Pascua item hæc Planicies peroportuna Gregibus Ovillis præbet; ex quibus Lana cum præcipua excellentia, tum incredibilis copia percipiuntur.
units.tr: In Cispadane Lombardy there are plains which in Livy, book XI, are called the Marri; Strabo (the old text read Naxpoi corruptly) the Kaʼ‬μ [Mapoi]; these, around Modena and Parma (as Columella indicates, book VII chapter II), are today the Valle di Montirono, as Leandro thinks, writing thus: "From Finale, as one advances upward, many marshes appear, and the very vast valley of Mantirono. This has on its right a bank, not indeed broad, but which runs out very far from the Emilian Way almost to the bank of the Po. The inhabitants call it the Ridge, abundant with a wonderful fertility of grain. This valley is closed on the west by that long hill, at a distance of five miles from Mirandola, which lies further to the south and west." We believe this wide and far-spreading plain, which the Italians call the Valem, to be the Nacrian Plains, mentioned by Strabo in book V, where he says they were accustomed to hold a market every year. He marks them out in this way: "Between Placentia and Ariminum lie Parma, Mutina and Bononia; in the middle of these lie some small towns, through which the road to Rome passes: Acara, Regium Lepidi, the Nacrian Plains, Claterna, and those that follow." Although Volaterranus, in book IV of his Commentaries on Urban matters, thinks these plains are where Carpi now is, I, says Leander, having carefully considered this plain with my own eyes and examined the words of Strabo, think these are the very Nacrian Plains; and that I hold this view, the great traces of antiquity and the most noble buildings adorned with mosaic work, as they call it, which we saw here, make clear: where also, every day, various coins, tessellated pavements, ancient vessels, and the ruins of ancient tombs with precious stones are found. And a little later: "This plain is wide and open, with no trees at all, and bears grass of a reddish colour and salty taste, which the inhabitants call Porcellana, and which is much sought after for sheep pasture; besides this, they make salt here from the earth, burnt by fire, with great skill. This level ground also supplies excellent pasture for flocks of sheep, from which wool is obtained both of outstanding quality and in incredible quantity."

units.la: Rosea Campus (hic enim appellatur Varroni, qui Livio lib. x Rosellanus Ager) in Umbria locatus legitur iuxta Lacum Velinum, unde apud Virgilium, Rosea Rura Velini, ad quem locum Servius notat, Lacum Velinum ei propinquum esse. Campus hic tantæ scribitur Fertilitatis; ut, auctore Varrone, Cæsar Vopiscus, quum Cautlam apud Censores ageret, Campos Rosea Italia dixerit esse Sumen: In iis enim (ut cap. iii. dixi) Perticam relictam postridie non apparere propter Herbam tantillo tempore succrescentem: quod etiam à Plinio commemoratur lib. xvii, cap. iiii. Pars huius Campi vel Agri videtur fuisse Amsanctii Vallis, de qua paullo ante.
units.tr: The Rosean plain (for Varro so calls it, and Livy, book X, the Rosellan territory) is said to lie in Umbria, beside the Lake Velinus, whence in Virgil we have "the Rosean fields of Velinus"; on which passage Servius notes that Lake Velinus is near it. This plain is said to be of such fertility that, on the authority of Varro, Caesar Vopiscus, when he was pleading the case of Cautla before the censors, called the Roseal plains of Italy a "sumen"; for in them (as I said in chapter III) a pole left behind the next day cannot be seen because of the grass that grows up in so short a time. Pliny also mentions this in book XVII chapter IV. Part of this plain or territory seems to have been the valley of Amsanctus, of which I spoke a little earlier.

units.la: Caudius Campus, quem in Venetia ponit Florus, ibidem Teutones ab C. Mario trucidatos scribens, hodie Candia dicitur, non longe à Pado, in Lacinellini oppidi tractu, ut Castilionius refert. Restituitur Floro ab Vineto Claudius. Rauds Campi leguntur apud Vell. Paterculum lib. ii. Nescio an designet Sidonius in Panegyrico, qui Maiorano dicatus: Perque Cavi quondam dictos de nomine Campos.
units.tr: The Caudian plain, which Florus places in Venetia, where he writes that the Teutones were slaughtered by Gaius Marius, is today called Candia, not far from the Po, in the district of the town of Lacinellino, as Castilionius reports. Floro's text is restored by Vineto as "Claudius." The "Rauds" plains are read in Velleius Paterculus, book II. I do not know whether Sidonius in his Panegyric, dedicated to Majorian, means these: "and through the Campi once called Cavi from their name."

units.la: Caninos Campos legit Sigonius lib. xviii Histor. Occident.
units.tr: Sigonius, book XVIII of his History of the West, reads "Caninos Campos" (the Canine plains).

units.la: In Romanula non longe ab Forcellis Prata longe lateque diffunduntur, quæ Salana vocant Adcolæ, quorum medio Propugnaculum est cum antiqua Turre; tenetque Vicinitatem Opinio Salam oppidum hoc olim exstitisse loco, unde Prata Salana nunc vulgo nuncupentur.
units.tr: In Romagna, not far from Forcelli, meadows spread far and wide, which the inhabitants call Salana; in the midst of them is a fortified tower with an ancient keep; and the neighbourhood holds the opinion that the town of Sala once stood in this place, whence the Salan meadows are now commonly named.

units.la: Viarum,
units.tr: Of the Roads.

units.la: Stellatis Campus Viarum, quæ per totam Italiam, atque adeo in ipsam usque Galliam ab Urbe ducebantur, quarumque hodie passim extant vestigia, enarratio potuisset etiam ad hoc Caput referri; sed commodior earum futura est explicatio in Latio, ubi quæ ad Romam (nam in Foro Romano ad Miliarum Aureum plerique Viæ sua erant initia & capita) eiusque spectant Magnitudinem, commemorantur.
units.tr: A description of the roads that ran from the City through all of Italy, and indeed as far as Gaul itself, and of which traces still survive in many places, could also have been referred to this chapter; but their explanation will be more convenient in the chapter on Latium, where those roads that relate to Rome and its greatness (for in the Roman Forum, at the Golden Milestone, most of the roads had their beginnings and heads) are recorded.

units.la: CAPVT VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: Italiæ Silvæ, Luci, Nemora.
units.tr: Forests, Groves and Woods of Italy

units.la: ET Montes, & Valles Campique, de quibus proxime dixi, sanè superbiunt Silvis, Lucis, Nemoribus, quorum non pauca apud Priscos, etiam suis Nominibus leguntur celebrata.
units.tr: The mountains, valleys and plains of which I have just spoken certainly boast of their forests, groves and woods, many of which are famous among the ancients under their own names.

units.la: In Etruria, qui hodie Saltus, vernacule Bosco di Monte Fiascone, Volsinio, quod vulgo Bolsena, Viterbium euntibus occurrit, Volsiniensium Lucum ab Antiquis ignoti probati Auctoris testimonio, nondum liquet appellatum tradit Leander; addens Etruria cognominatum apud Plinium, pravius lib. III cap. v lectum & intellectum: Quocunque notus fuerit nomine, videtur designari ab Ovidio in Fastis: Stat vetus & densa pra nubibus Arbore Lucus, Aspice, concedes Numinis esse locum: Aspicit Ara preces, votivaque Thura Priorum; Ara per antiquas facta sine Ante manus.
units.tr: In Etruria, the wood which today is called Bosco di Monte Fiascone in the vernacular lies on the way from Volsinium, commonly called Bolsena, to Viterbo. Leander reports that it is not yet clear by what name the ancients called the grove of Volsinii, on the testimony of an unknown but approved author, adding that Pliny calls it by the surname of Etruria, a reading and interpretation that is wrongly given in book III, chapter 5. By whatever name it was known, it seems to be indicated by Ovid in the Fasti: There stands an ancient grove, its dense tree rising above the clouds. Look, it shows that this is a place of divine presence: the altar receives the prayers and the votive incense of our forebears; the altar was made by ancient hands without iron.

units.la: In Cimino Etruriæ Monte quondam, calcari pauciens ob horrorem solita, fuit Silva, de qua sic Livius lib. IX: Silva erat Ciminia, magis tum invia atque horrenda, quam nuper fuere Germanici Saltus; nulli ad eam diem, ne Mercatori quidem, adita. Eam intrare haud fere quisquam praeter Ducem ipsum audebat. Confirmat Florus in Etrusco Sanniticoque bello Ciminium Saltum ante illa tempora invium plane, quasi Calidonium aut Hercinium, fuisse scribens. Hac tamen aetate, repurgatis munitisque locis illis, itemque habet non minus frequens atque tutum, quam olim infra Viterbum Via Cassia fuit, Romam Vetralla ducens. Post Vicum Bacchanum in Etruria silvosi se offerunt Saltus, qui Indigenis Bosco di Baccano, caedibus & latrocinio quondam perinfames. Veteres Mafsiam Silvam videntur appellasse. De ea Livius lib. I, Silva, inquit, Mafsia, Tuscis ademta. Et alibi pugnam Fabiorum contra Veientes explicans, ex Silva Mafsia vocem exauditam scribit. Olim ea commeare non sine summo discrimine licuit: sed hac nostra aetate partim quod maiori ex parte sit incendio vastata, partim quod per maximam Romanorum Pontificum curam & diligentiam, praecipueque Iulij II, Leonis X, Clementis VII & Pauli III, huc ibi excisa, tam est tuta, ut absque metu quovis tempore peragretur.
units.tr: On the Ciminian mountain in Etruria there was once a forest, which was often avoided out of dread. Livy speaks of it thus in book IX: There was the Ciminian forest, then more impassable and terrifying than the German woods have lately been. Up to that day no one had entered it, not even a merchant. Hardly anyone dared to go into it except the general himself. Florus confirms this, writing in his account of the Etruscan and Samnite war that the Ciminian wood had been entirely impassable before those times, like the Calydonian or Hercynian forest. In our own age, however, those places have been cleared and fortified, and the road from Viterbo to Rome through Vetralla is now as busy and as safe as the Via Cassia once was. Beyond the village of Baccano, in Etruria, wooded tracts present themselves, which the natives call Bosco di Baccano, once notorious for murders and robbery. The ancients seem to have called it the Massian Forest. Livy speaks of it in book I: The Massian forest, he says, was taken from the Etruscans. Elsewhere, describing the battle of the Fabii against the Veientes, he writes that a voice was heard from the Massian forest. Formerly it was possible to pass through it only at great risk. In our own age, partly because it was largely laid waste by fire, and partly because, through the great care and diligence of the Roman pontiffs, especially Julius II, Leo X, Clement VII and Paul III, it was cut down there, it is now so safe that it can be traversed at any time without fear.

units.la: In Latio apud Capenates Lucus fuit Feronia, quem canit Silius lib. XIII: Dives ubi ante omnes colitur Feronia Luco, Et sacer humectat fluvialia rura Capenas.
units.tr: In Latium, among the Capenates, there was the grove of Feronia, which Silius sings of in book XIII: Where rich Feronia is worshipped in a grove above all others, and the sacred Capenas waters the fields by the river.

units.la: Livius lib. XXVII in Agro Capenate prope Silvam Feroniae Signa quatuor diem & noctem sanguine tudavisse narrat. Iuxta Numicum Amnem Lucus erat Iovi Indigeti sacer, ut Plinius tradidit lib. III cap. v, quamquam mendose apud eum antea Locus legeretur, pro Lucus; quod Hermolaus Barbarus adnotavit; & ex Livio lib. I, Solino in Polyhist. Dionysio Halic. in Antiq. Rom. & Cicerone lib. III de Natura Deorum convincitur. Diana Aetolica Lucus Livio est lib. XXVII ad Anagninum Compitum. Nemus Silvam extra Urbem ad quartum Milliarium fuisse notat Festus. Ab ea nomen Porta Nevia. Extra Portam Capenam Camaenarum Lucus scribitur ab Livio lib. I. & Asconio Pædiano in Orat. Cicer. Luci Capeni Egeriaeque Nemus forte Virgilio lib. VII, ubi Servius notat iuxta Ariciam fuisse. An ex hoc Silij versu sinisterius intellecto? Egeria genitos immitis Aricia lucis.
units.tr: Livy in book XXVII relates that in the Capenate territory, near the Feronian Forest, four standards dripped with blood for a day and a night. Beside the river Numicus there was a grove sacred to Jupiter Indiges, as Pliny records in book III, chapter 5, although in that author the reading was once wrongly Locus instead of Lucus, as Hermolaus Barbarus noted; this is proved from Livy book I, Solinus in the Polyhistor, Dionysius of Halicarnassus in the Roman Antiquities, and Cicero in book III of On the Nature of the Gods. For Livy, the Grove of Diana Aetolica is in book XXVII, at the Anagninum crossroads. Festus notes that a wood, a nemus, lay outside the city at the fourth milestone, and the Nevian Gate took its name from it. Outside the Capene Gate the Grove of the Camenae is mentioned by Livy in book I and by Asconius Pedianus in his commentary on Cicero's orations. Perhaps Virgil in book VII means the grove of Lucus Capenus and Egeria, where Servius notes that it lay near Aricia. Or is this to be understood, less straightforwardly, from that verse of Silius: Aricia, cruel to the groves, born of Egeria?

units.la: Livius propius urbem locat, addens in eius medio fuisse Egeriae Fontem, quod & testatur Ovidius lib. XV Metamorph. Quod Alsidum Nemus Livio reliquisque Scriptoribus, hodie Selva del Aglio dicitur, consentientibus Mario Nigro & Leandro. Albuneam Silvam in altissimis Tiburtinis Montibus habet Servius ad vii Æneid. aliamque idem ad Georgica, in Laurentinorum agris, cognominem: Vide infra ubi de Fontibus cap. ii. Aegitia Nemus propinquum Albæ Marforum fuisse, significat Virgilius lib. vii. Æneid. Furina Lucus, Territorii Romani, est apud Ciceronem iii de Nat. Deor. & Cornelium Nepotem, ubi C Gracchum interfectum scribit. Furinarum Lucum habet P. Victor in xiiii. Regione Trans-Tiberiana. Plutarcho in Gracchi vita Furinarum Lucus ἄλσος Ἐρίννυος vocatur.
units.tr: Livy places it closer to the city, adding that in the middle of it was the Spring of Egeria, which Ovid also attests in book XV of the Metamorphoses. The Alsidian grove, which Livy and the other writers call that, is today called Selva del Aglio, as Mario Nigro and Leander agree. Servius, on Aeneid VII, places a Albunean forest on the highest Tiburtine mountains, and on the Georgics he places another of the same name in the fields of the Laurentines; see below, where I discuss springs in chapter 2. Virgil, in book VII of the Aeneid, indicates that the grove of Aegitia was near Alba of the Marsi. The Furina grove, in the Roman territory, is mentioned by Cicero in book III of On the Nature of the Gods and by Cornelius Nepos, where he writes that Gaius Gracchus was killed there. Publius Victor places the Furinae grove in the fourteenth region, across the Tiber. In Plutarch's life of Gracchus the Furinae grove is called a grove of the Erinys [ἄλσος Ἐρίννυος].

units.la: Vacunæ Nemora agnoscit iuxta Montem Fiscellum in Umbria Plinius.
units.tr: Pliny recognises the groves of Vacuna near Mount Fiscellum in Umbria.

units.la: Gaudent & suis Campani: cum primis Luco Sacro & Gallinaria Silva. Sacer Lucus Livio lib. xxiiii, ἀλσος ἱερὸν. Strabo ad Ostia Liris, qui hodie Hams, restibus Scipione Mazzello & Leandro Alberto. Tribus ab Cumis passuum millibus locat Livius, Nymphām Maricam ibi coli solitam scribit Strabo. Videndus & Servius ad Æneidem Virgilianam. Gallinariam Silvam nominant Cicero ad Patrum scribens & Strabo lib. v, qui Γαλλιναρίαν ὕλην vocat. Pomponius Sabinus, propius ad locum accedens, in Cumano Sinu fuisse air; addens, Trivia Lucum appellari ab Virgilio vi Æneid Sanfelicio hodie La Peneta de Patria dicitur. Pinus huius vitiosus apud Iuvenalem lib. i. Sat. iii Callinaria nuncupatur.
units.tr: The Campanians also have their own groves, above all the Sacred Grove and the Gallinarian Forest. Livy in book XXIV speaks of the Sacred Grove [ἀλσος ἱερὸν]. Strabo places the Liris, which is today the Garigliano, at the mouth, as Scipione Mazzella and Leander Alberti report. Livy places it three miles from Cumae, and Strabo writes that the nymph Marica was worshipped there. Servius on Virgil's Aeneid should also be consulted. Cicero, writing to Patrus, and Strabo in book V, who calls it the Gallinarian wood [Γαλλιναρίαν ὕλην], name the Gallinarian Forest. Pomponius Sabinus, coming closer to the place, says that it lay in the Gulf of Cumae, adding that Virgil in book VI of the Aeneid calls it the grove of Trivia. Today it is called La Peneta de Patria by Sanfelice. A pine of this place, faulty, is named in Juvenal book I, satire 3, as Callinaria.

units.la: Lucanorum sunt Silva Lucique Ebuli, Peregrinalis, Veliarum, Ebuli Silva perinfamis nomen habet ab Ebolo vicino oppido, quod tamen ultra flumen est in Campania seu Picentinis. Peregrinalis fauces excipiens Vallis Dianiæ, densitate arborum perobscura est; præsertim Ilicum, tantæ altitudinis, ut cœlum cacuminibus attingere videantur. Veliarum Lucos, ab Velia Lucanorum Urbe dictos, Hannibalem evasisse scribit Symmachus lib. ii. Epist. xii.
units.tr: The Lucanians have the Silva and the groves of Ebulus, the Peregrinalis and the Veliae. The Ebulus forest, notorious indeed, takes its name from the neighbouring town of Ebolus, which however lies across the river, in Campania or in the Picentine territory. The valley of Dianium, which receives the mouth of the Peregrinalis, is very dark with the density of its trees, above all of holm oaks, of such height that they seem to touch the sky with their tops. Symmachus, in book II, letter 12, writes that Hannibal escaped through the groves of the Veliae, named after Velia, the city of the Lucanians.

units.la: Bruttiorum est Rheginus vel Rheginorum Saltus; cuius meminit Solinus: Sila videtur dici Virgilio, & Vibio Sequestro; Sila Sallustio & Plinio; Σίλα Bruttis apud Strabonem lib. vi: Carminiacensis fortean in Libro Notitiarum, & Carmeianus in eo, qui de Limitibus. La Sila hodie per excellentiam ab Incolis vocari scribit Laurentius Ananiensis. Silvam hanc tanta Arborum varietate distinctam notat Gabriel Barrius in sua Calabria, ut id naturæ opus mortalium industria distributum videri possit. Patere in circuitu ad ducenta P.M. prodit Scipio Mazzella. Addit Strabo Picem Silvam hanc ferre optimam, arboribus esse præclare consitam, Aquæ copia præditam, 10 cc stadiis longam. Certe Picem Πρῖστοων quam memorant Scriptores, ex hac Silva colligi solitam, est verisimile. Dioscorides Βρυλλιον vocat cap. xcviii Vina Saltus huius laudat Cassiodor. lib. xii Variar.
units.tr: Among the Bruttii there is the Rhegine or the Rhegini forest, which Solinus mentions. Virgil and Vibius Sequester seem to call it Sila; Sallust and Pliny call it Sila; Strabo in book VI calls it Sila [Σίλα] among the Bruttii. Perhaps the Carminiacensis in the Book of Notitiae, and the Carmeianus in the one about the boundaries, refer to it. Laurentius Ananiensis writes that the inhabitants today call it, by preeminence, La Sila. Gabriel Barrius, in his Calabria, notes that this forest is so distinguished by the variety of its trees that the work of nature might seem to have been arranged by human industry. Scipione Mazzella reports that it extends around for about two hundred miles. Strabo adds that this forest bears the best pitch, is excellently planted with trees, is endowed with an abundance of water, and is 1,000 stades long. It is indeed likely that the pitch [πρῖστοων] which the writers mention was usually gathered from this forest. Dioscorides, in chapter 98, calls it brullion [Βρυλλιον], and Cassiodorus in book XII of the Variae praises the wines of this forest.

units.la: Apulorum Batinus sunt Saltus, & Lucus Gargani. Batinorum Saltuum, qui ab opido Apuliæ Batina dicti, meminit Horatius, cui Bantinos restituit ex M. SS. Codicibus Cruquius. De Luco Gargani sic scribit Leander Albertus in Apulia Daunia: Exteriora Crypta (quam, Michaelis Archangeli Domicilium, paullo ante delinearat) id est supremum eius Tectum virens densusque Lucus altissimis Arboribus operit; ex quibus multitudo maxima lapidum pendet, quos votis causa peregrinantes collo adligatos sursum in Montis tugum baiulant; itaque precibus patratis suspensos relinquunt. Admirationem profecto summam hac habet Silva, quod magno circumcirca spatio nullus ne frutex quidem appareat alius: quapropter Miraculum potius, quam res Naturalis habetur, tot & tam ingentes Arbores hic in vivum saxum radicatas. Pergit Leander: Mihi Adcola quum hic essem, narravere, circa Karolum viii Franciæ Regem, qui anno ab Christo nato ciↄ cccc xciiii Neapolitanum Regnum cepit, unam ab Gallo quodam Mlite casam, illamque protinus supplicio divino ex animatam concidisse.
units.tr: The Batinian woods and the grove of Garganus belong to the Apulians. Horace mentions the Batinian woods, named after the Apulian town of Batina; Cruquius restored the reading Bantinos from the manuscripts. Leander Alberti writes thus about the grove of Garganus in Apulia Daunia: The outer crypt (which he had described a little earlier as the dwelling of the Archangel Michael), that is, its uppermost roof, is covered by a green and dense grove of very tall trees, from which hang a very great number of stones. Pilgrims, for the sake of their vows, tie these to their necks and carry them up to the top of the mountain, and having finished their prayers they leave them hanging there. Indeed this wood has the greatest wonder, because for a wide area all around no other shrub at all appears; so that it is regarded as a miracle rather than a natural thing, that so many and such huge trees are rooted in the living rock. Leander goes on: When I was staying here as a resident, they told me that around the time of Charles VIII, King of France, who in the year of Christ 1494 took the kingdom of Naples, a hut of a certain French soldier was struck down at once by divine punishment, having been set on fire.

units.la: In Gallia Cis-Padana ubi Senius fluvius in Padusam Paludem defluit, Silva est Lucina; & prope confluentem cum Pado Renum, Pedanea Silva, quas Succinum flevisse fruitra credidit Antiquitas. Videndus Solinus in Polyhist. cap. xxiii.
units.tr: In Cisalpine Gaul, where the river Senius flows into the Padusan marsh, there is the Lucine Wood; and near the place where the Rhine joins the Po, the Pedanean Wood, which antiquity vainly believed to have wept amber. See Solinus, Polyhistor, chap. 23.

units.la: In Trans-Padana Castorum Lucum ad xii Lapidem distat ab Cremona apud Tacitum lib. xviii. Castorum Locus, inemendatius, Orosio lib. vii, cap. viii.
units.tr: In Transpadane Gaul, the Grove of the Castores lies twelve miles from Cremona, according to Tacitus, book 18. "Castorum Locus," less correctly, in Orosius, book 7, chap. 8.

units.la: Straboni denique apud Venetos suo sunt Luci, unus ab Iunone Argiva cognominatus; alter ab Diana Ætolica, alius ab Superiore, qui in Latio ad Anagninum Compitum.
units.tr: Finally, Strabo mentions among the Venetians their own groves: one named after Juno of Argos, another after Diana of Aetolia, and another after the Superior, who is at Anagninum Compitum in Latium.

units.la: CAPVT IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: Italiæ Sinus.
units.tr: The Gulfs of Italy.

units.la: QVÆ Terræ tribuenda notavi: succedunt, quæ Aquæ: ut sunt, Sinus, Portus, Navalia, Flumina, Vada, Paludes, Stagna, Fossa, Lacus, Fontes, Aqua, Balnea. Agmen ducunt Sinus.
units.tr: Having dealt with what I have noted as belonging to the land, I now turn to what belongs to the water: that is, gulfs, harbours, dockyards, rivers, fords, marshes, pools, ditches, lakes, springs, water, and baths. The gulfs lead the way.

units.la: Liguriæ præiacent Rapallinus, & Ericis. Rapallino, uti & Vallibidem, nomen ab Rapallo, nobili iuxta littus Vico. Ericis, sic ab Veneris cognomine dicti, mentio est apud Silium Italicum lib. viii & alios: hodie Golfo di Porto Venere vocatur. Vide quæ dicam in Portuum enumeratione.
units.tr: Off the coast of Liguria lie the Rapallinus and the Ericis. The Rapallinus takes its name, as does the nearby valley, from Rapallo, a noted town on the shore. The Ericis, so called from the surname of Venus, is mentioned by Silius Italicus in book 8 and by others. Today it is called the Gulf of Porto Venere. See what I say about it in the list of harbours.

units.la: Latio, Amyclanum Mare, ab Amyclis Latij quondam oppido dictum. Nominat Tacitus lib. iv Annalium. Non tam Mare est, quam Sinus, qui nunc Adcolis, ut notat Sanfelicius, il mare del Sperlunga.
units.tr: In Latium, the Amyclanum Mare is named after Amyclae, once a town of Latium. Tacitus mentions it in book 4 of the Annals. It is less a sea than a gulf, which the locals now call il mare del Sperlunga, as Sanfelicius notes.

units.la: Campaniæ, Baianus. Sic à Baiis Cumanorum oppido plerisque appellatur; qui Κυμαῖος à Strabone, cum inter Athenæum & Misenum Promontoria describente: addenteque eumdem ab Eratosthene Cumanum vocari. Hodie Golfo di Napoli. Lucrinum nuncupat Symmachus lib. ii. Epist. Quidam etiam Puteolanum & Avernum. In Itineraria Tabula Crater fluvius ter nominatur, Long. cIII, Lat. 7. Long. cIV, Lat. 6; Long. denique cv, Lat. 6. nonnulla confusione: videndum num scribere voluerit, quicumque exaravit Tabulam, Craterem Sinum; sed is locandus fuisset in eadem Tabula Long. xciv, Lat. 8.
units.tr: In Campania is the Baianus, so called by most people after Baiae, a town of the Cumaeans. Strabo calls it Κυμαῖος [Cumaean] when he describes the headlands between Athenaeum and Misenum, adding that Eratosthenes called it Cumanum. Today it is the Gulf of Naples. Symmachus, in book 2 of his Letters, calls it the Lucrinum. Some also call it the Puteolanum and the Avernum. In the Itinerary Table the Crater fluvius is named three times, at longitude 103, latitude 7; longitude 104, latitude 6; and finally longitude 105, latitude 6. There is some confusion here. Whoever drew the Table may have meant to write Craterem Sinum, but in that case it should have been placed in the same Table at longitude 94, latitude 8.

units.la: Ad Lucaniam est Peitanus. Sic cum aliis nominat Plinius: in Itineraria Tabula corrupte Pesianus scribitur: Græcis Ποσειδωνιάτης appellatur. Nomen est sortitus à Pæstio, Lucaniæ Urbe, quæ Græcis Ποσειδωνία. Hodie, ut Leandro videtur, Golfo Agropolitano; unde & quibusdam Acropolitanus Sinus; vel, ut Ananiensi placet & Mazzellæ, di Salerno. Incipit ab ora Picentinorum, ac inde flexu sinuatur usque ad Promontorium Posidoniate, ut Strabo, Plinius & Ptolemæus ostendunt.
units.tr: Near Lucania is the Peitanus. Pliny names it thus, along with others. In the Itinerary Table it is wrongly written Pesianus. The Greeks call it Ποσειδωνιάτης [Poseidoniates]. It takes its name from Paestum, a city of Lucania, which the Greeks called Ποσειδωνία [Poseidonia]. Today, as it seems to Leandro, it is the Gulf of Agropoli, whence some also call it the Acropolitanus Sinus; or, as Ananias and Mazzella prefer, the Gulf of Salerno. It begins at the shore of the Picentines and curves in a bend as far as the headland of Posidonia, as Strabo, Pliny and Ptolemy show.

units.la: Ad Brutiorum littora Hipponiates vficut Sinus. Ἱππωνιάτης ab Hippone oppido, quod Romanis postea Vibo Valentia (unde & Vibonensis) Straboni & Ptolemæo vocatur, qui Ναπηΐν ab Urbe Napitia apud Strabonem. Bruttius Marciano à Bruttiis Populis: Terinæus, ab Terina Civitate, hodie Teriana, Thucydidi lib. vi & Plinio lib. iii nat. hist. qui hunc cum Scyllaceo versus Orientem ex adverso Peninsulam Italiæ & Isthmum Stadiorum clx, ut notat Strabo, efficere scribit. Facta tamen locorum Plinij commissione, Vibonensis pars potius Terinæi, quam cum Terinæo idem. Ἀκροπολίτης Aristoteli lib. vii de Rep. cap. x, ab Lametinis, qui Lametiam Urbem habebant. Aut idem abesse ab Scylletio, itinere dimidiati diei. Hodie Golfo di S. Eufemia.
units.tr: On the shores of the Bruttii lies the Hipponiates, also called a Sinus. The Ἱππωνιάτης [Hipponiates] is named from the town of Hippo, which Strabo and Ptolemy call by its later Roman name Vibo Valentia (whence also Vibonensis). Strabo's Ναπηΐν [Napitin] comes from the city of Napitia. The Bruttius is named by Marcian from the Bruttii people. The Terinaeus, from the city of Terina, today Teriana, is mentioned by Thucydides in book 6 and by Pliny in book 3 of the Natural History. Pliny writes that it, together with Scylaceum, forms towards the east, opposite the peninsula of Italy, an isthmus of 160 stadia, as Strabo notes. Yet if we compare the places as Pliny describes them, the Vibonensis is rather part of the Terinaeus than the same thing as it. The Ἀκροπολίτης [Acropolites] is mentioned by Aristotle in book 7 of the Politics, chapter 10, and is named after the Lametini, who had the city of Lametia. Or it may be that it lies off Scylletium, half a day's journey away. Today it is the Gulf of Sant'Eufemia.

units.la: Ad oram Magnæ Græciæ Scylleticus est & Tarentinus: Σκυλλητικὸς Strabohi, qui hodie Golfo de Schilaci. Nomen illi ab Scylletio Urbe, quæ nunc Schylaci. Male nonnulli dictum volunt ab Scylla Scopulo, qui procul hinc ad Fretum Mamertinum. Versus meridiem Zephyrium, ad Septemtrionem Lacinium habet Promontorium, inque eo Crotonem Urbem. Superato Lacinio Sinus occurrit Tarentinus.
units.tr: On the coast of Magna Graecia lie the Scylleticus and the Tarentinus. The Σκυλλητικὸς [Skylletikos] of Strabo is today the Gulf of Squillace. It is named after the city of Scylletium, now Squillace. Some wrongly want it named after the rock Scylla, which lies far off, at the Strait of Messina. It has the Zephyrium headland to the south and the Lacinium headland to the north, and on that headland stands the city of Croton. Past the Lacinium the Tarentinus gulf comes into view.

units.la: Sic ab Tarento, urbe quondam nobilissima, Plinio vocatur; qui Thurinis ab Thurio, Salentinorum oppido, apud Ovidium lib. xv. Metamorph. Hodie Golfo di Taranto; vel, ut quidam notant, Mar grande; de qua appellatione dictum à me nonnihil Part. i. lib. iii cap. vi. Ingens eius est Ambitus vel Capacitas, inter duo Promontoria Lacinium & Iapygium. De eo Virgilius lib. iii Æneidos: Hinc Sinus Herculei, si vera est fama, Tarenti Cernitur.
units.tr: Pliny calls it thus after Tarentum, once a very noted city. Ovid, in book 15 of the Metamorphoses, speaks of it as the Thurinis, after Thurii, a town of the Salentini. Today it is the Gulf of Taranto, or, as some note, the Mar Grande, a name I discussed a little in Part 1, book 3, chapter 6. Its compass or capacity is immense, lying between the two headlands of Lacinium and Iapygium. Virgil speaks of it in book 3 of the Aeneid: "Hence the bay of Hercules at Tarentum is seen, if the report is true."

units.la: Tarentini pars est Sinus, qui nunc adcolis Golfo di Rosano, ab Civitate munitissima, Rosano, tribus ab mari P. M. sita.
units.tr: Part of the Tarentine gulf is the bay which the locals now call the Gulf of Rosano, after the well-fortified town of Rosano, set three miles from the sea.

units.la: Apuliam ornat Sinus, qui Frias Pomponio Melæ; hodie vero Golfo di Rode, nomen habens ab Roda oppido, quod Fria quondam Latinis, Τέγιον vel Τέγια Græcis, ut alibi àme notarum. Forum Iulium Tergestum, quem sic ab Tergeste Vrbe nominat Plinius; quique Ptolemæo, Luitarlio & Stephano Aquileia, ab Aquileia, Sinui adiacata. Prius nomen hactenus obtinuit. Dicitur enim hodie Golfo de Trieste. Intimus est Maris Hadriatici recessus.
units.tr: Apulia is adorned by a gulf which Pomponius Mela calls the Frias. Today it is the Gulf of Rodi, named after the town of Roda, which was once called Fria by the Latins and Τέγιον or Τέγια [Tegion or Tegia] by the Greeks, as I have noted elsewhere. Pliny names the Forum Julium Tergestum, after the city of Tergeste. Ptolemy, Lupiarius and Stephen call it Aquileia, after the city of Aquileia, which lies by the gulf. The former name has held so far, for today it is called the Gulf of Trieste. It is the innermost recess of the Adriatic Sea.

units.la: Iltriam denique Liburnia, cui illabitur Draconia fluvius: & Flanatius, sic Plinio dictus ab Flanatitus incolis: Φλανατικὸς Stephano; Polaticus Melæ, Libarnicus Crosio; Carnarium hodie, vulgo Quarnero vel Carnero, quam Carnivorum, ob violentiam maritimorum Fluctuum, inquit Leander, qua frequenter hic Naufragia fiunt, tamquam in hominum carnificina. Longitudinem habet millium lx; Latitudinem, inter Niam & Sintec-in Insulas, millium amplius xxx, utque ad xl; continetque moditas Insulas. Nominatur in Itineraria Tabula inter Iltriam & Liburniam Portus Planaticus, non ferendum Flanaticum.
units.tr: Finally, Istria has the Liburnia, into which the river Draconia flows, and the Flanatius, so called by Pliny from the Flanatitus inhabitants; Stephen gives Φλανατικὸς [Flanatikos]. Mela has Polaticus, Crosius Libarnicus. Today it is called the Carnarium, commonly the Quarnero or Carnero. Leander says it was once called the Carnivorum (the flesh-eating gulf), because of the violence of its sea waves, where shipwrecks happen often, as if it were a slaughterhouse of men. It is 60 miles long. Its breadth, between the islands of Nia and Sinte, is a little over 30 miles, and about 40 in places; it contains many islands. In the Itinerary Table, between Istria and Liburnia, the name Portus Planaticus appears, which should not be tolerated as Flanaticum.

units.la: Caput hoc in Freto hujus; ne nutquam hoc indicetur) quod Brutios inter Italiæ populos & Siculos Insulanos. Scilla dicitur Ciceroni lib. iii. de Nat. Deorum, Tacito lib. vi Annalium, & Plinio lib. xix. nat. hist. cap. 1: mentissime quod inter duas Scyllas. Nam Italiæ partem, à Brutiis aliisque Conregionalibus habitatam, etiam Scyllam apud Veteres Scriptores appellatam, tuo loco dicitur. Rhegium vocatur Stratoni ab Rhegis Iulio; Scyllaeum Athenæo lib. vii ab Scopulo Scylla, qui Freto versus Occidentem: Charybdis autem Thucydidi lib. iv ab altero, qui ad Orientem, à quibus multa Navigantibus pericula: unde & Fretum ipsum Naufragum cognominat Ovidius lib. xiii. Metamorph. Mazeda Homero & Apollonio lib. iv. Trajectus dicitur in Antonini Itinerario. Caulla nota: Lonia Benjamino. Hodie Faro de Messina, ab Messana Civitate, quæ Antiquis etiam Mamertina (unde Fretum ipsum quondam Mamertinum;) de quo nonnulla fortean Parte postrema, de Insulis, ubi de Sicilia. Describunt Aristoteles in Admirandis & Pausanias in Eliacis.
units.tr: This headland is in the strait of Italy (lest anyone think it is nowhere indicated), which lies between the Bruttii, among the peoples of Italy, and the islanders of Sicily. Cicero, in book 3 of On the Nature of the Gods, Tacitus in book 6 of the Annals, and Pliny in book 19, chapter 1, of the Natural History, call it Scilla: quite rightly, since it lies between two Scyllas. For the part of Italy inhabited by the Bruttii and their neighbours is also called Scylla by ancient writers, as will be said in its proper place. Strabo calls it Rhegium, after the Rhegians, Julius; Athenaeus in book 7 calls the Scylaeum after the rock Scylla, which lies to the west of the strait; and Thucydides in book 4 calls the Charybdis after the other, which lies to the east. From these comes the many dangers for sailors, and for this reason Ovid in book 13 of the Metamorphoses calls the strait itself the Naufragum (shipwrecking). Homer and Apollonius in book 4 call it Mazeda. It is called the Trajectus in the Itinerary of Antoninus. The Caulla is a known mark. Benjamin calls it the Lonia. Today it is the Faro di Messina, after the city of Messana, which the ancients also called Mamertina, whence the strait itself was once called the Mamertinum. I will perhaps say something more about this in the final part, on the islands, where I treat Sicily. Aristotle, in the Admirable Things, and Pausanias, in the Eliaca, describe it.

units.la: CAPVT X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: Italiæ Portus.
units.tr: The Ports of Italy.

units.la: POST Sinus nominavi Portus. Italiam plerisque in locis Λιμένων esse, scribit Strabo lib. vi; & quos habet Portus, magnos esse atque admirabiles, horum illud adversus Exterorum Incursiones utiu esse, hoc ad invadendos vicinos Exteros, & expeditam Mercaturæ copiam conducere. Portus igitur explicaturus, initium quam commodissime sumturum me arbitror ab Itinerario Portunum vel Positionem Navium, quod apud Antoninum ab Vrbe Niceam, & porro Arelatum usque producitur. Quum autem animus mihi sit in Portuum indicio ab Occasu versus Ortum, id est ab Vario Fluvio, qui Terminus hodie inter Liguriam & Galliæ Provinciam, ad Tiberim, qui inter Etruriam & Latium, progredi, necesse habeo Ordinem, qui apud Antoninum, invertere. Illud tamen hac Antonini notatione consequemur, ut certam tamen habituri cognitionem omnium Portuum, qui ad maritimas Liguriæ Etruriæque oras, olim senescente Imperio, fuerunt. Iter Antonini ad præpositerim seriem reductum, inque pauciora verba contractum, nec non cum Itineraria Tabula commissum, sic habet: Antonini Itinerar. | Itineraria Tabula. Hodierna Nomencl. Antipoli Niciam Plag. M. P. xvi. ......... Nizza Olivulam, Portus, M. P. v. .........
units.tr: AFTER the bays I come to the ports. Strabo, book VI, writes that in many places in Italy the harbours are called Λιμένων, and that the ports it has are large and remarkable: one serves to defend against incursions by foreigners, the other to attack neighbouring foreigners, and both provide convenient access for trade. Intending to explain the ports, I think it best to begin with the Itinerary of Antoninus, the Portunum or Positio Navium, which runs from the City to Nice and on to Arles. Since, however, I mean in this index of ports to proceed from west to east, that is from the river Varus, which today forms the boundary between Liguria and the Province of Gaul, to the Tiber, which lies between Etruria and Latium, I must reverse the order found in Antoninus. Nevertheless, by following this notation of Antoninus we shall gain a certain knowledge of all the ports which lay along the sea coasts of Liguria and Etruria when the Empire was growing old. The Itinerary of Antoninus, reduced to a continuous order, shortened into fewer words and compared with the Table of Itineraries, reads as follows: Antoninus' Itinerary | Table of Itineraries | Modern name. Antipolis to Nice, 16 miles ......... Nice. Olivula, Port, 5 miles .........

units.la: Surita legit ad Olbiam, cuius alij meminerunt. Sed Olbia Situs reclamat. Ptolemæus enim inter Cytharisten Promontorium & Argentij Fluvij Ostium Olbiam collocat: Strabo etiā inter Olbiam & Antipolin Navale Cæsaris Augusti statuit, Forum Iulij nuncupatum: adeo ut Olbia omnino pertinuerit ad Partem illam Galliæ Narbonensis, quæ Provinciæ nomen obtinuit. Anaonem Portus, M.P.XII. ....... Iulias Simlerus legit Naonem. Avisionem Portus; M.P.IV. ....... Monœco. Herculem Monœcum Portus. M.P.XXII. .......
units.tr: Surita reads "to Olbia", which others also mention. But the situation rules this out. For Ptolemy places Olbia between the Promontory of Cytharista and the mouth of the river Argentius; Strabo too places Caesar Augustus' naval station, called Forum Iulii, between Olbia and Antipolis. So Olbia certainly belonged to that part of Gallia Narbonensis which obtained the name of Province. Anaon, port, 12 miles ....... Iulias Simler reads Naon. Avision, port, 4 miles ....... Monoecus. Hercules Monoecus, port, 22 miles .......

units.la: Hæc olim vitiosissima scriptura in libris Antonini concepta legebantur. Meminerunt Tacitus, Plinius, Ptolemæus, & Ammianus. Sic Strabo lib. IV: ὁ δὲ ἐκ Μονοίκου λιμὴν ἐρημος ἐστιν, ὁ μὲν μεγάλως, ἀλλὰ πλάτος ναυσὶν, ἐχων ἱερὸν Ἡρακλέους Μονοίκου καλούμενον, &c. Albintimilium Plag. M.P.XVI. Albentimillum. Vintimiglia.
units.tr: This very corrupt reading was formerly found in the copies of Antoninus. Tacitus, Pliny, Ptolemy and Ammianus mention these places. So Strabo, book IV: "The harbour from Monoecus is deserted; it is large, but broad enough for ships, and has a temple of Hercules called Monoecus," etc. [ὁ δὲ ἐκ Μονοίκου λιμὴν ἔρημος ἐστιν, ὁ μὲν μεγάλως, ἀλλὰ πλάτος ναυσὶν, ἔχων ἱερὸν Ἡρακλέους Μονοίκου καλούμενον, &c.] Albintimilium, Plag. 16 miles. Albentimillum. Ventimiglia.

units.la: Consule Liguriam meam. Portus Mauritij, M.P.XII. ....... Porto Marifo.
