units.tr: See my Liguria. Port of Mauritius, 12 miles ....... Porto Marifo.

units.la: Portus non tam rei, quam nomine. Albingaunum Portus, M.P.XII. Albingaunum. Albenga. Vada Sabatia Portus, M.P.XVIII. Vadus Sabates. Vado.
units.tr: A port more in name than in fact. Albingaunum, port, 12 miles. Albingaunum. Albenga. Vada Sabatia, port, 18 miles. Vadus Sabates. Vado.

units.la: Adi Liguriam meam. Inter hunc & sequentem celebris hodie Portus est Savona, Gennam Portus, M.P.XXX. Genna. Genoa.
units.tr: See my Liguria. Between this and the following, the port that is famous today is Savona. Genna, port, 30 miles. Genna. Genoa.

units.la: Plene suo loco. Portum Delphini, M.P.XVI. ....... Porto sina.
units.tr: Fully in its place. Portus Delphini, 16 miles ....... Porto Sina (Porto Fino).

units.la: Meminit Plinius. Portum Veneris, M.P.XVIII. ....... Porto di Venere.
units.tr: Pliny mentions it. Portus Veneris, 18 miles ....... Porto di Venere.

units.la: Notus hic etiam in Latino Ptolemæo; quum tamen in Græco non habeatur.
units.tr: This is known here also in the Latin Ptolemy, though it is not found in the Greek.

units.la: Huic ex adverso Portus est Ericis: cuius meminit Ptolemæus. Porto di Frice; vel simpliciter Erice. Segestam Posit. M.P.XXX. ....... Sestri.
units.tr: Opposite this is the port of Ericis, which Ptolemy mentions. Porto di Frice, or simply Erice. Segesta, position 30 miles ....... Sestri.

units.la: De Liguriæ porro Portubus sic scribit Strabo lib. IV: ὁ λιμὴν δὲ ἡ ἀρχαία ἄνωθεν μέχρι τυρρηνίας ἀπὸ Μονοίκου λιμένος, ἐπὶ τὴν ἀλλὰ ἔπειτα, ἐν Ἡρακλείας ... Ἀντωνῖνος ad Etrur-iæ Portus sic pergit: Lunam ad Fluvium Macram. M.P.XXX. Luna.
units.tr: Strabo, book IV, writes thus about the ports of Liguria: "The ancient harbour from the harbour of Monoecus up to Etruria, ... then ... Heracleia ..." [ὁ λιμὴν δὲ ἡ ἀρχαία ἄνωθεν μέχρι Τυρρηνίας ἀπὸ Μονοίκου λιμένος, ἐπὶ τὴν ἀλλὰ ἔπειτα, ἐν Ἡρακλείας ...]. Antoninus, continuing with the ports of Etruria, goes on: Luna, at the river Macra, 30 miles. Luna.

units.la: Dicebatur ab hoc opido Portus Lunensis, Livio, Straboni, Plinio notus. Lunai Portum vocat Ennius 1 Annalium, & ex eo Persius Satyra VI: Lunai Portus est opera cognoscere Cives.
units.tr: From this town the port was called Portus Lunensis, known to Livy, Strabo and Pliny. Ennius, in book I of the Annals, calls it Lunai Portum, and from him Persius, Satire VI: "It takes effort to get to know the citizens of Luna's port."

units.la: Vide quæ noto ad eundem Poëtam.
units.tr: See what I note on the same poet.

units.la: Portum hunc amplitudine tanta testatur Strabo, ut omnibus, quæ toto Mari versantur, Navigiis excipiendis sufficiat: nec solum late vasteque patere; sed etiam tutissimum esse, quod iugis montium præcelsis undiquaque claudatur, ideoque longissimum, in omnes partes & utrumque Littus & Sardiniā prospectū habeat. Silius Italicus lib. VIII. Tunc quos à niveû exegit Luna Metallis Insignis Portu, quo non spatiosior alter Innumeras cepisse rates & claudere Pontû.
units.tr: Strabo attests that this port is so large that it is enough to receive all the ships that sail in the whole sea; and it not only lies wide and spacious, but is also very safe, because it is shut in on every side by the high ranges of mountains, and so it has a very long view in every direction, over both shores and over Sardinia. Silius Italicus, book VIII: "Then those whom Luna, famous for its snowy metals, sent forth, a port no more spacious than any other to receive countless fleets and enclose the sea."

units.la: Amplis eius faucibus Infula modica est obiecta, vim Austri Africique prohibens. Flumen in eum se exonerat Macra, contra quod in ostio Portus binæ iacent Infulæ aliæ modicæ, Tinus & Tinettus.
units.tr: At its wide mouth lies a small island, which blocks the force of the south and south-west winds. The river Macra empties into it there, and opposite it, at the mouth of the port, lie two other small islands, Tinus and Tinetus.

units.la: Portum Pisanum, M. P. IX. Huius nulla apud Veteres mentio: frequens autem in Pisanorum & Genuensium rebus, super Sardiniæ Infulæ imperio; & postea in expeditionibus Aragonensium Regum Maritimis, quibus Sardiniæ Regnum sibi adseruerunt.
units.tr: Port of Pisa, 9 miles. No mention of it among the ancients; but it is frequent in the histories of the Pisans and Genoese, in the contest over rule of the island of Sardinia, and later in the maritime expeditions of the kings of Aragon, by which they claimed the kingdom of Sardinia for themselves.

units.la: Vada Portus, M. P. XVIII. Vadis Volaterris. Vada.
units.tr: Port Vada, 18 miles. Vadis Volaterris. Vada.

units.la: Hodie Latine scribentibus Portus Ligurnus, vulgo Livorno. Sed Situs non patitur. Ligurnus est inter Pisas & Vada, medio fere itinere. Ligurnum Labronem appellare videtur Cicero ad Q. Fratrem lib. II. Epist. III. Liburnum Portum habent nescio unde Ptolemæi Interpretes; male etiam collocantes inter Lunam & Arnum. Censet Volaterranus Portum Ligurnum esse, quem Antoninus Salepronem nominat. Falso. Antoninus enim Iter Arelatense ab Urbe Roma describens Aurelia Via Salepronem ab Lacu Aprili abesse ostendit M. P. XII: at Ligurnus ab eo Lacu supra I millia distat. Reclamat etiam series, quæ in Itineraria Tabula. Celebris quidem Portus est; sed paucarum Navium capax, & nondum profunde effossus. Ante ingressum Turres quatuor, in mari tres ab Maximiliano Imp. dissectæ: quarta iam renovata, & impositā ei cu. stodia est. Plura apud Laurentium Schraderum, in monumentis Italiæ.
units.tr: Today writers of Latin call it Portus Ligurnus, commonly Livorno. But the position does not allow this: Ligurnus lies between Pisa and Vada, roughly halfway along the way. Cicero, in book II, letter III, to his brother Quintus, seems to call Ligurnum Labro. The editors of Ptolemy have a port Liburnum from I know not where, and they too wrongly place it between Luna and the Arnus. Volaterranus thinks that the port Ligurnus is the one Antoninus calls Salepro. This is false. For Antoninus, describing the Arles route from the City of Rome, shows that Salepro lies 12 miles from Lake Aprilis along the Aurelian Way; but Ligurnus is more than a thousand paces from that lake. The sequence in the Table of Itineraries also contradicts it. It is indeed a famous port, but it can hold only a few ships, and it has not yet been dug out deeply. Before the entrance there were four towers, three of them in the sea, demolished by the Emperor Maximilian; the fourth has now been rebuilt, and a guard placed in it. More on this in Laurentius Schrader, in his Monuments of Italy.

units.la: Populonium Portus, M. P. XXX. Populonia. Porto Ferrato. Vide plene Leandrum in Tuscia.
units.tr: Populonium, port, 30 miles. Populonia. Porto Ferrato. See Leandro fully on Tuscany.

units.la: Falesiam Portus, Faleria legitur Itinerarij Rutilij libro II.
units.tr: Falesia, port; Faleria is the reading in book II of Rutilius' Itinerary.

units.la: Scabros Portus, M. P. XVIII. Ptolemæo, aliisque Portus Trassanus dicitur.
units.tr: Scabros, port, 18 miles. Ptolemy and others call it Portus Trassanus.

units.la: Almam Flumen Posit. M. P. VI. Arbia fiume.
units.tr: The river Alma, position 6 miles. Arbia, river.

units.la: Lacrum Aprilem Posit. M. P. XVIII. Lacus ipse pictus est; Prille. sed suppressa nomine.
units.tr: Lake Aprilis, position 18 miles. The lake itself is depicted, but its name is suppressed: Prille.

units.la: Portum Telamonis, M. P. XVIII. Telamone. Telamone.
units.tr: Port of Telamon, 18 miles. Telamone. Telamone.

units.la: Telamon Portus etiam Polybio, Plinio, Melaque notus. Hinc Τελαμών Ptolemæo Promontorium. Scribit Plutarchus Marium in Portum Etruriæ
units.tr: The port Telamon is also known to Polybius, Pliny and Mela. Hence Τελαμών is the name of a promontory for Ptolemy. Plutarch writes that Marius, being carried into the port of Telamon in Etruria,

units.la: Lines numbered 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 stand in the right margin beside the text. rix Telamonem delatum, descensione facta, Servos ad Pileum vocasse. Alminam Fluvium Posit, | M. P. ..... | Albinia fl. | Albegna fiume.
units.tr: on landing, called his slaves to the cap of liberty. The river Almina, position ..... miles ....... Albinia river. Albegna, river.

units.la: Antoninus hic ex Itineraria Tabula vulgataque appellatione emendandus videtur. Domitianae Getariae Posit. | M. P. VIII. | | Portum Herculis, | M. P. III. | Port Herculus. | Porto Hercole.
units.tr: Antoninus here seems to need correcting from the Table of Itineraries and the common name. Domitiana Getaria, position 8 miles. Port of Hercules, 3 miles. Port Herculus. Porto Hercole.

units.la: Straboni est notus. 10 Arnimen fluvium Posit. | M. P. xxv. | Armenita fl. | Pescia, ni fallor. Regas Posit. | M. P. IIII. | ......... | ........
units.tr: Known to Strabo. The river Arnimen, position 25 miles. Armenita, river. Pescia, unless I am mistaken. Regas, position 4 miles.

units.la: An Pyrrhusae Strabonis? Quintianum Posit. | M. P. VI. | ........ | ........ Multinum Posit. | M. P. III. | ......... | ....... Gravisca Posit. | M. P. IIII. | Gravisca. | Monte alto.
units.tr: Is this Strabo's Pyrrhusa? Quintianum, position 6 miles. Multinum, position 3 miles. Gravisca, position 4 miles. Gravisca. Monte Alto.

units.la: Coralium hic nasci perhibet Plinius. Rapinium Posit. | M. P. VI. | ........... | .......
units.tr: Pliny says that coral is born here. Rapinium, position 6 miles.

units.la: In aliis est Rapinum. Algae Posit. | M. P.III. | ........... | .......... 20 Centumcellas Posit. | M. P. III. | Centum cellis. | Citta vecchia.
units.tr: In other copies it is Rapinum. Algae, position 3 miles. Centumcellae, position 3 miles. Centum Cellis. Civita Vecchia.

units.la: Vide Etruriam meam. Castrum Novum, | M. P. V. | Castro Nove. | Corneto. Fanapionem, | M. P. VII. | Punicum. | ........
units.tr: See my Etruria. Castrum Novum, 5 miles. Castro Nove. Corneto. Fanapio, 7 miles. Punicum.

units.la: Ania videtur Melae. Pyrgos Posit. | M. P. III. | Pyrgos. | ........ Portum Augusti: | M. P. XXXVIII. | Augustam habet Itineraria Tabula huius Portus sculpturam, sed nullum Nomen adscriptum. | Porto di Roma.
units.tr: Ania seems to be Mela's. Pyrgos, position 3 miles. Pyrgos. Port of Augustus, 38 miles. The Table of Itineraries shows a carving of this port, which it calls Augusta, but no name is written beside it. Porto di Roma.

units.la: 30 De eo plene dixi in Tuscia mea: ideoque non futurus hic in explicando prolixior: ad reliquos pergo.
units.tr: 30 I have dealt with this fully in my Tuscia, so I will not be more lengthy in explaining it here. I now turn to the rest.

units.la: Portus, Navium que Positiones Liguriae Tusciaeque hactenus commemoravi ex maritimo Antonini Itinerario: progredior iam, aliorum Auctorum sequutus vestigia, versus Euronotum, lectis Latij, Campaniae, reliquarumque Italiae ad Mare cum Inferum, tum Superum Regionum littoribus.
units.tr: I have so far mentioned the ports, and the stations of ships of Liguria and Tuscany, from the maritime Itinerary of Antoninus. I now proceed, following the footsteps of other authors, toward the south, and I survey the coasts of Latium, Campania, and the remaining maritime regions of Italy, both the Lower and the Upper.

units.la: Quod ad Latium, Neronem Principem Portum operis sumptuosissimi ad Antium fecisse, scribit in eius Vita cap. ix Suetonius. Aiaeis Aμβια habet Apollonius ad Circeium Montem: Aeaam ab Virgilio nominari, notat Servius, tribus Diphthongis ab spernantium voce, propter celebratas illic Corporum Mutationes. Caieta Portum fuisse celeberrimum, amplissimeque ab Antonino Pio Imperat. refectum, refert Spartianus. Hodie nullus est.
units.tr: As for Latium, Suetonius writes in the life of Nero, chapter 9, that the Emperor Nero built a harbour at Antium, a work of very great expense. Apollonius mentions Aeaea [Αἰαία] near Mount Circeius, and Servius observes that Vergil names it Aeaea, with three syllables, from the word of those who say it so, on account of the famous transformations of bodies that happened there. Caieta was a very famous harbour, and was greatly restored by the Emperor Antoninus Pius, as Spartianus reports. Today there is none.

units.la: 40 Portum Iulium, inquit Suetonius in Augusto, apud Baias immisso in Lucrinum & Avernum Lacum Mari, effecit. Virgilius in Georgicis,
units.tr: 40 The Julian harbour, says Suetonius in the life of Augustus, was made near Baiae by admitting the sea into the Lucrine and Avernus lakes. Vergil in the Georgics says:

units.la: Iulia qua Ponto longe sonat unda refuso.
units.tr: Where the Julian wave resounds far off, the sea poured in.

units.la: Iulium undam vocat Puteolanum Portum, ut addunt Servius & Philargyrius. Legendus de eo Mazzella, in Antiquitatibus Puteolanorum. Baianus Portus altissimus in littore conspicitur; qui licet aedificia nulla habeat circumpolita, numquam tamen de veteri celebritate quidquam remisit.
units.tr: The Julian wave is what Servius and Philargyrius say he calls the Puteolan harbour. On this, see Mazzella, in his Antiquities of Puteoli. The Baian harbour is seen on the shore, very deep; although it has no buildings around it, it has never lost anything of its old fame.

units.la: Velinum Portum, ab Velia, antiquo Lucaniae opido, quod periit, sic dictum, memorat Virgilius lib. vi Æn.
units.tr: The Velinian harbour, named after Velia, an ancient town of Lucania that has perished, Vergil mentions in Book 6 of the Aeneid:

units.la: 50 Portusque require Velinos.
units.tr: 50 and seek the Velinian harbours.

units.la: Utitur multitudinis numero, quod hoc littore plurimi sint Portus, quamquam exigui. Vide Agellium lib. x. noct. Attic. cap. xvi.
units.tr: He uses the plural, because on this shore there are many harbours, though small. See Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights, Book 10, chapter 16.

units.la: Herculis Portus prope Vibonem in Brutiis a Plinio describitur lib. iii. cap. v. Formiculas vocant Adcolae, ut tradit Barrius in sua Calabria. Metaurus Navium statio Straboni in Brutiis ad Metaurum Fluvium. Metaurum vocare videntur Pomponius Mela & Stephanus.
units.tr: The harbour of Hercules near Vibo in Bruttium is described by Pliny, Book 3, chapter 5. The local people call it Formiculae, as Barrius reports in his Calabria. Metaurus was a station for ships in Bruttium, by the river Metaurus, according to Strabo. Pomponius Mela and Stephanus seem to call it Metaurum.

units.la: Oresii Portus in Magna Graecia apud eumdem Plinium est: qui Ravagose ab Incolis colis dicitur, codé Barrio notante. Castra Hannibalis, Magnæ Græciæ Portum, celebrant Solinus & Plinius: hodie Le Castelle, ut opinatur Icander. Tarentinum Portum habet ibidem Plinius, ab nobilissima quondam Vrbe Tarento sic nominatum. Scribit Strabo lib. vi Portum hunc, maximum atque pulcherrimum, Ponte fuisse inclusum; itaduisque c amplitudine patuisse. Plura apud ipsum videat Lector. Nominatur vitiose Portus Salentinus in Tabula Itineraria; nisi κατ' ἐξοχὴν ita vocetur, quod ad Salentinorum Regionem.
units.tr: The harbour of Oresius in Magna Graecia is also in Pliny, which the inhabitants call Ravagose, as Barrius notes. The camp of Hannibal, a harbour of Magna Graecia, is mentioned by Solinus and Pliny; today it is Le Castelle, as Icander thinks. Pliny has in the same place the Tarentine harbour, so named after the once most noble city of Tarentum. Strabo writes in Book 6 that this harbour, the largest and most beautiful, was enclosed by a mole, and so opened out with a wide mouth. The reader may see more in Strabo himself. The Salentine harbour is wrongly named in the Itinerary, unless it is called so par excellence [κατ' ἐξοχήν], as belonging to the region of the Salentines.

units.la: Brundisium autem Salentinorum Vrbem Portu quondam fuisse nobilem, patet ex Ennij versu, qui apud Agellium lib. vi cap. vi:
units.tr: That Brundisium, a city of the Salentines, was once famous for its harbour is clear from a verse of Ennius, which Aulus Gellius quotes in Book 6, chapter 6:

units.la: Brundisium pulcro præcinctum præpete Portu. 10
units.tr: Brundisium, girded with a fair harbour open to the swift wind.

units.la: Sic Florus lib. i cap. xx: Salentini Picentibus additis, caputque Regionis Brundisium, incluso Portu, M. Attilio Duce. Plura ubi de Salentinis, cap. xxxii.
units.tr: So Florus in Book 1, chapter 20: The Salentines, with the Picentes added, and Brundisium, the capital of the region, with its harbour enclosed, under the leadership of Marcus Atilius. More on the Salentines is said where chapter 32 discusses them.

units.la: Garne Portus Italiæ, circa Garganum Montem, Plinio. ΓΑΡΝΗΤΑΙ sunt apud Goltzium in Nummis. Agasus, eidem Plinio, Portus in Apulia Pauna.
units.tr: Garne, a harbour of Italy near Mount Garganus, according to Pliny. There are ΓΑΡΝΗΤΑΙ [Garnētai] in Goltzius's coins. Agasus, also according to Pliny, is a harbour in Apulia Pauna.

units.la: Est iuxta Ancontanis hodie Portus, cum ab natura, tum ab humana industria munitus: aditu peropportunus, multarum Navium capax: ab Traiano Cæsare exstructus, adpositio etiam Arcu magni operis. Qualis eius fuerit structura, videre est in Traiani Nummis.
units.tr: Near Ancona there is today a harbour, fortified both by nature and by human industry: very convenient to approach, capable of many ships. It was built by Caesar Trajan, and an arch of great workmanship was set beside it. What its structure was like can be seen on the coins of Trajan.

units.la: Gloriatur Flaminia Portubus, cum aliis, tum Ariminensi; &, quem Bedesis Amnis, Bedesus à Plinio nominatus creat, Ravennate; de quo plenius in sequentibus. 20
units.tr: Flaminia takes pride in its harbours, both others and that of Rimini, and that of Ravenna, which the river Bedesis creates, called Bedesus by Pliny; of this more fully in what follows.

units.la: Sunt hodie in Marka Tarvisina Portus non pauci, alij tamen alijs celebriores: ut sunt qui vulgo, Porto Perotolo, Primetero, Magnazata, de Volame, della Fa, do Goro, del Tornase. Fossen, de Brondolo, de Chioza, de Malamoco, de S. Nicolo, de S Rasino, Treporte, de Piave, & alii.
units.tr: Today in the March of Treviso there are not a few harbours, some more famous than others, such as those commonly called Porto Perotolo, Primetero, Magnazata, de Volame, della Fa, do Goro, del Tornase, Fossen, de Brondolo, de Chioza, de Malamoco, de S. Nicolo, de S. Rasino, Treporte, de Piave, and others.

units.la: In Foro vero Iulio, qui Adcolis Porto de Livenza, S. Margareta, de Caorle, de Baseglego, de Taiamento, de Lignano, S. Andrea, de Busso, de Anfora, de Grado, de Canale.
units.tr: In Friuli, however, which the locals call Porto de Livenza, S. Margareta, de Caorle, de Baseglego, de Taiamento, de Lignano, S. Andrea, de Busso, de Anfora, de Grado, de Canale.

units.la: Ad Istriam denique Portus est Pola, Vallisque Forea, Africique & Flanaticus, quorum omnium, & aliorum, latiorem explicationem, ne nimium excrescat meum hoc Cosmographicum opus, prudens omitto; quum & plerique Portus post etiam in specialiore Vrbium designatione notentur. 30
units.tr: Finally, on the Istrian coast the harbours are Pola, Vallis Forea, Africi and Flanaticus. I wisely leave out a fuller account of all these and of others, so that this my Cosmographical work does not grow too large, since most harbours are also noted later in the more detailed description of the cities.

units.la: CAPVT XI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI.

units.la: Italiæ Flumina.
units.tr: The Rivers of Italy.

units.la: PORTVVM Enarrationi succedit Fluminum in quibus describendis, ea primum quæ in Tyrrhenum Mare se exonerant, indicabo; inde, quæ Ionium petunt Pelagus; postremo, quæ Hadriatico se miscent, indicabo. Præmonitum volo hic Lectorem, me ad Margines huius Capitis usurum Signo *; quod Flumini qualicumque præfectum, notat Nomen illud suum servare secumque in Mare deportare: Eo autem nudiatum, non Mare Flumen petere designat, sed cum Fluvio, qui proxime præcedit, Asterisco præmunitus, comiscetur, inque eo nomen amittere. 40
units.tr: After the harbours, the description of the rivers follows. In describing them I will first name those that empty into the Tyrrhenian Sea, then those that make for the Ionian Sea, and last those that mix with the Adriatic. I want the reader to be warned here that in the margins of this chapter I shall use the sign *. It marks a river of any kind that keeps its name and carries it with it into the sea. When the sign is absent, the river does not make for the sea by its own name but joins the river immediately before it, which is marked with an asterisk, and there loses its name.

units.la: Inter, quæ primi ordinis, locum primum obtinet Varus, non quidem dignitate vel amplitudine; minor enim est multis aliis: sed quod fines regat Galliarum & Italiæ; vel, ut specialius dicam, quod Limitem statuat inter Provinciam, & Liguriam; hanc Italiæ, illam Galliæ Regionem. Varus dicitur Lucano, Plinio, Melæ, Antonino, Itinerariæ Tabulæ, Latinisque ceteris; Ἄραξ Strabo, Ptolemæo, & aliis: Varo vernacule. Oritur in Alpium capite ex Monte Sallyo, supra villam D. Stephani. Rapide fluens, haud procul Nicæa, Massiliensium Mari immabitur. Nulla alia re memorabilis est Varus, quam quod, ut dixi, Italiæ Galliæque faciat discrimen, ut Veteres docent Scriptores. Inter eos Lucanus lib. i. de Bello Pharsalico: 50
units.tr: Among the rivers of the first rank, the Var holds the first place. It is not remarkable for its dignity or size, since it is smaller than many others, but because it marks the boundary between the regions of Gaul and Italy. More specifically, it divides Provence from Liguria, the former belonging to Gaul and the latter to Italy. The Var is called Varus by Lucan, Pliny, Mela, Antoninus, the Itinerary Tables and the other Latin writers. Strabo and Ptolemy call it Araxes [Ἄραξ], and the locals call it Varo. It rises at the head of the Alps, from Mount Sallium, above the villa of St Stephen. Flowing swiftly, it empties into the Sea of the Massilians not far from Nice. The Var is noteworthy for nothing else than what I have said: it makes the division between Italy and Gaul, as the ancient writers teach. Among them Lucan, in the first book of the Pharsalia:

units.la: Finis, & Hesperia, promoto milite, Varus.
units.tr: The boundary, and Hesperia, with the soldier advancing, the Var.

units.la: Plinius universæ Italiæ ambitum ab eo flumine ad Arsiam designat. Ptolemæus etiam Narbonensem Provinciam ad Ostia Vari terminat. Recipit, qua Occidentalior lior ejus ripa & Gallica, Fluvios, qui Vulgo Gallorum audiunt Caremp, Lazuire, Esseron: qua Orientalior & Italiam spectans, La Lince & La Vefubie: quorum alter in Itineraria Tabula Vulpi nominatur; posterior, credo. Sequuntur inde per Liguriæ Littora, Panion Pomponio, qui Pation hodie: ad Nicæam Maris misceens. Rutuba Lucano lib. 11. & Plinio lib. 111 cap. v notus: hodie Reta Leandro; Rodo ia Strumeç, Blondo, Ortelio. Merula Plinij subter Andoriam labitur; Vallem amœnam longamque M. P. viii. percurrens; mari jungitur, ubi Promontorio Merula nomen facit. Hodie Meira dicitur, ut Iustinianus & Leander notant. Nigro Centa est: Asfenta Stunicæ. Hoc fere loco scribitur in Itineraria Tabula Fluvius Lucus. Viterius Flumen est Portifera Plinio; Vulgo Porzevera. Oritur in Apennini lugis, curvaque millium xv Mare petit, Porsina corrupte Antonino. Fertor Plinio & Antonino, hodie Ferisano. Qui nunc Lazagna, & Itinerariæ Tabulæ, hodieque Latine scribentibus Labonis, Lavinia putatur Ptolemæo. Macra fluvius satis notus. Memincrunt præter alios Plinius, Antoninus in Itinerario Maritimo, & Tabula Peutingeriana. Strabo Maxpg, Ptolemæo Maxxaṁa, nescio an bene. Magra hodie. Celebratur & Livio, in cujus quibusdam Editionibus scribitur corrupte Mera. Profluit ex Apennino: Ligurianque ab Etruria dividens in Inferum provolvitur Mare. Tantus ejus est impetus, ut navigari commode nequeat, notante Sulpitio, in hæc Lucani: Calta Mer, nullasque vado qui Macramoriatus Alnus, zuina percurris in aquora Luna.
units.tr: Pliny marks the circuit of all Italy from this river to the Arsia. Ptolemy also ends the province of Narbonne at the mouths of the Var. On its western bank, which is Gallic, it receives the streams that the common people of Gaul call the Caremp, the Lazuire and the Esseron. On its eastern bank, which faces Italy, it receives the La Lince and La Vefubie; of these, the first is named Vulpis in the Itinerary Table, and the second, I believe, is the other one. Then along the coast of Liguria comes the Panion, which Pomponius mentions and which is today called the Pation; it mixes with the sea at Nice. The Rutuba, known from Lucan book 2 and Pliny book 3 chapter 5, is today called the Reta by Leander, and the Rodo by Strumeç, Blondus and Ortelius. The Merula of Pliny flows below Andora, running through a pleasant and long valley for eight Roman miles, and joins the sea where it gives its name to the promontory of Merula. Today it is called the Meira, as Justinian and Leander note. In Nigro it is the Centa; in Stunica, the Asfenta. Near this place the Itinerary Table writes the River Lucus. The Viterius, a river that Pliny calls Portifera and the common people call the Porzevera, rises in the ridges of the Apennines and makes for the sea in a winding course of fifteen miles. Antoninus corruptly calls it Porsina. The Fertor of Pliny and Antoninus is today the Ferisano. The river now called the Lazagna, and by Latin writers today Labonis, and in the Itinerary Table, is thought by Ptolemy to be the Lavinia. The Macra is a river well known. Among others, Pliny, Antoninus in the Maritime Itinerary, and the Peutinger Table mention it. Strabo calls it Makra [Μάκρα], Ptolemy Makxana; I do not know whether rightly. Today it is the Magra. It is also celebrated by Livy, in some editions of whom it is wrongly written Mera. It flows from the Apennines, and dividing Liguria from Etruria, rushes down into the Lower Sea. Its force is so great that it cannot be conveniently navigated, as Sulpitius notes on these lines of Lucan: The Macra, which the alder... and the river, which runs with shallows, flows into the waters of the moon.

units.la: Macram vocari ad eosdem versus scribit Omnibonus Vicentinus, quod ab Aquis maceat; ideoque, inquit, tum quia rapidior, tum quia vadosus, haud navigabilis est. Recipit Macra, præter alios, Laulam, Fagnonum, & Graceam. Connumerandus his qui Scaurt Ptolemæo: Vara Vulgo ex quorundam mente.
units.tr: Omnibonus of Vicenza writes, on the same lines, that the Macra is so called because it is "macerated" by its waters. Therefore, he says, it is not navigable, both because it is rapid and because it is shallow. Besides others, the Macra receives the Laula, the Fagnonus and the Gracea. The Scaurus of Ptolemy should be counted among these, and the Vara, according to the opinion of some.

units.la: Hactenus Flumina, vel quorum apud Ligures Ostia sunt, vel quis in alia Ingressus: sequuntur quæ Etruriæ consueverunt adcenseri. Hic primum ducunt agmen Lavenita & Frigidus. Prioris mentio in Itineraria Tabula, ubi tamen Avenita. Posterior Adcolis hodie Freddo. Post Versiliam inde Auler est Amnis; sic Plinio dictus & Cassiodoro, qui Aufur Rutilio, Ausus Straboni: Ofari vulgo. Leander tamen Serchium hodie dici notat; quem vide. Arnus mox succedit Livio lib. xxii, Plinio, & aliis memoratus: Arno Straboni & Ptolemæo: Arno vernacule. Nascitur, ut Strabo perhibet, ex Apennini latere dextro. Falteronam vocari Fontis locum, Auctores sunt Boccatius in libro Fluminum, Landinus Dantis Interpres in Purgatorio, & Facius Vbertus lib. 111. Cant vi. Modicis initijs principio inter Rupes horridas præcipitesque Convalles in Occasum tendit: deinde collectis Fontibus, Torrentibus, Amnibusque plurimis tumidior, magna cum Mole Florentinum ingreditur Agrum; Florentiaque & Pisa divisis, Mare petit. Multis adaugetur fluviis: quorum ad dextram illi ripam sunt inter alios Crasna; Solanus Rema, Refio, vulgo Refilho; Sera Mugellum lecans, receptis Ducaria & Ronta; Munio, Mugnone vernacule ex Apennino Florentiam adluens, ubi Arno jungitur; Terfola; Fisentium, cui Marina miscetur; Vmbro, Vmbrone vulgo, qui Stellæ junctim Arnum intrat; Pisita denique, Rivola dives, qui Pisinæ Valli dedit nomen: ad sinistram occurrunt Staggia; Corsolana; Archianum; Pilsilto; Clissa; Trinoga; Pesa, cui Fina & Greeva confluunt; Elsa denique & Era: quorum ille, paullum supra opidum Collis oriens, modico procursu tantum incrementi sumit, ut tres ingentes fumentarias fullonicasque Molas volvat; recipiens in alveum suum cum aliis Staggiam & Foeium. Post Arnum est Cecinna, Plinio Melaque laudatus. Visida, ni fallor corrupte, Itinerariæ Tabulæ, qui ex Montecti radicibus haud procul Mafia ortus, Agrum Volaterranum percurrens, ad Vrbem ipsam in Mare se præcipitat: hodie Cecina. Cornia ab Monte Rotundo profluit per Agrum Campilianum. Alma Antonino notus in Itinerario Maritimo, nomen retinens. Bruma, Prilis Plinio, ex Montibus Massæ vicinis prorumpens Lacus Prilis, de quo alibi, miscetur. Qui Vmbrone vulgo, Vmbro (alius ab eo, qui ad dextram Arno jungitur) est apud Plinium, Antoninum & in Itineraria Tabula, Οὐμβρων Stephano: ex Montibus oritur inter Senam & Aretium, supra Asciianum, juxta D. Guilmetij Castellumque Novum. Vmbronem Navigiorum aut capacem, memoratque Rutilius his versibus: xviii cap. xi, Via ab Urbe usque latere Consularis, quæ à Puteolis & ab Cumis Capuam ducit. Idem lib. iii cap. v. ibi de Campania loquitur. Laborini Campi sterminantur & in deliciis Alice politur a Mefio. Et lib. xvii cap. iv, Stipula crassitudinem tantam in Laborino Campo notat, ut incolæ ligni vice utantur. Describuntur ab Silio, Petronio, & Cornelio Severo. Fuit ibidem Stellatis Campus, Montibus & Fluminibus verba sunt Livii lib. xxii cuiusdam; meminit idem lib. ix & x. Stellatis Ager vocatur Suetonio in Cæsare. Sanctelicus ostendit cum hodie in Territorio Carmolo. Quod Mazzone vulgo dicatur, testis est Scipio Mazzella. De Campi Stellatis præstantia extat M. Tullii Testimonium in Oratione contra Rullum. Habet item Campania Agrum Falernum, de quo Plinius lib. xiv cap. vi: Falernus Ager a Ponte Campano læva petentibus Urbanam Coloniam Sullanam, nuper Capuæ contributam, incipit. Et addit: Faustianus autem circiter quatuor milliaria ab Vico prope Cedias, qui Vicus a Sinuessa vi millia abest. Nec ullum in Vino maior est clarritas: Faustianum Agrum circa Cumas locat Athenæus, ubi Vinum eius describit.
units.tr: So far the rivers whose mouths lie among the Ligurians, or which enter some other river. Next come those usually counted as belonging to Etruria. Here first lead the line the Lavenita and the Frigidus. The former is mentioned in the Itinerary Table, where however it is called Avenita; the latter is today called the Freddo by its neighbours. After the Versilia, the river next is the Auler; so called by Pliny and by Cassiodorus, who calls it Aufur, by Rutilius, and Ausus by Strabo; commonly it is called the Ofari. Leander notes, however, that today it is called the Serchio, which see. The Arno follows next, mentioned by Livy book 22, Pliny and others; it is the Arno for Strabo and Ptolemy, and the Arno in the vernacular. It rises, as Strabo says, from the right flank of the Apennines. Boccaccio in his book on rivers, Landino, the commentator on Dante's Purgatorio, and Fazio Uberti in book 3 canto 6 are authorities that the place of its source is called the Falterona. Starting from small beginnings, it first runs westward between steep rocks and precipitous valleys; then, gathering springs, torrents and very many streams, it swells and enters the Florentine territory with a great mass of water. Separating Florence from Pisa, it makes for the sea. It is increased by many rivers. On its right bank, among others, are the Crasna, the Solanus, the Rema and the Refio, commonly the Refilho; the Sera, which washes the Mugello, receiving the Ducaria and the Ronta; the Munio, which in the vernacular is the Mugnone, flowing from the Apennines past Florence, where it joins the Arno; the Terfola; the Fisentium, into which the Marina flows; the Umbro, in the vernacular Umbrone, which enters the Arno together with the Stella; and finally the Pisita, the Rivola, rich in water, which gave its name to the Pisine valley. On its left bank occur the Staggia, the Corsolana, the Archianum, the Pilsilto, the Clissa, the Trinoga and the Pesa, into which the Fina and the Greeva flow. Finally there is the Elsa and the Era. The Elsa, rising a little above the town of Collis, gains from a short course so much water that it turns three large mills for fulling and for making gunpowder; and into its bed, together with others, it receives the Staggia and the Foeius. After the Arno comes the Cecina, praised by Pliny and Mela. The Visida, unless I am mistaken in the corrupt reading of the Itinerary Table, rises at the foot of Montecti, not far from Massa; it runs through the territory of Volterra and throws itself into the sea at the city itself. Today it is the Cecina. The Cornia flows from Monte Rotondo through the Campiglia territory. The Alma is known from Antoninus in the Maritime Itinerary, keeping its name. The Bruma, which Pliny calls Prilis, bursting from the mountains near Massa, mixes with the Lake Prilis, about which I will speak elsewhere. That which is called the Umbrone by the common people, the Umbro (different from the one that joins the Arno on the right), is found in Pliny, Antoninus and the Itinerary Table; Stephanus has it as Oumbrōn [Οὐμβρων]. It rises from the mountains between Siena and Arezzo, above Asciano, near San Guglielmo and Castel Nuovo. Rutilius mentions the Umbro as capable of carrying ships, in these verses: book 18 chapter 11, the road from the city running alongside the Consular Way, which leads from Puteoli and Cumae to Capua. The same writer, book 3 chapter 5, speaks there of Campania: the Laborine Plains are laid waste and the Alice is polished by the Mefio. And book 17 chapter 4: he notes such a great thickness of stubble in the Laborine Plain that the inhabitants use it in place of wood. Silius, Petronius and Cornelius Severus describe them. There was also the Stellatine Plain, with its mountains and rivers, as Livy says in a certain passage of book 22; the same writer mentions it in books 9 and 10. Suetonius in his Caesar calls it the Stellatine Field. Sanctelicus shows that it is today in the territory of Carmolo, and that it is commonly called the Mazzone is attested by Scipio Mazzella. Cicero's testimony in his speech against Rullus gives evidence of the excellence of the Stellatine Plain. Campania also has the Falernian Field, of which Pliny writes in book 14 chapter 6: The Falernian Field begins on the left as one travels from the Campanian Bridge toward the Sullan colony of Urbana, recently added to Capua. And he adds: The Faustian field lies about four miles from the village near Cedia, which village is six miles from Sinuessa. Nor is there any greater renown for wine. Athenaeus places the Faustian Field near Cumae, where he describes its wine.

units.la: Visuntur in Langbardia Cisipadana Campi qui Livio lib. xli Macri: Str. boni Maxi: legebatur antea corrupte Ναυπου κάμπου: qui circa Mutinam & Parmam (ut Columella indicat lib. vii cap. ii) hodie Valle di Montirone, ut Leandro vocatur, sic scribent: A Finali sursum incedenti Paludes apparent multæ, vastissimaque Montironi Vallis: quæ ad dextram aggerem habet non latum quidem, sed qui longissime ab Amelia Via usque in Padi ferè ripam excurrat. Adcolæ Dorium vocant, Frumenti ubertate mirabili copiosum. Vallis hæc ab occasu longo illo clauditur tumulo, ab Mirandula, quæ superius inter Ambram & Occasum sita est, millibus quinque distante. Nos hanc longe latèque patentem Planitiem, Italis Valem appellatam Campos esse Nacros putamus, quorum meminit Strabo lib. v, ubi quotannis Forum habere solitum ait. Eos autem hoc modo designat: Inter Placentiam, inquit, & Ariminum sunt Parma, Mutina, Bononia, harum medio exigua quædam tacent opida, per quæ iter est Romam, Acara, Regium Lepidi, Nacri Campi, Claterna, & quæ sequuntur. Quamquam autem Volaterranus lib. iv Commentar. Urbanor. hos Campos ibi esse censeat, ubi nunc Carpi: Ego tamen, inquit Leander, exacte mecum hanc planitiem consideratam, Strabonisque verbis inspectis, hos ipsos esse Nacros Campos arbitror: idque ut sentiam, equidem maxima Antiquitatis vestigia, nobilissimaque ædificiorum opera musivo, ut vocant, ornatorum, quæ hic videmus, faciunt: ubi etiam indies Numismata varia, Pavimenta tessellata, vetusta Vasa, Sepulcrorum antiquorum ruinæ cum insignibus Lapillis inveniuntur. Et paulo post: Patent hi Campi latissime, nullis plane Arboribus, herbam ferentes colore rubellam, sapore salsam, Adcolæ Porcellanam vocant, ovina pastioni admodum expetitam: præterea que Salem hic ex terra igne decocta, magno tamen artificio, conficiunt. Pascua item hæc Planities peroportuna Gregibus Ovillis præbet; ex quibus Lana cum præcipua excellentia, tum incredibili copia percipiuntur.
units.tr: In Cisalpine Lombardy there are the plains which Livy in book 41 calls Macri, and which Strabo calls Maxi; the reading was formerly corruptly Naupou kampou [Ναυπου κάμπου]. These, around Modena and Parma (as Columella indicates in book 7 chapter 2), are today called the Valle di Montirone, as Leander names them. He writes thus: As one goes upward from Finale, many marshes appear, and the very vast valley of Montirone; this has on its right an embankment, not broad indeed, but which runs a very long way from the Amelian Way almost to the bank of the Po. The locals call it the Dorium, abundantly productive of wonderfully rich grain. This valley is closed on the west by that long hill, five miles from Mirandola, which lies further up, between the Ambra and the west. We believe that this plain, which stretches far and wide and which the Italians call the Valle, is the Nacri Plain, which Strabo mentions in book 5, where he says it used to hold a market every year. He describes them in this way: between Piacenza and Rimini lie Parma, Modena and Bologna; in the middle of these lie some small towns through which the road to Rome passes: Acara, Regium Lepidi, the Nacri Plains, Claterna, and those that follow. Although Volaterranus, in book 4 of his Urban Commentaries, thinks these plains are where Carpi now is, I, however, says Leander, having carefully considered this plain for myself and examined Strabo's words, think these are the very Nacri Plains. And I am convinced of this by the great remains of antiquity and the most noble buildings adorned with what is called mosaic work, which we see here; where also, every day, various coins, tessellated pavements, old vessels, and the ruins of ancient tombs with precious stones are found. And a little later: these plains extend very widely, quite without trees, bearing grass of a reddish colour and a salty taste, which the locals call Porcellana, and which is much sought after for sheep pasture. Moreover, the inhabitants make salt here from earth burned by fire, with considerable skill. This level ground also provides pasture very suitable for flocks of sheep, from which wool is obtained both in outstanding quality and in incredible quantity.

units.la: Rosea Campus (hic enim appellatur Varroni, qui Livio lib. x Rosellanus Ager) in Vmbria locatus legitur iuxta Lacum Velimum, unde apud Virgilium, Rosea Rura Velini, ad quem locum Servius notat, Lacum Velimum ei propinquum esse. Campus hic tantæ scribitur Fertilitatis; ut, auctore Varrone, Cæsar Vopiscus, quum Cautlam apud Centores ageret, Campos Roseos Italiæ dixerit esse Sumen: Injus enim (ut cap. iii. dixi) Perticam relictam postridie non apparere propter Herbam tantillo tempore succrescentem: quod etiam à Plinio commemoratur lib. xvii, cap. iiii. Pars huius Campi vel Agri videtur fuisse Amsanctis Vallis, de qua paulo ante.
units.tr: The Rosea Campus (for so Varro calls it, while Livy in book 10 calls it the Rosellanus Ager) is said to lie in Umbria, near the Lake Velimus, whence Virgil has "the rosy fields of Velinus"; Servius notes on this passage that the lake lies close by. This plain is written of as of such great fertility that, on the authority of Varro, Caesar Vopiscus, when he was conducting a lawsuit among the Centores, called it the Roseian Fields of Italy, Sumen: for (as I said in chapter 3) a pole left there the next day could not be seen because of the grass that grew up in so short a time. Pliny also records this in book 17, chapter 4. Part of this plain or field seems to have been the Amsanctian Valley, of which I spoke a little above.

units.la: Candius Campus, quem in Venetia ponit Florus, ibidem Teutones ab C. Mario trucidatos scribens, hodie Candia dicitur, non longe à Pado, in Lacinellini opidi tractu, ut Cathilionius refert. Restituitur Floro ab Vineto Claudius. Rauði Campi leguntur apud Vell. Paterculum lib. ii. Nescio an designet Sidonius in Panegyrico, qui Maiorano dicatus: Perque Cavi quondam dictos de nomine Campos.
units.tr: The Candian Plain, which Florus places in Venetia, when he writes there that the Teutones were slaughtered by Gaius Marius, is today called Candia, not far from the Po, in the district of the town of Lacinellinum, as Cathilionius reports. Vinetus restores "Claudius" in Florus's text. The Rauði Campi are mentioned in Velleius Paterculus, book 2. I do not know whether Sidonius in his Panegyric dedicated to Majorian means them: "and the fields once called Cavi after their name."

units.la: Caninos Campos legit Sigonius lib. xviii Histor. Occident.
units.tr: Sigonius, in book 18 of his History of the Western Empire, reads "Caninos Campos" (the Canine Fields).

units.la: In Romanula non longe ab Forcellis Prata longe latèque diffunduntur, quæ Salana vocant Adcolæ, quorum medio Propugnaculum est cum antiqua Turre: tenetque Vicinitatem Opinio Salam opidum hoc olim exstitisse loco, unde Prata Salæ nunc vulgo nuncupentur. Viarum, quæ per totam Italiam, atque adeo in ipsam usque Galliam ab Vrbe ducebantur, quarumque hodie passim exstant vestigia, enarratio potuisset etiam ad hoc Caput referri; sed commodior earum futura est explicatio in Latio, ubi quæ ad Romam (nam in Foro Romano ad Milliarium Aureum plerisque Viæ sua erant initia & capita) ejusque spectant magnitudinem, commemorantur.
units.tr: In Romanula, not far from the Forcellae, meadows spread out long and wide, which the locals call the Salanan meadows; in the middle of them is a fortress with an old tower. Opinion holds that the town of Sala once stood on this spot, and for that reason the meadows are now commonly called the Meadows of Sala. An account of the roads that ran from the City through the whole of Italy, and indeed into Gaul itself, and whose traces still survive here and there today, could also have been included in this chapter; but their explanation will be more suitable in the chapter on Latium, where those roads that lead to Rome (for in the Roman Forum, at the Golden Milestone, most roads had their beginnings and heads) and bear on its greatness are recorded.

units.la: CAPUT VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: Italiæ Silvæ, Luci, Nemora.
units.tr: The Woods, Groves and Copses of Italy.

units.la: ET Montes, & Valles Campique, de quibus proxime dixi, sunt superbiunt Silvis, Lucis, Nemoribus, quorum non pauca apud Priscos, etiam suis Nominibus leguntur celebrata.
units.tr: The mountains, valleys and plains of which I have just spoken abound in woods, groves and copses, many of which are celebrated in the writings of the ancients under their own names.

units.la: In Etruria, qui hodie Saltus, vernacule Bosco di Monte Fiascone, Volsinio, quod vulgo Bolsena, Viterbium euntibus occurrit, Lucum Vo sinensium ab Antiquis icinus probati Auctoris testimonio, nondum liquet, appellatum tradit Leander, addens Etruriæ cognominatum apud Plinium, pravius lib. III cap. V lectum & intellectum: Quocumque notus fuerit nomine, videtur designari ab Ovidio in Fastis: Stat vetus & densa pro nubibus Arbore Lucus, Aspice, concedes Nominis esse locum: Aspicit Ara preces, votivaque Thura Priorum; Ara per antiquas facta sine Arte manus.
units.tr: In Etruria, the wood which today is called in the vernacular Bosco di Monte Fiascone, and which meets travellers going to Viterbo from Volsinium (now Bolsena), is said by Leander to have been called by the ancients the Grove of the Volsinians. It is not yet clear, on the testimony of a reliable author, whether this is so. Leander adds that Pliny, in Book III, chapter V, gives it the surname of Etruria, though this is read and understood wrongly. Whatever its name, it seems to be referred to by Ovid in the Fasti: There stands an old grove, its tree dense as the clouds. Look, you will grant that it is a place worthy of the name. The altar looks upon the prayers and votive incense of our forefathers; an altar made by ancient hands without art.

units.la: In Cimino Etruriæ Monte quondam, calcari pauciens ob horrorem solita, fuit Silva, de qua sic Livius lib. IX: Silva erat Ciminia, magis tum invia atque horrenda, quam nuper fuere Germanici Saltus; nulli ad eam diem, ne Mercatori quidem, aditus. Eam intrare haud fere quisquam praeter Ducem ipsum audebat. Confirmat Florus in Etrusco Samniticoque bello Ciminium Saltum ante illa tempora invium plane, quasi Calydonium aut Hercinium, fuisse scribens. Hac tamen aetate, repurgatis munitisque locis illis, itaque habet non minus frequens atque tutum, quam olim intra Viterbum Via Cassia fuit, Romam Veiralla ducens. Post Vicum Bacchanum in Etruria silvosi se offerunt Saltus, qui Indigenis Bosco di Baccano, caedibus & latrocinio quondam perinfames. Veteres Mesiam Silvam videntur appellasse. De ea Livius lib. I, Silva, inquit, Mesia, Tuscia adempta. Et alibi pugnam Fabiorum contra Vejentes explicans, ex Silva Mesia vocem exauditam scribit, Olim ea commeare non sine summo discrimine licuit: sed hac nostra aetate partim quod maiori ex parte sit incendio vastata partim quod per maximam Romanorum Pontificum curam & diligentiam, praecipuèque Julii II, Leonis X, Clementis VII & Pauli III, huc ibi excisa, tam est tuta, ut absque metu quovis tempore peragretur.
units.tr: On Mount Ciminus in Etruria there was once a wood, which was often avoided because of its dread. Livy speaks of it thus in Book IX: There was the Ciminian Forest, then more impassable and terrible than the German forests have recently been. Until that day no one had access to it, not even a merchant. Scarcely anyone dared to enter it except the general himself. Florus confirms, in writing about the Etruscan and Samnite war, that the Ciminian Forest before those times was quite impassable, like the Calydonian or Hercynian. In our own age, however, those places have been cleared and fortified, and the road is now no less busy and safe than the Via Cassia once was within Viterbo, leading to Rome by way of Veii. After the village of Bacchanum in Etruria, wooded copses present themselves, known to the natives as the Bosco di Baccano, once notorious for murder and robbery. The ancients seem to have called it the Mesian Wood. Livy speaks of it in Book I: The Mesian Wood, he says, was taken from Tuscany. Elsewhere, describing the battle of the Fabii against the men of Veii, he writes that a voice was heard from the Mesian Wood. In the past it was possible to pass through it only at very great risk. In our own age, however, partly because most of it has been destroyed by fire, and partly because, through the very great care and diligence of the Roman Pontiffs, especially Julius II, Leo X, Clement VII and Paul III, it has been cut down here and there, it is so safe that it can be traversed at any time without fear.

units.la: In Latio apud Capenates Lucus fuit Feronia, quem canit Silius lib. XIII: Dives ubi ante omnes colitur Feronia Luco, Et sacer humectat flaviales rura Capenas.
units.tr: In Latium, among the Capenates, there was the grove of Feronia, which Silius sings of in Book XIII: Where Feronia, rich in her grove, is worshipped above all others, and her sacred place moistens the flowery fields of Capena.

units.la: Livius lib. XXVII in Agro Capenate prope Silvam Feroniae Signa quatuor diem & noctem sanguine sudavisse narrat. Iuxta Numicum Amnem Lucus erat Jovi Indigeti sacer, ut Plinius tradidit lib. III cap. V, quamquam mendose apud eum antea Locus legeretur, pro Lucus; quod Hermolaus Barbarus adnotavit; & ex Livio lib. I, Solino in Polyhist. Dionysio Halic. in Antiq. Rom. & Cicerone lib. III de Natura Deorum convincitur. Dianae Aetolicae Lucus Livio est lib. XXVII ad Anagninum Compitum. Naevium Silvam extra Urbem ad quartum Milliarium fuisse notat Festus. Ab ea nomen Porta Naevia. Extra Portam Capenam Camenarum Lucus scribitur ab Livio lib. I. & Asconio Pœdiano in Orat. Cicer. Luci Capeni Egeriaque Nemus forte Virgilio lib. VII, ubi Servius notat iuxta Ariciam fuisse. An ex hoc Silij versu sinisterius intellecto? Egeria genitos immitis Aricia lucis.
units.tr: Livy, in Book XXVII, tells that four standards in the territory of Capena near the Wood of Feronia sweated blood for a day and a night. Near the river Numicus there was a grove sacred to Jupiter Indiges, as Pliny records in Book III, chapter V, though earlier the word there was wrongly read as Locus instead of Lucus. Hermolaus Barbarus noted this, and it is proven from Livy Book I, Solinus in the Polyhistor, Dionysius of Halicarnassus in the Roman Antiquities, and Cicero in Book III of On the Nature of the Gods. Livy mentions the Grove of Diana of Aetolia near the crossroads of Anagnia in Book XXVII. Festus notes that the Naevian Wood lay outside the City at the fourth milestone, and that the Naevian Gate takes its name from it. Outside the Capene Gate the Grove of the Camenae is mentioned by Livy in Book I and by Asconius Pedianus in his commentary on Cicero's orations. The Grove of Lucus Capenus and the Egerian Nemus is perhaps in Virgil, Book VII, where Servius notes that it was near Aricia. Or is this line of Silius perhaps understood in a different sense? Aricia, cruel, begot from the grove of Egeria.

units.la: Livius propius urbem locat, addens in eius medio fuisse Egeriae Fontem, quod & testatur Ovidius lib. XV Metamorph. Quod Algidum Nemus Livio reliquisque Scriptoribus, hodie Selva del Aglio dicitur, censentibus Mario Nigro & Leandro. Albuncam neam silvam in altissimis Tiburtinis Montibus habet Servius ad vii Æneid. aliamque idem ad Georgica, in Laurentinorum agris, cognominem: Vide infra ubi de Fontibus cap. ii. Argitta Nemus propinquum Albæ Martiorum fuisse, significat Virgilius lib. vii. Æneid. Furina Lucus, Territorij Romani, est apud Ciceronem iii de Nat. Deor. & Cornelium Nepotem, ubi C Gracchum interfectum scribit. Furinarum Lucum habet P. Victor in xiiii. Regione Trans-Tiberiana. Plutarcho in Gracchi vita Furinarum Lucus ἄλσος Εὐμένης vocatur.
units.tr: Livy places it nearer the city, adding that in its middle there was the Fountain of Egeria, which Ovid also attests in Book XV of the Metamorphoses. The Algidian Grove, which Livy and other writers mention, is today called the Selva del Aglio, as Mario Nigro and Leander think. Servius, on Aeneid VII, places a wood named Albunea in the high Tiburtine mountains, and in his commentary on the Georgics he places another of the same name in the fields of the Laurentines. See below, where I speak of springs, chapter II. Virgil in Aeneid VII indicates that the Argitta Grove was near Alba of the Martians. The Furina Grove, in the Roman territory, is mentioned by Cicero in Book III of On the Nature of the Gods and by Cornelius Nepos, who writes that Gaius Gracchus was killed there. P. Victor mentions the Grove of the Furinae in the fourteenth region, Trans-Tiberina. In Plutarch's life of Gracchus, the Grove of the Furinae is called the grove of Eumenes [ἄλσος Εὐμένης].

units.la: Lacuna Nemora agnoscit iuxta Montem Fiscellum in Umbria Plinius.
units.tr: Pliny recognises the Lacunar Groves near Mount Fiscellum in Umbria.

units.la: Gaudent & luis Campani: cum primis Luco Sacro & Gallinaria Silva. Sacer Lucus Livio lib. xxiii, ἄλσος ιερόν. Strabo ad Ostia Liris, qui hodie Hami, testibus Scipione Mazzello & Leandro Alberto. Tribus ab Cumis passuum millibus locat Livius, Nymphām Maricam ibi coli solitam scribit Strabo. Videndus & Servius ad Æneidem Virgilianam. Gallinariam Silvam nominant Cicero ad Patrum scribens & Strabo lib. v, qui ταλ γραφεια ὑλὴ vocat. Pomponius Sabinus, propius ad locum accedens, in Cumano Sinu fuisse ait; addens, Trivia Lucum appellari ab Virgilio vi Æneid. Sanfelicio hodie La Peneta de Patria dicitur. Pinus huius vitiosus apud Iuvenalem lib. i. Sat. iii Gallinaria nuncupatur.
units.tr: The Campanians also delight in groves, above all the Sacred Grove and the Gallinarian Wood. Livy, in Book XXIII, speaks of the Sacred Grove [ἄλσος ἱερόν]. Strabo places it at the mouth of the Liris, which is today the Garigliano, as Scipione Mazzella and Leander Alberti attest. Livy places it three miles from Cumae, and Strabo writes that the Nymph Marica was worshipped there. Servius on Virgil's Aeneid should also be consulted. Cicero, writing to Patrus, and Strabo in Book V, which calls it a sacred wood [ταλ γραφεια ὑλή], mention the Gallinarian Wood. Pomponius Sabinus, coming closer to the place, says it was in the Cumaean gulf, adding that Virgil in Aeneid VI calls it the Grove of Trivia. Today it is called La Peneta de Patria, near Sanfelice. The pine of this grove, as Juvenal mentions in Satire III, Book I, is called Gallinaria.

units.la: Lucanorum sunt Silva Lucique Eboli, Peregrinalis, Veliarum, Eboli Silva perinfamis nomen habet ab Eboio vicino oppido, quod tamen ultra flumen est in Campania seu Picentinis. Peregrinalis fauces excipiens Vallis Dianiae, densitate arborum perobscura est; praesertim Ilicum, tantae altitudinis, ut caelum cacuminibus attingere videantur. Veliarum Lucos, ab Velia Lucanorum Urbe dictos, Hannibalem evasisse scribit Symmachus lib. ii. Epist. xii.
units.tr: The Lucanians have the Wood and Grove of Eboli, Peregrinalis, and of Velia. The notorious Eboli Wood takes its name from the nearby town of Eboium, which, however, lies beyond the river in Campania or among the Picentines. The Peregrinalis, which takes in the mouth of the Valley of Diania, is very dark because of the density of its trees, especially the holm oaks, which are so tall that their tops seem to touch the sky. Symmachus, in Book II, Letter XII, writes that Hannibal escaped through the groves of Velia, named after Velia, a city of the Lucanians.

units.la: Brutiorum est Rhegiruo vel Rheginarum Saltus, cuius meminit Solinus: Sila videtur dici Virgilio, & Vibio Sequestro; Sila Sallustio & Plinio: Σίλα Brutiis apud Strabonem lib. vi: Carminiaccensi fortean in Libro Notitiarum, & Carmeianum in eo, qui de Limitibus. La Sila hodie per excellentiam ab Incolis vocari scribit Laurentius Ananiensis. Silvam hanc tanta Arborum varietate distinctam notat Gabriel Barrius in sua Calabria, ut id naturae opus mortalium industria distributum videri possit. Patere in circuitu ad ducenta P.M. prodit Scipio Mazzella. Addit Strabo Piceum Silvam hanc ferre optimam, arboribus esse praeclare consitam, Aquae copia praeditam, 10 cc stadus longam. Certe Picem πίσσης, quam memorant Scriptores, ex hac Silva colligi solitam, est verisimile. Dioscorides Pinus vocat cap. xcviii Vina Saltus huius laudat Cassiodor. lib. xii Variar.
units.tr: Among the Bruttians there is the Rhegiruo or Rheginarum Saltus, which Solinus mentions. Virgil and Vibius Sequester seem to call it Sila; Sallust and Pliny also call it Sila; Strabo, in Book VI, calls the Bruttian Sila Σίλα. Perhaps in the Book of Notitiae it is called Carminiaccensi, and in the work on the Boundaries Carmeianum. Laurentius Ananiensis writes that today the inhabitants call it, par excellence, La Sila. Gabriel Barrius, in his Calabria, notes that this forest is so distinguished by its great variety of trees that it might seem to be a work of nature distributed by human industry. Scipione Mazzella reports that it extends about two hundred Roman miles in circumference. Strabo adds that this forest bears excellent pitch, is splendidly planted with trees, is rich in water, and is ten stades long. It is indeed likely that the pitch [πίσσα] which the writers mention was collected from this forest. Dioscorides calls it pinus in chapter 98. Cassiodorus, in Book XII of the Variae, praises the Vina Saltus of this region.

units.la: Apulorum Batinī sunt Saltus, & Lucus Gargani. Batinorum Saltuum, qui ab oppido Apuliae Batina dicti, meminit Horatius, cui Bantinos restituit ex M. SS. Codicibus Cruquius. De Luco Gargani sic scribit Leander Albertus in Apulia Daunia: Exteriora Crypta (quam, Michaelis Archangeli Domicilium, paullo ante delinearat) id est supremum eius Tectum virens densusque Lucus altissimis Arboribus operit; ex quibus multitudo maxima lapidum pendet, quos voti causa peregrinantes collo adligatos sursum in Montis tugum baiulant; ibique precibus patratis suspensos relinquunt. Admirationem profecto summam hac habet Silva, quod magno circumcirca spatio nullus ne frutex quidem appareat alius: quapropter Miraculum potius, quam res Naturalis habetur, tot & tam ingentes Arbores hic in vivum saxum radicatas. Pergit Leander: Mihi Adcola quum hic essem, narravere, circa Karolum viii Franciae Regem, qui anno ab Christo nato cIↄ cccc xciiii Neapolitanum Regnum cepit, unam ab Gallo quodam Multe caesam, illamque protinus supplicio divino ex animatum concidisse.
units.tr: Among the Apulians there are the Batini, which are woods, and the Grove of Garganus. Horace mentions the Batine Woods, named after the Apulian town of Batina, and Cruquius restores Bantinos from the manuscripts. Leander Alberti writes thus about the Grove of Garganus in his Apulia Daunia: the outer crypt (which he had described a little earlier as the dwelling of Michael the Archangel), that is, its upper roof, is covered by a green and dense grove of very tall trees. From these trees hangs a very great number of stones, which pilgrims making their vows carry up the slope of the mountain with stones tied round their necks, and there, after their prayers are said, they leave them suspended. This wood has the greatest wonder, because for a great distance all round no other shrub at all appears; therefore it is held to be a miracle rather than a natural thing that so many and such huge trees have taken root in the living rock here. Leander goes on: while I was staying here as a resident, people told me that, around the time of Charles VIII, King of France, who took the Neapolitan kingdom in the year of Christ 1494, a certain Frenchman cut down one of these trees, and that it at once fell, struck down by divine punishment.

units.la: In Gallia Cis-Padana ubi Senius fluvius in Padusam Paludem defluit, Silva est Lucina; & prope confluentem cum Pado Renum, Pedanea Silva, quas Succinum flevisse frustra credidit Antiquitas. Videndus Solinus in Polyhist. cap. xxiii.
units.tr: In Cisalpine Gaul, where the river Senius flows down into the Padusan marsh, there is the Silva Lucina; and near its confluence with the Po, the Rhine, there is the Pedanea Silva, which Antiquity vainly believed the amber (succinum) wept for. See Solinus, Polyhistor, chap. 23.

units.la: In Trans-Padana Caflorum Lucus ad xii Lapidem distat ab Cremona apud Tacitum lib. xviii. Caflorum Lucus, inemendarius, Orosio lib. vii, cap. viii.
units.tr: In Transpadane Gaul, the Caflorum Lucus lies twelve miles from Cremona, according to Tacitus, book 18. The Caflorum Lucus (the text is unemendable) is in Orosius, book 7, chap. 8.

units.la: Strabo denique apud Venetos suo sunt Luci, unus ab Iunone Argiva cognominatus; alter ab Diana Æstelica, alius ab Superiore, qui in Latio ad Anagninum Compitum.
units.tr: Finally, Strabo mentions groves among the Veneti: one named after Juno of Argos, Iunone Argiva; another after Diana Aestelica, Diana Æstelica; and another after the god called Superior, which in Latium stands at the Anagnine crossroads.

units.la: CAPUT IX.
units.tr: CAPUT IX.

units.la: Italiæ Sinus.
units.tr: The Gulfs of Italy.

units.la: QVÆ Terræ tribuenda notavi: succedunt, quæ Aquæ: ut sunt, Sinus, Portus, Navalia, Flumina, Vada, Paludes, Stagna, Fossæ, Lacus, Fontes, Aquæ, Balnea. Agmen ducunt Sinus.
units.tr: Having dealt with the things that belong to the land, I now turn to those that belong to the waters: these are gulfs, harbours, dockyards, rivers, shallows, marshes, pools, ditches, lakes, springs, waters, baths. The gulfs lead the procession.

units.la: Liguriæ præiacent Rapallinum, & Ericù. Rapallino, uti & Valli ibidem, nomen ab Rapallo, nobili iuxta littus Vico. Ericis, sic ab Veneris cognomine dicti, mentio est apud Silium Italicum lib. viii & alios: hodie Golfo di Porto Venere vocatur. Vide quæ dicam in Portuum enumeratione.
units.tr: Off the coast of Liguria lie the Rapallinum and the Ericus. The Rapallinum takes its name, like the nearby valley, from Rapallo, a noble town on the shore. The Ericis, so called from the epithet of Venus, is mentioned by Silius Italicus in book viii and by others; today it is called the Golfo di Porto Venere. See what I shall say in the enumeration of harbours.

units.la: Latio, Amyclanum Mare, ab Amyclis Latij quondam opido dictum. Nominat Tacitus lib. iv Annalium. Non tam Mare est, quam Sinus, qui nunc Adcolis, ut notat Santelicius, il mare del Sperlunga.
units.tr: In Latium is the Amyclanum Mare, named from Amyclae, once a town of Latium. Tacitus mentions it in book iv of the Annals. It is less a sea than a gulf, which the inhabitants now call, as Santelicius notes, il mare del Sperlunga.

units.la: Campaniæ, Baianus. Sic à Baiis Cumanorum opido plerisque appellatur: qui Κυμαῖος à Strabone, cum inter Athenæum & Misenum Promontoria describente, adenteque eumdem ab Eratosthene Cumanum vocari. Hodie Golfo di Napoli. Lucrinum nuncupat Symmachus lib. ii. Epist. Quidam etiam Puteolanum & Avernum. In Itineraria Tabula Crater fluvius ter nominatur, Long. cIII, Lat. 7. Long. cIV, Lat. 6; Long. denique cV, Lat. 6. nonnulla confusione: videndum num scribere voluerit, quicumque exaravit Tabulam, Craterem Sinum; sed is locandus fuisset in eadem Tabula Long. xcIV, Lat. 8.
units.tr: In Campania is the Baianus. Most call it so from Baiae, a town of the Cumaeans, whom Strabo, describing the promontories between Athenaeum and Misenum, calls Κυμαῖος [Kymaios]; and he adds that Eratosthenes called it Cumanum. Today it is the Golfo di Napoli. Symmachus in book ii of his Letters calls it the Lucrinus. Some also call it the Puteolanum and the Avernum. In the Itinerary Table the Crater river is named three times: long. 103, lat. 7; long. 104, lat. 6; and finally long. 105, lat. 6. There is some confusion here; one must consider whether the compiler of the Table meant to write Craterem Sinum, but in that case it should have been placed in the same Table at long. 94, lat. 8.

units.la: Ad Lucaniam est Pæstanus. Sic cum aliis nominat Plinius: in Itineraria Tabula corrupte Pestanus scribitur: Græcis Ποσειδωνιάτης appellatur. Nomen est sortitus à Pæstio, Lucaniæ Urbe, quæ Græcis Ποσειδωνία. Hodie, ut Leandro videtur, Golfo Agropolitano; unde & quibusdam Acropolitanus Sinus; vel, ut Ananiensi placet & Mazzella, di Salerno. Incipit ab ora Picentinorum, ac inde flexu sinuatur usque ad Promontorium Posidonia, ut Strabo, Plinius & Ptolemæus ostendunt.
units.tr: On the coast of Lucania is the Paestanus. Pliny names it so along with others; in the Itinerary Table it is wrongly written Pestanus. The Greeks call it Ποσειδωνιάτης [Poseidoniates]. It has its name from Paestum, a city of Lucania, which the Greeks called Ποσειδωνία [Poseidonia]. Today, as Leandro thinks, it is the Golfo Agropolitano, whence some also call it the Acropolitanus Sinus; or, as Ananiensis and Mazzella prefer, the di Salerno. It begins at the shore of the Picentines and curves in a bend as far as the promontory of Posidonia, as Strabo, Pliny and Ptolemy show.

units.la: Ad Brutiorum littora Hipponiates vīcitur Sinus. Ἱππωνιάτης ab Hippone opido, quod Romanis postea Vibo Valentia (unde & Vibonensis) Straboni & Ptolemæo vocatur, qui Ναπιτίης ab Urbe Napitia apud Strabonem. Brutius Marciano à Brutiis Populis: Terinæus, ab Terina Civitate, hodie Terriana, Thucydidi lib. vi & Plinio lib. iii nat. hist. qui hunc cum Scyllaceo versus Orientem ex adverso Peninsulam Italiæ & Isthmum Stadiorum CLX, ut notat Strabo, efficere scribit. Facta tamen locorum Plinii commissione, Vibonensis pars potius Terinæi, quam cum Terinæo idem. Λαμέτιος Aristoteli lib. vii de Rep. cap. x, ab Lametinis, qui Lametiam Urbem habebant. Aic idem abesse ab Scylletio, itinere dimidiati diei. Hodie Golfo di S. Eufemia.
units.tr: On the shores of the Bruttians the gulf is called the Hipponiates. The Ἱππωνιάτης [Hipponiates] takes its name from the town of Hippo, which Strabo and Ptolemy call by its Roman name Vibo Valentia (whence also Vibonensis), and which Strabo calls Ναπιτίης [Napitiës] from the city Napitia. The Brutius is so named by Marcian from the Bruttian people. The Terinaeus, from the city of Terina, today Terriana, is mentioned by Thucydides in book vi and by Pliny in book iii of the Natural History; Pliny writes that it, together with Scyllaceum, facing east across from the peninsula of Italy, forms an isthmus of 160 stadia, as Strabo notes. Yet when the places in Pliny are compared, the Vibonensis is rather a part of the Terinaeus than the same as it. The Λαμέτιος [Lametios] of Aristotle in book vii of the Politics, chapter x, is named from the Lametini, who had the city of Lametia. He says it lies half a day's journey from Scylletium. Today it is the Golfo di S. Eufemia.

units.la: Ad oram Magnæ Græciæ Scylleticus est & Tarentinus: Σκυλλητικὸς Strabohi, qui hodie Golfo de Schilaci. Nomen illi ab Scyllætio Urbe, quæ nunc Schylaci. Male nonnulli dictum volunt ab Scylla Scopulo, qui procul hinc ad Fretum Mamertinum. Versus meridiem Zephyrium, ad Septentrionem Lacinium habet Promontorium, inque eo Crotonem Urbem. Superato Lacinio Sinus occurrit Tarentinus. Sic ab Tarento, urbe quondam nobilissima, Plinio vocatur; qui Thurinus ab Thurio, Salentinorum opido, apud Ovidium lib. xv. Metamorph. Hodie Golfo di Taranto; vel, ut quidam notant, Mar grande; de qua appellatione dictum à me nonnihil Part. 1. lib. iii cap. vi. Ingens eius est Ambitus vel Capacitas, inter duo Promontoria Lacinium & Iapygium. De eo Virgilius lib. iii Æneidos: Hinc Sinus Herculei, si vera est fama, Tarenti Cernitur.
units.tr: On the coast of Magna Graecia are the Scylleticus and the Tarentinus. The Σκυλλητικὸς [Skyllētikos] of Strabo is today the Golfo de Schilaci. It takes its name from the city of Scyllaceum, now Schilaci. Some wrongly say it is named from the rock Scylla, which lies far off, at the Strait of Messina. On the south it has the Zephyrian promontory, on the north the Lacinian promontory, and on it the city of Croton. Past the Lacinian, the Tarentinus gulf comes into view. Pliny calls it so from Tarentum, once a most noble city; and Ovid in book xv of the Metamorphoses calls it the Thurinus, from Thurii, a town of the Salentines. Today it is the Golfo di Taranto, or, as some note, Mar grande; I have said something about this name in Part 1, book iii, chapter vi. Its circuit and capacity are immense, lying between the two promontories, Lacinium and Iapygium. Virgil speaks of it in book iii of the Aeneid: Hence, if the report is true, the gulf of Hercules' Tarentum comes into view.

units.la: Tarentini pars est Sinus, qui nunc adcolis Golfo di Rosano, ab Civitate munitissima, Rosano, tribus ab mari P. M. sita.
units.tr: Part of the Tarentine gulf is the one which the inhabitants now call the Golfo di Rosano, from the well-fortified town of Rosano, situated three miles from the sea.

units.la: Apuliam ornat Sinus, qui Frias Pomponio Melæ; hodie vero Golfo di Rode, nomen habens ab Rodæ opido, quod Fria quondam Latinis, Τέλον vel Τέλια Græcis, ut alibi à me notarum. Forum Iulium Forum Augusti, quem sic ab Tergeste Vrbe nominat Plinius: quique Prolemæo, Lultarcho & Stephano Aquileiensis, ab Aquileia, Sinui adlocata. Prius nomen hactenus obtinuit. Dicitur enim hodie Golfo de Trieste. Intimus est Maris Hadriatici recessus.
units.tr: A gulf adorns Apulia, which Pomponius Mela calls the Frias; today it is the Golfo di Rode, named from the town of Rodae, which was once called Fria by the Latins and Τέλον or Τέλια [Telon or Telia] by the Greeks, as I have noted elsewhere. The Forum Iulium, which Pliny calls the Forum Augusti after the city of Tergeste, and which Ptolemy, Plutarch and Stephanus call the Aquileiensis, after Aquileia, situated on this gulf. The former name has prevailed until now; for today it is called the Golfo de Trieste. It is the innermost recess of the Adriatic Sea.

units.la: Istriam denique Lygus, cui illabitur Draconia fluvius: & Flanaticus, sic Plinio dictus ab Flanaticus ideolis: Φλανατικος Stephano; Polaticus Melæ, Liburnicus Crotio; Carnarius hodie, vulgo Quarnero vel Carnero, quasi Carnivorus, ob violentiam marinorum Fluctuum, inquit Leander, qua frequenter hic Naufragia fiunt, tamquam in hominum carnificina. Longitudinem habet millium lx; Latitudinem, inter Niam & Sintecam Insulas, millium amplius xxx, usque ad xl; continetque modicas Insulas. Nominatur in Itineraria Tabula inter Istriam & Liburniam Portus Planaticus, non terrendum Flanaticum.
units.tr: Finally, Istria has the Lygus, into which the river Draconia flows; and the Flanaticus, so called by Pliny from the Flanatic island; Φλανατικος [Flanatikos] in Stephanus; the Polaticus in Mela; the Liburnicus in Crotius; and today the Carnarius, commonly called Quarnero or Carnero, as if Carnivorus, because of the violence of the sea's waves, which, as Leander says, causes frequent shipwrecks here, as though it were a slaughterhouse of men. It has a length of sixty miles and a breadth, between the islands Nia and Sintica, of more than thirty, up to forty miles; and it contains modest islands. In the Itinerary Table, between Istria and Liburnia, it is named the Portus Planaticus, not to be confused with the Flanaticum.

units.la: Caput hoc in Freto huiam (ne nusquam hoc indicetur) quod Brutios inter Italiæ populos & Siculos Insulanos. Sicilia dicitur Ciceroni lib. iii. de Nat. Deorum, Tacito lib. vi Annalium, & Plinio lib. xix. nat. hist. cap. 1: meritissime quod inter duas Siciliæ. Nam Italiæ partem, à Brutiis aliisque Conregionalibus habitatam, etiam Siciliam apud Veteres Scriptores appellatam, suo loco dicitur. Rhegium vocatur Strabono ab Rhegio Iulio; Scyllæum Athenæo lib. vii ab Scopulo Scylla, qui Freto versus Occidentem; Charybdis autem Thucydidi lib. iv ab altero, qui ad Oricutem, à quibus multa Navigantibus pericul& unde & Fretum ipsum Naufragum cognominat Ovidius lib. xiii. Metamorph. Mucedin Homero & Apollonio lib. iv. Traiectus dicitur in Antonini Itinerario. Caulla nota: Lonia Benjamino. Hodie Faro de Messina, ab Messana Civitate, quæ Antiquis etiam Mamertina (unde Fretum ipsum quondam Mamertinum;) de quo nonnulla fortean Parte postrema, de Insulis, ubi de Sicilia. Describunt Aristoteles in Admirandis & Pausanias in Eliacis.
units.tr: Here I should note, lest it be nowhere indicated, the headland in the strait which lies between the Bruttian peoples of Italy and the islanders of Sicily. Sicilia is the name used by Cicero in book iii of On the Nature of the Gods, by Tacitus in book vi of the Annals, and by Pliny in book xix of the Natural History, chapter 1, and rightly so, since it lies between two Sicilies. For the part of Italy inhabited by the Bruttians and other neighbouring peoples was also called Sicily by the ancient writers, as will be said in its place. The strait is called Rhegium by Strabo, from Rhegium Julium; Scyllaeum by Athenaeus in book vii, from the rock Scylla, which lies to the west of the strait; and Charybdis by Thucydides in book iv, from the other, which lies to the east; from these come many dangers for sailors, and for this reason Ovid in book xiii of the Metamorphoses also calls the strait itself Naufragum. Homer and Apollonius in book iv call it Mucedin. In the Itinerary of Antoninus it is called Traiectus. Caulla is a known name; Benjamin calls it Lonia. Today it is the Faro de Messina, from the city of Messana, which the ancients also called Mamertina, whence the strait itself was once called the Mamertinum. Something about this may perhaps be said in the final Part, on the islands, where I treat of Sicily. Aristotle in his Admirable Things and Pausanias in his Elian book describe it.

units.la: CAPVT X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: Italiæ Portus.
units.tr: The Harbours of Italy.

units.la: POst Sinus nominavi Portus. Italiam plerisque in locis ἀλίμενον esse, scribit Strabo lib. vi; & quos habet Portus, magnos esse atque admirabiles, horum illud adversus Exterorum Incursiones usui esse, hoc ad invadendos vicinos Exteros, & expeditam Mercaturæ copiam conducere. Portus igitur explicaturus, initium quam commodissime sumpturum me arbitror ab Itinerario Portuum vel Positionum Navium, quod apud Antoninum ab Vrbe Nicæam, & porro Arelatum usque producitur. Quum autem animus mihi sit in Portuum indicio ab Occasu versus Ortum, id est ab Vario fluvio, qui Terminus hodie inter Liguriam & Galliæ Provinciam, ad Tiberim, qui inter Etruriam & Latium, progredi, necesse habeo Ordinem, qui apud Antoninum, invertere. Illud sane hac Antonini notatione consequemur, ut certam timus habituri cognitionem omnium Portuum, qui ad maritimas Liguriæ Etruriæque oras, olim senescente Imperio, fuerunt. Iter Antonini ad præpositeram seriem reductum, inque pauciora verba contractum, nec non cum Itineraria Tabula commissum, sic habet: Antonini Itinerar. | Itineraria Tabula. Hodierna Nomencl. Antipoli Niciam Plag. M. P. xvi. ......... Nizza Olivulam, Portus, M. P. v. ........
units.tr: After the Gulfs, I have named the Harbours. Strabo, in book VI, writes that Italy is in most places without harbours (ἀλίμενον), but that the harbours it does have are large and remarkable. Some serve as protection against foreign attacks, others as a base for attacking neighbouring foreigners and for providing ready access to trade. To explain the Harbours, I think I should begin as conveniently as possible with the Itinerary of Harbours or Positions of Ships, which in Antoninus runs from the city of Nice onward to Arles. Since I intend in my account of the Harbours to go from west to east, that is, from the river Varus, which today is the boundary between Liguria and the Province of Gaul, to the Tiber, which lies between Etruria and Latium, I must reverse the order found in Antoninus. By following this notation of Antoninus we shall certainly gain a sure knowledge of all the harbours that existed along the seacoasts of Liguria and Etruria in the declining years of the Empire. The Itinerary of Antoninus, reduced to a continuous series, shortened into fewer words, and compared with the Itinerary Table, reads as follows. Itinerary of Antoninus | Itinerary Table | Modern names. Antipolis to Nicaea, 16 Roman miles ......... Nice. Olivula, harbour, 5 Roman miles ........

units.la: Surita legit ad Olbiam, cuius alii meminerunt. Sed Olbia Situs reclamat. Prolemæus enim inter Cytharisten Promontorium & Argentij Fluvij Ostium Olbiam collocat: Strabo etiá inter Olbiam & Antipolin Navale Cæsaris Augusti statuit, Forum Iulij nuncupatum: adeo ut Olbia omnino pertinuerit ad Partem illam Galliæ Narbonensis, quæ Provinciæ nomen obtinuit. Anaonem Portus, M.P.XII. ....... Iolias Simlerus legit Ņonem. Avisionem Portus, M.P.IV. ....... Monaco. Herculem Monæcum Portus, M.P.XXII. .......
units.tr: Surita reads "to Olbia", which some others also mention. But the position does not support Olbia. For Ptolemy places Olbia between the Cape of Cytharista and the mouth of the river Argentius. Strabo also places the naval station of Caesar Augustus, called Forum Julii, between Olbia and Antipolis. So Olbia belonged entirely to that part of Gallia Narbonensis which took the name of the Province. Harbour of Anao, 12 Roman miles ....... Simler reads Ionas for "Ņonem". Harbour of Avisio, 4 Roman miles ....... Monaco. Harbour of Hercules Monoecus, 22 Roman miles .......

units.la: Hæc olim vitiosissima scriptura in libris Antonini concepta legabantur. Meminerunt Tacitus, Plinius, Ptolemæus, & Ammianus. Sic Strabo lib. IV: ὁ δὲ ἦ Μονοίκου Ἀμφὶ ὄρμος ἐστὶν, ὁ μεγάλως, ἀλλ' ἐλλάς ἐαυτῶν, ἔχων ἱερὸν Ἡρακλέους Μονοίκου καλούμενον, &c. Albintimilium Plag. M.P.XVI. Albintimilium. Vintimiglia.
units.tr: This name, in the books of Antoninus, was once read in a very corrupt form. Tacitus, Pliny, Ptolemy and Ammianus mention it. So Strabo in book IV: "The harbour of Monoecus is a great harbour, but small in itself, having a temple of Hercules called Monoecus," etc. [ὁ δὲ τοῦ Μονοίκου ἀμφὶ ὄρμος ἐστὶν, ὁ μεγάλως, ἀλλ' ἐλλάς ἐαυτῶν, ἔχων ἱερὸν Ἡρακλέους Μονοίκου καλούμενον, κτλ.] Albintimilium, 16 Roman miles. Albintimilium. Ventimiglia.

units.la: Consule Liguriam meam. Portum Mauricis, M.P.XII. ....... Porto Marifo.
units.tr: See my Liguria. Harbour of Maurici, 12 Roman miles ....... Porto Maurizio.

units.la: Portus non tam rei, quam nomine. Albingaunum Portus, M.P.XII. Albingaunum. Albenga. Vada Sabatia Portus, M.P.XVIII. Vadus Sabates. Vadi.
units.tr: A harbour more in name than in fact. Albingaunum harbour, 12 Roman miles. Albingaunum. Albenga. Sabatian shallows, harbour, 18 Roman miles. Sabatian shallows. Vado.

units.la: Adi Liguriam meam. Leg. Sabatii.
units.tr: See my Liguria. Read Sabatii.

units.la: Inter hunc & sequentem celebris hodie Portus est Savona. Genuam Portus, M.P.XXX. Genua. Genoa.
units.tr: Between this place and the next is the harbour of Savona, famous today. Genua harbour, 30 Roman miles. Genua. Genoa.

units.la: Plene suo loco. Portum Delphini, M.P.XVI. ....... Porto sino.
units.tr: Fully in its place. Harbour of Delphinus, 16 Roman miles ....... Porto Fino.

units.la: Meminit Plinius. Portum Veneris, M.P.XVIII. ....... Porto di Venere.
units.tr: Pliny mentions it. Harbour of Venus, 18 Roman miles ....... Porto di Venere.

units.la: Notus hic etiam in Latino Ptolemæo; quum tamen in Græco non habeatur.
units.tr: This is also known in the Latin Ptolemy, though it is not found in the Greek.

units.la: Huic ex adverso Portus est Ericis: cuius meminit Ptolemæus. Porto di Erice, vel simpliciter Erice. Segestam Posit. M.P.XXX. ....... Sestri.
units.tr: Opposite it is the harbour of Erice, which Ptolemy mentions. Porto di Erice, or simply Erice. Segesta, position, 30 Roman miles ....... Sestri.

units.la: De Liguriæ porro Portubus sic scribit Strabo lib. IV: ὁ λῷ δὲ ἡ ... (Greek text continues) ... Antoninus ad Etruriæ Portus sic pergit: Lunam ad Fluvium Macram. M.P.XXX. Luna.
units.tr: Strabo, in book IV, writes thus about the harbours of Liguria: [ὁ λῷ δὲ ἡ ...]. Antoninus, going on to the harbours of Etruria, says: Luna, at the river Macra, 30 Roman miles. Luna.

units.la: Dicebatur ab hoc opido Portus Lunensis, Livio, Straboni, Plinio notus. Lunai Portum vocat Ennius i Annalium, & ex eo Persius Satyra VI: Lunai Portum est opera cognoscere Cives.
units.tr: From this town the harbour was called the Harbour of Luna, known to Livy, Strabo and Pliny. Ennius, in book I of the Annals, calls it the Harbour of Luna, and from him Persius, in Satire VI: It is worth the effort for citizens to know the harbour of Luna.

units.la: • Vide quæ noto ad eundem Poëtam.
units.tr: • See what I note on that same poet.
