units.la: Portum hunc amplitudine tanta testatur Strabo, ut omnibus, quæ toto Mari versantur, Navigiis excipiendis sufficiat: nec solū late vasteque patere, sed etiam tutissimum esse, quod iugis montium præcelsis undiqueclaudatur, ideoque longissimum, in omnes partes & utrumque Littus & Sardiniā prospectū habeat. Silius Italicus lib. VIII.
units.tr: Strabo testifies that this harbour is so large that it is sufficient to receive all the ships that sail in the whole sea. It not only spreads wide and far, but is also very safe, since it is enclosed on every side by the lofty ridges of mountains. For this reason it has a very long view in every direction, over both shores and over Sardinia. Silius Italicus, book VIII.

units.la: Tunc quos à niveis exegit Luna Metallis Insignis Portu, quo non spatiosior alter Innumeras cepisse rates & claudere Pontu.
units.tr: Then Luna, renowned for its harbour, which she drew from the snowy quarries; no other harbour was larger to take in countless fleets and enclose them in its sea.

units.la: Amplis eius faucibus Insula modica est obiecta, vim Austri Africique prohibens. Flumen in eum se exonerat Macra, contra quod in ostio Portus binae jacent Insulae aliae modicae, Tinus & Tinettus.
units.tr: A modest island lies before its wide mouth, keeping off the force of the south and south-west winds. The river Macra discharges into it, and opposite, at the mouth of the harbour, lie two other small islands, Tinus and Tinetto.

units.la: Portum Pisanum, M. P. IX. Huius nulla apud Veteres mentio: frequens autem in Pisanorum & Genuensium rebus, super Sardiniae Insulae imperio; & postea in expeditionibus Aragonensium Regum Maritimis, quibus Sardiniae Regnum sibi adseruerunt.
units.tr: The harbour of Pisa, 9 Roman miles. No ancient writer mentions it, but it is frequent in the affairs of the Pisans and Genoese, over the rule of the island of Sardinia, and later in the maritime expeditions of the kings of Aragon, by which they claimed the kingdom of Sardinia for themselves.

units.la: Vada Portus, M. P. XVIII. Vadis Volaterris. Vada. Hodie Latine scribentibus Portus Ligurnus, vulgo Livorno. Sed Situs non patitur. Ligurnus est inter Pisas & Vada, medio fere itinere. Ligurnum Labronem appellare videtur Cicero ad Q. Fratrem lib. II. Epist. III. Liburnum Portum habent nescio unde Ptolemaei Interpretes; male etiam collocantes inter Lunam & Arnum. Censet Volaterranus Portum Ligurnum esse, quem Antoninus Salepronem nominat. Falso. Antoninus enim Iter Arelatense ab Urbe Roma describens Aurelia Via Salepronem ab Lacu Aprili abesse ostendit M.P. XII: at Ligurnus ab eo Lacu supra I millia distat. Reclamat etiam series, quae in Itineraria Tabula. Celebris quidem Portus est; sed paucarum Navium capax, & nondum profunde effossus. Ante ingressum Turres quatuor, in mari tres ab Maximiliano Imp. diiectae; quarta jam renovata, & impositia ei custodia est. Plura apud Laurentium Schraderum, in monimentis Italiae.
units.tr: Vada harbour, 18 Roman miles. To Vada from Volterra. Vada. Today writers in Latin call it the Harbour of Ligurnus, commonly Livorno. But the position does not allow this. Ligurnus lies between Pisa and Vada, roughly halfway along the road. Cicero, in book II, letter III to his brother Quintus, seems to call it Ligurnum Labro. The interpreters of Ptolemy have a Liburnum harbour from I know not where, and they also place it badly between Luna and Arnus. Volaterranus thinks that the harbour of Ligurnus is the one which Antoninus calls Salepro. This is false. For Antoninus, describing the road to Arles from the city of Rome, shows that Salepro lies twelve Roman miles from the Lake Aprilis along the Aurelian Way, whereas Ligurnus is more than a thousand paces from that lake. The series in the Itinerary Table also contradicts this. It is indeed a famous harbour, but it can hold only a few ships and has not yet been dug deep. Before the entrance there are four towers, three of them built in the sea by the Emperor Maximilian; the fourth has been rebuilt and a guard placed in it. More on this in Laurentius Schrader, in the Monuments of Italy.

units.la: Populenium Portus, M. P. XXX. Populonia. Porto Ferrato. Vide plene Leandrum in Tuscia.
units.tr: Populenium harbour, 30 Roman miles. Populonia. Porto Ferraio. See Leandro's full account in Tuscia.

units.la: Falesiam Portus, Faleria legitur Itinerarij Rutilij libro II.
units.tr: The harbour of Falesia; the reading Faleria is found in book II of the Itinerary of Rutilius.

units.la: Scabros Portus, M.P. XVIII. Scarino. Ptolemaeo, aliisque Portus Traianus dicitur. Alsam Flumen Posit. M. P. VI. Arbiafiume. Lacrum Aprilem Posit. M.P.XVIII. Lacus ipse pictus est; Prille. sed suppresso nomine. Portum Telamonis, M. P. XVIII.
units.tr: Scabri harbour, 18 Roman miles. Scarino. Ptolemy and others call it the Harbour of Trajan. River Alsa, position, 6 Roman miles. Arbia River. Lake Aprilis, position, 18 Roman miles. The lake itself is drawn, but the name is omitted. Prille. The Harbour of Telamon, 18 Roman miles.

units.la: Telamon Portus etiam Polybio, Plinio, Melaeque notus. Hinc Τελαμών Ptolemaeo Promontorium. Scribit Plutarchus Marium in Portum Etruriae Telamone. Telamone. rit Telamonem delatum, descensione facta, Servos ad Pileum vocasse. Almunam Fluvium Posit, M. P...... Albinia fl. Albegna fiume. Antoninus hic ex Itineraria Tabula vulgaraque appellatione emendandus videtur. Domitianas Getarias Posit. M. P. VIIII. Portum Herculis, M. P. III. Port Herculus. Porto Hercole. Straboni est notus. Arnimen fluvium Posit. M. P. xxv. Armenita fl. Pescia, ni fallor. Regas Posit. M. P. IIII. ......... ......... An Pryaevitra Strabonis? Quintianum Posit. M. P. VI. ......... ........ Maltanum Posit. M. P. III. ......... ....... Gravisca Posit. M. P. IIII. Gravisca. Monte alto.
units.tr: The harbour of Telamon is also known to Polybius, Pliny and Mela. From this, Ptolemy has Telamon as a promontory. Plutarch writes that Marius, when he landed in the Etruscan harbour of Telamon, called the slaves to the cap of liberty when he disembarked. Telamone. River Almuna, position, Roman miles ...... River Albinia, Albegna. Here Antoninus seems to need correction from the Itinerary Table and common usage. Domitian's Getariae, position, 9 Roman miles. Harbour of Hercules, 3 Roman miles. Port Ercole. Porto Ercole. Known to Strabo. River Arnimen, position, 25 Roman miles. River Armenita, Pescia, unless I am mistaken. Regae, position, 4 Roman miles. ......... Is this Strabo's Pryaevitra? Quintianum, position, 6 Roman miles. ......... Maltanum, position, 3 Roman miles. ......... Gravisca, position, 4 Roman miles. Gravisca. Monte Alto.

units.la: Coralium hic nasci perhibet Plinius. Rapinium Posit. M. P. VI. ......... ....... In aliis est Rapionum. Algas Posit. M. P. III. ......... ......... Centumcellas Posit. M. P. III. Centum cellis. Citta vecchia.
units.tr: Pliny says coral is born here. Rapinium, position, 6 Roman miles. ......... In other copies it is Rapionum. Algae, position, 3 Roman miles. ......... Centumcellae, position, 3 Roman miles. Centum Cellae. Civitavecchia.

units.la: Vide Etruriam meam. Castrum Novum, M. P. V. Castro Novo. Corneto. Fanapionem, M. P. VII. Punicum. .........
units.tr: See my Etruria. Castrum Novum, 5 Roman miles. Castro Novo. Corneto. Fanapio, 7 Roman miles. Punicum. .........

units.la: Anio videtur Melae. Pyrgos Posit. M. P. III. Pyrgos. ....... Portum Augusti: M. P. XXXVIII. Augustam habet Itineraria Tabula huius Portus sculpturam, sed nullum Nomen adscriptum. Porto di Roma.
units.tr: Melas's Anio seems to be this one. Pyrgi, position, 3 Roman miles. Pyrgi. ....... The harbour of Augustus, 38 Roman miles. The Itinerary Table has a picture of this harbour labelled Augusta, but no name is written beside it. Porto di Roma.

units.la: De eo plene dixi in Tuscia mea: ideoque non futurus hic in explicando prolixior: ad reliquos pergo.
units.tr: I have spoken fully about it in my Tuscia, so I shall not be longer here in explaining it. I pass on to the rest.

units.la: Portus, Navium que Positiones Liguriae Tusciaeque hactenus commemoravi ex maritimo Antonini Itinerario: progredior iam, aliorum Auctorum sequutus vestigia, versus Euronotum, lectis Latij, Campaniae, reliquarumque Italiae ad Mare cum Inferum, tum Superum Regionum littoribus.
units.tr: Having so far recorded the harbours and positions of ships of Liguria and Etruria from the maritime Itinerary of Antoninus, I now proceed, following the footsteps of other authors, towards the south-east, reviewing the shores of Latium, Campania, and the rest of Italy on both the lower and upper seas.

units.la: Quod ad Latium, Neronem Principem Portum operis sumtuosissimi ad Antium fecisse, scribit in eius Vita cap. ix Suetonius. Ἀίας Ἀιδῖα habet Apollonius ad Circeium Montem: Αἴαιαν ab Virgilio nominari, notat Servius, tribus Diphthongis ab adipernantium voce, propter celebratas illic Corporum Mutationes. Caieta Portum fuisse celeberrimum, amplissimeque ab Antonino Pio Imperat. refectum, refert Spartianus. Hodie nullus est.
units.tr: As for Latium, Suetonius, in the life of Nero, chapter 9, writes that the emperor built a very sumptuous harbour at Antium. Apollonius calls the place by the name Aeaea near Mount Circeius; Servius notes that Virgil calls it Aeaea, with three diphthongs, from the word for those who swim about, because of the transformations of bodies celebrated there. Spartianus reports that Caieta was a very famous harbour, rebuilt at great expense by the Emperor Antoninus Pius. Today there is none.

units.la: Portum Julium, inquit Suetonius in Augusto, apud Baias immisso in Lucrinum & Avernum Lacum Mari, effecit. Virgilius in Georgicis,
units.tr: "He made the Julian Port," says Suetonius in Augustus, "by admitting the sea near Baiae into the Lucrine and Avernian lakes."

units.la: Iulia quas Ponto longe sonat unda refuso.
units.tr: "Where the Julian wave resounds from afar when the sea is poured in," (Virgil, Georgics).

units.la: Julium vndam vocat Puteolanum Portum, ut addunt Servius & Philargyrius. Legendus de eo Mazzella, in Antiquitatibus Puteolanorum. Baianus Portus altissimus in littore conspicitur: qui licet aedificia nulla habeat circumpolita, numquam tamen de veteri celebritate quidquam remisit.
units.tr: Virgil calls the Julian wave the Puteolan port, as Servius and Philargyrius add. On this, see Mazzella in his Antiquities of Puteoli. The Baian port, very deep, can be seen on the shore. Although no buildings stand around it, it has never lost anything of its old renown.

units.la: Velinum Portum, ab Velia, antiquo Lucaniae opido, quod periit, sic dictum, memorat Virgilius lib. vi Æn.
units.tr: The Velinian port takes its name from Velia, an ancient town of Lucania that has perished, as Virgil records in Aeneid book 6.

units.la: Portusque require Velinos.
units.tr: "And seek the Velinian harbours."

units.la: Vtitur multitudinis numero, quod hoc littore plurimi sint Portus, quamquam exigui. Vide Agellium lib. x. noct. Attic. cap. xvi.
units.tr: He uses the plural because there are many harbours on this shore, though they are small. See Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights, book 10, chapter 16.

units.la: Herculi Portus prope Vibonem in Brutiis à Plinio describitur lib. iii. cap. v. Formicules vocant Adcolae, ut tradit Barrius in sua Calabria. Metaurus Navium statio Straboni in Brutiis ad Metaurum Fluvium. Metaurum vocare videntur Pomponius Melā & Stephanus.
units.tr: The Port of Hercules near Vibo in the Bruttii is described by Pliny, book 3, chapter 5. The locals call it Formicules, as Barrius reports in his Calabria. Strabo mentions Metaurus, a naval station in the Bruttii on the River Metaurus. Pomponius Mela and Stephanus seem to call it Metaurum.

units.la: Oreslis Portus in Magna Graecia apud eumdem Plinium est: qui Ravagoso ab Incolis
units.tr: The port of Oreslis in Magna Graecia is also in the same Pliny. The inhabitants call it Ravagoso,

units.la: Brutiorum, Herculis.
units.tr: of the Bruttii, of Hercules.

units.la: Metaurus.
units.tr: Metaurus.

units.la: Mag. Graec. Oreste. lior ejus ripa & Gallica, Fluvios qui Vulgo Gallorum audiunt Carempt, Lavaire, Efleron: qua Orientalior & Italiam spectans, La Lince & La Fofubie: quorum alter in Itineraria Tabula Vulpi nominatur; posterior, credo. Sequuntur inde per Liguriæ Littora, Panion Pomponio, qui Panon hodie: ad Niceam Maris miscens. Rutuba Lucano lib. ii. & Plinio lib. iii cap. v notus: hodie Retu Leandro; Rodo ia Stunicæ, Blondo, Ortelio. Merula Plinij subter Andoriam labitur; Vallem amœnam longamque M P. viii. percurrens; mari jungitur, ubi Promontorio Merula nomen facit. Hodie Mera dicitur, ut Iustinianus & Leander notant. Nigro Centa est: Assenta Stunicæ. Hoc fere loco scribitur in Itineraria Tabula Fluvius Lucus. Viterius Flumen est Porcifera Plinio; Vulgo Porzevera. Oritur in Apennini lugis, curriqué millium xv Mare petit, Porfina corrupte Antonino. Fersio Plinio & Antonino, hodie Feriano. Qui nunc Lazagna & Itinerariæ Tabulæ, hodieque Latine tributibus Labonia, Lavinia putatur Ptolemæo. Macra fluvius satis notus. Meminerunt præter alios Plinius, Antoninus in Itinerario Maritimo, & Tabula Peutingeriana. Straboni Macra, Ptolemæo Macralia, nescio an bene. Magra hodie. Celebratur & Livio, in cujus quibusdam Editionibus scribitur corrupte Mera. Profluit ex Apennino: Liguriamque ab Etruria dividens in Inferum provolvitur Mare. Tantus ejus est impetus, ut navigari commode nequeat, notante Sulpitio, in hæc Lucam: Culta si er, nullaf que vado qui Macramoraus Alnos, ... ina percurris in aquora Luna.
units.tr: In Magna Graecia, Oreste. Its other bank is Gallic. The rivers that the people of Gaul call Carempt, Lavaire, Efleron; on the eastern side, facing Italy, La Lince and La Fofubie, of which the first is named Vulpi in the Itinerary Table, and the second, I believe, is the other. Next along the coasts of Liguria comes Panion, which Pomponius calls Panon today, mixing into the sea at Nice. Rutuba, known from Lucan book 2 and Pliny book 3, chapter 5, is today Retu according to Leander; Rodo according to Stunica, Blondus and Ortelius. Pliny's Merula flows below Andora, running through a pleasant valley eight miles long, and joins the sea, where at the promontory it gives its name to Merula. Today it is called Mera, as Justinian and Leander note. For Nigro it is Centa; for Stunica, Assenta. Roughly at this point the Itinerary Table writes Fluvius Lucus. Viterius is a river called Porcifera by Pliny, commonly Porzevera. It rises in the Apennine ridge and, running fifteen miles, seeks the sea; Antoninus corruptly calls it Porfina. Fersio in Pliny and Antoninus is today Feriano. What is now Lazagna, and in the Itinerary Table, and still today in Latin Labonia, is thought to be Ptolemy's Lavinia. The river Macra is well known. Besides others, Pliny, Antoninus in the Maritime Itinerary, and the Peutinger Table mention it. Strabo calls it Macra, Ptolemy Macralia, I do not know whether rightly. Today it is Magra. It is also celebrated by Livy, in some editions of whom it is corruptly written Mera. It flows from the Apennines, and, dividing Liguria from Etruria, rushes down into the Tyrrhenian Sea. Its force is so great that it cannot conveniently be navigated, as Sulpicius notes on the line of Lucan: "Culta si er, nullaque vado qui Macra moraus Alnos..." and so on "...percurris in aquora Luna."

units.la: Macram vocari ad eosdem vetus scribit Omnibonus Vicentinus, quod ab Aquis maceat; idcoque, inquit, tum quia rapidior, tum quia vadosus, haud navigabilis est. Recipit Maera, præter alios, Laulam, Fagnonum, & Graceam. Connumerandus his qui Ptolemæo: Vara Vulgo ex quorundam mente.
units.tr: Omnibonus of Vicenza writes that the same authors call it Macram, because it soaks up water from the springs. Therefore, he says, both because it is rather rapid and because it is shallow, it is not navigable. Besides others, Maera receives Laula, Fagnonum and Graceam. Among those who belong with these is what Ptolemy calls Vara, commonly, in the opinion of some.

units.la: Hactenus Flumina, vel quorum apud Ligures Ostia sunt, vel quis in alia Ingressus: sequuntur quæ Etruriæ confuaverunt adcenseri. Hic primum ducunt agmen Lavenna & Frigidus. Prioris mentio in Itineraria Tabula, ubi tamen Arvenna. Posterior Adcolis hodie Freddo. Post Versiliam inde Auser est Amnis; sic Plinio dictus & Cassiodoro, qui Ausur Rutilio, Straboni; Ofari vulgo. Leander tamen Serchium hodie dici notat; quem vide. Arnus mox succedit Livio lib. xxii, Plinio, & aliis memoratus: Straboni & Ptolemæo: Arno vernacule. Nascitur, ut Strabo perhibet, ex Apennini latere dextro. Fulteronam vocari Fontis locum, Auctores sunt Boccatius in libro Fluminum, Landinus Dantis Interpres in Purgatorio. & Facius Vbertus lib. iii. Cant vi. Modicis initijs principio inter Rupes horridas præcipitesque Convalles in Occasum tendit: deinde collectis Fontibus, Torrentibus, Amnibusque plurimis tumidior, magna cum Mole Florentinum ingreditur Agrum: Florentiaque & Pisa divisis, Mare petit. Multis adaugetur fluviis: quorum ad dextram illi ripam sunt inter alios Crana, Solanus Rena, Refus, vulgo Refibo; Sera Mugellum secans, receptis Ducaria & Ronta; Munio, Mugnone vernacule ex Apennino Florentiam adluens, ubi Arno jungitur; Terfola; Fisentium, cui Marina miscetur; Vmbro, Vmbrone vulgo, qui Stellæ jungitur Arnum intrat; Pisa denique, Rivola dives, qui Pilcinæ Valli dedit nomen: ad sinistram occurrunt Staggia: Corfolana; Archianum; Pallule; Claffa: Trioga; Pesa, cui Fina & Grieva confluunt; Elsa denique & Era; quorum ille, paullum supra opidum Collis oriens, modico procursu tantum incrementi sumit, ut tres ingentes frumentarias fullonicasque Molas volvat; recipiens in alveum suum cum aliis Staggiam & Foeium. Post Arnum est Cecinna, Plinio Melaque laudatus, Visida, ni fallor corrupte, Itinerarie Tabulæ; qui ex Monteti radicibus haud procul Malla ortus, Agrum Volaterranum percurrens, ad Urbem ipsam in Mare se præcipitat: hodie Cecina. Cornia ab Monte Rotundo profluit per Agrum Campilianum. Alma Antonino notus in Itinerario Maritimo, nomen retinens. Bruna, Pralu Plinio, ex Montibus Mallæ vicinis prorumpens Latui Prali, de quo alibi, miscetur. Qui Vmbrone vulgo, Vmbro (alius ab eo, qui ad dextram Arno jungitur) est apud Plinium, Antoninum & in Itineraria Tabula; Ομβρων Stephano: ex Montibus oritur inter Senam & Aretium, supra Asciianum, juxta D. Guifinetij CastelJumque Novum. Vmbronem Navigiorum aut capacem, memoratque Rutilius his versibus:
units.tr: So far the rivers whose mouths lie among the Ligurians, or whose entrances are elsewhere. What follows are those which are reckoned to belong to Etruria. Here the column is led first by Lavenna and Frigidus. The former is mentioned in the Itinerary Table, where however it is Arvenna. The latter is today called Freddo by the locals. After Versilia, next comes the river Auser, so named by Pliny and Cassiodorus, Ausur by Rutilius and Strabo, and commonly Ofari. Leander, however, notes that it is today called Serchium, which see. Arnus follows next, mentioned by Livy book 22, Pliny and others; in Strabo and Ptolemy it is Arno in the vernacular. It rises, as Strabo reports, from the right flank of the Apennines. That the place of the spring is called Fulterona is attested by Boccaccio in his book on rivers, by Landino, Dante's commentator on the Purgatorio, and by Fazio degli Uberti, book 3, canto 6. Starting from small beginnings, it runs westward between rugged cliffs and steep valleys; then, gathering springs, torrents and very many streams, it becomes swollen and enters the Florentine territory with great volume, and, separating Florence from Pisa, makes for the sea. It is increased by many rivers. On its right bank, among others, are Crana, Solanus, Rena, Refus, commonly Refibo; Sera, which cuts through the Mugello, taking in Ducaria and Ronta; Munio, Mugnone in the vernacular, which flows from the Apennines past Florence, where it joins the Arno; Terfola; Fisentium, into which Marina flows; Umbro, Umbrone commonly, which joins the Stella and enters the Arno; and finally Pisa, Rivola rich in water, which gave its name to the Pilcina valley. On the left come Staggia, Corfolana, Archianum, Pallule, Classa, Trioga, Pesa, into which Fina and Grieva flow; and finally Elsa and Era. Of these, the Elsa, rising a little above the town on a hill, gains so much from a short course that it turns three great mills for grain and fulling, taking into its bed, with others, Staggia and Foeium. After the Arno comes Cecinna, praised by Pliny and Mela; Visida, unless I am mistaken, is a corrupt form in the Itinerary Table. It rises from the foot of Monteti, not far from Malla, runs through the territory of Volterra and throws itself into the sea at the city itself; today it is Cecina. Cornia flows from Monte Rotondo through the Campiglia territory. Alma, known to Antoninus in the Maritime Itinerary, keeps its name. Bruna and Pralu, in Pliny, bursting out of the mountains near Malla, mingle with the Latui Prali, about which elsewhere. The Umbro (different from the one that joins the Arno on the right) is found in Pliny, Antoninus and the Itinerary Table; Stephanus has Omböron. It rises from the mountains between Siena and Arezzo, above Asciano, near Castel Nuovo of Signor Guifinetti. Rutilius mentions Umbro as capable of carrying ships, in these verses:

units.la: Tangimus Vmbronem, non est ignobile flumen, Quod tuto trepidas excipit ore rates. Tam facile pronus semper patet Aspera undis, In Pontum quoties saeva procella ruit.
units.tr: "We touch the Umbro, no ignoble river, which safely receives trembling ships at its mouth. So easily is the rough sea always open to the waves, whenever a savage storm rushes upon the Pontus."

units.la: Augetur Fluviis cum aliis: tum in dexteriore quidem ripa Arbia, qui in Montibus supra Castellinum ortus, historiis Florentinis celebris, Treffam, Sorram & Sriam recipit; item Mersa, in sinisteriore autem Ostia, quem Assius, Formoque, & alii ingrediuntur. Sequuntur hinc Osa; Albengia, supra Sempronianum oriens: Pefsa fortean Armine Antonino inter Pyrgos & Portum Herculis; Albinia autem Itinerarii Tabulae & Flora. Qui Marcha vulgo, notus etiam est Antonino in Itinere, ab Urbe per Tuscian & Alpes Maritimas Arelatum usque Via Aurelia, & alibi in tem Itinerarii Tabulae: sic nominatus, quod ex Lacu cognomine effundatur: Lora putatur dicti Ptolemaeo, alius ab Osi, de quo paulo ante. Qui Meqnone vulgo, Minio vocatur Virgilio lib. x. Aeneid. & Vibio. Munio dicitur Rutilio, qui audiendus:
units.tr: It is increased by other rivers: on the right bank, indeed, the Arbia, which rises in the mountains above Castellina, famous in Florentine histories, receives Treffa, Sorra and Sria; likewise the Mersa. On the left bank the Ostia, which Assius, Formo and others enter. Next come the Osa; Albengia, rising above Sempronian; Pefsa, perhaps the Armine of Antoninus between Pyrgi and the Port of Hercules; and the Albinia of the Itinerary Table, and the Flora. The river called Marcha commonly, also known to Antoninus in his Itinerary from Rome through Tuscany and the Maritime Alps to Arles along the Via Aurelia, and elsewhere in the Itinerary Table, is so named because it flows from the lake of the same name. Lora is thought to be the river named by Ptolemy, different from the Osi mentioned a little earlier. The river called Meqnone commonly, Minio, is named by Virgil, book 10 of the Aeneid, and by Vibius. Munio is named by Rutilius, who should be heard:

units.la: Paullus fer littus fugimus Munione vadosum Suspecto trepidant esta parva solo.
units.tr: "Hardly have we left the shore, the shallow Munio, when the small ships tremble on suspicious ground."

units.la: Eris, Caretanus est Plinio: Caeritis Amnis Virgilio lib. viii. Aeneid. Succedunt hinc Tiberim versus Vacina, Sanguinaria, & postremo loco Aron.
units.tr: Eris, the Caretanus, is Pliny's; the Caeritis Amnis is Virgil's, book 8 of the Aeneid. Next, towards the Tiber, come Vacina, Sanguinaria, and lastly Aron.

units.la: Ad Tiberim perveni Fluvium, limitem hic Etruriam inter & Latium. Nescio an Fluminum quid eo in historiis Romanorum celebratum. Varia leguntur ejus Nomina: quorum alia profani, ut sic loquar, generis, alia sacri. Prioris Classis sunt Tanus, Albula, Rumon, Tiberis: posterioris Serra, Ianum antiquissimis temporibus appellatum fuisse, tradit Athenaeus lib. xv, ab Iano, quem longe lateque ad ejus oras regnasse ferunt. Albulam fuisse dictum, patet ex Varrone lib. iv. de L. L. Plinio lib. iii. cap. iv, Virgilio lib. viii. Aeneid. Ovidio lib. iii. Fast. Silio lib. viii. Unde? Ab Albo Colore derivant Paullus Diaconus ex Festi fortean lib. i. & Servius ad viii Aeneid. An vere, cogitandum. Ego non difficulter adiciam: quamvis penitius intuito Color flavus adpareat: quod ipse etiam Servius notat ad Aeneid. vii; & confirmant Horatius lib. i. Carminum, Ode 11, & lib. ii. Od. iii, Silinsque Italicus lib. ix: unde & Flavae ejus Arenae apud Virgilium vii Aeneidos; vel Fulva apud Ovidium lib. xiii Metamorph. Caruleus etiam est Tiberis Virgilio eodem lib. vii, & Sidonio Carmine 11. Augustiore voce Ἀλβα vel Ἀλβη scribitur Stephano. Meminit & Albula M. Terentius Varro lib. i. apud Nonium in Animem. Quod Rumon fuerit dictum ab Ruminando, docet Servius ad viii Aeneidos. Omnibus his inuperhabitis nobilissimum nomen induit hic Fluvius Tiberis, cujus varia producuntur Etyma. Ab Tibri Aboriginum Rege trahunt quidam apud Servium ad viii Aeneidos; Tuscorum, Festus lib. xviii & Servius ipse ad librum a me laudatum: Ab Tiberino Silvio, Albanorum Principe, diducunt Livius lib. i, Ovidius ii Fastor. & xiiii Metamorph. Festus item lib. xviii, & Eusebius. Eorum sententias brevibus indicat Servius ad lib. viii Aeneid. Versum lxxii, refutans eadem, sub Livii nomine, ad indicati libri versum ccxxx, ubi pro Tiberio legendum Tiberino. Ab Τίβερις denique Tiberim, quasi τὸν ὕδωρ appellatum censet Servius, qui ejus Etymi duplicem indicat rationem lib. iii & viii, quem dixi, Aeneid. Varro lib. iv de L.L. Debebirim hunc fluvium ab nonnullis nominatum tradit ab Debebri, Veientum Regulo. Serram in Sacris nuncupatum memorat Servius ad eundem Aeneidos librum ab Secando. Ego sic vocatum autem dicere ab Etrusca vel Syriaca voce ΤΤΨ, quod nihil aliud, quam principatum habere, dominari. Tiberis Sara (sic enim scribendum arbitror) quod Princeps quasi esset, & Rex Fluviorum; ad quem Regnator Populus (sic Floro nominatur) habitabat: unde & elegantér idem Fluvius Regnator Aquarum ab Virgilio dictus. Partem Tiberis Terentum audisse scribit idem Servius ad viii Aeneid. Non video, quam recte. Quid enim Terentum, explicat, praeter alios, Festus lib. xviii. Haec de Nominibus: in quorum quarto illud notandum, aliquod observatum fuisse discrimen in prolatione Vocum Tiberis, Tibris & Tiberini. Tiberis enim communi sermone dicebatur; Tibris, poetice; Tiberinus in Sacris notante Servio ad viii Aeneid. quod tamen non ubique verum. Tevere vulgo. Variis inignitur Epitheris à Poetis aliisque. Eorum duo praecipua, Lydus & Tuscus. Lydus ab Lydis, clara bello gente, quae Sedibus in Italiam translatis, apud hunc fluvium habitavit: legendi Dionysius Halic. lib. 1, Virgil. 11. Æneid. & ibi Servius. Tuscus ab nobilissimo Populo, ipsius ad occidentaliorem ripam adcola. Sic dicitur Virgilio lib. 1 Georgic. Silio lib. viii, Martial lib. iiii Epigr. Tyrrhenum Flumen vocat Virgilius Æneidos. Tiberis, ut Strabo lib. v, Plinius lib. iii cap. iv, Sidonius Carm. 11. Servius ad viii Æneid. testantur; utque facile videre est, Caput quod extra Latium ponit Varro lib. iv de L.L. in Apennini jugis tollit, ex media propemodum ejus longitudine, finibus Aretinorum, eadem ferme parte, ubi fons Arni supra Aretium: &, ut Dionysius Halic. scribit lib. 1, initium ex ipsdem Apennini radicibus habet, in quibus etiam Liris, quamquam ostiis, per quas Mari miscetur utrque, stadiis 10 ccc vel P. M. c inter se distent. Tenuis admodum est initio & modici rivuli instar, lapsuque aliquamdiu paullum etiam incrementi adsumit, quod praeter exiguos Fonticulos Aquae grandes accedant nullae. ubi Fluminibus augeri incipit, paullatim crescens, navigabilis efficitur, non procul Tipherno, sed lintribus & naviculis tantum usque Romam. Procurrens non procul Tipherno, Perusia, Ocriculo. Etruriam ab Umbris Sabinisque dirimit: dein citra Romam P.M. fere xiii Veientes ab Crustuminis, & Fidenatibus; item Latium ab Vaticano separat: Romam tam grandis delatus, ut transiri, nisi Pontibus aut Navigio, nequeat, scribente Halicarnassaeo. Pergit inde ad Ostia sua, ubi in Mare Tyrrhenum evolvitur. Strabo lib. v. Curgum delineant Plinius lib. iii cap. iv, & Servius ad viii Æn. Videndi
units.tr: I came next to the river Tiber, which here forms the boundary between Etruria and Latium. I do not know whether any other river is more celebrated in Roman history. Several names for it are found, some of what I may call the profane kind and some of the sacred. Of the first kind are Tanus, Albula, Rumon, Tiberis. Of the second kind is Serra. Athenaeus, book xv, reports that in the most ancient times it was called Ianus, after Janus, who is said to have reigned far and wide along its banks. That it was called Albula is clear from Varro, On the Latin Language, book iv; from Pliny, book iii, chapter iv; from Virgil, Aeneid book viii; from Ovid, Fasti book iii; and from Silius, book viii. Why so? Paulus the Deacon, perhaps from Festus book i, and Servius on Aeneid viii derive the name from albo colore, "white colour". Whether this is true needs thought. I for my part would not hesitate to add that on closer inspection a yellow colour appears, which Servius himself notes on Aeneid vii. Horace, Odes book i, ode 11, and book ii, ode 3, and Silius Italicus, book ix, confirm this. Hence too the sands of the river are called "tawny" (flavae) by Virgil in Aeneid vii, or "yellowish" (fulva) by Ovid in Metamorphoses book xiii. The Tiber is also called "dark blue" (caeruleus) by Virgil in the same book vii, and by Sidonius in Carmen 11. Stephanus writes the name in a more ancient form, Alba or Albe [Ἄλβα, Ἄλβη]. Marcus Terentius Varro also mentions Albula, book i, cited by Nonius under "Animem". That Rumon was so called from "ruminating" Servius teaches on Aeneid viii. Above all these names, this river took on the most famous name, Tiberis, and various etymologies are given for it. Some, as reported by Servius on Aeneid viii, derive it from Tibris, a king of the Aborigines; Festus, book xviii, and Servius himself in the book I have cited, derive it from the Etruscans. Livy, book i, Ovid, Fasti book ii and Metamorphoses book xiv, Festus likewise in book xviii, and Eusebius derive it from Tiberinus Silvius, a prince of the Alban people. Servius, on Aeneid book viii, verse 72, briefly sets out these opinions and refutes them under the name of Livy, at the passage of that book, verse 230, where for Tiberio one should read Tiberino. Finally, Servius thinks that Tiberim was called from the Greek Tiberis, as if from to hudor [τὸν ὕδωρ], "the water". He gives a double reason for this etymology in books iii and viii of the Aeneid that I mentioned. Varro, On the Latin Language book iv, reports that some call this river Debebris, after Debebrus, a king of the Veientes. Servius on the same book of the Aeneid records that in the sacred usage it was named Serra, from "cutting" (secando). I, however, say that it was so called from the Etruscan or Syriac word meaning "to have the chief place, to rule". Hence Tiberis Sara (for I think this is how it should be written), because it was, as it were, the prince and king of rivers; and the people who ruled over it and lived beside it (Florus calls them the Regnator Populus) are so named. For this reason Virgil elegantly called the same river "Ruler of Waters". Servius, on Aeneid viii, writes that it heard the name Tiberis Terentum in part. I do not see how correctly, for Festus, book xviii, explains Terentum, among others. So much for the names. Under the fourth of these it should be noted that a distinction was observed in pronouncing the words Tiberis, Tibris and Tiberinus. Tiberis was used in common speech, Tibris by the poets, and Tiberinus in sacred usage, as Servius notes on Aeneid viii, though this is not true everywhere. In the vernacular it is Tevere. Poets and others have given it various epithets. The two chief are Lydus and Tuscus. The river is called Lydus from the Lydians, a people famous in war, who, when they moved their seats into Italy, lived beside this river. See Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book i; Virgil, Aeneid book ii, and Servius there. It is called Tuscus from the most noble people, whose neighbour it was on the western bank. So Virgil calls it in Georgics book i, Silius in book viii, and Martial in Epigrams book iv. Virgil in Aeneid calls it the Tyrrhenian River. Strabo, book v; Pliny, book iii, chapter iv; and Sidonius, Carmen 11, and Servius on Aeneid viii bear witness that the Tiber is so called. As is easy to see, the source, which Varro, On the Latin Language book iv, places outside Latium, rises on the ridges of the Apennines, from about the middle of their length, within the territory of the Aretines, in roughly the same part where the source of the Arno is above Arezzo. As Dionysius of Halicarnassus writes in book i, it has its beginning from the same roots of the Apennines, from which also the Liris rises; the mouths through which each empties into the sea are about 300 or 1,000 stades apart. At first it is very slender, like a small brook, and as it flows on for a while it gains a little increase, since no large waters join it apart from small springs. Where it begins to be increased by rivers, gradually growing, it becomes navigable, not far from Tifernum, but only by barges and small boats as far as Rome. Flowing past Tifernum, Perugia and Otricoli, it divides Etruria from the Umbrians and Sabines; then, about thirteen miles this side of Rome, it separates the Veientes from the Crustumini and Fidenates, and likewise separates Latium from the Vatican. Reaching Rome it has become so large that it cannot be crossed except by bridges or boat, as the Halicarnassian writes. It then goes on to its mouth at Ostia, where it rolls out into the Tyrrhenian Sea. Strabo, book v, and Pliny, book iii, chapter iv, and Servius on Aeneid viii describe its course. See also

units.la: & Florus lib. 1. Hist. Rom. cap. iv. & Varro lib. iv de L.L. Longitudo ejus ab Fonte ad Ostia P.M. ci. Latitudinem ad Urbem quatuor fuisse jugerum, notat Dionysius Halicarnass. Profunditas colligitur ex Plinij verbis lib. iii. cap. iv, ubi docet Tiberim Magnarum ex Italo Mari Navium fuisse capacem. Augetur, ut alij Fluvij, praecipue ab Imbribus, adeo ut suis Inundationibus maxima saepe Urbi detrimenta attulerit. De ijs multa Veteres Scriptores; praeter Livium & Iulium Obsequentem, Tacitus 1 Annalium & 1 Historiar. & Horatius lib. 1. Carm. Ode 11. Quae nostrorum temporum, notant Leander Albertus, Georgius Fabricius, Franciscus Schottus, quem vide. Inundationes hujusmodi Prodigijs adnumerare soliti Vereres, scribente Iulio Obsequente multis locis, praecipue cap. xlv, lii, liii. Et quamquam Prisci Romani gravissima sentirent damna ex crebris, quas dixi, Inundationibus; Tiberim tamen hoc suo Auctu Monitorem potius religiosum, quam saevum interpretabantur Tyrannum. Legendus Plinius lib. iii. cap. iv. Exstant Romae multis in locis Indicia Marmoribus incisa, ad quamtam altitudinem Tiberis proximis annis excreverit. Rerum omnium in toto orbe nasci cuiuum, inquit Plinius, Mercator placidissimus: etenim ab Ostia Naves adverso Flumine vel Remis vel Funibus subvehuntur. Plurimis adcolitur adspicituraque villis, opidis, Urbibus, praecipue Roma, quam in duas hodie partes dividit: Vetus venerans Septimontium ad Orientem; qua Occidens, Vaticanum & Ianiculum. Obervandum Tiberinam Aquam multis annis incorruptam servari solitam, suavissimam & salubernimam, quoties hauritur paullo supra Urbem usque ad Mare. Accidit hoc ex mistione Tiberis cum Aniene, quoniam hic Aquas habet multo infectas nitro; quod, ne putrescant, prohibet. Quique Tiberim supra Anienis Ostia adcolunt, utriusque Aquas Romano more, ne corrumpantur, miscent. De Piscibus Tiberinis Romanis peculiarem scripsit libellum Paulus Iovius. Praeter Pontes, qui Romae, etiam alios olim habuit. Inter eos unus est haud procul Ocriculo, ubi Pilae quaedam praegrandes hodieque visuntur, quibus quondam Pons sustinebatur, unus quaternorum e numero, quos Octavianus Augustus Via Flaminia perinsignes & magnificos aedificavit. Tiberis Riparum & Alvei Curatores primus instituit idem Augustus, docente in ipsius vita Suetonio c. xxxvii. Eorum frequens mentio in Monumentis, quae cum apud Martinum Smetium, tum apud Bartholemaeum Marlianum lib. v Topograph. Rom. cap. xiii. Consulendi & Dio lib. lvii & Tacitus sub finem lib. 1 Annal. Amnes vel Fluvios xl.ii in Tiberim influere, docet Plinius lib. iii. cap. iv. Inter eos nominatissimi ad Occidentaliorem ejus Ripam incedentii ab Fonte occurrunt Cierco infra Citernam, auctus Sovaria: Nero, qui, Marte recepto, in Tiberim exit contra Fratam adversa in ripa sitam: Nefler cui Caina, Genna, Ferseno, Fans, aliique miscentur. Clanis vel Glanus; sic enim Plinio in Tiberis descriptione dicitur, qui hodie Chiana: Appiano lib. 1s Κλάνις, Stephano, cui ... Alioquin instar se habet lenti pigrique Amnis, ut Palus videatur potius, quam Flumen, notante Boccatio de Fluminibus. Adcolis perquam noxius est Aëris gravitate, quam ob cœnosa Vada creat. Tiberim Arno conjungit. Agri plurimum amplectitur, Perusinorum & Senensium discrimen efficiens. Recipit Tifam, Foennam, Asfaronem, &, ut Blondus vult, Palam, vel, ut alij centent, à Palta recipitur Palta certe, qui vulgo Paglia, infra Redicofanum Montesque præcellos oritur, perque Convalles descendens tantum colligit incrementi, ut subjecta infestet loca. Qui hodie Treia vel Trisgia nominatur, Chitumnum putant nonnulli dictum Antiquis: eo conniti argumento, quod apud Plinium lib.11. cap.c.11. Clitumnus poni videatur in Falisci: quos ad dexteram Tiberis ripam in Etruria suas sedes, ubi nunc Civitas Castellana, habuisse fatis ex Veterum Monumentis est clarum. Sed quum, ut paullo post dicam, ex conceptissimis Servij ad 11. Georgic. verbis, Clitumnus fluvius sit in Mevania, quæ pars Umbriæ, partis Tusciæ, dicendum est, vel Plinium alium ejusdem virtutis designare Clitumnum; vel suum Falisci etiam ad Mevaniam tunc temporis fuisse Imperium; vel denique locum Plinij esse depravatum. Primum & alterum nullam habent Veri similitudinem; Tertium proxime ab eo, quod est, abest. Nam in veteribus Codicibus legitur: In Falisco omnis (non Clitumnus; aqua potata candidos Boves facit. An recte omnis Malim Amnis ut designet Plinius, Amnem esse apud Falisco: qui, aqua ipsius potata, colorem album Armentis conciliet; quemadmodum Clitumnus idem præstat in Umbria. Pergo. Cremeram; Fabiorum clade insignem, esse censet Leander Albertus Flumen illud, quod ex Bacchani Lacu prorumpens in Tiberim se exonerat, ad Pagum Varcam, unde & Varca nomen sortitur. Raphael Volaterranus putat eum Amniculum esse, qui hodie vicinus Primæ Portæ, quinto ab Urbe miliario, visitur. Tradit Ortelius Adcolas, ab ipso serio interrogatos, nomi aliud ulti Fluvio nomen dedisse, quam Fossa. Dionysius Amnem hunc parum ab Veiis distare notat. Cremeram sane vocant Scriptores omnes: Κρεμέραν dicitur Diodoro lib.xi. Pyrrhus Ligorius Cremeram putat Turiam esse vel Tutiam (sic enim legit Sigonius ad xxvi Livij librum ab V. C.) Silij lib.xiii; ubi inquit: Turia deducit tenuem sine nomine rivum, Et tacite Tuscis inglorius adfluit undis.
units.tr: Florus, Roman History book i, chapter iv; and Varro, On the Latin Language book iv. Its length from the source to Ostia is 101 miles. Dionysius of Halicarnassus notes that at Rome its breadth was four iugera. Its depth can be gathered from the words of Pliny, book iii, chapter iv, where he teaches that the Tiber could carry large ships from the Italian sea. Like other rivers it is increased, especially by rains, so much so that by its floods it has often done the greatest harm to the city. Many ancient writers have told of this, besides Livy and Julius Obsequens; Tacitus, Annals book i and Histories book i; and Horace, Odes book i, ode 11. Recent times are recorded by Leandro Alberti, Georgius Fabricius and Franciscus Schottus, whom see. The ancients were accustomed to count such floods among portents, as Julius Obsequens writes in many places, especially chapters 45, 52 and 53. And although the early Romans suffered very grievous losses from the frequent floods I have mentioned, they nonetheless regarded the Tiber in its flooding as a religious warner rather than a cruel tyrant. Read Pliny, book iii, chapter iv. At many places in Rome there still exist marks cut into marble showing how high the Tiber rose in recent years. "Of all things in the whole world," says Pliny, "the sea is the most peaceable merchant of all": for from Ostia ships are carried up against the current, either by oars or by ropes. It is lined and overlooked by very many villas, towns, cities, especially Rome, which today it divides into two parts: the old city, which faces the Septimontium to the east, and on the west the Vatican and the Janiculum. It should be observed that the water of the Tiber was customarily kept for many years uncorrupted, very sweet and healthful, whenever it was drawn a little above the city, all the way to the sea. This comes from the mixing of the Tiber with the Anio, since the Anio carries waters much tainted with nitre, which prevents them from rotting. Those who live beside the Tiber above the mouth of the Anio mix the waters of both, in the Roman manner, so that they do not spoil. Paulus Iovius wrote a special little book on the Tiberine fish of Rome. Besides the bridges at Rome, the river once had others too. Among them is one not far from Otricoli, where some very large piers may still be seen today, on which a bridge once rested: one of four, of which Octavian Augustus built along the Via Flaminia, very notable and magnificent. The same Augustus first appointed curators of the Tiber's banks and channel, as Suetonius teaches in Augustus's life, chapter 37. Their frequent mention is found in the monuments, both in Martin Smet and in Bartolomeo Marliani, Topography of Rome, book v, chapter 13. Dio, book lvii, and Tacitus at the end of Annals book i should also be consulted. Pliny, book iii, chapter iv, teaches that 42 rivers and streams flow into the Tiber. Among these the most famous, as one goes along its western bank from the source, are the Cierco below Citerna, increased by the Sovaria; the Nera, which, after receiving the Marta, flows into the Tiber opposite Fratta, lying on the opposite bank; and the Nestor, into which the Caina, Genna, Ferseno, Fans and others flow. The Clanis or Glanus (for so it is called by Pliny in his description of the Tiber) is today the Chiana; Appian, book i, calls it Κλάνις [Klanis], and Stephanus also. Otherwise it has the character of a slow and sluggish stream, so that it seems more a marsh than a river, as Boccaccio notes in his book on rivers. It is very harmful to those who live beside it because of the heaviness of its air, which it creates from its muddy shallows. It joins the Tiber to the Arno. It embraces a great deal of territory, forming the boundary between the Perugians and the Sienese. It receives the Tifa, Foenna, Asfarone and, as Biondo holds, the Pala; or, as others think, the Palta is received by it. The Palta certainly, which is commonly called the Paglia, rises below Radicofani and the very high mountains, and descending through the valleys gathers so much increase that it damages the lands lying beneath it. Some think the river now called the Treia or Tresgia was called Clitumnus by the ancients, relying on the argument that in Pliny, book ii, chapter 103, Clitumnus seems to be placed among the Falisci; and it is clear from ancient monuments that the Falisci had their seats on the right bank of the Tiber in Etruria, where Civita Castellana now is. But since, as I shall say a little later, from the very clear words of Servius on Georgics book ii, the river Clitumnus lies in Mevania, which is part of Umbria, part of Tuscany, we must say either that Pliny is referring to another Clitumnus of the same kind; or that the Falisci also had rule over Mevania at that time; or finally that Pliny's passage is corrupt. The first and second have no semblance of truth; the third is very close to what is the case, but falls short of it. For in the old manuscripts it is read: "In Falisco omnis" (not "Clitumnus") "water drunk makes white oxen." Whether it is right to read omnis I should prefer Amnis, so that Pliny means that there is a river among the Falisci which, when its water is drunk, gives the cattle a white colour, just as the Clitumnus does in Umbria. I go on. Cremera, notable for the defeat of the Fabii, Leandro Alberti thinks is that river which bursts out of Lake Baccano and discharges itself into the Tiber at the village of Varca, from which it also takes the name Varca. Raffaele Volaterrano thinks it is the little stream which is seen today near Prima Porta, at the fifth milestone from the city. Ortelius reports that when he seriously asked the inhabitants, they gave the river no name other than Fossa. Dionysius notes that this stream was not far from Veii. All writers certainly call it Cremera; it is called Κρεμέρα [Kremera] by Diodorus, book xi. Pirro Ligorio thinks that Cremera is Turia or Tutia (for so Sigonius reads it at Livy, book xxvi, ab urbe condita), in Silius, book xiii, where he says: "Turia leads down a slender stream without a name, and silently flows in, unrenowned, with the Tuscan waves."

units.la: Petrus tamen Marlus Turiam Rivulum esse dicit in via Appia, ut ab Urbe P.M; salso, ut opinatur Ortelius. Prope Cremeram cccvi Fabios, cum quinque Clientum, Servorumque millibus internecione ab Veientibus occisos, scribunt Livius lib.ii, Dionysius Halic. lib.ix, Ovidius 11 Fastorum, Florus lib.i. Histor. Rom. cap. xii, Orosius lib.ii. Hist. cap. v, Eutropius lib.i, Agellius lib.xvii. Noct. Attic. cap. xxi, Plutarchus in Vita Camilli, Silius Italicus lib. 11 & vii, Servius ad vi Æneid. & alij. Infra Romam est Galera Fluvius, qui haud procul Maliano Tiberu fit incola. Hi eum alijs ad Occidentalem Tiberis ripam conspiciuntur: sequentes, qua Oriens est, Tiberi adfluunt. Non magni nominis sunt Regia, Asinus, Rufina, Venita, & alij ibidem. Qui in Umbria Chiatus vel Chusfu hodie Latinè scribentibus, Vulgo autem Chiazzo, nec Afius est, ut falso quidam judicant. Ptolemæi: nec Aesis Strabonis, Plinij, Pomponiique Melæ; qui eum Semnonum flumen faciunt, locisque ad Mare Hadriaticum sitis adcenset, quemadmodum suo loco videbimus. Potest tamen Chiatius paullo Latinius vocari Afius, non quod ita Ptolemaeo nuncupetur, sed quod ex monte Afi profluat. Consulendus Landinus in Dantis Paradiso. Cant. Recipit in se præter Seircam, Rafinam, qui Larone augetur, Mactaiam & alios, Topinum ad Canariam, ejusque nomen extinguit, solo Chiaty retento; posteaque, opido Bertonio lustrato, prope Torsanam in Tiberim evolvitur. Qui nunc Topinus, Tinia (in quibusdam libris est Tinna) Plinio dicitur: Tiniας Strabonis. De eo Silius Italicus lib. viii: Tiniaque inglorius humor.
units.tr: Peter Marlus, however, says that the Turia is a small river on the Appian Way, P.M. (passus mille) from the City, and a salt stream, as Ortelius thinks. Near the Cremera, 306 Fabii, together with five thousand of their clients and servants, were slain to a man by the Veientes; so write Livy, book 2; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 9; Ovid, Fasti, book 2; Florus, Roman History, book 1, chapter 12; Orosius, History, book 2, chapter 5; Eutropius, book 1; Gellius, Attic Nights, book 17, chapter 21; Plutarch in the Life of Camillus; Silius Italicus, books 2 and 7; Servius on Aeneid 6; and others. Below Rome is the river Galera, which, not far from Malianum, becomes a tributary of the Tiber. Some of these are seen with others on the western bank of the Tiber; those flowing on the eastern side join the Tiber. The Regia, Asinus, Rufina, Venita, and others there are of no great note. The stream in Umbria called Chiatus or Chusfu by Latin writers today, and commonly Chiazzo, is not the Afius, as some wrongly judge. Nor is it the Aesis of Ptolemy, Strabo, Pliny, and Pomponius Mela, who make it the river of the Semnones and count it among the places on the Adriatic Sea, as we shall see in its place. Yet the Chiatius may be called Afius in a rather more Latin way, not because Ptolemy so names it, but because it flows from Mount Afius. Landino on Dante's Paradiso canto should be consulted. It receives, besides the Seircam and Rafina, which is increased by the Larone, the Mactaia and others, and the Topinus near Canaria; it extinguishes that name, the Chiaty alone being kept. Afterwards, having passed by the town of Bertonio, it rolls down into the Tiber near Torsana. What is now called the Topinus, Tinia (in some books Tinna), is called by Pliny; it is the Tinias of Strabo. Of it Silius Italicus says, book 8: "and the Tinia, humble stream without glory."

units.la: Quur ita? Quod non navigabilis, Rivulusque magis, quam Flumen. In Tinia ripis ingentes passim adparent Ædificiorum ruinæ, fundamentaque maximorum operum, quæ ab Romanis ad tutelam Viæ Flaminiæ quondam excitata. Augetur etiam Topinus ab alijs Fluvijs: inter quos vere Viri magni agnoscunt Clitumnum. Hic enim, notante Servio ad 11. Georgic. Fluvius est in Mevania, quæ Pars Umbriæ, partis Tusciæ. Iam vero Ateuniam opidum esse Umbriæ, quod hodie Serrania, dicam cam cap. xxiv. Oritur autem Clitumnus ex Trebulanis Collibus, in quibus olim veteres oliviteræque Mutilcæ, limpidissimo copiosissimoque erumpens Fonte, sequeintra Fulginum vel Fulgineum Topino commiscet. Nomen, quod hodie, in præsentia non occurrit. Philargyrius aut eum Umbriam ab Tuscia dividere. Quod apud Plinium male Falicis adscribatur, ante notatum. Constans apud Veteres fuit opinio, Aquam Clitumni a Bubus potatam albos creare Fœtus, experti sagmarique solitos ab Romanis ad Triumphalia Sacrificia. Virgilius lib. ii. Georgic. Hinc albi, Clitumne, greges, & maxima Taurus Victima, sæpe tuo persusi Flumine sacro, Romanos ad Templa Deum duxere Triumphos.
units.tr: Why so? Because it is not navigable and is more a brook than a river. Along the banks of the Tinia appear everywhere huge ruins of buildings and the foundations of very great works, which the Romans once erected to protect the Via Flaminia. The Topinus is also swollen by other rivers, among which learned men rightly recognise the Clitumnum. For, as Servius notes on Georgics 2, it is a river in Mevania, which is part of Umbria and part of Tuscany. Now, that Ateunia is a town of Umbria, which today is Serrania, I shall say in chapter 24. The Clitumnus rises from the Trebulan hills, where of old there were olive groves and mutilated... bursting forth from a very clear and very abundant spring, and then, near Fulginum or Fulgineum, mingles with the Topinus. The name which occurs today does not appear at present. Philargyrius says that it divides Umbria from Tuscany. That it is wrongly ascribed to the Falisci in Pliny has been noted before. It was a constant opinion among the ancients that the water of the Clitumni, drunk by oxen, produced white offspring, and these, once tested, were led by the Romans to triumphal sacrifices. Virgil, Georgics book 2: "Hence, Clitumnus, white herds, and the greatest bull, the victim often bathed in your sacred stream, led the Roman triumphs to the temples of the gods."

units.la: Propertius in Elegiis: Qua formosa suo Clitumnus flumina luco Integit, & niveo abiit unda Boves.
units.tr: Propertius in the Elegies: "Where the Clitumnus, lovely, covers its streams with its grove, and the water has made the oxen snow-white."

units.la: Silius Italicus de Bello Punico lib. viii: Et lavit ingentem perfusum Flumine Sacro Clitumnus Taurum.
units.tr: Silius Italicus, on the Punic War, book 8: "And the Clitumnus bathed the huge bull, drenched in its sacred stream."

units.la: Clitumnus sane Deus habitus, eique sacrata existimatur fuisse Ædes, quæ in propinquo visitur marmorea & antiquissima, nec non more Corinthio pulcherrime constructa, cujus Scenographiam & ornamenta varia curiose describit, Franciscus Schottus. Sequitur inde post Topinum aliusque Nar. Sic Virgilio, Strabon, Lucano, Tacito, Silio, Plinio, Procopio, aliusque nominatur, qui hodie Negra Italis αὶνΦοgοιν forte, quum Aquas habeat albas. Nar albus Aquaque Sulphurea, Virgilio lib. vii Æneidos, ubi Servius rationem Epitheti, vel ab Aqua sulfurea, vel ab Colore Saporeve sulphureo notat sumtam. Albescentes illi undas tribuit Silius lib. viii. Sulphureus Amnis canitur Martialis lib. vii. Ex Amiternis Montibus oriri notat Pomponius Sabinus ad vii. Æneid. Defluit, ex Leandri diffinitione, ex Apennini jugis; ibique, ut Plinius ait, ex Monte Fiscello, duobus erumpens Fontibus, qui foramina sunt in Saxo, natura sic excavato, ut naribus animalis, seu nasi spiraculis admodum sint similia. quamobrem etiam ab Antiquis Nar est vocatus: dein juxta Vacunæ Nemora descendens, ut Plinius testatur, per subjectam Vallem fluit, posteaque Tiberi conjungitur. Augetur prope tres Pontes ex Coriti Montis radicibus . Cum Lacu Velino conjungi scribit Tacitus. Narniam oppidum ab eo dici tradunt Livius & Stephanus in Urbium Syllabo. Supra Narem prætergressis Narniam adparent à dextris admirandi Pontis Fornices, qui duos præcelsos & abruptos Montes, subterlabente Flumine, solebat conjungere, ut æquali via transitus ab oppido Narnia pateret in montem adversum. Auctorem memorat Augustum Procopius; qui haud umquam altiores Pontis Arcus abse visos profitetur. Qualis quantusque fuerit, docent hodieque ex lapide quadrato prægrandi reliquiæ. Exaudiendus de eo Martialis Epigrammate ad Narniam: Sed jam parce mihi, nec abutere Narnia Quinto, Perpetuo liceat sic tibi Ponte frui.
units.tr: The Clitumnus was indeed regarded as a god, and a temple is thought to have been consecrated to him. It can be seen nearby, marble and very ancient, and also most beautifully built in the Corinthian manner; Francesco Schotto describes its stage-set and various decorations with care. After the Topinus follows the other river, the Nar. So it is named by Virgil, Strabo, Lucan, Tacitus, Silius, Pliny, Procopius, and others. It is today called Negra by the Italians, and perhaps by the Greeks [αἰνφοργοιν], since it has white waters: "The white Nar and the sulphurous water," Virgil, Aeneid book 7, where Servius notes the reason for the epithet, taken either from the sulphurous water or from the colour and taste of sulphur. Silius, book 8, gives it "whitening waves." Martial, book 7, sings of the "sulphurous river." Pomponius Sabinus notes on Aeneid 7 that it rises from the Amiternine mountains. According to Leandro's description it flows down from the ridges of the Apennines; there, as Pliny says, it bursts forth from two springs on Mount Fiscellus, which are openings in the rock, hollowed out by nature so as to resemble very closely the nostrils of an animal or the breathing holes of a nose; for this reason the ancients also called it Nar. Then, descending past the groves of Vacuna, as Pliny testifies, it flows through the valley below and afterwards joins the Tiber. It is increased near three bridges, from the roots of Mount Coritus. Tacitus writes that it joins the Lake Velinus. Livy and Stephanus in his list of cities say that the town of Narnia takes its name from it. Going past the Nar above, on the right as you approach Narnia, appear the arches of a remarkable bridge, which once joined two very high and steep mountains, the river flowing beneath, so that there was a level passage from the town of Narnia to the mountain opposite. Procopius, who records its builder as Augustus, professes that he never saw higher arches of a bridge. What its size and shape were is shown even today by the remains of huge square stone. Martial's epigram to Narnia should be heard on this point: "But now spare me, and do not abuse, Narnia, the Fifth; may you so enjoy your perpetual bridge."

units.la: Actum olim fuisse in Senatu de Nare in rivos deducendo tradit Tacitus lib. i. Annalium. Succedunt Nari Romam versus Himella, Fabaris, Allia, Rivus Solis, Anienus, & alij. Himella, cujus meminerunt Virgilius & Vibius, ijs in montibus Caput tollens, qui circa Velini Lacus exitus sunt, transcursa Sabinia, inter Ocriculum & Maliarum in Tiberim deflut. Qui Fabaris Virgilio Sidonioque, hodie Farfarus vocatur; quo nomine notus etiam apud Servium Plauto. Faber corrupte apud Vibium Sequestrum. Oritur ex Montibus, qui quondam Tetrici, ad opidulum, quod ab Amnis Fonte Caput Farfari. Plauti locus apud Servium hic est: Pussipabo te tamquam Folia Farfari.
units.tr: Tacitus, book 1 of the Annals, reports that once in the Senate there was a proposal to divide the Nar into channels. Towards Rome, after the Nar, follow the Himella, Fabaris, Allia, Rivus Solis, Anienus, and others. The Himella, which Virgil and Vibius mention, rises on those mountains which are the sources around the Lake Velinus; after crossing the Sabine country it flows into the Tiber between Ocriculum and Malliarum. The Fabaris, called by Virgil and Sidonius, is today called the Farfarus*, a name also known to Servius in Plautus. Faber is a corruption in Vibius Sequester. It rises from the mountains which were once called Tetrici, near a small town which takes its name from the spring of the river, Caput Farfari. The passage of Plautus quoted by Servius is this: "I shall pound you like leaves of the Farfarus."

units.la: Ex quibus patet Arborum circa flumen hoc frequentia, quæ gratissimas efficiunt umbras; unde Ovidio ——amœna Farsarus umbra.
units.tr: From these things it is clear that there are many trees along this river, which make the most pleasant shade; hence Ovid: "the pleasant shade of the Farfarus."

units.la: Sabiniam hæc ætate intersecat per pulcherrimos Campos, utrinque frondosis conseptos Arboribus; quarum perjucundis tegitur umbris. Allium Blondus & Volateranus esse volunt, qui Curefis hodie. Longe alia mens est Francisco Florido & Leandro Alberto; quibus Allia fluvius ille, qui hodie Caminato, vernacule. Alliam enim enum vixquarto ab Vrbe lapide Veteres locant Historiæ: Curesin autem vicesimo distare confirmat Floridus. Crustumenis defluit montibus. Ad interiora provolutus prope portum Mentis Rotundi M.P. ab Roma tribus, aut paullo amplius in Tiberim defertur. Meminerunt Allia nulli non Scriptores. Vnico L.scribendum docet in Orthographia Aldus. Quondam etiam, teste Leandro, Rivum Mussum, Rio di Mosio, pro Rivo Morsi, Rio di Monte appellare solent ab cruenta illa, ut volunt, Romanorum cum Brenno Gallorum Duce pugna, xv Kal. Sext. qui Dies Alliensis dicus. Legendi Livius lib. v, Plutarchus in Vita Camilli, & alij. Rivus Solis, Rivo del Sole, Blondo Leandroque videtur is, de quo Horatius lib.1. Epist. ad Lollium:
units.tr: In our time it cuts through the Sabine country across beautiful fields, enclosed on both sides by leafy trees, and is covered by their most delightful shade. Blondus and Volaterranus wish the Allia to be the river which today is called Curesis. Francesco Flora and Leandro Alberti think quite otherwise; for them the Allia is that river which today is called, in the vernacular, Caminato. For the ancient historians place the Allia barely four miles from the City, while Floro confirms that the Curesis is twenty miles away. It flows down from the Crustumine mountains. Having rolled into the interior, near the port of Mentis Rotundus, it is conveyed into the Tiber three miles, or a little more, from Rome. Every writer mentions the Allia. Aldus teaches in his orthography that it should be written with a single L. Formerly, too, as Leandro testifies, the people called it Rivus Mussus, Rio di Mosio, for Rivus Morsi, Rio di Monte, from that bloody battle of the Romans with the Gallic leader Brennus, as they say, on the 15th day before the Kalends of August, which is called the Day of the Allia. Read Livy, book 5, Plutarch in the Life of Camillus, and others. The Rivus Solis, Rivo del Sole, seems to Blondus and Leandro to be that of which Horace speaks in Epistles book 1, to Lollius:

units.la: Me quoties reficit gelidus Digentia rivus,Quam Mandella bibit rugosus frigore pagus,Quid sentire putas, quid credis, Amice, precari?
units.tr: "Whenever the cold Digentia brook refreshes me, which the wrinkled village of Mandela drinks in its frost, what do you think, my friend, what do you believe I pray for?"

units.la: Quos versus exponens Acron Mandellam Vicum in Sabinis esse scribit, ubi Rivus Solis, Horatio Digentia vocatus. Qui Anio dicitur apud Livium in libris ab V.C. non uno loco, Virgilium vi Æneidos, Horat.lib.1. Carm. Od. vii. Melam in Cosmographiâ. Silium Italicum lib.viii & xii, Propertium in Elegis. Plinium in libr. nat. historiæ; Anien autem apud Halicarnass. & Strabonem; Anienus apud Statium in Tiburtino; Anien apud Vibium Sequestrum; quemque Ναρόμον olim vocatum scribit, ni corruptus sit locus, Frontinus lib.ii. de Aquæductibus: hodie, Blondo, Leandro, aliisque censentibus, Teve one vocatur. Nomen illi, ex Silij Italici lib. xii sententia, ab Anio, Etruscorum Rege: ex Vibij Sequestri mente, ab Anione, Apollinis filio. Oritur, ut Plinius scribit lib. iii cap. xi, in montibus Trebanorum, tresque Lacus amœnitate nobiles, qui nomen dedere Sublacij, de quo alibi, deferet in Tiberim. Strabo eum ex Alba decurrere scribit præter Latinam Mariorum Vrbem, indeque per Campos propinquos in Tiberim defluere. Tacitus ab Montibus Simpruinis descendere, tribusque ab Roma millibus Tiberi conjungi dicit. Ad Trebam Vrbem manare tradit Frontinus ii Aquæductuum. Lacui Velinorum infundi scribit Vibius. Ad Tibur ex alta rupe, præcipite Aquæ delectu, qui καταρρακτης apud Strabonem lib. v, maximo cum fragore decidit in subiectam Convallem: indeque per plana & fructuosa loca fluit in Tiberim, Sabinos ab Latinis dividens; potu gratus, aspectu perjucundus, teste Halicarn.lib.v. cuius hæc verba: ὁ ναλίης ... (Greek). Transitum ejus quatuor conjungunt Pontes. Eorum unus in Via Tiburtina, Mammea vulgo dictus, tanquam Pons Mammea, qui primum ab Antonino Pio factus, dein ab Mammea, Alexandri xxv Imperatoris Matre restitutus, ac marmore sumtuose fuit exornatus, quo tamen nunc spoliatus cernitur; Alter paullo inferius Viam Nomentanam jungit. Eum quis condiderit, nondum constat. Integer est, sed ornamentis suis plane denudatus. Succedit infra Tertius in Via Salaria, tribus ab Vrbe Roma milliaribus, ab Narsete Iustiniani Imperatoris Augusti Legato, victis Gothis, fabricatus; quod docent positæ ibi Inscriptiones: quarum Prior, litteris ob longis & male proportionatis concepta, ita habet; IMPERANTE, D.N. PIISSIMO, AC. TRIVMPHALI. SEMPER. IVSTINIANO. PP. AVG. ANN. XXXVIII MARSES. VIR. GLORIOSISSIMVS. EX PRÆPOSITO. SACRI. PALATII, EX. CONS. ATQVE. PATRICIVS. POST. VICTORIAM. GOTHICAM. IPSIS, IORVM. REGIBVS CELERITATE. MIRABILI. CONFLICTV. PVBLICO, SVPERATIS, ATQVE. PROSTRATIS LIBERTATE. VRBIS. ROMÆ. AC. TOTIVS. ITALIÆ. RESTITVTA. PONTEM. VIÆ. SALARIÆ, VSQVE AD. AQVAM. A. NEFANDISSIMO. TOTILA. TYRANNO. DISTRVCTVM. FVRGATO FLVMINIS. ALVEO IN. MELIOREM. STATVM. QVAM. QVONDAM. FVERAT. RENOVAVIT
units.tr: Explaining these verses, Acron writes that Mandela is a village among the Sabines, where the Rivus Solis is, called by Horace the Digentia. The river called Anio in Livy, in the books from the foundation of the City, appears in more than one place: in Virgil, Aeneid 6; Horace, Odes 1, ode 7; Mela in his Cosmography; Silius Italicus, books 8 and 12; Propertius in the Elegies; and Pliny in his Natural History. Anien appears in Halicarnassus and Strabo; Anienus in Statius, in the Tiburtine poem; Anien in Vibius Sequester; and Frontinus, book 2 on Aqueducts, writes that it was once called Narmon, unless the place is corrupt. Today, according to Blondus, Leandro, and others, it is called Teverone. According to the opinion of Silius Italicus, book 12, its name came from Anio, king of the Etruscans; in the mind of Vibius Sequester, from Anio, son of Apollo. As Pliny writes, book 3, chapter 11, it rises in the mountains of the Trebani and, after three lakes famous for their charm, which gave their name to Sublaqueum (of which elsewhere), it flows into the Tiber. Strabo writes that it descends from Alba, past the Latin city of the Marsi, and thence flows through the neighbouring plains into the Tiber. Tacitus says that it comes down from the Simbruine mountains and joins the Tiber three miles from Rome. Frontinus, book 2 on Aqueducts, records that it runs to the city of Treba. Vibius writes that it pours into the Lake Velinus. At Tibur, from a high rock, with a headlong fall of water, which Strabo calls katarraktes in book 5, it drops with great roar into the valley below; thence it flows through level and fruitful places into the Tiber*, dividing the Sabines from the Latins, pleasant to drink and most delightful to look at, as Halicarnassus testifies in book 5, whose words are these: [Greek quotation garbled in the source]. Four bridges span its passage. One of them, on the Via Tiburtina, is commonly called the Mammea, as if it were the Mammean Bridge; it was first built by Antoninus Pius, then restored by Mammaea, mother of the emperor Alexander, and sumptuously adorned with marble, though it is now seen stripped of that. Another, a little lower down, joins the Via Nomentana. Who built it is not yet known. It is intact, but completely stripped of its ornaments. Further below, a third stands on the Via Salaria, three miles from the City of Rome, built by Narses, legate of the Emperor Justinian Augustus, after the defeat of the Goths; the inscriptions placed there show this. The first of these, written in letters too long and badly proportioned, reads thus: [Latin inscription in capitals, reproduced in the source; translated:] In the reign of our most pious, triumphant, and ever-august Emperor Justinian, Father of the Country, in the thirty-eighth year, Narses, most glorious man, ex-Praepositus of the Sacred Palace, ex-consul and patrician, after the Gothic victory, having overcome and struck down the Gothic kings themselves by wonderful speed and open combat, and having restored liberty to the City of Rome and to all Italy, renewed the bridge of the Via Salaria, destroyed as far as the water by the most wicked tyrant Totila, the channel of the river having been cleared and restored to a better state than it formerly was.

units.la: Altera litteris paullo melioribus sic sonat: QVAM. BINÆ. CVRVATI ⊕. DIRECTA. EST. SEMITA. PONTIS ⊕ ATQVE. INTERRVPTVM ⊕ CONTINVATVÞ. ITER ⊕ CALCAMVS. RAPIDAS ⊕ SVBIECTI. GVRGITIS. VNDAS ⊕ ET. LIBET. IRATÆ ⊕ CERNERE. MVRMVR. AQVÆ ⊕ ITE. IGITVR. FACILES ⊕ PER. GAVDIA. VESTRA. QVIRITES ⊕ ET. MARMOR. RESONANS ⊕ FLAVIVS. VBIQVE. CANAT ⊕ QVI. POTVIT. RIGIDAS ⊕ GOTHORVM. SVBDVRE. MENTES ⊕ HIC, DOCVIT. DVRVM ⊕ FLVMINA. FERRE. IVGVM ⊕
units.tr: The other, in slightly better letters, reads thus: "Since the path of the bridge has been straightened and the interrupted way is continued, we tread the rapid waters under the bent eddies, and it is pleasing to watch the murmur of the angry water. Go therefore, easy, through your joys, Quirites, and let the resounding marble sing of Flavius everywhere, who was able to subdue the stiff minds of the Goths. Here he taught the rivers to bear a hard yoke."

units.la: Ad Pontem hunc ferunt Hannibalem Imbrium inundatione perterritum, soluto obsidio, castra movisse ab Vrbe. Quartus Pons Tiburi, quam Romae, propinquior est, Lucanus; ubi Moles rotunda conspicitur, & praeclarum in marmore Pontis T. Plautii Silvani Elogium, quod commodiore adiicibam loco. Anienis Aquae multo infectae sunt Nitro: ideoque mistae iis Tiburinae bonitatem habent singularem, ut alibi dixi. Pausanias tradit Anienis Aquas ea esse natura, ut ad primum contactum gelidissimae, mox paullatim calescere videantur. Auctor est Martialis Eburi ablutum Anienis aqua Candorem accipere, similiterque Dentes humanos. Inter Anienis Arenas leguntur Amygdala, Anisum, Foeniculum, aliaque in Petram versa, ut in Romanorum convivijs in deliciis sint, ludantque arripientes, putantes se dulciaria Tragemata arripere, vocanturque paullim Confetti da Isvolt. Superioribus quoque annis Corporis Cadaver humani casum, & in flumen Anienem proiectum Arboris radici adhaerens in lapidem conversum est, & a putrefactione alienum, ut Titus Celsus, Patricius Romanus, abie visum adfirmat. Detraxit juxta Fluvium hunc memorabili Victoria Gallo Provocatori caelo Torquem aureum Torquatus, cognomen inde meritus Torquati, ut pluribus referunt Livius lib. vii, Florus lib. i. cap. xiii, Q. Claudius lib. i. Annal. apud Agellum lib. ix. cap. xii, Orosius lib. ii, c. ix, Eutropius lib. ii, Valer. Maximus lib. ii cap. ii, Auctor de VV. Inl. cap. xxviii. Delicatissimum Amnium vocat in Epistolis Plinius. Augetur cum aliis Fluviolis, tum Malliano & Veresi. Ὀυεφίος dicitur Straboni. Haud procul Tusculo Frascata est, olim L. Luculli Villa. Ibi non nulli Aqua Virginis, quae hodieque Romam accedit, Fontem repertum tradiderunt. Eam Aquam Plinius lib. xxxi. cap. iii M. Agrippam in Urbem adduxisse scribit ab octavi Lapidis diverticulo duobus P. M. Praenestina Via. Influit item ad Urbem Tiberim Aqua, quae Crabra, cujus apud M. Tullium & Frontinum est mentio. Hodie Lacus Marrana vocatur. Marancella dicitur Lucae Peto, libro Mensuris Romanis. Paullo infra Romam est Almo sive Almon Horatio, Ovidio, Silio, Ammiano, Prudentio, Hieronymo, & quibus non celebratus? Hodie Dachia nominatur. De eo Vibius Sequester: Almon Roma Fluvius, ubi Mater Deum vi Kalend. April. lavatur. Lucanus lib. i. Belli Pharsalici.
units.tr: They say that Hannibal, terrified by the flooding of the Anio, broke off the siege and moved his camp away from the City at this bridge. The Fourth Bridge, nearer to Tivoli than to Rome, is Lucanus, where a round mole can be seen and the famous inscription of T. Plautius Silvanus on the marble of the bridge, which I added in a more suitable place. The waters of the Anienis are heavily impregnated with nitre, and so the Tiburtine waters mixed with them have a singular goodness, as I have said elsewhere. Pausanias relates that the waters of the Anienis are of such a nature that at first touch they seem very cold and then gradually grow warm. Martial is the authority that Ivory washed in the water of the Anienis takes on whiteness, and human teeth likewise. Among the sands of the Anienis are found almonds, anise, fennel, and other things turned into stone, which are served at Roman banquets as delicacies, and people playing with them, grasping them, think they are seizing sweetmeats; they are called Confetti da Isvolt by degrees. In recent years too, a human corpse that had fallen and been thrown into the river Anienem, clinging to the root of a tree, was turned into stone and was free from putrefaction, as Titus Celsus, a Roman patrician, affirms he saw with his own eyes. Near this river, in the famous victory, Torquatus took from the Gallic challenger a golden torque, and earned the surname Torquatus from it, as many authors report: Livy book 7, Florus book 1 chapter 13, Q. Claudius book 1 of the Annals (in Gellius book 9 chapter 12), Orosius book 2 chapter 9, Eutropius book 2, Valerius Maximus book 2 chapter 2, the author De viris illustribus chapter 28. Pliny in his Letters calls it "the most delicate of streams" (Delicatissimum Amnium). It is increased by other small streams, both the Malliano & Veresi. Strabo calls it [Ὀυεφίος]. Not far from Tusculum lies Frascati, formerly the villa of L. Lucullus. Some have reported that the Aqua Virginis, which still reaches Rome today, was found there as a spring. Pliny in book 31 chapter 3 writes that M. Agrippa brought that water into the City from the branch of the eighth milestone, on the Praenestine Way. Also flowing into the City is the Tiber's Aqua, which is called Crabra; it is mentioned by Cicero and Frontinus. Today it is called Lacus Marrana. Lucas Peto, in his book on Roman measures, calls it Marancella. A little below Rome is the Almo, or Almon, celebrated by Horace, Ovid, Silius, Ammianus, Prudentius, Jerome, and by whom not? Today it is called Dachia. Of it Vibius Sequester says: "Almon is a river of Rome, where the Mother of the Gods is washed on the sixth day before the Kalends of April." Lucan, book 1 of the Pharsalia:

units.la: Et lotam parte revocant Almone Cybellen.
units.tr: And they bring back Cybele, bathed in the waters of Almo.

units.la: Hactenus de Tiberi, Fluminibusque variis; quae cum eo, nominibus amissis, Mare petunt: sequuntur reliqua Latii, ut antiquitus appellabantur, Numicus, Lorasina, Stura, Nymphaeus, Ufens. Numicium, vel ut alij scribunt, Numicum, in latio locant Virgilius, Ovidius, Plinius; in Agro Laurenti, Livius, idemque alio loco Ovidius, Vibius; haud procul Lavinio Halicarnassaeus lib. i. cui Νομίκιον vocatur, & Silius lib. viii: Numicium Stagnum habet Aurelius Victor. Rivo est hodie, ut vult Pyrrhus Ligorius. Notat ad Æneidem Virgilianam Servius Numicium ingentem fluvium ante mortem Ænaeae fuisse; ceterum post decrescendo paullatim in Fontem redactum, qui & ipse exaruerit, interceptis Sacris; Vestae quippe non nisi de hoc Fluvio libari licuisse. Lorasina Fluminis circa Antiates meminit Livius lib. xliii. De Stura sic scribit Festus, Stura Flumen in Agro Laurenti est, quod quidam Asturam vocant. Στυγὸς Straboni nuncupatur, & Livio lib. xxvi, cui sex millibus locatur ab Urbe. Apud Virgilium vii Æneidos pro Satura Palude nonnulli agnoscunt notante Servio, Asturam Paludem, eamque Flumen hoc interpretantur. Nomen hodie retinet, indicante Leandro, qui non recte confundit cum Nymphaeo Plinij. Nam Stura & Nymphaeus duo diversaque Plinio sunt Flumina. Ufens Fluvius est iuxta Terracinam & Privernum, Virgilio vii Æneid. Silio lib. i, Vibio Sequestro, Festo, alijs. Apud Straboncm Αὐφιδὸν scribitur, non sine errore, uti notant docti Viri. Baldino dicitur in Tabula Ligorij: aliis est Bandino. Hodie Ausente vocatur, uti tradit Leander Albertus. In Itineraria Tabula etiam notatur hujus Fluvij Cursus & Alveus, non adscripto tamen nomine.
units.tr: So much for the Tiber and its various rivers; those which, having lost their names with it, make for the sea. There follow the rest of Latium, as they were called in antiquity: the Numicus, the Lorasina, the Stura, the Nymphaeus, the Ufens. Virgil, Ovid and Pliny place the Numicium, or as others write, the Numicum, in Latium; Livy places it in the territory of Laurentum, and Ovid in another passage, and Vibius too; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 1, not far from Lavinium, calls it Νομίκιον, and Silius book 8 does likewise. Aurelius Victor has the Numicium Stagnum. It is today the Rivo, as Pyrrhus Ligorius thinks. Servius, in his notes on Virgil's Aeneid, observes that the Numicium was a huge river before the death of Aeneas, but afterwards, gradually diminishing, was reduced to a spring, which itself dried up, the sacred rites being cut off; for it was permitted to pour libations to Vesta only from this river. Livy book 43 mentions the Lorasina river near the Antiates. Festus writes of the Stura as follows: "The Stura is a river in the territory of Laurentum, which some call the Astura." Strabo calls it Στυγὸς [Stygos], and Livy book 26 places it six thousand paces from the City. In Virgil's Aeneid book 7, some recognise in place of the Satura Palude (as Servius notes) the Asturam Paludem, and they interpret it as this river. It keeps its name today, as Leander indicates, who wrongly confuses it with the Nymphaeus of Pliny. For the Stura and the Nymphaeus are two separate rivers in Pliny. The Ufens is a river near Terracina and Privernum, in Virgil Aeneid book 7, in Silius book 1, in Vibius Sequester, Festus and others. In Strabo it is written Αὐφιδὸν [Aphidon], not without error, as learned men note. It is called Baldino in Ligorio's map; for others it is Bandino. Today it is called Ausente, as Leander Albertus relates. Its course and bed are also marked in the Itinerary map, though no name is attached to it.

units.la: Sic ad Lirim, Latij terminum, Campaniæque initium, perventum nobis. Liris Plinio, Livio, Melæ; Λείρις Strabono, aliisque Græcis: Lyru per y scribitur in quibusdam Lucani & Taciti libris. Λείρις πολαμὸς, Κλαωις δ' ἰχαλῶν ποσσῶν, inquit Strabo; cui consentit Plinius, uti quidem ex Strabone emendandus: Colonia Minturnæ, Liris Amnæ divisa Glanis quondam appellato. Liternum etiam dictum putat Appianus Alexandrinus ι ἰμφυλ. Falso: vide infra. Hodie Garigliano. Nomen ab Gauro Monte non procul eius ortus natum exstimatur. Initium illi duobus e Fontibus: uno supra Soram viii P. M. in Apennino, non procul oppido Capitrello; altero millibus tribus Sora prope Castellum Petronium; & hinc est quod circa Soram erumpere notet Strabo. Laudat posteriorem Fontem mirifice Raffanus, numquam clariorem aut perlucidiorem Aquam sibi visam adferens: si quidem in ea, quantumvis & mirabili copia prorumpat, & altitudinem habeat non modicam, tamen quidvis etiam in fundo exiguum inter Pisces, mira cum spectantium voluptate discurrantes, posse discerni. Blondus originem eum ex Lacu Fucino vult trahere, uti quoque Plinius tradere videtur. Riviamborum cursu intra Soram delati confluunt; ita ut superius Peninsula relinquatur, in qua oppida sunt Pelcum, Poita, Lobrutullium, ipsaque Sora. Pergens inde per Fregellas, Minturnas (testantur idem etiam cum Strabone & Plinio, Porphyrius & Acron in Horatium) & Vettinos ad Lacum Frentalem Mari invehitur. Cæruleus dicitur Martiali: Cæruleus nos Liris amat, quem, autem Silva Marica Protegit; hunc Squilla maxima turba sumus.
units.tr: Thus we have come to the Liris, the boundary of Latium and the beginning of Campania. Liris in Pliny, Livy, Mela; Λείρις in Strabo and other Greeks. In some manuscripts of Lucan and Tacitus it is written Lyru with a y. Strabo says: Λείρις ποταμὸς, Κλαωις δ' ἰχαλῶν ποσσῶν [Leiris potamos, Klaois d' ichalon possōn], and Pliny agrees with him, though it should be corrected from Strabo: "the colony of Minturnae, on the Liris river, once called the Glanis." Appian of Alexandria thinks it is also called Liternum, wrongly, as see below. Today it is the Garigliano. The name is thought to come from Mount Gaurus, not far from its source. It has two sources: one above Sora, eight Roman miles away, in the Apennines, not far from the town of Capitrello; the other three miles from Sora near the little fortress of Petronius; and hence it is that Strabo notes that it bursts out near Sora. Raffanus praises the second spring wonderfully, saying he had never seen water clearer or more transparent; for although it gushes forth in such a marvellous abundance and has no small depth, yet even a tiny object on the bottom can be discerned among the fish darting about, to the wonderful delight of the onlookers. Blondus wishes it to draw its origin from Lake Fucinus, as Pliny also seems to report. Carried by the courses of the Riviambori, the streams flow together below Sora, so that the peninsula above is left, in which lie the towns of Pelcum, Poita, Lobrutullium, and Sora itself. Passing on from there through Fregellae, Minturnae (Porphyry and Acron on Horace also attest this, together with Strabo and Pliny) and Vettini, it is carried into the sea at Lake Frentanus. Martial calls it Cæruleus: "The blue Liris loves us, which the Marican wood protects; we are the very great crowd of shrimps."
