units.la: Su surenum vocat Silius lib. viii. Capiuntur in iis Fontium Rivis Carpiones; sed non, qua in Benaco, magnitudine. Suscipit dextra quidem Fibrenum, Cosam, Alatrum, Trernum, & alios; sinistra vero Casinum, Melfam, & Omnem. Fibreni meminit Silius lib. viii: At qui Fibreno misscentem flumina Lirem.
units.tr: Silius book 8 calls it Su surenum. In its waters, from the streams of the springs, carp are caught, but not as large as those in Lake Benacus. On the right it receives the Fibrenum, Cosam, Alatrum, Trernum, and others; on the left, indeed, Casinum, Melfam, and Omnem. Silius book 8 mentions the Fibreni: "But he who mingles the Liris with the waters of the Fibrenus."

units.la: Fluit inter Arpinum & Soram, coniungiturque Liri iii ab Arpino P. M. apud Villam S. Dominici, ubi M. Tull. in lucem editus. Eum vide lib. ii. de L. L, & lib. Epist. ad Attic. xiii. ubi & de Fibreno Arpinatem Insulam faciente. Fiume de la Posta, ait Sanfelicius. De Cosa: Κῶσα Φορενουν, Frutinum, ὁ Κέσας pὰ πολαμὸς, inquit Strabo. Hodie Pisia dicitur Leandro. Quod ad Trerum, Τρήρα Φαβεγανε̃ιαν, ait Strabo, ὁ Τρίρ ⊕ pὰ. De Casino idem Strabo: Γηγαμονα, inquit, ἐν συμβολῇ ἐωσῶν πολαμὸν κεμένων, Ἀειμησίς κὰι ἰνρα Κασινα. Quod illi hodie nomen, ignoro. Certe non Melfa, quod putat Ortelius. Nam qui Melfa vulgo, Straboni Μέλφας ibidem appellatur, Τῶσα Α'κίνηον ὁ Μέλφας, inquient, pὰ, πολαμὸς μίμαες; non idem, ut putat Leander, cum Melphe Plinij, qui circa Columnam Rhegiam. Melpa ex Apennino descendit per planiciem usque ad Fregellas, indeque non procul in Lirim evolvitur. Omnis Amnis iiii ab D. Germani P. M. iuxta D. Eliæ, propter Apenninum, caput tollit i modicis admodum initiis; sed permagnus, Aquis multorum Fontium exceptis: cursu P. M. fere xii confecto, in Lirim haud procul à Ponte Corvi cadit. Liri succedit Volturnus, Virgilio, Livio, Plinio (& quibus non?) notus. Οὐολτοῦρνος Straboni, aliisque Græcis. Volturnus Varroni, Βόλτουρνος. Volturno, hodieque. Οὐατυεγιν Plutarcho in Fabio Maximo, qui emendandus. Varie vertunt varii, variis usi codicibus: Notaronum Georgius Fabricius & Petrus Candidus, quem etiam probat Leander; Lotaronum Niger; Alocronum Cuspinianus in Cassiodorum. Kaσαλιω etiam vocatur Agathiæ lib. ii. de bello Gothico, ab opido fortean, quod in eius ripa situm. Videndi quoque Vibius Sequester, & Strabo lib. v. Sic item appellatur in Urna lapidea; cuius ad Vulturnum nobilem quondam Coloniam, hodie Castel al Mar di Botorno, Inscriptio ita habet: Aquas Cassilini Fluminis Mortuis gravatas suscepit Tyrrheni Maris Littus, quando Francorum gentem occidit Alfonsus Ensis, ubi misero hac gessit morem Bulting. Ab Apennino descendens, perexilis primo, Aquarum & Fontium accessione magnam & Latitudinem & Altitudinem nactus, inter Samnitium Montes tractu P. M. xxx in Agrum Venafranum, inde xx. P. M. in Alifanum, hinc xxv in Campanum evolvitur; Capuaque salutata, ad eum locum, ubi quondam Vulturnum fuit opidum, ut etiam post Varronem lib. iv. Strabo tellatur, in Mare se exonerat. Ab Vulturno Fonte ad Liris initium intervallum est modicum. Varro in Sammo oriri tradit. Fluens tribus ab Alifa P. M. antiquitus ibi Campaniæ Felicis & Samnij habebatur discrimen. Livius lib. xxii. dicit cum Falernum ab Agro Campano dividere. Vmnus est Vulturus Capua, inquit Pædianus in in Verrinam, tribus P. M. Ad Curtum pertinet quod Celer dicatur Lucano lib. ii; quodque Fluctu sonorum vocet Silius Italicus lib. viii. Iuxta Cumas in mare labi scribit Servius. Dionysius de Vulturno & Glani prodigium refert: eos, omisso naturali meatu, vertisse Curtus, aliquamdiu retrocedentes ab Ostiis ad suos Fontes. Nos Belgæ, qui Fluxum Refluxumque Maris novimus, hæc talia non miramur. Vulturnum Mare habet Plinius ad huius Fluminis ostium. Amnes Torrentesq; multos colligit: inter ceteros, dextra quidem Cusanum Corrcllum, sinistra Freddum: Pratellum, Sabbatum, Ifclerum, & alios. Cusanus Correctius ex Mathelio Monte ortus prope Pulianellum Vulturni se immergit Aquis. Freddus adversa ripa ibidem Vulturno se miscet, cognomine adlitum habens Opidum. Freddum sequitur alius; qui ortus ad Pedem Montis, vulgo Piedmont, fit per Agrum Alifanum iiii. P. M. curiu, tandem propter Alifam in Vulturnum se condit. Pratellus in radicibus nascitur Montis Mathelii, ab opido Pratello, quod iuxta est, nomen habens. Ab eius Fonte Cattellum Galli haud procul abest. Sabbatus, ut Antonino vocatur, ex Apennino oritur, qua regione luga eius Montes Tremuli nominantur: & per deprælla loca sinuosis flexibus, omnibus fere Beneventani Agri Fontibus uno alveo collectis, se tandem in Vulturnum, maximo ipsi inlato Incremento, exonerat. Hodie Fiume de Benevento dicitur; quod propter eam Urbem, perque eius fluat Agros. Sabbatus Incolas, ut sic loquar, habet varios, inter quos principis facile loci Calor, Antiquis notus. Sic etiam nominatur in Itineraria Tabula; sed cum Vulturni alveo ita imperite mistus, ut unus esse Fluvius videatur. A λαφ corrupte apud Appianum Alexandrinum. Ad Calorem Mansio est apud Antoninum, inter Nuceriam & Nerulum; qua Fluvium hunc designari certum est. Nomen hactenus retinet Ca ore. Hodie usque Pugna dicitur, inquit Paullus Diaconus. Testatur Ortelius in M. S. Codice Pugnam non esse Fluvij, sed Loci iuxta Fluvium nomen. Scipio Mazzella scribit Dentecane vulgo vocari: etsi, inquit, nonnulli sic vocent Tabernulam haud procul inde. Ex Amsanĉti Valle præcipitem ferri, inter opidum Aquariam & Pætianos Agros, Silaroque miscieri, tradit Pomponius Sabinus in vii Ænèid. Prope Beneventum ponunt Livius lib. xxiv sequenteque, & Vibius Sequester. In Sabbatum influit ccc fere passuum spatio supra Beneventum, prope Pontem Valentinum, qui Calorem transvit Valens Imperator. Augetur autem, antequam ab Sabbato suscipiatur, Tripalto, Misiano, Tamara alijs. Tripalto nomen ab opido Tripalta. Ad ripam eius dextram Silva est peringens & Latronum domicilio infamis, quæ ab Amne vicino Tripaltina. Exit, quemadmodum etiam Misianus, ex Monte Crepacorio. Tamarus notus quoque est Antonino, ubi Mansionem nominat Super Tamari fluvium. Male nonnulli Codices Super Mari flav. Tamarus Aquarum copia non est Calore minor. Præter Calorem sunt alij, qui Sabbato miscentur. Ad opidum sane Pontem Fontes sunt quatuor, qui corrivati uno ostio in Sabbatum feruntur; ex Apennino descendentes, Vicina Fontibus totidem sunt opida; Ad D. Laurentium, ad D. Lupum, Pons Landulphi, & Casilonium. Sabbatus sinistra sua ripa excipit, præter alios, Seritellam, ex Caudinis orientem Montibus. Iam relictis Vulturno etiam suis, ne prolixior sim, Ifuclere, Arnone, alijs, ad Glanum venio. De Glani Lycophron apud Stephanum (cui Γλάνις πόλεως Κύμης) ωὲι πίλεων:
units.tr: It flows between Arpinum and Sora and joins the Liris three miles from Arpinum, at the Villa S. Dominici, where M. Tullius was born. See his book 2 On the Laws, and his letter to Atticus, book 13, where he also speaks of the Fibrenus making Arpinum an island. Fiume de la Posta, says Sanfelicius. As for the Cosa: Strabo calls it Κῶσα, the Frutinus, and says it is ὁ Κέσας, a river. Leander says it is today called the Pisia. As for the Trerus, Strabo says it is Τρήρα, and that it is a river named Τρίρ. Of the Casinus, Strabo also says: Γηγαμονα, he says, where two rivers meet, the Ἀειμησίς and the Κασινα. I do not know what name it bears today. It is certainly not the Melfa, as Ortelius thinks. For the river commonly called Melfa is called Μέλφας by Strabo in the same place, and he says it flows from Τῶσα Α'κίνηον. It is not, as Leander thinks, the same as the Melphes of Pliny, which is near Columna Rhegia. The Melpa comes down from the Apennines across the plain as far as Fregellae, and from there flows into the Liris not far off. The Omnis, a river four miles from S. Germano, near S. Elia, beside the Apennines, rises from very small beginnings, but it becomes very large, having received the waters of many springs. After it has run about twelve miles, it falls into the Liris not far from the Ponte Corvo. After the Liris comes the Volturnus, well known to Virgil, Livy, Pliny (and who does not know it?). Strabo and other Greeks call it Οὐολτοῦρνος. Varro calls it Volturnus, and the Greeks Βόλτουρνος. It is still called Volturno today. Plutarch, in his Life of Fabius Maximus, calls it Οὐατυεγιν, which needs correcting. Various writers render it variously, using various manuscripts: Georgius Fabricius and Petrus Candidus give Notaronus, which Leander also approves; Niger gives Lotaronus; Cuspinianus, in his note on Cassiodorus, gives Alocronus. It is also called Καασαλιω by Agathias, book 2 of the Gothic War, perhaps from the town situated on its bank. Vibius Sequester and Strabo, book 5, should also be consulted. It is so called too on a stone urn, near the Vulturnus, where there was once a noted colony, today Castel al Mar di Botorno. The inscription reads: The shore of the Tyrrhenian Sea received the waters of the Cassilinus River, burdened with the dead, when Alfonso of the Sword slew the people of the Franks, where he performed this rite for the wretched... Descending from the Apennines, very slender at first, it gains great breadth and depth from the addition of waters and springs; it flows through the mountains of the Samnites for thirty miles into the Venafran territory, then twenty miles into the Alifan territory, and from there twenty-five miles into the Campanian. Greeting Capua, at the place where the town of Vulturnum once stood, it discharges itself into the sea, as Strabo also says in book 4, after Varro. The interval from the source of the Vulturnus to the beginning of the Liris is small. Varro reports that it rises in Samnium. Flowing three miles from Alifa, it was once the boundary between Campania Felix and Samnium. Livy, book 22, says that it divides the Falernian territory from the Campanian fields. Pædianus, in his commentary on the Verrines, says: The Vulturnus is at Capua, three miles away. To Curtius belongs the fact that Lucan, book 2, calls it swift, and that Silius Italicus, book 8, calls it the flood of sounds. Servius writes that it glides into the sea near Cumae. Dionysius tells of the wonder concerning the Vulturnus and Glanis: that, leaving their natural course, they turned back, for some time flowing backwards from their mouths to their sources, as Curtius reports. We Belgians, who know the ebb and flow of the sea, do not marvel at such things. Pliny places the Sea of the Vulturnus at the mouth of this river. It gathers many streams and torrents; among the others, from the right, the Cusanus Correctius, and from the left, the Freddus, the Pratellus, the Sabbatus, the Isclerus, and others. The Cusanus Correctius, rising from Mount Mathelius near Pulianellum, plunges its waters into the Vulturnus. The Freddus, from the opposite bank, joins the Vulturnus at the same place, having a town of the same name on its shore. Another river follows the Freddus; rising at the foot of the mountain commonly called the Piedmont, it runs four miles through the Alifan territory, and finally, near Alifa, hides itself in the Vulturnus. The Pratellus rises at the roots of Mount Mathelius and takes its name from the town of Pratellum, which lies nearby. Not far from its source is the Galli Cattellum. The Sabbatus, as Antoninus calls it, rises from the Apennines, where its ridges are called the Tremuli Mountains. Through deep valleys, in winding bends, collecting almost all the springs of the Beneventan territory into one channel, it at last discharges itself into the Vulturnus, bringing it a very great increase. Today it is called the Fiume de Benevento, because it flows past that city and through its fields. The Sabbatus has, so to speak, various inhabitants, among whom the chief place is Calor, known to the ancients. Thus it is also named in the Itinerary Table, but so carelessly mixed with the channel of the Vulturnus that it seems to be one river. Appian of Alexandria corruptly gives it from λαφ. There is a stage Ad Calorem in Antoninus, between Nuceria and Nerulum, and it is certain that this river is meant. It still keeps the name Calore. Today it is called Pugna as far as, says Paulus Diaconus. Ortelius testifies, in a manuscript, that Pugna is not the name of a river but of a place near the river. Scipio Mazzella writes that it is commonly called Dentecane: although, he says, some call the Tabernula, not far from there, by that name. Pomponius Sabinus, in his commentary on book 7 of the Aeneid, reports that it falls headlong from the valley of the Amsanctus, between the town of Aquaria and the fields of the Paetiani, and mingles with the Silarus. Livy, book 24 and following, and Vibius Sequester place it near Beneventum. It flows into the Sabbatus about three hundred paces above Beneventum, near the Valentine Bridge, which the emperor Valens crossed over the Calor. The Sabbatus, before it receives the Tripaltus, Misianus, Tamarus and others, is augmented. The Tripaltus takes its name from the town of Tripalta. On its right bank is a forest, infamous as a haunt of robbers, which is named after the neighbouring river, the Tripaltina. The Misianus likewise rises from Mount Crepacorium. The Tamarus is also known to Antoninus, where he names a stage Super Tamari fluvium. Some manuscripts wrongly read Super Mari flav. The Tamarus has no less water than the Calor. Besides the Calor there are others which join the Sabbatus. Near the town of Ponte there are four springs, which, gathered together, are carried into the Sabbatus through one outlet; descending from the Apennines, there are as many towns near the springs: Ad D. Laurentium, Ad D. Lupum, Pons Landulphi, and Casilonium. The Sabbatus receives on its left bank, among others, the Seritella, rising from the Caudine mountains. Now, to avoid being too long, having left aside the Vulturnus and its own tributaries, the Isclerus, Arnon and others, I come to the Glanis. Lycophron, in Stephanus (who calls it Γλάνις, city of Cumae), on cities:

units.la: Γλάνις τι ρύθρος διξίτιν πύγων χθονα:
units.tr: Γλάνις τι ρύθρος διξίτιν πύγων χθονα:

units.la: Et Poetarum Latinorum Princeps, Virgilius: Talem dives arat Capua, & vicina Vesevo Ora Iugo, & vacuis Clanis non æquus Acerris.
units.tr: And the Prince of Latin poets, Virgil: Such is the rich Capua that ploughs, and the shore near Vesuvius on its mountain ridge, and the Clanis, not kind to the barren Acerrae.

units.la: E montibus inter Nolam & Capuam, regione fere media, prorumpit. Amnis hic ille est, ut notat Leander, qui Via inter Capuam & Anversam occurrit; ac sæpenumero nunc in Acerrano Agro, sicut olim in Campano Atellanoque solebat, præsertim hibernis mensibus, stagnat: qua de causa ligneis Pontibus connexa multis in locis Itinera necessario sunt, qui Veterum Ædificiorum lapidibus ex Urbium propinquarum ruinis eo delatis plerumque sulciuntur & incumbunt. Meminit & Dionysius Halicarnassæus lib. vii, quum Glanem & Vulturnum, naturali quandoque Cursu omisso, contra ab ostiis ad Fontes refluxisse memoriæ prodit. Auctu suo Pestera meditari munarque Terris scribit cum Virgilio Vibius Sequester. Spatio ab Mari P.M. viii. a Hume effundit ur, Lacus intra latitudinem eorum terræ milium, quibusdam in locis; alibi etiam ideoque circum ostia, quibus in mare exit, vulgo Lacus Patriæ vocatur; Piscium abundantia, qui fere Neapolim deferre solent, uberrimus. De Lacu alibi Misenum cum alijs Glani Lucernus Amnis, cuius meminit, præter Strabonem, Livius lib. xx. ii & xxxvi. Hodie Patria ab opido, quod vernacule Torre della Patria, olim Liternum. Appianus lib. i E'μ{ϕ}υ. Liturn ... Occurrit hinc Sebethus, inter Vesevum Montem & Neapolim decurrens; vulgo Fiume de la Maddalena vocatur. Vicus im per Neapolitanam Urbem delabitur, omnibus Civibus usum præstans; & popularier Fornello dicitur. Memnerunt Sarnus Silvarum, Vibius Sequester, Columella in suo Horto, ubi Sebethus scribitur. Quod adjiciatur, docet ex Lapidibus Manutius in Orthographia. Mox Sarnus est. Sic Lucano, Silio, Statio; qui lib. i. Silv. Sarnetum e gnominat; Orosio, Vibio, alias appellatur; Σαρνο Straboni & Ptolemæo: qui hodieque Sarno, Leandro telle, qui Sarnus alibi interpretatur, ut & Erythræus, ab Sarnus, quæ ibi stationem habent, ad Viatores, qui Nuceriam cogitant, trajiciendos. Proximus Salernno est Irno; qui oritur ex Apennino supra Solefram. Sequitur inde Ibelo supra S. Licandrum prodiens Apennino. Opidum habet ad dextram ripam cognomine Xii hinc citer est m II. Sarno est. Sic Virgilio, Lucano, Silio, Plinio, Melæ, Tabulæ Itinerariæ: Σαλαο Straboni & Ptolemæo; Sinc Lucano item Vitio dictus; qui hodie ille, vel, ut alij pronuncient, vero. Oritur ad Lerfagernem in Apennino, parte citeriore, propemodum ex adverso Autido. Versus Meridiem decurrens in Tyrrhenum, Campaniam ab Lucania hodie dirimit. Campaniæ plerisque adscensitur: Lucania facit Pomponius Sabinus, addens in Mare extrve circa Leucasiam Insulam. Strabo cum Campanorum & Picentinorum facit terminum. Salernum prætere notat Sulpicius Verulam ex male intellecto Lucani loco, canentis lib. viii: Vestrum impu sus Aquis, radere fque Salerni Culta Siler.
units.tr: It breaks forth from the mountains between Nola and Capua, about the middle of the region. This is that river which, as Leander notes, meets the road between Capua and Aversa. Very often it stagnates, now in the Acerran territory, as once it did in the Campanian and Atellan, especially in the winter months; for this reason the roads in many places must be crossed by wooden bridges, and these are mostly propped up and supported with stones of old buildings carried there from the ruins of neighbouring cities. Dionysius of Halicarnassus also mentions it, book 7, when he records in memory that the Glanis and the Vulturnus, sometimes leaving their natural course, have flowed back from their mouths to their sources. Vibius Sequester, with Virgil, says that it meditates pestilence by its increase and is a plague to the lands. It discharges itself into the sea eight miles from the coast, and in some places it forms lakes within the breadth of its banks; elsewhere, also around the mouths by which it goes out into the sea, it is commonly called the Lake of Patria, and is very rich in fish, which people usually carry to Naples. Concerning this lake elsewhere, along with Misenum. The Glanis is the Lucernus River, which Livy mentions, book 22, and books 36, besides Strabo. Today Patria is named from the town, which in the vernacular is called Torre della Patria; formerly it was Liternum. Appian, book 1 of the Civil Wars: Liturnum. Here Sebethus comes into view, running between Mount Vesuvius and Naples; it is commonly called the Fiume de la Maddalena. It flows through the city of Naples, supplying all the citizens with water, and in the vernacular it is called Fornello. Sarnus is mentioned by Silvae, Vibius Sequester, and Columella in his Garden, where Sebethus is written. Manutius, in his Orthography, shows from inscriptions that the word should be added. Next is the Sarnus. So it is called by Lucan, Silius, Statius (who in book 1 of the Silvae calls it Sarnetum), and it is named otherwise by Orosius and Vibius; Strabo and Ptolemy call it Σαρνο. Today it is still called Sarno, as Leander testifies, who elsewhere interprets Sarnus, as does Erythraeus, from the boats there that carry travellers bound for Nuceria across. Next to Salerno is the Irnus, which rises from the Apennines above Solofra. Next follows the Ibelo, which issues from the Apennines above S. Licandro. It has on its right bank a town of the same name, Xii, and is less than two miles from the Sarno. So it is named by Virgil, Lucan, Silius, Pliny, Mela, and the Itinerary Table; Strabo and Ptolemy call it Σαλαο. Lucan also calls it Sinus, and it is named Vitius by others; today it is called that, or, as others pronounce it, vero. It rises at Lerfagerne in the Apennines, on the nearer side, nearly opposite Autido. Running south into the Tyrrhenian Sea, it now separates Campania from Lucania. Most people attribute it to Campania; Pomponius Sabinus makes it Lucania, adding that it enters the sea outside Leucasia Island. Strabo makes it the boundary between the Campanians and the Picentines. Sulpicius Verulanus notes that Salerno lies beyond it, from a misunderstood passage of Lucan, who sings in book 8: Vestrum impudens Aquis, radere quesque Salerni culta Siler.

units.la: Non enim Eburum vult Mœnia radere Salerni, quum ab eo abest xxiv P. M sed Salernitanorum Agros, qui huc usque extendebantur. Naturam eius Strabo, Plinius, Silius, ubique esse tradunt, ut in eum numeris Folia Virgiliique lapidescant, nec tamen in mutato colore vel forma; quamquam aliás ut adjicit Plinius eius Aquæ salubris sit potus. Defert secum Fontem Puernum & Nigrum, cui initium ex specu subterraneo iuxta Cauponam quandam, quæ vulgo Taverna della Tola ab opido Tolla, bi proximo.
units.tr: For Lucan does not mean the walls of Salernum (Eburum), since that is twenty-four Roman miles away, but the fields of the Salernitani, which extended as far as this point. Strabo, Pliny and Silius all report that the water there has the property that leaves cast into it turn to stone, though without any change of colour or shape; yet, as Pliny adds, its water is otherwise wholesome to drink. It carries with it the Fons Puernus and the Niger, whose source is a subterranean cave near a certain inn, commonly called Taverna della Tola, from the nearby town of Tolla.

units.la: Hactenus de Campaniæ Fluviis; quos Lucania habear, iamnunc ferutemur. Post Silaris oltia succedunt Pistia unde Caput Psiotaanum, quod olim Pyxuntum) Messe (qui Plinio Mephes, M. Ipes legunt membranæ) Cocci & Sapri. Putatur Sapri, qui Σαρ- Straboni; Lauf Plinio: quod haud procul vero esse video, si verba eorum bene expendantur. Lucanos dirimit à Brutijs; Lainum ab suis Suburbis, opidum in Lucanis, Suburbia in Calabris relinquens. Oritur prope Viminellum, Lucaniæ opidum, perque Montes asperos Meridiem versus Batilicatam vel Luciniam, ut dixi, ab Calabria dividens, in Mare Tyrrhenum profluit. Aquas habet perpetuo claras, adeo ut nullo unquam casu turbentur.
units.tr: So much for the rivers of Campania. Now let us go through those of Lucania. After the mouths of the Silarus come the Pistia, then the Caput Psiotaanum, which was formerly Pyxus (the manuscripts of Pliny read Mephes or Ipes for Messe), then the Cocci and the Sapri. The Sapri is thought to be the river Strabo calls [Σαρ-], and Pliny's Laus; and I see that this is not far from the truth, if their words are weighed carefully. It separates the Lucanians from the Bruttii, leaving Lainum with its suburbs (the town lies in Lucania, its suburbs in Calabria). It rises near Viminellum, a town of Lucania, and flows through rough mountains towards the south, dividing Basilicata (or Lucania, as I said) from Calabria, and so into the Tyrrhenian Sea. Its waters are always clear, so that they are never disturbed by any accident.

units.la: Sequuntur in Brutijs, eo enim delati fumus) tres Amnes, quorum Nomina non occurrunt: Primus ad Scalcam; Secundus ad Cirellam; Tertius ad S. Bonifacii, Mare petunt Tyrrhenum. Subeunt inde alij. Freddus cum eiusdem Nominis opido. Acheron ex Montis Radicibus, in quo Pandosii, nascens, per Vallem huic profundam, inter altissimos Montes, interque Martoranum & Altiliam: & tandem in Sinum Sanctæuphemianum evolvitur. Acherontem quidam, inter quos Leander, hodie Sarantum censent; Niger Baffentum; Barrius Capitanianum: alij Cerfinum. Ab eo Fluvio Adeolæ dicti Plinio Acherontini. Hic Fluvius est Acheron, ad cuius ripam: hæc ibidem Pandosia, in cuius Agro fatali casu functam accepit Cladem Alexander, Epiro arum Rex: Apollinis oraculo prænonitus, ut Acherusiam Aquam, utque Pandosiam vi arcerarus, non alium esse Acherontem, non aliam, quam in Epiro, Pandosiam. Vide Livium lib. viii, Trogum lib. xii, Straboneam, & alios. Ab Sanctæuphemia sexto Lapide Ostium est Lamas, alti latique Fluminis: inde octavo, perangentis item Angitula, cuius mentio apud Antoninum. Vulgo Acitola. Circumvectis Australius Termini vel Hipponiatis Sinus Cornu, occurrit Mesana. Sic vulgo vocatur Fluvius, qui Doctis Meduna; excipiens sinistra ripa praeter alios, paullum infra Rosarnum, Metaurum Amnem. Decimo hinc miliari Seminara vicitur, latum profundumque Flumen. Olim, ut censent Bonaccriolus & Leander, Metaurus, Metaurus Straboni, cuius ostium describit in Brutiis Plinius, exadverso Eoliarum Insularum. Idem tamen Leander, sui quasi oblitus, Metaurum esse vult in suo Insularum libello, qui hodie Metremo. Sed Metremus Metaurus esse nequit. Ottio namque ille ad Mare, quod Huius, ut dixi, Plinius delineat, caret, & ab Mesana ad Mare, amnis nomine detertur. Neteonan Paccasi- cus etiam fuerit dictus, quem Probus Grammaticus in Vergilij Vita ex 11. Caronis Originum scribit, Rhegiorum & Taurinorum Fines disjecere. In Mare se provolvit aliquo: auctus Annibus. Post nonnullos minoris momenti Fluvios, inter quos nescio an fuerint (nisi fabuloli sint centum) Ἀνάγαν, Lapodus, Micaee, Sadlanus, Iulianus, Acelegna & Agrade (Flumina continua inxia Rhegium Iulium, quibus Oreites purgatus fuit ab Matris nece, unde mnemorat Probus Grammaticus in Vita Poetica Virgilij, si Codici fides) aperiunt se alii Primo, qui vernacule Aesa. Ἀλης Thucydidi lib. iii, Strabo, Dionysio, & Antigono in Mirabilibus, Fluvium hunc statuent Finitorem inter Locrenses & Rhegnos. Haec tamen nuncupare videtur M. Tullius ad Trebatium. Ἀθραῖα nominat Theocritus. Inde qui Ἀσκλᾶς Polemaeo Meminit & Plinius, in cuius scriptionibus libris Locanus scribitur. Mox, qui vulgo dicitur Sagrianos; Sigra Plinio, Σαγρᾶς Strabon: a quo opidum Sagrianum. Sagra tamen Gabriel Barrius, Laurentio Anamenti & Mazzella Itaru est, Suethi antus Nigro. Hinc qui Casinus Plinio; Καχίνος Thucydidi lib. iii. Addit, sequitur quam Antigonus paullo ante Pausaniam in Elaeis Fluvium hunc esse, qui Locrensium Agrum ab Rheg no divisit. Ἀσκα a pella. Aelianus lib. viii. Var Histor. Non procul inde Cretalus est, Plinio notus. Hinc apud eundem Semirus, Aotha & Largues, qui hodie Tauna, quaeque e Montibus descendens in Sinum Scyllaceum evolvitur. Ifaru mox in oculos incurrit, qui Ἁλιμος Lycophroni, Theocrito, Straboni & Dionysio; Aelar Ovidio xv Metamorph. Theocriti Scholiastes dicit Fluvium hunc per mediam Vibonem Crotoniensem fluere. Putat Leander Ἀλαν appellari ab Thucydide lib. vii. Crotone iv. M. P. abest Natha, antiquum etiam, ut multa alia hoc tractu Flumina, nomen praeferens. Naxo Strabo, qui Nomen & aurae rationem indicat. Nestha Plinio, qui in secundo Europae Sinu collocat; Nicola Siciliae Fluvius est apud Theocriti Scholiasten, ob causam saepe indicatam: Suem ab Ovidio nominari nota Gabriel Barrius, qui apud Lycophronem etiam memoriam eius extare memorat: Nαχαρ apud eum legitur. Offerunt hunc se Latius legenti nonnulli minorum gentium, inter quos ab Cariathi, perhonesta Civitate, x iii lapide Triantes, latus ad usque Fluvius in Sinum erumpens cum reliquis Tarentinum. Τριάντης Thucydidis, de quo an e putare esse Gabriel Barrius.
units.tr: Next, in the land of the Bruttii (for we have come there), follow three rivers whose names are not recorded: the first at Scalea, the second at Cirella, the third at S. Bonifacio; they make for the Tyrrhenian Sea. Next come others: the Fredo, with the town of the same name. The Acheron rises at the foot of the mountains where Pandosia is; running through a valley deep between very high mountains, between Martirano and Altilia, it finally flows into the Gulf of Sant'Eufemia. Some, among them Leander, think the Acheron is today the Sarantus; Niger thinks the Bafento; Barrius the Capitanio; others the Cersino. From this river the people called by Pliny Acherontini take their name. This river is the Acheron, on whose bank stands Pandosia, in whose territory Alexander, king of the Epirots, met his death by a fatal accident, having been forewarned by Apollo's oracle to beware of the Acherusian water and of Pandosia, since there was no other Acheron and no other Pandosia than those in Epirus. See Livy book 8, Trogus book 12, Strabo, and others. Six miles from Sant'Eufemia is the mouth of the Lamas, a deep and wide river; then eight miles further, the equally narrow Angitula, which is mentioned by Antoninus and commonly called the Acitola. Having rounded the southern horn of the Gulf of Terina or Hipponium, one comes to the Mesana. This river is so called in common usage, though scholars call it the Meduna; receiving on its left bank, among others, a little below Rosarno, the river Metaurus. Ten miles from here, near Seminara, is a wide and deep river. Formerly, as Bonaccorsi and Leander think, this was the Metaurus, Strabo's Metaurus, whose mouth Pliny describes in the land of the Bruttii, opposite the Aeolian Islands. Yet Leander himself, as if forgetful of his own view, in his little book on the islands wants the Metaurus to be the river now called the Metremo. But the Metremus cannot be the Metaurus: for that river lacks the mouth to the sea which Pliny describes, as I said, and from the Mesana to the sea it is known by the name of that river. Neteon, which was also called Pacasicus, which Probus the grammarian writes in the Life of Virgil, citing the second book of Caro's Origines, marked the boundary between the territories of the Rhegians and the Taurinians. It flows into the sea, swollen by other streams. After several rivers of lesser importance, among which I do not know whether there were any (unless the hundred are fabulous), namely the Anagas [Ἀνάγαν], Lapodus, Micae, Sadlanus, Julianus, Acelegna and Agrade (rivers flowing continuously within Rhegium Julium, in which Orestes was cleansed of his mother's murder, as Probus the grammarian mentions in the Life of Virgil, if the manuscript can be trusted), there open up others. First is the one which in the vernacular is called the Aesa. Alex [Ἀλης] in Thucydides book 3, Strabo, Dionysius and Antigonus in the Mirabilia make this river the boundary between the Locrians and the Rhegians. Yet Cicero to Trebatius seems to name it thus. Athraea [Ἀθραῖα] is what Theocritus calls it. Then the Asclas [Ἀσκλᾶς], mentioned by Polemo and Pliny; in whose books it is written Locanus. Next, the one commonly called the Sagrianos: Pliny's Sigra, Strabo's Sagras [Σαγρᾶς], from which the town of Sagrianum takes its name. Yet Gabriel Barrius, Lorenzo Anamenti and Mazzella think the Sagra is the Itaru, and according to Niger it is the Suethus. Then the Casinus of Pliny; Kachinos [Καχίνος] in Thucydides book 3. He adds that Antigonus, a little before Pausanias, in the Elaeis, says this is the river that divided the territory of the Locrians from Rhegium. Aska [Ἀσκα], Aelian, Varia Historia book 8. Not far from there is the Cretalus, known to Pliny. Then in the same author the Semirus, Aotha and Largues, which today is the Tauna, and which, descending from the mountains, flows into the Gulf of Squillace. Next comes the Ifaru, which is called Halimos [Ἁλιμος] by Lycophron, Theocritus, Strabo and Dionysius, and Aelar by Ovid in Metamorphoses book 15. The scholiast on Theocritus says this river flows through the middle of Vibo of the Crotoniates. Leander thinks it is called Alan [Ἀλαν] by Thucydides in book 7. Four Roman miles from Croton is the Natha, which, like many other rivers in this region, bears an ancient name. Naxus in Strabo, who also indicates the origin of the name. Nestha in Pliny, who places it in the second gulf of Europe; Nicola is a river of Sicily in the scholiast on Theocritus, for a reason often given. Gabriel Barrius notes that Ovid names it Suem, and records that its memory also survives in Lycophron, where it is read as [Ναχαρ]. Several lesser rivers present themselves to the reader of Latin; among them, thirteen miles from Cariati, a very honourable city, is the Triantes, a river broad enough, bursting into the Gulf of Taranto along with the rest. Triantes [Τριάντης] in Thucydides; Gabriel Barrius asks whether this is the same river.

units.la: Magna iam a Triuntis ostio P. M. Rufillus occurrit: ab Rutillo quinque, qui Gratis vulgo; Crathis Ovidio in Fastis & Metamorphosi, Vibiosque Sequestro; Crateus Plinio; Κραθίς Theocrito, Herodoto, Straboni, Aeliano Siciliae Fluvium (quare, notum) dicit Eustathius in Dionysium: addens eum apud Sybarim sive Thurium fluere. Aelianus de Varia Historia nomen a Pastore quodam, sic dicto, accepisse scribit: Herodotus lib. i. nominatum tradit ad memoriam alius in Peloponneso Fluminis ita vocati. Fontem habet exiguum sensim ab Consentia milibus, Orientali latere; perque Montes altissimos ad Urbem accedit, quam paullum ab ortu contingit: hinc ad Septemtrionem se flectens Buscentum excipit; quo aliquique tandem amplitudinis tactus maximae, aspectuque terribilis, infra Bisignanum in Sinum Tarentinum, qui hodie Rosanus, se exonerat. Quam habeant ipsius Aquae Vim, alibi dicitur. Magnam Graeciam a Brutiis dividit. Augetur cum aliis, tum Busento, Septimo, Surdo, Finito Cuciari: Busenti, qui in Montibus Contentinis meridionali plaga nascitur, meminerunt Paullus Diaconus lib. xiii. Hist. Blondus lib. i. Sabellicus lib. ix. Ennead. vii, in Historia Funeris Alarici, Visigothorum Regis. Hic namque in Alveo Busenti positus scribitur. Nominant quidam in eius rei commemoratione Busentium; ignorantes Busentium alium esse a Busento. Hic enim Crathis miscetur; ille in Sinum Tarentinum se exonerat. Septimus & Surdus ex ipsidem Montibus orumoriuntur ad Opidum, quod vulgo Monte-Alto. Sinnus ad S. Agatham habet initium; & haud procul inde Cratas. Acantes hic & Macarum Annem rapidissimum praetereo. Antiquam Vrbem Sybaris, quæ eadem loco, Amnis sequebatur cognominis, qui nunc Coscile. Ort ut ad Scalæ Moranti, interque rupes altissimorum Montium in planitiem subiectam ferunt, per quam accelerante tandem Fontium ac Riuorum multarum aliarum Sinum Tarentinum influit. Ἰσπέρας Strabono; Siris Ovidio & Plinio. Quæ Visenus alibi nomen. Post Cerilium Amnis est, qui Adcolis Sino, vel, ut alii ceteri, Sennus; Σιρις Plutarcho & Strabono, qui Navigabilem dicit. Aris Plinio & Frontino. Ex Montium deleptus iugis in Sinum Tarentinum evolvitur. Olim illi Vrbs adpotita cognominis, ab Romanis, ut volunt, condita. Hinc Aeris sequitur, antiquum retinens nomen. A Ἀρις enim Strabono; Aeris est Plinio. In Littore os illi profundissimum latissimumque: quamobrem nec ibi transiri poterit; sed millariis duobus a Mari, ubi Pons Ligneus viam iungit. Ante succedit Salandra; Scalandrus Strabono & Plinio: qui nonnumquam ex Imbribus adeo abundat Aquis, ab declivi utrimque lugorum fastigio accedentibus, ut super Alveum excrescens totam Vallem Inundatione compleat, in faciem brachii Maris. Mox in ora Basentus Flumen iunt ostia Vulgo Basento. Basentinum vocat Paullus Diaconus. Casuentus est Plinio. Quinque aut circiter Basento milliaribus Bradanus occurrit; plurimum etiam hibernis mensibus augere solitus. Designat eum Appianus lib. v. Bell. Civil. ubi Cæsaris & Antonii congressum ad Metapontum Tarentumque, iuxta Flumen, quod inter eas Vrbes medium labitur, commemorat. Meminit Antoninus Itinere Mediolano ad Columnam. Iuxta Tarentum Stephano est Ἀγρας Fluvius. Paulianas etiam in Phocicis dicit Fluvium eodem nomine, quo Vrbs, vocari. Tarus hodieque ab Incolis dicitur, ut Galateus tellatur. Τέγειον corrupte legunt Diodori lib. xii. Codices.
units.tr: Already a great distance beyond the mouth of the Triuntis, Rufillus comes into view; five miles from the Rutillus, which is commonly called the Gratis. The Crathis in Ovid's Fasti and Metamorphoses, and in Vibius Sequester; the Crateus in Pliny; the Krathis [Κραθίς] in Theocritus, Herodotus, Strabo and Aelian. Eustathius, on Dionysius, says it is a river of Sicily (a well-known fact), adding that it flows near Sybaris or Thurii. Aelian, in his Varia Historia, writes that it took its name from a shepherd of that name; Herodotus, book 1, records that it was named in memory of another river of the same name in the Peloponnese. It has a small source a few miles from Consenza, on the eastern side; and through very high mountains it approaches the city, which it touches a little on the east. Then, bending northward, it receives the Busento; and at last, reaching its greatest size and a terrifying aspect, it discharges below Bisignano into the Gulf of Taranto, which today is the Gulf of Rosano. What power its waters have is said elsewhere. It divides Magna Graecia from the land of the Bruttii. It is increased by others, namely the Busento, Settimo, Surdo and the Finito Cuciari. Paul the Deacon (Histories book 13), Blondus book 1, and Sabellicus, Enneads book 9, book 7, in the account of the funeral of Alaric, king of the Visigoths, mention the Busento, which rises on the southern side of the Contentine mountains. For he is written to have been laid in the bed of the Busento. Some, in recounting this event, name it Busentium, not knowing that Busentium is a different river from the Busento: for the one mingles with the Crathis, while the other discharges into the Gulf of Taranto. The Settimo and the Surdo rise from these same mountains near the town commonly called Montalto. The Sinni has its source near Sant'Agata, and not far from there is the Crati. I pass over here the Acantes and the very rapid river Macara. The ancient city of Sybaris, which in the same place was followed by a river of the same name, now called the Coscile. Its source is near Scala di Morano; carried through the rocky cliffs of very high mountains into the plain below, through which, joined at last by many other springs and streams, it flows into the Gulf of Taranto. Ispera [Ἰσπέρας] in Strabo; Siris in Ovid and Pliny; which Visenus names elsewhere. After the Cerilium there is a river which the inhabitants call the Sino, or, as others do, the Sennus; Siris [Σιρις] in Plutarch and Strabo, who calls it navigable. Aris in Pliny and Frontinus. Descending from the ridges of the mountains, it flows into the Gulf of Taranto. Formerly a city of the same name, founded, they say, by the Romans, stood upon it. Then comes the Aeris, retaining its ancient name; for Strabo has Aris [Ἀρις], while Pliny has Aeris. On the shore its mouth is very deep and wide, so that it cannot be crossed there; but two miles from the sea, where a wooden bridge joins the road. Before it comes the Salandra; Scalandrus in Strabo and Pliny, which sometimes swells so much from the rains, with the sloping summits of the ridges on both sides descending into it, that overflowing its bed it fills the whole valley with flood, like an arm of the sea. Next on the coast is the river Basentus, whose mouth is commonly called the Basento. Paul the Deacon calls it the Basentinum; Pliny calls it the Casuentus. About five miles from the Basento the Bradano comes into view; it too is accustomed to swell greatly in the winter months. Appian (Civil Wars, book 5) marks it, where he records the meeting of Caesar and Antony near Metapontum and Tarentum, beside the river that flows between those cities. Antoninus mentions it in his Itinerary from Mediolanum to Columna. Near Taranto, according to Stephanus, is the river Agras [Ἀγρας]. Pausanias, in Phocis, also says that a river bears the same name as a city. The Tarus is still so called by the inhabitants, as Galateo testifies. The manuscripts of Diodorus, book 12, corruptly read Tegeion [Τέγειον].

units.la: Salentinorum oras legentibus tertio ab Vrbe Tarento lapide Galesus se offert. Quinto, dixit Livius lib. xxv, Hannibalem, capto Tarento, ad Galesum Flumen prosectum cum ceteris copiis ibi castra posuisse, scribens. Facile mutant Curtius suos Amnes: alia etiam fuit olim, quam hodie, Milliarum ratio: fecit denique Temporis iniuria, incuriaque Librariorum, ut depravatos habeamus Scriptorum Veterum Codices. Meminit Galesi Virgilius lib. iv. Georgic.
units.tr: Along the coast of the Salentines, as you read, the river Galesus presents itself three miles from the city of Tarentum. Livy, in book 25, writes that Hannibal, after taking Tarentum, marched to the river Galesus and there pitched his camp with the rest of his forces. Rivers easily change their names, and the measurement of miles was once different from what it is now. In short, the ravages of time and the carelessness of copyists have left us with corrupted manuscripts of the ancient writers.

units.la: Qua piger humectat flaventia culta Galesus. Vbi Servius notat, Galesum Amnem esse Calabriæ, non procul Tarento. Mentio eiusdem & apud Horatium, Martialem, Vibium. Lucotam nonnulli nominant, ut tradit Polybius lib. viii. Bagradam novo vocabulo appellat Ligorius in tabula Neapolitana. Præter Galesum, qui inter Magnam Græciam & Salentinos discrimen facit, etiam duos alios habent Salentini Amnes, unum quidem ad Littus Australis, qui ix Tarento lapide, ad Pulizanum, Sinum Tarentinum ingreditur: alterum, qui in ora Borealiore Hadriatico mucetur Mari, ad S. Marcum, decimo ab Vrbe Brundisina milliari.
units.tr: Virgil in book 4 of the Georgics mentions the Galesus: Qua piger humectat flaventia culta Galesus. There Servius notes that the Galesus is a river of Calabria, not far from Tarentum. It is also mentioned by Horace, Martial and Vibius. Some call it the Lucotam, as Polybius reports in book 8. Ligorio, in his map of Naples, calls it by a new name, Bagradam. Besides the Galesus, which marks the boundary between Magna Graecia and the Salentines, the Salentines have two other rivers. One of them, on the southern coast, enters the Gulf of Taranto at Pulizano, nine miles from Tarentum. The other, on the more northerly coast of the Adriatic, empties into the sea at S. Marco, ten miles from the city of Brindisi.

units.la: Iam Apulia Peucetia ab Fluviis valde est inops, unum tamen notatum video Cavam, xxv Brundisio lapide; xiv Egnatia. Exonerat se in Pelagus ad Corvinum. Pacilius hic nominatur Plinio. Pastum habet inemendate Itineraria Tabula, locans etiam vitioliore positu ultra Brundisium, quum eis esset. Quod sit in eadem Tabula inter Pacium & Aufidum Aveldum Flumen, nondum capio.
units.tr: Now Apulia Peucetia is very poor in rivers, yet I see one that has been noted, the Cava, twenty-five miles from Brindisi and fourteen from Egnatia. It discharges itself into the sea at Corvino. Pliny calls it Pacilius. The Antonine Itinerary's map has Pastum incorrectly, and places it even more wrongly beyond Brindisi, though it ought to be on this side. I do not yet understand what the Aveldum Flumen, which the same map puts between Pacius and Aufidus, is.

units.la: Peucetiam ab Daunia separat Aufidus. Sic Virgilio lib. xi. Æneid. Plinio, Melæ lib. ii, Antonino, Itinerariæ Tabulæ: Ἀυφίδος Polybio, Straboni, Ptolemæo dicitur; qui hodie L'Ofanto. In Hirpinorum Montibus oriri notat Ptolemæus. Solus, ut referunt Polybius lib. iii. & Plutarchus in Vita Hannibalis, Apenninum, in quo nascitur, secat. Apulia utraque divisa Hadriatico Mari inlabitur. Naturam eius, rapidumque currentis varieque se sinuantis Cursum describit Horat. lib. i. Sat. i.
units.tr: The Aufidus separates Peucetia from Daunia. So Virgil in book 11 of the Aeneid, Pliny, Mela in book 2, Antoninus, and the Itinerary map call it. Polybius, Strabo and Ptolemy call it Aufidus [Ἀυφίδος]. Today it is L'Ofanto. Ptolemy notes that it rises in the mountains of the Hirpini. Alone, as Polybius in book 3 and Plutarch in the Life of Hannibal report, it cuts through the Apennines, where it rises. Both Apulias are divided by it, and it flows into the Adriatic Sea. Horace in book 1, Satire 1, describes its nature, its rapid current and its winding course:

units.la: Quum ripa simul avulsos feras Aufidus acer.
units.tr: "When the fierce Aufidus carries away the uprooted trees together with its bank."

units.la: Et lib. iii. Carm. Od. xxx; Dicar, qua violens obstrepit Aufidus; Et qua pauper aqua Daunus agrestium Regnavit populorum.
units.tr: And in Book 3, Ode 30: "I shall be spoken of where the violent Aufidus roars, and where Daunus, poor in water, once ruled over a rustic people."

units.la: Lib. iv. Ode ix: Longe sonantem natas ad Aufidum.
units.tr: In book 4, Ode 9: Longe sonantem natas ad Aufidum.

units.la: Item eiusdem Libri Oda xiiii Sic Tauri formis volvitur Aufidus; Qui modo ... Lauus perflunt Appulo, Quum saevit horrendamque cultis Dimovitem meditatur Agris.
units.tr: Likewise, in the same book, Ode 14: "Thus the Aufidus rolls on in the shape of a bull, which now ... Lavinian... pours over Apulian lands, when it rages and threatens to tear the dreaded (ground) away from the cultivated fields."

units.la: Sic Silius Italicus lib. ix Belli Punici: At parte in dextra sinuat qua flexibus undam Aufidus, & curvo circumdat gurgite ripas.
units.tr: So Silius Italicus, Book 9 of the Punica: "But on the right side, where the Aufidus winds its course in bends and surrounds its banks with a curving flood."

units.la: Deo eo sic scribit eleganter Oculatus Testis Leander Albertus sub finem Apuliae Peucetiae: Oritur Apennino in Hirpinis modico fonte, non procul opidulo quodam Music: unde, non secus ac exiguus rivus, sic labitur, ut aestivis mensibus spatio P. M. xxx (cum enim decursum habet) vix eius agnoscatur fluvius: hieme tamen Fluminum & Torrentium aliorum accessione, itemque ex pluviis adeo plerumque crescit, ut, Alveo deiecto, saepe per latissimos Apulia Campos evagetur, & instar atis vastisque Pelagi ab antiquo Cannuso, quod ad ipsum Amnem erat in planicie, longo tractu Regionem inundet. Apuliam Peucetiam ab Daunia separans primum per Agrum Lacedamonium, deinde Melphitanum & Lavellinum; inde sinuosi flexibus per Campestria Loca prope Minervinum, tum ab Cannuso per Barulianum Agrum in Mare tribus infra ipsum Barulum mille passibus influens, ubi Pons Lapideus, mille passibus abest. Haec ille. Pons, quem nominat, alius censendus abeo, cuius meminit Antoninus Itinere, quod Benevento ducit Hydruntum. Quum enim, quem habet Leander, haud procul hodie sit mari, qui apud Antoninum, prope Venusiam sint, ubi in magnum gyrum evolvere se versus Caurum incipit Aufidus, xxxv aut circiter ab Hadriatico Sinu Milliaribus. Male editur in nonnullis Antonini Exemplaribus Pentaufidus; Aufidus Canna vocatur in Fastidio Cn. Marcii Carmine apud Livium lib. xxv. Octodecim ab Aufido milliaribus Candiarii visitur, quem cum Lacu Anduriano Strabonem, suppressis nominibus, indicare censeo: quum scribit inter Salapiam & Sipuntum Fluvium esse Navigationi satis oportunum & Lacus ingens ostiumque Cervaria mox est: qui Cerbulus Plinio. Cerbarium etiam Procopio lib. iii Goth. locus est in Apulia.
units.tr: Leander Albertus, an eyewitness, describes it elegantly at the end of Apulia Peucetia: It rises in the Apennines among the Hirpini, from a small spring not far from a little town called Music. From there it flows like a small brook, so that in the summer months, after about thirty Roman miles (for that is the length of its course), the river can hardly be recognised. In winter, however, with the addition of other rivers and torrents, and generally from the rains, it grows so much that, having broken its bed, it often spreads over the broadest plains of Apulia, and, like a vast and immense sea, floods the region for a long stretch from the old Cannusium, which lay on the river itself in the plain. Separating Apulia Peucetia from Daunia, it first passes through the territory of Lacedaemonia, then through Melfi and Lavello; then, winding in its bends through the plain near Minervino, and then from Canosa through the Barulian territory, it flows into the sea three thousand paces below Barolo, where the Stone Bridge is, a thousand paces away. So far he. The bridge he names must be taken to be another, the one mentioned in Antoninus's Itinerary, which leads from Benevento to Otranto. For the bridge that Leander has is not far from the sea today, whereas the one in Antoninus is near Venusia, where the Aufidus begins to wind in a great curve toward the northwest, about thirty-five miles or so from the Adriatic gulf. In some editions of Antoninus the name Pentaufidus is badly printed. The Aufidus is called Canna in the poem of Gn. Marcius on the Fasti, cited in Livy book 25. Eighteen miles from the Aufidus the Candiario is found, which I think, with the names suppressed, is what Strabo means by the Lake Andurianus, when he writes that between Salapia and Sipuntum there is a river fairly suitable for navigation, and a large lake and a mouth, Cervaria, soon after. Pliny calls this Cerbulus. Cerbarium is also a place in Apulia, according to Procopius in book 3 of the Gothic War.

units.la: Samnitium littora lustrantibus offert se primo loco Phiternus, quo Samnium ab Apulia dividitur: Fortore vulgo; Φιμπρος Prolemaeo; Tifernus Plinio & Mela. Eius in Tifermo Monte, qui nunc Bifanus, Fons est, haud procul a Boviano. Exonerat se in Mare Hadriaticum iuxta Lesinensem Lacum. Succedunt inde Flumina Trinius, quod Portusfum notat Plinius; Ajinella, Sentus, Sangrus. Qui Sangrus vel sanguinaus Latine scribentibus hodie, vernacule autem Sangro vel Sanguino; Σαγρος est Prolemaeo; Σαγρος Straboni, Saron Vibio Sequestro. Ex Apennino oriens, defcenfiqne, ut Strabo demonstrat, inter Aternum & Ortonem fluens, Frentanos Caracenoqne a Pelignis dividit, Hadriaticum tandem infusus. Varios convehit secum ad Mare Amnes: inter quos praecipui Rasinus, in Campis Furcae Palenae caput tollens, & Aventinus, qui ex Superequanis Pelignorum (sic enim olim vocati) Furcae Palenae finitimis oriturj recepto tamen ante Viridi, cuius in Maiella Monte Fons inter Monasterium D. Martini Castellumque Faranum. Mox bis mille passibus ab Ortona labitur Flumen Moras. Hoc loco in Itineraria Tabula Fluvius Ciorus scribitur, inter Anxanum & Ortonam. Sequitur inde exiguus Amnis Feltrinus. Ostia dein Fori; & nono inde lapide Senti; totidem hinc, qui vulgo Pescara. Aternum Varroni lib. iv de L.L. & Plinio: Αἴπηρος Strabono & Ptolemaeo. Nascitur ex plerorum Italiae Fluminum Parente Apennino, supra Aquilam, haud procul Monte Regali, qui subter eius est Fontem. Confluunt in Aternum vel Pisciariam multi Amnes. Ripa quidem Australiore cum primis duo, ortum habentes in Agro Sulmonensi, ad opida Pectoranum & Vallem Obscuram: unde uterque peculiari alveo ferme Sulmonem usque procedens, alter alteri inmersus unico Flumine extra Urbem per extentam planiciem, milliaque passuum vi latam, cursu fere millium xii absoluto, Fontibusque & Aquulis quibusdam prope Populum, ubi ligneo transitur Ponte, haud mediocriter adaucti, tandem in Aternum se exonerant: quemadmodum & xvii aut circiter hinc milliaribus ad eamdem ripam uno alveo Aternum iucunt Rafentus & Orta, ex Maiella Monte provoluti. VIII inde Lapide Liberata in Aternum se condit, binas item ex Maiella procurrentes Aquulas deferens: Tiperatam quoq; appellari hunc Fluvium monet Alexander Andreas. Ad Boreali horem vero ripam augetur Aternus duobus Amnibus, quorum unus Caput Aquae, Capo di Aquas; alter Nyrta prope Coenobium Casae Novae, Cistellini ordinis, capiens ini-tium.
units.tr: Coasting along the shores of the Samnites, the first river that presents itself is the Fiternus, by which Samnium is separated from Apulia. It is commonly called the Fortore; Ptolemy calls it Fimbrus [Φιμπρος]; Pliny and Mela call it Tifernus. Its source is on Mount Tifernus, which is now called Bifano, not far from Bojano. It empties into the Adriatic Sea near the Lake of Lesina. Next come the rivers Trinius, which Pliny notes as Portusfum; Ajinella, Sentus, and Sangrus. The Sangrus, which writers in Latin today call sanguinaus, and which in the vernacular is called Sangro or Sanguino, is Sangros [Σαγρος] in Ptolemy and Sagros [Σαγρος] in Strabo; Saron in Vibius Sequester. It rises in the Apennines, and as Strabo shows, flows down between Aternum and Ortona, dividing the Frentani from the Caraceni and the Peligni, and finally pours itself into the Adriatic. It brings several rivers with it to the sea, among which the chief are the Rasinus, which rises in the plains of Furca Palena, and the Aventinus, which rises in the upper parts of the Peligni (as they were once called), bordering on Furca Palena, but before it reaches the sea it receives the Viridis, whose spring is on the Mount Maiella between the monastery of St. Martin and the castle of Faranum. Soon, about two thousand paces from Ortona, flows the river Moras. In the Itinerary map a river called Ciorus is written here, between Anxanum and Ortona. Next comes the small river Feltrinus. Then the mouth of the Forum; and nine miles from there the Senti; and as many from there the one commonly called the Pescara. The Aternus is called by Varro in book 4 On the Latin Language, and by Pliny, and Aeperus [Αἴπηρος] by Strabo and Ptolemy. It rises, like most of the rivers of Italy, from its parent the Apennines, above L'Aquila, not far from Monte Regale, which lies below its spring. Many rivers flow into the Aternus, or Pescara. From the southern bank, especially, two rivers, which rise in the territory of Sulmona, near the towns of Pettorano and Valle Oscura, flow together, each in its own channel, nearly up to Sulmona. Then, having become one river beyond the city, across a wide plain and a width of many miles, after a course of about twelve miles, and greatly augmented by springs and small streams near Popoli, where it is crossed by a wooden bridge, they finally discharge themselves into the Aternus. In the same way, about seventeen miles from here, on the same bank, the Rafentus and the Orta, rushing down from Mount Maiella, join the Aternus in one channel. Eight miles from there the Liberata hides itself in the Aternus, likewise bringing two small streams that run down from the Maiella. Alexander Andreas advises that this river is also called Tiperata. On the northern bank the Aternus is increased by two streams, one of which, the Caput Aquae, now Capo d'Acqua, and the other, the Nyrta, begin near the monastery of Casa Nuova of the Cistercian order.

units.la: Candiarii, Cervariae, Samnitium, Fortorum, Tifernum, Trinium, Aprinea, Sentas, Sangrus, olim Sarno, Rasinus, Aventinus, Viridis, Morat, Feltrinus, Fori, Senti, Pescara, olim Aterno, Rafentus, Orta, Liberata, Caput Aquae, Nyrta, Sabinum. pigrique Amnis, ut Palus videatur potius, quam Flumen, notante Boccatio de Fluminibus. Adcolis perquam noxius est Aëris gravitate, quam ob cœnosa Vada creat. Tiberim Arno conjungit. Agri plurimum amplectitur, Perusinorum & Senensium discrimen efficiens. Recipit Fisam, Foennam, Asfaronem, &c, ut Blondus vult, Paltam, vel, ut alij censent, à Palta recipitur Palta certe, qui vulgo Paglia, infra Redicofanum Montesque præcelsos oritur, perque Convalles descendens tantum colligit incrementi, ut subjecta infestet loca. Qui hodie Treia vel Trogina nominatur, Clitumnum putant nonnulli dictum Antiquis: eo connisi argumento, quod apud Plinium lib.11. cap.cit. Clitumnus poni videatur in Falisci: quos ad dexteram Tiberis ripam in Etruria suas sedes, ubi nunc Civitas Castellana, habuisse, satis ex Veterum{10} Monumentis est clarum. Sed quum, ut paullo post dicam, ex conceptissimis Servij ad 11. Georgic. verbis, Clitumnus fluvius sit in Mevania, quæ pars Umbriæ, partis Tusciæ, dicendum est, vel Plinium alium ejusdem virtutis designare Clitumnum; vel suum Faliscis etiam ad Mevaniam tunc temporis fuisse Imperium: vel denique locum Plinij esse depravatum. Primum & alterum nullam habent Veri similitudinem: Tertium proxime ab eo, quod est, abest. Nam in veteribus Codicibus legitur: In Falisco omnis (non Clitumni, aqua potata candidos Boves facit. An recte omnis? Malim Amnis, ut designet Plinius; Amnem esse apud Faliscos: qui, aqua ipsius potata, colorem album Armentis conciliet; quemadmodum Clitumnus idem præstat in Umbria. Pergo. Cremeram, Fabiorum clade insignem, esse censet Leander{20} Albertus Flumen illud, quod ex Bacchani Lacu prorumpens in Tiberim se exonerat, ad Pagum Varcam, unde & Varca nomen sortitur. Raphael Volaterranus putat eum Amniculum esse, qui hodie vicinus Primæ Portæ, quinto ab Urbe miliario, visitur. Tradit Ortelius Adcolas, ab ipso serio interrogatos, non aliud isti Fluvio nomen dedisse, quam Fossa. Dionysius Amnem hunc parum ab Veiis distare notat. Cremeram sane vocant Scriptores omnes: Κρέμερα dicitur Diodoro lib.xi. Pyrrhus Ligorius Cremeram putat Turiam esse vel Tusiam (sic enim legit Sigonius ad xxvi Livij librum ab V. C.) Silij lib.xiii; ubi inquit: Turia deducit tenuem sine nomine rivum, Et tacite Tuscis ingloria adfluit undis.
units.tr: Candiarii, Cervariae, Samnitium, Fortorum, Tifernum, Trinium, Aprinea, Sentas, Sangrus, formerly Sarno, Rasinus, Aventinus, Viridis, Morat, Feltrinus, Fori, Senti, Pescara, formerly Aterno, Rafentus, Orta, Liberata, Caput Aquae, Nyrta, Sabinum. The sluggish river is more like a marsh than a stream, as Boccaccio notes in his book on rivers. Its air is very harmful to those who live near it, because of the heaviness it creates from its muddy shallows. The Tiberim joins the Arno. It takes in a great deal of territory, forming the boundary between the Perusini and the Senenses. It receives the Fisam, Foennam, Asfaronem, etc. As Biondo holds, it receives the Paltam, or, as others think, the Palta receives it. The Palta, certainly, which is commonly called the Paglia, rises below Radicofani and the very high mountains, and descending through the valleys it gathers such a flood that it harms the neighbouring places. What is now called the Treia or Trogina, some think was called the Clitumnum by the ancients, on the argument that in Pliny, book 11, chapter cited, the Clitumnus seems to be placed among the Falisci, whom it is clear from the ancient monuments had their seats on the right bank of the Tiber in Etruria, where the city of Civita Castellana now is. But since, as I shall say a little later, from the very clear words of Servius on Georgics 2, the Clitumnus is a river in Mevania, which is part of Umbria, part of Tuscany, we must either say that Pliny means another Clitumnus of the same kind; or that the Falisci's dominion at that time also extended to Mevania; or finally that the passage of Pliny is corrupted. The first and second have no probability. The third is very close to what is the case, for it is missing only a little. For in the old manuscripts it is read: In Falisco omnis (not Clitumni, aqua potata candidos Boves facit. Is omnis correct? I would prefer Amnis, so that Pliny means that there is a river among the Falisci which, when its water is drunk, gives cattle a white colour, just as the Clitumnus does the same in Umbria. I continue. Leander Albertus thinks that the Cremeram, famous for the defeat of the Fabii, is that river which, bursting from Lake Bacano, discharges itself into the Tiber near the village of Varca, from which it also takes the name Varca. Raffaele Volterrano thinks it is the small stream that today is seen near Prima Porta, five miles from the City. Ortelius reports that the residents, when he seriously asked them, gave that river no other name than Fossa. Dionysius notes that this river is not far from Veii. All writers, indeed, call it Cremera; it is called Κρέμερα [Kremera] by Diodorus in book 11. Pyrrhus Ligorius thinks the Cremera is the Turia or Tusia (for so Sigonius reads it at book 26 of Livy, from the foundation of the city). In Silius, book 13, where he says: Turia deducit tenuem sine nomine rivum, Et tacite Tuscis ingloria adfluit undis.

units.la: Petrus tamen Marius Turiam Rivulum esse dicit in via Appia, ut ab Urbe P.M; salso, ut opinatur Ortelius. Prope Cremeram cccvi Fabios, cum quinque Clientum, Servorumque millibus internecione ab Veientibus occisos, scribunt Livius lib.ii, Dionysius Halic. lib.ix, Ovidius ii Fastorum, Florus lib.i. Histor. Rom. cap. xii, Orosius lib.ii. Hist. cap. v, Eutropius lib.i, Agellius lib.xvi. Noct. Attic. cap.xxi, Plutarchus in Vita Camilli, Silius Italicus lib. ii & vii, Servius ad vi Æneid. & alij. Infra Romam est Galera Fluvius, qui haud procul Mariano Tiberis fit incola. Hi cum alijs ad Occidentaliorem Tiberis ripam conspiciuntur. Sequentes, qua Oriens est, Tiberi adfluunt. Non magni nominis sunt Reggia, Ajona, Rufina, Ventia, & alij ibidem. Qui in Umbria Chiatus vel Chiusa hodie Latine scribentibus, Vulgo autem Chiazzo, nec Ajus est, ut falso quidam judicant, Ptolemæi: nec Aesis Strabonis, Plinij, Pomponiique Melæ, qui eum Semnonum flumen faciunt, locisque ad Mare Hadriaticum sitis adcenseant, quemadmodum suo loco videbimus. Potest tamen Chiatus paullo Latinius vocari Ajus, non quod ita Ptolemæo nuncupetur, sed quod ex monte Asi profluat. Consulendus Landinus in Dantis Paradis. Cant. Recipit in se præter Scircam, Rufinam, qui Larone augetur, Marcaiam & alios, Topinum ad Canariam, ejusque nomen exstinguit, solo Chiaty retento; posteaque, opido Bertonio lustrato, prope Torsanam in Tiberim evolvitur. Qui nunc Topinus, Tinia (in quibusdam libris est Tinna) Plinio dicitur; Tinia Strabono. De eo Silius Italicus lib. viii:{50}
units.tr: Peter Marius, however, says that the Turia is a small stream on the Appian Way, P.M. from the city, salty, as Ortelius supposes. Near the Cremera, 306 Fabii, together with several thousand clients and slaves, were cut down by the Veientes, as Livy (book 2), Dionysius of Halicarnassus (book 9), Ovid (Fasti, book 2), Florus (Roman History, book 1, ch. 12), Orosius (History, book 2, ch. 5), Eutropius (book 1), Aulus Gellius (Attic Nights, book 16, ch. 21), Plutarch (in the Life of Camillus), Silius Italicus (books 2 and 7), Servius (on Aeneid 6) and others write. Below Rome is the river Galera, which becomes a tributary of the Tiber not far from Marianum. These, with others, are seen on the western bank of the Tiber. Those that flow in from the east are the following: the Reggia, Ajona, Rufina, Ventia and others there, none of them of great name. The one in Umbria called Chiatus or Chiusa by Latin writers today, but commonly Chiazzo, is not the Ajus of Ptolemy, as some wrongly judge; nor is it the Aesis of Strabo, Pliny and Pomponius Mela, who make it the river of the Semnones and count it among the places on the Adriatic Sea, as we shall see in its proper place. Yet the Chiatus may be called Ajus in a rather more Latin manner, not because Ptolemy so names it, but because it flows from Mount Asius. Landino on Dante's Paradiso, canto 1, should be consulted. Besides the Scirca and the Rufina, which is swollen by the Larone, it receives the Marcaia and others, and the Topinus near Canaria, losing its name there and retaining only the name Chiaty; afterwards, having washed the town of Bertonio, it rolls into the Tiber near Torsana. What is now the Topinus is called by Pliny the Tinia (in some books Tinna); Strabo calls it Tinia. Silius Italicus speaks of it in book 8:

units.la: Tiniaque ingloria humor.
units.tr: And the unrenowned moisture of the Tinia.

units.la: Quur ita? Quod non navigabilis, Rivulusque magis, quam Flumen. In Tinia ripis ingentes passim adparent Ædificiorum ruinæ, fundamentaque maximorum operum, quæ ab Romanis ad tutelam Viæ Flaminiæ quondam excitata. Augetur etiam Topinus ab alijs Fluvijs: inter quos vere Viri magni agnoscunt Clitumnum. Hic enim, notante Servio ad 11. Georgic. Fluvius est in Mevania, quæ Pars Umbriæ, partis Tusciæ. Iam vero Mevaniam opidum esse Umbriæ, quod hodie Bevagna, dicam cap. xxiv. Oritur autem Clitumnus ex Trebulanis Collibus, in quibus olim veteres oliviferæque Murticæ, limpidissimo copiosissimoque erumpens Fonte; sequeque infra Fulginum vel Fulgineum Topino committet. Nomen, quod hodie, in præsentia non occurrit. Philargyrius aut eum Umbriam ab Tuscia dividere. Quod apud Plinium male Falisci adscribatur, ante notatum. Constans apud Veteres fuit opinio, Aquam Clitumni a Bubus potatam albos creare Fœtus, experti lagunarique solitos ab Romanis ad Triumphalia Sacrificia. Virgilius lib. II. Georgic. Hinc alii, Clitumne, greges, & maxima Taurus Victima, sæpe tuo perfusi Flumine sacro, Romanos ad Templa Deum duxere Triumphos.
units.tr: Why so? Because it is not navigable, and is more a brook than a river. Along the banks of the Tinia there appear everywhere huge ruins of buildings and the foundations of great works, which were once erected by the Romans to protect the Via Flaminia. The Topinus is also swollen by other rivers, among which learned men rightly recognise the Clitumnus. For this, as Servius notes on Georgics 2, is a river in Mevania, which is part of Umbria, and part of Tuscany. That Mevania is a town of Umbria, now called Bevagna, I shall say in chapter 24. The Clitumnus rises from the Trebulan hills, where in former times there were olive groves, bursting forth from a most clear and abundant spring; and it joins the Topinus below Fulginum or Fulgineum. The name it bears today is not in use at present. Philargyrius, or perhaps he, divides Umbria from Tuscany. That Pliny wrongly assigns it to the Falisci has been noted before. It was a constant opinion among the ancients that cattle drinking the water of the Clitumnus produced white offspring; these were often used by the Romans for triumphal sacrifices. Virgil, Georgics book 2: "Hence, Clitumnus, many herds and the largest bull, the victim often bathed in your sacred river, have led Roman triumphs to the temples of the gods."

units.la: Propertius in Elegiis: Qua formosa suo Clitumnus flumina luco Intrgit, & niveo abluit unda Boves.
units.tr: Propertius in the Elegies: "Where the Clitumnus, lovely, enters its streams through its grove, and the water washes the snow-white oxen."

units.la: Silius Italicus de Bello Punico lib. VIII: Et lavit ingentem perfusum Flumine Sacro Clitumnus Taurum.
units.tr: Silius Italicus, on the Punic War, book 8: "And the Clitumnus bathed the great bull, drenched in its sacred stream."

units.la: Clitumnus sane Deus habitus, eique sacrata existimatur fuisse Ædes, quæ in propinquo visitur marmorea & antiquissima, nec non more Corinthio pulcherrime constructa, cujus Scenographiam & ornamenta varia curiose describit, Franciscus Schottus. Sequitur inde post Topinum aliosque Nar. Sic Virgilio, Strabone, Lucano, Tacito, Silio, Plinio, Procopio, aliisque nominatur, qui hodie Negra Italis Nera forte, quum Aquas habeat albas. Nar albus Aquaque Sulphurea, Virgilio lib. VII Æneidos, ubi Servius rationem Epithetí, vel ab Aqua sulfurea, vel ab Colore Saporeve sulphureo notat sumtam. Albescentes illi undas tribuit Silius lib. VIII. Sulphureus Amnis canitur Martiali lib. VII. Ex Amiternis Montibus oriri notat Pomponius Sabinus ad VII. Æneid. Defluit, ex Leandri diffinitione, ex Apennini jugis; ibique, ut Plinius ait, ex Monte Fiscello, duobus erumpens Fontibus, qui foramina tunc in Saxo, natura sic excavato, ut naribus animalis, seu nasi spiraculis admodum sint similia: quamobrem etiam ab Antiquis Nar est vocatus: dein juxta Vacunæ Nemora descendens, ut Plinius testatur, per subjectam Vallem fluit, posteaque Tiberi conjungitur. Augetur prope tres Pontes Corvo, ex Coriti Montis radicibus fluente. Cum Lacu Velino conjungi scribit Tacitus. Narniam oppidum ab eo dictum tradunt Livius & Stephanus in Urbium Syllabo. Supra Narem prætergressis Narniam adparent à dextris admirandi Pontis Fornices, qui duos præcelsos & abruptos Montes, subterlabente Flumine, solebat conjungere, ut æquali via transitus ab opido Narnia pateret in montem adversum. Auctorem memorat Augustum Procopius; qui haud umquam altiores Pontis Arcus abs se visos profitetur. Qualis quantusque fuerit, docent hodieque ex lapide quadrato prægrandi reliquiæ. Examiandus de eo Martialis Epigrammate ad Narniam: Sed jam parce mihi, nec abutere Narnia Quinto, Perpetuo liceat fictibi Ponte frui.
units.tr: The Clitumnus was certainly regarded as a god, and a temple is thought to have been consecrated to him; it can be seen nearby, marble and very ancient, and built most beautifully in the Corinthian style; Francesco Schotti describes its stage-set and various ornaments with care. After the Topinus and others comes the Nar. So it is named by Virgil, Strabo, Lucan, Tacitus, Silius, Pliny, Procopius and others; today it is called Negra by the Italians, perhaps Nera, since its waters are white. "The white Nar and its sulphurous water" (Virgil, Aeneid book 7), where Servius notes that the epithet is taken either from the sulphurous water or from the sulphurous colour and taste. Silius, book 8, gives it whitish waves. Martial, book 7, sings of the "sulphurous river." Pomponius Sabinus, on Aeneid 7, notes that it rises from the Amiternian mountains. According to Leandro's definition, it flows down from the ridges of the Apennines; and there, as Pliny says, bursting forth from two springs on Mount Fiscellus, which in the rock there are hollowed out by nature in such a way that they are very like the nostrils of an animal, or the breathing holes of a nose; for this reason the ancients also called it Nar. Then, descending near the groves of Vacuna, as Pliny attests, it flows through the valley below and afterwards joins the Tiber. It is swollen near Three Bridges by the Corvo, which flows from the roots of Mount Coritus. Tacitus writes that it joins Lake Velinus. Livy and Stephanus in his Syllabus of Cities report that the town of Narnia was named after it. Passing beyond the Nar, as one goes towards Narnia, there appear on the right the wonderful arches of a bridge, which once joined two very lofty and steep mountains, the river flowing beneath, so that there was a level passage from the town of Narnia to the mountain opposite. Procopius mentions the builder, Augustus; he declares that he never saw higher arches of a bridge. What its size and shape were, the remains of huge square stone still show today. Martial's epigram to Narnia should be examined: "But now spare me, and do not abuse, Narnia, Quintus; may it be allowed me to enjoy your bridge forever."

units.la: Actum olim fuisse in Senatu de Nare in rivos deducendo tradit Tacitus lib. I. Annalium. Succedunt Nari Romam versus Himella, Fabaris, Allia, Rivus Solis, Anienus, Fabara, & alii. Himella, cujus meminerunt Virgilius & Vibius, ijs in montibus Caput tollens, qui circa Velini Lacus exitus sunt, transcursa Sabinia, inter Ocriculum & Malianum in Tiberim defluit. Qui Fabaris Virgilio Sidonioque, hodie Farfarus vocatur; quo nomine notus etiam apud Servium Plauto. Faber corrupte apud Vibium Sequestrum. Oritur ex Montibus, qui quondam Terrici, ad opidulum, quod ab Amnis Fonte Caput Farfari. Plauti locus apud Servium hic est: Dissipabo te tamquam Folia Farfari.
units.tr: Tacitus, book 1 of the Annals, tells that once in the Senate it was proposed to divert the Nar into channels. Towards Rome from the Nar come the Himella, Fabaris, Allia, the Rivus Solis, the Anienus, the Fabara and others. The Himella, which Virgil and Vibius mention, rising in those mountains which are the outlets around the Lakes of Velinus, flows through the Sabine country, between Ocriculum and Malianum, into the Tiber. The Fabaris, which is named by Virgil and Sidonius, is today called the Farfarus; by this name it is known also to Servius on Plautus. Vibius Sequester corruptly writes Faber. It rises from the mountains which were once called Terrici, near the little town which is named from the source of the river, Caput Farfari. The passage of Plautus cited by Servius is this: "I will scatter you like the leaves of the farfarus."

units.la: Ex quibus patet Arborum circa flumen hoc frequentia, quæ gratissimas efficiunt umbras; unde Ovidio amœna Farfarus umbra.
units.tr: From this it is clear that there is a great abundance of trees along this river, which make very pleasant shade; whence Ovid's "the pleasant shade of the Farfarus."

units.la: Sabiniam hæc ætate intersecat per pulcherrimos Campos, utrimque frondosis conseptos Arboribus; quarum periucundis tegitur umbris. Allia Blondus & Volaterranus esse volunt, qui Curesi hodie. Longe alia mens est Francisco Florido & Leandro Alberto; quibus Allia fluvius ille, qui hodie Caminato, vernacule. Alliam enim vix quarto ab Vrbe lapide Veteres locant Historiae: Curesin autem vicesimo distare commemorat Horatius. Cunstumenis defluit montibus. Ad inferiora provolutus prope portum Mentis Rotundi M.P. ab Roma tribus, aut paullo amplius in Tiberim defertur. Meminerunt Aliae nulli non Scriptores. Unico L. scribendum docet in Orthographia Aldus. Quondam etiam, recte Leandro, Rivum Missum, Rivo di Molo, pro Rivo Morris, Rivo di Monte appellare tolent ab cruenta illa, ut volunt, Romanorum cum Brenno Gallorum Duce pugna xv Kal. Sext. qui Dies Alliensis dictus. Legendi Livius lib. v, Plutarchus in Vita Camilli, & alij. Rivus Solis, Rivo del Sole, Blondo Leandroque videtur is, de quo Horatius lib. i. Epist. ad Lollium: Me quoties reficit gelidus Digentia Rivus, Quam Mandella bibit rugosus frigore Pagus, Quid sentire putas, quid credu, Amice, precari?
units.tr: In our age it cuts through the Sabine country across most beautiful plains, enclosed on both sides by leafy trees, with which it is covered in very delightful shade. Blondus and Volaterranus wish the Allia to be the river now called Curesi. Francesco Fiorido and Leandro Alberti have a quite different view; for them the Allia is that river which today is called Caminato in the vernacular. For the ancient historians place the Allia barely four miles from the city, while Horace records that Cures is twenty miles away. It flows down from the mountains of Cunstumeni. Rolled down into the lower ground, near the harbour of Mentis Rotundus, three or a little more Roman miles from Rome, it is carried into the Tiber. Nearly every writer mentions the Allia. Aldus teaches in his Orthography that it should be written with a single L. Once, rightly according to Leandro, they call it the Rivus Missus, the Rivo di Molo, or instead of Rivo Morris, the Rivo di Monte, from that bloody battle, as they say, of the Romans with the Gallic leader Brennus, fought on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August, which was called the Day of the Allia. See Livy book 5, Plutarch in the Life of Camillus, and others. The Rivus Solis, Rivo del Sole, seems to Blondus and Leandro to be the stream of which Horace speaks in Epistles book 1, to Lollius: "Whenever the cold Digentia stream refreshes me, which the wrinkled village drinks in its frost at Mandela, what do you think, friend, what do you believe I should pray for?"

units.la: Quos versus exponens Acron Mandellam Vicum in Sabinis esse scribit, ubi Rivus Solis, Horatio Digentia vocatus. Qui Anio dicitur apud Livium in libris ab V.C. non uno loco, Virgilium vi. Aeneidos, Horat. lib. i. Carm. Od. vii. Melam in Cosmographia. Silium Italicum lib. viii & xii, Propertium in Elegiis, Plinium in libr. nat. historiae; Anien autem apud Halicarnass. & Strabonem, Anienus apud Statium in Tiburtino; Anien apud Vibium Sequestrum; quemque ναπάνον olim vocatum scribit, ni corruptus sit locus, Frontinus lib. ii. de Aquaeductibus: hodie, Blondo, Leandro, aliisque censentibus, Tere one vocatur. Nomen illi, ex Silij Italici lib. xii sententia, ab Anio, Etruscorum Rege: ex Vibij Sequestri mente, ab Anione, Apollinis filio. Oritur, ut Plinius scribit lib. iii cap. xi, in montibus Trebanorum, tetque Lacus amoenitate nobiles, qui nomen dedere Sublacij. de quo alibi, desere in Tiberim. Strabo eum ex Alba decurrere scribit praeter Latinam Marsorum Urbem, indeque per Campos propinquos in Tiberim defluere. Tacitus ab Montibus Simpruinis descendere, tribusque ab Roma millibus Tiberi conjungi dicit. Ad Trebam Urbem manare tradit Frontinus ii Aquaeductuum. Lacui Velinorum infundi scribit Vibius. Ad Tibur ex alta rupe, praecipite Aquae delectu, qui καταρράκτης apud Strabonem lib. v, maximo cum fragore decidit in subjectam Convallem: indeque per plana & fructuosa loca fluit in Tiberim, Sabinos ab Latinis dividens; potu gratus, aspectu perjucundus, recte Halicarn. lib. v. cuius haec verba: Οὐαλέρ ... ἐξ ἑνὸς ... Σαβίνων ... ποταμός ... καλὸς μὲν ἐφ᾽ ἑκάτερα, ψυχρὸς δὲ πίνειν. Transitum ejus quatuor coniungunt Pontes. Eorum unus in Via Tiburtina, Mammeae vulgo dictus, tamquam Pons Mammaea, qui primum ab Antonino Pio factus, dein ab Mammaea, Alexandri xxv Imperatoris Matre restitutus, ac marmore sumtuose fuit exornatus, quo tamen nunc spoliatus cernitur; Alter paullo inferius Viam Nomentanam jungit. Eum quis condiderit, nondum constat. Integer est, sed ornamentis suis plane denudatus. Succedit infra Tertius in Via Salaria, tribus ab Urbe Roma milliaribus, ab Narsete Justiniani Imperatoris Augusti Legato, victis Gothis, fabricatus; quod docent positae ibi Inscriptiones: quarum Prior, litteris ob longis & male proportionatis concepta, ita habet;
units.tr: Explaining these verses, Acron writes that Mandela is a village in the Sabine country, where the Rivus Solis is, called by Horace the Digentia. The Anio is so called by Livy in the books from the foundation of the city, in more than one place; by Virgil, Aeneid book 6; by Horace, Odes book 1, ode 7; by Mela in his Cosmography; by Silius Italicus, books 8 and 12; by Propertius in the Elegies; by Pliny in his Natural History; but Anien by Dionysius of Halicarnassus and Strabo; Anienus by Statius in the Tiburtine poem; Anien by Vibius Sequester; and Frontinus, book 2 on the Aqueducts, writes that it was once called Nanpanon (if the passage is not corrupt); today, according to Blondus, Leandro and others, it is called Tere one. Its name, according to Silius Italicus in book 12, came from Anio, king of the Etruscans; in the mind of Vibius Sequester, from Anion, son of Apollo. It rises, as Pliny writes in book 3, chapter 11, in the mountains of the Trebani, and makes the lakes famous for their pleasantness, which gave their name to Sublaci (about which elsewhere), and flows down into the Tiber. Strabo writes that it descends from Alba, past the Latin town of the Marsi, and thence flows through the nearby plains into the Tiber. Tacitus says it descends from the Simbruine mountains and joins the Tiber three miles from Rome. Frontinus, book 2 on the Aqueducts, reports that it runs down to the city of Treba. Vibius writes that it pours into the Lake of the Velini. At Tibur, from a high rock, by a steep fall of water, which Strabo (book 5) calls the cataract, it falls with a great roar into the valley below; thence it flows through level and fruitful country into the Tiber, dividing the Sabines from the Latins; pleasant to drink, most delightful to see, as Halicarnassus rightly says in book 5, whose words are these: "The Anio, from a single... of the Sabines... a river... beautiful on both sides, cold to drink." Four bridges span its crossing. One of them, on the Via Tiburtina, is commonly called the Mammaea bridge, as if the Bridge of Mammaea, which was first built by Antoninus Pius and then restored by Mammaea, mother of the Emperor Alexander, and sumptuously adorned with marble, though now it is seen stripped of it. Another, a little lower down, joins the Via Nomentana. Who built it is not yet known. It is intact, but completely stripped of its ornaments. Below it, a third follows on the Via Salaria, three miles from the city of Rome, built by Narses, legate of the Emperor Justinian Augustus, after the defeat of the Goths; this is shown by the inscriptions placed there, of which the first, composed in letters too long and badly proportioned, reads as follows:
