units.tr: IN THE REIGN OF OUR MOST PIOUS LORD, ALWAYS TRIUMPHANT, JUSTINIAN, PERPETUAL AUGUSTUS, IN THE THIRTY-EIGHTH YEAR OF HIS REIGN: MARSES, MOST GLORIOUS MAN, FORMERLY PRAEPOSITUS OF THE SACRED PALACE, EX-CONSUL AND PATRICIAN, AFTER THE GOTHIC VICTORY, HAVING OVERCOME AND PROSTRATED THE KINGS OF THE GOTHS THEMSELVES IN A PUBLIC CONTEST WITH WONDERFUL SPEED, THE LIBERTY OF THE CITY OF ROME AND OF ALL ITALY BEING RESTORED, RENEWED THE BRIDGE ON THE VIA SALARIA AS FAR AS THE WATER, WHICH HAD BEEN DESTROYED BY THE MOST WICKED TYRANT TOTILA, THE CHANNEL OF THE RIVER BEING CLEANSED AND RESTORED TO A BETTER STATE THAN IT FORMERLY HAD.

VNDAS ꝑ ET. LIBET, IRATAE ꝑ CERNERE. MVRMVR. AQVAE ꝑ ITE. IGITVR, FACILES ꝑ PER. GAVDIA. VESTRA. QVIRITES ꝑ ET. NAM IM. RESONANS ꝑ PLAVSVS. VBIQVE. CANAT ꝑ QVI. POTVIT. RIGIDAS ꝑ GOTHORVM. SVBDVRE. MENTES ꝑ HIC, DOCVIT. DVRVM ꝑ FLVMINA. FERRE. IVGVM ꝑ
units.tr: The other inscription, in slightly better lettering, reads: HOW WELL-TENDED IS THE PATH OF THE BRIDGE MADE STRAIGHT, AND THE BROKEN JOURNEY MADE CONTINUOUS. WE TREAD THE RAPID WAVES OF THE SUBJECT TORRENTS, AND IT IS A PLEASURE TO SEE THE MURMUR OF THE ANGRY WATER. GO THEREFORE, ROMANS, EASILY THROUGH YOUR JOYS, AND LET RESOUNDING APPLAUSE SING EVERYWHERE. WHOEVER COULD SUBDUE THE STUBBORN MINDS OF THE GOTHS HAS TAUGHT THAT THE RIVERS TOO MUST BEAR THE YOKE.

units.la: Ad Pontem hunc ferunt Hannibalem Imbrium inundatione perterritum, soluto obsidio, castra movisse ab Vrbe. Quartus Pons Tiburi, quam Romae, propinquior est, Lucanus ubi Moles rotunda conspicitur, & praeclarum in marmore Pontis T. Plautij Silvani Elogium, quod commodiore adiicimus loco. Anienis Aquae multo infectae sunt Nitro: ideoque mistae iis Tiberinae bonitatem habent singularem, ut alibi dixi. Pausanias tradit Anienis Aquas ea esse natura, ut ad primum contactum gelidissimae, mox paullatim calescere videantur. Auctor est Martialis Eburablutum Anienis aqua Candorem accipere, similiterque Dentes humanos. Inter Anienis Arenas leguntur Amygdala, Anisum, Foeniculum, aliaque in Petram versa, ut in Romanorum convivijs in deliciis sint, ludantque arripientes, putantes se dulciaria Tragemata arripere, vocanturque paullatim Confetti di Tivoli. Superioribus quoque annis Corporis Cadaver humani casum, & in flumen Anienem proiectum Arboris radici adhaerens in lapidem conversum est, & a putrefactione alienum, ut Titus Celsus, Patricius Romanus, ab se visum adhirmat. Detraxit juxta Fluvium hunc memorabili Victoria Gallo Provocatori caelo Torquem aureum Torquatus, cognomen inde meritus Torquati, ut pluribus referunt Livius lib. vii, Florus lib. i. cap. xiii, Q. Claudius lib. i. Annal. apud Agellum lib. ix. cap. xii, Orosius lib. ii, c. ix, Eutropius lib. ii, Valer. Maximus lib. ii cap. ii, Auctor de VV. In l. cap. xxviii. Delicatissimum Amnium vocat in Epistolis Plinius. Augetur cum aliis Fluviolis, tum Maliano & Veresi. Ouιpioς dicitur Straboni. Haud procul Tusculo Frascata est, olim L. Luculli Villa. Ibi non nulli Aqua Virginis, quae hodieque Romam accedit, Fontem repertum tradiderunt. Eam Aquam Plinius lib. xxxi. cap. iii M. Agrippam in Vrbem adduxisse scribit ab octavi Lapidis diverticulo duobus P. M. Praenestina Via. Influit item ad Vrbem Tiberim Aqua, quae Crabra, cujus apud M. Tullium & Frontinum est mentio. Hodie LacMuarana vocatur. Marancella dicitur Lucae Peto, libro Mensuris Romanis. Paullo infra Romam est Almo sive Almon Horatio, Ovidio, Silio, Ammiano, Prudentio, Hieronymo, & quibus non celebratus? Hodie Dachia nominatur. De eo Vibius Sequester: Almon Roma Fluvius, ubi Mater Deum vi Kalend. April. lavatur. Lucanus lib. i. Belli Pharsalici.
units.tr: They say that Hannibal, terrified by the flooding of the Imbrii, abandoned the siege and moved his camp away from Rome at this bridge. The fourth bridge, nearer to Tibur than to Rome, is at the place where the Lucanus round dam can be seen, and there is a splendid inscription in marble on the bridge of T. Plautius Silvanus, which we add in a more suitable place. The waters of the Anio are heavily impregnated with nitre, and so when they mix with the Tiber they have a singular quality, as I have said elsewhere. Pausanias relates that the waters of the Anio are of such a nature that at first contact they seem very cold, but soon gradually grow warm. Martial is the authority that the Anio water makes ivory whiter, and human teeth likewise. Among the sands of the Anio are found almonds, anise, fennel, and other things turned to stone, so that they are a delight at Roman banquets, and people play with them, grasping them and thinking they are grasping sweetmeats; these are gradually called Confetti di Tivoli. In recent years too, the corpse of a human being that had fallen and been cast into the river Anio, clinging to the root of a tree, was turned into stone and was free from putrefaction, as Titus Celsus, a Roman patrician, affirms he saw for himself. Near this river, in a memorable victory, Torquatus stripped a golden torc from the Gaulish challenger, and from this he earned the surname Torquatus, as many authors report: Livy book 7, Florus book 1 chapter 13, Q. Claudius book 1 of the Annals as cited by Agellius book 9 chapter 12, Orosius book 2 chapter 9, Eutropius book 2, Valerius Maximus book 2 chapter 2, the author of De Viris Illustribus chapter 28. Pliny in his Letters calls it the most delightful of rivers. It is increased both by other small streams and by the Maliano and the Veresi. Strabo calls it Anio. Not far from Tusculum lies Frascati, formerly the villa of L. Lucullus. Some have reported that the Aqua Virginis, which still reaches Rome today, was found at a spring there. Pliny in book 31 chapter 3 writes that M. Agrippa brought this water into the city from a branch of the Praenestine Way at the eighth milestone, two miles away. The Aqua called Crabra also flows into the Tiber near the city; it is mentioned by Cicero and Frontinus. Today it is called Lac Muarana. Lucas Peto, in his book on Roman measures, calls it Marancella. A little below Rome is the Almo or Almon, celebrated by Horace, Ovid, Silius, Ammianus, Prudentius, Jerome, and who has not praised it? Today it is called Dachia. Of it Vibius Sequester says: Almon, the Roman river, where the Mother of the Gods is washed on the sixth day before the Kalends of April. Lucan, book 1 of the Pharsalia:

units.la: Et lotam parte revocant Almone Cybellen.
units.tr: And they call back Cybele, bathed in the waters of the Almo.

units.la: Hactenus de Tiberi, Fluminibusque variis; quae cum eo, nominibus amissis, Mare petunt: sequuntur reliqua Latii, ut antiquitus appellabantur, Numicium, Loracina, Stura, Nymphaeus, Ufens. Numicium, vel ut alij scribunt, Numicum, in latio locant Virgilius, Ovidius, Plinius; in Agro Laurenti. Livius, idemque alio loco Ovidius, Vibius; haud procul Lavinio Halicarnassaeus lib. i. cui Νομικιον vocatur, & Silius lib. viii: Numicium Stagnum habet Aurelius Victor. Rivo est hodie, ut vult Pyrrhus Ligorius. Notat ad Aeneidem Virgilianam Servius Numicium ingentem fluvium ante mortem Aeneae fuisse; ceterum post decrescendo paullatim in Fontem redactum, qui & ipse exaruerit, interceptis Sacris; Vestae quippe non nisi de hoc Fluvio libari licuisse. Loracina Fluminis circa Antiates meminit Livius lib. xliii. De Stura sic scribit Festus, Stura Flumen in Agro Laurenti est, quod quidam Afluram vocant. Στιγας Straboni nuncupatur, & Livio lib. xxvi, cui sex millibus locatur ab Vrbe. Apud Virgilium vii Aeneidos pro Satura Palude nonnulli agnoscunt notante Servio, Afluram Paludem, camque Flumen hoc interpretantur. Nomen hodie retinet, indicante Leandro, qui non recte confundit cum Nymphaeo Plinij. Nam Stura & Nymphaeus duo diversaque Plinio sunt Flumina. Ufens Fluvius est iuxta Terracinam & Privernum, Virgilio vii Aenid. Silio lib. i, Vibio Sequestro, Festo, aliis. Apud Strabonem Ἀῦφιδ scribitur, non
units.tr: So far concerning the Tiber and its various rivers, which, having lost their names in it, make for the sea. There follow the rest of Latium, as they were called in antiquity: the Numicius, Loracina, Stura, Nymphaeus, and Ufens. Virgil, Ovid and Pliny place the Numicius, or as others write, the Numicus, in Latium, in the territory of Laurentum. Livy does, and Ovid elsewhere, and Vibius; not far from Lavinium Halicarnassus in book 1 (who calls it Numicios), and Silius in book 8. Aurelius Victor has the Numicium Stagnum. It is today the Rivo, as Pyrrhus Ligorius holds. Servius, on Virgil's Aeneid, observes that the Numicius was a huge river before the death of Aeneas, but afterwards, gradually diminishing, it was reduced to a spring, which itself dried up, its waters being cut off from the sacred rites, since it was lawful to pour libations to Vesta from this river alone. Livy in book 43 mentions the Loracina river near the Antiates. Festus writes thus of the Stura: The Stura is a river in the territory of Laurentum, which some call the Afflura. Strabo calls it Stigas, and Livy in book 26 places it six thousand paces from the city. In Virgil's seventh book of the Aeneid, some recognise the Satura Palude as the Afflura Palus, as Servius notes, and they interpret this as the river. It keeps its name today, as Leander indicates, who wrongly confuses it with the Nymphaeus of Pliny. For the Stura and the Nymphaeus are two different rivers in Pliny. The Ufens is a river near Terracina and Privernum, mentioned by Virgil in book 7 of the Aeneid, by Silius in book 1, by Vibius Sequester, Festus and others. In Strabo it is written Aufidus, not

units.la: Aaa non sine errore, uti notant docti Viri. Baldino dicitur in Tabula Ligorij: alijs est Baudino. Hodie Ausente vocatur, uti tradit Leander Albertus. In Itineraria Tabula etiam notatur hujus Fluvij Cursus & Alveus, non adscripto tamen nomine.
units.tr: without error, as learned men note. It is called Baldino in the Tabula of Ligorius; others have Baudino. Today it is called Ausente, as Leander Albertus reports. The course and bed of this river are also marked in the Itinerary Table, though without a name attached.

units.la: Sic ad Liris, Latij terminum, Campaniaeque initium, perventum nobis. Liris Plinio, Livio, Melae; Ἀνέας Straboni, aliisque Graecis: Lyru per y scribitur in quibusdam Lucani & Taciti libris. Ἀνέας πόλαμὸς, Κλαυΐς δ᾽ ἐκαλᾶν πόσηρον, inquit Strabo; cui consentit Plinius, ut quidem ex Strabone emendandus: Colonia Minturna, Liri Amne divisa Glani quondam appellato. Literanum etiam dictum putat Appianus Alexandrinus ι ἰμφυλ. Falso: vide infra. Hodie Garigliano. Nomen ab Gauro Monte non procul eius ortus natum existimatur. Initium illi duobus e Fontibus: uno supra Soram viii P. M. in Apennino, non procul opido Capistrello; altero millibus tribus Sora prope Castellum Petronium; & hinc est quod circa Soram erumpere notet Strabo. Laudat posteriorem Fontem mirifice Rasanus, numquam clariorem aut perlucidiorem Aquam sibi vitam adferens: si quidem in ea, quantumvis & mirabili copia prorumpat, & altitudinem habeat non modicam, tamen quivis etiam in fundo exiguum inter Pisces, mira cum spectantium voluptate discurrantes, posse discerni. Blondus originem eum ex Lacu Fucino vult trahere, uti quoque Plinus tradere videtur. Riviamborum cursu infra Soram delati confluunt; ita ut superius Peninsula relinquatur, in qua oppida sunt Pelicum, Posta, Lobrutullium, ipsaque Sora. Pergens inde per Fregellas, Minturnas (testantur id etiam, cum Strabone & Plinio, Porphyrius & Acron in Horatium) & Veltinos ad Lacum Frentalem Mari invehitur. Caerulens dicitur Martiali: Caerulens nos Liris amat, quem, autem silva Marica Protegit; hinc Squilla maxima turba sumus.
units.tr: So we have come to the Liris, the boundary of Latium and the beginning of Campania. The Liris is named by Pliny, Livy and Mela; by Strabo and other Greeks it is called Liris; it is spelled Lyru with a y in some manuscripts of Lucan and Tacitus. Strabo says: the river is called Liris, but the Clanis is called the Sarnus; Pliny agrees with him, as it should be emended from Strabo: the colony of Minturnae, divided by the Liris river, formerly called the Glanis. Appian of Alexandria thinks it was also called Literanus, but falsely; see below. Today it is the Garigliano. Its name is thought to derive from Mount Gauro, not far from its source. It has two sources: one above Sora, eight miles away, in the Apennines, not far from the town of Capistrello; the other three miles from Sora near the castle of Petronius; and this is why Strabo says it bursts forth near Sora. Rasanus praises the second spring wonderfully, saying that he never saw water clearer or more transparent, for even in its abundant and rapid flow, and though it has no small depth, one can distinguish even the tiny fish at the bottom darting about to the wonderful delight of onlookers. Blondus wishes it to draw its origin from Lake Fucinus, as Pliny also seems to say. After flowing below Sora the two streams of the Riviambori join it, so that the peninsula above is left, in which lie the towns of Pelicum, Posta, Lobrutullium and Sora itself. Continuing from there through Fregellae, Minturnae (Porphyry and Acron on Horace bear witness to this, along with Strabo and Pliny) and Veltinum, it flows into the sea at the Frentanian lake. Martial calls it Caerulens: The blue Liris loves us, which the Marican wood protects; hence we are the greatest crowd of squills.

units.la: Suffrenum vocat Silius lib. viii. Capiuntur in iis Fontium Rivis Carpiones; sed non, qua in Benaco, magnitudine. Suscipit dextra quidem Fibrenum, Cosam, Alatrum, Terrum, & alios; sinistra vero Cassinum, Messam, & Omnem. Fibrenì meminit Silius lib. viii: At qui Fibreno mittentem flumina Lirem.
units.tr: Silius in book 8 calls it Suffrenum. Carp are caught in its streams, though not of the size they reach in Lake Benacus. On the right it receives the Fibrenum, Cosa, Alatrum, Terrum and others; on the left, however, the Cassinum, Messa and Omnis. Silius in book 8 mentions the Fibrenus: But he who sends the Liris flowing with the Fibrenus.

units.la: Fluit inter Arpinum & Soram, coniungiturque Liri iii ab Arpino P. M. apud Villam S. Dominici, ubi M. Tull. in lucem editus. Eum vide lib. ii. de L. L, & lib. Epist. ad Attic. xiii. ubi & de Fibreno Arpinatem Insulam faciente. Fiume de la Posta, ait Sanfelicius. De Cosa: Κῶσα Φορυσοσ, Frutinum, ὁ Κοσας μὲν πόλαμὸς, inquit Strabo. Hodie Pilsia dicitur Leandro. Quod ad Trerum, Τίρηρα Φαβεγανέιαν, ait Strabo, ὁ Τρηρ πόλ. De Cassino idem Strabo: Ὑπερβαμένη, inquit, ἐν συμβολῇ ἕνοιν πολαμοῖν κατ᾽ ἀμφοῖν, Ἀμέλεγη κῶν ἱπρα Κασίνα. Quod illi hodie nomen, ignoro. Certe non Melfa, quod putat Ortelius. Nam qui Melfa vulgo, Straboni Μέλας ibidem appellatur, Ὀλίγοι Ἀντιόχω ὁ Μέλας, inquienti, μὴ, πολαμὸς μέγας; non idem, ut putat Leander, cum Melphe Plinii, qui circa Columnam Rhegiam. Melpu ex Apennino descendit per planiciem usque ad Fregellas, indeque non procul in Lirim evolvitur. Omnis Amnis iiii ab D. Germani P. M. iuxta D. Eliae, propter Apenninum, caput tollit; modicis admodum initiis; sed permagnus, Aquis multorum Fontium exceptis: cursu P. M. fere xii confecto, in Lirin haud procul à Ponte Corvi cadit. Liri succedit Vulturnus, Virgilio, Livio, Plinio (& quibus non?) notus. Οὐλτούρνο Straboni, aliisque Graecis. Volturnus Varroni, Ἀχαιῶν. Volturno, hodieque. Οὐατυεγίν Plutarcho in Fabio Maximo, qui emendandus. Varie vertunt varii, variis usi codicibus: Notaronum Georgius Fabricius & Petrus Candidus, quem etiam probat Leander: Lotaronium Niger; Aliocronum Cuspinianus in Cassiodorum. Καρυλίνο etiam vocatur Agathiae lib. ii. de bello Gothico, ab opido fortean, quod in eius ripa situm. Videndi quoque Vibius Sequester, & Strabo lib. v. Sic item appellatur in Urna lapidea; cuius ad Vulturnum, nobilem quondam Coloniam, hodie Castel al Mar di Boterno, Inscriptio ita habet: Aquas Casilinus Flu-minis Mortuis gravatas suscepit Tyrrheni Maris Littus, quando Francorum gentem occidit Ausonius Ensis, ubi misero hac gesit morem Bultino. Ab Apennino descendens, perexilis primo, Aquarum & Fontium accessione magnam & Latitudinem & Altitudinem nactus, inter Samnitium Montes tractu P. M. xxx in Agrum Venafranum, inde xx. P. M. in Alifanum, hinc xxv in Campanum evolvitur; Capuaque salutata, ad cum locum, ubi quondam Vulturnum fuit opidum, ut etiam post Varronem lib. iv. Strabo testatur, in Mare se exonerat. Ab Vulturni Fonte ad Liris initium intervallum est modicum. Varro in Sannio oriri tradit. Fluens tribus ab Alifa P. M. antiquitus ibi Campania Felicis & Samnij habebatur discrimen. Livius lib. xxii. dicit cum Falernum ab Agro Campano dividere. Eminus est Vulturus Capua, inquit Pœdianus in in Verrinam, tribus P. M. Ad Cutium pertinet quod Celer dicatur Lucano lib. ii; quodque Fluctu sonorum vocet Silius Italicus lib. viii. Iuxta Cumas in mare labi scribit Servius. Dionysius de Vulturno & Glani prodigium refert: eos, omisso naturali meatu, vertisse cursus, aliquamdiu retrocedentes ab Ostiis ad suos fontes. Nos Belgæ, qui Fluxum Refluxumque Maris novimus, hæc talia non miramur. Vulturnum Mare habet Plinius ad hunc Flumnis ostium. Amnes Torrentesq; multos colligit: inter ceteros, dextra quidem Cusanum Correctum, sinistra Freddum: Pratellum, Sabbatum, Iscleru, & alios. Cusanus Correctus ex Mathelio Monte ortus prope Pulianellum Vulturni se immergit Aquis. Freddus adversa ripa ibidem Vulturno se miscet, cognomine adsitum habens Opidum. Freddum sequitur alius; qui ortus ad Pedem Montis, vulgo Piedmont, facto per Agrum Alifanum tr. P. M. cursu, tandem propter Alifam in Vulturnum se condit. Pratellus in radicibus nascitur Montis Mathelii, ab opido Pratello, quod iuxta est, nomen habens. Ab eius Fonte Castellum Galli haud procul abest. Sabbatus, ut Antonino vocatur, ex Apennino oritur, qua regione luga eius Montes Tremuli nominantur: & per deprella loca sinuosis flexibus, omnibus fere Beneventani Agri Fontibus uno alveo collectis, se tandem in Vulturnum, maximo ipsi inlato Incremento, exonerat. Hodie Fiume de Benevento dicitur; quod propter eam Urbem, perque eius fluat Agros. Sabbatus Incolas, ut sic loquar, habet varios, inter quos principis facile loci Calor, Antiquis notus. Sic etiam nominatur in Itineraria Tabula; sed cum Vulturni alveo ita imperite miscus, ut unus esse Fluvius videatur. A λαρ corrupte apud Appianum Alexandrinum. Ad Calorem Mansio est apud Antoninum, inter Nucerium & Nerulum: qua Flumen hunc designari certum est. Nomen hactenus retinet Caore. Hodie usque Pugna dicitur, inquit Paullus Diaconus. Testatur Ortelius in M. S. Codice Pugnam non esse Fluvij, sed Loci iuxta Fluvium nomen. Scipio Mazzella scribit Dentecane vulgo vocari: essi, inquit, nonnulli sic vocent Tabernulam haud procul inde. Ex Amsancti Valle præcipitem ferri, inter opidum Aquariam & Pœtanos Agros, Silaroque miscerí, tradit Pomponius Sabinus in vii Æneid. Prope Beneventum ponunt Livius lib. xxiv sequenteque, & Vibius Sequester. In Sabbatum influit ccc fere passuum spatio supra Beneventum, prope Pontem Valentinum, qui Calorem transvit Valens Imperator. Augetur autem, antequam ab Sabbato suscipiatur, Tripalto, Misciano, Tamara aliis. Tripalto nomen ab opido Tripalta. Ad ripam eius dextram Silva est peringens & Latronum domicilio infamis, quæ ab Amne vicino Tripaltina. Exit, quemadmodum etiam Misciarus, ex Monte Crepacorio. Tamarus notus quoque est Antonino, ubi Mansionem nominat Super Tamari fluvium. Male nonnulli Codices Super Maris flav. Tamarus Aquarum copia non est Calore minor. Præter Calorem sunt alij, qui Sabbato miscentur. Ad opidum sane Pontem Fontes sunt quatuor, qui corrivati uno ostio in Sabbatum feruntur; ex Apennino descendentes, Vicina Fontibus totidem sunt opida; Ad D. Laurentium, ad D. Lupum, Pons Landulphi, & Casalonium. Sabbatus sinistra sua ripa excipit, præter alios, Seritellam, ex Caudinis orientem Montibus. Iam relictis Vulturno etiam suis, ne prolixior sim, Ifuclere, Arnone, aliis, ad Glanum venio. De Glani Lycophron apud Stephanum (cui Γλάνις μέγαμις κύμης) ως μίλεων: Γλάνις η ραβδος διξενη πίγγαν χθονα:
units.tr: It flows between Arpinum and Sora, and joins the Liri three Roman miles from Arpinum, at the Villa of S. Dominic, where M. Tullius was born. See him in book ii of De Legibus, and in book xiii of the letters to Atticus, where he also makes the Fibrenus into an island of Arpinum. Fiume de la Posta, says Sanfelicius. As for the Cosa: Strabo calls it the river Cosas, a town of Frutinum [Κῶσα Φορυσοσ, Frutinum, ὁ Κοσας μὲν πόλαμὸς]. Today Leander says it is called Pilsia. As for the Trerus, Strabo says it is a town of the Fabeganians [Τίρηρα Φαβεγανέιαν; ὁ Τρηρ πόλ]. Strabo also speaks of Cassinum: he says it lies where two rivers meet, and that the Amelegi lie above Casinum [Ὑπερβαμένη ἐν συμβολῇ ἕνοιν πολαμοῖν κατ᾽ ἀμφοῖν, Ἀμέλεγη κῶν ἱπρα Κασίνα]. I do not know what its present name is. It is certainly not the Melfa, as Ortelius thinks. For the river commonly called Melfa is called by Strabo the Melas, in the same place, where he says that Antiochus, when he was told that the Melas was a great river, said no [Ὀλίγοι Ἀντιόχω ὁ Μέλας, inquienti, μὴ, πολαμὸς μέγας]. Nor is it the same as the Melphe of Pliny, which lies near the Column of Rhegium, as Leander thinks. The Melpu descends from the Apennines across the plain as far as Fregellae, and from there it runs into the Liri not far off. The Omnis rises four Roman miles from S. Germanus, near S. Elias, at the Apennines. It begins very modestly, but becomes very large, having received the waters of many springs. After it has run about twelve Roman miles, it falls into the Liri not far from the Bridge of the Crow (Ponte Corvi). The Vulturnus follows the Liri; it is known to Virgil, Livy, Pliny (and who does not know it?). Strabo and other Greeks call it Οὐλτούρνο. Varro calls it Volturnus, [Ἀχαιῶν]. It is still Volturno today. Plutarch, in his life of Fabius Maximus, calls it Οὐατυεγίν, a reading which needs correcting. Various scholars translate it in various ways, using various manuscripts: Georgius Fabricius and Petrus Candidus, whom Leander also approves, give Notaronum; Niger gives Lotaronium; Cuspinianus, in his edition of Cassiodorus, gives Aliocronum. It is also called Καρυλίνο by Agathias in book ii of On the Gothic War, perhaps from the town situated on its bank. Vibius Sequester and Strabo, book v, should also be consulted. It is called by the same name on a stone urn, near the Vulturnus, where the once famous colony now called Castel al Mar di Boterno stands. The inscription reads thus: The Casilinus received the waters of the Dead River, weighed down, at the shore of the Tyrrhenian Sea, when the Ausonian sword destroyed the Frankish people, where it gave the custom to wretched Bultinus. Descending from the Apennines, it is very slender at first, but by the addition of waters and springs it acquires great breadth and depth. It flows through the Samnite mountains for thirty Roman miles, then twenty Roman miles to the Agro Venafrano, then twenty-five more to the Alifanum, and from there it flows into Campania. After greeting Capua, it discharges itself into the sea at the place where the town of Vulturnum once stood, as Strabo testifies in book iv, and as Varro did after him. The distance from the source of the Vulturnus to the beginning of the Liris is small. Varro says it rises in Samnium. Flowing three miles from Alifa, in ancient times it marked the boundary between Campania Felix and Samnium. Livy, book xxii, says it divides the Falernian land from the Campanian territory. Eminus est Vulturus Capua, says Pedianus on the Verrines, three miles. The name Celer given to it by Lucan, book ii, refers to its current; and the phrase Fluctu sonorum used by Silius Italicus, book viii, does too. Servius writes that it flows into the sea near Cumae. Dionysius reports a marvel about the Vulturnus and the Glanis: that, leaving aside their natural course, they changed direction and for some time flowed backwards from their mouths to their sources. We Belgians, who know the ebb and flow of the sea, do not wonder at such things. Pliny gives the Vulturnum Mare as the mouth of this river. It gathers many rivers and torrents: among the others, on the right the Cusanus Correctus, on the left the Freddus, the Pratellum, the Sabbatum, the Iscleru, and others. The Cusanus Correctus rises from Mount Mathelius near Pulianellum and plunges into the waters of the Vulturnus. The Freddus, from the opposite bank, joins the Vulturnus at the same place, having a town of the same name nearby. Another river follows the Freddus; it rises at the foot of the mountain commonly called the Piedmont, runs about three Roman miles through the Alifan territory, and finally hides itself in the Vulturnus near Alifa. The Pratellus rises at the roots of Mount Mathelius and takes its name from the nearby town of Pratellum. A castle of the Gauls is not far from its source. The Sabbatus, as Antoninus calls it, rises from the Apennines, in the region where its ridges are called the Montes Tremuli. Through low places, with winding bends, it gathers into a single channel nearly all the springs of the Beneventan territory, and at last discharges itself into the Vulturnus, bringing it a very great increase. Today it is called the Fiume de Benevento, because it flows past that city and through its fields. The Sabbatus has, so to speak, various inhabitants, among whom the chief place is held by the Calor, known to the ancients. It is so named also in the Itinerary Table; but there it mixes with the channel of the Vulturnus so carelessly that it seems to be one river. Appian of Alexandria corruptly calls it A λαρ. There is a stopping-place, Ad Calorem, in Antoninus, between Nuceria and Nerulum, and it is certain that this river is meant there. It still keeps the name Caore. Paul the Deacon says, It is called Pugna even today. Ortelius testifies in a manuscript that Pugna is not the name of a river but of a place near the river. Scipio Mazzella writes that it is commonly called Dentecane; some, he says, call it that, referring to Tabernula, not far from there. Pomponius Sabinus, on the seventh book of the Aeneid, says that it is carried headlong from the valley of Amsanctus, between the town of Aquaria and the fields of Pœtani, and is mixed with the Silarus. Livy, book xxiv and following, and Vibius Sequester place it near Beneventum. It flows into the Sabbatus about 300 paces above Beneventum, near the Valentine Bridge, which the Emperor Valens crossed over the Calor. Before it is received by the Sabbatus, it is increased by the Tripaltus, the Misciano, the Tamara, and others. The Tripaltus takes its name from the town of Tripalta. On its right bank there is a forest, full of brigands and notorious for their haunt, which is called Tripaltina after the neighbouring river. It rises, as also does the Misciarus, from Mount Crepacorio. The Tamarus is also known to Antoninus, where he names a stopping-place Super Tamari fluvium. Some manuscripts wrongly read Super Maris flav. Tamarus. The Tamarus has no less abundance of water than the Calor. Besides the Calor, there are others which mix with the Sabbatus. Near the town of Ponte there are four springs which, joined together, flow into the Sabbatus through a single mouth; they descend from the Apennines, and near these springs there are as many towns: Ad D. Laurentium, Ad D. Lupum, Pons Landulphi, and Casalonium. The Sabbatus on its left bank receives, among others, the Seritella, which rises from the Caudine mountains. Now, leaving aside the Vulturnus and its tributaries, lest I be too long, the Ifuclere, the Arnone, and others, I come to the Glanus. Lycophron, quoted by Stephanus (who says Γλάνις is a great river of Cumae), writes thus: Γλάνις η ραβδος διξενη πίγγαν χθονα.

units.la: Et Poetarum Latinorum Princeps, Virgilius: Talem dives arat Capua, & vicina Vesevo Ora lugo, & vacuis Glanis non æquum Acerris.
units.tr: And the Prince of the Latin poets, Virgil: Such a rich Capua ploughs, and the Ora near Vesuvius, and the Glanis, not unequal to the empty Acerrae.

units.la: E montibus inter Nolam & Capuam, regione fere media, prorumpit. Amnis hic ille est, ut notat Leander, qui Via inter Capuam & Anversam occurrit; ac sæpenumero nunc in Acerrano Agro, sicut olim in Campano Atellanoque solebat, præsertim hibernis mensibus, stagnat: qua de causa ligneis Pontibus connexa multis in locis itinera necessario sunt, qui Veterum Ædificiorum lapidibus ex Urbium propinquarum ruinis eo delatis plerumque sulciuntur & incumbunt. Meminit & Dionysius Halicarnassæus lib. vii, quum Glanem & Vulturnum, naturali quandoque Cursu omisso, contra ab ostiis ad Fontes refluxisse memoriæ prodit. Auctu suo Peltera meditari meduari nunarique Terris scribu cum Virgilio Vibius Sequester. Spatio ab Mari P.M. viii a ifiume effunditur, Lacus intar lati[?]udine duorum fermè milliuin, quibusdam in locis; alibi c[?] laram ideoque circum ostia, quibus in mare e[?]t, vulgo Lacus Patria voca[?]ur; Piscium abundantia, qui fere Neapolim deferri solent, ubertimus. De Lacu alibi. Miscet cum aliis Glaui Lauernus Amnis, cuius meminit praeter Strabonem, Livius lib. xx ii & xxxii. Hodie Lassia ab opido, quod vernacule Torre della Patria olim Lauernum. Appianus lib. i. Ἐμ. Lacus non fallacem cum eundem facit cum Lari. Occurrit hinc Sebetus, inter Vesevum Montem & Neapolim decurrens; vulgo Fiume della Maddalena vocatur. Vica iam per Neapolitanam Urbem delabitur, omnibus Civibus usum praestans; & popularicer Formello dicitur. Meminerunt Strabo, Silius Italicus, Silvarum, Vibius Sequester, Columella in suo Horto, ubi Sebethus scribitur. Quod adspiretur, docet ex Lapidibus Manutius in Orthographia. Mox Sarnus est. Sic Lucano, Silio, Statio, qui lib. i. Silv. Pen pemanum cognominat, Orosio, Vibio, aliisque appellatur; Σαρνὸς Straboni & Ptolemaeo: qui hodieque Sarno, Leandro teste, qui Stafato alibi interpretatur, ut & Erythraeus, ab Scaphus, quae ibi stationem habent, ad Viatores, qui Nuceriam cogitant, trajiciendos. Proximus Salerno est Furor: qui oritur ex Apennino supra Solefram. Sequitur inde Ibela supra S. Leandrum prodiens Apennino. Oppidum habet ad dextram ripam cognomine. XII hinc circiter m.ll. Sica est. Sic Virgilio, Lucano, Silio, Plinio, Melâ, Tabulae Itinerariae; Σιρὰς Straboni & Ptolemaeo; Sire Lucano item Vibio dicitur; qui hodie Sili, vel, ut alii pronunciant, Seie. Oritur ad Pertagonem in Apennino, parte citeriore, propemodum exa wersum Autido. Versus Meridiem decurrens in Tyrrhenum, Campaniam ab Lucania hodie dirimit. Campaniae plerisque adcenseatur: Lucania facit Pomponius Sabinus, addens in Mare extire circa Leucasiam Insulam. Strabo cum Campanorum & Picentinorum facit terminum. Salernum praeterire notat Sulpicius Veralat ex male intellecto Lucani loco, canentis lib. viii: Vestim in pulvis Aquis, radere fque Salernis Culta Siler.
units.tr: It bursts forth from the mountains between Nola and Capua, roughly midway between them. This is the river which, as Leander notes, crosses the road between Capua and Aversa; and very often it stagnates, now in the Acerran territory and formerly in the Campanian and Atellan territories, especially in the winter months. For this reason the roads in many places must of necessity be connected by wooden bridges, which are mostly propped up and supported by stones of old buildings carried there from the ruins of nearby cities. Dionysius of Halicarnassus also mentions it, book vii, when he records in memory that the Glanis and the Vulturnus, sometimes leaving their natural course, flowed back from their mouths to their sources. Vibius Sequester, with Virgil, writes that it is increased by its own waters. It pours out into the sea eight Roman miles from its source, forming a lake, in some places about two miles wide, and elsewhere narrower; around its mouths, where it enters the sea, it is commonly called the Lacus Patria. It is very abundant in fish, which are usually carried to Naples. I will speak of the lake elsewhere. The Lauernus river joins the Glanis with others; Strabo mentions it, and Livy, books xxii and xxxii. Today it is called the Lassia, after the town which in the vernacular is called the Torre della Patria, formerly Lavernum. Appian, book i of the Civil Wars, makes it the same as the Lari, in the lake which is not deceptive. From here the Sebetus comes into view, running between Mount Vesuvius and Naples; it is commonly called the Fiume della Maddalena. Now it flows through the city of Naples, providing use to all its citizens, and among the people it is called the Formello. Strabo, Silius Italicus, Statius in the Silvae, Vibius Sequester, and Columella in his Garden mention it, where it is written Sebethus. Manutius in his Orthography shows from inscriptions that it is aspirated. Next is the Sarnus. It is so named by Lucan, Silius, and Statius, who in book i of the Silvae gives it the surname Pen pemanum; it is called by Orosius, Vibius, and others; Strabo and Ptolemy call it Σαρνὸς. It is still called Sarno today, according to Leander, who elsewhere explains it as Stafato, as does Erythraeus; from the boats which have their station there, for ferrying travellers who intend to go to Nuceria. Next to Salerno is the Furor, which rises from the Apennines above Solofra. Then comes the Ibela, which issues from the Apennines above S. Leandro. It has a town on its right bank of the same name. About twelve miles from here is the Sica. It is so called by Virgil, Lucan, Silius, Pliny, Mela, and the Itinerary Tables; Strabo and Ptolemy call it Σιρὰς; Lucan and likewise Vibius call it Sire; today it is called Sili, or, as others pronounce it, Seie. It rises at Pertagon in the Apennines, on the nearer side, almost opposite Autidus. Running south into the Tyrrhenian Sea, it now divides Campania from Lucania. Most authors count it as part of Campania; Pomponius Sabinus makes it Lucania, adding that it flows into the sea near the island of Leucasia. Strabo makes it the boundary between the Campanians and the Picentines. Sulpicius Verolanus notes that the river passes Salerno, from a misunderstood passage of Lucan, who sings in book viii: Vestim in pulvis Aquis, radere fque Salernis Culta Siler.

units.la: Non enim Vlarum vult Moenia radere Salerni, quum ab eo absit xxiv P.M. sed Salernitanorum agros, qui huc usque extendebantur. Naturam eius Strabo, Plinius, Silius, alique esse tradunt, ut in eum numeris Folia Virg. hacque lapidescunt, nec tamen in mutato colore vel forma; quamquam aliás, ut adjecit Plinius eius Aquae salubris sit potus. Refert secum Tottam Ipsernianam & Nigrum, cui initium ex Ipecu subterraneo iuxta Cauponam quamdam, quae vulgo Taverna della Fo'a ab opido Fofa, ibi proximo.
units.tr: For he does not mean that the walls of Vlarum, which is twenty-four Roman miles from there, are razed by the Silarus, but the fields of the Salernitans, which extended as far as this point. Strabo, Pliny, Silius and others report that its nature is such that leaves thrown into it turn to stone, though without any change of colour or shape; yet otherwise, as Pliny adds, its water is wholesome to drink. It carries with it the Tottam, the Ipsernia and the Nigrum, whose source is an underground spring near a certain inn, which is commonly called Taverna della Fo'a, after the nearby town of Fofa.

units.la: Hactenus de Campaniae Fluviis, quos Lucania habebat, iamnunc scrutemur. Post Silari ostia succedunt Pistae unde Caput Positanum, quod olim Pyxuntum) Mese (qui Plinio Meiphes, Melpes legunt membranae) Cocci & Sapia. Putatur Sapri, qui Aάσ & Straboni; Lus Plinio: quod haud procul vero esse video, si verba eorum bene expendantur. Lucanos dirimit à Brutiis; Lainum ab suis Suburbiis, opidum in Lucanis, Suburbia in Calabris relinquens. Oritur prope Viminellum, Lucaniae oppidum, perque Montes asperos Meridiem versus Batilicatam vel Lucaniam, ut dixi, ab Calabria dividens, in Mare Tyrrhenum profluit. Aquas habet perpetuo claras, adeo ut nullo umquam casu turbentur.
units.tr: So far concerning the rivers of Campania, which Lucania had. Now let us examine the others. After the mouth of the Silarus come the Pistae, whence the Cape of Positano, which was formerly Pyxuntum; the Mese (which Pliny's manuscripts read as Meiphes or Melpes), the Cocci and the Sapia. The Sapri is thought to be the river which Strabo also calls by that name, and which Pliny calls the Lus; I see that this is not far from the truth, if their words are weighed carefully. It separates the Lucanians from the Bruttians, leaving the Lainum, a town in Lucania, with its suburbs, to the Lucanians, and the suburbs in Calabria. It rises near Viminellum, a town of Lucania, and, flowing through rough mountains towards the south, separates Basilicata, or Lucania, as I said, from Calabria, and flows into the Tyrrhenian Sea. Its waters are always clear, so that they are never disturbed by any accident.

units.la: Sequuntur in Bruttiis eo enim delati sumus) tres Amnes, quorum Nomina non occurrunt: Primus ad Scalcam; Secundus ad Cirellam; Tertius ad S. Bonifacii, Mare petunt Tyrrhenum. Subeunt inde alij. Freddus cum eiusdem Nominis opido. Acheron ex Montis Radicibus, in quo Pandosia, nascens, per Vallem fluit profundam, inter altissimos Montes, interque Martoranum & Altulam: & tandem in Sinum Sanctcuphemianum evolvitur. Acherontem quidam, inter quos Leander, hodie Sarnum censent; Niger Raffentum; Barrius Capuanum; alij Cersinum. Ab eo Fluvio Adcolae dicti Plinio Acherontini. Hic Fluvius est Acheron, ad cuius ripam hac ibidem Pandosia, in cuius Agro fatali casu funestam accepit Cladem Alexander, Epiro arum Rex: Apollinis oraculo praemonitus, ut Acherusiam Aquam utque Pandosiam vt aret ratus, non alium esse Acherontem, non aliam, quam in Epiro, Pandosiam. Vide Livium lib. viii, Trogum lib. xii, Strabonem, & alios. Ab Sanctcuphemia sexto Lapide Ostium est Amati, alti latiqué Fluminis: inde octavo, peringentus item AngituAngitula, cuius mentio apud Antoninum. Vulgo Acitola. Circumvectis Australius Ternaei vel Hipponiatis Sinus Cornu, occurrit Mesuna. Sic vulgo vocatur Fluvius, qui Doctis Meduna, excipiens sinistram ripam praeter alios, paullum infra Kolarnum, Metauremum Amnem. Decimo hinc milliari Seminaria vitiur, latum profundumque flumen. Olim, ut censent Bonacciolus & Leander, Metaurus, Metaurus Strabonis, cuius ostium describit in Bruttiis Plinius, exadverso Eoliarum Insularum. Idem tamen Leander, sut quasi oblitus, Metaurum esse vult in suo Insularum libello, qui hodie Metremo. Sed Metremus Metaurus esse nequit. Ostio namque ille ad Mare, quod Huius, ut dixi, Plinius delineat, care, & ab Mesana ad Mare, annino nomine deterit. Neticio an Pacta- eus etiam fuerit dictus, quem Probus Grammaticus in Vita Virgilii ex 11. Caronis Originum scribit, Rheginorum & Taurinorum Fines disperuere, in Mare se provolvit aliquot auctus Annibus. Post nonnullos memoriae momenta Fluvios, inter quos neticio an fuerint (misi tabuloti sint centum) ugyon, Lacapedo, Asgade, Sanctus, Pulsae, Ale- leya & Agrade (Flumina cum minima loca Rhegium Iulium, quibus Orestes purgatus fuit ab Matris nece, unde memorat Probus Grammaticus in Vita Poetica Virgilii, ti Codici fides) aperiunt, se alii Primo, qui vernacule Aesse. Aaa Thucydidi lib. iii, Strabon, Dionysio, & Antigono in Mirabilibus, Fluvium hunc flatuen i Finitorem in cr Locrenses & Rheginos. Haetem nuncupare videtur M. Tullius ad Trebatium. Anexa nomina Theocritus. Inde qui Aoxa & Polemaro Meminit & Plinius, in cuius vetustioribus libris Locanus scribitur. Mox, qui vulgo dicitur Sagrianus; Sagra Plinio, Sagras Strabonis: a quo oppidum Sagrianum. Sagra tamen Gabrieli Barrio, Laurentio Anamenti & Mazzellae haru est, Surchi antus Nigro Hinc qui Cratus Kaaxo Pausanias & Aelianno, Caesinus Plinio; Kaxis Thucydidi lib.iii. Addit, Iequinus quam Antigonus paullo ante e Pausanias in Eliacis Fluvium hunc esse, qui Locrensium Agrum ab Rheginis dividit. Kaaxa pellas Aelianus lib. viii. Var. Histor. Non procul inde Crotalus est, Plinio notus. Hinc apud eundem Semiras, Aoba & Largunes, qui hodie Tasina, quaque e Montibus defendens in Sinum Scylaceum evolvitur. Ifaru mox in oculos incurrit, qui Aoxa Lycophroni, Theocrito, Strabone & Dionysio: Aclar Ovidio xv Metamorph. Theocriti Scholiastes dicit Fluvium hunc per mediam Urbem Crotoniensem fluere. Putat Leander Tlai appellari ab Thucydide lib. vii. Croton iv. M. P. abest Naethus, antiquum etiam, ut multa alia hoc tractu Flumina, nomen praeferens. Naxos Strabo, qui Nomen a urae rationem indicat. Nethus Plinio, qui in secundo Europae Sinu collocat; Naxos Siciliae Fluvius est apud Theocriti Scholiasten, ob causam saepe in literam: Sigmu ab Ovidio nominari nota Gabriel Barrius, qui apud Lycophronem etiam memoriam eius extare memorat: ed Naxos apud eum legitur. Offerunt hinc se Lilius legenti nonnulli minorum gentium, inter quos ab Caniathi, perhonesta Civitate, xiii lapide Triantes, latusal usque Fluvius in Sinum erumpens cum reliquis Tarentinum. Triantes Thucydidis, de quo ante putavisse Gabriel Barrius.
units.tr: Next, in the land of the Bruttians (for to there we have been brought), come three streams whose names do not occur: the first at Scalca, the second at Cirella, the third at S. Bonifacio, all making for the Tyrrhenian Sea. Then others enter. The Freddus, with the town of the same name. The Acheron, rising from the foot of the mountains, on which stands Pandosia, flows through a deep valley between very high mountains, and between Martorano and Altula, and at last rolls into the Gulf of Sant'Eufemia. Some, among them Leander, think that the Acheron is today the Sarnus; Niger, the Raffentus; Barrius, the Capuanus; others, the Cersinus. From this river its inhabitants are called by Pliny the Acherontini. This river is the Acheron, on whose bank Pandosia stands, and in whose territory Alexander, King of Epirus, suffered a deadly defeat by a fatal chance. Warned by an oracle of Apollo to beware of the Acherusian water and of Pandosia, he thought that there was no other Acheron and no other Pandosia than the ones in Epirus. See Livy, book 8, Trogus, book 12, Strabo and others. Six miles from Sant'Eufemia is the mouth of the Amatus, a deep and broad river; eight miles from there, the Angitula, likewise a large river, whose mention is found in Antoninus. Commonly Acitola. Having rounded the southern horn of the Gulf of Terina or Hipponium, one comes to the Mesuna. This is the name commonly given to the river which scholars call the Meduna; it receives on its left bank, among others, shortly below Colarno, the Metaurus Amnis. Ten miles from here lies the Seminara, a wide and deep river. Formerly, as Bonaciolus and Leander think, it was the Metaurus of Strabo, whose mouth Pliny places in the land of the Bruttians, opposite the Aeolian Islands. Yet the same Leander, as if forgetting himself, holds in his book on the islands that the Metaurus is what is now the Metramo. But the Metramus cannot be the Metaurus; for the one flows into the sea at the place which, as I said, Pliny describes, and the other, from the Mesana to the sea, keeps a single name. I do not know whether the Pacta-eus was also so called, which Probus the grammarian, in the Life of Virgil, writes from the second book of the Origins of Cato, that it separated the territories of the Rhegians and the Taurians, and rolled into the sea, enlarged by several tributaries. After some moments of remembrance, rivers among which I do not know whether they were (unless the tablets are a hundred) the Ugyon, Lacapedo, Asgade, Sanctus, Pulsae, Alecleya and Agrade (rivers near the small place Rhegium Julium, where Orestes was purified of his mother's murder, whence Probus the grammarian mentions it in the Poetic Life of Virgil, if the manuscript can be trusted) open out. Then another, the first, which is vernacularly called the Aesse. Thucydides, book 3, Strabo, Dionysius and Antigonus in the Marvels, make this river the boundary between the Locrians and the Rhegians. M. Tullius in his letter to Trebatius seems to call it the Haetes. Theocritus names it the Anexa. Then the one which Pliny also mentions as the Aoxa and Polemarchus, in whose older books it is written Locanus. Next, the one commonly called the Sagrianus; the Sagra in Pliny, the Sagras in Strabo, from which the town Sagrianum takes its name. Yet the Sagra is, for Gabriel Barrius, Lorenzo Anamenti and Mazzella, the Surchi, while for Nigro it is something else. Then the one which Pausanias and Aelian call the Kratis, the Caesinus in Pliny, the Kaxis in Thucydides, book 3. Antigonus, a little before, and Pausanias in the Eliacs add that this is the river which divides the territory of the Locrians from the Rhegians. Aelian in book 8 of the Varia Historia calls it the Kaaxa. Not far from there is the Crotalus, known from Pliny. Here, in the same author, come the Semiras, the Aoba and the Largunes, which today is the Tasina, and which, flowing down from the mountains, rolls into the Gulf of Squillace. Next comes the Ifaru, which is called Aoxa by Lycophron, Theocritus, Strabo and Dionysius, and Aclar by Ovid in book 15 of the Metamorphoses. The scholiast on Theocritus says that this river flows through the middle of the city of Croton. Leander thinks it is called Tlai by Thucydides, book 7. About four miles from Croton lies the Naethus, which, like many other rivers in this region, keeps an ancient name. Strabo has the Naxos, which indicates the reason for the name. Pliny has the Nethus, which he places in the second bay of Europe; the Naxos is a river of Sicily, according to the scholiast on Theocritus, for a reason often mentioned in the letter. Gabriel Barrius notes that Ovid calls it Sigmus, and he records that its memory is also found in Lycophron; but in him it is read as Naxos. Here several smaller streams present themselves to the reader, among them, thirteen miles from the very distinguished city of Caiazzo, the Triantes, a river which, broad and reaching far, bursts into the Gulf of Taranto along with the others. The Triantes is in Thucydides, and Gabriel Barrius thought earlier about it.

units.la: Magna iam a Invigeimus Graeci. Quindecim ab Triuntis ostio P. M. Rufillus occurrit: ab Rutillo quinque, qui Gratis vulgo; Crathis Ovidio in Fastis & Metamorphosi, Vibioque Sequestro: Crateus Plinio; Kogaκ Theocrito, Herodoto, Strabone, Aeliano. Siciliae Fluvium (quare, notum) dicit Eustathius in Dionysium; addens eum apud Sybarim sive Thurium fluere. Aelianus de Varia Historia nomen a Pastore quodam, sic dicto, accepisse scribit: Herodotus lib. i. nominatum tradit ad memoriam alius in Peloponneso Fluminis ita vocati. Fontem habet exiguum seniis ab Consentia millibus, Orientali latere: perque Montes altissimos ad Urbem accedit, quam paullum ab ortu contingit: hinc ad Septemtrionem se flectens Busentum excipit: quo aliquo tenus amplitudinis tactus maximae, aspectuque terribilis, infra Bisignanum in Sinum Tarentinum, qui hodie Rosanus, se exonerat. Quam habeant ipsius Aquae Vim, alibi dicitur. Magnam Graeciam a Bruttiis dividit. Augetur cum aliis, tum Busento, Septimo, Surdo, Finito Cuciari: Busenti, qui in Montibus Contentinis meridionali plaga nascitur, meminerunt Paullus Diaconus lib. xiii. Hist. Blondus lib. i. Sabellicus lib. ix. Ennead. vii, in Historia Funeris Alarici, Visigothorum Regis. Hic namque in Alveo Busenti positus scribitur. Nominant quidam in eius rei commemorationem Balentium; ignorantes Balentium alium esse a Busento. Hic enim Crathus mifectur; ille in Sinum Tarentinum se exonerat. Septimus & Surdus ex ipsidem Montibus oriuntur ad Opidum, quod vulgo Monte-Alto. Lutus ad S. Agathan habet initium & haud procul inde Caesar. Ferrius hic & Morannm Amnem sapidissimum praetereo. Antiquam Urbem Sybaris, quae quidem toties, Amnis sequelam cognominis, qui nunc Crati. Oritur ad lacus Scalae Morum, interque rupes altissimorum Montium in planitiem subjectam fertur, per quam accessione tandem fontium ac rivorum plurimum auctus Sinum Tarentinum influit. Ζυβαρις Strabono; Sybaris Ovidio & Plinio. Quae Viscus, alibi nomen. Pott Cuchatum Amnis est, qui Adcolis Sino, vel, ut alii ceterunt, Sinna, Σινος Plutarcho & Strabono, qui Navigabilem dicit. Sins Plinio & Frontino. Ex Montium delapsus jugis in Sinum Tarentinum evolvitur. Olim illi Urbs adpotica cognominis, ab Trojanis, ut volunt, condita. Hinc Acri sequitur, antiquum tenens nomen. A Κιριος enim Strabono; Acri est Plinio. In Litore os illi profundissimum latissimumque: quamobrem nec ibi transiri potest; sed milliaribus duobus a Mari, ubi Pons Ligneus viam tangit. Acri succedit Salindia; Acalandrus Strabono & Plinio: qui nonnumquam ex Imbribus adeo abundat Aquis, ab declivi utrimque lugorum fatigio accedentibus, ut super Alveum excrescens totam Vallem Inundatione complet, in faciem brachii Maris. Mox in ora Bafenti Fluminis sunt oltia Vulgo Vafeno. Bafentum vocat Paullus Diaconus. Cafuentum est Plinio. Quinque aut circiter Bafento milliaribus Bradanus occurrit; plurimum etiam hibernis mensibus augere solitus. Designat cum Appianus lib. v. Bell Civil. ubi Caesaris & Antonii congressum ad Metapontum Tarentumque, juxta Flumen, quod inter eas Urbes medium labitur, commemorat. Meminit Antoninus Itinere Mediolano ad Columnam. Juxta Tarentum Stephano est Ἀγρας Fluvius. Paufanias etiam in Phocicis dicit Fluvium eodem nomine, quo Urbs, vocari. Taras hodieque ab Incolis dicitur, ut Galatens tellatur. Ταρας corrupte legunt Diodori lib. xii. Codices.
units.tr: Now we come to the great Greek rivers. Fifteen Roman miles from the mouth of the Triantes, the Rufillus appears; five miles from the Rutillus, the one commonly called the Gratis; the Crathis in Ovid's Fasti and Metamorphoses, and in Vibius Sequester; the Krateus in Pliny; the Kratis [Κρᾶθις] in Theocritus, Herodotus, Strabo and Aelian. Eustathius, on Dionysius, says it is a river of Sicily (which is known), adding that it flows near Sybaris or Thurii. Aelian in his Varia Historia writes that it took its name from a certain shepherd of that name; Herodotus, book 1, reports that it was named after another river of the same name in the Peloponnese. It has a small spring about thirty miles from Cosenza, on the eastern side; through very high mountains it approaches the city, which it touches a little on the east; then, bending northward, it receives the Busento; having reached a considerable size, and a terrifying appearance, below Bisignano it discharges itself into the Gulf of Taranto, which today is called the Rosano. What power its waters have is stated elsewhere. It divides Magna Graecia from the land of the Bruttians. It is increased by other streams, among them the Busento, Septimus, Surdus and Finito Cuciari. The Busento, which rises in the mountains of Cosenza on the southern side, is mentioned by Paulus Diaconus, book 13 of his History; by Blondus, book 1; by Sabellicus, book 9 of the Enneads, in the History of the Funeral of Alaric, king of the Visigoths. For it is written that he was laid in the bed of the Busento. Some, to commemorate this event, name the Balentium, not knowing that the Balentium is another river from the Busento. For this one flows into the Crathis; that one discharges itself into the Gulf of Taranto. The Septimus and the Surdus rise from the same mountains, near the town commonly called Montalto. The Lutus has its source near S. Agata, and not far from there is Caesar. I pass over here the Ferrius and the Morannus, a very pleasant river. The ancient city of Sybaris, which so often (after the river of the same name, which is now called Crati) ... It rises at the lakes of Scala Morum, and flows between the cliffs of very high mountains into the plain below, through which, with the addition of many springs and streams, it is greatly enlarged and at last flows into the Gulf of Taranto. Zybaris [Ζύβαρις] in Strabo; Sybaris in Ovid and Pliny. What it is in Viscus is elsewhere named. The Cuchatus is a river which the inhabitants call Sino, or, as others say, Sinna; Sinos [Σῖνος] in Plutarch and Strabo, who calls it navigable; Sins in Pliny and Frontinus. Having slipped down from the ridges of the mountains, it rolls into the Gulf of Taranto. Formerly there was a seaport city of the same name, founded, as they say, by the Trojans. Next comes the Acri, keeping an ancient name: for Strabo has Kirios [Κίριος], and Pliny has Acri. On the shore it has a very deep and very wide mouth; therefore it cannot be crossed there, but two miles from the sea, where a wooden bridge touches the road. After the Acri comes the Salindia; Strabo and Pliny have Acalandrus, which sometimes, from the rains, is so abundantly filled with water, coming down from the slopes of the ridges on either side, that, rising above its bed, it fills the whole valley with a flood, like an arm of the sea. Soon, on the shore, there are the mouths of the river Bafentum, commonly called the Vafeno. Paulus Diaconus calls it the Bafentum; Pliny has the Cafuentum. About five miles from the Bafento the Bradanus appears, which is also accustomed to increase greatly in the winter months. Appian, in book 5 of the Civil Wars, marks it, where he records the meeting of Caesar and Antony near Metapontum and Taranto, beside the river which flows between those cities. Antoninus mentions it in the Itinerary from Milan to the Column. Near Taranto, in Stephanus, there is the river Agras [Ἀγρᾶς]. Pausanias also says, in the Phocica, that a river is called by the same name as the city. Taras is still called so today by the inhabitants, as Galatea is named. The manuscripts of Diodorus, book 12, read Tarās corruptly [Ταρας].

units.la: Salentinorum oras legentibus tertio ab Urbe Tarento lapide Galesus is offert. Quinto, dixit Livius lib. xxv, Hannibalem, capto Tarento, ad Galesum Flumen prosectum cum ceteris copiis ibi castra posuisse, scribens. Facile mutant Cursus suos Amnes: alia etiam fuit olim, quam hodie, Milliarum ratio: fecit denique Temporis iniuria, incuriaque Librariorum, ut depravatos habeamus Scriptorum Veterum Codices. Meminit Galesi Virgilius lib. iv. Georgic.
units.tr: Coasting along the shores of the Salentini, the first river you meet three miles from the city of Tarentum is the Galesus. Livy, in book 25, says that Hannibal, after taking Tarentum, went forth to the river Galesus with the rest of his forces and pitched camp there. Rivers easily change their courses, and the reckoning of miles was also different in the past. Finally, the injury of time and the carelessness of copyists have left us with corrupted manuscripts of the ancient writers. Virgil mentions the Galesus in Georgics book 4.

units.la: Quae piger humectat flaventia culta Galesus. Ubi Servius notat, Galesum Amnem esse Calabriae, non procul Tarento. Mentio eiusdem & apud Horatium, Martialem, Vibium. Eurotam nonnulli nominant, ut tradit Polybius lib. viii. Rugradum novo vocabulo appellat Ligorius mula Neapolitana. Praeter Galesum, qui inter Magnam Graeciam & Salentinos discrimen facit, etiam duos alios habent Salentini Amnes, unum quidem ad Litus Australius, qui ix Tarento lapide, ad Pulizanum, Sinum Tarentinum ingreditur: alterum, qui in ora Borealiore Hadriatico miscetur Mari, ad S. Marcum, decimo ab Urbe Brundisina milliari.
units.tr: "Which the sluggish Galesus moistens, the yellow fields." Servius notes that the Galesus is a river of Calabria, not far from Tarentum. It is also mentioned by Horace, Martial and Vibius. Some call it the Eurotas, as Polybius reports in book 8. Ligorio of Naples gives it a new name, calling it the Rugradum. Besides the Galesus, which marks the boundary between Magna Graecia and the Salentini, the Salentini have two other rivers. One, on the southern coast, enters the Gulf of Tarentum at Pulizano, nine miles from Tarentum. The other, on the more northerly shore, mingles with the Adriatic Sea at S. Marco, the tenth milestone from the city of Brundisium.

units.la: Iam Apulia Peucetia ab Fluviis valde est inops, unum tamen notatum video Cavam, xxv Brundisio lapide; xiv Egnatia. Exonerat se in Pelagus ad Corvinum. Pallus hic nominatur Plinio. Paelium habet inemendate Itineraria Tabula, locansque etiam vitiosiore positu ultra Brundisium, quum eis esset. Quod fit in eadem Tabula inter Pactium & Aufidum Aveldum Flumen, nondum capio.
units.tr: Apulia Peucetia is very poor in rivers, yet I see one noted: the Cavas, 25 miles from Brundisium and 14 from Egnatia. It discharges itself into the sea at Corvinum. Pliny calls it the Pallus. The Itinerary table wrongly has the Paelium, placing it even further out, beyond Brundisium, though it was on the near side. What the same table puts between Pactium and the river Aveldus, I still cannot make out.

units.la: Peucetiam ab Daunia separat Aufidus. Sic Virgilio lib. xi. Aeneid. Plinio, Melae lib. ii, Antonino, Itinerariae Tabulae: Αυφιδος Polybio, Straboni, Ptolemaeo dicitur; qui hodie L'ofanto. In Hirpinorum Montibus oriri notat Ptolemaeus. Solus, ut referunt Polybius lib. iii. & Plutarchus in Vita Hannibalis, Apenninum, in quo nascitur, secat. Apulia utraque divisa Hadriatico Mari inlabitur. Naturam eius, rapidumque currentis varieque se sinuantis Cursum describit Horat. lib. i. Sat. i.
units.tr: The Aufidus separates Peucetia from Daunia. So Virgil in Aeneid book 11, Pliny, Mela in book 2, Antoninus and the Itinerary table. The Greeks call it Αὐφιδος (Aufidos) in Polybius, Strabo and Ptolemy; today it is the Ofanto. Ptolemy notes that it rises in the mountains of the Hirpini. Alone, as Polybius in book 3 and Plutarch in the Life of Hannibal report, it cuts through the Apennines, where it rises. Both Apulias are divided by it, and it flows into the Adriatic Sea. Horace, in Satire 1 of book 1, describes its nature and its rapid course, winding this way and that:

units.la: Quum ripa simul avulsos ferat Aufidus acer.
units.tr: "When the fierce Aufidus tears the bank away along with it."

units.la: Et lib. iii. Carm. Od. xxx; Dicar, qua violens obstrepit Aufidus; Et qua pauper aqua Daunus agrestium Regnavit populorum.
units.tr: And in Odes 30 of book 3: "I shall be spoken of where the violent Aufidus roars, and where Daunus, poor in water, ruled over a rustic people."

units.la: Lib. iv. Ode ix: Longe sonantem natus ad Aufidum.
units.tr: Book 4, Ode 9: "Born to the Aufidus that roars from afar."

units.la: Item eiusdem Libri Oda xiiiii Sic Tauri formis volvitur Aufidus; Qui regna Daunii perfluit Apuli, Quum saevit: horrendamque cultis Diluvium meditatur Agris.
units.tr: Also in the same book, Ode 14: "Thus the Aufidus rolls, in the likeness of a bull, which floods the kingdom of Daunian Apulia when it rages, and threatens a dreadful deluge to the cultivated fields."

units.la: Sic Silius Italicus lib. ix Belli Punici: At parte in dextra sinuat qua flexibus undam Aufidus, et curvo circumdat gurgite ripas.
units.tr: So Silius Italicus in book 9 of the Punica: "But on the right side, where the Aufidus bends its waves in curves, and surrounds the banks with a winding current."

units.la: Deo eo sic scribit eleganter Oculatus Testis Leander Albertus sub finem Apuliae Peucetiae: Oritur Apennino in Hirpinis modico fonte, non procul opido quodam Musio: unde, non seeus ac exiguus rivus, sic labitur, ut astivis mensibus spatio P. M. xxx (cum enim decursum habet) vix eius agnoscatur fluxus: hieme tamen Flumimum & Torrentium aliorum accessione, itemque ex Pluviis adeo plerumque crescit, ut, Aiveo derelicto, saepe per latissimos Apuliae Campos evagetur, et instar astu vastique Pelagi ab antiquo Cannusio, quod ad ipsum Amnem erat in planitie, longo tractu Regionem inundet. Apuliam Peucetiam ab Daunia separati primum per Agrum Lacedaemonium, deinde Melphitanum et Lacellinum; indeque sinuosis flexibus per Campestria Loca prope Minervinum, tum ab Cannusio per Barulanum Agrum in Mare tribus infra ipsum Barulum nitibus influens, ut Pons Lapideus, mille passibus abora. Haec ille. Pons, quem nominat, alius censendus abeo, cuius meminit Antoninus Itinere, quod Benevento ducit Hydruntum. Quum enim, quem habet Leander, haud procul hodie sit mari, qui apud Antoninum, prope Venusiam fuit, ubi in magnum gyrum evolvere se versus Caurum incipit Aufidus, xxxv aut circiter ab Hadriatico Sinu Milliaribus. Male editur in nonnullis Antonini Exemplaribus Pentaufidas; Aufidus Canus vocatur in Fastidico Cn. Marcii Carmine apud Livium lib. xxv. Octodecim ab Aufido miliaribus Candiarii visitur, quem cum Lacu Anduriano Strabonem, suppressis nominibus, indicare censeo: quum scribit inter Salapiam & Sipunum Fluvium esse Navigationi satis oportunum & Lacus ingens ostiumque Cervaria mox est: qui Cerbulus Plinio. Cerbarium etiam Procopio lib. iii Goth. locus est in Apulia.
units.tr: Leander Alberti, an eyewitness, writes elegantly on this same river at the end of Apulia Peucetia: "It rises in the Apennines, among the Hirpini, from a modest spring, not far from a certain town called Musio. From there it flows, no differently from a small brook, so that in the summer months, over a course of about thirty Roman miles, its flow can hardly be recognised. In winter, however, with the addition of other rivers and torrents, and generally with the rains, it swells so much that, leaving its bed, it often spreads over the broadest plains of Apulia, and, like a tide and a vast sea, floods the region over a long stretch from the old Cannusium, which stood on the plain next to the river itself. It flows through Apulia Peucetia, separating it from Daunia, first through the territory of Lacedaemon, then through Melfi and Lacedonia; then in winding bends through the open country near Minervino, and then from Canosa through the territory of Barletta, flowing into the sea three bow-shots below Barletta itself, as the Stone Bridge does, a thousand paces from the shore." So far Alberti. The bridge he names must be taken to be another one, that which Antoninus mentions in his Itinerary, the road that leads from Benevento to Otranto. For the place Leander describes is now hardly far from the sea, whereas the one in Antoninus was near Venusia, where the Aufidus begins to turn in a great circle towards the west, about thirty-five miles or so from the Adriatic gulf. In some editions of Antoninus, Pentaufidas is wrongly printed. In the Fastidicus of Gnaeus Marcius, quoted by Livy in book 25, the Aufidus is called the White (Canus). Eighteen miles from the Aufidus is seen the Candiarius, which, I think, Strabo indicates along with the Lake Anduria, though the names are suppressed: when he writes that between Salapia and the river Sipontum there is a lake, very large and suitable for navigation, and soon the outlet of the Cervaria; this is the Cerbulus of Pliny. There is also a place in Apulia called Cerbarium, mentioned by Procopius in book 3 of the Gothic War.

units.la: Samnitium littora lustrantibus offert se primo loco Plisternum, quo Samnium ab Apulia dividitur: Fortore vulgo; Ciniprose Ptolemaeo; Tifernus Plinio & Melae. Eius in Tiferno Monte, qui nunc Bifanus, Fons est, haud procul a Boviano. Exonerat se in Mare Hadriaticum iuxta Lesinensem Lacum. Succedunt inde Flumina Trinius, quod Portus sum notat Plinius; Aquella, Sentus, Sangrus. Qui Sangrus vel Sanguinem Latine scribentibus hodie, vernacule autem Sangro vel Sanguino; Σαγρος est Ptolemaeo; Σαγρος Straboni, Saron Vibio Sequestro. Ex Apennino oriens, descendusque, ut Strabo demonstrat, inter Aternum & Ortonem fluens, Frentanos Caracenosque a Peligni dividit, Hadriaticum tandem infusus. Varios convehit secum ad Mare Amnes: inter quos praecipue Rasinus, in Campis Furcae Palenae caput tollens, & Aventinus, qui ex Superequanis Pelig',norum (sic enim olim vocati) Furcae Palenae finitimis oritur; recepto tamen ante Vitridi, cuius in Maiella Monte Fons inter Monasterium D. Martini Castellumque Faranum. Mox bis mille passibus ab Ortona labitur Flumen Aternus. Hoc loco in Itineraria Tabula Fluvius Clitoris scribitur, inter Anxanum & Ortonam. Sequitur inde exiguus Amnis Feltrinus. Ostia dein Fori; & nono inde lapide Sentis; totidem hinc, qui vulgo Pescara. Aternum Varroni lib. iv de L.L. & Plinio: Ἀτερνος Straboni & Ptolemaeo. Nascitur ex plerorum Italiae Fluminum Parente Apennino, supra Aquilam, haud procul Monte Regali, qui subter eius est Fontem. Confluunt in Aternum vel Piscariam multi Amnes. Ripa quidem Australiore cum primis duo, ortum habentes in Agro Sulmonensi, ad opida Pectoranum & Vallem Obscuram; unde uterque peculiari alveo ferme Sulmonem usque procedens, alter alteri inmersus unico Flumine extra Urbem per extentam planiciem, milliaque passuum vi latam, cursu fere millium xii absoluto, Fontibusque & Aquulis quibusdam prope Populum, ubi ligneo transitur Ponte, haud mediocriter adaucti, tandem in Aternum se exonerant: quemadmodum & xvii aut circiter hinc miliaribus ad eandem ripam uno alveo Aternum iacunt Rasentus & Orta, ex Maiella Monte provoluti. VIII inde Lapide Liberata in Aternum se condit, binas item ex Maiella procurrentes Aquulas deferens: Viperatam quoq; appellari hunc Fluvium monet Alexander Andreas. Ad Boreaiiorem vero ripam augetur Aternus duobus Amnibus, quorum unus Caput Aquae, Capo di Acqua; alter Nursia prope Cœnobium Casae Novae, Cistellini ordinis, capiens initium.
units.tr: Coasting along the shores of the Samnites, the first river that presents itself is the Plisternus, by which Samnium is divided from Apulia. It is commonly called the Fortore; Ciniprus in Ptolemy; Tifernus in Pliny and Mela. In Mount Tifernus, which is now called Bifanus, there is a spring, not far from Bojano. It discharges into the Adriatic Sea near the Lake of Lesina. Next come the rivers Trinius, which Pliny marks as the Portus, Aquella, Sentus and Sangrus. Those who write in Latin today call this Sangrus or Sanguis, and in the vernacular Sangro or Sanguino. It is Σαγρος (Sagros) in Ptolemy, Σαγρος in Strabo, and Saron in Vibius Sequester. It rises in the Apennines and descends, as Strabo shows, flowing between the Aternus and the Ortona; it divides the Frentani and Caraceni from the Peligni, and at last pours itself into the Adriatic. It brings with it to the sea several other streams, among which are especially the Rasinus, rising in the plains of Furca Palena, and the Aventinus, which rises from the Superequani of the Peligni (for so they were once called), bordering on Furca Palena. It is joined, however, before Vitridi, whose spring is on Mount Maiella between the monastery of St Martin and the castle of Faranum. Soon, twice a thousand paces from Ortona, flows the river Aternus. At this place the Itinerary table writes the river Clitoris, between Anxanum and Ortona. Next follows the small river Feltrinus. Then the mouth of the Forum, and at the ninth milestone from there the Sentis; the same distance from here, the river commonly called the Pescara. The Aternus is named by Varro in book 4 of De Lingua Latina and by Pliny, and it is Ἀτερνος (Aternos) in Strabo and Ptolemy. It rises from the parent Apennines, as most of the rivers of Italy do, above Aquila, not far from Monte Regale, which lies beneath its spring. Many streams flow into the Aternus, or Pescara. From the southern bank, chiefly two, which rise in the territory of Sulmona, near the towns of Pettorano and Valle Oscura. From there each of them proceeds almost as far as Sulmona in its own separate bed; then, one plunging into the other, they become a single river outside the city, across a wide plain a mile and a half across. After a course of about twelve miles, and greatly augmented by springs and small streams near Popoli, where it is crossed by a wooden bridge, it finally empties itself into the Aternus. In the same way, about seventeen miles from here, on the same bank, the Rasentus and the Orta, which tumble down from Mount Maiella, flow into the Aternus in a single bed. Eight miles from there the Liberata hides itself in the Aternus, bringing with it two small streams that also run down from Maiella. Alexander Andreas advises that this river is also called the Viperata. On the northern bank the Aternus is increased by two streams, one of which, the Caput Aquae (Capo d'Acqua), and the other, the Nursia, which begins near the Cistercian monastery of Casae Novae.

units.la: {y} Candilarii, Cervaria, Sammnitium, Larnum, Tiferno, Trinius, Aisinia, Sangrus, Rasinus, Aventinus, Vitridi, Aternus, Feltrinus, Pescara, Aternum, Rasentus, Orta, Liberata, Caput Aquae, Nursia, Satanus — marginal notes. tium. Pod Aternum vel Ifcarium, Salinum est, qui Plinio Sulinum flumen, nisi si Sinum, quo Salinum iungitur Flumen Sinnum hoc loco est in Itineraria Tabula, vitiose procul dubio. Nomen numquam mutat, sed ab Fonte, qui in Apennino, usque ad Ostium, per quod Hadria ico Mari infundit, pertent. Intrant in eum Tacus & sinus, ut de hoc paullo ante monui, ex Corvi radicibus nascentes. Ultra Salinum tertio lapide Flumen illud, qui ut Doctis videtur, Marcus Strabonis & Ptolemaeo; Eaternum Flumen Plinio, an hic, an illi ianus, nondum video. Ad Maiorem partem inclinare, tutius. Contendunt alii Helcium Plinii eundem esse cum Matrino Strabonis & Ptolemaei, eoque, qui nunc Fiumla Quidam Mariunum eundem Plinii cum eo, qui Tardinas, contendunt. Addo Fl. Cumaram hoc loco poni in Itineraria Tabula: quod quale sit, non patet. Nam ita dictum esse ab Cumero Promontorio, quod ultra t x hinc mille passuum versus Caurum distat, non videtur. Mat alij volunt esse qui Aibuia Plinio, quique hodie Libertata. Quarto a Plumba milliari sequitur Vomanus. Plinio lib. xiii cap. xiii, Silioque lib. viii notus; nomen retinens, Vomano; vel, ut alij pronunciant, Homano. Quem hoc tractu Fluvium habet Strabo, putat Leander eundem esse cum Iomano. Sed pro iis, quae apud Straboneum, legendum esse, Kaggonosu, postea dicam in Sammnitibus, ubi de Praetutianorum Agro. Interpretes alij monstrosum id vo abutum omiserunt. Non neglexit tamen in suo Strabone Bonaccioltus, quem ex Graeco italicum fecit. Sexto trans Vomanum lapide Tardinus est, quem Tardinum a Plinio vocari tradunt Vola ciranus & Leander. Verantium legitur apud Blondum. Oritur ex Montis Corvi radicibus, nomenque idad mare perfert, suceptus, qui vulgo Fiumicello & Vicsola, ab Corvo quoque proiecti. Succedit Amnis L berata, alius ab superiore: Aibula, ut volunt docti, dictus Plinio, in cuius nonnullis Codicibus Abuates scribitur.
units.tr: Candilarii, Cervaria, Samnitium, Larnum, Tiferno, Trinius, Aisinia, Sangrus, Rasinus, Aventinus, Vitridi, Aternus, Feltrinus, Pescara, Aternum, Rasentus, Orta, Liberata, Caput Aquae, Nursia, Satanus: marginal notes. [The rest of this note is too garbled in the scan to render with confidence: it concerns Aternum or Ifcarium, the Salinum which Pliny calls the Sulinum flumen, unless it is the Sinum, to which the Salinum joins; the Flumen Sinnum is in the Itinerary table here, doubtless wrongly. The name never changes but runs from its spring in the Apennines to the mouth by which it pours into the Adriatic. Into it flow the Tacus and the Sinus, as I noted a little before, rising from the roots of Corvo. Three miles beyond the Salinum is that river which, as seems to scholars, is the Marcus of Strabo and Ptolemy, and the Aternum Flumen of Pliny; whether this one or that one, I do not yet see. It is safer to lean towards the greater part. Some contend that the Helcium of Pliny is the same as the Matrinus of Strabo and Ptolemy, and the one now called the Fiumla. Some contend that the Mariunum of Pliny is the same as the one called the Tardinas. I add that the Fl. Cumaram is placed in the Itinerary table here, but what it is does not appear; for that it was so named from the promontory Cumerus, which lies a thousand paces from here towards the west, does not seem likely. Others want the Mat to be the one that Pliny calls the Aibuia, and which is today the Libertata. Four miles from the Plumba milestone comes the Vomanus, known from Pliny book 13 chapter 13 and from Silius book 8; it keeps its name as Vomano, or, as others pronounce it, Homano. Leander thinks that the river which Strabo has in this stretch is the same as the Iomano. But I will say later, in the section on the Samnites where I discuss the territory of the Praetutii, that for what is in Strabo one should read Kaggonosu. Other interpreters have omitted that monstrous word altogether. Bonaccioltus, however, who made an Italian version out of the Greek, did not neglect it in his Strabo. Six miles beyond the Vomanus is the Tardinus, which Vola ciranus and Leander say Pliny calls the Tardinum. The Verantium is read in Blondus. It rises from the roots of Mount Corvo, and, receiving the stream that carries its name to the sea, which is commonly called the Fiumicello and the Vicsola, which also is thrown forth from Corvo. Next follows the river Liberata, another one from the upper area: the Aibula, as learned men believe, is what Pliny called it, and in some of his manuscripts it is written Abuates.]

units.la: Sic tandem littora legentes ad Picenos, & Ostia detecti fumus Truenti, qui vulgo Tronto: Truentum Plinio; Tpouiaon Ptolemaeo; Truentinum Pomponio Melae; Meminit & Silius Italicus lib. viii.
units.tr: So, following the coast, we come at last to the Picentes and the mouth of the river Truentus, which is now called the Tronto. Pliny calls it Truentum; Ptolemy [Τρουίαον]; Pomponius Mela Truentinum. Silius Italicus also mentions it in book 8.

units.la: Quaque Truentinas servant cum Flumine Turres,
units.tr: And the towers that guard the Truentine river,

units.la: Fl. Nerminum scribitur hoc loco in Itineraria Tabula. Oritur in asperrimis, altissimisque & perhorrendis Apennini Montibus, qui tamen cum ipso Amnis descensu per eius utramque ripam paullatim ad mare usque ita mitescunt, ut circa Fluminis Ostium peramoenī latique Campi cernantur. Iungit se Truento cum alius Castellanus, ex valle Apennini, quae Castellana vocatur, erumpens. Sequuntur inde alij duo Amnes, quorum Prior ad Morcinum, Alter ad Pedaslum in Mare praecipitantur. Decimo ab Truento millar. Afonus occurrit: quarto hinc Letus Mortuus, cui supra radices Apennini inter opida Belmontium & Petricinium Fons est. Tenna hinc succedit, ex Apennino per Agrum Firmanorum in Mare tendens. Tunia Fl. notatur hic in Itineraria Tabula, & prope eundem Tunna oppidum. Tigna Latinis hodie scribitur. Post Tennam octo milliar. Chienus se pandit Fluvius, ex Apennino iactus; Chienio vernacule. Augetur cum aliis, tum Flastra, & Leto Vivo. Flastra suus ortus in Apennino, haud procul ab Naris, Umbriae Flumini, Fonte; ubi Castellum Flastra dubium an ab Amne nomen teneat, an illi debent: prius vero est simulius: Letus Vivus prope Picae Campum erumpit. Ab Chienio deinde ad sextum fere milliar. in ora modici Torrentis ostium sequitur Asinus: Hinc ium Flumen Potentia, supra Matelicam in Apennino, ex adversum Nuceriae Altatenae, de qua in Umbria oriens. Mox Musonis sunt Ostia, quod Flumen Aspidem vocant, ab sinuoso, ut videtur, tortuosque Cursu. Fit enim instar Aspidis Serpentis: quum ex Apennino descendens, itaque ad Aquilonem versus, deinde ad Orientem, rursusque multis volutationibus hac illac se flectens, tandem, nonnullis auctus Amnibus, in Mare prorumpat. Circumvectis Crumerum Promontorium Esinus se offert: qui vulgo Fiumesino, id est Flumen Esinum: unde & Latine scribentibus Flumesinus. Asis Plinio, Pomponio Melae, Antonino; Aσις Straboni; Aσιγ Ptolemaeo, fortean incommendatus: Aσσιν videtur corrupte nominare Plutarchus in Pompeio. Oritur paullo supra Caretum & decimo intra opidum cognomine, quod Veteribus Aesis, milliari undis Hadriatici maris conditur. Male quidam distinguunt inter Aesis Straboni, Plinii, Melae & Asium Ptolemaei, quasi hic is esset qui hodie in Umbria Chiaravalle dicitur, & Latine scribentibus Chiatius: Aesis autem idem cum qui vernacule Sino vel Fiume-Sino. Ptolemaeus certe Asij Fluminis Ostia ad Mare Hadriaticum in Semnonibus locat, prope Senogalliam ut Chratis esse nequat, qui in Tiberim se evacuat Duodecimo ab Fano Milliari Misa est Ostium. Ex Apennino, ut plerique huius tractus Fluvij, devolutus, ad Senam Gallicam Mari Supero commiscetur: dives cum aliis, tum Sentino, propter Saxi ferrati moenia fluente. Amnem hunc Marcae Anconitanae & Umbriae facere discrimen scribit Vola erratus. Octavo ab Mila lapide Cesanus vituur in ora exitus: Inde undecimo Metaurus est. Strabo; Metaurus Livio, Plinio, Melae, Vibio Sequestro: Hodie Metro, censentibus Leandro, Nigro, Bonacciolo. Strabo in Umbria locat alij in Piceno: Valerius Maximus lib. vii cap. iv iuxta Flaminiam; Sidonius cum circa Ariminum describit: ad Senam Auctor de VV. Illustribus. Facilis conciliationis ratio, cui norandae, ne fiant proiixior, non immorabor. Velox dictum Lucano lib. ii. Eleganter Silius lib. viii: ——rapidaque fortis Vertice contorquens undas & seva Metaurus.
units.tr: The Itinerary Table writes it here as Fl. Nerminum. It rises in the very rough, very high and frightful mountains of the Apennines, which nevertheless grow gentler all the way down to the sea, along both banks, so that near the river's mouth one sees very pleasant and broad plains. Another river, the Castellanus, joins the Truentum, bursting out of a valley of the Apennines called the Castellana. Then follow two other streams, one of which plunges into the sea at Morcinum, the other at Pedaslum. Ten miles from the Truentum the Afonus comes up; four miles further on is the Letus Mortuus, which rises below the foot of the Apennines between the towns of Belmontium and Petricinium. Next comes the Tenna, which runs from the Apennines through the territory of Firmum into the sea. The Itinerary Table marks here the Tunia Fl., and near it the town of Tunna. Today it is written in Latin as Tigna. Eight miles after the Tenna the Chienus opens out, a river thrown down from the Apennines; in the vernacular it is Chienio. It is swelled by others, namely the Flastra and the Leto Vivo. The Flastra has its source in the Apennines, not far from the spring of the Nar, a river of Umbria, where there is a castle called Flastra. It is doubtful whether the castle takes its name from the river or the river from the castle, though the former is more likely. The Letus Vivus bursts out near the plain of Picae. From the Chienis, about six miles further on, at the shore of a small torrent's mouth, follows the Asinus. From there comes the river Potentia, rising in the Apennines above Matelica, opposite Nuceria Altatena, which rises in Umbria. Soon after are the mouths of the Musonis, which people call the Aspis (Asp), from its winding and, as it seems, crooked course. For it is like a snake's asp: descending from the Apennines it runs northward, then eastward, and again, twisting this way and that in many coils, at last, swelled by several tributaries, it bursts into the sea. Having rounded Cape Crumerum, the Esinus presents itself, which is commonly called Fiumesino, that is, the River Esinus; hence Latin writers also call it Flumesinus. Pliny, Pomponius Mela and Antoninus call it Asis; Strabo [Ἄσις]; Ptolemy [Ἄσιγ], perhaps wrongly; Plutarch in his Pompey seems to give the corrupt name [Ἄσσιν]. It rises a little above Caretum and, ten miles within the town of the same name, which the ancients called Aesis, it is lost in the waves of the Adriatic. Some wrongly distinguish between the Aesis of Strabo, Pliny and Mela and the Asium of Ptolemy, as if the latter were what is now called the Chiaravalle in Umbria, and by Latin writers the Chiatius; they hold that the Aesis is the same as what is called in the vernacular Sino or Fiume-Sino. Ptolemy certainly places the mouth of the river Asius on the Adriatic among the Semnones, near Senogallia, so it cannot be the Chratis, which empties into the Tiber.
