Twelve miles from Fanum is the mouth of the Misa. Descending from the Apennines, like most rivers of this region, it flows to Sena Gallica and joins the Upper Sea. It is rich in tributaries, among them the Sentino*, which flows past the walls of Saxoferrato. Vola the wanderer writes that this river forms the boundary between the Marche of Ancona and Umbria. Eight miles from the Mila stone the Cesanus lives, at the shore of its outlet; eleven miles further on is the Metaurus. Strabo writes Metaurus, as do Livy, Pliny, Mela and Vibius Sequester; today it is Metro, according to Leandro, Nigro and Bonacciolo. Strabo places it in Umbria, others in Picenum; Valerius Maximus (book 7, chapter 4) places it beside the Flaminian Way; Sidonius describes it near Ariminum; the author De Viris Illustribus places it at Sena. There is an easy way to reconcile these, but I will not linger on it, lest I make this too long. It is called Velox by Lucan in book 2. Silius Italicus, book 8, has it elegantly: "and the fierce Metaurus, whirling its rapid waters in a headlong eddy."

units.la: Ex Apennino radipissime se praecipitat, plurimumque Cantiano auctus praeter Forum Sempronii perpetuo citatus fertur, & tandem tribus infra Fanum milliaribus in Mare intrat. Ad hunc Amnem Livius Salinator & Claudius Nero Asdrubalem magna victoria superarunt, ut narrat Livius lib. xxvii. Ut Cantianus ab Apennino ortus Incola est Metaurus, sub Muro longe lateque patentis Leporum ab Friderico Vrbini Regulo confecti sic Cantiam ad Calnum Urbem Pofius ab Umbriae Vico Planello provolutus post Fanum Agla Fluvius in mare mergitur licab Terrae genere; quod Latinis Argilla, quam hic in Amnis solo aliam atque tenacem est videre, denominatus.
units.tr: It plunges headlong from the Apennines, and swelled especially by the Cantianus, flows on steadily past Forum Sempronii and, three miles below Fanum, enters the sea. By this river Livy Salinator and Claudius Nero defeated Hasdrubal in a great victory, as Livy relates in book 27. Just as the Metaurus, rising in the Apennines, is the inhabitant under the wall of Leporum, a vast and wide-spreading town destroyed by Frederick, the prince of Urbino, so the Cantianus* flows down to the city of Calnum from the village of Planellum in Umbria; after Fanum the river Agla is swallowed by the sea. It takes its name from a kind of earth, which the Latins call argilla (clay), which can be seen here in the river's bed, different and tenacious.

units.la: Flaminiae nunc indagemus Fluvios. Extra Pisauri portam, quae spectat in occasum, Amnis est Folia. Isaurus olim plerumque: Pisaurus Plinio, Vibio & Siculo Flacco. Oritur Apennino, fonte iuxta Cotili Arcem: Moenaque Pisauri adluit, ubi Pons lapideus Picenum cum Regione Flaminia iungit; moxque mari, Fluviis duobus auctus, inter eos Albi, inlabitur Ostio: saepe arena, Fluctibus deferentibus, adeo completo & obturato, ut vix exiguas recipere naviculas queat. Inveniuntur ultra Isaurum ex Apennino mare petentes primo Catolica: inde Vintinella mox Conca, Crustumium Lucano lib. ii. Plinio in viii Regione & Vibio Sequestro.
units.tr: Now let us survey the rivers of the Flaminian Way. Outside the Pisaurum gate, which faces west, is the river Folia. Formerly it was usually called Isaurus; Pliny, Vibius and Siculus Flaccus call it Pisaurus. It rises from the Apennines, from a spring near the citadel of Cotilus; it washes the walls of Pisaurum, where a stone bridge joins Picenum with the Flaminian region; and then, swelled by two streams, among them the Albi, it flows into the sea at its mouth. Often sand, carried by the waves, so fills and blocks the mouth that it can hardly admit small boats. Beyond the Isaurus, coming from the Apennines towards the sea, are found first the Catolica, then the Vintinella, soon the Conca, and the Crustumium of Lucan, book 2, Pliny in the eighth region, and Vibius Sequester.

units.la: Iamnunc, quae per Aemiliae Campos exspatiantur Flumina, videamus. In iis primi loci Marecia, vel, ut alij pronunciant, Marida: qui iuxta muros Arimini mari miscetur: portum exiguum, modicis tantum navigiis aptum propter Vada undique maris, efficiens. Ariminum Plinio Procopioque. Flaminiam Aemiliamque separat. Interrumpit eandem Aemiliam paullo post Plusia, Aprusa Plinio, Quondam hic Aemiliae transitus Ponte iungebatur lapideo; cuius ad hanc aetatem vestigia est cernere. Torrens succedit Rutrius. In proximo exiguus est Amnis Pisatellus. Sic hodie audit, qui Rubico Livio, Lucano, Caesari, Suetonio, Silio, Plinio, Itinerariae Tabulae, aliis: Ῥουβίκων Ptolemaeo, aliisque Scriptoribus Graecis: Ῥουβικῶν Straboni. De Pisatello sic Blondus: Pisatellum nunc qui sub Flaminia Via; Ruconem, qui supra adcolunt, vocant. Gaudentius Merula in sua Gallia Cisalpina scribit hac aetate ab Circumvicinis Populis materno Idiomate Rusium: pallo inferius, Rugesum, novissime non procul ab Sinu in quem influit, Pisatellum ingredi, per duo millia, iuxta Cesenam. Flumen est illud, quo antiquitus post translatos ab Aeti Amne Terminos, Italia finiebatur, auctore Plinio. Sic Lucanus lib. i. Puniceus Rubicon quum ferroida canduit aestas, Perque imas serpit Valles & Gallica certus Limes ab Ausonis disterminat Arva Colonis.
units.tr: Let us now look at the rivers that spread over the plains of Aemilia. Among them, first in order, is the Marecia, or, as others pronounce it, the Marida, which mixes with the sea by the walls of Ariminum, making a small harbour fit only for small craft because of the shoals on every side of the sea. Ariminum is in Pliny and Procopius; it separates Flaminia from Aemilia. A little further on the Plusia interrupts the same Aemilian Way; Pliny calls it Aprusa. Once a stone bridge joined the Aemilian road here; traces of it can still be seen in our own time. The Rutrius, a torrent, follows. Close by is the small stream Pisatellus. This is what today is heard as the Rubico in Livy, Lucan, Caesar, Suetonius, Silius, Pliny, the Itinerary Table and others; in Ptolemy and other Greek writers [Ῥουβίκων]; in Strabo [Ῥουβικῶν]. Blondus writes of the Pisatellus thus: "What is now called Pisatellum under the Flaminian Way, those who live above it call the Rucone." Gaudentius Merula in his Gallia Cisalpina writes that in this age the neighbouring peoples in their native tongue call it the Rusium; a little lower down, the Rugesum. Lastly, not far from the bay into which it flows, it enters the Pisatellus, for two miles, near Cesena. This is the river by which, after the boundaries were moved from the river Aesis, Italy was once bounded, according to Pliny. So Lucan, book 1: "When the Punic Rubicon glows with the fierce summer, and creeps through the lowest valleys, a sure boundary, it separates the fields of the Ausonian farmers from the Gallic."

units.la: Livius citra Rubiconem Italiam, ultra Galliam Cis-Alpinam (scilicet) esse prodit. Videndus & Appianus Alexandrinus lib. ii. Cis Rubiconem quondam Militibus Ducibusque à bello redeuntibus Arma ferre non fuisse licitum legimus absque S. P. Q. R. auctoritate; qui secus fecisset, hostis Reip. iudicabatur. Docet illud C. Iulij Caesaris, ex Galliis in Italiam parantis per Rubiconem reditum, Historia, quae apud ipsum Caesarem in Commentariis, Suetonium & Plutarchum in eius vita, Appianum Alexandrinum lib. ii, Lucanum lib. i, & alios. Pertinet huc Edictum Vetustissimum; quod in Rubiconis ripa ab se conspectum, annoque cIↄ Iↄ Ixv, quum Venetiis Romam rediret, diligenter exscriptum, testatur in Orthographia sua Aldus Manutius Pauli F: Tale:
units.tr: Livy states that Italy lies on this side of the Rubicon, and Gaul Cisalpine beyond it. Appian of Alexandria, book 2, should also be consulted. We read that on this side of the Rubicon soldiers and commanders returning from war were not permitted to bear arms without the authority of the Senate and People of Rome; whoever did otherwise was judged an enemy of the republic. The story of Julius Caesar's return through the Rubicon from Gaul into Italy, when he was preparing for war, proves this: it is found in Caesar's own Commentaries, in Suetonius and Plutarch in his life, in Appian of Alexandria, book 2, in Lucan, book 1, and in others. To this belongs the very ancient edict which, seen by him on the bank of the Rubicon, and carefully copied when in the year 1465 he was returning from Venice to Rome, Aldus Manutius, son of Paul, attests in his Orthography. It runs thus:

units.la: IVSSV. MANDVTVVE. P. R. COS IMP. MILI. TYRO. COMILITO MANIPVLARISVE. CENT. TVRMAEVE. LEGIONARIAE. ARMAT QVISQVIS. ES. HIC. SISTITO. VEXILLVM. SINITO. NEC. CITRA HVNC. AMNEM. RVBICONEM SIGNA. ARMA. DVCTVM. CO MEATVM. EXERCITVMQVE. TRADVCITO. SIQVIS. HVIVSCE IVSSIONIS. ERGO. ADVERSVS IERIT. SECERITVE. ADIVDICATVS. ESTO. HOSTIS. P. R. AC. SI. CONTRA. PATRIAM. ARMA. TVLERIT. SACROSQVE. PENATES. R. PENETRALIBVS. ASPORTAVERIT. SANCTIO. PLEBISCI. SENATVS VE. CONSVLTI. VLTRA HOS. SI NES. ARMA. PROFERRE. LICEAT NEMINI
units.tr: By order and command of the Roman people, consul and imperator. Recruit, fellow soldier, of the maniples and centuries, of the legionary cohorts, under arms, whoever you are, halt here and do not let your standard pass; let no one lead arms, standards, drawn troops, baggage, or army across this river Rubicon on this side. If anyone shall have gone against this order or turned aside, let him be adjudged an enemy of the Roman people. And if he bears arms against his country, or carries the sacred household gods away from their inner shrines, let the decree of the plebs, the senate or the consult apply. Beyond these, let no one be allowed to bring forth arms to no one

units.la: S. P. Q. R.
units.tr: S. P. Q. R.

units.la: Ne vero quis dubitet, utrum qui quomdam Rubico, sit hodie Pisatellus, an vero Plusa (nam illud controvertitur) e pendat velim Strabonem lib. v; ubi scribit Cesenam Ispi Fluvio propinquam & Rubiconi. Sic sane res hodie se habet: Cesena non inter Plusiam & Pisatellum locata, sed in ter Pisatellum & Sarsum. Nam qui Sarsus nunc temporis, Sapis Plinio & Silio Italico lib. viii. Ex Apennino rapidissime delapsus, cadentibus imbribus; Agros finitimos haud mediocriter infestat Cesenae muros fere adluit. Post Sapis Ostium Silva nobilis Pinca, vulgo Pignetta. Extra Pinetum Candiani Amnis, nunc Paludis, Ostium sequitur. Inde Torrens est Alia. Mox Bedesis Fluvius, Plinio notus, Aemiliam secans. In antiquis Plinii Exemplaribus Bedesis scribitur. Blondus in historiis Ronconum nominat, & Bidentem, cuius in Vitis S. Hilarii & Olybrij mentio; quique, nunc Portum creans Ravennatem, Theodorici Regis temporibus, eodem Blondo non uno loco auctore, Portulum appellabatur. Vt autem latus unum cingit hic Ravennae; sic alierum Montonus, qui hunc ad Aquaeductus, Plinianae Vitae dictus. Nascitur in Apennini jugis prope Tiberis Fontem
units.tr: Lest anyone doubt which river is the Rubicon (that is the point in dispute), whether it is now the Pisatello or the Pisa, let him consult Strabo, book 5, where he writes that Cesena lies near the Ispis river and the Rubicon. In fact the situation today is this: Cesena is not located between the Pisa and the Pisatello, but between the Pisatello and the Sarsus. For the river now called Sarsus is the Sapis of Pliny and Silius Italicus, book 8. It rushes down very swiftly from the Apennines when the rains fall, and it considerably harasses the neighbouring fields, washing almost the walls of Cesena. After the Sapis comes the mouth of the Silva, a famous pine wood, commonly called Pignetta. Beyond the pine wood follows the mouth of the Candiano river, now of the Paludi. Then comes the Torrens Alia. Soon after is the river Bedesis, known to Pliny, which cuts through Aemilia. In the old copies of Pliny it is written Bedesis. Blondus in his histories names it Ronco, and the Bidens, which is mentioned in the Lives of St Hilary and Olybrius. This river, now forming the port of Ravenna, was called Portulus in the times of King Theodoric, as Blondus, not in one place only, is the authority for this. Just as this river encloses one side of Ravenna, so another river, the Montone, which is called the Aquaeductus, encloses the other. It rises on the ridges of the Apennines near the source of the Tiber.

units.la: Perduxit nos tandem hier, quod ex Occidentalissima Liguria, per variorum Fluminum Ostia, circum Italiam ad penitiores Hadriatici Maris recessus instituimus littorale, in nobilissimum, quaeque omnes Europae Fluvios, ut Strabo asserit, docetque experientia, praeter Istrum magnitudine superat, Padum. Sic Latinis Scriptoribus, Livio, Virgilio, Ovidio, Tacito, aliis, Tabulaeque Itinerariae vocatur; qui Italis hodie Po. Padus dictus, non anie apud Plinium Metrodoro Scepsio, quod circa Fontem Arbor multa lit picea, quae Pades Gallice. Ἠριδανός olim Graecis Poetisque, ut Virgilio, Lucano, Senecae, aliisque: telibus Plinio lib. iii. cap. xvi, Solino in Polyhist. cap. vii, Vibio Sequestro, Polybio lib. v. Sic autem dictus, ut vult Servius, ab Solisfilio Phaetonte, qui anteaquam per cementiatem in hunc fluvium esset praecipitatus, Eridanus fertur appellatus. Et notat hunc Plinius Padum Phaetontis poena inlustratum: quam tamen Historiam Vistulae Flumini convenire docet in Hyperboreis Goropius Becanus. Eolin vero, teste Plinio, Liguribus vocabatur, quod Fundo careat: Ἀδῆς Polybio lib. iii. Padi Pater Mons Vesus, Antiquis omnibus Vesulus; ut docet Plinius lib. iii. cap. xvi. In Finibus Ligurum Gabienorum Fonte profluit, ut idem Plinius notat, τὸ ὑσεῖνδο; non qui proprio sic nomine, ut Leander putat, dictus, sed qui visu dignus & mirabilis, ut apud Marcianum Capellam. Ex Fonte suo (quem idem Plinius lib. ii, cap. cvi, medis diebus aestivis velut interquiescentem aut arere) nulli Amnium claritate inferior profluens, per angustas confragosaque Rupes, & arctas scopulosi Montis Convalles praecipitat; tantaque vi prorumpit, ut summam habeat admirationem. In Saxa hinc delabens, fragore strepituque maximo resonat. Mox in planiciem effusus Aquae Copia, quae versandae Molae Frumentariae sufficit, temere lateque, non uno certo Alveo discurrit, spatio trium fere milliar. usque ad Padanam, ubi quasi Cuniculis ita absorbetur, ut exigua plane supra Terram vestigia relinquat, post alterum vero milliar. rursus exoritur ad Paracolum (in Foro Vibienti Agro, inquit Plinius lib. II cap. xvi) unde pergens Aquilas, Torrentes, Amnesque ab Alpibus & Apenninis Montibus varios colligit, quibus tandem mirum in modum auctus altusque, mediam Langbardiam & Romanulae partem permeans, in Hadriaticum se exonerat Mare septem ostiis praegrandibus. Quia longius vomit, septem Maria efficere dictus, inquit Plinius, apud quem lib. III cap. xvi vide de Cursu plura, ut & apud Polybium lib. II, Strabonem lib. V, Pomponium Melam lib. III, Solinum in Polyhist. cap. VII, Leandrum Albertum, aliosque Novitios: inter quos optime Cursum hodiernum sic delineat M. Antonius Sabellicus lib. Histor. Venet. I. Decad. IV: Ab ipso Fonte suis latus Incrementis, uno Alveo Ficariorum usque de flumi (quod oppidum est haud multum infra Hustiliam) tum vero nimia Aquarum crapula i ictus paullulum sub ipsius Moenia luxuriari incipit; atque in duas sui ipsius partes primam Insulam facit; Ad oram Polesinum vocant, transfossa, ut opinor, si laba, ut quum Polesinum dicunt, Polynesum, id est longam seu multam Insulam dicere se credant; et, quia Ferraria non longe infra ipsum Aquarum divortium sedet, Ferrariensem Polynesum hanc vulgo nominant. Dexter Amnis, priusquam Urbem attingat, ob pleraque Flumina, quae brevi spatio se illis insinuant, amissas nuper vires pene ex integro reponit; quo fit, ut nova mole pressus, in ipsis oculis Civium, non praesentiam, non Urbis adhibita veritus, quasi nova seditione turbatus, in duas divisus partes, diversus abit: sitque recentiore hoc divortio altera Insula, qua Argentia oppidum, quaque item Comacium Magnis circumdatum includitur. Dextera pars Fluminis, quum Argentinos Fines perfirmavit aversa ripa, quae Insulam oppidum sedet, ex Foro-Cornelensi Agro Vatrenum Amnem accipit: nunc Adiola corrupto nomine Santernum vocant. Hic quasi omnis incrementi impatiens, non multo post, ubi, circa Comaclum, ad locum venit, quem Divum Albertum vocant, tantumdem pene Aquarum, quantum ex Vatreno acceperat, temere effundit, quae per stagna Ravennam progressa, navigabit Fluvio in Mare diabuntur: atque ita Ravenna Portus, unum ex Padi Ostiis dici potest. De reliquis ex Sabellico Portubus, paullo post: Navigabilis esse incipit Padus ab Urbe Taurino. Propter Imolam fluere, notavit inprudenter libro Fluminum Boccatius. Inusitata eius incrementa, quae proximis temporibus damnosa fuerunt Adcolis, notat Leander incidisse in annos, supra mille quingentos, xxii, xxiv, & xliv. Deiptius Auctu Sabellicus, quem antea dixi: Augent ipsum vehementer, praeter ipsa Flumina, liquata Nives, idque circa Canis ortum; nec, quum maxime innumerit, tam Navigius est infestus: quam Agris: quo fit, ut perpetuo Adcolarum labore utrumque coerceatur Aggeribus; in eo satis vicinis Campis aequus, quod nihil ex rapto sibi vindicat. Fluviorum Rex Eridanus, Virgilio IX Aeneidos. Non Minor hic Nilo canit lib. II Lucanus, cui paullo post ibidem. Non minor hic Istro. Padum maritimorum Commeatuum Italicis Subsidiis fidum vocat Invectorem Ambrosius. Appianus lib. I. bellor. Civilium Eridanum appellat intimum Maris Hadriatici Sinum. De septem Ostiis scribit loco iam indicato Plinius, quem ab aliis Scriptoribus nonnihil iuvabo & illustrabo. Ait ille: Quia largius vomit, Septem Maria dictus facere. Angusta Fossa Ravennam trahitur, ubi Padusa vocatur, quondam Masianicus appellatus (Padoa Polybio dicitur lib. II, fortean vitiosius; lornandes eam Asconis Fossam vocat. Novit etiam Padusam Amnem Virgilius lib. XI Aeneid. & Stagna Padusae Claudianus: Vibius Paludem appellat. Fossa sane est angusta, quae ex Pado Ravennam ducit: Hodie Canale di S. Alberto nominatur, Nigro teste. Extenditur in XII milia passuum, stagnans, vadosa, arta. Pergit Plinius:) Proximum inde Ostium Magnitudinem Portus habet, qui Vatreni dicitur: quo Claudius Caesar ex Britannia triumphans prægrandi illa domo versus, quam nave intravit Hadriam. Hoc ante Eridanum Ostium dictum est, alias Spineticum ab Urbe Spina (στῖν ... πόλεως Stephano. Spinonem novit & M. Tullius lib. III, de Nat. Deorum: legitur apud Dionysium Halicarnassaeum) Auget ibi Padum Vatrenus Amnis (hinc ostio nomen) ex ForoCornelensi Agro (a Pomponio videtur Magnus Padus appellari. Hieronymus Rubeus & Fabricius Primarium, Erythraeus, errans tamen in vero eius Situ, Premerinum, Primero Vulgus nuncupant) Proximum inde Caprasiae (hodie Magna Vaccha, Blondo & Leandro) Leandro) Dein Sagis (quem designer, non video: nam inter Caprasias & Volanem nullus est hodie Portus: Goras, ut censet in Itinere Romano Fabricius, esse nequit, quum secundus ille sit ab Volme, hodieque in Portuum numero sextus: expungendas existimarem, ut Glossema, duas voces, dein Sagis: ut & sequentes mox a Sagi; nisi quaedam dissuaderent: ideoque notas hic adponam Iudicij vel sententiae dilatorias ut ita loquar, N. L.) dein Volanc, quod ante Olane vocabatur (Volana hodie, teste Leandro: o'λαια & o'λαια est apud Polybium lib. ii.) Inde Ostia plenis, (cubant haec mihi in morbo: Si, quod verosimile, Plinius per Carbonariam, de qua mox subdit, Portum exaudiat, qui hodie del Fornase; praeterit sane duo, quae Volani & Carbonaria sunt interiecta, quae vulgo L'Aba & Goro: quorum Nomina si idem Plinius ignorans non exprellerit, facilis erit medicina, si legamus Inde Ostia lina, nimirum quae nunc L'Aba & Goro: sequitur in Plinio Carbonaria (Padi Brachium, quod hic Ostium facit, omnium primum infra Ficarolum diffunditur, indeque ad Fornaces in Mare profluit, unde Ostium vulgo Porto del Fornase: ut Plinius) ac Fossiones (vel Fossa) Philistinae, quod aliy Tartarum vocant. Hactenus de Padi Ostiis Plinius: sic tamen ut Fossiones Philistinae, quae Fossona hodie, Leandro Fabricioque testibus; Pistrina autem Rhodigino, in Ostiorum Padi numero non sint censendae: ad Athesin proprie pertinentes. Sic igitur septem ex Plinio, ut quidem emendandum, licet timidius, centeo, habemus Padi Ostia: Polybio bina tantum παδοαι (forte παδοαι) & o'λαιαι, exprimente; quemadmodum etiam patet ex iis, quae inlustrandis Plinii verbis in medium attuli
units.tr: At last we have come, by way of the mouths of various rivers, around Italy to the inner recesses of the Adriatic Sea, having set out from the most western part of Liguria, to the coast of the most noble river, which, as Strabo asserts and experience teaches, surpasses in size all the rivers of Europe except the Ister: the Po. Latin writers, Livy, Virgil, Ovid, Tacitus and others, and the Itinerary tables, call it thus; today the Italians call it Po. It was called Padus, not long before, by Metrodorus of Scepsis as Pliny reports, because around its source there are many pitch-bearing trees, which the Gauls call pades. The Greeks and poets of old called it Eridanus, as did Virgil, Lucan, Seneca and others; witnesses include Pliny, book 3, chapter 16, Solinus in the Polyhistor, chapter 7, Vibius Sequester, and Polybius, book 5. It was so named, as Servius holds, from Phaethon, son of the Sun, who, before he was hurled into this river by a thunderbolt, is said to have been called Eridanus. Pliny notes that this Po was made famous by the punishment of Phaethon; yet Goropius Becanus shows that this story fits the Vistula river among the Hyperboreans. Indeed, according to Pliny, it was called Eridanus by the Ligurians, because it lacks a bottom, which the Greeks in Polybius, book 3, call [Ἀδῆς]. The father of the Po is Mount Viso, which all the ancients called Vesulus, as Pliny teaches, book 3, chapter 16. It flows from a spring in the territory of the Ligurian Gabiani, as the same Pliny notes, and the Greek word [τὸ ὑσεῖνδο] is not, as Leander thinks, a proper name for it, but refers to its being worth seeing and wonderful, as in Martianus Capella. From its source (which the same Pliny, book 2, chapter 106, says rests and nearly dries up in the midday heat of summer), it flows forth, inferior to no river in fame, and plunges through narrow, rocky gorges and the confined valleys of a rugged mountain; it bursts out with such force that it arouses the greatest wonder. Falling from there onto rocks, it resounds with a great roar and din. Soon, spreading out onto the plain, it runs rashly and widely, not in one fixed channel, with a volume of water sufficient to turn a grain mill, over a distance of about three miles, as far as Padana, where it is so swallowed up as if into underground channels that it leaves only very slight traces above ground; but after another mile it rises again at Paracolo (in the territory of the Forum Vibii, says Pliny, book 2, chapter 16). From there it proceeds, gathering various torrents and rivers from the Alps and the Apennines, and having been increased and deepened in a remarkable way by these, it passes through the middle of Lombardy and part of Romagna and discharges itself into the Adriatic Sea through seven very large mouths. Because it empties so far out, it is said, according to Pliny, to make seven seas; see there for more on its course, as also in Polybius, book 2, Strabo, book 5, Pomponius Mela, book 3, Solinus in the Polyhistor, chapter 7, Leander Alberti, and other moderns. Among them, M. Antonius Sabellicus, in book 1 of the Venetian histories, decad 4, describes the present course excellently: From its very source it grows broad with its increments, flowing in a single channel as far as Ficarolo (a town not much below Hustilia). Then, when it is excessively drunk on its waters, it begins to revel a little beneath the very walls of that place, and it makes of itself a first island in two parts. They call the shore Polesine, having been dug through, I suppose, by a channel, so that when they say Polesine they believe they are saying Polynesum, that is, a long or large island; and because Ferrara sits not far below the very divergence of the waters, they commonly name this the Ferrarese Polynesum. The right-hand branch of the river, before it reaches the city, having lost its strength recently through the many rivers that join it in a short space, nearly recovers it entirely; whence it comes about that, pressed by a new mass of water, before the very eyes of the citizens, not fearing the presence of the city, as if disturbed by a new sedition, it divides into two parts and departs in a different direction. By this more recent division there is formed another island, on which the town of Argenta lies, and which is enclosed by the great branches around Comacchio. The right-hand part of the river, after it has strengthened the territory of Argenta, takes up on the opposite bank, which sits on the island town, the Vatrenus river from the territory of Forum Cornelii: they now call it Adiola, a corrupted name, Santerno. This river, as if impatient of any increase, not long after, when it comes near Comacchio to the place which they call Divo Alberto, rashly pours out about as much water as it had received from the Vatrenus, which, having passed through the marshes towards Ravenna, will be carried into the sea by a navigable channel; and thus the port of Ravenna can be called one of the mouths of the Po. Concerning the other ports, from Sabellicus, a little later: The Po begins to be navigable from the city of Turin. Boccaccio carelessly noted in his book on rivers that it flows past Imola. Leander notes that its unusual floods, which in recent times were harmful to the neighbours, occurred in the years 1522, 1524 and 1544. Sabellicus, whom I mentioned above, describes its growth as well: Besides the rivers themselves, melted snows greatly swell it, especially around the rising of the Dog Star; nor, although it is at its greatest, is it so hostile to navigation as to the fields; so that by the constant labour of its neighbours both are restrained by embankments; it is fair to the fields that are fairly near, because it claims nothing for itself from what it has seized. Eridanus, king of rivers, in Virgil, Aeneid 9. Lucan in book 2 sings: Not less than the Nile here, and soon after in the same place: not less than the Ister here. Ambrose calls the Po a faithful carrier of maritime supplies to the Italian garrisons. Appian, in book 1 of the Civil Wars, calls the Eridanus the innermost gulf of the Adriatic Sea. Pliny, whom I have already cited, writes about the seven mouths, and I shall somewhat aid and clarify him with other writers. He says: Because it pours out more widely, it is said to make seven seas. A narrow channel draws it to Ravenna, where it is called Padusa, once named Masianicus (Padoa is called in Polybius, book 2, perhaps more faultily; Jordanes calls it the Ditch of Ascon. Virgil also knows the river Padusa, Aeneid 11, and Claudian the pools of the Padusa; Vibius calls it a marsh. Indeed the channel which leads from the Po to Ravenna is narrow; today it is called the Canal of St Alberto, according to Nigro. It extends for twelve miles, stagnant, shallow and confined. Pliny continues: The next mouth has the size of a harbour, and is called Vatrenus: by it Claudius Caesar, triumphing from Britain, sailed into the Adriatic in that very large ship. This was formerly called the Eridanus mouth, and otherwise the Spinetic from the city of Spina (Stephanus: [Σπίνα] city... Marcus Tullius, book 3 of On the Nature of the Gods, also knows Spinon; it is read in Dionysius of Halicarnassus). There the Vatrenus river, which gives the mouth its name, enriches the Po, coming from the territory of Forum Cornelii (by Pomponius it seems to be called the Great Po. Hieronymus Rubeus and Fabricius Primarius, Erythraeus, though erring about its true position, call it Premerinum, the common people name it Primero). Next, Caprasia (today Magna Vacca, according to Blondus and Leander). Then Sagis (which I cannot see what it designates: for between Caprasia and Volane there is today no port; Goras, which Fabricius in his Roman Itinerary thinks it to be, cannot be, since it is the second from Volme, and today the sixth in the number of ports. I would think the two words dein Sagis should be struck out as a gloss, as also the following words soon after from Sagi, unless certain things argued against it; and therefore I put here marks of postponed judgement, so to speak, N. L.) then Volanc, which was formerly called Olane (Volana today, according to Leander: [ὠλαία] and [ὠλαῖα] occurs in Polybius, book 2). Then the Ostia plenis (these things lie heavily on me in my sickness: if, as is likely, Pliny by Carbonaria, which he mentions next, means the port which today is called Fornace; indeed he passes over two that lie between Volano and Carbonaria, which the people call L'Aba and Goro. If Pliny, not knowing their names, did not express them, the remedy will be easy, if we read Inde Ostia lina, namely what are now L'Aba and Goro. In Pliny there follows Carbonaria (an arm of the Po, which here makes a mouth, is first spread out below Ficarolo, and thence flows into the sea at Fornaces, whence the mouth is commonly called Porto del Fornase, as Pliny says), and the Philistine ditches (or Fossa), which others call Tartarum. Thus far Pliny on the mouths of the Po: yet the Philistine ditches, which today are called Fossona, according to the witnesses Leander and Fabricius, and the Pistrina, according to the Rhodigine, are not to be counted among the mouths of the Po, since they properly belong to the Adige. So from Pliny, with a more timid emendation than I might wish, I count the mouths of the Po as seven; Polybius expresses only two, the [πάδοαι] (perhaps [πάδοαι]) and the [ὠλαῖαι]; as is also clear from those things which I have brought forward in explaining Pliny's words.

units.la: De Septem Padi Ostiis dilucidissime Sabellicus lib. i Venetae Historiae: qui, quum probasset Ravennatem Eortum unum ex Padi Ostiis dici posse, sic pergit: Reliqua Pars ac longe maior (Padi) ex Alberto, recto ferme cursu in mare evolvitur, cuius Ostium Primarium Adcola appellant, olim Vatrenum dictum ab Fluvio, qui se illis insinuat. Lera pars Ferrariensis Eveortij, eo Aquarum impetu, quo ab Urbe digreditur, non amissis viribus, in mare decurrit; cuiusque Ostium Volanem vocant. Inter hoc & Primarium, Ostium Comacina Stagna habent: imo portum potius, quam Magna-vaccam appellant. Sed Aestuaria Maris illa sunt, quod ex Salis concretione datur intelligi. Redeo ad primam illam Flumi(nis) sed(i)uram, quam paululum infra Ficarioli moenia fieri dixi-mus, eam ut recentem esse existimem, non tam Roberti Neapolitani Regis, & Francisci Petrarchae Italiae figuratio fuit (in qua id Padi Divertium nequaquam fuisse Blondus adfirmat) quam Polybij, summi Viri, at illi ritu usquum duobus Ostiis Padum in Hadriaticum exire tradidit. Padusa & Volane, quae ad eum Fluvium, cuius proxime mentionem fecimus, attinere non est dubium. Sed nunc ad reliquam partem redeo, quae ad laevam inclinans Cursum, sine aliquo maiore detrimento, in Hadrianos Fines usque decurrit. Hic vero bifariam scissus, minor pars ad dextram flectens ipsam pene Hadriam adiit, ac priusquam Pelagus attingat, duobus Ostiis in Mare elabitur. Id quod Volana propinquum est Abbatis vocatur, reliquum vero Gotium. Maioris Fluminis Ostium, quod Hadriae finitrum, in mare decurrit, Pornaces Adcola appellant. Haec Sabellicus: quibus consimilia traduntur ab Volaterrano lib. iv. Comment. Vrbanorum. Videndus etiam Rubeus Ravennatium Histor. lib. i. cap. vi. De Pado sic universim Facius Vbertus lib. iii. Cant. xi: Lo Maggior Serpe, c' habbia quella Terra, Ridano è, che nasce sù inde l'osso, Che con trenta Figliuoli nel mar si ferra. Entra come Coniglio, e và nascosso Nel suo camino, e quando suor riesce Torbido corre, infino al suo ripasso. Nel Gemine, & nel Cancro, semper cresce, Adorna il suo bel letto al quanto d'oro, Benche ad haveri i spesso all' huom' incresce.
units.tr: On the Seven Mouths of the Po Sabellicus is very clear, in book i of his Venetian History. Having shown that Eortum near Ravenna can be called one of the Mouths of the Po, he goes on: The remaining part, and by far the greater (of the Po), runs in a nearly straight course from Alberto down into the sea. Its principal mouth, which they call Adcola, was once called Vatrenus after the river that flows into it. The Ferrarese part of Eveortius, without losing its strength, runs down into the sea with the same rush of water with which it leaves the city, and they call its mouth Volane. Between this and the principal mouth they have the Comacine Lagoons, or rather a harbour, which they call Magna-vacca. But those are estuaries of the sea, as the crystallised salt suggests. I return to that first cutting of the river, which I said was made a little below the walls of Ficarolo. I do not think it is recent, nor was it the work of King Robert of Naples or of Francis Petrarch, the Italian (Blondus asserts that the division of the Po did not exist at all in their time), but of Polybius, a man of great authority, who records that the Po then flowed into the Adriatic by two mouths. Padusa and Volane, which certainly belong to that river we mentioned just now, are not in doubt. But now I return to the rest of the river, which, bending to the left and without any great loss, runs on as far as the Adriatic borders. There it is split in two. The smaller part, turning to the right, almost reaches the Adriatic itself and, before it touches the open sea, flows out into it by two mouths. The one near Volana is called the Abbatis, and the other Gotium. The mouth of the greater river, which borders the Adriatic, runs into the sea, and they call it Pornaces Adcola. So far Sabellicus. Similar things are handed down by Volaterranus, book iv of his Commentaries on Urbanus. Rubeus, History of the Ravennese, book i, chapter vi, should also be consulted. Concerning the Po in general, Facio Uberti in book iii, canto xi, speaks thus: "The greatest serpent that this land possesses is the Po, which rises up from the Osso mountain, and with thirty sons plunges into the sea. It enters like a rabbit and goes hidden along its course, and when it emerges it runs muddy all the way to its outlet. In Gemini and in Cancer it always grows; it adorns its fair bed with a little gold, though it often irks men to have it." The poet read in the ancient writers that the Po sends thirty rivers into the Adriatic, a point made by Pliny, book iii, chapter xvi, Solinus, chapter vii, and others who record it in memory.

units.la: Quod de xxx canit Filiis, legerat Poëta apud Antiquos Scriptores, Plinium lib. iii. cap. xvi, Solinum cap. vii, & alios, qui Padum xxx Fluvios in Mare Hadriaticum deferre memoriae produnt. Ego supra L. memini me numerare, ijs exceptis, qui Confluentibus illi confluunt. Non omnes recensebo. Magni hoc esset laboris, exigui igni fructus. Præcipuos dabo. Provomuntur ex Apennini latere, versus dextram Padi ripam celebriores, Tanarus, Scrivia, Trebia, Tarus, Parma, Lenza, Secia, Panarus, Rhenus, Santernus, Senius, & alij. A Padi Fonte secundum Cursum ejus descendenti, post Vraytam, Mayram, Oranam, aliosque, occurrit, septimo quasi loco, Tanarus, qui hodie Tanaro. Plinius lib. iii. cap. xvi ex Apennino: Strabo ex Ligurum Alpibus, (quod idem) iaci tradit. Fons illi modica in Valle copiosus, tribus primum dimanans Rivisi qui jactus sagittæ spatio prolapti ad Convallis exitum coeuntes, unum creant Flumen: pergentque per angustas Montium fauces & altas rupes in planiciem postea effusus, collectis xii (quamquam xxx scripserit Sabellicus lib. iv Ennead. vi) Torrentibus, quatuor una, octo altera ripa (inter quos Pev, Stura, Porbus, Tom, Bellus, Ler, & Vrba vel Orbs; Vrbem habet Claudianus de Bello Getico ex Conjectura Abrahami Ortelij) tandem in Padum influit. Aurum gignit: quo conflatum Torquem maximi precij, Volaterranus lib. iv Commentar. Vrban. se vidisse scribit: ab Antonio Trotto Alexandrino, Equite Aurato, gestari solitum. Qui huic sæculo Scrivia, putat Georgius Merula in sua Montisferrati descriptione Tisum dici Iornandi; Hiriam Diacono lib. xvi ad Histor. Eutrop. Majoranum ibi occisum scribentibus. Ingenti cum fragore per Montes præcipitatus, eos magna vi dirumpit. Post Coronem inde, Scapham, Copam, Versam, & alios, Trebia se offert. Trebia Livio, Silio, Plinio, aliisque, Tρεβια Straboni. Initium juxta Montem Brunum in Apennino prope Cœnobium Sandaligerulorum, instituti D. Augustini tres Aquulæ duplices creant, & quingentis fere passibus prolapsæ coeuntes: unde post Amnis à Bobio in Agrum Placentinum descendens, ut Strabo quoque scribit, ultra Placentiam, Æmiliam secat Viam, ubi Ponte lateritio jungitur, Avanteque Torrente auctus, in Padum se exonerat. Occurrit hinc, Nuram, Clavennam, Lardam, cui Longina miscetur, Alfenam, Rigosam, aliosque transgressis Tarus, Plinio notus, Taro hodieque. Oritur Apennino juxta Zazen, & intervallo P. M. V; ab Urbe Parma fluens, Spurcana suscepto, Pado conjungitur. Ex hoc ad Iuliam Augustam Parmam Coloniam duxit Fossam nobilem Scaurus. Parma mox sequitur, qui ex nominato sæpe Monte supra Belvederium scaturiens, inde interrupta Via Æmilia, Parmaque Urbe Suburbiis divisa, in Padum defluit. Mirum ab Nemine Veterum esse nominatum. Incolam habet Lurnum, a quo oppidum ibi, ut quidam volunt, Colurnum tamquam Caput Lurni. Qui Lenza vel Lencia, Boiorum Limes, Nicia Plinio vocatur: Male & contra Plinianum ordinem, Nicram Plinij Cognatus & Gaudentius Merula interpretantur Nuram. Nura enim inter Trebiam & Tarum hodie: quum Nicia apud Plinium inter Tarum & Gabellum. Sic Plinio dicitur, qui nunc Secia, vel, ut alij scribunt, Sicia. Viam Æmiliam interrumpit. Panarus Livio lib. xi i Plinioq; lib. iii, Scultenna vocatur. In aliis Libris est Scutelnas. Σκυτέλνας appellatur Straboni. Ptolemæus eius, ut multorum hoc tractu, non meminit. Bernardinus Corius in vernaculis historijs Pugnam Rotaris cum Theodoro Exarcho narrans, Amnem hunc Aemilium vocat, cognominatque Scultennam ex Paullo Fortean Diacono; sed ei non Aemilius, verum Scultenna Aemilia (hanc sane Viam secat) dicitur. Appellationem antiquam Scultenna supra Viam Æmiliam nunc quoque retinet: infra in Panari mutavit. Scultenna Incola Fluvius est, qui Santurnum Frontino lib. ii Strategemat. Mutinam secans. Fuit & his locis Ἀαβινῶν, ad quem constituisse iii Viros R.P.C. Provinciasq: inter se distribuisse tradit Appianus lib. iv Civilium. Putat Niger esse, qui hodie Fromigo. Qui Reno vernacule, Plinio Rhenus est; Parvus Rhenus ad differentiam Germanici, Silio lib. viii. Nascitur ultra Porrectæ Fontem in Apennino, infra Pistorium, ut notat Leander; unde descendens propter Porrectæ Balnea, quorum Aquis augetur, deinde per Montes præceps ad alterum ab Urbe Bononia lapidem accedit, perque Campos late diffusus, Agri plurimum vastat; præsertim Autumnalibus Mensibus, quum Imbrium frequentia maxime solet extumescere; denique supra Ferrariam millibus quatuor in Padum exit. Rhenum hunc Calamos generare tradit Plinius lib. xvi. cap. xxxvi ii, quibus ad sagittas nulli alij sint aptioris, quod plurima ijs Medulla insit, Pondusque volucre, contra Flatus quoque pervicax libra. Post Savenam, Idicem (qui Ifex in Itineraria Tabula) Schiesam, Santernus est, qui Plinio Vaternus: Vaternus Martiali lib. iii. Prius Padum augebat, in Ostium eius influens, Eridanum antea, scribente Plinio, dictum, & ab aliis Spinetieum, ab Urbe Spina, qux quæ juxta fuit. Vatrenus adeo post ætatem ejusdem Plinij Cursum immutavit, ut hoc tempore quingentis ab Failla Zilio la pass. in Padum cadat, ostio xx fere millibus ab illo Vetere distando. Nascitur Vatrenus Apennino, in Silva Rhodigina, longa P. M. x; perque Foro-Cornelien-sem Agrum descendens, Æmiliam Viam intersecat, duobus ab Luco milliaribus. Semur ex Apennino, P. M V ab Alpibus, juxta Tortum (ita locum ibi Adcolæ vocant) oriens, Viam Æmiliam intersecat, & in Paduam Paludem defluit, ubi Silva Lucina est, & Futinianum, Calcagninorum Comitum ex Ferraria Cattellum. Ignorare nolo Lectorem Fluvios, quos hactenus commemoravi ex Apennino proiectos, plerosque aliis nominibus in Itineraria Tabula expressi, neque alios etiam conjici. Sunt illi, ut à Padi Fonte oriuntur, & quo modo 10 inibi scribuntur, recensam, Fevos, Lato, Lala, Varusa, Berfala, Odubria, Hadra, Nigella, Rigonus (non dubito, quin sit Rhenus, de quo paullo ante) Pasla, Saternus (proculdubio qui Vatrenus Antiquioribus) Animæ, Ifex (qui Idex hodie, si ordo pateretur) Siarus: de quibus, facta etiam cum Superioribus commissione, quid dicam? Non liquet.
units.tr: What the poet sings of the thirty sons he had read in the ancient writers, such as Pliny, Book 3, chapter 16, Solinus, chapter 7, and others, who record that the Po carries thirty rivers into the Adriatic Sea. I remember that I myself have counted more than fifty, leaving out those which flow into its tributaries. I shall not list them all; that would be great labour for little profit. I shall give the chief ones. From the flank of the Apennines, on the right bank of the Po, the more famous ones are: Tanarus, Scrivia, Trebia, Tarus, Parma, Lenza, Secia, Panarus, Rhenus, Santernus, Senius, and others. Descending from the source of the Po in its course, after the Vraytam, Mayram, Oranam and others, there comes, about seventh in order, the Tanarus, which today is the Tanaro. Pliny, Book 3, chapter 16, says it comes from the Apennines; Strabo says it is thrown from the Alps of the Ligurians, which is the same thing. Its source is copious in a small valley, first pouring out from three springs which, after running the distance of a arrow's flight, meet at the exit of the valley and make one river. It continues through narrow mountain gorges and high cliffs, and afterwards pours out into the plain, having gathered twelve torrents (although Sabellicus, Book 4, Ennead 6, writes thirty): four on one bank and eight on the other (among them the Pev, Stura, Porbus, Tom, Bellus, Ler, and the Vrba or Orbs; Claudian, in his On the Getic War, has Urbem, by the conjecture of Abraham Ortelius). At last it flows into the Po. It produces gold, and Volaterranus, Book 4 of his Commentaries on Urbanus, writes that he saw a necklace of the greatest value made from it, which was customarily worn by Antonio Trotto of Alessandria, a knight of the Golden Spur. The one which in this age is the Scrivia, Georgius Merula in his description of Montferrat thinks is called Tisum by Jordanes; writers who record that Majorian was killed there call it Hiria (Paul the Deacon, Book 16, on the History of Eutropius). Hurled down through the mountains with a great roar, it breaks them apart with great force. After the Corona, and then the Scapha, Copa, Versa and others, the Trebia presents itself. The Trebia is named in Livy, Silius, Pliny and others, and by Strabo as Τρεβια [Trebia]. Its source lies near Mount Bruno in the Apennines, near the monastery of the Sandaligerulorum of the Order of St Augustine, where three double springs form it; after running nearly five hundred paces they meet and make one stream. Thence, as Strabo also writes, the river, descending from Bobbio into the territory of Piacenza, beyond Piacenza cuts the Via Aemilia, where it is joined by a brick bridge; it is increased by the Avante torrent and empties itself into the Po. From here there run down the Nura, Clavenna, Larda, which is joined by the Longina, the Alfena, Rigosa and others; and across these, the Tarus, known to Pliny, which is still the Taro today. It rises in the Apennines near Zazo, at a distance of five Roman miles; flowing past the city of Parma, it is joined by the Spurcana, and then joins the Po. From here Scaurus led a famous ditch from the Via Aemilia to the Colony of Julia Augusta Parma. Next follows the Parma, which springs from the often-named mountain above Belvedere, and from there, the Via Aemilia being interrupted and the city of Parma divided by its suburbs, flows down into the Po. It is strange that no ancient writer has named it. It has a tributary, the Lurnum, from which the town there, as some think, is called Colurnum, as if it were the head of the Lurnum. The Lenza or Lencia, the boundary of the Boii, is called Nicia by Pliny; it is wrongly, and contrary to Pliny's order, that Pliny's kinsman and Gaudentius Merula explain Nicra as the Nura. For the Nura today lies between the Trebia and the Tarus, whereas in Pliny the Nicia lies between the Tarus and the Gabellus. The river which is now the Secia, or as others write, the Sicia, is named thus by Pliny. It cuts the Via Aemilia. The Panarus is called Scultenna by Livy, Book 41, and by Pliny, Book 3. In other books it is Scutelnas; Strabo calls it Σκυτέλνας [Skytelnas]. Ptolemy does not mention it, as he does not mention many in this region. Bernardino Corio, in his vernacular histories, narrating the battle of Rotari with Theodore the Exarch, calls this river the Aemilius, and surnames it Scultenna from Paul the Deacon; but it is not called the Aemilius by him, rather the Scultenna Aemilia, which indeed cuts this road. The ancient name Scultenna is still retained above the Via Aemilia; below, it has changed to Panari. The Scultenna is a river of the region, which Frontinus, Book 2 of the Stratagems, calls the Santurnus, cutting through Modena. In these places there was also the Ἀαβινῶν [Aabinon], at which Appian, Book 4 of the Civil Wars, records that three commissioners of the Roman Senate and People set up and divided the provinces among themselves. Niger thinks it is what is today the Fromigo. The one called the Reno in the vernacular is the Rhenus in Pliny; the Parvus Rhenus, to distinguish it from the German, in Silius, Book 8. It rises in the Apennines beyond the source of the Porrecta, below Pistoia, as Leander notes; descending from there past the baths of the Porrecta, whose waters augment it, it then comes headlong down through the mountains to a point one mile from the city of Bologna, and spreads widely through the plains, doing great damage to the fields, especially in the autumn months, when it is usually most swollen by frequent rains; finally, four thousand paces above Ferrara, it flows into the Po. Pliny, Book 16, chapter 38, reports that this Rhenus produces reeds, which are better suited to arrows than any others, because they have much pith and a light weight, yet a stubborn strength against the wind. After the Savena, Idex (which is the Ifex in the Itinerary Table), and the Schiesa, comes the Santernus, which in Pliny is the Vaternus; the Vaternus is in Martial, Book 3. Formerly it augmented the Po, flowing into its mouth, which, as Pliny writes, was called the Eridanus and by others the Spinetic, from the city of Spina, which was near it. The Vatrenus has so changed its course since the time of this same Pliny that now, five hundred paces from the Failla Zilio, it falls into the Po at a mouth about twenty miles from that old one. The Vatrenus rises in the Apennines, in the Rhodigine forest, ten Roman miles long; descending through the territory of Forum Cornelii, it intersects the Via Aemilia two miles from the grove. The Semur rises from the Apennines, five Roman miles from the Alps, near Tortum (the Adcolae call the place there thus), cuts the Via Aemilia, and flows down into the Paduan marsh, where there is the Lucina forest and the Futinian, the Cattel of the Counts Calcagnini of Ferrara. I do not wish the reader to be unaware that the rivers I have so far mentioned as thrown out from the Apennines are mostly expressed under other names in the Itinerary Table, nor that others are not even conjectured. These are, as they arise from the source of the Po, and as they are written in the same place: Fevos, Lato, Lala, Varusa, Berfala, Odubria, Hadra, Nigella, Rigonus (I do not doubt that it is the Rhenus I mentioned a little earlier), Pasla, Saternus (undoubtedly the one the older writers called Vatrenus), Animae, Ifex (which is today the Idex, if the order allowed), Siarus. What shall I say about these, even when the comparison is made with those above? It is not clear.

units.la: Fluvios hactenus, quos Apenninus generat, indicavi: videamus quos eiaculentur versus Padum Alpes. Primas inter eos obtinent, Veteribus etiam plerique celebrati, Doria Riparia, Stura, Orcus, Doria Baltea, Senza, Ticinus, Lambrus Addua, Ollius, Mincius, Tartarus. Post nonnullos enim obscurioris nominis Fluvios, Pallam, Cissolam, Sangonem, & alios, principis loci, famamque meritus occurrit Doria, Fluvius Plinio 20 notus; qui quum duplex fuerit, Antiqui, qui nobis ad manum, Riparam nominarunt. Meminit Strabo lib. iv (cui Δωρια, ut Ptolemæo Δωρια) cum ex adversa parte Druentij, qui Rodano inlabitur, caput tollere, perque Salallos & Alpes Gallia fluere scribens. Padum petit ad Taurinum: vulgo Dorietta, id est Minor Doria. Sequitur inde Stura, à Plinio etiam celebratus, Veterem appellationem hodieque servans: vestientibus ripas ejus utrimque Opidulis multis & Vicis. Malanum prætergressus offert le Orcus, vel, ut quidam efferunt, Orchus vel Orca. Plinius Morgnu nominat: M. S. Codices fanius Orgium scribunt, nec dubium quin M. hujus vocis capiti adhæserit ex præcedentis calce. Orsus est in Itineraria Tabula: sed vitiosius. Duriam, ad cujus ripam sinistram, prope confluxum cum Pado, Crescentinum 30 est opidum. Antiqui Baltheam & Matorem dixerunt, ad differentiam Superioris; ut merito duos hujus nominis Amnes, ex Alpibus in Padum decurrentes, Plinius nominarit. Hic caput elevat haud procul Hasturgia. Doria Baltia vulgo. Senza, vel, ut alij scribunt, Sesia, Sexta & Sicca, fluvius est, qui Plinio Sesites. Profluit ex Alpibus supra Burgum per Vallem Sectiam, cui nomen facit. Aliquot auctus Amnibus, inter quos Sarcis, Padum ingreditur, juxta Villam Novam. Ticinus Livio, Plinio, Silio Ticino, Polybio, Strabone, Plutarcho, Prolemæo, Stephano; Ticenus Tabulæ Itinerariæ, qui hodie Tesino: Finis hoc latere Infubrum, & Lybicorum initium. Oritur ex Monte Summano, qui nunc D. Gothardi nuncupatur unde &, in diversum tamen, eunt Renus, Rodanus Athetis, & alij. Ex illo Monte per Leponios 40 in Austrum inter præcipites rupes ad Bellinzonam opidum munitissimum fertur: inde copiosius accedit ione plurimorum Amnium ac Torrentium in Verbanum evolvitur Lacum, quem supermeat, ut Plinius auctor est lib 11 cap.cvi; ac tandem redditus per planiciem præcipua claritate Padum influit, quamquam non illa, quam ex Lacu trahit, abundantia quum derivationibus & fossis in irrigua passim exhauriatur. Tam est Aquis perlucidis, ut quidvis, etiam minimum, imo in fundo clare demonstret. Aurum quoque & Argentum ex eius arena percipitur. Piclem nobilitate est inclutus, nominatim laudatissimo Thymallo. Scribit Blondus in Italia Ticinum ex Alpibus effluentem prius Lacu Sebino, qui nunc Iseus, dein Verbano inlabi. Falso: quod clamant, cum maximum Sebino Verbanoque intercurrens 50 intervallum, tum profluens ex Sebino Ollius. Notat Livius lib. v. non procul hoc Fluvio Etruscos ab Gallis, Bellovefo Duce, fusos; item Pontem Romanos in eo Hannibalis expugnandi gratia struxisse: Præhumque juxta eum commissum, quo Patrem Scipio, qui postea Africanus, vulneratum cædi eripuit. Recipit cum alios, tum Athesim, quem Rheti Ὀτε Ὑπόουσα Itali La Mucia vocant. Influit autem Ticino paullo supra Bellizonam opidum. Lambrus Plinio notus, nomenque hodie servans, ab Eupili Lacu redditus, infra Larium in Padum defluit, Aquarum perpetua claritate
units.tr: So far I have listed the rivers that the Apennines produce. Let us now see which the Alps discharge into the Po. Among these the first place belongs to those that were also widely celebrated by the ancients: Doria Riparia, Stura, Orcus, Doria Baltea, Senza, Ticinus, Lambrus, Addua, Ollius, Mincius, Tartarus. After some rivers of less familiar name, Pallam, Cissolam, Sangonem and others, there comes the Doria, a river of leading rank and renown, known to Pliny. Since there are two of them, the ancients named the one nearer to us Riparia. Strabo mentions it in book iv (where it is Δωρια, as it is in Ptolemy), writing that it rises on the opposite side from the Druentia, which flows into the Rhone, and runs through the Salluvii and the Alps of Gaul. It makes for the Po at Turin. Commonly it is called Dorietta, that is, Minor Doria. Next follows the Stura, also celebrated by Pliny and keeping its old name even today; many small towns and villages line its banks on both sides. Passing Malanum, it presents itself as the Orcus, or, as some write it, Orchus or Orca. Pliny calls it Morgnu; the manuscripts more often write Orgium, and there is no doubt that the M of this word has clung to it from the end of the preceding word. Orsus is the form in the Itinerary Table, but it is more faulty. Then the Duria, on whose left bank, near its confluence with the Po, stands the town of Crescentinum. The ancients called the Doria Baltea and the Matora, to distinguish it from the upper one; hence Pliny rightly named two rivers of this name that run down from the Alps into the Po. This one rises not far from Hasturgia. It is commonly called the Doria Baltia. The Senza, or, as others write, Sesia, Sexta or Sicca, is a river which Pliny calls the Sesites. It flows from the Alps above Borgo, through the Valle Sesia, which gives it its name. Fed by several tributaries, among them the Sarcis, it enters the Po near Villanova. The Ticinus is named by Livy, Pliny, Silius (Ticinus), Polybius, Strabo, Plutarch, Ptolemy and Stephanus; the Itinerary Table has Ticenus, and today it is the Tesino. It is the boundary on this side of the Insubres and the beginning of the Lybici. It rises from Mount Summanus, now called Mount St Gotthard, from which the Rhine, the Rhone and others also rise, though they flow in different directions. From that mountain it runs southward through the Leponti, between steep cliffs, to the strongly fortified town of Bellinzona. From there it receives the waters of many more rivers and torrents, and rolls into Lake Verbanus (Lake Maggiore), which it crosses, as Pliny, book ii, chapter 106, reports. Finally, returned to the plain, it flows into the Po with especial brightness, though not with the abundance it has when it leaves the lake, since it is drawn off in many places by channels and ditches for irrigation. Its waters are so clear that anything, even the smallest object, can be seen plainly on the bottom. Gold and silver are also collected from its sand. It is renowned for the excellence of its fish, especially the highly praised thymallus. Blondus, in his Italia, writes that the Ticinus flows out of the Alps, first through Lake Sebinus, now called Iseo, and then into Verbanus. This is false, since Sebinus and Verbanus are separated by a very large distance, and it is the Ollius, which flows out of Sebinus, that does so. Livy, book v, notes that near this river the Etruscans were routed by the Gauls under their leader Bellovesus; he also records that the Romans built a bridge over it in order to attack Hannibal, and that a cavalry battle was fought near it in which Scipio, later called Africanus, rescued his father from being cut down after he had been wounded. It receives, besides others, the Athesis, which the Rhaetians call Ὀτε Ὑπόουσα and the Italians La Mucia. It joins the Ticino a little above the town of Bellinzona. The Lambrus, known to Pliny and keeping its name today, is drawn from Lake Eupili and flows down past Lario into the Po, shining with a constant clarity of waters and abounding in an excellent supply of fish.

units.la: Sirtrans tate nitens, copiaque Piscium optimorum abundans. Ex Lacu Lugano Lambrum effundi, scripsit imprudenter Blondus lib. xxi. Addua vel Abdua (variante scriptura, Posteriori Priorem praefero) Plinio Tacitoque nominatur, qui A'δδας Polybio & Straboni; Adda Vulgo. Cenomanos dividit ab Insubribus. Pater illi Mons Braulius. Notat inconsideratius Strabo nasci ex Adula Monte. Redditus è Lacu Lario, cuius Aquas supermeat, per planiciem in Padum tendit, deferens secum cum aliis, ut Piscilavonem, Mesram, Liram, Tartenem, Lecium orcum, Brembum, Serimortum (veniam peto si peccem in ordine tum Serium qui in Montibus supra Bergomum ortus, perque Seriana fluens, hibernis mensibus Cuniculis quibusdam se condit, rursusque juxta Cremam copiose exoriens, tandem in Addauam inlabitur: aestate tamen, liquescentibus ardore Solis Montium nivibus, adeo solet augere & abundare, ut non solum Meatus subterraneos impleat, sed etiam supra terram fluat perpetuo. Ollius Plinio, qui vernacule Oglio. Cernuntur in hoc flumine juxta Palatiolum Castrum frequens & lautum, ubi Pons Amnis transitum iungit, magno numero Excipuli seu Loculi confecti fabricatique Viminibus, in quo annuo certo tempore, deferentibus Aquis, Anguillae glomeratae cadunt, quae mirabili numero extractae saliuntur. Ortum eius investigare operosum. Opinio recepta est, duos modicos rivos ex Lacu Frigidulpho, qui inter Alpes est, profluere, unum ad dextram nomen Frigidulphi retinere, Olliuque tandem iungi alterum ad laevam in alium Amnem praecipitari, eumque ab Adcolis Olly principum constitui. Alii alia adferunt. In Ilcum Lacum influit, ubi Pisonum opidum; ecfusus in planiciem passim derivationibus exhauritur: quibus irrigua Brixiani & Cremonensis Agri sic adaquantur, ut ex icinnis atque calculosis optima benignaque fiant. Aquarum Olly perpetua claritas, nec ullo umquam tempore deficiens. Brixianum Agrum ab Cremonensi & Bergomate hac parte seiungit. Recipit alios supra xxxvii Amnes: inter quos celebriores dextra quidem Alcus, Deiwona, Comasfius: sinistra vero Rinus, Sanazara, Talabia, Grinia, Mella, Nauilio, Clusius (κλυσσος Polybio lib. II: Clusis vitiose in Itineraria Tabula; Chiese vulgo) quorum tres postremi multis etiam aliis augentur Torrentibus. Mincius Virgilio, Straboni, Plinio, Vibio Sequestro, D. Augustino ad Diioscorum, & aliisque Mencio vel Mentzo hodie Italis. Lacum ingressus Benacum praecipua claritate circumdata insigni stagno Mantua, xiii inde lapide in Padum evolvitur. Non praetereundus hic Atisis: sic Veteribus appellatus, Ατισις Graecis; Atisi. Epitomae Liviana, qui Tosa hodie, Bonaventura Castiglionco, Leandro Alberto, Gaudentio Merula aliisque tellantibus. Oritur ex Monte Iacere, non procul ab modico Lacu, supra D. Gothardi Sacellum. Nobilis est Cimbrorum clade, quos ad hujus ripam in Agro Novariensi locisque finitimis, non procul Urbe Vercellarum & Pado, C. Marius cum Q. Lutatio Catulo Conlega, praeclara victoria, caesis ad ext, captisque ad ix millia, devicit. Plutarchus in Marii vita & Apophthegmat. Lutatii Catuli. Male apud Florum Athesis, qui dierum etiam nonnullorum itinere hinc distat, appellatur. Inprudentius item Xylander & Cruserus, Plutarchum interpretantes, Atisonem eius vertunt Athesim. Assisa scribitur in Itineraria Tabula pro Atisone, vel saltem Athesi. Tartarus denique capit tollit in Agro Veronensi, juxta Glanum, olim Graecianum: pergens, interque Paludes quasdam labens, in duo scinditur Brachia; quorum laevum ad Pontem Molinum decurrit, dextrum ad Turrim Mediam: tandem tribus ultra P.M. uno Cornu per Ostiae Fossam, ut Priscianus scribit, in Padum deducitur. Hinc Ostium Padi Tartarum Plinio, quod & Fossiones Philistinae, ut alibi dictum. Fossam Philistinam describit Priscianus, quem dixi, lib. i. Antiquit. Ferrar. Quos hactenus ab Alpibus in Padum provolvi fluvios ex Plinio ceterisque notavi, aliis indicat nominibus Itineraria Tabula, uti de adversis etiam paullo ante monui; vel quod aliis appellationibus noti essent Theodosii Imperatoris principatu, vel quod alii sint ab Superioribus, vel denique quod depravata ipsorum sit ibi scriptura. Nam certi quid statuere nequeo. Sunt autem Orsus Adem cum Orco) Fetnelus, Victus, Novaria (an Maior Durias?) Ticenus (alias Ticinus) Ambrus (certum, Lambrum esse) Vbertus, Vmatta: qui sequuntur Medoscus & Luquentia, male in eadem Tabula in Padum traiuntur. Non autem Amnes tantum Apenninos Alpinosque Navigabiles, ut hactenus vidimus, capit Padus; sed Lacus quoque immensi in eum se exonerant, quales sunt Verbanus, Larius, Sebinus, Benacus, de quibus suo loco.
units.tr: Shining with a constant clarity of waters and abounding in an excellent supply of fish. Blondus carelessly wrote, in book xxi, that the Lambrus pours out of Lake Lugano. The Addua or Abdua (I prefer the latter reading to the former) is named by Pliny and Tacitus; Polybius and Strabo call it Ἄδδας; today it is the Adda. It divides the Cenomani from the Insubres. Its father is Mount Braulius. Strabo was too careless in saying that it rises from Mount Adula. It is drawn from Lake Lario, whose waters it passes over, and runs through the plain into the Po, carrying with it, among others, the Piscilavo, Mesra, Lira, Tarten, Lecius Orcus, Brembus and Serimortus (let me be forgiven if I err in the order). The Serius, which rises in the mountains above Bergamo and flows through the Val Seriana, hides itself in winter in certain underground channels, and then rises again in abundance near Crema, finally flowing into the Addua. In summer, however, when the snows of the mountains melt under the heat of the sun, it is accustomed to swell and overflow to such an extent that it not only fills its underground passages but also flows continuously over the surface of the earth. The Ollius, known to Pliny, is called Oglio in the vernacular. In this river, near the fortified and well-appointed little town of Palazzolo, where a bridge joins the two banks of the stream, can be seen a great number of wicker traps or baskets, made of osiers, into which, at a certain time every year, when the waters are high, eels gather and fall, and are caught in astonishing numbers and leap about. To investigate its source is a laborious task. The accepted opinion is that two small streams flow out of Lake Frigidulphus, which lies among the Alps: one on the right keeps the name Frigidulphus and at last joins the Ollius; the other on the left is thrown into another river, and that river, the inhabitants say, is the principal source of the Olly. Others put forward other views. It flows into Lake Iseo, where the town of Pisogne lies; poured out onto the plain, it is drained in many places by channels, and by these the irrigated lands of the Brescian and Cremonese territories are watered, so that from being barren and stony they become rich and fertile. The Ollius has a constant clarity of waters, never failing at any time. On this side it separates the Brescian territory from the Cremonese and the Bergamask. It receives more than thirty-seven other rivers, the more notable of which are, on the right, the Alcus, Deiwona and Comasfius, and on the left the Rinus, Sanazara, Talabia, Grinia, Mella, Nauilio and Clusius (Κλυσσος in Polybius, book ii; Clusis wrongly in the Itinerary Table; Chiese in the vernacular). The last three of these are increased by many other torrents. The Mincius, called Mencio or Mentzo by the Italians today, is named by Virgil, Strabo, Pliny, Vibius Sequester, St Augustine on Dioscorus, and others. Having entered Lake Benacus, it passes through the famous marsh beside Mantua, and after thirteen miles flows into the Po. The Atisis must not be passed over here: so called by the ancients, Ατισις by the Greeks, Atisi in the epitome of Livy; today it is the Tosa, as Bonaventura Castiglione, Leandro Alberti, Gaudentius Merula and others testify. It rises from Mount Iacere, not far from a small lake, above the chapel of St Gotthard. It is famous for the defeat of the Cimbri, whom Gaius Marius, together with his colleague Quintus Lutatius Catulus, overcame in a splendid victory on its bank, in the territory of Novara and the neighbouring places, not far from the city of Vercelli and the Po, when about 120,000 had been slain and 60,000 captured. See Plutarch in the life of Marius and in the Apophthegms of Lutatius Catulus. It is wrongly called Athesis by Florus, though it is some days' journey distant from it. Xylander and Cruserus, interpreting Plutarch, carelessly translate his Atisonem as Athesim. Assisa is written in the Itinerary Table for Atisone, or at least for Athesi. Finally the Tartarus rises in the territory of Verona, near Gualo, formerly Graecianum; running on, and flowing among certain marshes, it divides into two branches, of which the left runs down to the Ponte Molino and the right to the Torre di Media; at last, three miles beyond the Po, with one horn, it is led into the Po through the Ostia ditch, as Priscian writes. Hence the mouth of the Po is called the Tartarum by Pliny, and also the Fossiones Philistinae, as I have said elsewhere. Priscian describes the Fossa Philistina, as I mentioned, in book i of his Antiquities of Ferrara. Of the rivers that I have so far noted as flowing from the Alps into the Po, from Pliny and others, the Itinerary Table gives other names, as I also warned earlier about the rivers flowing from the opposite side: either because they were known by other names in the reign of the Emperor Theodosius, or because some of them are from earlier writers, or finally because the writing there is corrupt. For I cannot determine anything certain. The following are the names there: Orsus (the same as the Orcus), Fetnelus, Victus, Novaria (or is it the Greater Duria?), Ticenus (otherwise Ticinus), Ambrus (certainly Lambrus), Ubertus, Umatta*; and the ones that follow, Medoscus and Luquentia, are wrongly carried into the Po on the same table. But the Po does not receive only the navigable rivers of the Apennines and Alps, as we have so far seen; immense lakes also empty themselves into it, such as Verbanus, Larius, Sebinus and Benacus, of which in their proper place.

units.la: De Pado, Fluviisque, suas in ipsum Vndas deponentibus, hactenus: Addam reliquos, qui ad Padi ripam Septemtrionaliorem ad Italiam pertinent, in Hadriaticum Sinum se exonerantes. Sunt illi, ut plerosque cum Antiquis nominem, in Marka Tarvisana, Athesis, Atedoacus duplex, Anassus, Silis, Liquentia: in Foro Iulio, Romatinus, Tilaventus, Sontius, Frigidus, Natiso, Aesa, Turrus: in Istria denique Formio, Draconia, Quietus, Lemus, Arsia. Athesis Virgilio in Bucolicis & Æneide, Livio, Plinio, Auctorique, qui Panegyricum scripsit Constantino: Ἄδιγις autem Straboni: qui Italis hodie L'Adice, vel L'Adese; Germanis Etsch. Tradit Plinius Athesim ex Tridentinis Alpibus profluere. Initio perquam exilis lapsu vim magnam Aquarum colligit, accedentibus passim multis Amnibus: subter Bolzanum ad meridiem versus rapido se cursu flectit: dein ab Tridento lenius nonnihil per planiciem evolvitur; at mox iterum emensis campis inter montium angustias tanta cum violentia sævit, ut omnibus, quafluit, locis infeste minari videatur: eaque vehementia per Veronam præcipitat, infra quam in duo flumina diducitur; uno, quo Paludes petit, altero, quo in mare pertingit ad Fossiones, haud ignobilem Portum. Plura apud Leandrum. Ab Fonte Veronam usque ratibus navigabilis non est ob rapiditatem: Trabibus autem navigatur. Nam ingentes Larices Abietesque cum Alleribus maximis, aliaque prægrandia ligna compacta Tridentinis ex montibus eo deferunt: Verona porro usque ad Fossiones optime navigatur. De Athesi sic scribit Sabellicus lib. Hist. Venet. 1. Athesis, ex Tridentinis Montibus lapsus, Veronam mediam intersecat: inde infra Leniacum ad Caslagnarium derivatus, pars illa, qua Vicum perstringit, ad dextram flectens, Tartaro ex suis stagnis emerso occurrit, qui una mixtus non multum procedunt; quum alteram Athesis partem ad Maloperam majore alveo abruptam adsequuntur, atque ita uno ex pluribus fluminibus fit Rodigianam Polesinum a tergo claudunt: postremo in stagna dilapsi prorsus fluminum nomen amittunt: Athesi vero paululum supra Marchianam Turrim in duos Amnes divisa; dexter Lendenariam Rodigiumque perfluens, priusquam ad Caput Aggeris sit ventum, cognatis Aquis, quasi in gratiam reversus, se placide insinuat: hic mixto alveo per plagas & Paludes decurrens, ubi locum, quem Turrim Novam vocant, attigit, novissime duobus Ostiis in mare evolvitur: quorum dextrum Fossiones vocant; laevum vero Brundulum. Scribit in Cosmographia sua Sebastianus Munsterus, Italiam delineans, incredibilem cum aliorum Fluminum, tum præcipue Athesis Inundationem incidisse in Kalendas Novembris anni ab Christo nato 1 xc: addens maiorem non fuisse post Noachi tempora. Evagantem extra Alveum suum Athesim expertus sum ipse non sine magno vitæ periculo, mense Septembri, anno MDXXXV, quum cum CL. V. Petro Brederodio comitatus in Italiam proficiscerer. Torellus in Historia Veronensi Athesis Ἀτεσις vult esse Ptolemæi. Quibusdam idem etiam cum Athesi putatur esse Ἀδριας, qui apud Stephanum, Eustathium, Itacium in Lycophronem, & alios. Incolas habet plurimos: inter quos dextram quidem ripam petunt Pymna, Anagusa, Sulsum, sinistram vero Kyencza (auctus cum aliis, tum Tallero) Nevefus, Persona notus mihi ab Vita discrimine. Connumerandus etiam Posteriorum, Athesi se miscentium, Classi Vigisonus: qui male, quod monent Hermolaus Barbarus & Bernardinus Scardeonius, alique, Togisonus apud Plinium dicitur: In hodiernum enim diem Lacum esse, qui Usigiolo cognomine, Vigacolo nuncupatur aliis. Succedit illi versus Ortum & Mare Hadriaticum Lacus Anguillaria, per Vigisonem Superiori quasi adnexus. Vigisonus hodie vernacula lingua Sciocco vocatur, notante Leandro Alberto. Ad reliquos, qui in mare Hadriaticum se exonerant, Fluvios venio. Medoacus, qui Μεδοακος Straboni, duplex apud Plinium: Maior, qui Leandro aliisque Brenta; Minor, qui Bacchiglio. Major Brentesia vocatur Auctori de Progenie Augusti. Brintam novit hoc etiam loco Fortunatus. Manet antiquum Medoacus (cuius etiam mentio apud Livium; quemque Medoacum nominat Itineraria Tabula) nomen hodie in Metamauco, Venetiarum Portu. Brenta principium ab tribus simul Lacubus, decimo fere ab Tridento lapide, constituit, ipse aliquando meis oculis vidi. Bacchiglio, quem Bambilonem quidam Latine vocant, ab Alpibus, quemadmodum Brenta profluit Tridentinis, per planiciem ad Urbem Vicentiam: eamque percurrit. De cursu tam Brenta, quem Bacchiglionis, tale Schema posuit in Apodemica Methodo CL. V. Theodorus Zuingerus:
units.tr: Having dealt with the Po and the rivers that empty their waters into it, I will now add the remaining rivers that flow into the Adriatic Gulf and belong to the north bank of the Po. These are, to name most of them as the ancients did: in the March of Treviso, the Athesis, the two Atedoacus, the Anassus, the Silis and the Liquentia; in Friuli, the Romatinus, the Tilaventus, the Sontius, the Frigidus, the Natiso, the Aesa and the Turrus; and finally in Istria, the Formio, the Draconia, the Quietus, the Lemus and the Arsia. The Athesis is named by Virgil in the Bucolics and the Aeneid, by Livy, Pliny and the author of the panegyric delivered to Constantine. Strabo calls it Ἄδιγις [Adigis]; today the Italians call it l'Adice or l'Adese, and the Germans Etsch. Pliny says the Athesis rises in the Alps of Trent. It starts as a very slender stream, but gathers great volume as many rivers join it here and there. Below Bolzano it turns southward with a rapid course; then, from Trent, it flows more gently for a while across the plain; but soon, having crossed the plains again, it rushes between narrow mountain passes with such violence that it seems to threaten every place it flows past. With this fury it hurtles through Verona, and below that city it divides into two rivers: one, by which it makes for the marshes, and the other, by which it reaches the sea at the Fossiones, a not inconsiderable port. More on this in Leandro. From its source to Verona the river is not navigable because of its rapids, but it is used for floating timber: huge larches and firs, with very large logs and other massive timber bound together, are brought down to it from the Trentine mountains. From Verona down to the Fossiones, however, it is very well navigated. Sabellicus writes of the Athesis thus in book 1 of his History of Venice: "The Athesis, having fallen from the mountains of Trent, cuts Verona in half; then below Leniacum it is diverted toward Caslagnarium, and that part which skirts Vicum, bending to the right, meets the Tartarus, which has emerged from its own pools; mixed with it, they do not travel far, when they overtake the other part of the Athesis, which has broken off with a larger channel toward Maloperas; and so from several rivers one river is formed, which closes off the Polesine of Rovigo at its rear. Finally they flow into the pools and entirely lose the name of rivers. But the Athesis, divided into two streams a little above the Tower of Marchiana, the right branch, flowing past Lendenaria and Rovigo, before it reaches the head of the embankment, having returned as it were into favour with its kindred waters, quietly insinuates itself; here, flowing on with a mingled channel through the plains and marshes, when it reaches the place which they call the New Tower, it finally empties into the sea by two mouths: the right of these they call the Fossiones, the left Brundulum." In his Cosmography, describing Italy, Sebastian Münster writes that an incredible flood of other rivers, but especially of the Athesis, occurred on the Kalends of November in the year 1 (sic) xc [of our era], adding that there had been no greater since the time of Noah. I myself experienced the Athesis overflowing its bed, not without great danger to my life, in September 1535, when I was travelling to Italy in the company of the most distinguished Peter Brederode. Torelli, in his History of Verona, holds that the Athesis is the Ἀτεσις [Atesis] of Ptolemy. Some think that the same river is the Ἀδριας [Adrias] mentioned by Stephanus, Eustathius, Itacius on Lycophron, and others. It has very many tributaries. Among these, the Pymna, the Anagusa and the Sulsum join it on the right bank, and on the left the Kyencza (increased by others, and by the Tallerus), the Nevefus, and the Persona, known to me from my own peril of life. Among the later tributaries that mingle with the Athesis, the Vigisonus should also be counted in the fleet: it is wrongly called Togisonus by Pliny, as Hermolaus Barbarus and Bernardinus Scardeonius and others remind us; for to this day there is a lake which some call Usigiolo and others Vigacolo. To the east and towards the Adriatic Sea, next to it, lies the Lake Anguillaria, as it were joined to the upper Vigisonus. Leandro Alberti notes that the Vigisonus is today called Sciocco in the vernacular. I come now to the remaining rivers which empty into the Adriatic Sea. The Medoacus, which is Μεδοακος [Medoakos] in Strabo, is double in Pliny: the Greater, which Leandro and others call the Brenta, and the Lesser, which is the Bacchiglione. The Greater is called the Brentesia by the author of the Genealogy of Augustus. Fortunatus also knows the Brinta in this passage. The ancient name Medoacus (which is also mentioned by Livy, and which the Itinerary Table calls the Medoacus) survives today in Metamauco, the port of Venice. The Brenta takes its beginning from three lakes at about the tenth milestone from Trent; I myself have once seen this with my own eyes. The Bacchiglione, which some call Bambilo in Latin, flows from the Alps, just as the Brenta flows from the Trentine Alps, across the plain to the city of Vicenza, and runs through it. Concerning the course of both the Brenta and the Bacchiglione, the most distinguished Theodor Zwinger has set out such a diagram in his Apodemica Methodus:
