units.la: Brenta ex Tridentinum Alpibus delapsa, Limine, quinto ab Urbe (Patavio) miliaria dividitur. Et Alveo quidem. Dextro Patavium fertur, ubi Onerarias Naves excipit. Sinistra Roffam petit. Ibi obsecto obstaculo, rursum in Alveos duos divisus. Sinistra Vicum Stratum adiit. Dextra per Brentellam Fossam Patavium fertur, et non longe a Moenibus Bacchillioni iungitur. Coniunctus viribus ad Daulum Vicum fluit: ubi rursus, opposito obice partim. Dextra Mare petit. Sinistra Mole inserviens et transmissioni Onerariorum, Lizefusinam avit, ubi obice novo deflectens (per quem Onerariae machinis in Aestuaria transmittuntur) tandem in lacunas erumpit. Laevam partim: Moenia circumluit. Urbem ingreditur. Dextram per Agrum decurrit Patavinum: Batalcam usque, ibi rursus divisus, alveo. Maiore ad laevam, Bubulentam petit, et Brentae iunctus in Mare fertur; Portum faciens Metamaunum. Minore ad dextram Montem Silicem, Atbeslem, Montem Anianum alluens, ad Fraxinum Portum perducit.
units.tr: The Brenta, descending from the Tridentine Alps, is divided at Limine, five miles from the city (Padua). On one channel it flows past Padua on the right, where it receives the cargo ships. On the left it heads for Roffa. There, a barrier is placed in its way and it is again divided into two channels. The left channel goes to Vicus Stratus. The right channel flows through the Brentella ditch to Padua and joins the Bacchiglione not far from the walls. Joined in strength, it flows to Daulus Vicus, where it is again partly checked by a barrier placed across it. The right channel makes for the sea. The left channel, serving the dam and the passage of cargo vessels, reaches Lizefusina, where a new barrier turns it aside (through which cargo is carried by machinery into the lagoons). Finally it breaks out into the lagoons. Part of it, on the left, flows around the walls. It enters the city. The right channel runs through the Paduan countryside as far as Batalca, where it divides again into channels. The larger channel, on the left, makes for Bubulenta, and joined again with the Brenta flows into the sea, forming the port of Metamaunum. The smaller channel, on the right, passes Mons Silex, Atbesla and Mons Anianus, and brings the water to the port of Fraxinum.

units.la: Bachilio, ante 10 annos Retronus dictus (ut videatur nomen Germanicum esse) ex iisdem Montibus ortus, Urbs adpropinquans, Brentellam recipit.
units.tr: The Bachiglio, called Retronus ten years ago (it seems the name is German), rises from the same mountains. As it approaches the city, it receives the Brentella.

units.la: Addit deinde idem Zuingerus, diligentissimus locorum hoc tractu praelustrator, in Medea o exonerari Musenem, Tergulam, Lavendulam, Rusticam, Margenicum, Rivos amoenissimos et fecundissimos, qui a Septemtrione suos habent Fontes ad Campum S. Petri Bembi carminibus celebratos. Adscribit item Plavicum et Kofatam, Nonianam Villam Bembi tadentem: Tesinam denique, Pudinam, Cerisonum et Scandolam, irrigationi Molisque deservientes. Certe Patavinum Territorium ita ab Medoacis, aliisque Fluviis et Amnibus passim est scissum; ut, qui quos recipiant, quique contra quos dominentur et principatum obtineant, distincte dijudicare quis nequeat. Medoacis succedit Anafus: Sic Plinio dictus, qui hodie, ut Leandro, Sabellico, Cynthio Accedensi et Ioanni Flaminio videtur, Piavi, Piave vulgo: quem tamen Tiliaventum Minus esse putat Ioannes Candidus; Brentam, Castaldus; Lugnanum Marius Niger; Stellam esse volunt alii. Plavis etiam mentio apud Diaconum et Fortunatum. Oritur Alpibus, et medius inter Fectrium Bellunumque per confragosas Valles inquietus praecipitat; nec prius mitescit, quam in apertos Campos evolutus: quamquam sic quoque citatiore cursu inter Trinos Portus, et Liquentiani in Mare defertur, ut lib. iii. de situ Urbis Venetae scribit Sabellicus. Quum in planiciem evasit, Flaminius Imolanus auctor est, iterum rapido fluxu ab D. Salvatoris Altoque Colle provectum, mox in duo Cornua scindi tantae altitudinis, ut haudquaquam vado transiri queant, sed opus sit navigio: ac dein in Mare se effundere. Plavis vel Anassi Incolae, cum aliis, sunt Varamus et Silis. Varamus apud Plinium, ut Blondus et Volaterranus censent, est, qui Calorus hodie. Hunc ex Alpibus, quos Germani habent, orientem, quinque, aut circiter, augent Torrentes. Varramus scribitur in quibusdam Plinii Codicibus, duplici R. Silis Plinio, qui vulgo Sil. Erumpit, notante eodem, ex Montibus Tauriscanis. Olim Venetiae finem initiumque Carnorum fuisse testatur idem Plinius. Liquentia Plinio, Licenna corrupte in Itineraria Tabula; qui nunc Livensa Liquetis est apud Virgilium; probante scripturam hanc Servio, improbante Erythraeo. Oritur ex Montibus Opitergini, haud longè à Palcinico, Fontibus quibusdam, qui eodem prope loco largissime prorumpunt: & hinc adeo lenis fluit, ut vix commoveri videatur; uti Sabellicus in Carnorum Chorographia, librisque de Vrbis Venetæ Situ, itemque Candidus & Amafeus in Aquileiensibus Commentariis, exque ijs Leander Albertus in Marca Tarvisina, memoriæ produnt. Dividitur post in Cornua duo, quibus in stagna se condit ea, ubi Insula Æquilij modico ab Continente freto submovetur: uno enim hanc abscindit, altero autem in Paludes Insulæ Caprularum vicinas præcipitat, ibique Portum creat Plavis ab Ostio ejus cxi fere stadio.
units.tr: The same Zuingerus, the most diligent describer of the places in this tract, adds that the Musone, Tergola, Lavendula, Rustica, Marzenigo discharge into the Medoacus, along with the most pleasant and fertile streams, which have their sources in the north, near the Campus S. Petri celebrated in the verses of Bembo. He also lists the Plavico and Kofata, and the Villa Noniana, which Bembo praised, and finally the Tesina, Pudina, Cerisonus and Scandola, which serve for irrigation and mills. Certainly the Paduan territory is so cut up by the Medoacus and other rivers and streams everywhere that no one could clearly judge which ones receive which, which ones dominate over which, and which hold the leading place. After the Medoacus comes the Anaphus. Thus Pliny calls it, and today, according to Leandro, Sabellico, Cinthio Accedense and Giovanni Flaminio, it is the Piave, as it is commonly called. Yet Giovanni Candido thinks that the Tiliaventum Minus is this river; Castaldo, that it is the Brenta; Marius Niger, the Lugnanum; others want it to be the Stella. The Plavis is also mentioned by Diaconus and Fortunatus. It rises in the Alps and, flowing between Feltre and Belluno through rugged valleys, rushes down restlessly; nor does it grow calmer until it spreads out into open plains, although even so it runs down with a faster current between the Trini harbours and the Liquentia into the sea, as Sabellico writes in book iii of his work on the situation of the City of Venice. When it has come out onto the plain, according to Flaminio of Imola, it is carried on again with a rapid flow from the church of S. Salvatore and the high hill, and soon it is split into two horns of such depth that it cannot be crossed on foot, but a boat is needed; and then it pours itself into the sea. The inhabitants of the Plavis or the Anaxus call the Varamus and the Silis (rivers) among others. The Varamus in Pliny, as Biondo and Volaterranus think, is what is today the Caloro. It is increased by about five torrents or so as it rises from the Alps, which the Germans possess. In some manuscripts of Pliny it is written Varramus with a double R. The Silis of Pliny, which is commonly called the Sil, bursts forth, as the same author notes, from the Taurisci mountains. Pliny himself testifies that long ago the end and beginning of the Carni lay at Venice. The Liquentia of Pliny, corruptly Licenna in the Itinerary table, which is now the Livenza, is Liquetis in Virgil; Servius approves this reading, Erythraeus rejects it. It rises from the mountains of Oderzo, not far from Polcenigo, from certain springs which burst forth most abundantly in nearly the same place; and from here it flows so gently that it hardly seems to be moved at all, as Sabellico in his description of the Carni and in his books on the situation of the City of Venice, and likewise Candido and Amaseo in their Aquileian commentaries, and from them Leandro Alberti in the Marca Trevigiana, record in writing. Afterwards it is divided into two horns, by which it hides itself in marshes, where the island of Equilius is pushed away from the mainland by a narrow strait of sea: for one horn cuts off this island, and the other rushes into the marshes near the islands of the Caprulae and there creates a harbour, about 111 stadia from its mouth.

units.la: Ad Forum Iulium pertinent Fomatinum, Tilaventum, Sontius, Frigidus, Natisio, Alsa, Turrus, & alij. Romatinum, vel, ut alij scribunt, Romatum Plinij. Liminem dici vernacule notant Candidus, Amafeus, & Leander. Blondus ita nominatum scribit ab Limite Fori Iulij & Marke Tarvisinæ. Exsurgit in Carnis, ut Sabellicus indicat, lib. iii de Situ Vrbis Venetæ, moxque medium Portum Gruarium intersecans Concordiamque præstringens circa Caprulas mari infunditur. Tilaventum (quod Tilaventum Ptolemæo; Tilaubutse vitiose in Itineraria Tabula apud Plinium duplex est: Maius, quod ab Indigenis Tigliamento; Minus, quod Stella dicitur. Maius ex Monte Mauro nascitur supra Vicum Phornium, ubi Fons mirabilis, in quo Lignum dejectum lapideo cortice obducitur, & Virgulta Foliaque immersa lapidescunt. Amnes deinde Anisum, Decanum & Fellem; deinde ex angustis Alpium faucibus emergens, flumen Hydram accipit ex Agro Clemonensi; mox Argenum: quorum accessione navigabilis efficitur. Minus (hodie Stella) nascitur paullo infra Quadrinum, Cuniculis quibusdam ex Maiori Tilavento derivatus, ut auctor est Candidus. Aliter Sabellicus lib. iii de Situ Vrb. Venetæ, oriri in Carnorum Campis, magnaque ex parte corrivationibus Aquarum palustrium conflari scribit: Quod etiam Gregorius Amafeus in Regionis pictura videtur confirmare. Profluit ad Palatiolum tanta cum Aquarum mole, ut magnas naves capiat, sicque in Mare evolvitur. Sontius, cujus mentio apud Paullum Diaconum lib. xvi ad Eutropium, & Cassiodorum lib. i Variar. ad Domitianum & Voilam, fontem in Alpibus habet juxta lapidiam, quæ nunc Carnia vel Carniola: primum vero per præcipites rupes Vallesq; confragosas in occasum Solis hibernum tanto cum impetu & violentia provolvitur, ut ad cxx pene stadium nec pedibus, nec iumento transitum patiatur: dein crescens perpetuo stadia fere lx per Vallem Plitianam conficit: post eodem amplius spatio per asperrimas fauces ad Caporetum defertur, ubi Pons eximius Arcu uno pedum lx transitum jungit: hinc Vallem Caporetinam lxxx paullo minus stadiorum emetitur, multo lenior, adeo ut ubique transmittere commode liceat: porro circa finem hujus longissimæ Convallis apud Tulminam, Amnem excipit Tulminam, eoque non procul alium ex angustis faucibus prorumpentem Hydram insignem fluvium, ubi Argenti Vivi Metalla sunt: deinceps lxxx fere stadijs per Vallem Sontij, quam vocant Roncinam, labitur ad Pontem trium Arcuum, juxta quem annis superioribus Turrim struxit Goritianus Comes: hinc per artas Valles e regione Goritiæ, ubi Pons tribus Pilis lapideis innixus, lenis xi paullo amplius stadia defluit, usque dum Amnem Fipavum (qui Frigidus Antonino, Itinerariæ Tabulæ, & Claudiano in Panegyrico iii Consulatus Honorij; Socrati in Histor. Ecclesiast. & Nicephoro Callisto; Germanis Wipach) colligat, ex Alpibus per angustissimam Goritiæ Vallem accedentem: quo recepto navigabilis efficitur usque ad mare stadijs cxi. Tot Amnes Incolas deferens non procul Aquileia Natisoni inlabitur: nomen tamen nunc perferens; Natisone, qui una in mare delinit, exstincto: quamquam Candidus animadverterit e contra Veteres flumen hoc in Mare pertingens Natisonem appellasse, non Sontium, uti nunc omnibus dicitur. Qui Natiso Plinio Melaque; Ναυίσσ Straboni & Ptolemæo; hodieque Natisone dicitur. Oritur Alpibus post juga Ventionis ad Occasum Solis æstivi Solstitij versus, & lxxx fere stadijs prolapsus tum in Occasum hibernum flectit. Civitatemque Fori-Iulij mediam secat: mox ad orientem incedens post cxx fere stadia Sontio, quod dixi, Flumini inlabitur. Commiscentur illi Amphora, Ansa, Turrus. Qui nunc Ansa, Plinio & Sex. Aurelio in Annibaliano, Constantio & Constantino Alsa vocatur; Alsianum Cassiodoro lib. iv Variar. Alpe Codicibus Pauli Diaconi M. S. lib. iv. cap. x. Nam in Excusis Flave legitur; Alpha corrupte in Historia Miscella. Turrus Plinio, qui Torre Terre Adcolis; originem trahit ex Montibus Tarcentinis, & Natisoni infra Civitatem inlabitur. Post Sontiam ostium est Triveni Amnis, qui olim (ut censet Leander, legendus omnino) Timavus. De vero Timavi loco magna est inter Doctos aevi superioris nostriqe controversia. Blondus variis argumentis Timavum eundem facit cum Brenta. Contentiones praetereo, brevitatis gratia, quae inter Georgium Merulam & Domitium Calderinum: item quae inter Flaminium Imolensem & Ioannem Baptistam Pium Bononiensem. Antenoreus cognominatur ab Lucano lib. vii: Euganeus ab Martiale. Celebrant Livius lib. xli; Virgilius i. Æn. l. Florus, Plinius lib. iii. Pomponius Mela lib. ii, & alii. Describit diligenter Strabo lib. v.
units.tr: To the Forum Iulium belong the Fomatinum, Tilaventum, Sontius, Frigidus, Natisio, Alsa, Turrus, and others. Candido, Amaseo and Leandro note that the Romatinum, or, as others write, the Romatum of Pliny, is called Liminem in the vernacular. Biondo writes that it is so named from the Limite of the Forum Iulium and the March of Treviso. It rises in the land of the Carni, as Sabellico indicates in book iii of his work on the situation of the City of Venice, and soon, cutting through the middle of the Porto Gruario and skirting Concordia, it is poured into the sea near the Caprulae. The Tilaventum (which is the Tilaventum of Ptolemy; the Tilaubutse in the Itinerary table of Pliny is a corruption) is double: the Maius, which the natives call the Tagliamento; and the Minus, which is called the Stella. The Maius rises from Monte Mauro above the village of Phornium, where there is a marvellous spring, in which wood thrown in is covered with a stony crust, and twigs and leaves dipped in it turn to stone. Then it receives the rivers Anisus, Decanus and Fella; then, emerging from the narrow jaws of the Alps, it receives the river Hydra from the territory of Clemona; soon the Argenus, by whose addition it becomes navigable. The Minus (today the Stella) rises a little below Quadrinum, diverted from the Maius Tilaventum by certain underground channels, as Candido reports. Sabellico, in book iii of his work on the situation of the City of Venice, writes differently: that it rises in the plains of the Carni and is formed for the most part by the runoff of marsh waters. Gregorio Amaseo also seems to confirm this in his painting of the region. It flows to Palazzolo with such a great volume of water that it carries large ships, and so it rolls out into the sea. The Sontius, which is mentioned by Paulus Diaconus in book xvi to Eutropius, and by Cassiodorus in book i of the Variae to Domitian and Voila, has its source in the Alps near the place now called Carnia or Carniola. At first it rushes down through steep rocks and rugged valleys toward the winter sunset with such force and violence that for nearly 120 stadia it allows passage neither on foot nor by beast of burden. Then, growing steadily, it covers about 60 stadia through the valley of Plezzo. After another similar distance it is carried through very rough gorges to Caporetto, where a remarkable bridge with one arch of 60 feet joins the crossing. From here it measures out about 80 stadia less through the Caporetto valley, much gentler, so that it can be crossed conveniently everywhere. Further on, near the end of this very long valley, at Tolmino, it receives the Tolminus, and not far from there another noteworthy river, the Hydra, which bursts from narrow jaws and where there are mines of quicksilver. Afterwards, for about 80 stadia through the valley of the Sontius, which they call the Roncina, it glides to the bridge of three arches, near which the Count of Gorizia built a tower in earlier years. Then, through narrow valleys opposite Gorizia, where a bridge rests on three stone piers, it flows gently for a little more than 11 stadia, until it gathers in the Fiume (which is the Frigidus for Antoninus, the Itinerary table, and Claudian in the Panegyric on the third consulship of Honorius; for Socrates in his Ecclesiastical History and Nicephorus Callistus; and in German is Wipach), coming down from the Alps through the very narrow valley of Gorizia. With this received, it becomes navigable all the way to the sea, a distance of 111 stadia. Carrying so many rivers with it, it flows into the Natisone not far from Aquileia, though it now bears the name of the Natisone, which, having lost its own name, flows into the sea together with it. Candido has observed, however, that on the contrary the ancients called this river, which reaches the sea, the Natiso, not the Sontius, as everyone now says. This Natiso is called Natiso by Pliny and Mela, Nausis [Ναυίσσ] by Strabo and Ptolemy, and is still called the Natisone today. It rises from the Alps beyond the ridges of Ventimiglia, toward the summer solstice sunset, and, having run down about 80 stadia, it then bends toward the winter sunset. It cuts through the middle of the city of Forum Iulium, then, going eastward, after about 120 stadia it flows into the Sontius that I have mentioned. The Amphora, Ansa and Turrus join it there. The Ansa, which is now called the Alsa by Pliny and Sex. Aurelius in the Annibalianus, and by Constantius and Constantine; Alsianum in Cassiodorus book iv of the Variae; Alpe in the manuscripts of Paulus Diaconus, book iv, chapter x (for in printed editions it is read Flave; Alpha is a corruption in the Historia Miscella). The Turrus of Pliny, which the locals call the Torre, draws its origin from the Tarcento mountains and flows into the Natisone below the city. After the Sontia there is the mouth of the river Triveni, which in former times (as Leandro thinks, and it must certainly be read so) was the Timavus. There is great controversy among the learned of the earlier and our own age about the true place of the Timavus. Biondo, by various arguments, makes the Timavus the same as the Brenta. I pass over the disputes, for the sake of brevity, which exist between Giorgio Merula and Domizio Calderini, and likewise those between Flaminio of Imola and Giovanni Battista Pio of Bologna. The Antenoreus is the cognomen given by Lucan in book vii; the Euganeus by Martial. Livy in book xli, Virgil in the first book of the Aeneid, Florus, Pliny in book iii, Pomponius Mela in book ii, and others celebrate it. Strabo in book v describes it carefully.

units.la: Superstant pervestigandi Istriæ Fluvij, Risanus, Draconis, Quietus, Lemus, Arsia, Qui Risanus hodie, Pappios dicitur Ptolemæo, testibus Vergerio & Leandro. Distinum apud Nigrum, & Cisinum apud Blondum atque Volaterranum sequutores fecit ab Risano Typographorum incuria. Cuidam Anonymo in Tabula Venetijs excusa Alben vocatur; ut & Wolffgangus Lazius appellat. Hoc fortean Germanorum, illud Italorum est Idiomatis. Draconia nomen ab tortuoso tinuosoque lapsu, quo Draconi adsimilatur. Inlabitur in Sinum Largonem. Qui Quieto incolis, Latinis huius aevi Labatus nominatur; Italis Labovo; Germanis Laybach; Dalmatis Lubeana. Putant Blondus, Vergerius & Leander Fluvium hunc Antiquorum esse Nauportum, cuius meminit Plinius; sed contra sentiunt magni Viri. Profluit Quietus vel Labatus ex Alpibus, interque Montes praeceltos milia fere xii conficit: ab Taberna vero navigatur usque ad Mare: nam supra Tabernam, quae prope circa medium eius est, palustribus impeditur Vadis; sed infra commodam habet altitudinem, ut Fluvius appellari queat. Lemus Euripus magis, quam Flumen videtur. Inter Montes rapide fluit, saltuosque est usque ad Tabernam: inde supra quondam ad Castellum geminum opidum flexuoso per Montes Alveo videtur accessisse, &, quamvis nunc in Tabernam Aqua non influat usque ad Castellum geminum spatio millium v, pestilens tamen eo Lemi aura pervenit. Os Lemi latum est pass. mille, longum octo usque ad Tabernam, altitudine praecipua, & quae nec modicis convenit navibus. Qui Arsia Plinio & Itinerariae Tabulae, Arsia apud Curopalatem in Maximo; nomen hodie servat, Arsa dictus. Terminus est Italiae. Effluit ex Cosliaceno Lacu; definitque in Carnarium Sinum Ostio lato passibus mille: navigatur ab mari navibus onerariis ad sex millia; dein spatio millium iv modica tantum fert navigia. Istrum hic omittam, quem Istria fluvium nobis comminiscuntur cum alij, tum Diodorus Siculus, & Pomponius Mela; hic etiam addens, Istrum ex adverso Padi ostio in mare effluere, idque ratione duorum Fluminum Alvei dulce existere. Sequutum eos video Paullum Diaconum lib. ii. Langbard. qui hunc etiam Istrum nominat, adscribens amplioram cum, quam nunc, olim fuisse. Istrum autem fabulosum esse docet Plinius lib. iii. cap. xvi: Istriam cognominatam tradunt a Flumine Istro, in Hadriam effluente e Danubio Amne: eidemque Istro ex adverso Padi fauces, contrario eorum percussu Mari interrecto dulcescente, plerique dixere falso, & Nepos Cornelius etiam Padi adcola. Nullus enim ex Danubio Amnis in Mare Hadriaticum effunditur. Deceptos credo, quoniam Argo navis flumine in Mare Hadriaticum descendit; non procul Tergeste: nec tam constat (si verum tamen illud) quo Flumine. Humeris transvectam Alpes, diligentiores tradunt: Subisse autem Istro, dein Sao, dein Nauporto, cui nomen ex ea causa est, inter Emonam Alpesque exorienti. Dom. Marius, aliique de Istro persuasi, eundem esse illum cum Plinij Nauporto putant, & hodie Quieto dici. Sozomenus, Zosimus & Callistus, ut Ortelius notat, Αὐλὰς vocant; ex quo Aquilum & Aquilam ipsorum fecerunt Interpretes.
units.tr: There remain the rivers of Istria still to be investigated: the Risanus, Draco, Quietus, Lemus, and Arsia. The Risanus is today called the Pappios by Ptolemy, according to Vergerius and Leander. Through the carelessness of typographers, Nigrus has Distinum, and Blondus and the followers of Volaterranus have Cisinum, in place of Risanus. An anonymous author, in a map printed at Venice, calls it Alben, as Wolfgang Lazius also does. This is perhaps the German usage, and that the Italian. The name Draconia comes from the winding and twisting course by which it glides, which makes it like a dragon. It flows into the Gulf of Largo. What the inhabitants of Quieto, and the Latin writers of this age, call Labatus, the Italians call Labovo, the Germans Laybach, and the Dalmatians Lubeana. Blondus, Vergerius and Leander think this river is the ancient Nauportus, which Pliny mentions; but great men think otherwise. The Quietus, or Labatus, rises in the Alps and runs for nearly twelve miles between steep mountains. It can be navigated from the inn (Taberna) all the way to the sea; for above the inn, which lies roughly in the middle of its course, it is hindered by marshy shallows, but below it has sufficient depth to deserve the name of river. The Lemus seems more a strait than a river. It flows swiftly between mountains and is wooded as far as the inn. Above that it once seems to have come by a winding course through the mountains to the town of Castellum Geminum; and although now no water flows from the inn to Castellum Geminum, a distance of five miles, nevertheless the noxious air of the Lemus reaches that place. The mouth of the Lemus is a mile wide and eight miles long as far as the inn, of considerable depth, and suitable even for fairly large ships. The Arsia, which Pliny and the Itinerary Table call Arsia, is in Curopalates, in Maximus, and still keeps its name today, being called Arsa. It is the boundary of Italy. It flows out of the Lake of Cosliaceno and ends in the Gulf of Carnaro by a mouth a thousand paces wide. It can be navigated from the sea by cargo ships for about six miles; then, for a stretch of four miles, it bears only small vessels. I will omit here the Ister, which some others, as well as Diodorus Siculus and Pomponius Mela, invent for us as the river of Istria; Mela adds that the Ister flows into the sea opposite the mouth of the Po, and that because of the two rivers' channels the water there is sweet. I see that Paul the Deacon, book 2, Langobardic history, followed them; he also names this Ister, adding that it was once larger than it is now. But Pliny, book 3, chapter 16, teaches that the Ister is fabulous: they hand down that Istria took its name from the river Ister, which flows into the Adriatic from the Danube, and many, falsely, have said that the same Ister flows out opposite the mouths of the Po, where by the counter-pressure of the two streams the sea between them is held back and the water grows sweet; Cornelius Nepos, who lived beside the Po, says so too. For no river flows from the Danube into the Adriatic Sea. I believe they were deceived because the ship Argo descended by a river into the Adriatic, not far from Tergeste; yet it is not clearly established (if that is true at all) by which river. More careful writers relate that the ship was carried over the Alps on men's shoulders, and that it came by the Ister, then by the Sava, then by the Nauportus, which got its name from this event, rising between Emona and the Alps. Dominicus Marius and others persuaded that the Ister is that same Nauportus of Pliny, and think it is today called Quieto. Sozomen, Zosimus and Callistus, as Ortelius notes, call it Αὐλὰς [Aulas]; from this their interpreters made an Aquilus and an Aquila.

units.la: Ut supra. (marginal note mark omitted)
units.tr: As above.

units.la: CAPVT XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: Italiæ Lacus, Paludes, Stagna, Fossæ, Fontes, Aquæ.
units.tr: The Lakes, Marshes, Pools, Ditches, Springs and Waters of Italy.

units.la: MONSTRATIS, quæ per Italiam sunt, Fluminibus; sequitur, ut nonnulla diligentia deque Lacus aperiam, non quidem omnes, sed nominatissimos, quosque Veteribus etiam noti: adscripturus eodem capite singulis Regionibus propter similitudinem, quodque sæpe confundi consueverunt, quæ Paludum, Stagnorum, Fossarum & similium appellatione celebrantur: servato, quem in ipsis Regionibus paullo post fere tum secuturus, ordine.
units.tr: Having shown the rivers that are in Italy, it follows that I should set out, with some care, the lakes as well: not all of them, but the most famous, and those also known to the ancients. In this same chapter I shall add, for each region, the marshes, pools, ditches and similar waters that are commonly celebrated under those names and are often confused with one another, keeping, as far as possible, the order I shall follow shortly in the regions themselves.

units.la: Est igitur in Liguria, ab Albingauno quingentis fere passibus, ad Montis pedem, Lacus exiguus Ratenna: in quo circumiectis e iugis delabentes Aquæ stagnant. Piscibus fœcundus est optimis.
units.tr: In Liguria, then, about five hundred paces from Albingaunum, at the foot of a mountain, there is a small lake, the Ratenna. Waters running down from the surrounding ridges collect in it. It is rich in very good fish.

units.la: Viguntur in Etruria non pauci. Trasumenus Livio, alisque Trasimenus Silio lib. v. dicitur: qui hodie ab Urbe vicina Lago de Perugia. Trasimena Vada appellat idem Silius lib. xi; Lydis lib. xiii, Tyrrhena lib. xvii. Clitorus nominatur apud Diaconum in Langbardicis, mendose. Auno etiam Antiquis, ut innuit Silius lib. v. in cuius veteribus libris legitur Anno. Appiano in Hannibalicis appellatur. Mirum apud Cosmographos Trasimen: memoriam non referri, quum tamen pernobilis sit: ab Historicis tamen supra modum celebratur: propter Cladem, quam ad eum Romanis intulit Pœnorum Dux Hannibal, haud procul Opido, quod ab offibus Romanorum offarta dictum creditur. Legendi Polybius lib. iii, Livius lib. xxii, Plutarchus in Vita Hannibalis, Plinius lib. xv cap. xviii, & lib. xxxvii.cap.i, Strabo lib. vi, Lactant. lib. ii, cap. xvii, Silius Italicus lib. ix, Augustinus lib. iii de Civit. Dei cap. xix, Valerius Maximus variis locis, Frontinus lib. ii Stratag. cap. v, Auctor de VV. Illustr. cap. xlii. Scribit de hoc Lacu Campanus, eum in suo ambitu complecti circiter xxx P. M: lucidum esse & perspicuum, nec alienas recipere Aquas, nec refundere suas: Inlignem Aquæ esse Suavitatem, adeo ut vivo manante fonte videatur: Tribus Insulis adornari, earum duas sibi fere contiguas ad Septemtrionem vergere, unamque Maiorem, alteram Minorem vocari; Hanc inculltam & delectam, Templum tantum fere in acumine; Illam, quæ ad Coronensem spectat Agrum ducentis prope familiis habitare: Tertiam, quæ versus Meridiem consistit, maiorem ceteris hominibusque frequentem esse: Incolas solis fere Piscationibus incumbere: Frumentum vix serere, Vinetorum plantationem & curam non negligere; Lignarum pabulatumque in finitimos Campos Silvasque egredi: Insularum mentionem fieri in Archivis Ludovici I Imperatoris; ibique eas vocari Maiorem, Minorem & Pulvensem. Addit idem, Piscium genera in Lacu non esse multa: copia tamen inaudita; eaqueceteros Italiæ Lacus antecellere: Piscationes fieri toto anno, etiam ipso Brumæ tempore, quod nullus alius admittit in Italia Lacus: Pisces advehi hieme ad Etruscos, Umbros, Picentes; Romam quoque plurimos quotidie ab iumentis comportari: Lucium ibi capi vario colore, & quasi viridibus adspersum maculis; cum coire cum Serpentibus, indeque hunc varium sortiri colorem. De Piscatione totius anni negat Leander, scribens ab Kalendis Novembribus usque ad Pascha tantum concedi: ceteris vero temporibus, ut, quum opus est, abundantiam captura suppeditet, esse interdictam. Hunc Lacum aliquando totum arsisse tradit Plinius lib. ii. nat. histor. cap. cvii. Aprilis Lacus Antonino vocatur, qui hodie Fangosa Palude, ut notat Leander: Lago di Castiglione dicitur in Tabula Tuscana Hieronymi Bellarmati. Nomen illi ab Amne Prile. Confundunt eum cum Orbitello Lacu Flavius Blondus & Niger: male, quum Orbitellum, à quo denominari videtur, non ad hunc Lacum sit situm, sed ad Marinum, prope Montem Argentarium Marinus ille, qui & Satius, ab Strabone lib. iii nominatur: Lago d'Orbitello vernacule, ab opido, cuius ante meminî. ripæ ipsius adpositio. In Mare quibusdam faucibus se exonerat. Ante eum Cherrhonesus ingens seu Promontorium in Pelagus excurrit; Monte Argentato Adcolis. Fuit haud procul Tiberi Lacus, qui Vadimonis Livio, aliisque. Eum Leander esse censet, qui vulgo di Bassanello, Baffanello, tribus ab Horta P. M. in amœna planicie. Certe iuxta Amerina Prædia locant Plinius lib. 11 Nat. Hist. & alter lib. viii. Epist. ad Gallum suum, ubi eius innatantes describit Insulas. Antonius Massa notat eum in Agro Opidi Balsani esse, haud procul à Tiberi sub Collibus Amerinis. Vadimonis tamen Lacum Blondus putat eum, qui nunc Monte Rosei: nonnulli eum, qui hodie Bacchani; alij alium. Lacus Viterbiensis, de Viterbo, est Fabricio; qui hactenus Vadimono appellari scribit. Ciminius Italiæ Lacus apud Volsinios Strabonis: hodie Lago di Vico: notantibus Pomponio Sabino, eum circa Sutrium ponenti; Leandro, qui Elby Lacum ab Antonino dici addit; & Nicolao Erythræo, cui etiam Lago de Rossillon nominatur. Meminerunt Virgilius lib. vii Æneid. & Silius lib. viii Belli Pœnici. Nomen ab Cimino Monte, de quo alibi. De eius Origine sic Servius: Hercules, inquit, quum ad hos populos aliquando venisset, & à singulis provocaretur ad ostendendam virtutem, ferreum vectem, quo exercebatur, defixisse dicitur: qui quum terra esset adfixus, & à nullo potuisset auferri, etiam rogatus suitus, unde immensa vis Aqua sequuta est, quæ Ciminium Lacum fecit. Bulsinus Lacus Procopio & Agathiæ; Volsinensis Plinio; Vulsinensis Columellæ: qui iamnunc Lago di Bolsena. Circuitus eius xxiv milliar. Piscibus abundat; præcipue Anguillis. Est in eo Insula, modica quidem, at fertilis & peramœna: nobilis cæde Amalasiunte. Vide Procopium libro 1 Belli Gothici. Sabatus, Σαβάτος Strabonis; Sabatinus Columellæ, qui vulgo ab adiacentibus opidis, Lago di Braciano, uti censent Iovius & Leander; vel d'Anguillara, ut Blondus. Platina Latine vocat Angularem ab Angulis & Trigoni forma, quam habet: Plinio Lacus Tarquiniensis nuncupatur: Sabatia Stagna Silio Scribitur ab hoc Lacu quondam Sabatina Aqua Romam ducta. Septimo ab Luco lapide Palus est Bientina, ab opido adsito dicta, quondam in Lacum ab Florentinis conclusa; cui opidum imminet Monte Carlo. Caldana Palus haud procul est Plumbino. Nomen inditum putatur, quod calidas ecfundat Aquas. Memoratur fortean à Plinio lib. 11, ubi Paravinorum Aquis calidis herbas innatci virentes, Pisanorum Ranas, ad Vetulonios in Etruria non procul à mari Pisces, notat. Cornia, qui ab Monte Rotundo per Agrum Campilianum profluit, recepto, in Mare se exonerat, optimis fœcunda Piscibus. In Aretinorum Agris Palus est Ciana, quam Plinius de Tiberi scribens, Glanem vocat; Appianus Alexandrinus lib. 1. Glanium Fluvium, Instar habet lenti admodum & pigri Amnis, quam ob causam Paludem potius, quam Flumen dici debere scribit in libro Fluminum Boccatius. Adcolis perquam noxius est Aëris gravitate, quam, ut ante dixi, ob cœnosa Vada creat. Aretinum Stagnum videtur nominari ab Obsequente, quia Palos hæc Aretio vicina.
units.tr: Not a few are found in Etruria. Livy calls the Trasumenus, and others the Trasimenus, Silius in book 5; today it is the Lago de Perugia, from the nearby city. The same Silius calls it the Trasimena Vada in book 11, the Lydis in book 13, and the Tyrrhena in book 17. The Clitorus is named by Diaconus in his Lombard history, wrongly. The ancients also called it the Auno, as Silius hints in book 5, in whose old manuscripts it is read Anno. Appian in his Hannibalic books so calls it. It is strange that the cosmographers make no mention of the Trasimen, though it is very famous; yet the historians celebrate it beyond measure, on account of the defeat which Hannibal, the Carthaginian general, inflicted on the Romans near it, not far from the town which is believed to have been named Offarta from the bones of the Romans. Read Polybius book 3, Livy book 22, Plutarch in the Life of Hannibal, Pliny book 15 chapter 18 and book 37 chapter 1, Strabo book 6, Lactantius book 2 chapter 17, Silius Italicus book 9, Augustine book 3 of the City of God chapter 19, Valerius Maximus in various places, Frontinus book 2 of the Stratagems chapter 5, and the author of the Illustrious Men, chapter 42. The Campanian writes of this lake that its circuit embraces about thirty Roman miles; that it is clear and transparent, receiving no foreign waters and giving none back; that its water is remarkably sweet, so much so that it seems to be a living spring flowing up. It is adorned with three islands, two of which lie nearly side by side and face northward, and are called the Greater and the Lesser. The one of these is uncultivated and deserted, with only a temple almost at its peak. The other, which faces the territory of Corona, is inhabited by nearly two hundred families. The third, which lies toward the south, is larger than the others and crowded with people. The inhabitants apply themselves almost only to fishing; they can scarcely sow grain, but do not neglect the planting and care of vineyards; they go out into the neighbouring fields and woods for wood and fodder. The islands are mentioned in the archives of the Emperor Louis I, where they are called the Maiorem, Minorem and Pulvensem. The same writer adds that there are not many kinds of fish in the lake, but their abundance is unheard of, and that it surpasses the other lakes of Italy. Fishing is carried on the whole year, even in the very season of winter, which no other lake in Italy allows. Fish are brought in winter to the Etruscans, the Umbrians and the Picentines, and very many are carried daily from there on pack animals to Rome as well. There the pike is caught, of varied colour, as if spotted with green markings; it is said to mate with serpents, and from this it acquires its varied colour. Leander, writing about fishing throughout the year, denies it, saying that fishing is permitted only from the first of November until Easter; at other times, so that the catch may supply abundance when it is needed, it is forbidden. Pliny, in book 2 of the Natural History chapter 107, relates that this lake once burned entirely. The Aprilis Lacus is called by Antoninus the lake that today is the Fangosa Palude, as Leander notes; in the Tuscan map of Girolamo Bellarmato it is called the Lago di Castiglione. It takes its name from the river Prile. Flavio Biondo and Niger confuse it with the Orbitello lake, wrongly, since the Orbitellum, from which it seems to take its name, is not situated near this lake but near the Marinum, close to Mount Argentario; that Marinus, which is also called Satius, is named by Strabo in book 3. In the vernacular it is the Lago d'Orbitello, from the town of which I spoke earlier. It discharges into the sea through certain channels. Before it a great headland, or promontory, the Cherrhonesus, runs out into the open sea; the locals call it Monte Argentato. There was once a lake not far from the Tiber, which Livy and others call the Vadimonis. Leander thinks it is the one commonly called the di Bassanello or Baffanello, three miles from Orte, in a pleasant plain. Certainly Pliny, in book 2 of the Natural History, and another author, in book 8 of the Letters to his friend Gallus, place it near the Amerine estates, where he describes the islands floating on it. Antonio Massa notes that it lies in the territory of the town of Balsano, not far from the Tiber, under the Amerine hills. Blondus, however, thinks that the lake called Vadimonis is the one that is now the Monte Rosei; some think it is the one that today is the Bacchani; others another. The Viterbo lake, from Viterbo, is according to Fabricius, who writes that until now it has been called the Vadimono. The Ciminius, the lake of Italy near the Volsinians, is named by Strabo; today it is the Lago di Vico, as Pomponius Sabinus notes, who places it to the west of Sutrium; Leander, who adds that Antoninus calls it the Elby Lacum; and Nicolaus Erythraeus, by whom it is also called the Lago de Rossillon. Virgil in book 7 of the Aeneid and Silius in book 8 of the Punic War make mention of it. Its name is from Mount Ciminus, of which I shall speak elsewhere. Servius on its origin says this: Hercules, he says, when he once came to these peoples, and was challenged by individuals to show his strength, is said to have driven in an iron bar with which he was exercising; and when it was fixed in the ground and could not be removed by anyone, he was asked to pull it out, whereupon an immense flood of water followed, which made the Ciminian lake. The Bulsinus Lacus is named by Procopius and Agathias; the Volsinensis by Pliny; the Vulsinensis by Columella; today it is the Lago di Bolsena. Its circuit is twenty-four miles. It abounds in fish, especially eels. In it there is an island, modest indeed but fertile and very pleasant, famous for the murder of Amalasuntha. See Procopius, book 1 of the Gothic War. The Sabatus, the Σαβάτος of Strabo, and the Sabatinus of Columella, which the commonly called the Lago di Braciano from the neighbouring towns, as Jovius and Leander think, or the d'Anguillara, as Blondus says. Platina calls it in Latin the Angularem, from the angles and the triangular shape which it has. Pliny calls it the Lacus Tarquiniensis. Silius calls it the Sabatia Stagna. It is written that the Sabatine water was once brought to Rome from this lake. Seven miles from Lucca there is the Bientina marsh, named from the town situated near it, once enclosed into a lake by the Florentines; over it the town of Monte Carlo hangs. The Caldana Palus lies not far from Piombino. It is thought that its name was given because it pours out warm waters. Perhaps it is mentioned by Pliny in book 2, where he notes that green plants float on the warm waters of the Paravini, frogs of the Pisani, and fish near the Vetulonians in Etruria, not far from the sea. The Cornia, which flows from Monte Rotondo through the Campiglia territory, receives the stream and discharges into the sea, rich in very good fish. In the territory of the Aretines there is a marsh, the Ciana, which Pliny, writing about the Tiber, calls the Glanem; Appian of Alexandria, in book 1, calls it the Glanium Fluvium. It has the nature of a very slow and sluggish stream, for which reason Boccaccio, in his book on rivers, writes that it ought to be called a Paludem rather than a Flumen. It is very harmful to the neighbours because of the heaviness of the air, which, as I said before, it creates on account of its muddy shallows. The Aretinum Stagnum seems to be named by Obsequens, because this marsh lies near Arezzo.

units.la: Sunt & sui Latio Lacus. Hostilia Lacum habet Obsequens de Prodigiis ex Livij lib. xxviii. Stagno vulgo vocatur. Inter Marinum & Albam Longam Lacus est Albanus, cuius meminit Livius lib. v. Hodie Lago di Castel Gandolfo, ab opidulo Gandulpho, Lacu imminente, Veteris Albæ fundamentis impositio, cognominatus. Lacus hic ille est, de quo Vates Veiens Populo Romano cecinerat, priusquam ex Lacu Albano Aqua emissa foret, numquam potituram Veiis Romanum, ut memoriæ prodit Livius libro, quem indicavi. Ex hoc stagno per Fossam opere factam Amnis exit, non quidem frequentibus Aquis; sed qui propter locum fluens, ubi D. Paullus secuti percussus creditur (Tres Fontes hac memoria vocant) Paludum efficit, Aquas Salvias: ubi Monasterium D. Paulli, teste Adone. Quod tertio ut ab Urbe Lapide, & Gutta iugiter manans appelletur, testis est Baronius in Annalibus Ecclesiasticis. Aqua Silvia legiuntur mendose in Vita S. Gordiani. Ab Lacu Albano P.M. iv. Aricia est; totidem inde inter Montes Lacus vel Stagnum Nemorense, quemadmodum, ut magni Viri censent, Suetonius cap. xlvi appellat, quum Cæsarem in Nemorensi Villam ab fundamentis inchoatam, magnoque sumtu absolutam, quia non tota ad animum respondorat, diruisse scribit. Hodie Lago di Nemo, ut notat Erythræus; vel, ut vult Ciofanus in Ovidium, Lago di Ienfano. Trivia Lacus. Virgilio lib. vii Æneidos; scribentique in eum Servio, Speculum Diana: Alius Aricinus, ab Aricia Vrbe; Hippolyti, Statio lib. iii. Silvar. Diana Stagnum Ovidio iii Fast & xiii Metamorph. Instar Pelagi fluctuare notat Strabo. Iuturna Lacus Ovidio lib. ii Fastorum, qui Viturna Symmacho, corrupte, lib. 1. Epist. lxxxix. Iuturna Virgilio lib. xii Æneid, ad quem Servius Fontem esset docet Italiæ iuxta Numicium Fluvium. Gyraldus scribit ab nonnullis statui eo in loco, qui nunc vulgo Treglio, eosque non infirmis niti rationibus. Meminerunt Valerius Maximus, L. Florus, Lactantius, alij. Alius fuit Iuturna Fons in viii Vrbis Regione, testibus P. Victore & Paullo Marso. Regillus, ut indicant Plinius lib. iii, Livius lib. ii, Florus lib. i, Latij Lacus est, in Agro Tusculano ad Algidi Nemoris ingressum: Hodie, testibus Iovio & Leandro, Lago de S. Praxede; Nardo de S. Severa. Fucinus Virgilio lib. vii, Tacito lib. xii Annal. Plinio lib. iii. Ἀξκινος Dioni & Straboni, Ὀρμη commentanti in Lycophronem Ilacio; qui hodie ab locis adiacentibus Lago di Marso, id est Maisicn, quod Marsorum gentis, ut scribunt Niger & Volaterranus; Lago di Celano, uti censent Leander & Andreas Baccius, Lago di Rosfillon, vel di Tagliacozzo, ut Erythraeus interpretatur. Albanum etiam quidam vocant, quod prope Albam Albensium. Stadia ab Vrbe quingenta ad Lacum hunc numerat Ilacius. Haud longe ab Liri Flumine fuisse videtur ex lib. xii Annalium Taciti. Pisces in eo reperiuntur pinnis octo; quum ceteri quatuor tantum habeant; quod à Plinio inter Miracula commemoratur. Fluvium Invectum Fucinum Lacum transfire, tradit idem Plinius lib. ii. nat. hist. cap. cxiii. Fucini Lacus Emissionem in Tiberim concepit C. Iulius Caesar, non incepit, Suetonio scribente in eius Vita cap. xliv: nec rite perfecit Claudius, de quo Dion, Plinius lib. xxxvi cap. xv, Eusebius in Chronico; quoniam manus postea admovit & Hadrianus; teste in vita eius Spartiano. Consulendi de hoc Lacu Petrus Marius ad viii librum Silij Italici de Bello Punico & Leander Albertus in Italia. Pontina vel Pomptina (variat enim scriptura) Palus etiam in Latio describitur à Plinio. Meminit cum aliis Iuvenalis. Sic Lucanus lib. iii:
units.tr: There are also lakes in Latium itself. Obsequens, in his book on prodigies, takes from Livy book 28 the name Hostilia Lacus, which is commonly called the Stagno. Between Marinum and Alba Longa lies the Lacus Albanus, which Livy mentions in book 5. Today it is the Lago di Castel Gandolfo, named after the small town of Gandulpho, which overhangs the lake and was built on the foundations of Old Alba. This is the lake of which the Veientine seer had prophesied to the Roman people, before water was drawn off from the Lacus Albanus, that Rome would never become master of Veii, as Livy records in the book I have cited. From this lake an outflow runs through a channel made by human labour. It is not a stream with a large volume of water, but because it flows through a low-lying place, where St Paul is believed to have been struck after following the ... (the spot which people now call Tres Fontes), it forms the Paludes and the Aquas Salvias, where the monastery of St Paul stands, according to Ado. That it is called Gutta iugiter manans, and lies three miles from the city, is attested by Baronius in his Ecclesiastical Annals. The Aqua Silvia is wrongly read in the Life of St Gordian. From the Lacus Albanus it is four miles to Aricia; and from there, four miles more, lies the Lacus or Stagnum Nemorense among the mountains, which Suetonius, in chapter 46, calls by this name, as great men think, when he writes that Caesar pulled down a villa at Nemorensi, begun from its foundations and completed at great expense, because it did not wholly please him. Today it is the Lago di Nemo, as Erythraeus notes, or, as Ciofanus in his commentary on Ovid holds, the Lago di Ienfano. The Trivia Lacus is so called by Virgil in book 7 of the Aeneid; Servius, commenting on it, calls it the Speculum Diana. Another is the Aricinus, from the city of Aricia; the Hippolyti, in Statius, Silvae book 3; the Diana Stagnum in Ovid, Fasti book 3 and Metamorphoses book 13. Strabo notes that it surges like the open sea. The Iuturna Lacus is in Ovid, Fasti book 2, which Symmachus, in book 1, letter 89, corruptly calls the Viturna. The Iuturna is in Virgil, Aeneid book 12, where Servius teaches that it was a spring of Italy beside the river Numicius. Gyraldus writes that some have placed it in the place now commonly called Treglio, and that they rest on no weak arguments. Valerius Maximus, Florus, Lactantius and others mention it. There was another Iuturna Fons in the eighth region of the city, according to Publius Victor and Paulus Marsus. The Regillus, as Pliny in book 3, Livy in book 2 and Florus in book 1 indicate, is a lake of Latium in the territory of Tusculum, at the entrance to the Algidus grove. Today, according to Giovio and Leandro, it is the Lago de S. Praxede; Nardo calls it the de S. Severa. The Fucinus is in Virgil, book 7; Tacitus, Annals book 12; and Pliny, book 3. Dio and Strabo call it Ἀξκινος [Axkinos], and Horma, commenting on Lycophron, calls it Ilacius. Today, according to the neighbouring places, it is the Lago di Marso, that is, Maisicn, from the people of the Marsi, as Niger and Volaterranus write; the Lago di Celano, as Leander and Andreas Baccius think; or the Lago di Rosfillon or di Tagliacozzo, as Erythraeus explains. Some also call it the Albanum, because it lies near Alba Albensium. Ilacius reckons the lake at five hundred stades from the city. It seems to have lain not far from the river Liris, from Tacitus, Annals book 12. Fish are found in it with eight fins, whereas others have only four; Pliny mentions this among the marvels. Pliny the same, in Natural History book 2, chapter 113, says that the river Invectum crosses the Fucine Lake. Gaius Julius Caesar conceived the plan of draining the Fucine Lake into the Tiber but did not begin it, as Suetonius writes in his Life, chapter 44. Claudius did not carry it out properly, as Dio, Pliny in book 36, chapter 15, and Eusebius in his Chronicle report; afterwards Hadrian also put his hand to it, as Spartianus witnesses in his Life. On this lake, Petrus Marius on book 8 of Silius Italicus' Punica and Leander Albertus in his Italia should be consulted. The Pontina or Pomptina (for the spelling varies) Palus is also described in Latium by Pliny. Juvenal mentions it along with others, and Lucan says in book 3:

units.la: Et qua Pontinas Via dividit uda Paludes.
units.tr: And where the Appian Way divides the wet Pontine marshes.

units.la: Satura Paludem apud Virgilium vii Æneid. esse putant Hermolaus & Erythraeus: Sic Silius lib. viii: Qua Satura nebulosa Palus restagnat, & atro Litentes cœno per squalida turbidus arva Cogit Aquas Vfens, atque inficit aquora limo.
units.tr: Hermolaus and Erythraeus think that the Satura Palus is meant in Virgil, Aeneid book 7. So Silius, book 8: Where the misty Satura marsh stagnates, and the turbid one, driving the waters over the squalid fields that lie in black mud, fouls the waters with slime.

units.la: Hodie Ausente Palude, Leandro teste. Decennonia Paludes videntur dici, ut Celsus Citradinus censet, Cassiodoro lib. ii Variar. ad Senatum Vrbis. Vide paullo post Inscriptionem. Nomen à Pontia Vrbe deductum putat Strabo. Fit Palus ex Amnibus duobus, Aufido, ut Strabo vocat, aut Vfente, ut Plinius, & altero Minore. Circa Tarracinam esse docet Festus; circa Forum Appij, Vibius, cui Pontina nominatur. Longitudo xxvi milliaria amplectitur; Latitudo vi. Pontinam Paludem xxiv Vrbium fuisse, tradit ex Muciano Plinius, Neque mirum tot Opida spatio millium viii, vel paullo maiore exstitisse. Antiquis enim temporibus Civitates erant vel opida potius, ut hodie sunt Vici. Paludes hæ fertilissimi quondam Pomeftini erant Campi. Sic Livio aliisque appellantur, qui Pontini Silio lib. viii; Pomeftinus Campus Straboni; Pontinus Ager Floro lib. i. Hist. Rom. cap. xiii, & Agellio lib. ix. noct. Attic. cap. xi. Neglectis quippe Viis, quibus Aquæ huc propter Loca depressiora confluentes in mare se prius exonerabant, neque stagnare, ut nunc, poterant, Campi in palustrem hanc formam sunt redacti. Livius lib. xlvi ab Cornelio Cethego cos. Aquas quondam egestas maiore ex parte, Agrosque ad culturam reductos scribit. Postea tamen iterum, neglectis meatibus, effectæ Paludes; quas Theodoricus Rex Gothorum exsiccavit. Testatur Tabulæ Marmoreæ Inscriptio, Tarracinæ exstantis, quam Roma sibi missam ab Philippo Winghio scribit Ortelius: CAC. MAV. BASILIVM. DECIVM. V. INL. ET. ORDO. PAT. EXSICCASSE. PALVDES. DECENNOVII. VIA. APPIÆ. A. TRIT VSQ. TERRACENAM. Nunc denuo, nullo patente Aquarum ad Mare exitu, Amnes Fonteique plurimi vicinis è montibus orientes hic, ut Leander notat, stagnant, ingentemque faciunt Paludem, P. M. ab Roma distantem xl. Fundanum Lacum, partem quasi Pontinæ Paludis, habent Tacitus & Plinius. Pisces in eo capiuntur multi, cum primis raræ magnitudinis Anguillæ. Hodie Solum ibi esse Palustre, ita tamen ut Ædificiorum Vestigia ruinæque cernantur, scribit Hermolaus Barbarus; cui, ut & Leandro, vernaculæ Lago de Fundi vocatur. Vno ab Tiburte milliario Lacus est, cuius Aquæ sulphureæ, in quo Insulæ natantes hodie spectantur cum Caprís & Vaccis iisdem pascentibus. Mirantur intolerantiam Adcolæ; non Batavi nos, quibus magna natat
units.tr: Today it is the Ausente Palus, according to Leander. The Decennonia Paludes seems to be so called, as Celsus Citradinus thinks, from Cassiodorus, Variae book 2, to the Senate of the city. See a little later under the inscription. Strabo thinks the name is derived from the city of Pontia. The marsh is formed from two rivers, the Aufidus, as Strabo calls it, or the Ufens, as Pliny calls it, and another smaller one. Festus teaches that it lies near Tarracina, and Vibius that it lies near the Forum of Appius, where it is called the Pontina. It covers a length of twenty-six miles and a breadth of six. Pliny, from Mucianus, reports that the Pontina Palus once had twenty-four towns; nor is it surprising that so many towns existed in a space of eight or a little more miles. In ancient times the civitates were in fact towns, or rather villages, as the Vici are today. These marshes were once the very fertile Campi Pomestini. Thus they are called by Livy and others: Pontini in Silius, book 8; Pomestinus Campus by Strabo; Pontinus Ager in Florus, Roman History book 1, chapter 13, and in Gellius, Attic Nights book 9, chapter 11. Since the roads by which the waters, gathering here from the lower-lying places, had discharged themselves into the sea were neglected, and they could no longer stagnate as they do now, the fields were turned into this marshy state. Livy, book 46, writes that under the consul Cornelius Cethegus the waters were for the most part drained off and the fields brought back to cultivation. Afterwards, however, the channels were again neglected and the marshes were formed anew, and these were dried out by Theodoric, king of the Goths. The inscription on the marble tablet still standing at Tarracina attests this, which Ortelius writes was sent to Rome by Philip Winghius: "The Emperor Caesar Basilius Decius, Inlustris, and the order of senators, dried up the marshes of Decennovium along the Appian Way, from Tres Tabernae as far as Terracina." Now again, since there is no outlet for the waters to the sea, the many rivers and springs rising from the neighbouring mountains stagnate here, as Leander notes, and form a great marsh, forty miles from Rome. Tacitus and Pliny mention the Fundanus Lacus, which is part of the Pontine marsh, as it were. Many fish are caught in it, especially eels of unusually large size. Hermolaus Barbarus writes that today there is only marshy ground there, though the traces and ruins of buildings can still be seen; and it is called in the vernacular the Lago de Fundi, as it is also by Leander. One mile from Tibur there is a lake whose waters are sulphurous, in which floating islands are seen today, with goats and cows grazing on them. The inhabitants marvel at their hardiness; we, however, are not Batavians, whom a large part of Batavia, with its towns, villages, hamlets, inhabitants, travellers, animals, trees, crops, and whatever else, floats upon.

units.la: Tiberinus. natat pars Bataviæ cum Opidis, Pagis, Vicis, Incolis, Viatoribus, Animalibus, Arboribus, Frugibus, & quibus non? Cæcubum, Καικυβον Straboni, locus in Latio Palustris & vitifer, circa Caietanum Sinum: unde Cæcubi in Pontinis Paludibus sunt apud Plinium lib. xvii, cap. v. Hinc Finum Cæcubum eidem Plinio lib. xiv, cap vi, Athenæo lib. i. Horatio lib. i. Carm. Od. xx & xxxviii, Martiali, & aliis. Simbruina Stagna in Tiburtum finibus memorantur ab Tacito lib. Annalium xiiii: Nam quia dissumulantis Neronis apud Simbruina Stagna, cui Sublaqueum (quidam Sublacæum, alij Sublacum, nempe ob vicinatem Lacus) nomen est, illa Dapes, mensaque disiecta erat. Pertinet eo locus alius Taciti lib. xi: Fontesque Aquarum, Simbruinis Collibus deductos Urbi intulit, idque finibus Tiburtum acciderat. Ubi tamen V.Cl. Lipsius emendat, Sub Imbrutinis. Sublacenses Populos vocatos tradit Plinius ab tribus vicinis Lacubus, unde Fluvius Anio profluit.
units.tr: Tiberinus. Caecubum, which Strabo calls Καικυβον [Kaikybon], is a marshy and vine-bearing place in Latium, near the Gulf of Gaeta; hence the Caecubi in the Pontine marshes are mentioned by Pliny, book 17, chapter 5, and the Caecubum Fine by the same Pliny, book 14, chapter 6, by Athenaeus, book 1, by Horace, Odes book 1, odes 20 and 38, by Martial, and by others. The Simbruina Stagna are mentioned in the territory of Tibur by Tacitus, Annals book 14: "For at the Simbruina Stagna, where Nero was dissembling, and which is called Sublaqueum (some say Sublacaeum, others Sublacum, namely from the nearness of the lake), those feasts and tables were overturned." Another passage of Tacitus, book 11, relates to this: "He brought springs of water into the city, led from the Simbruine hills, and this happened in the territory of Tibur." Yet the most learned Lipsius corrects this to Sub Imbrutinis. Pliny reports that the Sublacenses were so called from the three neighbouring lakes from which the river Anio flows.

units.la: In Piceno ad latus Montis Victoris, qua in Orientem spectat, Lacus invenitur fama nobilitatus; Nurfinum dicunt. In eo Cacodæmones innatare Vulgus imperitum dictitat: quoniam Aquæ perpetuis moribus salire, & vicissim subsidere cernuntur, eorundem non sine ingenti illorum admiratione, qui causam ignorant. Fama hinc per Italiam, & alias quoque Mundi partes ab Idiotis sparsa, malignos Spiritus hic habitare, petentibusque dare Responsa. Superioribus iaculis, inquit Rallanus, quidam ex longinquis Regionibus levitate evecti lua, huc venerunt, sceleratorum ac detestabilium voluminum Cacodæmoni dedicandorum gratia: quo certis quibusdam flagitiosis optatis, utpote Divitiarum, Honorum, Voluptatum, aliorumve id genus potirentur: qui, quum multum sibi, saltamque Vulgi Famam cognovissent; pudorem ut averterent, neve laboris labores sumtusque perdituli viderentur, apud alios expleta sua desideria sunt mentiti. Addit idem Rallanus, se, quum harum rerum fidem exactius inquirere niteretur, ab Teutonis quibusdam doctis viris gnarisque, qui ipsi hunc locum Vulgi fama commoti adierant, ut cum Cacodæmone Carminibus impiis, Voti impetrandi gratia, magice operarentur, accepisse, ipsos, omnibus Superstitionis Legibus implicatos, orbeque descripto cum Signis peculiaribus nec ullo, quæ requiruntur, exsecrabilium Cerimoniarum genere praetermisso, nihil toto triduo audivisse quidquam, aut vidisse: Quam ob rem, quum Impositurām intelligerent, & indignarentur, quod Volumina, quibus pravæ Artis præcepta, Characteres, & Signa Magica continebantur, in Stagnum deiecta non fuisse reddita, Voto maximo numquam deinceps in huiusmodi Rebus quidquam fiduciæ habendi nunc cupato, & temeritatem gravissime accusasse suam, & Nugarum de Loco Auctores ob mendacia detestatos; simul omnes, qui Cacodæmonum, itemque Magicorum Voluminum ulla duceretur fide, diris exsecrationibus devovisse: enimvero, quod ad Motum Stagni attinet, eum ab Ventis creari, manifeste cognovisse, qui, quum Aquas angusti Lacus inter altissimos concluti Montes, agitant atque impellunt, ita fieri, ut summo sane cum stupore nunc intumescere, nunc subsidere videantur.
units.tr: In Picenum, on the side of Mount Victor facing east, there is a lake made famous by report, which they call Nurfinum. The ignorant common people keep saying that evil demons swim in it, because its waters are seen to leap up and sink back again in constant motion, to the great astonishment of those who do not know the cause. From this, a report spread by simple folk through Italy and other parts of the world holds that malignant spirits dwell here and give answers to those who seek them. Rallanus says: "A few years ago, some men from distant regions, carried away by lightness, came here to dedicate wicked and abominable books to the demon, so that by certain shameful wishes, such as riches, honours, pleasures or other things of that kind, they might obtain what they wanted. When they found that their hopes were vain and that the common rumour was empty, they lied to others that their desires had been fulfilled, so that they might avert their shame and so that their labours and wasted expense would not appear to be lost." Rallanus adds that when he tried to inquire more carefully into the truth of these things, he learned from certain learned and knowledgeable Germans, who had themselves come to this place, moved by the popular report, to practise magic with impious songs and the demon in order to obtain their wish, that they, entangled in every law of superstition, had drawn a circle with special signs and had omitted no kind of accursed ceremony that was required, yet heard and saw nothing at all for three whole days. Therefore, realising that they had been deceived and angry that the books, which contained the precepts of the wicked art, characters and magical signs, had been thrown into the lake and not returned, they vowed with the greatest prayer never afterwards to place any trust in such things. They bitterly condemned their own rashness and cursed the authors of the nonsense about the place for their lies. At the same time, they all devoted to dreadful curses anyone who might be thought worthy of any belief in demons or magic books. Indeed, as for the movement of the lake, they clearly learned that it is caused by the winds, which, striking and driving the waters of the narrow lake enclosed among very high mountains, make it seem, to the great astonishment of onlookers, now to swell and now to subside.

units.la: Habet præter Floridum, Lacum modicum, præcelsis cinctum Montibus, Umbria Velinum, cuius meminerunt Tacitus lib. i. Annalium, Silius lib. iv Belli Pœn. M. Tullius ad Atticum lib. iv. Epist. xv. Constituunt eius Initia extra Reate Velinus Amnis, cum aliis Aquarum rivulis, non paucis: qui tamen prius quam in Lacum confluant, Paludem quamdam (Reatinam videtur vocare Varro) efficiunt; ex qua deinde rursum emergentes, Lacui dant, ut dixi, principium. Collibus editioribus undique munitur, quamquam in præcelso Montium iacet ingo. Aquas habet claras; Saxum tamen per quod exoneratur, ita quandoque exercetur, ut id ferro repurgari sit necesse, quo semper exitus illi pateat, neve per vicina loca superstagnet. Ligna circum eum in Agris lapideo cernuntur obducta cortice. Affirmant, qui adhabitant, Lignum in eo defixum intra paucos dies lapide circumdari. Pisces optimos generat, præcipue Truttas & Tincas, eatque sine spinis, præterquam in contextu vertebrarum. Naviculas fert exiguas, quibus deportari ultro citroque Fructus solent. Adcolunt eum, teste Plinio, Sabini. Lacum hunc Italiæ Medium tenere, eiusque esse Umbilicum, affirmant Scriptores Veteres. De eo, considerata penitus Situs conditione, canit procul dubio Virgilius lib. vii:
units.tr: Besides Floridum, Umbria has a modest Lacum, surrounded by very high mountains, the Velinum, which is mentioned by Tacitus in the first book of the Annals, by Silius in the fourth book of the Punic War, and by Marcus Tullius to Atticus, book 4, letter 15. Its sources lie outside Reate: the Velinus Amnis, together with not a few other small streams. Yet before they flow together into the lake, they form a certain marsh (which Varro seems to call the Reatinam); from there they rise again and give the lake, as I said, its beginning. It is protected on all sides by higher hills, although it lies on the lofty ridge of the mountains. Its water is clear; but the rock through which it drains away is at times so worked that it must be cleared with iron, so that the outlet always stays open and the water does not spread over the neighbouring places. Around it, in the fields, wood can be seen covered with a stony crust. Those who live nearby affirm that a stick fixed in it is surrounded by stone within a few days. It breeds excellent fish, especially trout and tench, and these have no spines except in the structure of the backbone. It carries small boats, by which fruit is usually transported back and forth. According to Pliny, the Sabines dwell beside it. The ancient writers affirm that this Lacum holds the middle of Italy and is its navel. Virgil, in the seventh book, surely sings of it, having thoroughly considered the nature of its situation:

units.la: EH
units.tr: EH

units.la: Fit locus Italiæ in medio sub montibus altisNobilis, & fama multis memoratus in oris,Amsancti Valles;
units.tr: "There is a place in the middle of Italy, under high mountains, noble and remembered by many in the regions, the valleys of Amsanctus."

units.la: Reliqua cap. 11. In eos autem Virgilij Versus, ut ibi dixi, Servio Donatoque, contra receptissimos Geographos sentientibus, non magna est adhibenda fides. Hodie Lago del Pie de Luco, ut censet Leander ab opido adiacente; vel, ut Georgius Fabricius. Lago de Terni Septuagesimo ab Reate stadio opidum est, quod hodie Contigliano, olim Cutilia, de quo infra. Non procul ea Lacus erat amplitudine iugerum quatuor, immensæ vero profunditatis, numquam, etsi perpetuos effunderet rivos, decrescens, propter æternas in eo fontium scatebras. Veteres Numen illi credebant inesse, Victoriæque sacrum autumabant: quam ob causam etiam summa religione, atque adeo fossa vallo, circumducto Aditum eius custodiebant, ne cui præter Urbis Primores Accessus umquam pateret; iis quippe statis Sacrificiorum temporibus exiguam in eo Insulam, ambitu fere quingentorum, necamplius, pedum, sesquipede super Aquas eminentem, instabilem, & hac illac, ut Ventis impellebatur. Huc quantum ingredi tantum ex instituto moreque gentis fas erat. Herbida ea, Dumisque tecta erat humilibus; & præcipuam ferebat herbam caricî haud admodum dissimilem. Admiranda vero res illis videbatur, qui summæ Rerum gubernatricis Naturæ vires & facultates ignorabant, Miraculum inde potius nulli inferius, quam rem arbitrantes utitatam. Vide omnino Dionysium Halic. lib. 1. Antiq. Roman. cui Κοτυλία scribitur, Ἀ Βαπ esse notanti. De eius Aquis Strabo lib. v: Κωμ ὢ ... Lacus Cutiliensis Varroni lib. iv de L. L. Cutiliensium Macrobio lib. 1. Saturn. cap. vii; Cutilia Aqua & Cutilia Lacus Plinio; Cotilia Lacus Festo, Κωτυλίας appellat Strabo libro v. Sic enim legendum, non Κωποχολίας. Cutile etiam simpliciter Senecæ & Antonino, scilicet Aquæ; nisi apud hunc Opidum ipsum designetur, quod hodie, ut dixi, Contigliano: Lago di Contiglione dicitur vernacule. Aquas Cutilias etiam Sabinas nominat Dion. Inter Reate & Amiternum locat Livius lib. xxvi. Insulæ etiam mentionem faciunt præter Dionysium alij, Varro lib. iv. quem dixi, de L. L. Nympha Commotia ad Lacum Cutiliensem, ab Commotu, quod ibi Insula in aqua commoveatur. Plinius lib. iii. cap. xii: In Agro Reatino Cutilia Lacum, in quo fluctuet Insula, Italiæ Umbilicum esse, M. Varro tradit. Idem lib. ii. cap. xcv: Et apud Cutilias Aquas opaca Silva, quæ numquam die ac noctu eodem loco visitur. Seneca Quæst. Natur. lib. iii: Ipse ad Cutilias natantem Insulam vidi: & paullo post: Cutiliarum Insula & Arbores & Herbas nutrit. Sic Festus: Cotilia Lacus appellatur, quod in eo est Insula Cotilia nominata ab Græcis. His enim redditum fertur Responsum. Legitur illud apud eundem Macrobium loco, quem indicavi:
units.tr: The rest is in chapter 11. But in interpreting these verses of Virgil, Servius and Donatus, who think differently from the most accepted geographers, as I said there, must not be given much credit. Today it is the Lago del Pie de Luco, as Leander thinks, from the neighbouring town; or, as Georgius Fabricius says, the Lago de Terni. Seventy stadia from Reate is a town which is today Contigliano, formerly Cutilia, about which more below. Not far from it was a lake of four jugera in extent, but of immense depth, never decreasing, although it poured out perpetual streams, on account of the eternal bubbling of springs in it. The ancients believed a divinity dwelt in it and thought it sacred to Victory. For this reason they guarded its approach with the greatest reverence, surrounding it with a ditch and a rampart, so that access was never open to anyone except the chief men of the city. On the fixed days of the sacrifices there rose above the water a small island, about five hundred feet in circuit, no more, a foot and a half above the waves, unstable, and driven hither and thither by the winds. Only as many as the custom and practice of the people allowed could enter it. It was covered with grass and low bushes, and its chief plant was a kind of fig, not very unlike a caricus. The thing seemed wonderful to those who did not know the powers and faculties of Nature, the governing mistress of all things, and so they thought it a miracle rather than a natural phenomenon. Certainly see Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 1 of the Roman Antiquities, where it is written Kotylia, a form noted by those who correct the text. Strabo, book 5, speaks of its waters: [Κωμ ὢ ...]. Varro, book 4 of On the Latin Language, calls it the Lacus Cutiliensis; Macrobius, book 1 of the Saturnalia, chapter 7, the Cutiliensium; Pliny, the Cutilia Aqua & Cutilia Lacus; Festus, the Cotilia Lacus; Strabo, book 5, calls it Κωτυλίας. For so it should be read, not Κωποχολίας. Seneca and Antoninus also simply say Cutile, meaning the waters, unless the town itself is meant there, which today, as I said, is Contigliano; in the vernacular it is called Lago di Contiglione. Dion also names the Aquas Cutilias the Sabinas. Livy, book 26, places it between Reate and Amiternum. Besides Dionysius, others also mention the island: Varro, book 4, On the Latin Language, which I cited; the nymph Commotia at the Lacum Cutiliensem, named from Commotu, because the island is moved in the water there. Pliny, book 3, chapter 12: In the Reatine territory is Cutilia, a lake in which an island floats; Marcus Varro reports that it is the navel of Italy. The same author, book 2, chapter 95: And at the Cutilian waters there is a shady wood, which is never seen in the same place by day and night. Seneca, Natural Questions, book 3: I myself saw the island floating at Cutilia. And a little later: The island of Cutilia nourishes both trees and herbs. So Festus: The lake is called Cotilia, because in it is an island named Cotilia by the Greeks. For it is said that a response was given to them there. That verse is read in the same Macrobius, in the passage I indicated:

units.la: Στεχίη μαιόμβοι Σικελᾶν Σαληρίου αἶανἨ δ᾽ Ἀσσεργίνιον, Κοτύλη τ᾽ ἀγαθ᾽ ἐχέ᾽ ...
units.tr: [Στεχίη μαιόμβοι Σικελᾶν Σαληρίου αἶανἨ δ᾽ Ἀσσεργίνιον, Κοτύλη τ᾽ ἀγαθ᾽ ἐχέ᾽ ...]

units.la: Et sequuntur.
units.tr: And so on.

units.la: Blandusiæ Fons in Sabinis est Horatio lib. iii Carminum: ad quem Acroni Blandusiæ Regio est Agri Sabinensis. Sed Blandusiæ habere omnes M. SS. Codices notat Cruquius.
units.tr: The Blandusiae Fons is in the Sabine country, according to Horace, book 3 of the Odes; to which Acro says Blandusiae is a region of the Sabine territory. But Cruquius notes that all the manuscripts have Blandusiae.

units.la: Inter Lacus Paludesque, quæ Campaniæ, loci principis sunt Lucrinus & Avernus. Utriusque Situm, ut universim hoc præmittam, indicant Polybius & Strabo. Ille quidem lib. xlviii: Ἐν τῇ Κύμῃ τῇ Καμπανίδι χωρίον τι μεζόξὺ ... Lucrinus Virgilio, Valerio Maximo, Tacito, Silio, Plinio, Suetonio, Melæ; Λουκρῖνος Κόλπος, Straboni. Solent enim Græci κόλπους vocare Lucrinum & Avernum, quos Latini Lacus appellant. Lucrinum volunt nonnulli denominatum ab Lucro, quod ex eo, quia piscolus erat, percipiebatur. Λουκρῖνος Κόλπος, inquit, Strabo, σταδίων) μίχρι Baiæ, χώματι ἐρχόμενον ὁπὸ τ᾽ ἐξω Ἰουλίας ἐκ Ἰαδίῳ τὸ μῆ- κος, πλάτος δ᾽ ἀμαχλὺς πλατεῖας, ὁ Φασι Ἡρακλεια λίμνη, τὰς βὰς ἰλαύνειλα τὰς ἡμῶσιν· δεχεσθαι δ᾽ ὑπὸ πελάγης τὸ κῦμα τῆς χειμῶνος, ὡς τὴ μὴ πηλὸς ῥαδίως, Ἀχερ- οντας ἱπποδρομίαν. ἐσπαλεῶν δ᾽ ἐχὴ πλείως ἰλαφρίς, ἐσχρμιζας μὲν ἀχερ.ιᾶς, τ᾽ ἐσχάρω δὲ ἱνῶν ἐχων ἀφοναζωτῳ. Agger, quo Lucrinum ab reliquo mari arceri solitum notat Strabo, Opus fuit Julium: de quo Virgilius: An memorem Portus, Lucrinoque addita Claustra? Atque indignatum magnis fluctibus Alpheus? Julia qua Ponto longe sonat Unda refuso: Tyrrhenusque freto immittitur Aufidus Avernis.
units.tr: Among the lakes and marshes which are the chief places of Campania are the Lucrinus & Avernus. Polybius and Strabo indicate their position, which I shall state in general first. Polybius, book 48, certainly: [Ἐν τῇ Κύμῃ τῇ Καμπανίδι χωρίον τι μεζόξὺ ...]. Virgil, Valerius Maximus, Tacitus, Silius, Pliny, Suetonius and Mela call it Lucrinus; Strabo, Λουκρῖνος Κόλπος. For the Greeks are accustomed to call the Lucrinum & Avernum, which the Latins call Lacus, gulfs (κόλπους). Some hold that Lucrinum was named from Lucro, because profit was gained from it, since it was full of fish. Strabo says: the Lucrine Gulf, [about ... stadia] as far as Baiae, reached by an embankment that runs from outside Julia, a length of ... and a width of ..., which they say was the Heraclean lake, lying across the sea... receiving the wave of the storm, so that the water there is not easily... the Acheron horse-race... and it has a good harbour, fitted with ... Strabo notes that the embankment by which the Lucrine was usually kept apart from the rest of the sea was the work of Julius. Of it Virgil says: Shall I mention the harbours and the barriers added to the Lucrine? And Alpheus, indignant with the great waves? Where the Julian wave sounds far off with the sea poured back; and the Tyrrhenian Aufidus is sent into the Avernian waters by the strait.

units.la: Quos Versus exponens Servius, duos ait in Sinu Baiano Campaniæ contra Puteolos esse Lacus, Avernum & Lucrinum: unde propter uberes Piscatus amplissimum Vectigal percipiebatur: aliquando tamen maris undis impetu nimio intrantibus, & eadem celeritate refluentibus, abduci contigisse Piscem, & Vectigalia deteriora heri. Hac de causa Publicanis orantibus, ut provideretur, Julium Cæsarem misisse; ab eoque toto negocio perspecto, brachia duo iactis aggeribus ducta, quibus Æstus marinorum fluctuum arcerentur, angusto tamen ostio relicto per quod in Avernum Piscis convenire posset, Fluctus ingruere non possent: proinde Opus id Julium appellatum. De qua re Suetonius etiam memorat in Vita Iulij, Cæsarem Baianum Portum exstruxisse, immisso in Lucrinum, & Avernum Mari. Addit Strabo Lucrinum capturam habere Ostreorum copiosissimam. Sic Martialis: Non omnis landica pretiumque Aurata mercatur, Sed cum solus erit Concha Lucrina cibus.
units.tr: Explaining these verses, Servius says that in the Bay of Baiae in Campania, opposite Puteoli, there are two lakes, Avernus and Lucrinus, from which a very large revenue was drawn because of their abundant fish. Sometimes, however, the sea rushed in with great force and flowed back with equal speed, so that the fish were carried away and the revenues fell. For this reason the tax-farmers asked for a remedy, and Julius Caesar was sent. After examining the whole matter, he ran two arms out with embankments to keep out the surging of the sea, leaving a narrow mouth through which the fish could enter Avernus, while the waves could not burst in. That work was therefore called the Julian. Suetonius also mentions this in the Life of Julius: Caesar built the harbour of Baiae by letting the sea into Lucrinus and Avernus. Strabo adds that Lucrinus has a very rich oyster fishery. So Martial: "Not every spiny lobster or gilded fish is bought at a price, when the Lucrine shell alone is the meal."

units.la: Et alibi: Ebria Baiano veni modo Concha Lucrino, Nobile nunc sit o luxuriosa Garum.
units.tr: And elsewhere: "I come drunk on the Baian Lucrine oyster; now, o luxurious man, let garum be famous."

units.la: Plinius quoque lib. ix natur. Histor. cap. liv. Auratas & Ostrea Lucrini Baianique Sinus celebrat. Lucrinum Lacum Ἀίμνλυ esse Ἀχερουσίαν opinantur nonnulli apud Strabonem, vehementer, ut scribit Leander, errantes. Baianum Lacum habet Tacitus lib. xiv Annal. alium ab Lucrino. Ex Lucrino introitus olim erat in Avernum: ita Livio, Virgilio, Silio, Senecæ, Plinio, Suetonio, Melæ, Vibio Sequestro, aliis nominatum, qui Ἀόρνου Lycophroni, Aristoteli, Straboni, ceterisque Græcis. Ἀόρνυ vocat Antigonus, apud quem vide elegantem Timæi de eo locum. Styga quondam appellatum innuit Silius lib. xii: Ille olim Populis dictum Styga nomine verso, Stagna inter celebrem nunc mitia monstrat Avernum.
units.tr: Pliny too, in book ix of his Natural History, chapter liv, celebrates the gilt fish and the oysters of the Lucrine and Baian bays. Some, in Strabo, think the Lucrine lake is Acherusia [Ἀχερουσίαν], which, as Leander writes, is a serious mistake. The Baian lake is distinct from the Lucrine, as Tacitus has it in book xiv of the Annals. There was once a passage from the Lucrine into Avernus, and it is named this way by Livy, Virgil, Silius, Seneca, Pliny, Suetonius, Mela, Vibius Sequester and others, and by the Greeks, Lycophron, Aristotle, Strabo and the rest, it is called Aornos [Ἀόρνου]. Antigonus calls it Aornys [Ἀόρνυ]; there see Timaeus's elegant account of it. Silius in book xii hints that it was once called Styx: "That lake, once named Styx by the people under a changed name, now shows the gentle and famous Avernus among its pools."

units.la: Infernum Lacum vocat Virgilius iii. Æneid. Hodie Lago di Tripergola, ut notant Erythræus & Georgius Fabricius. Avernum dictus putatur, quasi Ἀόρνου, sine Avibus: quod Aves supervolantes odoris eius gravitate conciderent enecatæ. Legendi Servius in iii Æneid. Nonius Marcellus, Isacius in Lycophronem, Eustathius in Odyss. χ locum illum. ἐνθα μὲν εἰς Ἀχαιῶν. Virgilius lib. vi Æneidos. Inde ubi venere ad fauces graveolentis Averni Tollunt se celeres.
units.tr: Virgil in book iii of the Aeneid calls it the "infernal lake". Today it is the Lago di Tripergola, as Erythraeus and Georgius Fabricius note. Avernus is thought to be named as Aornos, that is, without birds, because birds flying over fell dead from the heaviness of its odour. On this, read Servius on Aeneid iii, Nonius Marcellus, Isacius on Lycophron, and Eustathius on that passage of the Odyssey, book x, beginning "There, where the Achaeans...". Virgil, Aeneid book vi: "Then, when they came to the mouth of foul-smelling Avernus, swiftly they raise themselves up."

units.la: Et paulo post: Quam super haud ulla poterant impune volantes Tendere iter pennis: talis sese halitus atris Faucibus effundens supra ad convexa ferebat: Unde locum Graij dixerunt nomine Avernum.
units.tr: And a little later: "Over which no birds could fly unharmed, beating their wings. Such was the breath pouring from its dark jaws, rising to the vault of heaven. Hence the Greeks named the place Avernus."

units.la: Sic Lucretius libro vi De Natura Rerum: Principio quod Averna vocant: non nomen id abre Impositum est: quia sunt Avibus contraria cunctis.
units.tr: So Lucretius in book vi, On the Nature of Things: "First, they call them Averna. That name was not imposed without reason, because they are hostile to all birds."

units.la: Formam eius rotundiorem describit Aristoteles περὶ Φυσικῆς. Περὶ τῆς Κύμης, τῶν ἐπὶ Γαλλίαν, λίμνη ἐστὶν ἡ πεζὸν ἀρξαμένη Ἀορνου. Αὕτη ὡς, ὡς ἔοικεν, οὐκ ἔχει ζώα ἡ Φυσικῆς. Ἐπεὶ γὰρ λέγω τῇ ἀυτῶν λέφυς κύκλῳ, τὸ ὕψος οὐκ ἐλάττον τεμάχῳ ταῖς ὡς ἐκ, ἡ αὐτῶν τῷ χημᾷ κυκλοπερῇ. Sic Lycophron Chalcidensis Cassandra: Λιμνὴν τι Ληθαιῶν ἱερὸν χλίστας, Λιμνὴν τ᾽ Ἀορνον ἀμφιπρωτῶν βροχῷ.
units.tr: Aristotle describes its rather round shape in his work on natural things. Concerning Cumae, those towards Gaul: there is a lake beginning from Avernus, which, as it seems, has no living creatures. For since its surface is round, its height not less than the thickness of the stone... (the rest of this passage is too corrupt to render with certainty). So Lycophron of Chalcis in the Cassandra: "a lake of the Lethaeans, sacred to the most holy, and the lake Avernus, encircled by its wet ..."

units.la: De Averno scribit in hanc sententiam Strabo lib. v, & aditu & fundo Sinum esse peropportunum, atque tam magnitudine, quam natura loci Portuum commoditissimum; usu tamen non frequentatum, quod Portus illi præiaceret Lucrinus.
