Addit deinde, Avernum undique ab Rupibus arduis, præterquam ad ostium, circumdari: Rupes illas olim horridis saltibus occupatas, Augusti tempore cultu diligente fuisse peramœnas: apud Adcolas quoque tamam increbuisse, Aves supervolantes χ ἀναφερόμενον exanimatas in eum decidere solitas, quemadmodum in Plutonis sit loci; indeque Stagnum Plutoni sacrum habitum: quinetiam vicinos illi Cimmerios fuisse, apud quos peractis rite Sacris, placatisque Diis Manibus ad Inferos Descensus esset: Sacerdotes enim in ea gente Duces itineris ad Plutonem exstitisse, eamque ob causam Oraculum eo loco fuisse: Fontem etiam ibi prorumpentem in mare defluxisse, ab cuius usu Regionis Incolæ, quod ζωὴς ὕδωρ arbitrarentur, abstinebant: ob propinquas enim ferventium undarum scaturigines & Paludem Acherusiam, πυρίφλεγμον esse existimabant. Multa alia, quæ de hoc Lacu apud Strabonem, prætereo. Scribit Servius in III Æneid. Avernum antea Silvarum densitate ita fuisse conceptum, ut inde per angustias odor Aquæ sulphureæ gravissimus exhalans Aves supervolantes enecaret: inde Avernum appellatum quasi ἀορνος: adjiciens Augustum Cæsarem, ea re intellecta, Silvis deiectis, è pestilentibus amœna hæc reddidisse Loca. Aqua Lacus Averni sapore falsa est, colore nigra: quod ob immensam Profunditatem accidere putatur; quum Fundum eius ictum non posse deprehendi Vibius Sequester adiérat. Testatur Leander ìe, quum hæc Loca peragraret, ex Adcolis accepisse, inventum Averni fundum ab curiosis quibusdam hominibus fuisse non pridem, Fune scilicet passuum xc, quos singulos Ulnæ quaternæ constituebant: ut sic altitudinem Stagni CCCLX Ulnarum esse constitutet. Boccatius libro de Lacubus rem narrat prodigiosam; se, Roberti Siciliæ, Neapolis & Hierosolymarum regis, temporibus, in littore circa eum lacum maximam vidisse Piscium enectorum multitudinem, Visceribus intus atro colore plane deformatis odorisque sulphurei tam gravis, ut accessum non permitterent: eos autem scaturigine recentis alicuius venæ sulphureæ contactos ictosque, dein undarum impetu ejectos in ripam, omnes censuisse. Infausto nomini non amplius hoc tempore respondet: quin Aves aquaticæ frequentes in eius undis natantes haud raro visuntur. Docet apud Strabonem Artemidorus Avernum Lacum Poëtis celebratissimum Αἰδου esse Ἀχερουσίαν, cuius mentionem sæpe facit Virgilius, præcipue libro vi: Vnum oro, quando hic Inferni Ianua Regis Dicitur, & tenebrosa Palus Acheronte refuso.
units.tr: Concerning Avernus, Strabo in book v writes to this effect: the bay is most convenient both for approach and for its bottom, and as a harbour it is most suitable as much for its size as for the nature of the place; yet it was not much used, because the Lucrine lay in front of that harbour. He adds that Avernus is surrounded on every side by steep cliffs, except at the mouth. Those cliffs, once overgrown with rough thickets, were made very pleasant in Augustus's time by careful cultivation. Among the neighbouring people it also became established that birds flying over, carried up, fell dead into it, as happens at the place of Pluto; for this reason the lake was held sacred to Pluto. Moreover, the Cimmerians, who lived near it, were there, where after the sacred rites had been duly performed and the spirits of the dead appeased, there was a descent to the underworld. For among that people the priests were the guides of the journey to Pluto, and for this reason there was an oracle in that place. A spring also bursting out there flowed down into the sea, and the inhabitants of the region abstained from its water, thinking it to be living water [ζωὴς ὕδωρ], because the neighbouring springs of boiling waves and the Acherusian marsh made them think it fiery [πυρίφλεγμον]. I pass over the many other things Strabo says about this lake. Servius writes on Aeneid iii that Avernus was formerly so enclosed by the density of the woods that the very heavy odour of sulphurous water exhaling through the narrow places killed the birds flying over; hence it was called Avernus, as if aornos [ἀορνος]. He adds that Augustus Caesar, having understood this, cleared the woods and made these pestilential places pleasant. The water of Lake Avernus is false in taste and black in colour; this is thought to happen because of its immense depth, since Vibius Sequester had reported that its bottom could not be reached. Leander testifies that when he travelled through these places he learned from the locals that the bottom of Avernus was not long ago reached by some curious men, with a rope of ninety fathoms, each of which they reckoned as four cubits; so they established the depth of the lake as 360 cubits. Boccaccio, in his book on lakes, tells a prodigious tale: in the time of Robert, king of Sicily, Naples and Jerusalem, he saw on the shore around that lake a huge number of dead fish, their insides plainly disfigured with a black colour, and a smell of sulphur so strong that they did not allow anyone to approach. All thought that the fish had been touched and struck by the spring of some fresh sulphurous vein, and then thrown onto the bank by the force of the waves. It no longer answers to its ill-omened name; indeed, aquatic birds swimming on its waves are often seen. Artemidorus, in Strabo, teaches that Lake Avernus, the most celebrated in the poets, is the Acherusia of Hades, of which Virgil often makes mention, especially in book vi: "One thing I beg: since here is said to be the gate of the Infernal King, and the shadowy marsh with Acheron overflowing..."

units.la: Ad quem locum Servius, Avernum Lacum ait à Poëta describi, quem Acheron Inferorum Fluvius efficit: ita dictus, quasi ἀ χαρᾶς, sine gaudio: cum locum revera haud longe à Baiis esse, undique Montibus septum, adeo ut nec Orientem, nec Occidentem Solem possit adspicere: sed tantum medium diem. Quæ Servius ibi ex Homero de inmolatis ad hanc Paludem Elpenore, Misenoque laudat, hic brevitati studens omitto. Paludem nominat Silius lib. viii, qua ad Acherontem fatur: Hinc vicina Palus fama est Acherontis ad undas Pandere Iter.
units.tr: On this place Servius says that the lake Avernus is described by the poet as formed by Acheron, the river of the underworld. It is so named as a-charas [ἀ χαρᾶς], without joy. In reality the place is not far from Baiae, surrounded on all sides by mountains, so that it can see neither the rising nor the setting sun, only midday. What Servius there cites from Homer about Elpenor and Misenus, sacrificed at this marsh, I omit, aiming at brevity. Silius names the marsh in book viii, where he speaks to Acheron: "Hence the neighbouring marsh, it is said, opens a way to the waters of Acheron."

units.la: Clanius Fluvius spatio ab mari P.M. viii latissime diffunditur, Lacus instar latitudine duorum ferme millium quibusdam in locis, alibi vero centum Ulnarum: ideoque circum Ostia, quibus in Mare exit, vulgo Lacus Patria, Lago della Patria, vocatur, Piscium abundantia, ut autea obiter monui, uberrimus. Lacum hunc Silius lib. vii Paludis nomine memorat: Hinc Linterna Palus
units.tr: The river Clanius spreads out very widely, eight Roman miles from the sea, like a lake, roughly two miles wide in some places and elsewhere a hundred cubits. So around its mouths, by which it runs out into the sea, it is commonly called Lake Patria, Lago della Patria, and it is very rich in fish, as I noted briefly before. Silius in book vii names this lake as a marsh: "Hence the marsh of Linterna."

units.la: Et libro viii. Stagnisque Palustre Linternum.
units.tr: And in book viii: "and Linternum, marshy with its pools."

units.la: Fuisse videntur & in Campania Statina Paludes, quarum meminit Statius lib. iii Silvarum. Iudicandum relinquit Lectori V. CL. Abrahamus Ortelius, an hæ Paludes non perierint apud Plinium lib. ii. cap. xxxix, ubi hodie legitur, alioque motu Terra Stagnum emersisse: Testatur enim in Vetustioribus Codicibus Statinas esse. Certe
units.tr: The Statina marshes seem also to have existed in Campania, which Statius mentions in book iii of the Silvae. The most distinguished Abraham Ortelius leaves it to the reader to judge whether these marshes have perished, in Pliny book ii, chapter xxxix, where today it reads "and by another movement of the earth a pool emerged"; for he testifies that in older manuscripts it reads Statinas. Certainly

units.la: Cette ab Statino Lacu vel Palude Statanum Vinum videtur dici, de quo cap. iv. Pompeiam Paludem, quam memorat his verbis Columella:
units.tr: This Statine lake or marsh seems to give its name to Statanum wine, of which in chapter iv. The Pompeian marsh, which Columella mentions in these words:

units.la: Qua dulcis Pompeia Palus, vicina Salinis Herculeis;
units.tr: "where the sweet Pompeian marsh lies, near the Herculean salt-pans."

units.la: ad mare circa Pompeianum fuisse in Campania, dicit ad illum locum Pomponius Fortunatus.
units.tr: Pomponius Fortunatus says that it lay by the sea near Pompeianum in Campania, at that place.

units.la: In Salentino, inquit Plinius lib. ii. cap. ciii, iuxta oppidum Manduriam Lacus ad margines plenus, neque exhauflu aquis minuitur, neque infusis augetur. Hodie, ut scribit Leander, Lago di Andurto, in Apulia Daunia; Versentino autem, si Alexandro Andreae fides. In Apulia Peucetia, haud procul Letina, Lacus est ab oppido cognominatus. Continet in ambitu M. P. xl. Piscium optimorum copia est foecundus; maximeque, quae praecipua sunt magnitudine, Anguillarum, quas Adcolae Captones vocant. Putant quidam Pantanum esse Lacum, quem Plinius circa Garganum Montem describit. Ego nihil temere volo adfirmare.
units.tr: In the Salentine, says Pliny in book 2, chapter 103, near the town of Manduria there is a lake full to the brim, which is neither lowered by drawing off water nor raised by pouring it in. Today, as Leander writes, it is the Lago di Andurto, in Apulia Daunia; Versentino, however, if we trust Alexander Andreas. In Apulia Peucetia, not far from Letina, there is a lake named after the town. It has a circuit of forty miles. It is rich in a plentiful supply of excellent fish, and especially of eels, which are particularly large and which the local inhabitants call captones. Some think that the lake Pliny describes near Mount Garganus is the Pantanum. I do not wish to assert anything rashly.

units.la: Habet Flaminia vel Romanula Paludes Fossasque non paucas, in quibus principem obtinent locum Septem-Maria. Sic appellant Indigenae Paludes, per quas Eridanus Fluvius septem Ostia (de quibus in Padi Historia) in Mare praecipitatur. Ita etiam nominantur in Itinerario Antonini. Επτα Τα Δελτα dicuntur Dionysio Halicarnassaeo: Hadriatica Stagna ab Hadriatico Mari, sunt apud Servium in lib. i. Aeneid. Gallica Paludes vocantur Vitruvio ab Italia Gallica, vel Gallia Cisalpina. Alias speciali-ores habent ab locis vicinis Appellationes. Atrianorum (ab Atria Urbe) Paludes, inquit Plinius lib. iii, cap. xvi, quae Septem-Maria appellantur. Tartari Flumina Paludes sunt Tacito lib. iii Historiarum; Ravennae Paludes Strabonis lib. v. Hodie Stagni de Venetia dicti notat Blondus. Describit Paludes hasce diligenter Cassiodorus lib. xii Variar. ad Maritimorum Tribunos. Septem-Martium mentionem facit etiam Herodianus libro viii, Iter Maximi ab Ravenna Aquileiam, ubi Maximi Pater & Filius interierant, referens. Eorum autem pars Padusa est Palus, ad Ravennam, haud procul Amne Montono. De ea Plinius lib. iii, cap. xvi: Padus, angusta Fossa Ravennam trahitur, ubi Padusa vocatur, quondam Metlanicus appellatus. Ea Fossa Naves, inquit Leander, ab Ravenna per spacium millium xii in Padum commeant. Meminit Virgilius: —— Piscosve Amne Padusa.
units.tr: Flaminia, or Romagna, has marshes and not a few ditches, of which the Septem-Maria hold the chief place. The natives call these marshes by this name, through which the river Po empties into the sea by its seven mouths (on which see the history of the Po). They are also so named in the Itinerary of Antoninus. Dionysius of Halicarnassus calls them [Επτα Τα Δελτα]; the Hadriatica Stagna, from the Hadriatic Sea, are mentioned by Servius on book 1 of the Aeneid. Vitruvius calls them the Gallica Paludes, from Italia Gallica or Gallia Cisalpina. They have other names taken from nearby places in a more specific way. The marshes of Atria (from the city of Atria), says Pliny in book 3, chapter 16, which are called the Septem-Maria. The Tartari Flumina Paludes are in Tacitus, book 3 of the Histories; the Ravennae Paludes in Strabo, book 5. Blondus notes that today they are called the Stagni de Venetia. Cassiodorus describes these marshes carefully in book 12 of the Variae, in his letter to the tribunes of the maritime region. Herodian also mentions the Septem-Martium, in book 8, where he recounts Maximus' march from Ravenna to Aquileia, where Maximus the father and son had perished. Part of them is the Padusa Palus near Ravenna, not far from the river Montonus. Of it Pliny writes in book 3, chapter 16: The Po is drawn by a narrow ditch to Ravenna, where it is called the Padusa, once named the Metlanicus. Leander says that ships sail from Ravenna into the Po through this ditch over a distance of twelve miles. Virgil mentions it: and the Padusa, rich in fish, by its river.

units.la: Vibius Sequester nomen illi a Pado vicino esse prodit, in quem se exonerat. Olim haec Palus tractum omnem inter Padum & Aemiliae Viae finitima loca occupabat: nimirum ab Fossa, quam dixi, prope Padum per l fere P. M. Occidentem versus: Fluminaque & Torrentes plurimos ex Apennino iactos ab Anemone usque ad Panarum colligebat; quibus ipsum Stagnum creabatur. Sed annis prope l superioribus adeo exsiccata terraque expleta est, ut exigua plane parte relicta sit: etenim ab Ravenna per multorum milliariorum spacium (quae loca quondam, ut Strabo perhibet, item Procopius lib. i. de Bello Gothico, omnia fuere paludstria) continens pridem adeo excreverat, ut vix illa, cuius memini, Fossa reperiretur: & quae ibi alia de Paludis huius exsiccatione. Haud procul Bononia, prope Flumen Labinium, Fossa est Ghironda, per quam paludstria quaedam hoc situ se exonerant loca. Excipit eam Labinius, quem dixi. Extra Pinetum Candiani Amnis, nunc Palude, exiguum est Ostium. Ante ιοccc ferme, vel ιοccc annos, in hoc Stagnum Sapis, qui nunc viii P. M. abest, inlabebatur. Portumque peroportunum efficiebat, auctore Blondo, circa quem Augustus Caesar ad tutelam Superi Maris tenebat classem, ut Suetonius in eius vita, Tacitusque lib. iv prodiderunt.
units.tr: Vibius Sequester reports that it takes its name from the nearby Po, into which it discharges. Formerly this marsh occupied the whole tract between the Po and the neighbouring lands of the Aemilian Way, namely from the ditch I mentioned, near the Po, for about fifty Roman miles westward. It gathered the rivers and many torrents thrown down from the Apennines, from the Anemo as far as the Panaro, and the lake itself was formed from them. But in nearly the last fifty years it has been so dried up and filled with earth that only a very small part is left. For from Ravenna, over a distance of many miles (these places were once, as Strabo reports, and Procopius in book 1 of the Gothic War, all marshland), the land had grown so much that scarcely that ditch I mentioned could be found. What other changes there were in the drying of this marsh, I shall leave aside. Not far from Bologna, near the river Labinius, there is the Fossa Ghironda, through which some marshy places discharge in this region. The Labinius, which I mentioned, receives it. Beyond Pineto is the mouth of the Candiano river, now a marsh, a small outlet. About nine or ten hundred years ago, the Sapis, which now lies eight Roman miles away, flowed into this lake. It made a very convenient harbour, according to Blondus, around which Augustus Caesar kept a fleet to guard the Upper Sea, as Suetonius in his life and Tacitus in book 4 have recorded.

units.la: In Aemilia seu Cispadana Langbardia Fossa sunt Phithorena & Mutinensis, per quas Aquae ex Locis superioribus corrivatae in Panarum Flumen exonerantur. Fossa Tarana, Torrente aucta Crustulo, per Vicum Suzariam in Padum iuxta Belfortium pertingit.
units.tr: In Aemilia, or Cispadane Lombardy, the ditches Fossa Phithorena and Mutinensis carry the waters gathered from higher places into the river Panaro. The Fossa Tarana, increased by the torrent Crustulo, reaches the Po through the village of Suzaria, near Belfortium.

units.la: Superat vero reliquas Italiae partes multitudine magnitudineque Lacuum Langbardia Transpadana. Deinde Plinius lib. iii. cap. xix: In hac Regione & x Lacus inclusi sunt, Aminesque eorum partus aut alumni, si modo exceptos reddunt, ut Addua Lacus, Ticinum Verbanus, Mincius Benacus, Ollius Sebinus, Lambrum Eupilis: omnes Incolae Padi. Sic Strabo lib. iv: Αμφιτας ... ἐν τοῖς ὀρεσι.
units.tr: Transpadane Lombardy, however, surpasses the other parts of Italy in the number and size of its lakes. Pliny says in book 3, chapter 19: In this region ten lakes are also enclosed, and the rivers that flow into them are either their offspring or their foster-children, if indeed they give back what they have received, such as the Adda to Lake Como, the Ticino to Verbanus, the Mincio to Benacus, the Oglio to Sebinus, the Lambro to Eupilis: all of them belong to the inhabitants of the Po. So Strabo in book 4: [Αμφιτας ... ἐν τοῖς ὀρεσι].

units.la: ἀπὸ μὲν Βρίζα ἐχὶ μέχρι πολισσοῦν ὁ πλάτος δὲ ἰκανὸν σταδίων [?]. ἐπεὶ δὲ πόλεως Μιγχίω ἡ δὲ ἐξῆς Οὐρίβαις, περαιώσιμον: πλάτος δὲ στάδια ἢ πρώτης [?], ἐξῆς δὲ πόλεων ἡ Τιλιτιον. Τέλη δὲ ἀπὸ Λαξ[?] μέχρι ἰσχύς τεταρτίας σταδίων, πλάτος δὲ τετρακοσίων πόλεως δὲ ἐξῆς μικρὰ Ἀδυαν: πωσ δὲ ὡς ἡ Πασσὼν σύμπαν. Verbanus, ut ab Occidentali illimo Præcipuorum ordiar, Plinio dicitur: Οὐιτάβανος Strabon, ut iam vidimus: qui hodie, quod reliquis in hoc tractu sit maior, Lago Maggiore Italis, Germanis autem Lang-See Itinerariæ Tabulæ videtur dici Cusius. Sunt qui hunc Lacum ab Virgilio Maximum vocatum putant, hoc versu:
units.tr: [ἀπὸ μὲν Βρίζα ἐχὶ μέχρι πολισσοῦν ὁ πλάτος δὲ ἰκανὸν σταδίων [?]. ἐπεὶ δὲ πόλεως Μιγχίω ἡ δὲ ἐξῆς Οὐρίβαις, περαιώσιμον: πλάτος δὲ στάδια ἢ πρώτης [?], ἐξῆς δὲ πόλεων ἡ Τιλιτιον. Τέλη δὲ ἀπὸ Λαξ[?] μέχρι ἰσχύς τεταρτίας σταδίων, πλάτος δὲ τετρακοσίων πόλεως δὲ ἐξῆς μικρὰ Ἀδυαν: πωσ δὲ ὡς ἡ Πασσὼν σύμπαν.] The Verbanus, to begin with the chief lakes from the western shore, is called the Verbanus by Pliny; Strabo calls it [Οὐιτάβανος], as we have already seen. Because it is larger than the others in this district, it is called the Lago Maggiore by the Italians, but by the Germans Lang-See. The Itinerary Tables seem to call it the Cusius. Some think that this lake is the one called Maximus by Virgil, in this line:

units.la: Anne Lacus tantus? te Lari, Maxime, &c.
units.tr: Is the lake so great? Larius, Maximus, etc.

units.la: dicuntque apud Poëtam vocem Maxime non esse Lari y Lacus Epitheton, sed proprium Lacus nomen. Verbanum dictum putant quidam ab diversis Verbis, hoc est varietate Sermonis, qua Lacus Adcolæ utuntur. Alij ab Verborum multitudine, quibus inter se gentes ad Lacum finitimæ conferre solerant indies propter Negociorum frequentiam. Nonnulli ab herba Verbena sacra, de sacro Capitolij loco sumta, quemadmodum ait Servius, qua coronabantur Feciales & Pater Patratus Fœdera facturi, vel Bella indicturi: proinde quoniam ex Herba Verbena Coronæ illæ fiebant, ideo Verbanum Euphoniæ gratia, unius litteræ commutatione nominatum hoc Stagnum, quod inter alia harum partium plurima dignitate, tamquam corona, præcellat. Non desunt, qui censeant Appellationem hanc ab verna temperie natam, quæ circa ripam Lacus perpetua; ceu Ver novi temporibus ubique constante virenteque Solo. Longitudinem eius ponit Strabo Stadiorum ccc; Canobius, cccxx; Machaneus, cccl xiii; Latitudinem maximam facit idem Strabo Stadiorum xxx; Machaneus, xxxiii; Canobius, lvi. Varietas inde, quod tortuosis Amfractibus Recessibusque multis sit implicitus. Altitudo plerisque locis tam est vasta, ut Fundo videatur carere. Initium eius ad Sextium oppidum, ubi Ticinus effluit. Hinc enim perpetuo tractu crescit, nunc se diffundens, nunc contrahens usque ad Magadinum, iuxta quod Ticinus inlabitur: quem invectum supermeare Verbano Plinius est Auctor libro iii cap. cvi. Maxima Procellarum vi sævit, ut & Benacus, præsertim ab Australi Vento, qui Incolis Liverna agitatus. Pisces generat optimos, cum primis Truttas permagnas, Lucios insignes; Chalcides vel Aquones, Phoxinos vel Veronos, Percas aurei coloris, & alios. Convestiunt Lacum huuc honestaOpida; Vicique, Colles, Campi, Prata, Nemora, summæ amœnitatis. Verbanum eiusque Situm accurate describunt Dominicus Machaneus, & Iulius Canobius IC. exque iis Leander Albertus. Hæc de Verbano, cui ad occidentem adiacet Ortanus ab Orta oppido, quod adsitum illi dictus. Exonerat se Strona Amne iuxta Omeniam, mille passibus ab Verbano in Athisonem, qui mox in Verbanum evolvitur. Idem D. Iuly nominatur ab æde in Lacus Insula sita, Divoque Julio sacra. Mentionem Insulæ facit etiam Paullus Diaconus lib. iiii. Histor. Langbard Minulphum Insulæ S. Iuly Ducem ab Agiulpho Langbardorum Rege, quod se Francis dedidisset, occisum scribens. Lacus in longum patet millibus ix, in latum v. Lacus porro Lacus Virgilio lib. ii Georg. Plinio, aliisque: Λαξ. Strabini, Ptolemæo, ceterisque Græcis, qui Comacenus ab Vrbe adiacente, PaulloDiacono & Antonino. Hodie Lago di Como Italis, Germanis autem Chumer-See. Pingitur in Tabula Itineraria, sed non addito nomine. Eius Etymon quod ex Catone Sempronioque suppositis ab Annio Viterbiensi Scriptoribus adfertur, nondum probare possumus. Nominatum nonnulli volunt ab Lario Ave, Græce sic dicta, Latinis Fulica, qua abundat. Benaco maior est, Verbano æqualis fere. Longitudinem Strabo stadiorum scribit ccc; Latitudinem, xxx: Noviti paullo aliter metiuntur. Excurrit ab Septemtrione in Meridiem; pronior tamen in Orientem. Situm Lacus Formamque delineant cum cura Angelus Mediolanensis, Iulius Canobius IC. Paullus Iovius, Leander Albertus, & ævi superioris alij: Antiqui autem Strabo lib. v, Plinius in Epistolis, Cassiodorus lib. vi Variar. Coronatur undique Montibus fructiferis, Silvisque Fetarum plenis Piscium optimorum est fertilis; maxime Truttis eximiis & grandibus abundans. Flumen Adduam, quod etiam notat Strabo, accipit ex Iugis Rheticis, quod Lacui invehitur supermeans, ut & Plinius auctor est, & oculis cernere licet: ac dein è Leuci redditum Pado inlabitur. In ipso Lario, millibus ab Como xvi, è regione Baibiani, Insula Comacena visitur, quam Paullus Diaconus lib. iii, iv & vi Histor. Langbard. nominat, scribens Principes Ducesq; multos cum Familiis & Thesauris in Propugnaculo, quod hic erat, se continuisse. Conspiciendos se præbent, inter Verbanum & Larium, Lacus quidam minorum gentium. Luganus Lacus, quem aliqui Lucanum Latine vocant, admodum est tortuosus, tribus præcipue ramis; quos totiusque Lacus accurate describit Leander. Pater est amnis Treilæ, qui hinc in Lacum Masorem tendit. Gaviratius Latitudinis passuum mille, Longitudinis ad sena millia, incola Verbani est, in quem iuxta Botiam supra Ilpratium Fossa P. M. V se exonerat. Ripæ adiidet Gaviratium Opidum, à quo Lacui nomen. Monattus dictus ab opido, quod in ripa situm, cognomine. Fossa quadam in Gaviratium evacuatur. Altius deinde Lacus est Trinattus, quem aliqui Latine Ternati vel Teriacum nuncupant. Sequitur alius ab opido denominatus, quod iuxta est in læva ripa, Trinattus cum Comebio, cuius dextra Corcinum & Varranum, à quibus etiam Corcini Varanique Lacus idem appellatur. Patet in longum stadius xvi, in latum viii; ab Sextio abest milibus xxxii; ab Gavratto Lacu, viii: ubi se exonerat quadam propter Blendronium exiguum opidum Fossa, seu potius Stagno 10 passuum, tantum ab Gavriatio lacu vicenum quinum intervallo: colliguntur enim hic Aquæ per abditos Meatus è Lacu manantes. Ad alterum Larij brachium supra Pontem Lecci modicus est Lacus exigua Fossa se in Adduam emittens. Haud procul inde Lacus occurrunt Chiva & Pusianus, ab Vico superposito nomen habens, Plinioque lib. iii. cap. xviii Enpilii vocatus: Lago di Pusciano Leandro quidem dicitur; sed di Monte Orphano, Erythræo; Mongutij sive Montù Acuti, Bernardino Sacco. Fossis Ostiisque Enpili coniuncti sunt, inque eum confluunt Cervianus & Segrennus. Minores alios præterco. Nobilioribus Langbardiæ Trani-Padanæ concenteri etiam consueverunt Lacus Sebinus & Benacus. Sebinus Plinio dictus lib. iii. cap. xix, Sevinus autem lib. ii, cap. cviii, qui hodie Lago d' Iseo, ab Iseo Castro, quod in eius ripa. Lacus hic exceptum ad Septemtrionem Ollium, rursus ad Austrum emovit. Insulas habet aliquot quorum una reliquas magnitudine superat, Rocca Pescheraque nobilis. Evacuantur in Sebinum per diversos Fluvios Lacus ignobiliores, qui vulgo Lago Mazefo, Lago Nodan, Lago di Areno. Benacus Virgilio, Plinio, Sex. Aurelio; Strabonis autem Ptolemæo, (ab Opido, quod hic olim, cuiusque hodie cernuntur Vestigia: Ego alibi.) qui Lydus Catullo ad Sirmionem suam, ab Lydo, id est Tyrrhenis, quos fama est quondam vicinos illi Agros coluisse: Lago di Garda, Italice; Gard Se Germanice ab Arce Orientali Ripæ adsita. Videndus præter alios Helias Capreolus lib. v. Histor. Brixianæ. Longitudo ex Strabonis indicio 10 Stadiorum; Blondo P.M. fere xxx. Latitudo eidem Strabonis ccc Stadiorum; Blondo, minor. Ex Georgij Iodoci Bergani Monachi & Iulij Canobij delineationibus inter opidum Pescheram & Rivam, quæ ad extrema sunt Capita, illud ab Meridie, hoc ab Septemtrione Longitudo P. M. xxxv per directum invenitur: Latitudo autem recta ab Salidio, quod in Occidentali ripa usque ab Gardam aut Lagisum, quæ in Orientali sunt, millia. censetur circiter yv. Perfluitur ab Mincio, qui Mencio nunc, vel Sarca. Nonnullæ sunt in eo Insulæ. Versus Meridiem inter Pescheram opidum & Peninsulam in qua Sirmio, Aquæ ex imo ipsius Lacus fundo ebulliunt sulphureæ. Sæpe ingentibus, commoti maris instar, Fluctibus æstuat; Ventis, qui circumiectorum Montium vallo inclusi, sævissimas frequenter procellas creantibus, ut merito Virgilius lib. ii Georgic.
units.tr: Some say that in the Poet Maxime is not an epithet of Lari and Lacus, but the proper name of the lake. Some think Verbanum was named from diverse words (verba), that is, from the variety of speech that the people living by the lake use. Others say it was named from the great number of words by which the neighbouring peoples around the lake were accustomed to deal with one another daily, because of the frequency of their business. Some derive it from the sacred herb verbena, taken from the sacred place on the Capitol, as Servius says, with which the fetial priests and the Pater Patratus were crowned when about to make treaties or declare war. Since those garlands were made from verbena, they say Verbanum, for the sake of euphony and by the change of one letter, was the name of this Stagnum, which surpasses the others of these parts in its great dignity, as a crown does. There are also those who think the name arose from the spring-like mildness of the air, which is constant along the shore of the Lacus, as if the soil were always green with a constant new spring. Strabo gives its length as 300 stadia; Canobius 320; Machaneus 353. Strabo gives its greatest breadth as 30 stadia; Machaneus 33; Canobius 56. It is called varied because it is intricate with many winding bends and recesses. In most places its depth is so great that it seems to have no bottom. Its beginning is at the town of Sextium, where the Ticinus flows out. From there it grows in one continuous stretch, now spreading out, now narrowing, as far as Magadinum, beside which the Ticinus flows in; and Pliny, in book 3, chapter 106, is the authority that this river, once it has entered, passes over the Verbanum. It rages with the greatest force of storms, as does the Benacus, especially from the south wind, which the inhabitants call Liverna. It produces excellent fish, above all very large trout and fine pike; chalcides or aquones, phoxini or veroni, perch of golden colour, and others. Splendid towns surround this Lacus, and villages, hills, plains, meadows and groves of the highest charm. Verbanum and its situation are described with care by Dominicus Machaneus and by Julius Canobius, jurist, and from them by Leander Albertus. So much for the Verbanum, to whose west lies the Ortanus, named after the town of Orta, which lies near it. The Strona river discharges itself near Omegna, a thousand paces from the Verbanum, into the Athiso, which soon rolls into the Verbanum. The same island is called by the name of St. Julius, from the church situated on the island of the lake and sacred to Divus Julius. Paulus Diaconus also mentions the Insula, in book 4 of his History, writing that the Lombard Minulphus, duke of the island of St. Julius, was killed by Agiulphus, king of the Lombards, because he had surrendered himself to the Franks. The Lacus extends lengthwise nine miles and across five. Virgil, in book 2 of the Georgics, Pliny and others call it Lacus; the Greeks, Strabo, Ptolemy and the rest call it Lax; it is Comacenus from the city lying next to it, by Paulus Diaconus and Antoninus. Today the Italians call it Lago di Como, and the Germans Chumer-See. It is drawn on the Itinerary Table, but without a name. We cannot yet prove the etymology that is brought forward from the spurious writings of Cato and Sempronius, attributed to Annius of Viterbo. Some want it named from the Larius; the bird Ave, called in Greek by that name and in Latin Fulica, abounds there. It is larger than the Benacus and roughly equal to the Verbanum. Strabo writes its length as 300 stadia and its breadth as 30; more recent writers measure it a little differently. It runs from north to south, though it slopes more towards the east. Angelus of Milan, Julius Canobius, jurist, Paulus Jovius, Leander Albertus and other writers of the more recent age have carefully described its position and shape; among the ancients, Strabo in book 5, Pliny in his Letters, and Cassiodorus in book 6 of the Variae. It is crowned on every side with fruitful mountains and woods full of wild animals, and it is fertile in excellent fish, abounding above all in choice and large trout. The river Adda, which Strabo also notes, takes its source from the Rhaetian ridges; it flows into the lake, passing over it as Pliny also attests, and this can be seen with the eyes; then after leaving Lake Lecco it flows into the Po. In the Larius itself, sixteen miles from Como, opposite Baibiano, the Insula Comacena is seen, which Paulus Diaconus in books 3, 4 and 6 of his Lombard History names, writing that many princes and dukes with their families and treasures kept themselves in the stronghold that stood there. Between the Verbanum and the Larius there appear certain smaller lakes. The Luganus Lacus, which some call Lucanum in Latin, is very winding, with three main arms; Leander describes accurately this lake and all of it. The river Treglia is its father, and from here it runs into the Lacus Masor. The Gaviratius, a thousand paces in breadth and about six thousand in length, belongs to the Verbanum; into it, near Bolgia above Ispra, the canal of the Po discharges itself. The town of Gavirate, from which the lake takes its name, lies on its bank. The Monattus is named from the town of the same name situated on its shore. Through a certain ditch it empties into the Gaviratius. Further up is the Lacus called Trinattus, which some in Latin name Ternati or Teriacum. Next follows another lake named from a town that lies near it on the left bank, the Trinattus with Comebio; on its right are Corcino and Varrano, from which the same lake is also called the Lakes of Corcino and Varano. It extends sixteen stadia in length and eight in breadth; it is thirty-two miles from Sextium and eight from the Gavratto Lacu. Here, near the little town of Blendrio, a ditch or rather a pool of ten paces empties itself, only twenty-five paces distant from the Gavriatio lacu; for the waters flowing out of the lake are collected here through hidden channels. Beside the other arm of the Larius, above the bridge of Lecco, there is a modest Lacus, which discharges itself into the Adda by a small ditch. Not far from there lie the Chiva and Pusianus, which has its name from the village situated above it, and which Pliny in book 3, chapter 18, called Enpilius. Leander indeed calls it Lago di Pusciano, but Erythraeus calls it di Monte Orphano, and Bernardino Sacco Mongutij or Montù Acuti. The Enpilius is joined by ditches and outlets, and into it flow the Cervianus and Segrennus. I pass over other smaller lakes. The lakes Sebinus and Benacus, which are also customarily reckoned among the more noble ones of Transpadane Lombardy, are also to be mentioned. The Sebinus is called by Pliny in book 3, chapter 19, but Sevinus in book 2, chapter 108; today it is Lago d'Iseo, from the castle of Iseo, which lies on its shore. This lake, after receiving the Ollius, pushes it back to the north and then again to the south. It has several islands, of which one surpasses the rest in size, the famous Rocca Pescheraque. Into the Sebinus empty by various rivers the less noteworthy lakes, which in common speech are called Lago Mazefo, Lago Nodan, Lago di Areno. The Benacus is named by Virgil, Pliny and Sextus Aurelius; by Strabo, however, and Ptolemy it is named Lydus (from the town which once stood here, whose traces can still be seen today; I shall speak of it elsewhere); Catullus calls it Lydus in relation to his Sirmio, from Lydus, that is, the Etruscans, who are said to have once inhabited the fields near it. Italians call it Lago di Garda, and Germans Gard See, from the eastern fortress that lies on its shore. Among others, Helias Capreolus in book 5 of the History of Brescia should be consulted. According to Strabo's indication, its length is 100 stadia; according to Blondus, almost thirty Roman miles. Its breadth is 300 stadia according to Strabo; according to Blondus it is less. From the delineations of George Jodocus Bergan, monk, and Julius Canobius, it is found that between the town of Peschiera and Riva, which are the extreme headlands, the one to the south and the other to the north, the length in a straight line is thirty-five Roman miles. The straight breadth, from Salò, which lies on the western shore, to Garda or Lazise, which are on the eastern, is reckoned at about five miles. It is flowed through by the Mincio, which is now called Mencio, or the Sarca. There are several islands in it. Towards the south, between the town of Peschiera and the peninsula on which Sirmio lies, sulphurous waters bubble up from the very bottom of the lake. Often it surges with huge waves, like a stirred sea, from the winds, which, enclosed by the barrier of the surrounding mountains, frequently raise the most savage storms, as Virgil rightly says in book 2 of the Georgics.

units.la: Fluctibus & Fremitu adsurgens Benacè marino.
units.tr: Rising with waves and roaring like the sea, Benacus

units.la: Hic Lacus, ut scribit ad Cardinalem Polum in quadam Epistola Alexius Vgonius, optimis Piscibus aliis præstat: amœnissimis Collibus circumseptus: undique fontes scatent; hac illac Nemora, Prata virentia, Vineæ, Olivæ, Abietes, Lauri, Cedri; Opida præterea, rebus omnibus necessariis referta in modum Coronæ illum ambiunt; ita ut nihil omnino illi desit ex hisce rebus, quæ Loca Campestria visu quidem pulcherrima & usu grata atque iucunda efficere possint, &c. De eo item Leander; Copia, inquit, Piscium optimorum abundat, imprimis Truttarum, itemque Carpionum, qui, ut ferunt, Auro vescuntur; nec alibi Piscis huius speciem invenisi creditur, præterquam in Peitano Lacu, prope Soram Aprutij, magnitudine tamen huic inferiorem. Inter Sebinum & Benacum Lacus est Idrinus, qui vulgo Lago d'Idro, vel Idro Lago. Nomen illi ab Idro Castello. Alij ab Hydra dictum censent, quam Hercules ex Iove & Alcumena natus hic perhibetur peremisse. Helias Caprecolus nomen putat inditum ab voce {a}τὸωρ, quæ Latinis Aqua. Piscibus abundat. Exonerat se in Idrinum per varios Amnes, Minores, qui vernacule Lago Cap, Lago Runcone, & alij. Nec illud silendum, describi à Ptolemæo ad caput Duriæ Fluminis Lacum Pœninum, pro quo in Itineraria Tabula vitiose legitur Lacus Henus, pro Pœnus vel Pœninus.
units.tr: Here the lake, as Alexius Vgonius writes in a letter to Cardinal Pole, surpasses the others in its excellent fish. It is surrounded by most pleasant hills, and springs gush forth on every side. Here and there are groves, green meadows, vineyards, olive trees, firs, laurels and cedars. Moreover, towns full of all necessary goods lie around it in the shape of a crown, so that nothing at all is lacking to it of those things which can make the level country both very beautiful to look at and pleasant and agreeable to use, etc. Leander says of it likewise: There is an abundance of the finest fish, especially trout, and also carp, which, as they say, feed on gold; nor is this kind of fish believed to be found anywhere else except in the Lake Penne near Sora in the Abruzzi, though that lake is smaller in size than this one. Between Sebinus and Benacus lies the lake Idrinus, commonly called Lago d'Idro or Idro Lago. It takes its name from the castle of Idro. Others think it was named from the Hydra, which Hercules, said to be the son of Jupiter and Alcmena, is here reported to have killed. Helias Caprecolus thinks the name was given from the word hydor [ὕδωρ], which in Latin is aqua (water). It abounds in fish. It discharges itself into the Idrinus through several smaller streams, which in the vernacular are called Lago Cap, Lago Runcone, and others. Nor should it be passed over in silence that Ptolemy describes at the head of the river Duria the Lacus Pœninus, for which the Itinerary Table wrongly reads Lacus Henus, in place of Pœnus or Pœninus.

units.la: Nec ius caret Lacolus F sssique Venetia. Vtitur in eius agris Virgiselus. Emittitur fossa per Valles hinc Turbanam & Sabadinam, inde Grandem cognominaras in alium, qui vulgo Lago di l'Anguilara. Occurrunt haud procul inde Fossa, quæ vulgo Fossa Monte Sefilana, Korega, Nova, Sergana, Paltana, & aliæ.
units.tr: Nor is Venetia without lakes or ditches. The Virgiselus makes use of its fields. A ditch is let out through the valleys of Turbana and Sabadina, and on the other side into another lake, called Grandis, commonly Lago di l'Anguilara. Not far from there occur ditches commonly called Fossa Monte Sefilana, Korega, Nova, Sergana, Paltana, and others.

units.la: Vt Caput hoc concludam, gloriatur unico Lacu Istria, cui nomen ab Costiaco, quod impositum illi cernitur, opido. Arsiam Flumen effundit.
units.tr: To conclude this chapter, Istria boasts of a single lake, which takes its name from the town of Costiacum, that is seen to have been given to it. The river Arsia flows out of it.

units.la: CAPVT XIII.
units.tr: CAPUT XIII.

units.la: De Variis, quæ cum in Terra, tum in Aquis Italiæ sunt, Miraculis.
units.tr: Concerning the Various Miracles Found Both in the Land and the Waters of Italy.

units.la: PARTES Italiæ, simpliciter nudeque, cum in Terra, tum in Aquis considerandas, notavi: earum iamnunc succedit Delineatio, quæ Miraculis pollent Virtutibusque singularibus, & diversæ sunt efficaciæ.
units.tr: I have noted the parts of Italy to be considered simply and plainly, both in the land and in the waters. Now follows a description of those places that are notable for miracles and singular virtues, and that have various powers.

units.la: Ad Aras Mutias, uti docet Plinius lib. iii nat. hist. cap. xxxviii, in Veiente, & apud Tusculanum, item in Silva Ciminia Loca sunt, in quibus Terra depacta non extabuntur. Quædam Terræ, eodem docente lib. ii. cap. xciv, ad ingressus tremunt, ut in Gabiensi Agro, non procul Urbe Roma Iugera ducenta Equitantium cursu, simultaneous in Reatino. In Umbria ad Naris ripam Terræ genus inveniri prodit inter Miracula Tullius, teste Plinio, quod Siccitate in Lutum, Pluviis in Pulverem solvatur. Scatent miraculis Viscera Campaniæ. In Agro Cumano Antrum est admirabili arte maximisque Sumtibus in Saxum excisum, quod hodie Sibylla Caverna nuncupatur. Designat Virgilius lib. vi Æneidos: At pius Æneas Arces, quibus altus Apollo Præsidet, horrendaque procul Secreta Sibylla, Antrum immane petit.
units.tr: Near the Altars of Mucius, as Pliny teaches in Natural History, book 3, chapter 38, in the Veientine country and near Tusculum, likewise in the Ciminian Forest, there are places where the trodden ground does not swell up. Some ground, as Pliny teaches in book 2, chapter 94, trembles at the entrances, as in the Gabian territory, not far from the city of Rome, where two hundred acres tremble under the running of horsemen, and at the same time in the Reatine country. In Umbria, on the bank of the river Nar, Tully reports, as Pliny attests, a kind of earth is found among the marvels, which dissolves into mud in dry weather and into dust in rain. The entrails of Campania teem with marvels. In the Cumaean territory there is a cave, cut into the rock with wonderful skill and at very great cost, which today is called the Sibyl's Cave. Virgil describes it in book 6 of the Aeneid: "But pious Aeneas makes for the heights where lofty Apollo presides, and for the awful hidden shrine of the Sibyl, a vast cave far off."

units.la: Et paullo post: Excisum Euboica latus ingens rupis in antrum, Quo lati ducunt Aditus centum, Ostia centum: Unde ruunt totidem voces, Responsa Sibyllæ.
units.tr: And a little later: "A huge cavern hewn from the Euboean rock, to which lead a hundred wide approaches and a hundred doors, from which as many voices pour forth, the responses of the Sibyl."

units.la: Et infra, Talibus ex Alyto dictis Cumæa Sibylla Horrendas canit Ambages, Antroque remugit, Obscuris Vera involvens.
units.tr: And below: "With such words from the shrine the Cumaean Sibyl chants dread ambiguities and roars in the cave, wrapping true things in obscurity."

units.la: Describit hoc Antrum Leander his verbis: Primum in eam partem Montis circa Lacum egressi, qua inter Septemtrionem & Occasum iacet, de qua Virgilius, Facilis Descensus Averni,
units.tr: Leander describes this cave in these words: "We first went out to that part of the mountain around the lake which lies between north and west, of which Virgil says, 'the descent to Avernus is easy.'"

units.la: ad medium Vepreti, quod ibi est, aut paullo infra inter Dumos & Urticas. Antrum exterius instar Aditus Sepulcri collapsi reperimus. In id ingressi per ruinas operum aliquamdiu procedentes, Viam elegantem in saxum excavatam, latitudine pedum x, altam xx, in longum 150 centum, vidimus; & quantum coniectura licet adsequi, quum obstructa muro sit, ulterius olim ad Lacum procedebat. Hanc esse crediderim, quam Strabo scribit Cocceium fecisse, quæ a Cumis & ab Averno Baias commeabatur. Ad cccl pedem Ostiolum in ea cernitur, a tum pedes v, latum iii, per quod eiusdem mensuræ Via, in saxum excisa, longitudine pedum lxxx, procedit. Ad eius finem, dextera, perbellum est Conclave, longum pedes xiiii, altum xii, latum viii. Intus exadversum ingressui iuxta parietem saxum a pavimento elevatum, instar exigui est Tori. Penetrale hoc olim, uti etiamnum ex parte cernitur, magnificentissime perfectum ornatumque fuit: summa Testudo Sile Attico cum auri notis depicta. Parietes Zophoros distinctis, ex Margaritarum conchis & Coralio compositis: infra Zophoros usque ad imum solum opere tessellato ex Gemmis, itemque Coralio & Margaritarum Conchis inductis erant, cuius operis etiamnum aliqua signa conspiciuntur, non minore sumtu quam artificio quondam facti. Vulgo fama est: hanc Sibyllae Cumanae habitationem fuisse. Ad laevam introitus eius Conclavis, eodem in pariete, quaedam alta Postula cernitur, paullo latior altius, per quam ad Cryptam aliam latitudinis pedum vi, longitudinis xxv, altae lata ped. iv, altae totidem, si d longa xl ducit. Inde tum via brevi & per angusta, sed altitudinis ped. iv, in quamdam Porticum, altam pedes viii, latam x, longam xxiv deveniunt, quae directo propemodum in alterum medium desinit, alta pedes xx, lata vi, longa vili. Contra eius introitum angustum item in saxo excavatum Sacellum est, latitudine pedum x, longitudine vi, altitudine totidem: ad cuius ingressum in eodem pariete dextra Alterum conspicitur, latum pedes ix, longum & altum, ut Superius. Huius in medio Lacuticulus Aquae est: iouisque tanta vi caloris aestuat, ut sudorem nemini non excutiat intranti. Qui Recessus hoc tenent, aiunt Sibyllam nubi votu operam dare consuevisse: mihi tamen Sudatorium versus fuisse videtur. Hucusque a primo ingressu, qui Lacum Avernum spectat, nullum omnino spiraculum est: sed obscura Caverna perpetua in saxum excisa, per quas oblique lucerna commeari nequit, & si quis ingrederetur alter, evadere profecto haud posset: uti cuidam accidisse constat, per cuius ossa nobis in iis angustiis necessario fuit incedendum. Prius etiam Exitus in fine nullius patebat: sed ad Ostium quo introibatur, retro erat commeandum, quod & prima vice nobis usu venit; nunc autem avulsa montis parte versus Baias Antrum apertum est angustum, per quod non tamen sine difficultate egredi licet, ut manifesto appareat hanc olim Via subterranea Baias ab Averno communis fuisse. Res est equidem admirationis plena, quae ratione tot Cuniculi Cryptaeque ferro petierint excisi, Sibylaeque casus egerit: quum praeter ullum spiraculum in tenebris Opus omne patratum sit. Vtrumque aut Cimmeriorum Habitationes, aut Antiquorum Vatum Adyta, vel Antrum Sibyllae, vel quidvis denique fuisse dicamus; certe res est, cum Arte Sumtuque, tum Raritate mirabilis. Audiamus & de hoc Antro Agathiam lib. i. de Bello Gothico: Spelunca erat utrinque patentior ac profunda, penitissimisque & amplissimis Penetralibus, Foraminibusque immensis in abruptum descendebas. Hanc ferunt Sibyllam Italicensem illam & magnam incoluisse, quae Phoebo capta & Spiritu divino inspirata potentibus futura praedixerat: siquidem & Aeneae Anchisa Fato traduntur ipsam adeuntis omnia praedixisse, quae illi in posterum essent occursura. Est & alius Sibyllae Specus in Piceno, haud procul Castello D. Mariae Gallicanae, in Apennino, immanis sane & horribilis. De eo Vulgi termo est, aut verius insulla & putida Fabula: hac ad Sibyllam patere Aditum; quae Regnum intus luculentum atque speciosum possideat, magnificis aedibus & Basilicis plenum, in quibus innumerae gentes versentur, oblectationibus Venerijs inter Choros Puellarum lascivientium, & per ea iucundissima Tecta & amoenissimos Hortos diffluentes: Id vero interdiu tantum accidere; noctu enim Viros Mulieresque pariter, atque una Sibyllam ipsam in terribiles mutari Draconess: simulque cum teterrimis illis belluis primum opere Veneris congredi ipsis necesse esse, qui intro admitti cupiunt; nec ante annum exactum quemquam contra voluntatem retineri, nisi quod unum omnino quotannis, ex numero, qui tum recepti fuerunt, manere oporteat: ad hanc porro auram inde reversis tantas Sibyllae praerogativas elargiri, ut felicissimo deinceps toto vitae cursu utantur. Vide Leandrum, & quae apud eum scribit Raffanus. Pergamus ad alia Italiae stupenda Loca. Spiracula vocant alii Charoneas Scrobes, mortiferum spiritum exhalantes. Sic Plinius lib. ii. nat. hist. cap. xciii, ubi ea in Sinuessano & Puteolano tractu describit. Eorum unum extat juxta Lacum Anianum, quod ita depingit Leander: Ad pedem altae rupis, quae Lacus cingitur, haud procul ob ipsis Aquis Scrobs aspicit in rupem excavata modice, nec lato profundave multum: posito signo praemunita, ne quis eo propius accedat, quod examinati repente concidunt ultra procedentes, uti intellectus saepe Animalium compertum fuit, & nos etiam oculis vidimus. Coliapsum tamen intus Animal si protinus educatur, affergine ex stagno Aquae vitales spiritus recuperat: sed auxilium ea in re vel quavis alia nullum, si commoretur plusculum. Adcola Karolum viii Galliae Regem, quam Alphonsum Aragonium Regno Neapolitano pepulisset, Asinum inquit iussisse mihi narraverunt, qui statim expiraverit. Ego puto Vapores noxios & graves hinc ex abditis aut Sulphuris, aut Aluminis, aut similis utriusque Metalli Venis perpetuo subiorientes, eo vehementiores intentioresque esse, quod consistant per angustum hic Specum exhalentur: quapropter quum vitales Animalium Spiritus subito comprimant atque suffocent, ut in Lacum mox immersis Vigorem pristinum restitui existimamus, tamquam alto somno obrutis, quem repentina ex- cutiat
units.tr: "To the middle of the thicket there, or a little below, among brambles and nettles. Outside we found an entrance like that of a collapsed sepulchre. Going in and advancing for some distance through the ruins of the works, we saw an elegant road cut into the rock, ten feet wide, twenty feet high, and one hundred and fifty feet long. As far as conjecture allows, since it is now blocked by a wall, it formerly continued further toward the lake. I believe this is the road which Strabo writes that Cocceius made, by which one passed from Cumae and from Avernus to Baiae. At about three hundred and fifty feet there is a small opening in it, five feet high and three wide, through which a road of the same measure, cut into the rock, proceeds for eighty feet in length. At its end, on the right, is a very fine chamber, fourteen feet long, twelve high, and eight wide. Inside, opposite the entrance, beside the wall, a rock rises from the floor like a small couch. This inner chamber was once, as is still partly visible, magnificently finished and adorned: the vaulted roof was painted with gold ornaments in Attic style. The walls were divided into zophori, composed of shells of pearls and coral; below the zophori, down to the floor, the pavement was inlaid with a mosaic of gems, likewise coral and pearl shells, and some traces of this work can still be seen, made at no less expense than skill. Common report holds that this was the dwelling of the Cumaean Sibyl. To the left of the entrance of this chamber, in the same wall, a certain high niche can be seen, somewhat wider above, through which a shorter way, six feet wide, twenty-five feet long, four feet high, and as deep as it is long, leads to another crypt, forty feet long. From there, by a short way and through a narrow passage four feet high, they arrive at a certain portico, eight feet high, ten wide, and twenty-four long, which ends almost directly in another middle space, twenty feet high, six wide, and eight long. Opposite its narrow entrance is likewise a small shrine cut into the rock, ten feet wide, six long, and as high. At its entrance, in the same wall on the right, another recess is seen, nine feet wide, and long and high as the one above. In its middle is a little pool of water, which seethes with such heat that it makes everyone who enters sweat. Those who hold this recess say that the Sibyl used to devote herself there to the nine-fold vow; to me, however, it seems to have been a sweat-bath. Up to this point, from the first entrance, which faces Lake Avernus, there is no opening at all; but there is a dark cavern cut continuously in the rock, through which a lamp cannot be carried obliquely, and if anyone went in the other way, he could surely not get out, as happened to a certain man, whose bones we had to tread upon in those narrow places. Formerly there was no exit at the far end either; but one had to go back to the door by which one entered, which also happened to us the first time. Now, however, with part of the mountain torn away toward Baiae, a narrow opening has been made, through which one can nevertheless go out only with difficulty, so that it is clear this underground passage once ran from Avernus in common to Baiae. Indeed the matter is full of wonder: by what reason so many tunnels and crypts were dug out with iron, and by what need the Sibyl's undertaking drove them, since the whole work was carried out in darkness without any opening. Whether we say these were dwellings of the Cimmerians, or shrines of the ancient seers, or the Sibyl's cave, or whatever else, the thing is certainly remarkable both for its art and expense and for its rarity."

units.la: Aliud Sybilla Antrum.
units.tr: Another Sibyl's Cave.

units.la: Charonea Scrobes nece affer-tes. cutat Aquarum adspersio, mora vero morte prorsus finitat. Vernacule Buco Velenoso dicitur, quasi dicas Antrum Venenosum: aliis Grotta de i Cani, eo quod Antri Naturam hoc Animali taepius experiantur Peregrini. Supra Balneum Ciceronianum in Rupe graduum aliquot adscentu Crypta invenitur, opere excisa, altitudine pedum vi. latitudine v, sed in longum sinuoso amfractu plurimum extenta, suavem & jucundum exhalans odorem: quam si quis erectus ingrediatur, repente sudabit, sin pronus & ad solum inflexus, refrigescet. Haud procul inde Specus adparet ad Meridiem vergens, ingressu vitandus: quippe si quis aliquantum in ima procedat, absque caloris vel frigoris excessu, absque Vento vel motu Aeris Vertigine concideret mortuus: caloreque iterum exsultante simul Cera Candelae deliquescet, simul lumen sponte deficiet. Ad finem ruinarum, quae prope Puteolos, sulphurarta est, locus ab conditione & natura sic dictus. Strabo Forum Vulcani (H Φουσα Α'γεγων) nominat, quum id Puteolis imminere dicit; & Campum esse planum, undique hagrantibus sulphure Collibus inclusum atque leptum, unde velut e Fornacibus Exhalationes cum ingenti fremitu proficiscuntur. Plinius hos ab Antiquis Campos Phlegraeos ait appellatos; quod etiam probat Silius lib. viii, quum inquit:
units.tr: Charonea, pits that bring death. The sprinkling of water ends the trance at once, but delay ends it utterly in death. In the vernacular it is called Buco Velenoso, as if you said Poisonous Cave; by others Grotta de i Cani, because foreigners often test the nature of the cave on that animal. Above the Ciceronian Bath, after climbing some steps up a cliff, one finds a crypt cut out by hand, six feet high and five wide, but extending a great distance in a winding passage. It gives off a sweet and pleasant smell. If someone enters it upright, he will sweat at once; if he goes in bent over and stooping to the floor, he will grow cold. Not far from there appears a cave facing south, which must be avoided. For if anyone goes some way into its depths, without any excess of heat or cold and without wind or any movement of air, he will fall dizzy and die. And when the heat flares up again, the wax of a candle melts at once and the light goes out of its own accord. At the edge of the ruins near Puteoli is a place called sulphurarta from its condition and nature. Strabo names it the Forum of Vulcan (ἡ Φουσα ἀγεγών), when he says it lies above Puteoli. He describes it as a level plain, enclosed on all sides by hills burning with sulphur and smoking, from which exhalations rise with a huge roar, as if from furnaces. Pliny says the ancients called these the Phlegraean Plains, which Silius also confirms in book 8, where he says:

units.la: Crypta sulfurea cassiana. Mortem adferens. Sulphurarta Forum Vulcani. Phlegraei Campi.
units.tr: Sulphurous crypt, Cassian. Bringing death. Sulphurarta, Forum of Vulcan. Phlegraean Plains.

units.la: illic quos sulphure pingues Phlegrai legere Sinus.
units.tr: there, which the Phlegraean bays, rich in sulphur, gathered.

units.la: Loci Naturam plane mirabilem scribunt, qui inspexerunt: primum Aream habere Ovi forma prolongiorem; extendi enim ferme ped. cio io; sed in latum non amplius cio patere: undique perpetuis altisque Collibus ita, tamquam opere, conseptum, ut Aditum unum, qua spectat Puteolos, tantum habeat: Solum Areae totum Sulphure vestitum esse, sponte ibi nato; ideoque & incessu crepitare, quum sit cavernosum, uti Vacua contactu solent omnia. In fine kiram Follam, verius rotundam, quam formae cujusquam alterius, adparere, Aquae nigrae spissaeque plenam, quae perpetuo fervet, magnaque vi Fumos ingentes emittit: de ea non solum Vulgi Famam, sed experientia quoque compertum esse, quicquid immergatur, protinus educ tectum, numquam tamen non aliqua parte deficiente. Adiceri apud Leandrum Hieronymus Linus Bononiensis: se, quaternis in eam immissis Ovis, tria tantum eduxisse. Addit Leander, Aquam non semper eodem in loco, neque qualis magnitudine, consistere: Se enim post annos x. quum iterum ea proficisceretur, parte ferme tertia minorem, quam prima vice conspexisse; eius rei causam Spissitatem Aquae esse; concrescentibus enim Sulphure ripis extremis, Imminutionem Variationemque contingere. Circa Follam porro undique Scrobes in Solo conspici; exque iis acutissimos Vapores sulphureos cum intento Calore prodire: in hac Area multas esse Officinas, quibus album Sulphur conficitur. In Tuscia tribus ab Lecia P. M. haud procul Senentium Monte Rotundo, inter Silvas Specus est in altitudinem vastissimus; ex quo certis anni temporibus Ventus tanto cum impetu ac vi prorumpunt, ut propinquos Arborum ramos convellant, ipsaque frequenter Arbores solo eruant. In Agro Thurino, inquit Plinius lib. xvi, cap. xxi, ubi Urbs Sybaris fuit, ex ipsa Urbe prospiciebatur Quercus una, numquam Folia dimittens, nec ante mediam Aestatem germinans. In Crustumino, inquit idem lib. ii cap. xcvi, natum Fenum ibi noxium, extra salubre est.
units.tr: Those who have examined the place describe its nature as truly remarkable. First, the area is shaped like an egg, somewhat elongated, for it extends about 1,000 feet in length but not more than 100 in breadth. It is enclosed on all sides by high, continuous hills, as if by a wall, and has only one entrance, on the side facing Puteoli. The whole floor of the area is covered with sulphur that grows there naturally, so that it crackles underfoot, since the ground is hollow, as all empty places are when touched. At the end there appears a pit, more round than of any other shape, full of black, thick water which boils constantly and sends out huge fumes with great force. Not only common report but experience has shown about this pit that whatever is dipped into it is at once drawn out whole, though never without some part being lost. Linus Hieronymus of Bologna is also mentioned by Leander: he says that when he put four eggs into it, he brought out only three. Leander adds that the water does not always stay in the same place or of the same size. He says that when he went there again ten years later, he saw it about one-third smaller than the first time. He attributes the cause to the thickness of the water: as sulphur gathers on the outer banks, the pool shrinks and changes. Around the pit, pits can be seen in the ground on every side, from which the sharpest sulphurous vapours come forth with intense heat. In this area there are many workshops where white sulphur is made. In Tuscany, three miles from Lecia P. M., not far from the Round Mountain of the Senenses, there is a very large cave among the woods. At certain seasons of the year wind bursts from it with such force and violence that it tears up nearby branches of trees and often uproots the trees themselves. In the territory of Thurii, says Pliny in book 16, chapter 21, where the city of Sybaris once stood, one oak could be seen from the city itself, which never sheds its leaves and does not sprout before midsummer. In Crustumium, says the same author in book 2, chapter 96, hay grown there is harmful, while elsewhere it is wholesome.

units.la: Haec quibusdam Italiae Terris Miracula: quid jam commemorem, quae in Aquis, Fluviis, Lacubus, Fontibus, & id genus aliis? Non omnibus me torquebo investigandis. Pauca ex multis sufficiant. Natura quarundam Aquarum est Indurare Insecta. Albuneus, Albula Aqua, Anten, ut affirmant Adcolae, vi quadam sua naturali non solum consolidant & adglutinant Corpora quaevis, verum etiam Virgulta, Ligna, Folia, Herbas, aliaque solidiora, quae perfluere contingit, cortice lapideo sensim obducunt. Quin & in Agro Tiburtino, circum Anienem, Scopuli Cautesque fiaculorum succesiu ex Aquis concreverunt; in Planicie vero Lacus atque Paludes multis in locis in solidum lapideumque Solum. In Tuscia Vlmenti Montis radicibus ex Saxo Fons prorumpit, cujus Aquae diebus xv spatio quidquid immersum lapideo tegunt cortice. Ibidem Eisa Fluvius, post Sena exigui Torrentis accessum, naturae est talis, ut iniectum ignum saxeo cortice obducat. Apud Campanos immersa in Stilarum Folia Virgultaque lapidescunt, uti tradunt Strabo, Plinius, alii; nec tamen inmutato colore vel forma: quamquam alias, quod adjicit Plinius, Potus eius sit salubris. De eo & Silius lib. viii Bell. Punic.: Nunc Silarus quos nutrit aquis, quo quaque tradunt Durescere lapidem mersis inolescere ramis.
units.tr: These are marvels in certain lands of Italy. Why should I now mention those found in waters, rivers, lakes, springs, and the like? I will not trouble myself to investigate all of them. A few out of many will suffice. It is the nature of certain waters to harden insects. The Albuneus, the Albula water, and the Anio, as the local inhabitants affirm, by a certain natural power not only bind and cement any bodies whatever, but also gradually coat with a stony crust twigs, wood, leaves, grass, and other more solid things that happen to be washed over by them. Indeed, in the territory of Tibur, around the Anio, rocks and crags have formed from the waters through the deposit of the streams, and on the plain, lakes and marshes in many places have turned into solid stony ground. In Tuscany a spring breaks out of the rock at the roots of Mount Ulmentum, whose waters within fifteen days cover in a stony crust whatever is immersed in them. In the same place the river Eisa, after it receives the stream of the small torrent Sena, has such a nature that it coats with a stony crust whatever fire is thrown into it. Among the Campanians twigs and leaves immersed in the Silarus turn to stone, as Strabo, Pliny, and others relate, yet without any change of colour or form, although otherwise, as Pliny adds, its water is wholesome to drink. Silius also speaks of this in book 8 of the Punic War: Now the Silarus, with the waters it nourishes, where they say stone hardens and branches dipped into it turn to stone.

units.la: Meminit & Neptuni Fontis, qui in Umbria prope Lacum Velinum, inter Miracula M. Tullius, Iamentorum Vngulas, si pluteulum in illo morentur, indurescere tradens. Eodem tractu Saxum, per quod Velinus Lacus exoneratur, ita quandoque ab Aquarum indole incrustatur, ut id ferro expurgari sit necesse, quo semper exitus illi pateat, neve per vicinos agros evagetur. In Foro Iulio Mons Maurus supra Vicum Phorum haud procul ortu Tiltaventi Maioris, Fontem habet mirabilem, in quo quidquid immersum lapidis induit naturam.
units.tr: Cicero also mentions among wonders the Spring of Neptune, which is in Umbria near Lake Velinus, and says that hooves of cattle, if they remain a little while in it, harden. In the same region the rock through which Lake Velinus discharges is sometimes so encrusted by the quality of its waters that it must be cleared with iron, so that the outlet always stays open and the water does not spread over the neighbouring fields. In the Forum Julii, Mount Maurus above the village of Phorum, not far from the source of the Greater Tiltavento, has a remarkable spring, in which whatever is immersed takes on the nature of stone.

units.la: Nonnullae aliae res conciliant Colorem. Auctor est Martialis Eburi ablutum Aquam Candorem accipere, similiterque Dentes Humanos. Memorat ad II Virg. Georgic. Servius iuxta Clitumnum, Amnem Mevaniae vicinum, Boves Albos nasci, Matribus ipso ex Fluvio potantibus. Videndus & Plinius lib. III Natur. Hist. cap. CVI. Crathidis, Bruttiorum Fluminis, Aquarum natura est, Capillum efficere flavum, uti e contra nigrum reddit Bisentus. Eandem horum Amnium Vim asserunt Adcolae in Serico etiam deprehendi: Nam eius F la fi Crathidis Aqua redordiantur, Album; si Bisentes, Fuscum accipere Colorem. Tribuit eandem quae Crathidis, efficaciam Sybari, qui iamnunc vulgo Cathilis, Ovidius in Metamorphosi: Crathis, & hinc Sybaris, nostra conterminus oris, Flectitur similes fas inter Auroque Capillos.
units.tr: Some other things change colour. Martial is the authority that water in which ivory has been washed takes on whiteness, and likewise human teeth. Servius, on Virgil's Georgics book 2, relates that near the Clitumnus, the river next to the town of Mevania, white oxen are born when their mothers drink from that river itself. Pliny, Natural History book 3, chapter 106, should also be consulted. The nature of the water of the Crathis, a river of the Bruttians, is to make hair blond, while conversely the Bisentus makes it black. The local people assert that this same power of these rivers is also found in silk. For when silk is re-dyed in the water of the Crathis it takes on a white colour; if in that of the Bisentus, it takes on a brown colour. Ovid, in the Metamorphoses, gives the same power to the Sybaris, which is now commonly called the Cathilis, the stream close to our shores, where the Crathis and the Sybaris turn between them hair like gold:

units.la: De Crathide etiam adfirmat Aristoteles: Κρᾶθις οὗν αἰθιοπίας ... καὶ ex eo Strabo lib. v: Κρᾶθις οὗν αἰθιοπίας ... Sybari aliam indem Virtutem adscribunt, ut postea dicam. Ἀσιναῖς apud Aelianum lib. x. Animal. cap. xxxix Thuriorum Fluvius, qui tametsi pellucidos habeat liquores: nigerrimos tamen Pisces procreat.
units.tr: Aristotle also affirms this of the Crathis: Κρᾶθις οὖν Αἰθιοπίας ... [Crathis, then, of Ethiopia...]. And Strabo in book 5 likewise. The Sybaris, as I will say later, is ascribed another virtue of the same kind. In Aelian, Animals book 10, chapter 39, the river of Thurii, which, although it has very clear waters, nevertheless produces the blackest fish.

units.la: Varium quoque vinum quendam habent. Plinii temporibus, ut ipse testatur lib. II cap. CV, in Agro Reatino Fons erat Nemesia, qui nunc hoc, nunc illo diversoque loco erumpebat; ea varietate mutationem Annonae significans. Haud procul Narnia quaedam Aquarum sunt scaturigines, quarum una Famis Vates. Nec enim solet erumpere nisi quum annus proximus gravem & difficilem Annonam est habiturus, uti etiam anno post Christum natum CIↄ Iↄ V, maxima indomitaque Fame toti Italiae calamitas fuit observatum. Apud Tuscos prope Leciam Aquae sunt; quae Fluvium densis & Lacum Vaporibus usque ad Nubes magna vi ematis, praenunciant caelo sereno Fumum rarum humilemque & per vicina te diffundentem exhalantes. Quid velle dicemus Amnes Sumentes fluentes? De Atrato scribit hoc M. Tullius II de Divinatione, de Amiterno, Obsequens in Prodigiorum Historia. An Aeternus utrobique reponendus, qui hodie apud Sammites Pescara? In Piceno idem accidisse tradit praeter Obsequentem, quem dixi, Plutarchus in Marcello.
units.tr: Some waters also have changing properties. In Pliny's time, as he himself testifies in book 2, chapter 105, there was in the territory of Reate a spring called Nemesia, which broke out now here, now there, in different places, signifying by this variation a change in the grain supply. Not far from Narnia there are certain springs, one of which is a prophet of famine. It breaks out only when the next year is going to bring a severe and difficult harvest, as was observed in the year of Christ 1005, when a great and unchecked famine was a calamity for all Italy. Among the Tuscans near Lecia there are waters which, sending up with great force vapours thick and dense as mist up to the clouds, forewarn of clear weather by exhaling a thin, low smoke that spreads over the neighbouring land. What shall we say the rivers Sumentes, Fluentes mean? Marcus Tullius writes this about the Atratus in book 2 of On Divination, and Obsequens in his History of Prodigies about the Amiternus. Should Aeternus be read in both places, which today among the Sammites is the Pescara? In Picenum, Plutarch in his Life of Marcellus reports that the same thing happened, apart from Obsequens, whom I mentioned.

units.la: In Tuscia prope Vicum Abbatiam, inter Florentinorum & Senensium Fines, bini vituntur Lacus, intervallo jactus sagittae disiuncti. Unus Aquas habet clarissimas, sed, ut aiunt Adcolae, Fundo caret: Alter, paullo minor, Aqua nigra Atramenti instar, partimque Vadorum omnino est, totus priori contrarius: quoniam intectum lignum extemplo in tenuem rapit, ut porro non appareat, Piscibus omnino carens. Prope Charoneas Scrobes in Campania Lacus est, undique ripis altissimis instar Amphitheatri conclusus. Fundum in eo deprehendi non posse, Boccatius etiam est testis. Nihil praeter Ranas quidquam generat. Ad Septemtrionem praecelsam habet Rupem, totam Saxo vestitam, ex qua primo Verae tot Serpentium convoluti globi decidunt, & in Aquas magno cum impetu provolvuntur, ut absque vehementi admiratione spectari nequeant. Quamquam autem magna pars in Stagnum delabatur, nullam tamen omnino conspici, ac ne signum quidem aliquod, postquam Aquas tubierunt, Locorum confirmant Adcolae. Aquam prope Eram Amnem, Deum ad Fundum iter bonum, sic describit Faetus Vberrus lib. III Cant. VIII. Nos crateras supra Eram, quando Ali fumosiatio unt Aqua, e per aliquo Contacto ex eius de novitate domando. Vsiña è qui fia noi; che cialchedumo, Che sa Cerchi da Vegge, ivi li moglia, E he sempre de dieci ne perda uno. E uum puo veder, chi quello tegna; L'un pensi che i Demoni gli afferra: E l'altro Acqua che da se l'ingoglia.
units.tr: In Tuscany, near Vico Abbatia, between the borders of Florence and Siena, there are two lakes, separated by the distance of an arrow's flight. One has very clear waters but, as the locals say, it has no bottom. The other, a little smaller, is as black as ink and partly shallow. It is wholly the opposite of the first, since a piece of wood left untied is at once dragged down and does not reappear. It has no fish at all. Near Charonea, in Campania, there is a lake enclosed on every side by very high banks, like an amphitheatre. That its bottom cannot be found, Boccaccio too bears witness. It produces nothing except frogs. To the north it has a towering rock, wholly covered with stone, from which first fall so many coiled balls of serpents that they rush into the waters with great force and cannot be watched without intense astonishment. Although a great part of them slides into the lake, the locals confirm that none of them can be seen at all, nor any sign of them, once they have plunged beneath the waters. Near the river Era, the water that Fazio Uberti describes in Book III, Canto VIII, of his Dittamondo, in this way, "Dio ad fundum" having a good road to the bottom: "We came upon craters above the Era, where the water boils up smoking, and through some passage of its own it ... Here is what we saw there: the boiling stones are cast up from the depths, and it always loses one of ten. One may see who holds that place: one thinks that demons seize them, and the other that the water swallows them of its own accord."

units.la: Apud Etruscos ad pedem Montis Rufoli Fons nitidus exsilit Aqua dulcis, in qua nullo unquam tempore quidquam impuri cernitur: tanta levitatis, ut ad trutinam cum ceteris huius litus Aquis examinata, cunctis pondere cedat. In Marka Tarvisina ad extum amplissimae Cavernae, quae prope Custodiam, Vicentini Agri Pagum, Lacus est Aqua tam tarda, ut tupinum Solum, ac si nihil obstaret, perlincat. Quibusdam in locis altitudine amplius pedum xx est, quemadmodum adferunt Adcolae, qui multa de Lacu, eiusque amplitudine fabulosa narrant. Pisces omnino nullos habet, praeter Squillas minimas, nec iis maximis dissimiles, quae vulgo Venetijs locantur vendi.
units.tr: Among the Etruscans, at the foot of Mount Rufolo, a clear spring gushes forth, sweet water, in which nothing impure is ever seen at any time. It is so light that, when weighed on a balance against the other waters of this shore, it outweighs them all. In the March of Treviso, at the mouth of a very large cavern near Custodia, a village of the Vicenza territory, there is a lake whose water is so sluggish that it spreads over the level ground as if nothing stood in its way. In some places it is more than twenty feet deep, as the locals report, who tell many fabulous stories about the lake and its extent. It has no fish at all, apart from very small crayfish, not unlike those that are commonly sold at Venice.

units.la: Anagniae, Latij oppido propinquus Fons est Trifurus; hieme, Celano Lacu glacie confisi cito fucus; autum o vere, ac aestate redundans, ut ab illo Lacu originem habere credi queat. Blondus sane Fontem hunc ab eo Lacu creari per abditas humo Vias coniectat: eiusque rei non vulgare videtur argumentum, quod, ut dixi, congelato Lacu, exsiccetur.
units.tr: Near Anagni, a town of Latium, there is a spring called Trifurus. In winter, when the lake of Celano is frozen over, it quickly dries up; in autumn and spring, and in summer, it overflows, so that it may be believed to have its origin in that lake. Blondus indeed conjectures that this spring is produced from that lake through hidden passages under the ground, and the evidence for this seems to be no small one: that, as I have said, when the lake freezes, it dries up.

units.la: Saporem Aquae quaedam habent singularem. Prope Linternum in Campania Acadulus ille Fons, de quo Plinius, hodieque invenitur: cuius Aquae, vini modo, fumantes mulcentos. Aquam in Caleni, quae Campaniae Urbs, Agro fluere homines inebriantem, ut Vinum, tradit Valerius Maximus, de Miraculis. In Agro Thurino, qui Magnae Graeciae, Aquaeductus adparet veterrimus, quem quidam volunt illius fuisse Fontis, a quo Thuriorum nomen acceptum. Huic Aetati vulgo Aqua che Favilla dicitur, fortalis ab dulcedine suavitateque summa. In Etruria prope Libbrianum Fons est, Aqua dictus, quem quod acidus, acutisque saporis & mordacis, nulla gustant Animalia.
units.tr: Some waters have a distinctive taste. Near Linternum in Campania is that sour spring, the Acadulus, of which Pliny speaks, which is still found today. Its waters, like wine, make the drinkers' spirits merry and cheerful. Valerius Maximus, in his chapter on miracles, reports that in the territory of Caleni, a city of Campania, there flows water that intoxicates men like wine. In the territory of Thurii, in Magna Graecia, there is a very ancient aqueduct, which some believe belonged to that spring from which the name of the Thurians was taken. In our age it is commonly called "Aqua che Favilla", perhaps from its very great sweetness and pleasantness. In Etruria, near Libbriano, there is a spring called Aqua Acida, which, because of its sharp, biting taste, no animals will taste.

units.la: In Magna Graecia Sternutamenta excitat Cochilis, qui quondam Sybaris. Aristoteles' ὁ μὲν Συβαρις τοῦ πνεῦμας ἀπ' αὐτοῦ πνυπηνὰς ἀναμισ: quae diffundens Strabo, ὁ Συβαρὶς, inquit, τοῦ πνεῦμας ἐπαισὶς ἀπ' αὐτοῦ πυρπνοῖς ποιεῖ: διὸ κὴν τὰς ἀχίλας ἀπειρήμεν ἀπ' αὐτοῦ.
units.tr: In Magna Graecia there is a stream, the Cochilis, which once belonged to Sybaris, that provokes sneezing. Aristotle's... [Ὁ μὲν Σύβαρις τοῦ πνεύματος ἀπ' αὐτοῦ πνυπηνὰς ἀναμισ] Strabo, expanding on this, says: "Sybaris," he says, "makes those who breathe its air sneeze, and for that reason the people there are forbidden to use it" [ὁ Σύβαρις ... τοῦ πνεύματος ἐπαισθάνεται ... ἀπ' αὐτοῦ πυρπνοῖς ποιεῖ].

units.la: Sunt quae supra modum frigent. In Umbria propter Narem Fontes sunt plurimi, varia natura & conditione. Est inter alios ex caverna magno cum impetu copiosissime prorumpens, tanta frigiditatu, tactum ut vix ferat. Amnis in Urbe Samnitium Telesia nascitur tam frigidus, ut nullum generet Piscem. Cutilias Aquas in Sabinis gelidissimas esse scribit Plinius lib. nat. Hist. xxxi. cap. ii.
units.tr: Some waters are exceedingly cold. In Umbria, near the Nar, there are very many springs of varied nature and condition. Among the others, one bursts forth from a cavern with great force and in great abundance, of such cold that it can scarcely be borne by touch. A river that rises in the city of the Samnite Telesia is so cold that it produces no fish at all. Pliny, in Book XXXI, chapter 2 of his Natural History, writes that the Cutiliae waters in the Sabine country are extremely cold.

units.la: Contrarium habent alias genus. In Agro Viterbiensi Aquae sunt Caiae, Veteribus nobilitatae, hodie Bollicane dictae; ut quarum ardore canit Facius lib. iii, Cant. ix: Io no' credea perche Pharsesse udito Senza provare il Bolicane fosse Accesso d'un bollor tanto infinito. Magnittavi un Monton acentro si cotte, In men che l'huomo andasse un quarto miglio, Ch'altro non vedevo, che proprio l'esse, etc.
units.tr: Other kinds have the opposite property. In the territory of Viterbo are the Caian waters, famous among the ancients and today called Bollicane, because of whose heat Fazio sings in Book III, Canto IX: "I did not believe, because I had heard it at Pharsesse, until I experienced at Bollicane an access of boiling so endless. I saw a ram so thoroughly cooked in less time than a man would walk a quarter of a mile that I could see nothing else but its bones, etc."

units.la: Haud procul Lecia quibusdam in locis Aquae tanto strepitu, tantaque violentia bulliunt, ut altitudine pedum x exsiliant, nec minore cum sonitu rursum cadant: praeterea tanti sunt ferveris, ut ins. Ebs Animalis Vivi Ossa extemporo carne nudata sursum emergant.
units.tr: Not far from Lecia, in some places, the waters boil with such noise and such violence that they leap up to a height of ten feet and fall back again with no less sound. Moreover, they are so hot that the bones of a living animal, stripped of flesh in an instant, rise up to the surface.

units.la: Mira quali sunt quaedam indolis. Tradit Pausanias Amenis Aquae ea esse natura, ut ad primum contactum gelidissima, mox paullatim calescere videantur. Sunt & in Tuscia prope Leciam Aqua claritatis praecipuae, quae quum bullire magna videantur vi, ad tactum tamen rigent.
units.tr: Some waters have wonderful qualities. Pausanias reports that the Amenus water is of such a nature that at first touch it seems very cold, but soon gradually seems to grow warm. There are also in Tuscany, near Lecia, waters of outstanding clarity which, while they seem to boil with great force, are nevertheless cold to the touch.

units.la: Quid iam dicam de Aquis, quae salutarem afferre medicinam solent Corporibus adfectis, quaeque variis conflictantur Morbis? In Campania quondam fuerunt innumerae, quarum multas cum variis hic ibi Terraemotibus haustas esse, tum Tripergulana Conflagratione, quæ in annum cIↄ Iↄ xxxvi incidit, intercidisse constat. Visuntur nihilominus circa Baias, locisque Averno vicinis adhuc magna copia. De Baiano universum Plinius lib. xxxi. cap. 11: Aqua nusquam largius, quam in Baiano Sinu, nec plurimis auxiliandi generibus: alia Sulphuris, alia Aluminis, alia Salis, alia Nitri, alia Bituminis, nonnulla acida salsave mixtura. Vapore quoque ipso aliquæ prosunt: tantaque eis est vis, ut Balneas calefaciant, & Frigidam etiam in Solis feruore reddant, quæ in Baiano Pollidianæ vocantur, nomine accepto a Caio Cæsaris Liberto. Obsonia quoque percoquunt. Vaporant & in Avernii ipso, quæ Licinii Crassi fuere: mediosque inter Fluctus existit aliquid Valitudini salutare, &c. Prope Baias ad oram Locus monstratur, ubi quondam splendida fuerunt Ædificia; Balnea Baiana vocant Adcolæ, Medici vero Sudatoria, in ripam nonnihil excavata. Iuxta eadem in ora littoris ampla Domus ad Rupis pedem in Saxum excisa conspicitur, ubi Balneum Tritoli (di Tritoli) Medicis dictum; sed vulgo vel Ciceronianum (di Cicerone) quod in Villa Ciceronis, Academiæ nomine clara, putetur exstare; vel Pratense, quod in Prato sit. Satis constat Cicerone vivo Fontes hos nondum fuisse apertos. Nam post eius excessum C.
