Antistio Vetere Villam possidente primum erupisse, carmineque Tullij Laureæ Ciceronis Liberti celebratos, Plinius est auctor. Versus adiiciendam, ut quid eo etiam tempore virium habuerint, non ignoremus: Quo tua, Romana Pindex clarissime Lingua, Silva loco melius surgere iussa viret; Atque Academiæ celebratam nomine Villam Nunc reparat cuius sub pastore Vetus: Hic etiam adparent Lymphæ non ante reperte, Languida quæ intuito Lumina Rore levant: Nimirum Locus ipse sui Ciceronis Honori Hoc dedit, hæc Fontes quum patefecit ope. Ut, quoniam totum legitur sine fine per orbem, Sint plures oculis quæ medeantur Aquæ.
units.tr: What shall I now say of the waters that are wont to bring healing medicine to diseased bodies, and that are used against various illnesses? In Campania there were once countless springs, many of which, as it is established, were swallowed up by various earthquakes here and there, and also by the conflagration at Tripergula, which fell in the year 1536 and is known to have destroyed them. Nevertheless, a great quantity still exists around Baiae and in the places near Avernus. Pliny, Book XXXI, chapter 11, writes generally about the Baian waters: "Water is found nowhere more abundantly than in the Bay of Baiae, nor with more kinds of healing power: some of sulphur, some of alum, some of salt, some of nitre, some of bitumen, and some with an acid or salty mixture. Some also work by their vapour alone, and their power is so great that they heat baths, and even make cold water warm in the heat of the sun. Those in Baiae are called the Pollidian waters, named after Gaius Caesar's freedman. They also cook food. Vapours rise also in Avernus itself, which belonged to Licinius Crassus; and amid the waves there is something beneficial to health, etc." Near Baiae, on the shore, a place is pointed out where splendid buildings once stood; the locals call them the Baian baths, but the physicians call them sudatoria, cut somewhat into the bank. Beside them, on the shore, a large house is seen, hewn out of the stone at the foot of the cliff, where the bath is called by physicians the Bath of Tritolus (di Tritoli); but commonly it is called either the Ciceronian (di Cicerone) bath, because it is thought to exist in the villa of Cicero, famous for the name of the Academy, or the Meadow bath, because it lies in a meadow. It is quite certain that these springs had not yet been opened while Cicero was alive. For after his death, while Gaius Antistius Vetus owned the villa, they first burst forth, as Pliny is the author, and were celebrated in verse by Tullius Laurea, a freedman of Cicero. Let me add the verses, so that we may not be ignorant of what power they had even at that time: "Where your Roman tongue, most famous Pindar, once ordered a forest to rise more fittingly, now the villa celebrated by the name of the Academy, once under the old shepherd, is restored here too; here appear waters not found before, which relieve weary eyes with dew at a glance. Surely the place itself gave this to the honour of its Cicero, when by his help he opened these springs, so that, since the whole world reads him without end, there may be more waters to heal the eyes."

units.la: Locus elegantiam habet summam; Cryptaque est mirabili artificio in saxum excavata: ubi & Imagines erant, Manus ad adfecta corporis loca tenentes, quibus Aquæ Facultas auxiliabatur. Nunc maiore ex parte dilapsa sunt omnia: nobilissimorum tamen Colorum, quibus Ædificium fuit depictum, indicia etiam nunc superstant. Fons interdum semel, & item noctu, cum Occasu Exortuque Lunæ, calidam ac fumantem Aquam in Balnei Lacum emittit: quo repleto pars in Mare quondam Rivulo defluit; pars ad Fontem revertitur. Ulterius ad dextram vergenti Aqua purissima, sed pene fervens & tactu vix innoxia offertur, quam plerique credunt in Balneum Ciceronianum vel Tritolinum Vijs occultis diffluere. Alia sunt hoc tractu Balnea Baiana dicta, quæ nunc omitto. Pleraque memorat Strabo, quum apud Baias Aquarum Calidarum Fontes, non solum adfectæ Valitudini multis modis auxiliantes; sed etiam Voluptati atque Delitijs oportunos, erumpere perhibet. Iam quæ vicinis Averno locis sunt, indagemus. Pandit se ibi primum ad Avernum lœva Balneum Arcus (Bagno dell' Arco) hic appellatum ab arcuata Ædificij forma. Sequuntur Aquæ Raverianæ (di Raverio) ita ab Inventore dictæ. Tum alio latere versus Puteolos Tripergulina erant Balnea ab Loci structura sic nominata, Domo nimirum tripartito divisa. Succedunt Aquæ D. Nicolai (di S. Nicolò) quæ quod, inquit Leander, inopibus auxilio esse solent, illius Divi more, quum alia Balnea Potentes plerumque petant, ita fuerunt vocatæ. Postea Balneum Scrofa est deinde D. Luciæ, salubberrimum oculis, unde quoque nomen creditur inditum; Vulgo Divæ huic Tutelam Oculorum tribuente. Occurrit inde Balneum Arcuis (dell' Arcolo) ab Ædificij forma denominatum, alterque D. Mariæ dictum. Hinc S. Crucis est, imprimis Pedibus, Manibus, Lateri salutare; & quod ex Christi in Cruce pendentis partes Vulneribus compunctæ fuerint, Crucis nuncupatum. In ora littoris sunt Aquæ Cantarellæ (di Cantarello) hic a Balneorum forma vocatæ: quibus ab latere Balneum Fontanum est (di Fontana) ita dictum, quod instar Fontis Aquæ eius perpetuo scaturiant. Sequitur ad litus juxta Templum D. Mariæ Balneum Oleï Petroleï, sic vulgo nominatum, quod is Liquor cum eius Aquis conjunctus esse tam aspectu, quam odoratu percipiatur. Culmanum inde juxta pedem celsissimi montis Culmæ est, vulgo propter altitudinem sic dicti, Templo D. Mariæ imminentis. In litore dein Sol & Luna occurrit ab Vi cognominatum, qua ceteris Aquis, uti Sol & Luna Stellis omnibus, antecellit. Succedit hinc Gibberosum (Bagno di Gimboro) ita vulgo ab Aditen forma, quæ tamquam Gibbus est, appellatum. Juxta eum Fons adparet Episcopale, Balneum ab Episcopo quodam ædificatum, quod Podagræ vehementer auxiliatur. Adiecentu deinde paludum aliquot Aquæ Fatorum (Bagni di Fato) nominantur, ita dictæ, quod repertas Fato credunt, vel uti alij censent, Etymo ex Italorum lingua ducto, quod epis Testudo opere lautissimo fit perfecta & elaborata. Haud procul inde Balneum Bracula. Nominis item Etymologiam ex Italorum Idiomate trahens, nimirum ab humilitate loci ac rotunditate. Post hæc Balneum Spelunea est, ita dictum, quod eius in Specu sit Lavacrum, cuius Aqua Cerebrum adjuvandi vim habet; &, uti Galenus tradit pondere quinque drachmarum pota quotidie, Vitijs tam infra, quam supra diaphragma medetur omnibus. Plurimi præterea situ hoc ab Agro Falerno usque ad Misenum saluberrimi, tam Calidarum quam Frigidarum Aquarum, Fontes erumpunt, quorum adhuc incomperta natura; tum quod Ædificiorum abditi ruinis latent, tum propter Adcolarum incuriam imperitiamque: quapropter æstimari potest Tractum hunc totum fere non nisi mediocris Aquas scatere. Multi etiam ultra Puteolos post Pilas, quæ vastissimæ in Mari conspicuntur, salubrium Aquarum Fontes prosiliunt, cum primis, quod D. Anastasia Balneum à propinquo ejus Divi Sacello vocant. Aquam cupientium in arena fodiendum est. Haud procul inde Caverna quædam Rupis Aquam habet longe salubernimam, obstructis Adcolarum incuria Fontis meatibus, in arena depereuntem & occultis in mare dilabentem: Vtips; quapropter uti volentibus contra Specum Lacus est egerendus, in quo latet. Vulgo propter mirabilem ad plurima medicam Virtutem Balneum Homo appellant, Bagno dell' Ajuto dell' Huomo. In alterius deinde Rupis latere Balneum Calaturæ est, ita dictum, quia Montem ipsum Calaturam vulgo vocitant. Sequitur sub Monte Rupis Petranum ob Aquarum eius Vim, quæ Calculum frangunt, denominatum. Mox in litore Falneolum est, ab modica Fontis forma sic dictum. Viterius Aquæ Iunctæ (Bagno di Iunara) quibus nomen ab Iunctis ibi nascentibus. Denique juxta litus Balneum Cryptæ est. Haud procul Mafico Monte, ubi nunc Turris Balneorum, Calidi quoque Fontes prorumpunt, ad plurima Morborum, ut Strabo scribit, genera salubres. Eas Aquas Tacitus Vesuvianas appellat, quum de Tigillini morte in hæc verba scribit: Tigillinus, accepto apud Aquas Vesuvianas suprema necessitatis nuntio, inter flupra Concubinarum & oscula & deformes mores, fœdis novissima fauces, infamem situm fædavit etiam exitu fero & inhonesto. Propinquo Sinuessæ loco supra Arcem Montis Draconis Aquæ Calidæ reperiuntur, quæ Balnea Caiana nunc Adcolis vocantur. De ijs, puto, loquitur Tacitus lib xii Annal. In ea mole cum arum Caudius altitudine advers ac oppidum, refovendisque corporibus mollitie cœli & salubritate Aquarum Sinuessam pergit. Hactenus Campanas Aquas, quæ medicinam Corporum Morbis Virtutemque faciunt, recensui: neque carent hujusmodi Naturæ Donis reliquæ Italiæ partes. In Latio subiecta Tiburi planitiesque propter Anienem plurimis Aquis gelidis scaturit, quas Albulæ vocant, multa medica virtute cum potæ, tum Balneo adhibitæ pollentes, ut scribit Strabo. Nomen Albularum ab Coloris albedine captum, quam Metallum Sulphuris, unde Fontes promanant, efficit. Martialis lib. 1 Epigr. Itur ad Herculei gelidas quæ Tiburis arces, Canaque sulphureis Albula fumat Aquis.
units.tr: The place has the highest elegance; the grotto is hollowed out of the rock with wonderful workmanship, and there were statues there too, holding their hands to the afflicted parts of the body, which the power of the water helped. Now for the most part everything has slipped away, yet traces of the most noble colours with which the building was painted still survive. Sometimes the spring, once and again at night, when the moon sets and rises, sends out warm, steaming water into the bath-pool; when this is full, part of it flows down into the sea by a rivulet, and part returns to the spring. Further on, to the right, there is offered water that is very pure but almost boiling and scarcely harmless to the touch, which most people believe flows by hidden channels into the Ciceronian bath or the Tritolinum. There are other baths in this tract called the Baian baths, which I now pass over. Strabo mentions most of them, when he reports that at Baiae there burst forth hot springs, not only helpful in many ways to diseased health but also suited to pleasure and delights. Now let us examine those places which are near Avernus. There first, on the left towards Avernus, opens the Bath of the Arch (Bagno dell' Arco), so called from the arched form of the building. Then come the Waters of Raverius (di Raverio), so named after their discoverer. Then, on the other side towards Puteoli, were the Tripergulina baths, named thus from the structure of the place, being evidently a house divided into three parts. The Waters of St Nicholas (di S. Nicolò) follow, which, as Leander says, since they are usually a help to the poor, were so called after that saint's custom, whereas the powerful generally seek other baths. Afterwards comes the Bath of Scrofa, then that of St Lucy, very wholesome for the eyes, from which it is also believed the name was given, since the common people ascribe the protection of the eyes to this saint. Thence the Bath of the Arcuis (dell' Arcolo) meets us, named from the form of the building, and another called after St Mary. From here is St Cross, healthful especially for the feet, hands and side; and because the parts of Christ hanging on the Cross were pierced with wounds, it is called the Cross. On the shore's edge are the Waters of Cantarella (di Cantarello), so called here from the form of the baths; beside them is the Fountain Bath (di Fontana), so named because its waters bubble up perpetually like a fountain. Along the shore, beside the church of St Mary, follows the Bath of Oil of Petroleum, so commonly named because that liquid is perceived to be mixed with its waters, both to sight and to smell. Next, below the foot of the very lofty mountain Culma, is Culmanum, commonly so called on account of its height, overhanging the church of St Mary. Then on the shore appears Sol and Luna, named from the power by which it surpasses all other waters, as the Sun and Moon surpass all the stars. From here follows Gibberosum (Bagno di Gimboro), so called commonly from the form of its building, which is like a hump. Near it appears the spring Episcopale, a bath built by a certain bishop, which greatly helps gout. Next, among some marshes nearby, the Waters of the Fates (Bagni di Fato) are named; they are so called because they believe them to have been found by fate, or, as others think, from an etymology drawn from the Italian language, because the tortoise-shaped structure is finished and elaborated with most elegant work. Not far from there is the Bath of Bracula, likewise taking its etymology from the Italian idiom, namely from the lowness and roundness of the place. After these is the Bath of Spelunea, so called because its washing-place is in a cave, whose water has the power of helping the brain; and, as Galen teaches, when five drachms by weight are drunk daily, it heals all faults both below and above the diaphragm. Moreover, in this region from the Falernian field as far as Misenum, very wholesome springs of both hot and cold waters break forth in many places, whose nature is still unknown, partly because they lie hidden under the ruins of buildings, and partly through the neglect and ignorance of the local inhabitants; wherefore it may be judged that almost this whole tract bubbles with only moderate waters. Also many beyond Puteoli, after the piers which are seen in the sea, very large, spring forth wholesome waters, chiefly those which they call the Bath of St Anastasia, from a little shrine of that saint nearby. One must dig in the sand for those who want water. Not far from there a certain cave in the rock holds water far more wholesome, which, through the neglect of the inhabitants, its channels being blocked, seeps away in the sand and slips secretly into the sea; therefore, for those who wish to use it, a pool must be dug opposite the cave where it lies hidden. Commonly, on account of its wonderful medicinal virtue against very many ailments, they call it the Bath of Man, Bagno dell' Ajuto dell' Huomo. Then on the side of another rock is the Bath of Calatura, so named because the common people call the mountain itself Calatura. Beneath the mountain's rock follows Petranum, named from the power of its waters, which break up stone in the bladder. Soon on the shore is Falneolum, so called from the small shape of the spring. Further on are the Joined Waters (Bagno di Iunara), named from the joined things growing there. Finally, beside the shore, is the Bath of the Cave. Not far from Mount Mafico, where now stands the tower of the baths, hot springs also burst forth, wholesome, as Strabo writes, for very many kinds of diseases. Tacitus calls these waters the Vesuvian waters, when he writes of Tigellinus' death in these words: "Tigellinus, having received at the Vesuvian Waters the final news of necessity, amid the debaucheries of his concubines and kisses and shameful manners, disfigured with a foul throat his infamous situation also by a savage and dishonourable end." Near Sinuessa, above the citadel of Mount Draco, hot waters are found, which are now called by the locals the Baths of Caiana. I think it is of these that Tacitus speaks in book 12 of the Annals: "In that mass, with Caudius' altitude opposite the town, he hastens to Sinuessa, to restore bodies by the mildness of the sky and the wholesomeness of the waters." Thus far I have reviewed the Campanian waters, which make medicine for bodily diseases and virtue; and the other parts of Italy are not lacking such gifts of nature. In Latium, the plain beneath Tibur and beside the Anio bubbles with very many cold waters, which they call the Albulae, powerful with much medicinal virtue both when drunk and when used for bathing, as Strabo writes. The name of the Albulae is taken from the whiteness of colour, which the metal of sulphur, from which the springs flow, produces. Martial, book 1 Epigrams: "One goes to the cold citadels of Hercules at Tibur, and the grey Albula steams with sulphurous waters."

units.la: Similes natura Labanis in Agro Nomentano, itemque aliis circa Eretum Aquis, ut Strabo memoriæ prodit. In Tuscia vicina Agillæ (ab Cære Veteri haud multum distantes) Caeretana Falnea describit Strabo salubernima: quæ hoc ævo Falnea Sabatina dicuntur, ab Lacu Sabatino. Ad Vmbronem Fluvium juxta Paganicum oppidum Balnea sunt Petriolæ, cum aliis in agro Senensi, quorum prisci temporibus & pretium & usus fuit. Patet hoc ex Oratione M. Tullij pro Cælio, Senensium Aquas memorantis. Sic Martialis ad Oppianum: Etruscis nisi tremulus laveris, Inlotus morieris Oppiane. Frequentantur etiamnum Ægris. Non procul Lecia Aquæ sunt, quarum Virtus, ut falsa & adsatim pota, moxque vel ore vel alio naturæ abscessu reddita, mirabilem in modum corpora malis plurimis emundent. Sterilitatem quoque Mulieribus auferunt, Fecunditate reposita. Ad Montem Vlmentum, prope Febianum Vicum, Fons est Aqua dulcis, potu {a}libertatem Lactis interim sum Nutricibus restituens. Refert ex Varrone Plinius ad Soractem esse Fontem Latitudinis pedum quatuor; & Sole Oriente exundare favent similem, Avel(que, aqua gustaverint, juxta mortuas concidere. Addit Leander eam rem à Blondo etiam in Italia confirmari, qui nec putandum aut tale quid fieri haud posse, quod & in Silvis Antijs, ubi Fons exiguus inter ingentes Ædificiorum ruinas, ipse oculis viderit, Aviculas duas, ut Aquam gustatis, repente tacuisse mortuas. Sunt & alterius in Etruria Fontis Agro Montis Politiani Aquæ, uti sermonibus aliorum accepisse se testatur Leander, quarum par omnino Vis & Natura. Sed quum his adfectæ post potum Aquis, Volucres jam, uti spiritu destituta, jacent, si mox alium in locum transferantur, Sensus Integritatemque recipiunt. In Vmbria, haud procul Narnia, multæ Fontium ostenduntur Scaturæ, nominatim quæ non ita pridem anno c1ɔ 10 vii repertæ, cujus Aquas Infirmi qui potassent, Morbis Malisque omnibus liberabantur: unde mox maximo concursu Ægri omnibus ex partibus huc confluere cœperunt, quibus haustl Fontis latices salutem impertiebantur. Hac de causa quum Narnienses Advenarum hospitio Tabernas Aquæ adjicere decrevissent effodiendis Novo operi Fundamentis Veterâ Ædificiorum sunt inventa, quo constituit etiam olim hunc in pretio Fontem fuisse. Alibi ibidem sunt Fontes in ripa Naris Montisque radicibus Hortam usque permulti, quorum fortassean Natura maxime quoque salutaris, quamquam incomperta. De Caetilis Aquis sic scribit Strabo lib. V. Τᾶς Κωλιάτις ὑγρᾶ, τ' ὕδατ' ἀφ' ἀνρῶν ὄντα, ... ἐν πλείστοις ἀποφυγάς. In Flaminia ad Sapin fluvium opidum est D. Mariæ in Balneo, ita cognominatum ab Aquarum medicatarum tam potu, quam lotione ad multas Infirmitates salubrium Balneis. In Romanula Balnea sunt Porrectana, opidum honestum; ubi ex Saxo Medicatæ Aquæ calidæ magna copia prorumpunt: quarum Vis omnibus notissima, Vulgi dicto hujusmodi celebrata: Chi beve l'Acqua della Porretta; Oche lo spazza, o che lo netta. Bovis ductu Fontem ab Agricola quodam anno c1ɔ ccc lxxxv repertum, docet pluribus Leander. In Langbardia Cis-Padana Mons est, Apennini portio, Zibius; supra quem ex Saxo latex prorumpit Olei cum Aqua misti specie, Vulneribus mirifice conferens. Aponus juxta Montes Euganeos, prope Vicum cognominem, multis scaturit locis; sed quinque maxime nobilibus: i Ad Radices Montis Ortonis Fonte exiguo; ii ad pedes Montagnoni, ubi Balnea amplissima, vivis lapidibus ab Theodorico Ostrogotho exstructa post exustionem Attilanam; iii inter utrumque humili clivo, in medio Agro, ubi Crater vivo saxo sub dio exstat, Aqua ferruginosa perpetuo Canale duas Molas Farinarias versante; iv prope Bataleam, ubi Fons ab S. Helena denominatus e Saxo scaturit; v ad D. Bartholomæi Ædem, ubi Limus sive Lutum Medicatum Artuum doloribus efficacissimum, eruitur. Celebrant Aponi Fontes Martialis, Claudianus, Suetonius. Exstat Epistola Theodorici Regis ad Aloysium Architectum Patavinum, de reparandis Aponi Balneis elegantissima apud Cassiodorum. Inter reliqua & illud, Furto ablatam Pecudem Fonti immersam prius detequi, quam Pilos amittere. Ad Aponi Fontem Divinationem exercere solitos Veteres, ex Suetonio notum; qui C. Cornelium Augurem Patavinum, jactis in Aponi Fontem Talis aureis, quum summum numerum ostendissent, Imperium Tiberio praedixisse testatur. Situm & Virtutes describit Bartholomæus Viotus. Iacobus Dondus Medicus, idemque Horologij Patavini artificiosissimi Inventor, ex Aquarum Aponi mille Libris Salis candidissimi Libram effici, absque majore coctione, edito libro docuit anno c1ɔ ccc xl. Ea causa structæ ibi Ædes Novæ, ubi Lacuna parva & ceteris magis salsa est, Carrariensium beneficio. Unde Balnea adhuc nomen retinent Casa Nova. Vocari nunc Bagni d'Abano notat Leander; vel Ebano, docet Savonarola. Aqua Patavina fortean Plinio; Ἀλλεῖδες Stephano.
units.tr: Similar waters are found at Labanae in the territory of Nomentum, and at other springs around Eretum, as Strabo records. In Etruria, near Agylla (not far from Caere Vetus), Strabo describes the Caeretan Falnea as very healthful; in this age they are called the Falnea Sabatina, after Lake Sabatinus. Near the river Umbro, beside the town of Paganicum, are the Petriolae baths, and others in the territory of Siena. These had both value and use in ancient times, as is clear from Cicero's speech for Caelius, where he mentions the waters of Siena. So Martial, writing to Oppianus: "Unless you bathe in the Etruscan waters while still trembling, you will die unwashed, Oppianus." They are still frequented by the sick. Not far off are the waters of Lecia, whose power, when they are drunk in quantity and then brought up, either by the mouth or by some other natural outlet, cleanses bodies of many ills in a remarkable way. They also take away barrenness in women, restoring fertility. Near Mount Ulmentum, close to the village of Febianum, there is a spring of sweet water which, when drunk, restores the flow of milk to nurses. From Varro, Pliny reports that at Soracte there is a spring four feet wide which, when the sun rises, overflows; and birds that have tasted its water fall dead beside it. Leander adds that Blondus also confirms this for Italy, and he says it should not be thought impossible, since in the Antian woods, where a small spring lies among huge ruins of buildings, he himself saw with his own eyes two little birds, which, after tasting the water, suddenly fell silent and died. There is also a spring of the same kind in Etruria, in the territory of Montepulciano, whose waters, as Leander says he learned from others, have altogether the same force and nature. But when birds that have been affected by drinking these waters lie there as if deprived of breath, if they are soon moved to another place they recover their senses and their wholeness. In Umbria, not far from Narni, many springs are shown, notably one discovered not long ago, in the year 1510, whose water, when the sick drank it, freed them from all diseases and ills; so soon a great crowd of sick people began to flow together to it from every direction, and by drinking from the spring they received health. For this reason, when the people of Narni decided to add taverns of water for the hospitality of strangers, while digging the foundations for the new work, remains of old buildings were found, which suggests that this spring was also highly valued in former times. Elsewhere in the same region there are very many springs along the bank of the Nar and at the foot of the mountains as far as Horta, whose natural power is perhaps also very healthful, though not well known. Strabo writes thus about the Caetilian waters in book 5: "The moist Colias, whose waters come from the heights ... in very many places escaping [Τᾶς Κωλιάτις ὑγρᾶ, τ' ὕδατ' ἀφ' ἀνρῶν ὄντα, ... ἐν πλείστοις ἀποφυγάς]." In Flaminia, by the river Sapis, there is a town of Santa Maria in Bagno, so named from its medicinal waters, both drunk and used for washing, healthful in baths for many infirmities. In Romagna there are the Porrettana baths, an honourable town, where hot medicinal waters pour out in great abundance from the rock. Their power is known to everyone and is celebrated in this popular saying: "Whoever drinks the water of Porretta, the goose sweeps it away, or cleans it." Leander teaches at length that a spring was discovered in the year 1385 by a certain farmer, under the guidance of an ox. In Cisalpine Lombardy there is a mountain, Zibio, a part of the Apennines; from the rock above it a liquid flows out in the appearance of a mixture of oil and water, wonderfully useful for wounds. Abano, near the Euganean hills, close to the village of the same name, bubbles up in many places, but five are especially noted: (i) at the foot of Mount Ortone, a small spring; (ii) at the foot of Montagnone, where very large baths, built of living stone by Theodoric the Ostrogoth after the burning by Attila, stand; (iii) between these two, on a gentle slope, in the middle of the field, where a crater rises from the living rock under the open sky, iron-bearing water runs through a constant channel, turning two grinding mills; (iv) near Bataglia, where a spring named after St Helena gushes from the rock; (v) at the church of St Bartholomew, where medicinal mud or clay, most effective for pains in the limbs, is dug up. The springs of Abano are celebrated by Martial, Claudian and Suetonius. There survives a most elegant letter of King Theodoric to Aloysius, architect of Padua, about repairing the baths of Abano, preserved in Cassiodorus. Among other things it mentions that a sheep stolen by thieves, when first dipped in the spring, reveals the theft before it loses its wool. That the ancients customarily practised divination at the spring of Abano is known from Suetonius, who records that Gaius Cornelius, an augur of Padua, when golden dice were thrown into the spring of Abano and showed the highest number, foretold the imperial power for Tiberius. Its situation and virtues are described by Bartolomeo Viotti. James Dondi, a physician and also the very skilful inventor of the Paduan clock, taught in a book published in the year 1340 that from a thousand pounds of the waters of Abano a pound of very white salt can be made without much boiling. For this reason new buildings were erected there, where the small pool is saltier than the others, through the generosity of the Carrara family. Hence the baths still keep the name Casa Nova. Leander notes that they are now called Bagni d'Abano; Savonarola teaches that they are called Ebano. Perhaps Pliny's "Aqua Patavina"; Stephanus's "Alleides".

units.la: CAPVT XIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV.

units.la: Italorum Genius & Indoles.
units.tr: The Genius and Character of the Italians.

units.la: REGIONIS ipsius cum Adjunctis, tum Partibus hactenus descriptis: flagitat Methodus, ut ad Incolas vertatur sermo. Hos considerabo & Gubernatos, & Gubernantes In iis Adjuncta perpendam, eaque partim Inhærentia, ut Indolem vel Genium; partim Adhærentia, ut Mores & Linguas.
units.tr: Method requires that, after the region itself with its accidents and the parts described so far, the discussion now turn to its inhabitants. I will consider them both as governed and as governing, and I will weigh their accidents: partly those that are inherent, such as their character or genius, and partly those that are adherent, such as their manners and languages.

units.la: Quod ad Indolem Geniumque, Itali Comitate, Convictus facilitate, facetis Colloquiis alios antecellunt Populos. Felici fecundoque nati Ingenio, supra modum prompti sunt in excogitando; & Docilitate percipiendis cum Litterarum studiis, tum variis Artibus præstant incredibili: Honoris ab omni ævo & Gloriæ sitientissimi, Laudisque præter alios adpetentes. Cum laete Voluptatem imbibentes, propensi sunt in Mollitiem; in Luxuriam prochives; in Venerem soluti. Vindictæ vehementer sunt cupidi, eamque Vita ipsa jucundiorem cententes, Testamentis suis mandare consuerunt Posteris.
units.tr: As to their character and genius, the Italians surpass other peoples in courtesy, ease of company, and witty conversation. Born with a happy and fruitful wit, they are exceedingly quick at invention. In docility for grasping both literary studies and various arts, they excel to an incredible degree. They have always been thirsty for honour and glory, and they seek praise above others. Joyfully drinking in pleasure, they are inclined to softness, prone to luxury, and loose in love. They are very eager for revenge, and they consider it more pleasant than life itself, and they are accustomed to entrust it to their posterity in their wills.

units.la: Mulieres porro variarum hic Civitatum depingit scite admodum Membrana quædam, quam suis Italiæ Monumentis adposuit V. Cl. Laurentius Schraderus Halberstadiensis. Ea, inter alia, hæc habet: Senenses, pulcræ; Florentinæ, delicatæ; Perusinæ, elegantes; Caietanæ, formosæ; Confentinæ, obstinatæ; Beneventanæ, rusticæ; Bononienses, arrogantiunculæ; Mutinenses, benignæ; Cesenates, rapaces; Genuenses, malaces; Cremenses, fallaces, Placentinæ, difficiles; Lucenses, castæ; Pistoriensis, faciles; Romanæ graves, Capuanæ, superbæ; Neapolitanæ, solicitæ; Brundusinæ, inertes; Ferrarienses, avidæ; Ravennatæ, humanæ; Urbinates, adfabiles; Vincentinæ, constantes; Parmenses, avaræ. Papienses, lucri-cupidæ; Mediolanenses, urbanæ; Pedemontanæ, procaces; Venetæ, petulantes; Veronenses, gratiosæ; Frisiana, diligentes; Formianæ, speciosæ; Laudenses, superstitiosæ; Cremonenses, sumtuosæ; Tarvisianæ, zelotypæ; Bergomates, astutæ; Arctinæ, tenaces; Putcolanæ, bellæ. Qui vero quales & quo modo ament, sequentibus eadem exponit Membrana: Proceram Mediolanenses, non zelotypi; Saltatricem Mantuanæ, solicitæ; Arrogantem Neapolitani, perditissimi; Pertinacem Lucenses, constantes, Carnosam Venetæ, libidinosissimi; Grandem Senenses, indefessi; Audacem Perusinæ, ardentes; Facundam Urbinates, cauti; Timidulam Brixienses, firmi; Candidam Calabræ, pertinaces; Exiguis mamillis Patavini, depereuntes; Elegantem Vincentinæ, diligentes; Lacertosam Genuenses, odiosi; Purpurillatam Mutinenses, gnavi; Gravem Bononienses, fideles; Iucundam Placentinæ, acres; Cantatricem Cremonenses, avidi; Blandam Veronenses, mollesi; Animosam Romani, infanti; Obsequentem Ravennates, cupidi; Ingenuam Pisanæ, vehementes; Pinguem Tarentini, profusi; Bene habitam Monopolitani, strenui; Pathicam Coronenses, furiosi; Rubicundam Pistoriensis, sedati; Nitidam Sarzonenses, placidi. Quibus denique Illecebris Philtrisque Hi Illi Amicas adliciant, his eadem Membrana docet: Mediolanenses, magnificentia; Florentini, rythmis; Lucenses, molestia; Senenses, lacrymulis; Urbinates, oratione; Mantuani, minis; Neapolitani, equis; Venetı, auctoritate; Perusini, blasphemiis; Veronenses, obsequiis; Bononienses, donis; Romani, iocis; Cremonenses, cantilenis; Vincentini, perpetua consectatione.
units.tr: A certain broadside, which the most distinguished Laurentius Schraderus of Halberstadt attached to his Italian monuments, describes the women of the various cities very cleverly. Among other things it says this: the Sienese women are beautiful; the Florentines delicate; the Perugians elegant; the Gaetans graceful; the Consentines obstinate; the Beneventans rustic; the Bolognese somewhat arrogant; the Modenese kind; the Cesenates rapacious; the Genoese spiteful; the Cremonese deceitful; the Piacentines difficult; the Lucchese chaste; the Pistoians easy; the Romans serious; the Capuans proud; the Neapolitans anxious; the Brindisians sluggish; the Ferrarese greedy; the Ravennates humane; the Urbinates affable; the Vicentines constant; the Parmesans avaricious; the Pavians eager for gain; the Milanese courteous; the Piedmontese bold; the Venetians wanton; the Veronese charming; the Friulians diligent; the Formians handsome; the Lodigians superstitious; the Cremonese lavish; the Trevisans jealous; the Bergamasks shrewd; the Arezzians tenacious; the Pozzuolans pretty. The same broadside sets out who loves whom and in what way: the tall Milanese women are not jealous; the dancing Mantuan women are anxious; the arrogant Neapolitan women are most profligate; the stubborn Lucchese are constant; the fleshy Venetian women are most lustful; the large Sienese are tireless; the bold Perugian women are ardent; the eloquent Urbinates are cautious; the timid Brescians are steadfast; the fair Calabrian women are stubborn; the Paduan women with small breasts dote; the elegant Vicentines are diligent; the muscular Genoese are hateful; the purple-clad Modenese are industrious; the dignified Bolognese are faithful; the pleasant Piacentines are sharp; the singing Cremonese are eager; the flattering Veronese are soft; the spirited Roman women are foolish; the obliging Ravennate women are desirous; the noble Pisan women are passionate; the plump Tarentine women are lavish; the well-kept Monopolitan women are vigorous; the sensual Coronese women are frenzied; the ruddy Pistoian women are calm; the neat Sarzanese women are placid. Finally, the same broadside teaches by what enticements and love-potions these men win their mistresses: the Milanese by magnificence; the Florentines by verses; the Lucchese by annoyance; the Sienese by little tears; the Urbinates by speech; the Mantuans by threats; the Neapolitans by horses; the Venetians by authority; the Perugians by blasphemies; the Veronese by attentions; the Bolognese by gifts; the Romans by jests; the Cremonese by songs; the Vicentines by unrelenting pursuit.

units.la: Color porro Italis varius, Statura non una. In Cis-Alpina Gallia, Venetoque recessu Color vulgo cādidus, Statura procerior: contra in plerā Etruria, Latio, Campania, Lucania & Brutijs, aquilus Color, Capillus niger, Statura brevior, quæ etiam deridiculo huiusce legitur Gallis. Eadem in Picentinis, aliisque qui Superi Mari soram adcolunt in Magnam usque Græciam: nisi quod in Apulis, Calabris, iisque, qui extremam tenent Italiam, Græcos fere æmulentur; Græci plurimum ipsi, origine.
units.tr: The colour of the Italians also varies, and their stature is not uniform. In Cisalpine Gaul and the Venetian recess the complexion is commonly fair and the stature taller. On the other hand, in most of Etruria, Latium, Campania, Lucania and the Bruttii the complexion is dark, the hair black, and the stature shorter, which the French also mock. The same holds for the Picentines and the others who dwell along the Adriatic coast as far as Magna Graecia; except that the Apulians, the Calabrians, and those who hold the farthest part of Italy nearly rival the Greeks, who themselves are very much so by origin.

units.la: Litterarum Cultores Itali, quantum in ipsis est, tuentur, fovent, alunt, ornant; iisque omnia bonorum Mæcœnatum exhibent officia. Hinc tot per Italiam Academia, quas suis commemoro locis, Romana, Mediolanensis, Bononiensis, Patavina, Papiensis, Neapolitana, Perusina, Salentitana, Pisana, Ferrariensis, Senensis, Florentina, Venetæ, uetia, Bergomensis, Mutinensis, Taurinensis; Nam Parmensis, Placentina, Anconitana, & Maceratensis magna ex parte interierunt. Inde item tanta Doctorum, summaque Eruditione variis Artibus & Disciplinis praestantium Virorum copia. Stupendum fuit ab ijs omne Aevum. Qui primi, qui medii, paucis per Satyram quasi colligam: quos nostrum vidit videtque, ad Patrias plerosque suas in sequentibus notabo. Non singularum Facultatum proferam hic Lumina. Theologos Medicosque tuos adferam locis. Notam mihi ingressuro arenam, Iurisconsultos dabo, tanquam in exemplum, utque vel ex ijs pareat solis, quot Soles huic Regioni nullo non tempore illuxerint. Legum scientia claruerunt olim, iuriqueNo... Ayignata solvendi fuerunt periti, Sex. Papirius, qui Leges Regias in unum collegit, unde Iuris Papiriano nomen: Ap. Claudius Sabinus Regiensis, unus ex X Viris, cuius maximum fuit in XII Tabulis conscribundis contulimus: Ap. Claudius Caecus, quem de Actionibus & Usurpationibus scripsisse traditum est: P. Sempronius, quem Pop. Rom. Σοφὸν cognominavit: P. Cornelius Scipio Nasica, Vir Optimus ab Senatu appellatus ingenio sapientissimus, unde vulgo Corculum dictus: cuique publica Domus in Via Sacra data est, quo facilius consulti posset. Q. Mucius Scaevola, qui Ciceroni Iurisconsultorum delectissimus: Ti. Coruncanius, qui Primus Ius profiteri coepit: Sex. & P. Aelii Peти Fratres, quorum ille Librum composuit, qui Tripertita inscribebatur, Cunabula iuris continentem, hic autem vocatum, quod Lege XII Tabularum praeposita, iungeretur Interpretatio: deinde subtexeretur Legis Actio: P. Atilius, qui Primus a Populo Sapiens est appellatus: M. Porcius Cato, Poteriae Familiae Princeps. Hos sequuti sunt P. Mucius Scaevola, M. Iunius Brutus, M. Manilius, insignes Iuris Fundatores; quorum Primus X Libellos reliquit, Secundus VII, Tertius III Manilius is, quem L. Crassus apud M. Ciceronem de Oratore III tranvertiose vidisse Foro ambulantem dicit; quod erat insigne, cum, qui id faceret, Civibus omnibus Consilij sui copiam faceret. Ab his profecti sunt P. Rutilius Rufus, quem Cicero magnum de Iure Munus sustinuisse, multaque praeclara de Iure scriptis tradidit: Publius Virginius, Q. Aelius Tubero, Stoicus, Sex. Pompeius, Cn. Pompei Magni Patruus, Stoicarum etiam rerum peritia clarus; L. Cassius Antipater; multorum etiam, inter illos L. Licinii Crassi Magister. Post hos Q. Mucius P.F. Scaevola, Pontifex Maximus, qui Ius Civile Primus constituit generatim in libros XVIII redigendo. Ejus Auditores fuerunt complures; sed praecipua auctoritatis C. Aquilius Gallus, maximi Populo aestimatus, qui Legem tulit de Dolo Malo; L. Lucretius Balbus, summus Stoicus; Sex. Papirius & C. Iuventius. Successit his Ser. Sulpicius, Balbi Gallique Discipulus, qui prope centum & octoginta libros reliquit. Ab hoc plurimi profecerunt; fere tamen hi Libros conscripserunt, P. Alphenus Varus; Caius; A. Ofilius, Q. Aelii Tuberonis Praeceptor; T. Cassius; Aufidius Tucca & Mamilius; Flavius Priscus; C. Atteius Capito; Pacia; Iulius Clemens; Q. Antistius Labeo; Cornelius Cinna; L. Gellius Publicola, quem Athenis scribit Cicero de Legibus Philosophos omnes convocasse, ipsumque Auctorem fuisse, ut aliquando Controversiarum aliquem facerent modum. Fuerunt eodem tempore C. Trebatius Testa, Cornelij Maximi Auditor; A. Cascellius; Q. Mucius, Volusij Discipulus. Secutus inde Q. Aelius Tubero, qui Ofilio dedit operam. Atteius Capito, & Antistius Labeo, primum duas quasi sectas fecerunt: hic multa innovavit, ille, in his quae tradita ipsi fuerant, perseveravit. Capitoni successit Masurius Sabinus (de quo Athenaeus lib. XIII. Δαπανοσοφ. Μαζούριος ... ) Labeoni Nerva, qui Dissensiones auxerunt: Sabino C. Cassius Longinus; Nerva Proculus: appellatique ab ijs sunt Cassiani & Proculeiani. Catllio quasi tutelectus Caius Sabinus; Proculo Pegasus; Caelio Priscus Iavolenus, Pegaso Celsus Patri Celso Celsus Filius & Neratius Priscus; Iavoleno Aburnus Valens, Tuscianus, Salvius Iulianus. Commemorat hos omnes Auctor. l. 2. D. de Orig. Iuris. Recentiores praeter Superiores, nonnulli, qui proxime sequuti, plerique Itali in Indice, qui Pandectis praefixus, Celsidius Scaevola, Papinianus, Pomponius, Mastanus, Mauricianus, Africanus, Marcellus, Florentinus, Venulejus, Tertullianus, Justus, Cyprianus, Paulus, Triphoninus, Callistratus, Menander, Marcianus, Gallus Aquilius, Modestinus, Tarruntenus Paternus, Macer, Arcadius, Rufinus, Maximus & Hermogenianus: ex quorum Scriptis Iuris Pandectae compositi sunt & conuncti: quibus, ut & Decretalibus illustrandis incredibilem suppeditarunt copiam variae Italiae Urbes & oppida. Gau-dent dent suis in Etruria Pisæ Francisco Tignum & Andrea. Plumbinum, Benedictus Luca, Hieronymo, Limbanoque, qui alius a Brixienti, Pistoria, Cyno, Florentia, Accursius, Laurentius ... Mugellum, Dyno & Ioanne Andrea; Mons Sansovinus, Fabianos Sena, Fredericus Petrutius, Bartholomeo Sozino, Martino alio ab Laudensi & Fanensi, Thomas Cro. Aretium, Gratianus, Fran[cisc]o de Arbergatti, alioque Francisco, sua ætate Iurisconsultorum Principe, Angelo de Ca[m]pellionibus & Bonagratia; Perusia, Baldo, qui B[artol]o fuit Discipulus, & Gregorij xi ante Pontificatum Præceptor, Ancelo, Benedicto Calla, Angelo de Perusio, Baldo Novello à Bartolinis, Ioanne Baptista, Ioanne Petruccio Nicolao ab Alexandro, Simone Bartholomeo, Petro Phaldo & Philippo Franco; Castrum, Paulo, qui inde Castellani; Oppidum denique D. Gemmani, Dominus & Nerus. Vidit in Latio Fortuna Livij Rainerium Bartoli Magnificum, & Argentinum. Mundo dederunt in Campania Minturnum Ricuperatum; Cumæ, Raphaelum; Neapolis, Nicolaum, Iacobum, Alexandrum ab Alexandro, Paulum à Puteo. Superbiunt Iuris in Piceno Firmum Ioannem Iacobum Bartholo, Ancona, Petro Gratianus; Saxoferratum, Bartolo, Iuris Lucernæ Fanum, Laurentium Pauli Rubei. Marco ... pic alio ab Laudensi & Senensi. Genuit Pons Castellanus, Vinbriæ oppidum, Ludovicum Fontanum. Alumnos habuerunt apud Samnites Beneventum Cedrum & Carleum; Æterna vero, Andream, nobilem Virum Feudalium Interpretum. Cœnetur apud Apulos S. Severi oppidum ab Ioanne Franc[isco] Bonæ & Ioanne Baptista Caccistopo. In venerandam Iustitiæ Officinam miserunt ex Romanula Bononienses Agonem, Gaudonem, Ioannem Calderinum, Petrum Andreæ Rumm, Manfredum à Mantigelis, Martinianum ab Arequidi, Iacobum Bovigarium, Bonconsum Andream, Lucidum, Florianum à S. Petro, Ioannem Anonimum, qui & Archidiaconus, Fredericum à Scala, Marcum Antonium Baverium, Iohannem Passagerium, Ioannem Campegium. Matheum Matheilanum, Petrum Andream Cambarum, Ludovicum Bolognanum, Andream Alciatum, & alios: Imolenses, Ioannem & Alexandrum; Ferrarienses, Ferrinum Sardum & Ludovicum Sardum. Illustrarunt legum scientia suas in Langobardia Cisalpina Patrias Regium quidem Philippus Caselia Parmam, Bernardus, Ioannes Lucianus, Ugolinus à Fontana; Placentiam, Raphael Fulgosius, Alberus de Ferraris, Ioannes Francischus Ponzinicus; Altam, Albertus Pernus, & Ioannes Nerulsinus.
units.tr: Italians who cultivate literature, as far as in them lies, protect it, foster it, nourish it and adorn it, and they show it every courtesy of good patrons. Hence there are so many academies throughout Italy, which I mention in their places: the Roman, Milanese, Bolognese, Paduan, Pavian, Neapolitan, Perugian, Salentine, Pisan, Ferrarese, Sienese, Florentine, Venetian, Vicentine, Bergamask, Modenese, and Turin academies. For the Parmesan, Piacentine, Anconitan and Macerata academies have for the most part perished. Hence also such a great number of learned men, and men of the highest erudition, excelling in various arts and disciplines. Their whole age has been astonishing. I will sum up, as it were in a satire, the first and middle ones and the few; most of those whom our age has seen and sees I will note in what follows, with their homelands. I will not set forth here the lights of each faculty. I will bring in your theologians and physicians in their places. As I am about to enter an unfamiliar arena, I will give jurists as an example, so that from them alone it may appear how many suns have shone upon this region at every time. They were once famous for the knowledge of the laws and were skilled in loosing the knots of law: Sextus Papirius, who gathered the royal laws into one, whence the Papirian law takes its name; Appius Claudius Sabinus of Regium, one of the Decemvirs, whose great contribution was in drafting the Twelve Tables; Appius Claudius Caecus, who is said to have written on actions and usucapions; P. Sempronius, whom the Roman people called wise; P. Cornelius Scipio Nasica, a most excellent man, called by the Senate the wisest in intellect, whence he was commonly called Corculum, and to whom a public house was given on the Via Sacra, so that he might be consulted more easily; Q. Mucius Scaevola, the most select of the jurists for Cicero; Ti. Coruncanius, who first began to profess law publicly; the brothers Sextus and P. Aelius Paetus, of whom the former composed a book called the Tripertita, containing the cradle of law, and the latter, because the interpretation was attached to the Law of the Twelve Tables and then the legal action was appended, was called so; P. Atilius, who was first called wise by the people; M. Porcius Cato, the Prince of the Plebeian Family. After them followed P. Mucius Scaevola, M. Junius Brutus, M. Manilius, distinguished founders of the law; of whom the first left ten little books, the second seven, the third three. This Manilius is he whom L. Crassus, in Cicero's On the Orator book III, says he saw walking in the Forum with a striking air, which was remarkable, since he gave all citizens the opportunity to consult him. From these came P. Rutilius Rufus, of whom Cicero reports that he bore the great office of law with distinction and wrote many excellent things on law; Publius Verginius; Q. Aelius Tubero, a Stoic; Sextus Pompeius, uncle of Gnaeus Pompey the Great, also famous for his knowledge of Stoic matters; L. Cassius Antipater; and, among many others, the teacher of L. Licinius Crassus. After these came Q. Mucius P.F. Scaevola, the Pontifex Maximus, who first set out the civil law by reducing it generally into eighteen books. He had many pupils, but of the greatest authority was C. Aquilius Gallus, esteemed highly by the people, who proposed the law concerning malicious deceit; L. Lucretius Balbus, a most eminent Stoic; Sextus Papirius and C. Iuventius. To these succeeded Servius Sulpicius, pupil of Balbus and Gallus, who left nearly one hundred and eighty books. Many profited from him; but these wrote books: P. Alfenus Varus; Caius; A. Ofilius, teacher of Q. Aelius Tubero; T. Cassius; Aufidius Tucca and Mamilius; Flavius Priscus; C. Ateius Capito; Pacia; Iulius Clemens; Q. Antistius Labeo; Cornelius Cinna; L. Gellius Publicola, of whom Cicero writes in On the Laws that at Athens he called together all the philosophers and was himself the author that they might at some time put an end to their disputes. At the same time lived C. Trebatius Testa, a pupil of Cornelius Maximus; A. Cascellius; Q. Mucius, a pupil of Volusius. Then followed Q. Aelius Tubero, who devoted himself to Ofilius. Ateius Capito and Antistius Labeo first made two schools, as it were: the former introduced many innovations, the latter persevered in what had been handed down to him. Capito was succeeded by Masurius Sabinus (of whom Athenaeus, book XIII of the Deipnosophists, speaks: "Masurius ..."); Labeo by Nerva, and they increased the dissensions; Sabinus by C. Cassius Longinus, and Nerva by Proculus; and from them they were called Cassians and Proculians. After Capito, Caius Sabinus as it were took the place of a guardian; after Proculus, Pegasus; after Caelius, Priscus Javolenus; after Pegasus, Celsus, and to the father Celsus, Celsus the son and Neratius Priscus; after Javolenus, Aburnus Valens, Tuscianus, Salvius Julianus. The author records all these in book 2 of the Digest, On the Origin of Law. Of the more recent jurists, besides the earlier ones, some who followed closely, and many Italians, are in the Index prefixed to the Pandects: Celsidius Scaevola, Papinian, Pomponius, Mastanus, Mauricianus, Africanus, Marcellus, Florentinus, Venuleius, Tertullian, Justus, Cyprian, Paul, Triphoninus, Callistratus, Menander, Marcian, Gallus Aquilius, Modestinus, Tarruntenus Paternus, Macer, Arcadius, Rufinus, Maximus and Hermogenianus; from whose writings the Pandects of law were composed and combined. Various Italian cities and towns have also supplied an incredible abundance for illustrating the Decretals. Pisa in Etruria has rejoiced in Francesco Tignoso and Andrea... Plumbino, Benedetto Luca, Girolamo, Limbano, who was other than the one from Brescia; Pistoia gave Cino; Florence Accursius, Lorenzo ...; Mugello gave Dino and Giovanni Andrea; Monte San Savino, Fabiani; Siena, Frederic Petrucci, Bartolomeo Sozzini, Martino, another from Lodi, and from Fano, Tommaso Cro... Arezzo, Gratiano, Francesco de Arbergati, and another Francesco, in his age the prince of jurists, Angelo de Canpellionibus and Bonagrazia; Perugia, Baldo, who was a pupil of Bartolo and teacher of Gregory XI before his pontificate, Ansel, Benedetto Calla, Angelo of Perugia, Baldo Novello of the Bartolini, Giovanni Battista, Giovanni Petruccio, Nicola of Alessandro, Simone, Bartolomeo, Pietro Faldo and Filippo Franco; Castro, Paolo, who was called from there Castellani; and finally the town of San Gemignano, Dominus and Nerus. In Latium the fortune of Livy saw Rainerius Bartoli the Magnificent and Argentinus. In Campania, Minturnae gave Ricuperatus to the world; Cumae, Raphael; Naples, Nicola, Giacomo, Alessandro of Alessandro, Paolo dal Pozzo. In Picenum, Fermo prides itself on Giovanni Giacomo Bartolo; Ancona on Pietro Graziano; Sassoferrato on Bartolo; Fano, the lamp of law, on Lorenzo Paolo Rubeo; Marco ... another from Lodi and from Siena. Pontecastello, a town of Vibrium, produced Ludovico Fontano. Among the Samnites, Benevento had Cedro and Carlo as its pupils; Eterna, Andrea, a noble interpreter of feudal law. Among the Apulians, the town of San Severo is to be honoured by Giovanni Francesco Bona and Giovanni Battista Caccistopo. Bologna sent from its own Romagna into the venerable workshop of justice Ago, Gaudo, Giovanni Calderino, Pietro Andrea Rumm, Manfredo of Mantigelli, Martiniano of Arequido, Giacomo Bovigario, Bonconsus Andrea, Lucido, Floriano of San Pietro, Giovanni Anonimo, who was also an archdeacon, Federico dalla Scala, Marco Antonio Baverio, Giovanni Passaggeri, Giovanni Campeggi, Matteo Matteilano, Pietro Andrea Cambaro, Ludovico Bolognese, Andrea Alciati, and others; Imola, Giovanni and Alessandro; Ferrara, Ferrino the Sardinian and Ludovico the Sardinian. In Cisalpine Lombardy, the native cities were made famous by the science of law: Regium, indeed, by Filippo Caselia; Parma by Bernardo, Giovanni Luciano, Ugolino dalla Fontana; Piacenza by Raffaele Fulgosio, Alberto de Ferraris, Giovanni Francesco Ponzinico; Alta by Alberto Pernus and Giovanni Nerulsino.

units.la: Arenam hanc ingrediti sunt ex variis Langobardiæ Transpadanæ Civitatibus, Mantua quidem Bonifacius à Vitalinis & Guido de Sufania; Mediolano, Philippus Decius, Bernardinus Lanzanus, Paulus Crasimus, Ioan Mayrus, Stephanus de Homodeo, Ioannes Lignanus; Cremona, Bistanus, Martinus, Richardus Malumbra, & Nicolaus; Brixia, Bartholomæus, Laurentius Cassarius, Lanfrancus, alius ab Lucenti, Marcus, Stephanus Fredericus; Papia, Iohannes a Curte, Stephanus Ceffa, Franciscus Curtius; Laude Pompeia, Obradus, Martinusque alius a Fanensi & Senensi: Vercellis denique Franciscus. Beatus in Marca Tarvisina Venetiæ Nicolaus Superantius, Petrus a Monte, Petrus Mauroceni; Vetonam Bartholomeus Cepolla & Iacobus de Arbizono: Paduam denique Franciscus Zabarella, Baptista a S. Biasio, Ioannes Lucianus Cantarus, Ioannes Franciscus, Ioannes Alexander, & Protasius Nemus. Prodierunt, ut concludam, ex Pedemontij Civitate Turino Andreas de Ipsitate, & Ioannes Cinaglius.
units.tr: They entered this arena from various cities of Transpadane Lombardy: from Mantua, Boniface of the Vitalini family and Guido de Sufania; from Milan, Philip Decius, Bernardino Lanzano, Paolo Crasimo, Giovanni Mayrus, Stefano de Homodeo, Giovanni Lignano; from Cremona, Bistano, Martino, Riccardo Malumbra, and Niccolò; from Brescia, Bartolomeo, Lorenzo Cassario, Lanfranco, another from Lucento, Marco, Stefano Federico; from Pavia, Giovanni a Curte, Stefano Ceffa, Francesco Curzio; from Lodi Pompeia, Obrado and Martino, another from Fano and another from Siena; and finally from Vercelli, Francesco. In the Trevisan March of Venice, Beatus: Niccolò Superanzio, Pietro da Monte, Pietro Mauroceni; from Vittorio, Bartolomeo Cepolla and Giacomo de Arbizono; and finally from Padua, Francesco Zabarella, Battista a San Biagio, Giovanni Luciano Cantaro, Giovanni Francesco, Giovanni Alessandro, and Protasio Nemus. To conclude, there came forth from the city of Turin in Piedmont Andrea de Ipsitate and Giovanni Cinaglio.

units.la: Historiis lectitandis memorandum apud Posteros nomen condiderunt M. Porcius Cato Censorinus, Q. Claudius Quadrigarius, L. Cornelius Sisenna, M. Terentius Varro, Q. Fabius Pictor, L. Calpurnius Piso Frugi, C. Fannius, C. Lælij Sapientis Gener, L. Cælius Antipater, Sempronius Asellio, Trib. plebis, C. Licinius Macer (quem Livius lib. vii. notat, ut studio lucis gentis ab Vero digressum) L. Valerius Antias, L. Cassius Hemina, Q. Aelius Tubero, C. Oppius, C. Sallustius Crispus (de quo Martialis, Hic erit, ut perhibent doctorum corda Virorum, Primus Romana Crispus in Historia)
units.tr: Those who won a memorable name among later generations by reading histories were Marcus Porcius Cato Censorinus, Quintus Claudius Quadrigarius, Lucius Cornelius Sisenna, Marcus Terentius Varro, Quintus Fabius Pictor, Lucius Calpurnius Piso Frugi, Gaius Fannius, the son-in-law of Gaius Laelius Sapiens, Lucius Caelius Antipater, Sempronius Asellio, tribune of the plebs, Gaius Licinius Macer (whom Livy, book 7, notes as having departed from the truth out of zeal for the people's cause), Lucius Valerius Antias, Lucius Cassius Hemina, Quintus Aelius Tubero, Gaius Oppius, Gaius Sallustius Crispus (of whom Martial says: He will be, as the hearts of learned men declare, the first Crispus in Roman history).

units.la: Cornelius Nepos, P. Nigidius Figulus (quem Agellius Romanæ Civitatis doctissimum vocat), M. Varro, Cornelius Matia? C. Asinius Pollio (quem Horatius ab recenti Belli Civilis Historia scribenda dehortatur lib. ii Carminum, Ode 1.) Fenestella, C. Attenus Capito, de quo alibi, Mosiens Sabinus, Sempronius Tuditanus, Cn. Gelius, Pompeius Trogus (qui totius Orbis Historiam scribere aggressus est, Herculea, ut inquit Iustinus, audacia); L. Cornelius Sulla, L. Cincius Alimentus, C. Iulius Hyginus, Sammonicus Serenus, T. Livius, C. Iulius Cassius, C. Plinius Paterculus, C. Cornelius Tacitus, Valerius Maximus, C. SuetoC. Suetonius Tranquillus, L. Iulius Florus, Fl. Eutropius, Paulus Orosius, Paulus Diaconus, Sex. Rufus, Aelius Spartianus, Iulius Capitolinus, Aelius Lampridius, Trebellius Pollio, Fl. Vopiscus, Volcatius Gallicanus, Ammianus Marcellinus, Sex. Aurelius Victor, Pomponius Laetus, Flavius Blondus, Aeneas Silvius, Nicolaus Machiavellus, Franciscus Guicciardinus, Joannes Pontanus, Gallearius Capella, M. Antonius Coccius Sabellicus, Raphael Volaterranus, Petrus Bembus: Alios infinitos praetereo.
units.tr: Cornelius Nepos, P. Nigidius Figulus (whom Aulus Gellius calls the most learned man of the Roman state), M. Varro, Cornelius Matia? C. Asinius Pollio (whom Horace discourages from writing a history of the recent civil wars, in Odes 2.1), Fenestella, C. Attenus Capito, of whom more elsewhere, Mosiens Sabinus, Sempronius Tuditanus, Cn. Gelius, Pompeius Trogus (who undertook to write a history of the whole world, with Herculean audacity, as Justin says); L. Cornelius Sulla, L. Cincius Alimentus, C. Iulius Hyginus, Sammonicus Serenus, T. Livius, C. Iulius Cassius, C. Plinius Paterculus, C. Cornelius Tacitus, Valerius Maximus, C. SuetoC. Suetonius Tranquillus, L. Iulius Florus, Fl. Eutropius, Paulus Orosius, Paulus Diaconus, Sex. Rufus, Aelius Spartianus, Iulius Capitolinus, Aelius Lampridius, Trebellius Pollio, Fl. Vopiscus, Volcatius Gallicanus, Ammianus Marcellinus, Sex. Aurelius Victor, Pomponius Laetus, Flavius Blondus, Aeneas Silvius, Nicolaus Machiavellus, Franciscus Guicciardinus, Joannes Pontanus, Gallearius Capella, M. Antonius Coccius Sabellicus, Raphael Volaterranus, Petrus Bembus. I pass over countless others.

units.la: Flagitat quis & quos tuae bearunt aeternamque Musae? Non omnes signabo. Operosum hoc mihi foret, onerosum Lectori. In memoria mihi vulgatum illud, Minimum de Tabula. Famam tibi tua vena peperererunt, rudi adhuc Roma. C. Livius Andronicus (qui Primus Bello Poenico II apud Latinos Fabulas docuit), Q. Ennius Rudinus (qui Primus annaeno Deluit ex Helicone perennis fronde Cororam, Per Gentes Italas hominum quae clara fuerunt,
units.tr: Who demands this, and whom have your Muses blessed and made immortal? I will not list them all. That would be laborious for me and burdensome for the reader. I recall that familiar saying about the smallest share of the tablet. Your own talent won you fame while Rome was still rough and unpolished. C. Livius Andronicus, who first staged plays among the Latins in the Second Punic War; Q. Ennius of Rudiae, who first brought down from Helicon a garland of evergreen leaves, to be famous among the peoples of Italy, as Lucretius sang of him;

units.la: ut de eo cecinit Lucretius) M. Accius Plautus Sarsinas (de quo apud Quintilianum lib. x cap. 1 Varro, In Comoedia, inquit, maxime laudamus, ut et Varro dicat Musas, Aelius Stolonis sententia, Plautino sermone loquuturas fuisse, si Latine loqui vellent) Cn. Naevius Campanus, in Proceres Civitatis Romanae maledicus; M. Pacuvius Brundisinus; Statius Caecilius Medio-lanensis (qui Ciceroni malus Auctor Latinitatis, cuique palmam inter Comicos tribuit Volcatius Sedigitus) L. Accius Pisaurus, (qui, referente Fabio lib. v cap. xiii, interrogatus, quur cautius non ageret, quum illi in Tragoediis tanta Vis esset, optime respondit, Quoniam, inquit, illa ea dicerent, quae vellet, in Foro essent dicturi Adversarii, quae minime vellet) C. Lucilius Aurunca-nus, quem Horatius Lutulentum & incompositum vocat; rectius est & candidius de eo Quintiliani iudicium, Satyra, inquit, tota nostra est, in qua Primus insignem laudem adeptus est Poeta Lucilius, qui quosdam ita dedicatos sibi habet Amatores, ut eum non cuiusquam modo operis Aetioribus, sed omnibus Poetis praeferre non dubitent. Ego quantum ab illis, tantum ab Horatio dissentio, qui Lucilium dicere lutulentum, & esse aliquid modo tollere possit, putat. Nam Eruditio in eo mira, Libertasque & Acerbitas & abunde Salis.) Sex. Turpilius, Cn. Matius, L. Afranius (Horatius: Dicitur Afrani Toga convenisse Menandro)
units.tr: M. Accius Plautus of Sarsina (of whom Quintilian, Book 10, chapter 1, says: "Varro, in comedy, we especially praise, so much so that Varro says the Muses, by the judgement of Aelius Stolo, would have spoken in the language of Plautus, if they had wished to speak Latin"); Cn. Naevius of Campania, a slanderer of the leading men of the Roman state; M. Pacuvius of Brundisium; Statius Caecilius of Milan (who was a poor authority on Latinity for Cicero, and whom Volcatius Sedigitus ranked first among the comic poets); L. Accius of Pisaurum (who, as Fabius reports in Book 5, chapter 13, when asked why he did not act more cautiously, given the great force of his tragedies, answered very well: "Because those characters say what he wishes, but in the forum his opponents will speak what he least wishes"); C. Lucilius of Aurunca, whom Horace calls muddy and unpolished. Quintilian's judgement of him is more correct and fairer: "Satire, he says, is wholly ours, and in it the poet Lucilius was the first to win distinguished praise. He has such devoted admirers that they do not hesitate to prefer him not only to the authors of any single kind of work, but to all poets. I disagree with them as much as I disagree with Horace, who thinks that Lucilius was muddy and could be surpassed in any respect. For his learning is remarkable, his freedom and sharpness are great, and his wit is abundant." Sex. Turpilius, Cn. Matius, L. Afranius (Horace: "The toga of Afranius is said to have suited Menander").

units.la: Q. Fulvius Dorsennus, M. Attelus (ab Licinio, ut testatur Cicero, Scriptor Ferreus dictus) Q. Trabea, Cn. Aquilius, C. Licinius Imbrex, Q. Novius (Atellanarum Scriptor in eo Argumenti genere, judice Macrobio, probatissimus.) Hos, Imperio aucto, puriorque aevo, sequuti sunt T. Lucretius Carus (de quo Ovidius: Carmina divini tunc sunt peritura Lucreti, Exitio terras quum dabit una dies)
units.tr: Q. Fulvius Dorsennus, M. Attelus (called an iron writer by Licinius, as Cicero attests), Q. Trabea, Cn. Aquilius, C. Licinius Imbrex, Q. Novius (judged by Macrobius the most highly approved writer of atellan farces in that genre). After these, when the empire had grown and the age was purer, came T. Lucretius Carus (of whom Ovid says: "The songs of the divine Lucretius will perish only when one day gives the lands to destruction").

units.la: L. Pomponius Bononiensis, verbis rudis, sensibus acer; D. Laberius, Eques Romanus, Mimorum Pater; Q. Catullus Veronensis; Cornelius Licinius Calvus; Q. Cornificius, C. Helvius Cinna, Smyrnae Auctor; M. Furius Bibaculus Cremonensis (cujus, ut & Catulli Carmina Caesarum relicta Contumelijs fuisse scribit Tacitus libro Annalium iv) C. Titida (Ovidius lib. ii Fastorum: Quid referam Ticidae, quid Memmi Carmina? apud quos Nomen adesse Rebus, Carminibusque Pudor.)
units.tr: Lucius Pomponius of Bologna, rough in words, keen in thought; Decimus Laberius, a Roman knight, father of the mime; Quintus Catullus of Verona; Gaius Licinius Calvus; Quintus Cornificius; Gaius Helvius Cinna, author of the Smyrna; Marcus Furius Bibaculus of Cremona (whose songs, like those of Catullus, Tacitus writes, were left to the insults of the Caesars, in book 4 of the Annals); Gaius Titius (Ovid, book 2 of the Fasti: "What shall I say of the songs of Ticida or Memmius? In them a name is present to things, and modesty to songs.").

units.la: A. Furius Antias, L. Iulius Calidius, Tullius Laurea (qui M. Tullij Ciceronis Vitam Academiam versibus celebrat apud Plinium) Gravido jam & laborante suis ingeniis Romanorum Imperio, claruerunt P. Virgilius Maro Mantuanus, Q. Horatius Flaccus Venusinus, C. Valgius Saturninus (De eo qui convixit ipsi Albius Tibullus Romanus: Est tibi, qui possit magnis se accingere rebus, Valgius, aeterno propior non alter Homero.)
units.tr: Aulus Furius Antias; Lucius Julius Calidius; Tullius Laurea (who celebrates the life of Marcus Tullius Cicero in verse, as Pliny records). When the Roman empire was already heavy and labouring under its own talents, there flourished Publius Vergilius Maro of Mantua, Quintus Horatius Flaccus of Venusia, and Gaius Valgius Saturninus (of whom Albius Tibullus, a Roman who lived with him, says: "There is for you, Valgius, one who can gird himself for great themes, no other closer to eternal Homer.").

units.la: M. Mallius, Sex. Aurelius Propertius Mevanius, L. Varius (cujus Thyesten Fabius cuilibet Graecorum comparari posse scribit) C. Cilnius Maecenas, P. Ovidius Naso Sulmonensis, Cassius Severus Parmensis (quem in studijs repertum missus ab Augusto Q. Varius interemit, ablato cum Libris eius Scrinio) Domitius Marsus, Cn. Cornelius Gallus, C. Germanicus Caesar, Cassius Bassus, Aemilius Macer Veronensis, C. Rabirius, L. Annaeus Seneca, C. Afinius Gallus, A. Persius Flaccus, Cornelius Severus, M. Annaeus Lucanus, L. Pomponius Secundus, Cn. Getulicus, Saleius Bassus, (quem Tacitus non modo Poëtam egregium & absolutissimum, sed etiam virum Optimum vocat) C. Clodius Sabinus, C. Pedo Albinovanus, Volusius Sedigitus, cuius hoc de Poëtis est iudicium apud Agellium lib. xv. Noct. Attic. cap. xxiv: Multos incertos certare hanc Rem videmus, Palmam Poëta Comico quos deferant. Eum, me Iudice, Errorem solvam tibi, Ut contra si qui sentiat, nihil sentias. Caecilio palmam statuo deferre Comico; Plautus secundus facile exsuperat ceteros; Dein Naevius, qui fervet, pretio in tertio est; Si quid quarto detur, dabitur Licinio, Post insequi Licinium facto Atilium; In sexto consequetur hos Terentius; Turpilius septimum, Trabea octavum obtinet; Nono loco esse facile facio Luscium; Decimum addo Antiquitatis causa Ennium.
units.tr: Marcus Mallius; Sextus Aurelius Propertius of Mevania; Lucius Varius (of whose Thyestes Fabius writes that it can be compared with any work of the Greeks); Gaius Cilnius Maecenas; Publius Ovidius Naso of Sulmo; Cassius Severus of Parma (whom, when he was found among his writings, Quintus Varius, sent by Augustus, destroyed, his writing case being taken away along with his books); Domitius Marsus; Gnaeus Cornelius Gallus; Gaius Germanicus Caesar; Cassius Bassus; Aemilius Macer of Verona; Gaius Rabirius; Lucius Annaeus Seneca; Gaius Asinius Gallus; Aulus Persius Flaccus; Cornelius Severus; Marcus Annaeus Lucanus; Lucius Pomponius Secundus; Gnaeus Geticus; Saleius Bassus (whom Tacitus calls not only an outstanding and most accomplished poet but also a most upright man); Gaius Clodius Sabinus; Gaius Pedo Albinovanus; Volusius Sedigitus, whose judgment on the poets is given by Gellius, book 15 of the Attic Nights, chapter 24: "We see many uncertain contestants striving over the prize for the comic poet. I will, in my judgment, resolve that error for you, so that if anyone thinks otherwise, you may think nothing of it. I award the palm among comic poets to Caecilius; Plautus comes second and easily surpasses the rest; then Naevius, who is full of fire, is third in worth; if a fourth place is to be given, it will go to Licinius; after Licinius, Atilius is placed; in sixth place Terence will follow these; Turpilius holds seventh, Trabea eighth; I make Luscius easily ninth; and for the sake of antiquity I add Ennius as tenth."

units.la: Successerunt iis, quos Paullo ante dixi, non eodem plane genio, nec eadem scribendi felicitate P. Papinius Statius, C. Valerius Flaccus Setinus, D. Iunius Iuvenalis Aquinas, L. Arruntius Stella Patavinus, Sentius Augur Romanus, Veltrius Spurina, Vocontius Victor, L. Paulus Pessicenus, T. Annianus, M. Marullus, A. Serenus, Virgilius Romanus, alius ab Mantuano. Declinante denique Imperio, Ingeniisque in hac Studiorum facultate paulatim flaccescentibus, vidit Italia Rufum Festum Avienum, Alphium Avitum, & alios, quos prudens praetereo; quique vixerunt, Musis pennato gradu iam ab Italis ad Afros, Gallos, Hispanosque abitum parantibus. De iis autem, qui nostra floruerunt aetate, sic canit Nicolaus Leonicus Siletius, Poëta doctus & elegans: Urbs Venetum Bembos loquitur Balbosque Poëtas; Naugeriosque suos; Mantua Virgilii Capilupos numine plenos, Castiliosque Duces; At Mollas Mutina, & Sadoletos iactat alumnos, Cortesiosque suos; Brixia Taygetos celebrat, Faustumque Sabaeum Caesare cum Duchio; Felsina cum Bochio commendat Achille Camillos, Flaminioque pio. Te, Dacti, simulemque tibi Florentia vena Praedicat Angelium; Te, Coeli, Bigumque canit Ferraria culta, Strozigenasque duos; Parva colis Vidam, lepidumque Cremona Faernum, Lampridiumque suum; Cum Fracastorio Cortam Verona recenset, Scaligerosque duos; Luca sed Alsitio, Maphaeo Lauda triumphas; Aonio Verulum; Sirenum Urbs Iioviane tuo, Syncereque plaudis Carmine Parthenope.
units.tr: To those whom I mentioned a little earlier there succeeded, not with quite the same genius nor the same felicity in writing: Publius Papinius Statius, Gaius Valerius Flaccus of Setia, Decimus Junius Juvenalis of Aquinum, Lucius Arruntius Stella of Padua, Sentius Augur of Rome, Veltrius Spurina, Vocontius Victor, Lucius Paulus Pessicenus, Titus Annianus, Marcus Marullus, Aulus Serenus, Virgilius Romanus (another than the one from Mantua). At last, as the empire declined and talents in this field of learning gradually withered, Italy saw Rufus Festus Avienus, Alphius Avitus, and others whom I wisely pass over; these had lived when the Muses, on swift wing, were already making their way from Italy to Africa, Gaul and Spain. As for those who flourished in our own age, Niccolò Leonico Tomeo, a learned and elegant poet, sings thus: "The city of Venice speaks of Bembo and the poets Balbo; and of its Navagero; Mantua boasts of Virgil's Capilupi, full of divine inspiration, and of the Castiglioni leaders; but Modena boasts of the soft Molza and of the Sadoleti, its pupils, and of its Cortesi; Brescia celebrates the Taygetes and Fausto Sabeo, with Caesar and Duke; Bologna, with Bocchi, commends the Camilli to Achilles and to pious Flaminio. Florence, you proclaim Dati, and Angeli as well, with your own vein; Ferrara, cultivated, sings of you, Coeli, and of Bigi, and the two Strozzi; you, Cremona, cultivate little Vida and charming Fasrno, and your own Lampridio; Verona recounts Cortese along with Fracastoro and the two Scaligeri; but Lucca triumphs with Alsitio, and Lodi with Maffeo; Verulum with Aonio; you, city of the Sirens, applaud your Giovio, and Naples, with its song, applauds Sincerus."

units.la: Hic sistam, ne Lectori sim molestus. Oratores ad suam usque aetatem enumerat Orator M. Tullius in Bruto, de Claris Oratoribus: Philosophos celebriores, Architam Tarentinum, Alcmaeonem, Philolaumque Crotoniates, & Hippasum Metapontinum, Graecos, in Italico solo natos, Diogenes Laertius: Grammaticos C. Suetonius Tranquillus: Alios Alij. Qui Italiae Populi quibus in Repub. litteraria Facultatibus Artibusque maxime dediti, Membrana notat, de qua paullo ante: In Literis amant Mediolanenses iurisprudentiam; Calabri, Linguam Graecam; Mantuani, Hebraeam: Veronenses, humanas; Bononienses, Mathesin; Patavini, Medicinam; Papienses, Sophisticam; Florentini, Philosophiam Naturalem; Neapolitani, Etruscam; Lucenses, Litteras Sacras; Vincentini Philosophiam Moralem: Venetii, Musicam; Senenses, Dialecticam; Perusini, Ius Pontificium.
units.tr: I will stop here, so as not to trouble the reader. Cicero the orator, in his Brutus, on famous orators, lists orators down to his own time. Diogenes Laertius lists the more famous philosophers: Architas of Tarentum, Alcmaeon, Philolaus of Croton and Hippasus of Metapontum, who were Greeks born on Italian soil. Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus lists the grammarians, and others list others. Membrana notes which peoples of Italy have been most devoted to which faculties and arts in the commonwealth of letters, as I said a little earlier: the Milanese love law in their studies; the Calabrians, the Greek language; the Mantuans, Hebrew; the Veronese, the humanities; the Bolognese, mathematics; the Paduans, medicine; the Pavians, sophistry; the Florentines, natural philosophy; the Neapolitans, Etruscan; the Lucchese, sacred letters; the Vicentines, moral philosophy; the Venetians, music; the Sienese, dialectic; the Perugians, pontifical law.

units.la: CAPUT XV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XV.

units.la: Italorum Mores in Rebus Sacris.
units.tr: The Customs of the Italians in Sacred Matters.

units.la: DIVNCTA Gubernatis Inhaerentia, Indolem, inquam, Geniumque aperui: Adhaerentia succedunt, Mores Linguaeque. Mores considerandi circa Res vel Sacras vel Profanas; hasque partim Publicas cum domi, tum militiae; partim autem Privatas.
units.tr: Having set out their connected qualities of government, I mean their disposition and genius, I now turn to what is adjacent to these: their customs and languages. Customs must be considered with regard either to sacred or to profane matters, and the profane ones are partly public, both at home and in military service, and partly private.

units.la: Quod ad Res Sacras; Itali quondam multis magnisque Superstitionibus ad stuporem usque leguntur fuisse dediti. Peculiariter id de Tuscis, Romanis, Sabinis Veterum docent Historiae, plenissimeque ex singulorum Delineatione in sequentibus patebit. Hodie Sacrorum Caerimonias ex Romanae Ecclesiae praescripto atque institutione religiosissime observant omnes: nisi quod in Australiore Italia pauci Graecorum sequantur ritus, & ipsi quidem Graeci generis. Nullum Italia novit alienum ab Roma Religione Dogma; nihilque permittit Librorum, qui Romanae Ecclesiae adversantur. Pontifex ibi Maximus ἱερεύς est, & Ecclesiarum omnium Caput, numerosam habens Familiam. Quoties procedit Gemmis conspicitur ornatus, & Sericis Vestibus (Verbis utar D. Bernardi ex Libro de Consideratione III, Papam Eugenius interpellantis) tectus Auro, vectus Equo albo, stipatus Milite, circumstrepentibus septus Ministris. Reliquis Sacerdotibus adhiranda ibi Dignitas & Auctoritas. Honorari magis eos animadverti, quam Nobiles. Cardinales, ut Petrus Messias, qui Silvam Variae Lectionis scriptis Venetiis editam, notat, in locum Consulum, qui Romanum olim Imperium administrabant, successerunt: Archiepiscopi Ducibus sunt adaequati: Episcopi Comitibus subjecti, eorum Vicarii Praesidum Imperij dignitatem: Praepositi Praefectorum vicem referunt: Archipresbyteri in locum Tribunorum Militum sunt substituti: Cancellarii Tribunos plebis repraesentant; Archidiaconi Munus Praetoris; Decani Centurionis, Subdiaconi locum Duum. Virum occupant. Alia apud eumdem Messiam; qui numerum Clericorum commemorat incredibilem. Plura Ego Capite de Gubernatione Sacra.
units.tr: As for sacred matters, the Italians were once given over to many great superstitions, to the point of astonishment, as the histories of the ancients teach, especially concerning the Tuscans, the Romans and the Sabines. This will become fully clear from the description of each people in what follows. Today all of them observe the ceremonies of the sacred rites most scrupulously, according to the prescription and institution of the Roman Church, except that in southern Italy a few follow Greek rites, and these are of Greek descent. Italy knows no doctrine foreign to the Roman religion, and it tolerates no books that oppose the Roman Church. There the Pope is the chief priest [ἱερεύς] and head of all the Churches, and he has a numerous household. "Whenever he goes forth, he is seen adorned with jewels, and clothed with silken garments," (I use the words of St Bernard from his book On Consideration, III, addressed to Pope Eugenius) "covered with gold, carried on a white horse, attended by soldiers, and surrounded by noisy ministers." The other priests there gain dignity and authority; I have noticed that they are more honoured than nobles. The cardinals, as Petrus Messias notes in his Silva Variae Lectionis, published at Venice, have succeeded to the place of the consuls who once administered the Roman empire. The archbishops are equal to dukes; the bishops are subject to counts, and their vicars hold the dignity of provincial governors; the provosts take the place of prefects; the archpresbyters have been substituted in the place of military tribunes; the chancellors represent the tribunes of the plebs; the archdeacons hold the office of praetor; the deans that of centurion; and the subdeacons occupy the place of the duumvirs. Messias also records other things, and he mentions the incredible number of clergy. I will say more in the chapter on sacred government.

units.la: CAPUT XVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVI.

units.la: Italorum Mores in Rebus Publicis, cum Domi, tum Militiae.
units.tr: The Customs of the Italians in Public Affairs, both at Home and in War.

units.la: TANTVM obiter de Ritibus Sacris: addam nonnihil de Profanis, ijsque Publicis, & domi, & militiae. Quod ad prius membrum; hoc solum dicam, breviterque in his talibus studens, Italiam Iure uti triplici, Pontificio, Caesareo, Municipali. Primum Alterumque quale, notum aliunde: Tertium ex Statutis constat & Legibus, quas Civitates sibi singulae condere sunt solitae. Sufficiant illa; non hic iurisconsultum agam; neque, quam profiteor Artem, cum ostentatione venditabo. Referam ad hoc Caput, quae de Variarum Civitatum Consiliis leguntur in Membrana, cuius antea feci mentionem: In Consiliis (scriptum ibi) Mediolanenses praestantes) stantes: Veneti, prudentes; Lucani, temerarij; Pisani, inconstantes; Placentini, providi; Florentini, lenti. Veronenses, fideles; Ferrarienses, cauti; Genuenses, ignari; Lucenses, utiles; Volsci, maligni; Bruti, stupidi; Mutinenses, acuti; Perusini, celeres; Senenses, tardi; Patavini, ambigui.
units.tr: I have said so much in passing about sacred rites. I will add a little about profane, that is public, matters, both at home and in war. As for the first part, I will say only this, and briefly, since I am keeping to such matters: Italy uses a threefold law: Pontifical, Imperial, Municipal. The first and second are known well enough elsewhere. The third is established by the statutes and laws which each city has been accustomed to enact for itself. Let these suffice. I will not play the jurist here, nor will I parade with a show the art I profess. I will bring into this chapter what is read about the counsels of the various cities in the parchment I mentioned earlier. In the counsels (so it is written there): the Milanese are outstanding; the Venetians, prudent; the Lucanians, rash; the Pisans, inconstant; the Placentines, provident; the Florentines, slow. The Veronese are faithful; the Ferrarese, cautious; the Genoese, ignorant; the Lucchese, useful; the Volscians, malicious; the Brutians, stupid; the Modenese, shrewd; the Perugians, quick; the Sienese, sluggish; the Paduans, ambiguous.

units.la: Quod ad posterius, quam quondam Bellicosi fuerint Itali Militiæque dediti, loquitur subactus ab its Orbis Terrarum; canente ad Gloriam hanc classicum Romano. Quales in Re Militari plerique sint Itali, quæque ad Expeditiones feliciùs suscipiendas confieuntque singuli conferant, quibus denique Hi, quam Illi magis valeant præstentque, docet elegantèr Membrana, quam dixi, hoc modo: In Re Bellica Perusini strenui; Calabri, præcipites; Spoletani, callidi; Senenses, felices; Bononienses efferi; Neapolitani, animosi; Faventini, Holti instantes; Pratenses, sacrilegi; Collenses, libidinosi; Piceni, rapaces; Aemiliani, inconsulti; Placentini crudeles; Romani, trucesi; Mediolanenses intrepidi; Romani, fortes; Vincentini, vindictæ cupidi; Pistorienses, sanguinei; Papienses, firmi. Ad Rem Bellicam conferunt Veneti Pecuniam; Mediolanenses, Galeas; Placentini, Carros; Cremonenses, Tentoria; Papienses, Lanceas; Pistorienses, Pugiones; Bononienses, Arundines; Florentini ..... Romani, Perseverantiam; Ferrarienses, Tormenta; Neapolitani, Equos; Parmenses, Clypeos; Tarvisini, Ensis; Viterbienses, Calcaria; Laudenses, Commeatum; Neapolitani, Industriam; Mediolanenses, Tolerantiam; Genuenses, Perfidiam. Præstant Mantuani Equitatu; Pistorienses excipiendo ictus Clypeis, Brixienses, extruendis Vallis; Genuenses, Classe; Lucenses, obsidendis Urbibus; Cremonenses, struendis Ordinibus; Veneti, adparanda Classe; Patavini, moderandis Equis; Bergomates, locandis Insidiis.
units.tr: As for the second part, how warlike the Italians once were and devoted to soldiering, the whole world they subdued bears witness, with the Roman sounding the trumpet for this glory. The same parchment I mentioned sets out elegantly what sort of men most Italians are in military affairs, what each contributes to undertaking campaigns more successfully, and finally in what respects these people excel or are stronger than those, in this manner: in warfare the Perugians are vigorous; the Calabrians, headlong; the Spoletans, crafty; the Sienese, fortunate; the Bolognese, fierce; the Neapolitans, spirited; the Faventines, instant at Holti; the Pratesi, sacrilegious; the Collesi, lustful; the Picenes, rapacious; the Emilians, imprudent; the Placentines, cruel; the Romans, savage; the Milanese, fearless; the Romans, brave; the Vicentines, eager for revenge; the Pistoiese, bloodthirsty; the Pavians, steadfast. For warfare the Venetians contribute money; the Milanese, galleys; the Placentines, wagons; the Cremonese, tents; the Pavians, lances; the Pistoiese, daggers; the Bolognese, arrows; the Florentines ..... the Romans, perseverance; the Ferrarese, artillery; the Neapolitans, horses; the Parmesans, shields; the Trevisans, swords; the Viterbese, spurs; the Laudesi, provisions; the Neapolitans, industry; the Milanese, endurance; the Genoese, treachery. The Mantuans excel in cavalry; the Pistoiese in receiving blows on their shields; the Brescians in building fortifications; the Genoese in fleets; the Lucchese in besieging cities; the Cremonese in drawing up battle lines; the Venetians in fitting out fleets; the Paduans in managing horses; the Bergamasks in laying ambushes.

units.la: CAPUT XVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVII.
