units.la: Italorum Mores in Rebus Privatis.
units.tr: The Customs of the Italians in Private Life

units.la: Sic se habent Itali in Rebus Publicis, cum domi, tum militiæ: videndum, quo modo se gerant in Rebus Privatis & Domesticis. Hic de Veteris Italia Moribus, sic canit Virgilius lib. ix. Æneidos: Quis Deus Italiam, quæ Vos Dementia adegit? Non hic Atrida, nec sandi Victor Ulysses, Durum a stirpe genus: Natos ad Flumina primum Deferimus, sævoque gelu duramus & undis: Venatu invigilant Pueri, Silvasque fatigant. Flectere ludus Equos, & spicula tendere cornu. At patiens operum, parvoque adsueta Iuventus Aut rastris terram domat, aut quatit oppida bello. Omne ævum ferro teritur, versaque invenchum Terga fatigamus hasta: nec tarda Senectus Debilitat Vires animi, mutatque vigorem: Canicien Galea premimus, semperque recentes Convectare iuvat Prædas & vivere rapto:
units.tr: This is how the Italians conduct themselves in public affairs, both at home and in war. Now we must consider how they behave in private and domestic life. Virgil sings of the customs of old Italy in the ninth book of the Aeneid: "What god, what madness drove you to Italy? Not here the sons of Atreus, nor Ulysses, the conqueror of Troy, a hard race from its origin. From the cradle they carry their children to the rivers and harden them against biting cold and the waves. The boys keep watch over the hunt and tire out the woods; they break horses and draw the bow with the cornel shaft. But the youth, patient of labour and used to little, either tills the soil with the mattock or shakes cities with war. All of life is spent with the sword, and we wear out the aged back with the turned spear; nor does slow old age weaken the strength of the mind or change its vigour; we press grey hair under the helmet, and it is always a joy to carry home fresh plunder and to live by rapine." And what follows.

units.la: & quæ sequuntur. Quis maiori Italia parti Arandi quondam modus fuerit, docet Plinius libro xviii, cap. xviii; quis Aribores serendi, lib. xvii, cap. xviiii; quis Vineas colendi, eodem, cap. xxiv; quis Vina condendi, libro xiiii cap.xix; quis Pinsendi, lib. quem dixi xvii, cap. x.
units.tr: Pliny, in book 18, chapter 18, shows what was the ancient measure of ploughing across most of Italy; in book 17, chapter 18, how trees were to be planted; in the same book, chapter 24, how vines were to be tended; in book 14, chapter 19, how wine was to be stored; and in the book I mentioned, book 17, chapter 10, how grain was to be pounded.

units.la: Hodie, quod ad Victum, sobrij sunt & frugalis vitæ; non operosi in adornandis struendisque Mensis, nisi quum necessitas flagitat. Vestitus non omnibus est unus: sæpe etenim pro tempore variatur, cum qualitate, tum forma & ritu. Venetis Vestitus est laxitate insigni & prolixitate: & in his Urbibus Municipali sumtuptior. Matronæ ibi ante paucos annos Vlnas, Brachia, Pectus, Humeros nudabant: nunc omnia contegunt, laxioribus utentes Manicis, & in Hispanicum degenerantes. Secundum Venetos civilis & nitidus Florentina, reliquæque Tuscia. Mediolanensibus totique Aemilia, Liguriaque floridior, sed paullo contractior. Roma Aulicus prolixitate colorumque varietate cunctos alios antecellit: Romanus ipse multo frugalior, cui tamen suus non deest nitor, praesertim in Feminis, quae Tuscum nuper adfectabant. Neapolis magis nitido utitur, quam sumtuoso. Cetera Italia simplicius vestitur. In tota Gallia Cis-Alpina Feminae Principes in Hispanico videri gaudent Habitu; Viri in Gallico malunt conspici. Constanti contenti sunt Itali Matrimonio; Repudium non permittentes, ex Urbe Roma, ad malos am inclinante Mores, Sp. Carvilij ductu quasi protectum. Regum Nobilium quoque Primogeniti, Instituto vetere, Principatus obtinent in privata fortuna viri-lis Iuris Liberi ex aequo tunc Heredes, modo legitimo nati Toro. Mercaturam summa exercet industria. Sed de privatoribus Civitatum in Italia Moribus; de selectiore quorundam Urbs & Vestitu; deque carumdem erga Hostes & Hospites Affectu, loquitur Exemplum Membranae, de qua ante dixi; ubi haec: Florentini pacis; Lucenses elegantes. Mantuani, viles, Anconitani, sordidi; Senenses, magnihci; Mediolanenses, copiosi; Neapolitani, luxuriosi; Vincentini, abundantes. Cremonenses, exquisiti; Neapolitani, splendidi; Genuenses, modici. Patavini, mediocres; Aretini, tenues. Veneti obtinentur parvo; Papienses, agrestes; Bononienses, lauti; Asienses, oppari; Perusini, delicati. Delectantur Florentini Caseo-lis; Lucenses, Pyris; Mantuani, Phaseolo; Arminenses, Anteribus; Tarvisani, Ranis; Cremonenses, Farcimine; Neapolitani, Caulibus; Genuenses, Lactucis; Patavini, Pisci-culis; Picenti, Poreis; Perusini, Piscibus, Papienses Caprio & Allio. In Vestitu Mediolanenses splendidi, Genuenses, elegantes. Mantuani, pueriles; Neapolitani, sumtuosi; Veneti, magnifici; Florentini, ridiculi. In perlequendis Injuriis Lucenses, mites; Mediolanenses, faciles; Perusini, dissimulantes; Fulginates, accensi. Mutinenses, placabiles; Senenses, magnanimi; Neapolitani, benigni. Ferrarienses, pertinaces; Veneti, tubdoli; Cremonenses, aperti. Picenti, maligni; Romani, iniqui: Erga Hospites Calabri inofficiosi; Lucenses, fideles, Senenses, amabiles; Veneti, blandi. Patavini, duri; Mediolanenses, incauti; Ferrarienses, alieni; Mantuani, deglabratores; Placentini, severi; Picenti, intenti; Neapolitani, benigni. Florentini protuli; Ptolemenses, benevoli, Sedetani, agrestes; Veronenses, studiosi; Papienses, rudentiores; Genuenses, inhospitales; Parmenses, inconstantes; Mutinenses, prolixi. Neapolitani inhumani. Sequitur ibi, quales singuli sint in Mercatura: Florentini, callidi; Genuenses, tolerantes; Mediolanenses, aperti; Lucenses, fideles; Veneti, splendidi, ...... cauti. Adiciam Coronidis loco elegantissimum, de hodiernis Italorum Genio Moribusque, Carmen Iulij Caesaris Scaligeri: Siticulosus Appulus; Croton sanus: Siculus dolosus: laniger Tarentinus: Picenus unctus: rusticus Ferentanus: Nebulosus Umber: Langobardus astutus: Carnus vorator: potor Ītrus: insanus Illurius, arrogantior Typhaeo: humus Capisque venti & gloria Ragusaeus: Venetus superba nobilis vetustate, Qui more Rodani carpis Arva vicina; Genuensis ofor pa is ac boni moris; Pisanus Britannus terreo Ligur cunctis, Saxicola, Pelagicus for, invidus, spurcus, Famelicosus, turpis, archipirata.
units.tr: Today, as far as food goes, the Italians are sober and lead frugal lives; they are not given to elaborate preparation and setting out of tables, except when necessity demands it. Dress is not the same for everyone: it often varies with the season, both in material and in cut and fashion. The Venetians dress in a notably loose and flowing style, and in their own cities the townspeople dress more lavishly. A few years ago the Venetian matrons went about with their arms, shoulders, breast and neck bared; now they cover everything, wearing looser sleeves and degenerating into Spanish fashions. After the Venetians, the Florentines and the rest of Tuscany dress with civility and neatness. The Milanese and all of Emilia and Liguria dress more showily, but a little more closely. Rome surpasses all others in courtly fashion, in length of garments and variety of colours; the Roman himself is much more frugal, yet he does not lack his own polish, especially the women, who lately aimed at Tuscan styles. Naples uses dress that is neat rather than sumptuous. The rest of Italy dresses more plainly. Across all of Cisalpine Gaul the noble ladies delight to be seen in Spanish dress, while the men prefer to be seen in French. The Italians are content with a constant marriage; they do not permit divorce, which, as is said, was introduced from the city of Rome under Spurius Carvilius, as a protection against a leaning towards bad morals. The firstborn sons of the nobles, by an old custom, hold the principalities, and in private estates the legitimate children born of the marriage bed then inherit equally, with equal rights of free men. They carry on trade with the greatest diligence. But concerning the private customs of the cities of Italy, and the more particular city and dress of some, and their attitude towards enemies and guests, the passage of the parchment I mentioned earlier speaks; it says this: the Florentines are peaceful; the Lucchese are elegant. The Mantuans are cheap, the Anconitans squalid, the Sienese magnificent, the Milanese wealthy, the Neapolitans luxurious, the Vicentines abundant. The Cremonese are refined, the Neapolitans splendid, the Genoese moderate. The Paduans are middling, the Aretines meagre. The Venetians get by on little; the Pavians are rustic, the Bolognese lavish, the Assisans frugal, the Perugians dainty. The Florentines delight in cheeses, the Lucchese in pears, the Mantuans in beans, the Arminians in ... the Trevisans in frogs, the Cremonese in sausage, the Neapolitans in cabbages, the Genoese in lettuces, the Paduans in little fish, the Picentines in pork, the Perugians in fish, the Pavians in goat and garlic. In dress the Milanese are splendid and the Genoese elegant; the Mantuans are childish, the Neapolitans sumptuous, the Venetians magnificent, the Florentines ridiculous. In forgetting injuries the Lucchese are mild, the Milanese easygoing, the Perugians dissembling, the Fulginates quick to anger. The Modenese are placable, the Sienese magnanimous, the Neapolitans kind. The Ferrarese are obstinate, the Venetians deceitful, the Cremonese open. The Picentines are malicious, the Romans unjust. Towards guests the Calabrians are discourteous, the Lucchese faithful, the Sienese lovable, the Venetians flattering. The Paduans are harsh, the Milanese incautious, the Ferrarese unfriendly, the Mantuans sleek, the Piacentines strict, the Picentines attentive, the Neapolitans kind. The Florentines are forward; the Ptolemenses are kindly, the Sedetani rustic, the Veronese studious, the Pavians rather simple, the Genoese inhospitable, the Parmesans inconstant, the Modenese long-winded. The Neapolitans are inhuman. There follows a description of how each sort of people is in trade: the Florentines are shrewd, the Genoese patient, the Milanese open, the Lucchese faithful, the Venetians splendid, ... cautious. By way of a crown, I will add a most elegant poem by Julius Caesar Scaliger on the present character and customs of the Italians: The Apulian is thirsty, Croton is healthy, the Sicilian crafty, the Tarentine a wool-worker, the Picene greasy, the Ferentanian a rustic, the Umbrian cloudy, the Lombard astute, the Carnian a glutton, the Istrian a drinker, the Illyrian mad, the Ragusan more arrogant than Typhoeus, earth and sea-wind and glory; the Venetian proud in his ancient nobility, who, like the Rhone, eats up the neighbouring fields; the Genoese arrogant and of bad manners; the Pisan a Briton, terrifying to all Ligurians, a stone-dweller, a sea-farer, envious, filthy, starving, foul, an arch-pirate.

units.la: CAPUT XVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVIII.

units.la: Linguae Italorum, quae olim, quae hodie.
units.tr: The languages of the Italians, what they were in former times and what they are today.

units.la: IN Linguis, quarum ab omni aevo ad nostra haec tempora per verum Mundi Occellum, cui post Italia nomen inditum, fuisse creditur usus, quam fieri potest commodissime explicandis, duo scrutandum censeo, quales fuerint olim, quales hodie:
units.tr: Of the languages which, from the earliest age down to our own times, are believed to have been used in that true jewel of the world to which Italy was later given its name, I think two things should be examined, so that they may be explained as conveniently as possible: what they were like in former times, and what they are like today.

units.la: Antiquissimis temporibus, quot Populi, tot fere fuerunt Linguae, quarum aliae
units.tr: In the most ancient times there were almost as many languages as there were peoples, some of which were

units.la: Cis-Tiberinæ (tamquam in Foro Romano vel Capitolio positus, loquor) aliæ TransTiberinæ. Cis-Tiberinæ, facta diligente variorum Scriptorum commissione, aliæ erant Principes, ut quidem ex antiquis constat Monimentis, quales Latina & Græca: aliæ Deincipes, ut Sabina & Campana vel Osca. Sed in Synopsin quæ dixi, quæque sum dicturus, docendi, commodiusque singula explicandi gratia, conjiciam:
units.tr: on this side of the Tiber (I speak as if standing in the Roman Forum or on the Capitol), and others beyond the Tiber. Of those on this side, after careful examination of various writers, some were principal, as is clear from ancient monuments, such as Latin and Greek; others were subordinate, such as Sabine and Campanian or Oscan. But in order to teach and to explain each point more conveniently, I shall set out in a synopsis what I have said and what I am about to say:

units.la: In Linguis, quibus ab omni ævo ad hæc usque tempora usa creditur Italia, commode explicandu, videndum jedulo, quales ex futuris
units.tr: On the languages which Italy is believed to have used from the earliest age down to the present times, to be conveniently explained and carefully examined: what they were like formerly and what they are like now.

units.la: Olim. Alia erant: Cis-Tiberina, eaque; Principes, quales; Latina, in qua perpendenda; Qualitas. Fuit enim Lingua Latina inutio: Rudu, in Vetustæ Scriptura, Pronunciatione. Sterilis. Sterilitati subrentum, petuo Incremento ab: Græcia, Etrusca. Dialecti Ex erant: Tusculana, Lanuvina, Prænestina, Formiana, Mutorum, &c. Græca: Eius Species: Sicula, Tarentina. Deinci-pes, ut: Sabina, Osca, Volsca, Campana, Brutiorum. Trans-Tiberina: Etrusca, cuius Species: Falisca, Rhetuca; Ligurum. Hodie: ubi explicatur, quibus gradibus ad communem Italicam devenitum.
units.tr: Formerly. There were these: on this side of the Tiber, and these were principal, such as Latin, whose quality is to be weighed. For the Latin language was at first rough, in its ancient writing and in its pronunciation; it was barren, and the barrenness was relieved by constant increase from Greece and Etruria. Its dialects were: Tusculan, Lanuvian, Praenestine, Formian, Mutine, and so on. Greek, and its species: Sicilian, Tarentine. Subordinate ones, such as Sabine, Oscan, Volscian, Campanian, and that of the Bruttii. Beyond the Tiber: Etruscan, whose species were Faliscan and Rhaetic; and that of the Ligurians. Today: where it is explained by what steps they came to the common Italian language.

units.la: In Latina Lingua, quam eorum fuisse censeo, qui primi Colonias in hanc Regionem duxerunt, quæque tandem contra alias obtinuit Principatum, duo considerabo, Qualitatem & Dialectos.
units.tr: Of the Latin language, which I think was that of those who first led colonies into this region, and which at last prevailed over the others as principal, I shall consider two things: its quality and its dialects.

units.la: Quod ad Qualitatem: fuit illa initio non solum valde rudis & inculta, verum etiam ieiuna supra modum, & sterilis. Rudiтatem & Incultum pono in ipsis Vocibus, Vetere Scriptura, Pronunciatione. Grammaticum hic non agam. Toti fuerunt in his tradendis alij. Brevibus pauca dicam. Ipsas Veteris Linguæ Voces, quas Carmenta, Fauni, Vates, Salij, hisque proximi, iunt loquuti, collegerunt industria singulari ex M. Terentio Varrone, Sex. Pompeio Festo, Nonio Marcello, reliquaque Grammaticorum Turba, Virorum Eruditorum non pauci. Ego ad Ennij mei Annales nonnullam etiam Symbolam contuli, & Catalogum, præter aliarum, feci quæ quondam Salius in usu. Studij quoque nonnihil, aliud tamen agendo, locavi in colligendis reliquis; quæ inventæ mihi immani numero, sed in privatorem meum usum, & Filiorum, qui fortean ijs aliquando, me Nuces has abjiciente, non invidebunt lucem. Merentur sane in ijs infinitæ, quæ cum summo reip. literariæ bono in usum revocentur. Scripturam Veterem huius Linguæ diversam ab Nova fuisse, partim Quantitate, additis detractive nunc Litteris, nunc Syllabis; partim Qualitate in commutatione Vocalium, Consonantium, Diphthongorum, docet insigni Methodo (ne cui tuam invideam laudem) V. CL. Franciscus Sylburgius, ad Dionysij Halicarnassæi Historiam Romanam: quem operæ pretium est, Lector, harum Rerum curiosior, adeat. Specimen Vocum Scripturæ Veteris præbet, præter xii Tabularum fragmenta, in quibus Antiquitati suæ restituendis varie ab variis laboratum, præterque Fœdera inter Romanos variosque Populos, Columna Rostrata, quæ Duilio ob Primam de Pœnis Victoriam Navalem in Foro ab S. P. Q. R. posita, quæque hodie visitur in Capitolio, cum Inscriptione, qua nihil antiquius, ob Vetustatem fere obliterata:
units.tr: As to its quality: at first it was not only very rough and uncultivated but also excessively meagre and barren. I locate its roughness and lack of cultivation in the words themselves, in the ancient writing, and in pronunciation. I shall not treat grammar here; others have devoted themselves entirely to that. I will say a few things briefly. The words of the old language, which Carmenta, the Fauns, the seers, the Salii and those nearest to them are said to have spoken, have been gathered with singular diligence from M. Terentius Varro, Sextus Pompeius Festus, Nonius Marcellus and the rest of the crowd of grammarians, along with not a few learned men. I too have added some contribution to my Ennius's Annals, and have made a catalogue, besides other things, of what the Salii once used. I also gave some effort, though occupied with other business, to gathering the rest, which I found in immense numbers; but these are for my private use and that of my sons, who perhaps will not grudge them the light when I one day set these nuts aside. Indeed, infinitely many of them deserve to be brought back into use for the great good of the literary commonwealth. That the ancient writing of this language differed from the new, partly in quantity, by additions and subtractions of letters or syllables, and partly in quality, by the change of vowels, consonants and diphthongs, is shown with remarkable method (lest I grudge anyone his due praise) by the most distinguished Franciscus Sylburgius, in his notes on Dionysius of Halicarnassus' Roman History; a reader more curious about these matters should consult him. He gives a specimen of the ancient writing, besides fragments of the Twelve Tables, over which various people have variously laboured to restore their antiquity; and besides the treaties between the Romans and various peoples, the Rostral Column, which the Senate and People of Rome set up in the Forum for Duilius's first naval victory over the Carthaginians, and which is seen today on the Capitol, with an inscription, than which nothing is more ancient, though almost obliterated by age:

Lucius... the consul Gaius Duilius... first... fleet and... first ships... won... the Carthaginian fleet... by the sea... the consul Gaius Duilius with his allies... seven ships and thirty... captured... the number of captives... the booty... the bronze... the naval spoils... given to the people of Rome, from the Carthaginians...

units.la: 30 Testatur Polybius, gravis inprimis Auctor, qui cum Africano Superiore vixit, se, quo tempore Historiam Romanam contexuit, vix unum aut alterum Romæ invenire potuisse; qui, quantumvis Antiquitatis curiosus, l'œdera quædam inter Romanos & Carthaginenses vetustissimis illis concepta verbis intelligeret, ac sibi tunc eam rem scribenti interpretaretur. Legitur etiam apud Quintilianum, Carmina Saliorum, quæ dicebantur ab ipso Numa compósita, novissimis Reip. temporibus vix ab suis quidem Sacerdotibus satis intellecta fuisse; tanta scilicet Antiquarum Vocum, & tunc pene obsoletarum, erant obscuritate involuta. De Vetere eiusdem Linguæ Pronunciatione multa, solide, ut solet, notat V. CL. Iustus Lipsius libello aureo de Recta Lingua Latina Pronunciatione: cuius Scrinia,
units.tr: 30 Polybius bears witness, an especially weighty author, who lived with Africanus the Elder, that when he composed his Roman History he could scarcely find one or two people in Rome who could understand certain treaties between the Romans and the Carthaginians, drawn up in the most ancient words, though they were very curious about antiquity, and who could interpret them for him while he was writing. It is also read in Quintilian that the Songs of the Salii, which were said to have been composed by Numa himself, were scarcely understood even by their own priests in the last times of the Republic; so thoroughly were they wrapped in the obscurity of ancient words, by then almost obsolete. Concerning the ancient pronunciation of the same language, much is noted soundly, as is his habit, by the most distinguished Justus Lipsius in his golden little book On the Correct Pronunciation of the Latin Language; whose storehouses,

units.la: 40 ad quæ Litteratori cuicumque Aditus, non compilabo. Iam Sterilitatem & inopiam Latinæ, ut aliarum consuevit Linguarum, immensam in ipsis incunabulis fuisse, extra omnem est controversiam. Probare posset hoc hodieque variis Argumentis, præcipue vero institutA cum Græca, Germanica, aliisque comparatione, vel mediocriter in iis versatus. Multa proferet Græcus, multa Germanus; ad quæ prorsus, tamquam elinguis, obmutesceret Latinus. Quæ stabilire non huius est loci. Rudis ille Horror, qui Linguæ recens ortæ adhæsit, diuque mansit, detersus est paulatim primo à Poëtis, Ennio, Pacuvio, Plauto; mox ab aliis magis magis, ab Historiographis inquam & Annalium Concinnatoribus; postremo studiosissime ab Oratoribus, palmam ferente M. Tullio, de quo Plinius, Sixtus, alii:
units.tr: 40 to which any literate person may have access, I shall not plunder. That the barrenness and poverty of Latin, as of other languages, was immense in its very cradle, is beyond all controversy. One could prove this even today by various arguments, especially by comparison with Greek, German and other languages, if one is at all versed in them. The Greek would bring forward much, and the German much; against which the Latin, as if tongueless, would be utterly struck dumb. These matters are not for this place to establish. That rude roughness which clung to the newly born language and remained for a long time was gradually wiped away: first by the poets, Ennius, Pacuvius and Plautus; then more and more by others, I mean the historians and compilers of annals; and lastly most diligently by the orators, with Marcus Tullius bearing off the palm, on whom see Pliny, Sixtus and others.

units.la: 50 adeo ut Augusti principatu Latinus Sermo elegantia sua & nitore gravida laboraret: a quo tempore magna ipsi rursus adnasci cœpit Scabrities, quia de re suo loco plura. Sterilitati obviam iam magnis viribus mitto, vel Novis quotidie, ut fieri solet, excogitatis Vocibus: vel facta ab Conregionalibus cum Græcis, tum Etruscis aliisque mutuatione. Novarum Vocum Excogitatio (præterquam quod Vulgo magna confuerit hic esse libertas) imprimis fuisse legitur penes viros, qui in Re vel Publica, vel Litteraria Principes, ad concilandum Novæ Proli maius pondus, solidioremque auctoritatem. Exempla quis me posset? Scribit M. Terentius Varro lib. iv de L L. ab Latino Rege confictum esse Vocabulum Negligere: Memoriæ prodit idem, ab Scaligero emendatior, Ennium Vocem excogitasse Caesari. De Ennio, de Catone, de Se quoque Horatius, Attem scribens Poeticam: — Ego quæ adquirere pauca, Si possem, invideor? quum Lingua Catonis & Ennii Sermonem patrium ditavere, & nova rerum Nomina protulerint. — —
units.tr: 50 So that under the principate of Augustus the Latin style, pregnant with its elegance and polish, was at its height; from which time a great roughness began to grow back upon it, of which more in its proper place. I now set about remedying the barrenness with great force, either by new words devised every day, as usually happens, or by borrowing from neighbouring peoples, both the Greeks and the Etruscans and others. The invention of new words (apart from the fact that commonly there is great licence here) is read to have belonged above all to men who were leaders in public affairs or in literature, so as to lend greater weight and more solid authority to the new offspring. What examples could I give? Marcus Terentius Varro writes in book 4 of On the Latin Language that the word "negligere" was coined by the Latin king; he also records, in Scaliger's more correct text, that Ennius devised the word "Caesari". Of Ennius, of Cato, and of himself too, Horace writes in the Art of Poetry: "Should I be envied if I could add a few words, when the language of Cato and Ennius enriched our native speech and brought forth new names for things?"

units.la: Non his addam, quæ florente iam Lingua, finxerint cum aliorum Imperatores ipsi, Augustus reliquique, de quibus abunde Suetonius: qui etiam de Claris commentans Grammaticis, memoriæ prodit, quum Pomponius, eius Artis Professor, Verbum quoddam Tiberii Principis reprehenderet, C. Atteium Capitonem I. C. affirmasse, & illud Latinum esse, &, si non esset, futurum esse ob Cæsaris auctoritatem & gratiam: ad hoc autem Pomponium subridendo repulisse: Iam inde mentitur Capito: Tu enim o Cæsar Civitatem Hominibus dare potes; Verba & Ipsum Linguam non potes. Quod ad Mutuationem, Latinos Veteres summa Vocum inopia laborantes, ab Confinalibus, maxime vero Græcis, infinita sumsisse iam est certum, ut etiam quosdam scripserint Latinam olim Linguam eamdem fere fuisse cum Græca, Declinatione parum mutata. Conferendæ, præter Dionysium Halicarnassæum lib. i. extremo, tristes Verrii Flacci vel Pompei Festi apud Paullum Diaconum, quæ ex inmani imperant Naufragio, Tabulæ. Græca, inquit Varro lib. iv de L L. ab Scaligero emendatus, fingit Latium: addens, dicis gratia, Ovum, Bulbum: Græcis enim hæc ᾠὸν, βολβός. Adhuc inveniuntur item Lana & Purpura; quæ Græcis ἄνθος, Doribus ἀᾶς, & πορφύρα. Plura quis petit: Dabo; non tamen omnia; sed de quibus controvertitur: dabo, inquam, ut pareat, frustra esse Varronem. Verrium Flaccum, Festum, alios, qui nimio Linguæ suæ obcæcati amore, radices in proprio Agro quæsierunt multarum Vocum, quæ pariter originis sunt Græcæ; quod ante omnes animadvertit ad Varronem suum magnus Scaliger. Tales sunt, ut per Classes colligam: Deorum quidem, Dis, Δίς, Ζεύς; Ops Dea, Ὀπς Hesychio; Ceres, Ῥέα, eidem, de qua voce vide & paullo post; Flora, Χλωρίς. Hominum autem, & eorum propriæ: Pater, Πατήρ, Mater, Μήτηρ; Frater, Φρᾶτωρ; Nepotes, Νέποδες, quod nisi ipse & fundamentum generis non essent: Levir, Δαήρ; Servus, ἐρῶ; Æolice addito sibilo, ut & Sermo, ἑρμός; Mens à Μέν; Umbilicus, ὀμφαλός; Cruor, Κρυόν; Gaudium, Ταδῶν, prisfcum; Somnus, Sopnus, Ὕπνος; Pæna, Ποινή, à Ποινῶν; Vibices, Ἰώκης, σημαί, Hesychio; Damnum, Dapnum, Δαπάνη; Sufarrus, Σύρραξ, priore duplicata: Gens à Γίνομαι; Populus, Πολύς priore geminata, ut in aliis; Pars à Φαίνω; Fama, Φήμη, Dorice Φαμά; Vis, is, aliis à Βία. Ad Animalia spectant Pecudes, Πεκάδες, quod tonderentur; Fos, Βοῦς: Forda, Φορδάδες, Taurus, Ταῦρος; Equus, ἵππος, mutato P. in Q. ut fit in multis; Ovis, ὄις, Arvum Ἄρνα, Ἄμνος Hesychio; Agnus Ἀμνός; Sus, Ὗς; Porcus, Πόρκος Aristophani: Canis, Κύων, κυνες; Lupus, Λύκος: Vulpes, Valopes, Falœnæ Æolice, Ἀλώπηξ Communiter: Cervus, Κέρας; Cornu, Κέρας: Columbus, Κολυμβός, ab gestu, inquit Scaliger, quem faciunt ea aves: Gallus, Κάλλος pala Galli gallinacei: Inundo, Veteribus Hebundo, χείλεσι: Penna, Πτέρις, Æolice Πέννης: Lutra, Λύτρα. Elementa, quæque inde nata notant Voces, quæ sequuntur: Ignis, Κάλω: Aer, Ἀήρ: Æther, Αἰθήρ: Ventus, Αἰών: Aurora, Αὔρα: Lux, Αὐγή: Crepum, quasi Κνεφαῖος, Κνέφας. Stagnum, Σταγών, quod Aquam continet, neque manare potest, σταγὼν enim Græcis, quod minime rimosum, & fidelitor quid continet. Locus ab Λέχος quod antiquis Græcis latere, unde λάθρα λεχῶ: Angulus, Ἀγκύλος: Humus, χαμαί, unde Humilis, χαμαλές: Colles, Κολῶναι. Rura, Ἀγρός: Pratum: Πεγαία, Dorice Πεγαία: Termini, Τέρματα; Ita, ita Apollonio: Campus, Καμπός, quæ vox Siculis Campus aut Hippodromus. Aurum, ab Αὐγὴς, quod vetus Græcum esse testatur Festus, unde remansit Θησαυρὸς, vel ab ὠσάν, custodire, ut vult Hyspicrates, sic enim legendum pro Hippocrates, apud Festum: Numinus, Νόμισμα: Dos, Δώς; Donum, Δῶρον. Cibos explicant: Panis, Πανὸς, vocabulum Magnæ Græciæ apud Athenæum; Puls, Πολτὸς Athenæo: & hinc Varro lib. iv de L L. Puls ita appellatur, quod ita Græci: Perna, Πτέρνη: Vinum, οἶνος: Herbas: Flos, Χλόη: Viola, Ἴον; ab Ἴος: Cucumis, Κικυός, Rapum vel Rapa, Ῥάφανος: Erafica, Πρασιά· Malva, Μαλάχη: Raudus, Rudis Virga, ῥαβδος. Vestimenta: Vestis, ἐσθης: Rica, ῥῖνος, ῥακος: Calamus, Κάλαμος: Ouxea, ab οκρειος: Pallium, inquit Tertullianus, de corona cap. 111, eis Graecum magis, sed iam penes Latium est: cum Voce Vestis intravit. Aedificia publica privataque: Templum, Τέμενος: Carcer, Καρχαρ: Turris Τυρρις, Τυρος: Termen (cuius vocisulum fuisse notat Varro in aliquot Italiae locis) Τέρμα, Terminus; Domus, Δόμα: Trapetes, ἀπὸ τῶν τραπέζων, Molae Olearia; Atrium, Αἴθριον: Trabes, Τράφη, Ennio Trafax vel Trifax. Suppellectilem denique: Patina, Πατάνη: Catinus, Κύλιξ: Cniugna, Κυλίχνη: Pelvis, Πέλυς: Simpulum, Simpo Antiquis, ab Σίφων: Cacabus, Κάκκαβος, Polluci & Athenaeo, Irpices, Vipices, Hurpices Catoni cap. x ab Ἀρπάξ καὶ Ἁρπαγή: Lectus, ab antiqua voce Αἴκτρον, teste Varrone. Voces Militares sunt; Cohors, χόρτος: Hyperiates apud M. Varronem lib. v. de L. L; Galea, Γαλέα, quod ex felina pelle fierent. γαλῆ enim feles: sic Kuvin, ixnotv, λυκιη, & similia. Cenus, Κάνος: Scutum, Σκύτος quod esset ὠμοβοεινον, Umbones, Ἀμβων. Nec Adiectiva desunt: Magnus, Μέγας: Pinguis, Παχύς: Macer Maxpis, quod Macris longior statura: Pauper, Παύρος, prima reduplicata: Parcus, Παρέχω: Laetus, Λαετος, qui cum corona publice vitulabat: Densus, Δασύς, Vidus, Τυφῶ, Vdor, Αἴθων, Αἴθος Dorice, Lilis communiter. Addam & Verba quaedam: Nisi, Antiquis Gnafis, ὠνεχ' τε γναικης, Otti ab ἐπει, unde ἐπομαι. Fari, Φάναι, unde Φραμί, Nara rare, Antiquis Ζῶ, ἀρ' τὸ ζῶμεν, Legere ἀπὸ τὸ λέγειν, Dicere, δείκνυμι, Docere, δοκεῖν, Disserere, ἀσκητήν: Lacere, Φαύω, Cirere, κίρνημι, Nosere, Antiquis Ginscere, γινώσκειν: Videre, εἶδον: Cernere, κρίνειν: Procare à πρὸς πωγῶν, Mereri, μεῖζον: Petere, πέτομαι, obsoletum: Fallere, Φαλλεῖν: Movere à μοιχεῖα τραχύς: Polor: Angere, ἀγχεῖν, Fremere, ξεμέω, Gemere γόμος, Tremere Τρεμεῖν: Murmurare, μορμύρειν: Arcere, ἀρκεῖν: Pulsare, πάλλειν: Meinere, μείων: Claudere, κλείειν, Liquere, unde Liquare, λείχειν, mutato p. in q. ut in aliis: Errare, ἐρρεῖν; Pitere, πίκειν, πικτήν, Linquere, λείχειν, unde & Lingua: Spargere, σπείρειν: Pasere, πάσχειν vel βόσκειν: Alligare, ἀμελγειν: Serere, σπεῖραι: vel ιπνη: Ruminare ab ρυκάω, Pinsere, Pisere Antiquis, πίσσειν: ilare, χαίρειν: Hiscere, χάσκειν: Frustrari, Φρεστάω, Φρυκτωρ: Fragere antiquum pro Frangere, Φρεγνυμι, unde Φραγμα. Nec sequentes praetermittendae voculae: Ferme, ἀχεῖ: At ab ἀπό: Am in Ambire, Ambactus, & similibus ab ἀμφί. Tales sunt Voces, quas cum aliis Latini Veteres, penuria presti, ex Graecorum Confinalium, Dorica Aeolicaque Dialecto plurimum utentium, fontibus in Latinos rivulos derivarunt: de quibus olim scripsit Hyperiates, ab M. Terentio Varrone in Libris de LL. Agellio lib. xvi. Noctium Atticarum, Pompeio Festo in Voce Aurum, ubi vitiose est Hipoeciates, cum honore laudatus. Neque solum Voces Latini multas ab Graecis mutuo sumserunt; verum etiam Characteres ipsos. Plinius lib. vii. nat. hist. cap. lvi de Litterarum agens Inventoribus: In Latium, inquit, eas attulerunt Pelasgi. Testatur idem indicati a Vnde fuit Latinus Characteres Libri cap. lviii, Veteres Graeci easdem pene fuisse, cum iis, quae tunc erant Latinae: addens, indicio esse Delphicam Tabulam antiqui aeris, quae eius aevo adhuc Romae servabatur in Palatio, dono Principum Minervae dicata, in Bibliotheca, cum Inscriptione tali:
units.tr: I will not add those words which the emperors themselves, Augustus and the others, coined when the language was already flourishing; Suetonius writes about these at length. In his book on famous grammarians he also records that when Pomponius, a professor of that art, found fault with a certain word of the emperor Tiberius, Gaius Ateius Capito, the jurist, maintained that it was Latin, and that even if it were not, it would become so on account of Caesar's authority and favour. Pomponius replied to this with a smile: Capito is already lying. For you, O Caesar, can give citizenship to men, but you cannot give words and language itself. As for borrowing, it is now certain that the early Latins, suffering from a great poverty of words, took an endless number from their neighbours, especially the Greeks, so that some have even written that the Latin language was once almost the same as Greek, with its inflection little changed. Besides Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 1 at the end, one may compare the sad tables of Verrius Flaccus, or of Pompeius Festus as preserved by Paulus the Deacon, which come from a great shipwreck. Greek, says Varro in book 4 of the De Lingua Latina, as corrected by Scaliger, forms Latin, adding, by way of example, egg, bulb (for the Greeks have ᾠὸν and βολβός). There are also still found wool and purple, which the Greeks call ἄνθος, the Dorians ἀᾶς, and πορφύρα. Who would look for more? I will give you more, though not all, only those about which there is dispute. I give them, I say, so that it may be clear that Varro's work is in vain. Verrius Flaccus, Festus and others, blinded by excessive love of their own language, sought the roots of many words in their own soil, though these words are equally of Greek origin; this was noticed before all others by the great Scaliger, against his Varro. Such words, to gather them by classes: of the gods, Dis (Δίς), Zeus; Ops, goddess (Ὀπς in Hesychius); Ceres (Ῥέα in the same, of which word see also a little later); Flora (Χλωρίς). Of men, and their own kin: father (Πατήρ), mother (Μήτηρ), brother (Φρᾶτωρ), grandsons (Νέποδες, which, were it not for them, would not be the foundation of the family), brother-in-law (Δαήρ), slave (ἐρῶ, with a hissing added in the Aeolic manner, as also in speech, ἑρμός); mind from Μέν; navel (ὀμφαλός); gore (Κρυόν); joy (Ταδῶν, an old form); sleep, sopnus (Ὕπνος); punishment (Ποινή, from Ποινῶν); weals (Ἰώκης, a sign, in Hesychius); loss, dapnum (Δαπάνη); sufarrus (Σύρραξ, the first syllable doubled); clan from Γίνομαι; people (Πολύς, its first syllable doubled as in other words); part from Φαίνω; rumour (Φήμη, in Doric Φαμά); force, of which the genitive is derived by others from Βία. Concerning animals: sheep (Πεκάδες), because they are shorn; ox (Βοῦς); pregnant cows (Φορδάδες); bull (Ταῦρος); horse (ἵππος), the P changed to Q as happens in many words; sheep (ὄις); lamb (Ἄρνα, and Ἄμνος in Hesychius); lamb (Ἀμνός); sow (Ὗς); pig (Πόρκος, in Aristophanes); dog (Κύων, κυνες); wolf (Λύκος); fox, valopes, falaenae (Aeolic forms, commonly Ἀλώπηξ); stag (Κέρας); horn (Κέρας); dove (Κολυμβός), from the diving motion, says Scaliger, which those birds make; cock (Κάλλος, the wattle of the domestic cock); to wet, which the ancients said hebundo (χείλεσι); feather (Πτέρις, in Aeolic Πέννης); otter (Λύτρα). The elements, and the words born from them, follow: fire (Κάλω); air (Ἀήρ); ether (Αἰθήρ); wind (Αἰών); dawn (Αὔρα); light (Αὐγή); twilight, as if from Κνεφαῖος, Κνέφας. Pool (Σταγών), because it holds water and cannot run out, for σταγὼν in Greek means something that is not at all leaky and holds what it is given faithfully. Place from Λέχος, because the ancient Greeks lay hidden, whence λάθρα λεχῶ; corner (Ἀγκύλος); ground (χαμαί), whence low (χαμαλές); hills (Κολῶναι). Fields (Ἀγρός); meadow (Πεγαία, in Doric Πεγαία); boundaries (Τέρματα); so, thus, in Apollonius; plain (Καμπός), a word which the Sicilians use for plain or racecourse. Gold, from Αὐγὴς, which Festus attests is an old Greek word, whence there remains Θησαυρὸς, or from ὠσάν, to guard, as Hyspicrates wishes; for so one must read, instead of Hippocrates*, in Festus. Money (Νόμισμα); dowry (Δώς); gift (Δῶρον). They explain foods: bread (Πανὸς, a word of Magna Graecia in Athenaeus); porridge (Πολτὸς in Athenaeus), and hence Varro in book 4 of the De Lingua Latina: porridge is so called because the Greeks so call it. Ham (Πτέρνη); wine (οἶνος). Of herbs: flower (Χλόη); violet (Ἴον), from Ἴος; cucumber (Κικυός); radish or turnip (Ῥάφανος); leek bed (Πρασιά); mallow (Μαλάχη); rod, rudis, a rod (ῥαβδος). Clothing: garment (ἐσθης); rag (ῥῖνος, ῥακος); reed (Κάλαμος); ox-hide (from οκρειος); cloak: Tertullian, in his De Corona, chapter 3, says that it is more Greek, but it already belongs to Latium, having entered with the word vestis. Public and private buildings: temple (Τέμενος); prison (Καρχαρ); tower (Τυρρις, Τυρος); boundary-post, whose diminutive Varro notes was in use in several places in Italy (Τέρμα, terminus); house (Δόμα); trapeza, from τῶν τραπέζων, the olive mills; atrium (Αἴθριον); beams (Τράφη, in Ennius trafax or trifax). Finally, household goods: dish (Πατάνη); bowl (Κύλιξ); small cup (Κυλίχνη); basin (Πέλυς); ladle, simpo to the ancients, from Σίφων; cauldron (Κάκκαβος, in Pollux and Athenaeus), irpices, vipices, hurpices in Cato chapter 10, from Ἀρπάξ and Ἁρπαγή; bed, from the old word Αἴκτρον, as Varro attests. Military words: cohort (χόρτος); hyperiates, in Marcus Varro, book 5 of the De Lingua Latina; helmet (Γαλέα), because they were made of cat-skin, for γαλῆ means cat; so also kuvin, ixnotv, lykiē, and similar words. Cenus (Κάνος); shield (Σκύτος), because it was ὠμοβοεινον, of raw hide; bosses (Ἀμβων). Nor are adjectives lacking: great (Μέγας); fat (Παχύς); lean (Maxpis), because it is longer in stature than Macris; poor (Παύρος, the first syllable doubled); sparing (Παρέχω); joyful (Λαετος), because with a garland they publicly celebrated the calf; dense (Δασύς); empty (Τυφῶ); water (Αἴθων, Αἴθος in Doric); smooth (Lilis, commonly). I will add some verbs too: unless, from the ancient Gnafis, ὠνεχ' τε γναικης; otti from ἐπει, whence ἐπομαι. To speak (Φάναι, whence Φραμί); to heap (ἀρ' τὸ ζῶμεν), from the ancient Ζῶ; to read, from the verb λέγειν; to say (δείκνυμι); to teach (δοκεῖν); to discuss (ἀσκητήν); to tear (Φαύω); to mix (κίρνημι); to know, in the ancients Ginscere (γινώσκειν); to see (εἶδον); to sift (κρίνειν); to beg, from πρὸς πωγῶν; to earn (μεῖζον); to seek (πέτομαι), now obsolete; to deceive (Φαλλεῖν); to move, from μοιχεῖα, rough; to choke (ἀγχεῖν); to roar (ξεμέω); to groan (γόμος); to tremble (Τρεμεῖν); to murmur (μορμύρειν); to ward off (ἀρκεῖν); to strike (πάλλειν); to diminish (μείων); to shut (κλείειν); to lick, whence to liquefy (λείχειν), the p changed to q as in other words; to wander (ἐρρεῖν); to drink (πίκειν, πικτήν); to leave (λείχειν), whence also tongue; to scatter (σπείρειν); to feed (πάσχειν or βόσκειν); to bind (ἀμελγειν); to sow (σπεῖραι, or ιπνη); to ruminate, from ρυκάω; to pound, in the ancients pisere (πίσσειν); to be cheerful (χαίρειν); to gape (χάσκειν); to frustrate (Φρεστάω, Φρυκτωρ); to break, the old form of frangere (Φρεγνυμι), whence φραγμα. Nor should the following little words be passed over: nearly (ἀχεῖ); at, from ἀπό; am in ambire, ambactus and similar words, from ἀμφί. Such are the words which the early Latins, lacking their own, drew from the springs of the Greeks, their neighbours who made much use of the Doric and Aeolic dialects, into Latin streams. Of these Hyperiates wrote long ago, as Varro in his books on the language mentions; Agellius, book 16 of the Attic Nights, praised them with honour, and Pompeius Festus in the word aurum, where the text is corrupt, reads Hipoeciates. Nor did the Latins borrow only many words from the Greeks; they borrowed the letters themselves too. Pliny, book 7 of the Natural History, chapter 56, speaking of the inventors of letters, says: The Pelasgians brought them into Latium. The same author, in chapter 58 of the book on whence the Latin letters came, attests that the ancient Greek letters were almost the same as those then in use among the Latins, adding as evidence the Delphic tablet of ancient bronze, which in his time was still kept at Rome on the Palatine, dedicated to Minerva as a gift of the princes, in the library, with the following inscription:

units.la: NAVCIKPATES TICAMENOV AΘENAIOC KOPAI KAI AΘENAI ANEΘEKEN.
units.tr: Naucrates, son of Timamenus, an Athenian, dedicated this to the maiden Athena and to Athena. [ΝΑΥΚΡΑΤΕΣ ΤΙΜΑΜΕΝΟΥ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΟΣ ΚΟΡΑΙ ΚΑΙ ΑΘΗΝΑΙ ΑΝΕΘΕΚΕΝ]

units.la: Ita & in Veteribus Tetradrachmis: ΑΘΕΙ. pro Α'θῆναι.
units.tr: So too on the old tetradrachms: ΑΘΕΙ, for Ἀθῆναι [Α'θῆναι].

units.la: Sic ab Graecis, Australioris Italiae quondam Incolis, Incrementum, Linguae suae quaesierunt Veteres Latini: Mutuationem quoque factam monui ab Etruscis, ad dextram Tiberis ripam longe lateque habitantibus: quos si constans doctorum virorum consensus vere tradat, Aramaea vel Syriaca usos priscis temporibus Lingua, non errarit meo iudicio, si quis censeat Originimis Tuscia esse Voces Latinas, quae hodieque in Lingua Syriaca suas habent radices. Earum quum vastum numerum aliquando collegissem, vastiorem multo monstravit mihi V. C. L. Guilielmus Coddaeus, Hebraicae Linguae in Academia Lugduno-Batava Professor, Collega mihi amicissimus. Operaepretium me facturum arbitror si nonnullam earum partem Meditationibus meis Cosmographicis, Loco Digressionem hanc non aversante, adiecripsi. Notandum in primis, quum Romani Veteres, uti ipsorum docent Historiae, Sacrorum ritus & caerimonias ab Etruscis, quos, Religionis ad superstitionem usque observ-
units.tr: In this way the ancient Latins drew the growth of their language from the Greeks, who were once inhabitants of southern Italy. I have also pointed out that they borrowed from the Etruscans, who lived widely and far along the right bank of the Tiber. If the constant agreement of learned men truly hands down that in early times they used the Aramaic or Syriac language, I think I would not be wrong if someone judged that the Latin words of Tuscan origin, which even today have their roots in the Syriac language, are such. When I had once gathered a large number of them, the most distinguished Guilielmus Coddaeus, professor of Hebrew at the Academy of Leiden and my dearest colleague, showed me a far larger number. I think I shall be doing something worthwhile if I add some part of them to my Cosmographical Meditations, in a place where this digression is not out of place. It should be noted first that the ancient Romans, as their histories teach, learned the rites and ceremonies of sacred things from the Etruscans, whom they observed with a religious devotion bordering on superstition

units.la: Eee obseruantissimos, Confinales ad alteram Tiberis ripam habebant, didicerint, missis etiam ad ipsos huius rei gratia singulis annis quibusdam suis iuvenibus: non mirum esse, multa quoque Deorum Dearumque Nomina una cum iis, ex Etruria Romam migrasse. Exempla suppeditant: Ianus, primus Vini plantator, ab יין, quod Vinum; Saturnus, ab סתר, abscondere, latere, Latini licet avide vocem hanc arripuerint, interpretantes tamen Latium dixerunt, ipsius autem Coniugem Latiam, ut videre est apud Agellium lib. xiii. cap. xxi; Terram denique & Patrimonium eius, quae Saturnia Tusce, Latium Vesta, ab אשתן, Ignis, Syro-Chaldaice: Cybele, ab קבלה, ab receptaculo, inquit Postellus, totius Naturae: Iovis antique, Iupiter, יהוה: Apello, ἀ λεξιας, obscurus est in Ecfatis, אפתח. & responsis: אפלה & אפל, Caligo, obscuritas, tenebrae; alias פלא, occultum esse, item mirabile, הפליא, mirificum fuit: Sol fortean à perpetuo ipsius adiccensu, à verbo סלל, adscendere, elevare; sic Ἡλιος Graecis, ab עלה, quod item adscendere: Luna, ab לוח, pernoctare, vel לנכה ab Alborc suo: Mercurius, venditor, negociator: מכר, vendere, quod Latini ר interponentes Mercari dicunt. Pallas, quae Virgilio Armipotens, Belli Praeses, forte à פלס, quod vibrare, agitare, quatere: Mars, Sabinum, מהרם; sic Ἀρης, ה-ם, destruere: πέλιμπῶ enim, id est Vrbis expugnanor: Aeolus, fortallis ab איל, Fortitudo, potentia; אילי, Aries: Adonis, filius Veneris, quid si ex ארון, Dominus? Ceres (de qua & in Graecis) Fruges reperit, ideoque spiceam coronam gestare solita: נריש Spicam virentem significat: vel ab הריש Arare: נ & ה saepe permutantur: Alii ab זרע trahunt, quod ferere, seminare, זרע Semen: Nonnulli ab כרש venter, quod haec Dea omnia, veluti ex Viero, pariat & procreet. Parca fortean à פרק abrumpere, rescindere: פרך alioquin Durtiem notat. Aesculapius ex quorumdam sententia ab voce הלף, innovare, instaurare, redintegrare, quod Mortuos solitus sit in Vitam revocare: Isis, אישה uxorem, feminam, Mulierem significat: Osiris, cui Bos sacrificabatur, fortallis ab שור, quae vox Bovem sonat: potest alioquin quis Μαχαιρίτα dicere ex אשר quod beatum praedicare. Musa, ab מוש, Hebraice vel Chaldaice perscrutari, investigare, indagare. Heros Etymon varie traditur: ארנא Chaldaeis idem est, quod ארץ apud Hebraeos, Terra: Heroes enim Veteribus erant Viri nobiles, qui Mortales quum essent, & Terra quasi geniti, rerum tamen gestarum magnitudine quamproximead Deos accederent; qualis habitus, praeter alios, Romulus, sic fortean nominatus ab רם, excelsus, sublimis, clarus; vel רמה, projicere, quod Avunculi iussu expositus & ad Tiberim cum Fratre Remo fuerit projectus. An ab hoc, ut volunt plerique, Roma vel potius ab רמה, Hasta, Lancea? Hinc Romani, Hastati; ut Quirites idem ab voce Sabina Quiris; quam Latini Hastam vocant. Quid si Roma ab רמם, exaltari, elevari? Videntur autem Dii, ex Etruria Romam cum suis Nominibus migrantes, nonnulla quoque, Sacris ibi peragundis secum abstulisse. Hinc, praeter quae non occurrunt, Sali Sacerdotes, ab בלל, exaltare, elevare: Mola, Far tostum & Sale conspersum, forte ab מלה, sal: Simpulum, Vas in Romanorum Sacris usurpari solitum. ab כפל, Phiala, Lagena, Hydria; unde Sephel, Simpel, Simpulum. Ad ea, quae Hominum, pergo: Rex, רנם, Princeps Maior: Nepos quibusdam, quod nihil possit, vel non Pes suae Familiae; forte à נפש, quae vox saepe pro libidine & desiderio animi capitur; vel ex נאף adulterare vel Adulterium committere: Nebulo, נבל, homo vilis, abiectus, stultus, improbus, perditus: Stultus, stultus, ut quidam volunt, ex סכל, pro quo & כסיל: Axilla, אזילה: Quae Animalium Camelus, נמל; Taurus, תור Chaldaice, pro quo Hebr. שור, Bos, Taurus, luvencus: Capra, עפר, Hinnulus, filius Cervi vel Capreae: Aranea, ארג, texere: Turtur, תור, gemi-natione facta: Corvus, κόραξ, קדן. luvandis Mortalibus faciunt Sicera, שכר. Potus inebriins; Byssus, כרפס; Sindon, סדין Linteum tam nocturnum, quam diurnum: Galbanum הלבנה חלב. Lac; הלב Pinguedo; Adeps; Vestimenti genus ab Albore: Saccus שק: Pelagus, פלג, Ager, אכר Agricola: Pratum, פרא multiplicare, fructificare: vel פרה crescere. Pyrus, פרי, generale Nomen Hebraeis, ad omnes Fructus pertinens: Taxus תחש: Nux לוז, mutato L in N, ut Lympha, Nympha: Hyssopus, אזוב: Casia, קציעה, nomen Aromatis: Canna, Arundo, קנה. Item Palatium, fortean ex פלט, evadere, eripere se: locus Perfugii בלטין: Turris, nescio an ab תור, explorare, scrutari, investigare: quod ex Turris maxima explorandi commoditas: an potius ab צור, quod Saxum, Petra: item Fortitudo, Moenia, מחנים. Vallia nam ה pura putaque adspiratio est, saepeque cruditi, Scala, סלם: Pala, Pars Anuli cava, qua Gemma vel Lapillus inseritur & quasi abscon-ditur, ditur, פלא, abscondere, latere: Fucus, פוך, Stibium, cuius ad venustandos oculos peculiaris usus: Falx, פרך: Iubilaeus, Iubilare, יובל. Monita מנה, numerare: Arrabo, ערב, spondere, idem iubere, oppignorare. Nenia, נהה queri, lamentari. Est & nonnihil, ut cum Grammaticis loquar, Adiectivorum: Gibbosus, גבן: Fortis, זר, Petra, Saxum, & metaphorice Fortis: Lassus, לאה, laborare, fatigari, molestè ferre: Nanus vel Gnarus, ערם, callidum esse: Amarum, מרה: Simius, סמל, Simulacrum, Sculptile, Idolum. Sunt & Verba quaedam: Mußiere, מסך: Latere, לאש, operire, tegere: Frangere, Fragere, פרק, conterere, lacerare, confringere: Labi, לבש, ruere, cadere. Agmen claudat vox Olim, non dubium quin ab עולם, quod Seculum, Perpetuum, Tempus Longum.
units.tr: most scrupulously. The Etruscans had neighbours on the other bank of the Tiber, and the Romans learned from them, sending some of their young men to them each year for this purpose. It is no wonder that many names of gods and goddesses also migrated from Etruria to Rome along with those rites. They offer examples: Ianus, the first planter of the vine, from יין [yayin], which means Vinum, wine; Saturnus, from סתר [satar], to hide away, to lie hidden. The Latini eagerly seized this word, though they interpreted it as Latium, and his consort as Latiam, as may be seen in Agellius, book 13, chapter 21. Then the earth and its patrimony, which the Tuscans call Saturnia, the Latins call Latium Vesta, from אשתן [ashtan], fire, in Syro-Chaldaic. Cybele, from קבלה [qabbalah], a receptacle, says Postellus, of all nature. Iovis, in older form Iupiter, from יהוה [YHWH]. Apello, from ἀ λεξιας [a-lexias], is obscure in his pronouncements and responses; from אפלה [aphelah] and אפל [aphel], darkness, obscurity, shadows; otherwise פלא [pala], to be hidden, and also to be wonderful, הפליא [hiphli], to be marvellous. Sol, perhaps from his constant ascent, from סלל [salal], to ascend, to raise up; so the Greeks call him Ἥλιος [Helios], from עלה [alah], which likewise means to ascend. Luna, from לוח [luach], to spend the night, or from לנכה [lenakah], from its Alborc. Mercurius, a seller, a merchant, from מכר [mekar], to sell; the Latins, inserting an ר, say Mercari, to trade. Pallas, who in Virgil is armipotent, president of war, perhaps from פלס [palas], to brandish, to shake, to strike. Mars, a Sabine word, from מהרם [mahoram]; so Ἄρης [Ares], from ה-ם [h-m], to destroy; for πέλιμπω [pelimpo], that is, a stormer of cities. Aeolus, perhaps from איל [ayil], strength, power; אילי [ayili], rams. Adonis, son of Venus; what if he is from אדון [adon], Lord? Ceres (who is also found among the Greeks) discovered grain, and so was accustomed to wear a crown of ears of corn; נריש [nerish] signifies a green ear of corn; or from הריש [harish], to plough, since נ and ה are often interchanged. Others derive her from זרע [zera], to sow, and זרע [zera], seed. Some from כרש [karash], belly, because this goddess, as from a womb, bears and produces all things. Parca, perhaps from פרק [perek], to break off, to cut away; פרך [perech], however, means hardship. Aesculapius, in the opinion of some, from the word הלף [halaph], to renew, restore, make whole again, because he was accustomed to call the dead back to life. Isis, from אישה [ishah], which means wife, woman, a female. Osiris, to whom an ox was sacrificed, perhaps from שור [shor], a word that means ox; otherwise one could call him Μακαρίτης [Makaritēs] from אשר [asher], to pronounce blessed. Musa, from מוש [mush], in Hebrew or Chaldaic, to search out, to examine, to investigate. The etymology of Heros is variously given: ארנא [arna] among the Chaldaeans is the same as ארץ [eretz] among the Hebrews, earth. For the Heroes were, among the ancients, noble men who, though mortal and as if born of the earth, yet by the greatness of their deeds drew as near as possible to the gods. Such a status belonged, among others, to Romulus, who was perhaps named from רם [ram], high, lofty, illustrious, or from רמה [ramah], to cast away, because by his uncle's order he was exposed and cast into the Tiber with his brother Remus. Is Roma, as most suppose, derived from this, or rather from רמה [ramah], a spear, a lance? Hence the Romani were the Hastati; and in the same way the Quirites take their name from the Sabine word Quiris, which the Latins call a spear. What if Roma comes from רמם [ramam], to be exalted, to be raised up? It seems that the gods, migrating from Etruria to Rome with their names, also carried away with them some things for performing the sacred rites there. Hence, besides those that do not occur, the Sali, priests, from בלל [balal], to exalt, to raise up; Mola, roasted spelt sprinkled with salt, perhaps from מלה [melah], salt; Simpulum, a vessel customarily used in Roman sacred rites, from כפל [kaphal], a bowl, a flask, a jug, whence Sephel, Simpel, Simpulum. Turning to the terms for human beings: Rex, from רנם [rnm], a greater chief or prince; Nepos, as some think, because he can do nothing, or because he is not the foot of his family, perhaps from נפש [nephesh], a word often taken for lust and the desire of the mind, or from נאף [naaf], to commit adultery. Nebulo, from נבל [nabal], a base, abject, foolish, wicked, lost man. Stultus, foolish, as some hold, from סכל [sakal], for which there is also כסיל [kesil]. Axilla, אזילה [azilah]. Of the animals: Camelus, from גמל [gamal]; Taurus, Chaldaic תור [tor], for which the Hebrew is שור [shor], ox, bull, steer; Capra, from עפר [afar]; Hinnulus, the young of a stag or roe deer; Aranea, from ארג [arag], to weave; Turtur, from תור [tor], with the doubling made by gemination; Corvus, κόραξ [korax], קדן [qadan]. To help mortals they make Sicera, שכר [shekar], strong drink, an intoxicating drink. Byssus, כרפס [karpas]; Sindon, סדין [sadin], linen cloth, used by night as well as by day. Galbanum, הלבנה [halbanah], from חלב [chalab], milk; הלב [helev], fat, grease; a kind of garment named from its whiteness. Saccus, שק [saq]. Pelagus, פלג [peleg]; Ager, אכר [ikar], a farmer. Pratum, פרא [para], to multiply, to make fruitful; or פרה [parah], to grow. Pyrus, פרי [peri], the general Hebrew word applying to all fruits. Taxus, תחש [tachash]. Nux, לוז [loz], with L changed to N, as in lympha, nympha. Hyssopus, אזוב [ezov]. Casia, קציעה [qetsiah], the name of an aromatic. Canna, a reed, קנה [qaneh]. Likewise Palatium, perhaps from פלט [palat], to escape, to snatch oneself away: a place of refuge, בלטין [baltin]. Turris: I do not know whether it is from תור [tor], to spy out, to search, to investigate, since from a tower there is the greatest convenience for exploring; or rather from צור [tsur], which means rock or stone, as well as strength. Moenia, city walls, מחנים [mechanim]. Since ה is a pure and light breathing, and is often dropped, Vallum ... Scala, סלם [sullam]. Pala, the hollow part of a ring in which a gem or stone is set and so, as it were, hidden, from פלא [pala], to hide, to conceal. Fucus, פוך [puch], stibium, whose special use is for beautifying the eyes. Falx, פרך [perek]. Iubilaeus, Iubilare, from יובל [yobel]. Monita, from מנה [mana], to count. Arrabo, from ערב [arab], to pledge, the same as to order, to pawn. Nenia, from נהה [nahah], to lament, to mourn. There is also a little of adjectives, to speak as the grammarians do: Gibbosus, from גבן [gaban], hunchbacked; Fortis, from זר [zar], a rock, a stone, and metaphorically strong; Lassus, from לאה [la'ah], to labour, to be wearied, to bear with difficulty; Nanus or Gnarus, from ערם [aram], to be cunning; Amarum, from מרה [marah], bitter; Simius, from סמל [semel], an image, a carved thing, an idol. There are also some verbs: Mußiere, from מסך [masakh], to cover; Latere, from לאש [la'ash], to cover over, to hide; Frangere, Fragere, from פרק [perek], to crush, to tear, to break in pieces; Labi, from לבש [labash], to fall, to collapse. The word Olim closes the list; there is no doubt it is from עולם [olam], age, eternity, a long time.

units.la: Hactenus de Latii Sermonis Qualitate, sequitur, ut de Dialectis pauca dicam. Eas fuisse censeo Tusculanam, Lanuvinam, Praenestinam, Formianam, Tarracinensem, Marsam, & si quae fuerint aliae. Latina quidem erant (nam qui iis utebantur, Latii erant Populi) sed peculiares quasdam ab aliis habebant Voces, quarum nonnullas laudant Grammatici: Tusculana leguntur apud M. Terentium Varronem lib. v. de LL. & Sex. Pompeium Festum lib. xv, Triatrus, Quinquatrus, Sevatrus, Septimatrus; Festa sic dicta, quod post diem tertium, quintum, sextum, septimum Idus. Ab Tusculano item Struppus, teste Festo in ea voce, vocatur, quod in Pulvinari ponitur Castoris. Citat quoque Varro lib. v. Verba haec solemnia ex Tusculanis Sacris: VINVM NOVVM NE VEHATVR IN VRBEM, ANTEQVAM VINALIA KALENTVR. Lanuvini apud Paullum ex Festo Testiculos nominant Nebrundines. Praenestina Voces sunt apud Paullum Nefrones, Testiculi; & Tonguo, Notio. Praenestinos decurtare solitos cum ritu audientium Vocabula Latina constat ex Plauti Truculento, Sc. Mirum videri, ubi Stratilax Servus: Ut Praenestinus Conia est Ciconia.
units.tr: So much for the character of the Latii Sermonis, the Latin language. Next I shall say a little about its dialects. I think these were the Tusculanam, the Lanuvinam, the Praenestinam, the Formianam, the Tarracinensem, the Marsam, and any others there were. They were all Latin (for those who used them were peoples of Latium), but they had certain words peculiar to themselves, and some of these grammarians praise. Tusculan words are read in Marcus Terentius Varro, book 5 on the Latin language, and in Sextus Pompeius Festus, book 15: Triatrus, Quinquatrus, Sevatrus, Septimatrus, festivals so called because they fall after the third, fifth, sixth, or seventh Ides. From Tusculum, too, Festus in that entry records that Struppus is the name given to what is placed on the pulvinar of Castor. Varro also cites from book 5 these solemn words of the Tusculan rites: the new wine must not be brought into the city before the Vinalia fall. The Lanuvians, according to Paulus from Festus, call the testicles Nebrundines. The Praenestine words in Paulus are Nefrones, testicles, and Tonguo, meaning notion. That the Praenestines were accustomed to clip Latin words, to the amusement of their hearers, is established by the Truculentus of Plautus, where the servant Stratilax says, to the wonder of the audience: as the Praenestine says, conia is ciconia.

units.la: Sic Attius Poeta apud Festum: Tammodo inquit Praenestinus, pro Tantummodo, Formianos Tigna, quibus eorum Pons surrectus erat, Sublicae appellasse, colligunt ex Festi Fragmentis in illa Voce docti Viri. Tarracina Numisianam appellabat quamdam uvae speciem, teste Plinio lib. xiiii, cap. ii. Marsis Herna sunt Saxa apud Festum lib. viii, unde Hernici Italiae populi. Notat idem de Sabinis Servius. Quum autem in omnibus Linguis saepe peculiare quid solet esse Feminis, Pueris, Rusticis: quod ad Latinum Sermonem, notat Festus libro xi. Potionem illam, quae Graece Nectar, Communiter autem Murrina dicebatur, ab Mulierilus Murrulam fuisse appellatam. Atta is, inquit Festus, quia Tata est Avi, id est Pater, ut Pueri usurpare solent. Meminit Martialis: Mammas atque Tatas habet Afra, sed ipsa Tatarum Dius & Mammarum Maxima Mamma poteit.
units.tr: So Attius the poet, in Festus: "Tammodo," says the Praenestine, for "tantummodo." The Formians, the men gather from the fragments of Festus under that word, called the beams (tigna) by which their bridge was raised "sublicae." Tarracina called a certain kind of grape "Numisiana," as Pliny testifies in book 14, chapter 2. Herna is the Marsian word for rocks, in Festus book 8, whence the Hernici, an Italian people. Servius notes the same about the Sabines. Since in every language something peculiar is often found among women, children and country folk, Festus notes in book 11 what belongs to the Latin speech. The drink which in Greek is nectar, but commonly called murrina, was named murrula by women. "Atta is," says Festus, "because it is tata, that is, father, of the grandfather," as children are accustomed to use it. Martial mentions it: "The African woman has mammas and tatas, but Dius is the greatest of the tatas, and the great Mamma of the mammas could..."

units.la: De Tata & Mamma plenius in Inferiore Germania. Inbutum est, inquit idem Festus, quod crassiam vel succum bibit: unde Infantibus an velint bibere, dicentes Bu syllaba contenta sunt. Varro Catone, de Liberis educandis: Quum Cibum ac Potionem Buas ac Papas vocent: Matrem, Mammam: Patrem, Tatam. A Papa Papare apud Plautum: Tum Puero dandum, quod papet.
units.tr: More fully on tata and mamma in the Lower Germany section. "Inbutum is," says the same Festus, what drinks a thick juice or broth; whence, when infants are asked whether they want to drink, they are answered with the syllable bu alone. Varro, in Cato, On the Education of Children: "When they call food and drink buas and papas, the mother mamma, the father tata." From papa comes papare in Plautus: "Then the boy must be given what he can eat (papet)."

units.la: Varro lib. vi de LL. ubi monet in pluribus Verbeis A ante E alios ponere, alios non, id est ea quae Diphthongo scribebantur, ab nonnullis simpliciter enunciari, adducis exemplis inter alia, Rusticus, ait, Pappum Mesum non Masum dicunt. Ita enim ea invertenda, pro quae in Vulgatis Pappum Masum, non Mesum. Indicat enim Festus proprie Rusticorum fuisse, Diphthongos non pronunciare. Sic Orum dicebant pro Auro & Orciulas pro Auriculis, teste Festo in Orata. Utitur Catullus: Vel Anseris medullula, vel imula Oricilla.
units.tr: Varro, book 6 On the Latin Language, where he notes that in many words some people put an A before an E and others do not; that is, words which were written with a diphthong were pronounced simply by some. Among other examples he adduces: "Country people," he says, "say Pappum Mesum, not Masum." For so those words should be reversed, for what the printed editions read as "Pappum Masum, not Mesum." Festus indicates that not pronouncing diphthongs was properly a habit of country people. So they said Orum for auro and orciulas for auriculis, as Festus attests under Orata. Catullus uses it: "Either the marrow of a goose or the little ear (oricilla)."

units.la: Paullus ex Festo: Insipere farinulam iacere pultis: inde Dissipare, Obsipare; ut quum Rustici dicunt, Obsipa Pullo Ffiam. Robus Rusticus apud eundem Festum Ros. Rustici, eodem scribente, in Ruminalis, appellabant Hedos subrumos, qui adhuc sub Mammis habebantur. De Hedo scribit & Varro lib. iv. de LL. de Sabinorum loquens Vocabus. It quod illic, apud Sabinos) Fedus, in Latio rure Hedus: quod in Urbe, ut in multis, A addito, Haedus. Solatum, ut apud eumdem legimus, genus Morbi maxime ab Rusticantibus dicitur, cuius meminit etiam Afranius. Syrus, inquit Nonius, ab Graeco Eleel magis tractum est, ἀπὸ τῆς σκιᾶς. Hanc Scopas, Rustici eo nomine Vros vocant. Subrigere, ait idem, significat sufsiam erigere: quo verbo Rustici utuntur, quum tritas Fruges ad ventilandum in areis eriguntur. Alias ne prolixior sim, praetereo. Plura enim huius classis apud Rerum Rusticarum Scriptores.
units.tr: Paulus, from Festus: "Insipere farinulam iacere pultis"; hence dissipare, obsipare, as when country people say obsipa... Robus, a rustic word in the same Festus: Ros, as country people say. The same writer, under Ruminalis, called the kids still kept under the teats hedos subrumos. Varro too writes about hedus in book 4 On the Latin Language, speaking of Sabine words: what among the Sabines is fedus, in the Latin countryside is hedus; in the City, as in many cases, with an A added, it is haedus. Solatum, as we read in the same author, is a kind of illness chiefly named by country folk, which Afranius also mentions. "Syrus," says Nonius, "is drawn more from the Greek eleel" [ἀπὸ τῆς σκιᾶς, from the shade]. Scopas: country folk call it vros by that name. "Subrigere," the same says, means to raise up a sufsia; country folk use this word when threshed grain is lifted in the threshing floors for winnowing. I pass over others, so as not to be too long; there are many more of this kind in the writers on rustic affairs.

units.la: Haec de Lingua Latina, succedit altera Principum, Graeca.
units.tr: So much on the Latin language. Next follows the other principal language, Greek.

units.la: Magnam Partem Vera Priterque Italiae una cum Sicilia aliquando sub nomine Magnae Graeciae cognomen fuisse, multis postea probabo Capite de ea singulari. Cerre quum ducti ex Graecia Coloni multi, ut inquit Festus, magnaque Civitates ibi, ab Tarento, ut notat Servius ad 1. Aeneidos, ad Cumas usque, condidissent, Linguam suam in Solo Italico non tantum retinuerunt (videndus Livius lib. xxxi) verum etiam in penitiorem Italiam longe lateque; arripientibus eam certatim Campanis, diffuderunt adeo ut cum primis Latini infinitas ex illo honte Voces in Arva sua derivarint, quae de re dicium in superioribus abunde. Haec enim est, ex qua non tantum multa Romani sunt mutuati, verum etiam quam sensim plenius exactiusque addidicerunt partim Commerciorum, ut heri solet, iure & beneficio, partim Doctoribus Praeceptia ad eam praeeuntibus. Ab Commerciis, quae ab Imperitoribus celebrari consueverunt, credo factum, ut germanam non fuerint adsequuti Graecorum Pronunciationem. Tetatur ex Festi lib. 1. de verb. significe. Paullus Diaconus, Romanos Veteres, Graecae Linguae nondum adsuetos, Alumentum dixisse pro Lauredonte; Mein pro Nilo; Catamitum pro Ganymede; Alphium pro Alpheo. Gloriatur hic apud Festum lib xv, se pavisse Romanos Graeca lingua: unde Graecos & Graios omnes iam eos vocabant: Contendunt Graeci Graios men o are solent sor: Quod Graeci Lingua longo per tempori tractus Hic patri. . . .
units.tr: For the greater part of true and older Italy, together with Sicily, was once under the name of Magna Graecia, which I shall prove in a later chapter devoted to it. When many colonists led out of Greece, as Festus says, and great cities, from Tarentum as far as Cumae, as Servius notes on Aeneid 1, had been founded there, they retained their language not only on Italian soil (see Livy book 31) but also far and wide in the interior of Italy. The Campanians took it up eagerly and spread it so widely that the Latins in particular drew countless words from that source into their own lands, as was said at length above. For this is the language from which the Romans borrowed not only many words but which they gradually learned more fully and exactly, partly by trade and commerce, as usually happens, partly through teachers who went before them in instruction. I believe that because they learned it from the dealings of the unskilled, they did not attain the genuine Greek pronunciation. This is shown from Festus, book 1, On the Meaning of Words. Paulus the Deacon: the old Romans, not yet accustomed to the Greek language, said Alumentum for Laomedon, Mein for Nilus, Catamitum for Ganymede, Alphium for Alpheus. Here, in Festus book 15, he boasts that he fed the Romans with the Greek language, whence they now called all the Greeks Graeci and Graii: "The Greeks contend that they are Graii..." The rest of the passage is corrupt.

units.la: Suetonius de Claris Grammaticis: Antiquissimi Doctorum quidem & Poeta & Oratores semigraeci erant. Livium & Ennium docuerunt, quo utraque Lingua domi forisque docuisse, adnotatum, et in nihilo piae, quam Graece interpretabantur. Et paullatim adeo invaluit eius Linguae addiscendae studium, ut M. Cato, qui & ipse Ennium habuerat Praeceptorem, in Scena cogi coactus fuerit exclamare, Se non posse pati Graecanicam Urbem. Huius Idiomatis sunt quae Aequipar aliquid tribuunt, nisi Messapii Lingua specialior eius fuerit Dialectus: Επιλογος inquit Stephanus, in Βρυτιων, ἀπὸ Ματαντίας ἢ Ελαιφος ἢ Σικελος, ut Σικέλος in δὲ πει γραστῶν: & hinc Βρεττιος, Latinis Brundisium, de quo suo loco. Sic Ταραντες, ἀπο Ταραντος inquit Athenaeus lib. ii. Μεταγραφεί, ἡ γὰρ πόλιν ὁ πρώτος αὐτῆς, ἡ πόλις τῆς ἐπαλλαγῆς. Deinde: ἡ Ῥωμαῖοι δὲ Ῥῶμα τῆς ἀποικίας. Quum autem variae fuerint Graecae Linguae Dialecti, ut suo loco dicemus, latius constat, & docent Scriptorum, qui in his Italiae locis floruerunt, Monimentia, eam quae cum Graecis Colonis eo invecta, fuisse Dorism. Eius Speciem ad Italiam pertinentes sunt Sicula & Tarentina, ad Graeciam, Terrae quidem Continentis, Laconica, Macedonica, Thessalica, quamvis non tota: Insularum autem, Cretensis & Rhodiana. De Prioribus Sicula & Tarentina hic nonnihil dicendum: de reliquis, in Graecia.
units.tr: Suetonius, On Famous Grammarians: "The most ancient teachers, both poets and orators, were half-Greek. They taught Livius and Ennius, and it is noted that they taught both languages at home and abroad, and in nothing more than in interpreting Greek." And gradually the zeal for learning that language grew so strong that Marcus Cato, who himself had Ennius as his teacher, was compelled on the stage to cry out that he could not bear a Greekified city (Graecanicam Urbem). Of this idiom are those things which some attribute to Aequipar, unless the Messapian language was a more special dialect of it. Stephanus says: Brettians, from Mataneia or Elaphos or Sikelos, as Sikelos in... and hence Brettian, which in Latin is Brundisium, of which in its place. So too Tarantines, from Taras; Athenaeus, book 2, says: "the first ruler of the city" (Metagraphei), "the city of the abandonment." Then: "the Romans from Rome of the colony." Since the dialects of Greek were various, as we shall say in its place, it is established more widely, and the monuments of writers who flourished in these parts of Italy teach that the language carried there by the Greek colonists was Doric. Species of it pertaining to Italy are the Sicilian and the Tarentine; to Greece, of the mainland, Laconian, Macedonian, Thessalian, though not wholly; of the islands, Cretan and Rhodian. Of the former, the Sicilian and Tarentine, something must be said here; of the rest, in the section on Greece.

units.la: Siculam ab Sicilia dictam, extra controversiam est. Sicilia nomen habuit olim, ut alibi moneo, non solum Insula, quae ab Italia exiguo freto separata: verum etiam totum illud quod ab Graecis, Brutiis, Calabris, quin & Campanis, aliisque Confinalibus, quondam habitatum. Siculos Trilingues appellat Apuleius lib. x i, an quod Graeco, Latino, Tertioque ex iis misto loquerentur? Sicelisare apud Plautum in Menechmis Sc. 1. Sicule loqui, Siculum sermonem imitari: Σικελίζειν Graecis. Momar (Μῶμαρ) virum Stultum vocant, inquit Festus lib. xi. Isidorus in Glossis Momar, Siculus, Stultus, qui cito movetur ad iram. Plautus, Quid tuo Momar, Sicule homo, prae- sus? Ubi legendum censeo: Momar Siculus Stultus; ut non Synonyma sint Momar, Siculus, Stultus; sed Momar appelletur Siculus, qui Latinis Stultus: unde & apud Plautum, quum nescio quis a quo Momar esset compellatus, ut cuius gentis ea vox esset, notaretur, additur Sicule homo. Omnis enim qui Momar dicebatur, Siculus erat: sed non omnis Siculus erat Momar. Si quis tamen stultum etiam Siculum apud Veteres fuisse nominatum contendat, non admodum pugnabo, ea tamen lege, ut vox Siculus non sit proprium gentis nomen, sed, ut ita loquar cum Grammaticis, appellativum: diminutum. vatum,ut antea indicavi,ex Hebraico סבל pro quo & בסיל. Pergo , Ἐ'πιπρον, inquit Varro lib. v, Vocabulum est Cibi, quo frequentius Siculi, quam Itali usi, Plautus Milite Gloriofo, Scena 1 : Ni unum Epiturum apud illum ejusmodi infanè edam. Sic enim apud Poetam legendum. Nam Vox Ene, quae addituar, explicat, quid ibi sit infane. Quo modo Ιαt Ἐπιπρον, docent M. Porcius Cato cap. de Re Rustica cxix. & Columella lib. xii. cap. xxvii. Hesychius ἐ'πιπεφα vocat fiacs & Olivarum magmata, id est τ ἰλαῶν ἱκμισματα : corrupte enim legitur, Ἐ πιπεφα , ἱκμισματα ἰλαων. Αἰπεζ Siculum esse vocem, docet Varro iv. de LL. Siculos ab Latinis, quibus est Lepus, tumsitle addens. Ναμεγη Sicula vox, unde Latinis Latina : Eubulus Comicus apud Pollucem & Athenaeum: Καὶ πωκτα Σικελικα ἀκταῖνα σωφρίματα.
units.tr: That the Sicilian is named from Sicily is beyond dispute. Sicily once had the name, as I note elsewhere, not only for the island separated from Italy by a narrow strait, but for the whole region once inhabited by Greeks, Bruttians, Calabrians, and even Campanians and other neighbours. Apuleius, in book 11, calls the Sicilians trilingual: was it because they spoke Greek, Latin, and a third language mixed from these? Sicelisare in Plautus, Menaechmi, scene 1: to speak Sicilian, to imitate Sicilian speech; the Greeks have sikelizein [Σικελίζειν]. Festus, book 11, says that they call a foolish man Momar [Μῶμαρ]. Isidore in his Glosses: "Momar, Sicilian, fool, who is quickly moved to anger." Plautus: "What is it to you, Momar, Sicilian man, you fool?" Where I think it should be read: "Momar, Sicilian, fool," so that Momar, Siculus, Stultus are not synonyms; but Momar is called Siculus, which for Latins is Stultus. Whence also in Plautus, when someone was addressed by another as Momar, and to note what nation the word belonged to, "Sicilian man" is added. For everyone who was called Momar was a Sicilian, but not every Sicilian was a Momar. If anyone maintains, however, that among the ancients a fool was also called a Sicilian, I shall not argue much, on this condition: that the word Siculus is not a proper name of a nation but, as I say with the grammarians, an appellative, a diminutive. As I indicated before, it comes from the Hebrew סבל [sakal], for which also בסיל [basil]. I go on: "Epiprum," says Varro in book 5, "is a word for food, which the Sicilians used more often than the Italians." Plautus, in Miles Gloriosus, scene 1: "Unless I eat one epiprum with him in such madness." For so it should be read in the poet, since the word ene that is added explains what infane means there. That epiprum is so, Cato teaches in his chapter on rustic matters (119), and Columella, book 12, chapter 27. Hesychius calls epipepha the dregs of figs and olives, that is, the liquid residue of olives; the text is corrupt, reading epipepha, the residues of olives. Varro, book 4, teaches that aipez is a Sicilian word, and that the Sicilians, as the Latins call the hare lepus, add tumsitle. Nameg is a Sicilian word, whence the Latin Latina. Eubulus the comic poet, in Pollux and Athenaeus: "and Sicilian cakes of..."

units.la: Καπνος, apud Varronem, Siculis Vas, ubi Asia ponebant: Latini Catinum dicebant. Νέμμος, Nummus Siculorum est. Pollux lib. ix. ὁ δὲ νέμμος ὁ δοκεῖ μὲν αἴναι Ῥωμαίων νόμισμα τῆς Νεμισματος : ἐπὶ δὲ Ἠπείρῳ, τ ω Ιταλια καὶ Σικελια διαφέρον. Ὁ Ἐπιχαρμος π γαρ ἐν ταῖς Χυτρεῖς Φησιν: Α ἡ εμως καλαὶ καὶ πεὶ ἀρηες, ὅρκυον ὀδ Μοικχή Νομμοις καὶ γαρ ἐνπ πωλαπας ταις μαπηες.
units.tr: Kapnos (καπνος), in Varro, is a vessel among the Sicilians, the one the Asians used for it; the Latins called it catinum, a bowl. Nemmos (νέμμος) is a Sicilian coin. Pollux, book 9: "The nemmos seems to be a Roman coin, of the kind called nemisma, but in Epirus, Italy and Sicily it differs." Epicharmus, in the Chytroi, says: "Are they not fine and handsome, the rams? Swear by Moirichē, nommoi, and indeed ... by the Muses." [Ὁ Ἐπιχαρμος ... ὅρκιον ... Μοικχή Νομμοις]

units.la: Καὶ παλιν: Καρυ̃ ὁ' Ἱὸυς ἱων τεριομαι δικα Νέμμων μεγ. ον καλην.
units.tr: And again: "... I ask for Nemmon, great and fair." [Καὶ παλιν ... Νέμμων μεγ(αν) ... καλὴν]

units.la: Sic Varro lib. iv. de LL. In Argento Nummi id a Siculis. Quare inepte Suetonius Tranquillus ab Numa Nummos appellari scribit. Οὐγκια, Nummi genus, Siculorum item est. Testatur Aristoteles apud Pollucem lib. ix. Καὶ μὴν ἐν Ἀκραγαντίνων πολιτεια Φησιν Ἀρίστωνδος : ζημιοῦσθαι τινα τέλαντον ἀργυρος ὀνααδε δὲ τὴν Λιτραν εδοκεν Αἰζαναῖος: ἀλλα μόνον ποτε ουπω τις ἀν ἐν τῇ Ἱμερας πολιτεια και ἀλλα ἀ ρει Σικελιων ὀνοματα, οιον Οὐγκια, ἐπει δωα, χαλκοῦν ἱνα, Δωρον Siculus, eodem Varrone scribente, Dos, quae nuptiarum causa data: ubi Δως legendum. Sic Theocritus: Δως αχαθη, Α ε πάχ ὁι καχη.
units.tr: So Varro, book 4 of De Lingua Latina: "In argento nummi id a Siculis": the word nummus for silver coin comes from the Sicilians. Hence Suetonius Tranquillus writes foolishly that nummi are named after Numa. The ounce (οὐγκια), a kind of coin, is likewise Sicilian. Aristotle attests this in Pollux, book 9: "In the constitution of the Akragantines, Ariston says, someone is fined a talent of silver ..., and Aristaeus the Ἀλεξανδρεύς (?) thought it should be called a litra; but only in the constitution of Himera ... and other Sicilian words, such as ounce, epidōa, chalkoun, ..." Sicilian also is Dōs (δῶς), a dowry, which Varro, writing in the same place, describes as "what is given for the sake of marriage"; here Δως should be read. So Theocritus: "Δως ἀγαθή..." [Δως ἀχαθη]

units.la: Siculi, & praecipue Syracusani Circum aut Hipped; omnium Καμπων, inquit ad Varronem suum Scaliger, cubabant ad flevu Flumorum & Quadrigarum, quae ibi cer-tabant: unde omnia Plana Καμπι dicta. Sicula, tam qui continentem habitabant, quam qui Insulam ipsam, moris erat adspiratas Consonantes mutare frequenter in suas Tenues. Vbi enim Communis Dialectus habebat χ φ, θ, vertere consueverant ipsi in κ, π, τ: ut κυτεγα, κυτεγαι Olla. χιτων, κιτων, τυλιχερμα, κρίμα, pecunia. Φημη, πημη fama, Θανατος, ταναγος, mors; & id genus alia. Declinabatur etiam ipsis Γυνη, Mulier, γυναικος, γυναι, γυναικων quum aliis diceretur γυνακ, γυναικος, γυναιων, γυναικα. Citat etiam Hesychius Siculorum vocem μεῖνον χαεῖν: & usurpari solitum ab ipsis Proverbium, Μεῖνον ἀντιμισον, quo significabatur Par Pari, & gratum animum sufficere ad rependendum beneficium. Μεινον, inquit, ἀντιμισον: sic emendandum pro ἰσον μισ) πικρομια Σικελεις. ἰ γαρ χαεῖς, μειτ: μεινον χαεῖν. Sic Varro lib. iv de LL. in fine: Si datur, quod reddatur, Mutuum, quod Sicu's μεινον. Ita scribit Sophron Μεινον ἀναπιμμεν. Sicula porro species est Syracusana, qua Ζαγχλη Syracusii, imo quod quidam notant, Siculis omnibus, Δεισαιτον, Falce: unde Zancle, Vrbs Siciliae. Pro Falce utitur Nicand. in Alexip. Nuncius, inquit, in Verborum Etymologiis, quae Coniectaneis ad Varronem coniecit, Scaliger, plane Syracusana vox, ut al. iv, ives, ἀγκια, sic a nes, νυγκ. Siculi declinarunt Carcer etiam Syracusana Λαπιμια dicebatur, testibus Varrone libro, quem dixi, de LL. & Festo lib. x. Vsurpat eamotione Plato Epist. ii.
units.tr: "The Sicilians, and especially the Syracusans, ... around Circum or Hipped; of all the Kampoi," says Scaliger to his Varro, "they lay by the river of Flumora and Quadriga, which raced there; whence all flat places were called kampoi. The Sicilians, both those who lived on the mainland and those on the island itself, regularly changed their aspirated consonants into their own tenues." For where the common dialect had χ, φ, θ, they were accustomed to use κ, π, τ instead: kytega, kytegai (a pot); chitōn, kitōn (tunic); tylicherma, krima (money); phēmē, pēmē (fame); thanatos, tanagos (death); and others of that kind. They also declined gynē (woman) as gynaikos, gynai, gynaikōn, whereas others said gynak, gynaikos, gynaiōn, gynaika. Hesychius also cites the Sicilian expression "μεῖνον χαεῖν" and the proverb they habitually used, "μεῖνον ἀντιμισον," by which was meant "like for like," and that a grateful mind is enough to repay a kindness. "Μεινον, he says, ἀντιμισον": so it should be emended in place of ἰσον μισ..., as the Sicilians say. Varro too, book 4 of De Lingua Latina, near the end: "If something is given to be returned, it is a loan, which the Sicilians call meinon." So Sophron writes meinon anapimmen. Further, a Sicilian dialect is the Syracusan, in which the Syracusans say zanchlē, and indeed, as some note, all Sicilians say deisaiton for sickle, whence Zancle, a city of Sicily. Nicander uses the word for sickle in his Alexipharmaca. "A messenger," says Scaliger in his etymologies of words, which he gathered in his Coniectanea on Varro, "is plainly a Syracusan word, as is ives, ankia, nes, nyg..." The Sicilians also declined carcer (prison); the Syracusans called it lapimia, as Varro attests in the book I mentioned, De Lingua Latina, and Festus in book 10. Plato uses the word in his second letter.

units.la: Haec de Siculis lutiticiant; non enim huius loci, non mei est instituti omnia conquirere: quod ad Tarentinam, ea Αραχτες vel Ἀραχιτια dicitur apud Hesychium, ἡ ἰαῖς πικτεαῖς ὑπηριτεὰ γυνη, ἡ Αἴτηκοι Μαλα καλὴν.
