Capys, inquit Scaliger ad Festum Graecum vel Tarentinum videtur Latine expressum per Falconem. Nam Καπυς ἀπ̃ξ ἡ ταπτεας, ἡεὼ καμπιλος, quod incurvi habeat pedes. Vt Siculis tribuunt Varro & Pollux: sic Tarentinis Aristoteles, de quo idem Pollux : Καὶ Ἀρισιτελης ἐν τῇ Ταραντινων πολιτεια Φησι, καλεῖσθαι Νεμισμα παρ αυτοις Νομμον, ἐφ' ἡ ὑπυτρασθαι Γαεμν τ Ποσειδωνο. δελφινι ἐπιοχημενον.
units.tr: These things I have gathered about the Sicilians, for it is neither the place nor my purpose to collect everything. As for the Tarentines, araches or arachitia is what Hesychius calls it: "a woman who is a seller of ..., and a Thracian (?) fine woman." Scaliger, on Festus, says: "Capys, the Greek or Tarentine word, seems to be rendered in Latin as falco (hawk), for kapys is named from kampē (bend), or kampylos, because it has curved feet." As Varro and Pollux assign these to the Sicilians, so Aristotle assigns them to the Tarentines. Pollux, of the same, says: "And Aristotle, in the constitution of the Tarentines, says that among them the coin is called nommos, on which a Tarentine dolphin is stamped, with Poseidon's trident(?) ..." [Καὶ Ἀρισιτελης ... Νομμον ...]

units.la: Non possum hic silentio praeterire, quosdam esse, qui memoriae produnt, Iapyges antiquissimos Italiae Orientalioris Incolas, quorum praecipui fuerunt Salentini, ante adventum eas in oras Idomenei, Linguam habuisse propriam, Litterasque peculiares:
units.tr: I cannot pass over in silence that some record that the Iapygians, the most ancient inhabitants of eastern Italy, among whom the chief were the Salentines, before the arrival of Idomeneus on those shores, had a language of their own and peculiar letters.

units.la: Graecafuccess. Iapygia. liares: Exemplum autem exstare in Tabula quadam marmorea, quam ante annos aliquot Vaticæ, quæ Salentinorum Vrbs, inventam testantur Ioannes Pontanus, Hermolaus Barbarus, Accius Synecrus, Charncus Summontius aliique qui eam viderunt: quorum quidam addunt, eandem post modum, inducta Græca interitus. Eius autem pars sic habet:
units.tr: There is an example of this on a certain marble tablet, which some years ago was found at Vaste (?), the city of the Salentines, as Giovanni Pontano, Ermolao Barbaro, Accio Sinecro, Carnico Summonzio and others who saw it attest; some of them add that it was afterwards lost, and that a Greek inscription was substituted. Part of it reads as follows:

units.la: ΚΑΘΗΓΙΣ Ο ΘΕΟΡΙΑ ΜΑΡΤΑΡΙΔΟΥ ΑΥΤΕΙΒΑΣΤΑ ΦΕΙΝΑΙΥ ΑΡΑΝΙΝ ΔΑΡΑΝΘΟΑΙΑΣ ΤΙΣ ΤΑΒΟΟΣ
units.tr: Kathēgis o theōria martyridou autei basta pheinai ... [ΚΑΘΗΓΙΣ Ο ΘΕΟΡΙΑ ΜΑΡΤΑΡΙΔΟΥ ΑΥΤΕΙΒΑΣΤΑ ΦΕΙΝΑΙΥ ΑΡΑΝΙΝ ΔΑΡΑΝΘΟΑΙΑΣ ΤΙΣ ΤΑΒΟΟΣ]

units.la: Iam Lucana Lingua Græca ne fuerit an Latina species, an vero prorsus ab ipsidem alia, certo statui nequit. Quum Magnæ Græciæ Lucani, quam Latio fuerint propiores, ad Græcam mallem, quam Latinam trahere. De ea Varro lib. iv. de LL. Vest, inquit, Lucana origo, et eundem illi, nostri ab ipsis et ece. Huc pertinet eiusdem Varronis locus ex lib. vi. ubi disputat, unde Luca Bos fuerit appellata, item quur Panthera & Leones non Luca, sed Afrinana Bestiæ dicerentur, quur denique Vesti Lucani potius, quam Luci vocarentur.
units.tr: Whether the Lucanian language was a Greek or a Latin form, or something entirely different from both, cannot be determined with certainty. Since the Lucanians of Magna Graecia were closer to Latium, I would rather class their language as Greek than as Latin. Varro, in book iv of De Lingua Latina, says of it: "Vestine origin is Lucanian," and he traces the rest to the same source. To this belongs another passage of the same Varro, from book vi, where he discusses why the Lucanian ox was so called, and why the panthers and lions were called not Lucanian but African beasts, and finally why the Vestines were called Lucani rather than Luci.

units.la: Principes, quæ antiquis cis Tiberim Italiæ Incolis, Linguas Latinam Græcamque expositi: succedunt Deinceps, Sabina, Osca, aliæ, quarum apud Grammaticos mentio. Et autem an peculiares fuerint, an vero vel Latini vel Græci sermonis Dialecti, non ausim, ego quidem, hoc tempore diffinire. Quod ad Sabinam, censet Isaacus Casaubonus ad initium lib. iii. Cæsarum Suetonii, plerasque eius Linguæ Voces originis esse Græcanicæ. Nam & ipsi, inquit, absque dubio avixabar Dores fuerunt e Peloponnesso orti. Non laborabo his vel confirmandis, vel refutandis. Nisi ex Græcis fontibus hæc Lingua originem habuerit, videntur sane Sabina nonnulla ab Græcis mutuati. Nam quod his Λ'λ.ξοvillis, Festo teste, Aipum est, Latinis Album. Aita Sabinorum vel Prænomen, vel Cognomen, ατ' ατα, quod suffire & nusquam fide pedem figere. Conferendi Festus lib. i. de Verbor: significat. & Suetonius in Tiberio cap. i. Nero Lingua Sabina Forte ac Strenuus, Suetonio notante in eiusdem principis vita, eodem capite. Vox Græca, inquit Casaubonus, originis. Græci enim hominem bonis lacertis vocant Νέρων. Eleganter Agellius lib. xiii. cap. xxii. Id autem sive Nerio sive Neriences est, Sabinum verbum est, eoque significantur Virtus & Fortitudo. Itaque ex Claudiis, quos a Sabinis oriundos accepimus, qui erat egregia & præstans fortitudine, Nero appellatus est. Sed id Sabini a Græcis accepisse videntur, qui vincula & firmamenta membrorum Νεῦρα dicunt: unde & nos quoque Latine Neruos appellamus. Nerio igitur Martis vis & potentia, & maiestas quaedam esse Martis demonstratur. Sed laudantur multa Sabinorum ab Latinis, quæ nihil cum Græcis habent commune. Eorum hic est Catalogus: Mamers Sabine, qui Latine Mars. Varro iv. de LL. Novit Lycophron, quum ait:
units.tr: The first peoples on this side of the Tiber whose languages are set out by the grammarians were the Latins and the Greeks. Next follow the Sabine, the Oscan and others, which the grammarians also mention. Whether these were distinct languages, or merely dialects of Latin or Greek, I would not venture to decide at present. As for the Sabine, Isaac Casaubon, at the beginning of book iii of Suetonius's Lives of the Caesars, holds that most of its words are of Greek origin. "For," he says, "the Sabines were without doubt Dorians, sprung from the Peloponnese." I shall not labour either to confirm or to refute this. Unless the language drew its origin from Greek sources, the Sabine words borrowed from the Greeks certainly seem to be several. For what the Sabines called aipum (as Festus testifies) the Latins called album, "white." The Sabine word ata, which was either a praenomen or a cognomen, means one who "is always on his feet and never plants his foot firmly." Compare Festus, book i, On the Meaning of Words, and Suetonius, Tiberius, chapter i: "Nero, in the Sabine tongue, means brave and strenuous," as Suetonius notes in the life of that emperor, in the same chapter. Casaubon says: "The word is Greek in origin, for the Greeks call a man with strong sinews Neron." Agellius, book xiii, chapter xxii, elegantly remarks: "Whether it is Nerio or Neriene, it is a Sabine word, and it signifies valour and courage. Thus Nero was the name given to one of the Claudii, whom we have received as descended from the Sabines, because he was outstanding and excellent in courage." But the Sabines seem to have taken this from the Greeks, who call the sinews and bands of the limbs neura, whence we too in Latin call them nervi. Nerio, therefore, is shown to be the force and power of Mars and a certain majesty of Mars. Yet many things of the Sabines are cited by the Latins that have nothing in common with the Greeks. Here is a list of them: Mamers in Sabine, which in Latin is Mars, as Varro says in book iv of De Lingua Latina. Lycophron knew this when he says:

units.la: Καὶ δαίον, ἡ Μαμέρτη ἐκ λίτλω λύκον.
units.tr: "And the wolf of Mamers, ... from the lot" [Καὶ δαῖον, ἢ Μαμέρτη ἐκ λίτλω λύκον.]

units.la: Item
units.tr: Likewise:

units.la: Πολλῶν δ' ἐναλλαξ πυμάτων ἀπάρξεῖ Καυδαῖος, ἡ μαμερης.
units.tr: "Of many, in turn, the Caudaean first, the Mamerta..." [Πολλῶν δ' ἐναλλαξ πυμάτων ἀπάρξεῖ Καυδαῖος, ἢ μαμερης.]

units.la: Feronia, inquit ibidem Varro, Minerva, Novemsiles a Sabinis paullo aliter ab eisdem dicimus Laram (alii Herculem legunt, Herem emendat Iosephus Scaliger) Vestam, Salutem, Fortem Fortunam, Fidem. Fa re (coniectat Scaliger Lares) Sabinorum Linguam olent, quæ Tatij Regis voto sunt Romæ dedicata. Nam, ut Annales dicunt, vovit Opi, Floraque, Duovi, Saturnoque, Soli, Lunæque, Volcano, Summanoquesitemque Larunda, Termino, Quirino, Vertumno, Larisbus, Diana, Cœsinaque. Et quæ nonnulla nomina in utraque Lingua habent radices: ut Arbores, quæ in confinio natae, in utroque agro serpunt. Potest enim esse Saturnus hic alia de causa distus, atque in Sabinis; & sic Diana. Sancus Sabina lingua, qui Deus Fidius Latina, notante eodem Varrone libro saepe iam indicato. Semonem eundem cum Sanco facit T. Livius lib. viii. Meminit omnium Ovidius in Fastis, ex emendatione Scaligeris
units.tr: Feronia, says Varro in the same place, Minerva and Novensiles; a little differently, the Sabines call the Lares (others read Hercules, but Joseph Scaliger corrects it to Herem), Vesta, Salus, Fortuna the Brave, and Fides. The Fa re (Scaliger conjectures Lares) savour of the Sabine language, and these were dedicated at Rome in fulfilment of a vow made by King Tatius. For, as the Annals relate, he vowed to Ops, Flora, Duonus, Saturn, the Sun, the Moon, Volcanus, Summanus, Larunda, Terminus, Quirinus, Vertumnus, the Lares, Diana and Caesina. Some names have roots in both languages, like arbores, which, born on the border, creep into the fields of both peoples. Saturn may be so called here for a different reason from the Sabine one, and likewise Diana. Sancus is Sabine, what in Latin is Deus Fidius, as Varro notes in the book already cited so often. T. Livy, book viii, makes Semo the same as Sancus. Ovid, in the Fasti, mentions them all, in the emendation of Scaliger:

units.la: Quærebam Nonas, Sanco Fidione referrem,
units.tr: "I was asking about the Nones, whether I should refer them to Sancus or Fidius,"

units.la: An tibi Semo-Pater:
units.tr: "Or to you, Father Semo?"

units.la: Sol Sabinum esse vocabulum testatur idem Varro libro nominato. Talus in Sabinorum nominibus Prænominis loco videtur fuisse, uti notat Festus lib. penultimo. Casus, acutus, Sabinis apud Varronem lib. vi. de LL. Circulus, inquit idem Varro lib. vi. quod multa mista farina iaseo & aqua circumsum aequaliter fundebant. Hoc quidam, qui magis incondite faciebant, vocabant Lixulas & Semilixulas, vocabulo Sabino: idque frequentius Sabini a globo farina dilatato. Scensu Scaliger legit Cesnas Sabini Cenas ducebant, ait Festus lib. xvii. Hircum, inquit Varro, quod Sabini Fircus; & quod illic Fedus, in Latio rure Hedus, quod in Urbe, ut in multis, A addito Hadus. Quae sequuntur, obscuriora sunt: Porcus, quod Sabini dicunt de Aprino Porco, porridus, unde Porcus: Veram Lectionem putat Scaliger: Porcus, quod Sabini dicunt Aprum Porcum, pronde Porcus. Hirpi Sabinu Lupi, Servio ad Virgilium indicante. Curis Sabinu Hasta: unde iuno Curis; item Quirinus, Romulus, quod Curs, id est Hasta, utereatur; Quirites Cives Romani cum Sabinis missi; Quiritare, Quiritium fidem clamando implorare; & similia: videndi Varro lib. iv. de LL. Festus in Celibari, Curis, Curitum, item in fragmentis vocis Quirinalis; & alii Cubam Sabini vocant, inquit idem Festus lib. iii, eam, quam Militia es Lectum; unde videtur dirivatum esse Cubiculum. Varro lib. iv. Item dicta Lepesta (sic enim corrigendum) etiam nunc in diebus (quid si edibus?) fuerit, Sabineis Vasa Vinaria in mensa Deorum sunt posita. Apud antiquos Scriptores Graecos invenio appellari poculi genus Aemiaeum. Quare vel unde radices in Agrum Sabinum & Romanum sunt profectae. Idem Varro lib. i. de Vita Populi Romani: Lepesta etiamnum Sabinorum Fanis pauperioribus plerisque aut fictiles sunt, aut aneae. Aixes meminerunt Athenaeus & Pollux. Aurum Sabinis Aurum, apud Festum. Sabinorum Lingua Herna Saxa vocantur, inquit Servius ad vii. Aeneid. Testatur idem de Mai(sorum Lingua Festus. Februum vocant apud Varronem lib. v. Sabini purgamentum. Cuprum apud eumdem lib. iv. Sabine bonum. Scaliger Cuprum vocem vult esse Syriacam; addens ea Lingua usos antiquitus Etruscos. Cascum, eodem teste lib. vi, Sabinus Verus; indeque Cassinum opidum, quod otii ab Sabinis Samnites tenuerunt: inde item Cassinum Forum, Vetus. Crepenum, eodem notante lib. v. & vi. de LL. Sabius, quod Latinis dubium: unde Crepusculum, dubium tempus. Sabinam Linguam, radices in Osciam egisse docet idem Varro lib vi. Sabinis Vocabulis delectatos Poetas Latinos, ex antiquis patet Grammaticis. Sabina Lingua Dialectus erat Samnitica. Nam quemadmodum ab Sabinis Samnites duxerunt originem, sic Linguam etiam, Genitoribus suis propriam & peculiarem, in novas sedes translati, secum asportarunt. Non enim solum Sabinis Lupi nominabantur Hirpi vel Irpi; sed etiam, ut notat ex Festo Paullus Diaconus lib. ix, Samnitibus.
units.tr: Varro, in the book named above, also testifies that sol is a Sabine word. Talus seems to have been used as a praenomen among the Sabine names, as Festus notes in the penultimate book. Casus and acutus are Sabine according to Varro, book vi of De Lingua Latina. "Circulus," says the same Varro in book vi, "because they spread a mixture of flour, sesame and water evenly in a circle. Those who made them less skilfully called them lixulae and semilixulae, using a Sabine word; and the Sabines more often used it of a ball of flour spread out." Scaliger reads, by an emendation, cesnas; the Sabines called cakes cenae, says Festus in book xvii. "Hircus," says Varro, "the Sabines call fircus; and what there is fedus in the country of Latium is hedus in the City, as in many words, with an A added, hadus." What follows is more obscure: "Porcus, which the Sabines say of the wild boar, porridus, whence porcus." Scaliger thinks the true reading is: "Porcus, which the Sabines call the wild boar porcus, whence porcus." Hirpi is Sabine for wolves, as Servius indicates on Virgil. Curis is Sabine for spear, whence Juno Curis; likewise Quirinus, Romulus, because he used a curis, that is a spear; Quirites, Roman citizens sent with the Sabines; quiritare, to invoke the faith of the Quirites by shouting. For similar examples see Varro, book iv of De Lingua Latina, and Festus under Celibaris, Curis, Curitum, and in the fragments under Quirinalis. Festus, book iii, says that the Sabines call a bed cuba, which the soldiers call lectus; whence cubiculum seems to be derived. Varro, book iv: "The lepesta (so the word should be corrected), which were also still in the temples (or houses?), with the Sabines the wine vessels were placed on the table of the gods." I find that among the ancient Greek writers a kind of cup is called aemiaeum. Whence or why the roots spread into the Sabine and Roman fields. The same Varro, book i of On the Life of the Roman People: "The lepesta, even now in the shrines of the poorer Sabines, are mostly of clay or bronze." Athenaeus and Pollux mention aixes. Aurum is Sabine for gold, in Festus. Servius, on Aeneid vii, says that in the Sabine language stones are called herna, and Festus attests the same of the language of the Marsi. Varro, book v, says the Sabines call the purgation februum. In the same author, book iv, cuprum is Sabine for "good." Scaliger wishes the word cuprum to be Syriac, adding that the Etruscans used that language in early times. Cascum, by the same witness, book vi, is Sabine for "true," and hence the town of Casinum, which the Samnites held after taking it from the Sabines; hence also the Forum Cassinum, the old one. Crepenum, as the same notes in books v and vi of De Lingua Latina, is Sabine for "doubtful," which is dubium in Latin; whence crepusculum, the doubtful time. Varro in the same book vi shows that the Sabine language had its roots in the Oscan. It is clear from the ancient grammarians that Latin poets took delight in Sabine words. The Sabine language was a dialect of the Samnite. For just as the Samnites derived their origin from the Sabines, so, having moved into new seats, they carried with them their own language, proper and peculiar to their forebears. For the Sabines were not the only ones called Hirpi or Irpi, that is, wolves; Paulus the Deacon, book ix, notes from Festus that this name was also given to the Samnites.

units.la: Haec de Sabina, ad Osciam venio. Osciam sermonem alium ab Latino fuisse docet Titinij versus: Osce & Volsce fabulantur: nam Latine nesciunt.
units.tr: So much for the Sabine; I come now to the Oscan. That the Oscan speech was different from Latin is shown by the verses of Titinius: "They speak Oscan and Volscian; for they do not know Latin."

units.la: Corruptior fuit, non plane diversus. Leguntur eius Linguae quaedam apud Grammaticos voces, Mamers lingua Osciorum Marsi & Mamercus praenomen secum, eo quod Osci Martem Mamertem appellarent, teste Festo lib. xi. Meddix, eodem scribente, apud Osces nomen Magistratus est. Ennius: Summus ibi capitur Meddix, occiditur alter.
units.tr: It was more corrupt, though not wholly different. Some words of this language are read in the grammarians: Mamers, in the Oscan language, is kept by the Marsi, and Mamercus as a praenomen, because the Oscans called Mars Mamers, as Festus says in book xi. Meddix, by the same writer, is the Oscan name for a magistrate. Ennius: "There the highest meddix is taken, the other is slain."

units.la: Famel Osci apud eumdem, servus. Sic Varro lib. iv. de LL. Quod supra Supparus; nisi quod id dicunt Osce. Vngulum ex Festi notatione lib. ult. Osciorum lingua significat Annulum ut Veia, Plaustrum. Multam, alit ex Festo Paulus, Osce dici putant poenam. Sic eidem Osce Pipatio, clamor plorantis; Sollum, totum & solidum: Mafius, Mensis Martius, Dalrum, insanum; Pirpi, quidquid: Petora, quatuor. Nam Osci T mutabant in P, ut Tis, Pis: Ti, Pit, unde Pirpi, quidquid; Oscae Petora; unde Petoritum, currus quatuor rotarum. Vide & supra libro iii. cap. xv. Notandum hic, quod peculiare Osci usu venisse notat Strabo lib. iv: inquit, ...Inde Oscum Ludicrum dicebatur: cuius meminerunt M. Tullius Epist. ad Marium, & Tacitus lib. iv. Annalium. Sunt qui idem censent cum Atellano: quia Atella Osciorum urbs. In Osciam Linguam radices suas Sabinam egisse tradit M. Terentius Varro lib. vi. de LL. Et inde Cassar Osci Senex: ab Casco, quae Vox Sabinis Verus. Vide & Festum in Cassar. Familiaris fuit Osca Lingua Brutiis; Estinques, inquit Festus, Brutates Ennius dixit, quod Bruti & Osce & Graece loquiu solitu sint: Item Canusini, Canulij, quod Apuliae Peucetiae opidum, Incolis: Horat. ——Canusini morebilinguis.
units.tr: Famel, among the Oscans, in the same author, means a slave. Varro says so in book iv of De Lingua Latina. What is supparus above, except that the Oscans say it differently. Vungulum, from Festus's note in the last book, in the Oscan language means a ring, as veia means a cart. Paulus, from Festus, thinks that multa is called poena in Oscan. Likewise in the same Oscan, pipatio is the cry of one weeping; sollum means whole and solid; mafius, the month of March; dalrum, mad; pirpi, whatever; petora, four. For the Oscans changed T into P, as tis, pis; ti, pit, whence pirpi, whatever; in Oscan petora, whence petoritum, a four-wheeled carriage. See also above, book iii, chapter xv. It should be noted here that Strabo, book iv, observes that this was a peculiar usage of the Oscans: "...Hence the Oscan play was so called," of which M. Tullius, in his letter to Marius, and Tacitus, book iv of the Annals, make mention. Some hold it to be the same as the Atellan, because Atella was an Oscan town. M. Terentius Varro, book vi of De Lingua Latina, records that the Oscan language had its roots in the Sabine. Hence Cassar is Oscan for "old man," from casco, which is a Sabine word for "true." See also Festus under Cassar. The Oscan language was familiar to the Bruttians; Ennius, says Festus, called the Bruttians Estinques, because the Bruttians and Oscans and Greeks used to speak together. Likewise the Canusini, Canulii, from the town of Canusium in Apulia and Peucetia: Horace: "the Canusian, two-tongued."

units.la: Ad quem locum Porphyrio vetus Horatij Interpres eadem fere scribit, quæ paullo ante laudata ex Festo: Bilingues inquit, dicuntur, quoniam utraque Lingua Campanis ei sunt, sicut per omnem illum tractum Italiæ, quem ex maiori parte Græci incoluerunt: ex quo Magna Græcia nomen accepit. Ideo ergo & Ennius & Lucilius Bruttiates bilingues dicerentur. Licet Campanam Linguam Dialectum fuisse Græci sermonis quis potuit dicere, quod apud Plinium Græci legantur tenuitè Campaniam: quodque Avernum Lacum in Magna Græcia describit Maximus Tyrius Orat. xxvi: eam tamen plerique docti Viri eandem cum Osca, vel saltem Osca faciunt speciem. Secundo, Falisci in Campania, aut Vario, abscondendo. Strena Campana, uvæ genus apud Plinium lib. nat. hist. xiiii, caput. An eandem cum Osca Linguam habuerint Vestini, adhuc incertum. Videtur inter eos nominibus fuisse distinctus. Tertius Fabula v, quam antea laudavi:
units.tr: Porphyrio, the old commentator on Horace, writes almost the same things at this passage as what was quoted a little earlier from Festus: "They are called bilingual," he says, "because both languages are at home among the Campanians, as they are throughout that whole stretch of Italy which the Greeks mostly inhabited, from which Magna Graecia got its name." So Ennius and Lucilius could both be called bilingual Bruttians. Yet who could say that the Campanian language was a dialect of Greek, since Pliny is read as saying that the Greeks only thinly inhabited Campania, and since Maximus of Tyre, in Oration 26, describes Lake Avernus in Magna Graecia? Still, many learned men make it the same as Oscan, or at least a form of Oscan. Second, the Falisci in Campania, or Vario, abscondendo [by hiding]. The Campanian strena, a kind of grape, in Pliny's Natural History, book 14, chapter... Whether the Vestini had the same language as Oscan is still uncertain; it seems they were distinguished from one another by their names. Third, Fabula 5, which I quoted before:

units.la: Qui Osce & Volsce fabulantur, Latine nescinunt.
units.tr: Those who speak Oscan and Volscian do not know Latin.

units.la: Volscorum, aut & Formianorum Vocabulo Tigna in latitudinem extenta Sublices dicebantur, teste Festo lib. de Verb. signif. c. xvii.
units.tr: By the word of the Volsci, or also of the Formians, beams laid out in width were called sublices, as Festus witnesses in his book on the meaning of words, chapter 17.

units.la: Hæc de Cit. Tiberinus Italiæ Linguis: succedit Transf. Tiberina, Tusca, Tuscos antiquos utos fuisse Aramæa vel Syriaca Lingua, constans Viris doctis mens est. Probat illud abunde ingens variarum Vocum numerus. Non illas hic repetam, quas notavi, quum de Incremento Latinæ Linguæ, pentiria laborans, ab Etruscis profecto, dissererem. Eas, Aramæi vel Syriaci Fontis, Tusci vero Vius, in Colonias suas transtulisse Veteres Latinos multas, non primus ego, monui. Quum tamen Scriptores antiquæ Voces, quas ibi memoravi, Tusci esse, concepte non tradant: pauculas hic adponam quæ Scriptoribus iisdem diversis verbis, sunt Etrusca, quæque suas habent in Aramaeæ sermone radices. Aesar Etrusca Lingua Deus, ut videre est apud Suetonium in Augusti Vita, cap. xcvii: ab עזר, Regnum, Dominium quod eum magis convenit, quam Deo? Quod Nepos Tuscus in Luxuriosus, constat ex Festi Fragmentis, si quidem legitimum Lacunæ eius ab doctis Viris supplementum acceperint. Hæc Vox meo iudicio manat ab Hebraica נפץ, quæ mihi aliud quam Dispergere, vel ab פוץ, quæ Conterere, Projicere, Evacuare significat: ut vere Nepotes Tusci, & ab iis hodie Latinis, sint perditi, luxuriosi, qui Patrimonium & rem familiarem nimia profusione dispergunt & evacuant. Nepos alia notione Latinis idem inter Agnationis Voces, quasi Non Pes, ut quibusdam videtur, nec fundamentum Generis. Ea autem Tuscum Cœlum, apud Festum lib. vi; Vox, ni fallor, ab Hebraico vocabulo derivata פלא, quod mirabile, difficile, arduum esse notat. Subuionem, quo utitur Ennius, Tusci Tibicinem esse, eiusque radices in Etruria, non in Latio quærendum esse, monet Varro de LL. lib. vi: quæ de re etiam Festus lib. xvii: fortean ab טמם, Tumescere Iniuri. Bastem, Tusum Charitius: Varro Baitea dixit, & Tusum Vocabulum aut esse, Rerum humanarum lib. xviii. an à בלא, Roborare, Confortare? Aliarum Vocum Origines aliis indagandas relinquo. Sunt enim plures, quæ ab Grammaticis: ut Tusca, laudantur. Ilia, Iuno, Etruscis Κυρία dicebatur, teste Strabone lib. v. Neptunus Tuscum, inquit in Coniecturis ad Varronem Iuum Vir Nob. Iosephus Scaliger, ut Volcanus. Nomina, quibus tres Veterum Romanorum Tribus designabantur, Taties, Ramnes, Luceres, Tusca esse, prodit apud Varronem lib. iv. de LL. antiquissimus Scriptor Voluminus. Inter Etrusca lingua Ludio apud Livium lib. vii. ab V. C. Lanista Tusca Carnifex, teste Ludoro in Etymologicis. Capa Tusca Vox, Hesychio notante. Ansa, Additamentum dicitur apud Festum Lingua Tuscorum, quod ponderi adiicitur; sed deterius, & quod lineullo est usu. Scaliger tamen negans Tuscum, adhuc purum putum esse Latinum pro Manuzeni a. Vox mihi Latina, sed ad Etruscismum inflexa. Ante Tusce Tuscorum lingua, ex urteignum sonare scribit ex Verrio Flacco Festus lib. i. de Verb. signif. Aliæ in præsentia non occurrunt. Suspicantur quidam Vocabula illa, quæ Arnobius lib. vii adversus Gentes recenset, de Victimis & earum partibus Originis esse Etruscæ: qualia sunt Apexabo, Longaeo: Tuccetum: Tania, Palasca, sive ut quidam nominant, Pasea, Iscia, Polimina, Africia, Gratilla, Catumicum, Fendica, Magnenta, Augmina, & id genus alia. Quæ Ioannes Annius Viterbiensis Etrusca vocabula nobis comminiscitur, & tubornatis Catonis adfingit fragmentis ut sunt Fonzo pro Pado, Puena pro Ancona, Larinum pro Metropoli, Loro pro Principe, Sagi pro Pontificibus & sacris Expiatoribus: mihi Nugæ sunt, Quisquiliæ, Butrubatta Nævii, nul-
units.tr: So much for the languages of the Italian peoples on this side of the Tiber. Next comes the Tuscan language across the Tiber. It is a settled view among learned men that the ancient Tuscans used the Aramaic or Syriac language. A huge number of words proves this amply. I shall not repeat here those I noted when, in my work on the growth of the Latin language, I discussed the words that the Latins derived from the Etruscans. I earlier pointed out that many of the ancient Latins had carried those words, which come from an Aramaic or Syriac source and were in use among the Tuscans, into their own colonies. Since the ancient writers do not say that the words I cited there were specifically Tuscan, I shall add here a few words that the same writers call Etruscan in different terms and that have their roots in the Aramaic tongue. Aesar, the Etruscan word for god, as may be seen in Suetonius, Life of Augustus, chapter 97: from [עזר], what could be more fitting for him than God, the one of kingdom and dominion? That nepos is Tuscan for a luxurious man is clear from the fragments of Festus, if scholars have supplied the correct filling of its lacuna. In my judgment this word comes from the Hebrew [נפץ], which to me means nothing other than to scatter, or from [פוץ], which means to crush, cast out or empty. Thus the Tuscan nepotes, and from them the Latins of today, are truly wastrels, luxurious men who scatter and empty out their patrimony and household property by excessive spending. In another sense, nepos among the Latins is one of the words for kinship, as if it meant "not foot", as some think, nor the foundation of a family. That word, caelum in Tuscan, in Festus book 6: the word, unless I am mistaken, is derived from the Hebrew [פלא], which means wonderful, difficult, arduous. Varro, in On the Latin Language book 6, warns that the subuo which Ennius uses means a flute-player in Tuscan, and that its roots must be sought in Etruria, not in Latium; Festus too deals with this matter in book 17. Perhaps it comes from [טמם], to swell, to be swollen. Charitius says bastum is Tuscan; Varro wrote baitea, and the Tuscan word is either from Rerum humanarum book 18, or from [בלא], to strengthen, to fortify? I leave the origins of other words to others, for there are many which the grammarians cite as Tuscan. Juno, called Ilia by the Etruscans, was called Kyria [Κυρία], as Strabo witnesses in book 5. Neptune is Tuscan, says the noble man Joseph Scaliger in his Conjectures on Varro, as Vulcan is. The names by which the three ancient Roman tribes were designated, Tities, Ramnes and Luceres, are Tuscan, as the most ancient writer Volumnius reports in Varro, On the Latin Language book 4. Among the Etruscan words, ludio in Livy book 7, from V. C. lanista, the Tuscan word for executioner, according to Ludorus in the Etymologica. Capa is a Tuscan word, as Hesychius notes. Ansa is called in Festus, in the language of the Tuscans, the addition that is attached to a weight, but it is worse, and it has little use. Yet Scaliger, denying that Tuscan is entirely pure Latin, takes it for a Latin word inflected towards Etruscan. Festus, book 1 of On the Meaning of Words, writes from Verrius Flaccus that before tuscae, the Tuscan language sounded something like urteignum. Others do not occur at present. Some suspect that those words which Arnobius lists in book 7 Against the Gentiles, concerning the victims and their parts, are of Etruscan origin: such as Apexabo, Longaeo, Tuccetum, Tania, Palasca or, as some name them, Pasea, Iscia, Polimina, Africia, Gratilla, Catumicum, Fendica, Magnenta, Augmina, and other things of that kind. The Etruscan words which John Annius of Viterbo invents for us, and which he adds to the spurious fragments of Cato, such as Fonzo for Po, Puena for Ancona, Larinum for metropolis, Loro for prince, Sagi for pontiffs and sacred expiators, seem to me mere trifles, rubbish, and the Butrubatta of Naevius, of no weight at all.

units.la: lius ius momenti. Tuscas Tragædias scripsisse Volumnium Poëtam, auctor est lib. iv. de LL. Varro. Mihi igitur, ut magnis Viris, Sermo Tuscus ab Aramæo sua habet primordia. Sunt qui ex Græcis fontibus dirivant, argumento vocum Falanti, Nepotum, & limilium: Quæ enim Falantum Nepotesque Tuscis, φαλαντυ & Νεποτες esse Græcis. Sed parum hæc probant. Fuerint enim ut hac lingua Græca quædam Vocabula, ut vere tuerunt, an necessum, ut ab Græca manarint? Sæpe multa ex una in aliam diffunduntur linguam propter vicinitatem Inter ea Lana Vestimenti genus, habitus duplicis, apud Tuscos, ut notat Festus, quæ Græcis χλαινα. Sic Lucumo, Tusium; & tamen origo ipsi Græca. Nam
units.tr: Varro, in On the Latin Language book 4, is the authority that the poet Volumnius wrote Tuscan tragedies. So, as with great men, I hold that the Tuscan speech has its beginnings in Aramaic. Some derive it from Greek sources, arguing from the words Falanti, Nepotes and similar: for they say that Falantum and Nepotes in Tuscan are Greek [φαλαντυ, Νεποτες]. But these arguments prove little. Even if certain words of the Greek language were used by the Tuscans, as indeed they were, does it follow that they came from Greek? Many words spread from one language into another because of nearness. Among these is lana, a kind of garment, a double garment, among the Tuscans, as Festus notes, which the Greeks call chlaina [χλαινα]. So too Lucumo and Tusius*, and yet their origin is itself Greek. For in Etruria and Latium there are Lucumones, who in Arcadia are the [Ανξαονες].

units.la: in Etruria & Latio Lucumones ii sunt, qui in Arcadia Ανξαονες. Quin tamen etiam habuit vires Græcorum vicinitas, ut Etrusci Progenitorum suorum Characteribus, qui erant Aramæi, carentes, alios ab iisdem Græcis Continalibus suis, quique Colonias etiam variasin Tusciam jam tunc duxerant, dicantur mutuati, sed mutatis, vel potius inversis, figuris: cum, ne iidem parerent, tum ut Majorum suorum in scribendo ritum, & consuetudinem æmulari aliquo modo viderentur. Repertæ fuerunt ante aliquot annos Eugubij in Umbria Tabulæ octoaenæ; quarum una litteris, quas dixi, erat concepta. Eius hæc pars est:
units.tr: Yet the nearness of the Greeks was strong enough to make the Etruscans, who lacked their own letters, which were Aramaic, borrow characters from those same Greeks, their neighbours on the coast, who had also already led colonies into Etruria. They borrowed the forms but changed them, or rather reversed them, both so that they would not be the same and so that they might seem in some way to imitate the custom and practice of their ancestors in writing. Some years ago, at Gubbio in Umbria, eight tablets were found, one of which was written in the letters I have mentioned. This is its first part:

units.la: Alphabetum, ab nonnullis cum veris rectisque litterarum Græcarum formis commissum, adponam: timidior tamen. Nam ego hic nihil ausim adfirmare. Licet enim Characterum cum vel Latinis Potestas reperiretur, tamen & Etrusca Lingua & eius Verba prisca funditus fere, paucis exceptis, exciderunt:
units.tr: I shall add an alphabet, put together by some people with the true and correct forms of Greek letters, but I am rather timid about it, for I should not dare to assert anything here. For although the power of the characters can be found with Latin ones, both the Etruscan language and its ancient words have almost wholly perished, with few exceptions.

units.la: [Alphabet display: Etruscan letters with Greek equivalents, Ω Φ Η Τ Σ Ρ Π Ο Ν Μ Α Κ Ι Ζ Ε Δ Β Α.]
units.tr: [Alphabet in display type: the Etruscan letters, each set beside its Greek equivalent.]

units.la: Eugubinæ Tabulæ Characteribus non multum absimiles extant Perusiæ in Etruria, cum publice lapide quadrato, tum ad domum quandam privatam, in qua Urnæ Etrusci litteris incisæ. Visuntur & similes Characteres Florentiæ in Palatio Reip. a l Scalam quandam in dextro pede Simulacri cuiusdam Chimæræ, quod cum in locum Aretio translatum. Elegantia vero extra controversiam Etrusca lin-gua, sed quæ paullatim iam ab Vetere degenerarat, specimina, Latinis concepta litteris, exhibent septem reliquæ, quas Eugubij in Etruria repertas dixi, Tabulæ. In Prima sunt hæc visuntur sculpta:
units.tr: Tablets with characters not very unlike those of the Eugubine tablets still exist at Perugia in Etruria, both the public one on a square stone and one on a certain private house, where urns bear inscriptions in Etruscan letters. Similar characters are also seen at Florence in the Palazzo della Signoria, on a ladder on the right foot of a certain statue of the Chimaera, which was moved from Arezzo to that place. But the seven remaining tablets, which I said were found at Gubbio in Etruria, present, written in Latin letters, specimens of the Etruscan language beyond dispute, though already gradually degenerating from the old form. The first of these tablets has the following carved on it:

ANGIOMP SOMO PORSEI NESIMEI VAPIRSVS AVILIIOEI EST EIST ANGIVIOSGMO VAPETEAVIENCIV IODCOMETYDER ANGIVTO HONDOMV.ASAMB DEVLIA.TODCOME TVDERLINE.TODCEIR.TVDERVS SEII ODRVHPEI. SERITV
units.tr: (The Etruscan inscription is printed in capitals as in the original. Its words cannot be rendered into English, and the author himself says that not even Oedipus could divine its meaning.)

units.la: Et quæ sequuntur. Quid autem sibi velint, ne Oedipus quidem, nisi forte Hebraici Rhetericque sermonis singulariter peritus, divinare posset. Hæc de Tusca lingua. Eius Species putantur Rhætia, Falisca, & si quæ fuerint aliæ. Ex Rhætica commodior dicendi erit locus in mea Germania. Falisci Etruriæ erant populi. Quemadmodum autem Tusculanus, Latii incolis Tertius, Sevirus, & Septenatus Festi dicebantur dies, quod post Tertium, Sextum, Septimum Iduum celebrarentur, ut ex Verrio scribit lib. xv. Festus; sic, eodem ibi notante, apud Falisios appellabatur, quod post diem decimum Iduum, Decimatus. Apud eosdem Falisios, memoriæ prodit ex Verrio Festus, diem Festum fuisse, qui vocabatur Struppearia; cauillam addens, quod coronati ambularent: & ab Tusculano, quod in pulvinari imponatur Castoris, Struppum nominari. Docent Exempla hæc duo Falisci Etruriæ & Tusculani Latii populis in Sermone multa tuisse communia. Iam Umbrorum Linguam Etruscam etiam censeo fuisse Dialectum; eo magis, quod octo Tabulæ, quas ante monui, Etrusca Lingua conceptas, & earum unam Etrusco quoque Charactere, Eugubii, quod Umbriæ oppidum, fuerint inventæ. Umbria certe Lingua Strebula Plauto appellantur apud Festum Covendice Hirsarum.
units.tr: And what follows. But what these words mean, not even Oedipus could guess, unless perhaps he were uniquely skilled in the Hebrew and Rhaetic tongues. So much for the Tuscan language. Its varieties are thought to be Rhaetian, Faliscan, and any others there may have been. A more convenient place to speak of the Rhaetian will come in my Germany. The Falisci were a people of Etruria. Just as the Tusculans, a tribe of Latium, called certain days the Tertius, Sevirus, and Septenatus festivals, because they were celebrated after the third, sixth, and seventh of the Ides, as Festus writes from Verrius in book 15, so, according to the same author, among the Falisci it was called the Decimatus, because it fell after the tenth day before the Ides. Festus also records from Verrius that among the same Falisci there was a festival day called the Struppearia, which he explains by the joke that people walked about crowned; and that it was named Struppum after the Tusculan practice of placing it on the couch of Castor. These two examples show that the Faliscan people of Etruria and the Tusculan people of Latium had many things in common in their speech. I also think the language of the Umbrians was a dialect of Etruscan, all the more because the eight tablets I mentioned earlier, written in the Etruscan language, with one of them also in Etruscan characters, were found at Iguvium, a town of Umbria. Certainly, in the Umbrian language, Plautus's "strebula" is called, in Festus, "Covendice Hirsarum."

units.la: Ligurum porro Linguam, quæ ex præscripta Synopsi restat, mere fuisse Gallicam, una vox probare potest Lodinus, qua Padum dici solum Liguribus scribit Plinius, quod fundo carerer. Eadem certe Gallis antiquis, hodieque Germaniæ & Inferioris & Superioris Populis nihil aliud, quam Fundus.
units.tr: Furthermore, that the language of the Ligurians which remains from the stated survey was purely Gallic, one word can prove: Lodinus writes that Pliny says the Po was called by the Ligurians alone "Padus", because it lacked a bottom. Certainly the same word means nothing other than "bottom" (fundus) for the ancient Gauls, and today for the peoples of Lower and Upper Germany.

units.la: Quales hodie per Italiam meo iudicio Linguæ fuerint, aliquo modo indicavi: restat, ut quibus Gradibus ad Communem Italicam devenitum, videamus. Lingua Latina, exiguus olim ut ipsa Gens, docente C. L. V. Liplio de Recta eius Pronunciatione, finibus contenta, circa Romam fere & finitima infero Tiberi hæsit. Italiam ceteram adeo non pervasit, ut, quemadmodum plene dictum doctumque, hinc Tuscii Liguresque, inde Magnæ Græciæ Incolæ aliique suæ indolis usi fuerint & diversissimo ab hac Sermone: quem diu, auctoritate etiam Imperio, tenuerunt. Nam Romanis etsi arma inferre finitimis acris cura fuit: non etiam Mores, Sacra, Linguam; quin contra aliquamdiu arcuisse illa videntur, & communicari ea cum aliis centuisse non pro bono. Certe ut Beneventum tandem indulserunt, & ad eam rem opus venia fuit, ac permissa. Livius lib. xl: Cumanis (Græca ipsorum Lingua fuit: quia Colonia Græcanica eo anno petentibus permissum, ut publice exaudiendum hoc de Scriptis Decretis Publicis) Latine loquerentur, Græcisque Latine vendendi usu esset. Narrat hoc Livius subannum 10 xxiii ab V. Caut videatur etiam tunc post Punica bella, finibus valde auctis haud valde auxilie Lingua. At mox immensum & diu coercita, velut rupto obice, se effudit: occasione quidem & causa duplici. Municipium primum Coloniarum, deinde Communione Civitatis. Nam de Coloniis, quum Romani eas spargerent, firmando Imperio per omnes Gentes: necessario una etiam Lingua spargebatur: quia numerosi illi Coloni, vel æquabant plerumque, vel superabant Civium Veterum partem. Ita si Commercia aut Colloquia inter eos futura aliorumque in aliorum Linguam migrare paulatim erat necesse: & quos potius, quam qui Victi? Hæc ratio incredibile, quam cito, quam late diffuderit Romanum hunc Sermonem. Quod ad Civitatis Communionem: Donati namque Civitatis Iure honeste cofrui non poterant sine Conscientia Linguae: non videbantur merito Cives Romani haberi censerique posse, nisi Romane & intelligerent & sonarent. Quin Nescisse id non turpe solum, sed periculo nunc tum: ut extent Exempla ob noxam hanc unam ademtæ Civitatis. Claudius Imperator, docente Suetonio in eius Vita cap. xvi: Splendidum Virum Græcaque Provincia Principem, verum Latini Sermonis ignarum, non modo Albo Iudicum erasit, sed etiam in Peregrinitatem redegit. Iaque Romani honorem suum agi palam censebant in honore suæ Linguæ. Itaque Legatis quidem, ut refert Valerius Maximus lib. II. cap. xi, Gentium exterarum permissum in Curia, nisi per Interpretem loqui: ipsaque Latine semper Responsa data. Idque servatum, non in Urbe tantum nostra, ait Valerius, sed etiam in Græcia & Asia: quo fulcret Latina fana Vocis honos per omnes Gentes venerabilior diffunderetur. Haec in Titulo Crucis Domini, quem scripsit Pilatus, Hebraice, Graece, Latine, primum obtinuit locum, uti testatur Nicolaus Papa in Epistola ad Michaelem Imperat. Tomo III Concilior. his verbis: Haec cum Hebraei & Graeca in Titulo Domini a reliquis discreta, insignem Principatum tenens, omnibus Nationibus praedicat IESVM NAZARENVM REGEM IVDAEORVM. Ego tamen hic timidior, quum alium in recensendis Linguis Ordinem Evangelistas observasse video: quos tamen volunt quidam non ordinem sequutos fuisse, sed tantum quod factum esset, insinuasse. Murcianus Imperator in Chalcedonensi Concilio, coram amplissimo Patrum Conventu concionaturus, licet homo Graecus, & inter Graecos, & in ditione Graecorum, eamdem Orationem Latine prius, postmodum Graece dixit, ut ex ipsius Synodi Actis constat. Legati etiam Romanae Ecclesiae Literas Romanorum Pontificum, ad Synodos Graecorum Episcoporum conscriptas, nonnisi Latine legi, ac coram omnibus ex scripto recitari iubere consueverunt: & nisi flagitantibus eius Concessus Episcopis, Graece reddere. Fidem facit vel unus ex Legatis Romanae Sedis Philippus Presbyter in Concilio Oecumenico Ephesino, ubi, recitatis Celestini Papae Litteris Latine scriptis, universi Episcopi petierunt, ut eadem Epistola Graece translata denuo recitaretur: tuncque interloquutus scribitur his verbis Philippus Legatus: Vetus consuetudo habet, ut Apostolica Sedis Diplomata Latine proponantur: & hoc fieri esse solet. Nunc vero quoniam Beatitudo vestra (ut Legitur) ut alterae aliae Graece itidem relegantur, necesse fuit vestra Beatitudini deferri satisfacere. Testatur etiam Nicolaus Papa, quem dixi, scribens ad Imperatorem Michaelem, penes Graecos in Missis celebrandis eam semper viguisse consuetudinem: ut tam Lectiones Evangelicae, quam Apostolicae, primum Latine, inde Graece eadem in Ecclesia publice recitarentur. Praesides Provinciarum aut Praetores non nisi Latine ius dicebant, &, quidquid publice, efferri solitum ea Lingua. Scripsit de Tiberio Suetonius cap. LXXI. Sermone Graeco quamquam alias promptus & faciliS, non tamen usque adeo usus est: abstinuitque maxime in Senatu, adeo quidem, ut Monopolium romanum, venia postulata, quod sibi Verbo percegrino uti non esset: atque in quodam Decreto Patrum, cum ἐμβολα recitaretur, commutandam censuerit vocem, & pro Peregrina Nostratem requirendam, aut si non reperiretur, pluris in & per ambitum Verborum rem ennuntiandam. Militem quoque Graece Testimonium interrogatum, nisi Latine respondere vetuit. Eadem fere de ipso testatur Dio lib. Histor. Rom. LVII. Bene igitur & vere Augustinus lib. XIX. de Civitate Dei, cap. VIII: Data est opera, ut Civitas imperata non solum Iugum, verum etiam Linguam suam domitis Gentibus per societatem (corrigendum censet Vir Magnus Iustus Lipsius, societatis aut certe, speciem societatis) imponeret. At Plinius lib. III. naturalis hist cap. V. Beneficentiam id accipit & in Italiae laudibus ponit: quod tot Populorum diversi ordines ferusque Linguas Sermonis commercio contraxerit ad Colloquia, & humanitatem hominum dederit. Sic sensum sparsa haec Lingua Bono generis humani, tam longe, late, ut Plutarchus scripserit omnes fere homines, suo aevo, ea usos. Pauca, sed notanda eius verba, in Quaestionibus Platonicis, haec, ὡς ὀχλα μεν ἀεὶ ταῦτα λέγει, ... ἀθωωσι χρῶν. Avide Asia Europaque nā versus Occidentem & Septemtriones maxime est (parva) arripuerunt: & inducto novo, paullatim abolitum iverunt Veterem Sermonem De Asu Apuleius in Floridis index. & Augustinus, Cyprianus, aliique, qui Plebem in Sacris Conventibus adloquuti Latine. Exstant Conciones. De Gallis, & quidem iam inde ab Augusti aevo, Strabo, quos negat dicendos ultra Barbaros, Μεταναστεύοντες τὴν πάλιν εἰς τὴν Ῥωμαίων τύχην καὶ τὴν γλῶτταν, τὴν βίος, πάντας δὲ καὶ τὴν πολιτείαν mutatos in Romanum morem & lingua & vitae, quibusdam & civili gubernatione. Spectat eo Ausonius in Mosella, Galliae Belgicae Fluvios:
units.tr: I have indicated in some measure, in my judgment, what kinds of languages there were throughout Italy: it remains to see by what steps the common Italian language was reached. The Latin language, once as small as the people itself, as C. L. V. Liplius teaches in his work on its correct pronunciation, kept within narrow limits and remained roughly around Rome and the neighbouring lands below the Tiber. It did not so far spread through the rest of Italy that, as is fully and learnedly said, the Tuscans and Ligurians on one side and the inhabitants of Magna Graecia on the other used their own character and a speech quite different from this one, which they long kept, even with the support of authority and empire. For although the Romans took keen care to carry arms against their neighbours, they did not in the same way carry their customs, rites and language; on the contrary, they seem for some time to have kept these away, and thought it wrong to share them with others. Certainly when they at last granted this to Beneventum, the matter needed and received permission. Livy, book xl: "The Cumaeans (their own language was Greek, because it was a Greek colony) were allowed, since they asked it that year, to speak Latin in public, and the use of Latin was to be applied to Greek public documents." Livy relates this in the year 523 from the founding of the city. Here it should be noted that even then, after the Punic wars and with the territory greatly enlarged, the language was not much helped. But soon, once the barrier was broken, it poured out, immensely and after long restraint: with a twofold occasion and cause, first the Latin colonies and then the common citizenship. For as the Romans spread their colonies to secure their empire over all peoples, the one language was necessarily spread with them, because those many colonists either equalled or mostly outnumbered the part of the old citizens. So if trade or conversation was to take place between them and others, it was necessary that others gradually pass over into their language; and which language would sooner be taken up than that of the victors? This method shows how incredibly quickly and widely it spread this Roman speech. As for the common citizenship: those who had been granted the rights of citizenship could not honourably enjoy them without knowledge of the language, and they could not rightly be regarded or counted as Roman citizens unless they both understood and spoke Latin. Indeed, not to know it was not only disgraceful but then also dangerous, so that there are examples of citizenship taken away for this one fault. The emperor Claudius, as Suetonius teaches in his Life, chapter xvi: "A distinguished man and the chief man of the Greek province, but ignorant of the Latin language, he not only struck from the roll of judges but even reduced to the status of a foreigner." And so the Romans openly held that their own honour was at stake in the honour of their language. Accordingly, Valerius Maximus, book II, chapter xi, reports that envoys of foreign nations were permitted in the Senate to speak only through an interpreter, and answers were always given in Latin itself. He says this was kept not only in our City but also in Greece and Asia, so that the honour of the Latin voice, a cause of strengthening, might spread more venerably among all nations. This priority was first held in the title of the Lord's Cross, which Pilate wrote in Hebrew, Greek and Latin, as Pope Nicholas testifies in his letter to the emperor Michael, in volume III of the Councils, in these words: Since the Hebrew and Greek were set apart from the rest in the title of the Lord, holding a distinguished primacy, they proclaim to all nations JESUS OF NAZARETH, KING OF THE JEWS. Yet I am more cautious here, since I see that the Evangelists followed another order in listing the languages; though some hold that they did not follow an order, but only indicated what had happened. The emperor Marcian, when about to preach at the Council of Chalcedon, before the most distinguished gathering of the Fathers, though he was a Greek man, among Greeks, and in the dominion of the Greeks, first spoke the same address in Latin and afterwards in Greek, as is clear from the Acts of that same Synod. Also the legates of the Roman Church, when letters of the Roman Pontiffs written for the synods of the Greek bishops were to be read, were accustomed to order that they be read only in Latin, and recited from the text before everyone, and rendered into Greek only if the bishops of that assembly demanded it. One legate of the Roman See, Philip the presbyter, bears witness to this in the Ecumenical Council of Ephesus, where, when the letters of Pope Celestine written in Latin had been read, all the bishops asked that the same letter, translated into Greek, be read again; and then Philip the legate is written as answering in these words: There is an old custom that the decrees of the Apostolic See are put forward in Latin, and this is usually done. But now, since your Blessedness (as is read) wishes the others also to be read again in Greek, it was necessary to satisfy your Blessedness. Pope Nicholas, whom I mentioned, also testifies, writing to the emperor Michael, that among the Greeks the custom always prevailed in celebrating Mass that both the Gospel and the Apostolic readings were read publicly in the church first in Latin, and then in Greek. The governors of provinces, or the praetors, pronounced judgment only in Latin, and whatever was customarily proclaimed publicly was carried out in that language. Suetonius wrote about Tiberius, chapter LXXI: "Although otherwise ready and fluent in the Greek language, he did not use it so much; and he abstained especially in the Senate, to such an extent that he asked pardon for the Roman custom, saying it was not his place to use a foreign word; and in a certain decree of the Fathers, when embola was being read, he judged that the word should be changed, and a native word sought instead of the foreign one, or, if none could be found, the matter should be expressed by a longer roundabout phrase." He also forbade a soldier, when questioned as a witness in Greek, to answer except in Latin. Dio, in book LVII of his Roman History, says much the same about him. Rightly and truly, then, Augustine, book XIX of The City of God, chapter VIII: "Care was taken that the ruling City should impose on the subdued nations not only her yoke but also her language, through a kind of association" (the great Justus Lipsius thinks it should be corrected to "association," or at least "the appearance of association"). But Pliny, book III of his Natural History, chapter V, takes it as a benefit and places it among the praises of Italy: "because it has drawn together the diverse orders of so many peoples and their wild tongues into a common conversation of speech, and given humanity to men." In this way the language, spread far and wide, has become a good of the human race; so much so that Plutarch wrote that almost all men in his age used it. His few but noteworthy words in the Platonic Questions are these: Ὡς ὄχλα μὲν ἀεὶ ταῦτα λέγει [as the crowd always says these things] ... ἀθωωσι χρῶν [using it without blame]. Eagerly Asia and Europe, and especially the regions toward the West and North, seized it, and once it was introduced, they gradually let the old speech go; Apuleius in the Florida, and Augustine, Cyprian and others who addressed the common people in the sacred assemblies in Latin, bear witness; their sermons survive. Concerning the Gauls, and indeed from the age of Augustus onward, Strabo, who denies that they should be called barbarians any longer, says that they had changed μεταναστεύοντες τὴν πάλιν εἰς τὴν Ῥωμαίων τύχην καὶ τὴν γλῶτταν, τὴν βίος, πάντας δὲ καὶ τὴν πολιτείαν [changing over to the Roman fortune and language, the way of life, and indeed the civil government], into Roman custom both in language and in life, and in some respects in civil government. Ausonius, in the Moselle, looks to this when he speaks of the rivers of Gallia Belgica:

units.la: Aemula te Latiae decorat facundia Linguae.
units.tr: Your rival eloquence adorns you, the eloquence of the Latin tongue.

units.la: De Hispanis idem Strabo: Οἱ πρὸς τὴν Βαῖτιν, πάλιν εἰς τὴν Ῥωμαίων μετασχόντες, τρόπον, ὥστε τὴν Διαλεκτόν σφέτερος ἐν μεμινῆμαι. De Pannoniis Velleius: In omnibus Pannoniis non disciplina tantum, sed Linguae quoque notitia Romanae. Nec ambigendum etiam de Britannis, ex Iuvenale: Gallia Causidicos docuit facunda Britannos.
units.tr: Strabo says the same of the Spaniards: "Those near the Baetis, having changed to Roman ways, have even forgotten their own language" [Οἱ πρὸς τὴν Βαῖτιν, πάλιν εἰς τὴν Ῥωμαίων μετασχόντες, τρόπον, ὥστε τὴν Διαλεκτόν σφέτερος ἐν μεμινῆμαι]. Of the Pannonians Velleius writes: In all Pannonia there was not only discipline but also knowledge of the Roman language. There is no doubt either about the Britons, from Juvenal: "Eloquent Gaul taught the British advocates."

units.la: qui idem quoque, etsi per Satyricum risum, ostendit de Thule. Germanorum denique plerosque Latinae sermoni fuisse gnaros ex aliquot locis patet doctissimi Scriptoris, Cornelii Taciti. Testantur etiam praeclarum hoc diffundendi studium Provinciales, quas Romani passim instituebant, Scholas, quales fuisse notavi Lugduni, Augustoduni, aliisque
units.tr: He also shows this, though in a satirical jest, about Thule. Finally, that most of the Germans were acquainted with the Latin language is clear from several passages of the most learned writer, Cornelius Tacitus. The eager spread of learning is also attested by the provincial schools which the Romans set up everywhere, of the kind I noted were at Lyon, Autun and other places

units.la: Mosellae Ausonii locus. lijsque locis & fuisse, dicam, in Batavia, haud procul Lugduno. Habebant huiusmodi Scholae suos Prefectos; in quorum numero fuit Latinus Pacatus, cuius extat ad Constantinum Imper. Panegyris. Inter eos etiam perhibetur fuisse Lactantius Firmianus, qui Crispum Caesarem, Constantini Augusti F. in Gallia docuit. Romanis omnes, qui alia, quam ipsorum Lingua utebantur, Barbari erant, praeter Graecos. Cicero in Epist. ad Q. Fratrem Afros, Gallos, Hispanos appellat Barbaros. Vegetius lib. II. de Re militari, cap. 11. Barbaricis Nationibus continet Gallos & Celtiberos.
units.tr: [Passage of Ausonius' Mosella.] and also in other places, I say, in Batavia, not far from Lyon. Such schools had their own prefects; among their number was Latinus Pacatus, whose panegyric to the Emperor Constantine survives. Among them too is said to have been Lactantius Firmianus, who taught Crispus Caesar, son of the Emperor Constantine, in Gaul. To the Romans all who used a language other than their own were barbarians, except the Greeks. Cicero, in his letter to his brother Quintus, calls Africans, Gauls and Spaniards barbarians. Vegetius, in book II of On Military Affairs, chapter 11, includes Gauls and Celtiberians among the barbaric nations.

units.la: Sparsa iam per Gentes tam varias, variavit & ipsa, nec patrium illum colorem diu tenuit, aut succum. Nec mirum. Ipsos Italos ab germanitate illa abiisse fatetur M. Tullius lib. III. de Oratore, quae in Romanu Praenestinos, ut ante dixi, Plautinus ille irridet in Truculento, Voces Tantum modo & Ciceriam vitiose efferentes. Pronunciationem germanam, suisque omnibus partibus inlaesam, peregre in Exteros migrasse verisimile est. & si quid germani fuerit, Hostes illud corruperunt & Barbari Gothi, Hunni, Vandali, aliique Septemtrionaliores (de Langobardis quidam addunt, sed falso. Eos enim eorumque Reges non solum Latinas, Graecasque Litteras supra modum fuisse delectatos; sed etiam Instituta Romanorum diligenter observasse, memoriae produnt illius aevi Scriptores, cum Galliae Hispaniaeque, tum Italiae non Arma solum intulerunt, sed Mores etiam & Linguam corruptis cum Pronunciatione, Verborumque sonis; saepe ex Varia face, miscella quadam & nova Lingua. Hinc origo Italicae, Gallicae, Hispanicae: in quibus clara Latiae Vestigia, semenque prisci ortus. Igitur Festus iure scripsit: Latine loqui a Latio dictum est, quae Loquutio adeo est versa, ut nec ulla eius pars maneat in nostris. Quae, fere est, ut asserant ante mille annos in usu & Vita fuisse Italicum Sermonem, languido aut emortuo Latino. Paret idem aliquo modo ex Narratione, quae in Historia Miscella, de rebus sub Mauritio Imperatore gestis In Exercitu, ait, quum animans cecidisset, clamante quodam TORNA, TORNA FRATER, unius sui Copias in fugam versus, ami quo illo Vocis Agnoscitur hic clare Italicismus. Argumentum etiam perspicuum ab Instrumento, quod Lutetiae in Bibliotheca Regis, quo Transactio continetur Stephani Tutoris cum Gratiano Pupillo scripta anno Iustinianae Imperij XXXVIII, & scripta hac vulgare Lingua: sed horridiore Paulli: tim enim ita ab Magnis Viris culta, ut ea hodie nihil elegantius, nihil tersius apud Tuscos praesertim in Agris Senesi & Florentino. Non magnopere mutarunt, quae scribit lib. II. Geograph. Sebastianus Munsterus. Littorali, inquit, Istriae era Veneta plurimum utitur Lingua, quae comta est & gravi, pluriumque Linguarum flore conflata, quod facile contigit in frequentissimo Italicarum Gentium commercio. Olim multo simplicior fuit, ac minus auribus grata. Carnicus Sermo plures sonat Linguas, & aliquid ab Italico diversum: dulcior auditu, quo Tarvisium, Patavium, Verona, Vincentia, Mantua, Ferraria, aluntur; sed in his Urbibus gratior Agrestii, Ravennae, Bononiae, & universa Aemiliae & Flaminiae Venustius Sermo: Picenis & Marsis crassior: Apulis, Lucanis, & Brutiis, ceteraque Italiae rudior Lingua, ac minus peregrinis imbuta, praeter Neapolim, ubi plerique Hispanicum adfectant. In Calabria corruptior est, quam ulla pars locorum. Haec ille. Quod de Calabrorum, idem etiam de Foro-Iuliensium Sermone dicere liceat. Pars Rhetorum, qui Alpes, inter Helvetiam & Galliam Cis-Alpinam, Helvetiis confoederati, incolunt, sua utuntur Lingua, Vetere illa, ut ante dixi, poteaque sum dictus, Tusca; sed quae, quo Italiae propior, Vocibus Italis mirum in modum, praecipue in Sacris, est infarcta: aut Italicismi species fere videatur. Scribit item Aeneas Pius, Valachos etiam Romanum esse Sermonem, sed magna ex parte mutatum, & Homini Italico vix intelligibilem. Succedit iam nunc Lingua Porтopиa, qua pleraque hodie utitur Etruria Exemplar, cum in Sanctissima illa IESV CHRISTI, pro Nobis mox morituri, ad Patrem Coelestem Precatione, tum, ut alibi factum, in Oratione Dominica, commisa cum hodierno non modo Foro-Iuliensium, corrupte loquentium: sed etiam Rhetorum, Italicissimum adfectantium Sermone.
units.tr: Once scattered among so many diverse peoples, the language itself also changed, and it did not long keep its native colour or flavour. Nor is this surprising. Marcus Tullius, in book III of De Oratore, admits that the Italians themselves had departed from that purity, which the Plautine comedian mocks in the Truculentus in the Romans of Praeneste, as I said before, who mispronounced the words tantum modo and Ciceriam. It is likely that the native pronunciation, intact in all its parts, migrated abroad among foreigners; and if anything of the genuine speech remained, enemies corrupted it, namely the barbarian Goths, Huns, Vandals, and other more northern peoples. (Some add the Lombards, but falsely. Writers of that age record that they and their kings were not only greatly delighted with Latin and Greek letters beyond measure, but also observed Roman institutions carefully.) Those who invaded Gaul and Spain, as well as Italy, brought not only arms but also customs and language, corrupting it in pronunciation and in the sounds of words; often from this various mixture a new and mixed speech arose. Hence the origin of the Italian, French and Spanish tongues, in which clear traces of Latin and the seed of their ancient origin remain. Therefore Festus rightly wrote: "To speak Latin" is named from Latium, but the speech has been so changed that no part of it remains in our own. Thus, as they assert, about a thousand years ago the Italian speech was in use and in life, with Latin languishing or dead. The same appears in some way from the narrative in the Historia Miscella about events under the Emperor Maurice: in the army, it says, when a certain animal had fallen, someone shouted TORNA, TORNA FRATER, and the troops of one of his own side turned in flight. From that cry an Italianism is clearly recognised here. There is also a clear proof from the document that is kept at Paris in the King's Library, containing the agreement of Stephen the Tutor with Gratian the Ward, written in the thirty-eighth year of Justinian's reign, and written in this vernacular language, but rougher than in Paulus; for then it had not yet been cultivated by great men as it is now, so that nothing today is more elegant or polished, especially among the Tuscans in the countryside of Siena and Florence. Not much changed is what Sebastian Münster writes in book II of his Geography: "The Littoral of Istria, which is Venetian territory, uses mostly a language that is elegant and weighty, blended from the flower of many languages, which easily happens in the very frequent commerce of Italian peoples. Formerly it was much simpler and less pleasing to the ear. The Carnic speech sounds more than one language, and something different from Italian; it is sweeter to hear, and it is the speech of Treviso, Padua, Verona, Vicenza, Mantua and Ferrara. But in these cities a more pleasing speech is found; in Ravenna, Bologna, and throughout Emilia and Flaminia the speech is more charming. Among the Picentes and Marsi it is cruder; among the Apulians, Lucanians and Bruttians, and the rest of Italy, the language is ruder and less imbued with foreign elements, except at Naples, where most affect Spanish. In Calabria it is more corrupt than in any other part of the region." So he. What is said of the Calabrians may also be said of the speech of the Friulians. A part of the Rhaetians, who live in the Alps between Helvetia and Cisalpine Gaul, allied to the Helvetians, use their own language, that old Tuscan one, as I said before and as I have since called it; but the closer it is to Italy, the more wonderfully it is stuffed with Italian words, especially in sacred matters, or it looks almost like a kind of Italianism. Aeneas Silvius also writes that the Wallachians too speak a Roman speech, but largely changed and scarcely intelligible to an Italian. Now comes the Tuscan language, which most of Etruria uses today, as an example, both in that most holy prayer of Jesus Christ, about to die for us, to the heavenly Father, and, as is done elsewhere, in the Lord's Prayer, compared with the present-day speech not only of the Friulians, who speak corruptly, but also of the Rhaetians, who affect the most Italian speech.

units.la: Ardentissimæ Iesv Christi Redemtione ignominiosissimæ Patrem Precatio. Joann.
units.tr: The most fervent prayer of Jesus Christ to the Father at his most ignominious redemption. John.

units.la: Italice.
units.tr: In Italian.

units.la: QVeste cose disse Iesv; poi alzò gli occhi suoi al Cielo, edisse Padre, l'Hora è venuta, glorifica il tuo Figliuolo, acciocche il tuo Figliuolo glorifichi Te.
units.tr: These things Jesus spoke; then he lifted up his eyes to heaven and said: Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son, so that your Son may glorify you.

units.la: Si come tu gli hai data Potestà sopra ogni carne, a sin ch'ei dui vita aterna a tutti quelli, che Tu gli hai dati.
units.tr: Just as you have given him power over all flesh, that he may give eternal life to all those whom you have given him.

units.la: E questa è la Vita aterna, che conoscano Te solo vero Iddio, & colui che Tu hai mandato, cioè, Iesv Christo.
units.tr: And this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and him whom you have sent, Jesus Christ.

units.la: Io Ti ho glorificato sopra la Terra, ho finito l'Opera che tu mi hai data à fare.
units.tr: I have glorified you on the earth; I have finished the work that you gave me to do.

units.la: Et hora tu Padre, glorificami appresso Te medesimo, con la Gloria, laquale Io havevo appresso di Te prima che il Mondo fusse.
units.tr: And now, Father, glorify me with yourself, with the glory that I had with you before the world existed.

units.la: Io ho manifestato il tuo Nome a gli Huomini, che Tu mi hai dati del Mondo. Essi erano tuoi, & Tu Me gli hai dati, & hanno osservata la tua Parola.
units.tr: I have made your name known to the men whom you gave me out of the world. They were yours, and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word.

units.la: Essi hanno hora conosciuto che tutto ciò che Tu mi hai dato, è da Te.
units.tr: Now they have come to know that everything you have given me is from you.

units.la: Percioche lo ho date loro le Parole che Tu hai date a me, & essi le hanno ricevute, & hanno veramente conosciuto, che lo sono uscito da Te, & hanno creduto che Tu mi hai mandato.
units.tr: For I have given them the words that you gave me, and they have received them, and have truly known that I came out from you, and have believed that you sent me.

units.la: Io prego per loro: Non prego già per il Mondo, ma per quelli che Tu mi hai dati: perciochè sono Tuoi.
units.tr: I pray for them. I do not pray for the world, but for those whom you have given me, because they are yours.

units.la: E tutto ciò ch'è Mio è Tuo, & il Tuo è Mio: & sono stato glorificato in essi.
units.tr: And all that is mine is yours, and what is yours is mine; and I have been glorified in them.

units.la: Et già Io non son più nel Mondo, ma essi sono nel Mondo, & lo vengo à te.
units.tr: And now I am no longer in the world, but they are in the world, and I am coming to you.

units.la: Padre ISTI, mox pro Generis Humani ima Crucis Morte mactandi, ad is cap. XVII.
units.tr: Holy Father, who is about to be put to death for the human race by the lowest death of the cross; see chap. XVII.

units.la: Latine.
units.tr: In Latin.

units.la: HÆc loquutus est Iesus; & sublevatis oculis in Cœlum, dixit: Pater, venit Hora, clarifica Filium tuum, ut Filius tuus clarificet Te.
units.tr: Jesus spoke these things, and, lifting up his eyes to heaven, said: Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son, that your Son may glorify you.

units.la: Sicut dedisti ei Potestatem omnis Carnis, ut omne quod dedisti ei, det eis, Vitam æternam.
units.tr: As you have given him power over all flesh, so that he may give eternal life to all whom you have given him.

units.la: Hæc est autem Vita æterna, ut cognoscant Te solum verum DEVM, & quem misisti, IESVM CHRISTVM.
units.tr: Now this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and him whom you have sent, Jesus Christ.

units.la: Ego te clarificavi super Terram; Opus consummavi, quod dedisti Mihi, ut faciam.
units.tr: I have glorified you on the earth; I have finished the work that you gave me to do.

units.la: Et nunc, Tu Pater, clarifica Me apud Temetipsum, Claritate, quam habui apud Te, prius quam Mundus esset.
units.tr: And now, Father, glorify me with yourself, with the glory that I had with you before the world was.

units.la: Manifestavi Nomen Tuum Hominibus, quos dedisti Mihi de Mundo. Tui erant, & Mihi eos dedisti, & servaverunt Sermonem tuum.
units.tr: I have manifested your name to the men whom you gave me out of the world. They were yours, and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word.

units.la: Nunc cognoverunt, quia omnia, quæ dedisti Mihi, abs Te sunt.
units.tr: Now they have known that all things which you have given me are from you.

units.la: Quia Verba, quæ dedisti Mihi, dedi eis; & ipsi acceperunt, & cognoverunt vere, quia à Te exivi, & crediderunt, quia Tu Me misisti.
units.tr: Because the words that you gave me I have given to them; and they have received them, and have truly known that I came out from you, and they have believed that you sent me.

units.la: Ego pro eis rogo: Non pro Mundo rogo, sed pro his, quos dedisti Mihi, quia sunt Tui:
units.tr: I pray for them. I do not pray for the world, but for those whom you have given me, because they are yours.

units.la: Et Mea omnia Tua sunt; & Tua Mea sunt: & clarificatus sum in eis.
units.tr: And all my things are yours, and yours are mine; and I have been glorified in them.

units.la: Et iam non sum in Mundo; & hi sunt in Mundo, & Ego venio ad Te.
units.tr: And now I am no longer in the world; but these are in the world, and I am coming to you.

units.la: Padre, Io desidero che quelli, che Tu M'hai dati, là doue sono Io, siano ancor essi con meco, acciocche contemplino la Gloria mia, laquâl Tu M'hai data, percioche tu M'hai amato innanzi à la fondation del Mondo.
units.tr: Father, I desire that those whom you have given me, where I am, may be with me also, so that they may behold my glory, which you have given me, because you loved me before the foundation of the world.

units.la: Pater, quos dedisti Mihi, volo, ut, ubi sum Ego, & illi sint mecum; ut videant Claritatem Meam, quam dedisti Mihi: quia dilexisti Me ante constitutionem Mundi.
units.tr: Father, those whom you have given me, I wish that, where I am, they too may be with me; that they may see my glory, which you have given me, because you loved me before the foundation of the world.

units.la: Padre giusto, il Mondo non T'ha conosciuto; ma Io T'ho conosciuto; & questi hanno conosciuto, che Tu M'hai mandato.
units.tr: Righteous Father, the world has not known you; but I have known you, and these have known that you sent me.

units.la: Pater iuste, Mundus Te non cognovit, Ego autem Te cognovi; & hi cognoverunt, quia Tu Me misisti.
units.tr: Righteous Father, the world has not known you, but I have known you; and these have known that you sent me.

units.la: Et Io ho fatto conoscer loro il Tuo Nome, & farollo conoscere: acciocche l'Amore, colquale Tu M'hai amato, sia in loro, & Io in essi.
units.tr: And I have made known to them your name, and I will make it known, so that the love with which you loved me may be in them, and I in them.

units.la: Et notum feci eis Nomen Tuum, & notum faciam: ut Dilectio, qua dilexisti Me, in ipsis sit, & Ego in eis.
units.tr: And I have made your name known to them, and I will make it known, that the love with which you loved me may be in them, and I in them.

units.la: Oratio Dominica,
units.tr: The Lord's Prayer,

units.la: Italorum, | Foro Iuliensium, | Rhetorum, | Latinorum PADRE Nostro, che sei ne Cieli, | PATRI Nostri, ch'e in Cyl. | BAB Nos, qui es in Cbefil, | PATER Noster, qui es in Coelis; Sia santificato il Tuo Nome. | Sanctificatur In Te Nom. | Sanctificetur Nomen Tuum. | Sanctificetur Nomen Tuum. Venga il Tuo Regno. | Veniat Regnum Tuum. | Veniat Regnum Tuum. Sia fatta la Tua Volontà, sì come in Cielo, così ancora in Terra. | Fiat Voluntas Tua, quemadmodum in Coelo, & in Terra. Dacci oggi il nostro Pane cotidiano. | Danos hac' i nostri Pan cotidian. | Da nobis hodie. | Panem nostrum quotidianum da nobis hodie. Et rimettici i Nostri Debiti, sì come anco Noi gli rimettiamo a i nostri Debitori. | Et perdona Nos glu nostri Debi, sic Nos perdonamus agl Nostri Debitori. | Pardona a Nos nos Debiti, sic Nos fam a Nos Debitoris. | Et dimitte Nobis Debita nostra, sicut & Nos dimittimus Debitoribus Nostris. E non ci indurre in Tentatione: | Et ne Nos inducas in Tentationem. Ma liberaci dal Male. Amen. | Ma libera Nos dal Mal. Amen. | Dimi per.. liberaci dal male. Amen. | Sed libera Nos à Malo. Amen.
units.tr: Italian | Friulian | Rhetian | Latin: Our Father, who art in heaven; Hallowed be your name. | Hallowed be your name. | Hallowed be your name. | Hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come. | Your kingdom come. | Your kingdom come. | Your kingdom come. Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. | Your will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth. | Your will be done, as in heaven and on earth. | Your will be done, as in heaven and on earth. Give us today our daily bread. | Give us this day our bread for each day. | Give us today. | Give us this day our daily bread. And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors. | And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. | Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. | And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors. And lead us not into temptation. | And lead us not into temptation. | And lead us not into temptation. | And lead us not into temptation. But deliver us from evil. Amen. | But deliver us from evil. Amen. | Deliver us from evil. Amen. | But deliver us from evil. Amen.

units.la: Addam hic ex Membrana illa, quam ante memoravi, quales in Loquela pleri-que tint Itali. Scriptum ibi inter alia: In Oratione Florentini inepti; Venetis putidi; Senenses, suaves; Bergomates, agrestes; Perutini, facetti. Spoletani, celeres; Novocomenses, balbi; Romani, clari; Consentini, dicaces; Narnienses, promti; Umbri, leves; Novarienses, rustici; Mediolanenses, rudes; Genuenses, ridiculi; Ferrarienses, inexhausti. Brixienses, duri. Bononienses, jucundi; Fulgmates, versuti, Capuani, graves; Pistorienses, festivi; Neapolitani, taxabundi; Picenti, vary; Apuli, Barbari; Ligures, mendaces.
units.tr: I will add here, from that parchment which I mentioned before, the kinds of speech that most Italians have. It says there, among other things: Florentines in speech are silly; Venetians vulgar; Sienese pleasant; Bergamasks rustic; Perugians witty; Spoletans quick; Como people stammering; Romans clear; Cosentines sharp-tongued; Narnians ready; Umbrians light; Novarese rustic; Milanese rough; Genoese ridiculous; Ferrarese inexhaustible; Brescians hard; Bolognese agreeable; Foligno people crafty; Capuans grave; Pistoians festive; Neapolitans chattering; Picentines varied; Apulians barbarous; Ligurians liars.

units.la: CAPUT XIX.
units.tr: CAPUT XIX.

units.la: Gubernatio Italorum Civilis & Politica.
units.tr: The Civil and Political Government of the Italians.

units.la: INCOLAS Italiae tamquam Gubernatos, coloribus adumbratos suis, explicui: flagitat ordo, ut Gubernantes illustrentur, tam qui priscis fuerunt, quam qui nostris sunt temporibus. Gubernationis & Imperij, sub quo vetustissimi fuerunt Italiæ Terræ Habitatores, non magna sunt apud Antiquos Scriptores Documenta, neque Notæ admodum indubitatæ. Ovum hic non quæram, nec temere fidem dabo tubernatis ab Annio Viterbiensi Auctoribus, Beroso, Manethoni, Q. Fabio, Myrsilo Lesbio, M. Catoni, C. Sempronio, & aliis. Multa eaque speciosa, Bonorum Scriptorum abusus auctoritate, sollicitatoque ad incredibilem patientiam suo Lectore, commentuerunt Vir ingeniosus quidem, sed ad gerras intricatque Imprudentioribus obtrundendas nimiumque compositus, de Comero, Primo in Regionem hanc Adversa, de Chamo, Iano, Sabatio Saga, Crano, Auruno, Malote Tage, Ofinde, Hercule, Tusco, Alteo, Kitim, Italo, Morgete, Roma, Romancspo, Iasio, & aliis; quorum apud probatos Historiarum Annaliumque Concinnatores nullum est vestigium. Quid igitur? Nihil hic dicere Timidi est: Omnia vero Temerarij: Si Magni Auctores non ausi quidquam in iis, quæ antiqua & ambigua, affirmare: certe nec ego temere audebo. Accipio, Fertur, Fama est, aliaque id genus (uti Græcis, ὡς ἀνκκα, κατα λέγεσι, & similia) excusabunt me, ut alios, ab Temeraria Eloquutione, & præcipiti fortean distinctione.
units.tr: I have described the inhabitants of Italy, sketched in their own colours, as the subjects of government. Order requires that the rulers also be set forth, both those of earlier times and those of our own. Concerning the government and empire under which the most ancient inhabitants of the land of Italy lived, the ancient writers offer no great records, and no very certain notices. I shall not seek the egg here, nor lightly give credit to the governments invented by Annius of Viterbo, and to the authors Berosus, Manetho, Q. Fabius, Myrsilus of Lesbos, M. Cato, C. Sempronius and others. That ingenious man, but one too well suited to confusing and crushing the less informed, has fabricated many splendid things, abusing the authority of good writers and wearing out his reader's patience past belief: concerning Comerus, the first to come to this region, Chamus, Janus, Sabatius Saga, Cranus, Auruncus, Malote Tage, Ofinde, Hercules, Tuscus, Alteus, Kitim, Italus, Morgetes, Roma, Romancspus, Iasius, and others; of whom there is no trace among the approved compilers of histories and annals. What then? To say nothing here is the mark of a timid man; to say everything is the mark of a rash one. If the great authors did not dare to affirm anything in matters so ancient and uncertain, then certainly I too shall not venture rashly. Expressions such as "I accept", "It is reported", "There is a tradition", and others of that kind (like the Greek ὡς ἔπος, κατὰ λέγεσι [as they say, as it is said] and similar), will excuse me, as they excuse others, from rash assertion and perhaps from hasty distinction.

units.la: Variorum igitur, cum Græcorum, tum Latinorum præcipuè Dionysij Halicarnassæi, Pompei Trogi, Solini Polyhistoris, & aliorum Monimentis diligenter perlustratis, didici multis ante Conditam Vrbem Ætatibus, varia Variorum in Italia Populorum, cum primis Siculorum; Aboriginum, Ligurum, Vmbrorum, Etruscorum vigusse Imperia: quæ cum ævo senescente vel in Romanorum ditionem, vel ad nihilum redacta: quibus gradibus, quam potero paucissimis indicabo.
units.tr: Therefore, having carefully gone through the monuments of various writers, both Greek and especially Latin, namely Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Pompeius Trogus, Solinus the Polyhistor, and others, I have learned that many ages before the founding of the City, various peoples in Italy, above all the Sicilians, the Aborigines, the Ligurians, the Umbrians and the Etruscans, enjoyed their own empires; these, as the age grew old, were either brought under the dominion of the Romans or reduced to nothing. I shall indicate, in as few steps as I can, by what stages this came about.

units.la: Nominat ante omnes Dionysius Halicarnassæus, quem dixi, lib. i Siculos, Barbaros tos agnoscens & gentem Indigenam. Aliunde tamen in Italiam venisse innuit Virgilius lib. viii Æneidos, versu cccxxviii, ubi Servius scribit Siceanos (sic enim Pœtæ dicuntur non ibi solum, sed & libro vii & xi) Siculo Duce, ex Hispania profectos in Italiam: eamque, exclusis Aboriginibus, tenuisse.
