Quamdiu Siculi fuerint dominati, qualemque habuerint Rep. formam, non constat. Ipsis certe docet idem Dionysius, diuturno bello victis, & in Insulam Trinacriam, quam inde Siculam ferunt nuncupatam, emotis Aboriginibus successisse. Manet nihilominus Regiom, in qua suas habuerant sedes, quæque post Magna Græcia fuit appellata, Sicilia nomen; manetque hodie in Principum Neapolitanorum Titulis, Sicilia cis Pharum vocata, ad differentiam Insulæ, quæ trans Pharum. Plinius hæc infra. Aborigines dicti, quasi sine origine, ut innuit Servius ad viii Æneidos; vel, ut ex Festo notat Paulus Diaconus, ab Errore, quasi Aberrigines; vel denique ab Montibus, quos Græci ὄρη vocant. Antiquissimi eorum Reges, quos ob Merita Deos grata fecit Posteritas, recensentur ab Dionysio, Iustino, aliisque, Janus & Saturnus. Janus, cuius Regis memi-nit Eusebius in Chronicis, Divum antiquissimum canitur Iuvenali Satyra vi. De eo cum alij, tum Macrobius lib. i. Saturnal. cap. ix. Saturnus, cuius, ut Regis, mentio apud eundem Eusebium, ad meliorem Vitæ rationem suos transduxisse memoratur Subditos. Certe quales sub eo Aborigines fuerint, scribunt Virgilius viii Æneid. Iustinus lib. xliii, Iuvenalis Satyra vi, & alij. Ab Saturno nomen retinuerunt Monte Saturnius, qui post Tarpeius & Capitolinus; inque eo oppidum Saturnia, cuius tria apud Varronem iv de L.L. vestigia; quemadmodum Ianiculum ab Iano. Utrumque reliquias monstrat Ænex Evander apud Virgilium libro, quem dixi, viii. Ab Saturno item Saturny Populi, Carmenque Saturnium Festo lib. xvii. Post Saturnum fama est regnasse Picum Priscum, Faunum Priscum, Latinum, & alios: de quibus Virgilius vii Æneidos; — — Rex Arva Latinus & Vrbes Iam senior longa placidas in pace regebat. Hunc Fauno & Nympha genitum Laurente Marica Accipimus, Fauno Picus pater, ipsque parentem Te Saturne refert, tu sanguinis ultimus Auctor.
units.tr: Dionysius of Halicarnassus, whom I have mentioned, in book i, names the Sicilians before all others, recognising them as barbarians and an indigenous people. Yet Virgil, in book viii of the Aeneid, at line 328, implies that they came into Italy from elsewhere, where Servius writes that the Siceani (for so the poets call them, not only there but also in books vii and xi) came from Spain under their leader Siculus into Italy, and held it, the Aborigines being shut out. How long the Sicilians ruled, and what form of commonwealth they had, is not established. Dionysius himself teaches that they were defeated in a long war and, the Aborigines having been removed, succeeded them in the island of Trinacria, which they are said to have called Sicily after themselves. Nevertheless the region in which they had their seats remains, and it was afterwards called Magna Graecia; the name Sicily remains, and it survives today in the titles of the Neapolitan princes, where it is called "Sicily this side of the Pharus", to distinguish it from the island which lies "beyond the Pharus". Pliny speaks of these matters below. The Aborigines are so called as if "without origin", as Servius hints on Aeneid viii; or, as Paulus the Deacon notes from Festus, from "error", as if "Aberrigines"; or finally from the mountains, which the Greeks call ὄρη. Their most ancient kings, whom posterity made gods on account of their merits, are listed by Dionysius, Justin and others: Janus and Saturn. Janus, whose king is mentioned by Eusebius in his Chronicles, is sung by Juvenal in Satire vi as the most ancient god; about him, among others, Macrobius, Saturnalia i, ch. ix. Saturn, whose kingship is likewise mentioned by the same Eusebius, is recorded as having led his subjects to a better way of life. Indeed, what the Aborigines were like under him is described by Virgil, Aeneid viii, Justin book xliii, Juvenal Satire vi, and others. From Saturn the Mons Saturnius, which came after the Tarpeian and Capitoline hills, retained its name, and in it the town of Saturnia, of which three traces are found in Varro, De lingua latina iv; just as the Janiculum takes its name from Janus. Evander, in Virgil, book viii, which I have cited, shows remains of both. From Saturn likewise come the Saturnian people and the Saturnian verse, in Festus book xvii. After Saturn, tradition says that Picus Priscus, Faunus Priscus, Latinus and others reigned; of whom Virgil, Aeneid vii: "King Latinus was ruling the fields and cities in peace, now aged and long." "We learn that he was born of Faunus and the nymph Marica of Laurentum; Picus, father of Faunus, and he himself refer you to Saturn, you the last author of the blood."

units.la: Consulendi & Iustinus lib. xliii. Suetonius in Vitellio cap. 1. Lactantius lib. 1. de falsa Relig. cap. xxii, Festus lib. xiii, Eusebius in Chronicis. Subditis autem Regum, quos memoravi, id est Aboriginibus adiunxerunt se paullatim, Dionysio Halicarlicarnassaeo, Sallustio, Solino scribentibus, Pelasgi, ex Peloponneso & Argis oriundi, a Pelasgo, Iovis & Niobes Filio, nominati: Secundo Arcades, ex urbe Arcadiae Pallanteo profecti: quorum Dux quum fuisset Euander, nonnihil etiam in his locis, adquisivit Gloriae. Nam Romanae conditor Arcis canitur Virgilio lib. viii: non quod Romam condiderit, sed quod fundamenta quasi futurae Urbi posuerit: condito ad Montem, qui post Palatinus, oppido Palanteo: de quo Virgilius, quem saepe dixi, libro viii, Iustinus lib. xli & Solinus cap. ii. Tertio Aborigenibus admisti leguntur Peloponnesiaci, Phenicae, Iberique, reduces cum victoria, Hercule Duce, ex Hispania: postque reditus in patriam desiderio. Adiociarunt te his Troiani, qui sub Laomedonte, bello Iliaco priore, fuerant ab Hercule capti. Quarto ad Aborigines se contulerunt Troiani, Troia diruta, Aeneas, Anchisae Veneriisque Filii (a quo Aenesi Veteribus appellati apud Festum lib. i. ductu & auspiciis in has oras compulsi. Hi ab Latino, cuius ante meminimus, cum suo Duce humaniter excepti, simulque Aborigines, quibus ille imperitabat, communi nomine Latini perhibenti nuncupati, Catone apud Servium ad i Aeneidos affirmante. Latinos hos Caseos nominat meus Ennius lib. i Annalium. Quum autem Aeneas Lavinium, unicam Latini Filiam, Uxorem duxisset, Turno, qui eam adamarat, Advenam sibi praelatum indignissime ferente, atrox ortum scribitur bellum; quo caesis non Turno solum, sed & Latino, Aeneas iure Successionis per Coniugem. Latinorum Rex factus, tres annos rerum tenuit gubernacula: condiitque de Coniugis nomine Lavinio, non amplius vitus (hoc de illo traditur) Successionem est nactus filium, qui dicebatur Euryleon Asca-nius cognomine Iulus, anno Troiani Excidii viii. Ab Iulo Iulia Gens Romae, uti testantur Virgilius i Aeneid, Ovidius iv Fast., Caesar apud Suetonium cap. vi, Isidorus lib. ix Etymolog. cap. iii. Ascanius, Alba condita, Albanorum condidit Regnum. Fatis functo successerunt ut notant Dionysius Halic. lib. i, Livius lib. i, Virgilius lib. vi Aeneidos, Ovidius lib. iiii Fastorum & xiiii Metamorph. Eusebius, Cassiodorus, Metlala Corvinus, Auctor Originis Augustae, meusque ad i Annalium Ennii Commentarius nobilissima serie Silvius a quo Reges Albani omnes Silvy cognominati, testibus eodem Virgilio vi Aeneidos, Festo lib. xvii & Isidoro lib. ix cap. iii; Aeneas quem a pietate & armis celebrat idem Poeta lib. vii; Latinus, Alba, Capetus (qui Livio Atys) Capis, Calpetus (alias Capetus iii) Tiberinus, qui nomen dedit Fluvio fertur in quo submersus; Agrippa (Remulus Ovidio) Alladius (Acrota Ovidio, Romulus Livio Aventinus, quem male Aborigenum Regem vocat Servius; Procas, qui Troianae gloriae gentis Virgilio lib. vi Aeneidos. Procas, duobus procreatis Filiis, Numitore & Amulio, natu Maiori Regnum vetustum Silviae Gentis legavit. Sed Vis ab Amulio & Patris evertit Voluntatem, & Aetatis Praerogativam hectae facit. Pulto Fratre, non modo Regnum invadit; sed teelus scelerī adcumulans, heu Fratris stirpem funditus tigi studet, ut Accio utar in Aegystho: Filioque eius interempto, Filiam, cui nomen Rea Silvia per speciem honoris Vestalem legit, ne nasceretur inde, quum perpetua teneretur Virginitate, futurus aliquando patrati flagitii vindex. Sed illa ab Marte, ut vetus est opinio, compressa Romulum & Remum parit. Hinc Romulus Ennio lib. ii Annalium:
units.tr: Justin, book xliii, should also be consulted, as well as Suetonius in Vitellius ch. i, Lactantius, De falsa religione i, ch. xxii, Festus book xiii, and Eusebius in the Chronicles. The subjects of the kings I have mentioned, that is, the Aborigines, were gradually joined by the Pelasgians, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Sallust and Solinus write; they were named after Pelasgus, son of Jupiter and Niobe, and came from the Peloponnese and Argos. Second came the Arcadians, who set out from the city of Pallantium in Arcadia; their leader Evander gained some glory in these places too. For he is sung by Virgil in book viii as "founder of the Roman citadel"; not because he founded Rome, but because he laid the foundations, as it were, for the future city, having founded on the hill which came after the Palatine, the town of Pallanteum; of which Virgil, whom I have often cited, in book viii, Justin book xli, and Solinus ch. ii. Third, the Peloponnesians, Phoenicians and Iberians are read to have been mingled with the Aborigines, returning with victory from Spain under the leadership of Hercules, and afterwards longing to return to their homeland. To these were added the Trojans, who had been captured by Hercules under Laomedon in the first Trojan war. Fourth, the Trojans came to the Aborigines after Troy was destroyed: Aeneas, son of Anchises and Venus (from whom the old writers called them "Aeneads", as in Festus book i), driven by leadership and auspices to these shores. These were kindly received by Latinus, whom we have mentioned before, together with their leader; and the Aborigines, over whom he ruled, were called by the common name "Latins", as Cato affirms in Servius on Aeneid i. My Ennius, in book i of the Annals, calls these Latins "Casci". When Aeneas married Lavinia, the only daughter of Latinus, Turnus, who had loved her, is written to have taken it very ill that a stranger had been preferred to him, and a savage war arose; in it, after Turnus and Latinus were slain, Aeneas, by right of succession through his wife, became king of the Latins, and held the reins of government for three years. He founded a city named after his wife Lavinium. He was not long afterwards (so it is handed down) succeeded by a son, who was called Euryleon Ascanius, with the surname Iulus, in the eighth year after the fall of Troy. From Iulus came the Julian clan at Rome, as Virgil attests in Aeneid i, Ovid in Fasti iv, Caesar in Suetonius ch. vi, and Isidore, Etymologies ix, ch. iii. Ascanius, having founded Alba, established the kingdom of the Alban people. After his death, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus book i, Livy book i, Virgil Aeneid vi, Ovid Fasti iv and Metamorphoses xiv note, there succeeded, in a most noble sequence, Silvius, from whom all the Alban kings were surnamed Silvius, as witnessed by the same Virgil in Aeneid vi, Festus book xvii, and Isidore book ix, ch. iii; Aeneas, whom the same poet celebrates for piety and arms in book vii; Latinus; Alba; Capetus (called Atys by Livy); Capys; Calpetus (otherwise Capetus iii); Tiberinus, who is said to have given his name to the river in which he was drowned; Agrippa (Remulus in Ovid); Alladius (Acrota in Ovid; Romulus in Livy); Aventinus, whom Servius wrongly calls "king of the Aborigines"; Procas, who in Virgil book vi of the Aeneid is "the glory of the Trojan race". Procas, having begotten two sons, Numitor and Amulius, bequeathed the ancient kingdom of the Silvian line to the elder, Numitor. But Amulius, by violence, overturned his father's will and made the privilege of age void. Having driven out his brother, he not only seized the kingdom but, piling crime upon crime, strove to root out his brother's line entirely, as Accius puts it in the Aegisthus. Having killed his son, he chose his daughter, named Rea Silvia, as a Vestal virgin under pretence of honour, so that, being bound to perpetual virginity, she would bear no child who might one day avenge the crime. But she, as the old opinion has it, was violated by Mars, and bore Romulus and Remus. Hence Romulus, in Ennius, book ii of the Annals:

units.la: Sanguen Dis oriundum.
units.tr: Descended from the gods through blood.

units.la: Amulius Ream, Incestus ream, in vincula compingit; Geminos in Tiberim abjici jubet. Tiberis secus refugiens, expositos, qui tanti Imperii futuri erant Auctores, in sicco deliquit. Sublatos ab littore Acca Laurentia (quam nomine vulgato inter Pastores Lupam vocatam scribunt Lactantius, D. Augustinus, & alii) Faustulus Coniux educat. Hi annos nati xvii, Eutropio teste, occasionem nacti, Amulium, Magnum Patruum, obtruncant, Numitori Avo Regnum restituunt; & confluente ad eos maxima Vicinorum multitudine, Romam Urbem, de qua suo loco, impetrata ab Avo benefici, loco nonnulla ad Tiberim in Latio parte Agri Albani, qui primum Populo Romano sufficeret, condunt. Ager Romanus, qui exiguus admodum, &, ut Strabo docet lib. V vix sex millibus passuum ab Urbe, qua longissime aberat, se extendebat, ab Occidente, ut diligenter delineat Onuphrius de Imperio Romano, Tiberi terminabatur; ab Septemtrione, Amene Amne, Vrbibusque Fidenis, Crustumeria, Antemnis, & Caenina; ab Oriente, Pedano, Tiburtino, Gabino, & Praenestino Agris; ab Meridie, Mare versus, Tellenis, Politorio, Ficanaque, earumque Agris finem habebat. Qua de re verba Strabonis ita Latine sonant: Intra quintum igitur & sextum Lapidem locus erat Felti appellatus, ubi Romani tunc Terminus monstrabatur Agri. Sacerdotes & hic, & alys in locis, perinde ac in Finibus eadem die Sacrificium absolvunt, quod Ambarvale vocant. Ficanam in Latio Via Ostiensi ad Lapidem xi olim fuisse tradit Sex. Pompeius: Rudia Saxa esse ad Portum, qui sit secundum Tiberim, ait Fabius Pictor, quem locum putat Labeo duci, ubi fuerit Ficana, Via Ostiensi ad Lapidem undecimum.
units.tr: Amulius throws Rea, accused of incest, into chains and orders the twins to be cast into the Tiber. The Tiber, flowing aside, leaves the exposed boys, who were to be the founders of so great an empire, stranded on dry ground. They were lifted from the shore by Acca Laurentia (whom the writers Lactantius, St. Augustine and others say was commonly called Lupa among the shepherds), and her husband Faustulus brought them up. When they were seventeen years old, according to Eutropius, they seized an opportunity, slew Amulius, their great-uncle, and restored the kingdom to their grandfather Numitor. A very large crowd of neighbours flocked to them, and, having obtained from their grandfather permission to do so as a favour, they founded Rome, a city of which I shall speak in its proper place, on a site on the Tiber in the part of Latium that belonged to the Alban territory, which first sufficed for the Roman people. The Roman territory, which was very small, extended, as Strabo teaches in book V, barely six miles from the city in the direction where it was farthest away. On the west, as Onuphrius carefully describes in his work on the Roman Empire, it was bounded by the Tiber; on the north by the Anio, and by the towns of Fidenae, Crustumerium, Antemnae and Caenina; on the east by the fields of Pedum, Tibur, Gabii and Praeneste; and to the south, toward the sea, it had as its limit the lands of Tellenae, Politorium and Ficana. Strabo's words on this matter run in Latin thus: Within the fifth and sixth milestone, therefore, there was a place called Feltis, where the Roman boundary stone of the territory was then pointed out. Here and in other places the priests, just as at the boundaries, complete on the same day a sacrifice which they call Ambarvale. Sextus Pompeius records that Ficana in Latium lay on the Via Ostiensis at the eleventh milestone: Fabius Pictor says that there are Rudia Saxa at the harbour which lies next to the Tiber, and Labeo thinks this is the place where Ficana was, on the Via Ostiensis at the eleventh milestone.

units.la: Sed quum omnis Potestas Consortis confuerit esse impatiens; Romulus, Fratre sublato, solus Imperium obtinuit annos xxxvii: quo temporis spatio acceptam ab Avo Ditionem egregie, ut Dionysius tradit, auxit cum Bello I Sabino, Caenina, Antemnis & Crustumerta debellatis; tum Latino, Cameria, Medullia, Fidenisque captis atque singulis in Colonias Romanas deductis, Agrique parte, quam suis divisit, multatis. Quum vero Veientes, nobilissimi potentissimique Etruriae Populi, Bellum tertium contra Romanos pro vindicanda Fidenatium Clade parantes, validum in Agros Romanos exercitum duxissent, victi fugatique Pacem ab Romulo petitam impetrarunt cum his, tum aliis Legibus, Ut Agrum Tiberi contiguum, qui vocabatur Septem-Pagi, Romanis traderent; utque Salinis, quae circa Fluminis erant Ostia abstinerent. Sic Romanus Ager propagatus ex Dionysii auctoritate, ab Romulo, tribus ductis Triumphis, trans Tiberim, Anienem prope, & in Latio Camerium versus. Romulo exstincto, quum annum unum Respubl. administrassent Interreges, subsectus est Numa Pompilius. Pomponius F. Sabinus, qui nulla Belli laude insignis, Pacis Religionisque studiis xliv annos floruit. Sequutus eum Tullus Hostilius, Hostilii F. Hostilii N. Alba eversa, Albanisque in Civitatem adscitis, Albanum Agrum Romano adiecit: Fidenates & Sabinos iterum rebellantes domuit, deque iis triumphavit. Idem Rex Bellum cum omnibus Latinis suscepit, qui xxx Urbium conventu regebantur: in cuius apparatu, anno principatus xxxii moriens Regni Bellique Latini Heredem habuit Ancum Marcium, Numae F. M. N, qui annos regnavit xxiv. Hic Politerium, Tellenas, Ficanam, Priscorum Latinorum Urbes, captas diruit: Civibusque Romam translatis, ipsorum Agros Romanis adiecit; Medulliam, quam Romulus Romanam fecerat Coloniam, ad Latinos regressam, iterum in Ditionem suam redegit; Fidenates & Sabinos, qui rebellarunt, bis victos triumphavit: Silvam Mesiam Veientibus iterum moventibus victisque ademit; Ostiam Urbem in ore Tiberis condidit, Salinasque circa exstruxit. Bellum Volscis Veliternis quum indixisset:
units.tr: But since every power is wont to be impatient of a partner, Romulus, having removed his brother, held sole rule for thirty-seven years. In this span of time, as Dionysius reports, he greatly enlarged the dominion he had received from his grandfather: in the first Sabine war Caenina, Antemnae and Crustumerium were subdued; then, in the Latin war, Camerium, Medullia and Fidenae were captured, each was settled as a Roman colony, and they were stripped of part of their land, which he divided among his own people. But when the Veientes, the most noble and most powerful people of Etruria, preparing a third war against the Romans to avenge the defeat of the Fidenates, led a strong army into the Roman lands, they were defeated and put to flight, and they obtained peace from Romulus, who sought it, on these and other terms: that they should hand over to the Romans the territory next to the Tiber, which was called the Seven Villages, and that they should keep away from the salt-works which were near the mouth of the river. Thus the Roman territory was extended, on the authority of Dionysius, by Romulus, who celebrated three triumphs, across the Tiber near the Anio, and toward Camerium in Latium. When Romulus had died, the interrexes governed the commonwealth for one year, and then Numa Pompilius was chosen. He was Pomponius Sabinus, son of Pompo, who, though distinguished by no glory in war, flourished for forty-four years in the pursuits of peace and religion. He was succeeded by Tullus Hostilius, son of Hostilius and grandson of Hostilius. After Alba was destroyed and the Albans were admitted into the citizenship, he added the Alban territory to the Roman lands; he again subdued the Fidenates and Sabines when they rebelled, and triumphed over them. The same king undertook war against all the Latins, who were governed by a league of thirty cities; in the course of its preparation, dying in the thirty-second year of his reign, he left as heir to the kingdom and to the Latin war Ancus Marcius, son of Numa's daughter, who reigned for twenty-four years. He destroyed by capture Politorium, Tellenae and Ficana, ancient cities of the Latins; he transferred their citizens to Rome and added their lands to the Roman territory. He brought back under his own power Medullia, which Romulus had made a Roman colony, but which had returned to the Latins. He twice defeated and triumphed over the Fidenates and Sabines who had rebelled. He again took from the Veientes, who were again stirring up trouble, the Silva Mesia, after defeating them. He founded the city of Ostia at the mouth of the Tiber and built the salt-works around it. When he had declared war on the Volscians of Velitrae:

units.la: Lumina fis oculis bonus Ancus reliquit:
units.tr: Good Ancus left light to your eyes:

units.la: ut de ipso loquitur libro Annalium tertio meus Ennius. Subsectus illi L. Tarquinius, Damarati F. qui postea Priscus dictus, xxx annos dominatus, Bellum primum cum Latinis gessit; Oppidum ibi Apiolas vi cepit, diruit, incendit; Agrum eius Romano adscripsit: Crustumeriam, Medulliam, Fidenas & Cameriam. Colonias rebellantes: Nomentum, Collatiam, Ficuneam Veterem, Corniculum, Scaptiam, Pitulum, Tifata, Ameriolam, Latinorum & Sabinorum Urbes Romanae fecit potestatis. Agrum Collatinum Sabinis ademit; universum denique Latium, ingentibus praelis superatum, domuit; Urbibus omnibus Latini Nominis in deditionem acceptis, Foedereque cum iis facto, suis vivere cas Legibus permisit: Sabinos & Etruscos, qui Latinis auxilio venerant, praelis aliquot profligavit; & cum plerisque iplorum Civitatibus Foedus pepigit. Subrogatus illi Ser. Tullius, Ser. F. xliv regnavit annos: Bellum xx annorum gessit cum Etruscis, terque de iis triumphavit. Novissime cum xii Etruria Populis pace facta, Belli concitatores, Veientes, Tarquiniensis & Caeretanos Agri parte multavit; isque, qui Romam ad habitandum venerant, distribuit. Regnum post Tullium adeptus L. Tarquinius Superbus Sabinos devictos triumphavit; Foedus cum Latinis renovavit: Iustum Bellum primus Volscis intulit; Suessamque Pometiam de iis vi cepit ac diruit: Gabios dolo Sex. Filii in deditionem accepit: Ardeam obsidens, Regno Bruti opera cum Uxore, Filiis, Familia, anno xxv est exactus.
units.tr: as my Ennius speaks of him in the third book of the Annals. He was succeeded by L. Tarquinius, son of Demaratus, who was afterwards called Priscus. He ruled for thirty years and waged the first war against the Latins. There he took the town of Apiolae by storm, razed it and set it on fire, and he added its territory to the Roman lands. He made Crustumerium, Medullia, Fidenae and Camerium, which had rebelled, into Roman colonies. He brought Nomentum, Collatia, Ficulea Vetus, Corniculum, Scaptia, Pitulum, Tifata and Ameriola, towns of the Latins and Sabines, under Roman authority. He took the Collatine territory from the Sabines; finally he subdued all Latium, which was overcome in great battles. When all the cities of the Latin name had surrendered, and a treaty had been made with them, he allowed them to live under their own laws. He crushed in several battles the Sabines and Etruscans, who had come to help the Latins, and he made a treaty with most of their states. He was succeeded by Servius Tullius, son of Servius, who reigned for forty-four years. He waged a war of twenty years with the Etruscans and triumphed over them three times. Finally, having made peace with the twelve peoples of Etruria, he punished the instigators of the war, the Veientes, Tarquinienses and Caeretani, by taking part of their land, and he distributed it among those who had come to live at Rome. After Tullius, L. Tarquinius Superbus obtained the kingdom; he triumphed over the Sabines, whom he had defeated, and renewed the treaty with the Latins. He was the first to wage a just war on the Volscians; he took Suessa Pometia from them by force and razed it. He received Gabii into surrender through the treachery of his son Sextus. While besieging Ardea, he was expelled in the twenty-fifth year, through the work of Brutus, together with his wife, sons and household.

units.la: Pulsis Regibus, partaque Libertate, primi Bello ab Sp. Cassio & Opitre Virginio Coss. domiti in ditionem Pop. Rom. venerunt anno ccli, Pometia capta funditusque deleta, Aurunci, vetustissimi Latinorum Populi, ut Plinius tradit lib. iii. cap. v: Fidenates, saepe victos, postremo, ut antea Legatorum, sic tunc Novorum Colonorum
units.tr: When the kings had been driven out and liberty won, the first war, waged under the consuls Sp. Cassius and Opiter Virginius, subdued them and brought them under the power of the Roman people, in the year 250. Pometia was captured and utterly destroyed. The Aurunci, the most ancient people of the Latins, as Pliny teaches in book III, chapter 5, and the Fidenates, who had often been defeated, were destroyed at last, just as earlier they had been destroyed for the murder of ambassadors, so then (as the new colonists were slain) by Mamercus Aemilius, dictator for the third time, in the year 328 from the founding of the city.

units.la: lonorum Ionorum cædę imbutos, delevit Mam. Æmilius Mamercinus Dictator iii, anno ab V. C. cccxxviii. Tricesimo post anno M. Furius Camillus Dictator, Falisci primum ac Capenatibus sulis & Caltris exutis, ad Veios profectus, cuniculo in arcem hostium acto, Urbem ipsam decimo ejus Belli anno cepit. Atque ita Veientes, qui ccc\u0331 annos Romanis negocium fecerant, sunt debellati. Sequuti sunt hos Præstinates, quos anno cccl.xxiv ad Allian fudit fugavitque, Urbe capta, T. Quinctius Cincinnatus Dictator & Tiburtes, quos Gallis Senonibus adhærentes aliquoties victos, tandem anno cccc, Suessula capta, ad deditionem, positis armis, adegit M. Fabius Ambustus Cos. iii. Anno cccc xi. M. Valerio Corvo iii & A. Cornelio Cossò Coss. Campani, quum bello ab Samnitibus urgerentur, auxiliumque adversus eos ab Senatu petitum non impetrassent, Urbem atque Agrum suum Populo Romano dediderunt. Hi post rebellionem Latinorum diu in fide Populi Romani permanserunt: Bello vero Punico ii post acceptam Cladem Cannensem, quum ad Hannibalem defecissent, quinquennio post à Q. Fulvio Proconsule Capua recepta est, atque in Campanos acriter lævitum: qui dein Romanorum fuere Servitia. Triennio post devicti sunt, commisso ad Veterem fluvium prælio, Latinis ab T. Manlio Imperiosio Torquato iii Cos. quum Collega ejus P. Decius Mus se pro Legionibus Romanis devovisset. Post hoc Bellum omne Latinum biennii intervallo ab Q. Publilio Philone Dictatore, L. Furio Camillo & C. Manlio Coss. domitum deinceps perpetua atque egregia in Romanos fide semper fuit. Ita sit, diuturno ac prope annorum Bello fessi, tandem anno cccxxv, Priverno capto, ab L. Æmilio Mamercino ii & C. Plantio Deciano subacti in ditionem venerunt Populi Romani. Q. Publilius Philo Primus Proconsul anno ab V. C. cccxxvii, Palæpolis capta, Opicos subjugavit: Hernicos, cum quibus Populus Romanus T. Sicinio & C. Aquillio Coss. bellare coeperat, tandem anno Urbis cccxlviii Q. Marcius Tremulus Cos. Anagnia capta, debellavit. Æqui quoque, qui adiunctis Volscis multa bella cum Populo Romano post Reges exactos gesserant, anno cccclii C. Iunio Bubulco Bruto Dictatore ad internecionem usque sunt deleti. Salinos anno cccclxiv M. Curius Dentatus Cos. intra eum tractum, qua Nar ambit, Fonteisque Velini, Hadriatico tenus Mari, igne ferroque vastatos omnino debellavit: qua Victoria tantum hominum, tantum agrorum redactum in potestatem, ut in utro plus esset, ne ipse quidem potest existimare, qui vicerat. Gallos Senones, qui superatis post Insubres, Cænomanos, Boios & Gessatas, Alpibus, cum Tuscis Umbrisque cæsis, Italiæ occuparant partem, quæ inter Amnes Rubiconem & Æsim, conditis ibi Mediolano, Como, Brixia, Verona, Bergomo, Tridento, Vicentia, & aliis oppidis, triumpharant jam post L. Furium Camillum Dictatorem varii Consules T. Quinctius, C. Sulpicius, C. Pœtelius, M. Popillius & Q. Fabius; aliique Romanorum Duces: Postremo, anno V. C. cccc. xxi, omnes eorum reliquias in Etruria ad Lacum Vadimonis P. Cornelius Dolabella delevit, ne quis exstaret in ea Gente, qui incensam ab Ie Romam Urbem gloriaretur. Senonibus cæsis, eorum Provincia in ditionem Romanam venit: quæ Mari, Tuscia, & Umbria, Amnibusque Rubicone & Æsi includebatur. Quo tempore etiam Italia, quæ Æsim fluvium non excedebat, ab Rubiconem usque extensa est; Senonumque Regio, ut inquit Strabo, Umbris attributa. Post Senones Tusci, quibuscum diuturnum fuerat jam inde ab Romuli tempore Bellum, anno cccclxxiv. Vulsinensibus & Vulcientibus, florentissimis Etruriæ Populis, victis, per Ti. Coruncanium Cos. Romano Nomini sunt adjecti: Imperio ea parte ad Arnum usque propagato. Post id tempus nullum cum Tuscis justum memoratur gestum fuisse Bellum. Quantæ fuerint Etruscis vires, quanta potentia, commemorant copiose Diodorus Siculus lib. vi & Livius lib. v. Ipsorum ante Romanum Imperium late terra marique opes patuisse, argumento esse præter alia, Mare cum Superum, tum Inferum; eorum enim hoc Tuscum communi Gentis vocabulo nominari solitum; illud autem Hadriaticum, ab Hadria, Tuscorum Colonia, Italicos Populos appellasse: in utrumque porro Mare vergentes incoluisse Urbibus duodenis (fuisse scribuntur ex Luca, Pisa, Popilonia, Volaterra, Aquillina, Fesulæ, Rusellani, Arretium, Perusia, Clusium, Pha-leria, & Volsinii) Terras prius eis Apenninum, ad Inferum Mare: postea trans Apenninum, totidem, quot capita originis erant, Colonus misisse, omnia, etiam quæ trans Padum, excepto Venetorum angulo, Loca usque ad Alpes tenuisse. Illud item Etruscarum rei amplitudinem satis superque loquitur, quod Populus Romanus in suos mores & Civitatem inde multa fuerat mutuatus, Praetextam, Trabeam, Vestem Palmatam, Equorum Phaleras, Fasces, Sellam Curulem, Tubas, ornamenta Triumphalia, Auguria, Muricam, aliaque plurima. Legendi praeter Livium, Dionysium Halicarnassaeum, Strabonem & alios, Florus lib. 1. & Silius Italicus lib. VIII. Tantam quoque Romanos de Tuscis opinionem habuisse tradunt Livius & Halicarnassaeus: ut Liberos suos primum in Etruriam Litteris Moribusque imbuendos, uti post in Graeciam, amandare consueverint. Samnitium Bello, de quo ante, pertinuis se contra Romanos conjunxerant Tarentini: a quibus Bellum illud Tarentinum, quod Lucani, Apulos, Bruttios, Picentes, Salentinos, aliosque, & cum iis omnibus Pyrrhum, clarissimum Graeciae Regem, una veluti ruina pariter involvit. Pyrrhum vicit Italiaque expulit M. Curius Dentatus Cos. Tarentinos, Lucanos, Samnitas, Bruttiosque, quum ab L. Papirio Cursore II & Sp. Carvilio Maximo II Coss. victi essent, Pax data est. Domiti deinde Picentes capto, capite Gentis, Asculo, ab Coss. P. Sempronio & Ap. Claudio. Salentini Picentibus additi, Metropolitanque Regionis Brundusium, nobilito Portu celebris, ab M. Attilio & L. Iulio Coss. vexata: quos anni sequentis Consules D. Junius & N. Fabius in potestatem redegerunt. Soli tunc omnium Italicorum superaverant Umbri, ad quos arma Romana nondum pertinuerant: qui, quum Romanis viribus opponere se tentarent, ab iisdem Coss. a quibus Salentini, Sallina erepta, sunt domiti. Atque ita anno CCCCXXXIX Italia omnis ab Freto Siculo ad Rubiconem & Arnum Tuscosque extremos, Ligurbus contines, in populi Romani ditionem devenit. Bellum Gallicum Cisalpinum initum est anno 19 XXIX ab V. C. L. Annilio Papo & C. Attilio Regulo Coss. Romani, Gallorum tumultu numerato, maximas, si umquam, Copias, auctore Polybio, comparaverunt. Tota enim Italia enixe pro Imperio Romano laboravit, solaque, tectae Tiruo sine externis ullis auxiliis, atque etiam tunc sine Transpadanis, Cenomanos & Venetos intelligit, qui ex Gallis soli pro Romanis stabant Equitum octoginta millia, Peditum septingenta armavit. Congressus primus tam fuit vehemens, ut Romani Gallorum quadraginta millia ceciderunt, decem millia ceperunt. Ab eo tempore Galli Cisalpini ab sequentibus Coss. ita paululum fracti fuerunt magnis victoriis, & debilitati: ut tandem Cisalpinam Galliam in Provinciae formam redegerit M. Claudius Marcellus Coss. anno 19 XXII. Rebellantes postea Gallos varii Duces Romani, praecipue L. Furius Purpureo Praetor, & C. Cornelius Cethegus Cos. compresserunt. Debellavit eos postremo anno 19 LVIII M. Claudius Marcellus Cos. eius, qui primo Galliam Provinciam fecerat, Filius; Cafteiis duodecimginta in deditionem acceptis. Boios, hi Galli Cisalpini Padum erant, qui saepius cum Transpadanis iam victis rebellarant, iidem Duces caeciderunt; eosque demum magnis cladibus adflictos domuit P. Cornelius Nasica Cos. anno 19 LXXII, denique ipsis in Magistratu triumphavit. Veneti diu in fide Pop. Romani permanserunt. Cum Carnis, Iapydibus & Istris, Bello suscepto, Marte vario pugnavit C. Claudius Pulcher Cos. anno 19 LXXVII: domuit eos postremo, & in Pop. Romani ditionem redegit anno 19 CXXV. C. Sempronius Tuditanus Cos. Ligurbus primum arma intulerunt L. Cornelius Lentulus Caudinus & Q. Fulvius Flaccus Coss. anno ab V. C. 19 XVII, eorum viginti quatuor millibus interfectis, quinqueque captis. Quum inde rebellantes saepe plures Romani Duces magnis cladibus per octoginta, & qui excurrunt, annos, aufecissent, tandem eos M. Aemilius Scaurus Cos. anno 19 CXXXIX in deditionem accepit. Salassos & Gentes Alpinas Ap. Claudius Pulcher Cos. anno 19 CXI bello vicit. Augustus postea Caesar ipsos non quiescentes delevit. Hac igitur ratione tercentum annorum intervallo Romanum suscepit iugum universa, quae nunc appellatur, ad Alpes usque Atriamque Fluvium, Italia. Subjugatae vero Italiae pleraque Oppida varias ab Victoribus conditiones suscepisse legimus. Alia enim pro ipsorum erga S. P. Q. R. Meritis vel Demeritis, Coloniarum jus mutuabant: alia Municipiorum, alia denique Praefecturarum, quaedam item Federata erant. Colonia dicebantur oppida, quo Populus Romanus ex Urbe Cives suos per ii. Vitos ad id electos, ad incolendum deducebat. Coloniarum duo erant genera: Quaedam Civium Romanorum; quaedam Latinae. Coloniae Romanae sive Civitas Romanorum appellabantur, quae donatae erant Iure Quiritium, hoc est, quae cu habebant Priva-
units.tr: The Ionian colonists, stained with slaughter, were destroyed by Mam. Aemilius Mamercinus, dictator for the third time, in the year 328 from the founding of the city. Thirty years later, M. Furius Camillus, dictator, after first stripping the Falisci and the Capenatibus of Sutrium and Caletrum, marched against Veios. He ran a mine under the enemy's citadel and took the city itself in the tenth year of that war. So the Veientes, who had given the Romans trouble for three hundred years, were utterly defeated. These were followed by the Præstinates, whom in the year 324 Dictator T. Quinctius Cincinnatus routed and put to flight at the Allia, and whose city he took. Then the Tiburtes, who had attached themselves to the Gallic Senones and were often defeated, were finally forced to surrender and lay down their arms in the year 400, when M. Fabius Ambustus, consul for the third time, took Suessula. In the year 411, under the consuls M. Valerius Corvus (for the third time) and A. Cornelius Cossus, the Campani, being hard pressed by the Samnites and having failed to obtain help against them from the Senate, surrendered their city and territory to the Roman people. After the revolt of the Latins they remained long loyal to the Roman people. In the Second Punic War, however, after the disaster at Cannae, they revolted to Hannibal. Five years later, after Capua had been recaptured by the proconsul Q. Fulvius, Campanos was severely punished, and they then became slaves of the Romans. Three years afterwards, in a battle fought near the river Veter, the Latinis were defeated by T. Manlius Imperiosus Torquatus, consul for the third time, after his colleague P. Decius Mus had devoted himself on behalf of the Roman legions. After this whole Latinum war, which was ended within two years by Q. Publilius Philo, dictator, and the consuls L. Furius Camillus and C. Manlius, they were ever afterwards faithful to the Romans in a steady and remarkable way. Ita sit: worn out by a long war lasting almost years, they finally came under the power of the Roman people in the year 325, when Priverno was taken and they were subdued by L. Aemilius Mamercinus, consul for the second time, and C. Plautius Decianus. Q. Publilius Philo, proconsul for the first time, in the year 327 from the founding of the city, took Palæpolis and subdued the Opicos. The Hernicos, with whom the Roman people had begun war under the consuls T. Sicinius and C. Aquillius, were at last subdued in the year 348 by Q. Marcius Tremulus, consul, who took Anagnia. The Æqui also, who with the Volsci had waged many wars against the Roman people after the kings were expelled, were utterly exterminated in the year 452 under C. Junius Bubulcus Brutus, dictator. In the year 464 M. Curius Dentatus, consul, subdued the Salinos (the Sabines) throughout the whole region where the Nar winds, and the springs of the Velinus, down to the Adriatic Sea, laying waste everything with fire and sword. By that victory so many men and so much land were brought under control that even the victor himself could not estimate which side had more. He also subdued the Gallos Senones, who, after defeating the Insubres, Cenomani, Boii and Gesatae, and after the Alps, with the Etruscans and Umbrians slaughtered, had occupied the part of Italy lying between the rivers Rubicon and Aesis. There they founded Mediolanum, Como, Brescia, Verona, Bergamo, Trent, Vicenza and other towns. Earlier, after Dictator L. Furius Camillus, various consuls, T. Quinctius, C. Sulpicius, C. Poetelius, M. Popillius and Q. Fabius, and other Roman commanders had already celebrated triumphs over them. Finally, in the year 421 from the founding of the city, P. Cornelius Dolabella destroyed all their remnants in Etruria at Lake Vadimo, so that no one should be left of that nation to boast that they had burned Rome, the city taken by the Gauls. With the Senones destroyed, their province came under Roman rule. It was bounded by the sea, Etruria and Umbria, and by the rivers Rubicon and Aesis. At that time Italia, which had not extended beyond the river Aesis, was extended as far as the Rubicon; and the region of the Senonumque, as Strabo says, was assigned to the Umbrians. After the Senones, the Tusci, with whom there had been a long war since the time of Romulus, were defeated in the year 474. The Vulsinensibus & Vulcientibus, most flourishing peoples of Etruriæ, were conquered under the consul Ti. Coruncanius and added to the Roman name, the empire being thereby extended in that region as far as the Arno. After that time no regular war with the Tuscis is recorded. How great the strength and power of the Etruscis were, Diodorus Siculus in book 6 and Livy in book 5 describe at length. That their wealth extended widely by land and sea before the Roman empire is shown, among other things, by the fact that both seas were named after them: the upper and the lower. The one was usually called the Tuscum, by the common name of the nation; the other, the Hadriaticum, from Hadria, a colony of the Tuscorum, which they called the Italian peoples. Moreover, dwelling on both seas, they are said to have had twelve cities (from Luca, Pisa, Popilonia, Volaterra, Aquillina, Fesulae, Rusellani, Arretium, Perusia, Clusium, Faleria, & Volsinii). They first held the lands from the Apennines down to the Lower Sea; afterwards, beyond the Apennines, they sent out as many colonies as they had cities of origin, and held all the places, including everything beyond the Po except the corner of the Veneti, up to the Alps. This also speaks amply enough of the greatness of the Etruscan state: the Roman people borrowed from them many of their customs and institutions, the purple-bordered toga, the toga picta, the palm-embroidered tunic, horse trappings, the fasces, the curule chair, trumpets, triumphal insignia, augury, the murex, and very many other things. Besides Livy, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Strabo and others should be read, and Florus, book 1, and Silius Italicus, book 8. Livy and Halicarnassensis also report that the Romans held the Etruscans in such high regard that they were accustomed to send their children to Etruria first to be educated in letters and manners, just as later they sent them to Greece. In the Samnite war, mentioned above, the Tarentines had joined themselves to the Romans' enemies. From this came the Tarentine war, which together with the Lucanians, Apulians, Bruttians, Picentes, Salentines and others, and with all of them, Pyrrhus, the most famous king of Greece, was drawn into one common ruin. M. Curius Dentatus, consul, defeated Pyrrhus and drove him out of Italy. When the Tarentines, Lucanians, Samnites and Bruttians had been defeated by L. Papirius Cursor for the second time and Sp. Carvilius Maximus for the second time, consuls, peace was granted to them. Afterwards the Picentes were subdued, their head town Asculum being taken by the consuls P. Sempronius and Ap. Claudius. The Salentines, joined with the Picentes, harassed Brundisium, the metropolis of the region and famous for its noble harbour, under the consuls M. Attilius and L. Julius; in the following year the consuls D. Junius and N. Fabius reduced them to submission. The only people of all the Italians who still held out at that time were the Umbrians, to whom Roman arms had not yet extended. When they tried to oppose Rome with their own forces, they were subdued by the same consuls who had defeated the Salentines, Sallina having been captured. Thus in the year 439 the whole of Italy, from the Sicilian Strait to the Rubicon and the Arno and the farthest Tuscans, bounded by Liguria, came under the power of the Roman people. The Cisalpine Gallic war began in the year 529 from the founding of the city, under the consuls L. Aemilius Papus and C. Atilius Regulus. Because of the Gallic uprising, the Romans, according to Polybius, raised the greatest forces ever, if ever. For all Italy strove zealously for the Roman empire, and without any foreign auxiliaries, and even then without the Transpadanes, he means the Cenomani and Veneti, the only Gauls who stood with the Romans. They armed eighty thousand cavalry and seven hundred thousand infantry. The first encounter was so fierce that forty thousand Romans fell and ten thousand were captured. From that time the Cisalpine Gauls were so weakened and worn down by the following consuls' great victories that at last M. Claudius Marcellus, consul, in the year 522, reduced Cisalpine Gaul to the form of a province. When the Gauls later rebelled, various Roman commanders, especially L. Furius Purpureo, praetor, and C. Cornelius Cethegus, consul, put them down. Finally, in the year 558, M. Claudius Marcellus, consul, son of the man who first made Gaul a province, finished them off, accepting the surrender of the Casteii and twelve thousand. The Boii, Cisalpine Gauls beside the Po, had often rebelled along with the Transpadanes who had already been defeated; the same commanders cut them down. Finally, broken by great disasters, they were subdued by P. Cornelius Nasica, consul, in the year 572, and he celebrated a triumph while still in office. The Veneti remained long loyal to the Roman people. C. Claudius Pulcher, consul, fought with varying fortune in a war against the Carni, Iapydes and Istri, undertaken in the year 577; finally he subdued them and brought them under Roman rule in the year 625. The Ligurians first took up arms against Rome under the consuls L. Cornelius Lentulus Caudinus and Q. Fulvius Flaccus in the year 617 from the founding of the city; twenty-four thousand of them were killed and five thousand captured. When they rebelled again and again, and for more than eighty years several Roman commanders had worn them down with great disasters, at last M. Aemilius Scaurus, consul, received them into surrender in the year 639. Ap. Claudius Pulcher, consul, defeated the Salassi and the Alpine peoples in war in the year 611. Later Augustus Caesar destroyed them when they would not keep quiet. In this way, over an interval of three hundred years, Italia took upon itself the Roman yoke, the whole of what is now called Italy, from the Alps to the river Atria. Now we read that most of the towns of the conquered Italiae received various terms from their victors. For according to their merits or demerits towards the Senate and People of Rome, some held the rights of colonies, others of municipalities, others of prefectures, and some were federated. Those towns were called colonies to which the Roman people sent their citizens from the City, chosen for the purpose by three commissioners, to live there. There were two kinds of colonies: some of Roman citizens and some of Latin right. The colonies of Roman citizens, or the Roman citizenship, were those granted the right of the Quirites, that is, those which had the Priva-

These consisted in the private right of liberty and marriage, as well as of inheritance, mancipation, nexum, usucapion, and of guardians and guardianships; but the public rights of citizenship belonged to those colonists assigned to them. By name they were Latin colonies, which had the right of Latium, that is, the power of voting, granted with permission to hold magistracies, or endowed with the right of Latium, and they held magistracies. The series of colonies in Italy, from Romulus down to the time when they were led out by command, is this: A.U.C.

units.la: In Coloniam autem deducti statim novam administrandæ Reip. rationem, ad exemplum fere Romanæ, constituebant. Posita enim erat plurimum in Legibus & Magistratibus. Leges non unius erat generis: aliæ quidem, quas Coloni vel ab ipso Populo Romano, vel ab Romanis Triumviris, qui Coloniam deduxerant, accipiebant; aliæ vero, quas ipsum Coloniæ Concilium, id est, Senatus Populusque sibi ferebat. Magistratus erant vel Sacri, vel Profani: Sacri vel Sacerdotes erant Pontifices & Augures. Hos enim in Coloniis cooptatos, testatur M. Tullii Ciceronis Agraria. An vero certus Sacerdotum fuerit numerus, an vero pro Coloniæ magnitudine variarit, parum explorata apud Antiquos est memoria. Profani erant, cum Decuriones, tum Duumviri, Censores, Ædiles, Prætores. Decuriones in Coloniis, ut & in Municipiis, erant illi, qui Romæ Senatores: sic nominati, quemadmodum notat Pomponius IC. quod decima Pars eorum, qui deducerentur, publici consilii gratia, solita esset conscribi. Eorum numerus an in omnibus Coloniis idem fuerit, certo sciri non potest. Hoc sane ex Plinio Iuniore paret in Decurionibus legendis non aliter, atque in Senatore Romano observatum fuisse Censum, qui centum erat nullum. Ex Decurionibus, singulis annis, duo plerumque, subinde quatuor Viri creabantur, iuxta Coloniæ magnitudinem vel parvitatem, qui II Viri, vel IV Viri I. D. id est Juri dicundo, vocabantur. Hi Consulum Romanorum speciem, vel certe Prætorum imaginem representabant. Eorum annuum erat Imperium. Meminerunt sæpe Antiqui Lapides & Numismata: Imo & iterati Duumviratus, ut apud Romanos Consulatus, sunt in iisdem notæ. Censores in Coloniis fuisse, nique iis Censum eos egisse manifestum est ex Livio. Ædiles Viarum, Ædificiorum publicorum, Annonæ, & locandorum Reddituum publicorum; Quæstores Ærarii publici habebant curam: quorum crebra exstat mentio in antiquis Marmoribus. Hæc de Coloniis; de Municipiis ut dicam, ordo postulat. Municipia Oppida erant iure Civium Romanorum donata: Festus lib. XI de Verborum significatu. Municipium id genus hominum dicitur, qui quum Romam venirent, neque Cives Romani essent, participes tamen fuerunt omnium rerum ad Munus fungendum una cum Romanis Civibus, præterquam de Suffragio ferendo, aut Magistratu capiendo, sicut fuerunt Fundani, Formiani, Cumani, Aeerrani, Lanuvini, Tusculani; qui post aliquot annos Cives Romani effecti sunt. Alio modo, quum id genus hominum distinguitur, quorum Civitas universa in Civitatem Romanam venit; ut Aricini, Cæritcs, Anagnini. Tertio, quum
units.tr: Those who were sent out to a colony immediately set up a new system for administering the commonwealth, modelled for the most part on the Roman one. Much of it rested on laws and magistrates. The laws were not all of one kind: some the colonists received either from the Roman People itself or from the Roman triumvirs who had founded the colony; others the council of the colony itself, that is, the Senate and People, enacted for themselves. The magistrates were either sacred or secular. The sacred ones, or priests, were the pontiffs and augurs, for Cicero's Agrarian Law attests that these were co-opted into colonies. Whether the number of priests was fixed, or varied according to the size of the colony, is little known from the memory of the ancients. The secular magistrates were the decurions, the duumvirs, the censors, the aediles and the praetors. The decurions in colonies, as in municipalities, were those who at Rome were senators; they were so called, as the jurist Pomponius notes, because the tenth part of those who were sent out was usually enrolled for the sake of the public council. Whether their number was the same in all colonies cannot be known for certain. It is clear enough from Pliny the Younger that in choosing decurions the census was observed in the same way as for a Roman senator, which was a hundred. From the decurions, two, and often four, men were created each year, according to the size or smallness of the colony; these were called duumvirs or quattuorvirs with judicial power (II Viri or IV Viri i.d., that is, for judging law). They represented the image of the Roman consuls, or at least of the praetors. Their power was annual. Ancient stones and coins often mention them; indeed, repeated terms of office as duumvirs, like repeated consulships at Rome, are recorded on the same monuments. That there were censors in colonies, and that they held the census, is clear from Livy. The aediles had charge of the roads, public buildings and the grain supply, and of letting out public revenues; the quaestors had charge of the public treasury. Mention of them is frequent in ancient marbles. So much for colonies; the order of the discussion now requires that I speak of municipalities. Municipalities were towns granted the rights of Roman citizens. Festus, book XI, On the Meaning of Words: a municipium is said of a class of men who, when they came to Rome, though they were not Roman citizens, nevertheless shared in all the duties of office together with Roman citizens, except voting or taking up magistracy; such were the people of Fundi, Formiae, Cumae, Acerrae, Lanuvium and Tusculum, who after some years became Roman citizens. In another sense, when a class of men is distinguished whose whole community came into Roman citizenship, as the Aricini, Caeriti and Anagnini. Thirdly, when

units.la: id genus hominum diffinitur, qui ad Civitatem Romanam ita venerunt, uti Municipia essent, ut sua cuiusque Civitatis & Co onia iura essent Tiburtes, Praenestini, Pisani, Arpinates, (in aliis sunt Vrbinates) Nolani, Bononienses,(in antiquiore Codice Bobiniensis legitur) Placentini, Nepesini, Sutrini, Lucenses. Triplex haec Festi vel Pauli Distinctio obscurior est, eamque non satis adsequor: certe Municipiorum duo erant genera: Vnum, quod ius Civitatis sine Suffragio habebat; alterum, cui idem ius cum Suffragij latione erat communicatum. Consulendi Agellius lib. xvi. cap. xiii & Sex. Pompeius Festus lib. de Verb. significat. xi.
units.tr: a class of men is defined who came into Roman citizenship on terms such that they were municipalities, so that each community had its own rights and its own colony: the Tiburtes, Praenestini, Pisani, Arpinates (in others, Urbinates), Nolani, Bononienses (read in an older codex, Bobiniensis), Placentini, Nepesini, Sutrini, Lucenses. This threefold distinction of Festus or Paulus is rather obscure, and I do not fully grasp it. Certainly there were two kinds of municipality: one which had the rights of citizenship without the vote; the other, to which the same right was granted with the right to vote. On this see Gellius, book XVI, chap. XIII, and Sextus Pompeius Festus, book XI, On the Meaning of Words.

units.tr: I. CARE, without the right of suffrage: Agellius, book 16, chapter 13, and Asconius Pedianus on Cicero's Verrines. Festus lists it among those prefectures to which the urban praetor used to send prefects. That this municipality had been granted citizenship with the right of suffrage before the Julian Law seems clearly hinted by Festus, since he writes that it was given the same status that Aricia received, and it is established from Livy that the Aricini were Roman citizens with the right to vote. Old inscriptions also mention this municipality. | CCCLXIII II. TUSCULUM, with suffrage: Sextus Pompeius Festus; Livy, book 6, and elsewhere, book 8; Valerius, book 9, chapter 10; Cicero, for Plancius. | CCCLXXIII III. LANUVIUM, with suffrage: Sextus Pompeius Festus; Livy; Cicero, for Murena. Afterwards it was made a colony from a municipality by Caesar the Dictator. | CCCCXVI IV. ARICIA, with suffrage: Livy, book 8; Velleius, book 1; Sextus Pompeius Festus. Aricia was afterwards made a colony from a municipality, as the rights and privileges of the municipalities faded away (as Agellius writes). | CCCCXVI V. NOMENTUM, with suffrage: Livy, book 8. | CCCCXVI VI. PEDUM, with suffrage: Livy, in the same place. | CCCCXVI VII. FUNDI, without suffrage: Livy, book 8, and Paterculus. Festus says that the Fundani were afterwards given the right of suffrage. | CCCCXVI VIII. FORMIAE, without suffrage: the urban praetor sent prefects from the City every year. | IX. CUMAE, without suffrage: Livy, books 8, 23 and 40. Festus lists this municipality among those to which citizenship with suffrage was afterwards given. An old inscription mentions it as a municipality. The same Festus also numbers it among the prefectures to which the people used to send prefects, and Augustus Caesar afterwards made it a military colony.

units.tr: XII. ACERRAE, without suffrage: Livy, book 8; Velleius Paterculus, book 2. Festus lists this municipality among those which first had citizenship without suffrage and afterwards received it with the right of suffrage. The same author counts it among the prefectures to which prefects were sent by the people. Augustus later made a colony of it, either from the prefecture or from the old municipality.

Idem Anagniam inter eas Praefecturas enumerat, in quas Praetoris Urbani auctoritate Praefecti ibant. xvi Trebula, sine Suffragii iure: Livius libro x. Civitatem autem Trebulanis sine Suffragio concessam fuisse, indicavit, quod multo tempore post Livium memoret Arpinates, quos cum Trebulanis eodem lib. x nominat, cum Suffragio Civitate donatos fuisse de Trebulanis vero nullam facta mentionem. xvi Atella, cum Suffragio: Festus libro xv, qui & libro de Verbor. significat. xiv Atellanam Praefecturis adscriptis in quas Praefecti, Populi Suffragiis creati mittebantur. Erumque esse potuit, ut primo Municipium, post autem bello Punico, cum reliquae, quae supra enumeravit, Praefectura fit facta. Augustus, ut plerasque alias, Coloniam deduxit.
units.tr: Livy, book 39, among those prefectures which Festus lists, to which the urban praetor sent prefects every year. Afterwards it was made a colony. | 339 | which were under their own law. XIV. ANAGNIA, without suffrage: Livy, book 9; Cicero, for Domus; inscription. Festus hints that Cyrus and Anagnia had suffrage in the same way that the Arpinates did. The same Festus also counts Anagnia among the prefectures to which prefects went by the authority of the urban praetor. XV. TREBULA, without the right of suffrage: Livy, book 10. That citizenship was given to the Trebulani without suffrage is shown by the fact that Livy, much later, mentions the Arpinates, whom he names together with the Trebulani in the same book 10 as having been granted citizenship with suffrage, but makes no mention of the Trebulani in this respect. XVI. ATELLA, with suffrage: Festus, book 15, who also, in his book on the meaning of words, lists Atella among the prefectures to which prefects chosen by popular vote were sent. It may be that it was first a municipality, and afterwards, in the Punic War, was made a prefecture along with the others he listed above. Augustus, as with many others, made it a colony.

units.la: Quae hactenus indicavi Municipia, certioris sunt temporis: sequentia quando fuerint facta, non latis constat. Commemorat praeter superiores Civitates inter Municipes Festus Tiburtes, Praenestinos, Ufanos, Nolanos, Bononienses, Placentinos, Nepesinos, Sutrinos, Lucenses. Ex his Tibur & Praeneste, quae Civitates Foederatae Latinae erant, suis Legibus relictae sunt: Pisae, Nola, Venenia, Placentia, Nepet, Sutrium, Luca Colonia deductae. Recententur ab Cicerone Municipia aliquot praeter ea, quae dixi, quae haud dubie post legem Iuliam facta sunt; ut Asculum in Oratione pro Sulla: Aquinum, Laetum, Gabii, Bovillae in secunda Philippica; Larinum in Oratione pro Cluentio, Ameria pro Sex. Roscio; Tarquinii pro Caecina; & quaedam alia. Tacitus quoque libro xvi Municipia Transpadana nominat Mediolanum, Novariam, Vercellas, & Eporediam. In Antiquis Marmoribus & Lapidibus Municipiorum Italorum, cum aliorum, tum sequentium frequens fit mentio: Segusini, Interamnatis, Nuburtis, Cafuentinorum, Tindentatum, Ortenses, Surrentini, Rhegini, Tiburtes, Hidruntini, Sepinates, Suessani, Foro Semproni, Coranii, Nolani, Atrinates, Allifani, Amerini, Bierani, Arretini, Clusini, Tifernates, Mavanae, & Mavaniola, Capenates, Urbini, Sassinates, Cassinates, Hispelli, Foro Flaminii, Normanenses, Asculani. Quam porro Municipia Reip. formam habuerint, non facile quis dixerit. Innuunt hoc saltem Veterum Scriptorum Monumenta, genus universum ex omnibus fere Rebuspublicis temperatum, Romanae propemodum fuisse simile. Erant in Municipiis, quemadmodum Romae, tres Ordines, Decuriones, Equites, Plebs. Decuriones idem erant, qui Romae Senatores; in quibus legendis summam adhibitam fuisse curam docet Cicero Epistola quadam libri vi, ad Leptam. Ex horum ordine Decem-primi legebantur; qui, uti scriptum est apud Hermogenianum IC. Tributorum Exactioni ita praeerant, ut si qua detrimenta Fiscus mortuorum causa contraheret, ipsi suis sumtibus resarcirent. Equitum celeberrimum ordinem in Municipiis fuisse patet ex Ciceronis Cluentiana. Iam Populi sive Plebis summum ius erat in Legibus ferendis, creandisque Magistratibus Municipalibus: cuius rei apud M. Tullium in Libris de Legibus, Oratione pro Cluentio, Epistolis aliquot extant testimonia. Erant vero Magistratus, Dictatores, Duumviri, Quatuorviri, Censores, Aediles, Quaestores. Scribit Spartianus, Imperatorem Hadrianum per Latina Oppida Dictatorem, & Aedilem, & Duumviros fuisse.
units.tr: The municipalities I have listed so far are of more certain date; when the following were made municipalities is not well established. Besides the above-mentioned states, Festus names among the citizens of the municipalities the Tiburtes, Praenestines, Ufani, Nolani, Bononienses, Placentini, Nepesini, Sutrini and Lucenses. Of these, Tibur and Praeneste, which were states allied to Latium, were left under their own laws; Pisa, Nola, Venafrum, Placentia, Nepet, Sutrium and Luca were made colonies. Cicero mentions several other municipalities besides those I have named, which were undoubtedly made after the Julian Law: Asculum in the speech for Sulla; Aquinum, Laetum, Gabii and Bovillae in the second Philippic; Larinum in the speech for Cluentius; Ameria, for Sextus Roscius; Tarquinii, for Caecina; and some others. Tacitus also, in book 16, names the Transpadane municipalities: Mediolanum, Novaria, Vercellae and Eporedia. In the ancient marbles and stones, the frequent mention of Italian municipalities, both of others and of the following, is common: Segusini, Interamnates, Nuburtes, Cafuentini, Tindentates, Ortenses, Surrentini, Rhegini, Tiburtes, Hydruntini, Sepinates, Suessani, Forum Sempronii, Coranii, Nolani, Atrinates, Allifani, Amerini, Bierani, Arretini, Clusini, Tifernates, Mavanae and Mavaniola, Capenates, Urbinates, Sassinates, Cassinates, Hispellates, Forum Flaminii, Normanenses, Asculani. What form of commonwealth the municipalities had, one can hardly say. The monuments of the ancient writers at least hint that their kind of government, mixed from nearly all the commonwealths, was almost like the Roman. In the municipalities, just as at Rome, there were three orders: decurions, knights and commons. The decurions were the same as the senators at Rome; that great care was taken in choosing them Cicero shows in a certain letter of book 6, to Lepta. From this order the Decemprimi were chosen, who, as is written in Hermogenianus, the jurist, presided over the collection of taxes in such a way that if the treasury suffered any loss on account of the dead, they made good the loss from their own resources. That the knights were a most distinguished order in the municipalities is clear from Cicero's Pro Cluentio. Now the highest right of the people, or commons, was in enacting laws and electing the municipal magistrates; evidence of this is found in Cicero's books On the Laws, in the speech for Cluentius and in several letters. The magistrates were dictators, duumvirs, quattuorvirs, censors, aediles and quaestors. Spartianus writes that the emperor Hadrian was dictator, aedile and duumvir through the Latin towns.

units.la: Incertioris.
units.tr: Of less certain date.

units.la: Municipiorum Reip.
units.tr: The constitution of the municipalities.

units.la: in Ordinibus.
units.tr: In the orders.

units.la: & Magistratibus. fuisse. Duum Viratus & Quatuor Viratus annus erat Magistratus: Censores, Aediles, Quaestores idem erant in Municipiis, qui in Coloniis. Sacerdotes item in Municipiis fuisse leguntur, cum primis autem Flamines; quorum frequens in Lapidibus est mentio. Quid inter Colonias & Municipia discriminis fuerit, docet Agellius lib. xvi. noct. Atticarum cap. xiii. Haec de Municipiis: succedit Praefecturarum Explicatio.
units.tr: and the magistrates. [They were?] The duumvirate and the quattuorvirate were annual magistracies. The censors, aediles and quaestors were the same in the municipalities as in the colonies. Priests, too, are read of in the municipalities, especially flamens, whose mention on inscriptions is frequent. What difference there was between colonies and municipalities Agellius teaches in Attic Nights, book 16, chapter 13. So much on the municipalities; the explanation of the prefectures follows.

units.la: Præfecturæ Oppida erant Italiæ, in quibus qui habitabant, nec suis Legibus, ut Municipes, vivebant; nec ullos de suo corpore Magistratus creare poterant, ut Coloni: sed ab Magistratibus Roma missis regebantur, iis Legibus quas Romanus Magistratus dixisset, qui quoniam Praefectus vocabatur, idcirco Praefecturae nominabantur. Ex quibus intelligitur Praefecturarum, inter omnes Italicas Civitates, conditionem ac fortunam fuisse durissimam. Sic enim ab Majoribus erat traditum, ut quae Civitates inquae ingratæve erga Pop. Rom. fuissent, ac fidem datam semel atque iterum fefellissent, ubi in potestatem dominemque essent adductæ, in Praefecturæ formam referrentur. Formula vero Praefecturæ non longe a Provinciæ formula videtur abfuisse. Ut enim quotannis in Provincias Praetores Roma mitti solitos in Praefecturas Praefectos, qui eas administrarent, ipsque iis dicerent. In exemplum veniat Capua, de cujus ante Coloniam co deductam conditione post Bellum Punicum II, sic scribit Livius lib. xxvi: De Urbe Agroque reliqua consultatio fuit, quibusdam deiendam censentibus, Urbem prava idam, propinquam, inimicam. Ceterum præsens status urbis, N. m propter Agrum, quem omni fertilitate Terra satis confabat primum in Italia esse, Vils ser vata est, ut esset aliqua Aratorum Sedes: Urbi frequentandæ multitudo Incolarum Libertinorumque & Institorum Opificumque retenta. Ager omnis & Tecta publica Populi Romani fuerunt. Ceterum habitari tantum, tamquam Urbem, Capuam, frequentariaque placuit: nullum Corpus Civitatis, nec Senatus, nec Plebis Concilium, nec Magistratus esse: sine Consilio publico, sine Imperio: Multitudinem nullius rei inter se sociam ad consensum inhabitandam fore: Præfectum ad Iura reddenda Roma quotannis mitti oportere. Quibus igitur Oppidis Italiæ huius generis Præfecti Roma missi jus reddebant, Præfecturæ dicebantur. Sex. Pompeius Festus lib. xv duas & viginti Præfecturas enumerat; in iis decem fuisse scribens, in quas Præfecti, Populi suffragiis creati mittebantur: quales erant Capua, Cumæ, Casilinum, Vulturnum, Linternum, Puteoli, Acerra, Suessula, Atella, & Calatia: duodecim vero, in quas Urbanus Praetor pro suo arbitrio Præfectos mittebat, leguntur hæ: Fundi, Formiæ, Cæræ, Venafrum, Allisæ, Privernum, Anagnia, Frusino, Reate, Saturnia, Nursia & Arpinum. Quæ fere omnes aut ex Coloniis & Municipiis Præfecturæ sunt factæ, aut ex Præfecturis in Colonias & Municipia redactæ. Ex his Capua Præfectura fuit a Bello Punico II ad Consulatum C. Cæsaris, a quo Colonia deducta est. Cumæ, Acerra, Suessula, Atella, Formiæ, Privernum & Anagnia tum Municipia, tum Coloniæ, Fundi vero, Cæræ & Arpinum Municipia tantum aliquando fuerunt: Casilinum, Vulturnum, Linternum, Puteoli, & Saturnia Coloniæ; Calatia vero, Venafrum, Allisæ, Frusino, Reate & Nursia Præfecturæ, dum Libertas Populi Romani staret, semper fuerunt. Nam quum post Legem Juliam, sociatis omnium Suffragiis, omni Italia data fuisset Civitas, Municipiorum, Coloniarum & Præfecturarum jura sunt obliterata; Nominaque hæc confundi cœpta, ut & Colonia pro Municipio & Municipium pro Colonia & Praefectura aliquando sint accepta. Cicero enim Placentiam in L. Pisonem; Seram & Casinum pro Plancio; Caenum in Rullum; Suessam in epist. ad Atticum; Casinum in Verrem Municipia vocat, quas Colonias fuisse deductas ostendi. Ad hæc Praefecturæ ipsæ, & Municipia & Veteres Coloniæ, deductis Militibus, Colonia omnes denuo ab L. Cornelio Sulla; deinde Cæsare, ut Virgilius, & Augusto factæ sunt, ut ex præcedentibus manifestum. Præter eas Praefecturas, quas ex Festo indicavi, Cere Praefectura Strabo lib. v, Claudia Plinius lib. iii, cap. v, Attinatis Cicero pro Plancio, Reatina idem de Natura Deorum, faciunt mentionem. In Praefecturis etiam, quemadmodum Municipiis, tres erant Ordines: Summus, Medius, Infimus. Summus Ordo Conventus dicebatur; Medius Equitum erat; Tertius Populi sive Plebis. Magistratus erant duplices: Alii enim Roma mittebantur: Alii ex Præfectura ipsa creabantur. Roma mittebantur, qui jus dicturi essent, quos Praefectos appellabant: creabantur, qui publicæ Curationi alicui præerant, ut Aediles & Quaestores, quorum Munera satis nota. Hæc de Praefecturis.
units.tr: The prefectures were towns of Italy whose inhabitants, unlike the municipes, did not live under their own laws, and could not create any magistrates from their own body, as the colonists could; instead they were governed by magistrates sent from Rome, under those laws which the Roman magistrate had prescribed. Because the magistrate was called a prefect, these places were accordingly named prefectures. From this it is understood that the condition and lot of the prefectures was the harshest of all the Italian states. For it had been handed down by our ancestors that those states which had been ungrateful or disloyal toward the Roman people, and had broken their pledged faith once or twice, when they had been brought under the power and dominion of Rome, were reduced to the form of a prefecture. The form of a prefecture, however, does not seem to have differed much from the form of a province. Just as praetors were accustomed to be sent from Rome each year into the provinces, so prefects were sent into the prefectures to administer them and to pronounce judgment for them. Take Capua as an example, whose condition before it was made a colony, after the Second Punic War, Livy describes in book 26 thus: "Concerning the city and the territory the rest of the deliberation was this: some thought the city should be destroyed as treacherous, close and hostile. But the present state of the city was preserved, on account of the land, which was judged by all to be the first in Italy for fertility, so that there might be some seat of ploughmen; a crowd of inhabitants, freedmen, traders and craftsmen was kept to people the city. The whole territory and public buildings were the property of the Roman people. But it was decided that Capua should be inhabited as a city only, and that it should be kept populous; that there should be no body of citizens, neither a senate, nor an assembly of the commons, nor magistrates; without a public council, without authority; that the multitude, sharing no common interest, would live together in harmony; and that a prefect should be sent from Rome each year to deliver judgments." So those towns of Italy to which a prefect was sent from Rome to deliver judgment of this kind were called prefectures. Sextus Pompeius Festus, in book 15, lists twenty-two prefectures; he writes that among them ten were those to which prefects chosen by the votes of the people were sent: such as Capua, Cumae, Casilinum, Volturnum, Liternum, Puteoli, Acerra, Suessula, Atella and Calatia. But twelve are read of to which the urban praetor sent prefects at his own discretion: these are Fundi, Formiae, Caere, Venafrum, Allifae, Privernum, Anagnia, Frusino, Reate, Saturnia, Nursia and Arpinum. Nearly all of these were made prefectures either from colonies and municipalities, or were reduced from prefectures into colonies and municipalities. Of these, Capua was a prefecture from the Second Punic War until the consulship of Gaius Caesar, by whom it was made a colony. Cumae, Acerra, Suessula, Atella, Formiae, Privernum and Anagnia were at different times both municipalities and colonies; Fundi, Caere and Arpinum were only ever municipalities at some time; Casilinum, Volturnum, Liternum, Puteoli and Saturnia were colonies; but Calatia, Venafrum, Allifae, Frusino, Reate and Nursia were always prefectures, for as long as the liberty of the Roman people lasted. For when, after the Julian Law, citizenship was given to all of Italy by the united vote of all, the rights of municipalities, colonies and prefectures were obliterated, and these names began to be confused, so that a colony was sometimes taken for a municipality, a municipality for a colony, and a prefecture too. For Cicero calls Placentia a municipality, in the speech against Lucius Piso; Sena and Casinum, in the speech for Plancius; Caenum, against Rullus; Sessa, in a letter to Atticus; Casinum, in the Verrines, municipalities, though I have shown that these were colonies that had been settled. Besides this, the prefectures themselves, and the municipalities and old colonies, were all made colonies again by Lucius Cornelius Sulla, then by Caesar, as Virgil says, and by Augustus, as is clear from what has gone before. Besides those prefectures which I have indicated from Festus, Strabo, book 5, mentions the prefecture of Caere; Pliny, book 3, chapter 5, mentions Claudia; Cicero, in the speech for Plancius, mentions Attinas; and the same author, in On the Nature of the Gods, mentions Reate. In the prefectures, as in the municipalities, there were three orders: the highest, the middle and the lowest. The highest order was called the Conventus; the middle was that of the knights; the third was that of the people or commons. There were two kinds of magistrates: some were sent from Rome, others were created within the prefecture itself. Those were sent from Rome who were to pronounce judgment, whom they called prefects; those were created who presided over some public office, such as aediles and quaestors, whose duties are well enough known. So much on the prefectures.

units.la: Reliqua omnia Italiæ oppida, quæ neque Coloniæ, neque Municipia, neque Præfecturæ erant, Fœderatæ Civitates vocabantur, ut Tibur & Præneste in Latio, Neapolis & pleraque aliæ, quæ suis Legibus & Magistratibus vivebant, diversisque Fœderibus aut Sponsione, aut Pactione, vario jure, Amicitiam cum Populo Romano contraxerant. Aliquæ enim erant omnino Liberæ, aliquæ Vectigales, aliquæ Stipendiariæ, aut plus vel minus gravatæ, prout Populo Rom. fuisset visum. Fœderatorum Civitatum Respublica in Legibus & Magistratibus consistebat: quales vero Leges, qualesque singulis Magistratus fuerint, est incertum. Aliis tamen alias Leges, aliosque Magistratus, pro rerum ac temporum ratione, proque cujusque natura & indole, fuisse vero limile est. Nam Tusculi Dictator & Consul, antequam Tusculani in Civitatem reciperentur, fuisse traditur. Narrat etiam Livius Capua, anteaquam deficeret, summum Magistratum Medix-tuticum fuisse; alioque loco Pratorum Capua Marium Blosium profitetur. Idem alibi etiam Pranestinum Pretorem commemorat. Habuisse eosdem Fœderatas Civitates etiam Censores, Ædiles & Quæstores ex Livio intelligitur & Strabone. Caruerunt autem omnia Fœderata oppida jure Civitatis Romanæ: quam ob causam multos ex Fœderatis Civitatibus nominatim Civitate donatos passim legimus.
units.tr: All the other towns of Italy, which were neither colonies, nor municipalities, nor prefectures, were called allied states, such as Tibur and Praeneste in Latium, Naples and many others. These lived under their own laws and magistrates, and had entered into friendship with the Roman people under various treaties, sworn agreements or pacts, with differing legal status. Some were wholly free, some tributary, some stipendiary, or burdened more or less heavily, as the Roman people saw fit. The constitution of the allied states consisted in their laws and magistrates. What those laws were, and what magistrates each state had, is uncertain. It is likely, however, that different states had different laws and magistrates, according to circumstances and times, and to each community's nature and character. For it is recorded that Tusculum had a dictator and consul before the Tusculans were received into citizenship. Livy also reports that Capua, before it revolted, had a chief magistrate called the Meddix tuticus; and elsewhere he names Marius Blosius as praetor of Capua. In another place he also mentions a Praenestine praetor. From Livy and Strabo it is understood that the allied states likewise had censors, aediles and quaestors. But all the allied towns lacked the right of Roman citizenship, which is why we read of many men from the allied states who were granted citizenship by name.

units.la: Omnia autem, quæ de Italiæ Municipiis, Coloniis, Præfecturis oppidisque Fœderatis dixi, tantum ante Bellum Marsicum locum habuerunt & Legem Iuliam: qua quum Italia omni Civitas data fuisset, omnes pari jure Civitatem sunt adepti. Illud ex eo patet, quod omnes in Comitiis Centuriatis jus, tempore Ciceronis, haberent. Quod ipse ostendit in oratione post Reditum ad Quiritès; ubi de Comitiis Centuriatis, quibus ab Exilio revocatus est loquens, ita scribit: Nullum in eorum reditu motus Municipiorum & Coloniarum factus: at me in patriam ter suis Decretis Italia cuncta revocavit. Et pro Sestio: Nullum erat Italiæ Municipium, nulla Colonia, nulla Præfectura, nulla Romæ Societas, nullum Concilium aut aliquod omnino commune Consilium, quod tum non honorificentissime de mea Salute decrevisset. Quod idem ex multis aliis ejus locis pro Murena, pro Sulla, pro Plancio intelligi potest. Nam quod Tranquillus in Cæsare scribit, ipsum, Quæstura finita, Coloniæ Latinæ de Civitate petenda agitantes adiisse, de Transpadanis intelligi debet; quibus Bello Marsico, quum Italiæ omni usque ad Rubiconem & Arnum, item Gallia Cis-Padana Civitas lege Iulia data esset, à Pompeio Strabone, ut in officio continerentur, Ius Latii datum fuerat: Quibus postea Cæsar, Dictator factus, additis Insubribus, Liguribus, Venetis & Carnis, id est universa Gallia Transpadana, Civitatem Romanam dedit.
units.tr: But everything I have said about the municipalities, colonies, prefectures and allied towns of Italy held good only until the Social War and the Julian Law, by which citizenship was granted to all of Italy, and all then obtained citizenship on equal terms. This is clear from the fact that in the time of Cicero all of them had the right to vote in the Centuriate Assembly. He shows this himself in his speech after his return to the Quirites, where, speaking of the Centuriate Assembly by which he had been recalled from exile, he writes thus: No disturbance of municipalities or colonies occurred at my return; but all Italy recalled me to my country by three decrees. And in the speech for Sestius: There was no municipality of Italy, no colony, no prefecture, no society at Rome, no council or any common assembly at all, which did not then decree most honourably for my safety. The same can be understood from many other passages of his, in the speeches for Murena, for Sulla and for Plancius. As for Suetonius's statement in his life of Caesar, that after finishing his quaestorship Caesar approached the Latin colonies which were seeking citizenship, this must be understood of the Transpadanes. In the Social War, when citizenship had been granted by the Julian Law to all of Italy as far as the Rubicon and the Arno, and likewise to Cisalpine Gaul, Pompey Strabo gave the Latin right to the Transpadanes to keep them in obedience. Afterwards Caesar, made dictator, added the Insubres, Ligurians, Veneti and Carni, that is, all of Transpadane Gaul, and gave them Roman citizenship.

units.la: Talis igitur habita sub Romanorum Imperio Italia: cujus viribus usa Urbs Roma plerum Terrarum orbem subjugavit. Mansit autem in Consulum, libera Respublica; inque Principum Romanorum, eadem oppressa, potestate; usque ad Imp. Cæsarem F. Momyllum Augustulum, quem quum abdicare jussisset Odoacer Herulus Gothorum Rex, nobilissimam Regionem in suam redegit Potestatem; cæsisque Theoderico, ipsiusque Successoribus possidendam reliquit. Fastos Consulum Romanorum, ut Italiæ Principum, hic adponerem, nisi omnibus essent in manu. Imperatorum Occidentis (nam Orientis Principes aperiam suo loco) Nomina adscribam; quod in ijs, eorumque Annis, Mensibus, Diebus, quibus imperarunt, recensendis multos supra modum errare videam. units.tr: Such, then, was Italy under Roman rule, and by its strength the city of Rome subdued almost the whole world. It remained a free commonwealth under the consuls, and afterwards was held under the power of the Roman princes, though oppressed by it, until the Emperor Caesar Flavius Momyllus Augustulus. When Odoacer the Herulian, king of the Goths, had made him abdicate, he brought that noblest region under his own power, and left it to be possessed by Theoderic and his successors. I would set out here the lists of the Roman consuls, as of the princes of Italy, were they not in everyone's hands. I shall give the names of the Emperors of the West (for I shall set out the Eastern emperors in their proper place), since I see that many err beyond measure in recording them, their years, months and days of rule. Beginning with C. Julius Caesar, I shall proceed to the Augustulus I have mentioned, and then go on to the princes of the Goths, the exarchs and the kings of the Lombards.
