units.la: Langbardi autem, praeterquam quod novas Leges, quas ab Se Langbardicas appellabant, ediderunt, Latinamque Linguam, Vocabula & Characteres immutare tentarunt, etiam totam, quam occuperant, Italiam in sex Satrapias seu Praefecturas distribuerunt: duas nominarunt Marckias, ceteras Ducatus. Marckia fuerunt Ancontana, quae Picenum; Tarvisina, quae Venetiae partem continebat. Ducatus erant Spoletinus, Taurinus, Foro-Iuliensis & Beneventanus. Lex haec erat Ducibus, ne arbitrio suo Successorem diligendi sibi haberet potestatem, sed is in Concilio totius Gentis declaretur: Marchiones ambo pari erant potestate, atque in alios etiam Duces sua utebantur auctoritate: praeterea qui vel ab Rege vel a Concilio communi locum illum nacti erant, his arbitrio voluntateque sua Heredem sibi decernere ius erat. Ita ducentis fere annis Langbardorum in Italia fterit Imperium, ut Paulus Diaconus, Blondus, Sabellicus, aliique commemorant. Urbs sola superserat Roma, in deditionem & ditionem ab Langbardis redigenda, quo toti Italiae imperitarent. Eam quum aliquamdiu acriter urfillent, nec ab Orientis Imperatoribus aliquid praesidii speraretur, Romani Pontifices ad Francorum Opes, longe lateque per totam Europam tunc pollentes, saepe confugerant: qui tandem, Karolo Magno Rege pro Hadriano I P. M. anno 1 o CCLXXIV, Italiam ingressi, Langbardis praelio victis, eorumque Rege Desiderio Mauo mense capto, Ticinoque Regni Metropoli in deditionem accepta, Langbardorum Regnum excluderunt: quo tempore Italia fere omnis in Francorum pervenit arbitrium; anno postquam Langbardi Italiam occuparant, CCVI & mense primo. Victoria parta, Karolus Magnus, Romanae Sedi Ravennam cum Exarchatu, Flaminiam & Picenum, Provincias de Langbardis captas scribitur largitus: ipse vicesimum ab eadem Sede magnis auctus honoribus; Francorum primo ab Stephano II, mox Langbardorum Rex ab Hadriano inunctus; Patritius inde Romanorum, quae tum suprema in Urbe dignitas erat, creatus: Imperator postremo Occidentis Augustusque ab Stephano III appellatus, VIII Kalendas Ianuarii, mense anno a partu Virginis 1 o CCCI, postea vero quam in Italia imperari desitum fuerat, anno CCCXXV. Quum autem assiduis Saxonum & Italiae Bellis esset implicitus, Filium suum Pipinum in Regno Italiae legit consortem; qui ab Hadriano P. M. XVII Kalendas Maii anno 1 o CC LXXXI, inunctos Venetos debellavit. Pipinum, qui ante Patrem Karolum obiit, sequutus est Filius Bernardus. Hic Karoli Avi voluntate ab Archiepiscopo Mediolanensi in Italia Regem coronatus, Patris exemplo Munus ab initio summa cepit administrare industria; post autem Adulantorum blanditiis incensus, quum Ludovicum
units.tr: The Lombards, besides issuing new laws, which they called Lombard laws, also tried to change the Latin language, its vocabulary and its letters; and they divided all of Italy that they had occupied into six satrapies or prefectures. Two they called marches, the rest duchies. The marches were the Ancona march, which contained Picenum, and the Trevisan march, which contained part of Venetia. The duchies were Spoleto, Turin, Friuli and Benevento. The law for the dukes was that they should not have the power to choose a successor at their own discretion, but that the successor should be declared in an assembly of the whole nation. The two marquises had equal power, and they also exercised their authority over the other dukes. Moreover, those who had obtained that position from the king or from the common assembly had the right to name an heir by their own choice and will. Thus the empire of the Lombards in Italy lasted for nearly two hundred years, as Paul the Deacon, Biondo, Sabellico and others record. Only Rome remained, to be brought under surrender and control by the Lombards, so that they might rule all of Italy. When they had pressed it hard for some time, and no help was hoped for from the emperors of the East, the Roman pontiffs often fled to the power of the Franks, which then flourished far and wide throughout Europe. At last, in the year 1000 CCLXXIV, under King Charlemagne, in the pontificate of Hadrian I, the Franks entered Italy, defeated the Lombards in battle, and after Desiderius, their king, was captured in May, and Pavia, the capital of the kingdom, had surrendered, they brought the Lombard kingdom to an end. At that time almost all of Italy came under the power of the Franks; this was in the 206th year, and the first month, after the Lombards had occupied Italy. Once victory was won, Charlemagne is recorded as having granted to the Roman See Ravenna with the Exarchate, Flaminia and Picenum, provinces taken from the Lombards. He himself, greatly honoured by the same See, was anointed by Stephen II as King of the Franks, and then by Hadrian as King of the Lombards; then he was created patrician of the Romans, which was at that time the highest dignity in the City; and finally he was called Emperor of the West and Augustus by Stephen III, on 8 December in the year 1000 CCCI from the birth of the Virgin; but after the emperors had ceased to rule in Italy, in the year CCCXXV. Since he was caught up in constant wars with the Saxons and in Italy, he chose his son Pepin as partner in the kingdom of Italy; Pepin, anointed by Hadrian I on 15 April in the year 1000 CCLXXXI, defeated the Venetians. Pepin, who died before his father Charles, was followed by his son Bernard. He, by the will of his grandfather Charles, was crowned King of Italy by the Archbishop of Milan; following his father's example he at first undertook the office with great diligence; but afterwards, inflamed by the flattery of his courtiers, when he began to block Emperor Louis, his uncle, from access to Italy, and to strip the kingdom of France, which he had long been persuaded belonged to him,

units.la: in Francorum ditionem redacta cum Imperatorem Patruum suum aditu Italiae prohibere, ac Regno Franciae, quod ad se pertinere jampridem persuasus erat, exucere institueret, ejus hostili adventu territus, & ab suis destitutus, armis abjectis, apud Caballinum Eduorum, urbem Burgundiae, ipsi se tradidit: a quo in Germaniam abductus & Aquisgrani juxta Leges Romanas & Salicas ad Capitis Supplicium condemnatus, sed vita donatus luminibusque orbatus, in Monasterium est inclusus, in quo paullo post moerore vitam finiit, xv Kalendas Mai anno ab Christo nato 10 ccccxviii. Post Bernardum Rex Italiae legitur Ludovicus II, qui a Patre Lotharto Imperatore, Ludovici Pii Primogenito, in Regni Italici consortium adsitus. Romae in Basilica S. Petri in Vaticano coronatus est ab Sergio Papa II, Idibus Aprilis, anno 10 ccclxiv. Hic, Militie coacto, contra Saracenos (Italiam omnem, quae Mari adluitur, miserè tunc vexantes) profectus, fortiter adversum eos & feliciter signa contulit. Sed quum, Exercitu magna ex parte Peste aliisque Morbis abstumto, defensionem Beneventi commendasset Adelgiso Langbardo, Salerni Principi; hic autem cum omnibus Samnij, Campaniae & Lucaniae opidis ad Graecos defecisset, hanc perfidiam ultrum in Italiam redit: & Adelgiso profligato, omnia recepit, deque Rebellanis sociis supplicium sumsit. Ceterum quum rerum trans Alpes nihil haberet, Italiam unam excoluit; eamque quanta maxima potuit cura & fide administravit, non solum Papiae, sed Mediolani quoque & in aliis complurius Langbardiae urbibus Iurisdictionis gratia versari solitus. Vita defunctus est Mediolani, pridie Kalendas Sextilis anno 10 ccccxxv. Imperante Arnulpho, quum Itali aliquot Principes ab Imperio Francico defecissent, Italiae sibi Regnum vindicantes, Imperij quoque Insignia & Titulos a Romanis Pontificibus per multos annos obtinuerunt. Eorum primus fuit Vvido quidam, Dux Spoletanus, Vir Langbardici Sanguinis, qui contra Arnulphum Competitorem Berengario fugato, Imperium sibi Italiae vindicans anno 10 ccclxxxviii Imperatoris quoque & Augusti nomine ab Romano Pontifice Stephano v coronatus adsumsit, ix Kalendas Martij anno 10 ccexci. Post quem etiam eius Filius Lambertus Italiae Regnum sub Augusti nomine ab Romano & ille Pontifice Formoso anno 10 ccccxciv inunctus, obtinuit. Quo mortuo, Berengarius ex Duce Foro Iulienti sub Augusti & Imperatoris titulis anno 10 ccccv Rem Italicam administravit. Huius tempore Italiam ingressi, non solum Saraceni Calabriam & Apuliam misere adflixerunt; verum etiam Hungari, Rege victo inque fugam conjecto, Venetias captas incenderunt. Post Berengarium Rudolphus Cunradi F. Burgundionum Rex, mense Ianuario, anno 10 ccccxxiii Hugo. Hlotharij F. Hlotharij Regis Hlotharingiae N. Hlotharij Imperatoris Ironepos, Comes Arelatensis anno 10 ccccxxvi; Hotharius, eius Filius, anno 10 ccccxxvii; Berengarius denique II, Adelberti Eporediae Marchionis F, Berengarij I ex Filia Nepos; eiusque Filius Adelbertus Regum nomine Italiam anno 10cccc L, obtinuerunt. Profligavit eos Otto Magnus, Imperator, ab Agapeto P. M. in Italiam evocatus. Berengarium iterum anno 10 ccccLvii moventem, ei udeliterque in quesquumque ixvientem, compescuit Ludolphus, ab Ottone Imperatore Patre in Italiam missus. Capitur tandem anno 10 ccccLxiv cum Coniuge Willa Berengarius ab ipso Imperatore, qui eum aliquamdiu in Monte Leonis obsederat: quum iam paullo ante Ioannes xii P. M. ab Imp. deficiens, Alberto, Berengarij Filio, Romam tradidisset. Patre in Germaniam relegato, Filius Libertati redditus, iterum anno sequente ab Italiae Proceribus Rex est appellatus: qui quadriennio post, praelio ab Ottone victus, Regno est exactus, anno 10ccccLxix. Sic Italia Imperio subiecta est ab Ottone I Germanorum. Sequentibus temporibus Ottones, Henrici & Friderici Imperatores multa ibi iunt perpessi adversa. Quum bonam iam partem Pontificiae Sedi Karolus Magnus (nam de Donatione Constantini parum fida sunt Documenta) donasset; egregiam etiam portionem, Langbardiae nimirum Tusciaeque ditionem cum Ferraria, Testamento legasset moritura anno cio cxv Iulio mense Mathildis, Bonifacij Filia, Dux Langbardiae & Tusciae, Marchionissa, ut ea utar voce, Parmae, Mantuae, Ferrariae, Etruriae, Spoleti, Anconae & Pisarum, Canusiae Comes; quae Romanorum Pontificum partes contra Henricum IV Caesarem pertinacissime foverat: aliorum membrorum sensim sequuntur sunt alienationes. Redacta est Apulia & Neapolis in Regnum Hereditarium: defecerunt ab Imperio Mediolanum, Florentia, Genua, Venetia, aliaeque Civitates, quae subinde rursum ad obedientiam retractae, iterum se iugo subtraxe-
units.tr: (this lands which had been brought under Frankish rule) ... Frightened by his hostile approach, and abandoned by his men, he laid down his arms and surrendered himself at Chalon-sur-Saône in Burgundy, a city of the Aedui. He was led from there into Germany and at Aachen was condemned to capital punishment according to Roman and Salic laws, but was granted his life and had his eyes put out, and was shut up in a monastery, where a little later he ended his life in grief, on 17 April in the year of Christ 1000 CCCCXVIII. After Bernard, Louis II is recorded as King of Italy, who was associated in the kingdom of Italy by his father, the Emperor Lothair, the eldest son of Louis the Pious. He was crowned at Rome in the basilica of St Peter in the Vatican by Pope Sergius II, on the Ides of April, in the year 1000 CCCLXIV. He, having gathered an army and set out against the Saracens, who then sorely harassed all of Italy along the sea, fought them bravely and successfully. But when, with the army greatly reduced by plague and other diseases, he had entrusted the defence of Benevento to Adelchis the Lombard, prince of Salerno, and Adelchis had then gone over with all the towns of Samnium, Campania and Lucania to the Greeks, he returned to Italy to punish this treachery, and, having routed Adelchis, recovered everything and exacted punishment from his rebellious allies. Otherwise, since he had nothing beyond the Alps, he cultivated Italy alone and administered it with all the care and loyalty he could, being accustomed to stay not only at Pavia but also at Milan and in several other cities of Lombardy for the sake of jurisdiction. He died at Milan on 31 July in the year 1000 CCCCXXV. Under Arnulf, when several Italian princes had revolted from the Frankish empire, claiming the kingdom of Italy for themselves, they also obtained the insignia and titles of the empire from the Roman pontiffs for many years. The first of them was one Guy, Duke of Spoleto, a man of Lombard blood, who, after Berengar had driven Arnulf the rival away, claiming the empire of Italy for himself, in the year 1000 CCCCLXXXVIII, was crowned and assumed the name of Emperor and Augustus by Pope Stephen V, on 21 February in the year 1000 CCCCXCI. After him his son Lambert also held the kingdom of Italy under the title of Augustus, anointed by Pope Formosus in the year 1000 CCCCXCIV. When he died, Berengar, from Duke of Friuli, governed the Italian realm under the titles of Augustus and Emperor in the year 1000 CCCCV. In his time not only did the Saracens enter Italy and miserably afflict Calabria and Apulia, but also the Hungarians, having defeated the king and put him to flight, captured and burned Venice. After Berengar, Rudolf, son of Conrad, King of the Burgundians, in January, in the year 1000 CCCCXXIII; Hugh, son of Lothair, grandson of Lothair, King of Lorraine, great-grandson of Emperor Lothair, Count of Arles, in the year 1000 CCCCXXVI; Hubert, his son, in the year 1000 CCCCXXVII; and finally Berengar II, son of Adalbert, Marquis of Ivrea, grandson through his daughter of Berengar I, and his son Adalbert, held Italy under the name of kings in the year 1000 CCCCL. They were routed by Otto the Great, Emperor, who had been summoned into Italy by Pope Agapetus. When Berengar again stirred up trouble in 1000 CCCCLVII, and dealt harshly with whoever resisted him, he was checked by Ludolf, sent into Italy by his father, Emperor Otto. At last, in 1000 CCCCLXIV, Berengar was captured with his wife Willa by the Emperor himself, who had besieged him for some time on Mount Leone; for shortly before, Pope John XII, having revolted from the Emperor, had handed Rome over to Alberic, son of Berengar. His father having been banished to Germany, the son was restored to liberty and, again in the following year, was called king by the nobles of Italy; but four years later, defeated in battle by Otto, he was driven from the kingdom, in 1000 CCCCLXIX. Thus Italy was made subject to the empire by Otto I of the Germans. In later times the Emperors Otto, Henry and Frederick suffered many adversities there. When Charlemagne (for the documents concerning the Donation of Constantine are little trustworthy) had already given a good part to the Roman pontiff's See, and a considerable portion as well, namely the domain of Lombardy and Tuscany with Ferrara, Mathilda, daughter of Boniface, Duchess of Lombardy and Tuscany, a marchioness, to use her own word, of Parma, Mantua, Ferrara, Etruria, Spoleto, Ancona and Pisa, Countess of Canossa, bequeathed it by will when she was about to die, in July 1115; she had most stubbornly supported the cause of the Roman pontiffs against Emperor Henry IV. Other parts were gradually lost by alienation. Apulia and Naples were turned into a hereditary kingdom. Milan, Florence, Genoa, Venice and other cities revolted from the empire; these, from time to time brought back to obedience, again withdrew from the yoke

units.la: Germanorum Imperatorum rebus adiectae. subtraxerunt. Invigilarunt quoque Venveti Pomeriis Dominationis suæ latius indies promovendis. Coeperunt item Imperatores nonnulli socordia singulari Civitates quasdam oppugnare; quosdam accepta pecunia, tacere liberas. Venceslaus Germaniam ab Imperio laceratam, tradidisse fertur Regi Franciæ: Ludovicus Bavarus Imp. acceptis sex aureorum millibus, liberos reddidit Florentinos: Karolus IV Bohemus, numinis exacerbatus, Vice-omitem Mediolanensem, qui Imperii Vasallus in Langobardia erat, Ducem creavit. De aliis acceto. Nam Italia, multis successu temporis calamitatibus cladibusque ab variis, cum ipsis Incolis, tum in ipsam aliunde irrumpentibus, Saraceni, Normanni, Franci, Germani, Hispani, aliisque dolendum in modum contectæ, quales partim in Imperatoribus, eorumque Filiis & Pontificibus, partim in diversis Principibus fuerint Domini, paret ex Blondo, Sabellico, Iovio & aliis; parcebatque speciatim ex singularum Regionum delineatione. Discerpta nunc est nobilissima Regio in varias Dynastias. Inter eos, sub quorum ditione nostro est ævo, præter Pontificem, Regem Neapolitanum, Liberasque Respublicas, Venetam, Genuensem, Lucensem & alias, primum facile obtinent locum in Septemtrionalibus, Principes Etruscis, Ferrarienses, Mantuanos, Mediolanenses, Montis-Ferratenses, Parmæ, Saluzzarum, Veronenses, in Australi multi sunt & innumerabiles Dynastiæ: quos, occasione oblata, suis recentoo locis. In Italiam, ut hoc addam, Avorum nostrorum temporibus variæ vexarunt mirum in modum Factiones: Etruriam Cancellarii & Panzatici, Picenum Albi & Nigri. Latium Colonnenses & Ursini; Infubrium Bracciani & Sforziani; potissimam partem Guelphi & Ghibellini. Sensit has furias aliquando Germania, sed non diu. In Italia extinguī non potuerunt, nec exstinguuntur facile, inquit Vir magni judicii, propter Gentis mores & genium, qui ad injuriam inferendam valde pronus, ad decernendum ulciscendi desiderium tardus. Tanta illius pestis vis est, ut Pueri etiam se vel harum vel illarum Partium esse professentur nec pietati Parentum, nec Cognatorum parcentes sanguini. Factionum, Cancellariorum & Panzaticorum nomina ad perniciem humani generis excogitata, primum, ut scribit Platina in Gregorio X, audita sunt Pistorii in Etruria. Ea Factio reliquarum, Nominibus tantum mutatis, pro Partium nobilitate & potentia, fons fuit; indeque infin ita pullularunt Mala, quæ universæ fere Italiæ fuerunt exitio; de quibus omnibus multi Auctores varia scribunt. Pistoriensis tanc Civitas maxime Cædibus recentibus madet.
units.tr: The cities were added to the affairs of the German Emperors, and they withdrew from them. The Venetians also took care to extend the boundaries of their dominion more widely every day. Some Emperors, through an extraordinary laziness, also began to attack certain cities, and for money they kept silent about others that were free. It is reported that Wenceslaus handed Germany, torn from the Empire, over to the King of France. Ludwig the Bavarian, Emperor, after receiving six thousand gold coins, gave back their freedom to the Florentines. Charles IV of Bohemia, provoked by the divine will, made the Viscount of Milan, who was a vassal of the Empire in Lombardy, a Duke. Of the others I say nothing. For Italy, over the course of time, suffered many calamities and disasters, both from its own inhabitants and from others who broke into it from outside: Saracens, Normans, Franks, Germans, Spaniards, and others, to a lamentable degree. Who ruled it, some in the persons of the Emperors, their sons and the Popes, and some in the various Princes, is clear from Blondus, Sabellicus, Jovius and others, and was set out in particular in the description of each region. The most noble region is now torn apart into various dynasties. Among those under whose rule we live in this age, besides the Pope, the King of Naples, and the free republics of Venice, Genoa, Lucca and others, the first place in the north is easily held by the Princes of Tuscany, of Ferrara, of Mantua, of Milan, of Monferrato, of Parma, of Saluzzo, and of Verona. In the south there are many and innumerable dynasties, which I shall mention in their proper places as the occasion arises. To add this too: in Italy, in the times of our grandfathers, various factions troubled it in a remarkable way. In Tuscany there were the Cancellieri and the Panzatici; in Picenum the Whites and the Blacks; in Latium the Colonna and the Orsini; in Lombardy the Bracceschi and the Sforzeschi; and in most of the country the Guelfs and the Ghibellines. Germany too felt these frenzies at one time, but not for long. They could not be extinguished in Italy, nor are they easily extinguished, says a man of great judgement, on account of the character and temper of the people, which is very prone to inflicting injury but slow to the desire of taking revenge when it has been decided on. So great is the power of that plague that even boys profess to belong to one or other of these parties, sparing neither the piety owed to parents nor the blood of kinsmen. The names of the Cancellieri and Panzatici factions, devised for the ruin of the human race, were first heard, as Platina writes in the life of Gregory X, at Pistoia in Tuscany. That faction was the source of the others, the names only being changed according to the nobility and power of the parties; and from there the evils sprang up endlessly, which were nearly everywhere the ruin of Italy. Many authors write various things about all of these. The city of Pistoia at that time was soaked with recent slaughter.

units.la: CAPUT XX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XX.

units.la: Gubernatio Italiæ Sacra vel Ecclesiastica.
units.tr: The Sacred or Ecclesiastical Government of Italy.

units.la: GUBERNATIONEM aperui Politicam: sequitur Ecclesiastica, in cujus explanatione futurus brevis.
units.tr: I have set out the political government. The ecclesiastical government follows, and I will explain it briefly.

units.la: Tusci, ad dextram Tiberis ripam in Italia locatis, omnium Europæorum Primus certam cordi curæque fuisse Religionem, adeo constans inter Doctos convaluit opinio, ut Græci quidem eos sic dictos fuerint arbitrati, Θεοσεβεῖς, quod Diis illi Immortalibus, acceptis ab ævo puriore, Deique, ut nonnullis videtur Populo ritibus sancte sacrificarent: quidam autem sic appellatos censuerunt, ab Ihure, quo, ut aliis etiam rebus, Sacra peragebantur: alii denique Tuscam dictam tradiderint, quasi Salutis Fontem: sic enim תשושה in Lingua Sancta sonare. Tusci tunc, ut ex infinitis Veterum Scriptorum constat Monumentis, summam olim habuerunt Divini Cultus peritiam & usum; eaque re omnes quondam superabant Gentes; quamquam Dionysius jam tum ævo suo Studium id Divinorum adeo apud eos exolevisse scribat, ut cunctarum Nationum uni haberentur Sacrorum incuriosissimi.
units.tr: The Tuscans, who lived on the right bank of the Tiber in Italy, were the first of all the peoples of Europe to take religion to heart and make it their care. Learned men were so firmly of this view that the Greeks thought they were named devout toward God [Θεοσεβεῖς], because they offered sacred sacrifices with careful ritual to the immortal gods, which they had received from a purer age. Some thought they were so called from incense, which was used for sacred rites as well as for other things. Others finally said they were called Tuscan, as if they were the spring of salvation, for תשושה sounds this way in the holy language. As is clear from countless monuments of the ancient writers, the Tuscans once had the greatest skill and practice in divine worship, and for this reason they surpassed all the nations of that time. Yet Dionysius already wrote in his own age that devotion to sacred things had so faded among them that they were regarded as the most careless of all nations in religious matters.

units.la: Fontes apud Priscos Etruriæ Populos devote excitati sensim cum in vicinos & confinales Agros, tum in remotiora totius Europæ Arva feruntur dimanasse. Inter Cometregionales erant Romani, qui post Tuscos nati proximi iis habitabant ad ripam Tiberis interfluentis sinistram. Hi quantum illis in Sacrorum Solemnibus Ritibusque tribuere consueverint, petere ab iis in rebus dubiis Augurum Vatumque Responsa soliti, docent partim M. Tullius cum libro 11 de Nat. Deorum, tum in libris de Legibus, ubi inter alia sic inquit. Prodigia, Portenta ad Etruscos & Haruspices, si Senatus iusserit, deferunto; Etruriaeque Principes Disciplinam docentes, qui eius Divi trecenti, procurantes, idemque Fulgura atque Obstrua prandio: partim Historiae de Oeno Caleno apud Plinium lib. xxviii cap. 11, Naevio Attio apud Dionysium lib. 11, Livium lib. 1, Florum lib. 1 cap. v, Ciceronem lib. 1. de Divinat. Valerium Maximum lib. 1 cap. iv, eundem Plinium lib. xxxiv, Lactantium lib. 11 cap. vii; denique Alii apud alios: Quod item Rerum Divinarum cognitionem ab eodem Romani acceperint, testatur idem Cicero lib. 1. de Divinatione, his verbis: In Sini Chaldaei cognitione Astrorum solertiaque Ingeniorum antecellunt. Etruria autem de caelo tacta fulgent, sine animadversione sunt: eademque interpretantur, quibusque ostenditur Monstris atque Portentis. Quaerenda bene apud Maiores nostros Senatus tum, quum florebat Imperium, decrevit, ut de Principum Filiis singulis Etruria Populis in Disciplinam traderentur, ne Artes tantum propter tenuitatem hominum a Religionis auctoritate abduceretur ad mercedem atque quaestum. Eadem de re Valerius Maximus lib. 1. Dictorum Factorumque Memorabilium cap. 1: Tantum autem Studium Antiqui non solum observandae, sed etiam amplexandae Religionis fuit, ut florentissima tum & opulentissima Civitate decem Principum filii s. c. singulis Etruriae Populis, percipiendae Sacrorum Disciplinae gratia traderentur. Auctor est apud Valerium numerus, quod quum initio Sex tantum, lapsu temporis auctis cum potentia Civibus, Decem ut mitterentur, fuerit decretum. Perdurarunt autem Romani aliquod saeculorum in Ritus, quos ab Etruscis acceperant, puritate, Simplicitatis amantissimi. Reverenter suos Deos habebant. Non apud eos Cum decantabatur ab Filiis castratus; non Saturnus Filiorum Parricida & Carnifex: non Iuppiter Patris insidiator: nulla apud eos audiebantur Deorum Bella, Vulnera, Caedes, Carceres, Servitutes: de quibus & pluribus plene Dionysius; concludens, puris Romanorum Ritibus nil Diis indignum fuisse in usu. Docet idem auctor, cum primis cautum fuisse Romae; ne quis Dei reperirentur Peregrini, nisi quos Oracula accersere iussissent, ut de Idaea Dea memoriae proditum; sed eam Romae receptam, Veteres illos, ne errarent, ritu Phrygio patrioque, non Romano, coli voluisse: abhorruisse praeterea summopere ab omni Fabularum genere, in quibus excogitandis facile principatum obtinebant Graeci: Vidisse enim, & parum inde manare utilitatis, & illud incommodi ex Graecanicis Fabulis oriri, ut Turba maximaque Populi pars, rerum ignara, aut contemneret Deos, Scelestibus & Passionibus infames, Bonisque Viris & Fortibus omnino dissimiles, Pejoresque deteriores; aut, si illos probaret & timeret, libenter imitaretur. Avertabantur item omnem Religionum & Caerimoniarum confusionem. Cautum enim erat, Cicerone indicante, Nequis separatim Deos haberet; neve Novos, sed ne Advenas, nisi publice adscitos, privatim coleret. Quemadmodum Romani ab Etruscis, sic Etrusci ab Hebraeis suos Sacrorum Ritus acceperant: unde factum, ut praeter unam Circumcisionem, nihil fere apud Hebraeos reperiretur; quod non usucatum etiam fuerit, salvis Caerimoniis, quae ubivis gentium diversae utplurimum sunt, ab Romanis. De Sabbato refertur Dion libro Historiae Romanae xxxvii; ejus, quod apud Judaeos, usum ad Graecos Romanosque fuisse translatum. Videre etiam est apud M. Tullium in Sacris Legibus, & apud Halicarnassaeum in Regum Institutis. Diem Romae fuisse sacram, Quieti dicatam Servitiorum & Animalium. Quum vero Romani paullatim à prioribus Initiis degenerassent, Graecarumque Fabularum, ex quibus primo Romana contaminari coepit Theologia, accepissent commercia: receptos ab Etruscis Ritus non solum supra modum mutarunt; verum etiam errores erroribus cumulantes, alios commenti, incredibiliter auxerunt, adeo ut Commentarios, in quibus Numa Pompilius, Secundus Romanorum Rex, simpliciores aevi sui Sacrorum Ritus perscripserat, multis post ipsius mortem aetatibus in Monte Ianiculo repertos, necesse fuerit ex S.C. publice comburi, ne quid inde curiosiora quorumdam ingenia sinisteriorum contra factam Mutationem, quae in Rebus Sacris maxime solet, ipsius Usus diuturnitate, habere locum, Suspicionis conciperent. Ut autem Etrusci Latinis in omnibus ad ipsissimam Simplicitatem; sic Latini, & sequuti ipsos Romani aliis, praecipue subjugatis Italiae Populis & Civitatibus ad varios Sacris Praefectos & multiplices Sacrorum Ritus, foecunda quadam seminatione, praeverunt: Sacrorum curam & administrationem, ut ad scopum tandem huius Capitis convertar, ante Romuli principatum habuisse leguntur in Latio, Luperci, Fratres Arvales, vel Ioni Sacerdotes, Ceréris Græca Sacerdos, quæ tunc Vito ætatem transigebat; Potitij & Pinarij, Hercules Sacerdotes; omnes ab Euandro, Arcadum Rege, institutj; Solemnibus, ut quidam ferunt, ex Arcadia translati. Accesserunt sub Romanorum Regibus, qui & ipsi Sacra quædam, tribuentibus Dionysio lib. II & V Liviōque lib. I & II, obibant, alij quales erant Fratres Arvales XII: Sacerdotes Pubinæ IX: bini nimirum ex singulis Curiis, quæ XXX erant, omnes quinquagenario majores: Augures III, singuli ex singulis Tribubus, quæ tres erant Ramnensium, Tatiensium, & Luceserum; auctitemporis lapsu ad XV: Haruspices VIII: Tribunus Celerum; quem Romulus quidem instituerat, sed Numa fecerat sacerdotem: Curiones XXX; qui totidem Curiis præerant, quorumque primus Curio Maximus dicebatur, cujus auctoritate ceteri Curiones regebantur. Salij Titij vel Titienses: Flamines XV; quorum tres Majores & Patricij vocabantur, quod semper ex eo ordine crearentur, Dialis Iovi sacer, Martialis Marti, Quirinalis Romulo vel Quirino; duodecim autem Minores, & Plebeij Volcanales Volcano, Carmentales Carmentæ, Floralis D. Florae, Palatualis Deæ Palatuæ, Falacer Divo Patri Falacri, Furinalis Deæ Furinæ, Volturnalis Deo Volturno, Tribualis Deo Virbio id est Hippolyto, Laurentinalis Accæ Laurentiæ, Larentalis, Ligularis vel Luculiaris, & Pomonalis Deæ Pomonæ: Flaminica XV: Vestales; quas quatuor ab Numa factas duabus additis auxit Ser. Tullius, quarumque prima Vestalis Maxima audiebat: Salij XII, cum Magistro Collegij Sacerorum: Martii sacrati; seu perque ex Patriciis legi solitu: Virgines Sacrae: Feciales XX cum Patre Patrato: qui Fœderum, Pacis, Belli, Induciarum, Oratorum Iudices erant: Pontifices XV, quorum quatuor initio Numa instituit, omnes Patricios, de Plebe quatuor adjecit anno ab V. C. CCCCXIV Lex Ogulnia, qui omnes Majores appellati, septem denique adpositis, qui Minores dicebantur, numerum ad XV auxit L. Cornelius Sulla Dictator: quorum unus Populi Romani suffragijs creabatur, ceteris præelatus, qui vocabatur Pontifex Maximus, omnibus Populi Romani Sacris Præfectus, inque omnes Sacerdotes maximam & supremam habens potestatem: Sa ij Agonenses vel Colinæ: & XV Viri Sacris faciundis, cum Magistra, qui Librorum Sibyllinorum curam gerebant. His omnibus, Libera Rep. Regibusque exactis, adjuncti sunt Rex Sacrorum, qui & Rex Sacrificulus, cujusque Vxor, Regina Sacrorum: Sacerdotes Bonæ Dea Feminæ: Galli Sacerdotes Dea Cybeles cum Archigallo: VII Viri Epulonum: II-Viri Sedis locandæ, faciundæ, dedicandæ: III-Viri Aedibus Sacris, incendio consumptis, adficiendis: III-Viri Sacris conquirendis, Donisque persequendis: Sacerdotes Deorum singulorum: Antistites denique, si & illi addendi, Templorum singulorum.
units.tr: The springs of devotion stirred among the ancient peoples of Etruria were carried gradually into the neighbouring and bordering fields, and then into more distant lands across Europe. Among their neighbours were the Romans, who were born after the Tuscans and lived next to them on the left bank of the flowing Tiber. How much they were accustomed to attribute to the solemn rites of sacred things, and how often they sought the answers of augurs and seers in doubtful matters, is shown partly by Marcus Tullius in the second book of On the Nature of the Gods, and partly in his books On the Laws, where among other things he says: Let portents and prodigies be referred to the Etruscans and the haruspices, if the Senate so orders; and the leaders of Etruria, teaching their discipline, who are three hundred in number, shall attend to these matters, and likewise to lightning and thunder. It is also shown partly by the histories of Oenus Calenus in Pliny, book 28, chapter 11; of Naevius and Attius in Dionysius, book 2; in Livy, book 1; in Florus, book 1, chapter 5; in Cicero, book 1 On Divination; in Valerius Maximus, book 1, chapter 4; in the same Pliny, book 34; and in Lactantius, book 2, chapter 7; and finally in others in other places. That the Romans likewise received knowledge of divine things from the same source is attested by Cicero himself in the first book On Divination, in these words: The Chaldaeans excel in knowledge of the stars and cleverness of mind. But the Etruscans interpret lightning that strikes from heaven, and whatever is shown by monsters and portents, and they are wise in these matters. Our ancestors, when the empire was flourishing, decided by the Senate that the sons of the leading men of each of the Etruscan peoples should be handed over to be taught this discipline, so that the art should not be drawn away from the authority of religion to pay and profit, because of the poverty of men. On the same matter Valerius Maximus, book 1 of Memorable Sayings and Deeds, chapter 1, writes: The ancients had such zeal not only for observing religion but for embracing it, that when the city was most flourishing and wealthy, the sons of ten leading men were handed over to each of the Etruscan peoples, by decree of the Senate, to be instructed in sacred discipline. Valerius reports the number, saying that at first only six were decreed, but as time passed and citizens grew in power, ten were ordered to be sent. The Romans, however, kept for some centuries the purity of the rites they had received from the Etruscans, being great lovers of simplicity. They revered their gods. Among them no song was sung of a castrated son; no Saturn was a parricide and butcher of his sons; no Jupiter was a plotter against his father. No wars, wounds, slaughters, prisons or servitudes of the gods were heard of among them. Dionysius treats these matters fully and at length, concluding that nothing unworthy of the gods was in use in the pure rites of the Romans. The same author teaches that above all it was carefully ordained at Rome that no foreign gods should be received unless the oracles had summoned them, as is recorded about the Idaean goddess. Yet when she was received at Rome, the ancients, lest they err, wished her to be worshipped in the Phrygian and native manner, not the Roman one. Moreover, they greatly shunned every kind of fable, in which the Greeks easily held first place. For they saw that little advantage came from such things, and that this harm arose from Greek fables: the crowd and the greater part of the people, ignorant of the facts, would either despise the gods, as infamous for crimes and passions and wholly unlike good and brave men, and worse than the worst; or, if they approved and feared them, would gladly imitate them. They likewise avoided all confusion of religions and ceremonies. For it was provided, as Cicero points out, that no one should have gods privately, nor worship new gods, nor foreign ones, unless they had been publicly adopted. Just as the Romans received their sacred rites from the Etruscans, so the Etruscans had received theirs from the Hebrews. Hence it came about that, apart from circumcision, almost nothing was found among the Hebrews that was not also in use among the Romans, though the ceremonies, which differ in most nations everywhere, did not pass over to them. Concerning the Sabbath, Dion in book 37 of his Roman History reports that its observance was transferred from the Jews to the Greeks and Romans. It may also be seen in Cicero in On Sacred Laws, and in Halicarnassensis in On the Institutions of the Kings. There was a day at Rome sacred to rest, dedicated to slaves and animals. But when the Romans gradually degenerated from their early beginnings, and admitted the traffic of Greek fables, from which Roman theology first began to be corrupted, they not only changed beyond measure the rites received from the Etruscans, but, heaping errors upon errors and devising others, they increased them incredibly. So much so that the commentaries in which Numa Pompilius, the second king of the Romans, had written out the simpler sacred rites of his age, found many centuries after his death on the Janiculum, had to be publicly burned by decree of the Senate, lest the more curious minds of certain men should conceive from them some suspicion against the change made in sacred matters, which usually takes place through the long duration of use. But just as the Etruscans kept everything among the Latins in the most exact simplicity, so the Latins, and the Romans who followed them, through a kind of fruitful sowing, handed on to other peoples, especially the subjugated peoples and states of Italy, various sacred officers and manifold sacred rites. To come at last to the purpose of this chapter: the care and administration of sacred things are read to have existed in Latium before the reign of Romulus, namely the Luperci, the Arval Brothers or priests of Jupiter, the Greek priestess of Ceres, who then spent her life in Vesta; the Potitii and Pinarii, priests of Hercules; all instituted by Evander, king of the Arcadians, and, as some say, transferred from Arcadia with the rites. Under the kings of Rome others were added, who themselves performed certain sacred duties, as Dionysius in books 2 and 5 and Livy in books 1 and 2 attribute: such as the twelve Arval Brothers; the nine priests of Pubina, namely two from each of the thirty curiae, all older than fifty; three augurs, one from each of the three tribes, the Ramnenses, Tatienses and Luceres, which number later grew to fifteen; eight haruspices; the Tribune of the Celeres, whom Romulus had instituted but Numa made a priest; thirty curiones, who presided over as many curiae, the first of whom was called Curio Maximus, and by whose authority the other curiones were governed; the Salii Titii or Titienses; fifteen flamens, of whom three were called greater and patrician, because they were always created from that order: the Dialis, sacred to Jupiter, the Martialis, to Mars, the Quirinalis, to Romulus or Quirinus; and twelve lesser and plebeian flamens: the Volcanalis to Vulcan, Carmentalis to Carmenta, Floralis to the goddess Flora, Palatualis to the goddess Palatua, Falacer to the divine father Falacer, Furinalis to the goddess Furina, Volturnalis to the god Volturnus, Tribualis to the god Virbius, that is Hippolytus, Laurentinalis to Acca Laurentia, Larentalis, Ligularis or Luculiaris, and Pomonalis to the goddess Pomona; fifteen flaminicae; the Vestals, whom Numa made four and Servius Tullius increased by two more, and of whom the first was called the Vestalis Maxima; twelve Salii, with a Master of the College of Sacred Rites, the sacred Martii, who were usually chosen from the patricians; the Sacred Virgins; twenty Fetiales with the Pater Patratus, who were judges of treaties, peace, war, truces and envoys; fifteen pontiffs, of whom Numa at first instituted four, all patricians, and in the year 414 from the founding of the city the Ogulnian law added four plebeians, all called greater; and finally, when seven more were added who were called lesser, Lucius Cornelius Sulla, the dictator, raised the number to fifteen. Of these one was created by the votes of the Roman people and was set above the rest, and was called Pontifex Maximus, presiding over all the sacred rites of the Roman people and holding the greatest and supreme power over all the priests; the Salii Agonenses or Colini; and the fifteen men for performing sacred rites, with a Master, who had charge of the Sibylline books. To all these, when the republic was free and the kings had been expelled, were added the King of Sacred Rites, also called the sacrificing king, and his wife, the Queen of Sacred Rites; the priestesses of the Good Goddess; the Gallus priests of the goddess Cybele with the Archigallus; seven men of the Epulones; two men for locating, making and dedicating sacred seats; three men for repairing sacred buildings consumed by fire; three men for seeking out sacred things and pursuing gifts; the priests of the individual gods; and finally, if these also are to be added, the officiants of the individual temples.

units.la: Iam Sacerdotes, Augures, & Pontifices ex Vrbe in Colonias & Municipia (procul dubio & in Præfecturas, fuisse disseminatos, ibique cooptari solitos, petet ex Ciceronis Agrariis. Habuisse & Flamines tuos Flaminicasque retinentur antiqua Marmora. Quin & ipsa Tirunia, quæ quondam mater fuerat & prima ovili formatrix Religionis Romanæ, debellata suos etiam cum Sacris Sacerdotes ab Lucipula vel mutuata est, vel suscipere fuit coacta. An vero certus Numerus Sacerdotum fuerit in Colonijs, Municipijs & Præfecturis, an vero pro ipsorum magnitudine varierit: parum explorata apud Antiquos est memoria.
units.tr: Now that priests, augurs, and pontiffs were scattered from the City into the colonies and municipalities (and without doubt into the prefectures too), and were accustomed to being co-opted there, may be learned from Cicero's Agrarian Speeches. Ancient marbles also attest that they had their flamens and flaminicae. Indeed Tirunia itself, which once was the mother and first shaper of the Roman religion, when it was conquered either borrowed its priests along with their rites from Lucipula, or was forced to receive them. Whether there was a fixed number of priests in the colonies, municipalities and prefectures, or whether it varied according to their size, is little explored in the memory of the ancients.

units.la: Manserunt Romæ Sacerdotes, quos enumeravi, omnes, quamdiu stetit florutque Respublica, & aliquot etiam ætates sub Imperatoribus. Prima Sublatio cœpit à Pontificatu Maximo. Quum enim, mortuo M. Æmilio Lepido, qui post eandem C. Julij Cæsaris honorem hunc per vim invaserat, Sacerdotium illud suscepisset Augustus, ejusque exemplum sequuti fuissent Principes omnes Successores; decessit, cum qui totius Imperij Possessionem adeptus erat, supremam quoque Divinarum Rerum Auctoritatem, quæ hoc Sacerdotio comprehendebatur, habere: Primus omnium Gratianus Imperator Edicto proposito (ut Zosimus docet) se Pontificem Maximum appellari vetuit: quamvis ante ipsius Principatum alij, Christianæ Religioni addicti, ut Constantinus, Constantius, Valentinianus, Valens & Gratianus id, Elogiu s adscriptum, non fuissent adjernati: itaque ejus Sacerdotij dignitas abolita in Imperatoribus defecit: sic tamen, ut postea renata fuerit in Præsulibus Romanis. Pontificem Maximum sequuti sunt Augures, Flamines & Flaminica. minis, Virgines Vestales, Pontifices ceteri Maiores Minoresque; quos cum reliquis Vetustae Superstitionis Sacerdotis Sacrisque sustulit circa annum cccxc Theodosius Imperator, nequidquam reclamante Senatu. Legendi Symmachus in Epistolis, & Ambrosius in Responsionibus. Diutissimi perseveraverunt in Rep. Romana Lupercì, quos omnium novissimos abolevit Gelasius Papa, Anastasio Imperatore & Theodorico Amalo Gothorum Rege in Italia regnante, circa annum cccccxv. At vero qui qualescunque remotis & abdicare iussis subrogati? Praevaluerat scilicet circa annum cc Christiana Religio; cuius magnus iam coeperat esse ab Salvatore passo per Italiam quoque gustus. Exercendae Sacrosanctae Christi Religionis veniam impetrarant Christiani ab Tiberio Imperatore, qui etiam ipse ad Senatum detulerat Christum Deorum numero adscribendum, cum praerogativa Suffragii sui, ut notat Tertullianus v Apologetico: sed Senatus, qui ipsum non probaverat, respuit. Nihil scilicet publice, absque Senatus Decreto, licebat: omnia privatim fiebant. Ecclesiae divinitus conlectae, praeter Presbyteros & Diaconos, suos habebant Pastores, doctrina, pietate, gravitate insignes, qui & Dispensatores Mysteriorum dicebantur, quod Verbum Domini docere, Sacramenta administrare, Disciplinam exercere ipsos oporteret: vocabantur & Episcopi, quod tamquam Inspectores Gregis communi curam gerere eosdem deceret. Legebantur illi iudicio Cleri Populique suffragio. Differt ea de re Cyprianus in Epist. Coram omni synagoga, inquit, iubet Deus constitui Sacerdotem, ac offendit Ordinationes Sacerdotales nonnisi sub Populi co[n]sentia fieri oportere, ut Plebe praesente detegantur Malorum Crimina, vel Bonorum Merita praedicentur & sit Ordinatio iusta & legitima, quae omnium Suffragio & Iudicio fuerit examinata; eaque hae Disciplina definita. Et lib. 1. Epist. iv: Diligenter, ait, de Traditione divina & Apostolica observandum & tenendum est, quod apud nos quoque, & per universas Provincias tenetur; ut, ad Ordinationes rite celebrandas, Praepositus ordinetur Plebe praesente, quae singulorum Vitam perspiciat, & uniuscuiusque Actum de eius Conversatione perspexit. Quod & apud nos factum videmus in Sacro Collegio nostro Ordinationis universae Fraternitatis Suffragio & de Episcopis, qui in praesentia convenerant, quaeque ad eos apud vos Litteris fere aut iudicium, ipsi opera ut ei deferretur, & Manus ei in locum Ejus dis imponeretur. Sic idem ait lib. iii. Epistol. xiii, Cornelium Dei iudicio, Cleri ac Plebis suffragio Episcopum ordinatum fuisse. Erant autem illi inter se coniunctissimi. Testatur Basilius Epistola xv ad Neocaesar. Episcopos Ecclesiae Caritatis zelo adeo vehementes aliquot saeculis praeditos fuisse, ut in modum Coronae uniti essent; quisque in Collegam suum Paedagogi & Ducis ministerii Munus obibat. Ipsi copius Presbyterorum. Presbyter Diaconum fraterne admonebat, & communi Consilio Ecclesiam regebant. Qui enim inter multos Presbyteros Episcopus dicebatur, tenebatur cum Presbyteris & Diaconis instre consilium, de iis, quae ad Ecclesiam gubernationem pertinebant: CHRISTUM, non Lucrum; Religionem, non Regionem; Episcopatus Onus, non Honorem; pro Dei Gloria Martyrium non otium, nedum Regnum Ecclesiae Rectores tunc adspectabant: sed Doctrinae & Disciplinae Exercitio ita incumbebant, ut nihil aliud sibi cibum oporteret ponere, quam in terra Deo servire fideliter, & pro eius Confessione fortiter mori: posteaque in Caelo ornari. Delegati sunt igitur ex communi consensu Presbyteri multis in Pagos fideles operarii, ut amplium Domini Messem collegerunt. Commissi vero ipsis Graecis quibus privatum publiceque fuerunt Moribus? De pingue paucis Plinius lib. x. epistola ad Trajanum: Affirmabant hanc fuisse Summam vel Culpae suae vel Erroris (sic ille nominat Christianam Religionem) quod essent solliti statu die ante lucem convenire, Carmenque Christo quasi Deo dicere secum invicem; seque Sacramento non in scelus aliquod obstringere: sed ne Furta, ne Latrocinia, ne Adulteria committerent, ne Fidem fallerent, ne Depositum appellari abnegarent: quibus peractis morem sibi discedendi fuisse, rursusque coeundi ad capiendum Cibum, promiscuum tamen & innoxium, quod ipsum facere desisse post Edictum meum &c. Pluribus haec Tertullianus, cui in Antiquitate Ecclesiastica plurimum est tribuendum, diffundit, infinitis locis, praecipue vero in Apologetico contra Gentes, & lib. ii ad Uxorem. Ex eo sane discimus, Veteres illos Christianos non prius discumbere solitos, quam ad Deum Preces sudissent: tantum Cibi cepisse, quantum esurientibus satis esset; tantum Potus, quantum sobrius expediret: ita saturari consuevisse, ut memoria tenerent, etiam per noctem sive esse surgendum ad nocturnos conventus celebrandos; in quibus convenichant ad Divinarum Scripturarum Institutionem, orabantque pro Imperatoribus, CHRISTI Hostibus; Vitam illis diuturnam precantes.
units.tr: The priests I have listed all remained at Rome as long as the Republic stood and flourished, and for some ages even under the emperors. The first removal began with the Pontificate Maximum. When, after the death of Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, who had seized this office by force after the honour of Gaius Julius Caesar, Augustus had taken up that priesthood, and all the later princes had followed his example, the supreme authority over sacred things, which was comprised in this priesthood, passed away from the one who had gained possession of the whole empire. The first of all was the emperor Gratian, who by a published edict (as Zosimus teaches) forbade himself to be called Pontifex Maximus; although before his reign others who were devoted to the Christian religion, such as Constantine, Constantius, Valentinian, Valens and Gratian, had not refused that title when it was added to their names. Thus the dignity of this priesthood was abolished and lapsed among the emperors, yet in such a way that it was later revived in the Roman bishops. The augurs, flamens and flaminicae followed the Pontifex Maximus, as did the Vestal virgins and the other pontiffs, greater and lesser; these, together with the rest of the priests and rites of the old superstition, were abolished by the emperor Theodosius about the year 390, though the Senate protested in vain. Read Symmachus in his Letters and Ambrose in his Replies. The Luperci persisted longest in the Roman Republic; the last of all of them were abolished by Pope Gelasius, while the emperor Anastasius and Theodoric the Amal, king of the Goths, reigned in Italy, about the year 495. But who were substituted for these men, of whatever kind, who were removed and ordered to stand down? Surely the Christian religion had prevailed by about the year 200; its great savour had already begun to be tasted throughout Italy too, from the suffering of the Saviour. Christians had obtained permission from the emperor Tiberius to practise the holy religion of Christ, and he himself had proposed to the Senate that Christ be counted among the gods, with the prerogative of his own vote, as Tertullian notes in the fifth book of his Apology; but the Senate, which had not approved of him, rejected it. Nothing, of course, could be done publicly without a decree of the Senate; everything was done privately. The churches, gathered by God's own act, besides the elders and deacons, had their own ministers, distinguished for teaching, piety and gravity, who were also called stewards of the mysteries, because they ought to teach the Word of the Lord, administer the sacraments and exercise discipline; they were also called bishops, because it was fitting that they, as overseers of the flock, should take common care of it. They were chosen by the judgement of the clergy and the vote of the people. Cyprian treats this matter in his Epistles: "In the presence of the whole congregation," he says, "God orders a priest to be appointed," and he observes that priestly ordinations ought to be made only with the consent of the people, so that, the people being present, the crimes of the wicked may be exposed or the merits of the good proclaimed, and the ordination may be just and lawful, having been examined by the judgement and vote of all; and this discipline was thereby settled. And in the first book, Epistle 4: "Carefully," he says, "we must observe and hold to the divine and apostolic tradition, which is also held among us and throughout all the provinces: that, for ordinations to be duly performed, the leader be ordained with the people present, who may know the life of each one, and who has examined the conduct of each man in his way of life. And we see this also done among us in our sacred college, by the vote of the whole brotherhood and of the bishops who had gathered in our presence; and the letters that were sent to you concerning them were almost a judgement, and the imposition of hands was done in his place." So he says in the third book, Epistle 13, that Cornelius was made bishop by the judgement of God and the vote of the clergy and people. Moreover, those bishops were very closely bound to one another. Basil testifies in his fifteenth Epistle to Neocaesarea that for some centuries bishops of the Church were so fervent in the zeal of charity that they were united as in a garland; each one performed the office of a tutor and guide towards his colleague. The presbyters of many of them gathered together, a presbyter admonished a deacon as a brother, and by common counsel they ruled the Church. For he who among many presbyters was called bishop was bound to hold counsel with the presbyters and deacons on those matters which pertained to the government of the Church. The rulers of the Church at that time looked to CHRIST, not to gain; to religion, not to region; to the burden of the episcopate, not to honour; to the glory of God, to martyrdom, not to leisure, much less to a kingdom of the Church. They devoted themselves so to the exercise of teaching and discipline that they judged nothing else should be set before them as food than to serve God faithfully on earth and to die bravely for his confession, and afterwards to be adorned in heaven. Therefore, by common consent, presbyters were sent out into many villages as faithful workers, so that they might gather in the wider harvest of the Lord. But what were the customs of the Christians, which were committed to them, both private and public? Pliny, in the tenth book, letter to Trajan, has a brief account: they affirmed that the sum of their fault or error (so he calls the Christian religion) was that they were accustomed to meet on a fixed day before dawn and to sing a hymn to Christ as to God, among themselves in turn; and that they bound themselves by a sacrament not to any crime, but not to commit theft, robbery or adultery, not to break faith, not to deny a deposit when it was claimed; after these things were done, it was their custom to depart and to come together again to take food, ordinary and harmless, which they had ceased to do after my edict, etc. Tertullian, to whom very much must be attributed in ecclesiastical antiquity, spreads these things abroad in very many places, especially in his Apology against the Gentiles and in the second book To His Wife. From him we certainly learn that those ancient Christians were not accustomed to recline at table before they had poured out prayers to God; they took as much food as was enough for the hungry, as much drink as sobriety required; they were accustomed to be so satisfied that they kept in mind that they must rise even at night to hold their nocturnal assemblies, in which they gathered for instruction in the divine Scriptures, and prayed for the emperors, enemies of Christ, asking for their long life.

units.la: {a} Eccl. pro: fuerint; ut ... (faint) sime persequutus est Isidorus libro de Ecclesiasticis Officijs, cap. xi. Alij Psalmista sive Cantores nominabantur, qui iussu Episcopi vel Presbyteri Cantandi munus obibant, & alijs praecinebant. Pij enim in Ecclesiasticis Conventibus, uti paret ex Tertulliano & Plinio, Hymnos Deo canebant, insigni cum Religione & Reverentia: non tantum ut Deo gratias agerent, sed ut in afflictionibus Consolationem, Fortitudinem, & Auxilium divinum implorarent. Erant denique Exorcistae, Subdiaconi, Ostiarij. Episcopo non licebat suam Ecclesiam deserere, neque in aliam transire, nisi id cum Ecclesiae consensu & multorum Episcoporum iudicio ad Dei gloriam promovendum fieret: quod postea in Canonem fuit relatum, uti docent Acta Concilij Antiocheni. Episcopo etiam peregre proficisci non licebat, & in alienam Ecclesiam versari absque litteris commendatitiis Presbyterij, quibus Causae Peregrinationis suscepte exponebantur. Ad Dogmata vero Pietatis & Disciplinae explorandum, Consensumque in illis retinendum, Episcopi & Presbyteri multarum Ecclesiarum bis saltem in anno conveniebant, ut communi consilio & consensu Opus Domini promoverent testantibus illud plene Actis Conciliorum Ancyrani & Neocaesariensis, quae quum Persequutionibus saeviretur, fuerunt celebrata.
units.tr: {a} Eccl. pro: fuerint; ut ... (faint) most diligently pursued by Isidore in his book On Ecclesiastical Offices, chapter 11. Others were called psalmists or cantors, who, at the command of the bishop or presbyter, performed the office of singing and led the others in song. For the pious, in the ecclesiastical assemblies, as is clear from Tertullian and Pliny, sang hymns to God with remarkable religious devotion and reverence, not only to give thanks to God, but to implore comfort, strength and divine help in their afflictions. Finally there were exorcists, subdeacons, and doorkeepers. A bishop was not permitted to desert his Church or to pass into another, unless this was done with the consent of the Church and the judgement of many bishops, for the promotion of God's glory; this was afterwards put into a canon, as the Acts of the Council of Antioch teach. Nor was it lawful for a bishop to travel abroad and to live in a foreign Church without letters of commendation from the presbytery, in which the reasons for the journey undertaken were set out. Moreover, to examine doctrines of piety and discipline, and to keep consent in them, bishops and presbyters of many churches met together at least twice a year, so that by common counsel and agreement they might advance the work of the Lord; this is fully attested by the Acts of the Councils of Ancyra and Neocaesarea, which were held while persecutions were raging.

units.la: Latum lapsu temporis in Concilijs, ut inter multos eiusdem Provinciae vel Regionis Episcopos eligeretur unus, qui Archiepiscopus vel Primarius Episcopus diceretur; penes quem inter alia esset, Coepiscopos in Synodum Provincialem convocare, non generalem: illam enim solus Imperator auctoritate sua indicebat.
units.tr: Over time, through the decrees of councils, it came to be the practice that from among the many bishops of the same province or region one was chosen who would be called the Archbishop or Primate. Among his other duties, he had the power to summon the fellow bishops to a provincial synod, but not a general one, since only the emperor could call that by his own authority.

units.la: Fuit autem Praesulum Romanorum, trecentorum fere annorum curriculo, usque ad Constantini Magni tempora, Conditio rerum humanarum spectatur splendor, miserrima. Multi Tyrannide sunt oppressi. Paucos indicabo. Cornelius sub Vibijs Tribonianis Gallo & Volusiano capite est truncatus: Caius Salonensis Dalmata, una cum Fratre Gabinio, sub Diocletiano & Maximiano Martyrio in Cryptis, in quibus vitandae Persequutionis causa latitarat, est affectus: ut & successor ipsius Marcellinus, qui, acta Poenitentia, quod Diis Gentium metu Mortus sacrificaret, in fide Christi ardentius persistens, & Sacrificia Gentium detestans, iussu Maximiani capitis subijt supplicium. Marcellus ab Maxentio in Pistrinum est coniectus; quo in opere ipse mox nudus & vix cilicio tectus, misere exspiravit. Alios praeterea. Nam Martyrium ob adsertionem constantis in Christum Fidei subijsse loquuntur Historiae Praesules propemodum omnes Romanos, usque ad Constantinum Magnum Imperatorem. Hic, parta veri Numinis ope contra Maxentium Victoria, Primus eos ex tenebris eduxit in luminis oras, quum antea in Cryptis fere latitarent, & nocturnos Conventus propter Tyrannorum Persequutiones colerent. Ornatam insigni huius beneficio (non loquor de Donatione, quam non veram esse probarunt non pauci) Urbem & Ecclesiam Romanam, Templisque instructam magnificis, & Nicaeni Concilij Legibus temperatam, suis reliquit Silvester Successoribus, quorum anceps postea variaque fuit conditio. Liberius enim in Concilio Mediolanensi damnatus fuit, & in exilium postea pulsus. Felix ii in locum Liberii exsulis factus est Episcopus: sed Liberum Imperatoris Constantij Arriani iussu liberatus Felicem loco movit. Damasus cum Ursicino ab Schismaticis Episcopi sunt designati, magno motu in Urbe concitato. Quum vero Alaricus Gothorum Rex Romam obsidione premeret, Innocentius ad Honorium Imperatorem est missus, ut de Pace componenda cum Hoste ageret: postea Bonifacius & Eulalius in Comitiis Schismaticis Episcopi sunt electi. Xystus Praetul variis ijsque capitalibus oneratus Criminibus vix legitur solutus. Talis fuit Episcoporum Romanorum ab Silvestro ad Xystum usque, emenso vix centum annorum curriculo, Status turbulentus sane & dubius. Quid Urbis & Ecclesiae quae fuit conditio? Alarico primum ad inducias pacis confirmandas quadraginta Librarum millia fuerunt persolvenda: sed postquam ab illo obsessa fuit Civitas, ingens eam Fames oppressit, Famem crudelis Pestilentia excepit: quumque passim omnia Cadaveribus implerentur, quod more solito extra Urbem recondi non possent, Lues ipsa dira odoris foeditate ingeminata est, Plebsque, stimulante Fame, in seipsam saevire coepit: & (quod horrendum dictu est) ab Romanis Gentilium Sacrificia (quae, & omnes Antiquorum Superstitiones aboleverat iam Constantinus magnam partem: nam omnia, nec ipse, nec Successores potuerant, manentibus adhuc multis veteri Superstitioni obligatis: neque forte voluerunt, nimiam hic Violentiam avorsati, unde hodieque Rituum Cærimoniarumque Veterum non pauca in Ecclesijs Romanis superant) sunt repetita, Senatusque in Capitolio Idolis sacrificavit: à quibus se conservari posse existimabat. Neque ita Romani Episcopi post Constantinum Imperatorem caput exercere potuerunt, ut non eorum multi variis calamitatibus fuerint iactati. Notæ sunt Historiæ cum aliorum, tum Silverij Pelagiique, quorum ille, capta Vrbe, proditionis suspectus in exilium est pulsus: hic, eius Successor, accusatus apud Iustinianum Imperatorem, quod Sylverium Antecessorem suum abdicandum curaret, & manus ei intulisset, comprehensus Principis mandatu in Græciam captivus est amandatus: Constantinopoli vero percussus alapa, fugit in Templum D. Euphemiæ, & columnam inibi amplexus est: sed inde abreptus, perque totam urbem tractus, clamante Plebe, Ecce Homicida, advenit Dominator Dominus, atque in Carcerem coniectus, modico pane & aqua vitam inisere tolerare est coactus. Quum vero Iustinianus, Cleri Romani precibus flexus, Vigilium dimisisset, & is in Siciliam Romam cogitans pervenisset, vitam ibi finivit, non sine mortis violentæ suspicione, qua Pelagius, qui ei successisset, est oneratus. Quo vero loco res fuerint Episcopi Romani, Mauritij Imperatoris tempore, testatur Epistola Gregorij I ad Constantiam Imperatricem: qua conqueritur se per annos xxvii inter Langbardorum vixisse gladios, illisque non Episcopum, sed Sacellarium fuisse. Cum huiusmodi igitur tempestatibus conflictati sunt fexcentos annos Antistites Romani, quos eleganter cum sui sæculi Pontificibus Maximus committit Poeta, qui temporibus scripsit Hadriani IV P. M. Is inter alia: Cogitet antiquos primæui temporis annos, Præteritosque dies & secula prisca revolvat: Num Petrus, aut Clemens, numcetera turba piorum Sceptra Latina dabat? Romanus tempore prisco Pauper erat Præsul: regali munere crevit; Nec tamen ut Fasces, & Regnitura Latini Vel dare præsumat, vel cuiquam tollere possit.
units.tr: For about three hundred years, until the time of Constantine the Great, the condition of the Roman bishops was, as one may observe in human affairs, most wretched rather than splendid. Many were oppressed by tyranny. I will name a few. Cornelius was beheaded under the emperors Gallus and Volusianus. Caius of Salona in Dalmatia, together with his brother Gabinius, was put to death under Diocletian and Maximian; he had been hiding in caves to avoid persecution. So too his successor Marcellinus, who, after doing penance because he had sacrificed to the gods of the Gentiles out of fear of death, then persisted more ardently in the faith of Christ, detested the sacrifices of the Gentiles, and by Maximian's order underwent capital punishment. Marcellus was thrown into a mill by Maxentius; there, stripped almost naked and barely covered with sackcloth, he died wretchedly from the labour. There were others besides. For nearly all the Roman bishops whom the histories mention suffered martyrdom for their steadfast confession of Christian faith, down to Constantine the Great. He, after winning victory against Maxentius by the help of the true God, first led them out of darkness into the light, since before this they had mostly been hiding in caves and holding night-time assemblies because of the persecutions of tyrants. The city and the Roman Church, adorned with his notable benefits (I do not mean the Donation, which many have shown to be not genuine), furnished with magnificent temples, and regulated by the laws of the Council of Nicaea, Silvester left to his successors, whose condition afterwards was uncertain and variable. For Liberius was condemned at the Council of Milan and later driven into exile. Felix was made bishop in the place of the exiled Liberius; but Liberius, freed by order of the Arian emperor Constantius, displaced Felix. Damasus and Ursinus were appointed bishops by schismatics, and great unrest was stirred up in the city. When Alaric, king of the Goths, pressed Rome with a siege, Innocent was sent to the emperor Honorius to negotiate peace with the enemy. Afterwards Boniface and Eulalius were elected bishops in rival assemblies. Xystus, a prelate burdened with various and even capital charges, is scarcely recorded as having been acquitted. Such was the state of the Roman bishops from Silvester to Xystus, in a span of barely a hundred years: certainly a turbulent and uncertain condition. And what was the condition of the city and the Church? At first forty thousand pounds had to be paid to Alaric to confirm the truce; but after the city was besieged by him, a huge famine overwhelmed it, and a cruel pestilence followed the famine. Since everything was filled everywhere with corpses, which could not be buried outside the city in the usual way, the dreadful plague was increased by the foulness of the smell, and the common people, goaded by hunger, began to turn against themselves. And (horrible to relate) the sacrifices of the Gentiles were restored by the Romans (Constantine had already abolished these, along with most of the superstitions of the ancients; but he and his successors could not do away with all of them, since many still remained bound to the old superstition, and perhaps they did not wish to, shrinking from excessive violence here; hence even today not a few of the old rites and ceremonies survive in the Roman churches), and the Senate sacrificed to the idols on the Capitol, believing that they could be preserved by these. Nor after the emperor Constantine could the Roman bishops exercise their office without many of them being tossed about by various calamities. The histories of Silverius and Pelagius are well known, as are those of others. Silverius, when the city was taken, was suspected of treachery and driven into exile. Pelagius, his successor, was accused before the emperor Justinian of having arranged for his predecessor Silverius to be deposed, and of having laid hands on him. Seized by the prince's command, he was sent as a captive to Greece. At Constantinople, however, he was struck with a slap, fled into the temple of St Euphemia, and clung there to a column. But he was dragged from there and hauled through the whole city, while the crowd shouted, "Behold the murderer! The Lord and Master has come!" Thrown into prison, he was forced to endure life on a small measure of bread and water. When Justinian, moved by the prayers of the Roman clergy, had released Vigilius, and Vigilius, intending to return to Rome, had reached Sicily, he ended his life there, not without suspicion of a violent death, which was also laid upon Pelagius, who had succeeded him. What the condition of the Roman bishops was in the time of the emperor Maurice is attested by the letter of Gregory I to the empress Constantina, in which he complains that for twenty-seven years he had lived among the swords of the Lombards, and that during that time he had been not a bishop but a sacristan. So the Roman prelates, for some six hundred years, were tossed about by such storms. The poet who wrote in the time of Pope Hadrian IV, most elegantly compares them with the pontiffs of his own age. Among other things he says: "Let him consider the years of the earliest age, and let him unroll the days gone by and the ancient centuries: did Peter, or Clement, or the rest of the crowd of the pious, give Latin sceptres? In early times the Roman prelate was a poor man; he grew through royal gift; yet he may not presume to give the rods and the kingdom that is to belong to the Latins, nor can he take them from anyone."

units.la: Pontifices Maximos nominavi. Nam Nomen illud iamdiu Gratiani Imperatoris Decreto sepultum, post annum circiter c cxxv renasci cœperat. Testis est Paulus Diaconus libr. xviii ad Petitionem Bonifacij Phocam, qui Mauricium Imperatorem, Dominum suum, cum omni Prole proditorie exstinxerat, & Imperium invaserat, statuisse, ut Sedes Romanæ Ecclesiæ Caput esset omnium Ecclesiarum: quia, inquit, Ecclesia Constantinopolitana primam se omnium Ecclesiarum scribebat. Sic Romanus Universalis & omnium Episcoporum Princeps, aliis frustra renitentibus, est designatus.
units.tr: I have named them Supreme Pontiffs. For that name, long buried by the decree of the emperor Gratian, began to be revived about the year 1125. Paul the Deacon, in book 18, is a witness: at the petition of Boniface, Phocas, who had treacherously destroyed his lord, the emperor Maurice, with all his offspring, and had seized the empire, ordained that the See of the Roman Church should be the head of all the churches; because, as he says, the Church of Constantinople was calling itself the first of all the churches. Thus the Roman bishop was appointed as the universal prince of all bishops, though others resisted him in vain.

units.la: Proximi Pontificibus in Ecclesia Romana sunt hodie Cardinales, qui unde sic dicti, quando cœperint, quibusque modis pauci initio ad numerum, qui iamnunc est, exercuerint, docent abunde alij, præcipue Onuphrius in eo, quem scripsit de Cardinalium Origine, aliòque de Episcopatibus, Titulis & Diaconis Cardinalium. Dignitas eorum maxime celebrari cœpit ex Decreto quodam Concilij Sutriensis, anno ciɔɔlxx. Quum autem circa annum cio cclxxvii potentissimus Imperator Fridericus II (uti Platina refert) Innocentij IV & Confœderatorum armis in Parmæ obsidione insigni clade affectus esset, Victor Pontifex voluit, ut Galero rubro in posterum Cardinales uterentur; utque, quemadmodum Purpura Antiquis Imperatoribus Imperatoriæ Potestatis testera erat, sic Pileus coccineus splendorem Cardinalibus adferret, qui progressu temporis Archiepiscopi & Episcopi sunt prælati. Cardinalium cognomen usurpant in Ecclesia Romana tres Clericorum Ordines, Presbyteri, Diaconi, & sequuti illos multo post tempore Episcopi, Presbyteri Cardinales omnium cententur antiquissimi. Præerant illi Titulis. Tituli nihil aliud quam Templa, Ecclesiæ, Loca Sacra in Sanctorum memoriam erecta, & per Vrbis Regiones ab Romanis Præsulibus distincta; in quibus animarum cura a Presbyteris, qui in ijs commorabantur, habebatur. Presbyteri autem hi Cardinales dicebantur, quasi Principales, similitudine à quatuor Ventis, ut quidam volunt, Cardinalibus, id est principalibus, deducta, du^a. Quum enim in unoquoque Titulo plures essent Clerici, qui Sacramenta Populis exhiberent, vel exhibentibus praesto essent, ut Presbyteri, Diaconi, Subdiaconi, is, qui omnibus praerat Presbyter, ab ceteris Clericis illius Tituli, dicebatur Cardinalis quod reliquis dignior principaliorve esset in eo Titulo commorantibus, ceterosque Clericos regeret vel gubernaret in Titulo ipsi commisso viventes. Huiusmodi Tituli propter Christianorum paucitatem initio pauci fuerunt: qui, crescente quotidie Fidelium numero, auxerunt ad xxviii. Hic numerus ad Avorum nostrorum tempora semper mansit. Veteres xxviii Titulos, quiante c1ɔc annum in Vrbe fuerunt, hos in Actionibus Synodi Romanae, quae sub Symmacho celebrata, & apud Anastasium Bibliothecarium legO.
units.tr: Next to the Pontiffs in the Roman Church today are the Cardinals. Others have amply taught why they are so called, when they began, and by what means a few at first came to the number that now exists, especially Onuphrius in his work on the origin of the Cardinals, and in another on the bishoprics, titles and deacons of the Cardinals. Their dignity began to be greatly celebrated from a certain decree of the Council of Sutri, in the year 1070. But when, about the year 1277 (as Platina reports), the most powerful emperor Frederick II had been struck by a notable defeat at the siege of Parma, by the arms of Innocent IV and his allies, Pope Victor wished that Cardinals should thereafter use a red hat, so that, just as purple was a token of imperial power for the ancient emperors, so a scarlet cap might bring splendour to the Cardinals, who in the course of time were promoted to archbishops and bishops. Three orders of clergy in the Roman Church claim the name of Cardinal: presbyters, deacons, and, long afterwards, bishops who followed them; the Cardinal presbyters are reckoned the most ancient of all. These presided over the titles. The titles were nothing other than temples, churches, and sacred places erected in memory of the saints, and distinguished by the Roman bishops across the regions of the city; in these the cure of souls was held by the presbyters who dwelt in them. These presbyters were called Cardinal, as if principal, the name being derived, as some hold, from the similarity with the four cardinal winds, that is, principal ones. For since in each title there were several clerics who administered the sacraments to the people, or who were at hand to assist those administering them, such as presbyters, deacons, and subdeacons, the one who presided over all of them was the presbyter, and he was called Cardinal by the other clerics of that title, because he was worthier and more principal than the rest who dwelt in that title, and because he ruled or governed the other clerics living in the title committed to him. Such titles were at first few, because of the small number of Christians; but as the number of the faithful grew daily, they were increased to twenty-eight. This number remained the same down to the times of our forefathers. The old twenty-eight titles, which were in the city about the year 500, I have read listed in the Acts of the Roman Synod, which was held under Symmachus, and in Anastasius the librarian.
