units.la: Noti sunt hodieque omnes, exceptis septem, S. Crescentiana, Fasciola, S. Cai, S. Matthaei in Merulana, S. Aemiliana, S. Nicomedis, & Tigridae, pro quibus in Actione Synodi Romanae sub Gregorio Papa i celebratae & apud Anastasium Bibliothecarium Septem alii leguntur repositi, S. Balbina in Monte Aventino, SS. Nerei & Achillei. S. Xysti, SS. Marcellini & Petri, S. Crucis in Hierusalem, S. Stephani in Monte Caelio, & SS. Quatuor Coronatorum. Qui omnes adhuc durant uno excepto S Cyriaci in Thermis Diocletiani, qui quum prae vetustate corruisset, Templo solo aequato, Titulus ab Xysto iv ad Ecclesiam SS. Quirici & Iuliae translatus est; ubi & nunc quoque manet. Videamus porro, quur neque plures, neque pauciores Tituli simul fuerint instituti. Veteres Romani Pontifices, uti patet ex libro Camerae Apostolicae, qui appellatur Provincialis, quinque in Urbe Roma maiores & praestantiores Basilicas, vel iam fabricatas eligentes, vel novas fabricantes, Patriarchales Ecclesiae appellarunt, Palatiaque illis adiuncta Patriarchia. Fuerunt ex, i Basilica Lateranensis, quae & Constantiniana, alias S Salvatoris, item S. Ioannis est appellata; ii Basilica S. Petri in Vaticano; iii Basilica S. Pauli extra muros Urbis, Via Ostiensi; iv Basilica S. Mariae Maioris, alias ad Praesepe; v Basilica SS. Stephani & Laurentii extra Muros Urbis, Via Tiburtina. Is numerus placuit ob quinque praecipuos orbis Patriarchas, Romanum, Constantinopolitanum, Alexandrinum, Antiochenum & Hierosolymitanum: ut quoties contigisset Generalia Concilia in Urbe celebrari, ad quae accedere Patriarchae ipsi tenebantur, vel Patriarchas ipsos pro arduis Reip. Christianae negocijs diffinicndis ad Urbem venire, eorum unusquisque Sedem, Palatium videlicet & Ecclesiam, tamquam in Natali solo, vel Provincia sua, Romae haberet praecipuam, quum ipsa Urbs communis totius Orbis Patria appellaretur. Prima Basilica Patriarchalis Romanam Ecclesiam elesiam repræsentat, ipsa Romani Pontificis quondam Sedes, ubi olim in Patriarchio, quod iuxta eandem Ecclesiam, per mille annos est commoratus, ad Clementis v usque Pontificatum, qui in Gallias Romanam Curiam transtulit; post cuius ad Vrbem reductionem sub Gregorio xi Romani Pontifices non amplius ad Lateranum, sed in Patriarchio prope S. Petrum permanserunt. Huic Lateranensi propter excellentiam septem Episcopi ex circumvicinis Civitatibus sunt adsignati, qui suis statis solemnibusque diebus singuli coram Romano Pontifice in eadem Ecclesia celebrarent divina Mysteria, vel Pontifici celebranti adstiterent, atque eam ob causam postea Episcopi Cardinales, id est principales, quod huic Ecclesiae & Romani Pontificis ministerio adscripti essent, appellari coeperunt. Sunt illi: i Episcopus Cardinalis Ostiensis, qui solus inter omnes Episcopos in Romani Pontificis Consecratione (haec enim ad eum pertinet) pallio utitur; ii Episcopus Cardinalis Portuensis; iii Episcopus Cardinalis SS. Rufina & Secunda, alias Silva Candida; iv Episcopus Cardinalis Sabinus; v Episcopus Cardinalis Praenestinus; vi Episcopus Cardinalis Tusculanus; vii Episcopus Cardinalis Albanus. Secunda Basilica Patriarchalis typum gerit Orientis vel Ecclesiae Constantinopolitanae: Ei adsignati sunt septem Presbyteri Cardinales, quod minoris esset dignitatis, quam Basilica Lateranensis, in qua erant Episcopi: Fuerunt autem: i Presbyter Cardinalis Tituli S. Mariae Trans-Tiberim; ii Presbyter Cardinalis Tit. S. Chrysogoni; iii Presbyter Cardinalis Tit. S. Caeciliae; iv Presbyter Cardinalis Tit. S. Anastasiae; v Presbyter Cardinalis Tituli S. Laurentii in Damaso; vi Presbyter Cardinalis Tit. S. Marci; vii Presbyter Cardinalis Tit. S. Martini in Montibus. Tertia Occidentem vel Ecclesiam Alexandrinam repraesentat, cuius Ministerio septem adsignati sunt Presbyteri Cardinales Titulorum, i S. Sabinae: ii S. Priscae: iii S. Balbinae: iv SS. Nerei & Achillei: v. Xysti: vi S. Marcelli: vii S. Susannae. Quarta Septentrionem vel Ecclesiam Antiochenam designat: cuius obsequio adstrieti sunt, septem Presbyteri Cardinales, i Basilicae SS. xii Apostolorum, ii S. Cyriaci in Thermis: iii S. Eusebii: iv S. Pudentianae: v S. Vitalis: vi SS. Marcellini & Petri: vii S. Clementis. Quinta denique Meridiem vel Hierosolymitanam Ecclesiam refert, cui datos constat reliquos septem Presbyteros Cardinales, i S. Praxedis; ii S. Petri ad Vincula: iii S. Laurentii in Lucina: iv S. Crucis in Hierusalem; v S. Stephani in Monte Caelio: vi SS. Iohannis & Pauli: vii SS. Quatuor Coronatorum. Episcopi igitur vii, Presbyteri vero xxxviii iuncti, erunt xxxv, Cardinales Sacerdotes; quibus accedentes xviii Diaconi, de quibus dicam, numerum conficiunt lxv. Mansit autem integer xxviii Presbyterorum Cardinalium numerus, ut notat Pandulphus Pisanus in Vita Gelasii ii usque ad Honorii ii Pontificatum, annumque Christi mcxxv: quo tempore supra modum labefactari coepit, atque adeo imminui ut tempore Nicolai iii tres tantum fuerint Presbyteri Cardinales. Post rursum sensim incrementum adquisivit. In Constantiensi Concilio cautum est ne plures, quam xxiv. Cardinales viventes simul essent. Primus Xystus iv, nulla habita Concilii, quod nominavi, ratione, numerum Cardinalium supra omnes amplavit: sequutus eum est Alexander vi, vita tamen ut numerum iiii non excesserint. Omnium Romanorum Pontificum Leo x primus, neglecta antiqui instituti ratione, Vererem iii numerum in magna illa xxxi Cardinalium creatione superavit. Nam sub illo plus minus lxv Cardinales simul viventes fuerunt. Eius exemplum sequuti sunt Paulli duo, iii & iv. Quum igitur Presbyteri Cardinales numerum xxviii excederent, novis etiam fuit opus Titulis, qui per diversos Pontifices fuerunt facti. Primus post mcd annorum intervallum Xystus iv novum Titulum addidit anno mcccclxxvii S. Nicolai inter Imagines prope Amphitheatrum sive Colosseum. Secundus Leo x in magna illa xxxi Cardinalium Creatione, anno mdxvii antiquissimum Titulum S. Matthaei in Merulana: qui per mille, & qui excurrunt, annos Titulus esse desierat, restituit. xi alios novos Titulos fecit, i. S. Iohannis ante Portam Latinam: ii S. Caesarii in Palatio; iii S. Hieronymi in Agone; iv S. Apollinaris; v S. Laurentii in pane & perna; vi S. Stephani in Campo Martio: vii S. Thomae in Parione; viii S. Pancratii: ix S. Calixti: x S. Bartholomaei in Insula, alias inter Pontes; xi S. Mariae de Capitolio alias de Ara Coeli. Tertio Papa Iulius iii anno Christi mdiii tres novos adiunxit Titulos, i S. Mariae in Via; ii S. Barbarae: iii S. Simeonis. Novissime Paullus iv anno mdlvii Titulum novum adpoluit, S. Mariae super Minervam. Tituli igitur xvii facti facii Novi unus ab Xysto iv, duodecim ab Leone x, tres ab Iulio iii, unusque à Paullo iv, compositi cum xxviii Antiquis, erunt omnino xlv. Presbyterorum autem Cardinalium antiquissimus appellari solitus est S. R. E. Archipresbyter Cardinalis. Haec de Presbyteris.
units.tr: All of them still survive today, except seven: St Crescentiana, Fasciola, St Caius, St Matthew in Merulana, St Aemiliana, St Nicomedes and Tigrida. In place of these, the Acts of the Roman Synod celebrated under Pope Gregory I, and the account of Anastasius the Librarian, record seven others as substitutes: St Balbina on the Aventine Hill, SS. Nereus and Achilleus, St Sixtus, SS. Marcellinus and Peter, the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, St Stephen on the Caelian Hill, and the Four Crowned Martyrs. All of these still survive, with one exception: St Cyriacus in the Baths of Diocletian, which, having collapsed through age and been levelled to the ground, had its title transferred by Sixtus IV to the church of SS. Quiricus and Julitta, where it remains to this day. Let us now consider why neither more nor fewer titles were established at one time. The ancient Roman Pontiffs, as appears from the book of the Apostolic Camera called the Provincial, chose five greater and more distinguished basilicas in the city of Rome, either already built or built anew, and called them Patriarchal churches, and attached palaces to them as Patriarchia. These were: (1) the Lateran Basilica, also called the Constantinian, otherwise named the Basilica of the Saviour or of St John; (2) the Basilica of St Peter in the Vatican; (3) the Basilica of St Paul outside the walls of the City, on the Ostian Way; (4) the Basilica of St Mary Major, otherwise called ad Praesepe; (5) the Basilica of SS. Stephen and Laurence outside the walls of the City, on the Tiburtine Way. This number was chosen because of the five principal Patriarchs of the world: Roman, Constantinopolitan, Alexandrian, Antiochene and Jerusalemite. The purpose was that whenever general councils happened to be held in the City, which the Patriarchs were bound to attend, or whenever the Patriarchs themselves came to Rome to settle weighty matters of the Christian commonwealth, each of them should have his own seat, namely a palace and a church, as in his native soil or his own province, at Rome, since the City itself was called the common fatherland of the whole world. The first Patriarchal basilica represents the Roman Church: it was the former seat of the Roman Pontiff himself, where for a thousand years the Pontiffs lived in the Patriarchium beside the same church, until the pontificate of Clement V, who transferred the Roman Curia to Gaul. After its return to the City under Gregory XI, the Roman Pontiffs no longer remained at the Lateran but in the Patriarchium near St Peter's. To this Lateran church, on account of its excellence, seven bishops from the neighbouring cities were assigned, who on their fixed and solemn days each celebrated the divine mysteries in the same church before the Roman Pontiff, or assisted the celebrating Pontiff. For this reason they later began to be called Cardinal Bishops, that is, principal ones, because they were enrolled for the service of this church and of the Roman Pontiff. They are: (1) the Cardinal Bishop of Ostia, who alone of all bishops wears the pallium at the consecration of the Roman Pontiff, since this belongs to him; (2) the Cardinal Bishop of Porto; (3) the Cardinal Bishop of SS. Rufina and Secunda, otherwise Silva Candida; (4) the Cardinal Bishop of Sabina; (5) the Cardinal Bishop of Palestrina; (6) the Cardinal Bishop of Frascati; (7) the Cardinal Bishop of Albano. The second Patriarchal basilica bears the image of the East or of the Constantinopolitan Church. Seven Cardinal Priests were assigned to it, because it was of lesser dignity than the Lateran Basilica, where the bishops were. They were: (1) the Cardinal Priest of the Title of St Mary Trans-Tiberim; (2) the Cardinal Priest of the Title of St Chrysogonus; (3) the Cardinal Priest of the Title of St Caecilia; (4) the Cardinal Priest of the Title of St Anastasia; (5) the Cardinal Priest of the Title of St Laurence in Damaso; (6) the Cardinal Priest of the Title of St Mark; (7) the Cardinal Priest of the Title of St Martin on the Mountains. The third represents the West or the Alexandrian Church, to whose ministry seven Cardinal Priests of titles were assigned: (1) St Sabina; (2) St Prisca; (3) St Balbina; (4) SS. Nereus and Achilleus; (5) Sixtus; (6) St Marcellus; (7) St Susanna. The fourth designates the North or the Antiochene Church, to whose service seven Cardinal Priests were bound: (1) the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles; (2) St Cyriacus in the Baths; (3) St Eusebius; (4) St Pudentiana; (5) St Vitalis; (6) SS. Marcellinus and Peter; (7) St Clement. Finally, the fifth represents the South or the Jerusalemite Church, to which it is agreed the remaining seven Cardinal Priests were assigned: (1) St Praxedes; (2) St Peter ad Vincula; (3) St Laurence in Lucina; (4) the Holy Cross in Jerusalem; (5) St Stephen on the Caelian Hill; (6) SS. John and Paul; (7) the Four Crowned Martyrs. Thus, seven bishops and thirty-eight priests together make thirty-five Cardinal Priests; adding the eighteen deacons, of whom I shall speak, they make up sixty-five. The number of twenty-eight Cardinal Priests remained intact, as Pandulf of Pisa notes in the Life of Gelasius II, down to the pontificate of Honorius II, in the year of Christ 1125. At that time it began to be weakened beyond measure and to diminish, so that under Nicholas III there were only three Cardinal Priests. Afterwards it gradually recovered its growth. At the Council of Constance it was provided that not more than twenty-four Cardinals should be living at the same time. Sixtus IV was the first, disregarding the rule of the council I have mentioned, to enlarge the number of Cardinals beyond all previous measure; Alexander VI followed him, though during his life they did not exceed forty-four. Of all the Roman Pontiffs, Leo X was the first, neglecting the ancient custom, to surpass the former number in that great creation of thirty-one Cardinals. For under him there were at one time about sixty-five living Cardinals. Paul II and Paul III and IV followed his example. Since the Cardinal Priests therefore exceeded the number of twenty-eight, new titles were also needed, and these were made by various Pontiffs. The first, after an interval of nearly 1,400 years, was Sixtus IV, who in the year 1477 added a new title, St Nicholas among the Images near the Amphitheatre, or Colosseum. The second was Leo X, who in the great creation of thirty-one Cardinals, in the year 1517, restored the most ancient title of St Matthew in Merulana, which had ceased to be a title for more than a thousand years. He made eleven other new titles: (1) St John before the Latin Gate; (2) St Caesarius on the Palatine; (3) St Jerome in the Agone; (4) St Apollinaris; (5) St Laurence in Pane e Perna; (6) St Stephen in the Campus Martius; (7) St Thomas in Parione; (8) St Pancras; (9) St Callistus; (10) St Bartholomew on the Island, otherwise between the Bridges; (11) St Mary of the Capitol, otherwise of the Ara Coeli. The third, Pope Julius III, in the year of Christ 1553, added three new titles: (1) St Mary in Via; (2) St Barbara; (3) St Simeon. Lastly, Paul IV in 1557 added one new title, St Mary above Minerva. Therefore the new titles made amount to seventeen: one by Sixtus IV, twelve by Leo X, three by Julius III and one by Paul IV; added to the twenty-eight old ones, they make forty-five in all. Of the Cardinal Priests, the oldest is customarily called the Archpriest Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church. So much for the priests.

units.la: Diaconi initio septem singuli binis Urbis Regionibus praerant. Exijs Primus lapsu temporis Archidiaconus, vel Diaconus Cardinalis, id est Principalis caput appellari. Is antiquissimis temporibus, uti liquet ex Actionibus Synodi Romanae sub Silvestro i celebrata unus tantum fuit. Quum autem Fidelium numerus indies crescieret, statutum fuit, ut in singulis Urbis Regionibus singuli essent Diaconi; sicque xiv sunt facti: quorum Primus dicebatur Archidiaconus vel Diaconus Cardinalis. Augeretque magis magis Christiana Religione, plures in unaquaque Regione Diaconi incernmore numero creari coepit; quorum dignissimus Diaconus Cardinalis ab ceteris eiusdem Regionis Clericis est nominatus: qua ratione factum, ut xiv postea pro Regionum numero Diaconi Cardinales fuerint. His aliquot post annis quatuor additi sunt alij Diaconi Cardinales: quorum unius tantum erat Lateranensi Basilicae ministrare, sicque xviii numerus est expletus: quum semel solus omnium Romanorum Pontificum excessit Paulus iii. Sub eo namque anno MDIX xlv Diaconi Cardinales xix viventes fuerunt. Quemadmodum enim xxviii Presbyteri Cardinales, sic xviii Diaconi fixus & praescriptus fuit numerus: qui eadem ratione, & eodem tempore quo Presbyterorum, paullatim post Honorij ii Pontificatum adeo diminutus est, ut non nisi tres Diaconi Cardinales viventes aliquando fuerint, quod tempore creationis Nicolai iv animadversum. Postea sentim, uti de Presbyteris dictum est, augere e x pit. Diaconias xviii, id est Ecclesias seu Templa ipsis adsignata, his nominibus expressas invenio: i S. Mariae in Dominica, ubi manebat Archidiaconus. | x S. Mariae in Porticu. ii S. Luciae in Circo iuxta Septisolium, quae nunc est vetustate consumta. | xi S. Nicolai in Carcere Tulliano. iii S. Mariae Novae. | xii S. Angeli in Piscina. iv SS. Cosmae & Damiani. | xiii S. Eustachy iuxta Pantheum. v S. Hadriani. | xiv S. Mariae in Aquiro. vi SS. Sergii & Bacchi. | xv S. Mariae in Via Lata. vii S. Theodori. | xvi S. Agathae in Equo Marmoreo. viii S. Georgii in Velabro. | xvii S. Luciae in Silice, alias Capite Suburae; alias Orphea. ix S. Mariae in Cosmedin, alias Schola Graeca. | xviii SS. Viti & Modestae in Macello Martyrum.
units.tr: Deacons were originally seven in number, each presiding over two regions of the City. Of these, the first came in time to be called the Archdeacon, or Cardinal Deacon, that is, the principal head. In the earliest times he was, as is clear from the Acts of the Roman Synod celebrated under Silvester I, the only one. But as the number of the faithful grew daily, it was decided that there should be a single Deacon in each region of the City, and so there were fourteen. The first of these was called the Archdeacon or Cardinal Deacon. As the Christian religion grew more and more, Deacons began to be created in each region in ever greater numbers, and the most worthy of them was named Cardinal Deacon above the other clergy of that region. In this way it came about that afterwards there were fourteen Cardinal Deacons, in proportion to the number of regions. A few years later four more Cardinal Deacons were added, one of whom alone was to serve the Lateran Basilica, and so the number was completed at eighteen. Pope Paul III alone among all the Roman Pontiffs went beyond this, for in the year 1549 there were forty-five Cardinal Deacons, nineteen of them living. For just as the twenty-eight Cardinal Presbyters were fixed, so the number of eighteen Deacons was fixed and prescribed. By the same reasoning, and at the same time as that of the Presbyters, their number gradually fell after the pontificate of Honorius II, to such an extent that at one time there were only three living Cardinal Deacons, which was noticed at the creation of Nicholas IV. Afterwards, as was said of the Presbyters, it began gradually to increase again. I find the eighteen Diaconiae, that is, the churches or temples assigned to them, listed under these names: i. St Mary in Domnica, where the Archdeacon lived; ii. St Lucy in Circo, next to the Septizonium, which is now destroyed by age; iii. St Mary the New; iv. Saints Cosmas and Damian; v. St Hadrian; vi. Saints Sergius and Bacchus; vii. St Theodore; viii. St George in Velabro; ix. St Mary in Cosmedin, also called the Greek School; x. St Mary in Portico; xi. St Nicholas in Carcere Tulliano; xii. St Angelo in Pescheria; xiii. St Eustace near the Pantheon; xiv. St Mary in Aquiro; xv. St Mary in Via Lata; xvi. St Agatha in Equo Marmoreo; xvii. St Lucy in Silice, also called Capo di Suburra, or Orphea; xviii. Saints Vitus and Modestus in Macello Martyrum.

units.la: Hae semper fuerunt: & numquam, vel additis Novis, vel Antiquis sublatis mutatae i usque ad Leonis x Pontificatum, qui Primus omnium Romanorum Pontificum Diaconiam unicam Novam adiunxit, S. Onuphry in Vaticano.
units.tr: These remained always the same, and were never changed, either by adding new ones or by removing old ones, until the pontificate of Leo X, who was the first of all the Roman Pontiffs to add a single new Diaconia, that of St Onuphrius in the Vatican.

units.la: Novissimi omnium Episcopi Cardinalis cognomen sunt adepti hac ratione. Quum septem ex circumvicinis Episcopis Laterani vel celebrantes, vel Romano Pontifici celebranti ministrantes, idem ibi munus habherent, quod Presbyteri Cardinales per ceteras quatuor Basilicas Patriarchales, indecens videbatur, Episcopos hos non aeque ac Presbyteros, Cardinales dici. Antecedunt hi omnes, quocunque terrarum sunt loco, Episcopos non-Cardinales, quin & Archiepiscopos & Patriarchas: quod sequius erat antiquis temporibus; quum, Titulo Cardinalis, nihil Dignitatis dante, eos tantum praecederent, qui post ipsos fuerant creati. Sunt illi, ut antea obiter indicavi: i Ostiensis, cui Ecclesia unita fuit Velitrena. | iv Sabinus. ii Portuensis. | v Praenestinus. iii SS. Rufina & Secunda, alias Silva Candida. | vi Tusculanus. vii Albanus.
units.tr: The title of Cardinal Bishop was the last to be acquired, and it came about in this way. Since seven of the neighbouring Bishops served at the Lateran, either celebrating or assisting the Roman Pontiff when he celebrated, and held there the same office that the Cardinal Presbyters held in the other four Patriarchal Basilicas, it seemed unfitting that these Bishops should not be called Cardinals in the same way as the Presbyters. All of them take precedence, wherever they are in the world, over the non-Cardinal Bishops, and indeed over Archbishops and Patriarchs. This was otherwise in earlier times, when the title of Cardinal conferred no dignity and they preceded only those who had been created after them. They are, as I indicated briefly above: i. Ostia, to which Velletri was united; ii. Porto; iii. Saints Rufina and Secunda, also called Silva Candida; iv. Sabina; v. Palestrina; vi. Frascati; vii. Albano.

units.la: Septem Episcopi Cardinalitium varias ob causas alij aliquando additi leguntur Episcopi: ut sub Leone ix & Paschali ii Episcopus Cardinalis Veliternus; sub Clemente iii Antipapa & Vrbano ii Episcopus Cardinalis Nepesinus: sub eodem Vrbano ii Labicanus: sub Paschali ii Parmensis: sub Innocentio ii Archiepiscopus Pisanus, Episcopi Mutinensis, Ortanus & Tiburtinus, novissime sub Leone x Reatinus, & iterum Tiburtinus, quum Ecclesias Sabinam & Praenestinam quam ab Iulio ii habuerant, recepisset idem Leo x, Episcopis Cardinalibus duobus ab Iulio ii privatis. Quum autem Ecclesia SS. Rufina & Secunda, alias Silvae Candidae, deficientibus propter crebras Barbarorum Incursiones Incolis, ab Callisto ii Portuensi esset adiuncta, non nisi sex Episcopi Cardinales ord narij fuerunt, qui numerus post Innocentij ii Papae tempora perduravit, ut non essent plures quam sex Episcopi Cardinales viventes; praesertim quum Ecclesia Veliterna, quae cum honorem aliquando habuerat, Ostiensi ab Eugenio iii sit adiuncta; & Tiburtina eo honore privata remanserit usque ad Leonem x; à quo necessitate flagitante, cum Reatina, semel tantum Cardinalis facta fuerit Ecclesia: verum necessaria causa sublata, utraque Ecclesia Cardinales esse desierunt sub eodem Leone. Reliquae vero Ecclesiae, quas Cardinales appellatas fuisse aliquando legimus, numquam postea cum honorem habuerunt, quum eum non habuerint ordinarie, sed necessitatibus quibusdam exigentibus. Quemadmodum vero Primus Presbyterorum Cardinalium Archipresbyter, Diaconorum autem Archidiaconus appellabatur: sic antiquissimus Episcoporum Cardinalium olim Prior Episcoporum Cardinalium, posterioribus vero temporibus Collegij Decanus nominatus est. Is autem semper fuit antiquissimus, qui Episcopus Cardinalis ordinatus erat, sive is esset Albanus, sive Praenestinus, sive Tusculanus, vel alius quilibet ex Episcopis Cardinalibus: unde pauci admodum Decanorum Collegij per quadringentos & quinquaginta annos fuerunt Episcopi Ostienses, quod non semper Episcopus Ostiensis Episcoporum Cardinalium fuerit antiquissimus. Primus autem Paulus iv instituit, ut non is Decanus haberetur, qui absolute Antiquissimus esset Episcoporum Cardinalium; sed qui moriente Decano antiquissimus esset ex Episcopis Cardinalibus in Urbe praesentibus. Absentium enim nullam voluit haberi rationem, nisi Ecclesiae causa essent absentes.
units.tr: Several other bishops are recorded as having been added at various times to the seven Cardinal Bishops, for various reasons: under Leo IX and Paschal II, the Cardinal Bishop of Velletri; under the antipope Clement III and Urban II, the Cardinal Bishop of Nepi; under the same Urban II, Labico; under Paschal II, Parma; under Innocent II, the Archbishop of Pisa, and the Bishops of Modena, Orte and Tivoli. Most recently, under Leo X, Rieti, and again Tivoli, since Leo X had received the churches of Sabina and Palestrina, which Julius II had held, from two Cardinal Bishops deprived by Julius II. But when the church of Saints Rufina and Secunda, also called Silva Candida, was joined to Porto under Callixtus II, because its inhabitants had failed through frequent barbarian incursions, there were only six ordinary Cardinal Bishops. This number lasted after the time of Pope Innocent II, so that there were never more than six living Cardinal Bishops, especially as the church of Velletri, which had at one time held that honour, was joined to Ostia by Eugenius III, and Tivoli, deprived of that honour, remained so until Leo X. From Tivoli, under pressing necessity, Rieti was made a Cardinal church once only. But when the necessary cause ceased, both churches ceased to be Cardinal sees under the same Leo. The other churches which we read were at some time called Cardinal never afterwards held that honour, since they had not held it as a regular thing, but only under certain pressing necessities. Just as the first of the Cardinal Presbyters was called the Archpresbyter, and the first of the Cardinal Deacons the Archdeacon, so the senior of the Cardinal Bishops was formerly called the Prior of the Cardinal Bishops, and in later times was named Dean of the College. He was always the one who had been ordained Cardinal Bishop first, whether he was Albano, Palestrina, Frascati, or any other of the Cardinal Bishops. Hence very few Deans of the College over four hundred and fifty years were Bishops of Ostia, since the Bishop of Ostia was not always the senior of the Cardinal Bishops. But Paul IV was the first to order that the Dean should not be the one who was absolutely senior among the Cardinal Bishops, but the one who, on the death of the Dean, was senior among the Cardinal Bishops present in the City. For he wished that no account be taken of absentees, unless they were absent on church business.

units.la: Sic se habet in ipsa Urbe Roma Latioque Ecclesiastica Gubernatio, quae vires suas in magnam hodie Terrarum Orbis partem extendit, praesertim in Italiam reliquam, suos habentem Archiepiscopos, quibus sui subsunt Episcopi Suffraganei. In Archiepiscopis enumerandis cum sequar ordinem, quo postea in Italia mea delineanda abstinere vendaque sum usurus: In Episcopis recensendis Alphabeticum. Sic non facile peccabo: qui namque quibus praeponendi, nondum mihi liquet. Nomina quidem habeo, sed legitima delit enumeratio, quum ad manum non sit Provinciale Romanum. Quibusdam etiam Gradus adscripsi cum Longitudinis, tum Latitudinis: ut facilius ipsorum Stationes in Tabulis Geographicis possint inveniri. Non enim perpetuum, ut in qua Regione suam habet Sedem Archiepiscopus, in eadem necessario sint omnes eius Suffraganei.
units.tr: Such is the ecclesiastical government in the City of Rome itself and in Latium, which today extends its power over a great part of the world, especially over the rest of Italy, which has its own Archbishops, under whom are their Suffragan Bishops. In listing the Archbishops I shall follow the order which I will use later when I describe Italy, and I shall refrain from it there; in listing the Bishops, I shall use alphabetical order. In this way I shall not easily go wrong, for it is not yet clear to me which should be placed before which. I have the names, but a proper enumeration is lacking, since the Roman Provincial is not to hand. For some I have also added the degrees of longitude as well as of latitude, so that their locations may more easily be found on the geographical maps. For it is not constant that all the Suffragans of an Archbishop must necessarily lie in the same region in which he has his see.

units.la: Hæc de Archiepiscopis, quoque ijs suffragantur, per Italiam, Episcopis. Plerorum ex his, aliorumque venientium aliunde Præsulum interventu celebrata legimus Universalia in variis Italiæ Civitatibus Concilia, Romana Lateranensiaque plurima, Telensè, Taurinense, Regiense, Aquileiense, Venetiacum, Tiburiense, & alia: de quibus abunde illi, qui colligendis in aliquot volumina Conciliis omnibus egregiam ante an nos aliquot navarunt operam.
units.tr: These are the archbishops, and the bishops who are their suffragans, throughout Italy. Of many of these, and of other prelates coming from elsewhere, we read that universal councils were celebrated in various Italian cities: the many Roman and Lateran councils, those of Telese, Turin, Reggio, Aquileia, Venice, Tibur, and others. On these, those who in recent years gathered all the councils into several volumes have done excellent work.

units.la: HActenus In genere Italiam descripsi: antea quam ad specialiorem singularum Partium delineationem me accingam, operæ precium putavi primum, Distributione proposita, indicare, quam in Membrorum enarratione sim Methodum sequuturus.
units.tr: Thus far I have described Italy in general. Before I set about the more detailed description of its individual parts, I thought it worth while first to set out the division I propose to follow in describing its parts.

units.la: Italiam aliter diviserunt. Catonem Sempronumque commeminisse Annius Viterbiensis Italiam partiri in Apenninam, Cis-Apenninam, Trans-Apenninam, & Alpinam; inque Prima Parte collocare Ligures cum Montanos, tum Apuanos, Umbros, Sabinos, Sabellos & Etruscos: Secundæ adscribere Ligures, & hic Montanos & Apuanos, Etruscos cosque Populonios & Turrhenos: item Lucanos, Picentinos & Cumanos: in Tertia ponere Gallium Cis-Alpinam, camque Trans-Padanam, Cis-Padanam, & Togatam: Postremam denique Alpes complecti Ligurinas, Pæninas inter Pœninum Ocramque Montes, & Taurisanas ab Ocra usque in Istriam. Ego his refutandis me non torquebo, quum absurda videam esse omnia, & nimium quantum intricata. Plinius lib. iii naturalis Historiæ cap. v. & quatuordecim sequentibus Divisionem recensét sui temporis, ab Divo Augusto Imperatore factam in xi Regiones: quarum i Latium Vetus Novumque & Campania: vi Umbri; ii Picentes; vii Etruriae; iii Lucani, Bruttij, Sallentini, Apulii viii Gallia Cis-Padana; iv Frentani, Marrucini, Peligni, Marsi, Vestini, Samnites, & Sabini; ix Ligures; v Picenum: x Venetia, Carni, Iapudes, Istriques; xi Gallia Trans-Padana.
units.tr: Italy has been divided in other ways. Annius of Viterbo records that Cato and Sempronius divided Italy into the Apennine, the Cis-Apennine, the Trans-Apennine and the Alpine regions. In the first part he places the Ligurians, both the mountain Ligurians and the Apuani, the Umbrians, Sabines, Sabellians and Etruscans; in the second he assigns the Ligurians (here again the mountain Ligurians and the Apuani), the Etruscans, with their Populonians and Tyrrhenians, and likewise the Lucanians, Picentines and Cumans; in the third he puts Gaul on this side of the Alps, which he calls Trans-Padane, Cis-Padane and Togata; finally, the last part he has embrace the Ligurian Alps, the Penine Alps between the Pennine and Ocra mountains, and the Taurisani from the Ocra as far as Istria. I shall not trouble myself to refute these, since I see that they are all absurd and far too tangled. Pliny, in book III of his Natural History, chapters 5 and the fourteen following, recounts the division of his own time, made by the deified emperor Augustus, into eleven regions: (1) Old and New Latium and Campania; (2) the Picentines; (3) the Lucanians, Bruttians, Sallentines and Apulians; (4) the Frentani, Marrucini, Peligni, Marsi, Vestini, Samnites and Sabines; (5) Picenum; (6) the Umbrians; (7) Etruria; (8) Gaul on this side of the Po; (9) the Ligurians; (10) Venetia, the Carni, Iapydes and Istrians; (11) Gaul beyond the Po.

units.la: Strabo Italiam in octo partitur Regiones i Venetiam, ii Liguriam, iii Picenum. iv Lucaniam, v Tusciam. vi Romam (quæ Latium aliis) vii Campaniam, viii Apuliam.
units.tr: Strabo divides Italy into eight regions: (1) Venetia; (2) Liguria; (3) Picenum; (4) Lucania; (5) Tuscany; (6) Rome (which others call Latium); (7) Campania; (8) Apulia.

units.la: Ex Imp. Cæsaris Traiani Hadriani Augusti Divisione xvii notat Sex. Rufus in Italia tribusque eius Insulis Provincias vel Dioeceses. Erant illæ: I Venetia, & Istria; | VII Campania: | XIII Rhetia Secunda; II Aemilia: | VIII Sicilia Insula: | XIV Samnij pars: III Liguria; | IX Apulia & Calabria; | XV Valeria: IV Flaminia, & Picenum, | X Samnium & Bruttij; | XVI Insula Sardinia; V Tuscia, & Vmbria: | XI Alpes Cottiae: | XVII Insula Corsica. VI Picenum Suburbicarium: | XII Rhetia Prima:
units.tr: From the seventeen divisions made by the emperors Trajan, Hadrian and Augustus, Sextus Rufus notes the provinces or dioceses in Italy and its three islands. They were: (1) Venetia and Istria; (2) Aemilia; (3) Liguria; (4) Flaminia and Picenum; (5) Tuscany and Umbria; (6) Suburbicarian Picenum; (7) Campania; (8) the island of Sicily; (9) Apulia and Calabria; (10) Samnium and the Bruttians; (11) the Cottian Alps; (12) Raetia Prima; (13) Raetia Secunda; (14) part of Samnium; (15) Valeria; (16) the island of Sardinia; (17) the island of Corsica.

units.la: Harum octo, quae primo loco, suos tunc habebant, ut obiter hoc addam, Consulares: Nona & Decima Correctores; reliquae septem suos Praesides: Ptolemaeus eandem non in Regiones, sed in Populos XLV distribuit: I Massilienses, | XVI Piceros, | XXXI Segusianos, II Tusios, | XVII Senones, | XXXII Nerusios, III Latinos, | XVIII Venetos, | XXXIII Surios, IV Campanos, | XIX Carnos, | XXXIV Vendeontios, V Piceentinos, | XX Istros, | XXXV Gallia Togata Incolas, VI Lucanos, | XXI Gallos Boios, | XXXVI Vmbros, VII Bruttios, | XXII Cenomanos, | XXXVII Sabinos, VIII Magna Gracia Gentes, | XXIII Becunos, | XXXVIII Aequicolos, IX Salentinos, | XXIV Infubres, | XXXIX Marsos, X Apulos, | XXV Salassos, | XL Praetutios, XI Teucetios, | XXVI Taurinos, | XLI Veitinios, XII Dauntos, | XXVII Lybicos, | XLII Caracenos, XIII Frentanos, | XXVIII Centrones, | XLIII Samnites, XIV Peligaos, | XXIX Lepontios, | XLIV Hirpinos, XV Marrucinos, | XXX Caturiges, | XLV Calabros.
units.tr: Of these eight, which were first in rank, as I may add here in passing, the first had consulars as their governors, the ninth and tenth had correctors, and the remaining seven had their own presidents. Ptolemy distributed the same region not into Regions but into forty-five Peoples: (1) the Massilienses; (2) the Tusci; (3) the Latini; (4) the Campani; (5) the Picentines; (6) the Lucanians; (7) the Bruttians; (8) the peoples of Magna Graecia; (9) the Sallentines; (10) the Apuli; (11) the Teucetii; (12) the Dauni; (13) the Frentani; (14) the Peligni; (15) the Marrucini; (16) the Piceni; (17) the Senones; (18) the Veneti; (19) the Carni; (20) the Istri; (21) the Gallic Boii; (22) the Cenomani; (23) the Becuni; (24) the Insubres; (25) the Salassi; (26) the Taurini; (27) the Lybici; (28) the Centrones; (29) the Lepontii; (30) the Caturiges; (31) the Segusiani; (32) the Nerusii; (33) the Surii; (34) the Vendeontii; (35) the inhabitants of Gaul Togata; (36) the Umbrians; (37) the Sabines; (38) the Aequicoli; (39) the Marsi; (40) the Praetutii; (41) the Veitinii; (42) the Caraceni; (43) the Samnites; (44) the Hirpini; (45) the Calabrians.

units.la: Corruptiorem nonnullorum scripturam alibi iuvo. Quam porro quidam adferunt Antonini in XVI Regiones Partitionem, plane vitiosa est, & ex aere, ut loquimur, obtorto collo nescio cuius audaculi manibus tracta. Imp. Caes. Fl. Constantinus Maximus Augustus omnium novissimus, uti constat cum ex aliis, tum ex Zosimi lib. Hist. II, novam excogitavit, ut totius Imperii, sic singularum Imperii Partium, Divisionem. Itaque certe Insulasque coniacentes, Hadriani sequutus exemplum in Provincias XVII distribuit: quarum I Venetia, & Istria: | VI Picenum Suburbicarium: | XII Rhetia Prima, II Aemilia: | VII Campania: | XIII Rhetia Secunda: III Liguria: | VIII Sicilia: | XIV Samnium; IV Flaminia, & Picenum Annonarium: | IX Apulia, & Calabria: | XV Valeria: V Tuscia, & Vmbria: | X Lucania, & Bruttii: | XVI Sardinia: XI Alpes Cottia, | XVII Corsica.
units.tr: I help a corrupted reading of some of these elsewhere. The division into sixteen regions that some people cite from Antoninus is plainly faulty, and, as we say, dragged out by the hands of some bold fellow by the neck from a bronze tablet. The Emperor Flavius Constantine the Great, the last of them all, as is clear both from others and from Zosimus, book II of the History, devised a new division, of the whole empire and of its individual parts alike. So, following the example of Hadrian, and leaving out the islands, he distributed Italy into seventeen provinces: (1) Venetia and Istria; (2) Aemilia; (3) Liguria; (4) Flaminia and Annonarian Picenum; (5) Tuscany and Umbria; (6) Suburbicarian Picenum; (7) Campania; (8) Sicily; (9) Apulia and Calabria; (10) Lucania and the Bruttians; (11) the Cottian Alps; (12) Raetia Prima; (13) Raetia Secunda; (14) Samnium; (15) Valeria; (16) Sardinia; (17) Corsica.

units.la: Harum I, II, III, IV Consulares erant, sub Vicario Italiae, V, VI, VII, VIII Consulares, sub Vicario Urbis Romae, IX & X Correctoriales, sub eodem: XI, XII, XIII Praesidiales, sub Vicario, quem dixi Italiae: reliquae quatuor eiusdem generis, sub Vicario, cuius meminí, Urbis. Octodecim Provincias lego apud Paulum Diaconum lib. II de Gestis Langobardorum, cap. XV & seqq. I Venetiam, cum Istria, & Foro Iulij: | IX Alpes Apenninae (Haec non est in Constantini Divisione) II Liguriam: | X Aemiliam; III Rhetiam Primam: | XI Flaminiam (adiungit Constantinus Picenum Annonarium) IV Rhetiam Secundam: | XII Picenum (Suburbicarium scilicet in Constantini Divisione) V Alpes Cottias: VI Tuscam, cum Aurelia, & parte Vmbria: | XIII Valeriam cum Nursia & Marsorum Regione; VII Campaniam: VIII Lucaniam, cum Bruttica; xiv Samnium; xv Apuliam, cum Calabria, & Salentina; xvi Siciliam; xvii Corsicam; xviii Sardiniam.
units.tr: Of these, the first four, I, II, III and IV, were under consulars, under the Vicar of Italy; V, VI, VII and VIII were under consulars, under the Vicar of the City of Rome; IX and X were under correctors, under the same vicar; XI, XII and XIII were under presidents, under the Vicar whom I have called the Vicar of Italy; the remaining four of the same kind were under the Vicar of the City whom I mentioned. I read of eighteen provinces in Paulus Diaconus, book II of the History of the Lombards, chapter 15 and following: (1) Venetia, with Istria and Forum Julii; (2) Liguria; (3) Raetia Prima; (4) Raetia Secunda; (5) the Cottian Alps; (6) Tuscany, with Aurelia and part of Umbria; (7) Campania; (8) Lucania, with the Bruttian land; (9) the Apennine Alps (this is not in Constantine's division); (10) Aemilia; (11) Flaminia (Constantine adds Annonarian Picenum); (12) Picenum (Suburbicarian, namely, in Constantine's division); (13) Valeria, with Nursia and the region of the Marsi; (14) Samnium; (15) Apulia, with Calabria and the Sallentine land; (16) Sicily; (17) Corsica; (18) Sardinia.

units.la: Distribuit apud Volaterranum Sacer Romanus Codex & apud Sebastianum Munsterum Rota Papæ Italiam in xii Partes, quarum i Marcka Trevisana, seu Venetia; ii Istria, cui Foro-Iuliensis adnectuntur; iii Langbardia, sive Gallia Transpadana; iv Liguria; v Romandiola, vel Gallia Cisalpina; vi Ducatus Spoletinus, qui Umbria. vii Aprutium, quod & Samninum; viii Campania, sive Latium; ix Terra Laboris, quæ Campania Propria, Itemque Leberia; x Calabria, vel Lucania; xi Apulia; xii Terra Hydruntina, quæ Salentinorum sedes.
units.tr: The Sacred Roman Codex, as cited by Volaterranus, and the Rota of the Pope, as cited by Sebastian Münster, divide Italy into twelve parts: (1) the March of Treviso, or Venetia; (2) Istria, to which Friuli is joined; (3) Lombardy, or Gaul beyond the Po; (4) Liguria; (5) Romagna, or Gaul this side of the Alps; (6) the Duchy of Spoleto, which is Umbria; (7) Abruzzo, which is also Samnium; (8) Campania, or Latium; (9) Terra di Lavoro, which is proper Campania, and likewise Liberia; (10) Calabria, or Lucania; (11) Apulia; (12) Terra d'Otranto, which is the seat of the Sallentines.

units.la: Blondus in xviii distribuit Regiones, i Liguriam: ii Etruriam, iii Latinam, seu Campaniam Maritimam; iv Umbriam, vel Ducatum Spoletinum: v Picenum, quod nunc Anconitana Marka: vi Romandiolam, olim Flaminiam: vii Aemiliam: viii Galliam Cisalpinam, quæ & Langbardia: ix Veneciam: x Italiam Transpadanam, quæ nunc Marka Tarvisina, vel Aquileiensis, vel Forojuliensis; xi Istriam: xii Samnium: xiii Terram Laboris; quæ Campania Vetus: xiv Lucaniam: xv Apuliam. xvi Salentinos, quorum Sedes nunc Terra Hydruntina: xvii Calabriam: xviii Bruttios.
units.tr: Blondus divides Italy into eighteen regions: (1) Liguria; (2) Etruria; (3) Latium, or Maritime Campania; (4) Umbria, or the Duchy of Spoleto; (5) Picenum, now the March of Ancona; (6) Romagna, formerly Flaminia; (7) Aemilia; (8) Gaul this side of the Alps, which is also Lombardy; (9) Venetia; (10) Italy beyond the Po, now the March of Treviso, or Aquileia, or Friuli; (11) Istria; (12) Samnium; (13) Terra di Lavoro, which is old Campania; (14) Lucania; (15) Apulia; (16) the Sallentines, whose seat is now Terra d'Otranto; (17) Calabria; (18) the Bruttians.

units.la: Leander Albertus Regiones ponit xix: i Liguriam, quæ nunc Italis Ora Genuensis: ii Etruriam, quæ & Tuscia: iii Vmbriam, quæ hoc tempore Ducatus Spoletinus: iv Latium, quæ iamnunc Campania Romana: v Campaniam Felicem, hæc hodie Terra Laboris: vi Lucaniam, Basilicata nuncaudit: vii Bruttios, quorum Sedes hodie Inferior Calabria: viii Magnam Græciam, quæ Calabria Superior nunc appellatur: ix Salentinos, ubi hodie Terra Hydruntina: x Apuliam Peucetiam, quæ Terra nunc Barriana: xi Apuliam Daunium, tunc Apulia plana vocatur. xii Samnites, quorum Regio nunc Aprutium: xiii Picenum, cui appellatio successit Anconitana Marka: xiv Flaminiam, quæ Romanula nunc, vulgo Romandiola: xv Aemiliam, hodie Langbardiam Cispadanam, xvi Galliam Transpadanam, quæ jam Langbardia Transpadana: xvii Veneciam, jamnunc Tarvisinam Markam: xviii Forum Iulii, quod nomen vulgo retinet, dicta & Patria: xix Istriam, nomen incorrupte servantem.
units.tr: Leander Albertus sets out nineteen regions: (1) Liguria, which Italians now call the Genoese Riviera; (2) Etruria, which is also Tuscany; (3) Umbria, which at this time is the Duchy of Spoleto; (4) Latium, which is now the Roman Campagna; (5) Happy Campania, today Terra di Lavoro; (6) Lucania, now called Basilicata; (7) the Bruttians, whose seat today is Lower Calabria; (8) Magna Graecia, now called Upper Calabria; (9) the Sallentines, where today is Terra d'Otranto; (10) Peucetian Apulia, now the land of Bari; (11) Daunian Apulia, then called Apulia Plana; (12) the Samnites, whose region is now Abruzzo; (13) Picenum, whose name has passed to the March of Ancona; (14) Flaminia, now called Romagnola, commonly Romagna; (15) Aemilia, today Cispadane Lombardy; (16) Gaul beyond the Po, now Transpadane Lombardy; (17) Venetia, now the March of Treviso; (18) Forum Julii, which keeps the name in the vernacular and is also called the Patria; (19) Istria, which keeps its name unchanged.

units.la: Alios prætereo. Ego Superiorum Divisiones partim sequuntur, partim nonnihil commutaturus, Italiam totam Methodice, Rebusque Romanorum virtute gestis convenienter, distribuam in Priscam vel Propriam, & Novam sive Accessoriam. Priscam statuo, quidquid hinc ab Arno, inde ab Rubicone est versus Euronotum, usque ad Promontoria Maris Ionici, Bruttium, Carcynium Zephyrium, Lacinium, Iapygium & Athenaeum: Nocam vero, quidquid ab isdem fluviis versus Cauram Alpiumque radices. Arnus igitur & Rubicon Termini inter Italiam Prisciam Nucamque illic, apud Internates; hic, Supernates: ab Infero Superoque Mari ita appellatos. Vocibus istis utor, Plinium Vitruviumque sequutus; quorum illi lib. xvi cap. xxx.x. Hunc vero libro iii, cap. ix, Infernas Alpes Supernas praefertur: & Microbium, apud quem lib. ii Saturnaliorum Superiores Adamas ab Augusto dicitur Macenas quam ob causam non huius est loci explicare. Quod ad Supernatem inter Italiam Vitelium Galliamque Togatam Limitem, is primus erat, ut obiter hoc ex nota ione Strabonis Plinii, Melaque dicam, Aesis. Strabonis verba lib. v sunt haec: ἡ προτέρα μὲν ... Plinii lib. iii, cap. xiv: Ab Ancona Gallicum ora incipit, Togata Gallia cognomine: Pomponii denique lib. ii, cap. iv. Ancon inter Gallias Italiasque Gentes quasi terminus interest. Ancon autem ad ripam Aesis fluvii dextram est locata: ut Plinius Melaque idem hac in re sentiant cum Strabone. Successit Aesi postea Rubicon, prolatis Imperii Romani finibus, omnemque Italiam ab Freto Siculo ad Rubiconem & Arnum, Tuscosque extremos, Liguribus confines in Populi Romani Ditionem circa annum ab V. C. cccexxcix redactam. Hinc est, quod Livius in libris ab V. C. tradat citra Rubiconem esse Italiam; ultra vero Galliam. Videndus item Ptolemaeus. Huc pertinet Inscriptio, quam ex Aldi Orthographia, potius capite huius libri xi, ubi de Italiae Fluminibus. Prisca porro mihi duplex vel Septemtrionalior est, vel Meridionalior; interfluentibus inter utramque ex Apennino, versus Tyrrhenum quidem Mare, Liris; versus Hadriaticum autem Trucuto: Meridionaliore Parte totum hodie Regnum Neapolitanum possidente. In Septemtrionaliore, quae quidem ab Montibus liberior, cis Apenninum, ad ripam Tiberis dextram, est Etruria, hodie Tuscana; ad sinistram Latium, nunc Campania Romana: trans Apennium, Picenum, vulgo Marca Anconitana: qua vero Montibus uniexior, ipsaque quasi immensa iacens, Umbria spectatur, nunc Ducatus Spoletinus. Meridionalior, quam dixi occupari nunc ab Regno Neapolitano, ad Mare Tyrrhenum cis Silarum quidem Campaniam habet Felicem, quae iamnunc Terra Laboris, trans autem eundem Fluvium Lucaniam, hodie Basilicatam; & Calabriam, tam Inferiorem, ubi quondam Bruttii quam Superiorem, ubi Magna Graecia: ad Hadriaticum Pelagus complectitur cis Phiternum Samnites, quorum hodie sedes Aprutium; trans idem flumen, partim utramque Apuliam, & Daunium, hodie Planam, & Peucetiam, nunc Terram Barianam: partim Salentinos, quorum hoc tempore Terra est Hydruntina. Moneo obiter, Halicarnassaeum lib. i. Italiam Orientalem vocare, quae est ab Iapygio Promontorio usque ad Fretum Siculum. Nota vel Accessoria, qua planior, versus Meridiem (ubi praesertim Antiquis Gallia Togata: Appiano item Italia Gallica) continet cis Padum quidem, Flaminiam, quae nunc Romandiola: & Aemiliam, quae hodie Lombardia vocatur Cis-Padanam; trans Padum vero Galliam, vel Lombardiam Trans-Padanam (mentio eius in Inscriptione, quae in horto Ducis Urbini, quamquam alibi ponam, ubi de Colonia Fanestri) & Venetiam, quae & Marca Tarvisina: versus Septemtrionem, cis Tergestinum Sinum, Forum Iulii: trans eundem Istriam: qua denique montosior Nova haec Italia, superbit antiqua illa Liguria (a qua Italia Ligustica Diodoro lib. xi.) cui nomen nunc Ora Genuensis; & Piedmontio, cuius pars Mons-Ferratus. Dictorum a me Schema sic habet. ITALIA consideranda vel Septentrionalior. Prisca & Propria Mo- ribus Libe- rior, eaque Mor bri Meridionalior, ad Mare Tyrr nu ub Ha- dria- ricū, Nova & Accessoria, eaq. Planior, & Montibus liberior, vertius Occasū quidem Ortum vero Montosior. ubi Lig Ped f Ab Cis. Apennina, ubi ad Ripam Tiberis. Dextram, Etruria; hodie Toscana. Sinistram, Latium; vulgo Campagna di Roma. Trans-Apennnia, ubi Picenum, nunc Marka Anconitana.
units.tr: I pass over the others. I will follow the divisions of our predecessors in part, but changing some of them a little, and I will distribute all of Italy in a methodical way, fitting the deeds of the Roman people by which they were won. I divide it into Old or Proper, and New or Added. I set as Old whatever lies on this side of the Arno and on that side of the Rubicon, extending southward to the promontories of the Ionian Sea: Bruttium, Carcinum, Zephyrium, Lacinium, Iapygium and Athenaeum. I set as New whatever lies beyond those same rivers, toward the north and the roots of the Alps. The Arno and the Rubicon are therefore the boundaries between Old Italy and New, the former called Lower and the latter Upper, from the Lower and Upper Seas. I use these words following Pliny and Vitruvius. Pliny, in book 16, chapter 30, and Vitruvius, in book 3, chapter 9, prefer Lower Alps and Upper Alps. Among those who call the Upper Adriatic the Upper, Macrobius, in book 2 of the Saturnalia, says that Augustus did so. Why this was so is not for this place to explain. As for the boundary between Upper Italy and Gallia Togata, the first of these was Aesis, as I will note in passing from Strabo, Pliny and Mela. The words of Strabo, book 5, are these: "The former..." [ἡ προτέρα μὲν ...]. Pliny, book 3, chapter 14: From Ancona the Gallic coast begins, called Gallia Togata. Finally, Pomponius, book 2, chapter 4: Ancona lies between the Gauls and the Italian peoples, as if it were a boundary. Ancona lies on the right bank of the river Aesis, so Pliny and Mela agree with Strabo on this point. Later, when the borders of the Roman Empire were extended, the Rubicon succeeded the Aesis as the boundary. In about the year 379 from the founding of the City, all Italy from the Sicilian strait to the Rubicon and the Arno, and the furthest Tuscans bordering the Ligurians, was brought under the power of the Roman people. Hence Livy, in the books from the founding of the City, says that Italy is on this side of the Rubicon, but Gaul is beyond it. Ptolemy should also be consulted. To this belongs the inscription which I shall give in its own place, from the Orthography of Aldus, at the eleventh chapter of this book, where I speak of the rivers of Italy. Next, my Old Italy is twofold, either more northern or more southern. Between these two, flowing from the Apennines, the Liris runs toward the Tyrrhenian Sea and the Trucuto toward the Adriatic. The more southern part now holds the whole of the Kingdom of Naples. In the more northern part, which is freer of mountains, Etruria, today Tuscany, lies on the near side of the Apennines, on the right bank of the Tiber; on the left lies Latium, now the Roman Campagna. Beyond the Apennines lies Picenum, commonly the March of Ancona. The part which is more bound up with the mountains, and lies as if sunk into them, is called Umbria, now the Duchy of Spoleto. The more southern part, which I said is now occupied by the Kingdom of Naples, has on the Tyrrhenian Sea, on this side of the Silarus, Campania Felix, now Terra di Lavoro; beyond the same river Lucania, today Basilicata; and Calabria, both the lower part, where the Bruttii once lived, and the upper part, where Magna Graecia was. On the Adriatic it takes in, on this side of the Frento, the Samnites, whose seat is now Abruzzo; beyond the same river, partly both Apulias, and Daunia, today the Tavoliere, and Peucetia, now Terra di Bari; partly the Salentini, whose land is at present the Terra d'Otranto. I note in passing that Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 1, calls Eastern Italy the part from the Iapygian promontory to the Sicilian strait. The New or Added Italy, which is flatter and lies toward the south (where among the ancients it was especially called Gallia Togata, and by Appian Gallic Italy), contains, on this side of the Po, Flaminia, now Romagna, and Aemilia, now called Lombardy on this side of the Po. Beyond the Po lies Gaul, or Transpadane Lombardy (it is mentioned in the inscription which is in the garden of the Duke of Urbino, though I shall place it elsewhere, where I speak of the colony of Fano), and Venetia, which is also called the March of Treviso. Toward the north, on this side of the Gulf of Trieste, lies Forum Iulii, and beyond the same gulf Istria. Finally, the more mountainous part of this New Italy is Liguria, the ancient name of which is still proud (from which Diodorus, book 11, calls it Ligurian Italy), now called the Riviera of Genoa; and Piedmont, part of which is the Monferrato. The diagram of what I have described stands thus: ITALY, to be considered as more northern or southern, old and proper, lower... [the diagram is garbled in the scan and continues in the following unit].

units.la: ntibus innexior, iisque quasi immersa iacens, ubi Vm-bria; Ducato di Spoleto. Cis Silarim quidem, Campania Felix, Terra di Lavoro. Trans Silarim vero: Lucania; vernacule Basilicata. Calabria: Inferior, Veterum Bruttiorum Sedes nunc Calabria inferiore. Superior, olim Magna Græcia: vulgo hodie Calabria Superiore. Cis Phiternum, Samnites: quorum Regio Italis nunc Abbruzzo. Trans Phiternum, ubi: Apulia: Daunia; vulgo Puglia Piana. Peucetia; nunc Terra di Bari. Salentini: quorum Regio hac tempestate Terra d'Otranto. Cis-Padana, ubi: Flaminia, nunc Romagna. Æmilia: vernacule Lombardia di qua del Po. Trans-Padana, quo tractu: Gallia Transpadana: hodie Lombardia di là del Po. Venetia: vulgo Marka Trivigiana. Cis Tergestinum Sinu, Forum Iulii, nunc Friuli vel Patria. Vltra eundem Sinu, Istria: nomen incorrupte servans.
units.tr: ...more bound up with the mountains, and lying as if sunk into them, where Umbria is; the Duchy of Spoleto. On this side of the Silarus, Campania Felix, Terra di Lavoro. Beyond the Silarus: Lucania, in the vernacular Basilicata. Calabria: Lower, the seat of the ancient Bruttii, now Lower Calabria. Upper, once Magna Graecia, now commonly Upper Calabria. On this side of the Frento, the Samnites, whose region is now called Abruzzo by the Italians. Beyond the Frento, where Apulia is: Daunia, commonly Puglia Piana. Peucetia, now Terra di Bari. The Salentini, whose region at present is Terra d'Otranto. Cisalpine, where Flaminia is, now Romagna. Aemilia, in the vernacular Lombardia di qua del Po. Transpadane, a region which is Gallia Transpadana, today Lombardia di là del Po. Venetia, commonly the March of Treviso. On this side of the Gulf of Trieste, Forum Iulii, now Friuli or Patria. Beyond the same gulf, Istria, keeping its name unchanged.

units.tr: ...which is now called the Riviera di Genova.

units.la: lemontium: Picdimonte: cuius pars Monsf. Ferratum, Monferrato.
units.tr: ...Piedmont: Piedmont, of which part is the Monferrato.

units.la: Occurrit in nostra Distributione loco primo Etruria, ex Descriptione Augusti, quam sequitur Plinius, Septima Italiae Regio: quae qualia temporibus antiquissimis habuerit Nomina vel Cognomina, anxie non quaeram. Comarum fuisse vocatam ab Comero Gallo, Iapeti Primogenito; Ianiculam vel Ianigenam ab Iano: Saturnbrorum, unde nescio; probet ex Fictitiis Beroso, Fabio Pictore, Myrsilo, & aliis Annius, Viterbiensis. Scilicet eo carebat Respublica Litteraria, ne Fabulis multisque careret Nugis. Unde item Tarcina nominetur Dionysio Halicarnassaeo solicite non disputabo. Nam quod Cranum Ratzenum ex Beroso suo doctis obtrudat idem Annius, apud me frustra est, & nullius fidei. Quod etiam quidam (inter quos Plinius lib. iii natur. histor. capit. v. memoriae prodant Umbros, Veteres horum late locorum Incolas, a Pelasgis, Pelasgos ab Lydis, Lydos ab aliis profligatos; ab ijsque Regionem hanc miris vicissitudinibus Umbriam, Pelasgiam, (quo nomine nota etiam est Halicarnassaeo) & Lydiam fuisse nuncupatam parvi apud me est momenti, fideque incerta. Illud certius est, fatisque constat, totam hanc Regionem antiquis Scriptoribus tribus praecipue nominibus celebrari, Tyrrhenia, Etruria, Tuscia. Tyrrhenia Τυρρηνία, ὅθεν Τυρρηνοὶ implicite Stephano, ἀπὸ τῆς Τυρρηνοῦ, τῆ Ἀτυος, inquit Strabo lib. v. τῶ γεληλατῷ ἐκ Λυδίας ἐκτισιας ἀπόρως, & quae ibi de Atye plura. Atys Herculis & Omphales filius e duobus Filiis, ἀπὸ λιμῶν ἐγγὺς ἀφορίας compulsus, forte iacta, alterum in regno retinuisse scribitur Lydum nominem; alterum in Italiam misisse, Coloniae deducendae, cui nomen Tyrrhenus, & ab eo Tyrrhenia Terra. Legendi Velleius Paterculus lib. i, Verrius Flaccus apud Festum lib. penult. Seruius ad ii, viii & xi Aeneidos, Iustinus ex Trogi libro xx, Seneca de Consolatione ad Albinam. Eleganter & brevibus, nonnihil tamen varians, Tacitus lib. iv Annalium: Sardianos inter Smyrnaeosque deliberatum. Sardiani Decretum Etruriae recitavere, ut Consanguinei. Nam Tyrrhenum Lydumque Atye Rege genitos ob multitudinem divisse gentem: Lydum patriis in terris recessisse; Tyrrheno datum, novas ut conderet Sedes: & Ducum e nominibus indita vocabula, illis per Asiam, his in Italia: auctamque adhuc Lydorum opulentiam, missis in Graeciam Populis, cuius mox a Pelope nomen &c. Sic Tertullianus de Spectaculis: Lydos ex Asia Transierunt in Etruriam consedisse Timaeus refert, duce Tyrrheno, qui Fratri successerat (legit C.L.V. Iustus Lipsius, cesserat; sive cesserat) Regni contentione. Addendus Dionysius libro i, qui inter alia scribit, Tyrrhenos antiquae originis ex aureo seculo esse, nec Lydorum Coloniam se arbitrari, quod argumenta id convincant, Diversitas Linguae, varius Numinum Cultus, variae Leges, varij Litterarum Characteres, aliaque multa, quibus ab Lydis manifesto differebant: proinde potius existimandum, cos non advenam fuisse Genem, sed antiquam Italiae indigenam. Sunt qui Tyrrhenos ab Tyrribus seu Tyrsit dictos censent, id est, Aedificios munitioribus, quibus uti erant soliti. Tegaria porro est apud Serapionem pro Τυρρηνία: videndus
units.tr: In our division there first occurs Etruria, from the description of Augustus, which Pliny follows: the Seventh Region of Italy. I shall not anxiously inquire what names or surnames it had in the most ancient times. That it was called Comara after Comer the Gaul, the firstborn of Iapetus; Ianicula or Ianigena after Janus; Saturnia, I know not from where: Annius of Viterbo tries to prove this from the fictions of Berossus, Fabius Pictor, Myrsilus and others. Clearly the Republic of Letters lacked nothing of this, lest it lack fables and many trifles. Nor will I anxiously dispute why Dionysius of Halicarnassus also calls it Tarchina. For what Annius, the same man, presses on learned readers from his Berossus, that Crano Ratzeno, is worthless to me and of no credibility. Likewise, that some (among whom Pliny, book 3 of the Natural History, chapter 5, hands down that the Umbrians, the ancient inhabitants of these wide lands, were driven out by the Pelasgi, the Pelasgi by the Lydians, and the Lydians by others; and that from these upheavals the region was called Umbria, Pelasgia (a name also known to Dionysius of Halicarnassus), and Lydia) is, to my mind, of little weight and uncertain faith. This is more certain, and it is agreed by all, that the whole region is celebrated by ancient writers under three names especially: Tyrrhenia, Etruria, Tuscia. Tyrrhenia [Τυρρηνία], whence the Tyrrhenians [Τυρρηνοί], as Stephanus implies, is from Tyrrhenus [ἀπὸ τοῦ Τυρρηνοῦ], son of Atys; as Strabo says in book 5, Atys, having been driven out of Lydia by famine [ἀπὸ λιμοῦ], ... and what is said there about Atys at greater length. Atys, son of Hercules and Omphale, is written to have kept one of his two sons, named Lydus, in the kingdom; and to have sent the other to Italy, by lot, to lead a colony, which was called Tyrrhenus, and from him Tyrrhenian Land. Velleius Paterculus, book 1, should be read; Verrius Flaccus, in Festus, the second-last book; Servius on Aeneid 2, 8 and 11; Justin from book 20 of Trogus; Seneca, On Consolation to Albina. Tacitus, in book 4 of the Annals, elegantly and briefly, though varying a little: Among the Sardians and the Smyrnaeans it was debated. The Sardians read a decree of Etruria, as kinsmen. For Tyrrhenus and Lydus, sons of King Atys, divided the nation on account of its numbers: Lydus remained in his ancestral lands; to Tyrrhenus was given the task of founding new seats; and names were given from the leaders, to the one through Asia, to the other in Italy; and the wealth of the Lydians, still growing, sent peoples into Greece, whose name soon came from Pelops, etc. So Tertullian, On the Spectacles: Timaeus reports that the Lydians passed from Asia and settled in Etruria, led by Tyrrhenus, who had succeeded his brother (Justus Lipsius reads cesserat, that is, yielded) in a contest for the kingdom. Dionysius, book 1, should also be added, who writes among other things that the Tyrrhenians are of ancient origin from the golden age, and do not think themselves a colony of the Lydians, since the arguments prove otherwise: the difference of language, the varied worship of the gods, the varied laws, the varied forms of letters, and many other things by which they clearly differed from the Lydians. Therefore it should rather be thought that they were not a foreign race but an ancient native people of Italy. Some hold that the Tyrrhenians were named from the Tyrsi or Tyrseni, that is, from builders of fortifications, which they were accustomed to use. Moreover, Tegaria in Serapion stands for Τυρρηνία; see

units.la: Dioscorides cap.de Resina. Iam Etruria dicta est, si Servio ad xi Aeneidos fides, quod eius Fines tendebantur usque ad primum ripam Tiberis; quasi Ἐτρουρία, per syncopam Ἐτρουρία. Nam Ἐτρῳ- est Alter, & ὀρῳ- Finis. Roma enim antea unam tantum Tiberis ripam tenebat. Juvenalis: Et qua, Imperii fines, Tiberinum Virgo natatit.
units.tr: Dioscorides, chapter on Resin. Now Etruria is said to have been so named, if we trust Servius on Aeneid xi, because its boundaries extended as far as the first bank of the Tiber; as if from Ἐτρουρία [Ἐτρουρία], by syncope. For Ἐτρῳ- [Ἐτρῳ-] means other, and ὀρῳ- [ὀρῳ-] means boundary. Rome, before that, held only one bank of the Tiber. Juvenal: And where, the limit of empire, the Virgin swims the Tiber.

units.la: Hinc putant nonnulli Etruria nomen cum adspiratione scribendum. Sed in melioribus Latinis Codicibus semper Etruria legitur, in Graecis Ἐτρουρία: ut mihi appellationis ratio videatur esse incertior. Sunt qui nescio quid differentiae statuunt inter Etruriam & Hetruriam: quod iis lubens relinquo. Gulielmus Postellus in suo de Etruria Regionis Originibus, Institutis Religionis, & Moribus, Etruriam scribendum monet, non Etruriam: addens sic Assyriam Assyriosque Aturim sive Eturim Lingua Chaldaica dici: illud autem Vocabulum, Duce Patre Universitatis Noacho, Ianove, in Italiam fuisse delatum: Quum autem hi Assyrii & Aurei Seculi Duces praestantissima fuerint Institutione Religionis, Etruriam Provinciam appellatam fuisse Tuscium, quasi Salutis Fontem: sic enim vocem תושיה in Lingua Sancta sonare. Ab Etrurim itaque sive Aturim, tandem Etrus, & demum ab utroque Vocabulo Etruscos, quasi Etruscos, invalescente Corruptione, fuisse nominatos: Graecos autem in ceteris Orbis Vocabulis externis litteris contentos, ad experimenda propria rerum Vocabula pro Etruris Turrhenos aut Tyrrhenos, Thyrsenosve dixisse. Haec flupeant, qui velint: perme licet. Ego ad alteram Appellationem pergo. Tuscia Latinis, Θυσκία Dionysio Halicarnassaeo lib. 1, ἀπὸ τῆς θυσίας, ab Sacrificando. Tusci, inquit Servius ad viii Aeneidos, ἀπὸ τῆς θυσίας. Et inde Plinius lib. iii cap. v Tuscos dictos notat ab Sacrificio ritu. Fuisse enim Etruscos prae ceteris Italiae Populis, eorum, quae ad Religionem & Sacra pertinebant, ad Superstitionem usque studiosos: quamquam Dionysius iam tum aevo suo Studium id Divinorum adeo apud eos exolevisse scribat, ut cunctarum nationum uni haberentur Sacrorum negligentissimi. Inde autem fit, ut nonnulli primam Nominis Litteram arbitrentur aspirandam. Alii Latinae faciunt originis, ab Ture derivantes: inter quos Paulus Diaconus de Gestis Langbardorum ii, cap. xvi. Unde & Facius Ubertus, doctissimus apud Italos Poeta, lib. iii Cantico ix: Tuscia dal Tuscè le su il Nome messo, Perche con quegli Antichi il tempo casso Devoti a i Dei sacrificavan spesso.
units.tr: Hence some think the name Etruria should be written with an aspirate. But in the better Latin manuscripts it is always read as Etruria, and in the Greek as Ἐτρουρία, so the reason for the name seems to me rather uncertain. Some lay down some distinction between Etruria and Hetruria; I gladly leave that to them. Guillaume Postel, in his work on the origins, religious institutions and customs of the region of Etruria, advises that it should be written Etruria, not Etruria. He adds that in the Chaldean language Assyria and the Assyrians are called Aturim or Eturim, and that this word was carried into Italy under Japhet, leader of the universal family, descended from Noah. Since these Assyrians, leaders of the golden age, were outstanding for their sound religious institutions, the province of Etruria was called Tuscium, as if it were the fountain of salvation; for the word תושיה in the Holy Tongue has that sense. From Etrurim or Aturim, then Etrus, and finally from both words Etruscos, as if Etruscos, the name came to be used as the corruption gained ground. The Greeks, content with foreign letters for the other names of the world, then said Turrhenos, Tyrrhenos or Thyrsenos for Etrur, in order to try out native words for things. Let whoever wishes marvel at this; I allow it. I now proceed to the other name. Tuscia in Latin, Θυσκία [Θυσκία] in Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 1, from θυσία [θυσία], from sacrificing. The Tuscans, says Servius on Aeneid viii, from θυσία [θυσία]. And from this Pliny, book 3, chapter 5, notes that the Tuscans were named from the rite of sacrifice. For the Etruscans were, beyond the other peoples of Italy, devoted to matters of religion and worship, indeed to superstition; although Dionysius writes that in his own day the study of divine things had so fallen away among them that they were regarded as the most negligent of all nations in these matters. From this some think the first letter of the name should be aspirated. Others derive it from a Latin origin, from tus (incense): among them Paulus Diaconus in his History of the Lombards, book 2, chapter 16. Hence also Fazio degli Uberti, the most learned poet among the Italians, book 3, canto 9: Tuscany took its name from Tusco, because in those ancient times men, devoted to the gods, often offered sacrifices.

units.la: Sex. Pompeius Festus Tuscium ab Tusco Rege, Herculis Filio, denominatam scribit: Eius Etymon ex Idiomate Babylonico, quo Tosca, Curia notatur Dominorum difficiliorum adytum, eruit Annius Viterbiensis cum alibi, tum in suis de Tuscia Quaestionibus: quem vide Lector, & cum doctis Viris quique lanioris iudicii, ride. Sed in Etymi nobilissimae Regionis ignoratione Salus non periclitatur publica: explicato Nomine, & quae conspectare videbantur, ad Res ipsas veniamus. Postremum sane hodieque retinet, Toscana namque vulgo audit.
units.tr: Sextus Pompeius Festus writes that Tuscium was named after Tuscus, a king, son of Hercules. Its etymology, from the Babylonian language, in which Tosca, Curia means the sanctuary of difficult lords, has been brought to light by Annius of Viterbo, both here and in his Questions on Tuscany. The reader should consult him, and laugh at him along with learned men and those of sounder judgment. But the public welfare is not endangered by ignorance of the etymology of this most noble region. With the name explained, let us come to the things themselves that seemed to call for our attention. Finally, it is still retained today, for it is commonly heard as Toscana.

units.la: Fines ex Berofo, Catone aliisque ab Annio suppositis Scriptoribus, non peram: ne quae vera non sunt, Lectoribus obtrudam, eorumque abutar patientia. Strabo, Polybius, Plinius, Ptolemaeus, Pomponius Mela, Solinus, alii multi in Macram cum Liguria, Occidentalem Terminum; Tiberim cum Latio, Orientalem (videndus & Livius lib. i, ubi Pacem inter Etruscos & Latinos convenisse ait, ut ipsis Adula quem polt Tiberim vocare coeperunt, finis esset) Apenninum, ubi Umbria, Galliaeque Togatae pars, Septemtrionalem: Infernum denique Mare, Sardiniam spectans, Meridionalem, unanimi consensu conspirant.
units.tr: I will not dwell on the boundaries as given by Berossus, Cato and the other writers that Annius has put forward, lest I impose on readers what is not true and abuse their patience. Strabo, Polybius, Pliny, Ptolemy, Pomponius Mela, Solinus and many others agree unanimously: the western limit is the Macra, with Liguria; the eastern is the Tiber, with Latium (see also Livy, book 1, where he says that peace was agreed between the Etruscans and the Latins on the condition that the Adula, which they then began to call the Tiber, should be the boundary); the northern is the Apennine, where Umbria and part of Togata Gaul lie; and finally the southern is the Tyrrhenian Sea, facing Sardinia.

units.la: Plinius inter Macram & Tiberim CCLXVIX Millia Passuum esse tradit: Blondus Etruriae Longitudinem CLXX M.P. scribit: Strabo Stadiorum bis mille quingentorum facit; quae si Milliario octona demus Stadia, summam efficiet Milliariorum circiter CCCXII. Ptolemaeus tres Gradus Longitudinis ponit, singulos millium paullo amplius XLVII; qui mensuram paullo maiorem millium passuum CXII faciunt. Facilis inter disidentes futura conciliatio: si dicamus, quosdam Longitudinem exigere, quam Navigatio propter oram habet, alios per Litus ipsum extremum & Sinus incedere; nonnullos per Mediterranea Loca; alios denique Situm ad Poli rationem aestimare. Latitudo eius certo non potest diffiniri. Maxima est inter Populonium Promontorium & Arni Fontes.
units.tr: Pliny says that between the Macra and the Tiber there are 269 miles. Biondo writes that the length of Etruria is 170 miles. Strabo makes it 2,500 stadia; if we give eight stadia to the mile, this comes to about 312 miles. Ptolemy sets down three degrees of longitude, each a little more than 47 miles, which makes a measure a little more than 112 miles. The disagreement is easily reconciled if we say that some measure the length along the course that navigation takes along the coast, others go along the very outermost shore and the bays, some through the inland places, and others finally estimate the position by the reckoning of the pole. Its breadth cannot be fixed with certainty. It is greatest between the Promontory of Populonia and the Springs of the Arno.

units.la: Circuitus septingenta habet Millia passuum, innuente Facio Vberto, cuius elegantissimos de Etruria Versus non possum, quin adscribam: Iovidi unscir la Magra delle fascie Del giogo d'Apennin rozido, è torbo, Che de l'acqua daius par che passe. Non voglio, disse Solin, che passi orbo, Da quello fiume Tosana commincia, Che ende in mare al monte de lo Corbo. E vo che sappi che questa Provincia Da venticinque Vef. ovadi ferra, Terren non so del tanto che la vincia. Dal Mezo giorno la cinge & afferra Il Mar Mediterran; poi l'Apennino Da ver Settentrion chinde la terra: E dal Levante come un Pellegrino Il Tebro in Mar, che surge in Falterona Compie Tosana, è tutto il suo camino. Il giro suo per quel che si ragiona, E misurato settecento miglia, E Roma qui, l'honor che l'incorona.
units.tr: The circuit has 700 miles, as Fazio Uberti suggests; and I cannot refrain from adding his most elegant verses on Etruria: "Where the Magra, from the ridges of the Apennine chain, rough and turbid, lets its waters pass as if they were running through a gap. I do not want, said Solinus, the one who passes blind, that Tuscany begins from that river, and runs into the sea at the mountain of Corbo. And I want you to know that this province, from twenty-five miles of coast, I do not know how much of the land it conquers. The Mediterranean Sea girds and grasps it from the south; then the Apennine closes the land from the north-east. And from the east, like a pilgrim, the Tiber, which rises at Falterona, runs into the sea, completing Tuscany, and is all its course. Its circuit, as far as we reckon it, is measured at 700 miles, and Rome here is the honour that crowns it."

units.la: Terra ipsa, qua Mari propior, planior est, oraeque spectatu iucundissimae; intus montosior: universim pulcra, nobilis, nullique Italiae Regioni sua Beatitudine postponenda Hanc Vbertate sua Soli sacratam voluit Marcianus: Latos latosque aperi Campos, rerum omnium fertiles; amoenissimas Valles: Montes, Collesque Vicis, Praedijs, Hortis, qui Arboribus omnis generis, praecipue Malis Medicis Citreisque consiti, supra modum nitentes. Vinetis abundat, Vina producentibus generosissima; in quis quae vulgo Fribiana, Apiana, Vofintensia, Senensia, & id genus alia. Fluvijs scatet Piscium optimorum foecundissimis, Arno, Boallo, Palia, alijsque, de quibus suo loco, ut & de Lacubus, in quorum numero principes, Perusinus, olim Thrasumenus, Vofintus, Sabatinus. Habet & salubberrima Balnea, nobilissimas Thermas, aliaque Aquas mirabili praeditas Virtute.
units.tr: The land itself, nearer the sea, is flatter, and the coast is most pleasant to behold; inland it is more mountainous. In general it is beautiful, noble, and not to be placed below any other region of Italy in its happiness. Marcianus wished this region consecrated to the sun for its fertility: broad and wide open plains, fertile in all things; most lovely valleys; mountains and hills, villages, estates and gardens, planted with trees of every kind, especially apple, citron and lemon, shining beyond measure. It abounds in vineyards producing the finest wines; among them are those commonly called Fribiana, Apiana, Volsiniensis, Senensis and others of that sort. It teems with rivers of the most abundant fish, the Arno, Bagnolo, Palia and others, of which in their place; likewise with lakes, the chief of which are Perugia, formerly Trasimene, Bolsena, and Bracciano. It also has very healthful baths, noble thermal springs, and other waters endowed with wonderful virtue.

units.la: Veteres Incolae universim dicti quondam Tyrrheni, Etrusci, Tusci: Tyrrheni ab Tyrrheno vel Tyrrhenis de qua ante: Etrusci ab Etruria; Tusci a Tuscia: noti passim ijs nominibus in omnium Scriptorum Graecorum & Latinorum Monimentis. Quod Pelasgi etiam fuerint generatim appellati, praeter Strabonem tradit ex Myrtilo Dionysius Halicarnassaeus lib. 1. Antiquit. Romanarum. Avões insuper nominatos, quod ex Lydia Tyrrheni ductu & auspicijs venerint, scribit Herodotus in Clio.
units.tr: The ancient inhabitants were in general once called Tyrrhenians, Etruscans and Tuscans: Tyrrhenians from Tyrrhenus or the Tyrrhenians, as mentioned above; Etruscans from Etruria; Tuscans from Tuscia. They are everywhere known by these names in the monuments of all the Greek and Latin writers. That they were also generally called Pelasgians, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 1 of the Roman Antiquities, reports from Myrtilus, apart from Strabo. Herodotus, in Clio, writes that they were also named Lydians, because the Tyrrhenians came from Lydia under the leadership and auspices of their king.

units.la: Etruscos porro Gentem Italiae opulentissimam Armis, Iuribus, pecunia esse aiunt Livius & Diodorus. Cerimonijs, Cultuique divino maxime semper addictos fuisse, constat ex antiquis scriptoribus, ut qui Sacrificia, Divinationes, Auguriaque primi Italorum invenerint, eaque Romanis tradiderint, notantibus Tullio de Divinatione, Dionysio Halicarnassaeo, Macrobio, Censorino, & alijs. Nota est Historia Tagetis, quem, quum in agro Tarquiniensi Terra paullo altius araretur, sulcique profundiores imprimerentur, repente exiluisse, ipsumque Aratorem adfatum commemorant. Tages autem puer effigie (uti Cicero ex Commentarijs Etruscorum tradit) apparuit, etsi prudentia quidem senili fuit. Verum quum ad eius speciem Bubulcus obstupesceret, edita voce, ut fit, maxima inclamavit: quo evenit, ut brevi tempore Magno concursu permulti ex Etruria eodem convenerint. Tum Tages idem, multis audientibus, complura loquutus dicitur, quae diligenti cura excepta sunt ac litteris commendata. Neque aliud Tagetis verba continebant, quam Aruspicinae disciplinam, quae multis subinde observationibus aucta, atque amplior facta est: sic ut ea Fulminum, Fulgurumque & Ostentorum scientia traderetur. Legendi de Tagete, praeter Ciceronem, Plutarchus, aliique plures. Ammianus Marcellinus Tagetis laudat libros, quibus Prodigia quaedam ac Portenta possent explanari; nari: qua in re officium Etrusci Vates atque Sacerdotes præstabant. Quin & Antistius Labeo Libros Tagetis exposuit, eiusque Disciplinam Etruscam quindecim Voluminibus est interpretatus: quod & Fulgentius ad Grammaticum Chalcidium refert, quo loco de Manali Lapide disserit. Vertumnus Etruriæ Deus celebratur a Varrone in libris de LL. & Propertio lib. iv:
units.tr: Livy and Diodorus say that the Etruscans, a people of Italy, were very wealthy in arms, laws and money. That they were always especially given to ceremonies and divine worship is clear from ancient writers, since they were the first of the Italians to invent sacrifices, divinations and augury, and passed them on to the Romans, as Cicero in his work On Divination, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Macrobius, Censorinus and others note. The story of Tages is well known: when the land at Tarquinii was being ploughed somewhat deeply and the furrows were being cut deeper, he suddenly leapt out and addressed the ploughman himself, as they record. Tages appeared as a boy in appearance (as Cicero tells from the Commentaries of the Etruscans), though in wisdom he had the prudence of an old man. But when the ploughman was astonished at the sight of him, he cried out loudly, as people do; as a result, in a short time a great crowd of many people came from Etruria to the same place. Then Tages, as many listened, is said to have spoken many things, which were taken down with careful attention and committed to writing. The words of Tages contained nothing other than the discipline of haruspicy, which, enlarged by many observations, grew and became fuller, so that the science of lightning, thunderbolts and portents was handed down. Concerning Tages, besides Cicero, Plutarch and many others should be read. Ammianus Marcellinus praises the books of Tages, by which certain prodigies and portents could be explained; in this matter the Etruscan seers and priests performed their duty. Indeed Antistius Labeo also expounded the books of Tages, and translated their Etruscan discipline into fifteen volumes; Fulgentius, in his commentary on the grammarian Chalcidius, where he discusses the Manalian stone, also refers to this. Vertumnus, god of Etruria, is celebrated by Varro in his books on the Latin language, and by Propertius, book 4.

units.la: Tuscus Ego, Tuscis ortus: nec pœnitet inter Prælia Volsinios deseruisse focos.
units.tr: I am a Tuscan, born of Tuscans; nor am I sorry that I deserted the hearths of Volsinii amid the battles.

units.la: Consulendi & Dionysius Halic. lib. v, Ovidius Fastorum i, Macrobius lib. i. Saturnal. Servius ad Aeneidem Virgilianam, & alij.
units.tr: To be consulted also: Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 5; Ovid, Fasti, book 1; Macrobius, Saturnalia, book 1; Servius on Virgil's Aeneid; and others.

units.la: Vires & Potentiam Etruscorum, Reliquæ ab ijs terra marique gestas, memorant copiosè Diodorus Siculus lib. vi, Livius locis infinitis, alijque Auctores quamplurimi. Amplitudinis Rei Etruscæ argumenta sunt; Primum, quod Maria, quibus Italia cingitur, ab iis denominationem acceperint, Inferum quidem, Tuscum, vel Tyrrhenum, ab ipsa Gente; Superum autem Hadriaticum ab Hadria Tuscorum Colonia: Alterum, quod Populus Romanus in suos Mores & Civitatem multa ab Etruscis traduxerit, Fasces, Trabeas, Sellas Curules, Annulos, Phaleras, Paludamenta, Prætextam, Ornamenta Triumphalia, Togas Pictas, Tunicas Palmatas, omniaque, ut paucis dicam, Decora & Insignia, quibus Imperij dignitas eminebat; quæ L.
