Tarquinium Priscum v Romanorum Regem, xii Etruriæ Populis subactis, Romam deportasse scribunt Strabo, Dionysius Halicarnassæus, Livius, Silius Italicus lib. viii, Florus lib. i, & alij: quodque idem Populus, ut præter Tullium in Divinatione & alios; tradunt Livius & Halicarnassæus, Liberos suos in Etruriam, tamquam ad Academiam & Scholam publicam, cum Litteris, tum Moribus imbuendos amandare fuerint soliti: Tertium, quod Tuscus Vicus Romæ, Tusculum & Tusculanum in Latio nomen ab ijs sumserint. Alia prætereo. Trecenta Umbrorum oppida ab ijs debellata leguntur, Plinio auctore, Duodenis Apenninum Urbibus habitantes ad Inferum Mare, totidem trans Apenninum condiderunt, Colonijs in eas missis, uti prodiunt Polybius, Livius, Halicarnassæus, & Plinius; qui hos, multosque alios Tuscorum Colonos nominat, Aretinos Veteres, Aretinos Fidentes, Aretinos Iulienses, Aquenses cognomine Taurinos, Agylleos, Alsios, Eleranos, Cortonenses, Caretanos, Capenates, Clusinos Novos, Clusinos Veteres, Cosanos, Falerios, Fluentinos, Fesulas, Ferentinum, Feliciniam, Fregenas, Graviscas, Hortanum, Herbanum, Lunam, Lucam, Nepe, Novem Pagos, Præfecturam Claudiam, Forum-Cassij, Pistorium, Pisas, Perusiam, Pyrgos, Suanenses, Saturninos an-ea Aurinos vocatos, Senenses, Sutrinos, Sudertanos, Statones, Tarquinienses, Tuscanienses, Vetulonienses, Veientanos, Vesentinos, Volaterranos cognomine Etruscos, Volsinienses, una cum Agro Cruslumino & Caletrano. Cum Tusci iam inde ab Romuli tempore Populus Romanus bellum gerere cœpit, perpetuoque temporum tractu gessit; adeo ut, rebus ad periculosissimum statum adductis, sæpe Dictatore contra ipsos fuerit opus. Anno Urbis cccclxxiv, Vulsiniensibus & Vulcientibus florentissimis Etruscorum Populis victis per Ti. Coruncanium Cos. Romano Imperio sunt adiecti, atque ea parte Imperium ad Arnum usque est propagatum. Neque post id tempus iuthum cum Tuscis bellum fuisse gestum memoratur. Ita subjugati constanter in fide Populi Romani manserunt. Inclinantibus Romanorum rebus, varias sunt Calamitates passi ab Gothis, Langbardis, Hungaris, alijs. Eo tandem ventum est, ut Etruria nunc, maiorem partem, Magno Etruriæ pareat Ducì, sub cuius Imperio nobilissimæ sunt Florentia, Pisæ, Sena, Pratum, Pistorium, Volaterra, Mons Politianus, Aretium, Cortona, Pescia, Pientia, Mons Alcinus, Liburnum, Plumbinum, aliaque quamplurima opida: Ad Summum Pontificem pertinet Patrimonium, quod vocant, S. Petri. Id ab Amne Pescia & ab S. Quirico capit initium, & ad Caparanum usque Castrum in Novo Latio non procul ab Liri Fluvio Producitur: Ditionis Hispaniarum Regis sunt Pontremulum iuxta Macræ Fluvij fontem, quod olim Ducum fuit Mediolanensium; deinde Portus Herculis, & Presidium, Mons Argenta-rius & Piumbini Arx. Caffeniana seu Graffiniana Vallis, sub Apenninio ultra citraque Serciam Amnem posita, in qua Castellum Novum est Granianum, cum plurimis alijs Castellis Vicisque, sub potestate est Ducu Ferrariensis: Sarzana apud Macram Fluvium ad Genuenses spectat. Massa & Carraria particularium sunt Marchionum, qui earum Titulis decorantur: Alia quoque sunt opida, Romanis quibusdam Proceribus subiecta, inter quæ Bracciannum Vfsinus Ducatus Titulum præstat,
units.tr: The power and might of the Etruscans, and the deeds they performed by land and sea, are recounted at length by Diodorus Siculus, book 6, by Livy in countless places, and by very many other authors. The following are evidence of the greatness of the Etruscan affairs. First, the seas that surround Italy took their names from them: the lower sea is called Tuscan or Tyrrhenian, from the people itself, and the upper sea is called Hadriatic, from Hadria, a colony of the Tuscans. Second, the Roman people took over from the Etruscans many things for their customs and their state: the fasces, the trabeae, the curule chairs, the rings, the phalerae, the paludamenta, the praetexta, the triumphal ornaments, the painted togas, the palm-tunics, and, to put it briefly, all the marks of honour and insignia by which the dignity of command stood out. Strabo, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Livy, Silius Italicus (book 8), Florus (book 1), and others write that Lucius Tarquinius Priscus, fifth king of the Romans, carried these to Rome after subduing the twelve peoples of Etruria. The same people, as Livy and Halicarnassus relate (and, besides Cicero in his On Divination and others), used to send their sons to Etruria, as to an academy and public school, to be imbued with letters as well as morals. Third, the Tuscan street at Rome, and Tusculum and the Tusculan estate in Latium, took their names from them. I pass over other points. Three hundred towns of the Umbrians are read to have been conquered by them, on the authority of Pliny. Those who lived along the lower sea in twelve cities each founded as many beyond the Apennines, sending colonies into them, as Polybius, Livy, Halicarnassus and Pliny report. Pliny names these and many other colonists of the Tuscans: the Aretini Veteres, the Aretini Fidentes, the Aretini Iulienses, the Aquenses surnamed Taurini, the Agylleans, the Alsians, the Eleranians, the Cortonenses, the Caretani, the Capenates, the Clusini Novi, the Clusini Veteres, the Cosani, the Falerii, the Fluentini, the Fesulae, the Ferentinum, the Felicinia, the Fregenae, the Graviscae, the Hortanum, the Herbanum, the Luna, the Luca, the Nepe, the Novem Pagi, the Praefectura Claudia, the Forum Cassii, the Pistorium, the Pisae, the Perusia, the Pyrgi, the Suanenses, the Saturnini, who are said to have been called the Aurini, the Senenses, the Sutrini, the Sudertani, the Statones, the Tarquinienses, the Tuscanienses, the Vetulonienses, the Veientani, the Vesentini, the Volaterrani surnamed Etrusci, the Volsinienses, together with the Ager Crusluminus and the Caletranus. From the time of Romulus onward the Roman people began to wage war against the Tuscans, and they waged it through a long stretch of time, so much so that, when affairs had been brought to the most dangerous state, a dictator often had to be appointed against them. In the year of the city 374, the flourishing peoples of the Etruscans, the Volsinians and the Vulcientes, were defeated by Tiberius Coruncanius, consul, and added to the Roman empire, and in that region the empire was extended as far as the Arnus. After that time, no war with the Tuscans is recorded. Thus subjugated, they remained steadfastly loyal to the Roman people. When the fortunes of the Romans declined, they suffered various calamities at the hands of the Goths, the Lombards, the Hungarians, and others. At last it came about that now, for the most part, Etruria obeys the Grand Duke of Etruria, under whose rule are the most noble cities Florence, Pisa, Siena, Prato, Pistoia, Volterra, Montepulciano, Arezzo, Cortona, Pescia, Pientia, Montalcino, Livorno, Piombino, and very many other towns. The Patrimony, as they call it, of St Peter belongs to the Supreme Pontiff. It begins at the river Pescia and at San Quirico, and extends to the castle of Caparanum in New Latium, not far from the river Liri. Under the rule of the King of Spain are Pontremoli, near the source of the river Magra, which once belonged to the Dukes of Milan; then Porto Ercole and Presidio, Monte Argentario and the citadel of Piombino. The Caffeniana or Graffiniana Valley, lying beneath the Apennines on both sides of the river Serchio, in which is the New Castle of Granaiolo, together with very many other castles and villages, is under the power of the Duke of Ferrara. Sarzana, on the river Magra, belongs to the Genoese. Massa and Carrara belong to particular Marquises, who are honoured with their titles. There are also other towns subject to certain Roman nobles, among which Bracciano holds the title of a Duchy under the Orsini.

units.la: Vt autem olim, sic hodieque Etrusci clarissimi sunt Belli Pacisque tempore: ad omnia summa tam in otio, quam negocio expeditissimi: ad litterarum Studia promptissimi, acumine ingenij mira sagacitate & astutia singulari praestantes: frugalis vitae, parsimoniaque laudabili: Idiomate utentes, quod ob elegantiam prae ceteris Italiae censetur nitidissimum, docentibus id abunde Poetis, Oratoribus, aliisque Scriptoribus, quos habuerunt, habentque cum purissimos, tum doctissimos.
units.tr: Just as they were formerly, so today the Etruscans are most distinguished in times both of war and of peace: they are most ready for all high affairs, both in leisure and in business; most eager for the study of letters; and outstanding for keenness of mind, remarkable shrewdness and singular astuteness. They lead a frugal life and practise a commendable thrift. They speak a dialect which, on account of its elegance, is considered the most refined of all in Italy, as the poets, orators and other writers whom they have had, and still have, abundantly demonstrate; they have been both the purest and the most learned of writers.

units.la: Etruscorum porro, de quibus hactenus generatim dixi, speciliores Populi leguntur vari, Vetentes, Faliscs, Tarquiniensis, cum multis aliis Vetentes, qui Bnos audiunt Plutarcho, Veientani Plinio lib. iii. cap. v. a Veio, id est Planstris, quibus omnia sua Scytharum more circumferre erant soliti, dictos quidam arbitrantur. Ego nihil affirmo. Alii ab Vejs derivant, principe ipsorum Urbe. Sedes habuerunt suas ab Janiculo ad Lacum usque Sabatum vel Tarquiniensem progressi inde versus Septentrionaliora facto Rosulum, Regnanum, Radiceique Sorac, & deinceps secundum Tiberim ad Janiculum quemadmodum patet ex variis Livii locis. Frequens ipsorum mentio apud Veteres Scriptores, praecipue Dionysium Halicarnassaeum & Livium; ex quibus aliisque constat, post diuturnum, varium & multiplex inter ipsos & Romanos bellum, tandem Mam. Aemilium Mamercinum Dictatorem iii anno ab V.C. cccxxviii eorum opes ita adflixisse, ut postero anno Inducias in xx annos petere fuerint coacti. Anno cccxlvii, quod ut inquit Livius, Inducias tempus exiit ille, Veientes ab Senatu impetrarunt, quia ipsi discordia intestina laborarent, ne Res ab se repeterentur. Sequente ergo anno Bellum Veiens motum ob superbum responsum Veientis Senatus, Legatis Romanis Res repetentibus datum. Id Patres aegre passi decreverunt, ut primo quoque tempore Tribuni Militum de Bello Veientibus indicendo ad Populum ferrent. Ita anno ab V.C. cccxlix circumscelli primum sunt Vej, atque inde per novem annos vario eventu ab Tribunis Militum res cum Veientibus gesta est, donec anno cccxviii M. Furius Camillus Dictator dictus, Faliscis primum & Capenatibus fusis castrisque exutis, ad Veios protectus, cuniculo in Arcem acto, Urbem ipsam decimo eius belli anno cepit; & maxima praeda potitus, Junonis etiam Signum Romam delatum in Aventino, exstructo ibi Templo, locavit; quum clarissimum de Veientibus in Urbem Triumphum equis albis vel o Curru invexisset. Atque ita Vej, qui cccc annis multum Romanis negocii fecerant, capta Metropoli sunt debellati. Legendi praeter Livium, Eutropium, Plutarchum, Diodorum, & Valerium, Florus lib. i. cap. xii, Auctor de VV. Illustribus cap. xxiii, Plinius lib. ii. cap. xcviii, lib. iii. cap. v, xii, xvii, Augustinus lib. i de Civit. Dei cap. xvii, & lib. iii. cap. xvii; apud quos aliosque alia multa de Veientibus leguntur, sed quae minoris momenti. Falisci, quos inter Veteres Etruria Populos secundo loco nominavi, Romanorum Historiis sunt notissimi. Φαλίσκοι cum aliis, tum Stephano: Φαλαῖκοι Diodoro. De iis Strabo lib. v; Ἔνιοι δ' ἀ Τυρρηνὸς φασι τὰς Φαλίσκους, ἀλλὰ Φαλίσκους ἰδίως ἰθι ... ubi pro οἱ δὲ ... Hermolaus Barbarus, vir doctissimus, ita emendat, οἱ δὲ αἰχεὶ Φαλίσκοι λέγουσι, quemadmodum apud alios aequos Falisci leguntur. Virgilius: Hi Fescenninas acies, Aequosque Falisco.
units.tr: Of the Etruscans, of whom I have so far spoken in general terms, various more specific peoples are read of: the Vetentes, Falisci, Tarquinienses, together with many others. The Vetentes, whom Plutarch calls Bneis, and the Veientani (Pliny, book 3, chapter 5), some think were named from Veii, that is, from wagons, on which they were accustomed to carry all their goods in the manner of the Scythians. I affirm nothing. Others derive the name from Veii, their chief city. They had their seats from the Janiculum to Lake Sabatinus or Tarquinii; then advancing from there towards the north, having made Rusellae, Regnano and the roots of Soracte, and then along the Tiber to the Janiculum, as is clear from various passages of Livy. Their mention is frequent among the ancient writers, especially Dionysius of Halicarnassus and Livy. From these and other sources it is established that, after a long, varied and manifold war between them and the Romans, Mamercus Aemilius Mamercinus, dictator in the year 328 from the founding of the city, so broke their power that in the following year they were compelled to ask for a truce of twenty years. In the year 347, as Livy says, when the truce period had run out, the Veientes obtained from the Senate that they should not be pressed to repay what was taken from them, because they were labouring under internal discord. So in the following year war against the Veientes was stirred up by the proud reply of the Senate, and it was given to the Roman envoys who demanded restitution. The Fathers, taking this badly, decided that at the first opportunity the military tribunes should bring a motion to the people for declaring war on the Veientes. So in the year 349 from the founding of the city, Veii was first besieged, and from then on for nine years the affairs with the Veientes were conducted by the military tribunes with varying outcome, until in the year 358 Marcus Furius Camillus, named dictator, having first routed the Faliscans and Capenates and stripped their camps, advanced to Veii, drove a mine into the citadel, and in the tenth year of that war took the city itself. Having gained great spoil, he also brought the statue of Juno to Rome and set it up in a temple built for it on the Aventine; and he rode into the city in a triumph over the Veientes, most celebrated, on a chariot drawn by white horses. Thus Veii, which for 400 years had given the Romans much trouble, was conquered once its capital had been taken. Besides Livy, one should read Eutropius, Plutarch, Diodorus, Valerius, Florus (book 1, chapter 12), the author of De Viris Illustribus (chapter 23), Pliny (book 2, chapter 98; book 3, chapters 5, 12, 17), Augustine (City of God, book 1, chapter 17, and book 3, chapter 17); in these and other authors many other things about the Veientes are read, but of lesser importance. The Falisci, whom I named second among the peoples of Etruria, are very well known from the Roman histories. Stephanus and others write Φαλίσκοι [Phaliskoi], while Diodorus writes Φαλαῖκοι [Phalaikoi]. Strabo, book 5, speaks of them: "Some say that the Tyrrhenians are the Falisci, but the Falisci are a distinct people..." [Ἔνιοι δ' ἀ Τυρρηνὸς φασι τὰς Φαλίσκους, ἀλλὰ Φαλίσκους ἰδίως ἰθι ...], where, in place of οἱ δὲ ... Hermolaus Barbarus, a most learned man, emends it thus: οἱ δὲ αἰχεὶ Φαλίσκοι λέγουσι [hoi de aiei Phaliskoi legousi]. Just as among other writers the Aequi Falisci are read. Virgil: "These lead the Fescennine battle-lines, and the Aequi Falisci."

units.la: Sic Silius Italicus de Bello Poenico: Hos iuxta Nepesina colors Aequique Falisci.
units.tr: So Silius Italicus in his Punic War: "Beside these came the Nepesine colonists and the Aequi and Falisci."

units.la: Non desunt tamen, qui de locis istis aliter sentiant. Ad rem. Falisos nomen Gentis esse; Falerios, Civitatis, constat etiam ex Plutarcho in Camillo & Livio lib. v. Solinus Gentem fuisse tradit; quae huc, Argivo Ductore, Physica, urbe Macedoniae, commigravit. Ovidius iv Fastorum Ducem appellat Alesium Argivum: Venerat Atrides Fatu agitatus Alesus: A quo se dictum Terra Falisca putat.
units.tr: Yet there are some who take a different view of these places. The point is this. That Falisos is the name of a people, and Falerios the name of a city, is established also from Plutarch in his Life of Camillus and from Livy, book 5. Solinus says the people were founded by a leader from Argos, who migrated here from Physica, a city of Macedonia. Ovid in book 4 of the Fasti calls the leader Alesius the Argive: "Alesus the Atreid had come, driven by fate, and from him, people think, the land of the Falisci takes its name."

units.la: Idem alibi in Elegia de Festo Junonis: Argiva est Tonipa facies; Agamemnone caso, Et sceleus & patrias fugit Alesus opes. Iamque per errati profugus terraque marique Moenia felici condidit altamanu. Ille suos docuit Junonia Sacra Falisco. Seles habuerunt ad dexteriorem Paliæ ripam, ad Vulsinium Lacum, longe latiusque vertus meridiem. Colebant Falisci, præter Iadimonem vel Veiouem, cum reliqui is Iuscus etiam Iunonem, unde Iunonis olea apud Ovidium vi Fastorum; Adde Senem Tatium, Iunonisque olasque Falisco s, Quos ego Romani succubuisse tuli:
units.tr: The same poet elsewhere, in his elegy on the Festival of Juno: "The face of Tonipa is Argive; after Agamemnon was killed, Alesus fled, both from crime and from his ancestral wealth. And now, a fugitive wandering over land and sea, he founded walls with a fortunate hand. He taught his people the sacred rites of Juno among the Falisci." The Seles lived on the right bank of the Paliae, near Lake Vulsinium, extending far and wide towards the south. The Falisci worshipped, besides Jupiter or Veiovis, Juno as well, whom the rest of the Italians also worshipped; hence the Juno of the olives in Ovid, book 6 of the Fasti: "Add Tatius the old, and the olives of Juno among the Falisci, whom I, Rome's own, have borne to be overcome."

units.la: Item Apollinem in Soracte Monte. Apud Falisços Familias fuisse, quæ Hirpi vocabantur hab Sacrificio annuo, quod Apollini sebat ad Montem Soractem, superaramtuliam Ligni ilim em ambulantes, non solitas aduri, & ob id perpetuo SC. Militiæ aliorumque Munerum vacationem habuisse memoria produnt Veteres Scriptores. Atuns apud Virgilium: Summe Deum, Cultos sacri Soractis Apollo, Quem primi colimus, ut pineus Ardor acervo Falsitur, & medium fert pietate per ignem Cultores multa premimus vestigia pruna.
units.tr: Likewise they worshipped Apollo on Mount Soracte. Ancient writers record that among the Falisci there were families called Hirpi, who had a yearly sacrifice offered to Apollo on Mount Soracte: walking barefoot over a pile of glowing embers, they were not burned, and for this reason they were always granted exemption from military service and other public duties by the senate. Virgil says: "Highest of gods, Apollo, worshipped on sacred Soracte, whom we first honour: as the pine-log's fire crackles on the heap, and in the middle the worshippers, through devotion, carry their steps over the glowing embers."

units.la: Silius Italicus libro v de Bello Punico: Tum Soracte satum præsentis corpore & armis Aequanum nosceus patrio cui rirus in arvo Quum prius arcitenens accerius gaudet accerius Exta ter umo vo late portare per ignes: Sic in Apollinea semper vestigia pruna Invio ata terat.
units.tr: Silius Italicus in book 5 of the Punic War: "Then a man born on Soracte, present in body and in arms, and known to the Aequi in his native land, when once the archer god rejoices in the sacrifice, to carry the entrails on his shoulders through the fire; so he always treads the path of Apollo's embers, unharmed."

units.la: & quæ sequuntur. In pretio erat apud eos & Pallas, de qua Ovidius iii Fastor. An quia per domum ad noscaptiva Falisca Venit——
units.tr: And what follows. Among them Pallas also was held in honour, of whom Ovid speaks in book 3 of the Fasti: "Or is it because a captive Falisca came into the house..."

units.la: De Iunone, cuius antea memini, item Tertullianus in Apologetico: Falisçorum in honorem est Pater Curis, unde accepit cognomen Iuno. Moribus & Institutis Falisci tam bene erant edocti, ut eam ob cautam Aequi quasi putentur cognominati. Loca id i mantua paullo ante laud. vi, de quibus aliis alia mens. In plerisque Veterum Argivorum moribus sutebantur, à quibus originem duxisse credebantur. Legendus Dionysius Halicarnassæus, qui quod dixi probat ab Re Falisçorum militari, variisque apud eos Armorum generibus. Tantæ apud Finitimos suos fuerunt existimationis, ut Leges ab iis (si Servio fides) & supplementum xii Tabularum Romani sumserint. Facit illud demonstrandæ Falisçorum potentiæ, quod Eutropius in i ne libri ii & Orosius lib. v dicant, uno prælio quindecim eorum millia fuisse cæsa, Q. Lutatio & A. Manlio Coss, ceteris pace concessa. Erat alioquin brevis admodum & angusta ipsorum Regio. Post multa feliciter & infeliciter gesta, tota tandem Falisçorum Regio cessit in ditionem Ecclesiæ Romanæ, vulgata illa Donatione, ut quidam contendunt, Constantini; vel, ut cum aliis auctor est Blondus Decadis i libro x, concessione Luitprandi Langobardorum Regis, Zachariæ, Romano tunc Pontifici, Divoque Petro facta, anno Christianæ salutis 1c cxiii; vel, quod vero magis consonat, longa Possessione, quæ ab Ludovico i Imperatore confirmata est anno ab Christo nato 1cccxv, tuti prebant ipsius Ludovici litteræ in Decretis Gratiani politæ, lxiii Distinct. c. Ego Ludovicus. Agri Falisci inter cetera proprium esse, Oves & Boves producere tentatur Plinius lib. xi. naturalis Historiæ. In Falisco, inquit, Herba depasta & Cutumini Amnis Aqua pota candidos Bos efficit. Ovidius in Fastis: Ducantur nivea Populo plaudente Juvenca, Quas alit Campis Herba Falisca suis.
units.tr: About Juno, whom I mentioned earlier, Tertullian also writes in his Apology: "Among the Falisci, Father Curis is honoured, from whom Juno received her surname." The Falisci were so well instructed in manners and institutions that they are thought to have been called by a name meaning "the wise" for their caution. The passages above have been cited, and different people have interpreted them differently. In most of their customs the Falisci followed the Argives, from whom they believed they were descended. Dionysius of Halicarnassus should be read, who proves what I have said from the Falisci's military affairs and the various kinds of arms among them. They were held in such esteem by their neighbours that the Romans took laws from them (if Servius is to be trusted) and the supplement to the Twelve Tables. What shows the power of the Falisci is that Eutropius, at the end of book 1 of book 2, and Orosius, book 5, say that in one battle fifteen thousand of them were slain, in the consulship of Q. Lutatius and A. Manlius, while peace was granted to the rest. Otherwise their territory was very small and narrow. After many successes and failures, the whole territory of the Falisci at last passed under the rule of the Roman Church, by the well-known Donation, as some contend, of Constantine; or, as Blondus also states in the first book of his tenth Decade, by the grant of Liutprand, king of the Lombards, made to Pope Zachary and to St Peter in the year of Christian salvation 713; or, what agrees more truly, by long possession, which was confirmed by the emperor Louis I in the year 815 after Christ's birth, as the letters of Louis himself, placed in Gratian's Decretum, Distinction 63, chapter "Ego Ludovicus," attest. Among other things peculiar to the Falisci territory, Pliny in book 11 of the Natural History says it is said to produce sheep and oxen: "In Falisco," he says, "grass grazed and water of the river Cutiminus drunk make the oxen white." Ovid in the Fasti: "Let the snow-white heifers be led forth, with the people applauding, which the Falisci grass feeds in their fields."

units.la: Idem alio loco: Colla rudes operum præbent ferienda Juvenci, Quo alunt campis Herba Falisca suis.
units.tr: Elsewhere he says: "They offer their necks, as untrained bullocks, to be struck for the works, which the Falisci grass nourishes in their fields."

units.la: Et lib. iii de Ponto: Agnaque tam lactens, quam Gramine pasta Falisco Vellima Tarpeios innuit ictafuros.
units.tr: And in book 3 of the Black Sea Letters: "The lamb, as milk-fed as the one pastured on Falisci grass, is said to be ready for the Tarpeian rock."

units.la: Agrum quoque eorum Lini copia fertilem denotat Silius Italicus, ——Induti sua Lina Falisci.
units.tr: Silius Italicus also indicates that their land was fertile in abundance of flax: "The Falisci, clad in their own flax."

units.la: Sic Gratius Poëta in libro de Venatione: At contra nostrū subellia Lina Falisci.
units.tr: So the poet Gratius in his book on hunting: "But on the other hand, the Falisci with flax seats."

units.la: Apud Falisros inventum Farciminis genus, de quo Papinius lib. iv. Silvarum: Non Lardum grave, debilisve Perna, Non Lucanica, non graves Falisci, Non Sal, Oxyporumve, Caseusve.
units.tr: A kind of sausage invented among the Falisci, of which Papinius speaks in book 4 of the Silvae: "Neither heavy bacon, nor a weakened ham, nor Lucanian sausage, nor the rich Falisci, nor salt, nor oxypor, nor cheese."

units.la: De Origine & Rebus Falisco rum scripsit circa annum cIↄ IↄXLIV Antonius Massa, Tarquiniensis, Falisci, Gallesius, Iurisconsultus. Tarquiniensis, qui tertio loco nominati, Infra Populos appellat Plinius libro naturę Histor. iii. cap. v, Fuerunt ubi hodie Tarquinia Urbis visuntur vestigia: Tarquene vulgo, in Etruria maritima. Multa inter Romanos & Tarquinienses gesta leguntur apud Veteres Scriptores. Ad alios venio. Capenates apud eundem sunt Plinium, indicato à me loco, & Livium libro v, xxvi & sequente: dicti à Capena ipsorum Metropoli, quæ hodie Canapina. Illorum sedes haud procul fuit Cimmia Silva & Cimino Lacu, colueruntque Monticulos, qui vernacule Montanea. Capenates cos esse, qui post Vaccanas ad sinistram partem habitant ab Roma eunti, tradit Pomponius Sabinus ad lib. vii Aeneidos. Municipii Capenatium meminit Inscriptio quæ in Falisco rum Monte Soratte, in Templo S. Oreslis in Tiburtino rudi, littera corrola:
units.tr: Antonius Massa of Tarquinii, a jurist of Gallesium, wrote about the origin and affairs of the Falisci around the year 1544. Tarquinii, which he named third, Pliny calls among the Infra peoples in book 3, chapter 5 of the Natural History; there are still traces of the city of Tarquinia to be seen where today it is commonly called Tarquene, in maritime Etruria. Many events between the Romans and the Tarquinienses are read in the ancient writers. I come to others. The Capenates are in the same Pliny (the passage I have indicated) and in Livy, book 5, chapters 26 and following; they were named after Capena, their metropolis, which today is Canapina. Their seat was not far from the Ciminian Forest and Lake Ciminus, and they inhabited the little hills, which in the vernacular are called Montanea. Pomponius Sabinus, on book 7 of the Aeneid, says the Capenates are those who live on the left-hand side, going from Rome, beyond the Vaccanae. The inscription which is on Mount Soracte among the Falisci, in the temple of St Oreste in the Tiburtine area, mentions a municipality of the Capenates, with the letters worn away:

units.la: V. M. SELICI. CLE MENTIS. SEVIRI MVNICIPIO. CA- PENAT. ARAM POSVERVNT PII LIBERTI
units.tr: To V. M. Selicius Clementis, seviir of the municipium of the Capenates: the dutiful freedmen set up this altar

units.la: Graviscani ab Gravisca, hodie Mortalto, haud procul Mari, ad Ossam Fluvium, qui vernacule Fiore. Mentio eorum in Inscriptione quæ Romæ in Vinea Cardinalis Carpensis, ubi L. Fabius Cilo Curator nominatur Reip. Nicomedensium, Interamnatium Nartium, item Gravisci anorum. Vide capite sequente, ubi de Interamnatibus Nartibus. Volsinii apud Strabonem & Auctorem de VV. Illustribus cap. xxxvi ab Volsino, quod Volsena hodie ad Volsiniensem & Lacum & Lucum, de quibus ante. Volsiniensium mentionem præter Plinium lib. iii, sæpe facit Livius, præsertim lib. ix & x. Ubi Pœtumium Consulem, Exercitu in Etruriam educto, primum Volsiniensium Agrum de populata, unipostea cum iis qui ex Urbe Finium tuendorum causa processerant, iuxta muros pugna decertasse, narrat. Quæ libro xi scribuntur, præterea. Volsinii apud Antoninum, ut & apud Tacitum libro iv Vulsinij: Vulsinij Fons apud Propertium pro Volsiniensi ponuntur Urbes, quam Caput Etruriæ quondam fuisse innuit Valerius Maximus Volsinies Seneca opulentissimos Etruriæ Populos nominat. Volsinienses etiam sunt in Marmoribus Romanis. Vide infra. Saturnini Plinio, quos Aurinos vocatos scribit, ab Saturnia, Tuscia Urbe mediterranea; cuius mentio apud Ptolemæum & alios, quæque & hodie nomen retinet, ut ex sequentibus parebit. Suanenses sunt apud eundem Plinium ab Suana, quæ Ptolemæo nota hodieque sic appellatur haud procul Glani Fluvio, ubi Stagnum Arctinum. Statones eidem Plinio, qui Statonenses Vitruvio ab Urbe Statonia, cuius meminit Strabo; hodie Scarlino: inde Statonensis Ager Varroni, & Statoniensis Lacus Seneca lib. ii. Naturali. Vetulonienses apud eundem sunt Plinium eodem loco ab Vetulonia, quod Οὐετύλωνοϲ Ptolemæo, Vetulonia Silio Italico; hodie Vetulia, locus de certus inter Pisas & Promontorium Populonium, tribus ab mari passuum millibus. Volaterrani, cognomine Ursi, qui in Volsiniensium sunt Regione, memorat idem Plinius loco sape indicato, apud quem in quibusdam Codicibus male Volaterrani. Tuscanenses eidem Plinio Populi Etruriæ, ubi nunc Opidum nobile, quod vulgo Tuscanell. Fasselli dicuntur nominari in Edicto Desiderii, Langbardorum Regis. Fluentini apud Linium Arno Fluminì adlocari ab Urbe, ut volunt, Fluentia; Florentini Tacito & Frontino, ut non nullis mens est: Populi satis noti. Quindecim porro Etruriæ Populorum meminit Inscriptionis Fragmentum, quod Vulsiniis extat hodieque mutilum.
units.tr: The Graviscani, from Gravisca, today Mortalto, not far from the sea, by the river Ossa, which in the vernacular is Fiore. Their name occurs in an inscription at Rome, in the vineyard of Cardinal Carpensis, which names L. Fabius Cilo as curator of the state of the Nicomedians, of the Interamnate Nartes, and likewise of the Gravisci. See the following chapter, where the Interamnate Nartes are discussed. The Volsinii, in Strabo and in the author of De viris illustribus, ch. 36, are named from Volsinus, which today is Volsena, near the Volsinian lake and grove, of which we spoke above. Apart from Pliny, book 3, Livy often mentions the Volsiniensians, especially in books 9 and 10, where he relates that the consul Poetumius, having led his army into Etruria, first ravaged the territory of the Volsiniensians, and then fought a battle near the walls with those who had come out of the city to defend its boundaries. What is written in book 11 follows. Volsinii in Antoninus, and Vulsinii in Tacitus, book 4. Propertius uses Vulsinii Fons for the Volsinian ... Valerius Maximus hints that this city was once the capital of Etruria, and Seneca names the Volsinians among the wealthiest peoples of Etruria. The Volsinienses also appear in Roman inscriptions; see below. The Saturnini of Pliny, whom he says were called Aurini, are named from Saturnia, an inland city of Tuscany; it is mentioned by Ptolemy and others, and it still keeps its name, as will appear from what follows. The Suanenses are also in Pliny, named from Suana, which is known to Ptolemy and is still so called, not far from the river Glanis, where there is the Arctine lake. The Statones of Pliny, whom Vitruvius calls Statonenses, are named from the city Statonia, which Strabo mentions; today it is Scarlino. Hence Varro's Statonensis ager and Seneca's Statoniensis lacus, book 2 of the Naturales Quaestiones. The Vetulonienses are in the same Pliny, in the same place, named from Vetulonia, which is Ptolemy's Οὐετύλωνος and Silius Italicus' Vetulonia; today it is Vetulia, a certain place between Pisa and the promontory of Populonium, three miles from the sea. The Volaterrani, with the surname Ursi, who lie in the region of the Volsiniensians, are also mentioned by Pliny in the passage already noted, where some manuscripts wrongly read Volaterrani. The Tuscanenses are, for the same Pliny, a people of Etruria, where now stands the noted town commonly called Tuscanell. The Fasselli are said to be named in the Edict of Desiderius, king of the Lombards. The Fluentini, placed by Livy on the river Arno, from the city which they think was Fluentia; the Florentini in Tacitus and Frontinus, as some think: peoples well enough known. Moreover, a fragment of an inscription, still extant at Volsinii though mutilated, mentions fifteen peoples of Etruria.

units.la: IN. ITALIA. VVLSINIENSIVM PATRIÆ. SVÆ. ITEM. FERENT ET. TIBVRTIVM. ITEM. COLON ITALICENSIVM. IN. PROV. BAETICA. PRAET. ETRVR. XV. POPVLORVM SACERDOTI. CAENENSIVM M. HELVIVS. M. F. CLEMENS. ARNENSIS DOMO. CARTHAGINE PRAEF. EQ. ALAE. PRIMAE CANNANEFATVM PRAESIDI. SANCTISS. ET CARISSIMO CVRA. AGENTE. L. ACONIO. CALLISTO TR. MIL. LEG. XIV. GEM. SEV
units.tr: In Italy: to the Volsiniensians, her homeland; likewise to the Tiburtines; likewise to the colony of the Italicenses in the province of Baetica; to the priest of the fifteen peoples of Etruria, of the Caenenses; M. Helvius Clemens, son of Marcus, of the Arnenses, from Carthage, prefect of the first ala of cavalry, governor of the Cannanefates, most holy and most dear, the business being carried out by L. Aconius Callistus, tribune of the soldiers of the fourteenth legion Gemina, Severan

units.la: De Tuscia generatim diximus: flagitat Methodus, ut sigillatim omnia persequamur: priore quidem loco, quæ ab Fluvio Macra ad Tiberim usque Littoribus proxima; inde quæ Mediterranea sunt, & intus magis se offerunt.
units.tr: We have spoken of Tuscany in general. Method requires that we go through each part in turn: first those districts that lie along the coast from the river Macra to the Tiber, and then those that are inland and present themselves further in.

units.la: Ab Macra iuxta Littus primum omnium Locus occurrit antiquæ nobilisque Vrbis Luna, cuius ingentes supersunt ruinæ, cum aliquot Piscatorum Casis. Luna Plinio: Ἄστε Straboni lib. v & Ptolemæo: Græcis etiam, uti notat Strabo, Σελήνη. Ex Luna ruderibus vicinum opidum Sarazanam, (Sergianam quidam Latine scribentes vocant) exstructum censet Volaterranus. Annius Viterbiensis, quum videret eo fere loco Cararam, fabricavit nobis illa Catonis, Cariara, quæ & Latine Luna addens in suo ad supposititium Autorem Commentario, Latine dici Lunam, Græce Selenen, Sago Etrusco vocabulo Cariaram nunc corrupte Carraram; esse enim Car, teste Hieronymo, Vrbem; & Iaram, Lunam; inde Car-Iaram nihil aliud esse, quam Vrbem Lunam. Ingeniose, sed an vere, ego in medio relinquo. Ab Luna autem Lunensis est Portus, de quo antea verba feci. De condita ab Trojanis Luna, excisaque ab Octaviano Augusto, multa fabulose circumferuntur. Certe ante Lucani tempora præceps ire coepérat, & labi. Canit is libro I Belli Pharsalici: quorum qui maxima nunc ævo Arunsincolunt desertæ mœnia Lunæ.
units.tr: Along the coast, from the Macra, the first place that meets us is the ancient and famous city of Luna, whose vast ruins survive, together with some huts of fishermen. Luna in Pliny; Ἄστε in Strabo, book 5, and in Ptolemy; the Greeks also, as Strabo notes, call it Σελήνη. Volaterranus thinks the neighbouring town of Sarazana, which some Latin writers call Sergiana, was built from the ruins of Luna. Annius of Viterbo, seeing that Carara lies almost on that spot, produced for us that passage of Cato, Cariara, which in his commentary on the supposed author he adds is Latin Luna, Greek Selene, and in the Etruscan language Cariara, now corruptly Carrara; for Car, he says, on the testimony of Jerome, means city, and Iara means Luna, so that Car-Iara is nothing other than the city Luna. This is ingenious, but whether it is true I leave undecided. Concerning Luna, founded by the Trojans and destroyed by Octavian Augustus, many fabulous tales are told. Certainly before the time of Lucan it had begun to decline and fall away. He sings in book 1 of the Pharsalia: "Of those who now dwell in the greatest numbers on the Arno, the walls of deserted Luna."

units.la: Meminerunt Lunæ multi Scriptores, cum primis Livius lib. xxxix & xli, ubi Coloniam eo deductam notat. Lunensem Caseum, celebrat Martialis: Caseus Etruscæ signatus imagine Lunæ Præstabit Pueris prandia mille tuis.
units.tr: Many writers mention Luna, above all Livy, books 39 and 41, where he notes that a colony was led there. Martial celebrates the Lunensian cheese: "A cheese stamped with the image of Etruscan Luna will provide a thousand dinners for your boys."

units.la: Plinius lib. xiv natur. Histor cap. vi in Vinorum censura palmam Etruria Lunam habere perhibet. Marmoris etiam candidi Fodinis celebris: unde Marmor Lunense. Intelligit Nonnus Διονυσιακ. 1 τῇ δὲ Σελήνης Εἶχε λίθον κα λιλλόν.
units.tr: Pliny, in book 14 of the Natural History, chapter 6, in his assessment of wines, says that Luna in Etruria holds the palm. It is also famous for its quarries of white marble, whence Luna marble. Nonnus in the Dionysiaca, book 1, refers to it: "She had a stone of the Selene, both bright and white" [τῇ δὲ Σελήνης Εἶχε λίθον καὶ λευκόν].

units.la: Legendum forte κα λιλλόν. Luna Patria fuit Eutychiani P. M. & Martyris. Vrbs quamquam interciderit, memoriam tamen eius servat Ager Confinalis, qui Lunana vulgo, nuncin Genuensium fere ditione.
units.tr: Perhaps one should read καὶ λευκόν. Luna was the homeland of Eutychianus, pope and martyr. Although the city has perished, its memory is kept by the surrounding district, which is commonly called Lunana, and now lies almost wholly within the territory of the Genoese.

units.la: Sequuntur in ora Ostia Larentia Frigidique, & Cervis Palus: dein Arx Motronis, Motrone, iuxta Versiliæ fauces; Propugnaculum vetus edito loco, quod Florentinis ademtum Karolus Siciliæ Rex Lucensibus restituit anno MCCCLXXV: iterumque Florentinos postea cepisse, scribit Blondus. Haud procul Arni ostio Portus est Liguranus, quem Cicero Labronem appellat ad Q. Fratrem lib. ii. Epist. iii scribens: apud quem pro Labrone male quidam reponunt Umbronem Fluvium. Umbro sane nimis magno Pisis distat intervallo, quam ut ab Cicerone coniungerentur. Ad Herculem videtur nonnullis dici ab Antonino, cuius Iter vide infra. Ptolemaeus tamen Ἠγεμονικὸν λιμὴν ponit inter Lunae Promontorium & Arni Fluminis Ostium: ergo multo verius Occidentem. Portus autem Ligurum hodie Livorno vocatur, de eo alibi plura.
units.tr: Along the shore follow the mouths of the Larentia and the Frigidi, and the marsh of Cervis; then the citadel of Motrone, near the narrow pass of Versilia: an old fortress on a high place, which Charles, King of Sicily, took from the Florentines and restored to the Lucchese in 1375; Blondus writes that the Florentines later took it again. Not far from the mouth of the Arno is the harbour of Liguranus, which Cicero, writing to his brother Quintus in book 2, letter 3, calls Labro; some wrongly substitute the river Umbro for Labro. The Umbro is certainly too far from Pisa to have been joined with it by Cicero. Some think the place is called Ad Herculem by Antoninus, whose itinerary see below. Ptolemy, however, places the harbour of Ἡγεμονικός between the promontory of Luna and the mouth of the Arno, so that the more correct view is the western one. The harbour of the Ligurians is today called Livorno; more on it elsewhere.

units.la: Intus tertio ab ora lapide stupendae vetustatis Urbs est Pisa. Sic Livio lib. xlv & alibi appellatur, quae Pisae Irogo, eidemque Livio nonnunquam loco, Virgilio, Lucano, Plinio, Solino, Pomponio Melae, Antonino, Itinerariae Tabulae, citeque Scriptoribus item Strabone lib. v, Polybio lib. ii, Dionysio Halicarnasseo lib. i, Agathio lib. x. de Bello Gothico & aliis. Ποσὶ, depravat. Prolemaeo. Condita vult Halicarnassaeus, quem nominavi, a Pisa Alpheo Peloponnesio; Plinius & Solinus a Pelope Pisaeque sive Attinatae, Graeca Gente; quos Pisa Arcadiae oppido, quod Alpheus Amnis adluit, protectos, cognominatos vocarunt Alpheos. Inde Pisa Virgilio lib. x. Aeneidos Alphea: inde Alphea Urbs Rutilio Itinerarii lib. i. Trogus item lib. xx. Pisa ab Graeca ornundas terbat. Strabo abus conditas Pisam notat qui ex Peloponneso cum Nestore ad bellum Trojanum profecti, quum excito Ilio domum redirent, erroribus acti per mare partim Mesapontum, partim Tyrrhenum Litus tenuerunt, Pisae omnes dicti. His consentanea quaedam legere est in Tabella, quae in Summo Templo pendebat. Incolae singulari valent memoria; quod Urbs crassiore sinatur aere. Iacet inter Amnes Auterem & Arnum, ut Strabo Plinuique notant. Contentit Rutilius Claudius Numatianus in Itinerario: Alpheae veterem qui nescit originem Troum, Quas circa quondam Arno et Aufidio aquae Con sul Pisae condita Flamma incendit, Intrari modica fonte capta est. Sed propinquum et ripas ab his ab opera ne nomen, Et Pontem sumptibus Arnae amnis, Ante dies quam Torquatus Fontana Pastor Laniorum Regno tuta iuste et. Dicet deinde et saepe Etruria Pisae, Nomine indicio tectisque tot genus.
units.tr: Inland, three miles from the coast, stands the city of Pisa, of astonishing antiquity. It is so called by Livy, book 45, and elsewhere; by Livy also on occasion, and by Virgil, Lucan, Pliny, Solinus, Pomponius Mela, Antoninus, the Itinerary Tables, and among Greek writers by Strabo, book 5, Polybius, book 2, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 1, Agathias, book 10, on the Gothic War, and others. Ptolemy has a corrupted form of the name. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, whom I have named, thinks the city was founded from Pisa on the Alpheus in the Peloponnese; Pliny and Solinus say it was founded by Pelops and the Pisaeans, or Attinates, a Greek people, who, protected by the Arcadian town of Pisa, which the river Alpheus washes, were called Alpheans. Hence Virgil in book 10 of the Aeneid calls it Alphea, and Rutilius, in book 1 of his Itinerary, calls the city Alphea. Trogus too, in book 20, says that Pisa was founded by Greeks. Strabo notes that Pisa was founded by men who set out from the Peloponnese with Nestor for the Trojan War, and who, on the fall of Troy and their return home, driven by storms, held partly the Messapian and partly the Tyrrhenian shore, all of them being called Pisans. Some things agreeing with this may be read on a tablet that hung in the great temple. The inhabitants are noted for an exceptional memory, which the thick air of the city is said to produce. It lies between the rivers Auser and Arnus, as Strabo and Pliny note. Rutilius Claudius Namatianus says in his Itinerary: "Who does not know the ancient origin of Alphean Pisa, which Trojan men once founded ... around which the waters of the Arno and Aufidius ... the city was taken and burned by fire ... and the bridge built at the expense of the Arno ..." The lines are too corrupt to render with certainty, but Rutilius goes on to say that Etruria will often name Pisa and show by its name and its many buildings the kind of people it was.

units.la: Hodie Arnus per eam fluit, tribus ornatus Pontibus: Spina, Fornicum quatuor; Verrum: Mars, quinque Vetustatem eius & Nobilitatem celebrat Dionysius Halic. lib. i. Commemorari solitam Primus xii Livoris Urbibus, tradunt alii. Navigationem ab Mari advertam habere Stadiorum xx. Civitatem quondam felicem & beatam fuisse nec tunc tempore vel ignobilem vel obscuram propter Frugum copiam, Saxorum opera, Navalem Materiam; & inter Etruscos belli gloria praecellunt Ligurumque finitimorum Gentem velut fuisse & irritamentum, memoriae produt Strabo. De ea sic Benjaminus in Itinerario: Dusan ab Gennua Pisae decorum diverum ittinere; magni Pisa, in quae Dominus fere decem mille Turres numerantur ad pugnandum apte & impune; si quando ei ipsius Pugnae necessitas exstat. Cives ipsi omnes fidelis, neque Regis, neque Principis sum parentes, sed Magistratus ab ipsis creato. Vixit Benjaminus ante quadringentos circiter & tringinta annos. Sic de eadem Franciscus Petrarcha, Pisarum Urbs, inquit, perantiqua habitatores & decora ipsae; & licet inter plana sita, non tamen, ut magna pars Urbium, pauca Turribus, sed tota communiter Aedificiis apparens, ut & Mari potens fuit: donec Patrum memoria non modo aeres aquereas, sed animos navigandi quae profisum, magno exit: pro in Genuensium, amisere. Antiqui splendoris adhuc monimenta supersunt Inclyta: marmoreis fulgentia Tecta Columnis; Turres & inclinata Fora, minitantesque ruinam Pendula, recta intus sit radentes Arcs longa, Gloria Romani Decimi quae maxima Turris Conditur ad ultra vicenos & quatuor horis Corpora consumi memorant hic obruta terris: Quin Nicodemi tua monstrant monumenta Sepulcri.
units.tr: Today the Arno flows through it, spanned by three bridges: the Spina, the Fornicum (four arches), and the Verrum, Mars, and five others. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 1, celebrates its antiquity and nobility. Others report that it was counted the first of the twelve cities of Etruria. Its navigable channel from the sea is twenty stadia long. Strabo records that the city was once fortunate and wealthy, and was neither obscure nor ignoble at that time, because of its abundance of crops, its stone quarries, and its timber for shipbuilding. Among the Etruscans it excelled in military glory, and it was a spur to the neighbouring Ligurian people. Benjamin, in his Itinerary, writes of it thus: "From Genoa to Pisa is a fine voyage of a day by sea. Pisa is a great city, in which the lord counts about ten thousand towers, fit for fighting and safe to use whenever the need of battle arises. The citizens themselves are all faithful, subject neither to king nor prince, but to a magistrate chosen by themselves." Benjamin lived about four hundred and thirty years ago. Francesco Petrarca likewise writes of the same city: "The city of Pisa is very ancient, and its inhabitants are noble. Although it lies on level ground, it is not, as most cities are, marked by a few towers, but it appears wholly built up with buildings in common, and it was also powerful at sea, until within living memory it lost not only its fleets and harbours but also its spirit for voyaging, and it went to ruin through the Genoese." Its ancient splendour survives in famous monuments: houses gleaming with marble columns, towers and leaning forums, and hanging structures threatening ruin, and long arcades with straight inner walls. The great tower of Pisa, the glory of Romans, is said to have been built with more than twenty-four hours of labour; and here bodies buried in the earth are said to be consumed, and the tombs of Nicodemus still show their monuments.

units.la: Sic inter alia de ea canit politissimus Poeta Nathan Chytraeus. Quae à Pisanis gestas, stadiantibus adhuc Romanorum rebus commemorant cum alii, tum Livius lib. ii, iii, iv, xxi, alibi, quae vero cum Imperio declinante, annisque nuper laptis, quamque; mari terraque, subiugatis Sardinia, Karthagine, Panormo, Salerno, aliis, fuerint semper potentes, docent Leonardus Aretinus, Flavius Blondus, Antoninus Archiepiscopus, Sabellicus, Plantina, Volaterranus, aliique multi: Scriptores Cladeab Genuensibus ad Lamellum iniata, adeo fuerunt tracti, ut post rehearte, utrumque recuperare pusillas numquam potuerunt. Libertatem, quam initio semper habuerant, salvam habuerunt ad annum usque 1310 vel 1220, quo Pisanam Tyrannide invalescente cum nomine Comitis Pisani Fig. Eum sequuti sunt alii: inter eos Joannes Ansaldus, qui Dux Pisanorum appellatus est, anno 1314. Tertius ab eo Gerardus Appianus Pisanus Joanni Galeatio Mediolanensium Ducis vendidit. Post per Joannem Gambartum in potestatem venerunt Florentinorum, qui anno 1406 ope Karoli VIII Galliarum Regis expulsi, aliquanto post obsessam Urbem anno 1499 recuperarunt; migrantibus civibus plerisque aliis alio, malentibusque sortis tuae fraui libertate, quam in Patria premi Servitute. Doctissimi multa pauci Julius Cæsar Scaliger: Pisa vetus, a tellure in Oriente emissa, Lydia arma tuae Troiae de rebus tuis. Si movent te ille annis fictor tamen ergo; Stet es est, inanis tutor, arbitrii loco. Mortales, ferae celeres, nec credere Fatis: Nam quod nos aliis, illa de terra nabis.
units.tr: In this way the most polished poet Nathan Chytraeus sings, among other things, about it. Those deeds of the Pisans which were performed while Roman affairs were still flourishing are recorded by several writers, and above all by Livy in books 2, 3, 4, 21, and elsewhere. That they were always powerful, both by sea and by land, after the Empire declined and after the years had slipped away, having subdued Sardinia, Carthage, Palermo, Salerno and others, is shown by Leonardo Bruni of Arezzo, Flavio Biondo, Archbishop Antonino, Sabellico, Platina, Volterrano, and many others. The writers say that after their defeat at Meloria by the Genoese they were so cast down that, although they later tried, they were never able to recover their former strength. They kept the liberty which they had always had from the beginning safe until about the year 1310 or 1320, when the tyranny of Pisa grew strong under the name of Count Fazio of Pisa. Others followed him: among them Giovanni Ansaldo, who was called Doge of the Pisans, in 1314. Third after him, Gerardo Appiani of Pisa sold the city to Giovanni Galeazzo, Duke of the Milanese. Afterwards, through Giovanni Gambacorta, it came into the power of the Florentines; in 1406, with the help of Charles VIII, King of the French, the Pisans expelled them. Some time later, after the city was besieged, the Florentines recovered it in 1499. Most of the citizens migrated elsewhere, preferring to lose their fortunes for the sake of liberty than to be oppressed by servitude in their homeland. The most learned Julius Caesar Scaliger wrote a few verses about it: "Old Pisa, sprung from the earth in the East, Lydian arms of your Troy, concerning your affairs. If those tales move you, yet they are fabricated for the sake of age; let it stand, as it is, a vain guardian in the place of judgement. Mortals, quick to flee, and not to trust the Fates: for what we are to others, that land is to us."

units.la: Archiepiscopatus floret dignitate: cui subiiciuntur Massanensis & Crostensis, praeter alios in Corsica Praesules. Archiepiscopus enim Pisanus Corsicæ est Primus. Academiam habent Pisanam Disciplinarum omnium, institutam anno 1343. Docuerunt ibi Petrus Sandeus, Franciscus Aretinus, Pilippus Decius, Partolus, & alii.—Cum Urbis fortuna laetam reddidit Cosmus Medices, vocatis eo ad iuris Protectionem Andreas Alciatus: ad Medicinæ, Mattheus Curtio: qui in Campo Sancto sepulti. Viros claros genuit non paucos, cum aliis, Eugenium III P.M., Raymerum & Bartholomæum, illum Pantheologiæ, hunc Summæ Catuum, ut vocant Conscientiæ, quæ Pisana dicitur, auctorem. Pisanorum appellat Nasum ut legere est apud Sex Pompeium Festum, Pa'ta contem e Pisi orundum Tyrannum: Cæsar (hic legendum pro caput) aliquin inde praefecti nunc Pisani dicuntur. Servatum hic aliquando nobilissimum illud Pandectarum Volumen, Constantinopoli ab ipsis adlatum, postea Florentiam portatum unde Pandectae hodie Florentinae. Bibliotheca apud Dominicanos est satis bona. Nobilitata fuit Pisa Concilio Generali, quod hic anno 1409, causa Schismatis inter duos Pontifices Gregorium XII & Benedictum XIII orti, celebratum. Inceptum hic quoque Concilabulum aliquot Cardinalium adversus Julium II, quæ res quum publice innotuisset, Populus, Armis arreptis, profugere coegit omnes, qui ea de causa convenerant. Pisa Magnus Etruriae Duxtaepe moratur; & in ea Domicilium habent Equites D. Stephani, ab Magno Duce institutum. In hac Urbe Otho I, Imperator septem Germanorum instituit Familias, quas & honoribus & facultatibus ornavit. Sunt ex Casa Maiola, Catania, Orlandi, Espa, Pisanae, Vicecomites, Gusmany, Dadi. Primarium Templum, quod Duomum vocant, ambitum habens 1xxl passuum, columnisque subnixum, x, & splendidas Praesulis Aedes ex Spolijs aedificarunt Pisani, quæ ieiunis ad Panormum Saracenis retulerunt. In eo Templo Octa iunt condita Henrici VI: Lucchesi, Imperatoris, Pisæ translata anno 1267, die Sextilis XXV. Est ibidem Sepulcrum Vladislai, illustrissimi Ducis Texanensis, qui obiit Pisis anno 1260, mense Aprili; ab Vladislao Duce Silesiæ Dominoque Texanensi renovatum anno 1300, Idibus Februarii. Monstrant ibidem Cives & Cadavera Gamaleontis, Vorumedo, & Aldae, Patris, Filii & Nepotis, Hierosolymis co traducta. Sepulcrorum pedes oblongum CCCCI XXXVI, latum CXX, pulcherrime exornatum Campus Sanctus dicitur: quod eius Terra, ut volunt, Hierosolymis fuerit transportata, Mortuorumque Cadavera ibi uno naturali die contumuntur. Ager suburbicarius Segetibus est perc omnimodis, adeo que fertilis, ut Eremum fere totam pateat, & Exteris etiam Annonam non neget. Vina ibi notae non admodum probae: Pepones optimi.
units.tr: The archbishopric flourishes in dignity; to it are subject the bishops of Massa and Crosseto, besides others in Corsica. For the Archbishop of Pisa is primate of Corsica. They have a university of all the disciplines, founded in 1343. There taught Pietro Sandeo, Francesco Aretino, Filippo Decio, Bartolo, and others. When Cosimo de' Medici made the city happy again, Andrea Alciato was called there for the protection of law, and Matteo Curzio for medicine; they are buried in the Campo Santo. The city produced not a few famous men, among them Pope Eugenius III, Raymer and Bartholomew, the first the author of a Pantheologia, the second of the Summa of Cases of Conscience, as they call it, which is called Pisana. Festus writes of the Pisans' nose, as one may read in Sextus Pompeius Festus. The Pisan... [the text here is corrupt]. Here once was preserved that most noble volume of the Pandects, brought from Constantinople by the Pisans, and afterwards carried to Florence, whence the Florentine Pandects today. The library among the Dominicans is fairly good. Pisa was made famous by a General Council, which was held here in 1409 because of the schism that had arisen between the two Popes, Gregory XII and Benedict XIII. A conciliabulum of some cardinals against Julius II was also begun here; when this matter became publicly known, the people, taking up arms, forced all who had gathered for that reason to flee. The Grand Duke of Tuscany often stays at Pisa, and the Knights of St Stephen, founded by the Grand Duke, have their home there. In this city the Emperor Otto I established seven families of the Germans, whom he adorned with honours and property. They are of the houses of Maiola, Catania, Orlandi, Espa, Pisane, Visconti, Gusmani and Dadi. The principal temple, which they call the Duomo, has a circuit of 1,070 paces and is supported by columns, and the splendid residence of the bishop was built by the Pisans from spoils, which they brought back from the Saracens after they had taken Palermo. In this temple are buried the bones of Henry VI, and the Emperor Lucchesi, transferred to Pisa in 1267 on the twenty-fifth of August. There is also the tomb of Ladislaus, the most illustrious Duke of Teschen, who died at Pisa in April 1260; it was renewed by Ladislaus, Duke of Silesia and lord of Teschen, in 1300, on the Ides of February. There the citizens also show the bodies of Gamaliel, Vorumedo, and Alda, father, son and grandson, brought there from Jerusalem. The Campo Santo is the name given to the oblong enclosure of the tombs, 436 feet long and 120 wide, most beautifully adorned; it is said that its earth was carried from Jerusalem, and that the dead bodies buried there are consumed within one natural day. The suburban land is wholly productive of crops, and so fertile that it nearly everywhere lies open to the desert, and it does not deny provisions even to foreigners. The wines there are not very good, but the melons are excellent.

units.la: Pei. Pisa in ora lequuntur, praeter crebros haud procul Ligurno Lacusculos ac Paludes, Mons Niger, Monte Nero, paullum ab Littore abitus: inde Rejimanum, Rejignano; Refignano ; & ulterius Vada. Sic Antonino, sicque hodie dicuntur, quæ Vada Volaterrana M. Tullio, Plinio, alijs. In Tabula Itineraria feriptum est, Vadis Volaterris; inter quæ & Pifæ notantur ibi alia loca, Turrita, Piscina, ad Fines & Veiuna, uti in medio videbimus hujus capitis. Fallitur Volaterranus, qui hoc loco scribit exstitisse quondam Etruriam Vrbem; quam meliores Scriptores ad Lacum Vadimonis signant; accedente Plinio, qui solum Vadam, Etruscæ gentis Oppidum, olim in Litore fuisse dicit. Visuntur quidem ad Vadam, recedentibus Marinis plus æquo Aquis, quorumdam Ædificiorum Rudera; sed ea putandum est Vadorum partem, vel aliud Volaterranorum opus. Succedit Ostium Cecinnæ, de quo dein Ab eo paullo interius ab ora Bulgarium est oppidum, Bulgari; frumenti Fructuumque copia mire adfluens, sed Aquarum dulcium supra modum inops. Iuxta est Castanietum, Castagneto, in colle; & ad littus S. Vincentij Turris, Torre di S. Vincenzo. Hanc inter & Promontorium Populonium tribus ab Littore passuum millibus, inter silvosos Saltus, Murus occurrit longus, spatium maximum complectens, grandibus Saxis, crassus pedes x, partim integer, partim conlapsus: cum magna Fontium Puteorumque copia; Amphitheatri parte. Lapide Etruscis Litteris inscripto multis denique nobilium Marmorum fustis, Capitulis praeruptis, Basibus, Tabulis, Abacis, Epistyliis, aliisque id genus Antiquitatis Monumentis: Vetulam Adcolæ nominant: nemorosoque Saltus Silvam Vetulam: unde conjicere licet cum Silva Vetuloni hic fuisse, cujus meminit Ptolemæus: Vetulonium appellat Silvam; de qua Populisque Vetulonensibus antea dixi.
units.tr: Pisa lies on the coast, and besides the frequent little lakes and marshes near Livorno, there is Monte Nero at a short distance from the shore; from there comes Rosignano, and further on Vada. So Antoninus calls them, and so they are called today; Cicero, Pliny and others call them Vada Volaterrana. The Itinerary Table has written Vadis Volaterris; between these and Pisae are marked other places, Turrita, Piscina, ad Fines and Veiuna, as we shall see in the middle of this chapter. The Volterran is mistaken, who writes in this place that there once existed a city Etruria; better writers locate it at the Lake of Vadimo, Pliny also agreeing, who says that only Vada, a town of the Etruscan people, was once on the coast. Indeed, at Vada, as the waters recede more than is fitting, the ruins of some buildings can be seen; but these must be thought to be part of Vada, or some other work of the Volaterrans. Next comes the mouth of the Cecina, of which more below. A little inland from the shore is the town of Bulgari, Bulgari, abounding wonderfully in grain and fruits, but very lacking in sweet water. Near it is Castanietum, Castagneto, on a hill; and on the shore the Tower of St Vincent, Torre di S. Vincenzo. Between this and the Promontory of Populonia, three miles from the shore, among wooded thickets, there appears a long wall, enclosing a very large space, built of large stones, ten feet thick, partly intact and partly collapsed, with a great abundance of springs and wells; part of an amphitheatre. Finally, there are a stone inscribed with Etruscan letters, many pieces of noble marble, cut capitals, bases, tablets, abaci, epistyles, and other monuments of antiquity of that kind; the neighbours call it Vetula, and the wooded thicket Silva Vetula. From this one may conjecture that the Silva Vetuloni of which Ptolemy speaks was here; he calls the forest Vetulonium, and I have already spoken before of it and of the Vetulonenses people.

units.la: Procurrit mox in æquor ora, Peninsulamque quasi facit: ubi quondam Colli imposita fuit antiqua Vrbs Populonia. Sic Livio, qui ejus meminit non semel, præsertim libro xxviii, Virgilio x Æneidos, Antonino, Rutilio lib. i, Melaque dicta, quæ Populonium Plinio & Itinerariæ Tabulæ; Straboni, Ptolemæo, Stephano. Vna fuit ex xii Etruriæ Vrbibus, princeps rei Navalis. Dictam volunt à Populorum multitudine, quæ in eius Agro; vel ab frequentibus Piratarum Populationibus. Qualis illi fuerit in Promontorio cognomine Situs, quo modo & quando Sullanis scilicet temporibus, dirutum fere totum, præter Sacras Ædes & paucas Domos, notat Strabo lib. v. Restauratum nonnihil plane subversum est ab Nicea Patritio Constantinopolitano, Imperatoris Præfecto, Bernardino Karoli Magni Nepote in Italia regnante. Iuxta Populonia Littus Vandalos cum Genserico Rege devictos à Bailio, Classis Imperatoris Leonis iii Præfecto, memorant Blondus & Sabellicus. Tradit Plinius libro xiv. cap. i in Vrbe Populonia Iovis fuisse Simulacrum una ex Vite, incorruptum multis annis conspectum. De Vestigiis hujus Vrbis, ex quibus ejus magnificentia facile potest æstimari, notatu digna leguntur ex relatione Zachariæ Zanchij Volaterrani apud Leandrum. De Populonia Ruinis Rutilius libro Itinerarij i: Pendula securum referat Populonia littus, Quas naturalem ducit in arva sinum. Nonillic positas extollit in aethera moles Lumine nocturno conspicienda Pharos: Sed speculum valida rupis sortita vetustas, Quas fluctus domitos arduus urget apex: Castellos geminos hominum fundavit in usus, Præsidium Terris, Indiciumque Fretis. Agnoscì nequeunt aevi monimenta prioris: Grandia consumsit Mœnia temptus edax. Sola manent interceptis vestigia muris: Ruderibus latis tecta sepulta jacent. Non indignemur mortalia Corpora solvi: Cernimus exemplis Opida posse mori.
units.tr: The coast soon runs out into the sea and forms a peninsula, where the ancient city of Populonia once stood on a hill. Livy mentions it more than once, especially in book 28; Virgil in book 10 of the Aeneid; Antoninus and Rutilius in book 1; Mela calls it Populonium, as do Pliny and the Itinerary Tables; Strabo, Ptolemy and Stephen also name it. It was one of the twelve cities of Etruria and the leader in naval affairs. Some hold that it took its name from the multitude of Populi in its territory, or from the frequent depredations of pirates. Strabo, book 5, notes what its situation was like on the promontory of the same name, and how and when, namely in the time of Sulla, it was almost entirely destroyed, except for the sacred buildings and a few houses. It was somewhat restored, but was later utterly overthrown by Nicea, a Patrician of Constantinople and prefect of the Emperor, while Bernard, grandson of Charlemagne, was reigning in Italy. Blondus and Sabellicus record that the Vandals, under King Genseric, were defeated near Populonia by Bailius, prefect of the fleet of the Emperor Leo III. Pliny, book 14, chapter 1, relates that in the city of Populonia there was a statue of Jupiter made from a single vine, which was seen unspoiled for many years. Notable accounts of the remains of this city, from which its magnificence may easily be judged, are found in the report of Zaccaria Zanchi of Volterra, cited by Leandro. Rutilius, in book 1 of his Itinerary, speaks of the ruins of Populonia: "Populonia, hanging over the shore, shows the safe bay that it makes into the fields. Here a tower raised to the sky, a Pharos to be seen by its light at night, stands; but ancient time, strong in its power, has taken hold of the rock, and its steep summit presses on the waves it has tamed. It founded two castles for human use, a defence for the lands and a sign for the sea. The monuments of an earlier age cannot be recognised; devouring time has consumed the great walls. Only traces remain where the walls were cut away; the buried roofs lie beneath the wide rubble. Let us not be indignant that mortal bodies dissolve; we see from examples that cities too can die."

units.la: In Situ Populonia labitur Blondus, eam ad Ostium Vmbronis Amnis ultra Plumbinum locans. Ad Populonia Rudera Palus est Caldana, supra quam versus Septemtrionem, ubi Corniam recipit fluvium, Campilia jacet, vulgo Campiglia; quam Auctore nullo, vel frigido, ut solet, Annius Capylium antiquitus vocatam scribit.
units.tr: Blondus places Populonia in the same position, beyond Piombino, at the mouth of the river Umbro. Near the ruins of Populonia is the marsh Caldana, and above it, toward the north, where it receives the river Cornia, lies Campilia, commonly called Campiglia; Annius, citing no author, or a worthless one as is his habit, writes that it was called Capylium in ancient times.

units.la: Altero Peninsulæ, de qua dixi, vel Promontorij latere major Maris Sinus panditur. Hic Paumlnum Sinum ipsum spectat, quod ob interitum Populony, ab cujus ruinis tribus Patauium a illibus est conditum, Populoniaque nomen adhuc quodam modo referre creditur. Ecclesia Romana Plumbinariam, Blondo teste, diu vocavit. Oppidum nobile lautumque latus, Mari adpositum, quo latere uno adluitur. Sub Principatu dudum fuit illustris Appianorum familiæ: hodie alius est potestatis.
units.tr: On the other side of the peninsula I have described, or on the side of the promontory, a larger bay of the sea opens out. This faces the bay called Paumlnum, which is believed to preserve in some way the name of Populonia, since after the ruin of Populonia*, from whose remains the Patavians were founded by Antenor, it was so named. The Roman Church long called it Plumbinaria, according to Blondus. It is a noble town and a well-washed one, set beside the sea, on the side where it is bathed by the sea. Under its lordship it was long the illustrious possession of the Appiani family; today it belongs to another power.

units.la: In interiore Sinus, cujus memini, recessu Scarlinum est, in Colle situm, Apianorum quondam ditionis: Scabra vel Snapra Antonini. Volaterranus hic fuisse Statonem Pinus opinatur.
units.tr: In the inner recess of the bay I have mentioned lies Scarlinum, situated on a hill, formerly under the rule of the Appiani; Antoninus calls it Scabra or Snapra. Pinus thinks that Volterrano was here Statonia.

units.la: In exitu Sinus Insula jacet Treiana, modico ab Continente separata Freto: vulgo Isola della Troia, vel Pisal; unde Lauterorum Imperium hoc usque pertinuisse quidam autumant.
units.tr: At the exit of the bay lies the island Treiana, separated from the mainland by a narrow strait; commonly called Isola della Troia, or Pisal; some claim that the rule of the Lauteri extended as far as this.

units.la: Alma funerato, Pinueres occurrit, quæ ab Fluvio Piano d'Alma. In ea Castellio Piscale est oppidum; Castiglione di Telaro; ad fauces altæ cœno Paludis, quam Lacum Apriam nominat Antoninus, cum in Itinerario Maritimo Portuum ab Vrbe Arelitum usque, cum Itinere ab Roma per Tuteam & Alpes Maritimas ad idem oppidum. Dixi alibi. Juxta eandem Paludem Burtanum est, mox Columna; de quibus post dicam in Itinere Antonini.
units.tr: Beyond the nourishing Alma, Pinueres comes into view, which takes its name from the river Piano d'Alma. In it is the town Castellio Piscale; Castiglione di Telaro, at the mouth of the high marsh of mud, which Antoninus names Lacus Apria, when he lists the harbours in his maritime itinerary from the city of Arelate onward, with the route from Rome through Tuteia and the Maritime Alps to the same town. I have spoken of this elsewhere. Near the same marsh is Burtanum, then Columna*; I will speak of these later in the Itinerary of Antoninus.

units.la: Hinc transito Bruno flumine ad oram redeunti secundum Paludem, modico ab ripa spatio, in colle Mons Tiscanus, Monte Pelano, adparet.
units.tr: Crossing the river Bruno here and returning to the shore beside the marsh, at a short distance from the bank, on a hill, appears Mons Tiscanus, Monte Pelano.

units.la: Ad ripam Vmbronis Occidentalem Grefetum est Oppidum, Ditionis Senensium, Episcopatus titulo clarum.
units.tr: On the western bank of the Umbro is the town of Grefetum, under the rule of the Sienese, famous for its bishopric.

units.la: Vitra Vmbronem Portus le offert Telamonis, Porto di Telamone, de quo alibi. Decimoquinto hinc lapide, Olim Albengamque transgressis occurrit Orbitellum, ad Lacum cognominemicum Cherronelus hic adjacet ingens & Promontorium, quod vulgo Monte Argentaro: cui uno in latere D.Stephani Optimum, S.Stefano: altero Portus Herculis, Porto d'Ercole, Antonino in Itinerario Maritimo celebratus.
units.tr: Beyond the Umbro, the harbour Telamonis, Porto di Telamone, presents itself, of which I speak elsewhere. Fifteen miles from here, after crossing the Albegna, one meets Orbitellum, near the lake of the same name; here lies a great headland and promontory, commonly called Monte Argentaro. On one side of it is the church of St Stephen, S. Stefano; on the other is the harbour of Hercules, Porto d'Ercole, celebrated by Antoninus in his maritime itinerary.

units.la: Haud procul Lacu, quem dixi, Cherroneloque Cossa fuit oppidum: sic vocatum Livio, Plinio, Pomponio, aliis, Cossa Straboni & Stephano; quod Kossa Ptolemæo: Cossa Vagino lib. x. Rutilio libro i, & Itinerariæ Tabulæ, Cosa Onuphrio. Volsiensium cognominat Plinus, cujus libro iii. cap. v hæc Loci his inlustrandis sunt verba: Vitare Nazzeronum ..., & ab eo (Litus legit ab Occidente versus Orientem) Forties Imbria, Portus Telamonis, Cossa Valentiensium (nam distinctio inter duas has voces expungenda: vitiose Codices Telamotosa, quali usus est Blondus) à Populo Romano deducta, Graviscæ, & quæ sequuntur. Cossa hæc Onuphrio Orbitellum putatur, de quo dixi; Lan edona, Nigro; Apolina, Leandro. Strabo certe post Populoniam in jugum Colle delitescit. Sunt qui Cosam ob multitudinem Murium delertam dixerunt. Fabulam censet Rutilius lib. i: Ce nemus antiquas nullo Cossa de ruinas, Et desertæ Mænia læva Colæ. Inde enim, clades, quod tanter forta causam Promere, sed risum dissimulare piget. Dicuntur Cives quondam in grave coacti, Muribus infestos deserere Lares. Credere malueram Pygmæa damna Cohortis, Et ventureta ut sua bella Grues.
units.tr: Not far from the lake I have mentioned, and from Cherrone, there was the town of Cossa; so called by Livy, Pliny, Pomponius and others, Cossa by Strabo and Stephen; Kossa by Ptolemy; Cossa by Vagino in book 10, by Rutilius in book 1, and in the Itinerary Tables; Cosa by Onuphrius. Pliny calls it Volsiensium, and in book 3, chapter 5, the words for illustrating this place are these: "to avoid Nazzeronum..., and from there (he reads the coast from west to east) Forties Imbria, the harbour of Telamon, Cossa Valentiensium (for the distinction between these two words must be removed: the manuscripts wrongly have Telamotosa, which Blondus used), derived by the Roman people, Graviscae, and what follows." Onuphrius thinks this Cossa is Orbitellum, which I have discussed; Nigro thinks it is Lanedona; Leander thinks it is Apolina. Strabo certainly places it on a hill beyond Populonia. Some have said that Cosa was deserted on account of the multitude of mice. Rutilius, book 1, considers this a fable: "This grove, Cossa, does not show the ancient ruins, nor the walls of the deserted Colaea on the left. For it is a shame to reveal the cause of such a great disaster, yet to hide the laughter. It is said that the citizens, once compelled by grave necessity, abandoned their household gods, troubled by mice. I would rather have believed that the cranes were the Pygmies' cohort, and that their wars were about to come."

units.la: In Argentarij Montis fine ad Litus Tabata est, Taglata: hinc modico ab ora intervallo in Colle Capalbium, Capalbo; Blondo Caput Alvium; Annio Caput Abantium, suo more hæc etiam nuper ...
units.tr: At the end of Mount Argentaro, on the shore, is Tabata, Taglata; then at a short distance from the coast, on a hill, Capalbium, Capalbo; Blondus calls it Caput Alvium; Annius Caput Abantium, in his own manner, and these things too recently...

units.la: Pecina Florique Amnibus transitis, ad orientalem posterioris ripam Castellum est, quod Aonte Ato vulgo, ubi, ut inquit Leander, pictura Ptolemæi Graviscas locare videtur. Sed aliud Montem. Itum esse, aliud Graviscas paret ex Itineraria Tabula, quæ paullo post ponitur. Testimonia autem, ne indictæ mihi abeant, Ptolemæo, & Graviscæ Livio, Silio lib. viii, Paterculo, Plinio, Antonino: quod in Strabonis
units.tr: Having crossed the Pecina and Flora rivers, on the eastern bank of the latter, there is a castle which is commonly called Aonte Ato, where, as Leander says, Ptolemy's map seems to place Graviscae. But it is one thing to have gone to Mons, and another for Graviscae to appear in the Itinerary Table, which is set down a little later. The witnesses, lest I leave them unmentioned, are Ptolemy, and Livy for Graviscae, Silius in book 8, Paterculus, Pliny, Antoninus; whereas in the manuscripts of Strabo, corruptly,

units.la: Codicibus corrupte Τεγαίσαν. Graviscæ ab cœli gravitate & intemperie putantur dictæ: unde Virgilio lib.x: Intempestaque Graviscæ.
units.tr: Tegaisan [Τεγαίσαν]. Graviscae are thought to be named from the heaviness and unhealthiness of the air; hence Virgil, book 10: "and unhealthy Graviscae."

units.la: Accinit Rutilius libro 1 Itinerarij: Inde Graviscarum vestigia rara videmus, Quas premit æstiva sæpe Paludis odor: Sed nemorosa viret densis vicinia Lucis, Pineaque extremis fluctuat Umbra Fretis.
units.tr: Rutilius sings in book 1 of his Itinerary: "Thence we see the scattered traces of Graviscae, which the summer odour of the marsh often oppresses; but the neighbourhood is green with dense grove, and the pine shade waves at the far edges of the sea."

units.la: Mentionem Graviscarum sæpe facit Livius, præsertim lib. xl, ubi eo Coloniam ab Romanis deductam scribit: cujus rei meminerunt etiam Velleius Paterculus & Sex. Iulius Frontinus. Idem Livius alibi fulmine percussos Muros & Portam Graviscarum narrat. Strabo inter Cosam & Graviscas Stadia esse ccc tradit. Plinius in Mari apud Graviscas Corallium nasci memorat; retibus evelli, ut hodieque, solitum.
units.tr: Livy often mentions Graviscae, especially in book 40, where he writes that a colony was led there by the Romans; Velleius Paterculus and Sextus Julius Frontinus also mention this. The same Livy elsewhere tells of walls and the gate of Graviscae struck by lightning. Strabo says there are 300 stadia between Cosa and Graviscae. Pliny records that coral grows in the sea near Graviscae, and that it was customarily gathered by nets, as it still is today.

units.la: Post Martam Fluvium interius paullo ab ora Cornetum est; in Colle, quo loco fuit Castrum Novum, cujus meminerunt Plinius, Mela, & Itineraria Tabula. Κάστρον Νέον appellat Ptolemæus; Castrum Inui Virgilius, ut notat Servius; Sic Rutilius lib. 1: Stringimus...... & fluctu & tempore Castrum Index semiruti Porta vetusta loci. Præsidit exiguî formatur imagine Lavi, Qui pastorali nomina fronte gerit. Multa licet prisci nomen deleverit ætas, Hoc Inui Castrum Fama fuisse putat. Seu Pan Tyrrhenus mutavit Menalas silvis, Sive sinus patriae incola Faunus init: Dum renovat largo mortalis semina fætu, Fingitur in Venerem promptior esse Deus.
units.tr: Beyond the river Marta, a little inland from the shore, is Cornetum, on a hill, where Castrum Novum once stood, which Pliny, Mela and the Itinerary Table mention. Ptolemy calls it Κάστρον Νέον [Kastron Neon]; Virgil calls it Castrum Inui, as Servius notes. So Rutilius, book 1: "We skirt... by wave and by time, Castrum, the sign of the half-ruined old gate of the place. It is guarded by the image of a small Lar, who bears a pastoral name on his brow. Although ancient time has blotted out much of its name, Fame thinks this was the Castrum of Inuus. Whether the Tyrrhenian Pan changed the Menalian woods, or Faunus, the native of the bay, came in; while the mortal renews the seed with abundant fruit, the god is imagined to be more ready for Venus."

units.la: Aliud est Castrum Novum, quod Antoninus Mari propius locat, & remotius paullo versus Vulturnum. Certe Cornetum esse Castrum Novum, de quo dixi, tam est certum, ut præter Situs rationem, quæ apud Ptolemæum, hodieque pars ibi superfit Veteris Appellationis. Urbs est in Colle sita, eoque modico tribus ab Mari passuum millibus, antiquis adhuc superbiens Mœnibus, multisque Turribus. Patria Gregorii v. P. M. & Roberti, eius (nam Episcopatus gaudet titulo) Præsulis, qui Symphoniarum Cantusque Ecclesiastici reformavit rationem.
units.tr: Castrum Novum is another place, which Antoninus places nearer the sea, and a little further inland towards the Vulturnus. That Cornetum is the Castrum Novum I mentioned is so certain that, apart from the evidence of its position in Ptolemy, part of the old name still survives there today. The town stands on a hill, only three miles from the sea, still proud of its ancient walls and many towers. It was the native place of Pope Gregory V and of Robert, its bishop (for the see still keeps the title), who reformed the system of church music and chant.

units.la: Superato Minione, Civitas occurrit Vetus, vulgo Citta Vechia, ubi Castrum Vetus fuit, uti Literæ saxo inscriptæ iussu Pij II. P. M. testantur. Nunc, inquit Leander, Cincellas vocant, pro Centum-Cellis, quæ apud Plinium Iuniorem, Ammianum Marcellinum, P.Rutilium, Antonium, & in Itineraria Tabula. Ponunt etiam Rerum antiquarum Curioli apud Leandrum Civitatem Veterem juxta eum locum, ubi tutissimus Centumcellensis Portus erat; quod modicum omnino inter hunc locum & Urbem Centum-Cellas spatium videtur comprobare. De Centum-Cellis, Portu, Locisque conjacentibus elegantér Plinius Secundus lib.vi, Epist. ad Cornelianum: Evocatus in consilium, inquit, ab Cæsare nostro ad Centum Cellas (hoc Loco nomen) magnam cepi voluptatem. Et paullo post: Villa (locus igitur id temporis nedum Opidi, sed ne Vici quidem nomen videtur absequutus) pulcherrima cingitur viridissimis Agris: imminet Littori, cujus in Sinu Portus, velut Amphitheatrum: Huius sinistrum brachium firmissimo Opere munitum est, dextrum elaboratur. In ora Insula adsurgit, quæ intatum Vento Mare obiacens frangat, tutumque ab utroque latere deursum navibus præstet. Adsurgit autem arte visenda, ingentia Saxa latissima Navis provehit: contra hæc alia super alia detecta ipso pondere manent, ac sensim quodam velut aggere construuntur. Eminet iam & adparet saxeum Dorsum, impactosque Fluctus in immensum elidit & tollit vastus illi fragor canumque circa mare. Saxis deinde Pila adiciuntur, quæ procedente tempore enatam Insulam imitentur. Habebit hic Portus & Nomen Auctoris, eritque vel maxime salutaris. Nam per longissimum spatium Litus impertuosum hoc Receptaculo utetur: Perfectius opus totum canit Rutilius lib.1:
units.tr: Beyond the Minio, one comes to Civitas Vetus, commonly called Citta Vechia, where Castrum Vetus was, as inscriptions carved in stone, set up by order of Pius II, attest. Now, says Leander, they call it Cincellas, for Centum-Cellae, which is named in Pliny the Younger, Ammianus Marcellinus, P. Rutilius, Antoninus, and the Itinerary Table. Antiquarians also place Civitatem Veterem, according to Leander, near the spot where the very safe Centumcellensis Portus was; this seems to prove that the distance between this place and the town of Centum-Cellae was quite small. On Centum-Cellae, its harbour and the places lying around it, Pliny the Younger writes elegantly in Book 6 of his Letters, to Cornelianus: Called into council, he says, by our Caesar to Centum Cellae (that is the name of the place), I took great pleasure. And a little later: The villa (the place at that time seems to have borne the name not even of a town, but not even of a village) is most beautifully surrounded by very green fields. It overlooks the shore, and in its bay is a harbour like an amphitheatre. Its left arm is protected by a very strong work, and the right arm is being built. On the edge rises an island, which, lying against the open sea, breaks the winds and gives ships a safe passage on either side. It rises by an art worth seeing: huge stones are brought by ship, very broad; others are laid above them, and, held in place by their own weight, they are gradually built up as if into a mound.
