Now a rocky ridge rises and shows above the water, and the vast roar of the waves dashing against it, and the white foam around, drives them out to sea. Afterwards piles will be added to the rocks, which, as time goes on, will look like a natural island. This harbour will also have the name of its builder, and it will be especially useful, for along a very long stretch of coast it will provide a refuge from the rough sea. Rutilius sings of the completed work in Book 1:

units.la: Ad Centum-Cellas forti deflexinus Austro, Tranquilla Puppes in Statione sedent. Molibus aquoreum concludit Amphitheatrum, Angustisque aditus Insula fatis tegit. Attollit geminas Turres, bifidoque meatu Faucibus arctatis pandit utrumque latus. Nec p. sinus esse satis laxo Navalia Portu, Ne vaga vel tutas venisset Aura Rates: Interior medias sinus instatus in aedes Insatiabilem fixis aera nescit aquis.
units.tr: Driven by the strong south wind we came to Centum-Cellae, and our ships rest in the harbour. Moles enclose the watery amphitheatre, and an island with its rocks hides the narrow entrance. It raises twin towers, and with a forked passage opens both sides of the narrowed mouth. Nor is the bay large enough for the dockyards in the harbour, lest a wandering breeze reach the safe ships. The inner bay, pressed into the midst of the buildings, with its fixed waters knows no insatiable bronze.

units.la: Centum-Cellas ab Saracenis deletas tempore Ludovici Imperatoris tradit Blondus lib. xii Historiarum. Instauratae postea nomen acceperunt Civitatis, ut dixi, Veteris, quae dein ob Aeris gravitatem pene deserta est. Munitissima hic Arx cernitur. Commemoratur in ea regione ab Strabone Pyrgos, Malaotis Pelasgis Regia, quae an ad Centum-Cellas pertineat, nondum liquet.
units.tr: Blondus, in Book 12 of his Histories, reports that Centum-Cellae was destroyed by the Saracens in the time of Emperor Louis. Later it was restored and took the name of the old town, as I said, which afterwards was nearly deserted because of the unhealthy air. A very strongly fortified citadel can be seen here. In that region Strabo mentions Pyrgos, the royal seat of the Pelasgians of Malaotis; whether it belongs to Centum-Cellae is not yet clear.

units.la: Ab Civitatis Veteris Portu aliisque locis illis vasta fundamenta ruderaque inveniuntur Murorum & Aedificiorum, ubi S. Marinella est: Pyrgos ibi fuisse conjicitur, tam ex Strabonis mensura inter Pyrgos & Graviscas, quod Stadiorum cxxc spatium esse scribit; quam ex cognomine, quod etiamnum hic Aedes Sacra retinet D. Maria Purgani Agri, del Territorio Purgano, vel, ut Castri Veteris Incolae proferunt, Vurgano. Pyrgi, Πύργοι, Straboni, Plinio, Ptolemaeo, Antonino, Itinerariae Tabulae, aliisque noti. Virgilius Pyrgos Veteres nominat. Rutilius lib. i:
units.tr: From the harbour of the old town and other places there, vast foundations and rubble of walls and buildings are found, where S. Marinella is. It is conjectured that Pyrgos was there, both from Strabo's measurement between Pyrgos and Graviscae, which he says is a distance of 120 stadia, and from the name which the sacred building still keeps here: S. Maria of the Purgano territory, or, as the inhabitants of Castrum Vetus pronounce it, Vurgano. Pyrgi (Πύργοι) is known to Strabo, Pliny, Ptolemy, Antoninus, and the Itinerary Table, and others. Virgil calls them the old Pyrgi. Rutilius, Book 1:

units.la: Altia praelegitur tellus, Pyrgique recedunt: Nunc Villae grandes, Oppida parva prius.
units.tr: The land of Alsium is passed, and Pyrgi recedes: now great villas, once small towns.

units.la: Coloniam Romanam facit Livius lib. xxxvi, deductam anno 1212, P. Scipione Nasica & M' Acilio Glabrione Coss.
units.tr: Livy, Book 36, makes it a Roman colony, founded in the year 1212, when P. Scipio Nasica and M'. Acilius Glabrio were consuls.

units.la: Occurrit mox ad Littus Ere Fluvius; haud procul inde fuit Emporium Caeretanorum, ad quod a Pyrgis Stadia xxx erant, ut Strabo scribit; addens exstitisse ibidem Lucinae Templum a Pelasgis conditum, olim opulentissimum, quod Dionysius Siciliae Tyrannus in transferendo spoliavit.
units.tr: Soon the Erus river appears on the shore; not far from there was the trading place of the Caeretans, which, Strabo writes, was thirty stadia from Pyrgi. He adds that there stood a temple of Lucina founded by the Pelasgians, once very rich, which Dionysius, tyrant of Sicily, despoiled when he carried it off.

units.la: Trans Erin Coenobium est S. Severa in Littore, instar Arcis, ubi forte ex Leandri sententia fuit Emporium, quod dixi; vel Turres Antonino nominatae.
units.tr: Across the Erus is the convent of S. Severa on the shore, like a citadel. There, perhaps in Leander's view, was the trading place I mentioned, or the towers named by Antoninus.

units.la: Interius hinc paullo in Colle Care Vetus, Cerveteri vulgo. Καῖρη Straboni; Care Virgilio. Festus auctor est ab hoc Oppido Ritus Sacrorum, Divinoque Cultus omnes, Caerimoniae appellatas; quod iis admodum addicti essent Caeretes. De Caeretanis multa in Historiis Romanis: quod, capta ab Gallis Senonibus Roma, Vestales cum aeterno Igne Sacrisque aliis Romanis profugas hospitio benigne suscepepint; quodque Gallos Senonas cum praeda domum redeuntes fuerint, Praedamque ereptam Romanis restituerint: pro quibus beneficiis Romani non dignam rependisse gratiam notantur, eorum, qui tum praerant, malignitate: Civitate quidem iis donata, sed sine Suffragii Iure: unde & alii, qui eodem cum Civibus Iure non fruebantur, in Caeretes Tabulas referri dicebantur. Videndi Agellius lib. Noct. Atticar. xvi cap. xiii, Asconius Paedianus in Verrinis, & alii. Legendus & Livius lib. i. xxviii, & alibi. S. P. Q. Caeres nominatur in Inscriptione, quae ibidem hodieque exstat:
units.tr: A little further inland, on a hill, lies old Caere, commonly called Cerveteri. Strabo calls it Καῖρη; Virgil calls it Care. Festus tells us that from this town all rites of sacred things and all divine worship were called caerimoniae, because the Caeretans were greatly devoted to them. Much is told of the Caeretans in Roman histories: when Rome was taken by the Gallic Senones, they kindly received the Vestals with the eternal fire and the other Roman sacred objects as fugitives in their hospitality; and when the Senones were returning home with their booty, they took it back and restored the plunder to the Romans. For these kindnesses the Romans are said to have repaid them with no fitting gratitude, through the malice of those who then held power: the town was indeed granted to them, but without the right of suffrage; hence others who did not enjoy the same right as citizens were said to be listed on the Caeretan tablets. See Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights, Book 16, chapter 13, Asconius Pedianus on the Verrines, and others. Livy, Book 1, chapter 28, and elsewhere, should also be read. The inscription which still survives there today names it S. P. Q. Caeres:

units.la: IMP. CAESARI DIVI F. AVGVSTO PONTIF. MAXIM S. P. Q. CAERES
units.tr: To Imperator Caesar Augustus, son of the Divine One, Pontifex Maximus: the Senate and People of Caere

units.la: Ceritum Municipium est in Tabula Marmorea Romae apud Cardinalem Maphaeum:
units.tr: This is the inscription for the municipium of Caere, on a marble tablet in Rome, in the possession of Cardinal Maffei:

units.la: VESBINVS AVG. L. PHETRIVM. AVGVSTALIBVS MVNICIPI. CAERITVM. LOCO ACCEPTO A RE. P SVA. INPENSA. OMNI EXORNATVM. DONVM. DEDIT DESCRIPTVM. ET. RECOGNITVM. FACTVM. IN. PRONAO. ADIS. MARTIS
units.tr: VESBINUS, freedman of Augustus, to Lucius Phetrius, of the Augustales of the municipium of Caere: a site received from the public, at his own expense, a gift fully adorned. Described and checked. Made in the forecourt of the temple of Mars.

units.la: Et quæ alia in eadem Tabula, alta palmos iii-s, lata vi-s, crassa digitos iii, reperta apud Caerites, anno cIↄ Iↄ xlviii. Strabo Caretana Balnea saluberrima, & Martialis Pernam Caretanam, Vinumque Caretanum laudant. Care quondam Agylla quoque nomen habuit ab Conditoribus Pelasgis, uti tradit Plinius lib. iii, cap. v. Urbis Agyllina meminit Virgilius lib. vii. Consulendi & Dionysius Halicarnassæus, lib. i, Trogus lib. xx, & Solinus in Polyhistore: Ἀγύλλα Græcis; Ἀγγύλλα Lycophroni. Quur inde Care dicta, aperiunt Dionysius lib. iii & Strabo lib. v. Inter xiii Etruriæ Capita fuit antiquitus. Splendidam quondam & gloriosam Civitatem, ætate sua vixdum Urbis vestigia retinuisse, ait Strabo; qui probandæ eius Magnificentiæ testatur ævo suo amplissima Agyllinorum Dona in Apollinis Templo adhuc visa. Alii diversam faciunt Agyllam ab Careti admodum exigua Urbis tantæ vestigia superesse scribentes.
units.tr: The same tablet, three and a half palms high, six palms wide and three digits thick, was found at Caerites in the year 1548, and contains other matters as well. Strabo praises the Caretana Balnea as very healthful, and Martial praises the Pernam Caretanam and the Vinumque Caretanum. Caere was once also called Agylla, from its Pelasgian founders, as Pliny relates in book 3, chapter 5. Virgil mentions the Urbis Agyllina in book 7. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 1, Trogus, book 20, and Solinus in the Polyhistor should also be consulted. The Greeks called it Agylla [Ἀγύλλα], Lycophron Aggylla [Ἀγγύλλα]. Dionysius, book 3, and Strabo, book 5, explain why it was called Caere. In antiquity it was one of the thirteen chief cities of Etruria. Strabo says it was once a splendid and glorious city, which in his own day had scarcely kept traces of its former greatness; and to prove its magnificence he attests that the very large gifts of the Agyllinorum were still to be seen in the temple of Apollo in his time. Others make Agylla a different place from Caere, writing that only very small remains of so great a city survive.

units.la: In littore mox ora Fluminum sunt Vacina & Sanguinaria. Ad Posterioris Latus Orientale, paullo interius exiguo in Colle Care est, Cere vulgo, olim Alsium vocatum Latinis, Ciceroni, Livio, Plinio, Itinerariæ Tabulæ, & aliis Ἄλσιον Straboni & Ptolemæo; quod primum Aborigines, deinde Pelasgi, postremo Tyrrheni tenuerunt, ut scribit Halicarnassæus lib. i. Antiquit. Romanarum. Nunc formam exigui Vici potius, quam Oppidi habet. Ab Caretanis Veteribus propinquis putatur evertsum; postea restauratum; dictumque sic simpliciter ad differentiam Veteris. Alsium Colonia vocatur ab Livio lib. xxvii, & Paterculo lib. i. Alsium denominatum ab Aleso Argivo, canit Silius Italicus libro Belli Punici viii: Nec non Argolico dilectum Litus Aleso Alsium.
units.tr: Right on the coast, next, are the mouths of the rivers Vacina and Sanguinaria. On the eastern side of the hill, a little inland, on a small hill, is Care, commonly Cere, once called Alsium by the Latins (Cicero, Livy, Pliny, the Itinerary Tables and others), and by Strabo and Ptolemy Ἄλσιον. The Aborigines first held it, then the Pelasgians, and last the Tyrrhenians, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus writes in book 1 of the Roman Antiquities. Now it has the appearance of a small village rather than a town. It is thought to have been overthrown by the nearby old Caretani, afterwards restored, and so called simply Alsium to distinguish it from the Veteris. Livy in book 27 and Paterculus in book 1 call it the colony of Alsium. Silius Italicus, in book 8 of the Punic War, sings that Alsium was named after the Argive Alesus: "And the shore of Alsium, chosen by the Argive Alesus."

units.la: Alesum Aurigam vel Agamemnonis Filium nominat Virgilius. Alsia Tellus est apud Rutilium: Alsiensis Villa Socrus Plinii Epistolarum lib. vi.
units.tr: Virgil names Alesus as the charioteer or son of Agamemnon. The Alsia Tellus is in Rutilius; the Alsiensis Villa is mentioned in Pliny's Letters, book 6, as the estate of his mother-in-law.

units.la: Hinc in ora Palus est, Palo vernacule; Oppidum, quod olim Fregena Livio; Fregena Silio lib. viii, Plinio, Antonino; Φρεγήνα Straboni lib. v. Colonia Romana est apud Livium lib. xix & xxxvi, Velleiumque Paterculum lib. i.
units.tr: Next, on the coast, is the Palus, called Palo in the vernacular; a town which Livy once called Fregena; Fregena in Silius, book 8, Pliny and Antoninus; Φρεγήνα in Strabo, book 5. It is a Roman colony in Livy, books 19 and 36, and in Velleius Paterculus, book 1.

units.la: Vltra Aronem, poltque Campum & Salinum (Campo & Salino vernacule) Portus est Romanus, Porto di Roma; ab Claudio Cæsare factus, uti in ipsius Vita memorat Suetonius cap. xx. Videndus & Plinius lib. xxxvi. Augusti cognominatur in Itinerario Portuum & Positionum Antonini, & apud Xiphilinum in Severo: Portus Urbis Æthico; Portus Urbis Romæ apud Cassiodorum lib. vii Variar. De eo Portu non pauca legere est apud Dionem lib. lx. quem perfecisse Claudium scribit magnitudine animi, & potentia Romana dignum; quod Loca circum Ostia Tiberis neque tuta Navibus appellendis essent, neque Portus oportunos haberent. Intelligit Rutilius Namatianus in Itinerario lib. i: Pande precor gemino placatum Castore Portum, Temperet æquoream dux Cytherea viam.
units.tr: Beyond the Aronem, and past the Campum and Salinum (Campo and Salino in the vernacular), is the Romanus harbour, Porto di Roma, made by the Emperor Claudius, as Suetonius records in chapter 20 of his Life. Pliny, book 36, should also be consulted. It is called Augusti in the Itinerary of Ports and Positions of Antoninus, and in Xiphilinus in the life of Severus: Portus Urbis Æthico; in Cassiodorus, book 7 of the Variae, Portus Urbis Romæ. Much can be read about this harbour in Dio, book 60, who writes that Claudius built it with a greatness of spirit worthy of Roman power, because the places around the mouth of the Tiber were neither safe for ships to land at nor had suitable harbours. Rutilius Namatianus in his Itinerary, book 1, refers to it: "Open, I pray, the harbour made calm by the twin Castors, and may Cytherea's guidance make the sea-route gentle."

units.la: Longius ab Urbe, quam Ostiam distare, paret ex Antonino. Ibi enim ab Vrbe in Portum quidem xviii M. P. signantur; Ostiam vero usque xvi. Procopius lib. i. Belli Goth. Portum ab Urbe Roma cxxvi Stadia abesse memorat; & decurlum Tiberis ad Portum describit, qui dextro Fluminis Brachio adiungebatur; Vrbem addens eo loco ab Romanis priscis constructam, muroque prævalido munitam, cui ab ipso Portu nomen inditum. Tradit idem Procopius ad lævam ex altera parte, qua in mare Tiberis secundo brachio influit, Urbem Ostiam adjacere, & eam Fluminis ripæ fuisse contiguam. Vrbis, quam ad Portum construxisse notat Procopius priscos Romanos, auctor censetur Optimus Princeps Trajanus; quem in melius Portum restaurasse, atque interius tutiorem sui nominis fecisse, scribit Commentator Vetus in Iuvenalem. Laudat quoque huic rei probandæ Nummum æreum antiquum Abrahamus Ortelius, qui Trajani Imperatoris Effigiem, & in postica parte Portum hunc depictum exhibet, adscribens se eadem forma Portum, etsi ruinis deformatum, aliquando vidisse. Pictura eius etiam aliquo modo est in Itineraria Tabula. Ab Vrbe Portuensi Episcopus nomen habet, unus ex Septem Cardinalibus, qui Pontifici Romano adstitunt. Natus ibi Formosus P. M. nomen retinens Porto dicitur. Insulam modicam hic efficit Tiberis, media ex parte palustrem. Procopius libro 1. de bello Gothico Insulam Sacram appellat. Multa ibi Marmorum frusta, magnæ vastitatis, exstantia partim, partim urticis, virgultis, rubis, vel humo conuecta, numeralibus duplici latere literis inscripta. De ea Insula Æthicus in Cosmographia: Tiberis Insulam facit inter Portum Vrbis (sic legendum, non Portum) & Ostiam Civitatem, ubi Populus Romanus cum Vrbis Præfecto vel Consule, Castorum celebrandorum causa egreditur, solemnitate iucunda. Castorum tunc numen iis locis colebatur, Ventorum Marisque gratia: unde auditus nobis ex Rutilio paullo ante, — gemino placatur Castore Portus.
units.tr: That the Ostiam lies farther from the city than the harbour is clear from Antoninus. For there the Portum is marked at eighteen Roman miles from the city, but Ostiam at only sixteen. Procopius, book 1 of the Gothic War, says the Portum is 126 stadia from the city of Rome, and describes the Tiber's course down to the Portum, which was joined to a right-hand branch of the river. He adds that a city was built there by the ancient Romans and fortified with a very strong wall, and that it was named after the harbour itself. The same Procopius says that on the other side, to the left, where the Tiber flows into the sea by a second branch, the city of Ostia lies adjacent and was next to the bank of the river. The city which Procopius says the ancient Romans built at the harbour is held to have been founded by the best of princes, Trajan; the old commentator on Juvenal writes that Trajan restored the harbour to a better state and made it safer inside, bearing his own name. Abraham Ortelius also cites an ancient bronze coin for this point, which shows the effigy of the Emperor Trajan and on the reverse this harbour depicted; he notes that he himself once saw the harbour in the same form, though deformed by ruins. A picture of it is also in the Itinerary Table in some way. The Bishop of Porto, one of the seven Cardinals who attend the Roman Pontiff, has his title from the city of Porto. Formosus, who was born there, is called Porto, keeping the name P. M. Here the Tiber forms a small island, partly marshy in the middle. Procopius in book 1 of the Gothic War calls it the Insulam Sacram. Many fragments of marble, of great size, stand there partly, partly lie covered with nettles, brambles, bushes or earth, inscribed with numerals on both sides. Concerning this Island, Aethicus in his Cosmography says: The Tiber makes an island between the Harbour of the City (so it should be read, not Portum) and the City of Ostia, where the Roman people go out with the Prefect of the City or the Consul to celebrate the rites of the Castors, a pleasant festival. The Castors were then worshipped as divinities in those places, for the sake of winds and sea; hence the line from Rutilius a little earlier is recalled: "the harbour is made calm by the twin Castors."

units.la: Sic pervenimus ad Tiberim, Limitem Etruriæ Orientalem. Quæ hactenus commemorata sunt à me Loca, plerAque leguntur apud Antoninum Itinere, quod Via Aurelia ab Vrbe ducit per Tuscium & Alpes Maritimas Arelatum usque. Eius Itineris tres sunt Partes: Prima ad Etruriam pertinet; secunda ad Liguriam; tertia ad Provinciam Gallicam. Posteriores suis posuit locis: Prima huius est Stationis. Ea sic habet: conlata cum Itineraria Peutingeri Tabula, quam ex tenebris eduxit Primus in Luminis oras Vir doctissimus Marcus Velserus, II Vir. Rcip. Augustanæ, Plinio, Ptolemaeo, Rutilio Numatiano, & Vulgata Nomenclatura: Antonini Itinerarium | Tabula Peutingeri | Plinius | Ptolemaeus | Rutilius | Vulgata Nomenclatura Roma Lortum, M.P. XII. | Lorio, XII. Villa Lorij alijs. | | | | Quid Nomen nis hodie habeat, ignoratur. Fregenæ. | | | | | Palo. 30
units.tr: So we come to the Tiber, the eastern boundary of Etruria. The places I have mentioned so far are mostly read in the Itinerary of Antoninus, which the Via Aurelia leads from the city through Tuscany and the Maritime Alps as far as Arles. This Itinerary has three parts: the first belongs to Etruria, the second to Liguria, the third to the Gallic Province. The later ones he set in their own places; the first is of this station. It reads as follows, compared with the Peutinger Itinerary Table, which the most learned man Marcus Velserus, duumvir of Augsburg, first brought out of darkness into the light, and with Pliny, Ptolemy, Rutilius Namatianus and the Vulgate nomenclature: Antonine Itinerary | Peutinger Table | Pliny | Ptolemy | Rutilius | Vulgate Nomenclature Rome – Lortum, 12 miles | Lorio, 12 | Villa Lorij (others) | | | What its name is today is unknown. Fregenae | | | | | Palo, 30

units.la: Consonant autem in hunc Numerum Eusebius & Eutropius. Capitolinus cum Antonino & Tabula Itineraria in Via Aurelia ponit, ibique educatum & mortuum scribit Antoninum Pium Imperatorem. Sualoris male legitur apud Iornandem, monente magno Viro Abrahamo Ortelio, pro Villa sua Loria: sic enim diuisim scribendum. ....... | Alsium, VI. | Alsium. | Ἀλσιον. | Alsia. | Ceri, ut vult Leander cū alijs. Ego 40 subdubito. Ad Turres, M.P. X. | | | | | S. Severa. Pyrgos, M.P. XII. | Pyrgos, VI. | Pyrgi. | πύργοι. | Pyrgi. | S. Marinella.
units.tr: Eusebius and Eutropius agree with this number. Capitolinus places it on the Via Aurelia together with Antoninus, and writes that the Emperor Antoninus Pius was brought up and died there. The name Sualoris is wrongly read in Jordanes, as the great man Abraham Ortelius points out, for his villa Loria; it should be written as two separate words. ....... | Alsium, 6 | Alsium | Ἀλσιον | Alsia | Ceri, as Leander and others hold. I myself doubt it at 40. To the Turres, 10 miles | | | | S. Severa. Pyrgos, 12 miles | Pyrgos, 6 | Pyrgi | πύργοι | Pyrgi | S. Marinella.

units.la: Vitiosus vel apud Antoninum, vel in Tabula Velseri censendus est numerus, ut & in seqq. multis. Castrum Nouum, M.P.VIII. | Punicum, VIIII. Castro Nouo, IV. | Castrum Nouum. | Κάστρον Νέον. | Castrum Novum. | Aliud est ab Castro Novo, quod Cornetum hodie. 50 Centum Cellas, M.P.V. | Centum Cellis. Turbata omnia hoc loco. | Centum Cellarum nomè recentius est, quam ut à Plinio recenseri potuisset: quum nec à Ptolemæo | Centum Cella. | Cincellas. Mindo earum fiat men tio. Mindo Fl. Legendum Minio. | | | Magnone fiume. Gravisca, ... | Gravi- fca. | Regio- ngi. | Gravi- fca.
units.tr: The number, whether in Antoninus or in Velserus' table, must be judged faulty, as in many of the following too. Castrum Novum, 8 miles | Punicum, 9 | Castro Novo, 4 | Castrum Novum | Κάστρον Νέον | Castrum Novum. It is different from Castro Novo, which is now Cornetum. Centum Cellas, 5 miles | Centum Cellis. Everything is confused at this point. The name Centum Cellarum is too recent to have been listed by Pliny, since it is not mentioned by Ptolemy either | Centum Cella | Cincellas. Mindo: mention is made of them. Mindo river: read Minio. | | | Magnone river. Gravisca, ... | Gravisca | Regio | Gravisca.

units.la: Ex Itineraria Tabula paret Gravifcas non esse hodie Monte Altum Gravifca enim inter Minium & Martham: Mons Altus magis Occidente versus, inter Martham & Floré. Tabellaria Isco, II. | | | Marta Furvius, II. | | | Marta, Hoc potius Monte Alto. Forte Pescia. Foro Aurelii, III. | | | Armenta Fl. III. | | | Ad Nonas. ....
units.tr: From the Antonine Itinerary it is clear that Gravisca is not today Monte Alto. For Gravisca lies between Minium and Marta, while Mons Altus lies further west, between Marta and Floré. Tabellaria to Isco, II. | | | Marta, Furvius, II. | | | Marta; this should rather be Monte Alto. Perhaps Pescia. Forum Aurelii, III. | | | Armenta River, III. | | | At Nonae....

units.la: Latere mihi videtur in his Tabulae Itinerariae vocibus Nomen Asedonia; nisi quis velit recentius esse, quam ut eius mihi fieri possit mentio. Cofsa, VIII. | Cossa vel Ascozi. | Cossa, | Dirura ad Lacum Salsum. Hercules Pertus, | Porto Hercole. Atens Argentatus. | Monte Argentato. Albinia, III | | | Allegna fiume.
units.tr: The name Asedonia seems to be hidden in these words of the Itinerary Table, unless someone wishes it to be too recent for me to mention it. Cossa, VIII. | Cossa or Ascozi. | Cossa. | Dirura at the Salt Lake. Hercules Pertus; Porto Ercole. Atens Argentatus; Monte Argentato. Albinia, III. | | | Allegna River.

units.la: Almina Antonino in Itinerario Maritimo. Telamone, VIII. | Portus Telamon. | Τέλαμων. | Telamone. Hasta. ... | Umbro fl. XII | Umbro fl. Prille Amnis. | Umbro. | Ombrone: Prille. Ad Lacum Aprilem, M. P. XII. | | | Salebronem, Saleborna, IX | | | Sequutus Itinerū & Antonini & Tabulae Filum, fere est, ut putem vel Furianum, vel Columnā esse ad Occidentalem Lacus Prillis ripam. Hoc certum, falli Volaterranum, qui putat Ligurnum Portum olim Salebronem appellatū. Salebrone enim inter Prillem est Lacum & Populonium Promontorium: Portus autem Ligurnus inter idem Promontorium & Arnum Fluvium. Erat vehementer Surita ad Antoninum; qui pro Salebrone legendum putat ad Umbronem. Nam si ab Urbe versus Pisas, id est ab Oriente ad Occidentem, cum Antonino progrediamur, Umbro Lacui Prilli est Orientalis; qui Occidentalis eidem futurus, si Emendationem illam admittamus. Deinde in Itineraria Tabula Umbro & Salebrone duo diversa sunt Loca.
units.tr: Almina, according to the Maritime Itinerary of Antoninus. Telamone, VIII. | Port Telamon. | Τέλαμων. | Telamone. Hasta.... Umbro River, XII. | Umbro River. Prille, a river. | Umbro. | Ombrone; Prille. To the Lake Aprilis, XII Roman miles. | | | Salebro, Saleborna, IX. | | | Following the thread of both the Itinerary of Antoninus and the Table, I think it is almost certain that it is either Furianum or Columna on the western bank of Lake Prille. This is certain: Volaterranus is wrong when he thinks that the port of Ligurnus was formerly called Salebro. For Salebro lies between the Lake Prille and the Promontory of Populonium, whereas the Port of Ligurnus lies between the same promontory and the River Arno. Surita is very vehement against Antoninus, who thinks that Umbro should be read for Salebro. For if we proceed with Antoninus from Rome towards Pisa, that is from east to west, the Umbro is east of Lake Prille, and it would be west of it if we admitted that emendation. Moreover, in the Itinerary Table, Umbro and Salebro are two different places.

units.la: Sic enim Rutilius Claudius Numatianus Itinerarij libro 1: Inde Triturita petimus, sic Villa vocatur Qua latet expulsis Insula pene Fretis. Pisas, M. P. XII. | Pisis. | Pisa. | Pisa. | Pisa.
units.tr: For so Rutilius Claudius Namatianus, in book I of his Itinerary: Thence we make for Triturita; so the villa is called, which lies hidden almost an island where the seas have been driven out. Pisae, XII Roman miles. | Pisis. | Pisa. | Pisa. | Pisa.

units.la: Vide & aliud Iter apud eumdem Antoninum, quod ab Roma tendit per Portum Centum-Cellas. Non absimile Superiori est apud eumdem Itinerarium Portuum vel Positionum Navium ab Vrbe Arelatum usque. Eius itidem tres sunt Portiones; Prima spectans Etruriam, Secunda Liguriam, Tertia trans Alpes Provinciam Gallicam. Postrema jam suum habuit locum libro huius Partis III, cap. xxxix; Secunda suum habitura hoc libro, cap. xxxix; Prima huc pertinet, sic se habens commissa cum Itineraria Tabula: Antonini Itiner. | Itineraria Tabula | Vulgata Nomencl. A Portu Augusti Pyrgos. Posit. M.P. XXXVIII. | A Portu Augusti Alsium, VIII. | Ceri. A Pyrgis Panapionem. Posit. M.P. III. | Pyrgos, VI. | S. Marinella. Punicum, VIII | Mansio incognita.
units.tr: See also another route in the same Antoninus, which runs from Rome through the port of Centum Cellae. The Itinerary of Ports or Positions of Ships from the City as far as Arelate, by the same author, is not unlike the foregoing. It too has three parts: the first concerning Etruria, the second Liguria, the third the Gallic Province beyond the Alps. The last has already had its place in this book of Part III, chapter 39; the second will have its place in this book, chapter 39. The first belongs here, and, set side by side with the Itinerary Table, reads thus: Antoninus' Itinerary | Itinerary Table | Common name. From the Port of Augustus to Pyrgi. Position, XXXVIII Roman miles. | From the Port of Augustus to Alsium, VIII. | Ceri. From Pyrgi to Panapion. Position, III Roman miles. | Pyrgos, VI. | S. Marinella. Punicum, VIII. | Unknown station.

units.la: Alter ex altero videtur hoc loco emendandus. Anio forte an Pomponio Mela. A Panapione Castrum Novum. Posit. M.P.VII. | Castro Novo, III. | A Castro Novo Centum-Cellas. Posit. M.P.V. | Centum-Cellis, .... | Cincellae. A Centum-Cellis Algas Posit. M.P.III. | Mindo fl. ... | Mognone fiume. Ab Algis Rapinium. Posit. M.P.III. Ab Rapinio Gravisce. Posit. M.P.VI. | Gravisca. .... A Gravisce Maltanum. Posit. M.P.III. | Tabellaria Vico, II | Marta Flumen hic succedit in Itineraria Tabula. | Marta fiume. A Maltano Quintianum. Posit. M.P.III. | ....... | Periit. Foro Aurelii. IV | Netcio an Monte Alto. A Quintiano Regas. Posit. M.P.VI. An Ἀγρίου Strabonis lib. v? A Regis Arnine fluvius habet | Armenita fl. .... | Pescia fl. forte. Posit.
units.tr: One of these seems to need correcting by the other at this point. Anio, perhaps, or Pomponius Mela. From Panapion to Castrum Novum. Position, VII Roman miles. | Castro Novo, III. | From Castrum Novum to Centum Cellae. Position, V Roman miles. | Centum Cellis.... | Cincellae. From Centum Cellae to Algae. Position, III Roman miles. | ....... | Lost. Forum Aurelii, IV. | Netcio, or Monte Alto. From Quintianum to Regae. Position, VI Roman miles. Or the Agrios of Strabo, book V? From Regae the Arnine river has its source. | Armenita River.... | Pescia River, perhaps. Position.

units.tr: Another route, the maritime Tuscan one.

units.tr: From Arnine to the Port of Hercules, XXV Roman miles. Port of Hercules, ....... XX. Porto Ercole. A place near Monte Argentario or the Salt Lake.

units.tr: From Domitianus, the river Almina has its source. Position, IX Roman miles. Albinia river, IV. Alagna River.

units.tr: From Scabris to Falesia, a port. XVIII Roman miles. ......... Somewhere near the Forest of Vetulonia.

units.la: Haec de Maritima & Exteriore perlustrandam se jamnunc offert Tuscia Interior & Mediterranea, quae, quod montosior, plus habitura in expeditione difficultatis. Ab Macra Limite Occidentalior Principium etto.
units.tr: These matters concerning the Maritime and Outer Tuscany are now offered for us to survey through Inner and Mediterranean Tuscany, which, being more mountainous, will have more difficulty in the journey. From the boundary of the Macra, the starting point lies further west.

units.la: Quarto ab Ottio Macrae Milliari Fortum ripa Orientalior. Oppidum est Sarzana, propter interitum Lunae conditum, ut ante ex Incolarum sententia memini. Illustravit Sarzanam Nicolaus V. P. M. Sedis Lunensis Episcopatus eo translat... Non procul hinc in alto Colle Sarzanellum, quod tanquam Sarzanae Arx, ab Castruccio Lucensium Principe primum aedificatum, Petrus Fregosus Genuensium Dux egregie munivit.
units.tr: Four miles from the Ottio, at the Macra milestone, on the eastern bank of the Fortum, lies the town of Sarzana, founded on the ruin of Luna, as I recalled earlier from the opinion of the inhabitants. Nicholas V, Supreme Pontiff, adorned Sarzana, transferring there the bishopric of the See of Luni.... Not far from here, on a high hill, lies Sarzanello, which, as the citadel of Sarzana, was first built by Castruccio, prince of the Lucchesi, and was splendidly fortified by Peter Fregoso, Doge of the Genoese.

units.la: Progredi facto Septentrionem versus, occurrunt oppida, quae vulgo S. Stefano, Tendae, Caprio, Luna, ad Fluvium cognominem, ubi Tegulam fuisse quidam volunt, Castagnio, Fornaco, tamquam Lunam Novam; Villa Franca; Vagnano Castellum, Fluvio nominis eiusdem adiacet: Filaterra, Melgra, Gragnola; & haud procul inde Castellum, quod vulgo cognominatum di Ponte Remuli, iuxta Macrae fontem. Hic ... Ligures ab Livio lib. x detexerit, ubi sempronium notat Pisas in Apuanos Ligures, vallando Vicos & Castella eorum, aperuisse Saltum usque ad Macram Flumen & Lunae Portum. Facit eorum mentionem idem Livius Libro XXXIX. Henricus Imperator anno 1 ... ex quo Cives transitum ipsi Romam cunti negaverant. Dum in Ditione sunt Ducum Mediolanensium.
units.tr: Proceeding northward, there come towns which are commonly called San Stefano, Tendae, Caprio, Luna, on the river of the same name, where some think Tegula once was; Castagnio, Fornaco, as New Luna; Villafranca; Vagnano, a castle lying by the river of the same name; Filaterra, Melgra, Gragnola; and not far from there a castle commonly called di Ponte Remuli, beside the source of the Macra. Here... Livy in book X has described the Ligurians, where he notes that Sempronius, having taken Pisa, opened a passage as far as the Macra river and the Port of Luna against the Apuan Ligurians, by fortifying their villages and castles. The same Livy makes mention of them in book XXXIX. The Emperor Henry in the year 1... after the citizens had denied him passage to Rome. While they are in the domain of the Dukes of Milan.

units.la: Ad Littus recurro. In conspectum hic se dant tertio ab ora lapide in colle Colle Orto Nuovo, Nicolai Castrum Nuovo; Fossa Nuova, quo loco Ποσειδών Παλαιόπολις Proelemaei fuisse putatur Volaterrano. Inde trans Lautum, inter montes Scirei ultraque Fiezano, Castrum, e Fossa, Ferrabia, altumque Cusiglano.
units.tr: I return to the coast. Here there appear, at the third milestone from the shore, on the hill Colle Orto Nuovo, Nicolai Castrum Nuovo; Fossa Nuova, in which place Poseidon Palaeopolis, the Proelemaeum, is thought by Volaterranus to have been. From there, across the Lautus, between the mountains of Scirei and beyond Fiezano, lies Castrum, from Fossa, Ferrabia, and high Cusiglano.

units.la: Denuo tum ab ora introrsum ad Montes vertus Massa, deinde Carrara, et irrea Phnio libro naturalis Historiae iii. cap. v, cum & Potentia dicitur. Succedit Montone, & altius aliquot quaedam Castella in Montibus edit Ilamsque vulgo La Montagnada Carrara & de Lunigiana. Marmorum Lapidis celeberrimum.
units.tr: Again, turning inland from the shore towards the mountains, lies Massa, then Carrara, and further on, as Pliny says in book III of the Natural History, chapter 5, where it is also called Potentia. Next comes Montone, and some castles set higher in the mountains, which are commonly called La Montagnada of Carrara and of Lunigiana. Very famous for its marble stone.

units.la: Transito Amne, cuius apud Arcem Motrones est ostium, in Orientali ripa intus Pietra Sancta opidum est nobile; quo loco censetur fuisse Αὐξ-Ῥεβόληα, Lunae Ieronia, Strabo, Ptolemaeus, Plinio nominatus: Lucoferonia in Libro de Limitibus. Sunt hae iterum ibi ...ulteriora in hoc aevo multa Antiquitatis Vestigia. Vicinus in Montibus Camaiore, quasi Capi Maior, & Libra fatta. Aperit se mox Lalla ... fluvius ultra utraque Flumen, Vicus multus & Castellis nitens. Altus est ... Castellum Nortum. Cognomina tum, Negotiatoribus frequens, cum alijs plurimis hunc tra-ctus, qui vrbem Bononiensium quondam, nunc in Ferrariæ Ducatu tenet. Ceterum inde est Lucensis, Alexandria Trenetania sepulta: quæ Loca maiore ex parte Malaspinæ Principes tenent.
units.tr: After crossing the river, at whose mouth near the citadel of Motrone lies, on the eastern bank inland, the noble town of Pietrasanta; in this place is thought to have been Auxe-Rhebolena, named by Strabo and Ptolemy as Luna's Ieronia, and by Pliny; Lucoferonia in the book On Boundaries. Here again there are... many further vestiges of antiquity in this age. Nearby in the mountains is Camaiore, as if Capi Maior, and Libra fatta. Soon Lalla opens out... a river beyond both streams, a populous village and bright with castles. There is high... the castle Nortum. Its names are then frequent with merchants, together with very many others in this district, which once held the city of the Bolognese and now lies in the Duchy of Ferrara. Moreover, from there is Lucca, where Alexandria Trenetania lies buried; these places for the most part are held by the Malaspina princes.

units.la: Trans Aufrem est Luca:
units.tr: Across the Auser lies Lucca.

units.la: Tuto in Deorum, Tutis latet inclusa Celi,
units.tr: Safe in the protection of the gods, enclosed in the secure sky,

units.la: inquit de ea Lilius Scaliger. Luca Latinus Græcique scriptores nominant Livio, Paterculo, Suetonio, Festo, Antonino, Itinerarij Tabulæ alias Strabone & Ptolemæo. Nomen retinet, litteris omnibus. Dicunt aut quidam volunt ab Scenis mauratis, quæ lumine collocata Urbs Turribus splendore Solis illustrata vel lucebant: vel, ut nomen ipsi videtur, ab Luce quodam nigra: vel, metaphorice ab Annio Viterbiensi Cato, ab Lusitano Lucemone. Alij alunde trahunt. Non hæc veritantur ovesque Ioannes. Vrbs Templis & Æ-dificijs ornata Pulchra, frequens, pulcherrimæ lanæ, Collibus undique circumdata. Lucus Lucce Lucarum nominant Strabo lib. v. Vrbs ἀπὸ τῆς ἀγρολῆς ... Lucca. Moenibus est trimetrica, quadrato strata litore, spatio parvo, sed Civibus arta & Negotiis nomini plena. Templum Primarium S. Cruci dicatum. Crux ibi aurea à Rep. Pisana Lucensibus oblata, redemptaque nunquam. Valere fertur xv milibus aur Coronat. Ibi monachi cum habent ibi Franciscani non contemnendam. Incolæ lauti sunt, prudentes, ingeniosi quoque Libertatem diu sapientissime conservarunt integram. Hoc Eminentiorum belli hand raro petiti. Livius lib. xxi Hannibalem in Ligures Scarpe Romanorum Pugnam Lucam eodem tempore concessisse memoriæ prodit. Senior Frontinus in Strategematibus T. Dominitium Calvinum Legatum Iguribus eldenfile, non solum natura loci & operibus, sed & valido Militum præsidio munitam. Coloniam eo deductam anno ab V. C. 1o LXXVII legimus apud eundem Livium lib. xl1. Paterculum lib. 1, Plinium lib. iii. cap. v. Festus Municipium (sive loca) vocat. Tradit Flavius lib. x 1 Historiarum, ab Gothis postea Nardetem Lunaschum tex mentibus oppugnatam, ante quam capere posset. Quos ab eo tempore Dominos Principesque in Carrarienses Cesarinos, Phasiolos, Catharios, Spinolos, Robertos, Scaligeros, Florentinos, Pisanos, Cranzi, quos habuerit, pluribus memorat Leander Albertus. Libertate recuperata iamnunc tranquillissime. Bene Pontanus lib. 1. Histor. Luccensium, inquit, Civitas non tam suis Consiliis liberas, quam aliena opibus atque Præsidio prima: dum Florentinorum ne accedat opibus, magna cura est ceteris. Tribunaria Imperatori Oligarchia administratur. Creantur aliquot Viri, quorum Dominatus biennis. Præfectus Urbi de Pænis Supplicijque decernunt: sed Iudicium est penes cxx Viros, sine quorum, vel maxima pars, auctoritas Capitis nemo damnatur. Episcopali gaudet dignitate. Inter Præsules leguntur Diverum adscripti numero Fratrum Ioannis & Ioannes. Multos quoque præclaros Viros; inter eos Lucam iii. P. M. Alij alios Pontifices addunt. Ioannes Hilario ... Lucam ortu suo nobilitavit Sanctus Paginus, Vir Lingvarum Orientalium peritissimus. Antoninus iter Lucæ ducit Ico-nam per viam Clodiam, per M P. cxxxvii. Idem alio loco ab Luca Pisas mm erat M.P. xiii Lunam, M.P. xxxiii Faventiam, M.P. cxx, Parmam M.P. c. Infra Lucam mare versus Templum erat Herculis amplissimum, quod circa tam describit Ptolemæus, hodieque obscurus quibusdam Volterranus rudens.
units.tr: Lilius Scaliger says of it. The Latin and Greek writers call it Luca: Livy, Paterculus, Suetonius, Festus, Antoninus, the Itinerary tables, and otherwise Strabo and Ptolemy. It keeps the name in all its letters. Some say, or wish to say, that it is named from the gilded stages (scenis mauratis) whose towers, set in the light, shone and were lit up by the splendour of the sun; or, as the name itself seems to suggest, from a certain black grove (luco); or, figuratively, from Annius of Viterbo's Cato, or from the Lusitanian Lucemo. Others derive it from elsewhere. John does not dispute these things. The city is adorned with temples and buildings, beautiful, populous, of the finest wool, and surrounded on every side by hills. Strabo in book 5 calls the grove of Lucca "Lucus Lucarum." The city is, from its walls, triangular (trimetrica), paved with square stone, small in extent but crowded with citizens and full of business. The principal temple is dedicated to the Holy Cross. There is a golden cross there, offered to the Lucchesi by the Republic of Pisa and never redeemed; it is said to be worth fifteen thousand gold crowns. There are monks there, and the Franciscans there are no mean body. The inhabitants are well-to-do, prudent and clever, and they have kept their liberty whole for a long time with great wisdom. Because of this, it was not rarely sought by the more powerful in war. Livy in book 21 records that Hannibal, at the same time, withdrew into Liguria from the Roman army and came to Luca. The elder Frontinus, in the Stratagems, says that Titus Dominitius Calvinus, legate, [took] the Ligurians, fortified not only by the nature of the place and its works but also by a strong garrison of soldiers. We read that a colony was led there in the year 577 from the founding of the city, in the same Livy, book 41; Paterculus, book 1; Pliny, book 3, chapter 5. Festus calls it a municipium (or a place). Flavius, in book 11 of the Histories, relates that it was later attacked by the Goths, with Nardes of Lunasco and the tents, before he could take it. Leander Albertus records at greater length the lords and princes it had from that time onward: the Carrara family, the Cesarini, the Fasioli, the Cattari, the Spinola, the Roberti, the Scaligeri, the Florentines, the Pisans, and the Cranzi. Now, with liberty recovered, it is most tranquil. Pontanus well says in book 1 of the History of the Lucchesi: the city of Luca, he says, is first not so much free by its own counsels as by the resources and protection of others, while the others take great care that the resources of the Florentines do not grow. It is governed by an oligarchy under the emperor's tribunes. Several men are created, whose rule lasts two years. A prefect of the city decides on penalties and punishments, but judgment lies with the hundred and twenty men, without whose authority, or that of the greater part of them, no one is condemned to death. It enjoys episcopal dignity. Among the bishops are read Diverus, counted among the brothers John and John. Many distinguished men also, among them Lucas III, P.M. Others add other pontiffs. Sanctus Paginus, a man most skilled in the Oriental languages, ennobled Lucca by his birth; John Hilario [likewise]. Antoninus gives the route from Luca to Ico-na by the Clodian way, 137 miles. The same writer, elsewhere, gives from Luca to Pisa 13 miles, to Luna 33 miles, to Faenza 120 miles, to Parma 100 miles. Below Lucca, toward the sea, there was a very large temple of Hercules, which Ptolemy describes in that region; it is still obscure to some, [and] rustic Volterra.

units.la: Luca versus Orientem Palus est Fresiana, in hanc hæc comacent Montes Colis, Alto Pelio, Pesita, Foveta, Phæsanos Pelasgos huic Conditores tribuunt nomen ... Pisaq, Pisana, Lucensis, Pisana.
units.tr: To the east of Lucca is the Fresian marsh, into which these hills of Colis, Alto Pelio, Pesita and Foveta descend; the Pelasgians of Phaesana are credited with founding the name... Pisa, Pisana, Lucensis, Pisana.

units.la: Ultra Pisam pulchra est Planities, in qua mixta Verbanus & Stellenus fluvios est Pisorum: sic Plinio & Antonino dictum; quod necessaria Ptolemæo, hodie Pisana. Pisanis vitiose scribitur in Itineraria Tabula ... Civitates & opidas Dictam alij volunt a Pisis, quæ Pisæ quas Cantiliæ, in agro Pisano, qua Florentinum spectat, describit ... Comme... apud quosdam Urbs nomen Vortex Graeci dicit ... quod hac in terminus, Clavisque & velut Claustrum Gallio Cisalpinæ. Mœnibus cincta ... plurimum legitur ab Desiderio Langobardorum Rege; idem post nudata ... Ilelle ... complanatis, ... Agro inter Florentinos & Lucenses diviso: Tandem Florentini totam suæ subjecerunt Ditioni, anno ab Christo nato cıɔ ccı, ut memoriæ prodit Leonardus Aretinus. Denique Civilibus Factionibus primo quidem Alborum & Nigrorum, deinde Cancellariorum & Panzaticorum adeo est labefactata, ut deserta nunc & Colonis destitura videatur: unde & Malegna quibusdam vocitata, Factionum, ut universim dicam, parens, Vindictæ cupidissima, atque, ut Hostem persequatur, Honoris, Opum, Vitæ prodiga. Arcem habet satis munitam. In Templo S. Iacobi Ara visitur argenteis Laminis & deauratis tecta: cum eiusdem Metalli Lampadibus xx. In Templo Humilitatis integræ cernuntur Effigies Leonis x & Clementis vii PP. MNI. Cosmi item & Alexandri Florentiæ Ducum. Viros eximios genuit non paucos: inter alios Sezomenum, & Cynum Dini Discipulum, Bartoli Præceptorem, qui in Summo Templo marmoreo conditur Sepulcro. Haud procul Pistorio Via Bononiensi magnifica cernitur Domus, quæ vulgo Igno, ab Antonio Pucio Cardinale, quum Pistoriensium esset Præsul, ædificata. Vallis ad hanc Vrbem, qua Florentiam itur, lata est, amœna, omni Fructuum genere abundans: Oppida, Pagos, Villas, Casas, Palatiaque in universum habens quadraginta quatuor millia: Sinui Bajano non absimilis.
units.tr: Beyond Pisa is a beautiful plain, in which the rivers Verbanus and Stellenus, mixed together, are the rivers of the Pisans; so called by Pliny and Antoninus, though Ptolemy has them differently, and today [it is] Pisana. In the Itinerary table it is wrongly written Pisanis... Some want the cities and towns to be named from Pisae, which Cantilia (in the Pisan territory) describes on the side facing Florence... Among some the city is called by the Greek name Vortex... because it lies at this boundary, and is as it were the key and barrier of Cisalpine Gaul. Surrounded by walls, it is read of most often under King Desiderius of the Lombards; afterwards, the same [city] was stripped and its... levelled, the land being divided between the Florentines and the Lucchesi. At last the Florentines subjected the whole of it to their rule, in the year of Christ 1406, as Leonardo Aretino records. Finally, by civil factions, first those of the Albi and the Neri, then those of the Cancellieri and the Panzatici, it has been so shaken that it now seems deserted and destitute of colonists; whence it is also called Malegna by some, the parent of factions, to speak generally, most eager for revenge, and, in order to pursue an enemy, lavish of honour, wealth and life. It has a citadel sufficiently fortified. In the church of St James an altar is seen, covered with silver and gilded plates, along with twenty lamps of the same metal. In the church of Humility there are to be seen the effigies of Leo X and Clement VII, popes, likewise of Cosimo and Alessandro, dukes of Florence. It produced not a few eminent men; among others Sezomenus, and Cino, pupil of Dino, teacher of Bartolo, who is buried in a marble tomb in the principal church. Not far from Pistoia, on the magnificent Bolognese road, there is a house commonly called Igno, built by Cardinal Antonio Pucci, when he was bishop of the Pistoiese. The valley leading to this city, by which one goes to Florence, is broad and pleasant, abounding in every kind of produce, and has in all forty-four thousand towns, villages, farms, houses and palaces; not unlike the Bay of Baiae.

units.la: Confinalia sunt Pistorio circumcirca Summano; Seravalle; Vitulino: Monte Catino, Opidum Victoria Vgottonis Phaseoli de Florentinis celebre; Monte Aterlo, Opidum ad Collem, Bartholemæi Valoris, Philippi Strozæ, multorumque Florentinorum Exsulum captura, ductu operaque Alexandri Vitellij, Cosmi Medicis Florentiæ Ducis Legati, inclutum; Prato denique, quod Amnis ex Apennino Bisentius adluit, Arni Incola. Imperatorem Fridericum ii condidisse scribit Collenutius lib. iiii. Histor. Neapolit. Censetur propter elegantiam & amplitudinem inter Castra quatuor Italiæ totius splendidissima Proverbio, quod ita habet: Larletta in Puglia; Fabriano nella Marca; Crema in Lombardia, & Prato in Toscana. De Clade Pratensi Ego in meo Synchronismo ad Annum cıɔ ıɔ xıı. Ditionis est Florentinorum. Clarum quoque Pratum cum aliis, tum Nicolao Cardinale, de quo multa Antoninus Archiepiscopus; & Arloto Scriptis illustri.
units.tr: Bordering Pistoia all around are Summano, Seravalle, Vitulino; Monte Catino, a town famous for the victory of Ugottone Fasioli over the Florentines; Monte Aterlo, a town on a hill, renowned for the capture of Bartolomeo Valori, Filippo Strozzi and many Florentine exiles, under the leadership and work of Alessandro Vitelli, legate of Cosimo de' Medici, duke of Florence; and finally Prato, which the river Bisenzio, from the Apennines, washes, a tributary of the Arno. Collenuccio, in book 4 of the Neapolitan History, writes that the emperor Frederick II founded it. On account of its elegance and size it is counted among the most splendid castles of all Italy, in the proverb which goes: Larletta in Puglia; Fabriano nella Marca; Crema in Lombardia, & Prato in Toscana. I have written about the defeat at Prato in my Synchronism for the year 1512. It belongs to the Florentines. Prato is also famous for, among others, Cardinal Niccolò, about whom Antoninus, archbishop, writes much; and for the writer Arlotto.

units.la: Ab Arno, cuius sæpe memini, percurrente secatur Florentia, Etruriæ caput & Metropolis. Sic Plinio lib. xiiii, cap. ii, Antonino non uno loco, Itinerariæ Tabulæ, (ubi cognominatur Tuscorum) xtaticque mediæ aliis, & omnibus nostræ Scriptoribus; Φλωρεντία Ptolemæo, Agathiæ lib. 1, & Procopio de bello Gothico libro iii, Φλωρέντια Suidæ dicitur: quam Fluentiam, ut nonnulli censent, vocat Florus, ubi de Bello Mariano: Fluentinorum ad Arnum tacientem mentionem Plinio lib. iii. cap. v. Florentinam Coloniam nominat Sex. Iulius Frontinus; & Florentinos inter Romanorum Colonias agnoscit Tacitus lib. 1 his verbis: Audiitaque, inquit, Municipiorum Coloniarumque Legationes, orantibus Florentinis, ne Clanis solito alveo demotus in amnem Arnum transferretur, idque ipsis perniciem adferret. Hodie vulgo Florenza, vel, ut alij pronunciant, Firenza. Mentio eius frequens in Inscriptionibus: duas adponam, quarum una in Palatio visitur hortoque Cardinalis Cæsij, in Vaticano, in Cippis oblongis è Tiburtino,
units.tr: Florence, the capital and metropolis of Etruria, is divided by the Arno, which I have often mentioned, as it flows through. So Pliny in book 14, chapter 2; Antoninus in more than one place; the Itinerary table (where it is named of the Tuscans); and Ptolemy in the middle; and all our writers. Ptolemy and Agathias, book 1, and Procopius, On the Gothic War, book 3, call it Φλωρεντία; Suidas says Φλωρέντια. Florus, where he speaks of the Marian war, calls it Fluentia, as some think: Fluentinorum, making mention of it on the Arno; Pliny, book 3, chapter 5. Sextus Julius Frontinus calls it Florentina Colonia; and Tacitus, book 1, recognises Florentinos among the Roman colonies, in these words: And he heard, he says, the embassies of the municipalities and colonies, the Florentines entreating that the Clanis, diverted from its usual channel, should not be turned into the Arno, and that this would bring ruin upon them. Today it is commonly called Florenza, or, as others pronounce it, Firenza. Its mention is frequent in inscriptions. I will add two, one of which is seen in the palace and garden of Cardinal Cesi, in the Vatican, on oblong cippi of Tiburtine stone,

units.la: Q. GARGENNIVS L. F. SCA CELER FLORENTIA. MIL COH. XI. PR VIX. A. XXV MILIT. A. V H. S. E
units.tr: Quintus Gargennius, son of Lucius, of the Sca tribe, Celer of Florence, soldier of the eleventh cohort, principal; lived 25 years, served 5 years. Here he lies.

units.la: altera Neapoli exstat, post S. Paulum, littera pulcra; atque adeo recenti, ut vix videatur antiqua: Mmm · C. CIS.
units.tr: the other is extant at Naples, after St Paul, in a fine letter, and so recent that it hardly seems ancient: Gaius Cispius, son of Gaius, of the Scaptian tribe, Severus of Florence, soldier of the third cohort, principal, lived 43 years, served 17 years.

units.la: C. CISPIVS. C. F. SCAPT. SEVERVS FLORENTIA MIL. COH. III PR. VIX. ANN. XLIII MILITAVIT. ANN. XVII.
units.tr: Gaius Cispius Severus, son of Gaius, of the Scaptian tribe, of Florence, soldier of the Third Praetorian Cohort; he lived forty-three years and served seventeen years.

units.la: Florentia nomen id habere putatur vel ab Flore, cui ob Felicitatem Florentemque Fortunam similis; vel ob florida ex cellentiaque Incolarum ingenia; vel denique (quæ mens est Politiano lib. 1. Epist. 11) quod ab Roma deducta esset omnium Vrbium fl. entissima. Si non vera hæc Etyma, certe Rebus Florentinæ rum prætentibus sunt convenientissima. Facius Vbertus lib. iii. Cant. vii Parentem eius fuit nescio quem Florinum. Initium illi ducunt Leonardus Aretinus principio Historiæ Florentinæ ab Romanis Sullæ Dictatoris Militibus; Volaterranus lib. v. ab Colonis, qui Trium-Virorum auspicijs co deducti; Laurentius Valla ab Fesulanis, commodiorem, relictis jugis, habitandi locum ad Arnum quærentibus: Annius Viterbiensis Catonis sui verbis innixus, ad Ianum Florentia primordium refert. Hos omnes conciliare conatur Leander Albertus. Ambitum habens sex millium, supra nonaginta millia continens Incolarum, æquali loco jacet ad Arnum; quo, ut jam monui, intersecatur, quatuor eximijs coniuncta Pontibus, Silice quadrato strata, latis ornata Platcis. Collibus cincta est Theatri instar ab Oriente & Septemtrione amœnissimus, quæque undique fructiferis vestiti Arboribus; qua Occidens est pulcram habet Planiciem: Cœli regione inter Aretium & Pisam media mistaque; quarum Vrbium prior acutissima fert ingenia, altera homines memoria valentes singulares. Munit eam contra Vim externam Hostiumque incursiones brachiis aliquot suis Apenninus. Geminos habuisse Muros tradit Christophorus Landinus suis in Dantem Commentationibus. Antiquos, quatuorque eorum Portas Majores, totidemque Minores fideli digito indicat Leander Albertus; ex Vberto, Leonardo Aretino, Christophoro Landino, Politiano & alijs; quo modo & quando antiqua Vrbis facies perierit, tenuissimeque præsentem induerit, adscribens. Splendore & elegantia summa est: ut voce incertoque Vulgi sermone feratur, Fiorenza la bella, totiusque Flos Italiæ. Locis, quæ divino Cultui sacrata, niter quam plurimis. Admirabile est Templum D. Maria Florida magnificentissimum: & inter tria Etruriæ nominatum totum ex Marmore albi, nigri, rufique coloris constat, cum Hemisphærio stupendi operis, quod ab Philippo Brunalitio Florentino singulari arte factum. Iuxta stat Turris eximia, tota marmorea. Modico post intervallo veterrimum Martij Templum, forma sexangulari magno ingenio constructum, & nunc D. Ioannis Baptistæ sacrum: ubi Lacus ex Marmore conspicuus, in quo Infantes baptizate lavantur. Situs est in hac Ædes Baltasar Cossa, quondam P. M. nomine Ioannis xxiii, decretoque Concilij Constantiensis Pontificatu abdicare iussus. Apud Portam, quæ est e regione Maioris Ecclesiæ, binæ cernuntur Columnæ Porphyreticæ; quas Pisani Florentinis, parta de Sarracenis victoria, honoris causa miserunt. Nobilia item sunt Fana D. Maria Novella, quod dedicatum ab Eugenio iv, anno cIↄ ccccxxvi Martij xxv; S. Spiritus; Fratrum Minorum; D. Laurenty, ubi situs est Cosmus Medices, suspensaque vi suntur cxxx Vexilla, Petro Strozzo in Prælio apud Senas olim commissio, erepta; & Annunciata, multis dotatum Privilegijs. Hic Insignia varia & Donaria ex Auro, Argento, Cera, Pannis; adeo ut ipsum complent. In Ambitu Cadavera quædam sunt exsiccata. Alia, ne tædium pariam, præterero. Inter Xenodochia, quæ xxxvii dicuntur numero, primi facile loci, quod D. Maria Nova. Parochiæ cententurxliv; Prioratus xii; Conventus Virorum Mulierumque Sacri lxxvi; Collegia Puerorum, quas Fraternitates vocant, ix; Virorum Sodalitates maximo numero. Ædificijs insuper nobilissimis, cum publicis, tum privatis est perornata. Palatia sunt infinita: inter illa Curia Senatus, amplissima Domus Medicea, Cosmi Opus; Strozzarum & Pitorum Ædes; Campi octo, S Crucis, S. Mariæ, S. Laurenty, Della Signoria, Del Prato, S Maria Novella, Mercato Vecchio, Mercato Nuovo. Suburbia quondam habuit non ignobilia: sed anno cIↄ Iↄ xxix deleta: Villas autem & nunc Suburbicarias habet innumeras; easque magnificentissimas; cum Structura & regio sumtu, tum Hortis, summam oculis delectationem, quod Myrto, Lauro, Rosa, aliisque, & opere Topiario decorati, praebentibus. Arx ibi duplex: Vetus, quae Urbem subtus despicit: Piscis cuiusdam Ossa continens mirae magnitudinis: Nova grandioris spacii, Fontibus, Molendinis, Turri, Propugnaculis, Tormentis, Annona, Rebusque aliis ad defensionem necessariis instructa. Auctores loquitur Inscriptio, quae ad Portam talis:
units.tr: Florentia is thought to have its name either from Flora, to whom it is similar in its happy and flourishing fortune; or from the floridness and excellence of its inhabitants' talents; or finally (which is the view of Politian, book 1, letter 11) because it was founded from Rome and was the most flourishing of all cities. If these etymologies are not true, they at least agree very well with the circumstances of the Florentines. Facio Uberti, in book 3 of the Cantica, c. 7, says that its parent was some Florinus or other. Leonardo Aretino, at the beginning of his Florentine History, traces its origin to Roman soldiers of Sulla the dictator; Volaterranus, book 5, to colonists sent there under the authority of the triumvirs; Lorenzo Valla to the people of Fiesole, who, leaving the heights, sought a more convenient place to live by the Arno; and Annius of Viterbo, relying on the words of his Cato, refers the beginning of Florentia to Janus. Leander Albertus tries to reconcile all of these. The city has a circuit of six miles and contains more than ninety thousand inhabitants. It lies on level ground beside the Arno, by which, as I have already said, it is divided, and is joined by four fine bridges, paved with square stone and adorned with broad squares. It is surrounded by hills, like a theatre, on the east and north, most pleasant and everywhere clothed with fruit-bearing trees; on the west it has a beautiful plain. It lies in a climate midway between Arezzo and Pisa, and mixes the qualities of both: of these two cities the former produces very sharp minds, the latter men of outstanding memory. The Apennines, with several of their arms, protect it against external force and the incursions of enemies. Christophorus Landinus, in his commentaries on Dante, reports that it once had two walls. Leander Albertus faithfully points out the old walls and the four major gates, and as many minor ones, drawing on Uberti, Leonardo Aretino, Christophorus Landinus, Politian and others, and he records how and when the ancient appearance of the city perished and took on its present, very slight, form. It is of the highest splendour and elegance, so that in the vague and common speech of the people it is said: Fiorenza la bella, the flower of all Italy. Among the places dedicated to divine worship there are very many. The church of Santa Maria del Fiore is most magnificent and admirable; it is named among the three of Etruria, is built entirely of white, black and red marble, and has a dome of stupendous workmanship, made with singular skill by Filippo Brunelleschi of Florence. Next to it stands an outstanding tower, wholly of marble. A short distance away is the very ancient temple of Mars, built in a hexagonal form with great ingenuity, and now sacred to St John the Baptist; there is a conspicuous marble font in which infants are washed when baptized. In this church lies Baldassare Cossa, once supreme pontiff under the name of John XXIII, who was ordered by the decree of the Council of Constance to resign the pontificate. Near the gate which faces the greater church there are two porphyry columns, which the Pisans sent to the Florentines as a mark of honour, after their victory over the Saracens. Also noteworthy are the churches of Santa Maria Novella, which was dedicated by Eugenius IV on 25 March 1436; of the Holy Spirit; of the Friars Minor; of San Lorenzo, where Cosimo de' Medici is buried; and of the Annunziata, endowed with many privileges. Here there are various insignia and gifts of gold, silver, wax and cloth, so many that they fill the place. In the cloister some corpses are preserved dried. I pass over others, so as not to weary the reader. Among the hospices, which are said to number thirty-seven, the first place is easily held by Santa Maria Nuova. There are forty-four parishes, twelve priories, seventy-six communities of religious men and women, nine colleges of boys, which they call confraternities, and very many associations of men. The city is also adorned with most noble buildings, both public and private. There are countless palaces: among them the Senate House, the very large Medici house, the work of Cosimo; and the houses of the Strozzi and the Pitti. There are eight squares: San Croce, Santa Maria, San Lorenzo, della Signoria, del Prato, Santa Maria Novella, the Old Market and the New Market. The city once had suburbs that were not unimportant, but these were destroyed in the year 1529. It now has countless country villas in the suburbs, and these are very magnificent, both in their construction and royal expense, and in their gardens, which give the eyes the greatest delight, being adorned with myrtle, laurel, roses and other plants and with topiary work. There is a double citadel there: the Old, which looks down on the city from below, and which contains the bones of a fish of remarkable size; and the New, of greater extent, equipped with fountains, mills, a tower, bulwarks, artillery, provisions and other things necessary for defence. The inscription at the gate, which reads as follows, tells who the builders were:

units.la: Quod faustum felixque sit, Carolus V. Rom. Imp. Victor ex Africa rediens, quum Alexandrum Medices Florentinorum Ducem, Generum suum, exstructa jam reliqua Arce, Turris huius Fundamenta locantem reperisset, primum victrici Manu Lapidem ponere non dedignatus est MDXXXX.
units.tr: May it be fortunate and happy. Charles V, Roman Emperor, returning victorious from Africa, when he found Alessandro de' Medici, Duke of the Florentines, his son-in-law, laying the foundations of this tower, the citadel having already been completed, did not disdain to lay the first stone with his victorious hand. 1540.

units.la: In Foro Novo Porticus est, Columnis xx sustentata, undique permeabilis; Cosmi Medicis Florentiae Ducis II opus, anno MDXLVIII exstructum. Prope Aedem D. Marci Equile est Ducis, vulgo L'Eyrrie in quo aluntur hodie Leones: Tygrides subflavi coloris, maculis nigris; Leopardi; Ursi; Boves Numidi. Incolae acuti, graves, facundi, bonarum artium studiosi; quibusque laus propria, quod Latinis litteris ab interitu vindicandis operae non parum contulerint. Pecuniae sunt studiosiores, cuius conquirendae desiderio in ultimis etiam terris negociantur. Mulieres forma pudicitiaque praestantes, earumque, ut & Virorum, Vestitus supra modum egregius & decorus. Nobili gente perpetuo frequentem, multaque honestas Familias hinc, tamquam ex uberrimo Fonte, in alias Italiae Urbes fuisse derivatas docet Christophorus Landinus, quem antea laudavi. Humanitate Etruscos omnes Florentini superant: quemadmodum & Sermonis elegantia. Quam varie periculosequae saepe jactata, quamque perniciosissimis nunc Alborum & Nigrorum, nunc Guelphorum & Gibellinorum Factionibus fuerit exagitata, docent plene Leonardus Aretinus, Antoninus Archiepiscopus, Nicolaus Machiavellus, & alij. Urbes Agrosque multos imperio subegit, Pisatorum, Aretium, Cortonam, Volaterras, Pisam, Portum Ligurinum, Bibienam, Agrum Clusentinum, Montem Politianum, aliaque plurima Tusciae Romanulaeque Opida. Anno MCXXII Incendium Florentiae duo millia Civium absumsit. Anno MCCCC Pestis ibidem triginta hominum millia e medio sustulit. Quum ab Gothis olim magnis cladibus fuisset adfecta, Karolus Magnus Imperator restauravit, mirumque in modum amplificatae binos creavit Consules annali imperio, addito Centum Patrum Senatu: postea anno MCCXX, ut Volaterranus numerat, vel, ut Blondus, MCCLIV, Decem-Viri sunt creati, qui Antiani dicebantur. Libertate post anno MCCXCVII ab Imperatore Rudolpho tenis aureorum nummum millibus, ut auctor est Platina in Vita Honorij IV, redemta, venturn est ad Octo-Viros, qui vulgo Priori dell' Arti audiebant, cum Praside Iustitiae uno bimestri, qui Confaloniere di Giustizia nominabatur. Qua Reip. forma aliquoties conversa atque immutata, tandem auctoritate Karoli V Caesaris Medicees Vibis Dominatus cessit.
units.tr: In the New Forum there is a portico, supported by twenty columns and open on every side, the work of Cosimo I de' Medici, Duke of Florence, built in the year 1548. Near the church of St Mark there is the Duke's menagerie, commonly called L'Eyrrie, in which lions are kept today, as well as tigers of a yellowish colour with black spots, leopards, bears and Numidian oxen. The inhabitants are sharp, serious, eloquent, and devoted to the liberal arts; their particular praise is that they have contributed not a little to rescuing Latin literature from destruction. They are keener on money, and in their desire to acquire it they do business even in the most distant lands. The women are outstanding for beauty and modesty, and their clothing, like that of the men, is unusually elegant and tasteful. Christophorus Landinus, whom I praised earlier, teaches that the city has always been crowded with noble families, and that many respectable families have been drawn from it, as from a most fertile spring, into other cities of Italy. The Florentines surpass all the Tuscans in courtesy, as well as in elegance of speech. How often the city has been tossed about in various and dangerous ways, and how it has been harassed by the most destructive factions, first of the Whites and Blacks, then of the Guelfs and Ghibellines, is fully described by Leonardo Aretino, Antoninus, the archbishop, Niccolò Machiavelli, and others. It subdued many cities and territories under its rule: Pistoia, Arezzo, Cortona, Volterra, Pisa, Porto Pisano, Bibbiena, the territory of Chiusi, Montepulciano, and very many other towns of Tuscany and of Romagna. In the year 1122 a fire in Florence consumed two thousand citizens. In the year 1400 the plague there carried off thirty thousand people. When it had once been struck by great disasters at the hands of the Goths, the Emperor Charles the Great restored it, and, greatly enlarged, it appointed two consuls with annual authority, with the addition of a Senate of one hundred elders. Later, in the year 1220, as Volterranus counts it, or, as Biondo has it, 1254, ten men were created, who were called the Antiani. After the liberty was bought back for a hundred thousand gold coins from the Emperor Rudolf, in the year 1297, as Platina reports in the life of Honorius IV, the government passed to eight men, who were commonly called the Priori dell'Arti, together with a single president of justice for two months, who was called the Gonfaloniere di Giustizia. This form of commonwealth was changed and altered several times, and at last, by the authority of Charles V Caesar, the rule of the Medici over the city came to an end.

units.tr: I read the following pedigree. Giovanni, son of Averardo, Captain of Justice. He died on the 10th day before the Kalends of March, 1478. His wife Picarda, daughter of Adorardo, died five years after her husband, on the 13th day before the Kalends of May. She is buried at St Lawrence, where her epitaph was set up by her sons Cosimo and Lorenzo. Cosimo de' Medici laid the first foundations of the splendour of the Medici family, and was named Father of his Country by public decree. He ruled his fellow citizens most happily while still wearing the toga, and was the great patron of scholars. He died in 1464, having lived 75 years, 2 months and 20 days. Fortune was so lavish to him that he was judged the richest and most fortunate man of his age. Lorenzo de' Medici, citizen of Florence. Piero de' Medici, a worthy emulator of his father, was raised to the helm of government, but conducted himself more as a private citizen than as a prince; he died in 1472. Piero de' Medici of Florence. Lorenzo de' Medici the Magnificent, prince of Florence, governed the republic together with his brother, by the arts of his father and grandfather; he died in 1492. Giuliano de' Medici, almost equal to his brother Lorenzo, younger by birth, was acclaimed prince of the young by the favour of the people. He was stabbed by the Pazzi in 1478. Lorenzo de' Medici, driven into exile together with his brother by Piero the prince. Giovanni de' Medici, in exile, became the most bitter enemy of Duke Piero, and against him and his homeland he followed the French party. He died in 1504. Piero de' Medici, prince of Florence, having degenerated from his father's diligence, was driven into exile and drowned at the mouth of the Liri in 1503. Giovanni de' Medici, cardinal, was raised to the Supreme Pontificate and took the name Leo X. Giuliano de' Medici, surnamed the Magnificent, died in exile in 1516. Giulio de' Medici, a posthumous son born of a concubine, was raised to the Supreme Pontificate and took the name Clement VII. He died in 1535. Ippolito, the illegitimate cardinal, exchanged life for death in 1541. Giovanni de' Medici, named Lodovico at the baptismal font, an outstanding duke and a vigorous warrior, departed this life in 1526. Cosimo de' Medici, an eighteen-year-old youth, was chosen by forty-eight men to succeed Alessandro, the agnate, in the principate of Florence, and governed the republic well and wisely. Pius V, the Supreme Pontiff, because he had supplied a great sum of money and other things needed for subduing rebels, created him Grand Duke of Tuscany, instead of Duke of Florence, on 26 August 1569; the pontiffs had these words inscribed on his crown by command: "Pius V, Supreme Pontiff, gave this on account of his exceptional affection, his zeal for the Catholic religion and his especial care for justice." He died in 1574. Cosimo de' Medici, put to death on account of his wandering lusts and adulteries. Lorenzo de' Medici, expelled together with his father, was made prince of Urbino by his uncle Leo X, and paid the debt of nature in 1519. Caterina de' Medici, wife of Henry II, King of the French, died on 5 January 1589. Alessandro de' Medici, a bastard, was restored by his father-in-law Charles V, after exile, and having assumed the title of prince, was stabbed in adultery in 1537.

Huic Principi inter alios liberos fuit Maria, quae nupta Christianissimo Galliarum Regi, Henrico IV. Ferdinandus Medices, Cardinalis depositopost Fratris morte Gallero, Magnus Dux Etruriae III. Lucretia Medices, Uxor Iordani Ursini, Ducis Bactianensis.
units.tr: Dukes of Florence. Francesco de' Medici, second Grand Duke of Etruria, was snatched away by death on 9 October 1587 (seventh day before the Ides of October, 1586). His wives were Joanna of Austria, daughter of Charles V, who died in 1578, and Bianca Cappello of Venice, who survived her husband by barely five hours. Among his other children this prince had Maria, who married Henry IV, the Most Christian King of France. Ferdinando de' Medici, cardinal, laid aside the purple after his brother's death and became the third Grand Duke of Etruria. He married Christina, daughter of Charles, Duke of Lorraine, on the first day of May 1589. Pietro de' Medici married a Medici, wife of Alfonso, Duke of Ferrara, and the daughter of the Duke of Baganti, Lucia. Lucrezia de' Medici, wife of Giordano Orsini, Duke of Bracciano.

units.la: Archiepiscopatus fulget hæc Vrbs dignitate: cui subsunt Netesinus, Castellanensis, Montis Falconis, Fiterbiensis, Castellanus, Valaterranus, Fesulanus, Zazanensis vel Lunensis, Sutri, Ortanensis, Cornetanensis, Tuscanensis, Anagninus, Ricentinensis, Pistoriensis, Binensis, Cortonensis, Balneoregensis, Frecentanus, Castrensis, Perusinus, Lucanus.
units.tr: This city is adorned with the dignity of an archbishopric, and under it are the sees of Nepi, Castellana, Montefalco, Viterbo, Castello, Volterra, Fiesole, Sarzana or Luni, Sutri, Orte, Corneto, Tuscania, Anagni, Rieti, Pistoia, Bina, Cortona, Bagnoregio, Ferentino, Castro, Perugia and Lucca.

units.la: Concilium Florentinum celebratum fuit sub Eugenio IV P. M. maxima Praesulum cum Latinorum, cum Graecorum Ecclesiarum, undique concurrentium, frequentia; praesente etiam Ioanne Palaeologo Imperatore cum Patriarcha. Testantur partim Diplomata, quod Graecis Latinisque litteris exaratum, manuque Pontificis & aliorum subscriptum, additis & Eugenii plumbeo, & Imperatoris aureo Sigillo in Bononiae Archivo publico servatur: partim Epigraphe, quae ad D. Matiae Novellae posita, his verbis:
units.tr: The Council of Florence was held under Pope Eugenius IV, with a very large gathering of prelates of the Latin Churches and of the Greek Churches, who came together from every side; the Emperor John Palaeologus was also present, with the Patriarch. Part of the evidence is a diploma, written in Greek and Latin letters and signed by the hand of the Pontiff and of others, with the lead seal of Eugenius and the golden seal of the Emperor added, which is preserved in the public archive at Bologna. Part of it is an inscription placed at Santa Maria Novella, with these words:

units.la: Generali Concilio Florentino celebrato post longas Disputationes Vnio Graecorum facta est in hac ipsa Ecclesia, die VI. Iulij, MCCCCXXXI, Praesidente eodem Concilio Eugenio P P. IIII. cum Latinis Episcopis, & Prælatis; & Imperatore Constantinopolitano cum Episcopis, Prælatis & Proceribus Graecorum, in copiosissimo numero; sublatisque Erroribus in unam eamdemque Fidem rectam, quam Romana tenet Ecclesia, consenserunt.
units.tr: At the general Council of Florence, after long disputations, the union of the Greeks was made in this very church on 6 July 1431, the Council being presided over by Pope Eugenius IV with the Latin bishops and prelates, and the Emperor of Constantinople with the bishops, prelates and nobles of the Greeks, in very great numbers; and, with errors removed, they agreed on one and the same right faith, which the Roman Church holds.

units.la: Florentiae Ignis Supplicio affectus est Hieronymus Savonarola, Theologus, anno MCCCCXCVIII. Mai XXII. Consequuti sunt Iesuitae amplissimum in hac Urbe Collegium anno MDLXI. Academiam habet Florentia apud omnes Europae Populos celebratissimam. Fundamenta eius iecit Cosmus Medices, Pater Patriae appellatus. Auxit magno studio, praeclaris Avi sui vestigiis insistens. Laurentius Magnus, Princeps Florentinus, quo Duce Hemerum in Italiam venisse, scribit Epistola ad ipsum Marsilius Ficinus: ab eodem cum Ioanne Argyropulo, Demetrio Chalcondyla, Pico, Angelo Politiano, aliisque doctissimis Viris, Florentiam evocatus. Bibliothecae in Urbe Florentina sunt tres. Prima S. Laurentii, quae Medicea appellatur, ab Clemente VII Medice, P. M. DD; adhuc inexplicata: Multi in ea Auctores, praesertim Graeci, qui excusi non sunt. Secunda S. Marci, Laurentii Medicis & Nicolai de Nicolis liberalitate & testamento instructa & aucta, Latinis, Graecis, Hebraeis, Armenicisque Libris superbiens: Aliquot ibi Theologorum Graecorum Opera nondum typis mandata. Debentur ei cum aliis multis Clementis Alexandrini Scripta. Tertia S. Benedicti, Libros Latinos habens optimos, adjuncta et Graeca, sed exigua. Quarta S. Crucis ab Sebastiano de Bacellis coepta in Litteris politioribus, tota Latina, praeclara sane. Quinta in domo Episcopi, Latinorum item Auctorum. Sexta denique Mariae Novellae, tota Latina. Pandectae Iuris Civilis, in Membranis emendatissime Latinis Litteris scripti, adservantur religiosissime in Palatio, quod habitat Magnus Dux Etruriæ; Pilis Florentinum cum reliqua præda translati. Græca Epistola bene longa illis est prefixa, Vetustate pene obliterata. Pandectas hos ab Antiquitate mirifice prædicant Angelus Politianus, Petrus Victorius, Antonius Augustinus & alij. Ad Libri Calcem legitur: Ego Marsilius Ficinus interfui, dum hoc reperiretur Opus; idque manu propria scripsi, 1x Aprilis anno Domini MCCCCLXXVI, Petro Bernhardo Bernhardis sedente Vexillifero Iustitiæ. Ab ipso Archetypo plura Præclarorum ope in orbem Christianum diffusa sunt: ante annos aliquot Exemplaria: in quibus quotquot hodie Litteræ, Syllabæ, Verba Maioribus Typis leguntur expressa, non ipsi Autographo, sed Laelij Taurelli diligentiæ debentur: æque accepta sunt ferenda. Æqualibus enim & paribus Litteris totum illud Pandectarum Libri sunt conscripti. Virorum insignium multorum genitrix fuit, estque hodie Florentia. Dedit inter alios Divorum numero adscriptos Iannem Gualbertum, Sodalitatis Vallis Umbrosæ Conditorem; Fernardum Vmbertum, Antoninum Archiepiscopum, Scriptorem non tenuendum: Produxit & ævo nostro Florentia Leonem x & Clementem vii Pontifices Maximos. Cardinales habuit plurimos: Albertum Alberti, Alemannum Adimarium, Franciscum Sederinum, Laurentium Puccium, Nicolaum Pandulphinum, Andream Fuiensem, Febertum & Antonium Puccios eiusdem Laurentij Fratrem & Nepotem, Nicolaum Audoenum, Hippolytum Medicæum, Iohannem Salviatum, Nicolaum Rudolphum & Nicolaum Caddum. Archiepiscopos, Episcopos, Abbates, aliosque Prælatos, quos Florentia genuit, longum esset referre: Celebriores in eorum numero fuerunt Angelus Arcievolus, Antistes Parmæ: Simon Saltarellus, Orivetus; Alexandrinus Cancellarius, Archiepiscopus Pisanus. Nati quoque hic Viri Eruditione Scriptisque clari, Aloysius Marsilius, Philosophus; Bartholomæus Lapacius, Theologus; Leonardus Statius; Robertus Fasius, Dominus Garbinus, Theodoricus Turrianus, Ianetus Manetus; Leo Alertus & Paulus Mathematici; Dantes Aligerus, Poëta. Egregie quoque Solum hoc suum Natale decorarunt Guido Catanus Cantes; Colutius Salutatus; Leonardus Datus; Donatus Acciaiolus, qui Vitas Hannibalis & Demetrij ex Plutarcho Latinas fecit, Commentariaque rebus in Aristotelis Ethica; Matthæus Palmerius, qui Supplementum Temporum Eusebio addidit, Libris etiam de Civili Vita quatuor conscriptis; Lapus Castiglionius, qui Vitas aliquot Plutarchi in Latinum Sermonem vertit; Nicolaus Nitolinus; Pallas Strozza; Angelus Accicvolus; Andreas Fuccius; Christophorus Landinus, qui Danos Comœdias Virgiliumque illustravit; Lucius Vibertus, Geographus & Poëta, Dictamundi Auctor; Ioannes Carolus, qui Clarorum Ordinis Prædicatorum Virorum Vitas condidit; Marsilius Ficinus, qui Platonem fecit Latinum; Adamannus Rinuccinus, qui Philostratum de Vita Apollonij Tyanei in Latinam vertit Linguam: Petrus Crinitus, Librorum de Honesta Voluptate Pateris; Bartholomæus Scala; Zenobius Acciaiolus, qui Iustinum Martyrem & alios Latine dedit; Lippus Rainaldus; Leonardus Nicolaus; Nicolaus Machiavellus. Longissime extra Italiam Florentiæ nomen extulit Americus Vespucius, Cosmographus, qui inventæ Quartæ Terrarum Orbis Partis nomen ab Se imposuit America. Florentinus fuit & Acciaiolus. Rupendus Iuris Cæsarei Enarrator, qui li Meliorum Litterarum cognitionem habuit, Miraculum profecto dubio fuisse: Naturæ: Filium habuit ille Franciscum, IC. etiam eximium. Concentiendus his aliisque Laurentius Rudolphus, qui Tractatum de Iure scripsit. Pictores insignes, quorum princeps fuit Iotus, Artis Reductor, defunctus anno MCCCXXXVI, & ad B. Mariæ Novellæ sitas, silentio præterreo. Neque commemorabo cum alios Artifices, tum qui Opticæ Arte Patriam suam nobilitarunt. Non denique irrarebo recentiendis iis, qui vel Externa rexerunt Imperia, vel Virtute Militari fuerunt admirabiles. Florentiam porro describunt lusque delineant coloribus, præter Leonardum Albertum, qui amplissime, Iovius Pontanus libro Historiarum i, Æneas Silvius de Rebus gestis Friderici iii, Natalis Comes lib. Histor. xxix. Flavius Blondus, & alij. Scriptaque in eamdem Variorum Elogia versibus scripta, Iulij Cæsaris Scaligeri, Petri Angelij Bargæi, Georgij Fabricij, Nathanis Chytræi, Nicolai Reuineri, & quorum non? Meretur enim omnium omnino Ingeniorum Laudes & Encomia Vrbs Florentinissima.
units.tr: At Florence, Girolamo Savonarola, a theologian, was put to death by fire on 23 May 1498. The Jesuits obtained a very large college in this city in 1561. Florence has an academy most celebrated among all the peoples of Europe.
