Cosimo de' Medici, called Father of his Country, laid its foundations, and he enlarged it with great zeal, following the excellent footsteps of his grandfather. Lorenzo the Magnificent, prince of Florence, under whose leadership, Marsilio Ficino writes in a letter to him, Hemerus came into Italy; he summoned him to Florence, together with Giovanni Argiropulo, Demetrio Calcondila, Pico, Angelo Poliziano and other most learned men. There are three libraries in the city of Florence. The first, of St Lawrence, which is called the Medicean, was dedicated by Pope Clement VII of the Medici; it is still unexplored, and contains many authors, especially Greek ones, which have not been printed. The second, of St Mark, was furnished and enlarged by the generosity and will of Lorenzo de' Medici and Niccolò de' Nicoli, and boasts of books in Latin, Greek, Hebrew and Armenian; there are some works of Greek theologians there not yet committed to print. To it, along with many others, belong the writings of Clement of Alexandria. The third, of St Benedict, has very good Latin books, with a few Greek ones, though few in number. The fourth, of Holy Cross, begun by Sebastiano de' Bacelli, is wholly in Latin and of more polished literature, and is truly distinguished. The fifth is in the bishop's house, likewise of Latin authors. Finally, the sixth, of Santa Maria Novella, is wholly Latin. The Pandects of Civil Law, written most accurately on parchment in Latin letters, are kept with the greatest care in the palace where the Grand Duke of Etruria resides; they were carried from Pisa to Florence with the rest of the spoils. A fairly long Greek letter is prefixed to them, almost obliterated by age. Angelo Poliziano, Pietro Vettori, Antonio Agustín and others extol these Pandects wonderfully for their antiquity. At the end of the book is read: "I, Marsilio Ficino, was present while this work was being found, and I wrote it with my own hand, on 9 April in the year of the Lord 1476, Pietro Bernardo de' Bernardi being standard-bearer of justice." Many copies have been spread throughout the Christian world from the original itself, through the help of distinguished men, some years ago; in these copies, whatever letters, syllables and words are read today printed in larger type, are owed not to the autograph itself but to the diligence of Lelio Torelli; they are to be accepted equally. For the whole of those books of the Pandects were written in letters that are uniform and equal. Florence has been, and is today, the mother of many outstanding men. Among others counted in the number of the saints it gave John Gualbert, founder of the Vallombrosan congregation; Ferdinand Umberto (?), and Antoninus, archbishop, an author not to be despised. In our own age Florence has also produced Popes Leo X and Clement VII. It had very many cardinals: Alberto Alberti, Alemanno Adimari, Francesco Soderini, Lorenzo Pucci, Niccolò Pandolfini, Andrea Fuiense, Feberto and Antonio Pucci, brother and nephew of the same Lorenzo, Niccolò Audoeno, Ippolito de' Medici, Giovanni Salviati, Niccolò Rodolfi and Niccolò Caddi. It would be long to list the archbishops, bishops, abbots and other prelates whom Florence has produced; the more notable among them were Angelo Arcivolo, bishop of Parma; Simone Saltarelli of Orvieto; Alessandro Cancelliere, archbishop of Pisa. Men born here and famous for learning and writings were also Luigi Marsili, philosopher; Bartolomeo Lapaccio, theologian; Leonardo Stazio; Roberto Fasi, Signor Garbino, Teodorico Turriani, Gianetto Manetti; Leo Alberti and Paolo, mathematicians; Dante Alighieri, poet. Florence's own children have also nobly adorned their native city: Guido Cattani, Cante; Coluccio Salutati; Leonardo Bruni; Donato Acciaiuoli, who made Latin lives of Hannibal and Demetrius from Plutarch, and commentaries on Aristotle's Ethics; Matteo Palmieri, who added a supplement of years to Eusebius, and also wrote four books on civic life; Lapo da Castiglionchio, who translated some lives of Plutarch into Latin; Niccolò Niccoli; Palla Strozzi; Angelo Ambrogini; Andrea Fucci; Cristoforo Landino, who illustrated Dante's comedies and Virgil; Lucio Vibio, geographer and poet, author of the Dittamondo; Giovanni Carlo, who composed the lives of illustrious men of the Order of Preachers; Marsilio Ficino, who made Plato Latin; Adamanno Rinuccini, who translated Philostratus's Life of Apollonius of Tyana into Latin; Pietro Crinito, author of the books On Honest Pleasure; Bartolomeo Scala; Zanobi Acciaiuoli, who gave Justin Martyr and others in Latin; Lippo Rinaldi; Leonardo Niccoli; Niccolò Machiavelli. Florence's name was carried far beyond Italy by Amerigo Vespucci, the cosmographer, who gave his own name, America, to the fourth part of the globe which he discovered. Acciaiuoli was also a Florentine, an expounder of Imperial law, who had knowledge of the better literature, a miracle of nature beyond doubt. He had a son, Francesco, also an outstanding jurist. Along with these and others should be counted Lorenzo Rodolfi, who wrote a treatise on law. I pass over in silence the famous painters, of whom the chief was Giotto, the restorer of the art, who died in 1336, and those at Santa Maria Novella. Nor shall I mention the other craftsmen, or those who made their homeland famous in the art of optics. Finally, I shall not hesitate to enumerate those who either governed foreign empires or were admirable for military valour. Moreover, Leonardo Bruni describes Florence and portrays her with lively colours in great detail; so too do Giovio, Pontano in the first book of his Histories, Aeneas Silvius in his deeds of Frederick III, Natale Conti in book twenty-nine of his Histories, Flavio Biondo and others. There are also various eulogies of the city written in verse by Julius Caesar Scaliger, Pierre Angiers du Bargès, Georg Fabricius, Nathan Chytraeus, Nicolas Reusner, and whom not? For the most splendid city of Florence deserves praise and commendation from every kind of talent.

units.la: Extra Florentiam haud procul in Apennini Colle Vestigia cernuntur Urbis Fesularum. Fesula Sallustio in Catilinaria Conjuratione, Livio lib.xxxii, Plinio lib.nat. hist. iii, cap.v, Antonino, & aliis Latinis Scriptoribus; Φαισόλαι Polybio lib.ii, Appiano lib. ii, Ptolemaeo; Fesula Silio Italico lib.viii de Bello Punico: quae hodie Fiesole. Nomen impositum Urbi volunt Volaterranus & Angelus Politianus ab Hyadum Atlantis Filiarum, & Bacchi Nutricum, una: Annius Viterbiensis, suo more arguens, ab Phefo & Fias Aramaeis Vocibus, quarum illam Transfensum, hanc autem Paludem significare notat. In Conditore variatur. Quibusdam est Iasus Dardani Frater; Facio Vberto & Politiano, Atlas. Erat in aprico & amoeno Colle, Fontibus exi-mijs, ut Vbertus, quem dixi, canit, abundante. Petrus Marsus ad Silium scribit olim hic Augures & Vates Etruscorum habitasse, Suffragantorem habens Politianum in quadam ad Petrum Medicem Epistola, lectu digna. Innuit haud obscure Silius Italicus loco, quem indicavi:
units.tr: Outside Florence, not far off on a hill of the Apennines, the remains of the city of Fesulae can be seen. Sallust in the Catilinarian Conspiracy, Livy book 32, Pliny Natural History book 3 chapter 5, Antoninus and other Latin writers call it Fesula; Polybius book 2, Appian book 2 and Ptolemy call it Phaisolai [Φαισόλαι]; Silius Italicus in book 8 of the Punic War calls it Fesula. Today it is Fiesole. Volaterranus and Angelo Poliziano think the city took its name from the Hyades, the daughters of Atlas and nurses of Bacchus, together. Annius of Viterbo, arguing in his usual way, derives it from the Aramaic words Phefo and Fias, of which he says the first means "crossing" and the second "marsh." The founder is disputed. For some it was Iasus, brother of Dardanus; Fazio Uberti and Poliziano name Atlas. It stood on a sunny, pleasant hill abounding in excellent springs, as Uberti, whom I mentioned, sings. Petrus Marsus, writing on Silius, says that the augurs and seers of the Etruscans once lived here, and he has Poliziano as a supporter in a certain letter to Piero de' Medici, which is worth reading. Silius Italicus clearly hints at this in the line I have cited:

units.la: Sacris Interpres Fulminis alis Fesula.
units.tr: Fesula, interpreter of the sacred rites of the lightning's wings.

units.la: Quo modo anno cIↄ xxv penerit, scribunt praeter Blondum Nicolaus Machiavellus lib. ii. & Sabellicus lib. ii. Ennead. cap. ii. Aedificia omnino pauca supersuNT: Tam potens olim, ut Stilicone, Romani Nominis Ducem, Gothus, quorum Rex erat Radagaisus, caedendis praecipue juverit. Eorum hic supra centum millia cruciata leguntur; reliqui pessime habiti. Collem, in quo fuit Urbs, Villae cum Hortis Florentinorum Civium haud ignobiles occupant: Templaque & Coenobia non pauca: in quis sumptuosissima est Abbatia, ut vocant, Fesulana, Cosmi Medicis opus. Nomen Fesularum locus adhuc cum Episcopatu servat. Passim ibi mirabilis Locorum amoenitas & ornatus. Pontanus & Joannes Cajus natam putant ex Fesularum ruinis Florentiam.
units.tr: That it was destroyed in the year 1125 is recorded by Biondo, and besides him by Niccolò Machiavelli, book 2, and by Sabellico, book 2 of the Enneads, chapter 2. Hardly any buildings survive. The city was once so powerful that the Goths, whose king was Radagaisus, were chiefly responsible for destroying Stilicho, the commander of the Roman name. Of them, more than a hundred thousand are said to have been crucified; the rest were treated very badly. Villas with gardens belonging to not unimportant Florentine citizens occupy the hill on which the city stood, as do not a few churches and monasteries. Among them the most sumptuous is the so-called Abbey of Fesulae, a work of Cosimo de' Medici. The place still keeps the name Fesulae together with a bishopric. Everywhere there is a wonderful loveliness and beauty of the place. Pontano and Giovanni Cai think Florence was born from the ruins of Fesulae.

units.la: Haud procul inde inter Colles Fesularum & ipsius Apennini luga Vallis conspicitur amoenissima, tota Villis Vicisque nobilibus nitens, Mugello vernacule: Coloniaque ejus Mugellani. Origo huic Ceno Mugellano, celebri turri contulto. Vallem hanc Sera medium perertit. Mugellana Regione oppidum, Via, quae Florentiam Bononia ducit, Scarperia est, anno cIↄ cccxxi sub Clemente v. conditum ab Florentinis; qui, capta Pistoria ut Blondus libro x tradit, quo finitimum Agrum tranquillum habérent, Adriano Propugnaculo, quod ab Vbaldina Gente emerant, everso, oppidum hoc in planitie, indito ob sitvum Scarperiae nomine, quod ad pedem Scarpamve, ut Itali vocant, Apennini hic positum, aedificarunt. Plenum est Fabris Ferrariis. Terraemotu totum pene concidit anno ab Christo nato cIↄ IↄXLIII, Die Julij iii.
units.tr: Not far from there, between the hills of Fesulae and the ridges of the Apennines itself, lies a most pleasant valley, shining throughout with noble villas and villages, called Mugello in the vernacular, and its inhabitants are the Mugellani. It owes its origin to the Cono Mugellano, a famous tower built on it. The river Sieve flows through the middle of this valley. In the Mugello region, on the road that leads from Florence to Bologna, is the town of Scarperia, founded by the Florentines in the year 1321 under Clement V. As Biondo relates in book 10, after taking Pistoia, they wished to have the neighbouring territory quiet, and having razed the fortress of Adriano, which they had bought from the Ubaldini family, they built this town on the plain, giving it the name Scarperia because it was placed at the foot (scarpa, as the Italians call it) of the Apennines. It is full of smiths and ironworkers. In the year of Christ 1543, on 3 July, an earthquake almost wholly brought it down.

units.la: • Ad Confluentes fere Sebam Rotamque, Nicolaium est, Niccolo; cui nomen ab duro Nicolai Pleniam obsidio, fortiliter tolerato, quod Blondus & Sabellicus describunt.
units.tr: • Near the confluence of the Sieve and the Rotta is Nicolaium, Niccolò; it takes its name from Nicholas, who held out bravely through the hard siege of Pieve, as Biondo and Sabellico describe.

units.la: Ad Rontam, Via qua itur Faventiam, ejusdem nominis est Vicus Ronta; sub quo Burgus est S. Laurentii, Italis Borgo S. Lorenzo.
units.tr: By the Ronta, on the road that goes to Faenza, is a village of the same name, Ronta; below it is the borough of S. Laurentii, which the Italians call Borgo S. Lorenzo.

units.la: Ager, qui inter Ducatum & Arnum Fluvios ad Aretinorum usque Fines patet, Caesentino dicitur vulgo. Eum Caesentinum esse appellandum ab Clusio Novo, probat ex Suo, non Litteratorum, Antonino Annius. Volaterranus lib.v. Comment. Vrban. hanc putat esse Terram, quae tò Nacrusoyon Strabonis libro v, qui tractus erat longus, quo in Tuscam Exercitus ex Gallis penetrare solebant, quoque Hannibal etiam transisse fertur. Xylander tò Nacrusoy Strabonis Latine vertit Transfumenum. Caesentinus Ager qua via ad Florentinorum ditionem venerit, exponit Blondus lib. viii. Peramaenus est & fertilis.
units.tr: The territory that stretches between the rivers Ducatus and Arno as far as the borders of the Aretines is commonly called Caesentino. Annius shows from his own, not the scholars', Antoninus that it should be called Caesentinum, after the New Clusium. Volaterranus, book 5 of his Commentaries on the City, thinks this is the land that Strabo, book 5, calls to Nacrusoyon, a long tract through which armies coming from the Gauls used to penetrate into Tuscany, and through which Hannibal is also said to have passed. Xylander translates Strabo's to Nacrusoy into Latin as Transfumenum. Biondo, book 8, explains how the Caesentine territory came under the dominion of the Florentines. It is very pleasant and fertile.

units.la: Supra Florentiam millia xv ad Arni ripam Opidum est Incisa, Francisci Petrarchae Patria. Nominem tamen Blondus putat ab incuso Obice laxeo, qui Cursum Arni sustinebat, quibusdam vestigiis adhuc se prodens. Nam priscis temporibus Planiciem hic Arno adpositam Paludes occupabant, quae post apertum ferro Saxum nunc exculta tota continaque nobilium Florentinorum est mstar. Vallem Arni, Valle d'Arno, vocant. Facit mentionem ejus Livius: Hannibalem hac cum difficultate & periculo transgressum, alteroque captum oculo memorans.
units.tr: Fifteen miles above Florence, on the bank of the Arno, is the town of Incisa, the homeland of Francesco Petrarca. Biondo, however, thinks it takes its name from the incusus barrier of rock that held back the course of the Arno, which still reveals itself by some traces. For in ancient times marshes occupied the plain lying beside the Arno here, but after the rock was opened with iron, the whole area is now cultivated and is the site of the country houses of noble Florentines. They call it the Vallem Arni, Valle d'Arno. Livy mentions it, recording that Hannibal crossed here with difficulty and danger, and was blinded in one eye.

units.la: Post Incisam, ad Arni dextram, in eadem Valle Opidum est Fichino, ab Florentinis tinis olim eversum, & ab Guidone Novello Comite restauratum anno cIↄ ccxcviii, scribente Volaterrano.
units.tr: After Incisa, on the right bank of the Arno, in the same valley, is the town of Fichino, once destroyed by the Florentines and restored by Count Guido Novello in the year 1298, according to Volaterranus.

units.la: Nobile huic Oppidum succedit D.Ioannis, Vino inclytum, quod Trebiani vulgo, suavissimum, si quod aliud, concentendo. Sequuntur mox Oppida Monte Farco & Guarantani[?] ultra Arnum Castel Franco (quod cum Fano D. Ioannis conditum ab Florentinis, circa annum cIↄ ccxcviii & Terra Nova, Patria Poggii, quam muro cinxit Guido Petramala, Episcopus Aretinorum.
units.tr: To this there follows a noble town, S. Giovanni, famous for its wine, which is called Trebbiano in the vernacular, the sweetest of all if one may judge. Next come the towns of Montefarco and Guarantani[?] beyond the Arno, Castelfranco (which, together with the Fano of S. Giovanni, was founded by the Florentines around the year 1298), and Terranova, the homeland of Poggio, which Guido Petramala, bishop of the Aretines, surrounded with a wall.

units.la: Occurrit mox cum Laterina, & Ponte Xano Canalicum quod ab Valle Umbrosa, dictu. Ortum inde Institutum Vitae Monasticae, Valli Umbrosae cognomento, anno cIↄ lxx.
units.tr: Next there comes Laterina, and Ponte Xano, a small canal which takes its name from the Valle Umbrosa. From there came the rule of monastic life called after the Valle Umbrosa, in the year 1070.

units.la: In Calentino insuper Agro multa sunt alia Castella Vicique quorum quae primi loci, sunt Romena, Borgo, Poppi olim in Comitum Guidonum ditione.
units.tr: In the Casentino territory, moreover, there are many other castles and villages, the chief of which are Romena, Borgo, and Poppi, formerly under the lordship of the Guidi counts.

units.la: Sub Arni Fonte, altera in ripa, visuntur Porcignano, Stia, Prato, Pecchio. Dein altissimus in Montibus Camaldulorum est Camaldulum, vulgo, di Camaldoli.
units.tr: Below the source of the Arno, on the other bank, are Porcignano, Stia, Prato, and Pecchio. Then, very high in the mountains, is the Camaldulum of the Camaldolese, in the vernacular Camaldoli.

units.la: Ad mittentem fere ie Arno Arcinianum, Bibbiena est, Larum in Monte Opidum. Haud procul inde Fanum est eximium D. Mariae Saxea, dal Sasso, mox Gelo & Corrreggio, Opida non magna.
units.tr: Near where the Arno receives the Arcinianus, is Bibbiena, a town on the hill of the Larus. Not far from there is the famous shrine of the Blessed Mary of the Rock, dal Sasso; then Gelo and Corrreggio, small towns.

units.la: Averni um locum habent Incolae religiosum; impressa memorantes ibi D.Francisco Christi Stigmata.
units.tr: The inhabitants have a religious place on Mount Alverna, recording that there the stigmata of Christ were impressed on St Francis.

units.la: Ad ea quae Florentiae sunt Meridionalia recurro: Ad Pesciam hinc inde sunt Laitra, Monte Lupo, Colina, Sambuca, Monte Cinello, Linaro, S. Donato, & alia.
units.tr: I return to the places south of Florence. Near Pesciola, on either side, are Lastra, Montelupo, Colina, Sambuca, Montecinello, Linaro, S. Donato, and others.

units.la: Ad Elsam sunt Empoli; Emporium Latine loquentibus dicitur: Castel Fiorentino, Certaldo, Boccatii Patria, Fiso, Barbermo, Francisci IC. ortu clarum, S. Miniato, cum cognomen Tedesco, fortean ab Teutonibus: Nam conditum legitur hoc Oppidum ab Desiderio Langbardorum Rege: Arcem ibi ab Imperatore Frederico II. factam memorat in Historia Neapolitana lib. iv. Pandulphus Collenutus: Nativitate superbiunt Cives Recuperati IC. & Laurentii, summi Astrologi, quem omnium Primum Iudicia in Annos singulos scripsisse notat Volaterranus.
units.tr: By the Elsa are Empoli, called Emporium by those who speak Latin; Castelfiorentino; Certaldo, the homeland of Boccaccio; Fiesole; Barberino, famous for the birth of Francesco the jurist; and S. Miniato, which has the surname Tedesco, perhaps from the Teutons, for this town is recorded as founded by Desiderius, king of the Lombards. Pandolfo Collenuccio, in his Neapolitan History, book 4, records that a citadel was built there by the emperor Frederick II. The citizens Recuperati, the jurist, and Lorenzo, the greatest astrologer, take pride in their birth. Volaterranus notes that he was the first to write the yearly prognostications.

units.la: Iuxta Elsae Fontem est Cafulo. Sunt ibidem Stagia & Poggibonsi. Posterius Latine loquentes Bonitium vocant. De Bonitio Blondus libro xviii memorat, ejus Excidium ab Karolo I. Siciliae Rege Florentinis pretio venditum, in contumeliam Pisanorum, qui id semel ab Florentinis eversum restaurarant. Ita tum Florentini hoc ad Pedem Collis, in cujus Vertice prius fuerat, haud pari tamen amplitudine, condiderunt: Poggibonsium pro Poggio Bonitio dictum, ut scribit Platina in Vita Clementis iv. Tradit Volaterranus olim ditionis fuisse Senensium.
units.tr: Beside the source of the Elsa is Cafaggiolo. There are also Staggia and Poggibonsi there. The latter those who speak Latin call Bonitium. Biondo, book 18, mentions Bonizio, whose destruction was sold to the Florentines for money by Charles I, king of Sicily, to the disgrace of the Pisans, who had twice restored it after the Florentines had destroyed it. Thus the Florentines then founded it at the foot of the hill, on the summit of which it had previously stood, though not of the same size; Poggibonsi was named for Poggio Bonizio, as Platina writes in the Life of Clement IV. Volaterranus relates that it once belonged to the Sienese.

units.la: Ad Austrahorem Elsae ripam Opidum est S.Geminiani, Senensium quondam, nunc Florentinorum. ab Desiderio Langbardorum Rege conditum, uti Tabula Viterbiensis, Langbardicis inscripta Literis, docet. Patria Ioannis & Vincentii, Ordinis Praedicatorij, quorum ille Libri de Rerum Similitudine est Auctor; Hic Vitae D. Antonij, aliorumque Operum.
units.tr: On the southern bank of the Elsa is the town of S. Gimignano, formerly of the Sienese, now of the Florentines, founded by Desiderius, king of the Lombards, as the Viterbo table, inscribed in Lombard letters, shows. It was the birthplace of Giovanni and Vincenzo of the Order of Preachers; the former is the author of the book On the Likeness of Things; the latter wrote the Life of St Antoninus and other works.

units.la: Ultra iunt Gambassio, Montec Atone, & Monte Opoli.
units.tr: Beyond these lie Gambassi, Montecatone, and Montepulciano.

units.la: Devenitur hinc ad Eram Fluvium; in cujus una ripa visuntur Pieve di Sacco, Feceiola, & Calcinara, cum quibusdam aliis Opidulis; in altera Calcina Pitam Agri, Lari, Terraccio; & haud procul Erae Fontibus antiquissima Vrbs Volaterra. Ciceroni, Livio, Plinio, aliis nota: ὀυολατέρραι, Ptolemaeo: Aquae Volaterna Itinerariae Tabulae. Vrbis Etymon petat ex Annio Lector, cui otium; addatque Volaterranum lib. v. Comment. Vrbanor Difficili asperoque lugo est impolita. De Situ sic Strabo lib.v: [Greek text, illegible, ~60 letters] Sic Paulus Iovius: Fummo, inquit, Montis Lugo quatuane praecipue Descendit, oblongo Dorso, ad infimos pertinent Campos: qui radiorum instar ad imaginem extenta cum digitis Palmae manus, interiecta profundissimis Vallibus, distinguuntur; ita ut Convalles transiri nequeant, quum abruptissimae sint, atque ita densis arboribus obsepta, ut Everittivus maxime fiant; quoniam ab hiis Additibus sulcet strata quum paululum adscenderis in proximas Vias, nullo modo ad mutuam opem ferendam transiri potest, quod praeaka Crepidines undique fuissent, ad quas commeantium oculi propter profunditatem facile cadunt.
units.tr: From here one comes to the river Era. On one bank are Pieve di Sacco, Fekiola, and Calcinaia, with some other small towns; on the other Calcina, the boundary of the territory, Lari, and Terriccio; and not far from the sources of the Era is the very ancient city of Volaterra, known to Cicero, Livy, Pliny and others; the Greeks call it Volaterrai [Οὐολατέρραι], Ptolemy; the Itinerary tables call it Aquae Volaterranae. The reader who has leisure may seek its etymology from Annius, and add Volaterranus, book 5 of his Commentaries on the City. It is set on a difficult and rough height. Strabo, book 5, describes the site thus: [Greek passage, illegible in the scan]. Paulus Jovius says: "From the top of the mountain, it descends by a long ridge to the lowest plains, which are divided, like the fingers of a palm stretched out in the likeness of rays, by very deep valleys in between. These valleys cannot be crossed, since they are so steep and so thickly covered with trees that they are especially hard to pass; for when you have climbed a little way up the nearest paths from them, one cannot in any way cross to bring mutual help, because on every side there are precipitous ledges, into which the eyes of travellers easily fall because of the depth."

units.la: Adhas Natura Munitiones acceserunt Mœnia antiquitus è quadrato Lapide constructa: quæ hodie suburbana præcingunt Tecta: quoniam Vrbs Noua, quæ hodie inhabitatur, post Calamitatum à Pannonis acceptam aliquanto adstrictior, quam antea, Muri ambitu munitur. Adfirmat etiam apud Leandrum Zacharias Zachius Volaterranus, Murorum formam humanæ Manus speciem sequi, quod Montis, in quo sitā, fastigium quinis adsurgat modicis Collibus, qui inter se parvis item Vallibus dissociati: omnes Muro claudi non esse, sed aliquos tantum. Mœnia porro quadratis constant Lapidibus, longitudinis senum sere pedum; qui elegantèr & adsabrè abque bitumine compositi. Quinis in Vrbem Portis Aditus datur: Pro singulis Fons eximius Aquas eiaculatur purissimas. Inter Colonias nominatur apud Frontinum. Est apud M. Tullium Epistola, qua pro Municipiis Volaterranis Q. Valerio Proprætori, Sullanam Legem antiquam restituere molienti, scribitur. Oratione etiam pro sua Domo Romam Volaterranis non solum ut Civibus, sed ut optimis Civibus, uti potuisse dicit idem Tullius. Quadam item ad Atticum Epistola gloriatur, Se in suo Consulatu Volaterranos & Aretinos in veteri possessione Agrorum, quos ademerat Sulla, nec diviserat, conservasse. De Rebus, quæ ad Volaterras olim gestæ, legendi Livius lib. x & xxviii, Strabo lib. v, & alij. Prima scribitur inter Etruriæ Civitates Fidem Christianam amplexa; Auctore D. Romulo, Divi Petri Apostoli Legato: quæ Arriana Labe postea nonnihil infecta, Iusti Africani Presbyteri, qui ipsius post Antistes, Virtute circa Leonis III Imperatoris tempora rursum est expurgata. Ab Vandalis primum, deinde ab Hunnis est vexata: quibus ex Italia profligatis, ab Othone I Imperatore, qui Othoniaum conatus est nominare, Antoniaum corrupte quidam vocant, iterum instaurata, & Muris artius septa, longo tempore per Cæsareos Legatos est administrata, demum ab Florentinis occupata, sæpe Detectionem molita creatis varie nunc hoc, nunc illo & nomine & numero Magistratibus, semper tamen in eorum retracta est potestatem; accepta etiam ab suis Victoribus Arce. Cum ijs inde subactis Volaterrani quoque in Ditionem venerunt Medicum, Magnorum hodie Etruriæ Ducum Antiquitatem ejus arguunt Muri, quibus adhuc cingitur, Sepulcra, Epitaphia Litteris Etruscis posita, Vererrimæ ex marmore Statuæ, Lapides elaborati, qui indies hic eruntur. Vrbis medio Vestigia maximi Theatri supersunt. In Via, quam Curjum Martium vocant, Signum Martis est marmoreum; cum Armis aliquot ex Alabastrite, in quibus Litteræ conspiciuntur Etruscæ: cujus generis, ut & Latinæ, multæ ibi passim Inscriptiones. Vrbs est Episcopalis, sub Archiepiscopo Florentino. Inlustrarunt Volaterras ortu suo Magni Viri inter quos Linus Horen a nus ex Maurorum Familia, & A. Persius. Vixerunt nuper Iacobus Cardinalis, dictus Tuscanensis, Raphaeli à Patria sua Volaterranus cognominatus; Zacharias Zachius, qui Res Volaterrarum memorabiles, ut Metallorum Fodinas, Aquas Medicatas, aliaque Singularia scripsit; Raphael Maffeus; & alij suis Monimentis nobiles.
units.tr: Moreover, nature has added fortifications: walls built in antiquity of square stone, which today surround the suburban buildings. Since the New City, which is inhabited today, after the calamity suffered at the hands of the Pannonians, is fortified by a circuit of walls somewhat narrower than before. Zacharias Zachius of Volterra also affirms, in Leandro, that the shape of the walls follows the likeness of a human hand, because the summit of the mountain on which it sits rises into five modest hills, which are separated from one another by small valleys. Not all of them are enclosed by the wall, only some. The walls, moreover, are made of square stones about six feet long, which are set elegantly and accurately without bitumen. There is access to the city through five gates; at each one an outstanding spring spouts the purest water. It is named among the colonies by Frontinus. There is a letter of M. Tullius in which he writes on behalf of the municipality of Volterra to Q. Valerius, propraetor, who was attempting to restore the old Sullan law. In a speech on behalf of his own house, the same Tullius says that the Volaterrans could have had recourse to Rome not only as citizens but as the best citizens. In a certain letter to Atticus he boasts that in his consulship he preserved the Volaterrans and Aretines in the old possession of their fields, which Sulla had taken away but had not divided. For the events that once took place at Volaterrae, one may read Livy, books 10 and 28, Strabo, book 5, and others. It is written that it was the first of the cities of Etruria to embrace the Christian faith, under the guidance of Romulus, legate of the blessed apostle Peter. Later it was somewhat tainted by the Arian stain, but through the virtue of Justus Africanus, presbyter, who afterwards became its bishop, it was cleansed again in the time of the emperor Leo III. It was harassed first by the Vandals and then by the Huns; when these had been driven out of Italy, it was restored by the emperor Otto I, who tried to name it Othoniaum, though some call it Antoniaum by corruption, and it was enclosed more tightly with walls. For a long time it was governed by imperial legates, and at last it was occupied by the Florentines, who often attempted to shake off their rule, and, with magistrates created now under this name and number, now under that, always fell back under their power, having also received the citadel from their conquerors. When those people had been subdued, the Volaterrans also came under the authority of the Medici, today the Grand Dukes of Etruria. Its antiquity is proved by its walls, with which it is still surrounded, by tombs, epitaphs inscribed in Etruscan letters, very ancient statues of marble, and carved stones which are dug up here every day. In the middle of the city the traces of a very large theatre survive. On the road which they call the Campus Martius, there is a marble statue of Mars, with some armour of alabaster, on which Etruscan letters can be seen; inscriptions of this kind, as well as Latin ones, are found here and there in abundance. The city is an episcopal see, under the Archbishop of Florence. Volaterrae has been made famous by the birth of great men, among whom are Linus Horanus of the family of the Moors, and A. Persius. Recently there lived Jacopo, called Cardinal of Tusculum, surnamed Volaterranus by Raphael from his homeland; Zacharias Zachius, who wrote the memorable things of Volterra, such as its metal mines, its medicinal waters, and other particulars; Raphael Maffeus; and others who are noble for their writings.

units.la: Trans Amnem Cæcinam in Colle Opidum est Marantium, quod vulgo Ripamaranæ; ab Volaterranis Muro cinctum. Inde tria milliaria Liblanum occurrit, in Monte, ubi Terra nigra foditur. Ulterius est Mons Rufolus, qui olim in Vertice summo Arcem habuit. Ab Marantio M.P.V Opidum est in Monte, quod vulgo Monte di Cerbero: hinc quarto lapide Castel Nuovo di Volterra: & paulo remotius Lecia. Tribus hinc milliaribus Senensium Opidum est, quod vernacule Monte Retundo. Oram versus Iustinianum est, & haud procul inde Sasseta, Latinis Saxeta ab Monte fortean saxoso, cui insidet. Hinc Soveretum Vino, Oleo, Frugibusque aliis abundans. Itinere ad maritimam Senensium Regionem inter Saltus, qui Senensium, in Colle Moscona visitur, quæ tota fere conlapsa in Pastorum Pecudumque habitationem abiit. Opidum olim fuisse perhonestum, indicant, præter magna Marmorum frusta, Columnasque fractas, Statuas mutilas, & eximii Fontis vestigia, semiruti ejus Muri quadrato lapide, cum ingenti Cisterna. Supersunt etiam Pavimentorum nobilium Partes, opere tessellato. Multa quotidie reperiuntur hic Antiquitatis Monimenta, plurimiqué Nummi. Secundum Collem Mare versus procedenti editiore loco Arx adparet dejecta, quæ Moscone fuisse creditur. Via, qua Senam itur Volaterris, quarto hinc lapide Opidum occurrit, quod Tuscis Monte Mitcuolo: inde mille passibus Spicciaiola: hinc tribus milliibus Castro Nuovo di S. Geminiano, viculq; Colliis Elsana Vallis, qui in Ditione est Senensium. Quarto inde lapide offert se
units.tr: Across the river Cecina, on a hill, is the town of Marantium, commonly called Ripamarana, walled by the Volaterrans. Three miles from there Liblanum appears, on a mountain where black earth is dug up. Further on is Mount Rufolus, which once had a citadel on its summit. Four miles from Marantium, on a mountain, is a town commonly called Monte di Cerbero; from there, four miles, Castel Nuovo di Volterra, and a little further away Lecia. Three miles from here is a town of the Sienese, which in the vernacular is called Monte Retundo. Toward the coast lies Iustinianum, and not far from it Sasseta, in Latin Saxeta, perhaps from the rocky mountain on which it sits. From here Soveretum, abounding in wine, oil and other crops. On the journey to the maritime region of the Sienese, among the woods that belong to the Sienese, on a hill, Moscona is seen, which has almost entirely collapsed and has passed into the dwelling of shepherds and flocks. That the town was once very distinguished is shown by large fragments of marble, broken columns, mutilated statues, traces of a splendid fountain, and the half-ruined walls of that town, of square stone, with a huge cistern. There also survive parts of noble pavements, in mosaic work. Many monuments of antiquity are found here every day, and very many coins. Going toward the sea along the hill, a citadel, apparently thrown down, appears on a higher spot, which is believed to have been Moscone. On the road by which one goes from Volterra to Siena, four miles from here a town meets the eye, which in Tuscan is called Monte Mitcuolo; from there, a thousand paces, Spicciaiola; three miles from here Castro Nuovo di S. Geminiano, and the village of Colliis Elsana Vallis, which lies in the territory of the Sienese. Four miles from there one comes upon

units.la: Vicus, qui vernacule La Badia inter fines Florentinorum, & Senensium. Volaterris Senam euntibus a tergo cellam lugo Sullanum adparet, Oppidum prænmunitum, saxoso in Monte quadrata forma conditum. Angulos singulos validæ tenent turres turque Arces; quinta que ceteris major Oppidi medio. Aditus ad ipsum est per difficilem, artam, sinuosamque Viam, Saxo incisam latitudine circiter trium pedum. Sullam Condito em Incolæ referunt; Volaterranus Petronii Senensis. Ab Sillano M, P. vi, in amœno Colle Oppidum est D. Armanij, S. Armatæ extra quod insigne Virginum conspicitur Cœnobium. Septimo inde lapide lautum est Oppidum Cassij, Volaterranæ Diœcesis, quamquam ditione Senensium habeatur. Statua hic L. Cornelii Sullæ Dictatoris marmorea cernitur. Altero ab Volaterris lapide Matolla Roncellaque sunt opida; verstque mare x, ab Roncolla P. M. Guardistallo; & e regione milibus duobus Mente Scudaa, Mons Scutarius Latinis. Octavo dein lapide Querceto: hinc tertio Ripa-bella.
units.tr: a village, which in the vernacular is called La Badia, between the borders of the Florentines and the Sienese. For those going from Volterra to Siena, behind them there appears on a rocky mountain the fortified town of Sullanum, built in a square shape. Each of its corners is held by strong towers, and the largest of them, in the middle of the town, is a citadel. The approach to it is by a difficult, narrow and winding road, cut through the rock, about three feet wide. The inhabitants say that Sulla founded it; Volaterranus says Petronius of Siena. Six miles from Sillanum, on a pleasant hill, is the town of S. Armanius, S. Armata, outside which a famous convent of virgins is seen. Seven miles from there is the bathing town of Cassij, in the diocese of Volterra, although it is regarded as under the authority of the Sienese. A marble statue of L. Cornelius Sulla the Dictator is seen here. One mile from Volterra are the towns of Matolla and Roncella; and ten miles toward the sea, from Roncolla, Guardistallo; and opposite, two miles away, Monte Scudaio, in Latin Mons Scutarius. Then, eight miles on, Querceto; from there, three miles, Ripabella.

units.la: Diœcesi Volaterrano nunc relicta, Senensium Territoria ingredimur; quæ propinquora Litroni, Maritima, Maremma di Siena, vocantur. Ibi Massa est Vrbs pervetusta. De Ferrario, quod quidam hic centum tunc ante a me dictum. Massanus vel Massaensis Episcopus legitur D. Cerlo, de quo Adcolæ Lacium, qui prope Abbatiam in Volaterrano morum Ditione, Itupenda quædam commemorant. Sequuntur Loca quædam exigui momenti Pena, Latti, Monte Massio, S. Fortuno, Strada, Monte Orsaio. Trans Vmbronem S. Lucano, Pereta, Migliano.
units.tr: Leaving the diocese of Volterra, we now enter the territories of the Sienese, which are nearer the coast and are called Maritima, Maremma di Siena. There Massa is a very ancient city. Concerning the Ferrarian matter, which some say was mentioned by me a hundred years ago, Massanus or Bishop of Massa is read in the time of Saint Cerlus, about whom the inhabitants of Lacium, who near the abbey in the territory of Volterra, recount certain marvels. Some places of little importance follow: Pena, Latti, Monte Massio, S. Fortunato, Strada, Monte Orsaio. Across the Umbrone: S. Lucano, Pereta, Migliano.

units.la: Ultra ad flumen Albengiam Saturniana, modicum nunc Opidum. Σατυρνία Ptolemæo; Saturnia Livio & Festo; Σατορνία Appiano lib. i. Belli Civilis. Huius Ruderra adhuc cerni in Finibus Tuscia, scribit Paulus Diaconus ad Eutropij Historiam. Collapsam refecere nonnihil Senenses, in quorum est Ditione. De Saturnino Pœsulo antea monui. Saturnianam præterfluunt Albengia, secundum quem ulterius ad Sempronianum devenitur. Nec procul inde Suana: Σύανα Ptolemæo; unde Suanenses Plinio, quorum ante meminni. Suanenses sunt Gregorius vii. P.M. Rursus a tergo ad Vmbronem sunt Ipsia, Campagnaticum, Paganicum, Bagni di Pitrio i. Supra juxta Ofennam Montem, est D. Quirici Oppidum, cum Arce, ab D. Quirici Æde, quam Zenoni Landrici filius potuisse fertur, denominatum. Hic memorandum est illud: Florentinam Remp. magno sumtu plurimos alere Leones: quorum si unus centesimum & unum annum supervixerit, ad eumque Montem & oppidum fuerit perductus, tum Senenses veteri quodam jure in Florentinorum futuros potestate. Dein Senam versus alto in Monte Oppidum est Mons Altinos, vulgo Monte Alcia; Vino, quod amœnisibi Collibus gignitur, nobile. Eo Avorum memoria principes Senensium Familiæ, oriunda ab Catatecanis & Florentinis Patria, commigrarunt; Sequeque, monte undique munito, contra omnem hostium Vim sub Gallorum Regis patrocinio sunt tutati. Iam Magno Etruria Duci cum Senu paret. Non procul inde Monte Oliveto, primo dio Instituti Monachorum Albornim inclutus, quod Montis Olivetti nuncupatur.
units.tr: Further on, toward the river Albegna, is Saturniana, now a modest town. Satyrnia [Σατυρνία] in Ptolemy; Saturnia in Livy and Festus; Satornia [Σατορνία] in Appian, book 1 of the Civil Wars. Paulus Diaconus, in his notes on the history of Eutropius, writes that its ruins can still be seen in the territory of Tuscany. The Sienese, in whose territory it lies, have partly restored it after its collapse. I have already spoken before about Saturninus the Bishop. Past Saturniana flows the Albegna, and beside it, further on, one comes to Sempronianum. Not far from there is Suana: Syana [Σύανα] in Ptolemy; whence the Suanenses in Pliny, of whom I have spoken before. The Suanenses are Gregory VII, pope and greatest. Back again, beyond the Umbrone, are Ipsia, Campagnatico, Paganico, Bagni di Petriolo. Above, near Mount Ofenna, is the town of S. Quirico, with a citadel, named from the church of S. Quirico, which is said to have been founded by the son of Zeno Landricus. Here that saying should be recorded: the Florentine Republic at great expense keeps very many lions; if one of them has survived to the hundred and first year, and has been led to that mountain and town, then the Sienese by an ancient right will come under the power of the Florentines. Then, toward Siena, on a high mountain, is the town of Mons Altinos, commonly called Monte Alcino, famous for the wine produced on its pleasant hills. In the memory of their grandfathers the leading families of Siena, which came from Catalonia and originally from Florence, migrated there; and, with the mountain fortified on every side, they defended themselves against every violence of the enemy under the protection of the King of France. Now Siena obeys the Grand Duke of Etruria. Not far from there is Monte Oliveto, the first house of the famous Order of Monks of Monte Oliveto, which is called Montis Olivetti.

units.la: Succedit explicanda iamnunc Sena. Σαίνα Ptolemæo, mediterranea Tuscia Vrbs lib. iii cap. 1. Sena Julia, Itinerariæ Tabulæ; Vulgo dicitur Siena. Hæc Senensis Colonia Plinio nominatur lib. iii, cap. v. ut aperte, quæ simul recensentur, Loca indicant. Alia est Senensis Colonia, quam diversis verbis locat ad Mare Superum Livius lib. xxvii; cuiusque meminit Tacitus lib. iv. Historiarum; ubi CL. V. Iusti Lipsij Editione scribitur Senensis. Hanc enim cum Superiore illa confundunt cum alii tum Albertus Leander. Quemadmodum Prior illa ab Sena, quæ Mari Tusco propior, quamque hoc loco delineabimus: hæ Posterior ab Sena, quæ ad Mare Hadriaticum: Sena simpliciter Floro ex Livio lib. xi, ubi notat Coloniæ esse deductas Castrum, Senam, Hadriam; Σλων Polybio; compositæ vero Σλωμφεσσα Strab. lib. v, & fortean etiam Σλωα ibidem paullo ante, innuentibus id aliquo modo, quæ connominantur ibi, locis; nisi scribendum Kuoloia. Senogallia Plinio lib. iii. cap. xiiii, Antonino, Paullo Diacono: divisim autem Σλωα Γαλλικα Ptolemæo lib. iii. cap. i. Sena Gallorum, Silio Italico: Sena Galli, Itinerariæ Tabulæ: hodie denique Senigaglia. Polybius initium Sanæ ad Gallos Senones, qui à Populo Romano devicti, referre videtur, quum eos alteram Vrbem Senam ædificasse, præter illam, quæ Hadriatico adposita Mari; tradit. Suffragantur Gothefredus in libro Memoriarum & Ioannes Sarisberiensis Policrat. lib. vi, cap. xvii. Non audiendus Blondus novam hanc esse Vrbem, & ab fenis ... de Perusina, Clusinensi, Aretina, Fesulana, Florentina, & Volaterrana Dioecesi, ab Ioanne xviii P.M. acceptis, dictam censens. Alij ab Karolo Martello conditam ajunt, quo tempore, quo modo, quam ob causam, non addentes. Alij initium ejus alio referunt, satis fabulose. Roma distans 10 ccc. Stadijs edito sita est loco, cis Arbiam, flexu sinuoso propter Montis dorsum, lateribus angustior & procliviot, tria habens quasi Cornua: quorum quod Meridiem spectat, latius est ijs, quae ad Ortum sunt & Occasum. Nam ea Vrbis pars, quae Septemtrioni obversa, exigua prae ceteris & plana. Valles intermediae ab Hortis fere occupantur. Coelo utitur benigno & salubri, nisi quod subinde noxijs infestetur. Ventis: Aere temperatissimo;
units.tr: Next I must now explain Sena. Ptolemy calls it Σαίνα [Saina], an inland city of Tuscany, book 3, chapter 1. The Itinerary Tables call it Sena Julia, and it is commonly called Siena today. Pliny names this Senensis Colonia in book 3, chapter 5, so that the places listed together clearly indicate it. There is another Senensis Colonia, which Livy places on the Upper Sea in book 27 using different words, and which Tacitus mentions in book 4 of the Histories, where in the edition of the most distinguished Justus Lipsius it is written Senensis. Several writers, including Albertus Leander, confuse this one with the former. The former is Sena, which lies nearer the Tuscan Sea and which we shall describe here; the latter is Sena, which lies on the Adriatic Sea. Florus, following Livy book 11, simply calls it Sena, where he notes that the colonies of Castrum, Senam and Hadria were founded. Polybius gives it as Σάλων [Salōn], and Strabo in book 5 gives the compound Senogallia form, and perhaps also the form Σάλωα a little earlier in the same place, where names are linked with places in a way that somewhat suggests this, unless the text should be read otherwise. Pliny in book 3, chapter 14, Antoninus and Paul the Deacon call it Senogallia; Ptolemy in book 3, chapter 1, gives Σάλωα Γαλλικά [Salōa Gallika]; Silius Italicus calls it Sena Gallorum, and the Itinerary Tables Sena Galli; today it is finally Senigaglia. Polybius seems to report that the beginning of Sena is to be traced to the Gallic Senones, who were defeated by the Roman People, and he relates that they built another city called Sena, apart from the one lying on the Adriatic Sea. Gotefredus in his book of Memoirs and John of Salisbury in Policraticus book 6, chapter 17, support this. Blondus should not be heeded, who thinks this city is new and that it was named from ... of the dioceses of Perugia, Chiusi, Arezzo, Fiesole, Florence and Volterra, which he holds were received from John XVIII, Supreme Pontiff. Others say it was founded by Charles Martel, but they do not add when, how or why. Others trace its beginning to something else, quite fabulously. Sena lies 300 stadia from Rome, on a hill on this side of the Arbia, in a winding bend beside the ridge of a mountain, narrower and steeper on its sides, and it has three horn-like parts. The part facing south is wider than those facing east and west. The part of the city that faces north is small compared with the rest and flat. The valleys between are mostly taken up by gardens. It enjoys a mild and healthy climate, except that it is sometimes troubled by unhealthy air. Its air is very temperate.

units.la: Fn l' Aer dolce lucida & serena,
units.tr: "The air sweet, bright and serene."

units.la: canit lib.iii. Cantic. viii Facius Vbertus. Italia Delicias multi vocant Poetae. Plurimum haec Civitas Germanis placer, cum ob alia, tum ob Situm Aerisque Temperiem ipsis adcommodatam. Portas habet complures, quarum quae spectat Septemtrionem Agrumque Florentinum, Chamolsa vocatur; ad Orientem conversa, Roma est, cui opponitur fere Occasum Solis versus ea, per quam Loca adeuntur Maritima & Planicies Rosciae: quae ad Meridiem, Vallem Arni Fluminis prospicit, figuram habens fere ovalem. Strata est Sena latere coctili, plateis recta & longa, alta Turribus. Plura sunt apud Natalem Comitem libro Histor. vi, Iov. Pontanum lib.i. Aeneam Silvium, & alios. Frequentia nitet nobilium Aedificiorum: ex quibus Templum D. Virgini sacrum splendidum est & sumtuosum. De ejus Ornamentis multa Silvius, quem dixi, & Laurentius Schraderus in Italia. De reliquis publicis Operibus audiamus Poetam Vbertum: Io vidi il Campo suo, ch'e molto bello, E vidi Fonte Branda, e Camelia, E l'Hospedal, del qual ancor novello: Vidi la Chiesa di santa Maria, Con intagli di marmo, e cio viduto In verso Arezzo fa la nostra via.
units.tr: So sings Fazio degli Uberti in book 3 of his Dittamondo, chapter 8. Many poets call Italy the delight of cities. This city pleases the Germans very much, both for other reasons and for its site and the temperate air that suits them. It has several gates. The one facing north and the Florentine countryside is called Chamolsa; the one turned to the east is Roma, and opposite it, almost towards the setting sun, lies the gate through which one goes to the maritime places and the plain of Roscia. The gate facing south looks onto the valley of the River Arno. The city is almost oval in shape. Sena is paved with brick, its streets straight and long, and it is high with towers. More is found in Natale Conti, book 6 of his Histories, in Giovanni Pontano, book 1, in Aeneas Silvius and others. The city shines with a crowd of noble buildings, of which the temple sacred to the Blessed Virgin is splendid and sumptuous. Much about its ornaments is told by the Silvius I have named, and by Lorenz Schrader in Italia. Let us hear the poet Uberti about the other public works: "I saw its Campo, which is very beautiful; and I saw the Fonte Branda, and Camelia, and the hospital, which is still new. I saw the church of Saint Mary, with carvings in marble; and, having seen this, on the road to Arezzo, our way lies."

units.la: Forum, quod Campi nomine celebrat Poeta, amplum & multorum est laterum; adeo ut propter angulorum inaequalitatem Forma ejus certe dici nequeat: in medio profundum, erectum e lateribus, ut pensile videatur: cui dignitatis non parum addit Fons Brandus, ex marmore. Cives cum suavissimis, tum elegantissimis sunt moribus, maximaque humanitate, erga Exteros etiam, praediti: Quaestui dediti & Civilis Vitae muneribus. Speciosissimae sunt Mulieres, inter quas semper aliquas est invenire, quæ forma venustate cunctas Italici generis fœminas superant: Lætæ porro placidæque, &, salva Pudicitia, benignæ, facundæ, quibusque multus inest Lepos: pfilii recitam, orare Latine, Carmen facere non indoctæ. Idioma Senensium pur ceteris Tuscis Populis elegans, & auditu gratum. Christianæ Fidei Fundamenta Primus hic potuisse scribitur D. Ansanus, Tranquilli Romani F. quem ad Arbiam Amnem Kalendis Decembris secum percutiliss ferunt Lytias Proprætor Episcopus, cuius Dignitatem quando consecuta sit Sena, non constat: hoc certum, Episcopum Senensem Ioannem recenseri inter xlvi plus minus Episcopos, qui Romanæ Synodo Primæ interfuerunt, sub Hilario Romano Præsule, i. anno cccc ixv. Marcus etiam Senensis Ecclesiæ Episcopus legitur inter cxxv Episcopos, qui subscripserunt Secundo Concilio Lateranensi, quod celebratum sub Martino i, anno 10 cli. Sic item Vitalianus Episcopus Ecclesiæ Senensis inter multos alios numeratur, qui subscripserunt Epistolæ Agathonis, Romani Pontificis, quam Legati ab eo ad Sextam Oecumenicam Synodum Constantinopolitanam celebrandam missi anno 10 clxxiii. secum attulerunt. Ecclesiam Senensem ex Episcopali in Archiepiscopalem evexit dignitatem Pius II P. M. anno cIↄ ccccLIX, ipse Senensis subjectis illi Suanensi, Cras- tanensi & Massanensi Episcopis. Concilium hic fuit Generale sub Nicolao II. P. M. cxxx Episcoporum. Est in hac Urbe Societatis Iesu Collegium, quod Francisci Mendozæ Cardinalis opera inchoatum, anno cIↄ 1· xv. Est ibidem Academia, quam Cardinalis Zabarella Iurisconsultus varias principio Vexationes perpessus, ut orta rursus interiret, tamen aliquando tandem constituisse scribit Clement. Dudum de Sepulcr. Testatur ibidem Petrus Anchoranus ieanne cIↄ ccclxxxvIII ab Senatu Senensi evocatum per triennium hic Decretales docuisse. Floruerunt ibidem & Nicolaus v. P. M. Abbas Panormitanus, Paulus Castrensis, Bartholemæus Sozinus, Philippus Decius, Dominus Angelus, Hugo Senensis, Augustinus Datus, Franciscus Philelphus. Scribit Caecialupus Sena in Collegio Sapientiæ, quod ab Andrea Galerano Cive Senensi initium sumsit, Studiosos ob Disputationes & privata Exercitia multum proficere. Aucta est interim in modum a Pio II. P. M. Templo juncta est Bibliotheca, ab eodem Pio Pontifice instituta; ubi Libri nondum expositi, neque magni fortean pretii. Hospitale est e regione Templi, in quod omnes omnium Nationum Infirmi 30 & Peregrini recipiuntur. Opus memoria dignum cœptum dicitur ab Sutore, auctumque lapsu temporis Variorum Collatione & Liberalitate, ut ipsius Reditum ad octingenta Ducatorum milia exurgere, ut fama. Viros illustres habuit multos, inque eorum numero D. Bernardinum, Minorum instituti Reformatorem, Divis adscriptum ab Nicolao v. Pontifices Romanos dedit Sena Alexandrum iii, duosque Pio II qui Aeneas Silvius, & iii ex Familia Pico omnes. Cardinales Sena habuit Alphonsum & Raphaelem ex Petrucci, Ioannem ex Pico omnes, Pij iii P. M. Nepotem. Archiepiscopos Episcoposque hinc oriundos recenlere nimis esset longum. Inter Viros eruditione claros fuerunt Ego, summus Philosophus & Medicus; Thomas Domus, qui vulgo Veritatis Doctor; item Fredericus Petrucci, Marianus Socinus ejusque F. Bartholemaus, Bulgarinus, Marianus, Senensis Iunior, omnes Iurisconsulti: quibus addendus Augustinus Datus, Philologus. Res ab Senensium gestas Victoriasque, quas ex hostibus sunt adepti, plurimas celebrant alij. Libera suaque iuris Avorum memoria fuit oppressa tyrannide Pandulphi Petrucci; quo defuncto, Filiisque ejus cum magna Nobilitatis parte expulsis, Libertatem recuperavit, accepto Caesareo Præfecto. Legendus omnino Aeneas Silvius. Agrum habet medium inter sterilem & feracem amœnum, Frumento cæterisque fructibus uberem. Qua in mare vergit, Maremma vulgo, copiam Frumenti præstat maximam; quamquam Colonis infrequentior, præcipue æstate & autumno propter Cœli vitium. Delineavit Urbem Senensem, ejusque Territorium, vulgata Charta, Cæsar Orlandinus IC. Senensis.
units.tr: The Forum, which the poet celebrates under the name Campo, is large and has many sides, so that because of the unevenness of its angles its shape cannot really be described. In the middle it is deep and sloping from its sides, so that it seems suspended. The Fonte Branda, made of marble, adds no small dignity to it. The citizens are both very agreeable and most elegant in their manners, and endowed with the greatest courtesy, even towards foreigners. They are devoted to trade and to the duties of civil life. The women are very beautiful; among them one can always find some who surpass all the women of the Italian race in beauty and grace. They are cheerful and calm and, while preserving their chastity, kind, eloquent, and full of charm. Some are not unlearned in reciting Latin, speaking it, or writing verse. The language of the Senese is more elegant than that of the other Tuscan peoples and pleasant to hear. It is written that the first to plant the foundations of the Christian faith here was Saint Ansanus, son of Tranquillus the Roman, whom they say was beheaded by the governor Lysias on the banks of the Arbia on the first of December. When Sena obtained its episcopal dignity is not known. It is certain that a bishop of Sena, John, is listed among the roughly forty-six bishops who attended the First Roman Synod under Hilary, bishop of Rome, in the year 465. Marcus, bishop of the Church of Sena, is also read among the 125 bishops who subscribed to the Second Lateran Council, celebrated under Martin I in the year 649. Likewise Vitalianus, bishop of the Church of Sena, is counted among many others who subscribed to the letter of Agatho, Roman Pontiff, which his legates carried with them to the Sixth Ecumenical Council at Constantinople in the year 673. Pope Pius II raised the Church of Sena from an episcopal to an archiepiscopal dignity in the year 1459, with the bishops of Suana, Crast and Massa made subject to it. A general council was held here under Pope Nicholas II, with 130 bishops present. In this city there is a college of the Society of Jesus, begun through the work of Cardinal Francesco Mendoza in the year 1515. There is also a university, which the jurist Cardinal Zabarella, after suffering various troubles at first so that it might arise again and then perish, writes was at last established, as Clement's Dudum de sepulturis attests. Peter Ancarano is witnessed here in the year 1388, summoned by the Senate of Sena, teaching the Decretals here for three years. Nicholas V, Supreme Pontiff, the Abbot Panormitanus, Paul of Castro, Bartolomeo Sozzini, Filippo Decio, Dominus Angelus, Hugo of Sena, Augustinus Datus and Francesco Filelfo also flourished here. Caecialupus writes that the college of Sapientia at Sena, which took its beginning from Andrea Galerano, a citizen of Sena, helps students greatly through its disputations and private exercises. Meanwhile it has been enlarged in the manner of Pius II, Supreme Pontiff, and a library, founded by the same Pope Pius, is attached to the temple; its books are not yet on display and are perhaps of no great value. Opposite the temple is a hospital, which receives the sick and pilgrims of every nation. A work worth remembering is said to have been begun by a cobbler and to have grown over time through the contributions and generosity of various people, so that its revenue, it is said, amounts to eight hundred thousand ducats. It has had many illustrious men, among them Saint Bernardino, reformer of the Franciscan order, who was enrolled among the saints by Nicholas V. Sena gave two Roman Pontiffs: Alexander III, and Pius II, who was Aeneas Silvius; and three from the Piccolomini family, all of them. Sena had as cardinals Alfonso and Raffaele Petrucci, and Giovanni Piccolomini, the nephew of Pope Pius III. To list the archbishops and bishops born here would be too long. Among men distinguished for learning were Ego, a most eminent philosopher and physician; Thomas Domus, commonly called Doctor of Truth; likewise Federico Petrucci, Mariano Sozzini and his son Bartolomeo, Bulgarino, Mariano the Younger of Sena, all jurists; and to these should be added Augustinus Datus, a philologist. Many others celebrate the deeds and victories of the Senese, which they won over their enemies. Their liberty and their ancestral rights were oppressed by the tyranny of Pandolfo Petrucci; when he died and his sons were expelled together with a large part of the nobility, they recovered their freedom, having received a Caesarean prefect. Aeneas Silvius is altogether worth reading. The territory has a middle character between barren and fertile, pleasant, and rich in grain and other crops. Where it slopes towards the sea, commonly called the Maremma, it yields the greatest abundance of grain, although it is less populated by farmers, especially in summer and autumn, because of the unhealthy air. The map of the city of Sena and its territory, a well-known chart, was drawn by Cesare Orlandini, jurist of Sena.

units.la: Hæc de Sena. Alio eamus. Trans Arbiam vel Septemtrionem est Mons Apertus inde itinere in Orientem, Umbrone superato, Asinanum: altiusque Rapolanum & Aquilonem versus Mons S. Sabini, vulgo Monte Sanfovino, Avorum memoria duobus Cardinalibus illustris, Antonio, hujusque Nepote Ioanne Maria. Altius sunt Cicerella & Batisfole: Deinde juxta Clanis ripam Martianum, superiusque Foliarum cum ad dextram Lucianum. Hoc Oppidum bello, quod Florentini cum Ioanne Galeatio Vicecomite, Primo Mediolani Duce, gesserunt, Bononienses, Arbitri ab Senensibus & Florentinis lecti, Florentinorum Ditioni adjudicarunt: Sed non multo post ad pristinos Dominos Senenses redijt. Infra deinde sunt Asina Longa, Turrita, Montes Fullonicus & Pulcianus; Latine scribentibus, ille Felcianus, hic Politianus. Postremum hoc, quum in Senensium esset ditione, à Pandulpho Petrucio, qui Urbis Principatum habebat, Florentinus traditum fuit, Iulio II Pontifice Maximo, qui ipsorum gratiam captabat, petente. Nobilitarunt hunc Locum Angelus, cognominatus inde Politianus, & Marcellus Cervinus Cardinalis. Non procul inde Chiancianum, Vino nobile: mox Pientia, Opidum à Pio II. P. M. sic dictum: Loco antea nomen erat Corsilianum. Ingentem ex Terræmotu Calamitatem accepit anno MDXLV. Hinc Clanem versus Sateanum est. Ulterius in alto & difficili Monte juxta Massicum ponit errore magno Servius ad librum Æneidos x) antiquissima vilitur Urbs Clusium. Sic dicitur Livio lib. II & alibi, Virgilio libro, quem notavi, x, Plinio non uno loco, Latinisque Scriptoribus aliis; καλλιστ Polybio, Strabone, Appiano lib. I, Plutarcho in Poplicola: item Procopio lib. II Belli Gothici; quod Chiusi hodie vulgo: Clusinum scribitur Silio Italico lib. VIII. & Orosio lib. II. cap. XIX: καλλιστ, incmendatius fortean, Diodoro libro IV. Meminit Lapis, qui ibi & nunc extat, Karolo Sigonio describente:
units.tr: These things concern Siena. Let us go elsewhere. Across the Arbia, or to the north, is Mons Apertus. From there, travelling east and crossing the Umbrone, lies Asinanum. Higher up, toward Rapolano and the north, is Mons S. Sabini, now called Monte Sanfovino, which in our grandfathers' time was made famous by two cardinals, Antonio and his nephew Ioanne Maria. Higher still are Cicerella and Batisfole. Then, beside the bank of the Clanis, comes Martianum, and higher up Foliarum, and on the right Lucianum. This town, in the war which the Florentinorum waged against Gian Galeazzo Visconti, the first Duke of Milan, was awarded by arbiters chosen by the Senenses and the Florentines to the rule of the Florentines; but not long afterward it returned to its former lords, the Senenses. Below these lie Asina Longa, Turrita, and the hills Fullonicus and Pulcianus, which in Latin writers are called Felcianus and Politianus respectively. This last, while it was under the rule of the Senensium, was handed over to the Florentinus by Pandolfo Petrucci, who held the principality of the city, at the request of Pope Julius II, who was courting their favour. The place was made noteworthy by Angelus, surnamed from there Politianus, and by the Cardinal Marcellus Cervinus. Not far from there is Chiancianum, famous for its wine; soon after comes Pientia, a town so named by Pope Pius II, who was its founder; previously the place was called Corsilianum. It suffered huge damage from an earthquake in the year 1545. From here, toward the Clanis, lies Sateanum. Further inland, on a high and difficult mountain near the Massicus, Servius, in his commentary on the tenth book of the Aeneid, mistakenly places the most ancient city of Clusium. It is so called by Livy in book II and elsewhere, by Virgil in the book I have noted (x), by Pliny in more than one place, and by other Latin writers; by Polybius, Strabo, Appian in book I, and Plutarch in the Life of Publicola, the best Greek writers; likewise by Procopius in book II of the Gothic War. Today it is commonly called Chiusi; Silius Italicus in book VIII and Orosius in book II, chapter XIX, write Clusinum; Diodorus in book IV perhaps writes it more correctly. The stone which still stands there commemorates it, as Carolus Sigonius describes:

units.la: Q. GAVIVS. Q. F. ARN. CLEMENS CLVSII. EVOK AVG. A. QVÆSTIONIBVS
units.tr: Quintus Gavius Clemens, son of Quintus, of the Arnian tribe, of Clusium, evocatus of Augustus, secretary for inquiries

units.la: An duo fuerint Clusia, Vetus, & Novum, disputent ex Catone supposititio alij. Mini fabricata videntur ab Annio, qui apud Plinium in Clusinos inciderat & Veteres & Nouos. Sic multa alia nobis comminiscendum esset Opida. Apud Livium lib. x legitur, Clusium, quod olim Camars appellabant. Hinc Catoni & Antonino adsingendum erat Clusium Vetus vocatum Camersolum; & ne quod Novum fuerit ignoraremus, additum ab Annio Cafentinum id hodie dici corrupte. Annius suis Commentis ita incertavit Italiam, ut, si ex ipsius Scriptis esset delineanda, aliam omnino haberemus ab ea, quam Strabo, Ptolemæus, ceterique Scriptores fidis coloribus pinxerunt. Nobilitavit Clusium Porsena celebribus quibusdam Operibus; inter quæ Labyrinthus, quem, Porsenæqui Sepulcrum (cujus Vestigia hodieque monstrari scribit Giraldus de Sepulcris) verbis Varronis describit Plinius lib. XXXVI. cap. XIII.
units.tr: Some others dispute whether there were two Clusiums, an Old and a New, relying on the pseudo-Cato. They seem to me to have been invented by Annius, who had come across the Clusinos in Pliny, as Veteres & Nouos. In this way we would have to invent many other towns. In Livy, book x, we read Clusium, quod olim Camars appellabant (Clusium, which they once called Camars). From this it would have to be supposed that Cato and Antoninus meant an Clusium Vetus called Camersolum; and lest we fail to know of a Novum, Annius added that it is today corruptly called Cafentinum. Annius so confused Italiam with his fabrications that, if one were to map it from his writings, we would have a picture quite different from the one that Strabo, Ptolemy, and the other writers painted in faithful colours. Porsenna made Clusium famous with certain well-known works, among which was the Labyrinth, which Pliny in book XXXVI, chapter XIII, describes in Varro's words as the tomb of Porsenna (whose traces Giraldus, in his book on tombs, writes can still be pointed out today).

units.la: Iuxta est Cetona: & in altissimis asperrimisque Montibus haud modico intervallo Rodicofanum, ab Desiderio Langbardorum Rege sic dictum, ut in Edicto ejus legi perhibetur: postea autem muris egregie munitum ab Hadriano IV P.M Platina teste. Ultimum id habetur ea parte Castrum Patrimonij, D. Petro ab Mathilde Comite donati.
units.tr: Near it is Cetona. And in the highest and roughest mountains, at no great distance, is Rodicofanum, so named by Desiderius, King of the Lombards, as is said to be read in his edict; afterwards it was strongly fortified by Pope Hadrian IV, according to Platina. This is considered the last castle of the Patrimony in that region, given to St Peter by the Countess Matilda.

units.la: Sub Tynni Montibus, qui hodie vulgo Montuniata, Oppidum est San Fiorium, quod olim Sfortia Attendulus Cotignolanus Bosio Filio largitus est, Comiti creato. Fossis hic Pater fuit alterius Bosij, quem Generum legit Paullus III. P.M junctâ ipsi Filia Constantia.
units.tr: Beneath the Tynni mountains, which today are commonly called Montuniata, there is a town, San Fiorium, which Sforza Attendolo of Cotignola once gave to his son Bosio, when he was made count. Fossis here was the father of another Bosij, whom Paul III, the Supreme Pontiff, chose as son-in-law, joining to him his daughter Costanza.

units.la: Inter Rodicofanum & præcelsos Montes Balnea sunt S. Philippi, vulgo Bagni di S. Filippo. Haud procul inde Vestigia monstrantur Rusellarum. Rusella, Livio, Ptolemæo, Rusellana Colonia Plinio lib. III Natur. Histor. Hinc Rusellanus Ager velut in aliis Exemplaribus scribitur Rosellanus, apud Livium lib. x, ab V. C.
units.tr: Between Rodicofanum and the very high mountains are the Balnea of S. Philippi, commonly called Bagni di S. Filippo. Not far from there the remains of Rusellarum are pointed out. Rusella in Livy and Ptolemy, Rusellana Colonia in Pliny, book III of the Natural History. Hence the Rusellanus Ager, which in other copies is written Rosellanus, in Livy book x, from the founding of the city.

units.la: Secundum Paliam hunc Vicus est Ricorso, Recursus; inde Ponte Sentine, vel ut vulgo Ponte Centena: ubi quondam Σύβαρις Strabo & Ptolemæo; unde Sentinates Plinio, aliisque Sentinas Ager, in quo P. Decius Cos. IV se, exemplum Patris imitatus, pro salute Populi Romani, Dijs Manibus devovit: de quo facto legendi Livius lib. x, Eutropius lib. II, Orosius lib. III. cap. XXI, Valerius Maximus lib. V. Dictorum Factorumque Memorabilium cap. VI, & alij. Sentinum tamen Nigro est Cerete; Francisco Pamphilo, Salso Ferrato. Livius Agri Sentini diverse ab Sentino in Falliscis facit mentionem.
units.tr: Next after this Palia is a village called Ricorso, Recursus; then Ponte Sentine, or as it is commonly called Ponte Centena, where once stood Sybaris, as Strabo and Ptolemy say. From here the Sentinates of Pliny and others, and the Sentinas Ager, in which P. Decius, consul for the fourth time, imitating his father's example, devoted himself for the safety of the Roman People to the gods of the dead. On this deed one should read Livy book x, Eutropius book II, Orosius book III, chapter XXI, Valerius Maximus book V, chapter VI of his Memorable Deeds and Sayings, and others. Sentinum, however, is Cerete to Niger and Salso Ferrato to Francesco Pamphilo. Livy mentions the Agri Sentini as distinct from the Sentino in the Falisci.

units.la: Nan Vkerius Viterius inter Montes ad Pelæ dextram Procenum occurrit, infraque Soranum; de inde propter Amnem incedenti furtim in Colle præcipitique Monte Civitas adparet Orivectum.
units.tr: Now, going up through the mountains to the right of the Paglia, Viterbo's Uckerius meets Procenum, and below it Soranum; then, travelling secretly along the river, a city appears on a hill and a steep mountain: Orivectum.

units.la: Orbitum vocari scribitur in Edicto Desiderij Langhardorum Regis; Oropitum, Antonino; Oropite, Catoni. Per me licet fides ab aliis fiet. Vrbevetanum, & Vrbs Vetana distinctum, videtur dici Procopio lib. 1. & 11, de Bello Gothico: Vrbs Vetus Paullo Diacono in Langbardicis. Herbannum forte Plinio lib. 111. nat. Hist. cap. v. De Herbano vide, si otium, quæ habet ex Myrsilo suo Annius Viterbiensis: adde, si lubet, quæ apud eumdem de Oropito. Leonardus Aretinus & Flavius Blondus scribunt Vrbem hanc ab Florentinis ortam, nec supra mille annos ante te natos ullam eius memoriam inveniri. Sita est in excelsi & præcipitis montis, quæque Flumine & Rivulis circumdatus, verticem plana, sine Muris, quorum vice Rupibus undique præruptis altiq, cingitur, natura hoc modo creatis, ut ex summa crepidine despectum in ima perquam horribilem habeant. Cœlo est iucundissimo, præterquam autumnali tempore, quum in Amne adcurrente Pelia Cannabis solet macerari: tum enim Aër fœtore illo correptus corruptusque Colonis est molestissimus. Templum primarium Porphyretico Marmore est incrustatum; Vestibulum Pario, quod elegantes Statuæ Picturæque summorum Artificum decorant: Templi Fenestræ sunt ex Alabastrite; nec aliter, ac Vitrum, perlucidæ. Sunt hic Ædes splendidissimæ ab Urbano v. P. M. anno cIↄ ccccxvii factæ. Fons ibidem profundissimus ab Clemente vii in rupe excisus; ad Introitum cuius legitur:
units.tr: Orbitum is said to be called so in the edict of Desiderius, King of the Lombards; Oropitum in Antoninus, Oropite in Cato. Let others judge whether this is credible; for my part I leave it. Vrbevetanum and Vrbs Vetana, distinguished from each other, seem to be named by Procopius in books I and II of the Gothic War; Vrbs Vetus by Paul the Deacon in his Lombard history. Herbannum perhaps in Pliny, book III of the Natural History, chapter v. About Herbano, if you have leisure, see what Annius of Viterbo has from his Myrsilus; add, if you like, what the same author says about Oropito. Leonardo Bruni of Arezzo and Flavio Biondo write that this city was founded by the Florentines, and that no memory of it can be found earlier than a thousand years before you were born. It is situated on the top of a high and steep mountain, surrounded by a river and streams; its summit is flat and without walls, for which rocks, steep on every side and high, serve instead, formed by nature in such a way that from the top edge they have a very frightful view down into the depths. The air is most pleasant, except in autumn, when the hemp is usually steeped in the river Paglia as it runs in; then the air, tainted and corrupted by that stench, is most troublesome to the inhabitants. The principal church is encrusted with porphyry marble; its vestibule is decorated with Parian marble and with elegant statues and paintings by the greatest artists; the church windows are of alabaster, and as transparent as glass. Here are very splendid buildings, erected by Urban V, Supreme Pontiff, in the year 1317. A very deep spring, cut into the rock by Clement VII, is there as well; at its entrance is inscribed:

units.la: Quod Natura Munimento inviderat, Industria adjecit:
units.tr: What Nature had denied as a defence, Industry added:

units.la: Profunditas dicitur ccliii. Cubitorum.
units.tr: The depth is said to be 253 cubits.

units.la: Pergamus Glanim transgressi: quem inter & Tiberim Opida sunt Garnaiolæ Monte Lion; Prœve, Latinè scribentibus Plebes; ulteriusque Cortona. Sic hodie, sic olim, notantibus Livio lib. ix & xxii, Silioque Italico lib. viii; sic Κορτώνα inquam, Polybio lib. iii, & Ptolemæo lib. iii. cap. i dicitur: quæ Κόρτων Stephano. Distinguit Dionysius Halicarnass. lib. i. Antiq. Roman, Κόρτων, ait, Colonia Romanorum Κορτώνα nuper appellata est. Κοζυρία exprimitur in Editione Roberti Stephani. Ab Cortona Cortonenses Plinio lib. iii. cap. v. Censet Volaterranus Cortonam antea dictum Cortum, cuius aliquoties mentio apud Virgilium: quod mihi non probatur. Alia est Κρότων Ptolemæo in Magna Græcia ad Sinum Tarentinum; quæ hodie Crotone; quamque Lauram quondam appellatam testatur Isacius Tzetza. Livius Cortonam, Perusiam, & Aretium Capita Etruriæ Populorum nominat libro ix. Episcopum huic Vrbi dedit Ioannes xxii. P. M. parte illi ex Diœcesi Aretina attributa. Leguntur Aretini cap-
units.tr: Passing the Glanis, we come to the towns between it and the Tiber: Garnaiola, Monte Lion; Prœve, which Latin writers call Plebes; and further on, Cortona. So it is named today and so it was named of old, as Livy notes in books 9 and 22, and Silius Italicus in book 8. Polybius in book 3 and Ptolemy in book 3, chapter 1, call it Κορτώνα [Kortōna]; Stephanus gives Κόρτων [Kortōn]. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, in book 1 of the Roman Antiquities, distinguishes the two: Κόρτων [Kortōn], he says, a Colony of the Romans, was lately called Κορτώνα [Kortōna]. Robert Estienne's edition gives Κοζυρία [Kozyria]. Pliny in book 3, chapter 5, gives the inhabitants as the Cortona Cortonenses. Volaterranus thinks that Cortona was formerly called Cortum, which Virgil mentions several times; I do not accept this. Ptolemy's Κρότων [Krotōn] is another place, in Magna Graecia on the Gulf of Taranto, today Crotone; Isaac Tzetzes records that it was once called Laura. In book 9 Livy names Cortonam, Perusiam and Aretium as the chief cities of the peoples of Etruriae. Pope John XXII made Cortona a bishopric, assigning to it part of the diocese of Arezzo. The Aretini are read

units.la: tam tám muris nudasse, pestimeque habitam duro tenuisse imperio. Principatum inde invasit Fgutio: quo ob infames Mores obtruncato Ladislaus Neapolitanorum Rex Vrbem, quae in ejus Ditionem venerat, vendidit Florentinis; quorum potestati jamnunc subjecta est. Nobilitarunt eam superioribus annis Silvius Cardinalis, & Jacobus Perusinorum Episcopus.
units.tr: ...to have stripped the city of its walls, and, having held it as a plague, kept it under a harsh rule. Afterwards Fgutio seized the principate; because of his infamous morals he was cut down, and Ladislaus, King of the Neapolitans, sold the city, which had come under his control, to the Florentines, to whose authority it is now subject. In recent years it has been made famous by Cardinal Silvius and by James, Bishop of Perugia.

units.la: Agro Cortonensi Petra Malã Castellum est, origine clarorum nobilis Familiae PetraMalarum Aretinae. Deinde est Crucifix Guidonis Petramalae opus, in loco edito. Est tamquam Porta ad multa alia Castella; & ad totum fere Imperium Florentinorum, quod ad eam spectat Partem, infestandum. Haud procul inde secundum Glanum occurrit Castiglione vulgo, Opidum Populo frequens; Iapi I. C, qui Vitas aliquot Plutarchi Latinas fecit, Patria.
units.tr: In the territory of Cortona is the castle of Petra Mala, the origin of the noble family of the Petramali of Arezzo, a family of distinguished men. Next is the Crucifix, the work of Guido of Petramala, in an elevated place. It serves as a gateway to many other castles, and to almost the whole Florentine dominion on that side, for harassing it. Not far from there, along the Glanis, lies Castiglione, as it is commonly called, a town crowded with people, and the birthplace of Iapis, the jurist who made Latin versions of several Lives of Plutarch.

units.la: Offert se mox Septemtrionem versus Arretium, ci co Stadijs Roma distans. Arezzo vocatur vernacule Opidum, quod Arezzo Polybio, Strabonio, & Ptolemaeo: Arretium Livio lib.ix & Plinio libro xxxv. cap. xii, retinere illud scribenti Valorum in Italia nobilitatem (qua de re & Martialis lib.i, alibique) Lateritium quoq; Mutum eidem tribuenti capite, quod mox ibi sequitur, xiv. Uvam denique ejus commendanti lib.xiii. cap.iii. Adretium mendosus legitur in Itineraria Tabula. Inde Aretini Etruriae Populi, eidem Plinio lib.iii. cap.v: cui triplices ibi, suis Cognominibus distincti, Veteres, Fidentiores, Iulienses. Horum autem nonnulli Codices Arretium scribunt. Sic Monimentum, quod Tiferni, vulgo Cita di Castello, in Umbria, in Ara marmorea praegrandi: C ANINIVS. C. F. POM. GALLVS DOMO ARRETIO. C. LEG. III SCHYTH. MILITAVIT. IN PR. AN. XVII EVOC. AN. II I. IN. LEG. IIII. SCHYTIC AN. XVIII. VIXIT AN. IX. MERV. AN. XXXVIII H. S. E. ATIMETVS. L EX TESTAMENTO. F. C
units.tr: Next the road turns north towards Arretium, which lies at a distance of ... stadia from Rome (the figure is garbled in the scan). It is now called Arezzo in the vernacular. Polybius, Strabo and Ptolemy give it its Greek name, while Livy in book 9 and Pliny in book 35, chapter 12, keep the older name Arretium. Pliny in that passage is writing about the nobility of the Varii in Italy (Martial also treats this in book 1 and elsewhere). In the following chapter, 14, Pliny assigns to the same place the Lateritium Mutum, and in book 13, chapter 3, he commends its grapes. The Itinerary Table reads Adretium, a mistake. From here come the Aretini, a people of Etruria, as Pliny says in book 3, chapter 5, where he distinguishes three divisions by their own surnames: the Veteres, Fidentiores and Iulienses. Some manuscripts of these write Arretium. So too the monument at Tifernum, now Città di Castello, in Umbria, on a very large marble altar, reads: Gaius Caninius Gallus, son of Gaius, of the Pomptine tribe, from Arretium, of the Third Legion Scythica, served as a soldier and was promoted; he served seventeen years and was called up for a second term at the age of ... ; he then served in the Fourth Legion Scythica for eighteen years. He lived nine years and earned thirty-eight years. Here he lies. Atimetus, his freedman, had this made at his own cost, according to the will.

units.la: Dictam volunt varie varij ab Arii, Aratura, Ariditate: Annius Viterbiensis suo more ab Veta Aretia, Iani Conjuge. Urbs hodie jucundis amoenisque in Campis sita; Agro, qui Frumenti, Vini, ceterarumque Frugum abunde fertilis. Magna quondam adfecit Clade L. Cornelius Sulla. Inde, Imperio Romano declinante, ab Gothis Langobardisque male admodum habitat imox Florentinorum Bellis non semel vexata; hinc civilibus agitata Factionibus Gibellinorum & Guelphorum ingentes accepit Calamitates, potestatem Urbis aliquamdiu tenentibus Ubertinis & Petramalis: postremo Florentinis vendita, postque defectionem ab ipsidem in ditionem aliquoties redacta, tandem Karoli V. Imperatoris auctoritate, ex voto Clementis VII. P. M. Alexandro Medici, quem Principem Florentinum ille appellarat, in perpetuum est concessa. Episcopatus floret dignitate. Fuit inter Praesules Arretinos D. Donatus; quem Martyrio hic affectum constat sub Valentiniano Augusto. Edidit Viros Claros non paucos: in quis Laurentius & Peregrinus ob Fidem in Christum sub Diocletiano necati, ibique siti: item Maecenas, quem Aretij natum Macrobius ex Epistola quadam Augusti docet; indicantibus idem Horatio, aliisque multis Scriptoribus. Nati & hic Ludovicus Brunus & Carolus Aretinus, qui, Florentinae Reip. à Secretis alter alteri succedens, multa è Graecis in Latinum transtulerunt sermonem. Aretini quoque sunt Ioannes Tertellius, Franciscus, qui praeter alia Phalaridis Epistolas Latinas fecit, Angelus Gambalionus I.C, Petrus Accoltus Cardinalis, Petrus Aretinus; omnes Scriptis nobiles.
units.tr: Various people have given various derivations of the name: from Arius, from ploughing (aratura), or from dryness (ariditas). Annius of Viterbo, in his usual way, derives it from Veta Aretia, the wife of Janus. The city today lies in pleasant, agreeable fields, and its territory is abundantly fertile in grain, wine and other crops. It once suffered a great disaster at the hands of L. Cornelius Sulla. Later, as the Roman Empire declined, it was very badly treated by the Goths and Lombards. Then it was often harassed by the wars of the Florentines, and, troubled by the civil factions of the Ghibellines and Guelphs, it suffered huge calamities, while the Ubertini and Petramali held power in the city for some time. At last it was sold to the Florentines. After revolting from them and being brought back under their rule several times, it was finally granted in perpetuity, by the authority of the Emperor Charles V and at the wish of Clement VII, supreme pontiff, to Alexander de' Medici, whom Clement had named Prince of Florence.
