The bishopric flourishes in dignity. Among the bishops of Arezzo was D. Donatus, who is known to have been martyred here under the Emperor Valentinian. The city has produced not a few famous men: Laurentius and Peregrinus, who were put to death under Diocletian for their faith in Christ and lie buried there; likewise Maecenas, whom Macrobius, from a certain letter of Augustus, shows to have been born at Arezzo, as Horace and many other writers also indicate. Born here too were Ludovico Bruni and Carlo Aretino, who, each succeeding the other as secretary of the Florentine Republic, translated much from Greek into Latin. Also from Arezzo are Giovanni Tortelli, Francesco (who, among other things, made Latin versions of the Letters of Phalaris), Angelo Gambiglioni the jurist, Pietro Accolti the cardinal, and Pietro Aretino; all are noted for their writings.

units.la: Haud procul Aretso, Tiberim versus, Opida sunt ad Fluvium Cerfonem, Citerna: & trans Souariam, Angularium, Anghiari vulgo, à quo ad Tiberim millia sunt iii. Sursum ad eumdem Fluvium Montedoglio, Monte-Doglio, se aperit: inde Fanum S. Stephani, & inter Montes Caprefium, Totilae Gothorum Regis morte inclutum. Vide Procopium lib. iii. de Bello Gothico, cui Capra nominatur. Altius hinc alia sunt exigua circa Tiberis Fontem Opida, non magni momenti. Infra Citernam Amnis est Ctereo: trans eum in Collibus Mons D. Mariæ; inde Mons Alianus & Sorbellum.
units.tr: Not far from Arezzo, towards the Tiber, lie towns on the river Cerfone: Citerna; and beyond the Sovara, Angularium, commonly called Anghiari, which is three miles from the Tiber. Further up the same river Montedoglio opens out; then Fanum S. Stephani, and among the mountains Caprefium, famous for the death of Totila, King of the Goths. See Procopius, book 3 of the Gothic War, where it is called Capra. Higher up from here are other small towns around the source of the Tiber, of no great importance. Below Citerna flows the river Ctereo. Beyond it, on the hills, is Mons D. Mariæ; then Mons Alianus and Sorbellum.

units.la: Nerone transito, Perusia in Colle cernitur: Mox in circuitu Thrasumeni Lacus Vici Opidaque multa nominatim Ossina, Opiarta, ab ossibus exterorum Romanorum, ut putatur, dicta. Nam eo loco Romanos Hannibal cecidit ob temeritatem C Flaminii, qui & ipse cum maxima Legionum parte occisus est, scribentibus plene Polybio lib. iii, Livio lib. xxii, Plutarcho in vita Hannibalis, Orosio libro iv. cap. xv, Eutropio in Historia Romana, Auctore de VV. Illustribus cap. xiii, Valerio Maximo lib. i. cap. vi, & lib. iii. cap. vii, M. Tullio de Divinatione lib. i; Silio Italico lib. v, Ovidio lib. vi. Fastor. Plinio lib. ii. cap. xxcv, Frontino libro Strateg. i. ii. iv. v & lib. iiii. cap. vii. Sunt ad eumdem Lacum, quæ vulgo Passignana, Forgiotto, Castiglione, Chiusino, Panicale: in Montibus Pantale & Monte Alera, reditque ad Lacum Monte Colonna: tum ultra Cortonam; mox antiquissima Civitas Perusia. Sic Plin. lib. iii. cap. v, Livio non uno in loco, Tacito lib. xvii, & aliis; nuova Ptolemæo lib. iii, πόλεις Appiano Alexandrino lib. v. vocatur, quæ Perusium Eutropio; Perusium
units.tr: Past the Nera, Perusia is seen on a hill. Soon, around the circuit of Lake Trasimene, there are villages and many towns, named Ossina and Opiarta, said to be named from the ossibus [bones] of foreign Romans, as is thought. For at that place Hannibal cut down the Romans, through the rashness of C. Flaminius, who was himself also killed with the greater part of his legions. This is related fully by Polybius in book 3, Livy in book 22, Plutarch in the Life of Hannibal, Orosius in book 4, chapter 15, Eutropius in his Roman History, the author of De viris illustribus, chapter 13, Valerius Maximus in book 1, chapter 6, and in book 3, chapter 7, Cicero in De divinatione book 1, Silius Italicus in book 5, and Ovid in Fasti book 6. Pliny in book 2, chapter 95, and Frontinus in the Strategemata, books 1, 2, 4 and 5, and book 4, chapter 7. Around the same lake are the places commonly called Passignana, Forgiotto, Castiglione, Chiusino, Panicale; on the mountains Pantale & Monte Alera; and Monte Colonna comes back down to the lake. Then beyond Cortonam; soon the most ancient city, Perusia. So Pliny in book 3, chapter 5, Livy in more than one place, Tacitus in book 17 and others; nuova [new town] in Ptolemy book 3; πόλεις [poleis] in Appian of Alexandria book 5; it is called Perusium by Eutropius; Perusium

units.la: Itinerariæ Tabulæ; πόλεις denique fortean Stephano: Hodie antiquo nomine Perugia, recepta Italis Pronunciatione, dicitur. Meminit Perusia Lapis, qui Romæ in domo Andreæ Cavaglieri, ad Campum Floræ:
units.tr: in the Itinerary Table; πόλεις [poleis] finally perhaps in Stephanus. Today it is called by its ancient name, Perugia, in the Italian pronunciation. Perusia is mentioned on a stone which is at Rome in the house of Andrea Cavaglieri, near the Campo de' Fiori:

units.la: C. VITRICIO. C. F. TRO. MAXIMO
units.tr: To Gaius Vitricius Maximus, son of Gaius, of the Tromentina tribe

units.la: P. PERVSIA. MIL. COH. V. FR. MIL. ANN. IIII VIX. ANNOS. XXIIII H. S. E.
units.tr: Publius Perusia, soldier of the fifth cohort, of the Fr... century, served four years and lived twenty-four years. Here he lies.

units.la: Perusiam dictam volunt alij à Perusio Troiano; alij à Perseo. Perusinos originem ab Achæis ducere scribit ex Trogi libro xx Instinus. A Tyrrhenis in Italia conditam, & inter xii Etruria Urbes fuisse, & ob id lunonem Tyrrhenorum more in ea Urbe colitam, memorat Appianus Alexandrinus lib. v. Bellor. Civil. Insigne Perusinorum est Gryphus: quod animal Scythica lingua Perus appellari dicitur. Colonia Vitelia scribitur in Porta Martia, ab C. Vitellio, Achæorum Duce, ut volunt; & Augusta Perusia in alia, ab C. Cæsare Augusto, qui obsessam & dirutam aliquanto post instauravit. Colli insidet Apennini: natura loci permunita. A dificia ficia habet cum publica, tum privata, valde nobilia, ampla, excelsa. Turribus est plena: ex quarum nulla cognosci tota prospectu potest; quod commune illi cum Urbino. Fora sunt bina; Rotundum & Kinenum: In Rotundo Fons est, & Palatium. In Ecclesiae Catedralis Sacrario S. Lucae Evangelium est in cortice scriptum, aureis litteris; & D. Herculani Monimentum, Martyris & Episcopi; cujus se Ossa servare perhibent Cives, uti & Benedicti XI. P.M. Beataeque Columbae. Episcopatus gaudet titulo. In Fundamentis Aedificiorum, quae a Pontifice diruta, repertum est Vulcani Templum, cujus apud Appianum lib. v. sit mentio. Alii volunt eo loco fuisse, ubi nunc D. Angeli Aedes, sub cujus Altari majore Saxum antiquum visitur, Romanis litteris incisum. Verba adscribam, quod ea Patronum Perusinorum praefe-
units.tr: Some hold that Perusia was named after Perusio the Trojan; others after Perseo (Perseus). Justinus, from book 20 of Trogus, writes that the Perusinos trace their origin to the Achæis (Achaeans). Appian of Alexandria, in book 5 of the Civil Wars, records that it was founded by the Tyrrhenis (Tyrrhenians) in Italy, that it was one of the twelve cities of Etruria, and that for this reason Juno was worshipped there in the Tyrrhenian manner. The emblem of the Perusinorum is the griffin, which animal is said to be called Perus in the Scythian tongue. Colonia Vitelia is written of at the Porta Martia, named after Gaius Vitellius, leader of the Achaeans, as some hold; and Augusta Perusia is written of at the other gate, named after Gaius Caesar Augustus, who restored it somewhat later, after it had been besieged and razed. The town sits on a hill of the Apennines, its position naturally well fortified. It has buildings, both public and private, very noble, spacious and lofty. It is full of towers, and none of them can be seen whole from any one viewpoint, a feature it shares with Urbino. There are two fora, the Rotundum and the Kinenum. In the Rotundum there is a fountain and a palace. In the sacristy of the cathedral church the Gospel of St Luke is written on bark in golden letters; there is also the monument of St Herculanus, martyr and bishop, whose bones the citizens claim to keep, as also those of Pope Benedict XI and of the blessed Columba. The bishopric enjoys the title. In the foundations of buildings pulled down by the Pope, a Temple of Vulcan was found, of which there is mention in Appian, book 5. Others think it stood where the church of St Angelo now is, beneath whose high altar an ancient stone can be seen, inscribed with Roman letters. I will set down the words, since they present the patron of the Perusians:

VELDVMNIANVS AVO. KARISSIMO. OB CVIVS DEDICATIONEM. DEDIT DECVRIONIB. *. IL. PLEBI. * I. L. D. D. D In Latere DEDIC. IDIB. IVI IMP. M. AVRELIO. ANTONINO. AVG. PIO. FEL. II Aiter Verjuf sub Terra latet, vel ex ipsus ejs.
units.tr: To Gaius Vibius Gallus Proculeianus, son of Gaius, of the Tromentina tribe, patron of the Perusians, patron of the Vetonenses, curator of the public affairs of the Veteronensians, judge, quinquennial?, decurion, patron of the college of the Centonarii. Vibius Veldumnianus gave this to his dearest grandfather, at whose dedication he gave to the decurions and to the common people, by decree of the decurions. On the side: dedicated on the Ides, in the consulship of the Emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus Pius Felix, for the second time. The rest lies buried under the ground, or from its own...

units.la: Incolae, quorum mediocris est frequentia, animis ingeniisque sunt sumtni; non minus ad Litteras, quam Arma promti. De Rebus, quae ad hanc Urbem olim, vel ab eius Incolis gestae, legendi Livius cum aliis locis, tum lib. vi, ix, x, xxviii, cxxv & sequente, Appianus lib. v. Bellor. Civilium, Florus lib. iv. Histor. Romanae, cap. vii, Eutropius lib. vii, Orosius lib. vi. cap. xvi, Suetonius in Octaviano Augusto cap. xiv, & seq. Plinius lib. vii cap. xiv, Solinus cap. iii. & Propertius lib. ii. Elegia i. Inter omnes Italiae Urbes Felicitatem scribitur a Blondo nacta fere inauditā: quod eamdem penes Status & Rerum conditionem, quae ante Romam conditam, & postea sub Regibus, Coss. Imperatoribus fuit, usque in hunc diem retineat: varias tamen saepius difficultates & calamitates experta, & tam ab externis, Gothis nimirum, Duce Totila (consulendus Procopius lib. iii. de Bello Gothico) Langobardis, & aliis pallas; quam civilibus conturbata Factionibus, praesertim Ghibellinorum & Nobilium Guelphorum. Legendus omnino Leander Albertus. Hodie in Pontificis Romani est Ditione, Arce, quam Cittadellam vocant, accepta cui emolumenta opera per Cives est communata, Nemine in Calce Lapidibusque portandis minuunt: Sacris & profanis aedibus dis-jectis, ut in utrumque Forum pateret. Administratur iustitia a Pontificis Gubernatore: cui xii ex Civium primorum numero, qualicumque Libertatis specie, adjunguntur; habitantes apud S. Laurentium. Academia Perusina circa annum ccxc florere coepit: iisdem ornata Privilegiis, quae in Lutica. C. de Professoribus, qui in Urbe Constantinop. docent, Constantinopolitanae Academiae tribuuntur; uti docent ad eam leg. Bartolus, qui & alibi Privilegia commemorat. Petrus Anchoranus inter Italiae Urbes Iurisprudentia honorabile Perusium scribit. Amplissima sunt Collegia, in quibus annuo Censu Vitae subsidia Studiosis suppeditantur. Est inter alia Collegium Vetus & Novum: vulgo Sapientia Vetus & Nova: quarum illa, D. Gregorio sacra, Episcopo loci, ut Provisori; Haec, D. Hieronymo dicata, Priori Canonico Cathedralis Perusinae, & Consulibus, Mercatoriae vulgo, patet. Apud S. Dominicum insignis est Bibliotheca. Clar-s Viros habuit Perusia non paucos: Sebastianum, Theologum & Astrologum: Nicolaum Columbum, Philosophum & Theologum; Paullum, qui, praeter Collationes, Numerum de Diis Græcorum Latinorumque scriptis; Baldum, Bartoli auditorem, Angeloque eius Filium & Nepotem; Petrum item Baldi Fratrem, & Matthæum Petri Filium: Baldum insuper alterum, cui Filij fuerunt tres ornatissimi, Nicolaus, Apostolicæ Rotæ Auditor, Matthæus magnus Iurisconsultus, & Sigismundus Eques auratus: Sequuti sunt hos Iso Sallustius & Ioannes Petronius ex nobili gente Montuperelli. Alios prætereo. Vixerunt etiam nuper ibi Restaurus Cataldus, & Iacobus Antiquarius, Franciscus Maturantius, Marius Podianus, Franciscus Camenus, Vincentius Herculanus, Gulielmus Pontanus, & alij Scriptis celebres. Agro Perusino, etsi multas adiit & lustravit Regiones Ioannes Campanus, nullam tamen cultiorem amœnioremque se umquam cognovisse scribit. Vasta omnia & montuosa prius intuenti, quum autem propius accedat, nihil cum Agrorum cultu tum benignitate cœli terræque ubertate felicius. Ager sane fructiferis jucunditateque adiungit Collibus, qui Vini, Olei, Ficuum, Pomorum, aliorumque optimorum Fructuum fertilis. Campi adjacent, Tritico ceterisque Frumento copioli. Peculiare de hac Urbe edidit Opusculum Marius Podianus, Orator insignis.
units.tr: The inhabitants, of whom there is a moderate number, are supreme in spirit and talent, no less ready for letters than for arms. Concerning the events that once took place in this city, or were done by its inhabitants, one should read Livy in various places, and especially book 6, 9, 10, 28, 125 and following; Appian, book 5 of the Civil Wars; Florus, book 4 of the Roman History, chapter 7; Eutropius, book 7; Orosius, book 6, chapter 16; Suetonius, in the Life of Augustus, chapter 14 and following; Pliny, book 7, chapter 14; Solinus, chapter 3; and Propertius, book 2, elegy 1. Among all the cities of Italiae (Italy), Blondus writes that Perusia has enjoyed an almost unheard-of felicity, because it has kept to this day the same state and condition of affairs that it had before Rome was founded, and afterwards under the kings, consuls and emperors. Yet it has often experienced various difficulties and calamities, troubled both by outsiders, namely the Goths under their leader Totila (consult Procopius, book 3, On the Gothic War), the Lombards and others, and by civil factions, especially those of the Ghibellinorum & Nobilium Guelphorum (Ghibellines and the Guelph nobles). It must be read in full by Leander Albertus. Today it is under the dominion of the Roman Pontiff. The citadel, which they call the Cittadellam, was received, and its profits were transferred by the citizens' labour; none of them spared work in carrying lime and stones, and sacred and profane buildings were demolished so that there might be an opening into both fora. Justice is administered by the Pope's governor, to whom twelve of the leading citizens are joined, with some sort of appearance of liberty; they live near St Laurence. The Academia Perusina (University of Perugia) began to flourish around the year 290, adorned with the same privileges as the one at Lutica. The law of the Code concerning professors who teach in the city of Constantinople is attributed to the Academy of Constantinople, as Bartolus teaches on that law, and he also records privileges elsewhere. Petrus Anchoranus writes that Perusia is honourable among the cities of Italiae for jurisprudence. The colleges are very large, and in them living support is given to students from an annual income. Among the others there is the Collegium Vetus & Novum, commonly called the Sapientia Vetus & Nova; of these the first, dedicated to St Gregory, the bishop of the place, is open to him as provost; the second, dedicated to St Jerome, is open to the prior, a canon of the Perusian cathedral, and to the consuls of the Mercatoriae (merchants' guild). There is a famous library at St Dominic's. Perusia has had not a few distinguished men: Sebastianum, theologian and astrologer; Nicolaum Columbum, philosopher and theologian; Paullum, who, besides collations, wrote a Number on the gods of the Greeks and Latins; Baldus, the hearer of Bartolus, and his son and grandson Angelus; likewise Petrus, brother of Baldus, and Matthaeus, son of Petrus; and another Baldus, whose three very distinguished sons were Nicolaus, auditor of the Apostolic Rota, Matthaeus, a great jurist, and Sigismundus, a gilded knight. Following these came Iso Sallustius and Ioannes Petronius of the noble family of Montuperelli. I pass over the others. Restaurus Cataldus, Iacobus Antiquarius, Franciscus Maturantius, Marius Podianus, Franciscus Camenus, Vincentius Herculanus, Gulielmus Pontanus and others famous for their writings have also lived there recently. Of the territory of Perugia, although Ioannes Campanus visited and surveyed many regions, he writes that he never knew any more cultivated or pleasant. At first sight everything is wild and mountainous, but as one comes nearer, nothing is more fortunate both in the cultivation of the fields and in the mildness of the sky and the fertility of the land. The land is indeed rich in fruitful hills and pleasant places, abundant in wine, oil, figs, apples and other excellent fruits. The plains adjoining it are well supplied with wheat and other grain. Marius Podianus, an outstanding orator, published a special little work on this city.

units.la: A Perusia deorsum inter Montes est Cerqueto. Mox trans Amnem Nestorem Opida, Monte Petriolo, Meriaiello, Monte Veiano, & Campignano; utraque Tiberim versus Marcia, inferius Colle Lungo, Ripabella, Monte Castello & Cerrara.
units.tr: Below Perusia, among the mountains, is Cerqueto. Soon, across the River Nestor, are the towns of Monte Petriolo, Meriaiello, Monte Veiano and Campignano, both towards the Tiber on the Marcia; further down, Colle Lungo, Ripabella, Monte Castello and Cerrara.

units.la: Aperit se inde trans Paliam Amnem Falisco rum Ager. De Falisci universim antea dixi. In eorum Opidis recensendis ab Mari ortus (relicta tamen ora littorali, quæ supra mihi descripta) Sortactem, qui limes Faliscos inter & Vejentes, versus incedam. Initium igitur esto Pittianum Opidum nobile Ursinorum, titulo Comitatus inclutum. Vicinum illi Farnesium, Gente Farnesiorum Romana, ex qua cum Paulo III. P. M. magni Viri prodierunt, clarum; Patria etiam Petri Ancharani IC. lic dicti, quod Ancharani Castelli esset Dominus. Paullum infra Farnesium Castrum est, adeo omni ex aditu rupibus cavernisque septum, ut accedentes in Speculum obscurum, Ferisque habitarum potius duci videantur, quam in Urbem, hominum cœtu cultam & frequentatam. Nobilitavit eam ortu suo Paulus IC. qui inde Castrensis. Deinceps Via, quæ Saxna Romam ducit, ad Paliam Flumen est Aqua pendens: Opidum oblongum, & in Monte positum; vulgo Acqua pendente: Ἀκκαλα Ptolemæo; unde Aquenses forte a Plinio, qui eos Taurinos cognominat.
units.tr: From there the territory of the Falisci opens up across the river Palia. I have already spoken of the Falisci in general. In listing their towns, starting from the sea (leaving aside the coastal shore, which I have described above), I will proceed inland towards the Sortacte, which forms the boundary between the Falisci and the Veientes. Let the beginning be Pittianum, a noble town of the Orsini, famous for its title of county. Near it is Farnese, famous as the seat of the Roman family of the Farnesi, from which came the great man Pope Paul III. Also the homeland of Pietro Ancarano, the jurist so called because he was lord of the castle of Ancarano. A little below Farnese is the castle of Faleria, so enclosed on every approach by rocks and caverns that those who approach seem to enter a dark cave and a dwelling of wild beasts rather than a town filled with a community of men. Paolo the jurist ennobled it by his birth, and from there he is called "of Castro". Next, the road that leads from Sassa to Rome reaches the river Palia, where there is Acquapendente: an elongated town set on a hill, commonly called Acquapendente; Ptolemy calls it Akkala, and perhaps the Acquenses are named from it by Pliny, who calls them Taurini.

units.la: Hinc ad Lacum Vulsinium Bolsena est, Vestigijs inædificatum antiquissimæ Vulsinensium Urbis; quæ Vo sinium Plinio; Ἀλτινων Strabonis, Ἰολτινων Ptolemæo; Volsinum, Itinerariæ Tabulæ; Vulsinum Livio; Vulsiny multitudinis numero eidem Plinio, Antonino, Capitolinus Tabulis, Tacito initio libri iv, ubi dicit Ælium Seianum Vulsinum natum. Sic Iuvenalis in Satyris: Quis tamet, aut timuit gelida Præneste ruinam? Aut positus nemorosa inter tuga Vollinijs, aut Simplicibus Gabiis, aut prono Tiburis arce?
units.tr: From there, towards Lake Vulsinius, is Bolsena, built on the traces of the ancient city of the Volsinienses, which is Volsinum in Pliny; Strabo's Altinon [Ἀλτινων], Ptolemy's Oltinon [Ἰολτινων]; Volsinum in the Itinerary tables; Vulsinum in Livy; Vulsinii by number of inhabitants in the same Pliny, in Antoninus, in the Capitoline tables; in Tacitus at the beginning of book 4, where he says that Aelius Sejanus was born at Vulsinii. So Juvenal in the Satires: "Who has feared the cold ruin of Praeneste? Or who, placed among the wooded hills of Volsinii, or the simple Gabii, or the steep citadel of Tibur?"

units.la: Sic Auctor de Viris Illustribus cap. xxxvi: Volsinij Etruriæ nobile oppidum. Volsiniensem Urbem, Caput Etruriæ vocat Valerius Maximus. A Postumio Cos. olim vastata legitur; deinde Servorum conspiratione aliquando occupata; quo tempore, Civibus auxilia a Pop. Ro. petentibus, Decius Murena cum exercitu missus Dominos ab Servorum Imperio vindicavit, ut tradunt, præter Livium, Florus lib. i Hist. Rom. cap. xxi, Eutropius lib. ii, Orosius lib. iv. cap. v, Auctor de V V. Illustr. cap. xxxvi, Valerius Maximus lib. ix, cap. i. Sed & Plinius lib. ii. nat. Hist. cap. xii hanc Urbem totam fere Fulmine concrematam tradit. Respicit ad Calamitatem illam Iuvenalis, quum ad superiora pergit: Nos Urbem columen tenui tibicine fultam Magna parte sus. Namsi labentibus obstat Villicus, & veteres rima contexit hiatum; Securos pendente tubet dormire ruina. Vivendum est illic, ubi nulla incendia, nulli Noctè metuq, Urbs nec mille pericula fœvæ.
units.tr: Thus the author of De Viris Illustribus, chapter 36: "Volsinii, a noble town of Etruria." Valerius Maximus calls the city of Volsinii the capital of Etruria. It is read that it was once laid waste by the consul Postumius, and later seized by a conspiracy of slaves. At that time the citizens asked the Roman people for help, and Decius Murena was sent with an army and freed the masters from the rule of their slaves, as they relate. This is recorded besides by Livy, Florus (Roman History, book 1, chapter 21), Eutropius (book 2), Orosius (book 4, chapter 5), the author of De Viris Illustribus (chapter 36), and Valerius Maximus (book 9, chapter 1). Pliny too (Natural History, book 2, chapter 12) records that this city was almost entirely burned by lightning. Juvenal refers to that disaster when he goes on to the lines above: "We live in a city propped up by a thin prop, and largely by a rotten beam. If the caretaker holds back the sagging walls, and a crack in the old wall covers the gap, he orders the careless to sleep beneath the hanging ruin. One must live there, where there are no fires, no nightly fear, and the city is free of a thousand savage dangers."

units.la: De Volsinis notandum & quod Plinius scribit ejusdem libri cap. xxiii: Exstat, inquit, Annalium memoria, Sacris quibusdam & Precationibus vel legi fulmina vel imperari, trari. Vetus fama Etruriæ est, impetratum, Volsinios Urbem Agris depopulatis subeunte Monitro, quod vocavere Voltam, evocatum & à Porsenafuo Rege. Antiquitatem Vrbis testantur vetustissima cum suis Inscriptionibus Marmora. Hodie deleta est, & in Villam propemodum conversa. Servare se dicunt Incolæ Corpus D. Christinæ Virginis: memorant etiam Hostia consecrata Miraculum, ab aliis descriptum. Plinius tantæ felicitatis Agrum Urbis esse perhibet, ut Oleæ ibi post primum, quo facæ, annum sint fœcundæ, & fructum ferant. Vina producit cum primis nobilia, præsertim vero Apiana.
units.tr: Also to be noted about Volsinii is what Pliny writes in the same book, chapter 23: "There is a record in the annals that by certain sacred rites and prayers the lightning could be called down or turned away. It is an old tradition of Etruria that the Volsinians obtained this when their fields were laid waste, a warning coming from Monitor, whom they called Volta, and that he was summoned out and driven off by King Porsenna." The ancient marbles with their inscriptions bear witness to the age of the city. Today it is destroyed and has almost been turned into a country house. The inhabitants say that they keep the body of the holy virgin Christina, and they also relate a miracle of a consecrated host, described by others. Pliny says that the land of the city was so fruitful that olive trees planted there bore fruit from the first year. It produces wines of the highest quality, especially the Apian.

units.la: Ad dextram Bolsenæ Opida se offerunt S. Laurentij, Grotte, Gradoli, in Collibus; paulloque ulterius, inter Montes, Valentano, Ditionis Farnesiorum. Rursus ad La cum Capo di Monte & Marta. Larthe seppolitito Catoni. Hinc versus Meridiem ad Martam Fluvium Tusanella est, pervetustum & nobile opidum, Ditionis Ecclesiæ Romanæ: Tuscana Itinerariæ Tabulæ. De eius Origine & Nomine Annius Viterbiensis; quibus, ut nec quæ apud Leandrum Albertum, hic recensendis non immorabor. Nugas avertari soleo, si quis alius, sed immorabor.
units.tr: On the right of Bolsena lie the towns of San Lorenzo, Grotte and Gradoli on the hills; and a little further on, among the mountains, Valentano, which belongs to the Farnese domain. Again toward Lake Bolsena, Capodimonte and Marta. Larthe ... to Cato. From here, toward the south, on the river Marta, is Tuscanella, a very ancient and noted town, in the jurisdiction of the Roman Church; it is the Tuscana of the Itinerary tables. Annius of Viterbo wrote about its origin and name; since I do not want to linger over these things, nor over what Leandro Alberti says, I pass them by. I usually turn away from such trifles, whoever writes them, but I will linger a little.

units.la: Superato Marta, furtum ad Lacum, itinere, quod Viterbum ducit, Lucum, qui Bosco di Monte Fiascone vulgo audit, transgressis occurrit Mons Fiasconus, vel, ut alij scribunt, Phasconus, vernacule Monte Fiascone, oppidum præcelso in Colle. Φαλισ- ser Straboni lib. v. Φαλίσκ, inquit Stephanus, πόλις Ιταλίας, ἀπεικ. Argiv. Colonia, ait Plinius lib. iii. cap. v, Falisca Argis orto ut auctor est Cato) quæ cognominatur Etruscorum. Frontinus de Coloniis: Colonia Junonia, quæ appellatur Falisca. Apud Diodorum Φιλίσκο. πόλιν reperio ἐκ τ Φαλίσκων ὄντες. Falisci multitudinis numero Eutropio libro 1, & Auctori de Viris Inlustr. cap. xxiii. Falery Plutarcho in Vitis, Macrobio lib. 1. Saturn. & Livio lib. v, cui Falisci sunt Populi, Falerij autem Faliscorum Vrbs. Faleros lego in Itineraria Tabula. Ex Variorum Auctorum collatione deprehenditur omnino esse ea, quam ob munitissimum loci naturam Situm longo bello L. Furius Camillus obsedit; eique Ludi magister, abductis clam in Hostium Castra Principum & Nobilissimorum Civium liberis, prodere est conatus. Legendi Livius libro indicato, Valerius Maximus lib. vi, cap. v, Frontinus lib. iv. cap. iii, Auctor de VV. Inlustr. cap. xxiii, Florus lib. 1 cap. xii, Plutarchus in Camilli Vita. Nonnulli tamen, inter quos Antonius Massa videndus & Leander Albertus) Faleros aliam ab Falisca Urbem statuentes, censent Faleriorum ruinas etiamnum hodie Falaro nomen retinere; & iuxta Campum esse Falartensem. Iuvare videtur eos nonnihil Solinus in Polyhist. cap. viii ab Alesso Argivo Faliscam, ab Falerio Argivo Faleros trahens. Certe quod Opidum Falery Livio & Φαλισια non uno loco Dionysio Halicarnasseo; Falisci vocatur in eadem Historia Eutropio, Auctorique de VV. Inlustr. Faleros autem vel Faliscum idem esse Opidum cum eo, quod hodie Mons Fiasconus, inde patet, quod Livius lib. v. scribat Faleros difficilioris fuisse aditus, asperis contragositque circa, & partim artis, partim arduis Vijs; quodque, ut canit Ovidius, difficilis Clivis Via in Urbem præbuerit Iter: non autem aliud in Faliscorum Montibus Opidum inveniatur eius naturæ, quam quod Mons Fiasconus vernacule. Conditum, Ovidius auctor est, ab Alesso, quum inquit: Argiva est Pompa facies: Agamemnone caso Et sceleus & patrias fugit Alesus opes. Iamque peregratus Profugus terraque marique Mænia felici condidit alta manu: Ille suos docuit Innonia Sacra Falisos.
units.tr: Having crossed the Marta, and going to the lake by the road that leads to Viterbo, one passes the grove called in common speech Bosco di Monte Fiascone, and there meets Monte Fiascone, or, as others write, Fiascone (in the vernacular Monte Fiascone), a town on a very high hill. Straboh (book 5) writes Φαλισ-; Stephanus says "Φαλίσκ [Falisk] is a city of Italy"; Pliny (book 3, chapter 5) calls it the colony of Argos, Falisca, as Cato says it was founded by Argives, and it is called the town of the Etruscans. Frontinus, in On Colonies: "The Junonian colony, which is called Falisca." In Diodorus I find Φιλίσκο, a city from the Falisci [Φαλίσκων]. Eutropius (book 1) and the author of De Viris Illustribus (chapter 23) speak of the Falisci as a people; Plutarch in the Lives, Macrobius (Saturnalia, book 1), and Livy (book 5) call the town Falery, for Livy's Falisci are a people and Falerii is the city of the Falisci. In the Itinerary tables I read Faleros. From comparing various authors it is clear that this is the place which L. Furius Camillus besieged in a long war, because of the very strong natural position; and the schoolmaster then tried to betray it, by secretly leading the children of the leading and most noble citizens into the enemy camp. Read Livy in the book indicated, Valerius Maximus (book 6, chapter 5), Frontinus (book 4, chapter 3), the author of De Viris Illustribus (chapter 23), Florus (book 1, chapter 12), and Plutarch in the Life of Camillus. Some, however, among whom Antonio Massa should be consulted, and Leandro Alberti, hold that Faleri was a different city from Falisca, and think the ruins of Faleri still today keep the name Falaro, and that Falerno lies near the plain. Solinus in his Polyhistor (chapter 8), deriving Falisca from Alesus the Argive and Faleros from Falerius the Argive, seems to lend these people some support. Certainly the town that Livy calls Falerii, and Dionysius of Halicarnassus in more than one place calls Φαλισια, is called Falisci by Eutropius and the author of De Viris Illustribus in the same history. That Faleros or Falisca is the same town as what is now Monte Fiascone is clear from this: Livy (book 5) writes that Faleros had a difficult approach, surrounded by rough and steep ground, partly on cliffs and partly on high roads; and as Ovid sings, the steep road offered the way into the city; no other town in the mountains of the Falisci has a site of this kind except Monte Fiascone, in the vernacular. Ovid is the authority that it was founded by Alesus, when he says: "The Argive procession has its appearance: after Agamemnon's death, Alesus fled both crime and his paternal wealth. And now, a wanderer and exile by land and sea, he built high walls with a fortunate hand. He taught the Falisci the rites of Juno."

units.la: Sic Solinus: Ab Alesso Argivo Faliscam; à Falerio Argivo Faleros. Ita Manuscriptum legit Volumen, quod optimæ notæ servatur in Bibliotheca Lugduno Batava: sequitur Vulgata, A Phalero Argiva Faliscam: malo contraque auctoritatem Ovidij. Falerij Simulacrum Iani Quadrifontis Romam advectum, notat Macrobius lib. 1. Saturnal. Ager huius Opidi peramœnus fructiferis nitet Collibus.
units.tr: Thus Solinus: "from Alesus the Argive, Falisca; from Falerius the Argive, Faleros." So the manuscript volume reads, which is kept in the Leiden library of the highest quality; the Vulgate follows: "from Phalerus the Argive, Falisca." I prefer the authority of Ovid. Macrobius (Saturnalia, book 1) notes that a statue of four-faced Janus was brought to Rome from Falerii. The land of this town, very pleasant, shines with fruitful hills.

units.la: Dextra tum inter Montes Balneo-Regium est, Ragnerea vulgo; Roda in Edicto Desideri Regis, si fides illi. Locus hic est, quem Plinius Novem-Pagos dicit. Male apud Volaterranum Decem-Pagi nominantur. Balneo-Regium ortu D. Bonaventura, Cardinalis & Doctoris ex Ordine Minorum, est nobile. Opida inde se offerunt, quæ vernavernacule Gratignano, Specciano, Ituerbiano, Romarzo, Minerano, Bassino: mox ad Confluentia Narìs & Tiberis Horta Civitas. Sic Paullo Diacono vocatur, quæ Hortanum, Plinio Orta, Antonio Massæ: Orti vel Horti, vulgo. Antiquissima licet sit, nulla tamen eius apud Veteres Scriptores mentio. Horti ad Meridiem Opidum est Basanello: à quo Lacus, Vadimonis olim cognominatus, hodie Lago di Vassanello. De eo alibi.
units.tr: On the right, among the mountains, is Bagno Regio, commonly called Ragnerea; Roda, in the edict of King Desiderius, if one trusts it. This is the place Pliny calls Novem-Pagi (Nine Villages). Wrongly, in Volaterranus, it is named Decem-Pagi (Ten Villages). Bagno Regio is noble for the birth of St. Bonaventure, cardinal and teacher of the Order of Friars Minor. From there the towns come into view which in the vernacular are called Gradignano, Specciano, Ituerbiano, Romarzo, Minerano, Bassano; then, at the confluence of the Nar and the Tiber, the city of Horta. Paul the Deacon calls it Hortanum; Pliny, Orta; Antonio Massa, Orti or Horti, in common speech. Although it is very ancient, there is no mention of it among the ancient writers. To the south of Horti is the town of Basanello, from which the lake, once called Vadimo, is now called Lago di Vassanello. I will say more about it elsewhere.

units.la: Sequitur versus Orientem Gallesium, Gallese vulgo. Patria Nicolai P. M. Referre creditur nomen Halesi, quem antea Falisca Gentis Auctorem ex Ovidio & Solino dixi. Adiudicatum est, quemadmodum & alia huius Regionis Opida, super Topho, tupis altissimis remanentibus, excisis: cuius figura in oblongum rendens Orbem, perinde similis est oblongo Pyrgo ita ut pars, quæ lactor, Orientem respiciat. Plura de hoc Opido Antonius Matta, ipse Gallesius.
units.tr: Next, toward the east, is Gallesio, in common speech Gallese. It is believed to be the homeland of Pope Nicholas III. It is thought the name recalls Halesus, whom I earlier said was the founder of the Falisci, according to Ovid and Solinus. It has been decided, as with other towns of this region, that it was cut out above the tufa, with very high cliffs left standing; its shape, stretching into an oblong circle, is much like an oblong tower, so that the part which is the left side faces the east. Antonio Massa, himself of Gallesio, writes more about this town.

units.la: Succedit huic Corchianum, quod ab Horchia, Etruriæ Dea; Pomona Latinis, dictum censetur: unde & aliud Vicorchianum, quam Vicus Horchianus sub Cymino Monte. Corchiano confinet Ignanelli, & ulterius Falerianum: item ad Tiberim Burgetum S. Leonardi, Vicus lautus, ad Ius Dominiumque Xenodochii S. Spiritus Saffiam Romæ pertinens, & ab Veneto Milite anno MDXXVII[?] incendio maiore ex parte vastatus. Tertio hinc per ripam Tiberinam lapide perve tusta est Turris, ubi transitus Tiberis, quæ della Regina cognominatur.
units.tr: Next comes Corchiano, which is thought to be named from Horchia, goddess of Etruria, called Pomona by the Latins; hence also another place, Vicorchiano, which is the village of Horchianus under Mount Cimino. Next to Corchiano lie Ignanelli, and further on Falerano; likewise on the Tiber Borghetto di San Leonardo, a pleasant village, under the jurisdiction and lordship of the hospice of the Holy Spirit in Sassia, which belongs to Rome, and which was largely laid waste by a great fire set by Venetian soldiers in 1527 [?]. Third from here, along the Tiber bank, is a tower of stone, very old, where the Tiber is crossed, which is called della Regina.

units.la: A Burgeto per antiquæ Viæ Flaminiæ Vestigia, post octavum Milliare Civitas Castellana præcelsis in rupibus occurrit. Putant quidam Veiorum hanc Urbem fuisse, decennium ab Romanis obsessam. Sed repugnare videntur Dionysius Halicarnassæus & Plinius. Is enim lib. II. scribit Veiorum Opidum non ultra centesimum ab Urbe Stadium abfuisse: hic autem lib. III. cap. VI. tradit, Veientes iuxta Tiberim, Urbemque Caenam ab Fidena, Vaticano, & Ianiculo P. M. XIII fuisse distantem. Civitatem autem Castellanam haud minus XXV P. M. Stadiisve ducentis Roma distare nullus, Locorum illius tractus non ignarus, ambigit. Alia Argumenta, quæ ex Livio, ubi de Irruere Trecentorum Fabiorum, quis colligere potest, præterco. Aliud igitur quærendum est antiquum huic Civitati Nomen. Verisimile, fuisse Urbem, quæ Fescennia Plinio; Φασκινιον Dionysio Halicarnassæo. Inde Fescennina Acies apud Virgilium lib. VII Æneidos, ad quem mirum est Servium Fescennium Opidum in Planicie scribere, quum & alia Loca, quæ Virgilius ibi memorat, & Civitas Castellana præcelsis in rupibus, ut antea dixi, sint sita. Dicendum forte Servium ignoratione quadam confundere cum Fescennio Falisiorum aliud Fescennium, quod in Campania. Ab Fescennio autem Etruscorum Fescennini dicebantur Versus: de quorum origine sic canit Horatius: Agricolæ prisci, fortes, parvoque beati, Condita post frumenta levantes tempore festo Corpus, & ipsum Animum spe finis dura ferentem, Cum Socio operum, & Pueris, & Coniuge fida Tellurem Porco, Silvanum Lacte piabant, Floribus & Vino Genium, memores brevis ævi. Fescennina per hunc inventa Licentia morem, Versibus alternis opprobria rustica fudit; Libertasque recurrentes accepta per annos Lusit amabiliter.
units.tr: From Borghetto, along the traces of the ancient Via Flaminia, after the eighth milestone, the town of Civita Castellana meets the eye on very high cliffs. Some think this city was Veii, which the Romans besieged for ten years. But Dionysius of Halicarnassus and Pliny seem to contradict this. For Dionysius (book 2) writes that the town of Veii was not more than a hundred stadia from Rome, and Pliny (book 3, chapter 6) reports that the Veientes lived by the Tiber, and that the city of Caenina was thirteen miles from Fidenae, Vatican and the Janiculum. Nobody who knows the region of that area doubts that Civita Castellana is at least 25 Roman miles, or two hundred stadia, from Rome. Other arguments which one can gather from Livy, where he speaks of the rush of the Three Hundred Fabii, I pass over. So another ancient name for this town must be sought. It is likely that it was the town which Pliny calls Fescennia, and Dionysius of Halicarnassus Φασκινιον [Phaskinion]. From this comes the Fescennine line in Virgil, Aeneid book 7, though it is strange that Servius writes that Fescennium is a town in the plain, when both the other places Virgil mentions there and Civita Castellana, as I said before, lie on high cliffs. Perhaps Servius through some confusion mixes it up with another Fescennium of the Falisci, which is in Campania. From the Fescennium of the Etruscans the Fescennine verses were named; Horace sings of their origin thus: The ancient farmers, brave and happy with little, when the grain was stored and they rested at the festive time, offered a sacrifice of their body, and their very soul bearing hard hope for the end, together with their fellow workers, their boys and their faithful wives, appeased the earth with a pig, Silvanus with milk, the Genius with flowers and wine, mindful of the brief life. Through this custom Fescennine license was invented, and with alternating verses poured out rustic taunts; and that freedom, received and recurring through the years, they played with in good humour.

units.la: Fescennini sanè Versus erant, per quos inductæ Rusticorum Personæ cum in Se, tum in alios iocola Convicia alternis canebant, non solum in Nuptiis, uti patet ex Festo, Senecæ Medea, Catullo in Epithalamio, Plinio lib. XV, Autonioque: verum etiam in Convivijs, atque hilarionibus hominum Conventibus, ut docent Horatii, quæ ante scripsi, Liviiique lib. VII, testimonia. Tam olim grati fuerunt Fescennini Versus, ut ne Octavianus quidem Augustus ab ijs scribendis abstinuerit. Unde apud Macrobium legimus lib. Saturnal. II, Temporibus Triumviralibus Pollionem, quum Fescenninos in eum Augustus scripsisset, dixisse, At ego taceo: non est enim facile in eum scribere, qui potest proscribere. Fescenninos omnium elegantissime fecit Ausonius Poeta. De eo Antonius in Centone Nuptiali: Nam quid Annum Fescennínos, quid antiquissimos Poetas Livij Eratosthenem Libros loquar? Fuit Ausonius Falisius, Probi GraunGrammatici Discipulus, Agellij (qui de eo, libro vii, & xx.) Amicus, per ea tempora, quibus ad Imperium Romanum evectus est Hadrianus. Versus aliquot eius ab Oblivionis iniuria vindicavit Terentianus: Cetera Pars superest mea Tibia dicere versus: Hac tunicta frequentius edent Anapaestica dulcia Metra; Quicumque libebit ut illos Triplices dare sic Anapaestos, Atque ille Poeta Falisçus, Quum Ludicra Carmina pangit: Uva, Uva tum, & Uva Falerna, Et ter feror, & quater anno. Libro quoque dixit eodem: Unde, unde Colonus? Eol A Flumine venit Orontæ.
units.tr: There were indeed Fescennine verses, by which rustic characters were introduced who sang jesting taunts at themselves and at one another in alternating lines. This happened not only at weddings, as is clear from Festus, Seneca's Medea, Catullus in his Epithalamium, Pliny book 15, and Ausonius, but also at banquets and merry gatherings of people, as the passages of Horace quoted above and of Livy book 7 show. Fescennine verses were so popular in earlier times that even Octavian Augustus did not refrain from writing them. Hence we read in Macrobius, Saturnalia book 2, that in the times of the triumvirs Pollio, when Augustus had written Fescennine verses against him, said: "But I am silent, for it is not easy to write against a man who can proscribe." Ausonius the poet wrote the Fescennine verses most elegantly of all. Antonius speaks of him in the Nuptial Cento: "For why should I speak of Annius's Fescennines, or of the most ancient poets, or of Livius's or Eratosthenes's books?" Ausonius was from Falerii, a pupil of the grammarian Probus, and a friend of Gellius (who speaks of him in book 7 and book 20), and he lived at the time when Hadrian was raised to the Roman throne. Terentianus rescued some of his verses from the injury of oblivion: "The rest of my part is to sing verses on the pipe. On this measure the anapaests will sound sweetest. Whoever pleases may give triple anapaests in this way, just as that Falerian poet does when he composes playful songs:" "Grapes, grapes then, and Falernian grapes, and I am carried three and four times a year." He says in the same book: "Whence, whence is the farmer? He comes from the river Orontes of the Aeolians."

units.la: Fuerunt haud procul Civitate Castellana Ara Murcia, quarum meminit Plinius libro ii. cap. xxxviii.
units.tr: Not far from the town of Civita Castellana there were the Ara Murcia, which Pliny mentions in book 2, chapter 38.

units.la: Ad Montem Soractem vel Falisco rum, de quo alibi, Strabonis aetate Feronia fuit: Τὰ δὲ τῷ Σωρακτε ἐρὶ Φερωνία πόλις ἐστὶ, ἐμώνυμος ἀπηχωρα τῷ Δαίμονι, προμηθὴν σφοδρὰ ... ἐχει. Γυμνοὶς γὰρ ... Innuit Feronium dictam ab Dea cognomine Feronia. Quod reliquum narrat ad Hirpos est referendum, de quibus antea. Putat Leander Feroniam eundem fuisse loco, quo nunc D. Silvestri Castrum, Castello di S. Silvestro. Antonius Matta arbitratur nulla hodie Feronia exstare vestigia. Nec certiora dici possunt de Flaviana, cuius eodem tractu meminit Silius lib. viii: Quique tuos Flaviana focos.
units.tr: Near Mount Soracte, or of the Falisci, of which elsewhere, in Strabo's time there was Feronia: "Near Soracte there is the city of Feronia, named after the goddess, which has ... for the priests walk barefoot..." [Τὰ δὲ τῷ Σωρακτε ἐρὶ Φερωνία πόλις ἐστὶ, ἐμώνυμος ἀπηχωρα τῷ Δαίμονι, προμηθὴν σφοδρὰ ... ἐχει. Γυμνοὶς γὰρ ...] He hints that Feronium was named after the goddess Feronia. The rest of what he says about the Hirpi must be referred to them, about whom above. Leander thinks Feronia was in the same place where now is D. Silvestri Castrum, Castello di S. Silvestro. Antonius Matta judges that no trace of Feronia survives today. Nothing more certain can be said about Flaviana, which Silius mentions in the same district in book 8: "and Flaviana, which tends your hearths."

units.la: Inde Flavinia Arva Virgilio lib. vii Aeneid. Hi Fescenninas Acies, Equitesque Falisci, Hi Soractis habent Arces, Flaviniaque Arva.
units.tr: Hence the Flavinia Arva in Virgil, Aeneid book 7: "These have the Fescennine battle line and the Falisci horsemen; these have the citadels of Soracte and the Flavinian fields."

units.la: Ad quae Verba Servio Flavinium, Locus est Tusciae in Italia.
units.tr: On these words Servius glosses Flavinium thus: "It is a place in Tuscany in Italy."

units.la: Quam fortunam Flaviana, fuibit etiam ipsidem locis Opidum, quod Ferentinum Tacito libro xvii, Plinio lib. iii. cap v, Aurelio Victori in Vita Othonis; Φερεντινὸν, Strabon: Φερωνία, Ptolemaeo: unde Ferentini apud eundem Plinium. Eos puto nominari in antiqua Inscriptione, quam Vultinus exscriptam posui folio 872, ubi de praecipuis Etruriae Populis. Ferentina fuerunt & alia. Commentator Vetus Horatii: Ferentinum inquit, est Campaniae, Tusciae, & Tertium in Via Lavicana ad xlviii Lapidem ab Urbe. De ceteris suo loco ex variis Auctoribus. Hoc interim Etruriae scribendum monent Viri docti Ferentium, vel Ferentiam. Sciendum tamen Urbes multas in Italia fuisse cognominies. Vide quae notavi ad Frentanos Samnitium. Ferentino Etruriae ortus scribitur Otho Imperator, scribente, praeter Tacitum in Annalibus & Sex. Aurelium Victorem, Suetonio in eius Vita. Fuit autem Ferentinum hoc, scribente ad Ortelium Celso Civitadino, inter Viterbium, Montem Soractem, Balneoregium & Flasconenses; exque ea tantum hodie Ecclesia superest, vocaturque Locus Ferento, quod sic pronunciatur, ut prima elevetur, reliquae Syllabae deprimantur. Locis Ferentio finitimis Opidum etiam erat, quod Plinio Festoque Trossulum: Troi- um fortean mendose apud Livium lib. x, ubi ab Carvilio memoratur expugnatum. Plinius Equites inde Trossulos deducit lib. xxxiii. cap. ii: Saepe variatum est, inquit, Equitum nomen: nam sub Romulo & Regibus appellati sunt Celeres; deinde Flexumines; postea Trossuli, quum in Tuscis citra Volsinos nono lapide opidum eius nominis sine Pedite ceperint. Vocis illius vis ultra C. Gracchum duravit. Maeoni, D. Anselmo incluti, quaedam adhuc Vestigia superstunt: Nominis memoriam retinente Campo, quem Planum Maeani, La Piana di Meana appellant. Inde Maeony, Tusciae Populi, apud Silium Italicum lib. ii. Ibidem Turrena Maeania fuisse putatur, quam Ovidius lib. iii. Metamorph. in Turrenorum Delphinorum Fabula commemorat. Opinantur quidam fuisse prope Tiberim, ubi nunc Montani nomen auditur, tamquam Maeoniani. Sunt nt. Sunt eo tractu & alia Oppida, Celino, Fabrica, Capreola: mox Nepet Civitas. Sic Livio non uno loco, Paterculo lib. 1, Plinio lib. iii. cap. v, PriscIano, & aliis dicitur; quæ Νέπητ, Ptolemæo; Νέπη Straboni lib. v; Νέπητ Dionysio Halicarnassæo, ex cuius libro xiii Νέπητ Stephano laudatur. Varie etiam scribitur in Antiquis Monumentis: quorum unum ibi, in ipso Templo, in Urna cineraria: HERENNIÆ C F F IVSTÆ M. APIITIVS. M. I. PAL. SABINVS. DVVMVIR VEIOS IIII. VIR. NEPETE VXXORI. SANCTISSIMÆ ET. PIENTISSIMÆ ET DE. SE. OPTIME. MERITÆ TESTAMENTO. FIERI IVSSIT
units.tr: The town Ferentinum also shared this fate of Flaviana in the same places; Tacitus mentions it in book 17, Pliny in book 3, chapter 5, and Aurelius Victor in the Life of Otho. Strabo calls it Ferentinon, and Ptolemy Pherōnia; hence the Ferentini in the same Pliny. I think they are named in an ancient inscription, which Vultinus copied and published on page 872, where he treats the chief peoples of Etruria. There were also other Ferentina. The old commentator on Horace says: "Ferentinum," he says, "is in Campania, in Tuscany, and a third in the Via Labicana at the forty-eighth milestone from the city." I will discuss the others in their place from various authors. Meanwhile learned men advise that Ferentium or Ferentiam should be written for the Tuscan town. One should know, however, that there were many cities in Italy with the same name. See what I have noted on the Frentani of the Samnites. The emperor Otho is said to have been born at Ferentinum in Etruria, as Tacitus in the Annals, Sextus Aurelius Victor, and Suetonius in his Life state. This Ferentinum, according to Celso Cittadini writing to Ortelius, lay between Viterbo, Mount Soracte, Bagnoregio and Fiascone; and of it only a church survives today, and the place is called Ferento, pronounced so that the first syllable is raised and the other syllables are lowered. Near Ferentium there was also a town which Pliny and Festus call Trossulum; perhaps it is wrongly written Troi-um in Livy book 10, where it is mentioned as taken by Carvilius. Pliny derives the Trossuli horsemen from it in book 33, chapter 2: "The name of the horsemen," he says, "has often changed: for under Romulus and the kings they were called Celeres, then Flexumines; afterwards Trossuli, when in Tuscany on this side of Volsinii, nine miles off, they took a town of that name without infantry. The force of that word lasted beyond Gaius Gracchus." Some traces of the Maeonians, famous to Saint Anselm, still survive: the plain, which they call Planum Maeani, La Piana di Meana, retains the memory of the name. Hence the Maeonii, a people of Tuscany, in Silius Italicus book 2. In the same place the Turrena Maeania is thought to have been, which Ovid in Metamorphoses book 3 mentions in the story of the Tyrrhenian Dolphins. Some think it was near the Tiber, where now the name Montani is heard, as if from Maeoniani. There are also other towns in that district: Celino, Fabrica, Capreola; and soon the city of Nepet. It is so called in Livy in many places, in Paterculus book 1, in Pliny book 3, chapter 5, in Priscian and others; Ptolemy calls it Nepet, Strabo in book 5 Nepe; Dionysius of Halicarnassus Nepet, and from his thirteenth book Stephanus cites Nepet. It is variously written in ancient monuments; one of these is there, in the temple itself, on a cinerary urn: "To Herennia Justa, daughter of Gaius, Marcus Appuleius Sabinus, son of Marcus, of the Pollian tribe, duumvir, quattuorvir of Veii, had this made by will for his wife, most holy and most dutiful, and most deserving of him."
