units.tr: Another in Rome, in the house of the Coritii in the Forum of Trajan, broken, of very white marble: "In the second consulship of Sergius Paullus, in the fifth year of the tribunician power, the soldiers named below made the seat and the tribunal. In the sixth consulship of Ite: Sextus Bolanius Quintianus of Tarentum; Marcus Tintorius Calendinus of Capua; Publius Fabius Saturnalis of Padua; Quintus Romanius Charito of Milan; Marcus Brittius Secundus of Nepet..." [the names are garbled in the scan]

units.la: Nepensis Colonia, alias Nepis, Frontino; cui restituenda Nepet ex Paterculi Vol. 1. Hanc Coloniam etiam commemorat Livius lib. xxv & xxix. Festus Nepet Municipium suis Iuris tuisse refert. Incolæ Nepetes, Procopio lib. iii de Bello Gothico; Nepesini in Bath, quæ in Foro Civitatis Nepesinorum erecta visitur: IMP CÆSARI L. SEPTIMIO SEVERO PERTINACI AVG PONTIF MAXIM TRIB POT II IMP III COS II P P NEPESINI OPTIMO FORTISSIMOQVE PRINCIPI SVO DEVOTI
units.tr: The colony of Nepet, called Nepesina, or Nepi, according to Frontinus; Nepet should be restored to it from Paterculus, volume 1. Livy also mentions this colony in books 25 and 29. Festus reports that Nepet was a municipium under its own law. The inhabitants are called Nepetes by Procopius in book 3 of the Gothic War, and Nepesini in a bath, which is seen erected in the forum of the city of the Nepesini: "To the Emperor Caesar Lucius Septimius Severus Pertinax Augustus, Pontifex Maximus, holder of tribunician power for the second time, imperator for the third time, consul for the second time, father of the fatherland, the Nepesini, devoted to their best and bravest prince."

units.la: Leguntur & in alia ibidem Bath, ex qua duo superiores Versus sunt erosi. Sic Municipes Nepesini in alio Lapide nominantur: NESTORI AVG. NEPETE HIC. LVDOS. FECIT ET. DEDICATIONE STATVÆ. PATRONI QVAM. IPSE. POSVIT ET. CLVPEI. SVI. ITERVM MVNICIPIBVS. NEPESINSIS EPVLVM. DEDIT Rempublicam denique Nepesinorum laudat Basis, quæ ibidem in Foro:
units.tr: They are also read in another bath there, from which the two upper verses have been eroded. Thus the citizens of Nepet are named on another stone: "To the Augustus Nestor; at Nepet he made the games here, and at the dedication of the statue of the patron, which he himself set up, and of his own shield, he gave a feast again to the citizens of Nepet." Finally, the base in the forum there praises Rempublicam the commonwealth of the Nepesini:

units.la: D. N. GALERI O. MAXIMI NO. NOB CÆS PRINCIP. IVV R. P. NEPESINO RVM
units.tr: To Our Lord Galerius Valerius Maximus, Most Noble Caesar, Prince of the Youth: the Republic of the Nepesines

units.la: Nepesina Cohors est apud Silium Italicum lib. VIII. Νεπησίνων, ἐθνικόν, apud Stephanum. Festus auctor est ab Gentis Insigni, quod erat Scorpius, nomen esse impositum. Livius Urbis memoriam multis in locis usurpat: præsertim lib. VI, ubi ab Valerio captam, Opidanisque, præterquam Defectionis Auctoribus, parcitum scribit; item lib. XX, quum inter XII numerat, quæ cum Populo Romano Hannibali se opponere noluerunt: libro quoque XXVIII, ubi cum ceteris anno sexto post duplum inferre compulsam notat.
units.tr: The Nepesina Cohors is mentioned by Silius Italicus, book VIII. Stephanus gives the ethnic Νεπησίνων [Nepesinōn]. Festus says the name was taken from the tribe's insignia, which was a scorpion. Livy often uses the name of the city, especially in book VI, where he writes that it was taken by Valerius and that the townspeople were spared, except the authors of the revolt. In book XX he counts it among the twelve communities that refused to side with the Roman people against Hannibal. In book XXVIII he notes that it was compelled, along with the others, to supply double (tribute) in the sixth year after that.

units.la: Rursus ab Nepete ū conversoad Occidentem itinere Planiciem amœnam repetas, Viterbium occurrit: cui quod olim fuerit nomen, valde nuper laboratum. Annius, Patriæ inlustrandæ non satis fideliter, neq; feliciter natus, quatuor hic quondam fuisse Urbes probat ex nescio quo Desiderij Langbardorum Regis Edicto, Longhulam Tussam, Vetulioniam, Turrenam Volturnam & Arbanum; addens eas ab eodem Rege uno Muro comprehensas Viterbi nomen accepisse. Annio Cœlum cum Terra miscenti, Opidaque, ex Aere quasi pro libitu rapta, Terris adsingenti suffragatur Leander Albertus, Vir alioqui diligens, & insignis Veritatis scrutator. Vetusfam antiquitus appellatam canit Facius Vbertus lib. III. Cant. x. Sed quum hoc Nomen nusquam apud bonos Scriptores reperiatur, non magni solet apud me esse momenti. Volaterranus Longholam hic ponit Livij, quem quum alij viderent lib. IX. Longulam collocare in Latio, ut Volaterranum nonnihil juvarent, duplex fecerunt istius nominis opidum; unum quidem Volscorum, circa Terracinam, scribi illud ajentes Longulam ab Longitudine: aliud Etruriæ Longholam, tamquam Hastaram, ἀπὸ τ λόγχης: sed omnia absque ulla Veterum auctoritate. Sabellicus lib. VII. Enn. IX & Platina in Clementis Vita Vetuloniam hoc loco fuisse notant, at ille cum Palinodia. Certe Vetuloniam alibi fuisse, alibi à me dictum. Hermolaus scribit Ptolemæo nominari Elby Vicum: sed is in Græcis Codicibus nusquam paret. Etruriam prius appellatum Viterbium, posteaque Flavium cognominatum, docet ex Desiderij Regis Edicto Angelus Brevetanus: sed Etruriam ex nescio quibus Myrsilo & Catone, maleque intellecto Livio fingere; Flavium autem ex Edicto solo, non erat satis. Inclinat & in eam sententiam, quod Viterbium Etruria antiquitus fuerit, Leander Albertus, qui hic probandæ Conjecturæ multus. Viterbium ex Foro-Cassij ruinis crevisse putat Paullus Iovius; omnium exactissime. Vnus Blondus Viterbium novam, vel non admodum vetustam censet Urbem: addens eius Nomen parvo in Castello ad annum suo tempore sexcentesimum Viturvium fuisse. Quæ mihi sit mens, puto ex superioribus satis liquere. Viterbium Annio, tamquam Vei Terbum, id est Curule Terbum: Aliis apud Annium, tamquam Vita Heroum, Vis trium Urbium, Vita Urbium, Vita herbidum, Vita inermium, Vis thermarum alia præterero. Rhenano Viterbium, quasi Wit Erbum, Germanico nomine. Iacet speciosō spaciosoque loco, Jugis Cyminijs (ca nunc Mons Viterbinus, Monte di Viterbo) à tergo imminentibus: Lapide quadrato ædificata; Turribus plena. Inter Opera Publica Fons est insignis, & maxima cum Spectantium admiratione copiosus. Viterbi multa sunt Epigrammata: inter ea Edictum Desiderij Langbardorum Regis, his verbis conceptum:
units.tr: Going on from Nepete in a westerly direction, across a pleasant plain, you come to Viterbium. What its former name was has been very much disputed of late. Annius, not very faithfully or happily in illustrating his homeland, claims that four cities once stood here, Longhulam, Tussam, Vetuloniam, Turrenam, Volturnam and Arbanum, citing some edict of King Desiderius of the Lombards that I cannot identify. He adds that these were enclosed by that king within a single wall and so received the name Viterbi. Leander Albertus, a man otherwise diligent and a notable seeker after truth, supports Annius, who mixes heaven with earth and conjures up towns, as if snatched from the air at will, and attaches them to the land. Facius Ubertus, book III, canto x, sings that it was anciently called Vetusfam. But since this name is nowhere found in good authors, it does not carry much weight with me. Volaterranus places Longholam here on the authority of Livy; but when others, to help Volaterranus somewhat, found Longulam in Latium in book IX of Livy, they made two towns of that name: one of the Volsci, near Terracina, which they say is written Longulam from its length (longitudo), and another of Etruria, Longholam, as if it were Hastara, from ἀπὸ τῆς λόγχης [from the spear]. But all of this is without any authority of the ancients. Sabellicus, book VII, Ennead IX, and Platina in the Life of Clement, note that Vetulonia was here, but the former with a recantation. Certainly I have said elsewhere that Vetulonia was somewhere else. Hermolaus writes that Ptolemy names Elby Vicum, but that name appears nowhere in the Greek manuscripts. Angelus Brevetanus teaches, from the edict of King Desiderius, that Viterbium was formerly called Etruria and afterwards surnamed Flavium. But to invent Etruria from I know not what Myrsilus and Cato, and from a badly understood Livy, is not enough, and Flavium rests on the edict alone. Leander Albertus, who is generous in arguing for this conjecture, leans towards the same view, holding that Viterbium was anciently in Etruria. Paulus Jovius, most exactly of all, thinks Viterbium grew out of the ruins of Forum Cassii. Blondus alone judges Viterbium a new city, or not very old, adding that its name was Viturvium, in a small castle, six hundred years before his time. What my own view is, I think is clear enough from what has been said above. Annius derives Viterbium from Vei Terbum, that is, Curule Terbum. Others, in Annius, derive it from Vita Heroum, Vis trium Urbium, Vita Urbium, Vita herbidum, Vita inermium, Vis thermarum, and I pass over others. Rhenanus derives Viterbium, as if it were Wit Erbum, from a German name. It lies in a fair and spacious place, with the Cyminian ridges (now Mons Viterbinus, Monte di Viterbo) rising behind it. It is built of square stone and full of towers. Among its public works is a notable fountain, abundant to the amazement of onlookers. At Viterbium there are many inscriptions, among them the Edict of Desiderius, King of the Lombards, conceived in these words:

units.la: {a} Nepe.
units.tr: {a} Nepe.

units.la: Revocamus Statuta Regis Astulphi contra Vetulones edita, ut Lacus non Tyrrenium, sed Vetulonum sit, qui Licus Magnus Italiæ dictus est; qui eorum Ager prius est Italia dicta, ab Ibi Sede Itali, & ut sua Longoli, non Lungobardolam sed cognomine sui Ampliatoris Tirrheni Terbum vocent, & sub uno Muro cingant tria Opida, Longolam, Vetuloniam, & Tirrheniam, Vulturnam dictam Etruriam, totamque Urbem nostra adiectione Viterbum pronunciant, ut Rhoda & Civitas Balneoregium dici iussimus. Permittimus Pecunijs imprimi Favi, sed amoveri Herculem, & poni Sᵗᵐ Laurentium eorum Patronum, sicut Roma & Bononia. Iubemus quoque reperari Cormentam, Dardanum, Assium, Faranium, Cormitum & Tuscanellum. Nos enim non sumus Tusciæ Destructores, ut nos apud Gallos accusat Hadrianus Papa. Nam ædificavimus à fundamentis, Vobis quidem Voltisphrenis, Calnellum, Vicum Orchianum, Balnearia, Barbaranum, & Gariophilum: Sentinatibus autem Ausedonias & Rodacofanum: Volatenis Rodocomalum: Lunæ Sergianum & Petram Sanctam, olim Fanum Feroniæ: Phocensibus SSᵗᵒˢ Geminianum & Miniatem: Iesulanis opidum, in quo vagos sparsos Arinianos & palantes Fluentinos collegimus rursus, plures antiquas nobiles Vrbes ampliavimus, & Muris cinximus, ut nunc agimus circa Lunam, Pistorium, Aretium, Orobitum, Etruriam nunc Viterbum; cuius Nomen, aut à nobis constituta Decreta si quis violaverit, aut capite puniatur, aut laqueo stranguletur. Hoc itaque non est Etruriam destruere, ut nos arguit Hadrianus, qui Pacem ultra à nobis oblatam repulit. Quare tibi Grimoalde, Præfecte Viterbiensis, præcipimus, ut quamdiu Pax dubia perseverat, iubeas omnes Tusciæ Milites paratos esse in armis, & commeatus ac stipendia sine avaritia in promtu fac habeas; ut non solum Hostibus occurrere, sed illos invadere possis, cives non gravabis novis exactionibus.
units.tr: We revoke the statutes issued by King Astulf against the Vetulones, so that the lake which was called the Great Lake of Italy shall be the Vetulonian, not the Tyrrhenian. And the land of those people, which was formerly called Italy, from the seat of the Itali there, and as its own Longoli, shall not be called Lombardy but, by the surname of its enlarger Tirrhenus, Terbum; and they shall enclose within one wall the three towns Longola, Vetulonia and Tirrhenia, Volturna called Etruria; and they shall proclaim the whole city Viterbum by our addition, just as we have ordered that Rhoda and the city Balneoregium be so called. We permit the coins to bear the image of Favus, but Hercules is to be removed and St Laurence, their patron, placed in his stead, as at Rome and Bologna. We also order that Cormenta, Dardanum, Assium, Faranium, Cormitum and Tuscanellum be restored. For we are not destroyers of Tuscany, as Pope Hadrian accuses us before the Gauls. For we have built from the foundations: for the men of Voltisphrene, Calnellum, Vicus Orchianus, Balnearia, Barbaranum and Gariophilum; for the Sentinates, Ausedonias and Rodacofanum; for the Volatenses, Rodocomalum; for the people of Luna, Sergianum and Petra Sancta, formerly Fanum Feroniae; for the Phocenses, Geminianum and Miniatem; for the Iesulani, a town in which we gathered together the scattered wandering Arinians and the roving Fluentines. We have also enlarged several ancient noble cities and fortified them with walls, as we now do around Luna, Pistorium, Arezzo, Orbetello, and Etruria, now Viterbum. Whoever violates its name, or the decrees we have established, shall either be punished by death or strangled with a noose. Therefore this is not destroying Etruria, as Hadrian accuses us, who has rejected the peace we offered. Wherefore, Grimoald, prefect of Viterbo, we command you, so long as the uncertain peace continues, to order all the soldiers of Tuscany to be ready under arms, and to see that provisions and pay are kept at hand without greed; so that you may not only meet the enemy but attack them, and you will not burden the citizens with new exactions.

units.la: Operam Edicto refigendo non dabo, ne ad Pœnas, quas decernit, poscar: hoc solum obiter dicam, Annium, illustrandæ nobilitandæque Patriæ, nimiam fingendi multa, doctiloqui auribus obtrudendi licentiam sibi sumsisse. Male cessit ipsi audacia, quod oculatius Seculum eius abitum excepit. Episcopum Viterbo primus dedit Cælestinus III. P. M. teste Platina in eius Vita. Ortu hac Urbe Petrus Antonius, Episcopus Signanus; Ioannes Annius, Sacri Palatii Magister; Facius Sanctior, Ecclesiæ Romanæ Cardinalis; & alij. Multa de hac Urbe, ciusque Agro & Internate, Supernate, idem Annius in suis Quæstionibus, variisque ad suppositicios Auctores Commentarius. Urbicarius illi Ager bonus & fertilis; Vino abundans & Frugibus; Fluminibus passim (uti Egelido, Rivo obscuro, Rivo Vrcerio, Alcione, Rosseno, Rivo Atlao, Albiano, Fessano, Catenace, Vetaque) & Fontibus irriguus, tam medicatis, quam alius generis. Principatu Urbis potiti diu leguntur Vici donec ab Ægidio Carila, Cardinale & Legato Ecclesiæ Romanæ, cuius tum in Gallia Sedes erat, pulsi. Eo tamen defuncto rursus ad Imperium venerunt. Vicis postea successerunt Gattinab Magancesio, ope Vrsinorum, aliquoties electi, sed ab Columnis iterum restituti: quorum Factionibus & Seditionibus Urbs adeo debilitata, adeoque flammis ferroque vastata, ut magna ex parte ruinis deformata nunc jaceat.
units.tr: I will not bother to reprint the edict, lest I be called to account for the penalties it decrees. I will only say in passing that Annius, eager to illustrate and ennoble his homeland, took to himself an excessive licence to invent many things and foist them on the ears of learned men. His boldness turned out badly for him, because a more discerning age received his work. Celestine III, supreme Pontiff, first gave Viterbo a bishop, as Platina witnesses in his Life. From this city came Pietro Antonio, bishop of Segni; Giovanni Annio, Master of the Sacred Palace; Fazio Sanzio, cardinal of the Roman Church; and others. Annius writes much about this city, its territory, and Internate and Supernate, in his Questions and in his various commentary on the supposititious authors. Its surrounding countryside is good and fertile, abounding in wine and crops, and watered throughout by rivers (such as Egelido, Rivo obscuro, Rivo Vrcerio, Alcione, Rosseno, Rivo Atlao, Albiano, Fessano, Catenace, Vetaque) and by springs, both medicinal and of other kinds. The Vici held the rule of the city for a long time, as the records say, until they were expelled by Ægidio Carila, cardinal and legate of the Roman Church, whose see was then in Gaul. But after his death they returned to power. The Vici were afterwards succeeded by Gattinab Magancesio, who, aided by the Orsini, was chosen several times, but was again restored by the Colonna. Through the factions and seditions of these families the city was so weakened, and so ravaged by fire and sword, that for the most part it now lies deformed by ruins.

units.la: Viterbo Passuum mil. xv. in Agro Cornetano Vestigia cernuntur Urbis quondam florentissimæ Tarquinia, nomen retinentia. Tarquinæ enim Adcolis audiunt: Ταρχυνία scribitur Straboni libro v; Ταρκύναι, Ptolemæo: Tarquinij Colonia, Frontino: Tarquiniense Municipium, M. Tullio pro Cæcina. Non dubito, quin idem sit cum Tarchonio, etiamsi Ταρκυνίαν & Ταρχωνιον duo Opida facere videatur Stephanus: Ταρχυνία inquit, πόλις Τυρρηνιῶν, ὁσὶ Ταρχῶν: τὸ ἐθνικον, Ταρκωνίων, ἡ Ταρκωνιὸς &c. Et postea suo ordine: Ταρχώνιον πόλις Τυρρηνίας, ὅση Τηλεφυ πιστοὶ Ταρχων, ὁ πολίτης Ταρχωνίων. Ego Stephanum ex variis Scriptoribus, de eadem Urbe, imprudenter, loqui censeo. Certe Ταρχώνιον Stephani, & Ταρκωνίαν Eustathij in Dionys. quin & Tarconam Silij Italici libro viii. eamdem cum Tarquinia esse, non obscure docet Strabo, Ταρκυνίας ab Tarconte, Tyrrhenię Præfecto conditam notans. Tarcon notus etiam Virgilio lib. x. & Tarco Latinius, ut Servius vult, eidem lib. viii. Sic Tarcona Silio lib. viii. Tarconis superbi domus. Eam tamen a Thessalis & Spinam bris Græcis conditam scripsit libro xx. Pompeius Trogus. Exiguum ab initio fuit Opidum, sed postea maximis incrementis auctum: testantibus id huic ævo Ruderibus. Crevisse putatur ex eius ruinis Cornetum. Demaratum Corinthium hic splendidissimam ædificasse Domum, tradunt Dionisius Halicarnass. lib. iii. & Strabo libro v. Orti ea duo Romanorum Reges, L. L. Priscus & Superbus: ambo Tarquinij inde nominati. Memoratur frequenter ab Livio, præsertim lib. vii. & xxvii. quum Tarquinius Porcum humano ore natum scribat. & lib. xxviii. ubi Tarquinienses ad Vela Classis, quam in Africam ducturus erat P. Cornelius Scipio, Lintea narrat contulisse.
units.tr: At Viterbo, fifteen miles away, in the territory of Corneto, traces of the once most flourishing city of Tarquinia can be seen, keeping its name. The inhabitants call it Tarquinae. Strabo, book V, writes Ταρχυνία [Tarchynia]; Ptolemy writes Ταρκύναι [Tarkynai]; Frontinus calls it Tarquinii Colonia, and Cicero in the speech for Caecina Tarquiniense Municipium. I do not doubt that it is the same as Tarchonium, although Stephanus seems to make Ταρκυνία and Ταρχώνιον two towns. He says: Ταρχυνία, a city of the Tyrrhenians, whose people are Ταρχῶν [Tarchōn]; the ethnic is Ταρκωνίων [Tarkōnioi], and the feminine Ταρκωνίς, etc. And later, in its own order: Ταρχώνιον, a city of Tyrrhenia, whose citizen is Ταρχωνίων [Tarchōnioi]. I think that Stephanus, speaking imprudently of the same city, drew on various writers. Certainly Strabo clearly teaches that Stephanus's Ταρχώνιον, and Eustathius's Ταρκωνία in his commentary on Dionysius, and even Tarcona in Silius Italicus, book VIII, are the same as Tarquinia, noting that Ταρκυνία was founded by Tarchon, prefect of the Tyrrhenians. Tarchon is also known to Virgil, book X, and Tarco is, as Servius holds, in the same poet's book VIII. So Silius, book VIII, has Tarcona: "the house of proud Tarcon". Pompeius Trogus, however, wrote in book XX that it was founded by Thessalians and Greeks from Spina. At first it was a small town, but later it grew by very great increases, as its ruins bear witness to this day. It is thought that Cornetum grew out of its ruins. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book III, and Strabo, book V, report that Demaratus of Corinth built a most splendid house here. From here came the two Roman kings, Lucius Priscus and Superbus, both called Tarquinius from this place. It is frequently mentioned by Livy, especially in books VII and XXVII, where he writes that Tarquinius gave birth to a pig with a human face; and in book XXVIII, where he relates that the Tarquinienses contributed sailcloth for the sails of the fleet which Publius Cornelius Scipio was about to lead into Africa.

units.la: Decem ab Viterbo passuum millibus, versus Meridiem, Bieda est: quæ Βλήρα Ptolemæo: unde Bleranı Plinio: Βλεράνι leguntur apud Strabonem: emendat Isaacus Casaubonus Βλερᾶτα. Habet & Bleram Antoninus: sed itinere, quod Benevento ducit Tarentum, putatque ibi Hieronymus Surita Bleram ex alieno loco in istam Antonini paginam forte delilisse. De Nominis Origine quædam frigide, ut de multis aliis, Annius.
units.tr: Ten miles from Viterbo, toward the south, is Bieda. This is Blera (Βλήρα) in Ptolemy, whence Bleranum in Pliny. Strabo is read as Βλεράνι, which Isaac Casaubon emends to Βλερᾶτα [Blerata]. Antoninus also has Blera, but on the road that leads from Benevento to Tarentum, and Hieronymus Surita thinks Blera may have slipped into that page of Antoninus from some other place. On the origin of the name, Annius says some things coldly, as he does about many others.

units.la: Sequitur inferius, oram versus, Barbaranum: item Vianum: utraque Tolfa Nova, quæ Φίρω κλαυδίας Ptolemæi Leandro putatur. Describi videtur à Plinio lib. iii. cap. v. sub Præfectura Claudij Foro-Clodij. Hic temporibus Pij ii. P. M. Metallum Aluminarium ab Ioanne Castro Langbardo repertum prodit Volatertanus. Inde ad Sabatum Lacum incedenti Bracianum occurrit: etiam Bracenum, Braceanum & Brignanum ab Eruditis Latine scribentibus vocatum. Ad Lacus ripam Orientalem est Anguillaria, nobile Opidum, à quo Lacui nomen; ad Septemtrionalem Trivilianum: ad Occidentalem Vicarellum, Διμάχιλον Ptolemæo, ut putat Leander: sed difsuadere videtur reliquorum ibi Locorum enumeratio, Vicarellum Volaterrano Vicus Aurelij nov-antiquo nomine.
units.tr: Further on, following the coast, is Barbaranum; likewise Vianum. Both are Tolfa Nova, which Leander thinks is Ptolemy's Φίρω κλαυδίας [Phiro Klaudias]. It seems to be described by Pliny, book 3, chapter 5, under the prefecture of Claudius Forum Clodii. Here, in the time of Pius II, Supreme Pontiff, the Volaterran reports that alum mining was discovered by John Castro, a Lombard. Advancing from there toward Lake Sabatus, one meets Bracianum, also called Bracenum, Braceanum and Brignanum by learned writers in Latin. On the eastern shore of the lake is Anguillaria, a noble town, from which the lake takes its name; on the northern shore is Trivilianum; on the western Vicarellum, which Leander thinks is Διμάχιλον [Dimachilon] in Ptolemy. The enumeration of the other places there seems to argue against this. The Volaterran calls Vicarellum the Vicus Aurelii, under its new-old name.

units.la: Quatuor Viterbo milliaribus Via, quæ ducit Romam, Canapina est opidum, quod Veteribus exististimatur Capena. Καπίνα, inquit Stephanus, Τυρρηνικὴ πόλις: λέγεται καὶ πληθωτικῶς. Τὸ ἐθνικὸν Καπινάτης. Capenates sunt apud Plinium lib. iii. cap. v. & Livium lib. v. vi. xxvi. & seq. Hinc Luci Capeni Virgilio lib. vii. De iis alibi.
units.tr: Four miles from Viterbo, on the road that leads to Rome, is the town Canapina, which the ancients are thought to have called Capena. Stephanus says: Καπίνα [Kapina] is an Etruscan city; it is also called by a plural form. Its ethnic is Καπινάτης [Kapinates]. The Capenates appear in Pliny, book 3, chapter 5, and in Livy, books 5, 6, 26 and following. Hence the Luci Capeni of Virgil, book 7. More on these elsewhere.

units.la: Haud procul Canapina versus Meridiem ad Lacum Ciminum Vicus est, vernacule Vico, unde Lacui nomen. Elby Vicum Ptolemæi esse vult Leander: sed Vicum hunc in Latinis expressum, in Græcis Ptolemæi Codicibus nusquam reperio. Ab Vico originem arbitratur esse idem Leander nobili Vicorum genti, quæ Viterbinæ Reip. principatum diu tenuit. Supra Viam Cassiam propter Ciminii juga Castellum Surianum est, Castel Soriano, ubi Arcem, Italiæ totius validissimam, construxit Nicolaus iii ex Vrsinorum Gente Pontifex Maximus: postea:que suæ Familiæ concessit, ut auctor est Volaterranus. Eam quo tempore Pontificia Sedes Avenione erat in Gallis, Brittones ab Cardinale Ceccebennensi, Gregorii xi. P. M. Legato, in Italiam adducti, occuparant: neque prius ulla vi exterrneri sibi sunt passi, quamvis ab Alberico Cunitate summo Libertatis Vindice reliquis Italiæ locis fuissent exturbati, quam Martinus v. P. M. Sedem Pontificiam ex Gallis Romam reduxisset. Is enim artibus, ingenioque ac muneribus id effecit, ut sponte excederent, Arcemque suæ Ditioni ac potestati restituerent: quemadmodum plene notant Blondus, Volaterranus, Sabellicus, alij.
units.tr: Not far from Canapina, toward the south, by Lake Ciminus, is a Vicus, in the vernacular Vico, from which the lake takes its name. Leander wants Elby Vicum to be Ptolemy's Vicus, but I cannot find this Vicus, as expressed in Latin, anywhere in the Greek codices of Ptolemy. The same Leander thinks the name Vico comes from the noble family of the Vicorum, which held the leadership of the Republic of Viterbo for a long time. Above the Via Cassia, below the ridges of Ciminus, is Castellum Surianum, Castel Soriano, where Nicholas III, Supreme Pontiff, of the Ursini family, built a citadel, the strongest in all Italy. Afterwards, as the Volaterran reports, he granted it to his family. At the time when the Papal See was at Avignon in Gaul, the Bretons, brought into Italy by the Cardinal of Ceccebennensis, legate of Gregory XI, Supreme Pontiff, had seized it. They did not allow themselves to be driven out by any force, although they had been expelled from the other places in Italy by Alberic of Cunio, the highest champion of liberty. This happened until Martin V, Supreme Pontiff, brought the Papal See back from Gaul to Rome. For he, by skill, ability and gifts, brought it about that they left of their own accord and restored the citadel to his dominion and power. Blondus, the Volaterran, Sabellicus and others note this fully.

units.la: Septem Viterbo milliaribus, versus Meridiem, Vetralla est, ut quibusdam placet, tamquam Vetus Aula dicta. Forum Cassii Antonio (supposititio ut cum Annio Leander censet; eo magis, quod in hodiernum usque diem Ædes ibi sit, quæ vulgo D. Maria Forensis.
units.tr: Seven miles from Viterbo, toward the south, is Vetralla, as some like to think, called Vetus Aula (the Old Court). Forum Cassii is in the Antonine Itinerary (a spurious work, as Leander with Annius judges), all the more so because to this day a church stands there, commonly called D. Maria Forensis.

units.la: Sequitur mox Roncillo vel Roncillonum in Colle; infraque Capranica, Basanum, Sutrium. Sic Livius, Itineraria Tabula, Latinique omnes nominant; Σουτρίον Ptolemæus, Diodorus, Strabo, Plutarchus, Stephanus, alij: quod Sutri vulgo. Meminit Ara Sepulcralis marmorea, quæ ibi in hortulo Summi Templi.
units.tr: Soon follows Roncillo, or Roncillonum, on a hill; and below it Capranica, Basanum, Sutrium. So Livy, the Itinerary Table and all Latin writers name it. Ptolemy, Diodorus, Strabo, Plutarch, Stephanus and others give Σουτρίον [Soutrion]; in the vernacular it is Sutri. A marble sepulchral altar is mentioned there, in the little garden of the high temple.

units.la: T. VALERIO. T. F. VEL. VICTORI DECVRIONI. SVRTI II. VIR. I. D. ITERVM Q. VIN Q. VENNALI CVRATORI. PECVNIÆ PVBLICÆ. PONTIFICI PATVLCIA. EXOCHE CONIVNX FECIT
units.tr: To Titus Valerius Victor, son of Titus, of the Velina tribe, decurion of Sutrium, duumvir with judicial power twice, and quinquennial curator of public money, pontiff: Patulcia Exoche, his wife, made this.

units.la: Multis locis Sutrii meminit Livius, præsertim libro vi; ubi Etruriæ Claustrum ob loci naturam, & belli adversus Etruscos gerendi opportunitatem appellat: Camillii, addens paullo post, audita Sutrinorum defectione, Multi edixisse, ut Annonam tridui secum in iter deferret, quo Celeritati profectionis adversus Sutrios obesse posset nihil. Hinc Plautinum Adagium in Catina, ut qui dierum aliquot Annonam secum deferunt, ire Sutrium dicantur: de quo & Festus lib. xvii. de Verbor. signif. Adjecit Livius tantam Camilli fuisse Celeritatem, ut eadem die Sutrium reciperet, ejectoque restitueret, qua erat ab Etruscis occupatum. Libro quoque ix. pugnatum inter Romanos, Etruscos & Umbros acerrime ad Sutrium notat idem Livius: amissaque ex Etruscis & Umbris, quorum pars capti, pars cæsi, hominum fere millia lx. Coloniam co deductam fuisse post septem annos, quam Galli Vrbem ceperant (is fuit annus ab V. C. cccLxxi) signat Velleius Paterculus. Mentionem Coloniæ faciunt & Frontinus & Plinius libro iii. cap. v. Livius item libro xvii & xxix. Tabula quoque marmorea, quæ hodieque Sutri in Summo Templo, sub Altari quodam, in qua inter alia hæc sculpta:
units.tr: Livy mentions Sutrium in many places, especially in book 6, where he calls it the gateway of Etruria because of the nature of the site and its suitability for waging war against the Etruscans. Shortly after, having heard of the revolt of the Sutrini, Camillus ordered many to carry food for three days with them, so that nothing might hinder the speed of his march against the Sutrini. Hence the proverb of Plautus in Catina: those who carry provisions with them for some days are said "to go to Sutrium"; Festus also mentions this in book 17, on the meaning of words. Livy adds that Camillus was so swift that on the same day he retook Sutrium, which the Etruscans had occupied, driving them out and restoring it. In book 9 the same Livy notes a very fierce battle near Sutrium between the Romans, Etruscans and Umbrians, in which about 60,000 men of the Etruscans and Umbrians were lost, some captured and some killed. Velleius Paterculus marks the founding of a Colonia there seven years after the Gauls had captured the city (that was the year 371 from the founding of the City). Frontinus and Pliny, book 3, chapter 5, also mention the colony, and Livy likewise in books 17 and 29. There is also a marble tablet which today stands at Sutri in the high temple, under a certain altar, on which, among other things, the following is carved:

units.la: PONTIFICES, A. COLONIA CONIVNC. IVLIA. SVTRIN. IN. ORD. RELAT
units.tr: PONTIFFS, ADMITTED FROM THE COLONY JULIA CONIVNCTA SUTRINA INTO THE ORDER

units.la: Habet & hunc Lapidem Onuphrius Panuinius in Imperio Romano:
units.tr: He also has this stone: Onuphrius Panvinius, in On the Roman Empire.

units.la: Q. FLAVIVS. Q. F. POLLINVS PONT. COL. SVTRINÆ
units.tr: Q. FLAVIUS, SON OF QUINTUS, POLLINUS, PONTIFF OF THE COLONY OF SUTRIUM

units.la: Huc pertinet quoque Silij illud Italici lib. viii. Belli Pœnici: Ciminique Lacu, qui Sutria tecta. Parum hac ætate frequentatur; Cavernis undique Topho, cui insidet, incisis cinctum.
units.tr: To this belongs also the line of Silius Italicus, book 8 of the Punica: and the Ciminian lake, which holds Sutrium's roofs. It is little visited in this age, and is surrounded on all sides by caves cut into the tufa on which it stands.

units.la: Veientes, de quibus antea dixi, inde incipiunt: in quorum Ditione Sutrio Viam Romanam pergenti quarto lapide Mons Roseus occurrit, Monte Rose vulgo. Lacui adjacet cognomini, quem falso Vadimonis censet Blondus. Mox in conspectum se dat Bacchanum, ad Lacum eiusdem nomenclaturæ qui Flumen modicum, Cremeram inquam, effundit versus Tiberim, totum ex Diverticulis Tabernis constans. Silvosi imminent Saltus, quos Bacchani vocant, cædibus & latrocinio perquam infames.
units.tr: The Veientes, of whom I spoke earlier, begin here. In their territory, on the Roman road as one goes from Sutrium, at the fourth milestone there is Mons Roseus, commonly called Monte Rosa. It lies beside the lake of the same name, which Blondus wrongly thinks is the lake of Vadimo. Next there comes into view Bacchanum, by the lake of the same name, which sends out a small river, the Cremera, toward the Tiber. The whole place consists of inns and taverns. Above it hang wooded glades, which they call the Bacchani, notorious for murders and robbery.

units.la: Dextra tum deorsum offerunt se Casanum, Formellum, Gallera. Fuit his locis olim Veientum Metropolis: Vej Livio, Floro, aliis, Entanum olim, mox Larthentanum, Veiens postea ab Romanis vocatu fuisse, tradit ex supposititiciis Scriptoribus, Catone & Antonino, Annius, Suffragatores etiam cum aliis, tum Leandrum Albertum, natus. Marthentano hodie eidem Annio & Leandro; Pontiana, Nardo; Civitata Castellana, aliis. Sed quo præcise loco Civitas Veientum olim sita fuerit, quis hodie conjectura adsequetur? quum canat suo tempore Propertius: Et Veii veteres, & Vos tum præda fuistis: Et vestro posita est aurea Sella foro. Nunc intra muros Pastoris Buccina lenti Cantat, & in vestris ossibus arva metunt:
units.tr: To the right, further down, Casanum, Formellum and Gallera present themselves. These places were once the metropolis of the Veientes: Livy, Florus and others call it Vei; Annius and Leandro Alberti, with others, say that it was once called Entanum, then Larthentanum, and afterwards Veiens by the Romans, relying on the spurious writers Cato and Antoninus. Today Marthentanum is given to the same Annius and Leandro, Pontiana to Nardo, and Civita Castellana to others. But who today could guess the exact place where the city of the Veientes once stood, since Propertius sang in his time: "And old Veii, and you were then plunder, and a golden chair was placed in your forum. Now within the walls the shepherd's horn sounds slowly, and they reap the fields over your bones"

units.la: quumque L. Florus lib. i. Hist. Rom. cap. xii. Nunc, aiat, Veientes fuisse quis meminit? quæ reliquiæ? quod vestigium? Laborat Annalium fides, ut Veios fuisse credamus. Certe ubicumque fuerit, satis certum Situm habuisse Urbem in edito Montis Iugo, Rupibus præcelsis abscissam, quæque, ut Dionysius Halicarnassæus libro ii. Antiq. Rom. scribit, Ambitu suo tantum complectebatur spatii, quantum olim Athenæ in Græcia. Nonnulli de Situ Conjecturæ initium dare possunt, quod apud Dionysium Colli impositæ legatur celso, vicinum habens Janiculum; centum fere Stadiis, vel paullo amplius P. M. xii. ab Urbe Roma. Fuit hæc Urbs, quam Populus Romanus decennium obsessam duce tandem Camillo expugnavit: unde tanta vis opum tunc delata Romam, quanta ccc l. annis ea in Urbe adhuc visa numquam fuerat. Livius lib. ii. Dionysius lib. ix, Eutropius lib. i. Florus loco indicato, Orosius lib. iii. cap. viii. Auctor de Viris Illustribus cap. xxiii. Augustinus libro de Civitate Dei ii. cap. xvii. & libro iii. cap. xvii. alique. Pertinet huc Ciceronis locus lib. i. de Divinatione. Veienti Bello, inquit, quum Lacus Albanus præter modum crevisset, Veientem quendam hominem nobilem profugisse Romam Annales testantur, eumque dixisse, ex Fatis, quæ Veientes scripta haberent, Veios capi non posse, dum Lacus is redundaret; & si Lacus emissus lapsu & cursu suo ad mare profluxisset, perniciosum Populo Romano; sin autem esset eductus, ut ad Mare pervenire non posset, tum salutare et hoc fore: ex quo illa admirabilis à Maioribus Albana Aqua facta deductio est. Quum autem Veientes bello fessi, Legatos ad Senatum misissent, tum ex his quidam dixisse dicitur: Non omnia illum Transfugam ausum esse Senatui dicere: in ipsdem enim Fatis scriptum Veientes habere, fore ut brevi ab Gallis Roma caperetur: quod quidem sexennio post Veios captos factum esse videmus. Pergo. Roma quondam ab Gallis capta, Livius lib. v. Auctor est, consilium habuisse Romanos Patriæ deserendæ, Domicilioque populariter Veios transferendi. Memoriæ proditum, quum Nero Imperator Domum ædificaret amplissimam, editos fuisse hos Versus: Roma Domus fiet, Veios migrate Quirites; Si non & Veios occupat ista Domus.
units.tr: And L. Florus, Roman History, book 1, chapter 12: "Now, who remembers that there were Veientes? What remains are there? What trace? The credibility of the annals labours to make us believe that Veii existed." Certainly, wherever it was, it is clear that the city stood on the high ridge of a hill, cut off by steep cliffs, and that, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus writes in book 2 of the Roman Antiquities, it enclosed as much space within its circuit as Athens once did in Greece. Some may find a starting point for locating it in the fact that Dionysius says it lay on a high hill, having the Janiculum nearby, about a hundred stadia, or a little more, that is, twelve Roman miles, from the city of Rome. This was the city which the Roman people besieged for ten years and at last took under the leadership of Camillus. From it so great a store of wealth was then carried to Rome that the city had never seen the like in the three hundred and fifty years that followed. See Livy book 2, Dionysius book 9, Eutropius book 1, Florus in the place indicated, Orosius book 3, chapter 8, the author On Illustrious Men, chapter 23, and Augustine, City of God, book 2, chapter 17, and book 3, chapter 17, and others. Cicero's passage in book 1 of On Divination belongs here: "In the Veientine war, Cicero says, when the Alban lake had risen beyond measure, the annals record that a certain noble man of Veii fled to Rome, and said that from the Fates, which the Veientes had written down, Veii could not be taken as long as that lake overflowed; and that if the lake were let out to flow by its own fall and course into the sea, it would be harmful to the Roman people; but if it were so drawn off that it could not reach the sea, then this too would be wholesome. From this came that admirable diversion of the Alban water which our ancestors made. But when the Veientes, weary of war, sent envoys to the Senate, one of them is said to have spoken thus: that the deserter had not dared to tell the Senate everything; for the same Fates say that the Veientes will have Rome taken by the Gauls within a short time, which we see indeed came to pass six years after Veii was taken." I go on. Livy, book 5, states that after Rome was once taken by the Gauls, the Romans considered abandoning their homeland and moving their dwelling to Veii. It is recorded in memory that when the Emperor Nero was building his very large house, these verses were posted up: "Rome will become a house; migrate, Quirites, to Veii, unless this house takes Veii too."

units.la: Agrum ignobilius & insipidum produxisse Vinum, innuunt Poëtæ. Horatius: Qui Veientanum Festis potare diebus Campana solitus Trulla.
units.tr: The poets imply that the land produced a wine of no great repute and little flavour. Horace: "Who used to drink the Veientine wine on festival days from a Campanian ladle."

units.la: Persius Satyra v: ——Veientanumque rubellum Exhalet vapida lasum pice sessilis obba?
units.tr: Persius, Satire 5: "...and exhales the reddish Veientine wine, sour with pitch, from a sitting-jar?"

units.la: Martialis in Epigr. Sed Veientani bibitur Fex crassa rubelli.
units.tr: Martial, in an epigram: "But the thick dregs of the reddish Veientine wine are drunk."

units.la: De eo Vino sic Columella lib. iv. Veientanæ Vvæ non ita rubent, ut Aminea, à quo colore Rubellane appellantur, eademque Fecennina, quod plus quam cetera Fecis habeant.
units.tr: Columella, book 4, on this wine: "The Veientine grapes are not as red as the Aminean, from whose colour they are called Rubellan; and they are the same as the Fecennine, because they have more lees than the others."

units.la: Transuerso ex his locis itinere ad Montem Soractem primo Malianum occurrit; deinde Mantianum, mox Stagia: tum ad pedem Montis Arminnum, Arignano vernacule. Obiit hic Hadrianus iv. P. M. scribente Platina. Ad ripam inde Tiberis sunt, quæ vulgo Pontiano vel Ponzano, Turrita, Nazano, Fiano, quod ortu Francisci celebris Historici & Poetæ, cuius Blondus meminit, nobile. Dextra tum in Mediterraneis Civitella, Limprimiano, Morlupo. Via porro Flaminiæ impositum cernitur Caitrum Nouum: hinc Arianum. Rursus Flaminia Romam tendenti Porta Prima occurrit, ubi Viæ strata Pars cum Vestigiis quibusdam, & ruinis Aedificiorum superest.
units.tr: Turning off from these places towards Mount Soracte, one first meets Malianum; then Mantianum, and soon after Stagia; then at the foot of the mountain Arminnum, called Arignano in the vernacular. Hadrian IV, as Platina writes, died here. Then on the bank of the Tiber are the places commonly called Pontiano or Ponzano, Turrita, Nazano, and Fiano, noted as the birthplace of Francesco, the famous historian and poet whom Blondus mentions. On the right, inland, are Civitella, Limprimiano and Morlupo. Further along the Flaminian Way Caitrum Nouum is seen, and from here Arianum. Again, for one going to Rome by the Flaminian Way, the Porta Prima comes into view, where part of the paved road survives with some traces and ruins of buildings.

units.la: Post Pontem Milvium Tiberis Alveus ad Ianiculum ducit. Terminus ibi Veientium. Sequitur secundo Tiberi Malianum, Ripæ adpositum: Locus peramoenus, quinto ab Urbe lapide, Pontificum oblectationi peculiaris. Opidum hinc Portus Romanus, de quo in Maritima Tuscia. Denique Tiberina Ostia, totius Etruriæ finis.
units.tr: Past the Milvian Bridge the channel of the Tiber leads to the Ianiculum. There is the boundary of the Veientium. Next, on the second stretch of the Tiber, is Malianum, placed on the bank. It is a very pleasant spot, five miles from the city, and a special delight of the Pontiffs. From here the town of Portus Romanus, which I will discuss under Maritime Tuscia. Finally Tiberina Ostia, the end of all Etruria.

units.la: Ad Etruriæ Mediterranea pertinet Iter, quod Antoninus per Viam Clodiam Lucam Romam ducit per M. P. cexxxviii. Adiiciebam collatum, quod a me fieri solitum, cum Itineraria Tabula, cui lucem Primus dedit Vir Nobilissimus Marcus Velserus ii-Vir. Reip. Augustanæ, & Vulgata Nomenclatura.
units.tr: To the inland parts of Etruria belongs the route which Antoninus leads from Luca to Rome by the Cassian Way, a distance of 238 Roman miles. I have added a comparison, as I am accustomed to do, with the Itinerary Table, to which Marcus Welser, a most noble man, duumvir of the Augsburg commonwealth, first gave light, and with the common nomenclature.
