units.la: CAPUT XXII. Latium.
units.tr: CAPUT XXII. Latium.

units.la: ETRVRIAM, quae in Italia Prisca, eaque Occidentaliore & CisApennina, ad Ripam Tiberis dexteram, perlustravi: offert se percurrendum, quod ibidem ad sinistram est, LATIVM, Italiae Regio, quae nullis non Auctoribus celebrata.
units.tr: I have now surveyed Etruria, which belongs to Ancient Italy, to its more western part on the cis-Apennine side, on the right bank of the Tiber. Next comes what lies on the left bank: LATIUM, a region of Italy celebrated by every author.

units.la: Latium dictum putatur ab Saturno, qui Patria profugus in his locis latuisse fertur. Legendus praeter alios Isidorus lib. xiiii. Erymolog. cap. iv. Saturnus, ut antea monui, quasi Deus latens, ab סתר Syriaca voce, quae Latinis Latere. De Laty Etymo Virgilius lib. viii. Æneidos: Primus ab aethereo venit Saturnus Olympo, Arma levis fugiens, & regnis Exsul ademtis: Is genus indocile, & dispersum Montibus altis Composuit, Legesque dedit: Latiumque vocari Maluit, his quondam latuisset tutus in oris.
units.tr: Latium is thought to be named from Saturn, who is said to have fled his homeland and lain hidden in these parts. Besides others, Isidore should be read, book 14 of the Etymologies, chapter 4: Saturn, as I said before, is as it were a hidden god, from the Syriac word satar, which in Latin is latere, to lie hidden. On the etymology of Lati, Virgil in book 8 of the Aeneid: First Saturn came from heaven's Olympus, fleeing arms and an exile from his stolen kingdom. He gathered into order the untamed race scattered over the high mountains and gave them laws, and he preferred that the land be called Latium, because he had once lain hidden safe on these shores.

units.la: Sic Ovidius libro i. Fastorum. Hæc ego Saturnum memini Tellure receptum: Cœlestibus Regnis ab Ioue pulsus erat. Inde diu Gens mansit Saturnia nomen: Dicta quoque est Latium Terra, latente Deo. At bona Posteritas Puppim formauit in Aere, Hospitis Aduentum testificata Dei.
units.tr: Ovid says the same in book 1 of the Fasti: I remember that Saturn was received by the earth, for he had been driven from the heavenly kingdoms by Jove. From him the race long kept the name Saturnian, and the land was also called Latium, because the god lay hidden there. But later generations fashioned a ship in bronze, to bear witness to the arrival of the god who had been their guest.

units.la: Sic Prudentius aduersum Symmachum, de Saturno: Num melius Saturnus Auos rexisse Latinos Creditur, Edictis qui talibus informauit Agrestes Animos, & barbara Corda Virorum? Sum Deus; aduenio fugiens, præbete Latebras, Occultate Senem Nati feritate Tyranni Detectum Solio: placet hic Fugitiuus, & Exsul Vt latcam: Genti atque Loco Latium dabo nomen.
units.tr: Likewise Prudentius, against Symmachus, on Saturn: Is Saturn believed to have ruled the Latins of old better, he who by such edicts shaped the rough minds of the rustics and the savage hearts of men? I am a god; I come in flight. Give me shelter, hide the old man, exposed on his throne by the savagery of his tyrant son. I am pleased to be a fugitive and an exile here, so that I may lie hidden; I will give a name, Latium, to the people and the place.

units.la: Adeo ut cum Solino quis merito interrogarit: Quis nescit a Saturno Latium atque Saturniam dictam? Ennius ex Emendatione nostra lib.1. Annalium: Saturnius illi Nomen erat, de quo Latium, Saturnia Terra.
units.tr: So that, with Solinus, one may rightly ask: who does not know that Latium and Saturnia were named from Saturn? Ennius, in our emendation, book 1 of the Annals: Saturnius was his name, from whom came Latium and the land of Saturnia.

units.la: Varroni placet Lati Nomen huic Regioni datum, quod inter Alpium & Apennini sublimes præcipitesque rupes, Mare, Tiberim atque Liris, tamquam abscondatur & lateat. Alii Latium ab Latino nominatur: quem Regem plerique habent. Orpheus autem quendam ex Argonautis, qui huc concesserit, cuiusque Filij Bello Trojano interfuerint. Nonnullis ab Latitudine derivatur, quod nulla Italiæ Regio Latius se inter Montes & Mare adipiscendam præbeat. Ab Latio Lataris, vel ut alia habent Exemplaria, Latialis Iupiter, Lactantio lib.1. Diuinar. Instit. cap. xxi. Latiare Concilium Symmacho lib.1. Epistola ix. Latiare Munus, Prudentio libro 1.in Symmachum: Latiaris Lingua eidem Symmacho lib. viii. Epist.xxii. Lataris de nique Facundia, eidem lib. ix. Epist. lxviii. Vocatur hodie Campagna di Roma, ad differentiam Campaniæ Felicis ab Roma, quasi dicas Territorium Romæ. Audit item apud Collenutium Latio vernacule, & Maremma.
units.tr: Varro holds that the name Latium was given to this region because it lies hidden and concealed between the lofty and steep rocks of the Alps and the Apennines, the sea, the Tiber and the Liris. Others derive Latium from Latinus, whom most count as its king. Orpheus, however, names a certain one of the Argonauts who came here, whose sons fought in the Trojan War. Some derive it from latitudo, breadth, because no region of Italy offers so wide a plain between the mountains and the sea as Latium does. From Latium come Lataris, or, as other copies have it, Latialis Jupiter, in Lactantius, Divine Institutes book 1, chapter 21; Latiare Concilium in Symmachus, book 1, letter 9; Latiare Munus in Prudentius, book 1 against Symmachus; Latiaris Lingua in the same Symmachus, book 8, letter 22; and finally Lataris Facundia, in the same, book 9, letter 68. Today it is called the Campagna di Roma, to distinguish it from Campania Felix, as though one said the territory of Rome. In Collenutius it is also heard in the vernacular as Latio, and Maremma.

units.la: Latium porro duplex legitur Vetus & Nouum. Vetus à Tiberi Circæsios (Fundos, aut Seruius) usque protendebatur: Nouum hinc ad Liris Fluuium; Plinio libro iii. & Strabone lib. v. Auctoribus: inde ulterius, isdem Tellibus: Sinuessam (quæ & Sinope) usque, in adiecto utpote Latio, ut idem Plinius hunc Tractum ultra Lirim, qui pars Campaniæ, nominat: quæ de causa forte Seruius hoc Latium ad Vulturnum usque Fluuium extendit.
units.tr: Moreover, Latium is read as of two kinds, Old and New. Old Latium extended from the Tiber to Circeii (Fundi, or, according to Servius, Terracina), while New Latium ran from there to the river Liris, according to Pliny, book 3, and Strabone, book 5. Beyond that, in the same lands, it reached as far as Sinuessa (also called Sinope), as an addition to Latium; so Pliny names this tract beyond the Liris, which is part of Campania. For this reason, perhaps, Servius extends this Latium as far as the river Volturnus.

units.la: Veriusque Latij Fines plerisque statuuntur ad Septemtrionem Apenninus Mons & Anio fluvius: ad Ortum Liris, qua Meridies est, Mare Tyrrhenum: qua Occasus, Tiberinum Flumen: ambientibus illud Populis, Tuscis, Sabinis, Marsis, Sammitibus, Præguttianis & Campanis.
units.tr: By most accounts the true boundaries of Latium are: to the north the Apennine mountains and the river Anio; to the east the Liris; to the south the Tyrrhenian Sea; to the west the Tiber river. Its neighbours were the Tuscans, Sabines, Marsi, Samnites, Praeguttians and Campanians.

units.la: Latium cognominat Virgilius lib.vii. Æneidos Hesperium: quam ob causam, parer ex iis, quæ dixi Cap.1.
units.tr: Virgil, in book 7 of the Aeneid, calls Latium Hesperium, for the reason which, as appears from what I said in chapter 1.

units.la: Fertilis & abundans est Regio: præterquam aliquibus in locis, propter Oram quibus cum aspera saxosaque habet multa, tum Paludes, & ex Paludibus Aerem vitiosum atque gravem. Le Qualitate legendus & Theophrastus lib.v. Histor Plantarum. Hæc est illa Regio, in qua totius Italiæ vetusta fuerunt Incunabula: quæ Genitrix Altrixque tot Ingeniorum: quæ totius Mundi sustinuit Arcem & Capitolium. Sed silere præstat, quam pauca pro dignitate dicere.
units.tr: The region is fertile and abundant, except in some places along the coast, where there is much rough and rocky ground, and marshes, and from the marshes an air that is foul and heavy. On its quality, Theophrastus, book 5 of the History of Plants, should also be read. This is that region in which the ancient cradle of all Italy lay, the mother and nurse of so many talents, which bore the citadel and Capitol of the whole world. But it is better to be silent than to say little that is worthy of its dignity.

units.la: Populi ad hæc usque tempora, præterquam in Ciuitatibus, plerumque rudes, moribusque agrestibus, animis audaces confidentesque: Viribus corporis, non minus quam olim, præstantes. Illi, antiquitus alij, Colonus sæpe mutatis, fuerunt, aliis temporibus. Nominantur in primis apud Dionysium Halicarnassæum libro i. Antiquit. Romanar. (nam eius ordo maxime placet) Siculi, Barbari, & Gens Indigena. Sicanos appellat Virgilius lib. viii. Æneid. ad quem legendus quoque Seruius: ut & in librum Æneidos xi. Siculos abunde in Italiam venisse, innuit idem Virgilius libro viii. Æneidos: ubi etiam Seruius scribit, Sicanos, Duce Siculo, ex Hispania in Italiam esse profectos, camque tenuisse exclusis Aboriginibus: agnoscens contra Dionysium Aborigines priores Siculis, Aborigines inquam Indigenas pulsos fuisse ab Siculis Advenis. Quidquid sit, latissimum fuit olim per Italiam Siculorum nomen. Ab iis enim Partem, quae obversa Trinacriae, Siciliam vocant Aelianus, Eustathius, Sudas, Theocriti Scholiastes, D. Hieronymus, Synodus Constantinopolitana, Stephanus, & alij. Scribit Plinius lib. iii. cap. xiii. & seq. eundem Galliae Togatae Partem occupasse ante Gallorum in eandem adventum: Siculas Urbes in Campania habet Livius libro xxiii. Supersunt etiam Siculorum vestigia post Marsorum & Aquilanorum fines, in Agro, ubi hodie, prima Nominis Littera mutata, Ciculi vocantur: Est item Valle Ciculiana, quae Praefectorum est, in Vestinis, qui sunt inter Aternum & Truentum Amnes. Sed haec suo loco. Siculi longo bello victis, atque demum in Insulam Trinacriam, quae ab iis deinde Sicania & Sicilia, exactis, succedunt apud Dionysium Halic. libro i. Aborigines: dicti quasi absque Origine, ut innuit Servius ad viii. Aeneidos: vel ab Errore, ut Paulus Diaconus ex Festi libro i. vel denique, ut nonnullis videtur, ab Montibus, qui ὄρη Graecis. Aborigines Servius, ut antea dixi, facit Indigenas: Arcadas esse, inque Italiam, Oenotro & Peucetio Ducibus, Lycaonis Arcadum Regis filiis, commigrasse, commemorat Dionysius libro i. Ab Oenotro Oenotria Italia Varrom, apud Servium i. Aeneidos; & Oenotry Virgilio, eodem libro. Dixi supra cap. i. Festus Aborigines dicit antiquissimam esse Italiae Gentem, & in Agro Romano habitasse: Iustinus etiam ex Trogi lib. xiiii. Aborigines facit Italiae Cultores Primos. Describit eos aliquo modo Sallustius in Conjuratione Catilinaria, Genus Hominum agreste, sine Legibus, sine Imperio, liberum atque solutum. Eorum antiquissimi Reges, quos ob Merita Deos fecit Posteritas, recensentur Ianus, Saturnus, Picus & Faunus: de quibus Lactantius libro i. de Falsa Relig. cap. xxii. Iustinus libro xliii. Suetonius in Vitellio cap. i. Ab Iano Ianiculum: ab Saturno Saturnia & Latium, Mons Saturnius, Oppidum Saturnia, Saturnij Populi, & alia: de quibus alibi. Aboriginibus paullatim se ad junxerunt Pelasgi, ex Thessalia in Italiam profecti, ut notant Dionysius libro i. & Plinius libro iii. cap. v. & Arcades, quibus ex Urbe Arcadiae Palanteo in Italiam tendentibus Dux fuit Evander: scribentibus eodem Dionysio Plinioque locis a me laudatis, & Virgilio lib. viii. Aeneidos. Ab horum Patria Urbs Palanteum in Monte, qui post Palatinus: testibus Iustino libro xliii. & Solino cap. ii. Depingit opidum illud Virgilius eodem libro viii. Sequuntur Pelasgos Arcadasque apud Dionysium Peloponnesiaci, Phenicae, Eperque, reduces cum Victoria, Hercule Duce, ex Hispania: politoque Reditus in Patriam desiderio: consulendus & Solinus cap. ii. His admisti erant, signante eodem Dionysio, Troiani, qui sub Laomedonte captivi, Bello Ilaco priore, ab Hercule facti fuerant. Quibus omnibus succesisse tandem, Troia diruta, Troiani, Aenea Duce; Latino jam Aboriginibus imperante, testibus ipsidem Dionysio, Iustino & Sallustio. Ab iis Troia, locus in Agro Laurente: quo primum in Italia Aeneas cum suis constitit apud Festum lib. penultimo. Hi Troiani appellati Veteribus Aenesi, eodem Festo scribente libro i. Αινιάδαι, ut notat Sudas. Troiani cum suo Duce ab Latino suscepti, & Aborigines communi nomine, ut M. Porcius Cato testatur apud Servium ad i. Aeneidos, nuncupati fuerunt Latini, qui & Πέλασγοι, scribente Dionysio libro i. Virgilius v. Aeneidos: —— Et Priscos docuit celebrare Latinos.
units.tr: Its peoples, down to these times, apart from those in the cities, are for the most part rude, with rustic manners, bold and confident in spirit, and no less outstanding in bodily strength than of old. Different peoples, some from ancient times and others by later colonization, have at various times inhabited it. Mentioned first by Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 1 of the Roman Antiquities (for I most approve of his order), are the Siculi, the Barbarians, and the Indigenous people. Virgil, book 8 of the Aeneid, calls them Sicani; on this see also Servius, and on book 11 of the Aeneid. The same Virgil, in book 8 of the Aeneid, hints that the Siculi came in great numbers into Italy; there Servius also writes that the Sicani, under a Sicilian leader, set out from Spain for Italy and took possession of it, driving out the Aborigines. Servius, contrary to Dionysius, acknowledges that the Aborigines were earlier than the Siculi, but that the Aborigines, I say the Indigenous, were driven out by the Siculi as newcomers. Whatever the case, the name of the Siculi was once very widespread through Italy. Indeed, Aelian, Eustathius, Suidas, the scholiast of Theocritus, St Jerome, the Council of Constantinople, Stephanus and others call by their name the part of the island that faces Trinacria, namely Sicily. Pliny, book 3, chapter 13 and following, writes that the same Siculi occupied part of Gallia Togata before the Gauls came to the same place. Livy, book 23, has Sicilian cities in Campania. Traces of the Siculi also survive beyond the borders of the Marsi and the Aquilani, in a district where today, with the first letter changed, they are called Ciculi; there is also the Valle Ciculiana, which belongs to the prefects, among the Vestini, who live between the rivers Aternus and Truentus. But these matters belong to their own place. According to Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 1, the Siculi, after a long war, were beaten and at last driven into the island of Trinacria, which was afterwards called Sicania and Sicilia, and the Aborigines took their place. The Aborigines are so called as if without origin, as Servius hints on Aeneid 8, or from wandering, as Paulus Diaconus has it from Festus, book 1; or finally, as some think, from the mountains, which the Greeks call orē. Servius, as I said before, makes the Aborigines Indigenous; Dionysius, book 1, records that they were Arcadians, who migrated into Italy under the leadership of Oenotrus and Peucetius, sons of Lycaon, king of the Arcadians. From Oenotrus, Varro, cited by Servius on Aeneid 1, derives Oenotria, Italy; and Virgil, in the same book, has Oenotria. I mentioned this above in chapter 1. Festus says the Aborigines were the most ancient people of Italy and lived in the Roman countryside; Justin also, from Trogus book 14, makes the Aborigines the first inhabitants of Italy. Sallust, in the Catilinarian Conspiracy, describes them in a way: a rustic race of men, without laws, without rule, free and unrestrained. Their most ancient kings, whom posterity made gods for their merits, are listed as Janus, Saturn, Picus and Faunus; concerning whom see Lactantius, book 1 of On the False Religion, chapter 22, Justin book 43, and Suetonius in Vitellius, chapter 1. From Janus comes the Janiculum; from Saturn come Saturnia and Latium, Mount Saturnius, the town of Saturnia, the Saturnian peoples, and other things, on which I will speak elsewhere. Gradually the Pelasgians, who set out from Thessaly for Italy, joined themselves to the Aborigines, as Dionysius, book 1, and Pliny, book 3, chapter 5, note; and the Arcadians, whose leader on their way to Italy from the Arcadian city of Pallanteum was Evander, as Dionysius and Pliny, cited by me, and Virgil in Aeneid book 8 write. From the homeland of these people comes the city of Palanteum on the mountain that was afterwards called the Palatine, as attested by Justin, book 43, and Solinus, chapter 2. Virgil describes that town in the same book 8. According to Dionysius, the Peloponnesians, Phoenicians and Epeans followed the Pelasgians and Arcadians, returning with victory from Spain under the leadership of Hercules; the longing for their homeland was then sharpened on the return. Solinus, chapter 2, should also be consulted. Mixed with these, as Dionysius points out, were the Trojans, who had been taken captive under Laomedon and made captives by Hercules in the earlier Ilian war. After Troy was destroyed, the Trojans, led by Aeneas, eventually succeeded all these peoples, while the Aborigines were already ruled by Latinus, as Dionysius, Justin and Sallust bear witness. From them comes Troy, a place in the territory of Laurentum, where Aeneas first halted with his men in Italy, according to Festus in the next-to-last book. These Trojans were called by the ancients Aenesi, as Festus writes in book 1: Αἰνιάδαι, as Suidas notes. The Trojans, with their leader, were received by Latinus, and both they and the Aborigines were called by the common name Latins, as Marcus Porcius Cato testifies, cited by Servius on Aeneid 1; they were also called Pelasgians, as Dionysius writes in book 1. Virgil, Aeneid book 5: and taught the old Latins to keep festival.

units.la: Prisci, inquit Festus, vocabantur proprie, qui priusquam Roma conderetur, fuerunt. Hi idem & Casci nominabatur. Ennius meus libro i. Annalium: Est Locus, Hesperiam quam Mortales perhibebant, Quam primum Catei Popoli tenuere Latini: Quos Homines quondam Laurentis Terra recepit.
units.tr: Prisci, says Festus, were properly called those who lived before Rome was founded. These were also called Casci. My Ennius, in book 1 of the Annals: There is a place which mortals called Hesperia, which the Catei Latin peoples first held. Men of old, these the land of Laurentum received.

units.la: Hieronymus ad Niceam: Nam rudes illi Italiae Homines, quos Cascos Ennius appellat, Vtrosque & Priscos & Cascos nominat M. Tullius libro i. Tusculanarum Quaest. Itaque unum illud erat insitum Priscis illis, quos Cascos appellat Ennius, esse in Morte Sensum, neque Excessu Vitae sic deleri Hominem, ut funditus interiret. Diu Latini, quod essent ingeniis ferociores, inimicitias acriter cum Romanis exercuerunt: sed compositá deinde Pace, maximo illis auxilio contra varios Populos in Bellis fuerunt: quemadmodum amplissime scribunt cum alij, tum Livius & Dionysius Halicarnass. Adduntur duntur apud Plinium lib. iii. cap. v. Superioribus in Veteri Latio Aurunci & Rutuli. Aurunci (qui Græcis Αὐρύγκαι) Italiæ Populi, inquit Servius ad viii. Aenidos, antiquissimi fuerunt. Auruncorum mentionem persæpe facit Livius: item Dionysius Halic. cum alibi, tum lib. vi. ubi Legatos ab iis Romam missos narrat, qui Agrum Nominis Volscorum, quem Ecetranis devictis Romani ademerant, restitui ab Senatu postularent: describens inde robustum hominum genus, membrorum firmitate præstantes, aspectu truci ac feroci; commemorans insuper Servilij Consulis ex iis Victoriam. Quia vero Ausonia nomen latissimum olim fuit, uti, quum generalia explicarem, dixi: factum est, ut Aurunci etiam Ausones fuerint habiti. Servius ad illud Virgilij vii. Æncidos: ——Et quos de Collibus altis Aurunci misere Patres ——
units.tr: Jerome, to Nicaea: For those rude men of Italy, whom Ennius calls Cascos. Marcus Tullius, in book 1 of the Tusculan Disputations, calls both Priscos and Cascos: So this one thing was implanted in those Priscis illustrious men, whom Ennius calls Cascos, that there is sense in death, and that a man is not so destroyed by the departure of life as to perish utterly. For a long time the Latins, because they were fiercer in temperament, waged bitter enmities with the Romans. But after peace was afterwards made, they were of the greatest help to them against various peoples in wars, as Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, among others, write at length. They are added by Pliny in book 3, chapter 5. Among the older peoples in Old Latium were the Aurunci and Rutuli. The Aurunci (called by the Greeks Aurynkai [Αὐρύγκαι]), peoples of Italy, says Servius on Aeneid 8, were very ancient. Livy often mentions the Aurunci; so too Dionysius of Halicarnassus, both elsewhere and in book 6, where he tells of envoys sent to Rome by them, who demanded that the territory of the Volscian name, which the Romans had taken from the Ecetrani after defeating them, be restored by the Senate; he describes there a robust race of men, excelling in firmness of limbs, fierce and grim in appearance, and he further recalls the victory of Consul Servilius over them. But since the name Ausonia was once very wide-ranging, as I said when I explained general matters, it came about that the Aurunci were also regarded as Ausones. Servius, on that line of Virgil's Aeneid 7: And those whom the Aurunci sent from the high hills, the Fathers.

units.la: Iiti, inquit, Græce Ausones nominantur: Hinc item quod Isacius & Tzetzes Ausoniam proprie Auruncorum Terram statuant, sitam inter Campanos & Volscos: Hinc denique quod Aurunca Festo scribatur condita ab Ausone, a quo nomen Ausonia. Nam vere Ausones, si strictius accipiantur, & Aurunci apud Plinium lib. iii. cap. v. sunt diversi: hi in Vetere Latio; illi in Novo, ultra Circeios. Ab Auruncis autem quuir Suessa Aurunca, Campaniæ Vrbs, dicta fuerit, suo dicam loco. Rutulos (quos Græci vocant Ῥουτούλους) etiam Italiæ Populos, ut Superiores, antiquissimos fuisse, testantur Veteres Scriptores. Ardeam cos habitasse, memorat Strabo lib. v. De rebus ab ipsis, eorumque Duce Turno feliciter & infeliciter gestis, multa idem Strabo, Dionysius lib. i. Livius lib. i. Virgilius, & alij. Daunos etiam vocatos paret ex Vibio Sequestr. De Daunis quædam apud Aristotelem in Admirandis. Et hæc de Populis, quos Plinius habet in Vetere Latio: in Novo, ultra Circeios nominat Volsços, Oscos, Ausones.
units.tr: They, he says, are called Ausones in Greek. Hence also Isacius and Tzetzes hold that Ausonia properly means the land of the Aurunci, situated between the Campanians and the Volsci. Hence finally, Festus writes that Aurunca was founded by Ausonus, from whom the name Ausonia comes. For truly the Ausones, if taken more strictly, and the Aurunci in Pliny book 3, chapter 5, are different: these in Old Latium, those in New Latium, beyond the Circeii. I shall say in its place how Suessa Aurunca, a city of Campania, was named after the Auruncis. That the Rutuli (whom the Greeks call Routoulous [Ῥουτούλους]) were also ancient peoples of Italy, like those above, the ancient writers testify. That they lived at Ardea Strabo records in book 5. Strabo, Dionysius in book 1, Livy in book 1, Virgil and others tell much about the deeds of the same people and their leader Turnus, both successful and unsuccessful. That they were also called Dauni appears from Vibius Sequester. Some things about the Dauni are in Aristotle's On Marvellous Things. And these are the peoples which Pliny lists in Old Latium; in New Latium, beyond the Circeii, he names the Volsci, Osci, Ausones.

units.la: Volsci Livio passim, Plinio, Eutropio, & Doctioribus emendatissime scribentibus qui Οὐόλσκοι Straboni: Οὐολσκοι Dionysio Halicarnassæo: Οὐόλσκοι Ptolemæo: Volci, L. Floro: Βαλσκοι Sudæ. Meminit Romanus Lapis: SEX. APVSIVS SEX. F. VET BÆBIVS VOLSCIS. LATIN
units.tr: The Volsci are called so by Livy throughout, by Pliny, Eutropius, and by the more learned writers most correctly; Strabo calls them Ouolskoi [Οὐόλσκοι], Dionysius of Halicarnassus Ouolskoi [Οὐόλσκοι], Ptolemy Ouolskoi [Οὐόλσκοι]; Lucius Florus calls them Volci; Suidas calls them Balskoi [Βαλσκοι]. A Roman stone mentions them: SEX. APVSIVS SEX. F. VET BÆBIVS VOLSCIS. LATIN

units.la: Item Neapolitanus, qui in Domo Petri Pighiole:
units.tr: Likewise the Neapolitan inscription, which is in the house of Pietro Pighioli:

units.la: M. PACCIVS. M. F. DOM. BASSVS.
units.tr: M. Paccius Bassus, son of Marcus, of the home (domo) Bassus.

units.la: AVGVR. ÆDIL. II. VIR. VOLSCIS. SIBI. ET. SVIS PACCIÆ. M. F. BASSÆ MANLIÆ. CN. F. RVFÆ PACCIÆ. L. F. MAXIMÆ PACCIÆ M. F. GRATÆ
units.tr: Augur, aedile, duumvir of the Volsci, for himself and his family: Paccia Bassa, daughter of Marcus; Manlia Rufa, daughter of Gnaeus, wife of Paccius; Paccia Maxima, daughter of Lucius; Paccia Grata, daughter of Marcus.

units.la: Italiæ in Littorali Latio Populi. De iis Virgilius lib. ii. Georgic.
units.tr: Peoples of Italy on the coast of Latium. Concerning them, Virgil in Georgics book 2:

units.la: Hac genus acre Virûm Marsos, Pubemque Sabellam, Adsuetumque malo Ligurem, Volscosque Verutis, Extulit; hæc Decios, Marios, magnosque Camillos, Scipiadas duros bello, & Te, Maxime Cæsar.
units.tr: From this land came forth the fierce race of men: the Marsi, the Sabine youth, the Ligurians inured to hardship, and the Volsci armed with javelins; from it came the Decii, the Marii, the great Camilli, the Scipios hard in war, and you, greatest Caesar.

units.la: Vbi de Volscis Servius, Italiæ Populi sunt, inquit, iaculo utentes in modum Vern; vel quia Verutis pugnant. Metropolis eorum Anxur sive Tarracina. Volsci, qui Bellum cum Romanis sub L. Tarquinio Superbo inchoatum per ducentos propè annos incredibili pertinacia & continuis motibus protraxerant, de quibus, supra xii. Triumphi acti fuerunt, postremo anno ab V. C. cccxxv. diuturno Bello defatigati, Priverno capto, ab Consulibus L. Æmilio Mamercino ii. & C. Plautio Deciano subjugati, in Ditionem venerunt Populi Romani: scribentibus plene Livio, Dionysio Halicarnass. Orosio, Eutropio, L. Floro, & alijs. Volscia Gens Romæ ab Volscis, teste Livio. De Oscis in Campania dicam. Nam & ibi nominat eos Plinius; ibique ex Variorum Scriptorum collatione potiores eorum fuerunt Sedes. De Ausonibus jam supra dictum: in sequentibus major dicendi dabitur occasio. Innotuerunt & successu temporis in Latio Hernici, Aequi, Marsi, & alij. Hernici Livio passim & Festo; Εῥνικες Straboni: qui Εῥνικες Stephano. Hernici, inquit Festus ex Verrio Flacco, dicti ab Saxis, qua Marsi Herna dicunt. Hinc Virgilius lib. VII. Quique altum Praenestè Viri, quique Arva Gabina Junonis, gelidumque Anienem, & rosida Rivis Hernica Saxa colunt, quos dives Anagnia pascit, Quos Amasene Pater: non illis omnibus Arma, Non Clypei, Currusve sonant: pars maxima Glandes Liventis Plumbi spargit, pars Spicula gestat Bina manu, fulvosque Lupi de pelle Galleros Tegmen habet capiti: Vestigia nuda sinistri Instituere pedis: crudus tegit altera pero.
units.tr: Where Servius speaks of the Volsci: They are peoples of Italy, he says, using the javelin in the manner of a spear; or because they fight with javelins. Their metropolis was Anxur, or Tarracina. The Volsci, who had begun war with the Romans under Lucius Tarquinius Superbus and had prolonged it for nearly two hundred years with incredible stubbornness and continual uprisings, against whom triumphs were celebrated in book 12 above, were at last worn out by a long war in the year 325 from the founding of the city; Priverno was taken, and they were subdued by the consuls Lucius Aemilius Mamercinus (for the second time) and Gaius Plautius Decianus, and came under the power of the Roman people. Livy, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Orosius, Eutropius, Lucius Florus and others write fully about this. A Volscian race at Rome, from the Volsci, according to Livy. I shall speak of the Osci in Campania, for Pliny also names them there, and there, from the comparison of various writers, were their chief settlements. Of the Ausones I have already spoken above; in what follows a greater opportunity for discussion will be given. In time there also became known in Latium the Hernici, Aequi, Marsi, and others. The Hernici are mentioned by Livy throughout and by Festus; Strabo calls them Hernikes [Ἑρνικες], and Stephanus likewise. The Hernici, says Festus, following Verrius Flaccus, were so named from the rocks, which the Marsi call herna. Hence Virgil in book 7: And the men of high Praeneste, and those who hold the Gabine fields of Juno, and cold Anio, and the Hernican rocks with their dewy streams, whom rich Anagnia feeds, whom the father Amasenus (feeds): not all of them have arms, not shields or chariots that clatter; most of them scatter leaden sling-bullets, some carry two javelins in hand, and wear on their head a cap of tawny wolf-skin; they set their bare left foot forward, while the other foot is covered by a raw-hide boot.

units.la: Vbi Servius, Sabinorum, inquit, lingua Herne Saxa vocantur. Quidam Dux Maius Cabinos de suis locis eiecit, & habitare secum fecit in Montibus saxosis, unde dicti sunt Hernici. Canit autem Virgilius Hernicos sinistro pede nudo in Acie stare solitos. Ad ea sic Servius: Atqui ipse est, ait, in pugnantibus primus. Sed bene nudus est: quia tegitur Scuto. Dextrum autem tectum esse conveniebat, quasi ab Armis remotum. Simile quid de Aetolis memoriae prodit Euripidis Interpres; Eos ῥ' ἀξίων μὲν ἄσπιδας ... ἔχειν ἀσπίδα. Thucydides item lib. III. de Plataensibus, noctu clanculum ex Civitate profugientibus, seque subripientibus, hoc modo scribit: ἔσαν ἱσαλὰς τε τῆς πόλεως, καὶ τὸν ἀσπίδα μόνον πόδα ἐποθηδιῶμοι, ἀσφαλείας ἕνεκα πρὸς τὴν πόλιν: Vbi Commentator: ὑπὸ ἰδίων τὸν μὲν ἐν τῶν ποδῶν δὲ ἀσφάλειαν, τὸν δ' ἔπειτα γυμνὸν ἔχειν ... Ea quoque de causa Hernicos altero pede nudo confligere solitos, est existimandum. Gens olim fuit longe potentissima, bellumque contra Romanos diu sustinuit. Bellare contra eos quum coepisset Populus Romanus, T. Sicinio & C. Aquilio Coss. tandem anno CCCCXLVIII. cos, Anagnia capta, debellavit Q. Marcius Tremulus Cos. ut legere est apud Livium, Dionysium, & alios. Hernica Terra nominatur Ovidio lib. III. Fast. Specialiores Hernicorum Populos persequar in sequentibus. Aequi erant in Latio Populi, qui postea Aequicolae dicti, Auctore Livio: Αἴκοι & Αἰκοῖοι, variante scriptura, Straboni; Αἰκλοι & Αἰκλοι Diodoro & Ptolomaeo: Aequiculani, Plinio lib. IV. cap. XII. Aecani, ni fallor, Antiquo Lapidi, qui Beneventi in aedibus Alphonsi Majorani:
units.tr: Where Servius says: In the language of the Sabines, he says, herne are called rocks. Some leader drove the Cabini out of their places and made them live with him in the rocky mountains, whence they were called Hernici. Virgil, however, sings that the Hernici were accustomed to stand in battle with the left foot bare. To this Servius says: But he himself, he says, is first among the fighters. But he is rightly bare, because he is covered by a shield. The right foot, however, ought to have been covered, as being removed from the arms. The interpreter of Euripides hands down something similar about the Aetolians; that they had shields... [ἀξίων μὲν ἄσπιδας ... ἔχειν ἀσπίδα]. Thucydides likewise, in book 3, writing of the Plataeans who fled from the city secretly at night and slipped away, puts it this way: they were ... and only the one foot they covered, for safety's sake towards the city [ἔσαν ἱσαλὰς τε τῆς πόλεως, καὶ τὸν ἀσπίδα μόνον πόδα ἐποθηδιῶμοι, ἀσφαλείας ἕνεκα πρὸς τὴν πόλιν]. There the commentator says: [ὑπὸ ἰδίων τὸν μὲν ἐν τῶν ποδῶν δὲ ἀσφάλειαν, τὸν δ' ἔπειτα γυμνὸν ἔχειν ...]. It must be thought that for this same reason the Hernici were accustomed to fight with one foot bare. It was a very powerful people by far, and sustained war against the Romans for a long time. When the Roman people had begun to make war against them, under the consuls Titus Sicinius and Gaius Aquilius, in the year 448, Anagnia was taken, and at last Quintus Marcius Tremulus, as consul, subdued them, as can be read in Livy, Dionysius and others. The Hernican land is named by Ovid in book 3 of the Fasti. I shall pursue the more particular peoples of the Hernici in what follows. The Aequi were peoples in Latium, who were afterwards called Aequicolae, on the authority of Livy; Strabo has Aikoi and Aikoioi, with variant spelling; Diodorus and Ptolemy have Aiklou and Aiklou; Pliny in book 4, chapter 12, has Aequiculani. The Aecani, unless I am mistaken, from an ancient stone which is in the house of Alfonso Majorano at Benevento:

units.la: C. OCTAVIO. C.F
units.tr: Gaius Octavius, son of Gaius

units.la: PAL. MODESTO AVGVR. II. VIR. I. D. QVAEST. II PRAEF. FABR. ROMAE. PRAEF COH. III. PANNONIOR. PRAEF COH. III. ITYREOS. TRIB. MIL. LEG. IIII. SCYTHIC. CVRAT. REI P. ACANOR. ITEM. HONORATO. AD. CVRAM. CALENDARI REIP. CANVSINOR. A. DIVO. TRAIANO. PARTHICO. ET. AB. IMP. HADRIANO. AVG.
units.tr: Pal. Modestus, augur, duumvir with judicial power, quaestor, prefect of engineers at Rome, prefect of the third cohort of Pannonians, prefect of the third cohort of Ityraeans, military tribune of the fourth legion Scythica, curator of the state of the Acanians, and likewise Honoratus, in charge of the calendar of the state of the Canusinians, by the deified Trajan Parthicus and by the Emperor Hadrian Augustus.

units.la: Et quae alia sequuntur. Meminit Aequorum & Ennius meus Annali IV. In praecelsis asperisque Laty Montibus habitabant. Describit Gentem Virgilius libro VII. Aeneidos: Horrida praecipue cui gens, adsuetaque multo Venatu Nemorum duris Aequicola glebis: Armati terram exercent, semperque recentes Convellere iuvat praedas & vivere rapto.
units.tr: And the others that follow. My Ennius also mentions the Aequi in Annals book IV: "They lived on the lofty and rugged mountains of Latium." Virgil describes the people in Aeneid book VII: "Chiefly a fierce race, used to much hunting in the woods, the Aequian dwellers with their hard clods; they work the land under arms, and always delight in fresh plunder and in living by rapine."

units.la: Aequi & Volsci plerumque conjunguntur apud Historiographos. Quae, quantaque gesserint contra Romanos, memoriae produnt cum alij, tum Livius infinitis locis. Post multa Bella tandem anno CCCCLII. ab C. Iunio Bubulco Bruto Dictatore non solum sunt victi & subacti, sed eorum etiam nomen ad internecionem usque prope fuit delectum. Legendus cum aliis Livius. Marsi Italiæ Populi non apud Geographos solum, Strabonem, Plinium, Ptolemæum: verum etiam Historiographos, Livium, Cæsarem, Tacitum, celebres. Auctor Gentis Marsus putatur, Ulyssis & Circes Filius, apud Plinium lib. vii. cap. ii. Silius Italicus Marsiam Phrygem celebrat libro Belli Pœnici viii:
units.tr: The Aequi and the Volsci are usually joined together by the historians. What great things they did against the Romans is recorded by others as well as by Livy in countless places. After many wars, finally in the year 452 from the founding of the city, under the dictatorship of C. Junius Bubulcus Brutus, they were not only conquered and subdued, but their very name was almost wiped out. Livy should be read along with the others. The Marsi of Italy are a famous people, known not only from the geographers Strabo, Pliny and Ptolemy but also from the historians Livy, Caesar and Tacitus. The founder of the people is thought to be Marsus, son of Ulysses and Circe, according to Pliny book VII chapter 2. Silius Italicus celebrates Marsia the Phrygian in book VIII of the Punic War:

units.la: Sed Populis Nomen posuit metuentior hospes, Quōnam fugeret Phrygias trans æquora Marsia, Crenos Migdoniam Phœbi superatus pectine Lotos.
units.tr: But a more fearful stranger gave the peoples their name, Marsia the Phrygian, who fled across the seas from the Phrygians, Lotos, conquered by the lyre of Phoebus, Crenos, Migdonia.

units.la: Alij alibunde derivant. Ferocissimos fuisse docent Res ab ipsis gestæ: quas diligenter notant cum alii, tum Livius, præcipue libro lxxii. ubi Marsos, quum Libertatem à Populo Romano petitam impetrare non potuissent, Picentibus, Vestinis, Peligns, Marucinis, Lucanis & Samnitibus ad Defectionem una concitatis, Auctores Belli Socialis, quod Marsicum inde appellatum, narrat; reliqua commemorans lib. lxxiii. & seqq. Legendus de Bello Sociali præter alios & Strabo lib. v. Marsorum Agrum vastat apud Livium lib. xxii. Hannibal: per Marsos idem transitum habet, quum ab vicinis Romæ locis rediret, eodem scribente libro xxvi. Catillos circa Anienem Livium locat Silius lib. iv. ubi Anienicolæ nominantur: fortean ab Catillo, quem Agri Tiburtini Montem habent Vibius Sequester & Servius, cui Catellus dicitur. Sanates, inquit Festus vel ex Festo potius Paullus, dicti sunt, qui supra infraque Romam 20 habitaverunt, quod nomen hīs fuit; quia, quum defecerent ab Romanis, brevi post redierunt in amicitiam, quasi sanata mente. Itaque in Duodecim tautum est ut idem juris esset Sanatibus, quod Forcitibus id est bonis, & qui nunquam defecerant a Populo Romano: ad quem legenda quæ scribit magnus Vir Iosephus Scaliger.
units.tr: Others derive the name from various sources. The fierce nature of the people is shown by the deeds they did, which are carefully noted by several writers, above all by Livy in book 72, where he relates that the Marsi, when they could not obtain liberty from the Roman people, roused the Picentes, Vestini, Peligni, Marrucini, Lucani and Samnites together to revolt, and became the authors of the Social War, which was called the Marsian war from them; and he recounts the rest in book 73 and following. Strabo book V should also be read on the Social War, among others. Livy in book 22 has Hannibal lay waste the land of the Marsi; he also has him pass through the territory of the Marsi when returning from the places near Rome, as Livy writes in book 26. Silius book IV places the Catilli near the Anio, where they are called Anienicolae, perhaps from Catillus, whom Vibius Sequester and Servius say held the mountain of the Tiburtine land, and who is called Catellus. "Sanates," says Festus, or rather Paulus from Festus, "were those who lived above and below Rome, a name they had because, when they revolted from the Romans, they soon returned to friendship, as if their minds had been healed. So in the Twelve Tables the Sanates had the same rights as the Forcites, that is, the good ones, who had never defected from the Roman people." On this see what the great man Joseph Scaliger writes.

units.la: Præter eos, quos commemoravi ex Antiquo Latio, multi Populi perierunt, adeo ut ne Vestigia quidem hodie adpareant, & quibus locis fuerint, nec conjectura quidem adsequi liceat. Recenset eos Plinius libro iii. cap. v. & itidem fere nominibus Dionysius Halicarnassæus. Nominat & passim T. Livius in libris ab V. C. Sunt autem, ut Plinij sequar ordinem: Albenses; Ἀλβανεῖς fortean Halicarnassæo libro viii. pro quibus Gelenius vertit Albiolanos; Sylburgius legit Labinatas: Albani; Albanorum Terram nominat Eustathius, ubi Mons Circæus est: Aesolani: Aesulum Italiæ Colonia est apud Velleium Paterculum, quod tamen Sigonius neciere se dicit, an idem sit cum Asculo Picentum: Acten-ses, in nonnullis Plinij Codicibus scribuntur Accensis, Akolani, Bubetani, Βουβετανοί, Dionysio Halicarnassæo lib. v. Bolani, Βολανοί Stephano & Halicarnassæo lib. viii. dicti ab Opido, quod Bola Virgilio, Βῶλα Stephano & Diodoro lib. xx. Bola Livio, qui Æquis adiberit, ut Diodorus Samnitibus, ad xiii. ab Urbe Lapidem statuit Plutarchi Coriolanus. Volani etiam videntur Livio lib. iv. Cusuctani, Coriolani, ab Coriolo, opido, sic Livius, Eutropius, Florus, alii appellant; quæ Coriola Auctori de VV. Inlustr. Κορίολα Dionysio Halic. Κορίολα Stephano: Ficulenses, Populi haud procul ab Urbe, Varroni ab Ficulnea Veteri Latij Urbe, quæ & Ficana. Hinc Ficelia in Urbe, Ficuleatum Statio, ut Græcostasis Græcorum, Fregellæ Fregellanorum, Fidenates, de his in Umbria dixi: Foretu, Forenses fortean Ovidio ab Forulis, ut nonnulli volunt, de quibus in Umbria: Hortenses: ab Ortona, ni fallor, quæ Livio lib. ii. & seq. Latinorum sive Æquorum Urbs: Βιέτονα Halicarnassæo lib. x. fortasis parum emendate: Latinienses, alij ab ipsis Latinii. His genus, Illis speciem constituentibus: Longulani, ab Longula, quæ Livio Volscorum Urbs, Λεγγύλα Halicarnassæo, haud procul Polutca, Manates, Macrales: in quibusdam Codicibus, Mlanales, Mutuencumenses, Munienses, Numinienses, Olbiculani, Octulani, Pedani, qui non Plinio solum, sed & Plutarcho in Coriolano sunt noti: hic dicta a Peda, quæ Stephano Ausonica Urbs: Latinorum autem, Livio lib. ii. & ix. cui Pedum scribitur: hinc Pedana Regio apud Horatium libro i. & Dionysium Halicarnassæum libro viii. Porphyrion dicit Opidum haud procul ab Urbe fuisse, nunc autem non esse: Regionem autem adhuc Pedanum vocant: Vetus Commentator, quem addit Cruquius, Regionem Pedanam fuisse notat inter Tibur & Præneste: Pedanos Scaptiam Urbem incoluisse auctor est Sex. Pompeius Festus: Pollustini: fortean a Pulusca, quæ Livio lib. ii. Volscorum Caput: Πόλυσκα Halicarnassæo lib. vi. Πόλυσκα eidem libro viii. Querquetulani: Κερκετυλανοί Halicarnassæo lib. v. Stcani, celccelebrati & Virgilio lib. x. Æneidos : de iis circa initium huius Capitis dixi : alibi etiam nonnihil additurus:Sifolenses: Tolerienses: meminit & Halicarnassæus lib.viii. Antiq. Rom. dicti ab opido,quod Τολιερον Plutarcho in Coriolano & Stephano de Vrbibus: Τελερινος etiam Halicarnassei lib. i. Tolerinos vertit Fridericus Sylburgius: Trebianos autem Gelenius: Tutienses, sic ab Fquo Tutsco (cuius aliquoties meminit Antoninus ; nominatos, fere est, ut opinetur Abrahamus Ortelius: Sed Equum Tuticum Apuliæ fuisse oppidum procul ab Latio (cuius sunt ex indicio Plinij Tutienses) parebit ex sequentibus. Agmen eorum, qui in Vetere Latio esse dicerunt, claudunt Vimitellarij, Velienses, Venetulani,& Vicellenses. Præmiserat xxxii Populus, quos in Antiquo Latio exstinctos iam enumeravi, clara ibidem Opida: quibuscum eosdem Populos Carnem accepere Latinis Ferus in Monte Albano fuisse solitos, quorumque penitus memoriam suo tempore, idem Plinus litteris mandat. Sunt ea Satricum, Pometia, Scaptia, Pitulum, Politorium,& alia. Satricum Latij opidum non semel nominat Livius: meminit & Orosius : Σατρικον forte Stephano, unde Σατρικανοι eidem ex Dionysio Halicarnasseo: sunt apud eundem libro viii. Α'τρικανοι quos Gelenius Satricanos interpretatur: sed & Σατρικανοι Dionysio sunt noti. Pometia mentionem facit & Virgilius lib.v. Æneidos: nominat hunc Pometinenses Populos Nonius Marcellus in Valgum, Mercatus & Simile: Pometinos Campos habet Livius: eosdem etiam Dionysius Halic. omnium Latinorum maximos ; Πομπτιον πεδιον apud Strabonem est lib.v. Pometia, Pomptina & Pontina Abrahamo Ortelio scriptura tantum differunt, non loco. Vide infra. Scaptiam, quæ tertio loco apud Plinium, memorat quoque Silius Italicus libro viii. Inde Σκαπτιενσες apud Dionysium Halicarnassæum lib.v.quos Scaptenses vertit Gelenius. Ab hac Urbe nomen Tribui apud Romanos Scaptia, Festo docente ; cuius Tribules Scaptienses Suetonio in Augusto. A Pitulo Pliniano Pitulanos quis non nepte formarit, ad exemplum eorum, de quibus in Umbria : nisi Pitulani Umbriæ sint ab Latij Pitulo. Nondum liquet. Politorium notum & Livio ; πολιτωριον Halicarnasseo & Stephano. Ex huius Opidi ruinis nunc Polim crediderim vocatum, inquit Volaterranus in Philologia. Quæ Tellena Plinio ; Τελλαινα Straboni lib. v. Τελλην dicitur Dionysio Halicarnassæo lib. iii. Tellensi Livio lib.i. Nobile Latinorum Opidum, ab Anco Marcio vi captum. Tifata legitur & apud Auctorem de de VV. Illustr. Statiumque lib. iv. Silvarum. Cenina, inquit Festus libro iii. de Verb. signif. Vrbs, quæ fuit vicina Roma, à Cenite Conditore appellata. Vide Caput de Vmbria, in fine. Ficana meminit quoque Livius; Φηκινα dicuntur Dionysio Afro. Opidum erat Via Ostiensi ad Lapidem xi. uti tradit Festus. Sigonius ad Livium eandem vult cum Ficulnea Livij libro i. De Crustumerio dicam in Umbria, sub finem. Ameriola Αμερωλα forsan ab Ameria, quæ in Umbria. Mentio eius & apud Livium. Medullia Tulli Hostilij ortu clara, Livio etiam & aliis nota; Μεδολλια Stephano & Halicarnassæo, qui Coloniam ab Romulo factam scribit. Corniculum. Ser. Tullij Patria, sic Plinio & Livio non uno loco dicitur ; quod Κορνικλον Halicarnasseo, Κορνικλω Stephano. Inde forte Κορνικλοι, Corniculi Montes, Halicarnasseo, prope Tibur: qui Κορνικαι, ni fallor, Zonarae lib. ii. ab Corvorum frequentia. Saturnia, ubi nunc Roma est, addit Plinius. Innuit fuisse in Monte, qui primo Saturnius, inde Tarpeius, postremo Capitolinus. Sic Ovidius libro vi. Fast.
units.tr: Besides those I have mentioned from Old Latium, many peoples have perished, so that not even traces of them appear today, and it is not possible to guess even roughly where they were. Pliny lists them in book III chapter 5, and Dionysius of Halicarnassus almost the same names. T. Livy also names them here and there in the books from the foundation of the city. Here, to follow Pliny's order, they are: the Albenses; Ἀλβανεῖς [Albanies] perhaps in Halicarnassus book VIII, for which Gelenius gives Albiolani, and Sylburgius reads Labinatae; the Albani; Eustathius mentions the land of the Albani, where Mount Circaeum is; the Aesolani: Aesulum is a colony of Italy in Velleius Paterculus, though Sigonius says he does not know whether it is the same as Asculum of the Picentes; the Actenses, which in some manuscripts of Pliny are written Accensis, Akolani, Bubetani, Βουβετανοί [Boubetanoi] in Dionysius of Halicarnassus book V; the Bolani, Βολανοί [Bolanoi] in Stephanus and Halicarnassus book VIII, named from the town Bola, which Virgil calls Bola, Βῶλα [Bola] in Stephanus and Diodorus book XX, and Bola in Livy, who assigned it to the Aequi, as Diodorus assigned it to the Samnites; Plutarch's Coriolanus places it at thirteen miles from the city. The Volani also seem to be in Livy book IV. The Cusuctani and Coriolani, named after the town Coriolus, as Livy, Eutropius, Florus and others call it; the author of De viris illustribus calls it Coriola, Κορίολα [Koriola] in Dionysius of Halicarnassus, and Κορίολα in Stephanus; the Ficulenses, a people not far from the city, according to Varro from Ficulnea, an old town of Latium, also called Ficana. From this come Ficelia in the city, and Ficuleatum, a station, as the Greek quarter is the Graecostasis of the Greeks; the Fregellae and the Fregellani; the Fidenates, about whom I have spoken in the chapter on Umbria; Foretu, the Forenses, perhaps from the Forulae in Ovid, as some think, of which I have spoken in the chapter on Umbria; the Hortenses, from Ortona, unless I am mistaken, which in Livy book II and following is a town of the Latins or Aequi; Βιέτονα [Bietona] in Halicarnassus book X, perhaps not correctly emended; the Latinienses, though others derive them from the Latins themselves. The one designates the genus, the other the species. The Longulani, from Longula, which in Livy is a town of the Volsci, Λεγγύλα [Lengylla] in Halicarnassus, not far from Polusca; the Manates, the Macrales; in some manuscripts Mlanales, Mutuencumenses, Munienses, Numinienses, Olbiculani, Octulani, Pedani, who are known not only from Pliny but also from Plutarch's Coriolanus. The latter are named from Peda, which Stephanus calls an Ausonian town; of the Latins, Livy book II and IX mentions it, where it is written Pedum; hence the Pedana Regio in Horace book I and Dionysius of Halicarnassus book VIII. Porphyrion says there was a town not far from the city but there is none now; the region is still called Pedanum. The old commentator, whom Cruquius adds, notes that the Pedanian region lay between Tibur and Praeneste. Sextus Pompeius Festus is the authority that the Pedani inhabited the city of Scaptia. The Pollustini: perhaps from Pulusca, which in Livy book II is the chief town of the Volsci; Πόλυσκα [Polyska] in Halicarnassus book VI and Πόλυσκα in the same author book VIII; the Querquetulani: Κερκετυλανοί [Kerketylanoi] in Halicarnassus book V; the Stcani, widely known also from Virgil book X of the Aeneid. I spoke of them near the beginning of this chapter and will add something more about them elsewhere; the Sifolenses; the Tolerienses. Halicarnassus also mentions them in book VIII of the Roman Antiquities. They are named from the town which Plutarch in Coriolanus and Stephanus in his work on cities call Τολιερον [Tolieron]; Τελερινος [Telerinos] also in Halicarnassus book I, which Frederick Sylburgius renders Tolerinos; Gelenius, however, renders Trebianos; the Tutienses, so named from the Equus Tuscus, of which Antoninus mentions several times; Abraham Ortelius thinks they were named after it. But that the Equus Tuticus was a town of Apulia far from Latium, of which the Tutienses were according to Pliny's evidence, will be clear from what follows. The list of those who are said to have been in Old Latium is closed by the Vimitellarii, Velienses, Venetulani and Vicellenses. Before them the people of the thirty-two towns, whom I have already listed as extinct in Old Latium, had named their famous towns: together with these peoples, the Carni received from the Latins the Ferus, who used to be on Mount Alban, and Pliny also commits their memory, long lost, to writing in his time. These are Satricum, Pometia, Scaptia, Pitulum, Politorium and others. Livy names Satricum, a town of Latium, more than once; Orosius also mentions it. Perhaps Stephanus has Σατρικον [Satrikon], whence Σατρικανοι [Satrikanoi] from Dionysius of Halicarnassus; they are in the same author book VIII, Ἀτρικανοι [Atrikanoi], which Gelenius translates Satricanos; but Σατρικανοι are also known to Dionysius. Virgil book V of the Aeneid mentions Pometia; Nonius Marcellus names the Pometinenses peoples in his notes on Valgus, Mercatus and Simile. Livy has the Pometine Plains; Dionysius of Halicarnassus also calls them the greatest of all the Latin peoples; Πομπτιον πεδιον [Pomption pedion] in Strabo book V. Pometia, Pomptina and Pontina differ only in spelling for Abraham Ortelius, not in place. See below. Scaptia, which Pliny names third, is also mentioned by Silius Italicus book VIII. Hence Σκαπτιενσες [Skaptiensēs] in Dionysius of Halicarnassus book V, which Gelenius renders Scaptenses. From this city the Romans' tribe received the name Scaptia, as Festus teaches; its tribesmen, the Scaptienses, are named by Suetonius in his Augustus. Who would not form Pitulani from Pliny's Pitulum, after the pattern of those in Umbria? Unless the Pitulani of Umbria are from the Latin Pitulum. It is not yet clear. Politorium is known also from Livy; πολιτωριον [politorion] in Halicarnassus and Stephanus. I would believe that Polis was named from the ruins of this town, says Volaterranus in his Philologia. Tellena in Pliny; Τελλαινα [Tellaina] in Strabo book V; it is called Τελλην [Tellen] in Dionysius of Halicarnassus book III; Tellensi in Livy book I, a noble town of the Latins, taken by Ancus Marcius. Tifata is also read in the author of De viris illustribus and in Statius book IV of the Silvae. Cenina, says Festus in book III of De verborum significatione, "a town near Rome, named after its founder Cenites." See the chapter on Umbria, at the end. Ficana is also mentioned by Livy; Φηκινα [Phekina] is what Dionysius the African calls it. It was a town on the Ostian Way at the eleventh milestone, as Festus relates. Sigonius, on Livy, wants it to be the same as Livy's Ficulnea in book I. I will speak of Crustumerium in the chapter on Umbria, near the end. Ameriola, Αμερωλα [Amerola], perhaps from Ameria, which is in Umbria. It is mentioned also by Livy. Medullia, famous for the birth of Tullus Hostilius, is also known to Livy and others; Μεδολλια [Medollia] in Stephanus and Halicarnassus, who writes that it was a colony founded by Romulus. Corniculum, the birthplace of Servius Tullius, is so called by Pliny and Livy in more than one place; Κορνικλον [Kornikklon] in Halicarnassus, Κορνικλω [Kornikklō] in Stephanus. From this perhaps come Κορνικλοι [Kornikloi], the Corniculan Mountains in Halicarnassus, near Tibur; these are Κορνικαι [Kornikai] in Zonaras book II, unless I am mistaken, from the abundance of crows. "Saturnia, where Rome now is," adds Pliny. He hints that there was a Saturnian hill, which was first called Saturnius, then Tarpeius, and finally Capitolinus. So Ovid in Fasti book VI:

units.la: A patre dicta meo quondam Saturnia Roma.
units.tr: Rome, once called Saturnian after my father.

units.la: Saturnia indicat Vestigia Varro lib. iv. de LL. etiam ævo suo solita monstrari tria: Saturni Fanum in faucibus Montis Capitolini, Saturniam Portam, quam Junius scribit, quæque post Pandana, post Ædem denique Saturni in Ædificiorum Legibus Parietes postici Muri scriptos, litterisque notatos. Eiusdem & Ianiculi Reliquias monstrat Æneæ Euander apud Virgilium lib. viii. Æn. Hæc duo præterea, disiectis oppida Murîs, Reliquias Veterumque Vides Monimenta Virorum. Hanc Ianus Pater, Hanc Saturnus condidit Arcem: Janiculum Huic, Illi fuerat Saturnia Nomen.
units.tr: Varro, in book 4 of On the Latin Language, notes that the traces of Saturnia were still shown in his own day in three places: the Temple of Saturn at the foot of the Capitoline Hill, the Saturnian Gate, which Junius writes about, and the back walls of the building that came after the Pandana, namely the temple of Saturn, inscribed and marked with letters in the Laws of Buildings. Euander, in Virgil, Aeneid book 8, also points out the remains of Janiculum that belonged to the same people. Besides these, he shows the ruins of towns with their walls levelled, and the monuments of ancient men: "Janus, our father, founded this citadel, and Saturn founded that one. Janiculum was the name of the one, and Saturnia the name of the other."

units.la: Incolæ Saturnij Festo: quod Nomen, Roma condita, mansit iis, qui in imo Clivo Capitolino Castrum incolebant. Antipolis, quod nunc, inquit Plinius, Ianiculum in parte parte Romæ. Ainia, quæ postea Tavíκλεον, ait Halicarnassæus: an de hoc Ianiculo, adhuc ambigo. Fit autem Antipolis prope rie in Tuscia. De Antemnis, quas & in Latio Vetere nominat Plinius, commodius dicam Capite, quo Umbria explicatur, in fine. Quod Camerium Plinio Tacitoque: Cameria, Livio & Halicarnassæo: Camerinum Ciceroni dicitur libro ad Atticum v i i i, Epist. x i i. ut item Festo, qui pulcrum esse Opidum ait. Vide Caput de Piceno. Collatiam in Umbria describo; Amiternum in Samnitibus. Quæ Norbe Plinio lib i i i. cap. v. Norba vocatur Livio lib. i i. Coloniam facienti. Latini Nominis Vrbs est Halicarnassæo lib. v i i. Campaniæ, Livio lib. x x x i i. fortasis non una. Nescio an ab Norbe Latij apud Plinium, eidem sint Norbani, quos paullo ante Norbes mentionem, nominat eodem capite. Alij sunt eidem Plinio Norbanenses in Calabria. Sulmonem, quam Superioribus addit Plinius, designat fortean Florus lib. i i i. Hist. Rom. cap. x x x i. Vetus Opidum Socium atque Amicum appellans. Licet autem hoc Latij Opidum perinde cum præcedentibus omnibus dicat Plinius: Pyrrhus tamen Ligorius sermonetam hactenus vocari adfirmat. Est etiam Sulmo, Ovidij Patria, Pelignorum in Samnitibus Opidum, de quo suo loco. Sacranas Acies à Populo quodam sic dictas habet Virgilius: de iis legendus est Servius, qui eos circa Romam vel Arsteam putat habitasse. Reate ortos memorat Festus.
units.tr: The inhabitants of Saturnia were called Festo's people. This name, from the founding of Rome, stayed with those who lived in the fortress at the foot of the Capitoline slope. Antipolis, which is now, says Pliny, is in the part of Rome called Janiculum. Halicarnassus says Ainia, which was later called Tavíκλεον; I am still uncertain whether he means this Janiculum. Antipolis is almost certainly in Etruria. I will speak more conveniently about the Antemnae, which Pliny also names in Old Latium, in the final chapter, where Umbria is explained. Pliny and Tacitus call it Cameria; Livy and Halicarnassus call it Cameria; Cicero, in book 8 of the letters to Atticus, letter 12, calls it Camerinum, as does Festus, who says it is a fine town. See the chapter on Picenum. I describe Collatia in Umbria and Amiternum among the Samnites. The town that Pliny in book 3, chapter 5, calls Norba, Livy in book 2, in the passage about founding a colony, calls Norba. Halicarnassus in book 7 places a city of the Latin name in Campania, and Livy in book 32 does so too, perhaps more than one. I do not know whether the Norbani that Pliny mentions in the same chapter, just after his mention of Norbe, are the same as the Norba of Latium. Other Norbanenses of Pliny's are in Calabria. Florus, in book 3 of his Roman History, chapter 31, perhaps indicates Sulmo, which Pliny adds to the places above, calling it an old town, an ally and a friend. Yet Pyrrhus Ligorius asserts that this town of Latium, although Pliny lists it along with all the preceding ones, has so far been called sermonetam. There is also Sulmo, the homeland of Ovid, a town of the Paeligni among the Samnites, about which I will speak in its place. Virgil mentions the Sacranae Acies as a people so called; Servius, who thinks they lived near Rome or Arsteia, should be read about them. Festus records that they came from Reate.

units.la: De Latij porro Iure, quod, ex Fœdere cum iis icto, ut M. Tullius pro Balbo memoriæ mandat, Sp. Cassio & Postumo Cominio Coss. anno C C L X I. multa continebat Privilegia, proximeque ad Civitatem accedebat Romanam, legenda, quæ ex variis Scriptoribus, præsertim Dionysio & Livio, notat vir Rerum Romanarum peritissimus & diligentissimus Indagator, Onuphrius Panuinius, in Opere, cui Titulum præscripsit Imperium Romanum.
units.tr: Concerning the law of Latium, which under the treaty made with them, as Marcus Tullius records in the speech for Balbus, in the consulship of Spurius Cassius and Postumus Cominius, in the year 261, contained many privileges and came closest to Roman citizenship, one should read what the man most skilled in Roman affairs and most diligent investigator, Onofrio Panvinio, has noted from various writers, especially Dionysius and Livy, in the work he entitled The Roman Empire.

units.la: Hæc de Latio universim: Hagitat Methodi ratio, speciatim ut perlustrem, orsus Vrbe, quæ Orbis quondam Compendium. Ea namque prima, in Antiquo Latio, Tiberim ex Etruria transgressa se cum incredibili hodieque Majestate offert, non ut debet (quis enim isti difficultati superandæ par futurus?) sed ut potest, summis inquam coloribus, delineandam. Præstaret alioquin de Ea, quod de Karthagine dixit Sallustius, Silere, quam pauca dicere. Nomen suum semel obtentum contra omnem Temporis & Fortunæ injuriam & nunc retinet. ROMA enim ubique terrarum ab omnibus Europæ, Asiæ, Africæque Populis, inflexa varie, nominatur. Alterum habuit Secretum, quod dicere Arcanu Cerimoniarum, ut inquit Plinius lib. i i i. cap. v. nefas habebatur: optimaque & salutari fide abolitum enunciavit Valerius Soranus, luitque mox pœnas. Adeundi, præter Plinium, loco indicato, & lib. x x v i i i. cap. i i. Solinus cap. i. Polyhist. Plutarchus Problem. l x. & Macrobius lib. i i i. Saturnal. cap. i x. Hoc tamen Romanensis fuisse fabulatur Annius ad fabulosum Berosum. Ille scilicet eo felicitatis adsurrexit, ut quod sæcula tam multa profundis sepultum fuerat tenebris, ipsi, si Diis placet, suus revelarit Berosus. ROMAM tub Amaryllidis nomine describere Virgilium in Eclogis notat Interpres Servius. Sed neque hoc D. Hieronymi omittendum duxi, ROMAM significari vocabulo Babylonis ab D. Petro Epistola 1. cap. v ubi scribit, Salutat Vos Ecclesia, quæ est in Babylone. Sed & Vrbs Babylonis Romana non semel meminit Liber de Limitibus. Sed ego cogitandum hic penitius censeo. Imperator Commodus ROMAM appellare voluit Coloniam Commodianam, docente Lampridio; Gothiam appellari voluit Athaulphus Gothorum Rex, ut Orosius prodit: Sed utrumque frustra. Vrbs per excellentiam dicitur omnibus Latinis Scriptoribus. Quæ ROMAM spectant, potissima excerpam ex Singulario Libello, quem olim, plenius otium nactus, de ea scripsi. De ipsius Appellatione, Primisque Conditoribus alij aliter sentiunt. Horum quinque mihi Classes: prima, qui Vrbem nominatam volunt non ab Conditore, sed ab eorum, qui Vrbem jam conditam incolebant, Indole & Natura. Nam, teste Pompeio Festo, Cumanæ Historiæ Scriptor ROMAM dictam scribit Valentiam ab Latina juventute, quod Nomen adventu Euandri Æneæque in Italiam interpretatum dici cœptum ROMAM. Videndi & Plutarchus in Romulo, & Iulius Solinus cap. i. ROMA igitur nomen ἀπὸ τῆς Ῥώμης, quæ Latinis Valentia & Robur. D. Hieronymus videtur non tam adprobare sententiam illorum, qui ἀπὸ τῆς Ῥώμης trahunt, quam derivare leni flexu ab Hebraico vocabulo co vocabulo רומה exaltari, elevari: quum ait contra Iovinianum, Roma autem Fortitudinis nomen est apud Graecos, aut Sublimitatis apud Hebraeos. Quid si Roma (ut & ego aliquid conferam) dicatur ab Syriaca voce רומה, quae Latinis Hasta. Certe adionat huic Coniecturae Nomen Quirus; sic Prisci Latini dicebant Hastam; à quo Cives Urbis, de qua nobis sermo Quirites sunt, ab Roma, Romani, qui nihil aliud, quam Hastati: bono omine, ut Urbs quam habitura aliquando esset Regiam Majestatem vel solo nomine in sui primordio tectaretur. Reges enim illo hoc aevo Hasta pro Insigni utebantur. Reliquarum Classium hae sunto Tabulae.
units.tr: So much for Latium in general. The order of the Method requires that I survey it in particular, beginning with the city which was once the epitome of the world. For Rome, which first in old Latium crossed the Tiber from Etruria, presents itself with an incredible majesty even today; it must be sketched not as it ought to be (for who would be equal to that difficult task?) but as it can be, with the highest colours, I mean. Otherwise it would be better to be silent about her than to say little, as Sallust said of Carthage. Once she had won her name, she has kept it even now, against all the injuries of time and fortune: for Rome, variously inflected, is named everywhere in the world by all the peoples of Europe, Asia and Africa. She had another secret, which it was forbidden to speak of, the "secret of the ceremonies," as Pliny says in book 3, chapter 5. Valerius Soranus, with the best and most wholesome good faith, disclosed it, and he soon paid the penalty. Besides Pliny, in the place indicated, and in book 28, chapter 2, one may consult Solinus, chapter 1 of his Polyhistor, Plutarch's Problems, question 60, and Macrobius, book 3 of the Saturnalia, chapter 9. Annius, however, makes up a story that this secret was Roman, relying on the fabulous Berossus. He evidently rose to such a height of good fortune that what had lain buried for so many ages in deep darkness was revealed, God willing, by his own Berossus. That Virgil, in the Eclogues, describes Rome under the name of Amaryllis, the commentator Servius notes. But I thought I should not omit this either, that Rome is signified by the word Babylon, from the first epistle of St Peter, chapter 5, where he writes, "The church that is in Babylon salutes you." The Roman city of Babylon is also mentioned more than once in the book On the Boundaries. But I think the matter needs to be considered more deeply here. The emperor Commodus wished to call Rome the Colony of Commodus, as Lampridius teaches; Athaulf, king of the Goths, wished it to be called Gothia, as Orosius reports; but both attempts were in vain. All Latin writers call the city the City, by excellence. I will excerpt the main points concerning Rome from a separate little work which I once wrote about her, when I had more leisure. Opinions differ about her name and her first founders. I divide these into five classes. The first consists of those who hold that the city was named not after its founder but after the character and nature of those who already lived in the city. For, according to Pompeius Festus, a writer of Cumaean history says that Rome was called Valentia by the Latin youth, and that this name, when Euander and Aeneas came to Italy, began to be interpreted as Rome. Plutarch in his life of Romulus and Julius Solinus, chapter 1, should also be consulted. So Rome's name comes from strength [ἀπὸ τῆς Ῥώμης], which for the Latins means Valentia and Robur. Jerome does not seem so much to approve the opinion of those who derive it from strength [ἀπὸ τῆς Ῥώμης], as to derive it by a slight bend from the Hebrew word רומה, to be exalted, raised high; for he says against Jovinian, "Roma is a name of fortitude among the Greeks, or of sublimity among the Hebrews." What if Rome (to add something of my own) is derived from the Syriac word רומה, which in Latin is hasta, a spear? Certainly the name Quirinus supports this conjecture; so the early Latins called a spear curis, and from this the citizens of the city we are discussing are called Quirites, and from Rome the Romans, who are nothing other than hastati, spearmen. It was a good omen, so that the city, which was one day to have royal majesty, might be sheltered in its very beginning by the name alone. For in that age kings used the spear as their insignia. The tables that follow are for the remaining classes.

units.la: II. Classis est.
units.tr: II. The second class.

units.la: Eorum, qui Urbem conditam volunt ab Romo,
units.tr: Of those who hold that the city was founded by Romus:

units.la: Antigonus, Italicae Historiae Scriptor: Xenagoras Historicus: Cephalon Gergithius, qui de Adventu in Italiam videtur conscripsisse; Consentiunt Cephalonis Demagoras, Agathyllus: Apollodorus in Euxenide: Incerti apud Dionysium Chalcidensem: Incerti: Incerti: Incerti apud Dionysium Chalcidensem: Alcinus: Incerti:
units.tr: Antigonus, writer of Italian history; Xenagoras, historian; Cephalon of Gergithus, who seems to have written about the arrival in Italy; in agreement with Cephalon are Demagoras and Agathyllus; Apollodorus in the Euxenides; unnamed authors cited by Dionysius of Chalcis; unnamed authors; unnamed authors; unnamed authors cited by Dionysius of Chalcis; Alcinus; unnamed authors.

units.la: Festo in Romam. Dionysio Halicarnassaeo lib. 1. Designat Plutarchus in Romulo; qui, quem Dionysius Ῥῶμον, appellat Ῥωμαῖον: Legendum forte Ῥῶμον &c. Dionysio libro eodem. Festus tamen ex Cephalonis sententia Romam appellat Aenea Comitem. Festo in Romam. Dionysio libro à me indicato. Plutarcho in Romulo. Dionysio Halic. laudato ante loco. Dionysio ibidem & Plutarcho in Romuli Vita. Festo in Romam. Plutarcho in Romulo, ubi legendum Ῥῶμον. Vna ex Captivis Trojanis, Eorum, qui conditam Vrbem scribunt: ab Roma Ilienfi Muliere: Ascanii Filia, Aeneae Nepte: Telephi Filia, Aeneae Coniuge: Profuga, potitis Troia Graecis, & deinde Latino Aboriginum Regi nupta: Latini Coniuge: Aeneae Filium, Fratrem ex Dextro Phorbantis: Eorum, qui Vrbis Conditorem Fratrem [illegible, ~4 letters] & [illegible, ~4 letters]
units.tr: Festus, on Rome. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 1. Plutarch designates him in the Life of Romulus, where he calls him Romaeus, which he (Dionysius) names Romos; perhaps we should read Romon, etc. Dionysius in the same book. Yet Festus, following the opinion of Cephalon, calls Rome the companion of Aeneas. Festus, on Rome. Dionysius in the book I have indicated. Plutarch in the Life of Romulus. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, cited in the passage above. Dionysius in the same place, and Plutarch in the Life of Romulus. Festus, on Rome. Plutarch in the Life of Romulus, where we should read Romon. One of the Trojan captives, of those who write that the city was founded by Roma a Trojan woman of Ilium: daughter of Ascanius, granddaughter of Aeneas: daughter of Telephus, wife of Aeneas: a fugitive, after the Greeks had taken Troy, and afterwards married to the Latin king of the Aborigines: wife of Latinus: son of Aeneas, brother by the right hand of Phorbas: of those who record the founder of the city as brother [illegible] and [illegible].

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: quod volunt Heraclides Lembus. Hunc designat Plutarchus in Romulo; ubi secundo loco quorundam de Vrbis Conditore commemorat opiniones. Eiusdem mentis facit Aristotelem Dionysius Halicarnassæus, qui fortean scribere voluit Heraclidis nomen. Sallustius etiam in Bello Catilinario videtur huius etle mentis: Αρίνυμος, cui suffragatur Damaites Sigæus: Agathocles Siculus, Cyzicenarum rerum Auctor: Incerti: Callias, Agathoclis rerum gestarum Scriptor. Galathas: Iulio Solino cap. 1; Festo in Romam. Dionysio Halicarnass. lib. 1. Plutarcho in Romulo, Solino Festoque locis indicatis. Plutarcho ibidem. Dionysio & Festo. Festo in Romam.
units.tr: which Heraclides of Lembus holds. Plutarch designates him in the Life of Romulus, where in second place he records the opinions of certain people about the founder of the city. Dionysius of Halicarnassus makes Aristotle of the same mind, though he perhaps meant to write the name Heraclides. Sallust also in the Catilinarian War seems to be of this view: Arinymus, supported by Damaites of Sigeum; Agathocles of Sicily, author of the history of Cyzicus; unnamed author; Callias, writer of the deeds of Agathocles. Galatians: Julius Solinus, chapter 1; Festus, on Rome. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 1. Plutarch in the Life of Romulus, and Solinus and Festus in the places indicated. Plutarch in the same place. Dionysius and Festus. Festus, on Rome.

units.la: IIII.
units.tr: IIII.

units.la: Incerti: Incerti: Plutarchum in Romulo, Dionysium Halicarn. lib. 1. Dionysium ibidem.
units.tr: Unnamed authors: unnamed authors. Plutarch in the Life of Romulus, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 1. Dionysius in the same place.

units.la: aliquot adgno-scüt qui dem Romulum, alium ta men ab Rea Filio scilicet Acmilii Filium, Aeneae & Lavinia Nepotem; | Cujus Sententiae | Incerti: | apud | Dionysium & Plutarchum ijsdem locis. ..... Filium, Aeneae Nepotem; | Incerti: | Dionysium laudato libro. Latini Filium, Telemachi Nepotem; | Incerti: | Plutarchü in eiusdem Romuli Vita. Ancillae, Tarchetij Albanorum Regis, Filium; | Promathion: | Auctorem indicatum;
units.tr: Some indeed acknowledge Romulus, but another, namely the son of Rhea, that is, the son of Aemilius, grandson of Aeneas and Lavinia; this opinion is held by unnamed authors, in Dionysius and Plutarch in the same places. ..... son of Aeneas, grandson; unnamed author; Dionysius in the book cited. Son of Latinus, grandson of Telemachus; unnamed author; Plutarch in the Life of the same Romulus. Son of a maidservant of Tarchetius, king of the Albans; Promathion; author indicated above.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Eorum, qui Nomen Urbi tribuunt im positum ab Romulo Rea Filio, cuius tamen Patrem faciunt Non-nulli Unum ex Procis: Legendus Dionysius lib. 1. Antiquitatum Romanarum. Amulium Patruum. Dionysius ibidem & Plutarchus in Romulo. Numen vel Genium Loci: Ijdem Auctores.
units.tr: Of those who say the city took its name from Rea's son Romulus, some make his father one of the suitors. Read Dionysius, book 1 of the Roman Antiquities. (They name him) Amulius, the uncle. Dionysius in the same place and Plutarch in the Life of Romulus. For the divinity or genius of the place, the same authors.

units.la: Onuphrius Panuinius Militem quemdam; qui putat ad Martem hoc relatum, quod Milites in Martis tutela. Videndus ille in Roma & Fastis.
units.tr: Onuphrius Panvinius (says it was) a certain soldier, and thinks this was referred to Mars because soldiers are under Mars's protection. See him in his work on Rome and the Fasti.

units.la: Plerique Martem: cuius cum Rea Silvia congressum describit graphice Ovidius libro III. Fastorum. Eundem congressum fabulosum putat Cicero 1. De Natura Deorum. Certe, quum incertus esset Pater, Mars fictus est, cluendae Turpitudinis Notae; & exstimulando, divinae Stirpis fiducia, ad maxima quaeque Humano Animo. Consulendi praeter alios Ovidius III. Fast. Varro III de Re Rustica, cap. 1, Solinus cap. 11, Isidorus lib. xv. cap. 1, cuius Verba emendantur à me ad mei Ennij Annales.
units.tr: Most (refer it to) Mars, with whose union with Rea Silvia Ovid gives a vivid account in book 3 of the Fasti. Cicero, in book 1 of On the Nature of the Gods, thinks that union was a fable. Certainly, since the father was uncertain, Mars was invented to cover the stain of shame, and to stir human minds to the greatest deeds by confidence in a divine ancestry. Consult, among others, Ovid, Fasti 3; Varro, On Agriculture 3, ch. 1; Solinus ch. 11; Isidore, book 15, ch. 1, whose words I correct by my own Ennius, the Annals.

units.la: Unde autem tanta in urbis Conditore Varietas? An quod non unus Romus, vel Roma, vel Romulus, sed alius, alio tempore? quod indicant indicati jam Scriptores. An quod non una Roma: sed eadem ab aliis capta, ab aliis renovata, ab aliis amplificata? Triplicem sane Romam ex Veterum Auctorum sententia signare videtur Dionysius Halicarnassaeus libro 1 Antiquitatum Romanarum. Primam & Antiquissimam, cuius meminit, eodem teste, Antiochus Syracusanus: Alteram, quae condita non multo post Belli Trojani tempora: Tertiam, quae renovata quasi, aetate post alteram illam quintadecima. Quae sint ita: certe Romani Nominis gloria debetur praecipue prosperoilli, quod Romulo datum, Augurio: maxime quum Annorum Ratio faciat cardinem Veritati, inquit Solinus cap. 11. Non unam Romam agnoscit etiam Pomponius IC. qui scribit Populum Romanum initio sine certa Lege, sine lure certo vixisse; omniaque manu à Regibus gubernata: postea Romulum superuenisse, & aliam Civitati formam induisse l. 2 necessarium §. 2. & 3. D. de origine Iuris. Non una autem Illa; vel, ut cum Dionysio Halicarnassaeo lib. 1. illud ancipiti animo dicam: Triplex Illa Roma, non solum varios ex variorum ut docui sententiis Conditores peperit: sed cautam etiam dedit immensae Varietati in notando Urbis conditae Tempore. Eleganter hac de re Solinus cap. 11. initio. De Varietate illa legendi Cicero in Bruto & Livius lib. 11. Antiquissima Roma, fingamus enim Triplicem fuisse, quando condita, colligi non potest ex Antiochi Syracusani (qui unus eius meminit Verbis, quæ apud Dionysium Halic. lib.1. Mediam illam designat: credo apud Dionysium Cephalon Gergithium, qui Romam conditam scripsit: secunda ætate post Ilium Trojanum. Cum eo autem de Tempore consentire notat ibidem Dionysius Demagoram, Agathyllum multosque alios. Ipse Dionysius, si tamen plures fuerint succedentes quasi sibi Romæ conditam significat, dubius tamen non multo post Ilii Trojani tempora in Alterutrius Incolas dignitatem quasi intendit Pomponius I C. vel quicumque Auctor censendus l.2.§.2.& 3. l.2. de Origine Iuris. Tempus, quam unicam plerique statuunt (τὸ πλαίσιον τῆς Ῥώμης γενέσεως εἰκοσμένον vocat Dionysius) conditæ temporis varie ab Variis indicatur, quod patet ex subiecta Synopsi:
units.tr: But whence such great variety about the founder of the city? Is it because there was not one Romus, or Roma, or Romulus, but another, at another time? The writers already cited indicate as much. Or is it because there was not one Rome, but the same city was taken by some, renewed by others and enlarged by still others? Dionysius of Halicarnassus, in book 1 of the Roman Antiquities, certainly seems to mark out a threefold Rome according to the opinion of the ancient authors. The first and most ancient, which, by the same witness, Antiochus of Syracuse mentioned; the second, founded not long after the time of the Trojan War; the third, renewed, as it were, in the age fifteen generations after that second one. However these things stand, the glory of the Roman name is owed chiefly to that auspicious omen given to Romulus, especially since the reckoning of years is the hinge of truth, as Solinus says in ch. 11. Pomponius the jurist also acknowledges that there was not one Rome. He writes that the Roman people at first lived without fixed law or sure right, and everything was governed by kings with their own hands; afterwards Romulus came along and gave the state another form (Digest 1.2.2 §§ 2 and 3, On the Origin of Law). But that was not the only one; or, to say it with Dionysius of Halicarnassus in book 1 with a wavering mind: that threefold Rome not only gave rise to various founders, according to the various opinions, as I have shown, but also gave cause for immense variety in fixing the time of the city's foundation. Solinus, ch. 11, at the beginning, speaks elegantly on this matter. On this variety see Cicero in the Brutus and Livy, book 11. Let us imagine that Rome was threefold when it was founded; it cannot be gathered from Antiochus of Syracuse (who alone mentions it, in words which Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 1, quotes, designating that middle Rome). I believe that in Dionysius, Cephalon of Gergithus, who wrote that Rome was founded in the second age after the Trojan Ilium, also (appears). Dionysius notes that Demagoras, Agathyllus and many others agree with him about the time. Dionysius himself, if indeed there were several successive (Romes), signifies that Rome was founded for himself, doubtfully, not long after the time of Trojan Ilium. Pomponius the jurist, or whatever author is to be regarded, (Digest 1.2.2 §§ 2 and 3, On the Origin of Law) intends the honour for the inhabitants of one or the other. The time, which most people establish as one (Dionysius calls it the framework of Rome's origin [τὸ πλαίσιον τῆς Ῥώμης γενέσεως]), is variously indicated by various authors, as is clear from the synopsis below:

units.la: Ante Primam Olympiadem anno xxxviii, eodem fere tempore, quo Karthago condita; Timæus Siculus, ὡς οὐδ' ἐπ' ἐκείνου Καρχηδὼν χρηματισμός, inquit Dionysius Halicarnassus lib. 1. Tempus autem illud Timæi incidit ex eiusdem Dionysii Calculo in annum ab Troia capta cc clxxi, in annum Procæ, xiv Latinorum vel Albanorum Regis, quartum. Olympiade VI. | Anno I. II.
units.tr: Before the First Olympiad, in year 38, at about the same time as Carthage was founded: Timaeus of Sicily, "for not even in his time was Carthage a matter of record," as Dionysius of Halicarnassus says in book 1. The time of Timaeus falls, by Dionysius's own calculation, in the year 271 after the capture of Troy, in the fourth year of Proca, fourteenth king of the Latins or Albans, in the sixth Olympiad, year 1, 2.

Iulius Cæsar Octavianus Augustus; uti probant partim quæ ab ipsis gesta, partim vero Ludi, quos celebrarunt, Sæculares. Ti. Claudius Cæsar Augustus; Fl. Domitianus Cæsar Augustus; L. Septimius Severus Cæsar Augustus; M. Iulius Philippus Cæsar Augustus: P. Velleius Paterculus: initio Voluminis i Historiæ Romanæ; C. Pomponius Atticus, Solino scribente cap.ii; Censorinus de die Natali cap. xiv, cruente Sententiam eius Onuphrio: Agellius lib. xviii Noct. Atticar. cap. xxi, volente eodem Onuphrio: Eusebius in Chronico: Eutropius lib.i. Historiæ Romanæ: Paullus Orosius; apud eundem Onuphrium. Paullus Diaconus; apud eundem Onuphrium.
