units.tr: M. Terentius Varro, cited by Censorinus in On the Birthday, ch. 14, and more fully by Onuphrius Panvinius in his commentary on the Roman Fasti, who also examines the opinions of the following writers. C. Julius Caesar Octavianus Augustus, as is shown partly by what he did and partly by the Secular Games he celebrated. Tiberius Claudius Caesar Augustus; Flavius Domitianus Caesar Augustus; L. Septimius Severus Caesar Augustus; M. Julius Philippus Caesar Augustus; P. Velleius Paterculus, at the beginning of the first volume of his Roman History; C. Plinius Secundus, to be consulted in Onuphrius; Plutarch, in the Life of Romulus; P. Cornelius Tacitus, consult Onuphrius; M. Tullius Cicero, according to Solinus ch. 3; Cassius Dio, as Onuphrius approves from his own writings; T. Pomponius Atticus, as Solinus writes, ch. 2; Censorinus, On the Birthday, ch. 14, whose opinion is set out by Onuphrius; Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights, book 18, ch. 21, as Onuphrius would have it; Eusebius in the Chronicle; Eutropius, book 1 of the Roman History; Paulus Orosius, as in the same Onuphrius; Paulus Diaconus, as in the same Onuphrius; Verrius Flaccus, as can easily be gathered from his own Fasti; Clement of Alexandria, book 1 of the Stromata; Eratosthenes of Cyrene, the affirmation of Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 1, and Solinus ch. 2 supporting it, in whom the number is to be corrected from Dionysius, and the reading should be "year 1 of the Seventh Olympiad" instead of "year 2"; Apollodorus, as Solinus notes, ch. 2; Julius

Solini Opinionem de Motu Siderum in Natalitio Vrbis die refutat Ioachimus Vadianus in Comment ad Pomponium Melam, lib. 11. cap. 1; M. Porcius Cato, docente id Onuphrio; Cornelius Nepos, C. Lutatius, apud Solinum; Diodorus Siculus, T. Livius, apud Onuphrium; Dionysius Halicarnassæus lib. 1. Antiquitatum Romanarum; Theophilus Antiochenus lib. 111. Disputationum contra Autolycum.
units.tr: {a}Julius Solinus, Polyhistor, ch. 11. Matthaeus Beroaldus especially approves this (view), book 2, ch. 11, Chronicle of Solinus. Joachim Vadian, in his commentary on Pomponius Mela, book 2, ch. 1, refutes Solinus's opinion about the motion of the stars on the birthday of the city. M. Porcius Cato, as Onuphrius teaches; Cornelius Nepos; C. Lutatius, in Solinus; Diodorus Siculus; T. Livy, in Onuphrius; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 1 of the Roman Antiquities; Theophilus of Antioch, book 3 of the Disputations against Autolycus.

units.la: Polybius Megalopolitanus, laudante sententiam ejus Dionysio Halicarnassæo, loco sæpe indicato.
units.tr: Polybius of Megalopolis, whose opinion Dionysius of Halicarnassus praises, in the passage often cited.

units.la: Q. Fabius Pictor, apud Solinum cap. 11, non notantem tamen, quoto Olympiadis v111 anno.
units.tr: Q. Fabius Pictor, in Solinus ch. 11, though he does not note in which year of the eighth Olympiad (it happened).

units.la: L. Cincius Vir Senatorij Ordinis apud Dionysium Halicarnassæum libro 1. Solinus cap. 11. scribit Cincio placere Vrbem Conditam x11 Olympiade; non indicato certo ejus Olympiadis anno.
units.tr: L. Cincius, a man of senatorial rank, in Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 1. Solinus, ch. 11, writes that Cincius held that the city was founded in the twelfth Olympiad, without a definite year of that Olympiad being indicated.

units.la: Ad tempus autem Vrbis Conditæ an Versus Enniani, quos citat M. Terentius Varro de Re Rustica lib. 111. cap. 1. pertineant, quæro ad ejusdem Poetæ Annal. librum 1. Hæc de Anno: addam nonnihil de Die. ROMAM conditam scribunt xi Kalendas Mai, id est Parilibus, Solinus cap. 11, Futropius lib. 1, Ovidius iv Fastorum, & alij: xii vero Kalendas Mai, id est pridie Paril. Plutarchus in Romuli Vita. Natalem Vrbis Diem Romanos quotannis celebrare solitos notant Dionysius lib. 1. & Plutarchus in Romulo. Hoc item adscribam, L. Tarrutium Mathematicum apud Iulium Solinum cap. 11 tradere ROMAM condi cœptam inter horas 11, & 111, Jove in Piscibus, Saturno, Venere, Marte, Mercurio in Scorpione; Sole in Tauro, Luna in Libra constitutis. Quæ vel Tarruntij, toto cœlo errantis, vel Solini, qui Tarruntium male exscripserit, gravi censura evertit Ioachimus Vadianus ad Libruml Pomponij Melæ. Versatur in eodem errore Sempronius de Divisione Italiæ; vel, ut verius loquar, Annius potius Viterbiensis, qui cum alijs Sempronium nobis subjecit, ἀστρολογικῶν & infulsisubdum agens Astronomum. ROMAM, quum Conditionem ejus molirentur quicumque fuerint. Libram Horoscopium habuisse, adfirmat Manilius Astronom. lib. 1v; Hesperiam: sua Libra tenet, qua condita ROMA, Orbis & imperium retinet, disrimine rerum Lancibus & positas Gentes tollitque premitque.
units.tr: Whether the Ennian verses which M. Terentius Varro cites in On Agriculture, book 3, ch. 1, refer to the time of the city's foundation, I ask from book 1 of the Annals of the same poet. So much for the year; I will add something about the day. Writers say Rome was founded on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, that is, at the Parilia: Solinus, ch. 11; Eutropius, book 1; Ovid, Fasti 4, and others. But on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May, that is, the day before the Parilia, (says) Plutarch in the Life of Romulus. Dionysius, book 1, and Plutarch in the Life of Romulus note that the Romans used to celebrate the city's birthday every year. I will also add this: L. Tarrutius the mathematician, in Julius Solinus ch. 11, relates that Rome began to be founded between the second and third hours, with Jupiter in Pisces, Saturn, Venus, Mars and Mercury in Scorpio, the Sun in Taurus, and the Moon in Libra. Joachim Vadian, in his commentary on the book of Pomponius Mela, overturns this, whether it is Tarrutius (who wandered over the whole sky) or Solinus (who miscopied Tarrutius badly), with severe criticism. Sempronius, On the Division of Italy, falls into the same error; or, to speak more truly, Annius of Viterbo, who with others has foisted Sempronius upon us, playing the astrologer and astronomer. When those who undertook its founding, whoever they were, were arranging Rome's foundation, Manilius, in book 4 of the Astronomica, affirms that Libra was Rome's horoscope: "Hesperia her own Libra holds, by which, Rome being founded, she keeps the world and empire, raising and pressing down the nations set in her balance by the scales of fate."

units.la: Recentiores certatim sub Leone ROMAM esse adiderunt. Conjecturam ait apud Vadianum Georgius Collimitius, minime frivolam: eo tempore, quo capta sit Vrbs condi, ascendens fuisse Cor Leonis, Regiam Stellam: in medio Cœli Solem in Tauro, Iovem in Piscibus in Nona, Orientalem; Mercurium in eadem Nona in Arete Orientalem: Venerem in Tauro Occidentalem, & in Medio Cœli; postremo Saturnum & Martem in Scorpione, in Domo Quarta. Vrbem fecit Romulus Quadratam; Testibus Dionysio lib. 1. Antiq. Romanar. Plutarcho in Vitis, & Solino cap. 11. Meminit ROMÆ Quadratæ meus Ennius libro 11. Annalium. Inde autem ampliori ROMÆ & florenti jam Locus mansit Quadrata Roma, in x: Vrbis Regione, uti videre est apud P. Victorem, qui Vrbi Domino, quum toti jam
units.tr: Recent writers have eagerly placed Rome under the sign of Leo. Georgius Collimitius, quoted by Vadianus, offers a conjecture that he calls by no means frivolous: at the time the city was founded, the Heart of the Lion, the royal star, was rising; the Sun was in Taurus in mid-heaven; Jupiter was in Pisces in the Ninth House, in the east; Mercury was in the same Ninth House, in Aries, in the east; Venus was in Taurus, in the west and in mid-heaven; and finally Saturn and Mars were in Scorpio, in the Fourth House. Romulus made the city square, as Dionysius in book 1 of the Roman Antiquities, Plutarch in the Lives, and Solinus in chapter 11 testify. My Ennius mentions "Square Rome" in book 11 of the Annals. Later, when Rome was larger and already flourishing, the name "Quadrata Roma" remained for a place in the tenth region of the city, as can be seen in P. Victor, who, when the city was already ruling the whole world, recalled the memory of the old city and pressed upon its lord how very uncertain its fortune had been in its infancy. Festus named that place; for how well he cites Ennius there, consult my commentary on the Annals of the poet.

units.la: Quo die.
units.tr: On what day.

units.la: Qua hora.
units.tr: At what hour.

units.la: Qua forma. jam Orbi imperaret, excitabat memoriam Veteris Vrbis, & dubiam admodum in Incunabulis Fortunam inculcabat. Nominabat eum Locum Festus, qui quam bene citet eo Ennium, meum ad Annales Poetæ consule Commentarium. Opidi apud Veteres Scriptores facta mentione, nihilque præterea addito, intelligi Quadratam Romam notat Scaliger in Appendice ad M. Terentium Varronem. Alioqui Vrbi nomen κατ' ἐξοχὴν gerebat, uti constat ex omnibus Scriptoribus; præcipue prolato jam Pomerio, quod pro incrementis Reip. protulerunt Varij T. Tatius Sabinorum Rex, adscitus in Regni societatem ab Romulo, Veteris Vrbis Pomerio Tarpeium Montem, qui extra Quadratam erat Romam, inclusit. Legendus cum aliis Livius. Tullus Hostilius III Romanorum Rex, Alba Longa diruta, & Albanis in Civitatem receptis, Montem Cælium, quem Romulus munierat, Pomerio addidit, testibus Dionysio libro III & Livio libro I. Cœlium Pomerio inclusisse Ancum Marcium, qui quarto regnavit loco, scribit Strabo libro V. Tacitus Tarquinio Priscō, v Regi illud tribuit libro IV. Ancus Marcius, Politorio Latinorum Opido excisō, & Latinis in Vrbem adscitis Montem Aventinum concessit habitandum, Pomerio tamen, quod ominosus, non inclusit: ut tradunt Dionysius libro III, Livius libro I, Strabo libro V, Auctor de VV. Inlustribus cap.I. Eutropius libro I. Idem Livius etiam lib. XLI Aventinum extra Vrbis Pomerium fuisse refert. Publicum adhuc fuisse, & Silvarum plenum notat Dionysius Halic. sub Cos. M. Valerio Maximo & Sp. Virginio Culmontano. Idem Rex Fossas circum Vrbem fecit, quæ Quiritium appellatæ sunt: ut memoriæ produnt Livius lib. I. & Festus lib. XV. Idem Janiculum & Trans-Tiberinam Regionem, facto super Tiberim Ponte Sublicio, Muro cinxit, & Pomerio prolato Vrbi addidit. Consulendi Dionysius Halic. lib.III I, Eutropius & Auctor de VV. Inlustribus cap.v. Latinus item Pacatus in Panegyrico. L. Tarquinius Priscus Vrbis Muros, ruderibus vilibusque structuris ad eam diem ædificatos, Primus cœpit Saxis magnis Albano, Tiburtino & Praenestino ad Regulam formatis, exstruere: quos Ser. Tullius Rex perfecit; ipsdem Auctoribus & Agellio lib.XIII. Noct. Attic. cap. XIV scribentibus. Ser. Tullius, quem dixi, Esquilias, Quirinalem & Viminalem Montes Vrbis pomerio adjunxit, docente Livio lib.I. Dionysius libro II Quirinalem ab Numa addiritum prodit: Strabo libro V Romulo illud tribuit. Auctor de VV, Inlustribus cap VII, & Eutropius lib.I. Livij sententiam sequuntur. Idem Rex Romam, ut idem tradunt, Aggere, Fossis & Muro Lapideo circumdedit. L. Tarquinius Superbus, inmenso ab Oriente Aggere addito, Romam tutiorem fecit. Plinius lib.III. cap.V. & Strabo lib.V. Quisautem fuerit illa ætate Vrbis Ambitus, docere conatur Onuphrius Panvinius in sua Roma. Post Ser. Tullium Regem usque ad Sullam Felicem Dictatorem tempora Pomerium non amplius prolatum scribit Dionysius Halic. lib. IX. L. enim Cornelius Sulla Primus post Reges exactos Pomerium protulit, testibus Tacito lib. III & Agellio loco, qui indicatus. Sullam hac in re sequutus C. Iulius Cæsar; de quo Dio lib. XVIII. & M. Tullius lib.XIII. Epist. non uno loco: item apud eumdem Dionem Antonius in Laudatione funebri. Errat Tacitus, qui Cæsarem præterit Sullam & Augustum: Excusat Scriptorem Magnum Vir Magnus Justus Lipsius. Certe Cæsarem Pomerium protulisse duobus locis, narrant diversis verbis Dio & Agellius. C. Iulij Cæsaris Octaviani Augusti in eodem studio industriam docent, præter Tacitum lib. III & Agellium notato à me libro, tres Cippi grandes, ejusdem fere & formæ & magnitudinis; qui hodieque Romæ visuntur, cum his Inscriptionibus: C. MARCIVS. L. F. L. M. CENSORINVS C. ASINIVS. C. F. GALLVS COS ET. S. C. TERMIN C. MARCIVS. L. F. L. M. CENSORINVS, ET. C. ASI NIVS. C. F. GALLVS. COS IX. S. C PIN. POMOR. TERMIN IMP.
units.tr: In what form. Already ruling the world, he called to mind the memory of the Old City and kept impressing upon his readers how very uncertain her fortune was in her infancy. Festus names the place, and to see how well he quotes Ennius there, consult my commentary on the Annals of the poet. Scaliger, in his Appendix to Marcus Terentius Varro, notes that when the ancient writers mention an town and add nothing further, Quadrata Rome is to be understood. Otherwise the city bore the name "the City" [κατ' ἐξοχὴν] by pre-eminence, as is clear from all the writers, especially since the pomerium was extended, which various men extended for the growth of the commonwealth. T. Tatius, king of the Sabines, admitted by Romulus into partnership in the kingdom, enclosed within the pomerium of the Old City the Tarpeian Hill, which lay outside Quadrata Rome. Livy should be read along with the others. Tullus Hostilius, the third king of the Romans, after Alba Longa had been destroyed and the Albans received into the citizenship, added to the pomerium the Caelian Hill, which Romulus had fortified; so Dionysius in book III and Livy in book I bear witness. That Ancus Marcius, who reigned in fourth place, enclosed the Caelian Hill within the pomerium, Strabo writes in book V. Tacitus assigns this to Tarquinius Priscus, the fifth king, in book IV. Ancus Marcius, after destroying the Latin town of Politorium and admitting the Latins to the city, allotted them the Aventine Hill to live on, but did not enclose it within the pomerium, because it was ill-omened; so Dionysius in book III, Livy in book I, Strabo in book V, the author of De Viris Illustribus chapter I, and Eutropius in book I report. Livy also, in book XLI, reports that the Aventine lay outside the pomerium of the city. Dionysius of Halicarnassus notes that it was still public and full of woods under the consuls M. Valerius Maximus and Sp. Virginius Culmontanus. The same king made ditches around the city, which were called Quiritium, as Livy in book I and Festus in book XV hand down. The same king also surrounded the Janiculum and the region across the Tiber with a wall, after building the Sublician Bridge over the Tiber, and added them to the city by extending the pomerium. Consult Dionysius of Halicarnassus in book III, Eutropius, and the author of De Viris Illustribus chapter V; also Latinus Pacatus in his Panegyric. L. Tarquinius Priscus was the first to begin building the city walls, which had been built to that day of rubble and cheap construction, with large stones of Alban, Tiburtine and Praenestine stone, cut to a square; these were completed by Servius Tullius, the king. The same authors write this, and so does Aulus Gellius in book XIII of the Attic Nights, chapter XIV. Servius Tullius, whom I have mentioned, added to the pomerium of the city the Esquiline, Quirinal and Viminal Hills, as Livy teaches in book I. Dionysius in book II reports that the Quirinal was added by Numa; Strabo in book V assigns it to Romulus. The author of De Viris Illustribus chapter VII and Eutropius in book I follow Livy's opinion. The same king, as the same authors hand down, surrounded Rome with an embankment, ditches and a stone wall. L. Tarquinius Superbus, by adding an immense embankment on the east, made Rome safer. Pliny in book III chapter V and Strabo in book V say so. What the circuit of the city was in that age, Onuphrius Panvinius attempts to show in his Roma. From the time of Servius Tullius the king down to the times of Sulla the Dictator, Felix, Dionysius of Halicarnassus in book IX writes that the pomerium was no longer extended. For Lucius Cornelius Sulla was the first, after the kings were expelled, to extend the pomerium, as Tacitus in book III and Aulus Gellius in the passage indicated bear witness. Sulla was followed in this matter by C. Iulius Caesar, about whom Dio in book XVIII and Cicero in several places in book XIII of his Letters speak; likewise Antony in his funeral oration in the same Dio. Tacitus is wrong, who passes over Caesar and mentions only Sulla and Augustus; the great man Justus Lipsius excuses the great writer. Certainly Dio and Aulus Gellius, in different words, relate that Caesar extended the pomerium in two places. That the diligence of C. Iulius Caesar Octavianus Augustus in the same undertaking is shown, apart from Tacitus in book III and Aulus Gellius, whom I have noted in my book, are three large cippi, of nearly the same shape and size, which are still seen at Rome today, with these inscriptions: "C. Marcius, son of Lucius, of the Lemonian tribe, Censorinus, and C. Asinius, son of Gaius, Gallus, consuls, by decree of the Senate, set this boundary stone of the pomerium." "C. Marcius, son of Lucius, Censorinus, and C. Asinius, son of Gaius, Gallus, consuls for the ninth time, by decree of the Senate, set the boundary of the pomerium, Imperator."

units.la: III. IMP. CÆSAR. DIVI. F. AVGVSTVS PONTIFEX. MAXIMVS TRIBVNIC. POTEST. XVII. EX. S. C. TERMINAVIT R. R. PROX. CIPP. PED. CLXVI S
units.tr: III. The Emperor Caesar, son of the deified Augustus, Pontifex Maximus, in his seventeenth year of tribunician power, by decree of the Senate, has set the boundaries of the city, at a distance of 166 feet from the stone markers.

units.la: Octaviano Augusto successit in hoc Stadio Claudius Imperator ; qui, admisso intra Vrbem Aventino, Pomerium protulisse putaret ex Agellio, Cornelio Tacito, Legeque Regia, quæ de Privilegiis Vespasiano ab S. P. Q. R. concessis lata. Eo pertinet Fragmentum Cippi, quod Romæ ad Cloacam S. Luciæ, non procul ab Campo Floræ, infernum Parieti Officinæ cuiusdam Aromatarij ; sic inscriptum:
units.tr: After Octavian Augustus, the Emperor Claudius followed in this course. He admitted the Aventine within the City, and believed he had extended the pomerium, as Agellius, Cornelius Tacitus and the Lex Regia, a law passed concerning the privileges granted to Vespasian by the Senate and People of Rome, make clear. To this belongs a fragment of a cippus, which was found in Rome, at the sewer of St. Lucia, not far from the Campus Florae, built into the wall of a certain perfumer's workshop, and inscribed thus:

units.la: TI. CLAVDIVS DRVSI. F. CÆSAR AVG. GERMANICVS PONT. MAX. TRIB. POT. VIII. IMP. XVI. COS. IIII. CENSOR. P. P. AVCTIS. POPVLI. ROMANI FINIBVS. POMERIVM AMPLIAVIT. TERMINAVITQ.
units.tr: Tiberius Claudius Caesar Augustus Germanicus, son of Drusus, Pontifex Maximus, in his eighth tribunician power, acclaimed Imperator sixteen times, consul four times, censor, Father of the Fatherland, with the boundaries of the Roman people enlarged, has extended the pomerium and set its limits.

units.la: Claudium excepit hic Imperator Nero ; Ponto Polemoniaco & Alpibus Cottijs Imperio Romano adiectis. Legendus Fl. Vopiscus in Vita Aureliani : qui idem testatur de Trajano Hadriano (quem æternant quoque Lapides) & Aureliano Imperatoribus. Arcadium & Honorium Principes præfert Elogium, quod Romæ supra Portam Portuensem S.P.Q.R. Pomerium ampliasse ex auctoritate Theoderici Gothorum Regis, scribit Cassiodorus in Epistol. Fl. Belisarium sub Imp. Iustiniano tertiam Murorum Urbis partem, Bello Gothico ab Totila Rege disiectam, refecisse, refert Procopius libro III. addens Fl. etiam Narsetem Urbis Moenia vetustate & ruinis conlapsa instaurasse. Post horum tempora Murorum Ambitus non amplius motus ; saepissime tamen vel vetustate vel Barbarorum vi disiectus, ab Romanis Pontificibus est renovatus. Inter eos um Novem Scriptores notant, Gregorius II, Hadrianus I, Leo IV (qui Moenia Urbis refecit ; xv Turres addidit ; Vaticanum, aucto Murorum Ambitu, cinxit, & Urbem Leoninam appellavit) Urbanus V, Nicolaus IV, Martinus V, Nicolaus V, Paulus II, Sixtus IV, Alexander V, Paulus III, qui novum Urbis Ambitum inchoatum reliquit imperfectum; Paulus IV, qui additis Aggeribus, Terreisque Propugnaculis Romam munivit; Bonifacius IX qui Hadriani Molem firmavit Alexander denique VI, qui Urbem, additis Fossa, Aggeribus, latioribusque Propugnaculis fecit tutiorem. De Moenibus Urbis, quæ hodie, consulendus Marlianus libro I. Topographiae Urbis Romae, cap. IX. Quod ad Suburbana notat Ammianus Marcellinus, Adventum describens Constantij Cæsaris ab Urbe Constantinopolitana Romam, Hormisdam genere Persam, Architecturæ peritissimum, in Cæsaris Comitatu dictum & omnium colloquio destitutum primaria quæque digniora Urbis Aedificia dum mente inspecta ordine sibi offendere iussum, ab Ocriculo Romam prius ingredi quam quo in loco Urbs inchoaret, discernere & intelligere potest. Iam multo ante Dionysius Halicarnassæus lib. IV, omnia circa Urbem habitata a tuisse loca ; multa ea & magna, facillimeque adventantibus Hostibus nere obnoxia. Si quis, ait (Latine exprimam eius verba) hæc sciens, avet Romæ Magnitudinem indagare, is & errare cogetur, & nihil certi habebit Signi, quo
units.tr: Imperator Nero followed Claudius; with Pontus Polemoniacus and the Cottian Alps added to the Roman Empire. One should read Flavius Vopiscus in the Life of Aurelian, who also bears witness concerning Trajan and Hadrian (whom stones also commemorate) and the Emperor Aurelian. An inscription that sets forth the Emperors Arcadius and Honorius, which at Rome above the Porta Portuensis records that the S.P.Q.R. extended the pomerium by the authority of Theoderic, King of the Goths, is recorded by Cassiodorus in his Letters. Procopius, in book III, reports that Flavius Belisarius, under Emperor Justinian, restored a third part of the city walls, which had been thrown down by King Totila in the Gothic War; he adds that Flavius Narses also repaired the city's ramparts, which had collapsed through age and ruin. After their time the circuit of the walls was no longer moved; yet very often, whether through age or the violence of the barbarians, it was thrown down and was renewed by the Roman Pontiffs. Among these the nine writers note Gregory II, Hadrian I, Leo IV (who rebuilt the walls of the city, added fifteen towers, enclosed the Vatican by enlarging the circuit of the walls, and named it the Leonine City), Urban V, Nicholas IV, Martin V, Nicholas V, Paul II, Sixtus IV, Alexander V, Paul III, who left the new circuit of the city begun but unfinished; Paul IV, who fortified Rome by adding embankments and earthen bulwarks; Boniface IX, who strengthened the Mole of Hadrian; and finally Alexander VI, who made the city safer by adding a ditch, embankments and broader bastions. Concerning the walls of the city as they stand today, Marlianus in book I of his Topography of the City of Rome, chapter IX, should be consulted. As to the suburbs, Ammianus Marcellinus notes, describing the arrival of Constantius Caesar from the city of Constantinople to Rome, that Hormisdas, a Persian by birth, most skilled in architecture, who was named in the Caesar's retinue and was excluded from everyone's conversation, was ordered to inspect in his mind and to show in order the chief and more notable buildings of the city. He entered Rome from Ocriculum before he could discern and understand where the city begins. Long before, Dionysius of Halicarnassus in book IV had said that all the places around the city were inhabited; many of these were large, and very exposed to enemies who approach easily. If anyone, he says (I shall express his words in Latin), knowing these things, wishes to investigate the greatness of Rome, he will be forced to wander and will have no certain sign by which

units.la: { } Suburbana Loca. quo dignescatur, quicunque sit hæc Vrbs progressa, aut unde esse non amplius Vrbis incipiat: ita Vrbs contexta est Regio, præsertim Spectantibus optimam extensam in infinitum Vrbu. Aristidis etiam quædam ita Latine tenant: Defenditur hæc Vrbs usque ad Mare, ubi commune Emporium, et omnium quæ terra exeunt, dispensatio: quacumque in parte eius Vrbis consistunt quis, nihil prohibet, quo non usus sit partem in medio: quidquid nunc Italiæ restat: completura efficiens videtur, unaque futura Vrbs, in Ienium Mare protensa.
units.tr: Suburban Places. By which one may determine, whoever has advanced into this city, or from where the city no longer begins; the city is so joined to the surrounding region, especially to those who look upon the very fine city extended without limit. Certain passages of Aristides also hold this in Latin: this city is defended as far as the sea, where there is a common market and the distribution of all that comes out of the land; wherever in that city people stand, nothing prevents it from being, in the middle, what no one has used; whatever of Italy now remains, it seems to make the whole and to be a city that will be one, stretched out into the Ionian Sea.

units.la: Vrbs condita non tantum ab Variis, ut docui, varie auctaque, sed & pro auctione & magnitudine diverse divisa in Partes quidem pauciores Cretcens sub Regibus, in plures, Florens, sub Imperatoribus. In Partes tris distribuit Romulus. Eas Tribus appellant Dionysius lib. II. & Livius lib. I. Partes vocat Varro lib. IV. de L L. Ex fuerunt: I Ramnium, qui & Ramnenses Varronii, II Tatium, qui & Tities Propertio, Tati Festo, Titiensis Livio & Plinio, III Lucerum, qui & Lucerenses & Lucomedi Festo. Vrbe amplificata quum tres Tribus Partesve non sufficerent, Tarquinius Priscus Veteres sub iisdem Nominibus duplicavit: Primoque & Secundos Ramnes, Tatios & Luceres constituit. Historia nota. Consulendi præter alios Livius libro I & Festus in Sex Vestæ. Ser. Tullius iterum minore numero in quatuor Partes distribuit: quas, reiectis antiquis Nominibus, non ab Auctore, vel Gentis Origine, sive Casibus: sed ab Locis, qui colebantur, appellavit: I Suburanam, in qua princeps Mons Cælius, Carinæ, Cerolicnsis, Subura: II Esquilinam, in qua Esquiliæ, quæ duo Montes habiti, Cispius & Oppius: III Collinam (Scaliger Collinam vocat) in qua Viminalis & Quirinalis: IIII Palatinam, in qua Palatium, Germalum, Velia, Sacri portus. Late hæc Varro lib. IV. de L L. & Dionysius lib. IV: ubi male Βασιλεύς & Καλαθιος: Livius item lib. I, qui earum Nomina non aperit. Vrbe mirum in modum aucta, novam eius excogitavit Divisionem Cæsar Augustus; qui in Regiones eam est partitus, Suetonio scribente in eius Vita cap. XXX: eatque XIV; uti legere est apud Plinium lib. III natur. hist. cap. V & Tacitum lib. XV Annalium, ubi de Neroniano Incendio. Mentionem XIV Regionum facit Lapis, qui anno CIↄ IↄLIV repertus ad Lacum Nemorensem, XV ab Vrbe Miliari:
units.tr: The city, founded not only by various men, as I have shown, and variously enlarged, was also divided, according to its growth and size, differently: into fewer parts under the Kings, as Cretensis taught, and into more parts under the Emperors, as Florus says. Romulus divided it into three tribes. Dionysius in book II and Livy in book I call these tribes; Varro in book IV of On the Latin Language calls them parts. They were: (1) the Ramnes, who are also called the Ramnenses by Varro; (2) the Tatienses, that is, the Tatii according to Propertius, Tatii according to Festus, and the Titienses according to Livy and Pliny; (3) the Luceres, who are also called Lucerenses and Lucomedi by Festus. When the city had been enlarged and three tribes or parts were not enough, Tarquinius Priscus doubled the old ones under the same names, and set up the Ramnes, Tatii and Luceres in a first and second group. The history is well known. Besides others, Livy in book I and Festus under the word Vesta should be consulted. Servius Tullius again divided it into four parts, with a smaller number; these, with the old names set aside, he named not after an author, or the origin of a people, or chance events, but after the places that were inhabited: (1) the Suburana, in which lies the chief hill, the Caelius, Carinae, Cerolicnsis, and the Subura; (2) the Esquilina, in which are the Esquiliae, which were regarded as two hills, the Cispius and the Oppius; (3) the Collina (Scaliger calls it Collina), in which are the Viminalis and the Quirinalis; (4) the Palatina, in which are the Palatium, Germalus, Velia, and the Sacri portus. Varro in book IV of On the Latin Language and Dionysius in book IV treat these at length, where Dionysius wrongly has Basileus and Kalathios. Livy likewise in book I, though he does not reveal their names. When the city had grown wonderfully large, Caesar Augustus devised a new division of it; he partitioned it into regions, as Suetonius writes in his Life, chapter XXX, and there were fourteen, as one may read in Pliny, book III of the Natural History, chapter V, and in Tacitus, book XV of the Annals, where he speaks of the Neronian fire. A stone found in the year 1554 near the Lake of Nemi, fifteen miles from the city, mentions the fourteen regions:

units.la: DIANÆ NEMORESI. VESTÆ SACRVM DICT
units.tr: Sacred to Diana of Nemi; dedicated to Vesta

units.la: IMP. NERVAE. TRAIANO, AVG GERMANICO. III. COS. PRAEF EIVS. T. VOLTEDIO. MAMILIANO QVAESTORIB. L. CAECILIO.VRSO. II. M. LVCRETIO SABINO II. AEDILIB. Q. VIBENNA. QVIETO TI. CLAVDIO. MAGNO P. CORNELIVS. TROPHIMVS. PISTOR ROMANIENSIS. EX REG. XIV. IDEM. CVR VICI. QVADRATI. ET. LANIA. C. F. THTONOE. CONIVX EIVS. VOTVM. LIBENS. SOLVERVNT
units.tr: In the consulship of the Emperor Nerva and Trajan Augustus Germanicus, for the third time: his prefect T. Voltedius Mamilianus; quaestors L. Caecilius Ursus; M. Lucretius Sabinus and Q. Vibenna Quietus, aediles for the second time; Ti. Claudius Magnus. P. Cornelius Trophimus, a baker of Rome from Region XIV, likewise overseer of the wards of Quadratus and Lania, daughter of Gaius, and Thtonoe, his wife, gladly paid their vow.

units.la: Alius item, qui sub Porticu Domus Conservatorum, in Capitolio, in Fasi Marmorea prægrandi:
units.tr: Another likewise, which is under the portico of the House of the Conservators on the Capitol, on a very large marble Fasti:

units.la: IMP. CAESARI. DIVI TRAIANI. PARTHICI. FIL. DIVI. NERVAE. NEPOTI TRAIANO. HADRIANO AVG. PONTIF. MAXIMO TRIBVNIC. POTESTAT. XX IMP. II. COS. III. P. P. MAGISTRI. VICORVM. VRBIS REGIONVM. XIIII
units.tr: To the Emperor Caesar Hadrian Augustus, son of the deified Trajan Parthicus, grandson of the deified Nerva, Pontifex Maximus, holding tribunician power for the twentieth time, Imperator for the second time, consul for the third time, Father of his Country, the magistrates of the wards of the City, of the fourteen regions.

units.la: Nominant Regiones illas Sex. Rufus (mutilus tamen: desunt enim illi x, xii, xiii & xiv) P. Victor, & Onuphrius Panvinius, qui plenissime delineat. Prima dicebatur Porta Capena: Secunda, Caelimontium; Tertia, Isis & Serapis Moneta; Quarta, Templum Pacis; Quinta, Esquilina cum Turre & Colle Viminali; Sexta, Alta Semita; Septima, Via Lata: Octava, Forum Romanum: Nona: Circus Flaminius; Decima, Palatium; Undecima, Circus Maximus; Duodecima, Piscina Publica; Decimatertia, Aventinus; Decimaquarta denique, Trans-Tiberina. Regiones haec regionum, fixis attentissime in praecipua quaeque oculis, obambulabo: si prius generalia quaedam Urbis praenotaro: in quibus priore loco quaeram, quae Romae ítatis locis: ea sunt Montes & Portae: deinde diffusius excurram in vias; hinc Aquas pervestigabo: post singulas Urbis Regiones percerrabo. Montes ix Veteri muro inclusi; Unus exclusus: illorum viiiis ii trans Tiberim. Cis-Tiberini sunt, Palatinus, Capitolinus, Quirinalis, Viminalis, Esquilinus, Caelius, Aventinus. Ab his vii Montibus Roma Septicollis quibusdam; Septimontium Varroni libro iv de LL. Septemgemina, Statio; Septena Arx, Latino Pacato Panegyr. Theodos. Ἑπτάλοφος Graecis Septem Iuga dicuntur Propertio. Arces nominantur, propter regias in illis olim Sedes constitutas, Virgilio libro vii. Aeneid. Romam Septem Colles nominare Horatium in Carmine Saeculari, testantur Acron & Porphyrion: Dominos Montes Septem vocat Martialis libro iv. Epigrammate lxxiv. Palatinus unde dicatur, sequens indicat Schema: Palanteo, / Palantio, / Παλαντίου. — Arcadum opido. — Livius libro ab V. C. i; Plinius libro naturalis Histor. iv, cap. vi; Dionysius Halicarn. libro i, Antiquit. Rom.
units.tr: The regions are named by Sextus Rufus (though his list is mutilated, since the tenth, twelfth, thirteenth and fourteenth are missing), by P. Victor, and by Onuphrius Panvinius, who describes them most fully. The first was called Porta Capena; the second, Caelimontium; the third, Isis and Serapis Moneta; the fourth, Temple of Peace; the fifth, Esquiline with the Tower and the Viminal Hill; the sixth, Alta Semita; the seventh, Via Lata; the eighth, Roman Forum; the ninth, Circus Flaminius; the tenth, Palatium; the eleventh, Circus Maximus; the twelfth, Piscina Publica; the thirteenth, Aventine; and the fourteenth, finally, Trans-Tiberina. I shall walk through these regions, keeping my eyes fixed most closely on the principal sights, if first I set out some general matters about the City: first I shall ask what the notable places of Rome are, namely its mountains and gates; then I shall run more fully through its roads; after that I shall trace its waters; and finally I shall go through each region of the City. Nine mountains lie within the old wall, and one outside it; of these, eight are on this side of the Tiber and two across it. On this side are the Palatine, Capitoline, Quirinal, Viminal, Esquiline, Caelian, Aventine. From these seven mountains Rome is called by some Seven-hilled; by Varro in book 4 of his work On the Latin Language, Seven-ridged; by Statius, Seven-twinned; by Latinus Pacatus in the Panegyric to Theodosius, Seven-fold Citadel. The Greeks call it Seven-hilled [Ἑπτάλοφος], and Propertius calls the hills Seven Ridges. They are called citadels because royal seats were once established on them, as Virgil says in book 7 of the Aeneid. That Horace, in the Secular Hymn, calls Rome Seven Hills, is attested by Acron and Porphyrion; Martial, in book 4, epigram 74, calls them the Seven Lord Mountains. The following scheme shows where Palatine takes its name: Palanteo, Palantio, [Παλαντίου] — a town of the Arcadians. See Livy, book 1 from the foundation of the City; Pliny, Natural History, book 4, chapter 6; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 1 of the Roman Antiquities.

units.la: Palantibus, qui cum Euandro in illa Loca venerant. Varro libro iv. de LL. Solinus cap. ii.Palatinus, qui & Aborigines. Varro lib. iv & Solinus cap. ii. Palante, vel Pallante — Euandri: Proavo, Virgilius libro viii. Aeneidos, vers. 54. Avo, Servius ad libr. viii. Aeneidos. Filio, illic sepulto. Quidam apud Servium, loco notato. Nepote, ex Dyna eius Filia & Hercule. Nonnulli, & in iis Polybius Megalopolitanus apud Dionysium Halic. lib. i. Arcadum Principe, Isidorus lib. xv. cap. iii. In isthoc Monte sepulto. Quidam apud Festum.
units.tr: The Palantes, who came with Evander to those places (Varro, book 4 On the Latin Language; Solinus, chapter 2). The Palatine people, also called the Aborigines (Varro, book 4, and Solinus, chapter 2). Palas or Pallas, of Evander: as great-grandfather, Virgil, Aeneid book 8, line 54; as grandfather, Servius on Aeneid book 8; as son, buried there, some in Servius at the passage noted; as grandson, by Dyna, his daughter, and Hercules, some, among them Polybius of Megalopolis cited in Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 1, call him prince of the Arcadians (Isidore, book 15, chapter 3); buried on this mountain, some in Festus.

units.la: Alij enim Pallantia Euandri Filia, ab Hercule viciata, & ibidem sepulta. Varro & alij apud Servium viii Aen.
units.tr: For others make Pallantia, Evander's daughter, ravished by Hercules and buried there (Varro and others in Servius on Aeneid book 8).

units.la: Palante, Hyperborei Filia, quæ ibi habitavit, & ex Hercule Latinum peperit. Quidam apud Festum: ubi pro Palante legendum esse Palante, satis docet Solinus cap. ii; qui idem hujus Montis Etymon citat ex Sileno.
units.tr: Palante, daughter of the Hyperborean, who lived there and bore Latinus by Hercules (some in Festus). That for Palante one should read Palante is sufficiently shown by Solinus, chapter 2, who also cites from Silenus the same etymology of this mountain.

units.la: Palatia, Latini Vxore. Quidam apud Varronem libro iv.
units.tr: Palatia, wife of Latinus (some in Varro, book 4).

units.la: Pale, Pastorali Dea. Quidam apud Solinum cap.ii.
units.tr: Pale, goddess of shepherds (some in Solinus, chapter 2).

units.la: Palando. Festus in Palatium, quod Palare Pecudes ibi solerent.
units.tr: Palando. Festus, under Palatium, says the flocks used to wander there.

units.la: Balando. Festus ibidem, quod ibi Pecus pascens Balare consuerit. Quidam apud Solinum cap. ii, quum inquit: sunt qui a Balatibus ovium. Sic de nonnullis Servius ad viii Aeneidos: Aiy, ait, a Balatu Ovium Balantenum volunt dictum, exinde per Ἀλαςκγες Palantenum. Innuit idem Etymon quidam apud Varronem libro iii, quum sic scribit: Eundem hunc locum a Pecore (vel addo, vel intellego Balante) dictum putant quidam. Itaque Nævius Balantium (Balantium retinuit Turnebus libro xx. cap.xxxvii) appellat.
units.tr: Balando. Festus in the same place: because a flock grazing there used to bleat. Some in Solinus, chapter 2, where he says: there are those who derive it from the bleating of sheep. So Servius on Aeneid book 8 says of some: They say it was called Balantenum from the bleating of sheep, and from that, through the Greek form [Ἀλαςκγες], Palantenum. The same etymology is hinted at by a certain writer in Varro, book 3, when he writes: Some think this place was named from the flock (or I add, or understand, from the bleating of the flock). Therefore Naevius calls it Balantium (Turnebus retained Balantium in book 20, chapter 37).

units.la: Collis Euandrius dicitur à Statio, quod Euander cum habitasse perhibeatur. Remulius appellatur Trebellio Pollioni & Vopisco in Gallieno Minore: unde, notum est. In eo Monte Sedes sunt Imperij & Domus Augustana; unde viuvenit, ut cujusvis Principis Aula, vel splendidioris hominis Domus Palatium nominetur. Secundi Montis tria Nomina: Antiquissimum Saturnius ab Saturno, Aboriginum Rege: Varro iv. de LL, Virgilius viii Aeneid. Festus lib. xvii. Solinus cap. ii. Medium, Tarpeius; vel à Tarpeo Duce, uti canit Propertius lib. iv; Eleg. iv; vel ab Tarpeia Virgine, ut vult cum multis aliis Varro libro iv de LL. postremum Capitolinus, à Capite invento, Varro idem loco indicato. Caput illud Totis fuisse scribit Arnobius adversus Gentes lib. vi. Capitis inventi Fabulam ad Gentis nobilitatem excogitatam censet Scaliger: & ait Capitolium Latinis esse, quod Græcis Ἀκρα. De hoc Monte elegantèr Virgilius libro viii Aeneid. Mons tertio loco a me nominatus, antiquitus, anteaquam in eum commigrarent Sabini Curibus venientes, dictus Agonalis; testibus Dionysio Halic. lib. i & Festo lib. i. & xv, qui emendandus; Quirinalis deinde fuit appellatus ab Curetibus, Curium Civibus, qui cum Tatio Romam prosecti Romanis multi Latiniore voce, ut quidam volunt, Quirites vocati. Varro libro iv & Festus lib. xv. Alij sic nuncupatum docent a Quirina, eiusque Fano, quod in illo Monte, Festus lib. xv, Horatius libro ii Epist. ad Iulium Florum, Ovidius libro ii Fastor. Aliæ Montis hujus appellationes, vel, quod malo, Partes, recensentur Varroni libro iv, Salutaris, Martialis, Latiaris, ex emendatione V. N. Iosephi Scaligeri. Constantino imperante dici cœpit Caballinus ab duabus Statuis Marmoreis Alexandri Magni, Bucephalum domantis; vulgo Monte Cavallo. Viminalis nomen habet ab Viminibus. Festus lib. ultimo de Verbor. signif. & Iuvenalis Satyra iii, Varro lib. iv de LL. duplex Etymon tradit vel ab Iove Viminio; cujus in illo Monte erant Arx, vel quod ibi Viminetā. Esquilinus nomen inditum vel ab Excubiis, quas Romulus, parum fidens T. Tatio, ibi habuit; Varro iv de LL. & Ovidius lib. iii Fastorum: vel ab Excolendo, quod excultus fuerit ab Ser. Tullio: idem Varro: vel denique ab Esculis, quarum fortean ibi ante culturam nonnulla copia. Septimontium duos Montes habitos, Cispium & Oppium, notat Varro iv de LL. ubi Septimus etiam Mons, tamquam Esquiliarum pars nominatur. Meminit & Cispii Paulus Diaconus ex Festi libro iii. Quin Esquiliæ Arx Horatio libro ii. Satyra vii quin Salubres eidem libro i. Sat. viii, alibi doceo. Hodie Mons S. Petri ad Vincula, vel. S. Mariæ Majoris. Sextus Mons in ordine nostro varie legitur appellatus, i. Querquetulanus, quod querna Silvæ frequens secundusque olim. Tacitus libro iv. Annalium. Cælius ab Cælio (quem Cælem alij nominant) Vibenno Tusco, qui Romulo, vel, ut alij, Tarquinio auxilium tulit. Varro lib.iv, Dionysius lib. ii, Festus lib. iii, Tacitus libro iv, Tabula Claudiana Lugdunensis. iii Augustus ab Ti. Augusto. Cassius indicant & Suetonius in eius Vita cap. xlviii, & Tacitus libro iv. Annalium. Perijt tertium nomen cum ignominioso Principis fine. Nam multo post Caelum vocant Martialis libr. xii & Sex. Rufus in Descriptione xiiii Urbis Regionum. Septimi Montis item varia Nomina. i Murcius, dictus ab Dea Murcia Sacello. Festus lib. xi. ii Aventinus ab Aventino Rege, vel Aborigenum, ut Servius notat ad Virgil. Aeneid. vii, vel Albanorum, ut tradunt Dionysius lib. i: Livius lib. i. Ovidius lib. iv Fastor. Paullus Diaconus ex Festi libro i, Anonymi apud Varronem libro iv de LL. Metlal Corvinus de Progenie Augusti; vel ab Avente, Sabinorum Fluvio, eodem Varrone scribente; vel ab Adventu, ut Ahonymis videtur apud eundem, quod Montis Etymon maxime probatur Iosepho Scaligero in Appendice ad Varronem; vel denique ab Advectu, uti censet ipse Varro lib. iv. Remurium etiam hunc Montem fuisse dictum, colligunt nonnulli ex Festi libro xvi. Sed designat Festus Locum in Summo Aventino. Cellam Dianae ab ejus Templo nominat Martialis lib. vii. Epigr. lxxi & libr. xii. Epigr. xviii. Nostro aevo Aventinus etiam dicitur. Haec de Septem principis loci Montibus, qui cis-Tiberini; sequuntur qui trans-Tiberim, Ianiculus & Vaticanus. Ianiculo nomen vel ab Iano, cujusve Opido vel Arce, scribentibus Macrobio lib. i. Saturnal. cap. vii, Solino cap. viii, Isidoro libro xv. cap. i. vel ab Ianua, quae ibi quasi ex Latio in Etruriam, ut tradit ex Festi lib. x Paullus Diaconus. Dicitur hodie Mons Aureus; Montorio vulgo, ab flavis arenis. Hujus Montis talis erat Situs, ut ex eo facile conspici posset Roma, canente Martiale libr. iv. Epigr. lxiv. Aliis infrequentiorem faciebat Aeris gravitas, ideoque habitabatur plurimum ab vili & sordida Plebecula, Circulatoribus, Scurris, & aliis, qui ignobiliora tractabant. Martialis lib. i. Epigr. xlii. & lib. vii. Epig. xcviii. Unus eius vertex temperatior erat. Idem Martial. lib. i. Epigr. lxiv. Vaticanus dictus putatur vel ab Vaticus, ut scribit Festus libro ult. de Verb. signif. vel ab Vaticinio, Agellio libr. xvi. cap. xvii; vel ab Vaticano Deo, Varroni in libris Divin. rer. apud eundem Agellium. Celebris hodie est Palatio Pontificio, D. Petri Basilica, Bibliotheca Vaticana, & infinitis admirandae Antiquitatis Monimentis. Et haec de Montibus Veteri Muro inclusis: exclusus (quem tamen inclusit serior aetas) restat. Collis Hortulorum; sic dictus ab Hortis proxime adjacentibus, vel potius a proximis Horti Sallustiani. Dictus etiam fuit aliquando Mons Pincius ab nobilissima Pinciorum familia, quae Romae floruit Constantini Principis tempore. Sunt & alij quidam Montes Romae, vel Monticuli potius. Citorus prope Columnam Antonini. Nominis ratio triplex indicatur a Bartholomaeo Marliano libro v. Topogr. cap. iv. Iordanus haud procul est Citro. Testaccus ab Testu. Consulendus idem Marlianus libro iv. cap. i. Haec de Montibus aequuntur Portae, quae vel Quadratae Urbis, vel Aurae: Quadratae Portas nonnulli ponunt tres, nonnulli quatuor. Plinius lib. iv. cap. v. i Mugionus Porta ab Mugitu Pecoris, Varroni libro iv de LL. Mugionia Festo, ab Mugito quodam derivanti; Mugonia Solino cap. ii. Dicitur & Trigonia Verrio Flacco ab tribus Angulis. ii. Romanula ab ipsa Roma, Varroni libro iv: Romana augustius Festo. iii. Ianualis ab Iano, Varroni & Festo. Palatii Portam nominant Livius libro i & Ovidius in Fastis. iv Carmentalis ab Carmenta Euandri Matre, Solino cap. ii. Scelerata postea. Cautiam notant Festus, non uno loco, Varro in libris de LL. Servius ad viii Aeneidos, & alij. Non desunt, qui Ratumenam nuncupant ex Festi libro xvi & Plin. lib. v iii. cap. xlvii. Antiquissimis Portis adnumerarunt quidam Saturniam, quae & Pandana, Salutarem, Stercorariam, Fenestralem, Piscularem, Catularium: de quibus sententiam meam alibi aperio. Quemadmodum Urbis Ambitus varios variis temporibus est consequutus Terminos: sic Stationes etiam suas & Novem multae mutarunt Portae. Portarum enim Urbis Auctiores aliae certum Locum hodieque servant, vel saltem ab antiquo Situ non multum distant; aliae incertioris sunt Loci. Quae certioris loci, alii Cis-Tiberina sunt, aliae Trans-Tiberina. Inter quae prioris generis, Prima Flumentana ab Flumine Tiberino dicta, cui haec Porta vicina. Festus lib. vi. Meminit non semel Livius. Hodie Porta Populi, ab Fano D. Mariae de Populo, quod illi adjacet. Secunda Collatina, ab Collatia, Sabinorum Opido. Festus lib. iii. Appellari postea caepit Pinciana, a Palatio Pinci Senatoris, quae nomine saepe Procopio nota. Tertia Quirinalis, ab Quirini Acde. Haec & Agonensis, Collina, Salaria, vii. Festus lib.1. & xv, Ovidius iv Fastorum, Iuvenalis Satyra vi, Livius lib. v, Procopius lib.1. Quarta Viminalis, ab Viminum Silva. Festus lib. ultimo. Hodie S. Agnetis. Quinta Querquetulana Plinio libro xvi cap. x. quæ Querquetularia Festo libro xv. Hodie clausa, & nullius usus. Sexta, Gabiusa, apud Livium; hodie D. Laurentij. Septima, Esquilina, cujus frequens apud Veteres Scriptores mentio: dicta ab Esquiliis, quibus impositæ: olim etiam Mataa. Sic nominat Plautus in Pseudolo. Item Labicana Plinio libro xxxv, cap. vi & Praenestina Procopio lib.1. non uno loco. Mataor hodie ab Ædificij magnificentia, cui hæc Porta suppositâ. Plerique hanc fuisse contendunt eam, quæ Veteribus Natta, quod falsum esse doceo variis Argumentis singulario de Vrbe Roma Libello. Esquilinæ subit octavo loco Cælimontana, ab Calio Monte dicta. Meminit Livius. Asinariam appellant Procopius lib.1. & iii. de Bello Goth. & Anastasius Bibliotb. in Vita Silvestri Papæ. Hodie D.Ioannis, ab nobilissimo eius Templo. Nona Latina est, dicta, quod duceret in Latium. Meminerunt multi. Decima Capena; cui nomen vel ab Capena Urbe, Solino vel Capenis Lucu, Servio ad vii Aeneid Virgil. vel Camena, tamquam Camena, Asconio, vel ab Capra, ut quidam volunt. Hodie S. Sebastiani. Mentio ejus apud infinitos Scriptores. Undecima Trigemina, sic nominata, quod Trigemini hac egressi contra Albanos. Commemorant crebro Veteres Auctores. Ostiensis ab nonnullis vocatur. Hodie D. Pauli ab eius Templo. Et hæc de Ostiensi-Tiberina Portis: sequuntur Transi-Tiberina, quarum Prima, vel inter omnes Duodecima; Natalis dicitur, ab Natalibus, Festo libro xii: Fortuensis Procopio, atque à Porta Romana, de quo alibi. Decimatertia S. Pancratij hodie; Pancratiana Procopio lib. 1. Laurentina, ut quidam volunt, Veteribus, Decimaquarta Fontinalis, cujus mentio apud Festum lib. vi, & Livium libro xxxv. Sic Lapis, qui ad Viam Appiam: DIS. MANIBVS A. ' APIDI MAISORIS TABELLARIS A. PORTA FONTINALI
units.tr: The Euandrian Hill is so called by Statius, because Evander is said to have lived there. Remulius is what Trebellius Pollio and Vopiscus call it in the Life of Gallienus the Younger, whence the name is well known. On this hill are the seat of empire and the Augustan house, and from this comes the custom that the court of any prince, or the house of any man of rank, is called a palace. The second hill has three names. The most ancient was Saturnius, from Saturn, king of the Aborigines (Varro, On the Latin Language, book 4; Virgil, Aeneid 8; Festus, book 17; Solinus, chapter 2). The middle one was Tarpeius, either from the leader Tarpeius, as Propertius sings (book 4, elegy 4), or from the virgin Tarpeia, as Varro holds with many others (On the Latin Language, book 4). The last is the Capitoline, from the head that was found there, as Varro says in the same passage. Arnobius, in Against the Gentiles, book 6, writes that this was the head of Tolus. Scaliger thinks the story of the found head was invented to lend nobility to the people, and he says that the Capitolium is for the Latins what the Akra is for the Greeks. Virgil describes this hill elegantly in Aeneid 8. The hill I have named third was in ancient times, before the Sabines who came from Cures settled on it, called the Agonalis, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus (book 1) and Festus (books 1 and 15, which needs correcting) attest. Afterwards it was called the Quirinalis, from the Curetes, that is, the Curi, citizens who went to Rome with Tatius, and who, as some think, were called Quirites by the Romans in a more Latin voice. So Varro (book 4) and Festus (book 15). Others teach that it was named from Quirinus and his shrine, which stood on that hill (Festus, book 15; Horace, Epistles 2, to Julius Florus; Ovid, Fasti, book 2). Other names of this hill, or parts of it, which I prefer to call parts, are listed by Varro (book 4): Salutaris, Martialis, Latiaris, according to the emendation of Joseph Scaliger, my late friend. Under Constantine it began to be called Caballinus, from two marble statues of Alexander the Great taming Bucephalus; commonly the Monte Cavallo. The Viminal has its name from the willows (Viminibus). Festus (last book, On the Meaning of Words) and Juvenal (Satire 3) say so; Varro (On the Latin Language, book 4) gives a double derivation: either from Jupiter Viminius, whose citadel stood on that hill, or because willow thickets grew there. The Esquiline received its name either from the guard posts (excubiis) which Romulus, having little trust in Titus Tatius, kept there (Varro, book 4; Ovid, Fasti, book 3), or from cultivation (excolendo), because it was cultivated by Servius Tullius (the same Varro), or finally from the oak-trees (esculis), of which there was perhaps a considerable number there before it was cultivated. Varro (book 4) records that the Septimontium comprised two hills, the Cispius and the Oppius, and names a seventh hill as part of the Esquiline. Paulus Diaconus, from book 3 of Festus, also mentions the Cispius. Horace (Satire 2, book 7) mentions the Esquiliae citadel, and the Salubres in book 1, Satire 8, which I explain elsewhere. Today it is the hill of St Peter ad Vincula, or of St Mary Major. The sixth hill in our order is variously called, namely the Querquetulanus, because it was once full of oak groves (quernae silvae); Tacitus, Annals, book 4. The Caelian is named after Caelius (whom others call Caeles), an Etruscan from Vibenna, who gave aid to Romulus or, as others say, to Tarquinius (Varro, book 4; Dionysius, book 2; Festus, book 3; Tacitus, book 4; the Claudian tablet of Lyons). The third name, Augustus, comes from Tiberius Augustus; Cassius and Suetonius (in his Life, chapter 48) and Tacitus (Annals, book 4) point this out. The third name perished with the shameful end of the prince. For much later they call it the Caelum, as Martial (book 12) and Sextus Rufus (in the Description of the Fourteen Regions of the City) do. The seventh hill also has various names. The first is Murcius, named after the goddess Murcia's shrine (Festus, book 11). The second is the Aventinus, named from King Aventino, either of the Aborigines, as Servius notes on Virgil, Aeneid 7, or of the Alban kings, as Dionysius (book 1), Livy (book 1), Ovid (Fasti, book 4), Paulus Diaconus (from Festus, book 1) and the anonymous writer cited by Varro (book 4, On the Latin Language) relate; or from Avente, a river of the Sabines, as the same Varro writes; or from Adventu (arrival), as an anonymous writer seems to think in the same place, which etymology Joseph Scaliger in his Appendix to Varro most strongly approves; or finally from Advectu (conveyance), as Varro himself thinks (book 4). Some gather from Festus (book 16) that this hill was also called Remurium, but Festus designates a place on the top of the Aventine. Martial (book 7, epigram 71, and book 12, epigram 18) names it Cellam Dianae from her temple. In our age it is also called the Aventinus. These are the names of the seven principal hills on this side of the Tiber. Next come those across the Tiber, the Ianiculus and the Vatican. The name Ianiculo comes either from Janus, or from his statue or citadel, as Macrobius (Saturnalia, book 1, chapter 7), Solinus (chapter 8) and Isidore (book 15, chapter 1) write; or from the Ianua (gate), which there, as it were, opens from Latium into Etruria, as Paulus Diaconus, from Festus (book 10), relates. Today it is called the Mons Aureus, and commonly Montorio, from its yellow sands. The site of this hill was such that Rome could easily be seen from it, as Martial sings (book 4, epigram 64). For others the heaviness of the air made it less frequented, and so it was mostly inhabited by the vile and squalid common folk, mountebanks, buffoons and others who practised the meaner trades (Martial, book 1, epigram 42, and book 7, epigram 98). Only its summit was more temperate (Martial, book 1, epigram 64). The Vaticanus is thought to be named either from the Vaticus, as Festus writes (last book, On the Meaning of Words), or from Vaticinio (prophecy), Gellius (book 16, chapter 17), or from the god Vaticano, as Varro in his books on Divine Things says, cited by the same Gellius. Today it is famous for the Papal Palace, the Basilica of St Peter, the Vatican Library and countless monuments of admirable antiquity. These are the hills enclosed within the old wall; the one left out (though a later age took it in) is the Collis Hortulorum, so called from the gardens lying nearest to it, or rather from the nearby Gardens of Sallust. It was also at one time called the Pincian Hill, from the most noble Pincian family, which flourished at Rome in the time of the emperor Constantine. There are also some other hills, or rather little hills, in Rome. The Citorus lies near the Column of Antoninus; the reason for its name is given threefold by Bartolomeo Marliani (Topography, book 5, chapter 4). The Iordanus is not far from the Citorus. The Testaccus is named from Testu (potsherds); Marliani (book 4, chapter 1) should be consulted. So much for the hills. The gates follow, which belong either to the Quadrata city or to the Aurelian wall. Some count three gates of the Quadrata, others four (Pliny, book 4, chapter 5). (1) The Mugionus Porta is named from the lowing (Mugitu) of cattle (Varro, On the Latin Language, book 4); Festus calls it Mugionia, deriving it from a certain Mugitus; Solinus (chapter 2) Mugonia. It is also called the Trigonia by Verrius Flaccus, from its three corners. (2) The Romanula, from Rome itself (Varro, book 4); Festus calls it the Romana in a more dignified form. (3) The Ianualis, from Janus (Varro and Festus). Livy (book 1) and Ovid (in the Fasti) call it the Gate of the Palatine (Palatii Portam). (4) The Carmentalis, from Carmenta, mother of Evander (Solinus, chapter 2). Later it was called the Scelerata. Festus, in more than one place, Varro in his books On the Latin Language, Servius on Aeneid 8, and others note its caution. There are some who name the Ratumenam from Festus (book 16) and Pliny (book 36, chapter 47). Some have counted among the most ancient gates the Saturniam, which is also called the Pandana, the Salutarem, the Stercorariam, the Fenestralem, the Piscularem and the Catularium; I set out my opinion on these elsewhere. Just as the circuit of the City has followed various boundaries at various times, so the gates have changed their positions and their number many times. Some of the older gates of the City still keep a certain place even today, or at least are not far from their ancient site; others are of uncertain place. Of those of certain place, some lie on this side of the Tiber, some across it. Among the first kind, the first is the Flumentana, named from the Flumine Tiberino (the Tiber River), near which this gate lies (Festus, book 6). Livy mentions it more than once. Today it is the Porta Populi, from the church of St Mary of the People, which stands beside it. The second is the Collatina, from Collatia, a town of the Sabines (Festus, book 3). Later it began to be called the Pinciana, from Pincius, a senator of the Palatine, and it is often known by that name to Procopius. The third is the Quirinalis, from the temple of Quirinus. This is also the Agonensis, Collina, Salaria (Festus, books 1 and 15; Ovid, Fasti 4; Juvenal, Satire 6; Livy, book 5; Procopius, book 1). The fourth is the Viminalis, from the Viminum (willow) grove (Festus, last book). Today it is the gate of St Agnes. The fifth is the Querquetulana (Pliny, book 16, chapter 10), which Festus (book 15) calls the Querquetularia. Today it is closed and of no use. The sixth is the Gabiusa in Livy; today it is the gate of St Lawrence. The seventh is the Esquilina, often mentioned by the ancient writers; it is named from the Esquiliae on which it was built, and formerly it was also called the Mataa. Plautus names it so in the Pseudolus. Likewise the Labicana (Pliny, book 35, chapter 6) and the Praenestina (Procopius, book 1, in several places). The Mataor today, from the magnificence of the building on which this gate rests. Most maintain that this is the gate which the ancients called the Natta, which I show to be false by various arguments in my separate little book on the City of Rome. After the Esquiline comes, eighth, the Cælimontana, named from the Caelian Hill (Livy mentions it). Procopius (book 1 and book 3, On the Gothic War) and Anastasius (Library, in the Life of Pope Silvester) call it the Asinariam. Today it is the gate of St John, from his most noble church. The ninth is the Latina, so called because it led to Latium; many mention it. The tenth is the Capena, whose name comes either from the city of Capena (Solinus), or from the grove of the Capenae (Servius on Virgil, Aeneid 7), or from the Camena, as if from the Camenae (Asconius), or from the goat (Capra), as some hold. Today it is the gate of St Sebastian. Its mention is found in countless writers. The eleventh is the Trigemina, so named because the triplets (Trigemini) went out through it against the Albans. The ancient authors often record it. Some call it the Ostiensis. Today it is the gate of St Paul, from his temple. These are the gates on the Ostian-Tiberine side; there follow the Trans-Tiberine gates, of which the first, or the twelfth among all, is called the Natalis*, from the Natalia (Festus, book 12); Procopius calls it the Fortuensis, and also from the Porta Romana, of which I speak elsewhere. The thirteenth is today the gate of St Pancras; Procopius (book 1) calls it the Pancratiana. The Laurentina, as some think, was known to the ancients. The fourteenth is the Fontinalis, which is mentioned in Festus (book 6) and Livy (book 35). Thus the inscription on the stone by the Appian Way: TO THE SPIRITS OF THE DEAD. TO APIDIUS MAISOR, TABELLARIUS, AT THE FONTINAL GATE.

units.la: Decimaquinta Triumphalis, ab Triumpho, qui per eam ducebatur. Meminerunt Suetonius in Augusto cap. c. & Tacitus lib.i: An & Basis Prænestina in Domo Episcopi? FORTVNÆ. SANCTA ATINIA. TYRANNIS SEMINARIA. A. PORTA TRIVMPHALE P. TERENTIVS. FORTVNATVS VIR. CLARISSIMVS
units.tr: The fifteenth is the Triumphalis, named from the triumph that was led through it. Suetonius in Augustus, ch. c, and Tacitus, book i, mention it. Also the Praenestine base in the Bishop's house? "To Fortune. Holy Atinia. Nurseries of tyrants. From the Triumphal Gate. P. Terentius Fortunatus, most distinguished man."

units.la: Et quæ ibi sequuntur. Decimasexta Aurelia, ab Via, quæ per eam exibat. Dicebatur & S. Petri, quod eius Templo propinquior. Videndus omnino Procopius. Portas aperui, quarum locus certior sequuntur, quæ incertioris: Navia, quod in Nemoribus Navus, Varroni lib.iv. de LL. Contra Varronis autem mentem, & Portarum apud eumdem ordinem, nonnulli Antiquarij Naviam confundunt cum ea, quæ hodie dicitur Maior. Randusculua, quod ærata fuerit. Æs enim Randus dictum, testibus Varrone iv. de LL. & Valerio Maximo lib.v. cap. vi. Aliunde derivat Paullus Diaconus, quem adi. Lavernalis ab Ara Laverna. Varro iv de LL. Naviam autem Portam eamdem fortean esse cum Latina; Randusculam cum Capena, Lavernalem cum Trigemina, doceo in mea Urbis Topographia. Minucia, quod proxima Sacello vel Arae Dei Minucij. Fest. lib. xi. Meminit Lampridius in Commodi Vita. De hujus Etymo quid sentiam, plenius expono in mea Roma. Sanqualis Porta, inquit Festus, lib. xvii. appellatur proxima Aedis Sangi. Sic enim emendandum. Eadem forte cum Collina, ut alibi doceo. Montes indicavi; portas aperui: postulat ordo, ut in Vias excurram. Inter ea, quæ Reip. utilissima ab Romanis quondam excogitata, non postremo loco censenda sunt Viæ: quarum Magnificentia per totam Italiam tanta fuit, ut Viarum Straturam tribus Fabricatum Romanæ Reip. Miraculis adnumeret Dionysius Halicarnassæus lib. iii Antiq. Rom. Viarum aliæ extra, aliæ intra Urbem. In iis enumerandis idem mihi servabitur ordo, qui in recensendis servatus Portis. Ordiar ab Flaminia, cuius principium à Porta Flumentana. Auctor eius alius fuisse scribitur C. Flaminius Censor, anno ab V.C. 1xxxiii. L. Veturio, C. Lutatio Coss. Epitoma Livij libri xx, Paull. Diacon. ex Festi lib. vi, Cassiodor. in Chronico alius C. Flaminius, Supernoris Filius, Consul cum M. Æmilio Lepido, anno ab V.C. 1 xvi. Strab. Geograph. lib v. Per Umbriam & Tusciam multaque nobilia Opida ducebat Ariminum usque. Strabo lib. v, Antonini Itinerarium, Suetonius in Augusto cap. xxx. Meminerunt præterea alios Ovidius de Ponto libro ii. Eleg. ix Martial. lib iv Epigr. lxiv. & lib. ix. Epigr. lviii, Festus in sacrum, Itineraria Tabula ad Urbem Romam, Ab hac Via Galliæ Togatæ Regio Flaminia. Ab Flaminia oriebantur, vel jungebantur illi, vel in ipsam incidebant Variæ: inter quas primi facile loci Æmilia Lepidi, strata ab M. Æmil. Lepido Cos. anno ab V.C. 1 xvi Strabo lib. v. Initium illi ab hinc Flaminia: excurrebat enim ab Ariminio per multa Opida Bononiam, & inde Aquileiam usque per Alpium radices ducto per gyrum circa Paludes opere. Strabo indicato loco. Paullo sequitur de ea Livius lib xxxix. Meminit cum aliis Capitolinus in Pertinace. Hæc Via Galliæ Togatæ Regioni nomen dedit Æmilia. Videndus Martialis lib. iii. Epigr. iv & lib. iv. Epigr. lxxxv Postumiam Viam in Gallia Togata haud procul Cremona & Hostilia, versus Flaminiam & Æmiliam, fuisse stratam colligitur ex Tacito. Eiusdem classis Via Cassia, ab Cassio Longino Censore anno 1 x ix strata, vel ab L. Cassio Longino Censore item 1 xxviii. Paullus ex Festi lib. iii. Mentio eius apud P. Victorem Committere non possum, quin huic loco Lapidem adponam, qui Auximi in Piceno (Osmam hodie vocant, decimo ab Ancona miliari) cum multis aliis visitur: quod cum Cassia Via, tum aliarum inibi fiat mentio.
units.tr: And what follows there. The sixteenth is the Aurelia, named from the road that went out through it. It was also called the Gate of St Peter, because it lies nearer to his temple. Procopius must certainly be consulted. I have opened the gates; those whose location is more certain come first, and then those whose location is less certain. The Navia is named from the Navus in the groves, according to Varro, book iv, On the Latin Language. Some antiquaries, however, contrary to Varro's view and to the order of the gates in the same author, confuse the Navia with the one now called the Maior. The Randusculua is so called because it was made of bronze, for randus meant bronze, as Varro, book iv, On the Latin Language, and Valerius Maximus, book v, ch. vi, attest. Paulus the Deacon derives it otherwise, and may be consulted. The Lavernalis is named from the altar of Laverna (Varro, book iv, On the Latin Language). I explain in my Topography of the City of Rome that the Navia gate may perhaps be the same as the Latina, the Randuscula the same as the Capena, and the Lavernalis the same as the Trigemina. The Minucia is so called because it lay next to the shrine or altar of the god Minucius (Festus, book xi). Lampridius mentions it in the Life of Commodus. I set out more fully in my Rome what I think of its etymology. "The Sanqualis gate," says Festus, book xvii, "is named from the nearby temple of Sancus." That is how the text must be emended. It is perhaps the same as the Collina, as I show elsewhere. I have pointed out the hills and opened the gates; the order now requires me to run through the roads. Among the most useful institutions devised by the Romans of old, the roads must not be counted last. Their magnificence was so great throughout the whole of Italy that Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book iii of the Roman Antiquities, counts the paving of the roads among the three marvels of the Roman state. Some roads lay outside the city, others inside. In listing them I shall keep the same order that I kept in reviewing the gates. I shall begin with the Flaminia, whose starting point was the Flumentana gate. It is written that its builder was another C. Flaminius, the censor, in the year 383 from the foundation of the city, in the consulship of L. Veturius and C. Lutatius (Epitome of Livy, book xx; Paulus the Deacon from Festus, book vi; Cassiodorus in the Chronicle). Another C. Flaminius, son of Supernor, was consul with M. Aemilius Lepidus in the year 516 from the foundation of the city. Strabo, Geography, book v, says it led through Umbria and Etruria and many notable towns as far as Ariminum. Strabo, the Antonine Itinerary and Suetonius in Augustus, ch. xxx, mention it; besides these, Ovid, From Pontus, book ii, Elegy ix; Martial, book iv, Epigram lxiv, and book ix, Epigram lviii; Festus under sacrum; and the Itinerary Table to the city of Rome. From this Flaminia road the Gallia Togata region takes its name. From the Flaminia there issued or joined it or ran into it various roads, the first of which, in the easiest place, is the Aemilia Lepidi, paved by M. Aemilius Lepidus, consul in the year 516 from the foundation of the city (Strabo, book v). It begins at the point where the Flaminia starts, for it runs from Ariminum through many towns to Bononia, and from there to Aquileia, led round the marshes by a detour along the foot of the Alps. Strabo, at the place indicated. Livy, book xxxix, speaks of it shortly afterwards. Capitolinus mentions it, among others, in the Life of Pertinax. This Aemilia road gave its name to the region of Gallia Togata. The Postumia Via must be consulted: Martial, book iii, Epigram iv, and book iv, Epigram lxxxv. It is gathered from Tacitus that the Postumia Via was paved in Gallia Togata, not far from Cremona and Hostilia, towards the Flaminia and the Aemilia. Of the same class is the Via Cassia, paved by Cassius Longinus, censor, in the year 619, or by L. Cassius Longinus, censor, likewise in the year 628 (Paulus, from Festus, book iii). I cannot refrain from mentioning, at this point, the inscription which is seen at Auximum in Picenum (today called Osma, ten miles from Ancona), together with many others, since it mentions both the Via Cassia and other roads there.

units.tr: Adlected by the most sacred Emperor Hadrian Augustus among the tribunicians; tribune of the praetorians; candidate of Augustus; legate of the province of Baetica; curator of the roads Clodia, Annia, Cassia, Ciminia, of the Three Traianae and of the Amerina; legate of the eleventh legion, Claudia, pious and faithful; propraetorian legate of Augustus of the province of Lusitania; proconsul of the province of Baetica; patron of the colony
