units.tr: Adlected as patron, and at the dedication of the statue, he gave a gift to the colonists.

units.la: Quas Lapis nominat Vias, Partes videntur fuisse Flaminia. Claudiam certe vel Claudiam Flaminia iunctam, restatur Ovidius lib. i. de Ponto: & ex Flaminia clare oritur in Itineraria Tabula. Meminit & Capitolinus in Vero Imperatore. Ex Annia iuxta Flaminiam, ortum duxisse Angustam, indicat Inscriptio, quæ ab aliis jam publici facta turis. Nescio an harum numerum referenda etiam Acmilia Scaura quam M. Aemi Scaurus, Censor anno 10c xlvi, duxit per Pisas & Lunam usque ad Sabbatos, quæque inde Derthonem tendebat, uti de ea scribit Strabo lib.v. Viam F... proximo loco sequitur inter Vias Principes, id est, quarum mitta in ipsa Urbe, vel ab Urbis Portis, Caelimontana dicta, quod duceret Caelium. Meminit Frontinus de Aquaeductibus. Tertia inter Principes Via Nomen Salaria ab Sale. Paullus ex Festi lib.xvii & Plinius lib. xxxi. nat. Hist. ca.vii. Initium eius ab Collina Porta, notante Tacito lib.xix. Stratam fuisse per Sabinos non magnæ longitudinis, tradit Strabo lib.v. Via Salaria memoriam servat contrata Tabula, quam ex pavimento Sacelli, quod est ad Templum S.Gregorii in Coelio Monte exceperiam potiu lib.ii.cap xvii, ubi de Atluria, Hispaniae parte. Pontis etiam Viae Salariae, tertio ab Urbe lapide super Anienem strati, meminit, praeter alios & Itinerariam Tabulam, Inscriptio, quam cum alia conspiciendam dedi capite huius libri xi, quod de Fluminibus Italiae. Quinctium & Iuniam eidem regionibus, quibus Salaria fuisse, indicat Dionysii Halicarn. lib.i. De Quinctia Vetus Marmor in Onuphrii Panuinii Commentariis: C. CVRTIVS. P. F. PAL. NERVA. IIII. VIR P. SILIVS. P. F. ARNIEN. PATINVS. IIII. VIR C. RVSTIVS. C. F. QVARTVS. VEL. IIII. VIR T. FLAVIVS. T. F. ARN. SABINVS IIII. VIR ARAM. ET. SIGN. VIA. QVINCT. D.D
units.tr: Those which the stone calls the Vias seem to have been parts of the Flaminia. Ovid, in book 1 of the Pontic Epistles, attests the Claudia, or the Claudia Flaminia joined together, and the Flaminia clearly appears in the Itinerary Table. Capitolinus also mentions it in his life of Verus. An inscription, already made public by others, shows that the Angusta arose from the Annia beside the Flaminia. I do not know whether the Aemilia Scaura should also be counted in this number. M. Aemilius Scaurus, censor in the year 646, led it through Pisae and Luna as far as Sabatum, and from there it ran to Dertona, as Strabo writes of it in book 5. The next road after these among the Principal Ways, that is, those whose starting point lay in the City itself or at one of its gates, is the Caelimontana, so called because it led to the Caelius. Frontinus mentions it in his work on the aqueducts. The third of the Principal Ways is the Salaria, named from sal (salt). Paulus, from Festus book 17, and Pliny, Natural History book 31, chapter 7, give this. Tacitus, in book 19, notes that its start was at the Colline Gate. Strabo, book 5, reports that it was paved through the land of the Sabines for no great distance. The Table of Contrata preserves the memory of the Via Salaria; I took it from the pavement of the shrine near the Church of St Gregory on the Caelian Hill, rather than from book 2, chapter 17, where Atluria, a part of Spain, is discussed. Apart from others, the Itinerary Table and an inscription, which I gave together with another to be looked at in chapter 11 of this book, on the rivers of Italy, also mention the Pons of the Via Salaria, paved over the Anio at the third milestone from the City. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 1, shows that the Quinctia and the Junia lay in the same districts where the Salaria was. About the Quinctia, an ancient marble in the Commentaries of Onuphrius Panvinius reads: Gaius Curtius, son of Publius, of the Palatine tribe, Nerva, quattuorvir; Publius Silius, son of Publius, of the Arnian tribe, Patinus, quattuorvir; Gaius Rustius, son of Gaius, Quartus, or quattuorvir; Titus Flavius, son of Titus, of the Arnian tribe, Sabinus, quattuorvir; the altar and statue on the Via Quinctia, by decree of the decurions.

units.la: Quarti in Principibus Vijs loci est Nomentana, quæ Nomentum ducebat. Ovidius lib. iv. Fastorum. Antiquitus dicebatur Ficulensis, Livio teste lib. iii. Apud Fretum Sabinorum Oppidum, supra Tiberim iacens, in Viam Salariam incidebat. Strabo lib.v. Meminerunt Suetonius in Nerone, cap.xlviii & Itineraria Tabula. Quinta Principum Tiburtina est in eadem Tabula, Tibur ducem, hodieque: Tiburs nominatur Horatio lib.i. Serm. Sat.vi. Inscriptio Tarraconensis in Templo S.Michaelis: L. OVINIO. L. F. QVIR RVSTICO. CORNELIANO COS. DES. PRAET. INTER TRIBVNICIOS. ADLECTO CVRAT. VIAE. FLAMINIAE LEG. LEG. VII CL. IN. MYS. INFERIOR CVRAT. VIAE. TIBVRTINAE
units.tr: The fourth of the Principal Ways in order is the Nomentana, which led to Nomentum. Ovid, Fasti book 4, mentions it. In earlier times it was called the Ficulensis, as Livy testifies in book 3. It met the Via Salaria near the Fretum Sabinorum, a town lying above the Tiber. Strabo, book 5, mentions it, as do Suetonius in Nero, chapter 48, and the Itinerary Table. The fifth of the Principal Ways is the Tiburtina, which is in the same Table; it led to Tibur, now still called Tiburs, as Horace names it in Satires book 1, satire 6. A Tarragona inscription in the Church of St Michael reads: Lucius Ovinius, son of Lucius, of the Quirine tribe, Rusticus Cornelianus, consul designate, praetor, adlected among the tribunes, curator of the Via Flaminia, legate of the Seventh Legion, Claudia, in Upper Moesia, curator of the Via Tiburtina.

units.la: Et quæ ibi alia. Sexta, Gabina, quæ Gabios tendebat. De ea Livius lib. ii & v. Brevem notat Strabo lib.v. Ultra viii ab Urbe Miliarium excurrisse docet Livius eodem lib. v. Septima, Praenestina, Praeneste ducens, cui initium a Porta Esquilina. Ibi enim hodieque Via bifurcata, cuius sinistrum Cornu Praeneste, dextrum Labicos vadit. Videndi Strabo lib. v & Capitolinus in Gordiano iii. Vitiole Prænestina scribitur in Itineraria Tabula. Octava, Labicana, quæ Labicos à Porta, quam jam nominavi, ducebat. Meminit Spartianus in Iuliano, sub finem. Laticanam præfert Itineraria Tabula. Nonam habet inter Principes Stationem Campana, quæ à Porta Collimontana Capuam vel in Campanium ibat. Mentio eius apud Suetonium in Augusto cap.xciv, ubi legendum Campana Via. Memoratur & cum Osticensi in Inscriptione quadam Neapolitana: M. BASSAEO. M. F PAL. AXIO PATR. COL. CVR. R. P II VIR. MVNIC. PROC. AVG VIAE. OST. ET. CAMP Reliqua lege cap. xxxxii, ubi de Hydrunto. Ex Via Campana exibat Tusculana, quæ Tusculum petebat. Vide Albium Tibullum lib. i. Valeriam etiam hac parte fuisse, paret ex Strabonis libro v. Duas autem Valerias habet P. Victor in Urbis Topographia. Decimo loco occurrit Latina, per quam iter erat in Latium. Initium illi a Porta cognomine. Latta dicitur Martialis lib. ix Epig. xxcv; Aufonia fortean eidem codem libro, Epig. civ. De Latina Lapis, quem Biæciæ compici in Hungaria, testatur Onuphrius Panuinius. Viam hanc mediam fuisse inter Valeriam & Appiam prodidit memoriæ Strabo lib. v. Mentio ejus apud Festum in Sacram & Retricibus, inque Tabula Itineraria. Albana etiam principium habuisse videtur a Porta Latina, vel talem ab ipsa Latina Via. Describit Tibullus lib. i. Elegiarum. Undecima inter Principes est Appia. sic dicta a Prænomine Ap. Claudy Cæci, qui Censorem strávit. Testes Livius lib. iii, M. Tullius pro Milone, Paullus ex Festi libro i, Procop. lib i, Pontius Paulinus, & alij. Initium ejus a Porta Capena, nonnullis Paullo Diacono & Frontino de Aquaeductibus; quin intra Urbem ab Septizonio Severi, indicante Spartiano in Vita Geta Imp. Protenditur Capuam apud Frontinum de Aquaeduct. lib. ii, & Brundusium apud Tacitum lib. ii. Annalium, Strabonem lib. v, Horatium lib. i. Epist. ii, Auctorem de VV: Inlustrib. cap. xxxxiv. Longitudinem, Latitudinem, & alia hujus Viæ singularia delineat Procopius lib. i. Statio ad Pollium scribenti dicitur
units.tr: And what else is there? The sixth is the Gabina, which ran to Gabii. Livy speaks of it in books 2 and 5. Strabo, book 5, notes it briefly. Livy in the same book 5 shows that it went out more than eight miles from the City. The seventh is the Praenestina, which leads to Praeneste and begins at the Esquiline Gate. There, even today, the road forks, and its left branch goes to Praeneste, its right to Labicos. See Strabo, book 5, and Capitolinus in Gordian III. In the Itinerary Table it is written Prænestina. The eighth is the Labicana, which ran from the gate I have just named to Labicos. Spartianus mentions it in Julian, near the end. The Itinerary Table prefers Laticana. Among the Principal Ways the ninth is the Campana, which ran from the Collina Gate to Capua or into Campania. Suetonius mentions it in Augustus, chapter 94, where we should read Campana Via. It is also recorded together with the Ostiensis in a certain Neapolitan inscription: Marcus Bassaeus, son of Marcus, of the Palatine tribe, Axius Patrus, colonist, curator of the public works, duumvir of the municipality, procurator of Augustus, for the Via Ostiensis and Campana. The rest read in chapter 42, where Hydruntum is discussed. From the Via Campana the Tusculana branched off, which went to Tusculum. See Albius Tibullus, book 1. That the Valeria was also in this region is clear from Strabo, book 5. Pompeius Victor, however, in his Topography of the City, has two Valeriae. In tenth place comes the Latina, by which the way lay into Latium. It begins at the gate of the same name. Martial, book 9, Epigram 95, calls it Latta. Perhaps the Aufonia is the same, in the same book, Epigram 104. Onuphrius Panvinius bears witness to a stone about the Latina, which is seen at Biecia in Hungary. Strabo, book 5, records that this road lay midway between the Valeria and the Appia. It is mentioned by Festus under Sacram and Retricibus, and in the Itinerary Table. The Albana also seems to have begun at the Latin Gate, or rather from the Latina Via itself. Tibullus describes it in book 1 of the Elegies. The eleventh among the Principal Ways is the Appia, so called from the praenomen of Appius Claudius the Blind, who paved it while censor. Livy, book 3, witnesses this, as does Marcus Tullius in Pro Milone; Paulus, from Festus book 1, Procopius, book 1, Pontius Paulinus, and others do too. Its start is at the Capene Gate, according to some, including Paulus the Deacon and Frontinus in his work on the aqueducts. Indeed, within the City it begins at the Septizonium of Severus, as Spartianus indicates in the Life of Geta Imperator. It extends to Capua, according to Frontinus, On the Aqueducts, book 2, and to Brundisium, according to Tacitus, Annals book 2, Strabo book 5, Horace, Epistles book 1, epistle 2, and the author of De Viris Illustribus, chapter 44. Procopius, book 1, describes its length, breadth, and other particular features. The station at Pollium is said to be written as...

units.la: Longarum Regina Viarum.
units.tr: The Queen of Long Roads.

units.la: Restituerunt Trajanus, unde & pars Appiæ Traianæ dicta versus Paludes Pomtinas, teste Dione: & Antoninus Pius, ut indicat Inscriptio Pontis, super Amnem Vulturnum. Meminerunt hujus Viæ nulli non Scriptores, ut & Itineraria Tabula. Vicinam Appia Minuciam facit non obscure Horatius lib. i. Epodon ad Lollium. Memorat M. Ciceroad Atticum. In Appiam etiam incidisse Viam Domitianam innuit Statius Papinius, qui ejus meminit in Campania, Neapolim versus, in Procemio lib. iv Silvarum. Scribit de hac Via ad Abrahamum Ortelium Celsus Cittadinus Angelerius his Verbis: Domitiana Via hodie fere integra permanet: initium habens a Via Appia & in ipsius dextra a Porta Vulturni, prope ubi sunt Casilini reliquiæ, & finem habet Puteolis. Longa est xx M. P. Recta est a Vulturno Linternum usque, nunc vulgo La Torre di Patria. Nam inter unius Sepulcri Scipionis repertus fuit Lapis, in quo scriptum erat hoc Verbum tantum P. TRIAMI: reliqua minuto adtritu legi non poterant. Duodecimam Principum facio Asinariam. Eam a Porta, quæ quondam Asinaria, exisse vero est simile. Finisse inter Latinam & Ardeatinam ostendit M. Porcius Cato apud Festum lib. xvi. in Retricibus. Decimamtertiam statuo Ardeatinam, quam post Asinariam fuisse colligitur ex Catonis verbis, quæ apud Festum loco, quem dixi. Dicta ab Ardea, quo ducebat. Decimamquartam habeo Laurentinam, cujus caput ab Radicibus Aventini. Ibat autem Laurentum. Ovidius lib. ii Fastor. Facit ejus mentionem & Plinius lib. ii. Epist. xvi. Principibus etiam concensenda Ostiensis, quæ Ostiam versus erat strata. Frequens ejus mentio apud Procopium. Loquitur & de ea Lapis Neapolitanus, quem paullo ante posui. Hostiensis appellatur vitiose in Tabula Itineraria. Hactenus Cf Tiberinas memoravi: sequuntur Transtiberinæ; quarum Prima Portuensis, a Portu Romano, de quo in Tuscia. Meminit P. Victor. Vitellia, quæ ex Janiculo, & fortean ex Porta Pancratiana, exiens ducebat ad Mare. Innuit Suetonius in Vitellio, cap. i. Aurelia erant duæ, Vetus & Nova. Habet utramque cum Cornelia & Triumphali Lapis, qui Tiburæ visitur, in Æde D. Pauli:
units.tr: Trajan restored it, whence the part of the Appia Traiana near the Pontine Marshes was so called, according to Dio. Antoninus Pius also restored it, as the inscription on the bridge over the river Vulturnus shows. Every writer mentions this road, as does the Itinerary Table. Horace in the first book of his Epodes, addressed to Lollius, clearly makes the Appia Minucia its neighbour. Marcus Cicero mentions it in his letters to Atticus. Statius Papinius, in the preface to the fourth book of his Silvae, where he speaks of it in Campania on the way to Naples, indicates that the Domitian Way also ran into the Appia. Celsus Cittadinus Angelerius writes about this road to Abraham Ortelius in these words: The Domitian Way remains almost intact today. It begins at the Appian Way, on its right side, from the Porta Vulturni, near where the remains of Casilinum are, and ends at Puteoli. It is twenty Roman miles long. It runs straight from the Vulturnus to Linternum, and is now commonly called La Torre di Patria. For a stone was found among the tombs of Scipio, on which only this word was written: P. TRIAMI; the rest was worn away too much to be read. I count the Asinarian Way as the twelfth of the principal roads. It probably left from the gate that was once called Asinaria. Marcus Porcius Cato, in the sixteenth book of Festus, under the heading "Retrices," shows that it ended between the Latin and Ardeatine roads. I place the Ardeatine Way as the thirteenth. From Cato's words in Festus, cited above, it can be gathered that it came after the Asinarian. It is named after Ardea, to which it led. The fourteenth I take to be the Laurentine Way, whose start was at the foot of the Aventine. It went to Laurentum. Ovid mentions it in the second book of the Fasti, and Pliny in the sixteenth letter of the second book. The Ostian Way, which was paved towards Ostia, must also be counted among the principal roads. Procopius often mentions it. The Neapolitan stone I quoted a little earlier also speaks of it. In the Itinerary Table it is wrongly called Hostiensis. So far I have mentioned the roads on the left bank of the Tiber; now come the Transtiberine roads. The first of these is the Portuensis, from the Roman harbour, which I will discuss in the section on Etruria. P. Victor mentions it. The Vitellian Way went from the Janiculum, and perhaps from the Porta Pancratiana, down to the sea. Suetonius hints at it in the life of Vitellius, chapter one. There were two Aurelian Ways, the Old and the New. A stone that is seen at Tibur, in the church of St Paul, bears both of them, together with the Cornelian and Triumphal Ways:

units.la: C. POPILIO. C. F. QVIR. CARO CEDONI. COS. VII. VIR. EPVLON SODALI. HADRIANALI. LEGATO Imp. CAES. ANTONINI. AVG. FIL. PROPR. GERMANIÆ. SVPER. ET. EXER CITVS. IN. EA. TENDENTIS. CVRATOR OPER. PVBLICOR. PRÆF. ÆRAR. SATVR CVRATORI. VIAR. AVRELIÆ. VETERIS. ET NOVÆ. CORNELIÆ, ET. TRIVMPHALIS Et quæ ibi alia : nam pleniorem alibi laudo. Exisse videntur ex Porta Aurelia. Meminerunt P. Victor, & non semel M. Tullius, præterim Philipp. xii, Eutropius, Capitolinus in Antonino Pio, Itineraria Tabula. Ab Aurelia haud procul fuisse Cornelium, indicat Inscriptio à me posita, junctim eas nominans. Sic duæ Statuarum Bases, quarum altera in Hortis Cæsianis servatur, altera in Palatio, quod vulgo Delia Capranica audit, abjecta jacent: C. SALLIO ARISTÆNETO. C. V. | C. SALLIO. ARISTANETO. V. C SEPTEMVIRO EPVLONVM | SEPTEMVIRO. EPVLON. SODALI SODALI. AVGVSTALI. IVRIDICO | AVG. IVRID. PER PICENVM. ET PER. PICENVM. ET. APVLIAM | APVLIAM. CVRATORI. VIAR CVRATORI. VIARVM. AVRELIA. | AVRE{ }. ET. CORNE{LIA}. TRIVMPHA CORNELIÆ. TRIVMPHALIS | LIS
units.tr: To Gaius Popilius, son of Gaius, of the Quirina tribe, Caro Cedon, consul, one of the seven Epulones, of the Hadrianic sodality, legate of the Emperor Caesar Antoninus Augustus, son of the deified one, praetorian legate of Upper Germany and of the army serving there, curator of public works, prefect of the treasury of Saturn, curator of the Aurelian Ways, the Old and the New, the Cornelian and the Triumphal. And whatever else is there; I praise a fuller one elsewhere. They seem to have left from the Porta Aurelia. P. Victor mentions them, and Marcus Tullius more than once, especially in the twelfth Philippic; so do Eutropius, Capitolinus in the life of Antoninus Pius, and the Itinerary Table. That the Cornelian Way was not far from the Aurelian is shown by the inscription I have quoted, which names them together. Likewise two statue bases, one kept in the Caesian Gardens and the other in the Palatine, which is commonly called the Palazzo Capranica, lie cast aside: C. SALLIUS ARISTAENETUS, clarissimus vir, / Gaius Sallius Aristaenetus, clarissimus vir, one of the seven Epulones, of the Augustal sodality, jurist for Picenum and for Apulia, curator of the Aurelian and Cornelian and Triumphal Ways.

units.la: Integriores dabo aliis locis. Cornelia succedit Triumphalis. Eum enim trium Viarum Aureliæ, Corneliæ & Triumphalis ordinem præterunt, quæ posui, Monimenta. Caput habebat à Ponte Triumphali, cujus vestigia hodieque in medio Tiberi. Meminerunt D. Hieronymus & Damasus in Vita Petri Apostoli. Ve Extra-Vrbanas finiam, P. Victor sex Vias nominat, quæ quibus locis fuerint, omnino ignoratur; Patinariam, Tiberinam, Galli anam, Gallicam, Latiniensem, & Flaviam. Hæc igitur de Viis, quæ extra Urbem sequuntur Vrbana, quæ vii numero. Inter eas Sacra censeri solet nobilissima, & maxime celebris: dicta, quod in ea fadus idum inter Romulum & Tatium Reges; vel quod eo itinere uterentur Sacerdotes Idulium Sacrorum conficiendorum causa. Festus lib. xvii. Oriebatur è Carinis. Varro lib. iv. Via hæc non integra, sed Pars tantum ejus Vulgo Romano erat nota, teste ibidem Varrone ea scilicet, quæ erat cunti à Foro, proximo Clivo: in antiquissimo Codice legitur, Primore Clivo: Ego restituendum puto Proxima Clivo, scilicet Capitolino vel Tarpeio. Meminerunt non pauci: quin & in antiquis Lapidibus frequens ejus memoria.
units.tr: I will give more complete ones in other places. The Cornelian Way follows the Triumphal. These are the monuments I have given, which pass over the order of the three Ways, Aurelian, Cornelian and Triumphal. The Triumphal Way began at the Triumphal Bridge, whose remains can still be seen today in the middle of the Tiber. St Jerome and Damasus mention it in the life of the apostle Peter. I will finish with the roads outside the city. P. Victor names six: the Patinarian, Tiberine, Gallicana, Gallic, Latiniensian and Flavian. Where these lay is quite unknown. So much for the roads outside the city; now follow the city roads, which are seven in number. Among them the Sacred Way is usually counted the most noble and most famous. It was so called either because the treaty between the kings Romulus and Tatius was made on it, or because the priests used it when they went to perform the sacred rites of the Ides. Festus, book seventeen. It began at the Carinae. Varro, book four. This way was not known to the Roman public in its entirety, but only in part, as Varro says in the same place, namely the part that ran from the Forum, by the nearest slope. In a very old manuscript it reads Primore Clivo; I think it should be restored as Proxima Clivo, that is, the slope of the Capitol or of the Tarpeian rock. Not a few writers mention it, and it is often recorded on ancient stones.

units.tr: In the gardens of St Sebastian, on the Appian Way, on a marble tablet: To the spirits of the dead. The curators of the Sacred Way, Decimius Faustus and Iortunutus, made this for themselves, for their freedmen and freedwomen, and for their descendants.

units.la: In Insula Tiberina, in Templo S. Bartholomæi: D. M: SETLIÆ. NICES VIX. ANN. XXXV MENS. VI. DIEB. XXI C. SETLIVS. ONESIMVS FLATVRAR. DE. VIA. SAC. CONIVGI. B. M P.
units.tr: In the Island of the Tiber, in the church of St Bartholomew: To the spirits of the dead. To Setlia Nice, who lived 35 years, 6 months and 21 days. Gaius Setlius Onesimus, a flaturarius of the Sacred Way, to his well-deserving wife, set this up.

units.la: Sic Tabula in domo Latini Iuvenalis:
units.tr: Such is the tablet in the house of Latinus Juvenal:

units.la: M. AEDICIVS IVCVNDVS | CLODIA. CYPARE AVRIZEX. DE SACRA VIA. VIX. A. XXX | DVLCISSIMA. SOROR C. ÆDISCVS. PRISCVS
units.tr: Marcus Aedicius Iucundus. Clodia Cypare, goldsmith of the Sacred Way, lived 30 years. Gaius Aedicius Priscus to his most sweet sister.

units.la: Summam Sacram Viam nominat Varro lib. i. de Rust. cap. ii, quæ eidem Sacra Via Caput lib. iv, de LL. Sacrazienses Festo in Octobr Equum, qui Sacram Viam habitabant. Via Nova duplex videtur Roma fuisse: una quidem ad Forum Romanum: altera vero ad Velabrum inter Palatinum & Aventinum Montes. Prior illa juncta fuit Foro Romano, canente Ovidio libro vi Fastor. De ea Livius lib. i. Posterior in Velabro, de qua Varro lib. iv. Hæc fortasis Nova Via est, cujus Caput ponit in xii Vrbis Regione P. Victor: unde etiam Spartianus Novam Viam agnoscit sub Thermis
units.tr: Varro, in the first book of On Agriculture, chapter two, names the Summa Sacra Via, and in the fourth book of On the Latin Language he mentions the same Sacred Way as the head of it. Festus, under October, mentions the Sacrazienses, who lived on the Sacred Way. There seem to have been two New Ways in Rome: one, indeed, by the Roman Forum, and the other by the Velabrum between the Palatine and Aventine hills. The former was joined to the Roman Forum, as Ovid sings in the sixth book of the Fasti, and Livy speaks of it in the first book. The latter lay in the Velabrum, and Varro speaks of it in the fourth book. This is perhaps the New Way whose head P. Victor places in the twelfth region of the city. Hence also Spartianus recognises a New Way beneath the Thermae

units.la: { } Thermis Antoninianis quae in eadem erant Regione. Via Fornicata Situm indicat Livius lib. xxii. Meminit Julius Obsequens de Prodigiis cap. xxxii. Viam Latam Augustus unam fecit ex xiiii Urbis Regionibus. Eius frequens mentio apud Anastasium Bibliothecarium. Via Recta ducebat per Longitudinem Campi Martii. Meminit Seneca de Morte Claudii. Fuisse vicinam Humiliae, indicat Martialis lib. viii. Epigr. lxxv. Alta Via vel Semita vestigia hodieque visuntur in Dorso Quirinalis. Eam Augustus Sextam fecit Urbis Regionem, ut indicat P. Victor. Polt Vias in propositia Methodo promisi Aquas. De Tiberi dixi, quum Generalia explicarem. Habebat autem Is suos in Urbe Pontes: quorum hodie restant Aelius, Ianiculensis, Tarpeius, Cestius, Palatinus: duorum Triumphalis & Sublicius vestigia tantum adparent. Aelius Pons dictus ab Aelio Hadriano Imp. qui Pontem hunc eo loco, quo hodie visitur, exstruxit; ut commodius per illum adiri posset superbissimum ipsius Sepulcrum, in altera Fluminis ripa positum. Spartianus in ejus Vita. Hodie Pons Cestius & S. Angeli appellatur. Hunc Pontem Nicolaus v. P. M. Domunculis quibusdam submotis, amphorem reddidit. Alexander vi angustissimam Portam tollulit, aliamque fecit augustissimam. Ianiculensis Pons dictus, quod per eum ex Urbe in Ianiculum esset aditus. Meminit P. Victor. Reparavit Aurelius Censor, qui Aurelium nuncupavit. Traditur hic Pons Marmoreus factus ab Antonino Pio Imp. Civilibus vero Bellis scribitur idem demolitus, & Rupi demanceps appellatus. Restitutum inde Sixtus iv. P. M. ab suo nomine, quod hodieque retinet, Sixti dixit Pontem. Tarpeius ab Tarpeio vocatus Monte, cui ad occasum proximus. Restituisse L. Fabricium, loquitur Elogium, quod ibi legitur his Verbis:
units.tr: The Antonine Baths, which were in the same region. The Via Fornicata is indicated in Livy, book twenty-two. Julius Obsequens mentions it in his book on Prodigies, chapter thirty-two. Augustus made the Viam Latam into one of the fourteen regions of the city; it is often mentioned by Anastasius the Librarian. The Via Recta ran along the length of the Campus Martius. Seneca mentions it in his Apocolocyntosis. That it was near the Humilia is shown by Martial, book eight, epigram seventy-five. The Alta Via, or Semita, can still be seen today on the ridge of the Quirinal. Augustus made it the sixth region of the city, as P. Victor shows. I promised in my plan to discuss the Vias; now I come to the Aquas. I spoke of the Tiber when I explained the general matters. It had its own Pontes in the city, of which the Aelius, Ianiculensis, Tarpeius, Cestius and Palatinus still stand today; the traces of the Triumphalis and the Sublicius are all that remain of two others. The Aelius Pons was named after the emperor Aelius Hadrian, who built this bridge where it is seen today, so that his very proud tomb, placed on the other bank of the river, could be reached more easily. Spartianus, in his life. Today it is called Pons Cestius and S. Angeli. Pope Nicholas V removed some small houses from this bridge and restored it to its former state. Alexander VI took away the very narrow gate and made another, much wider. The Ianiculensis Pons was so named because there was access through it from the city to the Janiculum. P. Victor mentions it. The censor Aurelius repaired it, and he gave it his name, calling it the Aurelian. It is said that this Pons was made of marble by the emperor Antoninus Pius. But it is written that in the civil wars it was demolished, and was called Rupi demanceps. Later Sixtus IV, Supreme Pontiff, restored it and, from his own name, which it still keeps, called it the Sixti bridge. The Tarpeius was named after the Tarpeian Mount, to whose west it is nearest. That L. Fabricius restored it is stated in the inscription that is read there in these words:

units.la: L. FABRICIVS. C. F. CVR. VIAR FACIVNDVM. COERAVIT IDEMQVE PROBAVIT
units.tr: L. FABRICIUS, son of Gaius, curator of the roads, had this built, and he also approved it.

units.la: Q. LEPIDIVS. M. F. M. LOLLIVS. M. F. COS. EX. SC. PROBAVERVNT
units.tr: Q. LEPIDIUS, son of Marcus, and M. LOLLIUS, son of Marcus, consuls, approved it by decree of the Senate.

units.la: Abeo Pons appellatus Fabricius; cujus meminerunt P. Victor, Horatius lib. ii. Sat. iii, & ibi Vetus Commentator. Dicitur hodie Pons quatuor Capitum, à quatuor Capitulus, vel Simulacro Quadrifronti, quod adscendentibus Pontem ab sinistra sese offert. Corruptum restituit Paulus iii. P. M. Cestius is est, qui Insulam conjungit cum Janiculo & Trans-Tiberina Regione. Mentio ejus apud P. Victorem. Instauratum aliquando ab Valentiniano, Valente & Gratiano Impp. Benedictoque Senatore indicant Inscriptiones, quae hodieque à dextra sinistraque Pontis:
units.tr: It was once called the Fabrician Bridge. P. Victor and Horace (Satires ii.3, with the old commentator there) make mention of it. Today it is called the Pons Quattuor Capitum, from the Four Heads, or from the four-faced statue (Quadrifrons) that meets those climbing the bridge on the left. Paul III, the highest pontiff, restored it when it had fallen into disrepair. The Cestian Bridge joins the island to the Janiculum and the Trans-Tiberine region; P. Victor mentions it. At some point it was restored by the emperors Valentinian, Valens and Gratian, and by the senator Benedictus, as the inscriptions still to be seen today on the right and left of the bridge show:

units.tr: Flavius Valentinian, pious, fortunate, greatest, victorious and triumphant, ever Augustus, supreme pontiff, greatest conqueror of the Germans, greatest conqueror of the Alamanni, greatest conqueror of the Franks, greatest conqueror of the Goths, holding tribunician power for the seventh time, acclaimed imperator for the sixth time, consul for the third time, father of the fatherland; and Flavius Valens, pious, fortunate, greatest, victorious and triumphant, ever Augustus, supreme pontiff, greatest conqueror of the Germans, of the Alamanni, of the Franks and of the Goths, holding tribunician power for the seventh time, imperator for the sixth time, consul for the second time, father of the fatherland; and Flavius Gratian, pious, fortunate, greatest, victorious and triumphant, ever Augustus, supreme pontiff, greatest conqueror of the Germans, of the Alamanni, of the Franks and of the Goths, holding tribunician power for the third time, imperator for the second time, consul, first father of the fatherland, have ordered this bridge to be established and dedicated for the use of the Senate and Roman people, named after the fortunate name of Gratian.

units.la: Vocatur hodie Pons S. Bartholomaei, ab vicino ejus Divi Templo, quod olim fuerat Aesculapij. Infra Insulam Tiberinam ad Passum lxxx visitur Pons, qui olim Palatinus, tinus, quod Palatino Monti proximus esset. Meminit P. Victor. De hoc Ponte cō-piendus Livius libro xxxix. Dictus legitur & Pons Senatorum. Vocatur hodie D. Maria Aegyptiaca, ab ipsius vicino Templo. Dixi duorum etiam Pontium vestigia & Pilas aliquot hodieque cerni in medio Tiberi. Eorum, quæ prope Vaticanum, ad eò iam intra Pontem Aelium, è regione Hospitalis S. Spiritus, fuerunt olim Pontis Triumphalis; sic dicti, quod Imperatores quondam Triumphantes per hunc Pontem in Urbem inveherentur. Meminit Iosephus, Triumphum delineans Vespasiani Imperatoris de Iudæis. Vaticanus etiam legitur appellatus à proximo Monte. Alternus Pontis hodie etiam confumtus Vestigia cernere est pedibus sexcentis infra Pontem Palatinum. Istuit Sublicius, omnium antiquissimus. Auctor ejus Ancus Marcius, qui lanicalum hoc Ponte cum Urbe coniunxit. Livius lib.1. Florus lib.1. cap. iv, & alij. Paullo post partam libertatem, solo Horatio vim Etruscorum sustinente, egre, quod Clavis compactior, sunt revulsus: ideoque in eius restauratione religionem fuit Clavos addere. Tellatur Plinius lib xxxvi, cap.xv. Sublicius dictus, ab Sublicio, de quibus Cæsar. Aemilius inde & Pons Lepidi, ab Aemilio Lepido, in Viro Reip. const. qui Primus cum lapideum fecit. Ita meminit P. Victor, non uno loco; ut & Lampridius in Vita Heliogabali. Disiectum impetu Fluminis restituit Tiberius Cæsar. Marmoreum fecit Antoninus Pius. Adeundus Capitolinus in ejus Vita. Et inde hodieque ipsius reliquiæ Romanis vocantur Ponte Marmorato. Putant nonnulli Pontem hunc appellatum olim Sacrum & Pontem Herculis. Consulendus, quem Dionysius Halicarnassæus in Antiquit. Romanis laudat, Epicardus. Superioribus Pontibus addo Milvium, quem Tiberis habet duobus ab Urbe Patri. Mulibus, in Via Flaminia. Auctor ejus M. Aemilius Scaurus, uti scribunt Auctor de VV. Inlustr. cap. lxxxii & Ammianus Marcellinus lib. xxvii. Meminerunt hujus Pontis Silius Italicus lib.11. Claudianus de Honorij, Sextum Consulatum adepti, in Urbem introitu, & alij. In antiquioris notæ & scripturæ libris M.SS. vocatur Milvius: hodie Ponte Italis. Fornices habet magnos quatuor, binos mediocres, totidemque parvos. Reliquarum Aquarum, præter Tiberim, quæ in Urbe quondam, aliæ dici possunt Religiosa, aliæ Profanæ, Religiosæ, quæ Sacris Vsibus plurimum erant consecratæ, ut Iuturna, Almo, Petronia, Mercurii Aqua. Iuturna nomen ab Iuturna, Italiæ Fonte prope Numicum, salubernimæ Aquæ, eamque ob causam ad omnia Sacra Romam adferri solitæ. Legendi Varro lib.iv. de LL. & Servius ad librum Aeneidos xii. P. Victor Iuturnæ Pontem vel Lacum collocat in vm Urbis Regione, id est in Foro; quod & alij confirmant; inter quos Ovidius vi Fastor. Lacum Iuturnæ designat Plautus in Curculione Act. iv. Sc.1. Confidentes, garrulique & mativoli supra Lacum. Frustra enim Lacum Curtium quidam interpretantur, qui tempore Plauti nullus erat. Alij exaudiendum putant Lucrinum, alij Servilium. Almo Fluvius fuit Romæ in 1. Urbis Regione, teste P. Victore. Erat enim extra Portam Capenam; & non procul ab Urbe cum Tiberi miscebatur. Ovidius iv Fastor. Inter religiosas Aquas habitus, quod quotannis pridie Kalendas Apr. Mater Deum in eo lavarentur. Ovidius ibidem, & Alij. Almo brevissimi erat Curtius, unde Parvus Almo Lucano lib.1. & Rivulus Prudentio in Martyrio Romani; & inde Minor Fluvius vel Amnis dicitur Ovidio respectu Tiberis, loco, quem notavi. Petronium Amnem describit Festus lib. xiv. de Verbor. signif. Mercurij Aquam elegantissime delineat Ovidius v. Fastorum. Profanas nomine, quæ quotidianis Vsibus erant dedicatæ. Eas in Urbe quondam sunt xxxiv restatur P. Victor, is, quem pleniorem edidit Onuphrius Panuinius. Nam Vulgati Codices agnoscunt tantum xx, alij xix, ut & Sex. Rufus, V. C. qui Diocletiani tempore vixit. An autem tot fuerint, an etiam plures, non facile divinari potest. Certe pauciores fuisse constat ex Frontino, qui vix ultra x nominat. Mihi præter alias lectæ Appia, Anio Vetus, Marcia, Tepula, Iulia, Crabra, Virgo, Alsietina, Augusta, Claudia, Anio Novus, Alix. Appia nomen ab Ap. Claudio Crasso, qui postea Cæcus cognominatus. Is enim Censor, ut scribit Frontinus, anno ab V.C. cccxxi post initium Belli Samnitici anno xxx (sic enim pro x legendum) Coss. M. Valerio Maximo & P. Decio Murena (reponend. Mure) hanc Aquam in Urbem induxit. Ejus Venas Primus invenerat C. Plautius Collega Ap. Claudij in Censura, cui ab illo studio Venecis cognomen datum. Cautam indicat Frontinus, quæ Aqua Aqua nihilominus Appia, non vero Plautia fuerit dicta. Auctorem huius Aquæ nominant etiam Appium Pomponius IC. in l. 2. §. 36. De orig. iuris, ubi tamen manifesta in Appio ἀνεφιλογραφία. Cœpiebatur in Agro Lucullano Via Prænestina inter Lapidem ab Urbe vi & viii, diverticulo sinistrorsus passuum 1 oxxc. Eius, quam secundo posui loco, nomen varie proferebatur: alijs Anio, alijs Anien, nonnullis Anienus; & hinc varia inflexio, Anionis, Anienis, Anient. Anio Vetus vocatus ad differentiam Novi, qui postea ab Claudio ductus. Veterem Urbi intulit M. Curius Dentatus Censor cum L. Papirio Cursore, anno ab V.C. ccccLXXXI, L. Papirio Cursore II & Sp. Carvilio Maximo Coss. ex Manubijs de Pyrrho captis, teste Frontino, apud quem concipitur supra Tibur xx. Miliario. Tubulus plumbeus Romæ:
units.tr: Today it is called the Pons S. Bartholomaei, after the nearby temple of that saint, which was formerly a temple of Aesculapius. Below the Tiber Island, at eighty paces, there is a bridge which was once the Palatine, because it lay next to the Palatine Hill; P. Victor mentions it, and Livy, book 39, should be consulted about this bridge. It is also read as the Pons Senatorum. Today it is called S. Maria Aegyptiaca, after the temple nearby. I have said that traces of two other bridges, and some piers, can still be seen today in the middle of the Tiber. Of those near the Vatican, close to the Aelian Bridge, opposite the Hospital of the Holy Spirit, there were formerly the Triumphal Bridges, so called because emperors once entered the City in triumph over this bridge. Josephus mentions it when describing Vespasian's triumph over the Jews. The Vatican bridge is also read as named after the neighbouring hill. The traces of another bridge, now also destroyed, can be seen six hundred feet below the Palatine Bridge. This was the Sublician Bridge, the most ancient of all. Its author was Ancus Marcius, who joined the Janiculum to the City by this bridge (Livy book 1, Florus book 1 ch. 4, and others). Shortly after liberty was won, when Horatius alone withstood the Etruscan army, it was torn apart with difficulty, because its clamps were too tightly fixed; so in its restoration it was a matter of religious scruple to add clamps. See Pliny book 36 ch. 15. It was called Sublician from the sublicae (wooden piles), of which Caesar writes. Next is the Aemilian Bridge, also the Pons Lepidi, named after Aemilius Lepidus, a man of the Republic, who first built one of stone. So P. Victor mentions it in more than one place, as does Lampridius in the Life of Heliogabalus. Tiberius Caesar restored it after it had been broken up by the force of the river. Antoninus Pius made it of marble; consult Capitolinus in his Life. From this, its remains today are still called by the Romans the Marble Bridge. Some think this bridge was formerly called the Sacred Bridge and the Bridge of Hercules; consult Epicardus, whom Dionysius of Halicarnassus cites in the Roman Antiquities. To the bridges above I add the Milvian Bridge, which the Tiber makes two miles from the City, on the Via Flaminia. Its author was M. Aemilius Scaurus, as the writer De Viris Illustribus (ch. 82) and Ammianus Marcellinus (book 27) record. Silius Italicus (book 11), Claudian on the entry of Honorius into the City after he had attained his sixth consulship, and others mention this bridge. In older manuscripts of more ancient hand it is called Milvius; today the Italians call it the Ponte Molle. It has four large arches, two medium and as many small. Of the waters of the City, other than the Tiber, some could be called Religious and others Profane. The Religious waters, which were largely consecrated to sacred uses, were Iuturna, Almo, Petronia and the Water of Mercury. Iuturna is named after Iuturna, a spring in Italy near the Numicus, of very healthful water, and for this reason customarily brought to Rome for all sacred rites. Read Varro, book 4 On the Latin Language, and Servius on Aeneid book 12. P. Victor places the bridge or the Lake of Iuturna in the eighth region of the City, that is, in the Forum; others also confirm this, among them Ovid, Fasti book 6. Plautus, in the Curculio act 4 scene 1, indicates the Lake of Iuturna: "Confident, chattering and fond of talk above the lake." For some wrongly interpret this as the Lacus Curtius, which did not exist in Plautus' time. Others think the Lucrine or Servilian lake should be understood. The river Almo was in Rome in the first region of the City, as P. Victor witnesses; for it lay outside the Capene Gate and was not far from the City when it mixed with the Tiber (Ovid, Fasti book 4). It was counted among the religious waters because every year, on the day before the Kalends of April, the Mother of the Gods was washed in it (Ovid there, and others). The Almo was the shortest of streams, whence Lucan (book 1) calls it the "little Almo" and Prudentius, in the Martyrdom of Romanus, a "rivulet"; and Ovid, with respect to the Tiber, calls it a "lesser river" or stream, in the passage I have noted. The Petronian stream is described by Festus, book 14 On the Meaning of Words. The Water of Mercury is elegantly portrayed by Ovid, Fasti book 5. The Profane waters are those named, which were dedicated to daily uses. Once there were thirty-four of these in the City; P. Victor records this, in the fuller edition published by Onuphrius Panvinius. For the common manuscripts recognise only twenty, others nineteen, as also Sex. Rufus, V.C., who lived in the time of Diocletian. Whether there were so many, or even more, cannot easily be determined. It is certain that there were fewer, according to Frontinus, who names scarcely more than ten. Besides others, I have read of the following: Appia, Anio Vetus, Marcia, Tepula, Iulia, Crabra, Virgo, Alsietina, Augusta, Claudia, Anio Novus, and [Alix]. The Appia takes its name from Appius Claudius Crassus, who was later surnamed Caecus. For he, as Frontinus writes, when censor in the year 321 from the founding of the City, in the thirtieth year after the beginning of the Samnite War (for thus x must be read for xxx), with the consuls M. Valerius Maximus and P. Decius Mus (to be restored as Mure), brought this water into the City. C. Plautius, colleague of Appius in the censorship, had first discovered its veins, and from that work he was given the surname Venox. Frontinus shows that this water was nonetheless called Appia, not Plautia. Pomponius the jurist (in l. 2 §36 De origine iuris) also names Appius as the author of this water, though there is a clear error in the attribution to Appius. It was collected in the Lucullan estate on the Via Praenestina, between the sixth and eighth milestones from the City, a diverticulum to the left, 1,000 paces. The name of the second water I listed was pronounced in various ways: by some Anio, by others Anien, by some Anienus, and hence the varied inflections Anionis, Anienis, Anient. The Anio Vetus (Old Anio) was so called to distinguish it from the New, which was later brought in by Claudius. M. Curius Dentatus, censor with L. Papirius Cursor, in the year 481 from the founding of the City, when L. Papirius Cursor and Sp. Carvilius Maximus were consuls, brought the Old Anio into the City from the spoils taken from Pyrrhus, as Frontinus testifies; in his work it is placed above Tibur at the twentieth milestone. units.tr: ANIO VETUS. Lucius Valerius, slave of the lead workshop (officina plumbaria), made this. 159

units.la: Ductis jam in Urbem Appia & Anione Vetere, quum incrementum Urbis exigere videretur majorem Aquæ modum, Marcio (sic enim apud Frontinum legendum est, pro M. Titio) mandatum ab Senatu est, ut curaret, quatenus alias Aquas posset, in Urbem perduceret, & ampliores Ductus faceret. Tertio igitur miliario opera Fabrorum eam duxit, cui ab ipso nomen Marcia, scribente praeter Frontinum Plinio libro xxxvi, cap. xv; qui etiam lib. xxxi. cap. iv. notat Aufeium olim dictam; Fontem vero Pucniam. Meminerunt Aquæ Marciæ Martialis lib. iv. Epig. xix, Propertius lib. iii, & alij. Leguntur de ea Romæ Inscriptiones, ad Portam Esquilinam:
units.tr: Once the Appian and Old Anio aqueducts had been brought into the City, and the growth of the City seemed to demand a greater volume of water, the Senate commissioned Marcius (for so it must be read in Frontinus, instead of M. Titius) to bring in, as far as he could, other waters and to make larger conduits. He therefore carried the work by the labour of the engineers (fabri) along the third milestone, and it was named the Marcia after him. Besides Frontinus, Pliny (book 36, chapter 15) writes of it, and in book 31, chapter 4, he notes that it was formerly called the Aufeius, and its source the Pucnia. The Marcian Waters are mentioned by Martial (book 4, epigram 19), Propertius (book 3), and others. Inscriptions concerning it are read at Rome, at the Esquiline Gate:

units.la: Aquam, cui Tepula nomen, in Vrbem perduxerunt Cn. Servilius Cæpio & L. Cassius Longinus Ravilla, Censores; M. Plautio Hypsæo; sic enim apud Frontinum est scribendum, & Fulvio Flacco Coss. anno ab V. C. ICCXXIX. Concipiebatur in Agro Lucullano, qui quibusdam Tusculanus, Via Latina, XI ab Vrbe milliario. Iuliam appellatam censent plerique, quod ab Iulio, incertum quo, fuerit inventa; ab Agrippa deinde ex variis Venis collecta in Agro Tusculano, & in Vrbem deducta, Via Latina, ad Milliarium ab Vrbe XII; Imp. Cæsare Augusto & M. Lælio Volcatio Coss. anno ab V. C. ICCXIX. Legendus Frontinus. Eius Ductus videtur fuisse is, qui à Porta Esquilina progreditur hodieque ad C. Marii Trophæa præter Caput Iulia transfluebat Crabra. Hanc Frontino scribente, Agrippa emisit, seu quia usum improbaverat, seu quod Tusculanis Possessoribus relinquendam crederet. Meminit Cicero oratione contra Rullum & libro XVI, Epist. XVIII. Aquam Virginem, uti Frontinus notat, in Vrbem maduxit Agrippa, C. Sentio & Sp. Lucretio Coss. post annum XIII, quam Iuliam. Virgo dicta, quod Herculaneum Rivum refugerit, ut censet Plinius lib. XXXI. cap. III. vel quod quærentibus Aquam Militibus eam, ut Frontinus vult, Virgo monstrarit. Concipiebatur Via Collatina, teste Frontino, ad milliar. VIII. palustribus locis: Viam Prænestinam nominat Plinius libro, quem indicavi. Obibat Campum Martium ut videre est apud Ovidium lib. I. Fast. Restituit Ti. Claudius Imp. Inscriptio, quæ in Hortulo Colotiano:
units.tr: The aqueduct called Tepula was brought into the City by Gnaeus Servilius Caepio and Lucius Cassius Longinus Ravilla, the Censors, in the consulship of Marcus Plautius Hypsaeus (for so it must be written in Frontinus) and Fulvius Flaccus, in the year 629 from the founding of the City. It rose in the Lucullan estate, which some call Tusculan, on the Via Latina, eleven miles from the City. Most authorities think Iulia was so named because it was discovered by someone named Julius, but it is uncertain whom. Later Agrippa gathered it from various springs in the Tusculan estate and brought it into the City by the Via Latina, at the twelfth milestone from the City, in the consulship of the Emperor Caesar Augustus and Marcus Lollius Volcatius, in the year 719 from the founding of the City. Read Frontinus. Its channel seems to have been the one that runs from the Esquiline Gate and still today flows past the Trophies of Gaius Marius, beside the head of the Iulia, the Crabra. While Frontinus was writing, Agrippa discharged this one, either because he had disapproved of its use or because he thought it should be left to the Tusculan landowners. Cicero mentions it in his speech against Rullus and in Letters, book 16, letter 18. Agrippa brought the Aqua Virgo into the City, as Frontinus notes, in the consulship of Gaius Sentius and Spurius Lucretius, thirteen years after the Iulia*. It was called Virgo either because it shrank from the Herculaneum stream, as Pliny thinks (book 31, chapter 3), or because, when soldiers were looking for water, a maiden showed it to them, as Frontinus would have it. According to Frontinus it rose on the Via Collatina, at the eighth milestone, in marshy places. Pliny names it the Via Praenestina, in the book I have cited. It passed across the Field of Mars, as can be seen in Ovid, Fasti book 1. Tiberius Claudius the Emperor restored it. The inscription in the little garden of Colotius reads:

units.la: TI. CLAVDIVS. DRVSI. F. CAESAR. AVGVSTVS. GERMANICVS PONTIFEX. MAXIM. TRIB. POTEST. V. IMP. XI. P. P. COS. III. DESIG. IV A. FUNDAMENTIS. NOVOS. FECIT. AC. RESTITVIT ARCVS. DUCTUS. AQVAE. VIRGINIS. DISTVRBATOS. PER C. CAESAREM
units.tr: TIBERIUS CLAUDIUS DRUSI FILIUS CAESAR AUGUSTUS GERMANICUS, PONTIFEX MAXIMUS, HOLDER OF TRIBUNICIAN POWER FOR THE FIFTH TIME, IMPERATOR FOR THE ELEVENTH TIME, FATHER OF HIS COUNTRY, CONSUL FOR THE THIRD TIME, CONSUL DESIGNATE FOR THE FOURTH TIME, MADE NEW FROM THE FOUNDATIONS AND RESTORED THE ARCHES OF THE CHANNEL OF THE AQUA VIRGO, WHICH HAD BEEN DISTURBED BY GAIUS CAESAR.

units.la: Scribit Ovidius lib. III Fastor. cos, qui in Campo Martio exercebantur, hac Aqua Sudorem & Pulverem abluere solitos; præcipue quum claustra jam essent Balnea, quod innuit Martialis. Ceræ Virginem Lavanti & Natanti fuisse commodissimam, testantur Plinius lib. XXXI. cap. III & Statius libro I Silvarum. Virgo simpliciter dicitur Martiali lib. V. Epig. XXI: Virgineus Liquor Ovidio lib. I de Ponto Eleg. IX. Virgineum Cruorem appellat idem Martialis libro IV Epig. LXIV:
units.tr: Ovid writes (Fasti book 3) that the men who exercised in the Field of Mars were accustomed to wash off sweat and dust in this water, especially when the baths were already closed, as Martial hints. That the Virgo was most convenient for bathing and swimming in wax is attested by Pliny (book 31, chapter 3) and by Statius in book 1 of the Silvae. Martial simply calls it Virgo (book 5, epigram 21), and Ovid calls it Virgineus Liquor, the maidenly liquid (Tristia? from the Black Sea, book 1, elegy 9). The same Martial calls it Virgineum Cruorem, maidenly blood, in book 4, epigram 64:

units.la: Et quod Virgineo cruore gaudet:
units.tr: And because it delights in maidenly blood:

units.la: Melius fortean Liquore. Qui enim Cruorem id est sanguineum Colorem referre potest hæc Virgo, cuius niveas Undas alio vocat loco Martialis lib. VII. Epigr. XXXI. Crudam nominat idem lib. VI. Epigr. XLII. forte quod turbidior propter limum, quodque non defæcata satis. Concipiebatur enim palustribus locis, ideoque Signino purgabatur, Frontino teste. Alsietinam in urbem induxit Augustus, unde & Augusta dicebatur, eodem Frontino scribente. Concipiebatur ex Lacu Alsietino, Via Claudia, miliario XXV. Nullius gratiæ erat, & parum salubris nusquam in usus Populi fluebat. Alia est Augusta, quam in supplementum Martiæ, quoties siccitates agerent, eiusdem bonitatis, opere subterraneo, perduxit Augustus, usque ad Martiam Rivum. Frontinum lege. Claudiam in Vrbem traxit C. Cæsar, qui Tiberio successerat; quum & publicis Usibus & privatis Voluptatibus Septem Aquarum ductus sufficere parum viderentur: altero Imperii sui anno, M. Aquilio Iuliano, P. Nonio Asprenate Coss. Ductum inchoavit, consummavit autem decennio post, & dedicavit Sulla & Titiano Coss. VI. Kalend. Augusti. Videndi præter Frontinum Suetonius in Caligula cap. XX, Plinius lib. XXXI. cap. III, Lampridius in Severo. Rudera Ruius hujus Aquæductus multa hodieque Romæ, ad Portam Esquilinam, quæ Major nunc dicitur: ubi de ea sequentes legūtur Inscriptiones:
units.tr: Perhaps Liquore, liquid, would be better. For this maiden cannot give back Cruorem, that is, the colour of blood, and Martial elsewhere calls her waters snowy (book 7, epigram 31). The same poet calls her Crudam, raw, in book 6, epigram 42, perhaps because she was rather muddy from silt and not sufficiently clarified. She rose in marshy places, and so was purified at Signia, according to Frontinus. Augustus brought the Alsietina into the City, whence it was also called the Augusta*, as Frontinus again writes. It rose from the Alsietine Lake, on the Via Claudia, at the twenty-fifth milestone. It was of no value and rather unhealthy, and it flowed nowhere into public use. Another is the Augusta, which Augustus, to supplement the Martia whenever droughts occurred, brought by an underground channel, of the same quality, as far as the Martian stream. Read Frontinus. The Claudia was brought into the City by Gaius Caesar, who had succeeded Tiberius, since the seven existing aqueducts seemed barely enough for both public needs and private pleasures. He began the channel in the second year of his reign, in the consulship of Marcus Aquilius Julianus and Publius Nonius Asprenas, but he finished it ten years later, and it was dedicated under the consuls Sulla and Titianus on the sixth day before the Kalends of August. Besides Frontinus, see Suetonius in Caligula, chapter 20; Pliny, book 31, chapter 3; and Lampridius in Severus. Many ruins of this aqueduct still survive today at Rome, at the Esquiline Gate, which is now called the Major. There the following inscriptions are read concerning it:

units.tr: The Emperor Titus Caesar Vespasianus Augustus, son of the deified Vespasian, Pontifex Maximus, holding tribunician power for the tenth time, acclaimed Imperator for the seventeenth time, Father of his Country, Censor, consul for the eighth time, had the Curtian and Caerulean Waters restored to the city. These had been brought in by the deified Claudius and later restored by the deified Vespasian, his father, but had collapsed through age from their source to the ground, and he had them led back in a new channel at his own expense.

units.la: Anienis Novi Ductus inchoatus ab C. Caesare, M. Aquilio Iulio & Nonio Aspernate Coss. consummatus vero ab Claudio, Sulla & Tiriano Coss. ut docet Frontinus; addens Novum dictum ad differentiam prioris Anienis, qui deinde Vetus appellari coepit. Concipiebatur, eodem notante, Via Sublacensi ad milliarium LXII. Iungebatur illi Rivus Herculaneus, & in Urbe cum Claudia confundebatur. De Superiorum Aquarum Longitudine, Altitudine, Cursu, cumque aliis subinde Concursu & Mistione, Fine locoque destinato, Qualitate, Erogatione, Modo Quinariarum, Signino, Piscinis, Reparatione, & Similibus, plene Frontinus Libello aureo de Aquaeductibus. Sunt & quas ille non nominat. Sabatina, ab Lacu Sabate ducta, & deducta Romam ex Angullariae Lacu, ut indicat Festus libro xvii. Ejus Ductus Vestigia hodieque extra Portam Pancratianam. Fontes ex hac Aqua in Arca D. Petri. Recentiores eam vocant Septimianam a Porta; Aurelianam, ab Via. Aqua Alexandrina ab Alexandro Imp. in Urbem fuit inducta; teste Lampridio in ejus Vita. P. Victori & hae nominantur: Damnata, Annia, Algentiana, Severiana, Antoniniana, Setina. Quid jam dicam de Balneis: quorum apud Romanos magna fuit & Copia & Luxuria? Scribit Victor per Quatuordecim Regiones fuisse ɪɔ ccclvi: Auctiorem numerum edit Onuphrius, qui notat in genere ɪɔ ccclx. Eorum non postremi loci fuerunt Palatina; de quorum Ruderibus ego alibi. Meminit Cicero Orationem pro Roscio Amer. Item Paulli, quorum mentio apud Iuvenalem Satyra vii; ubi in quibusdam Codicibus depravate Phoebi: Vestigia hodieque servant & tuentur aliquo modo Nomen. Dicunt enim Romani Bagna Poli, quasi Balnea Paulli. Laudantur etiam Balnea T. Claudii Etrusci ab Marmorum Precio, Aedificij magnificentia, Luminis immissione, & argenteis Fistulis, apud Statium lib. i. Silvarum & Martialem lib. vi. Epigr. xi.ii: apud quem passim Balneorum Romanorum frequens est mentio. Luxuriam Balneorum exagitat Seneca ad Lucill. libro xiii. Penfilia fecit Primus C. Sergius Orata. Valerius Maximus lib. ix. Cap.i, & Macrobius lib. iii. Sat. cap.xv. Argenteis Epistolis Aquam fundi in plebeis Fistulis; & in Libertinorum Balneis Gemmas collocari, indignatur Seneca. Parietes Balneorum sparsos fuisse a quibusdam Vnguento, notat Plinius lib. xiii. cap. iii; qui ibidem Solia temperata fuisse Vnguento ab Caio Principe, & quodam Neronis Servo, memorat. Quod ad Thermas: eas in Urbis Regionum Epilogo numerat xvi, Victor; quibus quatuor addit Onuphrius. Inter eas principatum obtinebant, in i Regione, Commodiana & Severiana; in iii, Titi, Trajani, Philippi, Caesarum: in vi, Diocletiani & Maximiani Imperatorum; in ix, Agrippae, Neroniana, Alexandrina, Deciana; in xii, Antoxx i, Antoniniana, de quibus omnibus, earumque Ruinis (quæ hodieque vastissimæ visuntur) ego in mea Vrbis nobilissimæ Topographia. Reliquat, quod ante promiseram, regionatim obambulandæ xiv Vrbis Regiones, Delineant eas, celebrioraque in iis Loca, cum Publica tum Privata, diligenter Sex. Rufus & P. Victor; iisque multo diligentius Onuphrius Panuinius, non adscriptis tamen Veterum Auctorum, qui singulorum faciunt mentionem, Testimonijs. Ea ego præcipuis, & quæ maximi videntur momenti, Locis, à me etiam locupletatis, obiter adponam ex meis Antiquitatum Romanarum Adversarijs. Nam omnia inde singulis, præcipue Templis, Ædibus Sacris, Ædiculisque, curiosius adscribere, hoc opus, hic labor effet; & nescio an Instituto meo satis conveniens. Sufficiat hic vel nudum Potiorum Testimoniorum Indicium. Pleniorem Singulorum explicationem singularius dabit a me Foetus. Hoc præmittam, universim Vicos Regionum i, x, xii, xiii & xiv, eorumque Curatores & Denunciatores describi in Basi marmorea prægrandi, quæ exstat sub Porticu Domus Conservatorum: i quidem x & xiii sinistro, dextro vero latere xii & xiv. A tergo fortean eodem modo reliquæ Regiones erant descriptæ; nulla tamen litterarum vestigia superliunt: putaque potest omnino omissas esse, eo quod pauciores aut nullos inlignores haberent Vicos. Certe Victor in libello suo de Regionibus Vrbis vix ullos præterquam in his quinque Regionibus Vicos numerat.
units.tr: The New Anio aqueduct was begun by Gaius Caesar, under the consuls Marcus Aquilius Julius and Nonius Asprenas, and completed by Claudius, under the consuls Sulla and Tirianus, as Frontinus records. He adds that it was called "New" to distinguish it from the earlier Anio, which then began to be called "Old." According to the same writer, it was channelled from the Sublacensian Way at the sixty-second milestone. The Herculaneum channel joined it, and in the city it was merged with the Claudian. Frontinus fully describes in his golden booklet on aqueducts the length, height and course of the upper waters, their occasional joining and mixing with others, their intended end and location, their quality, distribution and the measure of the quinaria, the sluices, the reservoirs, repairs and similar matters. There are also some he does not name. The Sabatina, drawn from Lake Sabate and brought to Rome from the Lake of Angullaria, as Festus indicates in book xvii, has traces of its course still outside the Porta Pancraziana today. Fountains are fed from this water in the Arca of St Peter. More recent writers call it the Septimiana after the gate and the Aureliana after the road. The Alexandrina aqueduct was brought into the city by the Emperor Alexander, according to Lampridius in his Life. P. Victor also names these: the Damnata, Annia, Algentiana, Severiana, Antoniniana and Setina. What more shall I say of the baths, of which there was a great abundance and luxury among the Romans? Victor writes that there were 856 across the fourteen regions; Onuphrius, who gives the general figure as 860, reports a larger number. Among them the Palatine baths were not the least, and I have written elsewhere about their ruins. Cicero mentions them in his speech for Roscius of Ameria. Likewise the baths of Paulus, mentioned by Juvenal in Satire vii, where some manuscripts wrongly read "Phoebi"; they still keep their trace, and in some way preserve the name, for the Romans call them Bagni di Polo, as if from Balnea Pauli. The baths of Titus Claudius Etruscus are also praised, for the price of their marbles, the magnificence of the building, the admission of light and their silver pipes, by Statius in book i of the Silvae and by Martial in book vi, epigram 42, where mention of Roman baths is frequent throughout. Seneca attacks the luxury of the baths in letter 86 to Lucilius. Valerius Maximus book ix, chapter 1, and Macrobius book iii of the Saturnalia, chapter 15, tell that Gaius Sergius Orata was the first to make suspended hot rooms. Seneca is indignant that water is poured through silver pipes in the baths of the common people and that gems are set in the baths of freedmen. Pliny, book xiii, chapter 3, notes that the walls of baths were sprinkled with perfume by some people, and he records that in the same place the tubs were warmed and perfumed by Caius the Prince and by a slave of Nero. As for the thermae, Victor counts sixteen in the epilogue on the regions of the city, to which Onuphrius adds four more. Among them the chief ones were: in region i, the Commodian and Severian; in region iii, those of the Caesars Titus, Trajan and Philip; in region vi, those of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian; in region ix, those of Agrippa, Nero, Alexander and Decius; in region xii, the Antoniniana and others, of all of which, and of their ruins (which are still seen today in great extent), I have written in my Topography of the most noble city. What I promised before remains: to walk through the fourteen regions of the city one by one. Sextus Rufus and P. Victor describe them, and the places in them, both public and private, that were most famous; Onuphrius Panvinius does so much more carefully, though he does not add the testimonies of the ancient authors who mention each one. I will set down briefly the chief and most important places, enriched by my own material, from my Adversaria of Roman Antiquities. For to ascribe everything from there to individual sites, especially temples, sacred buildings and shrines, would be a long and laborious task, and I doubt it would suit my plan. It is enough here to give a bare index of the more important testimonies. Foetus will give a fuller and more detailed explanation of each. I will first note that the vici of regions i, x, xii, xiii and xiv, with their curators and announcers, are recorded on a huge marble base which stands under the portico of the Conservators' house: of these, i, x and xiii on the left side, and xii and xiv on the right. Perhaps the other regions were recorded in the same way on the back, but no traces of letters survive, and it can be thought that they were omitted altogether because they had fewer or no notable vici. Certainly Victor, in his little book on the regions of the city, names hardly any vici except in these five regions.

units.la: Balnea Flaminiam, ortum duxisse Angustam, indicat Inscriptio, quæ ab aliis jam publici facta iuris. Nescio an harum numerum referenda etiam Acmilia Scauri quam M. Æmilius Scaurus, Censor anno 109 ex u.v, duxit per Pisas & Lunam usque ad Sabbatos, quæque inde Derthonem tendebat, uti de ea scribit Strabo lib.v. Viam Fl... proximo loco sequitur inter Vias Principes, id est, quarum initia in ipsa Vrbe, vel ab Vibis Portis, Constantina dicta, quod duceret Cellatiam. Meminit Frontinus de Aquæductibus. Tertiæ inter Principes Viæ Nomen Salaria, ab Sale. Paullus ex Festi lib.xvii & Plinius lib. xxxi. nat. Hist. cap.vii. Initium eius ab Collina Porta, notante Tacito lib.xix. Stratam fuisse per Sabinos non magnæ longitudinis, tradit Strabo lib.v. Viæ Salariæ memoriam servat contraria Tabula, quam ex pavimento Sacelli, quod est ad Templum S. Gregorii in Cœlio Monte exceptam posui lib.ii.cap xvii, ubi de Asturia, Hispaniæ parte. Pontem etiam Viæ Salariæ, tertio ab Vrbe lapide super Anienem strati, meminit, præter alios & Itinerariam Tabulam, Inscriptio, quam cum alia conspiciendam dedi capite huius libri xi, quod de Fluminibus Italiæ. Quintilium & Iuniam iisdem regionibus, quibus Salaria fuisse, indicat Dionysius Halicarn. lib.i. De Quintilia Vetus Marmor in Onuphrii Panvini Commentariis: C. CVRTIVS. P. F. PAL. NERVA. III I. VIR T. SILIVS. T. F. ARNIEN. PATINVS. III I. VIR C. RVSTIVS. C. F. QVARTVS. VEL. III I. VIR T. FLAVIVS. T. F. ARN. SABINVS III I. VIR ARAM. ET. SIGN. VIA. QVINCT. D.D
units.tr: That the baths of the Flaminian Way took their origin from the Angusta is shown by an inscription, which has already been made public by others. I do not know whether the Aemilian Way of Scaurus should also be counted among these roads, which the censor Marcus Aemilius Scaurus, in the year 109 from the founding of the city, led through Pisa and Luna as far as Sabatum, and which from there ran to Dertona, as Strabo writes of it in book 5. The Via Fl... comes next in the list of principal roads, that is, those whose beginnings lay in the city itself or at its gates, called the Constantine Gate, because it led to Cellatia. Frontinus mentions it in his work on aqueducts. The name of the third principal road is the Salarian Way, from salt. Paulus from the seventeenth book of Festus, and Pliny, Natural History, book 31, chapter 7. Its beginning was at the Collina Gate, as Tacitus notes in book 19. Strabo, book 5, reports that it was paved through the Sabines for a not very great length. The Salarian Way is kept in memory by the opposite table, which I took from the pavement of the chapel next to the Church of St Gregory on the Caelian Hill and placed in book 2, chapter 17, where I speak of Asturia, a part of Spain. Besides others, the Itinerary table also mentions the bridge of the Salarian Way, paved over the Anio at the third milestone from the city, and an inscription which, together with another, I have set out for viewing in chapter 11 of this book, concerning the rivers of Italy. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 1, indicates that the Quintilian and Junian roads ran through the same regions as the Salarian. Concerning the Quintilian Way there is an old marble in the commentaries of Onofrio Panvinio: Curtius, son of Publius, of the Palatine tribe, Nerva, triumvir three times; Silius, son of Titus, of the Arnian tribe, Patinus, triumvir; Rustius, son of Gaius, Quartus, or Flavius, son of Titus, of the Arnian tribe, Sabinus, triumvir, have made the altar and the sign of the Quintian Way, by decree of the decurions.

units.la: Quarti in Principibus Viis loci est Nomentana, quæ Nomentum ducebat. Ovidius lib. iv. Fastorum. Antiquitus dicebatur Fidulensis, Livio teste lib. iii. Apud Fretum Sabinorum Opidum, supra Tiberim lacens, in Viam Salariam incidebat. Strabo lib.v. Meminerunt Suetonius in Nerone, cap.xlviii & Itineraria Tabula. Quinta Principum Tiburtina est in eadem Tabula, Tibur ducere, hodieque Tibur nominatur Horatio lib.i. Serm. Sat.vi. Inscriptio Tarraconensis in Templo S.Michaelis: L. OVINIO. L. F. QVIR RVSTICO. CORNELIANO COS. DES. PRÆT. INTER TRIBVNICIOS. ADLECTO CVRAT. VIAE. FLAMINIAE LEG. LEG. VII CL. IN. MYS. INFERIOR CVRAT. VIAE. TIBVRTINAE
units.tr: The fourth of the principal roads is the Nomentan, which led to Nomentum. Ovid, book 4 of the Fasti. Anciently it was called the Fidulensian, as Livy attests in book 3. Near the Sabine Ford lay a town above the Tiber, which on the Salarian Way joined the road. Strabo, book 5. Suetonius in Nero, chapter 48, and the Itinerary table also mention it. The fifth principal road is the Tiburtine, which is in the same table and leads to Tibur, which is still called Tivoli today, as in Horace, book 1, Satires, satire 6. A Tarraconensian inscription in the church of St Michael reads: To Lucius Ovinius, son of Lucius, of the Quirine tribe, Rusticus Cornelianus, consul designate, praetor, chosen among the tribunes, curator of the Flaminian Way, legate of the Seventh Legion Claudia in Upper Moesia, curator of the Tiburtine Way.

units.la: Et quæ ibi alia. Sexta, Gabina, quæ Gabios tendebat. De ea Livius lib. ii & v. Bremvem notat Strabo lib.v. Ultra viii ab Vrbe Miliarium excurrisse docet Livius eodem lib. v. Septima, Pranestina, Prænestæ ducens, cui initium à Porta Esquilina. Ibi enim hodieque via bifurcata, cuius sinistrum Cornu Prænestæ, dextrum Labicos vadit. Videndi Strabo lib. v & Capitolinus in Gordiano iii. Vitiole Prænestina scribitur in Itineraria Tabula. Octava, Labicana, quæ Labicos à Porta, quam jam nominavi, ducebat. Meminit Spartianus in Juliano, sub finem. Larscanam præfert Itineraria Tabula. Nonam habet inter Principes Stationem Campana, quæ à Porta Cælimontana Capuam vel in Campaniam ibat. Mentio eius apud Suetonium in Augusto cap.xciv, ubi legendum Campana Via. Memoratur & cum Ostiensi in Inscriptione quadam Neapolitana: M. BASSAEO. M. F PAL. AXIO PATR. COL. CVR. R. P IIVIR. MVNIC. PROC. AVG VIAE. OST. ET. CAMP Reliqua lege cap. xxxii, ubi de Hydrunto. Ex Via Campana exibat Tusculana, quæ Tusculum petebat. Vide Albinum Tibullum lib. i. Valerium etiam hac parte fuisse, paret ex Strabonis libro v. Duas autem Valerias habet P. Victor in Vrbis Topographia. Decimo loco occurrit Latina, per quam iter erat in Latium. Initium illi a Porta cognomine. Latta dicitur Martiali lib. ix Epig. xxxv; Ausonia fortean eodem codem libro, Epig. civ. De Latina Lapis, quem Braccia conspici in Hungaria, testatur Onuphrius Panuinius. Viam hanc mediam fuisse inter Valeriam & Appiam prodit memoriæ Strabo lib. v. Mentio ejus apud Festum in Sacram & Retricibus, inque Tabula Itineraria. Albana etiam principium habuisse videtur à Porta Latina, vel saltem ab ipsa Latina Via. Describit Ἀπολλώνιος Tibullus lib. i. Elegiarum. Undecima inter Principes est Appia. sic dicta à Prænomine Ap. Claudy Cæci, qui Censor cam strauit. Testes Livius lib. iii, M. Tullius pro Milone, Paullus ex Festi libro i, Procop. lib i, Pontius Paullinus, & alij. Initium ejus à Porta Capena, nontantibus Paullo Diacono & Frontino de Aquæductibus; quin intra Vrbem ab Septizonio Severi, indicante Spartiano in Vita Getæ Imp. Protenditur Capuam apud Frontinum de Aquæduct. lib. ii, & Brundusium apud Tacitum lib. ii. Annalium, Strabonem lib. v, Horatium lib. i. Epist. ii, Auctorem de VV: Inlustrib. cap. xxxiv. Longitudinem, Latitudinem, & alia hujus Viæ singularia delineat Procopius lib. i. Statio ad Pollium scribenti dicitur
units.tr: And what else is there? The sixth, the Gabine, which led to Gabii. Livy speaks of it in books 2 and 5. Strabo, book 5, notes Bremen. Livy in the same book 5 shows that a milestone was set up more than eight miles from the city. The seventh, the Praenestine, leads to Praeneste, and its beginning is at the Esquiline Gate. For there, even today, the road forks, of which the left branch goes to Praeneste and the right to Labici. See Strabo, book 5, and Capitolinus in Gordian III. The Vitiole Praenestina is written in the Itinerary table. The eighth, the Labican, which led to Labici from the gate I have just named. Spartianus mentions it in Julian, near the end. The Itinerary table prefers Larscana. The ninth principal station is the Campanian, which went from the Caelian Gate to Capua or into Campania. It is mentioned by Suetonius in Augustus, chapter 94, where we should read Campana Via. It is also recorded together with the Ostian Way in a certain Neapolitan inscription: To Marcus Bassaeus, son of Marcus, of the Palatine tribe, Axius, patron of the colony, curator of the republic, duumvir of the municipality, procurator of Augustus for the Ostian and Campanian Ways. For the rest, read chapter 32, where it is about Hydruntum. From the Campanian Way branched the Tusculan, which made for Tusculum. See Albinus, Tibullus, book 1. That the Valerian Way was also in this part is clear from Strabo, book 5. But Publius Victor, in his Topography of the City, has two Valerian Ways. In the tenth place comes the Latin, by which the road ran into Latium. Its beginning is at the gate of the same name. It is called the Latta by Martial, book 9, epigram 35; perhaps the Ausonia in the same book, epigram 104. Concerning the Latin Way there is a stone, which is seen in Hungary at Bracchia, as Onofrio Panvinio testifies. Strabo, book 5, records that this road lay midway between the Valerian and the Appian. Its mention in Festus under "Sacred" and "Harlots," and in the Itinerary table. The Albana also seems to have had its beginning at the Latin Gate, or at least from the Latin Way itself. Apollonius describes it, Tibullus, book 1 of the Elegies. The eleventh among the principal roads is the Appian, so called from the praenomen Appius of Claudius the Blind, who as censor paved it. Witnesses are Livy, book 3, Marcus Tullius in the speech for Milo, Paulus from the first book of Festus, Procopius, book 1, Pontius Paulinus, and others. Its beginning was at the Capena Gate, as Paulus the Deacon and Frontinus in his work on aqueducts note; indeed, within the city it extends from the Septizonium of Severus, as Spartianus indicates in the Life of Geta. It stretches to Capua, according to Frontinus, On Aqueducts, book 2, and to Brundisium, according to Tacitus, Annals book 2, Strabo book 5, Horace, Epistles book 1, letter 2, and the author On Illustrious Men, chapter 34. Procopius, book 1, describes its length, breadth, and other peculiarities. The station at Pollium is said by the writer to be...

units.la: Longarum Regina Viarum.
units.tr: The Queen of Long Roads.

units.la: Restituerunt Traianus, unde & pars Appia Traiana dicta versus Paludes Pomtinas, teste Dione: & Antoninus Pius, ut indicat Inscriptio Pontis, super Amnem Vulturnum. Meminerunt hujus Via nulli non Scriptores, ut & Itineraria Tabula. Vicinam Appia Mimicam facit non obscure Horatius lib. i. Epodon ad Lollium. Memorat M. Ciceroad Atticum. In Appiam etiam incidisse Viam Domitianam innuit Statius Papinius, qui ejus meminit in Campania, Neapolim versus, in Proœmio lib. iv Silvarum. Scribit de hac Via ad Abrahamum Ortelium Celsus Cittadinus Angelerius his Verbis : Domitiana Via hodie fere integra permanet : initium habens a Via Appia & in ipsius dextra a Ponte Vulturni, prope ubi sunt Casilini reliquiæ, & finem habet Puteoli. Longa est xx M. P. Recta est a Vulturno Linternum usque, nunc vulgo La Torre di Patria. Nam inter vnianas Sepulcri Scipionis repertus fuit Lapis, in quo scriptum erat hoc Verbum tantum P. TRIAMI reliqua nimio aditu legi non poterant. Duodecimam Principum facio Asinariam. Fam a Porta, quæ quondam Asinaria, exisse vero est simile. Finisse inter Latinam & Ardeatinam ostendit M. Porcius Cato apud Festum lib. xvi. in Retricibus. Decimatertiam statuo Ardeatinam, quam post Asinariam fuisse colligitur ex Catonis verbis, quæ apud Festum loco, quem dixi. Dicta ab Ardea, quo ducebat. Decimamquartam habeo Laurentinam, cujus caput ab Radicibus Aventini. Ibat autem Laurentum. Ovidius lib. ii Fastor. Facit eius mentionem & Plinius lib. ii. Epist. xvi. Principibus etiam concensenda Ostiensis, quæ Ostium verfuserat strata. Frequens ejus mentio apud Procopium. Loquitur & de ea Lapis Neapolitanus, quem paullo ante posui. Hostensis appellatur vitiose in Tabula Itineraria. Hactenus Cs Tiberinas memoravi: sequuntur Transf-Tiberina; quarum Prima Portuensis, à Portu Romano, de quo in Tuscia. Meminit P. Victor. Vitellia, quæ ex Janiculo, & fortean ex Porta Pancratiana, exiens ducebat ad Mare. Innuit Suetonius in Vitellio, cap. i. Aurelia erant duæ, Vetus & Nova. Habet utramque cum Cornelia & Triumphalis Lapis, qui Tiburæ visitur, in Aede D. Pauli: C. POPILIO. C. F. QVIR. CARO CEDONI. COS. VII. VIR. EPVLON SODALI. HADRIANALI. LEGATO IMP. CAES. ANTONINI. AVG. PII. PROPR. GERMANIÆ. SVPER. ET. EXER CITVS. IN. EA. TENDENTIS. CVRATOR OPER. PVBLICOR. PRÆF. ÆRAR. SATVR CVRATORI. VIAR. AVRELIÆ. VETERIS. ET NOVÆ. CORNELLÆ, ET. TRIVMPHALIS Et quæ ibi alia: nam pleniorem alibi laudo. Exisse videntur ex Porta Aurelia. Meminerunt P. Victor, & non semel M. Tullius, præsertim Philipp. xii, Eutropius, Capitolinus in Antonino Pio, Itineraria Tabula. Ab Aurelys haud procul fuisse Cornelium, indicat Inscriptio à me polita, junctum eas nominans.
