units.tr: Trajan restored it, whence the part of it near the Pomptine Marshes was called the Appia Traiana, according to Dio; and Antoninus Pius did so as well, as the inscription on the bridge over the river Volturnus shows. Virtually all writers mention this road, as does the Itinerary Table. Horace in the first book of his Epodes, to Lollius, clearly points to the neighbouring Appia Mimica. Marcus Cicero mentions it in his letters to Atticus. Statius Papinius also hints that the Domitian Way ran into the Appian Way; he mentions it in Campania, towards Naples, in the Preface to the fourth book of the Silvae. Celsus Cittadinus Angelerius wrote about this road to Abraham Ortelius in these words: The Domitian Way remains almost intact today. It begins at the Appian Way, on its right, from the Bridge of the Volturnus, near where the remains of Casilinum are, and ends at Puteoli. It is twenty miles long. It is straight from the Volturnus as far as Linternum, now commonly called La Torre di Patria. For among the vineyards near the tomb of Scipio a stone was found on which only this word was written: P. TRIAMI; the rest could not be read, because access was too restricted. I make the twelfth of the principal roads the Asinarian. It probably left from the gate that was once called Asinaria. That it ended between the Latin and the Ardeatine Way is shown by Marcus Porcius Cato in Festus, book sixteen, in Retricibus. I count the thirteenth as the Ardeatine, which, from Cato's words in Festus at the passage I mentioned, is seen to have come after the Asinarian. It was named after Ardea, to which it led. The fourteenth I take to be the Laurentine, whose head lay at the foot of the Aventine. It went to Laurentum. Ovid mentions it in the second book of the Fasti, and Pliny mentions it in the second book of his Letters, letter sixteen. The Ostian Way must also be counted among the principal roads, since it was paved as far as Ostia. Procopius often mentions it. The Neapolitan stone I quoted a little earlier also speaks of it. In the Itinerary Table it is wrongly called Hostensis. So far I have mentioned the roads on this side of the Tiber; there follow those across the Tiber. The first of these is the Portuensian, named after the Roman Harbour, which I discuss under Tuscia. P. Victor mentions it. The Vitellian Way ran from the Janiculum, and perhaps from the Pancratian Gate, to the sea. Suetonius hints at it in the life of Vitellius, chapter one. There were two Aurelian Ways, the Old and the New. A stone that is seen at Tibur, in the church of St Paul, mentions both of them, together with the Cornelian and the Triumphal: Gaius Popilius Carus Cedonus, son of Gaius, of the Quirine tribe, consul seven times, septemvir of the Epulones, sodalis of the Hadrianales, legate of the Emperor Caesar Antoninus Augustus Pius, propraetor of Germania Superior and of the army stationed there, curator of public works, prefect of the treasury of Saturn, curator of the Aurelian Old and New, Cornelian and Triumphal Ways; and what else is there. I praise a fuller version of it elsewhere. They seem to have left by the Aurelian Gate. P. Victor mentions them, as does Marcus Tullius more than once, especially in the Philippics, book twelve; also Eutropius, Capitolinus in the life of Antoninus Pius, and the Itinerary Table. That the Cornelian Way lay not far from the Aurelian is shown by an inscription I have published, which names them together. Likewise two pedestal bases of statues, one of which is preserved in the Caelian gardens and the other in the palace commonly called the Capranica, lie next to each other: To Gaius Sallius Aristaenetus, clarissimus vir, septemvir of the Epulones, sodalis Augustalis, jurist for Picenum and Apulia, curator of the Aurelian and Cornelian and Triumphal Ways.

units.la: Integriores dabo aliis locis. Corneliæ succedit Triumphalis. Eum enim trium Viarum Aureliæ, Corneliæ & Triumphalis ordinem prætermisi, quæ postea Monimenta. Caput habebat à Ponte Triumphali, cujus vestigia hodieque in medio Tiberi. Meminerunt & Hieronymus & Damasus in Vita Petri Apostoli. Ut Extra-Urbanam finiam, P. Victor tex Viæ nominat, quæ quibus locis fuerint, omnino ignoratur; Patinariam, Tiberinam, Gallinam, Gallicam, Latiniensem, & Flaviam. Hæc igitur de Viis, quæ extra Urbem: sequuntur Viæ Vibana, quæ vii numero. Inter eas Sacra censeri solet nobilissima, & maxime celebris: dicta, quod in ea fuisse dictum inter Romulum & Tatium Reges; vel quod eo itinere uterentur Sacerdotes Idulium Sacrorum conficiendorum causa. Festus lib. xvii. Oriebatur è Carinis. Varro lib. iv. Via hæc non integra, sed Pars tantum ejus Vulgo Romano erat nota, teste ibidem Varrone: ea scilicet, quæ erat cunti à Foro, proximo Clivo: in antiquissimo Codice legitur, Primore Clivo: Ego restituendum puto Proxima Clivo, scilicet Capitolino vel Tarpeio. Meminerunt non pauci: quin & in antiquis Lapidibus frequens ejus memoria.
units.tr: I will give the more complete ones in other places. The Triumphal Way follows the Cornelian. For I have passed over the order of the three roads, Aurelian, Cornelian and Triumphal, which I will treat later as monuments. It had its head at the Triumphal Bridge, whose remains are still visible today in the middle of the Tiber. Both Jerome and Damasus mention it in the life of the apostle Peter. To finish with the roads outside the City: P. Victor names some roads whose locations are completely unknown: the Patinarian, Tiberine, Gallinian, Gallican, Latiniensian and Flavian. So much for the roads outside the City. There follow the roads of the Vibanian group, which are seven in number. Among them the Sacred Way is usually counted the most noble and most celebrated. It was called sacred either because a compact was made on it between the kings Romulus and Tatius, or because the priests used this route when performing the sacred rites of the Idulia. Festus, book seventeen. It began at the Carinae. Varro, book four. This road was not known to the Roman public in its entirety, but only in part, according to Varro in the same place: namely the stretch that ran from the Forum, by the nearest slope. In a very old manuscript it is read as Primore Clivo; I think it should be restored as Proxima Clivo, that is, by the Capitoline or Tarpeian slope. Not a few writers mention it, and its memory is frequent on ancient stones as well.

units.tr: To the spirits of the dead. To the spirits of the dead: Decimius Faustus and Setlia Nice, and Iortunutus, cabators (?) of the Sacra Via, who lived 35 years and flourished on the Sacra Via, 6 months and 21 days. For themselves and their freedmen and freedwomen, and for their descendants. C. Setlius Onesimus [set this up] for his wife, well deserving, [who was] of the Sacra Via. [This inscription is] to be paid for by the ... of the Sacra Via.

units.la: Summam Sacram Viam nominat Varro lib. i. de Rust. cap. ii, quæ eidem Sacra Via Caput lib. iv, de LL. Sacrazenses Festo in October Equus, qui Sacram Viam habitabant. Via Nova duplex videtur Roma fuisse: una quidem ad Forum Romanum: altera vero ad Velabrum inter Palatinum & Aventinum Montes. Prior illa juncta fuit Foro Romano, canente Ovidio libro vi Fastor. De ea Livius lib. i. Posterior in Velabro, de qua Varro lib. iv. Hæc fortasis Nova Via est, cujus Caput ponit in xii Urbis Regione P. Victor: unde etiam Spartianus Novam Viam agnoscit sub Thermis
units.tr: Varro, in book i of On Agriculture, chapter ii, names the whole Sacra Via, which is the same Sacra Via mentioned in book iv of On the Latin Language. Festus, under October Horse, says the Sacrani who lived on the Sacra Via [are meant]. There seem to have been two New Ways at Rome: one indeed leading to the Roman Forum, the other to the Velabrum between the Palatine and Aventine hills. The former was joined to the Roman Forum, as Ovid says in book vi of the Fasti; Livy speaks of it in book i. The latter, in the Velabrum, is mentioned by Varro in book iv. This is perhaps the New Way whose head P. Victor places in the twelfth Region of the City; whence also Spartianus recognises a New Way under the Thermae

units.la: Nova. Thermis Antoninianis quæ in eadem erant Regione. Via Fornicata Situm indicat Livius lib. xxii. Meminit Julius Obsequens de Prodigijs cap. xxxii. Viam Latam Augustus unam fecit ex xiiii Urbis Regionibus. Eius frequens mentio apud Anastasium Bibliothecarium. Via Recta ducebat per Longitudinem Campi Martij. Meminit Seneca de Morte Claudij. Fuisse viam Humina, indicat Martialis lib. viii. Epigr. lxxv. Alta Semita vel Semita vestigia hodieque visuntur in Dorso Quirinalis. Iam Augustus Sextam fecit Urbis Regionem, ut indicat P. Victor. Post Vias in propositā Methodo promuli Aquas. De Tiberi dixi, quum Generalia explicarem. Habebat autem Is suos in Urbe Pontes: quorum hodie restant Aelius, Ianiculensis, Tarpeius, Cestius, Palatinus: duorum Triumphalis & Sublicij vestigia tantum ad patent. Aelius Pons dictus ab Aelio Hadriano Imp. qui Pontem hunc eo loco, quo hodie visitur, exstruxit; ut commodius per illum adiri posset superbissimum iptius Sepulcrum, in altera Fluminis ripa positum. Spartianus in ejus Vita. Hodie Pons Castelli & S. Angeli appellatur. Hunc Pontem Nicolaus v. P. M. Domunculis quibusdam submotis, ampliorem reddidit. Alexander vi angustissimam Portam tollulit, aliamque fecit augustissimam. Ianiculensis Pons dictus, quod per eum ex Urbe in Ianiculum etiet aditus. Meminit P. Victor. Reparavit Aurelius Censor, qui Aurelium nuncupavit. Traditur hic Pons Marmoreus factus ab Antonino Pio Imp. Civilibus vero Bellis scribitur idem demolitus, & Rupis demunceps appellatus. Restitutum inde Sixtus iv. P. M. ab suo nomine, quod hodieque retinet, Sixti dixit Pontem. Tarpeius ab Tarpeio vocatus Monte, cui ad occasum proximus. Restituisse L. Fabricium, loquitur Elogium, quod ibi legitur his Verbis: tinus, quod Palatino Monti proximus esset. Meminit P. Victor. De hoc Ponte cautiendus Livius libro xxxix. Dictus legitur & Pons Senatorum. Vocatur hodie D. Maria Aegyptiaca, ab ipsius vicino Templo. Dixi duorum etiam Pontium vestigia & Pilas aliquot hodieque cerni in medio Tiberi. Eorum, quae prope Vaticanum, ad teli jactum intra Pontem Aelium, e regione Hospitalis S. Spiritus, fuerunt olim Pontis Triumphalis, sic dicti, quod Imperatores quondam Triumphantes per hunc Pontem in Urbem inveherentur. Meminit Iosephus, Triumphum delineans Vespasiani Imperatoris de Iudaeis. Vaticanus etiam legitur appellatus a proximo Monte. Alterius Pontis hodie etiam consumti vestigia cernere est pedibus sexcentis infra Pontem Palatinum. Is fuit Sublicius, omnium antiquissimus. Auctor ejus Ancus Marcius, qui Janiculum hoc Ponte cum Urbe conjunxit. Livius lib. i. Florus lib. i. cap. iv, & alij. Paullo post partam libertatem, solo Horatio vim Etruscorum sustinente, aegre, quod Clavis compactior, fuit revulsus: ideoque in ejus restauratione religiosum fuit Clavos addere. Testatur Plinius lib. xxxvi, cap. xv. Sublicius dictus, ab Sublicis, de quibus Caesar. Aemilius inde & Pons Lepidi, ab Aemilio Lepido, in Viro Reip. const. qui Primus eum lapideum fecit. Ita meminit P. Victor, non uno loco; ut & Lampridius in Vita Heliogabali. Dilectum impetu Fluminis restituit Tiberius Caesar. Marmoreum fecit Antoninus Pius. Adeundus Capitolinus in ejus Vita. Et inde hodieque ipsius reliquiae Romanis vocantur Ponte Marmorato. Putant nonnulli Pontem hunc appellatum olim Sacrum & Pontem Herculis. Consulendus, quem Dionysius Halicarnassaeus in Antiquit. Romanis laudat, Epicardus. Superioribus Pontibus addo Milvium, quem Tiberis habet duobus ab Urbe Passuum Milibus, in Via Flaminia. Auctor ejus M. Aemilius Scaurus, uti scribunt Auctor de VV. Illustr. cap. lxxii & Ammianus Marcellinus lib. xxvii. Meminerunt hujus Pontis Silius Italicus lib. ii. Claudianus de Honorii, Sextum Consulatum adepti, in Urbem introitu, & alij. In antiquioris notae & scripturae libris M. SS. vocatur Milvius: hodie Mole Italis. Formes habet magnos quatuor, binos mediocres, totidemque parvos. Reliquarum Aquarum, praeter Tiberim, quae in Urbe quondam, aliae dici possunt Religiosae, aliae Profanae, Religiosae, quae Sacris Ritibus plurimum erant consecratae, ut Iuturna, Almo, Petronia, Mercury Aqua. Iuturna nomen ab Iuturna, Italiae Fonte prope Numicum, salubernimae Aquae, eamque ob cautiam ad omnia Sacra Romam adferri solitae. Legendi Varro lib. iv. de LL. & Servius ad librum Aeneidos xii. P. Victor Iuturnae Fontem vel Lacum collocat in viii Urbis Regione, id est in Foro; quod & alij confirmant; inter quos Ovidius vi Fastor. Lacum Iuturnae designat Plautus in Curculione Act. iv. Sc. i.
units.tr: New, [near] the Antonine Baths, which were in the same Region. Livy in book xxii indicates the position of the Via Fornicata. Julius Obsequens, On Prodigies, chapter xxxii, mentions it. Augustus made one Viam Latam out of the fourteen Regions of the City; it is frequently mentioned by Anastasius the Librarian. The Via Recta ran along the length of the Campus Martius; Seneca mentions it in On the Death of Claudius. That there was a Humina road is shown by Martial in book viii, epigram lxxv. The traces of the Alta Semita, or Semita, are still seen today on the ridge of the Quirinal. Augustus then made the Sixth Region of the City, as P. Victor indicates. After the Vias, I have proposed in my plan to deal with the Aquas. I have spoken of the Tiberi when explaining generalities. The river had its own Pontes in the City, of which the following remain today: the Aelius, Ianiculensis, Tarpeius, Cestius, Palatinus; traces only of two, the Triumphalis and the Sublicij, can be seen. The Aelius Pons is named after the Emperor Aelio Hadriano, who built this bridge in the place where it is seen today, so that his very proud tomb, placed on the other bank of the river, could be approached more conveniently by it. Spartianus in his Life. Today it is called the Pons Castelli and S. Angeli. Nicholas V, having removed some small houses, made this bridge wider. Alexander VI took away the very narrow gate and made another very majestic one. The Ianiculensis bridge is so called because through it there was access from the City to the Janiculum. P. Victor mentions it. Aurelius the Censor repaired it, and named it the Aurelium. This Pons is said to have been made of marble by the Emperor Antoninus Pius. It is written that in the civil wars it was demolished, and was called the Rupis headlong. Afterwards Sixtus IV, Supreme Pontiff, restored it and, from his own name, which it still keeps today, called it the Sixti bridge. The Tarpeius is named after the Tarpeian Mount, to which it is nearest on the west. The inscription read there in these words says that Lucius Fabricius restored it. [Here the text is corrupt.] Because it was nearest to the Palatine Hill. P. Victor mentions it. On this bridge, see Livy in book xxxix. It is also read as the Pons Senatorum. It is today called S. Maria Egiziaca, after the neighbouring temple of the same name. I have said that traces of two other bridges, and some piers, can still be seen today in the middle of the Tiber. Of those which were near the Vatican, within a stone's throw of the Pons Aelius, opposite the Hospital of the Holy Spirit, were formerly the Pons Triumphalis, so called because triumphing Emperors were once carried into the City across this bridge. Josephus mentions it, describing the triumph of the Emperor Vespasian over the Jews. It is also read as the Vaticanus, named after the neighbouring Mount. Traces of the other bridge, now entirely destroyed, can be seen six hundred feet below the Palatine Bridge. This was the Sublicius, the most ancient of all. Its author was Ancus Marcius, who joined the Janiculum to the City by this bridge. Livy in book i, Florus in book i, chapter iv, and others. Shortly after liberty was won, when Horatius alone withstood the force of the Etruscans, it was torn up with difficulty, because the nails were too tight; therefore in its restoration it was considered religious to add nails. Pliny testifies to this in book xxxvi, chapter xv. It was called Sublicius from the sublicae, of which Caesar speaks. Hence also the Aemilius, and the Pons Lepidi, after Aemilius Lepidus, a man who held the state together, who first made it of stone. P. Victor mentions it in more than one place, and so does Lampridius in the Life of Heliogabalus. Tiberius Caesar restored it after it was swept away by the force of the river. Antoninus Pius made it of marble. Capitolinus should be consulted in his Life. And from this, the remains of it are still called by the Romans the Marble Bridge. Some think this bridge was formerly called the Sacred Bridge and the Bridge of Hercules. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, whom he praises in the Roman Antiquities, should be consulted, and Epicardus. To the bridges above I add the Milvius, which the Tiber has two miles from the City, on the Via Flaminia. Its author was M. Aemilius Scaurus, as the author of On Illustrious Men, chapter lxxii, and Ammianus Marcellinus in book xxvii, write. Silius Italicus in book ii, and Claudian in his account of Honorius' entry into the City after obtaining his sixth consulship, and others, mention this bridge. In books of older note and writing it is called the Milvius; today it is called Ponte Molle by the Italians. It has four large arches, two medium, and as many small. Of the other waters, apart from the Tiber, which were once in the City, some may be called sacred and others profane. Sacred are those which were much dedicated to sacred rites, such as the Iuturna, the Almo, the Petronia, and the Mercury water. The Iuturna takes its name from Iuturna, a spring in Italy near the Numicus, of very healthful water, which was therefore customarily brought to Rome for all sacred rites. See Varro in book iv of On the Latin Language, and Servius on book xii of the Aeneid. P. Victor places the spring or pool of Iuturna in the eighth Region of the City, that is, in the Forum; other writers confirm this, among them Ovid in book vi of the Fasti. Plautus in the Curculio, act iv, scene i, marks out the pool of Iuturna.

units.la: Confidentes, garrulique & mativoli supra Lacum.
units.tr: Confident, chattering and ill-disposed people above the Lake.

units.la: Frustra enim Lacum Curtium quidam interpretantur, qui tempore Plauti nullus erat. Alij exaudiendum putant Lucinum, alij Servilium. A mo Fluvius fuit Romae in i. Urbis Regione, teste P. Victore. Erat enim extra Portam Capenam; & non procul ab Urbe cum Tiberi miscebatur. Ovidius iv Fastor. Inter religiosas Aquas habitus, quod quotannis pridie Kalendas Apr. Mater Deum in eo lavaretur. Ovidius ibidem, & Alij. Almo brevissimi erat Curtius, unde Parvus Almo Lucano lib. i. & Rivulus Prudentio in Martyrio Romani; & inde Minor Fluvius vel Amnis dicitur Ovidio respectu Tiberis, loco, quem notavi. Petroniam Amnem describit Festus lib. xiv. de Verbor. signif. Mercurij Aquam elegantissime delineat Ovidius v. Fastorum. Profanas nomino, quae quotidianis Ritibus erant dedicatae. Eas in Urbe quondam suisse xxiv testatur P. Victor, is, quem pleniorem edidit Onuphrius Panvinius. Nam Vulgati Codices agnoscunt tantum xx, alij xix, ut & Sex. Rufus, V. C. qui Diocletiani tempore vixit. An autem tot fuerint, an etiam plures, non facile divinari potest. Certe pauciores fuisse constat ex Frontino, qui vix ultra x nominat. Mihi praeter alias lectas Appia, Anio Vetus, Marcia, Tepula, Iulia, Crabra, Virgo, Aufetina, Augusta, Claudia, Anio Novus, Alii. Appia nomen ab Ap. Claudio Crasso, qui postea Caecus cognominatus. Is enim Censor, ut scribit Frontinus, anno ab V. C. ccc cxli post initium Belli Samnitici anno xxx (sic enim pro xx legendum) Coss. M, Valerio Maximo & P. Decio Murena (reponend. Mure) hanc Aquam in Urbem induxit. Ejus Venas Primus invenerat C. Plautius Collega Ap. Claudij in Censura, cui ab illo studio Venocis cognomen datum. Causam indicat Frontinus, quur Aqua Aqua nihilominus Appia, non vero Plautia fuerit dicta. Auctorem huius Aquae nominat etiam Appium Pomponius IC. in l. 2. §. 36. De orig. iuris, ubi tamen manifesta in Appio αντιγραφία. Cocipiebatur in Agro Lucullano Via Praenestina inter Lapidem ab Urbe vi & viii, diverticulo sinistrorsus passuum ixxxc. Eius, quam secundo posui loco, nomen varie proferebatur: aliis Anio, aliis Anien, nonnullis Anienus; & hinc varia inflexio, Anionis, Anienis, Anieni. Anio Vetus vocatus ad differentiam Novi, qui postea ab Claudio ductus. Veterem Urbi intulit M. Curius Dentatus Censor cum L. Papirio Cursore, anno ab V.C. cccclxxxi, L. Papirio Cursore II & Sp. Carvilio Maximo Coss. ex Manubiis de Pyrrho captis, teste Frontino: apud quem concipitur supra Tiburx. Miliario. Tubulus plumbeus Romae:
units.tr: For some people wrongly interpret the Lake as Curtius's, though there was no such lake in Plautus's time. Others think Lucinus or Servilius should be understood. Almo was a river in Rome in the first region of the city, according to P. Victor. It lay outside the Capena Gate, not far from the city, and it mixed with the Tiber. Ovid (Fasti 4) says it was counted among the sacred waters, because each year on the day before the Kalends of April the Mother of the Gods was washed in it. Ovid says the same in that place, and others too. The Almo was a very short stream, which is why Lucan (book 1) calls it the little Almo, and Prudentius in his Martyrdom of the Romans calls it a rivulet. For this reason Ovid, with respect to the Tiber, calls it a lesser river or stream, in the passage I have noted. Festus (book 14, On the Meanings of Words) describes the Petronia as a river. Ovid, in Fasti book 5, describes the Water of Mercury very elegantly. I call them profane waters, meaning those dedicated to everyday rites. P. Victor, whose fuller edition Onuphrius Panvinius published, testifies that there were once twenty-four of these in the city. The common manuscripts recognise only twenty, others nineteen, as does Sex. Rufus, a man of distinction who lived in the time of Diocletian. Whether there were so many, or even more, cannot easily be determined. It is certain that there were fewer, according to Frontinus, who names scarcely more than ten. Besides others, I count the chosen waters as: Appia, Old Anio, Marcia, Tepula, Julia, Crabra, Virgo, Aufeia, Augusta, Claudia, New Anio, and others. The Appia took its name from Appius Claudius Crassus, who was later surnamed the Blind. For he was censor, as Frontinus writes, in the year 341 from the foundation of the city, in the thirtieth year after the start of the Samnite War (for thus we must read xxx instead of xx), in the consulship of M. Valerius Maximus and P. Decius Murena (we should restore Mure); he brought this water into the city. Its veins had first been discovered by C. Plautius, colleague of Appius Claudius in the censorship, to whom the surname Venox was given for that effort. Frontinus gives the reason why the water was nevertheless called Appia and not Plautia. Pomponius the jurist, in law 2, §36, On the Origin of Law, also names Appius as the author of this water, though there is a clear confusion of Appius there. It was collected in the field of Lucullus, on the Praenestine Way, between the sixth and eighth milestones, at a branch to the left, at a distance of 8,900 paces. The name of the second water I listed was pronounced in various ways: some said Anio, some Anien, some Anienus; hence the varied declensions Anionis, Anienis, Anieni. It was called Old Anio to distinguish it from the New, which was later brought in by Claudius. M. Curius Dentatus brought the Old Anio into the city as censor, together with L. Papirius Cursor, in the year 481 from the foundation of the city, in the consulship of L. Papirius Cursor (for the second time) and Sp. Carvilius Maximus, from the spoils taken from Pyrrhus, according to Frontinus. Frontinus places it above Tibur, at the milestone. A lead pipe at Rome:

units.la: ANIO. VET. L. VALERIO. SER. OF PLVMB. P.D. CCIX
units.tr: ANIO VETUS. L. VALERIUS, SON OF SERVIUS. LEAD PIPE. 209 FEET.

units.la: Ductis jam in Urbem Appia & Anione Vetere, quum incrementum Urbis exigere videretur majorem Aquae modum, Marcio (sic enim apud Frontinum legendum est, pro M. Tizio) mandatum ab Senatu est ut curaret, quatenus alias Aquas posset, in Urbem perduceret, & ampliores Ductus faceret. Tertio igitur miliario opera Fabrorum eam duxit, cui ab ipso nomen Marcia, scribente praeter Frontinum Plinio libro xxxvi, cap. xv; qui etiam lib. xxxi. cap. iv. notat Anfiam olim dictam; Fontem vero Pauciam. Meminerunt Aquae Marciae Martialis lib. iv. Epig. xix, Propertius lib. iii, & alij. Leguntur de ea Romae Inscriptiones, ad Portam Esquilinam:
units.tr: When the Appia and the Old Anio had already been brought into the city, and since the growth of the city seemed to require a greater supply of water, Marcius (for thus we must read in Frontinus, instead of M. Tizius) was ordered by the Senate to see how far he could bring other waters into the city and make larger channels. So at the third milestone he brought it in by the labour of the workmen, and it was named Marcia after him. Pliny (book 36, chapter 15) writes of it, besides Frontinus; and in book 31, chapter 4, he notes that it was formerly called Anfia, and its source Paucia. The Marcian Water is mentioned by Martial (book 4, epigram 19), Propertius (book 3), and others. There are Roman inscriptions about it, at the Esquiline Gate:

units.la: IMP. CAESAR. DIVI. IVLI. F. AVGVSTVS PONT. MAXIMVS. COS. XII TRIBVNIC. POTESTAT. XIX. IMP. XIIII. RIVOS. AQVARVM. OMNIVM. REFECIT Alia:
units.tr: THE EMPEROR CAESAR, SON OF THE DIVINE JULIUS, AUGUSTUS, PONTIFEX MAXIMUS, CONSUL FOR THE TWELFTH TIME, IN HIS NINETEENTH TRIBUNICIAN POWER, IMPERATOR FOR THE FOURTEENTH TIME, RESTORED THE CHANNELS OF ALL THE AQUEDUCTS.

RESTITVTA. FORMA. ADQ. VISITO. ETIAM. FONTE. NOVO. ANTONIANO IN. SACRAM. VRBEM. SVAM. PERDVCENDAM. CVRAVIT.
units.tr: Another: The Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Pius Felix Augustus, conqueror of the Parthians, conqueror of Britain, Pontifex Maximus, restored the Marcian Water, which had been hindered by various accidents and by age; its mountains had been cut through and pierced, and its form restored. He also visited the new Antonine spring and took care to bring it into his own holy city.

units.tr: The Emperor Titus Caesar, son of the divine Vespasian, Augustus, Pontifex Maximus, in his ninth tribunician power, imperator for the fifteenth time, censor, consul for the seventh time, designated consul for the eighth, restored the channel of the Marcian Water, which had collapsed through age, and brought back the water which had ceased to be in use.

units.tr: In the consulship of C. Aquilius Sabinus (for the second time) and Sex. Aurelius Anullinus

units.la: CASTEL. PRAET. L. VRVAS. OFF. PED. CCCLXXXIIII AQVA. MARC.
units.tr: Castellum of the Praetorian camp; L. Urvas, overseer of the pedestrian (?) ... 384 ; Aqua Marcia

units.la: Aquam, cui Tepula nomen, in Vrbem perduxerunt Cn. Servilius Cæpio & L. Cassius Longinus Ravilla, Censores ; M. Plautio Hypsæo (sic enim apud Frontinum est scribendum) & Fulvio Flacco Coss. anno ab V. C. 1cxxix. Concipiebatur in Agro Lucullano, qui quibusdam Tusculanus, Via Latina, xi ab Vrbe milliario. Iuliam appellatam centent plerique, quod ab Julio, incertum quo, fuerit inventa ; ab Agrippa deinde ex variis Venis collecta in Agro Tusculano, & in Vrbem deducta, Via Latina, ad Milliarium ab Vrbe xii ; Imp. Cæsare Augusto & M. Lælio Volcatio Coss. anno ab V. C. 1occxix. Legendus Frontinus. Eius Ductus videtur fuisse is, qui à Porta Esquilina progreditur hodieque ad C. Marij Trophæa Præter Caput Iulia transfluebat Crabra. Hanc, Frontino scribente, Agrippa emisit, seu quia usum improbaverat, seu quod Tusculanis Possessoribus relinquendam crederet. Meminit Cicero oratione contra Rullum & libro xvi, Epist. xviii. Aquam Virgineam, uti Frontinus notat, in Vrbem adduxit Agrippa, C. Sentio & Sp. Lucretio Coss. post annum xiii, quam Iuliam. Virgo dicta, quod Herculaneum Rivum refugerit, ut censet Plinius lib. xxx. cap. iii. vel quod quærentibus Aquam Militibus eam, ut Frontinus vult, Virgo monstrarit. Concipiebatur Via Collatina, teste Frontino, ad milliar. viii. palustribus locis: Viam Prænestinam nominat Plinius libro, quem indicavi. Obibat Campum Martium ut videre est apud Ovidium lib. i. Fast. Restituit Ti. Claudius Imp. Inscriptio, quæ in Hortulo Colotiano:
units.tr: The water called Tepula was brought into the City by Cn. Servilius Caepio and L. Cassius Longinus Ravilla, censors, in the consulship of M. Plautius Hypsaeus (for so it must be written in Frontinus) and Fulvius Flaccus, in the year 629 from the founding of the City. It was collected in the Lucullan estate, which some call Tusculan, on the Latin Way, at the eleventh milestone from the City. Most hold that it was named Julia, because it was discovered by someone named Julius, though it is uncertain who. Later Agrippa gathered it from various springs in the Tusculan territory and brought it into the City by the Latin Way, at the twelfth milestone, in the reign of the emperor Caesar Augustus and the consulship of M. Laelius Volcatius, in the year 719 from the founding of the City. Frontinus should be read. Its channel seems to have been the one that runs from the Esquiline Gate and still today flows past the trophies of C. Marius, beyond the head of Julia, the Crabra. Agrippa, while Frontinus was writing, let this go, either because he had disapproved of its use or because he thought it should be left to the Tusculan landowners. Cicero mentions it in his speech against Rullus and in book 16, letter 18. Agrippa brought the Virgin Water into the City, as Frontinus notes, in the consulship of C. Sentius and Sp. Lucretius, thirteen years after the Julia. It was called Virgin either because it avoided the Herculaneum stream, as Pliny thinks in book 30, chapter 3, or because, when soldiers were looking for water, a young girl showed them the spring, as Frontinus would have it. According to Frontinus it was collected on the Collatine Way at the eighth milestone, in marshy places; Pliny names it the Praenestine Way in the book I cited. It passed through the Campus Martius, as may be seen in Ovid, book 1 of the Fasti. Tiberius Claudius Caesar the emperor restored it. The inscription in the little garden of Colotius:

units.la: TI. CLAVDIVS. DRVSI. F. CAESAR. AVGVSTVS. GERMANICVS PONTIFEX. MAXIM. TRIB. POTEST. V. IMP. XI. P.P. COS. III. DESIG. IV
units.tr: TIBERIUS CLAUDIUS DRUSI F. CAESAR AUGUSTUS GERMANICUS, PONTIFEX MAXIMUS, TRIBUNICIAN POWER FIFTH, IMPERATOR ELEVENTH, FATHER OF HIS COUNTRY, CONSUL THIRD, DESIGNATED CONSUL FOURTH

units.la: A. FVNDAMENTIS. NOVOS. FECIT. AC. RESTITVIT ARCVS. DVCTVS. AQVAE. VIRGINIS. DISTVRBATOS. PER C. CAESAREM
units.tr: HE MADE NEW FROM THE FOUNDATIONS AND RESTORED THE ARCH OF THE CHANNEL OF THE VIRGIN WATER, DISTURBED THROUGH C. CAESAR

units.la: Scribit Ovidius lib. iii Fastor. eos, qui in Campo Martio exercebantur, hac Aqua Sudorem & Pulverem abluere solitos ; præcipue quum clausa jam essent Balnea, quod innuit Martialis. Certe Virginem Lavanti & Naranti fuisse commodissimam, testantur Plinius lib. xxxi cap. iii & Statius libro i Silvarum. Virgo simpliciter dicitur Martiali lib. v. Epig. xxi: Virgineus Liquor Ovidio lib. i de Ponto Eleg. ix. Virgineum Cruorem appellat idem Martialis libro iv Epig. xxiv:
units.tr: Ovid writes in book 3 of the Fasti that those who exercised in the Campus Martius were accustomed to wash off sweat and dust with this water, especially when the baths were already closed, as Martial hints. Certainly the Virgin Water was most convenient for bathing and swimming, as Pliny attests in book 31, chapter 3, and Statius in book 1 of the Silvae. Martial simply calls it "Virgin" in book 5, epigram 21; Ovid in book 1 of the Tristia, elegy 9, calls it "virgin liquid". The same Martial in book 4, epigram 24, calls it "virgin blood":

units.la: Et quod Virgineo cruore gaudet:
units.tr: And because it delights in virgin blood:

units.la: Melius fortean Liquore. Qui enim Cruorem id est sanguineum Colorem referre potest hæc Virgo, cuius niveas Undas alio vocat loco Martialis lib. vii. Epigr. xxxi. Crudam nominat idem lib. vi. Epigr. xlii. forte quod turbidior propter limum, quodque non defæcata satis. Concipiebatur enim palustribus locis, ideoque Signino purgabatur. Frontino teste. Alsietinam in urbem induxit Augustus; unde & Augusta dicebatur, eodem Frontino scribente. Concipiebatur ex Lacu Alsietino, Via Claudia, miliario xiv. Nullius gratiæ erat, & parum salubris nusquam in usus Populi fluebat. Alia est Augusta, quam in supplementum Martiæ, quoties liceritates agerent, eiusdem bonitatis, opere subterraneo, perduxit Augustus, usque ad Martiæ Rivum. Frontinum lege. Claudiam in Vrbem traxit C. Cæsar, qui Tiberio successerat; quum & publicis Vsibus & privatis Voluptatibus Septem Aquarum ductus sufficere parum viderentur: altero Imperii sui anno. M. Aquilio Iuliano, P. Nonio Asprenate Coss. Ductum inchoavit, consummavit autem decennio post, & dedicavit Sulla & Titiano Coss. vi. Kalend. Augusti. Videndi præter Frontinum Suetonius in Caligula cap. xx, Plinius lib. xxxi. cap. iii, Lampridius in Severo. Rudera hujus Aquæductus multa hodieque Romæ, ad Portam Esquilinam, quæ Major nunc dicitur: ubi de ea sequentes leguntur Inscriptiones:
units.tr: Perhaps "liquid" is the better reading. For this Virgin cannot really be said to show a blood-coloured hue; Martial elsewhere, in book 7, epigram 31, calls its snowy waves something else. The same poet in book 6, epigram 42 calls it "raw", perhaps because it is rather muddy from silt and not sufficiently clarified. For it was collected in marshy places, and therefore was purified at Signia, as Frontinus attests. Augustus brought the Alsietine water into the City; hence it was also called Augusta, as Frontinus again writes. It was collected from the Alsietine lake, on the Claudian Way, at the fourteenth milestone. It was of no value and rather unhealthy, and it flowed nowhere for public use. There is another Augusta, which Augustus brought by an underground channel, of the same quality, to supplement the Marcia, whenever the public games were held, as far as the Marcian stream. Read Frontinus. Gaius Caesar, who had succeeded Tiberius, drew the Claudia into the City, since the seven existing aqueducts seemed barely enough for public uses and private pleasures; this was in the second year of his reign, in the consulship of M. Aquilius Julianus and P. Nonius Asprenas. He began the channel, but completed it ten years later, and it was dedicated in the consulship of Sulla and Titianus, on the sixth day before the Kalends of August. Besides Frontinus, see Suetonius in Caligula, chapter 20; Pliny, book 31, chapter 3; Lampridius in Severus. Many remains of this aqueduct still survive today at Rome, at the Esquiline Gate, which is now called the Major; there the following inscriptions are read concerning it:

units.tr: The Emperor Titus Caesar Vespasian Augustus, son of the deified Vespasian, Pontifex Maximus, holding tribunician power for the tenth time, hailed Imperator for the seventeenth time, Father of his Country, censor, consul for the eighth time, had the Curtian and Caerulean aqueducts restored to the city at his own expense. They had been brought in by the deified Claudius and later by the deified Vespasian, his father, but had fallen into ruin from their source to their bed through age, and he had them rebuilt in a new form.

Aquilio Iulio & Nonio Asprenate Coss. cœptumque uero ab Claudio, Sulla & Titiano Coss. ut docet Frontinus; addens Novum dictum ad differentiam prioris Anienis, qui deinde Vetus appellari cœpit. Concipiebatur, eodem notante, Via Sublacensi ad milliarium LXII. iungebatur illi Rivus Herculaneus, & in Vrbe cum Claudia confundebatur. De Superiorum Aquarum Longitudine, Altitudine, Cursu, cumque aliis subinde Concursu & Miscione, Fine locoque destinato, Qualitate, Erogatione, Modo Quinariarum, Signino, Piscinis, Reparatione, & Similibus, plene Frontinus Libello aureo de Aquæductibus. Sunt & quas ille non nominat. Sabatina, ab Lacu Sabate ducta, & deducta Romam ex Anguillariæ Lacu, ut indicat Festus libro xvii. Ejus Ductus Vestigia hodieque extra Portam Pancratianam. Fontes ex hac Aqua in Area D. Petri. Recentiores eam vocant Septimianam à Porta; Aurrelianam, ab Via. Aqua Alexandrina ab Alexandro Imp. in Urbem fuit inducta; teste Lampridio in ejus Vita. P. Victori & hæ nominantur: Damnata, Annia, Algentiana, Severiana, Antoniniana, Setina. Quid jam dicam de Balneis: quorum apud Romanos magna fuit & Copia & Luxuria? Scribit Victor per Quatuordecim Regiones fuisse ID CCCLVI: Auctiorem numerum edit Onuphrius, qui notat in genere ID CCCIX. Eorum non postremi loci fuerunt Palatina; de quorum Ruderibus ego alibi. Meminit Cicero Oratione in pro Roscio Amer. Item Paulli, quorum mentio apud Iuvenalem Satyra VII; ubi in quibusdam Codicibus depravatè Phœbi: Vestigia hodieque servant & tuentur aliquo modo Nomen. Dicunt enim Romani Bugna Poli, quasi Balnea Paulli. Laudantur etiam Balnea T. Claudii Etrusci ab Marmorum Precio, Ædificij magnificentia, Luminis immissione, & argenteis Fistulis, apud Statium lib. I. Silvarum & Martialem lib. VI. Epigr. XIII: apud quem passim Balneorum Romanorum frequens est mentio. Luxuriam Balneorum exagitat Seneca ad Lucill. libro XIII. Pensilia fecit Primus C. Sergius Orata. Valerius Maximus lib. IX. Cap. I, & Macrobius lib. III. Sat. cap. XV. Argenteis Epistomijs Aquam fundi in plebeis Fistulis; & in Libertinorum Balneis Gemmas collocari, indignatur Seneca. Parietes Balneorum sparsos fuisse à quibusdam Vnguento, notat Plinius lib. XIII. cap. III; qui ibidem Solia temperata fuisse Vnguento ab Caio Principe, & quodam Neronis Servo, memorat. Quod ad Thermas; eas in Vrbis Regionum Epilogo numerat XVI, Victor; quibus quatuor addit Onuphrius. Inter eas principatum obtinebant, in I Regione, Commodiana & Severiana; in III, Titi, Trajani, Philippi, Cæsarum; in VI, Diocletiani & Maximiani Imperatorum; in IX, Agrippæ, Neronianæ, Alexandrinæ, Decianæ; in XII, Antoninianæ, &c.
units.tr: The New Anio aqueduct was begun by Gaius Caesar, in the consulship of Marcus Aquilius Julius and Nonius Asprenas, and was actually completed under Claudius, in the consulship of Sulla and Titianus, as Frontinus records. He adds that it was called "New" to distinguish it from the earlier Anio, which later began to be called the "Old." Its course, as the same writer notes, was begun on the Via Sublacensis at the sixty-second milestone, and the Herculaneum channel joined it; in the city it merged with the Claudian. Frontinus treats fully, in his golden little book On Aqueducts, the length and height of the Upper Waters, their course, the points where they subsequently met and mingled with others, their end and the place appointed for them, their quality, distribution, the size of the quinaria, the sluice-marks, the reservoirs, repairs and similar matters. There are also some that he does not name: the Sabatina, led from Lake Sabatus and brought to Rome from the Anguillara lake, as Festus indicates in book 17. Traces of its course can still be seen outside the Porta Pancraziana, and fountains in the Piazza of St Peter are fed by this water. More recent writers call it the Septimiana after the gate, and the Aurelia after the road. The Alexandrine aqueduct was brought into the city by the Emperor Alexander, according to Lampridius in his Life. Victor also names these: the Damnata, Annia, Algentiana, Severiana, Antoniniana and Setina. What shall I now say of the baths, of which the Romans had such great abundance and luxury? Victor writes that there were 856 in the Fourteen Regions; Onuphrius gives a larger number, noting 809 in general. Among these the Palatine baths were no mean ones; I have written about their ruins elsewhere. Cicero mentions them in his speech Pro Roscio Amerino. Likewise the Baths of Paulus, mentioned by Juvenal in Satire 7, where in some manuscripts the reading "Phoebi" is corrupt; these still preserve their name in some form and keep it, for the Romans call them Bugna Poli, as if "Baths of Paulus." The Baths of Titus Claudius Etruscus are also praised for the price of their marbles, the magnificence of the building, the admission of light, and their silver pipes, by Statius in Silvae book 1 and by Martial in book 6, epigram 13, where mention of Roman baths is frequent throughout. Seneca rails against the luxury of the baths in his letter to Lucilius, book 13. Gaius Sergius Orata was the first to build suspended baths, as Valerius Maximus (book 9, chapter 1) and Macrobius (Saturnalia book 3, chapter 15) relate. Seneca is indignant that water was poured through silver spouts into common pipes, and that gems were set in the baths of freedmen. Pliny (book 13, chapter 3) notes that the walls of some baths were sprinkled with perfume, and he also records that the tepid tubs were perfumed by Gaius Princeps and by a certain servant of Nero. As for the thermae, Victor counts sixteen in the summary of the City's Regions, to which Onuphrius adds four. Among them the chief ones were: in the first Region, the Commodian and Severan; in the third, those of Titus, Trajan, Philip and the Caesars; in the sixth, those of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian; in the ninth, those of Agrippa, Nero, Alexander and Decius; in the twelfth, the Antonine baths, etc.

The inscription on a marble tablet in the half-dome of the Church of St Martina (for that was formerly the Secretarium) tells who its author was and who restored it after the fire. In these words: With our lords Honorius and Theodosius, most victorious princes, the Secretarium of the most illustrious Senate, which the illustrious man Ilavianus had begun and the fatal fire had consumed, was restored by Ilavius Annius Eucharius Epifanius, V.C., ... and brought back to its former appearance.

units.la: Thermae Constantini in Colle, alias Constantinianae. Victor. De earundem reparatione servatur Inscriptio, littera longa & inaequali, in Aedicula deserta Sanctae Helenae, retro ipsas Thermas loquitur ea Petronium Perpetuum Magnum Quadratianum V. C. & Iul. Constantinianas Thermas, longa incuria & abolenda civilis, vel potius feralis cladis vastatione vehementer adflictas, ita ut agnitione sui omni ex parte perdita desperationem cunctis reparationis auferrent, deputato ab Amplissimo Ordine parvo sumtu, quantum publica patiebantur angustia, ab extremo vindi- caput eius, & prouinciae ... in proximum ... restituisse. Sex Rufo; P. autem Victori, paullo maiore numero, III CIↃ IↃC.
units.tr: Thermae Constantini in Colle, otherwise Constantinianae. Victor. An inscription concerning their restoration survives, in long and uneven letters, in the deserted little shrine of St Helena, just behind the baths themselves. It speaks of Petronius Perpetuus Magnus Quadratianus, vir clarissimus, and Iulius, prefect of the city, who, since the Constantinian baths had been severely damaged by long neglect and by the devastation of a civil, or rather deadly, disaster, so that they had lost all recognisable form in every part and had taken away all hope of repair, restored them at a small expense assigned by the most distinguished Order, as far as the public straits allowed, from the far end of the vindi- ... head of it, and of the province ... to the nearest ... to have restored. Baths of Paul. Victor, Rufus. Private baths: Victor 75, Rufus 65. Pools: 75, otherwise 76, Victor and Rufus. The Ulpian Library in the Baths of Diocletian: Vopiscus in the lives of Aurelian, Probus and Numerian. Granaries: 19, otherwise 18. Victor, Rufus. Fishponds: 23, otherwise 22, otherwise 12. Victor, Rufus. Houses: 115, otherwise 115. Victor, Rufus. Among these, the house of the Cornelii. Among other sources: Victor, Rufus; Cornelius Nepos in his Life; Marcus Tullius in certain letters to him; Gaius Sallustius; Titus Flavius Sabinus. Victor, Rufus, Marlianus, book IV, Topography of the City of Rome, chapter XXIII. Maximus. Martial, book VII, epigram LXXII. Gaius Julius Solinus, chapter II, writes that Numa Pompilius, the second king of the Romans, first lived on the Quirinal Hill. Islands: 3505 by Rufus; by Victor, with a rather larger number, 3600.

Victor, Rufus; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book iii, at the end; Cicero, book i, On Divination; Horace, book ii, Satires; Suetonius in Augustus, chapter lviii, and in Galba, chapter xx; Virgil in the Culex, not far from the end; Ovid, book iv, Fasti; Festus, Suidas, Papinius, and others. Varro should be corrected: where Rome now stands, the Septimontium, the lower, lowest place, is the Lake.

units.la: Hos versus in sequentibus Varro, quod ad Septemmontium, Infimus. Lacus &c. exponit. Lacus vocem addidi, quia Lacus Curtius videtur designari. Error natus ex similitudine vocum, quarum posteriorem, ut Glossema, quidam expuxerant. Sunt autem Versus Trochaici.
units.tr: These lines, which in what follows Varro explains with reference to the Septimontium ("the lowest, the Lake," etc.), I have explained. I added the word Lacus, because the Lacus Curtius seems to be meant. The error arose from the similarity of the words; some have removed the latter word as a gloss. These are trochaic verses.

units.la: Ad Ianum, secundum Tiberim. Varro lib. iii. de LL. Secundum Tiberim, inquit, Ianium, Forum Piscarium. Emendandum censeo ad Ianum. Nam Templum ... loco. vel ab Ian. celebri Mercatorum loco. Potest & legi ad Ianonem. à Templo Ianonis Martialis, aut Ædes Ianonis Monetae.
units.tr: Ad Ianum, secundum Tiberim. Varro, book iii, On the Latin Language. "Beside the Tiber," he says, "Janus, the Fish Market." I think it should be emended to ad Ianum, for the temple ... place, or from the famous place of the merchants of Janus. It may also be read ad Ianonem, from the Temple of Janonis, in Martial, or the shrine of Janus Moneta.

units.tr: In it was the Treasury of the Roman People. Many inscriptions mention it, among them one at Rome, in the Gardens of St Sebastian, on the Appian Way: "Marcus Aurelius Asclepiodotus, freedman of the Augusti, and Aelia Hygia his mother, made this monument for themselves and their own, for their freedmen and freedwomen and their descendants, whether by inscription or as a gift." Another, in Onuphrius: "Sanctus Salutaris?; Titus Petidius, son of Titus, of the Fabian tribe, Lucceius, man, aedile of the plebs, tribune, of the Fanorum (?) three times, of the Treasury, by decree of the Senate." Before the Treasury stood a bronze statue of Silvanus. Of the Divine Augustus. Rufus. Of Juno, Martial. The same, of the Lares. The same. Of Venus Genetrix, otherwise Venus and Anchises, with an altar. Rufus.

units.tr: The Circus Flaminius. Victor, Rufus. Suetonius calls this region the Campus Martius in the Life of Julius, ch. xxxix, and in Nero, ch. xii; perhaps Pliny too, in Natural History xxxiv, ch. vii. The Hill of the Gardens, otherwise called the Gardens. The Campus Martius. Victor, Rufus, and virtually all writers. The Via Formicata. The Via Recta. I have discussed these elsewhere. Wards: 30. Victor. Vicus ... Vicomagistri: 120. Victor. Curators: 2. Victor. Denunciators: 2. Victor. The Palus Caprea. Livy, book i, Plutarch in Romulus, and others who describe the rape of the Sabine women, that is, the disappearance of Romulus from among men, the king of the Romans. See also Festus on Caprilia. units.tr: As a garland to close, I shall add some praises of the city, the task of which taxes the pen, taken both from various writers and from what pertains to the city itself and its adjuncts. If we consider the city itself, it is called great by Virgil, Horace and Calpurnius Siculus; immense by Statius; the greatest city and cultivator of all the divinities by Arnobius, book VI; "the most philosophical city of the cities" [τὰς ἐκκυμάτις Φιλοσοφωτάτης πόλεως] by Polemo, in Athenaeus and Galen; lofty by Prudentius; exalted by Lucan; turreted, on account of the abundance of towers, which were once 240, by Sidonius, Carm. V; "most conspicuous" [Διαπρεπεστάτη] by Stephanus; renowned by Ennius and Virgil; a golden house by Ausonius; one to whom the greatest splendour belongs, in Cassiodorus, book XI, letter 2; light of the orb of the lands, by Cicero; the loveliest of things, by Virgil; prince of cities, by Horace; first among cities, by Ausonius; "the most joyful, the most philosophical city" [χαιρετάτη ἡ φιλοσοφωτάτη πόλις], Dionysius, book I; house of the gods, by Ausonius; the place of the gods, by Ovid; first of the lands, by Paulinus; mother of the world, by Rutilius; the temple of the whole world, by Ammianus; the summit of the world, by Sidonius, book I, letter 6; a seat wondrous through the whole orb, by Cassiodorus, book XI of the Variae, cap. 2. If we look at its inhabitants: Cassiodorus, whom I have cited, calls them blessed among noble peoples; Symmachus, book III, letter 12, calls the city mother of the best citizens; Evander to Hercules, in Livy, book I, calls them the most opulent people on earth; Prudentius calls them the richest; Rutilius, mother of men and gods; Claudian, mother of kings; Priscian, great home of kings; Dionysius the African and Eustathius, mother of leaders, Claudian. If we examine the prudence of the same inhabitants in magistracies, both sacred and secular: it is called the fount of the priesthood by the Emperor Justinian in the Code; mother of dignities, by Cassiodorus, book I, cap. 27; the court of dignities, by Sidonius, book I, letter 6; most adorned with senators, by Cassiodorus again. If we look at its laws: Sidonius, whom I have mentioned, in the same place, calls it the home of laws; Justinian the Emperor calls it the fatherland of laws; and, as the true augur says, "all other lands will seek help from this land," Ovid, book I of the Fasti. If we look at its military affairs: it is named Martial by Ovid and Ausonius; Martigena (born of Mars) by Silius Italicus; the temple of warlike Mars by Plutarch; warlike (bellatrix) by Ovid, Claudian and Sidonius, Carm. V; happy by Propertius, Cassiodorus, and an ancient inscription; on coins among the ancients, invincible, on the same coins; fierce by Horace; victorious on coins, which Hubert Goltzius reports; Ovid, book IV of the Fasti, portrays a statue of Victory at Rome, as if in colours, Georg Fabricius.

units.tr: {1} In the same vein, [epithets] of the times in the magistracies: Briet, Topogr., cap. 11. Others have other adjuncts: it is called home of virtues by Ammianus, book XIV; the Lar of virtues, in the same author, book XVI; the widest temple of all virtues, Cassiodorus, book I, cap. 39; fruitful mother of eloquence, in the same book I, cap. 29; gymnasium of letters, Sidonius, book I, letter 6. Now, to designate the Roman empire, the various expressions found among various writers: Rome is famed as augusta by Coppo and by Symmachus, book VI, letter 11; most august, in law 32 of the Theodosian Code on shipping; mistress, by Horace, Ovid, Arnobius and Nemesianus; ruling, by Silius; mistress of the nations, by Eumenius; mistress of things, by Ovid, Appian and Eunapius; mistress of the earth, by Ovid, Fasti IV; mistress of lands, by Ammianus, I; mistress of land and sea, by Dionysius of Halicarnassus; mistress of the whole world, by Ethicus; powerful, by Horace, book II, letter 1, Ausonius and Paulinus; most powerful, by Nazarius; royal, by Horace; queen, by Athenaeus and Ammianus; "queen of cities" [Βασιλις βασιλις]; queen city, in the Greek-Latin glossary, undoubtedly of Rome or Constantinople; Rome sits in the Itinerary Table as a queen, in the royal seat, wearing a crown on her head, holding the conquered orb in her right hand and a sceptre in her left. So she is called queen of cities by the same Athenaeus; queen of lands, by Ammianus and Nazarius; most beautiful queen of the world, by Rutilius, book I; "wisely loving" [Δαίφρων ἀγαπη], of Erinna of Lesbos, in Stobaeus; seat of empire, by Ovid, Fasti V; or seat, Florus, book I, cap. 7; Lar of the empire, Ammianus, book XVI; nurse of the empire, Corippus; head of the nations, Marcian; citadel of all nations, Nazarius; head of things, Livy, Ovid, Ausonius; head of lands, Florus, book II; head of the world, Lucan, book II, and Cassiodorus; head of the orb, Ovid, Fasti V, Livy in various places, Trogus in Justin, book XLIII, Gratius, Fortuna, Ethicus; head of the immense orb, the same Ovid; "the head of all, Rome" [ἡ πάντων κεφαλή, Ῥώμη], Dionysius of Halicarnassus, On the Ancient Romans.

Flori Prologus ad libros Historiae Romanae: Notat denique Vegetius lib. i. de Re militari cap. viii Romanum imperium Solis paene Regionibus & Mundi ipsius fine distentum. Roma. D. ad Municipalem, l. 6. §. 31. D. de Excusat. Tutor, Consule & Novellam lxxviii, cap. v, P. Rutilium libro i Itinerarii, Senecam de Consolatione ad Albin. cap. vi, Aristid. Laudat. ROMA nemini potest dici aliena, scribente Cassiodoro lib. i. Variar. Epist. xxxix. Et hinc paret, quae sit ratio, quod cui Patria interdictum, etiam Urbe abstinere debuerit l.7. §. 15. D. de Interdict. & Relegat. cuius Constitutionis Auctor Claudius Princeps, Suetonio notante cap.xxiii. quodque qui Roma profitetur, in Patris profiteri videatur. l. 9. D. de Vacat. & Excusat. Muner. Quid? quod decreti fuerint Vrbi Roma Divini Honores; quod Templa exstructa: quod Sacerdotes creati? Legendi Livius libro xliii. Tacitus libro iv. Annalium, Dio lib.li. in Actis annis ab V.C. 1ccccxxv. Suetonius in Augusto, Ammianus Marcellinus libro xvi. Spartianus in Hadriano, Sex. Rufus. Eleganter de hac Dea Prudentius: colitur nam Sanguine & ipsa More Dea, Nomenque loci ceu Numen haberi; Atque Vrbis Venerisque pari se culmine tollant Templa, simul geminis adolentur tura deabus.
units.tr: So Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Roman Antiquities book 10: "of the Romans, for rule, it is ancestral [Ῥωμαίων ἐπὶ ἀρχὴν, πατρίον ἐστ]." Livy, book 1 from the foundation of the City, writes that Rome labours under her own greatness. Also consult the Prologue of Florus to his books of Roman History. Finally, Vegetius, Concerning Military Affairs book 1, chapter 8, notes that the Roman empire is spread almost across the regions of the sun and to the very ends of the world. Hence the People itself is called "Prince" by Florus in the same Prologue, and in book 1 chapters 8 and 26, and book 2 chapter 2; "Prince of the lands and Preeminent" by Florus; "Ruler" by Livy, book 1; "Mistress of the sea and the land" by Arnobius, book 6, where he speaks of the name of the Capitol; "to possess the rule of the nations" by Lucan, book 1; "to obtain the rule of things" by Florus, book 1 chapter 1; and in Ovid, Fasti book 1: "when the world had been subdued and citizenship given to the peoples, Rome began to be called by the common and universal name of 'Fatherland'." This can be seen in Symmachus, book 5, letter 92; in Censorinus, On the Birthday, chapter 15 at the end; in the jurists, in law 3 "Roma" of the Digest, "To the Municipal", law 6 §31 of the Digest "On Excuses of Guardians"; in the Novel 78, chapter 5; in P. Rutilius, Itinerary book 1; in Seneca, Consolation to Albinus, chapter 6; in Aristides, Praise of the City. Cassiodorus, book 11, letter 2, calls it "the seat appointed to be the birthplace of the world"; Sidonius, book 7, letter 6, calls it "the one City of the whole world, in which only barbarians and slaves are foreigners." Cassiodorus, Variae book 1, letter 39, writes that Rome can be called alien to no one. From this it is clear why one who was forbidden his fatherland had also to abstain from the City (Digest 48, law 7 §15, "On Interdiction and Relegation", whose author of the constitution was the emperor Claudius, as Suetonius notes in chapter 23), and why one who professes himself a Roman is held to profess his fatherland (Digest 50, law 9, "On Vacation and Excuse from Public Duties"). Moreover, were not divine honours decreed to the City of Rome, temples built, and priests appointed? See Livy book 43, Tacitus Annals book 4, Dio book 51 in the events of the year 725 from the foundation of the City, Suetonius in Augustus, Ammianus Marcellinus book 16, and Spartianus in Hadrian, and Sextus Rufus. Prudentius speaks elegantly of this goddess: "for she is worshipped, and she herself is a goddess by her blood, and the name of the place is held as a divinity; and the temples of the City and of Venus rise to an equal height, and incense burns for both goddesses together."

units.tr: Martial names her "Goddess of the lands and Rome of the nations"; but Lucan, in book 1 of the Civil War, calls her "like a divine power."

units.la: Alma, in Basi quadam, quae hodie in Ponte Fabricio, rudibus alioquin litteris & inaequalibus exarata.
units.tr: "Nourishing" [Alma], on a certain base which today is on the Pons Fabricius, inscribed in otherwise rude letters and unevenly.
