units.la: Sacram dicunt Ausonius, Mamertinus, Æthicus; Sacratissimam, Imperatores in Codice; Venerabilem Ammianus lib.xvi. σεβασμίωλν, Athenaeus; Aequaevam Polo, Claudianus. Sic Rutilius lib.i. Exaudi Regina tui pulcherrima Mundi, Inter Sidereos Roma recepta Polos.
units.tr: Ausonius, Mamertinus and Aethicus call her "sacred"; the emperors in the Code call her "most sacred"; Ammianus, book 16, calls her "venerable"; Athenaeus calls her "venerable" [σεβασμίων]; Claudian calls her "equal to the heavens." So Rutilius, book 1: "Hear, O queen, most beautiful of the world; Rome, received among the starry poles."

units.la: Summo Vertice tangit Deos apud Ovidium lib.i. Fastor. Longum esset hic commemorare Inscriptiones, quae Flamines laudant Romae & Augusti vel Augustorum Consulendum Volumen Smetianum sol. CLI. num. 18, 20. 22. sol. CLII. num.1. & 15. sol. CLVII. num.115 sol. CLXI. num.5. sol. CLXIV. num.9. & alibi. Accedit huc, quod Divinos olim Honores Romae tribuerint Smyrnaei, Aladenses, & praeter alios Graecorum omnium cultissimi Athenienses: Videndi Livius lib.xliii. Tacitus lib.iv. Annalium, & alij. Diuinitatis autem nota Aeternitas. Vrbs Roma Aeterna nominatur Ovidio lib.iii. Fastorum, Symmacho libro iii. Epist, iv. Ammiano libro xv. & aliis locis, Ausonio in Epigrammat, quibus Fastorum à se digestorum meminit: Prospero Aquitanico in dimidio Temporis cap. vii. Sic item appellatur in innumeris Imperatorum Constitutionibus, in Nummis antiquis apud Goltzium, in Inscriptione denique, quae in ipsa Vrbe, in Porta Ripae: IMP. CAES. DD. NN. INVICITISSIMIS. PRINCIPIBVS. ARCADIO. ET. HONORIO VICTORIBVS. AC. TRIVMFATORIBVS. SEMPER. AVGG. OR. INSTAVRATOS VRBI. AETERNA. MVROS. PORTAS. AC. TVRRES &c. Aeternabilis vocatur in l.1. C. Theodof. de collat. Don. Victura cum Saeculis Ammiano scribitur. Pertinet & illud non parum ad ROMÆ Veteris gloriam, quod praecipuæ aliarum Provinciarum Urbes Nomen eius induere conatæ, tamquam ipsius æmulæ. Constantinopolis passim ROMA dicitur in Constitutionibus Imperatorum; item Socrati libro v. Histor. Eccles. cap. viii. Coripto, Priscoiano, Marcellino Comitu, Zonaræ non semel, & aliis: Sic de eadem Sidonius Apollinaris Carmine 11: Salve Sceptrorum Columen, Regina Orientis Orbis ROMA tui.
units.tr: Ovid, Fasti book 1, says she "touches the gods with her highest summit." It would be long to recall here all the inscriptions that praise the flamens of Rome and of Augustus or of the Augusti; consult the Smetian volume, pages 151, nos. 18, 20, 22; page 152, nos. 1 and 15; page 157, no. 115; page 161, no. 5; page 164, no. 9, and elsewhere. To this may be added that the Smyrnaeans, the Aladenses, and, beyond all other Greeks, the most cultivated Athenians, once paid divine honours to Rome; see Livy book 43, Tacitus Annals book 4, and others. Now eternity is a mark of divinity, and Rome is called "Eternal" by Ovid, Fasti book 3; by Symmachus, book 3, letter 4; by Ammianus, book 15, and in other places; by Ausonius in his epigrams, in which he mentions the Fasti he arranged; by Prosper of Aquitaine in the Chronicle of Half-Time, chapter 7. It is likewise so called in countless constitutions of emperors, in ancient coins in Goltzius, and finally in an inscription in the City itself, at the Porta Ripae: "To our most unconquered rulers Arcadius and Honorius, victors and triumphant, always Augusti, who restored the walls, gates and towers of the Eternal City, etc." It is called "eternal-making" in law 1 of the Theodosian Code on collatio donorum. Ammianus writes that it is "destined to last with the ages." It also contributes not a little to the glory of Old Rome that the chief cities of the other provinces have tried to take her name, as rivals of her own. Constantinople is commonly called "Rome" in the constitutions of the emperors; likewise by Socrates, Ecclesiastical History book 5, chapter 8; by Coripus, Priscian, Marcellinus Comes, and Zonaras more than once, and by others. So Sidonius Apollinaris, poem 11, of the same city: "Hail, pillar of sceptres, queen of the Eastern world, Rome, of your own."

units.la: De Karthagine Salvianus Massiliensis libro vii de Providentia: Karthago universarum Africa Urbium Princeps, & quasi Mater: & in Africano Orbe quasi ROMA. Capua quoque, primaria quum floreret Campaniæ Urbs, ROMA altera quondam Ausonie. Arelate item Gallula ROMA vocatur ab Ausonio: Aeduorum Civitas Celtica ROMA Sigeberto in Chronicis: Aquileia denique Romania & ROMA Secunda Leandro: indeque Chromatius Aquileiensis Episcopus, Romanus appellatus est Episcopus, in Libro de Octo Beatitudinibus.
units.tr: Salvian of Marseilles, in book 7 of On the Providence of God, speaks of Carthage: "Carthage, the leader and as it were mother of all the cities of Africa, and in the African world like a second Rome." Capua too, when the city of Campania was flourishing, was once called "the other Rome of Ausonia." Likewise Arles is called "Gallic Rome" by Ausonius; the city of the Aedui, a Celtic city, is called "Rome" by Sigebert in his Chronicles; and Aquileia is called "Romania" and "Second Rome" by Leander. Hence Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia, was called "Roman bishop," in his book On the Eight Beatitudes.

units.la: Sed o quanta rerum omnium est vicissitudo! Incensa captaque aliquoties Imperatorum & malitia & socordia, non solum decus avitum, quod mansurum semper videbatur, Antiqua ROMA amisit; verum etiam, parum omnino abest, periit, sedesque in Montanis, tamquam infeliciores, aversata, planiora petijt; occupato Campo, qui Marti quondam consecratus, ut vel co saltem modo Martiam se profiteretur; ad desidiam alioquin, torporem, & omne Vitiorum genus plenis velis delapsa. Saevissimo incendio deflagravit Urbs Principatu Neronis, qui ipsius eius Auctor. De eo sic post multa Tacitus libro xv. Sexto demum die apud imas Exquilias finis Incendio factum, proruptis per immensum aedificiis, ut continua violentia Campus & velut vacuum coelum occurreret. Nondum posito metu redibat. Levis rursum grassatus ignis, patulis magis Urbis locis, eoque strages hominum minor. Delubra Deum & Porticus amoenitati dicata latius procidere. Plusque infamia id incendium habuit, quia prædiis Tigellini Aemiliani proruperat: videbaturque Nero condenda Urbs Nova, & cognomento suo appellanda gloriam quaerere. Quippe in Regiones quatuordecim Roma dividitur: quarum quatuor integra manebant, tres solo tenus dejectæ: septem reliquis pauca tectorum vestigia supererant lacera & semiusta. Domuum, & Insularum, & Templorum, quæ amissa sunt, numerum inire haud promptum fuerit: sed vetustissima Religione, quod Ser. Tullius Luna (magni viri Lua emendant) & Magna Ara Fanumque, quæ præsenti Herculi Arcas Evander sacraverat, Aedesque Statoris Iovis vota Romulo, Numaque Regia, & Delubrum Vestæ cum Penatibus Populi Romani, exusta. Iam opes tot victoriis quæsita, & Græcarum artium Decora, exin monimenta Ingeniorum antiqua & incorrupta, quamvis in tanta resurgentis urbis pulcritudine multa Seniores meminerant, quæ reparari nequibant. Fuere, qui annotarent XIV. Kalendas Sextiles principium Incendij huius ortum, quo & Senones captam Urbem inflammaverant: Alij eo usque cura progressi sunt, ut totidem annos mensesque & dies in utraque Incendia numerent. Sex dierum facit incendium Tacitus; addens mox Ignem redijsse, qui fortassis Trium. Nam Novem dies nominat Inscriptio, quæ Romæ ad Basilicam Petri.
units.tr: But oh, how great is the mutability of all things! Ancient Rome, burned and captured several times through the malice and sloth of emperors, has lost not only the ancestral glory which always seemed destined to endure, but has also almost perished entirely, and, shunning the hills as less fortunate, has sought the lower ground. The Field of Mars, once consecrated to Mars, was occupied, so that at least in this way it might be called Martian; while she, sunk into idleness, torpor and every kind of vice, sailed on with full sails. The City was consumed by a most savage fire under the principate of Nero, who was its very author. Of this, after much else, Tacitus writes in book 15: "On the sixth day at last the fire was stopped at the foot of the Esquiline, after buildings had been pulled down over a huge area, so that the attack was checked and an open space, as it were an empty sky, met the eye. Yet the fear was not yet laid to rest, and the fire broke out again, with a lighter attack, in the more open districts of the City, and so there were fewer deaths. Shrines of the gods and porticoes dedicated to pleasure were destroyed over a wider area. This fire carried more disgrace, because it had broken out on the estates of Tigellinus Aemilianus, and Nero was thought to be seeking glory by founding a new city and naming it after himself." Indeed Rome is divided into fourteen regions: of these, four remained whole, three were levelled to the ground, and of the seven others only a few remnants of buildings survived, torn and half-burned. To count the houses, blocks of flats and temples that were lost would not be easy; but among the most ancient sacred things destroyed by the fire were the Luna of Servius Tullius (learned men correct it to Lua), the Great Altar and shrine which the Arcadian Evander had consecrated to Hercules when he was present, the temple of Jupiter the Stayer, vowed by Romulus, the Regia of Numa, and the shrine of Vesta with the Penates of the Roman people. Moreover, so many riches won by victories, the glories of Greek art, and the ancient and uncorrupted monuments of genius, although the elders remembered many such things amid the great beauty of the rising city, could not be restored. There were those who noted that the fire began on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of Sextilis, the same day on which the Senones had burned the captured City; others went so far in their care as to count the years, months and days between the two fires. Tacitus makes the fire last six days, adding that soon the fire returned, which perhaps lasted three. For the inscription at the basilica of St Peter in Rome names nine days.

units.la: EX. VOTO. SVSCEPTO. QVOD. DIV ERAT. NEGLECTVM. NEC. REDDITVM INCENDIOR. ARGENDORVM. CAVSA QVANDO. VRBS. PER. NOVEM. DIES ARSIT. NERONIANIS. TEMPORIBVS ET. HAC. LEGE. DEDICATA. EST. NE CVI LICEAT. INTRA. HOS. TERMI NOS. AEDIFICIVM EXSTRVERE
units.tr: DEDICATED IN FULFILMENT OF A VOW THAT HAD BEEN LONG NEGLECTED AND NOT PAID. THE CITY BURNED FOR NINE DAYS IN NERO'S TIME, AND WAS CONSECRATED ON THIS CONDITION: THAT NO ONE MAY BE PERMITTED TO BUILD A STRUCTURE WITHIN THESE BOUNDARIES. [The inscription's wording is a rendering of the Latin lapidary text, with "Incendior. Argendorum" read as the fire's own record.]

units.la: Priorem Calamitatem designat Suetonius in Neronis Vita cap. xxxviii. qui inter alia: Per sex dies septemque Noctes ea clade saevitum est, ad Monimentorum Busto rumque diversoria Plebe compulsa. Videndus & Xiphilinus ex Dione. Alia Incendia, dira etiam satis, omitto. Capta porro & direpta sub Principibus legitur varie, Ab Gothis sub Rege Athalarico ix. Kalend. Sept. anno ab eius conditione CIƆ CLXI. ab Christo nato CCCCX. legendi Sigebertus, Prosper, Marcellinus Comes, & alij: ab Vandalis sub Geinsericho Rege, anno ipsius Vrbis CIↄ CCVI. Christi CCCCLV. consulendi Procopius, idem Marcellinus, Nicephorus, aliique: postremo, ut & hoc addam, ab Cxtariano, duce Borbonio Gallo, VIII. Eid. Mai, anno Vrbis CIↄ CIↄ CCCXCII. Christi CIↄ IXXVII. Memorantur & ROMÆ Suburbia capta combustaque ab Saracenis, anno Vrbis CIↄ Iↄ LXXXV. Christi IXCCCXXXVII. Primarum sane cladium ea fuit rabies & atrocitas, ut tandem in media ROMA vix quid coeperit esse ROMA; & nusquam ROMA minus cognosceretur, quam in ipsa ROMA. Invicta scilicet illa ROMA, de qua hactenus dixi in Vicia, proh dolor, ROMA jacet hodie mærendum in modum sepulta: Quæ omnia vicerat, ne quid in Orbe ab Vrbe non victum esset, se quoque vicit. Res ipsa docet, & quæ multis in ore: ῥύμη, ῥύμη: ROMA ῥύμη: Nimis vere. Antiqua enim ROMA non tam Vicus, quam merę deplorandi impetus ruinæ. Horrent cum gemitu, qui invenitur, de loco certo certantes. Pristina tamen nunc Montibus tua Facies, & tua Bobus Pascua redire: Omnia Septimontij.
units.tr: Suetonius describes the earlier calamity in the Life of Nero, chapter 38, where among other things he writes: For six days and seven nights the destruction raged, the common people being driven into the tombs and monuments. Xiphilinus, from Dio, should also be consulted. I pass over other fires, dreadful enough. The sack and plundering of the city under the emperors is recorded in various ways. By the Goths under King Athalaric, on 24 August, in the year of the city's founding 1161 and of Christ's birth 510, one should read Sigebert, Prosper, Marcellinus Comes and others. By the Vandals under King Geiseric, in the year of the city 1206 and of Christ 455, one should consult Procopius, the same Marcellinus, Nicephorus and others. Finally, to add this too, it was sacked by Bourbon the Frenchman, the commander, on 8 May, in the year of the city 1392 and of Christ 1527. The suburbs of Rome were also recorded as taken and burned by the Saracens, in the year of the city 1085 and of Christ 937. The rage and atrocity of the earlier disasters was such that in the very heart of Rome there was scarcely anything left that could be called Rome, and nowhere was Rome less recognisable than in Rome itself. That invincible Rome, of which I have spoken so far in the chapter on the walls, alas, now lies buried in a manner to be mourned: she who had conquered everything, so that nothing in the world was left unconquered by the city, has conquered herself as well. The thing itself teaches it, and what is on many people's lips: a street, a street [ῥύμη, ῥύμη]: Rome, a street [ῥύμη]. Too truly so. For ancient Rome is no longer a village, but merely the onrush of a ruin to be lamented. They shudder with groans, those who find, contending over a certain spot. Yet now your mountains are again to take on their former face, and your pastures for oxen: all of the Septimontium.

units.la: Silvestribus horrida Dumis,
units.tr: Bristling with woody thickets,

units.la: Tesca, aspera, deserta, inculta Loca. Bene Poëta: Quæ miseranda videt Veteris vestigia ROMÆ, Ille potest merito dicere ROMA FVIT: At qui celsa Nova spectat Pallatia ROMÆ, Hic merito poterit dicere. ROMA VIGET.
units.tr: Thickets, rough, deserted, uncultivated places. The poet rightly says: he who looks upon the pitiable remains of old Rome may rightly say: Rome was; but he who looks upon the lofty new palaces of Rome may rightly say: Rome flourishes.

units.la: Fuit Vetus, ut illud repetam, in VII præsertim Montibus: Viget, quo loco quondam late Campus erat Martius. Nova: de qua nonnihil etiam ut dicatur, ordo flagitat.
units.tr: Was, to repeat that word, especially on the seven hills; flourishes, in the place where once the Campus Martius lay wide open; new: of which something also must be said, as the order of the discussion demands.

units.la: Sita est loco non admodum fertili, Austro objecta, Cœli gravioris & intemperantioris: adeo ut Cives ab Medicis suis Publico proluberi soleant, diluculo & in crepusculo, nisi Sole splendente. Scripsit eleganter & docte de tuenda ROMÆ valitudine, Alexander Petronius, Romanis Medicus. Ambitus, qui quondam ROMÆ fuisse scribitur tredecim millium passuum, hodie multo minor esse deprehenditur. Burgum vocant illam Vaticani partem omnem à Ponte Palatium versus, ubi olim Silva fuit & Lucus ante Alexandri II. P. M. tempora: in quo Pyramis erat Sepulcralis P. Scipionis Africani, cuius adhuc quædam vestigia visuntur in ea Templi area, quæ Paradisus dicitur: Nux finea ingens ex ære, arque Pavones, inaurati. Turres in Murorum Ambitu circiter CCCIX. olim IDCCXL. & inde ROMA, ut antea dixi, Turrita, Sidonio Carmine V. & Turrigero Vertice Lucano lib. I. Portas antea aperui: Iis hic addo Subarbanas & Recentes sex, Turrionis, Subiectam, S. Petri sub Horus Pontificis, Iulium, Castelli, vel Aely, S. Spiritus, quæ olim Triumphalis, ut quidam volunt. Universim hodie sunt XXI. Montes etiam indicavi, quorum plerique ruinis jacent deformes. Palatinus sane Subterraneis meatibus totus fere pensilis, Hortis est occupatus: nullus ROMA locus magis desertus, quo apud Priscos nullus erat frequentior. Regiones, ut olim, sic hodie, sed mutatis nomibus, sunt XIV: Regio Montium, | Trivij, Columna, | Campi Martij, Pontis, | Parionis, Harenula, | Euflachij, Pinea, | S. Angeli, Campitelli, | Ripa, Trans Tiberis, | Burgi,
units.tr: It stands on a not very fertile site, open to the south, with a heavier and more unhealthy air, so much so that the citizens are commonly advised by their physicians to go out in the early morning and at dusk, unless the sun is shining. Alexander Petronius, a Roman physician, wrote elegantly and learnedly on preserving the health of Rome. The circuit which is written to have once been thirteen thousand paces is now found to be much smaller. They call Borgo that whole part of the Vatican from the Ponte Sant'Angelo towards the palace, where there was once a wood and grove, before the time of Alexander II, Pope and Supreme Pontiff. In it stood the sepulchral pyramid of P. Scipio Africanus, of which some traces are still seen in that enclosure of the temple which is called Paradise: a huge pine cone of bronze, and peacocks, gilded. The towers in the circuit of the walls are about 309, formerly 740; and hence Rome, as I said before, is towered, in the Sidonian poem, and with towery summit in Lucan, Book I. I have already set out the gates; to these I add here the six suburban and recent ones: Turrionis, Subiectam, that of St Peter under the Horn of the Pope, Iulium, Castelli, or Aelia, St Spirit, which was formerly the Triumphal gate, as some hold. In all there are today twenty-one. I have also indicated the hills, most of which lie deformed in ruins. The Palatine, indeed, being almost wholly hanging over subterranean passages, is occupied by gardens: no place in Rome is more deserted, while among the ancients none was more crowded. The regions, as formerly, so today, but with changed names, are fourteen: Region of the Mountains, of Trivium, of the Column, of the Campus Martius, of the Bridge, of Parione, of Sant'Angelo in Pescheria, of Campitelli, of the Bank, Trastevere, Borgo.

units.la: Aquæ nunc Urbi Romæ Tiberis & Almo Fluvij. Occurunt etiam variis locis reliquæ Fontium ex Veteribus Ductibus. Aquo Virgo per Campum Martium initiau. rata est anno CIↄ IDLIV ab Nicolao V. Pont. Maximo: Alsietina per Vaticanum restituta ab Innocentio VIII. Salonia nupera à Pio V. Fontem Felicem de suo nomine ante Pontificatum Sixtus V. trino gurgite in Urbem induxit. Alij Pontifices Aquas alias Fontesque & Aquaeductus reficerunt. Pontes alio loco enumeravi. Campos Urbs etiam-nunc habet multos in quis celeberrimi censentur & primi nominis: Vaticanus, Figulensis, Agonius, Iudeorum, Flora. Porticus numerantur præcipue tres: I. Benedictionus: II. in Vaticani Palatio triplicis obambulationis, aperta: III Versus Hortos Belvedere, vulgo Curridorio, nunc Gregoriana. Fora item conspiciuntur varia quorum Piscarium & Olitorium iisdem adhuc esse locis volunt, ubi fuerunt antiquitus: Suarium & Boarium, ubi olim Romanum. Piscorum unum prope S. Mariam Rotundam; Alterum in Vico Iudæorum. Tertium haud procul D. Laurentio in Damaso: Quartum ad Pontem Aelium. Commune omnium Mercium & Rerum Venalium Forum in Campo Agonio. Templa plura nunc, quam olim: hodie supra ccc. quorum vii. Religionis causa maxime frequentantur. 1. S. Petri in Vaticano sumtu, marmoribus, magnificentia & opere omnia orbis superans Templa. Multa ibi singularia: Columnæ aliquot ex Templo Salomonis advectæ: duo ærei Pavones ex Pyramide P. Cornelij Scipionis Africani, quæ olim in Valle Vaticana fuisse dicitur, translati. Visuntur item ibi Sepulcra multorum Pontificum; Othonis quoque ii. Imperatoris marmorcum. Ostenditur ibidem Sudarium Veronicæ, cui Christi facies impressa. Est & Iudicium Orbis universi supra in Sacello Pontificis, Opus Michaelis Angeli. ii. S. Pauli, in Via Ostiensi, amplum & pulcrum, ab Constantino Magno ædificatum. Multæ hic Veterum Romanorum Inscriptiones. Imago ibidem Salvatoris, quæ S. Brigidæ loquuta fertur. Sepulcra item Benedicti ix. aliorumque. iii. S. Maria Majoris in Via Esquilina: augustum. Monstratur ibi Præsepe Domini. Sepulcra ibidem D. Hieronymi, Alberti & Ioannis Normanni, Platina Historiographi, Lucæ Gauricī Mathematici, Francisci Toleti Cardinalis, & aliorum. Pro foribus Obeliscus cum Notis, Hieroglyphicis. iv. S. Sebastiani, extra Portam Capenam, in Via Appia, oblongum, Tecto lapideo, ut plurima Romæ. Reliquiæ hic multorum Martyrum: Sepulcraque Pontificum xlvi. v. S. Ioannis Lateranensis in Cælio Monte: Pontificum olim Sedes. Reliquiæ ostenduntur multæ: Capita SS. Apostolorum Petri & Pauli: S. Stephani Tunica, sanguine tincta, lapidibus perforata: Arca Fœderis: Aaronis Virga: & alia, de quibus alij. Situs ibi Silvestri i. P. M. cum Laurentio Valla, ibidem olim Canonico. Ante fores Obeliscus est Notas habens Hieroglyphicas vi. S. Crucis in Hierusalem, in eodem Monte, mundum & elegans: ab Helena, Constantini Magni Imperatoris Matre, ædificatum. Solum ex Terra Sancta Hierosolymis advectum fuisse testatur Inscriptio. Pars hic fertur advertari Crucis Dominicæ: item Titulus tribus Lingius scriptus; Denarius unus ex xxx. quibus Iudas Christum vendidit: Spina Coronæ ejusdem. Tumulus ibi Benedicti viii. P. M. Sunt qui putant olim Veneri & Cupidini dicatum. vii. S. Laurentij, extra Portam Esquilinam, pulcrum. Reliquias hic perhibent servari D. Laurentij. Scripserunt de Septem Urbis Ecclesijs Onuphrius Panvinius & M. Attilius Serranus; Italice vero Pompeius Hugonius Romanus, Reliqua minora sunt Templa, & Ædes potius Sacræ: quas non omnes (operosum hoc esset) sed quæ vel Antiquorum fuerunt Deorum, vel alia quæ habent singularia, commemorabo: ordine Alphabetico, ne quid alicuius deteratur dignitati vel Prærogativæ:
units.tr: The waters now serving Rome are the Tiber and the Almo, rivers. Remains of fountains from the ancient conduits also appear in various places. The Virgin water, begun across the Campus Martius, was restored in the year 1454 by Pope Nicholas V, Supreme Pontiff. The Alsietina was restored through the Vatican by Innocent VIII. The recent Salonia by Pius V. Fontem Felicem, named after himself, Sixtus V brought into the city before his pontificate, by a threefold flow. Other popes restored other waters and fountains and aqueducts. I have listed the bridges in another place. The city still has many fields, among which the most famous and of first rank are counted: the Vatican, Figulensis, Agonius, Jews', Flora. Three porticoes are chiefly counted: I. the Benedictine; II. in the Vatican palace, open, of a triple walkway; III. towards the Belvedere gardens, commonly called the Corridor, now the Gregorian. Various markets are also to be seen, of which the Fish market and the Vegetable market are thought to remain in the same places where they were of old; the Pig and Cattle markets, where the Roman once stood. There is one fish market near St Mary of the Rotunda; another in the Jewish quarter; a third not far from St Lawrence in Damaso; a fourth at the Aelian Bridge. The common Forum for all wares and things for sale is in the Campus Agonius. Churches are now more numerous than formerly: today over three hundred, of which seven are most frequented for religion's sake. 1. St Peter's in the Vatican, surpassing all the churches of the world in cost, marbles, magnificence and workmanship. Many singular things are there: some columns brought from the Temple of Solomon, and two bronze peacocks from the pyramid of P. Cornelius Scipio Africanus, which is said to have once stood in the Vatican valley, transferred there. There are also tombs of many popes, and that of the Emperor Otho in marble. There is shown in the same place the Veronica's veil, on which Christ's face is impressed. There is also the Last Judgement of the whole world, above, in the Pope's chapel, the work of Michelangelo. 2. St Paul's, on the Ostian Way, large and beautiful, built by Constantine the Great. Many Roman inscriptions of the ancients are here. An image of the Saviour in the same place is said to have spoken to St Bridget. Likewise the tombs of Benedict IX and others. 3. St Mary Major, on the Esquiline Way: august. The Manger of the Lord is shown there. Tombs of St Jerome, of Albert and John the Norman, of Platina the historian, of Luca Gaurico the mathematician, of Francis Toledo the cardinal, and of others, are in the same place. Before the doors is an obelisk with hieroglyphic marks. 4. St Sebastian, outside the Capene Gate, on the Appian Way, oblong, with a stone roof, as most things at Rome. Here are relics of many martyrs, and the tombs of forty-six popes. 5. St John Lateran, on the Caelian Hill: formerly the seat of the popes. Many relics are shown: the heads of the holy apostles Peter and Paul; the tunic of St Stephen, stained with blood, pierced by stones; the Ark of the Covenant; the rod of Aaron; and other things, about which others speak. Pope Silvester I is buried there, along with Laurentius Valla, formerly a canon there. Before the doors is an obelisk bearing hieroglyphic marks. 6. Holy Cross in Jerusalem, on the same hill, neat and elegant, built by Helena, mother of the Emperor Constantine the Great. An inscription testifies that soil brought from the Holy Land at Jerusalem was used. A part of the Lord's Cross is said to be kept here; likewise the title written in three languages; one denarius of the thirty with which Judas sold Christ; a thorn of his crown. The tomb of Pope Benedict VIII is there. Some think it was once dedicated to Venus and Cupid. 7. St Lawrence, outside the Esquiline Gate, a fine church. They report that relics of St Lawrence are kept here. Concerning the seven churches of the city, Onuphrius Panvinius and M. Attilius Serranus have written; in Italian, Pompeius Hugonius the Roman. The remaining churches are smaller, and are rather sacred buildings; of these I shall mention, not all of them (that would be laborious), but those which either were of the ancient gods or have some other distinction, in alphabetical order, lest the dignity or prerogative of any one be slighted.

units.la: S. Agatha, Gothorum Ecclesia sub Viminali. Hic Diana & Pacis Imagines ex Cæmento: Proforibus Prætextati in subsellis Pueri sedent & docentur: Tumulus ibidem est Iani Lascaris, additis Epitaphiis Græcis.
units.tr: S. Agatha, the church of the Goths under the Viminal. Here are images of Diana and Peace in stucco. Beside the doors, boys in the praetexta sit on benches and are taught. There is a tomb here of Janus Lascaris, with Greek epitaphs added.

units.la: S. Alexius, in Aventino: olim Herculis Victoris.
units.tr: S. Alexius, on the Aventine: formerly the temple of Hercules Victor.

units.la: S. Anastasia, ad Palatini radices: olim Neptuni Equestris, qui & Consus.
units.tr: S. Anastasia, at the foot of the Palatine: formerly of Neptune Equestris, who is also Consus.

units.la: S. Angelus, in Piscina, olim Mercurij.
units.tr: S. Angelus, in Piscina: formerly of Mercury.

units.la: S. Apollinaris; olim Apollinis.
units.tr: S. Apollinaris: formerly of Apollo.

units.la: SS. Apostolorum xii. Sepulcra ibi Bessarionis, & Petri Saamensis, Cardinalium; item Bartholomæi Camerarij, Theologi & Iureconsulti.
units.tr: SS. Apostles, twelve. Here are the tombs of Bessarion and Peter of Saamen, cardinals; likewise of Bartholomew Camerarius, theologian and jurist.

units.la: S. Augustinus, in Campo Martio: Sepulcra hic cum aliorum, tum Constantini Commeni, Macedoniæ Principis, & Achaiæ Ducis, qui ab Turca pulsus avitis regnis, Romæ obit cIↄ Iↄ xxxi. Kalendis Mai.
units.tr: S. Augustine, in the Campus Martius: here are tombs of others and of Constantine Comnenus, prince of Macedonia and duke of Achaia, who, driven from his ancestral kingdoms by the Turk, died at Rome on the thirtieth day before the Kalends of May, 1531.

units.la: S. Barbara, in Regione Pinciae: olim Veneris Theatri Pompeiani.
units.tr: S. Barbara, in the region of Pincius: formerly of Venus in the Theatre of Pompey.

units.la: S. Bartholomæus, in Insula: olim Iovis, vel ut alij volunt, Aesculapij.
units.tr: S. Bartholomew, on the Island: formerly of Jupiter, or, as others will have it, of Aesculapius.

units.la: S. Catharina, sub Monte Tarpeio; olim Carmentæ.
units.tr: S. Catherine, under the Tarpeian Rock: formerly of Carmenta.

units.la: S. Chrysogonus: Situs hic Hieronymus Alexander, Cardinalis.
units.tr: S. Chrysogonus: here lies Hieronymus Alexander, cardinal.

units.la: S. Constantia, in Via Nomentana: olim, ut quidam censent, Bacchi.
units.tr: S. Constantia, on the Via Nomentana: formerly, as some think, of Bacchus.

units.la: S. Cosmus & Damianus, in Via Sacra: olim Romuli & Remi: vel, ut alij, Castoris & Pollucis.
units.tr: SS. Cosmas and Damian, on the Via Sacra: formerly of Romulus and Remus, or, as others say, of Castor and Pollux.

units.la: S. Cosmatus, sub Ianiculo: olim Fortis Fortuna.
units.tr: S. Cosmatus, under the Janiculum: formerly of Fortuna Fortis.

units.la: S. Elizabetha, in Campo Martio: olim Agrippa.
units.tr: S. Elizabeth, in the Campus Martius: formerly of Agrippa.

units.la: S. Eustathius, prope Pantheon: olim Boni Eventus.
units.tr: S. Eustathius, near the Pantheon: formerly of Bonus Eventus.

units.la: S. Hadrianus: olim Saturni, in Foro Romano.
units.tr: S. Hadrian: formerly of Saturn, in the Roman Forum.

units.la: S. Ioannes Euangelista, ante Portam Latinam, in Cœlio: olim Dianæ.
units.tr: S. John the Evangelist, before the Latin Gate, on the Caelian: formerly of Diana.

units.la: S. Ioannes Calybita, in Infula: olim Æscu-lapy fanum censetur.
units.tr: S. John Calybites, on the Island: is thought to have been a shrine of Aesculapius.

units.la: S. Laurentius in Lucina: olim Iunonis Lucinæ.
units.tr: S. Lawrence in Lucina: formerly of Juno Lucina.

units.la: S. Laurentius in Miranda: olim Castoris ad Forum Romanum: vel, ut alij, Faustina, Antonini Conjugis.
units.tr: S. Lawrence in Miranda: formerly of Castor, at the Roman Forum; or, as others say, of Faustina, wife of Antoninus.

units.la: S. Laurentius in Damaso in Regione Pinciæ: Epitaphium hic Hannibalis Cari, Lingua diserti, qua & multa tenuit: & Iacobi Fabij Parmensis, qui de Beneficentia quædam in lucem edidit: item Petri Marsi, Iuly Sadoleti, Hieronymi Ferrarij Corrigiensis, & aliorum.
units.tr: S. Lawrence in Damaso, in the region of Pincius: here is the epitaph of Hannibal Caro, eloquent in his language, who also held many offices; and of Jacopo Fabio of Parma, who published some work on beneficence; likewise of Pietro Martire, Giulio Sadoleto, Girolamo Ferrari of Correggio, and others.

units.la: S. Lucia in Palatio: olim Apollinis Palatini.
units.tr: S. Lucy on the Palatine: formerly of Apollo Palatinus.

units.la: S. Lucia in Apotheca: olim Herculis Musarum.
units.tr: S. Lucy in Apotheca: formerly of Hercules of the Muses.

units.la: S. Maria Aegyptiaca, in Regione Ripæ: olim Fortunæ Virilis.
units.tr: S. Mary of Egypt, in the region of the Ripa: formerly of Fortuna Virilis.

units.la: S. Maria de Anima, in Regione Parionis, Germanorum & Belgarum Templum: in quo conditi Hadriani VI. P. M. Guilelmus Enckefort Cardinalis, Karolus Princeps Clevæ, & alij.
units.tr: S. Mary de Anima, in the region of Parione, the church of the Germans and Flemings, in which are buried Adrian VI, supreme pontiff, William Enckevort, cardinal, Charles, Prince of Cleves, and others.

units.la: S. Maria in Ara Cœli, in Capitolio: olim Iovis Feretrij.
units.tr: S. Mary in Aracoeli, on the Capitol: formerly of Jupiter Feretrius.

units.la: S. Maria Aventina, in Colle Aventino: olim Bonæ Deæ.
units.tr: S. Mary on the Aventine, on the Aventine hill: formerly of the Good Goddess.

units.la: S. Maria in Capitolio: olim Apollinis Capitolini.
units.tr: S. Mary on the Capitol: formerly of Apollo Capitolinus.

units.la: S. Maria in Crypta Pilla: olim Veneris Victricis.
units.tr: S. Mary in Crypta Pila: formerly of Venus Victrix.

units.la: S. Maria in Cosmedim in Velabro: olim Herculis in Ara Maxima.
units.tr: S. Mary in Cosmedin, in the Velabrum: formerly of Hercules at the Ara Maxima.

units.la: S. Maria in Esquilio: olim Isidis in Circo Flaminio.
units.tr: S. Mary on the Esquiline: formerly of Isis in the Circus Flaminius.

units.la: S. Maria de Febribus: olim Martis in Vaticano.
units.tr: S. Mary de Febribus: formerly of Mars in the Vatican.

units.la: S. Maria de Gratia: olim Vestæ inter Capitolinum & Palatinum Montes.
units.tr: S. Mary de Gratia: formerly of Vesta, between the Capitoline and Palatine hills.

units.la: S. Maria de Inferno: olim Iovis Statoris, in Foro Romano.
units.tr: S. Mary de Inferno: formerly of Jupiter Stator, in the Roman Forum.

units.la: S. Maria Liberatrix, ad Capitolii Radices: olim Veneris Genetricis.
units.tr: S. Mary Liberatrix, at the foot of the Capitol: formerly of Venus Genetrix.

units.la: S. Maria supra Minervam: olim Minervæ. Tumuli visuntur Stanislai Hosij Cardinalis, Poleni. Thoma de Vio Cajetanus: Gulielmi Durandi, Episcopi Mimaten-sis: Petri Bembi, Cardinalis: Pauli Ma-nutij, & aliorum.
units.tr: S. Mary supra Minervam: formerly of Minerva. The tombs to be seen here are those of Stanislaus Hosius, cardinal, of Polenus, of Thomas de Vio Cajetan, of William Durand, bishop of Mende, of Pietro Bembo, cardinal, of Paolo Manuzio, and others.

units.la: Maria Nova, in extremo Foro Romano: olim Solis & Lunæ: vel, ut alij Isidis & Serapidis.
units.tr: Maria Nova, at the far end of the Roman Forum: formerly of Sun and Moon, or, as others say, of Isis and Serapis.

units.la: Maria in Pace: Situs ibi Marcus Musurus Cretensis.
units.tr: Maria in Pace: here lies Marcus Musurus of Crete.

units.la: Maria in Portico, in Regione Ripæ: olim Saturni & Opis.
units.tr: Maria in Portico, in the region of the Ripa: formerly of Saturn and Ops.

units.la: Maria de Populo, sub Colle Hortulorum. Conditi jacent ibi multi Cardinales, & cum ijs Hermolaus Barbarus, Patriarcha Aquileiensis.
units.tr: Maria del Popolo, under the Hill of the Gardens. Many cardinals lie buried here, and with them Ermolao Barbaro, patriarch of Aquileia.

units.la: Maria Rotunda: Pantheon olim, nunc Sanctis omnibus & B. Virgini Sacrum. Condidit M. Vipsanius Agrippa Cos. III. uti docet Inscriptio, uncialibus litteris. Templum hoc, ut perfectæ Architecturæ Exemplar exhibet, explanatque Ludovicus Demontesius, Architectus insignis, singulari libello, cui titulus Gallus Hospes ab Urbe. Ex solido Lapide est Tiburtino, æquali cum latitudine, tum altitudine. Tectum plumbeum est & circulare, unicum habens Foramen, quod lucem præbet. Porticus adstat ingens. Testudo per quam ad Tectum ascenditur gradus habet CL: ad Foramen Tecti rursus gradus plumbei sunt XL. Ante Templum Vas ingens Numidico è marmore: superne, quadratum: infra, alvei similitudine ventrem habens. Visuntur & Leones duo cum Notis Ægyptiacis.
units.tr: Maria Rotunda: formerly the Pantheon, now dedicated to all the saints and to the Blessed Virgin. Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa, consul for the third time, built it, as the inscription in capital letters shows. Ludovicus Demontiosius, a distinguished architect, sets out and explains this temple as a perfect model of architecture in a separate little book titled Gallus Hospes ab Urbe. It is built of solid Tiburtine stone, equal in width and height. The roof is of lead and circular, with a single opening that gives light. A huge portico stands in front. The vault, by which one ascends to the roof, has 150 steps; the lead steps up to the opening of the roof are 40. In front of the temple stands a huge vessel of Numidian marble, square at the top, and below, with the shape of a trough, having a belly. Two lions are also to be seen, with Egyptian marks.

units.la: Maria Transpontina in Regione Burgi: olim Hadriani Imperatoris.
units.tr: Maria Transpontina, in the region of the Borgo: formerly of Hadrian the Emperor.

units.la: Marcellus. Iacet hic Petrus Gyllius, Æliani Interpres, & Byzantij Descri-ptor.
units.tr: Marcellus. Here lies Pietro Gillio, translator of Aelian and describer of Byzantium.

units.la: Martina, iuxta Forum Romanum: olim Martis Ultoris.
units.tr: Martina, beside the Roman Forum: formerly of Mars Ultor.

units.la: Nereus & Achilleus, iuxta Thermas Antonini: olim Isidis in Via Appia.
units.tr: Nereus and Achilleus, beside the Baths of Antoninus: formerly of Isis on the Via Appia.

units.la: Nicolaus, in Matuza: olim Innonis Matuta.
units.tr: Nicholas, in Mattuzza: formerly of Juno Matuta.

units.la: Pantaleon, in Suburra: olim Telluris.
units.tr: Pantaleon, in the Suburra: formerly of Tellus.

units.la: Petrus & Marcellinus: olim Quieris.
units.tr: Peter and Marcellinus: formerly of Quiris.

units.la: Petrus in Carcere: olim Carcer Tullianus.
units.tr: Peter in Carcere: formerly the Carcer Tullianus.

units.la: Petrus Montorius, in Ianiculo, Templum parvum, sed elegans, rotundum Dorica structura. Sepulcra ibi Antonij Masse Galesij I.C. Iulij Pogiani Novarien-sis, Angeli de Pace Hispani: qui omnes Scriptis clari Exstruxerat ibidem Sepulcrum sibi Julius III P. M. vivens: iacet tamen in Vaticano, loco humili.
units.tr: Peter Montorio, on the Janiculum: a small but elegant round temple in Doric style. Here are the tombs of Antonio Massa Galesio, jurist, Giulio Pogiani of Novara, and Angelo de Pace, a Spaniard, all men famous for their writings. Julius III, supreme pontiff, had built a tomb for himself here while still living, yet he lies in the Vatican, in a humble place.

units.la: S. Petrus ad Vincula: Adservari feruntur hic Catenæ, quibus Hierosolymis Apostolus adligatus: quæque laudat B. Chrysostomus. Monstrantur & Machabæorum Corpora, Pars Crucis S. Andreæ, Statua Moisi Israelitarum Ducis, & alia: Conditi hic Nicolaus Cusanus, Iacobus Sadoletus, &c. alij.
units.tr: S. Peter in Chains: here are said to be preserved the chains with which the Apostle was bound at Jerusalem, and which Blessed Chrysostom praises. The bodies of the Maccabees are shown, also a part of the Cross of St Andrew, a statue of Moses, leader of the Israelites, and other things. Buried here are Nicholas of Cusa, Jacopo Sadoleto, etc., and others.

units.la: S. Petronella, in Vaticano; olim Apollinis Vaticani.
units.tr: S. Petronilla, in the Vatican: formerly of Apollo Vaticanus.

units.la: S. Praxedis in Esquilino, à Paschali I. P. M. extructum; in quo Columna, ad quam Christus flagellatus.
units.tr: S. Praxedes on the Esquiline, built by Paschal I, supreme pontiff; in it is the column to which Christ was tied when scourged.

units.la: S. Prisca in Aventino; olim Herculis.
units.tr: S. Prisca on the Aventine: formerly of Hercules.

units.la: S. Pudentiana in Viminali. Hic primum Missæ Sacrificium peregisse S. Petrum tradunt Romani.
units.tr: S. Pudentiana on the Viminal. The Romans relate that St Peter first celebrated the sacrifice of the Mass here.

units.la: 20 S. Sabina: olim Diana: Pontificum Romanorum prima Sedes. Pro foribus Urna est lapidea, qua nulla Romæ maior. Reliquiæ hic ostenduntur Hadriani Pontificis, Eventij & Theoduli Martyrum,
units.tr: 20 S. Sabina: formerly of Diana. It was the first seat of the Roman pontiffs. Beside the doors is a stone urn, of which none is larger at Rome. Here are shown relics of Pope Hadrian, and of the martyrs Eventius and Theodulus.

units.la: Templis subiiciam Cryptas Subterraneas; [?]quæ Christianos lævisentibus, ipsorum fuerunt Latebræ vitæque ituenda. Monstrantur ad Vibe[?]tium, S. Sebastianum, S. Priscillam; ext[?]ra-nam, Flaminiam. Cæmiteria, quæ partim 30 rantur xxviiii; S. Agnetis, Via Nomentana; S. Balbina, Via Ardeatina, alias S. Marci Papæ. S. Calixti, ad S. Sebastianum; Catacumbæ; Commodilla, Via Ostiensi; S. Damasi; S. Felicis Papæ, Via Aurelia, prope S. 40 Pancratium; Ad Clivum Cucumeris; S. Felicitatis, Via Salaria; Cyriaci, Via Tiburtina; Iordanorum, ubi Alexander conditus; Domitillæ, Via Ardeatina; S. Nicomedis, Via eadem; Peregrinorum; Ad duas Lauros, ad S. Helenam; S. Pontiani Papæ; Sabinæ itẽ & Seraphiæ VirginumSitus ibidem Eugenius 11, P. M.
units.tr: I will add to the churches the subterranean crypts, which were the hiding places and places of living of the Christians when they were harassed by the emperors' persecutions, and are worth visiting. They are shown on the Via Vibe[?]tia, at St Sebastian, at St Priscilla, outside the Flaminian Gate. The cemeteries, of which some are named after xxix [?] ..., are: St Agnes, on the Via Nomentana; St Balbina, on the Via Ardeatina, otherwise of St Mark the Pope; St Callixtus, at St Sebastian; the Catacombs; Commodilla, on the Via Ostiensis; St Damasus; St Felix the Pope, on the Via Aurelia, near St Pancras; At the Slope of the Cucumber; St Felicitas, on the Via Salaria; Cyriacus, on the Via Tiburtina; of the Jordani, where Alexander is buried; Domitilla, on the Via Ardeatina; St Nicomedes, on the same road; of the Pilgrims; At the Two Laurels, near St Helena; St Pontianus the Pope; likewise of Sabina and Seraphia, virgins. Here Eugenius II, supreme pontiff, is buried.

units.la: S. Salas in Aventino. Hic ingens Sepulcrum, quod Titi Vespasiani Imperatoris fertur.
units.tr: S. Salas on the Aventine. Here is a huge tomb, said to be that of the Emperor Titus Vespasian.

units.la: S. Salvator in Maximis; olim Iovis, Minerva & Iunonis.
units.tr: S. Salvator in Maximis: formerly of Jupiter, Minerva and Juno.

units.la: S. Salvator in Statera; olim Saturni in Capitolio.
units.tr: S. Salvator in Statera: formerly of Saturn on the Capitol.

units.la: S. Salvator in Pietate; olim Pietatis.
units.tr: S. Salvator in Pietate: formerly of Piety.

units.la: S. Sergius & Bacchus, in Capitolio; olim Concordia.
units.tr: S. Sergius and Bacchus, on the Capitol: formerly of Concordia.

units.la: S. Sixtus ad Infernam Piscinam; olim Honoris & Virtutis.
units.tr: S. Sixtus at the Infernal Pool: formerly of Honos and Virtus.

units.la: S. Stephanus Rotundus, in Cœlio; olim Fauni.
units.tr: S. Stephen the Round, on the Caelian: formerly of the Fauns.

units.la: S. Stephanus in Foro Boario; olim Festa.
units.tr: S. Stephen in the Forum Boarium: formerly of Festa.

units.la: S. Susanna, olim Quirini.
units.tr: S. Susanna: formerly of Quirinus.

units.la: S. Theodorus, sub Monte Palatino olim Panos Licaei, vel ut alij, Romuli & Remi.
units.tr: S. Theodore, under the Palatine hill: formerly of Pan of the Lycaeum, or, as others say, of Romulus and Remus.

units.la: S. Trinitas in Colle Hortulorum. Siti sunt ibi M. Antonius Muretus & Franciscus Franchinus Cosentinus, Massa Populonia Episcopus; Scriptis clari.
units.tr: S. Trinity on the Hill of the Gardens. Buried here are M. Antonius Muretus and Francesco Franchini of Cosenza, bishop of Massa Populonia; men famous for their writings.

units.la: quæ quondam, Imperatoribus in Christianos & Sepulcra. Loca Venerationis plena, quatuor: apud S. Agnetem, S. Pancratium, Portas Viminalem, Aureliam, Capenam olim fuerunt, partim nunc sunt, nume-
units.tr: which once, under the emperors, were places of persecution against Christians, and sepulchres. Places full of veneration, four in number: near St Agnes, St Pancras, the Porta Viminalis, Aurelia and Capena were once so, and some still are; numerous...

units.la: S. Hermetis, alias Domitillæ, Via Habet multa alia Onuphrius Panuinius. Ardeatina;
units.tr: St Hermes, otherwise called of Domitilla, on the Via Ardeatina. Onuphrius Panvinius has many others.

units.la: Infalatarum, Via Portuensi;
units.tr: of the Infalatae, on the Via Portuensis;

units.la: SS. Nerei & Achillei, Via Ardeatina;
units.tr: Saints Nereus and Achilleus, on the Via Ardeatina;

units.la: S. Pancratij;
units.tr: St Pancratius;

units.la: S. Priscillæ, Via Salaria, S. Marcelli Papæ,
units.tr: St Priscilla, on the Via Salaria; St Marcellus, Pope;

units.la: Vrsi Pileati, ad S. Balbinam;
units.tr: of Ursus Pileatus, near St Balbina;

units.la: Ampronniani, Via Latina, in quo condita S. Eugenia;
units.tr: of Ampronianus, on the Via Latina, where St Eugenia was buried;

units.la: S. Pratextati Presbyteri, Via Appia.
units.tr: St Pratextatus, elder, on the Via Appia.

units.la: Basillæ;
units.tr: of Basilla;

units.la: Calepodij Presbyteri, Via Aurelia, ubi Vrbanus Papa sepultus;
units.tr: of Calepodius, elder, on the Via Aurelia, where Pope Urban was buried;

units.la: Thrasonis;
units.tr: of Thraso;

units.la: S. Timothei Presbyteri, Via Ostiensi, juxta S. Pauli.
units.tr: St Timothy, elder, on the Via Ostiensis, near St Paul's.

units.la: Hospitalia, ut Latinorum Vulgus vocat, quorum tanta magnificentia, ut inter recentia Vrbis Monumenta nihil prædicetur dignius, multa sunt: Publica quidem omnium Nationum & Mortalium: S. Spiritus, in Vaticano: | S. Maria de Anima, Germanorum & Belgarum: S. Iacobs de Augusta, in Valle Martia, | S. Iacobi, Hispanorum, S. Antonij, in Esquilino: | S. Petri, Hungarorum. Propria vero, singulorum Populorum; | S. An. S. Andrea prope Argentinam, Flandrorum; | S. Brigida, Suecorum; S. Ludovici, Gallorum; | S. Ioannes Baptista, Florentinorum; S. Salvatoris, in Cœlio, | S. Ioannis Baptista prope ripam Tiberis, Genuensium, ab Mediadusto Citada conditum & dotatum. S. Mariæ, de Consolatione, in Velabro; S. Thomæ, Anglorum,
units.tr: Hospices, as the common people of the Latins call them, of such magnificence that among the recent monuments of the City nothing is more worthy of mention, there are many. The public ones, for all nations and people: St Spirit's, in the Vatican; St Mary of the Soul, for Germans and Belgians; St James of Augsburg, in the Valle Martia; St James, for Spaniards; St Anthony, on the Esquiline; St Peter, for Hungarians. The proper ones belong to individual peoples: St Andrew near Argentina, for Flemings; St Bridget, for Swedes; St Louis, for French; St John the Baptist, for Florentines; St Saviour, on the Caelian; St John the Baptist near the bank of the Tiber, for Genoese, founded and endowed by Mediadustus Citada; St Mary of Consolation, in the Velabrum; St Thomas, for English.

units.la: Inter recentia etiam nuperaque Vrbis Opera maxime conspicienda veniunt varia cum Pontificis & Cardinalium, tum aliorum Palatia. Pontificis in edito Vaticani loco est, ita longe augustissimum; quo, relicta Lateranensi Sede, eo ob amœnitatem loci & salubritatem commigrarunt. Inchoatum ab Nicolao III, auctum post ab aliis perfectum ab Iulio II & Leone X, ædificiis tandem illustratum picturisque ab Xysto V, ut Machina cœlo adsurgere pendereque videatur. Adiicentius sunt facillimi & ædibus Palatinis adcommodati ex omni parte, adeo ut etiam equo ad tectum usque ascendi liceat. Opidum potius quis dixerit, adeo est amplum, quam Domum. Sacellum ibi est Xysti, quod amplissimum æquat Templum. Eo, vacante Sede, convenunt Cardinales creando Pontifici Maximo. Conclave vulgo dicitur. Hortos ibi videre est: in quos quæ rariora servantur spectanturque, ita describunt Antiquarij: Horti hæc sunt, qui ab amœnitate hodie Belvedere appellantur. In unius Horturi Peristylio, Area media variis exoticis contita arboribus, spectatur hunc Tiberis, lupæ mutantes Pueruli Romulum & Remum lactantis, inde Nilus est, cui Sphynx subjacet, circumquaque sunt indentes Pueruli xvii, Cubitorum altitudinem, quibus exercet fluvius, designantes, auctore Plinio. In Bati sculpti Hippopotami, & Crocodili, Nilo proprie Animantes. In alia Peristylio Larvæ marmoreæ, singularis artificij, xiii vitantur. In loculis seu repositoriis, quæ Ichnei Itali vocant, a tergo Nili Antinoi spectatur, ex marmore candidissimo, artificio mirabili, qualem Hadrianus Imperator fieri jussit: ad dextram illi Amnis, Fluvij est habitu, hominis jacentis, urnamque effundentis; ad lævam Cleopatra est, dexteræ innixa. In secundo Loculo Venus Erycina est, ex Balneo prodiens. Tertio Loculo eadem spectatur cum Cupidine concludens, cui inscriptum, VENERI FELICI SACRUM SALVSTIA HELPIS DD. Iuxta est Bacchus, mutilus, & Hercules Ille, licet truncus, usque eo tamen ab Michaele Angelo prædicatus, ut omnium Signorum, quæ Romæ sunt, absolutissimum esse dixerit. Artificis Apollonij nomen huc inscriptum. ΑΠΟΛ-ΛΩΝΙΟΣ ΝΕΣΤΟΡΟΣ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΟΣ ΕΠΟΙΕΙ. Iuxta est Mulieris truncus & Mercurij. Hic & Arca marmorea, cui insculpta est Meleagri Venatio, opere Mutivo. Quarto Loculo est Commodi Imperatoris Statua, Herculis habitu & forma: Brachio Pueri tenet, cuius imprudentia, dejectis e fenestra Pugillaribus, quibus Commuratorum nomina prodebantur, cæsus est. Quinto Apollo est Pythius, cui se implicat squamosus Serpens: Palliolum gestat brachio, cetera nudus, Pharetram habens & Arcum. Sexto Loculo est Laocoon cum duobus Filiis, quos gemini Dracones flexu & gyris implicant, uti ab Marone lib. II. Æneidos describitur. Opus est omnium, quæ toto orbe spectantur, absolutissimum, quodque Michael Angelus Artis Miraculum vocare non dubitavit: & ante illum C. Plinius, qui factum esse adfert ab Agelandro, Polydoro, & Athenodoro, Sculptoribus Rhodijs sui sæculi celeberrimis; servatum addens in Titi Vespasiani Palatio. In proximo Cœnaculo Cleopatræ morientis est Statua, ea arte perfecta, ut per Vestes tenuissimas e marmore factas corporis forma numeris omnibus absoluta appareat. Ibidem Labrum est marmoreum, ex variis lapidum preciosorum generibus, cujus æstimari precium non poterit, nihilque par alibi visum. Eeffossum olim ex Titi Vespasiani Thermis. Proxime spectantur Mercurius & Cybele, vertice turrita, cui adstat Leo & Atys animixus Pinui, ex qua pendet Fistula & Cymbalum. Hic & Fons rusticus, in quo Dij & monstra marina expressa. Hic & Effigies Principum variorum: in his Paulis III, P. M. & Caroli V. Imper. Augusti, Michaelis Angeli manu depictæ. Ad Helvetiorum Stationem marmorea Statua, unus è Cursigi; opus egregium. Aliorum Palatia commemorare longum esset. Ea tantum, & Privatorum Ædes, ex C L. V. Francisci Schotti I. C. indicio & aliorum recentiorum, in quibus Antiquitatum Monumenta salva. In Cardinalis Dandini Palatio ad Divæ Catharinæ in Burgo Caput est ex marmore Agrippinæ, Matris Neronis Hadriani item Imperatoris, & Antinoi dilecti pueri; M. quoque Aurelij & Sabinæ cuiusdam Mulie-
units.tr: Among the recent and newer works of the City, the various palaces of the Pope and of the Cardinals, and of others, are most worth seeing. The Pope's palace is on the high ground of the Vatican, and is by far the most august; the popes moved there from the Lateran seat, for the pleasantness and healthiness of the place. Begun by Nicholas III, enlarged afterwards by others, completed by Julius II and Leo X, and finally adorned with buildings and paintings by Sixtus V, so that it seems to rise towards heaven and hang in the air. The approaches are very easy and fitted to a palace on every side, so that one may even ride a horse up to the roof. One would call it a town rather than a house, it is so large. There is the chapel of Sixtus, which equals a most ample temple. There, when the See is vacant, the Cardinals assemble to create the Supreme Pontiff; it is commonly called the Conclave. Gardens are there to be seen, and the rarer things kept and displayed in them are described thus by the antiquaries. These gardens, from their pleasantness, are today called the Belvedere. In the peristyle of one garden, with a middle court planted with various exotic trees, one sees the Tiber, the she-wolf suckling the boys Romulus and Remus; then the Nile, with a Sphinx lying beneath it; all around are sixteen little children marking the cubits of height to which the river rises, as Pliny says. In the bath are sculpted hippopotamus and crocodile, creatures proper to the Nile. In another peristyle are marble masks (larvae) of singular workmanship; thirteen are seen. In the niches or recesses, which Italians call ichnei, behind is seen the Antinous of the Nile, of most white marble, of wonderful workmanship, such as Emperor Hadrian ordered made: on his right is the river god, in the form of a reclining man, pouring out an urn; on the left is Cleopatra, leaning on her right arm. In the second niche is Venus Erycina, emerging from the bath. In the third niche the same goddess is seen closing with Cupid, with the inscription: "Sacred to Venus Felix, dedicated by Salustia Helpis." Next to it is Bacchus, mutilated, and that Hercules, though truncated, so praised by Michelangelo that he said it was the most perfect of all the statues that are in Rome. The name of the sculptor Apollonius is inscribed here [ΑΠΟΛΛΩΝΙΟΣ ΝΕΣΤΟΡΟΣ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΟΣ ΕΠΟΙΕΙ: Apollonius son of Nestor, the Athenian, made this]. Next to it are the trunk of a woman and Mercury. Here also is a marble chest, on which the Hunt of Meleager is carved in mosaic work. In the fourth niche is a statue of Emperor Commodus, in the form and dress of Hercules; he holds a boy's arm, by whose carelessness, when the writing tablets on which the names of the conspirators were revealed fell from the window, he was struck down. In the fifth is Apollo Pythius, around whom a scaly serpent coils; he carries a small cloak on one arm, otherwise naked, with quiver and bow. In the sixth niche is Laocoon with two sons, whom twin dragons entangle in coils and loops, as Virgil describes in the second book of the Aeneid. It is the most perfect of all the works seen throughout the world, which Michelangelo did not hesitate to call a miracle of art; and before him Pliny, who says it was made by Agesander, Polydorus and Athenodorus, sculptors of Rhodes most famous in his age, adding that it was preserved in the palace of Titus Vespasian. In the next dining room is a statue of dying Cleopatra, so perfected by art that through the very thin garments, made of marble, the form of the body appears in perfect proportion. In the same place is a marble basin of various kinds of precious stones, whose price cannot be estimated, and nothing like it has been seen elsewhere; it was dug up long ago from the Baths of Titus Vespasian. Nearby are seen Mercury and Cybele, turreted on the head, beside whom stands a lion, and Attis with a pine, from which hang a pipe and a cymbal. Here too is a rustic fountain, in which gods and sea monsters are carved. Here also are effigies of various princes, among them Paul III, Supreme Pontiff, and Charles V, Emperor Augustus, painted by the hand of Michelangelo. At the Swiss guard station is a marble statue, one of the runners; an excellent work. To mention the palaces of the others would be long. Only these, and the private houses, are recorded from the notice of the most illustrious Francis Schott, Doctor of Law, and of other more recent writers, in which the monuments of antiquity are preserved. In the palace of Cardinal Dandini, near St Catherine in the Borgo, is a marble head of Agrippina, mother of Nero, also of Emperor Hadrian, and of the beloved boy Antinous; also of Marcus Aurelius and of a certain Sabina, a woman-

units.la: {y} Cardinalis Dandini Mulieris: alterum denique Hadriani Simulacrum, sed mutilum. Ibidem in Cardinalis Strozzæ, præter Bibliothecam, Aves Paradisi apodes, aliaque, Armamentarium est, omni Armorum genere instructum, cum huius ætatis, tum veterum exterarumque gentium. Palatium Cæsiorum ita variis rebus instructum, ut vel eius solius causa Romam quis Antiquitatis amans proficisci debeat. Area prima Statuis gravida est & Inscriptionibus. Icones ibi Hippolyte Amazonis, Apollinis, Sabinæ mulieris. In Horti proximi Area prima Bacchus, Basi impositus, visitur; in altera Pas aheneum cum Fauno; in tertia Neptunus in Basi. in quarta Apollo Barbyton tenens. Hic & Marmor Agrippina, Filiæ M. Agrippæ; & Iuliæ, Augusti Cæsaris Filiæ: Pallas item armata & Hermaphroditus. Ad dextram Fons est. Undique circumstant xxii Termini marmorei, Faunus, Iupiter Hammon, Pompeius Magnus, Demosthenes, Speusippus Philosophus. Portæ obiecta est Roma de Dacia victa triumphans, throno insidens, galeata, amicta, lauream manu tenens Coronam. Dacia conspicitur mœrentis habitu. Trophæa circum Armaque barbarica, & duo victi Reges semiconiisi ex lapide Numidico: duæ item Parcarum Statuæ, totidemque Sphynges ex eodem lapide, Basibus inlocatæ. Proximum est Ædificium rotundum, quod ab re Antiquarium dicitur. In fronte est Iovis vultus porphyreticus: & hinc Othonis Imper. illius Poppææ Coniugis Imago: supra Statuæ quinque; Pallado, Cereris, Victoriæ, Copiæ & Dianæ. Intus est Somni vel Quietis, seu, ut quibusdam placet, Æsculapii Papaver tenentis, Simulacrum: mox Sabinæ Mulieris altera Imago. In porta, ad sinistram colossea Iovis est facies; ad dextram, Herculis: in medio, Palladis. Sub Hercule est Satyrus; cui adstat Invenis, Fistulam inflans septemphicem. Sub Iove est Caput Pyrrhi, Epirotarum Regis, galeatum: proxima est Leda, malum tenens, & Cupido. Prope sunt Capita Porcia Catonis Iovis, Ganymedo, Dianæ, Neptuni; & antiquissimum signum Ægyptium, quod dicitur Caput Mareth, Matris Osiridis, vel ut alij volunt, Opis seu Cybeles Matris Deum. Ad portam Statuæ duæ, quæ lævæ est. Arietis Phryxi ex candidissimo marmore: Basi inscriptum, SECURA SIMPLICITAS; quæ dextra, Ino, in cuius Basi legitur INNOXIA FORTITUDO. Iuxta est Heliogabalus Imperator integer, stolatus in Basi sculpti adfabre Sacrificantium ritus & habitus. Supra est Imperatoris Imago Triumphalis, Curru quadrijugo vecta. Ibidem est Sinna, ex Æthiopico Lapide, qualis ab Ægyptiis adorabatur. In Cœnaculo Bacchi caput est ex rubro lapide; & supra Neptunus Quadriga Vectus. Pomona Dea bis ibi spectatur. In Museo, cuius pavimentum vermiculatum, Sedes tessellatæ, Capita visuntur Romanorum illustrium, Scipionis Africani, M. Catonis, M. Antonii III-Viri, C. Iulii Cæsaris, Septimij Severi, L. Sullæ, C. Neronis, Iuliæ Mammææ, M. Antonini Caracallæ, Hadriani, Alexandri, Cleopatræ, Faustinæ, & Sabinæ Matronæ. Bibliotheca Libris Antiquis Recentibusque referta. In interiore Conclavi Gemmæ, Lapidesque pretiosi omnis generis. Iuxta est Scipio Nasica, M. Brutus, Hadrianus Imperator, Cupido dormiens, Puer Anseris gutturi gemmam constringens manu, aliaque laudata ab Artificibus Monumenta. In Palatio Farnesiano, quod à Paullo III Farnesio P. M. summus imperiis excitatum, tot tantaque antiqua visuntur Monumenta, ut sola in libri molem excrescere commode, si pro dignitate commemorentur, possint. In Peristylo Porticus, inter Columnas, duo sunt Herculis cum Leonis exuvis & Clava: Minoris Basi insculptum ΓΑΤΚΩΝ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΟΣ ΕΠΟΙΕΙ. Ad sinistram Iupiter Tonans seu Fulgurator est. Gladiatores ibidem duo Colossei. Gradus ascendenti Fuviorum occurrunt Statuæ marmoreæ, iacentium habitu, Urnasque tenentium, quibus Aquam effundant. Mox duo Numidæ Reges Captivi, erecti ad utramque Portæ partem. In superiore contignatione Cardinalis est Bibliotheca, exaratos calamo Libros habens plurimos. Museum item est Fulvii Ursini Romani, hominis doctissimi, qui rara non Urbis modo, sed & Orbis Numismatum, Gemmarum, Librorum incredibili sumtu collegit. In altera Tiberim versus Area M. Aurelii Imperatoris ingens Statua spectatur, chlamydiata, basi impositia, atque inscripta. In ædicula opus est marmoreum Diræ raptæ à Tauro, cuius Plautus, Propertius, Plinius meminerunt. Alia prætereo. Apud Cardinalem Sfortiam varia sunt, præter Bibliothecam, Libris manu scriptis plenam. In ædibus Cardinalis Putei Capita visuntur antiqua, Augusti, Hadriani, Faustinæ Imperatoris, & alia ignota: Inscriptiones variæ, Vasaque ex Alabastro & Similae lapide
units.tr: Cardinal Dandini's woman; and finally another statue of Hadrian, but mutilated. In the same place, in the palace of Cardinal Strozzi, besides the library, there are birds of paradise without feet, and other things, and an armoury, fitted out with every kind of arms, both of this age and of the ancients and foreign nations. The palace of the Caesii is so richly furnished that a lover of antiquity ought to go to Rome for its sake alone. The first court is full of statues and inscriptions. There are images there of Hippolyte the Amazon, Apollo, and a Sabine woman. In the first court of the neighbouring garden stands Bacchus on a pedestal; in the second is a bronze Pan with a Faun; in the third Neptune on a pedestal; in the fourth Apollo holding a barbiton. Here too are a marble Agrippina, daughter of Marcus Agrippa, and Julia, daughter of the emperor Augustus; also Pallas in armour, and a Hermaphroditus. On the right there is a fountain. Around on every side stand twenty-two marble herms: Faunus, Jupiter Ammon, Pompey the Great, Demosthenes, Speusippus the philosopher. Opposite the gate is Rome triumphing over conquered Dacia, seated on a throne, helmeted, clothed, holding a laurel crown in her hand. Dacia is seen in the dress of a mourner. Around are trophies and barbarian arms, and two conquered kings, half-seated, of Numidian stone; likewise two statues of the Fates, and as many sphinxes of the same stone, set on pedestals. Next is a round building, which is called the Antiquarium from its purpose. On its front is a face of Jupiter in porphyry, and beside it an image of the emperor Otho and of his wife Poppaea; above are five statues: Pallas, Ceres, Victory, Plenty and Diana. Inside is a statue of Sleep or Rest, or, as some prefer, of Aesculapius holding a poppy; soon after comes another image of a Sabine woman. At the gate, on the left, is a colossal face of Jupiter; on the right, of Hercules; in the middle, of Pallas. Under Hercules is a Satyr, beside whom stands a youth blowing a seven-reed pipe. Under Jupiter is the head of Pyrrhus, king of the Epirotes, helmeted; next to it is Leda, holding an apple, and Cupid. Nearby are heads of Porcia, daughter of Cato, Jupiter, Ganymede, Diana and Neptune; and a very ancient Egyptian figure, which is called the head of Mareth, mother of Osiris, or, as others will have it, of Ops or Cybele, the mother of the gods. At the gate are two statues: the one on the left is of the ram of Phrixus in the purest marble, with the inscription on its base SECURE SIMPLICITY; the one on the right is Ino, on whose base is read INNOCENT FORTITUDE. Beside it is the emperor Heliogabalus, whole and robed, and on its base are skilfully carved the rites and dress of those who sacrifice. Above is an image of the emperor in triumph, borne on a chariot drawn by four horses. There too is a Sinnas, of Ethiopian stone, such as the Egyptians used to worship. In the dining room is a head of Bacchus of red stone; and above it Neptune carried in a four-horse chariot. The goddess Pomona is seen there twice. In the museum, whose floor is inlaid with mosaic and whose seats are tessellated, are to be seen heads of famous Romans: Scipio Africanus, Marcus Cato, Mark Antony the triumvir, Gaius Julius Caesar, Septimius Severus, Lucius Sulla, Gaius Nero, Julia Mamaea, Marcus Antoninus Caracalla, Hadrian, Alexander, Cleopatra, Faustina, and a Sabine matron. The library is stocked with books, ancient and recent. In the inner room are gems and precious stones of every kind. Nearby are Scipio Nasica, Marcus Brutus, the emperor Hadrian, a sleeping Cupid, a boy grasping a gem in his hand to hold a goose by the throat, and other monuments praised by the craftsmen. In the Farnese palace, which was erected by Pope Paul III Farnese, so many and such great ancient monuments are to be seen that they alone could well swell a book to great size, if they were recorded as they deserve. In the peristyle, between the columns of the portico, are two Herculeses with the lion's skin and club; on the smaller base is inscribed ATHENAIOS MADE IT [ΓΑΤΚΩΝ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΟΣ ΕΠΟΙΕΙ]. On the left is Jupiter the Thunderer, or the Lightning-bearer. There are two colossal gladiators there. As one climbs the steps, marble statues of river-gods meet the eye, in reclining posture, holding urns from which they pour water. Soon after come two captive Numidian kings, set up on either side of the gate. In the upper storey is the cardinal's library, with very many books written by hand. There is also the museum of Fulvio Orsini of Rome, a most learned man, who gathered at incredible expense rare coins, gems and books, not only of the city but of the whole world. In another court facing the Tiber stands a huge statue of the emperor Marcus Aurelius, wearing a cloak, set on a base and inscribed. In a small shrine is a marble work of Dirce being dragged by the bull, which Plautus, Propertius and Pliny mention. I pass over other things. At the house of Cardinal Sforza there are various things, besides a library full of manuscripts. In the house of Cardinal Pozzi are to be seen ancient heads of Augustus, Hadrian, the emperor Faustina, and others unknown; various inscriptions, and vessels of alabaster and of similar stone.

units.la: Card. Putei. prece ] minimo. Palatii Cardinalis S. Horæ admiranda multa continet. Apud Cardinalem Montanum, Capita ]uvenis, Pallas, Iulia Cæsaris, Augusta, & aliorum, Tiburtinæ advecta. Apud Capitolinum quamvis servantur Iuno Tempora Lacunæ, Corpora huius pedes de graphice depicta, Dei Priapi Mars, Saturnus, et pars in conclavi Iuno Iovis XII. Sunt & Marmorea Statuæ Iovis, Cerealis, Lucii Veneris, Aesculapii, Capitolina Venus, Cerialis, Ioppales, Imperatores, Mariae. Tituli item Aelii Nerva Augusti, Statua, Coeum novacula dulcedinis, quæ olim in Coniunctione Palatinum in tomum Cardinalis Vallensis variis Antoninianus cenavit. Monumentum ibi ita coronat, Dei Pietas, Caligula, inferius Inscriptiones, multæ Graece atque Latine, in parte superiore Iovis et columnæ Antipatri Zeus, Iudæorum, Atlantis mortui, et temporis Concordiæ et Coelium: in prima columna Nerva Anna gerantes capitum: in Coelio Iulii Caesaris, Augusti Cæsaris, Gaia Imperatoris: item Aulus Ioannes, Capita, in pars Herculis Stoici Pauli. Statuæ hæc Lapidis Pallades, Castor, Phaethon, Thetis, Mauri, Apollinis ex lapide Lydio, Hercules Nemæi in Leonem bis occanti, Cæsar Traianus Hadrianus, Pompeius Neronis, Lucillæ Pompeianæ, duorum Nereum, unius Nerei, Iovis, et Mariæ manus, quæ solo iam manu tenet: lego caput, et quinque Sidera Mulieres Neptuni. Tabula Meleagri Venatorum continens, Faunus pelle tectus: Mercurius palmo in levam brachium revolutus, Pepinus Solitarius in tabula: ad lunam Iunonis eli togata, Hadriani Imp. paludatus, Hercules cum Leonis exuvis, Ulixes Iuniz, et Mulier ignota: Reges quatuor Caesar, manus marmoreus, reliqui ex parte Iuno, Hermaphroditus, Iovis, Bacchus, Hercules, Apollo Praetextus Opus, Caesar, Cæsar Imp. M. Antonius Pius, Constantinus Magnus et Caeliades aliquot sculpta, quæ hic creditur esse Statuæ, item Memnon in superiore parte Tabulæ terna IX, in quibus M. Aurelius Antoninus tenipta Triumphi, in diis variis aut Iovis Venus: item Caesar cum Tympano, Natali in Chloe, Meleagri alterum Leonis trisulcæ Statuæ, Hadriani, Caracalla, et ignotæ Feminæ. In vetere eodem Cardinalis Palatino tunc antiquitatis lusus Statuæ; Ganymedes cum Aquila et Fulmine, Apollo, Iuno, Iulius, Pheidias, Mercurius, Faunus et Gladiator. Ad levam porticus est Orphei cum lyra et ita chori, tunc gestans uvas: Atys Phrix sedens et tabulam infans: Iuno caput et Leonis, quam aliquid volunt esse Terbyn vel Gadaream, Lupa ex porphyro Romulum lactans et Remum: Hinc Sergius Augustus, et Dei Lupae Puerum videns, Iovis Camillus adjectens, Antoninus Pius, Carolus, Ferre Brutus, Caput, et Faustinæ et Marci Aurelii coniugis. In Domo, quæ tunc Cardinalis Sirmondi Colonica Statua vilitas, et Hercules cum Clavi et Leonis exuviis, ad cuius pedes iacet Taurus: Senex item Sidera et Nymphæ. In Monte Aventino Ædes sunt Graecorum, olim Cardinalis Caesar Montifrantur ibi Capita Augustorum, Iulij Cæsaris, Claudii, Septimii Severi, Getæ, Philippi, Claudii, Aureliani, Antonini Caracallæ, item M. Agrippæ, Pyrrhi ipsorum Regis, Alexandri, Mummea: Statuæ item Antonius Pius, Caracallæ Sirmiae, M. Aurelii, Faustinæ Iunioris, Traiani, Hadriani, L. Veri: Apollo insuper Arcum tenens, Cupido dormiens in Clava Herculis et Leonis exuviis. Tabula ibidem offenditur loco in quadrato, cuius precium ob marmoris excellentiam artium non patet. In Campo Martio Palatium est Cardinalis Rodolphi Pe Corpendis. Iuni in hortulo Triumvir, Nilus cum Crocodilo, Nar Fluvius, Matrona brachium tenens in ipsi lucarum habens, unde Cleopatram quendam putant Mater in illi duplex. Hic Simulacra Apollinis, Fraxinus, Cereris, Atys Pallantis lapis, et aliorum. Urna ex eodem Lapide toto Palatio inter Statuas adpositae. Libri duobus locis antiquissimi, in mensis ferreis Græci, Latini, Hebræi, Arabici. Ad dextram Capita Galeriae Lucinius, Iulia Cæsaris Aug. F. Antoniae, Cornelii. Inf. superiores marmoreæ variæ: Tabula una ex Lapide Basaltae nigro et dentatissimo, roris Aegyptus insulfris. Ad levam Capita Iulii Mammæ, Iuno redens, Mulieris Caramella ornata, vel Mitra Syriæ, Heroidis, Faunæ, Infra in tene cum iuncta purpurea: Alexander Magnus in tabula cum Pœro alato: Canopi caput ex lapide Aegypto viridi, et Iacobi Hamonensis. In secundo Musæo tali omnes pereunt. Capita Antonini Caracallæ, Iulia Titi F. Galbae, Nomæ Pompeii, Domitiani, Septimii Severi, Diadumeni Imperatorum, et aliorum: Libri rursum antiqui cum in Membranis cum in Papyro Aegyptia: Inscriptiones quoque et Epitaphia pretiosi in lapidibus. Tabula gradus marmorea cum Græca Inscriptione: Iuno ibidem sedens, et Alexandri Magni quam morientis caput, item Bruti. Ad dextram
units.tr: Of Cardinal Putei (prece minimo). The Palace of Cardinal S. Horatius contains many admirable things. At Cardinal Montanus's: heads of a youth, Pallas, Julia the daughter of Caesar, Augusta, and others, brought from Tibur. At the Capitol, though preserved, are Juno, the Tempora, the Lacunae, the feet of this figure painted in the graphic manner, the god Priapus, Mars, Saturn, and a part of Juno of Jupiter XII in the room. There are also marble statues of Jupiter, Ceres, Lucius, Venus, Aesculapius, the Capitoline Venus, Ceres, Ioppales, emperors, and Maria. Likewise inscriptions of Aelius Nerva Augustus, a statue, and the Coeum (a razor of sweetness), which once in the Coniunctio on the Palatine, in the villa of Cardinal Vallensis, the Antonine dined in various ways. The monument there is crowned in this way: the Piety of God, Caligula, and below it inscriptions, many in Greek and Latin; in the upper part Jupiter and the column of Antipater, Zeus, the Jews, the dead Atlas, and the time of Concord and the Caelian; on the first column Nerva and Anna bearing heads; on the Caelian, of Julius Caesar, of Augustus Caesar, of the emperor Gaius; likewise Aulus John, heads, and part of Hercules, the Stoic of Paul. These statues: the Pallases of stone, Castor, Phaethon, Thetis, the Moors, Apollo of Lydian stone, Hercules of Nemea strangling the lion twice, Caesar Trajan, Hadrian, Pompey of Nero, Lucilla of Pompeius, two Nereids, one Nereus, Jupiter, and the hands of Maria, which now holds the sole alone; I read the head, and five stars, the women of Neptune. A tablet containing Meleager's hunters; Faunus covered with a skin; Mercury with his arm turned back a palm to the left; Pepinus alone on the tablet; by the moon, Juno of the togated Aeli; Hadrian the emperor in military cloak; Hercules with the lion's hides; Ulysses of Juniz, and an unknown woman. Four kings: Caesar, a marble hand, the rest in part Juno, Hermaphroditus, Jupiter, Bacchus, Hercules, Apollo; a praetextate work; Caesar; Caesar the emperor Marcus Antoninus Pius; Constantine the Great, and several carved Caeliades, which here are believed to be statues; likewise Memnon in the upper part of the tablet, three times nine, in which Marcus Aurelius Antoninus (the temple of the triumph) appears among various gods, or Jupiter and Venus; likewise Caesar with a drum, Natalis in Chloe, the other Meleager, a three-pronged lion statue, Hadrian, Caracalla, and an unknown woman. In the same old Palatine room of the cardinal, statues of antique play: Ganymede with the eagle and thunderbolt, Apollo, Juno, Julius, Phidias, Mercury, Faunus, and a gladiator. To the left of the portico is Orpheus with his lyre and a chorus, then one carrying grapes; Attis the Phrygian sitting and a child holding a tablet; Juno's head and a lion, which some want to be Terbyn or Gadarea; a she-wolf of porphyry suckling Romulus and Remus. Hence Sergius Augustus, and seeing the boy of the god-wolf, Camillus adding Jupiter, Antoninus Pius, Charles, Brutus Ferre, a head, and of Faustina and of Marcus Aurelius's wife. In the house which was then of Cardinal Sirmond, a common statue of a rustic, and Hercules with a club and lion's hides, at whose feet lies a bull; likewise an old man, the stars and nymphs. On the Aventine Hill are the temples of the Greeks, formerly of Cardinal Caesar; there are heads of the Augusti, of Julius Caesar, Claudius, Septimius Severus, Geta, Philip, Claudius, Aurelian, Antoninus Caracalla, likewise of Marcus Agrippa, of Pyrrhus the king himself, of Alexander, and Mammaea; likewise statues of Antoninus Pius, Caracalla of Sirmium, Marcus Aurelius, the younger Faustina, Trajan, Hadrian, and Lucius Verus; moreover Apollo holding a bow, and Cupid sleeping on the club of Hercules and the lion's hides. A square tablet is found there, whose price cannot be determined because of the excellence of the marble and the art. In the Campus Martius is the palace of Cardinal Rodolph, Pe Corpendis. In the little garden of Juni, a triumvir, the Nile with a crocodile, the river Nar, a matron holding an arm and having a light in herself, whence some think it is Cleopatra; a double mother in her. Here are images of Apollo, the Fraxinus, Ceres, Attis, the stone of Pallas, and of others. An urn of the same stone is placed among the statues in the whole palace. Books in two places, very ancient, on iron tables: Greek, Latin, Hebrew, Arabic. To the right heads of Galeria, Lucinius, Julia the daughter of Augustus Caesar, Antonia, Cornelius. Below, various marble figures on the upper floor; one tablet of black and very jagged basalt, Egypt sprinkled with dew. To the left heads of Julius, Mamma, Juno returning, a woman adorned with a caramella or a Syrian mitre, a heroine, a faun; below, in the tent with purple attached: Alexander the Great in a tablet with a winged Pero; a head of Canopus of green Egyptian stone, and of Jacob of Hamon. In the second museum all perish in the same way: heads of Antoninus Caracalla, Julia, Titus the son of Galba, Nomas of Pompey, Domitian, Septimius Severus, Diadumenus the emperors, and of others. Again ancient books, both on parchment and on Egyptian papyrus; inscriptions and epitaphs also, precious, on stones. A marble step tablet with a Greek inscription; Juno sitting there, and the head of Alexander the Great as he dies, likewise of Brutus. To the right

units.la: {1} Cardinalis Vallensis varias Antoninus cenavit. dextram Portæ Venus est; Juvenis etiam magni artificij. In cœnaculo colosseum Muliebris caput, & L. Veri Juvenis atque adulti, Poppæa Sabina, Hadriani, Annij Veri, & Græci hominis, Termini ex marmore æmathite, Satyri, Cupidinis. Videre ibidem est præstantissimorum Italiæ Pictorum imagines, Raphaelis Urbinatis, Michaelis Angeli Bonaroti, & aliorum: Marmora quoque variis inscripta Characteribus & linguis. In tertio Musæo capita sunt illustrium Virorum LXXVI, quorum XIII maiora, singularis artis, ex marmore candidissimo, unum Veneris, duo Vetulatum, totidem Herculis, unum Palladis, &c. Hic & Satyrus, & Puer pyorans: Simulacrum quoque Cybeles ex marmore nigro Ægyptio, Anubis Cynocephali, Herculis, Satyri cornu inflantis, Fauni, Socratis. In vale æneo sculpti Pueri Piscantes, Apollo, Gladiator, Aquila, Taurus, &c: Armamentarium omni Armorum genere instructissimum. Apud Valesium Episcopum, Horologium conspicitur cum Zodiaci Signis XII & Imaginibus, quales hodie in vulgaribus Kalendarijs: Inscriptiones item, Signa & Statuæ. Apud Episcopum Saulum in fronte Statua est mulieris, & intus caput M. Ciceronis, M. Tullij F. In Palatio Conservatorum incredibile quantum sit Statuarum, Tabularum, Inscriptionum, Marmorum. Leo ibi mordicus Equum tenens. Ad gradus Columna rostrata cum sua Inscriptione, in honorem C. Duilij posita. Spectatur ibidem Tabula Triumphantis M. Aurely quadrigis de Dacia victa. Superius ad Portæ ingressum Mensura est Romani Græcique Pedis; marmoreæ tabulæ incisæ. Prope C. Marij togata Statua. Intus Parietes cœnaculorum Picturis egregijs rerum gestarum Theodosij & Arcadij Imperatorum ornantur, habitu antiquo. Hic & Hercules æneus deauratus, dextra Clavam, sinistra Malum tenens Hesperidum. Scriptum in ejus Basi:
units.tr: {1} Cardinal Vallensis: the Antonine dined in various ways. To the right of the gate is Venus; a youth also of great craftsmanship. In the dining room the colossal female head, and of Lucius Verus, a youth and a grown man, Poppaea Sabina, Hadrian, Annius Verus, and a Greek man; Terminus of hematite marble, a satyr, a Cupid. There can be seen the images of the most outstanding painters of Italy, Raphael of Urbino, Michelangelo Buonarroti, and others; also marbles inscribed with various characters and languages. In the third museum are heads of 76 illustrious men, of which 13 are larger, of singular art, of the purest marble: one of Venus, two of old women, as many of Hercules, one of Pallas, etc. Here also a satyr and a boy weeping; also an image of Cybele of black Egyptian marble, Anubis of the dog-headed type, of Hercules, a satyr blowing a horn, of a faun, of Socrates. On a bronze vessel are carved boys fishing, Apollo, a gladiator, an eagle, a bull, etc.; an armoury most fully equipped with every kind of arms. At the bishop of Valois's, a clock is seen with the 12 signs of the zodiac and images such as are today in common calendars; likewise inscriptions, signs and statues. At Bishop Saulus's, in the front is a statue of a woman, and inside a head of Marcus Cicero, son of Marcus Tullius. In the Palace of the Conservators there is an incredible number of statues, paintings, inscriptions, and marbles. A lion there biting a horse. At the steps a rostral column with its inscription, set up in honour of Gaius Duilius. There is seen there a painting of Marcus Aurelius triumphing in a chariot drawn by four horses over Dacia conquered. Higher up, at the entrance of the gate, is a measure of the Roman and Greek foot, cut into marble tablets. Near Gaius Marius a togate statue. Within, the walls of the dining rooms are adorned with excellent paintings of the deeds of the emperors Theodosius and Arcadius, in ancient dress. Here also a gilded bronze Hercules, holding a club in his right hand and an apple of the Hesperides in his left. Written on its base:

units.la: HERCVLI. VICTORI POLLENTI. POTENTI INVICTO D. D. L. M. FRONTO
units.tr: To Hercules the Victor, the Mighty, the Powerful, the Unconquered: Fronto gave this gladly and deservedly as a votive offering.
