units.la: 30 Ibidem Satyrus marmoreus caprinis pellibus, adligatus arboris trunco. Mox in Columna marmorea Statua est Viri inclinati æne a, Spinam è Pedis planta extrahentis: altera item laudatissima æ nea Lupa, Romulum Remumque lactantis, quæ olim in Comitio servabatur prope Ficum Ruminalem. Ingressu Peristylium Fasti illi occurrunt, toto terrarum orbe decantati, Magistratuum ac Triumphorum Romanorum Veterum. Nec illud silentio prætereundum legi ibidem Elogium Rerum præclare in Belgio gestarum ab Alexandro Farnesio, Octavij F. Duce Parmensi, cuius & Statua ibidem ostenditur. In vasto Cancellariæ Palatio, primo ingressu offert se duplex Colossea Statua: Opis & Cereris putantur. In superiore cœnaculo capita sunt Antonini Pij, Septimy Severi, Titi, Domitiani, Augusti, Getæ Imperatoris, Sabinæ Mulieris, Pyrrhi Epirotarum regis, Cupidinis, & Gladiatoris. In conclavi etiam variæ, & hominum ignotorum I Imagines. In Palatio S. Marci Labrum ingens est marmoreum, quod in Thermis Agrippæ inventum. Ad templi portam Fauna, vel, ut alij, Bona Dea statua. Palatium ascendenti multæ se offerunt Imagines, Signaque marmorea: Tabulæ item cum Sacrificantium ritu. In Circo Cleopatra est, Mulieresque circum plangentes, & alia miranda. In arca Xenodochij S. Ioannis Arca Araque ostenduntur marmoreæ; Labra Balneorum & Thermarum; Marmoribus incisæ Figuræ, Satyrorum Chori, Accubitus tacentium ritu, Amazonum pugnæ, Meleagri Venatio, aliaque id genus monumenta. In Sabellorum Domo, quæ est in Theatro Marcelli, sculptus ostenditur Leo in Tabula marmorea, cum tribus ad pugnam armatis: in Hortis Pilæ diversæ, 50 in quibus Herculis Labores; Imagines viriles, & Mercurij fragmenta. Apud Fabios prope S. Luciam Atlas Cœlum sustinet. Ostenduntur item Æsculapius, Caracalla Imperator, Bacchus sed fractus. In Palatio Mattheiorum videre est Capita inlustriorum virorum, cum pectoribus in suis Basibus, & alia LV absque pectoribus; Urnam Marmoream, Vasa, Pateras, Lucernas, Crateres, aliaque spectatu digna; Laocoontis insuper caput artificiosissimum: Tabulam marmoream, in qua Circus expressus cum suis Metis, Obeliscis, Dolijs & Aris; alteram item Discumbentium in Triclinio cum Syntheli. In Hortulis Statuæ sunt muliebres, Pan inpila grandi sculptus cum Syringe & Cupidinc. Plurima in eodem Palatio Antiquitatis Monimenta, Epitaphia, Inscriptiones. In Ædibus Maximorum Pyrrhi Statua est coloßea, galeata, armata, quam duobus Ducatorum millibus redemit olim Angelus de Maximis. Caput ibidem Julij Cæsaris marmoreum, Tabulæ, Sterna, Marmora, Vasa, Pictura: In Albertinorum, Inscriptiones variæ Statuaque Deorum: In Cinciorum, inter alia Vertumnus vilitur cum Liguine & Venabulo. Statua item Apollinis Pythij integra: In Norcinarum, Inscriptione non pauca, & Adonidis caput Baculum tenentis, canis item, qui spirare videtur ac vivere; cuius pretium quinque Ducatorum millibus æstimatur. Est ibidem Venus magni pecn. Diana Venatrix, succincta, Pharetra, Arcu, Sagittis ornata: Orcades item duæ, quæ Pharetras & Arcus gestant; Bene Tiberius Simulacrum, dextra Speculum, leva Sertum ex Spicis tenens, opus est Praxitelis absolutissimum: In Bufalorum, Signa sunt: Apollinis, Veneris cum Cupidine Lovis, Junonis, aliorumque Deorum; Capita Jovis, Pallados, Apollinis, Bacchi, Martis, Herculis, Mercurii & Atjia ... In hortulo præter alia singularia Colossæ tunc Statuæ, Cerberi Tricipitis, & Tripodis sunt & Imagines Dianæ, Fomnæ, Sacerdotis Flaminis, Veneris, Herculis, Sabinæ matronæ, Leæ ex lapide pretioso. in Cubiculo, Mariy (septies Cos.) Hadriani, M. Aurelij, Commodi, Maximini, Augustorum, Græca aliquanto infultus, Scipionis Africani, Hadriani Imperatoris: mox Herculis, Vespasiani, M. Aurelii, Getæ Imp. Antonini Pii, Ligæ Athenientium Oratoris, hoc titulo, ΑΥΣΙΑΣ: Ad Horti extremum Tabula marmorea, in qua tres Charites expressæ. Ad Fontem, qui Horto additus, tres Musæ sunt, & Caracalla Imperator: in Loculis vero repositi Demetrius, Maximinus, Philippus, & Claudius. In Domo Petri de Radicibus Pacchus ostenditur, Pampinis redimitus, Satyro innixus, dextra Vasculum tenens, Musæ tres, longis Instatus amictæ: una Librum, altera Musicum Instrumentum, tertia Larvam gestans; Caroli Magni caput: Fragmenta item Cupidinis, Herculis, Floræ: In Nicolai Guiffæ, Statua Nudi Hominis, quæ ab Cultro adjacente Vulgo Gladiatoris nominatur; putatur Gladiatoris esse dimicantis: In Georgij Serlupi ad S. Angelum caput est Vespasiani Imper. colossicum, marmoris candidissimi, operis absolutii. In propinqua Domo Gentilis Delphini multa illustrium Capita, L. Veri, & M. Aurelij Juvenis, Faunique; Pueri item suaviter ridentes, aliaque sex: Urna præterea Tabulaque variæ. Apud Valerium Crucium ad Iudæorum Vicum, in Hortulo visitur Hercules, & Hippolyta Amazonum una Equo insidens; Pan leonina indutus; cum Fistula vel Calamorum; in Pila Meleagri Venatio repræsentata; in Deambulacro varia Capita, ut & Apollinis Statua, & Herculis Anteum brachio sustinentis, quæ suis pedibus stat sine Basi; Faunus item æneus & Tigris marmorea: Apud Onuphrii Crucium Togati Statua ostenditur, cui adscriptum in Tabula, VALERIVS PVBLICOLA: Apud Hieronymum Crucium in Tabula sculpti quinque Fasces Consulares cum Securibus, uti adornatas indicat Titulus: item Medius Fidius. Honos quoque & Virtus, quos Amor comunget. In Ædibus Ceuoli Statuæ plurimæ supra in Conclavi: In Bindi Antonini, concinno ornine videntur Effigies Vespasiani, Mucij Scævolæ, Augusti Cæsaris, Antonini Caracallæ, Julij Cæsaris, Galeria Faustina, Marij septies Cos., Satyrorum: Cupido item Lupum tenens, & Antinoüs, aliaque Signa marmorea, Picturæque recentiores: In Petri Strozzæ, cum aliis, Meleager ingens & Atalanta, opus ex marmore laudatissimum. Pauli Iordanis Domus varia ostendit cum Novi, tum Antiqui operis Monimenta: Ardicin Statuam Viri elegantem. Palthio ad lævam inflexo: Vincentij Stampæ in Campo Phiceo, Imagines Lucretiæ, Iuliæ T. F., Iuliæ Mammeæ, Ælij Pertinacis, Drusi Hadriani, M. Aurelij, Elagabali, Neronis, Augusti, Palladis, Apollinis, Philippi Amyntæ Macedonis filij; Satyrus iuniper, Venus, Puer ridens, Faunus, Terminus, Tres Charites, & ignotiores supra xx Statuas. Apud Franciscum Liscam tres Statuæ Virginis Vestalis, Stola amictæ; Iuliæ Pompeii Magni uxoris togata; Panis semicapri, ad cuius pedes jacet Aries: Sub porticu Pomona, Silvanus nudus, Famæ, Bacchus, Arethusa Nympha, Cybele, Faunus, Iuno Lucina togata, Hebe Iunonis Filia, Apollo, Inscriptiones variæ. Apud Iordanem Boccabellum Getæ Imperator visitur, cum Dianæ trinepte, Iove, Cybele, Faustina, Marcia Otacilla, Pane, Herculè, Cupidine, aliis. Apud Lucam de Mattinis Capita monstrantur Octaviani Augusti, Tiberij, L. Severi, tria Neronis, Bruti Consulis, Iuliæ, Sabinæ, Marij, Asdrubalis, Faunī ridentis, & plus quam xl ignotorum hominum: Apollo item truncus, & Monstrum marinum.
units.tr: 30 Also there, a marble Satyr wrapped in goatskins, bound to the trunk of a tree. Soon, on a marble column, stands a bronze statue of a man bending over and pulling a thorn from the sole of his foot. Another, also most celebrated, is a bronze she-wolf suckling Romulus and Remus, which was formerly kept in the Comitium near the Ruminal fig tree. On entering the peristyle one meets those Fasti of the magistrates and triumphs of the ancient Romans, celebrated throughout the whole world. Nor should it be passed over in silence that I read there an inscription of the splendid deeds done in the Low Countries by Alexander Farnese, son of Octavio, Duke of Parma, whose statue is also shown there. In the vast Palace of the Chancery, at the first entrance, a double colossal statue presents itself; they are thought to be Ops and Ceres. In the upper dining room are heads of Antoninus Pius, Septimius Severus, Titus, Domitian, Augustus, the Emperor Geta, a woman of Sabina, Pyrrhus, king of the Epirotes, Cupid, and a gladiator. In the room there are also various images of unknown men. In the Palazzo of St Mark there is a huge marble basin, which was found in the Baths of Agrippa. At the temple door is a statue of Fauna, or, as others say, the Good Goddess. As one ascends the palace many images and marble statues present themselves, and also tablets showing the rite of the sacrificers. In the Circus there is Cleopatra, with women lamenting around her, and other marvels. In the chest of the hospice of St John are shown marble chests and altars; basins of the baths and thermae; figures carved in marble, choruses of satyrs, reclining figures in the manner of silent banqueters, battles of the Amazons, the Hunt of Meleager, and other monuments of that kind. In the house of the Sabelli, which is in the Theatre of Marcellus, a carved lion is shown on a marble slab, with three men armed for battle; in the gardens are various basins, on which are the Labours of Hercules; male images, and fragments of Mercury. At the Fabii, near St Lucy, Atlas holds up the heavens. Also shown are Aesculapius, the Emperor Caracalla, and Bacchus, but broken. In the Palazzo Mattei one can see heads of illustrious men with breasts on their bases, and fifty-five others without breasts; a marble urn, vases, dishes, lamps, mixing-bowls, and other things worth seeing; moreover a most skilful head of Laocoön; a marble slab on which the Circus is represented with its turning-posts, obelisks, barrels and altars; and another of people reclining at table in a dining room, with their coverlets. In the little gardens are female statues; Pan, carved on a large basin, with a pan-pipe, and Cupid. In the same palace are very many monuments of antiquity, epitaphs, inscriptions. In the house of the Massimi there is a colossal statue of Pyrrhus, helmeted and armed, which Angelo de' Massimi once bought back for two thousand ducats. There also is a marble head of Julius Caesar, tablets, pavements, marbles, vases, paintings. In the house of the Alberteschi, various inscriptions and statues of the gods. In the house of the Cenci, among other things, Vertumnus is seen with a mattock and a hunting-spear. Also an intact statue of Apollo Pythius. In the house of the Norcini, not a few inscriptions, and a head of Adonis holding a staff, and also a dog which seems to breathe and live; its price is valued at five thousand ducats. There too is Venus of great value; Diana the Huntress, girded up and adorned with quiver, bow and arrows; also two Oreads who carry quivers and bows; and a statue of Bene Tiberius, holding a mirror in the right hand and a garland of ears of grain in the left, a most perfect work of Praxiteles. In the house of the Buffalini there are statues of Apollo, Venus with Cupid, Jupiter, Juno, and of other gods; heads of Jupiter, Pallas, Apollo, Bacchus, Mars, Hercules, Mercury and Attis... In the little garden, besides other singular things, there are colossal statues of three-headed Cerberus and a tripod, and images of Diana, Fortune, a flamen priest, Venus, Hercules, a Sabine matron, Leda, in precious stone. In the bedroom, Marius (consul seven times), Hadrian, Marcus Aurelius, Commodus, Maximinus, of the Augusti, of Greek work, somewhat damaged; Scipio Africanus, the Emperor Hadrian; then Hercules, Vespasian, Marcus Aurelius, the Emperor Geta, Antoninus Pius, Lysias the Athenian orator, with this inscription, ΑΥΣΙΑΣ [AUSIAS]. At the far end of the garden is a marble slab on which three Graces are carved. At the fountain attached to the garden are three Muses and the Emperor Caracalla; in the niches are set Demetrius, Maximinus, Philip and Claudius. In the house of Pietro de Radicibus Bacchus is shown, crowned with vine-leaves, leaning on a satyr, holding a little vessel in his right hand; three Muses, clothed in long robes, one holding a book, another a musical instrument, the third carrying a mask; a head of Charlemagne; also fragments of Cupid, Hercules, Flora. In the house of Nicolò Giuffa, a statue of a naked man, which is commonly called a gladiator from the knife lying beside it; it is thought to be of a gladiator fighting. In the house of Giorgio Serlupi near St Angelo is a colossal head of the Emperor Vespasian, of the purest marble, a perfect work. In the nearby house of Gentile Delfini are many heads of illustrious men, Lucius Verus, and Marcus Aurelius as a youth, and of a Faun; also boys smiling sweetly, and six others; besides, an urn and various tablets. At the house of Valerio Cruci near the Jews' quarter, in the little garden, are seen Hercules and Hippolyta, queen of the Amazons, sitting on a horse; Pan clothed in a lion's skin, with a pipe or reeds; on a basin the Hunt of Meleager is represented; in the walkway various heads, as well as a statue of Apollo and of Hercules holding Antaeus aloft with his arm, which stands on its own feet without a base; also a bronze Faun and a marble tiger. At the house of Onofrio Cruci a statue of a man in a toga is shown, to which is inscribed on the tablet the name Valerius Publicola. At the house of Girolamo Cruci, carved on a tablet, are five consular fasces with axes, as the inscription indicates they are adorned; also Medius Fidius, Honour too and Virtue, whom Love joins together. In the house of Ceuoli, many statues upstairs in the room. In the house of Bindo Antonini, in an elegant arrangement, are seen effigies of Vespasian, Mucius Scaevola, Augustus Caesar, Antoninus Caracalla, Julius Caesar, Galeria Faustina, Marius (consul seven times), satyrs; Cupid also, holding a wolf, and Antinous, and other marble statues, and more recent paintings. In the house of Pietro Strozzi, along with others, a huge Meleager and Atalanta, a most praised work in marble. The house of Paolo Giordano shows various monuments both of modern and of ancient work; at Ardicini, an elegant statue of a man. Turning to the left through the palace: at Vincenzo Stampa's in the Campo Phiceo, images of Lucretia, Julia daughter of Titus, Julia Mamaea, Aelius Pertinax, Drusus, Hadrian, Marcus Aurelius, Elagabalus, Nero, Augustus, Pallas, Apollo, Philip son of Amyntas of Macedon; a juniper satyr, Venus, a laughing boy, Faunus, Terminus, the Three Graces, and more than twenty statues of lesser-known figures. At Francesco Lisca's, three statues: a Vestal Virgin, clothed in a stola; Julia, wife of Pompey the Great, in a toga; a half-goat Pan, at whose feet lies a ram. Under the portico: Pomona, naked Silvanus, Fame, Bacchus, the nymph Arethusa, Cybele, Faunus, Juno Lucina in a toga, Hebe daughter of Juno, Apollo, various inscriptions. At Giordano Boccabella's the Emperor Geta is seen, with a great-granddaughter of Diana, Jupiter, Cybele, Faustina, Marcia Otacilla, Pan, Hercules, Cupid, and others. At Luca de' Mattei's heads are shown of Octavian Augustus, Tiberius, Lucius Severus, three of Nero, Brutus the consul, Julia, Sabina, Marius, Hasdrubal, a laughing Faun, and more than forty of unknown men; Apollo also, a torso, and a sea monster.

units.la: Apud Marium Delphinum Gentilis F. multa Numismata visuntur & Inscriptiones. Habet Iulius Cæsarinus Adonidem nudum, Mulierem cum Vase, quam Cariatidem nominant, Venerem marmoream, Muliebres aliquot Figuras, Ianos bifrontes duos; item Propertij Poetæ Caput, Faustina Iunioris, Augusti Iuvenis, Bacchi cum pellibus; aliaque: Ambrosius Lilius, Pompeii caput, & in Tabula xii Herculis Labores, adfabre sculptos: Alianus Celsus, Bacchi Caput cum Pelle in humeris verveecina: Satyri Pueri ridentis Imaginem horibus redimitam: Servat apud se Cavallerius Faunum, Uvam altera manu tenentem, altera Pellem feminam, quæ uvis plena & fructibus; Silenum: Naturam Deam, alteri impositam, Mammis & Animalium Figuris ornatam; Herculem in Tabula marmorea cum Centauro pugnantem; Victoriam alatam, & alia: Hieronymus Alterius, Sacerdotem Cybeles stolatum, manu Vas tenentem; Herculem, spolijs indutum Leonis, trunco innixum; Fragmenta item Antiquitatis varia: Petrus Capoferratus ingentem Affculapium cum Puella & alia. In Fronte Domus Baldi Ferratini Galba Imper. est palmatus: duæ ibidem Vilæ & Tabulæ figuris variis insignes. Apud Io. Baptistam Galletum Statuæ Muliebres plurimæ; & in Tabula Affculapius, dextra Serpentem tenens: Femina item Serpentem comprimens & Pila diversis insculpta Figuris, in quis Herculis, geminos Tauros cornibus apprehendentes. Apud Archintum Statua visitur ænea Servulo: supra, Capita sunt variorum, Iovis Capitolini, & aliorum. In Agone apud Marium Melinum Pallas armata spectatur & galeata, aliæque Muliebres Statuæ, præterea Gladiator Nudus, Hercules, Sabinæ Mulieris Caput, Cupido, Alcibiadis Pueri figura, Silvani & Bacchi ludentes Capita Iovis, Drusi, aliorumque Decem ignota; Satyrus integer, singulari factus artificio. Apud Ioannem Baptistam Melinum tria capita egregia. Ad S. Aloisij apud Alexandrum Rufinum Julium Cæsar est, quasi colosseus, armatus; Augustus quoque Cæsar. Caput item aliud Iulij, & quatuor Virorum Muherumque. Apud Franciscum Ragaterium Capita sunt varia, Bacchi, Alexandri Magni duplex, Iovis, Naturæ, Satyri seu Panos; Imperatorum vero, Trajani, Hadriani, M. Aurelii Pueri, Getæ, hominumque ignotorum xx, & xi ab corporibus avulsa, & Iovis ex Porphyro. In eiusdem vinea ad Portam Flaminiam Inscriptiones variæ, Rex Numida captivus ex Porphyro Lapide: Thorax aneus alicuius Imperatoris. Apud Alexandrinum Cherubinum Inscriptiones & Vultum ridentis caput marmoreum. In Domo Mercelli Porcarij, ante ostium Statua Sedentis marmorea, & in angulo Terminus ingens, cum hac Epigraphe: c. livius. c. f. ivstvs &c. Visuntur ibidem & Visus marmoreus. Ovem devorans: Sacrificium, Marmor insculptum, Diana, summo artificio in Tabula: Candelabrum antiquum triangulare; Corpora trunca, Herculis, Hermaphroditus, Apollinis, Bacchi, Fauni, in Pilis variis Venatio Meleagri, Caucus, cauda Herculis boves attrahens, Herculis Labores. Capita quoque non pauca in conclavi; Inventum quidem Romuli, M. Bruti, M. Catonis, M. Agrippæ, M. Antonij & Cleopatræ. Imperatorem autem, Augusti, Tiberij, Othonis, Vespasiani, Nervæ, Hadriani, M. Aurelii, Lucillæ item & Antoniæ Augustarum. Plurima item alia Capita, Tabulæque marmoreæ. Apud Iulium Porcarium Tabulæ ostenduntur multæ; in quis etiam Meleagri Venatio. In pariete Tabulæ v, variis ornatæ figuris; ad dextram Pugnantium imago: hunc Taurus, Europam vehens. In domo Nicolai Stagni Hercules est, Leonina pelle & Caprae indutus, pedibus carens, Statua vel Iovis vel Neptuni & alia Antiquitatis rudera. Apud Leonardum Sabinum Hadrianus Imper. & Lucretia: Hercules & nudus & exuviis indutus Leonis; Caesaris & Octaviani caput, Pyrrhi que Regis galeatum; Faustina item & Galeria Augustarum. Apud Iulium Sabinum Ianus bifrons, Pallas, Livia, uxor Augusti, & Iulia Filia: nec non Augusti, Galbæ, Septimi Severi, Commodi, Gordiani Capita; Faustinæ duæ; Bacchus, Europa. In Domo Pauli de Castro Socratis caput visitur, Galeria Faustinæ, Veneris, Palladis, aliorum. Apud Iacomellum ad S. Magurum Atys spectatur, Pastor Idæus, Tibiam inflans; Faunus, ore exerto ridens, Hydram baculo percutiens, quæ mordicus uvam tenet; Medusa galeata: Faustina seniors Livia Drusilla, Augusti uxor: capita item Iani Bifrontis: Cornelij, uxoris Pompeij; Iulia, Iulij Cæsaris F. & uxoris Pompeij. C Cæsaris, qui M Agrippæ & Iuliæ Filius fuit. Apud Dominicum de Nigris Copia Cornu Statua, Nais Nympha dormiens, sinistra in urnam recubans; adjacens illi Nar Flavius, seminudus, læva tenens cornu copiæ: Bacchus Pampinis vin-ctus; {a}ætus. Hercules cum Clava; Capita item Neronis, Othonis, Hadriani. Apud Augustinum Rhegiensem & Papirium Papazuccam Imagines monstrantur Deorum, Imperatorumque quoque & Illustrium Virorum Capita magno numero. Franciscus de Alpia Statuam habet Capita & Pomonæ velitatarum. Bacchi simulacrum & Aristidæ Atheniensis: Thomas Sculptor, duo capita Faustinæ, duo Palladis galeatæ, & Silvani: Curtius Frangipanus, Mercurium petalatum, Cupidinem alatum, Arietem Phrygium; Capita Deorum Dearumque, in quis Iunonis, Iovis, Bacchi; Illustrium quoque Marii Cos. & Augusti Cæsaris, Hadriani, Caracallæ, Lucillæ, & aliorum. Apud Laurentium Mancitum Tabula magni precii, cum Cupidine inculpti, Leonis caput colosseum, rictu animal continens. Iuxta Maecenatis & Corvi, ubi olim Corvini Domus fuisse putatur, Domus est Marci Macaronei, in cuius porta caput est Alexandri Magni: In vestibulo sculptus Hercules, Virtutis ingressus viam: In Horto Ejus bene ornatus Lucretiae Simulacrum semiruptum, item Apollinis, Dianæ, Sphyngis, aliorumque Capita marmorea, Romuli, Herculis cum conjuge, Alexandri Magni, Iulii & Octaviani Cæsarum, Marcelli caput Nepotis, Trajani, Hadriani, Antonini, Zoroastris Astrologi Inventoris, Antonini Caracallæ. Apud Alcanium Magalotzam Capita sunt marmorea Sabinæ Mulieris: Alexandri, Mammeæ Iuliæ, Hadriani, L. Veri, Claudii, Iuppp. Bacchi ex rubro marmore, & alterius pampinus revinctus, Pueri humeris unam tabulam tenentis: in Tabulis Varium Tauriorum coniciens, Ariadne ebrius, Hercules rogo impositus. Visuntur ibidem & Termini duo, Marcia Otacilia, in loco tedens, sedens & Iulia Mammea velata. Capita Antinoi & Coloth, aliaque in Cœlio Montecœfoffa.
units.tr: At the house of Marius Delphinus, Gentilis F., many coins and inscriptions are to be seen. Julius Caesarinus has a nude Adonis, a Woman with a Vase, whom they call a Caryatid, a marble Venus, several female Figures, two two-faced Janus figures; also a Head of the poet Propertius, Faustina the Younger, Young Augustus, Bacchus with pelts, and others. Ambrosius Lilius has a head of Pompey, and on Table xii the Labours of Hercules, skilfully carved. Alianus Celsus has a head of Bacchus with a pelt over his shoulders, in green marble; an image of a laughing Boy Satyr crowned with flowers. Cavallerius keeps a Faun holding a bunch of grapes in one hand and a skin full of grapes and fruit in the other; a Silenus; Nature the Goddess, set on a pedestal and adorned with breasts and figures of animals; Hercules fighting a Centaur on a marble slab; a winged Victory, and others. Hieronymus Alterius has a priest of Cybele wearing a stole and holding a vase in his hand; Hercules, dressed in the lion's skin, leaning on a tree trunk; and various fragments of antiquity. Petrus Capoferratus has a huge Aesculapius with a girl, and others. On the front of Baldo Ferratini's house Galba the Emperor is wearing a palm wreath; there are also two vases and tablets there, notable for their various figures. Giovanni Battista Galletus has very many female statues, and on a tablet Aesculapius, holding a serpent in his right hand; also a woman pressing a serpent, and a ball carved with various figures, among them Hercules seizing two bulls by the horns. At Archinto's house a bronze statue of a slave is to be seen; above it are heads of various persons, of Capitoline Jupiter and others. In the courtyard at Marius Melinus's house an armed Pallas, helmeted, is on view, along with other female statues; besides these, a nude Gladiator, Hercules, the head of a Sabine woman, Cupid, a figure of an Alcibiades boy, playing heads of Silvanus and Bacchus, of Jupiter, Drusus, and ten others unidentified; an intact Satyr, made with singular skill. Giovanni Battista Melinus has three outstanding heads. At S. Aloisius's, at Alessandro Rufinus's house, there is Julius Caesar, almost colossal, armed; Augustus, also Caesar. Another head of Julius, and those of four men and women. Francesco Ragaterius has various heads: of Bacchus, a double head of Alexander the Great, of Jupiter, of Nature, of a Satyr or Pan; of emperors, Trajan, Hadrian, a Marcus Aurelius as a boy, Geta, of twenty unknown men, and of eleven torn from their bodies; and a Jupiter of porphyry. In the same man's vineyard at the Porta Flaminia there are various inscriptions, and a Numidian king captive, of porphyry; a bronze cuirass of some commander. Alessandrino Cherubino has inscriptions and a marble head of a laughing face. In Marcellus Porcarius's house, in front of the door, is a marble seated statue, and in a corner a huge Terminus with this inscription: C. Livius, C. F. Justus, etc. There is also to be seen a marble Visus devouring a sheep; a Sacrifice, marble carved; Diana, on a tablet of the highest art; an ancient triangular candelabrum; headless bodies of Hercules, Hermaphroditus, Apollo, Bacchus, and a Faun, on various pillars; the Hunt of Meleager, Caucus, Hercules dragging oxen by the tail, and the Labours of Hercules. In the room there are also not a few heads: indeed those of Romulus, M. Brutus, M. Cato, M. Agrippa, M. Antony and Cleopatra have been found. Emperors: Augustus, Tiberius, Otho, Vespasian, Nerva, Hadrian, M. Aurelius, likewise Lucilla and Antonia, the Augustae. Many other heads and marble tablets. At Julius Porcarius's many tablets are shown, among which also the Hunt of Meleager. On the wall, five tablets adorned with various figures; on the right an image of fighters, and opposite it a Bull carrying off Europa. In Nicolaus Stagnus's house is a Hercules, clad in a lion's skin and a goat's, lacking feet; a statue of either Jupiter or Neptune; and other rubble of antiquity. At Leonardus Sabinus's house are Emperor Hadrian and Lucretia; Hercules, both nude and clothed in the lion's hide; a head of Caesar and Octavian, and of King Pyrrhus wearing a helmet; also Faustina and Galeria, the Augustae. At Julius Sabinus's house are two-faced Janus, Pallas, Livia, wife of Augustus, and his daughter Julia; likewise heads of Augustus, Galba, Septimius Severus, Commodus, Gordian; two Faustinas; Bacchus, Europa. In Paulus de Castro's house a head of Socrates is seen, also Galeria Faustina, Venus, Pallas, and others. At Iacomellus's house at S. Magurus there is an Attis, the Idaean shepherd, blowing a pipe; a Faun, laughing with mouth open, striking a Hydra with a staff, which holds a grape in its teeth; a helmeted Medusa; Faustina the Elder, Livia Drusilla, wife of Augustus; also heads of two-faced Janus; of Cornelia, wife of Pompey; Julia, daughter of Julius Caesar and wife of Pompey; Caesar, who was the son of M. Agrippa and Julia. At Dominicus de Nigris's house is a statue of Copia with a Horn, a Naiad Nymph sleeping, reclining on an urn with her left hand; beside her Nar Flavius, half nude, holding a cornucopia in his left hand; Bacchus bound with vine-leaves; Hercules with a club; also heads of Nero, Otho and Hadrian. At Augustinus Rhegiensis's and Papirius Papazucca's house images of gods are displayed, and also many heads of emperors and illustrious men. Franciscus de Alpia has a statue with heads, and of Pomona of the vineyards; a statue of Bacchus and of Aristides the Athenian. Thomas the Sculptor has two heads of Faustina, two of helmeted Pallas, and of Silvanus. Curtius Frangipanus has Mercury with a petasus, Cupid winged, a Phrygian Ram; heads of gods and goddesses, among them Juno, Jupiter, Bacchus; also of illustrious men, of Marius the consul and of Augustus Caesar, Hadrian, Caracalla, Lucilla, and others. At Laurentius Mancitus's house is a tablet of great value, engraved with Cupid; a colossal lion's head, the animal holding something in its jaws. Next to Maecenas's and Corvus's houses, where the house of Corvinus is thought to have been, is the house of Marcus Macaroneus, at whose door is a head of Alexander the Great. In the vestibule, Hercules carved, entering the path of Virtue. In his garden a well-adorned, half-broken image of Lucretia; likewise marble heads of Apollo, Diana, a Sphinx, and others; of Romulus, Hercules with his wife, Alexander the Great, the Caesars Julius and Octavian, the head of the boy Marcellus, of Trajan, Hadrian, Antoninus, Zoroaster the astrologer and inventor, and Antoninus Caracalla. At Alcanius Magalotza's house there are marble heads of a Sabine woman, of Alexander, of Mammaea, Julia, Hadrian, L. Verus, Claudius, Jupiter; a Bacchus of red marble, and another with vine-leaves wound round him; a boy holding a tablet on his shoulders; on tablets a variety of bulls, Ariadne, a drunken Hercules laid on a pyre. Here are also two Termini, Marcia Otacilia standing in a place, seated, and Julia Mammaea veiled. Heads of Antinous and Coloth, and others, on the Caelian Hill at Montecoeffoffa.

units.la: Apud Euryalum Silvestrum Bacchus est, hedera coronatus; Sabinæ aliquot Mulierum: Capita Iovis, Augusti & Hadriani; Herculis; Diana cum Lunæ cornicu: Bacchus alius, pampinis redimitus, Scyphum manu gestans: Endymion, Antoninus Pius, Hadrianus & Antinoi Capita. Palladis quoque & Augusti Cæsaris, Dianæ lucem tela cum Pharetra ex humeris; Pan tibiens, M. Antonii in Viri caput, Cupidinis Pueri, suaviter ridentis, Iovis, Neptuni, Ledæ cum Cygno ludentis, Herculis, Lucretiæ, Gladiatoris cum Machæra. In ædibus Paulli Ponti, Via Flaminia, Aper offenditur Calydonius, ab Meleagro cæsus. Sunt ibidem Hercules cum Spolio Leonis, Apollo, Pomona, Cupido, Silvanus, Diana; hæc erata, Meleager alter mutilus, Pallas, Hermaphroditus, Adonis, Nox tenuunda, stellis coronata, Atalanta cum aprino capite, Silenus barbatus hederaque redimitus: Capita hic Poppæ Uxoris Neronis, Drusi Fratris Tiberii, Iovis Pueri ridentis, & alterius galeati, duarum Mulierum incognitarum, Iani Bifrontis: item Tigris æneî duo. Apud Franciscum Aragonium varia sunt Monumenta marmorea: in quis Pueri, Naiadis Nymphæ, urnam tenentis, Pomonæ. Apud Ambrosium Lilium Tabula spectatur pulcra Regis Indi antiqui in Tribunali: Herculis quoque Iunonis, Iubis tenens Caput equinum. Apud Antoninum Palatium Statua est Equi impingentis. Sunt & Capita Drusi, Iuliæ Augusti F, Galeriæ, Faustinæ Iunioris, Ernesti Prisci, Lentuli, Gallæ, & Sabinæ Hadriani. Herculis quoque, Bacchi, Silvani, & Mercurii; & in marmorea tabula Triumphus Tiberii Imperatoris expressus. Ad Iacobum Iacobatum Mulieris ignotæ statua; Capita Hadriani, Nervæ, M. Aurelii, Antonini Pii, Scipionis Africani, & Gladiatorum: Deorum quoque Iovis, Panis, Veneris marmoreum: aliaque visu digna.
units.tr: At Euryalus Silvester's house is a Bacchus crowned with ivy; several Sabine women; heads of Jupiter, Augustus and Hadrian; of Hercules; a Diana with the horns of the moon; another Bacchus, wreathed with vine-leaves, holding a cup in his hand; Endymion, Antoninus Pius, Hadrian, and heads of Antinous. Also of Pallas and of Augustus Caesar; Diana with a spear, her quiver on her shoulders; Pan playing the pipes; the head of a man, of M. Antony; a Cupid, a boy smiling pleasantly; Jupiter, Neptune; Leda playing with the swan; Hercules, Lucretia, a gladiator with a sword. In the house of Paulus Pontus on the Via Flaminia a Calydonian boar, slain by Meleager, is met with. There are also here Hercules with the lion's spoils, Apollo, Pomona, Cupid, Silvanus, Diana (this one is veiled), another Meleager, maimed, Pallas, Hermaphroditus, Adonis, Night, veiled and crowned with stars, Atalanta with a boar's head, a bearded Silenus wreathed with ivy. Here are heads of Poppaea, wife of Nero, of Drusus, brother of Tiberius, of a laughing boy Jupiter, and of another helmeted; of two unknown women; of two-faced Janus; also two bronze tigers. At Franciscus Aragonius's house there are various marble monuments, among which boys, a Naiad Nymph holding an urn, and Pomona. At Ambrosius Lilius's a fine tablet is seen of an ancient Indian king on a tribunal; also Hercules and Juno, Juba holding a horse's head. At Antoninus Palatius's house there is a statue of a horse rearing. There are also heads of Drusus, Julia daughter of Augustus, Galeria, Faustina the Younger, Ernestus Priscus, Lentulus, Galla, and Sabina, the wife of Hadrian. Also of Hercules, Bacchus, Silvanus and Mercury; and on a marble tablet the Triumph of Emperor Tiberius is depicted. At Iacobus Iacobatus's house is a statue of an unknown woman; heads of Hadrian, Nerva, M. Aurelius, Antoninus Pius, Scipio Africanus, and of gladiators; also a marble Jupiter, Pan, Venus; and other things worth seeing.

units.la: Apud Marcum Cafalem Statua Mulieris colossea, & Viri altera; Bacchum esse putant quidam, alii Apollinem, qui ibidem & integer est & pharetratus: Mulier Copiæ cornu tenens; elaboratissimum Iulii Cæsaris caput. In Domo Iacobi Colonæ Statuæ sunt & Inscriptiones variæ. Pompilius Narus Statuas habet Herculis & Veneris. Apud Desiderium Vriacum Diana Statua, vel Oreadis Nymphæ, Capreoli pellem tenens: & Orphei mutilus, aliaque visuntur. Apud Antonium Gabrielem Capita sunt Tiberii, Germanici, Trajani, Commodi, Pythagoræ antiquissimum. Catonis, Lucillæ, Otacillæ, M. Agrippæ, M. Tullii Ciceronis, Bacchi, Cupidinis, Ernesti Musæ, Cafonis, Faustinæ, Terminis, Satyri, & aliorum. Sunt item Hermaphroditus & Drusus, quem alii Romulum faciunt. Apud Dominicum Caponum varia sunt Simulacra, in quis Palladis vestiræ & Dianæ. Capita Iuny Bruti, Octaviani Augusti, Marini, Hadriani, Antonini, Septimi Severi, Iulia Mammeæ, Alexandri Severi, Cleopatræ, Veneris, Herculis, Apollinis, Silvani, Pueri plorantis, Iani Bifrontis, Parthorum Regis captivi, & Bacchi mindentis vasi. Apud Franciscum Aragonium in Hortulo ad Fontem Nilus est, lanifera innixus Crocodilo, utrumque duz duæ Statuæ Togatæ: hinc Capita plurima; rursum Capita xxiv in alio Hortulo. Apud Hieronymum Frangipanem Cupido alatus, Statuæ iv, & Hercules. In Pila sive Area sculptum est Iudicium Paridis: Mulier item Larvam tenens, & alia. Apud Hieronymum denique Celorium Nympha est. Dorso Monstri marini insidens, Dersdem alij, alij Galateam faciunt: Tabula marmorea cum Tauris duobus, quos viri duobus cornibus retinent: altera, in qua Iupiter cum Apro, quem Canis tenet: Victoria quoque Deæ Signum. Inscriptiones item variaque marmora. Ceterorum Civium Ædes satis sunt bellæ, Hortis: Fontibus, Nymphæis exornatæ. Arx Pontificis, quam Molem Hadriani seu Castellum S. Angeli appellant, triplici ratione munita, omnique instructa apparatu bellico. In ea tres dies Festi quotannis celebritate magna peraguntur, Funalibus passim accensis, jaciendis ignibus arte factis & emittendis bellicis Tormentis. Unus est SS. Petri & Pauli: reliqui duo, quibus illius temporis Pontifex Suffragis declaratus, & corona postea est ornatus. Arcis Custodia Viro spectato commendatur: qui post exactam septem annorum Præfecturam, dignitate aliqua decoratur, aut aliquot Aureorum donatur millibus.
units.tr: At Marcus Cafalis's house there is a colossal statue of a woman and another of a man. Some think it is Bacchus, others Apollo, and it is both intact and quivered. A woman holds a cornucopia. There is a very finely wrought head of Julius Caesar. In the house of Giacomo Colonna there are statues and various inscriptions. Pompilius Narus has statues of Hercules and Venus. At Desiderio Vriaco's there is a statue of Diana, or of an Oread nymph, holding a fawn's skin, and a mutilated Orpheus, and other things are to be seen. At Antonio Gabriele's there are heads of Tiberius, Germanicus, Trajan, Commodus, Pythagoras (very ancient), Cato, Lucilla, Otacilia, Marcus Agrippa, Marcus Tullius Cicero, Bacchus, Cupid, the Muse of Ernest, Cafo, Faustina, Terminus, a Satyr, and others. There are also a Hermaphrodite and Drusus, whom others make into Romulus. At Domenico Caponi's there are various images, among them Pallas in a robe and Diana. Heads of Junius Brutus, Octavian Augustus, Marinus, Hadrian, Antoninus, Septimius Severus, Julia Mamaea, Alexander Severus, Cleopatra, Venus, Hercules, Apollo, Silvanus, a weeping boy, Janus Bifrons, a captive king of the Parthians, and a Bacchus pouring from a vessel. At Francesco Aragonio's, in a small garden, there is the Nile leaning on a crocodile, holding a cornucopia; there are two togate statues, and from here many heads; again, 24 heads in another small garden. At Girolamo Frangipane's there is a winged Cupid, four statues, and Hercules. On the ball or area is carved the Judgment of Paris; also a woman holding a mask, and other things. Finally, at Girolamo Celorio's there is a Nymph sitting on the back of a sea monster; some call her Dersdem, others make her Galatea. There is a marble tablet with two bulls, which men hold by the two horns; another on which Jupiter is with a boar, which a dog holds; also a sign of the Victory of the goddess. There are inscriptions too, and various marbles. The houses of the other citizens are pleasant enough, adorned with gardens, fountains and nymphaea. The Pontiff's citadel, which they call the Mole of Hadrian or Castel Sant'Angelo, is fortified in a threefold way and equipped with a full military apparatus. Three feast days are celebrated there every year with great festivity: torches are lit everywhere, fireworks skilfully made are thrown, and artillery is fired. One is the feast of SS. Peter and Paul; the other two are those on which the Pope of that time was declared by vote and afterwards crowned. The guard of the citadel is entrusted to a man of standing, who after completing a seven-year prefecture is honoured with some dignity or given some thousands of gold coins.

units.la: De Hortis vero, qui multis Antiquitatum notis superbientes intra, qui extra Urbem, quid dicam? Quorumdam suis Palatiis, suis Domibus adfirorum memini. Sunt & alij, Vineæque in quibus plurima servantur Rerum Veterum monimenta. Ad Viam Flaminiam prope Portam Suburbanam Prædium exstruxit Iulius III P. M, omnia Romana opera superans. Ingredientibus occurrit vis magna Virorum Illustrium, Hirtij, Pansæ, Ciceronis, Cæsaris, aliorum. In Area variæ Icones, Herculis, Ganymedis, Veneris, Apollinis, Dianæ, Opis, Æsculapij, Bacchi, aliorumque, quæ in basibus rite conlocatæ sunt, Statuæ. Fons ibi summi artificij & incredibilis sumtus. Inscriptiones ibidem, sed novæ: duo Obelisci & Pyramis altissima. Hortus Inscriptionibus plenus & marmoribus: in quis Termius ex Alabastro Orientali candidissimo, & Sarta (Ægyptis Natura sic vocatur, facie velo tecta, & in pectore Animalia omnis generis. Major inde Hortus est, Vineis consitus, cum Termius ingentibus, qui sunt Hermæ, ab Græcis sic Mercurij nomine appellatæ, ut Alcibiades, Socratis, Aristophanis, & aliorum. In Farnesianis trans Tiberim spectatu digna duplex Venus marmorea: item Figuræ variæ Hominum, Leonum, Mulierum, novem Musarum, Ascendantium Satyrorum, Sinenebry, Puerorum uvas gestantium: Tabula marmorea, quæ Fasces & Secures consulares exhibet: Columna fracta cum Græca Inscriptione memorabili. Tibure advecta, vel, ut alij, Hierosolymis in Italiam translata. Ad Thermarum Diocletiani & Maximiani dextram Horti sunt Cardinalis Bellaij amœnissimi; in quorum ambulacris Statuæ visuntur Iovis, Apollinis, Orphei, Palladis, Bellonæ, Veriumni, Antinoi, aliorumque Deorum & Virorum Illustrium, basibus impositæ: in contignatione vero duarum Naiadum, Hebes, Vulcani, Ganymedis, Iovis, Apollinis, Sabinæ uxoris Hadriani principis, Lucillæ, Faustinæ Junioris, &c.
units.tr: As for the gardens, which are proud of many antiquities, both those within the City and those outside it, what shall I say? I remember some which were adorned by their owners' palaces and houses. There are others too, and vineyards, in which many monuments of ancient things are kept. On the Via Flaminia, near the Porta Suburbana, Pope Julius III built a villa surpassing all Roman works. As you enter, a great crowd of illustrious men meets you: Hirtius, Pansa, Cicero, Caesar, and others. In the courtyard are various images, of Hercules, Ganymede, Venus, Apollo, Diana, Ops, Aesculapius, Bacchus, and others, statues properly placed on bases. There is a fountain of the highest artistry and incredible cost. There are inscriptions there too, but new ones: two obelisks and a very tall pyramid. The garden is full of inscriptions and marbles, among them a Terminus of the purest white Eastern alabaster, and a Sarta (the Egyptians call it Nature; its face is veiled, and it has animals of every kind on its breast). Beyond is a larger garden, planted with vines, with great Termini which are Hermae, named by the Greeks after Mercury, such as Alcibiades, Socrates, Aristophanes, and others. In the Farnese gardens across the Tiber there is a double marble Venus worth seeing; also various figures of men, lions, women, the nine Muses, satyrs climbing, a sphinx, and boys carrying grapes. A marble tablet shows fasces and consular axes; a broken column with a memorable Greek inscription, brought from Tibur or, as others say, transferred to Italy from Jerusalem. To the right of the Baths of Diocletian and Maximian are the most pleasant gardens of Cardinal Bellai. In their walks are statues of Jupiter, Apollo, Orpheus, Pallas, Bellona, Vertumnus, Antinous, and other gods and illustrious men, set on bases. In the upper storey are two Naiads, Hebe, Vulcan, Ganymede, Jupiter, Apollo, Sabina, wife of the emperor Hadrian, Lucilla, Faustina the Younger, etc.

units.la: Ad Templum S. Sufannæ V a Quirinali Horti sunt Rodolphi Cardinalis Carpensis; ubi Statuæ multæ. Ad primam Portam Medusæ Caput, ad secundam Naturæ Simulacrum, mammosæ, variis Animalium Figuris & Florum ornatæ. Ad primos Palatij gradus Sphinx est, & Æsculapius e marmore. In Corte Hercules, Clavæ lævæ innixus, cum exuviis Leonis Senex quoque ignotus, cum Sandaliis; Pallas galeata, & prope Columbæ se insinuans; Vrania hinc & Tragœdia, & quinque continenter Termini seu Hermæ, interjectis matronis; Pluto tricipiti insidens Cerbero, & Mulier ex Lapide subnigro. In Cœnaculi porta Pastor dormiens. Ad Fontis ingressum Hercules est, continens manu mala Hesperidum; mox Faunus, Verem premens. Naias Nympha somnolenta ad Fontem dormit, Puero, qui blande adridet, adsit inte.
units.tr: At the Church of S. Susanna, near the Quirinal, are the gardens of Cardinal Rodolfo Carpi, where there are many statues. At the first gate is a head of Medusa; at the second, an image of Nature, many-breasted, decorated with various animal figures and flowers. At the first steps of the palace is a Sphinx and an Aesculapius in marble. In the court is Hercules, leaning on his left club, with the lion's skin; also an unknown old man, with sandals; Pallas in a helmet, and near her a dove slipping in; Urania from here, and Tragedy, and five Termini or Hermae in a row, with matrons placed between them; Pluto sitting on the three-headed Cerberus, and a woman of blackish stone. At the door of the dining room is a sleeping shepherd. At the entrance to the fountain is Hercules, holding the apples of the Hesperides; next is Faunus pressing a boar. A Naiad nymph, drowsy, sleeps by the fountain, with a boy beside her who smiles sweetly.

units.la: Ex altera parte Mulier vestita, cujus è vasculo Aqua scaturit limpida. Super Cisterna hinc inde Pomona & Flora stant: ad dextram Serapis. Ibidem Jupiter, pallio tectus; Capitaque Medusæ, Palladis, Iani Pifontis: & in tabula marmorea sculptus est Mithras, Persarum Deus, mactans Taurum. In Horti ingressu hinc Pallas, illinc Mulier est: in Porta Caput muliebre; & in tabula marmorea Hercules, vi comprimens capillos mulieris, in serpentes desinentes. In Horto Pallas altera vestita in urna, variis Animalium figuris decorata: Candelabrum ingens triangulare, cum tribus Figuris Herculis, Fauna & Fortuna. Ad dextram Apollo, cui ad pedes Anas est: alterum rursum Candelabrum triangulare, cum suis Figuris & Votis Iovi & Syriæ. Ad interpretum Vinea Nereis Nympha, incumbens Vinæ, sub qua Rapsus Proserpinæ. Hic Terminus cp. Lucretia Statua cum Leonis Ipolito; item Pallada, Livia Drusilla, Matris Augusti, Apollinis, Lidæ, Hermaphroditi, Faunæ. In un bracculis arborum Satyri Simulacrum, & Leonis egregium. Sunt & variæ Inscriptiones. In Monte Quirinali Horti sunt magnificentissimi Ferrarienses Cardinalis, quibus nullæ Romæ Arboribus splendidiores, ut Silvæ speciem præbeant & Labyrinthi. Hæc re vincunt Carpentes; licet Antiquitatibus præsertimque Inscriptionibus inferiores. In Parmenfis Ducis Hortulo Sacrum duplex vitatur, egregii operis, & supra in Tabula tre Curiata, Undeque gentibus innixa. Qua Suburram spectat Quirinalis Sacrum adhac exstructum Hortus Bartholomæorum, fornicatum, tessellato opere ex Conchylis venulis: in ne exterarum virorumque figuris Pisanus, Neptuno sacrum fonte putatur.
units.tr: On the other side is a woman clothed, from whose little vessel clear water gushes. On either side above the cistern stand Pomona and Flora; on the right, Serapis. There also is Jupiter, covered with a cloak; the heads of Medusa, Pallas, and Janus Bifrons; and on a marble tablet is carved Mithras, the god of the Persians, slaying a bull. At the entrance of the garden, on one side is Pallas, on the other a woman; in the gateway, a woman's head; and on a marble tablet Hercules, forcibly gripping the hair of a woman, which ends in serpents. In the garden is another clothed Pallas in an urn decorated with various animal figures; a huge triangular candelabrum with three figures, of Hercules, Faunus and Fortuna. On the right is Apollo, at whose feet is a duck; another triangular candelabrum again, with its figures and votive offerings to Jupiter and Syria. At the interpreter's vineyard is a Nereid nymph leaning on the vine, under which is the Rape of Proserpina. Here is a Terminus; a statue of Lucretia with a lion; also Pallas, Livia Drusilla, mother of Augustus, Apollo, Leda, Hermaphrodite, Faun. In the branches of the trees is a figure of a satyr and a fine lion. There are also various inscriptions. On the Quirinal hill are the most magnificent gardens of the Cardinal of Ferrara, with trees more splendid than any in Rome, so that they present the appearance of a forest and a labyrinth. In this respect they surpass those of Carpi, though they are inferior in antiquities, especially inscriptions. In the little garden of the Duke of Parma a double sacrifice is shown, of fine workmanship, and above, on a tablet, the Curiate ..., supported on all sides by peoples. Facing the Subura, on the Quirinal, is a sacrum still standing; the garden of the Bartholomei, vaulted, with tessellated work of shells and veined stones; in it are figures of foreign men and women. The Pisanus, believed to be the sacred fountain of Neptune.

units.la: Iuxta S. Mariæ Aventinæ Templum Vinea est Iana cornucopiæ, in qua Confessoris Statua duplex, sed altera minor: atque, quarum ignorantur nomina. Ad Tiberim Via Iulia est, hortus Brandi. In is non domus Bernardi Tiberiæ: in cuius Hortulo M. Catonem Caput est & Leo alianus Equo, qualis in Capitolio. In Horto Lutiæ Tuscanæ ad Campum Florae, Statuæ visuntur Traiani Imperatoris armata, Liviæ, Uxoris Augusti Lucretia Heroinæ, tenentis malum Hesperidum Sammeleta & Mineru Herculis cum Clivâ & Leonis Ipolito, duorum Consulum, totidemque Matronarum, aliæque: & plateam 1 Capita Imperatorum ac Virorum illustrium.
units.tr: Near the Church of S. Maria Aventina there is a vineyard with a Janus holding a cornucopia, in which is a double statue of a Confessor, one of them smaller; and others whose names are unknown. By the Tiber, along the Via Giulia, is the garden of Brandi. In it is not the house of Bernardo Tiberia; in whose little garden is a head of M. Cato, and a lion like the one on the Capitol, beside a horse. In the garden of Lutia Tuscana at the Campus Florae are seen statues of the Emperor Trajan in armour, Livia, wife of Augustus, Lucretia the heroine, holding an apple of the Hesperides, Sammeleta and Minerva, Hercules with his club and the lion's skin, two consuls and as many matrons, and others; and a square with heads of emperors and illustrious men.

units.la: Ad Iutrum Arantiorum apud Marium Deiphonum, Cientulis filium, horrus est Inscriptionis tesserulas: Ibidem Cæsaris Statua ex Smirne Lapide facta in Hydræ speciem, cum literis hieroglyphicis. In Hortis Iunii Caesaris Mulier est cum Vase, quam Cariatidem vocant, & Leonem quoque marmoreum. Mulebres Figuræ Iani duo Fratres omites. Ostenditur & Poëta: Propertii Caput; & Faustinæ Iuniori Augusti Hurentis Bacchi cum pellibus: aliaque. Sed de his satis. Veramque Romam, & Veterem & Novam, delinearunt Aristides Sophista Græce, P. Victor, Sex. Rufus, Poggius Florentinus, Fabricius Varthomus, Florus Bionius, Raphael Volaterranus, Franciscus Albertinus, Fr. Ostiensis, Fr. Serlius, Fabius Calvus Ravennas, Pyrrhus Ligorius, Bartholomæus Marlianus, Georgius Lucanus Lucius Faunus, Andreas Iuvenis. Andreas Palladius, Onuphrius Panvinus, Ioannes Lupus, Ivo Grangue Lazius, Iustus Lipsius in Admirandis. Lud. Vivus Dermuiense, Thomas Iolinus, Thomas Stapletonus Anglus. Tabulas æneas Antiquæ Romæ publicæ fecerunt juris Antonius Lanferius, Antonius Salamanca, Onuphrius Panvinus, Ioannes Ligorius, Michael Tramezzinus, & alii, quibus ego accessi nuper adjecta Marginibus succinctâ Veteris Romæ explicatione, ex prolixiore suisque locorum Urbis omnium, quam apud nos servo, commemoratione delucta. Inscriptiones Romanas, per orbem terrarum sparsas, collegerunt Petrus Appianus; Cyriacus Anconitanus, Mezenlius, Lucius Vifius ad librum de Romanis Legibus Antonii A gustini; Marcianus Smetius; cui Auctarium adjecit Iasus Lipsius; Ianus Gruterus antiquiens magnorum Virorum Iulipis Scaligeri & Marti Hefferi, in Viri Augustani. Consulendi & Manutius in Orthographia, Onuphrius Panvinus Commentar. in Fastos, Festus de Gente Cæcilia, Hieronymus ad Cæsarem, Wolfgangus Lazius, Hubertus Goltzius & alii.
units.tr: At the garden of the orange trees, at Marius Deiphonus's, son of Cientulus, there is a remarkable collection of inscribed tesserae. There too is a statue of Caesar, made of Smyrna stone in the shape of a hydra, with hieroglyphic letters. In the gardens of Junius Caesar there is a woman with a vase, whom they call a caryatid, and also a marble lion. Female figures of Janus, two companion brothers. A poet is also shown: the head of Propertius; and of Faustina the Younger, of Augustus, of a raging Bacchus with skins; and others. But enough of these. Both ancient and new Rome have been described by Aristides the Sophist, in Greek, P. Victor, Sex. Rufus, Poggius Florentinus, Fabricius Varthomus, Florus Bionius, Raphael Volaterranus, Franciscus Albertinus, Fr. Ostiensis, Fr. Serlius, Fabius Calvus Ravennas, Pyrrhus Ligorius, Bartholomaeus Marlianus, Georgius Lucanus, Lucius Faunus, Andreas Iuvenis, Andreas Palladius, Onuphrius Panvinus, Ioannes Lupus, Ivo Grangue, Lazius, Justus Lipsius in Admiranda, Lud. Vivus Dermuiense, Thomas Iolinus, Thomas Stapletonus the Englishman. Engraved bronze tablets of ancient public Rome were published by Antonius Lanferius, Antonius Salamanca, Onuphrius Panvinus, Ioannes Ligorius, Michael Tramezzinus, and others, to whom I recently added a brief explanation of old Rome, with notes in the margins, drawn from a fuller account of all the places of the City, which I keep among us. The Roman inscriptions, scattered throughout the world, were collected by Petrus Appianus; Cyriacus Anconitanus, Mezenlius, Lucius Vifius, in the book on Roman laws by Antonius Augustinus; Marcianus Smetius, to whom Justus Lipsius added a supplement; Janus Gruterus, a work of great men, Julius Scaliger and Martin Hefferus, in the Vir Augustani. One should also consult Manutius on orthography, Onuphrius Panvinus in his commentary on the Fasti, Festus on the Gens Caecilia, Hieronymus on Caesar, Wolfgangus Lazius, Hubertus Goltzius, and others.

units.la: Numos Veterum Romanorum decerunt Hubertus Goltzius, Iacobus Strada Mantuanus, Aeneas Vicus Parmensis, Sebastianus Erizzus, Adolphus Occo Augustanus, Antonius Augustinus Dialogis xi. Excellet hic aliquando noster Abrahamus Gorlaeus V. CL. apud quem unum plus Numorum Annulorumque Veterum in Urbe Delphensi, quam in tota fortean est Italia.
units.tr: Coins of the ancient Romans are discussed by Hubertus Goltzius, Jacopo Strada of Mantua, Aeneas Vicus of Parma, Sebastianus Erizzus, Adolphus Occo of Augsburg, and Antonius Augustinus in his eleven Dialogues. Our own Abrahamus Gorlaeus, a most distinguished man, excels here at times; in the city of Delft alone he has, perhaps, more ancient coins and rings than there are in all of Italy.

units.la: De ipsa Roma Veter Novaque differunt; si quæ ad Urbis tantæ Cives pertinent, animus jam mettet curiosus perlequi, Charta deflitueret. Brevis esse cogor. Flagitor hoc abunea Methodo. Pauca, ne Instituto Ordinique vis hæc, dicam. Romani ab Roma sua dicuntur Scriptoribus omnibus, & Ραυμοι Græcis; qui Stephanus, Byzantinus, Iulium, qui & Iurisconsultus Africanus, Æneæ Filius, Albanorum Regem designantu. Ut autem Romani qui Romæ nati sic Romanenses, teste Festo, qui Romæ negociabantur. Utitem Romani appellabantur universum, qui jus habebant Civitatis Romanæ, ubicumque terrarum: sic Quirites vocabantur, quibus Romæ tantum domicilium erat. Docent aliquot exemplorum millia. Quirites rite: sane Cives dixisse eos, qui ad populum Verba in Vrbe habebant, notat Strabo distertis verbis lib. v. Paret idem ex innumeris, quae apud varios Scriptores, Orationibus. Ut denique Romani generatim nominabantur, qui & domi morabantur, & militiae pro salute publica vigilabant: ita Quirites audiebant, qui domi tantum in pace atque vivebant otio: adeo ut exolum esset nomen istud viris, qui Castra sequebantur. Probrosum enim Milites censebant & ignominiosum, si Quirites ab Ducibus suis & Imperatoribus dicerentur, uti docent Suetonius in Iulio cap. ixx, Plutarchus in Caesare, Lucanus lib. v, Appianus lib. v. Bellor. Civil. Et illud est Verbum, quo uno Divum Iulium seditionem Exercitus sui compescuisse scribit lib.
units.tr: Writers, ancient and modern, differ about Rome itself. If I were to pursue everything that concerns the citizens of so great a city, my curious mind would gladly go through it, but the paper would run out, so I am forced to be brief. My plan requires this, so I will say only a few things, lest I depart from the purpose and order of this work. All writers call the people of Rome Romani after their city, and the Greeks call them Ῥωμαῖοι [Rhōmaioi]. Stephanus of Byzantinus and Julius, who is also called Africanus, say that Aeneas's son was the king of the Albans. Just as those born at Rome are Romani, so, according to Festus, are the Romanenses, those who did business at Rome. Those who held the right of Roman citizenship, wherever on earth they lived, were commonly called Romani; those whose only home was at Rome were called Quirites. Many thousands of examples show this. That they properly called Quirites those citizens who addressed the people in the city, Strabo states in plain words in book 5, and the same appears from countless speeches of various writers. Finally, just as those who both stayed at home and kept watch in the army for the public safety were generally called Romans, so those who lived only at home in peace and leisure were called Quirites. That name was so disagreeable to men who followed the camp that soldiers thought it shameful and disgraceful to be called Quirites by their leaders and commanders, as Suetonius in Julius ch. 70, Plutarch in Caesar, Lucan book 5, and Appian book 5 of the Civil Wars teach. And it is the word by which, as he writes in book, the deified Julius quelled the mutiny of his army.

units.la: 1. Tacitus: quem deinde imitatus legitur apud Lampridium Alexander Severus. Illud obiter addo ex Festo, Romanis morem fuisse in omnibus Sacrificiis Precibusque dici, Populo Romano Quiritibus: quod ex variis Auctoribus confirmat Barnabas Brissonius lib. i. de Formulis & solemnibus Populi Romani Verbis. Romani successu temporis variae distributi leguntur: i in Patricios & Plebeios; ii in Tribus, quae sensim numero xxxv; iii in Curias; iv in Classes & Centurias: v in Ordines, Senatorium, Equestrem, Plebeium: vi in Optimates & Populares; in Nobiles praeterea, Nobos & Ignobiles. Fit & mentio Ingenuorum, Libertorum & Libertinorum. In Romanis considerare solco Mores & Res gestas: Mores quidem & Domi & Militiae, Domi circa vel Divina vel Humana. In Divinis perpendere consuevi cum Deos ipsos, tum Deorum Cultum.
units.tr: 1. Tacitus, whom Lampridius later shows Alexander Severus imitating. I add in passing, from Festus, that it was the Romans' custom in all sacrifices and prayers to say, "To the Roman people, the Quirites," which Barnabas Brissonius confirms from various authors in book 1 of his work on the formulas and solemn words of the Roman people. Over time the Romans are read to have been divided in various ways: (1) into Patricians and Plebeians; (2) into tribes, which gradually came to number thirty-five; (3) into curiae; (4) into classes and centuries; (5) into orders: Senatorial, Equestrian, and Plebeian; (6) into Optimates and Populares. Besides these, there were nobles, new men, and ignoble persons. Mention is also made of freeborn men, freedmen, and libertines. In considering the Romans I am accustomed to look at their morals and their deeds: their morals both at home and in war, and at home both in divine and human matters. In divine matters I am accustomed to weigh both the gods themselves and the worship of the gods.

units.la: Du Romanorum Veterum quam Varii! Alii Domestici erant, alii Peregrini: Domesticorum alii Urbani, alii Rustici: Urbanorum alii quidem, Quibus in genere administratio rerum humanarum credebatur incumbere; quorum quidam Maiorum gentium, ut Selecti omnes, & cum Selectis tam Consentes, quam Adlecti, quales Ianus, Saturnus, Tellus, Iupiter, Juno, Apollo, Diana, Sol, Luna, Mercurius, Minerva, Mars (cui addi solent Bellona, Victoria, Nemesis, Venus) quam comitantur Cupido, Adonis, Gratiae, Liber-Pater, Ceres, Vulcanus, Vesta, Neptunus, Genius (cui conjunguntur Penates & Lares) Orcus sive Pluto (cui Sociae Parca & Furiae.) Sunt qui addunt horum Clatii fortunam: Quaedam Minorum sunt gentium; ipsque partim, Quos in Coelum Merita extulerunt, quales Hercules, Faunus, Carmenta, Evander, Castor & Pollux, Aesculapius, Acca Larentia, Quirinus, Anna-Perenna: partim propter quos hominibus dabatur adsensus in Coelum, ut Mens, Virtus & Honor, Pietas, Fides, Spes, Prudentia, Concordia, Pax, Quies, Salus, Felicitas, Libertas. Urbanorum deinde alii habebantur, Quibus sua singulis Munia erant tributa; quum quidam Praefectos se profitebantur Nuptiis, ut Iugatinus, Domiducus, Manturna, Virginensis, Cinxia, Mutinus, Subigus, Mater Prema, Viri placa; quidam Parturientibus, Mena, Fluonia, Lucina, Partunda, Latona, Egeria, Nixii, Prorsa, Postverta, Intercidona, Deverra, Mater Matuta, Bona Dea, Mana, Geneta, nonnulli Nascentibus & recens natis, Ianus, Opis, Nascio, Vaticanus, Levana, Rumina, Cunina, Potina, Educa, Offiago, Nundina, Statilinus, & Statanus, Labelanus, Carna, Iuventas, Orbona: alii aliis mille Actionibus, Murcia, Strenua, Stimula, Agonius, Horta, Asae Locutius, Catius, Volumnus & Volumna, Adeona, Abeona, Reduculus, Fugia, Vacuna, Vi Lupia, Vitula, Pellonia, Numeria, Fessonia, Febris, Viriplaca, Averruncus, Pavor & Pallor, Angeronia, Heres Martea, Stata Mater, Laverna, Lubentina, Anculi & Anculae, Cloacina, Nania. Isti Res Urbanas curare credebantur: Rusticas autem, praeter Superiorum nonnullos, Pales, Flora, Pomona, Vortumnus, Seia, Segetia, Tutanus, Tutilina, Robigus, Bonus Eventus, Populonia, Fulgora, Tempestas, Torna, Pulumnus & Picumnus, Sterculus, Bubona, Hippona, Mellona, Iugatinus, Collina, Vallonia, Rusina, Terminus, Pan, Silvanus, Priapus, & alij. Peregrini Dij censebantur Sancus vel Pius Fidius, Isis, Osiris, & Serapis. De quibus omnibus prolixius Ego in meis Antiquitatum Romanarum Tabulis. Scripserunt de Dys, eorumque Genealogiis Lilius Giraldus, Joannes Boccatius, Natalis Comes, Iulianus Aurelius, Georgius Victorius, Petrus Crinitus variis locis, & alij. Inter Veteres primi fuerunt Apollodorus, Hesiodus, Phurnutus, Palaephatus, Fabius Fulgentius: item Euhemerus & M. Terentius Varro. In Deorum cultu considerandae Causae & Adjuncta: Illae quidem cum Efficientes, tum Formalis: Efficientes partim Principales in Sacerdotibus, quales erant, ut temporis rationem observem, Luperci: Panos Lycaei vel Ianī Sacerdotes, Cereris Graeca Sacerdos; Potitii & Pinarii; Herculis Sacerdotes Fratres Arvales xii; Publicii Sacerdotes lxi Augures xv; Haruspices; Tribunus Celerum; Curiones xxx. cum Curione Maximo, Sodales Titii, Flamines xv; Virgines Vestales vi, quarum quæ prima Maxima dicebatur: Salii Palatini xii quis præerat Magister Collegii Salionum; Virgines Saliares. Fetiales xx. cum Patre Patrato: Pontifices, quorum caput Maximus audiebat; Sodales Collegii vel Agonenses xii; xv-viri sacris faciundis, cum Magistro; Rex Sacrorum, alias Sacrificulus; cujus uxor Regina Sacrorum. Sacerdotes Feminæ Bonæ Deæ, Galli & Archigalli; Sacerdotes Deæ Cybeles; viiviri Epulonum; ii viri Aedes lovandæ, sartiendæ, dedicandæ; iii-iii viri Aediles Sacræ incendio consumptis restituendi, & Sacra concurrendis; denique pestifer Pontifices denique & Sacerdotes Deorum & Sacrificia Templorum sanctorum: partim adjuvantes in Ministris: ut erant Camilli & Camillæ; Flaminii & Flaminæ, & Ædituus, qui & Aeditumus; Scriba Publici Pontificum; ab Commentariis xv-viri S F. Haruspices Haruspicum, Dictatores Sacerdotum; Tibicines & Tubicines, qui Sacris Publicis præsto erant. Pulli Pulli, Popa, Victimarii, Flaminis Diali Præcia, alias Præconi: Lictores Flaminum & Trigemina Vestalium: Præcones Pigmatores. Fidii denique & Vigilia. De his omnibus Ego copiosius in Methodicis Romanarum Antiquitatum Schematismis. Legendi interim Damianus Pio, ac Florentinus, Pomponius Læ-tus, Omphalus Panvinius in Civitate Romana & ad Fastos, aliquæ. Forma in ipsis erat sacrificiorum, quorum administratio stipendia plurimæ, Præcationum, Gratiarum a Deorum, Votorum, & innumerorum Ritibus: de quibus præter alios eleganter & plene Barnabas Brissonius lib. i Formularum. Adnexa erant in Instrumentis & Vasis, qualia, Aspergillum, Thuribula, Præfericula, Simpula, Capedines, Candelabra, Urnulæ, Paterae, Patellæ, Dapes, Scyphi, Scrinia, Embolia, Dolia, Ollæ, Ampullariæ, Ligula, Lituus, & ad genus alia, de quibus peculiarem librum scripsit Lilius Giraldus. Ioues singulorum sunt in Guilelmi Budæi Antiquitatibus, quæ Gallico idiomate sunt editæ. ii in Ioue & Vulcano, quarum multæ erant Species, Ferina, Suicidanea, Ambegna, Caesares, Prodigia, Ambarvalia, Imagines & aliæ: quæ Piebant, Dici, Ad hoc res Arie, Stare ad Aras, ab Iove Fugere, Terra, Cadere, Cadi Matlari, Ius, Lemulari in Sacrificijs dicebantur, Brissonio probante libro i. Formularum. iii in Locis Sacris; qualia erant Templa, Aedes Sacræ, Aedicula, Fana, Sacraria, Sacella, Delubra, Luci, Arae; de quibus ad superiora. iiii in Tempore, quod pertinebat in Feriis & Ludis. Feriæ aut Publicæ erant, aut Privatæ. Illæ triplices: Stativæ, Conceptivæ, Imperativæ. Stativa Vetus recentior Kalendarium, quod Romæ apud Cardinalem Mipherum a Paulo Manutio, Huberto Goltzio, aliaque rerum Antiquarum curiosis editum: Ianuario, Agonalia & Carmentalia. Februario, Lupercalia, Quirinalia, Feralia, Terminalia, Regifugium, Martio, Equirria, Liberalia, Quinquatrus, Tubilustrium: Aprili, Idus Maiæ Magnæ, quæ & Megalesia, Fordicidia, Cerealia, Parilia, Vinalia, Robigalia, Floralia: Maio, Compitalia, Lemuria, Agonalia, Tubilustria, Vestalia, Matralia. Quando iterum de ea rerum de præcedentibus omnibus Ovidius lib. Fastorum Libris. Quintili, Pepsifiona, Meditrinalia, velut alii, Mercuriales, Lucaria, Neptunalia, Furrinalia, Sextili, Portunnalia, Vinalia iterum, Consualia, Volcanalia, Opiconsiva dies, Volturnalia; Septembri, Mercurialia iterum, vel quod alii videtur Mercurio: hic enim compendiose in Kalendario scribitur REF.) Octobri, Meditrinalia, Augustalia, Fontinalia, Armilustrium: Novembri, Mercurialia 40 i. item, vel quod alii videtur, Mercurius: Decembri denique Agonalia, Saturnalia, Opalia, Sigillaria, Divalia, & Larentalia, vel ut alii Lucinalia. Conceptivæ erant Feriæ Latinæ, Paganalia, Sementinæ, Compitalia. Imperativæ, quæ ob Victoriam, Natalem diem Imperatoris & Successionem imperabantur. Copiose de his Lazius in Commentariis Reip. Romanæ. Rodolphus Hoffmannus, & Egnatius Tabulis. Ludorum duplex erat divisio, alia ab Forma iuncta, alia ab Fine. Priore, Ludi alii erant Circenses: ut Pugna, Cursus, Saltatio, Lucubratio, Decursio Equitum, Aurigatio, Naumachia, alii Scenici: ut Tragedia, Comoedia, Satyra, Mimus. Posteriore, alii hebant causa Pietatis cum erga Deos, ut erant Megalenses, Cerealeis, Floreales, Martiales, Apollinares, Capitolini, Romani, Plebei, Compitalitii, Augustales, Palatini, Seculares, Votivi, cum erga 50 Homines Defunctos, ut Funebres & Gladiatorii. Causa porro Exercitationis fiebant Triremes. De Ludis Romanorum scripsit diligentissime Omphalus Panvinius, qui & singularem librum edidit de Secularibus. Multa etiam de Ludis habet Iulius Caesar Scaliger lib. i. Poeticæ, & Petrus Faber. Plurima de Ludis Gymnicis tradit in suis de Arte Gymnastica libris Hieronymus Mercurialis, Medicus Patavinus, De Theatris & Amphitheatris, unde Ludi spectabantur, Iustus Lipsius, & Ioannes Serv...
units.tr: How varied the gods of the ancient Romans were! Some were domestic, others foreign. Of the domestic gods, some were urban and others rural. Of the urban gods, some were believed to preside over the general management of human affairs. Among these, some were of the greater gods, such as the Selecti, and with the Selecti both the Consentes and the Adlecti, such as Janus, Saturn, Tellus, Jupiter, Juno, Apollo, Diana, Sol, Luna, Mercury, Minerva, and Mars (to whom Bellona, Victoria, Nemesis, and Venus are usually added), accompanied by Cupid, Adonis, the Graces, Liber Pater, Ceres, Vulcan, Vesta, Neptune, and the Genius (to whom the Penates and Lares are joined), and Orcus or Pluto (with whom Parca and the Furies are associated). Some add the Fortune of the Clatii to these. Others belong to the lesser gods, and these were partly those whom their merits raised to heaven, such as Hercules, Faunus, Carmenta, Evander, Castor and Pollux, Aesculapius, Acca Larentia, Quirinus, and Anna Perenna; partly those through whom assent was given to men as to heaven, such as Mens, Virtus and Honos, Pietas, Fides, Spes, Prudentia, Concordia, Pax, Quies, Salus, Felicitas, and Libertas. Next, among the urban gods, were others to whom a particular duty was assigned each: some were said to preside over weddings, such as Iugatinus, Domiducus, Manturna, Virginensis, Cinxia, Mutinus, Subigus, Mater Prema, and Viriplaca; some over women in labour, such as Mena, Fluonia, Lucina, Partunda, Latona, Egeria, Nixii, Prorsa, Postverta, Intercidona, Deverra, Mater Matuta, Bona Dea, Mana, and Geneta; some over those being born and the newly born, such as Janus, Opis, Nascio, Vaticanus, Levana, Rumina, Cunina, Potina, Educa, Offiago, Nundina, Statilinus and Statanus, Labelanus, Carna, Iuventas, and Orbona. Others were assigned a thousand different actions: Murcia, Strenua, Stimula, Agonius, Horta, Aius Locutius, Catius, Volumnus and Volumna, Adeona, Abeona, Reduculus, Fugia, Vacuna, Vitula, Pellonia, Numeria, Fessonia, Febris, Averruncus, Pavor and Pallor, Angeronia, Heres Martea, Stata Mater, Laverna, Lubentina, Anculi and Anculae, Cloacina, and Nania. These were believed to take care of urban affairs. The rural gods, apart from some of the higher ones, were Pales, Flora, Pomona, Vertumnus, Seia, Segetia, Tutanus, Tutilina, Robigus, Bonus Eventus, Populonia, Fulgora, Tempestas, Torna, Pilumnus and Picumnus, Sterculus, Bubona, Hippona, Mellona, Iugatinus, Collina, Vallonia, Rusina, Terminus, Pan, Silvanus, Priapus, and others. The foreign gods were considered to be Sancus or Semo Sancus Dius Fidius, Isis, Osiris, and Serapis. I have treated all of these more fully in my Tables of Roman Antiquities. Writers on the gods and their genealogies include Lilio Gregorio Giraldi, Giovanni Boccaccio, Natale Conti, Giuliano Aurelio, Giorgio Vittorio, Pietro Crinito in various places, and others. Among the ancients the first were Apollodorus, Hesiod, Phurnutus, Palaephatus, and Fabius Fulgentius, likewise Euhemerus and M. Terentius Varro. In the worship of the gods one must consider the causes and the accompanying circumstances: the causes are both efficient and formal. The efficient causes were partly principal, in the priests, such as the Luperci, the priests of Pan of Lycaea or of Janus, the Greek priestess of Ceres, the Potitii and Pinarii, the priests of Hercules, the twelve Arval Brothers, the Publicii, the sixty-one priests, the fifteen augurs, the haruspices, the Tribunus Celerum, the thirty curiones with the Curio Maximus, the Sodales Titii, the fifteen flamines, the six Vestal Virgins, of whom the first was called Maxima, the twelve Salii Palatini, over whom presided the Master of the College of Salii, the Salian Virgins, the twenty Fetiales with the Pater Patratus, the Pontiffs, whose head was called the Maximus, the Sodales of the College or Agonenses, twelve, the fifteen men for performing sacred rites, with a Master, the Rex Sacrorum, also called Sacrificulus, whose wife was the Regina Sacrorum, the women priests of the Good Goddess, the Galli and Archigalli, the priests of the goddess Cybele, the seven men of the Epulones, the two men for building, repairing and dedicating temples, the three-men Aediles for restoring sacred things consumed by fire and for sacred matters, and finally the priests of the gods and the sacrifices of the holy temples; partly the assistants among the ministers, such as the Camilli and Camillae, the Flamines and Flaminicae, the Aedituus, also called Aeditumus, the scribe of the public Pontiffs, the fifteen men of the sacred books, the haruspices of the haruspices, the Dictatores of priests, the Tibicines and Tubicines, who attended the public sacred rites. Then the Pulli, Popae, Victimarii, the Praecia of the Flamen Dialis, otherwise called Praecones, the Lictors of the Flamens and the Trigemina of the Vestals, the Praecones Pigmatores, and finally the Fidii and the Vigilia. I have discussed all of these more fully in my Methodical Outlines of Roman Antiquities. Meanwhile, it is worth reading Damianus Pio and Florentinus, Pomponius Laetus, Onofrio Panvinio on the Roman citizenship and on the Fasti, and others. The form of the sacrifices themselves was also varied, the administration of which required many stipends, and the rites of prayers, thanksgivings to the gods, vows, and countless others; on these, Barnabas Brissonius, among others, writes elegantly and fully in book 1 of his Formulas. Attached to the rites were instruments and vessels, such as the aspergillum, censers, pitchers, ladles, baskets, candelabra, small urns, paterae, small plates, feasts, cups, chests, embolia, casks, pots, flasks, ligulae, the lituus, and many other kinds, on which Lilio Gregorio Giraldi wrote a special book. The gods of individual things are in Guillaume Budé's Antiquities, which were published in French. There were two kinds, in Jupiter and Vulcan, of which there were many species: Ferina, Suicidanea, Ambegna, Caesares, Prodigia, Ambarvalia, Imagines and others, which were said of such things as Piebant, Dici, Ad hoc res Arie, Stare ad Aras, Ab Iove Fugere, Terra, Cadere, Cadi Matlari, Ius, Lemulari in sacrifices, as Brissonius approves in book 1 of his Formulas. The third kind was in sacred places, such as temples, sacred buildings, small shrines, fana, sacraria, sacella, delubra, groves, and altars, which I have discussed above. The fourth concerned time, which pertained to festivals and games. Festivals were either public or private. Public festivals were threefold: stative, conceptive, and imperative. Of the stative, the older and more recent calendar, which was published at Rome from the library of Cardinal Mai by Paolo Manuzio, Hubert Goltzius, and others curious about antiquities, lists for January the Agonalia and Carmentalia; for February the Lupercalia, Quirinalia, Feralia, Terminalia, and Regifugium; for March the Equirria, Liberalia, Quinquatrus, and Tubilustrium; for April the Ides, May the Great Megalesia, Fordicidia, Cerealia, Parilia, Vinalia, Robigalia, and Floralia; for May the Compitalia, Lemuria, Agonalia, Tubilustria, Vestalia, and Matralia. Ovid treats all of the foregoing in the books of his Fasti. For July: the Pepsifiona, Meditrinalia (as some say, Mercuriales), Lucaria, Neptunalia, Furrinalia; for August: the Portunnalia, Vinalia again, Consualia, Volcanalia, the day of Opiconsiva, Volturnalia; for September: the Mercurialia again, or as some think, for Mercury (for it is abbreviated in the calendar as REF.); for October: the Meditrinalia, Augustalia, Fontinalia, Armilustrium; for November: the Mercurialia again, or as some think, for Mercury; and finally for December: the Agonalia, Saturnalia, Opalia, Sigillaria, Divalia, and Larentalia, or as others say, the Lucinalia. The conceptive festivals were the Latin Feriae, Paganalia, Sementinae, and Compitalia. The imperative festivals were ordained on account of a victory, the emperor's birthday, or his succession. Lazius treats these fully in his Commentaries on the Roman Commonwealth, and Rudolf Hoffmann and Egnatius in their Tables. The division of games was twofold, one according to their form and the other according to their purpose. In the first kind, some games were circus games, such as fighting, racing, dancing, night-revels, cavalry manoeuvres, chariot-racing, and naval battles; others were scenic, such as tragedy, comedy, satire, and mime. In the second kind, some were held out of piety, either toward the gods, such as the Megalesia, Cerealia, Floralia, Martial, Apollinarian, Capitoline, Roman, Plebeian, Compitalician, Augustan, Palatine, Secular, and Votive games, or toward the dead, such as funeral games and gladiatorial shows. Triremes were held for the sake of exercise. Omphalius Panvinius wrote most diligently about the games of the Romans, and he also published a separate book on the Secular Games. Julius Caesar Scaliger, in book 1 of his Poetics, has much on games, as does Pierre Faber. Hieronymus Mercurialis, a physician of Padua, gives very many details on gymnastic games in his books on the art of gymnastics.
