units.la: Ludi vilius lib. 1. de mirandis Antiquorum Operibus. Et sic se habebant apud Romanos Veteres Divina. Humana considerabantur in Rebus Publicis & Privatis. Ad Publica, praeter Comitia, quae trium erant generum, Curiata, Centuriata, Tributa (de quibus apud Veteres scripserunt M. Terentius Varro, & alij; aetate nostra praeter Onuphrium Panvinium, Iacobum Perpontum, Karolum Sigonium, Bichilium, Budaeum, altoque, Nicolaum Gruchium, pertinebant Magistratus cum suis Ministris, Leges, Iudicia. Magistratus (quorum Seminarium erat Senatus; de quo praeter alios Paulus Manutius cuiusque Principibus Onuphrius ad Fastos) erant vel Urbani, vel Provinciales: Urbani; Maiores, Minores: Maiores ordinarii, Extraordinarii. Ordinarij sub Regibus, cum ipsi Reges, qui septem numero, Romulus, Silvius, Numa Pompilius, Tullius Hostilius, Ancus Marcius, L. Tarquinius Priscus, Ser. Tullius, Superbus cum Praefectis vel Tribunis. Ceterum, L. Tarquinius, Praefectus Urbi, & Q. Aelius. Post Reges exactos Magistratus Maiores Ordinarij considerabantur Rep. vel Libera vel Occupata. Liberae quidem Resp. erant Consules II (horum Fastos scripserunt Cassiodorus, Marcellinus Comes, Sigonius, Nicephorus, Joannes Columna, & omnium diligentissime Karolus Sigonius, Onuphrius Panvinius, Hubertus Goltzius additis Icombus, Stephanus Vigilius, Corsus et II: Praetores, qui sensim facti XV; Occupatae vero Imperatores Caesares Augusti (quorum Icones vulgarunt Hubertus Goltzius, Ioannes Strada, Aeneas Vicus, Panvinius, Adolphus Occo & Augustinus) Donati Tribunicia Potestate; Nobilissimi Caesares, vel Principes Juventutis; & Praefectus Urbi. Extraordinary censebantur cum Interrege, Dictator & Magister Equitum, Tribunum Militum, utrique Consulari potestate; III-Viri, X-Viri Legibus scribendis, & Tribuni Militum, utrique Consulari potestate; III-Viri, X-Viri Legibus scribendis, & denique Rep. constituendae. Minores item Ordinarii erant & Extraordinarij. Ordinarii. Quaestores Urbani, II, & qui & Quaestores Aerarii. Tribuni Plebis, X; dediles plebis, II; Aediles Curules; Curatores omnium Tribuum; III-Viri Capitales; III-Viri Nocturni; III-Viri Vigintiviri; III-Viri Monetales; A. A. A. F. F.; IIII-Viri Viarum curandarum; V-Viri Cuc. Tribuni; X-Viri Statibus Iudicandis; V-Viri Iudices Iudicandi; Curatores. Praefecti Aerarii. Curatores Operum Publicorum. Curatores Aquarum Tiberis & Cloacarum. Praefectus Annonae, Praefectus Praetorio, Praefectus Frumenti, Populo dividendi; Praefectus Vigilum. Curatores Regionum; Denuntiatores Regionum; Magistri Vicorum; Vicorum Vies Regionum XIV. Ad eorum denique Fisci. Extraordinary erant, II-Viri Perduellionis, Quaestores Parricidii, vel Rerum Capitalium; Praefectus Annonae; V-Viri Mensarii; III-Viri Monetarii; II-Viri Navales; IIII-Viri, conquirendis ad Arma ferenda Iuvenibus; V-Viri Tarribus Muriscisque reficiundis; X-Viri, qui iudicarent super Sacramento & Libertate; X-Viri de Ibinendorum Donatoriorum; III-Viri legendi Senatus; III-Viri recognoscendi Armas Equitum Romanorum. Magistratus Provinciales erant Proconsules, Propraetores, Legati Proconsulum, & Propraetorum; Quaestores Provinciarum XII X; Pro Quaestores; Praefecti Aegypti; Praefecti Praefectorum; Consulares IV, quae per Italiam in Galliam Italiae; III-Viri, V Viri, VII-Viri, X-Viri Coloniae deducendae; V-Viri, VII-Viri, XX-Viri Agris dandis, adiudicandis; V-Viri, XV-Viri Agrorum metiendorum, Iudicandorumque, III-Viri, vel V-Viri ad Insulandos Fines, Litesque dirimendas, Magistrati porro Magistratuum erant Scribae, Accensi, Praecones, Lictores (de quibus V. Cl. Iustus Lipsius libro I Hector. cap.xx) Scriba publici, Viatores, Cornicines, Magistri Cursorum; & quorum in Comitiis usus erat, Nomenclatores, Distributores, Rogatores, Custodes & alij. De his omnibus Auctor l. 2. D. de Orig. Iuris, Notitia Imperii Romani cum Commentario Guido Panciroli; Pomponius Laetus: Andreas Dominus Focus, qui Fenestella nomine circumfertur, Factum Clodius in Roma Triumphante; Wolfgangus Lazius in Commentariis Resp. Romanae; Karolus Sigonius ad Fastos, item de antiquo iure Civium Romanorum, Italiae, Provinciarum, & alibi; Onuphrius Panvinius passim in Commentario ad Fastos, & in Civitate Romana; Iocosimus Perticus; Petrus Faber; Cl. Praesidius, Iunius Lipsius; & qui non, vel ex professo, vel data in emendandis illustrandisque Audoribus occasione? Haec de Magistratibus. Leges considerabantur partim Regiae, ut Romuli & aliorum, quae in unum collectae corpus, Iuris Papiriani appellatione cooperunt esse nobiles: partim Resp. Liberae, quarum causa Edictum duplex, cum Decemviri, tum alii, qui post illorum tempora Remp. administrarunt, Magistratus, ut Cos. Praetores, Duumviri, Tribuni Plebis. Decemvirorum erant Leges XII Tabularum, in quarum fragmentis hinc inde colligendis sudarunt varij. Reliquorum Magistratuum Leges. Leges de Rebus admodum varijs longum esset commemorare. Summa dabo capita. Latæ leguntur de Sacrorum Ritibus, Festis, Ludis & Sacerdotibus; item de Comitijs, Senatu, Magistratibus cuiuscumque generis; præterea de Legum Vi & Prærogatiua, de Nummis, Frumento, Negocijs Mercatorum: de Manumissionibus inuper, Iure Connubiorum, Tutelis, Vsucapionibus, Successionibus, Cessione Bonorum, Vsuris & Fœnore ius, de Criminibus denique Publicis; & alijs, quæ brevitati studens prætereo. His omnibus colligendis industriam adhibuerunt summam Pomponius Lætus, Conradus Celtes, Aemarus Ruvallius, Idaricus Zasius, Ludovicus Charondas Parisiensis, Paulus Manutius, Franciscus Hotomannus, Pardulphus Pratensis, Antonius Augustinus, Fulvius Ursinus alij. Iudicia, quæ inter Humana tertio potiri loco, vel Privata erant, vel Publica. Privata Causas habebant suas, & Controversias, de quibus instituebantur, suas Personas, quarum interventu peragebantur; suos denique Ritus, quibus fiebant. Publicorum Iudiciorum legibus comprehendebantur non solum Rep. id est Senatui, Populo, vel Magistratibus factæ sed etiam nonnullæ, quæ Privatis etiam inlatæ. Rep. directe facta dicebantur Crimina Maiestatis, Peculatus, Ambitus, Repetundarum, & Vis Publica: Privatim facta ad ie pertinere Populus exsultimabat Crimina inter Sicarios, Veneficij, Parricidij, Falsi, Adulterij, Plagij. Cotofius hæc omnia apud Varronem Sigonium, qui tres de Iudiciis Veterum Romanorum libros scripsit. Integram etiam Fori Romani Historiam quinque libris exposuit Franciscus Pulleus, Duacensis I.C. quos morte Auctoris imperfectos auxit, & ad finem perduxit ejus genér Phi-lippus Broudeus. Consulendus & cum alijs Barnabas Brissonius in Formulis, & alibi. De Iudicijs etiam scripserunt Jacobus Raverdus & Annaeus Rivallius: De Centumviralibus Iudicijs Stirandus Tetardus: de Suppliciis multa apud Petrum Fabrum libro II Semestrium. De Cruce Supplicio Iusto Lipsius, & Petrus Scriverius meus. Hactenus quæ Publica, tum perlequutus: Privatorum Ritus nunc vocant, quorum cognitio maximam etiam habet utilitatem, & incredibilem creare solet Antiquitatum studiosis suavitatem. De iis pauca dicam. Nam exponere copiosius singula, operosum esset, & ab instituto alienum. Spectabantur autem in Nuptiis, quarum ritus explicant Carolus Sigonius libro 1. de Antiquo Iure Civium Romanorum, & Andreas Tiraquellus in legibus Connubialibus; ediderunt & singularios de iis libros Barnabas Brissonius, Franc. Hotomannus, alij: In Natalitiis Nominumque Impositionibus, de quibus præcepta tradiderunt Onuphrius Panvinius, Carolus Sigonius, Fr. Robertellus, & alij; eo referre quis potest Onomasticum Romanum Ioannis Glandorpij: Familias item Richardi Strevvi, Antonij Augustini, & Fulvij Ursini: In Sepulchris, cujus partem exposuit in Vestalibus Lazarus Baysius: in Lectis & Lectisterniis Lipsius Electorum lib. 1: In Tondendi ratione, de qua Antonius Hotomannus; spectante eo & Hairiam Iurij Cornut: In Re Vestiaria, quam illustrant Lazarus, quem dixi, Baysius, singulari libello, sparsim item Aldus Manutius, Petrus Crinitus, Wolfgangus Lazius, Carolus Sigonius, Iustus Lipsius, Guilielmus Formenius, Rodolphus Hospinianus, & alij: In Conviviis, quorum Ritus fuse magnosatis volumine exponit Guilielmus Stuckius. De iisdem 40 Iustus Lipsius cum alibi, tum 111 Antiquarum Lectionum libro, Wolfgangus Lazius, cujus meminimus, in Commentario Rep. Rom. Hieronymus Mercurialis de Arte Gymnastica, Aldus Manutius in Quæstionibus per Epistolam; singularios de iis libros scripserunt Iacobus Cornarius, Petrus Cinetonius, Fuvius Ursinus: adeundi de Mensis Veterum Fr. Polletus, de Vita & Fictis Populi Romani Franciscus Robertellus; de Vitæ Naturæ Andreas Tacius: In Funeribus denique & Sepulcris quorum Ritus utraque quæ fuerint, docet Lilius Giraldi opus de Sepulcralibus: consulendi & Iustus Lipsius in Electis, & Barnabas Brissonius libro ult. Formularum. Huc referendi Ritus In Numeris, de quibus Matthaeus Horstius: In Mensuris & Ponderibus, de quibus, præter Volusium, Rhemnium & Prisicianum, Guilielmus Budaeus, Michael Neander, & Gul. Philander: In Nummis, quorum rationem aperit cum Vulpisio Metiano, Franciscus Hotomannus. De omnibus autem his copiosissime Lazius, quem sæpe nominavi, in Comment. Rep. Romanæ, Ioannes Rosinus decem illis non contemnendis Antiquitatum Romanarum libris, Egoque in meis earumdem Tabulis vel Schematismus. Hactenus Veterum Romanorum Mores delineavi Domesticos; quod ad Militares, Itupendi erant in Bello Suspiciendi, Gerendi, Finiendi. In Suspiciendis summam habebant curam Auspicionis, quæ fiebat per Patrem-Patratum & Feciales Clasaridiae.
units.tr: Ludi Vilius, book 1, On the Marvellous Works of the Ancients. In this way things stood among the ancient Romans. Divine and human matters were considered under public and private affairs. Public affairs included, besides the Assemblies, which were of three kinds, Curiate, Centuriate and Tribal (on these the ancient writers included M. Terentius Varro and others; in our own age, besides Onuphrius Panvinius, Jacobus Perpontus, Carolus Sigonius, Bichilius, Budaeus, and Nicolaus Gruchius, the subject is treated by others), the magistrates with their ministers, the laws and the courts. The magistrates (whose seminary was the Senate, on which, among others, Paulus Manutius wrote, and Onuphrius on its leaders in the Fasti) were either urban or provincial. The urban magistrates were either greater or lesser. The greater were ordinary or extraordinary. The ordinary magistrates existed under the kings, when the kings themselves, who were seven in number, were Romulus, Silvius, Numa Pompilius, Tullus Hostilius, Ancus Marcius, L. Tarquinius Priscus, Servius Tullius and Superbus, together with the prefects or tribunes. Besides these there were L. Tarquinius, prefect of the city, and Q. Aelius. After the kings were expelled, the greater ordinary magistrates were considered under a republic that was either free or seized. Under the free republic there were two consuls (their Fasti were written by Cassiodorus, Marcellinus Comes, Sigonius, Nicephorus, Joannes Columna, and most diligently by Carolus Sigonius, Onuphrius Panvinius and Hubertus Goltzius, with additions by Icombus, Stephanus Vigilius and Corsus), and two praetors, which gradually became fifteen. Under the seized republic there were the Emperors, the Caesars and Augusti (whose portraits were published by Hubertus Goltzius, Joannes Strada, Aeneas Vicus, Panvinius, Adolphus Occo and Augustinus), those granted tribunician power, the most noble Caesars or Princes of the Youth, and the prefect of the city. The extraordinary magistrates were considered to be the interrex, the dictator and the master of the horse, the military tribunes who held consular power; the triumvirs, the decemvirs for writing laws, and finally the decemvirs for re-establishing the republic. The lesser magistrates likewise were ordinary and extraordinary. The ordinary ones were the two urban quaestors, who were also the quaestors of the treasury; the ten tribunes of the plebs; the two plebeian aediles; the curule aediles; the curators of all the tribes; the triumvirs for capital cases; the triumvirs for the night watch; the triumvirs of the Twenty; the triumvirs of the mint; the A.A.A.F.F.; the quattuorvirs for the care of the roads; the quinqueviri tribunes; the decemvirs for judging the causes of status; the quinqueviri judges for judging; the curators; the prefects of the treasury; the curators of public works; the curators of the Tiber's waters and of the sewers; the prefect of the grain supply; the prefect of the praetorium; the prefect of the corn, for distributing to the people; the prefect of the watch; the curators of the regions; the announcers of the regions; the masters of the wards; the wardens of the wards, fourteen regions in all; and finally those belonging to their fiscus. The extraordinary ones were the duumviri for treason, the quaestors for parricide or for capital cases; the prefect of the grain supply; the quinqueviri for the banks; the triumvirs of the coinage; the duumviri for the navy; the quattuorviri for raising young men to bear arms; the quinqueviri for repairing towers and walls; the decemvirs who should judge concerning the oath and liberty; the decemvirs concerning the gifts of donors; the triumvirs for choosing the Senate; and the triumvirs for reviewing the arms of the Roman knights. The provincial magistrates were the proconsuls, the propraetors, the legates of the proconsuls and of the propraetors; the quaestors of the provinces, twelve or ten; the pro-quaestors; the prefects of Egypt; the prefects of the prefects; the consulars, four, who through Italy into Gaul were of Italy; the triumvirs, quinqueviri, septemviri and decemviri for founding colonies; the quinqueviri, septemviri and viginti-viri for assigning and adjudging lands; the quinqueviri and quindecimviri for measuring the fields and judging them, and the triumvirs or quinqueviri for marking out boundaries and settling disputes. The subordinate officials of the magistrates were the scribes, accensi, heralds, lictors (on whom see the most learned Justus Lipsius, book 1 of the Hector, chapter 20), the public scribe, the viatores, the cornicines, the masters of the couriers; and those whose service was used in the Assemblies: the nomenclators, distributors, rogators, custodians and others. On all these things see the author in book 2 of the Digest, On the Origin of Law; the Notitia of the Roman Empire with the commentary of Guido Panciroli; Pomponius Laetus; Andreas Dominus Focus, who circulates under the name of Fenestella; Factum Clodius in Rome Triumphant; Wolfgangus Lazius in his Commentaries on the Roman Republic; Carolus Sigonius on the Fasti, and also on the ancient right of Roman citizens, of Italy, of the provinces and elsewhere; Onuphrius Panvinius throughout his commentary on the Fasti and in On the Roman State; Iocosimus Perticus; Petrus Faber; Cl. Praesidius; Justus Lipsius; and who does not, whether professedly or on the occasion of emending and illustrating authors? So much for the magistrates. The laws were considered partly as royal, such as those of Romulus and others, which, once gathered into one body, came to be famous under the name of the Papirian Law; partly as those of the free republic, for which there was a double edict, one from the decemvirs and another from the others who governed the republic after their time as magistrates, such as the consuls, praetors, duumvirs and tribunes of the plebs. The laws of the decemvirs were the Twelve Tables, in gathering whose fragments here and there many have toiled. The laws of the remaining magistrates are likewise to be found. It would be tedious to recount the laws concerning the very various matters; I shall give the main heads. They are read as having been enacted concerning the rites of sacred things, festivals, games and priests; likewise concerning the assemblies, the senate, the magistrates of every kind; besides these, concerning the force and prerogative of laws, money, grain, the dealings of merchants; concerning recent manumissions, the law of marriages, guardianships, usucaptions, successions, cession of goods, interest and usury; and finally concerning public crimes; and others which, aiming at brevity, I pass over. Those who applied the greatest diligence to collecting all these were Pomponius Laetus, Conradus Celtes, Aemarus Ruvallius, Ulricus Zasius, Ludovicus Charondas of Paris, Paulus Manutius, Franciscus Hotomannus, Pardulphus Pratensis, Antonius Augustinus, Fulvius Ursinus, and others. Courts, which, among human matters, hold the third place, were either private or public. Private courts had their own causes and controversies, for which they were instituted, their own persons through whose intervention they were conducted, and finally their own rites by which they were carried out. The laws of public courts comprehended not only those acts done against the state, that is, against the Senate, the People or the magistrates, but also some which were brought even against private persons. Crimes said to be committed directly against the state were the crimes of treason, embezzlement, electoral bribery, extortion and public violence; those done privately, which the People judged to belong to the same class, were the crimes of assassination, poisoning, parricide, forgery, adultery and kidnapping. All these things are treated together by Varro and Sigonius, who wrote three books on the courts of the ancient Romans. Francis Pulleus, a Douai jurist, set out the whole history of the Roman Forum in five books, which, the author having died, were enlarged and brought to completion by his relative Philip Broudeus. Barnabas Brisson should also be consulted, in his Formulae, and elsewhere. On courts also wrote Jacobus Raverdus and Annaeus Rivallius; on the Centumviral courts Stirandus Tetardus; on punishments much is found in Petrus Faber, book 2 of his Semestria. On the cross as punishment Justus Lipsius, and my own Petrus Scriverius. Thus far I have run through those matters which were public; now I come to what they call the rites of private life, whose study is of very great use and usually creates an incredible pleasure for lovers of antiquity. I shall say a little about them, for to set out each one more fully would be laborious and beside my purpose. They were observed in weddings, whose rites are explained by Carolus Sigonius in book 1 of his On the Ancient Right of Roman Citizens, and by Andreas Tiraquellus in On the Laws of Marriage; Barnabas Brisson and Franciscus Hotomannus, and others, have also published separate books on them. In births and the giving of names, on which precepts were handed down by Onuphrius Panvinius, Carolus Sigonius, Fr. Robertellus and others; to this belongs the Roman onomasticon of Joannes Glandorpius; likewise the families of Richardus Strevius, Antonius Augustinus and Fulvius Ursinus. On tombs, part of which Lazarus Baysius set out in his On the Vestals; on couches and lectisternia, Lipsius in book 1 of his Electa; on the manner of shaving, on which Antonius Hotomannus; to which also Jurij Cornut's Hairiam pertains. On clothing, which Lazarus Baysius, whom I mentioned, illustrates in a single small book, and which is treated here and there by Aldus Manutius, Petrus Crinitus, Wolfgangus Lazius, Carolus Sigonius, Justus Lipsius, Guilielmus Formenius, Rodolphus Hospinianus and others; on banquets, whose rites Guilielmus Stuckius sets out fully in a large volume. On the same things Justus Lipsius, both elsewhere and in book 111 of his Antiquarian Lessons, and Wolfgangus Lazius, whom I have mentioned, in his commentary on the Roman Republic. Hieronymus Mercurialis in On the Art of Gymnastics, and Aldus Manutius in his questions by letter; separate books on these were written by Jacobus Cornarius, Petrus Cinetonius and Fulvius Ursinus. On the months of the ancients Fr. Polletus should be consulted, on the life and customs of the Roman people Franciscus Robertellus, and on the life and nature Andreas Tacius. Finally, on funerals and tombs, of which both the rites and what they were are taught by Lilius Giraldi in his work on sepulchral matters; Justus Lipsius in Electa and Barnabas Brisson in the last book of his Formulae are also to be consulted. To this belong the rites concerning numbers, on which Matthaeus Horstius; concerning measures and weights, on which, besides Volusius, Rhemnius and Priscian, Guilielmus Budaeus, Michael Neander and Gul. Philander; concerning coins, whose principles are laid open together with Vulpisius Metianus by Franciscus Hotomannus. On all these things most fully Lazius, whom I have often named, in his commentary on the Roman Republic; Joannes Rosinus in those ten not to be despised books of Roman Antiquities; and I myself in my tables and schemata of the same. Thus far I have sketched the domestic customs of the ancient Romans; as for the military ones, they were remarkable in war, in the taking of auspices, the conducting and the ending. In taking the auspices they took the greatest care, which was performed through the Pater Patratus and the Fetiales of Clusium.

units.la: Lazarus Bayfius, Nummi; Carolus Sigonius; Iustus Lipsius Electorum. rigando: Adparatus in Petunia. Commeatu, Armis: Dilectus denique Ducum Militumque In Gerendo dominabantur ipla Expeditio, Castrorum & Metatio & Motio, Disciplina Castrensis, Vigilia, Instructio Acies, Impugnatio, Itaque etiam Dvorum Tutelarium Evocatio, & Urbium Evertenturumque hostilium Devotio. Finiendi Belli partes, quae ad Victos, erant lenis modestaque in debellatos Hostes Animadversio, Coloniarum, Municipiorum (de utriusque exstat Sex Iulij Frontini Libellus, quem auctissimum mihi monstravit Petrus Scriverius Praef. Ararum, Provinciarumque (de quibus plene Sigonius & Onuphrius constitutae: quae ad Victores, Duces quidem Supplicatio, Triumphus, Ovatio, Arcus Triumphales, Trophaea, Statuae, Milites vero, praeter Laudationem, Praemiorum inter eos, qui rem bene gesserint, Distributio. La varia erant: cum primis Coronae Militares, Torques Armillae, Phaleræ, Hastae, Vexilla, Cornicula. Agmen militare, ut concludam, claudebant Exercitus Missio & in Agros promissi Deductio. Scripsit de Re Militari Flavius Vegetius libris iv. Eum cum xiii MSS. Codicibus in Gallijs anno cIↄ IↄLXXXII diligenter fideliterque conlatum, quintoque Libro de Praecentis Navalibus auctorem, familiariter nunc a me cum multis alijs, quae rariora conquisieram, commodato sumit (durius non dicam, ne Manes solicitem), Ludovicus Carrio: cujus Heredes, quicumque sint illi, pie iusteque facient, si quae jure optimo mea mihi curent restituenda. Legendi & de Re Militari Veterum Romanorum Wolfgangus Lazius Commentar. Reip. Rom. Joannes Rosinus Romanar. Antiq. libro ultimo, & alij: de Militis excasu Latius Taurellus: de Stipendio Militari Julius Lipsius libro Electior. i cap. ii: Haec de Moribus: jam Res gestae, quibus Romani Veteres primo Conregionales, inde totam Italiam, mox tenuem meliorem Terrarum orbis portionem contulerunt, suoque subjecerunt imperio, commorare non Cosmographi est; sed Historiographi. Describunt eas T. Livius, L. Florus, Eutropius, Plutarchus, Polybius, Appianus Alexandrinus, Sallustius, Dion Cassius, Caesar, Suetonius, Paterculus, Zonaras, Trogus, Valerius Maximus, Paulus Orosius, P. Cornelius Tacitus, & qui non? Addendi his, qui per Fastos Annorumque seriem omnia diligentissime notarunt, Karolus Sigonius, Onuphrius Panvinius, Stephanus Pighius. Sunt & mea quaedam tota in his recensendis, quae suo tempore lucem Ipero visura. Rerum gestarum Effecta parent, quo ad Italiam, in Coloniis, Municipiis, & Praefecturis; de quibus abunde capite hujus libri xix, quod de Gubernatione Italorum Civili & Politica: quod ad Regiones reliquas, manifesta sunt rerum a Pop. Rom. gestarum indicia, cum in Provinciis, & constitutis hic ibi Legionibus, tum in Coloniis extra Italiam ductis. Provincia dicebantur, quas Populus Romanus, prolatis extra Italiam armis, provicerat: in quas quotannis vel Proconsules vel Propraetores mittebantur; unde quaedam Consulares, quaedam Praetoriae dicebantur. Neutrum tamen fuit perpetuum. Non enim haec aut illa Provincia semper aut Consulares aut Praetorii, sed ita nomen mutabat, ut varie modo ab Consularibus, modo a Praetorijs administrabatur. Provinciae Populi Rom. ante C. Iulij Caesaris Dictatoris tempora xv fuisse, liquet ex Caelij Epistola, quae apud Ciceronem exstat.
units.tr: Lazarus Bayfius (on coins); Carolus Sigonius; Justus Lipsius (Electorum): preparation in money, supplies, arms, and finally the levying of commanders and soldiers. In waging war, the campaign itself held sway: the camp, its pitching and moving, camp discipline, watch, the arrangement of the battle line, the attack, and so too the summoning of the tutelary gods of the enemy and the devoting of enemy cities and armies. The parts of finishing a war concerned the vanquished: a mild and moderate punishment of the defeated enemy, of colonies and municipalities (a short book by Sextus Julius Frontinus on both exists, which Peter Scriverius, Praefectus Arae, showed me as the fullest), and of provinces (about which Sigonius and Onuphrius have written fully). For the victors, the commanders received thanksgiving, triumph, ovation, triumphal arches, trophies and statues; the soldiers, besides praise, received a distribution of rewards among those who had done well. These were various: above all military crowns, torques, armlets, phalerae, spears, banners and little horns. To conclude, the discharge of the army and the leading out to lands promised closed the military procession. Flavius Vegetius wrote On Military Affairs in four books; I, having carefully and faithfully collated him with thirteen manuscript codices in Gaul in 1582, and the author of the fifth book on naval matters, now take him, lent to me in friendship along with many other rarer things I had gathered, Ludovicus Carrio (I will not say more harshly, lest I disturb the dead). His heirs, whoever they are, will act piously and justly if they see to it that my property is returned to me, as is only right. For reading on the military affairs of the ancient Romans: Wolfgang Lazius, Commentarii Reipublicae Romanae; Johannes Rosinus, the last book of his Roman Antiquities; and others. On the discharge of soldiers see Latius Taurellus; on military pay see Justus Lipsius, Electorum book 1, chapter 2. So much for the customs. Now the deeds done, by which the ancient Romans first subdued their neighbours in the region, then all Italy, and soon a good part of the lands of the world, and brought them under their rule, is not for a cosmographer to dwell on but for a historian. They are described by Livy, Florus, Eutropius, Plutarch, Polybius, Appian of Alexandria, Sallust, Dio Cassius, Caesar, Suetonius, Paterculus, Zonaras, Trogus, Valerius Maximus, Paulus Orosius, Tacitus, and who not? To these should be added those who noted everything most carefully by fasti and the sequence of years: Carolus Sigonius, Onuphrius Panvinius, Stephanus Pighius. I also have some work of my own on these matters, which will, in due time, see the light. The effects of the deeds done appear, as far as Italy is concerned, in the colonies, municipalities and prefectures, of which I have said enough in chapter 19 of this book, on the civil and political government of the Italians. As for the remaining regions, there are clear signs of the things done by the Roman people, both in the provinces and in the legions stationed here and there, and in the colonies founded outside Italy. Those were called provinces which the Roman people, having extended its arms beyond Italy, had conquered; to these either proconsuls or propraetors were sent every year, whence some were called consular and some praetorian. Yet neither status was permanent: this or that province was not always consular or always praetorian, but its name changed, so that it was administered at one time by consulars and at another by praetors. That the provinces of the Roman people numbered fifteen before the time of Julius Caesar the dictator is clear from the letter of Caelius which survives in Cicero.

units.tr: 1. Sardinia and Corsica were made provinces between the First and Second Punic Wars by Titus Manlius Torquatus and Gaius Papirius Maso, consuls for the second time. 2. Sicily: part of it was made a province by Gaius Lutatius Catulus in the First Punic War, and the whole by Marcus Valerius Laevinus in the Second Punic War. 3. Cisalpine Gaul was made a province by Marcus Claudius Marcellus, consul for the fifth time. 4. Transalpine Gaul, by Quintus Fabius Maximus, called Allobrogicus. 5. Hither Spain was made a province by the victory of Scipio Africanus. 6. Further Spain. 7. Illyricum, Dalmatia, Istria and Liburnia were reduced to the form of a province by the victory of Lucius Anicius Gallus. 8. Africa and Numidia were made provinces by Scipio Africanus the Younger and Gaius Marius, consul for the seventh time. 9. Macedonia, Achaea, Thrace, Greece, Aetolia, Thessaly, Boeotia, Acarnania and Epirus were made provinces by the victories of Quintus Caecilius Metellus Macedonicus, Lucius Mummius Achaicus, Marcus Terentius Varro Lucullus and Marcus Fulvius Nobilior; for all these provinces were governed, under the law of Publius Clodius, by the man who presided over Macedonia. 10. Asia: Lydia, Ionia, Caria, the Hellespont, Pontus, Mysia and part of Phrygia were made provinces by the victories of Marcus Perperna and Marcus Aquillius.

units.la: x PONTVS, BITHYNIA, & PROPONTIDIS Pars, a Cn. Pompeio Magno Provinciæ factæ.
units.tr: 10. PONTUS, BITHYNIA and part of PROPONTIS were made provinces by Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus.

units.la: xii CILICIA, PAMPHYLIA, LYCAONIA & PHRYGIA Pars Victoriæ P. Servilij Isauricí & Cn. Pompeij Magni. PHRYGIAM in duas iurisdictiones dispertitam fuisse, ut una pars Ciliciæ, altera tribueretur Asiæ, itemque PAMPHYLIA & LYCAONIA partem sub Regibus, partem sub Ciliciæ Procon-
units.tr: 12. CILICIA, PAMPHYLIA, LYCAONIA and part of PHRYGIA, by the victory of Publius Servilius Isauricus and Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus. That PHRYGIA was divided into two jurisdictions, so that one part was assigned to Cilicia and the other to Asia, and likewise that PAMPHYLIA and LYCAONIA were partly under kings and partly under the proconsul of Cilicia.

units.tr: In the year 727 from the founding of the City, Augustus himself handed over the administration of all the provinces to the Senate and people of Rome. He handed over those that were pacified and settled, and kept all the armies in his own charge. The provinces of the Senate and Roman people, distinguished from his own, were these:

units.la: Et erant tunc temporis Imperij Limites Ister, Euphrates, Rhenus, Oceanus. De Istro & Euphrate ipse Augustus apud Iulianum in Menippea de Cæsaribus: Γ Greek text omitted here as illegible. Deinde reliquos Tacitus: Mari Oceano, inquit, aut Amnibus longinquis septum Imperium.
units.tr: At that time the limits of the empire were the Ister, Euphrates, Rhine and Ocean. Concerning the Ister and Euphrates, Augustus himself speaks in Julian's Menippus on the Caesars, quoting the Greek. Then Tacitus on the rest: The empire, he says, was enclosed by the Ocean sea or by distant rivers.

units.tr: Rightly, then, it is written that the Emperor Trajan extended the limits as far as the Red Sea. The unknown writer in Suidas puts it elegantly, in Greek. Tacitus, Annals book II: Then they came to Elephantine and Syene, once the barriers of the Roman empire, which now extends to the Red Sea.

units.la: Has omnes Provincias Imperatores cum Augustus, tum qui eum sequuti, validissimis Legionibus munire iunt soliti, & in eas Legatos suos Procuratoresque mittere. Legionum (subiectibo syllabum, praemonitos volens Lectores, adpositas Regiones urbesque signare Stationes, Primarum quidem xxv, ubi fuerint in Augusti distributione positae, reliquarum autem, ubi ab sequentibus Principibus primum institutae; quae omnes inde frequenter pro Imperatorum arbitrio Loca sua mutatle leguntur.
units.tr: Augustus, and those who followed him, were accustomed to secure all these provinces with very strong legions, and to send their legates and procurators into them. I will append a list of the legions, wishing readers to be forewarned, marking the regions and cities where the stations were assigned. Of the first twenty-five, the places are given where they were set by Augustus's distribution; of the rest, where they were first established by the later emperors. All of these were often moved from their places at the emperors' pleasure.

units.tr: The remaining colonies, those established after Alexander's reign by the later emperors, are listed in the Notitia of both Empires. I will not add them, since they are all set out there accurately. I would now add the colonies which the Romans founded outside Italy in various provinces and regions, but just as I gave their Italian colonies, so I will give each one to its own region; this could not conveniently be done with the legions. So much for the inhabitants of old Rome. As for present-day Rome, the chief place among its inhabitants is held by the Pontiff Maximus, whose court surpasses all the palaces of Christian princes in its splendour. In his household there are: Auditors of the Rota, 12. Writers of the Archive, 1. Wax-chandlers of the Chamber, 7. Masters of the Penitentiary, 3. Treasurer, 1. Secretaries of the Bulls or Briefs, 8. units.la: Pontificum Vitas Fastosque scripserunt Platina & Onuphrius; qui etiam, & alij, Icones ad vivum publicarunt. Tanta Pontifices est obiectvantia, ut ne Cardinales quidem Urbe exeant, nisi petita & habita licentia. De Coronatione Romani Pontificis, Ostensione Pedum ipsius, eiusdem Levatione seu Portatione legendus Iosephus Stephanus, Episcopus Oriolanus: de Insignibus autem Mitrarum, quæ Pontifex Maximus Principibus deferre consuevit, adeundus Stephanus Pighius. Cardinales dignitate Regibus comparari solent. Eorum incertior est numerus: pendet enim ab arbitrio nutuq; PonPontificis. In Vrbe semper ad minus sunt xl. Horum Fastos vulgarunt Onuphrius Panuinius & Alphonsus Ciacconius Hispanus: Icones autem & Elogia sculpsit Antverpiæ Theodorus Galłæus. Pergo Studia Facultatum omnium, inclitorumque litterarum ab omni ævo Romæ supra modum floruisse docent infinita Veterum Scriptorum Monumenta: quæ commemorare longum esset. Quanti precii fuerit Romanis ab Urbe usque condita Divinarum Rerum Studium, profanæ abunde tantus Deorum: Dearumque numerus, tanta Sacerdotum copia; tot Sacrificiorum Ritus & Cerimoniæ: & post Christum natum hodieque quæ non? Quanti momenti Iurisprudentia, patet ex solis xii Tabularum Legibus, quarum Libellum omnium Philosophorum Bibliothecas & auctoritatis pondere & utilitatis ubertate superasse, narrat, libro i. de Oratore sub persona Crassi M. Cicero. Certe manavit inde sensim etiam pium ex uberrimo fonte quid quid hodie in laudatissimis Rebuspublicis Legum & Constitutionum. Leges primus publice profiteri cœpit Ti. Coruncanius, ut scribit Auctor l. 2. D. de orig. iuris. § 35. Eum plurimi sunt secuti, in quis ex professo rec entendis totum sunt alii magni Viri. Quo loco Medicina fuerit, clamant cum alia, tum decreti tubinde Medicorum Diligentiæ Fideique Honores, & polita Elogia. Auctor est Cassius Hemina primum è Medicis Romam venisse Archagathum, Lysaniæ F. Peloponnesiacam, L. Aemilio & M. Livio Cos. anno ab V. C. 1 p xxxv, eiusque ius Quiritium datum. Per quos Vera Medicina, præsertim Herbarum, ad Romanos pervenerunt, docet Plinius lib. xxv natur. Hist. cap. 11 & alibi Cæsar, auctore Tranquillo, omnes Veram Medicinam Romæ prositentes Civitate donavit. Quid Historia commemorem curam? Scrip toribus recensendis non immorabor. Longum hoc esset & tædiosum. Præter alios, quorum memoria periit, Historiam Romæ docuisse perhibetur sub Hadriano & Antonino Impp. Fl. Arrianus, cognomine Xenophon Nicæus, vel Minor, Philosophus ex Nicomedia, Epicteti Discipulus, Honoribus ornatus consularibus. Nihil hic dicam de Grammatica, Rhetorica, Dialectica, aliis Artibus: quæ quantopere semper floruerunt, testantur partim Romani Cives, qui in iis excelluerunt, partim edita ab ipsidem Opera. Quum Crates, Attali Regis Legatus, inter ii & iii Bellum Punicum, per totum Legationis tempus singulis diebus Romæ doceret, ipsis quoque Romanis auctor fuit ut ad Grammaticæ Studium excitarentur, Scholamque instituerent, ubi tam necessaria ad Philosophiam via traderetur. Auctor est Strabo, Asclepiades, quum Pompei Magni Filios Romæ erudiret, Grammaticæ etiam Scholæ præfecit, omnibusque ea in re cumulate satisfecisse; mane Rhetoricam, mente Grammaticam profitentem, M. Antonius Gnipho Grammaticam docuisse traditur primum in C. Iulii domo Pueri adhuc; deinde in sua privata. Docuit & Rhetoricam ita ut quotidie præcepta Eloquentiæ traderet, declamaret vero non nisi in Nundinis. Scholam eius clarissimos quoque viros frequentasse ajunt, & in his M. Ciceronem, etiam quum Prætura fungeretur. Caecilius Epirota, Libertus Attici Equitis Romani, primus Virgilium & Poetas novos interpretatus legitur. Hinc illud Domitij Marsi:
units.tr: Platina and Onuphrius have written the lives and annals of the Popes, and they, along with others, have published their likenesses drawn from life. So great is the reverence paid to the Pontiff that not even the Cardinals leave the City without first asking for and obtaining permission. For the coronation of the Roman Pontiff, the showing of his foot, and its lifting up or carrying, one should read Joseph Stephanus, Bishop of Oriola; and for the insignia of the mitres, which the Pontiff Maximus is accustomed to bestow on princes, one should consult Stephanus Pighius. Cardinals are customarily compared in dignity to kings. Their number is rather uncertain, for it depends on the will and nod of the Pontiff. In the City there are always at least forty. Onuphrius Panvinius and the Spaniard Alphonsus Ciacconius have published their annals, while Theodorus Galle carved their likenesses and elogies at Antwerp. I proceed. That the study of all the faculties and of the renowned letters has flourished beyond measure at Rome in every age is shown by the countless monuments of the ancient writers, which would be too long to recount. How much value the Romans, from the founding of the City, placed on the study of divine things may be seen from the profane multitude of gods and goddesses, the great number of priests, and the many rites and ceremonies of sacrifice; and after the birth of Christ, what has not been kept up even today? How important jurisprudence was is clear from the Laws of the Twelve Tables alone, a little book which, as Marcus Cicero relates in the first book of De Oratore in the person of Crassus, surpassed all the libraries of the philosophers both in weight of authority and abundance of usefulness. Certainly from this source has gradually flowed, into all the most praised commonwealths of today, whatever is pious in their laws and constitutions. Ti. Coruncanius was the first to begin teaching the laws publicly, as the author of 2 D. de orig. iuris, §35, writes. Many followed him, and others, great men, have dealt with the whole subject professedly. As to where medicine stood, both other evidence and the honours and polished eulogies decreed from time to time to the diligence and faithfulness of physicians cry out. Cassius Hemina records that Archagathus, son of Lysanias, a Peloponnesian, first came to Rome from the physicians, in the consulship of L. Aemilius and M. Livius, in the year 535 from the founding of the City, and that the citizenship was granted to him. Through such men true medicine, especially of herbs, reached the Romans, as Pliny teaches in book 25 of the Natural History, chapter 11, and elsewhere; and Caesar, according to Suetonius, gave citizenship to all who professed true medicine at Rome. Why should I mention the care of history? I will not linger over the listing of writers; that would be long and tedious. Besides others whose memory has perished, Flavius Arrianus, surnamed Xenophon of Nicaea or the Younger, a philosopher from Nicomedia and a pupil of Epictetus, decorated with consular honours, is said to have taught history at Rome under the emperors Hadrian and Antoninus. I will say nothing here about grammar, rhetoric, dialectic and the other arts, which have always flourished to such a degree, as is attested partly by the Roman citizens who excelled in them and partly by the works they published. When Crates, ambassador of King Attalus, was at Rome between the Second and Third Punic Wars, he taught every day throughout the whole period of his embassy, and he also encouraged the Romans themselves to take up the study of grammar and to establish a school where the means so necessary for philosophy would be taught. Strabo relates that Asclepiades, when he was educating the sons of Pompey the Great at Rome, also put them in charge of a school of grammar, and that he satisfied everyone fully in this matter. Marcus Antonius Gnipho is said to have taught grammar first in the house of Gaius Julius, while still a boy, and afterwards in his own private house; he also taught rhetoric, so that he delivered the precepts of eloquence every day, but declaimed only on market days. They say that very distinguished men also attended his school, and among them Marcus Cicero, even while he was holding the praetorship. Caecilius Epirota, a freedman of Atticus the Roman knight, is recorded as the first to expound Virgil and the new poets. Hence that line of Domitius Marsus:

units.la: Epirota tenellorum nutricula Vatum.
units.tr: Epirota, the little nurse of tender poets.

units.la: Timagenes, Alexandrinus, sub Pompeo Romam ab Gabinio captivus ductus, & ab Fausto Sullæ Filio emtus, Grammaticam professus est usque ad Augustum; quia Cæcus propter nimiam in dicendo libertatem & arrogantiam Scholam Grammaticam excitaverat. Appion sub Tiberio & Claudio Theoni in Schola Grammatica successit: quando & Palaemon floruit, qui secum natas secumque interituras adfirmare audebat litteras. Scaurinum, celeberrimum Grammaticum, Præceptorem Romæ habuit Alexander Severus, auctore Lampridio. Valerius Probus privatim Grammaticam docuisse videtur; nec enim plures, quam quatuor aut quinque Discipulos admisit, quibus pomeridianis horis præleget; reliquum tempus studio & meditationi tribuens. Nam & magnam Silvam Observationum antiquarum reliquit. T. Castricius, Rhetoricæ Disciplinæ Doctor in Urbe temporibus Hadriani memoratur ab Agellio eius Discipulo lib. xi. Noct. Attic. cap. xiii, & lib. xiii cap. xx. Qui plura velit, Suetonium adeat de Claris Grammaticis. Iam de Mathematicis adeo certum est, ut aliquoties legantur, quemadmodum etiam Rhetores, sub Coss. & Impp. pulsis uti cum cura notant VV. CLL. Iustus Lipsius ad lib. 11 Annalium Taciti & Lævinus Torrentius variis ad Suetonij Cæsaris locis. Videndæ & I. Mathematicos. C. de Epite. audientia, & l. 2. C. de Malefic. & Mathemat. Mathematicarum Artium Professoribus Alexander Imperator Salaria & Honores proposuit. Rem tanc Pra tam maximæ fuit exstimationis & precij comprehans tot præclara felicitaque Poetarum ingenia. Primus Romæ Fabius docuit Livius Poeta, Claudio Centone Ap. Cæci F. & M. Sempronio Tuditano Coss. post 1 bellum Punicum, annis fere cccc post Romam conditam, statimque plures in hoc studio egregie laborarunt: Ennius, Pacuvius, Plautus, & qui varij sequuntur de quibus plene alij. Adeundi Cicero 1. Tuscul. Quæst. Horatius lib. 11. epist. 1 & alibi, Agellius lib. xvii, cap. ult. alisque. Exijs, quæ dixi, satis superque patet, Scholæ publicas Artium & Disciplinarum omnium Romæ fuisse multis ante Christum natum sæculis. D. Hieronymus Regulæ Monachorum cap. vi ante tua tempora Romæ antiquissima fuisse Gymnasia indicat. Scholæ quaedam nominantur in Vitis Topographia P. Victor & Sex. Rufus. Fuit ibidem posterioribus temporibus Athenæum. Pertinacem Imperatorem ad Athenæum, ut Poetas ibi audiret, tale fuisse, tradit in eius Vita Julius Capitolinus. Alexandrum Severum ad Athenæum, audiendorum & Græcorum & Latinorum Rhetorum vel Poetarum causa, frequenter proficisci, memoriæ prodit Ælius Lampridius. Gordianum, ubi adolevisset, in Athenæo controversias declamasse, audientibus Imperatoribus suis, narrat idem Capitolinus. Memorat & Athenæi B. Hieronymus ad Paulam scribens & Eustochium: Omnia Apostolorum simplicitate & puritate verborum, quasi ad Athenæum & ad Academiam conveniantur, ut pla-sus circumstantium suspiciantur. Ad adiecrendam Romanæ Academiæ Antiquitatem pertinent variæ in Digestis Codiceque Leges: l. fi longius 18 §. 1. D. de Iudiciis l. quum filius familias. 17 D. de reb. credit. l. fi duas habenti tutelas 6. §. 12 Legum Doctores. D. de excusat. §. item Romæ. 15. Instit. eodem. l. unica. C. de studijs liberalib. Urbis Romæ & Constantinopolitanæ. l. 1. C. Theodosiano de studijs: in quibus omnibus multa de Professorum Auditorumque Romæ Privilegijs. Scribitur ab Ælio Spartiano Hadrianus, quamvis esset in reprehendendis Musicis, Tragicis, Comicis, Grammaticis, Rhetoribus, Oratoribus facilis, tamen omnes Professores & honoratos & divites fecisse: in summa familiaritate Epicteti & Heliodori Philosophos, itemque Grammaticos, Rhetores, Musicos, Geometras, Pictores, Astrologos habuisse: præ ceteris eminente Favorino: Doctores insuper, qui Professiones suæ inhabiles videbantur, ditatos honoratosque à Professione dimissse. Alia ibi prætereo. Scholæ Romanæ neglectius, cum temporis injuria, tum variis bellorum calamitatibus habitas excitarunt iterum Pontifices Maximi. Evocavit Thomam Aquinatem Fratrum 1v, instituendæ ornandæque, quæ Romæ ante multos annos esse cœperat, Academiæ vti ejus Vita tradit Platina. Exstat Innocentij 1v Rescriptum cap. 11. de Privilegijs in vi. his verbis: Quum de diversis mundi partibus multi confluant ad Sedem Apostolicam, quasi ad Matrem: nos ad communem tam ipsorum, quam aliorum omnium commodum & profectum paterna sollicitudine intendentes, ut sit ut mora huiusmodi fructus, providimus, quod idem de cetero regatur & vigeat St. Divini Iuris Divini & Humani, Canonici videlicet & Civilis. Unde volumus & statuimus, ut Studentes in Scholis sui generis Sedem eandem talibus omnino Privilegia, Libertatem & Immunitatibus gaudeant quibus gaudent Studentes in Scholis, ubi generale regitur Studium, ac recipiant integre Prebendas suos Ecclesiasticos, fiant illi. Decretum in Concilio Viennensi Clementis v, ut Romæ ubicumque Romanam Curiam residere contingeret, Hebraica, Arabica, Chaldaica Lingua Professores haberentur. Eugenium iv, ut in ejus vita notat Platina, multas in Europa Academias instauravit, omniaque Gymnasia Litterarum quam diligentissime fovit; maxime Romanum, ad quod omne genus litteraturæ adhibuit. Quantum etiam fuerit ea in re studium Nicolai v docent illius ævi Scriptores, Perottus, Sabellicus, Volaterranus, Silvius, & alij. Leonem x totum in restituendis Græcis Litteris fuisse paret ex Epistola, quam scripsit Marco Musuro Cretensi. Gymnasium Sapientiæ ab Alexandro vi sic instauratum & dotatum, ut honeste omnium artium Professores alere possit. Sunt & Romæ xx Seminaria & Collegia omnium Nationum ab Gregorio xiii P. M. instituta: I Collegium Societatis Iesu, quo cc alun- | v Gracorum; tur, docenturque omnes Artes. units.tr: Timagenes, an Alexandrian, was taken to Rome as a captive by Gabinius under Pompey and bought by Faustus, son of Sulla. He taught Grammar until the time of Augustus, because Caecus, through excessive freedom and arrogance in his speech, had stirred up the Grammar School. Appion succeeded Theon in the Grammar School under Tiberius and Claudius, when Palaemon also flourished, who dared to claim that letters were born with him and would die with him. Alexander Severus, on the authority of Lampridius, had Scaurinus, a very famous grammarian, as his teacher in Rome. Valerius Probus seems to have taught Grammar privately; he admitted no more than four or five pupils, whom he lectured to in the afternoon hours, devoting the rest of his time to study and meditation. He left behind a great collection of ancient observations. T. Castricius, a teacher of Rhetoric in the City, is recorded in the time of Hadrian by Gellius, his pupil, in Attic Nights, book 11, chapter 13, and book 13, chapter 20. Whoever wants more should consult Suetonius, On Famous Grammarians. As for the Mathematicians, it is so well established that they were from time to time banished, just as the rhetoricians were, that the men who carefully note the consuls and emperors under whom they were expelled (the VV. CLL.) and Justus Lipsius on book 11 of Tacitus's Annals, and Lævinus Torrentius at various places in Suetonius's Caesars, make this clear. See also the Mathematicians in the law on hearing (C. de Epit. audientia) and in the second law on magic and mathematicians (C. de Malef. et Mathem.). Emperor Alexander offered salaries and honours to Professors of the Mathematical Arts. The poetic talents of so many illustrious and fortunate poets were held in the highest esteem and value at that time. Livius Fabius, a poet, was the first to teach at Rome, in the consulship of Claudius Centho, son of Appius, and M. Sempronius Tuditanus, after the first Punic War, roughly 400 years after the founding of Rome; and at once several men labored notably in this field: Ennius, Pacuvius, Plautus, and others who followed, about whom others have written fully. See Cicero, Tusculan Disputations book 1; Horace, Epistles book 2, epistle 1, and elsewhere; Gellius, book 17, last chapter, and others. From what I have said it is abundantly clear that public schools of all arts and disciplines existed at Rome many centuries before the birth of Christ. St. Jerome, in his Rules for Monks, chapter 6, indicates that gymnasia were very ancient at Rome long before his time. Certain schools are named in the topographical works of P. Victor and Sex. Rufus. In later times there was also an Athenaeum there. Julius Capitolinus, in the life of Pertinax, relates that he used to go to the Athenaeum to hear the poets. Aelius Lampridius records that Alexander Severus frequently went to the Athenaeum to hear both Greek and Latin rhetoricians or poets. Capitolinus also relates that Gordian, when he had grown up, declaimed controversies in the Athenaeum while his emperors listened. St. Jerome, writing to Paula and Eustochium, also mentions the Athenaeum: "All the things of the Apostles, with their simplicity and purity of words, are gathered as if to the Athenaeum and to the Academy, so that the applause of the bystanders may be admired." To the antiquity of the Roman Academy also pertain various laws in the Digest and Code: D. de Iudiciis, law "Fi longius" 18, §1; D. de reb. credit., law "Quum filius familias" 17; C. Tutelas, law "Fi duas habenti tutelas" 6, §12, for the Teachers of Law; D. de excusat., §item Romae; Institutes, same title, 15; C. de studiis liberalibus, unique law; the Theodosian Code, book 1 of the Code, on studies, of the City of Rome and Constantinople. In all these there is much about the privileges of Professors and students at Rome. Aelius Spartianus writes that Hadrian, although he was ready to censure musicians, tragedians, comedians, grammarians, rhetoricians, and orators, nevertheless made all professors both honoured and rich; that on intimate terms with Epictetus and Heliodorus, philosophers, he also kept grammarians, rhetoricians, musicians, geometers, painters, and astrologers, with Favorinus standing out above the rest; and that he dismissed from their profession with wealth and honours those teachers who seemed unfit for their work. I pass over other things here. The Roman schools, neglected both through the ravages of time and the various calamities of wars, were revived again by the Supreme Pontiffs. Pope Urban IV summoned Thomas Aquinas of the Friars to found and adorn the Academy that had begun to exist at Rome many years before, as Platina records in his life. There survives a rescript of Innocent IV, chapter 11, On Privileges, in the Sixth Book, in these words: "Since many from different parts of the world flock to the Apostolic See as to a mother, we, looking with paternal care to the common advantage and progress of them all, have provided that this may be so ordered and flourish... of Divine law, Human law, namely Canon and Civil." Hence we wish and decree that students in schools of this same kind shall enjoy the same privileges, liberties, and immunities as students in schools where a general study is conducted, and that they shall fully receive their ecclesiastical prebends. The Council of Vienne under Clement V decreed that wherever the Roman Curia happened to reside at Rome, there should be professors of the Hebrew, Arabic, and Chaldaic languages. Eugenius IV, as Platina notes in his life, restored many academies in Europe, and cherished the Gymnasia of Letters most diligently of all, especially the Roman one, to which he brought every kind of literature. The writers of that age, Perotti, Sabellicus, Volaterranus, Silvius, and others, show how great Nicholas V's zeal in this matter was. A letter Leo X wrote to Marcus Musurus of Crete shows that Leo was wholly devoted to restoring Greek letters. Alexander VI restored and endowed the Gymnasium of Wisdom in such a way that it could honourably support professors of all the arts. At Rome there are also twenty seminaries and colleges of all nations founded by Gregory XIII, the Supreme Pontiff: (1) the College of the Society of Jesus, where two hundred are supported and all the arts are taught. This college is divided into two schools: one for those over eighteen years of age, and the other its seminary; and the other for theology, philosophy, rhetoric and the humanities. The former is called Parthenia; it has in the church a theologian as its distinguished figure, kneeling, with Physics beside a globe of the earth and Mathematics with a celestial sphere, under the motto LEGES IMPONE SUBACTIS. (2) The German nation of the Anglo-... (3) The Neophytes from the Hebrews, Frisians; (4) of the Angels; (5) of the Greeks; (6) of the Maronites, from Mount Lebanon; (7) of the Illyrians; (8) Vienna, in Austria; (9) Prague, in Bohemia; (10) Graz, in Styria; (11) Olomouc, in Moravia; (12) Braunsberg, in Prussia; (13) Pont-à-Mousson, in Lorraine; (14) Vilnius, in Lithuania; (15) Cluj, in Transylvania; (16) Funai, in Japan; (17) the novitiate of the Society of Jesus at Usuki, in Japan; (18) Assiracense, in Japan; (19) Anzuchi, in Japan; (20) Fulda, in Hesse.

units.la: Quum autem absque Libris Bonæ Litteræ conservari, & ad posteros recte transmitti nequeant; omnem ab omni ævo leguntur Romani diligentiam adhibuisse conquirendis undique optimis Libris, Locisque, in quibus publice reponerentur, instituendis. Nihil hic dicam de studio Veterum in adservandis Libris Sibyllinis. Bibliothecas publicas numerant Urbis Topographi P. Victor, Sex. Rufus, & alii, xxix. Ut Peisistratus Tyrannis Athenis, sic Primus ROMÆ C. Asinius Pollio Disciplinarum monumentum Libros publice posuit legendos. Videndi Seneca lib. iiii Controversiarum Proœmio, & Plinius lib. xxxv nat. hist. cap. ii. C. Julius Cæsar Græcas & Latinas Bibliothecas exstruendi curam dedit M. Terentio Varroni; teste inde Vita Suetonio, cap. xliv & lvi. Octavianus Augustus in Palatio Latinam Græcamque Bibliothecam ex Apollinis Tuticanici Colossi ære nobilissimo instituit & exornavit, ut idem Suetonius scribit cap. xxix. Tiberiana Bibliotheca meminerunt Agellius, qui ea usus est, non uno loco, & Vopiscus in Probo. Domitianus, ut notat Suetonius in ejus Vita cap. xx, Bibliothecas, incendio absumtas, impensissime curavit reparari, Exemplaribus undique petitis, missisque Alexandriam, qui describerent emendarentque. Ulpius quoque Trajanus novas Bibliothecas exstruxit, ut auctor est Dion. Scribit Agellius lib. xi, cap. xvii, se in Bibliotheca Templi Trajani litteris operam dedisse. In Ulpia Bibliotheca Libri Lintei servabantur, teste Fl. Vopisco in Aureliano; & Flavianus, eodem scribente in Tacito. Mentio Bibliothecæ Ulpiæ ad Vopiscum in Probo, qui se depromtis ex ea Libris usum adserit. Paulus quoque Bibliothecam nominat Agellius, Præclara est illa Valentiniani, Valentis & Gratiani Constitutio ad Clearchum P. V. quæ exstat l. 2. C. Theodosiano, de Studiis Liberal. Antiquarios ad Bibliotheca Codices componendos, vel pro vetustate reparandos quatuor Græcos, & tres Latinos scribendi peritos legi jubemus: quibus de Caducis Populibus (& ipsi enim videntur à populo) competentes impertiantur Annona, ad eiusdem Bibliotheca custodiam conditionibus & requirendis & protinus adponendis. Non neglexerunt egregiam illam Romanorum Imperatorum erga lectissimos Libros curam Pontifices Maximi. Epistola legitur Athanasii ceterorumque Ægypti Præsulum ad Marcum, Antistitem Romanum; qua Canones Concilij Nicæni corrupti perditique ex Romana pontificum Bibliotheca repetuntur. Gregorius etiam Magnus Concilij Ephesini, ab Hæreticis depravati, verum purumque Exemplar Anastasio, Antiochiensium Episcopo, ex Romana Bibliotheca transmittere se scribit. Traditur Hilarius Sardus duas Bibliothecas reliquisse: Zacharias Græcus Bibliothecam S. Petri restituisse: Nicolaus v petiit universam fere Europam misisse Viros, in omni artium genere præstantissimos, qui Veterum Scriptorum libros conquirerent: promissis quinque Ducatorum millibus ei, qui Hebraicum D. Matthæi Apostoli Evangelium adferret. Leo x Joannem L. Scarem in Turciam misit, qui excussis omnibus ibi Bibliothecis Romanam valde ditavit.
units.tr: Since good letters cannot be preserved without books, nor correctly handed down to posterity, it is read that the Romans, from every age, took every care to seek out the best books from everywhere and to establish places in which they might be publicly kept. I will say nothing here about the ancients' care in preserving the Sibylline Books. Urban topographers, P. Victor, Sex. Rufus, and others, count twenty-nine public libraries. As Peisistratus did at Athens as tyrant, so first at Rome C. Asinius Pollio placed books of learning in public for reading. See Seneca, book 4, Preface to the Controversies, and Pliny, Natural History, book 35, chapter 2. C. Julius Caesar entrusted to M. Terentius Varro the task of establishing Greek and Latin libraries; Suetonius's Life, chapters 44 and 56, bears witness. Octavian Augustus founded and adorned a Latin and Greek library in the Palatine out of the bronze of the famous Colossus of Apollo at Tuticanum, as Suetonius also writes, chapter 29. Gellius, who used it on more than one occasion, and Vopiscus in the Life of Probus, mention the Tiberian library. Domitian, as Suetonius notes in his life, chapter 20, had the libraries, destroyed by fire, most carefully restored, with copies sought from everywhere and men sent to Alexandria to copy and correct them. Ulpius Trajan also built new libraries, as Dio attests. Gellius, book 11, chapter 17, writes that he had worked in the library of the Temple of Trajan. In the Ulpian Library linen books were kept, according to Flavius Vopiscus in the Life of Aurelian; and Flavian, the same author writing about Tacitus. The Ulpian Library is mentioned by Vopiscus in the Life of Probus, who says he used books taken from it. Gellius also names a library, Paulus. That famous constitution of Valentinian, Valens, and Gratian to Clearchus, Prefect of the City, which survives as law 2 of the Theodosian Code, On Liberal Studies, is also notable. We order that four Greek and three Latin antiquaries skilled in writing be chosen to compile codices for the library, or to restore them when they are old; to them, from the public funds of those who are fallen (for they too seem to belong to the people), let the grain allowance be granted, on condition that they both seek out and immediately put in place what is needed for the custody of the library. The Supreme Pontiffs also did not neglect the excellent care of the Roman emperors for the choicest books. A letter of Athanasius and the other bishops of Egypt to Mark, the Roman bishop, survives, in which the canons of the Council of Nicaea, corrupted and lost, are recovered from the Roman papal library. Gregory the Great also writes that he sent to Anastasius, bishop of Antioch, from the Roman library a true and pure copy of the Council of Ephesus, which heretics had corrupted. It is recorded that Hilarius of Sardinia left two libraries; Zacharias the Greek restored the library of St. Peter. Nicholas V sought to send men of the highest excellence in every kind of art throughout almost all Europe to collect the books of the ancient writers, promising five thousand ducats to anyone who brought him the Hebrew Gospel of the Apostle Matthew. Leo X sent Giovanni Lascaris to Turkey, who, after searching all the libraries there, greatly enriched the Roman one.

units.la: Sufficiant hæc de utraque ROMA: qua versus Meridionaliora egressio, Magnumque
units.tr: These things should suffice concerning both Rome: the exit from it towards the more southern parts, and the great

units.la: Seminaria & Collegia variorum Nationum, que petenti Marte sese offert xxii ab Vrbe Lapide ad fauces vel Ostia (unde nomen) Tiberis Vetus Opidum Ostia. Sic Latinis omnibus, ũ ne vero Græcis scribitur, quæ hodieque Ostia vulgo. In Tabula Itineraria Hostia legitur, auferendi, ut plerataque alia, calu, pro Hostiis. Conditor eius Ancus Marcius iv Romanorum Rex, uti memoriæ produnt Livius lib. i, Dionysius Halicarnass. in Antiq. Rom. Strabo, Florus lib. i. Plinius lib. iii nat. histor. cap. v. Pomponius Mela, alij. Sic meus Ennius lib. ii Annalium, ubi de Rege, quem dixi:
units.tr: Seminaries and colleges of various nations, which lies, as Mars would have it, twenty-two miles from the city by the stone, at the mouth (whence the name) of the Tiber, the old town Ostia. So it is written by all Latin writers, though not by the Greeks, and it is what people today commonly call Ostia. In the Itinerary Table it is read as Hostia, the initial letter having been lost, as in many other words, for Hostiis. Its founder was Ancus Marcius, the fourth king of the Romans, as Livy, book 1, Dionysius of Halicarnassus in his Roman Antiquities, Strabo, Florus, book 1, Pliny, Natural History, book 3, chapter 5, Pomponius Mela, and others, record. So my Ennius, in book 2 of the Annals, where he speaks of the king I mentioned:

units.la: Ostia munita est: idem Lun ma(?) ... Munda facta, Nautisque Mari quaesitus Viam
units.tr: Ostia was fortified; the same ... made clean, and sought by sailors for the sea-road

units.la: Sumptuosissimis lapsu temporis infractam ædificijs, sed ab Saracenis miserum in modum convulsam restauravit Leo iv Pontifex Maximus; largitus eam Colonis aliquot ex Corsica translatis incolendam. Turrim ibi in propugnaculo excitavit Martinus v. Munitissimam postremo reddidit, qualemque nunc videmus, fecit Iulius ii. Gravioris est cœli & pestilentis aëris. Constructa enim in Limo Tiberinis aquis inlato, ut Dionysius Halicarnass. notat: in ipso Maris Fluminisque Continio, ut Florus loquitur. Videre est ibi ruinas & veteris Portus, olim celeberrimi, cuiusque Fundamenta ex ipso Mari eminentia. Fuisse perhibetur ex admirandis Operibus, quæ unquam Romani extruxerunt. Evertisse tertur Gregorius Pontifex, ne Saracenis ad ipsorum irruptiones esset receptaculum. Ostia Castrorum Ædem fuisse, ibique sacrificari solitum Ventorum Maritque causa, patet ex Ammiano libro xix. Sacrum autem illud annuum fuisse, & Majumam post seculo dictum, docet Sudas: Μαιυμᾶς, παιτηρέας ἐχιτυ ... Μαῖα ... Respicit eo Æthicus in Cosmogr. Tiberis Infusum fuit inter Portam Urbis & Ostiam Civitatem; ubi Populus Romanus cum Urbis Praefecto et Consule, Castrorum celebrandorum causa egreditur, solemnitate iucunda. legendum inter Portum Urbis, &c. de quo in Etruria. Meminerunt Ostia sæpe Prisci. Legendus & de ea Natalis Comes libro Historiar. x. Ager Pēpones fert copiose; quorum, ut refert Capitolinus, Claudius Albinus Imperator uno prandio denos abtumsisse scribitur. Ab Ostia via Ostiensis; quæ inter Urbem & Ostiam ipsam celebria fuerunt Loca. Emporium ad Tiberim, cuius meminit Livius lib. xxxv & xli. Alexandri Vicus tertio ab Urbe Lapide, de quo Ammianus lib. xvii. Pomonal in Agro Solonio ad duodecimum lapidem, apud Festum; Ager Solonius est apud Livium lib. viii; Σηλᾶνοι etiam habent Dionysius lib. ii & Plutarchus in Mario inter Urbem & Ostiam: est & Solonij memoria apud M. Tullium ad Atticum lib. ii: idem fortean cum Solonio, quem variante Scriptura nominanti Ciceronis Codices i & ii. de Divinat. ubi apud focum Angues nundinari solent. Sextum denique Philippi, cujus in Territorio Romano inter Ostiam & Urbem, ubi fo Tiberis findit & Insulam facit, mentionem celebrat Æthicus. Adoni est Via Portuensis.
units.tr: Ostia, once crammed with very costly buildings, but wretchedly torn down by the Saracens, was restored by Leo IV, Pope, who granted it to some colonists brought from Corsica to inhabit. Martin V built a tower there as a bulwark, and Julius II finally made it as strong as we now see it. The air is heavier and pestilential, for it is built on mud brought down by the Tiber waters, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus notes, at the very meeting place of the sea and the river, as Florus puts it. There one may see the ruins of an old harbour, once very famous, whose foundations stand out of the sea itself. It is said to have been one of the most admirable works the Romans ever built. Pope Gregory is reported to have destroyed it, so that it should not become a refuge for the Saracens in their raids. That Ostia was the temple of the Camps, and that sacrifice was customarily offered there for the sake of the winds and the sea, is clear from Ammianus, book 19. That this sacrifice was annual, and was called Majuma a century later, Suidas teaches: Μαιυμᾶς, ... Μαῖα ... Æthicus in his Cosmography alludes to it: The Tiber flowed between the Gate of the City and the town of Ostia, where the Roman people with the Prefect of the City and the Consul go out to celebrate the festival of the camps, a pleasant solemnity. It should be read "between the Port of the City," etc., concerning which see under Etruria. The ancient writers often mention Ostia. Natalis Comes also should be read on it, book 10 of his Histories. The land produces Pepones abundantly; of these, as Capitolinus reports, the Emperor Clodius Albinus is written to have eaten ten at a single meal. From Ostia runs the Ostian Way; between the City and Ostia itself these were famous places. Emporium on the Tiber, which Livy mentions in books 35 and 41. Alexander's Village, three miles from the City, of which Ammianus speaks in book 17. Pomonal in the Solonian territory at the twelfth milestone, according to Festus; the Solonian field is in Livy, book 8; Dionysius, book 2, and Plutarch in his Life of Marius also have the Solanoi between the City and Ostia. The memory of the Solonium is also found in Cicero to Atticus, book 2; perhaps it is the same as the Solonium which the manuscripts of Cicero's On Divination, books 1 and 2, name with a variant spelling, where at the hearth snakes are usually sold at market. Finally, Æthicus records the Sextum of Philip, in the Roman territory between Ostia and the City, where the Tiber divides and makes an island. The Portuensian Way is near.

units.la: Ostiis relictis, reliqua Latij oppida, quæ mari fere adsident, pervagabor; ordinem sequutus, qui apud Plinium lib. iii, cap. v, Antoninum, & alios Geographos, quos inter se commutam. Adlocat ille post Ostia litori Laurentum, ut etiam (quod post ex generali Schemate parebit) Strabo, cui Λαύρεντον, Pomponius Mela. Antoninus & Itineraria Tabula. Λαύρεντον scribit Lacus ad Lycophronem. Laurentum Urbs Plinio vocatur libro ii ad Gallum. Meminit & Silius lib. viii: Sacra manus Eutuli ferit ante quæ Daunia regna, Laurentique domo guidem.
units.tr: Having left Ostia, I shall travel through the remaining towns of Latium, which sit mostly by the sea, following the order which Pliny, book 3, chapter 5, Antoninus, and other geographers use, though they differ from one another. He places Laurentum on the shore after Ostia, as also (as will appear later from the general scheme) Strabo does, who has Λαύρεντον, and Pomponius Mela, Antoninus and the Itinerary Table. Lycophron, in his commentary, writes Λαύρεντον for the lake. Pliny calls Laurentum a city in book 2 to Gallus. Silius also mentions it in book 8: "The sacred band of Eutulus strikes before the Daunian kingdoms, and the house of Laurentum indeed."

units.la: Hodie S. Laurenty memorat appellari Gabriel Barrius libro ii Calabriæ. Ex Urbe Laurento Publius & Marcus Indices producunt, apud Dionysium Halic. lib. v. Conjurationis Inopum & Servorum. A Pico Aboriginum Rege conditum notat Servius ad lib. vii Æneidos, unde, ——Laurentis Regia Pici.
units.tr: Today, Gabriel Barrius, in book 2 of Calabria, records that it is called Saint Lawrence. Publius and Marcus, the informers, bring forward from the city of Laurentum, in Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 5, the conspiracy of the poor and the slaves. Servius, on book 7 of the Aeneid, notes that it was founded by Picus, king of the Aborigines, whence "the royal palace of Picus of Laurentum."

units.la: In Littore Maris fuisse docet Valerius Maximus, ubi scribit Scipionem & Lælium Caietæ & Laurentis Conchulas & Umbilicos lectitasse. Idem non obscure colligitur ex Symmachi Epistola ad Filium, quæ ordine xv libro vii. Æneam hoc in loco primum consedisse auctor est Livius lib. i. Affirmat idem Strabo lib. v, scribens Æneam cum Anchife Patre Filioque Ascanio in Italiam delatum Laurenti cepisse terram; deinde xxiv ab mari Stadus opidum prope Ostiam conditum, Lavinium ab Lavinia Latini Filia nominatle. Inde Populus Laurens Ovidio libro vi Faltor. Laurentes Tabulae marmoreae, qui in Cubiculo Cardinalis Cæsij:
units.tr: That it lay on the shore of the sea Valerius Maximus teaches, where he writes that Scipio and Laelius were in the habit of gathering shells and sea-snails at Caieta and Laurentum. The same is clearly gathered from the letter of Symmachus to his son, which is letter 15 of book 7. Livy, book 1, is the authority that Aeneas first settled in this place. Strabo, book 5, also affirms it, writing that Aeneas, brought into Italy with his father Anchises and son Ascanius, took possession of the land of Laurentum; then, twenty-four miles from the sea, the town of Lavinium was founded near Ostia and named after Lavinia, the daughter of Latinus, Lavinium. Hence the Laurentine people, in Ovid, Fasti, book 6. The Laurentine marble tablets, which are in the bedchamber of Cardinal Cesi:

units.la: M. CORNELI. PAL. VALERIAN FLAMINI. PRÆTORI II. SACRA. VOLCANI DECVRION. LAVRENTIVM. VICI. AVG. EIVS PATRONO CORPORIS. LEMNIC. VIARIORVM AVXILIARIORVM. OSTIENSIVM
units.tr: To Marcus Cornelius Valerianus of the Palatine tribe, flamen, praetor for the second time, sacred to Vulcan, decurion of Laurentum, of the Vicus Augustus, patron of the corporation of the Lemnian auxiliary road-workers of Ostia.

units.la: Inde fortean & Laurentina Via Plinio in Epistolis libro ii & Valerio Maximo libro viii cap. v; Laurentina Palus, Virgilio; Laurentina Paludes, Paterculo; Laurentina Silva, Obsequenti & Symmacho: Quod si & Laurentium, Villa C. Plinij Secundi lib.
units.tr: Perhaps from this also comes the Laurentine Way, in Pliny, Letters book ii, and Valerius Maximus book viii, ch. v; the Laurentine Marsh, in Virgil; the Laurentine Marshes, in Paterculus; the Laurentine Forest, in Obsequens and Symmachus. But if Laurentium is also the villa of C. Pliny the Younger, book ii of the Letters, to Minucius Fundanus, which is also called Laurens, and in the same book to Gallus,

units.la: 1. Epist. ad Minutium Fundanum, quæ & Laurens eidem libro ii ad Gallum. Non procul Laurentio Lucus tunc Iovis Indigetis, innuente Plinio; iuxta Numicium Amnem, de quo alibi.
units.tr: 1. Not far from Laurentum there was then a grove of Jupiter Indiges, as Pliny indicates, beside the river Numicius, of which I shall speak elsewhere.

units.la: Laurento Lavinium subdunt Strabo & Peutingeriana Tabula: quin & Antoninus, apud quem tamen vitiose legitur Lanuvium, quod ibi locum habere non potest. Absurdum enim Lanuvium cogitanti petere Ostia & Laurentum. Nam Lanuvium in Mediterraneis erat, propius Viam Appiam inter Albanum Montem, Ariciam & Ardeam: Lavinium autem ad Mare, inter Ostia & Ardeam; in quam sententiam inclinant etiam Surita & Ortelius, si copiam habuissent Itinerariæ Tabulæ, quæ post editæ. Quod Lavinium Latinis omnibus; Aavinov dicitur Straboni: Aaʹ Cívtov Stephano; Appiano lib. i. & ii belli Civilis. Ab Urbe distat ad decimum lapidem. Appiano, ad xxi milliare Itinerariæ Tabulæ, recto itinere: nam quod per Ostia ducit, plurium est: ab Mari octo millibus separatur Servio: Certe haud procul inde fuisse, docemur ex Æneid. i & Metamorph. xv libro. Lavinij Fanum fuisse Veneris. Latinis omnibus commune, tradit Strabo lib. v. In Lavinio, ut scribit D. Augustinus de Civitate Dei lib. vii, cap. xxi Liber colebatur per totum Culmensem. Dekeribunt ejus initia Nominisque causam, præter Servium ad i Æneid. Dionysius Halic. lib. i, Virgilius lib. vii Æneid. Strabo lib. v, Varro lib. iv de L.L. Isidorus lib. xv. cap. i. Nunc pauccissima supersunt Urbis in monticulo vestigia. Hodie Lavinia, ut auctor est Philippus Pegafetta: vel, ut Celsus Civitatem Anglerius, Civita Lavina. Lavinium cum Laurento confundit Servius ad illa i Æneidos, ——— Lavinaque venit Litora.
units.tr: Strabo and the Peutinger Table place Lavinium next to Laurentum. Antoninus does too, though there it is wrongly read as Lanuvium, which cannot stand there, for it would be absurd to think of Lanuvium as something one reaches by way of Ostia and Laurentum. Lanuvium lay inland, nearer the Via Appia, between the Alban Mount, Aricia and Ardea; Lavinium, however, lay by the sea, between Ostia and Ardea. Surita and Ortelius also incline to this view, though they would have had the Itinerary Table had it been published later. Lavinium is called by all the Latins; Strabo calls it Lavinion [Λαβίνιον], Stephen Lavinion [Λαβίνιον], and Appian, in books i and ii of the Civil Wars, likewise. It lies about ten miles from the City: twenty-one miles by Appian and the Itinerary Table, by the direct road, for the road through Ostia is longer; Servius puts it eight miles from the sea. That it was not far from there we learn from Aeneid i and Metamorphoses book xv. The shrine of Lavinium was Venus's, as Strabo book v tells, common to all the Latins. In Lavinium, as Augustine writes in The City of God book vii, ch. xxi, Liber was worshipped throughout the Culmensian region. Its origins and the reason for its name are described by Servius on Aeneid i, Dionysius of Halicarnassus book i, Virgil Aeneid vii, Strabo book v, Varro De Lingua Latina book iv, and Isidore book xv, ch. i. Now very few traces of the city remain on the little hill. Today it is Lavinia, as Philip Pigafetta reports, or, as Celso Anglerio says, Civita Lavina. Servius, on those lines of Aeneid i, "and came to the Lavinian shores," confuses Lavinium with Laurentum.

units.la: Hæc Civitas, inquit, tria habuit nomina. Nam prius Lavinium dicta est, à Lavino Latini Fratre; postea Laurentum ab Lauro inventa à Latino, dum adepto imperio post Fratris mortem Civitatem augeret; postea Lavinium, à Lavinia uxore Æneæ: qui eadem habet paullo sequius ad illa vii Æneidos, Nec Prænestina fundator defuit arcis;
units.tr: "This city," he says, "had three names. For it was first called Lavinium, from Lavinus, brother of Latinus; afterwards Laurentum, from the laurel found by Latinus, while, having gained power after his brother's death, he enlarged the city; afterwards Lavinium again, from Lavinia, wife of Aeneas." He says much the same, with a little less clarity, on Aeneid vii: "Nor was there a founder of the Praenestine citadel."

units.la: Laurentum, ait inter alia, à Pico saltum est, ut Laurentis Regia Pici. Item à Lavino Latini Fratre est Lavinium dictum: idem à Latino Laurentum, item à Lavinia, Laurolavinium. Lavinium idem cum Laurolavinio esse, facile mihi persuadeo; sed idem esse cum Laurento, nondum possum. Servius Laurolavinium alibi sæpe nominat pro Lavinio, diserte ad illud vii Æneid. Latinus erat tecti medio in penetralibus altis;
units.tr: "Laurentum," he says among other things, "was named from Picus, as the palace of Picus was Laurentine. Likewise Lavinium was named from Lavinus, brother of Latinus; the same place was called Laurentum from Latinus, and also Laurolavinium from Lavinia. I readily believe that Lavinium is the same as Laurolavinium, but I cannot yet believe it is the same as Laurentum." Servius often elsewhere names Laurolavinium for Lavinium, and says so explicitly on Aeneid vii: "Latinus was in the deep recesses of his house."

units.la: Latinus, inquit, post mortem Lavini Fratris quum Lavinium amplificaret, ab inventa Lauro Laurolavinium appellavit. Laurolavinium Frontino Colonia est. Quemadmodum autem Lavinas forte ab Lavino vel Lavinio, sic ab Laurolavinio, LaurensLavinas. Sic urna depositoria oblonga Romæ, ante ædiculam Divi Nicolai, recto Cæsarinos: M. VALERIVS ACHILLEVS. L1 CTOR. PROXIMVS LAVRENS. LAVINAS AGENS. ANNVM. ÆTATIS. LXV. VIVVS. MIHI COMPARAVI. ET. POSVI
units.tr: "Latinus," he says, "after the death of his brother Lavinus, when he was enlarging Lavinium, named it Laurolavinium from the laurel he found." Frontinus calls Laurolavinium a colony. Just as Lavinas perhaps comes from Lavinus or Lavinium, so from Laurolavinium comes Laurens, Lavinas. So on an oblong burial urn at Rome, in front of the little shrine of St Nicholas, near the Caesarini: "M. Valerius Achilleus, nearest reader of Laurentum, pursuing the Lavinian business, aged 65, while alive, made this for myself and set it up."

units.la: Sic in Lapide, qui l eltriæ, ad Cathedrale Templum: C. FIRMIO. C. F. MENEN. RVFINO EQ. PVB. LAVREN. LAV DEC. FLAMIN. PATRONO COLLEGIORVM. FABR. CENT. DENDR. FELTRIÆ ITEM. QVE. BERVENS COLLEG FABR. ALTINATIVM PATRONO
units.tr: So too on a stone at Feltria, by the cathedral temple: "To Gaius Firmius, son of Gaius, of the Menenian tribe, Rufinus, public horseman, of Laurentum, Lavinian, decurion, flamen, patron of the colleges of smiths, centonarii and dendrophori of Feltria, and likewise of Beruens, patron of the smiths' college of Altinum."

units.la: Iam aliud esse Laurentum, aliud Lavinium, satis paret, ut dixi, ex Strabone, Antonino (quamquam apud eum corrupte Lanuvium sic scriptum, pro Lavinio) & Itineraria Tabula, utrumque nullo fere intervallo nominantibus. Adfirmat etiam, ut paullo ante scripsi, Strabo, Æneam in Italiam delatum Laurens terram cepisse, deinde xxiv ab mari stadiis Lavinium condidisse, dictum ab Lavinia Latini filia. Livius etiam & alij non semel, de Lavinio, & Laurento, atque etiam, ut hoc addam, Lanuvio tamquam diversis oppidis, loquuntur. Sic Ovidius lib. vi Fastorum:
units.tr: That Laurentum and Lavinium are different places is clear enough, as I have said, from Strabo, from Antoninus (though there, through a corruption, it is written Lanuvium for Lavinium), and from the Itinerary Table, all of which name them at almost no distance from each other. Strabo also affirms, as I wrote a little earlier, that Aeneas, carried to Italy, first took the land of Laurentum, and then, twenty-four stades from the sea, founded Lavinium, named after Lavinia, daughter of Latinus. Livy and others, more than once, speak of Lavinium and Laurentum, and even, I might add, of Lanuvium, as distinct towns. So Ovid in book vi of the Fasti:

units.la: Et Populus Laurens, Laviniumque meum.
units.tr: "And the Laurentine people, and my Lavinium."
