units.la: Sequitur apud Plinium Ardea. Sic Latinis, licque, Ἀρδέα, Ptolemæo & Stephano, quæ a dea Straboni. Quondam Rutulorum Urbs, ut Livius & Orosius tradunt. Meminerunt omnes ævi veteris Scriptores. Troiam quondam dictam, refert Stephanus: Dauni Urbem appellat Virgilius x Æneidos. Conditam ab Danae, Persei Matre, testatur post Virgilium Plinius lib. iii nat. Hist. cap. v, ab uno ex Vivis & Circensibus, ex Xenagora Dionysius. Nomen inditum ab Ardea Avis augurio, canit Virgilius libro vii:
units.tr: Next, in Pliny, comes Ardea. It is called Ardea by the Latins, and Ardea [Ἀρδέα] by Ptolemy and Stephen; Strabo calls it by the goddess's name. It was once a city of the Rutulians, as Livy and Orosius relate. All the writers of the ancient age mention it. Stephen reports that it was once called Troia; Virgil, in Aeneid x, calls it the city of Daunus. Pliny, after Virgil, in Natural History book iii, ch. v, testifies that it was founded by Danae, mother of Perseus; Dionysius, from Xenagoras, says it was founded by one of the Vivi and Circenses. The name was given from the omen of the bird Ardea, as Virgil sings in book vii:

units.la: Ardua it Rutuli ad muros, quam dicitur Urbem
units.tr: "Ardua the Rutulians go to the walls, which is called the city

units.la: Ac typhonas Danae fundasse Colonis,
units.tr: "and the Typhonians, founded by Danae's colonists,

units.la: Praesens delata Noto: locus Ardea quondam
units.tr: "borne by the south wind into view: once Ardea,

units.la: Dictus avis, & nunc magnum manet Ardea nomen.
units.tr: "was called after the bird, and now Ardea keeps its great name."

units.la: Virgilij sententiæ subscribunt Servius & Higinus. Consulenda & Ovidij Metamorphosis. Alij placet dictam Urbem ab Ardore, vel ἀέδω hoc loco vehementia. Innuere putatur hoc Martialis:
units.tr: Servius and Hyginus agree with Virgil's view. Ovid's Metamorphoses should also be consulted. Others think the city was named from ardor, or from ἀέδω, meaning vehemence here. Martial is thought to hint at this:

units.la: Ardea sollicito Pastanaque rura petantur,
units.tr: "Let Ardea be sought by those anxious, and the fields of Pastum,

units.la: Quaque Ciceronis sidere ferret ager.
units.tr: "and the land where Cicero's star bore fruit."

units.la: Ab Mari 10 e c Stadijs, ut Strabo tradit, distita; ab Vrbe cix, eodem notante, vel xviii milliario, Eutropio dignante, posita. Livius etiam inter Coloniae Romanas numerat, quae bello Punico Romanis auxilia denegarunt. Obtellam olim ab Tarquinio Superbo vi Romanorum Rege, scribunt Livius, Dionysius, alij. Pidutas Ardeatae Tempus, earumque auctorem M. Ludium celebrat Plinius lib. xxxv, cap. x, alijque locis. Nunc in ditione est Columniæ gentis. Nonnulli scribunt Ardea nomen retinere. In ejus agro Fontes sunt putidi, sulphurei aquis, teste Boccatio.
units.tr: It lay, as Strabo reports, ten and a half stades from the sea, and, as Eutropius records, eighteen miles from the City; Strabo notes sixty-one miles. Livy also counts it among the Roman colonies which refused the Romans help in the Punic War. Livy, Dionysius and others write that it was once besieged by Tarquin the Proud, sixth king of the Romans. Plinius, in book xxxv, ch. x, and elsewhere, celebrates the paintings of the Ardeatines and their author, M. Ludius. Now it lies in the domain of the Colonna family. Some write that Ardea keeps its name. In its territory there are foul springs, sulphurous in their waters, according to Boccaccio.

units.la: Post Ardeam erat Aphrodisium, cuius mentio apud Strabonem, Plinium Melam. Pandit le nox Antium. Sic plerique Latinis Scriptoribus nominatur: Graecis Ἀντίον: Ἀντέα autem & Ἀντίον Stephano, quae nunc Cabo d'Anzio, Caput Anty. Vocatum sic ab Ancio, uno ex Ulyssis & Circes Filius, notat ex Xenagora Dionysius lib.
units.tr: After Ardea came Aphrodisium, which is mentioned by Strabo, Pliny and Mela. Next comes Antium. Latin writers commonly name it so; the Greeks call it Antion [Ἀντίον], while Stephen gives Antea [Ἀντέα] and Antion [Ἀντίον]; it is now Cabo d'Anzio, Caput Anty. Dionysius, in book i, notes that it was so called from Ancius, one of the sons of Ulysses and Circe, according to Xenagoras.

units.la: 1. Alij putant sic dictum, quod ante alias Urbes in ipso littore fuerit sita. Colonia Romanorum Livio lib. viii. Tacito lib. xv. Appiano Alexandrino lib. 1. Plinio lib. iii. cap. v. alius. Sic COL. ANTIAT. LEG. iiii. ITALICA est in Nummo Neronis, apud Hubertum Goltzium in Thesauro. Dici itinere distare ab Urbe scribit Propopius, cui Antium in Samnitibus locatur: ccl x. Stadiis ab Ostia, Strabo. Celeberrimum ibi habuisse Fortunam Templum, memorat lib. iii. Annalium Tacitus. Innuit & Horatius lib. 1. Odarum: O Diva, gratum quae regis Antium, Praesens vel imo tollere de gradu Mortale corpus, vel superbos Vertere funeribus triumphos.
units.tr: Others think it was so called because it lay on the shore before other cities. It was a Roman colony, according to Livy book viii, Tacitus book xv, Appian of Alexandria book i, Pliny book iii, ch. v, and others. So the coin of Nero reads COL. ANTIAT. LEG. IIII. ITALICA, in Hubert Goltzius's Thesaurus. Procopius writes that it was a day's journey from the City, and places Antium among the Samnites: 150 stades from Ostia, says Strabo. Tacitus, in book iii of the Annals, records that it had a very famous temple of Fortune. Horace also hints at this in book i of the Odes: "O goddess, who rule grateful Antium, able to lift a mortal body from the lowest step, or turn proud triumphs into funerals."

units.la: Ibidem etiam in medio foro Castoris Pollucisque fuisse Templum lego apud Dionysium. Anty, Urbe Volscorum, exulasse Marcium Coriolanum, scribit idem libro viii. Ab T. Quinctio Cos. deditione captum, partemque agri eius adtributam Populo Romano, refert idem lib. ix. Instauravit Antium Claudius Nero Imp. Coloniis Impositis, Portuque facto operis summuosissimi, teste Suetonio cap ix. Eius stupenda hodie visuntur rudera. Navium, quibus Antiates bello fuerant usi, Rostra, ab Romano Victore in foro fixa, nomen fecerunt Loco ex quo Conciones haberi solitae ad Populum. Legendi Livius & alij. Narrat Philostratus de Vita Apollonij lib. viii. volume Anty, Oppido Italiae maritimo, adservatum, quo Phythagorae quaedam dogmata dicebantur perscripta; eaque de causa celebre fuisse Urbi nomen. Neroni ex Poppaea Coniuge natam ibi Filiam, Augustamque dictam, ait Tacitus lib. xv. Antij hodie nihil extare praeter ruinas, sed in eius vestigiis Neptunium nunc aedificatum, censent Volaterranus, Blondus, & Ciofanus. Memorat idem Blondus iuxta litus multas aedificiorum ruinas in Silvis adparere, loquentes ipsa re priscam Urbis amplitudinem. Silvae, quas dixi, Aprorum, Capreolorum, Leporum Venationi sunt aptae. Fuisse quondam ibi Lucum Iovis Indigetis, colligitur ex Plinio. Frequens Anty, Antiatumque mentio apud Veteres.
units.tr: I read in Dionysius that there was also a temple of Castor and Pollux in the middle of the forum there. The same writer, in book viii, says that Marcius Coriolanus went into exile from Anty, a city of the Volsci. In book ix he reports that it was taken by the consul T. Quinctius, through surrender, and that part of its land was assigned to the Roman people. Claudius Nero, the emperor, restored Antium, planting colonists there and making a harbour, a very splendid work, as Suetonius says, ch. ix. Its stupendous ruins can be seen today. The rostra of the ships which the Antiates had used in war, fixed in the forum by the Roman victor, gave the name to the place from which speeches were customarily made to the people. Read Livy and others. Philostratus, in the Life of Apollonius book viii, tells that a volume was kept at Anty, a maritime town of Italy, in which certain teachings of Pythagoras were written out; and for this reason the city's name was famous. Tacitus, in book xv, says that a daughter was born there to Nero by his wife Poppaea, and was named Augusta. Volaterranus, Biondo and Ciofano think that nothing of Antium survives except ruins, but that on its remains the temple of Neptune has now been built. Biondo also records that along the shore, in the woods, many ruins of buildings appear, speaking by their very existence of the city's former greatness. The woods I have mentioned are suited to hunting wild boar, roe deer and hares. That there was once a grove of Jupiter Indiges there is gathered from Pliny. Anty and Antiatum are frequently mentioned by the ancients.

units.la: Locatur post Antium Asturas; Plinio quidem Flumen cum Insula cognomine, Tabulae vero Itinerariae, si recte video, Oppidum, quod forte fuit vel ad Flumen in Continente, vel in Insula. De Astura Fluvio dixi supra. Asturae, ut Oppidi Fluviique, meminit, praeter M. Tullium ad Atticum, Servius ad finem vii Aeneidos: Haud longe a Terracina Oppidum est Astura, & eius cognomine Fluvius. Ἀστυρὶς forte Stephano, cui illa χώρα Ἰταλίας. Locus hic memorabilis cum indignissima M. Tullii Ciceronis, Antonium fugientis, caede, ut Livius, Plutarchus, aliique monumentis produnt; tum Corradini fato Henrici F. Friderici ii. Imperat. N. quem Karolus Eculisimensis, Primus Siciliae Rex, securi percussit. Quod Asturam quidam censent Κλώτες Ptolemaeo vocari, falluntur. Nam Astura & Cloelia Romana, interiecto Nymphaeo Flumine, sunt apud Plinium. In Tabula quoque Itineraria Astura & Cloelia interuallum habent ix. millium Passuum.
units.tr: Located after Antium Asturas. Pliny gives a river with an island of the same name, while the Itinerary tables, if I read them rightly, give a town, which was perhaps either on the river on the mainland or on the island. I have spoken of the Astura Fluvio above. Asturae, as the name of both the town and the river, is mentioned by Servius at the end of Book 7 of the Aeneid, besides Marcus Tullius in his letter to Atticus: Haud longe a Terracina Oppidum est Astura, & eius cognomine Fluvius. Perhaps Stephanus calls it Ἀστυρὶς [Ἀστυρὶς], for whom it is a region of Italy [χώρα Ἰταλίας]. This place is memorable for the most shameful killing of Marcus Tullius Cicero, who was fleeing Antony, as Livy, Plutarch and others record; and also for the fate of Conradin, son of Henry and grandson of the Emperor Frederick II, whom Charles of Anjou, the first King of Sicily, beheaded. Some think that Asturam is called Κλώτες [Κλώτες] by Ptolemy, but they are mistaken. For Astura & Cloelia Romana are in Pliny, with the Nymphaeum river lying between them. In the Itinerary table too, Astura & Cloelia are nine miles apart.

units.la: Cloelis succedit apud Plinium Circeum Promontorium, de quo antea. Fuit in eo quondam (quod hoc loco monendum) Oppidum, auctore Servio, Sacellumque Circes, & Minervae Ara. Κιρκαῖον dicitur Straboni Circeu Pomponio Melae Tabulaeque Itinerariae. Locat & in eodem Promontorio Circaeum, parvam Civitatem Ptolemaeus, Tarquinii Superbi Coloniam. Strabonis aetate Poculum ibi ostendebatur, quo bibisse dicebatur Ulysses. Opidi sensim conlapsi loco munitissima Arx condita, tutum Antiquis Pontificibus ab Tyrannorum saevitia refugium. Videndus Blondus in Historia Gelasij ii. Pontificis. In radicibus Montis Circaei Castellum est Sancta Felicitas, memoria Celestini ii. Pontificis clarum, uti notant Petracha & Platina.
units.tr: In Pliny, Cloelis is followed by the promontory Circeum, which I discussed earlier. On it there was once a town (which should be noted here), according to Servius, along with a shrine of Circe and an altar of Minerva. Strabo calls it Κιρκαῖον [Κιρκαῖον], and Pomponius Mela and the Itinerary tables call it Circeu. Ptolemy also places Circaeum, a small city and a colony of Tarquin the Proud, on the same promontory. In Strabo's time a cup was shown there, from which Ulysses was said to have drunk. On the site of the town, which had gradually collapsed, a very strongly fortified citadel was built, a safe refuge for the ancient pontiffs from the savagery of tyrants. See Blondus in his History of Pope Gelasius II. At the foot of Mount Circeo is the castle of Sancta Felicitas, famous for the memory of Pope Celestine II, as Petrarch and Platina note.

units.la: Interius abora Pometini erant Campi, cum Urbe Pometia: cuius meminerunt Plinius libro iii. nat. cap. v. & Virgilius libro v. Aeneidos. Coloniam Latinam vocat Pometiam Livius lib.ii. Ab ea Pometinenses apud Nonium Marcellum. Vide, quæ dicam in Campania, ubi de Suessa Pometia.
units.tr: Further inland, beyond the Pomptine fields, were the Pometini Campi, with the city Pometia. Pliny in Book 3, chapter 5 of his Natural History, and Virgil in Book 5 of the Aeneid, mention it. Livy in Book 2 calls Pometiam a Coloniam Latinam. From it come the Pometinenses in Nonius Marcellus. See what I say about Suessa Pometia in the section on Campania.

units.la: Post Paludem Pomptinam, Fluviumque Vfentem, de quibus suo loco, ponitur ab eodem Plinio Taracina, vel ut aliis exemplaribus & apud Tacitum lib.xix. & xx. Solinum in Polyhistore, Procopium lib.i. Spartianum in Hadriano, Pomponium Melam, & alios, geminata canina scribitur, Tarracina: Ταρράκινα, Straboni: Ταρρακινα, Ptolemæo: Ταρρακίνη, Stephano: Terracina per E., apud Antoninum & in Tabula Itineraria. Olim Τραχίνη, ut scribit Strabo. In aspero namque & saxoso Monte sunt locata. Trachas etiam vocatur Ovidio lib. xv. Metamorph. Volscorum (quorum erat caput in Latio, teste Diodoro) Lingua Anxur appellabatur, ut notant Plinius & Sex. Pompeius Festus, cuius hæc Verba: Anxur vocabatur, quæ nunc Terracina dicitur, Vosa gentis sicut ait Ennius:
units.tr: After the Pomptine Marsh and the river Ufens, which I will treat in their place, Pliny places Taracina. In other copies, and in Tacitus (Books 19 and 20), Solinus in the Polyhistor, Procopius (Book 1), Spartianus in the Life of Hadrian, Pomponius Mela and others, it is written with a double R, Tarracina: Ταρράκινα [Ταρράκινα] in Strabo, Ταρρακινα [Ταρρακινα] in Ptolemy, Ταρρακίνη [Ταρρακίνη] in Stephanus. It is written Terracina with an E in Antoninus and in the Itinerary table. Formerly it was Τραχίνη [Τραχίνη], as Strabo writes, for it lies on a rough and rocky mountain. It is also called Trachas by Ovid in Book 15 of the Metamorphoses. In the language of the Volsci (whose chief city in Latium was, according to Diodorus) it was called Anxur, as Pliny and Sextus Pompeius Festus note. Festus's words are: Anxur vocabatur, quæ nunc Terracina dicitur, Vosa gentis sicut ait Ennius: ("Anxur was the name of what is now called Terracina, of the Volscian people, as Ennius says:")

units.la: Volscula perdidit Anxur.
units.tr: Volscula perdidit Anxur. ("Anxur lost Volscula.")

units.la: Memorat eo nomine, præter Lucanum, Silium, Martialem, & alios, Livius lib. viii. inter Colonias numerans. Anxur sine N legitur in Numismate C. Vibij Pansæ. Terracina nomenclaturam hodie retinet, loco nonnihil mutato. Olim enim in Monticulo sita fuit, Mari circumfuso, ut legere est apud Solinum. Ad Situm pertinent Poëtarum Veterum quædam: Lucani lib.iii.
units.tr: Besides Lucan, Silius, Martial and others, Livy in Book 8 mentions it by this name, counting it among the colonies. Anxur, without the N, is read on a coin of C. Vibius Pansa. Today Terracina keeps the name, though the site has changed somewhat. For formerly it stood on a small hill surrounded by the sea, as can be read in Solinus. Some passages of the ancient poets refer to its position. Lucan, Book 3:

units.la: Iamque & præcipites superaverat Anxuris Arces:
units.tr: "And now he had passed the steep citadels of Anxur:"

units.la: Horatij libro 1. Sat.v.
units.tr: Horace, Satires, Book 1, Satire 5:

units.la: Millia tum pransi tria repimus atque subimusImpositum saxis Late candentibus Anxur:
units.tr: "Then, having dined, we crept three thousand paces and climbed up to Anxur, set upon the broad, gleaming rocks."

units.la: Martialis ad Faustinam libro x.
units.tr: Martial, to Faustinus, Book 10:

units.la: O Nemus, o Fontes, solidumque madentis arenaLitus, & aquoreus splendidus Anxur aquis:
units.tr: "O grove, o springs, and firm shore of the wet sand, and Anxur gleaming with its watery seas!"

units.la: Item post ad Frontinum:
units.tr: Likewise afterwards, to Frontinus:

units.la: Anxuris aquorei placidos, Frontine, recessus:
units.tr: "Anxuris aquorei placidos, Frontine, recessus:" ("The calm retreats of watery Anxur, Frontinus:")

units.la: Silij libro viii. de bello Punico:
units.tr: Silius, Book 8, on the Punic War:

units.la: Qui Circaa iuga & scopulosi verticis Anxur?
units.tr: "Qui Circaea iuga & scopulosi verticis Anxur?" ("What of the ridges of Circe and the rocky peak of Anxur?")

units.la: Sic Livius libro iv. ab V.C. Anxur fuit, quæ nunc Terracinæ sunt, Vrbs prona in paludes. Oppidum est exiguum, sed frequens & honestum. Quinquagesimo milliari ab Vrbe locatur apud Appianum lib.iii. bel. Ciuil. Muri ex quadrato silice absque cemento facti. Iovem ibi cultum olim, patet ex Virgilii lib.vii. Æneidos, cum Jupiter cognominatur Anxurus. Videndus Servius. Adfecti hic Martyrio Felix Presbyter & Eusebius Monarchus, Claudii Imperatoris iussu. Episcopatus gaudet dignitate. Portum Terracinensem ab Antonino refectum prodit Spartianus. Extra Vrbis hodie interna Theatrum vitiur forma quadrata. Ab Servilio Hala olim obiecta & direpta, auctore Livio lib.iv. qui etiam lib.viii. scribit, Militum manuum in Montis angustus, ad Laurulas non procul Anxure, conteduisse: deinde lib.ix. pugnatum ibi: post lib.xxvi. sub Adrubalis in Italiam aduentum immunitate donatam: insuper alibi lib.xxvii. Angues immensæ magnitudinis, Piscium modo, iuxta Portum Terracinæ conludere visos memorat. Narrat Suetonius in Tiberio cap.xxxix. Tiberium Imperatorem, in Prætorio prope Terracinam cœnantem, æger repentinum saxorum lapsum, quo multi Amicorum eius & Familiarium attriti sunt, effugisse: quia de re adeundus etiam Tacitus lib. iii. Annalium. Apud hoc etiam oppidum Tiberio Imperante xx. millia hominum Theatri ruina sunt oppressa. Terracinæ cæsus scribitur apud Spartianum Palmarius Consul, quod eadem in Hadrianum Imper. efficet molitus. Terracinensis Ager fœcunditissimus est & amœnissimus Vitibus, Aurantiis, Citris, Limonibus, aliisque id genus arboribus abundans.
units.tr: Thus Livy in Book 4 from the founding of the city: Anxur fuit, which is now Terracinae, a city sloping down toward the marshes. It is a small town, but populous and respectable. It lies fifty miles from the city, according to Appian in Book 3 of the Civil Wars. Its walls were made of squared flint without mortar. That Jupiter was once worshipped there is clear from Book 7 of Virgil's Aeneid, where Jupiter is called Anxurus. See Servius. Felix the presbyter and Eusebius the monk suffered martyrdom here by order of the Emperor Claudius. The see enjoys the dignity of a bishopric. Spartianus reports that the harbour of Terracina was restored by Antoninus. Outside the town today there are remains of a theatre of square shape. It was once besieged and plundered by Servilius Hala, according to Livy in Book 4. Livy also writes in Book 8 that soldiers' camps lay in the narrow pass of the mountain, at Laurulae, not far from Anxur. Then in Book 9 fighting took place there. Afterwards, in Book 26, it was granted immunity when Hannibal came into Italy. Moreover, elsewhere in Book 27, he records that snakes of immense size, like fish, were seen wrestling near the harbour of Terracina. Suetonius, in the life of Tiberius, chapter 39, relates that the Emperor Tiberius, who was ill and dining in a praetorium near Terracina, escaped a sudden fall of rocks, by which many of his friends and household were crushed. On this matter Tacitus in Book 3 of the Annals should also be consulted. At this same town, under Tiberius, twenty thousand men were crushed by the collapse of a theatre. At Terracina, according to Spartianus, the consul Palmarius was killed, because he had tried to do the same to the Emperor Hadrian. The territory of Terracina is very fertile and pleasant, abounding in vines, orange trees, citrons, lemons and other trees of that kind.

units.la: Tertio milliario ab Terracina, ut Commentator Horatianus indicat, Vrbs erat Feronia, cuius meminerunt Tacitus & Virgilius: Hic quidem vii. Æneidos: ille vero lib.iii. Historiarum, Isdem, inquit, dietus L. Vitellius positus apud Feroniam castris extidio Terracinæ imminebat. Feronia Lacus est Vibio, iuxta Terracinam: Feronia Lympha apud Horatium, tribus millibus ab Anxure. Feronia Fons Virgilio lib.vii. & Dionysio Halicarnassensi lib. iii. Feronia Templum spoliat apud Livium lib. xxviii. Hannibal, Karthaginiensium Dux: de quo & Silius Italicus lib. viii. Optato letis abitu iubet ire in agros, Diues ubi ante omnes colitur Feronia luco, Et sacer humectat fluuialia rura Capenas. Famaeit intaelas longaeui ab origine Fauni Creuisse in medium, congestis undique donis, Immen sum per tempus opes, lustrisque relictum Innumeris aurum solo seruante Pauore: Hac auidas mentes & barbara corda rapina Pollut, atque armat contemtu pectora Diuum.
units.tr: Three miles from Terracina, as the Horatian commentator points out, there was a city called Feronia, which Tacitus and Virgil mention. Virgil does so in Book 7 of the Aeneid, Tacitus in Book 3 of the Histories: "The same Lucius Vitellius, camped at Feronia, was threatening Terracina with destruction." Feronia is a lake of Vibius near Terracina. Feronia Lympha is in Horace, three miles from Anxur. Feronia Fons is in Virgil, Book 7, and in Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Book 3. The temple of Feronia was plundered by Hannibal, leader of the Carthaginians, in Livy, Book 28; Silius Italicus also speaks of him in Book 8: "He bids them go with a happy departure into the fields, where rich Feronia is worshipped above all in her grove, and the sacred river of Capena waters the fields. Report says that the wealth of long-lived Faunus, from ancient origin, grew to a great mass, heaped with gifts from every side, a vast treasure kept through time, and gold left in the woods, guarded by countless fear in the earth. This plunder pollutes greedy minds and barbarous hearts, and arms their breasts with contempt for the gods."

units.la: Olim hac in ora fuit antiquissima Vrbs Longula, Volscorum, Liuio nota; Λογγύλα Halicarnassæo: cuius hac ætate vestigium nullum. Inde Longulani Plinio. Ultima Ciuitatis Porta ultra Tarracinam in Appia reperitur, inter altissimam rupem & Mare, loco perangusto munitoque.
units.tr: Formerly on this coast there was a very ancient city, Longula, of the Volsci, known to Livy; Dionysius of Halicarnassus calls it Λογγύλα [Λογγύλα]. In this age no trace of it remains. Hence the Longulani in Pliny. The last gate of the city beyond Terracina is found on the Appian Way, between a very high rock and the sea, in a very narrow and fortified place.

units.la: Sequuntur apud Plinium Tarracinam Amyclæ. De iis Virgilibus lib.x. Æneidos:
units.tr: After Terracina, Pliny mentions Amyclae. Virgil speaks of them in Book 10 of the Aeneid:

units.la: ——Tacitus regnavit Amyclis:
units.tr: "——Tacitus regnavit Amyclis:" ("Tacitus ruled at Amyclae:")

units.la: ubi Seruius, Inter Caietam, inquit, & Tarracinam oppidum constitutum est à Laconibus, qui Gemites Castoris & Pollucis fuerunt; & ab Amyclis, Prouincia Ciuitate, est ei nomen inditum. Laconesque itaque isti quum secundum Pythagoram sectam à cede omnium animalium abstinerent (unde Inuenalis, A cunctis Animalibus Abstinuit) quumque, tamquam homines ex vicinis paludibus natas serpentes occidere nefas putarent, ab iisdem interemti sunt. (videndus est Plinius lib.11.cap.v.) Unde Amyclas taciturnas dicit, ad est, Pythagoreas. Nam Pythagorica Virtus est Quinquennale Silentium. Ab Amyclis Amyclanum Mare Tacito lib.iv. Annal.
units.tr: Servius says: "Between Caieta and Terracina a town was founded by the Laconians, who were the followers of Castor and Pollux; and it was named after Amyclis, a province-city. These Laconians, following the Pythagorean sect, abstained from killing any living creature (hence Juvenal: 'He abstained from all animals'); and since they thought it wrong to kill snakes, as if they were men born from the neighbouring marshes, they were destroyed by the very same creatures." (See Pliny, Book 11, chapter 5.) Hence he calls the Amyclas "taciturn", that is, Pythagoreans, for Pythagorean virtue consists of a five-year silence. From Amyclas comes the Amyclanum Mare in Tacitus, Book 4 of the Annals.

units.la: Post Amyclas apud Plinium est Spelunca de ea Tacitus loca à me indicato: Vescebatur in Villa, cui vocabulum Spelunca, Mare Amyclanum inter Fundanosque Montes. Mare illud hodieque Il Mare de Spelunga audit. Σπηλαιων etiam hoc loco meminit Strabo lib.v.
units.tr: After Amyclas, Pliny mentions Spelunca, of which Tacitus speaks in the passage I have indicated: "He was dining in a villa called Spelunca, between the Mare Amyclanum inter Fundanosque Montes." That sea is still called today Il Mare de Spelunga. Strabo in Book 5 also mentions the Σπηλαιων [Σπηλαιων] at this place.

units.la: Spelunca sufficit Plinius Lacum Fundanum. de eo alibi. Dictus autem ab oppido, quod Fundi Pompomio Melæ, Antonino & Tabulæ Itinerariæ, Φονδοι, Straboni: Φόνδα Stephano: Apud Frontinum Colonia est Romana, Fondi hodie. Fundanorum meminit Livius cum alibi tum lib. vii. Fundanum Vinum celebrat, cum Strabone & Martiale, Plinius lib. xiiii. nat. hist. cap.vi. Opidum hodie parvum, sed situ iucundum, ad Appiam Viam in planicie positum, satis commode habitatum. Donavit sub Ducatus Titulo Ferdinandus Aragonum & Neapolis Rex, ob fidelem operam, Prospero Columnæ. Ingentem calamitatem intulit anno MDXXXIV. Archipirata Caradinus Barbarossa, Classis Solimanni Turcarum Imperatoris Præfectus: abducere conatus frustra Iuliam Gonzagam, Vespasiani Columnæ, Prosperi Filii, Viduam, eandem Solimanno ob formæ præstantiam dono obtinendam. Ortus hac Vrbe Soter, Pontifex Maximus, qui suo incommodo, Imperatore Commodo, Ecclesiam ibi novem annos feliciter gubernavit.
units.tr: Spelunca is enough: Pliny calls it Lacus Fundanus; I will say more about it elsewhere. It takes its name from the town of Fundi, which Pomponius Mela, Antoninus and the Itinerary Table call Fundi, Strabo calls Φονδοι [Phondoi], and Stephanus calls Φόνδα [Phonda]. In Frontinus it is a Roman colony, Romana, Fondi today. Livy mentions the Fundani both elsewhere and in book 7. Strabo, Martial and Pliny (Natural History, book 14, chapter 6) celebrate the Fundanum wine. Today the town is small but pleasant in its site, lying on the plain beside the Appian Way, and fairly comfortably inhabited. Ferdinand, King of Aragon and Naples, gave it with the title of Duchy to Prospero Colonna in return for his faithful service. In 1534 the pirate chief Barbarossa, admiral of the fleet of the Turkish Emperor Suleiman, caused a great disaster there. He tried in vain to carry off Giulia Gonzaga, widow of Vespasiano Colonna and son of Prospero, intending to present her to Suleiman because of her outstanding beauty. Soter, bishop of Rome, was born in this city; he governed the Church there happily for nine years, under the Emperor Commodus.

units.la: Lacus Fundano subditur apud Plinium Caieta: Καιέτα Straboni. Hodie Gaietta vocatur. Αιητη quondam, tulte Diodoro. Αιμ⊙ etiam Homero, Ovidio, Sudæ: Laestrigonum incientibus Vrbem: ab Lamo, cuius ibi fuit Imperium. Caieta Typus est in Tabula Itineraria, non adscripto nomine. Oppidum cum suo Promontorio (de quo cap.vi. ubi & Ettymon indicatur) est quasi Penintula: ad Septemtrionem tantum continenti per Istmum angustiorem adnectitur: reliquum marinis fere aquis cingitur. Vrbs est munita cum primis: Arcem habens invictissimam, cum Turri altissima, summo in Monte, quem superioribus annis, Gallis profligatis, muro cinxit Ferdinandus, Aragonum & Neapolitanorum Monarcha, Caieta Sinum, Locique eius naturam describit his verbis B. Facius libro Histor. iiii. Mons est, ait, propemodum excelsus & præruptus undique: tribus enim fere partibus mari adluitur: reliquam partem, qua est Caietam aditus, Mons alter excelsior ac circumquaque proclivis communit. Hæc quoque pars muro cincta est, eam plurimum incolunt Agrorum culto res, atque infimæ sortis homines: Murus interius ductus hanc montem ab Vrbe dividit. In eo Turris sita est, quam Sufinimam appellant, iuxta D. Iuliam ædem, &c. Sinus ad Vrbem Caietanus audit, apud Strabonem. Portum ibi fuisse celeberrimum, amplissime ab Antonino Pio refectum, refert Spartianus. Hodie nullus est. Domus habet altissialtissimas perangustis divisas plateis: Porticusque perpetuas & Labyrinthos. Muri Domorum sunt tenues: sed firmissimi propter calcem & bitumen. In Monte meridiem versus Templum est S. Trinitatis: post quod descensus est in Sacellum S. Crucis, in Petra, terræmotu scissa, ædificatum. In Summo Templo multa monstrantur Donaria & Ornamenta. Inter ea Crater ingens, Formis adlatus, Cadorum plurium capax: ex Saxo Pario candidissimo cavatus: quo nunc Sacerdotes utuntur pro Sacri Baptismatis Lavacro. Auctorem loquitur Græca Inscriptio:
units.tr: After Lacus Fundanus, Pliny mentions Caieta: Καιέτα [Kaiéta] in Strabo. Today it is called Gaeta. Once it was Αιητη [Aiete], as in Diodorus; Αιμ⊙ [Aiai?] in Homer, Ovid and Suda, where the Laestrygonians are said to have founded the city, named after Lamus, whose rule was there. Caieta is a figure in the Itinerary Table, though no name is written beside it. The town, with its promontory (of which more in chapter 6, where its etymology is also given), is almost a peninsula. It is joined to the mainland only on the north, by a narrow isthmus, and is surrounded on the rest by the sea. The city is very strongly fortified, having a most impregnable citadel with a very high tower on the summit of a mountain, which Ferdinand, King of Aragon and Naples, walled round in recent years after the defeat of the French. B. Facius describes the bay and the nature of the place in these words, in book 4 of his Histories: "There is a mountain, he says, almost lofty and steep on every side. For it is washed by the sea on almost three sides. The remaining part, by which there is access to Gaeta, is defended by another mountain, higher and sloping on all sides. This part too is enclosed by a wall, and it is mostly inhabited by farmers and people of the lowest rank. A wall built on the inside divides this mountain from the city. On it stands a tower called Sufinima, next to the church of St Julia, etc." Strabo calls the bay by the city the Caietan Gulf. Spartianus reports that there was once a very famous harbour there, greatly restored by Antoninus Pius. Today there is none. The houses are very high and divided by very narrow streets, with continuous porticoes and labyrinths. The house walls are thin, but very firm because of the lime and bitumen. On the mountain to the south is the Church of the Holy Trinity; below it a way down leads to the chapel of the Holy Cross, built in a rock split by an earthquake. In the upper church many votive gifts and ornaments are shown. Among them is a huge bowl, brought from Formiae, large enough to hold many jars, hollowed out of the purest white Parian marble, which the priests now use as the font for holy baptism. A Greek inscription names its maker: "Salpion the Athenian made it".

units.la: ΣΑΛΠΙΩΝ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΟΣ ΕΠΟΙΗΣΕ.
units.tr: ΣΑΛΠΙΩΝ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΟΣ ΕΠΟΙΗΣΕ. [Salpion the Athenian made it.]

units.la: Sepultus ibi in Templo Arcis Dux Borbonius, ad Romam globo bellico ictus. Episcopus Urbi datus legitur ob Formias ab Saracenis excisas. Illustrarunt eam Gelasius 11. P. M. & Thomas Bionius, Cardinalis, Scriptis clarus. Pulcherrimas habet Mulieres. Magnis Cladibus adfecta legitur ab Gallis. Earum maxima incidit in annum c1ɔ cce xciv. Suburbium ipsi oblongum, iuxta littus protensum. Scauri Fundum, Agri Cajetani, donatile Xvltum iii. Ecclesiæ S. Mariæ Maioris, scribit Platina. Porto Ifiauro hodie vulgo dici putat apud Abrahamum Ortelium in Thesauro Geographico Philippus Winghus; quem idem Ortelius scribere notat, oftendi eius reliquias ad mare euntibus Gaieta Minturnas, parte dextra.
units.tr: In the castle church lies the Duke of Bourbon, who was struck by a cannonball near Rome. A bishop is recorded as given to the city after Formiae was destroyed by the Saracens. Gelasius II, Pope, and Thomas Bonius, the cardinal famous for his writings, have illustrated it. It has very beautiful women. It is recorded as having suffered great calamities at the hands of the French; the greatest of these fell in the year 1294. Its suburb is long, stretching along the shore. Platina writes that the estate of Scaurus, in the Gaetan territory, Xvltum iii, was given to the church of St Mary Major. Philip Winghe, in Abraham Ortelius's Geographical Thesaurus, thinks that the place commonly called Porto Ifiauro is meant; Ortelius notes that its remains are shown to those travelling by sea from Gaeta to Minturnae, on the right-hand side.

units.la: Caieta Formias sublocat Plinius. Sic etiam dictæ Ciceroni, Tacito, Pomponio Melæ, & Antonino: Frontino item, cui Colonia est Romana; Straboni Φοσμία: quæ Φωξμαι Ptolomæo: Formæ, Tabulæ Itinerariæ. Hormiæ olim dictas docent Strabo, Plinius, alij: sive ab frequentia bonitateque Stationum, ut Festo placet, quas ὁρμὰς Græci vocant: sive ab impetu Læstrigonum, quos humana carne victitasse scribit Plinius: vel denique ab Hormo Amne, illic prælabente. Mamurrarum Urbem appellat Horatius, ut putat Vetus eius Commentator. Originem inde traxit Mamurrana Gens Romæ, qua natus Mamurra is, quem Carminibus suis proscindit Catullus. Læstrigonum quondam fuit Sedes, scribentibus Plinio, Solino, Symmacho: unde Læstrigoniam vocat Cicero ad Atticum: Domus Antiphatæ nominatur Silio libro viii. Antiphates enim, Læstrigonum Rex, olim ibi imperasse perhibetur. Ἀακωνικὸν κτίσμα dicitur Straboni. Distabant ab Caieta Formiæ Stadia xl. ut Strabo notat. Ante ingressum inter sentes & spineta ruinæ adparent Sepulcrorum Veterum. Debellatis Campanis Romani in Præfecturæ formam Formias reduxerunt; quum prius tamen municipium fuisset, atque Civitatis Jus cum Suffragij latione obtinuisset, uti docet Livius lib. xxxix. Bello demum Civili, ut Frontinus auctor est, ab iii-Viris C. Julio Cæsare Octaviano, M. Antonio & M. Æmilio I epido inter Colonias Italiæ militares Formiæ fuerunt redactæ. Ab eo tempore sub Impp. semper propter cæli temperiem floruisse, constat ex Horatio, Martiale, aliisque Scriptoribus. Excisæ memorantur ab Saracenis anno 1ɔcce lvi, qua tempestate Episcopatum inde Cajetam transtulit, cum reliquis Erasmi Martyris, Gregorius iv. P. M. Legendus Blondus. Adscribam elegans Formiarum Encomium, quod apud Martialem libro x. Epigrammat. in quo plura Italiæ loca nominantur: O temperata dulce Formiæ littus: Vos, quum severi fugit oppidum Martis, Et inquietas fessus exuit curas Apollinaris, omnibus locis præfert. Non illè sanctæ dulce Tiburve xorus, Nec Tusculanos, Algidosve secessus, Prænestè nec sic, Antiumve miratur: Non blanda Circe, Dardanisve Cajeta Desiderantur: nec Marica, nec Liris, Nec in Lucrina lota Salmacis vena: Hic summa leni stringitur Thetis vento: Nec languet Aequor: vera sed quies Ponti Pictam Phaselon adjuvante fert aura.
units.tr: Pliny places Caieta next to Formiae. Cicero, Tacitus, Pomponius Mela and Antoninus also call it so, as does Frontinus, for whom it is a Roman colony. Strabo calls it Φοσμία [Phosmia], which Ptolemy calls Φωξμαι [Phoxmai]; the Itinerary Table calls it Formae. Strabo, Pliny and others record that it was once called Hormiae, either from the number and goodness of its anchorages, which the Greeks call ὁρμὰς [hormas], as Festus thinks, or from the attack of the Laestrygonians, whom Pliny says fed on human flesh, or finally from the river Hormus, which flows past there. Horace calls it the city of the Mamurrae, as his old commentator thinks. From here the Mamurrana family at Rome drew its origin, and from it came Mamurra, whom Catullus lashes in his poems. Pliny, Solinus and Symmachus write that it was once the seat of the Laestrygonians, which is why Cicero in his letter to Atticus calls it Laestrygonia. Silius, in book 8, calls it the house of Antiphates, for Antiphates, king of the Laestrygonians, is said to have ruled there once. Strabo calls it a Laconian foundation [Λακωνικὸν κτίσμα]. Formiae was forty stadia from Caieta, as Strabo notes. Before the entrance, among the brambles and thorn bushes, appear the ruins of ancient tombs. After the Campanians were subdued, the Romans reduced Formiae to the form of a prefecture; yet it had previously been a municipality and had obtained Roman citizenship with the right to vote, as Livy shows in book 39. Finally, in the civil war, as Frontinus records, Formiae was counted among the military colonies of Italy by the triumvirs Gaius Julius Caesar Octavian, Marcus Antonius and Marcus Aemilius Lepidus. From that time, under the emperors, it always flourished because of the mildness of its climate, as is clear from Horace, Martial and other writers. It is recorded that it was destroyed by the Saracens in the year 1056, at which time Pope Gregory IV transferred the bishopric from there to Gaeta, together with the relics of Erasmus the martyr; Blondus should be read on this. I will add the elegant encomium of Formiae which Martial gives in book 10 of his Epigrams, where many places in Italy are named: O sweet and temperate shore of Formiae, you whom the weary Apollinaris prefers to every place, when he flees the town of stern Mars and, tired, lays aside his restless cares. Neither holy Tibur, sweet to the wife, nor the Tusculan retreats or Algidus, nor Praeneste, nor Antium, does he admire; Circe's charms and Dardanian Caieta are not missed, nor Marica, nor the Liris, nor the Salmacis spring bathing the Lucrine lake. Here Thetis is touched by a gentle breeze, the sea does not grow sluggish, but a true calm carries the painted ship along with the favouring breeze.

units.la: & quae sequuntur. Formianorum mentionem facit Basis Statuae, litera absolutissima, quam, teste Martino Smetio, vidit & excripsit Molae Dionysius Harduinus:
units.tr: And what follows. A statue base mentions the Formiani; it is a most complete inscription, which Dionysius Harduinus saw and copied at Mola, as Martin Smet attests:

units.la: IMP. CÆSARI. DIVI HADRIANI. FILIO. DIVI TRAIANI. PARTHICI. NEP DIVI. NERVÆ. PRONEPOTI T. ÆLIO. HADRIANO Antonino. AVG. PIO. PONT. MAX. TRIB. POT. II. COS. III. P. P. FORMIANI. PVBLICE
units.tr: EMPEROR CAESAR, SON OF THE DEIFIED HADRIAN, GRANDSON OF THE DEIFIED TRAJAN PARTHICUS, GREAT-GRANDSON OF THE DEIFIED NERVA, TITUS AELIUS HADRIANUS ANTONINUS AUGUSTUS PIUS, PONTIFEX MAXIMUS, HOLDING TRIBUNICIAN POWER FOR THE SECOND TIME, CONSUL FOR THE THIRD TIME, FATHER OF HIS COUNTRY. THE FORMIANS (ERECTED THIS) AT PUBLIC EXPENSE.

units.la: Formianos Colles novit Horatius: Formianum Montem, Livius lib. xxxix. Vinum Formianum optimis adnumerat idem Horatius. Formianum, villa Ciceronis in Formianorum Agro, cuius frequens in Epistolis ad Atticum mentio: Hodie vulgo Ciceron.
units.tr: Horace knew the Formian hills (Formianos Colles); Livy, in book 39, the Formian mountain (Formianum Montem). Horace also counts Formian wine among the finest. Formianum was Cicero's villa in the territory of Formiae, often mentioned in his letters to Atticus; today it is commonly called Ciceron.

units.la: Jn eo tradit magnus Scriptor Laelium semper fere cum Scipione rusticari solitum: eosque, quoties huc ex Urbe, tanquam e vinculis, evolavisset, incredibiliter repuerascere solitos. Locus est peramoenus & perjucundus: hortis undique cultissimis consitus: in quo & veterum marmorum, & Aedificiorum, operumque amplissimorum vestigia passim videre licet.
units.tr: In it, the great writer reports, Laelius almost always used to take his country holidays with Scipio, and whenever they had flown out from the city, as if from chains, they used to become boys again to an incredible degree. The place is very pleasant and delightful, planted all round with most cultivated gardens, in which traces of ancient marbles, buildings and very grand works can be seen everywhere.

units.la: Inter Cajetam & Formias Itrum est Castellum, & Mola. Itrum amoenis in collibus, qui oleis, vitibus, ficubus, aliisque fructiferis arboribus convestiti, conspicitur longe inter Montes extensum; morte inclutum Hippolyti Medicis Florentini, Ecclesiae Romanae Cardinalis. Blondus magno errore Lamuras vocat, Horatij versum perperam legens & intellegens. Itri meminit Pomponius Sabinus. Olim Atrium dictum ait Scipio Mazzella. Hodie Itro Castello.
units.tr: Between Gaeta and Formiae lie the little town of Itri and Mola. Itri, seen on pleasant hills clothed with olives, vines, figs and other fruit trees, stretches far off among the mountains. It is famous for the death of Ippolito Medici of Florence, cardinal of the Roman Church. Blondus, through a great mistake, calls it Lamuras, misreading and misunderstanding a verse of Horace. Pomponius Sabinus mentions Itri. Scipio Mazzella says it was formerly called Atrium. Today it is Itro Castello.

units.la: Itro Mola distat P. M. v. via amoenissima, Hortis obsita, qui Citris, Limonibus, aliisque arboribus gravidi. Putant nonnulli Molam ex Formiarum ruinis crevisse: dictam ab Molarum frequentia: quas hic ex Montium radicibus profluentes continuo Aquae versant: unde apud Tullium Mola Formiana. Longus & percelegans est Vicus ad Viam Appiam.
units.tr: Mola is five miles from Itri by a most pleasant road, lined with gardens, rich in citrons, lemons and other trees. Some think Mola grew up from the ruins of Formiae, and that it takes its name from the number of mills (molae) which, fed by streams flowing from the foot of the mountains, turn constantly with water; hence Cicero's phrase "Mola Formiana." It is a long and very elegant village on the Appian Way.

units.la: Post Formias ponuntur apud Plinium Pyrae: aliis Pylae scribuntur.
units.tr: After Formiae, Pliny places Pyrae; others write Pylae.

units.la: Pylis (si quidem hic emendandum) succedunt apud eumdem Minturnae: sic Tacito, Plinio, Melae, Antonino; Μιντοῦρναι Straboni vocantur; quae Μίντουρνα Stephano, Menturna in Tabula Itineraria. Hodie Traietto, ut censent docti Viri. Alij aliter opinantur. Nardo Castro al Mar putatur: Sanfelicio, La Scafa del Garigliano. Sane ad Trajectum Antiquae, quaecumque tandem habenda, Urbis vestigia conspicuntur: inter alia Theatrum propemodum integrum: & sumptuosissimus Aquaeductus.
units.tr: After Pylae (if indeed the text should be emended here) Pliny places Minturnae. So Tacitus, Pliny, Mela and Antoninus; Strabo calls them Mintourna, Stephanus Mintourna, and the Tabula Itineraria Menturna. Today it is Traietto, as learned men think; others think otherwise. Nardo thinks it is Castro al Mar, and Sanfelicio La Scafa del Garigliano. Certainly, at Trajectum, whatever this ancient city is finally to be held to be, traces of the old city can be seen, among them an almost whole theatre and a most sumptuous aqueduct.

units.la: Liris oppidum medium olim intercluebat, ut Plinius & Strabo volunt: hodie paullo sequior est situs. Trajectus in colle est: Minturna in Valle erant, sive planicie; quod ex Theatri & Aquaeductuum, quorum meminit, reliquis est palam. Ex Minturnarum ruinis Trajectum esse aedificatum, sciebit etiam ad Ortelium Celsus Cittadinus.
units.tr: The Liris once cut through the middle of a town, as Pliny and Strabo maintain; today the site is somewhat lower. Trajectum lies on a hill, while Minturnae stood in a valley or plain; this is plain from the remains of the theatre and aqueducts that he mentions. That Trajectum was built from the ruins of Minturnae, Celso Cittadino will also know from Ortelius.

units.la: Coloniam Populi Romani Minturnas ad Ostium Liris factam Livius auctor est libro x. addens Immunitatem accepisse ob caeli gravitatem & vitium. Concilium Minturnis generale Marcellinus Pontifex Maximus anno ccxcvii. habuisse legitur.
units.tr: Livy, in book 10, says that Minturnae was founded as a colony of the Roman People at the mouth of the Liris, adding that it received immunity because of the heaviness and bad quality of its air. It is read that Pope Marcellinus held a general council at Minturnae in the year 297.

units.la: Juxta Minturnas Saracenos ab Christianis gravi pugna, cui Joannes x. P. M. & Albericus Tusciae Marchio interfuerunt, victos & profligatos fuisse, Italiaque pulsos, memoriae tradunt Blondus & Platina: exceptis Profugorum e praelio reliquiis, quae Garganum Montem occuparunt; in quo se diu postea tenuerunt, praedationibus & piratica vitam sustentantes. Castrum Trajecti non ita pridem Prospero Columnae cum ducatus Titulo donavit Ferdinandus, Aragonum Rex & Neapolitanorum.
units.tr: Near Minturnae, Blondus and Platina record, the Saracens were defeated and routed by the Christians in a fierce battle, in which Pope John X and Alberic, Marquis of Tuscany, took part, and were driven out of Italy. The remnants of the fugitives from the battle, however, occupied Mount Garganus, where they held out for a long time afterwards, sustaining themselves by plunder and piracy. The castle of Trajectum was not long ago given, with the title of duchy, to Prospero Colonna by Ferdinand, King of Aragon and of the Neapolitans.

units.la: Minturnense Flumen, quod censendum vide supra, ubi de Liri. Minturnense Paludem habet Seneca Declamatione iii. inde Minturnae, Palustres Horatio lib. i. Epist. v. In propinquis Minturnensium Paludibus Marium latitasse, quum inimicorum arma fugeret, fugerent, memorant Livius lib. lxxvii. Plutarchus in eius Vita, Lucanus lib. ii. Juvenalis Satyra x. Valerius Maximus lib. viii. alij.
units.tr: The Minturnian river, which should be understood as above, where we spoke of the Liris. Seneca, in Declamation 3, has the Minturnian marsh, and hence Horace, Epistles i. 5, has "Minturnae, Palustres." Livy (book 77), Plutarch in his Life of Marius, Lucan (book 2), Juvenal (Satire 10), Valerius Maximus (book 8) and others record that Marius hid in the nearby Minturnian marshes when he was fleeing from the weapons of his enemies.

units.la: Tertio dein lapide iuxta ripam Liris Speminum est opidum: inde octavo Frata: hinc totidem Pons Cervi, Fonte Cervo: Fregella quondam, ut volunt Sigonius & Leander. Aldus in sua Orthographia putat ex Fregellarum reliquis Ceperanum oppidulum esse extructum. Sunt, inter quos Ambrosius Leo, qui fuisse volunt, ubi nunc Arrigallo, Φρεγέλλα dicuntur Strabonis, cuius aevo vicus erat; olim Urbs nobilis ad Lirim Fluvium, teste Livio libro xxvi. Φρέγελλα Stephano, Fregellanum Antonino: Fregellani, Plinio. Coloniam factam docet Livius libro viii. Fregellae ob defectionem semel atque iterum diruta ab Romanis, scribitque idem lib. x & lx. De insulis lib. v.
units.tr: Three miles along the bank of the Liris is the town of Speminum; from there, eight miles on, Frata; from here as many miles to Pons Cervi, Fonte Cervo. Fregella was formerly here, as Sigonius and Leander think. Aldus, in his Orthography, thinks the little town of Ceperanum was built from the remains of Fregellae. There are some, among them Ambrosius Leo, who want Fregella to have been where Arrigallo now stands. Strabo calls it Phregella; in his day it was a village, but formerly a noble city on the river Liris, as Livy testifies in book 26. Stephanus calls it Phregella, Antoninus Fregellanum, and Pliny Fregellani. Livy, in book 8, shows that it was made a colony. Fregellae, after revolting once and again, was razed by the Romans, and the same writer records this in books 10 and 60. On the islands, book 5.

units.la: —Hunc tristes misere Fregellae.
units.tr: "Him the sorrowful Fregellae sent."

units.la: Et alibi lib. xi.
units.tr: And elsewhere, in book 11:

units.la: Et quae fumanti texere gigante Fregellae.
units.tr: "And Fregellae, which the smoking giant wove."

units.la: Inclutae sunt M. Sextilii Fregellani respondo, Senatui Romano pro xiix. Coloniis Bello Punico ii. dato, de quo Livius. Hinc Fregella, locus in Urbe, teste Festo, ab Fregellanis forte habitus, vel Fregellanorum Statio; ut Graecostasis, Graecorum; Ficulea, Ficulenatum.
units.tr: Famous is M. Sextilius of Fregellae, who gave the answer to the Roman Senate on behalf of the nineteen colonies in the Second Punic War, of which Livy speaks. Hence Fregella, a place in the City, as Festus says, perhaps inhabited by the Fregellans, or a station of the Fregellans, just as the Graecostasis was of the Greeks and the Ficulea of the Ficulenses.

units.la: Extremum Latij facit Plinius Sinuessam: de qua dicendum in Campania.
units.tr: Pliny makes Sinuessa the end of Latium; of it we shall speak under Campania.

units.la: Haec de Ora Latij maritima, deque quibusdam citra Lirim locis: antequam ad Mediterraneorum enarrationem veniam, committere inter se obiter decrevi Auctores, qui ordine quodam Littorales Latij Urbes commemorant: praepositurus Plinium, cum quod plenior ille ceteris, tum quod notatum ab ipso ordinem in superioribus praecipue fuerim sequutus.
units.tr: I have decided, in passing, to set side by side, before I come to the description of the inland places, the authors who name the coastal cities of Latium in a certain order, on this maritime shore of Latium and on certain places this side of the Liris. I shall put Pliny first, both because he is fuller than the others and because I have mainly followed the order he noted in the preceding passages.
