units.tr: Table comparing the coastal towns of Latium in Pliny, Strabo, Ptolemy, Pomponius Mela, Antoninus' Itinerary, the Tabula, the Vulgate and the Nomenclator: Ostia (colony; Ostia, sixteen miles from the City, Hostia, sixteen miles); Laurentum (Laurentum, ten miles; Laurentum, sixteen miles); Lavinium (Lanuvium, to be read Lavinium, sixteen miles; Lavinium, six miles; Lucus Iovis); remains survive near Fusianum and the places called Vicumori, the river Rivo, the Numicus, and Ardea; Ardea is said to keep its name today, as Anaclasia Saint; Aphrodisium, Antium (Antium beyond Neptunium, others read Calo Via, Antium); Astura, a river and island (Astura, seventeen miles; Stora, of the nymphaean river, now Paulo Fiume); Clostra (Clostra, nine miles, at the Towers, White Towers, three miles); Circei (Circeios, twenty-one miles, Monte Circello, at the Towers four miles; the Pomptine marsh; the river Ufens); Terracina or Anxur (Tarracina, eleven miles, Amycla); near Caluzam, Spelunca (Sperlunga, Pineto); Lacus Fundanus (Fundi, Fundos sixteen miles, Fundus thirteen miles, Fondi); Caieta (Itro Castello); Mola, which is said to come from Formia (Formias thirteen miles, Formis nine miles); Pyrae, others read Pylae; Minturnae (Minturnas nine miles, Menturnu, Traietto Castello); the Liris (Garigliano); Sinuessa, the end of Latium (Sinuessa nine miles; see Campania).

units.la: Mediterranea Latij loca perlustranti offert se xii. Roma lapide, Orientem versus Marinum, Columnarum Ditionis oppidum, in colle situm. Fuit ibi quondam, ut nonnulli censent, Mariana Villa, quæ tamen alius Castrum, quod vernacule Zagarola.
units.tr: To one travelling through the inland places of Latium, Marino presents itself twelve miles from Rome, towards the east. It is a town of the Colonna lordship, set on a hill. Some think that there was once the Villa Mariana there, though others call it a castle, which in the vernacular is Zagarola.

units.la: Marino P. M. viii. antiqua Civitas in Tumulo Velitræ: sic Livio passim & Suetonio in Octaviani Vita cap. i. atque lxxiv. dicitur Urbs: Οὐελίτραι Straboni lib. v. & Ptolemæo: Οὐαλίτραι Dioni lib. xlv. Βέλιτρα Stephano: quæ vulgo Belitre: vel, ut alij scribunt. Belletri. Oppidum vetustissimum Volscorum, in quo tamen pauca Antiquitatum nunc vestigia: alioquin amplum & populo latis frequens, Episcopatus fulgens dignitate. Venustissimi situs, jucundissimi prospectus: Mœnibus undique cinctum. Incolæ Livio & Plinio Veliterni: Veliterni, Suetonio in Augusto cap. xciv. ubi tamen quidam Codices Veliterni: Οὐελιτραῖοι Halicarnassæo. Coloniam ibi ductam notant idem Halicarnassæus lib. vii. Livius lib. ii. & Frontinus. De Rebus ab ipsis, vel contraptos gestis, legendi Dionysius lib. iii. vi. & vii. Livius cum alibi, tum lib. viii. & alij rerum Romanarum Scriptores. Extra Portam Follæ sunt angustis foraminibus & in profundum amplæ, quales sunt, in quibus condi conservarique consueverunt frumenta. Juxta Velitras ostendebatur adhuc tempore Suetonij Nutrimentorum Augusti Locus, in avito Suburbano, permodicus & Cellæ Penuariæ instar. Ager Fructuum omnis generis nunc etiam ferax est, ut olim propter Vrbis Romæ vicinitatem Villis & Hortis Nobilium expolitus. Veliterna Vina laudat Plinius lib. xiv. cap. vi. Ea nunc degenerarunt: propter cruditatem austeritatemque coqui alieno solita.
units.tr: Eight miles from Marino lies the ancient city of Velitrae on a mound. Livy throughout, and Suetonius in the Life of Octavian (chapters 1 and 74), call it a city. Strabo (book 5) and Ptolemy write Οὐελίτραι [Ouelitrai], Dio (book 45) writes Οὐαλίτραι [Oualitrai], and Stephanus writes Βέλιτρα [Belitra]. It is commonly called Belitre, or, as others write, Belletri. It is a very old town of the Volsci, which now has few traces of its antiquities, yet it is large, full of people, and famous for its bishopric. Its site is very pleasant and its views delightful, and it is surrounded on all sides by walls. Its inhabitants are called Veliterni by Livy and Pliny, and by Suetonius (Augustus, chapter 94), though some manuscripts there read Veliterni. Halicarnassaeus calls them Οὐελιτραῖοι [Ouelitraioi]. Halicarnassaeus (book 7), Livy (book 2) and Frontinus note that a colony was led there. On the events that happened there, or were devised there, one should read Dionysius (books 3, 6 and 7), Livy elsewhere and especially book 8, and the other writers of Roman history. Outside the Gate of Folla there are narrow openings that widen into deep pits, of the kind in which grain is usually stored and kept. Near Velitrae, in Suetonius' time, the "Storehouse of Augustus" was still shown, on his grandfather's suburban estate, very small and like a storeroom. The land is still fertile in every kind of produce, as it was once adorned with villas and gardens of the nobility because of its nearness to the city of Rome. Pliny (book 14, chapter 6) praises the Veliterna wines. These have now declined, since they are usually adulterated by the cook, owing to their harshness and roughness.

units.la: Quinto Velitris lapide ad lævam est Cora, in monte sita: Livio lib. ii. Silio libro viii. Solino, aliisque memorata: Κέραι Straboni. Nomen hodie retinet. Coranos (qui Κόραν Halicarnassæo lib. v. ab Dardano Troiano scribunt ortos Plinius lib. iii. cap. v. & Solinus in Polyhist. Servius ad Virgilium Coram, Catulli Tiburtiique Fratrem, Coræ Conditorem nominat.
units.tr: Five miles from Velitrae, on the left, is Cora, set on a mountain. It is mentioned by Livy (book 2), Silius (book 8), Solinus and others. Strabo calls it Κέραι [Kerai]. The name survives today. Halicarnassaeus (book 5) writes that the Coranians, whom he calls Κόραν [Koran], were descended from Dardanus the Trojan. Pliny (book 3, chapter 5) and Solinus in the Polyhistor also mention them. Servius on Virgil names Cora as the brother of Catillus and Tiburtus, and the founder of Cora.

units.la: Itinere hinc ad Velitras Nemus occurrit infame Latrociniis, spatio P M. vi. dein amœna planicie multum quinque ad Sermonettam, Castellum in Colle novi nominis, devenitur. Hoc justis Dominus ereptum, Filiæ impudicæ donavit Alexander vi. P. M. Putant quidam Sulmonem esse, oppidum Latij, quod sine vestigiis interiisse scribit Plinius iii. cap. v. Locat idem in Sulmonensi Agro Fabianum: quod quo loco fuerit, nescio.
units.tr: On the way from here to Velitrae one meets a grove notorious for robberies, six miles long. Then, through a pleasant plain, one comes after about five miles to Sermonetta, a castle on a hill, of recent name. Pope Alexander VI took this from its lord by justice and gave it to his shameless daughter. Some think it is Sulmo, a town of Latium, which Pliny (book 3, chapter 5) writes perished without a trace. The same author places Fabianum in the territory of Sulmo, but where it was I do not know.

units.la: Infra Sermonettam Taberna quædam & Vegistia veterum Ædificiorum. Ea Triuni Tabernarum esse putant docti Viri, quas memorant Cicero in Epistolis ad Atticum lib. ii. Antoninus, & Itineraria Tabula. Τρεῖς Ταβέρναι meminit Euangelista Lucas in Apostolorum Actis cap. ultimo. Tres Tabernæ in Baronii Annalibus est Cisterna, qui Vicus est in medio Appiæ Viæ, xxxvi. M. P. ab Urbe. Pighius ginus in Hercule Prodicio putat circa Casas Nouas fuisse, aut ipsas esse. Onuphrius in Chronic. Pontific. vocat Tres Tabernas, alias apud Nymphan. Apud Tres Tabernas Seuerum Imperatorem ab Aduersarijs occisum scribunt Eutropius, Zofimus, & alij.
units.tr: Below Sermonetta there is a certain tavern and the remains of ancient buildings. Learned men think this is the place of the Three Taverns, which Cicero (in his Letters to Atticus, book 2), Antoninus and the Itinerary Table mention. The evangelist Luke mentions Τρεῖς Ταβέρναι [Treis Tabernai] in the last chapter of the Acts of the Apostles. In Baronius' Annals, the Three Taverns is Cisterna, a village in the middle of the Appian Way, thirty-six miles from the City. Pighius, in his Hercules Prodicius, thinks it was around Casas Nuovas, or was those houses themselves. Onuphrius, in his Chronicle of the Popes, calls it Tres Tabernas, and elsewhere (in Nymphanus). Eutropius, Zosimus and others write that the emperor Severus was killed by his opponents at the Three Taverns.

units.la: Octodecim à Tribus Tabernis P. M. Forum Appy scribitur Antonino. Meminit eius &, præter Horatium in Hodeporico, Lucas Euangelista loco, quem indicaui: putatur hodie ibi esse quibuldam Taberna Marutz: alias L' Abbatia: nonnullis Fossa Noua, item Casa Noua.
units.tr: Eighteen miles from the Three Taverns is Forum Appii, as Antoninus writes. Besides Horace, in his account of the journey, the evangelist Luke also mentions it in the passage I indicated. Today there is said to be there a certain inn called Marutz, otherwise L'Abbatia; some call it Fossa Nuova, and also Casa Nuova.

units.la: Millia inde quinque occurrit editiore situm loco vetus Opidum Setia. Sic Liuio, Virgilio, aliisque Latinis: Σητία Ptolemæo, Σητία Straboni: quæ corrupte forte an Κετία l falicarnaffæo: Zezza vulgo, vel Secchi. Latinorum opidum mediterraneum, Volscis adscriptum. Incolæ Setini Plinio, Setia Colonia vel Setina Velleio & Frontino Setini Montes sunt apud Iuuenalem Sat. v. Vina Setina celebrant Strabo lib. v. Silius lib. viii. Plinius lib. xiv. cap. vi. & Martialis, qui & nonnihil de Situ: Pendula Pomtinos qua spectat Setia Campos, Exigua vetulos mittit ab Vrbe cados.
units.tr: Five miles further one comes to the ancient town of Setia, set on higher ground. So it is called by Livy, Virgil and other Latin writers. Ptolemy and Strabo write Σητία [Setia]; perhaps Halicarnassaeus, by a corruption, writes Κετία [Ketia]. It is commonly called Zezza, or Secchi. It is an inland Latin town, assigned to the Volsci. Pliny calls its inhabitants Setini; Velleius and Frontinus call it the colony Setia or Setina, and Juvenal (Satire 5) speaks of the Setine mountains. Strabo (book 5), Silius (book 8), Pliny (book 14, chapter 6) and Martial praise the Setine wines. Martial also says something about its situation: "Setia, hanging where it looks over the Pomptine plains, sends little old jars of wine from the City."

units.la: Monti enim altissimo est impolita. Inter Setiam & Casas Nouas adparent in radice montis Veteris Ædificii ruinæ, in Circi modum tactæ.
units.tr: Setia stands unadorned on a very high mountain. Between Setia and Casas Nuovas, at the foot of the mountain, appear the ruins of an old building, traced in the shape of a circus.

units.la: Setia Pipernum M. P. distat quinque. Sic vernacule vocatur Opidum, quod Priuernum Latinis: Πρίβερνον Ptolemæo: Πρίσσερνον Straboni: Prevernum in nummo C. Hyptæi. Opidum nunc in aspero situm monte: olim in planicie duobus ab hodierno passuum millibus versus Anagniam, uti fundamenta docent & maiorum operum vestigia. Iuxta Ousentem fluvium locatur Sex. Pompeio Festo: vicina Samnitibus Liuio: Priuernum Vetus ab Germanis & Britonibus excisum, auctor est Blondus. Colonia Romanis adscribentes Frontinus. Vetus Municipium & Præfectura ante fuit, scribente Festo. Incolæ Privernates Silio, Liuio: aliis: Πριβερνᾶτοι Strabo. Natalibus Camilla Regina, quæ Turno contra Æneam auxilio fuit, celebratum apud Virgilium lib. xi. Æneid. De Rebus, quæ a Privernatibus gestæ, passim Livius, inter alia memorans lib. viii. Privernates, ab S. P. Q. R. rogatos, qualem Pacem maxime optarent perpetuam, si bona foret & honesta: breve, ut turpis & infida, respondisse. Extra opidum in discensu montis pulcherrimus Fons est.
units.tr: Setia is five miles from Piperno. So the town is called in the vernacular, which the Latins call Privernum. Ptolemy writes Πρίβερνον [Priberno], Strabo Πρίσσερνον [Prisserno], and a coin of C. Hyptaeus has Prevernum. The town now stands on a rough mountain, but formerly it was on a plain, two miles from its present site towards Anagnia, as its foundations and traces of larger works show. Sextus Pompeius Festus places it near the river Ufens. Livy calls it a neighbour of the Samnites. Blondus says that Old Privernum was destroyed by Germans and Britons. Frontinus counts it among the Roman colonies. Festus writes that it was formerly a municipium and a prefecture. Its inhabitants are called Privernates by Silius and Livy; Strabo calls them Πριβερνᾶτοι [Privernatoi]. Camilla, the queen who helped Turnus against Aeneas, was a native of it, as Virgil celebrates in book 11 of the Aeneid. Livy, in many places and among other things in book 8, tells of the deeds of the Privernates. When the Senate and People of Rome asked them what kind of peace they most wished for, they answered that they wanted it lasting, if it were good and honourable; but brief, as one that is base and faithless. Outside the town, on the slope of the mountain, there is a most beautiful spring.

units.la: Locis deinde Piperno vicinis Opida Vicique reperiuntur, quæ vulgo Magienza: Rocca Gorgona: Rocca Secca, Thomæ Aquinatis instituto celebris. Hinc ad Sonninum millia quinque in alti montis vertice.
units.tr: In the places near Piperno there are towns and villages, commonly called Magienza, Rocca Gorgona and Rocca Secca, which is famous for having been the place of Thomas Aquinas' upbringing. From here it is five miles to Sonnino, on the top of a high mountain.

units.la: Vlterius versus Vulturnum iamnunc non tendens, finitimos Romæ agros repeto. In ijs Alba: sic Latinis omnibus nominata: Ἄλβα item Græcis, id est, Λευκα, ut inquit Halicarnassæus: Ἄλβα, Appiano. Nomen ab Alba Sue, quam cum Suculis triginta Æneæ in Italiam adpellenti volunt vitam. Conferendus præter alios Virgilius libro viii. Adeundi quoque Propertius lib. iii. Eleg. i. & Varra de LL. & de Re Rustica lib. ii. cap. iv. Longam cognominant Veteres Scriptores: ab Situ, ut loquitur Livius, porrectæ in dorso Vrbis. Sic ab altera eiusdem nominis Civitate, quæ in Marsis est, discernitur. Hodie Sauello, si Leandro fides: si aliis, Gandolfi, vel S. Gandolfo. Incolæ Albani, omnibus Ἀλβάνοι nominat Appianus. Conditor eius Ascanius, Æneæ filius, xxx post ædificatum Lauinium anno. Virgilius, libro, quem dixi: Iamque tibi ne vana putes hæc fingere somnum, Littoreis ingens inventa sub ilicibus Sus Triginta capitum fœtus enixa iacebit, Alba solo recubans, albi circum Vbera nati: Hic locus Vrbis erit: requies ea certa laborum Ex quo ter denis Vrbem redeuntibus annis Ascanius clari condet cognomine Albam.
units.tr: Not going further now towards the Volturno, I return to the fields near Rome. Among them is Alba, so named by all the Latins. The Greeks also call it Ἄλβα [Alba], that is, Λευκά [Leuka], white, as Halicarnassaeus says; Appian writes Ἄλβα [Alba]. It takes its name from the white sow, which, with thirty sucklings, they say Aeneas met when he came to Italy. Besides others, Virgil (book 8) should be compared, and Propertius (book 3, elegy 1), and Varro in On the Latin Language and On Farming (book 2, chapter 4). The ancient writers call it Longa, from its site, as Livy says, being stretched along the back of the city. In this way it is distinguished from the other city of the same name, which is among the Marsi. Today it is Sauello, if Leander is to be trusted; if others are, Gandolfi, or S. Gandolfo. Its inhabitants are the Albans; Appian calls them Ἀλβάνοι [Albanoi]. Its founder was Ascanius, son of Aeneas, thirty years after Lavinium was built. Virgil, in the book I mentioned, says: "And now, lest you think these things are the vain fictions of a dream: a huge sow, found under the holm-oaks on the shore, will lie there, having brought forth thirty young, lying on the ground, with the white sucklings around her udders. This will be the site of the city, and sure rest from your labours. When the Trojans have returned after thirty years, Ascanius the famous will found the city and call it Alba."

units.la: Confirmant Livius lib. i. & Dionysius libro i. Antiquit. Romanar. qui & inter initia condendæ Vrbis maximum accidisse prodigium narrat. Duodecimo ab Vrbe millario locatur apud Eutropium: decimo sexto, apud Appianum libro iii. Bellor. Civilium. Sub Monte Albano, ut Livius in Via Appia, ut Appianus innuit lib. 1. Bel. Civil. Inter Montem & Lacum scribitur Halicarnassæo; natura ipsa, tamquam muro tutissimo munita. Habuisse videtur ad numerum Porcellorum xxx. in ambitu Turres. Respicit eo Cassandra Lycophronis: κλεοί δὲ χώρεων ἐν τίμιος Βοφίζεων Τ᾽πὶρ Λαῦνας Δαυνίας τ᾽ ὠκισμένων, Πύργος τριάκοντ᾽ ἐξαμβαίνους γεὰς Σύες κελαινής, ἐν ἀπ᾽ Ἰδαίων λεύων Καὶ Δαρδανίων, ἐκ πίτων ναυσὶ λωστ᾽ Τὸ ἐμβιῶν Θεριβλέχον ἐν τένοις κάπρων,
units.tr: Livy (book 1) and Dionysius (book 1 of the Roman Antiquities) confirm this, and Dionysius also tells that the greatest portent happened at the beginning of the founding of the city. Eutropius places it twelve miles from Rome, while Appian (book 3 of the Civil Wars) gives sixteen miles. It lay under the Alban mountain, as Livy says of the Appian Way, and as Appian hints in book 1 of the Civil Wars. Halicarnassaeus writes that it lay between the mountain and the lake, and nature itself had fortified it like the safest wall. It seems to have had thirty towers in its circuit, matching the number of the piglets. Lycophron's Cassandra alludes to this: "And the famous, much-honoured land of the Bovesii, and of the Launians and the Daunians who dwell there: a tower of thirty ... black sows, of the Idaeans and Dardanians, which from the ships ... " [κλεοί δὲ χώρεων ἐν τίμιος Βοφίζεων Τ᾽πὶρ Λαῦνας Δαυνίας τ᾽ ὠκισμένων, Πύργος τριάκοντ᾽ ἐξαμβαίνους γεὰς Σύες κελαινής, ἐν ἀπ᾽ Ἰδαίων λεύων Καὶ Δαρδανίων, ἐκ πίτων ναυσὶ λωστ᾽ Τὸ ἐμβιῶν Θεριβλέχον ἐν τένοις κάπρων]

units.la: Albam Suem, unde nomen Urbi, nominant omnes: unus Lycophron Σύες κελαινής hic meminit. Condita tantis opum & fortunæ incrementis auxit, ut xxx. Oppidorum Latinorum, inter quæ ipsa Roma fuerit, Colonis emissis, Mater: & Reges habuerit xv. Eurycleonem Ascanium, Silvium, Aeneam, Latinum, Albam Capetum, Capyn, Calpetum, Tiberinum, Agrippam, Alladium, Aventinum, Procam, Amulium, Numitorem: Silvios omnes ab Secundo Rege, qui in Silvis natus erat, cognominatos; qui quales fuerint, quotque annos regnarint, prolixe tradit Halicarnassæus lib. 1. Consulendus & Livius lib. 1. Sub his Regibus, paucisque, qui sequuntur, Dictatoribus, quum supra quadringentos annos fuerunt Alba, tandem Senatus Romani Tullique Hostilij Romanorum Regis decreto propter Metij Suffetij proditionem, fuit excisa, Incolis Romam in Cœlium montem migrare iussis. Restauratam iterum ab Henrico iii. Imperatore Augusto everterunt Romani anno cIↄCLXVIII. temporibus Alexandri iii. P. M. uti Blondus scribit lib. xv. Historiarum. Nunc plane desolata jacet, nisi quod Savellam in angulo quodam Castellum modicum ex veteris urbis ruinis aedificatum putetur: unde nobilis Romæ Savellorum Familia, si Blondo credendum. Quanta certe eius olim fuerit magnificentia, Moles loquuntur & rudera. De Vuis Vinisque Albanis Plinius lib. xiiii. natur. Histor. Martialis, & alij.
units.tr: Everyone calls it Alba Longa, the White Sow, which gave the city its name; only Lycophron mentions it here as the "dark sow" [Σύες κελαινής]. Founded with such riches and such growth of fortune, it sent out colonists to thirty Latin towns, among them Rome itself, and was their mother. It had fifteen kings: Eurycleon, Ascanius, Silvius, Aeneas, Latinus, Alba, Capetus, Capys, Calpetus, Tiberinus, Agrippa, Alladius, Aventinus, Proca, Amulius and Numitor. All the Silvii were so named after the second king, who was born in the woods. Dionysius of Halicarnassus gives a full account of who they were and how many years each reigned, in book 1, and Livy in book 1 should also be consulted. Under these kings, and the few dictators who followed them, Alba stood for more than four hundred years. At last, by decree of the Roman Senate and of Tullus Hostilius, king of the Romans, because of the treachery of Metius Fufetius, it was destroyed, and its inhabitants were ordered to move to Rome, to the Caelian hill. Restored again by the emperor Henry III, it was overthrown by the Romans in the year 1168, in the time of Pope Alexander III, as Blondus writes in book 15 of his Histories. Now it lies wholly deserted, except that a small castle called Savella, built from the ruins of the old city, is thought to stand in a certain corner of it; from this, if we are to believe Blondus, came the noble Savelli family of Rome. How great its magnificence once was, the mounds and ruins bear witness. On the vines and wines of Alba see Pliny, Natural History book 14, Martial, and others.

units.la: Haud procul Alba fuit, si recte metior, Roboraria, cuius mentio apud Antoninum, cui illa inter Pictas & Urbem.
units.tr: Not far from Alba was, if I measure correctly, Roboraria, which is mentioned by Antoninus, whose route places it between Pictae and the City.

units.la: Ulterius in monticulo Civitas est Aricia: Sic Virgilio lib. vii. Aeneid. Horatio lib. 1. Satyra v. Livio passim, Ciceroni, Tacito lib. xx. Plinio, aliis: Ἀρίκια Appiano lib. 1. Straboni, Ptolemæo & Stephano dicta: quæ Rizza vel La Riccia vulgo. Colonia est Romana, Floro ex Livij Epitoma libri xxc. Eam autem conditionem induit ex antiquo Municipio: quo statu eius meminerunt Festus, Livius lib. viii. & Velleius lib. 1. Conditam ab Archilogo Siculo tradit ex Callio Hemina Solinus: denominatam ab Aricia, Hippolyti coniuge, addunt alij xx. M. P. ab Urbe locat vetus Horatij interpres: clx. Stadiis, Strabo: cxx. Dionysius Halicarnassæus libro vi. confirmante Philostrato lib. iv. de Vita Apollonij. Incolæ Arcini vocantur antiquis Scriptoribus. Dionysius libro iiii. Turnum Herdeontum Aricinum, Virum militarem & facundum, nominat. De Ariciinorum Gestis Dionysius cum alibi, tum lib. vii. Livius libro xviii. & alij. Nostra memoria parum frequentatur. Aricinam Brassicam, ut utilissimam, commendat Plinius libro xix. nat. hist cap. vii. Martialis eiusdem agri Porros celebrat. Nemoralis Aricia cognominatur ab Nemore ingenti, quod Urbi vicinum erat. In eo Vitellium Imperatorem libentissime versari solitum, notat libro xix. Cornelius Tacitus. Nemus hoc dictum erat Dianæ: de cuius simili Sacris, Sacerdote, Fano, & aliis sic scribit Strabo libro v. Τὸ δὲ Ἀρτεμίσιον ἐ καλῶσι νήμο, ἐν ξ ἐν ἱερισσά μίμως τὸ ἰδὲ ἐκ Ἀρικίας ἀναβαίνων, εἰς τ᾽ δ᾽ Ἀρτεμίδη τὸ ἱερὸν. Λέγεται δ᾽ εἶναι ἀφιδρύματος τ᾽ Ταυροπόλου. ἡ γὰρ ἡ Βασιλικὸν κρατεῖ ἡ Σκυθῶν τῶν τὸ ἱερὸν ἴδος. Καθίστα γὰρ ἐφεύς, ἐ ἥσθηκεν ἀπέσχε ἡ ἱερωμένη ἀσέπτην, ἐκ ἀπὸ ἀλλὰ ᾗ ἐξ Ἐφεσ ἐν ἔτι δὲ τῆς σπόροφ ἐπιμελέσι. τὸ δὲ ἱερὸν ἐν ἄλσει: ἀπόκειται δὲ Λίμνη πλαταμόνος. κυκλῷ δ᾽ ἐρυμὴ συνηχὴς ἐφεύς ἐστι, καὶ μία ὑλὴ, καὶ τὸ ἱερὸν καὶ τὸ ὕδωρ ἐπιλαμβάνεται ἐκ εἰλε πάντα καὶ βαθεῖ: & quæ sequuntur de Fontibus. Sic etiam Servius ad illud Virgilij vii. Æneidos,
units.tr: Further inland, on a little hill, is the town of Aricia. Thus it is called by Virgil, Aeneid book 7; by Horace, Satires book 1, satire 5; by Livy throughout; by Cicero, Tacitus in book 20, Pliny and others; Appian in book 1 calls it Ἀρίκια [Aricia], as do Strabo, Ptolemy and Stephanus. In the common speech it is now called Rizza or La Riccia. It is a Roman colony, as Florus shows from the Epitome of Livy book 90. It took this status from an earlier municipium, which is recorded by Festus, by Livy book 8, and by Velleius book 1. Solinus, from Callius Hemina, reports that it was founded by Archilochus the Sicilian; others add that it was named after Aricia, the wife of Hippolytus. The old commentator on Horace places it 20 miles from Rome; Strabo gives 160 stades; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, in book 6, gives 120 stades, confirmed by Philostratus, Life of Apollonius, book 4. The inhabitants are called Arcini by the ancient writers. Dionysius in book 4 names Turnus Herdonius of Aricia, a man skilled in war and eloquent. Dionysius treats the deeds of the Aricini both elsewhere and in book 7; so does Livy in book 18, and others. In our time it is little frequented. Pliny in Natural History book 19, chapter 7, commends Aricine cabbage as very useful; Martial celebrates the leeks of the same district. It is surnamed Nemoralis Aricia from the great grove (Nemus) that lay near the city. Tacitus, in book 19, notes that the Emperor Vitellius liked to spend his time there very much. This grove was called the grove of Diana. Strabo, in book 5, writes thus about its sacred rites, priest, temple and other things like it: "The place they call the Artemision grove (nemos), in which there is a sacred precinct... the ascent from Aricia to the temple of Artemis... It is said to be a copy of the Taurian Artemis, for the Scythian image of the goddess is said to have been brought here. The priest, who has killed the one who held the office before him, holds the office, and the priest is always a fugitive, ..." and what follows about the springs. [Τὸ δὲ Ἀρτεμίσιον ἄλσος καλοῦσι Νέμος, ἐν ᾧ ἐστιν ἱερὸν τῆς Ἀρτέμιδος, ἀνάβασις ἐξ Ἀρικίας...] Thus also Servius on that line of Virgil, Aeneid 7:

units.la: Latet Arbor opaca
units.tr: Hidden is the shady tree

units.la: Aureus, Licet in hoc ramo, inquit, qui de Sacris Proserpinæ scripsisse dicuntur, quidam esse Mysterium adfirmant, publica tamen opinio hoc habet: Orefles post occisum Regem Thoantem in Regione Tarnica, cum Sorore Iphigenia fuit, & Dianæ Simulacrum inde sublatum haud longe ab Aricia collocarunt. In luco Templi pòst multum tempus ritum Sacrificiorum fuit (Arbor quædam, de qua infringi ramum non licebat. Debatur autem fugitivo potestas, ut si quis exinde ramum potuisset auferre, monomachia cum fugitivo eius templi Sacerdote dimicaret. Nam fugitivus ille erat Sacerdos ad priscæ imaginem fugæ. Dimicandi autem dabatur facultas, quasi ad pristinum Sacrarii reparationem. Qui Δεχόμενος hastis Straboni, Sacerdos Nemorensis, Fugitivus Servius: Latinus proprio vocabulo Rex Nemorensis dicebatur. Is Sacerdotii Regnum tantùm per obtinebat, dum vertente anno fortior aliquis superveniens cum pugna superaret: qualem Caius Caligula ei, qui iam multos annos Sacerdotio præfuerat, subinde fuisse legitur apud Suetonium in eius Vita cap. xxxv. Respicit eo Ovidius lib. III. Fastor.
units.tr: Aureus says: "Although some affirm that there is a mystery in the branch that is said to have been written about the rites of Proserpina, public opinion holds the following. After Thoas the king was killed in the Tauric region, Orestes was with his sister Iphigenia, and they set up the image of Diana, taken from there, not far from Aricia. In the grove of the temple, for a long time afterwards, there was a rite of sacrifice. There was a certain tree, from which it was not permitted to break off a branch. The power over it belonged to a fugitive, so that if anyone could take a branch from it, he would fight a single combat with the fugitive, the priest of that temple. For that fugitive was a priest, in memory of the ancient flight. The chance to fight was given as if for the restoration of the earlier sanctuary." The one who held the spear, as Strabo puts it, was the priest of Nemi, the fugitive as Servius puts it; Latinus was called by his proper name the King of Nemi. He held the kingship of the priesthood only so long as, when the year turned, no stronger man came along and defeated him in combat. Such was the case with Caligula, who in later years repeatedly came against the man who had for many years presided over the priesthood, as is read in Suetonius, Life of Caligula, chapter 35. Ovid, Fasti book 3, alludes to this:

units.la: Regna tenent fortes manibus, pedibusque fugaces:
units.tr: The strong hold the kingdom with their hands, the fugitives with their feet:

units.la: Et periit exemplo postmodo quisque suo.
units.tr: And each afterwards perished by his own example.

units.la: Meminit etiam Lacus Ariciæ idem Ovidius lib. Fastorum IV. Trivia Lacus est Virgilio lib. VII. Speculum Dianæ Servio ibidem dicitur, Hippolyti Lacus Statio libro III. Silvarum; Dianæ Stagnum Ovidio libris I. Fastor. & lib. XIII. Metamorph. Hodie, ut vult Erythræus, Lago di Nemi. Distat ab Aricia circiter III. M. P.
units.tr: The same Ovid also mentions the Lake of Aricia in Fasti book 4. Virgil, Aeneid book 7, calls it the Trivian lake; Servius on the same passage calls it the mirror of Diana; Statius, Silvae book 3, calls it the lake of Hippolytus; Ovid in Fasti book 1 and Metamorphoses book 13 calls it the pool of Diana. Today, as Erythraeus thinks, it is the Lago di Nemi. It lies about three miles from Aricia.

units.la: Vetera Ariciam versus Meridiem est Lanuvium, cum Lavinio apud Græcos Latinosque Scriptores confundi solitum. Aliud enim Lavinium, de quo in Latii Litoralibus dixi; aliud Lanuvium, cuius hic institutur delineatio. De utriusque differentia consulendi Signonius in Livij librum VIII. Hermolaus Barbarus in Plinij librum III. Vrsinus de Familiis, ubi de Papiria Gente, Sinico Bolius in Epistolis ad Atticum, & alij. Illud certum, ubicunque mentio fiat Junonis Sospitæ, cum adscripto Urbis nomine, semper Lanuvium esse ponendum. Ælianus libro Animalium XI. cap. VI. Urbem, de qua agimus, Λαυίνιον vocat, addiditque eam merito Matrem primariam Urbis Romæ posse dici: errore duplici, in Nomine & Historia. Λαυσίνιον enim scribendum erat, quod tamen non Mater quasi Romæ, sed Lavinium. Legitur Lanuvium apud Antoninum, sed Lavinium ibi restituendum docent cum Itineris ratio, tum Itineraria Tabula cum Antonino commissa. Lanuvium in Marmoribus esse testis est V. Cl. Abrahamus Ortelius. Lavino male est apud Silium Italicum lib. XIII. pro Lanuvio, vel Lanuvo. Ego etiam Lanuvinos lego in Base marmorea, quæ ex Vico Corocollo inter Gabios Tiburtinosque anno MDXLIX cum aliis ad vecta, hodie in Vinca servatur Cardinalis Carpentisfic in fronte habens:
units.tr: Southeast of Aricia lies Lanuvium, which the Greek and Latin writers used to confuse with Lavinium. There is another Lavinium, of which I spoke in the Latin coastal region; and there is Lanuvium, whose outline is being given here. For the difference between the two, see Sigonius on Livy book 8, Hermolaus Barbarus on Pliny book 3, Ursinus in On Families, where he treats the Papirian gens, Sigonio Bolius in the Letters to Atticus, and others. This is certain: wherever mention is made of Juno Sospita together with the name of a city, it must always be taken to be Lanuvium. Aelian, in On Animals book 11, chapter 6, calls the city of which we speak Λαυίνιον [Lavinion] and adds that it could rightly be called the chief mother of the city of Rome; this is a double error, in the name and in the history. For it should have been written Λαυσίνιον, which is not Lanuvium but Lavinium, and it was not the mother of Rome in any sense. Lanuvium is read in Antoninus, but both the plan of the route and the Itinerary Table, compared with Antoninus, show that Lavinium should be restored there. That the form is Lanuvium on the marbles is attested by the most learned Abraham Ortelius. In Silius Italicus, book 13, Lavino stands wrongly for Lanuvio or Lanuvo. I also read Lanuvinos on a marble base, which was brought in with other things in the year 1549 from the Vicus Corocollo, between Gabii and Tibur, and is kept today in the vineyard of Cardinal Carpi, bearing this inscription on its front:

units.la: C. CÆSONIO. C. F. QVIR. MACRO. RVFINIANO
units.tr: C. Caesonius, son of Gaius, of the Quirine tribe, Macer Rufinianus

units.la: CONSVLARI. SODALI. AVGVSTALI. COMITI. IMP. SEVERI. ALEXANDRI. AVG. CVR. R. P. LANIVINOR.
units.tr: Consular, fellow of the Augustales, companion of Emperor Severus Alexander Augustus, curator of the public affairs of the Lanuvinians, and what follows there.

units.la: & quæ ibi sequuntur. Populus etiam Lanivinus nominari videtur in Fragmento Lapidis, quod hodie eo loco: ANI. F AIANI ICI NEP NERVÆ. PRONEP O. HADRIANO ONINO. AVG. PIO MAXVMO. TRIBVN AT. II. COS. II. P P. ES POPVLVSQVE VINVS VETERES
units.tr: A people called the Lanuvinians also seems to be named in a fragment of stone, which today in that place reads: ...son of ...ianus, grandson of Nerva, great-grandson of ... Hadrian Antoninus Augustus Pius Maximus, tribune with tribunician power for the second time, consul for the second time, father of the fatherland... and the people, the old...

units.la: Hodie ex Blondi, Leandri, Celsique Cittadinimente Indi ina cc. plus minus Stadus, hoc est xxv. M. P. ab Urbe tuste constat ex libro Diodori XIII. ubi aut Cilarcium; Locum sic dictum, haud procul hinc, teste Livio libro V., totidem Roma distare. Τρίτος ὁ αὐτὸς inquit Strabo, loquens de Aricia) τὸ μὲν Λαυινον, πόλις τυραννίς, ἐν ἐξέχῃ τὸ Ἀ Λαυίνιον ὀδός Legendum omnino Λαυινιον vel Λαυίσιον. Ab Lanuvio [illegible, ~6 letters], inquit idem, [illegible, ~8 letters]. Lanuvij Templum fuisse Junonis Sospitae prodit memoriae, praeter Plinium, Livius multis locis. In eo vexilla erant Lanuvinorum, quae sanguine tinxisse, tradit idem Plinius lib. xx. natur. Historiae: notans etiam libro xxxv. cap. iii. Lanuvij pictos fuisse cominus nudos Achillem & Helenam, excellentissimae formae. Lanuvium inter Municipia censetur apud Livium libro viii. & Sex. Pompeium Festum in Libris de Verb. significat. Meminit etiam, ut Municipij, Cicero pro Murena. Postea ex Municipio Coloniam ab Caesare dictatore factam, indicat Frontinus M. S. apud quem in vulgatis scribitur Lavinium. Nam id in Lauro-Lavinio paullo ante delineatum fuerat. Oriundam Lanuvio Gentem Murenarum Patriciam memorat Cicero in oratione, quam dixi.
units.tr: Today, according to Blondus, Leander and Celsus, the town of ... is about 200 stades, that is 25 miles, from Rome, as is clear from Diodorus, book 13, where it is called Cilarcium. Livy, book 5, says that a place of this name, not far from here, is the same distance from Rome. The same Strabo, speaking of Aricia, says: "Third, Lavinium, a tyrannical city, ... the Lavinium road" [Τρίτος ὁ αὐτός ... τὸ μὲν Λαυινον, πόλις τυραννίς, ... Λαυίνιον ὀδός]. It should certainly be read as Λαυινιον or Λαυίσιον. Strabo says that from Lanuvium ... Lanuvij is recorded as having had a temple of Juno Sospita; besides Pliny, Livy mentions it in many places. In it were the standards of the Lanuvinians, which Pliny tells us, in book 20 of his Natural History, were dyed with blood. In book 35, chapter 3, he also notes that at Lanuvij were painted, quite nude, Achilles and Helen, of most excellent beauty. Lanuvium is counted among the Municipia by Livy in book 8, and by Sextus Pompeius Festus in his books on the meaning of words. Cicero also mentions it as a Municipij in his speech for Murena. Afterwards, Frontinus, in a manuscript where the printed texts read Lavinium, shows that it was made a Municipio Coloniam by Caesar the dictator. For this was outlined a little earlier in Lauro-Lavinio. Cicero, in the speech I have mentioned, records that the patrician family of the Murenae came from Lanuvio.

units.la: Appia relicta, meditullium Latii petens, ut sensim ad Hernicorum agros deveniam, Viam adeo iamnunc Latinam. Ea, decimo ab urbe Lapide, fundamenta inveniuntur Columna Opidi: a quo magnifica Romae Columnarum Familia. Livio lib. ii. Columnae videtur appellari.
units.tr: Leaving the Appian Way and making for the middle of Latium, so that I may gradually reach the fields of the Hernici, I now take the Latin Way. At the tenth milestone from Rome, the foundations of the town of Columna are found; from it comes the noble Roman family of the Columnarum. In Livy, book 2, it seems to be called Columnae.

units.la: Fuerunt haud procul Columna Bovillae, de quibus Persius Satyra vi. & Martialis lib. ii. epig. vi. pauper Vicus, ad quem inter festus est ab Milone Clodius, ut scribunt Asconius Padianus; sic dictus a Boum multitudine, quasi Boum villa, ubi gentes multi stipem mendicabant. De Bovillis veteres Glossae ad vi. Persij Satyram. Hinc forte Bovillanum Fundus apud Ciceronem in Epist. ad Q. Fratrem. Aliae Bovillae nobiliores erant in Latio ad Lirim, de quibus suo loco. Inter Bovillas & Ariciam erat Virbii Clivus, quatuor ab Urbe Millibus: de quo Veteres, quas dixi, Glossae, Quatuor millibus nuncupant, ab Urbe est Urbis Clivus, quae iter est ad Ariciam & ad Nemus Dianae, ubi Urbis colitur, id est, Hippolytus, quod hic in vitam prolatus sit. Nota autem apud Virgilium Tabula est. Consulendus & Ovidius vi. Fastorum, cuius & illud Fastorum iii.
units.tr: Not far from Columna were Bovillae, which Persius mentions in Satire 6, and Martial in book 2, epigram 6: a poor village, where Clodius was killed by Milo, as Asconius Pedianus writes. It was so named from the number of oxen, as if it were Boum villa, where many beggars begged for alms. Ancient glosses on Persius' sixth Satire speak of the Bovillis. Perhaps from here comes the Bovillanum Fundus in Cicero's letter to his brother Quintus. Other, more famous Bovillae were in Latium by the Liris, which I will discuss in their place. Between Bovillae and Aricia was the Virbii Clivus, four miles from Rome. The ancient glosses I have mentioned call it the Quatuor millibus, from Rome; there is the Rome slope, which is the road to Aricia and to the grove of Diana, where Virbius is worshipped, that is, Hippolytus, because he was brought back to life here. Note also the Tabula in Virgil. Ovid, Fasti book 6, should be consulted, and also this from Fasti book 3:

units.la: Hic Latet Hippolytus furiis discerptus equorum;Unde Nemus nullis illud adiitur equis.
units.tr: Here lies Hippolytus, torn apart by the frenzied horses; hence that grove is approached by no horses.

units.la: Loquitur de Nemore Vallis Aricinae.
units.tr: Speaks of the grove of the Valley of Aricia.

units.la: Incipit co tractu Nemus Algidum: de quo ante. Supra illud in monte cognomine, xii. ab Urbe Lapide, ut notat Eutropius libro i. conspicitur Arx Papalis, vulgo Rocca del Papa: ubi quondam, ut viri docti volunt, Algidum; sic dictum ab situ loci, perpetuis coeli frigoribus propter altitudinem algentis. Meminerunt Algidi Horatius, saepe Livius, Dionysius Halicarnassaeus, Silius, alij. Ἄλγιδον Strabo & Dionysio; Stephano Ἄλγιδος dicitur: Algedon Procopio libro iii. Rerum Gothicarum. Male legitur apud Diodorum Siculum lib. xii. Αλγαδὸν pro Ἄλγιδον, in Historia Virgilij & Filiae ab ipso occisae.
units.tr: The Nemus Algidum begins in this district, of which I have spoken before. Above it, on the mountain of the same name, twelve miles from Rome, as Eutropius notes in book 1, rises the Arx Papalis, commonly called the Rocca del Papa. Where, as learned men think, the Algidum once was, so named from the nature of the place, because of the constant cold of the sky on account of its height. Algidi is mentioned by Horace, often by Livy, by Dionysius of Halicarnassus, by Silius and others. Strabo and Dionysius call it Ἄλγιδον; Stephanus calls it Ἄλγιδος; Procopius, in book 3 of his Gothic History, calls it Algedon. It is wrongly read in Diodorus Siculus, book 12, as Ἀλγαδὸν for Ἄλγιδον, in the story of Virgil and the daughter he killed.

units.la: In Hernicis, de quibus initio huius capitis dixi, est, ut notant Livius lib. ix. Strabo libro v. & Macrobius libro v. Saturnal. Anagnia. Sic cum aliis, tum Livio variis locis, Tacito libro xix. Ciceroni, Silio libro v. & alibi, Frontino, cui Colonia est, Antonino; Ἀνάγνια Strabo & Ptolemaeo vocatur; Anagnium Itinerariae Tabulae; quae Anagna vulgo. Incolae Anagnini Livio & aliis: Plinio item in Prima Italiae Regione: & Bali confractae, quae in ipso Opido, Parieti domus privatae ad S. Pauli lum inserta. πόλις ἀξιολογ, Strabo: Dives, Virgilio, ad quem Servius notat, Anagniam Divitem appellari, vel quod perfacunda sit, vel ad historia confirmationem. In ea enim Antonium, Augusti Sorore Fulvia contempta, Cleopatraque in Uxorem accepta, nummum percutit insigne. Muros & Portam Anagniae fulmine percussam scribit Livius lib. xxvii. alio loco, Terram ante Portam eiusdem Urbis iactam sine ullo ignis alimento arsisse; item lib. xlv. Terra quandoque ad eamdem urbem pluisse. Auctor est Plinius C. Septimulium, Graccho peramicum, Anagnia progenitum. Octavy Felicis, Anagnini, mentio in fragmento Tabellae marmoreae, quae in hortis Euryali Rufini ad Bulla Gallica. Varios genuit Pontifices: inter eos Innocentium iii. Gregorium ix. Alexandrum iv. Bonifacium viii. Cardinales insuper multos, Episcopos, aliosque praeclaros viros. Patria quoque haec Ioannis Anagnini, Bononiensis Archidiaconi, & Commentatoris Legum Pontificiarum, maximeque Decretalium: qui anno mccccclvii. Bononiae fato concessit. Hodie, licet Episcopatus dignitate fulgens, semidiruta tamen & deiolata jacet: civilibus & intestinis odijs maxime labefactata. Agri naturam exprimit aliquo modo Silius Italicus lib.viii. Quæris putris pingue sulcaru Anagnia glebis:
units.tr: Among the Hernici, of whom I spoke at the start of this chapter, is Anagnia, as Livy in book 9, Strabo in book 5, and Macrobius in book 5 of the Saturnalia note. Thus it is named by others as well as by Livy in various places, by Tacitus in book 19, by Cicero, by Silius in book 5 and elsewhere, by Frontinus, who calls it a colony, and by Antoninus. Strabo and Ptolemy call it Ἀνάγνια; the Itinerary Table gives Anagnium; commonly it is Anagna. Its inhabitants are the Anagnini in Livy and others, and in Pliny in the first region of Italy. Broken pieces of bronze, which are in the town itself, are set into the wall of a private house near St Paul's. Strabo calls it a notable city. Virgil calls it Anagniam Divitem, rich Anagnia, and Servius notes that it is so called either because it is very pleasant, or to confirm history. For in it Antony, having scorned Fulvia, Augustus' sister, and taken Cleopatra as his wife, struck a coin bearing this mark. Livy in book 27 writes that the walls and the gate of Anagniae were struck by lightning; in another place, that earth thrown before the gate of the same city burned without any fuel for fire; and in book 45, that earth once rained on the same city. Pliny records that C. Septimulius, a very great friend of Gracchus, was born at Anagnia. The name of Octavy Felicis, Anagnini is mentioned in a fragment of a marble tablet in the gardens of Euryalus Rufinus at Bulla Gallica. It produced several popes: among them Innocentius III, Gregorius IX, Alexander IV, Bonifacius VIII; also many cardinals, bishops and other distinguished men. It was also the home of Ioannis Anagnini, archdeacon of Bologna and commentator on the papal laws, above all the Decretals, who died at Bologna in 1457. Today, although it shines with the dignity of a bishopric, it lies half ruined and deserted, greatly weakened by civil and internal hatreds. Silius Italicus in book 8 describes the nature of its land in some way: You ask about Anagnia's rich fields, crumbling into fat clods.

units.la: Item:
units.tr: Likewise:

units.la: Frugiferis tete ante alias Anagnia glebis.
units.tr: Anagnia, rich above others in fruitful clods.

units.la: Anagninum habet M. Tullius in Epistolis, Prædium fortean in huius Vrbis agro. Propinquus Anagnia Fons Tofanus, de quo alibi.
units.tr: Marcus Tullius, in his Letters, has an Anagninum, an estate perhaps in the territory of this town. Near Anagnia is the Fons Tofanus, of which I will speak elsewhere.

units.la: Vltra Anagniam M. P. v. alia Hernicorum Vrbs in Colle est Ferentinum: Livio variis locis, Silio, Frontino, Antonino & Itinerariæ Tabulæ celebratum: Φερεντῖνον, Ptolemæo: Φερεντῖνος, Stephano ex Strabonis libro v. ubi tamen hodie legitur Φερεντῖνον, ut & in M. S. Frontino. Ferentino hodie. Vide, quæ noto ad Frentanas, Sammitium Populos. Incolæ Ferentinates Livio lib.xxxiii. Plinioque libro iii.cap.v. Ferentinensis Colonia est apud Frontinum. De Rebus gestis Livius libro iii. vii. & ix. Dionysius Halicarnassæus libro iii. in Foro Forentino Concilium scribit habitum.
units.tr: Five miles beyond Anagnia there is another town of the Hernici on a hill, Ferentinum, celebrated by Livy in various places, by Silius, Frontinus, Antoninus and the Itinerary Table: Φερεντῖνον in Ptolemy; Φερεντῖνος in Stephanus, from book 5 of Strabo, where however Φερεντῖνον is read today, as also in the manuscript of Frontinus. It is Ferentino today. See what I note on the Frentani and the Samnite peoples. Its inhabitants are the Ferentinates in Livy, book 33, and Pliny, book 3, chapter 5. The Ferentinensis Colonia is in Frontinus. Livy, in books 3, 7 and 9, writes of its deeds; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, in book 3, writes that a council was held in the Foro Forentino.

units.la: Hinc quinto lapide Frusinum abest. Φρουσινον, Straboni & Ptolemæo: Frusino, Livio, Silio, Festo, Antonino: Frasellono; vernacule. Frusinates Incolæ Livio lib.x, Plinioque in i. Italiæ Regione. Frusinone Colonia Frontino: in cuius membranis, quæ apud V. CL. Petrum Scriverium Fresenona. Frusini Livius lib. vii Puerum magnitudine, ut quatuor annorum videretur: & lib.xxi. Agnum cum Capite Suis natum, scribit. Patria duorum Pontificum Hormisda Iusti F. & Silverij Hormisda F.
units.tr: Five miles from here lies Frusinum. It is Φρουσινον in Strabo and Ptolemy; Frusino in Livy, Silius, Festus and Antoninus; Frasellono in the vernacular. Its inhabitants, the Frusinates, are mentioned in Livy, book 10, and Pliny in the first region of Italy. Frusinone Colonia is in Frontinus; in his manuscripts, which Petrus Scriverius possessed, it is Fresenona. Livy, book 7, writes of Frusini a boy of such size that he looked four years old; and in book 21, of a lamb born with a sow's head. It was the home of two popes, Hormisda son of Justus and Silverius son of Hormisdas.

units.la: Post M. P. xv. Latij hoc latere terminus est Ceparanum.
units.tr: Thirty miles beyond, on this side, the boundary of Latium is Ceparanum.

units.la: Hoc ipso tamen itinere dextra Sinuessanum (Zinazzano) Palianum (Pagliano) invenitur: quod annis superioribus Ascanio Columnæ Paulus iii. P. M. ademit.
units.tr: Yet on this same road, on the right, are found Sinuessanum (Zinazzano) and Palianum (Pagliano), which Pope Paul III in earlier years took away from Ascanio Colonna.

units.la: Sequuntur inde, quæ vernacule Serrono, Pillio, Agnto, Trivigliano. Colle di Po/Colle Podius) Anticolo & Veralo: Vrbs antiqua, quæ Verulanum Livio, in Hernicis, cuiusque Incolæ Verulani eidem Livio lib.ix. & Plinio lib.iii. Patria hæc Ennij Philonardi, Episcopi Verulani & Cardinalis. Verulas Coloniam habet Frontinus.
units.tr: Next come the places which in the vernacular are called Serrono, Pillio, Agnto, Trivigliano. Colle di Po (Colle Podius), Anticolo and Veralo. It is an ancient city, which Livy calls Verulanum, among the Hernici; its inhabitants are the Verulani, in the same Livy, book 9, and in Pliny, book 3. It was the home of Ennius Philonardi, bishop of Veroli and cardinal. Frontinus gives Verulas as a colony.

units.la: Succedit Castellum modicum Fumonus: à Petracha, Platina, Blondo, Sabellico, aliis frequenter nominatum in historia Celestini v. P. M.
units.tr: Next comes the small town of Fumonus, often named by Petrarch, Platina, Blondus, Sabellicus and others in the history of Celestine V, pope.

units.la: Mox Alatrium, quod vulgo Alatro: Ἀλάτριον Straboni: Alatrium Frontino, ut quidem in M. S. Nam in Vulgatis est Alatrum. Incolæ Alatrinates vel Alatrinates, Plinio, Ciceroni, Livio. Coloniam nominat Frontinus. Postea Municipij naturam induit. Docet Tabula marmorea, quæ ibi in Vestibulo Summi Templi:
units.tr: Then Alatrium, which is commonly called Alatro. Strabo gives it as Ἀλάτριον [Alatrion]. Frontinus writes Alatrium, at least in the manuscripts, though the printed editions have Alatrum. Its inhabitants are called Alatrinates or Alatrinates by Pliny, Cicero and Livy. Frontinus calls it a colonia. Later it took on the status of a municipium. A marble tablet in the vestibule of the main temple there attests this:

units.la: C. IVLIO. AVGVSTI. L HELENO
units.tr: To Gaius Julius Helenus, freedman of Augustus

units.la: EX. DECRETO. DECVR MVNICIPIL. ALETRINAT ET. POLLICITATIONE. SEVIR ET. MVNICIPIVM. ET. INCOLAR OB, MERITA, EIVS
units.tr: By decree of the decurions of the Alatrinate municipality, and by the offer of the Sevir, the municipality and the residents, on account of his merits.

units.la: Sevirum Augustalium Aletrinatium meminit Tabulæ marmoreæ fragmentum, quod ibidem in Sacra S. Ianuarij æde: Q. MINVCIVS. Q. L. ANTEROS. VI. V AVGVSTAL HIC. SEVIRIS. AVGVSTTAL. ALETRIN LEGAVIT. HS (D). QVOIVS. EX. RED QVOD. ANNIS. NATALI. SVO. VI. FEB. VESCERENTVR.
units.tr: A fragment of a marble tablet, found in the same place in the sacred church of St Januarius, mentions the Augustal seviri of Alatrium: "Quintus Minucius Anteros, freedman of Quintus, sixvir Augustalis here among the Augustal seviri of Alatrium, has bequeathed HS (D)..., from the income of which on his birthday, 6 February, they are to be given a feast."

units.la: Episcopatus gaudet titulo.
units.tr: The bishopric enjoys the title.

units.la: Hinc Babucum est: quod Bovilla Veteribus: quibus Bovilla duplicés, unæ haud procul Roma: alteræ prope Liris Fluvium. De Prioribus suo loco: Posteriores, quod nobiliores, puto designari à Plinio lib.cap.v. Βοΐλλαι sunt Appiano: Bovilla Colonia Frontino. Vulntur
units.tr: From here comes Babucum. The ancients knew Bovilla, and there were two places of that name: one not far from Rome, and another near the river Liris. I think the former is the one mentioned earlier, and the latter, being the more noted, is the one Pliny means in book 3, chapter 5. Appian has Βοΐλλαι [Boillai], and Frontinus calls it Bovilla Colonia. Remains are still to be seen.

units.la: Vide notas marginales ad loca citata.
units.tr: See the marginal notes for the passages cited.

units.la: Visuntur inde, quæ vulgo Nota, Turtio, Prose, Vico, Rippe, Porcigliano, Trevo & Fettino; Latine scribentibus Nota, Turritium, Profenum, Vicus, Ripa, Porcilianum, Trevum, & Fetinum.
units.tr: Next are seen the places commonly called Nota, Turtio, Prose, Vico, Rippe, Porcigliano, Trevo and Fettino; in Latin writers they are Nota, Turritium, Profenum, Vicus, Ripa, Porcilianum, Trevum and Fetinum.

units.la: Deinde repetita via, medio in Nemore Algido relicta, Valmontonium Castellum, vulgo Val-montono, inde colle cernitur. Labicum Virgilio; ut infra videbimus; Silio lib. v, viii, xiii; & aliis. Λαβικὸν Straboni. Huc pertinet illud principis Poetæ libro viii Æneidos:
units.tr: Then, returning to the road and leaving the Algidus grove in the middle, the castle of Valmontonium, commonly called Val-montono, is seen from the hill. Labicum is what Virgil calls it, as we shall see below; Silius (books 5, 8 and 13) and others do too. Strabo has Λαβικὸν [Labikon]. To this refers the line of the prince of poets in book 8 of the Aeneid:

units.la: Et Sacrane Acies, & picti Scuta Labici.
units.tr: "And the Sacran battle line, and the painted shields of Labicum."

units.la: Ad quem locum Servius, Glaucus, inquit, Minoïs filius venit ad Italiam; & quum sibi Imperium peferet, nec acciperet, idee quod nihil præstabat, sicut pater eius præstiterat, Zonam eius transmisit tendo, quum antehac disiunctæ essent; ostendit scutum militare, à quo & ipse Labicus dictus est, & ex eo Populi, ἀπὸ τοῦ λαβὴς, quam Latine Ansam vocamus. Labici mentionem sæpe facit Dionysius Halicarnassæus, præsertim libro viii, ubi ab Marcio Coriolano cum ceteris Albanorum Colonijs subactum scribit. Livius lib. iiii hanc Urbem expugnatam ab Q. Sulpicio Prisco Dictatore, direptamque scribit; & Colonijs eo Roma ex S. C. missis bina jugera singulis data. Labici Municipii meminit Cicero Philippica ii. Ab eo Labicana Via Romæ. Plinius Agrum Labicanum locat in i Italiæ Regione. Idem Ager olim ab Vvæ præstantia nomen habuit, cujus tres & viginti libras uno prandio Claudium Albinum abiumpsisse Capitolinus est auctor. Labicana Vina celebrant Spartianus & Frontinus. In Populis designandis nonnulla est apud Auctores Græcos Latinosque inconstantia. Nunc enim Labici & Labicani; nunc Lavici & Lavicani scribuntur. Subdinione hodie est Valmontonium Familiæ Comitum Romanæ.
units.tr: Servius, commenting on this passage, says: "Glaucus, son of Minos, came to Italy; and when he offered the command to Aeneas and was not accepted, because he was not as useful as his father had been, he sent his belt across the tents, though they had been separate before; he showed his military shield, from which Labicus was himself named, and from it the people, from ἀπὸ τοῦ λαβὴς [apo tou labēs], which we in Latin call the handle (ansa)." Dionysius of Halicarnassus often mentions Labicum, especially in book 8, where he writes that it was subdued by Marcius Coriolanus along with the other colonies of the Albans. Livy in book 4 writes that this city was taken and plundered by Quintus Sulpicius Priscus, the dictator, and that by decree of the senate two jugera were given to each of the colonists sent there from Rome. Cicero in the second Philippic mentions the municipality of Labicum, and from it the Labican Way at Rome takes its name. Pliny places the Labican territory in the first region of Italy. The same district once took its name from the excellence of its grapes; Capitolinus tells us that Claudius Albinus consumed twenty-three pounds of them at one meal. Spartianus and Frontinus praise the Labican wines. There is some inconsistency among Greek and Latin authors in naming the people: sometimes they are written Labici and Labicani, sometimes Lavici and Lavicani. Today Valmontonium lies under the lordship of a Roman family of counts.

units.la: Haud procul Valmontonio est Montefertinum; Castellum Monfortinorum; qui inter Patricios Romanos loci non postremi.
units.tr: Not far from Valmontonium is Montefertinum, a castle of the Monfortini, who are among the Roman patricians of no small standing.

units.la: Pandunt se mox Opida, quæ vulgo Zancato, Ganignano, & Segna. Hæc Segnia Livio: Σιγνία Straboni; Σίγνια; Stephano. Colonium deduxisse Signiam Tarquinium Superbum auctores sunt Livius libro i, ii, & xxvii, Dionysius lib. iv, Strabo lib. v, Frontinus de Colonijs, & Inscriptio, quæ apud Onuphrium Panvinium:
units.tr: Next open up the towns commonly called Zancato, Ganignano and Segna. This is Segnia in Livy; Strabo has Σιγνία [Signia], and Stephanus Σίγνια [Signia]. That Tarquinius Superbus founded a colony at Signia is attested by Livy (books 1, 2 and 27), Dionysius (book 4), Strabo (book 5), Frontinus in his work on colonies, and the inscription which Onuphrius Panvinius gives:

units.la: L. VOLVMNIO L. F. POMP IVLIANO. SEVERO IIII. VIRO. COL. SIGN. PATRONO. COLONIÆ, SVÆ SINATVS. POPVLVSQVE. SIGNINVS
units.tr: To Lucius Volumnius Julianus Severus, son of Lucius, of the Pomptine tribe, quadrumvir, colonist of Signia, patron of the colony; the senate and people of Signia.

units.la: Incolæ Signini Plinio, in i Regione. Dedit Signia Vitalianum P. M. Episcopatus claret dignitate. Vinum Signinum commendant Strabo & Plinius libro xiiii Nat. hist. cap. vi: quod vetus adstringebat ventrem. Marrialis: Potabis liquidum Signina morantia ventrem, Ne nimium sistant, sit tibi parca sitis.
units.tr: Pliny (book 1) calls the people of Signia Signini. Signia gave Vitalianus to the Church as a supreme pontiff. The bishopric is distinguished in dignity. Strabo and Pliny (Natural History, book 14, chapter 6) commend the Signine wine, which had the property of binding the bowels. Martial says: "You will drink clear Signine wine that checks the bowels; but do not let it stop you too much, and keep your thirst moderate."

units.la: Sic Silius Italicus libro viii de Bello Punico: Quos Cora, quos spumans inimico Signia musto.
units.tr: So Silius Italicus in book 8 of the Punic War: "Those whom Cora sent, and Signia with its foaming must, hostile to the drinker."

units.la: Inimicum Mustum, quod nimium sæpe adstringeret.
units.tr: "Inimicum mustum" (hostile must), because it strongly binds the bowels.

units.la: Post Signiam ulterius sunt Scarcula, Merulo, Sappino, Patria, Ceccano & Castrum Latij hic terminus.
units.tr: Beyond Signia further on are Scarcula, Merulo, Sappino, Patria, Ceccano and Castrum, which is the boundary of Latium here.

units.la: Flagitat jam ordo, ut Septemtrionalia Latij per Viam Valeriam Tiburtinam que peragremus.
units.tr: The order now requires that we travel through the northern parts of Latium along the Valerian Tiburtine Way.

units.la: Hic primo se offert loco Tibur. Ita Latinis omnibus dicitur. Τίβυρ, Prolemæo, Τίβυρς, Straboni; Τίβυρι ex Artemidoro; Τίβυρα ex Nicanore, & Τίβυρα ex nescio quibus: quæ Tivoli hodie. Ἀλυσίφανες olim vocatum tradit Stephanus; quam appellationem Strabo tribuit Prænestæ. Ineptiunt, qui Ἡράκλειον & Καπιτωλιον nominarum etiam ex Strabone contendunt; Auctoris mentem non satis adsecuti. Herculi tamen sacram fuisse, constat ex Suetonio in Caligulæ Vita cap. viii. Ejus pars est Σιβυλλῶν apud Dionysium Halicarnassæum. Incolæ Tiburtes plerisque, & altissimas perangustis divisas plateis: Porticusque perpetuas & Labyrinthos. Muri Domorum sunt tenues: sed firmissimi propter calcem & bitumen. In Monte meridiem versus Templum est S. Trinitatis: post quod descensus est in Sacellum S. Crucis, in Petra, terræmotu scissa, ædificatum. In Summo Templo multa monstrantur Donaria & Ornamenta. Inter ea Crater ingens, Formis adlatus, Cadorum plurimum capax; ex Saxo Pario candidissimo cavatus: quo nunc Sacerdotes utuntur pro Sacri Baptismatis Lavacro. Auctorem loquuntur Græca Inscriptio:
units.tr: Here Tibur first presents itself. All Latin writers so call it. Ptolemy has Τίβυρ [Tibyr], Strabo Τίβυρς [Tibyrs], Artemidorus Τίβυρι [Tibyri], Nicanor Τίβυρα [Tibyra], and others some other form; today it is Tivoli. Stephanus records that it was once called Ἀλυσίφανες [Alysiphanes]; Strabo gives this name to Praeneste. Those who insist, also on the authority of Strabo, that it was called Ἡράκλειον [Herakleion] and Καπιτώλιον [Kapitolion] are foolish, not having grasped the author's meaning well enough. Still, that it was sacred to Hercules is clear from Suetonius in the Life of Caligula, chapter 8. Part of it is the Σιβυλλῶν [Sibyllōn] mentioned by Dionysius of Halicarnassus. The people of Tibur are Tiburtes; for the most part the town is divided by very high and very narrow streets, with continuous colonnades and labyrinths. The house walls are thin, but very firm because of lime and bitumen. On the hill to the south is the Church of the Holy Trinity; beyond it a descent leads to the chapel of the Holy Cross, built into rock split by an earthquake. In the main church many votive offerings and ornaments are shown. Among them is a huge bowl, brought from Formiae, able to hold very many casks, hollowed out of the purest white Parian marble; the priests now use it as a font for holy baptism. A Greek inscription names its author:

units.la: ΣΑΛΠΙΩΝ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΟΣ ΕΠΟΙΗΣΕ.
units.tr: Salpion of Athens made it [ΣΑΛΠΙΩΝ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΟΣ ΕΠΟΙΗΣΕ].

units.la: Sepultus ibi in Templo Arcis Dux Borbonius, ad Romam globo bellico ictus. Episcopus Urbi datus legitur ob Formas ab Saracenis excisas. Inlustrarunt eam Gelasius II. P. M. & Thomas Vionius, Cardinalis, Scriptis clarus. Pulcherrimas habet Mulieres. Magnis Cladibus adfecta legitur ab Gallis. Earum maxima incidit in annum MCCCXCIV. Suburbium ipsi oblongum, iuxta litus protensum. Scauri Fundum, Agri Cajetani, donatae Xylum III. Ecclesiae S. Mariæ Maioris, scribit Platina. Porto Ifiauro hodie vulgo dici putat apud Abrahamum Ortelium in Thesauro Geograph. Philippus Winghius, quem idem Ortelius scribere notat, ostendi eius reliquias ad mare cunctibus Gaieta Minturnas, parte dextra.
units.tr: Duke Bourbon lies buried there in the Temple of the Citadel, struck by a cannonball near Rome. It is recorded that a bishop was assigned to the city because Formiae had been destroyed by the Saracens. Gelasius II, Supreme Pontiff, and Thomas Vionius, a cardinal famous for his writings, made it illustrious. It is said to have very beautiful women. It is recorded as having suffered great disasters at the hands of the French, the greatest of which fell in the year 1394. Its suburb is oblong and stretches along the shore. Platina writes that the estate of Scaurus, the fields of Gaeta, and the wood were given to the Church of St Mary Major. Philippus Winghius, whom Ortelius also cites as an author, notes that its remains are shown to everyone by the sea, at Gaeta, Minturnae, on the right-hand side. Ortelius, in his Thesaurus Geographicus, thinks Porto Ifiauro is what is commonly called by that name today.

units.la: Caieta Formiae sublocat Plinius. Sic etiam dictæ Ciceroni, Tacito, Pomponio Melæ, & Antonino: Frontino item, cui Colonia est Romana; Straboni Φορμίαι: quæ Φορμίαι Ptolomæo: Formia, Tabulæ Itinerariæ. Hormiæ olim dictas docent Strabo, Plinius, alii: sive ab frequentia bonitateque Stationum, ut Festo placet, quas ὁρμὰς Græci vocant; sive ab impetu Læstrigonum, quos humana carne victitasse scribit Plinius: vel denique ab Hormo Amne, illic praeterlabente. Mamurrarum Urbem appellat Horatius, ut putat Vetus eius Commentator. Originem inde traxit Mamurrana Gens Romæ, qua natus Mamurra is, quem Carminibus suis proscindit Catullus. Læstrigonum quondam fuit Sedes, scribentibus Plinio, Solino, Symmacho; unde Læstrigoniam vocat Cicero ad Atticum: Domus Antiphates nominatur Silio libro VIII. Antiphates enim, Læstrigonum Rex, olim ibi imperasse perhibetur. Ἀλκινόου πόλεμα dicitur Straboni. Distabant ab Caieta Formia Stadia XL. ut Strabo notat. Ante ingressum inter sentes & spineta ruinæ adparent Sepulcrorum Veterum. Debellatis Campanis Romani in Præfectura formam Formiae reduxerunt; quum prius tamen municipium fuisset, atque Civitatis Jus cum Suffragii latione obtinuisset, uti docet Livius lib. XXXIX. Bello demum Civili, ut Fronti-nus auctor est, ab III-VIIIS C. Julio Cæsare Octaviano, M. Antonio & M. Aemilio Lepido inter Colonias Italiae militares Formiae fuerunt redactæ. Ab eo tempore sub Imp. semper propter cæli temperiem floruisse, constat ex Horatio, Martiale, aliisque Scriptoribus. Excisæ memorantur ab Saracenis anno MCCCCLVI, qua tempestate Episcopatum inde Cajetam transtulit, cum reliquiis Erasini Martyris, Gregorius IV. P. M. Legendus Blondus. Adscribam elegans Formiarum Encomium, quod apud Martialem libro X. Epigrammat. in quo plura Italiae loca nominantur: O temperata dulce Formiæ litus: Vos, quum severi fugit oppidum Martis, Et inquietas fessus exuit curas Apollinaris, omnibus locis præfert. Non ille sanita dulce Tibur uxoris, Nec Tusculanos, Algidosve secessus, Prancite nec sic, Antiumve miratur: Non blanda Circe, Dardaniusve Cajeta Desiderantur: nec Marica, nec Laris, Nec in Lucrina leta Salmacis vena: Hic summa leni stringitur Thetis vento:
units.tr: Pliny places Caieta under Formiae. Cicero, Tacitus, Pomponius Mela and Antoninus also use this name, as does Frontinus, who calls it a Roman colony. Strabo calls it Φορμίαι [Phormiai], and Ptolemy likewise Φορμίαι; the Antonine Itinerary has Formia. Strabo, Pliny and others show that it was once called Hormiae, either from the crowded and good anchorages (the stations which the Greeks call ὁρμὰς [hormas]), as Festus thinks, or from the onslaught of the Laestrygonians, whom Pliny says fed on human flesh, or finally from the river Hormus, which flows past there. Horace calls it the city of the Mamurrae, as his old commentator thinks. The Mamurrana family at Rome took its origin from here, and from it came Mamurra, whom Catullus tears apart in his poems. Pliny, Solinus and Symmachus write that the Laestrygonians once had their seat here, and for this reason Cicero, in his letter to Atticus, calls it Laestrygonia. Silius, in book 8, names it the home of Antiphates, for Antiphates, king of the Laestrygonians, is said to have once ruled there. Strabo calls it the city of Alcinous [Ἀλκινόου πόλεμα, Alkinoou polema]. Formia was forty stadia distant from Caieta, as Strabo notes. Before the entrance, among the brambles and thickets, the ruins of ancient tombs appear. After the Campanians were defeated, the Romans restored Formiae to the status of a prefecture; yet it had previously been a municipal town and had obtained Roman citizenship with the right to vote, as Livy shows in book 39. Finally, in the civil war, as Frontinus records, Formiae was made one of the military colonies of Italy by the triumvirs Gaius Julius Caesar Octavianus, Marcus Antonius and Marcus Aemilius Lepidus. From that time on, under the emperors, it always flourished because of the mildness of its climate, as is clear from Horace, Martial and other writers. It is recorded that it was destroyed by the Saracens in the year 956, at which time Pope Gregory IV transferred the bishopric from there to Gaeta, together with the relics of the martyr Erasinus. Blondus should be read. I shall add the elegant panegyric on Formiae, which is found in Martial's tenth book of epigrams, in which many places of Italy are named. Martial prefers this shore to all other places: "O pleasant coast of Formiae, you whom the weary Apollinaris, when he flees the town of stern Mars and lays aside his restless cares, prefers to all places. He does not admire sane Tibur, sweet to his wife, nor the retreats of Tusculum or Algidus, nor Praeneste or Antium; neither the flattering Circe nor Dardanian Caieta is missed, nor Marica, nor Laris, nor the happy Salmacis of Lucrinus. Here the sea's surface is stirred by a gentle wind:"

units.la: Nec languet ⌒Aequor: vera sed quies Ponti Pictam Phaselon adjuvante fert aura.
units.tr: The sea is not sluggish, but has the true calm of the deep, and the breeze, helping, carries the painted boat along.

units.la: & quæ sequuntur. Formianorum mentionem facit Basis Statuæ, litera absolutissima, quam, teste Martino Smectio, vidit & exscripsit Molæ Dionysius Harduinus:
units.tr: & what follows. The inscription on a statue base, a most complete letter, mentions the Formiani; Dionysius Harduinus saw and copied it at Mola, as Martin Smectius testifies:

units.la: IMP. CÆSARI. DIVI HADRIANI. FILIO. DIVI TRAIANI. PARTHICI. NEP DIVI. NERVÆ. PRONEPOTI T. ÆLIO. HADRIANO Antonino. AVG. PIO. PONT. MAX. TRIB. POT. XX. COS. IIII. P. P. FORMIANI. PVBLICE
units.tr: IMPERATOR CAESAR, son of the deified Hadrian, grandson of the deified Trajan, conqueror of the Parthians, great-grandson of the deified Nerva, Titus Aelius Hadrianus Antoninus Augustus Pius, Pontifex Maximus, holding tribunician power for the twentieth time, consul for the fourth time, Father of his Country: the Formians, at public expense.

units.la: Formianos Colles novit Horatius; Formianum Montem, Livius lib. xxxix. Vinum Formianum optimis adnumerat idem Horatius. Formianum, villa Ciceronis in Formianorum Agro, cuius frequens in Epistolis ad Atticum mentio: Hodie vulgo Ciceron. In eo tradit magnus Scriptor Lælium semper fere cum Scipione rusticari solitum: eosque, quoties huc ex Urbe, tamquam e vinculis, evolavissent, incredibiliter repuerascere solitos. Locus est peramœnus & perjucundus: hortis undique cultissimis consitus: in quo & veterum marmorum, & Ædificiorum, operumque amplissimorum vestigia passim videre licet.
units.tr: Horace knew the Formian hills, and Livy, book 39, the Formian mountain. Horace also counts Formian wine among the finest. Cicero's villa in the territory of Formiae, often mentioned in his letters to Atticus, is commonly called today Ciceron. In it the great writer tells that Laelius almost always spent his country leisure with Scipio, and that whenever they flew out from the city, as if released from chains, they grew incredibly young again. The place is very pleasant and delightful, planted all round with the most carefully tended gardens, where traces of ancient marbles, buildings and very large works can be seen everywhere.

units.la: Inter Cajetam & Formias Itrum est Castellum, & Mola. Itrum amœnis in collibus, qui oleis, vitibus, ficubus, aliisque fructiferis arboribus convestiti, conspicitur longe inter Montes extensum; morte inclutum Hippolyti Medicis Florentini, Ecclesiæ Romanæ Cardinalis. Blondus magno errore Lamuras vocat, Horatij versum perperam legens & intellegens. Itri meminit Pomponius Sabinus. Olim ⌒Atrium dictum ait Scipio Mazzella. Hodie Itro Castello.
units.tr: Between Gaeta and Formia lie the castle of Itri and Mola. Itri, seen far off, stretches among the mountains over pleasant hills clothed with olives, vines, figs and other fruit trees. It is famous for the death of Ippolito de' Medici, the Florentine, cardinal of the Roman Church. Blondus, through a great error, calls it Lamuras, reading and understanding Horace's line wrongly. Pomponius Sabinus mentions Itri. Scipio Mazzella says it was formerly called Atrium. Today it is Itro Castello.

units.la: Itro Mola distat P. M. v. via amœnissima, Hortis obsita, qui Citris, Limonibus, aliisque arboribus gravidi. Putant nonnulli Molam ex Formiarum ruinis crevisse: dictam ab Molarum frequentia: quas hic ex Montium radicibus profluentes continuo Aquæ versant: unde apud Tullium Mola Formiana. Longus & perelegans est Vicus ad Viam Appiam.
units.tr: Mola is five miles from Itro by a most pleasant road, lined with gardens rich in citrons, lemons and other trees. Some think Mola grew up from the ruins of Formiae and was named from the great number of mills (molae), which here, flowing down from the roots of the mountains, keep the water constantly turning; hence "Mola Formiana" in Tully. It is a long and very elegant village on the Appian Way.

units.la: Post Formias ponuntur apud Plinium Pyra: aliis Pyla scribuntur.
units.tr: After Formiae, Pliny places Pyra; others write Pyla.

units.la: Pylis (si quidem sic emendandum) succedunt apud eumdem Minturnæ: sic Tacito, Plinio, Melæ, Antonino; Μινтypнa Straboni vocantur; quæ Μίντουρνα Stephano, Menturna in Tabula Itineraria. Hodie Traietto, ut censent docti Viri. Alij aliter opinantur. Nardo Castro al Mar putatur: Sanfelicio, La Scafa del Garigliano. Sane ad Traiectum Antiquæ, quæcumque tandem habenda, Urbis vestigia conspiciuntur: inter alia Theatrum propemodum integrum: & sumtuosissimus Aquæductus. Liris opidum medium olim inter luebat, ut Plinius & Strabo volunt: hodie paullo sequior est situs. Traiectus in colle est: Minturnæ in Valle erant, sive planicie; quod ex Theatri & Aquæductuum, quorum memini, reliquus est palam. Ex Minturnarum ruinis Trajectum esse ædificatum, scribit etiam ad Ortelium Celsus Citradinus. Coloniam Populi Romani Minturnas ad Ostium Liris factam Livius auctor est libro x. addens Immunitatem accepisse ob cæli gravitatem & vitium. Concilium Minturnis generale Marcellinus Pontifex Maximus anno ccxcvii. habuisse legitur.
units.tr: After Pyla (if that is the correct reading) come Minturnae in the same author, so called by Tacitus, Pliny, Mela and Antoninus. Strabo calls them Μινturna [Μινturna], Stephanus Μίντουρνα [Mintourna], and the Tabula Itineraria Menturna. Today it is Traietto, as learned men think; others think otherwise. Nardo puts it at Castro al Mare, Sanfelicio at La Scafa del Garigliano. Certainly at old Traiectum, whatever city it was, traces of a town can be seen: among other things an almost intact theatre and a very sumptuous aqueduct. Pliny and Strabo say the Liris once flowed through the middle of the town; today the site lies somewhat lower. Traiectus is on a hill, whereas Minturnae stood in a valley or on a plain, as is plain from the remains of the theatre and aqueducts I have mentioned. Celso Citradino also writes, in his letter to Ortelius, that Trajectum was built from the ruins of Minturnae. Livy, book 10, records that the colony of the Roman People at Minturnae was founded at the mouth of the Liris, and adds that it received an exemption because of the heaviness and unhealthiness of the air. It is recorded that Pope Marcellinus held a general council at Minturnae in the year 297.

units.la: Juxta Minturnas Saracenos ab Christianis gravi pugna, cui Joannes x. P. M. & Albericius Tusciæ Marchio interfuerunt, victos & profligatos fuisse, Italiaque pulsos, memoriæ tradunt Blondus & Platina: exceptis Profugorum è prælio reliquis, quæ Garganum Montē occuparunt, in quo se diu postea tenuerunt, prædationibus & piratica vitam sustentantes. Castrum Traietti non ita pridem Prospero Columnæ cum ducatus Titulo donavit Ferdinandus, Aragonum Rex & Neapolitanorum. Minturnense Flumen, quod censendum, vide supra, ubi de Liri. Minturnensem Paludem habet Seneca Declamatione iii. inde Minturnæ, Palustres Horatio lib. i. Epist. v. In propinquis Minturnensium Paludibus Marium latitasse, quum inimicorum arma fugeret, memorant Livius lib. lxxvii. Plutarchus in eius Vita, Lucanus lib. ii. Juvenalis Satyra x. Valerius Maximus lib. viii. alij.
units.tr: Near Minturnae, Blondus and Platina report that the Saracens were defeated and routed by the Christians in a fierce battle, in which Pope John X and Alberic, Marquis of Tuscany, took part, and were driven out of Italy. The survivors of the battle who escaped occupied Mount Gargano, where they held out for a long time afterwards, living by plunder and piracy. Ferdinand, King of Aragon and of the Neapolitans, not long ago gave the castle of Traetto, with the title of duchy, to Prospero Colonna. For the Minturnian river, which must be considered, see above, where I spoke of the Liris. Seneca in Declamation 3 has the Minturnian marsh, whence Horace in Epistles i.5 calls the Minturnians "marshy." Livy, book 77, Plutarch in his Life of Marius, Lucan, book 2, Juvenal, Satire 10, and Valerius Maximus, book 8, and others record that Marius hid in the nearby Minturnian marshes when he fled from the weapons of his enemies.

units.la: Tertio deinde lapide iuxta ripam Liris Speninum est opidum: inde octavo Frata: hinc totidem Pons Corvi, Ponte Corvo: Fregella quondam, uti volunt Sigonius & Leander. Aldus in sua Orthographia putat ex Fregellarum reliquiis Ceperanum oppidulum esse extructum. Sunt, inter quos Ambrosius Leo, qui fuisse volunt, ubi nunc Atrittaldo dicuntur Straboni, cuius aevo vicus erat; olim Urbs nobilis ad Liris fluvium, teste Livio libro xxvi. Stephano, Fregellanum Antonino: Fregellam, Plinio. Coloniam factam docet Livius libro viii. Fregellas ob defectionem semel atque iterum dirutas ab Romanis, scribit idem lib. x & lx. De iis Silius lib. v. Hinc tristes miserae Fregellae. Et quae fumanti texere gigante Fregellae.
units.tr: At the third milestone along the bank of the Liris lies the town of Speninum; from there, at the eighth, Frata; from here, as many miles, Pons Corvi, now Ponte Corvo. Fregella was formerly here, as Sigonius and Leander think. Aldus, in his Orthography, thinks the little town of Ceperano was built from the remains of Fregellae. Some, among them Ambrosius Leo, want it to be where Atrittaldo now stands, which in Strabo's time was a village but was once a noted city on the Liris, as Livy testifies, book 26. Stephanus calls it Fregellanum, Antoninus Fregellam, Pliny Fregellas. Livy, book 8, shows that it was made a colony. The same writer, in books 10 and 60, says that Fregellae, having revolted once and again, was razed by the Romans. Silius, book 5, speaks of it: "Hence the sad, wretched Fregellae," and "which Fregellae, smoking, wove with its giant..."

units.la: Inclutae sunt M. Sextilius Fregellanus relponso, Senatui Romano pro xiix. Colonis Bello Punico ii. dato, de quo Livius. Hinc Fregellae, locus in Urbe, teste Festo, ab Fregellanis forte habitus, vel Fregellanorum Statio; ut Graecostasis, Graecorum, Ficulea, Ficuleatum.
units.tr: Marcus Sextilius of Fregellae is famous; he gave the Roman Senate the answer on behalf of the nineteen colonies in the Second Punic War, of which Livy writes. Hence "Fregellae," a place in the city which, according to Festus, was perhaps occupied by the men of Fregellae, or the station of the Fregellani; just as Graecostasis is the station of the Greeks, Ficulea that of the Ficuleans.

units.la: Extremum Latij facit Plinius Sinuessam: de qua dicendum in Campania.
units.tr: Plinius makes Sinuessa the farthest point of Latium; this is to be discussed under Campania.

units.la: Haec de Ora Latij maritima, deque quibusdam citra Lirim locis: antequam ad Mediterraneorum enarrationem veniam, committere inter se obiter decrevi Auctores, qui ordine quodam Littorales Latij Urbes commemorant: praepositurus Plinium, cum quod plenior ille ceteris, tum quod notatum ab ipso ordinem in superioribus praecipue fuerim sequutus. Sinuessa, extremum Laty. | Σινόεσσα, | ..... | Sinuessa, | Sinuessam ix Sinuessa ix | vide Campaniam,
units.tr: Having dealt with the maritime coast of Latium and some places on this side of the Liris, I have decided, before I come to the description of the inland places, to set side by side the authors who list the coastal cities of Latium in some order. I will put Pliny first, both because he is fuller than the others and because I have mainly followed the order he noted in the preceding passages. Pliny, Strabo, Ptolemy, Pomponius Mela, the Antonine Itinerary, the Tabula Peutingeriana, and the Vulgate Nomenclature: Ostia, Colonia: Ostia (Ω ςια [Ostia]), 16 miles from the City, Hostis, Hostia; Laurentum (Λαυρεντον [Laurenton]), Laurentum, 10 miles from Laurentum, 16 miles; Lavinium: to be read Lavinium, 6 miles; the temple of Jupiter Indiges: its remains survive near Fusano and nearby places, by the stream of the river Numicius; Ardea (Ἀρδέα [Ardea]), Ardea, which some write still keeps the name, S. Anastasia; Aphrodisium and Antium (Ἀφροδίσιον Ἄντιον [Aphrodision Antion]), Antium, beyond Neptunium, by others placed at Capo d'Anzio; Astura, a river and island (Στόεγας [Stoegas]), Astura, 17 miles, Stora, the Nymphaean river, now a little river Paulo Fiume; Clostra, Roman (Κλαισερα [Klaisera]), Clostris, 9 miles from Circeii; Circeium (Κιρκαῖον [Kirkaion]), Kirkaion Akra, Circeii, Circeios, 21 miles, Monte Circello, at the Turres, 4 miles; the Pomptine Marsh; the river Ufens (Ἀνφιδ... [Amphid...]), now Anzente; Tarracina or Anxur (Ταρρακίνα [Tarrakina]), Tarracina, 11 miles, Tarracina; Amyclae, ..... ; near Caluzam, a cave (Σπηλαῖα [Spelaia]), Sperlunga; Pineto; Lake Fundanus; Caieta (Καιάττα [Kaiatta]), Caieta, ..... ; Itro Castello; Mola, which is said to be from Formia, (Φορμίαι [Formiai], Φώρμαι [Phormai]), Formia, Formiae 13 miles, Formis 9 miles, the remains of Formiae seem to have grown; some read Pyra as Pyla; Minturna (Μιντοῦρναι [Mintournai]), Minturnas on the Liris, Minturnas 9 miles, Menturnu; Traiette Castello; Garigliano; Sinuessa, the farthest point of Latium (Σινόεσσα [Sinoessa]), Sinuessa, Sinuessam 9 miles, Sinuessa 9 miles; see Campania.

units.la: Mediterranea Latii loca perlustranti offert se xii. Roma lapide, Orientem versus Marinum, Columnarum Ditionis opidum, in colle situm. Fuit ibi quondam, ut nonnulli censent, Mariana Villa, quæ tamen alius Castrum, quod vernacule Zagarola.
units.tr: Travelling through the inland places of Latium, the first town you meet, twelve miles from Rome towards the east, is Marino, a town in the lordship of the Colonna family, situated on a hill. There was once a Villa of Marius there, as some think, but another writer calls it a castle, which in the vernacular is Zagarola.

units.la: Marino P. M. viii. antiqua Civitas in Tumulo Velitra: sic Livio passim & Suetorio in Octaviani Vita cap. i. atque lxxiv. dicitur Urbs: Οὐελίτραι Straboni lib. v. & Ptolemæo: Οὐελιτραι Dioni lib. xlv. Βέλιτρα Stephano: quæ vulgo Belitre: vel, ut alii scribunt. Belletri. Opidum vetustissimum Volscorum, in quo tamen pauca Antiquitatum nunc viluntur vestigia: alioquin amplum & populo satis frequens, Episcopatus fulgens dignitate. Venustissimi situs, jucundissimi prospectus: Mœnibus undique cinctum. Incolæ Livio & Plinio Veliterni: Velitrini, Suetonio in Augusto cap. xciv. ubi tamen quidam Codices Veliterni: Οὐελιτραῖοι Halicarnassæo. Coloniam ibi ductam notant idem Halicarnassæus lib. vii.
