Livius lib. ii. & Frontinus. De Rebus ab ipsis, vel contra ipsos gestis, legendi Dionysius lib. iii. vi. & vii. Livius cum alibi, tum lib. viii. & alij rerum Romanarum Scriptores. Extra Portam Fossæ sunt angustis foraminibus & in profundum amplæ, quales sunt, in quibus condi conservarique consueverunt frumenta. Juxta Velitras ostendebatur adhuc tempore Suetonij Nutrimentorum Augusti Locus, in avito Suburbano, permodicus & Cellæ Penuariæ instar. Ager Fructuum omnis generis nunc etiam ferax est, ut olim propter Urbis Romæ vicinitatem Villis & Hortis Nobilium expolitus. Velterna Vina laudat Plinius lib. xiv. cap. vi. Ea nunc degenerarunt: propter cruditatem austeritatemque coqui alieno solita.
units.tr: Eight miles from Marino is Velitra, an ancient city on a hill, so called by Livy throughout and by Suetonius in the Life of Octavian, chapters 1 and 74, where it is named Urbs. Strabo (book 5) and Ptolemy call it Οὐελίτραι [Velitrae], Dio (book 45) Οὐελιτραι, and Stephanus Βέλιτρα [Belitra]. Today it is commonly called Belitre, or, as others write, Belletri. It is a very ancient town of the Volsci, though few traces of its antiquities are now to be seen. Otherwise it is large and fairly populous, and it is distinguished by its bishopric. Its site is most beautiful and its views most pleasant, and it is surrounded on every side by walls. Livy and Pliny call its inhabitants Veliterni, and Suetonius in Augustus chapter 94 calls them Velitrini, though some manuscripts there read Veliterni. Halicarnassensis calls them Οὐελιτραῖοι [Veliterraioi]. Halicarnassensis (book 7), Livy (book 2) and Frontinus record that a colony was led there. For the deeds done by them, or against them, one should read Dionysius (books 3, 6 and 7), Livy in several places, including book 8, and the other writers of Roman history. Outside the Gate there are ditches with narrow openings and wide inside, of the kind in which grain was customarily stored and kept. Near Velitrae, in the time of Suetonius, was still shown the Place of Augustus's Supplies, on his ancestral suburban estate, very small and like a storeroom. The whole countryside is still fertile in every kind of produce, as it once was, when it was adorned with the villas and gardens of the nobles because of its nearness to the city of Rome. Pliny (book 14, chapter 6) praises the Velitern wines, but these have now degenerated; because of their harshness and roughness they are usually mixed with other wines.

units.la: Quinto Velitris lapide ad lævam est Cora, in monte sita: Livio lib. ii. Silio libro viii. Solino, aliisque memorata: Κοῖρα Straboni. Nomen hodie retinet. Coranos (qui Κόρυνοι Halicarnassæo lib. v. Iab Dardano Troiano scribunt ortos Plinius lib. iii. cap. v. & Solinus in Polyhist. Servius ad Virgilium Coram, Catilli Tiburtiique Fratrem, Cora Conditorem nominat.
units.tr: Five miles from Velitrae, on the left, is Cora, set on a mountain, mentioned by Livy (book 2), Silius (book 8), Solinus and others. Strabo calls it Κοῖρα [Koira]. It still keeps the name. Halicarnassensis (book 5) writes that the Coranians (Κόρυνοι [Koryni]) descend from Iasus, a Trojan Dardanian. Pliny (book 3, chapter 5) and Solinus in the Polyhistor, and Servius on Virgil, name Cora as the founder, the brother of Catillus and Tiburtus.

units.la: Itinere hinc ad Velitras Nemus occurrit infame Latrocinijs, spatio P M. vi. dein amœna planicie millium quinque ad Sermonettam, Castellum in Colle novi nominis, devenitur. Hoc justis Dominus ereptum, Filiæ impudicæ donavit Alexander vi. P. M. Putant quidam Sulmonem esse, opidum Latij, quod sine vestigijs interiisse scribit Plinius iii. cap. v. Locat idem in Sulmonensi Agro Fabianum: quod quo loco fuerit, nescio.
units.tr: On the road from here to Velitrae one comes to a grove notorious for robbers, six miles in extent. Then, after five miles over a pleasant plain, one reaches Sermoneta, a castle on a hill of recent name. Pope Alexander VI took this from its lawful lord and gave it to his shameless daughter. Some think it is Sulmo, a town of Latium, which Pliny (book 3, chapter 5) writes perished without a trace. The same writer places Fabianum in the territory of Sulmo, but where it was I do not know.

units.la: Infra Sermonettam Tabernæ quædam & Vegistia veterum Ædificiorum. Ea Trium Tabernarum esse putant docti Viri, quas memorant Cicero in Epistolis ad Atticum lib. ii. Antoninus, & Itineraria Tabula. Τρεῖς Ταβέρναι meminit Euangelista Lucas in Apostolorum Actis cap. ultimo. Tres Taberne in Baronj Annalibus est Cisterna, qui Vicus est in medio Appiæ Viæ, xxxvi. M. P. ab Urbe. Pighius glius in Hercule Prodicio putat circa Casas Novas fuisse, aut ipsas esse. Onuphrius in Chronic. Pontific. vocat Tres Tabernas, alias apud Nymphaм. Apud Tres Tabernas Severum Imperatorem ab Adversarijs occisum scribunt Eutropius, Zosimus, & alij.
units.tr: Below Sermoneta are some taverns and remains of old buildings. Learned men think these are the Three Taverns, which are mentioned by Cicero in his Letters to Atticus (book 2), by the Antonine Itinerary, and by the Itinerary Table. The Evangelist Luke mentions Τρεῖς Ταβέρναι [Treis Tabernai] in the last chapter of the Acts of the Apostles. In Baronius's Annals, Tres Tabernae is Cisterna, a village in the middle of the Appian Way, 36 miles from the City. Pighius, in Hercules Prodicius, thinks it was near Casas Novas, or is Casas Novas itself. Onuphrius in his Chronicle of the Popes calls it Tres Tabernas, elsewhere Nymphaeum. Eutropius, Zosimus and others write that the Emperor Severus was killed by his enemies at the Three Taverns.

units.la: Octodecim à Tribus Tabernis P. M. Forum Appy scribitur Antonino. Meminit eius & præter Horatium in Hodœporico, Lucas Euangelista loco, quem indicavi: putatur hodie ibi esse quibusdam Taberna Mamurti, alias L' Abbatia, nonnullis Fossa Nova, item Casa Nova.
units.tr: Eighteen miles from the Three Taverns is the Forum of Appius, as Antoninus writes. Horace in his Hodoeporicon mentions it, and so does Luke the Evangelist, in the passage I have indicated. Today some think it is Taverna Mamurti, others L'Abbatia, others Fossa Nova, and likewise Casa Nova.

units.la: Millia inde quinque occurrit editiore situm loco vetus Opidum Setia. Sic Livio, Virgilio aliisque Latinis: Σετία Ptolemæo, Σετια Straboni: quæ corrupte forte an Σετια Halicarnassæo: Σετα vulgo, vel Setchi. Latinorum opidum mediterraneum, Volsci adscriptum. Incolæ Setini Plinio, Setia Colonia vel Setina Vellejo & Frontino Setini Montes sunt apud Iuvenalem Sat. v. Vina Setina celebrant Strabo lib. v. Silius lib. viii. Plinius lib. xiv. cap. vi. & Martialis, qui & nonnihil de Situ: Pendula Pontinus quæ spectat Setia Campos, Exigua vetuli maiit ab Vrle cados.
units.tr: Five miles on, on higher ground, lies the old town of Setia. So Livy, Virgil and other Latin writers call it; Ptolemy calls it Σετία [Setia], Strabo Σετια [Setia], which is perhaps a corruption for Σετια of Halicarnassensis, but commonly Σετα [Seta], or Setchi. It is an inland town of the Latins, assigned to the Volsci. Its inhabitants are called Setini by Pliny; Velleius and Frontinus call it the colony of Setia or Setina. The Setine Mountains are mentioned by Juvenal (Satire 5). Strabo (book 5), Silius (book 8), Pliny (book 14, chapter 6) and Martial celebrate the Setine wines. Martial also says something of the site: "Pontine Setia, which looks down on the hanging fields, sends small jars of wine to the old man."

units.la: Monti enim altissimo est impolita. Inter Setiam & Casas Novas adparent in radice montis Veteris Ædificii ruinæ, in Circi modum factæ.
units.tr: For it is unbuilt on the very high mountain. Between Setia and Casas Novas, at the foot of the mountain, appear the ruins of an old building, made in the manner of a circus.

units.la: Setia Piperum M. P. distat quinque. Sic vernacule vocatur Opidum, quod Privernum Latinis: Πρίβερνον Ptolemæo: Πρίβερνον Straboni: Preivernum in nummo C. Hyptzi. Opidum nunc in aspertimo situm monte: olim in planicie duobus ab hodierno passuum millibus versus Anagniam, uti fundamenta docent & magnorum operum vestigia. Iuxta Ufentem fluvium locatur Sex. Pompeio Festo: vicina Samnitibus Livio: Privernum Vetus ab Germanis & Britonibus excisum, auctor est Blondus. Coloniæ Romanæ adscribentes Frontinus. Vetus Municipium & Præfectura ante fuit, scribente Festo. Incolæ Privernates Silio, Livio: alias: Πριβερνίνοι Straboni. Natalibus Camillæ Regina, quæ Turno contra Æneam auxilio fuit, celebratum apud Virgilium lib. xi. Æneid. De Rebus, quæ a Privernatibus gestæ, passim Livius, inter alia memorans lib. viii. Privernates, ab S. P. Q. R. rogatos, qualem Pacem maxime optarent perpetuam, si bona foret & honesta: breve tum si turpis & infida, respondisse. Extra opidum in discensu montis pulcherrimus Fons est.
units.tr: Piperno is five miles from Setia. That is what the town is called in the vernacular; in Latin it is Privernum, Πρίβερνον [Priverno] in Ptolemy, and Πρίβερνον [Priverno] in Strabo; Preivernum on a coin of C. Hyptzus. The town now stands on a very steep mountain, but formerly it lay on a plain two miles from the present site, towards Anagni, as its foundations and traces of great works show. Sextus Pompeius Festus places it beside the river Ufens; Livy calls it neighbouring the Samnites. Blondus is the authority that Old Privernum was destroyed by the Germans and Britons. Frontinus assigns it to the Roman colonies. Festus writes that it was formerly a municipium and a prefecture. Its inhabitants are the Privernates (Silius, Livy); elsewhere Strabo calls them Πριβερνίνοι [Privernoi]. Virgil (Aeneid book 11) celebrates Camilla, queen of the Privernates, who helped Turnus against Aeneas, and her birthplace. Livy, in many places and especially in book 8, records the deeds done by the Privernates. Among other things he tells how, when the Privernates were asked by the Senate and People of Rome what kind of peace they most wished for, lasting if it was good and honourable, or brief if it was shameful and faithless, they answered that... Outside the town, at the foot of the mountain, there is a very beautiful spring.

units.la: Locis deinde Piperno vicinus Opida Vicique reperiuntur, quæ vulgo Magienza: Rocca Gorgona: Rocca Secca, Thomæ Aquinatis instituto celebris. Hinc ad Sonninum millia quinque in alti montis vertice.
units.tr: Next, towns and villages neighbouring Piperno are found, which are commonly called Magienza, Rocca Gorgona, and Rocca Secca, famous for the teaching of Thomas Aquinas. From here it is five miles to Sonnino, on the summit of a high mountain.

units.la: Vlterius versus Vulturnum jamnunc non tendens, finitimos Romæ agros repeto. In ijs Alba: sic Latinis omnibus nominata: Ἄλβα item Græcis, id est, Ἀλβανά, ut inquit Halicarnassæus: Ἄλβη, Appiano. Nomen ab Alba Sue, quam cum Suculis triginta Æneæ in Italiam adpellenti volunt vitam. Conferendus præter alios Virgilius libro viii. Adeundi quoque Propertius lib. iii. Eleg. i. & Varra de LL. & de Re Rustica lib. ii. cap. iv. Longam cognominant Veteres Scriptores: ab Situ, ut loquitur Livius, porrectæ in dorso Vrbis. Sic ab altera eiusdem nominis Civitate, quæ in Marsis est, discernitur. Hodie Savello, si Leandro fides: si alias, Gandolfi, vel S. Gandolfo. Incolæ Albani, omnibus. Ἀλβανοὶ Græcis nominat Appianus. Conditor eius Ascanius, Æneæ filius, xxx post ædificatum Lavinium anno. Virgilius, libro, quem dixi: Iamque tibi ne vana putes hæc fingere somnum, Littoreis ingens inventa sub ilicibus Sus Triginta capitum fœtus enixa iacebit, Alba solo recubans, albi circum Vbera nati: Hic locus Vrbis erit: requies ea certa laborum Ex quo ter denis Vrbem redeuntibus annis Ascanius clari condet cognomine Albam.
units.tr: Not continuing further towards the Volturnus now, I return to the fields near Rome. Among them is Alba, so named by all the Latins; the Greeks also call it Ἄλβα [Alba], that is Ἀλβανά [Albana], as Halicarnassensis says, and Appian Ἄλβη [Albe]. It takes its name from the white sow, which the old writers say bore thirty young to Aeneas when he landed in Italy. Besides others, Virgil (book 8) should be consulted, and also Propertius (book 3, elegy 1), and Varro in On the Latin Language and On Farming (book 2, chapter 4). The old writers call it Longa, from its site, as Livy puts it, stretched along the ridge of the city. It is distinguished in this way from the other city of the same name, which is among the Marsi. Today it is Savelli, if we trust Leandro, or otherwise Gandolfi, or San Gandolfo. Its inhabitants are all called Albani. Appian calls them Ἀλβανοὶ [Albanoi]. Its founder was Ascanius, son of Aeneas, thirty years after Lavinium was built. Virgil, in the book I mentioned: "And now, lest you think these things are vain fancies of a dream, a huge sow will be found under the holm-oaks on the shore, lying down and giving birth to thirty young, white, lying round her white udders. This will be the site of the city, and there will be certain rest from your labours. When thrice ten years have returned, Ascanius will found a city, and will call it Alba by its famous name."

units.la: Confirmant Livius lib. i. & Dionysius libro i. Antiquit. Romanar. qui & inter initia condendæ Vrbis maximum accidisse prodigium narrat. Duodecimo ab Vrbe millario locatur apud Eutropium: decimo sexto, apud Appianum libro iii. Bellor. Civilium. Sub Monte Albano, ut Livius; in Via Appia, ut Appianus innuit lib. 1. Bel. Civil. Inter Montem & Lacum scribitur Halicarnassæo; natura ipsa, tamquam muro rutilissimo munita. Habuisse videtur ad numerum Porcellorum xxx. in ambitu Turres. Respicit eo Cassandra Lycophronis: Κλυοί δὲ χώρᾳν ἐν πέντε βοεΐζεων Τ᾽ πὶρ Λαῦνας Δαυνίας τ᾽ ὠκισμένων, Πύργως τρικάρηνοι ἰζαρβημέρους γενάς Σύες κελαινῆς, ὧν ἀπ᾽ Ἰδαίων λεῶν Καὶ Ἀδρεδαίων, ἐκ πέτρων παιδ᾽ λώσει) Τὸν βωμῶν Θρίσσηλον ἐν πύλοις κάπρων,
units.tr: Livy (book 1) and Dionysius (book 1 of the Roman Antiquities) confirm this, and Dionysius also tells of a very great portent that happened at the beginning of the founding of the City. Eutropius places it twelve miles from the City; Appian (book 3 of the Civil Wars) sixteen. Under Mount Albanus, as Livy says; on the Appian Way, as Appian hints (book 1 of the Civil Wars). Halicarnassensis writes that it lay between the mountain and the lake, fortified by nature itself as with a very red wall. It seems to have had about thirty towers in its circuit, to match the number of the sow's piglets. Lycophron's Cassandra alludes to this: "...hear of the land of the black sows, inhabited about Launae and Daunian... three-headed towers, the pigs of the dark sow, from whom... " [Σύες κελαινῆς, Sues kelainēs]. Lycophron alone mentions the black sow here; all the Albans name the sow from which the city takes its name.

units.la: Albani Suem, unde nomen Urbi, nominant omnes: unus Lycophron Σύες κελαινῆς hic meminit. Condita tantis opum & fortunæ incrementis auxit, ut xxx. Oppidorum Latinorum, inter quæ ipsa Roma fuerit, Colonis emissis, Mater: & Reges habuerit xv. Euryleonem Ascanium, Silvium, Æneam, Latinum, Albam Capetum, Capyn, Calpetum, Tiberinum, Agrippam, Alladium, Aventinum, Procam, Amulium, Numitorem: Silvios omnes ab Secundo Rege, qui in Silvis natus erat, cognominatos; qui quales fuerint, quotque annos regnarunt, prolixe tradit Halicarnassæus lib. 1. Consulendus & Livius lib. 1. Sub his Regibus, paucisque, qui sequuti, Dictatoribus, quum supra quadringentos annos floruisset Alba, tandem Senatus Romani Tullique Hostilij Romanorum Regis decreto propter Metij Suffetij proditionem, fuit excisa, Incolis Romam in Cœlium montem migrare iussis. Restauratam iterum ab Henrico iii. Imperatore Augusto everterunt Romani anno cIↄCLXVIII. temporibus Alexandri iii. P. M. uti Blondus scribit lib. xv. Historiarum. Nunc plane desolata jacet, nisi quod Savellam in angulo quodam Castellum modicum ex veteris urbis ruinis aedificatum putetur: unde nobilis Romæ Savellorum Familia, si Blondo credendum. Quanta certe eius olim fuerit magnitudo, Moles loquuntur & rudera. De Ivis Vinifque Albanis Plinius lib. xiiii. natur. Histor. Martialis, & alij.
units.tr: All writers name the Alban Sow, from which the city took its name; only Lycophron mentions it here [Σύες κελαινῆς]. Alba grew so great in wealth and fortune that it sent out colonies to thirty Latin towns, Rome itself among them, and so became their mother city. It had fifteen kings: Euryleon, Ascanius, Silvius, Aeneas, Latinus, Alba, Capetus, Capys, Calpetus, Tiberinus, Agrippa, Alladius, Aventinus, Procas, Amulius and Numitor. All the Silvii were so named after the second king, who was born in the woods. Halicarnassus gives a full account of who they were and how many years each reigned (Book 1), and Livy (Book 1) should also be consulted. Under these kings and a few dictators who followed them, Alba had flourished for more than four hundred years. Then, by decree of the Roman Senate and of Tullus Hostilius, king of the Romans, it was finally destroyed because of the treachery of Metius Suffetius, and its inhabitants were ordered to move to Rome, to the Caelian hill. Henry III restored it, but the Romans overthrew it again in the year 1168, in the time of Pope Alexander III, as Blondus writes in Book 15 of his Histories. Now it lies entirely desolate, except that Savella, a small castle built in a corner of the old city from its ruins, is thought to be it; and from this, Blondus believes, came the noble Savelli family of Rome. What its greatness once was, its mounds and ruins indeed bear witness. On the Alban figs and wines see Pliny, Natural History Book 14, Martial, and others.

units.la: Haud procul Alba fuit, si recte metior, Roboraria, cuius mentio apud Antoninum, cui illa inter Fidenas & Urbem.
units.tr: Not far from Alba, if I measure correctly, was Roboraria, which Antoninus mentions, placing it between Fidenae and the City.

units.la: Ulterius in monticulo Civitas est Aricia: Sic Virgilio lib. vii. Æneid. Horatio lib. 1. Satyra v. Livio passim, Ciceroni, Tacito lib. xx. Plinio, aliis: Ἀρίκια Appiano lib. 1. Straboni, Ptolemæo & Stephano dicta: quæ Rizza vel La Riccia vulgo. Colonia est Romana, Floro ex Livij Epitoma libri xxc. Eam autem conditionem induit ex antiquo Municipio: quo statu eius meminerunt Festus, Livius lib. viii. & Velleius lib. 1. Conditam ab Archilogo Siculo tradit ex Callio Hemina Solinus: denominatam ab Aricia, Hippolyti coniuge, addunt alij xx. M. P. ab Urbe locat vetus Horatij interpres: clx. Stadus, Strabo: cxx. Dionysius Halicarnassus libro vi. confirmante Philostrato lib. iv. de Vita Apollonij. Incolæ Arcini vocantur antiquis Scriptoribus. Dionysius libro iiii. Turnum Herdeontum Aricinum, Virum militarem & facundum, nominat. De Aricinorum Gestis Dionysius cum alibi, tum lib. vii. Livius libro xviii. & alij. Nostra memoria parum frequentatur. Aricinam Brassicam, ut utilissimam, commendat Plinius libro xix. nat. hist cap. vii. Martialis eiusdem agri Porros celebrat. Nemoralis Aricia cognominatur ab Nemore ingenti, quod Urbi vicinum erat. In eo Vitellium Imperatorem libentissime versari solitum, notat libro xix. Cornelius Tacitus. Nemus hoc dicatum erat Diana: de cuius nibi Sacris, Sacerdote, Fano, & aliis sic scribit Strabo libro v. Τὸ δὲ Ἀρτεμίσιον ἐν ἁλσὶ ἀρχαῖον, ὡς τὸ Νέμορον, ἐκ τῶν ὑπὸ Ἀρικίας ἀναβαίνοντα, ὡς τ᾽ ἁλ᾽ Ἀρεκινὸν τὸ ἱερὸν. Ἀλ-
units.tr: Further on, on a little hill, is the town of Aricia. So it is called by Virgil (Aeneid Book 7), Horace (Satires Book 1, satire 5), Livy passim, Cicero, Tacitus (Book 20), Pliny, and others; by Appian (Book 1), Strabo, Ptolemy and Stephanus it is called Ἀρίκια [Ἀρίκια]. Today it is commonly called Rizza or La Riccia. It is a Roman colony, as Florus says from the Epitome of Livy, Book 90. It took that status from an older municipality, whose condition Festus, Livy (Book 8) and Velleius (Book 1) mention. Solinus, following Callias of Hemina, says it was founded by the Sicilian Archilochus; others add that it was named after Aricia, the wife of Hippolytus. The old commentator on Horace puts it twenty miles from the City; Strabo gives 160 stadia, and Dionysius of Halicarnassus (Book 6), supported by Philostratus (Book 4, On the Life of Apollonius), gives 120. Its inhabitants are called Arcini by ancient writers. Dionysius (Book 4) names Turnus Herdeonius of Aricia, a warlike and eloquent man. Dionysius, here and in Book 7, Livy (Book 18), and others write of the deeds of the Aricini. In our time it is little visited. Pliny (Natural History Book 19, ch. 7) commends the Aricine cabbage as very useful, and Martial praises the leeks of the same district. It is called Nemoralis Aricia from the great grove near the City. Tacitus (Book 19) notes that the Emperor Vitellius liked to spend his time there. This grove was dedicated to Diana, and Strabo (Book 5) writes thus of her rites, priest, temple and other things: "The Artemision in the grove is ancient, like the Nemus, rising from the places above Aricia, as also the sacred Aricinum [Τὸ δὲ Ἀρτεμίσιον ἐν ἄλσει ἀρχαῖον, ὡς τὸ Νέμορον, ἐκ τῶν ὑπὸ Ἀρικίας ἀναβαίνοντα]."

units.la: γίλ(ο) δ᾽ ἐκ ἀφιερώματα τὰ Ταυρόπολα. ἡ γὰρ ἡ Βασιλεῶν κρατεῖ ἡ Σκυθίων ἀπὸ τὸ ἱερὸν ἱδρῶ. Καθίσαντες γὰρ ἱερεύς, ἐ ἥμηθεὶς αὐτοὺς ἔ ἱεραμβὰν ἀπέπεμπεν, δέκα πηὺς ἄνδρ' ἐξιφέρης ἐν ἱερὸν ἐκ δεισοχώρων πᾶς ὀλιγίας, ἐπιμ.ρ. ἀμίνας. Τὸ δὲ ἱερὸν ἐν ἀλσοῖ: ἀπόκειται δὲ λίμνη πλαγίζουσα. κυκλῷ δ᾽ ἐρεψὴ συνεχὴς ἐξεῖνα. Καὶ μία ὑψηλὴ, καὶ τὸ ἱερὸν καὶ τὸ ὕδωρ ἐπλαμβάνοντα ἐκ κοίλων πάντων καὶ βαθεῖ: & quæ sequuntur de Fontibus. Sic etiam Servius ad illud Virgilij vii. Æneidos,
units.tr: "…not as offerings, the Tauropolia [Ταυρόπολα]. For the kingdom of the Scythians is held by the one who… from the sacred place. For when they had installed the priest, whoever he was, he sent him off as a fugitive, having first been a man who slew with the sword; and they say that ten men once came from the country with arms, in the sacred place… The temple lies in a grove; a lake lies beside it, and around it a continuous hedge… and one high place, and the temple and the water are set among hollows and deep places." And what follows about the springs. In the same way Servius, on that line of Virgil's Aeneid Book 7…

units.la: ——Lætes Arbor opaca
units.tr: ——Lush, shady tree

units.la: Aureus,
units.tr: Golden,

units.la: Licet in hac ramo, inquit, qui de Sacris Proserpinæ scripsisse dicuntur, quidam esse Mysterium adfirmant, publica tamen opinio hoc habet: Orestes post occisum Regem Thoantem
units.tr: Although some say that in this branch, which is said to have been written about the rites of Proserpina, there is a mystery, the common opinion holds this: Orestes, after killing King Thoas

units.la: iii in Regione Taurica, cum Sorore Iphigenia fuit, & Diana Simulacrum inde sublatum haud longe ab Aricia collocavit. In huius Templo post mutatum ritum Sacrificiorum fuit Arbor quaedam, de qua ramus infringi non licebat. Videbatur autem fugitivus potestas, ut si quis eximde ramum potuisset auferre, monomachia cum fugitivo eius templi Sacerdote dimicaret. Nam fugitivum tum erat Sacerdos ad priscam imaginem fuga. Dimicandi autem dabatur facultas, quasi ad priscum Sacrificii reparationem. Qui Aegyptius, ut ait Strabo, Sacerdotem Nemorensis, Fugitivus Servus: Latinus propriò vocabulo Rex Nemorensis dicebatur. Is Sacerdotem Regnum tenuit per obtinebat, dum vertente anno fortior aliquis superveniens cum pugna superaret; qualem Caius Caligula ei, qui jam multos annos Sacerdotio praefuerat, tulisse male legitur apud Suetonium in eius Vita cap. xxxv. Respicit eo Ovidius lib. iii. Fastor.
units.tr: III in the Taurian region, was with his sister Iphigenia, and placed the image of Diana, taken from there, not far from Aricia. In her temple, after the rite of sacrifices was changed, there was a certain tree, from which it was not allowed to break a branch. It was thought that whoever could take a branch from it had the right to fight in single combat with the runaway priest of that temple. For the priest then stood as a runaway, in memory of the ancient image of flight. The chance to fight was given as if to restore the ancient sacrifice. This Egyptian, as Strabo says, was the priest of Nemi, a runaway slave; in Latin he was properly called the King of Nemi. He held the priesthood and kept it until, as the year turned, some stronger man came along and defeated him in combat. Suetonius, in his Life (ch. 35), reads that Gaius Caligula was angry at such a man, who had already governed the priesthood for many years. Ovid, Fasti Book 3, alludes to this:

units.la: Regna tenent fortes manibus, pedibusque fugaces: Et periit exemplo patrimodo qualibet suo.
units.tr: Strong men hold the kingdom with their hands, and runaways with their feet; and one perishes by the same example as his predecessor.

units.la: Meminit etiam Lacus Ariciae idem Ovidius lib. Fastorum iv. Trivia Lacus est Virgilio lib. vii. Speculum Dianae Servio ibidem dicitur; Pappelyi Lacus Statio libro iii. Silvarum; Diana Stagnum Ovidio lib. iii. F. Ibid. & lib. xiiii. Metamorph. Hodie, ut vult Erythraeus, Lago di Nemi. Distat ab Aricia circiter mi. M. P.
units.tr: The same Ovid also mentions the Lake of Aricia, in Fasti Book 4. The Trivia Lake is named by Virgil in Aeneid Book 7; Servius on that passage calls it the Mirror of Diana; Statius (Silvae Book 3) calls it Pappelyus Lake; Ovid (Fasti Book 3 and Metamorphoses Book 14) calls it Diana's Pool. Today, as Erythraeus holds, it is Lago di Nemi. It lies about eight miles from Aricia.

units.la: Vltra Ariciam versus Meridiem est Lanuvium, cum Lavinio apud Graecos Latinosque Scriptores confundi solitum. Aliud enim Lavinium, de quo in Lat. Littoralibus diximus, aliud Lanuvium, cuius hic institutur delineatio. De utriusque differentia conferendi Synonymi in Livii librum vii. Hermolaus Barbarus in Plinii librum iii. Vitruvius de Familiis, ubi de Papia Gente, Simeo Botius in Epistolis ad Atticum, & alij. Illud certum, ubicumque mentio fiat Junonis Sospitae, cum adiecto Urbis nomine, semper Lanuvium esse ponendum. Aelianus libro Animalium xi. cap. vi. Urbem, de qua agimus, Aaxvior vocat, atque cum merito Matrem primariam Urbis Romae posse dici; errore duplici, in Nomine & Historia. Aaxeior enim scribendum erat, quod tamen non Matrem quasi Romae, sed Lanuvium. Legitur Lanuvium apud Antoninum, sed Lavinium ibi restituendum docent cum itineris ratio, tum Itineraria Tabula cum Antonino commutata. Lanuvium in Marmoribus esse testis est v. cl. Abrahamus Ortelius. Lavino male est apud Silium Italicum lib. xii. pro Lavino, vel Lanuvio. Ego etiam Lanuvinos legi in Balte marmorea, quae ex Vico Corocollo inter Gabios Tiburtinosque anno cIↄ Iↄ xlix cum aliis ad vectio, hodie in Vinea servatur Cardinalis Carpentensis, sic in fronte habens:
units.tr: Beyond Aricia, toward the south, is Lanuvium, which Greek and Latin writers have often confused with Lavinium. There is one Lavinium, of which we spoke in the Littoral Latium, and another Lanuvium, whose description is undertaken here. For the difference between the two, compare the commentaries on Livy Book 7 by Hermolaus Barbarus on Pliny Book 3, Vitruvius on families (where he speaks of the Papian clan), Simeon Bothius on the Letters to Atticus, and others. One thing is certain: wherever mention is made of Juno Sospita with the name of the city added, it must always be read as Lanuvium. Aelian (Animals Book 11, ch. 6) calls the city of which we are speaking Λαννούιον [Lanuvium], and rightly says it could be called the chief mother of the city of Rome; but this involves a double error, in the name and in the history. The Greek should have been written Λανούιον [Lanuvion], which refers not to Rome but to Lanuvium. Lanuvium is read in Antoninus, but the route and the Itinerary Table, which agrees with Antoninus, show that Lavinium should be restored there. That the name is Lanuvium on the marbles is attested by the very learned Abraham Ortelius. In Silius Italicus Book 12 the reading "Lavinum" is wrong, for "Lavinium" or "Lanuvium". I myself have also read Lanuvini on a marble tablet, which was found in the Vicus Corocollo between Gabii and Tibur in the year 1549, together with others, and is now kept in the vineyard of the Cardinal of Carpentras, bearing on its front this inscription:

units.la: C. CÆSONIO. C. F. QVIR. MACRO. RVFINIANO
units.tr: To Gaius Caesonius Macer Rufinianus, son of Gaius, of the Quirine tribe

units.la: CONSVLARI. SODALI. AVGVSTALI. COMITI. IMP. SEVERI. ALEXANDRI. AVG. CVR. R. P. LANIVINOR.
units.tr: Consul, sodalis of the Augustales, companion of the Emperor Severus Alexander Augustus, curator of the Lanuvians' public affairs.

units.la: & quae ibi sequuntur. Populus etiam Lanuvinus nominari videtur in Fragmento Lapidis, quod hodie eo loco:
units.tr: "...and whatever follows there." A Lanuvian people is also seen to be named on a fragment of stone that is today in that place:

units.la: ANI. F. AIANI ICI NEP NERVA. PRONEP O. HADRIANO ONINO. AVG. PIO MAXVMO. TRIBVN AT. II. COS. II. P P. ES POPVLVSQVE VINVS VETERES
units.tr: "...Ani son of Aianus, great-grandson of Nerva, of Hadrian Antoninus Augustus Pius Maximus, tribune for the second time, consul for the second time, father of the fatherland. And the people and the old Lanuvians..."

units.la: Hodie ex Blondi, Leandri, Celsique Citradini mente Indivina cc. plus minus Stadiis, hoc est xxv. M. P. ab Urbe fuisse constat ex libro Diodori xiiii. ubi ait Marcium: Locum sic dictum, haud procul hinc, tectè Livio libro v., tondem Roma distare. Τ ἐπὶ ἠξὲ ο αυτὸς (inquit Strabo, loquens de Aricia) ἐπὶ μὲν Λαυνιον, πόλις ἐμαυτῷ, ἐν ᾗ ἐστὶ ἐπὶ Ἀπιστίας ὁδὸς. Legendum omnino Λαυνιον vel Λανυσιον. Ab Lanuvio nuvio ἐωσᾶ, inquit idem, ἐν Ἰωλαπᾶ ἰσι, ἡ τὴ Ἀλβον. Lanuvij Templum fuisse Junonis Sospitæ prodit memoriæ, præter Plinium, Livius multis locis. In eo vexilla erant Lanuvinorum, quæ sanguine tudavisse, tradit idem Plinius lib. xx. natur. Historiæ: notans etiam libro xxxv. cap. 111. Lanuvij pictos fuisse cominus nudos Atlantem & Helenam, excellentissima forma. Lanuvium inter Municipia censetur apud Livium libro v111. & Sex. Pompeium Festum in Libris de Verb. significat. Meminit etiam, ut Municipy, Cicero pro Murena. Postea ex Municipio Coloniam ab Cæsare dictatore factam, indicat Frontinus M. S. apud quem in vulgatis scribitur Lanuvium. Nam id in Lauro-Lavinio paullo ante delineatum fuerat. Ortam Lanuvio Gentem Murenarum Patriciam memorat Cicero in oratione, quam dixi.
units.tr: Lanuvium is today said, on the authority of Blondus, Leander and Celsus Citradinus, to lie about 200 stadia, that is 25 miles, from the City, as Diodorus in book 14 shows, where he says Marcius... The place so named, not far from here, is at last a distance from Rome, as Livy says in book 5. Strabo, speaking of Aricia, says: "on the one hand to Lanuvium, a city, in which is the road of Appia..." [Ἐπὶ μὲν Λανούιον, πόλις ἐμαυτῷ, ἐν ᾗ ἐστὶ ἐπὶ Ἀππίας ὁδός]. Undoubtedly one should read Λανούιον or Λανυσιον. Strabo says that from Lanuvium... [Λανούιον]. Livy and Pliny, among others, record that there was a temple of Juno Sospita at Lanuvium. In it were the standards of the Lanuvians, which Pliny in book 20 of the Natural History says were dyed with blood; in book 35, chapter 111, he also notes that at Lanuvium there were paintings of Atlas and Helen, very beautiful and nearly nude. Lanuvium is counted among the municipalities by Livy in book 8, and by Sextus Pompeius Festus in his books On the Meaning of Words. Cicero, in the speech for Murena, also mentions it as a municipality. Frontinus, in a manuscript quoted, shows that it was afterwards made a colony from a municipality by Caesar the dictator, though in the printed texts it is written Lanuvium. For that name had been sketched a little earlier in Lauro-Lavinium. Cicero, in the speech I mentioned, records that the patrician family of the Murenae sprang from Lanuvium.

units.la: Appia relicta, meditullium Latij petens, ut sensim ad Hernicorum agros deveniam, Viam adeo jamnunc Latinam. Ea, decimo ab urbe Lapide, fundamenta inveniuntur Columna Opidi; a quo magnifica Romæ Columnarum Familia. Livio lib. 11. Columen videtur appellari.
units.tr: Leaving the Appian Way and making for the middle of Latium, so that I may gradually reach the lands of the Hernici, I now come to the Latin Way. At the tenth milestone from the city are found the foundations of the town of Columna, from which the magnificent Roman family of the Columnae takes its name. In Livy, book 2, it seems to be called Columen.

units.la: Fuerunt haud procul Columna Bovillæ, de quibus Persius Satyra vi. & Martialis lib. 11. epig. vi., pauper Vicus, ad quem inter sectus est ab Milone Clodius, ut scribit Asconius Paedianus; sic dictus a Boum multitudine, quasi Boum villa, ubi gentes multi stipem mendicabant. De Bovillis veteres Glossæ ad vi. Persij Satyram. Hinc forte Bovillianus Fundus apud Ciceronem in Epist. ad Q. Fratrem. Aliæ Bovillæ nobiliores erant in Latio ad Lirim, de quibus suo loco. Inter Bovillas & Ariciam erat Virbii Clivus, quatuor ab Urbe Millibus: de quo Veteres, quas dixi, Glossæ, Quatuor millibus, inquiunt, ab Urbe est Virbii Clivus, qua iter est ad Ariciam & ad Nemus Dianæ, ubi Virbius colitur, id est, Hippolytus, quod bis in vitam prolatus sit. Nota autem apud Virgilium Fabula est. Consulendus & Ovidius vi. Fastorum, cuius & illud Fastorum 111. Hic Latet Hippolytus furiis diserptus equorum; Unde Nemus nullis illud adiitur equis.
units.tr: Not far from there were Bovillae, the Columna Bovillae, of which Persius (Satire 6) and Martial (book 11, epigram 6) speak. It was a poor village, near which Clodius was killed by Milo, as Asconius Pedianus writes. It was so called from the great number of oxen, as if it were the villa of oxen, where many beggars begged for alms. The old glosses on Persius, Satire 6, speak of Bovillae. Hence perhaps the Bovillian farm in Cicero's letter to his brother Quintus. There were other, more famous Bovillae in Latium by the Liris, which I will discuss in their place. Between Bovillae and Aricia lay the Slope of Virbius, four thousand paces from the City. The old glosses I mentioned say of it: "Four miles from the City is the Slope of Virbius, where the road goes to Aricia and to the Grove of Diana, where Virbius is worshipped, that is Hippolytus, because he was brought back to life twice." The story is well known from Virgil. Ovid, Fasti book 6, should also be consulted, and Fasti book 3, where he says: "Here lies Hippolytus, torn apart by the frenzy of his horses; hence that grove is approached by no horses."

units.la: Loquitur de Nemore Vallis Aricinæ.
units.tr: He speaks of the Grove of the Valley of Aricia.

units.la: Incipit co tractu Nemus Algidum; de quo ante. Supra illud in monte cognomine, xi1. ab Urbe Lapide, ut notat Eutropius libro 1. conspicitur Arx Papalis, vulgo Rocca del Papa: ubi quondam, ut viri docti volunt, Algidum; sic dictum ab situ loci, perpetuis cœli frigoribus propter altitudinem algentis. Meminerunt Algidi Horatius, Iape Livius, Dionysius Halicarnassæus, Silius, alij. Ἀλγίδον Strabo & Dionysio; Stephano Ἀλγιδῶν dicitur: Algedon Procopio libro 111. Rerum Gothicarum. Male legitur apud Diodorum Siculum lib. xi1. Λαγαεῖω pro Ἀλγιδῳ, in Historia Virgilij & Filiæ ab ipso occisæ.
units.tr: Here begins the Algidus grove, which I discussed earlier. Above it, on the mountain of the same name, twelve miles from the City, as Eutropius notes in book 1, can be seen the Papal Citadel, commonly called the Rocca del Papa. There, as learned men think, once lay Algidum, so named from the site, since the place was always cold and chilled by its altitude. Algidum is mentioned by Horace, Livy, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Silius and others. Strabo and Dionysius call it Ἀλγίδον; Stephanus calls it Ἀλγιδῶν; Procopius in book 3 of his Gothic History calls it Algedon. Diodorus Siculus in book 14 wrongly reads Λαγαεῖω for Ἀλγιδῷ in the story of Virgil and of the daughter he killed himself.

units.la: In Hernicis, de quibus initio huius capitis dixi, est, ut notant Livius lib. ix. Strabo libro v. & Macrobius libro v. Saturnal. Anagnia. Sic cum aliis, tum Livio variis Locis, Tacito libro xix. Ciceroni, Silio libro v. & alibi, Frontino, cui Colonia est, Antonino; Ἀναγνία Strabono & Ptolemæo vocatur; Anagnium Itinerariæ Tabulæ; quæ Anagna vulgo. Incolæ Anagnini Livio & alijs: Plinio item in Prima Italiæ Regione; & Bati confracta, quæ in ipso Opido, Parieti domus privatæ ad S. Paullum inserta. πόλις ἀξιολόγος, Strabono: Dives, Virgilio, ad quem Servius notat, Anagniam Divitem appellari, vel quod perfacunda sit, vel ad historiæ confirmationem. In ea enim Antonium, Augusti Sororem Fulviam contempta, Cleopatraque in Uxorem accepta, nummum perculsi iniisse. Muros & Portam Anagniæ fulmine percullam scribit Livius lib. xxvi1. alio loco, Terram ante Portam eiusdem Urbis iactam sine ullo ignis alimento arsisse; item lib. x1 v. Terra quandoque ad eamdem urbem pluisse. Auctor est Plinius C. Septimulium, Graccho peramicum, Anagnia progenitum. Octavy Felicis, Anagnini, mentio in fragmento Tabellæ marmoreæ, quæ in hortis Euryali Rufini ad Bulla Gallica. Varios genuit Pontifices: inter eos Innocentium 111. Gregorium ix. Alexandrum iv. Bonifacium viii. Cardinales insuper multos, Episcopos, aliosque præclaros viros. Patria quoque hæc Ioannis Anagnini, Bononiensis Archidiaconi, & Commentatoris Legum Pontificiarum, maximeque Decretalium: qui anno MCCCCLVII. Bononiæ fato concessit. Hodie, licet Episcopatus dignitate fulgens, semidiruta tamen & deiohata jacet: civilibus & intestinis odijs maxime Vsurtur inde, quæ vulgo Nota, Turtio, Prose, Vico, Rippe, Porcigliano, Trevo & Fettino Latine scribentibus Nota, Turrtium, Profeum, Vicus, Ripa, Porcilianum, Trevum, & Fettinum.
units.tr: Among the Hernici, of whom I spoke at the beginning of this chapter, lies Anagnia, as Livy in book 9, Strabo in book 5 and Macrobius in book 5 of the Saturnalia note. It is so named by Livy in many places and by Tacitus in book 19, by Cicero, by Silius in book 5 and elsewhere, by Frontinus, to whom it is a colony, and by Antoninus. Strabo and Ptolemy call it Ἀναγνία; the Itinerary Table calls it Anagnium; commonly it is Anagni. Its inhabitants are called Anagnini by Livy and others, and by Pliny in the first region of Italy. A broken Roman inscription, now set into the wall of a private house at the Church of St Paul in the town itself, also names the city. Strabo calls it a notable city [πόλις ἀξιολόγος]; Virgil calls it Dives (rich), on which Servius remarks that Anagnia is called rich either because it is very pleasant or to confirm the history. For in it Antony, having scorned Augustus's sister Fulvia, took Cleopatra as his wife and was struck from his command of the coinage. Livy in book 27 writes that the walls and gate of Anagnia were struck by lightning; elsewhere he says that earth thrown before the gate of the same city burned without any fuel to feed the fire; and in book 45 that it once rained earth on the same city. Pliny records that Gaius Septimulius, very close to Gracchus, was born at Anagnia. The name of Octavius Felix of Anagni is mentioned in a fragment of a marble tablet found in the gardens of Euryalus Rufinus at Bulla Gallica. The town produced several popes: among them Innocent III, Gregory IX, Alexander IV and Boniface VIII; also many cardinals, bishops and other distinguished men. It was also the homeland of John of Anagni, archdeacon of Bologna and commentator on the laws of the Popes, and especially on the Decretals, who died at Bologna in 1357. Today, although it shines with the dignity of a bishopric, it lies half ruined and deserted; it is especially harassed by civil and internal hatreds. From there, the places commonly called Nota, Torcio, Prosa, Vico, Ripa, Porcigliano, Trevi and Fettino, which Latin writers call Nota, Turtium, Profeum, Vicus, Ripa, Porcilianum, Trevum and Fettinum, are held in turn.

units.la: Deinde repetita via, medio in Nemore Algido reliƈa, Valmontonium Castellum, vulgo Val-montono, inde colle cernitur. Labicum Virgilio: ut infra videbimus; Silio lib. v, viii, xiii & aliis. Λαβικὸν Straboni. Huc pertinet illud principis Poetæ libro vii Æneidos: Et Sacrana Acies, & pilli Scuta Labici.
units.tr: Then, taking the road back, through the middle of the Algidus grove that was left, the castle of Valmontone, commonly Valmontono, can be seen from the hill. Labicum is mentioned by Virgil, as we will see below, and by Silius in books 5, 8 and 13 and elsewhere. Straboo calls it Λαβικόν. To this place belongs the passage of the prince of poets in book 7 of the Aeneid: "And the Sacranian host, and the shields of Labicum with their crests."

units.la: Ad quem locum Servius, Glaucus, inquit, Minoi filius venit ad Italiam; & quum sibi Imperium peteret, nec acciperet, ideo quod nihil prestabat, sicut pater eius prestiterat, Zonam eius transmittendo, quam antehac distinctum esset, ostendit scutum militare, à quo & ipse Labicus dictus est, & ex eo Populi, ἀπὸ τῆς λαβῆς, quam Latine Ansam vocamus. Labici mentionem sæpe facit Dionysius Halicarnassæus, præsertim libro viii, ubi ab Marcio Coriolano cum ceteris Albanorum Colonijs subactum scribit. Livius lib. iii hanc Vrbem expugnatam ab Q. Sulpicio Prisco Dictatore, direptamque scribit; & Colonijs eo Roma ex S. C. missis bina jugera singulis data. Labici Municipii meminit Cicero Philippica ii. Ab eo Labicana Via Romæ. Plinius Agrum Labicanum locat in 1 Italiæ Regione. Idem Ager olim ab Vvæ præstantia nomen habuit, cuius tres & viginti libras uno prandio Claudium Albinum absumpsisse Capitolinus est auctor. Labicana Vina celebrant Spartianus & Frontinus. In Populis designandis nonnulla est apud Auctores Græcos Latinosque inconstantia. Nunc enim Labii & Labicani; nunc Lavici & Lavicani scribuntur. Subditione hodie est Valmontonium Familiæ Comitum Romanæ.
units.tr: On this passage Servius says: "Glaucus, son of Minos, came to Italy; and when he sought command and did not receive it, because he had nothing to offer as his father had, he showed by sending his belt, which had been fastened before, a military shield, from which Labicus himself was named, and from it the people, from ἀπὸ τῆς λαβῆς, which we call in Latin the handle [ansa]." Dionysius of Halicarnassus often mentions Labici, especially in book 8, where he writes that it was subdued by Marcius Coriolanus together with the other colonies of the Albans. Livy in book 3 writes that this city was stormed and plundered by Quintus Sulpicius Priscus, the dictator, and that two acres each were given to the colonists sent there from Rome by a decree of the Senate. Cicero in the second Philippic mentions the municipality of Labici. From it the Labican Way at Rome takes its name. Pliny places the Labican territory in the first region of Italy. The same territory once had its name from the excellence of its grapes; Capitolinus says Clodius Albinus consumed twenty-three pounds of them at one meal. Spartianus and Frontinus praise the Labican wines. There is some inconsistency among Greek and Latin authors in naming the peoples: sometimes they are written Labii and Labicani, sometimes Lavici and Lavicani. Today Valmontone belongs to the Roman family of the Counts.

units.la: Haud procul Valmontonio est Montefortinum; Castellum Monfortinorum; qui inter Patricios Romanos loci non postremi.
units.tr: Not far from Valmontone is Montefortino, the castle of the Montefortini, who are among the Roman patricians of no small standing.

units.la: Pandunt se mox Opida, quæ vulgo Zancato, Gavignano, & Segna. Hæc Segnia Livio: Σιγνία Straboni; Σίγνια; Stephano. Coloniam deduxisse Signiam Tarquinium Superbum auctores sunt Livius libro i, ii, & xxvii, Dionysius lib. iv, Strabo lib. v, Frontinus de Colonijs, & Inscriptio, quæ apud Onuphrium Panuinium:
units.tr: Soon there open out the towns commonly called Zagarolo, Gavignano and Segni. Segni is Signia in Livy; Σιγνία in Strabo; Σίγνια in Stephanus. That Tarquinius Superbus founded the colony of Signia is attested by Livy in books 1, 2 and 27, by Dionysius in book 4, by Strabo in book 5, by Frontinus On Colonies, and by an inscription which Onofrio Panvinio records:

units.la: L. VOLVMNIO L. F. POMP IVLIANO. SEVERO
units.tr: To Lucius Volumnius Julianus Severus, son of Lucius, of the Pomptine tribe

units.la: IIII. VIRO. COL. SIGN. PATRONO. COLONIÆ, SVÆ. SENATUS. POPVLVSQVE. SIGNINVS
units.tr: Quadrumvir of the colony of Signia, patron of the colony. The senate and people of the Signians (set this up) to their own patron.

units.la: Incolæ Signini Plinio, in 1 Regione. Dedit Signia Vitalianum P. M. Episcopatus claret dignitate. Vinum Signinum commendant Strabo & Plinius libro xiiii Nat. hist. cap. vi: quod vetus adstringebat ventrem. Martialis: Potabis liquidum Signina morantia ventrem, Ne nimium fluant, sit tibi parca fluis.
units.tr: Pliny, in the first region, calls the inhabitants Signini. Signia gave the Church Vitalian, Pontifex Maximus, and its bishopric is distinguished by its dignity. Strabo and Pliny, Natural History book 14, chapter 6, commend the wine of Signia, which used to bind the belly. Martial: "You will drink clear Signine wine, which checks the belly; so that it does not flow too much, let your flux be sparing."

units.la: Sic Silius Italicus libro viii de Bello Pœnico: Quos Cora, quos spumans inimico Signia musto.
units.tr: So Silius Italicus, book 8 of the Punic War: "Those whom Cora sends, and Signia foaming with hostile must."

units.la: Inimicum Mustum, quod nimium sæpe adstringeret.
units.tr: Hostile must, which often constipated too much.

units.la: Post Signiam ulterius sunt Scrcula, Merulo, Sappino, Patria, Ceccano & Castrum, Latij hic terminus.
units.tr: Beyond Signia lie Sezze (Scrcula), Merulo, Sappino, Patria, Ceccano and Castrum; here is the boundary of Latium.

units.la: Flagitat jam ordo, ut Septemtrionaliora Latij per Viam Valeriam Tiburtinam que peragremus.
units.tr: The order of the work now requires that we traverse the more northern parts of Latium along the Via Valeria Tiburtina.

units.la: Hic primo se offert loco Tibur. Ita Latinis omnibus dicitur. Τίβυρ, Prolemæo, Τίβυρις, Straboni: Τίβυρη ex Artemidoro; Τίβυρ ex Nicanore, & Τίβυρ ex nescio quibus: quæ Tinoli hodie. Ἀρελυστίφανον olim vocatum tradit Stephanus; quam appellationem Strabo tribuit Præneste. Ineptiunt, qui Ἡρόκλεον & Καπιτώλιον nominatum etiam ex Strabone contendunt; Auctoris mentem non satis adsequuti. Herculi tamen sacram fuisse, constat ex Suetonio in Caligulæ Vita cap. viii. Ejus pars est Σιβυλλαν apud Dionysium Halicarnassæum. Incolæ Tiburtes plerisque,
units.tr: Here Tibur presents itself first. All Latin writers so call it. Ptolemy has Τίβυρ [Tibur], Strabo Τίβυρις [Tiburis], Artemidorus Τίβυρη [Tiburē], Nicanor Τίβυρ [Tibur], and others of unknown name Τίβυρ [Tibur]; today it is Tivoli. Stephanus says it was once called Ἀρελυστίφανον [Arelystiphanon]; Strabo gives that name to Praeneste. Those who contend, also on Strabo's authority, that it was called Ἡρόκλεον [Herakleon] and Καπιτώλιον [Kapitōlion] are silly, not having grasped the author's meaning. Nevertheless, that it was sacred to Hercules is clear from Suetonius in the Life of Caligula, chapter 8. Part of it is the Sibyl, in Dionysius of Halicarnassus. The inhabitants are for the most part called Tiburtes,

units.la: Antiquis Inscriptionibus: Tiburtini Plinio, in iv Italiæ regione. Conditam volunt quidam à Phocensibus alij ab Catillo Arcade, Evandri Classis Præfecto: non nulli ab Argivis nominatum autem à Tiburto. Catilli Filio, Amphiarai vatis Nepote, Fratre vero Coræ & Catilli. Legendus Seruius ad illa libri vii Aeneidos: Tum gemini Fratres Tiburtia moenia linquunt; Fratris Tiburti dictam cognomine gentem, Catillusque, acerque Coras, Argiva Iuuentus.
units.tr: as in ancient inscriptions; Tiburtini in Pliny, in the fourth region of Italy. Some hold that it was founded by the Phocaeans, others by Catillus the Arcadian, prefect of Evander's fleet; some say by the Argives. It was named after Tiburtus, son of Catillus, grandson of the seer Amphiaraus, and brother of Cora and Catillus. Servius should be read on those lines of Aeneid 7: Then the twin brothers leave the Tiburtine walls; the people was named from brother Tiburtus by its surname, and Catillus, and fierce Coras, the Argive youth.

units.la: Videndus & Silius libro v 1. Horatius etiam Catili Mœnia Tibur appellat. Antiquitatem tectantur, quæ scribit Plinius lib. xvi, ætate sua duratile apud Tiburtes tres lites, apud quas eius Conditor Tiburtus fuerat inauguratus. Urbs ad Anienem Fluuium. Romæ distans c. t. stad. js. Procopio; cxlvii, Stephano; xvi lapide, aliis: ἐν ἀφ ἐνεπ... Strabone & idem paulo post de Tibure & Prænestæ: ... Cœlo est temperatissimo locoque ob Aquarum Fontiumque copiam salubcrrimo. Inter Fontes extra Vrbem in monte sublimi est Albunea: a quo sibylla Albunea Tiburtina cognominata, aliæque complures Aquulæ mediæ, quas Albulæ vocant. Episcopatus Titulo est nobile. Patria Simplicij P. M. & aliorum, quos commemorare longum esset. Tibure Fanum fuisse Herculis, Græcanici generis Dei, notat Strabo: Autumant periti Antiquitatum esse rotundum & Vetustissimum illud, quod sub monte ad Viam Tiburtinam conspicitur, D. Virgini sacrum. Viderunt & cultus Tibure Hercules, Saxanus cognomine, cuius ibidem meminit Tabella Marmorea; Parieti Diversorii publici infecta.
units.tr: Silius, book 5, should also be consulted. Horace too calls it the walls of Catillus, Tibur. Its antiquity is attested by what Pliny writes in book 16: in his own time there were three holm oaks among the Tiburtines, where its founder Tiburtus had been inaugurated. The city lies on the river Anio. Its distance from Rome is given by Procopius in stadia (the figure is unclear in the text), 147 stadia by Stephanus, and 16 miles by others. It has a very temperate climate and, because of its abundance of water and springs, a very healthy site. Among the springs outside the city, on a high mountain, is Albunea, from which the Tiburtine Sibyl was called Albunea; there are also several smaller waters, which they call the Albulae. The bishopric makes it noble. It was the native place of Simplicius P.M. and of others too many to mention. Strabo notes that at Tibur there was a shrine of Hercules, a god of the Greek kind. Experts in antiquities think that the round and very ancient building, seen beneath the mountain by the Via Tiburtina, is sacred to the Blessed Virgin. People have also seen the cult of Hercules at Tibur under the surname Saxanus, mentioned on a marble tablet fixed to the wall of a public inn.

units.la: HERCVLE SAXANO SACRVM SER. VLPI IVS TROPHIMVS ÆDEM ZOTHECAM CVLINAM PECVNIA SVA A SOLO RESTITVIT IDEMQVE DEDICAVIT K. DECEMBR. L. TVRTILIO DEXTRO, M. MÆCIO AVITO COS VTACHIVS SIR PERAGENDVM CVRAVIT
units.tr: SACRED TO HERCULES SAXANUS. SERGIUS ULPIUS TROPHIMUS, AT HIS OWN EXPENSE, RESTORED FROM THE GROUND THE TEMPLE, THE STOREROOM AND THE KITCHEN, AND DEDICATED THEM ON 1 DECEMBER, IN THE CONSULSHIP OF LUCIUS TURTILIUS DEXTER AND MARCUS MAECIUS AVITUS. UTACHIUS SAW TO ITS COMPLETION.

units.la: Putatur eius Aedes fuisse in Saxo vel Rupe, Rotunda illa sine Tecto. sumtuosi operis ex marmore, artisque eximiæ: ex eius Porticu xii adhuc Columnæ superfuere. Porticum Herculis Templi meminit Suetonius in Augusto cap. lxxi. De Hercule iane Tiburtino Victore loquitur Inscriptio, quæ ibi ad S. Vincentium in Balii:
units.tr: It is thought that its temple stood on the rock, that round building without a roof, of costly work in marble and of exquisite art; twelve columns of its portico still survive. Suetonius, in the Life of Augustus, chapter 71, mentions the portico of the Temple of Hercules. The inscription at S. Vincenzo in Balii speaks of Hercules Tiburtinus Victor:

units.la: HERCVLI TIBVR. VICT. ET. CETERIS. DIS FRAT. TIBVRT L. MINICLVS NATALIS COS. AVGVR LEG. AVG. IR. PR. PROVINCIA MOESIA. INFER. VOTIS. SVBSC
units.tr: TO HERCULES TIBURTINUS VICTOR AND THE OTHER GODS, THE TIBURTINE BROTHERS. L. MINICLUS NATALIS, CONSUL, AUGUR, LEGATE OF AUGUSTUS WITH PROPRAETORIAN POWER, IN THE PROVINCE OF LOWER MOESIA, FULFILLED HIS VOW WILLINGLY.

units.la: In æde S. Archangeli. SS. Silvestri & Vincentij multæ sunt Inscriptiones antiquæ, quæ ab aliis publicatæ; quemadmodum & illa, quæ est in sepulcro marmoreo Plautiorum. Stupendus visitur Tibure præceps Anienis ex aliis Rupibus in subiectos Campos maximo cum fragore lapsus. Cascatam vocant Itali, corrupta ex Cataracta voce. Bella Tiburtium & Romanorum, Pacemque inter cos factam, commemorat Livius libro vii. Quam ob causam Virgilius lib. vii Aeneidos Tibur voce Superbum explicat Seruius, scilicet historiam per transitum tangere: quoniam aliquando, quum à Senatu auxilia poscerent Tiburtes sub commemomemoratione beneficiorum, hoc tantum responsi tulerunt, Superbi estis. In ditionem Populi Romani quondam redacta; multis post seculis ab Germanis eversa, & ab iisdem restaurata auctaque, tandem Arce munitissima, quae Vibem subtus despicit, a Pio II. P. M. ornata legitur. Ingentia Tiburtina Villa in huius Vibis Agro visuntur secundo milliario rudera, sumtuosissima, & opidi ambitum complexa. Adparent inter ruinas Fornices & Loca concamerata, partim picturis, partim incrustationibus marmoreis adhuc ornata. Testatur Spartianus, Hadrianum in ea Villa & provinciarum & Locorum celeberrima nomina inscripsisse; velut Lycium, Academiam, Prytanium, Canopum, Poecile, Tempe, &, ut nihil praeteriret, etiam Inferos in ea finxisse. Nunc tota passim sentibus, Agris, Pratis occupata iacet, praeter exiguam inter ruinas semitam. Incolae rerum ignari Domum, Saccellum, Fontem, Campum Sibyllae Tiburtinae illic fuisse fingunt, Tivoli Vecchio appellantes, opinione falsa. Intra Tibur multa vetustatis inveniuntur Monimenta, interque alia Marmor insigne, quo Leo cum Equo tam apte commissus exprimitur, ut vera pugna videatur. Inter eos certatum ferunt de Tiburtinorum & Romanorum Imperio, sed Equum Victorem, Leone pluribus vulneribus sauciato, opes Tiburis ad rem Romanam traduxisse. Sumtuosissimos Hortos, quos hoc loco Hippolytus Aldobrandinus, Ferrariensis Cardinalis, in clivo montis cum magnifico Praetorio, Statuis Antiquis, Picturis, regiaque profusus Supellectile ante annos aliquot instruxit, describunt accurate & eleganter Vbertus Folietus, Franciscus Schottus, & alii. Corona Pighius Picturam Praetorii & Hortorum Romae typis aeneis publicavit. De Tibure multa docte Fulvius Cardulus in notis ad S. Getulij Passionem.
units.tr: In the church of St Archangel, and of Ss. Silvester and Vincent, there are many ancient inscriptions published by others, as is also the one on the marble tomb of the Plautii. At Tibur one can see the Anio plunging headlong from the rocks onto the plains below with a great roar. The Italians call it the cascata, corrupted from the word cataracta. Livy, book 7, records the wars of the Tiburtines and Romans and the peace made between them. For this reason Servius, on Virgil's Aeneid 7, explains the word superbum as touching briefly on history: when the Tiburtines once asked the Senate for help, recalling their services, they received only this answer, You are proud. Once brought under the power of the Roman people, it was many centuries later destroyed by the Germans, and afterwards restored and enlarged by the same people; at last it is adorned by Pius II, P.M., with a very strong citadel that looks down upon the city. Huge ruins of the Tiburtine Villa are seen in the territory of this city at the second milestone, very sumptuous and covering the whole circuit of the town. Among the ruins appear arches and vaulted chambers, some still adorned with paintings, others with marble incrustations. Spartianus testifies that Hadrian, in that villa, inscribed the most famous names of provinces and places, such as Lyceum, Academy, Prytaneum, Canopus, Poecile, Tempe, and, so that nothing should be left out, even fashioned the Underworld there. Now it lies everywhere overgrown with brambles, fields and meadows, except for a narrow path through the ruins. Ignorant of these things, the locals imagine that a house, a shrine, a fountain and the field of the Tiburtine Sibyl were there, calling the place Tivoli Vecchio; this is a false belief. Within Tibur many monuments of antiquity are found, and among other things a notable marble on which a lion and a horse are joined so aptly that it looks like a real fight. They say the two contended over the empire of the Tiburtines and the Romans, and that the horse, the victor, with the lion wounded by many blows, transferred the power of Tibur to the Roman cause. The most sumptuous gardens, which Hippolytus Aldobrandini, Cardinal of Ferrara, laid out some years ago on the slope of the mountain with a magnificent palace, antique statues, paintings and lavish royal furnishings, are described accurately and elegantly by Ubertus Folietus, Franciscus Schottus and others. Pighius published at Rome, with copper engravings, a picture of the palace and gardens. Fulvius Cardulus has much learned material about Tibur in his notes on the Passion of St Getulius.

units.la: Supra Tibur in Latio arduis asperisque Montibus habitarunt Aequicoli: quos initio huius capitis descripsi. Primum eius gentis oppidum inter montes ad dextram Anienis est, quod vernacule Vico-varo; Latine forican Vicus Varronis; Sabellicus vocat Vicum Valerium. Castellum nunc est, cum natura loci, tum opere munitissimum; in cuius oppugnatione anno MDXXXIII globo ictus interiit Ludovicus Gonzaga, Legionum Clementis VII P.M. Ducor. Nomen loci nobilitavit ortu M. Antonius Coccius Sabellicus.
units.tr: Above Tibur, in Latium, the Aequicoli lived on steep and rough mountains; I described them at the beginning of this chapter. The first town of that people among the mountains, on the right of the Anio, is what in the vernacular is called Vico-varo, in Latin Vicus Varronis; Sabellicus calls it Vicus Valerius. It is now a castle, fortified as much by its natural site as by its works. In its siege in 1533, Ludovico Gonzaga, commander of the legions of Pope Clement VII, was killed by a cannon ball. The place was made famous by the birth there of M. Antonius Coccius Sabellicus.

units.la: Ultra Vicum Valerium, vel Varronis, inter rupes Opida parva sunt, quae vulgo Precella & Cantalupo dein aspero in monte Rizo Freddo, Rizus Frigidus: supra quem altissima iuga multis vel editissimis totius Apennini cacuminibus inferiora; Puteis perfossa plurimis, magnae profunditatis, ad emittendum Fucinum Lacum: quorum auctor Claudius Imperator, uti notant Suetonius cap. xx & Plinius lib. natur. histor. xxxvi, cap. xv.
units.tr: Beyond Vicus Valerius or Varronis, among the rocks, are small towns commonly called Precella and Cantalupo; then, on a rugged mountain, Rizo Freddo, Rivus Frigidus. Above it rise the highest ridges, surpassing many of the loftiest peaks of the whole Apennines. The mountain is pierced by very many wells of great depth, made for draining the Lake Fucinus; their author was the Emperor Claudius, as Suetonius (chapter 20) and Pliny (Natural History book 36, chapter 15) note.

units.la: Post Rivum frigidum recta devenitur Arceolum; iuxta quod in montium verticibus amoena incipit planicies. Hic quondam Carseoles fuisse putant viri docti. Carseoli dicuntur Livio, variis locis; Καρσιόλαι item Straboni: qui Καρσίολα Ptolemaeo; Carsulae Itinerariae Tabulae; Capsioli corrupte Antonino; Carseolis singulariter Ovidio libro iv Fastorum. Coloniam vocant Livius lib. x, xxvii, xxix & Velleius Paterculus libro i. Paullus Marsus ad Ovidium dicit in Via Valeria esse, medio spatio inter Vrbem & Marsorum Municipium, ubi se natum addit. Ad Fucinum Lacum est Ligorio. Incolae Carseolani, Aequicolanorum Populi, cum Livio, tum Plinio in quarta Italiae Regione. Bithim, Regis Thraciae Filium, Obsidem Pop. Romano datum, Carseolis in custodia degisse scribit Livius libro xl. Agri indolem describit Ovidius lib. iv Fastorum: Frigida Carseolis; nec olivis apta ferendis Terra; sed ad segetes ingeniosus Ager.
units.tr: Past Rivus Frigidus one comes straight to Arceolum, beside which a pleasant plain begins among the mountain peaks. Learned men think that Carseoli once stood here. Livy in various places calls it Carseoli; Strabo has Καρσιόλαι [Karsiolai], Ptolemy Καρσίολα [Karsiola], the Antonine Itinerary Carsulae; Antoninus corruptly has Capsioli, and Ovid in book 4 of the Fasti has the singular Carseolis. Livy, books 10, 27 and 29, and Velleius Paterculus, book 1, call it a colony. Paulus Marsus, on Ovid, says it lies on the Via Valeria, midway between Rome and the municipality of the Marsi, and adds that he was born there. Ligorio places it near Lake Fucinus. The inhabitants, the Carseolani, are a people of the Aequicoli, according to Livy and also Pliny, in the fourth region of Italy. Livy, book 40, writes that Bithus, son of the king of Thrace, given as a hostage to the Roman people, was kept in custody at Carseoli. Ovid, in book 4 of the Fasti, describes the nature of the land: "Cold Carseoli, a land not fit to bear olives, but a field clever for crops."

units.la: Hinc summo in vertice sunt Cella, difficillimo aditu.
units.tr: From the highest summit lie Cella, very hard to reach.

units.la: Sequuntur mox Stencula, Pereto, Tagliacozzo; quod Taliaquitium Sabellicus nominat libro i. Ager hic peramoenus & fecundus, Vitibus undique, Ficubus, Pomis, Pyris, aliisque id genus Arboribus consitus. Imperium agnoscitur hic Columnarum.
units.tr: Next come Stencula, Pereto, Tagliacozzo, which Sabellicus calls Taliaquitium in book i. This district is very pleasant and fertile, planted everywhere with vines, fig trees, apple trees, pear trees and other trees of that kind. Here the rule of the Colonna family is recognised.

units.la: Aequicolis succedunt Marsi, de quibus supra. Eorum olim caput Marruvium, ad Fucinum Lacum exiguis nunc se prodit vestigiis: quae Marso vulgo nominant; ut scribit Leander: Marsico, ut Erythraeus, qui addit a Bononiensibus Maragofio vocari.
units.tr: Beyond the Aequicoli come the Marsi, of whom I spoke above. Their former chief town, Marruvium, now shows itself on the shore of Lake Fucinus only in scanty remains, which the common people call Marso, as Leander writes; Marsico, as Erythraeus has it, who adds that the people of Bologna call it Maragofio.

units.la: Schaduw. vocari. Marrubium plerisque dicitur; Μαρούιον Straboni, aliisque Græcis, Marrubium Virgilio & Itinerariæ Tabulæ. Marruvium Halicarnassæus Aboriginibus adscribit, in intima locans palude: xı Stadijs à Septem Aquis. Marruvy Plinio dicuntur Incolæ: de quibus Servius ad illud Virgilij, lib. vii Æneidos.
units.tr: ...called. Most people say Marrubium; Strabo and other Greeks write Μαρούιον [Marouion], and Virgil and the Itinerary Table write Marrubium. Halicarnassus assigns Marruvium to the Aborigines, placing it in the middle of a marsh, eleven stades from Septem Aquae. Pliny calls the inhabitants Marruvy; on whom Servius comments on that line of Virgil in book vii of the Aeneid.

units.la: Quin & Marrubia venit de gente Sacerdos:
units.tr: Nor does the priestess come from the Marrubian people:

units.la: Scilicet Medea, inquit, quando relictis Colchis Iasonem sequuta est, dicitur ad Italiam pervenisse, & populos quosdam circa Fucinum ingentem Lacum habitantes, qui Marrubij appellabantur, quasi circa mare habitantes, propter Paludis magnitudinem, docuit remedia contra Serpentes: quamquam alij Marrubios ab Rege dictos velint. Et paullo post: Sunt autem isti Marsorum Populi.
units.tr: Namely, he says, when Medea left Colchis and followed Jason, she is said to have come to Italy, and to have taught remedies against serpents to certain peoples living around the vast Lake Fucinus, who were called Marrubians, as if 'dwelling around the sea', on account of the size of the marsh. Others, however, want the Marrubians to be named after a king. And a little later: Now these are the peoples of the Marsi.

units.la: In Marsis Valerium describit Strabo; Patriam Bonifacij IV P. M. Ab ea mediæ ætatis Scriptoribus, Gothicis temporibus Regio circumjecta Valeria.
units.tr: Strabo describes Valerium among the Marsi, the homeland of Pope Boniface IV. By medieval writers the surrounding region is called Valeria, in Gothic times.

units.la: Ab Talicquitio per amœnos Colles descenditur in amœnam planiciem, ubi juxta Montis pedem ad Viam lævam Sentula est; Σεντουλα Straboni.
units.tr: From Talicquitium one descends through pleasant hills to a pleasant plain, where, at the foot of the mountain, on the left of the road, is Sentula; Σεντουλα [Sentoula] in Strabo.

units.la: Duobus hinc passuum millibus, eodem montis latere, in tumulo Malianum eminet: cujus in dextra Planities, de qua paullo ante, ab Montium radicibus ad Fucini Lacus ripas usque pandi-tur: Campos Palentinos appellat Blondus, Legionibus Corradini Siciliæ Regis Filij, fusis inclutos: in cujus rei memoriam Karolus victor Cœnobium ibi sumptuoli operis fecit D. Mariæ Victoriæ. Vulgo dicitur S. Maria della Vittoria, frequente terræ motu conquassatum hodie jacens.
units.tr: Two miles from here, on the same side of the mountain, Malianum rises on a hillock. On its right lies the plain of which I spoke a little before, spreading from the foot of the mountains to the banks of Lake Fucinus. Blondus calls it the Plains of Palentia, famous for the rout of the legions of Conradin, son of the King of Sicily. In memory of this, Charles the victor founded there a monastery of costly construction, dedicated to St Mary of Victory. Commonly called S. Maria della Vittoria, it now lies shaken and ruined by frequent earthquakes.

units.la: Ad exitum Camporum, quos dixi; Via Valeria tribus ab Lacu millibus in colle circa Anienis Fontes Alba conspicitur. Alba Latinis & Itinerariæ Tabulæ: ut & Ἄλβα Straboni. Ad differentiam cognominum in Italia Urbium, Albensium Plinio appellatur libro iii cap. xii, ab Incolis, qui Albenses Varroni: vel Albanenses Plinio, Livio, Festo: ut Alba, quæ in Latio: Albani: quæque in Gallia Togata, Albenses. Alba Fucentia Sofipatro dicitur, ab Fucino Lacu, qui tertio inde lapide: quod cognomen corrupte legitur apud Prolemæum & Antoninum: apud hunc quidem Alba Tucentia, pro Fucentia: apud illum vero Ἀλφαζύκης, pro Ἄλβα Φυκεντius. Albam scribit Coloniam cum Sora factam, Livius libro x, qui ejusdem etiam meminit libro xxvii & xxviii, ut & Florus Epitoma libri lxxii. Agrum describit quodam modo Silius lib. viii.
units.tr: At the end of the plains I mentioned, the Via Valeria, three miles from the lake, can be seen on a hill near the sources of the Anio: Alba. Alba is the Latin form, used also in the Itinerary tables, and Strabo has Ἄλβα [Alba]. To distinguish it from the other cities of the same name in Italy, Pliny in book 3, chapter 12, calls its inhabitants Albensians, while Varro calls them Albenses, and Pliny, Livy and Festus call them Albanenses, as the Alba that is in Latium has Albani, and the one in Gallia Togata has Albenses. Sofipater calls it Alba Fucentia, from the Fucine Lake, which lies three miles off. This surname is corruptly read in Ptolemy and Antoninus: in the latter it is Alba Tucentia for Fucentia, and in the former Ἀλφαζύκης [Alphazýkēs], for Ἄλβα Φυκεντία [Alba Fykentia]. Livy writes in book 10 that Alba was made a colony together with Sora, and he also mentions it in books 27 and 28, as does Florus in the Epitome of book 72. Silius, in book 8, describes its territory in a certain way.

units.la: Interiorque per udos Alba sedet campos, pomisque rependit arillas:
units.tr: Inland across the watery plains Alba sits, and in return for apples it yields dried figs.

units.la: quibus Poeta innuit, Urbis Agrum non tam frumentarium esse, quam vbertate pomorum fructuosum. Albam hanc, quod ἐν βάθει & χώρας sita, & permunita undique esset, tradit Strabo, Romanos ibi, qui custodiendi erant, tamquam Carcerem adsignare consuevisse. Unde Perseum Regem cum Alexandro Filio iussu Senatus eo ab Q. Cassio deductum, libro xlv; Bithuntem autem Avernorum Regem ibidem servatum, lib. lxi memoriæ prodit Livius: qui & libro xxvii Albam hanc inter xxii recenseт Colonias, quæ tempore Belli Punici Romanis auxilia non dederunt. Ruinis nunc tota fere collapsa jacet. Quædam veterum Mœniorum ex quadrato lapide partes, quanta fuerit Urbs, facile loquuntur. Angitia Nemus Alba vicinum fuisse canit Virgilius lib. viii Æneidos.
units.tr: By these words the poet hints that the territory of the city is not so much productive of grain as rich in abundance of fruit. Strabo reports that this Alba, because it lies in a hollow [ἐν βάθει] of the countryside [χώρας] and is strongly fortified on every side, was accustomed to have the Romans assign to it those who were to be kept in custody, as in a prison. Hence Livy records in book 45 that Perseus the king, together with his son Alexander, was taken there by Quintus Cassius on the orders of the Senate; and in book 61 he records that Bituitus, king of the Arverni, was kept there. Livy also, in book 27, counts this Alba among the twenty-two colonies that gave no help to the Romans during the Punic War. Now it lies almost wholly collapsed in ruins. Some parts of the old walls, built of square stone, readily tell how large the city was. Virgil, in book 8 of the Aeneid, sings that the Angitian grove was near Alba.

units.la: Circa Fucinum porro Castella sunt, quæ vulgo S. Aperito, S. Giona, Paterno, Transacio, Gatano, Avezzano & Atalliano, de quo ante: quæ omnia cum populi frequentia, tum opibus longe superat Celanum, juxta Montium editissimorum pedem, in colliculo, meridiem versus. Possidetur ab Ciborum Genuentium familia, Fucinoque Lacui indit hoc ævo nomen.
units.tr: Around the Fucine Lake there are further small towns, which are commonly called S. Aperito, S. Giona, Paterno, Transacio, Gatano, Avezzano and Atalliano, of which I spoke above. All of these, both in the number of their people and far more in their wealth, are surpassed by Celano, which lies on a little hill at the foot of the very high mountains, facing south. It is held by the family of the Ciboni of Genua, and in this age it gives its name to the Fucine Lake.

units.la: Quatuor Alba milliaribus opidulum est Cesa, Petri Marsi Patria, cum aliis, tum Commentarijs in Silium celebris.
units.tr: Four miles from Alba is the small town of Cesa, the homeland of Petrus Marsus, famous both for other works and for his commentaries on Silius.

units.la: Occidentalior a Lacui Celano vel Fucino Loca repetentibus occurrunt, quæ vernaculæ Rocca dalle Carve; Capranica, opidum Capranicorum, Romæ Nobilium origine clarum: Gnadagnolo, Poli, Casa Corbula, S. Georgio, Rocca delli Tricis, Cesisano, Sambucca, Saraunesco, Rocca de Mutti, Girano, Cereto (Κερέτη) Straboni; Cercate Marsa, Municipium ab S. Mario, apud Frontinum de Coloniis: Sic Plinius libro iii cap. v. Cerretum, Cerretanum, quia Marsi cognominantur: Alter ex altero emendandus.) Anticolo, Rinate, Affile, Civitella, Oliteana (multæ amœnitatis) Prifisano & Santuto, juxta Fontem Liris Fluvij dexteriorem.
units.tr: Further west, for those who go back from Lake Celano or the places of Fucinus, there occur Rocca dalle Carve; Capranica, a town of the Capranicans, famous for the noble families of Rome; Gnadagnolo, Poli, Casa Corbula, S. Georgio, Rocca delli Tricis, Cesisano, Sambucca, Saraunesco, Rocca de Mutti, Girano, and Cereto (Κερέτη [Kerete] in Strabo); Cercate Marsa, a municipium named after St Marius, in Frontinus's work on colonies. So Pliny in book iii, chapter v: Cerretum, Cerretanum, because the Marsi are so surnamed. One must be corrected from the other. Anticolo, Rinate, Affile, Civitella, Oliteana (of great charm), Prifisano and Santuto, near the right-hand source of the river Liris.

units.la: Supra inter excelsos Montes Opidum est, quod hodie Sollago vel, ut alij pronunciant, Sublaco; Latinis Sub-Lacum, ab situ ad Lacum. Meminerunt, sed corruptius, Veteres. Pro Sublaqueo Plinij libro iii.cap.xii reponit Hermolaus Barbarus Sublacum, quod ab Frontino de Aquaeductibus Via Sublacensis nominetur; quodque nomen loco dedisse docet idem Plinius, Lacus tri amoenitate notabilis. Sublacensis item Villa Neroniana est apud Frontinum de Aquaeductibus. Tacitus libro xiiii Annalium: Nam quia disiumbentis Neronis apud Simbrivina Stagna, cui Sublaqueum nomen est, ibi dapes, mensaque defecta, idque finibus Tiburtum accideret unde paterna Planto origo. Legit V.Cl. Iustus Lipsius Sublacum; rationem addens Emendationis quia ab Lacu Simbrivino etiam habet Silius libro viii Belli Poenici, & Simbrivinos Colles idem Tacitus libro xi; pro quibus tamen Lipsius mavult Imbrivium & Imbrivines Colles, ex melioribus codicibus cum Tacito, tum Livij libro viii. Ego hic haereo; non ignorans interim Imbrium Livij aliud esse ab Silij Simbrivio, Tacitique Simbrivinus, cum collibus, tum Stagnis. Sofagium, ut eo redeam, Opidum est perhonestum, Lacui, de quo dixi imminens, Monasterio D. Benedicti, qui vitam hic egit, celebre, ubi D. Gregorij Dialogi memorant. Huc aliquot temporis mutandi aeris grata, secedunt Monachi Farfenses. Farfa monasterium est sumptuosum ab Monachis habitatum Germanis, ad Fluvium Farfarum & Vallem Lucretilem situm, quibus Mons cum Silva ejusdem nominis, Blandusiaeque Fons, de quibus suo loco, adjacent.
units.tr: Above, among the high mountains, is a town which today is called Sollago, or, as others pronounce it, Sublaco; in Latin Sub-Lacum, from its position below the lake. The ancients mention it, but in a more corrupt form. In place of Sublaqueo in Pliny's book iii, chapter xii, Hermolaus Barbarus substitutes Sublacum, which Frontinus in his work on aqueducts calls the Via Sublacensis; and the same Pliny shows that this name was given to the place, since he says the lake is notable for its charm. There is also a Sublacensis Villa Neroniana in Frontinus's work on aqueducts. Tacitus in book xiv of the Annals: For since Nero was dining at the Simbrivian Pools, which are called Sublaqueum, there the feast and the table failed, and this happened within the territory of Tibur, whence the family of Plautus is descended on his father's side. The most learned Justus Lipsius reads Sublacum, adding a reason for the emendation: Silius in book viii of the Punic War also has the Lacus Simbrivinus, and the same Tacitus in book xi has Simbrivinos Colles. Yet Lipsius prefers Imbrivium and Imbrivines Colles, from the better manuscripts, both of Tacitus and of Livy in book viii. I hesitate here, not unaware that the Imbrium of Livy is different from Silius's Simbrivium and Tacitus's Simbrivinus*, both as to the hills and the pools. Sofagium, to return there, is a very respectable town, famous for the monastery of St Benedict, who lived his life here, where the Dialogues of St Gregory mention it. Here the Farfa monks retreat for some time, for a change of air which they find pleasant. Farfa is a sumptuous monastery inhabited by German monks, situated by the river Farfarus and the Lucretilian Valley, to which adjoin the mountain with the forest of the same name, and the Fountain of Bandusia, of which I shall speak in its place.

units.la: Praenestae jam nunc me vocat. Sic Latinis constanter appellatur, Νεγίνες autem Straboni, Ptolemaeo: quae hodie Palestrina. Conditum à Praeneste, Latini Filio, Ulyssis Nepote, tradit apud Solinum Xenodotus. Praenestum Latinum, Ulyssis & Circes Filium, dicit Stephanus. Plutarchus in Parallelis ex Aristotelis rerum Italicarum iii Telegonum, Ulyssis & Circes Filium, quem & Tusculum condidisse volunt, Deorum oraculo monitum, etiam hoc opidum condidisse tradit, ubi saltantes cum coronis Colonos invenerat; & tum appellatione coronae ligneae Prinisium nominasse, & hinc Praenestinos Romanos postea vocitasse. Quapropter & Stephane Graecis quondam dicta fuit, teste Plinio; vel, ut Strabo vult, Polystephanos, quasi multarum coronarum. Ab Caeculo Vulcani Filio, aedificatum canit Virgilius libro vii Aeneidos. De Caeculo longum Fabulam habet Servius, qui nomen Urbis derivat ἀπὸ τῆς πέτρας, ab Ilicibus, quibus Ager ibi abundabat. Malunt alij ἀπὸ τῆς ἀγρῶν dictam, quod pronus & declivis sit locus, in quo sita est. Festus autem vocatam ait, quod locus, in quo posita, montibus praestet: unde & altum Praeneste Virgilio. Situs ejus in declivi Montis ad Venestrim fluvium, olim longe fuit & amoenissimus & iucundissimus: ideoque florente Re Romana frequenter Imperatores Augusti huc animi gratia secessisse leguntur. Videndus, praeter alios, Suetonius in Octaviano, cap. lxxii. Hinc Praenestina Secessio apud Symmachum libro i, Epist. ii; & Praenestinum Diversorium apud eundem libro iii Epist. v, lib. vii. Epist. xxxv, lib ix Epistol. lxxviii. Infaustus Antonino Pio locus fuit propter Veri Caesaris, septennis Filij, interitum de quo Capitolinus in ejus Vita. Mons, in quo conditum, quondam Arentinus, ut Sequester ait, nunc Aretinus. Arx summo Monti impositae est xviii ab Urbe milliario locat Eutropus, hodie xxii numerantur: ὑπὲρ τῶν ἐν Ῥώμῃ cum Tiburte & Tusculo est apud Strabonem; qui paullo post abesse Roma notat c i Stadijs Praeneste apud Festum Municipium est sui juris. Appianus Italico bello cum Tiburtinis in Civitatem acceptos Praenestinos diterte scribit. Non tamen diu post L. Sulla victor, quantum ex Tullij Agraria & Catilinaria colligimus, Opido caedibus atque proscriptionibus exhausto Colonos imposuit, agrumque eorum omnem divisit. Apud Agellium lib. xvi, cap. xiii legimus Praenestinos ab Ti. Augusto impetrasse, ut ex Colonia in pristinum Municipij statum redigerentur. Coloniam appellat, qui cum multis alijs ibi, Lapis:
units.tr: Praeneste now calls me. It is consistently so named in Latin; Νεγίνες [Neginês] in Strabo and Ptolemy; it is today Palestrina. Xenodotus, in Solinus, reports that it was founded by Praeneste, son of Latinus, grandson of Ulysses. Stephanus calls it Praenestum Latinum, son of Ulysses and Circe. Plutarch, in the Parallels, from Aristotle's work on Italian matters, book iii, reports that Telegonus, son of Ulysses and Circe, whom they also think founded Tusculum, warned by an oracle of the gods, also founded this town, where he found colonists dancing with garlands; and from the name of the wooden garland he called it Prinisium, and afterwards the Romans called the Praenestines by this name. For this reason it was once called Stephane by the Greeks, as Pliny witnesses; or, as Strabo wants, Polystephanos, as if "of many garlands". Virgil in book vii of the Aeneid sings that it was built by Caeculus, son of Vulcan. Servius has a long fable about Caeculus, and he derives the name of the city from ἀπὸ τῆς πέτρας [from the rock], from the holm oaks, of which the land there abounded. Others prefer that it was called from ἀπὸ τῆς ἀγρῶν [from the fields], because the place where it lies is sloping and inclined. Festus, however, says it was so called because the place where it is situated stands out above the mountains; whence also Virgil's altum Praeneste. Its site on the slope of the mountain by the river Vestrinus was long ago very pleasant and most delightful; therefore, while the Roman state flourished, the emperors are often read to have retired there for their enjoyment. Suetonius, in the life of Augustus, chapter lxxii, is to be consulted, among others. Hence the Praenestine Retreat in Symmachus, book i, letter ii; and the Praenestine Lodging in the same author, book iii, letter v, book vii, letter xxxv, and book ix, letter lxxviii. The place was unlucky for Antoninus Pius, because of the death of the seven-year-old son of Verus Caesar, of which Capitolinus speaks in his Life. The mountain on which it is founded was once called Arentinus, as Sequester says, and now Aretinus.
