Eutropius places the citadel on the top of the mountain eighteen miles from the City; today twenty-two are counted. Strabo, in a passage about Rome along with Tibur and Tusculum, says that Praeneste is a hundred stades away from Rome, and a little later. Festus says Praeneste is a self-governing municipium. Appian clearly writes that the Praenestines were received into citizenship with the Tiburtines in the Italian War. Not long afterwards, however, L. Sulla, the victor, as we gather from Cicero's Agrarian and Catilinarian speeches, after the town had been drained by slaughter and proscriptions, settled colonists there and divided all its land among them. In Aulus Gellius, book xvi, chapter xiii, we read that the Praenestines obtained from Tiberius Augustus that they should be brought back from a colony to their former state as a municipium. Those who go there among many others call it a Colonia, as the inscription says:

units.la: Giranum. Ceretum. Amiternum. Rusicam. Apte. Carsulae. Ostiam. Sulmona.
units.tr: Giranum. Ceretum. Amiternum. Rusicum. Apte. Carsulae. Ostia. Sulmo.

units.la: Farfa, Monasterium.
units.tr: Farfa, a monastery.

units.la: Praeneste, Opidum, Vadediani. Situs.
units.tr: Praeneste, a town; Vadediani. Situation.

units.la: Distantia ab Urbe. Municipium. Colonia.
units.tr: Distance from the City. Municipium. Colonia.

units.la: M. BARBI. FASTI CONSVLARIS PATRONI COLONIÆ PRÆNESTINORVM FILIÆ OPTIMÆ MERITÆ PRÆNESTIN D. D.
units.tr: M. Barbus. Consular Fasti, Patron of the Colony of the Praenestines, to his most excellent and deserving daughter, of Praeneste. Dedicated.

units.la: Prænestinos, quorum frequens passim mentio, Nucula esse nuncupatos auctor est Festus. Multæ hic, præsertim in Domo Episcopali, Antiquitatum reliquiæ, Imagines, Coronæ, Aræ, Tabulæ, Cippi marmorei, cum suis Elogijs & Inscriptionibus. Templum hic sumtuosissimum habuit Fortuna, in quo Simulacrum ejus fuisse notat Plinius, inauratum: ab cujus operis præstantia Bractæ crassissimæ dicebantur Prænestinæ. Lithostratum etiam in Fortuna Prænestina delubro factum ab L. Cornelio Sulla commemorat idem lib. xxxvi cap. xxv inter nobilia Pavimentorum genera. units.tr: Festus states that the Praenestines, who are often mentioned, were called Nucula. Here, especially in the Episcopal Palace, are many remains of antiquity: images, crowns, altars, tablets and marble cippi with their inscriptions and epitaphs. Here Fortuna had a most magnificent temple, and Pliny notes that her statue there was gilded; from the excellence of this work the thickest gold leaf was called "Praenestine." In the shrine of the Fortuna Praenestina, the same author (book 36, chapter 25) also records a mosaic pavement made by Lucius Cornelius Sulla, among the noble kinds of paving. On a marble base there used to be read a poem, which today is in the Bishop's Palace, and runs thus: You, Fortune, who dwell near the thundering god, ever the avenger of my vows, receive these prayers, and grant gifts to one who deserves them. I give the effigy of our parent, the one whose name shall not be silent but be remembered in writing: Caesius, here, and likewise Titus, the first, who is called the one who gathers the harvests of bountiful Ceres and the bronze-fruited abundance, in whom fame and faith agree, and whose fury surpasses riches; who is accustomed to go through those ports, with care and devoted labour, who gives the most sheltering shores to the weary ship; known in the sacred city, and known also in those regions which the Umbrian ploughs and the Tuscan farmer tills. Every year, after the custom of vows, he adds a hundred crowns, as the number grows, honouring Fortune, the images, the altars of Apollo and of fierce Jupiter, in whom majesty agrees, promising long times of life. Accept this, posterity, so that you may tell of it after your ages: Taurinus, ordered by the affection of his beloved parent, set up this gift, which neither the sentence of death nor the highest power of the fathers shall be able to overcome, but it shall remain with the people's rumour always safe.

units.la: De Prænestinorum Sortium Historia & Superstitione, ejusque initio legendus Cicero libro ii de Divinatione. Meminit Suetonius in Tiberio cap. lxiii, & ibi Torrentius. Consulendus & Petrus Crinitus lib. xxii. cap. iii, D. Agapetus hic genitus, & annorum xv adulescens Imperatoris Alexandri jussu martyrio coronatus traditur. Episcopatus hodie gaudet dignitate: estque Antistes Prænestinus inter septenos, qui Romano Pontifici adstiterunt. A Pœnis olim obsessa fuit Urbs, ut auctor est Livius lib. xxiii, quo tempore fide erga Populum Romanum fuit singulari. Quæ autem aliis Urbibus magno solent esse usui & tutelæ, Situs loci montuosissimus maximaque murorum firmitas: ea huic postea fuerunt calamitati & exitio; ut Strabo memorat propter Bella Romanorum Civilia; quum factiosi Cives huc, veluti in arcem, confugerent Opidumque simul sua clade involverent. Visuntur adhuc Cuniculi Specuque subterranei ab opido per vicinos montes ad plana perfossi, tam auxilii intromittendi, quam clandestinæ fugæ causa. In quorum uno C. Marius Iunior obsessus, quum fugæ nulla pateret via, ne caperetur vivus, cum amico Pontio Telesino dimicans cecidit. Videndus Livius libro lxxxvii & seq. Eadem de re Lucanus libro ii. ——Vidit Fortuna Coloros Prænestina suos cunctos simul ense recīsos, Vnus Populum pereuntem tempore mortis.
units.tr: For the history and superstition of the Praenestine Lots, and their origin, read Cicero, On Divination, book 2. Suetonius mentions them in Tiberius, chapter 63, and Torrentius there. Petrus Crinitus, book 22, chapter 3, should also be consulted. D. Agapetus is said to have been born here, and at the age of fifteen, under the order of the Emperor Alexander, to have been crowned with martyrdom. The see today enjoys the dignity of a bishopric, and the Bishop of Praeneste is one of the seven who stand by the Roman Pontiff. The city was once besieged by the Carthaginians, as Livy records in book 23, at which time it showed singular loyalty to the Roman People. But the features that usually bring great help and protection to other cities, namely a very mountainous site and great strength of walls, proved for this city later to be a calamity and a ruin, as Strabo recounts, on account of the civil wars of the Romans, when factious citizens fled here as into a citadel and at the same time involved the town in their destruction. Underground tunnels and caves can still be seen, running from the town through the neighbouring mountains down to the plain, made both for bringing in help and for secret escape. In one of these, Gaius Marius the Younger, besieged, and with no way of flight open, fought and fell with his friend Pontius Telesinus, so that he should not be taken alive. Livy, book 87 and following, should be seen. Lucan also treats the same matter in book 2: "Fortune of Praeneste saw her Coloni all cut down together by the sword, one people perishing in the same hour of death."

units.la: Vulgi etiamnum opinio manet in Cuniculis illis Saxa cæsorum ibidem adhuc cruore rubere quum tamen in his vicinisque montibus tam Tusculanis, quam Albanis mollior lapis omnis sua natura rubeat obscure. Post, ut scribit Volaterranus libro vi cap. i, à Bonifacio viii. P. M. Ioannis & Iacobi Columnarum Cardinalium, Sciaræ item Columnæ odio, Vrbs est eversa; ac dein rursus restaurata: quumque receptum illic haberent Poncelenus & Nicolaus Fortebracius, aliquè Populi Romani Hostes, tandem funditus est delecta: quæ nunc eodem in loco restituta quidem aliquantulum; sed nec ea amplitudine, nec murorum limitate, qua olim fuit, cernitur: ut ex murorum ingentium adparet vestigijs. Sub ditione hodie Columnarum est. In radice Montis, cui quasi adfixum est opidum, Castellum fuit Aquæ, cui Fornices novem alti & ampli, singuli quatuor habentes ostia, conspiciuntur. Ante ingressum Castelli xxi Fenestellæ sunt, quibus Statuas Imaginum suarum Veteres imposuerunt. Fuit in Prænestinis Montibus Horatii Poetæ Villa, ubi nunc Ecclesia S. Ioannis in Campo Horatij: vel ut alij dicunt, S. Mariæ in Villa. Ab hac Vrbe Porta dicebatur, Viaque Prænestina Romæ, de quis alibi.
units.tr: There is still a popular belief that in those tunnels the stones are red with the blood of the slain, even though in these and the neighbouring mountains, both Tusculan and Alban, every stone is naturally of a softer, dimly reddish kind. Afterwards, as Volaterranus writes in book 6, chapter 1, the town was overthrown by Boniface VIII, Supreme Pontiff, at the instigation of the cardinals John and James Colonna, and likewise from hatred of the Sciarra Colonna. It was then rebuilt again; but because Poncelenus and Nicholas Fortebraccio, enemies of the Roman People, had been received there, it was at last utterly destroyed. It has now been restored on the same spot, to some extent, but it is seen neither with the same extent nor with the same narrow compass of walls as it once had, as can be seen from the vast traces of the walls. Today it lies under the rule of the Colonnas. At the foot of the mountain, to which the town is as it were attached, there was a fort of water, where nine tall and wide arches can be seen, each having four openings. Before the entrance to the fort there are twenty-one small windows, in which the ancients placed statues of their ancestors. In the mountains of Praeneste there was the villa of the poet Horace, where now stands the church of St John in the Field of Horace, or, as others say, of St Mary in the Villa. From this city the gate and the Praenestine Way at Rome were named, concerning which more elsewhere.

units.la: Supra Prænestè Capitulum, Καστιτλεὶ, Hernicorum Vrbs, est Straboni & Plinio. Capitolium Frontino inter Coloniae censetur.
units.tr: Above Praeneste is Capitulum, a city of the Hernici, according to Strabo and Pliny. Frontinus counts Capitolium among the colonies.

units.la: Circa Prænestè item Sacriportus erat, ubi Marium oppressum scribunt Florus, Velleius & Appianus: qui ἱερὸν λίμνην vocat.
units.tr: Near Praeneste there was also the Sacriportus, where Florus, Velleius and Appian write that Marius was overwhelmed; Appian calls it the sacred lake [hieron limnen].

units.la: Nefas sit inditum hic habere Tusculum, opidum multis olim nominibus insigne, quod haud procul ab Frusciata abfuisse censent ex ruderibus, quæ hodieque visuntur, Viridoctiss. Tusculum Scriptoribus Latinis Græcisque notissimum. Τύσκλον Diodoro Siculo, Dionysio Halicarnassi. Straboni, Ptolemæo, aliis: Τύσκλ & Τύσκλαν Stephano. Opus, ut norant Veteres Scriptores, Telemachi, quem Vlyssis & Circes ferunt filium. Annius Viterbiensis ab Tusco conditum vult & denominatum. Tusculum quidam quasi Discoloi dictum putant, quod aditus esset difficilioris. Roma abest Stadijs centum, numerante Dionysio: loco situm amoenissimo, salubri, aqua abundante, in Albani montis dorso: versus Orientem collibus circumdatum, ceteris partibus planicie & silva. Strabo Tusculi collem fecundum aquis, & regijs aedificijs abundasse, refert, continuaque esse loca, quæ ad Albanum vergunt montem. Incolæ Plinio Tusculani: Τύσκλανοι Halicarnasseo lib. v. Magna olim fuit ejus, ut memorant Dionysius & Livius, æmulatio cum exoriente Roma: à qua deinceps in potestatem est redacta: quo pacto, scribit Diodorus libro xi. Primum omnium Municipium cum Suffragij latione fuit Tusculum, cui quum, ut inquit Festus, primo sine suffragio Civitas data esset, post aliquot annos pleno jure Cives Romani facti sunt Tusculani. Meminit Livius libro vi ad annum ccclxxiii & cccl xxvii. Videndi idem Livius libro viii, Cicero pro Plancio, Valerius Maximus libro ix cap. x. Tusculum postea, Romæ Fortuna Majestateque sub Cæsaribus propemodum conlapsa, sensim adeo crevit opibus & potentia, ut, præter alias insignes Victorias, Friderici i Imperatoris junctâ copiis, magnam, Raymonis Principis ductu, Romanorum ediderit stragem: cujus injuriæ, Blondo scribente, memores Romani Vrbem tandem post annum septimum flamma ferroque vastatam solo æquarunt, ut vix fundamenta relinquerent. Post illud tempus paullatum instaurari quidem coepit, auspicijs præcipue Paulli iii, sed minore multis partibus, quam antiqua, amplitudine. Tusculi Agnum cum Vbere lactanti natum prodit Livius lib. xxvii. Tusculanus fuit Octavius Mamilius. Latinorum Princeps: cui, ut regnum suum stabiliret, Filiam suam locavit Tarquinius Superbus, vii Romanorum Rex. Legendi Livius lib. ii & alij. Ex Tusculo quoque celebres Familiæ, quæ Romæ summos adeptæ sunt honores, prodierunt, Porciorum & Cornuncanorum, ut memoriæ produnt Cicero & Tacitus lib. xi. quamquam hic Cornuncanos, non Tusculo scribat, sed Camerta oriundos. Videndus & Auctor de VV. Illustribus cap. xlvii. Tusculanus item fuit L. Furius, qui, ut refert Plinius, suæ Civitatis consul, ea adversus Pop. Romanum arma parante, Romam transfugit; ibique Cos. designatus, uno eodemque anno Romæ Tusculanique Magistratum illum adeptus est, deque Tusculanis triumphavit. Fuit item Tusculum Patria Benedictorum viii & ix & Ioannis xiix. Nominantur inter Suburbana Loca & in Tusculano Territorio Villa Horatii Poetæ, haud procul Tusculo in montanis posita; eadem procul dubio cum Superiore. Item uno ab Vrbe milliari Tusculanum Ciceronis erat Prædium: ubi nunc est D. Mariæ Cryptæ Ferratæ Cænobium (vulgo S. Maria de Grotta Ferrata) quo ita se delectari scribit Vir magnus, ut sibimet ipse tum denique, quum illo veniret, placere esse solitus. Inhabitatur ab Monachis Calabris, regulam imitantibus, D. Basilij, Sacraque Græcorum ritu facientibus. In horto tria Sepulcra antiqua, in quorum uno homines insident Elephantis, Camelis, Leonibus: & Basis cum Virorum Mulierumque imaginibus pulcherrima L. Luculli Villa fuisse putatur, quo loco hodie Frascata: ubi nonnulli Aquæ Virginis, quæ etiamnum Romam accedit, fontem repertum tradunt.
units.tr: It would be wrong to pass over Tusculum here, a town once famous under many names, which the very learned men think lay not far from Frascati, judging from the ruins which can still be seen today. Tusculum was very well known to Latin and Greek writers. Diodorus Siculus and Dionysius of Halicarnassus call it Tuskulon [Τύσκλον], Strabo, Ptolemy and others likewise; Stephanus gives Tuskla and Tuskla­n [Τύσκλα, Τύσκλαν]. It was, as the ancient writers knew, the work of Telemachus, whom they say was the son of Ulysses and Circe. Annius of Viterbo holds that it was founded and named by Tuscus. Some think it was called as it were "Discoloi," because its approach was more difficult. Rome lies, according to Dionysius, a hundred stadia away. It was situated in a very pleasant and healthy place, abundant in water, on the back of the Alban mountain; surrounded by hills towards the east, and on the other sides by plain and forest. Strabo reports that the hill of Tusculum was fertile in waters and abounded in royal buildings, and that the places which slope towards the Alban mountain are continuous with it. Pliny calls its inhabitants Tusculani; Halicarnassian Dionysius, in book 5, calls them Tuskla­noi [Τύσκλανοι]. As Dionysius and Livy record, it once had a great rivalry with the rising Rome, to which it was afterwards brought under subjection; in what manner, Diodorus writes in book 11. Tusculum was the first of all municipalities to have the right of voting; and since, as Festus says, it had first been given citizenship without the vote, a few years later the Tusculans were made Roman citizens with full rights. Livy mentions this in book 6, under the years 373 and 327 of the city. Livy, book 8, Cicero, Pro Plancio, and Valerius Maximus, book 9, chapter 10, should be consulted on the same point. Tusculum afterwards, with its Roman fortune and majesty almost collapsed under the Caesars, gradually grew so in resources and power that, besides other notable victories, when it joined the forces of the Emperor Frederick I, under the leadership of Prince Raymond it inflicted a great slaughter on the Romans. Blondus writes that the Romans, mindful of this injury, at last after seven years destroyed the town with fire and sword and levelled it with the ground, so that they scarcely left the foundations. After that time it began to be restored little by little, chiefly under the auspices of Paul III, but with a far smaller extent in many respects than the ancient one. Livy, book 27, reports that a lamb was born at Tusculum with its udder still giving milk. Octavius Mamilius, prince of the Latins, was a Tusculan; to him, so that he might strengthen his kingdom, Tarquin the Proud, seventh king of the Romans, gave his daughter in marriage. Livy, book 2, and others should be read. From Tusculum also came famous families which obtained the highest honours at Rome, the Porcii and the Cornuncanii, as Cicero and Tacitus, book 11, record in their memoirs, although Tacitus writes that the Cornuncanii were from Camerta, not from Tusculum. The author On Illustrious Men, chapter 47, should also be seen. Lucius Furius was likewise a Tusculan, who, as Pliny reports, was consul of his own state; when that state was preparing arms against the Roman People, he deserted to Rome, and there, as consul-designate, in one and the same year obtained that magistracy at Rome and among the Tusculans, and triumphed over the Tusculans. Tusculum was also the native place of the Benedicts, eighth and ninth, and of John the nineteenth. Among the suburban places and in the territory of Tusculum are named the villa of the poet Horace, situated in the mountains not far from Tusculum; it is without doubt the same as the one mentioned above. Likewise, one Roman mile from the city, there was Cicero's estate at Tusculum, where now stands the monastery of D. Mariae Cryptae Ferratae (commonly S. Maria de Grotta Ferrata), in which, as that great man writes, he took such delight that he used to think himself pleasing only when he came there. It is inhabited by Calabrian monks, who follow the rule of St Basil and perform the sacred rites in the manner of the Greeks. In the garden there are three ancient tombs, in one of which men sit with elephants, camels and lions; and a base with very beautiful images of men and women is thought to have belonged to the villa of Lucius Lucullus, at the place which is today Frascati; here some report that the spring of the Virgin Water, which still flows to Rome, was found.

units.la: Floruit haud procul his locis Gabiorum Vrbs: quam Marlianus, Blondus & Leander fuisse arbitrantur, ubi hodie Callicanum: Onuphrius, ubi Zagarolum, errore manifesto; Celsus denique Cittadinus suis ad Orticelium litteris, ubi La Colonna. Gabij dicuntur omnibus & Græcis & Latinis, Gabinæ Vrbs Ovidio lib. ii Fastorum. Gabij vitiose scribuntur in Itineraria Tabula. Incolæ Gabini Plinio lib. iii. cap.v, aliisque. Vrbs est Volscorum in Latio: Campaniæ falso tribuit Servius. Municipium vocat Cicero Philippica i. Coloniam fuisse probare nititur ex antiquo Lapide, qui Zagaroli extat, Onuphrius Panvinius, his verbis conceptus:
units.tr: A city of the Gabii Gabiorum Vrbs flourished not far from these places. Marlianus, Blondus and Leander think it was on the site of what is today Callicanum. Onuphrius places it at Zagarolum, which is a manifest error. Finally, Celsus Cittadinus, in his letters to Orticelius, places it at La Colonna. The people are called Gabij by both Greeks and Latins, and Ovid in book 2 of the Fasti calls it the Gabinæ Vrbs. In the Itinerary Table the name is wrongly written Gabij. Pliny (book 3, chapter 5) and others call the inhabitants Gabini. It was a city of the Volsci in Latium; Servius wrongly assigns it to Campania. Cicero, in the first Philippic, calls it a Municipium. Onuphrius Panvinius tries to prove that it was a Coloniam from an ancient stone which exists at Zagarolo, worded as follows:

units.la: CN. ARRIO. CN. F. IVS. AXIMIO PATRONO. ORDIN. ET. COLON.
units.tr: To Gnaeus Arrius, son of Gnaeus, Ius Aximius, patron of the order and of the colony.

units.la: Inter Romam & Præneste medium ponunt Strabo & Appianus libro v bellorum Civilium. Centum Stadiis ab Vrbe, Halicarnassæus libro iv: Iuxta Lucretilem Amnem Acronii locatur. Conditam notat Solinus cap. viii Polyhist. ab Galatio & Bio Siculis Fratribus: auctam ab Albanis Regibus, Dionysius, ab Sex. Tarquinio Superbi Filio, simulato transfugio, in potestatem Populi Romani redactam, Livius lib.i. & ii, Dionysius lib. iv, Orosius lib.ii cap. iiii, Eutropius lib. i, Valerius Maximus lib.vii. cap.iiii, Frontinus lib. i. Strateg. cap.i, Ovidius lib. ii Fastor. & alij. Ab hac Vrbe Gabinus Cinctus, quem describunt apud Ioannem Meursium meum in Spicilegio ad Theocritum Servius ad v & vii Æneidos. Veterus Persij Interpretes ad Satyram v, Isidorus libro xix cap.xxiv. Nobilis sane & augustus; usurpari solitus apud Veteres Romanos ab Consulibus, non solum honorem ineuntibus, uti innuit Claudianus lib. iii de Consulatu Honorij: verum etiam bellum indicturis, canente Virgilio libro Æneidos viii; item ab Exercitu pugnaturo, teste Festo in Procinctu, & Claudiano iv Consulatu Honorij; ab Sacerdotibus, ut scribunt Isidorus indicato à me loco & Valerius Maximus lib. i. cap.i. ab Imperatoribus denique, ævo posteriore, uti colligere est ex Corripi libro iv. Ab Gabijs item Gabina Via, de qua suo loco.
units.tr: Strabo and Appian, in book 5 of the Civil Wars, place it midway between Rome and Praeneste. Halicarnassus, in book 4, places it at a hundred stadia from the city, near the river Lucretilis at Acronium. Solinus, in chapter 8 of the Polyhistor, says it was founded by the Sicilian brothers Galatius and Bius. Dionysius says it was enlarged by the Alban kings; Livy (books 1 and 2), Dionysius (book 4), Orosius (book 2, chapter 4), Eutropius (book 1), Valerius Maximus (book 7, chapter 4), Frontinus (book 1 of the Strategemata, chapter 1), Ovid (book 2 of the Fasti) and others say it was brought under the power of the Roman people by Sextus Tarquinius, son of Superbus, who got in by a pretended desertion. From this city came the Gabinus Cinctus, which Servius describes on Aeneid 5 and 7, and which is described in the works of John Meursius, my own book Spicilegium on Theocritus. The old interpreters of Persius describe it on Satire 5, and Isidore in book 19, chapter 24. It was indeed a noble and august form of dress, customarily used by the Consuls among the ancient Romans, not only when they entered office, as Claudian indicates in book 3 on the Consulship of Honorius, but also when they were about to declare war, as Virgil sings in book 8 of the Aeneid. It was likewise used by an army about to fight, as Festus testifies under Procinctus, and Claudian in the fourth Consulship of Honorius. Priests used it, as Isidore (in the passage I have indicated) and Valerius Maximus (book 1, chapter 1) write. Finally, in a later age, Emperors used it, as may be gathered from book 4 of Corippus. From the Gabii also comes the Gabina Via, of which I shall speak in its place.

units.la: Et hæc de Latio, per quod ab Vrbe varia ducit Itinera Antoninus cum alijs quæ vel in Campaniam vel in Samnites porro pergunt, missa. Ea operæpretium ducat Geographicorum Studiosus exemplo meo cum Itineraria consere Tabula. Non ego possum, nec debeo omnia; ne sim prolixior. Vnum adjiciam, quod Via, Prænestina ab Vrbe per Latium & Samnites ducit Beneventum: compositum cum Itineraria Augustanæ Bibliothecæ Tabula. Antoninus. | Itineraria Tabula. Latium: Prænestina, Ab Vrbe Beneventum usque M.P. CLXXXVIII. sic Roma, | Prænestina, vitiose | XII. Cabios, CM.P. XII. Cabios, | XI. Alijs omnibus Auctoribus Gabij nominantur. Praneste, M. P.xi. | Praneste, ... Sub Anagniam, M.P.xxiiii. | Anagnino, viii.
units.tr: And so much for Latium, through which Antoninus leads various routes from the city, and I pass over those which go further on into Campania or into the Samnites. The student of geography will do well to compare them with the Itinerary Table, following my example. I cannot and should not do everything, lest I become too long. I will add one thing: the Praenestine Way leads from the city through Latium and the Samnites to Beneventum. I have compared it with the Itinerary Table of the Augsburg Library. Antoninus: Latium, Praenestine Way, from the city to Beneventum, 188 miles, thus: Rome, Praeneste (wrongly written as Praenestine), XII Cabios, 12 miles (XI in all other authors, where it is called Gabii), Praeneste, 11 miles, below Anagnia, 24 miles, Anagnino, 8. Thus some suburb, perhaps Anagnia, or another station not far from there, is noted. Frusino, 7 miles, Ferentino, 7. I shall discuss it elsewhere. Fregellanum, 14 miles, (blank), (blank). Others call it Fregellae. Fabrateria, 3 miles, Febrateriae, 4. Petrus Marsus, on book 8 of Silius Italicus, notes that it keeps its name. Melfel, 4; Aquinum, 8 miles, Aquino, 9; Casinum, 7 miles, Casino, 8; Venafrum, 16 miles, at Flexum, 8; Teanum, 18 miles, Teano Scedicino, 8, wrongly. See below, chapter 29, where I treat the Samnites. Alifas, 17 miles, Ebutiana, 9, Adlefas, 6; Telesia, 25 miles, Telesie (blank), in a very confused order; Sepinum, 12; Sirpium, 18; Beneventum, 18 miles, Benebento (blank).

units.la: Sic Suburbium forte Anagnia, vel alia haud procul inde Statio notatur. Frusinonem, M.P.vii. | Ferentino, vii.
units.tr: Thus Suburbium, perhaps Anagnia, or some other station not far from there, is noted. Frusino, 7 miles. | Ferentino, 7.

units.tr: Deco elsewhere. Fregellanum, 14 miles. | ...... | ......

units.tr: Elsewhere, Fregellae. Fabrateria, 3 miles. | Febrateriae, 4.

units.la: Nomen retinere notat Petrus Marsus ad librum viii Silij Italici. | Melfel, iiii Aquinum, M.P.viii. | Aquino, viiii. Casinum, M.P.vii. | Casino, viii Venafrum, M.P.xvi. | Ad Flexum, viii Teanum, M.P.xviii. | Teano Scedicino, viii corrupte. Vide infra caput xxix ubi de Samnitibus. Alifas, M.P.xvii. | Ebutiana, ix | Adlefas, vi. Telesiam, M.P.xxv. | Telesie, ... turbatissimo ordine. Sepinum, xii. | Sirpium, xviii Beneventum, M.P.xviii. | Benebento, ....
units.tr: Petrus Marsus, in his note on book 8 of Silius Italicus, says the name is retained. Melfel, 4. Aquinum, 8 miles. | Aquino, 9. Casinum, 7 miles. | Casino, 8. Venafrum, 16 miles. | At Flexum, 8. Teanum, 18 miles. | Teano Scedicino, 8, corruptly. See below, chapter 29, where the Samnites are discussed. Alifae, 17 miles. | Ebutiana, 9. | Adlefas, 6. Telesia, 25 miles. | Telesie, ... in a very confused order. Sepinum, 12. | Sirpium, 18. Beneventum, 18 miles. | Benebento, ....

units.la: Leguntur apud eumdem Antoninum alia duo Latij Itinera, quæ ab Vrbe ducunt, unum quidem Via Labicana, Beneventum; alterum, Latina, ad Decimum.
units.tr: The same Antoninus records two other roads through Latium that lead from the city: one, the Labican Way, to Beneventum; the other, the Latin Way, to Decimum.

units.la: CAPVT XXIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIII.

units.la: Picenum.
units.tr: Picenum.

units.la: ITALIAM Priscam, eamque Occidentaliorem & ab Montibus liberiorem, cis Apenninum, perlustravi in Etruria & Latio, sequitur, quod ejusdem naturæ trans eumdem Montem, Picenum.
units.tr: Having surveyed Old Italy, and its western part, which is freer of mountains, on this side of the Apennines, in Etruria and Latium, there follows, beyond the same mountain and of the same nature, Picenum.

units.la: PICENVM
units.tr: PICENUM

units.la: PICENVS nominatur Livio Tacito, Plinio, Melæ, Latinisque Scriptoribus omnibus: Πικηνὸς Ptolemæo, ceterisque Græcis: Πικηνὸν etiam Straboni. Picena Regio apud Sex. Pompeium Festum. Pentapolis Provincia appellatur in Synodo vi Constantinopolitana.
units.tr: Picenus is the name used by Livy, Tacitus, Pliny, Mela, and all the Latin writers. Ptolemy and the other Greeks write Picenos [Πικηνὸς], and Strabo writes Picenon [Πικηνὸν]. Sextus Pompeius Festus calls it the Picene Region. In the Sixth Council of Constantinople it is called the Province of Pentapolis.

units.la: Picenum autem, ut apud Strabonem aliosque legere est, dictum ab auspicato Pici Martij omine, qui in vexillis Picenorum, quum ex Sabinis, à quibus orti sunt, Asculum commigrarent, conspicuus dicitur. Alij à Pico, Saturni Filio, Gentis Duce & Auctore, derivant. Nonnulli à Piceno; Vibe huc olim circa Aesis Fluvii ostium primaria. Regionem volunt denominatam: Pelasgis antea cultam & habitatam, uti Silio placet libro viii. Postea ab Langobardis Marchia Anconitana nomen accepit, ab Ancona Emporio celeberrimo, quod sedem & domicilium dabat Marchionibus universæ Regionis Dominis & Moderatoribus; uti & Firmiana, testibus Blondo libro xiii Historiarum, & Platina in vita Gregorij vii, ab Firmo, quod totius Piceни caput.
units.tr: As one can read in Strabo and others, Picenum is said to take its name from the auspicious omen of Picus Martius, who is said to have been conspicuous on the standards of the Picenes when they migrated from the Sabines, from whom they were descended, to Asculum. Others derive it from Picus, son of Saturn, leader and founder of the people. Some hold that the region was named from Picenum, once the chief town here near the mouth of the river Aesis, which was formerly inhabited and settled by the Pelasgians, as Silius thinks in book 8. Later the Lombards gave it the name Marchia Anconitana, from Ancona, a very famous market town, which provided the seat and dwelling of the margraves, the lords and rulers of the whole region. Likewise Firmiana, from Firmo, which was the head of all Picenum, as attested by Blondus in book 13 of his Histories and by Platina in the life of Gregory VII.

units.la: Confinales Picentibus sunt ad meridiem quidem Sabini, Vmbri, Vmbricum Apennino Monte; ad Occidentem Galli Cis-Alpini cum Hauro Fluvio: qua Septemtrio est, Sinus illos pulsat Adriaticus: in Orientali Limite statuendo variatur. Plinius Aternum ponit Amnem & Ancona; Ptolemæus Matrinum fluvium cum Ancone: Novitij, in quis princeps Leander, Truentum signat Finitorem inter hos & Præcutianos; quem ego æquat addo Strabonem Æsin navigabilem Amnem & Leastrum longitudine per oram 1500 Stadiorum, item Mare & Montes, inæquali tamen latitudine constituere.
units.tr: The neighbours of the Picentes are: to the south the Sabines and Umbrians, bordering on the Umbrian Apennine; to the west the Cisalpine Gauls, along the river Hauro. On the north, the Adriatic beats upon those bays. The eastern boundary varies depending on how it is set. Pliny places the river Aternus and Ancona there; Ptolemy places the river Matrinus with Ancona; the Novitii, whose leader is Leander, mark Truentum as the boundary between these and the Praecutiani, which I too consider accurate. I add that Strabo describes the Aesis as a navigable river, and the Leastrum, with the sea and the mountains, as forming a region of 1500 stadia along the coast, though of unequal breadth.

units.la: Maioris multo longitudinis est, quam latitudinis.
units.tr: It is much longer than it is broad.

units.la: Ager Picenus ut cum Livio loquar libro xxiii) rerum omnino fertilis: fructibus tamen lignarijs, quam frumentarijs, Præstantior. Nobilissimum vinum ad Sirolum oppidum colligitur, quod Plinius Anconitani Vini celebrat nomine.
units.tr: The Picene land, to use Livy's words in book 23, is entirely fertile, though it is more productive of timber fruits than of grain. The finest wine is gathered near the town of Sirolum, which Pliny celebrates under the name Anconitanum Vinum.

units.la: Populi Picentes dicuntur Livio passim, Pomponio Melæ aliisque: Picentes Verrio Flacco. Sunt autem Picenti diversi à Picentinis, Tyrrheni Maris Adcolis; eo ex Piceno translatis, de quibus suo loco. Auximates ab Auximo, hodie Osimo. | Cuprentes cognomine Montanos: à Cupra Montana. | Plinius Picenus incolas facit. Beregranos; ubi hodie Mons Granarus. | Falerienses hodie Falerone. Cingulanos, ab Cingulo oppido. | Firmanos ab Firmo Piceno. |
units.tr: The people are called Picentes by Livy throughout, by Pomponius Mela and others; Picentes by Verrius Flaccus. The Picenti, however, are different from the Picentini, neighbours of the Tyrrhenian Sea, who were transplanted there from Picenum, of whom more in their place. The Auximates are named from Auximum, today Osimo. The Cuprenses, with the surname Montani, from Cupra Montana. Pliny makes the inhabitants of Picenum the Beregrani, where today there is Mons Granarus. The Falerienses, today Falerone. The Cingulani, from the town of Cingulum. The Firmani, from Firmum in Picenum.

units.la: Paufulanos; à Paufulis prope Potentiam. Ricinenses; ab Ricina opido everso, cujus vestigia prope Maceratam.
units.tr: The Paufulani, from Paufulae near Potentia. The Ricinenses, from the destroyed town of Ricina, whose traces are near Macerata.

units.la: Pleninenses: ubi fuerint, ignoro. Testatur Ortelius tres suos codices habere Plynienses, Plynienses, & Plinienses, Membranas autem Laevini Torrentij Planienses. Salvianos: ab Salvia Urbe.
units.tr: The Pleninenses: where they were, I do not know. Ortelius testifies that his three codices have Plynienses, Plynienses and Plinienses, but the manuscript of Laevinus Torrentius has Planienses. The Salviani, from the city of Salvia.

units.la: Pollentinos; à Pollentia, quae & Potentia diruta. Septempedanos: à Septempeda diruta, ubi nunc San-severinum.
units.tr: The Pollentini, from Pollentia, which is also Potentia, destroyed. The Septempedani, from Septempeda, destroyed, where Sanseverino now stands.

units.la: Tollentinates: ab Tollentino opido.
units.tr: The Tolentinates, from the town of Tolentinum.

units.la: Triaccenses. Qui sint, nescio. Traianenses malunt Pintianus. Traiana est Ptolomaeo circa Anconam. Trea Antonino.
units.tr: The Triaccenses. Who they are, I do not know. Pintianus prefers Traianenses. Traiana is in Ptolemy near Ancona. Trea is in Antoninus.

units.la: Idem Plinius Pincentiu Civitates recesser, Asculum, de eo in Samnitibus, Novanam: Citta Nova. Clusanam; quae sit, nondum liquet. Potentiam; infra suo loco. Numanam: ab Siculis conditam: hodie Humana. Anconam. Nomen retinet. Adrium. Atri. Cupram; quum duplex esset, Maritima & Montana; illam intelligit, quae Crypta hoc aevo. Castellum Firmanorum: suo loco.
units.tr: The same Pliny mentions the states of Picenum: Asculum, which is in the land of the Samnites; Novana, Citta Nova; Clusana, whose identity is still unclear; Potentia, see below in its place; Numana, founded by the Siculi, today Humana; Ancona, which keeps its name; Hadria, Atri; Cupra, which was of two kinds, Maritima and Montana. He means the one that is today Crypta. The Castellum of the Firmani, see in its place.

units.la: Vberrimae sane quondam multitudinis fuisse testatur Plinius: ccclx Picentium millia in fidem Populi Romani venisse olim, addens.
units.tr: Pliny testifies that in former times the population was indeed very large: he adds that three hundred and sixty thousand Picentes once came into the allegiance of the Roman people.

units.la: Res à Picentibus gestas describunt cum alij, tum Livius passim, praecipue libr. xxii, xxiii, xxv. Incolae hodie feroces sunt animo, bellicosi: Agriculturae Armisque potius, quam negotiationibus & artificijs vacantes.
units.tr: Other writers describe the deeds of the Picentes, Livy throughout, especially in books 22, 23 and 25. The inhabitants today are fierce in spirit and warlike, occupied more with agriculture and arms than with trade and crafts.

units.la: Regio majore ex parte sub ditione summi est Pontificis: cujus in ea esse lego Anconam, Recanatum, Fanum D. Mariae Laurett, Camerinum, Fanum Fortunae, Tolentinum, Firmum, Maceratam, & alia quaedam opida: Engubium, Caglium, Forum Sempronij, S. Leo, Senogallia, Urbinum, aliaque nonnulla sub aliorum sunt principatu.
units.tr: Most of the region is under the authority of the supreme Pontiff. I read that the following towns are in it: Ancona, Recanati, Fano di Santa Maria di Loreto, Camerino, Fano della Fortuna, Tolentino, Fermo, Macerata, and certain other towns: Gubbio, Cagli, Fossombrone, San Leo, Senigallia, Urbino. Some others are under the rule of other princes.

units.la: Specialiorem Regionis Delineationem ordiar ab Truento; qui limes illi, ut dixi, Orientalior. Occurrit ibi primo loco Portus Asculi, Arcis propugnaculo ad Locorum, quae vicina, praesidium validus.
units.tr: I shall begin a more detailed description of the region from the Truentum, which, as I said, is its more eastern boundary. There first occurs Porto d'Ascoli, a strong defence of the citadel for the places nearby.

units.la: Tertio inde iecundum littus lapide Castrum visitur D. Benedicti: agro beatum amoenissimo.
units.tr: Three miles further along the coast, a castle called San Benedetto is seen, blessed with a very pleasant countryside.

units.la: Intus dein non procul Truento Mons Brandonus, Ioannis Marchiani Monachi ortu nobilis.
units.tr: Then, inland, not far from the Truentum, is Monte Brandone, noted for the birth of John of Marche, a monk.

units.la: Hinc tribus milliaribus celebre est opidum Aqua-Viva, inlustri Aquavivana inclutum familia.
units.tr: Three miles from here is the famous town of Acquaviva, renowned for the illustrious Acquaviva family.

units.la: Ulterius ad Truentum Arquata visitur in Apennino: & xxv hinc lapide Acumulum: & infra Truenti fontem in monte Amatricanum, in Samnitibus describitur.
units.tr: Further along the Truentum, Arquata is seen in the Apennines, and twenty-five miles from here Acumulum; and below the source of the Truentum, on the mountain Amatrice, which is described among the Samnites.

units.la: In ora iterum ab Truenti ostiis Auscul-ique Portu Castellum sequitur, Crypta Latinis dictum, Grotte vulgo. Duas habet his locis Κύπρας Ptolemaeus, Μαξίμηαν & Μεντάνας, sed utraque ad Orientaliorem Truenti ripam in Tabulis vitiose ponitur: quum ad Occidentaliorem sint locandae: quod patet cum ex Strabonis ab Occidente versus Orientem pogredientis, poltque Κύπρον Truentinum amnem ponentis, enumeratione; tum ex Itineraria Tabula, quam in fine Capitis adscribo cum Ptolemaeo conlatam. Cupra igitur Maritima, vel ut in Augustana Itinerum Tabula, quam dixi, nominatur, Marina, fuisse putatur, quo loco hodie Crypta; Montana vero, ubi Templum D. Virgini cognomine di Loreto, dicatum. De Maritima potius, quam, ut alij censent, de Montana sic Strabo libro v: Ἐ Φιξῆς δὲ (post Castellum Firmanum: hoc enim intelligit Ε Κύπρας Καστέλλιον nominans Firmi Piceni) τὰ δ' Κύπρας ἱερὸν, Τυρρηνῶν ἱδρυμα ἡ πτισμα. Ἡ δ' ἡ ἐαν ἐκεῖνος Κύπρας καλεῖσθαι. Pintianus ex Cupra Maritima duas facit apud Ptolemaeum urbes: quod nollem ab illo factum. Maritimam intelligit Pomponius Mela, quum Cupram in Piceni littoribus cum aliis Vrbibus nominat: ut frustra sit idem Pintianus, qui Maritimam fabricat ex adjecto illo Senogalliae vocabulo. Ab Cupra Montana Cuprenses Plinio cognomine Montani, ut antea vidimus. Audiatur jamnunc, & excutiatur scribens ad Ortelium suum Roma Celsus Cittadinus Angelerius: Si descriptio Ptolomaei fidelis est (atqui fidé fide, ut ante dixi, laborat) conferem Cupram Maritimam fuisse, ubi nunc locus appellatus S. Benedicto : non ubi est Grotta. Nam Ptolemaeus ponit eam inter Fortunum Trientum, nunc Tronto, & Matrinum, nunc Piomba (sed male, uti perspicuum cum ex locorum, quae apud Strabonem Scriptorem diligentissimum, enumeratione, accedentibus etiam Plinio Melaque; tum ex Itineraria Tabula, quae, ut saepe in Mediterraneis, sic raro fallere solet in Littoralibus) & Grotta est inter Firmanum Portum & Truentum (sed ibidem etiam est D. Benedictus, cui cum Cupra Marina, nihil esse poterit commune, si legitima sit apud Ptolemaeum, ut censet Cittadinus, locorum notatio: sin illegitima non magnopere laboro, utrum Cupra sit hodie Crypta, an vero D. Benedictus; sed tribuendum arbitror nonnihil vocum similitudini. Pergit inde:) Cupra Montana vero non potest esse Domus Laureti. Nam a Ptolemaeo ponitur similiter ultra Truentum (sed vitiose) paullo, in Mediterraneis, ubi nunc Cafirum appellatur La Colonnella (concedo, si Locorum apud Ptolemaeum fideliore non egeat positu. Sed vacillans Celtus sic porro scribit) Strabo autem, Mela & Plinius videntur ponere (& recte ponunt, ut etiam Tabula Itineraria fidem facit) inter Firmanum portum & Truentum &c. Maritimam porro hanc Litoreum Cupram appellat Silius Italicus lib. Belli Punici VIII. Progrediamur.
units.tr: On the shore again, from the mouths of the Truentum and the harbour of Ascoli, there follows a castle called Crypta by the Latins, commonly Grotte. Ptolemy has two places here, Kypras [Κύπρας], Maximena [Μαξίμηαν] and Mentanas [Μεντάνας], but both are wrongly placed in the Tables on the eastern bank of the Truentum, whereas they ought to be placed on the western bank. This is clear both from Strabo's enumeration, in which he proceeds from west to east and places Cupra on the river Truentum, and from the Itinerary Table, which I append at the end of this chapter, collated with Ptolemy. Cupra Maritima, or, as it is named in the Augustan Itinerary Table I mentioned, Marina, is thought to have been there, in the place where Crypta is today; Montana, however, is where the temple dedicated to the Blessed Virgin with the surname of Loreto is. Strabo in book 5 speaks of Maritima rather than, as others think, of Montana in these words: "After Firmum (for he means this when he names the Castellum of the Firmani in Picenum), Cupra, a sanctuary, a foundation or a city of the Tyrrhenians. And it is called Cupra..." [Ἐ Φιξῆς δὲ ... Κῦπρα δ' ἱερὸν, Τυρρηνῶν ἵδρυμα ἢ πόλισμα· ἡ δ' ἐκαλεῖτο Κῦπρα]. Pintianus makes two cities out of Cupra Maritima in Ptolemy, which I would have preferred he had not done. Pomponius Mela means Maritima when he names Cupra on the coasts of Picenum together with other cities, so that Pintianus, who manufactures Maritima from the added word Senogallia, is wrong. The Cuprenses from Cupra Montana are called Montani by Pliny, as we saw before. Let us now hear, and examine, what Celsus Cittadinus Angelerius, writing from Rome to his Ortelius, says: "If Ptolemy's description is faithful" (but it labours, as I said before, under unfaithfulness), "I would compare Cupra Maritima to the place now called San Benedetto, not where Grotta is. For Ptolemy places it between the river Fortunus, now the Tronto, and the Matrinus, now the Piomba" (but wrongly, as is clear both from the enumeration of places in Strabo, the most diligent writer, with Pliny and Mela agreeing, and from the Itinerary Table, which, as it often fails in inland places, so rarely errs on the coast) "and Grotta is between the harbour of Fermo and the Truentum" (but San Benedetto is also there; and this cannot have anything in common with Cupra Marina, if Ptolemy's notation of places is correct, as Cittadini thinks; but if it is incorrect, I do not greatly trouble myself whether Cupra is today Crypta or San Benedetto, though I think some weight should be given to the similarity of the names). He goes on: "Cupra Montana cannot be the house of Loreto. For Ptolemy places it similarly beyond the Truentum" (but wrongly) "a little, inland, where it is now called Castrum Cafirum, La Colonnella" (I concede this, if Ptolemy's positions of places do not need a more faithful location. But the wavering Celtus writes further as follows:) "Strabo, Mela and Pliny seem to place" (and they place it rightly, as the Itinerary Table also confirms) "between the harbour of Fermo and the Truentum," etc. "This Cupra on the shore Silius Italicus calls Maritima, in book 8 of the Punic War." Let us go on.

units.la: Cryptae succedunt in Litore Pedassum & Civitas Nova: hinc Asoni Fluminis Ostia P. M. a Truento x.
units.tr: Next along the coast come Pedassum and Civitas Nova. From here it is 10 miles to the mouth of the river Asonus, measured from Truentum.

units.la: Ad Ostium inde exigui cujusdam Amnis sequitur Morcinum; paulloque magis intus aliud, Ripa Traiana, situ & moenibus permunitum: supra, honestum aliud Cofinianum; indeque tertio lapide Cissa, natura loci validum.
units.tr: From the mouth of a small stream the next place is Morcinum. A little further inland is another town, Ripa Traiana, well protected by its position and walls. Above it is another respectable town, Cofinianum, and three miles beyond that is Cissa, strong by the nature of its site.

units.la: Editissimi passim hic Montes Apennini, quorum in uno Castellum D. Mariae Gallicanae, S. Maria in Gallo: cui propinquus immanis horribilisque Specus Sybilla Cavernam vocant, de qua multas Adcolae narrant Fabulas, non satis, ut meis his adponantur, dignas: quod idem de Lacu Nurfino pronuncio, qui haud procul inde ad latus Montis Victoris.
units.tr: Here the Apennine mountains are everywhere very steep. On one of them is the little castle of S. Maria in Gallo, the Castle of Our Lady of Gaul. Near it is a huge and frightening cave, which the locals call the Sibyl's Cave. They tell many stories about it, but they are not worth setting down in these pages. I say the same of Lacus Nurfinus, not far from there at the foot of Mount Victor.

units.la: Intus deinde supra Pedassum occurrunt Mons Floris, Mons Novus, Mons Altus, Mons Fortis Communalium.
units.tr: Inland, above Pedassum, lie Mons Floris, Mons Novus, Mons Altus and Mons Fortis Communalium.

units.la: Sub Amnis Asoni fonte in Apenninini vertice Mons Monachus, Monte Monico, honestum Opidum; transitoque Asono Flumine in Mediterraneis Servitianum & ad D. Victoriam: supraque Mons Falco. Tum mare versus descendenti prope Asonum Mons Rubianus occurrit.
units.tr: Beneath the source of the river Asonus, on the summit of the Apennines, is Mons Monachus, Monte Monaco, a respectable town. Crossing the river Asonus inland are Servitianum and ad D. Victoriam, and above them Mons Falco. Then, going down towards the sea near the Asonus, one meets Mons Rubianus.

units.la: In ora inde Leti Mortui Fluminis Ostium, prope quod Obscura quaedam Urbis, non, ut videtur, modicae, vestigia. Adcolae Picenum, unde Regioni nomen, olim hic fuisse opinantur. De Piceno Civitate nihil apud probatos Auctores legi.
units.tr: Along the shore from there is the mouth of the river Letus Mortuus, near which are the traces of some obscure city, not a small one, as it seems. The locals believe that Picenum, from which the region takes its name, once stood here. Nothing about the city of Picenum is read in approved authors.

units.la: Per oram deinceps in Agrum Firmanorum devenitur. Eorum Urbs, Episcopalis hodie, tribus ab mari distans P. M. Firmum Cicconi ad Atticum lib. VIII, Epistola XII, Velleio Paterculo Pomponio Melae, Antonino, aliis: Φίρμον Procopio libro II & III de Bello Gothico: Φίρμον πόλις Straboni libro V. Firmum Vicenum, vitiose in Itineraria Tabula. Hodie Firmo dicitur. Hinc Firmiani Livio de Bello Punico II: vel Firmani, Plinio. Firmianum fuit Caelius Lactantius. Procopius dicit dici iter ab Auximo distare. Celenijs Romanorum accenset Velleius libro I: eaque conditione notum est Livio libro XXVIII, Veteriique Inscriptioni, quae ita habet:
units.tr: Continuing along the coast, one comes to the territory of the Firmani. Their city, now an episcopal see, is three miles from the sea. It is called Firmum by Cicero to Atticus, book VIII, letter XII; by Velleius Paterculus, Pomponius Mela, Antoninus and others; Φίρμον [Phirmon] by Procopius in books II and III of the Gothic War; and Φίρμον πόλις [Phirmon polis] by Strabo in book V. The Itinerary Table wrongly calls it Firmum Vicenum. Today it is called Fermo. From it come the Firmiani in Livy's Second Punic War, or the Firmani in Pliny. Caelius Lactantius was from Firmianum. Procopius says the road is said to be at a distance from Auximum. Velleius, in book I, counts Celenijs among the Roman colonies, and it is known by that status from Livy, book XXVIII, and from an old inscription which reads:

units.la: T ARRO. T. APPÆO. T. F. VEL ALFINIO. SECVNDO PROC. AVGVST. XX. HERED PROC. ALP. ATRECTIANAR. PRÆF.VEHICVL.SVB. PRÆF CLASS.PRÆT.RAVINN. PR ALÆ.I AVG.THRACTRIB.CCH I. ALIÆ. BRITTON. PRÆF COH. IIII.GALLOR.PATRON COLON. FLAMINI. DIVOR OMNIVM. AVGVRI II VIR.QVINQ. BIS OB. MERITA. EIVS
units.tr: To Titus Arrius Appaeus Secundus, son of Titus, of the Velina tribe, or Alfinius Secundus, procurator of Augustus for the twentieth time, heir-procurator of the Alpine Atrectian estates, prefect of the vehicles, sub-prefect of the fleet at Ravenna, prefect of the first ala of Augustan Thracians, prefect of the fourth cohort of Gauls, patron of the colony, flamen of all the deified emperors, augur, duumvir with quinquennial powers twice, on account of his merits.

units.la: Sic Colonia Augusta Firma legitur, teste Goltzio, in Galbæ Principis Nummo. In Romanorum potestate & ditione semper fuit, vsque ad Gothorum & Langbardorum in Italiam adventum: à quibus ea, scribente Procopio libro II de Bello Gothico, sub jugum redacta; ipsidemque profligatis in Cæsarum venit arbitrium: hinc ab Moglianis & Olegijs, uti legere est in antiquissimis Bononiensium Amalibus, aliquamdiu vi possessa demum Pontificum Romanorum administrata Imperio, usque ad Francisci Sfortiæ tempora; qui Vrbe occupata, Arcem in ea Gironis munitissimam ædificavit: quæ tamen non ita multo post in ditionem redijt Pontificum: sub quibus diu florens opibus & fortuna, tandem ab Oliverotijs conturbata prorsus & perniciosissimis Civium Popularium-que factionibus supra modum est adflicta & lacerata, ut nunc tota fere jaceat desolata. Hieronymus Rubeus mentionem facit in Agro Firmiano Pausuli; à quo Pausulani Plinio, Picent Populi. Leguntur & Pausula in Itineraria Tabula xv P. M. ab Firmo Piceno.
units.tr: So Colonia Augusta Firma is read, according to Goltzius, on a coin of the emperor Galba. It was always under Roman power and rule until the coming of the Goths and Lombards into Italy. Procopius, writing in book II of the Gothic War, says that it was reduced to subjection by them, and when they were defeated it came under the control of the Caesars. Then it was held for some time by force by the Moglians and Olegians, as one may read in the oldest annals of the Bolognese, and finally it was administered by the Roman Pontiffs, down to the time of Francesco Sforza. He took the city and built in it a very strong citadel, the Girone. Not long afterwards, however, it returned to the authority of the Pontiffs. Under them it flourished for a long time in wealth and fortune, but was then utterly thrown into confusion by the Oliverotti and by the most pernicious factions of the citizens and the common people. It was so beaten down and torn apart that now almost the whole place lies deserted. Hieronymus Rubeus mentions Pausulum in the territory of Firmum, from which the Pausulani (Pliny) and the Picentes people take their name. Pausula is also read in the Itinerary Table, fifteen miles from Firmum Picenum.

units.la: Sequitur in ora Tennæ Fluminis Ostium: ad quod ripa dextra Opidulum Portus Firmianus est, Porto Fermano; Portu tamen carens. Nam litus hic universum Anconem usque est vadosum. Videtur aliquando majoris fuisse usus. Nam Navale Firmi Opidi, ponit hic Strabo, cui Καστέλλον simpliciter, Castellum Firmianum est apud Antoninum & in Itineraria Tabula. Castellum Firmanorum dicitur Plinio.
units.tr: Next along the coast is the mouth of the river Tenna. On its right bank is a small town, Portus Firmianus, Porto Fermano, though it has no harbour. The whole shore from here as far as Ancona is shallow. It seems to have been of greater use at one time. Strabo here mentions the Naval of the town of Firmum, which he calls simply Καστέλλον [Kastellon]; Castellum Firmianum is found in Antoninus and in the Itinerary Table. Pliny calls it Castellum Firmanorum.

units.la: Intus cum in continenti haud procul Tenna, ad alteram ripam Opidum est D. Maria Georgiana, S. Maria in Georgio, ubi quondam Vetus Vrbs Tignum, Cæsari libro I bellorum Civilium nominatum.
units.tr: Inland, not far from the Tenna, on the opposite bank, is the town of S. Maria in Georgio, Our Lady in George, where the old city Tignum once stood, named by Caesar in book I of the Civil Wars.

units.la: Multa præterea Firmianorum ultra citraque Tennam sunt opida; inter quæ ad ipsum Amnem Mons D. Martini: & altius tertio lapide Penna. indeque fere ad quartum, juxta primos Apennini colles Mandola.
units.tr: Many other towns of the Firmiani lie on both sides of the Tenna. Among them, at the river itself, is Mons S. Martini, and higher up, three miles away, Penna. From there, almost four miles on, close to the first hills of the Apennines, is Mandola.

units.la: Post Tennam vii millibus in ora Chienti fluminis Ostia. Supra Fontem eius Seravallis visitur; altiusque Vetus Civitas & frequens in Apennini jugo, munitissimo sita loco, Camerinum. Sic cum alijs, tum Ciceroni libro viii ad Atticum epist.xii. & Antonino, in Via Flaminia locanti, dicitur: quod Καμάρινον Ptolemaeo, Camerium Tacito & Plinio; Cameria Livio & Lionysio Halicarnasseo: Camerino vernacule: Καμέρτη Straboni, ἐκ αὐτῆς τῆς ὀρείας τ' Ἰλικαρνασσοῦ ὄρεσι, addenti. Alij, in quis Ptolemaeus, hanc Vrbem in Vmbria recensent. Camerini Cives Camertes habet Plinius lib.iii. cap. xiii & Inscriptio, quæ ibi ad fores Templi, in Pasi Statuæ.
units.tr: Seven miles beyond the Tenna are the mouths of the river Chienti. Above its source lies Seravalle, and further up, on the Apennine ridge in a very strongly defended position, is the old and populous city of Camerinum. It is so called by Cicero, book VIII to Atticus, letter XII, and by Antoninus, who places it on the Flaminian Way. Ptolemy has it as Καμάρινον [Kamarinon]; Tacitus and Pliny have Camerium; Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus have Cameria; in the vernacular it is Camerino. Strabo has Καμέρτη [Kamerte], adding that it lies on the mountains of the Ilicarnassians, ἐκ αὐτῆς τῆς ὀρείας τ' Ἰλικαρνασσοῦ ὄρεσι [ek autes tes oreias t' Ilikarnassou oresi]. Others, including Ptolemy, count this city in Umbria. Pliny, book III, chapter XIII, has the citizens of Camerinum as Camertes, and so does an inscription which stands at the doors of a temple, on the statue of Pasius.

units.la: IMP. CÆSARI L. SEPTIMIO SEVERO PIO PERTINACI AVG. ARABIC. ADIAB. PARTHIC. MAX. BRIT. MAX. TR. POT. XVIII. IMP. XII. COS. III. P.P. CÆLESTI. LIVS. ISPVL GENTIA. IN. ALTERNAM SALVTEM. ATQVE GLORIAM. IVRE. A. QVO. SOLDERIS. SIBI CONSECRATO CAMERTE
units.tr: To the Emperor Caesar Lucius Septimius Severus Pius Pertinax Augustus, Arabicus, Adiabenicus, Parthicus Maximus, Britannicus Maximus, holder of tribunician power for the eighteenth time, acclaimed Imperator twelve times, consul three times, father of his country; the Camertine people, to Caelestis (?) Livius Ispulus (?), for eternal safety and glory, by the right from which the soldiers... consecrated to himself at Camerte

units.la: Camertium frequens mentio apud Livium cum alibi, tum libro ix & xxiv, Res ab ipsis gestas commemoratum. Camertem ab Ambro & Patre, id est ab Re Mutina & Arimino vocari: Silius Italicus libro viii. Coloniam Romanam fuisse ab Romulo Pastoque regibus tradit Onuphrius Panvinius in Imperio Romano. Hanc Urbem Episcopatum habet, sub Tucanis multo diu obtinuit familia Varranentis.
units.tr: Camertes is frequently mentioned in Livy, both in other places and in books 9 and 24, where the deeds done by them are recounted. The Camertes are called from Ambrus and Patrus, that is, from the places Mutina and Ariminum. Silius Italicus in book 8 says it was a Roman colony founded by the kings Romulus and Pastor, as Onuphrius Panvinius also reports in his Imperium Romanum. This city has a bishopric; for a long time under the Tucani it was held by the family of the Varranentes.

units.la: Ad Hadriam, qui in Ghienum se encerat, Camelum est Amni cognomen; & quo loco mittentur, Camelum.
units.tr: Near the Hadria, which encloses itself in Ghienum, Camelus is the surname of the river; and at the place where they are sent, Camelus.

units.la: Sunt & alii prope Clienum loca, Ad S. Iulianum, ad D. Iustum, Mons Granarius. Huius Incolæ putarunt olim tutte qui Aregnati Plinio, in eius antiquorum Libris legantur Eregnati. Eregnatum esse Caesarem habet. Eiam Liber Limitum. Altius propter Apenninum Colles ad D. Ouarfum est, interiusque Serre Alto infra quam Vetus Urbs Atha. Sic Aeolia, tenet Candrochrum, quæ Atin Atha Plinio, Οἴκοι Σαλαρια forte Σαλαρία Ptolemæo, in cuius translatis ab his, ab illis corrupte Codicibus Ipsa Ruheria vocatur: Ruheria memorandus. Procopio libro ii de Bello Gothico, Vels Salvia Ancomo; Vele Salvia denique, auferendo eatus, ut solet, in Itinerario Tabula. Hunc, ut tuli, Salvium apud alios Auctores. Dirimit, ut tenuit Procopius, Aborienus Godorum sex; addens arae sua paucas eius superstitiose reliquias, cum modica Porta. Nunc Theatrorum vagorum aliorumque Operum vestigia ibi vestiga.
units.tr: There are also other places near Clienum: Ad S. Iulianum, Ad D. Iustum, Mons Granarius. The inhabitants of this place were once thought to be those whom Pliny calls Aregnati; in the books of the ancients they are read as Eregnati. Caesar has Eregnatum. Also the Liber Limitum. Higher up, on account of the Apennine hills, is Ad D. Ouarfum, and more inland Serre Alto, below which lies the old city Atha. So Aeolia holds Candrochrum, which is Atin Atha in Pliny, and perhaps Salaria Ptolemy's Οἴκοι Σαλαρια; in the translations of these and the corrupt manuscripts of those, it is itself called Ruheria: Ruheria is worth recalling. In Procopius, book 2 of the Gothic War, Vels Salvia Ancomo; finally Vele Salvia, with the ending removed, as is usual, in the Tabula of the Itinerary. This Salvium, as I have carried it, is found in other authors. Procopius says that Aborienus, the sixth of the Goths, divided it, adding a few superstitious remnants of its altar, with a modest gate. Now traces of theatres, baths and other works are to be seen there.

units.la: Viterius secundum Anaem mirum trium runa occurrunt nobilissimi quomam Camerti Caesaris.
units.tr: Further on, according to Anaem, three wonderful... very noble men of Camerte Caesar occur.

units.la: Ad Iteram Chienu ripam Mons Cassianus, paulloque post Morum, inde tertio lapide Marnura, ob Helviæ Reginæ aut Blondus interitum una cum Reginæ comitæ: frequens, totaque regione Cancellariatus Sede Marchiæ Legati celeberrimi. Haber & Episcopatum & Academiam, sed non adeo nobilem. Altius ad quintum Lapidem Mons Loanus est, honestum. Opidum, quondam ab Francisco Sforzia, ut Blondus notat, directum. Succedit Atantia, præsignis Varranorum Vicus: supraque hunc Tolentinum Vetus Opidum: cuius incolæ Tolentinates; qui D. Nicolai Tolentinæ Ossa apud se servari affirmant. Nobilitarunt eum suo Francisco Pricalphum, Viri litterati; Nicolaus item Matruus & Ioannes Franciscus cognomine Tolentinas, Militiae gloria Rebuplicæ gentis magn. Ternoo supra Tolentinum lapide Castellum est Ie fortunæ. Spectantur inde ad Asinum Flavium P. Mariæ Cassianæ Castellum, S. Maria in Castro; & ha d procul Mari nobilissimum Opidum trequenterque in Monte Cronus Nora, quæ Neuma Plinio appellatur, ut Pamphilo videtur.
units.tr: At the river Itera on the Chienu bank is Mons Cassianus, and a little after Morum; from there, at the third milestone, Marnura, because of the death of Queen Helvia, or as Blondus says, together with the queen's companions; a frequent place, and in the whole region the seat of a chancellery, where the very famous legates of the Marches are. It has both a bishopric and an academy, but not so noble. Higher up, at the fifth milestone, is Mons Loanus, an honest town, once founded by Francesco Sforza, as Blondus notes. Next comes Atantia, a distinguished village of the Varranes; and above it the old town of Tolentinum, whose inhabitants are the Tolentinates, who affirm that the bones of St. Nicholas of Tolentino are kept among them. They were ennobled by their Francesco Pricalpus, a man of letters; likewise Nicolaus Matruus and Johannes Franciscus, surnamed Tolentinas, of military glory for the republic of the Gentiles. Three miles above Tolentinum at Ternoo is a castle of Ie Fortuna. From there one sees, toward the Asinus Flavius, the castle of P. Mariae Cassianae, S. Maria in Castro; and from afar, the very noble town of Mari, and often on Mount Cronus Nora, which Pamphilus thinks is called Neuma by Pliny.

units.la: Hanc tam in Ora Flumen Potentia, juxta cuius ostium Urbs olim fuit cognominis Potentia, inter præcipua Picenti Opida memorata. Potentia Ciceroni pro Plancio, Plinio libro iii, Paterculo lib. 1. Antonino; Ηοτεντία Straboni, & Ptolemæo, Pollentia: Livio lib. xxxi, Potentia in Itineraria Tabula, & apud Orosium libro ii, cap. xxvii. Potens a S. Lepido interpretatur Ligerus: Potentia a hoc tractu hodie vocari, legitur apud Franciscum Pamphilum, xxx P. M. ab Mari Hadriatico. Volaterranus lib. vi Commentar. Urb. Potentiam Traianam scribit dictam: sed Nororia & Tegeiza duae sunt Ptolemaeo Urbes: illa ad Litus; haec in Mediterraneis. Colonia eo deductam eodem anno cum Pisauro tradunt iidem Livius & Velleius Paterculus. A Pollentia Pollentini Plinio. Pollentinos Agros hinc etiam habet Prudentius lib. ii. contra Symmachum. Lego in Itineraria Tabula, novem P. M. a Polentia Pausulas: hinc Pausulani apud Plinium.
units.tr: On this coast is the river Potentia, near whose mouth there was once a city of the same name, Potentia, mentioned among the chief towns of the Picentes. Potentia is mentioned by Cicero in the speech for Plancius, by Pliny in book 3, by Paterculus in book 1, by Antoninus; Ηοτεντία by Strabo and Ptolemy, Pollentia by Livy in book 31; Potentia in the Itinerary Table, and in Orosius book 2, chapter 27. Ligerus interprets Potens as from S. Lepidus; that it is today called Potentia from this stretch is read in Francesco Pamphilo, 30 miles from the Adriatic Sea. Volaterranus, book 6 of his Commentaries on the City, writes that it was called Potentia Trajana; but Nororia and Tegeiza are two cities of Ptolemy: the former on the coast, the latter inland. Livy and Velleius Paterculus themselves report that a colony was led there in the same year as Pisaurum. Pliny has Pollentini from Pollentia. Prudentius in book 2 against Symmachus also has the Pollentine fields from this. I read in the Itinerary Table that Pausulae is nine miles from Pollentia: hence Pausulani in Pliny.

units.la: Intus Potentia Fluvius sub primis Apennini collibus ad duo milllia remotum habet Montecellum: infraque Montem D. Honorati, opidum Marchianorum: supra inter colles Apennino finitimos nobile Opidum Sanseverinum, ex antiquae Urbis Septempeda ruinis, ut volunt Volaterranus, Leander Albertus, Fr. Pamphilus, Caesar Baronius, & alij. Septempeda Antonino; Σεπτέμπεδα Straboni & Ptolomaeo. Inde Septempedani Plinio. Hoc opidum, ut tradunt aevi medij Scriptores, everterunt Langbardi.
units.tr: Inland from Potentia, the river has Montecellum, two miles away, at the foot of the first hills of the Apennines; below it Mont St. Honorat, a town of the Marchians; above, among the hills bordering the Apennines, the noble town Sanseverino, from the ruins of the ancient city Septempeda, as Volaterranus, Leander Alberti, Fr. Pamphilus, Caesar Baronius and others think. Septempeda in Antoninus; Σεπτέμπεδα in Strabo and Ptolemy. From it come the Septempedani of Pliny. This town, as the writers of the Middle Ages relate, was destroyed by the Lombards.

units.la: Dehinc in ora Ostia sunt Musonis, cujus utroque latere opida sunt multa. Intus vicinum illi Ricinetum, quod Reccanato, vel Recanati, vel Ricanati Italis hodie, expiscopatus clarum titulo. Ricinetum Blondus dictam ait, quod quum Gothi Helvetiam Ricinam, Opidum ab Imp. Helvio Pertinace refectum, Coloniisque instauratum excidissent, deletae Urbis Incolae in hoc longum Collis jugum migrantes Urbem condiderint, Ricinetum exigua mutatione in Ricina memoriam appellantes. Ab antiqua Ricina, cujus etiam mentio in Itineraria Tabula. Plinio sunt Ricinenses. Marmor apud Maceratam repertum sic vidit, legit, & exscriptit Dionysius Harduinus, uti testatur in Thesauro suo Smetius:
units.tr: Next, on the coast, are the mouths of the Musone, on each side of which there are many towns. Inland, near it, is Ricinetum, which today the Italians call Recanato, or Recanati, or Ricanati, a bishopric famous by its title. Blondus says Ricinetum was so called because when the Goths had destroyed Helvia Ricina, a town rebuilt by the emperor Helvius Pertinax and restored with colonists, the inhabitants of the destroyed city, migrating to this long ridge of the hill, founded a city and, with a slight change, named it Ricinetum in memory of Ricina. From the old Ricina, which is also mentioned in the Itinerary Table, come the Ricinenses of Pliny. Dionysius Harduinus saw, read and copied a marble found near Macerata in this form, as Smetius attests in his Thesaurus:

units.la: IMP. CAESARI L. VERI. AVG. FIL. DIVI. FIL. NEP. DIVI HADRIANI. PRON. DIVI TRAIANI. PARTH. ABNEP. DIVI. NERVAE. ADNEPOTI L. SEPTIMIO. SEVERO PIO. PERTINACI. AVG. ARABI C. ADIAB. PARTHIC MAXIMO. P. M. TRIBUNIC POTEST. XVII. IMP. XII. COS. III P. P. COLONIA. HELVIA. RICINA CONDITORI. SVO
units.tr: To the Emperor Caesar L. Verus Augustus, son of the deified son, grandson of the deified Hadrian, great-grandson of the deified Trajan, Parthicus, great-great-grandson of the deified Nerva, adoptive descendant; to Lucius Septimius Severus Pius Pertinax Augustus, Arabicus, Adiabenicus, Parthicus Maximus, Pontifex Maximus, holding tribunician power for the 17th time, acclaimed Imperator for the 12th time, consul for the 3rd time, Father of his Country; the Colony of Helvia Ricina to its founder, its own

units.la: Ricinetum Emporium est celeberrimum, venientibus eo bis ad Nundinas, statis anni temporibus, ex tota Europa Asiaque pleraque Mercatoribus. Stupenda Helviae Ricinae vestigia passim in itinere per agros monstrantur; inter alia lateritium Amphitheatrum ingens in ripa fluminis Potentiae, aliaque magnorum aedificiorum rudera.
units.tr: Ricinetum is a very famous market town, to which merchants come twice a year for the fairs, at fixed seasons, from almost all of Europe and Asia. Astonishing remains of Helvia Ricina are shown here and there along the road through the fields; among them a huge brick amphitheatre on the bank of the river Potentia, and other ruins of great buildings.

units.la: Inter Septempedam & Auximum quod sequitur Trea locatur ab Antonino; quae Τέγεια Ptolemaeo: hinc Trajanenses Plinio, quos pro Traiacensibus putat reponendos Pintianus.
units.tr: Between Septempeda and Auximum, the next place is Trea, which Antoninus places; it is Tegeia [Τέγεια] in Ptolemy. Hence Pliny has the Trajanenses, whom Pintianus thinks should be replaced by the Traiacenses.

units.la: Inter Ricinetum & Mare, haud procul ab Musone Fanum adparet in edito colle D. Mariae Lauretanae, vulgo S. Maria di Loreto; fortissimis muris cinctum, propugnaculis, turribus, fossis, bellicisque machinis, opera praecipue Alexandri VI, Julii II, Sixtique V probe munitum cum Vico, quem fere Caupones & Strabularij colunt ad Convenas, quiex omni Europa Religionis causa votis solvendis eo catervatim confluunt, excipiendos. Delubrum, & quod in eo est, arcanum conclave, unde & a quo in ea loca advectum, quae sit intervitendi Fani ratio, aliaque multis verbis describunt Horatius Turselinus Societatis Iesu in Historia Lauretana, na, Baptista Mantuanus initio historiæ, Leander Albertus in Piceno, Laurentius Schraderus, Franciscus Schottus, & alij; ideoque eain re pluribus Lectorem non morabor. Putat Leander, ut ante monui, olim hoc loco fuisse Vrbem, quæ Κίνγα μοντύνα Ptolemæo. Nonnulli quoque Potentiam, de qua supra dixi, hic designant. Lauretana dicitur ab Laures Silva, quæ olim hic fuisse perhibetur. Episcopatus flo- ret dignitate.
units.tr: Between Ricinetum and the sea, not far from the Musone, there appears on a high hill the Fanum of D. Mariae Lauretanae, commonly called S. Maria di Loreto. It is surrounded by very strong walls, and well fortified with bulwarks, towers, ditches and war engines, chiefly the work of Alexander VI, Julius II and Sixtus V, together with the village which innkeepers and tavern keepers mostly inhabit near the Convenae. People flock there in crowds from all over Europe to fulfil their vows for religion's sake, and must be received. The shrine, and the secret chamber within it, whence and by whom it was brought to that place, and the manner of visiting the sanctuary, and other matters, are described at length by Horatius Turselinus of the Society of Jesus in his Historia Lauretana, by Baptista Mantuanus at the start of his history, by Leander Albertus in his Piceno, by Laurentius Schraderus, Franciscus Schottus and others; so I will not detain the reader further on this point. Leander thinks, as I said earlier, that a town once stood on this spot, which Ptolemy calls Kinga Montuna [Κίνγα μοντύνα]. Some also identify here the Potentia I mentioned above. Lauretana is so called from the Laures Silva (Laurel Wood), which is said to have once grown here. The bishopric flourishes in dignity.

units.la: Ad Mutonem porro in colle, cujus radices adluit Amnis, x ab Mari milliaribus, antiqua visitur & Episcopalis Civitas Auximum, quæ vulgo Osimo, Auximum Lucano, Velleio & Antonino; Ausimum Itinerariæ Tabulæ; Αὔξιμον Plutarcho: Αὔξιμον Straboni; Oximum Livio libro xli; Ausimas apud Baldum de Limitibus. Scribit Procopius Metropolin etiam Romanis dicta solitam; & ab Ionico xxc distare Stadiis. Hinc Auximates Plinio, in cujus nonnullis Codicibus corrupte Ansinates. Colonia adcenitur apud eundem Velleium Paterculum. Meminerunt, ut Colonia, multæ quæ ibi Inscriptiones: inter quas nobilis illa, quæ & aliorum eo tractu, locorum facit mentionem: M. OPPIO. CAPITONI Q. TAMVDIO. Q.F. T.N T. TRON. VEL. ANINIO. SEVERO EQVO. PVBL. IVDICI. SELECT EX. V DECVR. TRIB. LEG. VIII AVG. IRAE. FABR. PATRONO COL. AVXIM. ET. COL. ASIS IT. MVNIC. NVMANAT ORDO. ET. PLEBS. TREIENS PATRONO. MVNICIPI CVRATORI. DATO. AB IMP. ANTONINO. AVG L. D. D. D
units.tr: Further on, towards the Musone, on a hill whose foot is washed by the river, ten miles from the sea, stands the ancient episcopal city Auximum, commonly called Osimo. Auximum in Lucan, Velleius and Antoninus; Ausimum in the Itinerary Table; Auximon [Αὔξιμον] in Plutarch and Strabo; Oximum in Livy, book 41; Ausimas in Baldus de Limitibus. Procopius writes that it was used to be called the metropolis even by the Romans, and that it is 90 stades from Ancona. Hence Auximates in Pliny, in some manuscripts of whom corruptly Ansinates. It is mentioned as a Colonia in Velleius Paterculus. Many inscriptions there also mention it as a Colonia, among them the noted one which also makes mention of other places in that district: To Marcus Oppius Capito, Quintus Tamudius, son of Quintus, of the Tribe Tromentina, Titus Aninius Severus, equestrian, public judge, chosen from the five decuries, tribune of the Eighth Legion Augusta, Iraean, Fabian, patron of the colony of Auximum and of the colony of Asisium, Munic. Numanas; the order and the people of Treia (appointed by the Emperor Antoninus Augustus), patron of the municipality, curator. Dedicated by decree of the decurions.

units.la: Addam & Fragmentum hoc: III VIR. IN. COL AVXIM. BIS
units.tr: I will add also this fragment: Triumvir in the colony of Auximum, twice.

units.la: Plinius libro xi, natur. histor. Auximati Cafeo inter laudata genera gloriam tribuit. Summam loci Antiquitatem testantur passim plurima nuper reperta hic Epitaphia & Elogia. Occuparat Auximum, patriæ Vrbis, principatum superioribus annis Bocalinus Guzonius: sed gravissima, Ioannis Galeatij Sforziæ, Mediolani Ducis, ope, pressus obtidione tandem se suaque omnia Pontifici dedere est coactus.
units.tr: Pliny, in book 11 of his Natural History, gives Auximate cheese its praise among the famous kinds. Many inscriptions and eulogies recently found here everywhere attest the great antiquity of the place. Some years ago Bocalinus Guzonius had seized the leadership of Auximum, the native city; but, pressed by a very grave siege with the help of Giovanni Galeazzo Sforza, Duke of Milan, he was at last forced to surrender himself and all his possessions to the Pope.

units.la: Supra Auximum sub Apennini collibus, in monte tamen, offert se Cingulum ad Musonem. Meminerunt Cicero ad Atticum, Cæsar in libris Bellorum Civilium, & alij. Hinc Cingulani Plinio. Blondus Cimbalum vocat. Hodie Cingole. Condidit T. Labienus, qui C. Cæsaris Proconsulis Legatus in Gallia longo bello tantum libi corraserat ex prædis divitiarum, ut Opidum hoc privata impensa condiderit: cuius imaginem numis argenteis expressam, cum Conditoris Titulo, vidi apud Cl.V. Abrahamum Gorlærum, Amicum meum, cui stupendus, cum aliarum rerum, tum Veterum Numismatum Thesaurus.
units.tr: Above Auximum, beneath the hills of the Apennines, yet on a mountain, there lies Cingulum by the Musone. Cicero in his letter to Atticus, Caesar in his books on the Civil War, and others mention it. Hence Cingulani in Pliny. Blondus calls it Cimbalum. Today it is Cingole. It was founded by T. Labienus, who as lieutenant of C. Caesar the proconsul in Gaul had gained so much wealth from the spoils of a long war that he founded this town at his own private expense. I have seen its image stamped on silver coins, with the founder's title, in the collection of my friend the distinguished Abraham Gorlaeus, whose treasury of ancient coins, as well as of other things, is remarkable.

units.la: Inter Cingulum & Auximum honestum est opidum Staphilum infraque inter Colles Montemque Apennino vicinum Castellum Vetus Rapirum.
units.tr: Between Cingulum and Auximum lies the respectable town of Staphylum, and below, among the hills and close to the Apennines, the old fortress of Rapirum.

units.la: Deinceps in ora iii P.M ab Osilio Mutonis Vrbs fuit Humana. Sic Melæ dicta, quæ Numana Plinio, Antonino, Itinerariæ Tabulæ, & Silio Italico lib. viii, cui Scopiosa audit: Νούμανα Ptolemæo. Ab Siculis conditam notat Plinius, Municipium appellat Inscriptio, quæ paullo ante, ubi de Auximo, polita. Humana hodie vocatur, Episcopali dignitate celebris.
units.tr: Next, on the coast, three miles from Osilium, was the city of Humana on the Musone. It is called thus by Mela, and is Numana in Pliny, Antoninus, the Itinerary Table and Silius Italicus, book 8, who calls it Scopiosa; Noumana [Νούμανα] in Ptolemy. Pliny notes that it was founded by the Sicilians, and an inscription, which was set up a little earlier where he speaks of Auximum, calls it a municipium. Today it is called Humana and is noted for its episcopal dignity.

units.la: Non procul hinc juxta littus in Promontorio Anconitano Sirolum est Opidum, Vino, quod Plinius Anconitani nomine laudat, nobile. Altero ejus Promontorij latere Castellum Ficardum est.
units.tr: Not far from here, beside the shore on the Ancona promontory, lies the town of Sirolum, famous for its wine, which Pliny praises under the name of Anconitani. On the other side of that promontory is the fortress of Ficardum.

units.la: Sub Cumero Promontorio, de quo alibi, qua se in Mare torquet, Vrbs Episcopalis jacet Ancona. Sic Catiari lib. 1 & alibi, Tacito libro 111 Annal. Plinio, Antonino, & aliis: quae Αγκων Ptolemaeo, Procopio lib. 111 de bello Gothico, Lucano lib. 11, Silio lib. v 111. & Itinerariae Tabulae, ubi Ancone scribitur auferendi casu; Hodie nomen retinet: quod impositum Vrbi ab orae ibi flexu, Cubiti formam, ut Strabo, Plinius & Mela testantur, efficiente. Nam is Αγκων Graecis dicitur. Oppolita Promontorio Cumero, Mari simoque Portu clauditur a Septemtrione: Portis porro, Propugnaculis, Murisque undique munitissima, Pontificum praesertim Romanorum industria. Preticum fuit Italis Gallisque discrimen: Nam, ut Mela tradit, Italia hic quondam inebatur: incipiebantque Galli Senones cum Gallia Togata. In ratione Munitionis convenit illi cum Massilia Galliarum, Ragusiaque Dalmatiae. Strabo, Plinius, Solinus Graecum Vrbem, & ab Syracusanis, Dionysij tyrannidem fugientibus, conditam memorant: unde & ab Juvenale Dorica nuncupatur. Portum inprimis habet, qui natura arteque validus: aditu peropportunus: multarum navium capax, ab Trajano Cæsare exstructus: adjecto etiam Arcu magni operis Qualis ejus fuerit structura, videre est in ejus Principis Numismis. Propugnaculis Vrbs sex superbit; quae vulgo Il Ribellino del Porto, Il Cavalliero di S. Stephano, La Fortezza del Cassaro, Il Cavalliero della Porta del Calamo, Il Ribellino di S. Agostino, Il Lazaretto: omnia suis tormentis bene instructa. Est ibi Domus, quae vulgo della Farina, quam incolunt qui ab Legato Pontificio in consilium adhibentur, nobiles Anconitani, quorum Magistratus tres durat menses. Continua Graecorum, Illyricorum, Pannonum, imo totius Europae mercatura praesignis, viis longissimis, sed angustis, frequens habitatur. Genuit Augustinum, Ordinis Eremitarum, Theologum; Franciscum & Nicolaum Stalamontios, lureconsultos; Cyriacum, singularem Antiquitatis indagatorem. Sub Imperio maxime floruit Romanorum: a quibus Colonia co ductam, paret ex Plinij libro 111. natur. historiae cap. xiii, Libroque de Limitibus: item ex Basi cujusdam Statuae, quam C. SALLIO ARISTANETO V. C. multis honoribus illustri (ut ex ipsa manifestum Inscriptione, quae Romae in Palatio della Capranica) posuerunt.
units.tr: Under the Cumerus promontory, which I shall discuss elsewhere, where the land bends into the sea, lies the episcopal city of Ancona. So it is called in Catiari, book 1 and elsewhere, in Tacitus, Annals book 3, Pliny, Antoninus and others; it is Ancon [Αγκων] in Ptolemy, in Procopius, book 3 of the Gothic War, in Lucan book 2, Silius book 8, and in the Itinerary Table, where it is written Ancone in the ablative case. It keeps the name today, which was given to the city by the bend of the shore there, forming the shape of an elbow (cubit), as Strabo, Pliny and Mela attest. For the Greeks call the elbow Ancon [Αγκων]. Facing the Cumerus promontory, it is enclosed by the sea and a safe harbour on the north side; it is also most strongly fortified on every side with gates, bulwarks and walls, chiefly through the diligence of the Roman Pontiffs. It was once the boundary between the Italians and the Gauls: for, as Mela relates, Italy ended here, and the Gallic Senones began beyond it with Gallia Togata. In its fortifications it resembles Massilia in Gaul and Ragusa in Dalmatia. Strabo, Pliny and Solinus record that it was a Greek city, founded by Syracusans fleeing the tyranny of Dionysius; hence Juvenal calls it Dorica. It has above all a harbour, strong by nature and by art, very convenient in its approach and able to hold many ships, built by the Emperor Trajan; an arch of great workmanship was also added. What its structure was like can be seen on the coins of that emperor. The city boasts six bulwarks: Il Ribellino del Porto, Il Cavalliero di S. Stephano, La Fortezza del Cassaro, Il Cavalliero della Porta del Calamo, Il Ribellino di S. Agostino, Il Lazaretto, all well equipped with artillery. There is a building which is commonly called della Farina, inhabited by the noble Anconitans who are summoned to advise the papal legate; their magistracy lasts three months. Renowned for its continuous trade with the Greeks, Illyrians, Pannonians, and indeed all of Europe, it is densely inhabited, with very long but narrow streets. It produced Augustinus, a theologian of the Order of Hermits, Franciscus and Nicolaus Stalamontius, jurists, and Cyriacus, an outstanding investigator of antiquity. It flourished especially under Roman rule, by which it was made a colony, as is clear from Pliny, book 3, Natural History, chapter 13, and from the book de Limitibus; also from the base of a statue which, to C.
