Sallius Aristaneus, a distinguished man of many honours (as the inscription itself, which is in Rome in the Palazzo della Capranica, makes clear), they set up.

units.la: DECVRIONES. ET. PLEBS COLONIAE. ANCONITANORVM. PROP. TVR. HVMANITATEM. ABSTINENTIAM. EFFICACIAM
units.tr: THE DECURIONS AND COMMONALTY OF THE COLONY OF ANCONA. PRAISED FOR HUMANITY, ABSTINENCE AND EFFICACY

units.la: Postea, quemadmodum variorum docent Historiae, praecipue Procopij libro 111, Blondique libro v, vii & xi, ab Gothis diu obsessa, non modo expugnari plane non potuit, sed & Classis Gothicae Navium xlvii Victrix evasit: ex quibus vix decem fuga sunt elapsae, ceteris omnibus aut captis, aut in mari submersis. Sequenti deinceps aetate Langbardorum Dominatum sustinuit, qui Sedem in ea Marchionatus habuerunt. Iisdelectis profligatisque, in fidem se dedit Caesarum Germanicorum. Ab Saracenis hinc incenta, at non ita multo post instaurata, & populo opibusque aucta, suae facta est potestatis: salvo tamen Clientelari jure Pontifici Romano: sub cujus imperio postea, omnino esse coepit, arte doloque Bernardini Barbae, Episcopi Catalensis, & Ludovici Gonzagae, Clementis vii Legionum Praefecti. Ager suburbicarius cum rerum omnium, tum Vini generosi, Straboni Plinioque celebrati, est fertilis. Jam quid apud Antoninum, inter Anconam & Penogalliam sit Ultra Anconam, non video: nisi locus censendus, qui venientibus ex Sammitibus ultra Anconam. Quicumque habendus sit, fuit certe haud procul, Casa Cremata.
units.tr: Afterwards, as various histories show, especially Procopius book 3 and Biondo books 5, 7 and 11, Ancona was besieged for a long time by the Goths. It not only could not be taken, but it became victorious over the Gothic fleet of forty-seven ships. Of these, scarcely ten escaped by flight, all the others being either captured or sunk in the sea. In the following age it endured the rule of the Lombards, who held the seat of their march there. When these had been driven out and overthrown, it gave itself into the faith of the German Caesars. Then, though it was laid waste by the Saracens and restored not long after, it grew in people and wealth and became its own master, saving however the client right owed to the Roman Pontiff. Under his rule it afterwards began to be wholly subject, by the art and deceit of Bernardino Barba, Bishop of Catalensis, and Ludovico Gonzaga, prefect of the legions of Clement VII. The suburbicarian territory is fertile in all things, and especially in noble wine, celebrated by Strabo and Pliny. Now what Ultra Anconam is in Antoninus, between Ancona and Penogallia, I do not see, unless it is to be taken as a place, namely the one for those coming from the Sammites beyond Ancona. Whatever place it is to be held to be, it was certainly not far away: Casa Cremata.

units.la: Finiebatur, uti constat ex Strabone, Plinio, Melaque, Picenum olim Aesi Amne, qui nunc Fiume Esino dicitur: & occurrebant ad Occidentaliorem ejusdem Amnis ripam Umbri, & inde Senones. Erat enim Umbria, quod clarum cum ex aliis tum ex Strabone, quasi duplex, Cis-Apennina & Trans-Apennina: illa ad Inferum erat Mare, separatim capite xxiv explicanda: hæc ad Mare Superum ab Ravennatum agris ad Æsin usque pertinebat, nobilia hoc situ amplectens loca, Sarsinam, Arminum, Senam, Camerinum, Montem Cignum, Sentinum, Metaurum Amnem, Fanum Fortunæ cum Æsi Flumine, ubi primos Italiæ terminos statuunt veteres, ut alibi dictum, Scriptores. Umbri igitur Transf. Apennini ex notatione Strabonis inter Æsin & Ravennates. Iam cum Plinio etiam Ptolemæus Tractum omnem inter Ancona seu Amnem Æsin & Rubiconem: Senonum Gallorum esse scribit: discrepans tamen ab eodem Plinio, quum Gallium Togatam inter Rubiconem & Trebiam Amnes concludit: Plinio Senones ipsos Galliam vocante Togatam. Quum igitur Marka An contana se extendat ad Foliam usque Fluvium, qui antiquis Isaurus, necessarium erit, ut etiam Umbres de Transf. Apennini loquor, Senonesque, quatenus inter Æsin Isaurumque sedes habuerunt, in eadem Marka explicemus; reliqua ipsorum ultra Isaurum loca Romanula datari: ut ipsorum hic fines sint Æsis cum Piceno ab exortu, Isaurus cum parte Senonum, quæ nunc Romanula, ab occasu; ab meridie Apenninus, qui Umbres Cas. Apennines ab his, itemque ab Senonibus diuidit, ab Septemtrione denique Sinu claudantur Hadriatico. Addam ad Hadriaticum Mare ponere etiam Umbres Athenæum & Stephanum, cuius hæc sunt verba: Ὁ μὲν Ἀδρίας, ἦ ... (sic enim legendum pro Ἴαχωκ.) Ἀσχολ, καὶ Ὁ μεγάλ. Sic Silius Italicus lib. viii: —Cari se ventente) Montibus Vmbri, Hos Æsi Sapessque lætant.
units.tr: As is clear from Strabo, Pliny and Mela, Picenum was once bounded by the River Aesis, which is now called the Fiume Esino. On the western bank of the same river the Umbri came up to it, and beyond them the Senones. For Umbria, as is clear from other writers and from Strabo, was as it were double, Cis-Apennina and Trans-Apennina. The former lay towards the Lower Sea and is to be explained separately in chapter 24. The latter lay towards the Upper Sea and extended from the fields of Ravenna as far as the Aesis, embracing in this position the noted places Sarsina, Ariminum, Sena, Camerinum, Mons Cyneus, Sentinum, the River Metaurus, and Fanum Fortunae with the River Aesis, where the ancient writers, as stated elsewhere, set the first boundaries of Italy. The Umbri of Trans-Apennine Umbria, then, according to Strabo's indication, lay between the Aesis and the Ravennates. Now with Pliny, Ptolemy also writes that the whole tract between Ancona, or the River Aesis, and the Rubicon belonged to the Senones of Gaul, though he differs from the same Pliny when he includes Gallia Togata between the Rubicon and Trebia rivers, whereas Pliny calls the Senones themselves Gallia Togata. Since, then, the March of Ancona extends as far as the River Foglia, which the ancients called the Isaurus, it will be necessary, as I speak also of the Umbri of Trans-Apennine Umbria, to treat of the Senones too, insofar as they had their seats between the Aesis and the Isaurus, in this same March. Their other places beyond the Isaurus are to be assigned to Romagna. So their boundaries here are: the Aesis with Picenum on the east; the Isaurus with the part of the Senones which is now Romagna on the west; the Apennine on the south, which divides the Umbri of Cis-Apennine from these and also from the Senones; and finally on the north the Adriatic Gulf encloses them. I add that Athenaeus and Stephanus also place the Umbri on the Adriatic Sea, and Stephanus's words are these: "The Adriatic, ... (for so it should be read instead of Iachok) Ascholi, and the great ..." [Ὁ μὲν Ἀδρίας, ἦ ... (sic enim legendum pro Ἴαχωκ.) Ἀσχολ, καὶ Ὁ μεγάλ.] So too Silius Italicus, book 8: "The Umbri, dwelling on the mountains dear to him, rejoice in the Aesis and in Sapis."

units.la: Apud Isidorum etiam lib. xiiii Etymolog. cap. iiii Umbria in jugis Apennini Montis sita, in parte Italiæ, iuxta Meridiem. Vniuersim igitur de Umbris postea, ubi ce Apenninus angustiore loco dicturus, speciatim hic indicabo Transf. Apennininarum.
units.tr: In Isidore also, book 14 of the Etymologies, chapter 4: Umbria, situated on the ridges of the Apennine mountains, in a part of Italy, near the south. I will speak of the Umbri in general later, where I am about to describe the Apennine in its narrower part; here I will indicate in particular the Trans-Apennine places.

units.la: Primum ad Anconitani Agri fines in ora Æsis est, qui Fiumesino hodie de quo alibi. Propter huius Ostium Arx est (Rocca vulgo) ab Anconitanis ad Agri finitimi tutelam condita, tormentisque contra Prædonum excursiones instructa. Sequitur in ora inde Casa Bruciata, Cremanam Latini dicunt, diuersoria Taberna, fortissimo munita muro propter Piratarum Turcarumque metum. In continenti tum quingentis ab Æsi passibus opidum est præcelso in monte Sanquirican: ulterius que ex aduersum Fabrianum: inde sexto lapide Matelica; cuius Incolæ Plinio libro iii cap. xiv Matelicate in Sexta Regione cum Umbris recensentur. Matelica nullus omnino, vel in publicis vel in priuatis ædificiis, cuius. Regitur a quadam Othonum familia ex qua erant xxii adeoque idem ius pertinebat, sed administrandi honor ad raru maiorem temper deferri soler.
units.tr: First, at the border of the territory of Ancona on the coast of the Aesis, is what today is Fiumesino, about which elsewhere. Near its mouth there is a citadel (commonly called the Rocca), built by the Anconitans to guard the neighbouring territory and equipped with artillery against the raids of pirates. Next along the coast is Casa Bruciata, which the Latins call Cremana, an inn, strongly fortified with a wall because of the fear of pirates and Turks. Inland, five hundred paces from the Aesis, there is a town on the very high mountain of Sanquirico; further on, opposite it, Fabriano; then six miles off, Matelica, whose inhabitants are listed by Pliny in book 3, chapter 14, among the Umbri of the Sixth Region. Matelica has no ... either in public or in private buildings ... It is ruled by a certain family of the Ottoni, of which there were twenty-two, and the same right applied, but the honour of administering was usually conferred on a few.

units.la: Laterc tum, qua Gualdum Umbriæ opidum iter, sub Apennini jugis Eremita, nobile Fratrum Minorum Cænobium, se visendum præbet ædificiis stupendum.
units.tr: Then, on the road that leads to Gualdo, an Umbrian town under the ridges of the Apennine, there appears the hermitage, a noble monastery of the Friars Minor, remarkable for its buildings and worth a visit.

units.la: Inter eiusdem Apennini Colles, Æsi fluuio versus Caurum, Æsis Vrbs inuenitur Æsis Strabone & Ptolemæo: Hodie Giesi, Episcopali gaudens dignitate. Hinc Æsinates Plinio Umbriæ Populi, libro iii natur. Histor. cap. xiiii. Colonijs adiectetur in Antiquis Interpretationibus, quarum unam paullo ante fixi.
units.tr: Among the same hills of the Apennine, towards the north-west on the River Aesis, is the city of Aesis, known to Strabo and Ptolemy as Aesis. Today it is called Iesi and enjoys episcopal dignity. Hence the Aesinates, a people of Umbria, according to Pliny, book 3 of the Natural History, chapter 14. The name is added among the colonies in the ancient interpreters, one of which I quoted a little earlier.

units.la: Vitra sub primis Apennini Collibus, atque adeo inter ipsos est Fabrianum; Latine scribentibus Fabertana; Opidum quatuor nobilissimis Italiæ Castellis ob ædificiorum splendorem connumerari solitum. Ea sunt Crema Langbardiæ, Pratum Tusciæ, Baruluna Apuliæ, Fabrianum Markæ. Ædificatum volunt ob Sentini, veteris Vrbis cuius ad sextum lapidem reliquiæ supersunt, interitum. Opificum tabernis frequens, quæ ita distributæ sunt, ut Vici singulî proprias habeat uno in loco, Fabri suas, Calceolarii suas, Cartarii suas De Baptista Claraesio, cuius aliquando Principe, quemque habuerunt vitæ exitum, & quæ inde sequuntur prodit memoriæ Blondus lib. xxv Historiarum. Insignia Ciuitatis iam imaginem vidi, malleum tenentis, & tanquam Incudi suppositæ impressuri. Inter præclaros viros habuit Constantium, Prædicatorum ordinis Monachum, a Pontificibus in Diuorum numerum relatum: de quo li. v de Vitis Illustribus eiusdem Ordinis.
units.tr: Below the first hills of the Apennine, and indeed among them, is Fabriano, which writers in Latin call Fabertana. It is a town usually counted, on account of the splendour of its buildings, among the four most noble castles of Italy. These are Crema in Lombardy, Prato in Tuscany, Barletta in Apulia, and Fabriano in the March. They say it was built after the destruction of Sentinum, an ancient city whose remains survive about six miles away. It is full of workshops, which are so distributed that each trade has its own place in one district: the smiths their own, the shoemakers their own, the paper-makers their own. Blondus, book 25 of his Histories, gives an account of Baptista Claresio, once their prince, and of the end of his life and what followed from it. I have already seen the city's insignia, an image of a man holding a hammer, as if about to strike it on an anvil placed beneath. Among its distinguished men it had Constantius, a monk of the Order of Preachers, who was enrolled among the saints by the Pontiffs; concerning him see book 5 of the Lives of Illustrious Men of the same Order.

units.la: In ora deinceps ab Cata Cremata viii circiter milibus, Vrbs est Episcopalis Senogallia. Senam prius appellatam fuisse, patet ex Polybii lib. iv, Liuio multis locis, præcipue libro xxvii, res ibi ab M. Liuio Salinatore contra Hasdrubalem Pœnorum rum ducem gestas commemorante, Strabone libr. v, Lucano libro II, & aliis. Deinde vero ad differentiam alterius, quæ in Etruria (vide quæ ibi dixi) Senogallia coepit audire. Sic Plinio, Melæ Antonino, Paulo Diacono, aliisque nominatur, Σιναγαλλια autem Straboni; quæ Σηνα ταλλικα divisim Ptolemæo; & Sena Galli mutilate in Itineraria Tabula, Hodie Sinigaglia vocatur, vel Senegaglia. Unde? Indicat Silius.
units.tr: Next along the coast, about eight miles from Casa Cremata, is the episcopal city of Senigallia. That it was formerly called Sena is clear from Polybius, book 4, from Livy in many places, especially book 27, where he recounts the deeds done there by M. Livius Salinator against Hasdrubal, the Carthaginian leader, from Strabo book 5, from Lucan book 2, and from others. Later, however, to distinguish it from the other Sena, which is in Etruria (see what I said there), it began to be called Senogallia. So it is named by Pliny, Mela, Antoninus, Paulus Diaconus and others; Strabo calls it Σιναγαλλια; Ptolemy, separately, Σηνα ταλλικα; and the Itinerary Table, in mutilated form, Sena Galli. Today it is called Sinigaglia or Senegaglia. Whence the name? Silius indicates it:

units.la: ——qua Sena relictumGallorum à populis traxit per secula nomen.
units.tr: "The place where Sena, left by the Gauls, took its name from the peoples through the ages."

units.la: Et alibi:
units.tr: And elsewhere:

units.la: Clanius & Rubico, & Senonum de nomine Sena.
units.tr: Clanius and Rubico, and the Senones, from whose name Sena comes.

units.la: Sunt autem ii Senones, quos facta in Italiam irruptione, Urbem captam incendisse loquuntur Historiæ. Opidum Cælum habet grave. Parvum, ab Occasu Misa flumine adiuntur; muro validum lateritio, valde crasso, vallo item propugnaculis. Penuria laborat propter Maris vicinitatem Aquarum dulcium; importatis uti coacta. Deductam hoc Coloniam, quo tempore Cæsium & Hadriam; docet ex Livio Florus. Et hinc Colonia Senensis ad Superum mare ponitur ab Livio libro xxvii, cujus etiam meminit Tacitus libro iii Histor. Prope est Mons Hasdrubalis, nomen ex clade ipsi hic illata retinens; & tota illa Planicies, Fanumque pertingens, longa x milliaribus; Mala Rotta inde denominata: pars scilicet Planicei illius amœnæ, Apenninis Montibus & Germanis Alpibus circumdatæ, Padoque Fluvio divisa; quam exacte multis verbis describit Polybius libro ii.
units.tr: The Senones are those who, in their invasion of Italy, are said by the histories to have captured and burned the City. The town of Cælum has a heavy air. It is small and is bordered on the west by the river Misa. It is strong, with a thick wall of brick, and likewise a rampart with bulwarks. Because of the nearness of the sea it suffers from a lack of fresh water and is forced to use imported water. Florus shows from Livy that this was founded as a colony at the time when Caesium and Hadria were founded. From this, the Colonia Senensis is placed on the Upper Sea by Livy in book 27, and Tacitus also mentions it in book 3 of the Histories. Near it is Mons Hasdrubalis, which keeps its name from the defeat inflicted on him here. The whole plain stretching to Fanum, about ten miles long, is called Mala Rotta after this. It is part of that pleasant plain, surrounded by the Apennine mountains and the German Alps and divided by the river Po, which Polybius describes exactly and at length in book 2.

units.la: Ad Misam Amnem, cujus meminit, multa sunt Opida, in quis honestiora Mons Novus, Mons Bodius, Cormalum, & Arx Contraria.
units.tr: Near the river Misa, which he mentions, there are many towns, of which the more notable are Mons Novus, Mons Bodius, Cormalum, and Arx Contraria.

units.la: Ad Sentinum, qui Misæ fluentis miscetur, Saxum-Ferratum est Opidum, ab Cavernis seu Fodinis ferrariis, quæ olim hic fuerint, uti nonnullis mens est, dictum. Celeberrimum est Bartholi I. C. Alexandri Monachi, & Nicolai Perotti Sipontini Præsulis ortu. Putant quidam hoc loco fuisse Ptolemæo Ἰέφικον. Adhuc quæro, an idem cum Tuficum, quod in libro de Limitibus, & an hinc Tuscani, Plinio, Umbriæ (Transapenninæ) Populi.
units.tr: Near the Sentinus, which mixes its waters with the Misa, is the town of Saxum-Ferratum, named after the caverns or iron mines that were once here, as some think. It is very famous as the birthplace of Bartholomew, a jurist, of Alexander the Monk, and of Nicholas Perotti, bishop of Siponto. Some think that Ptolemy's Ἰέφικον [Iephikon] was located here. I still ask whether it is the same as Tuficum, which is in the book De Limitibus, and whether the Tuscani, the people of Umbria (across the Apennines) mentioned by Pliny, came from here.

units.la: Supra Saxum-Ferratum duorum intervallo Stadiorum ad Sentinum Amnem in Via, quæ Follatum ducit, Umbriæ opidum, locus occurrit, ubi quondam Urbs antiqua Sentinum. Σίντινον Straboni & Ptolemæo: unde Sentinates Plinio in vi Regione. In hujus Opidi Agro nobilis ille fuit conflictus Romanorum, Samnitium, Gallorum, Umbrorum, & Etruscorum, coss. Q. Fabio Maximo & P. Decio Mure, qui se Patris exemplum sequutus tunc pro Rep. devovit. Vide præter alios Livium libro x. Ob Sentinum ab Langbardis delictum, ut post Procopium scribit Blondus, Saxum-Ferratum est conditum, & Fabrianum: de quibus ante.
units.tr: Two stadia above Saxum-Ferratum, on the road to Follatum by the river Sentinus, there is a town of Umbria, where the ancient city of Sentinum once stood. Straboand Ptolemy call it Σίντινον [Sintinon], and from it Pliny in book 6 calls its people the Sentinates. In the territory of this town was that famous battle of the Romans, Samnites, Gauls, Umbrians and Etruscans, in the consulship of Q. Fabius Maximus and P. Decius Mus, who, following the example of his father, then devoted himself for the republic. Besides others, see Livy, book 10. Because Sentinum was destroyed by the Lombards, as Blondus writes after Procopius, Saxum-Ferratum and Fabriano were founded, about which I have written before.

units.la: In ora deinceps sequuntur Cæsani Fluminis Ostia: ad cujus utrimque ripas multa Opida Mondulphium, Mondavium, Orzanum, Ad D. Laurentium, Cerefium, Ad D. Constantium; juxtaque Cæsani fontem Pergula.
units.tr: Next along the coast come the mouths of the river Cesano. On each of its banks are many towns: Mondulphium, Mondavium, Orzanum, Ad D. Laurentium, Cerefium, Ad D. Constantium; and near the source of the Cesano is Pergula.

units.la: Post in montibus, qui inter Metaurum Amnem Isaurumque & Apenninum sunt, Castellum visitur Carda cum aliis quibusdam non magni momenti locis, uti sunt Ralpaganta, Miraldella, Sorbum-longum, Ad D. Martini, Brasiliana, Befortium, Campus, Turris Fossati, Paganticum, Pelunum.
units.tr: Afterwards, in the mountains between the river Metaurus and the Isaurus and the Apennines, there is seen the castle of Carda, together with certain other places of no great importance, such as Ralpaganta, Miraldella, Sorbum-longum, Ad D. Martini, Brasiliana, Befortium, Campus, Turris Fossati, Paganticum, and Pelunum.

units.la: Dein propter Apenninum est Alercadellum; supraque asperrima in via, quæ per editos Flaminiæ Montes in Tusciam ducit, Opidum Amola.
units.tr: Then, near the Apennines, is Alercadellum; and above it, on the very rough road that leads through the high Flaminian mountains into Tuscany, is the town of Amola.

units.la: Rassano, Blondo; alii Tractus hic Massa Trebaria nominatur, tamquam Massa Trebium, quod Peringentes Abietes ad Templorum Ædiumque structuras olim hic cæsi confuxerint, hodieque cædantur.
units.tr: Blondus calls this district Rassano; others call it Massa Trebaria, as if it were Massa Trebium, because pine trees growing tall were once cut here for the building of temples and houses, and are still cut today.

units.la: In propinquo est hoc sinu Castellum D. Angeli Vadani, S. Angelo in Vado, Negotiatorum commercio frequens: Tipherum Metaurum olim: uti constare adierit. Fredericus Bavarius hic natus, ex quibusdam Annalibus Pontificumque Epistolis.
units.tr: Nearby, in this bend, is the castle of D. Angelo Vadano, S. Angelo in Vado, busy with the trade of merchants. Formerly it was Tifernum Metaurum, as it is clear from what we have learned. Frederick of Bavaria was born here, according to certain annals and the letters of the popes.

units.la: Millibus ab hoc opido quinque Planicies ternitur pulcra, peninsulam habens, quam Metaurus efficit. In ea Durantium est, conditum & denominatum ab Gulielmo Durante, Carnotensi Decano, Speculi Auctore, Nuncio & Thesaurario per Romanulam Martini iv. P. M.
units.tr: Five miles from this town there is a beautiful plain, which has a peninsula formed by the Metaurus. In it is Durantium, founded and named after William Durand, dean of Chartres, author of the Speculum, who was nuncio and treasurer in Romagna under Pope Martin IV.

units.la: Secundum litus deinde itinere P. M. iii ad Fanum devenitur, Opidum Episcopale,
units.tr: Then, along the coast, three Roman miles farther on, one comes to Fanum, an episcopal town,

units.la: Bbbb 4 scopale, non magnum, in monte situm, quod vulgo Fano. Fanum simpliciter Caesari lib. 1. Procopio, aliis, Φάνα Stephano. Fanum Fortunae Tacito libro x, Plinio lib. iii cap. xiiii, Antonino, Itinerariae Tabulae, Φάνον Φορτούνας Ptolemaeo: Fanestris Fortuna est in Libro de Limitibus. Graece expressit Strabo Ἱερὸν τῆς Τύχης. Hinc Fanestres Incolae sunt apud Aggenum. Colonus adcenunt Plinius indicato à me loco & Pomponius Mela lib. 1. cap. ii. cui Fanestris Colonia dicitur. Sic Inscriptio, quae Pisauri in horto Ducis Vrbini, in Basi Statuae sex pedibus altae: C. LVXILLIO. C. F. POMPT SABINO. EGNATIO PROCVLO. CN. CVA. RER PVBLICAE. PISAVR. ST. FANEST
units.tr: not large, situated on a hill, which is commonly called Fano. Caesar in book 1 simply calls it Fanum; Procopius and others likewise; Stephanus Φάνα [Phana]. Tacitus in book 10, Pliny in book 3 chapter 14, the Antonine Itinerary and the Itinerary Tables call it Fanum Fortunae; Ptolemy Φάνον Φορτούνας [Phanon Phortounas]; the book De Limitibus has Fanestris Fortuna. Strabo expressed it in Greek as Ἱερὸν τῆς Τύχης [Hieron tēs Tychēs]. From this, the inhabitants are called Fanestres, as among Agennus. Pliny, in the place I have indicated, and Pomponius Mela in book 1 chapter 2 mention it as a colony, which is called Fanestris Colonia. So too an inscription at Pesaro, in the garden of the Duke of Urbino, on the base of a statue six feet high: To Gaius Luxillius Sabinus Egnatius Proculus, son of Gaius, of the Pompt-ine tribe, Cn. Cu... for the public affairs of Pisaurum and of Fanestris.

units.la: & versibus quibusdam interjectis: PATRONO. COLONIARVM PISAVR. IT. FANEST
units.tr: And, with some verses in between: To the patron of the colonies of Pisaurum and Fanestris.

units.la: Plenius Colonia Iulia Fanestris vocatur in Tabula marmorea, quae in ipso Opido in ambitu Monasterii Augustinensium: Q.GOLIVS Q. L. NICOMEDES MEDI. VS. OCVLARIVS. SEX. VIR. COL. IVL. FENESTRIS GOLIA. Q. L. SALVIA. VXSOR Q.GOLLVS Q. F. POL. FANESTR. FILIVS VELIA. Q. L. TRISCA. VXSOR EX. TESTAMENTO. FANESTRIS. FILI
units.tr: It is called more fully Colonia Iulia Fanestris on a marble tablet which is in the town itself, in the precinct of the Augustinian monastery: Quintus Golius, son of Quintus, of the Nicomedes family, Mediolanum...ocularius, sixvir of the Colonia Iulia Fanestris; Golia Salvia, wife; Quintus Gollus, son of Quintus, of the Pollian tribe, of Fanestris, son; Velia Trisca, wife; by the will of Fanestris, son.

units.la: Iterum plenius in alia tabella marmorea. L. TITVLENVS. L. L TERTIVS. ORIVNDVS COLONIA. IVII. FANO FORTVNAE. SEX. VIR L. TITVLINVS. TITVLENI. L:B VASIO. ANNORVM. XII
units.tr: Again, more fully, on another marble tablet: Lucius Titulenus, son of Lucius, Lucius Tertius Orundus, of the colony of Fanum Fortunae, sixvir; Lucius Titulinus, son of Titulenus; Basio, aged twelve years.

units.la: Fuit procul dubio inter xxiiii Coloniae quas Augustum duxisse auctor est Tranquillus. Fani, quod ibi Fortunae sumtuosissimum olim dedicatum, adhuc magna monstrantur vestigia. Ab Totila Gothorum Rege cum Pisauro eversum, & à Belisario restitutum scribit Blondus. Vitiatur ibidem Arcus ex marmore, sumtuoso nobilisque opere factus, altus cubitos xxx, latus xx. Fastigio, quod mirabili arte elaboratum concidit, insculptum legitur Constantino Imperatori Elogium, quod apud alios. Fanum hoc Plinius & Strabo Umbriae tribuunt. Principatus eius quum diu suisset in Malatestarum familia postea Sfortiarum, devenit tandem ad Ecclesiam Romanam. Adluitur ab Argilla Fluvio. Mulieres habet lectissimas & à pulchritudine commendatas.
units.tr: It was without doubt among the twenty-four colonies which, the writer Suetonius says, Augustus founded. Great remains of the very splendid temple of Fortune, which was once dedicated there, can still be seen. Blondus writes that it was overthrown together with Pisaurum by Totila, king of the Goths, and restored by Belisarius. On the spot an arch of marble is decaying, made with sumptuous and noble workmanship, thirty cubits high and twenty wide. On its pediment, which fell down, carved with wonderful skill, there was read an inscription to the emperor Constantine, which is recorded elsewhere. Pliny and Strabo assign this Fanum to Umbria. Its rule was for a long time in the family of the Malatesta, afterwards of the Sforza, and it finally came to the Roman Church. It is washed by the river Argilla. It has very choice women, commended for their beauty.

units.la: Occurrit ad Metauri sinistram, Via Flaminia, quae ab Fano in Meridiem flectit, ad xv lapidem Fossombrunum, Fossumbrunum. Sic Opidum Episcopale hodie vocatur, quod olim Forum Sempronii, Antonino, aliisque Latinis, ut & Itinerariae Tabulae: Φόρον Σεμπρωνίου Strabonis: Φορῶ Σεμπρωνίου Ptolemaeo. Hinc Forosempronienses Plinio: qui Umbriae tribuit, in Sexta Regione, Strabo & Ptolemaeus Vilumbris. Vestigia ibi Antiquitatis quamplurima, praeter Aquae ductus, Vias Silicatas, Columnas & alia. Marmora multa cernuntur diligenter cum antiquis Inscriptionibus, quae ab aliis collectae. Novum Opidum, Veteris fundamentis non esse aedificatum, docet Leander. Possedit quondam Malatestarum Familia; post jure Emtionis ad Vrbinates pervenit. Extra Opidum Pons lapideus Metauri jungit ripas. Supra ad Cantiani ripam est Furlum; sic dictum, tamquam Saxum Foratum; de quo, Viaque Flaminia Leander Albertus multa habet lectu digna, hic brevitatis gratia a me omissa.
units.tr: On the left bank of the Metaurus, the Flaminian Way, which turns south from Fanum, meets Fossombrunum, Fossumbrunum, fifteen miles away. This is what the episcopal town is called today; it was once Forum Sempronii for Antoninus and other Latin writers, as also in the Itinerary Tables; Strabo calls it Φόρον Σεμπρωνίου [Phoron Semproniou], and Ptolemy Φορῶ Σεμπρωνίου [Phorō Semproniou]. From it, Pliny calls its people the Forosempronienses, whom he assigns to Umbria in the sixth region; Strabo and Ptolemy call them Vilumbri. There are very many remains of antiquity there, besides an aqueduct, paved roads, columns and other things. Many marbles, with ancient inscriptions carefully collected by others, may be seen. Leander says that the new town was not built on the foundations of the old one. The Malatesta family once held it; afterwards, by right of purchase, it came to the Urbinates. Outside the town a stone bridge over the Metaurus joins the banks. Above, on the bank of the Cantianus, is Furlum, so called as if it were Saxum Foratum, about which Leander Albertus, in his Via Flaminia, has many things worth reading; I have omitted them here for brevity.

units.la: Paullo altius ad Cantianum in amoena planicie, quae Calium usque spatio fere P. M. x extenditur, Vicus occurrit Aqualania, diversorias habens Tabernas ab exiguo Castello Aqualania dictas, quod haud procul in colle situm distat. Prope sunt Campi, in quibus cruento certamine superatus est ab Narsete, Justiniani Imperatoris Legato, Totila Gothorum Princeps. Lege Procopium libro iii. Hist. 10 Gothicae. Blondus, Sabellicus, aliqueque falso ad Tanetum, Agri Regiensis, pugnatum adierunt. Altius deinde, non procul tamen ab Aqualiana, Mons Falco est.
units.tr: A little higher up, on the Cantianus, in the pleasant plain that extends nearly ten Roman miles as far as Calium, there appears a village, Aqualania, which has inns called after the small castle of Aqualania, which stands on a hill not far off. Near it are the fields where Totila, prince of the Goths, was defeated in a bloody battle by Narses, the legate of the emperor Justinian. Read Procopius, Gothic War, book 3, chapter 10. Blondus, Sabellicus and others have falsely placed the battle at Tanetum, in the territory of Reggio. Higher up, though not far from Aqualania, is Mons Falco.

units.la: Sequitur mox Calum, Vrbs Episcopalis, vulgo Cagio, Calle Viius Antonino: Calli Procopio lib. iii belli Gothici, apud quem in nonnullis exemplaribus vel Interpretis, vel Typographi vitio calli minusculo scribitur, quasi Via, non Opidum designaretur. Ad Calem lego in Itineraria Tabula. Calium Boafus ab Septemtrione, ab ortu Cantianus adluit, ut tamquam in peninsula relinquatur. Vetus Opidum deletum constat; a quo, incertum. Novum quo tempore conditum testantur his verbis ejus Annales: Anno clo cc lxxxix die Mercurij, ix Februarij inter Primam & Quintam Horam matutinam Civitas Calij translata fuit in locum, in quo nunc est, & incepta prima fundamenta & Domorum constructio, & dicta Civitas S. Angeli Papalis, tempore Pontificatus Domini Nicolai Papae iiii, Domino Ioanne de Columnia, Rectore Marchiae. In Vrbinatium est ditione.
units.tr: Soon comes Calum, an episcopal city, commonly called Cagio; Antoninus calls it Calle Viius; Procopius in book 3 of the Gothic War calls it Calli; in some copies of him, through the fault of the translator or the printer, it is written with a small letter, calli, as if a road and not a town were meant. I read Ad Calem in the Itinerary Table. The Boafus flows around Calium from the north, and the Cantianus from the east, so that it is left as if on a peninsula. The old town is known to have been destroyed; by whom, is uncertain. The time when the new town was founded is attested by its annals in these words: "In the year 1289, on Wednesday, 9 February, between the first and fifth hour of the morning, the city of Calium was transferred to the place where it now is, and the first foundations and construction of houses were begun, and the city was called S. Angelo Papale, in the time of the pontificate of Lord Pope Nicholas IV, with Lord John de Colonna as rector of the March." It lies in the dominion of the Urbinates.

units.la: Oculis se mox offert Candianum cum Arce in Colle. Conditum ob urbis Luceolorum, quae ulterius ad Cantianum erat amnem, interitum. Ejus Pontem transgressus ad alterum fere Lapidem, Luceolorum adparent vestigia; unde Pontis nomen vulgo corruptum, Riz. ole. Luceolis Eleutherium, Exarchum ab Heraclio Imperatore ordinatum, Ravennates Milites propter affectati Imperii suspicionem confodisse tradit Paullus Diaconus lib. v Histor. Langbard.
units.tr: Soon Candianum, with its citadel on the hill, presents itself to the eyes. It was founded after the destruction of the city of the Luceolorum, which lay further on, by the river Cantianus. Crossing its bridge, at about one mile, traces of the Luceolorum appear; hence the bridge's name, corrupted in common speech into Riz. ole. Luceolis. Paul the Deacon, in book 5 of the History of the Lombards, relates that the Ravennate soldiers killed Eleutherius, the exarch appointed by the Emperor Heraclius, at Luceolis, on suspicion that he aspired to empire.

units.la: Supra Forum Sempronii P. M. viii Firmianum est, Vrbinatis Agri Opidum, quod Metaurus adluit. Iuxta est Mons Hasdrubalis, de quo ante dixi:
units.tr: Above Forum Sempronii, eight Roman miles away, lies Firmianum, a town in the territory of Urbino, which the Metaurus washes. Nearby is Mons Hasdrubalis, of which I have spoken before.

units.la: 30 Ad oram redeo, ubi prope Ifaurum Pisaurum Vrbs Episcopalis. Sic Livio passim, Caesari in Commentariis, Plinio, Melae, Vibio Sequestro, Antonino, Itinerariae Tabulae, & aliis dicitur: Πισαυρον Ptolemaeo & Agathiae: quae hodie Pesaro. Sic, quod prope Ifaurum, vocatum videtur. Plinius tamen fluvium ipsum etiam Pisaurum appellat: ut alteri ab altero forte nomen. Servius ab Auro, quod Galli Senones Camillo adpenderunt, nuncupatum autumat. Ptolemaeo est in Senonibus; Plinio in Umbris, vi Regione. Emporium Italiae celebre, mercimonijs dives, amplum, splendidum, pulcris aedificijs ornatum, plateis perelegans, situ peramoeno maximeque fertili: Caeli tamen gravitate laborans; mentibus, potissimum astivis subexortum Sirij, Vrbi valde inimicum & lethalem; unde & Catullo morbunda sedes Pisauri dicitur. Condita in longitudinem, cum in modum, ut ex foro ad quatuor opidi vias prospectus pateat; ea tamen quae ad Ifauri pontem tendit, ceteris longiore. Praeter Curiam tumultuosam, aliasque nobiles Aedes, Arcem ad littus habet, munitam & pulchram, ab Ioanne Sforzia conditam. In Ducis Palatio instructissimum est Armamentarium. Ratione munitionis respondet nonnihil Patavio. Portus propter Vada & Arenas onusta maioraque navigia non admittit; ut ab Agasonibus & Mulionibus, qui merces invehunt, magis quam ab Nautis Vrbs frequentetur. Describit eam Fr. Guicciardinus lib. xii Histor. 40 Coloniam factam docent Livius libro xxxix, Plutarchus in Antonio, & Velleius Paterculus lib. i. Eandem ejus conditionem testantur Inscriptiones. Apud Ortelium ex antiquo lapide est COLONIA. IVL. FELIX. PISAVRVM. Inter Colonos fuisse L. Attium Poetam Tragicum, Libertinis parentibus natum, tradit Eusebius de Temporibus. Paulo ante bellum Actiacum, quum eo M. Antonius iii vir Colonos rursum deduxisset, terra inani absorptam periisse, prodit memoriae Plutarchus in Antonio. Diruram a Totila, refectamque a Belisario, scribunt Procopius & Blondus. Post Malatestarum imperio diu habita est, mox a Sfortijs; hinc a Porgijs possessa: post quos in potestate fuit Pontificum Romanorum: ab his tandem
units.tr: 30 I return to the coast, where near the Ifaurus lies Pisaurum, an episcopal city. It is so called by Livy throughout, by Caesar in the Commentaries, by Pliny, Mela, Vibius Sequester, Antoninus, the Itinerary Table and others; Πισαυρον by Ptolemy and Agathias; today it is Pesaro. It seems to have been named from its nearness to the Ifaurus. Pliny, however, also calls the river itself Pisaurum, so perhaps one name was taken from the other. Servius thinks it was named from the gold (aurum) which the Gallic Senones hung on Camillus. Ptolemy places it among the Senones; Pliny among the Umbrians, in the sixth region. It is a famous market of Italy, rich in merchandise, large, splendid, adorned with fine buildings, with very elegant squares, in a most pleasant and very fertile site. Yet it suffers from the heaviness of its air, especially in summer, when the Dog Star rises, which is very hostile and deadly to the city; hence Catullus calls it "the dying seat of Pisaurum". The city is laid out lengthwise, so that from the forum the view extends down four streets; the one leading to the bridge over the Ifaurus is longer than the rest. Besides the turbulent Curia and other noble buildings, it has a citadel by the shore, fortified and handsome, built by John Sforza. In the Duke's palace is a very well-equipped arsenal. In its fortifications it somewhat resembles Padua. Because of shallows and sandbanks the harbour does not admit large ships, so the city is frequented more by carters and muleteers who bring in goods than by sailors. Francesco Guicciardini describes it in book 12 of his Histories. 40 Livy in book 39, Plutarch in the Life of Antony, and Velleius Paterculus in book 1 show that it was made a Colonia. Inscriptions attest the same status; Ortelius gives an ancient stone reading: COLONIA IVL. FELIX. PISAVRVM. Eusebius in his work On Times reports that L. Attius, the tragic poet, born of freedmen parents, was among the Colonos. Plutarch in the Life of Antony records that shortly before the battle of Actium, when Mark Antony as triumvir had again sent out Colonos, the land was swallowed up by an empty chasm and perished. Procopius and Biondo write that it was destroyed by Totila and restored by Belisarius. After a long period under the Malatesta, it was held by the Sforza, then possessed by the Porzi; after them it was under the power of the Roman Pontiffs, and at last by them

units.la: dem Marijs tradita. Ingenia tulit magno numero celebria: præter alios Andreinum, summum Medicum ; Pandulphum Collenutium, qui inter alia scriplit Historiam Regni Neapolitani, & de Machinis Tormentariis Inventione; Petrum Bassinianum, Poetam. Viam Pisaurensem iterit, Templumque Iovis Pisauri edit cat apud Livium libro xl. Fulvius Flaccus cos.
units.tr: was handed over to the Mari. It has produced many famous men of genius: among others, Andreinus, a very great physician; Pandulphus Collenutius, who among other things wrote a History of the Kingdom of Naples and a work on the invention of siege engines; Petrus Bassinianus, a poet. Livy, in book 40, mentions the Viam Pisaurensem and the Temple of Iovis Pisauri, which Fulvius Flaccus, consul, built.

units.la: Supra Pisaurum ad Isaurum Mons Abbatis est. Castella dein inter Isaurum, &c, quo augetur, Album in agro Pisaurio & Urbinate sunt multa: in quis celeberrimum Monte Fiorum, Monte di Fabri.
units.tr: Above Pisaurum, on the Isaurus, lies Mons Abbatis. Then, between the Isaurus and the Album, which is increased by it, there are many castles in the territory of Pisaurum and Urbino; among them the most famous are Monte Fiorum and Monte di Fabri.

units.la: Mox vtendum te præbet, alto situm monte & inæquali loco inter eosdem Amnes, Vrbinum; Tacito libro xix in bello Vitellliani descriptione, Procopio libro ii Belli Gothici, alisque notum. Dubitat Leander Albertus num sit Suaca, quam Ptolemaeus inter Senones prope Pisaurum in colle designat. Incolæ Vrbinates Plinio in sexta Italiæ Regione; Metaurenses & Hortenses cognominati. Vrbinatium Metaurensium meminit Tabula, quæ confracta cernitur Romæ in pavimento Sacelli, quod est ad Templum S. Gregorij in Cœlio Monte. Ejus Tabulæ partem priorem posui supra libro ii cap. xvi, ubi de Attuta: reliqua cum principio sic habent:
units.tr: Next you come to Urbinum, a town set on a high mountain and uneven ground between the same rivers. It is known from Tacitus, book 19, in his description of the war of Vitellius, from Procopius, book 2 of the Gothic War, and from others. Leander Albertus doubts whether it is Suaca, which Ptolemy places among the Senones near Pisaurum on a hill. The inhabitants are the Urbinates in Pliny's sixth region of Italy, surnamed Metaurenses and Hortenses. The Table mentions the Urbinatium Metaurensium, and it can be seen broken in the pavement of a chapel in Rome, which is next to the Church of St Gregory on the Caelian Hill. I set out the first part of that Table above in book 2, chapter 16, where I discussed Attuta. The rest, with its beginning, reads as follows:

units.la: L. RANIO, OTTATO. V. C. COS. &c. CVRATORI. VIÆ SALARIÆ. ET. CVRATORI. REIP. VRVINATIVM METAVRENSIVM. LEGATO. PROVINCIÆ ASIÆ. PRÆTORI. TRIBVNO. PLEBI QVÆSTORI. PROVINCIÆ. SICILIÆ.
units.tr: To Lucius Ranius Ottatus, most illustrious man, consul, &c., curator of the Via Salaria and curator of the state of the Urbinates Metaurenses, legate of the province of Asia, praetor, tribune of the plebs, quaestor of the province of Sicily.

units.la: Vrbs est lautissima, splendideque satis ædificata, bono & fœcundo agro. Arcem habuerunt extra eam Vrbinates lautissimam, quam Guidobaldus dux, ne noxia esset, dejecit. Novam, Vetere diruta, intra muros ab fundamentis extruxit Fridericus Dux, ædibus Episcopi & Templo D. Dominici contiguam; ita ædificatam, ut possit equo in Turres & ad Tectum ipsum ire; quem admodum Venetijs Turris D. Marci, Romæ Pontificis Palatium, in Hannonia Arx Fosiniana. Conclavia ibi cc lxxiii, ampla & magnifica. Illustrat eam præcipuè Bibliotheca, libris optimis & multis referta. Ornamentis suis ab Cæsare Valentino Borgia, Alexandri vi P. M. Filio, Ipsoranni atque etiam translatam rettulit postea Iulius ii. Describe Vrbem ejusque Arcem in Aulico suo Latinas: Castiliensis. Episcopatus gaudet titulo. Inter præclaros, quos ulti, Viros Raphael Pictor celeberrimus, cum Vetero-bus, ut opera passim per Italiam, præcipue vero Romæ in Basilica Pontificia ad D. Petri clamant, committendus. Olim à Belisario Iustiniani Imper. Duce, obsessam, captamque scribit Procopius libro ii de Bello Goth. Post id tempus diu fuit in ditione Comitum Montis Feltrii, qui Duces postea Vrbini creati ab Sixto iv P. M. inter quos fuit Fridericus Guidobaldus, qui Vrbem illustri ornavit, quam dixi, Bibliotheca. Post Monteferetrum & Pesaro Vrbs ab Cesare Borgia aliquamdiu possessa, dein ab Francisco Maria Rovere, auctoritate Iulij ii P. M. post ab Laurentio Medicæo sub Leone x P. M. occupata, eoque tandem mortuo, ab Maria & Hæredæ ejus Filio Guidone Ubaldo recepta.
units.tr: The city is very splendid and handsomely built, with good and fertile land. The Urbinates had a very splendid citadel outside it, which Duke Guidobaldo pulled down so that it would do no harm. Duke Fridericus, with the old one demolished, built a new citadel from the foundations within the walls, adjoining the bishop's palace and the Temple of St Dominic. It was built so that one can ride on horseback up into the towers and onto the roof itself, as in Venice the Tower of St Mark, at Rome the Pope's Palace, and in Hainault the citadel of Fosiniana. There are 273 rooms there, spacious and magnificent. It is chiefly distinguished by its library, filled with the best and many books. Its furnishings were carried off by Caesar Valentino Borgia, son of Pope Alexander VI, and afterwards Julius II had them brought back. Baldassare Castiglione describes the city and its citadel in his Courtier. The bishopric enjoys the title. Among the illustrious men it has produced is Raphael, the most famous painter, who is to be named alongside the ancients, as his works proclaim everywhere in Italy, especially at Rome in the papal basilica of St Peter. Procopius, in book 2 of the Gothic War, writes that it was once besieged and captured by Belisarius, general of the emperor Justinian. After that time it was for a long while under the rule of the Counts of Montefeltro, who were later created Dukes of Urbino by Pope Sixtus IV, among whom was Fridericus Guidobaldus, who adorned the city with the library I mentioned. After Montefeltro and Pesaro, the city was held for some time by Cesare Borgia, then was taken by Francesco Maria della Rovere, by authority of Pope Julius II, and afterwards was occupied by Lorenzo de' Medici under Pope Leo X. When he died, it was finally recovered by Maria and her heir, her son Guidobaldo.

units.la: Redeunti hinc Pisaurum multa offerunt se Castella: inter quæ Mons Barotius, Monte Barozzo, & Novilaria, vel Nobili Asia ab Cœli bonitate, nobilique Aere nominata.
units.tr: On the way back from here to Pisaurum, many castles present themselves: among them Mons Barotius, Monte Barozzo, and Novilaria, or Nobili Asia, named for the goodness of its sky and its noble air.

units.la: Picenum clausurus, adscribam, quod eo pertinet, iter Littorale ex Itineraria Tabula, ab Fluvio Rubicone, quem Isaurum alij vocant, cuiusque Occidentalioni ripa adfidet in Romanula Pisaurum, ad Truentum usque: Iter Littorale. Itineraria Tabula. | Prolemæus: | Vulgata Nomenclat. Pisauro, VIII | Nimadeor. | Pesaro. Fl. Nelurum: Emend. Pisaurum. | | Fossa, Flume. Fano Fortuna, II. | Φάνο Φορ Ἀνου. | Fano. Flavium
units.tr: To close Picenum, I shall add, since it belongs there, the coastal route from the Itinerary Table, from the river Rubicone, which others call the Isaurus, whose western bank borders on Romagna, to Pisaurum, and as far as the Truentum: the Coastal Route, from the Itinerary Table. | Ptolemy | Vulgate names | Pisaurum, 8 | Nimadeor | Pesaro. units.la: Umbria.
units.tr: Umbria.

units.la: REGIONES Italiae Primae, quae versus occidentem ab Montibus sunt liberiores, Etruriam, Latium, & Picenum percurri: sequitur, quae superioribus Montanosior, UMBRIA: sic Latinis omnibus scriptoribus dicitur, quae ὈΜΒΡΙΑ Graecis.
units.tr: Of the regions of Italy, those called the First, which toward the west are freer of mountains, have been traversed: Etruria, Latium and Picenum. Next follows Umbria, which is more mountainous than the regions above it. All Latin writers so call it, and the Greeks call it Ὀμβρία [Ombria].

units.la: Umbria nomen ab Umbro fluvio, scribente Plinio lib. iii. cap. v. vel ἀπὸ ἕ ὄμβρων, ut docet Isidorus lib. xiv. cap. iv. quod tempore aquosae Cladis, inquit, imbribus superfuerint, & ob hoc Umbria Graece cognominata. Aliis ab Umbra dicitur, quod ob montium altitudinem & vicinitatem regio sit umbrosa. Guilielmus Postellus in sua Etruria putat Umbrorum nomen ab Graecis loco Hebraici & vem suppositum: הָ enim notat fluctum significare & aquarum copiam: inde Ombrios sive Imbrios olim vocatos Gallim, impluviatos; quos posteritas vocavit Gallos:
units.tr: Umbria takes its name either from the river Umbro, as Pliny writes in book 3, chapter 5, or ἀπὸ τῶν ὄμβρων [from the rains], as Isidore teaches in book 14, chapter 4: "because in the time of the watery disaster they survived the rains," and for this reason Umbria was called in Greek by that name. Others say it is named from umbra (shade), because the region is shady owing to the height and nearness of its mountains. Guilielmus Postellus, in his Etruria, thinks that the name of the Umbri was put in by the Greeks in place of a Hebrew word, since the Hebrew term means a flood and an abundance of waters. From this, he says, the Ombrii or Imbrii, who were once called Galli, meaning "rain-fed" people, were later called Gauls.

units.la: Latissimos Umbria fines olim habitos, non obscure docet Strabo libro v his verbis: ὁ δ' Ὀμβρικοὶ μέσον μὲν χωρὶς ἀπὸ Σαβίνης καὶ τ' Τόπλωιας μηχέ Λ' ἐμμινα καὶ Ρ' ἀ- μίνης πεσοσία ἐπιτρέπαλλοντες τὸ ὄρη. Idem paullo post: Τὴν δὲ Τυρρηνία μεγάλην ... ὡς τὸ πρὸς τὸ μέσον ... ὁ Ὀμβρικὸς, ... ἀλλ' Ἀμμινον λαβεῖν, καὶ ἐπὶ περιτρέπειν μεγάλ' ὡς Ἀδεῖα. Ἀλλ' γὰρ δὴ Ραυίνης ἀξιαμάτοι καταχωρίζων ἐπὶ τὸ πλήσιον, ἐφηκῆς, Σαβινὰς, Ἀρμινὸν, Σίνας καὶ Καμαρίνον. Αὐτὴ δ' ἐστὶ καὶ ὁ Ἀπὸς πεταμὲς, ἡ τὴ Τυγγῆσον ἀρρ, ἡ Σενῖνον, ἡ Μεζωροῖ, πλάμος, ἡ τὸ Ἰερὸν τ Τυχῃ. & quae ibi sequuntur de Longitudine & Latitudine. Plinius libro iii. cap. xiv. Umbriam angustioribus includit terminis. nam ab finibus tantum agri Ariminensis Anconam usque per Litus Superi Maris incedens in Adriae fonte consistit, omnemque Continentis tractum per Apenninj juga Ameriam usque adjicit: ut ex horum notatione Umbri quasi duplices videantur fuisse, Cisapennini & Transapennini. Ptolemaeus duas hic statuens gentes, Umbros & Vilumbros, Ὀμβρες & Οὐιλάμβρος: His quidem, qua Meridies est, Tiberim; qua Oriens, Anienem; qua Septentrio, Montem Apenninum: qua denique Occidens, Umbros facit Limites: illis autem ad Occasum Gallos Togatos; ad Septentrionem, Senones; ad Ortum, Vilumbros, ad Meridiem Etruscos adlocans conregionales. Ptolemaei descriptionem sequi est animus: ipsdem finibus servatis, Umbros & Vilumbros hoc capite complectar, quum jam Transapenninos Umbros in Piceno descripserim.
units.tr: That the Umbrians once held very wide borders is clearly shown by Strabo in book 5, in these words: the Umbri, separated in the middle from the Sabines and ..., extend across the Apennine ridges. The same author a little later says: Etruria is large... toward the middle... the Umbrian... but they hold Ameria, and beyond it extend as far as Hadria. Then he lists the places near the sea: Ravenna, Sena, Sarsina, Ariminum and Camerinum. The river Apsus is also there, the Tinia, the Sena, the Metaurus, a plain, and the temple of Juno... and what follows there about length and breadth. Pliny, in book 3, chapter 14, confines Umbria within narrower limits. For he says that, from the borders of the Ariminian territory down to Ancona, along the coast of the Upper Sea, and standing at the source of the Adriatic, it takes in the whole stretch of the mainland as far as Ameria along the ridges of the Apennines. From this description the Umbri seem to have been as it were of two kinds, the Cisapennine and the Transapennine. Ptolemy, who sets up two peoples here, the Umbri and the Vilumbri (Ὀμβρες and Οὐιλάμβρος), gives these boundaries: to the Umbri on the south the Tiber, on the east the Anio, on the north the Apennine mountain, and on the west the Umbri form the limit; to them on the west are the Togate Gauls, on the north the Senones, on the east the Vilumbri, and on the south the Etruscans as neighbouring regions. It is my intention to follow Ptolemy's description. Keeping the same boundaries, I shall include the Umbri and Vilumbri in this chapter, since I have already described the Transapennine Umbri in Picenum.

units.la: Regio ab Apennino majore ex parte occupata, in situs sui varietate se quodam modo videtur oblectare. Nunc enim altis asperisque quasi horret Montibus; nunc collibus vestitur, qui Vini, Olei, Ficuum, aliorumque fructuum mirum quam fertiles; nunc denique amoenissimas pandit planicies, nihil non frugum abunde ferentes. Bonitatem Vbertatemque Umbria mirifice extollit Stephanus Auctorem citans Aristotelem.
units.tr: The region, for the most part occupied by the greater Apennine, seems in the variety of its situation to delight itself in a certain way. For now it bristles with high and rugged mountains; now it is clothed with hills, which are wonderfully fertile in wine, oil, figs and other fruits; and now at last it opens out most pleasant plains, bearing abundantly every kind of crop. Stephanus, citing Aristotle, extols Umbria's goodness and fertility in remarkable terms.

units.la: Incolae reliquis Italiae Populis sunt bellicosiores. Umbri quondam universim audiebant: uti videre est apud omnes Latinos Scriptores, innuente id quoque Stephano, apud quem, λέγει Ὀμβροι ... ἀλλὰ τὰς Γαλλικὰς συγγραφεῖς: alioquin Ὀμβρικοι nominantur eidem Stephano. Ombricos, ut antiqui Codices praeferunt, non Imbrios, scripserat ex Theophrasto Plinius lib. xxxi. cap. vii. ubi dicit invenire se apud Theophrastum Imbrios Harundinis & Iunci cinerem decoquere aqua solitos, donec exiguum superesset humoris. Umbrorum Gentem antiquissimam existimari Italiae, legimus apud Plinium lib. iii cap. xiiii, ut quos (addit) Umbrios ab Graecis putent dictos, quod inundatione terrarum imbribus superfuissent. Sic M. Antonius apud Solinum in membranis cap. viii. Bocchus adserit Gallorum veterem propaginem Umbros esse, qui tempore aquosa cladis imbribus superfuerunt. Sed fabulosum hoc, quum diluvium fuerit universale, nullaque terrae pars tunc supereminuerit.
units.tr: The inhabitants are more warlike than the other peoples of Italy. The Umbri were once universally heard of, as may be seen in all Latin writers, and Stephanus also indicates this, where he says: "the Ὀμβροι ... but the Gallic writers"; otherwise the same Stephanus calls them Ὀμβρικοί [Ombrikoi]. Pliny, in book 31, chapter 7, following Theophrastus, wrote Ombricos, as the old manuscripts have it, not Imbrios. There he says he found in Theophrastus that the Imbrii were accustomed to boil the ash of reed and rush in water until a little moisture remained. We read in Pliny, book 3, chapter 14, that the Umbrian people is thought to be the most ancient of Italy, "as those whom (he adds) the Greeks think were called Umbrii, because they survived the flooding of the lands by the rains." So M. Antonius, in Solinus, chapter 8 of the manuscripts: "Bocchus asserts that the Umbri are the ancient offspring of the Gauls, who survived the watery disaster by rains." But this is fabulous, since the flood was universal and no part of the earth then stood above the waters.

units.la: Memoriam Umbrorum celebrat Dionysius Halicarnassaeus libro i, Genremque supra cæteras omnes magnam vetustamque, ac multos Italiæ locos infeditîe, perhibet Plinius item loco indicato memoriæ prodit Umbros agro Palmenti, Præturiano, Adrianoque, Siculos atque Eburnes expulsos; ipsos vicissim pulsos ab Etruscis; illos a Gallis: præterea, quod ante montem antiquissimos esse, ut quorum ccc oppida debellarunt. Livius quoque frequenter Umbros commemorat, præsertim lib. ix, ubi per deditionem eos in Romanorum venisse potestatem narrat; præterea cum lib. xv, obsidionem Urbi Romæ commminatos scribit.
units.tr: Dionysius of Halicarnassus, in book 1, celebrates the memory of the Umbri, and says that this people was greater and more ancient than all the others and had occupied many places in Italy. Pliny, in the place already noted, likewise records that the Umbri drove the Siculi and Aborigines out of the land of Palmensis, Praeturia and Hadria, and were in turn driven out by the Etruscans, and they by the Gauls. He adds that they were the most ancient of all, since they had conquered three hundred towns. Livy also often mentions the Umbri, especially in book 9, where he tells that they came into the power of the Romans by surrender, and in book 15, where he writes that they threatened a siege of the city of Rome.

units.la: Umbrorum Fratres, Proles vel Coloni sunt, quos enumerat Alphabetico ordine Plinius libro iii. cap. xiiii:
units.tr: The brothers, offspring or colonists of the Umbri, are those whom Pliny enumerates in alphabetical order in book 3, chapter 14:

units.tr: Attidiates.

units.la: Asinates: Legendum Asinates, ab Asio, quorum etiam mentio in Tabula marmorea, in foro ibi collocata:
units.tr: Asinates: the reading should be Asinates, from Asium, and they are also mentioned on the marble tablet set up in the forum there:

units.la: IOVI. PAGANICO. SACR. EX. INDVLGENTIA. DOMINORVM SVCCESSVS. PVBLICVS. MVNICIPIVM ANNINATIVM. SER. AMOENIANVS ARDIEN. CVM. PORTICIBVS. A SOLO DVA. PBC. FECIT ITEM. MENSAM. ET ARAM D. D.
units.tr: To Jupiter Paganicus, sacred. By the indulgence of the lords, the public success of the municipium of the Anninates. Ser. Amoenianus of Ardea, with the porticoes, from the ground up, at his own expense, has built; likewise the table and the altar. D.D.

units.la: Ainates, ab Arna Opido, cujus meminit Silius libro viii, quodque Ptolemæo inter Vilumbrio Civitates.
units.tr: Ainates, from the town of Arna, which Silius mentions in book 8, and which Ptolemy lists among the cities of the Vilumbrians.

units.la: AEsinates, ab Opido Umbrorum, quod Ptolemæo: Hodie Cesi.
units.tr: AEsinates, from the town of the Umbrians, which Ptolemy names; today it is Cesi.

units.la: Camertes. Nomen his ab Urbe, quæ in Umbrorum montibus Καμέρτη Strabonis. De his ego in Piceno.
units.tr: Camertes. The name comes from the city in the mountains of Umbria, which is Strabo's Καμέρτη. I have written about these in the account of Picenum.

units.la: Casuentillani, quos Casuentinos scribunt, ut ait Abrahamus Ortelius, tres veteres Codices, cafitias, ni fallor, addens. Eorum mentio in antiquo Marmore, quod Interamnæ ad Summum Templum: T. FLAVIO. T. F. CLV. ISIDORO ♁ EQROM. PATRI. DIVORVM. EQ. PVB OMNIBVS. HONORIBVS. HONES E FVNCTO. QVINQ. II. AVGVRI SACER. PONT. PRAEF. SACROR PATRONO. MVNICIPII. INTE RAMNAT. NART. CASVENTI NORVM. VINDENATIVM
units.tr: Casuentillani, whom they write as Casuentini, as Abraham Ortelius says, adding that three old codices have "cafitias", I think. Mention of them is found on an ancient marble at Interamna, at the Summum Templum: To Titus Flavius Isidorus, son of Titus, of the Claudian tribe, Roman knight, father of the deified emperors, knight of the public horse, who held all honours honourably, quinquennial, augur, sacred pontiff, prefect of the sacred rites, patron of the municipium of Interamna Nartium Casuentinorum, the Vindenatian [tribe].

units.la: Carsulani, non Plinio solum, sed & Tacito: Κασζυλαι autem Straboni: olim, ubi nunc Cassia, notante Icandro. Dolates, qui S lentini cognominati: Veteribus Plinij Codicibus Dolates. Fulginates, à Fulginia, cujus infra descriptio. Foro-Flaminienses ab Foro Flaminy, de quo post. Foro-Julienses, cognomine Concubienses. Foro-Bremitiani. Foro-Sempronienses, à Foro Sempronij, quod hodie Fossumbrinuo. Iguvini ab Opido, quod Iguvium Ciceroni, Ingivium Silio, Iguvio Prolemæo: Eugubio hodie. Pro Iguvini antiqui Plinij codices habent Ingvinos. Iguvini videntur nominari in Inscriptione, quæ Fulinguæ in Vmbria:
units.tr: The Carsulani, named not only by Pliny but also by Tacitus; Strabo calls them Κασζυλαι; they were formerly where Cassia is now, according to Icander. The Dolates, surnamed Slentini; in the old codices of Pliny they are Dolates. The Fulginates, from Fulginia, which is described below. The Forum Flaminienses, from the Forum of Flaminius, of which more later. The Forum Julienses, surnamed Concubienses. The Forum Bremitiani. The Forum Sempronienses, from the Forum of Sempronius, which is today Fossombrone. The Iguvini, from the town which Cicero calls Iguvium, Silius Ingivium, Ptolemy Iguvio; today it is Gubbio. In place of Iguvini, the old codices of Pliny have Ingvinos. The Iguvini seem to be named in an inscription which is at Fulginia in Umbria:

units.la: P. ÆLIO. P. F. PAPIR MARCELLO CENT FAVM. SVB. PRINCIPE PEREGRINORVM. ADSTATO ET. PRINCIPI. ET. PRIMIPILO LEG. VII GEM. PIÆ. FEL. ADLEC TO. AD. MVNERA. PRAEF. LEGG. VII. CLAV. ET. PRIMÆ ADIVTRICIS. V. F. FLAMINI LVCVLARI. LAVREN. LAVINA PATRONO. ET. DECVRIONI. COLONIÆ. ARVLESIVM. PATRONO CIVIT. FORO. FLA. FVLGINIA ITEMQVE. IGVVINORVM. SPLEN DIDISSIMVS ORDO. FORO. FLAM. CIVIS. DEDICAT. DECVRIONIBVS ET. LIBERIS. ROR VM. PANEM ET. VINVM. S S XX. M. ITEM MVNICIPIBVS. S S LIII. DEDIT.
units.tr: To Publius Aelius Marcellus, son of Publius, of the Papirian tribe, centurion, chief of the foreign troops under the emperor, adlected for the offices, prefect of the Legions VII Gemina and VII Claudia, and of the First Adiutrix, Pious and Faithful, flamen of Lucullus, patron of Laurentum and Lavinium, and of the decurions of the colony of Arulesium, patron of the citizens of Forum Flaminium and Fulginia, and likewise of the Iguvini. The most splendid order of Forum Flaminium, citizens, dedicated this, to the decurions and the freedmen of the Romans, bread and wine, 20 sesterces each; and likewise to the municipia 53 sesterces each. He gave it.

units.la: Inscriptionem hanc, ut & alias, integras pono, quod multorum simul locorum Vmbriæ in ijs fiat mentio.
units.tr: I set out this inscription, as I do the others, in full, because in these mention is made of several places of Umbria at once.

units.la: Interamnates, ab Interamna, de qua post, Nartes cognominati, ab Nar Flumine, cui adjacent. Memorant eos varij Lapides: inter quos, qui Romæ in Vinea Cardinalis Carpensis: L. FABIO. M. F. GAL. CILONI. SEPTI MINO, & post magnum Elogium: X. VIR. STLIT. IVDIC. CVR. R. P. NICO MEDENSIVM. INTERAMNA TIVM. NARTIVM. ITEM GRAVI SCANORVM TI. CL. AMBRELIANVS. 7. LEG. V MACEDONICÆ. OB. MERITA
units.tr: Interamnates, from Interamna, of which more later; surnamed Nartes, from the river Nar, on which they lie. Various stones record them, among which is the one at Rome in the vineyard of the Cardinal of Carpi: To Lucius Fabius Gallus Ciloni Septiminus, son of Marcus, of the Claudian tribe... and after a long eulogy: decemvir for judging suits, curator of the public affairs of the Nicomedenses, of the Interamnates, of the Nartes, and likewise of the Graviscani; Tiberius Claudius Ambrelianus, of the Seventh Legion, of the Macedonian Fifth, on account of his services.

units.la: Alius, qui Interamnæ in Foro ad Officinam Aromatariam, in Basi marmorea: A. POMPEIO. A. F CLV. Q. PATRONO MVNICIPI. INTERAMNAT NAHARTIS. QVOD. EIVS OPERA. VNIVERSVM MVNICIPIVM. EX. SVMMIS PERICVLIS. ET. DIFFICVLTATIBVS. EXPEDITVM ET. CONSERVATVM. EST TESTAMENTO. L. LICINI. T. F. STATVA. STATVTA. EST
units.tr: Another, at Interamna, in the forum by the apothecary's shop, on a marble base: To Aulus Pompeius, son of Aulus, of the Claudian tribe, patron of the municipium of the Interamnates Nartes, because through his work the whole municipium was set free and preserved from the greatest dangers and difficulties. By the will of Lucius Licinius, son of Titus, a statue was set up.

units.la: Est ibidem & alia Basis marmorea ad Summum Templum.
units.tr: There is also another marble base at the Summum Templum.

units.la: Mevan tes, ab Mevania Opido.
units.tr: Mevantes, from the town of Mevania.

units.la: Mevanienses, alij ab Superioribus, pro quibus alij codices Mevanionenses. IVLIÆ. LVCILIÆ L. IVLI. IVLIANI FIL PATRONI. MVNICIPI CVIVS PATER THERMAS. OCRICVLA NIS. A. SOLO. EXTRVCTAS SVA. PECVNIA. DONAVIT DECVR. AVG. PLEBS L. D. D. D
units.tr: Mevanienses; some derive them from the above, and for these other codices have Mevanionenses. To Julia Lucilia, daughter of Lucius Julius Julianus, patron of the municipium, whose father built the baths of Ocriculum from the ground up at his own expense; the decurions, the Augustales and the common people [set this up] by decree of the decurions.

units.la: Ostrani ab Vrbe, quæ o᷑s᷒ Ptolemæo. Pitulani, Pisuertes & Morgentini cognominati.
units.tr: Ostrani, from the town which Ptolemy names. Pitulani, Pisuertes and Morgentini are surnames.

units.la: Pesestini olim ubi, Tractus qui hodie Plesteia, inter Iguvium, Spoletum, & Fulginium; ubi Probigo opidum. In aliis Plinij Codicibus scribuntur Pestini, Pestini & Palastini, inemendatius.
units.tr: Pesestini: formerly where the district now called Plesteia is, between Iguvium, Spoletum and Fulginium, where the town of Probigo is. In other codices of Pliny they are written Pestini, Pestini and Palastini, less correctly.

units.la: Sentinates, ab Sentino.
units.tr: Sentinates, from Sentinum.

units.la: Sasinates ab Sarsina Paluti Patria. Ortelius vetusta Plinij exemplaria libro xxx cap. xiiii legere notat Farsinates. Vide infra.
units.tr: Sasinates, from Sarsina, the homeland of Plautus. Ortelius notes that old copies of Pliny, book 30, chapter 14, read Farsinates. See below.

units.la: Spoletini à Spoletio. Basis marmorea Romæ, in domo Iulij Porcarij ad Minervam.
units.tr: Spoletini, from Spoletium. A marble base at Rome, in the house of Julius Porcarius near Minerva.

units.la: ASTERII
units.tr: ASTERIUS

units.la: L. TVRCIO. AFRONIANO. V. C FILIO. L. TVRCI. AFRONIANI. V. C PRÆFECTI. VRBIS. NEPOTI L. TVRCI. SECVNDI. C. V. CONSVLIS QVÆSTORI. PRÆTORI. QVINDECEM VIRO. SACRIS. FACIVNDIS. CORRECTORI. TVSCIÆ. ET. VMBRIÆ. OMNI VIRTVTE. PRÆSTANTI. STATVAM EX. AERE. ORDO. SPOLETINORVM AD. MEMORIAM. PERPETVI. NOMINIS CONLOCAVIT CVRANTIBVS. FL. SPE. V. PE. ET. CONDO NIO. TAVRO. IVN POST. AMANTI. ET. ALBINI. CONS
units.tr: To Lucius Turcius Afronianus, of senatorial rank, son of Lucius Turcius Afronianus, of senatorial rank, prefect of the city, grandson of Lucius Turcius Secundus, of consular rank: quaestor, praetor, quindecemvir for the sacred rites, corrector of Tuscia and Umbria, distinguished for every virtue. The order of the Spoletines set up this bronze statue to his memory, for a name that will last forever. Overseers: Fl. Spe... V.P.E., and Condonius Taurus Junius Post Amantius and Albinus, consuls.

units.la: Suarrani.
units.tr: Suarrani.

units.la: Sestinates, fortean à Sestino, cujus, & aliorum Locorum in Ara marmorea, quæ in Vineâ Cardinalis Carpensis, mentio:
units.tr: Sestinates, perhaps from Sestinum, of which, and of other places, there is mention on the marble altar in the vineyard of Cardinal Carpensis.

units.la: Narnienses, ab Narnia. Narniates Stephano.
units.tr: Narnienses, from Narnia. Stephanus calls them Narniates.

units.la: Nucerini, quorum etiam meminit Livius libro xxvii, quique corrupte Lucerini Auctori de VV. Illustrib. cap. xxxii, ab Nuceria, qui Favonienses & Camelani cognomine.
units.tr: Nucerini, whom Livy also mentions in book 27, and whom the author of De Viris Illustribus, ch. 32, wrongly calls Lucerini. From Nuceria, they have the surnames Favonienses and Camelani.

units.la: Ocriculani ab Ocriculo. Basis ibi Statuæ: CALLICANO ET VETERE. COS VI ID. IAN. COIL. I. PR. P SATRI. CEMO. T. MISSI HONESTA. POSTHVMI. VII M. BLRO. COS L. CENSORINO. IVSTVS. VIRVNO T. FLAVIO. TO Y. CLV. ISIDORO PATRONO. MVNICIPI. INTE RAMNAT. NART. CASVENTI NORVM. VINDENATIVM
units.tr: Ocriculani, from Ocriculum. The base of a statue there bears an inscription, garbled and hard to read, with the names of consuls and of a patron of the municipality.

units.la: Nominantur Plinio postremo loco Vicentini.
units.tr: The Vicentini are named by Pliny in the last place.

units.la: Sul ater.
units.tr: Sul ater.

units.la: Tadinates, in aliis libris Sadinates nominantur.
units.tr: Tadinates; in other books they are named Sadinates.

units.la: Trebiates.
units.tr: Trebiates.

units.la: Tuficani, ab Vrbe Tifca, quod in libro legitur de Lunitibus. Vide Iuficum in Piceno.
units.tr: Tuficani, from the city Tifca, which is read in the book on the Lunitae. See Iuficum in Picenum.

units.la: Tiferinates, a T.Ferro, cognomine Tiberini & Metaurenses; pro Tiberinis apud Plinium alij Codices habent Tiburinos, inemendate. Tifernum cognomine Tiberinum est apud eundem Plinium libro iv cap. 1. ut infra dicam.
units.tr: Tiferinates, from T. Ferrus, surnamed Tiberini and Metaurenses. Other manuscripts of Pliny have Tiburinos instead of Tiberinis, which is incorrect. Tifernum, surnamed Tiberinum, is mentioned by the same Pliny in book 4, ch. 1, as I shall say below.

units.la: Vellientates: in aliis Vellinonates
units.tr: Vellientates; in other books, Vellinonates.

units.la: Vrbinates, ab Vrbino, cognomine Metaurenses & Hortenses. Elogium legitur Romæ in Pavimento Sacelli, quod est ad Templum S. Georgij in Cœlio Monte, potcum L. RANIO. OPTATO. V. C. COS CVRATORI REIP. VRVINATIVM. METAVRENSIVM
units.tr: Urbinates, from Urbinum, surnamed Metaurenses and Hortenses. An inscription is read at Rome on the pavement of a chapel by the church of St George on the Caelian Hill, with the name of Lucius Ranius Optatus, of consular rank, curator of the state of the Urbinates and Metaurenses.

units.la: Vindenates is Plinio dicuntur, qui Vindenates Bah marmoreæ, quam Interamnæ Nahartium, vulgo Terni, descriptam paulio ante repræsentavi, postcam
units.tr: The Vindenates are named by Pliny. I have already shown, a little earlier, the marble base of the Vindenates, which is described at Interamna Nahartium, commonly called Terni, and after it...

units.la: Sed & hos seu idem Plinius interiisse scribit Felsgnates, & eos, qui Clusiolum tenuerunt supra Interamnam: Suuatates, cum opidis Acerris, quæ Vafria cognominabantur, Turnes, ue, quod etiam Tiernum: item Solmates, Suuatus, Falisnates, Apenna-nes Aternates, cum Crustoreaa: Ilbutuanus, Pancenses, Pesinates, qui in quibusdam Libris Pilaters & Ciclinus Umbriae gentem etiam Sabinos esse; tradit Dionysius Halicarnassæus lib. ii. De iis speciatim infra hoc eodem capite. Sabini item antea ri font solvi: Cuirinum & Fidenates, de quibus etiam ego post Sabinos exlin ansi scities.
units.tr: But Pliny also writes that these, or the same people, have perished: the Felsgnates, and those who held Clusiolum above Interamna; the Suuatates, with the towns of Acerrae, which were surnamed Vafria, and Turnes, which is also Tiernum; likewise the Solmates, Suuatus, Falisnates, Apennanes, Aternates, with Crustoreaa; Ilbutuanus, Pancenses, Pesinates. In some books the Pilaters and Ciclinus are mentioned. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, in book 2, says that the people of Umbria are also Sabines. I shall discuss these in detail below in this same chapter. The Sabines likewise were formerly... the Cuirinum and the Fidenates, of whom I too shall speak after the Sabines.

units.la: Vindeuam hodie, quamvis non totam, Ipeleinum Ducatum appellant; vulgo Ducato di Spoleto, ab Vrbe Spoleto, quæ olim Regia fuit Ducum Langbardorum.
units.tr: Today they call the whole of Umbria, though not all of it, the Duchy of Spoleto, commonly Ducato di Spoleto, from the city Spoleto, which was once the royal seat of the Lombard dukes.

units.la: Hæc de Vmbria universim: ordo postulat, ut ad singula speciatim explicanda veniatur.
units.tr: These are general remarks on Umbria. Order requires that we now come to explain each place in particular.

units.la: Primum ab Tiberis intimo versus inferiora Pratolinum est opidum: infraque mille perripam pasibus cum Lauta, tum permunita Civitas, Borgo di S. Sepolcro; non magni ævi. Sunt qui putant, inter quos Blondus, locum hic esse, ubi Plinius lumior Fest. lib. iv Villam habuisse se significat, ad Apennini radices, iuxta Tiberim, Montibus ibi spectaculum mittat Theatri efficientibus. Alij negant. Quidam volunt Strappiae esse Ptolemæi, qui tamen eam inter mediterraneas Tusciæ Vrbes numerat. Batiueba scribitur in Itineraria Tabula, vitiose. Vide omnino quæ notavi ad Iter Antonini, quod in fine posui Capitis de Tuscia. Diu hanc Vrbem Ecclesia Romana sub sua ditione tenuit, donecab Eugenio iv P. M. xii autreetarum nummum millibus Florentinus fuit oppignerata. Nobilitavit eam Mariscilla Cinanensis IC. præsitantissimus, & Camertium Præsul.
units.tr: First, from the innermost part of the Tiber going downstream, there is the town of Pratolinum. A little less than a thousand paces further on is the city of Borgo di San Sepolcro, both elegant and well fortified, not of great antiquity. Some think, among them Biondo, that this is the place where Pliny the Younger, in book 4 of his letters, says he had a villa, at the foot of the Apennines, beside the Tiber, where the mountains there form a natural theatre. Others deny it. Some want Strappiae to be the place of Ptolemy, who nonetheless counts it among the inland towns of Tuscany. In the Itinerary Table it is written as Batiueba, wrongly. See everything I have noted on the Itinerary of Antoninus, which I have added at the end of the chapter on Tuscany. For a long time the Roman Church held this city under its rule, until Pope Eugene IV, for twelve thousand gold pieces, pledged it to the Florentines. It was made famous by Mariscilla of Cinanensis, a most excellent jurist, and by the bishop of Camerino.

units.la: Sequitur Civitas Cacellana, Citta di Castello. Sic, vel etiam Castello simpliciter, hodie dicitur, quæ, ut placet Zachariæ Lilio, Blondo, Platinæ, Leandro, Cello Citso Cittadino Angelerio apud Ortelium, & alijs, Tifernum Plinio lib. iii. cap. v, cui inde Tifernates, eodem libro cap. x. iii : Τιφερνον Ptolemaeo; Plinio denique lib. iv. Epist. i, addito cognomine, Tifernum Tiberinum; qui addit se sua pecunia Templum ibi excstruxisse. Huc pertinent illa Sex. Iulij Frontini de Coloniis, quae adscribamtur, uti legenda centeo: Ager Tifernas (legitur Tifernus) Centurns just adsignatus: postea, iussu Imp. Tiberij Caesaris, cutque, prout occupavit miles: defficientibus his, alijs paucioribus est adsignatus: Termini plerique, quod ratione observationis tantum ascendunt, quantum rectura limitum. Ornarunt hanc Urbem Gregorius ciusque discipulus Lælius, Scriptis utrque ex Graeco in Latinum sermonem versis clari. Urbis
units.tr: Next comes the city of Cacellana, today called Città di Castello, or simply Castello. This is Tifernum in Pliny, book 3, ch. 5, according to Zacharias Lilius, Biondo, Platina, Leander, Cellus, Citso, Cittadino, Angelerius, as cited by Ortelius, and others. From it come the Tifernates, in the same book, ch. 10; Ptolemy calls it Τιφερνον [Tiphernon]. Finally, in Pliny, book 4, letter 1, with the added surname, it is Tifernum Tiberinum, and he adds that he built a temple there at his own expense. To this belongs the passage of Sextus Julius Frontinus on colonies, which I think should be read as follows: "The territory of Tifernas (the reading is Tifernus) was assigned to a centurion; later, by order of the Emperor Tiberius Caesar, it was assigned in the same way as the soldier had occupied it. When these failed, it was assigned to others, fewer in number. The boundaries are for the most part marked, since they rise as far as the straight line of the limits." Gregory, and his disciple Lelius, both famous for writing translated from Greek into Latin, adorned this city. The Urbis

units.la: principatum diu tenuit nobilis Vitelliorum gens, de cujus Virtutibus Rebusque gestis consulendus Leander Albertus.
units.tr: For a long time the principate of the city was held by the noble family of the Vitelli, about whose virtues and deeds Leander Alberti should be consulted.

units.la: Succedit mox Montontum, Montone vulgo; summorum Ducum, inter quos primas tenet Bracius, ortu incluctum. Post Montonium Fratta est.
units.tr: Next comes Montone, called Montone in the vernacular, of great and distinguished leaders, among whom Braccio holds the first place, a native of the place. After Montone comes Fratta.

units.la: Tiferno r. m. xx versus Orientaliora abest Eugubium, ad Apennini radices positum: aditum praestante amoena pulcraque Planitie. Sunt qui volunt esse, quod Iuginium Silio libro viii; Igunium Ciceroni libro vii ad Atticum, epist. xiii, Iguvium Ptolemaeo lib. iii. Dominicus tamen Niger Eugubium idem fuisse cum eo; quod Ptolemaeo paullo ante Iguvium. Legitur & apud Caesarem Ignium, pro quo quidam reponunt Iguvium. Τὸ Ῥυγγίνον ἔθος nominatur apud Strabonem libro v. non dubito, quin scripserit Ῥυγγετν vel Ῥυγγίνον; & is sic, in quo nunc D. Vbaldi Fanum;
units.tr: Twenty Roman miles east of Tifernum lies Gubbio, set at the foot of the Apennines, offering access through a pleasant and beautiful plain. Some think it is what Silius, in book 8, calls Iuginium, and what Cicero, in letter 13 of book 7 to Atticus, calls Igunium, and Ptolemy in book 3 calls Iguvium. Dominicus Niger, however, holds that Eugubium is the same as what Ptolemy called Iguvium a little earlier. Caesar also has Ignium, for which some substitute Iguvium. Strabo, in book 5, mentions τὸ Ῥυγγίνον ἔθος [to Ruggínon éthos], which I do not doubt he wrote as Ῥυγγετν or Ῥυγγίνον. This is the place where the church of St Ubaldus now stands.

units.la: cuius adiacet radicibus Eugubium, perversus Opidum, multis Antiquitatem suam testanshodieque vestigijs. Visuntur enim ibi cum aliquot Rudera Templorum & Theatri, tum Tabulae octo, ante annos aliquot repertae: quarum una litteris, ut videtur, Graecis invertis; Linguaque, ut quidam autumant, Aeolicae; alij volunt Characteres esse Etruscos. & Tuscorum Linguam; reliquae vero litteris quidem Latinis, sed lingua, ut putatur, Etrusca sunt scriptae. Exempla sunt apud Martinum Smetium folio xxxix verso, & seq. Eugubij, quod diruptum aliquando in eam, qua nunc est, amplitudinem excrevit, magnificum est, artisque summae opus, Caria Priorum, ubi Fons pereximus, supra cunctas aedificij partes exiliens. Frequens hodie. Incolis industria summa Lanariam Negociationem tractantibus. Quis
units.tr: At the foot of this lies Gubbio, a town that tells of its antiquity to many even today by its remains. For there can be seen some ruins of temples and of a theatre, and eight tablets found some years ago, one of which is written in Greek letters, apparently reversed, in a language which some say is Aeolic, while others hold that the characters are Etruscan and the language Etruscan. The rest are written in Latin letters, but in a language which is thought to be Etruscan. Examples are in Martin Smetius, folio 39 verso and following. Gubbio, which was once broken down and afterwards rebuilt to its present size, is splendid, and a work of the highest skill, especially the Palace of the Priors, where a fountain, rising above all parts of the building, is a remarkable sight. It is populous today, and its inhabitants, with great industry, carry on the wool trade.

units.la: post Ecclesiam Romanam ex Monfeltriis & aliis Principibus habuerit Eugubium, docet Leander, Patriam hanc tuam illustravit D. Vbaldus, Civis eius & Antistes. Episcoparus enim gaudet dignitate. Ager Campestris partim, partim Collinus; Frumenti undique ferax.
units.tr: After the Roman Church, Gubbio was held by the Montefeltro and other princes; Leander shows this. St Ubaldus, a citizen and bishop of this place, made your fatherland famous. For the city enjoys the dignity of a bishopric. The land is partly flat and partly hilly, and everywhere fertile in grain.

units.la: Supra Eugubium Brancha est; & in Via Flaminia, quae Romam ducit, Scheccia: tum loco vicino D. Pedrintiani Fanum, S. Pedrizano, propemodum in Apennino: cuius latus prosequenti Costaciarum Agri Eugubini Opidum occurrit; paulloque ulterius Sigellum, Perusini: mox Fossatum in praecelso Apennini Colle; iuxtaque quarto lapide in eodem Colle Gualdum, quod Blondus ab Langbarbis conditum scribit, Vallido Urbe loco finitimo diruta.
units.tr: Above Gubbio lies Branca, and on the Via Flaminia, which leads to Rome, Scheggia; then, in a nearby place, the church of San Pietro Pedrintiani, called San Pedrizano, almost in the Apennines. Along its side, as you go on, you meet Costacciaro, a town of the territory of Gubbio, and a little further Sigillo, belonging to Perugia. Soon after comes Fossato, on a high hill of the Apennines, and next to it, four miles off on the same hill, Gualdo, which Biondo writes was founded by the Lombards, after the nearby city of Vallido was destroyed.

units.la: Post Gualdum Apennini Opida paullatim elongari incipiunt. Deinde Civitas est Nuceria, lateri item Apennini adhaerens. Sic Livio libro xxvii, qui deletam scribit, dicitur; quae Νουκερία Ptolemaeo, Umbrorum in Piceno Urbs; Straboni, in Via Flaminia. Nucerium Tabulae Itinerariae. Nocera vulgo. Inde Nucerini, de quibus ante. Nuceria Constantia muro ducta colonia scribitur a Frontino, iussu Imp. Augusti. Alphaternum etiam dictam ex Livio notant Volaterranus, Blondus, Niger, Leander, alij. Sed Alphaternam apud Livium legendum docet ex Diodoro Karolus Sigonius. Nuceriam Strabo commendat ab Vasis ligneis.
units.tr: After Gualdo the towns of the Apennines gradually begin to thin out. Then there is the city of Nuceria, also clinging to the side of the Apennines. So it is called in Livy, book 27, who writes that it was destroyed; Ptolemy calls it Νουκερία [Nouketia], a city of the Umbrians in Picenum; Strabo places it on the Via Flaminia. The Itinerary Table calls it Nucerium. Today it is Nocera. From it come the Nucerini, of whom I spoke before. Frontinus writes that Nuceria was made a colony, walled by the constant effort of the Emperor Augustus. Volaterranus, Biondo, Niger, Leander and others note that it was also called Alphaternum, from Livy. But Karl Sigonius teaches, from Diodorus, that Alphaternam should be read in Livy. Strabo praises Nuceria for its wooden vessels.

units.la: Haud procul inde in amoena Planitie Fulignum se offert; Fuligno vernacule. Φυλίνιον Appiano libro v bell. Civilium; sexaginta supra centum stadiis Perusia distans. Fulginia Silio Italico libro ix, & antiquo Lapidi apud Smetium. Is supra positus. Inde Fulginates Plinio, ut antea dixi.
