Marius Niger, Dalechampius, & Zacharias Lilius putant idem esse cum Foro Flaminij, cuius Plinius & Festus quoque meminerunt; quodque Strabo Φόρου Φλαμινίου vocat. Sed in Lapide, de quo dixi, Fulginia & Forum Flaminij sunt diversa. Tinna dividitur, Flumine parvo & inglorio. Conditum est hoc opidum in Orbem, tribusque partibus habet Monasteria D.D.D. Augustini, Francisci, Dominici: Templum item D. Feliciani, Opus novum, latque pulcherrimum. Ad huius pertinet Silij illud: ——pareque j. cem fine mænibus arvo
units.tr: A little beyond that, Fulignum presents itself on a pleasant plain; the locals call it Fuligno. Appian in book 5 of the Civil Wars calls it Fulinium [Φυλίνιον], lying one hundred and sixty stadia from Perusia. Silius Italicus in book 9, and an ancient inscription cited by Smetius, call it Fulginia, and it lies above that place. Hence the Fulginates of Pliny, as I said before. Marius Niger, Dalechampius and Zacharias Lilius think it is the same as the Forum Flaminii, which Pliny and Festus also mention, and which Strabo calls Forum Flaminium [Φόρου Φλαμινίου]. But in the inscription I mentioned, Fulginia and Forum Flaminii are different places. The town is divided by the Tinna, a small and undistinguished river. The town was founded in a circle and has three monasteries of the Augustinians, Franciscans and Dominicans, as well as the temple of St Felician, a new work and very handsome. To this place belongs that line of Silius: ——and a field equal in extent to the walls of Fulginia.

units.la: Fulginia.
units.tr: Fulginia.

units.la: Quem locum enarrat Marsus, urbe quidem Silij muris eam carmine; postea vero pul. herrimus & optimus arc incœtam. In Foro Palatij sunt tria. In uno habitant V I-VIII Fe[?] ad quos primum Civiles deferuntur Controversiæ, Magistratus fungentes bimestris: in altero Præctor, qui graviores causas duplicat, cuius munus sex iurat mentes: in tertio Gubernator, cum summa potestas Pontificis nomine tribuitur. Ipse opus stans fulget titulo. Inluit avit plurimum nomen huius Vrbis Gentile. Memorius Scriptis, quæ edita, celebris. Exeilam a Perufinis anno c10 cc xxxv tertiam Blondus Libro I Hist. xvi[?] non sine gravissima indignatione Martini V P.M. qui Perufinos Anathemate perculsos exire noluit, nisi restitutis Vrbi novis mænibus. Ab eo tempore Fulginum tempe florum. Centuntur Fulgiuntes eximiæ præ ceteris gentibus Tragemata ex Saccaro conficere, quæ vulgo Fuiginata vocant.
units.tr: Marsus describes this place, a city that Silius praised in verse for its walls, but later it was built up with a most beautiful and excellent citadel. In the Palace Forum there are three bodies. In one, the seven or eight men sit who first hear civil disputes and serve as magistrates for two months at a time; in another sits the praetor, who hears the weightier cases and whose office is sworn to by six men; in the third is the governor, in whose hands supreme power is exercised in the name of the Pontiff. The work itself shines, standing in its inscription. The city's Gentile name has greatly illuminated it. It is famous for its written records, which have been published. Blondus, in book 1 of his History, says that in 1235 it was driven out by the Perugians, to the great indignation of Martin V, the Supreme Pontiff, who would not allow the Perugians, struck by anathema, to leave unless the city had new walls restored. From that time Fulginum enjoyed its flourishing age. The Fulginates are said to excel all other peoples in making sweetmeats from sugar, which they commonly call Fuiginata.

units.la: Quinque a Fuligno p. M. ex arta situm est Hispellum: hic Sylo Plinioque scribitur: Strabonis Ἱσπέλλον, Ptolemæo Ἱσπελλὸν quod Spello vernacule: Spellum, ut hodie, vocat Hyginus de Limitibus constituendis: Spellates autem Incolas. Colonia Iulia Hispella exstat in quadam antiqua Inscriptione, quæ in Thesauro Hubert. Gruteri. In imperio est & ditione Perusinorum: ideoque anno c10 10 xxix ductum a Philiberto Arausiorum Principe, Karoli V Cæsaris Legato; anno autem c10 10 xxxvi, Pauli III P.M. Ius, mœnibus nudatum: eaque forma nunc jacet.
units.tr: Five miles from Fuligno, on a steep site, lies Hispellum. Silius and Pliny write it thus; Strabo has Hispellon [Ἱσπέλλον], Ptolemy Hispellon [Ἱσπελλὸν], which in the vernacular is Spello. Hyginus, in his work on fixing boundaries, calls it Spellum, as it is still called today, and its inhabitants Spellates. An ancient inscription, which is in the Thesaurus of Hubert Gruter, records the colony of Julia Hispella. It is under the rule and jurisdiction of the Perugians; therefore in 1529 it was taken by Philibert, Prince of Orange, legate of Emperor Charles V, and in 1536, under Paul III, its walls were stripped and it now lies in this form.

units.la: Quinto ab Hispello lapide ostentat sese edito loco Assisium, dictum ab Asi monte proximo. Ἄσισιον Ptolemæo & Procopio: Ἄσσις Straboni: Axu, ut putat Zacharias Lilius in suo Orbis Breviario, apud Propertium: Scanderitisque Axis consurgit vertice muris.
units.tr: Five miles from Hispellum, Assisium shows itself on a high site, named from Mount Asius nearby. Ptolemy and Procopius have Asision [Ἄσισιον], Strabo Assis [Ἄσσις]; Zacharias Lilius in his Breviary of the World thinks it is Axus, as in Propertius: Axis rises with its walls on the climbing summit.

units.la: Assisi vulgo & Assi. Ab Assio autem Assisinates, de quibus ante. Assisium Episcopatus dignitate clarum. Patria est D. Francisci, qui Familiæ Minorum Conditor; Templo ibi hic nestatus iam ruoditissimo. Vexarum adeo Civilibus legitur discordiis, ut pene interierit. Ibi & hic Sepulcrum Reginæ Cypri item ix Sociorum D. Francisci: bibliotheca inter instructissima: Domus quoque vetusta, quam Iocus Pagan Templum fuisse memorant.
units.tr: It is commonly called Assisi, or Assi. From Assium come the Assisinates, of whom I spoke before. Assisium is famous for the dignity of its bishopric. It is the birthplace of St Francis, founder of the Order of Friars Minor; the church there, now very ancient, is named after him. It was so harassed by civil discords that it nearly perished. Here too are the tomb of the Queen of Cyprus and of the nine companions of St Francis; the library is among the best furnished. There is also an old house which Pagan Joco records was a temple.

units.la: Rursus ab Fuligno ulterius læva in parte secundum Apenninii latus Trevi inveniuntur. Olim hoc eiusdem Mutusca dicebatur. Virgilius lib. vii Æneid. Tuscis manuit amnis aliusque aque Mutuscæ.
units.tr: Again, on the left side of the Apennine slope, further on from Fuligno, lie Trevi. Formerly this same place was called Mutusca. Virgil in book 7 of the Aeneid: The Tuscan river and the waters of Mutusca.

units.la: Ad quem locum Servius, primum Mutusca, deinde Trebiam, quæ nunc Trebula, dictam fertur, ad quam Romani ab Hannibale Karthaginensium duce cæsi. Vere Servius priora, posterioria fallo. Mutusca quidem Trebula post dicta; sed hæc Trebia non sunt Trebia, ad quam clades illata ab Hannibale Romanis. Trebia enim Calamitatis Romanæ memoria celebris. Fluvius est ultra Placentiam in Gallia Togata docentibus id omnibus Historiographis: Mutusca autem Virgilij procul a Trebia haud in Umbris, prope Sabinos, qua & Trebula. Et hinc Plinius lib. iii cap. xii. Trebulani, qui cognominantur Mutuscani, & qui Suffenates. Hæc est Τρεβούλα (ita legendum, non Τρέουσα) quam in Sabinis agnoscit Strabo libro v; Hæc Trebula, quam eadem memorat libro iii. adversus Gentes Arnobius: Hæc Τεβουλα, cuius meminit Halicarnassæus, Reate ix Iladris distantis: Hæc denique, quæ duplici nomine Trebula Mutusca, apud Obsequentem de Prodigiis & in Veteri Lapide, quem in Auctario publicavit Lipsius. Putant Erythræus, Villanovanus, & I eandem Trebiam hanc eamdem esse cum Trebula Ptolemæi. Sed errant. Τεβουλα (ita enim scribitur) Ptolemæo, ut & Livio, adscribitur Campaniæ Urbibus: cuius Incolas Plinius libro iii cap. iv Balnuenses cognominat; ut hos cap. x i, quemadmodum dixi, Mutuscani & Suffenates. Suffenas vocat Dionysius, ut annotat Sigonius de Iure Italiæ libro i. cap. xviii. Martialis Trebulanum Caseum loquentem facit his verbis: Trebula nos genuit, commendat gratia duplex; Sive lens flamma, sive domantur aqua. Humidam Trebulam vocat alibi idem Poëta. Humida quæ gelidas submittit Trebula Valles. Et viridis Caneri menstrua alget ager.
units.tr: On this passage Servius says that it was first called Mutusca, then Trebia, which is now called Trebula, near which the Romans were slain by Hannibal the Carthaginian general. Servius is right about the earlier names, wrong about the later. Mutusca was indeed afterwards called Trebula; but this Trebia is not the Trebia near which Hannibal inflicted defeat on the Romans. For the Trebia is famous for the memory of Roman disaster. It is a river beyond Placentia in Cisalpine Gaul, as all the historians teach. But Virgil's Mutusca is far from the Trebia, not in Umbria but near the Sabines, where also is Trebula. Hence Pliny in book 3, chapter 12: the Trebulani, who are surnamed Mutuscani, and the Suffenates. This is Trebula [Τρεβούλα] (so it should be read, not Τρέουσα), which Strabo in book 5 places among the Sabines; this is the Trebula which Arnobius mentions in book 3 against the Gentiles; this is the Tebula [Τεβουλα] mentioned by the Halicarnassian, nine miles from Reate; this is finally the one which, under the double name Trebula Mutusca, appears in Obsequens on Prodigies and in an old inscription published by Lipsius in his Auctarium. Erythraeus, Villanovanus and others think this same Trebia is the Trebula of Ptolemy. But they are wrong. Tebula (for so it is written) is assigned by Ptolemy, as by Livy, to the cities of Campania; Pliny in book 3, chapter 4 surnames its inhabitants Balnuenses, as he calls these, in chapter 11, as I said, Mutuscani and Suffenates. Dionysius calls them Suffenas, as Sigonius notes in his De Iure Italiae, book 1, chapter 18. Martial makes the Trebulan cheese speak in these words: Trebula bore us, and two gifts commend us: whether a lentil is boiled in fire or tamed in water. The same poet elsewhere calls it damp Trebula: Damp Trebula, which sends its cold valleys down, and the green field of Caneros lies chilled in its monthly phase.

units.la: E regione Trevi Mons Falco est oppidum amœnus in Collibus; Novum quidem, sed Incolis frequens: quo S. Clara, Eremitarum Ordinis virgo, fertur orta.
units.tr: Opposite Trevi lies Monte Falco, a pleasant town on the hills; it is new, but full of inhabitants, and St Clare, virgin of the Order of Hermits, is said to have been born there.

units.la: Tum in radicibus ejus Collis, Viaque quondam Flaminia Bevania est; Bevagna vulgo: Mevania Livio, Tacito, Solino, Suetonio, Antonino, & aliis Latinis, Straboni & Ptolemæo. Mevanie Itinerariæ Tabulæ, corruptius. Inde Mevaniates, de quibus antea dixi. Plinio: cui & Laterensis Martius Mevania celebratur libro xxxv. cap. xiii. Mevania natus est Propertius ipso canente libro iiii: Umbria me notis antiqua penatibus edit, Mentior? an patriæ tangitur ora tuæ? Qua nebulosa tuo irrorat Mevania Campo, Et Lacus estivo tepet Umber aquis Scandentesque Avii?
units.tr: Then at the foot of that hill, on the old Via Flaminia, is Bevania, now Bevagna in the vernacular: Mevania in Livy, Tacitus, Solinus, Suetonius, Antoninus and other Latin writers, and in Strabo and Ptolemy. The Itinerary tables have Mevanie, more corruptly. From it come the Mevaniates, of whom I spoke earlier. Laterensis Martius also celebrates Mevania in Pliny, book 35, chapter 13. The poet Propertius was born at Mevania, as he sings himself in book 4: Umbria, an ancient land, bore me with its familiar household gods. Am I lying? Or is the shore of your homeland touched? Where misty Mevania waters your plain, and the Umbrian lake grows warm with summer waters, and the Avii, climbing slopes?

units.la: Non prorsus insuperhabendum quod notat Servius ad illud Virgilij libro ii Georgic.
units.tr: What Servius notes on that line of Virgil in book 2 of the Georgics should not be dismissed entirely.

units.la: Hinc albi Clitumni greges
units.tr: Hence the white herds of Clitumnus.

units.la: Clitumnus Fluvius est, inquit, in Mevania quæ pars est Umbriæ, partis Tusciæ: de quo Fluvio discet Plinius in Historia Naturali, quod Animalia, quæ cum potaverint, albos Fœtus creant. Docemur enim Mevaniam esse Umbriæ portionem, cui primaria Urbs cognominis Mevania. De Regione etiam exaudiendi Lucanus & Silius: Ille lib.i. Et qui tauriferis ubi se Mevania Campis Expandit;
units.tr: Servius says: Clitumnus is a river in Mevania, which is part of Umbria, part of Tuscany; from this river Pliny learns, in his Natural History, that animals which have drunk from it produce white offspring. We learn that Mevania is a portion of Umbria, whose chief city bears the same name, Mevania. Lucan and Silius also speak of the region: Lucan in book 1: And where Mevania spreads over the bull-bearing plains.

units.la: Hic autem libro vii. ——Et late Mevania Pratis.
units.tr: Silius, in book 7: And Mevania broadly across its meadows.

units.la: Mevania Territorium Armentorum Gregumque hodieque est ferax.
units.tr: Mevania is still today a fertile territory for herds and flocks.

units.la: Viam porro per amœnam Planiciem, ubi Fulignum & Trebula, pergenti, læva parte Spoletum occurrit, à quo Ducatus Spoletini nomen Umbriæ tributum. Vulgo Spoleto. Σπολήτιον Straboni lib.iv & Ptolemæo; Spoletium Antonino & reliquis Latinis. Colonum agnoscunt Florus in Epitoma Liviana libri xx, Paterculus libr. i, Cicero in Balbiana, Frontinus de Coloniis. Situm est Spoletum inæqualiter, partim in plano, partim in colle, cui & Arx insidet munitissima; ex vetusto quodam Amphitheatro quod hic erat, facta, uti Blondus censet libro vi Histor. Ex Urbe lapideo aditur Ponte, qui magno artificio ingenioque factus pilis grandibus xxiv sustinetur: urbisque partem editiore loco positam cum Arce, quæ in alio est colle, quem modica ab Urbe submover convallis, adnectit. Arx à propinquioribus Pontificis temper gubernatur. Urbs hodie splendida est, & omnium rerum affluit copia. Prætorium Spoleti splendidissimum ab Theodorico Gothorum Rege (cui hic locus summopere placebat) ædificatum; ab Gothis deinde una cum Regia cversum; Narsetis autem opera post restauratum, auctores sunt Blondus & Sabellicus. Videre ibidem licet præter alia magni ævi ædificia & Antiquitates reliquas, Theatri fundamenta, vetustissimum extra Urbem Concordiæ Fanum, Formæ: ibidem sublimes ac solidas Aquæductuum ex Apennini cofis partim excisas, partim opere lateritio ex ima Valle fornicibus in altum subductas. Spoletum frustra ab Hannibale obtentum memorat Livius lib.xxi. Spoleti Marem in Feminam commutatum refert idem lib.xxiv. Spoletum gravissimis bellorum Punicorum temporibus auxilia Populo Romano præbuisse, recenset idem libro xxvii. Quas, declinante Imperio, passum fuerit Spoletum Calamitates ab Gothis, commemorant Blondus & Sabellicus. Insignem etiam Cladem accepit ab Frederico Ænobarbo, quod Alexandro iii. P. M. fuerat; & anno cIↄ cccxxiv à Perusinis, uti tradit Bernardinus Corius parte iii. Histor. In Prætorio jus dicunt vii-Viri Spoletini, quibus in consilio adsunt alij lx, forma Reip. Summa tamen potestas est penes Gubernatorem Pontificis. Spoleti nomen inlustrarunt P. Cornutus Orator, de quo Cicero de Claris Oratoribus; C. Melissus, quem Grammaticis adcensent Suetonius & Eusebius. Alios multos prætereo. Martyrio coronati in hac Urbe leguntur sub Diocletiano Carpophorus, Abundius, Sabinus, Exsuperantius, Marcellinus, Pontianus cum Vxore & Liberis, Gregarius, plurimique alij. Episcopatus claret dignitate.
units.tr: Continuing along the pleasant plain, past Fulignum and Trebula, on the left side appears Spoletum, from which the name Ducatus Spoletini is given to Umbria. Now Spoleto. Strabo in book 4 and Ptolemy have Spoletium [Σπολήτιον]; Antoninus and the other Latin writers have Spoletium. Florus in his epitome of Livy book 20, Paterculus in book 1, Cicero in the Balbiana, and Frontinus On Colonies recognise it as a colony. Spoletum lies unevenly, partly on the plain and partly on a hill, on which a very strong citadel also sits; made, as Blondus thinks in book 6 of his History, from an old amphitheatre that was here. From the city one approaches by a stone bridge, which is supported on large piers, twenty-four in number, with great skill and ingenuity, and it joins the part of the city set on higher ground with the citadel, which stands on another hill, separated from the city by a short valley. The citadel is always governed by those nearest the Pontiff. The city today is splendid and abounds in every kind of goods. The praetorium of Spoletum, most splendid, was built by Theodoric, king of the Goths, who was greatly pleased with this place; it was afterwards overthrown by the Goths together with the royal palace, and restored after by the work of Narses, as Blondus and Sabellicus relate. Here one may see, besides other buildings and remaining antiquities of a great age, the foundations of a theatre, the most ancient temple of Concord outside the city, and the Forma: there too are lofty and solid aqueducts, partly cut from the Apennine slopes and partly built of brick, carried up on arches from the valley floor. Livy in book 21 records that Spoletum was attacked in vain by Hannibal. The same author in book 24 reports that Spoletum changed a male into a female. In book 27 he lists that Spoletum gave aid to the Roman people in the most grievous times of the Punic wars. Blondus and Sabellicus recall the calamities that Spoletum suffered from the Goths when the Empire was declining. It also received a notable defeat from Frederick Barbarossa, because it had been on the side of Alexander III, the Supreme Pontiff; and in 1324 it was defeated by the Perugians, as Bernardino Corio relates in part 3 of his History. In the praetorium the seven men of Spoleto give judgment, with sixty others as their council; yet the supreme power in the state lies with the Pontiff's governor. Those who have made the name of Spoleto famous include P. Cornutus the orator, of whom Cicero speaks in his Brutus; and C. Melissus, whom Suetonius and Eusebius count among the grammarians. I pass over many others. Crowned with martyrdom in this city under Diocletian are read the names of Carpophorus, Abundius, Sabinus, Exsuperantius, Marcellinus, Pontianus with his wife and children, Gregarius, and very many others. The bishopric is distinguished in dignity.

units.la: Inter Montes, supra Fulginum, Opidum est, quod vulgo Capo di Acqua, ab fonte cotidiano I lavis, qui hac oritur, denominatum.
units.tr: Between the mountains, above Fulginum, there is a town, commonly called Capo di Acqua, named after a daily spring of the river Lavis, which rises here.

units.la: Pullo altius. o v Fla idm est, vernacule Col Fordo
units.tr: A little further back, o v Fla idm is in the vernacular Col Fordo.

units.la: Inter Trebulam & Spoletum Castella tant plurima Spoletini Agri, & inter alpestres altissimos Montes Ceretum, novi nominis Opidum, sed frequens: a quo Ceretani vocantur Istriones, qui nunc per universam Italiam discurrentes sanctitatis religionisque praetexta variis urbibus emungere stipem consueverunt. Plura Leander.
units.tr: Between Trebula and Spoleto there are very many small castles of the Spoletine territory, and among the high Alpine mountains lies Ceretum, a town of recent name but populous. From it the Ceretani are called mountebanks (Istriones), who now roam all over Italy under the pretext of holiness and religion and are accustomed to squeeze alms out of various cities. More on this in Leander.

units.la: Intra Ceretum Pons Castellanus est, Ponte Castello, ab Ceretanis condatum, & à Ponte Naris, utramque ripam coniungente, dictum. Fo orti Ludovicus & Paulus, nitidi ingenio, item Iohannes Fontanus, Vir magni nominis & omni disciplinarum genere praestantissimus.
units.tr: Within Ceretum is the Pons Castellanus, Ponte Castello, founded by the Ceretani and named after the Ponte Naris, which joins the two banks. Born there were Ludovicus and Paulus, men of bright talent, and likewise Iohannes Fontanus, a man of great name and outstanding in every branch of learning.

units.la: Sexto hinc lapide Cassia, Opidum frequentissimum, quod Corvo adiuvatur. Recens putat Blondus, antiquum Volaterranus: quae Leandro mens, centum nerit Cassiae nomen, de quibus antea dictum, esse sedem. De Cassia imperio aeternae quondam dictum praesertim inter Spoletinos & Nursinos: utrique potestatem ibi vindicantibus. Legendus Blondus.
units.tr: Six miles from here is Cassia, a very populous town, which is supported by Corvo. Blondus thinks it is recent, while the older Volaterranus places it earlier; Leander's view is that the name of Cassia belonged to the seat of the peoples mentioned earlier. There was once a dispute about jurisdiction over Cassia, especially between the Spoletines and the Nursini, each claiming power there. Blondus should be read.

units.la: Post Cassiam m. x. v. i inter Montes maximos Urbs est, quae vulgo Norsia, Nursia Latinis dicitur, Nursia Ptolemaeo. De ea Virgilius lib. vii Aeneid.
units.tr: Ten miles beyond Cassia, among the largest mountains, is a city commonly called Norsia, in Latin Nursia, and Nursia by Ptolemy. Virgil speaks of it in book 7 of the Aeneid:

units.la: Qui Tiberim fatalemque lubent, quos frigida misit
units.tr: Those who love the Tiber and the fated (river), whom cold Nursia sent.

units.la: Nursia.
units.tr: Nursia.

units.la: Ad quem locum Servius, Nursia, inquit, Urbs in Picena est, Frigidaque dicta: vel quia reverta talis, vel quia nocens. Gravibus enim nibique in concionibus fuit Nursinos fecerunt appellavere. Quod hanc Urbem in Picentibus collocet, ex Plinij facit sententia, à quo Regionis III tributum. Alijs auctoribus in Umbria; alijs, inter quos Ptolemaeus in Sabinis est. Parum refert. Adscribenda diversitas Regionum vicinitati, quae hic confines. Frigida vero Virgilio dicitur propter montium circumiectorum, qui nivibus perpetuo occupantur, ingentesque propinquis locis frigus concinunt, altitudinem: unde & eodem libro à Virgilio dicuntur Montosa Nursia. Ab Nursia Nursina Plinio in IV Regione. Livius libro xxviii Umbriae populos, & praeter hos Nursinos & Reatinos, & Amiternes, Sabinumque agrum, omnes pollicitos finitimae multas memoriae prodit. Tradit idem libro xxxviii Nursinos Scipioni militès ad instruendas naves Africano bello paratas misisse. Nursinas rapas celebrat praeter Martialem, Plinius libro xviii cap. xiii. Nursiam illustrarunt Sertorius ille, militans apud Romanos gloria celeberrimus: Benedictus, Monachorum pater: Vespasia Polla Imp. Vespasiani mater. Discordijs civilibus pessime nunc afsecta iacet.
units.tr: On this passage Servius says: "Nursia is a city in Picenum, and it is called Frigida, either because it is of such a cold temperament or because it is harmful." For the Nursini made their name from the grave and unhealthy (?) meetings that took place there. That Pliny places this city among the Picentes, from whom he takes the tribute of the third region, follows his opinion; other authors place it in Umbria, and others, including Ptolemy, in the Sabines. This matters little. The variation is to be attributed to the closeness of the regions, which border here. Virgil calls it Frigida because of the height of the surrounding mountains, which are always occupied by snow and which make the nearby places cold; for this reason in the same book Virgil also calls it Montosa Nursia, mountainous Nursia. Pliny, in the fourth region, calls the people Nursina, from Nursia. Livy in book 28 records that the peoples of Umbria, and besides these the Nursini, the Reatini and the Amiternini, and the Sabine territory, all promised many men to the neighbouring (Romans). The same Livy, in book 38, relates that the Nursini sent soldiers to Scipio to equip ships prepared for the African war. Pliny, book 18, chapter 13, celebrates the Nursian turnips, besides Martial. Nursia was made famous by Sertorius, who fought among the Romans and was most celebrated for glory; by Benedict, father of the monks; and by Vespasia Polla, mother of the emperor Vespasian. Now it lies in a very sorry state, wrecked by civil discord.

units.la: Supra Cassiam deinde m. p. x. Conisia novi nominis est oppidum, montoso situ, frequens admodum.
units.tr: Beyond Cassia, then ten Roman miles away, is Conisia, a town of recent name in a mountainous site, quite populous.

units.la: Relictis montibus Spoletum repropero. A quo r. m. xvi versus Africum distat Interamna. Sic Tacito lib. xviii. & seq. Plinioque dicitur, non uno loco; Interamna, Strabonis; Interamna, Ptolemaeo; Interamnia, Antonino, Interamnium Itinerariae Tabulae: quae vulgo Terni vel Terrani, Ἰντεραμνία. Dicta, quod inter Amnes, Altissimam scilicet ex Nare Fossam, ipsumque Narem sita. Ab ea Interamnates, de quibus supra: quorum & meminit Tacitus. Conditionis tempus notarat in antiqua Inscriptione, quae ibidem ad Cathedralem Ecclesiam servatur in Tabula Marmorea, lata pedes vii, alta pedes iv:
units.tr: Leaving the mountains I hurry on to Spoleto. Sixteen miles from it, toward the southwest, lies Interamna. It is called so by Tacitus in book 18 and following, and by Pliny in more than one place; Interamna by Strabo; Interamna by Ptolemy; Interamnia by Antoninus; Interamnium in the Itinerary Table. It is now commonly called Terni or Terrani, Ἰντεραμνία [Interamnia]. It is named because it lies between rivers, namely the very deep ditch of the Nar and the Nar itself. Its people are the Interamnates, mentioned above, and Tacitus also mentions them. An ancient inscription, kept on a marble tablet in the cathedral church there, seven feet wide and four feet high, marks the date of its founding:

units.la: SALVTI. PERPETVÆ. AVGVSTÆ LIBERTATIQVE. PVBLICÆ POPVLI ROMANI GENIO. MVNICIPI. ANNO POST INTERAMNAM. CONDITAM DCCIII. AD. CN. DOMITIVM AHENOBARBVM COS PROVIDENTIÆ. Ti. CÆSARIS. AVGVSTI. NATI. AD. ÆTERNITATEM ROMANI. NOMINIS. SVBLATO. HOSTE. PERNICIOSISSIMO. P. R. FAVSTVS. TITIVS. LIBERALIS. VI. VIR. AVG. ITER. S. F. C.
units.tr: TO THE SAFETY OF THE EVERLASTING AUGUSTA AND THE PUBLIC LIBERTY OF THE ROMAN PEOPLE, TO THE GENIUS OF THE MUNICIPALITY, IN THE 703RD YEAR AFTER INTERAMNA WAS FOUNDED, WHEN CN. DOMITIUS AHENOBARBUS WAS CONSUL; UNDER THE PROVIDENCE OF TI. CAESAR AUGUSTUS, SON OF THE DIVINE (AUGUSTUS), FOR THE ETERNITY OF THE ROMAN NAME, THE MOST PERNICIOUS ENEMY HAVING BEEN REMOVED, P. R. FAUSTUS TITIUS LIBERALIS, SEXVIR OF THE AUGUSTALES, (SET THIS UP) BY VOW, S. F. C.

units.la: Urbem olim fuisse maiorem, veterum Ædificiorum ruinæ, quæ circa sunt, loquuntur. In foro Statua conspicitur, cujus basi incisum:
units.tr: The ruins of old buildings that are around it show that the city was formerly larger. In the forum a statue can be seen, on whose base is incised:

units.la: NEPTVNO SACRVM
units.tr: TO NEPTUNE, SACRED

units.la: Rebus omnibus ad Vitam necessariis abundat: Incolis frequens. Ingenia magno numero tulit: cum primis Ioannem A... cinellum, Virum doctum & prudentem, Apostolicæ Cameræ quondam Auditorem. Commendantur hujus Urbis Columbæ cum ob insignem magnitudinem, tum ob carnis præstantiam. Episcopatus gaudet titulo. Agro insignis ab fluviis est fertilitas. Vinum notæ optimæ Vernaccia. Scribit Plinius libro xviii. cap. xxviii, Prata, quæ hic sunt, irrigua, quartum quæ non, tertium annuo tempore secari.
units.tr: It abounds in all things necessary for life and is populous with inhabitants. It has produced many men of talent, chiefly Iohannes A...cinellus, a learned and prudent man, once Auditor of the Apostolic Chamber. The pigeons of this town are commended both for their remarkable size and for the excellence of their flesh. The town enjoys the title of a bishopric. The land is distinguished by fertility from its rivers. The wine is of excellent quality, Vernaccia. Pliny, book 18, chapter 28, writes that the meadows here are irrigated; those that are not are cut a fourth time in the year, and the irrigated ones a third time.

units.la: Ad ripam Tiberis, unde versus Orientaliora iter, redeo. Ibi in collis supra Tiberim latere post Tinnæ confluentem, Druida castellum apparet. Dicitur ab Latine dici quibusdam placet. In pretio sunt hujus Loci Vasa fictilia: Maiorica Vulgus Italicum vocat, quod artis initium, ex una Balearium insula Maiorica prodierit.
units.tr: I return to the bank of the Tiber, from which the route goes further east. There, on a hill above the Tiber, on the side beyond the confluence of the Tinna, appears the castle of Druida. Some are pleased to think it is said to be named from the Latin word for ... (obscure). The earthenware vessels of this place are in high esteem; the Italian populace calls them Maiorica, because the art began on the island of Majorca in the Balearics.

units.la: Via deinde, qua Perusia itur Narniam properanti, vetusta civitas in colle occurrit Tuder, Sic Plinio libro iii. cap. xiv, & Silio Italico libro vii, & alibi, item Tabulæ Itinerariæ: Τύδιτ Procopio libro ii. Belli Goth. dicitur; Tudernum etiam Latine scribentibus; Τύρδι Ptolemæo; Τυρδίλα Plutarcho in Crassi vita: quod Todi vulgo. Τυρδενλως πόλις legitur apud Strabonem; pro quo Nobilissimus Scaliger & doctissimus Casaubonus legunt, Τύδιτ, Οὐλεις vel Ὀγχης πόλις, optimo sensu, ut apud Silium:
units.tr: Then, on the road by which one goes from Perugia to Narni, an ancient city appears on a hill, Tuder. It is so called by Pliny, book 3, chapter 14, and by Silius Italicus, book 7 and elsewhere, as well as in the Itinerary Tables; Τύδιτ [Tudit] in Procopius, book 2 of the Gothic War; Tudernum also among Latin writers; Τύρδι [Tyrdi] by Ptolemy; Τυρδίλα [Tyrdila] by Plutarch in the Life of Crassus. It is now commonly called Todi. The phrase Τυρδενλως πόλις [Tyrdenlos polis] is read in Strabo; for this the most noble Scaliger and the most learned Casaubon read Τύδιτ [Tudit], Οὐλεις or Ὀγχης πόλις [Ouleis or Onchēs polis], which makes good sense, as in Silius:

units.la: Sed domus haud obscura Tuder.
units.tr: But Tuder, a house not obscure.

units.la: Tuder Fida Colonia est apud Frontinum. Censet etiam Albertus Leander, quæ Maluven & Τίωνα apud Halicarnas. libro i. eadem esse cum Tuderno. Incolæ Tudertes Silio libro viii. Tudertis Populi meminit Inscriptio:
units.tr: Tuder is a Faithful Colony in Frontinus. Albertus Leander also thinks that Maluven and Tiona in Halicarnassus, book 1, are the same as Tuderno. The inhabitants are called Tudertes by Silius, book 8. An inscription mentions the Tudertis Populi:

units.la: PRO. SALVTE COLONIÆ. ET. ORDINIS DECVRIONVM. ET. POPVLI TVDERTIS. Iovi. OPT. MAX CVSTODI. CONSERVATORI
units.tr: FOR THE WELFARE OF THE COLONY, THE ORDER OF DECURIONS, AND THE PEOPLE OF TUDER. To Jupiter, Best and Greatest, Guardian and Preserver.

units.la: & quæ ibi sequuntur. Martem coluisse Tudertes canit idem Silius, loco indicato. Martis Tudertis mentio in Basi marmorea, quæ Calligliani, Tudertium vico:
units.tr: "and what follows there." The same Silius sings that the Tuderates worshipped Mars, in the passage cited. Mention of Mars of Tuder is made on a marble base, which is at Calligliano, in the village of the Tuderates:

units.la: L. IVLIO.
units.tr: L. JULIUS.

units.la: L. IVLIO. L. F. CLV. MARCIANO AED. II. VIR. TVDER VICANI. VICI. MARTIS TVDERT. EX. AERE. COLL. OB. MERITA. EIVS. L. D. D. D. CVRAM. AGENTIBVS L. IVLIO. PRIVAT. PATRE. ET. L. IVLIO. PRIMINO. AMICO
units.tr: L. JULIUS. To Lucius Julius Marcianus, son of Lucius, of the Claudian tribe, aedile, duumvir, the men of the village of Tuder, of the village of Mars at Tuder, from bronze contributed by subscription, on account of his services, by decree of the decurions. Erected under the care of Lucius Julius Privatus, his father, and Lucius Julius Primus, his friend.

units.la: Fr probare videtur Dionysius Oraculum Tiο a antiquissimum Martis fuisse scribens haud absimile Dodonæo. Situm est Tuder in amœno fructiferoque colle. Ad situm pertinent Silij illa libro vi: ——Celses Umbras atque arva petebat Hannibal, exceiso summus qua vertice montis Deve um lateri pendet Tuder.
units.tr: Dionysius seems to confirm this too, writing that the most ancient oracle of Tion belonged to Mars, not unlike the one at Dodona. Tuder lies on a pleasant and fruitful hill. To its situation belong those lines of Silius in book 6: "Hannibal was making for the shadows and fields on high, where the summit of the mountain, cut away, hangs over Tuder at its side."

units.la: Civilibus discordijs hoc tempore propemodum subversum jacet, indignissime acceptum Avorum memoria ab Alrotello, indigno patriæ alumno: de cuius immanissimo tandem supplicio legendus omnino Leander. Episcopatus claret honore. Tuder ortu suo illustravit Martinus i. P. M, ut Platina & Petracha notant: Blondus Martinum iii dicit. Natus etiam hic Antoninus, Vir Græce Latineque doctissimus; reliquantibus id aliquot Plutarchi Vitis, Latio ab ipso donatis.
units.tr: In recent civil discords it has lain almost overthrown, shamefully treated in the memory of our forebears by Alrotellus, an unworthy son of his country; of whose most savage punishment one should by all means read Leander. The bishopric is distinguished by its honour. Tuder adorned itself with the birth of Martin I, supreme pontiff, as Platina and Petrarch note; Blondus says Martin III. Antoninus, a man most learned in Greek and Latin, was also born here, as several Lives of Plutarch, which he gave to Latin readers, attest.

units.la: Hinc finitimos inter montes ad Tiberim Castella sunt plurima; interque cætera modico in colle Alviannum, insignis munitaque Arx.
units.tr: From here, among the neighbouring mountains by the Tiber, there are very many castles; and among the rest, on a modest hill, Alviano, a notable and fortified citadel.

units.la: Quarto-decimo inde Lapide versus Meridiem inter Tiberim & Narim antiqua civitas est Amelia in Colle: sic vulgo audit, quæ Ameria Ciceroni, Plinio libro iii cap xiv, Festo, Tabulæ Itinerariæ; item Tabulæ Marmoreæ, quæ apud Cardinalem Maphæum, repertæ apud Cæretes anno cIↄ Iↄ XLIIXI; Ἀμέλια Straboни & Ptolemæo; Ἀμέλιον, Stephano: Amerinum, Servio. Ameriam Cato apud Plinium loco indicato prodit ante Persei Bellum conditam Annis ıɔccccı xıv. Ortus Ameria Restitui, quem sua facundia defendit M. Tullius. Episcopatui dat Sedem. Ager Amerinus, qui lege Imp. Augusti adsignatur Veteranis apud Frontinum de Coloniis, uber est, & bonus, frumento, vino, oleo abundans; collibusque nitens amœnis, quæque vitibus & arboribus fructiferis passim vestiti. Virgilius i Georg. Atque Amerina parat lenta retinacula viti:
units.tr: Fourteen milestones from there towards the south, between the Tiber and the Nar, lies the ancient city of Amelia on a hill; so it is commonly called. It is Ameria to Cicero, in Pliny book 3 chapter 14, in Festus, and in the Itinerary tables; likewise in the marble tables found at Cere, which are at Cardinal Maffei's. Ἀμέλια [Amelia] to Strabo and Ptolemy; Ἀμέλιον [Amelion] to Stephanus; Amerinum to Servius. Cato, in the passage of Pliny cited, says Ameria was founded before the war with Perseus, some four hundred and more years earlier. Ameria was restored after its destruction, a cause which Marcus Tullius defended with his eloquence. It gives its seat to the bishopric. The Amerine territory, which by the law of the Emperor Augustus was assigned to veterans, according to Frontinus on colonies, is rich and good, abounding in grain, wine and oil; it shines with pleasant hills, and everywhere is clothed with vines and fruit trees. Virgil, Georgics book 1: "And the Amerine (land) readies the pliant ties for the vine."

units.la: Quem locum exponens Servius, Retinacula hæc virgulti genus esse notat; quo ligabantur vites; & Ametinus ager abundabat.
units.tr: Explaining this passage, Servius notes that these retinacula are a kind of twig by which vines were tied, and that the Amerine land abounded in them.

units.la: Via qua Tuderno Narniam itur, passim in montibus adparent obscura quædam nulliusque momenti oppidula: media autem Via Castellum Tudertinum, Castel Tudino; locus exiguus; utraque S. Gemini, honestum quondam oppidum; sed ab Venetis anno cIↄ Iↄ xxvii, pessime habitum. Sequitur hac ipsa via altissimi montis radicibus adpositum oppidum Cesia, Cresa vulgo, cum Arce, præcelso in monte sita. Deinde secundum huius montis pedem ad oppidum pervenitur Aquam Spartam: quo locum scribit Matthæus Cardinalis suis in Sententias Commentarijs.
units.tr: On the road from Todi to Narni, here and there in the mountains appear some obscure little towns of no account. In the middle of the road is the Castle of Tuder, Castel Todino, a small place. Both are S. Gemini, once an honourable town, but treated very badly by the Venetians in 1527. Along this same road, set at the foot of a very high mountain, is the town of Cesi, commonly Cresa, with its citadel placed on a steep peak. Then, along the foot of this mountain, one comes to the town of Acquasparta; Matthaeus Cardinalis writes of this place in his commentaries on the Sentences.

units.la: Ad exitum deinde Viæ Flaminiæ Pons ex latere cocto Naris ad Narniam transitum jungit. Nec procul eodem in amne grandissimæ innixi Pilis Arcus quidam ingentes adparent nobilis ac vetusti Pontis, mirabili arte facti ex lapide quadrato permagno; quo ab collis, qui citra flumen est, radicibus per amnem ad Narniam commeabatur. Maximum id opus fuisse indicant rudera. Celebratur à Martiale libro vi epigrammat. Sed tam parce mihi, nec abutor Narnia Quinto, Perpetuo ducat fit mihi Ponte frui. Scribit & Procopius libro 1. belli Goth. haud unquam Pontis Arcus altiores sibi visos. Ædificatum ex Cimbricis Spoliis ab Augusto clamant Narnienses.
units.tr: Then, at the end of the Via Flaminia, a bridge of baked brick over the Nar gives passage to Narni. Not far off, in the same river, stand certain huge arches resting on very great piers, the remains of a noble and ancient bridge, made with marvellous skill from very large square stone; by it people used to cross the river from the foot of the hill on this side to Narni. The ruins show this was a very great work. Martial celebrates it in book 6 of his epigrams: "But I am spared, and do not abuse it, Narnia; may a perpetual bridge be mine to enjoy." Procopius also writes, in book 1 of the Gothic War, that the arches of the bridge never seemed to him higher. The Narnians declare that Augustus built it from the spoils of the Cimbri.

units.la: Cum Vmbria solet explicari, tamquam Pars ejus, Regio, quæ hactenus Sabinia; ab Antiquissimis Italiæ Populis, qui Scriptoribus omnibus Sabini. Illi unde dicti, variant Auctores. Ab Sabo derivant Dionysius Halicarnass. libro II & Silius Italicus libro VIII: Ibant, & kei pars Sinclum voce canebant Auctorem gentis: pars laudes ore ferebant Sabe tuas, qui de patrio cognomine primus Patrise populos magna ditione Sabinos.
units.tr: Sabinia, the region which hitherto has been reckoned as part of Umbria, is usually explained as a part of it. It takes its name from the most ancient peoples of Italy, who by all writers are called Sabines. Authors vary as to whence they were named. Dionysius of Halicarnassus in book 2 and Silius Italicus in book 8 derive them from Sabus: "Some went, and some sang with voice the author of the race; others bore your praises on their lips, Sabus, who first, from his paternal surname, ruled the Sabines, the peoples of Sabinia, with great dominion."

units.la: De hoc Sabo multa Annius ex suis Berosio, Xenophonte, Catone, & Sempronio, quæ prætereo. Plinius lib. III. Natur. Hist. cap. XII Ἀπὸ δὲ τῆς θέας, quasi Selinos, ab Religione, Deorumque cultu dictos censer. Strabo lib. V initium eos ex Etruria & ab Tiberi habuisse opinatur. Zenodotus Trezenius Historicus Advenas quosdam ex Vmbris in Agrum Reatinum profectos tradit, ubi quum aliquandiu consedissent, tandem a Pelasgis expulsos in hanc Regionem, quæ Sabinia appellabatur, concessisse, ab eaque Sabinos deinde vocatos. Termini Gentis ex commutatione temporum valde diversi reperiuntur. Quos Cato Sempronius que statuunt, quia summi pedes sunt, non rectè.
units.tr: Annius says much about this Sabus, drawing on his Berosus, Xenophon, Cato and Sempronius, which I pass over. Pliny, Natural History book 3 chapter 12, thinks they were named from the Greek ἀπὸ δὲ τῆς θέας [from the sight], as if they were called Selinoi, from religion and the worship of the gods. Strabo, book 5, thinks they originally came from Etruria and the Tiber. Zenodotus of Troezen, a historian, relates that some newcomers from the Umbrians went out into the Reatine territory, and that after settling there for a time, they were at last driven out by the Pelasgians and moved into this region, which was called Sabinia, and from it they were afterwards called Sabines. The boundaries of the people are found to differ widely according to changes in time. Those which Cato and Sempronius lay down are not rightly so, since they are the extreme limits.

units.la: Dionysius Halicarnass. lib. II, Sabinorum primas omnino sedes Testrena in Vico fuisse non procul Amiterno, memoriæ prodit: addens, ijs deinde relictis in Agrum Reatinum profectos cum Aboriginibus habitasse; postea quoque Cotiliam Oppidum nobile, vi occupasse, Reatinos agro suo depulisse, Civitates quoque aliquot munitas, inter quas Cures, ædificasse; senserim inde potentia divitiisque adeo esse auctos, ut Tractum omnem ab illa urbe ad Adriaticum mare peringentem spatio centum LXI stadiorum in latum, & fere cio in longum occupaverint: quam regionem Dionysii etiam temporibus habebant. Apud Plinium libro III. cap. XII. Sabinorum populi recensentur Amiternini, Curenses, Forum Decii, Forum Novum, Fidenates, Interamnates, Nursini, Nomentani, Reatini, Trebulani, qui cognominantur Mutuscæ, & qui Suffenates, Tiburtes, Tarinates. De plerisque dixi: de reliquis suo loco dicturus.
units.tr: Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 2, records that the very first seats of the Sabines were at Testrina, in a village not far from Amiternum; adding that after leaving these they went out into the Reatine territory and lived there with the Aborigines. Later, he says, they also seized by force the noted town of Cotilia, drove the Reatines from their land, and built several fortified cities, among them Cures. I suppose that from this they grew so great in power and wealth that they occupied the whole tract reaching from that city to the Adriatic Sea, a hundred and sixty-one stadia in breadth and about three hundred in length; this was the region they still held in Dionysius's time. In Pliny, book 3 chapter 12, the peoples of the Sabines are listed as: the Amiternini, Curenses, Forum Decii, Forum Novum, Fidenates, Interamnates, Nursini, Nomentani, Reatini, Trebulani, who are called Mutuscae, and the Suffenates, Tiburtes and Tarinates. I have spoken of most of these; I shall speak of the rest in their place.

units.la: Idem Plinius paullo post: Velinos adcolunt Lacus rusticis collibus: addens Apenninī jugis undique vallatos, infra quos sit Latium, à latere Picenum, à tergo Vmbria. Ἡ Ζαβίνη, inquit Strabo libro V, μεταξὺ τῶν Λατίνων καὶ τῶν Ὀμβρικῶν: ἐκτείνεται ἡ ἐξ αὐτῆς πρὸς τὰ Σαμνιτικὰ ἔθνη, καὶ μάλιστα συναπτὴ τοῖς Ἀππενίνοις. Et postea: Σαβῖνοι ἢ γενικῶς οἰκοῦσι χώραν, ὅπερ μέγα. Leander Albertus Sabinorum fines notat Narem, Apenninum, Tiberim & Anienem: hoc tempore Sabinum appellari indicans, quidquid inter Lacum Velinum, Reate, Tiberim, Narem & Anienem continetur. Totam Sabinorum regionem egregie fertilem esse oleis ac vitibus, multumque ferre glandis, & pecori producendo aptam esse scribit Strabo.
units.tr: The same Pliny a little later: "The Lake Velinus is surrounded by rustic hills," adding that they are enclosed on all sides by the ridges of the Apennines, below which lies Latium, on one side Picenum, and behind them Umbria. Strabo, book 5, says: "Ἡ Σαβίνη [Sabine land] lies μεταξὺ τῶν Λατίνων καὶ τῶν Ὀμβρικῶν [between the Latins and the Umbrians]; it extends from there towards the Samnite nations, and is especially joined to the Apennines." And afterwards: "Σαβῖνοι [the Sabines] ἢ γενικῶς οἰκοῦσι χώραν [generally inhabit a land], ὅπερ μέγα [which is great]." Leander Albertus marks the boundaries of the Sabines as the Nar, the Apennines, the Tiber and the Anio, indicating that at this time the name Sabina is applied to whatever is contained between Lake Velinus, Rieti, the Tiber, the Nar and the Anio. Strabo writes that the whole Sabine region is excellently fertile in olives and vines, bears a great deal of acorn-mast, and is suited to rearing livestock.

units.la: Sabinorum frequens mentio apud Rerum Romanarum Scriptores; ex quibus universim patet, prudentes admodum fuisse, audaces, & ad omnia aptos: ut merito Romulus omnem dederit operam, quo eos adiunctos sibi & Imperij socios adsciseret. Factum illud anno ab V. C. VIII. receptio in urbem T. Tatio Sabino. Legendi, præter alios, Dionysius Halic. libro II, Livius libro I, Florus libro I. cap. I. Lapsu temporis, immemores factæ sub Tatio Adhinitatis, Populum Romanum sub Regibus, deinde eis exactis sæpe lacessierunt: triumphati aliquoties potius, quam victi: postremum etiam contagio belli Latinis se adjudgentes. Eos M' Curius Dentatus Cos. intra eum tractum, qua Nar ambit Fontesque Velini, Hadriatico tenus mari, igne ferroque vastavit. Qua victoria tantum hominum, tantum agrorum redactum in potestatem, utin utro plus esset, ne ipse poterat æstimare, qui vicerat. Consulendi cum aliis Florus libro I. cap. XV, Orosius libro III cap. XXII, Eutropius libro II, Frontinus libro I. Ex quibus docemur Sabinos tandem omnino fuisse debellatos, ijsque Civitatem datam sine Suffragio, quod Paterculo notatum.
units.tr: The Sabines are frequently mentioned by the writers of Roman history, from whom it appears in general that they were very prudent, bold, and fit for every undertaking; so that Romulus deservedly took great pains to join them to himself and admit them as partners in his empire. That happened in the year 8 from the founding of the City, when Titus Tatius the Sabine was received into the city. Besides others, read Dionysius of Halicarnassus book 2, Livy book 1, and Florus book 1 chapter 1. As time passed, they forgot the affinity made under Tatius, and under the kings, and then after the kings were expelled, they often harassed the Roman people; more often they were triumphed over than conquered; and at last they even joined the Latins, drawn in by the contagion of war. Manius Curius Dentatus, as consul, laid them waste with fire and sword throughout that tract where the Nar winds round and the springs of the Velinus lie, as far as the Adriatic Sea. By that victory so many men and so much land were brought into subjection that he who had conquered could not himself judge which was the greater. For further reading, see Florus book 1 chapter 15, Orosius book 3 chapter 22, Eutropius book 2, and Frontinus book 1. From these we learn that the Sabines were at last wholly subdued, and that citizenship was given to them without the right of suffrage, which Paterculus notes.

units.la: Hæc de Sabinis universim: postulat Methodus, ut singulatim de ipsorum urbibus opidisque agam.
units.tr: These are the general points about the Sabines. My method requires that I now deal with their towns and settlements one by one.

units.la: Principem locum obtinet Reate. Sic dicta Silio libro VIII, Tacito in Annalibus, Suetonio. livium certe nomen restituit M. Porcio Catoni de Re Rustica cap. cxxxv Nobilissimus Vir Iosephus Scaliger in Coniectaneis ad M. Terentij Varronis librum de L.L. iv. Plura Dionysius quondam hoc situ opida dicit floruisse „quae calamitate temporum jam tum ejus aetate prorsus perierant. Relicto Agro Reatino, expatiemur ad reliqua Sabinorum.
units.tr: The chief place is held by Reate. Silius in book 8, Tacitus in the Annals and Suetonius all call it so. The most noble Joseph Scaliger certainly restored the name Lavinium in his Coniectanea on Varro's book De Lingua Latina iv, citing Marcus Porcius Cato, De Re Rustica, ch. 135. Dionysius says that many towns once flourished in this region, "which by the calamity of the times had already utterly perished in his age." Leaving the territory of Reate, let us range through the rest of the Sabines.

units.la: Ad laevam Velini Lacus partem, ubi Aquae ex edito colle praecipitatae. Nari inlabuntur, Opidum in Tumulo cernitur, quod Colle Scipionis Litteratis, Celle di Scipio vernacule appellatur; frequens, opibusque adfluens. Scipionem condidisse nonnulli putant. Sequuntur inter Montes Opidula, quae vulgo Monte Buono & Tarano, ad Himellam Amnem.
units.tr: On the left side of Lake Velinus, where the waters, plunging headlong from the high hill, flow into the Nar, there is a town on a hill, which the learned call Colle Scipionis and which is called Celle di Scipio in the vernacular. It is populous and abounds in wealth. Some think Scipio founded it. Among the mountains follow small towns, commonly called Monte Buono and Tarano, near the river Himella.

units.la: Post Collem Scipionis supra in aspero, saxoso & praecelso Monte, Urbs antiqua visitur Nequinum olim, ut Livius lib. x, & Plinius lib. iii tradunt. Vitiose apud Stephanum ex Dionysij Halicarnass. xvii Antiquit. Romanar. Νικαια, πολις ὁ Μεζηκων: Post Narnia Livio variis locis, Silio Italico lib. viii, Tacito, Martiali, Antonino, & aliis; Ναρνια Ptolemaeo, Stephano, Procopio; Νάρνα Strabon, forte Nappia: Narni hodie. Ut ab Narnia Narnienses & Narnistes, de quibus ante; sic olim ab Nequino, Nequinates. Νεχνιατης est apud Stephanum. Narnia ab Nare, scribente cum aliis Livio; ... inquit Stephanus, ... Neguinum infame Nomen, sive ab incertibus, & pravis opidanorum moribus, sive ab loci, in quo Urbs sita est, asperitate; sive ab Cladis acceptae iniquitate. Ab cos. Apuleio frustra obsessam Urbem, paulo post tamen in Pop.Rom. potestatem fuisse redactam, deducta eo Colonia anno cccc.iv (quo tempore cum Samnitibus per M. Fulvinum Patrinum Cives triumphati leguntur) notant Livius lib. x & Plutarchus in T. Quinctio. Meminit ut Colonia idem Livius lib. xxvii & xxix. Narniam cccl.i itadijs ab Urbe Roma abesse, auctor est Procopius de bello Gothico lib. i. Urbs est alti, saxosi, praecipitisque Montis impolita dorso, rupes, qua meridies est, habens, despectuosque horrendos, quorum imo in hiatu Nar Amnis per Scopulos confragoso alveo labitur; ab Septemtrione Colles imminent amoeni, Arboribus fructiferis, Vitibus, Oleis, Ficubus, & id genus aliis nitentes. De Situ Servius ad vii Aeneid. In Via Flaminia Civitas, inquit, Narnia in montibus posita, quibus subest Nar fluvius. Silius lib. viii: — & duro monti per saxa recumbens Narnia. — Martialis libro viii: Narnia, sulphureo quam gurgite Candidus amnis Circuit, ancipiti vix adeunda sugo. Claudianus: — celsa dehinc prospectans Narnia Campum Regali calcatur equo, rarisque coloris Non procul Amnis abest, urbi qui nominis auctor.
units.tr: Above Colle Scipionis, on a rough, rocky and very lofty mountain, there is seen an ancient city, Nequinum in former times, as Livy in book 10 and Pliny in book 3 relate. Stephanus, drawing on Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Roman Antiquities book 17, wrongly gives Νικαια [Nikaia], city of the Mezekians. After Narnia in Livy in various places, in Silius Italicus book 8, in Tacitus, Martial, Antoninus and others; Ναρνια [Narnia] in Ptolemy, Stephanus and Procopius; Νάρνα [Narna] in Strabo; perhaps Nappia: today Narni. As from Narnia come the Narnienses and Narnistes, mentioned before, so formerly from Nequino came the Nequinates. Νεχνιατης [Nechniates] is in Stephanus. Narnia is derived from the river Nar, as Livy and others write. Stephanus says ... Neguinum was an infamous name, either from the unreliability and wicked morals of its townsmen, or from the roughness of the place where the city lies, or from the unfortunate outcome of a defeat suffered there. Under the consul Apuleius the city was besieged in vain, but shortly afterwards it was brought under the power of the Roman people, when a Colonia was led there in the year 404 (at which time, through M. Fulvius Paetinus, citizens are said to have been triumphed over together with the Samnites). Livy in book 10 and Plutarch in his life of T. Quinctius note this. The same Livy mentions it as a Colonia in books 27 and 29. Procopius, On the Gothic War book 1, states that Narniam is 51 miles distant from the city of Rome. The town stands on the unpolished back of a high, rocky and steep mountain, having cliffs on the south side and horrible precipices, at the bottom of which the Nar flows through rocks in a rough channel. Pleasant hills overhang it on the north, gleaming with fruit trees, vines, olives, figs and other such things. On its situation, Servius on Aeneid 7 says: "In Via Flaminia Civitas," he says, "Narnia in montibus posita, quibus subest Nar fluvius" ("On the Via Flaminia is the city of Narnia, set in the mountains, beneath which flows the river Nar"). Silius, book 8: "...and Narnia, lying on the hard mountain among the rocks." Martial, book 8: "Narnia, which the bright river encircles with a sulphurous whirlpool, scarcely to be approached by a doubtful passage." Claudian: "...then, looking down from on high on Narnia, the plain is trodden by the royal horse; not far off is the river of rare colour, which gave the city its name."

units.la: Patrum memoria deserta quodammodo jacebat cum Armis hostilibus, tum Discordijs civilibus labefactata: hodie refecta nonnihil Aedificijs satis elegans est & rerum copia lauta. Cathedrale Templum D.Iuvenalis dicatum est, visiturque Monasterium extra portas D. Hieronymi pulcherrimum. Narnia viros tulit praeclaros & illustres non paucos: inter alios Ioannem xiii P. M, Petrarcha cum aliis teste. Sunt tamen, qui Romanum perhibent, sed prius Narniensem fuisse Praesulem. Episcopatus enim dignitate gaudet Narnia Adduntur huic Bernardus & Paullus, Cassij, Cardinales; Bernardus Cardulus, Angelus & Cellavinus Pater & Filius Cassij, omnes Episcopi: Franciscus & Marcus Cardul, viri ingenio litterisque pollentes, stupendae memoriae, Galeottus Orator & Philosophos, Scriptis clarus. Alios praetereo. Ager Narniensis bonus ad utramque Naris ripam partim collinus, partim planus. Invenitur ibi Terrae genus, quod siccitate Lutum fit, pluvijs in Pulverem solvitur, M. Tullius inter miracula prodit apud Plinium.
units.tr: In our fathers' time it lay somewhat deserted, weakened both by hostile arms and by civil discords. Today, partly restored with buildings, it is fairly elegant and has an ample supply of goods. The cathedral temple is dedicated to D. Iuvenalis, and outside the gates is visited the very beautiful monastery of D. Hieronymi (St Jerome). Narnia has produced many distinguished and illustrious men, among them Ioannem XIII, Supreme Pontiff, as Petrarch and others attest. There are, however, those who say that he was Romanum, but that first he was Narniensem Praesulem (bishop of Narni). For Narnia enjoys the dignity of a bishopric. To these are added Bernardus & Paullus, Cassij, cardinals; Bernardus Cardulus, Angelus & Cellavinus, father and son of Cassius, all bishops; Franciscus & Marcus Cardul, men excelling in talent and learning, of remarkable memory; Galeottus, orator and philosopher, famous for his writings. I pass over others. The Narniensis territory is fertile on both banks of the Nar, partly hilly and partly flat. There is found there a kind of earth which becomes mud when dry and dissolves into powder when rained on. Marcus Tullius reports it among the marvels, according to Pliny.

units.la: Sequitur Via inter fructiferos Colles Flaminia Ocriculum. Ὀκρίκολον Ptolemaeo; Ὀκρίκλων Strabonis libro v, & paullo ante inemendatius Ὀχνλοι: Ὀκρικολα, πολις Τυρρηνων (latius enim olim Etruscorum erat Imperium) Stephano ex Dionysio; Ocricoli Antonino, Multitudinis numero; cui in quibusdam Codicibus Vtricul: quod Otricolum Livio lib. xxii & Tacito: Otriculi autem Italis, Ortigoli Adcolis. Inde Ocriculani, de quibus alibi. Ocriculani Municipij vetusta Monumenta, maximaeque ruinae prostrantur ad Viam Flaminiam, Turrium, Templorum, Thermarum, Aquæductuum, Porticus, Theatri, Amphitheatri, & aliorum Ædificiorum quæ vel ex parte, vel prorsus confracta mole stant testantur, quanta Urbis olim fuerit amplitudo & magnificentia, quum florente adhuc Imperio staret. Falluntur, qui Ocrea vel Interocrea rudera putant. Certe Ocriculi esse, probant antiquæ Statuarum Inscriptiones duæ, Patri ac Filiæ, propter Thermas, quæ privato sumtu ibidem exstructæ, & Resp. donatæ. Ea sic habent: L. IVLIO. L. F. PAL IVLIANO III. VIR. ÆD IIII. VIR. I. D. III. VIR. QVINQ. QVINQ. II. DEST PATRONO MVNICIPI PLEBS. OB. MERITA L. D. D. D IVLIÆ. LVCILIÆ L. IVLI. IVLIAN. FIL PATRONI. MVNICIPII CVIVS. PATER THERMAS. OCRICVLA IIS. A. SOLO. EXSTRVCTAS SVA. FECVNIA. DONAVIT DEC. AVG. PLEBS L. D. D. D
units.tr: Next along the Flaminian Way, among fruitful hills, lies Ocriculum. Ὀκρίκολον [Okrikolon] in Ptolemy; Ὀκρίκλων [Okriklōn] in Strabo book 5, and a little earlier, less correctly, Ὀχνλοι [Ochnloi]; Ὀκρικολα [Okrikola], city of the Etruscans (for the empire of the Etruscans once extended more widely), in Stephanus from Dionysius; Ocricoli in Antoninus, by the number of the multitude, and in some codices Vtricul, which Livy in book 22 and Tacitus call Otricolum. The Italians call them Otriculi, and their neighbours Ortigoli. Hence the Ocriculani, of whom elsewhere. The ancient monuments and great ruins of the municipality of Ocriculani lie scattered along the Flaminian Way: towers, temples, baths, aqueducts, porticoes, a theatre, an amphitheatre and other buildings which still stand, wholly or partly broken down, and testify how great the size and magnificence of the city was when it stood, with the empire still flourishing. Those are mistaken who think these are the ruins of Ocrea or Interocrea. That they belong to Ocriculum is certainly proved by two ancient inscriptions on statues, of a father and his daughter, near the baths, which were built there at private expense and given to the public. They read as follows: To Lucius Julius Julianus, son of Lucius, of the Pollian tribe, triumvir, aedile, quattuorvir, duumvir, quinquennial, and twice prefect, patron of the municipality, the commons by his merits (decreed this); and to Julia Lucilia, daughter of Lucius Julius Julianus, patron of the municipality, whose father gave the baths of Ocricula built from the ground up at his own expense; by decree of the Augustales, the commons (set this up).

units.la: Quod nunc Ocriculi dicitur, in Monte est: Antiqui vestigia, de quibus jam dixi, in planicie ut ea Tiberim visuntur dispersa.
units.tr: What is now called Ocriculum lies on a mountain. The remains of which I have already spoken are seen scattered on the plain towards the Tiber.

units.la: Rursum si ad Montes revertamur Reati finitimos, Casperia ad Himellam occurrit. Sic Virgilio libro vii, Vbique dicitur, sic hodie; sic proculdubio Casperula Silio libro viii: Hunc Amerina cohors, & Bacchis nomina ducens Casperula. —
units.tr: Turning back to the mountains bordering Reate, Casperia meets us at the Himella. So Virgil in book 7; it is called so everywhere, and so today. So undoubtedly Casperula in Silius, book 8: "Hunc Amerina cohors, & Bacchis nomina ducens Casperula..." ("this one the Amerine cohort, and Casperula, which takes its name from Bacchis...").

units.la: A Casperula Bactrianæ oppido: ut notat Pomponius Sabinus ad lib. vii Æneid. Aliunde ducit Marsus ad Silium.
units.tr: Casperula is a town of Bactria, as Pomponius Sabinus notes on Aeneid book 7. Marsus derives the name from elsewhere, in Silius.

units.la: Sequuntur Foruli, canente Virgilio vii Æneidos: Casperiamque colunt, Forulosque & Flumen Himellæ;
units.tr: Next come the Foruli, as Virgil sings in Aeneid book 7: "They inhabit Casperia and Forulus and the river of Himella;"

units.la: & succinente Silio, libro viii, quem antea nominavi: Casperula, hunc Foruli,
units.tr: and Silius in book 8, mentioned above, echoes: "Casperula, the Foruli..."

units.la: &c. Forulorum meminit & Livius libro xxvi. Sabinorum Forulo (Θεραπευτής) habet Strabo lib. v. Saxa ad rebellionem, quam habitationem, ut ... nata magis & ab natura facta.
units.tr: Livy also mentions the Foruli in book 26. Strabo in book 5 has the Forulum of the Sabines (Θεραπευτής [Therapeutes]). Rocks suited to rebellion; a dwelling, as ... more natural than made by nature.

units.la: Inter Tabarum (qui hodie Fasfaro) & Himellam Vacuna est, nobilis olim Vicus. Vacunæ Fanum Horatio Epistola ad Aristium: Hic tibi dissilabam post Fanum putre Vacunæ:
units.tr: Between Tabarum (today Fasfaro) and the Himella lies Vacuna, once a noted village. Horace refers to a shrine of Vacuna in his Epistle to Aristius: "Here I was telling you two syllables after the rotten shrine of Vacuna:"

units.la: quem locum explicans Interpres, Vacunam notat ab Sabinis cultam, Deam, quæ Minerva quibusdam, aliis Diana seu Venus habita. Varro de rebus Divinis lib. i Victoriam fuisse memoriæ prodit; cui qui in acquirenda sapientia studiose diligenterque vertati eam consequuti essent, tamquam Ignorantiæ Victores jam vacando laeundoque vota solvebant.
units.tr: Explaining this passage, the commentator notes that Vacuna was a goddess worshipped by the Sabines, whom some held to be Minerva and others Diana or Venus. Varro, in De Rebus Divinis book 1, reports that she was Victory: those who had studiously and diligently applied themselves to acquiring wisdom, and had obtained it, paid their vows as victors over ignorance, now at leisure and rejoicing.

units.la: Supra Himellam versus dextram haud procul Tiberi Maglianum spectatur in edito asperoque monte: hoc ævo princeps Sabiniæ Civitas, frequens lautaque.
units.tr: Above the Himella, towards the right, not far from the Tiber, Magliano is seen on a high, rough mountain. In this age it is the chief town of Sabina, populous and wealthy.

units.la: Descendenti ab Monte, cui insidet Malianum, ad mediterranea Sabiniæ, spatiosa quædam Convallis offertur, in qua prope Fluvium Himellam D. Maria Templum itemque D. Fatimæ, Sabinianæ Diœcesis. D. Gregorius ad Gratiosum Nomentanum Episcopum scribens, se rationem ejus aut habuisse, communis illa Ecclesia D. Fatimæ in Curibus, agro Sabinorum, cura. Dextra certe D. Eurimij Oppidum est Turre vel Turres: sic Vulgus Italicum, inquit Leander, perperam pronunciat, nunciat, pro Cures. Κύες, inquit Strabo libro v, νὸν μὲν χώμιόν ἐστιν: ἣν δὲ πόλις Σαβινῶν ἐξ ἧς ἀφιλεῖνε ἐι τ Ῥώμης βασιλεύσαντος, τῖτ Ταῦ κὴ Κυμᾶς Πομπηΐ. ἐστησὶν δὲ ἡ Κυᾶς ὁνομάζωσιν εἰ Δημηρικῆς τῆς Ῥωμαίας. Quis condiderit, & unde nomen habuerit, tradunt cum alij, cum M. Terentius Varro apud Dionysium Halicarnass lib. 11. Curenses inde, de quibus alibi.
units.tr: Going down from the mountain on which Malianum sits, towards the inland parts of Sabina, there opens a spacious valley, in which, near the river Himella, there is a temple of St Mary and likewise one of St Fatima, in the diocese of Sabina. Gregory, writing to Gratiosus, bishop of Nomentum, says that he took account of it: the care of that common church of St Fatima at Cures, in the territory of the Sabines, was his. To the right is certainly the town of St Eurimius, Turre or Turres; thus, says Leander, the Italian populace wrongly pronounces the name for Cures. Κύες [Kyes], says Strabo in book 5, is now a village, but was formerly a city of the Sabines, from which Tatius came, who reigned at Rome together with Romulus; and the Romans were called Quirites from it. Who founded it and whence it got its name, others relate, and Marcus Terentius Varro, cited by Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 2. Hence the Curenses, of whom elsewhere.

units.la: Sequitur Nomentum. Sic Livio variis locis, Virgilio lib. vii, Itinerariae Tabulae; Νωμεντον Strabom & Ptolemaeo; Νώμῆον Stephano appellatum, quod vulgo hodie Lamentano, ut scribit Leander. xii ab Urbe esse lapide, tradit Rhegino. Albanorum olim Colonia, a tribus fratribus deducta, teste Dionysio. Incolae Nomentani, quos in quarta Italiae Regione locat Plinius lib. iii, cap. xii, quorumque excursiones per Agrum Romanum memorat Dionysius Halic. lib. iii: scribens tandem ab Tarquinio debellatos, & in rantas redactos angustias, ut, conditionibus acceptis, se dedere cogerentur. Sic Livius lib. i. tubactum, notat Nomentum una cum Corniculo, Ficulnea, Cameria, Crustumerio, Ameriola, Medulliaque, Veterum Latinorum Opidus. Ortus Nomento Crescentius, Romani Imperii Vindex, de quo multa in Historia. Auctor fuit nobilis Familiae Romanae Crescentiorum. Praedium se habuisse in huius Urbis Agro non semel significat Martialis libris i, ix, & aliis. Nomentanum Rus decimo lapidis diverticulo ab Urbe, apud Plinium lib. xiv. cap. iiii, & Aemilium Probum in Pomponio Attico.
units.tr: Next comes Nomentum. Livy calls it this in various places, Virgil in book 7, and the Itinerary Tables likewise. Strabo and Ptolemy call it Νωμεντον [Nomenton], and Stephanus calls it Νώμῆον [Nomeon]. Today it is commonly called Lamentano, and Rhegino reports that it is twelve miles from the City, as Leander writes. Dionysius says it was once a colony of the Albanorum, founded by one of three brothers. Its inhabitants were the Nomentani, whom Pliny places in the fourth Region of Italy in book 3, chapter 12, and whose raids across the Roman territory Dionysius of Halicarnassus records in book 3. Dionysius writes that they were at last defeated by Tarquin and reduced to such straits that, to save themselves, they were forced to surrender on whatever terms they could get. Livy in book 1 likewise mentions Nomentum together with Corniculum, Ficulnea, Cameria, Crustumerium, Ameriola and Medullia, all towns of the ancient Latins. Crescentius, the champion of the Roman Empire, about whom much is written in history, was born at Nomentum. He was the author of the noble Roman family of the Crescentii. Martial, in books 1 and 9 and elsewhere, shows more than once that he had an estate in the territory of this city. The Nomentanum Rus is mentioned by Pliny in book 14, chapter 4, at a branch road ten miles from the City, and by Aemilius Probus in his life of Pomponius Atticus.

units.la: Supra Cutes in Montibus ad laevam opidum se offert, haud temnendum, quod vulgo Stroncono: deinde Monte Calvo, itemque S. Pietro. Ad dextram infra, Coranello, Roca Antica, Aspera, & ultra montes Rucignario, & Castello di S. Pietro
units.tr: Above Cutes, on the mountains to the left, there appears a town not to be despised, which is commonly called Stroncono; then Monte Calvo, and likewise S. Pietro. Below, on the right, are Coranello, Roca Antica, Aspera, and beyond the mountains Rucignario and Castello di S. Pietro.

units.la: Mox inter Calentinum Torrentem & Malianum Opidum est Col Vecchio; item Stermiliana, Furano, Salvanano. Post Calentinum in Colle Poggio Mirteto.
units.tr: Soon, between the Calentine stream and the town of Malianum, is Col Vecchio; likewise Stermiliana, Furano and Salvanano. Beyond the Calentine, on a hill, is Poggio Mirteto.

units.la: Haud procul Torrens modicus fluit, qui Digentia a Horatio dicitur, hodie Rivo del Sole. De eo alibi a me dictum, Ad ripam illius Mont. pelis est & Pubina. Opidum hoc ortu suo nobilitavit Petrus Odo, maximus Grammaticus, Carminibus, quae non pauca in lucem edidit, Horatij Flacci, & Ovidij Naionis aemulus.
units.tr: Not far off flows a modest stream, which Horace calls the Digentia, today Rivo del Sole. I have spoken of it elsewhere. On its bank is Mont. pelis and Pubina. This town was made famous by its birth of Petrus Odo, the greatest grammarian, who published not a few poems, a rival of Horace Flaccus and Ovid the Nasonian.

units.la: Ad Farfarum pulcro in Colle Coenobium sumtuose quondam aedificatum Farfa: inde haud procul Nerula, perhonestum Opidum; supra id Scandinella Civitas, mox Topia, Monte di S. Maria, Frascho, Poggio Lonadeo, patria Francisci Floridi, qui multis Doctrinae monumentis relictis mortem obiit in Gallijs cIↄ Iↄ xlvii. Sequitur Sa ifano cum Poggio Mariano.
units.tr: On a fine hill near the Farfa stands the monastery of Farfa, once sumptuously built. Not far from it is Nerula, a most respectable town; above it the town of Scandinella, then Topia, Monte di S. Maria, Frascho, and Poggio Lonadeo, the homeland of Francesco Florido, who, having left many monuments of his learning, died in France in 1547. Next comes Sa ifano with Poggio Mariano.

units.la: Trans Alliam, qui nunc Caminato & Rio di Mosso, Crustuminorum fuisse putatur initium. Eorum Sedem clare, meo quidem judicio, indicat Plinius lib. iii cap. v ubi de Tiberi, Etruriam, inquiens, ab Umbris ac Sabinis, mox Urca xiii M. P. Urbs Veientum Agrum ab Castramino dein Fidenate, Latiumque a Vaticano dirimens. Crustumini igitur supra Romanos Fidenatesque versus Septemtrionem in Sabinis; vel, si ab his separandi, Sabinis versus Meridiem adhaerentes. Dionysius sane Halicarnassaeus Crustumerium Albanorum vocat Coloniam, eamque haud procul ab Urbe in Sabinis locat, ut quoque Livius; cui inconstanti Scriptura Crustuminum, Crustumerium, & Crustumeria nominatur: nisi vel Librariorum hoc incuriae & supinitati sit adscribendum, vel diversa Opida sunt censenda. Nam & Crustumerium habet Plinius in Prima Regione inter clara, ut inquit, Latij Opida; & Crustuminum in Tuscia fuisse docet idem libro iii. cap. v, ubi notat, Crustuminum Agrum Veteris Opidi nomen retinere in Tuscia, quod & Cicero confirmat Orat. pro Flacco. Crustumini, de quibus hic agimus, cum Romulo foedere se junxerunt, inque Romanorum fide constanter ad Tarquinium usque permanserunt; quo tempore Latinos sequuti, mox tamen ad Pop. Romani nomen & amicitiam sunt reversi. Legendus praeter alios Livius libro i, qui Crustuminorum etiam alijs locis meminit, praesertim libro xli, ubi scribit Avem Sanqualem in Crustumino adparuisse. Calsius Hemina apud Servium, nuper Petri Danielis auspicijs editum, scribit Siculum nomine Vxoris suae Clutumnestra condidisse Clutemnestram, mox corrupto nomine Crustumerum dictum. Fides sit penes Grammaticum. In Crustumino, inquit Plinius libro ii cap. xcvi natum Fenum, ibi noxium, extra salubre est. Crustumini Montes Livio, ex quibus Allia Flumen praealto defluit alveo. Ab Crustumino Tolus nomen accepit Crustumium vel Clusumina, de qua alij, cum ex antiquis Scriptoribus, tum ex Lapidibus.
units.tr: Across the Allia, what are now Caminato and Rio di Mosso are thought to have been the beginning of the territory of the Crustuminorum. Pliny, in book 3, chapter 5, where he speaks of the Tiber, clearly indicates (in my judgment) where they lived. He says that Etruria is bounded by the Umbrians and Sabines, and then, thirteen Roman miles off, Urca; the city of the Veientes separates the territory of Castramen, then of Fidenae, and Latium from the Vatican. So the Crustumini lay beyond the Romans and Fidenates, toward the north among the Sabines; or, if they are to be separated from these, they adhered to the Sabines toward the south. Dionysius of Halicarnassus indeed calls Crustumerium a colony of the Albans and places it among the Sabines not far from the City, as does Livy too. Writers vary in their spelling of it, calling it Crustuminum, Crustumerium and Crustumeria, unless this is to be ascribed to the carelessness and negligence of copyists, or unless they were different towns. For Pliny also mentions Crustumerium in the First Region, among the famous towns of Latium, as he says; and in book 3, chapter 5, the same author shows that Crustuminum existed in Etruria, where he notes that the territory of Crustuminum keeps the name of the old town in Etruria, which Cicero also confirms in his speech for Flaccus. The Crustumini, of whom we are speaking here, joined themselves to Romulus by treaty and remained constant in their loyalty to the Romans until the time of Tarquin; at that time they followed the Latins, but soon returned to the name and friendship of the Roman people. Besides others, Livy in book 1 should be read; he also mentions the Crustumini in other places, especially in book 41, where he writes that a sanqualis bird appeared in Crustuminum. Calpurnius Hemina, cited by Servius, published recently under the auspices of Pierre Daniel, writes that a Sicilian named Clytemnestra founded Clutemnestra, named after his wife, and that the name was later corrupted into Crustumerum. The truth of this is for the grammarian to judge. Pliny in book 2, chapter 96 says: hay grown in Crustuminum is harmful there, but outside it is wholesome. Livy mentions the Crustumine mountains, from which the river Allia flows down in a very deep channel. Tolus took its name from Crustuminum; Crustumium or Clusumina, about which others write, both from the ancient writers and from inscriptions.

units.la: Crustuminis {a}Montem Rotundum adnumerant: Livio lib. xxvi, Virgilio lib. vii Æneid. Valerio Maximo, Itinerariæ Tabulæ & alijs Fretum, Strabon & Stephano nam dictum. Sic censent Hermolaus Barbarus, Volaterranus, Erythræus, Leander: & convenit Sextus. Nam Fretum Dionysius (cui, ut & Stephano, Sabinorum est Oppidum) lib. iii Stadio cvii ab Urbe distiungit xvii Miliari Antoninus Itinere, quo lab Urbe duxit Hadrian. Strabo Salariam non magnæ latitudinis constitutam fuisse, inque eam Nomentanam incidisse apud Fretum Sabinorum Vicum supra Tiberim jacentem, notat. Fretum Pomponius Sabinus ad vii Æneid. Vicum esse scribit ad ripam Tiberis haud longe ab Urbe, Via Salaria, ubi jungitur Nomentanæ. Eretri Nomen ab lunone Era, quæ hoc loco celebrabatur, factum ait Servius. Locus nunc in Vrsinorum est ditione. Iuxta est Palumbaria, Savelliorum, patritiæ Familiæ Romanæ Patrimonium.
units.tr: Among the Crustumini they count the Round Mountain: Livy in book 26, Virgil in book 7 of the Aeneid, Valerius Maximus, the Itinerary Tables and others call it the Strait (Fretum), and Strabo and Stephanus also name it so. Hermolaus Barbarus, Volaterranus, Erythraeus and Leander think so, and Sextus agrees. For Dionysius (to whom, as to Stephanus, the town belongs to the Sabines), in book 3, places the Strait at 107 stadia from the City, which is 17 miles by the Antonine Itinerary, by which Hadrian led his road from the City. Strabo notes that the Salarian Way was not of great width, and that the Nomentan Way joined it near the Strait, the village of the Sabines lying on the Tiber. Pomponius Sabinus, on book 7 of the Aeneid, writes that the village lies on the bank of the Tiber not far from the City, on the Salarian Way, where it joins the Nomentan. Servius says that the name Eretum comes from Juno Era, who was worshipped in this place. The place is now in the power of the Orsini. Nearby is Palombara, the patrimony of the Savelli, a patrician Roman family.

units.la: Inter Crustuminos & Romanos ad Tiberim fuisse Fidenates, probant quæ paulo ante ex Plinio laudavi. Fidenates tunc Eutropius ab Urbe locat Milliario nunc sexto, nunc septimo: Halicarnassæus lib. ii Stadijs xi, quæ quinque tantum millia efficiunt. Eorum Metropolis Fidena. Sic Livio patrium, Tacito, Suetonio, aliis vocantur: Fidenæ vero Straboni libro v & Ptolemæo hunc Latio adscribit, errore permanifesto quæ Fidena Virgilio lib. vi Æneid. Olim Oppidum nobile ad Tiberis & Anienis, ut Dionysius tradit libro iii, confluentes: Strabonis antetis ætate Pagus & Privatorum Domicilium. Romulus Fidenatibus insigni præmio superatis, Urbeque eorum capta, Fidenas Coloniam Romanam fecit, Idibus Aprilis, anno A. V. C. xiii, duobus millibus & quingentis Colonis eo deductis. Olim Albanorum fuerat Colonia, deducta ab maximo natu ex tribus Fratribus Albanis, quorum alter Crustuminam, alter Nomentum Coloniam fecerant. Videndi Dionysius lib. ii, & Plutarchus in Romulo. De aucto post, anno ab V. C. cccxxvi, Colonorum numero legendus Livius libro iv. Biennio vero post novi Coloni ab Fidenatibus occisi Urbi excidium attulerunt. Livius, Dionysius, alij. Suetonius in Vita Tiberij cap. xi Fidenis Amphitheatri lapsu xx millia hominum gladiatorio Munere scribit attrita, Adeundus idem in Caligulæ Vita cap. xxxi. Plinius lib. x. cap. xxix Ciconias in Fidenate Agro juxta Urbem non facere nidos commemorat. Erythræus putat Fidenas esse, quod hodie vulgo Castel Iubileo. Censet Leander hac ætate ne vestigia quidem ejus ulla superesse, ut nec aliarum plurium, quas olim his in locis exstitisse notat Strabo.
units.tr: Between the Crustumini and the Romans, on the Tiber, were the Fidenates, as the passages I quoted from Pliny a little earlier prove. Eutropius places the Fidenates from the City at one time six, at another seven miles. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, in book 2, gives eleven stadia, which make only five miles. Their metropolis was Fidenae. Thus Livy, Tacitus, Suetonius and others call them Fidenae; but Strabo in book 5 and Ptolemy assign it to Latium, an error that is quite evident, since Virgil in book 6 of the Aeneid calls it Fidena. Once it was a noted town at the confluence of the Tiber and the Anio, as Dionysius reports in book 3; in Strabo's time it was a village and a dwelling of private persons. Romulus, having defeated the Fidenates with a notable prize and captured their city, made Fidenae a Roman colony on the Ides of April in the year 13 from the founding of the City, with 2,500 colonists led there. Earlier it had been a colony of the Albans, founded by the eldest of three Alban brothers, of whom one had founded Crustuminum and another Nomentum. See Dionysius in book 2 and Plutarch in the life of Romulus. Concerning its later enlargement in the year 326 from the founding of the City, with an increase in the number of colonists, read Livy in book 4. Two years afterwards the new colonists were killed by the Fidenates, and this brought destruction upon the City, as Livy, Dionysius and others relate. Suetonius, in the life of Tiberius, chapter 11, writes that when the amphitheatre at Fidenae collapsed, 20,000 men were crushed at a gladiatorial show; the same may be read in the life of Caligula, chapter 31. Pliny in book 10, chapter 29 records that storks in the Fidenate territory near the City do not build nests. Erythraeus thinks that Fidenae is what is commonly called today Castel Giubileo. Leander holds that in this age not even any traces of it survive, nor of the many others which, as Strabo notes, once existed in these places.

units.la: Inter eas Collatia. Sic Latinis, Livio, Plinio, Auctori de VV. Illustribus, alijs dicitur; & Κολλᾶα Straboни; quæ Κολλᾶα Halicarnassæo, Conlatia Festo. Sabinorum Oppidum Livio, Latij in Via Tiburtina, Plinio. Olim Oppidum; Pagus & Privatorum Domicilium ætate Strabonis, cui inter xxx & xl Stadium ab Urbe locatur. Hinc Collatina & Porta & Via Romanis. Conlatium Vicum habet Ausonius Epistola xv. Collatia Vim attulit Lucretiæ Sex. Tarquinius: scribentibus præter alios Livio & Dionysio Halicarnassæo, in Antiquitatibus Romanis.
units.tr: Among these was Collatia. It is so called by the Latins, by Livy, Pliny, the author De viris illustribus, and others; Strabo calls it Κολλᾶα [Kollatia]; Dionysius of Halicarnassus calls it Κολλᾶα [Kollatia], and Festus calls it Conlatia. Livy calls it a town of the Sabines, Pliny a town of Latium on the Tiburtine Way. It was once a town; in Strabo's time it was a village and a dwelling of private persons, placed by him between thirty and forty stadia from the City. Hence the Collatine Gate and Way among the Romans. Ausonius in letter 15 mentions the village of Collatium. Sextus Tarquinius used violence against Lucretia at Collatia; this is told by Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, among others, in their Roman Antiquities.
