units.la: Erant item hic Cænina, Antemna, & aliæ Urbes. Cænina Urbs, inquit Festus, Cæninæ Romæ: Κανιον Stephano & Halicarnassæo, cui ea in Sabinis ponitur: Plinio autem in Latio. Inde Caeninensis quorum Res gestæ leguntur apud Livium & alios. Colonia memoratur omnium prima ab Romulo facta bello Sabino, anno ab V. C. iv, teste, præter alios, Dionysio Halicarnassæo: vide & Solinum in Polyhistore cap. ii.
units.tr: Here were also Caenina, Antemna, and other cities. Festus says Caenina was a city of Rome; Stephanus and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, who place it among the Sabines, give the name as Kanion [Κανιον]; Pliny places it in Latium. From it come the Caeninenses, whose deeds are read in Livy and others. It is recorded that it was the first colony of all, founded by Romulus in the Sabine war in the year 4 from the founding of the City (ab V. C. iv), as Dionysius of Halicarnassus, among others, attests. See also Solinus, Polyhistor, chap. ii.

units.la: {Antemna} quibusdam Latine scribentibus: Ἀντέμνα Stephano; quæ Antemnæ Plinio libr. iii cap. v, Varroni libro iv de LL, Virgilio libro vii. Æneid. (cui Turrigera cognominantur) Ἀντέμναι Dionysio Halicarnassæo, Plutarcho, Straboni. Hanc Urbem Veteriorem esse Roma, scribit ex Varrone Priscianus. Nomen illi, quod ante Amnem sita, qui influit in Tiberim, ut notant Varro, Servius, Isidorus libr. xix cap. ii. Amnis ille fortean Anio. In bello male acceptum hoc Oppidum consenuit, scribente Varrone. De Rebus contra Antemnates gestis plene Historiæ Romanæ. Hæc eodem anno, quo Cænina, bello primo Sabino finito Colonia ab Romulo deducta fuit. Vrbs fuerat Graecorum Aboriginum, qui Siculos expulerant, quemadmodum Caenina. Trecentos eo Cives Colonos fuisse deductos anno iv tradit Dionysius lib. ii.
units.tr: Antemna, as some Latin writers have it. Stephanus gives Antemna [Ἀντέμνα]. Pliny (book iii, chap. v), Varro (book iv, On the Latin Language), and Virgil (Aeneid, book vii, where it is given the epithet "tower-bearing") call it Antemnae. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Plutarch, and Strabo give Antemnai [Ἀντέμναι]. Priscian, citing Varro, writes that this city was older than Rome. It took its name because it lay in front of the river that flows into the Tiber, as Varro, Servius, and Isidore (book xix, chap. ii) note. That river may perhaps be the Anio. This town, badly treated in the war, grew old, as Varro writes. The deeds against the Antemnates are fully recorded in the Roman histories. It was in the same year as Caenina, at the end of the first Sabine war, that the colony was led out by Romulus. The city had been a city of the Greek Aborigines, who had driven out the Sicels, just as Caenina had. Dionysius, book ii, reports that three hundred colonists citizens were led there in the fourth year.

units.la: Alias praetereo. Certe Strabonis, Dionysij, & Plinij saeculis, ut ipsi memoriae prodiderunt, multa ruinis conlapsa jacebant in Agro Sabinorum Opida. Reteram huc iter, quod ab Vrbe Ariminum ducit Antoninus per Vmbriam & Picenum, hoc modo: Antoninus: | Vulgata Nomenclatura Vmbria, Ab Vrbe Reflratam Villam, M.P. XXIIII | Rignano, Castello, ni fallor. Ocriculum Civ. M. P. XXV | Otriculi, Castello. Narniam Civ. M. P. XII | Narni, Citta. Interamnium Civ. M.P.VIII | Terni, Citta. Spoletium Civ. M. P. XVIII | Spoleto, Citta. Forum Flaminij Vicum, M.P.XVIII | Foligni, Castello. Helvillam Vicum, M.P.XXVII | ........ Picenum, Callem; Vicum, M.P.XXIII | Cagli. Forum Sempronij. M.P.XVIII | Fossombruno. Fanum Fortunae, M.P. XVI | Fano, Citta. Pisaurum, M. P. VIII | Pesaro, Citta. Flamin. Ariminum, M.P. XXIIII | Rimini, Citta.
units.tr: I pass over the others. Certainly, in the times of Strabo, Dionysius, and Pliny, as they themselves recorded, many towns lay in ruins in the territory of the Sabines. I will here retrace the route that Antoninus gives from the City to Ariminum through Umbria and Picenum, as follows. Antoninus: | Common name, Umbria. From the City, to Reatina Villa, 24 M.P. | Rignano, a castle, unless I am mistaken. Ocriculum, city, 25 M.P. | Otricoli, a castle. Narnia, city, 12 M.P. | Narni, a city. Interamna, city, 8 M.P. | Terni, a city. Spoletium, city, 18 M.P. | Spoleto, a city. Forum Flaminii, village, 18 M.P. | Foligno, a castle. Helvilla, village, 27 M.P. | ........ Picenum, Calle; village, 23 M.P. | Cagli. Forum Sempronii, 18 M.P. | Fossombrone. Fanum Fortunae, 16 M.P. | Fano, a city. Pisaurum, 8 M.P. | Pesaro, a city. Flaminia, Ariminum, 24 M.P. | Rimini, a city.

units.tr: CAPUT XXV.

units.la: Campania Felix.
units.tr: Campania Felix.

units.la: ITALIAM hactenus, quae in Prisca Propriaque, ut sic loquar Occidentalior, pro virili mea explicui; succedit quae Orientalior.
units.tr: I have now set out, as well as I can, Italy as it is in its ancient and proper character, or as I may call it, its more western part. What follows is the more eastern part.

units.la: Ea ad Occasum communes habet cum Occidentaliore Limites, Truentum & Vfentem Fluvios; reliqua ejus Latera Mari cum Infero Superoque; tum Ionio circumluuntur.
units.tr: To the west this region shares its boundaries with the western part: the rivers Truentus and Ufens. Its other sides are washed by the Adriatic (with its lower and upper parts) and then by the Ionian Sea.

units.la: Totum hoc dimidiam fere complectens Italiae universae portionem, REGNVM NEAPOLITANVM ab Urbe Primaria, de qua post, nuncupatur. REGNVM etiam quibusdam audit APVLIA, ab triplici Apulia, Daunia, Peucetia, & Salentina, quae partem ejus constituunt non ignobilem. REGNVM item dicitur, SICILIA CIS PHARVM vel CITERIORIS, ad differentiam Siciliae ultra Pharum vel Ulterioris, quae ipsa Siciliae est Insula. Reges enim nonnulli, qui & Neapolitanis & Siculis sunt dominati, in suis Titulis se Utriusque Siciliae Reges cis & ultra Pharum vocare consueverunt.
units.tr: This whole region, which takes up nearly half of all Italy, is called the KINGDOM OF NAPLES, after its chief city, which I will discuss later. Some also call it the KINGDOM OF APULIA, after the three Apulias, Daunia, Peucetia and Salentina, which form a considerable part of it. It is also called the KINGDOM OF SICILY ON THIS SIDE OF THE STRAIT, or the Cisfarine (Citerior), to distinguish it from Sicily beyond the Strait, or the Ultrafarine (Ulterior), which is the island of Sicily itself. For some kings, who ruled both the Neapolitans and the Sicilians, were accustomed to style themselves in their titles Kings of both Sicilies, on this side and beyond the Strait.

units.la: Ambitus ejus & Circumnavigatio colligitur à quibusdam Milliarium cIↄ cccc LXVIII: ab aliis cIↄ cccxiv.
units.tr: Its circuit and the distance around its coast are reckoned by some at 1468 miles, and by others at 1314 miles.

units.la: Cœlestis Situs idem illi fere cum universa Italia, præter misso aliquot Parallelis ad Septemtrionem, aliquotque Meridianis ad Occidentem.
units.tr: Its celestial position is nearly the same as that of all Italy, except that it lies some parallels further north and some meridians further west.

units.la: Regio universim tum montuosa est, tum campestris: Cœli temperie, Aquarum scaturiginibus, Ingeniorum præstantia, Corporum robore, Rerum omnium ubertate varietateque felix & beata. Nobiles habet Portus, Promontoria stupenda, Montes insignes & admirandos, Fluvios fœcundos, Fontes jucundos & salubres; De quibus omnibus alibi.
units.tr: The region as a whole is partly mountainous and partly flat. It is happy and blessed in the mildness of its climate, its springs of water, the excellence of its people's minds, the strength of their bodies, and the abundance and variety of all its produce. It has famous harbours, astonishing headlands, notable and admirable mountains, fertile rivers, and pleasant and healthful springs. I will speak of all these elsewhere.

units.la: Regnum hoc varietatem pallium est in suis Principibus maximam. Nam post Imperium Romanum, sub quo multa secula floruerant hujus Regni Regiones, declinationem, sub Gothorum primum, ut aetatis mediæ Scriptores memorant, & Langobardorum fuit ditione: Ab his ad Græcos pervenit & Saracenos, qui illud sub sua habuerunt potestate usque ad Normannorum in Italiam adventum. Hi cum armato exercitu Apuliam ingressi sunt anno cIↄ xxxiv, mense Februario, Drogone, Tancredi F. Duce, qui Normannorum Comes dicebatur. Hic, vectis ad Aufidum Amnem Constantinopolitani Imperatoris Ducibus, Primus Normannorum Locum in Apulia pedem fixit cum Fratribus suis, seque Apulia Comitem appellavit. Qui Drogoni successerint, sequens docet Schema:
units.tr: This kingdom has the greatest variety of rulers of any region. For after the decline of the Roman Empire, under which the regions of this kingdom had flourished for many centuries, it first fell, as the writers of the Middle Ages relate, under the rule of the Goths and the Lombards. From them it passed to the Greeks and the Saracens, who held it under their power until the coming of the Normans into Italy. These, with an armed force, entered Apulia in the year 1034, in the month of February, under Drogo, son of Tancred, who was called Count of the Normans. He, having been brought to the river Aufidus by the commanders of the Emperor of Constantinople, was the first of the Normans to fix his foot in Apulia, together with his brothers, and he called himself Count of Apulia. Those who succeeded Drogo the following table shows:

units.la: Tancredo Richardi F. Normannorum Comes, ex duabus Uxoribus, quarum nomina sunt obliterata, XII procreavit Filios, III Filias. Eorum, qui ad institutum nostrum pertinet, Nomina hæc sunt: Drogo, Primus ex Normannis in Italia Comes. | Gulielmus Comes, qui propter Fortitudinem Ferreum id est Fortubras dictus. | Humfridus, Secundus ex Normannis in Italia Apuliæ Comes, &c. | Rocerius Guiscardus, Quartus Apuliæ Comes, Bajelardo ejecto. | Regerius, cognomine Gibbolus, Vir militiæ gloria clarus. Bajelardus Tertius Apuliæ Comes, à Pattuo expulsus. | Hic Primus Ducis Titulum usurpavit, adprobante Nicolao II P M. obiit anno 1135. Sepultus Salerni. Sexagenarius. Duas legitimas habuisse Conjuges, Alberadam Francam & Gilherardam, Sororem Gisulphi, Principis Salernitanam. Natu ex
units.tr: Tancred, count of the Normans, son of Richard, had twelve sons and three daughters by two wives, whose names have been lost. Of those who pertain to our purpose, the names are these: Drogo, the first Norman count in Italy. | Gulielmus, count, who because of his strength was called Ironarm, that is, Fortebras. | Humfrid, the second Norman count of Apulia in Italy, etc. | Robert Guiscard, the fourth count of Apulia, after Bajelard had been driven out. | Regerius, surnamed Gibbolus, a man famous for his military glory. Bajelardus, the third count of Apulia, who was expelled from Pattuo. | He was the first to assume the title of Duke, with the approval of Pope Nicholas II. He died in the year 1135 and was buried at Salerno, aged sixty. He had two lawful wives, Alberada the Frank and Gilherarda, sister of Gisulf, prince of Salerno. Children by ...

units.la: Priore: Bohemundus, Princeps Tarentinus, qui in maxima Belli Sacri expeditione, capta Adeiphi. Dux Antiochenus factus est anno cIↄ xcviii. Obiit cIↄ cvii. Vixit illi in connubio Constantia, Philippi Franciae Regis Filia. Bohemundus II. Princeps Antiochenus. Cecidit in proelio cum Rodoano Turco, Salapiae Sultano, anno cIↄ cxxxi. Sepultus Antiochiae. Vxor illi Halis, Balduini II Solymorum Regis Filia. Constantia, Heres Principatus Antiocheni, nupta. I Raimundo, Aquitaniae & Pictonum Duci: ex quo natus II Reinaldo Castilioneo, ex quo procreata Bohemundus III Princeps Antiochenus. Maria Vxor Manuelis Comeni, Constantinopolitani Imperat. Posteriore: Rogerius II, Secundus Robertus Apuliae Calabriaeque Dux: Siciliam recepta, Comitem quoque Siciliae se dixit. Vitam cum morte commutavit Salerni anno cIↄ cx mense Februario, quum annorum esset quinquaginta; ibidem sepultus. Vxor illi Adelheida, Roberti Frisonis Flandriae Comitis Filia, Vidua Canuti Daniae Regis. Guilielmus III. Apuliae Calabriaeque Dux, Salerni sine liberis decedens, Principatum Testamento reliquit Agnato Rogerio II. Rogerij Gibbosi Filio. Mortuus est mense Iulio anno cIↄ cxxvii, triginta annorum. Sepultus in Avito Monumento. Ludovicus & Guitcardus in annis pueri-libus obierunt.
units.tr: The elder line: Bohemund, Prince of Taranto, who during the great expedition of the Holy War, after the capture of Adeiphi, became Duke of Antioch in 1098. He died in 1107. He had as his wife Constance, daughter of Philip, King of France. Bohemund II, Prince of Antioch, fell in battle against Rodoan the Turk, Sultan of Aleppo, in 1131. He was buried at Antioch. His wife was Alice, daughter of Baldwin II, King of Jerusalem. Constance, heiress of the principality of Antioch, was married to Raymond, Duke of Aquitaine and Poitou. From this marriage was born Reginald of Châtillon, and from him was begotten Bohemund III, Prince of Antioch. Maria, wife of Manuel Comnenus, Emperor of Constantinople. The later line: Roger II, the second son of Robert, Duke of Apulia and Calabria. After taking Sicily he also called himself Count of Sicily. He exchanged life for death at Salerno in February 1150, at the age of fifty; he was buried there. His wife was Adelaide, daughter of Robert the Frisian, Count of Flanders, and widow of Canute, King of Denmark. William III, Duke of Apulia and Calabria, died without children at Salerno and by his will left the principality to his kinsman Roger II, son of Roger the Hunchback. He died in July 1127, at the age of thirty, and was buried in the ancestral tomb. Ludovicus and Guitcardus died in boyhood.

units.la: Simon Comes Siciliae. III. Comes Siciliae; & ex Testamento Guilielmi Agnati Dux Apuliae Calabriaeque. Neapolim post longam obsidionem Imperatori Byzantino sub finem mentis Sept. anno cIↄ cxxx eripuit; renunciatus eam ob causam ab Anacleto II P. M. Beneventi Rex Neapolis & Siciliae. Regis Italiae titulo, quem autectatarat, repudiato, Sacramentum ipsi de Regnis dixit Clientilare: quod tamen non eas habuit vires, ut bella averruncare potuerit, quae varia gestit cum tribus Pontificibus, aliquotque Aborum Regulis; tam felicitec, ut ubique Victor Gladio suo interemit iussit: Apulus & Calaber, Siculus mihi servit & Afer. Vita defunctus est Panormi in Sicilia, propridie Kalendas Martij cIↄ cLIII, quum regnasset annos xxxv, ibidem sepultus in Ecclesia primaria. Vixit annos LVIII, Mense v. Dies totidem. Vxores habuit tres, Albuinam, Sibyllam Ducem Burgundiae, & Beatricem Comitem de Retelste. Rogerius, Dux Apuliae ante Patrem obiit, anno cIↄ cxl viii. Sepultus Panormi. Vxor Maria, Roberti Comitis Alerij in Apulia, Filia; ex qua unica illi nata est Filia. Tancredus Princeps Tarentinus, obiit ante patrem. Guilielmus, cognomine Malus, Princeps, Capuanus, Secundus Siciliae Rex, eis & uls Pharum, Patre vivo inauguratus xii. Mal anno cIↄ cL. Ab Hadriano II P. M. diris devotus, mox in gratiam receptus, Tunetum vastavit. Ob Tyrannidem ab Regni Proceribus captus, sed paullo post rebus suis restitutus, diem obiit pridie Kal. Mai cIↄ cLXVI, aetatis XLVI. Sepultus Panormi. Vxor illi Margareta Garsiae, Navarrae Regis Filia. Henricus. Constantia. Constantia, quae quinquagenaria jam ab Celestino III. P. M. Coronata, Regni Siciliae Heres nuncupata, & Henrico II, Friderici Barbarossae Filio desponsata. Tancredus, ex Concubina natus, Comes Alcetij: testamento Guilielmi Boni Rex utriusque Siciliae creatus est: sed quum Pontificis gratiam demereri non posset, prae moerore amissi Filij obiit, nono imperij anno, qui ab Christo nato erat cIↄ cxcIv. Vxor Sibylla. Fridericus II Imp. Rom. Rex Neapolis & Siciliae. Ducta in Vxorem Iole, Ioannis Brennij, Hierosolymorum Regis, Filia, Ius Hierosolymitani Regni tibi Rogerius Dux Apuliae, Rex Siciliae contra Patrem per tumultum militarem nominatus; non multo post, dum eum varium & mutabile semper Vulgus iterum reiicere conatur, fortuito casu est interemtus. Guilielmus II, cognomine Bonus Rex utriusque Siciliae, Princeps pius, prudens, inhibitae auctoritatis, coronatus Kal. Mai cIↄ cIxxvi. Obiit anno cIↄ cLxxvi, aetatis suae xxxii, sepultus Panormi. Vxor Ioanna, Henrici II Angliae Regis Filia, quae Matrimonio. Robert. Henricus, Principes Capuani, Improles defuncti.
units.tr: Simon, Count of Sicily. He was the third Count of Sicily and, by the will of his kinsman William, Duke of Apulia and Calabria. After a long siege he wrested Naples from the Byzantine Emperor toward the end of September 1130. For this reason he was proclaimed King of Naples and Sicily by Anacletus II, Pope. He rejected the title of King of Italy, which he had claimed, and swore an oath of allegiance to the Pope concerning his kingdoms. However, he did not have the strength to avert the wars that he waged with three popes and several petty princes of the region, and he was so successful that everywhere he had his victorious sword slay them, as the saying went: "Apulian and Calabrian, Sicilian and African serve me." He died at Palermo in Sicily on 28 February 1153, after reigning thirty-five years, and was buried there in the cathedral church. He lived fifty-eight years, five months and the same number of days. He had three wives: Albuina, Sibylla, the Duchess of Burgundy, and Beatrice, Countess of Rietberg. Roger, Duke of Apulia, died before his father in 1148 and was buried at Palermo. His wife was Maria, daughter of Robert, Count of Alife in Apulia; from her he had one daughter. Tancred, Prince of Taranto, died before his father. William, surnamed the Bad, Prince of Capua, second King of Sicily, was crowned during his father's lifetime in 1150 (?). He was placed under a curse by Adrian II, Pope, but was soon received back into favour. He laid waste to Tunis. Seized by the nobles of the kingdom on account of his tyranny, he was restored to his position shortly afterward. He died on 30 April 1166, at the age of forty-six, and was buried at Palermo. His wife was Margaret, daughter of Garcia, King of Navarre. Henry. Constance. Constance, who, already in her fifties, was crowned by Pope Celestine III and named heiress of the kingdom of Sicily, was betrothed to Henry II, son of Frederick Barbarossa. Tancred, born of a concubine, Count of Alcamo, was created King of both Sicilies by the will of William the Good. But since he could not win the favour of the Pope, he died of grief over the loss of his son in the ninth year of his reign, which was the year 1194 after the birth of Christ. His wife was Sibylla. Frederick II, Emperor of the Romans, King of Naples and Sicily. He married Iolanda, daughter of John of Brienne, King of Jerusalem, and thereby acquired the right to the kingdom of Jerusalem. Roger, Duke of Apulia, was proclaimed King of Sicily by a military uprising against his father; not long afterward, while the fickle and ever-changing common people were trying to cast him out again, he was killed by a chance event. William II, surnamed the Good, King of both Sicilies, a pious and prudent prince of restrained authority, was crowned on 1 May 1166. He died in 1189, at the age of thirty-two, and was buried at Palermo. His wife was Joan, daughter of Henry II, King of England, who was married to... Robert. Henry, Princes of Capua, died without offspring.

units.la: II ex Imperatoribus Germaniae. adquisivit. Ab eo tempore Regey Siciliæ se quoque Reges Hierosolymorum scripserunt. Multa gessit cum aliis bella. Quum magnæ ætatis iam ex morbo decumberet, ab Manfredo, Filio Notho, Tarentinorum Principe, est suffocatus. Nonis Decembris, anno ᴐᴐᴐ ᴄᴄ L.
units.tr: Second of the Emperors of Germany. He acquired... From that time the kings of Sicily also styled themselves kings of Jerusalem. He waged many wars against others. When, already of great age, he lay sick, he was smothered by Manfred, his natural son, Prince of Taranto. On the Nones of December, in the year 1250.

units.la: Rogerius, a Patre Rex utriusque Siciliæ creatus, sed brevi post ante Patrem mortuus anno cIↄ cxcIV. Uxor Irene Isaaci Imperatoris Constantinopolitani filia. Guilielmus III Alius Rex Siciliæ post Patrem, captus ab Henrico VI Imp est exceatus & cvitatus; in quo Stemma Normannorum in Sicilia defecit, Anno cIↄ cxcV.
units.tr: Roger, created King of both Sicilies by his father, but died shortly after, before his father, in the year 1194. His wife was Irene, daughter of Isaac, Emperor of Constantinople. William III, the other son, King of Sicily after his father, was captured by Henry VI, Emperor, and blinded and deposed; with him the line of the Norman kings in Sicily came to an end, in the year 1195.

units.la: Stemma III Regum, ex Francis, utriusque Siciliæ.
units.tr: Stemma of the Three Kings from the Franks, of both Sicilies.

units.la: Karolus, Hludovici IIX Matris Regis Francorum F. Philippi II Augusti N, S. Hludovici Regis Frater, Rex utriusque Siciliæ contra Manfredum ab Vibano IV P. M. creatus.
units.tr: Charles, son of Louis VIII, King of the Franks, and of Blanche, mother of the king; nephew of Philip II Augustus; brother of King Louis IX. He was created King of both Sicilies by Pope Urban IV against Manfred.

units.la: Karolus, II, cognomine Claudus, Princeps Salernitanus, Rex Utriusque Siciliæ. Princeps benignus & liberalis. Siciliam recuperare conatus ab Rogerio Lora Calabro, Petri Aragonum Regis Ammi alio, VII Idus Aprilis anno cIↄ cc LXXXIV navali prælio victus, & cum magno Nobilium numero est captus, ex quibus ducenti in ultionem Conradini capite sunt truncati. Ipse quoque morte adjudicatus post quadraginta demum captivitatem beneficio Constantiæ Reginæ, quæ Aragonensi erat nupta, dimissus est certis, quis antea indicavi conditionibus. Obiit IV Nonas Maii, anno cIↄ cccIX, quum annos regnasset XXV, quatuorque menses. Uxor illi Maria Filia & Hæres Stephani Regis Hungariæ, quondam librorum Mater. Ex iis ad institutum nostrum pertinent: Karolus Martellus, Hungariæ Rex XXI, ex matrina Successione. Karolus Robertus, Rex Hungariæ. Hludovicus Rex Hungariæ. obiit cIↄ ccc LXXXII Andreas Primus Mantua Ioannæ I Reginæ Siciliæ. obiit cIↄ cccXLV. Robertus Dux Calabriæ, & Rex Neapolitanus, Heres Regni Siciliæ, quam post Iacobi Aragonij mortem recuperare conatus, sed victus ab Fridenco Iacobi germano nil amplius tentandum ratus, contentus Neapoli Siciliam reliquit. Obiit Neapoli IV Kal. Februarij cIↄ cccXLIII anno Regni XXXIV, ætatis, ut plerique volunt, LXIIX. Uxores illi fuerunt II: Violanta Ioannes Princeps Achaiæ Dux Dyrrachij. Philippus princeps Tarentinus. Ludovicus Tarentinus, Marrius Ioannæ Reginæ Secundus. Petri Aragonum Regis F. & Sanctia Majoricarum F. Priore genitus,
units.tr: Charles II, surnamed the Lame, Prince of Salerno, King of both Sicilies. He was a kindly and generous prince. Trying to recover Sicily, he was defeated by Roger de Loria, Calabrian, admiral of Peter, King of Aragon, in a naval battle on 9 April 1284, and was captured with a great number of nobles. Of these, two hundred were beheaded in revenge for Conradin. He himself was condemned to death, but after forty months of captivity he was released, through the kindness of Queen Constance, who was married to the Aragonese, on the conditions I have described earlier. He died on 4 May 1309, having reigned for twenty-five years and four months. His wife was Mary, daughter and heir of Stephen, King of Hungary, mother of many children. Of these, those relevant to our purpose are: Charles Martel, King of Hungary, the twenty-first, by hereditary succession through his mother; Charles Robert, King of Hungary; Louis, King of Hungary, who died in 1382; Andrew, the first husband of Queen Joanna I of Sicily, who died in 1345; Robert, Duke of Calabria and King of Naples, heir of the kingdom of Sicily. After the death of James of Aragon he tried to recover Sicily, but was defeated by Frederick, brother of James, and, judging that nothing more could be attempted, he was content to leave Sicily and remain at Naples. He died at Naples on 29 January 1343, in the thirty-fourth year of his reign and, as most would have it, in his sixty-eighth year. He had two wives: Violante, and Ioannes, Prince of Achaea, Duke of Durazzo, Philip, Prince of Taranto, and Louis of Taranto, husband of Queen Joanna II. (Of the first wife, a son of Peter, King of Aragon, and Sancia, daughter of Majorca, was born earlier.)

units.la: Karolus, Dux Calabriae, qui ante Patrem Neapolitanum ipso aetatis flore est extinctus vi. Eid. Nov. anno cIↄ CCC XXVIII. Duas habuit Conjuges: Mariam Valesiam, Sororem germanam Philippi VI Francorum Regis, & Catharinam Alberti I Imp. Filiam, inprolem. Ex priore nata illa
units.tr: Charles, Duke of Calabria, who died at Naples before his father, cut down in the prime of his life, on 10 November 1328. He had two wives: Mary of Valois, full sister of Philip VI, King of the Franks, and Catherine, daughter of Albert I, Emperor; he had issue by her. Of the first wife was born that

units.la: Ioanna I, Neapolis Regina Avi testamento designata, hac lege ut nuberet Andreae Hungaro, Principi Agnato: quem quum strangulatum, ab Levito Ludovico Hungariae Rege regno est ejecta: quod Clementis VI P. M. ope postea recuperavit, ab eodem coronata cum Ludovico Tarentino, altero Marito v. Kal. Iunij, anno cIↄ CCC LII: quo defuncto nuptiis Jacobo Tarraconensi, Infanti Majoricarum & mox hoc repudiato, Othoni Brunsvigio. Quum vero ne hoc quidem defensore se satis tutam videret, explendo, quod in Agnatos conceperat, odio, adoptavit Ludovicum Andegavensem. Importuna hac ejus levitate offensus Vrbanus VI P. M. Ludovicum è Pannonia revocavit; qui aetatem obtendens Carolum Dyrrachinum armavit: a quo illa capta, & eodem in loco, quo primum ipsa Maritum ii. Hocarat, est strangulata, VII Eid. Iunias CIↄ CCC LXXXI.
units.tr: Joanna I, Queen of Naples, designated by her grandfather's will, on condition that she marry Andrew of Hungary, a prince of her own house. When he was strangled, Louis, King of Hungary, expelled her from the kingdom. She later recovered it with the help of Pope Clement VI, and was crowned by him with Louis of Taranto, her second husband, on 27 May 1352. When he died, she married James of Tarragona, infant of Majorca, and soon repudiated him, and then Otto of Brunswick. But seeing that not even this man was a sufficient protector, she, in order to satisfy the hatred she had conceived against her kinsmen, adopted Louis of Anjou. Offended by this reckless fickleness of hers, Pope Urban VI recalled Louis from Pannonia; he, pleading his age, armed Charles of Durazzo against her. She was taken by him and, in the same place where she had first strangled her husband, was strangled herself, on 7 June 1382.

units.la: Ladislaus de Dyrrachio ex Duce Calabriae, mortuo Patre, adhuc puer sub tutela Matris Margaretae Rex Siciliae creatus est I I. Kal. Martij CIↄ CCC XXXVI. Regnavit contra Regem Ludovicum annos II mens. v. dies. XI obiit Perusij VIII Eid. Augusti. CIↄ CCCC XIV.
units.tr: Ladislaus of Durazzo, Duke of Calabria, became King of Sicily on 1 March 1386, while still a boy, after his father's death, under the guardianship of his mother Margaret. He reigned against King Louis for two years, five months and eleven days, and died at Perugia on 6 August 1414.

units.la: Ioanna II, de Dyrrachio, post mortem Fratris regnum obtinuit, coronata ab duobus Episcopis Francisco Politiano Aretino, & Angelo Romano Anagnino, Nuncijs Martini P. M. anno CIↄ CCCCXIX Regnavit annos XX. Obijt CIↄ CCCC XXXIV Neapoli. Quum liberos non haberet, adoptavit primo Alphonsum Regem Aragonum Regemque Siciliae designatum post mortem suam haeredem instituit mense Sept. anno CIↄ CCCCXX; mox quum inter se dissidere coepissent, eius adoptione antiquata Ludovicum III Ducem Andegavensem, Ludovici I Hostis Patris & Fratris suorum, Regis Siciliae Filium adoptavit, Regemque post se designavit anno CIↄ CCCC XXXIII, quo ante obitum suum sine liberis mortuo ejus fratrum Renatum, Lotharingiae Ducem, eadem lege adoptavit, & non multo post diem obiit Neapoli anno CIↄ CCCC XXXIV.
units.tr: Joanna II, of Durazzo, obtained the kingdom after the death of her brother. She was crowned by two bishops, Francis Politian of Arezzo and Angelo of Rome, bishop of Anagni, envoys of Pope Martin V, in the year 1419. She reigned for twenty years and died at Naples in 1434. Having no children, she first adopted Alfonso, King of Aragon, and designated him King of Sicily and her heir after her death, in September 1420. Soon, when they began to fall out, she revoked this adoption and adopted Louis III, Duke of Anjou, son of Louis I, enemy of her father and brother, and in 1433 she named him King after herself. Before her death, when his brother René, Duke of Lorraine, died without children, she adopted him on the same condition, and not long after she died at Naples in 1434.

units.la: Stemma IV Regum ex Ducibus Andegavensibus, Siciliae cis Pharum.
units.tr: Stemma of the Four Kings from the Dukes of Anjou, of Sicily on this side of the Pharos.

units.la: Ludovicus Valesius, Ioannis Regis Francorum II F. Philippi VII Valesij N. Dux Andegavensis, adoptatus, ut antea dixi, in Filium ab Ioanna, Siciliae Regina, quae inprolis erat, consensu Antipapae Clementis VII anno ab Christo nato CIↄ CCC LXXIX, Rexque Hierosolymorum & Siciliae. Comesque Provinciae designatus est, post mortem ipsius coronandus. Defuncta Regina Regis titulum adsumens, regnavit titulo tenus contra Karolum III Dyrrachinum annos II, Menses II, dies IX, nimirum ab IIII Eidus Iunij anni CIↄ CCCLXXII, quo die Regina est occisa, ad XII Kal. Octobris anni CIↄ CCC LXXXIV. Vxor illi Lucia, Filia Barnabae Vicecomitis.
units.tr: Louis of Valois, second son of John, King of the Franks, grandson of Philip VII of Valois, Duke of Anjou, adopted as son, as I said before, by Joanna, Queen of Sicily, who had no children, with the consent of the antipope Clement VII, in the year of Christ 1379. He was designated King of Jerusalem and Sicily and Count of Provence, to be crowned after her death. When the Queen died in 1382, he took up the royal title and reigned in name only, against Charles III of Durazzo, for two years, two months and nine days, namely from 10 June 1382, the day the Queen was killed, to 21 September 1384. His wife was Lucia, daughter of Bernabò Visconti.

units.la: Ludovicus Postumus, ex Duce Andegavensi, mortuo Patre, Regni Siciliae, contra Karolum III Dyrrachinum, Titulum adsumsit XII Kalendas Octobris, anno CIↄ CCC LXXXIV; coronatusque fuit Avenione ab Clemente P. M. anno CIↄ CCC LXXXIX. Vxor Violenta Aragonum Filia.
units.tr: Louis the Posthumous, Duke of Anjou, after his father's death, took up the title of the Kingdom of Sicily against Charles III of Durazzo on 21 September 1384. He was crowned at Avignon by Pope Clement VII in 1389. His wife was Violante, daughter of Aragon.

units.la: Ludovicus III Dux Andegavensis, mortuo Patre, titulo tenus Rex Siciliae appellatus est; adoptatus ab Ioanna II, postquam Alphonsum Aragonum Regem Adoptione ob osta dissidia privasset, anno CIↄ CCC XXXIII. Obiit Consentiae in Brutijs, anno CIↄ CCC XXXIV.
units.tr: Louis III, Duke of Anjou, after his father's death, was called King of Sicily in name only. He was adopted by Joanna II, after she had deprived Alfonso, King of Aragon, of his adoption, because of their quarrels, in 1433. He died at Cosenza in Bruttium in 1434.

units.la: Renatus Dux Lotharingiae titulo-tenus & Andegavensis, Comes Provinciae, Fratre Ludovico III mortuo. Regni Siciliae jura suscepit, adoptarus ab Ioanna II anno CIↄ CCCC XXXIV, Regnavit in Schismate contra Alphonsum Regem Aragonum & Siciliae annos XLVI. Obiit CIↄ CCC XXC mense Ianuario; Ludovicum XI Francorum Regem, Comitatus Provinciae Regnique Siciliæ hæredem relinquens. Vxor eius fuit Isabella.
units.tr: René, Duke of Lorraine in name only and of Anjou, Count of Provence, after his brother Louis III died, took up the rights of the Kingdom of Sicily, adopted by Joanna II in 1434. He reigned during the Schism, against Alfonso, King of Aragon and Sicily, for forty-six years. He died in January 1480, leaving Louis XI, King of the Franks, as heir of the county of Provence and the Kingdom of Sicily. His wife was Isabella.

units.la: Ioannes, Dux Andegavensis, titulotenus Dux Calabriæ, qui ante Patrem obiit in Gallia.
units.tr: John, Duke of Anjou, Duke of Calabria in name only, who died in Gaul before his father.

units.la: Stemma v Regum ex Valesijs Franciæ Regibus, Siciliæ cis Pharum.
units.tr: Stemma of the Five Kings from the Valois Kings of France, Kings of Sicily this side of the Strait.

units.la: Karolus v Valesius, cognomine Sapiens, Primus ex Regys Filijs Franciæ Delphinus, Paternæ Regni Hæres & Successor. Obiit anno MCCCLXXX. Karolus vi Valesius, Benenatus cognomine, Pater defuncti in Regno Successor. Obiit MCCCCXXII. Ludovicus Valesius, Dux Aurelianensis & Turonensis. Alenconij & Vertuci Comes: mucdatus per Sicanos ab Ioanne Burgundo Patruele subornatus, anno MCCCCVII. Karolus vii Valesius, Rex Franciæ. Alij. Obiit MCCCCLX, xi Kalendas Augusti. Karolus Valesius, Dux Aurelianensis, Hæres Comitatus Mediolanensis. Obiit anno MCCCC XXI. Ioannes Valesius, Comes Angolismorum. Vita defuncta est anno MCCCC LXVIII. Ludovicus xi Valesius, Rex Franciæ. Hunc Renatus Dux Lotharingiæ, Siciliæ Rex. Provinciæque Comes Heredem & Successorem testamento reliquit. Obiit propinde Kal. Sept. MCCCCLXXXIII. Ludovicus xii Valesius, Dux Aureliæ & Mediolani, postque Karoli viii Agnati mortem Rex Franciæ, Siciliæ, &c. Obiit MCCCCXXV. Karolus Valesius, Comes Angolismensis: defunctus anno MCCCCXCIV, duobus relictis ex Ludovica, Filia Philippi Comitis Brettiani, Ducis Sabaudiæ Liberis, Francisco & Margareta. Claudia Valesia Karolus viii Valesius, cognomine Gibbosus, Rex Franciæ, Siciliæ, &c. Franciscus i Valesius, Angolismorum Comes, Ludovico xii sine masculo prole defuncto, cujus & Filiam habuit Vxorem Rex Franciæ, Siciliæ, &c. Obiit pridie Kalendas Aprilis MDXLVII. Franciscus Delphinus Franciæ, ante Patrem obiit iv Eid. Sept. anno MDXXXVI. Henricus ii Valesius, Rex Franciæ, Siciliæ, &c. Obiit ex vulnere anno MDLIX Eidib Iulij relictis inter alios ex Katharina Medicea. Karolus Dux Aurelianensis. Obiit non sine Veneni suspicione anno MDXLV. Franciscus ii Valesius, qui Rex post Patrem Franciæ, Siciliæ, &c. Obiit ex Apostemate cerebri inprolis MDLX Nonis Decembris. Karolo Maximiliano ix Valesio, Fratris in Regno Franciæ Siciliæque Successore. Periit acuta febre iii Kalendas Iunij, MDLXXIV. Henricus iii Valesius, Rege Poloniæ: &c., Fratre defuncto, Franciæ, &c. Obiit Kalend. Sextilis MDLXXXIX, venenato cultello confossus, Rege Navarræo, Henrico Borbonio, quem sibi fidelissimum fuerat expertus, primum impositæ corona Successore nominato, qui hodie Illustrissime regnat.
units.tr: Charles V of Valois, surnamed the Wise, the first of the king's sons to be Dauphin of France, heir and successor to his father's kingdom. He died in 1380. Charles VI of Valois, surnamed the Beloved, father of the late king and his successor in the kingdom. He died in 1422. Louis of Valois, Duke of Orléans and Touraine, Count of Alençon and Vertus, murdered in 1407 by the Scots, at the instigation of his cousin John of Burgundy. Charles VII of Valois, King of France. Others say he died on 22 July 1461. Charles of Valois, Duke of Orléans, heir to the County of Milan. He died in 1421. John of Valois, Count of Angoulême. He died in 1468. Louis XI of Valois, King of France. René, Duke of Lorraine and King of Sicily, and Count of Provence, left him as heir and successor in his will. He died on 1 September 1483. Louis XII of Valois, Duke of Orléans and Milan, and after the death of his cousin Charles VIII, King of France, Sicily, etc. He died in 1525. Charles of Valois, Count of Angoulême, who died in 1494, leaving two children by Louise, daughter of Philip, Count of Bresse and Duke of Savoy: Francis and Margaret. Claudia of Valois. Charles VIII of Valois, surnamed the Hunchback, King of France, Sicily, etc. Francis I of Valois, Count of Angoulême, succeeded Louis XII, who died without a male heir; he had a daughter by his wife, the King of France, Sicily, etc. He died on 31 March 1547. Francis, Dauphin of France, died before his father on 10 September 1536. Henry II of Valois, King of France, Sicily, etc. He died of a wound on 10 July 1559, leaving among others children by Catherine de' Medici. Charles, Duke of Orléans. He died in 1545, not without suspicion of poison. Francis II of Valois, who became king after his father, King of France, Sicily, etc. He died of a brain abscess, without issue, on 5 December 1560. Charles IX of Valois, successor in the kingdoms of France and Sicily to his brother. He died of a high fever on 30 May 1574. Henry III of Valois, King of Poland, etc., and after his brother's death, of France, etc. He died on 1 August 1589, stabbed with a poisoned knife by the King of Navarre, Henry of Bourbon, whom he had found to be most loyal to him, having first named him successor to the crown; he now reigns most illustriously.

units.la: Stemma v. Regum Arragoniae in Regno Siciliae.
units.tr: Stemma of the Five Kings of Aragon in the Kingdom of Sicily.

units.la: Ferdinandus cognomine [?] Regis cIↄ ccccxvi.
units.tr: Ferdinand, surnamed [?], King, 1416.

units.la: Alphonsus, cognomine Magnanimus, Patre defuncto Aragoniae, Cataloniae, Valentiae, Navarrae & Siciliae Regna gubernare coepit, adhuc valde iuvenis. Ex Sardinia, ubi Genuenses oppugnabat, Neapolim accersitus, quum virtute sua Ludovici Andegavensis & Sforzae vim repressisset, ab Ioanna in Filium & Regni Successorem est adoptatus. Quum autem Hostibus veniam postulantibus facilis condonasset, Reginam supra modum offendit: quam quum placare nequiret, palam armis oppugnavit, Neapolique extrudavit: quoties cum ceu ingratum & impium Regina exhaeredi-tavit, & priore Adoptione rescissa. Ludovicum Andegavensem in eius locum adscivit. Hinc gravissima sequuta sunt bella, in quibus alternante fortuna, nunc Aragonij, nunc Andegavenses Neapoli sunt potiti. Ad extremum Alphonsus Victor Regni possessionem transmisit ad Ferdinandum Filium Naturam. Obiit Neapoli iv Kal. Quint. anno cIↄ ccccxviii.
units.tr: Alphonsus, surnamed Magnanimus, on his father's death began to govern the kingdoms of Aragon, Catalonia, Valencia, Navarre and Sicily while still very young. Summoned from Sardinia, where he was attacking the Genoese, to Naples, he restrained by his valour the force of Louis of Anjou and Sforza. He was adopted by Joanna as her son and successor to the kingdom. When he readily pardoned the enemies who asked for mercy, he gave great offence to the queen. Unable to placate her, he openly attacked her with arms and drove her out of Naples. Many times she disinherited him as ungrateful and impious, and rescinded the earlier adoption, and in his place adopted Louis of Anjou. From this came very serious wars, in which, as fortune alternated, now the Aragonese and now the Angevins held Naples. At last Alphonso the Victor transferred possession of the kingdom to Ferdinand, his natural son. He died at Naples on 28 July 1418.

units.la: {y} Ferdinandus vel Ferrandinus, Dux Calabriae, Patris Regum, ex Aragoniæ Regibus, Siciliæ cis Pharum, vel Neapolis. Iustus & Honestus, Rex Aragoniæ, &c. Vita decessit iv Nonas ApriIoannes ii Rex per Coniugem Blancam Navarræ, & Fratre Alphonso absque legitima Prole defuncto, Siciliæ Aragoniæque. Obiit xiv Kalend. Feb. MCCCCLXXIX. | Alij Ferdinandus Rex Aragoniæ & Siciliæ, ducta in Uxorem Isabella Henrici iv Castellæ & Legionis Sorore germana, ab cius obitu Regna utriusque Hispaniæ Ulterioris & Citerioris copulavit, anno MCCCCLXXVII. Princeps felicissimus, continuo victoriæ cursu primo Granatæ Regnum, Saracenis penitus exterminatis, mox Neapolitanum quoque, Oranum in Africa, Hispaniolæ & Americæ Regna, Fortunatas itemque Insulas, aliasque quatuor in Oceano meridionali sitas suo adjecit Imperio. Obiit x Kalend. Ianuarij, MDXVI, ætatis suæ LXIV. | Alij Ioannes Princeps Hispaniæ post contractas cum Margareta Maximiliani I Imperatoris F. nuptias diem obiit anno MCCCCXCVII. Isabella Alphonso IV, dehinc Emanuelis Lusitaniæ Regibus nupta obiit MCCCCXCVII, ex magno partus dolore. Ioanna, conjux Philippi Archiducis Austriæ Ducisque Burgundiæ, quibus ditiones Belgicas regno Castellæ univit. Obiit anno MDV. | Alij Karolus V Romanorum Imperat. Rex Castellæ, Legionis, Aragoniæ, Navarræ, Valentiæ, Granatæ, Siciliæ ultra & cis Pharum, &c. Obiit MDLVIII. | Ferdinandus Cæsar Augustus Rex Hungariæ & Bohemiæ. Obiit anno MDLXIV. Philippus Rex Hispaniæ, Siciliæ, Neapolis, Hierosolymæ, Portugalliæ, Magnus Dux Austriæ, Dux Burgundiæ, &c. Obiit anno MDXCVIII | Maria — Maximilianus Roman. Imperat. Rex Hungariæ, & Bohemiæ.
units.tr: Ferdinand or Ferrante, Duke of Calabria, father of the kings, of the Aragonese line, Kings of Sicily this side of the Strait, or of Naples. Just and honourable, King of Aragon, etc. He died on 2 April 1479. John II, King of Aragon and Sicily, by his wife Blanche of Navarre, and his brother Alphonso having died without legitimate issue. He died on 19 January 1479. Others say Ferdinand, King of Aragon and Sicily, who married Isabella, full sister of Henry IV of Castile and León, and after his death joined the kingdoms of both Hispanic realms, Further and Hither, in 1477. A most fortunate prince, in a continuous course of victory, first Granada, the Saracens being utterly driven out, then also the Kingdom of Naples, Oran in Africa, the kingdoms of Hispaniola and America, the Fortunate Islands, and four others in the southern ocean, he added to his empire. He died on 23 December 1516, in the sixty-fourth year of his age. Others say John, Prince of Spain, after contracting marriage with Margaret, daughter of the Emperor Maximilian I, died in 1497. Isabella, married first to Alphonso IV and then to Emmanuel, Kings of Portugal, died in 1497 from the great pain of childbirth. Joanna, wife of Philip, Archduke of Austria and Duke of Burgundy, by whom she joined the Belgian lands to the kingdom of Castile. She died in 1505. Others say Charles V, Roman Emperor, King of Castile, León, Aragon, Navarre, Valencia, Granada, Sicily beyond and this side of the Strait, etc. He died in 1558. Ferdinand, Augustan Caesar, King of Hungary and Bohemia. He died in 1564. Philip, King of Spain, Sicily, Naples, Jerusalem, Portugal, Grand Duke of Austria, Duke of Burgundy, etc. He died in 1598. Mary. Maximilian, Roman Emperor, King of Hungary and Bohemia.

units.la: testamento in Regno Neapolitano Successor constituturus, prælio conserto cum Ioanne Andegavensi, Neapolim eum relinquere coegit. Obiit Neapoli viii Kal. MCCCCXCIV. Anna — Rudolphus II | Ernestus, alijque Fratres Archiduces Austriæ. Philippus Rex Hispaniæ, Siciliæ, Neapolis, &c. Alphonsus II Rex Neapolis ab Ioanne Borgia Cardinale Claremontano coronatus. Subditos sibi ob crudelitatem adversos habuit. Fredericus Ferdinandi Fratuelis in Regno Neapolitano Successit, anno MCCCCXCVII ab Ludovico XII Gallorum Rege & Consalvo Hispano pariter impetitus, quum neutri se parem cognosceret, ad Ludovicum Holtem in Galliam
units.tr: intending by his will to appoint a successor in the Kingdom of Naples; when battle was joined with John of Anjou, he forced him to leave Naples. He died at Naples on 25 December 1494. Anne. Rudolf II; Ernest, and other brothers, Archdukes of Austria. Philip, King of Spain, Sicily, Naples, etc. Alphonso II, King of Naples, was crowned by John Borgia, Cardinal of Clermont. He had subjects who were hostile to him because of his cruelty. Frederick, cousin of Ferdinand, succeeded in the Kingdom of Naples in 1497, attacked at the same time by Louis XII, King of the French, and by the Spaniard Gonzalo; since he did not think himself a match for either, he went to Louis in France

units.la: bens, suisque distitudens rebus. Regem deiectum, fugit in S. Iohannem, ibique nomine Regis, post Mediolanum, Mantuam ... anno ... mense Iulio.
units.tr: taking with him and dividing his goods. Having fled from his deposed kingdom, he went to Saint John, and there, in the name of the King, after Milan and Mantua ... in the year ... in the month of July.

units.la: Ferdinandus II Rex Neapolitanus ab Ludovico VIII Galliarum Regem repulsus, post ejus fata Hispanorum ac Venetorum auxilijs, Gallis pulsis, Neapolim recepit, mortuus in ipso Victoriae calida VIII Kal. Oct. anno MCCCCXCVII.
units.tr: Ferdinand II, King of Naples, driven out by Louis VIII, King of the French, after that king's death, with the help of the Spaniards and the Venetians, the French having been expelled, recovered Naples, and died in the very heat of victory on 24 September 1497.

units.la: Alphonsus Dux Calabriae Tarenti ab Consulvo captus est anno MCCCCXIII, ductusque in Hispaniam, & Valentiae hoc libertis mortuus. Regnum Hispanae Regibus potiendum reliquit, Karolo V. ceterisque Successoribus.
units.tr: Alphonso, Duke of Calabria and Taranto, was captured by Gonzalo in 1503 and taken to Spain, and died a prisoner at Valencia. He left the kingdom of Spain to be possessed by the kings, Charles V and his other successors.

units.la: Totius porro Regni Metropolis est Neapolis, de qua post. Domicilium ibi non solum plerisque Principibus & Nobilibus, verum etiam Regis Legato, quem Vice-Regem nominant, variisque Conciliis.
units.tr: The metropolis of the whole kingdom is Naples, of which more later. There reside not only most of the princes and nobles, but also the king's legate, whom they call the Viceroy, and various councils.

units.la: Septem Principales sunt Magistratus, qui Regi comitdere solent: ad dextram quidem I Magnus Comestabilis, II Magnus Admiranus, III Magnus Protonotarius: ad sinistram I Magnus Iustitiarius, II Magnus Cubicularius, III Magnus Cancellarius: ad pedes denique Regis, Magnus Senescalus. Magnus Comestabilis, vulgo Gran Connestabile, principem obtinens locum, generalis est Praefectus Rei Militari, Bellicoque Apparatu. Creatum Rex, por recto Gladio, verbis adloquitur, quae Latine sic sonant: Accipe Sacrosanctum hunc Gladium, quo confectes Hostes Populi mei. Magnus Iustitiarius, Gran Giustiziere, iurisdictionem habet in causis & Civibus & Criminalibus, eique hic parent subjectique sunt omnes Principes, Duces, Marchiones, Comites, Barones, Dynastae, & alii. Vicarius ejus vulgo dicitur Regente della Vicaria, Magnus Admiranus, Gran Ammiraglio, vel Admiraglio, rebus praeest universim Maritimis, mera etiam praeditus iurisdictione. Magnus Cubicularius, qui vernacule Gran Ciamberlano, vel Camerlingo, curam gerit non solum Penetrare Regiae, ejus Lecti & Vestimentorum; verum etiam Vitri, Reditium, Vectigalium, idque genus aliorum. Subest illi nobilis Cubicularium & Thesaurariorum Cohors. Magnus Protonotarius, Gran Protonotario, Chartarum Regiarum est custos, auctoritatem habens creandi Notarios Iudicesque, & Nothos legitimandi. Rex Catholicus dignitatem hanc transtulit ad Cancellariam Regiam. Magnus Cancellarius, Gran Cancelliere litteras scribit Regis Secretiores: Sigillo Magno munit Privilegia ab Rege Subditis concessa Academicos in oculis gerit. Magnus denique Senescalus, vernacule Gran Siniscalco, Maior-Domo, & Maestro di Casa nominatus, Regiam Domum gubernat, procurans quaecumque ad Victum Amictumque Familiae Regiae, ejusque castigans & puniens Delicta.
units.tr: There are seven principal magistrates, who are customarily attendant upon the king: on his right, (1) the Great Constable, (2) the Great Admiral, (3) the Great Protonotary; on his left, (1) the Great Justiciar, (2) the Great Chamberlain, (3) the Great Chancellor; and finally at the king's feet, the Great Seneschal. The Great Constable, in the vernacular Gran Connestabile, holding the chief place, is the general commander of military affairs and the war apparatus. When he is created, the king addresses him with a drawn sword, in words which in Latin run thus: Receive this most sacred sword, with which you shall crush the enemies of my people. The Great Justiciar, Gran Giustiziere, has jurisdiction in civil and criminal causes, and to him all princes, dukes, marquises, counts, barons, dynasts and others render obedience and are subject. His deputy is commonly called the Regent of the Vicaria. The Great Admiral, Gran Ammiraglio, or Admiraglio, presides over maritime affairs in general, and is also endowed with pure jurisdiction. The Great Chamberlain, in the vernacular Gran Ciamberlano or Camerlingo, has charge not only of the royal bedchamber, bed and clothing, but also of the treasury, revenues, taxes and other such things; a noble company of chamberlains and treasurers serves under him. The Great Protonotary, Gran Protonotario, is the keeper of the royal charters, having authority to create notaries and judges and to legitimate bastards. The Catholic King transferred this dignity to the royal chancery. The Great Chancellor, Gran Cancelliere, writes the king's more secret letters and authenticates with the great seal the privileges granted by the king to his subjects; he keeps watch over the academies. Finally the Great Seneschal, in the vernacular Gran Siniscalco, called Majordomo or Maestro di Casa, governs the royal household, providing whatever is needed for the food and clothing of the royal family, and punishing and correcting its offences.

units.la: Supra quidem cap. XXI, quum in genere agerem de Gubernatione Italiae Sacra vel Ecclesiastica, quot in Regno Neapolitano sint Archiepiscopatus, quique & quot sub Singulis Episcopatus, qua potui tunc fide indicavi: sed quia interea temporis ad meas venit manus Libellus, Neapoli impressus, in quo ijdem majore forsan fide sunt perscripti, non gravabor transsumptos inde hoc loco in Lectoris gratiam ponere, quo ordine, quibusque appellatibus sunt concepti; additus a me Latinis:
units.tr: Earlier, in chapter 21, when I was treating the sacred or ecclesiastical government of Italy in general, I stated as well as I could, on the information I then had, how many archbishoprics there are in the Kingdom of Naples and how many bishoprics are subject to each. But since a booklet printed at Naples has since come into my hands, in which these matters are set down perhaps with greater authority, I will not hesitate to set out here, for the reader's benefit, the extracts from it, in the order and under the names in which they are given there, with the Latin forms added by me.

units.tr: The nobility of this kingdom is so numerous and abundant that the pen would scarcely suffice. Of the princes only, dukes, and the rest of lesser dignity and inferior rank: Cassano; Nicastro; Catanzaro; Cerrano; Tropea; Oppido; Gerace; Squillace; Nicotera; Bova; Cosenza. The following bishopric is subject to Cosenza: Martirano. Rossano has no subject bishoprics. The Bishop of Bisignano is subject to no one. San Severino. The following bishopric is subject to it: Umbriatico. San Marco; Belcastro; Strongoli; Isola; Fiorentino; Strangoli; Mileto; Cariati.

units.tr: The bishopric of the island of Lipari is united with that of Patti, and both are subject to the Archbishop of Messina.

units.la: Baronum Nobiliumque Familiarum incredibilis est per totum hoc Regnum numerus: quemadmodum suis parebit locis.
units.tr: The number of barons and noble families throughout this kingdom is incredible, as will be shown in their places.

units.la: Concilia sunt sex: 1. Viceregis, quod Collaterale dicitur, in quo gravissima tractantur totius Regni Negocia, aliaque, quæ eo evocantur. Caput est Vicerex: Adsessores nonnulli Comites. 2. S. Clara, quod ita ab loco, quo cogi solitum, vocatur: Sacrum etiam nominatum. Præses hic & Consiliarij cognitionem habent Causarum omnium, quæ ab Vicaria per Provocationem eo devolvuntur. 3. Vicaria: Hic ab Regente Neapolitano, qui Vicarius est Magni Justitiarij, quatuorque Juris Doctoribus, qui singulis annis renovantur, Ius dicitur, Iustitiaque administratur omnibus Regni Subditis, per Appellationem ab Inferioribus Iudicibus eo venientibus. 4. Summaria: Hic Ratiocinarium est, ibique quæ ad Fiscum & Regni Vectigalia pertinent, curantur. Constat ex Vicario, sex Præsidibus, octo Rationariis, decem, ut vocant, Clericis, & aliis. 5. Admiralitatis: Hic toti Maris Præfecturæ est Domicilium, Iurisdictionem exercet in Nautas & quæcumque ad illos, tam Criminalem, quam Civilem. 6. Monetarium: in quo cognoscitur & civiliter & Criminaliter cum de aliis, tum de Regni totius Monetis, Ponderibus, Mensuris, idque genus aliis. Caput illi Præfectus Rei Monetariæ: cui adiunt Magistri, ut loquuntur, Rationales, Probitatis Monetæ Examinatores, Pensitator, & alij.
units.tr: There are six Councils: (1) the Viceregal council, which is called the Collaterale, in which the most weighty affairs of the whole kingdom are handled, along with other matters referred to it. The head is the Viceroy, with some counsellors who are counts. (2) The S. Clara, so named from the place where it was customarily convened; it is also called the Sacred council. Its president and councillors hear all cases which are brought before it on appeal from the Vicaria. (3) The Vicaria: here justice is declared and administered to all subjects of the kingdom, on appeal from inferior judges who come before it, by the Neapolitan regent, who is the deputy of the Grand Justiciary, together with four doctors of law, who are renewed every year. (4) The Summaria: this is the exchequer, where matters pertaining to the treasury and the revenues of the kingdom are managed. It consists of the vicar, six presidents, eight accountants, ten so-called clerks, and others. (5) The Admiralitatis: here is the seat of the whole maritime prefecture, which exercises jurisdiction over sailors and all things pertaining to them, both criminal and civil. (6) The Monetarium: in which cases are heard, both civil and criminal, concerning the coinage, weights, measures of the whole kingdom, and similar matters. Its head is the Prefect of the Mint, with whom are associated the so-called Masters of Accounts, the examiners of the purity of the coin, the assayer, and others.

units.la: Et hæc de Meridionalhore Italia, id est de Regno Neapolitano universim: Regiones autem, quæ toti huic Parti adscensentur, aliæ, ut quæ dixi cap. xxi. obiter hic repetam, ad Mare sunt Tyrrhenum, aliæ ad Hadriaticum: Tyrrheno eis Silarum adiidet Campania: trans idem flumen Lucania, Calabriaque Inferior & Superior: Hadriatico eis Phiternum adlocati sunt Samnites; trans eundem amnem Apulia utraque vilun-tur & Salentini.
units.tr: And these things concerning Southern Italy, that is, concerning the Kingdom of Naples in general. The regions which are assigned to this whole part, some (as I said in chapter 21, which I will briefly repeat here), lie on the Tyrrhenian Sea, others on the Adriatic. On the Tyrrhenian side, from the river Silarus, lies Campania; beyond the same river, Lucania and Lower and Upper Calabria. On the Adriatic side, from the Phiternum, the Samnites are situated; beyond the same river both Apulias are found, and the Salentines.

units.la: C A M P A N I A (quæ & Καμπανία Straboni, Ptolemæo, aliis: quæque etiam in Antiqua Inscriptione sub Prænestæ in Via publica, qua Albam iter est, cum Umbria, Piceno, Brutiis, Calabria, & Apulia nominatur) plerisque dicta censetur ab florentissima quondam Metropoli Capua, cuius Incolæ Scriptoribus omnibus Campani, quibus originem tribuit Græcam Trogus apud Iustinum libro xx. Nonnulli hic vocatam volunt, quod Campestribus ita pandat locus. Eustathius ad Dionysium ab Campo Civitate derivat: Capuam, ni fallor, designans. Vide & Paullum Diaconum lib. ii. de Reb. gest. Langhardor. cap. xvii.
units.tr: CAMPANIA (which Strabo, Ptolemy and others call Καμπανία [Kampania]; and which also in an ancient inscription on the public road from Praeneste, on the way to Alba, is named together with Umbria, Picenum, the Bruttii, Calabria, and Apulia) is thought by most to be named from the once most flourishing metropolis Capua, whose inhabitants all writers call Campani. Trogus, in Justin book 20, assigns them a Greek origin. Some want the name to come from the level plain (campestres) which the place so spreads out. Eustathius, in his commentary on Dionysius, derives it from the city Campus, meaning Capua, unless I am mistaken. See also Paul the Deacon, book 2 of the Deeds of the Lombards, chapter 17.

units.la: Felix Plinio lib. iii. cap. v. nuncupatur ab felice beataque Regionis amœnitate, de qua paullo post. Antiqua quibusdam dicitur ad differentiam Novæ, quæ Campania Romana vel Lalium. Terra Laboris, vernacule Terra di Lavoro, audit hodie ab Laborinis, qui Capuæ quondam vicini & suburbani, Campi, quorum mentionem facit Plinius lib. iii. nat. histor. cap. v. lib. xvii. cap. iv. & lib. xv. ii. cap. xi. De ipsis ego alibi. Quidā parum solide ab Labore laborant Laborinos trahere: vel quod ad Culturæ Labores idonea sit: vel quod facillime colitur & arctur, Italis illud Lavorare vocantibus Narcitius. Narcissus Medicus apud Sebastianum Munsterum ab Lepore & elegantia autumat sic appellatum.
units.tr: Felix is what Pliny, book 3, chapter 5, calls it, from the happy and blessed pleasantness of the region, of which I shall speak a little later. Some call it Antiqua, to distinguish it from the New Campania, which is the Roman Campania or Latium. Today it is called in the vernacular Terra di Lavoro, from the Laborini, who were once neighbours and suburbs of Capua, the Campi, whom Pliny mentions in book 3, chapter 5, book 17, chapter 4, and book 15, chapter 11. I speak of them elsewhere. Some, without much solidity, labour to derive Laborini from labour: either because the land is suited to the labours of cultivation, or because it is very easily tilled and worked, the Italians calling this lavorare, as Narcitius does. Narcissus the physician, in Sebastian Münster, claims it was so named from charm (lepos) and elegance.

units.la: Fines eius, ut videre est apud Strabonem, Ptolemaeum, & alios, ad Occasum Liris, Latium ad alteram relinquens oram: ad Septemtrionem, Samnitium Montes; qua Ortus est, Silarus Fluvius, Lucaniam hinc dirimens, parteque Agri Samnitium, quos dixi: qua Meridies; Mare Tyrrhenum sive Inferum.
units.tr: Its boundaries, as may be seen in Strabo, Ptolemy and others, are: to the west, the Liris, leaving Latium on the other bank; to the north, the mountains of the Samnites; to the east, where it rises, the river Silarus, separating it from Lucania, and part of the territory of the Samnites I mentioned; to the south, the sea, the Tyrrhenian or Lower Sea.

units.la: Vere Campus est Campania, in quem Natura luxurians ecfudisse videtur largissimo Sinu quidquid usquam est Deliciarum, Amoenitatum, Gaudiorum & Oblectationum. Paradisus vere Italiae. Tam incredibilis ibi rerum est fertilitas. Visuntur spatiosi feracesque Campi: aprici fructiferique Colles, amoena odorataque Nemora, jucundi salubresque Fontes: & quid non Miraculorum? Ea suis locis commemorabimus. Scribit Strabo libro v. Campaniam cum omnium Rerum ad Usus humanos affluentia, tum Amoenitate omnes Italiae partes partibus multis superare. Depingit eandem his coloribus Florus lib. 1. Histor. Rom. cap. xvi. Omnium non modo Italia, sed toto orbe terrarum pulcherrima Campania plaga est. Nil mollius Caelo, nil ubertius Solo, nil hospitalius Mari: denique bis Floribus vernat: ideo Liberi Cereresque Certamen dicitur. Hic illi nobiles Portus, Caieta, Misenus & tepentes Fontibus Baiae: Lucrinus & Avernus quadam Maris otia. Hic amicti Viribus Montes Gaurus, Falernus, Massicus, & pulcerrimus omnium Vesuvius, Aetnae Ignis imitator. Urbes ad Mare Formiae, Cumae, Neapolis, Herculanum: Pompeii, & ipsa caput Urbium Capua, quondam inter tres Maximas Romam Karthaginemque numerata. Dionysius Halic. libro 1. tribus anni cuiuque temporibus, Vere, Aestate, Autumno, Fructus in ea colligi suis oculis vidisse se testatur. Strabo rursus accedat, scriptum se reperisse memorans, quibusdam Campania locis Zeam, Frumenti speciem, iterum eodem anni seri, tertioque Panicum, sed & quarto Olerum eodem in Arvo Semina. Urbium summa hic Nobilitas. De iis universim Propertius: Et te mirantem Thesproto subdita Regno Proxima Misenis Aequora nobilibus.
units.tr: Campania is truly a plain, into which Nature seems to have poured out in lavish abundance, from a most generous bosom, whatever delights, pleasures, joys and enjoyments there are anywhere. It is truly the paradise of Italy. Such incredible fertility of produce is found there. Spacious and fruitful fields are to be seen; sunny and fruitful hills, pleasant and fragrant groves, agreeable and healthful springs; and what of wonders does it not have? We shall mention these in their places. Strabo, in book 5, writes that Campania surpasses all other parts of Italy in many respects, both in the abundance of everything useful for human needs and in its pleasantness. Florus, in book 1 of the Roman History, chapter 16, paints the same region in these colours: Campania is the most beautiful tract not only of Italy, but of the whole world. Nothing is milder than its sky, nothing more fertile than its soil, nothing more hospitable than its sea; in short, it blooms with two springs; hence it is said to be the contest of Liber and Ceres. Here are those noble harbours, Caieta and Misenum, and Baiae warm with springs, and Lucrinus and Avernus, the calm pools of the sea. Here are the mountains clad with vines, Gaurus, Falernus, Massicus, and Vesuvius, the most beautiful of all, an imitator of the fire of Etna. The cities on the coast are Formiae, Cumae, Naples, Herculaneum, Pompeii, and Capua itself, the head of cities, once counted among the three greatest, with Rome and Carthage. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, in book 1, testifies that he had seen with his own eyes the fruits gathered there in each of the three seasons: spring, summer and autumn. Strabo, again, may be added, recording that he had read that in some places of Campania spelt, a kind of grain, is sown twice in the same year, and millet a third time, and even vegetables and seeds a fourth time in the same field. Here is the highest nobility of cities. Propertius speaks of them in general: And you, marvelling, placed under the Thesprotian kingdom, the waters nearest to noble Misenum.

units.la: Intelligit enim per Misenas Nobiles, omnes illas Urbes, quae in tractu Neapolitano erant, Cumas, Baias, Puteolos, & alias: ut Varro per Tarentinas Nobiles, Urbes tractus Tarentini, in quibus Croton & ipsum Tarentum. Circumferuntur etiam de plerisque Campaniae Urbibus hi versus: Castellani Caietani. | Pignatari son da Sessa. Belle Femine son de Mola. | Papari de Castello. Cefali de Patria. | Asinari de Buzolo. Cernati de Ischia. | Fogatori de Prochyta. Gentilezze a Napoli. | Buen Graco fa la Torre. Meglo fa Li Somma. | Castel a mare ne amico, ne compare. Avvico porta pane contico. | Surrente stinge li denti. Massa jaluta & passa. | Sarraini son de Capre. Fico de donna grana. | Marinari de Pasitano. Vogatori de Preano. | Samigothi de Cythara. Taglia borsi di Salerno. | Zeppolan son de Agropoli.
units.tr: For by noble Misenum he means all those cities which were in the Neapolitan district: Cumae, Baiae, Puteoli, and others; just as Varro, by noble Tarentines, means the cities of the Tarentine district, among which are Croton and Tarentum itself. There also circulate about most of the cities of Campania these verses: Castellani of Gaeta. | Pot-makers come from Sessa. Fine women come from Mola. | Simpletons of Castello. Mullets of Patria. | Donkeys of Buzolo. Cernati of Ischia. | Stokers of Procida. Gentility at Naples. | Good grace makes Torre; better, Somma. | Castellammare is neither friend nor kinsman. Avvico brings bread with it. | Sorrento blunts the teeth. Massa, the envious, passes by. | Saracens come from Capri. Figs of Donna Grana. | Sailors of Positano. Oarsmen of Praiano. | Samigothi of Cythara. Purse-cutters of Salerno. | Fritter-makers come from Agropoli.

units.la: Aliorum Encomia brevitati studens praetereo.
units.tr: Passing over the praises of others for the sake of brevity, I say nothing more of them.

units.la: Principatum habuerunt olim in hac Regione varij Populi, de quibus Strabo libro v. Geograph. & Plinius libro iii. cap. v. Opicos, cognomine Ausones, Campaniam tenuisse docet Strabo ex Antiochi sententia Opicos Ausonios fuisse dictos refert Aristoteles lib. vii. Politicor. cap. x. Loca ad Tyrrhenum Mare tenuisse scribens; cui suffragatur Dionysius Halicarnass. libro 1. qui in Latium usque protendit. Opicos & Ausones diversos tradit Polybius apud eundem Strabonem, utrosque addens habitasse juxta Sinum Crateris. Pausanias in Achaicis notat Cumas Opica esse Terra. Videndus & Thucydides libro vi. Οἰνώτροι Italiae Populi etiam Stephano noti. Ausonia testibus Livio & Festo ea pars olim Italiae, in qua Beneventum & Cales: vel, uti scribit Isaacius in Lycophronem, proprie Aurunciorum Terra, inter Campanos & Volscos juxta Mare sita. Aurunciorum, qui Αὐρῆγκαι Graecis scribuntur, meminit etiam Virgilius lib. v i i. Æneid. non uno loco, ubi Servius notat antiquissimos Italiæ Populos; & Græcè Ausones nominari. Mentio eorundem passim apud Livium & Dionysium. Hic sane lib. vi. Auruncos robustum hominum genus, membrorum firmitate præstantes, adipectu truci & feroce, describit. Dixi etiam de Aurunci in Latio. Ab Ausonibus hic non solum universa Italia quondam Ausonia, verum etiam Ausonium Mare dictum refert Strabo libro v. quod idem auctor suo tempore Siculū fuisse appellatum scribit lib. vi. & Tyrrhenum, uti memoriæ prodit Halicarnass. libro i. Opicos Ausones volunt Incertiores apud Strabonem ab Oscis subactos. Osci, o'erui, Latinis Græcisque Scriptoribus satis celebrati. Osci, inquit Paulus Diaconus ad Festum in Masiis, à regione Campania, quæ est Oscos, vocati sunt. Oscos Verrius apud Festum antiquitus Opscos fuisse vocatos notat ex Ennio, cuius hoc Hemistichium libro viii. Annalium, in mea editione:
units.tr: Various peoples once held power in this region. Strabo, in book 5 of his Geography, and Pliny, in book 3, chapter 5, speak of them. Strabo teaches that the Opici, also called Ausones, held Campania; following the opinion of Antiochus, he reports that the Opici were called Ausonian. Aristotle, in book 7, chapter 10 of the Politics, writes that they held places on the Tyrrhenian Sea, and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, in book 1, supports this, extending their territory as far as Latium. Polybius, quoted by the same Strabo, treats the Opici and the Ausones as different peoples, adding that both lived near the Gulf of Crater. Pausanias, in the Achaica, notes that Cumae is the land of the Opici. Thucydides, book 6, should also be consulted. The Oenotrians, peoples of Italy, are known to Stephanus as well. According to Livy and Festus, Ausonia was once the part of Italy in which Beneventum and Cales lay; or, as Isaac writes on Lycophron, it was properly the land of the Aurunci, situated by the sea between the Campanians and the Volsci. Virgil, in book 7 of the Aeneid, mentions the Aurunci, who are called Auruncae by the Greeks, in more than one place, and Servius notes that they were among the most ancient peoples of Italy and are called Ausones in Greek. Mention of them is frequent in Livy and Dionysius. Livy, in book 6, describes the Aurunci as a robust race of men, excelling in the firmness of their limbs, of a savage and fierce appearance. I have also spoken of the Aurunci in my treatment of Latium. Strabo reports that from the Ausones not only all Italy was once called Ausonia, but the sea was also called the Ausonian Sea. The same author, in book 6, writes that in his own time it was called the Sicilian Sea, and, as Halicarnassus records in book 1, the Tyrrhenian. Some less certain writers, cited by Strabo, hold that the Opici Ausones were subdued by the Oscans. The Osci are well known to Latin and Greek writers. Paulus Diaconus, in his note on Festus under Masii, says that the Osci were so called from the region of Campania. Verrius, quoted by Festus, notes that the Oscans were formerly called Opsci, from Ennius, whose half-line from book 8 of the Annals, in my edition, is this:

units.la: De Mæris res gerit Opicus.
units.tr: The Opican wages war concerning the Maeri.

units.la: Oscos sinus etiam cognominibus fuisse distinctos, plerosque autem periisse, præter eos, qui Sidicini dicebantur, ex Strabone facile colligitur lib. v. Notat enim ille Teanum Sidicinum ipso cognomine ostendere, ac ad Sidicinos pertinere: Sidicinos autem esse Oscos Gentem Campaniæ superstitem: atqui tradiderat idem paullo ante universum Gentem Oscorum periisse: Sermonem tamen eorum superfuisse apud Romanos, sed Scenicum & in Mimis. Sic Osci erant, qui Capuenses appellabantur. Servius ad illud Virgilii lib. vii. Æneid Oscorumque manus: Capuenses inquit, dicit, qui antea Ophici appellati sunt, quod illic plurimi abundavere Serpentes. Nam Græce ὄφις dicitur Serpens. Vocabantur fortean & Ausones, si tamen, ut censent nonnulli, Osci ijdem fuerint cum Opicis, de quibus ante, quod Crucis disputandum relinquo. Oscos scribit Strabo profligatos ab Cumanis, de quibus in Cumarum delineatione. Cumanos Plinius antiquos Campaniæ Populos enumerans, Græcos vocat.
units.tr: That the Oscan peoples were also distinguished by surnames, and that most of them perished except those who were called Sidicini, is easily gathered from Strabo, book 5. For he observes that Teanum Sidicinum shows by its very surname that it belonged to the Sidicini, and that the Sidicini were a surviving Oscan people of Campania. Yet the same author had said a little earlier that the whole Oscan nation had perished; their language, however, survived among the Romans, but only in the theatre and in farces. So the Osci were those who were called Capuans. Servius, on the line of Virgil's Aeneid book 7, and the bands of the Oscans, says: "He means the Capuans, who were formerly called Ophici, because very many serpents abounded there; for in Greek ophis means serpent." They were perhaps also called Ausones, if indeed, as some think, the Osci were the same as the Opici mentioned above; but I leave that question for another place to discuss. Strabo writes that the Oscans were routed by the Cumaeans, of whom I shall speak in the description of Cumae. Pliny, listing the ancient peoples of Campania, calls the Cumaeans Greeks.

units.la: Cumanos magna ex parte ab Tuscis, de quibus ante, fuisse pulsos, narrat idem Strabo. Hos Plinius loco à me indicato Umbros specialius appellat. Autumat Strabo Commutationum harum causam fuisse Regionis ubertatem & præstantiam; eiusque desiderio tam varias Gentes provocatas Sedes in ea quæsiisse. Addit idem, Tuscos ibi dominantes, Urbibus xii. eximiis conditis, omnem Principatum Capuæ tribuisse: Tuscos autem, nimia Agrorum felicitate languescentes & enervatos, ab Samnitibus fuisse exactos: Hos autem postremum à Pop. Rom. debellatos.
units.tr: Strabo also relates that the Cumaeans were for the most part driven out by the Tuscans, of whom I spoke above. Pliny, in the passage I have indicated, calls these more specifically Umbrians. Strabo thinks the cause of these shifts of population was the fertility and excellence of the region, and that from desire for it so many different peoples sought homes there. He adds that the Tuscans, who ruled there, founded twelve notable cities and gave the whole primacy to Capua; but that the Tuscans, weakened and enervated by the excessive prosperity of their fields, were expelled by the Samnites, and that these last were finally subdued by the Roman people.

units.la: Habitatur hodie ab multa magnaque Nobilitate. Nam præter Principes, Duces, Marchiones & Comites, quos antea huius Regni commemoravi, in Campania Baronum ingens numerus. Vulgatas dabo Nomenclaturas ex Libello, cuius antea feci mentionem:
units.tr: It is inhabited today by a large and great nobility. For besides the princes, dukes, marquises and counts, whom I have already mentioned for this kingdom, Campania has an immense number of barons. I shall give the common names from the little book of which I made mention before:

units.la: Baroni di
units.tr: Barons of
