units.la: Hæc in genere paucis de Campania: jam nunc specialior me vocat eius Descriptio: quam ab Liris (hic enim communis inter Latium & Campaniam Limes) ostiis au- spicabor.
units.tr: These things, in brief and in general, concern Campania. Now its more detailed description calls me, which I shall begin from the mouths of the Liris, for this is the common boundary between Latium and Campania.

units.la: De Liri supra dixi. Fuisse quondam in eius ora memorant quidem Vrbem Ausoniam, cuius nescio an quis Veterum praeter Livium lib. ix. de quo post, meminerit. Sanfelicius putat æquatam solo.
units.tr: I have spoken of the Liris above. On its shore they do indeed record that there was once a city Ausonia, of which I do not know whether any of the ancients except Livy, in book 9 (of which more later), made mention. Sanfelicius thinks it was levelled with the ground.

units.la: Fuerunt ibidem Vestina & Minturnæ. Livius loco indicato Ausoniam, Vestinam (in quibusdam Codicibus Vescia legitur exaratum. Consule Ambrosium Leonem lib. 11. cap. 111. de Nola Vrbe) & Minturnas uno bello scribit subactas; Minturnas quidem conservatas: Vestinam autem cum Ausonia deletam, idque per Ducum contiguè absentiam. Vestinæ Incolæ Vestini, uni Livio noti. Nam quos nominant Strabo, Plinius, Ptolemæus, ad Mare erant Superum, circa Matrinum Fluvium. Ab Vestinis Campaniæ ad Mare Inferum Vestinus Mons appellatur, circa Minturnas, cuius meminit Hyginus de Limitibus. Inde item Vestinus Saltus Livio libro x. De Minturnis dictum in Latio. Describitur in Agro Minturnensium Straboni Lucus Sacer, Ἀλσος Ἱερον, de quo alibi: ut & de Monte Gauro, qui paullum ab Liris abest Ostio.
units.tr: Vestina and Minturnae were also there. Livy, in the place indicated, writes that Ausonia, Vestina (in some manuscripts the reading is Vescia; consult Ambrosius Leo, book 2, chapter 3, on the city of Nola) and Minturnae were subdued in one war: Minturnae indeed were spared, but Vestina was destroyed along with Ausonia, and this through the absence of the commanders in turn. The inhabitants of Vestina, the Vestini, are known only from Livy. For the Vestini whom Strabo, Pliny and Ptolemy name lived on the Upper Sea, near the River Matrinus. From the Vestini a Vestine Mountain is named on the Lower Sea of Campania, near Minturnae, which Hyginus mentions in his work on boundaries. Likewise there is the Vestine Forest, in Livy, book 10. I have spoken of Minturnae in my treatment of Latium. In the territory of the Minturnenses Strabo describes the Sacred Grove, Alsos Hieron, of which I shall speak elsewhere; likewise of Mount Gaurus, which lies a little way from the mouth of the Liris.

units.la: Iunctre Minturnis ad Gaurum inter illas & Sinuessam Trifanum erat, quod Livius nominat libris ab V.C. viii. & xi.
units.tr: Between Minturnae and Gaurus, and between those places and Sinuessa, lay Trifanum, which Livy mentions in books 8 and 11, ab urbe condita.

units.la: Hinc Sinuessa, Minturnis lxxx. distans stadiis. Sic Latinis, cum aliis, tum Melæ, Antonino, & Itinerariæ Tabulæ dicitur, quæ Σινόεσσα Ptolemæo per o:nā per u, Σέτοσα alia ab hac est in Mediterraneis: nisi forte pro Σέτοσα legendum sit Σινόεσσα. Livius libro x. describit eam juxta Agrum Falernum; addens Græcam fuisse Vrbem, Synopen dictam: deinde ab Colonis Romanis Sinuessam appellatam. Videndus & Plinius. Coloniam etiam nominat Frontinus. Sinuessa Silio libro viii. Tepens vocatur, ad Aquis proculdubio calidis. Quod hodieque Sinuessa nuncupetur, tradunt Marius, Leander, & Hubertus Goltzius, qui oculatus testis totam interiisse affirmat apud Ortelium, tantumque superesse inter eius ruinas exiguum, sed munitissimum metu Piratarum, Opidulum, quod vulgo Rocha de Monte Dragone, pallibus ab Marille. Incolæ Sinuessani Lapidi, quem apud Petrinum Sinuessanum servari notat Apianus:
units.tr: Then comes Sinuessa, eighty stadia from Minturnae. So it is called by the Latins, by Mela, Antoninus and the Itinerary Tables, among others; Ptolemy writes it Sinoessa with an omicron, not an upsilon, and there is another Setossa in the interior, unlike this one, unless perhaps for Setossa we should read Sinoessa. Livy, book 10, places it beside the Falernian field, adding that it was a Greek city called Synope, and afterwards, by Roman colonists, named Sinuessa. Pliny should also be consulted. Frontinus also calls it a colony. Silius, book 8, calls Sinuessa tepid, undoubtedly because of its warm waters. That it is still called Sinuessa today is reported by Marius, Leander and Hubert Goltzius, who, as an eyewitness, affirms in Ortelius that the whole town has perished, and that only a small but very well fortified little town remains among its ruins, for fear of pirates, which is commonly called Rocca di Monte Dragone, and is distant from the Marille by a short distance. The Sinuessani, the inhabitants of Sinuessa, are mentioned in the stone which Apianus notes is preserved at Petrinum Sinuessanum:

units.la: L. PAPPIVS. L. F. TER POLLIO. II. VIR L. PAPPIO. L. F. FAL. PATRI MVLSVM. ET. CRVSTVM COLONIS SINVESSANIS. ET CEDIANIS. OMNIB. MVNVS GLADIATORIVM. COENAM COLONIS. SINVESSANIS. ET PAPIENIS. MONVMENTVM &c.
units.tr: L. PAPPIUS, son of Lucius, of the Terentine tribe, duumvir. To Lucius Pappius, son of Lucius, of the Falerian tribe, his father: a pair of wrestlers, and a gladiatorial show for the colonists of Sinuessa and Cedia, for all of them; a banquet for the colonists of Sinuessa and Papia; a monument, etc.

units.la: Σινόεσσα Polybio apud Strephanum. Hinc Sinuessana Aqua Plinio in Campania: quarum etiam meminerunt Livius lib. xxii. Tacitus lib. xvii. (ubi male in vulgatis Codicibus Sucssane, indicante Lipsio) & Martialis lib. xi. hodie Acque de Monte Dragone, ut vult Ben. Falconius. Sinuessana Prata nonnullis celebrantur, quod Sinuessa Vina Massica & Falerna premerentur. Sinuessani Fundi mentio non semel apud M. Tullium in Epistolis ad Atticum.
units.tr: Σινόεσσα [Sinoessa] in Polybius, as cited by Stephanus. Hence Sinuessana Aqua, in Campania, in Pliny; Livy in book 22, Tacitus in book 17 (where the common manuscripts wrongly read Sucssane, as Lipsius points out), and Martial in book 11 also mention these waters. Today they are Acque de Monte Dragone, as Ben. Falconius holds. Sinuessana Prata are celebrated by some, because Sinuessa produced the Massic and Falernian wines. The Sinuessani Fundi are mentioned more than once by M. Tullius in his Letters to Atticus.

units.la: Ab Sinuessa, quæ, ut dixi, Ptolemæo Σέτοσα, vel, uti legendum forte monebám Σινόεσσα, Suessa Aurunca, alia est Suessa, eadem Σuéssa in Mediterraneis & Septemtrionalior. Binominis plerisque, nunc Suessa Pometia, nunc Suessa Aurunca. Nam Pometinos ab L. Tarquinio Romanorum Rege, Pometia, de qua in Latio, deleta, pulsos in eam commigrasse, tradit Dionysius Halicarnassaeus libro 1. Antiq. Rom. unde Pometia cognominata: sicque Tacito, Floro, Plinio lib. vi. cap. xvi Auctori de VV. Inlustr. cap. viii. aliisque nota. Postea Aurunca vel Aurunearum coepit dici, teste Livio lib. viii. quum Aurunci, ab T. Manlio Cos. Sidicinis opem ferente victi, cum Liberis & Coniugibus eo, Patria deserta, confugissent. Suessa Aurunca meminit idem Livius libro xxxii. Suessa nihilominus simpliciter vocatur cum aliis, tum Plinio libro natur. Histor. iii cap. v. simplexque hodie nomen retinens, Sessa dicitur, posita in Agro Vestino, Situ inaequali, ad Montes Massicum & Calenum, in Via Appia, in Regione amoena & fertili. Ducatus & Episcopatus honore decorata. Nobilitavit eam ortu suo Augustinus Niphus, insignis Philosophus, Scriptis clarus. Inter Volscorum quondam Urbes nominata, Roma ipsa antiquior, tandem Romanis cessit, factaque Colonia circa annum ab V. C. cccxl. ut ex Livio paret. Velleius deductam notat triennio post Luceriam. Pasla deinde multas Clades Bellis Punicis. Colonia censetur in Inscriptione, quae ibi servatur:
units.tr: Distinct from Sinuessa, which, as I have said, is Σέτοσα [Setosa] in Ptolemy (or perhaps, as I suspected, we should read Σινόεσσα [Sinoessa]), is Suessa Aurunca; another Suessa, the same Σούεσσα [Souessa], lies inland and farther north. Many cities had two names, sometimes Suessa Pometia, sometimes Suessa Aurunca. For Dionysius of Halicarnassus, in book 1 of the Roman Antiquities, tells us that the Pometini, driven out by L. Tarquinius, king of the Romans, after Pometia, the town in Latium, was destroyed, migrated to this place, and that is why it was called Pometia. So it is known to Tacitus, Florus, Pliny in book 6, chapter 16, the author of De viris illustribus, chapter 8, and others. Later it began to be called Aurunca or Aurunci, according to Livy in book 8, when the Aurunci, defeated by T. Manlius the consul, who was aided by the Sidicini, fled there with their children and wives, having abandoned their homeland. Livy mentions Suessa Aurunca again in book 32. Yet it is also called simply Suessa, by others and by Pliny in book 3, chapter 5 of the Natural History. Today, keeping the simple name, it is called Sessa. It lies in the Vestine territory, on uneven ground, near the Massic and Caleni mountains, on the Appian Way, in a pleasant and fertile region. It is adorned with the honour of a duchy and a bishopric. Augustinus Niphus, an outstanding philosopher and famous for his writings, ennobled it by his birth. Once numbered among the cities of the Volsci, older than Rome itself, it at last yielded to the Romans, and became a colony about the year 340 from the founding of the city, as Livy makes clear. Velleius notes that it was settled three years after Luceria. Afterwards it suffered many losses in the Punic Wars. It is shown to be a colony by an inscription preserved there:

units.la: C. TITIO. CHRESIMO. AVG. LIB.
units.tr: C. TITIUS CHRESIMUS, freedman of Augustus.

units.la: HVIC. ORDO. DECVRIONVM QVOD. PRO. SALVTE. ET. INDVLGENTIA. IMPERAT ANTONINI. PII. FELICIS. AVG. ET. VOLUNTATE. POPVLI MVNVS. FAMILIAE. GLADIATORIA. EX. PECUNIA. SVA DEDIT. PRIVATVM. SECVNDVM. DIGNITATEM. COLONIAE EDIDERIT. HONOREM. BIS. ILLI. QVOD. QVIS. OPTIMO. EXEMPLO IN. COLONIA. SVESSA. HABVIT. ET. VT. AQVA. DICITVR IN. DOMO. EIVS. FLVERET, &c.
units.tr: To him the council of decurions, because for the safety and indulgence of the emperor Antoninus Pius Felix Augustus, and by the will of the people, gave from its own money a gladiatorial show for the family, and afterwards, in keeping with the dignity of the colony, gave a public honour twice, which anyone would have had in the colony of Suessa with the best example, and as the water is called, flowed in his house, etc.

units.la: Suessanorum etiam meminit Inscriptio, quae ibidem legitur:
units.tr: An inscription read in the same place also mentions the Suessani:

units.la: IMP. CAES. L. SEPTIMO SEVERO. PERTINACI PIO. P. P. SVESSANI
units.tr: To the emperor Caesar Lucius Septimius Severus Pertinax Pius, Father of his Country, the Suessani.

units.la: Suessanorum Municipium Alia, in fragmento Cippi Marmorei, littera palmari:
units.tr: The municipality of the Suessani, called Alia, appears in a fragment of a marble cippus, in letters a palm high:

units.la: RTHICI. FIL. DIVI. NERVAE. NEP. TRAIANI. HADRIANI AVG. PONTIF. MAX TRIB. POT. VI. COS. III VIAM. SVESSANIS MVNICIPIBVS SVA. PEC. FECIT
units.tr: ...son of Divus Nerva's grandson, Trajan Hadrian Augustus, Pontifex Maximus, holding tribunician power for the sixth time, consul for the third time, made the road to the municipalities of the Suessani at his own expense.

units.la: CVRATOR R. P. SVESSANORVM nominatur L. CAESONIVS C. FIL. QVIRINA. LVCILLVS in Basi Marmorea, quae hodie in Vinea Cardinalis Carpensis: translata eo cum duabus aliis ex Vico Corocollo, inter Gabios & Tiburtinos, anno cIↄ IↄXLIX. Inter alia Antiquitatum Monimenta, multae Suessae visuntur Inscriptiones Marmoreae, pulcerrimae & integrae, si quae alibi.
units.tr: L. CAESONIUS C. F. QVIRINA LVCILLVS is named as curator of the public affairs of the Suessani, on a marble base which today is in the vineyard of the Cardinal of Carpi. It was moved there, with two others, from the village of Corocollo, between Gabii and Tibur, in the year 1549. Among other monuments of antiquity, many very fine and intact marble inscriptions of Sessa are to be seen, if any are found elsewhere.

units.la: Octo P. M. ab Sinuessa oppidum se offert in Campo, qui quondam Stellatis, de quo alibi, Carinula. Sic hodie, ut volunt Blondus, Niger & Leander, vocatur: quod Calenum Plinio: Καλλωὶ Strabono. Incolae Καλλωὶ Plutarcho in Hannibale. Ager eius Calenum, nobile Vini genus, ferebat, Plinio laudatum libro xiv. cap.vi. Meminit Horatius, cui Molle Calenum; Vuam etiam Pralo Domitam Caleno laudans. In eiusdem Opidi Agro Aquâ fluere, quæ non secus ac Vinum homines inebriabat, antea, ubi de miraculosis Italiæ Aquis, dixi ex Valerio Maximo.
units.tr: Eight miles from Sinuessa, a town presents itself in the plain, which was once Stellatis, of which I speak elsewhere, and Carinula. Today, as Blondus, Niger and Leander hold, it is called Calenum, which Pliny calls Calenum and Strabo Καλλωὶ [Kalloi]. Its inhabitants are Καλλωὶ [Kalloi] in Plutarch's Life of Hannibal. Its territory produced Calenum, a noted kind of wine praised by Pliny in book 14, chapter 6. Horace mentions it, calling it Molle Calenum (soft Calenum), and praises the grape Vuam as well as the wine Pralo Domitam Caleno (tamed by the Calenian press). I have already said, when discussing the miraculous waters of Italy, citing Valerius Maximus, that in the territory of this town there flowed a water which made men drunk just as wine did.

units.la: Vicinis locis Calatia erat, cuius variis locis Livius, Cæsar, Appianus, Plutarchus in Hannibale, Silius lib.viii. qui parvos ei muros tribuit, alii que meminerunt: Calatia Plinio; Calatie Itinerariæ Tabulæ; Calatia Colonia, Frontino: Gajazo hodie, Leandro & Sanfelicio, qui de hac Urbe in elegante de Campania Libello consulendus. Capua viii. Neapoli xxiv. Italicis distat miliaribus. Antiquum & celebre quondam Opidum. Polybius lib.iii. Caulas enumerans Adventus Hannibalis in Campaniam, hanc quoque addit, ut potirentur nobilibus Urbibus Capua, Atella & Calatia. Extat adhuc magna Veterum Murorum pars, qui ex quadratis Lapidibus sine Calce, vel alio Ferruminationis genere structi. Cognomen dedit Attilia Genti, in qua legitur præter alios A. Atilius Calatinus, bis Consul & Dictator, de quo cum alij, tum Valerius Maximus lib.iiii. cap.vi. & alibi. Hippiam, Philoxeni F. Calatinum, Hospitem & necessarium suum Legeque Calatinorum, quibus vetabatur, ne quisquam Publicum, nisi publico nomine, possideretur, celebrat Epistol.lib.xiii. M. Tullius Cicero. Veteranos, quoque Calilni & Calatia sunt, perducit ad suam sententiam Octavianus apud Ciceronem lib.xvi. ad Atticum, Epist.vii. Multa hic Antiquitatis Monumenta, Veteresque Inscriptiones. Visitur inter alia in Foro Simulacrum Priapi lapideum, paucos ante annos in Ruderibus antiquissimi Templi Veneris repertum. Fuit Calatia, primis Ecclesiæ Crescentis temporibus, Episcopatus titulo insignita; uti ex publicis patet Tabulis, quæ circa annum ccc. confectæ, mentionem Episcopatus Calatini facientes. Inter primos Episcopos fuisse censetur S. S. Ferdinandus Hispanus & Stephanus Italus.
units.tr: Near these places was Calatia, which Livy, Caesar, Appian, Plutarch in his Life of Hannibal, Silius in book 8 (who gives it small walls), and others mention in various places. Pliny calls it Calatia; the Itinerary Table Calatie; Frontinus Calatia Colonia. Today it is Gajazo, according to Leander and Sanfelicius, who should be consulted about this city in the elegant little book on Campania. It is twenty-four Italian miles from Naples and ten from Capua. It was once an ancient and famous town. Polybius in book 3, listing the stratagems of Hannibal's arrival in Campania, adds this as well: that by these means they might take the noble cities of Capua, Atella and Calatia. A large part of the old walls still stands, built of square stones without lime or any other kind of cement. It gave its surname to the Attilia family, in which, among others, is read A. Atilius Calatinus, twice consul and dictator, of whom Valerius Maximus in book 4, chapter 6, and others elsewhere speak. Cicero in his letters, book 13, celebrates Hippias, son of Philoxenus, his Calatinum host and friend, and the law of the Calatinorum, by which it was forbidden that anyone should possess public land except in the public name. In book 16 of his letters to Atticus, letter 7, Octavian brings the veterans of Calilnum and Calatia round to his opinion, as Cicero reports. Many monuments of antiquity and old inscriptions are found here. Among other things, in the forum there is a stone image of Priapus, found a few years ago among the ruins of the very ancient Temple of Venus. Calatia was honoured with the title of a bishopric in the earliest times of the growing Church, as is clear from public records made about the year 300, which mention the Episcopatus Calatini (the bishopric of Calatia). Among its first bishops are counted S. S. Ferdinandus the Spaniard and Stephanus the Italian.

units.la: Ager extendit se huc usque ex Samnitibus Venafranus, de quo alibi. Propinqua sunt illi conjacentque Gallusium (ab obsesso Rogerio, Rogerij Siciliæ Comitis Filio; captoque per Gulielmum Calabriæ Ducem obsesli Filium ipso Obsessore, Innocentio ii. P. M. clarum) Conca, Minianum, Præsentianum & Varianum; hæc uno latere: altero Sellus.
units.tr: Extending as far as this is the territory of Venafrum, among the Samnites, of which I speak elsewhere. Near it and lying beside it are Gallusium (named from the siege of Roger, son of Roger, Count of Sicily, and famous because Gulielmus, Duke of Calabria, captured the son of the besieger himself, in the time of Innocent II, supreme pontiff), Conca, Minianum, Præsentianum and Varianum; these lie on one side, and on the other Sellus.

units.la: Superius ultra Vulturnum est Alliphæ, de qua commodiore loco in Samnitibus. Suessam repeto, cui vicinum est, cum Turri Fracolisa, Teanum: ad alterius in Apulia differentiam, Sidicinum ab Strabone, cui Σιδικινών, Plinioque cognominatum. Teanum Sedicinum, corruptius in Itinerario Tabula. Meminit sæpe Livius. Coloniam eo deduxisse Augustum, Liber indicat Coloniarum. CURATOR R. P. TEANENS. nominatur C. CASONIVS C. F. QVIRINA MACER RVFINIANVS in Basi marmorea, quæ visitur in Vinca Cardinalis Carpensis. Desertum hodie Theano vernale dicitur; Episcopatus nihilominus titulo nobile. Capuæ pæne æquat Strabo, in Via locans Appia.
units.tr: Beyond the Vulturnus, further up, is Alliphæ, which I will discuss in a more suitable place among the Samnites. Returning to Suessa, near it lie Turris Fracolisa and Teanum. To distinguish it from the other in Apulia, Strabo calls it Sidicinum (Σιδικινών), and Pliny gave it the surname. The Itinerary Table, more corruptly, calls it Teanum Sedicinum; Livy often mentions it. Augustus is shown by the Book of Colonies to have settled a colony there. C. CASONIUS C. F. QVIRINA MACER RVFINIANUS is named as curator of the public affairs of the Teanenses on a marble base, which is seen in the vineyard of the Cardinal of Carpi. Today it is called Theano, a deserted place, said to be a spring retreat; nevertheless it is noble with the title of a bishopric. Strabo, placing it on the Appian Way, almost equals it with Capua.

units.la: Ultra Cafilinum fluvium Calvi sunt, Opidum Episcopatus dignitate superbiens: Cales, numero multitudinis, Virgilio lib. vii. Æneidos: Καλὴς, Ptolemæo; Calis, Frontino, ut & Itinerariæ Tabulæ, cui Cale auferendi calu. Auctor canitur ab Silio lib.viii. Calais, Boreæ F. post Argonautarum reditum in hæc loca profectus. Livius lib.viii. & Festus Ausones primos Calium Incolas fuisse tradunt. Coloniam eo deductam anno cccccxx. scribit eodem libro Livius, qui eiusdem meminit lib.xxvii. & xxix. Cicero in Rullum & Frontinus Municipium vocant.
units.tr: Beyond the river Clanius are Calvi, a town proud of the dignity of a bishopric: Cales (in Virgil, book 7 of the Aeneid, because of the number of inhabitants); Καλὴς [Kales] in Ptolemy; Calis in Frontinus, as in the Itinerary Tables, to which Cale is to be preferred. Its founder is sung by Silius in book 8: Calais, son of Boreas, who came to these parts after the return of the Argonauts. Livy in book 8, and Festus, say that the Ausones were the first inhabitants of Calium. Livy writes in the same book that a colony was settled there in the year 420, and he mentions it again in books 27 and 29. Cicero against Rullus and Frontinus call it a Municipium.

units.la: Sequitur Caianellum, quod Calliculam Veteribus dictum ait Leander. Callicula Jugi meminit Livius lib.xxii. circa Cafilinum: nescio an idem cum Gallicano Monte, qui & Masficus & Gaurus.
units.tr: Next comes Caianellum, which Leander says was called Calliculam by the ancients. Livy in book 22 mentions Callicula Jugi near Casilinum; I do not know whether it is the same as the Gallicanus mountain, which is also called Massicus and Gaurus.

units.la: Fuit haud procul inde Casilinum, Latinis & Itinerariæ Tabulæ: Καστλινον Strabono, Appiano, Plutarcho: Baσιλινας corrupte apud Zonaram. Urbs haud procul Vulturni Ostio. Meminit sæpe Livius, nominatim lib.xxxiii. duobusque seq. Ductus eo fuit errore, ibique conclusus Hannibal, quum Casinum cogitaret; sedente tunc ad Turrim Fracolisam Fabio Maximo. Nota est Historia. Legendi præter alios Livius lib.xxii. & Plutarchus in Hannibale. Coloniam ab M. Antonio deductam, tradit Cicero Philippica ii. Auctore Festo, Vetus fuit Præfectura. Hodie, ut volunt Sanfelicius & Leander Albertus, Cassellunzo.
units.tr: Not far from there was Casilinum, in Latin and in the Itinerary Table; Καστλινον [Kastlinon] in Strabo, Appian and Plutarch; Basilinas [Βασιλινας] corruptly in Zonaras. It was a city not far from the mouth of the Vulturnus. Livy often mentions it, especially in book 33 and the two following. Hannibal was led there by error and shut in there, when he intended to go to Casinum, while Fabius Maximus sat at Turris Fracolisa. The story is well known. Among others, Livy in book 22 and Plutarch in his Life of Hannibal should be read. Cicero, in the second Philippic, says it was made a colony by M. Antonius. According to Festus, it was formerly a prefecture. Today, as Sanfelicius and Leander Albertus hold, it is called Cassellunzo.

units.la: Vlterius
units.tr: Further on

units.la: Viterus ad Oltia Vulturni Flumnis finiltra, Vulturnum fuit Opidum. Sic Livio, Plinio, Mela, Itineraria Tabula, alioque Latinis dicitur: quod οὐόλτυρνον Dionysio, Strabone & Ptolemæo. Hodie Castello al Mar di Beturno, ad differentiam Castelli Volturni, ultra Neapolim. Colonia Frontino Liviōque libro xxxiv. Capua jam nemo oserre se delinquendum: Veterem dico, nullum non Latinorum Scriptorum, ut le acceptat Talulcinotam. Sic Καπύα Stephano: Καπύη Ptolemæo, Dionysio Halicarnasseo, Appiano: Campania Ides Virgilio lib. x. Quod Vulturnum antea, fuerit dicta, no ait Livius lib. iv. & Plutarchus in Hannibale. Sueposlis aliquando vocata fuisse legitur apud Sigonium. Dicta autem Capua, vel ab Capy Aneæ Socio, ut centent Virgilius lib. x. Æn. & ejus Servius, Lucanus libro ii. Silius Italicus lib. ii. Dionysius lib. i. accedente & Inscriptione, quæ apud Suetonium in Cæsare cap. lxxxi. Livius lib. xl v. Capua Samnitum Ducum vocat, vel ab Agro Campestri, ut putant Livius libro iii. Strabo, Plinius, Festus. Nonnulli se appellatam volunt, quod Caput et ex alius xi. Urbs quæ ab Etruscis constituta. Legendus Strabo libro v. Quondam ab Capue dirivant, qui prima Tuscorum lingua Capys dicebatur. Alii, maiores quos Diodorus, ab Capuaticate trahunt & abundantia rerum omnium, quam loquuntur varia ejus apud Ciceronem, ii. in Rullum, quum diffluaderet ne ex Præfectura in Coloniam mutaretur, Encomia: Subsidium Belli, Fundamentum Vectigalium, Herreum Legionum, Solatium Annona. Splendor ejus, Amplitudo & Magnificentia ab omnibus summopere passim celebratur. Non dicam omnia. Capua, ait Florus libro i. Hist. Rom. cap. xvi. & ipsa Caput Urbium, quondam inter tres maximas Romam Carthaginemque numerata. Altera Karthago Capua, inquit Silius libro vi. Altera Roma, Ausonius. Sic Magio apud Livium libro xxiii. dicit Capuam non Campanæ modo, sed Italiæ Caput, post addictam Cannensi pugna Reipublicæ Romanorum. Livius omnium Urbium Italiæ secundam Romam principem nominat libro, quem dixi. Alii apud alios Nimia Felicitas Intolentiæ sæpe Mater. Capua Fortunam nacta obsequentissimam, Arrogantiæ Protervitasque vitio corrupti laborare. Testatur M. Tullius Agraria ii. contra Rullum Campanos semper superbos fuisse bonitate Agrorum & Fructuum magnitudine, Urbis salubritate & pulcritudine, ornatamque ex eadem Copia, rerumque omnium adfluentia Adrogantiam, quæ alterum Urbis Romæ Consulem e Capua postulavit: eamque Luxuriem natam, quæ ipsum Hannibalem, Armis invictum, voluptate vicit & enervavit. Legendi præter alios Livius libro xxxi, Valerius Maximus lib. ix. cap. i. Silius Italicus libro xv. copiosissime, Auctor de VV. Illustr. cap. xlii. Pergens Cicero eleganter Capuam appellat Domicilium Superbiæ & Sedem Luxuriæ. Verum nimis illud apud Silium libro viii.
units.tr: Liternum, at the mouth of the river Volturnus on the left bank, was a town called Vulturnum. Livy, Pliny, Mela, the Itinerary Table and other Latin writers use this name, while Dionysius, Strabo and Ptolemy write it in Greek as [Οὐόλτυρνον]. Today it is Castello al Mar di Beturno, to distinguish it from Castello Volturno, beyond Naples. Frontinus and Livy in book 34 call it a Colonia. No one now dares to say Capua is wrongly written; I mean the old form, which every Latin writer uses, as Talucinus also accepts. Stephanus writes Καπύα [Kapya], while Ptolemy, Dionysius of Halicarnassus and Appian write Καπύη [Kapyē]. Virgil in book 10 calls it Campania Ides. Livy in book 4 and Plutarch in his life of Hannibal say it was formerly called Vulturnum. It is read in Sigonius that it was sometimes called Sueposlis. It was called Capua either after Capys, the companion of Aeneas, as Virgil in book 10 of the Aeneid and his commentator Servius think, and as Lucan in book 2, Silius Italicus in book 2 and Dionysius in book 1 relate, with support also from the inscription that Suetonius gives in his life of Caesar, chapter 81; or, as Livy in book 45 calls it, Capua of the Samnite leaders; or after the open countryside (Ager Campestris), as Livy in book 3, Strabo, Pliny and Festus think. Some want it named because it was the head of the other cities; Livy in book 11 calls it a city founded by the Etruscans. Read Strabo in book 5. Some derive it from Capys, which in the Tuscan language was the word for a head. Others, including Diodorus, derive it from the abundance of all good things, which Cicero in the second speech against Rullus calls its various praises, when he argued against changing it from a prefecture into a colony: support of war, foundation of revenues, nursery of legions, solace of the grain supply. Its splendour, greatness and magnificence are everywhere celebrated by all. I will not mention everything. Capua, says Florus in book 1 of his Roman History, chapter 16, was itself the head of cities, once counted among the three greatest, Rome, Carthage and Capua. Another Carthage is Capua, says Silius in book 6. Another Rome, says Ausonius. So Magius in Livy, book 23, says that Capua was the head not only of Campania but of all Italy, after the Roman state had been given over at Cannae. Livy in the book I mentioned calls Capua the second city of all Italy after Rome. Others among other writers say that excessive good fortune is often the mother of insolence. Capua, having obtained most obedient fortune, suffered from arrogance and wantonness that had corrupted it. Marcus Tullius in the second speech on the agrarian law against Rullus testifies that the Campanians were always proud, from the goodness of their fields, the size of their crops, the healthiness and beauty of their city, and from the same abundance and flow of everything; this pride demanded a consul of Rome from Capua; and that luxury, born of this, conquered and enervated Hannibal himself, unconquered in arms, by pleasure. Read, among others, Livy in book 31, Valerius Maximus book 9 chapter 1, Silius Italicus book 15, who is very full, and the author of On Illustrious Men, chapter 42. Cicero elegantly calls Capua, in his continuing discourse, the home of pride and the seat of luxury. But more true is what Silius says in book 8:

units.la: Capua hen rebus servare serenis- Inconsulta modum, & parvo perritura tumore.
units.tr: Capua, unable to keep measure in serene circumstances, and destined to perish from a small swelling.

units.la: Tam enim olim potens & superba tandem ab Romanis, quorum Imperij fuerat æmula, post bellum Punicum ii. Præfectura conditionem accepit, scribente Livio libro xxvi. qui de Capua obsidione, obsessorumque Fortitudine & Magnanimitate, quæ Urbi Magnæ Fortuna fuerit sequuta, omnino legendus. Præfectura manet ad Consulatum utque C. Julij Cæsaris, qui cos. cum M. Calpurnio Bibulo anno 1xcxcv. Coloniam eo deduxit, ut videre est apud Paterculum, Suetonium in Cæsare cap. xx. & Frontinum de Coloniis, cui Capua Julia Felix dicitur. Ut Coloniæ meminerunt Cicero ii. in Rullum, & ii. Philippica, Suetonius in Cæsare cap. lxxxi. & in Octaviano cap. iv. Resurgens postea auspicis Imperatorum reflorere nonnihil corpit sub P. R. porectate, donec ab Genserico Vandalorum Rege capta subversaque, ab Ostrogothis dem occupata: atque hus pulsus ab Narsete restaurata; tandem post annos fere centum ab Langobardis iterum excita sunt atque deleta. Stantem potenter, cadentemque miserabiliter, canit fere magnus Poeta Ausonius Magnus: Nec Capuam Pelago, Cultuque, Pennaque potentem Deliciis, Opibus, Famaque priore silebo: Fortuna variante et eo, quæ fida secundis Nescivit fereque Medium, nunc subdita Romæ, Æmula tunc Fidei memor, an infida Senatum
units.tr: For Capua, once so powerful and proud, was at last reduced by the Romans, whose rival in empire she had been, to the status of a prefecture after the Second Punic War. Livy, book 26, who describes the siege of Capua and the courage and magnanimity of the besieged, which followed the great fortune of the city, should be read in full. The prefecture lasted until the consulship of Gaius Julius Caesar, who was consul with Marcus Calpurnius Bibulus in the year 695 of the city, and who established a colony there, as can be seen in Paterculus, Suetonius in his life of Caesar, chapter 20, and Frontinus on colonies, where it is called Capua Julia Felix. Cicero in the second speech against Rullus and in the second Philippic, and Suetonius in his life of Caesar, chapter 81, and in his life of Augustus, chapter 4, mention it as a colony. Later, rising again under the auspices of the emperors, it began to flourish somewhat under the power of the Roman people, until it was taken and overthrown by Genseric, king of the Vandals, then occupied by the Ostrogoths; when they were driven out, it was restored by Narses; but about a hundred years later it was again stormed and destroyed by the Lombards. The great poet Ausonius sings of it, standing powerfully and falling miserably: "Nor will I pass over in silence Capua, powerful in the sea, in culture, and in wings, in delights, in wealth and in her former fame: fortune changing, she who was faithful to success and almost never knew the middle way, now subject to Rome, then a rival, mindful of her faith, or faithless, hesitating whether to scorn or to cherish the Senate. Capua, proud of her curule magistrates, dared to challenge the Roman people with her own auspices, and with one of her own Consuls aimed to raise the empire of the divided world; she also drove back Rome, again her mistress and mother of the wide world, warring with the Roman..."

units.la: Speneret Sperneret, an coleret, dubitans: sperare CurulesCampanus ausa auspicijs: unoque suorumConjiciat: ut Imperium divisi attollerent Orbis.Sigtn etiam Iterum Dominam, Latyque ParentemAd[?]ertus bello, Ducibus non freta Togatis;Parrhabalu juratz armis: deceptaque in HostisSere[?]rtum demens specie transfivit heredi:Moxque in occasum vitiis communibus actlCorrumperet Poeni Luxu, Campania Fastu,(Ut[?] manquam: flabilem fortia superbia Sedem)Nam potens opibusque valens, Roma altera quondam,Cumera quae paribus petiit fastigia comis,Ostatum rejecta locum aux ponc tuetur.
units.tr: ...and the Carthaginian general, not trusting the togaed leaders, swore an oath to Hannibal with arms, and, deceived by the appearance of an enemy, crossed over to the heir in mad fashion; and soon, in the common vices of the west, Capua was corrupted by the Carthaginian with luxury, Campania with pride; (as fierce pride is a fickle seat of strength) for powerful in wealth and strong, she, once another Rome, who had sought the heights of the Consuls on equal terms, now holds her place beneath Rome's feet, rejected as a stranger.

units.la: Cautas etiam Interitus tantae Urbis paucis indicat Silius Italicus:
units.tr: Silius Italicus also indicates briefly the causes of the ruin of so great a city:

units.la: Luxus & infamis nutrita Ignavia Lustris,Consumptusque Pudor peccando, unisque relictusDira quid probrosus Honor, laceravit hiantemDelphin Capuam, ac resolutam Legibus UrbemProximaque exitio truculenta superbia semper.Nec Vitiis deerant vires: non largior ullaAnsuta Populo (sic tum Fortuna favebat)Aurique Argentique modus: madefacta venenoManibus Vestis: medioque dierumRegales Epulae: atque ortu Convivia SolisDeprensa: & nulla macula non inlita Vita:Tum Populo savi Patres: Plebesque SenatusIncedia lucra: &, conlidens dissona corda, Seditio: sedenum interea temeraria PubesDelicta angebat: pollutior ipsa Senectus;
units.tr: Luxury, and disgraceful idleness fostered by brothels, and shame used up by sinning, and honour left alone, though infamous, has torn gaping Capua, and the city dissolved from its laws, and fierce pride always near to ruin. Nor were the vices lacking in strength: no more lavish dress was ever sewn for the people (fortune then favoured them), and no limit on gold and silver; garments soaked in poison for the hands; royal feasts at midday; banquets begun at sunrise, caught out; and life smeared with every stain. Then the wise fathers were cruel to the people, and the common people to the senate; greedy profits, and sedition, quarrelling hearts, rash in discord; meanwhile the reckless youth hurt the sins of the older people; old age itself was more defiled.

units.la: & quae ibi alia. Vituntur hodie eius altero ab Nova Capua lapide peringentes Ruinae, juxta Templum D. Mariae Gratiarum. Exstant Portae semirutae, Amphitheatrum, quod aliquo modo describit Laurentius Schraderus in Italiae Monumentis, immensa Porticuum, Thermarum, et Aedificiorumque Publicorum rudera: praeterea longa vallaque Aquarum Receptacula subterranea & Castella, quae, qualis & quanta fuerit antiqua Urbs, abunde restantur. Capitoly Capuam mentio apud Suetonium in Tiberii Principis Vita cap. XL. Aurea, Argentea, Aerea Numismata, Gemmae, Marmora, aliaque summi Luxus indicia quotidie ab Incolis effodiuntur. Ex Antiquae autem dirutae Ruinis Novae erpi exstrui, feliciterque crescere, quam conspicere jam nunc est adiitam sinistrae Vulturni ripae, duodecimo ab Mari lapide, in planicie, satis magnificam, commode habitatam, sed infrequentius; stratam Silicibus, Plateas habentem amplas & rectas, aliaque Aedificia. Adluit eam ab Ortu & Septentrione Vulturnus, indeque in Oceanum reflectitur. Pons est supra amnem ex lapide insignis. Templum S. Benedicti dicatum fuisse creditur Isidi. Regitur ipsidem Magistratibus, eademque Resp. forma, qua Neapolis. Civium Mores superbia ab Antiquis non differunt. Eius Mannia Conradus, Friderici I. Imp. F. dejecit, Urbemque directam calamitate affecit magni. Causam exponit Blondus libro XVI. Hist. Aliam deinde non minorem cladem sustinuit sub Alexandro VI. P. M. Videndus Sabellicus. Episcopatum Capuae Novae evexit in Archiepiscopatum Joannes XIV. P. M. quum Othoni II. Imper. Aug. Coronam imponeret. Legendi Blondus & Platina. Huic qui suffragentur, alibi a me dictum. Capuam Novam ortu suo nobilitarunt Raimundus, Praedicatorum Generalis Magister XXXII. & Ioannes Antonius Campanus, Scriptis clari. Multae ibi nobiles Familiae, quae vulgo: Antiquam, d'Arienzo, d'Azzia, di Capua, d'Iboli, di Falco, Feramosca, Ferrara, Gattazzi, Gallo, Dinganno, delli Leoni, Lanza, Marchesi, Maggio, Olimpio, Pantaleani, Pelegrini, Pettonato, di Rinaldo, Rossi, Semifacho, di Tomase, delle Vigne, Vitelli; & aliae. Post Urbem Romanam nullo in loco plures Inscriptiones, sed vetustate admodum consumtae. Campanos quondam Osos fuisse nuncupatos, notat Servius ad lib. VII. Æ neid. Virgil. Laudem olim mercebantur Campani, (nam & hic Capuæ Incolæ audiunt) Fagitas, teste Suetonio in Augusto cap. xcvIII. & in Caligula cap. xvIII.
units.tr: And other things there. Today there are still remains of that ancient city, lying a stone's throw from New Capua, beside the church of St Mary of the Graces. There survive half-ruined gates, an amphitheatre, which Laurentius Schraderus describes to some extent in his Monuments of Italy, the vast ruins of colonnades, baths and public buildings; besides these, long and wide underground water reservoirs and castles, which sufficiently show what and how great the ancient city was. Suetonius mentions Capua in the life of the emperor Tiberius, chapter 40. Gold, silver and bronze coins, gems, marbles and other signs of the greatest luxury are dug up daily by the inhabitants. New Capua, rising from the ruins of the old city and happily growing, can now be seen on the left bank of the Volturnus, twelve miles from the sea, on a plain; it is fairly magnificent, conveniently inhabited, but rather thinly; paved with flints, with broad and straight streets, and other buildings. The Volturnus washes it on the east and north, and then turns back into the sea. There is a notable stone bridge over the river. The temple of St Benedict is believed to have been dedicated to Isis. It is governed by its own magistrates, with the same form of government as Naples. The manners of its citizens do not differ from those of the ancients in pride. Conrad, son of the emperor Frederick I, cast down its walls and inflicted great disaster on the city; Blondus in book 16 of his History explains the cause. Then it suffered another no less grievous disaster under Alexander VI, Supreme Pontiff; see Sabellicus. Pope John XIV raised the bishopric of New Capua to an archbishopric when he placed the crown on Otto II, august emperor. Read Blondus and Platina. Those who favour this I have discussed elsewhere. New Capua was made famous by its natives Raimundus, thirty-second Master General of the Preachers, and Giovanni Antonio Campano, famous for his writings. Many noble families are there, commonly called: Antiqua, d'Arienzo, d'Azzia, di Capua, d'Iboli, di Falco, Feramosca, Ferrara, Gattazzi, Gallo, Dinganno, delli Leoni, Lanza, Marchesi, Maggio, Olimpio, Pantaleani, Pellegrini, Pettonato, di Rinaldo, Rossi, Semifacho, di Tomase, delle Vigne, Vitelli; and others. After the city of Rome there is no place with more inscriptions, but they are very much worn by age. Servius on book 7 of Virgil's Aeneid notes that the Campanians were once called Osci. The Campanians of old, as Suetonius testifies in his life of Augustus, chapter 98, and in his life of Caligula, chapter 18, used to be paid for praise; for the people of Capua too are still hearing this.

units.la: Orta ab Capua Milliaribus, quis Campus Stellatis, Agriqué Leborini percurrun-tur, Vrbs nova vocatur Anversa, Veteris Atellæ ruinis ædificata. Atella Livio multo loco, Silio lib.xii. alijqueaut & Itinerariæ Tabulæ, Avia Strabon & Ptolemæo. Sanctelius Atellam tuisse censet, ubi hodie S. Arpino. Incolæ Atellani Plinio in Prima Regione. Meminit aliquoties Livius, præcipue libro xxvii, ubi Atellanos ab Senatu Calatiam migrare jussos scribit. Abeca Atellanæ fabulæ quales exponunt Livius lib.vii. Varro, Agellius, Macrobius, Iuvenalis, & alij. Earum Scriptores Ciceronis ævo, L. Pomponius Bononiensis. In collapsa Vrbe veligus Robertus Guiscardus Normannorum Dux (vel, ut Pandulphus Collenutius lib. iii. Hist. appellat, Ranno, Tristani Normanni Successor) quum Capuæ hunc, inde Neapolis Imperio imminerent, Castra munivisse, Novæque Vrbis nomen potuisse tradi-tur: Anversaque ab re, uti adversus illa Oppida exstructam, appellasse. Hodie nonnulla immutatione Anversa vel Aversa dicitur. Diruta usque ad fundamenta Karolus I. Neapolis Rex, ob Reburia Gentis rebellionem, tèste Collenutio lib.v. Describit hanc Vrbem P. Iovius libro Hist. iv. Paucis etiam Baptista Mantuanus, his verbis:
units.tr: Starting from Capua, after a distance of some miles, one passes through the Campus Stellatis and the Leborine fields to reach the new town called Aversa, built from the ruins of old Atella. Atella is mentioned by Livy in many places, by Silius in book 12, and by others, and by the Itinerary Tables; Strabo and Ptolemy call it Avia. Sanctelius thinks Atella was where San Arpino stands today. Pliny places the people of Atella in the First Region. Livy mentions it several times, especially in book 27, where he writes that the Atellans were ordered by the Senate to migrate to Calatia. What the Atellan farces were like is described by Livy in book 7, by Varro, Gellius, Macrobius, Juvenal and others. Their writers in Cicero's time included L. Pomponius of Bologna. When the town had fallen into ruin, Robert Guiscard, Duke of the Normans (or, as Pandulph Collenuccio calls him in book 3 of his History, Ranno, successor of Tristan the Norman), pitched camp there while Capua and then Naples were threatened by his power. He is said to have given the new town its name, and to have called it Aversa because it was built against those other towns. Today it is called Anversa or Aversa, with a slight change in spelling. Charles I, King of Naples, razed it to the ground because of the rebellion of the Reburrian people, as Collenuccio reports in book 5. P. Giovio describes this town in book 4 of his History, and Baptista Mantuanus does so briefly in these words:

units.la: Appula Campano tellus ubi jungitur Agro,
units.tr: Where the Apulian land joins the Campanian field,

units.la: Est locus, Atellæ retinens cognomina prisca:
units.tr: There is a place that keeps the old name of Atella,

units.la: Sive Atella vetus, nam fors mutata locorum
units.tr: Whether it is old Atella, for perhaps the places have changed

units.la: Prisca loca, dedit & prisci nova nomina terris.
units.tr: And the old sites have given new names to the old lands.

units.la: Urbs in colle sedet validis circumdata muris,
units.tr: The town sits on a hill, surrounded by strong walls,

units.la: Civefrequens, Pecorum locuples, gleba ubere dives.
units.tr: Crowded with citizens, rich in flocks, fertile in its rich soil.

units.la: Episcopus gaudet dignitate. Templum habet Cathedrale satis amplum: huic olim Theatrum ingens, cuius nihil nunc reliquum. Nobiles ibi Familiæ, quæ sequuntur: Altimari | Marco | Silvestri Cutinaro | Mauro | Simonelli Gargani | Pacifici | Tusi Grimaldi | Ricciardo | Della Valle Landolfi | Scaglioni
units.tr: The bishop enjoys the dignity of his office. The cathedral church is rather large. Once there was a huge theatre here, of which nothing now remains. Noble families living there include the following: Altimari, Marco, Silvestri, Cutinaro, Mauro, Simonelli, Gargani, Pacifici, Tusi, Grimaldi, Ricciardo, Della Valle, Landolfi, Scaglioni.

units.la: Non procul Atella Septemtrionem versus Avella fuit, Silio Italico nota lib.viii. Ἀτέλλα Strabonis libro v. & Ptolemæo; Avellanum Servio ad ii. Georgic. Incolæ Plinio Avellani, qui alij ab Abellinatibus ejusdem Campaniæ, vel Avellinatibus Lucanæ Populis, quemadmodum aliud Avellinum Ἀβέλλινον, ab Avella: illud enim Ptolemæo Hirpinorum in Aprutio Opidum: hodie Avellino. In libro Fisci Pontifici Vrbs nomen Frietal Avellinus dicitur; ut Abellini in Hirpinis Avellinensis. Macrobius Avellanas Nuces ab hac Vrbe nomen habere censet. Spectat eo fortean Virgilius lib.vii. Æneidos:
units.tr: Not far from Atella, to the north, was Avella, known from Silius Italicus, book 8. Strabo, book 5, and Ptolemy call it Ἀτέλλα. Servius on Georgics 2 calls it Avellanum. Pliny calls its people Avellani; others call them Abellinates of the same Campania, or Avellinates of the Lucanian peoples, just as there is another Avellinum, Ἀβέλλινον, named after Avella. That one, according to Ptolemy, was a town of the Hirpini in Apulia, and is today Avellino. In the Book of the Papal Treasury the town is called Frietal Avellinus, just as the Abellini among the Hirpini are called Avellinenses. Macrobius thinks that the Avellan nuts take their name from this town. Perhaps Virgil refers to it in book 7 of the Aeneid:

units.la: Et quæ malifera despectant mœnia Abellæ.
units.tr: And the walls of Abella, rich in apples, look down.

units.la: In Vulgatis hæc nomen legitur Bellæ, probante etiam & interpretante Scripturam hanc, sed fraudine Servio. Patria hæc Ambrosio Leoni, qui de ea tres scripsit libros, tradens etiam Prisci Græcis Ἀέλλαι ab venti vertigine, hunc tractum perflante, dictam; à posteris Latinis vero Binsertum.
units.tr: In the printed editions this name is read as Bellae, which the Vulgate translator also approves and explains as the Scripture, but this is due to a mistake by Servius. This is the homeland of Ambrogio Leone, who wrote three books about it. He also reports that the Greeks of old called it Αἴελλαι from the whirling of the wind that blows across this tract, and that later Latins called it Binsertum.

units.la: Juxta Turrim Patriæ, vulgo Torre del Patria, ubi cum Turre unica tantum est Taberna diversoria, aliquotque Piscatorum Casæ Linternı, Veteris urbis, superstes memoria, situ peramæno & jucundo: Linternum Silio & Pomponio Melæ: Liternum Plinio, aliis, ut & Itinerariæ Tabulæ: Λιτέρνον Ptolemæo. Colonus Livio lib.xxxiv. & Frontino: Præfecturam aliquando fuisse, eodem jure quo Vulturnum, referit Festus. P. Cornelium Scipionem Africanum huc in voluntarium exsilium concessisse, notare præter alios Livius, Plutarchus, Strabo. Scribitur item quibusdam apud Livium libro xxxviii. ibidem sepultus: quod etiam videtur non obscure colligi ex Strabonis v. Valerio Maximo libro vi. cap. de Ingratis, Seneca Epistol. lxxxvii. ad Lucilium, Testatur Plinius libro xvi. capite ultimo sua ætate in Liternino durasse Prioris Africani manu sa. tas Olivas; item Myrtum ejusdem in Luco conspicuæ magnitudinis: & sub ea Specum fuisse dicit, in quo Manes ejus custodire Draco ferebatur. Ab eo Linterna Palus Silio libro vii: hodie Lago della Patria. Dixi alibi. Linternum Fluvij nomen hoc tractu Straboni & Livio libro xxxii: oppidum vulgo Linternum Ciceronis in Epistolis ad Atticum, Prædium fortean in suburbicario Linterni Agro. Meminit Plinius libro xiiii cap.iiii.
units.tr: Near the Tower of the Fatherland, commonly called Torre del Patria, where there is only one tavern with lodgings, and a few fishermen's houses, lies the memory of the old town of Linternum, in a very pleasant and agreeable situation. Silius and Pomponius Mela call it Linternum; Pliny and others call it Liternum, as do the Itinerary Tables; Ptolemy gives it as Λιτέρνον. Livy in book 34 and Frontinus call it a colony. Festus reports that it was at one time a prefecture, under the same law as Volturnum. That P. Cornelius Scipio Africanus retired here into voluntary exile is noted, among others, by Livy, Plutarch and Strabo. Some write, as Livy does in book 38, that he was buried here; this also seems to be clearly inferred from Strabo, book 5, from Valerius Maximus, book 6, chapter on the ungrateful, and from Seneca, Letter 87 to Lucilius. Pliny, in book 16, last chapter, testifies that in his own day olive trees planted by the hand of the elder Africanus were still surviving at Liternum, as was a myrtle of his in the grove of remarkable size; and he says that beneath it was a cave in which a dragon was said to guard his shade. From him comes the Linterna Palus of Silius, book 7; today it is the Lago della Patria. I have written about this elsewhere. Linternum is the name of a river in this district for Strabo and for Livy, book 32; it is also the name of a town, commonly called Linternum, in Cicero's Letters to Atticus, perhaps an estate in the suburban territory of Linternum. Pliny mentions it in book 14, chapter 4.

units.la: Hinc Itinere juxta Mare Millibus passuum quinque usque Cumas, Villa fuit Servilij Vaccæ, Hominis nobilis & opulenti, sed ignavi & lethargi: de quo Seneca Epistola lv.
units.tr: From here, along the coast, five miles brings you to Cumae. There was a villa here of Servilius Vacca, a man of noble birth and wealth, but idle and lethargic; Seneca speaks of him in Letter 55.

units.la: Sequitur inde locus antiquissimæ Urbis Cumarum. Cumæ Livio, Tacito, Silio Plinio, Solino, Melæ, Antonino, Itinerariæ Tabulæ, & quibus non Latinorum? Κύμαι Straboni, Ptolemæo, Dionysio, aliisque Græcis: Cumæa Urbs Virgilio libro iii. Conditores ejus Cumaei Euboici; qui Ducibus Hippocle & Megasthene, cum Chalcidensibus in Italiam venerunt, testibus Dyonisio lib. viii, Livio libro viii, Strabone, Plinio, Solino, Servio ad lib.iii & vi Æneidos: quo notante, Cumæ dictæ vel Κύμη & Κυοντ., id est prægnante (nam ibidem prægnans Mulier inventa fœcunditatis omen ipsis dederat) vel ab Vndis, quas Græci Κῦμα vocant. Legendi Strabo, Dionysius, Livius, alij. Cumæ in Monte adscenso difficili arduoque politas & ad Mare spectavisse, tradit Agathias lib. i. Belli Gothici. Intimam fluctus marini adluebant: superiora Muris, Turribus, aliisque molibus adeo erant circumvallata & munita, ut locus expugnatu esset difficillimus. Nunc omnia fere concidérunt, oppletaque jacent ruinis, ut tamen undique amplissimorum operum vestigia satis agnoscantur. Erat in vertice Rupis urbe media celeberrimum Apollinis Templum, de quo Virgilius libro v Æneid. At pius Æneas Arces, quibus altus Apollo Præsidet, horrendæque procul secreta Sibylla Antrum immane petit.
units.tr: Next comes the site of the very ancient city of Cumae. Cumae is the name used by Livy, Tacitus, Silius, Pliny, Solinus, Mela, Antoninus, the Itinerary Tables, and by Latin writers generally; Κύμαι by Strabo, Ptolemy, Dionysius and other Greeks; Virgil in book 3 calls it the Cumaean city. Its founders were the Cumaeans of Euboea, who came to Italy with the Chalcidians under the leaders Hippocles and Megasthenes, as Dionysius, book 8, Livy, book 8, Strabo, Pliny, Solinus, and Servius on Aeneid 3 and 6 testify. Servius notes that Cumae was called either Κύμη or Κυοντ., that is, "pregnant" (for a pregnant woman was found on the spot, which had given them an omen of fertility), or from the waves, which the Greeks call Κῦμα. Strabo, Dionysius, Livy and others should be read. Agathias, book 1 of his Gothic War, says that Cumae was built on a steep and difficult hill, and looked out towards the sea. The sea washed the lower part; the upper parts were so surrounded and fortified with walls, towers and other great structures that the place was very difficult to take by assault. Now nearly everything has collapsed and lies buried in ruins, though everywhere traces of very magnificent works can be sufficiently recognised. On the top of the rock, in the middle of the city, was the most famous temple of Apollo, of which Virgil speaks in book 5 of the Aeneid: But pious Aeneas makes for the citadels over which high Apollo presides, and for the cave, vast and terrifying, of the Sibyl hidden away far off.

units.la: Quos versus exponens Servius in Arce munitissima Cumis Ædem Apollinis fuisse scribit. Cumarum mentionem facit non raro Dionysius Halicarnass. nominatim lib.vii Antiq. Roman. ubi multa de Aristodemo Malaco, Cumanorum Duce, Rebusque ab Cumanis gestis. L. Tarquinium Superbum ad eumdem Aristodemum, Cumanorum Principem confugisse, scribunt idem libro vi & Livius lib ii, qui alibi libro iv Romanos Vibem Cumas ab Græcis habitatam expugnasse commemorat: item libro viii Cumanos atque Sinuessanos eadem lege, qua Capuam habere, Senatum censuisse. Cumanorum item Fidem erga Populum Romanum narrat idem libro xxiii. Tradit etiam Strabo Cumanos in potestatem olim ab Campanis fuisse redactos. Cumæ Vetus aliquando Municipium, aliquando Præfectura fuit, testibus Livio & Festo: postea Coloniam eo ab Augustofuisse deductam, paret ex Frontino. Ab Cumis Cumanus Campus & Cumanus Sinus, de quibus alibi: & Cumanum, Villa circa Cumas, cujus meminit Cicero in Epistolis.
units.tr: Servius, explaining these verses, writes that in the citadel of Cumae, which was very strongly fortified, there was a temple of Apollo. Dionysius of Halicarnassus often mentions Cumae by name, notably in book 7 of the Roman Antiquities, where he tells much about Aristodemus Malacus, leader of the Cumaeans, and the deeds of the Cumaeans. Both Dionysius, book 6, and Livy, book 2, write that Lucius Tarquinius Superbus fled to the same Aristodemus, prince of the Cumaeans. Livy, elsewhere in book 4, records that the Romans took by storm the city of Cumae, which had been inhabited by Greeks. In book 8 he also records that the Senate decreed that the Cumaeans and the Sinuessans should have the same law that Capua had. The same Livy, book 23, tells of the loyalty of the Cumaeans towards the Roman people. Strabo also reports that the Cumaeans were once brought under the power of the Campanians. Cumae was at one time a municipal town and at another a prefecture, as Livy and Festus testify; that Augustus later settled a colony there is clear from Frontinus. From Cumae come the Cumanus Campus and the Cumanus Sinus, of which I have written elsewhere, and the Cumanum, a villa near Cumae, which Cicero mentions in his Letters.

units.la: Ab Cumis dein ad Avernum usque Lacum nihil invenitur scitu dignum præter Sibylla (quæ ab Cumis, Patria, Cumæa, omnibus decantata, Cavernam, ut vocant. Meminerunt hujus Antri Virgilius vi Æneidos libro, & Symmachus lib. iiii Epist.xxxiii. Describit autem plene Leander Albertus in Campania; qui inter alia censet Viam hic fuisse ab Cumis per Avernum Baias subterraneam, quam Cocceius fecisse notat Strabo; Cymmerios his locis olim habitasse in Antris & Specubus subterraneis, quas Argyllas nominabant, addens.
units.tr: From Cumae as far as Lake Avernus there is nothing worth knowing except the Sibyl (who, being from Cumae, her homeland, is sung of by everyone, and whose cave, as they call it... ). Virgil in book 6 of the Aeneid and Symmachus in book 4, letter 33, mention this cave. Leander Alberti describes it fully in his work on Campania; among other things he thinks there was a road here from Cumae through Avernus to Baiae, underground, which Strabo notes was built by Cocceius. Strabo also says that the Cimmerians once lived in these places, in caves and underground hollows, which they called Argyllae, adding ...

units.la: Tribus Cuma Urbe millibus Hamarum Silva fuit; Sacer Lucus antiquis. Dixi supra. Hamæ Livio nota libro xxxii. Ruinas conspici hactenus in arduo Monte, qui à Balneis Tripergulanis abest P. M. cto 10. scribit Dalechampius. Videndus item Scipio Mazzella de Puteolanorum Antiquitatibus.
units.tr: Three miles from the city of Cumae there was the Hamarum Silva, formerly a sacred grove, as I said above. Livy mentions Hamae in book 32. Dalechampius writes that ruins may be seen so far on a steep hill, which is 10 miles from the Tripergulan baths. Scipio Mazzella on the antiquities of Puteoli is also worth consulting.

units.la: Haud procul inde Mare Mortuum, Sinus Batanus, Lucrinus & Avernus, de quibus alibi. Chersonnesum quamdam faciunt ab Cumis incipientem, uti ab Strabone describitur.
units.tr: Not far from there are the Dead Sea, the Bay of Baiae, Lake Lucrinus and Lake Avernus, which I discuss elsewhere. They form a kind of peninsula beginning at Cumae, as Strabo describes it.

units.la: In ejus Chersonnesi radicibus Baiæ erant, Latinis Græcisque notissimæ, Acris temperie, Romanorum frequentia, Ædificiorum ornamentis celeberrimæ. Q. Horatius Flaccus: Il Conte de { Alvito. | Matera. | Pulicastro. Aversa. | Mignano. | Rocca dell' aspro. Aquino. | Mileto. | Ruvo. Belcastro. | Miscingna. | S. Angelo de Lombardi. Borrello. | Monte Calvo. | Santa Severina. Briatico. | Montella. | San Valentino. Cavazzo. | Monte Miletto. | Saponara. Canosa. | Montorio. | Sarno. Carinola. | Morcone. | Serino. Caserta. | Muro. | Simari. Castro. | Nerulani. | Sinopoli. Condiani. | Nicastro. | Torella. Consa. | Nicotera. | Trevento. Cusuperfano. | Noia. | Vgento.
units.tr: At the roots of that peninsula lay Baiae, well known to Latins and Greeks alike, celebrated for its mild climate, its crowds of Romans and the splendour of its buildings. Quintus Horatius Flaccus: The County of Alvito; Matera; Pulicastro; Aversa; Mignano; Rocca dell'Aspro; Aquino; Mileto; Ruvo; Belcastro; Miscingna; S. Angelo de Lombardi; Borrello; Monte Calvo; Santa Severina; Briatico; Montella; San Valentino; Cavazzo; Monte Miletto; Saponara; Canosa; Montorio; Sarno; Carinola; Morcone; Serino; Caserta; Muro; Simari; Castro; Nerulani; Sinopoli; Condiani; Nicastro; Torella; Consa; Nicotera; Trevento; Cusuperfano; Noia; Vgento.

units.la: Baronum Nobilumque Familiarum incredibilis est per totum hoc Regnum numerus: quemadmodum suis parebit locis.
units.tr: The number of barons and noble families throughout this kingdom is incredible, as will be shown in their proper places.

units.la: Concilia sunt sex: I. Viceregu, quod Collaterale dicitur, in quo gravissima tractantur totius Regni Negocia, aliaque, quae eo evocantur. Caput est Vicerex: Adiectores nonnulli Comites. II. S. Clare, quod ita ab loco, quo cogi solitum, vocatur: Sacrum etiam nominatum. Praeses hic & Consiliarij cognitionem habent Causarum omnium, quae ab Vicaria per Provocationem eo devolvuntur. III Vicaria: Hic ab Regente Neapolitano, qui Vicarius est Magni Justitiarii, quatuorque Juris Doctoribus, qui singulis annis renovantur, Ius dicitur, Iustitiaque administratur omnibus Regni Subditis, per Appellationem ab Inferioribus Iudicibus eo venientibus. IV. Summaria: Hic Rationocinarium est, ibique quae ad Fiscum & Regni Vectigalia pertinent, curantur. Constat ex Vicario, sex Praesidibus, octo Rationarijs, decem, ut vocant, Clericis, & alijs. V. Admiralitatis: Hic toti Maris Praefecturae est Domicilium. Iurisdictionem exercet in Nautas & quaecunque ad illos, tam Criminalem quam Civilem. VI. Monetarium: in quo cognoscitur & civiliter & Criminaliter cum de aliis, tum de Regni totius Monetis, Ponderibus, Mensuris, idque genus alijs. Caput illi Praefectus Rei Monetariae: cui adiunt Magistri, ut loquuntur, Rationales, Probitatis Monetae Examinatores, Pensitator, & alij.
units.tr: There are six councils. I. The Viceregal council, called the Collaterale, which handles the gravest affairs of the whole kingdom and any other matters referred to it. Its head is the Viceroy; some add counts as members. II. The council of S. Clare, so named from the place where it was customarily convened; it is also called the Sacred council. Its president and councillors hear all the cases that are brought to it on appeal from the Vicaria. III. The Vicaria: here justice is declared and administered to all the subjects of the kingdom by the Neapolitan Regent, who is the deputy of the Grand Justiciar, and by four doctors of law, who are renewed every year, on appeals from the lower judges. IV. The Summaria: this is the Exchequer, where matters concerning the treasury and the kingdom's revenues are dealt with. It consists of the Vicar, six presidents, eight auditors, ten so-called clerks, and others. V. The Admiralty: this is the seat of the whole maritime command. It exercises jurisdiction over sailors and over everything touching them, both criminal and civil. VI. The Mint: here both civil and criminal cases are heard concerning coinage, weights, measures and similar matters throughout the whole kingdom. Its head is the Prefect of the Mint, with the so-called rational masters, examiners of the purity of the coinage, a weigher and others as assistants.

units.la: Et haec de Meridionalliore Italia, id est de Regno Neapolitano universim: Regiones autem, quae toti huic Parti adscensentur, aliae, ut quae dixi cap. xxi. obiter hic repetam, ad Mare sunt Tyrrhenum, aliae ad Hadriaticum: Tyrrheno cis Silarum adiidet Campania: trans idem flumen Lucania, Calabriaque Inferior & Superior: Hadriatico cis Phiternum adlocati sunt Samnites: trans eundem amnem Apulia utraque vilun-tur & Salentini.
units.tr: And this is what I have to say of southern Italy, that is, of the Kingdom of Naples in general. The regions that belong to this part, however, I will briefly repeat here from what I said in chapter 21: some lie on the Tyrrhenian Sea, others on the Adriatic. On the Tyrrhenian, on this side of the Silarus, lies Campania; beyond the same river lie Lucania and Lower and Upper Calabria. On the Adriatic, on this side of the Frento, the Samnites are settled; beyond the same river are both Apulias and the Salentines.

units.la: CAMPANIA (quae & Καμπανία Straboni, Ptolemaeo, aliis: quaeque etiam in Antiqua Inscriptione sub Praenestae in Via publica, qua Albam iter est, cum Umbria, Piceno, Brutiis, Calabria, & Apulia nominatur) plerisque dicta censetur ab florentissima quondam Metropoli Capua, cuius Incolae Scriptoribus omnibus Campani, quibus originem tribuit Graecam Trogus apud Iustinum libro xx. Nonnulli sic vocatum volunt, quod Campestribus se pandat locus. Eustathius ad Dionysium ab Campo Civitate derivat: Capuam, ni fallor, designans. Vide & Paulum Diaconum lib. ii. de Reb. gest. Langhardor. cap. xvii.
units.tr: CAMPANIA (which is also called Καμπανία [Kampania] by Strabo, Ptolemy and others, and which also appears in an ancient inscription on the public road from Praeneste towards Alba, together with Umbria, Picenum, the Bruttii, Calabria and Apulia) is commonly thought to be named from the once most flourishing city of Capua, whose inhabitants are called Campani by all writers; Trogus, in Justin book 20, traces their origin to the Greeks. Some hold that the name comes from the fact that the place lies open on the plains (campestribus). Eustathius, on Dionysius, derives it from the city of Campus, meaning, I think, Capua. See also Paul the Deacon, book 2, On the Deeds of the Lombards, chapter 17.

units.la: Felix Plinio lib. iii. cap. v. nuncupatur ab felice beataque Regionis amoenitate, de qua paullo post. Antiqua quibusdam dicitur ad differentiam Novae, quae Campania Romana vel Latium. Terra Laboris, vernacule Terra di Lavoro, audit hodie ab Laborinis, qui Capuae quondam vicini & suburbani, Campus, quorum mentionem facit Plinius lib. iii. nat. histor. cap. v. lib. xvii. cap. iv. & lib. xviii. cap. xi. De iis ego alibi. Quidam parum solide ab Labore laborant Laborinos trahere: vel quod ad Culturae Labores idonea sit: vel quod facillime colatur & arcetur; Itali illud Lavorare vocantibus Narcelius. Narcissus Medicus apud Sebastianum Munsterum ab Lepore & elegantia autumat sic appellatam.
units.tr: Pliny, book 3, chapter 5, calls it Felix from the happy and blessed pleasantness of the region, of which I shall speak a little later. Some call it the Old Campania, to distinguish it from the New, which is Campania Romana or Latium. Today it is called in the vernacular Terra di Lavoro, from the Laborini, who once lived near Capua and in its suburbs, the Campus people, whom Pliny mentions in book 3 of the Natural History, chapter 5, and in book 17, chapter 4, and book 18, chapter 11. I discuss them elsewhere. Some rather weakly try to derive Laborini from labour, either because the land is suited to the labours of cultivation, or because it is very easily tilled and irrigated; Narcelius says the Italians call this lavorare. Narcissus the physician, quoted by Sebastian Münster, thinks they were so called from Lepore and elegance.

units.la: Finescius, ut videre est apud Strabonem, Ptolemaeum, & alios, ad Occasum Liris, Latium ad alteram relinquens oram: ad Septemtrionem, Samnitium Montes; qua Ortus est, Silarus Fluvius, Lucaniam hinc dirimens, parteque Agri Samnitium, quos dixi: qua Meridies; Mare Tyrrhenum sive Inferum.
units.tr: The Finescius, as is seen in Strabo, Ptolemy and others, lies to the west of the Liris, leaving Latium on the other shore; to the north are the mountains of the Samnites; where it rises is the river Silarus, which separates Lucania from it, and part of the territory of the Samnites I have mentioned; to the south is the Tyrrhenian Sea, also called the Lower Sea.

units.la: Vere Campus est Campania, in quem Natura luxurians effudisse videtur largissimo Sinu quidquid usquam est Deliciarum, Amoenitatum, Gaudiorum & Oblectationum. Paradisus vere Italiae. Tam incredibilis ibi rerum est fertilitas. Visuntur spatiosi feraceque Campi; aprici fructiferique Colles, amoena odorataque Nemora, jucundi salubresque Fontes: & quid non Miraculorum? Ea suis locis commemorabimus. Scribit Strabo libro v. Campaniam cum omnium Rerum ad Usus humanos affluentia, tum Amoenitate omnes Italiae partes partibus multis superare. Depingit eandem his coloribus Florus lib. i. Histor. Rom cap. xvi. Omnium non modo Italia, sed toto orbe terrarum pulcerrima Campania plaga est. Nil mollius Coelo, nil uberius Solo, nil hospitalius Mari: denique bis Floribus vernat: ideo Liberi Cereriscque Certamen ditatur. Hic illi nobiles Portus, Caieta, Misenus & tepentes Fontibus Baia: Lucrinus & Avernus quadam Maris ostia. Hic amicti Vitibus Montes Gaurus, Falernus, Massicus, & pulcerrimus omnium Vesuvius, Aetnae Ignis imitator. Urbes ad Mare Formiae, Cumae, Neapolis, Herculanium: Pompeii, & ipsa caput Urbium Capua, quondam inter tres Maximas Romam Karthaginemque numerata. Dionysius Halic. libro i. tribus anni cuiusque temporibus, Vere, Aestate, Autumno, Fructus in ea colligi suis oculis vidisse se testatur. Strabo rursus accedat, scriptum se reperisse memorans, quibusdam Campania locis Zeam, Frumenti speciem, iterum eodem anni seri, tertioque Panicum, sed & quarto Olerum eodem in Arvo Semina. Urbium summa hic Nobilitas. De iis universim Propertius:
units.tr: Campania is truly a plain, into which nature seems to have poured out with the most lavish hand whatever delights, pleasures, joys and enjoyments there are anywhere. It is truly the paradise of Italy. Its fertility is so incredible. There are broad and fruitful plains to be seen, sunny and fruitful hills, pleasant and fragrant groves, and wholesome, delightful springs; and what of the wonders? I shall mention these in their places. Strabo, in book 5, writes that Campania surpasses all other parts of Italy in many respects, both in the abundance of everything needed for human use and in its pleasantness. Florus, in book 1 of his Roman History, chapter 16, paints the same region in these colours: Campania is the most beautiful stretch of land not only in Italy but in the whole world. Nothing is softer than its sky, nothing more fertile than its soil, nothing more hospitable than its sea. It is always in flower twice a year, and so it is the field of contest between Liber and Ceres. Here are those noble harbours, Caieta and Misenum, Baiae warm with its springs, Lucrinus and Avernus, mouths of the sea. Here are the mountains clad with vines, Gaurus, Falernus, Massicus, and Vesuvius, the most beautiful of all, rival of Aetna's fire. The cities by the sea are Formiae, Cumae, Naples and Herculaneum; Pompeii too, and Capua itself, head of cities, once counted among the three greatest, with Rome and Carthage. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, in book 1, testifies that he saw with his own eyes the fruits gathered in it in each of the three seasons, spring, summer and autumn. Let Strabo be added again, who recalls that he had read that in certain places in Campania, Zea, a kind of wheat, is sown twice in the same year, and a third time millet, and even a fourth time seeds of vegetables in the same field. The highest nobility of cities is here. Of them in general Propertius speaks:

units.la: {y} Et te mirantem Thesproto subdita Regno / Proxima Misenis Aequora nobilibus.
units.tr: And you, marvelling, the waters near the noble cities of Misenum, subject to the Thesprotian kingdom.

units.la: Intelligit enim per Misenas Nobiles, omnes illas Urbes, quae in tractu Neapolitano erant, Cumas, Baias, Puteolos, & alias: ut Varro per Tarentinas Nobiles, Urbes tractus Tarentini, in quibus Croton & ipsum Tarentum. Circumferuntur etiam de plerisque Campaniae Urbibus hi versus: Castellani Caietani. | Pignatari son da Sessa. Belle Femine son de Mola. | Papari de Castello. Cefali de Patria. | Asinari de Buzolo. Cernati de Ischia. | Fogatori de Prochyta. Gentilezze a Napoli. | Buen Gracofa la Torre. Megliofa la Somma. | Castela mare ne amico, ne compare. Avico porta pane contico. | Surrente stinge li denti. Massa salute & passa. | Sarraini son de Capre. Fico de donna grana. | Marinari de Pasitano. Vogatori de Preano. | Samigothi de Cythara. Taglia borsi di Salerno. | Zeppolan son de Agropoli.
units.tr: For by Misenas Nobiles he means all those cities that lay in the Neapolitan district, Cumae, Baiae, Puteoli and others, just as Varro by Tarentine nobles means the cities of the Tarentine district, among them Croton and Tarentum itself. Verses are also circulated about most of the cities of Campania: Castellani of Gaeta. Pignatari, from Sessa. Beautiful women are from Mola. Papari from Castello. Cefali from Patria. Asinari from Buzolo. Cernati from Ischia. Fogatori from Procida. Gentlemen at Naples. Good wine at La Torre. Better at La Somma. Castellamare: be neither friend nor kinsman. Avico gives bread with a pinch. Sorrento blunts the teeth. Massa is health and passes. Sarracens are from Capri. Fig of a donna grana. Sailors of Positano. Rowers of Praiano. Samigothi of Cythara. Cutpurses of Salerno. Zeppolani are from Agropoli.

units.la: Aliorum Encomia brevitati studens praetereo.
units.tr: I pass over the praises of others, out of regard for brevity.

units.la: Principatum habuerunt olim in hac Regione varii Populi, de quibus Strabo libro v. Geograph. & Plinius libro iii. cap. v. Opicos, cognomine Ausones, Campaniam tenuisse docet Strabo ex Antiochi sententia Opicos Ausonios fuisse dictos refert Aristoteles lib. vii. Politicor. cap. x. Loca ad Tyrrhenum Mare tenuisse scribens: cui suffragatur Dionysius Halicarnassi, libro i. qui in Latium usque protendit. Opicos & Ausones diversos tradit Polybius apud eumdem Strabonem, utrosque addens habitasse juxta Sinum Crateris. Pausanias in Achaicis notat Cumas Opica esse Terra. Videndus & Thucydides lib. vi. Ὀμβροὶ Italiae Populi etiam Stephano noti. Ausonia testibus Livio & Festo ea pars olim Italiae, in qua Beneventum & Cales: vel, uti scribit Isaacus in Ycephronem, proprie Aurunncorum Terra, inter Campanos & Volscos juxta Mare sita. Aurunci, qui Αὐρόγκοι Graecis scribuntur, meminit etiam Virgilius lib.vii. Aeneid. non uno loco, ubi Servius Aruncos notat antiquissimos Italiæ Populos; & Græce Ausones nominari. Mentio eorumdem passim apud Livium & Dionysium. Hic sane libro vi. Aruncos robustum hominum genus, membrorum firmitate præstantes, adspectu truci & feroce, describit. Dixi etiam de Aruncis in Latio. Ab Ausonibus his non solum universa Italia quondam Ausonia, verum etiam Ausonium Mare dictum refert Strabo libro v. quod idem auctor suo tempore Siculum fuisse appellatum scribit lib.vi. & Tyrrhenum, uti memoriæ prodit Halicarnass. libro i. Opicos Ausones volunt Incertiores apud Strabonem ab Osciis subactos. Osci, o'ɛucs, Latinis Græcisque Scriptoribus satis celebrati. Osci, inquit Paulus Diaconus ad Festum in Massius, a regione Campania, quæ est Osca, vocati sunt. Osicos Verrius apud Festum antiquitus Opsicos fuisse vocatos notat ex Ennio, cuius hoc Hemistichium libro viii. Annalium, in mea editione:
units.tr: In this region various peoples once held sway, of whom Strabo in book 5 of the Geography and Pliny in book 3, chapter 5, speak. Strabo teaches that the Opici held Campania, following Antiochus' opinion. Aristotle, in Politics book 7, chapter 10, relates that the Opici were called Ausonii, writing that they held places on the Tyrrhenian Sea; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 1, supports him, extending their range as far as Latium. Polybius, cited by the same Strabo, says that the Opici and the Ausones were different peoples, adding that both lived near the Gulf of Crater. Pausanias in the Achaica notes that Cumae is an Opican land. Thucydides book 6 should also be consulted, as should the Umbrians [Ὀμβροὶ], an Italian people also known to Stephanus. According to the testimony of Livy and Festus, Ausonia was once that part of Italy in which lie Beneventum and Cales; or, as Isaac writes on Lycophron, it was properly the land of the Aurunci, situated between the Campani and the Volsci by the sea. Virgil in book 7 of the Aeneid, mentions the Aurunci, who are written Αὐρόγκοι [Aurongkoi] by the Greeks, in more than one place; Servius notes that the Aruncoi were the most ancient peoples of Italy, and are called Ausones in Greek. They are mentioned here and there in Livy and Dionysius. Indeed, in book 6 the latter describes the Aruncoi as a sturdy race, outstanding for the firmness of their limbs, with a fierce and savage look. I have also spoken of the Aruncians in Latium. Strabo in book 5 reports that from these Ausones not only the whole of Italy was once called Ausonia, but also the sea was called the Ausonian Sea; the same author writes that in his own time it was called the Sicilian sea, in book 6, and the Tyrrhenian, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus records in book 1. Some less well-known writers, cited by Strabo, hold that the Opici Ausones were subdued by the Osci. The Osci, Ὀσκοί [Oskoi], are well enough known to Latin and Greek writers. The Osci, says Paul the Deacon on Festus, under Massius, were so called from the region of Campania, which is Osca. Verrius, cited by Festus, notes that the Osicos were formerly called Opsicos, from Ennius, whose half-line from book 8 of the Annals, in my edition, is this:

units.la: De Mœris res gerit Opscus.
units.tr: Opscus carries on the war about Mœris.

units.la: Osicos fuisse etiam cognominibus fuisse distinctos, plerosque autem periisse, præter eos, qui Sidicini dicebantur, ex Strabone facile colligitur lib.v. Notat enim ille Teanum Sidicinum ipso cognomine ostendere, sic ad Sidicinos pertinere: Sidicinos autem esse Osicos Gentem Campaniæ superstitem: atqui tradiderat idem paullo ante universim Gentem Osicorum periisse: Sermonem tamen eorum superfuisse apud Romanos, sed Scenicum & in Mimis. Sic Osci erant, qui Capuenses appellabantur. Servius ad illud Virgilii lib.vii. Aeneid Osicorumque manus: Capuenses inquit, dicit, qui antea Ophici appellati sunt, quod illic plurimi abundavere Serpentes. Nam Græce ὄφις dicitur Serpens. Vocabantur fortean & Ausones, si tamen, ut censent nonnulli, Osci idem fuerint cum Opicis, de quibus ante, quod Criticis disputandum relinquo.Osicos scribit Strabo profligatos ab Cumanis, de quibus in Cumarum delineatione. Cumanos Plinius antiquos Campaniæ Populos enumerans, Græcos vocat.
units.tr: That the Osici were also distinguished by surnames, and that most of them perished except those who were called Sidicini, is easily gathered from Strabo, book 5. For he observes that Teanum Sidicinum shows by its very surname that it belonged to the Sidicini, and that the Sidicini were Osici, a people of Campania that survived. Yet the same writer had said a little earlier that the nation of the Osici had perished as a whole. Their speech nevertheless survived among the Romans, but only in the theatre and in mimes. So the Osci were those who were called Capuenses. Servius, on that line of Virgil in book 7 of the Aeneid, and the bands of the Osci, says: he means the Capuenses, who were formerly called Ophici, because very many serpents [ὄφις] abounded there. For in Greek a serpent is called ὄφις. They were perhaps also called Ausones, if indeed, as some think, the Osci were the same as the Opici mentioned above; this I leave for the critics to dispute. Strabo writes that the Osici were routed by the Cumani, of whom I shall speak in the description of Cumae. Pliny, listing the ancient peoples of Campania, calls the Cumani Greeks.

units.la: Cumanos magna ex parte ab Tuscis, de quibus ante, fuisse pulsos, narrat idem Strabo. Hos Plinius loco à me indicato Umbros speciatim appellat. Autumat Strabo Commutationum harum causam fuisse Regionis ubertatem & præstantiam; eiusque desiderio tam varias Gentes provocatas Sedes in ea quæsisse. Addit idem, Tuscos ibi dominantes, Urbibus xii. eximiis conditis, omnem Principatum Capuæ tribuisse: Tuscos autem, nimia Agrorum felicitate languescentes & enervatos, ab Samnitibus fuisse exactos: Hos autem postremum à Pop. Rom. debellatos.
units.tr: Strabo also relates that the Cumani were for the most part driven out by the Tuscans, of whom I spoke above. Pliny, in the passage I have indicated, calls these specifically Umbrians. Strabo supposes that the cause of these changes of masters was the fertility and excellence of the region, and that from desire for it so many different peoples sought homes there. He adds that the Tuscans, who ruled there and had founded twelve notable cities, gave the whole leadership to Capua; but the Tuscans, growing feeble and enervated by the excessive happiness of their fields, were expelled by the Samnites, and these at last were subdued by the Roman people.

units.la: Habitatur hodie ab multa magnaque Nobilitate. Nam præter Principes, Duces, Marchiones & Comites, quos antea huius Regni commemoravi, in Campania Baronum ingens numerus. Vulgatas dabo Nomenclaturas ex Libello, cuius antea feci mentionem:
units.tr: It is inhabited today by a great and numerous nobility. For besides the princes, dukes, marquises and counts, whom I mentioned earlier for this kingdom, there is in Campania an immense number of barons. I shall give the common nomenclatures from the little book of which I made mention before:

units.la: Baroni di
units.tr: Barons of
