units.la: Haec in genere paucis de Campania: iam nunc specialior me vocat eius Discriptio: quam ab Liris (hic enim communis inter Latium & Campaniam Limes) oltus auspicabor.
units.tr: These things, in brief, concerning Campania in general. Now its more particular description calls me; I shall begin it from the Liris (for this is the common boundary between Latium and Campania), going round by the coast.

units.la: De Liri supra dixi. Fuisse quondam in eius ora memorant quidem Vrbem Ausonian, cuius nescio an quis Veterum praeter Livium lib. ix. de quo post, meminerit. Sanfelicius putat aequatam solo.
units.tr: I have spoken of the Liris above. On its shore they do indeed record that there was once a city Ausonia, which I do not know whether any of the ancients except Livy, book 9, of whom more later, mentions. Sanfelicius thinks it was levelled with the ground.

units.la: Fuerunt ibidem Vestina & Minturna. Livius loco indicato Ausoniam, Vestinam (in quibusdam Codicibus Vescia legitur exaratum. Consule Ambrosium Leonem lib. ii. cap. iii. de Nola Vrbe) & Minturnas uno bello scribit subactas; Minturnas quidem conservatas: Vestinam autem cum Ausonia delectam, idque per Ducum contiguè absentiam. Vestina Incolae Vestini, uni Livio noti. Nam quos nominant Strabo, Plinius, Ptolemaeus, ad Mare erant Superum, circa Matrinum Fluvium. Ab Vestinis Campaniae ad Mare Inferum Vestinus Mons appellatur, circa Minturnas, cuius meminit Hyginus de Limitibus. Inde item Vestinus Saltus Livio libro x. De Minturnis dictum in Latio. Describitur in Agro Minturnensium Straboni Lucus Sacer, de quo alibi: ut & de Monte Gauro, qui paullum ab Liris abest Ostio.
units.tr: There were also Vestina and Minturna there. Livy, in the place indicated, writes that Ausonia, Vestina (in some manuscripts it is read as Vescia; consult Ambrosius Leo, book 2, chapter 3, on the city of Nola) and Minturnae were subdued in one war; Minturnae were indeed spared, but Vestina was destroyed together with Ausonia, this happening through the continued absence of the commanders. The inhabitants of Vestina were the Vestini, known only from Livy. For the Vestini whom Strabo, Pliny and Ptolemy name lived on the upper sea, near the river Matrinus. From the Vestini, on the lower sea of Campania, there is called the Vestine Mountain, near Minturnae, which Hyginus mentions in his work on boundaries. Thence likewise the Vestine Wood, in Livy book 10. Minturnae was described in Latium. In the territory of the Minturnenses Strabo describes the Sacred Grove, of which I shall speak elsewhere; likewise of Mount Gaurus, which is a little distant from the mouth of the Liris.

units.la: Iunere Minturnis ad Gaurum inter illas & Sinuessam Trifanum erat, quod Livius nominat libris ab V.C. vii. & xi.
units.tr: On the road from Minturnae to Gaurus, between those places and Sinuessa, was Trifanum, which Livy mentions in books 7 and 11 from the founding of the City.

units.la: Hinc Sinuessa, Minturnis lxxx. distans stadiis. Sic Latinis, cum aliis, tum Melae, Antonino, & Itinerariae Tabulae dicitur, quae Σίνουσσα Ptolemaeo per o:nā per u, Σίνουσσα alia ab hac est in Mediterraneis: nisi forte pro Σίνουσσα legendum sit Σινούσσα. Livius libro x. describit eam iuxta Agrum Falernum; addens Graecam fuisse Urbem, Synopen dictam: deinde ab Colonis Romanis Sinuessam appellatam. Videndus & Plinius. Coloniam etiam nominat Frontinus. Sinuessa Silio libro viii. Tepens vocatur, ad Aquis proculdubio calidis. Quod hodieque Sinuessa nuncupetur, tradunt Marsus, Leander, & Hubertus Goltzius, qui oculatus testis totam interiisse adfirmat apud Ortelium, tantumque superesse inter eius ruinas exiguum, sed munitissimum metu Piratarum, Opidulum, quod vulgo Rocha de Monte Dragone, pallibus ab Mari mille. Incolae Sinuessani Lapidi, quem apud Petrinum Sinuessanum servari notat Apianus:
units.tr: Hence Sinuessa, eighty stades distant from Minturnae. It is so called by the Latins, both by others and by Mela, Antoninus and the Itinerary Tables; Ptolemy writes Σίνουσσα with an o rather than a u [Σίνουσσα]. Another Sinuessa, different from this one, lies inland; unless perhaps for Σίνουσσα one should read Σινούσσα. Livy, book 10, describes it near the Falernian field, adding that it was originally a Greek city called Synope, and afterwards, when Roman colonists came, called Sinuessa. Pliny should also be consulted. Frontinus also calls it a colony. In Silius, book 8, Sinuessa is called tepid, undoubtedly on account of its warm waters. That it is still called Sinuessa today is reported by Marsus, Leander and Hubert Goltzius, who, as an eyewitness, affirms in Ortelius that the whole town has perished, and that among its ruins there remains only a small but very well fortified little town, for fear of pirates, which commonly goes by the name Rocca di Monte Dragone, two miles from the sea. The inhabitants of Sinuessa [call it?] ... by the stone which Apianus notes is preserved at Petrinum Sinuessanum:

units.la: L. PAPPIVS. L. F. TER POLLIO. II. VIR L. PAPPIO. L. F. FAL: PATRI MVLSVM. ET. CRVSTVM COLONIS SINVESSANIS. ET CEDIANIS. OMNIB. MVNVS GLADIATORIVM. COENAM COLONIS. SINVESSANIS. ET PAPIENIS. MONVMENTVM &C.
units.tr: L. PAPPIUS L. F. TER. POLLIO, DUUMVIR, TO L. PAPPIUS L. F. FAL., HIS FATHER: A FEAST OF HONEYED WINE AND PASTRY FOR THE COLONISTS OF SINUESSA AND CEDIA, AND FOR ALL OF THEM A GLADIATORIAL SHOW, A DINNER FOR THE COLONISTS OF SINUESSA AND PAPIA, A MONUMENT, ETC.

units.la: Σινουσσανοὶ Polybio apud Stephanum. Hinc Sinuessana Aqua Plinio in Campania: quarum etiam meminerunt Livius lib. xxii. Tacitus lib. xvii. (ubi male in vulgaris Codicibus Suessane, indicante Lipsio) & Martialis lib. xi. hodie Acque de Monte Dragone, ut vult Ben. Falconius. Sinuessana Prata nonnullis celebrantur, quod Sinuessa Vina Massica & Falerna premerentur. Sinuessani Fundi mentio non semel apud M. Tullium in Epistolis ad Atticum.
units.tr: Σινουσσανοὶ [Sinoussanoi] in Polybius, cited by Stephanus. Hence Sinuessana Aqua in Pliny, in Campania; these are also mentioned by Livy, book 22, and Tacitus, book 17 (where the common manuscripts wrongly read Suessane, as Lipsius points out), and by Martial, book 11. Today they are the Acque de Monte Dragone, as Ben. Falconius holds. Some celebrate the Sinuessana Prata, because the Massic and Falernian wines were pressed at Sinuessa. The Sinuessani Fundi are mentioned more than once by M. Tullius in his Letters to Atticus.

units.la: Ab Sinuella, quae, ut dixi, Ptolemaeo Σέσσα, vel, uti legendum forte monebam Sinuessa, Σινόεσσα, Suessa Aurunca, alia est Suessa, eadem Σuεσσα in Mediterraneis & Septentrionalior. Binominis plerisque, nunc Suessa Pometia, nunc Suessa Aurunca. Nam Pometinos ab L. Tarquinio Romanorum Rege, Pometia, de qua in Latio, deleta, pulsos in eam commigrasse, tradit Dionysius Halicarnassaeus libro 1. Antiq. Rom. unde Pometia cognominata: sicque Tacito, Floro, Plinio lib. VII. cap. XVI Auctori de VV. Illustr. cap. VIII. aliisque nota. Postea Aurunca vel Aurunmarum coepit dici, teste Livio lib. VIII. quum Aurunci, ab T. Manlio Cos. Sidicinis opem ferente victi, cum Liberis & Coniugibus eo, Patria deserta, confugiTent. Suessa Aurunca meminit idem Livius libro XXXII. Suessa nihilominus simpliciter vocatur cum aliis, tum Plinio libro natur. Histor. III cap. V. simplexque hodie nomen retinens, Sessa dicitur, posita in Agro Vestino, Situ inaequali, ad Montes Maslicum & Calenum, in Via Appia, in Regione amoena & fertili. Ducatus & Episcopatus honore decorata. Nobilitavit eam ortu suo Augustinus Niphus, insignis Philosophus, Scriptis clarus. Inter Volscorum quondam Urbes nominata, Roma ipsa antiquior, tandem Romanis cessit, factaque Colonia circa annum ab V. C. CCCCXL. ut ex Livio patet. Velleius deductam notat triennio post Luceriam. Passa deinde multas Clades Bellis Punicis. Colonia censetur in Inscriptione, quae ibi servatur:
units.tr: Distinct from Sinuella, which, as I said, Ptolemy calls Σέσσα [Sessa], or, as I was suggesting may be read, Sinuessa (Σινόεσσα [Sinoessa]), is Suessa Aurunca, another Suessa, the same as Σουεσσα [Souessa] in the inland and more northern parts. It has two names in most authors: now Suessa Pometia, now Suessa Aurunca. For Dionysius of Halicarnassus, in book 1 of his Roman Antiquities, reports that the Pometines, driven out by the Roman king Lucius Tarquinius when Pometia in Latium was destroyed, migrated to this place; hence it was called Pometia. So it is known to Tacitus, Florus, Pliny (book 7, chapter 16), the author De Viris Illustribus (chapter 8), and others. Later it began to be called Aurunca or Auruncum, according to Livy, book 8, when the Aurunci, defeated by T. Manlius, consul, bringing help to the Sidicini, fled from their homeland with their children and wives. Livy mentions Suessa Aurunca in book 32. Nevertheless it is also called simply Suessa, by others and by Pliny in book 3, chapter 5 of his Natural History. Still keeping the simple name, it is today called Sessa. It stands in the Vestinian territory, on uneven ground, near the mountains Maslicum and Calenum, on the Appian Way, in a pleasant and fertile region. It is adorned with the honour of a duchy and a bishopric. Augustinus Niphus, a distinguished philosopher famous for his writings, ennobled it by his birth. Once numbered among the cities of the Volsci, older than Rome itself, it finally yielded to the Romans and became a colony about the year 440 from the founding of the city, as Livy shows. Velleius notes that it was founded three years after Luceria. It then suffered many defeats in the Punic Wars. It is styled a colony in the inscription preserved there:

units.la: C. TITIO. CHRESIMO. AVG. LIB.
units.tr: GAIUS TITIUS CHRESIMUS, FREEDMAN OF AUGUSTUS.

units.la: HVIC. ORDO. DECVRIONVM QVOD. PRO. SALVTE. ET. INDVLGENTIA. IMPERAT ANTONINI. PII FELICIS. AVG. ET. VOLVNTATE. POPVLI MVNVS. FAMILIÆ. GLADIATORIÆ. EX. PECVNIA. SVA DIEM. PRIVATVM. SECVNDVM. DIGNITATEM. COLONIÆ EDIDERIT. HONOREM. BIS. ILLI. QVOD. QVIS. OPTIMO. EXEMPLO IN. COLONIA. SVESSA. HABVIT. ET. VT. AQVÆ. DICITVR IN. DOMO. EIVS. ILVERET, &c.
units.tr: TO HIM THE ORDER OF DECURIONS, BECAUSE, FOR THE HEALTH AND INDULGENCE OF THE EMPEROR ANTONINUS PIUS FELIX AUGUSTUS, AND BY THE WILL OF THE PEOPLE, HE GAVE FROM HIS OWN MONEY A GLADIATORIAL TROUPE FOR A SINGLE DAY, IN KEEPING WITH THE DIGNITY OF THE COLONY; THE HONOUR OF TWICE BEING... WHICH SOMEONE HELD IN THE COLONY OF SUESSA, AND, AS IT IS SAID, LET IT SHINE IN HIS HOUSE, ETC.

units.la: Suessanorum etiam meminit Inscriptio, quae ibidem legitur:
units.tr: The inscription found there also mentions the Suessani:

units.la: IMP. CAES L. SEPTIMO SEVERO. PERTINACI PIO. P. P. SVESSANI
units.tr: THE EMPEROR CAESAR LUCIUS SEPTIMIUS SEVERUS PERTINAX PIUS, FATHER OF THE FATHERLAND: THE SUESSANI.

units.la: Suessanorum Municipium Alia, in fragmento Cippi Marmorei, littera palmari:
units.tr: Another inscription, on a fragment of a marble cippus, in letters a palm high, names the Suessanorum Municipium:

units.la: RTHICI. FIL. DIVI. NERVÆ. NEP. TRAIANI. HADRIANI AVG. PONTIF. MAX TRIB. POT. VI. COS. III VIAM. SVESSANIS MVNICIPIBVS SVA. PEC. FECIT
units.tr: ... PARTHICUS, SON OF THE DEIFIED NERVA, GRANDSON OF TRAJAN, HADRIAN AUGUSTUS, PONTIFEX MAXIMUS, HOLDER OF TRIBUNICIAN POWER FOR THE SIXTH TIME, CONSUL FOR THE THIRD TIME, MADE THE ROAD AT HIS OWN EXPENSE FOR THE MUNICIPALITIES OF THE SUESSANI.

units.la: CVRATOR R. P. SVESSANORVM nominatur L. CÆSONIVS C. FIL. QVIRINA. LVCILIVS in Basi Marmorea, quæ hodie in Vinea Cardinalis Carpensis; translata eo cum duabus aliis ex Vico Corocollo, inter Gabios & Tiburtinos, anno CIO IO XLIX. Inter alia Antiquitatum Monimenta, multæ Suessa visuntur Inscriptiones Marmoreæ, pulcerrimæ & integræ, si quæ alibi.
units.tr: L. CAESONIUS, SON OF GAIUS, OF THE QUIRINA TRIBE, AND LUCILIUS, are named as curators of the republic of the Suessani on a marble base which today is in the vineyard of the Cardinal of Carpi. It was moved there, along with two others, from the village of Corocollo, between Gabii and Tibur, in the year 1549. Among other monuments of antiquity, many Suessan inscriptions, very fine and intact, are to be seen, if any are anywhere.

units.la: Oco P. M. ab Sinuella opidum se offert in Campo, qui quondam Stellatis, de quo alibi, Carinula. Sic hodie, ut volunt Blondus, Niger & Leander, vocatur: quod Calenum Plinio: Καλαῖον Straboni. Incolæ Καλαῖοι Plutarcho in Hannibale. Ager eius Calenum, nobile Vini genus, ferebat, Plinio laudatum libro xiv. cap. vi. Meminit Horatius, cui Molle Calenum; Vnam etiam Prælo Domitam Caleno laudans. In eiusdem Opidi Agro Aquâ fluere, quæ non secus ac Vinum homines inebriabat, antea, ubi de miraculosis Italiæ Aquis, dixi ex Valerio Maximo.
units.tr: Oco P. M. From Sinuella a town presents itself in the plain, which was once called Carinula, the Stellatis (of which elsewhere). Today, as Blondus, Niger and Leander think, it is called Calenum, which Pliny calls Calenum and Strabo Καλαῖον [Kalaion]. Its inhabitants are the Καλαῖοι [Kalaioi] in Plutarch's Hannibal. Its territory produced Calenum, a noble kind of wine, praised by Pliny in book 14, chapter 6. Horace mentions it, calling it Molle Calenum, and praising the Vnam wine that was Prælo Domitam Caleno, tamed by the press at Calenum. In the territory of this same town, a water flows which, like wine, made men drunk; I said this earlier, when speaking of the miraculous waters of Italy, citing Valerius Maximus.

units.la: Vicinis locis Calatia erat, cuius varijs locis Livius, Cæsar, Appianus, Plutarchus in Hannibale, Silius lib. viii. qui parvos ei muros tribuit, aliique meminerunt: Calatia Plinio; Calatie Itinerariæ Tabulæ; Calatia Colonia, Frontino: Gajazo hodie, Leandro & Sanfelicio, qui de hac Vrbe in elegante de Campania Libello consulendus. Capua viii. Neapoli xxiv. Italicis distat miliaribus. Antiquum & celebre quondam Opidum. Polybius lib. iii. Causas enumerans Adventus Hannibalis in Campaniam, hanc quoque addit, ut potiretur nobilibus Vrbibus Capua, Atella & Calatia. Extat adhuc magna Veterum Murorum pars, qui ex quadratis Lapidibus sine Calce, vel alio Ferruminationis genere structi. Cognomen dedit Attilia Genti, in qua legitur præter alios A. Attilius Calatinus, bis Consul & Dictator, de quo cum alij, tum Valerius Maximus lib. iii. cap. vi. & alibi. Hippiam, Philoxeni F. Calatinum, Hospitem & necessarium suum Legesque Calatinorum, quibus vetabatur, ne quandam Publicum, nisi publico nomine, possideretur, celebrat Epistol. lib. xiii. M. Tullius Cicero. Veteranos, quique Casilini & Calatia sunt, perducit ad suam sententiam Octavianus apud Ciceronem lib. xvi. ad Atticum, Epist. vii. Multa hic Antiquitatis Monimenta, Veteresque Inscriptiones. Visitur inter alias Foro Simulacrum Priapi lapideum, paucos ante annos in Ruderibus antiquissimi Templi Veneris repertum. Fuit Calatia, primus Ecclesiæ Crescentis temporibus, Episcopatus titulo insignita; uti ex publicis paret Tabulis, quæ circa annum ccc. confectæ, mentionem Episcopatus Calatini facientes. Inter primos Episcopos fuisse censetur S. S. Ferdinandus Hispanus & Stephanus Italus.
units.tr: Nearby was Calatia, which Livy, Caesar, Appian, Plutarch in Hannibal, Silius in book 8 (who gives it small walls), and others mention in various places. Pliny calls it Calatia; the Itinerary Table calls it Calatie; Frontinus calls it Calatia Colonia. Today it is Gajazo, according to Leander and Sanfelicius, to be consulted on this city in the elegant little book on Campania. It is twenty-eight Italian miles from Capua and twenty-four from Naples. It was once an ancient and famous town. Polybius, in book 3, listing the causes of Hannibal's coming into Campania, adds this also: that he might seize the noble cities Capua, Atella and Calatia. A large part of the ancient walls still stands, built of squared stones without lime or any other kind of binding. It gave its surname to the Attilia family, in which, among others, A. Attilius Calatinus is read, twice consul and dictator; of him Valerius Maximus, book 3, chapter 6, and others, speak. M. Tullius Cicero, in book 13 of his Letters, celebrates Hippias, son of Philoxenus, Calatinus, his host and close friend, and the laws of the Calatini, by which it was forbidden that any public land be held except in the public name. Octavian, in Cicero's letter 7 of book 16 to Atticus, brings the veterans who are at Casilinum and Calatia over to his opinion. Many monuments of antiquity and old inscriptions are here. Among other things, a stone statue of Priapus is seen in the forum; it was found a few years ago in the ruins of an ancient temple of Venus. Calatia was, in the early times of the growing Church, adorned with the title of a bishopric, as appears from public records, made around the year 300, which mention the Episcopatus Calatini. Among its first bishops are counted S. S. Ferdinandus the Spaniard and Stephanus the Italian.

units.la: Ager extendit se huc usque ex Samnitibus Venafranus, de quo alibi. Propinqua sunt illi conjacentque Gallutium (ab obtleo Rogerio, Rogerij Siciliæ Comitis Filio; captoque per Gulielmum Calabriæ Ducem obsessi Filium ipso Obsessore, Innocentio ii. P. M. clarum) Conca, Mintanum, Præsentianum & Variaanum; hæc uno latere: altero Sestus.
units.tr: The territory extends from here as far as Venafrum in the Samnites, of which elsewhere. Near it and lying close by are Gallutium (named after Roger, son of Roger, Count of Sicily; and famous for Innocent II, supreme pontiff, who was besieged there by the son of the besieger himself, after being captured by William, Duke of Calabria), Conca, Mintanum, Praesentianum and Variaanum. These lie on one side; on the other is Sestus.

units.la: Superius ultra Vulturnum est Alluphia, de qua commodiore loco in Samnitibus.
units.tr: Further up, beyond the Volturnus, is Alluphia, of which in a more suitable place among the Samnites.

units.la: Suessam repeto, cui vicinum est, cum Turri Fracolisa, Teanum: ad alterius in Apulia differentiam, Sidicinum ab Strabone, cui Σιδικινον, Plinioque cognominatum. Teanum Sedicinum, corruptius in Itinerario Tabula. Meminit sæpe Livius. Coloniam eo deduxisse Augustum, Liber indicat Coloniarum. CVRATOR R. P. TEANENS. nominatur C. CASONIVS C. F. QVIRINA MACER RVFINIANVS in Basi marmorea, quæ visitur in Vinea Cardinalis Carpensis. Delectum hodie Theano vernale dicitur; Episcopatus nihilominus titulo nobile. Capuæ pæne æquat Strabo, in Via locans Appia.
units.tr: Returning to Suessa: near it lie, together with Turris Fracolisa, Teanum, to distinguish it from the other in Apulia, Sidicinum, called so by Strabo, who gives it the name Σιδικινον [Sidikinon], and by Pliny, who gives it the surname. The Itinerary Table calls it, more corruptly, Teanum Sedicinum. Livy often mentions it. Augustus is shown by the Book of Colonies to have settled a colony there. C. CASONIUS, SON OF GAIUS, OF THE QUIRINA TRIBE, MACER RUFINIANUS, is named as curator of the republic of the Teanenses on a marble base seen in the vineyard of the Cardinal of Carpi. Today it is called Theano, and its spring fair is famous; nevertheless it is distinguished by the title of a bishopric. Strabo, placing it on the Appian Way, almost equals it with Capua.

units.la: Vltra Casilinum fluvium Calvi sunt, Opidum Episcopatus dignitate superbiens: Cales, numero multitudinis, Virgilio lib. vii. Æneidos: Κάλης, Ptolemæo; Calis, Frontino, ut & Itinerariæ Tabulæ, cui Cale auferendi casu. Auctor canitur ab Silio lib. viii. Calais, Boreæ F. post Argonautarum reditum in hæc loca profectus. Livius lib. viii. & Festus Ausones primos Calium Incolas fuisse tradunt. Coloniam eo deductam anno cccxx. scribit eodem libro Livius, qui eiusdem meminit lib. xxvii. & xxix. Cicero in Rullum & Frontinus Municipium vocant.
units.tr: Beyond the river Casilinum are Calvi, a town proud of the dignity of a bishopric: Cales, in the plural, in Virgil, book 7 of the Aeneid; Κάλης [Kales] in Ptolemy; Calis in Frontinus, as also in the Itinerary Table, where it is Cale in the ablative. Its founder is sung of by Silius, book 8: Calais, son of Boreas, who came to these parts after the return of the Argonauts. Livy, book 8, and Festus say the Ausones were the first inhabitants of Calium. Livy writes in the same book that a colony was founded there in the year 320, and mentions it again in books 27 and 29. Cicero, in his speech against Rullus, and Frontinus call it a Municipium.

units.la: Sequitur Caianellum, quod Calliculam Veteribus dictum ait Leander. Callicula Jugi meminit Livius lib. xxii. circa Casilinum: nescio an idem cum Gallicano Monte, qui & Massicus & Gaurus.
units.tr: There follows Caianellum, which Leander says was called Calliculam by the ancients. Livy, book 22, mentions Callicula Jugi near Casilinum; I do not know whether it is the same as Mount Gallicanus, which is also called Massicus and Gaurus.

units.la: Fuit haud procul inde Casilinum, Latinis & Itinerariæ Tabulæ: Κασίλινον Straboni, Appiano, Plutarcho: Βασιλίνας corrupte apud Zonaram. Vrbs haud procul Vulturni Ostio. Meminit sæpe Livius, nominatim lib. xxxiii. duobusque seq. Ductus eo fuit errore, ibique conclusus Hannibal, quum Casinum cogitaret; sedente tunc ad Turrim Fracolisam Fabio Maximo. Nota est Historia. Legendi præter alios Livius lib. xxii. & Plutarchus in Hannibale. Coloniam ab M. Antonio deductam, tradit Cicero Philippica ii. Auctore Festo, Vetus fuit Præfectura. Hodie, ut volunt Sanfelicius & Leander Albertus, Castellucio.
units.tr: Not far from there was Casilinum, called so by the Latins and in the Itinerary Table; Κασίλινον [Kasilinon] in Strabo, Appian and Plutarch; Βασιλίνας [Basilinas] corruptly in Zonaras. It was a town not far from the mouth of the Volturnus. Livy mentions it often, especially in book 33 and the two following. Hannibal was led there by error and was shut in there while he was planning to attack Casinum, Fabius Maximus then sitting at Turris Fracolisa. The story is well known; besides others, read Livy, book 22, and Plutarch in Hannibal. Cicero, in the second Philippic, says a colony was founded there by Mark Antony. According to Festus, it was formerly a prefecture. Today, as Sanfelicius and Leander Alberti think, it is called Castellucio.

units.la: Vlterius
units.tr: Further

units.la: Viterius ad Oltia Vulturni fluminis finitra, Vulturnum fuit Oppidum. Sic Livio, Plinio, Mela, funerariæ Tabulæ, alioque Latinus dicitur: quod οὐλτουρνος Dionysio, Strabone & Ptolemæo. Fuisse Castellum ad differentiam Castelli Volturni, citra Neapolim. Colonia Frontino Livioque libro xxxiv. Capua jam nunc offert se delineandam: Veterem dico, nulli non Latinorum Scriptorum, ut Itinerariæ Tabulæ notant. Sic κάπυα Stephano: Καπύη Ptolemæo, Dionysio Halicarnasseo, Appiano: Campana Vrbs Virgilio lib. x. Quod Vulturnus antea fuerit dicta, nomen Livius lib. iv. & Plutarchus in Hannibale. Neapolis aliquando vocata fuisse legitur apud Sigonium. Dicta autem Capua, vel ab Capi Ænea Socio, ut censent Virgilius lib. x. Æn. & ita Servius, Lucanus libro ii. Silius Italicus lib. ii. Dionysius lib. i. accedente & Inde nomine, quæ apud Suetonium in Cæsare cap. lxxxi. Livius lib. xxvi. Capua Samnitum Tuscorum vocat, vel ab Agro Campestri, ut putant Livius lib. xxiii. Strabo, Plinius, Plutarchus. Nonnulli sic appellatam volunt, quod Capys et alias ait. Vrbi nomen a Lanuvio constituta. Legendus Strabo libro v. Quidam ab Capua derivant, qui prima Tuscorum lingua Capys dicebatur. Alii, inter quos Diodorus, ab Capacitate trahunt & abundantia rerum omnium, quam loquuntur varia eius apud Ciceronem ii. in Rullum, quum dissuaderet ne ex Præfectura in Coloniam mutaretur, Encomia: Subsidium Belli, Fundamentum Rei publicæ, Horreum Legionum, Solatium Annonæ. Splendor eius, Amplitudo & Magnificentia ab omnibus tamenpore pathum celebratur. Non dicam omnia. Capua, ait Florus libro i. Hist. Rom. cap. xvi. & ipsa Caput Vrbium, quondam inter tres novissimo Romam Karthaginemque numerata. Altera Karthago Capua, inquit Silius libro xi. Altera Roma, Ausonius. Sic Mago apud Livium libro xxiii. dicit Capuam non Campaniæ modo, sed Italiæ Caput post adflictam Cannensi pugna Rem Romanam. Livius omnium Urbium Italiæ secundam Romam principem nominat libro, quem circa. Alia apud alios. Nimia Felicitas Intolerantia sæpe Mater. Capua Fortunam nacta obsequentem finitam, Arrogantiæ Proterviæque vitio caput laborare. Tettatur M. Tullius Agrarii ii. contra Rullum Campanos semper superbos fuisse hortatus Agrorum & Fructuum magnitudine, Vrbis salubritate & pulchritudine, nataque omnium rerum Copia, rerumque omnium adfluentia Arrogantiam, quæ alterum Vrbi Romæ Consulem e Capua pollutavit: eamque Luxuriem natam, quæ ipsum Hannibalem, Armis invictum, voluptate vicit & enervavit. Legendi præter alios Livius libro xxxi. Valerius Maximus lib. ix. cap. i. Silius Italicus libro xv. copiosissime, Auctor de V V. Illustr. cap. xlii. Pergens Cicero eleganter Capuam appellat Domicilium Superbiæ & Sedem Luxuriæ. Verum nimis illud apud Silium libro viii.
units.tr: Further on, at the mouth of the river Volturnus, on its border, Vulturnum was a town. Livy, Pliny, Mela, the funerary inscriptions and other Latin writers so call it, and Dionysius, Strabo and Ptolemy call it Volturnum. There was a small fort of this name, to distinguish it from the Castello di Volturno on this side of Naples. Frontinus and Livy in book 34 mention a colony. Capua now presents itself for description; I mean the old city, which all Latin writers mention, as the Itinerary tables note. Stephanus gives it as Capua, Ptolemy, Dionysius of Halicarnassus and Appian as Capue, and Virgil in book 10 calls it the city of Campania. That it was earlier called Volturnum, Livy in book 4 and Plutarch in his Life of Hannibal say. Sigonius reads that it was at one time called Neapolis. The name Capua is derived either from Capys, the companion of Aeneas, as Virgil in book 10 of the Aeneid thinks, and Servius likewise, and Lucan in book 2, Silius Italicus in book 2 and Dionysius in book 1 agree, with the addition of the name from Suetonius in Caesar chapter 81; or from the Campestrian field, as Livy in book 23, Strabo, Pliny and Plutarch think. Some want it so named because Capys and the others were so called. Strabo in book 5 should be read on the name of the city, which was founded by Lanuvium. Some derive Capua from Capys, the name it bore in the Tuscan language. Others, among them Diodorus, derive it from the capacity and abundance of all things. Cicero in his second speech against Rullus gives its many praises, when he dissuaded the Campanians from being transferred from a prefecture to a colony: the support of war, the foundation of the republic, the granary of the legions, the solace of the grain supply. Its splendour, greatness and magnificence have been celebrated by all for a long time. I shall not say everything. Capua, says Florus in book 1 of his Roman History, chapter 16, was itself the head of cities, once numbered among the three greatest, after Rome and Carthage. Silius in book 11 says: "Capua is another Carthage." Ausonius: "Another Rome." So Mago in Livy, book 23, says that Capua is the head not only of Campania but of Italy, since the Roman state was shaken by the battle of Cannae. Livy, in the book around this place, names Rome first and Capua second among all the cities of Italy. Other things are said by others. Excessive good fortune is often the mother of intolerance. Capua, having obtained a compliant fortune, suffered from the vice of arrogance and insolence. Marcus Tullius, in the second book of his Agrarian speeches against Rullus, urges that the Campanians had always been proud, from the size of their fields and their produce, the healthiness and beauty of the city, and the abundance and plenty of all things; and this arrogance, which gave Rome a consul from Capua, and that luxury which conquered and enervated Hannibal himself, invincible in arms, through pleasure. Among others, Livy in book 31, Valerius Maximus in book 9, chapter 1, Silius Italicus in book 15 very fully, and the author De viris illustribus, chapter 42, should be read. Cicero, continuing elegantly, calls Capua the home of pride and the seat of luxury. But the verse of Silius in book 8 is too true:

units.la: Capua heu relius servare serenis Inconsulta modum, & parvo pertitura tumore.
units.tr: Capua, alas, could not keep its measure in prosperous times, unmindful of restraint, and was doomed to fall by a small swelling.

units.la: Tam enim olim potens & superba tandem ab Romanis, quorum Imperii fuerat armula, post bellum Punicum ii. Præfectura conditionem accepit, scribente Livio libro xxvi. qui de Capua obsidione, obsessorumque Fortitudine & Magnanimitate, quæ Urbi Magnæ Fortuna fuerat secuta, omnino legendus. Præfectura manuit ad Consulatum usque C. Iulij Cæsaris, qui cos. cum M. Calpurnio Bibulo anno mdcxcv. Coloniam eo deduxit, ut videre est apud Paterculum, Suetonium in Cæsare cap. xx. & Frontinum de Colonis, cui Capua Julia Felix dicitur. Ut Colonia meminerunt Cicero ii. in Rullum, & ii. Philippica, Suetonius in Cæsare cap. lxxxi. & in Octaviano cap. iv. Resurgens postea auspiciis Imperatorum reflorere nonnihil caput sub P. R. potestate, donec ab Genserico Vandalorum Rege capta subversaque, ab Ostrogothis dein occupataque hispulsis ab Narsete restaurata: tandem post annos fere centum ab Langobardis iterum excita fuit atque deleta. Stantem potenter, cadentemque miserabiliter, canit scite magnus Poëta Ausonius Magnus: Nec Capuam Pelago, Calisque, Penumque potentem Delectis, Opibus, Lamaque priore siche. Fortuna variante ei, quæ freta fecunda Nescivit servare Medoma, nam subdita Romæ, Credula tunc Fidei memor, an insula Senatum Sperneret. Spumeret, an celeret, dubitans: sperare Curules Campanis aula auspiciis: unaque suorum Corsale ac Imperium divisi attolleret Orbis. Saepe etiam Rerum Dominam, Latiqve Parentem Aggrediunt bello, Ducibus non freta Togatis Cannensi clade mutatas armis deceptaque in Hostis Sera rursum demens specie transfert herilis: Moxque in occasum vitus communibus actis Corruerent Pani Luxu, Campania Tastu, (Et a sinu quam flabilem sortita superbis Sedem) Ista paucae, opibusque valens, Roma altera quondam, Ponere quae paribus petuit fastigia comis, Obstantum rejecta locum vix pone tuetur.
units.tr: For Capua, once so powerful and proud, was at last, after the Second Punic War, reduced by the Romans, whose empire it had been a little part of, to the condition of a prefecture. Livy, book 26, who describes the siege of Capua, the courage and magnanimity of the besieged, which followed the great fortune of the city, must be read in full. The prefecture lasted until the consulship of Gaius Julius Caesar, who, as consul with Marcus Calpurnius Bibulus in the year 695 of the city, led a colony there, as may be seen in Paterculus, in Suetonius's Caesar chapter 20, and in Frontinus On Colonies, where it is called Capua Julia Felix. Cicero in his second speech against Rullus and in the second Philippic, and Suetonius in Caesar chapter 81 and in Augustus chapter 4, mention it as a colony. Afterwards, rising again under the auspices of the emperors, it somewhat revived its head under the power of the Roman people, until it was taken and overthrown by Genseric, king of the Vandals, then occupied by the Ostrogoths, and restored after they were driven out by Narses. At last, after nearly a hundred years, it was again roused and destroyed by the Lombards. Great Ausonius sings wittily of it, standing powerful and falling wretchedly: "Nor Capua, powerful by the sea, and Cales and Pennus, chosen for its wealth and its former Lamae..." Fortune, changing, did not know how to keep the fertile seas of Medoma; for when it was subject to Rome, uncertain whether the island, mindful of faith, would spurn the Senate or boast, it hoped for curule offices under the Campanian auspices, and together with its own people wished to raise the whole divided world to its rule. Often they attacked the mistress of things and the parent of Latium in war, with leaders not in togas; after the Cannaean disaster, changed by arms and deceived into the hostile. Again the mad slave, in the appearance of his master, carried them over; and soon, with their vices common to their deeds, they fell into the west: Pani by luxury, Campania by its taste, and the seat they had obtained from a windy bay, proud. Capua, small and strong in resources, once a second Rome, which sought to set its gables level with the equal combs, scarcely holds its ground, cast out from its position of resistance.

units.la: Cautas etiam Interitus tantae Urbis paucis indicat Silius Italicus: Lucro & infamis nutrita Ignavia Luxu, Coniunctisque Pudor peccando, unique relictus Dedecus probrosus Honor, laceravit huantem Deluta Capuam, ac resolutam Legibus Urbem Proximaque exitio truculenta superbia semper, Nec Virtus decerant vires: non largior ulli Auxilia Populo (sic tum Fortuna favebat) Aurique Argentique modus: madefactaque veneno Assyrio manibus Vestis: medioque dierum Regales Epula: atque ortu Convivia Solis Deprensa: & nulla macula non inlita Vita: Tum Populo favet Patres: Plebesque Senatus Invidia lacera: & conlidens dissona corda, Sedatio: sedemi interea temeraria Pubes Delicta augebat: pollutior ipsa Senectus;
units.tr: Silius Italicus also briefly indicates the causes of the ruin of so great a city: its ignorance, nourished by gain and infamous luxury, shame joined to sinning, and the disgraceful honour left alone, tore the wretched Capua, a city dissolved in laws, and fierce pride, always near to destruction. Its virtue did not lack strength; no people received larger help (such was Fortune's favour then), and there was no measure of gold and silver. Clothes were soaked in Assyrian poison by hand, royal feasts were held in the middle of the day, and banquets were detected at sunrise, and life was smeared with every stain. Then the Senate favoured the people, and the commons, torn by envy of the Senate, and discordant hearts clashing, sedition; meanwhile reckless youth increased their crimes, and old age itself was more polluted.

units.la: & quae ibi alia. Vituntur hodie eius altero ab Nova Capua lapide peringentes Ruinae, juxta Templum D. Mariae Gratiarum. Exstant Portae semirutae, Amphitheatrum, quod aliquo modo describit Laurentius Schraderus in Italiae Monumentis, immenta Porticuum, Thermarum, Aedificiorumque Publicorum rudera: praeter haec longa vastaque Aquarum Receptacula subterranea & Castella, quae, qualis & quanta fuerit antiqua Urbs, abunde restantur. Capitoly Capuani mentio apud Suetonium in Tiberii Principis Vita cap. xl. Aurea, Argentea, Aerea Numismata, Gemmae, Marmora, aliaque summi Luxus indicia quotidie ab Incolis effodiuntur. Ex Antiquae autem diruta Ruinis Nova coepit excitari, feliciterque crevere, quam conspicere jamnunc est aedificatam limitrae Vulturni ripae, duodecimo ab Mari lapide, in planicie, latus magnificam, commode habitatam, sed infrequentius; stratam Silicibus, Plateas habentem amplas & rectas, altaque Aedificia. Adiunt eam ab Ortu & Septemtrione Vulturnus, indeque in Oceanum reflectitur. Pons est supra amnem ex lapide insignis. Templum S. Benedicti dicatum fuisse creditur Isidi. Regitur ipsum Magistratibus, eademque Resp. forma, qua Neapolis. Civium Mores superbia ab Antiquis non differunt. Eius Moenia Conradus, Friderici II. Imp. F. dejecit, Urbemque directam calamitate adfecit ingenti. Cautam exponit Blondus libro xvii. Hist. Aliam deinde nominem cladem sustinuit sub Alexandro vi. P. M. Videndus Sabellicus. Episcopatum Capuae Novae evexit in Archiepiscopatum Ioannes xiv. P. M. quum Othoni ii. Imper. Aug. Coronam imponeret. Legendi Blondus & Platina. Huic qui suffragentur, alibi a me dictum. Capuam Novam ortu suo nobilitarunt Raimundus, Praedicatorum Generalis Magister xxxiii. & Ioannes Antonius Campanus, Scriptis clari. Multae ibi nobiles Familiae, quae vulgo: Antignani, d' Aricenzo, d' Azzia, di Capua, d' Lboli, di Falco, Feramosca, Ferrara, Gaiazzi, Gallo, Dinognano, delli Leoni, Lanza, Marchesi, Maggio, Olimpio, Pantoleani, Pelegrini, Pettenato, di Rinaldo, Roffi, Sintisale, di Tomasi, delle Vigne, Vitelli; & aliae. Post Urbem Romam nullo in loco plures Inscriptiones, sed vetustate admodum consumtae. Campanos quondam Oppos fuisse nuncupatos, notat Servius ad lib. vii. Aeneid. tas Olivas; item Myrtum ejusdem in Luco conspicuæ magnitudinis: & sub ea Speculum fuisse dicit, in quo Manes ejus custodire Draco serebatur. Ab eo Linterna Palus Silio libro vii: hodie Lago della Patria. Dixi alibi. Linternum Fluvij nomen, hoc tractu Straboni & Livio libro xxxii: patria vulgo Linternum Ciceroni in Epistolis ad Atticum, Prædium fortean in subburbicario Linterni Agro. Meminit Plinius libro xiiii cap. iiii.
units.tr: And many other things there. Today its ruins, which still stand on the other side of the new Capua, are pointed out, near the church of Santa Maria delle Grazie. The half-ruined gates remain, an amphitheatre, which Laurentius Schraderus describes in some way in his Monuments of Italy, the vast remains of porticoes, baths and public buildings; besides these, the long and vast underground water reservoirs and castles, from which the extent and size of the ancient city can be sufficiently judged. Mention of the Capitol of Capua is made by Suetonius in the Life of the emperor Tiberius, chapter 40. Gold, silver and bronze coins, gems, marbles and other signs of the greatest luxury are dug up daily by the inhabitants. From the ruins of the old city the new one began to be raised and grew happily; it can now be seen built on the bank of the Volturnus, twelve miles from the sea, on a plain, a large city, conveniently inhabited, though rather thinly; paved with flints, with broad and straight streets and tall buildings. The Volturnus flows past it on the east and north, and then turns back into the sea. There is a notable stone bridge over the river. The church of St. Benedict is believed to have been dedicated to Isis. It is governed by magistrates, and its form of republic is the same as that of Naples. The morals of its citizens do not differ from those of the ancients in pride. Conrad, son of the emperor Frederick II, threw down its walls and inflicted a huge calamity on the city, which was thus laid low. Blondus in book 17 of his History describes this disaster. Afterwards it suffered another calamity under Alexander VI, the Supreme Pontiff; Sabellicus should be consulted. John XIV, the Supreme Pontiff, raised the bishopric of New Capua to an archbishopric, when he placed the crown on Otto II, the august emperor. Blondus and Platina should be read. Those who favour this I have discussed elsewhere. Raimundus, Master General of the Preachers, the thirty-third, and John Antony Campanus, famous for his writings, ennobled New Capua by their birth. Many noble families are there, commonly called: Antignani, d'Aricenzo, d'Azzia, di Capua, d'Lboli, di Falco, Feramosca, Ferrara, Gaiazzi, Gallo, Dinognano, delli Leoni, Lanza, Marchesi, Maggio, Olimpio, Pantoleani, Pelegrini, Pettenato, di Rinaldo, Roffi, Sintisale, di Tomasi, delle Vigne, Vitelli, and others. After the city of Rome there is no place with more inscriptions, but they are much worn away by age. Servius, on book 7 of the Aeneid, notes that the Campanians were once called Opi; likewise the olive trees and a myrtle of remarkable size in the grove, and under it he says there was a mirror, in which it was said a dragon guarded its shades. From this comes Linterna Palus in Silius, book 7; today it is Lago della Patria. I have spoken of it elsewhere. Linternum is the name of a river, in this region mentioned by Strabo and Livy in book 32; the country people call it Linternum, and Cicero in his Letters to Atticus mentions it, perhaps as an estate in the suburban region of Linternum. Pliny mentions it in book 14, chapter 4.

units.la: Hinc Iunere juxta Mare Millibus passuum quinque usque Cumas, Villa fuit Servilij Vaccia, Hominis nobilis & opulenti, sed ignavi & solitarij: de quo Seneca Epistola lv.
units.tr: From here, along the sea near Iunere, five miles to Cumae, there was the villa of Servilius Vaccia, a man of noble birth and wealth, but idle and solitary. Seneca writes of him in Letter 55.

units.la: Sequitur inde locus antiquissimæ Vrbis Cumarum. Cumæ Livio, Tacito, Silio Plinio, Solino, Melæ, Antonino, Itinerariæ Tabulæ, & quibus non Latinorum? Κύμη Straboni, Ptolemæo, Dionysio, aliisque Græcis: Cumæa Urbs Virgilio libro iii. Conditores ejus Cumæi Euboni; qui Ducibus Hippocle & Megasthene, cum Chalcidensibus in Italiam venerunt, teste Dyonisio lib. viii, Livio libro viii, Strabone, Plinio, Solino, Servio ad lib. iii & vi Æneidos: quo notante, Cumæ dictæ vel ἀπὸ τῆς κύων, id est prægnante (nam ibidem prægnans Mulier inventa fœcunditatis omen ipsis dederat) vel ab Cudis, quas Græci Κύμαται vocant. Legendi Strabo, Dionysius, Livius, alij. Cumæ in Monte adscensu difficili arduoque positas & ad Mare spectavisse, tradit Agathias lib. i. Belli Gothici. Infimam fluctus marini adluebant: superiora Muris, Turribus, aliisque molibus adeo erant circumvallata & munita, ut locus expugnatu esset difficillimus. Nunc omnia fere concidêrunt, oppletaque jacent ruinis, ut tamen undique amplissimorum operum vestigia satis agnoscantur. Erat in vertice Rupis urbe media celeberrimum Apollinis Templum, de quo Virgilius libro v Aeneid. At puus Aeneas Arces, quibus altus Apollo Præsidet, horrendæque procul secreta Sibyllæ Antrum immane petit.
units.tr: Next comes the site of the very ancient city of Cumae. It is called Cumae by Livy, Tacitus, Silius, Pliny, Solinus, Mela, Antoninus, the Itinerary tables, and what Latin writer does not? Kyme [Κύμη] in Strabo, Ptolemy, Dionysius and the other Greeks. Virgil in Book 3 calls it the Cumaean city. Its founders were the Cumaean Euboeans, who came to Italy with the Chalcidians under their leaders Hippocles and Megasthenes, as Dionysius (Book 8), Livy (Book 8), Strabo, Pliny, Solinus, and Servius on Aeneid 3 and 6 attest. Servius notes that Cumae was named either from κύων, that is pregnant (for there a pregnant woman had been found, which gave them an omen of fertility), or from Cudis, which the Greeks call Kymata. Strabo, Dionysius, Livy, and others should be read. Agathias (Book 1 of the Gothic War) says that Cumae lay on a mountain, reached by a difficult and steep climb, and faced the sea. The waves washed its lowest part, while the upper parts were so surrounded and fortified with walls, towers and other structures that the place was very hard to take. Now almost everything has fallen and lies buried in ruins, though traces of its vast works can still be recognised everywhere. On the summit of the rock, in the middle of the city, stood the famous temple of Apollo, of which Virgil writes in Aeneid Book 6: "But pious Aeneas makes for the citadels over which lofty Apollo presides, and for the vast cave of the dread Sibyl, far off."

units.la: Quos versus exponens Servius in Arce munitissima Cumis Ædem Apollinis fuisse scribit. Cumarum mentionem facit non raro Dionysius Halicarnass. nominatim lib. vii Antiq. Roman. ubi multa de Aristodemo Malaco, Cumanorum Duce, Rebusque ab Cumani gestis. L. Tarquinium Superbum ad eundem Aristodemum, Cumanorum Principem confugisse, scribunt idem libro vi & Livius lib. ii, qui alibi libro iv Romanos Urbem Cumas ab Græcis habitatam expugnasse commemorat: item libro viii Cumanos atque Sinuessanos eadem lege, qua Capuam haberi, Senatum censuisse. Cumanorum item Fidem erga Populum Romanum narrat idem libro xxxiii. Tradit etiam Strabo Cumanos in potestatem olim ab Campanis fuisse redactos. Cumæ Vetus aliquando Municipium, aliquando Præfectura fuit, testibus Livio & Festo: postea Coloniam eo ab Augusto fuisse deductam, paretex Frontino. Ab Cumis Cumanus Campus & Cumanus Sinus, de quibus alibi: & Cumanum, Villa circa Cumas, cujus meminit Cicero in Epistolis.
units.tr: Explaining these lines, Servius writes that in the most strongly fortified citadel of Cumae there was a temple of Apollo. Dionysius of Halicarnassus often mentions the Cumaeans, especially in Book 7 of the Roman Antiquities, where he tells much about Aristodemus Malacus, leader of the Cumaeans, and the deeds of the Cumaeans. The same author in Book 6, and Livy in Book 2, write that Lucius Tarquinius Superbus fled to this same Aristodemus, prince of the Cumaeans. Livy elsewhere, in Book 4, records that the Romans took the city of Cumae, inhabited by Greeks; and in Book 8 he reports that the Senate decreed that the Cumaeans and the Sinuessans should be held under the same law by which Capua was held. The same author, in Book 33, tells of the loyalty of the Cumaeans toward the Roman people. Strabo also states that the Cumaeans were once brought under the power of the Campanians. Cumae was at one time a municipality and at another a prefecture, as Livy and Festus testify; later, Frontinus records, Augustus led a colony there. From Cumae come the Cumaean Plain and the Cumaean Gulf, of which more elsewhere; and the Cumanum, a villa near Cumae, which Cicero mentions in his Letters.

units.la: Ab Cumis dein ad Avernum usque Lacum nihil invenitur scitu dignum præter Sibyllæ (quæ ab Cumis, Patria Cumæa, omnibus decantata) Cavernam, ut vocant. Meminerunt hujus Antri Virgilius vi Aeneidos libro, & Symmachus lib. iiii Epist. xxxiii. Describit autem plene Leander Albertus in Campania; qui inter alia censet Viam hic fuisse ab Cumis per Avernum Baias subterraneam, quam Cocceium fecisse notat Strabo; Cymmerios his locis olim habitasse in Antris & Specubus subterraneis, quas Argyllas nominabant, addens.
units.tr: From Cumae as far as Lake Avernus nothing worth knowing is found, except the cave of the Sibyl, as it is called, who was sung of by all, a native of Cumae. Virgil in Book 6 of the Aeneid and Symmachus in Book 4, Letter 33, mention this cave. Leander Albertus describes it fully in his work on Campania. Among other things he thinks that there was a road here from Cumae through Avernus to Baiae, underground, which Strabo notes was made by Cocceius. He adds that the Cimmerians once lived in these places, in caves and underground hollows, which they called Argyllae.

units.la: Tribus Cuma Urbe millibus Hamarum Silva fuit; Sacer Lucus antiquis. Dixi supra. Hama Livio notæ libro xxiii. Ruinas conspici hactenus in arduo Monte, qui à Balneis Tripergulanis abest P. M. cio io. scribit Dalechampius. Videndus item Scipio Mazzella de Puteolanorum Antiquitatibus.
units.tr: Three miles from the city of Cumae was the Hamarum Silva, the sacred grove of the ancients, as I said above. Hama is known from Livy, Book 23. The ruins can be seen to this day on a steep mountain, which is about P. M. 1010 from the baths of Tripergula, according to Dalechamps. Scipione Mazzella's work on the antiquities of Puteoli should also be consulted.

units.la: Haud procul inde Mare Mortuum, Sinus Batanus, Lucrinus & Avernus, de quibus alibi. Chersonnesum quamdam faciunt ab Cumis incipientem, uti ab Strabone describitur.
units.tr: Not far from there are the Dead Sea, the Batanian Gulf, Lucrinus and Avernus, of which elsewhere. They form a kind of peninsula beginning at Cumae, as Strabo describes it.

units.la: In ejus Chersonnesi radicibus Baiæ erant, Latinis Græcisque notissimæ, Aeris temperie, Romanorum frequentia, Aedificiorum ornamentis celeberrimæ. Q. Horatius Flaccus: Nullus in orbe Sinus Baijs pralucet amœnis, Si diuit deees, Lacus & Mare sentit amorem Fœminaque bene. cui fi rtisofa libido Fecerit auspicium, &c.——
units.tr: At the roots of this peninsula lay Baiae, very well known to Latins and Greeks, celebrated for the mildness of its air, the crowds of Romans, and the adornments of its buildings. Quintus Horatius Flaccus: "No bay on earth shines more brightly than the lovely Baiae's; if the Lake and Sea feel a lover's passion for the goddesses and for good women, then whatever wanton desire has made a beginning..."

units.la: Sic Martialis: Littus beata gentis aureum Baiæ: Baiæ superba blanda dona Naturæ Vt mille tandem, Hæc e versus Baiæ: Laudatro digne non tamen satis Baiæ.
units.tr: Thus Martial: "Baiae, the golden shore of a blessed people; Baiae, the proud and charming gift of Nature; a thousand times Baiae, though never sufficiently praised..."

units.la: {a}Vestigia superstant ingentium nimirum Pelago demersa operum fundamenta, cum Plateis silicatis. Vrbis Interitus ab Terræmotuum exortus vt fertur. Nominis originem a Baio quodam Vlyssis Socio hic sepulto fluxisse scribit Strabo. Silius Italicus in libris de bello Punico: Primores adsunt Capuæ: docet ille tepentes Unde ferant nomen Baiæ: comitemque dedisse Dulcibus Fuppii flagne sua nomina monstrat.
units.tr: {a}Remains of enormous works still stand, foundations sunk beneath the sea, together with paved streets. The city's ruin is said to have arisen from earthquakes. Strabo writes that the origin of the name is to be traced to a certain Baius, a companion of Ulysses, who was buried here. Silius Italicus, in his books on the Punic War: "The leading men of Capua are present; he shows where the warm waters are, from which Baiae takes its name, and he has given a companion to the sweet pools of Puteoli, showing their own names."

units.la: Balarum descriptio extat apud Callixodorum libro ix Variarum ad Primiscrinium. Synodus Constantinopolitana vi habita sub Constantino Magno Imp. has Baias Siciliæ tribuit. Baiæ Insulas & Civitates circa Siciliam habet Hacius in Lycophronem. Rationem alibi aperit. Baiensis Vici Episcopus Ajacipus est apud Gennadium.
units.tr: A description of Balae exists in Cassiodorus, Book 9 of the Variae, to the Primicerius. The Synod of Constantinople, the sixth, held under the Emperor Constantine the Great, assigns these Baiae to Sicily. Hacius, on Lycophron, gives Baiae islands and cities around Sicily; he explains the reason elsewhere. Ajacipus is the bishop of the Baian village, according to Gennadius.

units.la: Iuxta vicinas Rupes in Littore varia sunt Balnea, cum quæ Baiana vocant Accolæ, Medici Stufæ: tum quæ Medicis Bagni di Tritoli, vulgo di Cicerone, item di Prato. Aquarum Ciceronianarum meminit Plinius libro xxxi Nat. Hist. cap. 11. Sic autem dicebantur ab Villa Ciceronis, Academiæ nomine clara, cuius meminit apud eundem Plinium, Spartianum & Philostratum libro viii Apollon. Hodie Stadio dicitur, ut refert Ferd. Lofredus, sed Ciceroniano, testibus Fr. Lombardo & Antonio Sanfelicio. Alia præterea, quæ Strabo commemorat, non solum adfectæ valitudini auxiliantia, verum etiam quæ Voluptati & Deliciis oportuna. De Portu Baiano alibi ut de Sinu vel Lacu Lucrino, qui etiam Baianus cognominatur. Ad Baianum Sinum Templum Herculis Bauli fuisse antiquissimum, rotunda forma, constat ex Strabone & Plinio. Baulis locus circa Baias Plinio, Ciceroni, Silio, Suetonio, Dioni, aliis: Tacito item lib. xiv locanti cum inter Misenum Promontorium & Bajanum Lacum. De iis Martialis: Dum petit à Baulis mater Caræa Baias, Occidit insani crimine mersa freti. Gloria quanta periit cum Neroni monstra Nec quondam tulisse præ, sterilis aquæ.
units.tr: Along the nearby cliffs on the shore there are various baths: some the locals call Baiana, which physicians call Stufae, and others which physicians call Bagni di Tritoli, commonly di Cicerone, and likewise di Prato. Pliny mentions the Ciceronian waters in Natural History Book 31, chapter 11. They were so called from the villa of Cicero, famous under the name of Academy, which Pliny, Spartianus and Philostratus (Life of Apollonius, Book 8) also mention. Today it is called Stadio, as Ferdinando Lofredo reports, but Ciceroniano, according to Fr. Lombardo and Antonio Sanfelice. Strabo also records other springs, useful not only for sick health but also for pleasure and luxury. The Baian Harbour is treated elsewhere, as is the Gulf or Lake Lucrinus, which is also called Baian. It is established from Strabo and Pliny that there was a very ancient temple of Hercules at Bauli, round in shape, by the Baian Gulf. Bauli is a place near Baiae, mentioned by Pliny, Cicero, Silius, Suetonius, Dio and others; Tacitus also mentions it in Book 14, placing it between the promontory of Misenum and the Lake of Baiae. Martial speaks of these: "While Caraea, the mother, was making for Baiae from Bauli, she perished, drowned by the crime of the mad sea. How much glory was lost when the monsters were not shown to Nero, nor the once barren water."

units.la: Sic Silius Italicus libro xii de bello Punico: ——ludet Herculeos in littore Baulos.
units.tr: Thus Silius Italicus in Book 12 of the Punic War: "...he will play at Hercules' Bauli on the shore."

units.la: Symmachus: ——Inde recens atque Baulis Baulos Nuncupat.
units.tr: Symmachus: "...Then the newly named Bauli names Bauli..."

units.la: Ex eodem constat Hortensij prius fuisse Villam. A Puteolis distare xxvi stadiis, notat Zonaras libro ii: Nomen hodie retinere tellatur Ferd. Lofredus. Bagola, inquit Ortelius, vocabat Nauta, cuius opera Sinum Puteolanum navigabat. Alii Monte Barbaro vocatur, sed male, eundem Ortelij iudicio, Alexandrum Imperatorem splendidissimam Villam in Sinu Bajano cum Stagno Mammeæ Matri adificasse, quod etiam sua memoria nomine Mammeæ celebrabatur, tradit Spartianus eumdem & alia in Bajano opera magnifica in gratiam & honorem continguncorum Stagnaque mirabilia admisso Mari fecisse notans.
units.tr: From the same source it is clear that this was formerly the villa of Hortensius. Zonaras, Book 2, notes that it was 26 stadia from Puteoli. Ferdinando Lofredo says the name is still kept today. Ortelius says that the sailors called it Bagola, and by their work they navigated the Gulf of Puteoli. Others call it Monte Barbaro, but wrongly, in Ortelius's judgement. Spartianus records that the Emperor Alexander built a most splendid villa in the Baian Gulf, with a pool, for his mother Mammaea, and that in his own time it was celebrated under her name. He notes that he also did many other magnificent works in Baiae, in favour and honour of the bathers, and made wonderful pools by admitting the sea.

units.la: Visitur prope Baias Ædificium descendentis gradum xi in ipsis Terræ viscerbus, operis admirandi, latere calceque factum, quatuor columnarum ordinibus. Adcolis Piscina Mirabilis dicitur. Credunt nonnulli Piscinam hanc olim fuisse Lucullj Baianam, ubi ille mensibus hibernis agere erat solitus. Legendus Plutarchus in eius Vita Vitruvianæ Villam deferretur ingravescente morbo, ut illic Tiberium Imperatorem, auctor est Tacitus libro iii.
units.tr: Near Baiae one can see a building with eleven steps descending into the very bowels of the earth, a work of wonderful construction, made of brick and lime, with four rows of columns. The locals call it the Wonderful Fishpond. Some believe this fishpond was once the Baian villa of Lucullus, where he used to spend the winter months. Plutarch should be read in his Life. Tacitus, Book 3, says that the Emperor Tiberius, as his illness grew worse, was carried to the Vitruvian villa there.

units.la: Sunt & ad Avernum Lacum, vicinisque Locis multa Balnea, quæ vulgo Bagni dei dell' Arco,di Raverio, di Triperçola,di S. Niccolo,di Scrofa,di S. Lucia,dell' Arculo, vel di S. Maria,della Croce,di Cantarello,di Fontana,dell' olio Petrolio,Di Culma,del Sole & della Luna di Gimlorefo,dei Vefio,di Fatu,di Bracula,della Spelunca, & alia.
units.tr: Also at Lake Avernus and in the places nearby there are many baths, commonly called Bagni dell' Arco, di Raverio, di Triperçola, di S. Niccolo, di Scrofa, di S. Lucia, dell' Arculo, or di S. Maria, della Croce, di Cantarello, di Fontana, dell' olio Petrolio, di Culma, del Sole and della Luna di Gimlorefo, dei Vefio, di Fatu, di Bracula, della Spelunca, and others.

units.la: In Viis,quae Puteolos ducunt,tum in ora Littoris, tum intus in continenti colli- busque tam multae splendidissimorum Operum ruinae conspiciuntur, ut Sinum intuentibus mirifice ituporem. Inter alia Amphitheatrum occurit ex quadrato lapide propemodum integrum, sed inaequali forma. Longitudo enim areae pedes CLXXII, latitudo xc1 continet. Suetonius addit eatum testatur ad Ludos in honorem Vulcani, quos etiam Augustus spectavit. Hodie proscissum Aratro Frumento est constitum.
units.tr: Along the roads that lead to Puteoli, both on the shore and inland over the plain and hills, so many ruins of magnificent works are visible that they strike the viewer of the bay with wonder. Among other things, an Amphitheatre appears, almost entire, built of square stone but of irregular shape. Its arena measures 172 feet in length and 91 in breadth. Suetonius adds that it was used for the games in honour of Vulcan, which Augustus also attended. Today it has been ploughed up and is planted with grain.

units.la: Non procul hinc subterraneum est Aedificium,multis instructum Cellis, Labyrinthum Adcolis vocatum.
units.tr: Not far from here is an underground building, fitted with many cells, which the locals call the Labyrinth.

units.la: In proximo sunt Puteoli Sic Livio,Plinio,Tacito,Melae, Vitruvio, Itinerariae Tabulae,aliis dicitur Herculei Straboni,Ptolemaeo, Stephano:quae Pozzuolo vernacule. Δικαιαρχεια ab administratione Iustitiae,tanctissimoque Imperio quondam nuncupatam,tribunt cum aliis Strabo, Paulus, Stephanus,cui Δικαια quoque dicitur. Dicarchia legitur apud Silium: Dicarchia apud Petronium. Ceadilla corrupte apud Hieronymum de Locis Hebraicis. Dicaearchia Minor etiam appellata fuit, ut tradit Festus:ab Sanus conditam addens,in fine Olympiados lxii,ut numerat Eusebius in Chronic. adstipulante Stephano Byzantio. Emporium Cumanorum celeberrimum. Idem Festus Puteolos unam ex his Praefecturis aliquando fuisse dicit, in quas Praefecti Populi Romani Suffragiis creati mittebantur. Coloniam eo deductam primum a Q.Fabio Maximo notat Livius libro v;mox P. Cornelio Scipione Africano II.& Ti.Sempronio cos. anno ab u. c. 191x scribit idem libro xxxiv cum Velleio Paterculo lib. 1. Colonis eorumque Posteris intermortuis, Colonia esse desinit,ad Municipale Ius transgressa. Cicero Oratione pro Coelio: Nam quod est objectum Municipibus adoescentem non esse probatum suis; nemini umquam praesenti Puteolani maiorem honorem habuerunt. Iterum novis ab Augusto Colonis adscriptis, Augusta fuit cognominata,teste Frontino:auctoque rursum ipsidem ab Nerone, cognomen ab eodem est adepta,scribente Tacito libro xiv.Meminerunt ut Coloniae Veteres Inscriptiones,quaeque Neapoli hodie leguntur: AB COLONIA. DEDVCTA. ANNO. XC. N. FVFIDIO. N. F. M. PVLLIO. DVO, VIR P. RVTILIO. CN. MALLIO. COS OPERVM. LEX. II
units.tr: Nearby is Puteoli, as Livy, Pliny, Tacitus, Mela, Vitruvius and the Itinerary tables call it; others call it Herculea, following Strabo, Ptolemy and Stephanus. In the vernacular it is Pozzuolo. Strabo, Paulus and Stephanus, among others, say it was once called Dicaearchia [Δικαιαρχεια], from the administration of justice and its most sacred government. Stephanus also calls it Δικαια. Dicarchia is the reading in Silius, and Dicarchia in Petronius. Ceadilla is the corrupt form in Jerome's book on Hebrew places. It was also called Dicaearchia Minor, as Festus relates, adding that it was founded by Sanus at the end of the sixty-second Olympiad, as Eusebius counts it in his Chronicle, with Stephanus of Byzantium agreeing. It was a very famous trading place of the Cumaeans. Festus also says that Puteoli was at one time one of those prefectures to which prefects were sent, chosen by the votes of the Roman people. Livy, in book 5, notes that it was first settled as a Coloniam by Q. Fabius Maximus; then, as the same Livy writes in book 34 along with Velleius Paterculus in book 1, it was settled again under P. Cornelius Scipio Africanus the Younger and Ti. Sempronius, consuls, in the year 191 from the founding of the city. When the colonists and their descendants had died out, it ceased to be a Colonia and passed over to the Municipale Ius. Cicero, in his speech for Caelius: "For as to what is objected to the townsmen, that the young man was not approved by his own people, no one present ever had greater honour from the Puteolani." When new colonists were enrolled again by Augustus, it was surnamed Augusta, as Frontinus testifies; and when it was enlarged again by Nero, it took its name from him, as Tacitus writes in book 14. Old inscriptions of the Coloniae remember this, and those still read today at Naples say: "FROM THE COLONY LED OUT IN THE YEAR 90. N. FUFIDIUS N.F. M. PULLIUS, DUUMVIR P. RUTILIUS, CN. MALLIUS, CONSULS. WORK OF THE LAW, SECOND."

units.tr: FOR THE SAFETY, VICTORY OF THE AUGUSTI, TO THE GREAT GOD GENIUS OF THE COLONY OF PUTEOLI, AND OF HIS OWN NATIVE LAND

units.la: Q. AVRELIVS. HERMADION. SEVIR. AUGUSTALIS. ET. CURATOR. EORVM EXSTRVXIT. ET. DONVM. DAT
units.tr: Q. AURELIUS HERMADION, SEVIR AUGUSTALIS AND CURATOR OF THEM, BUILT THIS AND GIVES IT AS A GIFT.

units.la: Puteoli nomen esse innuit Strabo libro v Ἀπὸ τῶν Φρεάτων, vel ex aliorum mente, Ἀπὸ τῆς δυσωδίας τῶν ὑδάτων, id est,ut, quo respicit Auctor, Etymon aperiamus, a Puteis, vel à Putore salientium Aquarum sulphureo. Videndus Festus. Incolae Puteolani cum aliis, tum Inscriptionibus quarum una,quae Populonij extat, sic inter alia habet: VIRI PERFECTISS.ET PRINCIPALES.ET.SPLENDIDISSIMVS. ORDO. ET POPVLVS. PVTEOLANORVM. Sita est haec Vrbs in excelsa Rupe,quae undique praeceps. Inexpugnabilem efficiunt cum Mare, tum Murus,quo circumdata. Vnus modo est aditus,isque angustus per Pontem. Maiorem olim fuisse loquuntur quae in proximo visuntur ingentes aedificiorum ruinae. Vrbis medio Templum antiquissimum,opere Corinthiaco,ex quadrato lapide cernitur;crebrorum Terraemotuum impetu nonnihil deformatum: Christiani D.Proculo sacrarunt,Augusto ante dicatum;quod mutila testatur Inscriptio:
units.tr: Strabo in book v hints that the name of Puteoli comes from Ἀπὸ τῶν Φρεάτων [from the wells], or, in the opinion of others, Ἀπὸ τῆς δυσωδίας τῶν ὑδάτων [from the stench of the waters]; that is, to uncover the etymology to which the author refers, it comes either from Puteis [wells] or from Putore [stench] of the sulphurous bubbling waters. Festus should be consulted. The inhabitants are called Puteolani, as both other sources and inscriptions show; one of these, which exists at Populonia, says among other things: THE MOST PERFECT MEN AND LEADERS, AND THE MOST SPLENDID ORDER AND PEOPLE OF PUTEOLI. This city is situated on a high rock, steep on every side. Both the sea and the wall with which it is surrounded make it impregnable. There is only one approach, and that is narrow, across a bridge. The huge ruins of buildings which are seen nearby say that it was larger formerly. In the middle of the city stands a very ancient temple, of Corinthian work, made of square stone; it has been somewhat disfigured by the force of frequent earthquakes. Christians consecrated it to St. Proculus, though it was earlier dedicated to Augustus, as a mutilated inscription testifies:

units.la: {y} Puteolani, Incolae, Situs, Publica opera, Unde dicti, Municipium, Colonia iterum, Labyrinthus, Conditores, Praefectura, Colonia, Amphitheatrum: marginal catchwords.
units.tr: Puteolani, Inhabitants, Situation, Public works, Whence named, Municipality, Colony again, Labyrinth, Founders, Prefecture, Colony, Amphitheatre.

units.la: LIBER I. TEMPLVM AVGVSTO, CVM ORNAMENTIS D.D.
units.tr: BOOK I. THE TEMPLE OF AUGUSTUS, WITH ITS ORNAMENTS, DEDICATED TO THE GODS

units.la: Operis Architectus qui fuerit, loquuntur quæ in pariete Templi sinistro leguntur his Characteribus: L. COCCIVS. L C. POSTVMI. L AVCTVS. ARCHITECT
units.tr: Who the architect of the work was is stated by the letters read in these characters on the left wall of the temple: L. COCCIVS. L C. POSTVMI. L AVCTVS. ARCHITECT.

units.la: Templum Neptuni magnificentissimum ibidem fuisse constat ex Cicerone: visunturque eius adhuc rudera vasta ad eandem D. Francisci, Testudines, Arcus, Statuarum Loculi. Visuntur hic ossa quaedam humana stupendæ magnitudinis, Pomponij Lætì carmine celebrata. Commendat Silvæ arundinum Puteolanum Plinius lib. xxxii, cap. ult. Purpurissum autem Puteolanum laudat idem libro xxxv, cap. vi. Episcopatus gaudet dignitate. Nobiles ibi Familiæ, quæ vulgo audiunt: Aquileri, Capomazza, Pesce. Bufi, Cesianzi, Rogli, & aliæ.
units.tr: That there was once a very magnificent temple of Neptune here is established from Cicero; and its vast ruins are still to be seen near the church of St Francis: vaults, arches, and niches for statues. Here are seen certain human bones of astonishing size, celebrated in a poem by Pomponius Laetus. Pliny, book 32, last chapter, commends the Puteolan reeds (silvae arundinum). The same author, book 35, chapter 6, praises the Puteolan purple-dye (purpurissum). The bishopric enjoys dignity. Noble families are there which are commonly called: Aquileri, Capomazza, Pesce, Bufi, Cesianzi, Rogli, and others.

units.la: Quanta fuerit olim Portus Puteolanus commoditas, docet Strabo libro v. Ejus nulla ferme hodie supersunt vestigia. In Mari xiiii vastissimæ Pilæ Turrium instar ex latere structæ, & in quibusdam Arcus semiruti cernuntur: ex adverso ijs Pilæ, quæ item in æquore juxta Baias adparent. Pontem hic ab Caligula Imperatore superinjectum quo transitus per tria millia sexcentos fere passus a Puteolano litore in Baianum sinum jungebatur, memorat multis Suetonius. Edidit Libellum Ferdinandus Lofredus Marchio Trevicensis, Regiæ Majestatis in rebus Bellicis Consiliarius, cum hoc Titulo Le Antichità di Pozzuolo & Luoghi convicini.
units.tr: How great the convenience of the Puteolan harbour once was, Strabo teaches in book 5. Scarcely any traces of it survive today. In the sea, fourteen very vast piers built up from the side like towers are to be seen, and in some of them half-ruined arches; opposite them are piers which likewise appear in the water near Baiae. Suetonius, in many places, records the bridge thrown across here by the Emperor Caligula, by which the crossing from the Puteolan shore to the Baian gulf, a distance of about three thousand six hundred paces, was joined. Ferdinando Lofredo, Marquis of Trevico, councillor of His Royal Majesty in military affairs, published a little book under this title: Le Antichità di Pozzuolo & Luoghi convicini.

units.la: Post Pilas, quas dixi, ultra Puteolos in littore multi salubrium Aquarum Fontes prorumpunt, quorum præcipui, qui vulgo Bagni di S. Anastasio, dell'Argento dell'huomo, di Calestura, di Pietra, acqua Cerota.
units.tr: Beyond Puteoli, along the shore, past the piers I have mentioned, many springs of healthful waters burst forth; the most notable of these are commonly called Bagni di S. Anastasio, dell'Argento dell'huomo, di Calestura, di Pietra, acqua Cerota.

units.la: Haud procul Monte Astruno ad Viam eunti, quæ Puteolis Neapolim ducit, Villæ Ciceronianæ locus occurrit, ubi Hadrianum Imperatorem sepultum, quum apud Baias excessisset, Templumque illi pro Sepulcro constitutum, auctor est Spartianus.
units.tr: Not far from Monte Astruno, on the road that leads from Puteoli to Naples, there occurs the site of the Villa Ciceroniana, where, according to Spartianus, the Emperor Hadrian was buried after he died at Baiae, and a temple was built for him to serve as his tomb.

units.la: Eadem via pergenti Villæ L. Luculli, quam prope Neapolim habebat, ut Plutarchus memorat, ingentia adparent rudera.
units.tr: Along the same road, for one going on, appear the huge ruins of the Villa of L. Lucullus, which he had near Naples, as Plutarch records.

units.la: Succedit inde Mons Pausilypus, cum subterranea Crypta mirabili; de quibus suo loco.
units.tr: Next comes Mount Pausilypus, with its wonderful underground grotto; of which in its proper place.

units.la: Secundo inde lapide Neapolis est, ab Græcis Latinisque Scriptoribus multis encomiis celebrata. Cumanos vicinos eam primum condidisse, Parthenopemque ab Sirenarum una ibidem sepulta nominasse, Strabo, Virgilius, aliique Authores consentiunt. Subversam deinde fuisse volunt ab ipsis Conditoribus, quum nimium effloresceret, & augeri propter Agri ubertatem, Marremque vicinam Cumas sensim supplantaturā videretur. Quo facto Cumanos immani Peste vexatos, oraculoque monitos ferunt, ut Urbem restituerent: sicque, quum restaurassent, Neapolin voce Græca tum appellari ab re cœpisse, volunt. Errat Solinus, qui Urbem ab Augusto restauratam Neapolin dictam scribit; quum frequens ante Augusti Principatum Neapolis apud varios fiat mentio, præcipue apud Lycophronem, qui ætate Ptolemæi Philadelphi claruit. Livius etiam de Neapolitanis multis locis scribit, quæ sæculis aliquot ante Augustum contigerunt. Idem Lycophron in Alexandra fiat Phaleri Murum hanc Urbem appellat; & adjicit cius Interpres Isacius Tzetzes, Phalerum Siciliæ Tyrannum Neapolin in Italia condidisse. Ab Hercule extructam testantur Diodorus Siculus & Oppianus, qui ad Urbis nomen alludens in Poemate tuo de Venatione, Novum Herculis Campum Neapolin appellat. Νέαπολις in Numismatibus dicitur. Nomen hodie retinet, Napoli vulgo audiens. Caput est Campaniæ, Regiumque Metropolis. Spatium amplectitur magnum inter mare collium-que que amcenissimorum radices aedificata magnifice; Muris firmissimis, Propugnaculis, Turribus Castellisque, praeterum illi Karoli v, cujus jam nunc paret Nepoti, ut sit quasi inexpugnabilis munita. Fossas habet lxxx pedes profundas. Portae sunt octo: Capuana pulcerrima, Carmelitarum, S. Coeli, & S January. Fora sunt ampla: quorum unum famosissimum La Piazza del Vino, prope Castrum Novum. Fontes publici, ex quibus Aqua limpidissima nunc lanceae altitudine, nunc duorum capitum crassitudine, nunc per centum fistulas prosilit, sunt innumeri. Forma est oblonga, sequem in modum Dimidiatae Lunae incurvans. Circuitus olim 111; nunc, prolato pomerio, v milliarum Aere gaudet permolli & placido Hiemem vix sentit. Romanos aliosque in hanc Urbem vel Studiorum, vel Otii vel Voluptatis & Deliciarum, atque etiam Sanitatis gratia solitos secedere, patet ex Strabone. Sic de Neapoli Silius Italicus: Parthenope Portus Statio fidissima Nautis, Nunc molles Vrbis Vitae atque hospita Musis Otia, & exemptum curis gravioribus aevum. Sirenum dedit una summ & memorabile nomen Parthenope muris Achelois: aequore cuius Regnaverè diu cantus: quum dulce per undas Exitium miseris canerent non prospera Nautis.
units.tr: Two miles further on is Naples, celebrated with many praises by Greek and Latin writers. Strabo, Virgil and other authors agree that the Cumaeans, their neighbours, first founded it, and named it Parthenope after one of the Sirens buried there. They hold that it was afterwards destroyed by the founders themselves, when it grew too luxuriant and seemed likely, because of the fertility of the land and the nearby Marra, gradually to supplant Cumae. After this, they report, the Cumaeans were troubled by a dreadful plague, and, warned by an oracle, rebuilt the city; and so, when they had restored it, they hold that it began then to be called Neapolis in Greek, from the new city. Solinus is wrong when he writes that the city restored by Augustus was called Neapolis, since the name Neapolis is frequently mentioned before the principate of Augustus by various authors, especially by Lycophron, who flourished in the age of Ptolemy Philadelphus. Livy too writes of the Neapolitans in many places, and these events happened some centuries before Augustus. The same Lycophron, in his Alexandra, calls this city Phaleri Murum; and his interpreter Isaac Tzetzes adds that Phalaris, tyrant of Sicily, founded Neapolis in Italy. Diodorus Siculus and Oppian testify that it was built by Hercules; and Oppian, alluding to the name of the city in his poem on hunting, calls it the New Field of Hercules, Neapolis. In coins it is called Νέαπολις [Neapolis]. It still keeps the name, commonly called Napoli. It is the capital of Campania and the royal metropolis. It occupies a large area, magnificently built between the sea and the foot of the most pleasant hills; it is fortified as if impregnable, with very strong walls, bulwarks, towers and castles, especially that of Charles V, under whose grandson it now stands. It has ditches eighty feet deep. There are eight gates: the very beautiful Capuana, Carmelite, St Clare, and St January. Its markets are large, the most famous of which is La Piazza del Vino, near the New Castle. The public fountains, from which the clearest water springs now to the height of a lance, now as thick as two heads, now through a hundred pipes, are innumerable. Its shape is oblong, curving like a half-moon. Its circuit was once 111 [miles]; now, with the pomerium extended, it measures five miles. It enjoys a very mild and gentle air, and hardly feels winter. That the Romans and others used to retreat to this city for study, leisure, pleasure and delight, and also for the sake of health, is clear from Strabo. Thus Silius Italicus writes of Naples: "Parthenope, most trusty harbour for sailors, now the soft leisure and hospitable life of the city, friendly to the Muses, and an age freed from heavier cares. One of the Sirens gave her name, a famous one: Parthenope, Achelois by the walls, over whose sea their songs reigned long, when they sang sweet destruction through the waves to wretched sailors who did not prosper."

units.la: Vitam apud Neapolitanos degisse leguntur P. Virgilius, qui Georgicorum libros hic composuit; T. Livius, Horatius Flaccus, Annaeus Seneca, Claudius Claudianus, Agellius (quem vide libro ix Noct. Attic. cap. xv) Franciscus Petrarcha, Antonius Beccadellus Bononiensis, cognomine Panormitanus, Laurentius Valla, Porcellius Romanus Poeta, Blondus Foroliviensis, Bartholomaeus Facius Sulmonensis, & infiniti alii. Idem hodie mos. Hac enim aetate Principes, Duces, Marchiones, Comites, Barones, illustresque Viri totius Regni Neapolitani maiorem anni partem hic exigunt; adeoque plerique habent splendidissimas, ut non sine causa inter Italiae Urbes Nobilis audiat. Incredibile sane est, quantus Nobilium Familiarum, praeter Majorum Gentium, sit in hac Urbe numerus. Quum enim tota in suas Curias vel Basilicas (quae Seggi vulgo, quoque Principes, Duces, Marchiones, omnesque reliqui Ordines ad consultandum de rebus publicis conveniunt) sit distributa, singulis sua adscribitur Nobilitas. Eam ex Libello, cuius paullo ante mentionem feci, hic enotabo; uti vernaculo sermone concepta:
units.tr: It is read that many lived among the Neapolitans: P. Virgil, who composed the books of the Georgics here; T. Livy, Horace Flaccus, Annaeus Seneca, Claudius Claudianus, Agellius (see book 9 of the Attic Nights, chapter 15), Francis Petrarch, Antonio Beccadelli of Bologna, surnamed Panormita, Lorenzo Valla, the Roman poet Porcellio, Biondo of Forlì, Bartolomeo Fazio of Sulmona, and countless others. The same custom holds today. In this age princes, dukes, marquises, counts, barons and the illustrious men of the whole Neapolitan kingdom spend the greater part of the year here; and so most of them have very splendid houses, so that it is not without reason that it is counted among the noble cities of Italy. It is truly incredible how great is the number of noble families in this city, apart from the greater nations. For since the whole city is divided into its own Curiae or basilicas (which are commonly called Seggi, where the princes, dukes, marquises and all the other orders gather to consult about public affairs), each has its own nobility assigned to it. I shall note these here from the little book of which I made mention a little while ago, as it was written in the vernacular:
