units.la: Ædes hæc Vrbs cum Divorum, tum Hominum habet ornatissimas: Arces invictissimas. {a}Mirabile est opus Templum D. Clare (S. Chiara) cum Parthenone perampio, ab Agnete Regina Hispana (alijs Sanctia) Roberti Regis Conjuge factum. Sepulcra in eo multa conspiciuntur Regum, Reginarum, Regiorum Liberorum ex illustri Dyrrhachina domo, Karolique, qui S. Ludovico Francorum Regi fuit frater, Progenie. Vetustissimum est S. Pauli, quod olim Castoris & Pollucis. Insigne & S. Dominici Fanum. Servantur in eo Pharppi Imper. Constantinopolitani, Alphonsi 1, Ferdinandorum 1 & 11, Isabellæ, Ducis Mediolanensis, Ferrandi Davali Marchionis Petcharæ, Marchionis del Guasto, qui Regem Galliæ in Acie prope Papiam cepit, aliorumque Principum & illustrium hominum Ossa. In Deiuhro Fratrum Montis Oliveti (Frati di Monte Oliveto) sepultus legitur Alexander ab Alexandro I. C. Voluminis Geniallum dierum Auctor. In Templo D. Ioannis in Carbonaria (S. Giovanni in Carbonara) Fratrum Fremmanorum, monimentum visitur magnificentissimum Roberti Regis & Ioannæ 1 Sororis, ex Marmore candido. Pari celebritate sunt Cathedrale, quod Episcopo (nam Archiepiscopatus floret dignitate) vulgo vocant; D. Laurentij, Fratrumque Minorum D. Francisci. Alia prætereo.
units.tr: This city has most adorned buildings, both of the saints and of men, and most invincible citadels. The church of St Clare (S. Chiara), together with a very spacious convent, is a wonderful work, built by Agnes, Queen of Spain (others say Sanctia), wife of King Robert. Many tombs of kings, queens and royal children of the illustrious house of Durazzo can be seen in it, and of the line of Charles, who was brother of St Louis, King of the French. The church of St Paul is the oldest, which was once that of Castor and Pollux. The church of St Dominic is also notable. In it are preserved the bones of Philip, Emperor of Constantinople, of Alphonso I, of Ferdinand I and II, of Isabella, Duchess of Milan, of Ferrante Davalos, Marquis of Pescara, of the Marquis del Guasto, who took the King of France in battle near Pavia, and of other princes and illustrious men. In the church of the Monks of Monte Oliveto (Frati di Monte Oliveto) is buried Alexander ab Alexandro, jurist, author of the Geniales dies. In the church of St John in Carbonara of the Fremmanorum friars there is seen a most magnificent monument of white marble to King Robert and his sister Joanna I. The cathedral, which they commonly call the Episcopal church (for the archbishopric flourishes in dignity), is equally famous, as are the church of St Lawrence and that of the Friars Minor of St Francis. I pass over the rest.

units.la: Templa Monacharum sunt xv, inter quæ pulcerrima D. Framisii, S. Spiritus, S. Crucis. Ἀπηρόχωρα visitur, Templo Annunciatæ Virginis Mariæ iunctum, magnitudine & structura amplo opidi instar 1 in quo supra duo pauperum millia, omnis generis, Aegroti, Senes, Debiles alluntur curanturque: plusquam octingenti utriusque sexus Orphani & Expositi in eodem ab infantia & litteris imbuuntur, & variis artibus pro cuiusque genio & indole diligenter ad aetatis usque maturitatem instituuntur. In reditibus habet xvii. mill. Ducat. Alit Nutrices 100 pro expositis. Ex Virginibus, quae plerumque ccc, quotannis tres cum dote elocantur. Parochiae sunt xi. Tribunalia sunt vi. S. Pauli, in quo levia debita expediuntur; La Zecha, ubi ea, quae ad Mercaturam; La Vicaria, ubi Causae Iudiciariae Civiles & Criminales tractantur; Camera, ubi de Patrimonio Regis; Sacrosancta, ubi liturgia & Controversiae decidantur. Arces fortissimae sunt hae: Castellum Novum (CastelNuovo) in ipso Urbis ingressu, forma quadrangulari, Lapide Tiburtino, fossa duplici, ab Karolo I. Caesarum, Rege Neapolitano, anno MCCCLXV aedificatum, ab Alphonso I. instauratum, maximisque operibus instructum, ut inter firmissimas Italiae Arces habeatur. Aula ibi speciosissima, in qua quotannis Conventus Regni celebratur, & Prorex bis sin ... Supplicationes, ut ea vocentur, & Querelas variorum suscipiens, iudiciumque exercens. Iuxta est Turris, in qua conservantur Caesaris localia, ut sic loquatur; Sceptrum aureum; Ensis, habens capulam & Vaginam auream gemmis elaboratam; Corona, gemmis incredibilis magnitudinis ruitans; Fomum Caesareum, vetustum; Cappa Imperialis; Crux aurea, Poculum magnum, Gemmis undique ornatum; Poculum minus, Smaragdis, Rubinis, Sapphiris & Unionibus decoratum; Caesaris denique Effigies, ad vivum expressa. Magnus in hac Arce apparatus bellicus. Visuntur ibi aliquot aenea Tormenta, Hen. ori Saxoniae Ioanni Friderico in pugna ad Witebergam erepta. Capuanum (Castello Capuano vel Vetus, ad portam, quae Capuam emittit, sinum olim munitum satis, nunc Conciliis habendis, & Imperii Civitatisque negotiis attributum est. Armamentarium hic est, & inter alia Navalia Regis Francisci ad Ticinum capti elegantissima. Custodiunt hanc Arcem ducenti Hispani. Ovi, Castello dell' Ovo ab ovali dictum forma, modico extra urbem spatio in Scopulo (Μυαγεγα) Veteres appellabant, vel a Planta Sylvestris nomine, vel ob loci atque situs conditionem difficilemque elapsus, quasi captorum munitipulum) Mari cinctum, ab Gulielmo III. Normanno conditum, diuque Normannicum vocatum. Restauravit ornavitque Alphonsus I. Servatur ab Hispanis L. Sanctemerense (Castello di S. Herme) ab Roberto Rege in Rupe Moenibus imminente, ante annos CCL locatum, superioribus annis ab Karolo V. Imper. mirifice Propugnaculis maximis communitum: Urbi, ampliato Pomerio, ab Philippo Hispaniarum Rege iunctum. Vocatur etiam hoc Castrum Brigia quasi dicas Frenum Equitis. Karolus enim V. Imperator ex Africa reversus, quum Neapolim ingressus videret plures equos absque Freno, non ignorans Symboli vim, continuum cepit ferocem & temerarium hunc Equum constringendi, ne aliquando domino pollet reluctari. Cepit itaque sub specie Domus voluptariae & Templi Castrum hoc extruere, & Equum indomitum, hoc est Neapolitanos, indocto fieno, domare. Extra Muros australi parte Moles in Mari, opus arte summa factum spectatur: a Karolo II. exstructa sed ab Alphonso I. maiorem in modum aucta, ad Portus tutelam: ex quo Miseno, Minervaque Promontorium, celebrisque ac iucundus Insulae Capreae, Ischia, & Prochyte sereno coelo iunt conspicua. Sunt etiam Neapolitanae summa tuosissima Regis Equilia, in quibus generosi Equi centum numero, stabulantur, domantur, docenturque. Ex his quotannis XII Regi donantur. Inter Hortos, qui innumeri, principem obtinet locum, qui Carria Tor- spatio peramplus, cultu singularis. Academiam habet Neapolis ab Frederico III. Imp. Aug institutam ad quam Studiosorum ex toto Regno magnus fit concursus. Imperator quum instituisset, ut florentissimam redderet, decrevisse legitur non solum, Ne quis extra Regnum illud studiorum causa proficisceretur; sed ... , ne in trivialibus Regni Scholis maiores Disciplinae traderentur. Restauravit Robertus Rex sapientissimus; & centum post annis nonnihil per bella collapsum Alphonsus Aragonum Rex. Sunt & Bibliothecae aliquot: in quis primi loci D. Dominici. Servat Libros non paucos Ioannis Pontani, ab Eugenia Filia in doctissimi Patris memoriam ibi dicatos. Inter Palatia magnatum primi fere loci, Principis Sciernitani, quod Emtionis titulo Iesuitae nunc habent; deinde Sulmonensis, Tolentini, Gratianensis, Caetani. Sunt & privatioribus superba aedificia, in quis reliqua superant Hadriani de Gaiteino, Carapha, Gonsalvi de Bernardo, Tiberii de Bacie, Cafara Cardinal. Hoipina porro vilia & incommoda. Plateas habet, tribus exceptis, quæ latæ & miræ longitudinis, majore ex parte strictas & angustas: olim lignibus, nunc lapide coctili stratas. Fabri atque Artifices, qui vel strepitu vel sordibus molesti sunt, in extremis Urbis partibus suas habent Regiones: reliquam Urbis partem Nobiliores atque Cives habent. Singulis propemodum Ædificiis Fontes sunt, salientes copiosa saluberrimaque aqua. Manant ex Sebetho fluviolo, quem præter alios Vetevus prosomit. Mulieres habet Neapolis deformes plurimum, sparso ore, magnis natis. Ortu hanc Urbem suo nobilitarunt Bonifacius ix, ex nobili Tomacellorum familia; Ioannes xxiii, ex illustri Collarum Domo: item Octavius Carrafa, Vincentius Carrafa, Andreas Mathæus Palmerius, Marinus Caraciola, Antonius Sanseverinas, Ioannes Petrus Carrafa, Ioannes Vincentius Aquavivanus, Cardinales: Omitto Patriarchas, Archiepiscopos, Episcopos. Fuit etiam Neapolitanus Statius Papinius Poeta, item Sannazarus. Neapolitani in Fide & amicitia Populi Romani & Imperatorum constantissime quamdiu fuerunt, manseræ, offendunt Livius lib. viii, xx, xxiii & xxiv, Blondus, Sabellicus, & Collenutius. Coloniam eo deductam Vetusta loquuntur Epigrammata, apud Onuphrium. Inclinante Imperii Romani Majestate Urbem primum ab Gothis subactam, & à Belisario recepiam Procopius auctor est lib. i. Hist. Goth. Postea sub Langobardorum; hinc que pulsi, sub Graecorum & Saracenorum fuit possellate, usque ad Normannorum in Italiam adventum, ex quibus aliique qui fuerunt, qui nati Reges & Principes, pluribus commemorati huius capitis initio. Extant antiquorum Ædificiorum priscæ Reliquiæ plures, Epitaphia, Statuæ, Cippi, Columnæ, Aræ, Marmora sculpturis artificiis preciosa. Videndæ cum primis magnæ illæ quadratæ Cattorum Templi (cujus obiter antea[?] memini) ruinæ, incendijs deformatæ. Conspicitur ibi Porticus viii Columnarum, opere Corinthiaco. In Tympano figurantur, partim integræ, partim fractæ: Apollo ad Tripodem. In angulis ad dextram jacet Terra cum Cornu Copiæ, velificante supra Caput Linteo: ad sinistram Fluvius, sub cujus Cubito vasaquam effundens, tenet Cannam manu: reliqua discerni nequeunt. Adscripta leguntur hæc:
units.tr: The city has fifteen convents of nuns, among which the most beautiful are those of St Francis, the Holy Spirit and the Holy Cross. The Aperochora [Ἀπηρόχωρα] is seen, joined to the church of the Virgin Mary of the Annunciation, a large building, in size and structure like a small town, in which more than two thousand poor people of every kind (the sick, the old and the infirm) are fed and cared for. More than eight hundred orphans and foundlings of both sexes are brought up there from infancy in letters, and are carefully trained in various crafts, according to each one's bent and talent, until they reach adulthood. It has an income of seventeen thousand ducats. It maintains 100 wet-nurses for the foundlings. Of the virgins, who number about 300, three are each year given in marriage with a dowry. There are eleven parishes and six tribunals: the Tribunal of St Paul, where minor debts are settled; La Zecca, where matters concerning trade are dealt with; La Vicaria, where civil and criminal lawsuits are heard; the Camera, which deals with the royal patrimony; and the Sacrosancta, where liturgical and ecclesiastical disputes are decided. The strongest citadels are these: Castel Nuovo (Castel Nuovo), at the very entrance to the city, square in plan, built of Tiburtine stone with a double moat, built in 1365 by Charles I, King of Naples and of the Caesars, and restored by Alphonso I, and equipped with very great works, so that it is counted among the strongest citadels of Italy. There is a most splendid hall there, in which the assembly of the kingdom is held each year, and the Viceroy receives the petitions, as they are called, and complaints of various people, and exercises judgement. Next to it is a tower, in which are kept the Emperor's, so to speak, regalia: a golden sceptre; a sword whose hilt and golden scabbard are worked with gems; a crown glittering with gems of incredible size; an ancient Caesarean cloak; an imperial cape; a golden cross; a large cup, adorned all over with gems; a smaller cup decorated with emeralds, rubies, sapphires and pearls; and finally a likeness of the Emperor, drawn from life. There is a great stock of weapons in this citadel. Several bronze cannon can be seen there, taken from John Frederick, Elector of Saxony, in the battle near Wittenberg. Capuano (Castello Capuano, or Vetus), at the gate which leads out to Capua, was once sufficiently fortified, and is now assigned to holding councils and to the affairs of the Empire and the city. There is an armoury here, and among other things the very elegant naval equipment of King Francis, taken at the Ticino. Two hundred Spaniards guard this citadel. Ovo, Castel dell'Ovo, named from its oval shape, stands a short distance outside the city on a rock (the ancients called it Megaris), surrounded by the sea; either from a wild plant, or because of the difficult nature and position of the place, as if a stronghold of captives; it was founded by William III the Norman and for a long time was called the Norman. Alphonso I restored and adorned it. It is kept by Spaniards. Sanctemerense (Castello di S. Herme), placed on a rock overhanging the walls by King Robert about 250 years ago, was in recent years wonderfully fortified by the Emperor Charles V with very great bulwarks; it was joined to the city by Philip, King of Spain, when the boundary was enlarged. This castle is also called Brigia, as if you would say "the bridle of the horse". For the Emperor Charles V, returning from Africa, when he entered Naples and saw many horses without bridles, not unaware of the power of the emblem, began to restrain this wild and reckless horse, lest at some time it should resist its master. So under the appearance of a pleasure house and a temple he took it upon himself to build this castle, and to tame the unbroken horse, that is, the Neapolitans, with unlearned hay. Outside the walls, on the southern side, a mole in the sea is seen, a work of great skill: built by Charles II, but greatly enlarged by Alphonso I, for the protection of the harbour; from it Misenum, the promontory of Minerva, and the famous and pleasant islands of Capri, Ischia and Procida can be seen under a clear sky. There are also the royal stables of Naples, most splendid, in which a hundred noble horses are stabled, broken and trained. Each year twelve of these are given to the King. Among the gardens, which are innumerable, the chief place is held by the one called Carraia, very spacious and singularly cultivated. Naples has an academy, founded by the Emperor Frederick III Augustus, to which a great crowd of students comes from the whole kingdom. When the Emperor had established it to make it flourish, it is recorded that he decreed not only that no one should leave that kingdom to go abroad for study, but also that the higher disciplines should not be taught in the ordinary schools of the kingdom. It was restored by King Robert, the most wise, and a hundred years later, having somewhat collapsed through wars, by Alphonso, King of Aragon. There are also several libraries, of which the first place belongs to that of St Dominic. It keeps not a few books of Giovanni Pontano, dedicated there by his daughter Eugenia in memory of her most learned father. Among the palaces of the nobles, the first place belongs to that of the Prince of Sciernitani, which the Jesuits now hold by purchase; then those of Sulmona, Tolentino, Graziano and Caetani. There are also magnificent buildings of private persons, among which those of Hadrian de Gaiteino, Carafa, Gonsalvo de Bernardo, Tiberius de Bacie and Cardinal Carafa surpass the rest. The houses of the poor are cheap and uncomfortable. The city has streets, except three, which are wide and of wonderful length, but for the most part narrow and cramped; formerly paved with wood, now with burnt brick. Smiths and craftsmen, who are troublesome by their noise or their filth, have their districts in the outer parts of the city; the nobles and citizens have the rest of the city. Almost every building has fountains, gushing with abundant and very healthful water. They come from the little river Sebeto, which, among others, Vitruvius mentions. Naples has very many women who are ugly, with wide mouths and large noses. This city was ennobled by its natives: Boniface IX, from the noble family of the Tomacelli; John XXIII, from the illustrious house of the Colonna; likewise Octavius Carafa, Vincent Carafa, Andrew Matthew Palmerius, Marinus Caracciolo, Antony Sanseverino, John Peter Carafa, John Vincent Aquaviva, cardinals. I omit the patriarchs, archbishops and bishops. Statius Papinius, the poet, was also a Neapolitan, likewise Sannazaro. The Neapolitans remained most constant in faith and friendship towards the Roman people and the Emperors for as long as they existed, as Livy (books 8, 20, 23 and 24), Blondus, Sabellicus and Collenuccio relate. Ancient inscriptions speak of a colony led there, as recorded by Onuphrius. As the majesty of the Roman Empire declined, Procopius (Gothic History, book 1) tells that the city was first subdued by the Goths and recovered by Belisarius. Afterwards it was under the Lombards, and then, when they were driven out, under the Greeks and the Saracens, until the coming of the Normans into Italy, from whom came several kings and princes, mentioned in more detail at the beginning of this chapter. Many remains of ancient buildings survive: epitaphs, statues, cippi, columns, altars, and marbles precious for their artistic carving. Especially worth seeing are the great square ruins of the Temple of the Cattans (of which I recalled something earlier), disfigured by fires. There can be seen a portico of eight columns, in the Corinthian style. On the tympanum are figured, partly whole and partly broken: Apollo beside the tripod. In the corners, on the right, lies Earth with a cornucopia, with a cloth billowing above her head; on the left a River, under whose elbow a jar pours out water, and holds a reed in his hand; the rest cannot be made out. These words are read as inscribed:

units.la: ΤΙΒΕΡΙΟΣ ΙΟΥΛΙΟΣ ΤΑΡΣΟΣ ΔΙΟΝ ΚΟΙΝΟΙΣ ΚΑΙ ΤΗΙ ΠΟΛΙΤΩΝ ΝΑΟΝ ΚΑΙ ΤΑ ΕΝ ΤΩΙ ΝΑΩΙ ΠΕΛΑΛΑΟΝ Σ ΒΑΣΤΟΤ ΑΠΕΛΑΥΘΕΡΟΣ ΚΑΙ ΕΠΙΤΡΟΠΟΣ ΣΥΝΤΕΛΕΣΑΣ ΕΚ ΤΩΝ ΙΔΙΩΝ ΚΑΘΙΕΡΩΣΕΝ
units.tr: TIBERIUS IULIUS TARSUS, freedman and steward, from his own resources completed and dedicated the temple for the common good of the citizens, and the things in the temple [ΤΙΒΕΡΙΟΣ ΙΟΥΛΙΟΣ ΤΑΡΣΟΣ ΔΙΟΝ ΚΟΙΝΟΙΣ ΚΑΙ ΤΗΙ ΠΟΛΙΤΩΝ ΝΑΟΝ ΚΑΙ ΤΑ ΕΝ ΤΩΙ ΝΑΩΙ ΠΕΛΑΛΑΟΝ Σ ΒΑΣΤΟΤ ΑΠΕΛΑΥΘΕΡΟΣ ΚΑΙ ΕΠΙΤΡΟΠΟΣ ΣΥΝΤΕΛΕΣΑΣ ΕΚ ΤΩΝ ΙΔΙΩΝ ΚΑΘΙΕΡΩΣΕΝ].

units.la: Ager suburbicarius, Vicinique Colles amœnissimi sunt & jucundissimi a Frumenti, Vini, Variorum Fructuum, Herbarum, Florum, rerumque omnium, ad Hominum Animalium quæ necessitatem, Voluptatem, delicias facientium feracissimi. In Agro circumquaque fertili, præsertim littoreo, videre est stupenda Principum Nobilium quæ Pratoria: inter alia Marcionis Vicensis & Ferdinandi Marizzani. Superbit autem præ aliis Palatium exstructum olim ab Rege Ferdinando Aragonio: quod vulgari voce Pagum vocant Itali. Præterea Fontium Ædiculas, Antra Nymapharum, Piscinas, Porticus, Ambulacra, & id genus alia. Altero ab Neapoli lapide Via Puteolana, prope fauces perfossæ per Paufilypum Cryptæ, Monimentum fuisse Virgilii, scribit Servius. Locum nunc ostentant Adcolæ: monstrantque ex vicinis hortis S. Severini. Nec procul inde Attij Syncerus Sannazarus Poetæ Domus visitur quæ ex testamento in Cœnobium abiit, Templumque D. Virgini dicatum. Est ibi marmoreum Sepulcrum, actabre sculptum. Hinc Orpheus, seu Apollo, illinc Sibylla sive Musæ, ex marmore candente: cum hoc Petri Bembi Cardinalis Epigrammate;
units.tr: The suburban countryside and the neighbouring hills are most pleasant and delightful, and most fertile in corn, wine, various fruits, herbs, flowers, and all things that serve the needs, pleasures and delights of men and animals. In the surrounding fertile country, especially along the shore, one may see the amazing country villas of noble princes; among others, those of Marcione of Vico and Ferdinando Marizzano. But the palace built long ago by King Ferdinand of Aragon surpasses the rest; the Italians call it, in the vernacular, the Pagum. Besides these there are little shrines of fountains, grottoes of the Nymphs, fishponds, porticoes, walks, and other things of that kind. Servius writes that one mile from Naples, on the Puteolan road, near the mouth of the grotto dug through Posillipo, was the tomb of Virgil. The locals now point out the place, and from the neighbouring gardens of San Severino they show it. Not far from there one visits the house of the poet Attius Syncerus Sannazarus, which by his will passed to a monastery and a temple dedicated to the Blessed Virgin. There is a marble tomb there, carved in relief: on one side Orpheus or Apollo, on the other the Sibyl or the Muses, in gleaming marble; with it this epigram of Cardinal Pietro Bembo:

units.la: Dafacro Cineris flores: hic ille Maroni Syncerus Musa proximus, ut Tumulo.
units.tr: Flowers from the ashes of Dafacrus: here lies that Syncerus, the Muse nearest to Maro, as his tomb tells.

units.la: Historiam Regni scripsit Paulus Collenutius. Iplam Urbem delineant Iovianus Pontanus libro Histor. vi, & alii. Edidit quoque Libellum Benedictus de Falco Neapolitanus, patria lingua cum Titulo, Descrittione de i Sacri Antiqui di Napoli, & del suo ametamento disposito. Circumfertur & Libellus, cujus ante mentionem feci, sine Auctoris nomine, cum hac Inscriptione: Nomi delle Provincie, Città, Terre, & Castella del Regno di Napoli: De Vigiovadi e Principi, Duchi, Marchesi, Conti, Baroni, e Signori. Sagro- i, che ci sono: Delle Famiglie Nobili della Città di Napoli, & di tutto il Regno.
units.tr: Paulus Collenutius wrote the history of the kingdom. Giovanni Pontano describes the city itself in book 6 of his History, and others do too. Benedetto de Falco of Naples also published a little book in the native tongue, with the title Descrittione de i Sacri Antiqui di Napoli, & del suo ametamento disposito. There also circulates a little book, which I mentioned before, without the author's name, with this inscription: Nomi delle Provincie, Città, Terre, & Castella del Regno di Napoli: De Vigiovadi e Principi, Duchi, Marchesi, Conti, Baroni, e Signori. Sagro- i, che ci sono: Delle Famiglie Nobili della Città di Napoli, & di tutto il Regno.

units.la: Extra Vrbem ad Orientem mille circiter pass. a Mari fuit olim Parthenopis. Non procul Neapoli describit Livius libro viii, utrumque Oppidum inhabitatum ab una eademque Gente Cumana; Palaepolim autem ab Graecis expugnatam, à P. vero Palatio cos. receptam, addens. Putat Ambrosius Leo libro i Palaepolim olim fuisse, ubi nunc Turris Lapparellorum, tribus Neapoli. P. M. Leander Albertus non procul abfuisse censet a Foro Regali, nobilissimo Palatio, quod, ut antea dixi, Ferdinandus Aragonius, Primus Neapolis Rex, exstruxit: eo enim loci non pauca veterum Aedificiorum Vestigia hodieque superesse.
units.tr: About a thousand paces outside the city to the east, a mile from the sea, there was once Parthenope. Not far from Naples, Livy in book 8 describes both towns as inhabited by one and the same people, the Cumaeans; adding that Palaepolis was taken by the Greeks, but was received by the Romans into the Palatium under the consuls. Ambrosio Leone, in book 1, thinks Palaepolis once stood where the Tower of the Lapparelli now is, three miles from Naples. Father Leandro Alberti thinks it was not far from the Foro Regale, the most noble palace, which, as I said before, Ferdinand of Aragon, the first King of Naples, built; for in that place many traces of ancient buildings still survive to this day.

units.la: Inter Vesevum Montem & Anversam, de qua ante, sunt Marianum & Acerrae. Quod Marigliano vernacule, Marianum Latine scribentibus; Mutanum vocare videtur Paulus Diaconus lib. ii Langbardic.
units.tr: Between Mount Vesuvius and Avella, of which I spoke earlier, lie Marianum and Acerrae. The place called Marigliano in the vernacular seems to be what writers in Latin call Marianum; Paul the Deacon, in book 2 of the Lombard history, seems to call it Mutanum.

units.la: Acerrae (quae hactenus nomen retinent) Livio lib. xxiii, xxvi & alibi, Virgilio in Georg. Silio lib. viii, aliisque; quae Acerrae Appiano lib. i bellor. Civilium Acerrae Strabeni. Ad Clanium Amnem, non longe ab Neapoli, situm notat ad Virgilium suum Servius: addens Clanium adiduus inundationibus Agrum Acerranum infestare solitum: unde & deletum oppidum, ac potius intrequentem Pagum videri, quam Urbem, aut Probus. Olim in Monte erant, nunc in plano: inquit ad eundem Virgilium Pomponius Sabinus. Colonia Romana est Frontino. Plinius Acerranos in Prima locat Regione. Meminit eorum & Livius libro xxviii.
units.tr: Acerrae, which still keeps its name, is mentioned by Livy in books 23 and 26 and elsewhere, by Virgil in the Georgics, by Silius in book 8, and by others; Appian in book 1 of the Civil Wars calls it Acerrae, and Strabo calls it Acerrae. Servius, on his Virgil, notes that it lies by the River Clanius, not far from Naples, adding that the Clanius, by its constant flooding, used to harm the Acerran territory; hence the town was destroyed, and it seems more a crowded village than a city, as Probus says. Pomponius Sabinus, on the same Virgil, says it was once on a hill, and now is on the plain. Frontinus calls it a Roman colony. Pliny places the Acerrans in the First Region. Livy also mentions them in book 28.

units.la: Ab Acerris P. M. iv abest Suessula, cujus meminit, praeter Strabonem, Livius multis locis, praesertim libro vii, viii & xxiii: item Itineraria Tabula. Colonia est apud Frontinum. Hodie Sessula, oppidum pene nunc conlapsum. Suessulani Plinio etiam noti.
units.tr: Four miles from Acerrae lies Suessula, which Livy mentions in many places, especially in books 7, 8 and 23, besides Strabo, and also the Itinerary Table. Frontinus lists it as a colony. Today it is Sessula, a town now almost fallen down. The Suessulans are also known to Pliny.

units.la: Supra Convallem Taburni, quae flumen Isclerum spectat, Castellum est, quod Colle di Pace vulgo: in Valle inter Montem & Amnem, ad dextram Lunatula: in Monte Avola, Comitatus titulo decorata.
units.tr: Above the valley of Taburnus, which faces the River Isclero, there is a castle, commonly called Colle di Pace. In the valley, between the mountain and the river, on the right, is Lunatula; on the mountain is Avola, adorned with the title of a county.

units.la: Qua parte Montes, Tifata antiquis, Meridiem spectant, quaedam sunt Opida in ipsis radicibus. in quis Maronda, & Caserta, Episcopatus dignitate clara, nobilibusque Familijs, quae vernacule, d'Aloe, d'Amico, Cafoa, Clementi, de Guido, Mugliarefi, Sasi: & aliis. Sunt ibidem Matalana Opidum Comitatus titulo insignitum, cujus principatum possidet Gens Neapolitana Caraffarum, Durazzanum, Ratanorum; Argentum Castellum, Stendardorum Peculium.
units.tr: On the side where the mountains, the ancient Tifata, face south, there are some towns right at their foothills, among them Maronda and Caserta, famous for the dignity of their bishopric and for their noble families, which in the vernacular are called d'Aloe, d'Amico, Cafoa, Clementi, de Guido, Mugliarefi, Sasi, and others. There too is Matalana, a town distinguished by the title of a county, whose principality is held by the Neapolitan family of the Caraffa, Durazzo and Ratano; and Argenta, a castle, the property of the Stendardi.

units.la: Hinc per amoenos Campos Neapolim incedenti Sancta Agathae Castellum ab Gothis, ut perhibent, aedificatum, se offert. Iuxta est Marianum, de quo paulo ante; infra Argentum; & ad medium Collis opidum Cancelli; supraque Forinum.
units.tr: Coming from there through the pleasant fields toward Naples, one meets Sant'Agata, a castle which, they say, was built by the Goths. Nearby is Marianum, mentioned a little earlier; below is Argenta; and halfway up the hill the town of Cancelli; and above it Forino.

units.la: In declivi Titiatarum descensu Sarnum est, opidum ab Amne Sarno denominatum.
units.tr: On the downward slope from the Tifatine hills lies Sarno, a town named after the River Sarno.

units.la: Reditu ab Sarno in planitiem Vetus Urbs Nola, Nola, visitur antiquis Scriptoribus, praecipue Livio multis locis, Plutarchoque in Vitis Marcelli & Hannibalis, celebrata. Locat Strabo in Campania, Plinius in Prima Regione; Ptolemaeus in Picentibus, in Samnitibus Livius libro xxx. Conciliationis ratio ab vicinate. Condinam tradit ab Iapygis Trogus ab Tuscis, Solinus. De hac Urbe sic canit Silius libro v: Campo Nola sedet, crebris circumdata in Orbem Turribus, & tesse factiem tutatur adire Planitiem Vallo.
units.tr: Returning from Sarno to the plain, one sees the old city of Nola, Nola, celebrated by ancient writers, especially Livy in many places, and by Plutarch in the Lives of Marcellus and Hannibal. Strabo places it in Campania, Pliny in the First Region, Ptolemy among the Picentines, and Livy in book 30 among the Samnites. The reason for these different attributions is their proximity. Trogus says it was founded by the Iapygians, Solinus says by the Tuscans. Silius sings of this city in book 5: Nola sits in the plain, surrounded by a circle of many towers, and defends its face, which can be approached only across the plain, with a rampart.

units.la: De eadem sic Facius libro Historiarum v: Abest Nola ab Neapoli non plus duodeviginti milibus passuum: Urbs Antiqua, & Hannibalis crebris celebris, & ad servandos Neapolitanos perquam opportuna. Quinta fuerit olim, qualiqua forma, conatur eruere Ambrosius Leo libro i, multa adscribens de ipsius Antiquitate, Publicisque Operibus. Nola Templum Augusto ab Tiberio Principe dedicatum, scribit Suetonius libro iii cap. xl. Recentiores inter Coloniae Frontinus, Augustae tribuens cognomen Amicam Romae dicit D. Paullinus in S. Felicis Natali Tertia. Memoriae prodit Livius libro ix hanc Urbem ab C. Livio cos. receptam; lib. vero xxiii ab Hannibale bis oppugnatam, sed ab Marcello liberatam. Vide & Auctorem de V V. Illustr. cap. xiv. Narrat Suetonius Augustum ex Capreis adiecta valetudine Nolam delatum: ibique in eodem cubiculo, quo pater Octavius, obiisse. Videndus & Tacitus lib.
units.tr: Of the same city Facius writes in book 5 of his Histories: Nola is not more than eighteen thousand paces from Naples: an ancient city, famous for Hannibal's frequent attacks, and very well placed for keeping the Neapolitans safe. Ambrosio Leone, in book 1, tries to bring to light what sort of city it once was, adding much about its antiquity and public buildings. Suetonius, in book 3, chapter 40, writes that a temple at Nola was dedicated to Augustus by the Emperor Tiberius. Among the more recent writers Frontinus counts it among the colonies, giving it the name Augusta; Paulinus, in his Third Poem on the Birthday of St Felix, calls it a friend of Rome. Livy in book 9 records that this city was received by the consul Gaius Livius; in book 23 that it was twice attacked by Hannibal, but was freed by Marcellus. See also the author On Illustrious Men, chapter 14. Suetonius tells how Augustus, his health failing on Capri, was carried to Nola and died there in the same bedroom in which his father Octavius had died. Tacitus, book 1, should also be consulted.

units.la: 1. Senatus Populique Nolanorum mentionem faciunt Veteres Inscriptiones ; quæ apud Onuphrium Panvinium: L. RANIO. ACONTIO. L. F. | L. SICINIO L. F. IVEL. OPTATO. VIR. CLAR. | SER. VALENTI COS. ORDIN. CVRATORI. REIP. | PATRONO. MVNICIPI NOLANORVM. CVR. PEC. P. | CVRAT.REIP.NOLANORVM XV. VIR. SACRIS. FACIVND. PATRONO | S. P. Q_NOLANORVM R. P. III. VIRO. AD. AGR. DIVIDEN. | D. D. X. VIRO.STLITIBVS.IVDICANDIS STAT. EX. ÆRES. P. Q_NOLAN. D. D.
units.tr: Ancient inscriptions mention the Senate and People of the Nolans; these are found in Onofrio Panvinio: L. RANIO. ACONTIO. L. F. | L. SICINIO L. F. IVEL. OPTATO. VIR. CLAR. | SER. VALENTI COS. ORDIN. CVRATORI. REIP. | PATRONO. MVNICIPI NOLANORVM. CVR. PEC. P. | CVRAT. REIP. NOLANORVM XV. VIR. SACRIS. FACIVND. PATRONO | S. P. Q. NOLANORVM R. P. III. VIRO. AD. AGR. DIVIDEN. | D. D. X. VIRO. STLITIBVS. IVDICANDIS STAT. EX. ÆRES. P. Q. NOLAN. D. D. [Lucius Ranius Acontius, son of Lucius; Lucius Sicinius Julius Optatus, son of Lucius, distinguished man, consul, curator of the state, patron of the municipality of the Nolans, curator of the public money, fifteen-man commission for sacred rites, patron; the Senate and People of the Nolans; three-man commission for dividing the land; ten-man commission for judging lawsuits; a statue at public expense, by decree of the Senate and People of Nola.]

units.la: Episcopatus fulget dignitate; nobilibusque Familijs, quæ vulgo: Albertini. | Fontanarosa. | De Notariis. Baroni. | Giudice. | De Pier-Gionanni. Cesarini. | Griffi. | De Risi. Felicibus. | Miglrilli.
units.tr: The bishopric shines with dignity; the noble families, commonly called: Albertini, Fontanarosa, De Notariis, Baroni, Giudice, De Pier-Gionanni, Cesarini, Griffi, De Risi, Felici, Migliarilli.

units.la: Vnos tulit multos cum doctrina, tum virtute bellica nobiles; quos enumerat libro III Ambrosius Leo apud quem plura de hac Vrbe.
units.tr: This city has produced many men, noble both in learning and in military valour; Ambrosio Leone, who writes more about this city, lists them in book 3.

units.la: Ad Litus reverto. P. M. ab Vrbe Neapolitana VIII. Turris Graca est, vulgo Torre di Greco, sic ut nonnulli censent, dicta ab Conditore, qui nomine vel origine Græcus; vel quod Vinum Græcum ibi proveniat optimum; vocatur & Turris Octava, quod octavo ab Neapoli Lapide. Putant Viri docti, inter quos Ambrosius Leo, Sanfelicius, Leander, quondam hic Herculaneum fuisse. Sic Sifennæ apud Nonium in Fluvius, Ciceroni, Plinio, Melæ dicitur, quod Ἡρακλέων nominatur Straboni libro V, & Halicarnass. libro I; ubi Nominis ratio indicatur. Herculanum vetus est in Itineraria Tabula, Herculanensis Turris mentio apud M. Tullium Epistola ad Pætum: Herculaneum tamen arbitrantur Blondus, Raffanus & Collenutius fuisse, ubi hodie militibus hinc octo Torre di Nunziata. Turris sane Graca, Castellum elegans, juxta quod Oppidum Stabiae, Monti aliquanto vicinius & ab Mari remotius, fuisse volunt Viri locorum illorum gnari. Stabiæ vocat Itineraria Tabula. Memoriam Stabiarum servari in Castello Al ... di Stabie censet Leander Albertus. Meminit Stabiarum in Agro Cumano Ovidius lib.xv Metamorph. Celebrat Stabiae Columella lib.x, ab Fontibus, quos ad Furcas Caudinas decurrere notat ad eundem Pomponius Fortunatus. Deleras ab L. Cornelio Sulla Bello Sociali, pridie Kalendas Mai, Cn. Pompeio & L. Porcio Catone cos. sensimque in Villas abiisse, auctor est Plinius. Stabiensis Episcopus in Libro Fidei Romani delectus legitur. Stabiarum Littus habet Seneca, libro VI Natur.
units.tr: Returning to the shore: eight miles from the city of Naples lies Torre Greca, commonly Torre di Greco, so called, as some think, from its founder, who was either a Greek by name or origin, or because excellent Greek wine is produced there; it is also called Turris Octava, because it is eight miles from Naples. Learned men, among them Ambrosio Leone, Sanfelice and Leandro, think that Herculaneum was once here. Thus the river Sebethus is called Herculaneus by Cicero, Pliny and Mela, and by Strabo in book 5 and Halicarnassus in book 1 it is named Ἡρακλέων, where the reason for the name is given. Herculanum is an old name in the Itinerary Table, and the Herculanean Tower is mentioned by Marcus Tullius in his letter to Paetus; yet Biondo, Raffano and Collenuccio think Herculaneum was where Torre di Nunziata now stands, about eight miles from here. The men who know those places hold that Torre Greca is certainly a fine castle, and that near it lay the town of Stabiae, somewhat closer to the mountain and further from the sea. The Itinerary Table calls it Stabiae. Leandro Alberti thinks the memory of Stabiae is kept in the castle called Castello al... di Stabia. Ovid in book 15 of the Metamorphoses mentions Stabiae in the Cumaean territory. Columella in book 10 celebrates Stabiae for its springs, which Pomponius Fortunatus, on the same passage, notes flow down toward the Caudine Forks. Pliny reports that it was destroyed by Lucius Cornelius Sulla in the Social War, on the day before the Kalends of May, in the consulship of Gnaeus Pompeius and Lucius Porcius Cato, and that it gradually shrank into villas. A bishop of Stabiae is found in the list of the Roman council. Seneca, in book 6 of the Natural Questions, mentions the shore of Stabiae.

units.la: Haud procul hinc Pompeji fuerunt: Sic Straboni, Plinio, Melæ Xiphilino, Itinerariæ Tabulæ, aliis nominatur; quod Pompeium Sallustio, Tacito, Senecæ. Solinus ita notat nominatos ab Hercule, quod Vir ex Hispania Pompeianum eo duxisset. Haud procul ab Monte Vesevo ponit Plinius; prope Sarnum, Pomponius Fortunatus ad librum x Columellæ, Sarno adiunxit Strabo. Plinius Municipium facit: Coloniam fuisse colligi posse videtur ex Ciceronis pro Sulla. Idem Cicero Legem Agrariam dissuadens, nullo modo ferendam aut, Pompeios, ut i multimum uberrimumque Pop. Ro. fundum, Decem-virorum Nundinationi permittit. Terræmotu subversum hoc oppidum maiori ex parte temporibus Neronis, notat Tacitus libro xxv: obrutum autem cum Herculaneo cinere Vesevi Montis, Dio. Celebrat Pompeiana Vina Plinius libro XIV. nat. Hist. cap. VI. Pompeianæ Pæpulus hinc habet Appianus lib.1 Civil. An non prope Pompeios, & ab iis itercan Pompeianum, Ciceronis Villa; cujus memineruntcum Ipsi non tamen ad Atticum, tum Sallustius oratione in ipsum? Prope S. Mariam Nunciatam locant Blondus & Baptista Porta Neapolitanus: Ambrosius Leo Pompeianum hoc appellari opinatur. Pompeianum Stabis eras dicemtum, inquit Plinius lib.vi Epist. ad Lactum sinu medio. An idem cum Pompeiano? ait Abrahamus Ortelius: Pompeiam Paludem, cujus mentio apud Columellam, ad Mare circa Pompeianum fuisse, scribit ad eundem Auctorem Pomponius Fortunatus.
units.tr: Not far from here were the Pompeii. Strabo, Pliny, Mela, Xiphilinus, the Itinerary Table and others name it thus, while Sallust, Tacitus and Seneca call it Pompeium. Solinus notes that it was named after Hercules, because a man from Spain had led his Pompeian followers there. Pliny places it not far from Mount Vesuvius. Pomponius Fortunatus, on book 10 of Columella, places it near the Sarnus, and Strabo joins it to the Sarnus. Pliny calls it a municipium, but it may be gathered from Cicero's speech for Sulla that it was a colonia. The same Cicero, arguing against the Agrarian Law, said it must in no way be allowed, and he hands the Pompeii, a very rich and fertile estate of the Roman people, over to the auction of the decemvirs. Tacitus, in book 25, notes that this town was for the most part overthrown by an earthquake in the times of Nero, and Dio says it was buried under the ash of Mount Vesuvius together with Herculaneum. Pliny, in book 14 of the Natural History, chapter 6, celebrates the Pompeian wines. Appian, in book 1 of the Civil Wars, mentions the Pompeian plain from here. Is it not near the Pompeii, and from them is it not called the Pompeian villa of Cicero, which he mentions both in his letters to Atticus and in Sallust's speech against him? Blondus and Baptista Porta of Naples place it near S. Maria Nunziata. Ambrogio Leone thinks this place is called Pompeianum. Pliny, in book 6 of his letters, to Lactus, writes of Pompeianum, which lay in the middle of the bay. Is it the same as the Pompeianum? asks Abraham Ortelius. Pomponius Fortunatus, on the same author, writes that the Pompeian marsh, mentioned by Columella, lay by the sea near Pompeianum.

units.la: Veteri Montis, de quo supra, pedi adpositum est opidum Summa in Mediterraneis: à quo Mons ipse Summa us, vulgo Monte di Summa.
units.tr: At the foot of Mount Vetere, mentioned above, lies the town of Summa in the inland hills, from which the mountain itself is called Summa, commonly Monte di Summa.

units.la: Rubos, quos canit Horatius libro 1. Sat. v Campaniae etiam Opidum fuisse, notant Magni Viri. Videndus & Servius ad 1. Georgic. Vingilij, cui hinc Rubea Virga. Iam quid in Itineraria Tabula Pons Campaniae, Vibana, Ad Nonum, Inumia, Oplonti, Icentic, alijs quaerendum relinquo.
units.tr: Rubi, which Horace sings of in book 1, Satire 5, were also a town of Campania, as the great men note. See also Servius on Virgil, Georgics 1, from which comes the "Rubea Virga." As for what is to be sought in the Itinerary Table (Pons Campaniae, Vibana, Ad Nonum, Inumia, Oplonti, Icentia, and others), I leave that to others.

units.la: Solent cum Campanis explicari Picentini, quorum Ager, Pars quaedam Campaniae, Principatus nunc appellatur, testibus Collenutio & Leandro. Fines Gentis Strabo, Ptolemaeus alij constituunt ad Occasum Campaniam; ad Septemtrionem, Hirpinos, qua Ortus est, Silarum Amnem & Lucaniam; qua Meridies, Tyrrhenum Mare, inter quos limites Regio concluditur latitudine P. M. xvi, longitudine xxx, ut auctor est Plinius. Picentines à Piceno in haec loca transductos, scribit Strabo; Picentes etiam nominant ut & Pomponius Mela. Caput Gentis Picentiam, unde Nomen illi, fuisse tradit Plinius: quae Nixerria Straboni; Nixerrov, Phiegonti apud Stephanum. Faciunt Picentie mentionem etiam Silius Italicus & Pomponius Mela. Hodie Picenis, notaribus Leandro & Mazzella. Dividitur nunc haec Regio, Principatus inquam, in Citeriorem & Ulteriorem; singuli que, praeter Principatus, Ducatus, Marchionatus & Comitatus, de quibus in genere supra, sui etiam sunt Baronatus: Citerioris q. idem, Pimonte. | Olivito. | Alfano. Pascetano. | Cornito. | Romagnano. Castello de Laureto. | Rescino. | Castello de Benati Vietre. | Filetto. | Fennachio. Acciaro. | Campora. | Acquaviefe. Mandia. | Toracia. | Porcile. Turrecursare | Trituirella | Cameleto. Perriano. | Casaletto. | S. Pietro. Lavrino. | Cugniano. | Santo Memnano. Pella. | Cotrone. | Agropoli. S. Giorgio. | Bracigliano. | Patechia. Sicigna o. | Vidanella. | Lancusiori. Santo Angelo Fasavelle. | Casella. | Casale de centule. Castro Nuovo. | Forte. | Casali de Capo Grasse. Casal Nuovo. | Senerchia. | Casals de Prignani. Prisiotta. | Santo Magno. | Castiello de Deastri. Schifato. | Valva.
units.tr: The Picentini are usually explained together with the Campanians. Their territory, a part of Campania, is now called the Principato, according to the testimony of Collenuccio and Leandro. Strabo, Ptolemy and others set the boundaries of the people: to the west Campania; to the north the Hirpini, and the Silarus river and Lucania where it rises; to the south the Tyrrhenian Sea. Within these limits the region is enclosed, 16 Roman miles in breadth and 30 in length, as Pliny says. Strabo writes that the Picentines were transferred to these places from Picenum. Pomponius Mela also calls them Picentes. Pliny reports that the chief town of the people was Picentia, from which they took their name; Strabo calls it Nixerria, and Phlegon, in Stephanus, Nixerron. Silius Italicus and Pomponius Mela also mention Picentia. Today it is Picenis, according to Leandro and Mazzella. This region, the Principato as I say, is now divided into Citra and Ultra. Each of them, besides the principalities, dukedoms, marquisates and counties (of which above, in general), also has its own baronies. Of Citra, the baronies are: Pimonte, Olivito, Alfano, Pascetano, Cornito, Romagnano, Castello de Laureto, Rescino, Castello de Benati Vietre, Filetto, Fennachio, Acciaro, Campora, Acquaviefe, Mandia, Toracia, Porcile, Turrecursare, Trituirella, Cameleto, Perriano, Casaletto, S. Pietro, Lavrino, Cugniano, Santo Memnano, Pella, Cotrone, Agropoli, S. Giorgio, Bracigliano, Patechia, Sicigna, Vidanella, Lancusiori, Santo Angelo Fasavelle, Casella, Casale de Centule, Castro Nuovo, Forte, Casali de Capo Grasse, Casal Nuovo, Senerchia, Casals de Prignani, Prisiotta, Santo Magno, Castiello de Deastri, Schifato, Valva.

units.la: Vlterioris vero:
units.tr: Of Ultra, indeed:

Cervinara. | Villa Marina. | Sorbo. Bisavia. | Pandarono. | Santo Giorgio de Monte Fuscilo. Castiello Pote. | Molinara. | Mirabella. Santo Magno. | Paglio. | Santa Maria di Tloro. Fossaceca. | Fono Albergo. | Monte Falcone. Cassiano. | Arpaia. | Prata. Valio Vitulano. | Monti ma'o. | Chianetella. Monte Falcone. | Santo Martino. | Santo Nicolao Menfreda. Sumonti Balzenara. | Lacidonia. | Petruno. Rocha Balzenara. | Guardia Lombarda. Melite. | Lapio. Chiancheterelle. | Genestra de Monte Fuscolo. | Santo Barbato. Malecalzalis. | Forino. | Mancusio. Carise. | Tuso. | Porcarino. Frangito de Monteforte. | Castro de Franchi. Quæ Ticentinorum Specialiora jam nunc videamus.
units.tr: Solofra, Castiello Franco, Casale de Monte Rochette, Monte Viridi, S. Marco di Cavoti, S. Maria in Grisone, Castello de la Baronia, Toccamisio, Coppalono, Cervinara, Villa Marina, Sorbo, Bisavia, Pandarono, Santo Giorgio de Monte Fuscilo, Castiello Pote, Molinara, Mirabella, Santo Magno, Paglio, Santa Maria di Tloro, Fossaceca, Fono Albergo, Monte Falcone, Cassiano, Arpaia, Prata, Valio Vitulano, Monti Mao, Chianetella, Monte Falcone, Santo Martino, Santo Nicolao Menfreda, Sumonti Balzenara, Lacidonia, Petruno, Rocha Balzenara, Guardia Lombarda, Melite, Lapio, Chiancheterelle, Genestra de Monte Fuscolo, Santo Barbato, Malecalzalis, Forino, Mancusio, Carise, Tuso, Porcarino, Frangito de Monteforte, Castro de Franchi. Let us now look at the places of the Picentines more closely.

units.la: Ostium Sarni transgressus post duo millia Castellum Almarinum est, Stabiense cognominatum, vulgo Castel al Mare di Stabie; quod propinquo loco Stabiæ fuerint, ut ante dictum, ad differentiam alterius Almarini Vulturnien sium. Situm est in angulo Gauri Montis, ubi in Occasum ille vergere incipit, Minervæ Promontorium efficiens.
units.tr: Having crossed the mouth of the Sarnus, after two miles, is the Castellum Almarinum, surnamed Stabiense, commonly Castel al Mare di Stabie. It is so called because Stabiae were near that place, as said before, to distinguish it from the other Almarinum of the Vulturnians. It lies in the corner of Mount Gauro, where that mountain begins to slope westward, forming the Promontory of Minerva.

units.la: A litore tum introrsum in Mediterraneis Nuceria Civitas est, ab Mari P. M. ix; ab Sarno, iv. Nota Strabonı, Appiano lib. i, ii, iv de Bello Civili, Ptolemæo (quibus Nuceria) Tacito lib. xiii, L. Floro de Bello Spartaco, Procopio lib. iii. de Bello Gothico, Silio libro viii, Antonino, itinerariæ Tabulæ, & aliis. Hodie Nuceria, vel Nocera de' Pagani, de quo Cognomine Volaterranus lib. vi Commentar. Vrbanor. Cicero ad Atticum non semel Luceriam videtur appellare. Coloniam Romanam notat Livius libro xxvii. Episcopatus floret inuio. Memorat Nucerinos aliquoties Livius, præcipue libro xxii & xxviii: Nucerini autem Agri præstantiam Cicero, Legem dissuadens Agrariam. Est sane vberrimus, amœnissimus Pagis refertissimus. Nobiles Nuceria huic Familiæ, Castaldi. | Marini. | Di Rinaldo. Lamberti. | Pagani. | Virgari & aliæ. Magliani.
units.tr: Inland from the shore, in the Mediterranean hills, is the city of Nuceria, nine miles from the sea and four from the Sarnus. It is noted by Strabo, Appian in books 1, 2 and 4 of the Civil Wars, Ptolemy (who calls it Nuceria), Tacitus in book 13, L. Florus on the war with Spartacus, Procopius in book 3 of the Gothic War, Silius in book 8, Antoninus, the Itinerary Table, and others. Today it is Nuceria, or Nocera de' Pagani, concerning which surname Volaterranus, in book 6 of his Commentaries on Urban Matters, writes. Cicero, in letters to Atticus more than once, seems to call it Luceria. Livy, in book 27, notes it as a Roman colony. The bishopric flourishes. Livy mentions the Nucerini several times, especially in books 22 and 28, and Cicero, arguing against the Agrarian Law, praises the excellence of the Nucerini's agri. It is indeed very fertile and very pleasant, and full of villages. Noble families of Nuceria are: Castaldi, Marini, Di Rinaldo, Lamberti, Pagani, Virgari and others, Magliani.

units.la: Supra Nuceriam Montes sunt; inter quos Intermontium Castellum, vulgo Tramonte, sicab situ dictum.
units.tr: Above Nuceria there are mountains, among which lies the Intermontium castle, commonly Tramonte, so called from its situation.

units.la: Lœva tum propinqua in Convalle ad Collis latus haud procul opidum est San-Severinum, unde Nobilissimæ San-Severinatium Familiæ Origo. Archiepiscopatus gaudet dignitate. Nobiles ibi: Abbatessa. | Pescara. | Sarno. Antinori. | Prignano. | Villani. Capasino. | San-Barbato.
units.tr: On the left, near at hand in a valley at the foot of a hill, not far off, is the town San-Severinum, from which the most noble San-Severinates family takes its origin. It enjoys archiepiscopal dignity. Noble families there are: Abbatessa, Pescara, Sarno, Antinori, Prignano, Villani, Capasino, San-Barbato.

units.la: Amœna jucundaque hic Vallis, Vino, quod San-Severinate, nobilis, in cujus fine Castellum est Aqua Malorum, vulgo Castello dell' Acqua della Mella. Illustravit Ortu suo Iacobus, Ordinis Prædicatorum Monachus, qui temporibus Eugenij iv P. M. in Concilio Florentino cum Græcis dimicavit.
units.tr: This valley is pleasant and agreeable, with the noble wine of San-Severinate, at whose edge is the Castellum Aqua Malorum, commonly Castello dell' Acqua della Mella. It was made famous by its native son Iacobus, a monk of the Order of Preachers, who in the time of Pope Eugene IV struggled with the Greeks at the Council of Florence.

units.la: Dextra in Monte, supra Convallem Cava est, Civitas Episcopalis; sic ab situ dicta. Iuxta visitur antiquum diversique Cœnobium, Civitati cognomine; cujus mentio in Canonibus. Lintrea Cave texta valde solent commendari; ipsíque etiam Cavenses Architectura. Nobiles ibi Familiæ: Anna. | Ponzi. | Recchi. De Curtis. | Lamberti. | Tolsone. Longhi.
units.tr: On the right, on the mountain above the valley, is Cava, an episcopal city, so named from its situation. Nearby is seen an ancient and separate monastery, named after the city, whose mention is found in the Canons. Linens woven at Cava are usually much commended, and the Cavenses too for their architecture. Noble families there are: Anna, Ponzi, Recchi, De Curtis, Lamberti, Tolsone, Longhi.

units.la: Ad Littus redeo. Relictis obiter Grimano & Letterano Opidulis Surrentum videamus: positis primum Nobilibus, quæ Grimani, Familiis: Amiato. | Marchesi. | Miri. Aurea. | Marino. | Riminì. Baroni. | Medici. | Sicardi. Comparato.
units.tr: I return to the shore. Having passed by the small towns of Grimano and Letterano, let us look at Surrentum. First, the noble families of the Grimani: Amiato, Marchesi, Miri, Aurea, Marino, Riminì, Baroni, Medici, Sicardi, Comparato.

units.la: Surrentum vocant Tacitus libro iv, Plinius, Mela, Silius libro viii, Itineraria Tabula, aliique: quod Σύρρεντον, simplici R, Ptolemaeus. Nomen retinet. Ab Graecis conditam ait Higinus. Non, cujus olim, amplitudinis esse, monstrant Veterum Ædificiorum hic ibi rudera. Colonus adnumerat Liber Coloniarum. Calcum nobilitate Surrentum celebrari solitum, docet Plinius lib. xxxv. Nat. Histor. Hinc Martialis:
units.tr: Surrentum is called so by Tacitus in book 4, Pliny, Mela, Silius in book 8, the Itinerary Table and others. Ptolemy writes it with a single R, Σύρρεντον [Syrrenton]. It keeps its name. Hyginus says it was founded by the Greeks. The ruins of ancient buildings here and there show that it was once not of great size. The Liber Coloniarum counts it among the colonies. Calcum (lime) from Surrentum was commonly celebrated for its quality, as Pliny teaches in book 35 of the Natural History. Hence Martial:

units.la: Accipe non vili Calices de pulvere natos,Sed Surrentinae laeve torneuma reta,
units.tr: Take these cups, made not from cheap dust, but from the smooth turning of the Surrentine wheel.

units.la: Archiepiscopatus hodie Sedes. Nobiles habet Familias, quae vulgo: Acciapazzi. Domini Marte. Orefice. Accio. Esipio. Pellegrini. Amoni. Falanghi. Della Porta. Anfora. Fieri. Romani. Borso. Guardati. Rota. Branzi. Marzati. Serfali. Capeci. Maestro giudici. Spasiani. Cortesi. Muligiuani. Tracci. Curiali. Nobilione. Visfo. Vulcani, & aliae.
units.tr: Today it is an archiepiscopal see. It has noble families, which in the vernacular are called: Acciapazzi, Domini, Marte, Orefice, Accio, Esipio, Pellegrini, Amoni, Falanghi, Della Porta, Anfora, Fieri, Romani, Borso, Guardati, Rota, Branzi, Marzati, Serfali, Capeci, Maestro Giudici, Spasiani, Cortesi, Muligiuani, Tracci, Curiali, Nobilione, Visfo, Vulcani, and others.

units.la: Nobilitavit hoc Opidum Crassitius, Libertinae conditionis, cognomine Pasides, qui Romae Grammaticam docuit, teste Suetonio. Ager uberrimus Vitibus, Citris, aliisque Arboribus. Vina Surrentina, propter tenuitatem & salubritatem, celebrant, praeter Strabonem & Martialem, Plinius libro iiii cap.vi, & libro xxiii cap. i. Lenia vocat Persius Satyra iii. Surrentinos Colles nominat Columella; Surrentinum Promontorium Tacitus libro iv.
units.tr: This town was made famous by Crassitius, a freedman, with the surname Pasides, who taught grammar at Rome, as Suetonius attests. The countryside is very fertile in vines, citrons and other trees. Surrentine wines are celebrated for their thinness and wholesomeness, besides by Strabo and Martial, by Pliny in book 4, chapter 6, and in book 23, chapter 1. Persius in Satire 3 calls them Lenia. Columella names the Surrentine hills, and Tacitus in book 4 the Surrentine promontory.

units.la: Ab Surrento M. P. novi nominis Opidum est Massa; cujus Ager Vino, quod Massicanum dicitur, idem cum Surrentino, abundat.
units.tr: Massa, a town of recent name, lies about a Roman mile from Surrento. Its territory abounds in the wine called Massican, which is the same as the Surrentine.

units.la: Sequitur Vicus, exiguum Opidum; sic dictum, quod Vicus prius fuerit non ignobilis. Et Vico & Massa, licet obscurioribus, Episcopi tamen sunt sui, Archiepiscopo Surrentino suffraganei.
units.tr: Next comes Vico, a small town, so called because it was formerly a not inconsiderable village. Vico and Massa, though less well known, nevertheless have their own bishops, who are suffragans of the Archbishop of Surrento.

units.la: Offert se mox Ritellum; novum Opidum, sed Ædificiorum splendore & Episcopatu praeligne: multisque superbiens Nobilibus Familiis, quae vernaculae: Aconzagiaco. Frezza. Pirenta. Appenditane. Fusca. Roga Dio. Bove. Grizona. Ruffola. Castalda. Marra. Rustica. Campanile. Muscetolla. Storbagioco. Confaloni. Oferia. Della Vitte. Fogia. Pepone.
units.tr: Next presents itself Ritellum, a new town, but excelling in the splendour of its buildings and its bishopric, and taking pride in many noble families, which in the vernacular are called: Aconzagiaco, Frezza, Pirenta, Appenditane, Fusca, Roga Dio, Bove, Grizona, Ruffola, Castalda, Marra, Rustica, Campanile, Muscetolla, Storbagioco, Confaloni, Oferia, Della Vitte, Fogia, Pepone.

units.la: In Littore, sub montibus, Civitates sunt duae: cum Ædium magnificentia, tum Agrorum amoenitate nobiles: Major & Minor dictae.
units.tr: On the shore, beneath the mountains, there are two cities, noted both for the magnificence of their buildings and the pleasantness of their fields. They are called Major and Minor.

units.la: Mox circa medium ferme hujus Orae, juxta littus, Amalphi jacet; Urbs lautissima: à qua circumjecti Tractus, quem Leander curiose delineat, appellatio fluxit. Malfitanum Opidum est apud Volaterranum, qui putat Plinij Asfellanos esse. Ego secus sentio. Asfellani enim Plinio Hirpinorum Populi, ad Mare Hadriaticum. adeo ut etiam non possint esse Melphis Incolae in Lucania, ut quidam putant. De Amalphi Blondus libro Historiarum xv. Amalphitanos quondam magnos fuisse Negociatores, testantur multa Siciliae Loca, in quis suas habuerunt Ædes, propriasque Apothecas, & Mercium Promptuaria. Ioannem Goiam, Civem Amalphitanum, Magnetis usum, navigantibus perneccessarium, reperisse circa annum cio cce perhibent. Archiepiscopatus superbit dignitate. Amalphitanae Ecclesiae meminit Gratianus Decret. ii Cauf. xxxv. Cives Offa D. Andreae se servare adfirmant. Nobiles ibi familiae D'Afflitto & Dello Riccio.
units.tr: Soon, about the middle of this coast, close to the shore, lies Amalfi, a most elegant city, from which the name of the surrounding district, which Leander describes with care, derives. The town of Malfi is mentioned by Volaterranus, who thinks it is Pliny's Asfellani. I think otherwise. For according to Pliny the Asfellani are a people of the Hirpini, on the Adriatic Sea, so that they cannot be the inhabitants of Melfi in Lucania, as some think. On Amalfi see Biondo, book 15 of the Histories. Many places in Sicily testify that the Amalfitans were once great merchants, having their own houses there, private shops and storehouses for goods. They say that John Gioia, a citizen of Amalfi, who used the magnet, which is very necessary to sailors, discovered it around the year 1302. The archbishopric takes pride in its dignity. Gratian mentions the Church of Amalfi, Decretum part 2, cause 35. The citizens affirm that they keep the bones of St Andrew. Noble families there are the D'Afflitto and Dello Riccio.

units.la: Amalphi Salernum per Continentem incedenti Vicus Veterum occurrit vel Vetus Vrbs, ubi plurimæ passim Villæ, cum lautissimæ, tum amœnissimæ.
units.tr: Going from Amalfi through the mainland towards Salerno, one meets the Vicus Veterum, or Vetus Urbs, where very many villas are scattered about, both most elegant and most pleasant.

units.la: Succedit antiqua Civitas Salernum, Veteribus celebratum Scriptoribus Plinio, Lucano lib. II, Silio libro VIII, Itinerariæ Tabulæ, alijs. Σάλερνον Straboni & Ptolomæo: Salernus Paullo Diacono libro II de Gest. Langbardor. cap. XVII. Coloniis concensent Livius libro XXXIV, Paterculus: Frontinus. Vrbs & Principatus & Archiepiscopatus Titulum sustinet. Academiam habet, quæ consulta aliquando ab Anglorum Rege de Conservanda valitudine, Consilium, quod exstat Typis excusum, transmisit. In ea superioribus annis docuit Augustinus Niphus, celebris Philosophus: Iurisprudentiam ibi professus est Robertus Moranta, Speculi Aurei auctor. Nunc temporis injuria & aliarum Academiarum, quæ vicinæ sunt, splendore valde est obscurata. Primarium Templum D. Matthæo dicatum, cujus ibi corpus servari fertur. Nobilitarunt Patriam Salernam, præter alios, Iacobus Solimenius Medicus, cum Antonio Filio: Bartholomæus Salvanius, Pandectarum Medicinalium Auctor, aliique multi. Familiæ Nobiles hic non paucæ, quas in vulgato Libello sic lego conceptas:
units.tr: Next comes the ancient city of Salerno, celebrated by ancient writers: Pliny, Lucan in book 2, Silius in book 8, the Itinerary Table, and others. Strabo and Ptolemy call it Σάλερνον; Paul the Deacon, in book 2 of the History of the Lombards, chapter 17, calls it Salernus. Livy in book 34, Paterculus and Frontinus agree that it is among the colonies. The city holds the title of principality and of archbishopric. It has an academy, which once, when consulted by the King of England about preserving health, sent him a consultation that survives in print. In recent years Augustinus Niphus, a famous philosopher, taught there; Robertus Moranta, author of the Speculum Aureum, professed jurisprudence there. Now, through neglect and through the splendour of other academies nearby, it is greatly overshadowed. Its chief temple is dedicated to St Matthew, whose body is said to be preserved there. Besides others, Jacobus Solimenius, a physician, with his son Antonio, ennobled their homeland Salerno; also Bartholomaeus Salvanius, author of the Medicinal Pandects, and many others. There are not a few noble families here, which I read in a popular little book as follows:

units.la: Nel Seggio di Porta Ritesa.
units.tr: In the Seggio of Porta Ritesa.

units.tr: In the Seggio del Campo:

units.tr: Castellonico. | Guardati. | Solimele. Cavafelice. | Di Ruggio. | Spitilli. Granito. | Sciabiga. | Trentacapilli. Grillí.

units.la: Nel Seggio di Porta Nova.
units.tr: In the Seggio of Porta Nova.

units.la: Aversani. | Comiti. | Del Giudice. Capogrossi. | Grilli. | Longhi. Mazza. | Pinti. | Scattaretici. Di Mora. | Protogiudici. | De Vicarijs. Pagani. | Santo Mango.
units.tr: Aversani. | Comiti. | Del Giudice. Capogrossi. | Grilli. | Longhi. Mazza. | Pinti. | Scattaretici. Di Mora. | Protogiudici. | De Vicarijs. Pagani. | Santo Mango.

units.la: Ager infinitis Pomorum variorumque Fructuum generibus, quæ recensèt Leander Albertus, abundat.
units.tr: The land abounds with countless kinds of apples and various other fruits, which Leander Alberti lists.

units.la: Ab Salerno per amœnam Planitiem decem millia emenso offert se Ebolum, haud procul Amne Silaro opulentum Opidum Reperitur in Geographia Ptolemaica Bernardi Silvani. Sed Glossema esse loquuntur meliores Fidei editiones, ab ipso celebrandæ Patriæ, adjectum.
units.tr: Ten miles from Salerno, across a pleasant plain, there presents itself Ebolum, a rich town not far from the river Silarus. It is found in Ptolemy's Geography in the edition of Bernardo Silvani. But the better editions say that this is a gloss, added by Silvani himself to celebrate his own homeland.

units.la: Anteaquam Campania excedam, adscribam ex Antonino Itinera Tria: quorum Priora ad eam solam pertinent; Postremum cum alio mistum ducitur ex Latio per eam in Lucaniam.
units.tr: Before I leave Campania, I will add from the Antonine Itineraries three routes. The first of these pertain to this region alone; the last, combined with another, is taken from Latium through Campania into Lucania.

units.la: T
units.tr: T

units.la: Antoninus: | Itineraria Tabula. | Vulgata Nomencl. Iter à Tarracina Neapolim M.P. LXXXVII sic: | Terracina, | XIII. | Fundi, | ..... | Fondi. Formis, | VIIII. | Menturnis. | VIIII. | Trajetto. Sinuessam, M.P.XXIIII. | Sinuessa, | VII. | Rocha di Monte Dragone. Safo Fl. | XII. Vulturno, | XII. | Castello al Mar di Boterno. Liternum, M.P.XXIIII. | Literno, | VI. | Vbi nunc Torre del Patria. Cumas, M.P.VI. | Cumas, | .... | Periere. Puteolos, M.P.III | Putcolis, | .... | Pozzuolo. Neapolim, M.P.X. | Neapoli, | .... | Napoli.
units.tr: Antoninus, Itinerary Table (Vulgate nomenclature). The route from Tarracina to Naples, 87 Roman miles, runs thus: Terracina, 13 (Fundi); Fundi, Fondi; Formiae, 9; Minturnae; Trajectum (Traetto); Sinuessa, 24 miles; Sinuessa, 7; Rocca di Monte Dragone; Savo river; Vulturnus, 12; Castello al Mar di Volturno; Liternum, 24 miles; Literno, 6; now Torre del Patria; Cumae, 6 miles; Cumae; Pericles (Parete?); Puteoli, 3 miles; Puteoli, Pozzuolo; Naples, 10 miles; Neapolis, Napoli.

units.la: II
units.tr: II

units.tr: Antoninus, Itinerary Table (Vulgate nomenclature). From Liternum to Misenum, 22 miles, thus: Cumae, 6 miles; Liternum to Cumae, 3; Pericles (?). Baiae, 3 miles; the remaining stages are missing, though traces survive. Misenum, 3 miles; Monte Miseno.

units.tr: III The route which leads from the City by the Appian Way to the Column, among other stages, reads thus:

Ad Nonum, VI | ........ Casilino, III. | Castelluzzo. Capuam, M.P.XXVI. | Capua, VIII. | Casals de Capua. Suessula, VIIII. | Sessulla. Nolam, M.P.XXI. | Nola, V. | Noli. Ad Teglanum, VIIII. | ....... Nuceriam, M.P.VI. | Nuceria. | Nuceria dei Pagani. In medio Falerno ad Tanarum, M.P.XXV. | ....... | ........
units.tr: Antoninus, Itinerary Table (Vulgate nomenclature). Minturnae, 9; Minturnae to Sinuessa, 9 miles; Sinuessa; Rocca di Monte Dragone. To the Campanian Bridge, 3, faultily. To Nonum, 6; Casilinum, 3; Castelluzzo. To Capua, 26 miles; Capua, 8; Casal di Capua. Suessula, 9; Sessula. To Nola, 21 miles; Nola, 5; Nola. To Teglanum, 9; Nuceria, 6 miles; Nuceria; Nocera dei Pagani. In the middle of the Falernian land, at the Tanarus, 25 miles.

units.la: De hac Mansione vide Conjecturam Hieronymi Suritæ, qui doctum & elaboratum scripsit Commentarium ad Antonini Itinerarium.
units.tr: On this stage see the conjecture of Girolamo Surita, who wrote a learned and elaborate commentary on the Itinerary of Antoninus.

units.la: Tria, quæ ex eadem Campania ducunt in Samnites, alibi videbimus. Non prætermittenda hic Inscriptio: quæ, uti ab Exscriptore Celso Cittadino Angelerio habere se dicit Abrahamus Ortelius, exstat in Agro Atinati, inserra pariet cuiusdam Cauponæ, vulgo L'Hosteria; vel, ut Regnicolis appellatur, La Taverna della Polla, ab Opido Polla, ibi proximo juxta quam exijt specu subterraneo Fluvius Tanager, vulgo aliique Scriptores. Quales ipserum mores fuerint, docet Iustinus ex Trogi libro xxiii his verbis: Lucani ipsidem legibus Liberos suos, quibus & Spartani instituere solebant: quisque ab initio pubertatis in silvis inter Pastores habebantur, sine munere ferre secum, sine veste, quam induerent, vel cum lavabantur, ut a primis annis duri & parsimoniaque sine ulla vi sua adsuefierent. Cibus his praeda venatica, potus Mellis & Lactis & Fontium liquor erat, sed ad labores bellicos indè alebantur: & quae sequuntur. Lucani Scuta sua e Vimine faciebant, corioque tegebant, Salustio teste. Plinius Lucanorum Coloros nomin at Atinates, Bantinos, Eburinos, Grumentinos, Polentinos, Sontinos, Sirinos, Tegilanos, Vfentinos, Volcentanos, Numestianos. De Atinatium, Grumentinis, Polentinis, Vfentinis infra. Eburinorum, Sontinorum, Sirinorum, Tergilianorum, Scriptorum nullus praeter Plinium facit mentionem. Qui Bantini Plinio, Stephano fortean Bantini) ab Opido, quod eidem nascerentur. Bantinus Salinus habet Horatius. De Volcentanis ita scribit ad V.C.L. Abrahamum Orielium Roma Celsus Citradinus Anglerius: Non sine ratione addunt Plinii textum hoc in toto siant & in aliis plurimis corruptum esse; & pro Volcentanis, Volcentani scribendum esse, ut in antiquis inscriptionibus, nisi forte ab Oppo Plinio a Volcetio Volcentani faciebant; tempore illius autem inferiores Volciani. Vencentes vel Vfifcientes, quos Livius lib. xxvii cum Hirpinis & Lucanis numerat, easdem cum Volcentanis vel Volcianis arbitrantur Viri docti. Vide quae infra dicam de Volcejo opido. Numestrani vel Numistrani ab Opido, quod Numistro apud Livium libro xxvii & Frontinum libro ii cap. ii; Nεμιστρων Ptolemaeo Numistra putatur nonnullis. Addidit Plinius lib. iii cap. xi: Praeterea inter ipse Thebanas Lucanas Cato auctor est: & Pandosiam Lucanorum urbem suisse Thebempur, in qua Alexander Epirotes occubuit.
units.tr: The three routes that lead from the same Campania into the Samnites we shall see elsewhere. An inscription must not be passed over here. Abraham Ortelius says that it was copied by Celso Cittadino Angelerio; it stands in the Atinate land, in the inner wall of an inn, commonly called L'Hosteria, or as the people of the kingdom call it, La Taverna della Polla, near the town of Polla, close to which the river Tanager emerges from an underground cave, as other writers also say. What their customs were, Justin shows in the words of Trogus' twenty-third book: "The Lucanians brought up their free children by the same laws by which the Spartans also trained theirs: from the beginning of puberty each was kept among the shepherds in the woods, carrying nothing with him, without the clothing he would put on, even when bathing, so that from their earliest years they became hardy and frugal and accustomed to no luxury. Their food was game from the hunt, their drink honey, milk and spring water, and from these they were then nourished for warlike labours," and what follows. "The Lucanians made their shields of wicker and covered them with leather," on the testimony of Sallust. Pliny names the Lucanian peoples as the Atinates, Bantini, Eburini, Grumentini, Polentini, Sontini, Sirini, Tegilani, Ufentini, Volcentani, and Numestiani. Of the Atinates, Grumentini, Polentini and Ufentini, see below. Of the Eburini, Sontini, Sirini and Tegilani, no writer except Pliny makes mention. The Bantini of Pliny (perhaps Stephanus' Bantini) are named from a town of that name, where they were born. Horace has "Bantine salt." About the Volcentani, Celso Cittadino Angelerio writes from Rome to the learned Abraham Ortelius thus: "Not without reason do they add that the text of Pliny is corrupted throughout this passage and in many others, and that for Volcentanis we should write Volcentani, as in the ancient inscriptions, unless perhaps from the town of Volcetium, which Pliny mentions, they were called Volcentani; but in his time the later form was Volciani." The Vencentes or Ufificientes, whom Livy in book 27 counts with the Hirpini and Lucanians, learned men think are the same as the Volcentani or Volciani. See what I say below about the town of Volcei. The Numestrani or Numistrani are named from the town which Livy in book 27 and Frontinus in book 2, chapter 2, call Numistro; some think Ptolemy's Nεμιστρων is Numistra. Pliny added in book 3, chapter 11: "Besides, Cato is the authority that among the Lucanians themselves there were Thebes and Pandosia, a city of the Lucanians, where Alexander of Epirus fell."

units.la: Haec generatim de Lucanis: speciatim quae ad eos persequar, orius ab Silaro, ubi est Occidentalissima.
units.tr: These things in general about the Lucanians. Specifically, I shall follow those places that belong to them, beginning from the Silarus, where it is most westerly.

units.la: In Silari Fausibus Locus visitur, ubi olim Iunonis Argiva Templum: uti Strabo referr, ab Iasone conditum. Plinius in Picentibus id locat, fortean propter vicinitatem.
units.tr: At the mouth of the Silarus there is a site where once stood the temple of Argive Juno, founded by Jason, as Strabo reports. Pliny places it among the Picentes, perhaps because of its proximity.

units.la: Hinc i Stadiis antiquis Temporibus fuit Pastum. Sic Latinis dicitur (Pestus nominatur Paulo Diacono lib. ii. Langbardic. cap. xvii) quae Gracis Ποσειδωνια, ut notat Plinius. Emendandus hic Agellius lib. xiiii cap. vi, ubi agit de immutatis Vrbium Regionumque Vocabulis: quod, inquit inter alia, Sesson Ποσειδαννον legendum Paeston vel Pastum. Pasti memnit multis locis Livius, praecipue libro viii, xxvi, xxvii. Deco Virgilius lib. iii Georg.
units.tr: Hence, in ancient times, there was a town at a distance of about five stadia, called Pastum. Thus it is called in Latin (it is named Pestum by Paul the Deacon, Lombard History, book 2, chapter 17), but in Greek Poseidonia, as Pliny notes. Agellius, book 14, chapter 6, needs correction here, where he treats of names of cities and regions that have changed: "Sesson, he says among other things, should be read as Poseidannon, or Paeston or Pastum." Livy mentions Pastum in many places, especially in books 8, 26 and 27. Virgil also mentions it in the third book of the Georgics:

units.la: Bissaque rosa in Pasti.
units.tr: "and roses twice in bloom at Paestum."

units.la: Ad quem locum Servius Pæsum Calabriae facit Civitatem ubi bis quotannis Rosae generantur. Lucanam enim Calabria, universim sumpta, Magni Viri concensent. Maritima Lucanae Vrbs est Philargyrio. Strabo conditam Locridem tradit in litoreab Sybaritis; Solinus ab Dorensibus. Inter Cominas est Livio lib. xii i & Herculo lib. i. Incolæ Pastani Livio lib. xxvi & aliis; vel Posidoniates eidem Livio lib. xv. Pastanum fuisse Parmenidem, qui Olympiade xcii vixit, docent Halicarnass. lib. ix & Diodorus Siculus lib. xi. A Pæsto Pastanae Valles, Solino; Pestanus Sinus Plinio, aliis Posidoniates, qui hodie Golfo Acropolitano apud Leandrum, di Salerno apud Ananientem & Mazzellam, ab Opidis vicinis; de quorum Priore mox dicendum, de Posteriore ante dictum. Pastanae Rosae leguntur apud Ovidium de Arte Amandi: unde & Vifera Rosaria Pasti apud Virgilium, ut supra memini; & Odorata Rosaria Pasti apud Propertium. Hoc Opidum Acropoli Pontano censetur; Gripos Nigro: Nomen retinet apud Leandrum Posidonia certe nunc tota propemodum extinctata jacet, vestigiaque tantum quibusdam partibus superessunt, cum Moemorum, tum Antiquorum Ædificiorum; uti adsirmant mihi, qui ijs in locis diu versati.
units.tr: On this passage Servius makes Paestum a city of Calabria, where roses are produced twice a year. For great men agree that Lucania is, in general terms, Calabria. Philargyrus says Maritima is a Lucanian city. Strabo records that Locri was founded on the shore by the Sybarites; Solinus says by the Dorians. Among the Cominates is in Livy, book 12, and in Hercules, book 1. The inhabitants are Pastani in Livy, book 26, and others, or Posidoniates in the same Livy, book 15. That Parmenides, who lived in the ninety-second Olympiad, was a native of Pastum is taught by Halicarnassus, book 9, and Diodorus Siculus, book 11. From Paestum come the Pastanian valleys, according to Solinus; the Paestan Gulf according to Pliny, and the Posidoniates according to others; today it is the Gulf of Acropoli near Leandro, and the Gulf of Salerno near Ananiente and Mazzella, named from neighbouring towns, of which the former will be discussed shortly, the latter has been mentioned before. Pastanian roses are read of in Ovid's Art of Love, whence also the "rosebeds of Paestum" in Virgil, as I mentioned above, and the "fragrant rosebeds of Paestum" in Propertius. This town is thought by Pontano to be Acropolis; by Nigro to be Gripos. Posidonia retains its name at Leandro, but now it lies almost wholly destroyed, and only traces remain in some parts, both of modern and ancient buildings, as those who have long lived in those places assure me.

units.la: In Littore porro post sex millia Opidum est Acropolis, ab Silari estio M. xii. Aere gaudet prastantissimo. Originis esse Græcæ, ut hoc tractu plerique; ipsum indicat Nomen.
units.tr: Further along the coast, six miles beyond, is the town of Acropolis, twelve miles from the mouth of the Silarus. It enjoys a most excellent air. That it is of Greek origin, like most places in this region, its very name shows.

units.la: Deinde quarto Lapide Castellum Albatis est, Castello de l'Abbate: hinc octavo Turris Martha Brucæana, Torre di Mare di Brucca. Sunt qui putant Vestam, antiquum Opidum, hoc loco fuisse. Strabo loquens lib. vi de Sinu, qui post Posidoniatem: ἐστὶ, inquit, πόλις, ἡ οἱ μὲν κτίσαντες Φωκαεῖς Τίλυε; οἱ δὲ ἐ Ἀλλων ἀποικίαν πυθ; οἱ νῦν.
units.tr: Then, four miles on, is the little castle of Albati, Castello de l'Abbate; from there, eight miles on, the tower of Martha Brucaeana, Torre di Mare di Brucca. Some think that Vesta, an ancient town, was in this place. Strabo, speaking in book 6 of the gulf which comes after Posidonia, says: "There is a city which the Phocaeans who founded it called Tilye, but others say it was a colony of the ... now" [ἐστὶ, inquit, πόλις, ἡ οἱ μὲν κτίσαντες Φωκαεῖς Τίλυε; οἱ δὲ ἐ Ἀλλων ἀποικίαν πυθ; οἱ νῦν].

units.la: Gggg 4 · di vir Vlterius in Collium flexu non procul a Mari Vrbs est Capacia, olim frequens admodum, & opulenta, Ducatus Episcopatuique (qui Caputaquensis) titulo insignis sed hac tempestate propemodum deserta, propter Adluviones.
units.tr: Further on, in a bend of the hills not far from the sea, is the city of Capaccio, once very populous and wealthy, distinguished by the title of a duchy and a bishopric (the Bishopric of Capaccio), but in these times almost deserted because of floods.

units.la: Ab Sanct-Atleno m. r. ad pedem Collis San-Petrium est, S. Pietro, inde SanRussum, S. Russo: hinc quaternis millibus in Apennini Colle, Dianium, Diano, est, Oppidum dives & nobile; a quo Valli, quam dixi universiae nomen.
units.tr: From Sant'Arsenio, a mile and a half, at the foot of the hill, is San Pietro, San Pietro; then San Rufo, San Rufo; and then, four miles up on the Apennine hill, Diano, Diano, a rich and noble town, from which the valley I mentioned takes its general name.

units.la: Duobus Diano milliaribus Castellum S. Iacobi est, S. Giacopo; hinc uno Sanctinum.
units.tr: Two miles from Diano is the little castle of San Giacomo, San Giacomo; one mile from there, Sanctinum.

units.la: Vlterius Bonum habitaculum est, Buon-Habitaculo, in dextra Vallis Dianiae postremum.
units.tr: Further on is Buon Abitacolo, Buon-Habitaculo, the last place on the right of the Valley of Diano.

units.la: Ad eiusdem Vallis laevam, si a Pola Septemtriones versus declines, ad millia xxx, inter Montes Potentia reperitur, Potenza vulgo, hac parte Lucaniae Finis. Meminerunt Ptolemaeus (cui Potentia) Antoninus, & Itineraria Tabula. Potentiae item habent Plinius lib. iii cap. v.
units.tr: On the left of the same valley, if you bear north from Pola, about 30 miles off, between the Potentia mountains, commonly called Potenza, is the border of this part of Lucania. Ptolemy (who calls it Potentia), Antoninus and the Itinerary Table mention it. Pliny, book 3, chapter 5, likewise has Potentiae.

units.la: In Vallem Dianam redeunti, sinistra secundum Colles, quatuor Pola miliaribus Atenum adparet: cuius Incolae Atinates Plinio lib. iii cap. xi: inde totidem Cala, Salernitani Principis Castellum: hinc rursus eodem spatio Padula Oppidum, Marchionatus inclutum dignitate.
units.tr: Returning into the Valley of Diana, on the left along the hills, Atenum comes into view four miles from Pola. Its inhabitants are the Atinates (Pliny, book 3, chapter 11). Then, equally far on, is Cala, a castle of the Prince of Salerno. From here, again at the same distance, is Padula, a town famous for its marquisate's dignity.

units.la: Sequitur mox spatio quatuor item milliar. Montesanum, ubi Vallis coartari incipit, usque ad finem decrescens.
units.tr: Next, after another four miles, is Montesanum, where the valley begins to narrow and keeps shrinking until its end.

units.la: Postremum eodem intervallo Casale Novum est, Casal Nuovo.
units.tr: Last, at the same interval, is Casale Novum, Casal Nuovo.

units.la: Silva Peregrinali peragrata, Itinereque octo miliarum per praecelsos & difficiles Lucaniae Montes, Antiquis celebratissimos, facto, offert sese Lacus Niger, Lago Negro oppidum: cuius ad dextram Turturellae: & Mare versus Laurinum: postea Iuta, Giogia, Nocaque.
units.tr: After crossing the Peregrinal forest and making an eight-mile journey through the very lofty and difficult mountains of Lucania, most celebrated among the ancients, there appears Lacus Niger, the town of Lago Negro. On its right is Turturellae, and toward the sea Laurinum; afterwards come Iuta, Giogia and Nocaque.

units.la: Ad Lacum Nigrum Itinere inter Montes tendenti, quatuor ab Mari p. m. Cucarum, dein Rufrenum & Casellae se dant in conspectum.
units.tr: On the journey between the mountains toward Lacus Niger, four miles from the sea, Cucarum comes into view, and then Rufrenum and Casellae.

units.la: Ad eiusdem Lacus Nigri dextram, inter luga Saponaria Castellum est, ubi Grumentum quondam fuisse magni censent Viri. Grumenti meminerunt Livius, Florus, Macrobius, Plinius lib. xiii, ubi de Vinis Italiae, Antoninus, Itineraria Tabula, alij. Γρύμεντον Appiano, Ptolemaeo, aliisque Graecis: Δεύμεντον passim apud Strabonem scribi notavit V. C. L. Isaacus Casaubonus; quemadmodum etiam apud Senecam lib. iii de Benef. cijs. Grumentinum Plinio noti.
units.tr: On the right of the same Lacus Niger, among the ridges of Saponaria, is a castle where distinguished men think Grumentum once stood. Grumentum is mentioned by Livy, Florus, Macrobius, Pliny (book 13, where he speaks of the wines of Italy), Antoninus, the Itinerary Table and others. Appian, Ptolemy and other Greeks write it Γρύμεντον [Grýmenton]. The distinguished Isaac Casaubon noted that Strabo throughout writes it Δεύμεντον [Deúmenton], as also does Seneca in book 3 of On Benefits. Pliny knows the name Grumentinum.

units.la: Iuxta haec deinde Mons Morus est & San-Clericum.
units.tr: Next to these are Mons Morus and San-Clericum.

units.la: Hinc ab Lacu Nigro quatuor milliar per horridos Montes emenso Rivellum occurrit: inde Luria; ad cuius dextram est Trechina; infraque inter Montes, Mare versus uno fere milliar Maratia.
