units.tr: From Lacus Niger, after four miles through rugged mountains, Rivellum comes up; then Luria, on whose right is Trechina; and below, among the mountains toward the sea, about a mile off, Maratia.

units.la: Ad Luriae laevam Latronicum, cum Claro-Montio, cernitur.
units.tr: On the left of Luria, with Claro-Montio, Latronicum is seen.

units.la: Eosdem inter Montes Lusillum est, a quo Silva Lusillina.
units.tr: Among the same mountains is Lusillum, from which the Silva Lusillina takes its name.

units.la: Sequitur Lainum Opidum cum Suburbiis, quae ab ipso opido, Lucanosque a Brutiis dividit Sapris Fluvius, antiquis Laus, de quo alibi. Lainum, Laus Plinio, Λαός Herodoto & Apollodoro apud Stephanum, cui τὸ Ἐθνικὸν Λαῖνον: Λαῖος Straboni lib. vi πόλις ἰσχάτη τῶν Λευκανῶν, Lucanicarum ultima.
units.tr: Next comes the town of Lainum with its suburbs. The river Sapris, anciently called Laus (of which more elsewhere), divides the town itself and the Lucanians from the Bruttians. Lainum, Laus in Pliny; Herodotus and Apollodorus, according to Stephanus, write Λαός [Laós], whose ethnic form is Λαῖνον [Laînon]; in Strabo, book 6, it is Λαῖος [Laîos], a city Λευκανῶν [Leukanôn] ἰσχάτη [ischátē] (the furthest of the Lucanian cities).

units.la: Ad Lucaniam pertinet Pars Itineris, quod Antoninus Mediolano ducit ad Columnam, id est Traiectum Siciliae; Portioque Alius, quod ab Urbe Appia Via recto itinere ad eandem tendit Columnam. De iis alibi. Nominantur praeter Polentiam & Grumentum, de quibus ante, in Priore quidem Acidy, Semuncla (pro quo Semunda legit Sigonius; Nerulum (quod Livius etiam libro ix notat ab Aemilio Cos. captum: Nerulos vocat Itineraria Tabula, unde Nerulonensis Mensarius apud Suetonium in Augusto cap. iv. Celsus Citradinus, scribens ad Ortelium, id esse censet, quod hodie Lagonero, in Via Aquilia, quae a Capua ad Rhegium tendebat) & Summuranum, Castrol illari nunc, ut idem putat Citradinus, & Scipio Mazzella: In Posteriore autem Marcelliana (parum ultra Atinam, uti idem Celsus arbitratur) & Cesariana.
units.tr: Part of the route which Antoninus leads from Mediolanum to Columna, that is, the crossing to Sicily, belongs to Lucania; so does the other route, from the Appian Way by a direct road to the same Columna. Of these more elsewhere. Besides Polentia and Grumentum, already mentioned, the following are named: in the former itinerary, Acidy, Semuncla (Sigonius reads Semunda instead), Nerulum (which Livy also records in book 9 as taken by the consul Aemilius; the Itinerary Table calls it Nerulos, whence the Nerulonensis Mensarius in Suetonius, Augustus, chapter 4. Celsus Citradinus, writing to Ortelius, thinks it is what is today Lagonero, on the Aquilian Way, which ran from Capua to Rhegium), and Summuranum, now Castrol illari, as Citradinus and Scipio Mazzella also think. In the latter itinerary are Marcelliana (a little beyond Atina, as Celsus also thinks) and Cesariana.

units.la: Non procul Summurano Syphei Opidi, cuius meminit Livius libro xxx vestigia conspici Gabriel Barrius Franciscanus Calaber confirmat; & ex eius ruinis Summuranum Opidum constructum coniicit; idque Sybarim Fluvium praeterfluere.
units.tr: Not far from Summuranum, Gabriel Barrius, a Franciscan of Calabria, confirms that traces of the town of Syphei, which Livy mentions in book 30, can still be seen. From its ruins he conjectures that the town of Summuranum was built, and he says that the river Sybaris flows past it.

units.la: CAPVT. XXVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVII.

units.la: Brutij.
units.tr: The Bruttii.

units.la: HÆC de Lucania: sequitur CALABRIA; eaque duplex, Inferior, quæ BRVTIORVM olim Sedes, hodie proprie Calabria Inferior; quum Magna Græcia sit Superior. Calabria ab Calabris, quos Magnæ Græciæ partem Salentinis adhærentem ad Ionium Æquor circa Iapygium Promontorium tenuisse, ex Ptolemæo est manifestum. Quin & Plinius, Ptolemæus & Solinus auctores sunt Calabriam Græcis Messapiam ab eo um Duce vocatam. Ex quibus paret, Calabriam quoque Partem esse Italiæ circa Iapygium Promontorium. Dauniorum, Iapygū & Salentinorum Regiones sub Calabrorum nomine contineri scribit Tzetza Chiliade 1 num. 27. Divinant quidam Appellationem factam Καλὰ τᾶ χωρα vel ἐφ' ἑω, quasi Regio omnibus rebus affluens & abundans. Fert enim utraque Calabria, ubertate quadam felicitateque stupenda, quidquid Vitæ ex voto transigendæ, deliciisque fruendis necessarium: Triticum Hordeum, aliaque Frumenti genera; Vinum varium, Oleum, Saccarum, Manna, Mel, Ceram, Sal nativum Factitiumque, Ficus, Poma Medica & Citria, Limones, aliosque Fructus nobilissimos: item Aurum, Argentum, Lanam, Gossipium, Crocum, Sericum, Linum, & quid non? Flumina passim oportuna, Fontes gratissimi, calidarum Aquarum Scaturigines, Pascua florentissima, Montes frugiferi, pingues Colles, densa Nemora, Valles fœcundissimæ: ingens Populi ubique frequentia. Meminerunt Calabriæ Inscriptiones Veteres: inter quas, quæ Neapoli his verbis concepta: M. BASSÆO. M. F PAL. AXIO PATR. COL. CVR. R. P IT VIR. MVNIC. PROC. AVG VIÆ. OST. ET. CAMP. TRIB. MIL. LEG XIII GEM. PROC. CALABR OMNIB. HONORIB. CAPVÆ. FVNC. PATR. COL. LVPIENSIVM. PATR MVNICIP. HYDRENTINORVM, &c.
units.tr: So much for Lucania. Next comes CALABRIA, which is double: Inferior, which was formerly the seat of the BRUTTII and is today properly called Calabria Inferior, since Magna Græcia is the Superior. That Calabria takes its name from the Calabri, who held the part of Magna Græcia adjoining the Salentines, by the Ionian Sea near the Iapygian promontory, is clear from Ptolemy. Indeed Pliny, Ptolemy and Solinus state that Calabria was called Messapia by the Greeks, after a leader of that name. From these sources it is plain that Calabria too is part of Italy around the Iapygian promontory. Tzetzes, in Chiliad 1, no. 27, writes that the regions of the Daunians, Iapygians and Salentines are included under the name of the Calabri. Some guess that the name was derived from Καλὰ τᾶ χωρα [Καλὰ τᾶ χωρα] or ἐφ' ἑω [ἐφ' ἑω], as if to say a region abounding and overflowing in all things. For both parts of Calabria bear, with a wonderful fertility and richness, whatever is needed for living as one wishes and for enjoying pleasures: wheat, barley and other kinds of grain; wine of various sorts, oil, sugar, manna, honey, wax, natural and manufactured salt, figs, medlars and citrons, lemons, and other most excellent fruits; likewise gold, silver, wool, cotton, saffron, silk, flax, and what not? Rivers suitable for use are everywhere, springs most pleasant, hot-water springs, very lush pastures, fruitful mountains, rich hills, dense woods, very fertile valleys, and everywhere a great crowd of people. The ancient inscriptions mention Calabria. Among them is one from Naples, worded thus: To Marcus Bassaeus, son of Marcus, of the Palatine tribe, Axius, patron of the colony, curator of the republic, procurator of Augustus for the Via Ostiensis and Campania, tribune of soldiers of the thirteenth legion Gemina, procurator of Calabria, holding all honours, priest for life of the colony of the Lupienses, patron of the municipality of the Hydrentini, etc.

units.la: Sic, quæ sub ipsa Præneste, in Via publica, qua Albam itur: T. FLAVIO. T. F. GERMANO
units.tr: So too the inscription just below Praeneste, on the public road that goes to Alba: To Titus Flavius Germanus, son of Titus.

units.la: & paullo post: PROC. AD. ALIMENTA. BRVTI. CALABR. ET. APVLIÆ &c.
units.tr: And a little after: procurator for the provisions of Bruttium, Calabria and Apulia, etc.

units.la: Calabriæ huius inferiora versus Mare Mediterraneum tenent Bruttij; quibus unde nomen impositum, variant Veteres Auctores. Strabo lib. vi alijque sic dictos putant ab Lucanis, qui Bruttios sua lingua vocabant Apoštatas, Rebelles & Fugitivos. Lucanorum enim Pastores & Servi, rebus tempore Dionysij turbatis, ab ijs defecerant; & aufugientes sese pro liberis gerere coeperant. Iustinus ex Trogi libro xxiii à Bruttia Muliere quadam, cujus proditione quum ab hostibus peterentur, Castellum quoddam expugnarant, eos dirivat. Regnum fuisse vult Paullus Diaconus lib. ii Langbardic. cap. xvii. Stephanus à Bretto Herculis Filio censet dictos. Alij sic appellatos arbitrantur à Bruto Vmbro. Βρέττιοι nominantur Ptolemæo: Brutij non semel vocantur in Codice Theodosiano: Brettij leguntur in Numismatibus: Βρέττιοι Aristophani: Βρεττίοι sunt apud Dionysium Afrum, & ipsius commentatorem Eustathium, Diodorum item libro xvi. Bruttates apud Sex. Pompeium Festum. flum. Βρέττια ipsi nominatur Regio apud Polybium lib. xr. Βρέττια Straboni lib.vi. Sicilam vocari a Stephano, Theocriti Scholiaste, aliisque inde patet, quod Fluvios Opidaque non pauca in hoc Tractu Sicilia adscribunt. Hodie etiam in Titulis Regum Hispaniae Sicilia cis Pharum appellatur ad differentiam Insulae, quae ultra Pharum. Olim Bruttiorum fines inter Laum & Fretum Siculum fuerunt, Stadiorum cIↄ ccc, inquit Strabo. Ptolemaeus Recentiorésque signant Bruttiorum regionem ab Amne Lao, qui ipsis ad Occidentem, per Tyrrheni Maris oram, quae Austro obiacet ad Fretum Siculum: qua Oriens est, parte Maris Adriatici; qua denique Septemtrio, Magna Graecia & Amne Crathi claudituř. Bruttios Saltus habet Seneca de Tranquillitate Vitae: Bruttia Saxa Persio Satyra vi dicuntur Scopuli Bruttys Italiae Populis Lucanisque proximi. Bruttiana Tarma Festo, quibus Bruttij sunt usi. Bruttia Vada, id est Mare Bruttium Senecae in Hercule Oetaeo Choro Actus II. Bruttia Pinus meminit Dioscorides: eam Plinius ad Vasa Vino condendo maxime probasi adfirmat. Res à Bruttiis gestas commemorat praeter alios Romanarum Rerum Scriptores, Livius plurimis in locis; cum primis lib. xii, xiii, xv, xxiv, xxx. Meminerunt & Bruttiorum Silius lib.xi, aliique Auctores. Huc pertinent illa Paulli Diaconi ex Festi lib. ii: Bruttiani dicebantur, qui officia servitia Mugisfratitum praestabant: eo quod hi primum se Hannibali tradiderant, & cum eo perseverarunt usque dum recederet de Italia. Vide & Agellium lib. x. cap. iii, Iustum Liptium ad lib. ii Annalium Taciti, & lib. i. Electorum cap. xxii, Petrum Crinitum lib. ii. de honesta Disciplina cap. vii, & alios. Bruttates Bilingues Ennio Poetae apud Festum, quod Brutij & Osci & Graeci loqui essent soliti.
units.tr: The lower parts of this Calabriæ towards the Mediterranean Sea are held by the Bruttij; the ancient authors differ about where their name came from. Strabo, book 6, and others think they were so called by the Lucanians, who in their own language called the Bruttios Apoštatas [Apostates], Rebelles [rebels] and Fugitivos [runaways]. For the Lucanian shepherds and slaves, when affairs were disturbed in the time of Dionysius, had revolted from them, and, having fled, had begun to pass themselves off as free men. Justin, from book 23 of Trogus, derives them from a certain Bruttia woman, through whose betrayal they had captured a certain stronghold when they were being attacked by enemies. Paulus Diaconus, book 2 of the Lombard history, chapter 17, wants them to have been a kingdom. Stephanus thinks they were named after Bruttus, a son of Hercules. Others believe they were called after Brutus the Umbrian. They are called Βρέττιοι [Brettioi] by Ptolemy; the Brutij are called so more than once in the Theodosian Code; the Brettij are read of on coins; Βρέττιοι [Brettioi] by Aristophanes; Βρεττίοι [Brettioi] in Dionysius Afer and his commentator Eustathius, and likewise in Diodorus, book 16. Bruttates in Sextus Pompeius Festus. The region itself is called Βρέττια [Brettia] by Polybius, book 11, and by Strabo, book 6. That Sicily is called so by Stephanus, the scholiast of Theocritus, and others, is clear from the many rivers and towns they assign to this tract in Sicily. Even today in the titles of the kings of Spain, Sicily on this side of the Pharos is so named, to distinguish it from the island beyond the Pharos. Formerly the boundaries of the Bruttii lay between the Laus and the Sicilian Strait, 1,300 stadia, says Strabo. Ptolemy and more recent writers mark the region of the Bruttii as bounded by the river Laus, which lies to its west along the coast of the Tyrrhenian Sea facing the south wind, as far as the Sicilian Strait; to the east by the part of the Adriatic Sea; and to the north by Magna Græcia and the river Crathis. Seneca, in his De tranquillitate animi, mentions the Bruttian woods; in Persius, Satire 6, the Bruttian rocks are named as reefs, the Bruttii being peoples of Italy nearest to the Lucanians. Festus has the Bruttian tarmac, that is, what the Bruttii used. Seneca, in the Oetaean chorus of his Hercules Oetaeus, act II, has the Bruttian shallows, that is, the Bruttian sea. Dioscorides mentions the Bruttian pine, which Pliny asserts was especially approved for making vessels to store wine. Livy mentions the deeds of the Bruttii in many places among the other Roman historians, especially in books 12, 13, 15, 24 and 30. Silius, book 11, and other authors also mention the Bruttii. To this belong those words of Paulus Diaconus from Festus, book 2: the Bruttiani were those who performed the menial services of the magistrates, because they first surrendered themselves to Hannibal and remained with him until he withdrew from Italy. See also Aulus Gellius, book 10, chapter 3; Justus Lipsius on book 2 of Tacitus' Annals, and book 1 of his Electa, chapter 22; Petrus Crinitus, book 2 on honest discipline, chapter 7; and others. The poet Ennius, in Festus, calls the Bruttates bilingual, because the Bruttii were accustomed to speak Bruttian, Oscan and Greek.

units.la: De Calabria Natura, Situ doribus peculiaribus, & Antiquitatibus scripserunt Gabriel Barrius & Antonus Galateus. Bruttiorum etiam Terram seu Calabriam celebravit eleganti Encomio Franchinus Consentinus.
units.tr: Gabriel Barrius and Antonius Galateus have written about the nature, situation, peculiar customs and antiquities of Calabria. Franchinus Consentinus has also celebrated the land, or Calabria, of the Bruttii in an elegant encomium.

units.la: Ad Calabriam, vel, si cui magis id placet, Apulias referendi sunt, quos nominat Plinius, aliis nullam eorum mentionem facientibus, Egetini (qui in vulgatis Codicibus scribuntur Aegetini) Deciani, Ermuleffini, Nar bonenses, Sturnini & Tutini. De Butuntinensibus, qui ibidem commemorantur, infra in Apulia Peucetia. Habet etiam Plinius Aprusianos, Brettiorum Populos.
units.tr: To Calabria, or, if anyone prefers, to Apulia, must be referred the peoples Pliny names, while others make no mention of them: the Egetini (written Aegetini in the common texts), Decianos, Ermuleffini, Narbonenses, Sturnini and Tutini. The Butuntinenses, who are also mentioned there, are dealt with below under Apulia Peucetia. Pliny also has the Aprusiani, a people of the Bruttii.

units.la: Ad specialiora Bruttiorum venio; orsus ab Lai, quo separantur, ut dixi, ab Lucanis, ostio.
units.tr: I come to the more particular places of the Bruttii, beginning at the mouth of the Laus, by which, as I said, they are separated from the Lucanians.

units.la: Hic prima Bruttiorum Urbs in Littore Temesa. Ἀ'πὸ γὰρ Ἀάς, inquit Strabo lib. vi, πρώτη πόλις ἐστὶ τῆς Βρεττίας Τέμεσα: Τέμψαν δὲ οὕτω καλοῦσιν, Ἀὐσόνων κτίσμα: Τεμέση Homero apud Strabonem & Stephanum; Temese item Ovidio lib. xv. Metamorph. Statio in Silvis, ubi de Statua Equestri Imperatoris Domitiani, Pomponio Melae, aliis: Τέμσα Pausaniae lib. ii Eliacor. Nunc Tamosa, nunc Τέμσα Lycophroni: ut etiam notat ejus commentator Isacius: Τεμσία Polybio: Tempsa Ciceroni, Livio lib. xxxiv & aliis locis, Plinio, Prolemaeo: Temsa Itinerariae Tabulae. Tempsam primi coluerunt, ut notat Strabo, Ausones; inde Aetoli, qui Thoantem sequebantur: Aetolisautem pulsis Bruttij successerunt. Bruttij ab Hannibale & Romanis fuerunt attriti. Videndus omnino Livius libro xxxiiii; qui Coloniam Romanam docet factam. Vina Tempsa genita Plinius gloria non carere scribit. Metallorum fuisse divitem, paret ex Ovidio libro xv. Aliquando Metaurum vocatum, sed nunc S. Marco dici docet Gabriel Barrius. Malrito tradit hodie nominari Laurentius Ananiensis. Longobuco ab nonnullis censeri, memorat in Historia Neapolitana Pontanus. Sunt qui sitam fuisse putant, ubi nunc Policastrum, inquit Leander, eosdem refutans. Scribit Strabo prope Temesam Sacellum fuisse conceptum Olcastris, Politae Ulyssis Comiti dicatum, qui fraude Barbarorum circumventus ingenium bellorum fuit causa.
units.tr: Here, on the coast, is the first city of the Bruttii, Temesa. For "from Laus," says Strabo, book 6, "the first city of Bruttian territory is Temesa; they call it Tempsa, a foundation of the Ausones" [Ἀ'πὸ γὰρ Ἀάς, πρώτη πόλις ἐστὶ τῆς Βρεττίας Τέμεσα: Τέμψαν δὲ οὕτω καλοῦσιν, Ἀὐσόνων κτίσμα]. Homer, in Strabo and Stephanus, has Temese; Ovid, book 15 of the Metamorphoses, likewise has Temese. Statius, in the Silvae, where he speaks of the equestrian statue of the emperor Domitian; Pomponius Mela, and others. Pausanias, book 2 of the Eliaca, has Τέμσα [Temsa]; Lycophron has Nunc Tamosa and Τέμσα [Temsa], as his commentator Isaac also notes; Polybius has Τεμσία [Temsia]; Cicero, Livy in book 34 and elsewhere, Pliny and Ptolemy have Tempsa; the Itinerary Table has Temsa. The first to inhabit Tempsa, as Strabo notes, were the Ausones; after them the Aetolians, who followed Thoas; but when the Aetolians were driven out, the Bruttii succeeded them. The Bruttii were worn down by Hannibal and the Romans. Livy, book 34, must certainly be consulted, where he tells that a Roman colony was founded there. Pliny writes that the wines grown at Tempsa are not without their renown. That it was rich in metals is clear from Ovid, book 15. It was once called Metaurum, but Gabriel Barrius teaches that it is now called San Marco. Laurentius Ananiensis reports that it is today named Malrito. Pontanus, in his Neapolitan history, reports that some think Longobucco is it. Leander, refuting the same views, says there are those who think it stood where Policastro is now. Strabo writes that near Temesa there was a shrine, established at Olcastris and dedicated to Polites, the companion of Ulysses, who, deceived by the treachery of the barbarians, was the cause of the war by his cleverness.

units.la: Ταύτης δὲ, inquit Strabo, loquens de Tempsa, σωεχῆς Τεῖνα: Sic item vocatur Diodoro, Plinio, Melae: quae Terriana Leandro; Terina Nova Iovio; Mantes, Nigro. Nuceriam prope Terina reliquias statuit Gabriel Barrius. Τεῖνα κτίσμα Κροτωνιατῶν, teste apud Stephanum Phlegonte. Urbem captam evertit Hannibal, quum teneri posse dissideret, ut scribit Strabo: quum & Herdoneam forte: Vide Livium libro xxvii & Stephanum. Ab hac Sinus Terinaeus dictus Plinio & Thucydidi. Tempsa igitur & Terina Strabonis aliorumque Veterum temporibus Vrbes in Bruttiis fuerunt: flagitat ordo, ut quæ nunc exstant, commemorem.
units.tr: "Next to this," says Strabo, speaking of Tempsa, "continuously is Terina" [Ταύτης δὲ ... σωεχῆς Τεῖνα]. It is called so likewise by Diodorus, Pliny and Mela; Leander calls it Terriana; Jovius Terina Nova; Nigro Mantes. Gabriel Barrius places the remains of Nuceria near Terina. Terina was "a foundation of the Crotoniates," as Phlegon, quoted by Stephanus, testifies [Τεῖνα κτίσμα Κροτωνιατῶν]. Hannibal captured and destroyed the city, since he despaired of being able to hold it, as Strabo writes; and Herdonea likewise, perhaps. See Livy, book 27, and Stephanus. From this city the Terinaean gulf was named by Pliny and Thucydides. So Tempsa and Terina were towns of the Bruttii in the time of Strabo and the other ancients; the order of the work requires that I now mention those that still exist.

units.la: Circa Littus quidem sunt: primum Scalea, Episcopatus titulo insignis: decem inde passuum milibus Citrium; totidem hinc Adamantium, Diamante, cujus in agro Saccharum provenit: octavo inde Belvedersum: unde milliario semi Bonifactum. Hinc decem millibus Cetraum Abbatiæ Montis Caffini, Opidum in edito loco super saxum mari incumbens, sinum. Putat Barrius esse quod Λαμπτεία Polybio apud Stephanum: Clampetia scribitur Plinio & Pomponio, Dampetus Livio: utri emendatius & fanius? Va ietas orta, inquit Ortelius, ex elementorum similitudine apud Græcos Δ & Λ, apud Latinos d & cl.
units.tr: Along the coast there are, first, Scalea, distinguished by the title of a bishopric; ten miles from there Citrium; as many from here Adamantium (Diamante), in whose territory sugar grows; eight miles from there Belvedersum, and from there half a mile to Bonifactum. Ten miles from here is Cetraum, an abbey of Monte Cassino, a town on a raised site, leaning over the sea on a rock, a gulf. Barrius thinks it is what Polybius, as cited by Stephanus, calls Λαμπτεία [Lampteia]; Clampetia is written by Pliny and Pomponius, Dampetus by Livy. Which is the more correct and the more sound? The variation, says Ortelius, arose from the similarity of the letters among the Greeks Δ and Λ, and among the Latins d and cl.

units.la: Post totidem millia Opidum Paula, cujus Ager Vinum gignit optimum. Paulam ortu suo nobilitavit D. Franciscus cognomine Paulanus, Ordinis Minimorum Fratrum Auctor.
units.tr: After as many miles lies the town Paula, whose fields produce excellent wine. Saint Francis of Paola, founder of the Order of Minim Friars, ennobled Paula by his birth.

units.la: Post Paulam quarto lapide Castrum est illustris familiæ Carrafarum Neapolitanæ Sanlucidum, S. Lucido, generoso vino inclutum.
units.tr: Four miles beyond Paola is the castle of Sanlucidum, S. Lucido, famous for its fine wine, belonging to the illustrious Neapolitan family of the Carafas.

units.la: Pari hinc intervallo Fredus Amnis abest, cum eiusdem nominis Opido: in cujus Agro Horti admirabilissimi, Medicis, Citris, Limonibus, & id genus aliis consiti nitent: ut & Terminorum, in quo Teimontium, quod Fredo millia abest quatuor: Belmontioque totidem Mantia, opidum munitissimum, cum insigni Arce, olim Napitia, uti censet ex Antiochi sententia apud Strabonem, Gabr. el Barrius. Sed vide Abrahamum Ortelium. Scipio etiam Mazella in Neapolitani Regni descriptione notat Gabrielem Barrium falli, ubi Napitium interpretatur Amantheam: Pitzo hodie vominari Napitium addens. Amanthia porro, Calabriæ Vrbis, meminit Cedrenus, quum scribit ab Nicephoro Saracenis ereptam.
units.tr: At the same distance from here is the river Fredus, with the town of the same name. In its territory are very wonderful gardens, full of citrons, lemons and similar fruits. Also in the territory of Terminus lies Teimontium, four miles from Fredus, and four miles from Belmonte is Mantia, a strongly fortified town with a notable citadel, formerly Napitia, as Gabriel Barrius thinks, following the opinion of Antiochus in Strabo. But see Abraham Ortelius. Scipio Mazella, too, in his description of the Kingdom of Naples, observes that Gabriel Barrius is wrong where he interprets Napitium as Amantheam, adding that Napitium is today called Pitzo. Cedrenus also mentions the city of Amanthia in Calabria, when he writes that it was seized from the Saracens by Nicephorus.

units.la: Post Manthiam Opida sunt, mille quingentis à Mari passuum millibus Castilio: dein itinere per littus, Sanctæ Euphemiæ Fanum, quod propinquo Mari dedit cognomen. Arbitratur Gabr. Barrius esse Λαμετία Lycophronis, sic dictam, ut Stephanus notat, ab Lameto Flumine. Inde Lameti us Sinus apud Aristotelem libro vii Politicor. cap.x, qui ait abesse ab Scylletico itinere dimidiati diei.
units.tr: After Mantia there are towns: Castilio, fifteen hundred paces from the sea. Then, by the coast road, comes the shrine of Sanctae Euphemiae, which gave its name to the nearby sea. Gabriel Barrius thinks it is the Lametia [Λαμετία] of Lycophron, so called, as Stephanus notes, from the river Lametus. Hence the Lametus Sinus in Aristotle, Politics book 7, chapter 10, who says it lies half a day's journey from the Scyllaean road.

units.la: Ab Angiola Flumine tria Passuum millia emenso exiguum terræ brachium se offert Promontorium in mare procurrens, cui modicum insidet Castellum Lepitium. Vernis illi litoribus quotannis Mense Majo Thuni incredibili frequentia capiuntur.
units.tr: After three miles from the river Angiola, a narrow neck of land appears, a promontory running out into the sea, on which sits a small castle, Lepitium. Every year in May, in the spring waters off this shore, tunny are caught in incredible numbers.

units.la: Ab Lopitio per oram ad exiguum Opidum Bizonam millia Pass. sunt quatuor. Nomen illi natum videtur ab Vibone antiqua Vrbe, de qua paullo post.
units.tr: From Lopitio along the coast to the small town Bizona is four miles. The name seems to have come from Vibo, an ancient city, of which a little later.

units.la: Post duodecim millia Chersenesus est, in qua Tiopia pulcerrima Civitas & Episcopalis: à Tropæis dicta, ut nonnulli volunt.
units.tr: After twelve miles there is a Chersonese, on which stands Tiopia, a very beautiful city and an episcopal see, called from the Tropaea (trophies), as some hold.

units.la: Haud procul inde a rare Strabonis Hercules fuit Portus, Plinio quoque memoratus libro iii cap.x. Formiculas vocant Adcolæ, ut notat Gabriel Barrius.
units.tr: Not far from there was the Portus Herculis of Strabo, also mentioned by Pliny, book 3, chapter 10. The locals call it Formiculas, as Gabriel Barrius notes.

units.la: Strabo scribit hoc situ Medamam Locrorum Opidum fuisse, cum Fonte magno ejusdem nominis. Medma Plinio in melioribus exemplaribus: Μέδμη Stephano. Nicotera Gabrieli Barro & Scipioni Mazellæ: sed verius Capo di Baticam Leandro: sic vocata, quod ab Canibus, id est, Paganis & Infidelibus (sic enim vocari soliti) fuerit excita. Fons, quem ibi quoque locat Strabo, etiamnum adparet.
units.tr: Strabo writes that Medama, a town of the Locri, stood in this position, with a great spring of the same name. In the better copies of Pliny it is Medma; in Stephanus, Medma [Μέδμη]. Gabriel Barrius and Scipio Mazella say it is Nicotera, but Leandro more truly says it is Capo di Baticam, so called because it was raised by the Canibus, that is, by pagans and infidels, for so they were commonly called. The spring which Strabo also places there still appears.

units.la: Post octo millia per Littus in latere Montis Opidum occurrit Nicotera (Victrix) Antonino notum: hodie Episcopatus dignitate clarum.
units.tr: After eight miles along the shore, on the side of a mountain, the town of Nicotera (Victrix) comes into view, known to Antoninus, and today distinguished by its episcopal dignity.

units.la: Ab Nicotera P. M. viii Iola, Gioia cernitur introrsum ab littore nonnihil remota.
units.tr: Eight Roman miles from Nicotera, Iola, now Gioia, can be seen inland, somewhat away from the shore.

units.la: Ab Ioia Seminariam Fluvium, qui Metaurus quondam, ut alibi dixi, transgressis Palma Vicus occurrit: exin Bantaria, Bagna; mox Scylleum Promontorium, de quo suo loco.
units.tr: From Gioia, after crossing the river Seminarius, which was once the Metaurus, as I have said elsewhere, one comes to the village of Palma. Then Bantaria, now Bagna; and soon the Scylleum Promontorium, of which in its own place.

units.la: Flexu dein circum littus Freti, quod nunc Pharum Messanensem appellat Vulgus, Columna fuit Rhegia, centum ab Rhegio stadiis. ἡ τῶν πηγῶν Στήλης Straboni libro vi. Columna Rhegia Ciceroni pro Sestio, Plinio lib. iii cap. v (in cujus corruptionibus Codicibus legitur Corona Rhegia) Pomponiæ Melæ: Columna simpliciter & κατ' ἐξοχὴν Antonino, qui duo ad eam ducit Itinera; unum quidem Mediolano per Picenum ad Campaniam, longum milliaria; alterum ab Vrbe, Via Appia utrumque celeberrimum, Locorumque nobilium. Columella vocatur in Antiqua Inscriptione, quæ Tegeani visitur in Calabria, quamque supra descripti. Authors Columnam suo tempore nominatum scribit Diaconus libro de Reb. Langhardic. iii. cap. xxxiii. sed fabulas addit. Tradit Strabo in more Prisci fuisse Ditiones & Imperia certis terminis distinguere; quemadmodum ab Rheginis factitatum, qui Columellam id est exilem Turrem in littore Freti, Peloro Siciliæ Promontorio adversam exstruxerant. De ea sic scribit Hermolaus Barbarus in doctissimus Plinii Castigationibus Græcum locum Stylidam id est Columellam vocant: ea turricula modo erecta ex adverso Turrem in Peloro sitam respicit: hodieque à multis Stylarion appellatur.
units.tr: Then, bending round the shore of the strait, which the common people now call the Lighthouse of Messina, there was the Columna Rhegia, a hundred stadia from Rhegium: the Stele of the springs [ἡ τῶν πηγῶν Στήλη] in Strabo, book 6. Columna Rhegia is what Cicero calls it in Pro Sestio, and Pliny, book 3, chapter 5 (in whose corrupt manuscripts it is read as Corona Rhegia), and Pomponius Mela. Antoninus calls it simply Columna, and by preeminence, and gives two routes to it: one from Milan through Picenum to Campania, long in miles, and the other from the City by the Appian Way; both are very famous and pass noble places. In an ancient inscription, which is seen at Tegeanum in Calabria, and which I described above, it is called Columella. The author Diaconus, in his book on the deeds of the Langobards, book 3, chapter 33, writes that Columna was named in his time, but adds fables. Strabo relates that the men of old were accustomed to distinguish domains and empires by fixed boundaries, as the Rhegians did, who had built a Columellam, that is, a slender tower, on the shore of the strait, opposite the promontory of Pelorus in Sicily. Hermolaus Barbarus, in his learned Castigationes of Pliny, writes of it thus: The Greek text calls it Stylis, that is, Columella; this little tower, set up alone, looks towards the tower situated on Pelorus opposite; even today it is called Stylarion by many.

units.la: Dehinc ab Silio P. M. viii, ab Rhegio vii Turris cujusdam visuntur ruinæ, ubi nunc Taberna diversoria, Catonam vocant, è regione Messanæ: frequens hinc in Siciliam ex Italia Trajectus, freto haud ampliore lenis passuum millibus.
units.tr: Then, eight Roman miles from Silio and seven from Rhegium, there are to be seen the ruins of a certain tower, where now there is an inn; they call the place Catonam, opposite Messina. From here there is a frequent crossing from Italy to Sicily, over a smooth strait of only a few miles.

units.la: Septimo ab Carona lapide Urbs est Rhegium, ad Fretum loco prominente sita. Rhegium simpliciter Scriptoribus multis Latinis Græcisque, item Itinerariæ Tabulæ, & Inscriptionibus: quod Regium Julium Plinio & Melæ; Appiano lib. iv & v, Polybio libro i, Philostrato, Straboni libro vi, & Ptolemæo. Cum adspiratione scribi in prima docet in Orthographia sua Manutius. Vulgo Rezzo dicitur. Aschenaz olim vocatam docet ex Iosepho Gabriel Barrius: addens ab Antiocho apud Halicarnassum Neptunium sive Posidonium nuncupatam. Incolæ Rhegini. Docet Probus Grammaticus in Vita Virgilij ex Catonis Originibus Incolas Taurocinos ab Flumine præterfluente nominatos. Ipsa Regio Rhegina Eustathio. Ager Rheginus Cicerone i. Philippica & alijs, qui latissime olim patebat ad Amnem usque Alicem; ubi, ut Geographi signant, Rheginorum erat terminus. Rhegina Littora leguntur apud Salium Italicum libro xiii. Rheginos nominat Salius Solinus. Quur Siciliæ faciat Urbem Hieronymus de Locis Hebraicis, antea docui. Conditam Strabo Solinusque perhibent ab Chalcidensibus. Strabo Rhegium dictum, Æschylo teste, scribit Ἀπὸ τῆς ῥήξεως, quod hic violentia Terræmotuum Siciliam ab Italia divulserit: cuius rei Auctores etiam sunt Trogus libro iiii, Sex. Pompeius Festus, Eustathius, Servius in iii Æneidos, alique. De ratione huius Divulsionis multa lectu digna Strabo. Alii sic vocatum putant, quod regia esset urbs, multis aliis imperans. Describit eam Cassiodorus lib. xii Variarum. Res ab Rheginis gestas legere est apud Livium varijs locis, præcipue libro xxiv, Diodorum libro xii, & alios. Potentissima fuit olim urbs, Strabone teste, validissimumque contra Siculos, Turribus Castellisque munitum propugnaculum: multarum Mater Coloniarum: Addit Strabo postea ab Dionysio Rege solo æquatam, & ab Dionysio Juniore Filio partem eius restauratam, Φοιβίανque dictam. Cladem postea ingentem ab D. Iubellio, Campani exercitus Ductore, accepisse notant Thucydides lib. vi. Polybius lib. i. Livius lib. xii. Terræmotibus concussam paullo ante Bellum Marsicum refecit postea C. Iulius Cæsar, Coloniisque plurimis, quos inter Socios Navales habuerat, instauravit, ut scribit Strabo; unde & Rhegium cognominatum Julium. Nuper etiam anno cIↄ Iↄ xliii magnam huic Urbi calamitatem attulit Caradinus Turca, Solimanicæ Classis Præfectus: ita ut hodie infrequentior sit & deserta pene. Quin & anno cIↄ Iↄ xciv ab Turcis incendio est vastata. Archiepiscopatus gaudet hodie dignitate. Orti hinc leguntur præter alios apud Aristotelem lib. ii Politicor. Andredanus, qui Chalcedonensibus in Thracia Leges scriptit: & apud Plinium lib. xxxiv. cap. viii Pythagoras Statuarius.
units.tr: Seven miles from the milestone at Carona is the city of Rhegium, set on a projecting point by the strait. Rhegium is the plain name in many Latin and Greek writers, and likewise in the Itinerary tables and inscriptions; Regium Julium in Pliny and Mela; in Appian, books 4 and 5; in Polybius, book 1; in Philostratus, in Strabo, book 6, and in Ptolemy. Manutius teaches in his Orthography that it is written with an aspirate in the first syllable. It is commonly called Rezzo. Gabriel Barrius, following Josephus, teaches that it was formerly called Aschenaz, adding that Antiochus, in Halicarnassus, named it Neptunium or Posidonium. Its inhabitants are the Rhegini. The grammarian Probus, in the Life of Virgil, teaches from Cato's Origines that the inhabitants, the Taurocinos, were named from a river flowing past. The region itself is called Rhegina by Eustathius. The Ager Rheginus in Cicero's first Philippic and elsewhere once extended widely as far as the river Alex, where, as geographers mark, was the boundary of the Rhegini. The Rhegina Littora are read of in Silius Italicus, book 13. Solinus names the Rheginos. Why Jerome, in his Hebrew Places, makes it a city of Sicily I explained before. Strabo and Solinus report that it was founded by the Chalcidians. Strabo writes that Rhegium was so named, with Aeschylus as witness, from breaking [Ἀπὸ τῆς ῥήξεως], because here the violence of earthquakes tore Sicily away from Italy. Trogus, book 4, Sextus Pompeius Festus, Eustathius, Servius on Aeneid 3, and others are also authorities for this. Strabo has much worth reading on the manner of this separation. Others think it was so called because it was a royal city, ruling over many others. Cassiodorus describes it in Variae, book 12. The deeds of the Rhegians may be read in Livy in various places, especially book 24, in Diodorus, book 12, and in others. It was once a most powerful city, according to Strabo, and a very strong bulwark against the Sicilians, fortified with towers and castles; mother of many colonies. Strabo adds that it was later levelled to the ground by King Dionysius, and that part of it was restored by his younger son Dionysius, and called Phoebia [Φοιβίαν]. Thucydides, book 6, Polybius, book 1, and Livy, book 12, note that it later suffered a huge defeat at the hands of D. Iubellius, leader of the Campanian army. Shaken by earthquakes shortly before the Marsian War, it was afterwards rebuilt by C. Julius Caesar, who restored it with many colonists, among whom were the naval allies he had; as Strabo writes, whence it was also surnamed Julium. Recently, too, in the year 1543, Caradinus the Turk, prefect of Soliman's fleet, brought great calamity on this city, so that today it is rather sparsely populated and almost deserted. Indeed, in the year 1594 it was laid waste by fire at the hands of the Turks. It now enjoys archiepiscopal dignity. Men born here are read of, among others, in Aristotle, Politics book 2: Andredanus, who wrote laws for the Chalcedonians in Thrace; and in Pliny, book 34, chapter 8, Pythagoras the sculptor.

units.la: Hactenus Bruttiorum Littoralia sumus persequuti: succedunt Mediterranea: quorum explicationem aggrediar ab Lao, communi inter Lucaniam Bruttiosque termino.
units.tr: Thus far we have followed the coastal parts of the Bruttii; the inland parts follow, and I shall begin their description at Laus, the common boundary between Lucania and the Bruttii.

units.la: Post Laum igitur, vel, ut hodie vocant, Lainum statim inter Montes saxosos difficilesque Colles est exiguus orbicularis specie, cui Opidum insidet Rotunda ab forma, quod res loquitur, dicta: Castellutio Lucaniæ Opido P. M. distans quatuor. Pari hinc spatio item inter Montes Vallis D. Martini amœna, Fontibus scatus purissimarum aquarum.
units.tr: After Laus, or Lainum as they call it today, there lies at once, among rugged mountains and difficult hills, a small valley of roughly circular shape, on which sits the town Rotunda, named from its form, as the name itself says; it is four miles from the Lucanian town of Castellutio. At the same distance, again among the mountains, lies the pleasant Vallis D. Martini, abounding in springs of the purest water.

units.la: Inde in Montium jugis Silva quædam, & ad eius finem jucunda planicies, Campus Temesis, Campo Temesi, antiquis Temesanus, ex sententia Ioannis Babtistæ Martorani, apud Leandrum, qui eum accurate describit.
units.tr: From there, on the ridges of the mountains, is a certain wood, and at its edge a pleasant plain, the Campus Temesis, the Campo Temesi, anciently Temesanus, according to Giovanni Battista Martorano, cited by Leandro, who describes it carefully.

units.la: Hhhh Ab Rotunda xii P. M. Moranum est Opidum item inter Montes situm, Agro undique peramœno. Quarto inde lapide via quoque per Montes, Castrum Villare succedit, editissimo impositum jugo, Ducatus Titulum ab Karolo v. consequutum.
units.tr: Twelve miles from Rotunda, to the south-east, is Moranum, a town also set among the mountains, with a very pleasant countryside on every side. Four miles beyond it, by a road also running over the mountains, comes Castrum Villare, placed on a very high ridge, which obtained the title of a duchy from Charles V.

units.la: Patre tum, qua Campus Temesis, ab Castro Villari Millia xii. inter Montes Murus Magnus est: inde quatuor eodem tractu montano Papasiderum. Dein reditu ad Viam, quæ Consentiam ducit, ad dextram in Apennino Saracina: inde quatuor millium intervallo, eiusdem viæ dextra præcelso in vertice est Altomontium, Altomonte: unde Salis Fodinæ mille passibus absunt.
units.tr: On the side where the Campus Temesis lies, twelve miles from Castrum Villare, among the mountains, is the Murus Magnus. Four miles from there, along the same mountain tract, is Papasiderum. Then, returning to the road that leads to Cosenza, on the right in the Apennines is Saracina. Four miles from there, on the right of the same road, on a very high peak, is Altomonte, from which the salt mines are a thousand paces away.

units.la: Elaro transito in Apennino Malvetum se offert: inde quarto milliari Sancti-Agatha: Opidum Episcopale: demum eodem itinere per Montes, octavo San-Genitum, S. Genito: hinc quatuor Mare versus Inferum millibus montano quoque situ San-Bonifacium est: inde rursum millibus tribus reditu ad viam, a qua discessi, Civitas est D. Marci, Episcopalis. Ab Altomontio porro P. M. x. modico in Colle Rugianum est. Ab Rugiano millibus iii. in montibus Turranum est Opidum. Via inde per Montes, qui in Septemtrionem vergunt, Regina invenitur, in cuius Agro maxima Olei copia nascitur. Itinere dein ab Regina trium millium in Monte Mons Altus cernitur: Ducatus titulo nobilis. Incolæ hic passim fortunis inopes, moribus agrestes, ruditer habitantes.
units.tr: After passing through Elaro, in the Apennines, Malvetum presents itself. Four miles from there is Sant'Agata, an episcopal town. Then, by the same route over the mountains, eight miles on is San Genito. From there, four miles towards the Lower Sea, is San Bonifacio, also set on a mountain. Then, three miles further back to the road I left, is the episcopal city of San Marco. From Altomonte, ten miles to the west, is Rugiano, on a modest hill. Three miles from Rugiano, in the mountains, is the town of Turrano. From there the road over the mountains that slope to the north brings you to Regina, in whose territory a very great quantity of olive oil is produced. Then, three miles from Regina, on a mountain, is Montalto, famous for its ducal title. The inhabitants here are everywhere poor in means, rustic in manners, and live in a rough way.

units.la: Quinque ab Monte Alto milliaribus supra Consentiam, secundum Apenninum. Pandosia vestigia conspiciuntur, antiquæ Urbis in Monte. Παυδοσία Straboni, aliisque Græcis: Παυδασία Plutarcho de Fortuna Romanorum. Mardoniam ab Theopompo appellari, scribit Marius Niger. Pandosia munitissimo loco sita erat, ubi tres exigui Colles Acherunte Fluvio cincti, ut indicat Livius, qui sæpe eius meminit: apud quem etiam libro xxix. Pandosiani una cum Consentinis in potestatem Populi Romani ultro concessisse leguntur. Oenotria quondam fuisse notat Strabo. Haud procul hinc Alexandrum, Epiri, Regem, ab Exule Lucano interfectum misere periisse, tradunt Livius libro viii. Trogus libro xii. Strabo libro vi. Hodie Castro Franco, quod mille passibus abest, Gabrieli Barrio; Mendicino, Prospero Parisio.
units.tr: Five miles from Montalto, above Cosenza, along the Apennines, are to be seen the remains of Pandosia, an ancient city on a mountain. The Greeks, Strabo and others, write it Παυδοσία [Pandosia]; Plutarch, in his work on the Fortune of the Romans, writes Παυδασία [Pandasia]. Marius Niger writes that Theopompus called it Mardonia. Pandosia was situated in a very well fortified place, where three small hills are girt by the river Acheron, as Livy indicates, who often mentions it; in his twenty-ninth book we read that the Pandosians, together with the Consentines, voluntarily surrendered themselves into the power of the Roman people. Strabo notes that it was formerly Oenotria. Not far from here, Alexander, king of Epirus, was killed by an exile from Lucania and perished miserably; Livy in book eight, Trogus in book twelve, and Strabo in book six, relate this. Today, Castrofranco, which is a thousand paces away, is assigned by Gabriele Barrio, and Mendicino by Prospero Parisio.

units.la: Busento Fluvio non ignobili transito, statim in urbem Consentiam est ingressus. Consentia Livio, Plinio, Melæ, Antonino, aliisque Latinis: Κοσεντία Appiano, Straboni, Ptolemæo, Græcisque ceteris: quæ Consenza hodie. Caput & Metropolis Bruttiorum, ut testatur Strabo: hodieque Sita circa declivitatem pene Appennini, colles amplectens septem, quibus maxima Urbis ædificiorum pars imposita: unde & septenis collibus pro Insigni vititur. Urbem uno latere Crathis, altero amnis includit Busentus, qui ipsam ab Suburbiis separat. Arcem habet in Montis jugo australi regione munitissimam. Summo Templo dignitas Archiepiscopalis est adtributa.
units.tr: After crossing the not undistinguished river Busento, you immediately enter the city of Cosenza. Livy, Pliny, Mela, Antoninus and other Latin writers call it Consentia; Appian, Strabo, Ptolemy and the other Greeks Κοσεντία [Kosentia]. Today it is Cosenza. It is the head and metropolis of the Bruttii, as Strabo attests, and today too it lies near the slope of the Apennines, embracing seven hills, on which the greater part of the city's buildings are placed; hence it uses the seven hills as its emblem. The Crati encloses the city on one side and the Busento, which separates it from its suburbs, on the other. It has a citadel, very strongly fortified, on the southern ridge of the mountain. The principal church has the dignity of an archbishopric.

units.la: Capta quondam ab Hannibale, mox ad Pop. Romani societatem & amicitiam una cum Thuriis est reducta, ut Livius memorat, apud quem Consentia Consentinorumque, & rerum ab iis gestarum frequens est commemoratio, præsertim libro v. viii. xxix. Ingentem, ut Blondus notat libro xiii. Histor. calamitatem passa est ab Saracenis, Ioannis xiii. P. M. & Ottonis Imp. Augusti temporibus. Consentini fuerunt Petrus Paullus Parrhasius I. C. Patavij Bononiæque Professor, inde Auditor Apostolicæ Camerae Paulli iii. P. M. postea Cardinalis: Ioannes Paullus Parrhasius, Latinis Græcisque litteris eruditissimus: Ioannes Crasius, Orator eximius: Antonius Telesius: Antonius & Nicolaus Giardini, omnes Græce Latinæque doctissimi: Ioannes Baptista Martoranus, Poëta Italus. Nobiles ibi Familiæ: Bernardi. | Longhi. | San-Felice. Cavalcanti. | Martirani. | Sarsali, alias di Surrento. Chiachio. | Matera. | Scaglioni. Ciozi. | Migliarezi. | de Tarsia. Ferai. | Morelli. | Tilesii. Ferrari, | Quatromani.
units.tr: Once taken by Hannibal, it was soon brought back, together with Thurii, into the alliance and friendship of the Roman people, as Livy relates; in his work the Consentines and the deeds they performed are often recorded, especially in books five, eight and twenty-nine. As Blondus notes in book thirteen of his Histories, it suffered a huge disaster at the hands of the Saracens in the times of John XIII, pope, and of the emperor Otto. Natives of Cosenza were: Pietro Paolo Parrasio, doctor of civil law, professor at Padua and Bologna, afterwards auditor of the Apostolic Chamber under Pope Paul III, and later a cardinal; Giovanni Paolo Parrasio, most learned in Latin and Greek letters; Giovanni Crasio, an outstanding orator; Antonio Telesio; Antonio and Nicola Giardini, all most learned in Greek and Latin; and Giovanni Battista Martorano, an Italian poet. The noble families there are: Bernardi, Longhi, San Felice, Cavalcanti, Martirani, Sarsali (otherwise di Sorrento), Chiacchio, Matera, Scaglioni, Ciozi, Migliarese, de Tarsia, Ferrari, Morelli, Tilesio, Ferrari and Quatromani.

units.la: Ager Frugum omnium Fructuumque optimorum, Vini (Plinio etiam celebrati lib. xiiii. cap. vi) Olei ferax: Moris item arboribus abundans ad Vermium nutricationem, qui sericum faciunt. In eodem Agro tot Vici Villæque sunt, ut perpetua videatur esse Civitas. Refert Martoranus apud Leandrum amplius centenos nos esse Vicos in vicenas Jurisdictiones, quæ vulgo Prætoria, divisos: omnes ad Consentinam Diæcesin pertinentes. Ea sic se habent. Donicorum Jurisdictioni subsunt tres Pagi Aprilliani, decem: Filenì, quatuor: Mangoni, duo: Roblani, quinque: Tessani duo: Dipani, sex; Paterni, quinque; Naleti, duo: Grimaldi, tres, in quibus Altilia, reliquis populi frequentia antecellens: Gauranum porro tribus præpositum est Vicis: Cornum, duobus; Tompanum, tribus: Robertum, totidem: itemque Celicum: Spetianum Maius, uni, Spetianum Minus, undecim: Pedagium, quatuor; Fetra ficta, totidem; Siciliianum denique, octo.
units.tr: The territory is rich in all kinds of crops and the finest fruits, productive of wine (which Pliny also celebrates in book fourteen, chapter six) and of olive oil; it is likewise abundant in mulberry trees for feeding the silkworms that make silk. In the same territory there are so many villages and farmhouses that it seems to be one continuous city. Martorano, cited by Leandro, reports that there are more than a hundred villages, divided into some twenty jurisdictions, which are commonly called Prætoria, all belonging to the diocese of Cosenza. They are arranged thus. Under the jurisdiction of Donico lie three hamlets; Aprilliano ten; Fileni four; Mangone two; Roblano five; Tessano two; Dipano six; Paterno five; Naleto two; Grimaldi three, among which Altilia, excelling the rest in population. Gaurano, moreover, has three villages set over it: Cornus two; Tompano three; Roberto as many, and likewise Celico. Spezzano Maggiore has one, Spezzano Minore eleven; Pedagio four; Fetra Ficta as many; and lastly Sicilianum eight.

units.la: Passuum millibus ab Confentia xvi in Apennino vetus est Civitas, Marturanum, Episcopalis ubi nobiles Familiæ, d' Angelis, Martirano, Scagliono, de Serrento.
units.tr: Sixteen miles from Cosenza, in the Apennines, is the ancient episcopal city of Martirano, where the noble families are d'Angelis, Martirano, Scaglione and de Sorrento.

units.la: Tribus Marturano millibus Clocentum est: cum Motta Porciana, haud procul: sex, inter Montes, Lucerta: octo, Aielum. Ab Motta xii lapide Ferulentum sequitur, in Montibus: deinde pulcra in convalle Taberna, frequens oppidum, Episcopatus titulo clarum qui unitus est cum Cathacensi. Octo Taberna P. M. ornatissimum se offert Opidum Catanzarum: hinc xii ix. P. M. ab Mari tribus Nicastrum est, Civitas Episcopalis, splendida, perelegantis Agri: inde per amœna loca duobus millibus incedenti San-Blasium occurrit: unde ad decimum lapidem juxta collem modicum, sub Apennini radicibus, opidum frequens est Maida: hinc millibus octo Franca-Villa sequitur in Apennino: inde tribus, Mons Sanctus: ab eo quatuor, Badiatum Castellum: decem hinc Laconia: post eam Arx Argitolana, quatuor, fuisse putatur hic Κεφαλη Lycophronis: octo inde Mons Leo cognominatus, Comitatus Episcopatusque (cum quo unitus est Melitensis) dignitate insignis.
units.tr: Three miles from Martirano is Clocento, with Motta Porciana not far off; six miles away, among the mountains, is Lucerta; eight, Aiello. Twelve miles from Motta comes Ferulento, in the mountains; then, in a beautiful valley, Taverna, a populous town famous for its episcopal title, which has been united with that of Catanzaro. Eight miles from Taverna, a very well-appointed town, Catanzaro, presents itself. From here, three miles towards the sea, is Nicastro, a splendid episcopal city in a very elegant countryside. From there, on going two miles through pleasant places, you meet San Biagio; from there, at the tenth milestone, beside a modest hill at the foot of the Apennines, is the populous town of Maida. Eight miles from here comes Francavilla in the Apennines; then, three miles on, Monte Santo; from it, four miles, the castle of Badiato. Ten miles from here is Laconia; after it the fortress of Argitolana, four miles further. Here, it is thought, was the Κεφαλη [Kephale] of Lycophron. Eight miles from there is the town called Monteleone, distinguished by its rank as a county and by its bishopric, with which the see of Mileto has been united.

units.la: Fuit olim hus locis in Apennini Colle Hippon sive Vibo Valentia; quod clamant cum Loci situs, ad antiquam descriptionem optime conveniens; tum Veterum Ædificiorum vestigia, quæ hic etiamnum visuntur ad Opidum usque Bivonam, de quo supra, Mari adjacentem, cui nomen proculdubio ab Vibone diruta inditum. Nec absentiunt de Situ Ptolemæus Straboque. Quin Bivonam antiquam Vibonem facit Celsus Cittadinus ad Abrahamum Ortelium scribens. Hippo vel Hipponium quondam, post Vibo Valentia Strabo: Μετὰ δὲ τ Κωτρωνιάν Ἱππώνιον, Λοκρῶν κτίσμα. Βρεττίους δὲ καταχεντας ἀφέλεν Ῥωμαίοις, καὶ μετανέμασαν Οὐιβῶνα Οὐαλεντίαν. Ἱππώνιον cum Appiano libro iii. & iv. tum Stephano, ἡ μετωνόμασθη, addenti, ὑπὸ Ῥωμαίων Οὐιβῶν καὶ Οὐαλεντία. Lege, Strabonem sequutus, Οὐιβῶνα Οὐαλεντία. Hippo, ait Plinius, quod nunc Vibonem Valentiam appellamus. Hippo, nunc Vibon, inquit Mela libro ii. Leg. potius, Hippon, nunc Vibo. Οὐιβῶν Οὐαλεντία Ptolemæo. Vibona Balentia, Itinerariæ Tabulæ. Vibo simpliciter Livio, qui libro xxxv Coloniam eo ab Romanis ductam scribit. Vibo item apud Antoninum, in nonnullis Codicibus Vibona. Valentini hinc Calabriæ Populi apud Plinium libro iii. cap. xi. in fine. Navale
units.tr: Formerly, in these places on a hill of the Apennines, there was Hippo, or Vibo Valentia. This is asserted both by the position of the site, which agrees very well with the ancient description, and by the remains of ancient buildings still to be seen here, down to the town of Bivona, mentioned above, which lies by the sea; it certainly took its name from the ruined Vibo. Ptolemy and Strabo do not disagree about the situation. Indeed, Celso Cittadino, writing to Abraham Ortelius, makes ancient Bivona to be Vibo. Strabo calls it Hippo or Hipponium once, and afterwards Vibo Valentia: Μετὰ δὲ τὴν Κωτρωνιᾶτιν Ἱππώνιον, Λοκρῶν κτίσμα. Βρεττίους δὲ καταλαβόντας ἀφεῖλεν Ῥωμαίοις, καὶ μετωνόμασαν Οὐιβῶνα Οὐαλεντίαν [After the Cotroniate territory comes Hipponium, a foundation of the Locrians. The Romans took it from the Bruttii who had seized it, and they renamed it Vibo Valentia]. Appian in books three and four, and then Stephanus, who adds ἡ μετωνομάσθη ὑπὸ Ῥωμαίων Οὐιβῶν καὶ Οὐαλεντία [which was renamed by the Romans Vibo and Valentia], agree. Following Strabo, one should read Vibo Valentia. Pliny says: Hippo, which we now call Vibo Valentia. Mela in book two says: Hippo, now Vibo; one should rather read Hippon, now Vibo. Ptolemy writes Οὐιβῶν Οὐαλεντία; the Itinerary Tables Vibona Balentia. Livy simply says Vibo, and in book thirty-five writes that a colony was led there by the Romans. Antoninus also has Vibo, and in some manuscripts Vibona. Hence the Valentini, a people of Calabria, in Pliny, book three, chapter eleven, at the end.

units.la: hic fuisse ab Agathocle Siculorum Tyranno ædificatum, idem notat Strabo.
units.tr: That this was built by Agathocles, tyrant of the Sicilians, Strabo likewise notes.

units.la: Quod in hujus Vibus Agro Prata essent præclara, Floribus abundantia, finxit, scribente eodem, Antiquitas, venisse eo ex Sicilia Florum legendorum gratia Proserpinam.
units.tr: Antiquity, which Strabo also records, feigned that Proserpina came here from Sicily to gather flowers, because the meadows of this Vibo's territory were splendid and abounding in flowers.

units.la: Octavo ab Monte Leone milliario Philocasium est, Filocaso: inde tribus millibus quingentis Panalia, Panaria: unde Bel-Fortium Opidum milia quatuor: quod Subsicivum Antonini esse putat Barrius, teste ad Antoninum Surita. A Bel-Fortio Surianum abest decem.
units.tr: Eight miles from Monte Leone is Philocasium, now Filocaso. Three and a half thousand paces further is Panalia, now Panaria, and from there Bel-Fortium, a town four miles away. Barrius thinks this is the Subsicivum of Antoninus, as Surita notes in his commentary on Antoninus. Surianum is ten miles from Bel-Fortium.

units.la: Decimo post Surianum lapide Missanium est, Missano: hinc sexto Mellitium; inde quarto Burellum: altoque impositum monti duobus abora millibus, sex a Bivona, honestum Opidum Briaticum, agro beatum fœcundo.
units.tr: At the tenth milestone after Surianum is Missanium, now Missano. Six miles from there is Mellitium, and four miles beyond that is Burellum. Then, set on a mountain two miles up, six miles from Bivona, is the respectable town of Briatico, blessed with a fertile countryside.

units.la: Juxta est modicum Castellum, Calimera, Briaticani Reguli: quatuor hinc P. M. Rosarnum invenitur, felicis Agri. Occurrit mox Politlena, Castellum frequens: utraque millibus duobus in Apennino San-Georgium: octo hinc juxta radices Apennini Terra-Nova, Opidum populo frequens.
units.tr: Nearby is a small castle, Calimera, belonging to the petty lords of Briatico. Four miles from here, Rosarno is found, a town in a fruitful district. Soon after comes Polistena, a populous castle. Each is two miles from San Giorgio in the Apennines. Eight miles from here, near the foot of the Apennines, is Terranova, a town well populated.

units.la: Deinde à San-Georgio senis P. M. loca altiore Grotaria est: decem inde Castellum Vitreum; hinc senis Motta Læta; post Mottam quaternis tillum.
units.tr: Then, six miles from San Giorgio, on higher ground, is Grotteria. Ten miles from there is Castelvetere, and from here six miles to Motta Lata. After Motta, four miles brings you to Tillum.

units.la: Santerne Amne transmisso, atque ad præcelsum Montem Seminaria invenitur, Opidum haud infrequens, Agri cultissimi. Taurianum, cujus meminerunt Pomponius Mela & Plinius libro iii. cap. v. (apud quem tamen in nonnullis codicibus Taurocentum legitur) olim fuisse, censet Gabriel Barrius: inde Taurianus Scopulus hoc loco apud Ptolemæum, quem Terinæum vocat Plinius: hodie Pietra della Nove Ligorio, & Nove simpliciter Barrio.
units.tr: After crossing the river Sant'Erne and reaching the very high mountain, one finds Seminara, a town not thinly peopled, with very well-cultivated land. Taurianum, which Pomponius Mela and Pliny (book 3, chapter 5, where some manuscripts read Taurocentum) mention, was, Gabriel Barrius thinks, formerly on this site. From there, Taurianus Scopulus is named here in Ptolemy, which Pliny calls Terinaeum. Today it is Pietra della Nave according to Ligorio, and simply Nave according to Barrius.

units.la: P. M. ab Seminaria xiiii. parvo à montis vertice descensu Flumaria Mori (Fiumara di moro) Pagus, ab Moris Arboribus dictus occurrit: unde Fretum adspicitur Siculum, per quod à Catona Messanam frequentissimus est Traiectus.
units.tr: Fourteen miles from Seminara, after a short descent from the mountain top, comes the village of Fiumara di Muro (Flumaria Mori), named from its mulberry trees. From here the Sicilian strait can be seen, and across it from Catona to Messana is the most frequented crossing.

units.la: Ad Bruttios porro vel Calabriam Inferiorem pertinet postrema Pars Itineris, quod apud Antoninum Medialano per Picenum & Campaniam ducitur ad Columnam, id est Trajectum Siciliæ M. P. ccccclvi. secunda item eius, quod ab Urbe, Appia Via, pergit recto itinere ad Columnam per M. P. ccccv. tertia denique eius, quod ab Equotutico per M. P. ccccclxx. tendit Rosicianum Rhegium. Nominantur præter Consentiam, Nicoteram & Columnam, indicata jam loca in Prima quidem Caprasia, quæ in Itineraria Tabula Caprasia, hodie Tarsia, ut putat Gabriel Barrius: Ad Turres, jamnunc eidem Barrio Fanum S. Blasii, de quo ante ad Mallias, qui locus quis sit nemo adhuc, quod sciam, divinavit. In Secunda eadem sunt loca cum ijs, quæ in Prima, nisi quod Vibo Civitas hic legatur pro Fluvius Angitula, qui ibi. In Tertia pleraque sunt alius ab superioribus appellationis & obscurioris situs. De Scyllacio sane ibidem & Cocintho, si quidem Promontoria, alibi à me dictum.
units.tr: The last part of the route belongs to the Bruttii, or Lower Calabria. In Antoninus it runs from Mediolanum through Picenum and Campania to Columna, that is, the crossing to Sicily, 456 miles. Its second route, from Rome by the Appian Way, runs in a straight line to Columna, 405 miles. Its third, from Equotuticum, runs 470 miles to Rhegium (Rosicianum). Besides Consentia, Nicotera and Columna, the places already indicated are named. In the first route, Caprasia, which in the Itinerary Table is Caprasia, is today Tarsia, as Gabriel Barrius thinks; Ad Turres is now, according to the same Barrius, Fanum S. Blasii, which I mentioned before, under Ad Mallias. Who this place is, so far as I know, nobody has yet guessed. The second route has the same places as the first, except that Vibo Civitas is read here in place of the river Angitula, which is there. Most of the names in the third route differ from those above and have more obscure positions. I have already spoken elsewhere about Scyllacium and Cocinthus, which are there, if indeed they are promontories.

units.la: Tacinam ex scriptis Celsi Cittadini Ortelius scribit Fluvij esse nomen, qui prope Scyllacium in mare defertur. Succeianum nemo præter Antoninum nominat. Subsi-civi antea mentio mihi facta. Altanum Gabrieli Borrio hodie Soreto. Pro Hipporo (quod Felum Pagum esse arbitratur idem Barrius) substituendum fortean Hipponium, quod postea Latinis Vibo Valentia. Nihil affirmo. Decastidium denique, vel, ut alij scribunt, Decastadium, S. Annam esse idem censet Barrius, qui, quur Decastidium scribat, ignoro, quum de nominis ratione clarum.
units.tr: Ortelius, from the writings of Celso Cittadini, says that Tacina is the name of a river that flows into the sea near Scyllacium. Nobody but Antoninus names Succeianum. I have already mentioned Subsicivum. Altanum is today Soreto, according to Gabriel Barrius. In place of Hipporo (which the same Barrius thinks is the village Felo), perhaps Hipponium should be read, which was later called Vibo Valentia by the Latins. I affirm nothing. Finally, Decastidium, or as others write, Decastadium, Barrius thinks is S. Anna. Why he writes Decastidium I do not know, since the derivation of the name is clear.

units.la: De Calabriæ Principibus vide supra, ubi de Regno Neapolitano generatim.
units.tr: On the princes of Calabria, see above, where the Kingdom of Naples is treated in general.

units.la: CAPVT. XXVIII.
units.tr: CAPUT XXVIII.

units.la: Magna Græcia.
units.tr: Magna Graecia.

units.la: SIc se habet Calabria, quæ Inferior, Bruttiorum quondam Sedes; sequitur Superior, quæ olim MAGNA GRÆCIA. Maior dicitur Silio lib.xi. & ex Festo ex Veteri Flacci scriptis.
units.tr: Such is Calabria, the Lower one, once the seat of the Bruttii. Next comes the Upper, which was once MAGNA GRAECIA. It is called Maior by Silius, book 11, and by Festus, from the old writings of Flaccus.

units.la: Nomen Regioni inditum, ea de causa, ut Straboni lib.vi. & M. Tullio lib.ii. de Oratore placet, quod Pythagoras Philosophus Græcus ibi habitarit aut, ut Synesio oratione de Dorio videtur, quod viros & Philosophos & Militares aluerit. Athenæo potius credendum, qui scribit propter ingentem Græcorum hominum numerum, in hac regione habitantium, sic vocatam. Græci, inquit Trogus, non partem, sed universam fere Italiam olim occupaverunt. Græci de ea, ait Plinius, judicavere, genus in gloriam suam effusissimum, quotam partem ex ea (Italia) appellando Græciam Magnam. Sic Festus: Maior Græcia dicta est Italia, quod eam Siculi obtinuerunt, vel quod in ea multæ magnaque Civitates fuerunt ex Græcis profectæ. Ad quem locum Iosephus Scaliger: Quare Græcia dicta sit, non dubitatur, sed quare Maior Græcia. Certissimum est ita vocatam à Romanis, quia propior ea esset illis, quam transmarina Græcia: quemadmodum contra Græcos Italos ipsi Græci transmarini vocabant Ἐξωτικὸς, id est Barbaros. Nam Messenio Servus apud Plautum vocat Exoticam Græciam, quam Romani Maiorem Græciam, non quidem ex persona sua: nam erat Siculus, neque vocasset consulto se ipsum Barbarum: sed μηνιικῶς ex persona Græcorum ipsorum, qui Siculos & Calabros vocabant Ἐλλὼας ἐξωτικὰς: ut Plautus quum se vocat Barbarum & Barbariam Italiam, non ex consuetudine Romanorum dicit: quis enim sanus se Barbarum vocet? sed ex persona Græcorum, qui Βαρβάρους ἡμᾶς ἐξωτικὰς Italos vocabant, quod ex Plutarcho in Vita Pyrrhi cognoscimus. Hæc Magnus Vir. Servius ad i. Æneid. Italia μεγάλη Ἑλλὰς appellata est, quia à Tarento usque ad Cumas omnes Civitates Græci condidere. Seneca de Consolatione: Totum Italiæ latus, quod Infero Mari adluitur, Magna Græcia fuit. Sic Hieronymus Epistola ad Paullinam, Platonem, scribit, in Italiam venisse ad Architam Tarentinum, ca regione, quæ Magna Graecia quondam appellabatur, habitantem. Fusissime autem & illustratum Trogus libro xx. Tusorum Populi, qui oram Inferi Maris possident, à Lydis venerunt: & Venetos, quos Incolas Superi Maris videmus, capta & expugnata Troja, Antenore duce misit: Adria quoque Illyrico mari proxima, quæ & Adriano mari Nomen dedit, Graeca Vrbs est: Argos Diomedes, excisō Ilio, naufragio in illa loca delatus, condidit. Sed & Vscā in Liguribus Graecos Auctores habent; & in Tuscis Tarquinij a Thessalis & Spinambris: Perusini quoque originem ab Achaiis ducunt. Quid Ceren urbem dicam? Quid Latinos Populos, qui ab Aenea conditi videntur? Iam Falisci, Nolani, Abelani, nonne Chalcidensium Coloni sunt? Quid Tractus omnis Campaniæ? Quid Brutij Sabinique? Quid Tarentini: quos Lacedæmone profectos Spurijsque vocatos accepimus. Thurinorum Vrbem condidisse Philoctetem ferunt: ibique adhuc eius Monumentum visitur, & Herculis Sagittæ in Apollinis Templo, quæ fatum Troiæ fuere. Metapontini quoque in Templo Minervæ ferramenta, quibus Epeus, à quo conditi sunt, Equum Trojanum fabricavit: propter quod omnis illa pars Italiæ Major Graecia appellata est. Vt vere admodum cecinerit Ovidius iv. Fastorum:
units.tr: The region got its name, according to Strabo (book 6) and Cicero (De Oratore, book 2), because the Greek philosopher Pythagoras lived there. According to Synesius in his speech on Dio, it was because it nourished men who were both philosophers and soldiers. I would rather trust Athenaeus, who writes that it was so called because of the huge number of Greeks living in this region. "The Greeks," says Trogus, "occupied not a part but almost the whole of Italy once. The Greeks, as Pliny says, judged that the race had spread out most widely to its own glory, calling a large part of it (Italy) Magna Graecia." So Festus: "Italy was called Greater Greece because the Sicilians held it, or because many large cities in it were founded by Greeks." On this passage Joseph Scaliger remarks: "It is not doubted why it was called Greece, but why Greater Greece. It is most certain that it was so called by the Romans, because it was nearer to them than transmarine Greece, just as, conversely, the transmarine Greeks themselves called the Italian Greeks Exotic, that is, barbarians [Ἐξωτικὸς]. For in Plautus the slave Messenio calls Greece Exotic, which the Romans call Greater Greece; not indeed in his own person, for he was a Sicilian and would not have deliberately called himself a barbarian, but in the manner of the Greeks themselves, who called the Sicilians and Calabrians foreign Greeks [Ἐλλὼας ἐξωτικὰς]. Just as Plautus, when he calls himself a barbarian and Italy barbary, does not speak according to the custom of the Romans (for who in his right mind would call himself a barbarian?) but in the person of the Greeks, who called us Italians barbarians, as we learn from Plutarch's Life of Pyrrhus. So far the great man." Servius, on Aeneid book 1: "Italy was called Great Greece [μεγάλη Ἑλλάς] because the Greeks founded all the cities from Tarentum to Cumae." Seneca, in his Consolation: "The whole flank of Italy that is washed by the Lower Sea was Magna Graecia." So Jerome, in his letter to Paulina, writes that Plato came to Italy to visit Archytas of Tarentum, who lived in that region once called Magna Graecia. Trogus, however, treats the matter most fully and clearly in book 20: "The peoples of the Tusci, who hold the coast of the Lower Sea, came from the Lydians; and the Veneti, whom we see living by the Upper Sea, were sent by Antenor as leader after Troy was taken and stormed. Adria too, close to the Illyrian sea, which also gave its name to the Adriatic, is a Greek city; Argos was founded by Diomedes, after he destroyed Ilium and was carried by shipwreck to those parts." But also the authors record Greek founders for Vsca among the Ligurians, and for Tarquinii among the Etruscans, by Thessalians and Spinambrians; the people of Perusia also trace their origin to the Achaeans. Why should I mention the city of Caere? Or the Latin peoples, who seem to have been founded by Aeneas? And the Falisci, the Nolani and the Abellani, are they not colonists of the Chalcidians? What of the whole district of Campania? What of the Bruttii and the Sabines? What of the Tarentines, whom we learn came from Lacedaemon and were called Parthenians? They say that Philoctetes founded the city of Thurii, and his tomb is still shown there, as well as the arrows of Hercules in the temple of Apollo, which were the fate of Troy. Also the Metapontines, in the temple of Minerva, keep the iron tools with which Epeus, by whom they were founded, built the Trojan horse; for this reason that whole part of Italy was called Greater Greece. Ovid rightly and most truly sang in book 4 of the Fasti:

units.la: Italiam Tellus Graecia Maior erat.
units.tr: Italy by its land was Greater Greece.

units.la: Fines Magnæ, de qua nos agimus, Graeciæ Sinui circumiectæ Tarentino, Locrensi & Scyllaceo, patentiqueque in longitudinem m. p. lxxxxii. ut ex Varronis sententia tradit Plinius: multo quondam, quam hodie, fuisse amphores, patet ex Strabone lib. vi. Plinio lib. iii. cap. ix. Ptolemæo in Tabulis Geogr. quos aliosque recentioris ævi sequutus, hos ego statuere solco nobilissimæ Regioni terminos: ad Solis exortum Aequor Adriaticum ad Meridiem Aliceam Fluvium & Bruttios; qua Occasus est, Crathidem Amnem cum Apennino & Lucanis; qua Septemtrio, Sinum Tarentinum cum Apulis Peucetijs.
units.tr: The bounds of Magna Graecia, of which we are speaking, lie around the Gulf of Tarentum, Locri and Scyllaceum, and extend in length 92 Roman miles, as Pliny reports from Varro's opinion. That it was once much larger than today is clear from Strabo, book 6, and Pliny, book 3, chapter 9. Following Ptolemy in his Geographical Tables, and others of more recent times, I am accustomed to set these boundaries for this most noble region: to the east the Adriatic Sea; to the south the river Alice and the Bruttii; to the west the river Crathis with the Apennines and the Lucanians; to the north the Gulf of Tarentum with the Apulian Peucetians.

units.la: Florucrunt in hac Regione Architas, Pythagoras, Parmenides, Zeno, Pythagoricique multi Philosophi: Poeta item Ennius, & alij.
units.tr: In this region flourished Archytas, Pythagoras, Parmenides, Zeno, and many Pythagorean philosophers; also the poet Ennius, and others.

units.la: Ad huius Graeciæ differentiam nominat Livius lib. vii Graeciam Vlteriorem, quæ vere Graecia: ut hæc sit Citerior.
units.tr: To distinguish it from this Greece, Livy, book 7, names Greece Beyond, which is truly Greece, so that this one is the Nearer.

units.la: Italia, inquit Joannes Juvenis in sua Tarentina Historia, dicebantur non prisci & germani Italiæ Populi, qui Itali dicuntur: sed Graeci, qui postea eo advenerant, & eam partem occupaverant, quæ aliis Magna Graecia appellabatur. Sic dicimus Siciliotas & Phthiotas, differentes à Siculis & Phthijs.
units.tr: The name Italia, says John the Younger in his Tarentine History, was given not to the ancient and true peoples of Italy, who are called Italians, but to the Greeks who came there later and occupied that part which was called by others Magna Graecia. So we speak of the Siciliotae and Phthiotae, to distinguish them from the Sicilians and Phthians.

units.la: Nomen hodie Magnæ Graeciæ periit. Nam una cum Bruttiis nobilis hæc Italiæ portio Calabria censetur nunc appellatione.
units.tr: The name Magna Graecia has now disappeared. For together with the Bruttii, this noble part of Italy is now called by the name Calabria.

units.la: Ad particularem, præmissis his, Delineationem venio, ab Alice orsus, quo Magna Graecia à Bruttijs terminatur. De ipso Fluvio alibi. Inter cum & Herculis Promontorium Brancaleonium (Branca Leone) est Opidum: à quo tribus milliaribus læva introrsum in mediterraneis nobilissimum abest D. Mariæ Tridentinæ (Maria di Tredetti) Cænobium, Sodalium D. Basilij, ab Templo denominatum, quod hic fuit, Neptuni, cui Maris imperium & Tridentem Veteres tribuebant.
units.tr: Having set out these things, I come to a particular description, beginning from the Alice, where Magna Graecia is bounded by the Bruttii. About the river itself, elsewhere. Between it and the promontory of Herculis lies the town of Brancaleone (Branca Leone). Three miles to the left, inland, in the interior, is the very noble abbey of St. Mary of Tridentum (Maria di Tredetti), of the Brothers of St. Basil, named after a temple which was here of Neptune, to whom the ancients assigned rule of the sea and the trident.

units.la: In ora Bursanum Caput (Cavo di Bursano) sequitur, Zephyrium olim: quod alibi notatum.
units.tr: On the coast follows Cape Bursanum (Cavo di Bursano), once Zephyrium, which is noted elsewhere.

units.la: Post Zephyrium locus antiquæ Vrbis Locrorum. Locri, Αοκροί Latinis Graecisque Scriptoribus, quos longum esset & taediosum commemorare, satis celebrati. Conditam ab Graecis ex Sinu Cretaeo profectis, Euanthe Duce, Diodorus lib. xii. & xiii. Strabo lib. vi. Eustathius tradunt, aliique Scriptores. Alij Locrorum Auctores volunt Ajacem Oileum, eiusque Comites Narynios. Consulendi Virgilius iii. Aeneid. & Solinus in Polyhist. Et inde Narynia Locrorum regio Ovidio lib. xv. Met. & alijs. Cives, Locrenses Livio ceterisque, Ἐπιζεφύριοι cognominabantur, ut apud Strabonem legitur, à Promontorio, cui erant adiuti. In Bruttiis Livio libro xxxvii, propter vicinitatem: idem etiam libro xxiv Locros Graecis Vrbibus conferunt. Hinc ad Rhegium Stadia numerantur apud veteres Geographos 10c. Res ab iis gestas commemorant ex Trogo Iustinus libro xx. Livius libro xxvii. & xxix. aliisque locis. Locros omnium primos scriptis Legibus usos exstitisse, atque Remp. optimis fundatam institutis habuisse notat Strabo. Gymnasium in hac Vrbe Litteratorum fuisse paret ex Platone. Locrorum nomen multi rarae virtutis homines illustrarunt: inter alios Agesidamus, nobilis Olympionices, in quem Pindarus Hymnum cecinit: Euthymus, à quo lapidem ingenti magnitudine qui Locris ostendebatur, gestatum Plinius, Pausanias & Ælianus libro vii. scripserunt. Locris augustissimum Templum erat Proserpinæ, cuius honorifica mentio apud Livium lib. xxix. & xxxi. Locrorum Opidum, quod Niger, Parisius, Pyrrhus Ligorius & Gabriel Barrius volunt, hodie vulgo Gerazi, Latinè scribentibus Hieracium, de quo mox: Sed Vrbis exigua nunc vestigia vix superesse, ubi Palapolis, censet Leander.
units.tr: After Zephyrium is the site of the ancient city of the Locri. Locri [Lokroi] is sufficiently well known to Latin and Greek writers, and it would be long and tedious to recount them. Diodorus, books 12 and 13, Strabo, book 6, Eustathius and other writers relate that it was founded by Greeks who set out from the Cretan Gulf under the leader Euanthes. Others want the founders of the Locri to be Ajax the son of Oileus and his companions the Naryni. See Virgil, Aeneid 3, and Solinus in the Polyhistor. And hence Narynia, the region of the Locri, in Ovid, Metamorphoses, book 15, and others. The citizens, called Locrenses by Livy and others, were surnamed Epizephyrii [Epizephyrioi], as is read in Strabo, from the promontory near which they lived. Among the Bruttii, in Livy book 37, on account of their proximity; the same Livy also in book 24 counts the Locri among the Greek cities. From here, according to the ancient geographers, the distance to Rhegium is 100 stadia. Justin, book 20, from Trogus, recounts their deeds, and Livy, books 27 and 29, and in other places. Strabo notes that the Locri were the first of all to use written laws, and that their state was founded on the best institutions. From Plato it appears that there was a gymnasium of letters in this city. Many men of rare virtue have made the name of the Locri famous; among others Agesidamus, a noble Olympic victor, for whom Pindar sang a hymn. Pliny, Pausanias and Aelian, book 7, wrote that Euthymus carried a stone of huge size which was shown at Locri. At Locri there was a most august temple of Proserpina, of which Livy honourably mentions in books 29 and 31. The town of the Locrians, which Niger, Parisius, Pyrrhus Ligorius and Gabriel Barrius identify, is today commonly called Gerace, and by Latin writers Hieracium, of which more shortly. But Leander thinks that hardly any traces of the city survive now, where Palaepolis was.

units.la: Supra Locros in Mediterraneis Opidum nobile fuit Mamertium, Μαμέρτιον à Bruttiis habitatum, ut scribit Strabo. Intercidisse notat Leander: Martirano est Gabrieli Barrio & Prospero Parisio, qui in Tabula sua Magnæ Græciæ Nummum adponit cum Inscriptione, ΜΑΜΕΡΤΙΝΩΝ ΒΡΕΤΤΙΩΝ, id est Mamertinorum in Bruttiis, ob vicinitatem. Mamertini, Genti ferocissimæ, quæ fraude Zanclen Siciliæ Vrbem, hodie Messanam occupavit, originem ab his esse, tradunt Siculorum Rerum Scriptores. De Rebus Mamertinorum. Livius lib. xiv. xvi. & alibi.
units.tr: Above the Locri, inland, there was a noted town, Mamertium, inhabited by the Bruttii, Mamertion [Mamertion] as Strabo writes. Leander notes that it has perished; Martirano is its name for Gabriel Barrius and Prosper Parisius, who in their map of Magna Graecia add a coin with the inscription ΜΑΜΕΡΤΙΝΩΝ ΒΡΕΤΤΙΩΝ [MAMERTINŌN BRETTIŌN], that is, of the Mamertines in the Bruttii, because of their proximity. The historians of the Sicilian affairs relate that the Mamertines, a most fierce people who by treachery occupied Zancle, the city of Sicily now called Messina, are descended from these. On the affairs of the Mamertines: Livy, books 14 and 16, and elsewhere.

units.la: Occurrit inde alto in colle, tanquam Promontorio, ab Mari 10 P. Opidum Rocella; juxtaque Castellum Vetus, Castello Vecchio. Mox introrsum ab ora millibus quatuor Stillum, honestum in Monte Opidum. His locis passim Auri, Argenti, Ferri Fodinæ. Inde juxta Sagram Fluvium, de quo alibi, Sagrianum.
units.tr: From there, on a high hill that stands like a promontory, one comes after 10 miles from the sea to the town Rocella, and beside it is Castellum Vetus, Castello Vecchio. Soon, about four miles inland from the shore, is Stillum, a respectable town on a mountain. Throughout these places there are gold, silver and iron mines. Then, near the River Sagra, of which I shall speak elsewhere, is Sagrianum.

units.la: Post Sagram Mons Aulon est; cuius in vertice olim, ut tradit Higinus, Caulonia fuit. Μετὰ δὲ τὸν Σάγραν, inquit Strabo, Ἀχαιῶν κτίσμα Καυλωνία, ἀστηρὸν δ' Ἀυλωνία λεγομένη, ἀπὸ τῆς ἀπεκέμενοι Αὐλῶνα. Καυλωνία, ait Stephanus, πόλις Ἰταλίας, ἣν Αὐλωνίαν Ἐκαταῖος καλεῖ ἀπὸ μίσθου Αὐλῶνα εἶναι. Καυλωνία Thucydidi: Caulonia Melæ & aliis: Caulon Plinio, Virgilio lib. iii. Æneid. & Itinerariæ Tabulæ. Solinus Auctores eius Crotonienses perhibet. Bruttiis adtribuit Livius lib. xxvii. ob vicinitatem; oppugnatam scribens ab Hannibale Poenorum Duce. Opidi solum vestigia exstitisse innuit Plinius: desertum fuisse suis temporibus notat Strabo. Porhyrius Agrum eius vini nobilitate celebratum scribit. Castro Vetere vel Veto putatur Barrio & Ananiensi.
units.tr: After the Sagra comes Mount Aulon, on whose summit Caulonia once stood, as Hyginus relates. "After the Sagras," says Strabo, "is Caulonia, a foundation of the Achaeans, which was called Aulonia in a looser form, from the Aulon that lies near it" [Μετὰ δὲ τὸν Σάγραν, Ἀχαιῶν κτίσμα Καυλωνία, ἀστηρὸν δ' Ἀυλωνία λεγομένη, ἀπὸ τῆς ἀπεκέμενοι Αὐλῶνα]. "Caulonia," says Stephanus, "is a city of Italy, which Hecataeus calls Aulonia, because the Aulon is near it" [Καυλωνία, πόλις Ἰταλίας, ἣν Αὐλωνίαν Ἐκαταῖος καλεῖ ἀπὸ μίσθου Αὐλῶνα εἶναι]. Thucydides calls it Caulonia; Mela and others Caulonia; Pliny Caulon; Virgil in Aeneid book iii and the Itinerary Table also Caulon. Solinus says its founders were from Croton. Livy in book xxvii assigns it to the Bruttians because of its proximity, writing that it was attacked by Hannibal, the Carthaginian general. Pliny hints that only traces of the site remained; Strabo notes that in his day it was deserted. Porphyry writes that its land was celebrated for the excellence of its wine. Barrio and the Ananian think it is Castro Vetere or Veto.

units.la: Dein in Agro Locrorum mediterraneo, dextra, ferme ad octavum lapidem est Hieracium, titulo Marche natus nobile; dictum, ut nonnullis videtur, ab visò Accipitris augurio, dum conderetur. Gierazzo vulgo.
units.tr: Then, in the inland territory of the Locrians, on the right, about the eighth milestone, is Hieracium, a noble town bearing the title of a marquisate. It was named, as some think, from the sight of a hawk taken as an omen when it was founded. Commonly called Gierazzo.

units.la: Postea non procul ab littore, Castella quædam sunt, vernacule dicta, Torre Bruttiana Motta Brutiana, Bianco, Crepacuore, Panduro, Careno, Motta Rubalina, Condoianne.
units.tr: Afterwards, not far from the shore, there are certain small castles, called in the vernacular Torre Bruttiana, Motta Brutiana, Bianco, Crepacuore, Panduro, Careno, Motta Rubalina, Condoianne.
