units.la: In ora Caput Stilli, Capo di Stillo, succedit, quod Carinum olim Promontorium; post hoc autem Scyllaceum de utroque suo loco. In hoc vetus Urbs fuit Scyllatium. Σκυλλήτιον, ait Strabo, ἀπὸ οἰκιστοῦ Ἀ Θησέως τ' μετὰ Μενεσθέως, νῦν δὲ Σκυλάκιον καλεῖ. Sic Plinius: Dein Sinus Scylaceum, Scylletium Athenienses, quum conderent, dictum. Postea Coloniam Romanam huc ductam notat Paterculus. Σκυλλήτιον, inquit Stephanus, πόλις Σικελίας, ὡς Εὐδοξος ἐκτῃ. Siciliæ tribuit Eudoxus ob rationem 40 antea sæpe indicatam. Meminerunt eius Ptolemæus, Solinus, Mela, alij; Veteres item Nummi. Scyle est in Itineraria Tabula, utrum Urbs, an Promontorium? De Situ consule Cassiodorum lib. xii. Variar. qui eam Primam Bruttiorum vocat. Causam sæpe aperuit. Τὸ ἐθνικὸν, Σκυλλαῖος, Stephano; unde Scyllateni Episcopi meminit Concilium Romanum, sub Hilario Pontifice: Squillatinus est in Decretis. Hoc enim Opidum Squillaci hodie, teste Leandro Alberto. Hinc Scyllaceus Sinus Scriptoribus nominatus, non ab Scylla, ut Servius putat. Scylla enim procul hinc ad Fretum est Siculum.
units.tr: On the coast follows Caput Stilli, Capo di Stillo, which was formerly the promontory Carinum; after it comes Scyllaceum, each in its own place. In this district there was an ancient city, Scyllatium. "Scylletion," says Strabo, "from its founder Theseus together with Menestheus, but now it is called Scylacium" [Σκυλλήτιον, ἀπὸ οἰκιστοῦ Θησέως μετὰ Μενεσθέως, νῦν δὲ Σκυλάκιον καλεῖ]. So Pliny: "Then the Gulf of Scylaceum; the Athenians, when they founded it, called it Scylletium." Paterculus notes that a Roman colony was later led there. "Scylletion," says Stephanus, "is a city of Sicily, as Eudoxus states" [Σκυλλήτιον, πόλις Σικελίας, ὡς Εὐδοξος ἐκτῃ]. Eudoxus assigns it to Sicily for the reason often indicated earlier. Ptolemy, Solinus, Mela and others mention it, as do ancient coins. Is Scyle in the Itinerary Table a city or a promontory? On its position consult Cassiodorus, Variae book xii, who calls it "the first of the Bruttians." He often explains the matter. The ethnic is Σκυλλαῖος in Stephanus, whence the Roman council under Pope Hilary mentions the Scyllatenus bishop; Squillatinus is in the Decretals. This town is today Squillaci, according to Leandro Alberti. Hence the Gulf of Scyllaceus was so named by writers, not from Scylla, as Servius thinks; for Scylla lies far from here, at the Sicilian Strait.

units.la: Intus dein in Agro Scyllaceo milliaribus ab mari octo Belicastrum est Civitas. Fuit hic olim Petelia, Πετηλία Sic Appiano, Ptolemæo, Valerio Maximo, Itinerariæ Tabulæ dicitur, quæ Petilia Virgilio lib. iii. Æneid. & Silio Italico. Πέτελλα corrupte est apud Plutarchum in Annibalicis, ubi recte vertit Xylander Peteliam. Hinc Petelinos vocat Livius libro xxii. eosque Samnitibus tribuere videtur; Bruttus vero idem libro xxiii. & xxix. Belicastro est, ut dixi, Leandro, quem sequor: Pelina Nigro, Petigliano Erythræo: Policastro Mazzellæ & Barrio; Strongili Pyrrho Ligorio: Bellicastro, quod in Lucanis, Angelerio. Petelinos Montes habet Plutarchus in Crasso. Caput Lucanorum fuisse tradit Strabo. Causæ notæ. Idem Strabo, Solinus, & ad libro iii. Æneid. Servius ab Philoctete conditam scribunt. Tradit quoque que Strabo suis temporibus fuisse frequentissimam: nunc prorsus interijt.
units.tr: Inland then, in the territory of Scyllaceum, eight miles from the sea, is the city Belicastrum. Here formerly stood Petelia, Πετηλία in Appian, Ptolemy and Valerius Maximus; it is called Petilia in the Itinerary Table, and by Virgil in Aeneid book iii and Silius Italicus. Πέτελλα is a corrupt form in Plutarch's Life of Hannibal, where Xylander rightly renders it Petelia. Hence Livy calls the people Petelini in book xxii, and seems to assign them to the Samnites; but the Bruttians, in the same book xxiii and in xxix, are named too. Belicastrum is, as I said, according to Leandro, whom I follow; Pelina according to Nigro; Petigliano according to Erythraeus; Policastro according to Mazzella and Barrio; Strongili according to Pyrrhus Ligorio; Bellicastrum, which is among the Lucanians, according to Angelerius. Plutarch in his Life of Crassus has the Petelini Montes. Strabo says it was the head of the Lucanians. The causes are known. Strabo, Solinus, and Servius on Aeneid book iii write that it was founded by Philoctetes. Strabo also records that in his time it was very populous; now it has utterly perished.

units.la: Auctor idem est Strabo Crimisam, Κρίμισα quoque hoc situ conditum fuisse Philoctete; idque Apollodorum confirmare. Meminit & Crimisa apud Stephanum Lycophron, cui Κρίμισα tribuitur. Putatur hodie Gabrieli Barrio Cirra sive Cire. Fuit & haud procul inde Thonis, oppidum ab eodem Philoctete conditum, ut Strabo notat, cui Χῶνις scribitur: Χῶνα Lycophroni apud Stephanum: ipsi vero Stephano Χῶνη, Oenotrijs tribuenti. Chones, Χῶνες Incolae Adcolaeque Stephano: unde & Regio ipsa Χῶνη. Beltcastro censetur Barrio.
units.tr: Strabo is again the authority for Crimisa, Κρίμισα, which was also founded on this site by Philoctetes; Apollodorus confirms this. Lycophron also mentions Crimisa in Stephanus, to whom Κρίμισα is attributed. Gabriele Barrio today thinks it is Cirra or Cire. Not far from there was also Thonis, a town likewise founded by Philoctetes, as Strabo notes; he writes it Χῶνις. Lycophron has Χῶνα, as cited in Stephanus, while Stephanus himself writes Χῶνη, attributing it to the Oenotrians. The Χῶνες are the inhabitants and neighbours in Stephanus, and the region itself is named Χῶνη from them. Beltcastro is considered by Barrio to be this place.

units.la: Via deinde per oram Scyllaeum Sinus P. M. xii. Oppidum se offert Simaris, ubi Sybarim antiquam fuisse Marturanus autumat: quod Leandro non probatur, uti ex sequentibus patebit.
units.tr: Then along the coast of the Gulf of Scyllaceum, 12 miles, the town Simaris presents itself, where Marturanus claims ancient Sybaris once stood; Leander does not accept this, as will be clear from what follows.

units.la: Ab Tacina fluvio, spatio P M. xii. oppidum sequitur Castella: quod Plinium Castrum Hannibalis dicere, persuasum habet Leander. In Itineraria Tabula scriptum est: Annibali. Castella hodie propter multitudinem, quae ibi, Turrium.
units.tr: Twelve miles from the river Tacina follows the town Castella; Leander is persuaded that Pliny calls it Castrum Hannibalis. In the Itinerary Table it is written Annibali. Castella, today called Turrium on account of the many towers there.

units.la: Sensu hinc P. M. oppidum est Insula: totidem inde Caput Columnarum, olim Lacinium Promontorium, cuius alibi delineatio.
units.tr: Twelve miles from there is the town Insula; as many from there is Caput Columnarum, formerly the promontory Lacinium, whose drawing is given elsewhere.

units.la: Ab Lacinio Promontorio c L. Stadijs, itinere secundum Tarentini Sinus oram Croton fuit. Croton Livio passim, Silio, Plinio, Κρότων Thucydidi lib. vii. Dionysio Halicarnassaeo variis locis, Straboni libro vi. Ptolemaeo, aliis: quae Croto Melae: Κρότωνα Diodoro lib. xiii. Crontona vitiosius in Itineraria Tabula: Crotone vulgo. An Κρότων haec Magnae Graeciae Stephano etiam nota, non autem adfirmare. Triplex certe illi Κρότων: una Ἰταλίας prope Ἥραν: altera Τυρρηνίας μητρόπολις: Tertia Ἰταλίας: Si in hanc etiam digitum intendat: putarum Tertiae significatione intelligendam. Nomen derivat Rassanus ab Κρότῳ, quae Graecis planctus & iucundissimo: olim enim Crotonia plaudendi saltandique studium magno in usu fuisse. Eadem Laura dicta scribitur ab Ifacio Tzetza. Antiochus apud Strabonem ab Miscello Achivorum Duce conditam scribit. Docet idem cum Ovidio libro xv. Metamorphos. Dionysius Halicarnass. libro. ii. qui addit Conditionem huius Urbis medium in annum iv. Numae Pompilij Secundi Romanorum Regis, tertium autem Olympiados x. De ipsius Situ, Amplitudine, Arce, Aliisque multa Livius libro xxiv. Res ab iis gestae memorantur ab eodem, praeterum libro xxiv. & xxix. Silioque Italico lib. xi. Coloniam Crotonem deductam docet idem Livius libro xxxv. Cives Crotoniatae: Κροτωνιᾶται Strabono, Stephano, aliis. Haec Urbs prodigiosa quadam raraque praestantium hominum multitudine claruit. Seq tem enim uno die Victores Olympico certamine habuit, ut memorat Strabo: unde Proverbium ortuum: Κροτωνιατῶν ἐξέλατο, πρῶτον τὴν τῶν ἄλλων ἐλλάδων. Firmitatem corporis & virium huius Urbis Incolis optima caeli constitutio salubritasque creabat, ut Plinius libro ii. cap. xcviii. testatur, unde vetus Adagium: Υγίεστερον Κρότωνος. Ab Robore corporis noti sunt in Historiis non pauci, cum primis Milo, Pythagorae discipulus, de quo cum alii, tum Diodorus lib. xii. Strabo lib. vi. Agellius libro xv Ifamachus, qui Olympiade lxviii. & sequente vicit: Tisicrates, qui lxxi. Astylus, qui lxxiii. de quibus praeter Pausaniam, Dionysius Halicarnass. libris v. vi. viii. Fuit & Crotoniates Democedes, Medicus in summo apud Polycratem Samiorum Tyrannum & Darium Persarum Regem honore habitus, auctore libro iv. Herodoto. Ibidem etiam natum Alcmaeonem, celeberrimum Medicum ex Pythagorae Discipulis, qui primus de ratione Naturae scripsit, tradit in omnimoda historia Favorinus. Orpheum ex Crotone Poetam, Philostrato Tyranno clarum, Argonautica, Dicaearcham, aliaque scripsisse, notat ex Asclepiade Sudas. Alios recentiore nunc esset longum. Pythagoras hic post i. Olympiadem, ut auctor est Halicarnassaeus, Philosophorum instituit Gymnasium. Croton hodie non tam, ut olim, celebris, neque tam ampla: nomen tamen celebre titulumque habet Marchionatus. Arcem munitissimam juxta littus ad Orae maritimae tutelam inchoavit Karolus v. anno MDXLIII.
units.tr: From the promontory of Lacinium, 150 stadia along the shore of the Gulf of Tarentum, lay Croton. Livy uses Croton throughout, as do Silius, Pliny, and Κρότων in Thucydides book vii, Dionysius of Halicarnassus in various places, Strabo in book vi, Ptolemy and others; Mela has Croto; Diodorus in book xiii has Κρότωνα; the Itinerary Table has the more faulty Crontona; the common form is Crotone. I do not affirm whether Stephanus also knew Κρότων as this city of Magna Graecia. He certainly has three places called Κρότων: one in Italy near Hera, another a metropolis of Tyrrhenia, and a third in Italy; if one points a finger at this one too, it should be understood in the sense of the third. Rassanus derives the name from κρότος, which in Greek means applause and delight, for in early times the Crotoniates had a great zeal for clapping and dancing. The same city is called Laura, according to Isaac Tzetzes. Antiochus, in Strabo, writes that it was founded by Myscellus, leader of the Achaeans. The same is taught by Ovid in Metamorphoses book xv. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, in book ii, who adds that the founding of this city fell in the fourth year of Numa Pompilius, the second king of the Romans, but in the third year of the tenth Olympiad. Livy in book xxiv treats its situation, size, citadel and much else; the deeds done by its people are recorded by the same author in book xxiv and xxix, and by Silius Italicus in book xi. Livy in book xxxv teaches that a colony of Croton was led out. The citizens are Crotoniatae, Κροτωνιᾶται in Strabo, Stephanus and others. This city shone with a remarkable multitude of outstanding men. For it had seven victors in the Olympic contests on a single day, as Strabo recounts; whence the proverb arose: "of the Crotoniates, the first of the other Greeks" [Κροτωνιατῶν ἐξέλατο, πρῶτον τὴν τῶν ἄλλων ἐλλάδων]. The firmness of body and strength of the inhabitants was produced by the excellent constitution and healthfulness of the climate, as Pliny testifies in book ii, chapter 98; whence the old saying "healthier than Croton" [Υγίεστερον Κρότωνος]. Not a few men known in histories for bodily strength came from it, above all Milo, a disciple of Pythagoras, about whom Diodorus in book xii, Strabo in book vi, and Aulus Gellius in book xv, among others, speak. Ischomachus, who won in the sixty-eighth Olympiad and the following one; Tisicrates, who won in the seventy-first; Astylus, who won in the seventy-third; concerning these, besides Pausanias, Dionysius of Halicarnassus in books v, vi and viii. There was also Democedes of Croton, a physician held in the highest honour by Polycrates, tyrant of Samos, and by Darius, king of the Persians, as Herodotus records in book iv. Favorinus in his universal history relates that Alcmaeon, the most famous physician among the disciples of Pythagoras, who first wrote on the nature of things, was also born there. Suidas, from Asclepiades, notes that the poet Orpheus of Croton, renowned under the tyrant Philostratus, wrote the Argonautica, Dicaearchus and other works. To list others of more recent times would be tedious. Pythagoras here, after the first Olympiad, as the Halicarnassian writes, established a school of philosophers. Croton today is not as celebrated as it once was, nor so large; yet its name is famous and it holds the title of a marquisate. Charles V began the very strongly fortified citadel beside the shore, for the protection of the coast, in the year 1543.

units.la: Crotone relicto, quatuor ab littore millibus Cutrum sequitur, Oppidum alto impositum Montis vertici. Per oram deinde incedenti amnes occurrunt Ffarus cum Portu & Neethus, de quibus alibi. In Mediterraneis laeva Croton Oppidum est Severina. Post id Bernalda, cum aliis quibusdam Castellis Vicisque, veluti Averna, Mesuraca, Amiri, Longoluco, Virginio, ubi candidum caeditur Marmor, aliaque loca.
units.tr: Leaving Crotone, four miles from the shore, one comes to Cutrum, a town set on the summit of a high mountain. Then, continuing along the coast, the rivers Ffarus, with its harbour, and Neethus come into view; of these, more elsewhere. Inland, on the left of Crotone, is the town of Severina. After it come Bernalda and some other castles and villages, such as Averna, Mesuraca, Amiri, Longoluco and Virginio, where white marble is quarried, and other places.

units.la: Crimisa, Clonia, Simaris, Castella olim Castrum Hannibalis, Insula, Caput columnarum, Crotona, unde dicta, olim & Laura appellata, Conditores, quando condita, Situs, &c., Res gestae, Colonia, Cives Crotoniatae, Clari Viri, Philosophorum Gymnasium, Croton hodie, Marchionatus, Arx munitissima, Severina, Bernalda, Averna, Mesuraca, Amiri, Longoluco, Virginio. loca. Tum per oram Sinus, quatuor ab Nectho millibus Opidum est Strongoli. Post id tex millibus tamquam Promontorium adparet, in quo Pagus Hippizirsus, Piscuis admodum opportunus: xv hinc lapide Turris Imperatoria est: quarto inde Cariathis, opidum Comitatus titulo insigne. Ab Cariathi xiv. P. M. ostia sunt Fluvij Trinutis. Inde millibus tribus, ab mari mille quingentis Pass. Calopittatum, Calopizzato opidum agri foecundi & amoeni, ab Rosano milliaribus distans octo.
units.tr: Crimisa, Clonia, Simaris, the castles, formerly Hannibal's camp, the Island, the Head of the Columns, Crotona, from which it was named, formerly also called Laura, its founders, when it was founded, its situation, etc., its deeds, its colony, the citizens of Croton, famous men, the school of the philosophers, Croton today, the marquisate, the very strong citadel, Severina, Bernalda, Averna, Mesuraca, Amiri, Longoluco, Virginio, and other places. Then, along the coast of the gulf, four miles from Nectho, is the town of Strongoli. After it, six miles off, a promontory comes into view, on which is the village of Hippizirsus, very suitable for fishing. Fifteen miles from here is the Turris Imperatoria. Four miles beyond that is Cariathis, a town distinguished by the title of county. Fourteen miles from Cariathis are the mouths of the river Trinutis. Three miles from there, a thousand five hundred paces from the sea, is Calopittatum, now Calopizzato, a town of fertile and pleasant land, eight miles from Rosano.

units.la: Trans Crathin Locus occurrit, ubi quondam Sybaris, Σύβαρις Latinis Graecisque Scriptoribus satis nota. Crotone distabat, ut Strabo Pliniusque monent, c l. Stadiis Conditores nominat Strabo Achivos, Duce Ilchicto: Troezenios & Sagarin Ajacis Locri filium, Solinus. Hi, quod ex Strabone facile est colligere, fortean condiderunt: illi autem amplificarunt. Situm male indicant Ptolomaei Tabulae, ultra Crotonem, ubi nunc Symari contra Diodorum lib. 11. Strabonem & Plinium, qui inter Crathin & Sybarin locant. Sybaris, ut testes sunt Strabo lib. xvi. Diodorus lib. xii. Herodotus lib. v. & vi. aliique: opibus atque potentia tam egregie quondam floruit, ut quatuor finitimis gentibus imperitarit, Civitatesque xxv. ditionis suae fecerit, & contra Crotoniatas ccc. hominum millia in aciem eduxerit. Quo bello superati Sybaritae, quum toti diffluerunt otio & luxuria, una cum urbe sua funditus sunt deleti ob dissolutos effeminatosque mores omnibus gentibus & Civitatibus exosi, adeo ut Proverbio locum dederint, quum molles vitaeque dissolutioris homines appellati fuerint Sybaritae. Quo anno Milium ex Oleo & Garo repererunt (quem ob id Sybariticum vocabant) eodem natere turpiterque perierunt. Itaque Nova urbs non procul ab Vetere postea ad mare condita est: Thuriumque ab Fonte proximo dictum. Thurium diu opibus & pace floruit, suisque liberum vixit legibus ab Lucanis post subiactum: quos quum Tarentini vehementer infestarent, Romanorum Colonia est facta; qui novo nomine Copias eam vocarunt. Sic Varro Sybari, inquit de Re Rustica lib. i. cap. vii. qui nunc Thury, cui suffragatur Plutarchus in Pericle. Stephanus: Θούριοι, πόλις Ιταλίας, ἡ πρότερον Συβάρις, ἀπὸ Θουρίας πηγῆς· ὑστερον δὲ Κωπία. Λέγει καὶ Θουρίας χ' Θούριον. Eadem tufius apud Strabonem, qui Κωπάς habet. Thurium Plinio, Melae, aliisque Latinis: Θούριον Ptolemaeo, Graecisque caeteris: Thuri Antonino: Θούριοι Thucydidi lib. vi. & vii. Appiano libro v. Straboni lib. vi. Diodoro item, cui & Θούριον: Turis Itinerariae Tabulae, pro Turis vel Turiis. Thuria Livio, cui & Thurinum & Thurini lib. xxv. Floroque de Bello Spartaco. Addit Stephanus Thurinum etiam Αθειου dici a Pausania: male. Pausanias enim hoc de Thure Messenica loquitur, non de Thuriis Italico. Thury urbs in Salentinis Livio libro x. propter vicinitatem. Vere enim est in Magna Graecia. Incolae Thury, Θούριοι, Stephano & aliis. De hac Urbe scribit Diodorus loco saepe indicato: Eam in quatuor Foris secundum longitudinem fuisse distinctam: quorum primum appellabant Heracleam: ii. Aphrodisiadem: iii. Olympiadem: iv. denique Dionysiadem: in latitudinem vero tribus Foris distributam: quorum nomina erant, i. Heroa, Ἡρῴα: Thuria: iii. Thurina. Thuriis in Italia Historiam suam Herodotus condidit, ut libro xii. cap. iv. scribit Plinius. Thurij hodie exigua supersunt vestigia, iuxta littus. Terram Novam hoc tempore dici notant Scipio Mazella, & Gabriel Barrius: non bene, quum Terra Nova sit in Mediterraneis: Thurium autem ad Mare fuerit, quo loco nunc, ut magni viri volunt. Buffalaria; In Agro Thurino, inquit Plinius lib. xvi. cap. xxii. ubi Sybaris fuit, ex ipsa Urbe profluebatur. Quercus una, numquam folia demittens, nec ante mediam aestatem germinans. In eodem Agro aestivo tempore ex Arborum truncis Folijsque hodie Manna legitur. Adparet his in locis Aquaeductus adhuc veterrimus, qui putatur illius fuisse Fontis a quo Thuriorum nomen acceptum. Aqua Fabulina, Acqua che Favella hodie dicitur. Supra locum, ubi Thury quondam fuerunt, Regio nunc est, quae vulgo Torrana: sic procul dubio ab antiquo Opido nunc eupata. Thurinus Pagus & Thurina Regio apud Suetonium in Octaviano. Ab hac Urbe Θουρίνον Οῖνον, Thurinum Vinum, Straboni libro vi. etiam apud Stephanum: quod in precio fuisse testatur Plinius libro. xiv. cap. vi. Thurios Montes habet Appianus libro i. Bellor. Civilium. Thurinus denique Sinus ab hac Urbe: de quo alibi.
units.tr: Across the Crathis is a place where once stood Sybaris, Σύβαρις [Sybaris], well known to Latin and Greek writers. As Strabo and Pliny note, it was 150 stadia from Crotone. Strabo names its founders as the Achaeans under their leader Ilchicto; Solinus names the Troezenians and Sagaris, son of Ajax the Locrian. These, as may easily be gathered from Strabo, perhaps founded it, while the others enlarged it. Ptolemy's tables wrongly indicate its site, beyond Crotone, where Symari now is, contrary to Diodorus (book 11), Strabo and Pliny, who place it between the Crathis and Sybaris. Sybaris, as Strabo (book 16), Diodorus (book 12), Herodotus (books 5 and 6) and others attest, once flourished so remarkably in wealth and power that it ruled four neighbouring peoples, made twenty-five cities subject to itself, and led three hundred thousand men into the field against the Crotoniates. In that war the Sybarites were defeated. Since they had wholly dissolved in idleness and luxury, they were utterly destroyed together with their city, hated by all peoples and cities for their dissolute and effeminate manners, so much so that they gave a proverb: men who are soft and live loose lives are called Sybarites. In the same year they discovered millet grown with oil and salt (which for that reason they called Sybaritic), and they perished there shamefully. Therefore a new city, Thurium, named after the nearby spring, was later founded by the sea, not far from the old one. Thurium flourished for a long time in wealth and peace, and lived free under its own laws after being subjected by the Lucanians. When the Tarentines harassed it severely, it became a Roman colony, which they called Copias by a new name. Thus Varro, On Farming, book 1, chapter 7: "Sybaris, which is now Thury." Plutarch in Pericles agrees. Stephanus: Θούριοι [Thourioi], a city of Italy, formerly Sybaris, from the spring Θουρία [Thouria]; later Κωπία [Kopia]. He also says the Θουρίας [Thourias]... The same is more clearly stated in Strabo, who has Κωπάς [Kopas]. Thurium in Pliny, Mela and other Latin writers; Θούριον [Thourion] in Ptolemy and the other Greeks; Thuri in Antoninus; Θούριοι [Thourioi] in Thucydides (books 6 and 7), Appian (book 5), Strabo (book 6), and likewise in Diodorus, who also has Θούριον [Thourion]; Turis in the Itinerary tables, for Turis or Turiis. Thuria in Livy, who also has Thurinum and Thurini (book 25), and in Florus on the Spartacus war. Stephanus adds that Thurinum is also called Ἀθηνῶν [Athenon] by Pausanias, but wrongly: Pausanias speaks of Thouria in Messenia, not of Thurii in Italy. Thury, a city among the Salentines in Livy (book 10), is so called because of its nearness; in truth it is in Magna Graecia. Its inhabitants are Thury, Θούριοι [Thourioi], according to Stephanus and others. Diodorus, in the passage often cited, writes of this city that it was divided lengthwise into four quarters: the first they called Ἡρακλέα [Herakleia], the second Ἀφροδισιάς [Aphrodisias], the third Ὀλυμπιάς [Olympias], and the fourth Διονυσιάς [Dionysias]; across its breadth it was divided into three quarters, whose names were: first Ἡρῷα [Herôa], second Thuria, third Thurina. Herodotus composed his history at Thurii in Italy, as Pliny writes (book 12, chapter 4). Few traces of Thurii remain today, beside the shore. Scipio Mazella and Gabriel Barrius note that it is now called Terram Novam, but not rightly, since Terra Nova lies inland, whereas Thurium was by the sea, in the place where, as great men maintain, it now is. Buffalaria. "In the Thurian territory," says Pliny (book 16, chapter 22), "where Sybaris was, there flows from the city itself..." One oak, never shedding its leaves and not sprouting before midsummer. In the same territory, in the summer season, manna is still gathered today from the trunks and leaves of trees. In these places there appears a very ancient aqueduct, which is thought to have belonged to that spring from which the name Thurii was taken. It is called Aqua Fabulina, today Acqua che Favella. Above the place where Thury once stood there is now a district commonly called Torrana; thus, without doubt, named after the ancient town. Thurinus Pagus and Thurina Regio in Suetonius, Augustus. From this city comes Θουρίνον Οἶνον [Thourinon Oinon], Thurinum wine, in Strabo (book 6) and also in Stephanus; that it was valued Pliny testifies (book 14, chapter 6). Appian (Civil Wars, book 1) has the Thurios Montes. Finally, the Thurinus Sinus takes its name from this city; of which elsewhere.

units.la: Post Thurios, inquit Strabo, Lagaria, Λαγαρία, est Opidum: Epei & Phocensium Colonia: unde Vinum, addit, Lagarianum, dulce ac lene, cuius quoque Plinius meminit
units.tr: After Thurii, says Strabo, is Lagaria, Λαγαρία [Lagaria], a town, a colony of the Epeans and Phocians; whence, he adds, comes the Lagarian wine, sweet and mild, which Pliny also mentions.

units.la: Strongoli, Hippizirsus, Turris Imperatoria, Cariathis, Calopittatum, Sybaris, Conditores, Situs, Potentia. Resurgentia, Diruta Thurii peperit, quod Colonia Romanorum facta, Thurium, Thurij, Vestigia hodie, Ager, Fons Thurium, Thurina Regio, Thurinum vinum, Montes, Sinus, Lagaria. minit lib.xiv.cap.vi. Λαχαρία, inquit Stephanus, Φρούριον Σικελίας (quur Siciliæ tribuat, alibi dictum) πλήσιον Θεζίων, & Ἑπεὶς καὶ Φωκεῶν κτίσμα, ὡς Στρεφῶν: non procul Grumento, apud Plinium. Gabriel Barrius dicit locum nunc vacuum, sine Habitatoribus: Mons vero, cui Civitas impolita, Adcolis Cirnisfaso nominatur, ab Fluvio Cylistarno præterfluente.
units.tr: Strongoli, Hippizirsus, Turris Imperatoria, Cariathis, Calopittatum, Sybaris, its founders, situation, power; its revival; Thurii destroyed, which, having been made a Roman colony, produced Thurium, Thurii, the remains today, the territory, the spring of Thurium, the Thurina Regio, the Thurinum wine, the mountains, the gulf, Lagaria. Pliny mentions it in book 14, chapter 6. Λαγαρία [Lagaria], says Stephanus, a fortress of Sicily (why he assigns it to Sicily is said elsewhere), near Thurii, and a foundation of the Epeans and Phocians, as Strabo says. Not far from Grumentum, in Pliny. Gabriel Barrius says the place is now empty, without inhabitants; but the mountain on which the town was built is called Cirnisfaso by its neighbours, from the river Cylistarnus flowing past it.

units.la: Amni, qui hodie Sinus, olim Siris dictus, Opido adpositum fuit cognomine Σίρις, à Troianis condita, quod Palladium huc ex Ilio delatum indicabat, Videndus Strabo: qui addit, Ionex Lyderum Imperium pertæsos eo venisse. Urbemque expugnantam, quam Aborigines seu Chones tenebant prius, πόλιον appellasse: πλήρη legitur apud Aristotelem in Mirabil. Pelicori recentiore nomine dicitur Pyrrho Ligorio. Sirin postea Tarentum subegerunt, Coloniamque inde deduxerunt Heracleam. Legendus Livius libro viii.
units.tr: To the river which today is called the Sinus, but was formerly called Siris, was joined a town of the same name, Σίρις [Siris], founded by the Trojans, as the Palladium carried here from Ilium indicated. See Strabo, who adds that the Ionians, weary of Lydian rule, came there. The city they took, which the Aborigines or Chones held before, they called πόλιον [polion]; πλήρη [plêrê] is read in Aristotle's Mirabilia. In more recent times it is called Pelicori, as Pyrrho Ligorio names it. Afterwards the Sirites subdued Tarentum and from there led out a colony, Heraclea. Livy, book 8, should be read.

units.la: Fuit etiam ætate Strabonis ab Siri xxiii. à Thurijs cccxxx Stadiis, non plane juxta littus, Ηράκλεια: quæ Livio, Melæ, Antonino, Itinerariæ Tabulæ, aliis Heraclea; Ηράκλεια Plutarcho: Colonia, ut jam dixi, Tarentinorum. Olim πόλις εμπόριον Τωικὴ, inquit Strabo. Heracleam Appianus inter Metapontum & Tarentum statuit: Plinius libro iii. cap.xi. inter Sirin & Acirin Fluvios locat: & Sirin quoque appellatam refert: Sirin & Heracleam unam eandemque (vide & Diodorū lib.xii.) censens Urbem, ut quæ primo Siris, post Heraclea fuerit dicta: sed diversas fuisse, aperte docet Strabo. Nonnulli duas Heracleas hoc loco ponunt, xxiv. Stadijs ab invicem distantes: earum unam, quæ & Troia) alterius facientes Navale, quod hodie Amygdalariam vocari testatur Barrius. Heracleam, Tarentinorum coloniam, ab Alexandro Epiroto captam, testantur Livius lib.viii. & Diodorus lib.xii. Incolæ ab Finitimis Μισθοφόροι vocabantur, teste, Athenæo lib. xii.cap.viii.
units.tr: In Strabo's time there was also, twenty-three miles from Siris and 330 stadia from Thurii, not quite on the shore, Ἡράκλεια [Herakleia]: in Livy, Mela, Antoninus, the Itinerary tables and others, Heraclea; Ἡράκλεια [Herakleia] in Plutarch; a colony, as I have already said, of the Tarentines. Formerly, says Strabo, it was a Tyrrhenian trading city, πόλις ἐμπόριον Τυρρηνική [polis emporion Tyrrhênikê]. Appian places Heraclea between Metapontum and Tarentum. Pliny (book 3, chapter 11) places it between the rivers Siris and Aciris, and reports that it was also called Siris, thinking Siris and Heraclea one and the same city (see also Diodorus, book 12), since it was first Siris and afterwards was called Heraclea. But Strabo clearly shows that they were different. Some place two Herakleias here, twenty-four stadia apart from each other: one of them, which is also Troy, and the other a shipyard, which Barrius testifies is today called Amygdalaria. That Heraclea, a colony of the Tarentines, was captured by Alexander of Epirus is attested by Livy (book 8) and Diodorus (book 12). Its inhabitants were called Μισθοφόροι [Misthophoroi], mercenaries, by their neighbours, as Athenaeus (book 12, chapter 8) testifies.

units.la: Anteaquam ulterius progrediar, obiter Mediterranea, Veteribus non admodum nota, percurram.
units.tr: Before I go further, I will briefly survey the inland places, which were not very well known to the ancients.

units.la: Post Confeccentiam eis Crathin primum est Castilio opidum, Casiglio: tum inter juga Rose: mox millibus inde iv. Lilucium, peramœni agri.
units.tr: After Confeccentia, the first town toward Crathis is Castilio, now Casiglio. Then, among the ridges of Rose, comes Lilucium, a very pleasant district, four miles from there.

units.la: Succedit post in Colle montibus editissimis propinquo Bisinianum, Bisignano, forma septiquetra, Arce præditum, Titulisque Principatus Episcopatusque ornatum.
units.tr: Next, on a hill near very high mountains, lies Bisinianum, now Bisignano, of seven-cornered shape, with a citadel and adorned with the titles of a principality and a bishopric.

units.la: Sequitur fenis a Bisiniano milliaribus inter montes Opidum Tarsia: antiquum, frequens, opulentum. Quinque hinc P. M. ab mari vero xii. inter montes item, est Terra Nova. Opidum dives. Pari dein ab ora spatio aliud est Agri. Post id quaternis milibus in planiciem mare versus descendenti perpulcrum occurrit D. Mauri, S. Mauro, magnificentissimo Bisiniani Principis splendens Palatio.
units.tr: Next, about fifteen miles from Bisignano among the mountains, is the town of Tarsia: ancient, populous and wealthy. Five miles from here, toward the sea, and twelve miles from the sea, again among mountains, is Terra Nova, a rich town. Another place, Agri, lies the same distance from the coast beyond it. Four miles further, descending toward the plain and the sea, there appears a very handsome palace of San Mauro, the magnificent residence of the Prince of Bisignano.

units.la: Via tum per planiciem P. M. ab mari quatuor ad Corliánum venitur: agri Opidum amœni. Adluit Amnis Corlianetus. In agro Corlianæ Argenti sunt Fodinæ.
units.tr: Then, by a road across the plain, four miles from the sea, one comes to Corliano, a pleasant town in the country. The river Corlianetus flows past it. In the territory of Corliano there are silver mines.

units.la: Offert se hinc Orientem versus Rosanum, vel Rossanum, Civitas munitissima, tribus ab Mari P. M. Antonino Rosciānum dicitur: ut putat Gabriel Barrius. Procopius lib. iii. de Bello Goth. Blondusque lib.vi. Historiæ. Ruscianum hanc vocant Urbem. Sedem habet Archiepiscopalem, cui multi sunt Suffraganei. Valerianum, Episcopum Rossanensem interfuisse Synodo Constantinopolitanæ vi. sub Agathone, prodit memoriæ Agathias lib.iv. Nobileshic Familiæ: Amarellis. | Foggia | Rapano, Armingari. | Longhi. | Risi. Briti. | Maleni. | Tagliaferro. Campagna. | Manarini. | Toscani, Capofachi. | Muro. | Zuo. Citi. | Negri. Corti. | Protospatari.
units.tr: From here, toward the east, lies Rosanum, or Rossanum, a very strong city, three miles from the sea. Antoninus calls it Rosciānum, as Gabriel Barrius thinks. See Procopius, book 3 of the Gothic War, and Blondus, book 6 of his History. They call this city Ruscianum. It has an archbishop's see, to which many suffragans are subject. Agathias, book 4, records that Valerianus, bishop of Rossano, took part in the sixth Synod of Constantinople under Agatho. Noble families: Amarellis, Foggia, Rapano, Armingari, Longhi, Risi, Briti, Maleni, Tagliaferro, Campagna, Manarini, Toscani, Capofachi, Muro, Zuo, Citi, Negri, Corti, Protospatari.

units.la: Ulterius inter Montes xii. milliario Casanum est, ad Bisiniani quoque Principis Imperium spectans, & Episcopatus fulgens dignitate.
units.tr: Further on, among mountains twelve miles away, is Casanum, which also belongs to the rule of the Prince of Bisignano and is distinguished by its bishopric.

units.la: Dehinc inter altissima juga dives Opidum Cerciaria, Cerchiara, Marchionis Montis Sarchij, ex Neapolitana Carrafarum gente.
units.tr: Then, among very high ridges, is the wealthy town of Cerciaria, now Cerchiara, belonging to the Marquis of Monte Sarchio, of the Carafa family of Naples.

units.la: Inde millibus quatuor ad Sinum Rosanū descendenti in montis latere, quod Sinū spectat, Castellum Novum visitur, tribus à Mari P. M. Milerinæ Comitis ex illustri Neapolitana Sanseverinatum Familia. Vltra Cochilem Amnem ad jactum lapidis Opidum Trebisatium est,Trebisazzi vulgo: juxtaque montes Albidona, millibus mari quatuor: dein Amygdalaria duobus à mari milliaribus, nomen illi ab Amygdalarum copia. In ditione est Marchionis Sarchini. Illustravit suo ortu Pomponius Latus.
units.tr: Four miles from there, descending toward the Gulf of Rosano on the mountainside that faces the gulf, is seen the little castle of Castellum Novum, three miles from the sea, belonging to the Count of Milerina, of the illustrious Sanseverino family of Naples. Beyond the river Cochilis, within a stone's throw, lies the town of Trebisatium, commonly called Trebisazzi. Next to it, among the mountains, lies Albidona, four miles from the sea. Then comes Amygdalaria, two miles from the sea, named for its abundance of almond trees. It is in the domain of the Marquis of Sarchio. Pomponius Latus made it famous by his birth.

units.la: Quæ sequuntur Loca Lucania potius, quam Magna Gracia tribuenda censent non pauci. Ego non magnopere in veritate quærenda me torquebo. Laborant enim hic Indigenæ ipsi; Viri etiam eruditi.
units.tr: Many people think that the places which follow should be assigned to Lucania rather than to Magna Graecia. I will not trouble myself much over seeking the truth here, for even the natives themselves are confused about it, and learned men too.

units.la: Passibus ab mari mille, juxta montis, de quo dixi, latus, Arx est Imperialis, sic dicta, quod ab Imp. Friderico Siciliæ Rege sit condita. Alphonsus etiam 11. Neapolis Rex, Calabriæ Dux, validissimam hic erexit Arcem.
units.tr: A thousand paces from the sea, beside the mountain I mentioned, stands the Imperial Citadel, so called because it was founded by the Emperor Frederick, King of Sicily. King Alfonso II of Naples, Duke of Calabria, also built a very strong citadel here.

units.la: Inter montes sunt, quæ vulgo Feleta, Nucara, Cana, Ruino, Franca-Villa, ubi splendidum Carthusianorum Cœnobium. Mox ad montis pedem Noia. Succedunt vestigia Pelicoris, ubi modica etiamnum Arx. Intus inter montes sunt S. Arcango, Bocca Nova, Vaturno Græcorum domicilium, Castro Nuovo, Episcopia, Carinia, Teanis, Chiaramonte, Senesi, Collivali, Torfe. Ruinæ Petrolæ adamnem Salandram monstrantur. Sequitur ultra Salandram Graco. tum ulterius inter montes sunt S. Mauro, Acremira, Cantiano mille passibus ab Amne Bafentio: deinde Ferrandina, Castellum, ab Ferrandino Calabriæ Duce, Alphonsi 11. Neapolitanorum Regis Filio, conditu, & nominatum, haud procul eo loco, ubi prius Vegianum fuit, terræmotibus subversu & absumtum. Exin inter montes Pelice.
units.tr: Among the mountains are the places commonly called Feleta, Nucara, Cana, Ruino, and Franca-Villa, where there is a splendid monastery of Carthusians. Soon, at the foot of the mountain, is Noia. Next come the remains of Pelicoro, where a small citadel still stands. Inland, among the mountains, are San Arcangelo, Bocca Nova, Vaturno, a settlement of Greeks, Castro Nuovo, Episcopia, Carinia, Teanis, Chiaramonte, Senesi, Collivali and Torfe. The ruins of Petrola are shown by the river Salandra. Beyond the Salandra comes Graco. Then, further inland among the mountains, are San Mauro, Acremira, and Cantiano, a thousand paces from the river Basentius. Then comes Ferrandina, a castle founded and named after Ferrandino, Duke of Calabria, son of King Alfonso II of Naples. It lies not far from the place where Vegianum once stood, which was overthrown and swallowed up by earthquakes. After this, among the mountains, is Pelice.

units.la: Paullo ultra Basentium, 19. ab mari passibus Turris Marina, Torre di Mar, nunc deserta, cernitur: pauca quædam superstunt inopum Tuguria.
units.tr: A little beyond the Basentius, nineteen paces from the sea, can be seen the Marine Tower, Torre di Mare, now deserted. Only a few poor huts remain.

units.la: Non procul hunc Campus ingens & amœnus sternitur, ab mari 19. passibus, in quo Metapontum, fuisse fertur, urbs nobilissima nullis non Scriptoribus Græcis Latinisque celebrata. Metaponti hac ætate nulla (quod mirandum de tanta Vrbe) vestigia; præter vetus cocti lateris rudus cum atra terra, supersunt: quam ob causam sunt, qui suisse volunt, ubi hodie Pelicoris. Sed fallo. Pelicoris enim inter montes fuit: Metapontum autem juxta mare Thebesaze; Trebisazi potius dicendum erat) Castellum hoc loco nunc esse scribit Niger. Metapontum porro plerisque; Μεταπόντιον Straboni & Ptolemæo: Vibo aliquando vocata fuit, Solino teste: & sic eam quoque nominat Cæsar lib.111. bell. Civil. Siris etiam Σιρις nomen habuisse tradunt Stephanus & Eustathius: inde Sirini Plinio eius Incolæ. Μεταπόν olim vocatam tradit apud Strabonem Antiochus. Tzetza Chiliade xi 1.num.404. illam etiam Ἀλύβας appellat, ut & Stephanus. Metapontum Strabo conditum scribit à Pyliis: qui huc, Nestore Duce, Troia sunt profecti: Solinus ab Locris notat factum, ab ipsaque Metapontum vocatum, & ætate sua Iubium: Ephorus ab Daulio, Crisæ Delphis propinquæ Tyranno, ait: Antiochus à Metaponto, Siliphi Filio, quem Barbari Metabum vocabant: primoque nominatum Siritum memorat Eustathius. Non desunt, qui nuncupatum arbitantur ab extremitate maris, ac si Meta Ponti diceretur. Vrbis Natalem Feriis, quæ Neleida dicebantur, celebrabant. Templi Junonis hic columnis Vitigineis stetisse tradit Plinius lib. xiv.cap.1. Tantæ Metapontinorum fuerunt opes, tanta potentia: ut, quod refert Strabo, aureiam Aestatë Apollini Delphis obtulerint. Testatur Trogus lib.xx. Metapontinos in Minervæ Templo Ferramenta, quibus Equum Troianum Epeus, à quo conditi erant, fabricaverat, ostentasse: propter quod omnis illa pars Italiæ, nimirum in qua Metapontus, Maior Gracia vocabatur. Res ab Metapontinis gestas, eorumque clades recensent Herodotus lib.xxi. Antiochus apud Strabonem, Livius lib.xxv.& xxvii. atque alij. Metapontum à Spartaco direptum narrat L.Florus Hippasis Pythagoræ discipuli ortu fuit nobilitatum, teste Demetrio in Homonymis. Pythagoram ipsum hic supremam ætatem exegisse, quum Crotonemigrasset, ubi annos xx. constiterat, testis est Trogus lib.xx. addens eumdem in tanta Metaponti fuisse admiratione, ut & ædes eius dedicarentur, & divinis ipse honoribus coleretur. A quo tanta Urbs fuerit eversa, non invenitur.
units.tr: Not far from here stretches a vast and pleasant plain, nineteen paces from the sea, where Metapontum is said to have stood, a most noble city celebrated by almost all Greek and Latin writers. Today there are no remains of Metapontum (a strange thing for so great a city), except some old rubble of baked brick with black soil. For this reason some want it to have been where Pelicoro is today. But they are wrong. For Pelicoro lay among the mountains, whereas Metapontum lay beside the sea, near Thebesaze (it should rather be called Trebisazi). Niger writes that there is now a castle in this place. Most writers, however, call it Metapontum, Μεταπόντιον in Strabo and Ptolemy [Metapontion]. It was once called Vibo, as Solinus testifies, and Caesar also names it so in book 3 of the Civil War. Stephanus and Eustathius say that Siris also had the name Σιρις [Seiris]; hence its inhabitants are called Sirini by Pliny. Antiochus, as reported in Strabo, says it was once called Μεταπόν [Metapon]. Tzetzes, in his Chiliades 11, line 404, also calls it Ἀλύβας [Alybas], as does Stephanus. Strabo writes that Metapontum was founded by the Pylians, who set out from Troy under Nestor as leader. Solinus says it was founded by the Locrians and named after one of their own, and that in his own day it was called Jubium. Ephorus says it was named after Daulius, tyrant of Crisa, near Delphi. Antiochus says it was named after Metapontus, son of Siliphus, whom the barbarians called Metabus. Eustathius records that it was first called Siritis. Some think it was named from the end of the sea, as if it were called Meta Ponti. They celebrated the city's birthday at the festivals called Neleida. Pliny, book 14, chapter 1, reports that a temple of Juno stood here with columns of vine wood. The wealth and power of the Metapontines were so great that, as Strabo reports, they offered a golden ear of grain to Apollo at Delphi. Trogus, book 20, testifies that the Metapontines displayed in the temple of Minerva the tools with which Epeus, their founder, had made the Trojan horse. For this reason that whole part of Italy, namely where Metapontum lies, was called Magna Graecia. Herodotus, book 21, Antiochus in Strabo, Livy, books 25 and 27, and others record the deeds of the Metapontines and their defeats. L. Florus relates that Metapontum was sacked by Spartacus. Hippasus, a disciple of Pythagoras, made it famous by his birth, according to Demetrius in his Homonyms. Trogus, book 20, is a witness that Pythagoras himself spent his last years here, after he had left Croton, where he had lived for twenty years. He adds that Pythagoras was so admired in Metapontum that his house was dedicated and he himself was worshipped with divine honours. By whom so great a city was overthrown is not recorded.

units.la: Reliqua, quæ succedunt Tarentum usque nunc Magna Gracia, nunc Apulia, Ptolemæi insistentes vestigiis, concensent Magni viri.
units.tr: The remaining places which follow, from Tarentum onward, are now called Magna Graecia, now Apulia. Great men have agreed to these names, following the footsteps of Ptolemy.

units.la: Post cum locum, ubi quondam Metapontus, ad quartum lapidem, mille passibus ab ora, Columnæ marmoreæ xx. prægrandes altæque conspiciuntur, ordine duplici, ubi Gymnasium Architæ Tarentini fuisse quondam vulgo creditur. Intus in montibus est opidum Bernalda, propinquum ad teli iactum Basentio. Tum ab eo flumine millibus duobus iuxta pedem montis Pomarium est: & in ipsis Collibus Meliorcum, Principis Bisiniani: senis inde millibus Crotolum, Ducis Traiectini Castellum: ulterius Graffanum, & Mons Scaliosus, Monte Scagliofo, mille passibus a Bradano.
units.tr: Beyond the place where Metapontum once stood, at the fourth milestone, a thousand paces from the shore, twenty very large and tall marble columns are seen in a double row. It is commonly believed that these were once the gymnasium of Archytas of Tarentum. Inland, among the mountains, is the town of Bernalda, within a spear's throw of the Basentius. Then, two thousand paces from that river, at the foot of the mountain, is Pomarium. On the hills themselves is Meliorcum, belonging to the Prince of Bisignano. Six miles from there is Crotolum, a castle of the Duke of Trajetto. Further on are Graffanum and Mount Scaliosus, Monte Scagliofo, a thousand paces from the Bradanus.

units.la: Dein mare versus incedenti Tricaricum juxta Montis radices occurrit, sex a Graffano passuum millibus Opidum in ditione Principis Bisiniani.
units.tr: Going on toward the sea, Tricaricum is met at the foot of the mountains, a town six miles from Graffanum, in the domain of the Prince of Bisignano.

units.la: Itinere hinc secundum ulteriorem Bradani ripam, sursum, Opidum in jugis invenitur Mons Pelosus, Ducis Traiectini: quod Bradanus adluit.
units.tr: From here, following the farther bank of the Bradanus upward, a town is found on the ridges, Mons Pelosus, belonging to the Duke of Trajetto, which the Bradanus washes.

units.la: Hinc eadem Via sex millibus inter montes Gravina est: titulo Ducatus & Episcopatus dignitate nobilis.
units.tr: From here, along the same road, six miles away among the mountains, is Gravina, noted for its dukedom and the dignity of its bishopric.

units.la: Millia inde sex numerantur ad Altam-Villam, antiquo Petelia loco sitam, ut nonnulli sentiunt: non recte, & contra Ptolemaei Tabulas, ubi Petelia in Agro Scyllaceo octo circiter P. M. ab Mari locatur. Videnda & Locorum enumeratio apud Virgil. lib. III. Aeneid. consulendi item Strabo & Plinius. Opidum hoc Principatus habet Titulum. Nulli in Sacrorum jure Episcopo, sed Ecclesiae Romanae & eius paret Archibres bytero.
units.tr: Then six miles are counted to Altam-Villam, situated, as some think, on the ancient site of Petelia. This is not right, and it contradicts the Tables of Ptolemy, where Petelia is placed in the territory of Scyllaceum, about eight Roman miles from the sea. The list of places in Virgil, book 3 of the Aeneid, should also be consulted, as should Strabo and Pliny. This town has the title of a principality. It has no bishop with rights over sacred matters, but it is subject to the Roman Church and to its archpresbyter.

units.la: Itinere hinc per Apenninum P. M. XII. Vallis invenitur pulcra: in qua urbs Matera, frequens & opulenta: quondam, ut auctor est Collenutius, Archerontia. De Situ Murorum referr nonnulla Leander Albertus. Archiepiscopatus Titulum obtinet. In ditione est Ducis Gravinensis. Dirutam ab Saracenis, memoriae prodit Blondus lib. XIII. Historiar. Urbis Incolae Materani Plinio in Secunda Regione.
units.tr: Three Roman miles further on, through the Apennine, you come to a fine valley in which lies the city of Matera, populous and wealthy. It was once, according to Collenutius, Archerontia. Leander Albertus reports some details about the situation of its walls. It holds the title of an archbishopric. It lies within the lordship of the Duke of Gravina. Blondus, in book 13 of his Histories, records that it was destroyed by the Saracens. The inhabitants of the city are the Materani, as Pliny calls them in the Second Region.

units.la: Ab Matera dein ad XII. milliar. Castrum est Tertianum. Postad XI x item a Matera, totidemque a Tarento, Castellanetum in Apennino, Episcopatus honore superbiens.
units.tr: From Matera, twelve miles off, is the fortress of Tertianum. Eleven miles from Matera, and as many from Taranto, is Castellanetum in the Apennine, proud of the honour of an episcopal see.

units.la: Inde per Apennium ad VI. Tarentoque XII. Motula, Civitas item Episcopalis.
units.tr: Through the Apennine, six miles on, and twelve from Taranto, is Motula, also an episcopal city.

units.la: Tum ad oram versus III. milliari, Tarentoque XII. in planicie reperitur Palescanum: lavaque juxta flexum ad Aquilonem Tarentini Sinus in Apennino, v. ab mari millibus, a Palesano III. Tarentoque IX exiguum est, sed munitum valde, Castellum Masafra, ubi male contra Plinium & alios quidam antiquam locant Messapiam, quum in Salentinis ea fuerit, ultra Tarentum.
units.tr: Then, three miles toward the coast, and twelve from Taranto, on the plain, is Palescanum. Near the bend of the Gulf of Taranto, toward the north, in the Apennine, five miles from the sea and three from Palesano, and nine from Taranto, is the small but very strongly fortified castle Masafra. Some men, wrongly and against Pliny and others, place the ancient Messapia* here, although it lay among the Salentines, beyond Taranto.

units.la: Alia huius Tractus Loca minoris dignationis, ne sim prolixior, praetereo; qualia sunt, quae vulgo, Ginosa, Colubrano, Alianello, Aliano, Guarda,
units.tr: I pass over other places of this district of lesser importance, so as not to be too long; such as those commonly called Ginosa, Colubrano, Alianello, Aliano, Guarda.

units.la: In ea demum antiquissima nobilissimaque Urbs est Tarentum; cui non Scriptorum Veterum multis encomiis celebrata? Tarentum plerique dicitur: Ταράντ Appiano Alexandrino libro v: Τάραντ Straboni libro VI, Ptolemaeo, Ne mismati, quod apud se esse scribit Abrahamus Ortelius. Taranto hodie. Oebaliam ab Virgilio vocari, testatur Servius, & ab Ovido Scopas: sed Oebaliam Arcem esse Tarentinam, notat Philargyrius. Urbem volunt conditam Plinius libro III. cap. XI, L. Florus, & Orosius lib. III, cap. I ab Lacedaemoniis, ab Heraclidis Solinus, ab Cretensibus Antiochus, & ab uno eorum Duce Tarentum appellatam. Alii ab Tarento Amne, v ab Urbe P. M. praeterfluente, denominatam censent: Nonnulli, inter quos Varro, ab Sabina voce, quae molle significat, unde & Molle Tarentum Horatio Flacco, propterea quod, ut nonnulli volunt, in Agro Tarentino & Nuces & Lanae mollissimae proveniant. Plerique Tarenti auctorem faciunt Tarantem Neptuni filium, ab ea nomen addentes accepisse. Legend. Servius ad III Aeneid. & IV Georgic. Calabriae, sive Magnae Graeciae Urbem faciunt omnes: Sudas & Alianus in Militaribus Siciliae adscribunt. Caussam alibi aperui. Calabriae quondam & Apuliae, totiusque Lucaniae Caput, L. Floro. Describunt abfabre Strabo lib. VI, L. Florus lib. I cap. XVIII Procopius lib. III. Bell. Gothic. aliique, Situs eius notatur in intimo recessu Sinus, qui ab ipsa Urbe dicitur Tarentinus, in ipsis Maris Hadriatici faucibus, inquit Florus. Portum, quem habuit maximum, pulcerrimum, tutissimum, describit curiose Strabo lib. VI. Hodie visitur obturatus saxis ingentibus, adeo ut parvis tantum navigiis pateat: quod qua de causa sit factum, & a quo, nondum legi. Maxima nunc in eo Portu Piscium ubertas. De antiqua etiam ibidem Arce, Statuisque inibi & Signis positis, quae cum Karthaginiensis, tum Romani abstulerunt, lectu etiam digna apud Strabonem, & alios. Theatrum item habuisse prope portam, Stadium lucylentissimum. Forum amplissimum, Colossum ex ære artis summæ, notant Florus lib.1. cap.xviii. Strabo libro vi. alij. Cives Tarentini Latinis, Ταραντῖνοι Græcis. Spurios vocatos scribit ex Trogo Iustinus; Parthenias dictos notat Servius ad iii Æneid. Rationem indicant Historiographi; inter alios Antiochus. Φαλαντιάδας appellatos tradit Stephanus, à Palantho, quo duce Lacones eo advenientes Urbem conditam valde auxerunt. Initio popularI administrata Imperio, tantis opum potentiæque incrementis valuit, ut finitimas Gentes omnes (multis, quæ sequuntur, commemorant Strabo lib.vi. & apud eum Ephorus & Antiochus: Herodotus lib.iii. Livius infinitis locis, præcipue lib.ix.xii.xiii. xiv.xv.xxv.xxvii.xlix. Plutarchus in multorum Vitis, præsertim Pyrrhi, Hannibalis, & Fabij Maximi: Iustinus ex Trogi lib.iii. Silius Italicus lib.xi. & xv. Valerius Maximus lib.xii.cap.ii. Auctor de VV. Illustribus cap.xxv. xliii. lxv. L. Florus lib.i. cap.xviii. Augustinus lib.i. de Civit. Dei, cap.vi. Orosius lib.iii.cap.i. & seqq. Blondus lib.vi. & xxv. Histor. Sabellicus lib.iv. Ennead.viii. rerum gestarum amplitudine & gloria longe superaret: magnis bellis patratis cum Messapus & Lucanis itemque cum Romanis; quibus quum imparem se videret, Pyrrhum Epirotarum Regem in auxilium vocavit: quo superato, ab Romanis occupata, dein proditione capta ab Hannibale, ac non ita multo post ab Q. Fabio Maximo recepta, tandem Populi Romani Colonia est facta. Ab eo tempore Imbelle esse coepit, ut etiam Horatius appellat, cui & Molle dicitur. Byzantinis deinde Imperatoribus diu paruit usque ad Saracenorum Incursiones, qui Italiam fere totam occuparunt. Quibus postea ejectis in Principum suorum (ex quibus Vrsini fuerunt, gente Romana oriundi) moxque Regum Neapolitanorum fuit potestate. Quis posteriore seculo Tarentum, potentissimam quondam Urbem everterit, & in eam redegerit speciem, qua nunc est, ut Castellum videatur in peninsula tribus lateribus conclusa mari, non facile dixerim. Urbs enim exigua admodum hodie, si ad Veteris amplitudinem conferatur. Postrema in parte, qua continentem spectat, ubi prisca Urbs erat, Arx visitur munitissima, marinis cincta Aquis, nuper ab Ferrando Arogonio primo Neapolitanorum Rege refecta. Celebrarunt ortu suo hanc Urbem cum alij, tum Archytas Pythagoricus, diu Civitatis Principes, qui Platonem, quum mortem ipsi machinaretur Dionysius Tyrannus, per epistolam eripuit, ut auctor est lib.viii. Laertius. De eo Hieronymus ad Paullinā. Ortus etiam hinc Aristoxenus, qui celebrem Philosophiæ Scholam Mantinææ diu habuit, & prælatum sibi ab Aristotele Theophrastum perique tulisse dicitur. De eo Sudas. Tarentini quoque fuerunt Nicomachus Mathematicus, qui de Arithmetica & Musica scripsit, Lucitus Philosophus celeberrimus, Heraclides Musicus. Alios, nam innumeri sunt, præterea Neptunum Tarenti Custodem vocat Horatius in Oda ad Architam Tarentinum. Herculeum nominat Tarentum Virg.lib.iii. Æneidos. Servare apud se D.Cataldi, Urbis quondam Antistitis, ossa adfirmant Incolæ. Hodie Archiepiscopatus floret dignitate. Extra Tarentum haud procul Ædicula subterranea visitur: Fama regionem tenet ab D. Petro Apostolo factam: cum, enavigato mari, primum hic in terram egressum: hincque Romam iter arripuisse. Ager Tarentinus, qui rerum omnium fertilis, Salem generat, quem Plinius lib.xxxi.cap.vii. uti suavissimum candidissimumque, præ ceteris generibus commendat. Ab Varrone Mel Tarentinum laudatur. Macropius lib.iii. Sat. Nucem Tarentinam adeo fragili esse putamine, ac ita mollem scribit, ut vix attrectata rumpatur. Favorinus Nuces item & Oves molles Sabinorum lingua Tarentinas vocari dixit. Lanas mollissimas in Agro Tarentino provenire constat cum ex aliis, tum Martiale Poëta. Respicit eo Persius Satyra ii. Calabri Velleris faciens mentionem. Et affirmat Varro Oves ibi pellibus tegi solitas, ne Lana inquinaretur. Porrum Tarentinum nominant Martialis & Plinius lib.xv. Ficus etiam Tarentinas laudat idem, ut & Castaneas. Purpuram item Ager Tarentinus producit, quæ ab loco Tarentina vocatur.
units.tr: Finally, the most ancient and noblest city in that region is Tarentum. Why should it not be celebrated with many encomia by the ancient writers? Most call it Tarentum; Appian of Alexandria, in book 5, calls it Ταράντ [Tarant]; Strabo, in book 6, and Ptolemy call it Τάραντ [Tarant], a mistake which Abraham Ortelius writes is found among his own copies. Today it is Taranto. Servius testifies that Virgil calls it Oebalia, and Ovid calls it Scopas; but Philargyrius notes that Oebalia is the citadel of Tarentum. Pliny in book 3, chapter 11, Lucius Florus, and Orosius in book 3, chapter 1, hold that it was founded by the Lacedaemonians; Solinus says by the Heraclidae; Antiochus says by the Cretans; and that it was named after one of their leaders, Taras. Others think it was named after the river Tarentum, which flows past the city, five miles from it. Some, among them Varro, derive the name from a Sabine word meaning soft, whence Horace Flaccus also calls it Molle Tarentum, because, as some say, both nuts and very soft wool are produced in the territory of Taranto. Most make Tarantus, the son of Neptune, the founder of Tarentum, and add that it received its name from him. See Servius on Aeneid 3 and Georgics 4. All make it a city of Calabria, or Magna Graecia; Suidas and Aelian list it among the cities of Sicily in their writings on military matters. I have explained the cause elsewhere. According to Lucius Florus it was once the capital of Calabria and Apulia and of all Lucania. Strabo in book 6, Lucius Florus in book 1, chapter 18, Procopius in book 3 of the Gothic War, and others describe it accurately. Its site is noted at the innermost recess of the gulf, which is called the Tarentine gulf from the city itself, at the very jaws of the Adriatic Sea, as Florus says. The harbour it once had, very large, very beautiful, and very safe, is carefully described by Strabo in book 6. Today it is seen to be blocked by huge rocks, so that it is open only to small boats; I have not read why or by whom this was done. Now the fish in that harbour are very abundant. Also worth reading in Strabo and others is what they say about the ancient citadel there, and the statues and images placed in it, which the Carthaginians and then the Romans carried off. Strabo and others also mention that there was a theatre near the gate and a very splendid stadium; Florus, book 1, chapter 18, Strabo, book 6, and others mention a very spacious forum and a colossus of bronze of the highest workmanship. The citizens are called Tarentini in Latin, Ταραντῖνοι [Tarantinoi] in Greek. Justin writes, from Trogus, that they were called Spurii; Servius on Aeneid 3 notes that they were called Parthenii; the historians, among others Antiochus, give the reason. Stephanus reports that they were called Φαλαντιάδαι [Phalantiadai], from Phalanthus, under whose leadership the Laconians who came there greatly enlarged the founded city. Governed at first by the common people, it became so powerful through such great increases of wealth and strength that it surpassed in extent and glory all the neighbouring peoples. (Strabo in book 6, and in him Ephorus and Antiochus, mention many things that follow; also Herodotus in book 3; Livy in countless places, especially books 9, 12, 13, 14, 15, 25, 27 and 49; Plutarch in the lives of many, especially Pyrrhus, Hannibal and Fabius Maximus; Justin from Trogus, book 3; Silius Italicus, books 11 and 15; Valerius Maximus, book 12, chapter 2; the author of De viris illustribus, chapters 25, 43 and 65; Lucius Florus, book 1, chapter 18; Augustine, De civitate Dei, book 1, chapter 6; Orosius, book 3, chapter 1 and following; Blondus, books 6 and 25 of the Histories; Sabellicus, book 4 of Ennead 8.) Having waged great wars with the Messapians and the Lucanians, and likewise with the Romans, against whom it saw itself unequal, it called in Pyrrhus, king of the Epirots, for help. When he was defeated, it was occupied by the Romans, then taken by treachery by Hannibal, and not long after recovered by Quintus Fabius Maximus; at last it became a colony of the Roman People. From that time it began to be unwarlike, as Horace also calls it, and it is also called soft. Afterwards it obeyed the Byzantine emperors for a long time, until the incursions of the Saracens, who occupied almost all of Italy. When these had been driven out, it came under the power of its own princes (among whom were the Ursini, of Roman stock), and soon after under the kings of Naples. I could not easily say in what later century it was overthrown and reduced to the condition it now has, so that it looks like a castle on a peninsula enclosed on three sides by the sea. For the city today is very small, if it is compared with the size of the old one. In the last part, which faces the mainland, where the ancient city stood, there is seen a very strongly fortified citadel, surrounded by sea waters, recently restored by Ferdinand of Aragon, the first king of Naples. Among others, Archytas the Pythagorean, for a long time a leader of the city, made this city famous by his birth; he rescued Plato by a letter when Dionysius the Tyrant was plotting his death, as Laertius reports in book 8. Jerome writes about him to Paulina. Aristoxenus also came from here; he held a famous school of philosophy at Mantinea for a long time, and is said to have preferred Theophrastus to himself, as Aristotle did. Suidas writes about him. The Tarentines also included Nicomachus the mathematician, who wrote on arithmetic and music, the very famous philosopher Lucitus, and the musician Heraclides. Of the others, for there are countless, Horace in his Ode to Archytas of Taranto calls Neptune the guardian of Tarentum. Virgil in Aeneid book 3 calls Tarentum Herculean. The inhabitants affirm that the bones of St Cataldus, once bishop of the city, are kept there. Today the archbishopric flourishes in dignity. Not far outside Tarentum is seen a small underground chapel; report holds that the region was evangelised by the Apostle Peter, who, having sailed across the sea, first landed here and from here set out on his journey to Rome. The territory of Tarentum, which is fertile in all things, produces salt, which Pliny in book 31, chapter 7, commends above other kinds as the sweetest and whitest. Varro praises Tarentine honey. Macrobius in book 3 of the Saturnalia writes that the Tarentine nut has so thin a shell, and is so soft, that it breaks when hardly touched. Favorinus said that nuts, and also sheep, which are soft, are called Tarentine in the Sabine language. It is established that the softest wool comes from the territory of Tarentum, as shown by other writers and by the poet Martial. Persius alludes to this in Satire 2, mentioning the Calabrian fleece. Varro affirms that the sheep there were customarily covered with skins, so that the wool would not be soiled. Martial and Pliny in book 15 name the Tarentine leek. The same author also praises Tarentine figs, and likewise chestnuts. The territory of Tarentum also produces purple, which is called Tarentine from the place.

units.la: Florus lib.1. cap.xviii.
units.tr: Florus, book 1, chapter 18.

units.la: CAPVT XXIX. Samnites.
units.tr: CAPVT XXIX. Samnites.

units.la: REGIONES, quæ in Prisca Propriaque Italia versus Orientem ad Mare Tyrrhenum, qua potui diligentia percurri: peragrandæ succedunt, quæ Hadriatico sunt adiacæ Pelago: inter quas Tabula nostra priore loco cis Phiternum Samnitivm aperit agros.
units.tr: Having gone through, as carefully as I could, the regions of ancient and proper Italy that face east toward the Tyrrhenian Sea, I now turn to those that border the Adriatic. Among them our Table first opens the lands of the Samnites on this side of the Phiternus.

units.la: Hos initio, nomine ab Sabinis Progenitoribus per diminutionem deducto, Sabelli sunt dicti; post autem Romanos quidem ab Samnio Monte Samnites cos appellasse, Græcos vero Σαυνίτας, sicut τῶν Σαυνίων, veteres tradunt Scriptores. Strabo lib. v: εἰσὶ δὲ ... Σαυνίτας δὲ ... ὡς οἱ Ἕλληνες Σαυνίτας καλοῦσι. Sic enim legendum cum Cl. V. Casaubono. Vulgati libri perpetuo, quod mirum, Σαυνίτας habent: quod & apud Polybium locis aliquot offendet Lector. Σαυνῖται etiam dicuntur Stephano. Plinius lib. iii cap. xii: Samnitium, inquit, quos Sabellos, & Græci Sauniras dixere. Eustathius in illud Dionysii.
units.tr: These people were at first called Sabelli, a name derived by diminution from their Sabine forefathers. Later the Romans called them Samnites after Mount Samnius, and the Greeks called them Σαυνίτας, as in τῶν Σαυνίων, according to the ancient writers. Strabo, book 5: "They are ... and the Greeks call them Σαυνίτας ..." For so it should be read, with the distinguished Casaubon. The printed texts everywhere, strangely, have Σαυνίτας, and the reader will find the same in several places in Polybius. Stephanus also says Σαυνῖται. Pliny, book 3, chapter 12: "Of the Samnites," he says, "whom they called Sabelli, and the Greeks Sauniras." Eustathius on Dionysius: "The Σαυνῖται ... one ... Mize ..." he says, ... the middle country of the Saunitai ... as the Romans say otherwise; as the writing of Diodorus shows. But whence? Festus indicates it, or Paulus the Deacon from Festus: "The Samnites," he says, "were called after the spears (hastae), which the Greeks call Σαυνία. For they were accustomed to carry these; or from the hill Samnium, where they settled after coming from the Sabines." This must be understood so that the Σαυνῖται are the Greeks' τῶν Σαυνίων, while the Latins called them Samnites after Mount Samnius. On the origin of the Samnites from the Sabines, and on the occasion and cause of their migration from their ancestral seats, read Strabo, book 5, and Pliny, book 3.

units.la: Σαυνῖται δὲ ... μίαν ... Μίζε ... inquit, Συδαερίας μέσην χώραν εἰκεῖν εἰ Σαυνῖται, ὡς ἀλλ' Ἔ μοι Ῥωμαῖοι λέγουσιν: ὡς ἐκ γεαφῆς ἡ Διοδώρου δηλοῖ. Unde autem? Indicat Festus, vel ex Festo Paulus Diaconus: Samnites, inquit, ab Hastis appellati sunt, quas Græci Σαυνία appellant. Has enim ferre adsueti erant: sive à Colle Samnio, ubi ex Sabinis adventantes consederunt. Quæ ita accipienda, ut Σαυνῖται Græcis sint τῶν Σαυνίων, Samnites autem Latinis ab Samnio Monte. De Samnitium ab Sabinis origine, deque Migrationis ex patriis sedibus occasione & causa, legendi Strabo lib. v & Plinius lib. iii. Alii, ut idem Strabo notat, Samnites ab Tarentinis ortos volunt, eosque Παvalas olim vocatos fuisse contendunt. Samnitium ingens olim fuit potentia, quemadmodum passim scribunt Livius, L. Florus, aliique Historiographi. Non enim solum multis populis suum superinduxerunt nomen, verum etiam Populum Romanum continuis fere bellis Victoriisque innumeris fatigarunt: ex quibus illa, quæ ad Furcas Caudinas accepta singularis fuit & omnino memorabilis; qua Romanos, locorum angustia circumventos, sub jugum miserunt: quam tamen ignominiam Romani non ita multo post magna ipsorum clade abolevernt; Samnitibus vicissim sub jugum missis, ipsidemque cum Urbibus & Colonis per Fabios & Papirios fundi-tus
units.tr: Others, as the same Strabo notes, hold that the Samnites were descended from the Tarentines, and insist that they were once called Παvalas. The power of the Samnites was once great, as Livy, Florus and other historians write everywhere. For they not only imposed their name on many peoples, but also wore down the Roman people with almost continual wars and countless victories. Among these, the one at the Caudine Forks was singular and altogether memorable, in which they trapped the Romans, hemmed in by the narrowness of the place, and sent them under the yoke. Yet the Romans wiped out this disgrace not long afterwards by a great slaughter of the Samnites, who in turn were sent under the yoke; and at last the Samnites themselves, together with their cities and colonists, were utterly destroyed by the Fabii and Papirii.

units.la: Ioan. 3. tus tandem exstinctus. Florus lib. 1. cap. xvi Victoriam de hac Gente L. Papirii Cursoris commemorans, addit ea urbium Samniticarum ruinas ita fuisse deletas, ut ætate sua Samnium in loco Samnio requireretur. Prodit postremum memoriæ Strabo, Sullana Dominatione quadam Samnitium Vrbes, mœnibus æquatis, in Vicos redactas, plerasque etiam stirpitus eversas; ut suis videbimus locis. Samnitium Legem in Matrimoniis contrahendis recitat idem Strabo. Fines universi Samnij constituti solent ab Ortu Apuli Daunij cum amne Phiterno; ab Occasu Sabini & Piccentes cum Trento flavio: qua Septemtrio est, Mare Hadriaticum; qua Meridies Picentini, Campani, Marsi, Æquicoli, secundum Apenninum Montem ultra citraque ex parte habitantes. Samnites medios esse inter Picenum, Campaniam & Apuliam, testis est Eutropius libro 11, centesimo fere & tricesimo ab Urbe mulliari. Vicinos Privernatibus scribit Livius lib. viii. Regio summa gaudet cœli salubritate & incredibili Incolarum frequentia: amœna est & commoda versus Mare: sed Montibus aspera in Mediterraneis. Præter alia Crocum abunde nitet, nutritque Animalia innumera, Montes hic nonnulli sunt memorabiles: Ai ucle altissimus Apennino adjacens; & Mons Virginis præcelsus, superansque altitudine sua ipsum Apenninum. Aprutios Regionem ipsam Aprutium, Abruzzo vernacule) hodie vocant Itali; vel, ut augurantur, quod Bruti non sint: vel quod in his quoque sit Præcutini, translato a parte ad totum vocabulo; vel denique ab Montium Saltuumque asperitate, in quibus Apri plerumque apricantur; Vide omnino Iov. Pontanum Histor. lib. 1; ubi Aprutium diligenter suis coloribus delineatur.
units.tr: Ioan. 3. ... was at last wiped out. Florus, book 1, chapter 16, recalling the victory over this people won by Lucius Papirius Cursor, adds that the cities of the Samnites were so thoroughly destroyed that in his own time Samnium was sought in the place where Samnium had been. Strabo, the last to record it, reports that under the domination of Sulla the cities of the Samnites were levelled to their walls, reduced to villages, and most of them uprooted from the ground, as we shall see in their proper places. The same Strabo recites the Samnite law on contracting marriages. The boundaries of all Samnium are usually set: on the east, by the Apulians of Daunia and the river Phiternus; on the west, by the Sabines and the Picentes, with the river Trento; on the north, by the Adriatic Sea; on the south, by the Picentines, Campanians, Marsi and Aequicoli, who live along the Apennine Mountain on both its sides. That the Samnites lay between Picenum, Campania and Apulia is attested by Eutropius, book 11, near the one hundred and thirtieth year from the founding of the City. Livy, book 8, writes that they were neighbours of the Privernates. The region enjoys the highest healthfulness of air and an incredible density of inhabitants; it is pleasant and convenient towards the sea, but rough with mountains in the inland parts. Among other things it abounds in saffron, and it feeds countless animals. Several mountains here are notable: Ai ucle, very high, adjoining the Apennines; and Mount Virgo, very lofty, surpassing the Apennines themselves in height. Italians today call the region itself Aprutium (in the vernacular, Abruzzo), either, as some guess, because the Bruttians are not there, or because the Praecutini are also there, the name being transferred from part to whole, or finally from the roughness of the mountains and thickets, in which boars commonly bask in the sun. See above all Giovanni Pontano, Histor. book 1, where Aprutium is carefully portrayed in its own colours.

units.la: Samnitibus porro nomen magnum aliquando fuit & peramplum. Plinius eorum appellatione comprehendit Ferentanos, cumque iis Carentinos, Peligno, Vestinos, Marrucinos, Pratuttianos, Hirpinos, & vocabulo strictius sumto Samnites. De singulis, ut ad specialiora deveniam, ordine agam; qui sint, quisque ipsis fines, urbes, oppida, aliaque singularia, cum fide diligentiaque explicaturus.
units.tr: Indeed the name of the Samnites was once great and very wide. Pliny includes under their name the Ferentani, together with them the Carentini, the Peligni, the Vestini, the Marrucini, the Pratuttiani and the Hirpini, and, taking the name in a narrower sense, the Samnites. I shall treat each of these in order, as I come to the more particular matters, explaining faithfully and carefully who they are, what their boundaries are, and their cities, towns and other distinctive features.

units.la: Primo loco sunt Frentani. Sic Cæsari in Comment. libro 1, Livio multis locis, præcipue libro xx, ubi de rebus ab ipsis gestis; Silio lib. viii. Plinio lib. iii. cap. xii, & Pomponio Melæ, prope Daunios locanti: Φρεντανοὶ Straboni libro v, Σαυνιτῶν addenti, & Ptolemæo lib. iii, tabula vi: qui Φερεντανοὶ Appiano lib. 1. Φερεντῖνος ἢ Φερεντίνοι, ἐθνικον, inquit Stephanus in voce Φερεντῖνος. Alij sunt, ut discussis Veterum Recentiorumque Scriptorum Monimentis didici, Frentani, alij Ferentinates, alij Ferentini. Frentani, de quibus paullo ante dixi, Samnitium erant Populi. Horum Vrbs, nescio an bene, Φεντράνος Stephano, πόλις Σαυνιτῶν inquiunt, & Ferentinum Veteri ad Horatium Commentatori in Via Labicana ponenti, Φερεντὸν Dionysio Halicarnassæo, & Ferentum Valerio lib. 11, Φερεντὸς Diodoro libro x x. Ferentinates Latij erant, notantibus Livio lib. xxxiv & Plinio lib. iii natur. histor. cap v Eorum Vrbs item Φερεντινὸν Ptolemæo, qui Hernicis Latij Populis tribuit. Ferentinum item Livio variis locis, Horatio, Silio, Frontino, Antonino, Itinerariæ Tabulæ, Commentatoribus, quem dixi, qui tamen Campaniæ adscensi, propter vicinitatem: Φερεντῖνον Stephano ex Strabonis lib. v, ubi tamen hodie Φερεντίνο, ut & in Manuscripto Frontino. Et hinc Ferentina Aqua meminit Livius lib. 1. Ferentini denique Etruriæ Populi Plinio & Veteri Lapidi; quorum Vrbs Φερεντία Ptolemæo, in Falisci locanti; Ferentinum Plinio lib. iii cap. v; Suetonio in Othone cap. 1, Aurelio Victori in Othone, Commentatoriano, & Frontino; Φερεντῖνον Strabonis. Iam ad quos horum referendi Φραγεντῖνοι, ἐθνικον Ἰταλίας, apud Stephanum, nondum video. Hæc de variis his Populis habebam ego: adscribam, non reprehendendi, sed committendi gratia, quæ Roma mittit ad Ortelium suum Celtus Cittadinus: Similitudo Nominis inter Frentanos seu Ferentanos & Ferentinates & Ferentinos ansam præbuit Librariis errandi in Scriptura & confundendi hæc Nomina. Frentani itaque seu Ferentani sunt Populi Samnitium, vulgo uno communi nomine Abruzzezi appellati, inter Hirpinos & Marracinos. Ferentinates sunt Populi Hernicorum, quorum Oppidum Sedem Episcopalem habet, & Ferentino penultima gravi appellatur, in Campagna di Roma est in Via Latina supra collem inter Anagniam & Frusinonem. Latine dicitur Ferentinum prima brevi & reliquis dactylo. Horatius Epist. xvii lib. 1 Ferentini fuerunt Etruriæ Populi, & illorum Vrbs Ferentium sive Ferentia, Patria Othonis Imp. Suetonio, Tacito & alys. Erat inter Viterbium, Montem Soractem, Balneoregium & Faliscos. Hodie ex ea tantum Ecclesia superest, vocaturque hodie locus Ferento, sic pronunciato, ut antepenultima attollatur, reliqua deprimantur. De his consulendi etiam Hermolaus Barbarus ad iii Plinii cap. v, Sigonius ad ix Livii, Caesar Baronius in Martyrologio ad xiiii Mai. Frentanos ab Opido prope Teanum Apuliae Frentano denominat Petrus Marius ad librum Silij Italici viii. Eos autem Ptolemaeus (quem sequi statuimus in Finibus regundis) his Limitibus includunt ab Oriente Phiterno fluvio vel Apulia Daunia ab Occidente Saro Amne, & Pelignis (Plinius ad Aternum fluvium producit, ut ipsius aetate latius haec gens videatur patuisse, quam a Ptolemaeo describatur) a Septentrione Sinu Adriatico; ab Meridie denique Apennino, ubi Plinius Carentinos etiam recenset in Supernates & Infernates divisos; qui cum Frentanis solent explicari. Καρκυλωι forte Ptolemaeo; & sic etiam nonnulli legunt apud Plinium, cujus haec sunt verba libro iii. cap. xii: In ora Ferentanorum a Triferno Flumen Trinium portuosum: Opida Histonium, Buca, Ortona, Aternus Amnis. Intus Auxani, cognomine Frentani, Carentini Supernates & Infernates, Lanuvium. Horum igitur & reliquorum, quae ad Frentanos, explicationem jam dabo.
units.tr: First come the Frentani. So Caesar in his Commentaries, book 1; Livy in many places, especially book 20, where he discusses the deeds done by them; Silius, book 8; Pliny, book 3, chapter 12; and Pomponius Mela, who places them near the Daunians; Φρεντανοὶ in Strabo, book 5, adding them to the Samnites; and Ptolemy, book 3, table 6. Appian, book 1, calls them Φερεντανοί. "Φερεντῖνος or Φερεντίνοι, an ethnic," says Stephanus under the word Φερεντῖνος. Some writers, as I learned after examining the records of ancient and recent authors, say Frentani, others Ferentanates, others Ferentini. The Frentani, of whom I spoke a little earlier, were a people of the Samnites. Their city, I do not know whether rightly, Stephanus calls Φεντράνος, "a city of the Samnites"; and Ferentinum is given by the ancient commentator on Horace, who places it on the Via Labicana; Φερεντὸν by Dionysius of Halicarnassus; Ferentum by Valerius, book 2; Φερεντὸς by Diodorus, book 20. The Ferentinates were of Latium, as Livy, book 34, and Pliny, book 3, chapter 5, of his Natural History note. Their city is likewise Φερεντινὸν in Ptolemy, who assigns it to the Hernici of Latium. Ferentinum is also mentioned by Livy in various places, by Horace, Silius, Frontinus, Antoninus, the Itinerary Table, and the commentators I have mentioned, though these are assigned to Campania because of their proximity; Φερεντῖνον in Stephanus, from Strabo, book 5, where, however, today it reads Φερεντίνο, as also in the manuscript of Frontinus. And from this Livy, book 1, mentions the Ferentine Water. Finally, the Ferentini were a people of Etruria, according to Pliny and an ancient inscription; their city is Φερεντία in Ptolemy, who places it among the Falisci; Ferentinum in Pliny, book 3, chapter 5; in Suetonius, Life of Otho, chapter 1; in Aurelius Victor, Life of Otho; in the commentator Cruquius, and in Frontinus; Φερεντῖνον in Strabo. As to which of these the Φραγεντῖνοι, an ethnic of Italy, in Stephanus, should be referred, I do not yet see. I have given these details about the various peoples; I add, not to criticise but to entrust them to judgement, what Celtis Cittadinus has sent from Rome to his Ortelius: "The similarity of name between the Frentani or Ferentani and the Ferentinates and Ferentini has given scribes an occasion to err in writing and to confuse these names." Therefore the Frentani or Ferentani are a people of the Samnites, commonly called by one common name the Abruzzesi, lying between the Hirpini and the Marrucini. The Ferentinates are a people of the Hernici, whose town has an episcopal see; its name is pronounced with the penultimate syllable heavy, Ferentino, and it lies in the Campagna di Roma on the Via Latina above a hill between Anagni and Frosinone. In Latin it is called Ferentinum, with the first syllable short and the rest dactylic. Horace, Epistles, book 1, letter 17. The Ferentini were a people of Etruria, and their city Ferentium or Ferentia, the native place of the Emperor Otho, according to Suetonius, Tacitus and others. It lay between Viterbo, Mount Soracte, Bagnoregio and the Falisci. Today only a church survives from it, and the place is called Ferento, pronounced with the antepenult raised and the rest lowered. On these matters one may also consult Ermolao Barbaro on Pliny, book 3, chapter 5; Sigonius on Livy, book 9; and Cesare Baronio in the Martyrology for 14 May. Petrus Marius, on Silius Italicus, book 8, derives the Frentani from a town near Teanum in Apulia, Frentano. Ptolemy, whom I have decided to follow in fixing the boundaries, encloses them within these limits: on the east, the river Phiternus or Daunian Apulia; on the west, the river Saro and the Peligni (Pliny extends them to the river Aternus, so that in his day this people seems to have spread more widely than Ptolemy describes); on the north, the Adriatic Gulf; and on the south, the Apennines, where Pliny also lists the Carentini, divided into Supernates and Infernates, who are usually explained together with the Frentani. Perhaps Καρκυλωι in Ptolemy; and so some also read in Pliny, whose words in book 3, chapter 12, are these: "On the coast of the Ferentani, from the Trifernus, the river Trinius, with a harbour; the towns Histonium, Buca, Ortona, the river Aternus. Inland, Auxanum, surnamed Frentanum; the Carentini Supernates and Infernates; Lanuvium." I shall now give an explanation of these and of the rest that pertain to the Frentani.

units.la: Primus Frentanorum a Phiterno in ora est Campus Martinus. Deinde Opidulum Terminus; Termine vel Termole vulgo: Docti, Latine scribentes, Termulas appellant: situm in peninsula, firmitate Moenium, naturaque Loci bene munitum: Ducatus habet dignitatem.
units.tr: The first town of the Frentani on the coast, after the Fortore, is Campus Martinus. Next is the small town Terminus, called Termine or Termole in the vernacular; scholars who write in Latin call it Termulae.
