It lies on a peninsula, is well fortified by its walls and the natural strength of the site, and has the dignity of a duchy.

units.la: Intus milie passibus a Phiterno, millibus octo ab Mari Castellum est Guillinia-cum: & altius pari intervallo Guarda, Alfenia dicta: supra quam, Luparia, Lupara; Cargaboratum: Carga Botazzo; Lucisum, Lumefanum, Castellum Pinianum, Rocketa, Casale Reparandum, Lubinetum, Tornaquisium.
units.tr: Inland, a mile from the Fortore and eight miles from the sea, is Guillinia-cum. A little higher up, at the same distance, is Guarda, called Alfenia. Above it lie Luparia (Lupara), Cargaboratum (Carga Botazzo), Lucisum, Lumefanum, the castle of Pinianum, Rocketa, Casale Reparandum, Lubinetum and Tornaquisium.

units.la: Ultra Botanum Civitas doctis Bovianum dicta: de qua post.
units.tr: Beyond Botanum is the city which the learned call Bovianum, of which more later.

units.la: Rursus in ora post Termulas, Amnis ostium Triny, quem Portuosum appellat, ut audivimus. Plinius.
units.tr: Again on the coast, after Termulae, is the mouth of the river Trinius, which Pliny calls Portuosum, as we have heard.

units.la: Ab eo laeva millibus iiii, totidemque ab mari Castellum visitur Mons Niger: tum supra Castelluttum; & Arx Vivaria, cum nobili Opido Trivento, Comitatu Episcopatuque Titulo insigni. Hoc quidam Τάτιων esse volunt apud Ptolemaeum. Sed de ea nos in Apulia Daunia.
units.tr: Four miles from it on the left, and as many from the sea, is seen Mons Niger. Then above it are Castelluttum, the citadel of Vivaria, and the noble town of Trivento, with a county and a bishopric of distinguished title. Some want this to be the Τάτιων [Tation] of Ptolemy. But we shall treat of that place in Apulia Daunia.

units.la: Altius offerunt sese Salcitum, Fossa Sicca, Baniolum & Civitas Nova.
units.tr: Higher up present themselves Salcitum, Fossa Sicca, Baniolum and Civitas Nova.

units.la: Inter Trinium & Afinellam Opidula sunt primum in ora Monasterium D. Stephani: tum intus Turinum, Casale, Burdinum, Polustrum, Sernium, Casalangra, Pelicornum, inque ora ad Afinellam Opidum Penna.
units.tr: Between the Trinius and the Afinella, along the coast, are small towns: first Monasterium S. Stephani; then inland Turinum, Casale, Burdinum, Polustrum, Sernium, Casalangra and Pelicornum; and on the coast at the Afinella the town of Penna.

units.la: Aliud inde se offert pernobile Guastum Amonium, vernacule Guasto di Amone. Plinio Melaque Histonium. Ιστονιον Ptolemaeo sine aspiratione: ut & Istonium Tabulae Itinerariae. Histonensis Municipij meminit Antiqua Inscriptio apud Vrsinum in Imaginibus Virorum Illustrium. Histonienses scribuntur (vitiosius fortean Sculptoris culpa: nisi velimus inemendatiores esse, quod non videtur, Plinium & Ptolemaeum, Cives in Antiquo Lapide, qui hodieque ibidem:
units.tr: Next there appears the very famous Guastum Amonium, in the vernacular Guasto di Amone. Pliny and Mela call it Histonium; Ptolemy writes Ιστονιον [Istonion] without the aspirate, as does the Itinerary Table with Istonium. An ancient inscription in Ursinus's Images of Illustrious Men mentions the Histonian municipality. The people are written Histonienses, perhaps more faultily through the carver's fault, unless we want to say (which does not seem right) that Pliny and Ptolemy were less accurate. The citizens are named on an ancient stone which is still there today:

units.la: L. VALERIO. L. F. PRVDENTI
units.tr: L. VALERIUS, SON OF LUCIUS, PRUDENS

units.la: HIC. CVM. ESSET. ANNORVM XIII. ROMAE. CERTAMINE IOVIS. CAPITOLINI. LVSTRO SEXTO. CLARITATE. INGENII CORONATVS. EST. INTER POETAS. LATINOS. OMNIBVS SENTENTIIS. IVDICVM HVIC. PLEBES. VNIVERSA HISCONIENSIVM. STATVAM AERE. COLLATO. DECREVIT
units.tr: HERE, WHEN HE WAS THIRTEEN YEARS OLD, AT THE CONTEST OF THE CAPITOLINE JUPITER IN THE SIXTH LUSTRUM, BY THE BRILLIANCE OF HIS GENIUS, HE WAS CROWNED AMONG THE LATIN POETS, THE JUDGES' VOTES BEING UNANIMOUS. THE WHOLE PEOPLE OF THE HISTONIENSES DECREED HIM A STATUE IN BRONZE, FUNDS HAVING BEEN COLLECTED.

units.la: Supersunt hic quædam antiquorum operum, Theatri cum primis & Prætorij veftigia. Marchionatus habet Titulum.
units.tr: There remain here some traces of ancient works, especially of a theatre and a praetorium. The place has the title of a marquisate.

units.la: Intus deinde juxta flumen Asinellam modicum Castellum est Mons Dorifius, Monte Dorife. Comitatus titulo clarum: utraque Amnem fontem versus Gessum; Campino, Campignano; Vasilea, Gelinum, Tripalum.
units.tr: Further inland, beside the river Asinella, is the small castle of Mons Dorifius, Monte Dorife, famous for its title of county. Toward the source of the river, both are Gessum, Campino (Campignano), Vasilea, Gelinum and Tripalum.

units.la: Cis Sarum porro in Frentanis fuisse olim Opidum, quod Ptolemæo Ἀνξανον, cuiusque Incolæ Plinio Anxani cognomine Frentani, indicant ejusdem Ptolemæi Tabulæ: Pstura tamen, ut sæpe, corruptiore, quæ ultra Sarum collocat in Pelignis. Falluntur enim, qui Anxanum cis Sarum olim positum fuisse contendunt, ubi hodie Lanciamum trans eundem fluvium. Fieri tamen potuit, ut ob interitum Anxani conditum remotiore loco fuerit Lancianum, de quo infra. Alia sane exempla nobis, si prolixioribus esse liceret, novarum Vrbium, longissimis intervallis ab Veterum, quarum illæ nomen acceperunt, ruinis distantium, non desunt. Anxanum fuisse arbitror, ubi nunc Palictum, aut circiter, ad dextram Sari ripam.
units.tr: Moreover, on this side of the Sangro, there was once in the land of the Frentani a town which Ptolemy calls Ἀνξανον [Anxanon], and whose inhabitants Pliny calls Anxani, with the surname Frentani. The tables of the same Ptolemy indicate this, though the text there is corrupt, as often happens, and places it beyond the Sangro among the Peligni. Those who maintain that Anxanum once stood on this side of the Sangro, where Lanciamum stands today across the same river, are mistaken. It could, however, be that Lancianum, of which more below, was founded in a more distant place because Anxanum had been destroyed. Other examples of new cities, separated by long distances from the ruins of the old ones from which they took their names, are not lacking, though I would have to be more lengthy to give them. I think Anxanum was where Palictum now is, or near it, on the right bank of the Sangro.

units.la: Fuit etiam cis Sarum Frentanorum Opidum, quod, ut antea dixi, Φερετὸν Diorylio Halicarnassæo; Ferentum, Valerio Maximo lib. 11; Φέρεντα, Diodoro lib. xix; Ferentinum, Veteri ad Horatium Commentatori; Φερεντῖνος denique Stephano, πόλις Σαυνιτῶν addenti. Quidam male locant ubi Franca-Villa prope Ortonam, quæ in Pelignis.
units.tr: There was also on this side of the Sangro a town of the Frentani which, as I said before, is called Φερετὸν [Fereton] by Diorylus of Halicarnassus; Ferentum by Valerius Maximus, book 2; Φέρεντα [Ferenta] by Diodorus, book 19; Ferentinum by the old commentator on Horace; and finally Φερεντῖνος [Ferentinos] by Stephanus, who adds that it was a city of the Samnites. Some wrongly place it where Franca-Villa stands near Ortona, which is in the land of the Peligni.

units.la: Vlterius ad Maiellæ montis, de quo alibi, radices Palumbarium est: & in montano jugo supra ad Pinna Opidum, Saro propinquum, cuius meminit Silius lib. viii: juxta Sarum dein ad ejus dextram Atissa, Tornaticumque Castella.
units.tr: Further on, at the foot of the Maiella mountain, of which we speak elsewhere, is Palumbarium. On the mountain ridge above is the town of Pinna, near the Sangro, which Silius mentions in book 8. Next to the Sangro, then, on its right, are the castles of Atissa and Tornaticum.

units.la: Sub Sari in Apennino Fonte Opida sunt Asserulum, Pescum, Opum, Vallis Regia, Civitella, Rocca.
units.tr: Below the source of the Sangro in the Apennines are the towns Asserulum, Pescum, Opum, Vallis Regia, Civitella and Rocca.

units.la: Trans Amnem deinde antiquissima Caracenorum, ut Ptolemæus indicat, Vrbs Aufidena Livio, Antonino, Itinerariæ Tabulæ memorata: Ἀυφιδηνα Ptolemæo, Vi captam ab Cn. Fulvio Cos. scribit Livius libro x. Hinc Aufidenates Plinio. Coloniam Romanam facit Onuphrius.
units.tr: Beyond the river, next, is the most ancient city of the Caraceni, as Ptolemy indicates: Aufidena, mentioned by Livy, Antoninus and the Itinerary Table. Ptolemy calls it Ἀυφιδηνα [Aphidena]. Livy, book 10, writes that it was taken by force by Gnaeus Fulvius, consul. From it come the Aufidenates of Pliny. Onuphrius makes it a Roman colony.

units.la: In Frentanis hinc mare versus ad Sarum vestigia reperiuntur Vrbis antiquæ, inquit Leander, Sari, quemadmodum adhuc vocatur locus Sari huius nescio an quis Veterum meminerit.
units.tr: In the land of the Frentani, toward the sea from the Sangro, traces of an ancient city are found, says Leander, at a place still called Sari; I do not know whether any of the ancients mentions it.

units.la: Supra est Palictum Opidum ob superiorem urbem deletam, ut idem sentit Leander, ædificatum. Sane haud procul inde Anxanum fuisse, antea dixi.
units.tr: Above it is the town of Palictum, built, as Leander also thinks, because the upper city was destroyed. Indeed, I said before that Anxanum was not far from there.

units.la: Altius secundum Sari alveum Mons Planus, editissimus ex Apennino oriens adspicitur; in cuius declivitate supra Sarum Arca est Opidum: aliaque in eodem Monte hæc: Bemia, Colmetium, Transf Rivum, Mons Ferrandus, & Petra Ferracina: deinde trans Fontem Amnis supra Petram Ferracinam Castellum Pilum, Civitasque Bucellum, & Pescolanum Penatarium: item ad D. Angelum Pescolanum, S. Angelo di Pescoli, cum Opido Iudico, Giudice, cunis superbiente Iacobi Caldora Domini, cuius facta describunt Blondus, Sabellicus, Corius, alij.
units.tr: Higher up, along the bed of the Sangro, is seen Mons Planus, the highest peak rising from the Apennines. On its slope above the Sangro is the town of Arca. Also on the same mountain are these: Bemia, Colmetium, Transf Rivum, Mons Ferrandus and Petra Ferracina. Then, across the river's source above Petra Ferracina, are the castle of Pilum, the city of Bucellum, and Pescolanum Penatarium; likewise at S. Angelo, Pescolanum (S. Angelo di Pescoli), with the town of Iudicum (Giudice), proud of the cradle of Jacopo Caldora, lord of it, whose deeds Blondus, Sabellicus, Corius and others describe.

units.la: Flexu hinc lævorsum in arduo difficilique Monte Castellum succedit Capracotta: & in intima valle prope Montem Maiellam aliud pernobile Agnonium, Agnone, vel, ut alijs scribitur, Angluna: quod nonnullis (inter quos Leander & Niger) putatur Aquilonia, ab Livio memorata libro x, ubi scribit, L. Papirio cos. cum Samnitibus bellum gerente, eosdem ad Aquiloniam omnem exercitum indixisse, militemque collectum ibi sacramento diroque carmine in exsecrationem sui Capitis jurare coactum: ita Legionem millium xvi, quum vir virum legisset, effectam, dictamque Linteatam. Secus sentit Celsus Cittadinus, cujus hæc ad Ortelium verba: Errat Leander, credens Aquiloniam fuisse, ubi nunc est Agnone: nam Agnone est in Frentanis prope Pelignos; Aquilonia autem Ptolemæo erat in Hirpinis, media inter Beneventum, Luceriam & Avellinum. Errat etiam Niger: nam Angelone est Vrbs Episcopalis in finibus Lucania & Brutiorum: quantum mea conjectura valet, putarem Aquiloniam fuisse, ubi nunc Laquedonia Latine, vulgo Lacedogna, Vrbs Archiepiscopalis in Hirpinis,
units.tr: From here, bending to the left, on a steep and difficult mountain, the castle of Capracotta comes next; and in a deep valley near Mount Maiella, another very noble town, Agnonium (Agnone), or, as others write it, Angluna. Some (among them Leander and Niger) think this is Aquilonia, which Livy mentions in book 10, where he writes that when Lucius Papirius was consul and waging war with the Samnites, the Samnites summoned their whole army to Aquilonia, and the soldiers who were gathered there were forced to swear by a solemn oath and a dreadful formula, calling down a curse on their own heads; so that a legion of 16,000 men was formed by each man choosing another, and it was called the Linteata. Celsus Cittadinus thinks otherwise; his words to Ortelius are these: "Leander is wrong in believing that Aquilonia was where Agnone now is, for Agnone is in the land of the Frentani near the Peligni; but Aquilonia, according to Ptolemy, was among the Hirpini, midway between Beneventum, Luceria and Avellino. Niger is also wrong: for Angelone is an episcopal city on the borders of Lucania and the Bruttii. As far as my conjecture is worth anything, I would think Aquilonia was where Laquedonia now is, in Latin, and in the vernacular Lacedogna, an archiepiscopal city among the Hirpini."

units.la: Succedit D. Petrus Avellanus, & alia deinceps circa Sarum Opida: quorum in Pelignis commemoratio.
units.tr: Next comes St Peter Avellanus, and then other towns around the Sangro, whose mention belongs among the Peligni.

units.la: De Buca & Ortona, quas Frentanis adnumerat Plinius: ego, Ptolemæum sequutus, in Pelignis dicam. Nam ampliores Plinius Frentanis tribuit limites ad Aternum usque extendens, quam Ptolemæus, qui Sarum non transilit.
units.tr: About Buca and Ortona, which Pliny counts among the Frentani, I shall speak among the Peligni, following Ptolemy. For Pliny gives the Frentani wider boundaries, extending them to the Aternus, than Ptolemy does, who does not cross the Sangro.

units.la: De Lanuensibus etiam Plinianis nihil habeo, quod addam.
units.tr: Concerning the Lanuenses of Pliny I have nothing to add.

units.la: Frentani Carentinique vel Caraceni jam explicatis succedunt ex Ptolemæi notatione Peligni. Sic Latinis dicuntur. Πελίγνοι Straboni & Ptolemæo; Πελιγνοι autem male, inquit Ortelius, apud Memnonem: qui Pælna nunc vulgo, uti tradit Ciofanus in Sulmonis Urbis descriptione Pælnensi, ut Leander notat. Prosectos huc quidam scribunt ex Illyrico ductu Vollinii Regis Lucullı: ei duos fuisse Nepotes Pacinum & Pælnum; ab hoc Pelignos, ab illo nomen accepisse Pacinates. Vide Festum. Fortissimæ Pelignorum gentis meminerunt nulli: non Veteres Scriptores, cum primus Livius. Later Pelignorum appellatio in quibusdam huius Regionis locis, Palena, Forca di Palena, Leto di Palena: quin totus Ager Pelignorum hodie corrupte Palena dici perhibetur. Peligni ab Oriente Flumen est Sarus, cum Frentanis Caracenisque; ab meridie, Vestini ab Occidente, Amnis Aternus cum Marrucinis; ab Septemtrione Sinus Adriaticus. Acrem Pelignum nominat Silius lib. viii Belli Punici. De his ita Plinius lib. iii cap. xii: Pelignorum Corfinienses, Superaequani, Sulmonensis.
units.tr: After the Frentani and Carentini, or Caraceni, now explained, comes the people which Ptolemy calls the Peligni; so they are named in Latin. Πελίγνοι [Peligni] in Strabo and Ptolemy; but Πελιγνοι [Peligni], Ortelius says, is a wrong form in Memnon. Today the town is commonly called Pælna, as Ciofanus reports in his description of the city of Sulmo, "Pælnensi," as Leander notes. Some write that the people came here from Illyria, led by Vollinius, king of the Lucullians; that he had two grandsons, Pacinus and Pælnus, and that the Peligni got their name from the one, and the Pacinates from the other. See Festus. None of the old writers mentions this very brave nation, except Livy, who is the first. The name Pelignorum survives in some places in this region: Palena, Forca di Palena, Leto di Palena; indeed the whole territory of the Peligni is said to be called Palena today, in a corrupted form. The Peligni have the Sangro as their eastern river, with the Frentani and Caraceni; to the south are the Vestini; to the west the river Aternus, with the Marrucini; to the north the Adriatic gulf. Silius, book 8 of the Punica, names them "the sharp Peligni." Pliny, book 3, chapter 12, says of them: "the Corfinienses, Superaequani and Sulmonenses of the Peligni."

units.la: Quod ad specialiora Pelignorum loca, juxta fontem Sari, ad Septemtrionaliorem ejus ripam Scontronum est cum Valle Regia: subjectisque locis parum ab amnis alveo D. Maria Quinque Millium; supraque Arx Quinquemilium, de cinque miglia.
units.tr: As for the more particular places of the Peligni: beside the source of the Sangro, on its northern bank, is Scontronum with Valle Regia; in places a little below the river's bed is S. Maria Quinque Millium; and above it the citadel of Quinquemilium, "de cinque miglia."

units.la: Propinqua Rasio Amni, de quo alibi, Arx Rasini est, Rocca de Rasino.
units.tr: Near the river mentioned elsewhere, the Rasio, is the Arx Rasini, Rocca de Rasino.

units.la: Mare versus incedenti ad Sarum prope littus Cænobium occurrit D. Ioannis, ubi quondam celeberrima Veneris ædes fuisse fertur: Supraid Fossa Casa, cum Arce D. Ioannis.
units.tr: Going from the coast towards the Sarus, near the shore, you meet the Cænobium of D. Ioannis, where a very famous temple of Venus is said to have once stood. Above it are the Fossa Casa, with the Arce D. Ioannis.

units.la: Paullo altius ad eundem amnem vestigia cernuntur antiquæ urbis, quæ Buca Plinio, Frentanis adnumeranti, quod huc usque Frentanorum fines ipsius & Strabonis ætate, extenderentur, qui contractiores postea facti. Βῶκα Straboni, ἡ αὐτὴ Φρεντανων: Bucara Pomponio Melæ. Βάκα Ptolemæi eandem esse cum Buca reliquorum, quod Villanovanus censet, non puto; quum supra Iltonium inter Sarum & Phiternum eam Ptolemæus collocet; Fucam autem reliqui inter Sarum & Aternum: vel, ut propius accedam, inter Sarum & Ortonem.
units.tr: A little higher up the same river, traces of an ancient city can be seen. Pliny, who counts it among the Frentanis, calls it Buca. The Frentani extended their territory this far, both in Pliny's time and in Strabo's, though their borders were later reduced. Strabo calls it Βῶκα, which is the same as the Frentani's. Pomponius Mela calls it Bucara. I do not think, as Villanovanus holds, that Ptolemy's Βάκα is the same as the Buca of the others, since he places it above the Iltonius, between the Sarus and the Phiternus. The others place Fucam between the Sarus and the Aternus, or, to be more exact, between the Sarus and the Ortonus.

units.la: Ad Aventini Amnis initium oppidum est Furea cognomine di Palena, Palena, quasi Peligna, quod ortu suo illustravit Nicolaus Furcanus, Eremita, ante annum c l. Lege Blondum.
units.tr: At the source of the Aventinus stands the town Furea, surnamed di Palena, Palena, as if it were Peligna. Nicolaus Furcanus, a hermit, made it famous by his birth, about 150 years ago. Read Blondus.

units.la: Sunt etiam hoc situ Castella Letum Palenæ & Palenum; in quis, uti dixi, Peligno-rum memoria adhuc videtur conservari.
units.tr: In this same region are the villages Letum Palenæ & Palenum, in which, as I said, the memory of the Peligno-rum still seems to survive.

units.la: Visuntur ad Sarum oppida Altinum, Arx Scalonia, Scalogna; Geffum; Turricella, Pinna Hominis, Penna di Huomo, Mons Niger, cum vico Bona-Notte, Buona Notte, ubi Pons qui Sari ripas iungit: Mox Mons Labianus, Falum; altiusque in editissimis montis faucibus Lnparilla, munitum natura oppidum. Supra hinc Quartum; Muferatum, Gambatarium, Petra, Ausonia: Post ad ripam Aventini, qua Viridem excipit, Casale Oppidum: altiusque ad alteram ripam Collis Macina cum Falasculo.
units.tr: Along the Sarus are the towns Altinum, Arx Scalonia, Scalogna; Geffum; Turricella, Pinna Hominis, Penna di Huomo, Mons Niger, with the village Bona-Notte, Buona Notte, where a bridge joins the banks of the Sarus. Next come Mons Labianus, Falum, and higher up, in the steep gorge of the mountain, Lnparilla, a town fortified by nature. Above here are Quartum; Muferatum, Gambatarium, Petra, Ausonia. Afterwards, on the bank of the Aventinus where it receives the Viridis, is the town of Casale, and higher up, on the other bank, Collis Macina with Falasculum.

units.la: Ad Radices Maiellæ, supra Viridis amnis egressum duo sunt oppidula Civitella & Lama.
units.tr: At the foot of the Maiella, above the outflow of the Viridis, are two small towns, Civitella & Lama.

units.la: In Borealiore Maiellæ Montis latere Campus est, cui nomen La Pianura della Rocca, Rupis Planities: ubi opida frequentia, Pescum, Constantium, Rivus Sonulus.
units.tr: On the northern side of the Maiella is a plain called La Pianura della Rocca, Rupis Planities, where there are many towns: Pescum, Constantium, Rivus Sonulus.

units.la: Inde peracta difficilique Via in Planiciem devenitur Quinque Millium, sic a Quinque Millium passuum longitudine, quam habet, appellatam, in Superaequanis Pelignis valde celebrem, æstivo tempore amœnam, hieme deformem & periculosam.
units.tr: From there, by a difficult road that has been travelled, you come down to the plain of Quinque Millium. It is named after the length of Quinque Millium passuum (five miles) that it covers. It is very famous in the Superaequanis Pelignis, pleasant in summer, but in winter ugly and dangerous.

units.la: Sed relictis montibus, ad Littus redeo. Hic in ora Civitas est antiqua Ortona. Sic Plinio hodieque dicitur, quæ Ὠρτῶν Ptolemæo & Straboni, cui Ἐπίνειον Φρεντανῶν. Idem etiam Ὧλον vocat, Prædonibus & Piratis infestum. Servare se gloriantur Cives in augusta æde D. Thomæ Apostoli reliquias. Adpellunt huc Naves ex Epiro, Dalmatia aliisque partibus, Merces ad Lanciani mercatum deferentes.
units.tr: But, leaving the mountains, I return to the coast. Here on the shore is the ancient city of Ortona. Pliny still calls it that today. Ptolemy and Strabo call it Ὠρτῶν, and Strabo also calls it Ἐπίνειον Φρεντανῶν. He also calls it Ὧλον, and it was troubled by pirates and robbers. The citizens boast that they keep relics of St Thomas the Apostle in their magnificent church. Ships come here from Epirus, Dalmatia and other regions, bringing goods to the market at Lanciano.

units.la: Non procul ab Ortona opidum est Franca-Villa; ubi Blondus & alij Vrbem Frentanum fuisse opinantur. Sed de ea nos supra.
units.tr: Not far from Ortona is the town of Franca-Villa, where Blondus and others think the city of Frentanum stood. But we have spoken of it above.

units.la: Introrsum dein Majellam versus Givianum, Aretium, Arevacrum; supraque haec Opida Casa Candidella: tum altius ad D. Martinum, Falletum, & alia. Hinc inter Morum Amnem & Ortonam sunt Gracum, & altius Ariellum, Orsonia, Ad D. Apollinarem, Frisium. Castellum Novum Lanciani, vulgo Lanzano Novo. Dein supra Mori initia duobus fere p. M. Opidum est Guardagallum, Guarda di Gallo.
units.tr: Further inland, towards the Maiella, are Givianum, Aretium, Arevacrum, and above these towns Casa Candidella. Then higher up, D. Martinum, Falletum, and others. From here, between the Moro river and Ortona, are Gracum, and higher up Ariellum, Orsonia, Ad D. Apollinarem, Frisium. Castellum Novum Lanciani, commonly called Lanzano Novo. Then, above the sources of the Moro, about two miles away, is the town of Guardagallum, Guarda di Gallo.

units.la: Prope Felerinum Amnem in littore Castellum est D. Viti Lanciani: medioque hoc intervallo Civitas vulgo Lanciamum, P. M. ab Saro iv, totidemque distans ab Ora, ob Anxani fortean interitum aedificatum. Celebre est Emporium: quo quotannis mensibus Maio & Augusto Italiae, Illurici, Siciliae, Graeciae, Asiae, & reliquarum Mundi Partium Negotiatores ad frequentissimum conveniunt Mercatum. Urbs Archiepiscopum habet, cui nullos subesse Episcopos lego.
units.tr: Near the Felerinus river, on the coast, is the castle of D. Viti Lanciani. Midway between this and the sea lies the city commonly called Lanciamum, four miles from the Sarus and as far from the shore. It was perhaps built after the destruction of Anxani. It is a famous trading centre, where merchants from Italy, Illyricum, Sicily, Greece, Asia and other parts of the world meet every year in May and August for a very crowded market. The city has an archbishop, to whom, as far as I know, no bishops are subject.

units.la: In ora dein ad Fori Amnis ostium Tullonum est: supraque Militanicum & altius Farum ulterius Rapinum; Opidumque Maiellae propinquum Pinna; Penna vulgo.
units.tr: Next, at the mouth of the Foro river on the coast, is Tullonum. Above it are Militanicum, and higher up Farum, and further on Rapinum. There is also the town Pinna, commonly called Penna, near the Maiella.

units.la: Sequitur inde Lentum Flumen, ad cujus ripam Borealem P. M. ab mari v Villa Maina occurrit: supra quam sub Maiella Praetorium est opidum: juxta id Arx Montis Plani; supraque fontem Lenti amnis Castellum Menale; intra in Mediterraneis aliud Bucianicum.
units.tr: Next comes the Lentus river. On its northern bank, four miles from the sea, is Villa Maina. Above it, under the Maiella, is the town of Praetorium. Near it is the Arx Montis Plani, and above the source of the Lentus is Castellum Menale. Further inland is another, Bucianicum.

units.la: In Boreali ore Lenti ripa sub Maiella Coenobium est amplissimum cum Fano D. Liberatoris, ubi antiquissima quaedam servantur volumina, Langbardicis litteris exarata.
units.tr: On the northern mouth of the Lentus, on the bank under the Maiella, is a very large monastery with the shrine of D. Liberatoris, where some very ancient books are kept, written in Lombardic script.

units.la: Hinc tum Sulmo Civitas est. Sic Latinis scribitur, Σulmῶν Ptolemaeo: Σάλμων Strabonis libro v. Apellationis origo ab Solymo Phrygio, Ænea Comite. Ovidius lib. iv Fastorum: Huius erat Solymus, Phrygia comes unus ab Ida, A quo Sulmonis moenia nomen habent; Sulmonis gelidi patria, Germanice, nostra: Me miserum Scythico quam procul illa solo est.
units.tr: From here is the city of Sulmo. Thus it is written in Latin; Ptolemy calls it Σulmῶν, and Strabo in book 5 Σάλμων. The name comes from Solymo, the Phrygian, companion of Aeneas. Ovid, Fasti book 4: "Of this man was Solymus, one companion from Ida in Phrygia, from whom the walls of Sulmo have their name. Sulmo, the cold homeland of Germanicus, is ours; alas, how far away it is from me, on Scythian soil."

units.la: Sic Silius de bello Poenico libro ix: Huic domus & gemini fuerant Sulmone relicti Matris in uberibus Nati, Mancinus & una Nomine Rhetaeo Solymus: nam Dardana origo, Et Phrygio genus a proavo, qui sceptra secutus Aenea claram muris fundaverat urbem; Ex sese dictam Solymon; celebrata colonis Mox Italis paulatim attrito nomine Sulmo.
units.tr: So Silius, in book 9 of the Punic War: "For him there were a home and twin sons left at Sulmo, Mancinus and Solymus, of one name with Rhaetus, sons nursed at one mother's breast. Their origin was Dardanian, and their race Phrygian from their great-grandfather, who, following the sceptre of Aeneas, had founded the famous city with walls; from himself it was called Solyma, and it was celebrated by its colonists. Soon, by the Italians' gradual wearing down of the name, it became Sulmo."

units.la: Hodie Sulmona est, teste Leandro: aliquibus male Sermona dicitur, notante Ciofano, in pulcherrima huius Urbis descriptione. Septem ab Corfinio P. M. distare scribit Caesar. Urbs est pulchritudine loci, frequentia populi, aquarum abundantia in primis nobilis. Mentionem eius saepe faciunt cum alij, tum Livius, praecipue lib. xxvi. Sulmonenses Plinio noti. Ovidij patria, ipso teste lib. iiii Trist. Eleg. x: Sulmo mihi patria est, gelidis uberrimus undis, Millia qui novies distat ab urbe decem.
units.tr: Today it is Sulmona, according to Leander. Some wrongly call it Sermona, as Ciofanus notes in his fine description of this city. Caesar writes that it is seven miles from Corfinium. The city is especially noted for the beauty of its site, the crowds of people and its abundance of water. Many writers mention it, including Livy, especially in book 26. The Sulmonenses are known to Pliny. Ovid's homeland, as he himself says in Tristia book 4, elegy 10: "Sulmo is my homeland, very rich in cold waters, which is ninety miles from the city."

units.la: Inde, quia Sulmo in Pelignis erat, eleganter Martialis i Epig. Nasone Peligni sonant.
units.tr: Because Sulmo was in the land of the Peligni, Martial elegantly says in Epigram 1 about Naso: "The Peligni resound."

units.la: Et alibi ipse Alumnus: Mantua Virgilio gaudet, Verona Catullo, Pelignae gentis gloria dicor ego. Quem sua libertas ad honesta coegerat arma: Quum timuit socias anxia Roma manus. Atque aliquis spectans hospes Sulmonis aquosi Moenia: qua campi ingera pauca tenent: Qua tantum, dicet, potuisti ferre poetam; Quantulacumque estis vos, ego magna voco. Episcopum habet, qui Valvensis dicitur, quod Sulmonensis ager cum parte quoque vicinorum Valva nominetur. Legendi Blondus & Rassanus. Nobiles ibi sunt Familiæ, non pauce, quæ vulgo: Amone, | de Corbo. | de Ranaldo. d'Aristotile, | de Martino. | Rissa. de Canibus. | de Matteis. | Sarda. de Capite. | Melioratti. | de Sanita. Capograsi. | Merlino | de lo Tinto. Columbino. | Quadraro. | & alii.
units.tr: And elsewhere Ovid himself, the native: "Mantua rejoices in Virgil, Verona in Catullus; I am called the glory of the Peligni people, who, when anxious Rome feared her allied forces, had been driven by their freedom to honourable arms. And some stranger, looking at the walls of watery Sulmo, where the fields hold only a few heaps, will say: 'Such a poet as you could bear? However small you are, I call you great.'" It has a bishop, called the Bishop of Valva, because the territory of Sulmo, together with part of its neighbours, is called Valva. Read Blondus and Rassanus. There are not a few noble families there, commonly called Amone, de Corbo, de Ranaldo, d'Aristotile, de Martino, Rissa, de Canibus, de Matteis, Sarda, de Capite, Melioratti, de Sanita, Capograsi, Merlino, de lo Tinto, Columbino, Quadraro, and others.

units.la: Iuxta flumen, quod Sulmone provolvitur, oppidum est Pratula, Abbatiæ S. Spiritus fratrum Cælestinorum. Sequitur aliud Popului, oppidum perhonestum, prope quod Aternus ligneo ponte transitur; ubi Arx utramque fluminis ripam supra modum munit. Ibidem pons fuisse videtur tribus à Corfinio P. M. de quo Cæsar lib. 1 bell. Civ. cuiusque mentio apud Lucanum lib. 11 & Strabonem libro v, quem à Corfinio distare scribit xxiiii stadiis.
units.tr: Beside the river that flows past Sulmo is the town of Pratula, of the Abbey of the Holy Spirit of the Celestine brothers. Next comes another, Popului, a very handsome town, near which the Aternus is crossed by a wooden bridge. There a citadel fortifies both banks of the river exceedingly well. Here there seems to have been the bridge three miles from Corfinium, of which Caesar writes in book 1 of the Civil War, and which Lucan also mentions in book 2. Strabo, in book 5, writes that it is twenty-four stadia from Corfinium.

units.la: Incedenti per Planciem tribus à Populo P. M. occurrunt Veteris Corfinij vestigia, quæ nunc Campi de S. Petrino, vel, ut aliter, Pentinia. Meminit honeste corfini Strabo libro v, Vestinos, Marsos, Pelignos, Marrucinos, & Frentanos ob negatum ius Civitatis à Populo Rom. defecisse: itaque bellum intulisse Sociale, memorans; quo Corfinium Peligorum caput (μητρόπολις inquit Strabo, Caput Imperij Velleius) omnibus Italis communis Civitas appellata, Italiaque (Ἰταλία vitiose legitur apud Diodorum) novo nomine dicta, ubi Arx & Propugnaculum belli contra Romanos esset, ubi & in conventibus Imperatores deligebantur. Bellum hoc Marsicum dictum est, quod biennio amplius duravit, donec Civitatis Romanæ jus iis Populis concederetur. Corfinium, Livio, Cæsari, Lucano, Silio, aliis; Κορφίνιον Diodoro, Appiano, Straboni, Ptolemæo: Ὀφέινιον Dionysio Halicarnassæo fere esse putat Fr. Sylburgius. Corfinates Plinio. Scribit ad Ortelium Celsus Cittadinus, Corfiny hodie nihil remanere, quam Vicum cum Ecclesia & paucis Domibus, vulgoque appellari S. Petrino. Ingentium Aedificiorum ruinas passim ibi cerni, addit Leander.
units.tr: Going across the plain, three miles from Popului, you find the remains of old Corfinium, which are now the fields of San Petrino, or, as others call them, Pentinia. Strabo in book 5 mentions corfini with honour: when the Vestini, Marsi, Paeligni, Marrucini and Frentani revolted from the Roman people because citizenship had been refused them, they waged the so-called Social War. He says that Corfinium, the capital of the Paeligni (which Strabo calls μητρόπολις, and Velleius the capital of the empire), was made a city common to all Italians and that Italy (Ἰταλία, wrongly read in Diodorus) got its new name there. It was the stronghold and bulwark of the war against the Romans, and the generals were chosen there at assemblies. This war is called the Marsian War, because it lasted more than two years, until Roman citizenship was granted to those peoples. Corfinium is the name used by Livy, Caesar, Lucan, Silius and others; Κορφίνιον by Diodorus, Appian, Strabo and Ptolemy. Fr. Sylburgius thinks that Dionysius of Halicarnassus almost certainly wrote Ὀφέινιον. Pliny calls its people the Corfinates. Celsus Cittadinus writes to Ortelius that nothing of Corfinium remains today except a village with a church and a few houses, which is commonly called San Petrino. Leander adds that the ruins of huge buildings can be seen everywhere there.

units.la: A Populo deinde, si Majellam versus pergas quarto fere milliari prope Aternum amnem, Toccum est: & post in mediterraneis Cantalupum circa montis pedem, ubi Oleum Petronicum colligitur. Haud procul Lucus est, paulloque altius in Aterni ripa Castellum Turris; & ad confluentes Rafentam & Ortam, de quibus alibi, Caramanicum, Antonij Monachi Prædicatoris fama inclutum. Supra sub Maiella Arx Morisii est; paulloque inferius Cusanum.
units.tr: From Popoli you go toward the Maiella, and about four miles from there, near the river Aterno, lies Toccum. Further inland, at the foot of the mountain, is Cantalupo, where Petronian oil is collected. Not far off is a grove, and a little higher on the bank of the Aterno lies Castello Turris. At the confluence of the Rafenta and the Orta (of which elsewhere) is Caramanico, famous for the reputation of the preaching friar Antonio. Above, under the Maiella, is the fortress of Morisio, and a little lower down, Cusano.

units.la: Haec intus sunt; ad oram revertor. Edito in Colle ab Mari vii P. M. Urbs est Archiepiscopalis, quæ vulgo Chieti, vel Civita Chieto. Sic Leander, Collenutius & Nigerhodie vocari scribit, quæ Teatia Straboni & Ptolemæo. Teatinos habet Plinius: Teates Apulos Livius lib. viii. Marrucinum hanc urbem tribuunt Strabo & Ptolemæus: velle videntur idem Plinius Siliusque lib. viii. Marrucina simul Frentanis æmula pubes Corfini populos magnumque Teate trahebat.
units.tr: So much for the inland places; I return to the coast. On a hill seven miles from the sea stands the archiepiscopal city commonly called Chieti, or Civita Chieti. Leander, Collenuccio and Niger write that this is what it is called today; Strabo and Ptolemy called it Teatia. Pliny has the Teatini, and Livy in book 8 has the Teates Apuli. Strabo and Ptolemy assign this city to the Marrucini, and Pliny and Silius in book 8 seem to agree: "The Marrucine youth, rivals of the Frentani, drew with them the peoples of Corfinium and great Teate."

units.la: Item Statius ad Marcellum de Vesuvij Conflagratione:
units.tr: Likewise Statius, to Marcellus, on the eruption of Vesuvius:

units.la: Necdum letale minari Cessat Apex: procul ista tuis Tifata, Teate, Nec Marrucinos agat hac insania montes.
units.tr: Nor does the peak yet cease to threaten deadly destruction. Far from your Tifata, Teate, let this madness not drive the Marrucine mountains.

units.la: Sic apud Antoninum Teate Marrucinum; & corrupte in Itineraria Tabula Tea Nomaructnoccio, ubi legendum Teate Marucinorum; nisi sit Teanum Marucinorum. Mirum, quum Teate in Australiore Aterni sit ripa, ubi inter eundem Aternum & Sarum, ex notatione ipsius Ptolemæi, Pelignorum fuit Sedes, quam Marrucinos eam tribuant Tabulæ, ad Septentrionalem Aterni ripam habitantibus: nisi velimus Teatea Marucinorum diruta, aliam cognominem in Pelignorum agris fuisse conditam. Quidquid sit, urbem hanc à Pipino Karoli Magni Patre eversam legimus, quod rebus Langbardicis perpetuo studuisset; restauratam vero postea adeo Normannis ob amoenitatem loci placuisse, ut sedem hic potissimum collocarent, auctore Blondo.
units.tr: So in Antoninus, Teate of the Marrucini; and corruptly in the Itinerary Table, Tea Nomaructnoccio, where one should read Teate Marucinorum, unless it is Teanum Marucinorum. It is strange, since Teate lies on the southern bank of the Aterno, where, between the same Aterno and the Sagrus, by Ptolemy's own indication, was the seat of the Paeligni, whom the Table assigns to the Marrucini, who lived on the northern bank of the Aterno. Unless we suppose that the Teatea of the Marrucini was destroyed and another city of the same name was founded in the territory of the Paeligni. Whatever the case, we read that this city was overthrown by Pepin, father of Charlemagne, because he had been constantly active in Lombard affairs; but that later, when it was restored, it so pleased the Normans for the pleasantness of the site that they chose it as their chief seat, according to Biondo.

units.la: De Superaquanis, quos Pelignorum populos nominat Plinius, nihil habeo quod dicam; cum; nisi quod Super Equam oppidum etiam notum sit libro Limitum: quod, ubi fuerit, ignoro.
units.tr: About the Superaquani, whom Pliny names as a people of the Paeligni, I have nothing to say, except that the town Super Equam is also known from the book of Limites. Where it was, I do not know.

units.la: Fuit haud procul Teate in ostio fluminis Aterni oppidum cognomine Aternum, Livio lib. xx. x & Antonino notum. Strabo etiam Aternum oppidum cum flumine eiusdem nominis, Piceno vicinum, memorat. Hodie ibi Pescara est, exiguum castellum, a quo fluvio etiam nomen, de quo alibi.
units.tr: Not far from Teate, at the mouth of the river Aterno, there was a town of the same name, Aternum, known to Livy in book 20 and to Antoninus. Strabo also mentions the town Aternum, with the river of the same name, neighbouring Picenum. Today Pescara stands there, a small castle, from which the river also takes its name, of which more elsewhere.

units.la: Pelignis ablatus, Vestinos videamus. Vestini Latinis, ὀ Οὐεστῖνοι Strabonis, Οὐεστῖνοι Ptolemæo. Eorum frequens apud Livium, Appianum, Florum, aliosque mentio. Hinc Vestina Juventus Silio celebratur lib. viii. Vestinus Cascus Martialis. De Vestinis sic Plinius lib. iii cap. xi: Vestinorum Angulani, Pinnenses, Peltuinates, quibus iungUntur Aufinates Cismontani. Confinales huic genti signare solent Geographi ex Ptolemæi tabulis aliisque Scriptoribus a Septentrione Pelignos, ab Ortu Samnites specialius iuntos, qua Meridies est, Campaniæ Latinæque populos, qua Occidens, Præcutinos, Marsos, & Sabinos. Fecit autem, ut semel hoc dicam, eorum vicinitas, ut Loca, quæ Vestinorum, ab Auctoribus nunc Sabinis, nunc Campanis, nunc alius adscribantur: quemadmodum parebit in Amiterno, Pinna, Angelo: & hinc Vestinorum designatio nonnullos esse solet difficultatis.
units.tr: Having left the Paeligni, let us look at the Vestini. The Vestini in Latin; Ouestinoi in Strabo, Ouestinoi in Ptolemy. They are frequently mentioned in Livy, Appian, Florus and others. Hence the Vestina Juventus is celebrated by Silius in book 8, and Vestinus Cascus by Martial. Pliny speaks thus of the Vestini in book 3, chapter 11: The Vestini Angulani, Pinnenses, Peltuinates, to whom the Aufinates Cismontani are joined. Geographers, following Ptolemy's tables and other writers, usually mark this people's neighbours: to the north the Paeligni, to the east the Samnites more particularly, to the south the peoples of Campania and Latium, and to the west the Praecutini, the Marsi and the Sabines. Their proximity, to say this once for all, means that places belonging to the Vestini are ascribed by authors now to the Sabines, now to the Campanians, now to others, as will appear in the cases of Amiternum, Pinna and Angelus. For this reason the delimitation of the Vestini is often a source of some difficulty.

units.la: Ut singularia oi diar cum primis locus apud eos, ubi olim Amiternum, nunc maximarum ædium ruinis horridus. Amiternum Livio, & Plinio. Ἀμίτερνον Hacarnassæo lib. ii, Straboni v, Ptolemæo. Amiternum Samnitium urbs est apud Livium lib. x. Strabo Emporium nominat Frentanorum; Vestinus adcenset Ptolemæus; Satini tribuit Dionys. Halic. Plinius etiam Amiternos habet inter Sabinos. Sabinorum forte an fuit antiquissimis temporibus, quæ postea Samnitium; &, ut specialius dicam, Vestinorum facta. Amiternum perpetuo montis insidebat dorso, ubi hodieque fundamenta ostenduntur magnorum Operum, Theatri præcipue & Templorum aliquot; ex quibus, quam ampla fuerit, facile iudicare Spectator potest. Laurentius Ananiensis Pescara ex eo facit. Amiternum, inquit Baptista Fonteius in Cæsia Familia, quod diruta Aquilam urbem auxit. Hinc Amiterni Plinio, qui Amiternini Livio & M. Terentio Varroni, qui sic dictos notat, quod circum Aternum flumen habitarent. A Sp. Consule quondam expugnatam, cæsis Samnitium cIↄ cIↄ ICCC, captisque cIↄ cIↄ cIↄ cIↄ CCXXC, auctor est Livius lib. xi, qui & Amiternos cum Umbris, Nursinis & Reatinis, L. Scipioni in Africam ituro militaria suppeditasse auxilia commemorat. Amiterna cohors legitur apud Virgilium lib. vii & Silium Italicum lib. viii. Ortu suo nobilitarunt cum alij, tum Sabinus Crispus & Victorinus, Martyr sub Nerone, Urbis Episcopus. Amiternum Agrum civiusque Napos celebrat Martialis in Apophoretis: Nos Amiternus Ager fecundus educat hortis: Nulla fines potens parvus esse rapas,
units.tr: To take the particulars first: the place among them where Amiternum once stood, now grim with the ruins of great buildings. Amiternum in Livy and Pliny; Amiternon [Ἀμίτερνον] in Dionysius of Halicarnassus in book 2, in Strabo in book 5, and in Ptolemy. Amiternum Samnitium is a town in Livy, book 10. Strabo calls it an emporium of the Frentanorum; Ptolemy counts it among the Vestinus; Dionysius of Halicarnassus assigns it to the Satini. Pliny also places the Amiternos among the Sabinos. Perhaps in the most ancient times it was Sabinorum, afterwards Samnite, and, to be more specific, made Vestinorum. Amiternum sat on the ridge of a mountain, and even today the foundations of great works are shown there, especially a theatre and several temples; from these a spectator can easily judge how large it was. Laurentius of Anagni derives Pescara from it. Amiternum, says Battista Fonteio in the Caesian family, which, when destroyed, enlarged the city of L'Aquila. Hence the Amiterni in Pliny, who are called Amiternini by Livy and by M. Terentius Varro, who notes that they were so called because they lived around the river Aternum. Livy in book 11 reports that it was once taken by a consul, Spurius, with 2,300 Samnites slain and 4,220 captured. He also records that the Amiternos, together with the Umbrians, Nursini and Reatines, supplied military aid to L. Scipio when he was going to Africa. The Amiterna cohors is read of in Virgil, book 7, and in Silius Italicus, book 8. Others ennobled it by their birth, such as Sabinus Crispus and Victorinus, martyr under Nero and bishop of the city. Martial in the Apophoreta celebrates the Amiternum Agrum and its citizen turnips: The fertile Amiternian field raises us in its gardens; we are small turnips, yet powerful, knowing no bounds.

units.la: Flumen ex Amiterno facit Pomponius Sabinus ad librum vii Æneid. quod Vestinos & Marrucinos, a sinistra habet, supra sunt Pelligni: ex Livii proculdubio loco, qui libro xxiv, male intellecto, ubi auctor scribit, Flumen Amiterni cruentum fluxisse: quæ verba quid velint, vel pueri norunt.
units.tr: Pomponius Sabinus, on book 7 of the Aeneid, makes the river from Amiterno, which has the Vestinos and Marrucinos on its left, while the Paeligni are above it. He surely took this from the passage of Livy in book 24, which he misunderstood, where the author writes: The river of Amiternum flowed bloody. What these words mean even boys know.

units.la: Quinto ab Amiterni Ruderibus lapide alto in monte iacet Episcopalis Urbs Aquila, nunc huius tractus Caput, ab Sulmone xxx P. M. versus Apenninum sita. Natam volunt ex Amiterni ruinis & Forconij, quod P. M. viii hinc abeeat, altero latere contra Amiternum, versus Piscariam amnem; qui locus nunc quoque magna operum fundamenta ex lapide quadrato habet, appellatus Forconum. Condidisse autem perhibent Aquilam Langbardos; Karolum inde Martellum, vel, ut aliis placet, Fridericum ii Imperat. mœnibus cinxisse, munisseque; Colonis Civium jure, & Civitati Aquila nomine attignato ab signo Cæsareo, vel potius ab fausto Aquila nomine. Ea autem brevi maximis incrementis ita auxit, ut Civitatum reliquarum principatum in hac regione facile nunc obtineat. Ab Ludovico Montorio Comite aliquamdiu fuit possessa sub auspiciis Ferrandi Aragonum regis. Hodie in ditione est Philippi Regis Hispaniarum. De eius conditione, primordio, nominis ratione, rebusque gestis plura Raffanus, Blondus, Leander, Collenutius lib. iii Hist. Reg. & Iovianus Pontanus lib. v Hist. Colitur ab Civibus D. Bernardini, Minorum Ordinis Monachi, Corpus. Claruit Aquila ante paucos annos Ioanne Aquilano Prædicatore, Scriptis claro. Ager mira cum aliarum rerum, tum Croci copia est fœcundus.
units.tr: Five miles from the ruins of Amiternum, on a high mountain, lies the episcopal city Aquila, now the capital of this district, situated thirty miles from Sulmo towards the Apennines. They think it was born from the ruins of Amiternum and of Forconium, which is eight miles from here, on the other side opposite Amiternum, towards the river Pescara. That place still has large foundations of square stone and is called Forconum. They say that Aquila was founded by the Lombards; then Charles Martel, or, as others prefer, Emperor Frederick II, surrounded it with walls and fortified it, settling colonists with citizens' rights, and the city was named Aquila from the imperial eagle, or rather from the auspicious name of the eagle. It grew so quickly, with great increases, that it can now easily hold the primacy among the other cities of this region. For some time it was held by Count Lodovico Montorio under the auspices of Ferrante, king of Aragon. Today it is under the rule of Philip, king of Spain. More about its condition, origin, the reason for its name and its deeds is given by Raffanus, Biondo, Leander, Collenuccio in book 3 of the Histories of the Kings, and Giovanni Pontano in book 5 of the Histories. The citizens venerate the body of St Bernardino of the Order of Minor Friars. Aquila flourished a few years ago through the preacher John of Aquila, famous for his writings. The land is fertile in a remarkable abundance of other things, and of saffron.

units.la: Subter fontem dein Aterni in Apennino Mons Regalis est: nec procul inde Pyrus fastigiata, de qua nonnihil capite de Fluminibus, ubi de Aterno.
units.tr: Below the source of the Aterno, in the Apennines, is Mons Regalis; and not far from there is Pyrus fastigiata, of which something in the chapter on rivers, where the Aterno is discussed.

units.la: De Peltuinatibus & Aufinatibus Cismontanis, Vestinorum Populis, apud Plinium, nihil habeo quod dicam; nisi Peltuinos etiam nominari in antiquo Lapide, qui in Aulario Lipsij ad Smetij Inscriptiones. De Angolanis & Pinnensibus, quos Vestinis idem Plinius concenset, nos iam nunc in Marucinis.
units.tr: About the Peltuinatibus and the Aufinatibus Cismontanis, peoples of the Vestinorum in Pliny, I have nothing to say, except that the Peltuinos are also named in an ancient inscription in the Aularium of Lipsius, among the Inscriptions of Smetius. About the Angolanis and Pinnensibus, whom the same Pliny counts among the Vestinis, we shall now turn to the Marucinis.

units.la: Hi enim Vestinis succedunt explicandi. Marucini Cæsari, Livio, Statio, aliisque Latinis scriptoribus dicuntur; Μαρούκινοι Straboни; Μαρούκινοι Ptolemæo: qui Marrucini Plinio, Teatinos adsignantes; cuius rei vestigia, sed corruptissima, etiam deprehendo in Itineraria Tabula; ubi, ut antea indicavi, sic legitur, Tea Nomarucinoceto: emendandum Teate Marucinorum: Μαρούκινοι Diodoro. Corrupte μαρούκινοι apud Memnonem, inquit Ortelius. Marrucini, ut Ptolemæus & alij delineant, ab ortu sunt Peligni cum Aterno; ab meridie Vestini & Præcutini; ab occasu Piceni cum Truento; ab Septemtrione Adria. Res ab iis gestas memorat Livius libro ix, ubi Marrucinos, Marsos, Pelignos & Frentanos pacem amicitiamque Populi Romani impetrasse scribit.
units.tr: For the Marrucini come next to be explained after the Vestini. The Marrucini are mentioned by Caesar, Livy, Statius and other Latin writers; Marroukinoi in Strabo; Marroukinoi in Ptolemy. They are the Marrucini in Pliny, who assigns Teatinos to them. I also detect traces of this, though very corrupt, in the Itinerary Table, where, as I indicated before, it reads Tea Nomarucinoceto, which should be emended to Teate Marucinorum. Diodorus has Marroukinoi. Ortelius says that marroukinoi is corrupt in Memnon. The Marrucini, as Ptolemy and others delineate them, are bounded on the east by the Paeligni along the Aterno, on the south by the Vestini and Praecutini, on the west by Picenum along the Truentus, and on the north by the Adriatic. Livy in book 9 records their deeds, where he writes that the Marrucinos, Marsos, Pelignos and Frentanos obtained peace and friendship with the Roman people.

units.la: Particularis sequitur delineatio, capto ab arduis circa Piscariam vel Aternum montibus initio. In adscensu igitur illorum sunt Ratanum, Vertorium, Carapellum, mediterranea. Tum infra duobus ab Aterno millibus Capistranum est; inter alia duo Castella Offenum & Buxum (Supo) ad amnem, qui vulgo Capo d' Acqua, situm.
units.tr: A detailed description follows, beginning at the steep mountains around the Piscaria and the Aternus. Going up along them are Ratanum, Vertorium and Carapellum, inland towns. Then, two miles below the Aternus, is Capistranum. Between two other small castles, Offenum and Buxum (Supo), lies a river commonly called Capo d' Acqua.

units.la: Dein ad Piscariam sunt Cajatio, Turris Antonelli, Petrancum, Alardum, & Rosanum.
units.tr: Then, along the Piscaria, are Cajatio, Turris Antonelli, Petrancum, Alardum and Rosanum.

units.la: Sub Nuriæ, Aterno se commiscentis, fonte Monasterium est Casa Nova, ædificiorum pulchritudine, reditibusque amplissimis nobile.
units.tr: Below the spring of the Nuria, where it joins the Aternus, is the monastery of Casa Nova, noted for the beauty of its buildings and its very rich revenues.

units.la: Ad Septemtrionaliorem Nuriæ ripam oppida sunt Cambaronum, Planellum, Musconum, Mons Silvanus, & Spoletorium.
units.tr: On the northern bank of the Nuria are the towns Cambaronum, Planellum, Musconum, Mons Silvanus and Spoletorium.

units.la: Inter Tanum porro & Sinum amnes, media prope regione, iv ab ora P. M. Civitas Penne, Civitas Penne, nobile & antiquum Opidum. Pinna Ptolemæo; Pinna Silo, Pinnis Paullo Diacono lib. ii Langbardic. cap. xix. Pinnenses Plinio in Vestinis locantur. Meminit eorum & Valerius Maximus.
units.tr: Between the rivers Tanus and Sinus, in a region near the middle, four Roman miles from the coast, is Civitas Penne, Civitas Penne, a noble and ancient town. It is Pinna in Ptolemy, Pinna in Silius, and Pinnis in Paul the Deacon, Lombard History, book ii, chapter xix. Pliny places the Pinnenses among the Vestini. Valerius Maximus also mentions them.

units.la: Non procul dein ab Tavo Lauretum in Collibus adparet, Ducatus insigne titulo; itemque Colle Corvinus.
units.tr: Not far from the Tavus, Lauretum appears on the hills, a place distinguished by its ducal title; likewise Colle Corvinus.

units.la: Ad ripam Tavi dexteram jacent Valvanum, Serra, Corvinianum, Bisentum, Pinianum, Mons Siccus, Casilentum.
units.tr: On the right bank of the Tavus lie Valvanum, Serra, Corvinianum, Bisentum, Pinianum, Mons Siccus and Casilentum.

units.la: Prope Salinum fluvium duobus ab ora milliaribus Opidum Episcopale Portus S. Angeli. Ἀγγέλου est Ptolemæo, ut censent Orlandus, Volaterranus, Blondus, Leander, alij. Angelum, ut quibusdam videtur, Antonini. Angulani sunt apud Plinium, in Vestinis eos ponentem.
units.tr: Near the river Salinus, two miles from the shore, is the episcopal town Portus S. Angeli. It is Angelou [Ἀγγέλου] in Ptolemy, as Orlandus, Volaterranus, Blondus, Leander and others judge. Some think it is Angelum in Antoninus. The Angulani are in Pliny, who places them among the Vestini.

units.la: Propinquo Plumbæ Amnis loco Castellum jacet Illice: tum intus ad eumdem amnem Celinum, & prope fontem Schiranum: nec procul ab ostio Plumbæ Portus Adriæ, vulgo Porto di Adria, vel, ut alij, Porto de Atri. Ἐπίνειον τῆς Ἀδρίας Straboni, ad Matrinum, qui nunc Plumba, illud locanti. Supra dein, Castellum Silvium est.
units.tr: Near the mouth of the river Plumba lies the castle Illice. Further inland, on the same river, are Celinum and, near its spring, Schiranum. Not far from the mouth of the Plumba is Portus Adriae, commonly Porto di Adria, or, as others say, Porto de Atri. Strabo calls it the port of Adria [Ἐπίνειον τῆς Ἀδρίας], placing it near the Matrinus, which is now the Plumba. Above it is the castle Silvium.

units.la: Plumbam transgressis inter ipsum & Vomanum amnem medio spatio occurrit Adria, vulgo Atri (alia ab ea, quæ in Transpadanis) Urbs Episcopalis: arduo montis inlocata jugo. Adria Livio, Plinio, Melæ, Silio lib. viii, Itinerariæ Tabulæ: Ἀδρία Stephano in Νεαπολιτία & Eustathio. Adriam hanc Plinius vii P. M. ab Mari locat. Livius lib. xi Coloniam agnoscit Romanorum; alibi etiam lib. xxv eius faciens mentionem. Hinc Adriani eidem Livio lib. xxvii. Ortus hinc Adrianus Imperator, ipso teste apud Spartianum. Legendi & Aurelius Victor Paulusque Diaconus, lib. ii. cap. xix, qui imprudenter hanc Urbem confundunt cum ea, quæ in Romanula, de qua suo loco; adferentes inde Adriatico Sinui nomen factum. Non bene. De Adriani tamen Imperatoris Patria alii aliter. Adriani etiam hinc Ager mentio apud Livium lib. xxii & Plinium lib. iii cap. xiii. Plinius, Strabo, Ptolemæus hanc in Piceno collocant, quoniam Matrino amne, ut Strabo vocant & Ptolemæus, vel, ut Plinius, Helvino, vel, ut hæc ætas, Plumba Trætutia nam Regionem finiri, & Picenum incipere tradunt.
units.tr: Crossing the Plumba, midway between it and the river Vomanus, you come to Adria, commonly Atri (not the one in Transpadane Italy), an episcopal city set on the ridge of a high mountain. Adria is named by Livy, Pliny, Mela and Silius (book viii) and in the Itinerary Table; Stephanus (under Neapolitis) and Eustathius call it Adria [Ἀδρία]. Pliny, book vii, chapter 3, places this Adria on the sea. Livy, book xi, recognises it as a Roman colony, and mentions it again in book xxv. Hence the Adriani in Livy, book xxvii. The Emperor Hadrian came from here, as he himself says in Spartianus. Aurelius Victor and Paul the Deacon, book ii, chapter xix, should also be read; they carelessly confuse this city with the one in Romagna, which I will discuss in its place, and they derive the name of the Adriatic Sea from it. That is wrong. Opinions differ about the homeland of the Emperor Hadrian. The Adriani territory is also mentioned by Livy, book xxii, and Pliny, book iii, chapter 13. Pliny, Strabo and Ptolemy place this town in Picenum, since they say the region ends and Picenum begins at the river Matrinus (as Strabo and Ptolemy call it), or the Helvinus (as Pliny calls it), or, as this age calls it, the Plumba Trætutia.

units.la: Prætutios igitur subiungamus, quos post agrum Adrianum Adriamque Coloniam & flumen Vomanum nominat Plinius. Prætutium, qui Περιουτία Ptolemæo, Prætutiani alii, ad ortum sunt Vestini, ad meridiem Sabini; qua occatus est, Truentum flumen, qua Septentrio, Maruccini cum Adriatico Sinu. Inde Prætutianus .i.e. Plinio lib. iii cap. xiii. Prætutiana Regio apud Livium lib. xxii, quæ Περιαυτία Stephano, χωρίον aienti & Ἀεργία, de quo ante; addentuque τὰ ἐν τῷ εἰκόνι, Περιπνοαῖος, Περιπνοῖα. Vina Prætutiana nobilitas inter optima gradum habere, notat Plinius lib. xiiii cap. vi.
units.tr: Let us next take up the Praetutii, whom Pliny names after the Adrian territory, the colony of Adria and the river Vomanus. The Praetutium, which Ptolemy calls Περιουτία [Perioutia], and others call the Praetutiani, lies to the east of the Vestini and to the south of the Sabines. It is bounded on the west by the river Truentum, and on the north by the Marrucini and the Adriatic Sea. Hence the Praetutianus, as in Pliny, book iii, chapter 13. The Praetutiana Regio is in Livy, book xxii. Stephanus calls it Περιαυτία [Periautia], a place, as he says, and Aergia, of which I spoke before; he adds the things in the image, Περιπνοαῖος [Peripnoaios] and Περιπνοῖα [Peripnoia]. Pliny, book xiv, chapter 6, notes that Praetutian wines hold a rank among the best.

units.la: Speciatim huius gentis explicemus. Post Plumbam fluvium in ora ostium est Vomani: cui versus Austrum adiident Motula, Mons Vitula, Mons Gualdus: surumque ad fontem amnis, Vici Pagique multi & Castella frequentia: inter quæ Mejanum, Caput Tofium, & Poggium, Opida.
units.tr: Let us now describe this people in detail. After the river Plumba, on the coast, is the mouth of the Vomanus. Towards the south lie Motula, Mons Vitula and Mons Gualdus. Up towards the source of the river are many villages and hamlets and frequent castles, among which Mejanum, Caput Tofium and Poggium are towns.

units.la: Trans Vomanum in ora sexto lapide Turdini Fluminis est ostium.
units.tr: Across the Vomanus, six miles along the coast, is the mouth of the river Turdinus.

units.la: Sunt inter Vomanum & Turdinum Opida multa: quorum ab supremo ad infimum hic fere est ordo; Roseneum, Poggium, Vincretium, Ripes Montoriana (Rocca di Mostorio i Mon o tum, Ferat'um, Collis Vetus, Rapinum, Manum, Forcella, Cantianum, Transmundinum, Castellum Vetus, Castellum Novum, Guardia Vomani, Loccarisinum, & Morum.
units.tr: Between the Vomanus and the Turdinus are many towns. From top to bottom their order is roughly this: Roseneum, Poggium, Vincretium, Ripes Montoriana (Rocca di Mostorio), Monotum, Ferat'um, Collis Vetus, Rapinum, Manum, Forcella, Cantianum, Transmundinum, Castellum Vetus, Castellum Novum, Guardia Vomani, Loccarisinum and Morum.

units.la: Sequitur Amnis Turdinus: inter quem & Viciolam Turdino se miscentem Civitas est Teranum, spatio ab ora x: i P. M. Caput Prætorianorum, Ducatus & Episcopatus titulo clarum. Ab situ Interamnia Plinio, Interamna Ptolemæo.
units.tr: Next is the river Turdinus. Between it and the Viciola, which flows into the Turdinus, is the city Teranum, ten Roman miles from the shore. It is the chief town of the Praetorians and is famous for its ducal and episcopal title. From its site it is called Interamnia by Pliny and Interamna by Ptolemy.

units.la: Ad initium Flumicelli (qui ab Viciola in Turdinum defertur) Castellum est Campium: supraque fontem amnis Burgum Novum & Bisantum.
units.tr: At the source of the Flumicellus (which flows from the Viciola into the Turdinus) is the castle Campium. Above the spring of the river are Burgum Novum and Bisantum.

units.la: Haud procul Turdino circa littus Opidum est fere desertum Flavianum, ubi quondam Urbs, quæ Ptolemæo Κάσπερι Castrum Novum Plinio, Antonino, & Itinerariæ Tabulæ. Reduxit hanc Urbem apud Strabonem libro v, Manus doctissimi Casauboni. Nam pro monstrosis istis, εἰπε ἐκ τρευσῶν, ex quibus nonnulli Flumen fuerunt, restituit, εἰπε Καστρινῶν, quod omnino probo. De eo sic scribit ad Ortelium Celtus Civitatis Anglerius: Appellatum hoc fuit postea Castrum S. Fabiani; & eo diruto ob aeris malignitatem, iussu Iulii Aquaviva, Arrianorum Ducis (vulgo de Atri ex illius ruinis aedificata fuit summitatis eiusdem Ducis Iulia Nova, Opidum in Mediterraneis, ad tertium fere milliarium.
units.tr: Not far from the Turdinus, near the shore, is the almost deserted town Flavianum, where once stood the city which Ptolemy calls Κάσπερι [Kasperi], Castrum Novum in Pliny, Antoninus and the Itinerary Table. The most learned Casaubon restored this city's name in Strabo, book v. In place of those monstrous words εἰπε ἐκ τρευσῶν [eipe ek treusōn], from which some made a river, he restored εἰπε Καστρινῶν [eipe Kastrinōn], which I wholly approve. Concerning it, Celtus Civitatis Anglerius writes thus to Ortelius: "This place was afterwards called Castrum S. Fabiani; and when it was destroyed because of the unhealthy air, by order of Giulio Acquaviva, Duke of the Atri (from whose ruins the town of Atri was built), a new town called Julia Nova was founded on the heights of the same Duke, an inland town about three miles away."

units.la: Parvo hinc intervallo abest Mons Paganus; inque Mediterraneis Mosanum, Ripatonium, Villantium.
units.tr: A short distance from here is Mons Paganus. Inland are Mosanum, Ripatonium and Villantium.

units.la: Salino fluvio ad Meridiem adlocatum est Montorium, titulo Comitatus ornatum.
units.tr: On the south of the Salinus river lies Montorium, adorned with the title of a county.

units.la: Supra Monterium deinde Poggium Morellorum, Poggio de i Morelli; altiusque Troia est,
units.tr: Above Montorium is Poggium Morellorum (Poggio de i Morelli), and higher still is Troia.

units.la: Post in montibus haud procul ab amne, dextra, munitissimum est Opidum Cinitella, super Clivo præalto sita, qua meridiem ex una, ex altera parte Orientem prospectat. Eius descriptio apud Natalem Comitem Historiarum lib. x.
units.tr: Afterwards, among the mountains not far from the river on the right, is the very strongly fortified town Cinitella, set on a very high slope, looking south on one side and east on the other. Its description is in Natale Conti, Histories, book x.

units.la: Iuxta amnem Libratam in dextra sunt Caropeilum & Neretum; in sinistra vero Tuturetum, Ad D. Tomerum, & ad D. Aegidium haud procul a fonte.
units.tr: Along the river Libratus, on the right, are Caropeilum and Neretum. On the left are Tuturetum, Ad D. Tomerum and Ad D. Aegidium, not far from the source.

units.la: Secundum littus ad Truentum properanti locus occurit ubi Opidum D. Floriani erat, superioribus annis ab Iulio, duce Adriano, ob aeris inclementiam subuersum, cui successit eiusdem auspiciis aliud tribus ab ora P. M. Iulia Nova.
units.tr: Hurrying along the coast towards the Truentum, you come to the place where the town of D. Floriani stood. In recent years it was overthrown by Giulio, Duke of Atri, because of the unhealthy air. In its place, under his auspices, another town was built three miles from the shore: Iulia Nova.

units.la: Ad dextram Truenti primum Opidum est Columella. Ductum sequutus Itineris, quod Antoninus describit ab Urbe Mediolanensi per Italiæ longitudinem ad Columnam vel Traiectum Siciliæ, omnino censeo hoc fere loco tuisse ante quam Civitatem Truentum. Accedit & Itineraria Tabula, in qua eodem loco scriptum est, Castro Trentino, vitiose pro Castro Truentino. Nam & Castrum Truentinum habet ibidem M. Tullius lib. viii Epist. ad Atticum. Truentum opidum etiam Plinio Pomponioque notum. Truentinas Turres nominat Silius lib. viii.
units.tr: On the right bank of the Truentum the first town is Columella. Following the route which Antoninus describes from Milan through the length of Italy to Columna or the strait of Sicily, I judge that this place was on the road before the city of Truentum. The Itinerary Table agrees, for in the same place it is written Castro Trentino, wrongly for Castro Truentino. Cicero (M. Tullius), in book viii of his Letters to Atticus, also has Castrum Truentinum there. The town of Truentum was also known to Pliny and Pomponius. Silius, book viii, names the Truentine towers.

units.la: Supra Columellam sunt Contraguerra, Ancharanum, Morrum, Murrumque Trajjinum.
units.tr: Above Columella are Contraguerra, Ancharanum, Morrum and Murrumque Trajjinum.

units.la: Mox ad confluentem cum Truento Castellanum offert sese Asculum, antiquissima Civitas, Episcopatus dignitate nobilis. Asculum quidem Strabo, Plinius & Ptolemæus in Piceno collocant: sed quia ad australiorem Aterni ripam est positum, Picenum autem ad Borealiorem initium capit, malui coeptum sequutus institutum Samnitium concenere. Asculum Cæsari lib. i. Commenta. Silio lib. viii, Livio passim. Ἀσκλὸν Ptolemæo; Ἄσκλον Stephano. Asculum Antonino; Ascu-us Paulo Diacono lib. ii Langobardic. cap. xix. Asculo Piceno in Itineraria Tabula, ob vicinitatem. Plinius nobilissimam Piceni Colonia appellat. Iacet plano patuloque campo, munitissimo in loco, moenibus firmis. Ab una parte Mons sublimis in quo sita est Arx; ab altera Truentus ripis praealtis munit. Res ab Asculanis & contra ipsos gestas describunt Livius libro lxxxi, lxxxvi, & alibi, L. Florus lib. iii cap. xviii alique Scriptores. Imperium Urbis diu Romana Ecclesia tenuit, primumque hic ipsius Domini Temporalis, ut vocant, initium. Asculani fuerunt T. Betutius Barrus, quem omnium extra urbem Romam eloquentissimum appellat M. Tullius in Bruto; Ventidius Bassus, bello Parthico Legionum Romanarum Imperator; de quo cum alij, tum Iuvenalis Sat. vi; Nicolaus iiii P. M; Cæcus, Astrologus quam Poeta, melior; Enoch Orator eloquens, Orationum aliquot & Epistolarum auctor, GratiaDei Theologus & Philosophus, Scriptis itidem clarus: & alij. Aliud est Asculum in Apulia.
units.tr: Soon, at the confluence with the Truentum, a castle presents itself: Asculum, a very ancient city, noted for its episcopal dignity. Strabo, Pliny and Ptolemy indeed place Asculum in Picenum. But since it lies on the southern bank of the Aternus, while Picenum begins on the northern bank, I preferred to follow the starting point of the Samnites and count it among them. Asculum is in Caesar, Commentaries, book i; in Silius, book viii; and in Livy throughout. Ptolemy has Ἀσκλὸν [Asklon], and Stephanus has Ἄσκλον [Asklon]. Antoninus has Asculum; Paul the Deacon, Lombard History, book ii, chapter xix, has Ascu-us. The Itinerary Table has Asculo Piceno, because of its nearness. Pliny calls it the most noble colony of Picenum. It lies on a flat, open plain, in a very well protected place, with strong walls. On one side is a lofty mountain on which the citadel stands; on the other the Truentus protects it with steep banks. Events concerning the Asculans, and wars waged against them, are described by Livy, books 81 and 86 and elsewhere, by L. Florus, book iii, chapter xviii, and by other writers. The Roman Church held dominion over the city for a long time, and here was the first beginning of what they call its temporal lordship. Asculans include T. Betutius Barrus, whom Cicero in the Brutus calls the most eloquent man outside the city of Rome; Ventidius Bassus, commander of the Roman legions in the Parthian war, of whom Juvenal (Satire vi) and others speak; Nicholas IV; Caecus, an astrologer rather than a poet, but a better one; Enoch, an eloquent orator and author of several orations and letters; Gratia Dei, a theologian and philosopher, likewise famous for his writings; and others. Asculum in Apulia is a different place.

units.la: Per Vallem deinde Castellanam Amatricum devenitur, infra Truenti fontem. Ad Castellani ripas Oppida sunt Mons Sanctus, Machia, Buffarum, & Ad D. Viti. Ablativimus quos litorales aliquo modo dicere possumus Samnitium Populos, Frentanos, Carentinos, Peligos, Vestinos, Marucinos, & Pracutinos: sequuntur, qui nulla parte oram attingunt, sed plane mediterranei etiam in alteram Apennini partem, quod Regioni Italiæ nulli præterea commune, se extendunt Hirpini, & Samnites (speciatim sic dicti, junctim ob limitum incertitudinem & indiscretam utriusque gentis vicinitatem explicandi. Hirpinos, ab Coloniæ Ductore Lupo, qui Samnitibus Hirpus, nomen habuisse, auctores sunt Strabo lib. v & Festus libro ix. Hirpini Plinio lib. v cap. xi, Livio multis locis, Silo lib. xi: Ἱρπῖνοι Straboni libro v; Ἱρπῖνοι Ptolemæo & Appiano libro i. Strabo Agrum illis tribuit Lucanis confinalem. Plinius in Secunda loco Italiæ regione, in qua & Beneventum. Samnium citra Hirpinos est, à quo tota regio Samnitium nomen adepta. Quidam Urbem fuisse Regionis Caput Samnium, nunc delerant; indeque Samnites huius tractus Incolas esse vocatos. Conregionales Hirpinis, Samnitibusque hic, ab Ortu sunt Lucani; ab Meridie, Campani & Picentini ab Occasu, Sabini & Vestini; ab Septemtrione, Apuli Dauni in Apennino. De Samnitibus his sic scribit Plinius libro v cap. xiii: Samnitium, quos Sabello, & Græci Saunitæ dixere, Colonia Bovianum Vetus, & alterum cognomine Undecumanorum, Aufidenate, Fernini, Fagi, Fugalæ, Ficolenses, Sepinates, Treventinates. Alij pro duobus Fagi, Fugali, legunt Fagifulani, de quibus præterea nil habeo.
units.tr: Then, through the Castellana valley, one comes to Amatrice, below the source of the Truentus. On the banks of the Castellana lie the towns of Mons Sanctus, Machia, Buffarum, and Ad D. Viti. The peoples of the coast, whom we may in some sense call Samnite peoples, are the Frentani, Carentini, Peligni, Vestini, Marrucini, and Praetutii. Next come those who touch the coast nowhere but are wholly inland, extending also to the other side of the Apennines, a feature shared by no other region of Italy: the Hirpini and the Samnites. They are treated separately, though grouped together to explain the uncertainty of their boundaries and the close, unseparated neighbourhood of the two peoples. Our authorities say that the Hirpini took their name from the leader of the colony, Lupus, whom the Samnites called Hirpus: Strabo, book 5, and Festus, book 9. Pliny, book 5, chapter 11, and Livy in many places, and Silius, book 11, call them Hirpini. Strabo, book 5, calls them Hirpinoi; Ptolemy and Appian, book 1, have the same form. Strabo assigns them land bordering the Lucanians. Pliny places them in the second region of Italy, in which Beneventum also lies. Samnium lies on this side of the Hirpini, and the whole region took the name of the Samnites from it. Some have said that Samnium was once the chief city of the region, but that it has now been destroyed, and that the people of this tract were named Samnites after it. The neighbours of the Hirpini and the Samnites are: to the east, the Lucanians; to the south, the Campanians and Picentines; to the west, the Sabines and Vestini; to the north, the Apulians and the Daunians in the Apennines. Pliny writes of these Samnites as follows, book 5, chapter 13: "Of the Samnites, whom the Sabellians, and the Greeks as Saunitae, called: the colony of Old Bovianum, and another with the surname of the Undecumani, Aufidena, Fernium, Fagum, Fugala, the people of Ficulea, Sepinum, Trebula." Others read "Fagifulani" instead of the two names Fagum and Fugala, but I have no further information about them.

units.la: A Beneventa Archiepiscopali Civitate principium nobis esto. Id Malventum olim dictum, post Beneventum dici coepit. Beneventum, ait Plinius lib. i: i cap. xi auspicatius mutato nomine, quæ quondam appellata Maleventum. Βενεβεντος, inquit Stephanus, ἡ ἠχ Μαλεβεντος, &c. Festus libro ii: Beneventum Colonia quum deduceretur appellari coeptum est melioris ominis causa. Namque eam urbem antea Græci incolentes Μαλοεντον (sic legendum) appellarunt. Vide Nobilis. Virum Iosephum Scaligerum. Procopius libro i de bello Gothico ab Malo Vento deducit, quem injuriosum & horribilem sæpe patitur. Non defuerunt, qui Maleventum prius appellatum putent propter ingentem stragem, hic à Sulpitio Petiliòque coss. editam, cuius descriptio apud Livium lib. ix. Imprudenter. Maleventi prisci nominis mentionem facit Livius libro ix & x. Idem libro xiii & Plinius libro x Beneventum notant vocari coepisse, quum eo Colonia deduceretur, boni ominis gratia. Beneventum Livio passim, Tacito lib. xv, Antonino, Vibio Sequestro, aliisque notum; Βενεβεντον & Ουενεβεντ Ptolemæo: Beneventi vulgo. Conditum ab Diomede, testibus Solino in Polyhistore & Servio ad viii Aeneidos: inde χωρίον Διομηδ̈ς apud Stephanum. Olim Argyrippam vocatum scribunt Sudas & Cedrenus, non sine errore. De Argyrippa alibi. Situ urbs est admodum oportuno & amœno, summa agrorum bonitate præstans. In Hi pinus, eorumque Colonia esse scribit Plinius: in Samnio ponunt Strabo & Ptolemæus: Campanum Beneventum nominat Antonius his versibus: Caucaconsentiunt Pedes Saturnia: Confini. in bronaque fuit cum pore Tr clias; Vrat: fentrentin pars sam et Hermaphroditum: Edit nutrientem Phæbi in ad agnum: Nescitis ut tum, quæ Campano in Beneventó Tum Ephesio nunc ergo repente fuit.
units.tr: Let us begin with Beneventum, an archiepiscopal city. It was formerly called Malventum, and only later began to be called Beneventum. Pliny, book 3, chapter 11, says: "Beneventum, its name changed to a more auspicious one, which was once called Maleventum." Stephanus says: "Beneventum, which was formerly Maleventum." Festus, book 2: "When a colony was led there, it began to be called Beneventum for the sake of a better omen. For the Greeks who once inhabited it called it Maloenton (so it should be read)." See the noble man Joseph Scaliger. Procopius, book 1 of the Gothic War, derives the name from Malum Ventum, since the place often suffers harm and terror from the winds. There were some who thought it was called Maleventum earlier because of the great slaughter made here under the consuls Sulpicius and Petilius, described in Livy, book 9. (Imprudently.) Livy mentions the older name Maleventum in books 9 and 10. Livy, book 13, and Pliny, book 10, note that it began to be called Beneventum when a colony was led there, for the sake of a good omen. Beneventum is well known from Livy throughout, from Tacitus, book 15, from Antoninus, from Vibius Sequester, and from others. Ptolemy has Greek forms of the name, and the people are commonly called Beneventi. It was founded by Diomedes, according to Solinus in his Polyhistor and Servius on Aeneid 8; hence Stephanus has "the place of Diomedes." Suidas and Cedrenus write that it was once called Argyrippa, not without error; more on Argyrippa elsewhere. The site of the city is very suitable and pleasant, and it excels in the richness of its fields. Pliny writes that it lay in Hirpinia and was a colony of the Hirpini; Strabo and Ptolemy place it in Samnium. Antonius calls Beneventum Campanian in these verses, which are too corrupted in the scan to be rendered with confidence: "Nescitis ut tum, quae Campano in Beneventó..." (you do not know how, then, in Campanian Beneventum...).

units.la: Ab Neapoli Beneventum xxx fere M. P. intercedunt. Coloniam Civium Romanorum deductam Beneventum, quo tempore & Arimmum, auctores sunt Livius lib. xiiii, & Velleius lib. ii, quam ob eaultam & Colonia Plinio dicitur, & in antiquo lapide Cnmago etiam commemorat Coloniarum Liber, quem vide. Concordia cognominatur apud Frontinum. Cives maximam olim virtutis & disciplinae militaris optimorum apud Romanos habuisse, notum est ex historiis. Ordo Beneventanus est in Bath, quæ ibi ante summum Templum:
units.tr: About thirty Roman miles lie between Naples and Beneventum. Livy, book 14, and Velleius, book 2, are the authorities that Beneventum was made a colony of Roman citizens at the same time as Ariminum. For this reason Pliny also calls it a colony, and the Book of Colonies, which see, mentions it on an ancient inscription. It is known from the histories that its citizens once had the highest reputation among the Romans for courage and military discipline. The Beneventan order is in the inscription found there, before the chief temple:

units.la: CLAVDIO. IVLIO PACATO. V. C. CONS. CAMP OB. ACVITATEM. IVDICII ET. PATROCINIA. IAM. PRIVATI ORDO. BENEVENTANVS PATRONO. POST. FASCES. DEPOSITOS CENSVIT. COLLOCANDAM
units.tr: TO CLAUDIUS IULIUS PACATUS, OF CONSULAR RANK, CONSUL, FOR HIS KINDNESS, JUDGEMENT AND PATRONAGE, NOW A PRIVATE CITIZEN; THE BENEVENTAN ORDER VOTED THAT THIS SHOULD BE SET UP TO ITS PATRON AFTER HE LAID DOWN THE FASCES.

units.la: Plebem Beneventanam nominat alia Bisis, quæ in Vico Fabrum Ferrariorum:
units.tr: Another inscription, in the Vicus of the Smiths (Fabri Ferrariorum), names the Beneventan plebs:

units.la: T. AVONIO. MARCELLINO V. C. CONS. CAMP. PATRONO. DIGNISSIMO. OB. INSIGNIA. BENEFICIA. QVI BVS. LONGA. POPVLI. TÆDIA. SEDAVIT VNIVER- SA. PLEBS. BENEVENTA- NA. CENSVIT. PONENDAM
units.tr: TO T. AVONIUS MARCELLINUS, OF CONSULAR RANK, CONSUL, MOST WORTHY PATRON, BECAUSE OF HIS DISTINGUISHED BENEFITS, WHO CALMED THE LONG WEARINESS OF THE PEOPLE; THE WHOLE BENEVENTAN PLEBS VOTED THAT THIS SHOULD BE SET UP.

units.la: Martyrio Beneventi adfectus est cum aliis Januarius, Episcopus sub Diocletiano Nobilitatur hanc urbem orto suo Oratius Grammaticus, Magister ætate Ciceronis plagiatus; Gregorius VIII P. M: Roffredus & Odofredus, iurisconsulti celeberrimi. Nobiles hic Familiæ non paucæ, quæ vulgo: Capo-bianchi. Manfelli. Pescie. Condeftabili, Mafcambruni. Savariani. Centrovieri. Mazzili. Velota. Di Gregorio. Di Pacca. & aliæ.
units.tr: Januarius, bishop, suffered martyrdom at Beneventum along with others under Diocletian. The city is also made famous by its natives: Horatius the grammarian, a teacher in Cicero's time, whom some call a plagiarist; Pope Gregory VIII; and Roffredus and Odofredus, very celebrated jurists. Several noble families are found here, commonly called Capobianchi, Manfelli, Pescie, Condestabili, Mascambruni, Savariani, Centrovieri, Mazzili, Velota, Di Gregorio, Di Pacca, and others.

units.la: Uiam à Beneventó Brundisium usque Nervam Traianum fecisse, loquitur viæ Terminus, qui Alculi:
units.tr: The milestone of the road, which stands at Alculi, tells that Nerva Trajan made the road from Beneventum to Brundisium:

units.la: IMP. CÆSAR DIVI. NERVÆ. F. NERVA. TRAIANVS AVG. GERM. DACIC PONT. MAX. TR. POT. XIII. IMP. VI COS. V P. P. VIAM A. BENEVENTO BRVNDISIVM. FECIT SVA. FECIT
units.tr: Emperor Caesar Nerva Trajan Augustus, son of the deified Nerva, conqueror of Germany and Dacia, Chief Pontiff, holding tribunician power for the thirteenth time, acclaimed Imperator for the sixth time, consul for the fifth time, Father of his Country, built the road from Beneventum to Brundisium at his own expense.

units.la: Ager suburbicarius vulgo dicitur Valle, vel Destretto di Benevento; multorum millium. Beneventum Vrbs ab Hannibale primum (Videndus Livius lib. xxii, xxiv, xxv & xxvii) direpta, dein ab Totila Gothorum Rege (Blondus lib. vi. Histor.) eversa, & ab Langbardis postea est refecta, qui, tota Italia occupata, sedem & domicilium Imperij sui una cum Beneventani Ducatus nomine hic constituerunt, quod annos stetit fere ducentos; donec sublata ab Karolo Magno eorum Dominatione, in potestatem ac ditionem venit Regum Italicorum. Iterum aliquot annis post ab Saracenis vexata est & cremata: ijs deinceps Italia pulsis, instaurata denuo; sed non ita multo post ab Othone II Imperatore vi expugnata est, & vastata. Blondus lib.xiii Histor. Tandem ab Gulielmo Normanno, qui Regnum Siciliae post adeptus, reædificata, Pontificis Romani Imperio parere est justa: quam tamen aliquanto post rursus ab Friderico II Imp. direptam eversamque esse, Platina in Vita Hadriani iv, & Gregorij ix, & Blondus libro xv & xvii testatur. A quo postea refecta sit, non legitur.
units.tr: The district is commonly called the Valle, or Destretto di Benevento, of many thousands. The city of Beneventum was first plundered by Hannibal (see Livy, books 22, 24, 25 and 27), then destroyed by Totila, king of the Goths (Blondus, Histories, book 6), and was afterwards rebuilt by the Lombards, who, once they had occupied all of Italy, established the seat and home of their empire here, together with the name of the Duchy of Benevento.
