This lasted nearly two hundred years, until Charlemagne abolished their rule and the city passed under the power and authority of the kings of Italy. A few years later it was harassed and burned by the Saracens; after these were driven out of Italy it was restored again, but not long afterwards it was taken by storm and laid waste by the Emperor Otto II (Blondus, Histories, book 13). At last it was rebuilt by William the Norman, who afterwards obtained the kingdom of Sicily, and it was made subject to the rule of the Roman Pontiff. Yet some time later it was again plundered and overthrown by the Emperor Frederick II, as Platina in the lives of Hadrian IV and Gregory IX and Blondus in books 15 and 17 attest. By whom it was afterwards restored is not recorded.

units.la: Sex a Benevento P. M. inter Colles Opidum est Mons Fasciolus, supraque id Turris & Mons Militum.
units.tr: Six miles from Benevento, in the hills, lies the town of Mons Fasciolus, and above it Turris and Mons Militum.

units.la: Circa Vallem, quam Sabbatus perfluit, Benevento propinquam, sunt Mons Falo, Candida, Serpitum; supraque altissimus in montibus Tremulis, Episcopalis Civitas Vulturnata.
units.tr: Around the valley, which the Sabato flows through near Benevento, lie Mons Falo, Candida and Serpitum; and above them, on the high mountains of the Tremuli, the episcopal city of Vulturnata.

units.la: Supra Beneventum ad Calorem visuntur Iapygium, Cusanum, Castellum Vetus, & altius Montella Opidum, Comitatus titulo clarum.
units.tr: Above Benevento, on the Calore, are seen Iapygium, Cusanum, Castellum Vetus, and further up the town of Montella, famous for its county title.

units.la: Ad alteram Caloris ripam sunt Apirium, Mirabella, Taurasum, Cusanum aliud, Baniolum (Vagnolo) Cassanum & Noscum.
units.tr: On the other bank of the Calore are Apirium, Mirabella, Taurasum, another Cusanum, Baniolum (Vagnolo), Cassanum and Noscum.

units.la: Sabbatum transgressio se offert, Tripalto, Fluvio vicinum, Opidum Tripalta, Ferrariis officinis notum, Marchionatusque dignitate ornatum. Cives Hippolyti Martyris ossa in primario templo servare se gloriantur.
units.tr: Crossing the Sabato there presents itself Tripalta, a town near the river of the same name, known for its ironworks and adorned with the dignity of a marquisate. Its citizens boast that they keep the bones of the martyr Hippolytus in their chief church.

units.la: Sequitur ad Tripaltum amnem silva Latronibus infamis Tripaltina: & supra eam prope flumen Fonettum, Crypta (Grotta) Menarda, Flumarium, Miletum, Amandum, Iunculum, & in Apennino Mons Grumus, quondam ita dictus, nunc Crepacotius.
units.tr: Next to the river Tripalto lies the Tripaltina forest, notorious for robbers; and above it, near the river, Fonettum, Crypta (Grotta) Menarda, Flumarium, Miletum, Amandum and Iunculum; and in the Apennines Mons Grumus, formerly so called, now Crepacotius.

units.la: Iuxta Fluvios Tripaltum & Miscanum Opida jacent Cursanum, Mons Calvus, Arianum, Colli alpero & difficili insitum, olim, ut Volaterranus vult, Ara Iani, nihil tamen antiquitatis prae se ferens. Titulum nunc habet Comitatus.
units.tr: Beside the rivers Tripalto and Miscano lie the towns of Cursanum, Mons Calvus and Arianum, set on a steep and difficult hill. Formerly, as Volaterranus holds, it was Ara Iani, though it shows no trace of antiquity. It now has the title of a county.

units.la: Haud procul inde trans Miscanum in Valle Mons Malus, Benalbergium, Casale Arborii, & Castellum Francum.
units.tr: Not far from there, across the Miscano, in the valley lie Mons Malus, Benalbergium, Casale Arborii and Castellum Francum.

units.la: Pergo porro ad Tamarum Fluvium, cui adsident ad Orientalem quidem ripam Padula, Ad D. Gregorii, Molinaria, Castle Lani, Rignanum, Ad D. Maria, Collis, Cerculum, Coffianum, ad Crucem Sanctam: ad Occidentalem vero; Petra Pulcina, Pavonium, Peftulonium, Farnelum, Campus Lotharius, Monasterium Iulectorum (di Giulleri) Marconium, Savum Honorij; & in Apennino Sepinum; quod antiquum nomen retinet. Sepinum enim dicitur Livio libro x, ubi res ad opidum illud gestas victoriamque Papirij piri} commemorat: Σαίμιτν Ptolemæo. Sepinum etiam in antiquo Marmore. Hinc Sepinates Plinio. Coloniam esse docet Frontinus. Illustravit ortu suo Angelus Sepinas, Philosophus & Medicus insignis.
units.tr: I proceed further to the river Tamarus, on whose eastern bank sit Padula, Ad D. Gregorii, Molinaria, Castle Lani, Rignanum, Ad D. Maria, Collis, Cerculum, Coffianum and Ad Crucem Sanctam; and on the western bank Petra Pulcina, Pavonium, Peftulonium, Farnelum, Campus Lotharius, Monasterium Iulectorum (di Giulleri), Marconium and Savum Honorij; and in the Apennines Sepinum, which keeps its ancient name. For Livy in book 10 calls it Sepinum, where he recounts the events at that town and the victory of Papirius; Ptolemy calls it Saipinon [Σαίπινον]. The inscription on ancient marble also has Sepinum. Hence the Sepinates in Pliny. Frontinus teaches that it was a colony. Angelus Sepinas, a distinguished philosopher and physician, made it famous by his birth.

units.la: Sequitur Alta-Villa, Principatus titulo celebris: supra quam in Apennini jugo Castellum Vetus est.
units.tr: Next comes Alta-Villa, famous for its principality; above it, on the ridge of the Apennines, is Castellum Vetus.

units.la: Ad Sabbati dextram infra in planitiem redeunte sub colle Mille Pass. ab amne, antiquum se pandit Oppidum Telesia. Sic apud Livium, inter Samnij oppida libro xxi & xxiv referentem, Antoninus, aliaque scribi video. Telesia autem apud Strabonem, Venafro adjungentem: quæ duplici ar Τελεσία Ptolemæo. Telese est in Itineraria Tabula, pro Telesia. Colonys commemorat Frontinus. Hodie Telese, Episcopatus titulo horens.
units.tr: Lower down, where the Sabato returns to the plain on the right, under a hill a mile from the river, the ancient town of Telesia reveals itself. I see that Livy, listing the towns of the Samnites in books 21 and 24, and Antoninus and others, write it this way. Strabo, however, who joins Telesia with Venafrum, writes it differently; Ptolemy has Telesia [Τελεσία]. The Itinerary Table has Telese for Telesia. Frontinus mentions it as a colony. Today it is Telese, flourishing with the title of a bishopric.

units.la: Haud procul inde ad Sabbatum versus ortum Opidum est Lumata: hinc ad Fontem quatuor intercedunt Torrentes, qui convertuntur uno ostio in Sabbatum feruntur: quorum fontibus vicina sunt, Ad D. Laurentium, Ad D. Lupum, Pons Landulphi, & Casalonium.
units.tr: Not far from there, toward the east, on the Sabato, is the town of Lumata. From here to Fontem four streams run in, which unite at one mouth and flow into the Sabato. Near their sources lie Ad D. Laurentium, Ad D. Lupum, Pons Landulphi and Casalonium.

units.la: Sabbatum transgredior, cui ad meridiem miscetur Seritella ad cujus ripas oppida visuntur Castellum Popponum, Peticola, Mons Saticulus. Saticula Livio libro vii & ix: Σατικυλα Diodoro lib. xix & Stephano. Colonia vocat Paterculus. Saticulae ager Virgilij est, referente Servio, in Campania, fortean ob vicinitatem. Saticulanum ager est apud Livium libro ab Urbe condita xxiii.
units.tr: I cross the Sabato, into which the Seritella flows from the south. On its banks are seen the towns of Castellum Popponum, Peticola and Mons Saticulus. Livy in books 7 and 9 calls it Saticula; Diodorus in book 19 and Stephanus have Saticula [Σατικύλα]. Paterculus calls it a colony. Servius reports that Virgil's ager Saticulae lay in Campania, perhaps on account of its proximity. In Livy's history from the founding of the city, book 23, there is ager Saticulanus.

units.la: In proximo deinde Caudini Vallis est, quæ Benevento, inter fluente Amne, P.M. octo ferme abest, nunc Valle di Gardano dicta, testibus Collenutio & Leandro. Visuntur ibi antiquæ urbis vestigia, quæ Caudium Livio libro ix & aliis in locis, Καudes Straboni (male apud eum uno loco Καλύδιον) & Ptolemæo: quorum Interpretes male vertunt Clusium. Caudinum Colonia adcensetur Frontino; ubi M. S. Codices, indicante Scriverio meo, Caudium, rectius. Hinc Caudini Populi circa Hirpinos nominantur Plinio. Caudina Furca vel Furcula Livio, qui libro ix scite depingit, Floro, Valerio Maximo, Lucano, Plinio in Epistolis, & aliis: insignis Romanorum, quorum Legiones sub jugum hic miserunt T. Veturio Calvino & Sp. Postumio Coss. Samnites, ignominia nobiles. Historiam narrant præter alios Livius lib. ix. Caudinæ Fauces dicuntur Silio lib. viii. Hodie Stretto di Arpaia, Angustiae Harpadij nominant ab Opido propinquo, & ubi sub jugum Romani transierunt Jugum dicitur D. Mariæ. Caudinum Jugum etiam est apud Quintilianum.
units.tr: Next is the Caudine Valley, about eight miles from Benevento, through which a river flows. It is now called Valle di Gardano, according to Collenuccio and Leandro. There are visible remains of an ancient city, which Livy in book 9 and elsewhere calls Caudium, Strabo calls Caudes [Καύδαι] (wrongly, in one place, Kalydion [Καλύδιον]), and Ptolemy also; their interpreters mistranslate it as Clusium. Frontinus counts Caudinum among the colonies, where my manuscripts, as my friend Scriverius points out, have the more correct Caudium. Hence the Caudini Populi, named near the Hirpini in Pliny. Livy, in book 9, describes it skilfully as the Caudina Furca or Furcula; so do Florus, Valerius Maximus, Lucan, Pliny in his Letters, and others. It was notorious for the shame of the Romans, whose legions were sent under the yoke here by Titus Veturius Calvinus and Spurius Postumius, consuls, and the Samnites were made famous by this disgrace. Among others Livy in book 9 tells the story. Silius in book 8 calls them the Caudinae Fauces. Today they are called the Stretto di Arpaia, the Angustiae Harpadij, from the neighbouring town; and the place where the Romans passed under the yoke is called Jugum D. Mariae. The Caudinum Jugum also appears in Quintilian.

units.la: Haud procul etiam à Monte Saticulo Civitas est Harpadium, vulgo Harpaia: Antiquis Harpinum, ut Blondus tradit. Irpinum apud Ciceronem est, sine adspiratione.
units.tr: Not far from Mount Saticulus is the town of Harpadium, commonly Harpaia; to the ancients it was Harpinum, as Blondus reports. In Cicero it is Irpinum, without the aspirate.

units.la: Sequuntur ab alia parte Vallis Caudinæ Opida Ad D. Martini, Penna Sturnina, Ad D. Angeli Scalarum, dalle Scale.
units.tr: On the other side of the Caudine Valley follow the towns of Ad D. Martini, Penna Sturnina and Ad D. Angeli Scalarum, dalle Scale.

units.la: In Valle Amnis, qui de Monte Virginis altissimo in Sabbatum fluit, Opida sunt Alta-Villa, Monsque Freddanus & in propinqua Convalle vetus Civitas Abellinum. Sic Plinio vocatur Αβέλλανον etiam Ptolemæo; cui, ut & Straboni, alia est Αβέλλα in Campania, ut ibi dictum. Hodie Avellino. Hinc Abellinates Plinio, Protropi & Marsi cognominati: Avellinates Lucano. In libro Fisci Pontificij Urbis hujus Antistes Avellinensis dicitur Episcopus: alterius in Campania, Avellinus. In Glossario Græco-Latino hæc lego: Αβέλλιτ; Ἐπίσκοπος Beneventanum. Nescio an scripserit Αβέλλανος, cujus quidem utius in Agro Beneventano, unde Beneventanum; sed quod Abellini parabatur, unde Αβελλανὸν.
units.tr: In the valley of the river which flows from the high Mount Virginis into the Sabato lie the towns of Alta-Villa and Monsque Freddanus, and in the neighbouring small valley the ancient city of Abellinum. Pliny calls it so, and Ptolemy calls it Abellanon [Αβέλλανον]; Strabo, too, and Ptolemy have another Abella [Αβέλλα] in Campania, as is noted there. Today it is Avellino. Hence the Abellinates in Pliny, and the surnames Protropi and Marsi; the Avellinates in Lucan. In the register of the papal fisc the bishop of this city is called the bishop of Avellinensis; the other Avellino, in Campania, is Avellinus. In a Greek-Latin glossary I read these words: Abellit[es] [Αβέλλιτ]; bishop of Benevento. I do not know whether it was written Abellanos [Αβέλλανος], whose inhabitants in the territory of Benevento are called Beneventani; but it was prepared at Abellinum, whence Abellanon [Αβελλανὸν].

units.la: Altius dein aspero in loco Mercuriale est opidum, cujus apud Antoninum est mentio.
units.tr: Further up, in a rugged place, is the town of Mercuriale, which is mentioned in Antoninus.

units.la: Hinc in alia Convalle Nigra Palus, & Serinum: nec procul inde locus, qui Forino vernacule, cum Cœmeterio D. Felicissimi.
units.tr: From here, in another small valley, lie Nigra Palus and Serinum; and not far from there the place which in the vernacular is Forino, with the cemetery of St Felicissimus.

units.la: Occidentalior hinc Petam Loca Silari Vulturnique Fontibus vicina: in quis non poltremæ claslis sera. Sic Latinis scribitur; Σάγα Græcis. Plinius in i Regione memorat, ubi Latium, inquo recensi etiam Ptolemæus; Strabo in Campania Felice. Alij, quibus & ego consentio, Samnitibus tribuunt, cum quod in Vestinis, Samnitium gente, sit, ut alibi dictum: tum quod ab Samnitibus de Volcis capta legatur apud Livium lib. x. Vicina est Liri Amnis populo haud infrequens, utroque tuloque Ducatus & Episcopatus ornata. Coloniam eo ab Romanis ductam, notant Livius lib. ix & x, Paterculus libro 1, Frontinus de Colonijs: ideoque Colony annumeratur à Plinio libro iii cap. v. Soram Cicero pro Plancio Municipium vocat. Diu sub Imperio Romano floruit. Direptam crematamque ab Friderico II Imper. auctores sunt Blondus lib. xvii Histor. & Platina in Vita Gregorij ix. Quis postea refecerit, non legi.
units.tr: Further west from here, near the sources of the Sele and the Volturno, lies Petra, in which there is no little cold. Thus it is written in Latin; the Greeks have Saga [Σάγα]. Pliny in the first region mentions it, where Latium is, in which Ptolemy also lists it; Strabo puts it in Campania Felix. Others, to whom I too agree, assign it to the Samnites, partly because it lies among the Vestini, a Samnite people, as is said elsewhere, and partly because it is read in Livy, book 10, that it was taken from the Volsci by the Samnites. Near it is the river Liri, not without people, adorned with both a duchy and a bishopric. Livy in books 9 and 10, Paterculus in book 1 and Frontinus in his work on colonies note that the Romans made it a colony; therefore Pliny in book 3, chapter 5, counts it among the colonies. Cicero in his speech for Plancius calls Sora a municipium. It flourished for a long time under the Roman empire. Blondus in book 17 of his Histories and Platina in the life of Gregory IX are the authorities that it was plundered and burned by the Emperor Frederick II. By whom it was afterwards rebuilt I have not read.

units.la: Confluunt paullo infra Soram duo Amnes, qui Liri praebent initium; itá ut Peninsulam quasi faciant, in qua praeter Soram sunt Pescum, Possa, Lobrutallium.
units.tr: Just below Sora, two streams join to form the Liri, so that they enclose a kind of peninsula. In it, besides Sora, lie Pescum, Possa, Lobrutallium.

units.la: Hinc Peninsulae ad Ortum peramoena & fertilis est Regio, quam Comitum dicunt, ab Antiqua Urbe Comitro, cuius meminit Livius libro x & alibi.
units.tr: To the east of this peninsula is a very pleasant and fertile region, which they call Comitum, after the ancient city Comitro, which Livy mentions in book x and elsewhere.

units.la: Castella hic non infrequentia, Trebulum, Alvetium, Ad D. Donati, ad Septem Fratres, Priniestum, Calinarium, Casale Teerum, & Arina, civitas antiquissima, cujus meminerunt Virgilius libro vii inter Urbes quae Turnum armis iuverunt, Livius multis locis, praecipue libro is, & Silius libro viii. Pomponius Sabinus eam in excelso colle describit post Fabateriam versus Itrum. Arinates Plinius in prima notat Regione. Ptolemaeus Arinam etiam in Latio ponit. in Campania juxta Pomptinas Paludes locat Servius: Alij commodius in Samnitibus: Creat diversitatem hanc vicinitas. Colonys concenser Frontinus.
units.tr: There are not a few small towns here: Trebulum, Alvetium, Ad D. Donati, ad Septem Fratres, Priniestum, Calinarium, Casale Teerum, and Arina, a very ancient city. Virgil in book vii names it among the cities that aided Turnus in arms; Livy mentions it in many places, especially in book ix; and Silius in book viii. Pomponius Sabinus describes it as standing on a high hill beyond Fabateria, towards Itri. Pliny, in the first region, notes the Arinates. Ptolemy also places Arina in Latium. Servius puts it in Campania, near the Pomptine marshes; others, more reasonably, among the Samnites. The neighbourhood creates this disagreement. Frontinus counts it among the colonies.

units.la: Sub Casali Ivero ad Melphem modicum invenitur Castellum Solaceum, Schiarone infraque asperrimo in colle Arpinum (Arpas hodie inter Soram & Aquinum) Opidum Livio multis locis, praecipue libro ix, aliquè celebratum. Hinc Arpinates Plinio in prima Regione, & Silio lib. viii. Colonium eo deductam scribit Livius libro ix. Arpinates Civitate donatos tradit idem libro x & xxxviii. De Municipio Arpino M. Tullius pro Plancio & de Claris Oratoribus. Festus Arpinum inter eas numerat Praefecturae, in quas Praetor singulis annis Praefectos mittebat, itemque interea Municipia, quae sui erant juris. Celeberrimum hoc Opidum ortu C. Marij, septies Consulis, de quo nulli non Scriptores. In huius Agro Arpinatem Fundum nominat Cicero ad suam Terentiam.
units.tr: Below Casale Ivero, near Melfa, a small castle is found, Solaceum, Schiarone; and further down, on a very rugged hill, stands Arpinum (Arpas today, between Sora and Aquinum), a town made fairly famous by Livy in many places, especially in book ix. Hence the Arpinates in Pliny in the first region, and in Silius, book viii. Livy writes in book ix that a colony was led there. The same Livy, in books x and xxxviii, records that the Arpinates were granted citizenship. M. Tullius speaks of the Municipio Arpino in his speech for Plancius and in the Brutus. Festus counts Arpinum among those Praefecturae to which the praetor sent prefects every year, and likewise among the Municipia, which were under their own law in the meantime. This very famous town was the birthplace of C. Marius, seven times consul, about whom every writer speaks. Cicero, in his letter to his Terentia, names an Arpinatem Fundum, an estate near Arpinum.

units.la: Sorae versus Austrum est Villa D. Dominici, ubi Fibrenus Liri miscetur: tribus ab Arpino P. M. ubi M. Tullium in lucem editum, ait Petrus Marius. Ipse sane de Natali loco sic scribit lib. ii de LL. Sed ventum in Insulam est: hac vero nihil est amoenius: ut enim hoc quasi rostro findetur Fibrenus, & divisus aequaliter in duas partes lutera haec alluit, rapideque diapsus cito in unum confluit, & tantum complectitur, quod satis sit modica palaestra loci: quo effecto, tamquam id habuerit operis ac muneris, ut hanc nobis efficeret sedem ad disputandum, statim praecipitat in Lirem, & quasi in Familiam Patritiam venerit, amittit nomen elapsurus, Lirèmque multo geldiorem facit. Nec enim ullum hoc frigidi flamen attigi, quum ad multa accesserim, ut vix pede tentare id possim, quod in Phaedro Platonis facit Socrates. Paullo vero prius idem his verbis fuerat usus: Haec est mea & hujus Fratris mei germani Patria: hinc enim orti sumus antiquissima familia, hic Sacra, hic Genus, hic Maiorum multa Vestigia: quid plura? hanc vides Villam, ut nunc quidem est, lautius aedificatam Patris nostri studio: qui quum esset infirma valetudine, hic fere aetatem egit in literis, sed hoc ipso in loco quum: Actus viveres, & antiquo more parva esset villa, ut illa Curiana in Sabinis, mensito esse natura.
units.tr: South of Sora is the Villa D. Dominici, where the Fibrenus mingles with the Liri, three miles from Arpinum, where, Petrus Marius says, M. Tullius was born. Cicero himself writes of his birthplace thus in book ii of the De Legibus: "But we came to the island. Nothing is more pleasant than this place. For the Fibrenus is split as if by a beak, and, divided equally into two parts, washes this land; then, rushing swiftly, it flows together again into one and embraces just enough ground for a modest exercise-ground. Having done this, as though it had taken on the task of providing us this seat for discussion, it at once plunges into the Liri, and, as if it had entered a patrician family, it loses its name, about to vanish, and makes the Liri much colder. For I have never touched a cold breeze here, although I have been to many places; so I can scarcely test it with my foot, as Socrates does in the Phaedrus of Plato." A little earlier, the same writer had used these words: "This is my own homeland and that of my brother, a true brother. For here we were born of a most ancient family; here are our sacred rites, here our stock, here many traces of our ancestors. What more? You see this villa, now more handsomely built thanks to the zeal of our father, who, being in weak health, spent most of his life here in his studies. But in this very place, when he was living a busy life, and the villa was small in the old fashion, like that of Curius among the Sabines, he was content with it as it was by nature."

units.la: Sub Arpino prope Melphem Opida sunt Fontanum & Arceum: supraque, ubi duo Liris capita in unum cocunt Insula Castrum: olim, ut censent Blondus, Leander, Cittadinus, Niger, & alij, quod inter duos Amnes, Interamnia Ιντεραμνιον Straboni, quod ad confluentes Liris & Casini. Colonium factam docent Livius lib. ix & x, Paterculus lib. 1, & antiquus Lapis. Hinc Interamnates Plinio, cognomine Succusani Lirinates, ut sine copula legit Ortelius. De ijs Inscriptio, quae apud Onuphrium in Imperio Romano: P. TVRCIO P. F. STEL. SEVERO II VIRO. CVRAT. REIP. INTERAMNAT LIRIN. EORVMDEM. PATRONO, COL CASSINATES
units.tr: Below Arpinum, near Melfa, are the towns Fontanum & Arceum; and above, where the two heads of the Liri come together, the Insula Castrum. Formerly, as Blondus, Leander, Cittadinus, Niger and others think, it was Interamnia (Ιντεραμνιον in Strabo), because it lies between two rivers, at the confluence of the Liri and the Casinus. Livy, books ix and x, Paterculus, book i, and an ancient stone show that it was made a colony. Hence the Interamnates in Pliny, surnamed Succusani Lirinates, as Ortelius reads it without a conjunction. There is an inscription about them, given by Onuphrius in his Imperium Romanum: "To P. Turcius Severus, son of Publius, of the Stellatine tribe, duumvir, curator of the state of Interamnia Lirinum, their patron, the Casinates [set this up]."

units.la: Secundum ejusdem fluminis decursum Opida visuntur Turris, Campus Largus, Pa-faletta.
units.tr: Along the course of the same river are seen the towns Turris, Campus Largus, Pafaletta.

units.la: Occurrit ab his locis versus Ortum procedenti Aquinum. Sic Latinis dictum; inter alios Silio Italico libro viii, Antonino, & Itinerariæ Tabulæ: Ἀ̓κουῖνον Ptolemæo: Ἄκουϊνον, inquit Strabo, μεγάλη πόλις ἐστι, ὡς ἡν ὁ Μελέτης ἐμ πόλεως μέγας. Legendum ex Ptolemæo Ἀ̓κουῖνον. In Latio ponit Ptolemæus, in Prima regione Plinius. Municipii jus habuisse paret ex Ciceronis Oratione pro Plancio. Coloniam inde factam, testantur Frontinus & Plinius lib. iii cap. v. Hinc Colonia Aquinas Livio libro xxvi & Tacito libro xvii. Aquinates hunc Silio lib. xii. Natus hic Pefcennius Niger Imperat. testibus Herodiano & Iuvenale; & Villorinus, summus Geometra. Nobilitavit etiam eam Patriam suam Thomas, magnus Philosophus; Aquinas hinc cognominatus. Nomen tenemus collapsa pene jacet, vestigia præterea pristinæ amplitudinis: Comitatus Episcopatusque habens titulum.
units.tr: Proceeding eastward from these places, one comes to Aquinum. So it is called by the Latins, among them Silius Italicus in book viii, Antoninus, and the Itinerary tables; Ptolemy writes Ἀκουῖνον. Strabo says Akouinon is a great city, as Meletes was a great man of the city. It should be read as Akouinon from Ptolemy. Ptolemy places it in Latium, Pliny in the first region. That it had the rights of a Municipii appears from Cicero's speech for Plancius. That a colony was made there afterwards is attested by Frontinus and by Pliny, book iii, chapter v. Hence Colonia Aquinas in Livy, book xxvi, and Tacitus, book xvii. Silius, book xii, calls them the Aquinates. Born here was Pescennius Niger, the emperor, according to Herodian and Juvenal; and Villorinus, a very great geometer. Thomas, the great philosopher, also ennobled this, his homeland, and from it he is surnamed Aquinas. The name remains; the place lies almost in ruins, with traces of its former size. It has a county and a bishopric bearing its title.

units.la: Haud procul inde in vertice Montis locus monstratur, ubi quondam Casinum, Meminit cum aliis Silius Italicus libro xii de Bello Punico: ——— Nymphasque habitata Catini
units.tr: Not far from there, on the top of a mountain, a spot is pointed out where Casinum once stood. Silius Italicus, among others, mentions it in book xii of his Punic War: "and the nymphs of the inhabited Catinus."

units.la: Rura.
units.tr: Rura.

units.la: Expressi est & in Itineraria Tabula. Casinum, inquit Varro, Forum Vetus appellant. Ἀ̓κανα Agathias libro ii quæ Κασλῶν scribitur in M. S. Codice CL. V. Bonaventuræ Vulcanij, hodiernus Græcarum Literarum in Academia Lugdunensi Interpretis, Collegæ mihi amicissimi. In Casinensi Castro, inquit Paulus Diaconus lib. i. Rerum Langobardicarum cap xxvi, quod Narum appellatur; dicitque x millibus distare ab Sublaco. Pro Haram legit Abrahamus Ortelius Arum ex Floriacenti, quod Avarum apud Marianum Schotum, & Banum apud Blondum lib. vi Dec. cap. i. Κάσινον Strabo præclaram Latinorum Urbem vocat, & xix stadiis ab Capua distare scribit: Plinius in Prima numerat Regione: Casinum habet Livius circa Campaniam. Romanorum Coloniam testatur idem Livius libr. ix. Sic Vetus Inscriptio:
units.tr: It is also found in the Itinerary Table. Casinum, says Varro, they call Forum Vetus. Agathias, book ii, writes it Ἀ̓κανα [Akana], which in the manuscript codex CL of Bonaventura Vulcanius, the present interpreter of Greek literature at the Academy of Leiden and my dearest colleague, is written Κασλῶν [Kaslōn]. In the Casinensian Castle, says Paulus Diaconus, book i of the History of the Lombards, chapter xxvi, which is called Narum; and he says it is ten miles from Subiaco. For Haram, Abraham Ortelius reads Arum from the Floriacensis manuscript; Marianus Scotus has Avarum, and Blondus, book vi of the Decades, chapter i, has Banum. Strabo calls Κάσινον [Kasinon] a famous city of the Latins, and writes that it is 19 stades from Capua. Pliny counts it in the First Region. Livy places Casinum near Campania. The same Livy, book ix, attests that it was a Roman colony. So an ancient inscription:

units.la: P. TVRCIO. P. F. STEL. SEVERO II. VIRO. CVRAT. REIP. INTERAMNAT LIRIN. EORVMDEM. PATRONO. COL CASSINATES
units.tr: P. TVRCIO. P. F. STEL. SEVERO II. VIRO. CVRAT. REIP. INTERAMNAT LIRIN. EORVMDEM. PATRONO. COL CASSINATES

units.la: Cicero pro Plancio Municipium appellat. Ædes hic fuisse scribitur Apollinis; ubi postea magnificum Casinense Monasterium, sic ab Urbe dictum Benedictus Nursinus, Monachorum in Italia Pater, fundavit situs ibidem cum Scholastica Sorore. De varia Templi hujus Fortuna Paullus Diaconus lib. vi Histor. Helias Capreolus lib. v Histor. Brix Blondus lib. xii & xvii Hist. Volaterranus libro xxi Comment. Urban. D. Gregorius libro ii Dialog. Casina Arx in Samnio, ubi Monasterium, inquit Eginarthus, D. Benedicti, quod etiam Casinense vocat. Prodigium, quod Casini accidit, narrat Plinius libro vii Nat. Histor. cap. iv. Casinas Mons est in Campania, Platinæ in Vita Pelagij i, P. M.
units.tr: Cicero in the speech for Plancius calls it a municipium. It is written that there was formerly a temple of Apollo here; later Benedict of Nursia, father of the monks in Italy, founded there, with his sister Scholastica, the famous Casinense Monasterium, so named from the city. On the varied fortunes of this temple, see Paulus Diaconus, book vi of the History; Elias Capreolus, book v of the History; Biondo Flavio, books xii and xvii of the History; Volaterranus, book xxi of the Commentaries; and Pope Gregory, book ii of the Dialogues. Casina, a citadel in Samnium, where the Monastery, says Eginhard, of St. Benedict, which he also calls the Casinense. Plinius, book vii of the Natural History, chapter iv, tells of the portent that happened at Casinum. Mount Casinas is in Campania, according to Platina in the Life of Pelagius I.

units.la: Sequitur in radicibus Casini Montis Orientem versus D. Germani Castrum, Fontium copia abundans. Incolæ majori ex parte Fabri sunt Aeuum.
units.tr: Next, at the foot of Mount Casinum, toward the east, is the Castle of St. Germanus, abounding in springs. Most of its inhabitants are smiths and carpenters.

units.la: Vulturni jam alveum utrimque perlustremus, quatenus ad Samnites pertinet.
units.tr: Let us now survey the bed of the Volturnus on both banks, as far as it belongs to the Samnites.

units.la: Circa initium Vallis est Rotunda: quam sequuntur Aqua Fundata, S. Vincentij, Mons Niger, Rivus Niger, Mons Aquilae, Arx Ravennola, Ferulum, Fanum D. Mariae Oliveti-na, & alia: postea Venafrum in Colle. Sic Livio, Plinio, Silio, Antonino, aliis dicitur; quod Οὐενάφρον cum Appiano & aliis, tum Ptolemæo, cui Hirpinorum Urbs est in Samnitibus. In Regione i Plinius, in Campania locat Acron ob vicinitatem. Campanum etiam cognominatur Martiali: Hoc tibi Campani sudavit bacca Venafri, Vinguentum quales fumus, & illud ole.
units.tr: Near the beginning of the valley is Rotunda, followed by Aqua Fundata, S. Vincenzo, Mons Niger, Rivus Niger, Mons Aquila, Arx Ravennola, Ferulum, the shrine of St. Mary of Oliveto, and others. Then Venafrum on a hill. It is so called by Livy, Pliny, Silius, Antoninus and others; Appian and others, as well as Ptolemy, call it Οὐενάφρον [Venaphron], and for Ptolemy it is a city of the Hirpini among the Samnites. Pliny places it in the First Region, but in Campania because of its proximity to Acerrae. Martial also gives it the surname Campanum: For you the berry of Campanian Venafrum sweated, the oil with which we anoint ourselves, and that olive oil.

units.la: Venafrum unam ex antiquis Præfecturis, in quas Præfectos mittere quotannis erat solitus Prætor, tradit Festus. Colonia jus postea accepit, ut paret ex Frontino Plinioque nioque libro 111 cap. v. Venafri vulgo, Episcopatus habens titulum. Olum celebratur Iuvenali.
units.tr: Festus records Venafrum as one of the ancient prefectures, to which the praetor used to send prefects every year. That it later received the rights of a colony appears from Frontinus and Pliny, book iii, chapter v. In common speech Venafro has the title of a bishopric. Olum is celebrated by Juvenal.

units.la: A Vulturno 111 P.M. Furnelium cit, frequens & opulentum Opidum.
units.tr: Three Roman miles from the Volturnus, Furnelium is a crowded and wealthy town.

units.la: Ex advertum huic Castello Vallis Porcina conspicitur, inque ea magnae cuiusdam Vrbis Cadaver. Aesernam dico, uti vocant Dionysius Halicarnassaeus, Strabo (apud quem male Aisegnia in Vulgatis libris) Appianus libro 1, Ptolemaeus, alij; Isernia Silio libro viii; Isernum Itinerariae Tabulae. Vitiose apud Diodorum libro xx Σεγερνια, pro Εσερνια. Sernicum legebatur apud Antoninum & Serra sed restitutum ex Regio Exemplari V. Cl. Hieronymus Surita. De Sernico tamen ampliandum censeo, quum Sernicianum Vinum inde denominare videatur Plinius lib. xiiii Nat. Hist. cap. vi. Hodie Segna. Isernini hinc Plinio & Nonio Marcello. Vulturno Flumini adiacet, auctore Livio libro xab v. c. Ptolemaeus in Samnitibus locat: Plinius Isernanus in iv regione memorat. Colonia est apud Frontinum, Velleium Paterculum libro 1, Florum ex Livii libro xvi, lxxii, & seq. Illustravit Patrum nostrum memoria hoc Opidum Andreas Alfeminus I.C.
units.tr: Opposite this fortress one sees the Porcine Valley, and in it the corpse, as it were, of a great city. I mean Aesernia, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Strabo (in whom the printed books wrongly have Aisegnia), Appian in book i, Ptolemy and others call it; Isernia in Silius, book viii; Isernum in the Itinerary Table. Wrongly in Diodorus, book xx, Σεγερνια [Segernia] for Εσερνια [Esernia]. Sernicum was read in Antoninus and Serra, but it was restored from the royal copy by the most learned Girolamo Surita. I think, however, that Sernicum should be enlarged on, since Pliny, book xiv of the Natural History, chapter vi, seems to name the Sernician wine after it. Today it is Segna. Isernini is used by Pliny and Nonius Marcellus. It lies next to the river Volturnus, according to Livy, book xxv. Ptolemy places it among the Samnites; Pliny mentions the Isernani in the fourth region. It is a colony according to Frontinus, Velleius Paterculus book i, and Florus from Livy, book xvi, lxxii and following. Our fathers' generation saw this town illustrated by Andrea Alfeminus, a jurist.

units.la: Occurrunt inde ad Pratellum Crapaia, Pratum. Masfratum, Compl'e ia, quam vi captam ab Fabio cum Telesia scribit Livius lib. xxiv. In aliis libris legitur Compulteriae.
units.tr: From there, toward Pratellum, one meets Crapaia, Pratum, Masfratum, Compl'eia, which Livy, book xxiv, writes was captured by Fabius together with Telesia. In other books it is read Compulteriae.

units.la: Ab Aesernia deinde versus ortum xx ferme lapide, Bovianum occurrit, nobilissima quondam Samnii Vrbs, Vetus cognomine: nam aliud fuit Fundi humanorum. Bovianum Livio passim, Silio libro viii, Plinio, aliisque Latinis; Bobianus Frontino; Bobianum Itinerariae Tabulae, incmendatius; Βοιανον Straboni libro v; Βοιανον Ptolemaeo: Bo ano hodie: Opidum Episcopale. Bovianum Livius libro ix Pentrorum (in aliis Codicibus Pentrorum, & Pentiorum legitur) appellat caput; opulentissimum & potentissimum eius gentis Opidum describens. Coloniam ab Iulio Caesare ducta, paret ex Frontino, & Plinio lib. ii cap. xii, eam in Regione iv locante.
units.tr: About twenty miles east of Aesernia comes Bovianum, once the most noble city of the Samnites, called Vetus to distinguish it from another, which was the Fundi of the humans. Bovianum appears throughout Livy, in Silius book viii, in Pliny and other Latin writers; Bobianus in Frontinus; Bobianum in the Itinerary Table, less correctly; Βοιανον [Boianon] in Strabo, book v, and in Ptolemy. Today it is Bojano, an episcopal town. In book ix Livy calls Bovianum the capital of the Pentri (other manuscripts read Pentrorum and Pentiorum), describing it as the most wealthy and powerful town of that people. That it was made a colony by Julius Caesar appears from Frontinus and from Pliny, book ii, chapter xii, who places it in the fourth region.

units.la: Adiicribam huc iter, quod ab Vrbe Via Salaria per Vmbriam in Samnites Hadriam duxit Antoninus; commissum cum Itineraria Tabula, vulgataque Nomenclatura. Antoninus. Itineraria Tabula. Vulgata Nomencl. Ab Vrbe Hadriam usque M. P. | Roma, | XI. | Monte Ritundo. Eretum M. P. XVIII. | Foro, XIII. | Riete. Vicum Novum M. P. XIII. | Ad Novas, XVI. | Lago di Contiglione, vel Lago de Pie de Luco, ut alij. Beate, M. P. XVI. | Beate, VIII. | Interdocho. Cutilias, M. P. XVIII. | Aquae Cutiliae VII. | S. Silvestri in Phalacrino. Sic etiam simpliciter Senecam in Quaest. Naturalib. lib. iii. | Sic etiam vocat Plinius libro xi, cap. xcv. | Ducatu Spoletino. Interocrium, M. P. VI. | Interocrio, XII. | Falacrinum, M. P. XVI. | Palacrinis, XVI. | Legendum Falacrinis, Vicum Badien M. P. IX. | Ad Martis, ... | ........... Forte, Vicum Martis. | | Ad Centesimum, M. P. X. | Magna confusio. | Asculum. M. P. XII. | Nam ab Vrbe versus Occidentem hoc Iter primo ducitur inde reflectitur in Orientem; quum in Septentrionem primo mox in Orientem suisset ducendum. | Asculiso Aliis Asculum, & Asculum scribitur. | | Abruzzo. Samnii. | | cum; mti quod Super Equam opidum etiam notum sit libro Limitum: quod ubi facit, ignoto.
units.tr: I shall add here the route which Antoninus gives from the city by the Via Salaria through Umbria to the Samnites and the Adriatic, compared with the Itinerary Table and the common nomenclature. Antoninus. Itinerary Table. Common Nomenclature. From the city to the Adriatic, Roman miles: Rome, XI; Monte Ritundo; Eretum, 18 miles; Forum, XIII; Rieti; Vicus Novus, 13 miles; Ad Novas, XVI; Lago di Contiglione, or Lago de Pie de Luco, as others have it; Beate, 16 miles; Beate, VIII; Interdocco; Cutiliae, 18 miles; Aquae Cutiliae, VII; S. Silvestro in Falacrino. Seneca too simply calls it so in Natural Questions, book iii. Pliny also calls it so in book xi, chapter xcv. Duchy of Spoleto; Interocrium, 6 miles; Interocrio, XII; Falacrinum, 16 miles; Palacrinis, XVI; read Falacrinis; Vicus Badien, 9 miles; Ad Martis...; perhaps Vicus Martis; Ad Centesimum, 10 miles. Great confusion. Asculum, 12 miles. For this route, from Rome, first leads toward the west, then turns back to the east; whereas it ought to have led north and then straight east. Asculiso; others write Asculum. Abruzzo. Samnium. ... since the town Super Equam is also known from the book of Limites, but where it lies is unknown.

units.la: Fuit haud procul Teate in ostio fluminis Aterni opidum cognomine Aternum, Livio lib. xx & Antonino notum. Strabo etiam Aeternum opidum cum flumine eodem nomine, Plinio vicinum, memorat. Hodie ibi Pescara est, exiguum oppidulum, à quo fluvio etiam nomen, de quo alibi.
units.tr: Not far from Teate, at the mouth of the river Aternus, there was a town of the same name, Aternum, known from Livy, book xx, and from Antoninus. Strabo also mentions the town Aeternum, with a river of the same name, which Pliny places nearby. Today there is Pescara there, a small town, named after the river, of which more elsewhere.

units.la: Feligni absolutis, Vestinos videamus. Vestini Latinis, vicinos Strabonis Vestini Ptolemæo. Eorum frequens apud Livium, Appianum, Florum, aliosque mentio. Hunc Vestinum Lucentem Silio celebratur lib. viii. Vestinum Caput Martialis. De Vestinis hic Plinius lib. iii cap. x. Vestinorum Angulam, Pinnenses, Peltuinates, qui ut tangantur Aufidenate, Cismontani. Continales huc genti signare solent Geographi ex Ptolemæi tabulis aliisque Scriptoribus a Septentrione Peligni, ab Ortu Samnites spectatius tantos, qua Meridies est, Campanos, Latinque populos, qua Occidens, Præcutinos, Marsos, & Sabinos. Fecit autem, ut tempore hoc etiam, eorum vicinitas, ut loca quæ Vestinorum, ab Auctoribus nunc Sabinis, nunc Campanis, nunc alius adscribantur: quemadmodum patebat in Aquerno, Pinna, Angelo: & hanc Vestinorum designatio nonnullos esse solet difficultatis.
units.tr: Having finished with the Peligni, let us look at the Vestini. The Vestini are the neighbours of the Vestini of Strabo for the Latin writers, and of Ptolemy. Their name is frequent in Livy, Appian, Florus and others. Silius celebrates this Vestinum Lucens in book viii; Martial calls it Vestinum Caput. Pliny, book iii, chapter x, speaks here of the Vestini. The Vestinorum Angula, Pinnenses, Peltuinates, which are touched on by the Aufidenates, are Cismontane. Geographers, following Ptolemy's tables and other writers, usually assign this people by the north to the Peligni, by the east to the Samnites (more particularly the Frentani), toward the south to the Campanians and the Latins, and toward the west to the Praecutini, Marsi and Sabines. Because of their proximity, however, the places of the Vestini are at times ascribed by authors now to the Sabines, now to the Campanians, now to others, as is clear in the case of Aquernum, Pinna and Angelus; and this uncertainty about the Vestini is often a source of difficulty.

units.la: Ut singularia ordiar cum primis locus apud eos, ubi olim Amiternum, nunc maximarum ædium ruinis horridus. Amiternum Livio, & Plinio. Appianus. Hadrianus Hadrianus lib. ii, Strabo v, Ptolemæo. Amiternum Samnitium urbs est apud Livium lib. x. Strabo Emporium nominat Frentanorum; Veltina adscribit Ptolemæus; Salutis tribuit Dionysius. Hinc Plinius etiam Amiternos habet inter Sabinos. Sabinorum forte ab sunt antiquissimis temporibus, quæ postea Samnitium, &, ut specialius dicam, Vestinorum facta. Amiternum perpetuo montis inlidebat dorso, ubi hodieque sunt monumenta ostenduntur magnorum Operum, Theatri præcipue & Templorum aliquot; ex quibus, quam ampla fuerit, facile iudicare Spectator poterit. Laurentius Anastasius Pescara ex eo facit. Amiternum, inquit Baptista Fonteius in Catia Familia, quod dicitur Aquilam urbem auxit. Hinc Amiternus Plinio, qui Amiternum Livio & M. Terentio Varroni, qui hic dictos notat, quod circum Aeternum flumen habitarent. A Sp. Consule quondam expugnatam, captis Samnitium eo eo locos, captisque eo eo eo eo cexxc, auctor est Livius lib. xi qui & Amiternos cum Umbris, Nursinis & Reatinis, L. Scipioni in Africam ituro militaria suppeditasse auxilia commemorat. Amiterna cohors legitur apud Virgilium lib. vii & Silium Italicum lib. viii. Ortu suo nobilitarunt cum alii, tum Sabinus Crispus & Victorinus, Martyr sub Nerone, Urbis Episcopus. Amiternum Ager cumque Nasos celebrat Martialis in Apophoretis: Non Amiternus Ager frugiferus educat hortos: Nunc hortos potens parum esse capax,
units.tr: To begin with the more notable places, first there is the site where Amiternum once stood, now bleak with the ruins of great buildings. Amiternum is named by Livy and Pliny, Appian, Hadrian in book ii, Strabo in book v, and Ptolemy. Amiternum of the Samnites is a city in Livy, book x. Strabo calls it an emporium of the Frentani; Ptolemy assigns it to the Veltini; Dionysius gives it to the Salutares. Hence Pliny also places the Amiterni among the Sabines. It was perhaps in the most ancient times Sabine, later made Samnite and, to speak more exactly, Vestinian. Amiternum lay on the ridge of a mountain, where there are still displayed the remains of great works, especially a theatre and several temples; from these a spectator can easily judge how large it was. Laurentius Anastasius derives Pescara from it. Amiternum, says Battista Fonteius in the Catia family, which is said to have enlarged the city of Aquila. Hence Amiternus is used by Pliny, who notes Amiternum with Livy and Marcus Terentius Varro, who say the people were so called because they lived around the river Aternus. Livy, book xi, records that it was once stormed by the consul Spurius, with the capture of Samnite places and the taking of many thousand men; and he also records that the Amiterni, together with the Umbrians, Nursini and Reatini, supplied military aid to Lucius Scipio when he was going to Africa. The Amiterna cohort is read in Virgil, book vii, and in Silius Italicus, book viii. By their birth they ennobled, among others, Sabinus Crispus and Victorinus, the martyr under Nero and bishop of the city. Martial, in the Apophoreta, also celebrates the Amiternian field and Nasos: The fertile Amiternian field does not produce gardens: now the gardens are too small to hold its power.

units.la: Flumen ex Amiterno facit Pontus unius Sabinus ad librum vi; Ænead. quod Vestinos & Marrucinos, a sinistra habet, supra sunt Peligni: ex Livii procul dubio loco, qui libro xxiv, male intellecto, ubi auctor scribit, Flumen Amiterni crescentem fluxisse: quæ verba quid velint, vel pueri norunt.
units.tr: Pontus Sabinus, on book 6 of the Aeneid, says the river flows out of Amiternum, and that the Vestini and Marrucini lie on its left and the Peligni beyond them. This is without doubt based on a place in Livy, book 24, which he misunderstood, where the author writes that "the river of Amiternum flowed in flood." Even schoolboys know what those words mean.

units.la: Quinto ab Amiterni Ruderibus lapide alto in monte iacet Episcopalis Urbs Aquila, nunc huius tractus Caput, ab Sulmone xxx P. M. versus Apenninum sita. Natam volunt ex Amiterni ruinis & Forconij, quod P. M. viii hinc aberat, altero latere contra Amiternum, versus Pliciariam amnem, qui locus nunc quoque magna operum fundamenta ex lapide quadrato habet, appellatus Forconum. Condidisse autem perhibent Aquilam Langobardos; Karolum inde Martellum, vel, ut alii placet, Fridericum ii Imperat. moenibus cinxisse, munisseque; Colonis Civium iure, & Civitati Aquila nomine adlignato ab ligno Cæsareo, vel potius ab fausto Aquila nomine. Ea autem brevi maximis incrementis ita auxit, ut Civitatum reliquarum principatum in hac regione facile nunc obtineat. Ab Ludovico Montorio Comite aliquamdiu fuit pollicita sub auspiciis Ferrandi Aragonum regis. Hodie in ditione est Philippi Regis Hispaniarum. De eius conditione, primordio, nominis ratione, rebusque gestis plura Raffanus, Blondus, Leander, Collenutius lib. iii Hist. Reg. & Iovianus Pontanus lib. v Hist. Colitur ab Civibus D. Bernardini, Minorum Ordinis Monachi, Corpus. Clarum Aquila ante paucos annos Ioanne Aquilano Prædicatore, Scriptis claro. Ager mira cum aliarum rerum, tum Croci copia est fœcundus.
units.tr: Five miles from the ruins of Amiternum, on a high mountain, lies the episcopal city of Aquila, now the chief town of this district, situated thirty Roman miles from Sulmo towards the Apennines. Some think it arose from the ruins of Amiternum and of Forconium, which was eight miles away from here, on the other side, opposite Amiternum, towards the river Plisciaria. That place still has large foundations of building work made of squared stone and is called Forconum. They say the Lombards founded Aquila, and that Charles Martel, or, as others prefer, Frederick II the Emperor, surrounded it with walls and fortified it. It was given citizen rights to its colonists, and it took its name Aquila from the imperial eagle, or rather from the auspicious sign of the eagle. In a short time it grew so greatly that it now easily holds first place among the cities of this region. For some time it was held by Count Ludovico Montorio, under the protection of Ferdinand, king of Aragon. Today it is under the rule of Philip, king of Spain. More about its condition, origin, the reason for its name and its history can be found in Raffanus, Blondus, Leander, Collenutius (book 3 of the Historia Regni) and Giovanni Pontano (book 5 of his History). The body of St Bernardine, a monk of the Franciscan Order, is venerated by the citizens. Aquila was famous a few years ago for John of Aquila, a preacher famous for his writings. The countryside is remarkably fertile, both in many other things and in an abundance of saffron.

units.la: Subter fontem dein Aterni in Apennino Mons Regalis est: nec procul inde Pyrus fufigiata, de qua nonnihil capite de Fluminibus, ubi de Aterno.
units.tr: Below the spring of the Aterno in the Apennines is Mons Regalis, and not far from there is the Pyrus fufigiata, about which something was said in the chapter on rivers, where the Aterno is discussed.

units.la: De Peltuinatibus & Aufivatibus Cafmontanis, Vestinorum Populis, apud Plinium, nihil habeo quod dicam; nisi Peltuinas etiam nominari in antiquo Lapide, qui in Auario Lipsij ad Smetij Inscriptiones. De Angolanis & Pinnenfibus, quos Vestinis idem Plinius concenset, nos iam nunc in Marucinis.
units.tr: About the Peltuinates and the Aufivates Cafmontani, peoples of the Vestini in Pliny, I have nothing to say, except that Peltuinas is also named on an ancient stone, which is in Lipsius's Auarium on the Inscriptions of Smetius. About the Angolani and Pinnenses, whom the same Pliny counts among the Vestini, we shall now speak under the Marrucini.

units.la: Hi enim Vestinis succedunt explicandi. Marucini Cæsari, Livio, Statio, alijsque Latinis scriptoribus dicuntur; Μαρύκινοι Straboni; Μαρσύκλου Ptolemæo: qui Marrucini Plinio, Tearmes ita assignanti; cuius rei vestigia, sed corruptissima, etiam deprehendo in Itineraria Tabula; ubi, ut antea indicavi, sic legitur, Tea Nemarucinoceto: emendandum Teate Marrucinorum: Μαρύκινοι Diodoro. Corrupte Μαρρύκινοι apud Memnonem, inquit Ortelius. Marucini, ut Ptolemæus & alij delineant, ab ortu sunt Peligni cum Aterno; ab meridie Vestini & Præcutini; ab occasu Piceni cum Truento; ab Septemtrione Adria. Res ab iis gestas memorat Livius libro ix, ubi Marrucinos, Marsos, Pelignos & Frentanos pacem amicitiamque Populi Romani impetrasse scribit.
units.tr: For these are explained next, after the Vestini. The Marrucini are called by Caesar, Livy, Statius and other Latin writers; Strabo calls them Μαρύκινοι [Marykinoi]; Ptolemy calls them Μαρσύκλου [Marsyklou]; Pliny, who assigns them Tearmes, calls them Marrucini. Traces of this, though very corrupt, I also detect in the Itinerary Table, where, as I pointed out before, it reads: "Tea Nemarucinoceto," which should be emended to "Teate Marrucinorum." Diodorus calls them Μαρύκινοι [Marykinoi]; Memnon, Ortelius says, wrongly calls them Μαρρύκινοι [Marrykinoi]. As Ptolemy and others describe them, the Marrucini are bordered on the east by the Peligni along the Aternus; on the south by the Vestini and Praecutini; on the west by the Picenes along the Truentum; and on the north by the Adriatic. Livy, book 9, records their deeds, where he writes that the Marrucini, Marsi, Paeligni and Frentani obtained peace and friendship from the Roman people.

units.la: Particularis sequitur delineatio, capto ab arduis circa Piscariam vel Aternum montibus initio. In adiacentu igitur illorum sunt Ratanum, Vertorium, Carapellum, mediterranea. Tum infra duobus ab Aterno millibus Capsiranum est; inter alia duo Castella Offenum & Buxum (Bufio) ad amnem, qui vulgo Capo d'Acqua, situm.
units.tr: There follows a detailed description, beginning from the steep mountains around the Pescara or the Aternus. In the neighbourhood of these lie Ratanum, Vertorium and Carapellum, inland towns. Then, two miles below the Aternus, is Capsiranum. Between two other small castles, Offenum and Buxum (Bufio), set by the river commonly called Capo d'Acqua.

units.la: Dein ad Piscariam sunt Cajanio, Turris Antonelis, Petramcum, Alardum, & Rofanum.
units.tr: Then, on the Pescara, are Cajanio, Turris Antonelis, Petramcum, Alardum and Rofanum.

units.la: Sub Nuriæ, Aterno se commiscentis, fonte Monasterium est Casa Nova, ædificiorum pulcritudine, reditibusque amplissimis nobile.
units.tr: Below the spring of the Nuria, where it mingles with the Aterno, is the monastery Casa Nova, famous for the beauty of its buildings and its very rich revenues.

units.la: Ad Septemtrionaliorem Nuriæ ripam opida sunt Cambatoneum, Planellum, Mussofanum, Monte Sirmanus, & Spoletortum.
units.tr: On the northern bank of the Nuria are the towns Cambatoneum, Planellum, Mussofanum, Monte Sirmanus and Spoletortum.

units.la: Inter Tanum porro & Sinum amnes, media prope regione, iv ab ora P. M. Civitas Penne, Citta di Penne, nobile & antiquum Opidum. Pinna Ptolemæo; Pinna Silo, Pinnis Paullo Diacono lib. ii Langbardic. cap. xix. Pinnenses Plinio in Vestinis locantur. Meminit eorum & Valerius Maximus.
units.tr: Between the rivers Tanus and Sinus further on, in the middle of the region, four miles from the coast, is the Civitas Penne, Citta di Penne, a noble and ancient town. Ptolemy calls it Pinna; Silius, Pinna; Paulus Diaconus, Pinnis (book 2 of the History of the Lombards, chapter 19). Pliny places the Pinnenses among the Vestini. Valerius Maximus also mentions them.

units.la: Non procul dein ab Tavo Lauretum in Collibus adparet, Ducatus insigne titulo; itemque Colle Corvinus.
units.tr: Not far from the Tavo, Lauretum appears on the hills, a duchy notable for its title; likewise Colle Corvinus.

units.la: Ad ripam Tavi dexteram jacent Valvianum, Serra, Corvinianum, Risentum, Pinianum, Mons Siccus, Casilentum.
units.tr: On the right bank of the Tavo lie Valvianum, Serra, Corvinianum, Risentum, Pinianum, Mons Siccus and Casilentum.

units.la: Prope Salinum fluvium duobus ab ora milliaribus Opidum Episcopale Portus S. Angeli. Ἀγγελος est Ptolemæo, ut censent Orlandus, Volaterranus, Blondus, Leander, alij. Angeium, ut quibusdam videtur, Antonini. Angulani sunt apud Plinium, in Vestinis eos ponentem.
units.tr: Near the river Salinus, two miles from the coast, is the episcopal town of Portus S. Angeli. Ptolemy calls it Ἄγγελος [Angelos], as Orlandus, Volaterranus, Blondus, Leander and others think. Antoninus calls it Angeium, as some think. Pliny has the Angulani, placing them among the Vestini.

units.la: Propinquo Plumbæ Amnis loco Castellum jacet Illice: tum intus ad eumdem amnem Celinum, & prope fontem Sebiranum: nec procul ab ostio Plumbæ Portus Adriæ, vulgo Porto di Adria, vel, ut alij, Porto de Atri. Ἐπίνειον Ἀδρίας Straboni, ad Matrinum, qui nunc Plumba, illud locanti. Supra dein, Castellum Silnium est.
units.tr: Near the mouth of the river Plumba lies the castle Illice; then inland, on the same river, Celinum, and near its spring Sebiranum. Not far from the mouth of the Plumba is Portus Adriae, commonly called Porto di Adria, or, as others say, Porto de Atri. Strabo calls it Ἐπίνειον Ἀδρίας [Epineion Adrias], placing it near the Matrinus, which is now called the Plumba. Above it, further on, is the castle Silnium.

units.la: Plumbam transgressis inter ipsum & Vomanum amnem medio spatio occurrit Adria, vulgo Atri (alia ab ea, quæ in Transpadanis) Vrbs Episcopalis: arduo montis inlocata jugo. Adria Livio, Plinio, Melæ, Silio lib. viii, Itinerariæ Tabulæ: Ἀδρία Stephano in Ηεγίστεια & Eustathio. Adriam hanc Plinius vii P. M. ab Marsi locat. Livius lib. xi Coloniam agnoscit Romanorum; alibi etiam lib. xxv eius faciens mentionem. Hinc Adriani eidem Livio lib. xxvii. Ortus hinc Adrianus Imperator, ipso teste apud Spartianum. Legendi & Aurelius Victor Paulusque Diaconus, lib. ii. cap. xix, qui imprudenter hanc Vrbem confundunt cum ea, quæ in Romanula, de qua suo loco: adferentes inde Adriatico Sinui nomen factum. Non bene. De Adriani tamen Imperatoris Patria alii aliter. Adriani etiam hinc Agri mentio apud Livium lib. xxii & Plinium lib. iii cap. xiiii. Plinius, Strabo, Ptolemæus hanc in Piceno collocant, quoniam Matrino amne, ut Strabo vocant
units.tr: Having crossed the Plumba, between it and the river Vomanus, at a central point, is Adria, commonly called Atri (a different place from the one in Transpadane Italy), an episcopal city set on the ridge of a steep mountain. Adria is so named by Livy, Pliny, Mela, Silius (book 8) and the Itinerary Table, and Ἀδρία [Adria] by Stephen in his Hegesteia and by Eustathius. Pliny places this Adria seven Roman miles from the Marsi. Livy, book 11, recognises it as a colony of the Romans, and mentions it again elsewhere, in book 25. From it come the Adriani mentioned by Livy, book 27. From here came the Emperor Hadrian, by his own testimony in Spartianus. Aurelius Victor and Paulus Diaconus, book 2, chapter 19, should also be read; they carelessly confuse this city with the one in Romagna, which I will discuss in its place, and derive the name of the Adriatic Sea from it. This is wrong. But on the homeland of the Emperor Hadrian, others think differently. There is also mention here of the Adrianus field in Livy, book 22, and Pliny, book 3, chapter 14. Pliny, Strabo and Ptolemy place this in Picenum, because, as Strabo and Ptolemy call it, the river Matrinus, or, as Pliny calls it, Helvinus, or, as this age calls it, Plumba, is said to bound the region and the Apennines to begin there.

units.la: Ager. cant & Ptolemæus, vel, ut Plinius, Helvino, vel, ut hac ætas, Plumba Trattua nam Regionem finiri, & Pirenæi incipere tradunt.
units.tr: Ager. Pliny, Strabo and Ptolemy also say that the region is bounded by the Matrinus, which Strabo and Ptolemy call..., or Helvinus per Pliny, or, as this age calls it, Plumba; and that the Apennines begin there.

units.la: Pirenæi vero igitur subiungamus, quod post agrum Adrianum Adriamque Coloniam & flumen Vomanum recipiunt Plinius. Pretutium, quod Regio est Ptolemæo, Praetutiani alius, ad ortum habet Vestinum, ad occidentem Sulmo, qua occasus est, Truentum flumen, quae Septentrio Marrucini & Adriaticum Sinum. Inde Tra- ... go Plinio lib. 1. cap. xiii. Praetutiana Regio apud Livium lib. xxii, quae Pegasus Stephano, ... de quo ante addendoque ... Pegasus, Pegasus. Ibi Praetutiana ut habitata antea optima gradum habere, notat Plinius lib. xiiii cap. vi.
units.tr: Now let us add the Apennine region, which, after the Adrian field, the city of Adria and the river Vomanus, Pliny includes. Pretutium, which is a region for Ptolemy, the Praetutiani for others, has the Vestini to the east, Sulmo to the west, where the river Truentum flows to the setting sun, the Marrucini to the north and the Adriatic Sea. Livy, book 22, mentions the Praetutian region; Stephen calls it Pegasus... Pliny, book 1, chapter 13. Pliny, book 14, chapter 6, notes that the Praetutian region, as formerly inhabited, held the best rank.

units.la: Speculabor iam nunc gentis explicemus. Post Plumbam fluvium in ora ostium est Vomanum: cum versus Auctrum adiident Matrila, Mons Fundi, Mons Gradus: tum omnemque ad tonitrum annus. Vici Fragaque multi & Castella frequentia: inter quae Magnum, Caput Tophum, & Porcum, Opida.
units.tr: Now let us explain the peoples. After the river Plumba on the coast is the mouth of the Vomanus. Towards the south lie Matrila, Mons Fundi and Mons Gradus; then, all the way to the Tronto, many villages, hamlets and frequent castles, among which Magnum, Caput Tophum and Porcum are towns.

units.la: Trans Vomanum in ora texto lapide Turdini Flumen est ostium.
units.tr: Across the Vomanus, on the coast, at a marked stone, is the mouth of the river Turdinus.

units.la: Sunt inter Vomanum & Turdinum Opida nauta: quorum ab supremo ad infimum hic fere est ordo; Rofenum, Tegenum, Tinerarium, Kepes Montoriana (Rocca de Materio Mon o tum, Pera toi um, Collis Fetus, Rapinae, Mirnum, Foveella, Cantarinum, Trasfummo, Castellum Ferni, Castellum Novum, Curatum Fonsant, Locarisium, & Morem.
units.tr: Between the Vomanus and the Turdinus are the towns of the seafaring folk. From north to south the order is roughly this: Rofenum, Tegenum, Tinerarium, Kepes Montoriana (Rocca de Materio Mon o tum), Pera toi um, Collis Fetus, Rapinae, Mirnum, Foveella, Cantarinum, Trasfummo, Castellum Ferni, Castellum Novum, Curatum Fonsant, Locarisium and Morem.

units.la: Sequitur Amnis Turdinus: inter quem & Vicinam Turdino se miscentem Civitas est Teranum, ipsum ab ora x. 1 P. M. Caput Praetoriarum, Ducatus & Episcopatus titulo clarum. Ab fine Interamnia Plinio, Interamnia Ptolemæo.
units.tr: Next comes the river Turdinus. Between it and the Vicina, which flows into the Turdinus, is the city of Teranum, ten miles from the coast, famous as the head of the Praetorian region and bearing the title of a duchy and bishopric. From its end it is called Interamnia by Pliny and Interamnia by Ptolemy.

units.la: Ad sinistrum Flumicelli qui ab Vicinia in Turdinum defertur) Castellum est Campanum: iuxtaque fontem amnis Burgum Novum & Infimum.
units.tr: On the left of the Flumicellus, which runs from Vicinia into the Turdinus, is the Campanian castle, and beside the river's source are Burgum Novum and Infimum.

units.la: Haud procul Turdino circa littus Opidum est fere desertum Flavianum, ubi quondam Urbs, quae Ptolemæo Κάστρον, Castrum Novum Plinio, Antonino, & Itinerariae Tabulae. Reduxit hanc Urbem apud Strabonem libro v, Manus doctissimi Calaubori. Nam pro monitoribus illis, ... ex quibus nonnulli Flumen fuerunt, retinent, ... quod omnino probo. De eo sic scribit ad Ortelium Celsus Cittadinus Anglerius: Appellatum hoc fuit postea Castrum S. Fabiani; ... ob aeris malignitatem, infra Iulii Aquarum ... Arrianorum Ducis vulgo de Atri ex illius ruinis edificata fuit sumtibus eiusdem Ducis Iulia Nova, Oppidum in Mediterraneis, ad littus fere militarium.
units.tr: Not far from the Turdinus, near the shore, lies the town of Flavianum, now almost deserted, where once stood the city that Ptolemy calls Kastron, Pliny Castrum Novum, and Antoninus and the Itinerary Table likewise. The most learned Calaubor restored this city in Strabo, book v. For those monitors... some of whom were rivers, they keep... which I entirely approve. Celsus Cittadinus Anglerius writes about it thus to Ortelius: "This was afterwards called Castrum S. Fabiani; ... because of the unhealthy air, below Iulii Aquarum ... it was built from its ruins at the expense of the Duke of the Arriani, commonly called of Atri, as Iulia Nova, a town in the interior, almost on the shore of the soldiers..."

units.la: Parvo huic intervallo abest Mons Paganus; inque Mediterraneis Mesanum, Ripatonum, Tabernaru.
units.tr: A short distance from this lies Mons Paganus; and inland are Mesanum, Ripatonum and Tabernaru.

units.la: Saline fluvio ad Meridiem adlocatum est Monterium, titulo Comitatus ornatum.
units.tr: On the Saline river, to the south, lies Monterium, adorned with the title of county.

units.la: Supra Monterium deinde Pegnum Morellorum, Poggio de i Morelli: altiusque Treia est.
units.tr: Above Monterium is Pegnum Morellorum, Poggio de i Morelli, and higher up is Treia.

units.la: Post in montibus haud procul ab amne, dextra, munitissimum est Opidum Cistella, supra Clivo praealto sita, qua meridiem ex una, ex altera parte Orientem prospectat. Ius descriptio apud Natalem Comitem Historiarum lib. v.
units.tr: Afterwards, in the mountains not far from the river on the right, is the very strongly fortified town of Cistella, set on a steep high slope, which looks towards the south on one side and the east on the other. Its description is in Natalis Comes, Histories, book v.

units.la: Iuxta amnem Libratam in dextra sunt Carapellum & Nerelum; in sinistra vero Tvettoretum, Ad D. Tomasium, & ad D. Algidum haud procul a fonte.
units.tr: Beside the river Librata on the right are Carapellum and Nerelum; on the left are Tvettoretum, Ad D. Tomasium, and Ad D. Algidum, not far from the source.

units.la: Secundum littus ad Truentum properanti locus occurit ubi Opidum D. Floriani erat, superioribus annis ab Iulio, duce Adriano, ob aeris inclementiam subversum, cui successit eiusdem auspiciis aliud tribus ab ora P. M. Iulia Nova.
units.tr: Hastening along the shore towards the Truentus, one comes to a place where there was the town of St Florian, overthrown in earlier years by Julius, the duke Hadrian, because of the unhealthy air. In its place, under the same auspices, another town was built three miles from the shore: Iulia Nova.

units.la: Ad dextram Truenti primum Opidum est Colonia Ductum sequutus Itinerarius, quod Antoninus describit ab Urbe Mediolanensi per Italiæ longitudinem ad Columnam vel Traiectum Siciliæ, omnino centeo hoc fere loco fuisse ante quam Civitatem Truentum. Accedit & Itineraria Tabula, in qua eodem loco scriptum est, Castro Trentino, vitiose pro Castro Truentino. Nam & Castrum Truentinum habet ibidem M. Tullius lib. viii Epist. ad Atticum. Truentum opidum etiam Plinio Pomponioque notum. Truentinae Turres nominat Silius lib. viii.
units.tr: On the right of the Truentus the first town is Colonia. The itinerary Antoninus describes, from the city of Milan through the length of Italy to the Column or the Strait of Sicily, followed this route, and it was certainly at this place, before the city of Truentum. The Itinerary Table agrees, in which the same place is written Castro Trentino, wrongly for Castro Truentino. Marcus Tullius, in book viii of the Letters to Atticus, also has Castrum Truentinum there. The town of Truentum is known also to Pliny and Pomponius. Silius, book viii, names the Truentine towers.

units.la: Supra Columnellam sunt Contrigueria, Ancharanum, Morrum, Murumque Trasimum. Mox ad confluentem cum Truento Castellanum offert sese Asculum, antiquissima Civitas, Episcopatus dignitate nobilis. Asculum quidem Strabo, Plinius & Ptolemaeus in Piceno collocant: sed quia ad australiorem Aterni ripam est positum, Picenum autem ad Borealiorem initium capit, malui coeptum sequutus institutum Samnitibus concenseri. Asculum Caesari lib. 1. Commenta. Silio lib. viii, Livio passim Ἄσκουλον Ptolemaeo; Ἀσκλὰ Stephano Asculum Antonino; Asculus Paulo Diacono lib. ii Langobardic. cap. xix. Asculo Piceno in Itineraria Tabula, ob vicinitatem. Plinius nobilissimam Picenorum colonium appellat. Iacet plano patuloque campo, munitissimo in loco, moenibus firmis. Ab una parte Mons sublimis in quo sita est Arx; ab altera Truentus ripis praealtis munit. Res ab Asculanis & contra ipsos gestas describunt Livius libro lxxxii, lxxxvi, & alibi, L. Florus lib. iii cap. xviii aliique Scriptores. Imperium Urbis diu Romana Ecclesia tenuit, primumque hic ipsius Domini Temporalis, ut vocant, initium. Asculani fuerunt T. Betutius Par-rus, quem omnium extra urbem Romam eloquentissimum appellat M. Tullius in Bruto; Ventidius Bassus bello Parthico Legionum Romanarum Imperator; de quo cum alii, tum Iuvenalis Sat. vi; Nicolaus iiii P. M; Cerus, Astrologus quam Poeta, melior; Enoch Orator eloquens, Orationum aliquot & Epistolarum auctor, Gratia-Dei Theologus & Philosophus, Scriptis itidem clarus: & alij. Aliud est Asculum in Apulia.
units.tr: Above Columnella are Contrigueria, Ancharanum, Morrum and Murum Trasimum. Soon, at the confluence with the Truentus, Castellanum presents itself, and then Asculum, a most ancient city, noble for its episcopal dignity. Strabo, Pliny and Ptolemy indeed place Asculum in Picenum; but since it lies on the more southern bank of the Aternus, while Picenum begins on the more northern side, I preferred to follow the arrangement I had begun and count it among the Samnites. Asculum in Caesar, book i of the Commentaries; in Silius, book viii; in Livy passim; Askoulon in Ptolemy; Ask la in Stephanus; Asculum in Antoninus; Asculus in Paul the Deacon, Lombard History, book ii, chapter xix. Asculo Piceno in the Itinerary Table, on account of its proximity. Pliny calls it the most noble colony of the Picentes. It lies on a flat, open plain, in a very well-protected place, with strong walls. On one side is a high mountain on which the citadel stands; on the other the Truentus defends it with steep banks. The affairs of the Asculani, and what was done against them, are described by Livy in book lxxxii, lxxxvi and elsewhere, by L. Florus, book iii, chapter xviii, and by other writers. The Roman Church held dominion over the city for a long time, and here was the first beginning of its temporal lordship, as they call it. Among the Asculani were T. Betutius Parrus, whom Marcus Tullius in the Brutus calls the most eloquent man outside the city of Rome; Ventidius Bassus, commander of the Roman legions in the Parthian war, of whom both others and Juvenal, Sat. vi, speak; Nicolaus IV, Pope; Cerus, better as an astrologer than as a poet; Enoch, an eloquent orator and author of several orations and letters; Gratia-Dei, a theologian and philosopher, likewise famous for his writings; and others. Asculum in Apulia is another place.

units.la: Per Vallem deinde Castellanam Amatricum devenitur, infra Truenti fontem. Ad Castellani ripas Oppida sunt Mons Sanctus, Machia, Buffarium, & Ad D. Viti. Ablolvimus quos litorales aliquo modo dicere possumus Samnitium Populos, Frentanos, Carentinos, Peligncs, Vestinos, Marucinos, & Praecutinos: sequuntur, qui nulla parte oram attingunt, sed plane mediterranei etiam in alteram Apennini partem, quod Regioni Italiae nulli praeterea commune, se extendunt Hirpini, & Samnites (speciatim sic dicti, junctim ob limitum incertitudinem & indiscretam utriusque gentis vicinitatem explicandi. Hirpinos, ab Coloniae Ductore Lupo, qui Samnitibus Hirpus nomen habuisse, auctores sunt Strabo lib. v & Festus libro ix. Hirpini Plinio lib. v cap. xi, Livio multis locis, Silio lib. xi: Ἱρπινοὶ Straboni libro v; Ἐμνίτες Ptolemaeo & Appiano libro i. Strabo Agrum illis tribuit Lucanis confinalem. Plinius in Secunda locat Italiae regione, in qua & Beneventum. Samnium citra Hirpinos est, a quo tota regio Samnitium nomen adepta. Quidam Urbem fuisse Regionis Caput Samnium, nunc deletam: junt, indeque Samnites huius tractus Incolas esse vocatos. Conregionales Hirpinis, Samnitibusque hic, ab Ortu sunt Lucani; ab Meridie, Campani & Picentini; ab Occasu, Sabini & Vestini; ab Septemtrione, Apuli Dauni in Apennino. De Samnitibus his sic scribit Plinius libro v cap. xii: Samnitium, quos Sabello, & Graeci Saunitas dixere, Colonia Bovianum Vetus, & alterum cognomine Undecumanorum, Aufidenates, Ffernini, Fagi, Fugali, Ficolenses, Sepinates, Treventinates. Alij pro duobus Fagi, Fugali, legunt Fagifulani, de quibus praeterea nil habeo.
units.tr: Then through the Castellan valley one comes to Amatricum, below the source of the Truentus. On the banks of the Castellanus are the towns Mons Sanctus, Machia, Buffarium and Ad D. Viti. We have dealt with the peoples of the Samnites whom we may in some way call coastal: the Frentani, Carentini, Peligni, Vestini, Marrucini and Praecutini. Those follow who touch the coast nowhere but extend wholly inland, even across to the other side of the Apennine, a feature shared with no other region of Italy: the Hirpini and the Samnites (named separately here, though discussed together because of the uncertainty of their boundaries and the close, indistinct neighbourhood of the two peoples). That the Hirpini took their name from Lupus, the leader of the colony, who was called Hirpus among the Samnites, is attested by Strabo, book v, and Festus, book ix. The Hirpini appear in Pliny, book v, chapter xi, in Livy in many places, and in Silius, book xi; Hirpinoi in Strabo, book v; Emnites in Ptolemy and in Appian, book i. Strabo assigns them land bordering the Lucani. Pliny places them in the second region of Italy, in which Beneventum also lies. Samnium lies on this side of the Hirpini, and from it the whole region took the name of the Samnites. Some hold that Samnium was the capital of the region, now destroyed, and that the Samnites of this tract were named after it. The neighbours of the Hirpini and Samnites here are: to the east, the Lucani; to the south, the Campani and Picentini; to the west, the Sabini and Vestini; to the north, the Apulian Daunians in the Apennine. Pliny writes thus about these Samnites in book v, chapter xii: "Of the Samnites, whom the Sabelli and the Greeks called Saunitae, the colonies are Bovianum Vetus, and another with the surname Undecumanorum, Aufidenates, Ferrini, Fagi, Fugali, Ficolenses, Sepinates, Treventinates." Others, for the two names Fagi and Fugali, read Fagifulani, about whom I have nothing further.

units.la: A Benevento Archiepiscopali Civitate principium nobis esto. Id Maleventum olim dictum, post Beneventum dici coepit. Beneventum, ait Plinius lib. iii cap. xi auspicatius mutato nomine, quae quondam appellata Maleventum. Βενεβεντῶ, inquit Stephanus, ἡ πρὸς Μαλεντῶ, &c. Festus libro ii: Beneventum Colonia quum deduceretur appellari coeptum est melioris ominis causa. Namque eam urbem antea Graeci incolentes Μαλοέντον (sic legendum) appellarunt. Vide Nobilis. Virum Iosephum Scaligerum. Procopius libro i de bello Gothico ab Malo Vento deducit, quem injuriosum & horribilem saepe patitur. Non defuerunt, qui Maleventum prius appellatum putent propter ingentem stragem, hic à Sulpicio Petilioque coss. editam, cuius descriptio apud Livium lib. ix. Imprudenter. Maleventi prisci nominis mentionem facit Livius libro ix & x. Idem libro xiii & Plinius libro x Beneventum notant vocari coepisse, quum eo Colonia deduceretur, boni ominis gratia. Beneventum Livio passim, Tacito lib. xv, Antonino, Vibio Sequestro, aliisque notum; Βενεβεντὸν & Ὀυενεβεντῶ Ptolemaeo: Beneventi vulgo. Conditum ab Diomede, testibus Solino in Polyhistore & Servio ad viii Aeneidos: inde χωρίον Διομήδες apud Stephanum. Olim Argyrippam vocatum scribunt Sudas & Cedrenus, non sine errore. De Argyrippa alibi. Situ urbs est admodum oportuno & amoeno, summa
units.tr: Let our starting point be Benevento, an archiepiscopal city. It was formerly called Maleventum; afterwards it began to be called Beneventum. "Beneventum," says Pliny, book iii, chapter xi, "the name having been changed to a more auspicious one, was once called Maleventum." Stephanus says: "Beneventon, which is near Maletum," etc. Festus, book ii: "Beneventum, when a colony was led there, began to be so called for the sake of a better omen. For the Greeks who formerly inhabited that city called it Maloention" (so read). See the noble man Joseph Scaliger. Procopius, book i of the Gothic War, derives the name from Malum Ventum, the ill wind which often troubles it, harmful and dreadful. There were those who thought it was called Maleventum earlier because of the huge slaughter made there by the consuls Sulpicius and Petilius, whose account is in Livy, book ix. Imprudently... Livy, books ix and x, mentions the old name Maleventum. The same author, in book xiii, and Pliny, book x, note that it began to be called Beneventum when a colony was led there, for the sake of a good omen. Beneventum is known from Livy passim, Tacitus, book xv, Antoninus, Vibius Sequester and others; Beneventon and Ouenebenton in Ptolemy; Beneventi commonly. It was founded by Diomedes, as Solinus in the Polyhistor and Servius on the Aeneid, book viii, testify; hence the "place of Diomedes" in Stephanus. Suidas and Cedrenus write that it was formerly called Argyrippa, not without error. More on Argyrippa elsewhere. The city's site is very suitable and pleasant, distinguished by the greatest

units.la: {¹} Asculum Picenum; Episcopatus cuius gentis. summa agrorum bonitate praestans. In Hispania, eorumque Coloniam esse scribit Plinius: in Samnio ponunt Strabo & Ptolemaeus. Campanum Beneventum nominat Antonius his versibus: Cum esset erat Proles Saturnia: Confiss [illegible, ~8 letters] Ioduu quae Corpore Trelias; Tum sucrum etiam Satyri Sarm et Hermaphroditum: Vidit monstrum etiam Ius nero, sed agnum: Nec satis serum, quod Campano in Beneventro Ius plebs Iphseo ius est ergo sepente fuit.
units.tr: {¹} Asculum Picenum; bishopric of which people. ...excelling in the goodness of its fields. In Spain, and Pliny writes that it was their colony; Strabo and Ptolemy place it in Samnium. Antonius names Campanian Beneventum in these verses: ...(the remainder of this footnote is too garbled in the scan to be rendered with confidence).

units.la: Ab Neapoli Beneventum xxx fere M.P. intercedunt. Coloniam Civium Romanorum deductam Beneventum, quo tempore & Arimanum, auctores sunt Livius lib. xxiii, & Velleius lib. ii; quam ob causam & Colonia Pinto dicitur, & in antiquo lapide Coloniae etiam commemoratur Colonarum Liber, quem vide. Concordia Colonia cognominatur apud Frontinum. Cives maximam olim virtutis & disciplinae militaris opinionem apud Romanos habuisse, notum est ex historiis. Ordo beneventanus est in Italia, quae ibi ante summum Templum:
units.tr: From Naples to Benevento there are about thirty Roman miles. That Benevento was settled as a colony of Roman citizens, at the same time as Arimanum, is attested by Livy, book 23, and Velleius, book 2; for this reason it is also called the Colony of Pinto, and the Book of Colonies, which see, also mentions it on an ancient inscription. Frontinus gives it the surname Concordia Colonia. That the citizens of old held the greatest reputation for courage and military discipline among the Romans is well known from the histories. The Beneventan order is in Italy, which there stands before the highest temple:

units.la: CLAVDIO. IVLIO PACATO. V. C. CONS. CAMP OB. AEQVITATEM. IVDICII ET. PATROCINIA. IAM. PRIVATI ORDO BENEVENTANVS PATRONO. POST. FASCES. DEPOSITOS CENSVIT. COLLOCANDAM
units.tr: TO CLAUDIUS JULIUS PACATUS, VIR CLARISSIMUS, CONSUL, CAMPANIAN... The Beneventan order voted that this be set up for their patron, now a private citizen, after he had laid down the fasces, because of his fairness in judging and his patronage.

units.la: Plebem Beneventanam nominat alia Bisis, quae in Vico Fabrum Ferrariorum:
units.tr: Another inscription, the one at Bisis which is in the Vicus of the Fabri Ferrarii, names the Beneventan commons (plebs):

units.la: T. AVONIO. MARCELLINO V. C. CONS. CAMP. PATRO NO. DIGNISSIMO. OB. IN SIGNIA. BENEFICIA. QVI BVS. LONGA. POPVLI. TÆ DIA. SEDAVIT VNIVER SA. PLEBS. BENEVENTA NA. CENSVIT. PONENDAM
units.tr: To T. Avonius Marcellinus, a most distinguished man, consul, most worthy patron of the Campus, in return for his remarkable benefits, by which he long calmed the whole people, the entire Beneventan commonalty voted that this be set up.

units.la: Martyrio Beneventi adfectus est cum aliis Ianuarius, Episcopus sub Diocletiano. Nobilitarunt hanc urbem ortu suo Orosius Grammaticus, Magister aetate Ciceronis plagiolus; Gregorius VIII P.M; Koffredus & Odofredus, Iureconsulti celeberrimi. Nobiles hic Familiae non paucae, quae vulgo: Capo-bianchi. | Mansellii. | Pesciey. Condestabili. | Mascambruni. | Savariani. Controvieri. | Mazzilli. | Velata. Di Gregorio. | Di Pacca. | & aliae.
units.tr: Ianuarius, bishop under Diocletian, was put to death at Benevento together with others. Orosius the grammarian, a petty plagiarist and teacher in the age of Cicero, ennobled this city by his birth; so did Gregory VIII, Pope; and Koffredus and Odofredus, most celebrated jurists. Several noble families are also found here, commonly called: Capo-bianchi; Mansellii; Pesciey; Condestabili; Mascambruni; Savariani; Controvieri; Mazzilli; Velata; Di Gregorio; Di Pacca; and others.

units.la: Viam à Beneventô Brundisium usque Nervam Traianum fecisse, loquitur viae Terminus, qui Alculi:
units.tr: That Nerva Trajan built the road from Benevento all the way to Brundisium is attested by the milestone at Alculi, which reads:

units.la: IMP. CÆSAR DIVI. NERVÆ. F. NERVA. TRAIANVS AVG. GERM. DACIC PONT. MAX. TR. POT. XIII. IMP. VI COS. V P. P.
units.tr: EMPEROR CAESAR, SON OF THE DEIFIED NERVA, NERVA TRAJAN AUGUSTUS, CONQUEROR OF GERMANY AND DACIA, SUPREME PONTIFF, HOLDER OF TRIBUNICIAN POWER FOR THE THIRTEENTH TIME, IMPERATOR FOR THE SIXTH TIME, CONSUL FOR THE FIFTH TIME, FATHER OF HIS COUNTRY.

units.la: VIAM A. BENEVENTO BRVNDISIVM. PICVM SVA. FECIT
units.tr: He made the road from Benevento to Brindisi at his own expense.

units.la: Ager suburbicarius vulgo dicitur Valle, vel Dell'retto di Beneveto; multorum millium. Beneventum Vrbs ab Hannibale primum (Videndus Livius lib. xxii, xxiv, xxv & xxvii) directa, dein ab Totila Gothorum Rege (Blondus lib. vi. Histor.) eversa, & ab Langbardis postea est refecta, qui, tota Italia occupata, sedem & domicilium Imperij sui una cum Beneventani Ducatus nomine hic constituerunt, quod annos stetit fere ducentos; donec sublata ab Karolo Magno eorum Dominatione, in potestatem ac ditionem venit Regum Italicorum. Iterum aliquot annis post ab Saracenis vexata est & cremata: ijs deinceps Italia pulsis, instaurata denuo; sed non ita multo post ab Othone II Imperatore vi expugnata est, & vastata. Blondus lib. xiii Histor. Tandem ab Gulielmo Normanno, qui Regnum Siciliae post adeptus, reaedificata, Pontificis Romani Imperio parere est jussa: quam tamen aliquanto post rursus ab Friderico II Imp. direptam eversamque esse, Platina in Vita Hadriani iv, & Gregorij ix, & Blondus libro xv & xvii testatur. A quo postea refecta sit, non legitur.
units.tr: The district is commonly called Valle or Dell'retto di Beneveto, and it is many miles in extent. Beneventum was first destroyed by Hannibal (see Livy, books 22, 24, 25 and 27), then overthrown by Totila, king of the Goths (Blondus, Histories, book 6), and afterwards rebuilt by the Lombards. When they had occupied all of Italy, they established the seat and centre of their rule here, together with the name of the Duchy of Benevento, which lasted nearly two hundred years, until Charlemagne abolished their dominion and the town came under the power and authority of the kings of Italy.
