A few years later it was harassed and burned by the Saracens; after these were driven out of Italy it was restored again, but not long after, Emperor Otto II took it by force and laid it waste (Blondus, Histories, book 13). At last it was rebuilt by William the Norman, who afterwards won the kingdom of Sicily, and it was ordered to obey the Roman pontiff. Yet some time later Emperor Frederick II plundered and overthrew it again, as Platina in the lives of Hadrian IV and Gregory IX, and Blondus in books 15 and 17, attest. By whom it was afterwards restored is not recorded.

units.la: Sex a Benevento P. M. inter Colles Opidum est Mons Fasciolus, supraque id Turrus & Mons Militus.
units.tr: Six miles north-west of Benevento, among the hills, lies the town Mons Fasciolus, and above it Turrus and Mons Militus.

units.la: Circa Vallem, quam Sabbatus perfluit, Beneveto propinquam, sunt Mons Falco, Candida, Serpinum; supraque altissimis in montibus Tremulis, Episcopalis Civitas Vulturata.
units.tr: Around the valley which the river Sabbato flows through, near Benevento, lie Mons Falco, Candida and Serpinum; and high up in the mountains, at Tremulis, is the episcopal city Vulturata.

units.la: Supra Beneventum ad Calorem visuntur Iapygium, Cusanum, Castellum Vetus, & altius Mentella Opidum, Comitatus titulo clarum.
units.tr: Above Benevento, on the Calore, are seen Iapygium, Cusanum, Castellum Vetus, and higher up the town Mentella, famous for its countship.

units.la: Ad alteram Caloris ripam sunt Apicium, Mirabella, Taurasum, Cusanum aliud, Raniolum (Pagnolo) Cusanum & Noscum.
units.tr: On the other bank of the Calore lie Apicium, Mirabella, Taurasum, another Cusanum, Raniolum (Pagnolo), Cusanum and Noscum.

units.la: Sabbatum transigreslo se offere, Tripalco, Fluvio vicinum, Opidum Tripalta, Ferrariis officinis notum, Marchionatusque dignitate ornatum. Cives Hippolyti Martyris ossa in primario templo servare se gloriantur.
units.tr: Crossing the Sabbato, one meets Tripalta, a town near the river Tripalco, known for its iron foundries and adorned with the dignity of a marquisate. Its citizens boast that they keep the bones of the martyr Hippolytus in their principal church.

units.la: Sequitur ad Tripaltum amnem Silva Latronibus infamis Tripaltina: & supra eam prope flumen Fenettum, Crypta (Grotta) Menarda, Flumarium, Mileum, Amandum, Iunculum; & in Apennino Mons Grumus, quondam ita dictus, nunc Crepacotus.
units.tr: Following the river Tripalto comes the forest Tripaltina, notorious for robbers; and above it, near the river Fenettum, are Crypta (Grotta) Menarda, Flumarium, Mileum, Amandum and Iunculum; and in the Apennines Mons Grumus, formerly so called, now Crepacotus.

units.la: Iuxta Fluvios Tripaltum & Miscanum Opida jacent Cursanum, Mons Calvus, Arianum, Colli aspero & difficili insitum, olim, ut Volaterranus vult, Ara Iani, nihil tamen antiquitatis prae se ferens. Titulum nunc habet Comitatus.
units.tr: Beside the rivers Tripaltum and Miscanum lie the towns Cursanum, Mons Calvus and Arianum, set on a rough and difficult hill, which was once, as Volaterranus holds, Ara Iani, though it shows no sign of antiquity. It now has the title of a county.

units.la: Haud procul inde trans Miscanum in Valle Mons Malus, Bonalbergium, Casale Arboris, & Castellum Francum.
units.tr: Not far from there, across the Miscanum, in the valley lie Mons Malus, Bonalbergium, Casale Arboris and Castellum Francum.

units.la: Pergo porro ad Tamarum Fluvium, cui adsident ad Orientalem quidem ripam Padula, Ad D. Gregorij, Molinaria, Castle Ini, Rignanum, Ad D. Mariae, Colles, Cericelum, Coffianum, ad Crucem Sanctam: ad Occidentalem vero; Petra Paticina, Pavonum, Pestulonium, Farnelum, Campus Lotharius, Monasterium Iuliorum (de Giuliis) Marconium, Saxum Honorij; & in Apennino Sepinum; quod antiquum nomen retinet. Sapinum enim dicitur Livio libro x, ubi res ad opidum illud gestas victoriamque Papirij piri} commemorat: Σεἰμνττ Ptolemæo. Sepinum etiam in antiquo Marmore. Hinc Sepinates Plinio. Colonriam esse docet Frontinus. Inlustravit ortu suo Angelus Sepinas, Philosophos & Medicus insignis.
units.tr: I proceed further to the river Tamarus, on whose eastern bank sit Padula, Ad D. Gregorij, Molinaria, Castle Ini, Rignanum, Ad D. Mariae, Colles, Cericelum, Coffianum and Ad Crucem Sanctam; on the western bank are Petra Paticina, Pavonum, Pestulonium, Farnelum, Campus Lotharius, Monasterium Iuliorum (de Giuliis), Marconium and Saxum Honorij; and in the Apennines Sepinum, which keeps its ancient name. For Livy in book 10 calls it Sapinum, where he recounts the events at that town and the victory of Papirius; Ptolemy gives it as Σήπινον [Sepinum]. Sepinum is also found on an ancient marble. Hence the Sepinates of Pliny. Frontinus teaches that it was a colony. Angelus Sepinas, a notable philosopher and physician, made it famous by his birth.

units.la: Sequitur Alta-Villa, Principatus titulo celebris: supra quam in Apennini jugo Castellum Vetus est.
units.tr: Next comes Alta-Villa, famous for its title of principality; and above it, on the ridge of the Apennines, is Castellum Vetus.

units.la: Ad Sabbati dextram infra in planiciem redeunt sub colle Mille Passuum ab amne, antiquum: se pandit Oppidum Telesia. Sic apud Livium, inter Samnij opida libro xxi & xxiv referentem, Antoninum, aliosque scribi video: Τελεσία autem apud Straboneum, Venafro adjungentem: quae duplici σ τηλεσία Ptolemæo, Telesia est in Itineraria Tabula, pro Telesia. Colonys connumerat Frontinus. Hodie Telesia, Episcopatus titulo florens. 10
units.tr: Down on the plain, to the right of the Sabbato, below the hill a thousand paces from the old river-bank, lies the town Telesia. This is how Livy, Antoninus and others write it, when they list the towns of the Samnites in books 21 and 24; but Strabo, who joins it to Venafrum, writes Τελεσία [Telesia]. Ptolemy has it with a double sigma, Τηλεσία, and in the Itinerary Table it is Telesia. Frontinus counts it among the colonies. Today it is Telesia, flourishing with the title of a bishopric. 10

units.la: Haud procul inde ad Sabbatum vetus ortum Oppidum est Limata: hinc ad Pentem quatuor intercedunt Torrentes, qui conrivati uno ostio in Sabbatum feruntur: quorum fontibus vicina sunt, Ad D. Laurentium, Ad D. Lupam, Pons Landulphi, & Casalonium.
units.tr: Not far from there, near the Sabbato, stands the old town Limata. From here to Pente there are four streams, which join and flow into the Sabbato through a single mouth. Near their sources lie Ad D. Laurentium, Ad D. Lupam, Pons Landulphi and Casalonium.

units.la: Sabbatum transgredior, cui ad meridiem miscetur Scutellaria cujus ripas opida visuntur Castellum Potonium, Pescolia, Mons Saticulus. Saticula Livio libro vii & ix: Σατικυλα Diodoro lib. xix & Stephano. Colonia vocat Paterculus. Saticulus asper Virgilii est, referente Servio, in Campania, fortean ob vicinitatem. Saticulanus Ager est apud Livium libro ab Urbe condita xxiiii.
units.tr: I cross the Sabbato, into which the Scutellaria flows from the south. On its banks are seen the towns Castellum Potonium, Pescolia and Mons Saticulus. Livy in books 7 and 9 calls it Saticula; Diodorus in book 19 and Stephanus write Σατικυλα [Saticula]. Paterculus calls it a colony. Servius, citing Virgil's Saticulus asper, places it in Campania, perhaps because it is nearby. The Saticulan territory is mentioned in Livy's history from the founding of the city, book 24.

units.la: In proximo deinde Caudini Vallis est, quae (Benevento, interfluente Amne, P.M. octo ferme abest: nunc Valle di Gardano dicta, testibus Collenutio & Leandro. Visuntur ibi antiquae urbis vestigia, quae Caudium Livio libro ix & aliis in locis, Καυδιον Straboni (male apud eum uno loco καλλιον) & Ptolemæo: quorum Interpretes male vertunt Cinsium. Caudinum Colonys adcensetur Frontino; ubi M. S. Codices, indicante Scriverio mco Caudium, rectius. Hinc Caudini Populi circa Hirpinos nominantur Plinio. Caudina Furca vel Furcula Livio, qui libro ix scite depingit, Floro, Valerio Maximo, Lucano, Plinio in Epistolis, & aliis: insigni Romanorum, quorum Legiones sub jugum hic miserunt T. Veturio Calvino & Sp. Postumio Cos s. Samnites, ignominia nobiles. Historiam narrant praeter alios Livius lib. ix. Caudinæ Fauces dicuntur Silio lib. viii. Hodie Stretto di Arpaia, Angustias Harpadis nominant ab Oppido propinquo; & ubi sub jugum Romani transierunt Iugum dicitur D. Maria. Caudinum Iugum etiam est apud Quintilianum. 30
units.tr: Next comes the Caudine Valley, which lies about eight miles from Benevento, with a river flowing between them. It is now called Valle di Gardano, as Collenutio and Leandro testify. There are visible remains of an ancient city, which Livy in book 9 and elsewhere calls Caudium; Strabo writes Καυδιον [Caudion] (wrongly, in one place, καλλιον [kallion]), and Ptolemy likewise; their translators wrongly render it Cinsium. Frontinus counts Caudinum among the colonies, where the manuscripts, as my friend Scriverius points out, read Caudium, which is more correct. Hence the Caudini Populi are named by Pliny as near the Hirpini. The Caudine Fork or Little Fork is named by Livy, who describes it skilfully in book 9, and by Florus, Valerius Maximus, Lucan, Pliny in his Letters and others: a notable disgrace to the Romans, whose legions were sent under the yoke here by T. Veturius Calvinus and Sp. Postumius, consuls, and the Samnites were made famous by the shame. Livy in book 9, among others, tells the story. The Caudine Gorges are named by Silius in book 8. Today they are called Stretto di Arpaia, the Narrows of Harpadium, from the nearby town; and the place where the Romans passed under the yoke is called Iugum D. Maria. The Caudine Yoke is also mentioned by Quintilian. 30

units.la: Haud procul etiam à Monte Saticulo Civitas est Harpadium, vulgo Harpaia: Antiquis Hirpinum, ut Blondus tradit. Irpinum apud Ciceronem est, sine adspiratione.
units.tr: Not far from Mount Saticulus is the city Harpadium, commonly Harpaia; in antiquity it was Hirpinum, as Blondus relates. Irpinum in Cicero is written without the aspirate.

units.la: Sequuntur ab alia parte Vallis Caudinæ Opida Ad D. Martini, Penna Sturnina, Ad D. Angeli Scalas, dicitur Scalæ.
units.tr: On the other side of the Caudine Valley follow the towns Ad D. Martini, Penna Sturnina and Ad D. Angeli Scalas, which is called Scalae.

units.la: In Valle Amnis, qui de Monte Virginis altissimo in Sabbatum fluit, Opida sunt Alta-Villa, Monsque Freddanus & in propinqua Convalle vetus Civitas Abellinum. Sic Plinio vocatur Ἀβέλλινον etiam Ptolemæoi, cui, ut & Straboni, alia est Ἀβέλλα in Campania, ut ibi dictum. Hodie Avellino. Hinc Abellinates Plinio, Protropi & Marsi cognominati: Avellinates Lucano. In libro Fisci Pontificij Urbis huius Antistes Avellinensis dicitur Episcopus: alterius in Campania, Avellinum. In Glossario Graeco-Latino haec lego: Ἀσρμαϊ ... Ἀβέλλανος Beneventanum. Nescio an scripserit Ἀβέλλανος, cujus quidem usus in Agro Beneventano, unde Beneventanum; sed quod Abellini parabatur, unde Ἀβελλανὸν. 40
units.tr: In the valley of the river which flows from the high Mount Virgil into the Sabbato lie the towns Alta-Villa and Monsque Freddanus, and in a nearby hollow the ancient city Abellinum. Pliny calls it so, and Ptolemy Ἀβέλλινον [Abellinon]; Strabo likewise, though there is another Ἀβέλλα [Abella] in Campania, as is said there. Today it is Avellino. Hence the Abellinates of Pliny, surnamed Protropi and Marsi; Avellinates in Lucan. In a book of the Papal Fisc the bishop of this city is called the Bishop of Avellinensis; the other Avellinum is in Campania. In a Greco-Latin glossary I read: Ἀσρμαϊ ... Ἀβέλλανος [Abellanos], Beneventan. I do not know whether he wrote Ἀβέλλανος [Abellanos], which is in use in the territory of Benevento, whence Beneventanum; but what was prepared at Abellinum was called Ἀβελλανὸν [Abellanon]. 40

units.la: Altius deinde aspero in loco Mercuriale est opidum, cujus apud Antoninum est mentio. 50
units.tr: Higher up, in a rough place, is the town Mercuriale, which is mentioned by Antoninus. 50

units.la: Hinc in alia Convalle Nigra Palus, & Serinum: nec procul inde locus, qui Forino vernacule, cum Cæmiterio D. Felicissimi.
units.tr: From here, in another hollow, lie Nigra Palus and Serinum; and not far from there is the place which in the vernacular is Forino, with the cemetery of St Felicissimus.

units.la: Occidentaliora hinc Petam Loca Silari Vulturnique Fontibus vicina: in quis non postremæ classis Sora. Sic Latinis scribitur; Σώρα Græcis. Plinius in i Regione memorat, ubi Latium, in quo recenset etiam Ptolemæus; Strabo in Campania Felice. Alij, quibus & ego consentio. Samnitibus tribuunt, cum quod in Vestinis, Samnitium gente, sit, ut alibi dictum: tum quod ab Samnitibus de Volcis capta legatur apud Livium lib.x. Vicina est Liri Amni; populo haud infrequens, titulo-que tuloque Ducatus & Episcopatus ornata. Coloniam eo ab Romanis ductam, notant Livius lib. ix & x, Paterculus libro 1, Frontinus de Colonijs: ideoque Colonys annumeratur à Plinio libro iii cap. v. Soram Cicero pro Plancio Municipium vocat. Diu sub Imperio Romano floruit. Direptam crematamque ab Friderico II Imper. auctores sunt Blondus lib. xvii Histor. & Platina in Vita Gregorij ix. Quis postea refecerit, non legi.
units.tr: Further west from here, towards the sources of the Silarus and Volturnus, lies Sora, not the least of the fleet. The Latins write it so; the Greeks Σώρα [Sora]. Pliny mentions it in the first region, where Latium is, and Ptolemy also places it in Latium; Strabo puts it in Campania Felix. Others, with whom I agree, assign it to the Samnites, partly because it lies among the Vestini, a Samnite people, as is said elsewhere, and partly because Livy in book 10 says it was taken from the Volsci by the Samnites. It lies near the river Liris, is not sparsely populated, and is adorned with the title of a duchy and of a bishopric. Livy in books 9 and 10, Paterculus in book 1, and Frontinus in his work on colonies note that the Romans established a colony there; hence Pliny in book 3, chapter 5, counts Sora among the colonies. Cicero in his speech for Plancius calls Sora a municipium. It flourished for a long time under Roman rule. That it was plundered and burned by Emperor Frederick II is attested by Blondus in book 17 of his Histories and by Platina in the life of Gregory IX. By whom it was afterwards restored I have not read.

units.la: Confluunt paullo infra Soram duo Amnes, qui Liri praebent initium; itá ut Peninsulam quasi faciant, in qua praeter Soram sunt Pescum, Posta, Lobrutallium.
units.tr: Just below Sora two rivers join to form the source of the Liris, so that they make a kind of peninsula, in which, besides Sora, lie Pescum, Posta, Lobrutallium.

units.la: Hinc Peninsulae ad Ortum peramoena & fertilis est Regio, quam Comitium dicunt, ab Antiqua Urbe Comita, cuius meminit Livius libro 4 & alibi.
units.tr: From the peninsula eastward lies a very pleasant and fertile district, which they call Comitium, after the ancient town Comita, which Livy mentions in book 4 and elsewhere.

units.la: Castella hic non infrequentia, Vitulum, Alatium, Ad D. Donati, ad Septem Fratres, Piscinestum, Calinarium, Casale Iocrum, & Atina, civitas antiquissima, cujus meminerunt Virgilius libro VII inter Urbes quae Turnum armis iuverunt, Livius multis locis, praecipue libro IX, & Silius libro VIII. Pomponius Sabinus eam in excelso colle describit post Fabateriam versus Ictum. Atinates Plinius in prima numerat Regione. Ptolemaeus Atinum etiam in Latio ponit, in Campania juxta Pomptinas Paludes locat Servius: Alij commodius in Samnitibus: Creat diversitatem hanc vicinitas. Colonys concenset Frontinus.
units.tr: There are not a few small settlements here: Vitulum, Alatium, Ad D. Donati, ad Septem Fratres, Piscinestum, Calinarium, Casale Iocrum, and Atina, a very ancient town. Virgil in book 7 mentions it among the towns that aided Turnus in arms, Livy mentions it in many places, especially in book 9, and Silius in book 8. Pomponius Sabinus describes it on a high hill beyond Fabateria, towards Ictus. Pliny counts the Atinates in the first region. Ptolemy places Atinum in Latium, while Servius places it in Campania near the Pomptine Marshes; others more suitably place it among the Samnites. The neighbourhood of these places creates this disagreement. Frontinus reckons it among the colonies.

units.la: Sub Casali Vero ad Melphem modicum inveniturt Castellum Sclaterum, Sclia-rone infraque asperrimo in colle Arpinum Arpino hodie inter Soram & Aquinum) Opidum Livio multis locis, praecipue libro ix, aliisque celebratum. Hinc Arpinates Plinio in prima Regione, & Silio lib. v. ii. Coloniam eo deductam scribit Livius libro ix. Arpinates Civitate donatos tradit idem libro x & xxxviii. De Municipio Arpino M. Tullius pro Planco & de Claris Oratoribus. Festus Arpinum inter eas numerat Praefectura, in quas Praetor singulis annis Praefectos mittebat, iremque interea Municipia, quae sui erant juris. Celeberrimum hoc Opidum ortu C. Marij, septies Consulis, de quo nulli non Scriptores. In huius Agro Arpinatem Fundum nominat Cicero ad suam Terentiam.
units.tr: Below the settlement of Casalis, near Melpha, there is a small castle called Sclaterum, Sclia-rone. Further down, on a very steep hill, lies Arpinum, today Arpino, between Sora and Aquinum, a town celebrated by Livy in many places, especially in book 9, and by others. Hence the Arpinates in Pliny's first region, and in Silius book 5 (ii). Livy writes in book 9 that a colony was led there; in book 10 and book 38 he says the Arpinates were granted citizenship. M. Tullius speaks of the municipality of Arpinum in his speech for Plancius and in De claris oratoribus. Festus counts Arpinum among those prefectures to which the praetor used to send prefects every year, while the municipalities, which were their own masters, remained in the meantime. This town is very famous as the birthplace of C. Marius, seven times consul, of whom every writer speaks. Cicero, in a letter to his Terentia, names the Arpinatem Fundum in this territory.

units.la: Sorae versus Austrum est Villa D. Dominici, ubi Fibrenus Liri miscetur: tribus ab Arpino P. M. ubi M. Tullium in lucem editum, ait Petrus Marius. Ipse sane de Natali loco sic scribit lib. II de LL. Sed ventum in Insulam est: haec vero nihil est amoenius: ut enim hoc quasi rostro findetur Fibrenus, & divisus aequaliter in duas partes latera hac alluit, rapideque diffusus cito in unum confluit, & tantum complectitur, quod satis sit modica palaestra loci: quo effectio, tamquam id habuerit operis ac muneris, ut hanc nobis aequaret sedem ad disputandum, statim praecipitat in Lirem, & quasi in Familiam Patritiam venerit, amissis nomen obscurius, Liremque multo gelidiorem facit. Nec enim ullum hoc frigidius flumen attigi, quum ad multa accesserim, ut vix pede tentare id possim, quod in Phaedro Platonis fecit Socrates. Paullo vero prius idem his verbis fuerat usus: Haec est mea & huius Fratris mei germani Patrimonium: hinc enim orti sirpe antiquissima sumus, hic Sacra, hic Genus, hic Maiorum multa Vestigia: quid plura? hanc vides Villam, ut nunc quidem est, lautius aedificatam Patris nostri studio: qui quum esset infirma valetudine, hic fere aetatem egit in litteris: sed hoc ipso in loco quum Atius viveret, & antiquo more parva esset villa, ut illa Curiana in Sabinis, mescito esse natum.
units.tr: South of Sora is the Villa of St. Dominic, where the Fibrenus mingles with the Liris, three miles from Arpinum, where Petrus Marius says M. Tullius was born. Cicero himself writes about his birthplace in this way in book 2 of De legibus: "But we came to the island; and indeed nothing is more pleasant than this place. For the Fibrenus is split as if by a beak, and, divided equally into two parts, washes these banks on either side, and then, rapidly spreading out, quickly flows together again into one, and encloses only so much ground as is enough for a modest exercise-ground. As if it had taken on this task and office, so that it might give us a seat equal to debate, it at once plunges into the Liris, and, as if it had come into a patrician family, having lost its more obscure name, makes the Liris much colder. For I have never touched a river that is colder, though I have approached many, so that I can scarcely test it with my foot, as Socrates did in Plato's Phaedrus." A little earlier the same author had used these words: "This is my own and my brother's ancestral estate; for from here we have sprung from a very ancient stock; here are our sacred rites, here our family, here many traces of our ancestors. Why say more? You see this villa, as it now is, built more splendidly through the zeal of our father, who, being in poor health, spent most of his life here in study. But in this very place, while Atius lived, and the villa was small in the old manner, like that Curian villa among the Sabines, I was born, as it were."

units.la: Sub Arpino prope Melphem Opida sunt Fontanum & Arceum: supraque, ubi duo Liris capita in unum coeunt Insula Castrum: olim, ut censent Blondus, Leander, Cittadinus, Niger, & alij, quod inter duos Amnes, Interamnia Straboni, quod ad confluentes Liris & Cafini. Coloniam factam docent Livius lib. ix & x, Paterculus lib. 1, & antiquus Lapis. Hinc Interamnates Plinio, cognomine Sucusani Lirinates, ut sine copula legit Ortelius. De ijs Inscriptio, quae apud Onuphrium in Imperio Romano:
units.tr: Near Melpha, below Arpinum, are the towns Fontanum and Arceum. Above them, where the two heads of the Liris join into one, is Insula Castrum. Formerly, as Blondus, Leander, Cittadinus, Niger and others think, it was Interamnia of Strabo, so called because it lies between two rivers, near the confluence of the Liris and the Casinus. Livy in books 9 and 10, Paterculus in book 1, and an ancient stone show that it was made a colony. Hence Pliny has the Interamnates, with the surname Sucusani Lirinates, as Ortelius reads it without a conjunction. There is an inscription about them, which is found in Onuphrius in Imperium Romanum:

units.la: P. TVRCIO P. F. STEL. SEVERO II VIRO. CVRAT. REIP. INTERAMNAT LIRIN. EORVMDEM. PATRONO, COL CASSINATES
units.tr: P. TURCIUS SEVERUS, SON OF PUBLIUS, OF THE STELLA TRIBE, DUUMVIR, CURATOR OF THE STATE OF THE INTERAMNATES ON THE LIRIS, AND THEIR PATRON: THE CASSINATE COLONISTS

units.la: Secundum ejusdem fluminis decursum Opida visuntur Turres, Campus Largus, Infuleta.
units.tr: Following the course of the same river are the settlements Turres, Campus Largus, Infuleta.

units.la: Occurrit ab his locis versus Ortum procedenti Aquinum. Sic Latinis dictum; inter alios Silio Italico libro viii, Antonino, & Itinerariæ Tabulæ: Akuïnov Ptolemæo: Akuïnov, inquit Strabo, μεγάλη πόλις ... Legendum ex Ptolemæo Aquinum. In Latio ponit Ptolemæus; in Prima regione Plinius. Municipiū jus habuisse paret ex Ciceronis Oratione pro Plancio. Coloniam inde factam, referunt Frontinus & Plinius lib. iii cap. v. Hinc Colonia Aquinas Livio libro xxvi & Tacito libro xvi. Aquinates hinc Silio lib. xii. Nati hic Pesceunius Niger Imperat. retulibus Herodiano & Iuvenale; & Vitruvius, summus Geometra. Nobilitavit etiam eam Patriam suam Thomas magnus Philosophus; Aquinas hinc cognominatus. Nomen retinens collapsa pene jacet, vestigia præterens pristinæ amplitudinis: Comitatus Episcopatusque habens titulum.
units.tr: Proceeding eastward from these places one comes to Aquinum. It is so called in Latin by, among others, Silius Italicus in book 8, by Antoninus, and in the Itinerary Tables; Ptolemy writes it Ἀκουῖνον [Akuinon]; Strabo says, μεγάλη πόλις [megale polis], "a great city". It should be read from Ptolemy as Aquinum. Ptolemy places it in Latium; Pliny in the first region. That it had the rights of a municipality appears from Cicero's speech for Plancius. Frontinus and Pliny in book 3, chapter 5, report that a colony was made there. Hence the Colonia Aquinas in Livy book 26 and Tacitus book 16. The Aquinates are mentioned from here by Silius in book 12. Born here were Pescennius Niger, the emperor, according to Herodian and Juvenal, and Vitruvius, the greatest geometer. It also made its homeland famous through Thomas, the great philosopher, who is surnamed from Aquinas. Keeping its name, it lies almost fallen to ruin, showing traces of its former grandeur; it has the status of a county and an episcopal see.

units.la: Haud procul inde in vertice Montis locus monstratur, ubi quondam Casinum, Meminit cum aliis Silius Italicus libro xii de Bello Punico: Nymphisque habitata Catini
units.tr: Not far from there, on the summit of a mountain, a place is pointed out where Casinum once stood. Silius Italicus, among others, mentions it in book 12 of the Punic War: "and Catinum, haunted by nymphs".

units.la: Rura.
units.tr: The Countryside.

units.la: Expressi est & in Itineraria Tabula. Casinum, inquit Varro, Forum Vetus appellant. Καίσινα Agathiæ libro ii quæ Καυλον scribitur in M. S. Codice CL. V. Bonaventuræ Vulcanii, fidelissimi Græcarum Litterarum in Academia Lugdunensi Interpretis, Collega mihi amicissimi. In Casinensi Casino, inquit Paulus Diaconus lib. i. Rerum Langobardicarum cap xxvi, quod Narum appellatur; dicitque i millibus distare ab Sublaco. Pro Harum legit Abrahamus Ortelius Arum ex Floriacensi, quod Avarum apud Marianum Schotum, & Rauram apud Blondum lib. vi Dec. cap. i. Καίρας Strabo præclaram Latinorum Urbem vocat, & xix stadiis ab Capua distare scribit: Plinius in Prima numerat Regione: Casinum habet Livius circa Campaniam. Romanorum Coloniam testatur idem Livius lib. ix. Sic Vetus Inscriptio: P. TVRCIO. P. F. STEL. SEVERO II. VIRO. CVRAT. REIP. INTERAMNAT LIRIN. EORVMDEM. PATRONO. COL CASSINATES
units.tr: It is also shown on the Itinerary Table. Varro says, "They call Casinum Forum Vetus" (Old Market). Agathias, book ii, writes it as Καυλον [Kaulon] in the manuscript codex CL. V. Bonaventura Vulcanius, most faithful interpreter of Greek literature in the Academy of Leiden and my very dear colleague, but Καίσινα [Kaisina] in the text. Paulus Diaconus, book i of the History of the Lombards, chapter 26, says "in the Casinum of Casinum, which is called Narum," and places it one mile from Subiaco. Abraham Ortelius reads Arum for Harum, following the Floriacensis manuscript; Marianus Scotus has Avarum, and Blondus, book vi of the Decades, chapter 1, has Raura. Strabo calls Καίρας [Kairas] an excellent city of the Latins and writes that it is nineteen stadia from Capua. Pliny counts it in the First Region. Livy places Casinum near Campania, and the same Livy, book ix, testifies that it was a Roman colony. So the old inscription: "To P. Turcius Severus, son of Publius, of the Stellatina tribe, duumvir, curator of the state of Interamna Lirinas, patron of the same, the colonists of Casinum."

units.la: Cicero pro Plancio Municipium appellat. Ædes hic fuisse scribitur Apollinis; ubi postea magnificum Casinense Monasterium, sic ab Urbe dictum Benedictus Nursinus, Monachorum in Italia Pater, fundavit: litus ibidem cum Scholastica Sorore. De varia Templi hujus Fortuna Paulus Diaconus lib. vi Histor. Helias Capreolus lib. v Histor. Brix Blondus lib. xi & xvii Hist. Volaterranus libro xxi Comment. Urban. D. Gregorius libro ii Dialog. Casina Arx in Samnio, ubi Monasterium, inquit Eginarchus, D. Benedicti, quod etiam Casinense vocat. Prodigium, quod Casini accidit, narrat Plinius libro vii Nat. Histor. cap. iv. Casinas Mons est in Campania, Platina in Vita Pelagii i, P. M.
units.tr: Cicero in his speech for Plancius calls it a municipium. It is written that there was a temple of Apollo here; later Benedict of Nursia, father of the monks in Italy, founded on this site the famous Monastery of Casinum, so named from the city, together with his sister Scholastica. Paulus Diaconus, book vi of the Histories, Helias Capreolus, book v of the Histories, Biondo Flavio, books xi and xvii of the Histories, Volaterranus, book xxi of the Commentaries on Urbanus, and St. Gregory, book ii of the Dialogues, tell of the various fortunes of this temple. Eginhard calls Casina a citadel in Samnium, where there is a monastery of St. Benedict, which he also calls Casinense. Pliny, book vii of the Natural History, chapter 4, tells of the portent that happened at Casinum. Platina, in the Life of Pelagius I, calls Casinas a mountain in Campania.

units.la: Sequitur in radicibus Casini Montis Orientem versus D. Germani Castrum, Fontium copia abundans. Incolæ majori ex parte Fabri sunt Aeuum.
units.tr: Following at the foot of Mount Casinum, toward the east, is the castle of St. Germanus, abundant in springs. Most of its inhabitants are smiths.

units.la: Vulturni jam alveum utrimque perlustremus, quatenus ad Samnites pertinet.
units.tr: Let us now survey both banks of the Volturnus, as far as it belongs to the Samnites.

units.la: Circa initium Vallis est Rotunda: quam sequuntur Aqua Fundate, S. Vincentij, Mons Niger, Rivus Niger, Mons Aquibus, Arx Ravinieola, Fornuli, Fanum D. Mariae Oliveti, & alia: postea Venafrum in Colle. Sic Livio, Plinio, Silio, Antonino, aliis dicitur; quod Οὐενάφρον cum Appiano & aliis, tum Ptolemæo cui Hirpinorum Urbs est in Samnitibus. In Regione i Plinius, in Campania locat Acron ob vicinitatem. Campanum etiam cognominatur Martiali: Hoc tibi Campani sudavit baccα Venafri; Unguentum quoties sumis, & illud ole.
units.tr: Near the beginning of the valley is Rotunda, followed by Aqua Fundate, San Vincenzo, Mons Niger, Rivus Niger, Mons Aquibus, the citadel Ravinieola, Fornuli, the shrine of St. Mary of the Olive, and others. Then Venafrum, on a hill. Livy, Pliny, Silius, Antoninus and others so call it; the Greeks, Appian and others, write Οὐενάφρον [Ouenaphron], and Ptolemy, for whom it is a city of the Hirpini among the Samnites, does likewise. Pliny in the First Region places it in Campania, because of its nearness to Acerrae. Martial also gives it the surname Campanum: "The Campanian Venafrum's grape sweated this for you; whenever you use an unguent, it is this oil."

units.la: Venafrum unam ex antiquis Præfecturis, in quas Præfectos mittere quotannis erat solitus Prætor, tradit Festus. Colonia jus postea accepit, uti paret ex Frontino Plinioque libro iii cap. v. Venafri vulgo, Episcopatus habens titulum. Venafranum Olium celebratur Iuvenali.
units.tr: Festus reports that Venafrum was one of the ancient prefectures to which the praetor used to send prefects every year. Later it received the status of a colony, as appears from Frontinus and Pliny, book iii, chapter 5. Venafrum is commonly known as having the title of a bishopric. Juvenal celebrates Venafran oil.

units.la: A Vulturno iii P.M. Furnellium cit, frequens & opulentum Opidum.
units.tr: Three Roman miles from the Volturnus lies Furnellium, a populous and wealthy town.

units.la: Ex adversum huic Castello Vallis Porcina conspicitur, inque ea magnæ cuiusdam Urbis Cadaver. Aufernam dico, uti vocant Dionysius Halicarnassæus, Strabo (apud quem male Aιαρνια in Vulgatis libris) Appianus libro i, Ptolemæus, alij: Fernia Silio libro viii; Fernum Itinerariæ Tabulæ. Vitiosè apud Diodorum libro xx Σερνια, pro Εερνια. Sernatum legebatur apud Antoninum & Serri sed restitutum ex Regio Exemplari V. Cl. Hieronymus Surita. De Sernico tamen amplianda censeo, quum Serniatanum Vinum inde denominare videatur Plinius lib. xiii Nat. Hist. cap. vi. Hodie Sergna. Iferninum hinc Plinio & Nonio Marcello. Vulturno Flumini adiacet, auctore Livio libro xab v. c. Ptolemæus in Samnitibus locat: Plinius Fernatus in iv regione memorat. Colonia est apud Frontinum, Velleium Paterculum libro i, Florum ex Livii libro xvi, lxxii, & seq. Illustravit Patrum nostrum memoria hoc Opidum Andreas Aliserninus I C.
units.tr: Opposite this castle the Porcine Valley comes into view, and in it the carcass of a great city. I mean Aufernum, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Strabo (in whom the printed books wrongly have Αιαρνια [Aiarnia]), Appian in book i, Ptolemy and others call it. Silius in book viii calls it Fernia; the Itinerary Table calls it Fernum. Diodorus in book xx wrongly has Σερνια [Sernia] for Εερνια [Eernia]. Antoninus and Serrius had Sernatum, but Hieronymus Surita restored it from the royal copy of a very learned man. Yet I think Sernicum should be reconsidered, since Pliny, book xiii of the Natural History, chapter 6, seems to derive the Serniatan wine from it. Today it is Sergna. Pliny and Nonius Marcellus have Iferninum from here. It lies next to the Volturnus River, according to Livy, book xxxv. Ptolemy places it among the Samnites; Pliny mentions Fernatus in the fourth region. It is a colony according to Frontinus, Velleius Paterculus in book i, and Florus from Livy, book xvi, chapters 72 and following. In our fathers' memory the lawyer Andreas Aliserninus illustrated this town.

units.la: Occurrunt inde ad Pratellum Crapiaia, Pratum. Masliranum, Compluteria, quam vi captam ab Fabio cum Telesia scribit Livius lib. xxiv. In aliis libris legitur Compulteria.
units.tr: From there, toward Pratellum, one meets Crapiaia and Pratum, Masliranum, and Compluteria, which Livy, book xxiv, writes was taken by force by Fabius together with Telesia. In other books it is read as Compulteria.

units.la: Ab Æsernia deinde versus ortum xx ferme lapide, Bovianum occurrit, nobilissima quondam Samnii Urbs, Vetus cognomine: nam aliud fuit Vndeumanorum. Bovianum Livio passim, Silio libro viii, Plinio, alùsque Latinis; Bovianus Frontino; Bovianum Itinerariæ Tabulæ, memendatius; Bοιανον Strabone libro v; Βοιανον Ptolemæo: Bovano hodie: Opidum Episcopale. Bovianum Livius libro ix Pentrorum (in aliis Codicibus Pentrorum, & Pentiorum legitur) appellat caput; opulentissimum & potentissimum eius gentis Opidum describens. Coloniam ab Iulio Cæsare deductam, paret ex Frontino, & Plinio lib. ii cap. xii, eam in Regione iv locante.
units.tr: Then, about twenty miles east of Aesernia, appears Bovianum, once the most noble city of the Samnites, called Vetus (Old) to distinguish it from another, which was Undeumanorum. Bovianum is the form used by Livy throughout, by Silius in book viii, by Pliny and other Latin writers; Frontinus has Bovianus; the Itinerary Table has Bovianum, more correctly; Strabo in book v has Βοιανον [Boianon]; Ptolemy has Βοιανον [Boianon]. Today it is Bovano, an episcopal town. Livy in book ix calls Bovianum the chief town of the Pentri (other codices read Pentrorum and Pentiorum), describing it as the most wealthy and powerful town of that people. That it was a colony founded by Julius Caesar appears from Frontinus and Pliny, book ii, chapter 12, who places it in the fourth region.

units.la: Adscribam huc iter, quod ab Urbe Via Salaria per Vmbriam in Samnites Hadriam duxit Antoninus; commissum cum Itineraria Tabula, vulgataque Nomenclatura. Antoninus. | Itineraria Tabula. | Vulgata Nomencl. Ab Vrbe Hadriam usque M. P. CLVI. sic: | Roma, xi. | Eroiam, M. P. XVIII. | Freo, XIIII P. | Monte Ritundo. Vicum Nouum, M. P. XIII. | Ad Novas, XVI. | ......... Reate, M. P. XVI. | Beate, VIII. | Riete. Cutiliae, M. P. XVIII | Aquae Cutiliae, VII. | Lago di Contiglione, vel Lago de Pie de Luco, ut alij. Sic etiam simpliciter Seneca in Quæst. Naturalib. lib. iii. | Sic etiam vocat Plinius libro xi, cap. xcv. | Interocrium, M. P. VI. | Interocrio, XII. | Interdocho. Falacrinum, M. P. XVI. | Palacrinis, XVI. | S. Silvestri in Phalacrino. Legendum Falacrinis. Vicum Badies: M. P. IX. | Ad Martis, ... | .......... Forte, Vicum Martis. Ad Centesimum, M. P. X. | Magna confusio. | .......... Nam ab Urbe versus Occidentem hoc iter primo ducitur, inde reflectitur in Orientem; quum in Septemtrionem primo mox in Orientem fuisse ducendum. Asculum. M. P. XII. | Asciolim Alius Ασκουλον, & Asculum scribitur. Castrum Trucntinum, M. P. XX. | Castro Tremino, ... | Columella. Castrum Novum, M. P. XII. | Castro Nevo. XII. | Flaviano. Had ram. | Hadria. | Atri.
units.tr: I shall add here the route which Antoninus led from the city by the Via Salaria, through Umbria, into the Hadrian territory of the Samnites. It is compared with the Itinerary Table and the common nomenclature. Antoninus | Itinerary Table | Common Nomenclature. The distance from the city to Hadria is 156 Roman miles, as follows: Rome, 11. Eroia, 18 miles. Freo, 14 miles. Monte Ritundo. Vicus Novus, 13 miles. Ad Novas, 16. ......... Reate, 16 miles. Beate, 8. Riete. Cutiliae, 18 miles. Aquae Cutiliae, 7. Lago di Contiglione, or Lago de Pie de Luco, as others call it. Seneca also simply calls it this in Natural Questions, book iii. Pliny also calls it this in book xi, chapter 95. Interocrium, 6 miles. Interocrio, 12. Interdocho. Falacrinum, 16 miles. Palacrinis, 16. S. Silvestri in Phalacrino. We should read Falacrinis. Vicus Badies, 9 miles. Ad Martis, ... ........... Perhaps Vicus Martis. Ad Centesimum, 10 miles. Great confusion. .......... For this route first leads from the city toward the west, then turns back toward the east; whereas from the north it should have led first and immediately toward the east. Asculum, 12 miles. Asciolim, another form, Ασκουλον [Askoulon], and Asculum is written. Castrum Trucentinum, 20 miles. Castro Tremino, ... Columella. Castrum Novum, 12 miles. Castro Nevo, 12. Flaviano. Hadram. Hadria. Atri.

units.la: Aliud, quod mox apud eundem Antoninum sequitur, ab Urbe Hadriam, Via Valeria.
units.tr: Another route, which in the same Antoninus follows next, from Rome to Hadria by the Via Valeria.

units.la: Antonius: | Itineraria Tabula: | Vulgata Nomencl. Ab Vrbe Hadriam usque M. P. CXI VIII, sic | Roma ..... | Trivoli. Tibur. M. P. XX. | Tibors, VIII. Legend. Tibure. | Arceola. Varia, V. | Lamnas, X. Carseolas M. P. XII. | Carsulu, VI. Legend. Carseolis. | Campagna di Roma,
units.tr: Antoninus: the Itinerary Table; the common names (Nomencl.). From Rome to Hadria, 118 miles, as follows: Rome ..... | Tivoli (Tibur), 20 miles. | Tibors, 8. Read Tibure. | Arceola. Varia, 5. | Lamnas, 10. Carseolae, 12 miles. | Carsulu, 6. Read Carseolis. | Campagna di Roma.

units.la: Livius lib. x Carseolas in agrum Æquicolarum deductam Coloniam perhibet. Ptolemæo itē in Æquicolis Καρσιόλοι. Carseolani Plinio Populi Æquiculanorum. Strabo Carseolas cum Alba in Via Valeria collocat. Albam Fucentiam, M. P. XXV. | Ingens hic iterum confusio in Itineraria Tabula. | ........ʌ Cefsinnia, M. P. XXIII. | Cirfenna. | ........
units.tr: Livy, book 10, says that Carseoli was founded as a colony in the territory of the Aequicoli. Ptolemy likewise places the Καρσιόλοι [Karsiolloi] among the Aequicoli. Pliny calls them the Carseolani, the people of the Aequiculani. Strabo places Carseoli with Alba on the Via Valeria. Alba (Fucentia), 25 miles. Here again there is great confusion in the Itinerary Table. ........ | Cefsinnia, 23 miles. | Cirfenna. | ........

units.la: Alij non meminerunt. Corfinium, ... M. P. XVIà. | Corfinio. Progressu hactenus facto in Orientem, ad hanc Mansionem recurritur iterū in Occidentem; magna confusione. | Campo di S. Pelino Interbromium M. P. XI. | Inter Primum | ........
units.tr: Others do not mention it. Corfinium, ... 16 miles. | Corfinio. Having progressed eastward until now, the route returns westward to this stage; a great confusion. | Campo di S. Pelino: Interbromium, 11 miles. | Inter Primum | ........

units.la: Ultrum melius, nondum video. Teate Marrucinum, M. P. XVII. | Tes Ngmarucinoceio, Leg. Teate Marrucinorum. | Chieti. Confusio. Hadriam, M. P. XIIII. | Hadria. | Atri.
units.tr: I do not yet see which reading is better. Teate of the Marrucini, 17 miles. | Tes Ngmarucinoceio [Teate Marrucinorum]; read Teate Marrucinorum. | Chieti. Confusion. Hadria, 14 miles. | Hadria. | Atri.

units.la: Tertium denique à Septempeda Castrum Truentinum, M. P. LXXIV.
units.tr: Thirdly, from Septempeda to Castrum Truentinum, 74 miles.

units.la: Antoninus: | Itineraria Tabula: | Vulgata Nomencl. Picenum. Vrbem Salviam M.P.XII. | Vrbe Salvia. .... | Alia. Ad Aquas, IX, | Marca Ancon. Surpicano, XV. Firmum, M.P.XVIII. | Firmo Viceno, XII. | Fermo. Leg. Piceno. Cupra Marina XII | Grotte, vel Gritto. Samnites. Asculum, M P.XXIV. ......... | Ascoli. Castrum Truentinum, M. | Castro Trentino. | Abruzzo. Columella. P. XX. | Leg. Truentino.
units.tr: Antoninus: | Tabula Itineraria: | Vulgate nomenclature, Picenum. The city Salvia, 12 miles. | From the city Salvia. .... | Another: To the Waters, 9. | Marca Ancona: Surpicanum, 15. Firmum, 18 miles. | From Firmum to Vicenum, 12. | Fermo. Read Picenum. Cupra Marina, 12. | Grotte, or Gritto. Samnites. Asculum, 24 miles. ......... | Ascoli. Castrum Truentinum, [miles blank]. | To Castro Trentino. | Abruzzo. Columella, 20 miles. | Read Truentinum.

units.la: Huc item pertinet Pars Itineris, quod ab Vrbe Via Praenestina Beneventum ducit Antoninus, nota & explicata superius, Loca continens, Aquinum, Casinum, Venafrum, Tesnum, Allisas, Telesiam & Beneventum.
units.tr: To this also belongs the part of the itinerary that Antoninus gives from the city by the Via Praenestina to Beneventum, which was noted and explained above. It contains the places Aquinum, Casinum, Venafrum, Tesnum, Allifae, Telesia and Beneventum.

units.la: CAPVT XXX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXX.

units.la: Apulia Daunia.
units.tr: Apulia Daunia.

units.la: HÆc de Samnitibus, quos Distributio mea in Prisca Italia, eaque Orientaliore locarat priore loco cis Phiternum ad Mare Hadriaticum: perlustrandas sistit nunc ordine mea Methodus ibidem trans Phiternum Apulias.
units.tr: So much for the Samnites, whom my Distribution placed in Ancient Italy, in its more eastern part, first on this side of the Piternus toward the Adriatic Sea. My Method now requires that I survey, in the same order, the Apulias beyond the Piternus.

units.la: APVLIAM nonnulli dictam opinantur ab A privativa particula & Pluvia, tamquam Apluvia: &, si Dis placet, rationem addunt, quod in ea rarissime pluat. Alij nomen ab Apulo Rege volunt ortum, huc multis ante Bellum Troianum aetatibus profecto. Apulia, inquit Diaconus libro 11 rerum Langbardicarum cap. xi à Perdrione nominatur. Ctine enim ibi Solis feroribus terra virentia perduntur. אפוליא scribitur in Chaldaica Paraphrasi, Ezech. cap. xxvii. Sic exstat in Veneta Editione in Commentarius Kimchi. Complutensis Codex rectius אפוליא: de quo Elias, Videtur mihi, inquit, esse Provincia illa, quae dicitur אוליא, Pouilla, in Regno Neapolitano, Apuliae totius Fines constituunt ad Ortum quidem, Salentini, ad Meridiem, Lucani, Hirpini, Samnites; ad Septemtrionem, Sinus Hadriaticus; ad Occasum Phiternus Amnis. Caracenorum & Frentanorum, de quibus suo loco, terminus. Finibus autem, quos indicavi, concluditur quidquid ab variis Scriptoribus tributum Apuliae, quae duplex; cis Aufidum quidem Fluvium DAVNIA: trans idem Flumen PEVCETIA.
units.tr: Some think Apulia was named from the privative particle A and pluvia, as if it were "Apluvia," and, God willing, they add the reason that it very rarely rains there. Others hold that the name came from a king Apulus, who lived there many ages before the Trojan War. "Apulia," says Diaconus in book 11 of the History of the Lombards, chapter 11, "is named from Perdrio, for there green lands are destroyed by the heat of the sun." In the Chaldee paraphrase of Ezekiel 27 it is written [אפוליא]. So it stands in the Venetian edition of Kimchi's commentary, but the Complutensian codex has the more correct [אפוליא]. On this, Elias says: "It seems to me that this is the province called Pouilla in the Kingdom of Naples." The borders of the whole of Apulia are: to the east, the Salentini; to the south, the Lucani, Hirpini and Samnites; to the north, the Adriatic gulf; to the west, the river Piternus, the boundary of the Caracenes and Frentani, of whom more in their place. Within the limits I have indicated lies whatever various writers have attributed to Apulia, which is twofold: on this side of the river Aufidus it is called Daunia, and beyond the same river Peucetia.

units.la: Hic antequam ad sequentium me accingam explicationem, monere Lectorem operaeprecium duxi, Plinium libro III. natur. Histor. cap. xi triginta sex, aut circiter, enumerare Populos, qui utrum ad Apulos, an vero ad Samnites sint referendi, non satis constat. Eos hic malui recenlere, quam nusquam. De certis quorundam locis, perlpicuum est. Aquiloni enim, Abellinates cognomine Protropi, Cantiani, & Caudini suas habuerunt Vrbes inter Samnites, quae vulgo Agnone, Aquiltone, Campagna & Vetus Caudinum, quemadmodum praecedente Cap. vidimus: suas etiam habituri, ut duobus sequentibus videbimus, in Dannia quidem Arpani, Herdonienses, Hyrini, & Lirinates: puta, quae vulgo Arpi, Cedogna, Rode, Larino; accedentibus & Mateolanis, quos ad Garganum montem ipse locat Plinius: in Peucetia vero Cannenses, ubi Canna Veteres, Silvini item prope Andorum, & Venusini ubi hodie Venosa. Reliquant igitur xx circiter Populi, qui utrum Samnitibus sint adcenadcensendi an Apulo. adhuc ambiguum est; Posteriorībus malim, verbis Plinij bene expensis: sed utrum Daunij, an Penicij, vel qui quibus, adhuc haereo. Totum nomenclatura haec est. Aecolani (pro his Ausfeculanos habere tria Exemplaria testatur Ortelius. Male. Nam Anxanum urbem habet Ptolemæus, Anxanus Appianus: Eclanum Antoninus xxv P. M. ab Equoteutico: Aeclanum legit Solinus: Ex hinc Aecanensis Ager in Libro de Limitibus. Fuerunt forte Apulæ Daunij.) Sunt inde apud Plinium, Ligures, qui cognominantur Cornelians, quinque Bebiani. Sic Frontinus de Coloniis, uti in M. S. Codice aliquot mihi servari legitur, Ligures Cabiani & Cornatenses in iro ducti, &c. Fistellani, Frentani, Aufidenates, Atinates, Arpani. Horum meminit Lapis, qui Beneventi in Ædibus Alphonsi Materani.
units.tr: Before I proceed to what follows, I think it worth warning the reader that Pliny, in book 3 of his Natural History, chapter 11, lists some thirty-six peoples, or thereabouts, and it is not altogether clear whether they belong to the Apulians or to the Samnites. I preferred to list them here rather than nowhere. For some of them the places are certain. The Abellinates, surnamed Protropi, the Cantiani and the Caudini had their cities among the Samnites, which are now commonly called Agnone, Aquiltone, Campagna and Vetus Caudinum, as we saw in the preceding chapter. As the two following chapters will show, they also had their own in Daunia: the Arpani, Herdonienses, Hyrini and Lirinates, that is, what are now commonly called Arpi, Cedogna, Rode and Larino; to these must be added the Mateolani, whom Pliny places near Mount Garganus. In Peucetia were the Cannenses, where the ancients placed Canna, also the Silvini near Andria, and the Venusini, where Venosa stands today. So about twenty peoples remain, and it is still uncertain whether they should be counted among the Samnites or the Apulians. I would rather count them among the latter, if Pliny's words are weighed carefully; but whether they are Daunians or Peucetians, or which of these, I am still unsure. The whole list reads thus: Aecolani (for this, three copies have Ausfeculanos, as Ortelius reports, wrongly; for Ptolemy gives the city Anxanum, Appian Anxanus, Antoninus Eclanum in the 25th mile from Equotuticum, Solinus reads Aeclanum, and from this comes the Aecanensis Ager in the book on boundaries. Perhaps they were Daunian Apulians.) Then in Pliny there are the Ligures, who are surnamed Cornelians, and five Bebiani. So too Frontinus, in his book on colonies, as I read in a manuscript copy preserved to me: Ligures Cabiani and Cornatenses led in the same ... etc. Fistellani, Frentani, Aufidenates, Atinates, Arpani. An inscription at Benevento, in the house of Alfonso Materano, mentions these:

units.la: C. OCTAVIO. C. F. PAL. MODESTO
units.tr: To Gaius Octavius Modestus, son of Gaius, of the Palatine tribe

units.la: AVGVR. II VIR. I. D. QVAEST. PRAEF. FABR. ROMA. PRAEF. COH. III. ITYREOS. TRIB. MIL. LEG. III SCYTHIC. CVRAT. REI P. ÆCANOR. ITEM. HONORATO. AD. CVRAM. CALENDARI REIP. CANVSINOR &c.
units.tr: Augur, duumvir, quinquennial, quaestor, prefect of engineers at Rome, prefect of the third cohort of Ityraeans, military tribune of the third legion Scythica, curator of the state of the Aecani; also to Honoratus, in charge of the calendar of the state of the Canusini, etc.

units.la: Afellani porro Plinij sunt qui Amalphitanos esse volunt, Amalphi in Campania Incolas: alij Cives contendunt esse Malphi vel Melphi in Lucania. Sed reclamat utrumque situs & enumeratio, quæ apud Plinium, Hirpinis Samnitibusque Afellanos concenseret. Nominantur inde Plinio Atinates, Bovianī (Hermedani tacet horum etiam Auctorem Strabonem: sed Bovianos nusquam apud eum reperio) Collatini, Corninenses (in M. S. sunt Carrinenses) Divini, Ferentani (an qui Ἀφροδισιάς Artemidoro apud Stephanum?) Genusini, Hirnates (de his etiam paullo ante eodem cap. scripserat Plinius) Nercetini (alij ab Nercetino. Salentinorum Populis, quos eadem nomine ut Plinius in fine capitis) Olfatini (noti sunt & Lucano. Hinc, ut teramus hunc Littorales, Matium im Littus, Matina Palus, Matina Cacumina apud Horatium, cui & Matinus Mons notus in Epodis, quem tamen Interpretes in Calabria fixerunt. Vide nonnihil capite sequenti, ubi de Battna Urbe) Rubutini (M. SS. suos Codices Trabuinos habere monet Ortelius: sed Rubutini Agri mentionem quoque hic in Libro de Limitibus) Strapatini, Turmentini, Tiburnes (Exemplaria quaedam Vibrinates praeterre, lugerit Ortelius, eodemque etiam & lacere Hermolao Barbaro ab Oppido Viarna, Varini denique postremo, inter hos incertorum situs Populos, loco.
units.tr: Next, Pliny's Afellani are those whom some wish to be the Amalphitans, inhabitants of Amalphi in Campania; others maintain they are the citizens of Malphi or Melphi in Lucania. But both location and the list object, since in Pliny the Afellani are reckoned among the Hirpini and Samnites. Then Pliny names the Atinates, the Bovianī (Hermedanus is silent about them, and Strabo, the author of this, too; but I find Bovianos nowhere in him), the Collatini, the Corninenses (in manuscripts they are Carrinenses), the Divini, the Ferentani (are they the [Ἀφροδισιάς] of Artemidorus in Stephanus?), the Genusini, the Hirnates (Pliny had written about these also a little earlier in the same chapter), the Nercetini (others take them from the Nercetini, a people of the Salentini, whom Pliny names in the same way at the end of the chapter), the Olfatini (known also to Lucan). Hence, to touch on this coastal region, there are Matium on the shore, the Matina Palus, the Matina Cacumina in Horace, and the Matinus Mons known from his Epodes, which the commentators, however, have placed in Calabria. See a little in the following chapter, where I speak of the city of Battum. Then the Rubutini (Ortelius warns that his manuscripts have Trabuinos, but the Rubutini Agri is also mentioned here in the book on boundaries). Then the Strapatini, the Turmentini, the Tiburnes (Ortelius reports that some copies omit Vibrinates, and Hermolaus Barbarus has the same, from the town of Viarna), and finally the Varini, whose place among these uncertain peoples I leave here.

units.la: : Daunia Nomen, ut scribit Plinius ab antiquissimo, vel Rege vel Duce Daunio, Diomedis Socero, qui, ut Festus notat, ex Illyrica gente Vir clarus, Patria propter seditionem excedens, hanc Italiæ partem occupavit, eamque cum Diomede Genero est partitus. Plene de ea Strabo, qui tamen in ejus, tamquam non visæ, descriptione indiligentior: Plinius, Ptolemæus, Pomponius Mela, alij. Itali hodie Puglia Piana vocatur. Plana ab latissimis Campis, & maiore, quam in Peucetiis, æquore Agrorum, quæ fertiles hic supra modum Tritici aliorumque Frumenti generum. Fines illi ab Oriente Apulia Peucetia, intercurrente Aufido; ab Meridie, Apenninus, cum Hirpinis & Samnitibus; ab Occidente Frentani, Caracemque, nunc Aprutii, cum Pinnetinis ab Septentrione Hadriaticum vel Ionium Mare. Scribit Plinius lib. III. cap. XI Diomedem in hac Regione deleviæ Gentes Monedorum Dardorumque, & Urbes duas, quæ in Proverbii ludicrum vertere, Apsenum & Trucium.
units.tr: Daunia: the name, as Pliny writes, comes from the very ancient Daunius, either king or leader, the father-in-law of Diomedes, who, as Festus notes, was an illustrious man of the Illyrian people. Leaving his homeland because of a sedition, he occupied this part of Italy and shared it with his son-in-law Diomedes. Strabo describes it fully, though he is rather careless in his description of a region he had not seen. Pliny, Ptolemy, Pomponius Mela and others also write of it. Today the Italians call it Puglia Piana, Plana from its very wide plains and the flatter expanse of its fields, which here are fertile beyond measure in wheat and other kinds of grain, more than in Peucetia. Its boundaries are: on the east, Apulia Peucetia, with the Aufidus running between; on the south, the Apennine, with the Hirpini and Samnites; on the west, the Frentani and the Caracenes, now the Abruzzi, with the Pinnetini; on the north, the Adriatic or Ionian Sea. In book 3, chapter 11, Pliny writes that Diomedes, in this region, conquered the warlike peoples of the Monedi and Dardi, and two cities which became a joke in a proverb, Apsenum and Trucium.

units.la: Specialiora jam nunc persequar, absolutus ea per partes suas principes, quas hujus
units.tr: I shall now pursue the more particular matters, having first set out the principal parts of this region, which I usually establish as

units.la: Note: marginal entries are small and largely illegible in the scan. hujus Regionis statuere solco in Ora, Monte Gargano, Capitanita. Ab Ora ordiar, ortum spectante.
units.tr: of this region: Ora, Monte Gargano, and Capitanata. I shall begin with Ora, facing east.

units.la: Vicenis ab Aufido P. M. Veteris Salapia locus invenitur. Salapia Livio, Plinio, Vitruvio; Σαλαπια Straboni: quæ Σαλαπια Ptolemæo. Conditorem ejus Varro Diomedem, alij Rhodium Elphiam tradunt. Meminit sæpe Livius, præcipue libro xxvi, xxxvi, xxxvii. Plinius meretricio Hannibalis amore inclutam scribit. Strabo Ἀργυρίππα ἔποικον fuisse scribit. Salapinam Paludem habet hoc tractu, &tu Lucanus lib. v. Belli Pharsalici. Quod locum mutarit, Cæli fecit, ut Veteres Authores memorant, inter quos Strabo, gravitas. Nam quotannis pestilentia ingruente, M. Hostilianus ab S. P. Q. R. petijt, ut Urbem quaternis P. M. caprandæ salubritati introrsum in Continentem transferre liceret. Quo impetrato, novum Opidum in Mediterraneis condi cœptum, quod ab desolato prorsus priore Salpe nunc appellatur. Opidum Episcopatus titulo nobile.
units.tr: Twenty miles from the Aufidus, the Old Roman location of Salapia is found. Livy, Pliny and Vitruvius call it Salapia; Strabo calls it Σαλαπια [Salapia], and Ptolemy likewise. Varro reports that Diomedes founded it, while others name the Rhodian Elphias. Livy mentions it often, especially in books 26, 36 and 37. Pliny writes that it was famous for Hannibal's love for a prostitute. Strabo writes that it was a colony of Argyrippa [Ἀργυρίππα]. It has a Salapine Marsh in this district, which Lucan also mentions in book 5 of the Civil War. As ancient authors record, among them Strabo, the town changed its site because of the heaviness of the air. For each year, when pestilence struck, M. Hostilianus petitioned the Senate and People of Rome for permission to move the city four Roman miles inland onto the mainland, to secure its health. When this was granted, a new town began to be built in the interior, which is now called Salpe, the former Salapia having been entirely deserted. It is a town noble by the title of a bishopric.

units.la: Sequitur Lacus Andurianus, Lago di Ardoria, ab Opido vicino Anduria, quod Mandurium Plinio, Lacum etiam describenti, quod ad Margines sit plenus, neque exhaustis aquis minuatur: neque augeatur infusis. Meminit & Lacus hujus cum Fluvio quem hodie Candelarem vocant, Strabo inter Salpiam & Sipuntem eum ponens.
units.tr: Next is Lacus Andurianus, Lago di Ardoria, named after the nearby town of Anduria, which Pliny calls Mandurium. Pliny also describes the lake as full up to its margins, neither diminished when its waters are drawn off nor increased when water is poured in. Meminit and this Lacus is linked with the Fluvio that people today call the Candelarem, which Strabo places between Salpia and Sipuntum.

units.la: Hinc ad Manfredonium millia octo sunt. Urbs ea luta sane populoque frequens, in rupe Sinus marini, quem Gargani Montis Hexus efficit, sita. Condidit Manfredus Rex, Friderici II Imp. Filius, anno circiter 1Ɔ0 cc, qui Manfredoniam ab se denominavit, quum prius locus hic Capitaniata Portus vocaretur, teste libro IIII Hist Reg. Collenutio. Conditam constat ob Siponti interitum; translata etiam Archiepiscopo Archiepiscopi Sipontini Sede; unde Sipontini Antistitis nomen hodieque manet Manfredoniano. Invictam ad Litus habet Arcem. Moles extra muros in mari jacta, magnæ artis opus, securam præstat stationem navibus, in quas per gradus descenditur. Nobiles ibi Familiæ: Avantaggio. | Calvano, | Minadoi. Beccarino. | Festa. | Nicastro. Caraczuolo. | Florio. | Selvaggio. Cessa. | Gentile. | Et aliæ.
units.tr: From here it is eight miles to Manfredonia. That town is quite fine and populous, set on a rock of the sea-bay which the headland of Monte Gargano forms. King Manfred, son of the Emperor Frederick II, founded it about the year 1260, and named it Manfredonia after himself, whereas this place had previously been called the Port of Capitanata, as Collenuccio records in book 4 of the Histories of the Kings. It is established as a fact that it was founded because of the destruction of Siponto, and the see of the Archbishop of Siponto was also transferred there; hence the title of Bishop of Siponto still remains today for the Archbishop of Manfredonia. It has an unconquered citadel on the shore. A mole built out into the sea outside the walls, a work of great skill, provides a safe anchorage for ships, to which one descends by steps. Noble families there include: Avantaggio, Calvano, Minadoi, Beccarino, Festa, Nicastro, Caraczuolo, Florio, Selvaggio, Cessa, Gentile, and others.

units.la: Ab Manfredonia per oram incedenti M. P. ad Gargani Montis radices saxosa in rupe Siponti ruinæ ostenduntur. Sipontum Livio, Plinio, Cassiodoro, Itinerariæ Tabulæ, quæ Sipontium Paullo Diacono de gestis Langbard, lib. II cap. xxi; Sipus Silio lib. viii Belli Pœnici; Σιπους Ptolemæo. Audiamus Strabonem lib. vi: Δεσπα ... Innuit non jam amplius ita ab Græcis dici, sed Σιπους. Sic Pomponius Mela: Sipuntum, vel, ut Graeci dixere, Sipyus; quid si Sepius? Σιπους, inquit Stephanus, πολις Δαυνιων. Siponto hodieque, teste Leandro. Dicta, ut ex Strabone audivimus, ab multitudine Sepiarum, quæ hic in litus ejiciuntur: quod hodieque videre est. Hodie plane conlapsa jacet; monstrantibus nihilominus ruderibus magnificam fuisse Urbem. Summum Civitatis Templum adhuc omnibus suis partibus fere integrum. Sipontum Coloniam Romanorum fuisse ductam notat libro xxxiv Livius; qui eius etiam meminit libro xxxv. Interitus varie narratur: aliis alio referentibus, ad Saracenorum irruptiones, ad intestinas contentiones, ad Terræ-motuum violentiam.
units.tr: Proceeding along the coast from Manfredonia for three miles, one comes to the foot of Monte Gargano, where the ruins of Siponti are shown on a rocky crag. Livy, Pliny, Cassiodorus and the Itinerary Tables call it Sipontum; Paulus Diaconus, in his history of the Lombards (Book II, chapter 21), calls it Sipontium; Silius (Book VIII of the Punic War) calls it Sipus; and Ptolemy calls it Σιπους [Sipous]. Let us hear Strabo, Book VI: "Δεσπα ..." [Despa ...]. He implies that it was no longer called by the Greeks by that name but Σιπους [Sipous]. So Pomponius Mela says: Sipuntum, or, as the Greeks have said, Sipyus. What if it is Sepius? Stephanus says Σιπους [Sipous] is a city of the Daunians. It is still called Siponto, according to Leandro. It was named, as we have heard from Strabo, after the multitude of cuttlefish (sepiae) which are cast up on this shore, as may still be seen today. Today it lies quite collapsed, yet the rubble nevertheless shows that the city was once magnificent. Its main cathedral is still nearly whole in all its parts. Livy, in Book XXXIV, notes that Sipontum was founded as a Roman colony, and he also mentions it in Book XXXV. Its destruction is variously reported: some ascribe it to the Saracen incursions, others to internal strife, others to the violence of earthquakes.

units.la: A Siponto per litus procedenti Locus Apenestli sese offert, plane nunc deleti. Meminit situs Ptolemæus, cui Απηνεστης scribuntur. Hinc Apenestini Plinio, qui vitiose in vulgatis Apamestini.
units.tr: Proceeding from Siponto along the shore, the site of Apenestli presents itself, now quite destroyed. Ptolemy records the place, where it is written Απηνεστης [Apenestes]. Hence the Apenestini of Pliny, which in the printed editions is wrongly given as Apamestini.

units.la: Montis Gargani, de quo alibi, Opida sequuntur explicanda.
units.tr: Montis Gargani, of which elsewhere, is followed by towns that need explaining.

units.la: Reperiuntur in eo Lacus aliquot piscosi, inter ceteros Varanus, Varrano, ambitu M. P. xxx, quem Caprinum, Cognatium, Iscitella Opida coronant.
units.tr: In it are found several fish-filled lakes, among them Varanus, or Varrano, thirty miles in circuit, which is encircled by the towns Caprinum, Cognatium and Iscitella.

units.la: Tum in fronte Promontorij Bestia est Civitas; sic dicta, pro Vesta, cuius hic putatur fuisse ædes.
units.tr: Then at the front of the promontory is the city of Bestia, so named in place of Vesta, whose temple is thought to have stood here.

units.la: Post x millia Vestice Castellum sequitur.
units.tr: Ten thousand paces past Vestice follows a small fortress.

units.la: Flexum Promontorij totum emensis se offert Rode Civitas: olim Hyrium. Τεγεον Ptolemæo & Dionysio Afro; Τεγη, Herodoto & Eustathios Hyria, Varroni & Plinio libro iii nat. histor. cap. xi; Οὐρνον, Straboni, cujus tempore modicum erat Strabo & ex Trogo Iustinus lib. xx. Sarpi dicitur Nigro; Monte S. Angelo, Erythraeo. Hinc Arpini Livio. ΑΡΠΑΝΩΝ, Arpanorum, Numismata exhibet in sua Magna Graecia Hubertus Goltzius. Ardanum Agrum nominat Plinius, in quo latum frumentum non nascitur. In editione Veneta est Harpanus: Arpanum esse in M. S. Codice & quibusdam excusis reperitur Ortelius ab Arpi fortean. Putant quidam Diomedium, quae Διομήδεια Stephano, eamdem esse cum Arpis Urbem. Sed reclamat ipse Stephanus, cujus quae in ea voce sunt mutila, sic supplenda censeo: Ἐ'ὰ κὴ Διομήδεια, σπλιον Ἀργυρίππης. Sunt enim Ἀργυρίππη & Διομήδεια Daunio-rum ad Sinum Ionium vel Hadriaticum. Et Diomedium potius, quam, quod quidam arbitrantur, Aipos, designare puto Virgilium lib. vii Aeneid. & Ovidium lib. xiii. Metam. quum Diomedis Urbem nominant. Utraque certe ab Diomede est condita.
units.tr: Having passed the whole bend of the promontory, the city of Rode presents itself; formerly it was Hyrium. Ptolemy and Dionysius Afer call it Τεγεον [Tegeon]; Herodotus and Eustathius call it Τεγη [Tege], Hyria; Varro and Pliny (Natural History, Book III, chapter 11) give Hyria; Strabo, in whose time it was of modest size, gives Οὐρνον [Ournon]; and Justin, from Trogus, Book XX. It is called Sarpi by Nigro, and Monte S. Angelo by Erythraeus. Hence the Arpini of Livy. Hubert Goltzius, in his Magna Graecia, gives coins bearing ΑΡΠΑΝΩΝ [Arpanon], of the Arpanorum. Pliny names the Ardanum Agrum, in which broad-leaved grain does not grow. In the Venetian edition it is Harpanus; Ortelius finds Arpanum in a manuscript and some printed editions, perhaps from Arpi. Some think that Diomedium, which Stephanus calls Διομήδεια [Diomedeia], is the same city as Arpi. But Stephanus himself objects, and I think the mutilated part of his entry in that word should be supplied thus: Ἐ'ὰ κὴ Διομήδεια, σπλιον Ἀργυρίππης [Ea kai Diomedeia, a fortress of Argyrippe]. For Ἀργυρίππη [Argyrippe] and Διομήδεια [Diomedeia] are cities of the Daunians on the Ionian or Adriatic Gulf. I think Virgil in Book VII of the Aeneid, and Ovid in Book XIV of the Metamorphoses, when they name the city of Diomedes, designate Diomedium rather than Aipos, as some believe. Both were certainly founded by Diomedes.

units.la: Millibus à Foggia xii Occasum versus adparet in exiguo colle Opidum, nunc Episcopale, Luceria. Sic Livio, Plinio, Paulo Diacono lib. ii cap. xxi Rerum Langbard. aliisq; Latinis dicitur: Ἀυκεια, Straboni ceterisque Graecis, Ἀυκαεία Polybio lib. iii teste Stephano. quae Λυκεία Diodoro lib. xvii. incmendatius; ut & Νυκεία Ptolemaeo, & Νuceria Suetonio. Nuceriae Apulae Itinerarii Tabulae, vitiosiore Scriptura, pro Nuceria Apula. Luceriam quidam volunt dictam à Lucendo, quod editiore loco sita lux quasi & fax esset totius Apuliae. Coloniam eo ab Romanis ductam scribit Livius libro ix, mentionem etiam ejus faciens libro xxii. Fano Minervae (cui Lanificium curae est. Nam Lanas optimas tonderi solitas prope nobilem Luceriam, canit Horatius lib. iii Carmin. Oda xv) celebris, Strabonis temporibus jam diruta jacebat, post ex veteribus ruinis restituta ab Constantino ii Orientis Imperatore (Legendi Paulus Diaconus lib. v & Blondus libro ix Histor.) denuo excita, rursus post hanc cladem instaurata Saracenis, ex Africa deductis, (eodem Blondo scribente libro xvii) concessa est; unde vulgo Luceria de i Saraceni cognominata: quibus tandem expulsis ab Karolo ii utriusque Siciliae Rege, nomen Urbi nomen datum est, ut D. Mariae Civitas, Citta di S. Maria, diceretur, monumentum Victoriae ab Saracenis reportatae, ipso xviii Kalend. Sept. die Virgini Matri sacro. Sed pristinum Luceria nomen in hunc diem praevaluit. Quingentis ab Urbe passibus Imperator Fridericus modico in Colle munitissimam exstruxerat Arcem; quae ingentibus ruinis deformata nunc jacet, & prorsus deserta. Rudera, quae hodieque passim eo loco, priscam docent Urbis amplitudinem.
units.tr: Twelve miles from Foggia, toward the west, appears on a small hill the town now an episcopal see, Luceria. It is so called by Livy, Pliny, Paulus Diaconus (Book II, chapter 21, of the History of the Lombards) and other Latin writers; Strabo and the other Greeks give Ἀυκεια [Aukeia]; Polybius (Book III, according to Stephanus) gives Ἀυκαεία [Aukaeia]; Diodorus (Book XVII) gives the less correct Λυκεία [Lykeia], as also Ptolemy Νυκεία [Nykeia] and Suetonius Nuceria. The Itinerary Tables have Nuceriae Apulae, a more corrupt reading for Nuceria Apula. Some want Luceria to be named from lucendo (shining), because, set on a higher site, its light was as it were a torch for all of Apulia. Livy, in Book IX, writes that the Romans made it a colony, and he mentions it again in Book XXII. Its temple of Minerva, to whom wool-working was sacred (for Horace, Book III of the Odes, Ode XV, sings that the finest wools were shorn near the noble Luceria), was famous; in Strabo's time it already lay in ruins, and afterward it was restored from the old ruins by Constans II, Emperor of the East (read Paulus Diaconus, Book V, and Biondo, Book IX of the History). It was reopened again, but after this disaster it was rebuilt, and it was granted to Saracens brought over from Africa (as Biondo writes in Book XVII). Hence it was commonly called Luceria de' Saraceni. When these were at last expelled by Charles II, King of both Sicilies, the city was given the name D. Mariae Civitas, Citta di S. Maria, as a monument of the victory won over the Saracens, on the day sacred to the Virgin Mother, the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September. But the old name Luceria has prevailed to this day. Five hundred paces from the city, the Emperor Frederick had built a very strong citadel on a modest hill; it now lies wrecked by huge ruins and quite deserted. The rubble still found scattered there today shows the former size of the city.

units.la: Succedit in Apennino Teanum Apulum; sic cognominatum ad differentiam ejus, quod in Campania Sidicinum. Τεανὸν Ἀπύλων Strabono & Ptolemaeo: Teanum, Livio; Tianum, Pomponio Melae & Antiquis Numismatibus; Theanum Apulum, cum adiectu. M. Tullio & priscis Lapidibus. Hodie Teano vel Tiano. Incolae Teanenses Livio libro viii & ix. Teanensis Respublica est in Basi marmorea, quae in Vinea Cardinalis Carpensis: alibi à me posita. Τυαῖτας nominat Polybius libro iii, ubi Vetus Interpres Calatinos legit. Nobiles ibi Familiae: D'Agnelo. | Carigli. | Di Martino. Abenavoli. | Caluccio. | De Monte. Baratuzi.
units.tr: In the Apennines follows Teanum Apulum, so surnamed to distinguish it from the Sidicinum in Campania. Strabo and Ptolemy give Τεανὸν Ἀπύλων [Teanon Apylon]; Livy gives Teanum; Pomponius Mela and the ancient coins give Tianum; Cicero and the old inscriptions give Theanum Apulum, with the addition. Today it is Teano or Tiano. Its inhabitants are the Teanenses (Livy, Books VIII and IX). The Teanensis Respublica is on a marble base in the vineyard of Cardinal Carpensis, which I have set down elsewhere. Polybius, Book III, names Τυαῖτας [Tyaitas], where the old interpreter reads Calatinos. Noble families there: D'Agnelo, Carigli, Di Martino, Abenavoli, Caluccio, De Monte, Baratuzi.

units.la: Ab Luceria P. M. viii itinere Campestri in Septemtrionem Opidum invenitur Farentinum, quod Blondo Ferensuola, recens omnibus habitum, Colonis infrequens, & magna parte conlapsum: inclutum nihilominus morte Friderici ii Imper. de qua legend. Collenutius lib. iii Histor. Reg. & alij.
units.tr: Eight miles from Luceria by the plain road toward the north is found Farentinum, which Biondo calls Ferensuola; it was recently inhabited by everyone, yet is thinly peopled by colonists and for the greater part collapsed. It was nevertheless famous for the death of Frederick II, Emperor (on which read Collenuccio, Book III of the History of the Kings, and others).

units.la: Ab Ferensuola itinere xviii P. M. ad exiguum Collem vestigia cernuntur Civitatis Civitati, Civitato; non ita pridem delectae. Aedes Cathredalis superest.
units.tr: Eighteen miles from Ferensuola, on a small hill, traces of a city are seen, Civitati, Civitato, which was abandoned not long ago. The cathedral church survives.

units.la: Ad Luceriam commeantibus retro juxta latus Apennini versus Orientem, inter alia sunt: Castellutium, Castelluzo, Petra-motta, Mons Corvinus, Vulturnum, aliud Castellutium, Licellaria, Fortinum, Castellum Francum, Alberettum, Eiccarinum.
units.tr: For those travelling back from Luceria, along the side of the Apennines toward the east, among other places are: Castellutium, Castelluzo, Petra-motta, Mons Corvinus, Vulturnum, another Castellutium, Licellaria, Fortinum, Castellum Francum, Alberettum, Eiccarinum.

units.la: Dein ab Luceria P. M. viii Civitas est opulentissima, Troia, fœcundi agri. Instauratam vel potius conditam à Bubagiano, Michaelis Constantinopolitani Imp. Praefecto, circa tempora Stephani viii P. M. tradit lib. xiii Historiar. Blondus. Vetustissima tustissima Bononiensis Vrbs Chronica ab Duce quodam Imperatoris Basilii in- stituta, produnt. Utrumque verum esse potest. Quum enim Michael Batilius successisset, potuit Bubagiacus suisse Legatus, & sub uno quidem capite, perse calle s. s. alterò. Hanc fuisse loquuntur Bononiensium Chronica, ab Consentino Leandro iste consirmata. Hannibalis Castra, quæ ab Guidone Ravennate, Collenutio lib. III Hist. Reg. & Volaterrano in Cæsar. hic ponuntur, ab nullo Veteranorum prorum in hac Regione, sed in Magna Græcia, ut vidimus, nominantur. Helium hic Conciliam Urbanus II P. M. depravatissimos Clericorum mores corrigenti, teste Blondo lib. XXII Histor. & Platina in Pontificum Vitis. Vrbs Consantia & Episcopatus titulo clara.
units.tr: Then, eight miles from Luceria, is the very wealthy city of Troia, with fertile fields. Biondo (Book XIII of the Histories) says it was restored, or rather founded, by Bubagianus, prefect of Michael, Emperor of Constantinople, around the time of Pope Stephen VIII. The very ancient chronicle of Bologna says it was founded by a certain commander of the Emperor Basil. Both may be true: since Michael had succeeded Batilius, Bubagiacus could have been legate, and one account refers to one ruler, the other to another. The chronicles of Bologna say it was this city, as Leandro of Cosenza confirmed. The Hannibalis Castra, which Guido of Ravenna, Collenuccio (Book III of the History of the Kings) and Volaterranus in Caesar place here, are named by none of the ancient writers in this region, but in Magna Graecia, as we have seen. Here Urban II, Pope, correcting the most depraved morals of the clergy, held a council, according to Biondo (Book XXII of the History) and Platina in the Lives of the Popes. The city of Consentia is famous for its title of bishopric.

units.la: Secundum Apenninum descendum in Meridiem procedenti quarto lapide Castel- lum occurrit Vista, perinde deinceps intervallo Berinum Civitas: inde tertio Dæretum Oppidum: hinc tertio Asculum Vrbs, titulo Ducatus & Episcopatus inclutà. Asculum L. Floro, Tarentinum Bellum scribenti; Appiano Alexandrino, Stephano: Asculum vulgo, sed cognomine Sarrianò, teste Mazzella, ad differentiam alterius, quod in Piceno. Colonia jus habet apud Plinium, & in antiqua Tabula, quæ in Hortis Cæsianis: C. SALLVSTIO. ARISTAENETO. C. V & post aliquot versus: nam alibi integram poluit: DECVRIONES. ET. PLEBS. COLONIÆ. ASCVLANO EVM. PROPTER. HVMANITATEM. ABSTINENTIAM
units.tr: Going south along the Apennines, at the fourth milestone one meets the castle of Vista; at the same interval afterward the city of Berinum; thence at three miles the town of Dæretum; thence at three miles the city of Asculum, famous for its title as a duchy and a bishopric. Asculum is given by Florus, writing of the Tarentine War; by Appian of Alexandria, and by Stephanus; it is commonly Asculum, but by the surname Sarriano, according to Mazzella, to distinguish it from the other Asculum, which is in Picenum. It has the status of a colony in Pliny and in an ancient inscription, which is in the Caesian gardens: "C. SALLVSTIO. ARISTAENETO. C. V." and after a few lines, for it was once complete: "DECVRIONES. ET. PLEBS. COLONIÆ. ASCVLANO. EVM. PROPTER. HVMANITATEM. ABSTINENTIAM" [the decurions and the common people of the colony of Asculum, for his humanity and abstinence]. It was overthrown by Roger, son of Guiscard, on account of its rebellion, and restored, according to Biondo (Book XXII of the History), but not with its former size. The Asculani are named among the Italian peoples in other authors, and in the Capitoline Fasti; the Lapis, which is praised elsewhere, especially shows the commonwealth of the Asculani.

units.la: Eversum ab Rogerio Guiscardi F. ob defectionem, teste Blondo libro XXII Hist. restauratum est, sed non quâ fuerat, amplitudine. Asculani nominantur cum in aliis Inter ipsi noribus, tum in Fastis Capitolinis, Asculanorum Remp. præsert Lapis, qui alioquin laudatus loco.
units.tr: Razed by Roger, son of Guiscard, because of its revolt, it was restored, as Blondus reports in book 22 of his Histories, but not to its former size. The Asculani are named both in other inscriptions and in the Capitoline Fasti. The stone, which is praised elsewhere in its place, bears the public record of the Asculani.

units.la: Itinere hinc per Campelltria versus oram, quatuor ab ea P. M. augustum est D. Leonardi Templum, ab Frederico II Imp. fundatum cum nobili cœnobio, quod Equitibus Teutonicis D. Mariæ Prossianæ maximis redditibus ille concesserat: Exstimetis ijs Commendationis jure locus caput habeat.
units.tr: From here, travelling through Campelltria towards the coast, four miles from it stands the church of St Leonard, built by the Emperor Frederick II with a noble monastery, which he had granted, with very large revenues, to the Teutonic Knights of St Mary of Prussia. You may judge whether the place is the head of that estate by right of commendam.

units.la: Inde XIX lapide Ordinaria est, Ordinaria copiarum Ludovici XII Francorum Regis clade anno MCCCXIII mente Malo facta, nobiles.
units.tr: Nineteen miles from there is Ordinaria, famous for the disaster that befell the forces of Louis XII, King of the French, in the year MCCCXIII, brought about by ill counsel.

units.la: Hic Apulia Dauniæ, cum Littoriis, tum Gargani Montis, & Capitanatæ Locis Leandri Scriptoris & Delineatoris Italiæ diligens enumeratis, quartam quasi adum partem Iapygiam. Servius enim ad illud Virgilii, Victor Garganı condebat Iapygis arces;
units.tr: Here, with its coastal places and those of Mount Gargano and Capitanata, carefully listed by Leandro, the writer and mapmaker of Italy, Apulia of Daunia forms almost a quarter part of what is called Iapygiam. For Servius, on that line of Virgil about the victor of Garganus founding the citadels of the Iapygians,

units.la: notat Iapygiam ipsa est Salentinorum: partem esse Apuliæ, in qua Mons Garganus. Hujus igitur initium ab ipso ponitur Campus Pascuus Oppidum. Comitatus dignitate clarum in medio Montium, qui eis Apenninii iunc juga, positum, à Boviano XVIII P. M. intervallo.
units.tr: notes that Iapygiam is the land of the Salentini itself, and that it is a part of Apulia in which Mount Gargano lies. Its beginning is therefore placed at the town of Campus Pascuus, a place famous for the dignity of its county, set in the middle of the mountains that are the ridges of the Apennines, eighteen Roman miles from Bojano.

units.la: A Campo-Basso Luceriam versus incedenti quarto lapide Campus Petratus, Campo di Pietra, occurrit: texto deinceps Oppidum Petra Catella, præcelsi Montis impositum verticem: inde quinto Macra; itemque decimo texto à Campo-Basso Celenza; septimo hinc Riccia; è Regione Gambariglia: dein octavo Castellum Motta, ac postea secundo Buturaria.
units.tr: Going from Campobasso towards Lucera, at the fourth milestone one meets Campus Petratus, Campo di Pietra. Next along the road is the town of Petra Catella, set on the summit of a very high mountain; then at the fifth milestone Macra; likewise at the tenth from Campobasso Celenza; at the seventh from here Riccia, and opposite it Gambariglia; then at the eighth Castellum Motta, and after that at the second Buturaria.

units.la: Ad Apuliam quoque Vinculatorum, Vinculatore pertinet, ab initio Tiferni Amnis intervallo VI M. P. pariterque a Boviano. Sequunturque ulterius Faranellum, Buxum, Buxinum, Recceria, Mons Sagianus; Monte Sagiano; Petrella, Castellinetum, Morronum; Lovenza, Cerrana.
units.tr: Vinculatorum, Vinculatore, also belongs to Apulia, six Roman miles from the source of the river Tifernus, and likewise from Bojano. Further on follow Faranellum, Buxum, Buxinum, Recceria, Mons Sagianus, Monte Sagiano; Petrella, Castellinetum, Morronum; Lovenza, Cerrana.

units.la: In Campis porro, qui XVI P.M. patent usque ad Mare, vestigia reperiuntur, teste Leandro, antiquissimæ Vrbis, quæ Cerya vel Gerion Livio libro XXII & alibi; Ceryna Stephano, cui & Ceryna: Geronium est in Itineraria Tabula. Polybio est in Apulia, decem stadiis ab Aufido flumine & ducentis ab Luceria Vrbe distans. Livius item & Appianus Apuliæ adscribunt. Cirignola nonnullis dicitur, teste Laurentio Anagnienti. Cellius Cittadinus Romæ scribens ad Orcelium Gerunia vix nomen, nec dum vestigia superesse notat.
units.tr: Further out in the plains, which extend sixteen Roman miles to the sea, traces are found, according to Leandro, of a very ancient city, which Livy in book 22 and elsewhere calls Cerya or Gerion; Stephanus calls it Ceryna, and also Ceryna; Geronium is its name in the Itinerary Table.
