Polybius places it in Apulia, ten stadia from the river Aufidus and two hundred from the city of Luceria. Livy and Appian likewise assign it to Apulia. Some call it Cirignola, according to Laurentius of Anagni. Cellius Cittadinus, writing at Rome to Orcelius, notes that Gerunia is scarcely more than a name, and that no traces of it survive.

units.la: Hinc ad alterum lapidem Casalenda se offert: postque sex milliaria, aliud recens Larinum, loco ab Veteri, quod nunc deletum, milliar. duorum. Larinum Ciceroni, Plinio Itineraria Tabulæ, aliis: Λαρῖνον Ptolemæo. Cicero pro Plancio Larinum xiii x P. M. distare docet ab Theano Apuliæ. Videdus & Plinius. Λάρινα πόλις Λαξνίων Stephano; emendā Δαυν.αν. Hinc Larinates cognomine Frentani, Livio, Cæsari, Plinio, Silioque, cuius & hoc: Quæque iacet Superi Larinas adrola Ponti.
units.tr: From here, at the second milestone, Casalenda presents itself; and after six miles, another recent place, Larinum, a town two miles from the old one, which is now destroyed. Cicero and Pliny and the Itinerary Table, and others, call it Larinum; Ptolemy calls it Λαρῖνον [Larinon]. Cicero, in his speech for Plancius, shows that Larinum is thirteen Roman miles from Teanum in Apulia; Pliny does too. Stephanus has Λάρινα πόλις Λαξνίων [Larina polis Laxnion]; read as Δαυνίων [Daunion], Daunian. Hence the Larinates, surnamed Frentani, in Livy, Caesar, Pliny and Silius, and Silius also has this line: "which lies where the waves of the Upper Sea wash the Larinian shores."

units.la: Larinus Ager eidem Ciceroni eadem Oratione; qui Larinatis Ager apud Livium lib. xxii & xxvii. Periit hoc Opidum in vulgatis Melæ libris. Nam ubi libro II Lucinum legitur reponendum est Larinum. Dauny autem, inquit, Tifernam Aminem, Clusernam, Lucrinum, Theanum Opida; Montemque Garganum. Novum Larinum Ditionis est Vrsinorum, Familiæ Romanæ.
units.tr: Silius, in the same speech, has the Larinian territory; Livy, in books 22 and 27, has the territory of the Larinates. This town has dropped out of the common texts of Mela. For where book II reads Lucinum, Larinum must be restored. But, he says, Daunia has the towns Tifernum Amnem, Clusernam, Lucrinum, Theanum, and Montem Garganum. The new Larinum belongs to the lordship of the Orsini, a Roman family.

units.la: Ab Littore P. M. iv est Lesina, à Piscatoribus vicini Stagni primum coepta; sed ita progressu temporis ampliata, ut frequens & honestum factum fuerit Opidum, & Episcopum etiam acceperit. Diruta ab Saracenis, restituta est, sed non qua quondam amplitudine. Hodie ab Colonis propemodum deserta, sedem tamen retinet Episcopalem. Nomen Vibi ab Lesina, Inlurici Insula: unde primi Habitatores in adversam hanc Continentem migrasse feruntur.
units.tr: Four miles from the shore is Lesina, which began as a settlement of fishermen on the nearby lagoon; but in the course of time it grew so that it became a populous and respectable town and even received a bishop. Destroyed by the Saracens, it was restored, but not to its former size. Today it is almost deserted by its inhabitants, yet it keeps its episcopal see. The name of Vibi comes from Lesina, an island of Illyricum, from which the first inhabitants are said to have migrated to this opposite mainland.

units.la: In Continenti deinde iv Vibe Lesina millibus, unoque à Phiterno Serra Caprecla conspicitur in alti Montis vertice decantatum passim Opidum, quod Pecudū gregibus, qui in Apuliam hibernandi gratia ducuntur, hac transire, adpenso Portorio, quod Dogana dicitur, sit necesse. Episcopalem habet Sedem.
units.tr: On the mainland, four miles from Vibe Lesina and one from Phiternum, Serra Caprecla is seen on the top of a high mountain, a town known everywhere. Flocks of sheep led to winter in Apulia must pass through it, and must pay the toll that is called the Dogana. It has an episcopal see.

units.la: Deinde paullo altius, quædam sunt Castella haud procul à Phiterno: ad D. Iulianum, Coloronum, Matia, Petra Caella, Gedanum, & alia parvi momenti: quorum quædam superius etiam memorata.
units.tr: A little further inland are some villages not far from Phiternum: ad D. Iulianum, Coloronum, Matia, Petra Caella, Gedanum, and others of little importance, some of which have already been mentioned above.

units.la: Secundum Amnem sursum procedenti læva, multo altius prope ipsum Fluminis Fontem Circus Marr est, juxtaque dein Amnis, Apulia Daunia terminus.
units.tr: Going upstream along the river, on the left, much higher up, close to the very source of the river, is Circus Marr; and next to it the river marks the boundary of Apulia Daunia.

units.la: Quæ Ἐρδωνία Ptolemæo in Mediterraneis Apulorum Dauniorum Vrbs; Ἐρδωνία Straboni Ardonea Livio libro xxiv multitudinis numero, ut & Erdonia Antonino; Ardona Limitum libello; ea hodie Codogna censetur Celso Cittadino in confinio Apulorum & Hirpinorum. Cerugno vocatur ab Nigro. Ab Herdonia sane vel Erdonia, Herdonienses Plinio, Apulorum Populisn antiquis Codicibus sunt Herdonenses; in vulgatis etiam nonnullis Erdonienses & Hordonienses.
units.tr: What Ptolemy calls Ἐρδωνία [Erdonia], a city of the Daunian Apulians inland, Strabo calls Ἐρδωνία [Erdonia], and Livy in book 24 Ardonea, as to its number of people, as does Antoninus Erdonia; the Limitum libellus has Ardona. Today it is thought to be Codogna, according to Celso Cittadino, on the border of the Apulians and the Hirpini. It is called Cerugno by Nigro. From Herdonia or Erdonia, Pliny has Herdonienses, and in the old manuscripts the people of the Apulians are Herdonenses; in some of the common printed texts Erdonienses and Hordonienses.

units.la: Adscribam hic Iter quod in Itineraria Tabula Littorale ducitur ad Mare Superum cum per utramque Apuliam & Daunum & Peucetiam, tum Salentinorum Regionem: ab Larino, quod paullo ante descripsi, Hydruntum usque: ea mente, ut corruptiora inibi emendem, obscura nora inlustrem, simulque Lectorem benevolum mecum in plenioreum ducam Locorum, quæ in Daunia dicta, quæque in Peucetia & Salentina sunt dicenda, cognitionem: Itineraria Tabula. Vulgat. Nomencl. Larinum, xii | Larino. Teneapulo, xviii | Teano. Latet Teanum Apulum. Ergitium, xxv | Arpi. Legendum esse Argosippion, antea monui. Siponto, viii | Siponto.
units.tr: I shall set down here the route that is traced along the coast on the Itinerary Table, by the Upper Sea, through both Apulia, Daunia and Peucetia, and the region of the Salentini, from Larinum, which I described a little earlier, as far as Hydruntum. My purpose is to correct the corrupt readings, to clarify the obscure ones, and at the same time to lead the kindly reader with me to a fuller knowledge of the places mentioned in Daunia and of those that are to be described in Peucetia and Salentina. Itinerary Table | Common names Larinum, xii | Larino. Teneapulo, xviii | Teano. Teanum Apulum lies hidden. Ergitium, xxv | Arpi. I have already said that Argosippion should be read. Siponto, viii | Siponto.

units.la: Sequitur nonnihil confusionis in Anxano, quod Ferentanorum apud Ptolemæum Opidum; & in Sar.., quæ sequiore hic loco, Ptolemæo sunt inter Sipontum & Aunernam, in Mediterraneis.
units.tr: Some confusion arises over Anxanum, which Ptolemy gives as a town of the Ferentani; and over Sar.., which in this later place Ptolemy puts between Sipontum and Aunerna, inland.

units.la: {y} Dauniae. Fl. Aufidus, | vi | Lofanto Fiume. Bardulos, | viii | Videntur Barulum vel Baruli signari. | | Barlette. Turenum, | vi | Trani. Natiolum, | viiii | ubi Marfetta. Bartum, | xx | Barri. Turris Cafaris, | ix | inter S.Georgium & Molam. Dertum, | ix | inter S.Vitt & Polisanum. Gnatie, | xxi | Nace vel Nazo. Legend. Gnatiæ. Spelunis, | xxviii | inter Egnatiam & Villam Nevam. Legend. Speluncis. Brindisi. | x. | Brindisi. Emend. Brindisio. Fl. Pastum. | .... | ............ Balentium, | xv | Torre di S. Cataldo, aut circiter. Luppia, | xxv | ............ Videntur. | viii | Otranto.
units.tr: {y} Of Daunia. Fl. Aufidus, | vi | Lofanto river. Bardulos, | viii | It seems that Barulum or Baruli is meant. | | Barletta. Turenum, | vi | Trani. Natiolum, | viiii | where Marfetta is. Bartum, | xx | Barri. Turris Cafaris, | ix | between S. Giorgio and Mola. Dertum, | ix | between S. Vito and Polignano. Gnatie, | xxi | Nace or Nazo. Read Gnatiae. Spelunis, | xxviii | between Egnatia and Villa Nova. Read Speluncis. Brindisi, | x. | Brindisi. Emend to Brundisio. Fl. Pastum, | .... | ............ Balentium, | xv | Torre di S. Cataldo, or thereabouts. Luppia, | xxv | ............ It seems. | viii | Otranto.

units.la: CAPVT XXXI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXI.

units.la: Apulia Peucetia.
units.tr: Apulia Peucetia

units.la: Sic se habet Apulia, quæ eis Aufidum Fluvium Occidentalior, Daunia dicebatur: sequitur explicanda jam nunc, quæ trans eundem Fluvium Orientialior, cognominari solet Peucetia.
units.tr: Such is Apulia, which on the western side of the River Aufidus was called Daunia. What remains to be described is the region beyond the same river to the east, which is usually called Peucetia.

units.la: Nomen illi a Peucetio Lycaonis Filio, Oenotri Fratre, xvii ante Bellum Troianum ætatibus huc profecto, utinemoriæ produnt cum alii, tum Dionysius Halicarnassus libro 1 Antiquit. Roman. Dicitur nunc vernacula Italorum lingua Terra Barina, Terra di Bari, ab Urbe Bario primaria, ceterarumque Capite.
units.tr: It takes its name from Peucetius, son of Lycaon and brother of Oenotrus, who came here seventeen generations before the Trojan War, as both others and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, in book 1 of the Roman Antiquities, record. In the vernacular Italian it is now called Terra Barina, Terra di Bari, from the city of Bari, its chief town and the head of the others.

units.la: Regio hæc stupenda Agrorum ubertate, admirandaque nobilissimorum Fructuum copia cum reliqua fere Italia communi potest. Sunt tamen ibi, ne quid sit omni ex parte beatum, loca quædam, quæ pluviis, aquisque laborant, ut merito Horatius Sustinulosam vocet Apuliam, & Persius jure cecinerit Satyra 1,
units.tr: This region, remarkable for the richness of its fields and the abundance of very fine produce, may be compared with almost the rest of Italy. Yet, lest anything be wholly blessed, there are some places that suffer from lack of rain and water, so that Horace rightly calls Apulia "thirsty" (sustinulosam), and Persius, in Satire 1, rightly sang:

units.la: Nec lingua tantum sitiat Canis Apula.
units.tr: "Nor does the Apulian dog thirst only in its tongue."

units.la: His locis antea Aetolos ex Græcia ortos habitasse ferunt, qui expulerant Pediculos. Sic Plinio lustrinoque scribuntur; Πεδίκλοι Straboni, Πελίχαι corrupte Appiano. Memorant autem Adolescentes eos fuisse ix, totidemque Virgines ex Illurico ortos, ab iis progenitos fuisse xiii Populos, multaque Oppida condita.
units.tr: These places, they say, were formerly inhabited by Aetolians who had come from Greece and had driven out the Pediculi. So Pliny and Lustrinus write; Strabo has Pedicli [Πεδίκλοι], and Appian, corruptly, Pelichae [Πελίχαι]. They record that there were nine young men and as many virgins, sprung from Illyricum, and that from them thirteen peoples were descended and many towns founded.

units.la: Ora Regionis huius Littoralis primum percurria: post, quæ in Mediterraneis perlustrabo. Ab ea parte, quæ Orientem spectat, ordiar.
units.tr: I shall first survey the coast of this region, and afterwards describe what lies inland. I shall begin from the side that faces the east.

units.la: A Portu Brundusino flexus primum est Aquinonem versus per litus Oftuni; de quo iv P.M. in Mediterraneis at sito, alibi. Villa Nora hic, Portus Oftuncensis, quo ex illa urbe Merces deferri solent in Naves.
units.tr: From the harbour of Brindisi the coast first bends towards Aquinum, along the shore of Ostuni. Ostuni lies four Roman miles inland; more on it elsewhere. Here is Villa Nora, the harbour of Ostuni, through which the goods of that city are usually carried down to ships.

units.la: Dein spatio P.M. xiiii. antiquissimæ Civitatis Egnatiæ vestigia. Egnatia Plinio, Mela, Antonino; Ἐγνατία Straboni & Ptolemæo dicitur, quæ Gnatia Horatio libro 1 Sat. v. & Antonino alio quam supra loco: Gnatiæ in Itineraria Tabula. κωμη apud Strabonem. Hodie conlapsa jacet: sed ejus Bustum non procul ab ora inter vepres & dumeta Nazo vocatur Nigro: Natta, Ananiensi: Iovenazo Collemutio & Pontano: Anazzo Ligorio. Celsus Cittadinus & Volaterranus putant ex ejus ruinis extructam Monopolim.
units.tr: Then, at fourteen Roman miles, are the traces of the very ancient city of Egnatia. Egnatia in Pliny, Mela and Antoninus; Egnatia [Ἐγνατία] in Strabo and Ptolemy, which is Gnatia in Horace, Satires book 1, poem 5, and in Antoninus at another place than the one above: Gnatiae in the Itinerary Table. A village [κωμη] in Strabo. Today it lies in ruins, but its remains, not far from the shore among brambles and thickets, are called Nazo by Nigro, Natta by the Ananiensian, Iovenazo by Collenuccio and Pontano, and Anazzo by Ligorio. Celsus Cittadinus and Volaterranus think Monopoli was built from its ruins.

units.la: Inter Egnatiam & Villam Novam, nisi conjectura fallit, Speluncæ fuerunt, quarum mentio apud Antoninum. In Itineraria Tabula Spelunæ scribitur, pro Speluncis.
units.tr: Between Egnatia and Villa Nova, unless conjecture deceives, there were caves, whose mention is found in Antoninus. In the Itinerary Table it is written Spelunae, for Speluncis.

units.la: Quarto ab Egnatia ruinis milliari modica visitur Arx D. Stephani; in maris scopulo, brachij instar in altum procurrente, sita: Equitum D. Ioannis Rhodiorum.
units.tr: At four miles from Egnatia, among the ruins, is seen a small fortress of St Stephen, set on a rock in the sea, jutting out into the deep like an arm. It belongs to the Knights of St John of Rhodes.

units.la: Altero ab hinc lapide per littus Vrbis Nova Monopolis Episcopalis & Marchionatus titulo celebris; non quidem magna sed pulchra, splendida, aedificiorumque magnificentia nobilis. Illustrarunt nomen Vrbis Bartholomeus Sibylla, Monachus, Philosophus, & Theologus; & Hieronymus cognomine Monopolitanus, Professor primum Patavij & Neapoli; post Archiepiscopus Tarentinus; Scriptis celebres. Ager Monopolitanus Olei feracissimus.
units.tr: Another milestone along the shore brings us to the new city of Monopolis, a bishopric and famous for the title of marquisate: not large, but beautiful, splendid, and noble for the magnificence of its buildings. The city's name has been made illustrious by Bartholomeus Sibylla, monk, philosopher and theologian, and by Hieronymus, surnamed Monopolitanus, professor first at Padua and then at Naples, afterwards archbishop of Taranto, famous for his writings. The territory of Monopoli is very fertile in olive oil.

units.la: A Monopoli P. M. v per littus Polinianum, Polignano, succedit, Civitas Episcopalis, edita licet praeruptaque & saxosa in rupe sita, lauta tamen & populo frequens. Adiderunt Cives servare sc Viti, Crescentij, Moacsliqueque Martyrum Corpora.
units.tr: From Monopoli, five Roman miles along the coast, comes Polinianum, Polignano, a bishop's city, set on a steep, rocky cliff; although it is high and stony, it is nonetheless elegant and full of people. The citizens add that they keep the bodies of the martyrs Viti, Crescentij and Moacsliqueque Martyrum.

units.la: Ab Egnatia xv, a Bario, quod sequitur xxii Arnestum fuit, Oppidum Antonino notum. Apeneste legit Sigonius. Ἀρνησσος sane, quae apud Ptolemaeum, ad Apuliam Daunian pertinent. An Arnetium sit legendum, dubitat Cittadinus, teste Ortelio.
units.tr: Fifteen miles from Egnatia and twenty-two from Bari, which comes next, was Arnestum, a town known to Antoninus. Sigonius reads Apeneste. Indeed Arnessos [Ἀρνησσος], which in Ptolemy belong to Daunian Apulia. Whether Arnetium should be read, Cittadinus doubts, as reported by Ortelius.

units.la: Per oram hinc lapide vii pernobilis & antiqua Aedes D. Viti succedit.
units.tr: Along the coast, seven miles from here, follows the very noble and ancient church of St Vitus.

units.la: Inter Polinianum & S. Viti Fanum Dertum fuit, quod in Tabula Itineraria nominatur.
units.tr: Between Polignano and the shrine of St Vitus was Dertum, which is named in the Itinerary Table.

units.la: Ab D. Viti intervallo P. M. ii Mola sequitur in litore, frequens quidem aedificiis, sed colonis agrestibus. Condidit Arcem ibi superioribus annis Marchio Polinianus ad Orae tutelam.
units.tr: From St Vitus, at two Roman miles, follows Mola on the shore, thick with buildings, but inhabited by rustic farmers. A citadel was built there in recent years by the Marquis of Polignano, to guard the coast.

units.la: Inter Molam & S. Georgij Fanum, quod ibidem in litore, Turres fuerunt, quas nominat Antoninus in Itinere, ab Equotutico Hydruntum. In Itineraria Tabula Turris Cesare scribitur, cum Portu cognomine Turris.
units.tr: Between Mola and the shrine of St George, which stands on the shore there, were Turres, the Towers, which Antoninus names on the road from Equotuticum to Hydruntum. In the Itinerary Table it is written Turris Cesare, with the added name Portu, that is, Turris Portus.

units.la: Ab Mola P. M. x antiqua Civitas Barium. Barium Horatio, Tacito lib. xvi, Pomponio Melae libro ii, Antonino, Itinerariae Tabulae: Barion, Plinio libro iii nat. hist. cap. xi. ante Iapyx, addenti, a Dedali Filio, a quo & Iapygia: Βαριον, Straboni & Ptolemaeo: Βαρηνς, Strabonis Epitomae: Βαρις, inquiens Stephanus, πολις, an hanc designet, nescio: Βαρις Cedreno etiam. Baris legitur apud Acronem Horatij Interpretem, qui addit ex Theotiisto Grammatico hodie Adbaris nominari. Alius Horatij Commentator, quem Cruquius edidit, Barin hanc notat aliam a Bario esse, quod & Xylandro placet ad librum vi Strabonis. Barri vulgo. Fa est pulchritudine, populique frequentia, ut Regionis universae teneat principatum, eique nomen ab se terra Bariana largiatur. Fanum habet augustissimum D. Nicolai Mireani Antistitis, in quo ipse sepultus perhibetur. Archiepiscopali gaudet dignitate. Familias habet nobiles, non paucas, in quis: D'Affatati. | D'Ffrem. | Di Massime. D'Alisio. | Filipucio. | Palombi. Arcamonte. | Gerunda. | Pascalina. Carducci. | Glori. | Rossi. Carettoni. | Lamberti. | Taurisano. De Caris. | Lampugnani. | Trefia. Dottola. | Di Marsilia.
units.tr: Ten Roman miles from Mola is the ancient city of Barium. Barium in Horace, in Tacitus book 16, in Pomponius Mela book 2, in Antoninus, and in the Itinerary Table; Barion in Pliny, Natural History book 3, chapter 11, where he adds "before Iapyx", from the son of Daedalus, from whom Iapygia also took its name. Barion [Βαριον] in Strabo and Ptolemy; Barenes [Βαρηνς] in the Epitome of Strabo; Baris [Βαρις], says Stephanus, a city; whether it designates this one I do not know. Baris also in Cedrenus. Baris is read in Acro, the interpreter of Horace, who adds, on the authority of the grammarian Theotiscus, that today it is called Adbaris. Another commentator on Horace, whom Cruquius published, notes that Barin is a different place from Barium; Xylander too agrees, on book 6 of Strabo. Commonly Barri. It is so beautiful and so populous that it holds the leadership of the whole region, and grants its name to the land, the Bari land. It has a most venerable shrine of St Nicholas, bishop of Myra, in which he is said to be buried. It enjoys archiepiscopal dignity. It has not a few noble families, among which: D'Affatati, D'Ffrem, Di Massime, D'Alisio, Filipucio, Palombi, Arcamonte, Gerunda, Pascalina, Carducci, Glori, Rossi, Carettoni, Lamberti, Taurisano, De Caris, Lampugnani, Trefia, Dottola, Di Marsilia.

units.la: A Basilio & Constantino Imperatoribus Byzantinis olim, ut Blondus memorat lib. xiii. Histor. capta direptaque, dein opibus aucta & aedificiis instaurata, aliquamdiu in potestate ditioneque fuit Sforziarum: a quibus tandem Aragonijs dotis nomine, est restituta. Tradunt Historiographi ab Gulielmo i Siciliae Rege funditus deletam: cujus cladis mentionem facit & in Itinerario suo Benjamin, ut Barium sit idem cum ipsius Mtquoles Devar רכר מיקולם, Nomen latet in litteris בר. Addit Benjamin suo adhuc tempore Incolis vacuam. Farium quoque nobile Syllani morte, Senatoris clarissimi, qui diro Neronis imperio mori iussus, pectus Centurioni praebuit feriendum. Celebris est haec urbs inauguratione Regum Siciliae & Neapolis. Ora hic importuosa. Barium Horatio Ustiosum dicitur libro i Satyra v. Agri Vbertas incredibilis. Strabo a Brundisio Barium 300 Stadiorum spatium designat. Antoninus a Bario per compendium Tarentum numerat M. P. lx.
units.tr: Once taken and plundered by the Byzantine emperors Basil and Constantine, as Blondus records in book 13 of his Histories, and afterwards enriched by its wealth and restored with buildings, it was for some time under the power and rule of the Sforzas, from whom at last it was restored to the Aragonese as a dowry. Historians relate that it was utterly destroyed by William I, King of Sicily. Benjamin also mentions this disaster in his Itinerary, and this is thought to make Barium the same as his Mtquoles Devar [רכר מיקולם]; the name lies hidden in the letters bar [בר]. Benjamin adds that in his own time it was empty of inhabitants. Farium too was notable for the death of Syllanus, a most distinguished senator, who, ordered to die under the cruel rule of Nero, offered his breast to the centurion to be struck. This city is famous for the inauguration of the kings of Sicily and Naples. The coast here is unsafe for ships. Horace calls Barium Ustiosum in book 1, Satire 5. The fertility of the land is incredible. Strabo puts the distance from Brundisium to Barium at 300 stadia. Antoninus, counting by the shorter route, gives 60 Roman miles from Barium to Tarentum.

units.la: Sequitur in ora xii lapide Iuvenatium, Guevenazzo, Vrbs Episcopalis: Agro fertili.
units.tr: On the shore, twelve miles further, follows Iuvenatium, Guevenazzo, an episcopal city with fertile land.

units.la: Tertio hinc milliari in ora est Marfetta; vel, ut alijs scribitur Merfitta, vel Melfatta. Principatus hodie titulo floret. Fuit hoc loco Natiolum, quod in Itineraria Tabula.
units.tr: At a third milestone from here, on the shore, is Marfetta; or, as others write it, Merfitta or Melfatta. It now flourishes with the title of principality. In this place was Natiolum, which is named in the Itinerary Table.

units.la: Inde quinto milliari ad littus praecelsis in rupibus oppidum est Episcopale, quod vulgo Bisegle: Latinis video scribi Virgilia. Apud se servari dicunt Cives Ossa Mauri Episcopi, Sergij & Pantaleonis Martyrum.
units.tr: Then, at a fifth milestone from there, on the shore, on very high rocks, is an episcopal town, commonly called Bisegle; I see that in Latin it is written Virgilia. The citizens say they keep the bones of Mauri Episcopi, Sergij & Pantaleonis Martyrum.

units.la: Post quintum deinde milliare Civitas Archiepiscopalis Tranum se offert Sic Latini hodie vocant, quae vulgo Trani. In Itineraria Tabula legitur Turenum. Volaterranus scribit nonnullis Trinium dici apud Plinium: cui tamen Trinium fluvius est, non Oppidum, Trasanopolita quondam fuisse nominatam testatur ex Collenutio Leandro. Inscriptio supra Portam Vrbis haec legitur, non magni aevi.
units.tr: After the fifth milestone the archiepiscopal city Tranum presents itself, as the Latins call it today; it is commonly Trani. In the Itinerary Table it is read Turenum. Volaterranus writes that by some it is called Trinium in Pliny, but Trinium is a river, not a town. He attests, from Collenuccio and Leandro, that it was formerly named Trasanopolita. An inscription above the city gate reads as follows; it is not of great age.

units.la: TRANVM A TYRRHENO FILIO DIOMEDIS CONDITVM ET A TRAIANO INSTAVRATVM.
units.tr: TRANUM, FOUNDED BY TYRRHENUS, SON OF DIOMEDES, AND RESTORED BY TRAJAN.

units.la: Ab aedificijs est pulcherrima: sed hodie majore ex parte deserta. Cautiam vide apud Leandrum. Arcem Fridericus II Imper. struxit. Hic Ophium parari scribit Platearius. Nobiles ibi Familiae: D'Angelo. | Cunio. | Passafepe. Belingieri. | Fliezavio. | Sifo i. Bonifacio. | Filingeri. | Staffa. Portoni. | Lambertino. | Stanga. Campatello. | Malardicio. | Pentura. Palagani. | Et aliae.
units.tr: It is very handsome in its buildings, but today for the most part deserted. For its caution, see Leander. Frederick II, Emperor, built the citadel. Platearius writes that Ophium was prepared here. Noble families live there: D'Angelo, Cunio, Passafepe, Belingieri, Fliezavio, Sifoi, Bonifacio, Filingeri, Staffa, Portoni, Lambertino, Stanga, Campatello, Malardicio, Pentura, Palagani, and others.

units.la: Portus olim satis commodus, hodie arena est oppletus, nemine curante, Silvae Olearum & Amygdalorum ab huius Oppidi Agro propemodum Tarentum usque pertinent.
units.tr: The harbour was once quite convenient, but today it is filled with sand, and nobody cares. The groves of olive and almond trees of this town's territory extend almost as far as Taranto.

units.la: Deinceps in ora post vi Lapidem Oppidum est nobile & frequens Barulum Barleta vulgo. Condidit, ut quidam volunt, Fridericus II Imper. Collenutius abijs, qui Canusium deseruerant, aedificatum scribit. Barduli scribuntur hoc loco in Itineraria Tabula. Medio Opidi Foro Statua ex aere armati Regis, x Pedum altitudine: Eam Incolae dicunt Imperatoris esse Heraclij: quis autem posuerit, ignorant. Barulum inter quatuor Italiae nobilissima censetur Caltella: Fabriano, inquiunt Itali, nella Marca: Prato, in Toscana: Crema, in Lombardia: Barletta, in Puglia. Et hic sua magnae Nobilitati Sedes: Acanciagiore. | Gentili. | Santa Croce. Delli Falconi. | Delli Marra. | Strazza. Galiano. | Pappaletterre. | Et aliae.
units.tr: Next, along the coast, six miles on, is the noble and populous town commonly called Barulum Barleta. Frederick II, Emperor, founded it, as some hold. Collenutius writes that it was built by those who had abandoned Canusium. Barduli is the name written for this place in the Itinerary Table. In the middle of the town's forum stands a bronze statue of an armed king, ten feet tall. The inhabitants say it is a statue of the Emperor Heraclius, but who set it up they do not know. Among the four most noble towns of Italy, Barulum is counted, the Italians say: Fabriano, nella Marca; Prato, in Toscana; Crema, in Lombardia; Barletta, in Puglia. Here too is the seat of a great nobility: Acanciagiore, Gentili, Santa Croce, Delli Falconi, Delli Marra, Strazza, Galiano, Pappaletterre, and others.

units.la: Illustravit ortu suo Gabriel Monachus, ex Praedicatorum Classe: sub cujus nomine extant Conciones. Qua usum fuerit proximis annis fortuna, memorat Sabellicus libro ultimo Enead. Littus vadosum hic & absque ullo Sinu.
units.tr: Gabriel the Monk, of the order of Preachers, made it famous by his birth; sermons under his name survive. Sabellicus, in the last book of the Enneads, records the fortune it enjoyed in recent years. The shore here is shallow and without any bay.

units.la: Haec de Littoralibus: sequuntur Mediterranea; non religioso, propter locorum situm, ordine. Ordiar ab Orientaliore plaga, qua Brundisium Tarentumque; progressurus ad Aufidum, qui limes Peucetia Apulia Occidentalior.
units.tr: These are the coastal places. The inland places follow, in an order that is not strictly religious because of the lie of the land. I shall begin from the more eastern region, where Brindisi and Taranto lie, and proceed to the Aufidus, which is the boundary of Peucetian Apulia on the western side.

units.la: Iter igitur per Continentem à Brundisio xxiii P. M. silvis dumisque horridus emensis Civitas occurrit populo frequens, Ostunum, Episcopali Sede clarum, parvo in colle situm.
units.tr: So, travelling inland from Brindisi, twenty-three Roman miles, through a rough country of woods and thickets, one comes to the town of Ostunum, populous and famous for its episcopal see, set on a small hill.

units.la: Haud procul inde Fanum est D. Alicandri, Ecclesiæ D. Nicolai Barianæ patrimonium.
units.tr: Not far from there is the shrine of D. Alicandri, a property of the church of St Nicholas of Bari.

units.la: Post id in colle Martina, xvii ab Ostuno P. M, ab Monopoli xvi.
units.tr: After that, on a hill, is Martina, seventeen Roman miles from Ostuni and sixteen from Monopoli.

units.la: Vlterius in fine collis antiqua succedit Civitas Cœlum, Cælo: Cœla Ptolemaeo. In cjus ejus Agro Crocum nasci scribunt. Oltunum versus quarto lapide D. Vitus item in Colle. Caravinea Caravigo: ulterius Cisternum, Cisternino: Lucus Rotundus: Putilianum, Opidum D. Ioannis Equitum: inde tertio milliari Castellum Nucis: Castel della Nuce; Ibi Pecuaria notum: postea vetus Opidulum Turium, nunc non magni momenti: ulterius Castellum, Ioia, Gioia, Comitatus honore splendens: frumento abundans: Aream hic extruxit Fridericus II Imper. Venationis ductus studio.
units.tr: Further on, at the end of the hill, lies the ancient town of Cœlum, Cælo; Cœla in Ptolemy. They write that saffron grows in its territory. Towards Ostuni, four miles off, is St Vitus, also on a hill. Then Caravinea (Caravigo), and further on Cisternum (Cisternino), Lucus Rotundus, Putilianum, the town of St John of the Knights; from there, three miles off, the Castle of the Nut (Castel della Nuce), known for its livestock; then the old little town of Turium, now of no great importance; further on the Castle of Gioia (Ioia), splendid with the honour of a county, abounding in grain. Frederick II, Emperor, built a palace here, out of his zeal for hunting.

units.la: Ioiae ad dextram x circiter lapide: xxx, Oltuno: xv, Bario Conversanum est Opidum, Episcopali Sede Comitatusque titulo clarum: nec non Nobilibus aliquot Familiis, in quis Della Forza, De Manerio, Rubiolo, De Tarsia.
units.tr: About ten miles to the right of Gioia: thirty from Ostuni and fifteen from Bari, is Conversanum, a town famous for its episcopal see and its title of county, and also for several noble families, among them Della Forza, De Manerio, Rubiolo, De Tarsia.

units.la: Sexto inde lapide Noia vilitur, in Comitis Ioiae ditione, à Bario P.M.x.
units.tr: Six miles from there is Noia, in the lordship of the Count of Gioia, ten miles from Bari.

units.la: Duobus hinc milliaribus, & à Bario x, Rontilianum jacet, sub imperio Ecclesiae D. Nicolai Bariensis.
units.tr: Two miles from here, and ten from Bari, lies Rontilianum, under the authority of the church of St Nicholas of Bari.

units.la: Inde per planiciem amoenissimam incedenti Aqua-Viva se offert, Bario P.M. xv. in ditione Comitis Ioiae.
units.tr: As one goes on through a most pleasant plain, Aqua-Viva presents itself, fifteen Roman miles from Bari, in the lordship of the Count of Gioia.

units.la: Sequitur inde Cassanum: hinc ad octavum lapidem Altus Murus, Alta-Mura: paulloque post inter montes Gravina: de quorum nonnullis etiam in Magna Graecia. cui an Apuliae Peucetiae; ea sint concensenda, adhuc ambigitur.
units.tr: Next comes Cassanum; from here, at the eighth milestone, Altus Murus, Alta-Mura; and a little after, among the mountains, Gravina. Some of these are also in Magna Graecia, so it is still uncertain whether they should be counted as belonging to Peucetian Apulia.

units.la: Ab Gravina P.M. viii Spinaccola vilitur, agri opimi, magnamque frumenti copiam producentis.
units.tr: Eight Roman miles from Gravina is Spinaccola, a town of rich fields that produces a great quantity of grain.

units.la: Hinc Civitas Episcopalis est Venusia. Sic Plinio, Livio, Antonino; Στρατ. Strabone, Ptolemaeo, Plutarcho vocatur: quod Venusium Horatio. Utrumque modo legitur apud Appianum. Venusie scribitur in Itineraria Tabula, pro Venusia vel Venusio. Venosa hodie. Dictum volunt quidam Venusinum, ab Veneris cultu ejusque Fano. Locat inter Apuliam & Lucaniam Acron Horatii interpres. Distat Canusio P. M. xv. Coloniis connumerat Velleius Paterculus. Venusianos Populos habet Appianus lib.1. Bellor. Civilium; Venusinos Plinius libro iii cap.xi. Patria Q. Horatii Flacci, Poetae Lyrici, qui ab ea Venusinus. In hanc Urbem, victis ad Cannas ab Hannibale Romanis, fugit cum Equitibus quinquaginta M.Terentius Varro cos. L.Aemilio Paullo in acie caesus. Legendi praeter alios Livius libro xxii & Plutarchus in Vitis Scipionis Africani & Hannibalis. Agrum Venusinum describit libro Hiltor.
units.tr: From here comes the episcopal city of Venusia. Plinius, Livy and Antoninus call it so; Strabo, Ptolemy and Plutarch call it Στρατ. [Strat.]; Horace calls it Venusium. Both forms are read in Appian. Venusie is written in the Itinerary Table, for Venusia or Venusio. Today it is Venosa. Some hold that it was called Venusinum from the worship of Venus and her shrine there. Acron, the commentator on Horace, places it between Apulia and Lucania. It is fifteen Roman miles from Canusium. Velleius Paterculus counts it among the colonies. Appian, in the first book of the Civil Wars, mentions the Venusian people; Plinius, in book iii, chapter xi, mentions the Venusini. It was the homeland of Q. Horatius Flaccus, the lyric poet, who is called Venusinus from it. After the Romans were defeated by Hannibal at Cannae, the consul M. Terentius Varro fled to this city with fifty horsemen; L. Aemilius Paullus was killed in the battle. Besides others, one should read Livy, book xxii, and Plutarch in the Lives of Scipio Africanus and Hannibal. Horace describes the Venusian country in his book of Epistles.

units.la: 1. Pentanus.
units.tr: 1. Pentanus.

units.la: Venusinae Civitati vicinam facit Acron Batinam, cujus mentio apud Horatium: Campam Apuliae adscribens, indeque, addens. Matinos Campo dici, pro Batinus. abusive, Batinos Saltus habet idem Horatius, qui Bantini in Manu-scripto. Βάτινα dicitur haec Urbs apud Plutarchum in Marcello, & Livium libro xxvii. Vide num quid his lucis ab iis, quae supra ubi de Apuliae Populis in genere, de Matinis inquam.
units.tr: Acron places Batina, a town near the Venusian city, which Horace mentions, "assigning it to the plain of Apulia"; and then he adds that Matinos Campo is said for Batinus, improperly. Horace also has Batinos Saltus, which in some manuscripts is Bantini. This city is called Βάτινα [Batina] by Plutarch in the Life of Marcellus, and by Livy in book xxvii. See whether anything here is clarified by what was said above about the peoples of Apulia in general, about the Matini, I mean.

units.la: Sex ab Venusia milliari, tertioque ab Aufido Lavellum est, Episcopale Opidum; Patria Tartalia, quo Copiarum suarum Duce diu usus Franciscus Sforza, Dux postea Mediolanensis.
units.tr: Six miles from Venusia, and three from the Aufidus, is Lavellum, an episcopal town. Its native son was Tartalia, whose forces Francesco Sforza, later Duke of Milan, long used as his commander.

units.la: Superius inter asperrimos Apennini Montes est Acherontia, Sede Archiepiscopali incluta. Agerentia vitiose Paullo Diacono lib.11. cap.xxi, Langbardic. Hanc alij in Hirpinis locant.
units.tr: Higher up, among the very rough mountains of the Apennines, is Acherontia, renowned for its archiepiscopal see. Paul the Deacon, book ii, chapter xxi, of the Lombard History, wrongly calls it Agerentia. Others place it among the Hirpini.

units.la: Ab hinc P. M. xv item inter Montes Atella est; alia, quam quae prope Neapolin.
units.tr: Fifteen Roman miles from here, also among the mountains, is Atella, a different place from the one near Naples.

units.la: Rursum ab Venusia xv lapide Aufidum versus Cannarum vestigia visuntur exigua: licet Cathedralis Ecclesia sit Cannarum, à qua Cannensis Episcopus nominatur. In Argyrippae Territorio fuisse scribit Tzetza in Variis suis: In Apulia Dauniorum, Campo Diomedeo ad Aufidi Ostia, Zonaras lib. 11. Insignis Clade Romana Vicus, de qua nulli non Scriptores, cum primis Livius libro xxii, Plutarchus in Vitis Hannibalis & Scipionis, Silius Italicus lib.ix.
units.tr: Again, fifteen miles from Venusia, towards the Aufidus, slight traces of Cannae can be seen, although the cathedral church is of Cannae, from which the bishop is named Cannensis. Tzetzes, in his Miscellanies, writes that it lay in the territory of Argyrippa, in the Apulia of the Daunians, in the Diomedean plain at the mouths of the Aufidus. Zonaras, book ii: a village notable for the Roman defeat, of which almost every writer speaks, above all Livy in book xxii, Plutarch in the Lives of Hannibal and Scipio, and Silius Italicus in book ix.

units.la: Distabat ab Cannarum Vico xxv stadijs, ut Procopius scribit, Canusium. Ita Plinius, Pomponius Mela, Paullus Diaconus, Antoninus vocant: Καυσιον Ptolemaeus; quod Καυσιον Straboni. Καυσιον, inquit Stephanus, μεγίστη πόλις τῆς Ἰταλιωτίδος; & addit, Στρᾶβων ἐπὶ τῇ. Quod verum. Scribit enim ille, quod non procul à mari in planicie duae sint sitae Urbes, quae, ut ambitus earum docent, quondam, Ἰταλιωτίδων fuerunt maximae, Καυσιον & Ἀργυρίππη. Haud ita procul Mari, πρὸς τ᾽ ποταμὸν Ἀυφίδιον, ut idem Strabo paullo ante dixerat: quod item testantur Plinius & Pomponius Mela. Apuliae Daunia adscribit Ptolemaeus; male; quum omnis ultra Aufidum ripa, in qua Cannusium, Peucetiis ab omnibus tributatur. Nomen Ganola quidam retinere notat. Nonnulli circa Farfetum fuisse centent. Cannusium idem esse cum Cannarum urbe adiciunt Leander: qui ti Livium, Plutarchum, Strabonem, Plinium, & alios, utrumque & Canusii & Cannarum facientes mentionem, hunc expendisse, aliud proculdubio fuisset mentis. De Cannusina Lana Martialis in Apophoretis. Plinius libro xxxv cap. vi. de coloribus nativis & fictitijs agens, Cannusinum Purpureissimum utilissimum commendat.
units.tr: Canusium was, as Procopius writes, twenty-five stadia from the village of Cannae. Thus Plinius, Pomponius Mela, Paul the Deacon and Antoninus call it; Ptolemy calls it Καυσιον [Causion], which is also the form in Strabo. Stephanus says: Καυσιον [Causion] is the greatest city of Italiotis; and he adds, "Strabo, at this point." This is true. For he writes that not far from the sea, on the plain, there are two cities which, as their circuits show, were once the greatest of the Italiotic cities: Καυσιον [Causion] and Ἀργυρίππη [Argyrippe]. Not very far from the sea, towards the river Aufidus, as Strabo himself had said a little before; Plinius and Pomponius Mela likewise bear witness to this. Ptolemy assigns Canusium to Daunian Apulia, wrongly, since every bank beyond the Aufidus, where Canusium stands, is by everyone attributed to the Peucetians. Some note that a certain Ganola preserves the name. Some think it lay near Farfetum. Leander adds that Canusium is the same as the city of Cannae; but if he had weighed Livy, Plutarch, Strabo, Plinius and others, who mention both Canusium and Cannae as separate places, he would doubtless have thought otherwise. On the Canusian wool, see Martial in the Apophoreta. Plinius, book xxxv, chapter vi, discussing natural and artificial colours, commends the Canusian purple as most useful.

units.la: Itinere dein per Campeltria mare versus occurrit Filetum, Civitas Episcopalis nec procul inde Medonum, Medogno: unde non magno intervallo Castellum Palus.
units.tr: Then, by a route through the plains of Campeltria towards the sea, one comes to Filetum, an episcopal city, and not far from there Medonum (Medogno), from which, at no great distance, is the little town of Palus.

units.la: Viterius Civitas est, quae vulgo Bitonto vel Botonto; nobilis, frequens, Episcopatus & Marchionatus dignitate clara. Butontum Antonino; in aliis libris legitur Budruntum: unde Butuntinensis Plinio, magna M. S. S. Codicum concordia, & unanimi consensu. Illustrarunt ortu suo Antoninus & Marianus, Monachi, Ordinis hic Praedicatorum, ille Minorum. Nobiles ibi Familiae, quae vulgo: D'Abenante. | Padula. | Tacola. Barone. | Perisio. | Valeriano. Bozzi. | Di Pice. | Di Veritati. Girardi. | Regna. | Vulpiano. Di Labino. | Ripa. | Planeta. Di Lucio. | Rogadio. | Et aliae. Di Maggiori. | Scattaglio.
units.tr: Further on is a city commonly called Bitonto or Botonto, noble, populous, and famous for its dignity as a bishopric and marquisate. Antoninus calls it Butontum; other books read Budruntum, whence Plinius has Butuntinensis, with great agreement and unanimous consent of the manuscripts. Antoninus and Marianus, monks, one of the Order of Preachers here, the other of the Minorites, made it famous by their birth. Noble families live there, commonly called: D'Abenante, Padula, Tacola, Barone, Perisio, Valeriano, Bozzi, Di Pice, Di Veritati, Girardi, Regna, Vulpiano, Di Labino, Ripa, Planeta, Di Lucio, Rogadio, and others, Di Maggiori, Scattaglio.

units.la: Abest Bitonto M. P. vii pulcrum Opidum Terlitium unde tertio Civitas est; quae vernacule Rino vel Rubo. Rubi Antonino. Horatius Canusio se Rubos venisse ostendit libro i. Satyra v,
units.tr: Bitonto lies seven miles off, then the pretty town of Terlizzi, from which the city is the third; in the vernacular it is called Rino or Rubo. Rubi is the Antonine name. Horace shows in Satire 5 of Book 1 that he came to Rubi from Canusium.

units.la: Inde Rubos fessi pervenimus: utpote longum
units.tr: Thence we came, weary, to Rubi, since the journey was long

units.la: Cassentes iter & factum corruptum imbri.
units.tr: and the road was spoiled by rain.

units.la: ubi imprudenter Campaniae tribuit V. CL. Dionysius Lambinus. Populi Plinio Rubustini, qui in Exemplari Toletano Rubustini. Inde Rubea vel Rubea Virga Virgilio libro i Georgic.
units.tr: Here V. CL. Dionysius Lambinus imprudently assigned it to Campania. The people are Pliny's Rubustini, which in the Toledo copy is written Rubustini. Then there is Rubea, or Rubea Virga, in Virgil, Georgics Book 1.

units.la: Nunc facilis Rubea texatur fissina virgi.
units.tr: Now the Rubean osier is easily woven into baskets.

units.la: Hinc quatto milium Quarata, vel Corato, Marchionis Aquinatis Opidum: inde septimo Iudrum Civitas, titulo Ducatus & Episcopatus incluta. Fictilia Andry vasa ob elegantiam operis in summa apud omnes sunt existimatione.
units.tr: Four miles from here is Quarata, or Corato, a town of the Marquis of Aquino. Then, seven miles on, is Giovinazzo, a city renowned for its title of duchy and bishopric. The earthenware vessels of Andria are held in the highest esteem by everyone for the elegance of their workmanship.

units.la: Opidum haud procul hinc fuit, quod Silvium Antonino, Itinere à Benevento Tarentum; Silvium Straboni & Diodoro: unde Silvini Populi Plinio. Scribitur & Ad Silvianum Antonino; Itinere Beneventano Hydruntum.
units.tr: Not far from here there was a town which Antoninus calls Silvium, on the route from Benevento to Tarentum; Strabo and Diodorus also call it Silvium, whence the Silvini people in Pliny. It is also written Ad Silvianum in Antoninus, on the Beneventan route to Hydruntum.

units.la: Montes deinde versus incedenti itinere secundum Aufidum millium xii. exiguo in colle, tribus ab ipso amne miliaribus, ab Lauello autem novem, Cannusium Cannusio, invenitur, non tamen Vetus illud, de quo supra: quum id in planicie fuerit situm; hoc autem in Colle sit, nullo prorsus Antiquitatis argumento nobile.
units.tr: Then, as one proceeds on the road towards the mountains, along the Aufidus, twelve miles on, on a small hill three miles from the river itself and nine from Lavello, is found Canusium, the Canosa of today. It is not, however, that ancient town mentioned above, since that was situated on a plain; this one stands on a hill and is noted for no evidence of antiquity whatever.

units.la: Sequitur ad tertium lapidem Aufidus, medius inter Peucetiam & Daunian limes; de quo alibi.
units.tr: Next, at the third milestone, comes the Aufidus, the middle boundary between Peucetia and Daunia, of which more elsewhere.

units.la: Referam huc Iter; quod à Benevento Hydruntum describit Antoninus.
units.tr: I will set out here the route that Antoninus describes from Benevento to Hydruntum.

units.la: Antoninus: Itineraria Tabula. Vulgata Nomencl.
units.tr: Antoninus: Itinerary Table. Common Nomenclature

units.la: A Benevento Hydruntum m. | Benevento. p. clxv. Aeclanum, m.p.xxv, Eclano, xvi. In aliis libris legitur Eclanum. Ἀικ-λανον Prolemaeo. Hinc Aeclani Plinio, & Eclanensis.
units.tr: From Benevento to Hydruntum, miles: Benevento, 165 paces. Aeclanum, 25 Roman miles; Eclano, 16. In other books it is read as Eclanum. Ptolemy has Aiklanon [Ἀικλανον]. Hence Aeclani in Pliny, and Eclanensis.

units.la: Apulia. Ager libro de Limitibus? Sub Romulam. M.P. XI. | Subromula, | XI. Eadem cum Pomula Livij libro x. Stephano Παμυλία dicitur. | Aquilonia, | VI. Pontem Aufidi M.P. XXII | Ponte Aufidi, | XVIII. Vitiosis admodum gyris & circumductionibus. Alij Codices Ponte Aufidi; alij Fonte; nonnulli Pontaufido; quidam Pentaufido. Venusia, M.P. XVIII. | Venusie, | XXXV Venosa. De ea alibi. Legend. Venusia. Ad Smicroanum, M.P. XX. | Siutum, | XXV. Sequenti itinere Silvium. Emenda Silviano. Sub Lupatia, M.P. XXI. | Sublubatia, | XI. Sublupatia, Sigonius: Sub Luparia, vel Sub Lupantia, Surita. Canales, M.P. XIII. | Maximum hic Intervallum Meminit & D. Athanasius in concilio Sardiano. Hydruntum, M.P. XXV. | Tdrunte, | Otrante.
units.tr: Apulia. Field, in the book on Limits? Under Romula, 11 miles. Subromula, 11. This is the same as Pomula in Livy Book 10; Stephanus calls it Pamylia [Παμυλία]. Aquilonia, 6. The bridge over the Aufidus, 22 miles; Ponte Aufidi, 18. The turns and detours are very faulty. Other manuscripts have Ponte Aufidi, others Fonte, some Pontaufido, some Pentaufido. Venusia, 18 miles; Venusie, 35, Venosa. Of it elsewhere. Read Venusia. To Smicrum, 20 miles; Siutum, 25. In the following route it is Silvium; emend to Silviano. Under Lupatia, 21 miles; Sublubatia, 11. Sublupatia is Sigonius's reading; Sub Luparia or Sub Lupantia is Surita's. Canales, 13 miles. Here he mentions a very great interval, as does St Athanasius in the Council of Sardica. Hydruntum, 25 miles; Tdrunte, Otranto.

units.la: CAPUT XXXII. Salentini.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXII. The Salentini.

units.la: ORDINE in Prisca Propriaque Italia, qua Orientem spectat, versus Mare Hadriaticum trans Phiternum, post Apulias, explicanda succedit SALENTINORUM Sedes.
units.tr: In the order of ancient and proper Italy, facing east towards the Adriatic Sea beyond Phiternum and after the Apulias, the seat of the Salentini comes next to be described.

units.la: Hanc variis olim nominibus appellatam fuisse libro VI refert Strabo. Primum enim Iapygia Messapiaque; inde Calabria & Salentinorum Regio fuit dicta. Iapygia (Ἰαπυγία Aristoteli, Herodoto, aliis) ab Iapygilus, qui nominis Auctorem Iapygem quemdam Dædali filium, scribuntur habuisse ab Strabone libro VI, Appiano libro I. Bellor. Civilium, Plinio libro III, Solino, aliis. Hinc Iapygium Promontorium, de quo suo loco. Messapiam (Μεσσαπία) dictam notant Solinus, quem dixi, & Servius ad VIII Æneid. ab Messapo, Græcorum Ductore; cujus etiam meminit Virgilius eodem libro. Sed alio, quam qui Servio in oculis loco. Μεσσαπία unico S. scribitur Stephano: cujus hæc verba. Μεσσαπία χώρα Ἰαπυγίας, προσεχὴς Ταράντι. Calabria (sic enim postea vocatam memoriæ prodit Solinus) unde dicta, alibi expositi.
units.tr: Strabo, in book VI, reports that this region was once called by various names. First it was called Iapygia and Messapia, and afterwards Calabria and the land of the Salentini. Iapygia (Ἰαπυγία in Aristotle, Herodotus and others) is said to take its name from the Iapygians, who, according to Strabo in book VI, Appian in book I of the Civil Wars, Pliny in book III, Solinus and others, had as their founder a certain Iapyx, son of Daedalus. Hence the Iapygian Promontory, of which in its place. Messapia (Μεσσαπία) is said to be named, as Solinus (whom I have mentioned) and Servius on Aeneid VIII note, from Messapus, leader of the Greeks, whom Virgil also mentions in the same book. But this is another Messapus from the one Servius has in view. Stephanus writes Μεσσαπία with a single S, and his words are these: "Messapia, a region of Iapygia, adjoining Tarentum." Calabria (for Solinus records that it was later called by this name) took its name from a cause I have explained elsewhere.

units.la: Salentinos (Σαλεντίνος) Festus ab Salo derivat, quod Salentini pene circumquaque mari ambiantur. Alij appellatos sic volunt ab Fædere, quod inter Idomeneos & Cretenses in Salo, id est, Mari initum fuit: quoniam in hanc oram Lytium Idomeneum commigrasse, testis est Virgilius libro III Æneid. Salentinos ab Lytiis conditos tradit Solinus. Referam huc quod Isacio in Lycophronem notatur; Μεσσαπίη, scribenti alio nomine Ἰαπυγη, postea Σαλαπία, postremo Καλαβρία nominata est. Addit idem alio loco Ὀταλντίαν etiam nuncupatam. Salantinos per A legunt vetusta apud Hubertum Goltium Numismata. Sallentini per duo LL scribuntur
units.tr: Festus derives Salentini (Σαλεντίνος) from salum, because the Salentini are surrounded by the sea almost on every side. Others want them so called from a covenant (foedus) made between the Idomeneans and the Cretans in the Salum, that is, the sea; for Virgil, in book III of the Aeneid, bears witness that Lyttius, the follower of Idomeneus, migrated to this coast. Solinus says that the Salentini were founded by the Lyttians. I will add here what Isacius notes on Lycophron: Messapia, which some call by another name, Iapygia, was afterwards called Salapia, and finally Calabria. The same writer elsewhere adds that it was also called Otalntia. Ancient coins, according to Hubert Goltz, read "Salantini" with an A. Salentini is written with two L's.

units.la: L III 4 buntus buntur in Fastis Capitolinis; & apud Stephanum Σαλεντινοι. Salentinorum frequens mentio apud Livium, præcipue libro 11, xv, 112. Salentinorum Populos nominat Plinius lib.111 cap.xi Aletinos, Batferbinos, Neretinos, Valentinos, Veretinos. De Aletino, Neretino, & Veretino ad suas Vibes. Batferbini, ubi fuerint, ignoro. Valentini nominati vel ab Vibone, Valentia, quæ in Bruttiis; vel à Valentia, Vrbe ibi delera, quod innuere videtur Ifacius. Salentini Campi & Salentina Littora sunt apud Pomponium Melam: illi etiam apud Virgilium libro 111 Aeneidos. Nomen item huic Regioni Apulia datum legimus. Unde Apulia dicta, alibi dictum. Recentissimum nunc Italis ab Hydrunte, Terra Hydruntina, vulgo Terra d'Otranto.
units.tr: Salentini is written with a double L in the Capitoline Fasti, and in Stephanus as [Σαλεντινοι]. The Salentini are often mentioned in Livy, especially in book 11, chapter xv, 112. Pliny, book III, chapter xi, names the peoples of the Salentini: the Aletini, Batferbini, Neretini, Valentini and Veretini. On the Aletini, Neretini and Veretini, see their own cities. I do not know where the Batferbini were. The Valentini are named either from Vibo Valentia, which lies among the Bruttii, or from Valentia, a city there that has been destroyed, which Isacius seems to suggest. The Salentine Plains and Salentine Shores are mentioned by Pomponius Mela, and also by Virgil in book III of the Aeneid. We also read that this region was given the name Apulia. Why Apulia was so named has been said elsewhere. Most recently, Italians call it, from Hydruntum, the Hydruntine Land, commonly Terra d'Otranto.

units.la: Habet hæc Regio ab Meridie Tarentum & Mare usque ad Promontorium Salentinum, ab Oriente idem Promontorium cum Mari Ionio: quod etiam & Hadriatico, qua Septentrio est, adluitur ab Hydrunte Brundisium usque; qua Occidentem respicit Apulia illi adiacet Peucetia, cum Magnæ Græciæ portione. Sic Peninsula quædam his terminis efficitur, Ionio Hadriaticoque mari circumscripta, latitudine inter Brundisium & Tarentum xxx P. M. ut Plinius; vel xl ut alii. Quo modo Peninsula hæc totius Italiæ speciem referat, exponit eleganter Galateus de lapygiæ Situ. Strabo latitudinem diurnum aut esse expedit Viatoris iter. Littus omne ab Tarento Brundisium ambitu P. M. cc, vel, ut alij exc, colligitur; magisque in hyemem Solis exortum quam æstivum procurrens.
units.tr: This region has Tarentum and the sea to the south, as far as the Salentine Promontory; to the east, the same promontory and the Ionian Sea; it is also washed by the Adriatic on the north side, from Hydruntum as far as Brundisium. On the west it borders Apulia, with Peucetia and a part of Magna Graecia. Thus a certain peninsula is formed within these limits, enclosed by the Ionian and Adriatic seas, with a breadth between Brundisium and Tarentum of 30 miles according to Pliny, or 40 according to others. How this peninsula resembles the shape of all Italy, Galateo explains elegantly in his account of the situation of Iapygia. Strabo says that the breadth is about as far as a traveller can go in a day. The whole coast from Tarentum to Brundisium measures about 200 miles around, or, as others reckon, 250; and it projects further towards the winter sunrise than the summer one.

units.la: Tota Iapygia saluberrimo gaudet aere, cœloque sudo & sincero, præterquam in ora, quæ ab Lacu Hydruntino Brundisium usque; ubi plerisque in locis juxta mare sunt Paludes. Non sunt Flumina, inquit Antonius Galateus; non Valles, non Lacus, nec ubique Torrentes, qui ingentes pluvias recipere possint. Instituti Natura cavernas in locis Voragines; haec tamen sunt Fossæ, nulli videntur hiatus, ideo nulli animalium permissi sunt. Ha Aquas aliquandiu continent, donec à cæcis quibusdam spiramentis ex intimis terræ recessibus spiritum erigunt, atque eruunt. Hic magno impetu atque ingente fragore aperit aquis aditus: illas per subterraneos meatus in mare profluere credibile est, ut & multa flumina, quæ terra absorbet, deinde iterum emittit, aut occulte in mare projicit, ut dicunt de Nilo, & de Alpheo, Helide & Arethusa. Explosa est ab Aristotele Veterum Philosophorum sententia, qui Tartarum intra terram ponebat: locum enim aquarum, ad quem omnes decurrunt, mare est. Ha Voragines crebræ, ubi plani & latissimi sunt Campi: ut sunt Mandurini. Si hæ non essent, magnam Regionis partem aut Paludes obtinerent, aut incolitam esse Regionem foret necesse: nam per Sementis tempora Noti flare solent, & pluvias ciere. Regio fertilis & opima, xiii, ætate Strabonis, honestissimis superbiens ut bibus, quæ jam tum illius tempore præter Brundisium & Tarentum ita perierant, ut exigua essent Opida. Hodie Aletium principem obtinet locum. Incolæ moribus sunt simpliciores.
units.tr: All of Iapygia enjoys a very healthy air and a dry, clear sky, except on the coast from the Lake of Hydruntum to Brundisium, where in many places near the sea there are marshes. "There are no rivers," says Antonio Galateo, "no valleys, no lakes, and nowhere torrents that could receive great rains. Nature has made caverns in places, chasms; but these are ditches. No openings seem to exist, so no animals are allowed in them." These hold water for some time, until through certain blind vents they draw up and expel air from the deepest recesses of the earth. Here, with great force and a huge roar, the air opens a way for the waters. It is credible that they flow through underground channels into the sea, as many rivers do which the earth swallows, then sends out again, or secretly casts into the sea, as is said of the Nile, and of Alpheus, Helis and Arethusa. The view of the ancient philosophers, who placed Tartarus inside the earth, was refuted by Aristotle: the sea is the place of the waters, to which all streams run down. These chasms are frequent where the plains are flat and very wide, such as the Mandurini. If there were none, marshes would cover a large part of the region, or the region would have to be uninhabited; for during the sowing season the south winds are wont to blow and stir up rains. The region is fertile and rich, and in Strabo's time it was proud of very noble oxen, which by then had so perished, apart from Brundisium and Tarentum, that the towns were few. Today Aletium holds the chief place. The inhabitants are simpler in their manners.

units.la: Describunt hunc Italiæ, vel, ut Horatio in Odis dicitur, Terrarum Angulum Strabo; & fusissime, peculiari libello Antonius Galateus, Philosophus & Medicus.
units.tr: Strabo describes this part of Italy, or, as Horace says in the Odes, the "corner of the lands"; and Antonio Galateo, philosopher and physician, describes it most fully in a separate little book.

units.la: Ad singulorum jam nunc venio explicationem, ab Litoralibus, quæ ad Australius Apennini latus, initium sumturus; ïcque totam oram circumiturus: ingressurus inde Mediterranea.
units.tr: I now come to the explanation of the individual places, beginning with the coastal towns on the southern flank of the Apennines, and so I will go round the whole shore and then enter the inland places.

units.la: Post Tarentum, Via P. M. v nobile Cœnobium est, ab D. Vito, cujus ibi caput servari volunt, dictum.
units.tr: After Tarentum, five miles along the Via, is the noble monastery named after St. Vitus, whose head they hold is kept there.

units.la: Ad quintum inde lapidem Monacitium, Monacuccio se offert, M. P. ab littore: Arcem habens invictam.
units.tr: At the fifth stone from there, Monacizio (Monacuccio) presents itself, a mile from the shore, with an impregnable citadel.

units.la: A Tarento introrsum per continentem mille passibus & amplius plurimæ quoque Villæ reperiuntur, quas Regionis Incolæ Casalia vocant, cum singulis Turribus ad Agrorum tutelam & contra Piratarum incursiones. In his est Litiamum, ab Monacitio quatuor P. M. dictum, ut quidam volunt, ab Lytijs, quorum meminit Solinus: vel Lytio Idomeneo, cujus Virgilius lib.111 Æneid.
units.tr: Inland from Tarentum, through the mainland, a thousand paces and more, very many farmhouses are found, which the inhabitants of the region call casali, each with its towers for guarding the fields and against raids by pirates. Among these is Litiamum, four miles from Monacizio, named, as some hold, after the Lyttians, whom Solinus mentions, or after Lyttius Idomeneus, whom Virgil mentions in book III of the Aeneid.

units.la: Sequitur inde Pulsanum, & Leuranum, Fontibus nobile.
units.tr: Next follow Pulsanum and Leuranum, noted for their fountains.

units.la: Viterius ab Monacitio 1111, ab Mari 111 Castellum est Marucium, nec procul ab littore antiquum D. Petri Fanum.
units.tr: Farther on, four miles from Monacizio and three from the sea, is the castle of Marucium, and not far from the shore, the ancient shrine of St. Peter.

units.la: In ora rum Gallipolis, P. M. ab Tarento xlii. Gallipolis Melæ Plinioque, quæ nunc Auxa, addenti. Anca etiam Livio libro xxiv sunt in Apulia. Hodie Callipoli. Alijs Callipolis scribitur, tamquam Vrbs pulcra. Sed vere ab Gallis Cenomanis, ut indicat Plinius;
units.tr: On the coast is Gallipoli, 42 miles from Tarentum. Gallipolis, which Mela and Pliny call Auxa, is now so named; Anca, also in Livy book XXIV, is in Apulia. Today it is Callipoli. Some write Callipolis, as if it meant "beautiful city." But it was truly named by the Gallic Cenomani, as Pliny indicates;

units.la: {a} Apulia Terra di Terra d'Otranto Plinius dicta, quibus expulsis successerunt Graeci. Munitissimum habet natura situm. Scopulo etiam insidet seu Insulae modicae, quae mari undique cingitur; Continenti Ponte adharens, saxis fulto ingentibus. Describit peculiari libello hanc Urbem Antoninus Galateus, de quo paullo ante, nimis tamen ibi in Vita Moribusque suis delineandis. Nobiles ibi Familiae. Chrisogiovanni. | Pepi. | Sermaistri. De Magis. | Ro. chi. | Valderavano. Nandy. | Scaglioni. | & aliae.
units.tr: (a) Apulia, Terra di Terra d'Otranto, called so by Pliny. After the Cenomani were expelled, the Greeks succeeded them. Nature has given it a very strongly fortified site. It also sits on a rock, a small island surrounded on all sides by the sea, attached to the mainland by a bridge supported on huge stones. Antonio Galateo, mentioned a little earlier, describes this city in a separate booklet, though there he spends too much time on his own life and manners. Noble families there are: Chrisogiovanni, Pepi, Sermaistri (De Magis), Ro. chi, Valderavano, Nandy, Scaglioni, and others.

units.la: Per bella Alphonsi Senioris numquam ab fide defecit. Quinto post captum ab Turcis Hydruntum anno ab Venetorum classe capta & directa est. Episcopum habet qui per vices nunc originis gentisque Graecanicae, nunc Latinae creari solitus. In Sacris administrandis Instituta Ritusque Graecorum plurimum obtinent. Ager optimus est & fertilissimus.
units.tr: Through the wars of Alfonso the Elder it never fell away from the faith. In the fifth year after the Turks took Hydruntum, it was captured and recovered by the Venetian fleet. It has a bishop, who is customarily created in turn, sometimes of Greek origin and race, sometimes of Latin. In administering the sacred rites, the institutions and rites of the Greeks mostly prevail. The land is very good and most fertile.

units.la: Hinc P. M. xxx per litus Promontorium est D. Mariae quod Salentinum & Iapygium Veteribus dictum, alibi dixi.
units.tr: From here, thirty miles along the coast, is the Promontory of St. Mary, which the ancients called Salentine and Iapygian, as I have said elsewhere.

units.la: Ab Capite D. Mariae per oram M. P. xx Civitas succedit Castrum, quod cladem memorabilem accepit anno MDXXXVII a quodam Solimannicae Classis Praefecto. Episcopatus dignitate gaudet; Mercatoribus frequens, Olei coemendi.
units.tr: From the Cape of St. Mary, twenty miles along the shore, follows a town, Castrum, which suffered a memorable defeat in 1537 at the hands of a certain prefect of Soliman's fleet. It enjoys the dignity of a bishopric; it is frequented by merchants who buy oil.

units.la: A Castro deinde per oram Millia xx Caput est Leuca, cui nomen ab Opido, quod Strabono & Lucano libro IV Leuca, Leucas in maritimo Antonini Itinerario. Dicta putatur ab albedine & nuditate scopulorum. Episcopatus hodieque titulo floret. Ab Leucae Promontorio Sasson, Insula maris Ionij non procul Apollonia Epiri Opido, abest. L. P. M.
units.tr: From the castle the coast runs twenty miles to Caput Leuca, named after the town of Leuca, which Strabo and Lucan (book 4) call Leuca, and which is Leucas in the maritime itinerary of Antoninus. It is thought to take its name from the whiteness and bareness of its rocks. It still holds the title of a bishopric. Opposite Cape Leuca, not far from the town of Apollonia in Epirus, lies the island of Sasso in the Ionian Sea, about fifty miles away.

units.la: Ex his locis brevissimam in Graeciam esse transmissionem scribit Plinius lib. III nat. hist. cap. III: quod intervallum LX circiter milliar. pedestri continuare transitu, pontibus factis, primum Pyrrhus Epiri rex cogitavit; post eum M. Terentius Varro, quum Cn. Pompei classibus bello Piratico praefuit: utrumque tamen, inquit Plinius, alia cura impedierunt. Virgilius lib. III Aeneidos: Provehimur Pelago vicina Ceraunia juxta, Unde iter Italiam, cursusque brevissimus undis.
units.tr: Plinius, in book 3, chapter 3 of his Natural History, writes that the shortest crossing to Greece is from these places. The distance is about sixty Roman miles, and Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, was the first to think of crossing it on foot by building bridges. After him Marcus Terentius Varro thought of it when he commanded Pompey's fleets in the pirate war. But, as Pliny says, other concerns prevented both of them. Virgil, in book 3 of the Aeneid: We sail across the sea near the Ceraunian cliffs, from where the way to Italy lies and the shortest passage by water.

units.la: Quos versus explicans Servius eius Interpres, inter mare Ceraunios & Italiam intervallum esse tam exiguum notat, ut commode spatio mediae notis transmittatur; quum non amplius inter Italiam Graeciaque Continentem sit, quam LX P. M. inter capedo.
units.tr: Explaining these lines, Servius, Virgil's commentator, notes that the gap between the Ceraunian sea and Italy is so narrow that it can easily be crossed in a short time by those who make the journey. Between Italy and mainland Greece there is no more than sixty Roman miles of sea.

units.la: Haud procul Basta fuit Opidum, cujus mentio apud Plinium lib. III cap. XI. Vasta dicitur Galateo, qui de eo sic scribit: Hinc (ab Urbe D. Petri) vit M. P. abest Vastae opidum, totidem ab Hydruntum distans: alii Vastam dicunt, alii Vastem, alii Vastan: & hac nunc vicinus est, vix quinque in locis habitatus. Urbs mediocris ac juxta fuerat ambitus; ejus pars in humili clivo, pars in plano posita erat. Extra urbem innumera reperiuntur sepulcra, fictilibus vasculis elegantissimarum formarum, & ossibus & cineribus hominum plena, & in quibusdam Arma aenea vetustate consumpta & anuli aurei rudes, nec satis perpoliti. Reperta fuit ibidem superioribus annis Inscriptio marmorea, Characteribus & lingua (ut Pontanus, Hermolaus Barbarus, Accius Syncerus, Charneus, Summontius, & alij, qui eam viderunt, illius temporis docti Viri existimarunt) Mesapia, solae & unicae ex tota illa lingua antiquissimae reliquiae. Partem ejus posui supra capite hujus libri decimo-octavo: totam videre licet apud Martinum Smetium sol. XI. numero III.
units.tr: Not far from Basta there was a town, which Pliny mentions in book 3, chapter 11. Galateo calls it Vasta, and writes of it thus: "Thirty-six miles from the city of St Peter, one comes to the town of Vasta, which is as far from Otranto. Some call it Vasta, others Vastem, others Vastan. It is now nearby, and hardly inhabited in five places. It was once a town of moderate size and of considerable circuit; part of it lay on a gentle slope and part on the plain. Outside the town countless tombs are found, full of earthenware vessels of most elegant shapes, and of bones and ashes of men; in some of them there are bronze weapons consumed by age and rough gold rings, not yet well finished. In recent years an inscription in marble was found there, in characters and a language which (as Pontanus, Hermolaus Barbarus, Accius Syncerus, Charneus, Summontius and others who saw it, learned men of that time, judged) is Messapian, the only and unique very ancient remnant of that whole language. I have set down part of it above in the eighteenth chapter of this book; the whole can be seen in Martin Smet, page 11, number 3."

units.la: Quarto dein ab Leucae Promontorio milliari per mare Hydruntum occurrit. Sic Plinio & Antonino dicitur, quae Ὑδροῦς Straboni libro VI, Appiano lib. I. Bell. Civil. Procopio libro I Belli Gothici, Ptolemaeo Stephano, aliis. Hydrus Melae, ubi pro Mons legendum forte Mox lib. II. cap. IV: Idrus Itinerariae Tabulae: Hydron Cassiodoro libro I Variar. ad Theonem, Fui, inquienti, Tyrus est Hydron Italica: non nomine, sed historia; ob purpurae nempe utrobique positarum. Plinio etiam, ut & Antonino Hydrus videtur dici; sed diversas urbes esse apud Plinium contendit Pintianus. Hodie Otranto. Caput Regionis, cui nomen a se praebuit Terra Hydruntina, ut antea dictum. Vrbs est vetustissima, cœloque potitur clementissimo. Præter Portum satis capacem, Aquilone flante non satis tutum, Arcem habet in Saxo, quo mari imminet, Hydrentum. Lapis Neapolitanus: M. BASSÆO. M. F PAL. AXIO PATR. COL. CVR. R. P II. VIR. MVNIC. PROC. AVG VIÆ. OST. ET. CAMP. TRIB. MIL. LEG XIII. GEM. PROC. REG. CALABR. OMNIB. HONORIB. CAPVÆ, VNC. PATR. COL. LVPIENSIVM. PATR. MVNICIPI. HYDRENTINORVM VNIVERSVS. ORDO. MVNICIP. OB REM. PVBL. BENE, AC. FIDELITER. GESTAM HIC. PRIMVS. ET. SOLVS. VICTORES CAMPANIÆ. TRATIS. ET. ASTIM ................. PARIA. GLADIAT. EDIDIT E. L. D. D. D
units.tr: Four miles further along the coast from Cape Leuca, by the sea, one meets Otranto. Pliny and Antoninus call it Hydrus; Strabo (book 6), Appian (book 1 of the Civil Wars), Procopius (book 1 of the Gothic War), Ptolemy, Stephanus and others call it Hydrous [Ὑδροῦς]. Mela has Hydrus, where perhaps Mox should be read for Mons (book 2, chapter 4). The Itinerary Table has Idrus, and Cassiodorus (book 1 of the Variae, to Theon) has Hydron: "I say," he writes, "that Tyre is the Hydron of Italy," meaning not the name but the story, namely the purple dye produced in both places. In Pliny and Antoninus it also seems to be called Hydrus, though Pintianus maintains that Pliny speaks of two different cities. Today it is Otranto. It is the chief town of the region which, as was said before, takes its name, Terra Hydruntina, from itself. It is a very old city and enjoys a most mild climate. Besides a harbour large enough, though not very safe when the north wind blows, it has a citadel on a rock overhanging the sea, called Hydrentum. There is a Neapolitan stone with this inscription: "To Marcus Bassaeus, son of Marcus, of the Pollian tribe, Axius, patron of the colony, curator, duumvir of the municipality, procurator of the Augustan road and the camp, military tribune of the Thirteenth Legion Gemina, procurator of the region of Calabria, holder of all honours at Capua, patron of the colony of the Lupienses, patron of the municipality of the Hydrentini: the whole order of the municipality, for having administered public business well and faithfully, here first and alone, [...] the victors of Campania [...] gladiators' games [...] gave this at public expense, by decree of the decurions."

units.la: Archiepiscopali superbit dignitate. Ab Saracenis & Turcis, ex Aulone Macedoniæ Opido, duce Achamato, profectis multere direpta est anno cIↄ cccc xxcı tertio Eidus Sextilis; Civibus omnibus ad internecionem cæsis, in Valle propinqua quæ Martyrum vocatur, Pueris & Mulieribus in acerbissimam abductis servitutem. Recepta iterum de Turcis, ab Alfonso II. Aragonum Rege, paulatim incolis reficì, novisque Colonis, quì e diversis locis eo commigrarunt, frequentari coepit. Vide Leandrum Albertum, Antonium Galateum, & alios. Ager illi amoenus & fertilis.
units.tr: It takes pride in the dignity of an archbishopric. On the third day before the Ides of August in the year 1481, Saracens and Turks, who had set out from Aulon, a town in Macedonia, under their leader Achmat, plundered it. All the citizens were slaughtered, and the boys and women were led away into a most bitter slavery, in the nearby valley called the Valley of the Martyrs. It was recovered from the Turks by Alfonso II, king of Aragon, and gradually its inhabitants were restored; it began to be populated again by new colonists who had moved there from various places. See Leandro Alberti, Antonio Galateo and others. Its countryside is pleasant and fertile.

units.la: Hydrunte P.M. VIII munitissimum est in maris scopulo Castellum Rocca. Munivit Gualterius Brehena, ex Galateo in Iapygia.
units.tr: Eight miles from Otranto, on a rock in the sea, there is a very strongly fortified castle called Rocca. It was fortified by Walter Brehena, from Galatea in Iapygia.

units.la: Octavo hinc milliario per oram Vicus sequitur D. Cataldus ubi Turris Aletio tamquam Portus usus præbens, a quo P. M. VIII distat. Cataldus Tarentinorum fuit Archiepiscopus. Floruit haud procul hinc Batentium, quod in Itineraria Tabula.
units.tr: Eight miles further along the coast from here comes the village of D. Cataldus, where a tower serves the Aletium as a harbour; it is eight miles from Otranto. Cataldus was archbishop of the Tarentines. Not far from here flourished Batentium, which is in the Itinerary Table.

units.la: Hinc tum VIII fere P.M. Civitas est Brundusium, icapud Livium Cæsarem, Tacitum, Silium, Plinium, Solinum, Melam, Antoninum aliosque Latinos Scriptores vulgo dicitur, quum in ipsorum exaratis manu Codicibus & Antiquioribus Editionibus Brundisium plerumque scribatur. Sic in Termino Viæ, qui Arculi descriptus legitur apud Onuphrium Panuinum: IMP. CÆSAR DIVI. NERVÆ. F NERVA. TRAIANVS AVG. GERM. DACICO PONT. MAX. TR. POT XIII. IMP. VI. COS. V | In alio Exemplari P. P | IIII. COS. II VIAM. A. BENEVENTO BRVNDISIVM. FECVIT SVA. FECIT Brindisi legitur in Itineraria Tabula pro Brindisio. Bryndisium Veteribus Nummis. Βρεντέσιον est Ptolemæo: Βρεντήσιον Stephano. Barnicàs, בר נדס vocatur I enfammo in Itinerario. Brindisi hodie. Brinde nuncupant ad annum cIↄ Ↄ xxxviii mense Septembr. Ephemerides Karoli v, quæ apud me M. SS. servantur. Bruna sive; inquit Paullus ex Festo, quidam Poeta brevitatis causa Brendam dixerunt: in aliis libris Brundam scriptum reperio. Brunda vel Brenda est apud Arnobium lib. r. Βρέντη antiquum Opidi nomen fuisse videtur N. v. Iosepho Scaligero; cui vox illa Cretensium Idiomate Cerus. Βρεντέσινοι, Cives. Lapis, qui ibi pro foribus adium Diomedis Athenæi Medici: ΕΥΚΡΑΤΙΔΑΣ ΠΕΙΣΙΔΑΜΟΤ ΡΟΔΙΟΣ ΦΙΛΟΣΟΦΟΣ ΕΠΙΚΟΥΡΕΙΟΣ ΤΟΝ ΤΟΠΟΝ ΤΗΣ ΒΡΕΝΔΕΙΝΩΝ ΒΟΤΑΝΗΣ. ΕΙΣ ΤΑΦΗΝ ΨΗΦΙΣΑΜΕΝΟΣ EVCRATIDAS. PISIDAMI. F. RHODIVS PHILOSOPHVS. EPICVREVS
units.tr: About eight miles from here is the city of Brundusium, as it is commonly called in Livy, Caesar, Tacitus, Silius, Pliny, Solinus, Mela, Antoninus and other Latin writers, although in the manuscripts written by their own hands and in the older editions it is mostly written Brundisium. So on the boundary stone of the road, described as read in Onuphrius Panvinius from Arcole: "Imperator Caesar, son of the deified Nerva, Nerva Trajan Augustus, Germanicus, Dacicus, Pontifex Maximus, holder of tribunician power for the thirteenth time, Imperator for the sixth time, consul for the fifth time (in another copy: father of the country, consul for the fourth time, consul for the second time), made the road from Benevento to Brundisium, and made it at his own expense." In the Itinerary Table one reads Brindisi for Brindisium. On old coins Bryndisium. Ptolemy has Brentesion [Βρεντέσιον], Stephanus Brentesion [Βρεντήσιον]. It is called Barnicàs [בר נדס] in the Hebrew itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela. Today it is Brindisi. In the year 1538, in the month of September, they called it Brinde, in the journals of Charles V which are kept by me in manuscript. Paulus, from Festus, says: "Some poet, for brevity's sake, called it Bruna or Brenda"; in other books I find it written Brundam. Brunda or Brenda is found in Arnobius, book 1. Joseph Scaliger thinks Brentē [Βρέντη] was the ancient name of the town, a word which in the Cretan dialect means cerus. The citizens are Brentesinoi [Βρεντέσινοι]. There is a stone which stood at the doors of the house of Diomedes the physician of Athenaeus, with this inscription: "Eukratidas, son of Peisidamos, the Rhodian philosopher, the Epicurean, having decreed that the place of the Brendeinian grove be a tomb" [ΕΥΚΡΑΤΙΔΑΣ ΠΕΙΣΙΔΑΜΟΤ ΡΟΔΙΟΣ ΦΙΛΟΣΟΦΟΣ ΕΠΙΚΟΥΡΕΙΟΣ ΤΟΝ ΤΟΠΟΝ ΤΗΣ ΒΡΕΝΔΕΙΝΩΝ ΒΟΤΑΝΗΣ. ΕΙΣ ΤΑΦΗΝ ΨΗΦΙΣΑΜΕΝΟΣ]: "Eucratidas, son of Pisidamus, Rhodian philosopher, Epicurean, decreed this place for a tomb."

units.la: L. P. D. D. D.
units.tr: L. P. D. D. D.

units.la: Ζὸ Ἐθνικὸν, inquit Stephanus Βρεντέσιον: cuius & hæc. Ἀπὸ Βρέντου Ἡ ἐαχλ ἐιε, ὃ ὡς ἐνλιρῳ ἀὸι ἔν γὰρ σέματι λιμένες ποιλοι συγκλείει. Βρεντιον γὰρ πρὸς Μεσαπίας ἡ ἐλαφου κεφαλὴ, ὡς Σέλευκος. Ἐν οὐτερῷ γλωσσῶν. Conditam primum scribit Trogus ab Actolis, qui Dion eidem sequuti fuerant: hos autem expulsos fuisse ab Apulis. Aerem habet Clementissimum. Portus olim illi inclutus, ut cum vocat Florus; ex quo Romanis tutissimus quondam fuit, ut omnes docent historiæ, in Græciam transitus. De eo præter alios Ennius meus, libro vi Annalium:
units.tr: Stephanus gives the ethnic as Βρεντέσιον, and adds this: "from Brention (?), which is in fact a bay, for in its sea it encloses many harbours. For Brention, towards Messapia, is a stag's head, as Seleucus says." [Βρεντέσιον] In another book of the glosses. Trogus writes that the town was first founded by the Aetolians, and Dion, who followed him, agrees, but says they were driven out by the Apulians. The air is very mild. The harbour was once famous, as Florus calls it; from it was once the safest crossing to Greece for the Romans, as all the histories show. Among others my Ennius speaks of it in Book vi of the Annals:

units.la: Brundisium pulcro præcinctum prepete portu:
units.tr: Brundisium, girded with a fair and swift harbour.

units.la: Laudat Agellius lib. vi. cap. vi. Hinc Ἐυλιμένος Stephano. Describunt cum Lucanus, Strabo, Sabellicus, Leander. Nunc repletus est: adeo ut vix Triremibus per eum currere liceat. Obturasse dicitur Ioannes Antoninus, Princeps Tarentinus, bello, quod inter Alfonsum & Venetos gestum est: oneraria Nave ingentibus onusta lapidibus in ipso ore demersa: timens, ne Urbs in Venetorum seu Alfonsi potestatem deveniret. Ferdinandus & Alfonsus conati sæpe sunt demersa effodere; sed frustra. Ad Portum quondam Fontem fuisse Navigantibus incorruptas præbentem aquas, auctor est Plinius. Adhuc in Urbe juxta Portum binæ stant Columnæ ingentes; quæ qua de causa fuerint erectæ, incertum. Arx Urbi munitissima, quam Castellum Insulæ, Castel dell' Isola vocant, Ferrandi Primi Neapolitanorum Regis opus. Patria scribitur M. Pacuvii, Poetæ antiquissimi. Tantis opibus, tantaque quondam potentia, scribente Floro, ut Salentinorum habita fuerit Caput, & frequentata ab Asiaticis Græcisque populis: nunc deserta propemodum & conlapsa jacet: odiis & dissensionibus labefactata civilibus. Archiepiscopum habet, cui unitus est Archiepiscopus Ocrensis. Nobiles ibi Familiæ non paucæ: in quis. Del Palzo. | Fornari. | Salvatore. Curacciolì. | Pando. | Scolmafora. Catignani. | Di Raimondo. | Tomasini Di Fiorenza. | Sacchi. | Villa-Nova.
units.tr: Agellius praises this in Book vi, chapter vi. Hence Stephanus calls it Εὐλιμήν [a good harbour]. Lucan, Strabo, Sabellicus and Leander describe it. It is now so silted up that triremes can hardly pass through it. It is said that Giovanni Antonio, Prince of Taranto, blocked it during the war waged between Alfonso and the Venetians, by sinking a merchant ship loaded with huge stones in the mouth of the harbour, fearing the town would fall into the power of the Venetians or of Alfonso. Ferdinand and Alfonso often tried to dig the sunken ship out, but in vain. Pliny is the authority that there was once a spring near the harbour that gave clean water to sailors. Still in the town, beside the harbour, stand two huge columns; why they were erected is uncertain. The citadel, the most strongly fortified part of the town, which they call the Castle of the Island, Castel dell' Isola, is the work of Ferdinand I, King of Naples. The town is said to be the birthplace of Marcus Pacuvius, the very ancient poet. Florus writes that it was once so rich and so powerful that it was regarded as the capital of the Salentines, and was frequented by Asiatic and Greek peoples; now it lies almost deserted and in ruins, weakened by civil hatreds and dissensions. It has an archbishop, to whom the Archbishop of Ocre is joined. There are not a few noble families there, among them: Del Palzo; Fornari; Salvatore; Curacciolì; Pando; Scolmafora; Catignani; Di Raimondo; Tomasini Di Fiorenza; Sacchi; Villa-Nova.

units.la: Quod ad res gestas. Strabo ab Cretensibus initio habitatum refert, è Cnosso cum Theseo huc profectis: eorum autem regio habitam imperio; ab Lacedæmoniis postea fuisse occupatam Phalante Duce, quem Tarento pulsum ab suis Brundisini receperunt. Coloniam deinde Populi Romani Brundisium esse deductam notat Livius lib. xix, quæ Bello Punico ii & milite & pecunia Populum Romanum plurimum mum adjuvit, ut idem scribit lib. xxvii. Eo in loco Cn. Pompeius ab C. Julio Cæsare obsessus, præsidiisque dilectis vix urbe elapsus in Thessaliam fugit. Historia ab multis descripta, Cæsare præsertim ipso lib. 1 belli Civilis. Ager ipsi fertilissimus olelque feracissimus. Antoninus a Brundisio Tarentum ad littus numerat M. P. xliiii. Ad hancque Urbem Via Appia perducta legitur. Alibi dixi.
units.tr: As to its history: Strabo reports that it was first inhabited by the Cretans, who came here from Cnossus with Theseus; their region was held under their rule.
