Later it was occupied by the Lacedaemonians under their leader Phalanthus, whom the Brundisians received when he had been driven out of Tarentum by his own people. Livy, in Book xix, notes that Brundisium was then made a colony of the Roman People, and in Book xxvii he writes that in the Second Punic War it gave the Roman People great help with both soldiers and money. In this place Gnaeus Pompey, besieged by Gaius Julius Caesar and having barely escaped from the town with his guards, fled to Thessaly. The story has been told by many, above all by Caesar himself in Book i of the Civil War. Its land is very fertile and very rich in olive oil. Antoninus counts 44 miles from Brundisium to Tarentum along the coast. A Via Appia is known to have been led to this town. I have said more elsewhere.

units.la: Videndum iam, quo modo se habeant Salentinorum Mediterranea.
units.tr: We must now see how the inland parts of the Salentines stand.

units.la: Via Brundisio Tarentum versus P. M. viii ad radices exigui collis Opidum est Mili-signo; Latine scribentibus Messania. Putat Leander hic olim fuisse Messapium, quam cum Alcio Plinius in Mediterraneis locat hujus Regionis; cui nomen inde impositum Messapiæ. {10}
units.tr: On the road from Brundisium towards Tarentum, eight miles from the town, at the foot of a small hill, is the town Mili-signo; in Latin writers Messania. Leander thinks that this was once Messapium, which Pliny with Alcius places inland in this region, and from which the name Messapia was given to the whole region.

units.la: Quatuor inde P. M. Letianum invenitur, Lezano vernacule: & ulterius in Colle Oria Tarentum spectans, unde tamen P. M. xxiv abest. Οὐρία apud Strabonem libro vi dicitur Herodoto, qui addit conditam ab Cretensibus. Locus Herodoti est lib. vii, ubi tamen hodie non Οὐρία, sed Θρίη legitur: quo pertinere videtur, quod notat Eustathius Θρίον pro Θρίην dici solitum. Οὐρία ipsi Strabo: ea enim docto Scriptori Scriptura ex sententia Causabboni reponenda, quum vulgo fit Θουρίον. Nolim tamen dissimulare multos Vrium & Thurium vel Thurcam distinguere, & duo facere Opida. Varia exstat in Vulgatis Plinii Codicibus libro iii. cap. xi legendum Vrii: Sic apud Livium lib. x, ubi Cleomenes in Italiam profectus Thurcam Salentinorum Urbem legitur cepisse; scribendum forsan est Vriam. Spectat Vriam Arx in Colle valida, Marchionis ex nobili gente Balciorum. {20}
units.tr: Four miles further on is found Letianum, in the vernacular Lezano; and further on, on a hill, Oria, facing Tarentum, though it is still 24 miles from there. In Strabo, Book vi, it is called Οὐρία [Ouria], and Herodotus adds that it was founded by the Cretans. Herodotus's passage is in Book vii, where today the reading is not Οὐρία but Θρίη [Thriē]; to this, it seems, belongs what Eustathius notes, that Θρίον was commonly used for Θρίην. Strabo himself has Οὐρία, and in the view of Casaubon that is the reading to restore in that learned writer, since the common text has Θουρίον. Yet I would not wish to hide that many distinguish Vrium and Thurium or Thurca and make two towns. Varia stands in the common editions of Pliny, Book iii, chapter xi, where Vrii should be read. So too in Livy, Book x, where it is read that Cleomenes, having sailed to Italy, took the Salentine town of Thurca; perhaps it should be written Vria. Vria is overlooked by a strong citadel on a hill, belonging to the Marquis of the noble family of the Balci.

units.la: Ab Oria P. M. v situm est ad radices collis, qui Tarentum spectat, Opidum Francavilla, quam etiam Marchio Balcius possidet.
units.tr: Five miles from Oria, at the foot of the hill that faces Tarentum, lies the town Francavilla, which also belongs to the Marquis Balcius.

units.la: Inde P. M. viii ad radices ejusdem Collis Opidum occurrit Crotalis, Tarentinorum Ecclesiæ D. Caraldi subjecta.
units.tr: Eight miles further from there, at the foot of the same hill, the town Crotalis comes into view, subject to the church of St Caralus in Tarentum.

units.la: Tractu hoc, ut Ptolemæi indicant Tabulæ, Rudiæ fuit. Quæ Rudiæ Plinio, Ῥουδίαι Ptolemæo; Ῥουδίαι Stephano; Ῥαδαῖον Straboni lib. vi: Rudiæ dicuntur Pomponio Melæ. Ab Lupiis vix duobus millibus distare scribit Galateus, hodieque Ruie nominari. Rufæ habet Hieronymus Columna in Ennii Vita, locum dicens esse, ubi Lateritiæ Moles, Aggeres, Rudera, Busta, hětribus vasculis offibulisque plena, ostenduntur. Ennij mei Patria. Pomponius Mela libro ii; Ennio Ciræ nobiles Rudiæ. {30} Strabo lib. vi: Ἐξελαύνεται δὲ πόλιξ σὺν πυρὶ ... Ῥαδαῖαι, πόλεως Ἐπιδαύρου, ἐξ ἧς ἡ Ποιητὴς Ἐννίου. Silius Italicus lib. xii. ——Rudiæ genuere vetustæ: Nunc Rudiæ solo memorabile nomen Albanio.
units.tr: In this tract, as the tables of Ptolemy show, was Rudiae. These Rudiae are called Ῥουδίαι by Ptolemy and Stephanus, and Ῥαδαῖον by Strabo, Book vi; Pomponius Mela calls them Rudiae. Galateus writes that they are scarcely two miles from Lupiae, and are still called Ruie today. Hieronymus Columna, in the Life of Ennius, has Rufae, saying that the place where brick walls, mounds, rubble and ruins are shown, full of small vessels and clasps, is the spot. It was the homeland of my Ennius. Pomponius Mela, Book ii: "the noble Rudiae to Ennius, Cirae." Strabo, Book vi: "the town is driven out with fire ... Radaiai, a town of Epidaurus, from which came the poet Ennius." Silius Italicus, Book xii: "Rudiae bore the ancient ... Now Rudiae is a name remembered only by the Albanian soil."

units.la: Hinc hominem Rudium appellat Ennium M. Tullius in orationem pro Archia Poeta; & Rudinum Ausonius in Monosyllabis: Unde Rudinus aut: Divum Domus alis sanum Cal.
units.tr: Hence Marcus Tullius, in his speech for the poet Archias, calls Ennius a Rudian man; and Ausonius, in his Monosyllables, calls him Rudinus: "Unde Rudinus aut..." and "Divum domus alis sanum Cal...."

units.la: Eusebius tamen in Chronicis ad annum quartum Olympiados cxxiv Ennium Ta-rentii natum notat. Calabros Montes generatim nominat Ovidius lib. iii de Arte amandi: {40} Ennius emeruit, Calabris in Montibus ortus.
units.tr: Yet Eusebius, in his Chronicle, at the fourth year of the 124th Olympiad, notes that Ennius was born at Tarentum. Ovid, in Book iii of the Art of Love, generally names the Calabrian Mountains: "Ennius earned his fame, born in the Calabrian mountains."

units.la: Pergendum. Rodium ager est in Libro Limitum.
units.tr: We must go on. Rodium is a field in the Book of Boundaries.

units.la: Lupiæ, quarum paullo ante meminí, Pomponio Melæ & Antonino dicuntur Αὔξιμα Straboни libro vi: quæ Lupia Plinio, cui & Statio militum: Auxia Pausaniæ, Luppia Itinerariæ Tabulæ; Ἀῦξμοι Appiano Alexandrino lib. iii: Ἀξείαι Ptolemæo, quæ etiam fere scriptura legiuntur in nonnullis Plinij editionibus Lispia: Hermolao Barbaro Lubiam cafligante. Sed restituendæ Ptolemæo Ἀῦξμιαι, Plinio Lupiæ uti meliores ipsius præferunt Codices. Lipia sunt in Epist. D Paullini de Niceræ obitu: incmendarius etiam. Ptolemæus in Tabulis hoc Opidum xxv. ab Tarento distare, & maritimum esse demonstrat. Strabo mediterraneum dicit. Utrque vere: {50} si quidem non in ipso situm littore, sed in continente fuerit, haud procul tamen ab ora. Sane non procul ab Aletio abfuisse, paret ex Antonino, Lupiæ scribente ab Hydrunte esse xxv P. M. quot quoque sunt, aut paullo minus, ab Hydrunte Aletium. Nulla nunc Lupiarum vestigia. Nam qui Aletium ipsius inædificatum fundamentis censent, inter quos Galateus, fallunter. Aletium enim & Lupiæ diversas urbes fuisse, clarum ex Plinio Pomponioque Mela.
units.tr: The Lupiae, which I mentioned a little earlier, are called Αὔξιμα [Auxima] by Pomponius Mela and Antoninus, and by Strabo in book vi. Pliny calls them Lupia, and also Statio militum. Pausanias calls them Auxia, the Itinerary Table Luppia, and Appian of Alexandria in book iii Ἀῦξμοι [Auxmoi]. Ptolemy gives Ἀξείαι [Axeiai], a form which in some editions of Pliny is also read almost as Lispia, as Hermolaus Barbarus corrected it to Lubiam. But Ptolemy's form should be restored as Ἀῦξμιαι [Auxmiai], and Pliny's as Lupiae, as the better manuscripts of Pliny show. Lipia appears in Paulinus's letter on the death of Nicer, and that too is a corrupt reading. Ptolemy, in his Tables, shows that this town lies 25 miles from Tarentum and is on the coast. Strabo says it is inland. Both are right, provided the town was not situated on the shore itself but on the mainland, though not far from the coast. Indeed, that it was not far from Aletium is clear from Antoninus, who, writing of Lupiae, gives the distance from Hydruntum as 25 Roman miles, which is about the same, or a little less, as the distance from Hydruntum to Aletium. There are no traces of the Lupiae today. Those who think that Aletium was built on its foundations, among whom is Galateus, are mistaken, for it is clear from Pliny and Pomponius Mela that Aletium and Lupiae were different towns.

units.la: Iam quod Aletium Plinius, Ἀλήτιον Ptolemæus nominat; hodie Leze & Leccie vulgo vocatur. Faletium corrupte apud Pomponium Melam. Hinc Aletini Populi Plinio libro iii. cap.xi. Brundisio distat m.p. xxiv; ab Morì, viii; ab Iapygio Promontorio xxx. Dictum creditur nonnullis ab Lytiis quibusdam, huc ex Asia profectis; aliis autem ab Lisio Idomeneo, cujus meminit Virgilius lib.iii. Æneid. ubi plura Servius. Salentinorum hodie primaria: non Episcopo solum, quem vulgus Lecciensem appellat, decorata; verum etiam Concilio totius Apuliæ Regio, Foroque perpetuo: Procerum totius hujus tractus Domicilium, multorumque Sedes Nobilium; in quis: Aiello. De Aimeni. Ammiraati. De l'Achaia. Della Barbera. Baroni. Carbonerii. Castromediani. Corsi. Dello Doce. Delli Falconi. Francons. Frisari. Di Giorgio. Delli Guidi. Guarini. Guidani. Lobelli. Maramonti. Di Matteo. Mereschalchi. Della Monica. De Mosto. De Muro. De Noia. De Paladini. Perroni. Petraroli. Della Porta. Prati. Priuli. Raino. San Biagio. Saracini. Scifio. Tusuri. Verardi. Zimara. Nobilitavit ortu suo Robertius, Aquinatium Episcopus, cujus Conciones typis editae.
units.tr: Now, what Pliny calls Aletium, Ptolemy calls Ἀλήτιον [Aletion]; today it is commonly called Leze and Leccie. In Pomponius Mela it is corruptly Faletium. Hence the Aletini as a people in Pliny, Book iii, chapter xi. It is 24 miles from Brundisium, 8 from Mori, and 30 from the Iapygian promontory. Some believe it was named from certain Lytians who came here from Asia; others from Lisio Idomeneus, whom Virgil mentions in Book iii of the Aeneid, where Servius says more. Today it is the chief town of the Salentines, adorned not only by a bishop, whom the common people call the Bishop of Lecce, but also by the council of the whole region of Apulia, and by a permanent market; it is the home of the nobles of the whole district and the seat of many noble families, among them: Aiello; De Aimeni; Ammiraati; De l'Achaia; Della Barbera; Baroni; Carbonerii; Castromediani; Corsi; Dello Doce; Delli Falconi; Francons; Frisari; Di Giorgio; Delli Guidi; Guarini; Guidani; Lobelli; Maramonti; Di Matteo; Mereschalchi; Della Monica; De Mosto; De Muro; De Noia; De Paladini; Perroni; Petraroli; Della Porta; Prati; Priuli; Raino; San Biagio; Saracini; Scifio; Tusuri; Verardi; Zimara. Robertius, Bishop of Aquino, also made it famous by his birth, and his published sermons survive.

units.la: Ulterius Hydruntum est, de quo ante.
units.tr: Further on is Hydruntum, about which I spoke earlier.

units.la: Inde tum M. P. VIII, flexu ad caput D. Mariae, VI ab mari, Castellum est Busardum: ab eo III, Andranum: hinc totidem Tricassum; hinc item III Alexanum: ulterius 10 P. Mons Sardus; hinc Villa S. Mariae, plurimique alij Vici.
units.tr: From there, eight Roman miles on, with a bend toward the cape of Santa Maria, six miles from the sea, is the castle Busardum. Three miles from it is Andranum, and from there as many to Tricassum. From Tricassum, again three miles to Alexanum. Ten miles further is Mons Sardus, and from here Villa S. Maria, and many other villages.

units.la: Civitas inde Minervium, ab mari P. M. XII, Episcopatu nobile.
units.tr: The city Minervium, twelve Roman miles from the sea, is noted for its bishopric.

units.la: Itinere ab Monte Sardo ad alterum lapidem Galianum, Gagliano, invenitur.
units.tr: On the way from Mons Sardus to the first milestone you come to Galianum, Gagliano.

units.la: Hinc ad septimum via, quae Vxentum ducit, Pagi se offerunt plurimi, quibus Graeci habitant; Gens moribus linguaque ab Italis diversa.
units.tr: From here, at the seventh milestone, the road that leads to Uxentum passes many villages inhabited by Greeks, a people differing from the Italians in customs and language.

units.la: Peragratis inter pulcerrimos Vicos octo millibus Episcopalis Civitas in colle edito succedit Vxentum; Οὐξεντον Ptolemaeo: hodie Vsento, Vgenti, Ugento, variante scriptura. Ampliorem olim fuisse antiqua monstrant Aedificiorum rudera. Nunc perexigua est. Subarbium in plano jacet. Abest ab Iapygiae Promontorio M. P. xx: totidem ab Gallipoli. Ejus in agro Fanum D. Mariae, quo loco Veretum olim, ut docti censent Viri. Veretum Itinerariae Tabulae: Οὐέρετον Ptolemaeo. Βάρας etiam quondam, teste Strabone lib. VI. Hinc Veretini Plinio libro III cap. XI in fine. Hodie, ut dixi, S. Maria, teste Leandro, cognomine quoque de Vereto: quod item ad Ortelium Roma scribit Celsus Cittadinus. Vetranam nominat Ciofanus in lib. XV Metamorph. Ovidij. Alij pro eo Vsano vertunt.
units.tr: After passing through very beautiful villages for eight miles, you come to the episcopal city Uxentum, on a high hill. Ptolemy calls it Uxentum [Οὐξεντον]; today it is Usento, Vgenti, or Ugento, the spelling varying. The ruins of buildings show that it was once larger; now it is very small. Its suburb lies on the plain. It is twenty Roman miles from the Promontory of Iapygia and as many from Gallipoli. In its territory is the shrine of Santa Maria, which learned men think was formerly the site of Veretum. Veretum appears in the Itinerary tables, and Ptolemy calls it Ouereton [Οὐέρετον]. Strabo, in book VI, also names it Baras [Βάρας]. From it come the Veretini of Pliny, book III, chapter XI, near the end. Today, as I said, it is S. Maria, which Leander says is also called de Vereto. Celsus Cittadinus writes this to Ortelius from Rome. Ciofanus, in book XV of Ovid's Metamorphoses, calls it Vetrana, while others translate the name as Vsanum.

units.la: Sexto ab Vxento lapide Specianum sequitur: ultra tertio, Ruffanum; inde quinto, Coranum; hinc totidem Corlianum, Coregliano vel Corliano vernacule; Hydrunto P. M. XIII, in dorso modici collis situm.
units.tr: Six miles from Uxentum comes Speciano. Three miles further is Ruffano, and then five miles on is Corano. From Corano as many miles bring you to Corliano, called Coregliano or Corliano in the vernacular. It lies thirteen Roman miles from Hydruntum, on the back of a modest hill.

units.la: Dein a Gorliano V. P. M. nobile Castellum est in Valle amoenissima, quod vulgo S. Pietro in Gallatina.
units.tr: Then, five Roman miles from Gorliano, is a noble castle in a very pleasant valley, commonly called S. Pietro in Gallatina.

units.la: Abest hinc mille passibus Soletum, Plinio notum lib. III, cap. XI; qui suo tempore desertum scribit. Nomen hodie retinet, Leandro teste in aspero & aquarum indigo situm jugo. Amplum fuisse docent Murorum vestigia: nunc parvum est oppidulum, quod quondam, ut ajunt, erat Episcopale, nunc etiam, inquit Galateus, caput Comitatus. Nominat post Soletum Plinius Fratuertium, cujus nullum hodie indicium.
units.tr: About a thousand paces from here is Soletum, known to Pliny, book III, chapter XI, who writes that in his time it was deserted. It keeps its name today, according to Leander, and is set on a rough ridge that lacks water. Remains of its walls show it was once large. Now it is a small town, which was once, they say, an episcopal see, and which is now, Galateo says, the chief town of a county. After Soletum, Pliny names Fratuertium, of which there is no trace today.

units.la: Ad tertium deinde milliare Sternatia succedit; Hydrunto P.M. XIII.
units.tr: At the third milestone then comes Sternatia, thirteen Roman miles from Hydruntum.

units.la: Inter Sternatiam & Hydruntum multi passim Vici, Pagi, Castellaque reperiuntur: tur : inter alia Scurianum, octo P. M. à Baffardo, unde Castrum Neta munitissimo situm loco conspici potest.
units.tr: Between Sternatia and Hydruntum there are many villages, hamlets and castles scattered about. Among them is Scurianum, eight Roman miles from Baffardo, from where the castle Neta, set in a very strongly fortified place, can be seen.

units.la: Hinc tum tenis passuum millibus Conuertinum ; ab eo quaternis Leucanum ; unde totidem Velia : tenis ab ea D. Ioannis Castellum, S. Gianazzo, hinc totidem Turrus ab Vria pari intervallo distans.
units.tr: From here, ten miles further, is Convertinum. From it, four miles, Leucanum; from there as many to Velia; ten miles from Velia is the castle of St John, S. Gianazzo. From here as many miles to Turrus, which is the same distance from Uria.

units.la: Tum iterum mare versus ab Mesiania v milliari Cilinum : inde quarto Curreiorum, hinc octavo Lettum, exiguo inter capedine Capua ; ultraque quarto milliari Gunannum invenitur.
units.tr: Then, toward the sea again, from Mesiania at the fifth milestone is Cilinum. From it, at the fourth milestone, Curreiorum; from here, at the eighth, Lettum. With a small gap between them lies Capua, and beyond it, at the fourth milestone, Gunannum is found.

units.la: Itinere ab D. Petri Tarentum versus ad v lapidem Galatina, aliis Galatana, Galatena, Galata : ortu Antony cui, qui Galateum inde, Philosophi, Medici, Oratoris, Poetae, Cosmographi nobilis. Ab Calata Gallipolin ix sunt M. P. Haec Vrbs septem res habere, inquit Galateus, se jactat croceo coloris : Crocum ipsum, Mel, Caseum, Vinum, Oleum, Caricas, & Vvas passas.
units.tr: On the road from St Peter toward Taranto, at the fifth milestone, is Galatina, called by others Galatana, Galatena, or Galata. Antonio, who from this place was called Galateo, was born here; he was a noble philosopher, physician, orator, poet and cosmographer. From Galatina to Gallipoli is nine Roman miles. This city, Galateo says, boasts of seven products: saffron itself, honey, cheese, wine, oil, figs, and raisins.

units.la: Ab Galatina sex P. M. Paravua Castellum abest : ab mari septem.
units.tr: Six Roman miles from Galatina lies the castle Paravua, seven miles from the sea.

units.la: Ad laevam vero ab Galatina P. M. tribus : ab ora Sinus Tarentini, quatuor : ab Lupiis, quindecim : ab Tarento, quadraginta quinque, Vrbs est antiquissima Nardum : populo frequens & lauta : in amoenissima jacens planicie. Ptolemaeo. Ab D. Caesarea nomen habere scribit Galateus. Hinc Neritini vel Neretini apud Plinium Populi in Salentinis, libro iii cap.xi : in fine. Nam ibidem alii sunt Neretini, Hirpinorum Populi. Episcopum habet, qui Latinorum vulgo Neritoniensis. Abest ab Gallipoli M. P. novem ; ab mari, quatuor. Ducatus dignitate nobilis. Ortus hinc Franciscus Nardus, Philosophus & Theologus scriptis clarus.
units.tr: Three Roman miles to the left of Galatina, four from the shore of the Gulf of Taranto, fifteen from Lupiae, and forty-five from Taranto, lies the very ancient city Nardum. It is populous and prosperous, set on a most pleasant plain; so Ptolemy. Galateo writes that it took its name from Caesarea. Hence come the Neritini or Neretini, peoples of the Salentini, in Pliny, book III, chapter XI, near the end. For in the same passage there are other Neretini, a people of the Hirpini. It has a bishop, whom the Latins call Neritonensis. It is nine Roman miles from Gallipoli and four from the sea. It is noble through the dignity of its duchy. From here came Francesco Nardo, a philosopher and theologian famous for his writings.

units.la: Nerito Tarentum versus xxv M.P. Casalnovum abest. Mandurium hic fuisse putant Leander, Galateus & Ananiensis. Quae Mandura Plinio Salentinorum : Μανδύζον est Stephano Iapygiae : Μανδόνιον Messapiorum Plutarcho. Mandurii meminit Livius libro xxvii.
units.tr: Twenty-five Roman miles from Nerito on the way to Taranto lies Casalnovum. Leander, Galateo and Ananiensis think Mandurium was here. Mandura in Pliny belongs to the Salentini; Stephanus gives Mandyzon [Μανδύζον] for Iapygia, and Plutarch gives Mandonion [Μανδόνιον] for the Messapii. Livy mentions Mandurium in book XXVII.

units.la: Ad Apulias proprie pertinet Iter, quod ab Equestrico Hydruntum ducit Antoninus hoc Modo, per M. Peucetia | Canusium, M.P.XXVI. | ........... | Perijt. Rubos, M.P.XXIII. | Rubos, XIII. | Rivo. Budruntum, M.P.XI. | Butuntos, | Bitonto. Barium, M.P.XII. | Barium, XX. | Fari. 40 Turres, M.P.XXI. | Turris Cafaru, IX. | Inter Molam & D.Georgii. Egnatiam, M.P.XVI. | Dertum. IX. | Inter Polignano & S.Vitt. Speluncis, M.P.XX. | Gnatie. XXI. | Nazo. Spelunis, XXVIII. Leg. Speluncis. | Inter Egnatiam & Villam Novam. Salentinorum | Brundisium, M.P.XIX. | Brindisi, X. Legend. Brindisio. | Brindisi. 50 Fl. Pastum. | Balentinum, XV. | Lupias, M.P.XXV. | Luppia, XXV. | Nulla huius Opidi hodie vestigia. Hydruntu, M.P.XXV. | Tdrunte, VIII. | Otranto.
units.tr: The road that properly belongs to Apulia runs from Equestrico to Hydruntum, as Antoninus gives it, through 235 Roman miles. In the Antonine route and the Itinerary table, with the names of the Vulgate and the modern towns: Apulia, Daunia: Ecas, 18 miles, and Erdonias, 18 miles, which is Erdonia. Peucetia: Canusium, 26 miles, which has perished. Rubos, 23 miles (Rubos, 13, now Rivo). Budruntum, 11 miles (Butuntos, now Bitonto). Barium, 12 miles (Barium, 20, now Fari). Turres, 21 miles (Turris Cafaru, 9, between Mola and S. Giorgio). Egnatia, 16 miles (Dertum, 9, between Polignano and S. Vito). Speluncis, 20 miles (Gnatie, 21, now Nazo; Spelunis, 28, to be read as Speluncis, between Egnatia and Villa Nova). Salentinorum: Brundisium, 19 miles (Brindisi, 10, to be read as Brundisio, now Brindisi). Fl. Pastum: Balentinum, 15 miles; Lupias, 25 miles (Luppia, 25; no trace of this town survives today). Hydruntum, 25 miles (Tdrunte, 8, now Otranto).

units.la: CAPUT XXXIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXIII.

units.la: Flaminia vel Romanula.
units.tr: Flaminia, or Romanula.

units.la: ITALIAM Priscam & Propriam, tam Septemtrionaliorem, quam quæ Meridionalior, ad utrumque Mare, intercurrente Apennino, Tyrrhenum & Hadriaticum in xii nobilissimis Regionibus vidimus: perluitranda succedit Nova. Eam sic appello, quod Prisca sensim adcreverit, Italiæque etiam nomine, cum ævo senescente, ea perit audire & innotescere.
units.tr: Having seen Italy, both its northern and its southern parts, in its old and proper form, on both seas, the Tyrrhenian and the Adriatic, with the Apennines running between them, in twelve most noble regions, we now come to New Italy, which must be described in turn. I call it so because the old Italy gradually grew, and, as the age grew old, the name of Italy itself also came to be heard and known in a different way.

units.la: 10 Hæc autem duplex statui à me solet vel Planior, vel Montibus innexior. Planior & ab montibus liberior olim propriè Gallia dicebatur Cis-Alpina. Gallia quidem ab Gallis Boiis, Senonibus, Insubribus, Cenomanis, aliisque, à quibus quidquid Alpium radicibus Rubiconisque fluentis intercipitur, pullis veteribus colonis, occupatum, longoque post tempore fuit habitatum. Sunt illi, qui remotiorem gentium primi Romanis arma intulerunt, Urbemque Romam captam incenderunt; scribentibus Polybio, lib. ii, Livio libro v, Trogo Pompeio lib. xx, & aliis. Cis-Alpina vero dicta, quod prisci Itali, Romanisque Scriptoribus, de ea differentibus cis esset Alpes: quum alia trans Alpes, de qua libro præcedente, habitaretur. CisAlpina hæc, qua Septemtrionalissima Montibusque adhæret propius, Sub-Alpina cognominatur Plinio libro xvi. cap. xii: qua Australissima, ab nobili ibidem urbe, Arminum Livio, cujus libro xxviii hæc verba: Arminum, ita Galliam appellabant, Sp. Lucretio obtigit. Ad Carnos usque suos extendebat limites. Togatam enim ab Venetis & Carnis coli scribit Pomponius Mela. Citerior etiam appellatur Gallia Sallustio, Cæsari, Hirtio; ob causam jam antea indicatam. Veterem quoque Galliam nominat Autonius ad Gratianum Imperatorem scribens; quod Romanis multo prius, quam Trans-Alpina fuerit cognita. Italia Gallica, γαλατικὴ vocatur Appiano in Hannibalicis. Galliam autem κατ' ἐξοχὴν nuncupat Livius libro xlv, & alibi. Mediterraneam Italiam vocat Notitia Provinciarum; non quod, ut falsa quibusdam mens est, Mediterraneo adposita mari, sic enim nomen illud potius mereretur Italia Prisca, hactenus a me delineata, undique mari cincta: sed quod hæc in locis mediterraneis cincta, qua Septemtrio, Occidens, Meridiesque sunt, Alpibus & Apenninotumescente; qua Oriens est, Mari Hadriatico.
units.tr: This region is usually divided in two: one part is flatter and freer of mountains, the other more closely bound to them. The flatter part, free of mountains, was once properly called Gallia Cisalpina. It was called Gallia after the Gallic Boii, Senones, Insubres, Cenomani, and others, who occupied whatever lies between the foot of the Alps and the stream of the Rubicon, after the old inhabitants were driven out, and who lived there for a long time afterwards. These were the first of the more distant peoples to take up arms against the Romans and to burn the city of Rome when they captured it, as Polybius (book 2), Livy (book 5), Trogus Pompeius (book 20) and others write. It was called Cisalpina because the ancient Italians and the Roman writers who spoke of it were on this side of the Alps, while the other region beyond the Alps, of which I spoke in the previous book, was inhabited. The part of this Cisalpina that lies farthest north and clings more closely to the mountains is called Subalpina by Pliny (book 16, chapter 12). The part that lies farthest south is named after the famous city there, Arminum, by Livy, in book 28, where he says: "Arminum, for so they called Gaul, fell to Spurius Lucretius." It extended its limits as far as its Carni. For Pomponius Mela writes that the Togata was inhabited by the Veneti and the Carni. Sallust, Caesar and Hirtius also call it Citerior Gallia, for the reason already given. Autonius, writing to the emperor Gratian, names it Gallia Vetus, because it became known to the Romans much earlier than the region beyond the Alps. Appian, in his Hannibalic history, calls it Italia Gallica, galatikè. Livy, in book 45 and elsewhere, names it simply Gallia par excellence. The Notitia Provinciarum calls it Mediterranea Italia. This is not because, as some have falsely supposed, it lies on the Mediterranean Sea; in that case the name would fit the old Italy I have described so far better, since it is surrounded by sea on every side. It is so called because it is enclosed in inland places: on the north, west and south by the Alps and the Apennines, and on the east by the Adriatic Sea.

units.la: Polybius & Plinius toti huic tractui Gallico formam tribuunt triangularem: cujus Apicem faciunt Alpes & Apenninus Montes: Basin, Sinus Hadriaticus.
units.tr: Polybius and Pliny give this whole Gallic tract a triangular shape, whose apex is formed by the Alps and the Apennine mountains, and whose base is the Adriatic Gulf.

units.la: Florentissimum Italiæ latus appellat Tacitus. Ubique arboriferam hanc Regionem, pecori patcendo aptam, & multis irrigari fluviis, testis est Plutarchus in Camillo. Describunt accurate pleneque Strabo lib. v. Polybius libro iii, aliisque. Audiamus hic M. Tullium Philippica iii: Nec vero de virtute, constantia, gravitate Gallia tacere potest: etenim ille sios Italia, illud firmamentum Imperii Romani, illud ornamentum dignitatis. Perelegantèr autem naturam ejus delineat Karolus Sigonius libro i de Regno Italiæ: Regio, inquit, est in Italia cum vetera Agrorum Urbiumque nobilitate, tum spectata Virorum Armorumque potentia celebris, Galliæ olim Cis-Alpinæ nomine appellata: Hanc Alpibus & Apennino monte tribus à lateribus, quasi quibusdam altissimis mœnibus cinctam Padus interfluit, Fluvius eximia magnitudine sua, & fabulosis Græcorum Poetarum carminibus inclutus. Et post Padi descriptionem: Campi vero adeo culti & uberes intercedunt: ut satis constet haud temere alios reperisse aut naturæ feraciores, aut rebus necessariis ad hominum usum instructiores.
units.tr: Tacitus calls it Florentissimum Italiae latus, the most flourishing flank of Italy. Plutarch, in his Life of Camillus, bears witness that this region everywhere bears trees, is suited to pasturing livestock, and is watered by many rivers. Strabo, book 5, describes it carefully and at length, as does Polybius, book 3, and others. Let us hear Marcus Tullius in the third Philippic: "Nor indeed can Gaul be silent about its virtue, constancy and dignity; for that region is the sinews of Italy, that support of the Roman empire, that ornament of its rank." Karl Sigonius describes its nature very elegantly in book 1 of his De regno Italiae: "A region," he says, "lies in Italy, famous both for the old nobility of its fields and cities and for the renowned power of its men and arms, and once called by the name of Cisalpine Gaul. It is enclosed on three sides by the Alps and the Apennine mountain, as by very high walls, and the Po flows through it, a river of great size and made famous by the fabulous songs of the Greek poets." And after describing the Po he says: "The fields between them are so well cultivated and fertile that it is clear enough that others have not been found, either more productive by nature or better equipped with what is needed for human use."

units.la: 50 Addit deinde idem Sigonius antiquos ejus Principes fuisse Ligures & Etruscos, mox Galos; postremo Romanos: his Gothos successisse: Gothis iterum Romanos, Romanis Langbardos. Videndus & Sabellicus libro Historiæ Venetæ i, Decade iiii.
units.tr: Sigonius then adds that its ancient rulers were the Ligurians and the Etruscans, then the Gauls, and finally the Romans; after these the Goths succeeded, then the Romans again, and after the Romans the Lombards. The reader should also consult Sabellicus, Venetian History, book 1, decade 4.

units.la: Hanc Italiæ partem multum adhuc frugalitatis antiquæ (quæ scilicet in Trans-Alpinis Gallis erat, Cis-Alpinorum progenitoribus) retinere scribit Plinius ad Iunium Mauricum suum.
units.tr: Pliny, in his letter to his friend Junius Mauricus, writes that this part of Italy still retains much of the ancient simplicity of life that belonged to the Transalpine Gauls, the ancestors of the men of Cisalpine Gaul.

units.la: Qui qualesque quondam habitarint, parebit in ipsis partibus. Polybius libro ii de iis universim agens, inter Padum & Alpes habitasse scribit Laos, mox Lebetios, de hinc ingentem Insubrum nationem; post non longe ab ripa fluminis Cenomanos Loca vero Mari Hadriatico vicina antiquum ex Paphlagonia genus habuisse Veneti: rursus inter Padum & Apenninum, primo Anares, post Boios, inde Ägones, postremo Senones, juxta Hadriaticum mare extremos omnium Gallorum incolui-se, eorumque caput fuisse Senam. Comprehendebantur olim sub ea Ligures, quos antiquitus ad Padum usque habitasse, veteres tradunt: hodie per Apenninum juga excluduntur.
units.tr: What sort of peoples once lived here will be clear from the regions themselves. Polybius, in book 2, speaking of them in general, writes that between the Po and the Alps lived the Laevi, then the Lebecii, and after them the great nation of the Insubres; then, not far from the bank of the river, the Cenomani. The places near the Adriatic Sea, he says, were held by the Veneti, an ancient people from Paphlagonia. Again, between the Po and the Apennines lived first the Anares, then the Boii, then the Agones, and finally the Senones, who dwelt along the Adriatic Sea and were the most remote of all the Gauls; their chief city was Sena. Once the Ligurians were included under this name; the ancients report that they lived as far as the Po, but today they are shut out by the ridges of the Apennines.

units.la: In hac ex D. Augusti Divisione Regiones Italiae sunt ⅠTuscia, Nona, Decima, & Undecima.
units.tr: In this division of Italy made by the deified Augustus, the regions of Italy are: Tuscia, the Ninth, the Tenth and the Eleventh.

units.la: Gallia porro Cis-Alpina versus Occasum duplex est Strabonis, Plinio, aliis, vel Cis-Padana vel Trans-Padana; illa quod cis: haec, quod trans-Padum. Cis-padana nobiliores Partes hodie Flaminia & Almitia.
units.tr: Moreover, Gaul on this side of the Alps, toward the west, is double, according to Strabo, Pliny and others: either Cispadana or Transpadana; the first because it is on this side of the Po, the second because it is beyond the Po. The more noteworthy parts of Cispadana today are Flaminia and Aemilia.

units.la: Primo loco FLAMINIAM dabo, sic dictam ab Via Flaminia, quam C. Flaminius, Consul Romanus, opere munivit, ut Strabo libro v & Livius libro ix notant; cum, Liguribus devictis, pacque cum finitimis gentibus firmata, ne mules interni ono languescerent, Viam ab Urbe Roma per Etruriam & Umbriam usque Ariminum lapide stravisse tradentes. Flaminia meminerunt cum alii, tum Capitolinus in Gordiano. Hodie, Karoli Magni Imperatoris & Romani Pontificis beneficio atque auspiciis, Romaniola dicitur vel Romandiola, quod prae reliqua Gallia Romanorum ritibus, legibus & institutis firmius inhaereret, Imperiique Romani dignitatem, nomen & maiestatem acrioribus armis contra Langobardorum tyrannidem defendisset. Vide eleganter Leandrum in ejus delineatione.
units.tr: First I shall take up FLAMINIA, so called from the Via Flaminia, which C. Flaminius, a Roman consul, built, as Strabo (book 5) and Livy (book 9) note, when, after the Ligurians had been conquered and peace had been secured with the neighbouring peoples, so that the vigour of the Roman people might not weaken through idleness at home, he laid a road paved with stone from the city of Rome through Etruria and Umbria as far as Ariminum. Many writers mention Flaminia, among them Capitolinus in his life of Gordian. Today, by the favour and under the auspices of Charlemagne the emperor and the Roman pontiff, it is called Romaniola or Romandiola, because it held more firmly to the customs, laws and institutions of the Romans than the rest of Gaul, and because it defended the dignity, name and majesty of the Roman empire with sterner arms against the tyranny of the Lombards. See Leandro Alberti's description of it, which is elegantly done.

units.la: Romaniola Limites ex communi sententia ad Septemtrionem quidem Paludes Veronenses & Patavinae, usque ad Fornaces, Ostium Padi ultimum, una cum parte Maris Hadriatici; ad Orientem Isaurus, qui vulgo Foliu una cum Piceno; ad Meridiem Apenninus, cum Etruria. In Occidentali variatur. Quidam ultra Varrinum flumen cis Forum Cornelii non procedunt; manstiliunt nonnulli (inter quos Peregrinus Priscianus Ferrariensis libro i de Antiq. Ferr.) Sculien nam, nunc Panarium; in eo plerique, quorum numero Leander Albertus, sistunt. Hos sequar; Longitudinem ejus ex milliarium, aut circiter, pertinuit inter Foliam & Panatium, quod dixi Latitudinem autem vel mille, vel paulo minus, inter Apenninum & quarum memini, Paludes. Quae vero hucusque ultra Padum, docet Leander Romaniola igitur appellatio multo latior hodie, quam olim Flaminia. Flaminia namque de nit appellari haec Italiae pars ad Ariminum. Ibi enim Via Flaminia finis: initium autem Aemilia, adeo ut quae nunc Romaniola incidat in nonnullam Flaminiae, in maximam vero Aemiliae partem.
units.tr: By common opinion the limits of Romaniola are: on the north, the Veronese and Paduan marshes, as far as the Fornaces, the last mouth of the Po, together with part of the Adriatic Sea; on the east, the Isaurus, which is commonly called the Foglia, together with Picenum; on the south, the Apennines, with Etruria. The western boundary varies. Some do not go beyond the Varrinus river, on this side of Forum Cornelii; some extend it further (among them Peregrinus Priscianus of Ferrara, book 1, De antiquitatibus Ferrariae) to the Sculiena, now the Panaro; most, including Leandro Alberti, stop at this one. I shall follow these. Its length, by my estimate, extends roughly some thousand miles between the Foglia and the Panaro, which I mentioned; its breadth, however, is a thousand or a little less, between the Apennines and the marshes I mentioned. As to what lies beyond the Po, Leandro explains it. So the name Romaniola today is much wider than Flaminia was in the past. For Flaminia was properly the name of this part of Italy as far as Ariminum; there the Via Flaminia ended, and Aemilia began. Hence what is now Romaniola takes in a part of Flaminia, but most of Aemilia.

units.la: Quod ab Regionis qualitatem, Agros habere optimos scribit Leander, omniumque frugum, tam quae ad vitam necessariae quam quae ad humanas voluptates opportunae & delitias, ferules. Campi hic latissimi; fructiferis arboribus omne genus consiti: Colles peramoeni; Vitibus, olea, Ficu nitentes. Silvae munificae, herbidaque prata cum dumis Venationi aptae; salubres passim aquae; Salinae cum circa litus, tum intus frequentes; Mare Fluminaque plurima navigabilia, & piscibus foecunda: Metallorum fodinae innumeraque praeterea naturae dotes eximiae, quae, nisi longissima narratione, commemorari haud possent.
units.tr: As for the quality of the region, Leandro writes that it has excellent fields and produces every kind of grain, both what is necessary for life and what serves human pleasure and delight. The plains here are very wide, planted with every kind of fruit tree; the hills are very pleasant, shining with vines, olives and figs. The woods are generous, and the grassy meadows with thickets are suited to hunting; the waters are healthy everywhere; there are salt-pans, both along the shore and inland, in great numbers; the sea and the many rivers are navigable and rich in fish. There are mines of metals, and countless other outstanding gifts of nature, which could not be recounted without a very long narrative.

units.la: Flaminia vel tota vel pars ejus etiam, Plinio & Ptolemaeo notantibus, Togata dicebatur; quod illi, ut Italiae pleraque, Toga, Romanorum vestis, esset communis. Statuit Togata Fines Plinius quidem inter Anconam & Ariminum, ulterius etiam ab Rubiconem usque diffiniens; Ptolemaeus autem uno latere placentiam, altero Rubiconem ejusdem ponit terminum, tum hinc usque Ravennam per eram Hadriae Gallos Boios complectens.
units.tr: Flaminia, whether as a whole or in part, was also called Togata, as Pliny and Ptolemy note, because the toga, the dress of the Romans, was common there, as in most of Italy. Pliny sets the bounds of Togata between Ancona and Ariminum, and extends them further as far as the Rubicon. Ptolemy, however, places its boundary on one side at Piacenza and on the other at the Rubicon of the same region, and so takes in the Gallic Boii from there as far as Ravenna, along the shore of the Adriatic.

units.la: Romaniola igitur, ut quae dixi docent, duplex, Cisp-adana & Transpadana. Cispadanam col. ille quondam Senones & Boios, auctores sunt Polybius & Ptolemaeus. De Senonibus verba feci in mea Gallia cap. xxiiii. Eorum in Italia caput fuit Sena. Scribit Trogus lib. xx. Galli Senones, quum in Italiam venissent, sedibus expulisse Tuscos, & Mediolanum, Comum, Brixiam, Veronam, Bergomum, Tridentum, Vicentiam condidisse. Videndus & Livius lib. v. De Boys dixi ibidem cap. xxvi & xxxiv. Utrinque ex Gallis in hanc Italiae partem, Alpibus superatis, penetrarunt.
units.tr: Romagna then, as my preceding account shows, is double: Cisp-adana and Transpadana. The authors Polybius and Ptolemy say that Cispadana was once occupied by the Senones and the Boii. I discussed the Senones in my Gallia, chapter 24. Their chief town in Italy was Sena. Trogus, book 20, writes that the Gallic Senones, when they came into Italy, drove the Tuscans from their seats and founded Mediolanum, Comum, Brixia, Verona, Bergamo, Trent and Vicenza. Livy, book 5, should also be consulted. I spoke of the Boii in the same work, chapters 26 and 34. Both peoples came from the Gauls into this part of Italy, crossing the Alps.

units.la: Sed particularia Romanulæ videamus; orsi ab Isauro Amne; qui, Folia vulgo, limes inter Picenum est & Flaminiam.
units.tr: But let us look at the particulars of Romagna, beginning at the river Isaurus, which, commonly called the Foglia, forms the boundary between Picenum and Flaminia.

units.la: Ab Isauro igitur modico spatio, in colle, qui uno latere spectat Orientem: Septemtrionem & Hadriaticum Mare altero, superbum illitur Palatium, Poggio Imperiale vulgo vocatum, quod Fridericus III Imperator primum fundamento lapidem, petente id Constantino Pisauri Domino, jecerit: auctum postea, & ædificiis splendidis ornatum ab Francisco Maria Roboreo, Urbini Duce, Pisaurique Dynasta.
units.tr: A short distance from the Isaurus, on a hill that faces east on one side, and north and the Adriatic Sea on the other, stands a proud palace, commonly called the Poggio Imperiale. Emperor Frederick III laid its first stone at the request of Constantine, lord of Pesaro. It was later enlarged and adorned with splendid buildings by Francesco Maria Della Rovere, Duke of Urbino and lord of Pesaro.

units.la: Sursum hinc ad Pisauri sinistram Putcus est, Pozzo vernacule.
units.tr: Above this, to the left of Pesaro, is the Pozzo, as it is called in the vernacular.

units.la: Tum inter Isauram & Concam Amnes Mons Lurus, cælis Nicolai Picinini copiis apud Blondum & alios inclutus.
units.tr: Then, between the Isaurus and the Conca, lies Monte Luro, famous from the campaign of Niccolò Piccinino's forces near Biondo and others.

units.la: Ad Viam Flaminiam descendenti Mons se Pisauri offert in meridiem prospectans, antiquis Promontorium Fo. aria dictus, quatuor gelitans Opida, quæ vulgo Granaruolo, Castello di Mezzo, Gabizze, Hi en zuola.
units.tr: Descending towards the Via Flaminia, a mountain presents itself at Pesaro, looking south. The ancients called it the Promontory of Fo(r)tuna(?)... It holds four towns, commonly called Granaruolo, Castello di Mezzo, Gabbice and Gradara.

units.la: Dein ad alteram viæ ripam è regione Montis ex colle modica quædam passim est cernere Castella, quæ vernacule Tomba, Pian del monte, Monte Calvo, Pie del Cam-po Sasso, Carbaro, & Macerata di Monte Feluro.
units.tr: Then, on the other bank of the road, opposite the mountain, several small castles can be seen scattered over a hill, called in the vernacular Tomba, Pian del Monte, Monte Calvo, Piè del Campo Sasso, Carbaro and Macerata di Monte Feltro.

units.la: Ad occasum pergenti ipsa in Via sub Monte Pisauri, Catholica Vicus occurrit, Arce superbiens. Spectantur hic sub aquis mari tranquillo Moenia, Turriumque & aliorum ædificiorum fastigia demersæ superioribus annis urbis Concæ.
units.tr: Going west along the road itself, below the mountain of Pesaro, one meets the village of Cattolica, proud of its citadel. Under the calm sea one can see the walls, and the tops of towers and other buildings, of the city of Conca, which sank in recent years.

units.la: Intus excelso in Colle Palatium eminet, ab grato aere dictum, Grataria, Sigismundi Malatestæ, Pandulphi Filii, Pisauri Dynastæ, opus.
units.tr: Inside the town, on a high hill, rises a palace named Gradaria* from the pleasant air, built by Sigismondo Malatesta, son of Pandolfo, lord of Pesaro.

units.la: Ultra Catholicam primo flumen est Vintinella; dein Conca, quod Plinio Lucanoque Crustumium.
units.tr: Beyond Cattolica the first river is the Vintinella; then comes the Conca, which is the Crustumium of Pliny and Lucan.

units.la: Hic in Collibus sunt S. Giovanni in Marignano, Mondiano, Saludetio, Monte Gridolfo: tum aspero in Monte Germano, Tauleto, Pian di Castello, Castel Nuovo, Monte Tavesco, Certaldo, Piagnano. Certaldum Petri Turci, viri docti; Planianum Francisci Planiani, summi litteratique Ducis est patria. Sequitur Pian di Meledo, cuius Karolus, qui sub Innocentio VIII P. M. Legionibus fuit Præfectus, nobile.
units.tr: On the hills here lie San Giovanni in Marignano, Mondaino, Saludecio and Montegridolfo; then, on the rugged mountain, Montegermano, Tavoleto, Pian di Castello, Castelnuovo, Montetassi, Certaldo and Piagnano. Certaldo is the native place of Pietro Turchi, a learned man, and Pianiano of Francesco Pianiani, a most distinguished and learned duke. Next comes Pian di Meleto, notable for Carlo, who was commander of the legions under Pope Innocent VIII.

units.la: Sunt etiam hoc situ Petra Rubbia, & Carpegno: ab eo mons Carpenianus, quem ab Apennino Marecia fluvius dividit: reliquos Italiæ, ab Apennino abscissos, altitudine sua vincentem. Sub eo sunt Castellaria, Monte Cerognone, ubi multa veterum ædificiorum vestigia, & Monasterium Sestinum.
units.tr: In this region are also Petra Rubbia and Carpegna. From the latter runs the Carpegna mountain, which the river Marecchia separates from the Apennine. It surpasses in height the other peaks of Italy that are cut off from the Apennine. Beneath it are Castellaro, Monte Cerignone*, where many traces of ancient buildings remain, and the Sestine Monastery.

units.la: Trans amnem porro Concam conspiciuntur S. Clemente, Aggello, Ceriano, Monte Scutulo, Albareto, Gessio, Tomba di Gusana, Monte Zardino, Sasso, Monte Germano, Monte di Tasso, Monte Copiolo.
units.tr: Further on, beyond the river Conca, one sees San Clemente, Agello, Ceriano, Montescudo, Albereto, Gessio, Tomba di Gusana, Monte Zardino, Sasso, Montegermano, Montetassi and Monte Copiolo.

units.la: Descensu dein ad Viam Flaminiam Fanum est Trinitatis.
units.tr: Descending then to the Via Flaminia is Fano della Trinità.

units.la: Sunt etiam ibidem Castella Seravalle, Verruchio, S. Marino.
units.tr: There are also castles here: Serravalle, Verucchio and San Marino.

units.la: Hinc en Agro Montis-Feltrij sursum nonnihil, hæc cernuntur, Monte Maggio, Macerata, Pietra Acutula, Torano & Sanctum-Leo. Civitas hæc Episcopalis, verticì insidens præcelsi montis, qui undique, præterquam quo latere aditur, rupibus circumcisus: adeo ut naturali situ Urbs invicta videatur. Meminit præter alios Luitprandus in historijs libro VI.
units.tr: Then, a little way up from the territory of Montefeltro, the following can be seen: Montemaggio, Macerata, Pietracuta, Torano and San Leo. This is an episcopal city, sitting on the summit of a very high mountain, cut off on every side by cliffs except on the one side from which it is approached. So much so that by its natural position the town seems invincible. Luitprand, among others, mentions it in book 6 of his histories.

units.la: Sequitur hinc Stanino Verruchio, Coane, Pena de Billi & Maiolo.
units.tr: Next from here come Stignano, Verucchio, Coriano, Penna di Billi and Maiolo.

units.la: Situ quoque hoc sunt Ciconaria, Montirone, & Mercato di Ranchi.
units.tr: In this region also lie Cerreto, Montiróne and Mercato di Ranchio.

units.la: In ora conspiciendum se præbet maritimum Oppidum antiquæ notæ, Ariminum. Sic Cæsari, Livio, Lucano, Tacito, Plinio, Pomponio Melæ, Antonino dicitur; Ἀρίμινον Polybio, Straboni, Ptolemæo, Appiano passim, Procopio lib. III, Agathiæ lib. 1: quod hodie truncato capite Rimeni Incolis; Rumelen Germanis. Nomen illi ab Amne, quo adluitur, cuius alibi facta est mentio. Alij aliunde trahunt: quorum sententias, quod parum habeant fundamenti, non referam. Inter eos sane ex plodendus mihi Annius Viterbiensis, qui nonnihil nobis auctorum subornavit, ad ostentandum, quod alioqui felicissimum ipsi fuit, ingenium. Urbs in planicie sita, imminentibus ab meridie collibus amoenis & frugiferis; ab Ortu Occasuque latissimi lætissimique se pandunt Campi, Frumenti feraces: pulsatur, qua Septemtrio est, Hadria. Rerum omnium copia supra modum abundat. Ædificia habet memorabilia, cum primis ad portam, quæ Orientem & Pisaurum spectat, Arcum Triumphalem cum suis Elogijs; Theatri partem ex latere coćto, mare versus In littore post Portum Cefenaticum, qui exiguis tantum navigijs excipiendis est idoneus, opidum jacet loco palustri, cæloque gravi Cervia, quam Phycolim olim dictam, doceri ex Ravennatis Ecclesiæ Privilegijs, idque referre loannem Petrum Feneirum Ravennatem, Milentem Episcopum, tradit Leander. Videndus & Rubeus in Ravennarium historia, & apud eum Pyrrhus Ligorius. Cervia majori ex parte talarij sunt Artifices, tanto quaestu, ut Pontifex annuatim inde habeat 1x millia Coronatorum. Antiquum non est, quum primus omnium, ni fallor, mentionem ejus faciat Blondus lib. x Histor. Cathedrale Templum, licet vilior ipsi sit structura, magnis tamen redditibus est dotatum. Ante fores Templi Sepultura visitur, antiqua forma pyramidali, in cujus uno latere duo pueri mœsti jacent, facem accensam una manu: altera coronam, tenentes: adposita Inscriptione, non magni ævi. Licet ob incommodorem situm sit infrequens, Episcopali tamen superbit dignitate, sub Archiepiscopo Ravennate. Inter Episcopos fuit D. Hierontius Martyr, cujus ossa Calij perhibentur servari. Scribitur Cervia primum ad Ecclesiæ Ravennatis patrimonium pertinuisse; post in potestate fuisse Bononiensium; hinc in Forolivensium, item Polentanorum Ravennæ Principum ditionem devenisse; mox Malatestas, flatimque Venetos habuisse; hodie denique Pontifices Romanos agnoscere Dominos.
units.tr: On the coast there presents itself a maritime town of ancient renown, Rimini, called Ariminum by Caesar, Livy, Lucan, Tacitus, Pliny, Pomponius Mela and Antoninus, and [Ariminon] by Polybius, Strabo, Ptolemy, and Appian in many places, Procopius in book 3, and Agathias in book 1. Today, with its head cut off, it is called Rimeni by its inhabitants and Rumelen by the Germans. It takes its name from the river on which it lies, which I have mentioned elsewhere. Others derive the name from other sources, but I will not report their opinions, since they have little foundation. Among them, I must certainly reject Annius of Viterbo, who put together some passages from the authors on our behalf, in order to show off a talent that otherwise was very fortunate for him. The city lies on a plain, with pleasant and fruitful hills overhanging it to the south; to east and west wide and very fertile fields of grain stretch out; the Adriatic beats on the north side. It has an abundance of all good things beyond measure. It has notable buildings, above all at the gate facing east and Pesaro, a triumphal arch with its inscriptions; part of a theatre built on the side towards the sea. On the shore, after the Cesenatico harbour, which can take only small vessels, lies the town of Cervia, in a marshy place with an unhealthy climate. Leander reports, on the authority of Giovanni Pietro Feneiri of Ravenna, bishop of Milet, that it was once called Phycolis, as the privileges of the Church of Ravenna show. See also Rubeus in his history of Ravenna, and Pirro Ligorio there. The majority of the people of Cervia are salt-workers, with such profit that the Pope receives from it 9,000 crowns every year. It is not ancient: Blondus, book 10 of his histories, is, I think, the first of all to mention it. Its cathedral church, although its structure is rather plain, is endowed with large revenues. Before the doors of the church there is a tomb, in the old pyramidal form, on one side of which two sorrowful boys lie, holding a lit torch in one hand and a crown in the other, with an inscription beside them that is not of great age. Although it is little frequented because of its inconvenient situation, it nonetheless takes pride in its episcopal dignity, under the archbishop of Ravenna. Among its bishops was St. Hieronymus, a martyr, whose bones are said to be kept at Calci. It is written that Cervia first belonged to the patrimony of the Church of Ravenna; afterwards it was under the power of the Bolognese; from there it came under the rule of the Forlivesi and likewise of the Polenta, princes of Ravenna; soon it had the Malatesta, and immediately the Venetians; today at last it acknowledges the Roman Pontiffs as its lords.

units.la: Ultra Cerviam in ora quinto lapide Savij fluminis, de quo alibi, ostium sequitur. Classem hac in ora ad tutelam Superi maris collocatam habuisse Augustum, auctor est Suetonius.
units.tr: Beyond Cervia*, on the coast, five miles away, comes the mouth of the river Savio, which I shall discuss elsewhere. Suetonius is the authority that Augustus stationed a fleet on this coast to guard the upper sea.

units.la: In ipsa mox AEmilia ad pedem Collis juxta fluvium Sapin Urbs Cesena conspicitur. Sic Plinio, Antonino, & alijs; Καισαρια autem Ptolemaeo, Καισηνα Straboni vocatur: quæ hodie plerisque Cesena, alijs Cesenadigo, tertijs denique Cesna, dissyllabicas. Curva etiam cognominatur cum ab Antonino in Itinere ab Arimino Dertonam, tum in Itineraria Tabula, ubi Cesena scribitur. Flavia Curva Papia dicitur in Vita S. Mauri Episcopi. Secundam in Cesena sine diphthongo scribendam, docet in Orthographia Aldus Manutius Paulli F. cum ex alijs, tum ex sequenti Inscriptione, quæ nescio an in rerum fuerit natura: ego certe, notas habens hujusmodi Patriciorum artes, de fide valde dubito. Est autem talis: A. LVCRETII. HISTORICI. AC. POETÆ CONDITORIS. VERISSIMI CVI. OB. EXCELLENTIAM. INGENII STATVA. CONDONATA AG. CIVITATI. CAESENÆ ROMAN. COLONIA. DEDVCTÆ IN. HOC. SACRO. MONTE. DEDICATA
units.tr: Right in Aemilia, at the foot of a hill beside the river Savio, is seen the city of Cesena. It is so called by Pliny, Antoninus and others; Ptolemy calls it [Kaisaria] and Strabo [Kaisena]. Today most call it Cesena, others Cesenadigo, and others finally Cesna, in two syllables. It is also surnamed Curva*, both by Antoninus in his itinerary from Ariminum to Dertona and in the Itinerary Table, where it is written Cesena. In the Life of St. Maurus, the bishop, it is called Flavia Curva Papia. Aldus Manutius, son of Paulus, teaches in his Orthography that the second vowel in Cesena should be written without a diphthong, showing this both from other sources and from the following inscription. I do not know whether it ever existed; for my part, knowing the arts of such patricians, I greatly doubt its authenticity. It reads: "To A. Lucretius, historian and poet, most true founder, on account of the excellence of his genius, the statue was granted to the city of Caesena, a Roman colony led into this sacred mountain, dedicated."

units.la: Dictam sic volunt ab caedendo, quod exiguo amne cæsa: aut quod amnibus duobus, Sapi & Rubicone, sit divisa. Plinius in vIII. Regione. Ptolemæus in Tegata nominat Gallia: Procopius libro 1. de bello Gothico Cæsenam ab Ravenna Itadijs ccc abesse tradit. Civitatibus, quæ majoris quam Opida dignationis censeri solent, adcenset in magno illo Itinere, quod Mediolano per Picenum & Campaniam ducit ad Columnam, id est Trajectum Siciliæ, Antoninus, ut non immerito Aldus Manutius indignetur Cesenam ab Hadriano Turnebo, homine Trans-Alpino, minimum & frigidissimum dici opidum, quum & Strabo inter nobiles Civitates eam numeret. Hodie sane Civitas est admodum frequens: annis superioribus à Bernardo Rubrio Parmensi, quum angustius habitaretur, augusta, qua Occidentem Septemtrionemque spectat, aucta. Arx urbi ex Colle, qua Auster est, valida imminet, ab Friderico II. Imperat. teste Collenutio libro iv, condita. Hospitale etiam visitur ibi sumtuosissimum. Incolas habet nobiles, ingenio opibusque pollentes. Cesena sub fide Romanorum diu floruit, Langbardis totam Italiam occupantibus. A Britonibus post, quos Cardinalis Gebennensis, Gregorij xi Legatus in Italiam adduxerat, magnis adfecta est calamitatibus, & patum aberat, desolata, scribentibus Blondo. Platina,
units.tr: They say it was named thus from caedendo (cutting), because it was cut by a small stream, or because it is divided by two rivers, the Sapis and the Rubicon. Pliny mentions it in the eighth region. Ptolemy names it in Gallia Togata. Procopius, in book 1 of the Gothic War, reports that Cesena is 300 miles from Ravenna. Antoninus counts it among the towns that are usually thought of as more important than villages, on the great road that leads from Milan through Picenum and Campania to the Column, that is, the crossing to Sicily. Aldus Manutius rightly complains that Hadrian Turnebus, a man from beyond the Alps, calls Cesena "the smallest and coldest town," since Strabo also counts it among the noble cities. Today it is certainly a very populous city: in recent years, when it had become rather cramped, it was enlarged by Bernardo Rubrio of Parma, on the side facing west and north, making it grander. A strong citadel rises above the town on the hill on the south side, built by Emperor Frederick II, according to Collenuccio, book 4. A most sumptuous hospital is also to be seen there. Its inhabitants are noble, powerful in talent and wealth. Cesena* flourished for a long time under the protection of the Romans, while the Lombards occupied all of Italy. Afterwards, after it had been struck by great calamities from the Britons, whom the Cardinal of Geneva, legate of Gregory XI, had brought into Italy, it was almost deserted, as Blondus and Platina write, and was reduced to almost nothing.

units.la: Ars. Hodie, Incola. Ravenne. tina, aliis. Dein a Bononiensibus in deditionem accepta hinc aliquamdiu dominata pressa Sulenanorum, Ordelaffurum, Malatestarum, tandem in Pontificum Romanorum venit potestatem, quorum Alexander VI eam filio donavit Cæsari Borgiæ, ante quem maxima Civium pars factionibus erat divisa Tibertorum & Martinellorum. Episcopatus titulo floret. Videre est ad D. Francisci Bibliothecam insignem, Malatestæ Novelli opus, omnis generis mss. libris, inter quos quidam rarissimi, abunde instructam. In vestibulo Symbolum legitur Malatestarum hoc: Elephas Indus non curat murem. Ager suburbicanus Vino generoso, quod Cæsennate vocat Plinius libro XIIII, cap. VI, est nobilis.
units.tr: Ars. Today, the inhabitants... Ravenna... Platina, and others. Then, once taken into surrender by the Bolognese, it was ruled for some time by the Sulenani, the Ordelaffi and the Malatesta, and at last came under the power of the Roman Pontiffs. Of these, Alexander VI gave it to his son, Cesare Borgia, before which time the greater part of its citizens had been divided by the factions of the Tiberti and the Martinelli. It flourishes with the title of a bishopric. At the library of St. Francis one may see the notable library of Malatesta Novello, well furnished with manuscript books of every kind, among which are some very rare ones. In the vestibule is read this device of the Malatesta: The Indian elephant does not care for the mouse. The suburban countryside is famous for its noble wine, which Pliny, in book XIV, chapter VI, calls Caesennas.

units.la: Haud procul Cæsena Oppidum est, quod Latine scribentibus Forum Saracenum, vulgo autem Mercato Saracino ab Negociatoribus ex finitimis agris commerciorum gratia frequentari solitum.
units.tr: Not far from Cesena is a town which writers in Latin call Forum Saracenum, but which commonly goes by Mercato Saracino, because it is customarily frequented by merchants from the neighbouring countryside for the sake of trade.

units.la: Tum altius ad Apennini radices Urbs est Sarsina: Plauti, Poetæ Comici, Patria. Sic Latinis nominatur, Σάρσινα Straboni quæ vulgo nomen retinens, Sarsina Sassinam, non Sarsinam scribendum docet Iacobonius in Historia Cæsia: & suffragantur Inscriptiones & Fasti Triumphales, in quibus Sassinates sculpuntur, Municipy etiam Sassinatis meminit Lapis, qui ad Summum ibi Templum: D M SEX. TETTI. SEX. L HERME VI. VIRI. PATR. COLLEG. CENT. MVN. SASS. TORASIA. C. F. SABINA CONIVGI. INCOM. PARABIL. ET. SIBI HAVE: HERME. HOMO. BONE
units.tr: Further up, at the foot of the Apennines, is the city of Sarsina, the home of Plautus, the comic poet. So it is named in Latin; Strabo gives it as Σάρσινα. Retaining the name in the vernacular, Iacobonius, in his History of Cesena, teaches that it should be written Sassina, not Sarsina, and the inscriptions and the Triumphal Fasti support him, in which Sassinates is carved. A stone at the principal temple there also mentions the Municipium Sassinatis: To the Divine Spirits of Sextus Tettius, Sextus son of L. Hermes, sixvir, patron of the college of the centuries of the municipium of Sassina; Torasia Sabina, daughter of Gaius, to her husband, inconsolable, and to herself. Hail, Hermes, good man.

units.la: Videtur ibidem Ara marmorea ad Apennini radices: posita D. M. CETRANIA P. F. SEVERINÆ, SACERDOTI DIVÆ MARCIANÆ, cujus sinistrum latus MVNIC. SASSI etiam facit mentionem. Sarsinates leguntur apud Plinium libro III cap. XIIII. ubi tamen antiquiores codices Farsinates habent: sed priorem scripturam præferendam ordo Alphabeticus clamat, à Plinio in Populis recensendis usurpari plurimum solitus. Gaudentius Merula haud procul fonte Rubiconis statuit: Plinius in VI Regione, Strabo in Umbris locat. Sic Martialis: Nympha sacri Regina lacus, cui grata Sabinus Et mansura pio munere templa dedit: Sic montana tuos semper colat Umbria fontes, Necnon Rajanas Sarsina malit aquas: &c.
units.tr: There is also a marble altar at the foot of the Apennines there, set up to the Divine Spirits of Cetrania, daughter of Publius, Severina, priestess of the goddess Marciana, on whose left side is also a mention of the Municipium Sassinatum. The Sarsinates are read in Pliny, book III, chapter XIV, where however older manuscripts have Farsinates. But alphabetical order calls for the former reading to be preferred, since Pliny very often used this order when listing peoples. Gaudentius Merula places it not far from the source of the Rubicon; Pliny locates it in the Sixth Region, Strabo among the Umbrians. So Martial: Queen of the sacred lake, nymph, to whom Sabinus gave his welcome gift of a temple that will endure: so may mountainous Umbria always tend your springs, and may Sarsina prefer the waters of Rajana, etc.

units.la: Urbs est Episcopalis, cujus Præsul aliquando fuit Vicinus Ligur. Corpus ejus in Ecclesia Cathedrali servare se perhibent Cives. Episcopatui Sarsinæ Castelli subsunt xx, quem Regionis tractum una cum Civitate nunc vulgo Bisbum vocant, tamquam Forum seu Boseorum agrum. De Sarsinatum auxiliis, quæ contra gentes quasdam ex Alpibus irruentes pro Populo Romano contraxerunt, scribit Polybius lib. II. Imperio diu Malatestarum habita, tandem ad Pontifices Maximos cum Arimino pervenit, donata postremo ab Leone X Alberto Pio, Carpensi Comiti. Ager Urbis uber Vinæ, Oleæ, Arboribusque omnis generis fructiferis.
units.tr: It is an episcopal city, whose prelate was once Vicinus the Ligurian. The citizens claim to keep his body in the cathedral church. Twenty castles are subject to the bishopric of Sarsina; the district together with the city is now commonly called Bisbum, as if it were the territory of Forum or of the Boii. Polybius, book II, writes about the auxiliaries of the Sarsinates whom they raised for the Roman people against certain tribes rushing down from the Alps. Long under the rule of the Malatesta, it at last came with Rimini to the Supreme Pontiffs, and was finally granted by Leo X to Alberto Pio, Count of Carpi. The fields of the city are rich in vines, olives and trees of every kind bearing fruit.

units.la: Viterius secundum Sapin ad Opidum Via ducit D. Mariæ in Balneo, sic ab aquis medicatis dictum.
units.tr: Further on, according to Sapis, the road leads to the town of St. Mary in the Baths, so called from its medicinal waters.

units.la: Visitur mille hinc passibus in Valle, quam Sapis perfluit, perhonestum opidum D. Petri in Balneo.
units.tr: A thousand paces from here, in the valley which the Sapis flows through, is a very handsome town, St. Peter in the Baths.

units.la: Vallis quam dixi, tota Comitum, qui à Balneis & Iacolo cognominabantur, olim fuit potestatis: post universa fere dimidia facta est Florentina. Supra vallem opidum adparet Sarianum, quod in potestate Malatestarum.
units.tr: The whole of the valley I have mentioned belonged of old to the Counts, who were named from Bagni and Iacolo; afterwards almost the whole of it became Florentine. Above the valley appears the town of Sariano, which is in the power of the Malatesta.

units.la: Hinc in ora post Sapis ostium Nemus est vastissimum, Pinis mirae altitudinis frequens. Pinetum vocat Paullus Diaconus libro xvi.
units.tr: From here, on the coast beyond the mouth of the Sapis, is a very vast wood, thick with pines of wonderful height. Paulus Diaconus, book XVI, calls it Pinetum.

units.la: Extra Pinetum Candianum Amnis, nunc Paludis ostium sequitur. Turris hic olim fuit Pharea, cujus usus, inquit Plinius lib. xxxvi cap. xii nocturno Nautarum usui ignem offendere ad praenuncianda vada Portusque introitum. Classem autem ibi ab Augusto ad utelam Maris Superi collocatam, celebrant varij Scriptores, cum primis Suetonius in Augusti Vita cap. xlix, & Tacitus lib. iiii Annalium. Ravennas dicebatur Classis, quod vicina esset Ravennae, quae illi versus Occidentem. Videndi Separtianus in Didio Juliano, Vegetius lib. iv de re militari cap. xxx., sequentque, & alij. Classi vero est navium tutissimam ibi stationem fuisse auctor est Dio, & ex eo lornandes. Hinc Praefectus Classis Ravennatum in Notitia Imperij; qui in Notis Magnonis Paullique Diaconi sic notatur, p. cl. r. Fecit quondam Portus celebritas, quum valde frequentaretur, ut aedificia fuerint adstructa, quae post etiam muribus circumdata formam Opidi non contemnendi effecerunt. Nomen illi ab Classe, quam dixi, impositum Classis. Fuit, ut multa alia; tamque plane interiit, ut praeter sumtuosum D. Apollinaris Fanum nulla Aedificiorum vestigia supersint. Quin & ipsius Portus facies ita periit, ut Sidonij aevo & ante illud spaciosissimos Hortos ostenderet, Arboribus plenos, de quibus non Vela, sed Poma pendebant. A Blondo libro Romae restaurata iii locus, ubi olim Classis fuit, Candiano vocatur; ab Candiano Amne, qui nunc Palus. Non procul ea loco, ubi Classis Opidum fuit, vestigia cernuntur Caesarea, cujus Blondus meminit libro v. ii Historiarum. Visitur jam ibi Monasterium S. Mariae Porti, tribus ab Classe P. M. Opidorum Classis & Caesarea, Civitatisque Ravennae talis erat ad celeberrimam Navium Stationem Situs, ut Ravennae ipsi esset ad occasum, Classis ad ortum; medium autem versus meridiem ad intimum Stationis recessum obtineret Caesarea; ita ut continuata quasi ab Ravenna Classem usque videretur Civitas: ut mirum non sit, toto illo spatio innumera spectari Antiquitatum audera. Ex iis, quae dixi, paret Lornandem male ex tribus, Ravenna, Caesarea & Classe, trinominem facere Ravennam his verbis: Trino Urbs ipsa vocabulo gloriatur, tergeminaque posituone exsultat, id est prima Ravenna, ultima Classis, media Caesarea, inter urbem & mare plana mollitie, arenaque munita, rectionibus apta. Alia enim Ravenna, ut dixi, alia Caesarea, alia Classis. Ab Caesarea autem Caesaris Via apud Sidonium lib. i. Epist. v. quae Ravennam ducebat, eamque vel ab Novo Portu discernebat, vel cum eo potius connectebat, ut suo loco videbimus.
units.tr: Beyond the Pinetum flows the river Candianus, which now follows the mouth of the marsh. Here there was once a tower, the Pharos, whose use, says Pliny, book XXXVI, chapter XII, was to kindle a fire at night for sailors, to signal shallows and the entrance to the harbour. That a fleet was stationed there by Augustus to guard the Upper Sea is recorded by various writers, above all Suetonius in the Life of Augustus, chapter XLIX, and Tacitus, book IV of the Annals. The fleet was called Ravennas, because it lay near Ravenna, which is to the west of it. See Spartianus in the Life of Didius Julianus, Vegetius, book IV of the Military Art, chapter XXX, and those that follow, and others. That there was a very safe station for ships there is attested by Dio, and from him Jordanes. Hence the Prefect of the Fleet of Ravenna in the Notitia of the Empire, who is so noted in the notes of Magnon and Paulus Diaconus: p. cl. r. The port once made a town of it, since it was very much frequented, so that buildings were erected, which afterwards, surrounded by walls, made the form of a not contemptible town. It took its name, Classis, from the fleet I have mentioned. It fell, like many other things, and so utterly perished that, apart from the sumptuous shrine of St. Apollinaris, no traces of buildings survive. Indeed the very face of the port has so vanished that in the age of Sidonius, and before it, it showed very spacious gardens, full of trees, from which hung not sails but apples. Blondus, in book III of his Rome Restored, says the place where the fleet once was is called Candiano, from the river Candianus, which is now a marsh. Not far from that spot, where the town of Classis was, traces of Caesarea can be seen, which Blondus mentions in book V of his Histories. There is now a monastery of St. Mary of the Port there. Of the two towns of Classis and Caesarea, and the city of Ravenna, the situation was such at this most famous station of ships that Ravenna itself lay to the west, Classis to the east, and Caesarea, in the middle, toward the south, held the inner recess of the station; so that the city seemed to be continuous, as it were, from Ravenna all the way to Classis. It is no wonder, then, that countless remains of antiquity are to be seen over that whole space. From what I have said it is clear that Lornandes wrongly makes Ravenna three-named, out of three, Ravenna, Caesarea and Classis, in these words: The city itself glories in a triple name and exults in its threefold position, that is, first Ravenna, last Classis, middle Caesarea, between the city and the sea, with a level softness and a sandy fortification, fit for ... For Ravenna is one thing, as I said, Caesarea another, Classis another. From Caesarea, however, runs the Caesar's Way mentioned by Sidonius, book I, letter V, which led to Ravenna and either separated it from the New Port or rather joined it to it, as we shall see in its place.

units.la: Relicta ora, intus in Aemilia via, quam Torrens interrumpit Avefa, Opidum est, quod Plinio Forum-Pompilij, vel Popilij. Vitra scriptura praeferenda sit, adhuc ambigo: ad posteriorem magis inclino, quod vulgata appellatio Forum Popilii nonnihil suffragetur. Habent quidam Plinij codices Forum Populi corrupte. Iacet in Aemilia Via, campis peramenis. Unum est ex quatuor Foris, quae Aemiliae memorat Plinius. Fora ducebantur, quod in his olim Magistratus Populi Romani Fora agere solebant, Auctorum primorum his plerumque impositio cognomine. Pontificibus, in quorum olim fuit ditione, eripuit Grimoaldus Langbardorum Rex, pridie Paschatis, anno ab Christo nato 1ccc. Legendus Paullus Diaconus lib. v. Histor. Langbard. qui solo aquatum notat. Restauratum inde ab Foro-Liviensibus evertit iterum Aegidius Canis, Hispanus, Cardinalis, totiusque Italiae Legatus Pontificis Maximi, qui tunc Avenione sedem habebat, adeo ut & Ararum solo inducerent, Salemque insereret anno cIↄ ccclxx, Episcopali sede in Forum Truentinorum translata. Post xx vero annum reaedificatum legitur qua nunc est forma, ab Stimbaldo Ordelasso, Foro Livien-sium Principe, addita post insigni Arce. Habuit inter Antiistites Kofilum, Sanctorum Classi adscriptum. Genuit Forum hoc Antonellum Armutium, qui ex Rustico per gradus munerum militarium ad Praefecturam pervenit Equitatus Pontificij, acceptis praemiorum loco D. Mauri & Talamellarum opidis. Consulenda Iacobi Volaterrani Cardinalis Commentaria.
units.tr: Leaving the coast, inland on the Aemilian Way, which the river Ariminus interrupts, lies the town which Pliny calls Forum Pompilii, or Popilii. I am still unsure which reading is to be preferred; I incline more to the latter, since the common name Forum Popilii lends some support to it. Some manuscripts of Pliny have Forum Populi, corruptly. It lies on the Aemilian Way, in very pleasant fields. It is one of the four Fora which Pliny mentions in Aemilia. They were called Fora because the magistrates of the Roman people used to hold their business in them there, the names being usually given by the earliest authors. King Grimoald of the Lombards snatched it from the Pontiffs, under whose rule it once was, on the day before Easter, in the year of Christ 1ccc. Paulus Diaconus, book V of the History of the Lombards, should be read; he records it as a place of waters only. Afterwards, restored from Forum Livii, it was again overthrown by Egidius Albornoz, a Spaniard, Cardinal and Legate of the Supreme Pontiff throughout Italy, who at that time had his seat at Avignon, so much so that they even brought the plough over the site of the altars and sowed salt in the year 1370, the episcopal see having been transferred to Forum Truentinorum. Twenty years later, however, it is read to have been rebuilt in the form it has now, by Stimbaldo Ordelaffi, Prince of Forum Livii, with a famous citadel added afterwards. Among its bishops it had Kofilus, who is enrolled among the Saints. This Forum produced Antonello Armuzio, who rose from a peasant, through the grades of military offices, to the prefecture of the Papal cavalry, and received the towns of St. Maurus and Talamello as the reward of his services. The Commentaries of Cardinal Jacopo Volterrano should be consulted.

units.la: Mille quingentis ab Foro-Pompilij Palfibus opidum in Colle jacet Bretinorum, quod Plinio Forum Truentinorum. Brittanorum legunt Marius & Blondus; ex vulgari fortean Latinum facientes. FORODAVLNT. oltendit antiqua apud Goltzium Inscriptio. Petram urbem habet in Piceno Procopius libro II de Bello Gothor. quam Brentinore vulgo dici scribit L. Aretinus in suo de ijsdem lib. III. Posita cernitur in tumulo, Arcem habens munitissimam, Friderici II Imp. opus. Vibs mirę salubritatis, ferax ingeniorum, fixis ibi propter summam loci amœnitatem sedibus, post pacem cum Pontifice factam, Fridericus Ahenobarbus, rogatu Alexandri III P. M. Ecclesiæ restituit. Inde in Foro-Livienfium venit ditionem post Malatestarium, cujus gentis ultimus Nocellus Ecclesiæ Romanæ reddidit. Donavit tandem filio Cæfari Borgia, cum multis aliis, Alexander VI P. M. Post ejus excessum factionibus Saccorum & Zatulorum pene diiceptum tandem in potestate Comitum Carpersium esse cœpit. Episcopalem habet sedem, quæ eo ex Foro-Pompiliano translata, ut antea dixi. De hoc opido lege omnino quæ scribit Landinus Commentario ad Dant. in Purgator. Can. XIV.
units.tr: Fifteen hundred paces from Forum Pompilii, on a hill, lies the town of Bretinorum, which Pliny calls Forum Truentinorum. Marius and Blondus read Brittanorum, perhaps making it Latin from the vernacular. An ancient inscription in Goltzius shows FORODAVLNT. Procopius, in book II of his work on the Gothic War, gives the city of Petra in Picenum, which L. Aretinus, in book III of his work on the same events, writes is called Brentinore in the vernacular. It is set on a mound and has a very strong citadel, the work of Emperor Frederick II. The town has remarkable healthiness and produces men of talent, since its inhabitants settled there because of the great charm of the site. After peace was made with the Pope, Frederick Barbarossa restored it to the Church at the request of Pope Alexander III. Afterwards it came under the rule of the Forlivesi, following the Malatesta family, the last of whom, Nocello, handed it back to the Roman Church. Finally Pope Alexander VI, along with many other places, gave it to his son Cesare Borgia. After his death, it was torn between the factions of the Sacchi and the Zatuli, and at last it began to be in the power of the Counts Carpersi. It has an episcopal see, which, as I said earlier, was transferred there from Forum Pompilianum. On this town read everything that Landino writes in his commentary on Dante, Purgatorio canto XIV.

units.la: Duobus ab Foro-Truentinorum versus meridiem millibus Opidum adparet subcolle Polenta, Gentis Polentanæ, Ravennæ quondam Principum, origine clarum.
units.tr: Two miles south of Forum Truentinorum, the town of Polenta appears below a hill, famous in origin for the Polentani family, once rulers of Ravenna.

units.la: Post ostium Bedetis Amnis, de quo dixi cap. XI, sequitur antiquissima Civitas Ravenna. Sic Livio, Tacito multis locis, Plinio, Melæ, Antonino Itinerariæ Tabulæ, aliisque Latinis, atque etiam vulgo hodieque dicitur: Ραβενα Strabo lib. V. (cui & Ραυεννα paullo post) Appiano lib. III & V, Agathiæ; Ραβενα Stephano: quæ Ραβενναη Ptolemæo; Ραυεννα Hermippo apud Stephanum. Nonnullis Navennam dicti ab Navibus, scribit H. Rubeus in sua Ravennatum historia. Apud Zosimum Rhene vocatur, quod Aquæ eam ex omni parte circumfluant. Iornandes trimonimen facit in historia Gothica; dici tradens Ravennam, Classem Cæsaream. Classem & Cæsaream alia ab Ravenna fuisse opida, patet ex præcedentibus; nisi quis velit Classem ab Iornande dici Novum Portum, Cæsaream vero Cæsarii viam. Conditores faciunt alios: quidam Tubalem Lamechi filium: nonnulli, inter quos Iacobus Voragmentis, Filios Nimrodi Tyranni: Carinus Pentapolin Trojanum, ab eoque Pentapolin dictam; simulque, ne frustra tale Auctoris nomen habere videretur, quinque vicinarum urbium imperio fuisse præpositam. Quadratus in Marco & Olympiodorus ab Reno conditam notant; quorum sententiam rejicit Zosimus libro V. Strabo lib. V. ab Thessalia cœptam tradit; postea vero Sabinorum Umbrorumque ditione habitam, quos primi urbis coloni sibi conjunxerunt, quum perpetuis Tuscorum incursionibus pares esse non possent: Hinc Sabinorum eam Coloniam nominat Plinius. Quidquid sit, antiquam Civitatem testantur omnes; & disertis verbis Zosimus quem dixi. Sic Claudianus: Dixit, & antiquæ muris egressa Ravennæ.
units.tr: After the mouth of the river Bedesis, of which I spoke in chapter XI, comes the very ancient city of Ravenna. So it is called by Livy, Tacitus in many places, Pliny, Mela, the Antonine Itinerary, and other Latin writers, and it is still called so commonly today. Strabo in book V calls it Rabena [Ραβενα] (and Ravenna [Ραυεννα] shortly after); Appian in books III and V and Agathias likewise; Stephanus gives Rabena [Ραβενα]; Ptolemy gives Ravennaea [Ραβενναη]; Hermippus, cited by Stephanus, gives Ravenna [Ραυεννα]. Some, as H. Rubeus writes in his history of the Ravennates, say it was named Navenna from ships. Zosimus calls it Rhene, because waters flow round it on every side. Jordanes, in his Gothic history, makes a tripartite name, stating that Ravenna is called Classis and Caesarea. That Classis and Caesarea were other towns apart from Ravenna is clear from what has gone before, unless one wishes to say that Jordanes means by Classis the New Harbour, and by Caesarea the Road of Caesarius. Others name different founders: some say Tubal, son of Lamech; some, including James Voragine, say the sons of the tyrant Nimrod; Carinus says it was founded by the Trojan Pentapolis, and that the name Pentapolis came from him, and that, so that his name would not seem to have been given in vain, five neighbouring cities were placed under his rule. Quadratus in Marcus and Olympiodorus record that it was founded by the Rhine, whose opinion Zosimus rejects in book V. Strabo in book V says it was begun by Thessalians, but afterwards held under the rule of the Sabines and Umbrians, whom the first colonists of the city joined to themselves, since they could not match the constant incursions of the Tuscans. For this reason Pliny calls it a colony of the Sabines. Whatever the case, all writers attest that it is an ancient city, and Zosimus, whom I mentioned, does so in plain words. So Claudian: "He spoke, and out of ancient Ravenna's walls he went."
