units.la: Veterem etiam Civitatem appellat Sidonius Apollinaris lib. I. epist. V. Immunitam, vel suis munimentis senio terræve motu, vel aquis imminutam Portis Murisque novis munitæ Claudium Imperatorem, testatur Titulus Portæ Marmoreæ, quam Speciosam, vel Aueam vulgus ob architecturæ vel artificii pulchritudinem appellat, quondam inculptus: TI. CLAVDIVS. DRVSI. FIL. CAESAR. AVGVSTVS. GERMANICVS PONT. MAX. TRIB. POT. II. COS. II. DESIG. III. IMP. III. P. P. DEDIT
units.tr: Sidonius Apollinaris, in book I, letter V, also calls it the old city. An inscription that was once carved on the Marble Gate, which the common people call the Speciosa or Aurea because of the beauty of its architecture and workmanship, attests that it was unwalled, either by age or earthquake, or diminished by the waters, and that it was fortified with new gates and walls by the Emperor Claudius: TI. CLAUDIUS DRUSI FILIUS CAESAR AUGUSTUS GERMANICUS PONTIFEX MAXIMUS, TRIBUNICIA POTESTATE II, CONSUL II, DESIGNATUS III, IMPERATOR III, PATER PATRIAE, DEDIT.

units.la: Ab Galla Placidia, Theodosij Magni Cæsaris Filia, amplificatam: item ab Valentiniano II, ac Tiberio, Gallæ Placidiæ Filio, plurimum auctam, Murisque passim refectis, aliisque præclaris Monimentis relictis, quin & XII ipsi Civitatibus subjectis memoriæ prodit Blondus libro III. Historiar. Ostrogotthorum etiam Reges, cum primis Alaricus & Theodericus supra modum eam exornarunt Regijs, Templisque tumultosissimis passim exstructis. De Odoacro etiam vide Paullum Diaconum, Iornandem cap. XVII, Ennodium in Panegyrico. De Situ multa Strabo libro V; Littoribus adiacere maris Hadriatici, palustri in loco, Aquis ubique subtus intercurrentibus, ideoque Pontibus ac Lembis peragrari solere: Paludes tamen Aerem nihil inficere, propterea quod crebris cum Fluviorum, tum Maris inundationibus sordes abluantur:
units.tr: It was enlarged by Galla Placidia, daughter of Theodosius the Great, and greatly increased by Valentinian II and by Tiberius, son of Galla Placidia, who also repaired the walls in many places and left other notable monuments. Blondus, in book III of his Histories, records that twelve cities were also subject to it. The kings of the Ostrogoths, especially Alaric and Theodoric, adorned it beyond measure with royal buildings and with many splendid temples built in various places. On Odoacer see Paulus Diaconus, Jordanes chapter XVII, and Ennodius in his Panegyric. Strabo in book V says much about its situation: it lies on the shore of the Adriatic Sea, in a marshy place, with waters flowing everywhere beneath, and therefore people usually travel about it by bridges and boats. Yet the marshes do not taint the air, because the filth is washed away by the frequent floods of both the rivers and the sea.

units.la: Ampliatio ... Situs. luantur: eamque ob caussam, teste eodem Strabone, Gladiatoribus educandis exercendisque locum hunc Romanos Principes praecipue diligere solitos. Paludosam appellat Silius libro VIII: Quique gravi remo limosis segniter undis Lenta paludosae proscindunt flagna Ravennae.
units.tr: Enlargement ... Situation. are washed clean, and for this reason, according to the same Strabo, the Roman emperors especially liked this place for raising and training gladiators. Silius, in book VIII, calls it marshy: "Those who with heavy oar slowly cut through the muddy waves, the sluggish pools of marshy Ravenna."

units.la: Paludicolam etiam vocat Sidonius lib. VII, Epist. XVII. Hodie Paludes adeo exsiccatae, ut nunc undique patentes & fructiferi Campi appareant, frumenti mira ubertate foecundi. De situ item Sidonius lib. I. Epist. V: Oppidum duplex, pars interiusi Padi, cetera pars alluit. Qui ab alveo principali molium publicarum disiectus objectu, & per eosdem derivatis tramitibus exhaustus sic dividua fluenta pariuntur, ut praebeant maenibus circumfusa praesidium, adfusa commercium. De Pado quod dicit: Ravennam is per Paduam trahitur: urbem alioquin Amnes duo cingunt: unus dextrum latus Besedus, alter laevum tenet Montonus. Dixi cap. XI. Piceni caput aliquando fuisse, testatur vetus Inscriptio, quae Romae in domo quondam Augustini Mafei: CRONIO. EUSEBIUS, V. C. CONSULARIS, AMILIA. ADDITA. PRAEDICTAE. PROVINCIAE CONSULARI. VIGILANTIA. LT. IUSTITIA EIUS. ETIAM. RAVENNATIVM. CIVITATE. QUAE ANTEA. PICENI. CAPUT. PROVINCIAE. VIDEBATUR VICARIO. ITALIAE. QUAE. POSTEA. SUPRADICTO VIRO. OB.TESTIMONIUM. ANTEACTI. HONORIS EST. ATTRIBUTA. PETITIONE. SENATUS. CONTEMPLATIONE. VITAE. ADQUELOQUENTIAE EIUS. AB. IN VICTISSIMIS. PRINCIPIBUS EST. DELATA
units.tr: Sidonius also calls it marsh-dwelling, in book VII, letter XVII. Today the marshes are so drained that fertile fields appear spread out on every side, rich with wonderful abundance of grain. On its situation, Sidonius again, in book I, letter V: "The town is double: one part lies within the Po, and the other part is washed by it. The river, separated from its main channel by the public dykes and drained by channels diverted through them, splits into separate streams, so that they give protection to the walls around them and trade to the waters that flow to them." As for what he says about the Po, that it is drawn through the Padus to Ravenna: otherwise two rivers surround the city, one, the Bedesis, holding its right side, and the other, the Montone, its left. I spoke of these in chapter XI. An ancient inscription, once in the house of Augustino Mafei in Rome, attests that Ravenna was once the capital of Picenum: "Cronio Eusebius, a man of most distinguished rank, consular: by his vigilance and justice, Aemilia was added to the aforesaid consular province, and the city of the Ravennates, which formerly seemed to be the capital of Picenum, was assigned to the aforesaid man, as a testimony of his earlier honour, to the Vicar of Italy, which afterwards was given by request of the Senate, in view of his life and eloquence, by the most invincible emperors."

units.la: Templa hæc urbs habet nobilissima, imprimis Archiepiscopale vel Cathedrale S. Anastasii, opus rarum, splendidum, immensi pretii. Succedit illi, quod D. Vitali sacratum, forma rotunda constructum. Ibi inter alias columnas est tantæ raritatis, ut propemodum omnia pretiosorum lapidum genera, veluti porphyritidis, ophitis, granati, iaspidis rubentis viridisque, ac citrini, aliorumque colorum, item achatæ rubini, chalcedonij, reliquorumque id genus in se continet: cui vix alia similis invenitur. Iuxta Templum hoc non procul Theatrum vetustum est C. Cæsaris, & Æd es Divis Gervasio Protasioque ab Galla Placidia constituta. Inter varia ibi Sepulcra, ipsius etiam Gallae, Filiorumque duorum visuntur, pretiosissimi Marmoris, artifique singularis. Circa Forum D. Mariæ in Portu peramplum visitur Cænobium, & Dantis Aldigerij, Etrusci Poetæ nobilis, sepulcrum marmoreum, à Bernardo Bembo Veneto, Ravennatum quondam Prætore excitatum. Alia cum Templa, tum eximia Antiquitatis Monimenta, ut Sepulcra, Tymbos, Inscriptiones, magno numero praetereo. Adeundus, qui pleraque descripsit, Desiderius Spretus libro III. Spectatur ibi inter alia in Cratere Fontis, Herculis Horarii vel Astrologi Statua; qui, posita clava, velut Atlas innixus genu sinistro, e terra semet erigens, ambobus lacertis atque cervice gestat Horologium solare, semirotundum & convexum: in cujus concavitate per gnomonis seu umbulici solis umbram horae diurnae lineis distinctis demonstrabantur. Additus est Inscriptio: HIERONYMUS DONATUS PRAEFECTUS HERCULIS HORARII RELIQUIAS IX HERCULANAE REGIONIS ANGIPORTU IN FORUM TRANSTULIT, ET RAVENNATIVM ANTIQUITATI D. D.
units.tr: This city has very noble temples, above all the archiepiscopal or cathedral church of St. Anastasius, a rare and splendid work of immense value. Next to it is the church dedicated to St. Vitalis, built in a round shape. There, among other columns, is one of such rarity that it contains nearly all kinds of precious stones, such as porphyry, ophite, garnet, red and green jasper, citrine, and other colours, likewise agate, ruby, chalcedony and the like; hardly any other like it is found. Near this church, not far off, is the old Theatre of Gaius Caesar, and the church built by Galla Placidia for Gervasius and Protasius. Among the various tombs there, those of Galla Placidia herself and of her two sons may be seen, made of most precious marble and of singular workmanship. Around the Forum of St. Mary in Porto there is a very large monastery, and the marble tomb of the noble Tuscan poet Dante Alighieri, erected by Bernardo Bembo of Venice, once governor of the Ravennates. I pass over many other churches and remarkable monuments of antiquity, such as tombs, tympana and inscriptions. Whoever wishes to know most of them should consult Desiderius Spretus, book III. Among other things there is seen, in the basin of a fountain, a statue of Hercules Horarius or Astrologer. He, having set down his club, leaning on his left knee like Atlas, raising himself from the ground, carries on both arms and neck a sundial, half-round and convex, on whose hollow surface the hours of the day were shown by distinct lines through the shadow of the gnomon or navel of the sun. An inscription was added: "Hieronymus Donatus, prefect of Hercules Horarius, moved the remains of the Hercules of the Herculean region from the alley into the Forum, and dedicated them to the antiquity of Ravenna."

units.la: Arx ibi munita, Turribus aliquot per tormenta bellica dejectis, bello cum Gallis gesto. Portum habuit non incelebrem; qui Novus appellatus ad differentiam veteris illius capacissimi, de quo, quum de Classe agerem, verba feci. De eo sic scribit bit Sidonius lib. 1. epistola sæpe laudata: Ravennam paullo post cursu dextrorsum subeuntes: quo loci veterem Civitatem Nozumque Portum media via Cæsaris amnis, utrum connectebat an sejungeret. Vbi Via Cæsaris, quæ ab Cæsarea Opido, de quo ante, huc ducebat, Ravennamque Vrbem vel ab Novo Portu separabat, vel potius connectebat. Et hinc nonnulla interpretatione juvandus Iornandes, cujus verba ante posui: ut Trinominem faciens Vrbem, Ravennam, Classem, Cæsaream: Classis ipsi sit Novus Portus, vetus scilicet nomen retinenti; Cæsarea autem Cæsaris Via, quæ inter Novum Portum & Ravennam veterem. Novus hic Portus Portellus nunc vulgo dicitur; Caesarea, quod priore illo multo minor. Aquaeductum Theodorici Regis opus Ravennae fuisse scribit Cassiodorus in Chronico: Arcadio Iunio & Probo Coss. D. N. Rex Theodoricus Aquam Ravennam perduxit, cuius formam sumto proprio instauravit, quae longo ante fuerat ad solum redacta temporibus. Sic vetus Chronog. Anno Anastasii Aug. xii 1. Theodoricus Aquam Ravennam perduxit. Meminit & Sidonius Epistola sæpe indicata. Vrbs est Archiepiscopalis. Archiepiscopi, Canonici, Monachique sunt diutissimi, totamque ferme ditionem sibi vindicarunt. Inlustrarunt ortu suo Ravennam multi cum eruditione, tum aliis virtutibus præstantes viri: quorum non pauci Antistites ibi fuerunt, etiam in Divorum numerum relati. Enumerat eos Leander Albertus. Ravennates item fuerunt: Ioannes xvii P. M. Cassiodorus Senator; Faustinus, Martiali notus: Aspasius, temporibus Alexandri Imperatoris Sophista, Pantomimae ac Hippodromi discipulus, quem Suidas, adversus Aristonem & alios aemulos Orationes multas scripsisse perhibet: Petrus Damianus, Cardinalis Episcopus Ostiensis; Gulielmus, excellens Medicus, scriptis Pauli Vergerii laudatus; Ioannes Grammaticus, insignis Orator: Desiderius Spretus, qui de amplitudine, vastatione & instauratione Vrbis non indocte scripsit: Ioannes Petrus Ferrettus, Milensis Antistes, qui multa elucubravit, de Institutis Ecclesiasticis nominatim, & de eorum honesta disciplina; Breviarium insuper ab Vrbe condita ad sua usque tempora, tresque Decades Historiarum Ravennatum. Ravennatium frequens in lapidibus mentio. Habuerunt Ravennam initio Thessali, & evocati ab ijs Umbri Sabinique. Hos ejecerunt post ea Galli Boji: Boios Romani, quibus, imperio stante, constanter adhæsit. Colonia adscensus Strabo libro v. Duxit eam Octavianus Augustus, quum Classem eo loci tuendo Mari Supero collocaret. Occidentis imperio Sedem, relicta urbe Roma, constituit eam Honorius: quod institutum Successores quoque illius custodierunt tam Imperatores Romani, quam Reges Gothorum. Gothis Italia ejectis, hic ab Narsete Exarchorum Afacifrarum est constitutus, Duce Fl. Longino Patricio, quem Iustinus Imperator Narsetis loco Italiae praeesse voluit, anno ab Christo nato 1 o 1 i x. Duravit Exarchatus in Italia annos CLXXV, usque ad Leonem III, sub quo Ravennam Astulphus Langobardorum Rex cepit: qui à Pipino Francorum Rege bello victus urbem Romano Pontifici dedit, una cum Exarchatu toto, qui haec Opida Locaque continebat, Cæsaream, Arminum, Cesenam Forum Livii, Forum Pompili, Faventiam, Forum Cornelii, Bononiam, Agrum Mutinensem, cuius opidum semirutum jacebat, Regium Lepidi, Parmam, Placentiam, aliaque. Exarchatu rursus ab Langobardis occupato, postquam Desiderium ipsorum Regem superasset Karolus Magnus, sub populari aliquamdiu fuit Imperio, quod non ita multo post Bononiensibus cessit; inde Venetis, quibus ad Ripaltam cæsis, tandem Pontifici Romano cum Cervia reddita est Ravenna: cujus adhuc, frustra ab Venetis recepta, ditioni est subjecta. Legendi Procopius, Agathias, Blondus, Sabellicus, Platina. Pugna ad Ravennam commissa, qua Iulius II. P. M. commissus cum Ludovico XII Galliarum Rege ad sedecim millia suorum militum amisit, incidit in ipsum Paschatis diem anni c 1 o 1 3 x 1 i. Describunt multi. Rasponorum & Lunardorum Factiones Ravennam ingenti calamitate adflixerunt, quae temporibus Leonis x P. M. enatae caedibus ac flammis, urbem non semel funestarunt. Pascua ad urbem optima: ex quibus magna Lactis, Butyri, Casei copia. Miram esse Ravennatis Vitis naturam scribit Strabo a Palude celeriter producti, multumque fructus ferre, sed intra quadriennium aut ad summum quinquennium, perire. Vinum Ravennate vituperat Martialis lib. III.
units.tr: There was a fortress there, after some towers had been brought down by siege engines in the war waged against the Gauls. It had a harbour of no small repute, called the New Port, to distinguish it from that old and very capacious one of which I spoke when I was discussing the Fleet. Sidonius writes of it thus in book 1, in the letter often cited: "Shortly afterwards, running to the right, we came to Ravenna. There, in the middle of the road, the Caesar's river either joined or separated the old city and Nozum Port." Here the Via Caesaris, which led from the town of Caesarea mentioned earlier, either separated the city of Ravenna from the New Port or rather joined them. Jordanes, whose words I quoted before, needs some interpretation here too. Making the city three-named, Ravenna, Classis and Caesarea: Classis is the New Port itself, keeping its old name; Caesarea, however, is the Via Caesaris, which lies between the New Port and old Ravenna. This New Port is now commonly called Portellus; Caesarea is much smaller than that former port. Cassiodorus writes in his Chronicle that the aqueduct to Ravenna was the work of King Theodoric: "In the consulship of Arcadius Junius and Probus, our lord King Theodoric brought water to Ravenna, and restored it in its former form at his own expense, having been long before reduced to ruin by the passage of time." So the old Chronographer: "In the twelfth year of Anastasius Augustus, Theodoric brought water to Ravenna." Sidonius, in the letter often indicated, also mentions it. The city is an archiepiscopal see. The archbishops, canons and monks have been there for a very long time, and have claimed almost the whole of the surrounding territory for themselves. Many men, outstanding both for learning and for other virtues, have brought lustre to Ravenna by their birth. Not a few of its bishops were there, and some were even numbered among the saints; Leander Alberti lists them. The following were also Ravennates: John XVII, Supreme Pontiff; Cassiodorus the Senator; Faustinus, known to Martial; Aspasius, a sophist in the time of the Emperor Alexander, a pupil of pantomime and of the hippodrome, who, according to Suidas, wrote many orations against Aristo and other rivals; Peter Damian, Cardinal Bishop of Ostia; William, an excellent physician, praised in the writings of Paulus Vergerius; John the Grammarian, a distinguished orator; Desiderius Spretus, who wrote learnedly on the extent, devastation and restoration of the city; and John Peter Ferretti, bishop of Milan, who produced many works, in particular on the ecclesiastical institutions and their honourable discipline, as well as an abridged history from the founding of the city down to his own times, and three decades of the Histories of Ravenna. The Ravennates are frequently mentioned on inscriptions. At first Ravenna was held by the Thessalians, and by the Umbrians and Sabines whom they summoned. Afterwards these were driven out by the Gallic Boii; the Romans, whom the Boii constantly adhered to while the empire stood, followed them. Strabo, in book 5, calls it a colony. Octavian Augustus established it as a colony when he stationed the fleet there to guard the Upper Sea. When the empire of the West was established, Honorius made it his seat, leaving the city of Rome; his successors kept this arrangement, both the Roman emperors and the kings of the Goths. When the Goths were driven out of Italy, Narses established it as the seat of the Exarchs, with Flavius Longinus the patrician as commander, whom the Emperor Justinian wished to preside over Italy in place of Narses, in the year 569 after the birth of Christ. The exarchate lasted in Italy for 175 years, until Leo III, under whom Astulf, king of the Lombards, took Ravenna. He was defeated in war by Pepin, king of the Franks, and gave the city to the Roman Pontiff, together with the whole exarchate, which comprised these towns and places: Caesarea, Ariminum, Cesena, Forum Livii, Forum Popilii, Faenza, Forum Cornelii, Bologna, the territory of Modena, whose town lay half in ruins, Reggio of Lepidus, Parma, Piacenza, and others. The exarchate was again occupied by the Lombards, but after Charlemagne had defeated their king Desiderius, it was for some time under the popular rule of the empire, which not long afterwards yielded to the Bolognese; from them it passed to the Venetians, who were routed at Ripalta, and at last Ravenna was returned to the Roman Pontiff together with Cervia; even though the Venetians later recovered it for a time, it is still subject to his rule. One should read Procopius, Agathias, Blondus, Sabellicus and Platina. The battle fought at Ravenna, in which Julius II, Supreme Pontiff, lost some sixteen thousand of his soldiers in alliance with Louis XII, king of the French, fell on Easter Day in the year 1512. Many have written of it. The factions of the Rasponi and the Lunardi afflicted Ravenna with a great calamity: in the time of Leo X, Supreme Pontiff, they broke out in slaughter and fire, and more than once brought misery upon the city. The pastures around the city are excellent, and yield a great abundance of milk, butter and cheese. Strabo writes that the nature of the Ravenna vine is remarkable: it grows quickly from the marsh and bears fruit abundantly, but it perishes within four years, or at most five. Martial, in book 3, finds fault with the Ravenna wine.

units.la: Sit Cisterna mihi, quam Vinea, malo Ravennæ:Quum possim multo vendere pluris aquam.
units.tr: I would rather have a cistern at Ravenna than a vineyard, since I could sell water for much more.

units.la: Commendat contra idem Poëta Ravennates Asperagos: Mollis in aquorea quae crevit spina Ravenna, Non erit inculta gratior Asparagis.
units.tr: The same poet, on the other hand, praises the Ravenna asparagus: "Ravenna's soft thorn, which grows in watery ground, will be no less pleasing than uncultivated asparagus."

units.la: Eosdem quoque laudat Plinius. De Ranis Ravennatibus sic canit idem Martialis lib. iii. epig. 11: Quum comparata vilibus tuis ora Nilhacus habeat Crocodilus anguilla: Meliusque Ranae garriant Ravennates, Et Hadriaticus dulcius culex cantet.
units.tr: Pliny also praises the same asparagus. Martial, book iii, epigram 11, sings thus of the frogs of Ravenna: "Although the crocodile of Nile, with its eel-like jaws, is compared with your cheap fare, and the Ravenna frogs chatter more sweetly, and the Adriatic gnat sings more sweetly."

units.la: Municipales Ranas nominat Sidonius lib. 1. Epist. viii. ad Candidianum. Plinius lib. ix. Natural. histor. cap. liv. optimi saporis Rhombum haberi Ravennae captum tradit. Concludam meas de Ravenna notas cum fassis Sidonij de ea verbis, quae exstant indicata à me Epistola: Te Ravenna felicius exsultantem anribus Padano Culice (Nam Ravenna in Padi paludibus sub aere calido sita, culicibus infestatur) perfossis Municipalium Ranarum loquax turba circumsilit: in qua palude indesinenter rerum omnium lege perversa Muri cadunt, Aqua stant; Turres fluunt, Naves sedent; Aegri deambulant, Medici jacent; algent Balnea, Domicilia conflagrant; sitiunt Vivi, natant Sepulti; Vigilant Fures, dormiunt Poteitates; fenerantur Clerici, Syri psallunt; Negociatores militant, Milites negociantur; fludent pila Sensi, alea Iuvenes, armis Eunuchi, literis Foederati.
units.tr: Sidonius, in book 1, letter 8, to Candidianus, names the "municipal frogs". Pliny, in book 9 of the Natural History, chapter 54, reports that a turbot caught at Ravenna is considered of the finest flavour. I shall conclude my notes on Ravenna with the words of Sidonius about it, which are found in the letter I have indicated: "While you, rejoicing more happily at Ravenna, are pierced by the Po gnats (for Ravenna, set in the marshes of the Po under a hot sky, is infested by gnats), the chattering crowd of the municipal frogs swarms about you. In that marsh, by a perverse law governing all things, walls fall, water stands still; towers flow, ships sit still; the sick walk about, the physicians lie down; baths grow cold, homes burn down; the living thirst, the buried swim; thieves keep watch, magistrates sleep; clergy lend at interest, Syrians sing psalms; merchants serve as soldiers, soldiers trade; the pleasures of the senses flourish, young men gamble, eunuchs bear arms, and allies are learned."

units.la: Tu vide qualis sit Civitas, ubi tibi Lar familiaris incolitur: qua facilius Territorium potuit habere, quam Terram. Videre est extra urbem Ædem rotundam, D. Mariae Virginis, antiquissimam & pulcerrimam, forma rotundam.
units.tr: Look at what sort of city it is, where your household god dwells; it could more easily have a territory than a land. Outside the city one can see the round church of the Blessed Virgin Mary, very ancient and very beautiful, round in form.

units.la: Intus, haud procul tamen ab Mari, Opidum Umbrorum erat Butrium, Plinio notum, Butrium Straboni, Ptolemaeo, Stephano. Reliquiae eius in exiguo Castello, quod hodieque Butrio vernacule, prope Cotignolam & Lucum. Terminus hic erat Umbrorum, qui hinc ad Aesin usque amnem fines habuerunt, auctore Strabone libro v. Alibi plura.
units.tr: Inland, though not far from the sea, was the town of the Umbrians, Butrium, known to Pliny; Strabo, Ptolemy and Stephanus also mention Butrium. Its remains are in a small castle, which to this day is called Butrio in the vernacular, near Cotignola and Lugo. This was the boundary of the Umbrians, who, according to Strabo, book v, had their territory from here as far as the river Aesis. More elsewhere.

units.la: Introrsum in Aemilia Pontis ruinae visuntur, quo per Roncum fluvium Via illa solebat iungi. Prope est Aedes cum Fossa loco edito super Amnis ripam, ubi olim Roncum fuit Opidum, cujus memihit in Mediolanensi Historia Bernardinus Corius.
units.tr: Further inland in Emilia, the ruins of a bridge can be seen, where the road used to cross the river Ronco. Near it is a church with a moat, on a raised spot above the bank of the river, where Roncum once stood as a town; Bernardino Corio mentions it in his Milanese History.

units.la: Rursum ad collis radices in introitu faucium Meldola iacet opidum munitum & lautum, agrum habens copiosum. Diu in potestate fuit Malatestarum, Principum Ariminensium: à quibus in Venetorum, ab his in Pontificum venit cum Arimino potestatem. Concessit Alberto Pio Comiti Carpensi Leo x. Cladem accepit maximam ab Karolo Borbonio, Exercitus Karoli v Imperatoris Praefecto, quum Romam infestus tenderet, anno MDXXVII.
units.tr: Again, at the foot of the hill, at the entrance to the gorge, lies the fortified and elegant town of Meldola, with a rich territory. For a long time it was in the power of the Malatesta, princes of Rimini; from them it passed to the Venetians, and from these, together with Rimini, to the Pontiffs. Leo X granted it to Alberto Pio, Count of Carpi. It suffered a very great defeat from Charles of Bourbon, commander of the army of the Emperor Charles V, when he marched in hostility towards Rome, in the year 1527.

units.la: Ulterius inter montes exiguum occurrit Castellum Cuserculum, ubi Pons Amnem jungit.
units.tr: Further on, among the mountains, a small castle called Cusercolo appears, where a bridge spans the river.

units.la: Ad alteram ripam visitur Civitella: indeque secundo lapide Galeata. Hinc Salutus Galliani, Aquinates cognominati Plinio, in Octava Regione.
units.tr: On the other bank is Civitella; and from there, two miles off, Galeata. From here are the Saluti Galliani, called Aquinates by Pliny, in the Eighth Region.

units.la: Ad exitum Vallis arx munitissima colli insidet Planetum: juxtaque sub ea D. Mariae Planetinae Fanum: denique inter Montes altius Castellum D. Sophiae.
units.tr: At the exit of the valley, a very strongly fortified citadel sits on the hill, Planetum. Just beneath it is the shrine of St. Mary of Planetum, Mariae Planetinae Fanum. Higher up, among the mountains, is the castle of St. Sophia, Castellum D. Sophiae.

units.la: Rursum in Aemilia Via Montoni Amnis dextra Civitas est Forum-Livii. Sic Plinio, Antonino, Itinerariae Tabulae, aliisque dicitur, quod hodie Forli. Nominatur & in Latino Ptolemaeo: licet in Graeco non habeatur. Memorat primordia eiur ex antiquissimus Annalibus Leander; conditum esse ab L. Hermio, Veterano milite: eum Ducis sui, Livij Salinatoris cos. nomen dedisse. Servat in Urbis foro memoriam rei Statua, cum Elogio: Livius ecce fui Romanus conditor Urbis Huius, & hanc volui Terram colnisse Quirites Magnanimos, Populusque dedi cognomen & arma.
units.tr: Again, on the Aemilian Way, on the right bank of the Montone river, is the city of Forum-Livii. Pliny, Antoninus, the Itinerary Tables and others call it this, and today it is Forli. It is also named in the Latin Ptolemy, though it is not found in the Greek. Leander recounts its beginnings from very ancient annals: it was founded by L. Hermius, a veteran soldier, who gave it the name of his commander, the consul Livius Salinator. A statue with an inscription preserves the memory of the event in the city's forum: "Behold, I, Livius, a Roman, was the founder of this city, and I wished this land to be inhabited by you, Quirites, great of soul; and the people gave me a name and arms."

units.la: Urbs natura & situ, rerumque omnium ubertate praestans inter duos Amnes Ronocum ab ortu, & Montonum ab occasu sita: aere fruens optimo. Templum Cathedrale S. Crucis; item S. Domini, S. Francisci, S. Mariae Carmenta notissima sunt.
units.tr: The city, outstanding for its natural situation and its abundance of all things, lies between two rivers, the Ronco to the east and the Montone to the west. It enjoys a very good air. The cathedral church of the Holy Cross, and likewise the churches of St. Dominic, St. Francis and St. Mary of Carmel, are very well known.

units.la: Praetorium hic sumtuosissimum in Foro, ab Aegidio Cardinale aedificatum, & semirutum Catharinae Sforziae iussu in caedis mariti ultionem. In eo Pictura duorum manibus junctis vel fœdus incuntium, vel injurias remittentium cum Inscriptione non magni ævi: Sextus Tit. Livius Saltuator cos. S. R. jussu Claud. Neronis Collega recon-ciliatus jujurando pollicetur, se Reipubl. contra Annibalem ac Asdrubalem fratres egregie defensurum. Episcopatus gaudet titulo. Illustrarunt ortu suo Forum-Livii multi præstantes Viri D. Valerianus, Eques & Martyr: Stephanus Nardinus & Christophorus, Ecclesiæ Romanæ Cardinales: Ioannes Rufus Theodorus, Archiepiscopus Confentinus, Ecclesiæ Romanæ Thesaurarius, & Karoli v. Capellanus: Ludovicus, Thomas Aflius, Alexander Nugatius, ipsius urbis Episcopi; Nicolaus Afflus, Riccierii; Bartholemaus Morasinus, Fori Truentinorum; Antonius Arculanus, Cariatis; Antonius Nymphalus, Alternæ; Philippus Arculanus, Alatri; Hieronymus Theodulus, Calcis Hispaniæ Antistites. Edidit insuper Forum-Livii Cornelium Gallum, Poetam celeberrimum: Hieronymum, Prædicatorij Ordinis Theologum, & Historicum; Raimundum Arsinetum, Iurisconsultum maximum, Bartoli Saxoferratensis Præceptorem; Iurisperitos item, Franciscum Kultrum, Nerium Morandum, Ioannem Sellenum, & Guilelmum Lambertellum: Medicos Iacobum Turrium, Guidonem Pepum Stellam, Bartholomæum Lombardinum: Historicos, Flavium Blondum, multis scriptis celebrem & Paulum Quirinum, qui res Foro-Livienjium memorabiles collegit, scriptisque prodidit; Item Guidonem Bonatum Astrologum summum; Hieronymum Maffurium, Philologum excellentem: Iacobum Alegrettum, Poetam jucundum; Faustum Andrelinum, Poetam item suavissimum, ab Ludovico xii Francorum Rege Laurea coronatum: Vgolinum denique Orivetanum. Musicum, Scalæ Modulorum in manus articulis inventorem. Nihil hic dicam de celebribus in re militari Ducibus; quos Leander Albertus recenset. Servare fe aiunt Foro-Livienses ossa D. Mercurialis, Episcopi quondam Urbis & Patroni, item D. Sigismundus Regis, cuisque Coniugis & Filiorum duorum; D. Roffili, Foro-Pompilienfium Antistitis, D. Grati Diaconi, D. Marcelli Subdiaconi, & B. Iacobi Veneti, ex ordine Prædicatorum Monachi. In fide olim fuit Populus Romani: sui deinde juris & tutelæ facta sub imperio Exarchorum in tantum sensim crevit opibus & potentia, ut non solum cum Finitimis sæpe bella gereret, sed & in alias Civitates jus sibi usurparet: Cervia, Foro Truentinorum, Foroque Popilij subactis; conditus item cum aliis, tum Sadurano, Melidonio, Caminateque opidis. In potestatem deinde redacta est Bononiensium anno cioccxlviii; & aliquanto post cio cc xcvi ab Ordelaphis possessa, qui urbis primum Vicarij, deinde Principes à Populo sunt appellati. Tandem multis fracta calamitatibus imperio subjugata Pontificum Romanorum. Legendi Bernardinus Corius, Blondus in Historijs, Platina in Vita Innocentij vi. Factionibus aliquamdiu gravissime laboravit Numaliorum & Moratinorum perniciofissimus. Agrum habet, qui Frumenti, Vini, Olei feracissimis; Coriandrum etiam, Anisum, FœnumGræcum, Cuminum, Rubiam, Glastum, aliaque hujus generis gignens.
units.tr: Here in the forum is a very sumptuous town hall, built by Cardinal Egidio and half destroyed by order of Caterina Sforza in revenge for her husband's murder. In it is a painting of two men joining hands, either making a covenant or remitting injuries, with an inscription not of great age: "Sextus Titus Livius Salinator, consul, reconciled at the order of the Senate and Roman people, with his colleague Claudius Nero, pledges on oath that he will defend the Republic nobly against the brothers Hannibal and Hasdrubal." The bishopric enjoys the title of a see. Many outstanding men have adorned Forum-Livii by their birth: St. Valerian, knight and martyr; Stefano Nardini and Cristoforo, cardinals of the Roman Church; Giovanni Rufo Teodoro, archbishop of Cosenza, treasurer of the Roman Church and chaplain of Charles V; Ludovico, Tommaso Aflio, and Alessandro Nugazio, bishops of the city itself; Niccolò Aflio, of Ricci; Bartolomeo Morasino, of Fermo of the Truentines; Antonio Arculano, of Cariati; Antonio Ninfalo, of Alterna; Filippo Arculano, of Alatri; Girolamo Teodulo, of Calahorra in Spain, prelates. Forum-Livii has also produced Cornelius Gallus, a most celebrated poet; Girolamo, a theologian and historian of the Dominican order; Raimondo Arsineto, a very great jurist, teacher of Bartolo of Sassoferrato; likewise the jurists Francesco Cultro, Nerio Morando, Giovanni Sellen and Guglielmo Lambertello; the physicians Giacomo Turri, Guido Pepo Stella and Bartolomeo Lombardino; the historians Flavio Biondo, famous for many writings, and Paolo Quirino, who gathered the memorable events of Forum-Livii and handed them down in writing; also Guido Bonatto, a leading astrologer; Girolamo Maffurio, an excellent philologist; Giacomo Alegretto, a pleasant poet; Fausto Andrelino, likewise a most sweet poet, crowned with the laurel by Louis XII, king of the French; and finally Ugolino of Orvieto, a musician, inventor of the scale of notes on the joints of the hand. I will say nothing here of the famous commanders in war, whom Leander Alberti lists. The people of Forum-Livii say they keep the bones of St. Mercurialis, once bishop and patron of the city; also those of St. Sigismund, king, of his wife and two sons; of St. Roffillus, bishop of Forum-Popilii; of St. Gratus, deacon; of St. Marcellus, subdeacon; and of Blessed Giacomo Veneto, a monk of the Dominican order. In olden times the people were under the faith of the Roman people; afterwards, placed under the authority and protection of the Exarchs, they gradually grew so strong in resources and power that they not only often waged wars with their neighbours but also usurped rights over other cities: after Cervia, Forum Truentinorum and Forum Popilii were subjected, and they founded, along with others, the towns of Sadurano, Meldonio and Camino. Then it was brought under the power of the Bolognese in the year 1248; and a little later, in 1296, it was held by the Ordelaffi, who were first called vicars of the city and then princes by the people. At last, broken by many calamities, it was subjected to the rule of the Roman Pontiffs. Read Bernardino Corio, Biondo in his Histories, and Platina in the Life of Innocent VI. For some time it suffered very grievously from the factions, the most destructive being those of the Numali and the Moratini. It has land very fertile in grain, wine and oil, and it produces also coriander, anise, fenugreek, cumin, madder, woad, and other things of this kind.

units.la: Ad Æmilia dextram in Apennini latere, quod Septemtrionem ipsetat, Castrocarum est; Veteribus, uti volunt Blondus, Raffanus, Leander, Salsubium, quod ibi Aquæ salsæ Fons exiliar. Olim sub Foro Livienjium fuit; post sub Florentinis esse cœpit.
units.tr: On the Aemilian Way, on the right, on the side of the Apennines that faces north, is Castrocaro. In ancient times, as Biondo, Raffanus and Leander wish, it was called Salsubium, because a fountain of salt water springs there. Formerly it was under Forum-Livii; afterwards it began to be under the Florentines.

units.la: Sequitur inde Dudola, honestum Opidum; tum altius inter montes D. Caffiani Fanum; & inter asperrima luga Portieu, ab Ambrosio Monacho Scriptis celebri inlustratum.
units.tr: Next comes Dudola, an honourable town; then higher up among the mountains the shrine of St. Caffianus; and among the very rugged hills Portico, made famous by the writings of the monk Ambrose.

units.la: Ad Flavij, qui vulgo Lamonis, quemque Plinius & Antoninus Anemonem vocant, dextram, Vicus est Traversaria, Ravennatus agri; a præclara Traversariorum gente factus, nisi hinc ipsa traxerit nomen.
units.tr: On the right of the Flavio, which is commonly called the Lamone, and which Pliny and Antoninus call the Anemo, is the village of Traversara, in the territory of Ravenna. It was named after the illustrious family of the Traversari, unless it rather drew its name from that place.

units.la: Non procul deinde, ad alteram Amnis ripam Raniacavallum est, antea Tiberiacum & ad Caballos dictum, ut memoriæ produnt Blondus, Sabellicus, Niger, Rubeus, Leander, qui & Gabrum olim appellatum tradit ex Tabulis Ecclesiæ Ravennatis, judicioque Ioannis Petri Ferretti Milensis Episcopi. Opidum est pereleegans, lautum & opulentum, ditioni subjectum Ferrariensis Principis.
units.tr: Not far from there, on the other bank of the river, is Ragnacavallo, formerly called Tiberiacum and Ad Caballos, as Biondo, Sabellico, Nigro, Rubeo and Leander record, the last of whom also reports that it was once called Gabrum, on the authority of the registers of the Church of Ravenna and the judgment of Giovanni Pietro Ferretti, bishop of Mileto. It is a very elegant, handsome and wealthy town, subject to the rule of the Prince of Ferrara.

units.la: Succedit in Æmilia Via Civitas Faventia. Sic Livio lib. lxxxviii, Silio libro viii, Spartiano in Hadriani Vita, Capitolino in Ælij Veri, Antonino, Tabulæque Itinerariæ dicitur; Φαυτία Strabonì libro v, Appiano lib. i bel. Civil. Ptolemæo, qui in Gallia Togata ponit, Agathiæ libro i. de bell. Gothico; Φαβιΐα Stephano; Faventina Civitas Cassiodoro in Variis: quæ hodie Faenza. Faventinos habet in Octava Italiae Regione Plinius. Honesta est & frequens: Salinis Saxonicis non male comparari solita. Secat eam Amnis Anemo. Inter opera publica Templum habet magnificum, Cathedrale & Episcopatus titulo celebre: Arcem ab Friderico II Imperatore conditam, Pandulpho Collenutio teste libro IIII Histor. Reg. Pontem lapideum, sane pulcrum, duabusque Turribus munitum; quo & Vrbs Suburbijs cohaeret, & Aemilia Via continuatur. Altor Manfredus Vrbem ab Friderico II nudatam auctioribus firmavit moenibus, altaque & lata cinxit fossa, idemque Praetorium in Foro splendidum construxit. Figulinis celebrata est passim Faventia praestantissimis, quae etiam Aretinis praeferuntur. Vber inde Incolis quaestus.
units.tr: On the Aemilian Way follows the city of Faenza. It is so called by Livy in book 88, by Silius in book 8, by Spartian in the Life of Hadrian, by Capitolinus in the Life of Aelius Verus, by Antoninus, and in the Itinerary Tables; Strabo in book 5 calls it Phautia [Φαυτία], Appian in book 1 of the Civil Wars, likewise; Ptolemy, who places it in Cisalpine Gaul, and Agathias in book 1 of the Gothic War; Stephanus calls it Phabia [Φαβιΐα]; Cassiodorus in the Variae calls it the city of Faventia. Today it is Faenza. Pliny places the people of Faventia in the Eighth Region of Italy. It is an honourable and populous town, which is customarily compared not badly with the Saxon salt-works. The river Anemo cuts through it. Among its public buildings it has a magnificent cathedral church, famous for its episcopal see; a citadel founded by the Emperor Frederick II, as Pandolfo Collenuccio testifies in book 4 of his Histories of the Kingdom. It has a stone bridge, indeed a fine one, fortified with two towers, by which the city is joined to its suburbs and the Aemilian Way is continued. The lord Manfred, having restored the city, which had been stripped by Frederick II, strengthened it with larger walls and surrounded it with a deep and wide ditch; he also built a splendid town hall in the forum. Faventia is famed everywhere for its most excellent pottery, which is even preferred to that of Arezzo. From this the inhabitants have a rich income.

units.la: 10 Populus studiosus admodum reipublicae, animis omnium ad pacem & quietem spectantibus, factionesque detestantibus. Ex Faventia originem maternam suisse Aelio Vero, Imperatori, scribunt Spartianus & Capitolinus. Ingenia tulit multa. Fuit inter alios Mengus, summus Philosophus & Medicus, qui in Logica Paulli Veneti Commentaria scripsit. Primis temporibus in fide semper fuit Imperij Romani; post Bononiensibus aliquamdiu paruit: hinc Factionibus Lambertatiorum & Gremetorum apud eos exortis, in libertatem se urbs recepit: post anno cIↄ cc lxxxvi in Manfredorum venit potestatem; inque ea mansit usque ad Caesarem Borgiam; qui, Manfredis eiectis trucidatisque, ope Alexandri VI P. M. Patris, Urbis dominatum occupavit; a quo tamen, mortuo Pontifice, rursum ea defecit, Manfredo adhuc uno
units.tr: 10 A people very devoted to the commonwealth, with every mind set on peace and quiet, and detesting factions. Spartianus and Capitolinus write that Faventia was the maternal origin of the emperor Aelio Vero, Aelius Verus. It produced many men of talent. Among others there was Mengus, a most eminent philosopher and physician, who wrote commentaries on the Logic of Paulus Venetus. In early times it always remained loyal to the Imperij Romani, the Roman Empire. Afterwards it obeyed the Bononiensibus, the Bolognese, for some time. Then, when the factions of the Lambertatiorum & Gremetorum, the Lambertazzi and Geremei, arose there, the city recovered its liberty. In the year 1286 it came under the power of the Manfredorum, the Manfredi, and remained under them until Caesarem Borgiam, Cesare Borgia, who, with the Manfredi expelled and slain, seized rule of the city with the help of Pope Alexander VI, his father. Yet after the Pope's death it revolted from him again, and with only one of the family, Manfredo, Manfredo, still surviving, he was brought back into the city and greeted as prince. He afterwards handed the rule of the city over to the Venetos, the Venetians. But when these were defeated by Louis XII, King of the French, it returned to the authority of the Popes.

units.la: 20 superstite in urbem reducto, Principeque salutato, qui postea in Venetos Urbis imperium transtulit: his autem ab Ludovico XII Gallorum Rege caesis, in Pontificum ditionem est reversa. Magnis calamitatibus adfecta legitur ab Gothis, a Brittonibus, ab Friderico II, Imperatore, qui anno cIↄ ccxl post longam arctamque obsidionem, Muros solo aequavit: Arce, de qua dixi, in ea, praesidij causa, aedificata. Consulendi Blondus & Sabellicus. Ager illi opimus, frumenti vinique fertilis; maxime vero Lini candidissimi, a Plinio etiam celebrati.
units.tr: 20 It is recorded to have suffered great calamities: from the Gothis, the Goths; from the Brittonibus, the Britons; and from Frederick II, the Emperor, who in 1240, after a long and close siege, levelled its walls with the ground. The citadel of which I spoke was built in the city for its defence. For further reading consult Blondus and Sabellicus. Its land is rich, fertile in grain and wine, and especially in very white flax, which Pliny also celebrates.

units.la: Supra Faventiam, quarto lapide, fructiferis adsitum collibus visitur Oriolum.
units.tr: Above Faventia, four miles away, on fruitful hills, lies Oriolum, Oriolo.

units.la: Infra Oriolum, vetus opidum, quod Marzanus torrens adluit, Modiana spectatur: Mutilum Livio libro xxxi & xxxiii: Mutila Obsequenti de Prodigijs. Iuris est hodie Florentinorum, olim Comitum Guidonum.
units.tr: Below Oriolum lies the old town of Modiana, which the Marzanus stream washes. It is called Mutilum by Livy in books 31 and 33, and Mutila by Obsequens in his book on prodigies. Today it belongs to the Florentines; formerly it belonged to the Counts Guidi.

units.la: Inde supra Faventiam prope flumen Anemonem Vallis se offert Lamonis, sic hodie ab Fluvio, quem dixi, corruptius nominata pro Anemonis, quidquid hic de Lamonibus ex suo suppositio Sempronio adferat audax Viterbiensis. Amoena est, colonis referta, opidis plena castellisque: in iis Brefegella, ortu clara insignium Ducum; inter quos principis loci cum Dionysius Naldus, primum Alfonso, Ferrandinoque Neapolitanis Regibus, post autem Venetis militia sua fidus; tum Vincentius Naldus, item Carlinus Galasius & Ioannes Raboni. Horrendam accepit calamitatem hoc Castellum anno cIↄ Iↄ ix ab Francisco Alidosio, Copiarum Iulij II P. M. ductore, spoliatis vinctisque contra fidem publicam Civibus.
units.tr: Beyond it, above Faenza, near the river Anemo, there opens the valley of the Lamones. It is called by that name today, more corruptly, after the river I mentioned, instead of Anemonis. Whatever the bold Viterbian has to say about the Lamones from his own conjecture about Sempronius, it is not to be trusted. The valley is pleasant, full of farms, towns and castles. Among them is Brisighella, famous for its noble lords. The foremost of these was Dionysius Naldus, who served faithfully in arms first for Alfonso and Ferrante, the Neapolitan kings, and afterwards for the Venetians. Then there was Vincentius Naldus, and likewise Carlinus Galasius and Ioannes Raboni. This castle suffered a dreadful disaster in the year 1509, when Francesco Alidosi, commander of the forces of Julius II, the Supreme Pontiff, plundered and bound its citizens, in breach of their public pledge.

units.la: 40 Opida sunt ibidem alia Rontana, Castellio, Grataria; item Vici Marate, Bifurcatum, & alij.
units.tr: 40 In the same district are other towns, Rontana, Castellio and Grataria, and also the villages Marate and Bifurcatum, and others.

units.la: Sub Apennino inde Crispinum, ubi Abbatia magnis decorata praerogativis.
units.tr: Below the Apennine, beyond that, is Crespino, where there is an abbey adorned with great privileges.

units.la: Infra Viam Aemiliam sub Faventia non ignobile opidum est Solariolum, Sigismundo Gonzagae Cardinali ab Leone X P. M. donatum.
units.tr: Below the Via Aemilia, near Faenza, is the not unknown town of Solarolo, given by Pope Leo X to Cardinal Sigismondo Gonzaga.

units.la: Ad dextram Senij Amnis parvum quidem, sed nobile opidum est Cotignola, alta septum fossa, murisque firmissimis anno cIↄ cccc lxxi ab Ioanne Aucutho Praefecto, cui cum Baniolo ab Gregorio XI donatum teste in Mediolanensi historia Corio. Originem hinc traxit incluta Sforziarum gens, uti docet Petrus Cotignolanus, Ioannes Simoneta, Bernardus Cornus, Franciscus Philelphus, Sabellicus, Platina, & alij, qui multos alios referunt hinc oriundos. Principatum opidi diu habuerunt Mediolani Duces; inde in Pontificum Maximorum fuit ditione; hodie in Ferrariensium Ducum, si bene meminí, est potestate.
units.tr: On the right of the river Senio, a small but noble town, Cotignola, lies, enclosed by a deep ditch and very strong walls. In the year 1471 it was given by Pope Gregory XI to Giovanni Acuto, its prefect, together with Bagnacavallo, as Corio testifies in the Milanese history. The famous Sforza family drew its origin from here, as Pietro Cotignola, Giovanni Simonetta, Bernardo Cornazzano, Francesco Filelfo, Sabellico, Platina and others teach, and they name many other men who came from here. For a long time the Dukes of Milan held the lordship of the town; afterwards it was under the rule of the Supreme Pontiffs; today, if I remember rightly, it is under the power of the Dukes of Ferrara.

units.la: 50 Secundo hinc lapide Lucus opidum, cum Civibus, tum rebus tuendae vitae necessariis abundans; inceptum tamen. Territorium cui inaedificatum, stagnare solitum fertur ab Aquis, ex Apennino defluentibus: quod argumentum, novum esse, fabulamque censendam, Lucum hic olim fuisse Dianae. Principes eius olim Bononienses, inde Pontifices Maximi, mox Ferraria Reguli. Ortu superbit Vincentij Archerij, ex Prædicatorum familia Monachi, Scriptis clari, qui ibidem obijt anno cIↄ ƖↄXI. Ager illi magna frumenti, tuliæ, vinique copia uber.
units.tr: 50 Two miles from here is the town of Lugo, rich both in citizens and in the things necessary for sustaining life, yet unfortified. The land on which it was built is said to have been flooded by waters flowing down from the Apennine, which is proof that the claim that Lugo was once a sacred grove of Diana is a new idea and should be counted a fable. Its lords were formerly the Bolognese, then the Supreme Pontiffs, and soon the Ferrarese princes. It takes pride in its birth of Vincenzo Archeri, a monk of the Dominican order, famous for his writings, who died there in the year 1511. The countryside around it is rich in grain, flax and wine.

units.la: Haud procul Lucô Ægnaria vilitur, Florentini exercitus clade nobilis; scribentibus Blondo libro xxii Historiar. Sabellico libro 1 Ennead. cap. x & Platina in Vita Martini v. P. M.
units.tr: Not far from Lugo lies Ghiaiolo, famous for the defeat of the Florentine army, as Biondo writes in book 22 of his Histories, Sabellico in book 1 of his Enneads, chapter 10, and Platina in the Life of Martin V, Supreme Pontiff.

units.la: Duobus inde P. M. in Senij ripa locus monstratur, ubi olim Castellum fuit Cumiam, rebus ab Alberico Cumae magno duce contra Britones, qui in Italiam irruperant, gestis nobile. Eversum legitur a Bononiensibus, qui illud potuebant anno cIↄ ccxxvii, militantatum inde Alberici Comitis tempore, post denuo excisum, planeque delerum, mentibus vix memoriam loci Fotia, qua cingebatur, Templo, paucaque tecta, quae tamen recenter excitata.
units.tr: Two miles from there, on the bank of the Senio, is a place where once there was a castle called Cumiae, noted for the deeds of Alberic, the great leader of Cumae, against the Britons who had invaded Italy. It is recorded that it was overthrown by the Bolognese, who were able to capture it in the year 1227, and afterwards, in the time of Count Alberic, it was attacked again, and then completely destroyed and wiped out. Hardly any memory of the place survives in men's minds, except the moat by which it was surrounded, a temple, and a few houses, which have been built recently.

units.la: Prope vestigia videre est opidum Barbianum, quod Cumatum Comitum patrimonium, ab Ioanne xxiv P. M. anno cIↄ cccɔ exeunt.
units.tr: Near these remains one can see the town of Barbiano, which was the patrimony of the Counts of Cunio. Pope John XXIII gave it up in the year 1413.

units.la: Ad Viam Flaminiam recurrenti Fons D. Proculi. Senio in locatus, se offert; duplici Bononiensium itinerariis anno cIↄ ccc lxxv ab Faventinis, Lambertiatorum & Foro-Livienium auxiliis, inlata celebris.
units.tr: Turning back to the Via Flaminia, there is the Fountain of St Proculus, situated on the Senio. It is famous for the Bolognese expedition of the year 1375, which was brought against it by the men of Faenza, with the help of the Lamboni and the men of Forlimpopoli.

units.la: Pontem transgresso Castellum occurrit Bononiense, lautum & opulentum, à Bononiensibus anno cIↄ ccc lxxxvii conditum, testibus Hieronymo Albertutio in Chronicis, aliisque rerum Bononiensium Scriptoribus.
units.tr: Having crossed the bridge, one comes to the castle of Bagnara di Bologna, handsome and prosperous, founded by the Bolognese in the year 1387, as witnessed by Girolamo Albertucci in his Chronicles and other writers on the affairs of Bologna.

units.la: Surrium ad Apenninum Sufenanum vitatur, Magiunardi Patria, qui Faventiæ, Cesenæ, Forique Cornelii principatum tenuit, titulo tamen Capitanei.
units.tr: Near the Apennine, in the district of Sorrivoli, is Sufenano, the homeland of Magiunardo, who held the lordship of Faenza, Cesena and Forlimpopoli, though with the title of captain only.

units.la: In ipso Apennino Palatiolum est, ditionis olim Vbaldinorum.
units.tr: In the Apennine itself is Palazzuolo, formerly under the rule of the Ubaldini.

units.la: Succedit iterius in Æmilia Via ad ripam Amnis Saterni Imola. Sic hodie, testibus Leandro, Sigonio, aliis, dicitur, quod olim Forum Cornelii. Ita vocant M. Tullius libro xvi Epistola ad Cattium. Plinius lib. iii nat. hist. in viii portus regione, Antoninus in Itinerario, Procopius lib. ii de Bello Gothico, quod Ἐμολα Κορνηλίου Ptolemæo, in Gallia Togata locanti; Φορον Κορνηλιον Strabon lib. v. Meminit & Aedula marmorea Romæ, in ædibus Alteriorum juxta S. Marcum: D . M . C. PAPIRIVS. C LIB. FELIX. FORO CORNELI. MILIT. COH. VI. VIG. AN VI. VIX. ANN. XXIII M. III . D. XI HERES. EIVS. P. M. F
units.tr: Next, on the Via Aemilia, on the bank of the river Santerno, is Imola. Today it is so called, as Leandro Alberti, Sigonio and others attest, but formerly it was Forum Cornelii. Marcus Tullius calls it that in book 16 of his Letters to Cassius; Pliny in book 3 of his Natural History, in the eighth region of Italy; Antoninus in his Itinerary; Procopius in book 2 of the Gothic War, where he calls it Emola Cornelii [Ἐμολα Κορνηλίου], placing it in Cisalpine Gaul; and Strabo in book 5 calls it Forum Cornelium [Φορον Κορνηλιον]. It is also mentioned in a marble tablet at Rome, in the house of the Altieri near S. Marco. It reads, in substance: To the spirits of the dead. Gaius Papirius Felix, freedman, of Forum Cornelium, soldier of the sixth cohort of the vigiles, served six years, lived 23 years, 3 months and 11 days. His heir had this made.

units.la: Inde Foro-Cornelienses Plinio. Imola nomen ab Arcis appellatione natum, post ForumCornelii ab Antiocho Narsetis Præfecto excisum, docent Blondus libro viii Historiar. & Pomponius Laetus lib. ii. Ædificatum quidam fabulantur (nam sine probato Auctore) ab Troianis, post eversum Ilium. Conditor proculdubio Cornelius quidam, qui juris dicundi gratia eo Romam miserat. Sita est ad Santernum Amnem, agro frumentario, vini, olei, aliarumque frugum ferace: Fossa, Aqua, muris munita, non abhinc Wittebergae, nobilissimae Saxonum Civitati. Incolae lauti, opulenti, actis ingenij, virtutis eximiae, summae industriae, quocumque animum adplicent, ad litteras, militiam, mercaturam, alia. Episcopatus gaudet dignitate. Claros genuit viros, non paucos: in quis Benevenutus, Philosophus & Poeta, Dantis illustrator; item Ioannes ab Imola dictus, & Alexander Tartagnus, summi Iuris consulti; Hieronymus Clarutius, Poeta, Urbanus, Grammaticus; Ioannes Antonius Flaminius, Orator & Poeta, cujus filius M. Antonius, summus Philosophus, Graecis litteris pererudinitus, uti scripta probant. Quos laude militari inclutos habuit, omitto. Multorum loco sint Beltramus & Lippus Aldoph: Franciscus & Ioannes Saxatellis; Guido Vannus, ejusque filius Dominicus. In fide olim Populi Romani quum diu floruisset, post in Langobardorum est redacta potestatem; quibus Italia profligatis, in ditionem venit Bononiensium, sub quibus varie ab Alidosijs, Manfredis & Galeatijs habita, tandemque ab Romanis Pontificibus subjugata, uti pluribus docent ipsorum Annales. Legendi & Dantes in Paradiso, Cantico xv: Blondus lib. xxi Historiar. Marius Zquicola in Historia Mantuana; Leander Albertus, qui haec accurate: atque. Fede non ita pridem vastata lacerataque ab Saxatellorum, quibus Ioannes Princeps & Vanorum, quibus Guido praerat, factionibus; quum aliquot maximo universa Italiae ornamento esse potuisset.
units.tr: Pliny therefore calls its people the Forum-Cornelienses. Biondo in book 8 of his Histories and Pomponio Leto in book 2 teach that the name Imola came from the word for a citadel, and that after Forum Cornelii had been destroyed by Antiochus, prefect of Narses, the town was called Imola. Some tell fabulous stories that it was built by the Trojans after the fall of Troy, but they have no reliable author. Its founder was without doubt some Cornelius, who went to Rome to administer justice. The town lies on the river Santerno, in a land rich in grain, wine, oil and other crops. It is protected by a ditch, water and walls, and is not far from Wittenberg, the most noble city of the Saxons. Its inhabitants are wealthy, prosperous, clever in affairs, of outstanding courage and very great industry, and whatever they turn their minds to, whether letters, war or trade, they excel. The town enjoys the dignity of a bishopric. It has produced many distinguished men, among whom are Benvenuto, philosopher and poet, the illustrator of Dante; also Giovanni da Imola and Alessandro Tartagni, most eminent jurists; Girolamo Chiarucci, poet and grammarian of Urbino; Giovanni Antonio Flaminio, orator and poet, whose son Marcantonio, a most learned philosopher, was thoroughly versed in Greek letters, as his writings prove. I pass over those whom it has made famous for military renown. Let Beltrame and Lippo Adolfo, Francesco and Giovanni Sassatelli, Guido Vanni and his son Domenico stand for many. Once it was faithful to the Roman people for a long time, but afterwards it was brought under the power of the Lombards; when they were overthrown, it came under the rule of the Bolognese, under whom it was variously held by the Alidosi, the Manfredi and the Galeazzi, and at last it was subjected to the Roman Pontiffs, as their own annals teach at length. Dante in Paradise, Canto 15, should also be read, as should Biondo in book 21 of his Histories, Marco Equicola in his History of Mantua, and Leandro Alberti, who records these things accurately. Recently it was laid waste and torn apart by the factions of the Sassatelli, over whom Giovanni was prince, and of the Vanni, whom Guido led, though the whole of Italy could have been greatly adorned by it.

units.la: Septem ab Imola milibus Santerni ripae adlidet opidum, quod Latine scribentibus Tabellarium olim Ceteterum, post Ecclesiae Romanae potestatis, ortu clarum Petri Tauisignani, praestantis Medici.
units.tr: Seven miles from Imola, on the bank of the Santerno, lies a town which in Latin writers was formerly called Tabellarium, but later Ceteterum. It is under the power of the Roman Church, and is famous as the birthplace of Pietro Tavagnini, an excellent physician.

units.la: In colle hinc modico Castellum est Reum, ab Francisco Alidosio, Cardinale & Bononiae Legato, Fratribusque ejus Opizone & Riccardo, Opizonis denique filijs Cesare, Nicolao, Octaviano, & Alexandro valde nobilitatum.
units.tr: On a low hill from there is the castle of Riolo, greatly ennobled by Francesco Alidosi, cardinal and legate of Bologna, and by his brothers Opizzo and Riccardo, and finally by Opizzo's sons Cesare, Niccolò, Ottaviano and Alessandro.

units.la: Mille quingentis a Tauisignano Pattibus Gorgnanum Vicus est, Ioannis cognomine Tauisignani, Episcopi Ferrariensis, patria.
units.tr: A thousand five hundred paces from Tavagnini, toward Pattis, is the village of Gorgnano, the homeland of Giovanni, called Tavagnini, bishop of Ferrara.

units.la: Hinc inter Apennini Colles Opida vinearum aliquot & Vici in quis Fons, Casula, Saxatellum, unde Sanatellorum apud Foro-Cornelienses origo.
units.tr: From here, among the hills of the Apennine, are several towns and villages with vineyards, among which are Fonte, Casola and Sassatello, from which the Sassatelli of Forlimpopoli take their origin.

units.la: Ad aliam Vatrem ripam in monte Ceturi est Ranci, ulterioque Planum Caldulum.
units.tr: On the other bank of the Vatra, on Mount Cetura, is Ranco, and further on, Pianocaldoli.

units.la: Descendentium ad radices Apennini Forrestila se offert, Opidum novum, ab Florentinis, quibus subjectum, coniunctum, laurum & elegans. Porro quidem Fidentium olim dictam, neque corrupte Serenti Iun appellari pro Fidentiet.
units.tr: Descending to the foot of the Apennine, Forlimpopoli presents itself, a new town, handsome and elegant, under the Florentines, to whom it is subject and joined. Indeed, it was formerly called Fidentia, and it is not corruptly called Serenti Iun instead of Fidentiet.

units.la: Haud procul inde ex Apennini jugo Cajaie Fanmanum adparet in Agro Bononiensi.
units.tr: Not far from there, from the ridge of the Apennine, Caiaia Fanmano appears, in the territory of Bologna.

units.la: Padusam repetenti pandit se Mesa Lambardorum, circa annum cıɔ cc xxxıı, Friderici ıı Imperatoris principatu concessit, ab Familijs quibusdam Langbardicis, ob censuum acerbitatem ex agris Brixiano Mantuanoque profugis.
units.tr: Heading back toward the Po, there opens up Mesa Lombarda, which was granted around the year 1232, under the principate of Frederick II, Emperor, to certain Lombard families who had fled from the lands of Brescia and Mantua because of the harshness of the taxes.

units.la: Prope est Consilice, voce corrupta, tanquam Caput Silvae. Huc usque enim Via Silice strata, longitudine ab Ima la P. M. xıı, perducebatur.
units.tr: Near it is Consilice, a corrupted word, as if it meant Caput Silvae (the head of the wood). For as far as this place the Via Silice, a paved road, was carried, twelve Roman miles from Ima.

units.la: Propter Amnem Silerum in Agro Bononiensi Castellum Guelphum jacet, nobilis Familia Malvetiorum.
units.tr: Beside the river Silerus in the territory of Bologna lies Castellum Guelphum, the noble family of the Malvezzi.

units.la: Ad eundem Castellum D. Petri est, anno cıɔ cc conditum a Bononiensibus.
units.tr: Near the same river is Castellum D. Petri, founded by the Bolognese in the year 1200.

units.la: Ad alia eius ripam in colle, qui Aemiliam spectat, opidum visitur Dotia; sequiturque in montibus Flagnanum.
units.tr: On the hill on the river's other bank, which faces Aemilia, is the town Dotia; and in the mountains follows Flagnanum.

units.la: Clateram tranigresus offert se locus, ubi quondam Opidum Claterna. Sic Ciceronem lib. xı Epist. ad Cassium, Plinio, Antonino, Pomponio Melae, alijs; Ptolemaeo dicitur: quae Strabonis: Glacerima & Glacerina in quibusdam Antonini libris, corrupte. Crepit ejus inclinatio jam inde ab Gratiani temporibus, uti docet in Bononiensium historia Leander. Superant hodie Fani cuiusdam veteris Muri & Via lapide strata.
units.tr: After crossing the Claterus, a place presents itself where the town Claterna once stood. Cicero mentions it in book 11 of the Letters to Cassius, and so do Pliny, Antoninus, Pomponius Mela and others; Ptolemy calls it by the name Strabo gives, Glacerima and Glacerina in some books of Antoninus, corruptly. Its decline began in the times of Gratian, as Leander shows in his history of Bologna. Today there survive the remains of an old temple, a wall and a road paved with stone.

units.la: Occurrit hinc ab Aemilia Padulam versus cunctı Castellum Medicina, a Bononiensibus anno ab Christo nato cıɔ ccc xxcvı aedificatum.
units.tr: From here, on the way from Aemilia toward Padula, comes into view the castle Medicina, built by the Bolognese in the year of Christ 1296.

units.la: Altero latere Brutium est opidum opulentum, muris a Bononiensibus cinctum anno cıɔ ccc lxııı. Patria Antoniaa Barrie, praestantissimi iureconsulti.
units.tr: On the other side is Brutium, a rich town, walled by the Bolognese in the year 1363. It was the native town of Antonio Barri, a most distinguished jurist.

units.la: Viam Viam Aemiliam hinc ad Apennini colles Varignana est, opidum Petri Varignani Medici ortu nobile.
units.tr: From here, on the Via Aemilia, toward the hills of the Apennines, is Varignana, a town made noble by the birth of Pietro Varignani, a physician.

units.la: Ad Idicem flavium trans Aemiliam in tumulo Castellum adparet, quod vulgo Brutii. Arx olim, ut censet Leander, urbs Bristia, cuius meminit apud Blondum lib. ıı Histor. Agnellus in libro de Rebus Ravennae, qui eam commemorat Civitatibus Archiepiscopo Ravennati suffraganeis. Superstite praeter Abbatiam pervetterem aliquot antiquorum Operum vestigia.
units.tr: Across the river Idex, beyond Aemilia, a castle appears on a mound, commonly called Brutii. It was once a citadel, which Leander thinks was the city Bristia, of which Blondus makes mention in book 2 of his Histories. Agnellus, in his book on the affairs of Ravenna, also records it among the cities subject to the archbishop of Ravenna. Apart from a very old abbey, some traces of ancient works survive.

units.la: Visitur haud procul inde Vetianum, unde nomen antiquae Vetianorum Bononiensium familiae.
units.tr: Not far from there is Vetianum, from which came the name of the ancient Bolognese family of the Vetiani.

units.la: In adversa Idicis ripa Camburatium est.
units.tr: On the opposite bank of the Idex is Camburatium.

units.la: Ad Sapinam Amnem itinere, quo Bononia itur Florentiam Vicus est Planorum, cui nomen i tanore Virgiliano fabulatur Annus Viterbiensis ad fictitium Semproniū. Docent vestigia Aream hic fuisse, quam propter opidanorum defectionem anno cıɔ ccc lxxvıı Bononienses cum Loiano, Zapelino, Monteque Marmio diruerunt.
units.tr: On the road from Bologna to Florence, near the river Sapina, is the village Planorum, to which the Viterbo annalist, following his fictitious Sempronius, gives a name taken from a line of Virgil. Remains show that there was once an area here, which the Bolognese destroyed in 1377, together with Loiano, Zapelino and Monte Marmio, because its townsfolk had revolted.

units.la: Nnnn
units.tr: Nnnn

units.la: Occurrit post Loianum eodem itinere Scaricalasinum, à Bononiensibus conditum anno cIↄ ccxlvi.
units.tr: Beyond Loiano, on the same road, lies Scaricalasinum, founded by the Bolognese in 1246.

units.la: Hinc eadem via pergenti, læva, prærupto in colle, Opidum se offert Cauretum; ultraque Petra-Malx vicus.
units.tr: Continuing on the same road, on the left, on a steep hill, the town Cauretum presents itself; beyond it is the village Petra-Malx.

units.la: Succedit mox x à Bononia P. M. Bentivolum, sumtuosa Villa cum Turre, sic ab Ioanne Bentivolo II Restauratore nuncupatum: antea Fons Voledranus dicebatur.
units.tr: Soon, ten Roman miles from Bologna, comes Bentivolum, a sumptuous villa with a tower, so named by Giovanni Bentivoglio II, its restorer; before that it was called Fons Voledranus.

units.la: Inde ad Malalbergum, ubi initium Paduæ; quod antea, ut Peregrinus Priscianus libro I Antiquitatum Vrbis Ferrariæ tradit, Maletum audiit.
units.tr: Then comes Malalbergum, where the Padua begins. Before that, as Peregrinus Priscianus relates in book 1 of his Antiquities of the City of Ferrara, it was called Maletum.

units.la: Hinc ad Turrim Follæ navigranti Turris Vecllini ab læva relinquitur, à Bononiensibus anno cIↄ ccxlii condita.
units.tr: From here, for those sailing to the Tower of Folla, Turris Vecllini is left on the left hand. It was founded by the Bolognese in 1242.

units.la: Haud procul inde Poggium Lambertinorum, nobilis Bononiensium gentis, item ad D. Proßerum & ad D. Venantium antiquæ familiæ Bononiensis Platenium Patrimonium: ultra Galerus Vicus.
units.tr: Not far from there is the Poggium Lambertinorum, of the noble Bolognese clan of the Lambertini; likewise ad D. Prosperum and ad D. Venantium, the Platenian patrimony of an ancient Bolognese family. Beyond these is the village Galerus.

units.la: Sequitur mox opidum olim præclarum Plebis; indeque spatio P. M. superato Rheno, Centum, cujus appellationem aperit Leander. Meminit Blondus libro x Histor.
units.tr: Next comes the town Plebis, once famous; and then, after crossing the Reno over a distance of three Roman miles, Centum, whose name Leander explains. Blondus mentions it in book 10 of his Histories.

units.la: Via, quæ Bononia Ferrariam ducit Castellum est D. Georgy, à Bononiensibus extructum, ultraque cum Corticella.
units.tr: On the road that leads from Bologna to Ferrara is the castle of D. Georgy, built by the Bolognese, and beyond it Corticella.

units.la: Hinc tribus millibus nobilis & antiqua jacet Bononia. Sic Ciceroni lib. xII, Epistola ad Cassium; Livio passim, nominatim lib. xxxix; Tacito lib. xii, & seq. Strabo lib. v; Ptolemæo; Plinio lib. iii; Appiano lib. iii bell. civil. Dioni lib. xlix; Suetonio in Augusti, & Neronis Vitis; Pomponio Melæ lib. ii; Trebellio Pollioni in Censorino; Procopio lib. xiii. de Bello Gothico; Paullo Diacono lib. vi; Antonino in Itinerario, & aliis appellatur: quæ Bologna vulgo. Sic Inscriptiones Romanæ: xv. Legendus & Livius libro xxxiii. Galliæ Togatæ facit Ptolemæus: Æmiliæ, Zosimus: Plinius Octavæ tribuit Regioni. Ptolemæus eam describit Climate vi, gradu Longitudinis xxxiii medioque Latitudinis fere xliiii. Apennini radicibus adposita, ad Amnem Rhenum, Aposa torrente mediam Urbem interlabente: tota Orienti exposita, qua Auster est: montes imminent vitiferi: qua reliquæ partes, Agri patent longe lateque, omnis generis frugum feraces. Cœlum illi non admodum salubre. Circuitus vii miliarium; olim multo minor. Speciem habet onerariæ Navis, cujus partes explicat Leander. Portas habet xii. Potens est nobilitate, ædibus magnifica, porticibus frequens. Multa sunt Urbis hujus ornamenta & præclara, cum quæ rei divinæ, tum quæ Civium utilitati serviunt, ædificia. Primi ordinis sunt Divorum Petri Petronij quæ illius, Ecclesiæ hujus, Urbis Patroni, Fanum: Petri Episcopi Sedes est; Petronij, maximum & ornatissimum: inde S. Michaelis mirabilissimum; S. Francisci, splendidissimum: S. Salvatoris, elegantissimum, D. Ioannis Montani, pulcherrimum: D. Stephani, vetustissimum, olim Isidi & Serapidi dicatum: Alterius, Curia Senatus amplissima; Turrisque altissima intra Urbem, Asinelle nomine nota, ad quam adscensus est per gradus lineos ccccxlviii. Vi.na est Garisenda, inclinata nonnihil; arte an casu, dubium est. Inter publica medii ævi monimenta notatu dignum illud, quod Henrici, Sardiniæ & Corsicæ Insularum Regis, Henrici ii Romanorum Imperatoris Filii, non solum captivi à Bononiensibus, verum etiam in ipso defuncti & honorifice sepulti, statuaque honorati, servat memoriam, his verbis: Orto inter Bononienses & Mutinenses bello, Cæsar Henricus Secundus Romanorum Imp. Filium Henricum, Sardiniæ & Corsicæ Insularum Regem, Mutinensibus supplicas ferre jubet; qui instos apud D. Ambrosij Pontem certamine à Bononiensibus capitur, nulloque re ut dimittatur, impetrat, quum Pater mini, deinde precibus & precio de precatoribus utcunque, quum tantum auri pro redimendo filio polliceretur, quantum ad mœnia Bononiæ circulo aureo cingenda sufficeret. Sic captivus xxii annes, Menses ix, Dies xvi tenetur, a. regio more publica Bononiensi impensa, sic defunctus munificentissime ac pientissime funeratus, hic tumulatur. Præterea simulacrum hoc in perpetuum & hosti & captivo monumentum S. P. Q. Bononiensis posuit Anno salutis M. CCLXXII, II Id. Martij. Hoc volebam, ut sires: abi ac vale. Posuit aere publico, Ioanne Francisco Adjutorio Dictatore. Monimenta spectantur in variis Templis insignium luriconsultorum, Oratorum, aliorumque. In S. Dominici Templo siti sunt Ioannes Lignanus, Ioannes Andreas, Ioannes Calderinus, Bartholomæus Salicetus, Alexander Tartagnus, Petrus Ancharanus, & Ioannes Crottus Montil-Ferratensis: in Claustro, Florianus Sampetrus, Dinus Mugellanus, Cynus Pistoriensis, Ioannes Imolanus, Hippolytus Marsilius, Hieronymus Zanettus; omnes Iurisconsulti: item Ioannes Garzonius, Ioannes Antonius Flaminius, & Ioannes Andreas Garisendus, Oratores: Iacobus Petra Melara, Medicus & Astrologus; Alfonsus Lucensis Statuarius: ante Fanum Rolandini Passagerii & Azzonis Fuscarij, Iurisconsultorum stant sepulcra. In S. Francisci collocati leguntur Rolandinus Romanticus, Odofredus, Accursius Iurisperitissimi: In Servorum Templo Ioannes Ananias & Ludovicus Gozadinus, ICC. Apud Eremitas duo Nicolaus Faby, Philosophi. In Porticu Cœnobij D. Salvatoris, Antonius Codrus Præcius: In D. Ioannis Montani Karolus Ruinus IC. Domus Civium sumtuosissimæ. Visuntur ibi Vetusta Langbardorum ac vasta ædificia. De ejus initiis multa tradunt fabulose Hieronymus Albertutius in Annalibus Latinis, Ioannes Garzonius in Histor. Bononiensi, aliique; item, quos obtrusit Reip. literariæ Annius Viterbiensis non necessarios, Manethon, Cato, Sempronius. Quidquid sit, Colonia est Romanorum Livio libro xxxvii, Tacito lib.xii, Velleio Paterculo, Plinio, Pomponio Melæ, aliis: facta anno ab V C.10 lxv, M. Fulvio Nobiliore & Cn. Manlio Vulsone coss. Festus Bononiam Municipium sui juris appellat. Romanis fidi Bononienses in Antonicorum erant clientela, ut alij in aliorum; teste Suetonio in Cæsare cap.xvi. Bello Civili exorto Antonianas aliquamdiu sequuta legitur partes. Post illa Gratiano imperante, quum in libertatem se vindicare conaretur, ab Asclepio Cæsaris Præfecto in potestatem est redacta: non multo post rebellans ab Theodosio Imp. tota propemodum est subversa; anno demum ab Christo nato cccc xxxiii hortatu D. Petronij iterum ab Theodosio ii instaurata, magnaque sui parte aucta, & nobili Academia est ornata. Mansit deinde Urbs in fide de Romade Romanorum Imperatorum usque ad Leonem III, sub quo Langobardorum subdita ditioni; ijdemque vi erepta a Pipino Francorum Rege, & ab hoc datum Pontifici Romano adtributa: mox in Cesarum potestatem iterum redacta ab Karolo Magno & Lothario I, fideliter denuo Pan if. Max. committit, salvo tamen jure principatus sui: à quo tempore forma Reip. saepius mutata, Lumbertatiorumque & Cercmeiorum factionibus concussa partim per Duces suos Populos, Vicecomites, Comitatos: partim per Legatos Praesidesque Pontificios, magna varietate fuit administrata. Regitur Civitas ab Legato Pontificio, cui adjunguntur XI viri ex Nobilitate, qui singulis duobus mensibus creantur & appellantur Consules vel Confalonieri della Giustitia, qualicumque libertatis specie.
units.tr: Three miles from here lies the noble and ancient Bononia. So Cicero in book 12, in the letter to Cassius; Livy often, and by name in book 39; Tacitus in book 12 and following; Strabo in book 5; Ptolemy; Pliny in book 3; Appian in book 3 of the Civil Wars; Dio in book 49; Suetonius in the Lives of Augustus and Nero; Pomponius Mela in book 2; Trebellius Pollio in the life of Censorinus; Procopius in book 13 of the Gothic War; Paul the Deacon in book 6; Antoninus in the Itinerary; and others call it Bononia, which is commonly Bologna. So the Roman inscriptions. Livy in book 33 should also be read. Ptolemy places it in Gallia Togata, Zosimus in Aemilia, and Pliny assigns it to the eighth region. Ptolemy describes it in the sixth climate, at a longitude of 33 degrees and a latitude of about 44 degrees. It lies at the foot of the Apennines, beside the river Reno, with the torrent Aposa flowing through the middle of the city. It is wholly exposed to the east, where the south wind blows; vine-bearing mountains hang over it, and the rest of the fields stretch far and wide, fertile in every kind of crop. The air is not very healthy. Its circuit is seven miles; formerly it was much smaller. It has the shape of a merchant ship, whose parts Leander explains. It has twelve gates. It is powerful in nobility, magnificent in its buildings, and full of porticoes. There are many fine and famous ornaments of the city, both sacred buildings and those that serve the use of the citizens. Of the first rank are the temple of the saints Petrus and Petronius: that of Petronius, patron of this city and church, is the shrine, while Peter's is the seat of the bishop; that of Petronius is the largest and most richly adorned. Then there is the most wonderful church of S. Michaelis; that of S. Francisci is the most splendid; that of S. Salvatoris is the most elegant; that of D. Ioannis Montani is the most beautiful; and that of D. Stephani is the most ancient, once dedicated to Isis and Serapis. Of another kind are the very spacious Senate House and the tallest tower within the city, known by the name Asinelle, to which the ascent is by 448 stone steps. The tower Garisenda leans somewhat; whether this is by art or by chance is uncertain. Among the public monuments of the Middle Ages, that one is worth noting which preserves the memory of Henrici, King of the islands of Sardinia and Corsica, son of the Roman Emperor Henry II, who was not only taken prisoner by the Bolognese but also died there and was honourably buried, and was honoured with a statue, in these words: "When war broke out between the Bolognese and the Modenese, Caesar Henry II, Emperor of the Romans, ordered his son Henry, King of the islands of Sardinia and Corsica, to bring help to the Modenese. He was captured by the Bolognese in a battle at the bridge of St Ambrose, and could not be released by any means, although his father sent envoys and begged, and by whatever prayers and payment from the envoys, he promised as much gold to ransom his son as would suffice to encircle the walls of Bologna with a golden ring. So he was held captive for twenty-two years, nine months and sixteen days, and at public expense of the Bolognese, in royal manner, when he died he was buried most generously and most piously; here he lies entombed." Besides, "the Senate and People of Bologna set up this statue in the year of salvation 1272, on the 2nd of the Ides of March, as a monument to be kept forever, both for the enemy and for the captive. This is what I wanted you to see: go and farewell." It was set up at public expense, with Giovanni Francesco Adjutorio as dictator. Monuments of distinguished jurists, orators and others are to be seen in various churches. In the church of St Dominic are placed Ioannes Lignanus, Ioannes Andreas, Ioannes Calderinus, Bartholomaeus Salicetus, Alexander Tartagnus, Petrus Ancharanus, and Ioannes Crottus of Montferrat; in the cloister, Florianus Sampetrus, Dinus Mugellanus, Cynus Pistoriensis, Ioannes Imolanus, Hippolytus Marsilius, Hieronymus Zanettus, all jurists; likewise Ioannes Garzonius, Ioannes Antonius Flaminius and Ioannes Andreas Garisendus, orators; Iacobus Petra Melara, physician and astrologer; and Alfonsus of Lucca, sculptor. Before the church stand the tombs of Rolandini Passagerii and Azzonis Fuscarii, jurists. In the church of St Francis lie Rolandinus Romanticus, Odofredus and Accursius, most learned in law. In the church of the Servites, Ioannes Ananias and Ludovicus Gozadinus, jurists. At the Hermits' church, two, Nicolaus Faby, philosophers. In the portico of the monastery of St Salvator, Antonius Codrus Praeclarus; at St John of Monte, Carolus Ruinus, jurist. The houses of the citizens are very sumptuous. There are seen there ancient and vast buildings of the Lombards. Many fabulous things about its origins are told by Girolamo Alberti in the Latin Annals, by Giovanni Garzoni in the Bolognese History, and by others; also by those whom Annius of Viterbo, to the great inconvenience of the republic of letters, thrust upon it, namely Manetho, Cato and Sempronius. Whatever the truth, it was a Roman colony, as Livy in book 37, Tacitus in book 12, Velleius Paterculus, Pliny, Pomponius Mela and others say; it was founded in the year 565 from the founding of the city, in the consulship of M. Fulvius Nobilior and Cn. Manlius Vulso. Festus calls Bononia a municipality with its own rights. The faithful Bolognese were under the patronage of the Romans, as others were of others, as Suetonius attests in the Life of Caesar, chapter 16. When civil war broke out, they are read to have followed the party of Antony for some time. After that, under the emperor Gratian, when it tried to win back its liberty, it was reduced to subjection by Asclepius, the prefect of the Caesar; not long after, rebelling against the Emperor Theodosius, it was almost entirely destroyed; at last, in the year of Christ 433, at the urging of St Petronius, it was restored by Theodosius II, greatly enlarged in its part, and adorned with a noble academy. The city then remained loyal to the Romans, and to the Roman emperors, until Leo III, under whom it was made subject to the Lombards; and it was taken from them by force by Pepin, king of the Franks, who gave it to the Roman pontiff and assigned it to him. Soon it was brought back under the power of the Caesars by Charlemagne and Lothair I, and again faithfully committed by the emperors to the Supreme Pontiff, saving however the right of its own principality. From that time the form of the republic was often changed, shaken by the factions of the Lambertazzi and the Geremei, and governed partly through its own dukes, lords and counts, partly through the papal legates and presidents, with great variety. The city is governed by a papal legate, to whom are joined eleven men from the nobility, who are chosen every two months and called consuls or Confalonieri della Giustitia, with some semblance of liberty.

units.la: Episcopatus floret dignitate. Academiam instituit D. Petronij hortatu Theodosius Imperator, anno CCCCXXIII, quim in Privilegio, quod ibi legitur, eam Serenarum omnium Fontem, & Arcanorum sanctam Armarium nominat. Conlapsam quodammodo renovavit Karolus Magnus. Fridericus Barbarossa odio Bononiensium transferre conatus est Patavium.
