Eam paullatim summorum Pontificum Caesarumque munificentia ita exornavit, ut bonarum artium parens atque altrix, Legumque nutrix censeri coeperit.
units.tr: The bishopric flourishes in dignity. The Emperor Theodosius founded the university in 423, at the urging of Petronius, and in the privilege that is read there he calls it the fountain of all the sciences and the holy storehouse of secrets. Charlemagne restored it after it had in some measure fallen into ruin. Frederick Barbarossa, out of hatred for the Bolognese, tried to transfer it to Padua. Little by little, through the generosity of the supreme Pontiffs and the Emperors, it was so adorned that it began to be regarded as the parent and nurse of the liberal arts and the nursery of the law.

units.la: Sed & ex Lotharij Imperatoris Decreto Legum & Iuris Scholae unus fuit & Cura Bononia. Quamquam vero, quum Ius Romanum toto ferme Occidente celebraretur, multae Civitates ejus interpretationem susciperent: nullo tamen loco vel illustrium Doctorum cum laude: vel majore luventuris celebritate id fiebat, quam Bononiae, adeo ut nec Scholae Auditoribus, nec Aedes Habitatoribus in Urbe sufficerent, quemadmodum ex Clementis P. M. Decreto docemur.
units.tr: Moreover, by a decree of the Emperor Lothar, Bologna was one of the schools and the care of law. Although the Roman law was studied almost throughout the whole of the West, and many cities took up its interpretation, nowhere was this done with greater renown for illustrious teachers, or with a larger crowd of young people, than at Bologna. So much so that neither the lecture halls could hold the students nor the houses the residents of the city, as we are taught by the decree of Clement the Great.

units.la: Bononienses etiam primi Pandectas inventos ex superiore loco exponere, primumque Glossas in eos scribere instituerunt, ut Irnerius, Bulgarus, Hugo, Martinus, Iacobus aliique. De ea sic scribit Laonicus Chalcondylas: Bononia optimus & reliqua felicitate praestantis Italia Urbibus non cedit; litterarum vero studiis superat. Petrus Anchoranus eam veram studiorum Matrem vocat, ut nulla Italiae Civitas litterarum gloria cum ea comparari queat. Azo, Bononia, inquit, Legum studiorum semper Monarchiam tenuit. Glossa I. sin. C. de Testamentis Legum Nutricem appellat. Baldus mille annos ante suam aetatem floruisse scribit.
units.tr: The Bolognese were also the first to set out the Pandects, which had been discovered, from a higher chair, and the first to begin writing glosses on them, namely Irnerius, Bulgarus, Hugo, Martinus, Jacobus and others. Laonicus Chalcondylas writes of it thus: Bologna is the equal of the best cities of Italy, and of any other city in Italy in prosperity; but in the pursuit of letters it surpasses them. Peter Anchoranus calls it the true mother of studies, so that no city of Italy can be compared with it in the glory of letters. Azo says: Bologna has always held the sovereignty of the study of law. The Gloss on I. sin. C. de Testamentis calls it the nurse of the laws. Baldus writes that it flourished a thousand years before his own time.

units.la: Decrevit Clemens V. in Concilio Viennensi, ut in Academia Bononiensi, praeter omnium liberalium artium studia, Hebraica, Arabica, Chaldaica Linguae publice traderentur. Docuerunt ibi Joannes Andreae, Cynus, Azo, Bartolus, Accursius, Martinus Sociatus, Saliceius, & alij. Est Bononiae Collegium Hispanorum, in quo alunt multi studiosi, & Rectorem ipsi creant, qui secundas ab Academiae Rectore tenet, de quo Didacus Covarruvias lib. III Variar. Resolut. cap. I & Hieronymus Cygas in tractatu de Pensione, quaest. XXIII. Est & Germanorum Superiores intelligo & Inferiores Socictas, qui singulis annis binos Procuratores, Consiliarios quatuor legunt.
units.tr: Clement V, in the Council of Vienne, decreed that in the University of Bologna, besides the study of all the liberal arts, Hebrew, Arabic and Chaldee should be taught publicly. There taught John Andreae, Cynus, Azo, Bartolus, Accursius, Martin Sociatus, Saliceius, and others. At Bologna there is the Spanish College, in which many students are supported, and they elect for themselves a Rector, who holds second place after the Rector of the University; concerning this see Diego Covarrubias, Variae Resolutiones book III, chapter 1, and Hieronymus Cygas in his treatise on Pensions, question 23. There is also the society of the Germans, the Superiores, I mean, and the Inferiores, who each year elect two proctors and four counsellors.

units.la: Bibliothecae publicae sunt duae: una ad S. Salvatorem, Hebraicis, Graecis, Latinisque libris instructa; Altera apud S. Dominicum, in qua plurimi libri Iurisconsultorum, & illa Pandectarum Exemplaria, quibus usus est Georgius Haloander Zuicaviensis: item Archetypon Bibliae Efdrae in albo Corio ab Efora Scriba tempore Cyri conscriptae.
units.tr: There are two public libraries: one at S. Salvatore, furnished with books in Hebrew, Greek and Latin; the other at S. Dominic, in which are very many books of the jurists, and those copies of the Pandects which Georg Haloander of Zwickau used; also the archetype of the Bible of Ezra, written on white leather by the scribe Esdras in the time of Cyrus.

units.la: Martyres alioque Sanctorum numero adscriptos Poronia recensetur Agenum, Cajum, Vitalem, Hermolaum, Hermetum, Proculum, Iulianam Viduam, Bonentum Abbatem, Guarinum Episcopum Praeneflinum, & alios. Pontifices dedit Honorium II, Lucium II, Gregorium XIII: Cardinales, Bartholomaeum Medicaeum, Iacobum Isidianum, Nicolaum Alexandrinum, Achillem Craliun, Laurentium Campegium: Archiepiscopos, Bartholomaeum, Armeniae; Aegidium, Galatiae Cretae; Franciscum Prolapsum, Mediolani; Felicem Trophimum, Theatus: Quid dicam de Episcopis, cum qui patriae hic suae Episcopatus floret titulo Bononia tum qui aliis in locis praefuerunt?
units.tr: Among those who suffered martyrdom and were enrolled among the saints, Bologna lists Agenus, Caius, Vitalis, Hermolaus, Hermes, Proculus, Juliana the widow, Bonentus the abbot, Guarinus bishop of Palestrina, and others. It gave Popes Honorius II, Lucius II and Gregory XIII; cardinals Bartholomew Medici, James of Isidian, Nicholas of Alexandria, Achilles Craliun, Laurence Campeggio; archbishops Bartholomew of Armenia, Giles of Galatia and Crete, Francis Prolapsus of Milan, Felix Trophimus of Thea. What shall I say of the bishops, both those who here flourish with the title of their own see of Bologna and those who presided in other places?

units.la: Quid Protonotarios memorabo Apostolicos? quid Auditores Rotae? quid Advocatos Consistoriales, quos Bononia tulit? Doctorum tanc Virorum, qui Scriptis suam Patriam nobilitarunt, incredibilis est apud Leandrum numerus. Theologi: Angelus, Alexander, Bombolognius, Bartholomaeus Comanus, Eustachius Plateosis, Gerardus & Mi hoc sei cent, Paulus Matthaeus, Thomas Trentaquatrius: Iurisconsulti; Accursius Marsiotus, Albertus Kamponius, Alexander Patrensis, Andalus Andalus, Andreas Bovius, Andreas Manzolinus, Antonius Butrius, Bartholomaeus Saliceius, Bartholomeus de Pratis, Bartholomeus Bolognius, Bartholomaeus
units.tr: Why should I mention the apostolic protonotaries? Why the auditors of the Rota? Why the consistorial advocates whom Bologna has produced? Of learned men who have ennobled their homeland by their writings the number, as Leandro tells us, is incredible. Theologians: Angelus, Alexander, Bombolognius, Bartholomew Comanus, Eustachius Plateosis, Gerard and Mihoc sei cent, Paul Matthew, Thomas Trentaquatrius. Jurists: Accursius Marsiotus, Albertus Kamponius, Alexander Patrensis, Andalus Andalus, Andreas Bovius, Andreas Manzolinus, Antonius Butrius, Bartholomew Saliceius, Bartholomew de Pratis, Bartholomew Bolognius, Bartholomew

Hieronymo, Ioannes Calderinus, Ioannes Sulimanus, Ioannes Platcanus, Ioannes Bonsignorius, Ioannes Barberius, Ioannes Arbotenus, Ioannes Fantutius, Ioannes Sangeorgius, Ioannes Salanus, Ioannes Campegius, Ioannes Antonius Bottonus, Guido Bansius, Hippolytus Marsilius, Lambertinus Ramponius, Laurentius Pineus, Ludovicus Bolognínus, Ludovicus Mozolitus, Ludovicus Gozadinus, Ludovicus Ludovitius, Maciagnanus Affliguido, Martinus Sulimanus, Matthaeus Matthesilanus, Melchior Megius, Odofredus Odofredus, Paulus Eleazarus, Paulus Poltanus, Petrus Crenedolus, Petrus Anzolanus, Petrus Bonpetrius, Raphael Primaditius, Richardus Salicetus, Richardus Malumbra, Rolandinus Passageius, Rolandinus Romancius, Thomas Formaticus, Troilus Malvetius, Hugolinus a Prato, Vincentius Paleotus, Vincentius Saloncius: Medici; Christophorus Honestus, Dominicus Varignanus, Astor Taufignanus, Gaspar Varignanus, Hieronymus Raynutius, Ioannes Blanchinus, Ioannes Garzonius, Iacobus Montevalius, Ludovicus Leo, Mundinus Lucius, Nestor Morandus, duo Nicolai Fabij, Petrus Zanetinus & Petrus Varignanus: Historici; Benedictus Morandus, Ioannes Garzonus, Hieronymus Albertinus, Nicolaus Fabrutius, Guido Ghisilerius, Guido Gusnicellus, N. Huneus, Petrus Crescentius, Semperbonus, Thomas Caesellanus: Philosophi; Alexander Achinus, Bartholemaeus Manzolus, Hieronymus Gazo, Laurentius Spata, Tiberius Bazelerius, Ludovicus Bolcaferrius, Florianus Certoius: Arithmetici; Scipio Ferreus & Ioannes Maria Cambius: Astrologi; Iacobus Benatius, Julius Machiavellus, Marcus Scrilanarius: Chiromanta; Bartholemaeus Cocles: Oratores & Poeta: Andreas Magnanius, Angelus Coffus, Bartholemaeus Blanchinus, Benedictus Morandus, C. Rufticellus, Gamillus Falcottus, Iacobus Crucem, Ioannes Baptista Pius Andalus, Ioannes Andreas Garisendus, Lucius Pomponius, Laurentius Rufus, Petrus Megius, Philippus & Philippinus Beroaldi, Philippus Phagamanus, Pomperius Fofararius, Rufus denique, cujus mentio apud Martialem: Antiquarij: Alexander Caluma, Bartholemaeus Maffinus, Gaspar Fantutius, Ioannes Philotheus Achillinus: Architecti; Aristoteles Albertus, Ioannes Beroaldus, Ioannes Acciusius & Iacobus Raynutius: Pictores; Hercules, Franciscus Francia, Ioannes Maria Chiodarolus, Marcus Antonius Raymundus, Amicus Aspertus, Blasius Pupinus: Statuarij; Dominicus Aymon Varignanus, & Hieronymus Cortellinus. Nec defuerunt Bononiae Mulieres litteratae, inter quas Ioanna, Matthaei Blanchetti Filia, Bonsignori Bonsignorii uxor; Novella, Ioannis Andreae Filia, Ioannisque Lignani Conjux, quae Patre per alia occupato munus ejus ex suggestu docendi sustinebat. Genuit & haec Urbs Militiae Duces praestantissimos, quorum qui sequuntur nominatissimi: Agamemnon Senensis, Albertus Gallutius, Albertus Platensis, Annibal Bentivolus primus & alter, Antonius Maria Cignanus, Bartholemaeus Manzinus, Baptistorius Pelacanus, Camillus Gozadinus, Aeneas Blanchinus, Gaspar Malvetius, Iacobus Pepolus, Ioannes Ignanus, Ioannes Pepolus, Ioannes Ludovicus, Julianus Malvetius, Gualengus Ghisilerius, Hector Panicinus, duo Hercules Bentivoli, Hercules Malvetius, Hermes Bentivolus, Ludovicus Malvetius, Lucius Malvetius, Pompeius, Ramaciotti filius, Romeus Pepolus, Ramaciottus Scaricalcinus, Spinatus vel Alexander Clarius. Thomas Ramponus, Hugo Pepolus, & alij; quorum omnium praeclara militiae gesta ab alijs fuse commemorantur. Celebrarunt porro Bononiam suis scriptis Scipio Balbus, Antonius Codrus Urceus, Nicolaus Brutus. Deca sic Hadrianus Cardinalis: Urbs antiqua, ingens, Etruscà Regia quondam Felsina; tum Boii fato irrumpentibus impar, Accepisse novum fertur Boionia nomen: Verum ubi suns Boij Romano milite pulsi, Barbariem excusat, capitque Bononia dici. Subditur ad Boream radicibus Apennini, Planicie adclive procumbens Solis ad ortus, Inter aquas Sapinae & Rheni; quarum utraque in Urbem Ducta vehit revehitque rates, pistrinaque versat, Aemilia Aemilię decus, & belli pacisque patrona: Dives opum variarum, & nullius indiga cultus, Musarum domus, atque omnis nutricula Iuris.

Hieronymo, John Calderinus, John Sulimanus, John Platcanus, John Bonsignorius, John Barberius, John Arbotenus, John Fantutius, John Sangeorgius, John Salanus, John Campegius, John Antony Bottonus, Guido Bansius, Hippolytus Marsilius, Lambertinus Ramponius, Laurence Pineus, Ludovicus Bolognínus, Ludovicus Mozolitus, Ludovicus Gozadinus, Ludovicus Ludovitius, Maciagnanus Affliguido, Martin Sulimanus, Matthew Matthesilanus, Melchior Megius, Odofredus Odofredus, Paul Eleazarus, Paul Poltanus, Peter Crenedolus, Peter Anzolanus, Peter Bonpetrius, Raphael Primaditius, Richard Salicetus, Richard Malumbra, Rolandinus Passageius, Rolandinus Romancius, Thomas Formaticus, Troilus Malvetius, Hugolinus a Prato, Vincent Paleotus, Vincent Saloncius. Physicians: Christopher Honestus, Dominic Varignanus, Astor Taufignanus, Gaspar Varignanus, Hieronymus Raynutius, John Blanchinus, John Garzonius, James Montevalius, Ludovicus Leo, Mundinus Lucius, Nestor Morandus, the two Nicholas Fabius, Peter Zanetinus and Peter Varignanus. Historians: Benedict Morandus, John Garzonus, Hieronymus Albertinus, Nicholas Fabrutius, Guido Ghisilerius, Guido Gusnicellus, N. Huneus, Peter Crescentius, Semperbonus, Thomas Caesellanus. Philosophers: Alexander Achinus, Bartholomew Manzolus, Hieronymus Gazo, Laurence Spata, Tiberius Bazelerius, Ludovicus Bolcaferrius, Florian Certoius. Arithmeticians: Scipio Ferreus and John Mary Cambius. Astrologers: James Benatius, Julius Machiavellus, Marcus Scrilanarius. Palmist: Bartholomew Cocles. Orators and poets: Andreas Magnanius, Angelus Coffus, Bartholomew Blanchinus, Benedict Morandus, C. Rufticellus, Camillus Falcottus, James Crucem, John Baptist Pius Andalus, John Andrew Garisendus, Lucius Pomponius, Laurence Rufus, Peter Megius, Philip and Philippinus Beroaldi, Philip Phagamanus, Pomperius Fofararius, and Rufus, finally, he whom Martial mentions. Antiquaries: Alexander Caluma, Bartholomew Maffinus, Gaspar Fantutius, John Philotheus Achillinus. Architects: Aristoteles Albertus, John Beroaldus, John Acciusius and James Raynutius. Painters: Hercules, Francis Francia, John Mary Chiodarolus, Marcus Antonius Raymundus, Amicus Aspertus, Blasius Pupinus. Sculptors: Dominic Aymon Varignanus and Hieronymus Cortellinus. Nor have learned women been lacking at Bologna, among whom were Joanna, daughter of Matthew Blanchettus, wife of Bonsignorus Bonsignorius; Novella, daughter of John Andrew, and wife of John Lignanus, who, while her father was occupied elsewhere, discharged his duty of lecturing from the rostrum. This city also has produced most distinguished military commanders, of whom the most famous are these: Agamemnon of Siena, Albertus Gallutius, Albertus Platensis, Annibal Bentivolus the first and the second, Antonius Maria Cignanus, Bartholomew Manzinus, Baptistorius Pelacanus, Camillus Gozadinus, Aeneas Blanchinus, Gaspar Malvetius, James Pepolus, John Ignanus, John Pepolus, John Ludovicus, Julianus Malvetius, Gualengus Ghisilerius, Hector Panicinus, the two Hercules Bentivoli, Hercules Malvetius, Hermes Bentivolus, Ludovicus Malvetius, Lucius Malvetius, Pompeius, son of Ramaciotti, Romeus Pepolus, Ramaciottus Scaricalcinus, Spinatus or Alexander Clarius, Thomas Ramponus, Hugo Pepolus, and others; the glorious military exploits of all of whom are recounted at length by others. Moreover, Scipio Balbus, Antonius Codrus Urceus and Nicolaus Brutus have celebrated Bologna in their writings. Cardinal Hadrian sings thus: an ancient, mighty city, once the royal Etruscan Felsina; then, unequal to the Boii as they burst in by fate, it is said to have received the new name Boionia; but when the Boii were driven out by the Roman soldiery, it excuses its barbarism and is called Bologna. It lies to the north, at the foot of the Apennines, sloping down into a plain toward the rising sun, between the waters of the Savena and the Reno; and both of these, led into the city, carry boats to and fro and turn the mills. Emilia, the glory of Aemilia and the patroness of war and peace, rich in varied wealth and needing no outside cultivation, the home of the Muses, and the nurse of all law.

units.la: Aliorum Poëtarum Encomia prætereo. Haud procul Vrbe apud confluentes Rheni & Labinij amnium in Insula quadam exigua tres Romanorum Exercituum Duces M. Antonius, M. Æmilius Lepidus, C. Iulius Cæsar Octavianus convenientes junctis manibus conjurationem inierunt, Populique Romani Imperium inter se diviserunt. Nec magno Bononia intervallo Olivetum est, locusque, qui quondam Batiditium Castellum. Hæc de clarissima sufficiant Civitate: pergendum jam nunc ad reliqua.
units.tr: I pass over the eulogies of other poets. Not far from the city, at the confluence of the Rhine and the Labinius rivers, on a small island, three commanders of the Roman armies, Mark Antony, Marcus Aemilius Lepidus and Gaius Julius Caesar Octavianus, met, joined hands, entered into a conspiracy, and divided the empire of the Roman people between them. Not far from Bologna is Olivetum, and the place which was once the castle of Batiditium. Let these things about this most famous city suffice: we must now proceed to the rest.

units.la: In adversa Rheni ripa Caselicium Vicus visitur.
units.tr: On the opposite bank of the Reno lies the village Caselicium.

units.la: Hinc per Vallem Rheni ad magnificam Rubriorum Villam venitur, à Bartholomæo Rubrio loco commodissimæ amœnitatis cœptam, ab Mino ejus Filio auctam; inde, quum bellorum injuriis lacerata esset, ab Ludovico Mini filio restitutam.
units.tr: From here, through the Valley of the Reno, one comes to the magnificent Villa of the Rubrii, begun by Bartholomew Rubrius in a place of very pleasant charm and enlarged by Minus, his son. Later, when it had been torn apart by the damage of wars, it was restored by Ludovicus, son of Minus.

units.la: Succedit hinc Castellum Episcopi, Opidum olim, nunc Vicus.
units.tr: Next comes Castello Episcopi, once a town, now a village.

units.la: Inde altissimam rupem, quæ ferro secta, emensoo offert se Saxum Glosina, Sasso di Glosina: sequitur mox Pagus Vergatus.
units.tr: Beyond this rises a very high rock, cut by iron and smoothed, Saxum Glosina, Sasso di Glosina; soon after it comes the village of Vergatus.

units.la: Altius inde Balnea Porrettana, Bagni della Porretta, Opidum non contemnendum, calidis Aquis, de quibus alibi, nobile.
units.tr: Higher up is Bagni della Porretta, Balnea Porrettana, a town not to be despised and famous for its hot waters, of which more elsewhere.

units.la: Iis finitimi sunt Pagi, qui vulgo Garnaglio, Caprone, Capugnano, Casula, Casio, Bargi, Castiglione, Monte Agut, Paragazza, Bombiano.
units.tr: Near it are the villages commonly called Garnaglio, Caprone, Capugnano, Casula, Casio, Bargi, Castiglione, Monte Agut, Paragazza, Bombiano.

units.la: Decimo à Bononia lapide Crispellianum est Opidum, altiusque millibus quatuor in colle non magno Baciano, Bazzano, Arce, quam Ioannes Bentivolus II tecit, munitum.
units.tr: Ten miles from Bologna is the town Crispellianum, and four miles further up, on a hill not large, is Baciano, Bazzano, fortified with a citadel which John II Bentivoglio built.

units.la: Duobus P. M. à Baciano Mons Velius est, Monte Vellio: inde Savinianum occurrit.
units.tr: Two miles from Bazzano is Mons Velius, Monte Vellio; from there Savinianum comes into view.

units.la: Fuerunt & olim hoc tractu alia quædam Opidula à Bononiensibus eversa, Mons Maior, Mons D. Ioannis, Mons D. Petri, Mocia, Bonaciarium, Zapoinum, & alia.
units.tr: In this district there were also formerly certain other small towns, destroyed by the Bolognese: Mons Maior, Mons D. Ioannis, Mons D. Petri, Mocia, Bonaciarium, Zapoinum, and others.

units.la: Mille ab Æmilia Via Passu. Castrum est Piumatium, Castello Piumazzo, quod quibusdam olim Castellum Columbanum, alijs ad D. Columbanum, Bononiensium opus anno MCDLXVII.
units.tr: A thousand paces from the Via Aemilia is the Castrum of Piumatium, Castello Piumazzo, which some formerly called Castellum Columbanum and others ad D. Columbanum; it was a work of the Bolognese in the year 1467.

units.la: Hinc v milliari in ipsa Via Castellum Francum visitur.
units.tr: Five miles from here, on the Via itself, the Castellum Francum is seen.

units.la: Haud procul inde fuit olim vel Vicus, vel Opidum, quod veteribus Forum Gallorum, Ἀγορὰ Κελτῶν Appiano libro III bell. Civilium, Hirtium Consulem eo divertisse scribenti. Meminerunt Frontinus & M. Tullius libro XII Epist. ad Familiar. Alij alio fuisse loco contendunt. Mihi, & alijs, verisimile, si non Castellum Francum, sane haud procul inde fuisse.
units.tr: Not far from there there was formerly either a village or a town, which the ancients called Forum Gallorum, [Ἀγορὰ Κελτῶν], as Appian says in Book III of the Civil Wars, where he writes that the consul Hirtius lodged there. Frontinus and Marcus Tullius, in Book XII of the Letters to Friends, mention it. Others contend that it was in some other place. To me and to others it seems likely, if not at Castellum Francum, then certainly not far from there.

units.la: Castellum D. Ioannis in Perficeto, quod etiam in Agro Bononiensi, peramplum olim fuit, sed à Bononiensibus ob defectionem ad miseram conditionem præcipitatum. Nobilitarunt ortu suo Gasparus, Ordinis Prædicatorum Monachus, Imolanus Episcopus, & Andreas Bernardus, scriptis clarus.
units.tr: Castellum D. Ioannis in Perficeto, which is also in the territory of Bologna, was once very large, but was reduced to a wretched condition by the Bolognese because it had defected. Its birth made famous Gasparus, a Dominican friar and Bishop of Imola, and Andreas Bernardus, famous for his writings.

units.la: Vlterius ad alterum fere lapidem Castellum est D. Agathæ.
units.tr: Further on, about a mile away, is the Castellum of D. Agathæ.

units.la: Hinc Æmiliam repetenti Manzolinum exiguum Castellum se pandit.
units.tr: Heading back toward the Via Aemilia, the small castle Manzolinum opens into view.

units.la: Tertio à Castello D. Ioannis lapide Crocetta Vicus est; cujus læva via Bonportum ducit, dextra; ad Opidum Crevalcorem, quod prius Alcegralcore, Antonio nobili Pictore clarum.
units.tr: Three miles from Castello San Giovanni is the village Crocetta. Its left-hand road leads to Bonportum, its right-hand road to the town Crevalcorem, formerly Alcegralcore, famous for the noble painter Antonio.

units.la: Austrum versus inter Crevalcoris Viam & Æmiliam Noramula visitur, insigni quondam sumtuosoque Cœnobio, quod Anselmus, Arhaulphi Langbardorum Regis Cognatus, circa annum 10 CCLXXX condiderat, superbiens. Opidum olim in Bononiensium, post in Ferrariensium cœpit esse ditione.
units.tr: Toward the south, between the road to Crevalcore and the Via Aemilia, lies Noramula, once famous for a notable and sumptuous monastery, which Anselm, a kinsman of Arhaulphus, King of the Lombards, founded about the year 780 with considerable pride. The town was formerly under the rule of the Bolognese, and afterwards came under that of the Ferrarese.

units.la: Hactenus Cis-Padanam perambulavimus Romanulam: sequitur Transf-Padana; cui ab Ortu Mare Hadriaticum; à Septemtrione Paludes Paravinorum, Vicentinorum, & Veronensium; earumque pars usque ad Padum ab Occasu; à Meridie Padus. Habitarunt olim, indicante Polybio libro II, Trigaboli, Egones, Ananes, Boi, Senones, de quibus alibi.
units.tr: So far we have traversed Cis-Padana, the Romagna; there follows Trans-Padana. It is bounded on the east by the Adriatic Sea; on the north by the marshes of the Paravini, the Vicentines and the Veronese; on the west by part of these marshes as far as the Po; and on the south by the Po. Formerly it was inhabited, as Polybius indicates in Book II, by the Trigaboli, Egones, Ananes, Boii and Senones, of whom more elsewhere.

units.la: Hic ad Primarium, quod primum Padi in Hadriaticum pelagus fluentis ostium, Spina fuit opidum: Σπίνα Straboni & Stephano, cui sic dictum ab Amne Spino, qui prope fluebat. Initium Vrbis, progressum & excidium describit Dionysius Halicarnassæus libro i Antiquit. Romanarum. Plinius ab Diomede factum notat libro iii, cap.xv. Dionysius Pelasgos Conditores tradit. Strabonis ætate jam ex Vrbe in Vicum degeneratat. Locus hodie partim Vallù, partim Dorsum Spinæ nuncupatur.
units.tr: Here, at the first mouth of the Po where it flows into the Adriatic sea, was the town Spina, [Σπίνα] in Strabo and Stephanus, so called from the river Spinus, which flowed nearby. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, in Book I of the Roman Antiquities, describes the beginning, growth and destruction of the city. Pliny records that it was founded by Diomede, in Book III, chapter 15. Dionysius hands down that the Pelasgi were its founders. In Strabo's time it had already declined from a city to a village. The site today is partly called Vallù and partly Dorsum Spinæ.

units.la: In Padi ripa Vicus D. Alberti est: Castellum prius, anno cIↄ cccc ab Nicolao Marchione conditum.
units.tr: On the bank of the Po is the village Vicus D. Alberti: it was formerly a castle, founded in 1400 by Marquis Nicholas.

units.la: Spatio xx Mill. ab D. Alberti, passim multi Vici Pagique: in quis Humana, Fossa Putula, Longastrinum, Filium, cui nomen ab directo Amnis cursu sex fere millium: ulterius sunt Rotta, & ad S. Blasium e regione Fossæ Zilioliæ Bastiæque.
units.tr: Within twenty miles of Sant'Alberto there are many villages and hamlets scattered about, among them Humana, Fossa Putula, Longastrinum and Filium, which is named after the river's straight course of about six miles. Further on are Rotta and ad S. Blasium, opposite Fossa Zilioliae and Bastia.

units.la: Quarto inde Milliari Castellum Argenta cernitur, cui, ut quidam volunt, nomen ab Argento, quod Incolæ quotannis Ravennati pendunt Antistiti. De ipsius Dominis legendi Blondus libro xx Histor. Platina in Vita Benedicti xii, Sabellicus lib. viii, Ennead. ix.
units.tr: Four miles from there the castle of Argenta is seen. Some hold that it takes its name from Argento [silver], which the inhabitants pay each year to the Bishop of Ravenna. For its lords, read Blondus, Book XX of the Histories; Platina, in the Life of Benedict XII; and Sabellicus, Book VIII, Ennead IX.

units.la: Altero ab Argenta lapide ad Padi ripam sumtuosum Ferrariensium Principum Palatium est Boccaleo: inde ad tertium milliare Cossandolum. Haud procul hinc Hospitaletum, Monasteriolum, Ad D. Nicolaum, aliique Vici.
units.tr: Two miles from Argenta, on the bank of the Po, is Boccaleo, the sumptuous palace of the Princes of Ferrara; from there, at the third mile, is Cossandolum. Not far from here are Hospitaletum, Monasteriolum, Ad D. Nicolaum and other villages.

units.la: In Insula, quam duo Padi cornua faciunt, quæque Polesino di San Giorgio vernacule, tribus à Cosandolo millibus Palatium spectatur splendidissimum Calcagninorum, cognomine Benvegnantium, aliaque præclara ædificia: item D. Georgij Burgum, ad quod translati primo Fori Alieni (quod haud procul inde fuit ubi nunc Viceventia Pagus) coloni. Forum Alienum memorat Tacitus. Vide & Bocatium libro de Fluminibus. Allieni dicitur Numismatibus. Burgum hoc D. Georgy quoque etiam Ferrariola legitur nuncupata; cujus in Archivo Inlustrium Marchionum Academiæque Bononiensis Codicillis, ab Theodosio Imperatore concessis, mentio.
units.tr: On the island which the two horns of the Po form, and which in the vernacular is called Polesino di San Giorgio, three miles from Cossandolo there can be seen the most splendid palace of the Calcagnini, surnamed Benvegnanti, along with other notable buildings. Likewise there is the D. Georgij Burgum, to which the colonists of the Fori Alieni (which was not far from where the village Viceventia now stands) were first moved. Tacitus mentions Forum Alienum. See also Boccaccio's book on rivers. On coins it is called Allieni. This Burgum of D. Georgy is also read as named Ferrariola; it is mentioned in the archive of the illustrious Marquises and in the codicils of the Bolognese Academy, granted by the Emperor Theodosius.

units.la: In eadem Insula juxta litus Stagnum spectatur ambitu milliumxii, in quo Civitas Comaclum, Priscis, ut quidam volunt, dicta Cymaclum, quod in Vndis sita. De rebus ab ea gestis, ejusque excidio Blondus in Historiis. In ditione est Ateflinorum Principum. Piscibus Cephalis, Anguillis, aliisque capiundis, Saliquæ coquendo dant operam Comaclini.
units.tr: On the same island, near the shore, lies a lake with a circuit of twelve miles, on which stands the town Comaclum, called by the ancients, as some think, Cymaclum, because it is situated among the waves. Blondus, in his Histories, tells of its doings and its destruction. It is in the territory of the Princes of Este. The people of Comaclini busy themselves catching cephali (mullet), eels and other fish, and boiling salted fish.

units.la: Sequitur hinc ad secundum Padi ostium alia Insula, in qua multi Vici, nominatim Massa, Fossa Arborum, Milianeum, Miliarinum, & Medelana; supraque Portum, Belriguardum, Viroveria.
units.tr: From here, at the second mouth of the Po, follows another island, in which there are many villages, namely Massa, Fossa Arborum, Milianeum, Miliarinum and Medelana; and above them Portum, Belriguardum and Viroveria.

units.la: In Insula ad Gaurum, tertium Padi Brachium, Pagi frequentes: in quis Arianum, & Codicorum, sic dictum tamquam Caput Gauri; Maxentia, & Pomposa Monasterium.
units.tr: On the island at the Gaurus, the third branch of the Po, there are many villages: among them Arianum and Codicorum, so called as if it were the Caput Gauri (Head of the Gaurus); also Maxentia and the monastery of Pomposa.

units.la: Ferrariam Vidcamus: cui unde nomen datum, valde variatur. Quidam à Fratte, quæ lingua vernacula Vrgulta, Prunaque Silvestria: nonnulli à Fabro quodam Ferrario: sunt qui à Ferro dirivant, quotannis ab Incolis olim Census nomine Ravennatibus pendi solito: uti Argenta ab Argento: Auriolum ab Auro præstando. Veritati maxime consentaneum Ferrariam nuncupatam ab Ferrariola, quæ, ut supra dixi, trans Padum erat, Colonis, huc ex Theodosij Imperatoris decreto translatis anno ccccxxxiii: quo tempore Vicus fuit absque muris ab Smaragdo Exarcho, uti Blondus & Volaterranus memorant; circa annum 10 xcv fossa mœnibusque septus; paulatimque ita auctus, ut tandem in nobilissimam Civitatem commutatus fuerit; Vetere Præsulatu ab Vitaliano P. M. huc circa annum 10 clviii traducto, aliisque duodecim Pagis finitimis illi subjectis ab Constantc 11 Imperat. qui multa ipsi largitus est Privilegia. Legendi Blondus, Sabellicus, Peregrinus Priscianus, alij. Hodie Ferrara audit. Conditam ab Trojanus cum Mutina, Cremona, Atestè, Vicentia, Placentia, Verona, Aquileia, Concordia, Mantua, & alijs, adserit ex novitijs Scriptoribus Gabriel Venetus. Adsidet ripæ Padi Amnis, quo qua Ortum Austrumque respicit, adluitur. Cœlum ipsi crassius, obsitum paluström. Plateas habet rectas, longas, amplas, quarum plerasque Leonellus Marchio primum coctis stravit lateribus. Ædificijs cum publicis, licet non magnis, tum privatis supra modum est ornata. Maximum est Vrbis Fanum. Arx illi duplex, una ad flumen, altera è regione S. Georgij, Ducis Sedes; utraque satis munita. Populo frequens, rebus ad vitam necessarijs abundat. Non inamœna inter primas Italiæ Vrbes merito censenda; Caput Sedesque Ducatus Atestinæ familiæ, nobilitatis & antiquitatis stupendæ. Familias habet celebres & opulentas. Legitur olim in fide fuisse Cæsarum, Pontificum Romanorum,& Exarchorum. His aliquoties auxilio fuit contra Langbardos, quorum Regem Desiderium quum Karolus Magnus debellasset, Opidaque Exarchatus Romano tradita essent Pontifici, hæc Cæsareo fere paruit Imperio: dein circa annum cIↄ i ab Henrico III Imp. bello subacta, & Mathildæ Comitii adtributa, ab eaque rursum Pontifici Romano donata, & aliquamdiu possessa; tandem circa annum cIↄ cxcv Marchionum Atestinorum subdita est imperio, rursusque anno cIↄ Iↄxcviii Clementis viii P. M. opera Sedis Apostolicæ restituta. Consulendi præter alios Platina in Pachale i. Concilium hic celebrarunt Eugenius IIII, P. M. anno cIↄ ccccxxxviii; cui Græcorum Imperator Ioannes Palæologus & Iosephus Patriarcha Constantinopolitanus interfuere. Gravi Terræmotu concussa est anno cIↄ Iↄ lxx, & intra biduì spatium prope funditus vastata. Principes enumerat à prima origine Leander Albertus, & apud eum alij. Academiam ibi instituit Fridericus II Imperator in Bononiensium contumeliam. Florucrunt in ea magna Ingenia: Angelus Aretinus, Bartholemaeus Salicetus, Felinus Sandeus, Andreas Alciatus, Guarinus Veronensis, Theodorus Gaza, Celius Calcagninus, Baptista Guarinus, Nicolaus Leonicenus, aliique. Bibliotheca est apud Carmelitas, non contemnendam habens veterum Codicum copiam. Nobilitarunt Urbis nomen Viri maximi: Antonius Beccarius, Scodræus Episcopus, Ordinis Prædicatorum Monachus; Felinus Sandeus Episcopus IC, Hieronymus Savonarola, Franciscus Silvester, summus Antistes Sodalitatis Prædicatorum; Io. Maria Riminaldus, IC; Peregrinus Priscianus, Patriæ Inlustrator, Ludovicus Ariostus, Poeta, Auctor Orlandi Furiosi; Celius Calcagninus, Orator & Poeta; Lilius Gregorius Giraldus, Latine Græcequè doctissimus, & memoriæ tenacissimæ; Ludovicus Bigus, Poeta; Alexander Guarinus; Casparus Sardus, Historicus. Planiciem habet circa se maximam, sed sterilem.
units.tr: We come to Ferrara, and there is great disagreement about where its name comes from. Some derive it from Fratte, which in the vernacular is called Vrgulta and Prunaque Silvestria [brambles and wild plums]; others from a certain smith, Fabro Ferrario; some derive it from Ferro [iron], since the inhabitants used to pay a customary tax to the Ravennates each year, just as Argenta is named from Argento and Auriolum from Auro [gold], which was paid as a tribute. But what agrees most with the truth is that Ferrara was named after Ferrariola, which, as I said above, lay across the Po, whose colonists were moved here by decree of the Emperor Theodosius in the year 433. At that time it was a village without walls, under the Exarch Smaragdus, as Blondus and Volaterranus record. About the year 995 it was enclosed by a ditch and walls, and gradually grew until at last it became a most noble city. The old episcopal see was transferred here by Pope Vitalian about the year 1158, and twelve neighbouring villages were made subject to it by the Emperor Constans II, who granted it many privileges. For reading, see Blondus, Sabellicus, Peregrinus Priscianus and others. Today it is called Ferrara. Gabriel Venetus, among the more recent writers, asserts that it was founded by Trojanus, along with Modena, Cremona, Este, Vicenza, Piacenza, Verona, Aquileia, Concordia, Mantua and others. It sits on the bank of the Po, and is washed by that river on the side facing east and south. Its air is rather thick, and it is surrounded by marshes. It has straight, long, wide streets, most of which Marquis Leonello first paved with baked bricks. It is decorated beyond measure with buildings, both public, though not large, and private. The city's largest temple is the cathedral. It has a double citadel: one by the river, the other opposite St George's, the seat of the Duke; both are quite strong. It is populous and abounds in the necessities of life. Not unpleasant, it is rightly counted among the first cities of Italy, the head and seat of the Duchy of the family of Este, of astonishing nobility and antiquity. It has famous and wealthy families. It is read that it was once in the allegiance of the Caesars, Roman Pontiffs and Exarchs. Several times it gave them help against the Lombards; when Charlemagne had defeated their King Desiderius and the towns of the Exarchate were handed over to the Roman Pontiff, this city mostly obeyed the Imperial power. Then about the year 1001 it was subdued in war by Henry III, Emperor, and assigned to the Countess Matilda; from her it was again given to the Roman Pontiff and held for some time. At last, about the year 1195, it was subjected to the rule of the Marquises of Este, and in 1598 it was restored to the Apostolic See through the efforts of Pope Clement VIII. Consult, besides others, Platina in the Life of Paschal I. Pope Eugenius IV, the Supreme Pontiff, held a council here in the year 1438, which the Greek Emperor John Palaeologus and Joseph, Patriarch of Constantinople, attended. It was shaken by a severe earthquake in 1570 and within two days was almost utterly destroyed. Leander Albertus lists its princes from their first origin, and others do so with him. Frederick II, Emperor, founded an academy there to the discredit of the Bolognese. Great minds flourished in it: Angelus Aretinus, Bartholomaeus Salicetus, Felinus Sandeus, Andreas Alciatus, Guarinus Veronensis, Theodorus Gaza, Celius Calcagninus, Baptista Guarinus, Nicolaus Leonicenus, and others. There is a library at the Carmelites, with no small store of old codices. Very great men have ennobled the city's name: Antonius Beccarius, Bishop of Scodra, a Dominican friar; Felinus Sandeus, Bishop and doctor of law; Hieronymus Savonarola; Franciscus Silvester, supreme head of the Dominican confraternity; Io. Maria Riminaldus, doctor of law; Peregrinus Priscianus, illustrator of his homeland; Ludovicus Ariostus, poet, author of Orlando Furioso; Celius Calcagninus, orator and poet; Lilius Gregorius Giraldus, most learned in Latin and Greek and of most retentive memory; Ludovicus Bigus, poet; Alexander Guarinus; Casparus Sardus, historian. It has around it a very large plain, but a barren one.

units.la: Visuntur in Agro Ferrariensi nobiles Pagi, inter quos Francolinum, non spernendum olim Propugnaculum, de quo Volaterranus libro IIII Vrbanorum Commentar. Sunt item Corbula & Crispinum: item Fossa Pelasella, victoria nobilis contra Venetos anno cIↄ IↄIX; intra quam Pagus pulcer est Orcanus.
units.tr: In the territory of Ferrara there are noble villages, among which is Francolino, once a not contemptible stronghold, of which Volaterranus speaks in book 4 of his Commentaries on Urban Matters. There are also Corbula and Crispinum, and Fossa Pelasella, a noted victory over the Venetians in the year 1509; within its bounds lies the fine village of Orcano.

units.la: Pergenti per Padi ripam occurrunt Pagi, Pons Lacus obscuri, Oculus Bellus, & alij.
units.tr: Proceeding along the bank of the Po, one meets the villages of Ponte, Lago Oscuro, Occhio Bello, and others.

units.la: Sequitur inde Ficarolum, quondam Vicus Aricoli dictus, ut vult Priscianus lib.i. Antiquit. Ferrar. sine auctore certo.
units.tr: From there one comes to Ficarolo, formerly called Vicus Aricoli, as Priscianus holds in book 1 of his Antiquities of Ferrara, though without a certain author.

units.la: Inter quartum Padi ostium & Athesim spectantur antiquæ Civitatis Adria vestigia. Adria Livio, Trogo, Tacito, Plinio, reliquisque Latinis; Ἀδρία Straboni & Polybio; Ἀτρία Ptolemaeo, & emendatioribus Plinij Codicibus, teste Hermolao Barbaro in Castigat. Αἰδρίων quoque dictam notat Stephanus. Scribit Torellus hodieque Adri vocari in agro Ferrariensi. Stephanus ab Diomede conditam adseruit. Venetorum Urbs Ptolemaeo; Tuscorum, Plinio; Colonia Romanorum, Livio; Tuscorum, Polybio lib. IIII; Græcorum, Trogo libro xx. Inlustris admodum fuit olim; adeo ut Adriaticum Mare nomen inde sortitum, testibus Livio, Polybio, Trogo, Strabone, Plinio, Eustathio; quem honorem Adriæ Marucinorum, de quo supra dixi, tribuit Aurelius Victor in Ælio Hadriano; sed solus. Restant paucissima ejus rudera: quod non mirum, quum jam Strabonis ævo pene periisset.
units.tr: Between the fourth mouth of the Po and the Adige can be seen the remains of the ancient city of Adria. Adria is its name in Livy, Trogus, Tacitus, Pliny and the other Latin writers; Ἀδρία in Strabo and Polybius; Ἀτρία in Ptolemy and in the more correct manuscripts of Pliny, as Hermolaus Barbarus witnesses in his Castigations. Stephanus also notes that it was called Αἰδρίων [Aidrion]. Torelli writes that it is still called Adri today in the territory of Ferrara. Stephanus asserts that it was founded by Diomedes. It is the city of the Veneti in Ptolemy, of the Tuscans in Pliny, a colony of the Romans in Livy, of the Tuscans in Polybius book 4, and of the Greeks in Trogus book 20. It was once very famous, so much so that the Adriatic Sea took its name from it, as Livy, Polybius, Trogus, Strabo, Pliny and Eustathius bear witness; and Aurelius Victor, in his life of Hadrian, ascribes this honour to Adria of the Marrucini, which I mentioned above, but he alone does so. Very few of its ruins remain, which is no wonder, since it had almost perished already in Strabo's time.

units.la: In eadem Insula Opidum est Rhodigio, dives; Bartholemaei Roverella, Ravennatium Archiepiscopi, & Ludovici Calij ortu superbiens. Visitur ibidem Castellum Venetum: ulterius Lendenaria & Abbatia. Alia minoris momenti praetereo.
units.tr: On the same island is the town of Rovigo, a wealthy place, which takes pride in Bartolomeo Roverella, Archbishop of Ravenna, and in Ludovico Celio. There may be seen there the Venetian castle; farther on are Lendinara and the Abbey. Other places of lesser importance I pass over.

units.la: CAPVT XXXIV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXIV.

units.la: Æmilia vel Langbardia Cis Padana.
units.tr: Aemilia or Langobardia Cis-Padana.

units.la: PRIOREM Galliæ Cis-Padanæ portionem perlustravimus in Flaminia: succedit percurrenda posterior in ÆMILIA vel LANGBARDIA, quæ ab situ CISPADANA, ratione alterius, quæ trans Padum, de qua capite sequenti. Generalia prius dabo, post specialiora persequar.
units.tr: We have gone through the first part of Cisalpine Gaul in Flaminia. The second part follows, in ÆMILIA or LANGOBARDIA, which is called Cispadane from its position, in contrast with the region beyond the Po, which I will treat in the following chapter. I will first give general matters and afterwards go through the particulars.

units.la: Varias adferunt nonnulli appellationes; quas non omnes probare possum. Quod Bianora fuerit dicta ab Otho Bianoro nobili Tuscorum Duce: quod Bianoræ pars Ravennam usque Felsina, ab Etruriæ Principe, cui id erat nominis, quod item suis temporibus Doria, Aurelia & Æmilia, ab Doria, Tusca Familia, Romanisque Ducibus audierit, tradunt supposititi ab Annio Viterbiensi, Reique publicæ litterariæ obtrusi, Cato & Sempronius. Æmilium nihilominus vocat Paullus Diaconus lib. 11 de Gestis Langbardorum cap. xviii. Lang-bardia cum sequente Provincia appellatur ab Lang-bardis, ex Germania huc Iustiniani principatu profectis; qui ad utramque Padi ripam multos annos suas cum imperio habuerunt, ejectis incolis, Sedes. Hodie Euphoniæ gratia Lombardia dicitur. Hæc, de qua nihil termo, vocatur ab situ Cis-Padana; vulgo Di qua del Po.
units.tr: Some writers give various names, and I cannot approve of all of them. They tell us that Bianora was so called after Otho Bianoro, a noble Tuscan leader; that the part of Bianora extending as far as Ravenna was called Felsina after the prince of Etruria who bore that name; and that in their own times it was also known as Doria, Aurelia and Æmilia, after Doria, a Tuscan family, and the Roman leaders. These claims are made by Cato and Sempronius, forgeries put out by Annius of Viterbo and foisted on the literary public. Paulus Diaconus, nevertheless, calls it Æmilium in book 11 of his History of the Lombards, chapter 18. Langobardia, along with the following province, takes its name from the Langobardi, who came here from Germany in the reign of Justinian and for many years held their seats and rule on both banks of the Po, after the inhabitants had been driven out. Today it is called Lombardy for the sake of euphony. This region, about which nothing more need be said, is called Cispadane from its position; in the vernacular, Di qua del Po.

units.la: Fines ejus ab Ortu Scultenna seu Panarius fluvius cum Romanula, superiore capite explicata ab Septemtrione Padus: qua Occasus est Padus idem cum Alpibus, Galliam Ulteriorem ab Citeriore dirimentibus; qua Meridies, Apenninus cum Etruriæ Liguriæque portione.
units.tr: Its boundaries are: on the east, the river Scultenna, or Panaro, together with the Romagna, explained in the previous chapter; on the north, the Po; on the west, the same Po and the Alps, which separate Transalpine from Cisalpine Gaul; on the south, the Apennines with part of Etruria and Liguria.

units.la: Regio hæc ob admirandam amœnitatem, incredibilem rerum omnium copiam, gratam deliciarum varietatem, stupendam ingeniorum excellentiam, cum primis Italiæ censenda. Colles ibi videre jucundissimum, vitæ, ficu, olea, aliisque arboribus gravidos; Campos tritico, hordeo, faba, ceterisque frumenti generibus convestitos; Incolas rei litterariæ juvandæ, tractandis armis, mercaturæ exercendæ plane ad naturam factos; Urbes lautas, & ab natura atque bene munitas; Opida Pagosque populo frequentes.
units.tr: This region deserves to be counted among the first of Italy, on account of its wonderful pleasantness, its incredible abundance of all things, its agreeable variety of delights, and its remarkable excellence of talent. There you see most pleasant hills laden with vines, figs, olives and other trees; plains covered with wheat, barley, beans and other kinds of grain; inhabitants made by nature for promoting literature, handling arms and carrying on trade; elegant cities, well fortified by nature and by art; and towns and villages crowded with people.

units.la: Specialiora memoraturus a Panaro, de quo inter Fluvios, ordiar.
units.tr: Since I am going to deal with particulars, I shall begin with the Panaro, among the rivers.

units.la: Quo loco is Padum ingreditur, Castrum est Ferrariensium Principum, Bondenum; olim, uti censet Blondus, Bodincomagum, quod & Industria vocabatur tempore Plinij, ubi, ut ipse inquit, præcipua Padi altitudo incipiebat; lingua Ligurum Bodincum vocari scribens Padum, quod fundo careret: sequius sentiunt alij, inter quos Marius Niger & Leander Albertus. Quidquid sit, Bondenum Opidum est satis lautum; superioribus annis ab Leonis x P. M. milite occupatum; post autem cIↄ Iↄ xxI ab Alfonso Atestino, Ferrariæ Duce, recuperatum.
units.tr: At the place where it enters the Po stands the castle of the princes of Ferrara, Bondeno. Formerly, as Blondus thinks, it was Bodincomagus, which was also called Industria in the time of Pliny, where, as he himself says, the greatest depth of the Po began. Pliny writes that the Ligurians called the Po Bodincus, because it has no bottom; but others think otherwise, among them Marius Niger and Leander Albertus. Whatever the truth, Bondeno is a fairly handsome town. In earlier years it was occupied by the soldiers of Pope Leo X; but afterwards, in 1521, it was recovered by Alfonso d'Este, Duke of Ferrara.

units.la: Ad dextram Panari ripam Castellum Finale situm, ab Mutinensibus conditum anno cIↄ ccxiii; Nicolai, Prædicatorij Ordinis Monachi, & Scipionis Balbi, quos sua scripta nobilitarunt, patria.
units.tr: On the right bank of the Panaro lies the Castello Finale, founded by the Modenese in 1213. It was the native place of Nicolò, a Dominican friar, and Scipione Balbi, who have made it famous by their writings.

units.la: Haud procul inde Bon-Portus, Fossæ Mutinensis spectans cum Panaro commissionem.
units.tr: Not far from there is Bon-Portus, facing the Modenese canal where it meets the Panaro.

units.la: Fossæ ripam pergenti offert se Mutina: Livio multis locis, Ciceroni in Epistolis ad Cassium, Tacito, Plinio, Silio Italico, Floro in Spartac. bello, Pomponio Melæ, aliisque nota: Inscriptionibus item, Mutinensi, apud Carolum Sigonium de antiquo iure Italiæ: * Q. AMBILIVS. T. F. POL. TIRO. MVTIN. MILES. COHORT. VII. PR. 7. GRÆCINI. VIXIT. ANN. XXXII. MILITAVIT. ANN. XII. Romanæ, in ædibus Colorianis. M. BALLONIO. M. F. POL. PAVLLO MVTINA MIL. COH. X. PR. 7 FRONTONIS. MIL ANN. VIIII. VIX. ANN XXXVI. T. P. I
units.tr: As one goes along the bank of the canal, Mutina presents itself. It is known from many passages in Livy, from Cicero in his letters to Cassius, from Tacitus, Pliny, Silius Italicus, Florus in his account of the Spartacus war, Pomponius Mela, and others. It is also known from inscriptions from Modena, given by Carlo Sigonio in his work on the ancient law of Italy: * Quintus Ambilius, son of Titus, of the Pollian tribe, Tiro, soldier of Mutina, of the seventh cohort, century of Graecinus, lived 32 years, served 12 years. At Rome, in the Coloriani house. Marcus Ballonius, son of Marcus, of the Pollian tribe, Paullus, of Mutina, soldier of the tenth cohort, century of Fronto, soldier for 9 years, lived 36 years.

units.la: Mutina quibusdam Antonini Codicibus: Μότινα Dioni libro LXIV, Straboni lib. v, Appiano Alexandrino libro III & v bellorum Civilium, Ptolemæo. Vulgo Modena à movendo, ut quidam intulse conjiciunt; eo quod diluvio quondam tota fuerit submersa; qua de re dignus auctore suo Versiculus, Mutina submersa fuit olim gurgitus unda:
units.tr: In some Antonine codices it is called Mutina; in Dio, book 64, in Strabo book 5, in Appian of Alexandria, Civil Wars books 3 and 5, and in Ptolemy it is called Μότινα [Motina]. The vulgar name is Modena, from movere (to move), as some conjecture, because it was once entirely submerged by a flood; on this matter there is a verse worth its author: "Mutina was once submerged by the waves of a whirlpool."

units.la: vel quod ab veteris Vrbis, quam Langobardi omnino delerunt, vestigiis hodie nonnihil sit remota. Ptolemæo Galliæ Togatæ Vrbs: Plinio in Octava Regione. Sita est haud procul Apennino. Attingit eam Formigo torrens. Olim altiore versus Montes fuit loco; docentibus id veterum ædificiorum vestigiis. Lauta est & splendida. Fores Ecclesiæ Cathedralis admirandæ sunt, cum ob alia, tum ob insignes Adami Evæque ex marmore statuas. Episcopatus floret dignitate. Academiam habet non ignobilem, in qua docuit Azo Iuris-consultus, qui se iuris arcana in hac Vrbe reserasse scribit ad l. unicam C. de stud. liberal. art. Vrb., Rom. & Constantinopol. Quomodo autem eo venerit, explicat ad Titul. C. de Municip. & Originar. his verbis: Quum essem Pononiæ, ibique iuris præcepta compluribus Auditoribus traderem, cursumque mei magisterii fere in trienniun traherem, quodam die occurrit mihi Mutina, quæ Iuris adamantes semper diligere consuevit, benignissimoque vultu talibus me adloquuta est: Quid hic facis Iuvenis? quur tantis & tam importabilibus injuriis agitaris? non convenit adolescentiæ tuæ tam graves tamque adsiduas molestias sustinere: accede igitur ad me, quum tui similes consuevi dulciter affectuosque amplecti, & te ac socios tuos ab his omnibus liberato. Statimque mihi prope centum marcas obtulit argenti pro munere. Cui petitioni vix post multas contentiones tamen adnui, & me ad ipsam iturum promisi, &c. Bononienses vero quum hoc intelligerent, veluti aliud agentes, decrevisse ait, ne quis suorum Professorum proximo biennio extra Bononiam iurisprudentiam doceret. Ipse tamen Mutinam profectus, non solum viva voce plurimos erudivit, verum etiam in tres posteriores libros Codicis Commentaria conscripsit. Dedit Mutina Herculem Rangonum ab Leone x; Iacobum Sadoletum, Virum exquisitæ eruditionis, Gregorium Cortesium ex Ordine Benedictinorum, Thomam Badiam, Sodalitatis Prædicatorum, a Paullo III P. M. Cardinales lectos. Nobilis est & Karolo Sigonio Viro doctissimo, magnoque Historico. Genitrix item Ygonis Rangoni, Regiensium Præsulis; Francisci Mariæ Molzæ, Ioannis Francisci Furnij. Bellica laude celebres produxit Nicolaum Rangonum & Gerhardum; Hannibalem & Guidonem Nicolai filios. Multas habet nobiles Familias, in quibus præ ceteris inlustris Rangonum gens. Quod ad res gestas: Tusci, qui primum condiderant, expulsis, ab Gallis Boiis est occupata: his profligatis, ab Romanis; qui Coloniam eo, ut & Parmam duxerunt, anno ab V. C. 13 LXXI, Q. Fabio Labeone & M. Claudio Coss. Clare Livius lib. XXXIX. Ejus, ut Colonia, mentionem faciunt Polybius libro III, M. Tullius Philippica VII, Plinius libro III, cap. XV, Pomponius Mela libro II, cap. II. Obsedit in ea anno 10 CCXI M. Antonius D. Brutum; post ab Cæsare Octaviano, juvene adhuc, itemque A. Hirtio & C. Pansa Coss. liberatum; M. Antonio ibidem castris exuto & fugato. Mox inita ab eodem Octaviano, M. Antonio & M. Aemilio Lepido Triumviratus societate, male fuit habita. Magnis adfecta cladibus ab Constantino Magno, quod faveret Maxentio, post Victoriā est restituta; Sacrisq; Christianis susceptis,
units.tr: Or it may be named from the remains of the old city, which the Lombards completely destroyed, and which today lies somewhat distant. In Ptolemy it is a city of Gallia Togata; in Pliny, in the Eighth Region. It lies not far from the Apennines. The torrent Formigo touches it. Formerly it stood on higher ground toward the mountains, as the remains of ancient buildings show. It is elegant and splendid. The doors of the cathedral are admirable, both for other reasons and for the remarkable marble statues of Adam and Eve. The bishopric flourishes in dignity. It has a not undistinguished academy, in which Azo the jurist taught, who writes that he unlocked the secrets of law in this city, in the note on the single law of C. de studiis liberalibus urbis Romae et Constantinopolitanae. He explains how he came here, in his note on the title C. de municipibus et originariis, in these words: "When I was at Bologna, teaching the precepts of law to many students, and was drawing out the course of my teaching for almost three years, one day Modena met me, which has always been accustomed to love the adamant of the law, and with a most kindly face she addressed me thus: 'What are you doing here, young man? Why are you harassed by such great and intolerable injuries? It is not fitting for your youth to endure such grave and constant troubles. Come therefore to me, since I am accustomed to embrace sweetly and affectionately those like you, and free yourself and your companions from all these troubles.' And at once she offered me nearly a hundred marks of silver as a gift. To this request I scarcely yielded after much dispute, and I promised that I would go to her, etc." When the Bolognese understood this, he says, they pretended not to notice and decreed that none of their professors should teach law outside Bologna for the next two years. He, however, went to Modena and not only taught very many by his living voice, but also wrote commentaries on the last three books of the Code. Modena has given to the Church three cardinals chosen by Pope Leo X: Ercole Rangoni; Jacopo Sadoleto, a man of exquisite learning; and Gregorio Cortese of the Benedictine order; and by Pope Paul III, Tommaso Badia of the Dominican order. It is also noble because of Carlo Sigonio, a very learned man and a great historian. It was also the birthplace of Ugo Rangoni, bishop of Reggio; of Francesco Maria Molza; and of Giovanni Francesco Fornio. Renowned for military glory it has produced Niccolò Rangoni and Gerardo; and Annibale and Guido, sons of Niccolò. It has many noble families, among which the Rangoni family is outstanding. As for its history: the Tuscans, who first founded it, were expelled by the Gallic Boii, who occupied it; when these were defeated, the Romans took it, and in the year 571 from the founding of the city, in the consulship of Quintus Fabius Labeo and Marcus Claudius, they made it a colony, as they also did Parma. Livy clearly relates this in book 39. Polybius in book 3, Marcus Tullius in the seventh Philippic, Pliny in book 3, chapter 15, and Pomponius Mela in book 2, chapter 2, mention it as a colony. In the year 711 Mark Antony besieged Decimus Brutus in it; afterwards it was relieved by Caesar Octavian, still a young man, and likewise under the consuls Aulus Hirtius and Gaius Pansa, Mark Antony being driven from his camp there and put to flight. Soon afterwards, the triumvirate alliance formed by the same Octavian, Mark Antony and Marcus Aemilius Lepidus was ill used there. It suffered great disasters from Constantine the Great, because it had favoured Maxentius; after his victory it was restored, and having received Christian rites,

units.la: {y} ... susceptis. Geminianum Episcopum spectatæ virtutis Virum tulit. Ab Gothis ferro igneque vestata, ab Langbardis omnino est subversa deletaque. His ab Karolo Magno Italia ejectis, a quibusdam Civibus, quorum nominibus portæ fuerunt insignitæ, ædificari de integro quasi cœpit, remotiore nonnihil loco ab veteris Urbis vestigiis, quæ sui initio juris suæque potestatis. Romani solum nominis auctoritatem sequens, multa contra vicinos, præcipue Bononienses, pro Finibus suis gessit. Postea circa annum cIↄ ccLxxxviii Dominos agnoscere cœpit Atessinos, Ferrariæ Ducēs, voluntate Civium ipsiusque Præsulis: anno cIↄ cccxii Mirandulanos, auctoritate Cæsaris: anno cIↄ cccxix Bonacossius, Mantuæ Tyrannos, Guelphorum ope, vi coacta: anno cIↄ cccxxxi Pios, usurpato nomine primum Capitanci, deinde Principis. Hos sequuti rursum anno cIↄ cccxxxvi Atestini, Ferrariæ Marchiones, venia Pontificis Romani, qui imperarunt usque ad annum cIↄ Iↄx, quo Julius II. P. M. Urbem cepit, & Maximiliano I. Imperatori cessit, à quo deinceps anno cIↄ Iↄ xiv Leoni x P. M. pro decem millibus aureorum nummum pignori data. Anno denique cIↄ Iↄ xxvii, quum in Hadriani mole Clemens ab Cæsarianis obsideretur, Atessinorum armis est recepta, à quibus aucta ædificiis, mœnibusque & fossis munita, ad splendorem, qui jam nunc sensim excrevit. Hæc cum antiquis, Livio præsertim, novisque Scriptoribus, Blondo, Corio, Platina, Sabellico, Volaterrano & Leandro; tum ex ipsius Urbis Bononiæque Annalibus, paucis descripta. Mira Agri est fertilitas ab Frugibus, Tritico, Faba, & aliis, Vinoque optimo, quod Tribianum dicitur.
units.tr: ... received. It produced Geminianus, a bishop of proven virtue. Laid waste by the Goths with sword and fire, it was utterly overthrown and destroyed by the Lombards. When the Lombards had been expelled from Italy by Charlemagne, it began to be rebuilt afresh by certain citizens, whose names gave the gates their titles, in a place somewhat distant from the remains of the old city; at its beginning it was under its own law and power. Following only the authority of the Roman name, it waged many wars against its neighbours, especially the Bolognese, over its boundaries. Later, about the year 1288, it began to acknowledge as lords the Estensi, dukes of Ferrara, by the will of the citizens and of its own bishop; in 1312 the Mirandolesi, by the authority of the emperor; in 1319 the Bonacossi, tyrants of Mantua, by the aid of the Guelphs, by forced violence; in 1331 the Pii, who first usurped the title of Captain and then of Prince. After these, again in 1336, the Estensi, marquises of Ferrara, by permission of the Roman Pontiff, who ruled until the year 1510, when Pope Julius II took the city and yielded it to the Emperor Maximilian I, from whom it was afterwards pledged to Leo X, Pope, in 1514 for ten thousand gold coins. Finally, in 1527, when Clement was besieged by the imperial forces in the Mole of Hadrian, it was taken by the arms of the Estensi, by whom it was enlarged with buildings, fortified with walls and ditches, and raised to the splendour which has since gradually grown. I have described these matters briefly, drawing on the ancient writers, especially Livy, and on newer writers, Blondus, Corio, Platina, Sabellico, Volaterranus and Leandro, and also on the annals of the city itself and of Bologna. The fertility of the territory is remarkable, in grain, wheat, beans and other crops, and in excellent wine, which is called Trebbiano.

units.la: Per Padi lævam incedenti quinque à Bondeno P. M. Stellata Arx se offerr, ab Nicolao III Atestino, Ferrariæ Marchione, condita; ab Legionibus autem Julij II P. M. & Venetorum majore ex parte subversa.
units.tr: Advancing along the left bank of the Po, five miles from Bondeno, the fortress Stellata Arx comes into view. Nicholas III of Este, Marquis of Ferrara, founded it, but the legions of Julius II, Supreme Pontiff, and the Venetians largely destroyed it.

units.la: Succedit inde nonnullo intervallo Castellum Sermitum, Serminus, Blondo Leandroque judicibus, apud Antoninum in Itinerario.
units.tr: At some distance beyond this comes the castle Sermitum (Serminus, according to Blondus and Leander), which is named in Antoninus's Itinerary.

units.la: Hinc in Padi ripa recens Opidum visitur Roverum, lautum & elegans.
units.tr: From here, on the bank of the Po, one sees the recently built town Roverum, handsome and elegant.

units.la: Spacio, quod inter Panarum, Seciam, Padum fluvios, Viamque Æmiliam, nonnihil est opidorum, in quis non postremæ classis haud procul Finali, munitissimum est D. Felicis, de cujus Dominis variaque fortuna legendi sunt Corius & Leander.
units.tr: In the area between the rivers Panaro and Secchia and the Via Emilia there are several towns. Among them, not far from Finale and not of the lowest rank, the most strongly fortified is D. Felicis. For its lords and its varied fortunes, one should consult Corio and Leander.

units.la: Spectatur eodem situ locus, qui Adcolis Bocca Civitatis, quo loco quondam Ansa Regina fuisse perhibetur; agro, uti scribit Peregrinus Priscianus, Bondenino; testantibus id ingentium ædificiorum vestigiis.
units.tr: In the same position lies a place which the locals call Bocca Civitatis, where Ansa Regina is said to have once stood, in the territory of Bondeno, as Peregrinus Priscianus writes. The traces of huge buildings there bear witness to this.

units.la: Occurrunt inde post Campos Nacros, de quibus alibi, ingentia Arva, in quibus lautum honestumque Opidum Mirandula. Conditum fertur principatu Constantis Imperatoris, Magni Constantini Filij. Mens illa cum aliis, tum Francisco Pico, Joannis Pici Patrui Vitam scribenti. Primus auctor perhibetur Manfredus, qui Furide Constantij Filia clam in uxorem abducta, huc locorum confugerat; mox
units.tr: Beyond the Campi Nacri, of which I write elsewhere, there are vast fields, and in them lies the handsome and respectable town of Mirandula. It is said to have been founded in the reign of the Emperor Constans, son of Constantine the Great. This view is held by others, and by Francesco Pico, who wrote the life of his uncle Giovanni Pico. The first founder is said to have been Manfredus, who had secretly carried off Furida, daughter of Constantius, as his wife and had fled to this region. Soon

units.la: ab eodem Constantio, Aquileiam cum copiis cogitante, Eques creatus: indeque, recognita, Comes & Marchio factus, ibi auspicijs ipsius Castellum ædificavit, nomine ob admirabilem ejus rei casum Miranda imposito, quæ post Mirandula. Auxit brevi ea familia, ut paucis post annis Patres-familias in ea nobiles essent xl. Majoris partis nomina hæc sunt: Prendi parte, Lanfranco, Paganello, Manfredi, Pontio, Guido, Coslante, Azolino, Tossio, Aldobrandino, Arnero, Giovanni, Marcello, Constanzo, Corrado, Bonifacio, Matteo, Oderio, Egidio, Nevo, Opizzone, Roberto, Guasredi, Capino, Azzone, Cossantino, Baolo, Berardo, Artuso, Panaro, Lanzono. Ab ijs Curia Quarantula vocata est. Diu hic Principes egerunt Pici, à prima ejus conditione usque ad annum cIↄ Iↄ LVIII, quo Galeottus, Ludovici Pij filius, Mirandulæ imperio pro certis quibusdam in Gallia reditibus sponte cessit Henrico Francorum Regi. De his & pluribus consulendum Mutinensium Annales, Merulæ, Æquicolæ, Corijque Historias; Leandri Italiam, aliorumque Scripta. Sita est loco amœno, qui frumenti, vinique supra modum fertilis. Incolæ humani, venusti, liberales, tractandis armis strenui. Ex Pici celeberrimi & eruditione præstantissimi fuerunt Joannes Picus, & Joannes Franciscus Nepos.
units.tr: afterwards, by the same Constantius, who was then planning an expedition to Aquileia, he was made a knight. Then, having been recognised, he was made count and marquis, and there, under his auspices, he built a castle. Because of the remarkable chance of the event, he gave it the name Miranda, which was afterwards changed to Mirandula. His family grew quickly, so that within a few years there were forty noble heads of households there. The names of most of them are these: Prendi parte, Lanfranco, Paganello, Manfredi, Pontio, Guido, Coslante, Azolino, Tossio, Aldobrandino, Arnero, Giovanni, Marcello, Constanzo, Corrado, Bonifacio, Matteo, Oderio, Egidio, Nevo, Opizzone, Roberto, Guasredi, Capino, Azzone, Cossantino, Baolo, Berardo, Artuso, Panaro, Lanzono. From them the Curia Quarantula took its name. For a long time the Pici ruled here, from its first foundation until 1558, when Galeotto, son of Lodovico Pico, voluntarily gave up the rule of Mirandula to Henry, King of the French, in return for certain revenues in France. On these matters and more, one should consult the Annals of Modena, Merula, Equicola and the histories of Corio; also Leander's Italy and the writings of others. The town lies in a pleasant place, extraordinarily fertile in grain and wine. Its inhabitants are courteous, charming and generous, and vigorous in the use of arms. From the Pici, very famous and outstanding in learning, came Giovanni Pico and his nephew Giovanni Francesco.

units.la: Ultra Mirandulam altero lapide, in dextra Seciæ ripa Castellum visitur novi nominis Concordia, cujus imperium Pici Mirandulani multos annos tenuerunt. Excidit, cršo Ioanne Francisco, Galeottus Picus Ludovici Filius, anno cIↄ IↄXXXIV.
units.tr: Two miles beyond Mirandola, on the right bank of the Secchia, a castle of recent name is seen, Concordia, whose rule the Pici of Mirandola held for many years. It was lost when Giovanni Francesco was killed by Galeotto Pico, son of Lodovico, in the year 1534.

units.la: Æmiliam Viam versus pergenti supra Mutinam per dextram Panari ripam post VIII M. P. Sylibertum le offert. Opidulum non ignobile ad Rangones pertinens, olim Spinum Lamberti, uti testatur antiquæ notæ Codex, in quo vita Hadriani, à P. M. qui ex Gallijs redux hic obijt, periicripta servatur, in Nonantulæ Cœnobio.
units.tr: Going toward the Via Emilia above Modena, along the right bank of the Panaro, after eight miles Sylibertum presents itself. It is a not undistinguished little town belonging to the Rangoni, formerly Spinum Lamberti, as an ancient codex attests. That codex, which preserves the life of Hadrian, a Supreme Pontiff who died here on his return from Gaul, is kept in the monastery of Nonantula.

units.la: Quarto dein lapide Viniola est, quæ Luitprando Levitæ Papiensi libro II Histor. Nerola vocatur.
units.tr: Four miles further on is Viniola, which Liutprand the deacon of Pavia, in book II of his History, calls Nerola.

units.la: Succedit hinc Maranellum; mox secundo lapide Marenum; & in Apennini jugis 10 duodecimo ferme Pattanum, hinc quarto Lo.orttanum. Inter Montes Arx est. Sexto ab ea milliari Æmiliam versus Castellum Novum jacet: hinc quatuor millium intervallo Formigo: Altius Speciannum & Floranum sunt: item in Apennino Foitanum cum Turre Anserina.
units.tr: From here comes Maranello; soon, two miles on, Marano; and on the ridges of the Apennines, about twelve miles off, Pattano, and four miles from there Lo.orttanum. Among the mountains there is a fortress. Six miles from it, toward the Via Emilia, lies Castelnuovo; four miles from there is Formigine. Higher up are Speciano and Floriano; likewise on the Apennines are Foitanum and the Tower of the Goose.

units.la: Post illa rursum in Æmilia Via ad Seciam exiguum vicitur Castellum Marzalia per quam sursum procedenti occurrit Mareda, quintoque inde milliario D. Maria Saxatina Fanum, sic dictæ ab Saxula, nobili Castello, quod hinc quingentis abest passibus, ad Apennini radices, læva Seciæ ripa.
units.tr: After these, back on the Via Emilia toward the Secchia, a small castle is seen, Marzalia. Going up past it one meets Mareda, and five miles beyond that, the shrine of D. Maria Saxatina, so called from Saxula, a noble castle which lies five hundred paces away, at the foot of the Apennines, on the left bank of the Secchia.

units.la: In ipso Apennino haud procul Petra Bisoniana, Castellum est Busonia. Inde trium milliariorum intervallo Opidum est Negonum, agro Parmensi finitimum. 20 Succedit hinc Opidum Care, in Apennini, necnon Parmensis & Fiviciani Agri confinio situm: Sequitur mox Aquarium, Agro Mutinensi vicinum, medicatis aquis notum.
units.tr: On the Apennine itself, not far from the Petra Bisoniana, is the castle Busonia. Three miles from there is the town Negonum, bordering on the territory of Parma. Next comes the town Care, situated on the Apennines at the boundary of the territories of Parma and Fivizzano. Soon after is Acquario, near the territory of Modena, known for its medicinal waters.

units.la: Tertio hinc versus meridiem lapide Menatium est, alto in montis jugo, propter Apenninum.
units.tr: Three miles from here toward the south is Menatium, high on a mountain ridge near the Apennines.

units.la: Inde spatij tantumdem est ad Castellum Piolum: mille hinc passibus Lingoncium pagus.
units.tr: From there the same distance takes you to Castellum Piolum; a thousand paces from here is the village of Lingoncium.

units.la: Itinere deorsum ad planitiem, Seciam transgressis offert se nobile Opidum Carpi: quo fere loco Ἀxapμ Strabonis exstitisse centet Leander. Habuit eius principatum diu Pragens ex Manfredi & Euridis, de quibus supra, posteris.
units.tr: Going down by the road to the plain and crossing the Secchia, the noble town of Carpi presents itself. Leander thinks that Strabo's place called [Ἀxapμ] once stood near this spot. For a long time its lordship was held by the descendants of Manfredus and Eurida, mentioned above, the Pragens family (that is, the Pio).

units.la: A Carpis Nori succedunt, Arx olim munitissima. 30
units.tr: From Carpi come Nori, once a very strongly fortified castle.

units.la: Haud procul inde Corregium spectatur, honestum Opidum. Putant quidam hic Regiates fuisse, quos Plinius nominat lib. III cap. XV; ubi tamen Vegiates reponendos esse, suadet litterarum ordo, à Plinio cum ibi, tum aliis locis observatus. Imperium ejus apud Correggiam gentem; cui an ab Opido, an vero huic ab ea nomen, incertum est.
units.tr: Not far from there Correggio is seen, a respectable town. Some think that the Regiates were here, whom Pliny names in book III, chapter 15. But the order of the letters, observed by Pliny both there and elsewhere, suggests that Vegiates should be read instead. Its lordship belonged to the Correggia family. Whether the family took its name from the town, or the town from the family, is uncertain.

units.la: Eodem tractu, ubi Crustulus Taranæ fossæ commiscetur, Castellum est non magnum Regiolum.
units.tr: In the same district, where the Crostolo joins the ditch of the Taro, there is a small castle, Regiolum.

units.la: Est ibidem Gonzaga, Vicus, ubi splendidissima Gonzagarum, Principum Mantuanorum est Villa.
units.tr: There too is Gonzaga, a village, where stands the most splendid villa of the Gonzagas, princes of Mantua.

units.la: Hinc amplum, nobileque & opulentum Cœnobium D. Benedicti Podolironi, à Bonifacio Mathildis Comitis Patre conditum, & ab eadem Mathilde, cujus ibi sepulcrum est, auctum. Consulendi Platina in Benedicto x, Benevenutus Imolanus Commentationibus in Dantem, Bernardinus Corius de Henrici III temporibus, Æquicola lib. I Histor. Gonzag. & alij. 40
units.tr: From here comes the large, noble and wealthy monastery of D. Benedicti Podolironi, founded by Boniface, father of the Countess Matilda, and enlarged by Matilda herself, whose tomb is there. One should consult Platina on Benedict X, Benvenuto of Imola in his commentaries on Dante, Bernardino Corio on the times of Henry III, Equicola book I of the History of the Gonzagas, and others.

units.la: Post Transfimariæ vel Taranæ Ostium Luzaria visitur pagus: inde Guardistallum, duobus Conciliis sub Vrbano II & Paschale II P. M. nobilitatum; testibus Platina in ipsorum Vitis & Blondo lib. XIII Histor.
units.tr: After the mouth of the Transfimaria or Taro, the village Luzzara is seen. Then comes Guastalla, made famous by two councils held under Urban II and Paschal II, Supreme Pontiffs. Platina in their lives and Blondus in book XIII of his Histories are witnesses to this.

units.la: Vlterius in Padi ripa Brixellum occurrit. Sic Plinio libro III, Plutarchoque in Othone, Βεζελλον Ptolemæo, Tacito, Suetonio, Antonino, Paulloque Diacono vocatur, quod vulgo Bresello. Civitas olim, docentibus id apud Leandrum Ravennatis Ecclesiæ Codicillis. Captam ab Anthare Langbardorum Rege, æquatis solo mœnibus, tradit Paullus Diaconus, Eutropium continuans, libro XXVIII. Adeundus & Blondus libro VIII Historiarum. 50
units.tr: Further on, on the bank of the Po, Brixellum comes into view. It is called Brixellum by Pliny in book III, by Plutarch in his Life of Otho, Bezellon [Βεζελλον] by Ptolemy, and by Tacitus, Suetonius, Antoninus and Paul the Deacon; commonly it is called Bresello. It was once a city, as the documents of the Church of Ravenna, cited by Leander, show. Paul the Deacon, continuing Eutropius, book XXVIII, tells how it was captured by Anthari, king of the Lombards, and its walls levelled to the ground. Blondus in book VIII of his Histories should also be consulted.

units.la: Læva Lenciæ ripa Tannetum est. Sic Livio multis locis scribitur; iterumque Plinio, qui hominem ibi repertum ait CXX annos natum; Antonino, & Itinerariæ Tabulæ, inter Regium & Parmam locantibus: Tanetus, Polybio; Ταννου, Ptolemæo: vulgo Tanedo. Hinc Tanetani Populi, apud Plinium. Eversum ab Cesi Langbardorum Rege, scribit Paullus Diaconus. Restauratum formam, qua jam-nunc est, Vicique speciem induit.
units.tr: On the left bank of the Lenza is Tannetum. It is written thus in Livy in many places, and again by Pliny, who says that a man of 120 years was found there; by Antoninus and the Itinerary Table, which place it between Reggio and Parma; Tanetus by Polybius; Tannou [Ταννου] by Ptolemy; and commonly Tanedo. Hence the Tanetani people in Pliny. Paul the Deacon writes that it was overthrown by Cesi, king of the Lombards. Restored, it took the form it has now and the appearance of a village.

units.la: Ad eamdem ripam sursum versus, Monteecium jacet, & in medio Baniolum, Novilavia, Ad D. Martinum.
units.tr: Up along the same bank lies Montecchio, and in the middle Banzolo, Novilavia, Ad D. Martinum.

units.la: In dextra Secia Campus Cajanus spectatur cum Soleria: ex-adversum Monteccio, Ceritus vel Cheruinus, lautum Opidum.
units.tr: On the right bank of the Secchia the Campus Cajanus is seen, with Solaria. Opposite Montecchio is Ceritus, or Cherinus, a handsome town.

units.la: Iter per indicatam Seciae ripam continuanti Castrum se offert firmissimum, Ruberia, doctis Herberia a Bajardis, ut quidam volunt: ab Rubrus Parmenfibus, ut alii, condictum: varios expertum dominos, anno cio io xxiii pervenit ad Ferrariae Duces: inclutum Antonio Cadro, viro Graecarum Latinarumque literarum doctissimo.
units.tr: Continuing along the indicated bank of the Secchia, a very strong fortress presents itself, Ruberia. Learned men call it Herberia, from the Bajardi, as some want; others say it was founded by the Rossi of Parma. It has had various lords. In the year 1523 it came to the Dukes of Ferrara, famous through Antonio Cadro, a man most learned in Greek and Latin literature.

units.la: Æmilia dein via pergenti, dextra Seciae ripa omissa, Regium Lepidi occurrit, ripae Crustuli laevae adjoicum. Regium Lepidi M. Tullio Epistola ad Cassium, aliisque; Regium Lepidum, Tacito; Pήγιον Αἰμίλιον, Straboni lib. v; Pήγιον Αἰμίλιον, Ptolemaeo, cui Colonia Regium simpliciter Antonino: Hodie Reggio vocatur. Sincadipiratione scribendum monet in sua Orthographia Manutius. Forum Lepidi eo loco fuisse quondam notat Festus. Incolae Regienses, ab Lepido apud Plinium: quemadmodum Regini, ab Regio Julio. Urbs est lauta, nobilis, frequens: solo sita valde fertili, loco pulcro, amoeno, planeque regio, unde illi, quorundam judicio, nomen. Conditores feruntur Tusci, quibus, ut Livius & Polybius tradunt, ejectis occuparunt Galli; hique, Romani quorum auspicis Coloniam (legendus idem Livius lib. xxxv) eo duxerunt Trium-Viri M. Æmilius Lepidus, a quo cognomen accepit, T. Ebutius Carus, & L. Quinctius Crispinus. Ab Langobardis Gothisque vastatum, ut Italia profligatis, restauratum est circa annum 1000. Liberum fuitque juris usque ad annum 1100 ccl xxxvi, inde Comitum & Principum habere coepit imperio, primo Canossum, hinc Atestinorum, Caesarum, Regum Galliae; mox Pontificum Romanorum: in ie Foraneos, Salimbeni, Gonzagas, Galcatios, & Orthobonos habuit Dominos; a quibus ad Atestinos redit, ab his ad Pontifices; Hadriano vi morituo; rursum ad Atestinos. Adeundi Cornus parte ii Histor. Blondus & Antoninus in Histor. Placina in Vita Bonifacii ix, Sabellicus lib. ix Ennead. ix. Episcopatus floret dignitate. Nobilitarunt hanc Urbem D. Maximus, Episcopus: Guido Sapiranus, Philippus Callus, Jacobus Columbus, Carolus Rhinus, Franciscus Brinus, Julius Scarlatinus, luriliconsulti, Sebastianus Corradus. Latinae Graecaeque literaturae doctissimo; Bartholomaeus Crotus. Poeta. Celebris est Calcaribus, quae hic fabricantur venustissimo, ac etiam aliis rebus, quae ex ollibus confiunt supra modum polite. Ager per-quam uber, frumento, faba, hordeo, ceterisque frugibus; Vino item cum albo, tum helvolo abundans.
units.tr: Going on along the Via Emilia, leaving the right bank of the Secchia, one meets Reggio di Lepido, lying on the left bank of the Crostolo. Cicero in his letter to Cassius and others call it Regium Lepidi; Tacitus Regium Lepidum; Strabo in book V Rhegion Aimilion [Ῥήγιον Αἰμίλιον]; Ptolemy the same, while Antoninus calls it simply the colony Regium. Today it is called Reggio. Manutius, in his Orthography, advises that it should be written without an aspirate. Festus notes that the Forum of Lepidus was once in that place. The inhabitants are called Regienses after Lepidus, as in Pliny, just as the Regini are called after Regium Julium. The city is handsome, noble and populous, set on very fertile soil, in a beautiful, pleasant place, and on a flat plain, whence, in some people's judgment, its name. The Etruscans are said to have founded it; when they were driven out, the Gauls occupied it, as Livy and Polybius relate. Then the Romans, under whose auspices the colony was led there (see Livy again, book XXXV), were the triumvirs M. Aemilius Lepidus, from whom it took its surname, T. Ebutius Carus, and L. Quinctius Crispinus. It was laid waste by the Lombards and Goths, and when Italy had been ruined, it was restored around the year 1000. It was free and under its own law until the year 1100, 236 (?) and then began to be ruled by counts and princes: first by Canossa, then by the Este, the Caesars and the kings of France, and afterwards by the Roman Pontiffs. Among its lords were the Foranei, Salimbeni, Gonzagas, Galcatii and Orsini; from them it returned to the Este, and from them to the Pontiffs, and when Hadrian VI died, it returned again to the Este. Cornus, part II of his History, Blondus and Antoninus in their Histories, Platina in the Life of Boniface IX, and Sabellicus in book IX of the Enneads should be consulted. The bishopric flourishes in dignity. This city has been made famous by Saint Maximus, bishop; by Guido Sapiranus, Philippus Callus, Jacobus Columbus, Carolus Rhinus, Franciscus Brinus, Julius Scarlatinus, jurists; and by Sebastianus Corradus, most learned in Latin and Greek literature; and by Bartholomaeus Crotus, the poet. It is famous for the very fine spurs made here, and also for other goods made of clay, which are exceptionally elegant. The land is very rich, abundant in wheat, beans, barley and other grains, and in wine, both white and yellowish.
