units.la: Supra Viam Æmiliam ad Amnis Seciae dextram sunt, Lora Bassium que & sub Apennino Castellum Novum interque colles tribus ab Secia P. M. Castellaranum; & ulterius Carpinetum, Balistae monti vicinum; praeterea Toanum.
units.tr: Above the Via Aemilia, on the right bank of the river Secchia, are Lora, Bassium, and, under the Apennines, Castel Nuovo; between the hills, three miles from the Secchia, Castellaranum; and further on Carpineto, near Mount Balista; besides these, Toano.

units.la: Ab Ruberia, de qua ante, tribus P. M. non procul ab Secia spectatur Salvaterra: post in Apennino tribus supra Castellaranum P. M. Castellum D. Valentini, juxtaque Seciam ad primos Apennini colles Dinamitanum, & ulterius Casale Magnum.
units.tr: From Ruberia, mentioned above, Salvaterra can be seen three miles off, not far from the Secchia. Afterwards, in the Apennines, three miles above Castellaranum, is Castel San Valentino; and beside the Secchia, at the first foothills of the Apennines, Dinamitanum, and further on Casal Maggiore.

units.la: Haud procul inde Turricella & Scandianum, quod Opidi Dynasta Matthaeus Maria Bejardus, Civis Regiensis, Vir doctus inlustravit.
units.tr: Not far from there are Turricella and Scandiano, which Matteo Maria Boiardo, a citizen of Reggio and a learned man, made famous as lord of the town.

units.la: Sequitur altius in montibus Caranum, inde Cianum. Fuit hoc loco Naxeja, quae Ptolemaeo Galliae Togatae Urbs, testantibus id cum Nummis antiquis, qui hic inveniuntur, tum Rivo Luxuria, Rivo de Lufera, nominis memoriam, aliquo modo servante.
units.tr: Further on, higher in the mountains, comes Caranum, and then Ciano. In this place once stood Naxeja, which Ptolemy calls a city of Gallia Togata; this is attested both by the ancient coins found here and by the Rio Luxuria and the Rio di Lufera, which preserve the memory of the name in some way.

units.la: Succedunt inde Leviciaunm, Sarzanumi, & Castellum Novum.
units.tr: Next come Levizzano, Sarzano, and Castel Nuovo.

units.la: Ab Æmilia Via sursum prope Lenciam fluvium conspiciuntur Borzanum, Ad D. Paulli, Ammea, Mozadella; altiusque Gessium.
units.tr: Up from the Via Aemilia, near the river Lenza, can be seen Borzano, Sant'Paolo, Ammea and Mozzadella; and higher up, Gessio.

units.la: Iuxta sunt Arundinaria, Rhasena; propiusque ad amnem Canossa, munitissimum Castellum, de quo Blondus libro xiii Histor. & Platina in Vita Gregorii vii. Sunt co tractu quatuor Apenninicolles, in quibus totidem opida,ab Mathilde Comite fundata, Bibianellum, Castellum Vitreum, Mons Iamu, (Monte Zano) Mons Lucius, (Monte Luzzo) omnia sub ditione Comitum Canossæ.
units.tr: Nearby are Arundinaria and Rasena; and nearer to the river is Canossa, a very strongly fortified castle, of which Biondo (book 13 of his Histories) and Platina (in the Life of Gregory VII) write. In this district are four Apennine hills, on each of which stood a town founded by the Countess Matilda: Bibianello, Castel Vetro, Monte Jamu (Monte Zano), Monte Lucio (Monte Luzzo), all of them under the rule of the Counts of Canossa.

units.la: In dextra Parmæ fluminis ripa a Pado furtim versus litum est Colurnum, cui nomen ab Torrente Lurno, quasi, ut nonnullis mens, Caput Lurni, hic in Parmam, qui Urbem ab Suburbiis discernit, exeuntis.
units.tr: On the right bank of the river Parma, a little away from the Po, lies Colorno, named after the torrent Lurno, or, as some think, Caput Lurni (the head of the Lurno), which flows here into the Parma and separates the city from its suburbs.

units.la: In Æmilia porro Via, quinque ab Apennino P. M. Parmam est videre. Sic Livio, M. Tullio Epistola ad Cassium, Plinio, Antonino; Παρμα, Straboni, Ptolemæo, Agathio lib. v dicitur. Nomen illi ab Amne Parma: ex aliorum mente, ab figura, quod Parmam, hoc est, breve scutum referat. Ædificijs est splendida, plateis ornata rectis largisque; rebus ad vitam necessarijs affluens; Incolarum nobilitate, civiumque frequentia celebris. Situ est admodum plano, cœlo summe salubri; adeo ut Plinius Parmenses tradat, tres quidem annos cxx, duos vero cxxx vixisse. Eam neque hiems, neque æstas adfligit. Castrum habet munitissimum: Principum & illustrium Familiarum Palatia non pauca. In Foro satis amplo, Fons pulcerrimus; & Templum ad imitationem S. Petri Romani exstructum; Campana tribus impositá columnis; Turris persimilis Bononiensi. Separatur ab suis Suburbiis fluvio cognomine. Conditam ab Chryso Trojano, Pallantis Comite, & ab eo Chrysopolin dictam scribit Sicardus Cremensis. Albertutius libro de Urbibus Italiæ Chrysum illum Placentinum fuisse memorat. Notat Isidorus Clarius pleraque ibi Familias ab Romanis originem trahere. Patria Casfy Poeta, & Mairoby. Genuit & Parma Blasium, excellentem Philosophum & Astrologum; Albertum Galeottum, Bernardum Parmensem, Gulielmum Aremundum, Iacobum Arenanum, Iurisconsultos, Scriptis claros: Gerardum Blancum, Cardinalem circa annum cIↄ cc lxxx; Guidantonium Arcimboldum, Mediolani Archiepiscopum, & inde Cardinalem; Hieronymum Palavicinum, Laudensem Antistitem, Bernardum Rubrium, Tarvisinum Episcopum: Ioannem, Generalem Ministrum Ordinis Minorum, & Ioannem, Prædicatorij Ordinis Menachum; Theologos, scriptis celebres: Gregorium Anselmum, Medicum & Philosophum: item Antonium Camaldulensem, Græcæ Latinæque litteraturæ doctissimum, Franciscum Marium Grapaldum, Thadeum Volettum, Nicolaum Brucium, Franciscum Carpesanum. Militares Viros dedit cum primis Rubrios; puta, Orlandum, Petrum, Petrum Mariam, Guidonem. Episcopatus floret titulo. Incolæ venusti, nobiles, Martij, animosi, genio ingenioque præstantes. De ijs Iulius Cæsar Scaliger: Inventum medijs præclarum nomen in armis, Prædita quo sit gens igna Marte docet. Ingenium rapidum facili flammatur ab ira; Sed viget in patulo pectore purus amor. Magnanimo precium est non displicuisse pudori, Hoc satis officio cedere turpe putat.
units.tr: Further along the Via Aemilia, five miles from the Apennines, is Parma. It is so called by Livy, by Cicero in his letter to Cassius, by Pliny and by Antoninus; Strabo, Ptolemy and Agathias (book 5) call it Parma [Παρμα]. The name comes from the river Parma; others think it comes from its shape, because it resembles a parma, that is, a small round shield. It is splendid in its buildings, adorned with straight and wide streets, abundant in the necessities of life, and famous for the nobility of its inhabitants and the number of its citizens. It lies on very level ground and has an extremely healthy climate, so much so that Pliny reports that Parmenses have lived, some three hundred years, others a hundred and thirty. Neither winter nor summer troubles it. It has a very strong citadel and not a few palaces of princes and illustrious families. In the fairly large forum there is a very beautiful fountain, and a temple built in imitation of St Peter's at Rome; a bell hung on three columns; and a tower very like that of Bologna. It is separated from its suburbs by a river of the same name. Sicardus of Cremona writes that it was founded by Chrysus the Trojan, Count of Pallas, and called Chrysopolis after him. Albertutius, in his book on the cities of Italy, records that this Chrysus was the one from Piacenza. Isidoro Clario notes that many of the families there trace their origin to the Romans. Native to Parma were the poet Casfy and Mairoby. Parma also produced Blasius, an excellent philosopher and astrologer; Albertus Galeottus, Bernardus Parmensis, Gulielmus Aremundus, Jacobus Arenanus, jurists famous for their writings; Gerardus Blancus, a cardinal around the year 1280; Guidantonius Arcimboldus, archbishop of Milan and afterwards cardinal; Hieronymus Palavicinus, bishop of Lodi; Bernardus Rubrius, bishop of Treviso; Johannes, minister general of the Order of Minorites, and Johannes, a Dominican monk; theologians famous for their writings; Gregorius Anselmus, a physician and philosopher; likewise Antonius Camaldulensis, most learned in Greek and Latin literature; Franciscus Marius Grapaldus, Thadeus Voletus, Nicolaus Brucius and Franciscus Carpesanus. It has given many military men, above all the Rossi: Orlandus, Petrus, Petrus Maria, Guido. Its bishopric flourishes in title. Its inhabitants are elegant, noble, warlike, spirited, and outstanding in talent and wit. Of them Julius Caesar Scaliger says: "A famous name, found among the middle peoples in arms, the nation endowed with fire shows by its warlike spirit. Their wit is quick and kindled by easy anger, but a pure love thrives in an open heart. It is worth much to a great soul not to have displeased honour; it thinks it shameful to yield to such a duty."

units.la: Dendrophori Parmenses nominantur in Inscriptione, quæ in ipsorum opido mutila: PRÆF. LEG. XX. VALEN VICTR. PRIMIP. LEG X. GEM. PIÆ. FIDEL CENT. LEGION. III. SCY THICÆ. XI. CLAVD. XIIII. GEM VII. GEM PATR. MVNICIPIORVM. FORODRVENT. ET. FORO NOVANTR. PATR. COLLEGIOR. FABR. ET. CENT ET. DENDROPHOR. PARMENS. COL. CENT. MERENTI EXERCITORES. RATIVM. VLPIAN
units.tr: The Dendrophori of Parma are named in an inscription, which is damaged in their town: "Prefect of the legion XX Valeria Victrix; Primigenia of the legion X Gemina Pia Fidelis; of the century of the legion III Scythica; XI Claudia; XIIII Gemina; VII Gemina; of the Patrons of the Municipia, of the Forum Druentinum and of the Forum Novanorum; Patrons of the Colleges of the Smiths and of the Centuries; and of the Dendrophori of Parma, Colony; to the deserving century of the Exercitores, Accounts, Ulpian..."

units.la: Ab Thuscis, ut multæ his locis aliæ Civitates, condita, à Boys inde possessa, lapsu temporis Romanos habuit Dominos: qui anno 1 LXX, quo tempore Mutinam, eo Coloniam, ut Livius tradit libro xxxix, duxerunt. Calamitatem ab L. Antonio inlatam deplorat M. Tullius Philippica ultima. Conlapsa, auctoritate Romani nominis libera cum aliis coepit esse: sequuta nunc Cæsares, nunc Pontifices Romanos, Bononienfibus semper amica & conjuncta. Gravem passa est totum biennium obsidionem ab Friderico 11 Imp. circa annum cIↄ ccxlviii, quod partium esset Pontificiarum. Eo inde profligato, varios habuit Regulos, Corregios, Scaligeros, Atestinos, Vicecomites, Galeatios, Sforzas, Gallos denique, quibus cum sæpe de Urbis dominatu certavit Pontifex Romanus, qui ope & auxilio Karoli v Imperatoris, Gallis tota Italia pulsis, rerum solus deinceps in Urbe est potitus. Hodie suos habet Duces, quorum primus à Pontifice Maximo institutus est Petrus Aloysius Farnesius, Pauli 111 P. M. Filius, quo crudeliter intra biennium cæso, subrogatus est Octavius Filius, eique defuncto Alexander, Belgicæ Gubernator; cui mortuo sitæcessit ante aliquot annos Filius. Legendi Pandulphus Collenutius lib. iiii. Histor. Regni Neapolitani. Blondus libro viii. Historiar. Platina in Vita Innocentij iiii, Merula libro iv & viii Histor. Sabellicus, & alij. Haud procul Urbe Amphitheatrum fuit, ut Agathius refert libro i Belli Gothici. Ager suburbicarius amœnus est, & frugum vitiumque optimarum fertilis, aquis medicatis pascuisque lætissimis felix: cujus Cascus & Vellera summam merentur commendationem. Laudat Vellera Martialis: Tondet & innumeros Gallica Parma greges.
units.tr: Founded by the Tuscans, as many other cities in these parts were, and then possessed by the Boii, it came over time under the Romans, who in the year 570 of the city, when they led a colony there as Livy reports (book 39), took Mutina as well. Marcus Tullius, in his last Philippic, laments the disaster brought upon it by Lucius Antonius. Having been ruined, it began to be free with the others by the authority of the Roman name; afterwards it followed now the Caesars, now the Roman Pontiffs, always friendly and allied with the Bolognese. It suffered a grievous siege for two whole years by Frederick II, Emperor, around the year 1248, because it was on the side of the Papal party. When that was overthrown, it had various petty lords: Corregi, Scaligeri, Estensi, Visconti, Gonzaga, Sforza, and finally French rulers, for whom the Roman Pontiff often contended over lordship of the city. With the help and support of the Emperor Charles V, the French having been driven out of all Italy, the Roman Pontiff afterwards alone held power in the city. Today it has its own Dukes, the first of whom was appointed by the Supreme Pontiff, Pietro Luigi Farnese, son of Pope Paul III, who was cruelly murdered within two years; Ottavio, his son, succeeded him, and after his death Alessandro, governor of the Netherlands; when he died, some years ago his son succeeded. Read Pandolfo Collenuccio, book 4 of his History of the Kingdom of Naples; Biondo, book 8 of his Histories; Platina, in the Life of Innocent IV; Merula, books 4 and 8 of his Histories; Sabellico and others. Not far from the city there was an amphitheatre, as Agathias reports in book 1 of his History of the Gothic War. The suburban territory is pleasant, fertile in crops and the best vines, favoured by healthy waters and very rich pastures; its cheese and wool deserve the highest praise. Martial praises the wool: "The Gallic Parma shears countless flocks."

units.la: Idem, censuram instituens Lanarum: Velleribus primis Appulia, Parma secundis Nobilis, Altinum tertia laudat ovis.
units.tr: The same poet, in drawing up a ranking of wools: "Apulia takes the first fleeces, noble Parma the second, and Altinum praises the sheep of the third rank."

units.la: Lanam Gallicanam vocat M. Terentius Varro lib. viii de lingua Latina.
units.tr: Marcus Terentius Varro, in book 8 of his work on the Latin language, calls it Gallic wool.

units.la: Supra Viam Æmiliam ad lævam Lenciæ ripam Guardasanum visitur: & ulterius in Apennino ad fontem Amnis Relvedertum.
units.tr: Above the Via Aemilia, on the left bank of the Lenza, Guardasone is seen; and further on in the Apennines, at the source of the river, Relvedere.

units.la: Altius ultra Bagantiam torrentem & Parmam fluvium Zisanum occurrit; & ad Parmæ initia Berzum,
units.tr: Higher up, beyond the Baganza torrent and the river Parma, Zisa comes into view; and at the beginning of the Parma, Berzo.

units.la: Iacet in læva Tari amnis Carona: ulterius Forum Novum.
units.tr: On the left of the river Taro lies Carona; further on, Forum Novum.

units.la: Remotiore loco ad dextram Bagantiæ ripam Cafecum se offert, & in Tari læva Petra Maliana: hinc Belfortium; & in Apennino Cajale: ad Tari denique fontem Castellum Zizs.
units.tr: Somewhat further off, on the right bank of the Baganza, Cafecchio presents itself; and on the left of the Taro, Pietra Maliana; from here Belforte; and in the Apennines Cagliale; finally, at the source of the Taro, the castle Zizzo.

units.la: Ab Tari ostio pergenti læva Padi ripa Castellum occurrit Arx Alba; dein Regariola: inde ad Lardæ ostium Polescum; mox Caput Vrsi.
units.tr: Going from the mouth of the Taro along the left bank of the Po, a castle appears, Arx Alba; then Regarola; from there, at the mouth of the Larda, Polesco; soon after, Caput Ursi.

units.la: Dextra Tari ripa sursum D. Secundi Castrum est cum Arce valida: altius Grumum & Nasetum adparent.
units.tr: Up the right bank of the Taro is the castle of San Secondo with a strong citadel; higher up, Gruno and Naseto come into view.

units.la: Supra Leciam torrentem Borbum, Copianum, Mons Arsinus, D. Maria visuntur.
units.tr: Above the Lecchia torrent appear Borbo, Copiano, Monte Arsino and Santa Maria.

units.la: Ad dextram Conij Amnis D. Andreas est: interque Conium & Sestronium fluvios Fontanellatum: iuxta Arx Lanzanum.
units.tr: On the right of the river Conio is Sant'Andrea; and between the rivers Conio and Sestrone, Fontanellato; near it the citadel of Lanzano.

units.la: Hinc, Æmilia via transita, Castellum Guelfum sequitur, ab Guelfis nominatum Conditoribus: Octavo inde lapide sursum Septonium falsum, ab aquæ salsæ fontibus dictum.
units.tr: From here, having crossed the Via Aemilia, comes the castle of Guelfo, named after the Guelfs, its founders; eight miles up from there, Salsomaggiore, so called from the springs of salt water.

units.la: In ipsa Via Æmilia Burgum est Sancti Domini: infra dein, Padum versus, Turricula spectatur.
units.tr: On the Via Aemilia itself is the village of San Donnino; below it, towards the Po, Turricola can be seen.

units.la: Rursus supra Viam Æmiliam Mons Lanzonus: & altius Varanum Malagrorum, Varan dei Melagri: utraque Viani & Apecium: hinc inter altos montes Landesium & Coparinum: mox Bardi: superius Teinm & Tamucola; juxtaque Conij fotem Casalestinum, Casaleio; item Rninum, Rovino; sub quo Carisium.
units.tr: Again, above the Via Aemilia lies Mount Lanzonus, and higher up Varanum Malagrorum, Varan dei Melagri; both are Viani and Apecium. From here, between high mountains, lie Landesium and Coparinum; soon Bardi; higher up Teinm and Tamucola. Near the source of the Conio lies Casalestinum, Casaleio; likewise Rninum, Rovino, below which lies Carisium.

units.la: Infra Viam Æmiliam in planicie dextra Sestroni ripa Sorania (Sorigna) jacet, Marchionatus titulo nobilis.
units.tr: Below the Via Aemilia, in the plain on the right bank of the Sestrone, lies Sorania (Sorigna), noble by the title of a marquisate.

units.la: Inter Sestronum & Longenam torrentem Castellum Novum visitur; & sub Via Gibellum, Oppidum à Gibellinis extructum ad Castelli Guelfi æmulationem.
units.tr: Between the Sestrone and the Longena torrent is Castellum Novum; and below the road is Gibellum, a town built by the Ghibellines to rival the Guelf castle.

units.la: Hinc ad Æmiliam incedenti altero lapide Buxetum se offert: ab Gallis anno cIↄ ıo xx direptum.
units.tr: Going from here towards the Aemilia, at the second milestone Buxetum presents itself; it was plundered by the Gauls in the year 1520.

units.la: Succedunt inde ad D. Columbanum; & in Æmilia Via Firenzola; ϑιδωδια Ptolemæo: Fidentia Livio lib. xxcviii & Antonino, uti volunt Leander & Georgius Fabricius. Videtur & Antonino dici alio loco Fidentiola Vicus. Hinc iane Fidentini Plinio.
units.tr: Next come D. Columbanus, and on the Aemilia Way Firenzola; Fidentia in Ptolemy [Φιδεντια]; Fidentia in Livy book 98 and in Antoninus, as Leander and Georgius Fabricius hold. It seems that Antoninus also mentions Fidentiola Vicus in another place. Hence also the Fidentini in Pliny.

units.la: Sequitur haud procul Apennino Visolenqum.
units.tr: Not far from the Apennines follows Visolenqum.

units.la: Ad Viæ Æmiliæ lævam in primis Apennini collibus Castellum jacet Arquatum: mille hinc passibus Vicus amœnus abest Luraniannum, Lugagnano.
units.tr: On the left of the Via Aemilia, on the first slopes of the Apennines, lies the castle Arquatum; a thousand paces from here is the pleasant village Luraniannum, Lugagnano.

units.la: Dein sub Æmilia Via Castrum adparet Curia Maior; spatio dehinc aliquot milliar. Pontinnurum, Ponte-nuro, à Ponte, qui Nurę fluvio ibi impositus. Per ripam hinc eius amnis secundam ad Monticellium devenitur. 18
units.tr: Then under the Via Aemilia appears the castle Curia Maior; after a few miles comes Pontinnurum, Ponte-nuro, named from the bridge built there over the river Nura. From here one reaches Monticellium by the second bank of that stream. 18

units.la: Æmiliam Viam transgressis prope radices Apennini offerunt se Roncoverium, Roverium, Nuceta, Torciaria, Feltinum.
units.tr: Crossing the Via Aemilia near the foot of the Apennines present themselves Roncoverium, Roverium, Nuceta, Torciaria, Feltinum.

units.la: Venimus tandem ab ostio Nurę secundum Padum, ad vetustam nobilemque Civitatem Placentiam, Sic Livio multis in locis. Cornelio Tacito lib. xv, xvii, xviii, & alibi, Silio lib. viii, Plinio, Antonino, Trebellioni Pollioni in Aureliano; πλακεντία Polybio, Straboni lib. v, Appiano lib. i & ii, Plutarcho in Vita Scipionis & Hannibalis, Ptolemæo, aliisque: quæ vulgo Placenza. Dictam volunt (inter quos Festus Alexandrinus) a Placentulo quodam Trojano, Conditore: deinde, ut notat Hieronymus Albertutius Bononiensis in libro de Civitatibus Italiæ, à Peucentio Gallo Instauratore Peucentiæ nomen accepisse. Aliis tamen magis placet à Placendo vocatam, ob loci amœnitatem, pulcritudinem, copiamque rerum omnium admirabilem. Veterem nobilitatem, inquit Ambrosius in Epist. ipso adhuc nomine servat. Iuxta Padum, à quo distat circiter M. P. jacet, loco peramœno; agrorum bonitate, Civiumque, inter quos Landi, Scoti, Anguiscioli & Fontani, claritate superbiens. Muri novi sunt; Propugnacula ampla, Munitiones insignes. Inter Plateas Farnesia principis est loci. Quod spectetur dignum est Monasterium novum, sumtuose nuper exstructum ab Philippo Hispaniarum Rege. Arcem habet munitissimam ab Duce eius t cœptam, & ab Imperatore Karolo v absolutam. Fons in urbe vetustus & limpidus, ab Augusto Cæsare nomen habens. Episcopatus gaudet titulo. Gymnasium habet omnium disciplinarum. Claros produxit viros varios: antiquioris notæ Tincam, hominem facetissimum, cuius in Bruto meminit M. Tullius, item L. Calpurnium Pisonem, C. Iulij Cæsaris Socerum: recentioris autem Gregorium x P. M. Americum, Vincentium Baraterium, Thomam Radinum, Theologos: Raphaelem Fulgosum, Iurisconsultum; Guilelmum, Medicum: Georgium Vallam & Ioannem Castronum, Græcæ latinæque linguæ peritissimos; Antoniam Cornaciarum & Nicolaum Fontanum, Poetas. Quod ad gesta: antiquissimum illud, quod Colonia legatur Romanorum. Ea de re sic scribit Asconius Paedianus in Pisonianam: In Annalibus eorum, qui Punicum Bellum Secundum scripserunt, tradi video Placentiam Coloniam deductam pridie Kal. Ianuarij Ti. Sempronio Longo & P. Cornelio Scipione Patre Africani cos. primo anno eius belli, Urbis 1 xxxxvi. Sex millia hominum, novi Coloni deducti sunt, in quibus Equites. Deducendi fuit causa, ut opponerentur Gallis, qui eam partem Italiæ tenebant. Deduxerint iii Viri P. Cornelius Asina, P. Papirius Maso, & Cn. Pompeius, alias Cn. Cornelius Scipio: eamque Coloniam iiii deductam esse invenimus. Deducta est autem Latina. Factum illud sub adventum in Italiam Hannibalis, notat Velleius Paterculus lib. i. Videndi & Polybius libro iii, Plutarchus in Hannibale, Plinius lib. iii cap xv, Florus Epitomæ libri xx. Meminerunt item ut Coloniæ Livius libro xxxi & Tacitus lib. xxix. M. Cicero in Pisonem Municipium vocat: Festus Municipium sui juris. Hanc Livius libro xxvii Populo Romano, quum bellis adflige retur Punicis, cum xviii alijs Coloniis subsidia contulisse memorat; frustraque ab Hannibale obsessam magis, quam oppugnatam; ac denceps, ut idem Livius docet libro xxxi, ab Gallis Insubribus, Cenomanis, & Boijs, exctis Salyis Ilnaribus, reliquisque Ligusticis populis. Hamilcare Pœno Duce, qui ijs in locis de Asdrubalis exercitu subsiterat, magna ex parte direptam atque per iram fuisse incensam. Instaurata denuo Nomini addicta fuit Romanæ, quamdiu majestas ejus, Exarchatusque Ravennatis dignitas fuit incolumis: quibus conlapsis, ad reliquarum eo tractu Vibium exemplum Gothicum & Langbardum, videndus Procopius libro iii belli Gothici, suscepit jugum; quo rursum excussoa cusso, captoque Langbardiæ Rege Desiderio auspicijs Karoli Magni, primum Italiæ Regum, deinde Cæsarum subjecta fuit Imperio: post libera quodammodo facta, sub hac constituta Imperij Romani, partim suorum Civium, partim Externorum dominatu oppressa, ut Palavicinorum, Landorum, Scotorum, Galeatiorum, Sforziarum, magna fortunæ varietate, suaque haud mediocri calamitate, ab Gallis demum anno MCCCCXCIX subactâ inde anno MDXII a Pontifice Romano, iterumque ab Gallis, quibus Italia bello Sociali profligatis Ecclesiæ Romanæ fuit restituta; licet ab Karolo V Cæsare aliquamdiu possessa, & per Præsides vicariosque administrata. Anno tandem MDXLV Ducem cum Parma à Paulo III P. M. ex Alosio accepit. Consulendi Merula, Cornus, Blondus, Sabellicus, Simonetta, Platina, &c. Pulcherrimum fuit extra Urbem Amphitheatrum, quod bello Orthoniano, uti Tacitus testatur, in acerrima oppugnatione conflagravit. Urbis ager vini, olei, frumenti, omniumque generis fructuum fertilissimus est, propter copiam aquarum: multos habens fontes, fluvios, rivulos, palcus irrigandis facientes. Placentini Casei, qui in omnem Europam exportari solitus, summa est bonitas, summaque commendatio: uti & Parmensis, atque Laudensis. Habet & Ager Placentinus aquæ tales fontes, ex quibus Sal candidissimum conficitur: item Ferri-fodinas, Saltuque venatu Ferarum aptissimos.
units.tr: At last, from the mouth of the Nura, we come along the Po to the ancient and noble city of Placentia, so called by Livy in many places, by Cornelius Tacitus in books 15, 17 and 18 and elsewhere, by Silius book 8, by Pliny, Antoninus, and Trebellius Pollio in the life of Aurelian; Πλακεντία [Placentia] by Polybius, Strabo book 5, Appian books 1 and 2, Plutarch in the Lives of Scipio and Hannibal, Ptolemy and others; commonly called Piacenza. Some (among them Festus of Alexandria) hold that it was named after a certain Trojan founder, Placentulus; then, as Girolamo Alberti of Bologna notes in his book on the cities of Italy, it took its name from Peucentius the Gaul, restorer of Peucentia. Others, however, prefer that it was named from placere (to please), on account of the pleasantness of the place, its beauty, and the admirable abundance of all things. Ambrose, in his letter, says it keeps its old nobility even in its name. It lies beside the Po, from which it is about a mile distant, in a very pleasant spot, proud of the fertility of its fields and the distinction of its citizens, among whom are the Landi, Scoti, Anguissola and Fontana families. The walls are new; the bastions large and the fortifications notable. Among the squares is the Farnese square, the chief of the place. What is worth seeing is the new monastery, lavishly built not long ago by Philip, King of Spain. It has a very strongly fortified citadel, begun by its Duke and completed by Emperor Charles V. In the city there is an ancient and clear spring, which has its name from Augustus Caesar. The bishopric enjoys its title. It has a university of all disciplines. It has produced distinguished men of various kinds: of older note, Tinca, a most witty man, whom Marcus Tullius mentions in the Brutus; also Lucius Calpurnius Piso, father-in-law of Gaius Julius Caesar; of more recent note, Gregory X, supreme pontiff; Americus, Vincentius Baratterius and Thomas Radinus, theologians; Raphael Fulgosius, jurist; Guilelmus, physician; Georgius Valla and Ioannes Castronus, most skilled in Greek and Latin; Antonia Cornacchiari and Nicolaus Fontanus, poets. As for deeds, the most ancient is that it is read to have been a Roman colony. Asconius Pedianus writes on this in his commentary on Piso: "I see it handed down in the annals of those who wrote of the Second Punic War that Placentia was founded as a colony on the day before the Kalends of January, when Tiberius Sempronius Longus and Publius Cornelius Scipio, father of Africanus, were consuls, in the first year of that war, in the year of the city 536. Six thousand men, new colonists, were led there, among them knights. It was founded so that they might be set against the Gauls, who held that part of Italy. The triumvirs who founded it were Publius Cornelius Asina, Publius Papirius Maso, and Gnaeus Pompeius, otherwise called Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio; and we find that this colony was founded in the fourth [year]." It was a Latin colony. This event took place at Hannibal's arrival in Italy, as Velleius Paterculus notes in book 1. See also Polybius book 3, Plutarch in Hannibal, Pliny book 3 chapter 15, and Florus, Epitome book 20. They also mention it as a colony: Livy in book 31 and Tacitus in book 29. Marcus Cicero in Against Piso calls it a municipium; Festus, a municipium of its own right. Livy in book 27 records that when the Roman people were afflicted by the Punic Wars, it, along with eighteen other colonies, gave aid to Rome, and that Hannibal besieged it in vain, rather than storming it. Afterwards, as Livy also teaches in book 31, it was ravaged by the Gallic Insubres, Cenomani and Boii, after they had driven out the Salyes, the Ilvates and the other Ligurian peoples. Under the Carthaginian leader Hamilcar, who had remained in those regions from Hasdrubal's army, it was for the most part plundered and burned in anger. Restored again, it remained subject to the Roman name as long as its majesty and the dignity of the Exarchate of Ravenna were unharmed. When these collapsed, it took upon itself the Gothic and Lombard yoke, as did the other places of that district (see Procopius, book 3 of the Gothic War). Again the yoke was thrown off, and with King Desiderius of the Lombards captured under the auspices of Charlemagne, it was first subjected to the Kings of Italy, then to the Emperors, and afterwards was made somewhat free, placed under the rule of the Roman Empire. But it was oppressed, partly by its own citizens and partly by foreign lordship, such as the Palavicini, Landi, Scotti, Galeazzi, Sforza families, with great changes of fortune and no small calamity to itself. It was finally subdued by the French in 1499, then in 1512 by the Roman Pontiff, and again by the French; when the French were overthrown in the Social War in Italy, it was restored to the Church of Rome, although for some time it was held by Emperor Charles V and governed through prefects and vicars. At last, in 1545, it received a Duke together with Parma from Pope Paul III, from Alessandro. Consult Merula, Cornus, Blondus, Sabellicus, Simonetta, Platina, etc. There was a most beautiful amphitheatre outside the city, which, as Tacitus testifies, burned in the fiercest assault in the Othonian war. The land of the city is most fertile in wine, oil, grain and every kind of fruit, because of its abundance of water: it has many springs, rivers and streams that make the meadows irrigated. Piacenza cheese, which is customarily exported to all of Europe, is of the highest quality and highest repute, and so too Parmesan and Lodi cheese. The Piacenza territory also has springs from which the whitest salt is made; it also has iron mines and woods most suited to hunting wild beasts.

units.la: Non procul extra Placentiam Vicum-Vis, Empotium, fuisse, paret ex Livio libro XXI.
units.tr: That Vicum-Vis, Empotium, lay not far outside Piacenza appears from Livy book 21.

units.la: Lœva Trebiæ ripa sursum Opida se pandunt quæ vernacule Ritualgare, Ponizza, Arvia, Riva.
units.tr: Up the left bank of the Trebbia lie towns which in the vernacular are called Ritualgare, Ponizza, Arvia, Riva.

units.la: Spectantur inde Raffiriane, Apeppian, Cela, Crosc, Boriano, Mombruno.
units.tr: From there are seen Raffiriane, Apeppian, Cela, Crosc, Boriano, Mombruno.

units.la: Dextra Trebiæ Roncomero & Robio (ubi nobile D. Galli Abbatis Cœnobium) Vmberti JC. ortu nobile.
units.tr: On the right of the Trebbia are Roncomero and Robio (where is the noble monastery of St Gall the Abbot), and Umberti, famous as the birthplace of the jurist.

units.la: Haud procul Organasso est, & altius Ottuno, cum Gioveno.
units.tr: Not far off is Organasso, and higher up Ottuno, with Gioveno.

units.la: Ad confluentem cum Avanto Algretiam Opidum jacet D. Joannis.
units.tr: At the confluence with the Avanto lies the town Algretia of St John.

units.la: Ad Apenninum dehinc Tarvelum est: ulterius Bosomasco; infra Albian & Stella; mox ad caput Copis amnis Bricolaro; dextraque Copis antiquum Opidum Classidium. Sic Livio libro XXI & XXXII; Κλασίδιον Polybio & Straboni; quod vulgo Chieseggio. Apud Plutarch. in Marcello male Καξιόν scribitur. Livius libro XXXVI uno in loco Legurum, altero Galloram dicit; propter vicinitatem.
units.tr: Next, at the Apennines, is Tarvelum; further on Bosomasco; below it Albian and Stella; then, at the source of the Copis river, Bricolaro; and on the right of the Copis the ancient town Classidium. So Livy in books 21 and 32; Κλασίδιον [Klasidion] in Polybius and Strabo, which is commonly called Chieseggio. In Plutarch's Marcellus it is wrongly written Καξιόν [Kaxion]. Livy in book 36 calls it Legurum in one place and Galloram in another, on account of its nearness.

units.la: Altius inde quæ vulgo Troncosara, Torre, Albiano, Pancaran, Nazzan, Vorco.
units.tr: Higher up from there are what are commonly called Troncosara, Torre, Albiano, Pancaran, Nazzan, Vorco.

units.la: Dextra tum torrentis Stafora lautum Opidum Poghera, Latine scribentibus Vicheria, quasi Vicus Iria. Iri a Plinio & Antonine; Ειρία Ptolemæo.
units.tr: On the right of the torrent Stafora is the pleasant town Poghera, which Latin writers call Vicheria, as if Vicus Iria. Iri in Pliny and Antoninus; Ειρία [Eiria] in Ptolemy.

units.la: Supra hein sunt Riva & Sessima.
units.tr: Above these lie Riva and Sessima.

units.la: Ad Curonem tortentem Opida spectantur, quæ vernacule sermone Ponte Curone & Casele, quod Frontino Cossium.
units.tr: Near the river Curone are towns that in the vernacular are called Ponte Curone and Casele, which Frontinus calls Cossium.

units.la: Succedunt ulterius Muleta, Castellazzo, Tauriga, & S. Cassano.
units.tr: Further on come Muleta, Castellazzo, Tauriga, and S. Cassano.

units.la: Iuxta caput Scrinix, qui Latinis Iria, Castellum Novum est, ab Gothis ædificatum, opulentum Opidum; Vincenty Bandelli ejusque Nepotis Matthæi natalibus decoratum.
units.tr: Near the source of the Scrivia, which in Latin is Iria, Castellum Novum, is a wealthy town built by the Goths, adorned by the birthplaces of Vincenty Bandelli and his nephew Matthæi.

units.la: Non procul inde Sale est Opidum, Gothorum item opus.
units.tr: Not far from there is the town of Sale, also a work of the Goths.

units.la: Hinc in Apenníni flectentis se jugi cubito Dertona Civitas est, non admodum formosa. Sic Plinio lib. III nat. hist. cap. V, aliisque Latinis Scriptoribus vocatur; Δερτῶνα, Ptolemæo; Δερτὼν, Stephano: Δέρτων Straboni; Tertona, in Libro Notitiarum: quæ Tortona vernacule. Tertrionensis Civitas, & incmendatius Tetrionensis legitur apud Paullum Diaconum. Condita perhibetur ab Ligaribus; vel, ut alij volunt apud Hieronymum Albertutium, ab Gallis, & ab his primum Antilia, deinde Tertona ad tribus domus, id est miraculis eius urbis denominata: quorum primum in Saxo, quod copiose oleum emittebat; secundum in Fonte, quotannis festo Natalis D. Ioannis Baptistæ largissime fluente; tertium, quod paullo ante, quam nobiles aliquot viri mortem essent oppetituri, panis sectus sanguinem stillaverat. Ego hæc in medio relinquo. Apud Plinium Colonia est Romanorum. Colonia Iulia Dertona legitur in Goltzij Thesauro. Ab Friderico Ahenobarbo Cæsare funditus olim eversa, post ab Mediolanensibus ad pedem collis in planitie recti-
units.tr: From here, where the ridge of the Apennines bends like an elbow, lies the city of Dertona, which is not very handsome. So Pliny calls it in Book 3, chapter 5 of his Natural History, and so do other Latin writers; Ptolemy calls it Dertona [Δερτῶνα], Stephanus Dertón [Δερτὼν], and Strabo Derton [Δέρτων]. The Book of Notitiae has Tertona, which in the vernacular is Tortona. Tertrionensis Civitas, and the less correct Tetrionensis, is read in Paul the Deacon. It is said to have been founded by the Ligurians, or, as others hold (Hieronymus Albertutius), by the Gauls, and at first was called Antilia, and then Tertona, named from the three houses, that is, the three wonders of the city. The first of these is a stone that copiously gave out oil; the second is a spring that flows very abundantly every year on the feast of the Nativity of St John the Baptist; the third is that bread, cut shortly before some noblemen were to face death, dripped blood. I leave these matters open. In Pliny it is a Colonia of the Romans. Colonia Iulia Dertona is read in Goltzius's Thesaurus. Once it was utterly overthrown by Frederick Barbarossa, and afterwards the Milanese rebuilt it on the plain at the foot of the hill. See Blondus, Corio, and the Annals of Lodi.

units.la: guta. Videndi Blondus, Corius, Annales Laudenses. In colle, qui Urbis Arx
units.tr: On the hill that holds the city's citadel...

units.la: ccm cem habet, Ædes est pervetusta D. Virginis Matris. Episcopalis est Sedes, quam praeter alios D. Martianus nobilitavit. Servari volunt corpus eius in Æde Do. Apolloniæ, Virginis & Martyris. Ager suburbicarius bonus & fœcundus, tritici, hordei, aliarumque frugum, vini item & glasti fertilis.
units.tr: has a very old church of the Blessed Virgin Mother. It is an episcopal see, ennobled among others by St Martianus, whose body they wish to be preserved in the church of St Apollonia, virgin and martyr. The suburban land is good and fruitful, rich in wheat, barley and other grains, and in wine and woad.

units.la: Post Dertonam in Montis jugo, dextra Servia Amnis, Opidum est Seravallis, sic nominatum, quod angustas hic montium Vallisque fauces, tamquam fera, clandat.
units.tr: Beyond Dertona, on the ridge of the mountain, with the river Scrivia on the right, lies the town of Serravalle, so named because here it shuts the narrow jaws of the mountains and valley, as a wild beast would.

units.la: Altius hinc Buffuta Insula, & ad Apenninum Totila spectatur.
units.tr: Higher up from here, Buffuta island and Totila are seen toward the Apennines.

units.la: Ad confluentem cum Pado Servicm Castellum quondam fuit Cibellinum, ab Matthaeo Vicecomite Mediolani Regulo conditum anno cIↄ CC XIII in Gibelina factionis gratiam.
units.tr: At the confluence with the Po there was once the castle of Cibellinum, founded in 1213 by Matteo Visconti, lord of Milan, to favour the Ghibelline faction.

units.la: Incipit dextra fluminis Tanari peramoena Vallis, longa M. P. VII, circa principium nobile Opidum quod vulgo Caresia, Latine loquentibus Garesium, olim Monf-Cardinus dictum, Marchionatus titulo nobile.
units.tr: On the right of the river Tanaro begins a very pleasant valley, seven miles long. Near its start is a noble town, commonly called Caresia, in Latin Garesium, once called Monte Cardinale, notable for the title of marquisate.

units.la: Transito Petriola Castello Vallis Fanasci occurrit, ab Opido Bonisco, quod ibi, dicta.
units.tr: After passing the castle of Petriola, one meets the valley of Fanasco, named from the town of Bonisco that is there.

units.la: Incipit mox a Tanaro peramoena & fœcunda Regio Mons Ferratus, sic dictus, uti censet Leander, quasi Monsferax, ab modicorum Collium, quos habet, fertilitate: vel a Ferro, similitudine quadam, quod uti Ferrum cetera Metalla vi ac duritie vincit: ita ille finitimos ubertate cum aliorum fructuum, eorumque nobilitate & suavitate, tum vero vini, longo superer. Fuerunt olim in hoc tractu septem Marchionatus, tum ab Othone II Imperatore instituti: Montis-ferrati, Ceva, Poncioni, Buf bi. Saluttarum, Savonæ, & Finarij, singuli septem filiis Alerami Saxonum Ducis adlignati. Montis-ferrati Marchionatum tenuit primum Palæologa stirps usque ad annum cIↄ Iↄ XXXIV: quo, defuncto San Georgio Palæologorum ultimo, Karolus V Imperator Mantuæ Ducem legitimum Montis-ferrati Heredem declaravit. Erectus fuit Marchionatus in Ducatum anno cIↄ Iↄ LXXV ab Maximiliano Imperatore, primusque Montis-ferrati Dux dictus est Gulielmus III, Mantuæ Princeps. Describit Montem-Ferratum Merula lib. VI. Antiquitatum Vicecomit. hoc modo: Mons est perpetuis expansus jugis, totus amoenus & fructifer, omniumque rerum ad vitam utilium fertilis, & colonis admodum frequens. Incipit diurno fere itinere ab Alpibus, planicieque separatur, quae inter hos Colles & Alpes intercedit. Nihil hic inculcum quidquam propter summam Sali bonitatem opportunitatemque. Lævam Tanarus, dextram Padus adluit, nec ullius alveum Regio egreditur. Quanto magis autem ab Amnibus abscedunt Colles, tanto maiores amoeniorcsque Campi inter eos panduntur, quos haud male Meiopotamiam queas dicere, quippe quod amnibus utrimque sint conclusi.
units.tr: Soon beyond the Tanaro begins the very pleasant and fertile region of Monferrato, so called, as Leander thinks, as if it were "Monsferax", from the fertility of its small hills; or from iron, by a certain likeness, because just as iron surpasses other metals in strength and hardness, so this region surpasses its neighbours in fertility, both of other fruits and of their excellence and sweetness, and above all in wine, by a long way. In this district there were once seven marquisates, established by the Emperor Otto II: Monferrato, Ceva, Ponzone, Buffa-lora, Saluzzo, Savona, and Finale, each assigned to one of the seven sons of Aleramo, Duke of the Saxons. The marquisate of Monferrato was first held by the Palaeologus line until 1533, when, after the death of Giorgio Palaeologus, the last of the Palaeologi, the Emperor Charles V declared the legitimate heir of Monferrato to be the Duke of Mantua. The marquisate was raised to a duchy in 1575 by the Emperor Maximilian, and the first Duke of Monferrato was called William III, Prince of Mantua. Merula describes Monferrato in Book 6 of the Antiquities of the Visconti in this way: "The mountain stretches in unbroken ridges, all pleasant and fruitful, fertile in all things useful for life, and very populous with farmers. It begins, after almost a day's journey, from the Alps, and is separated from the plain that lies between these hills and the Alps. Nothing here is barren, because of the great goodness and convenience of the soil. The Tanaro washes it on the left, the Po on the right, and the region does not leave the bed of any river. The further the hills withdraw from the rivers, the larger and pleasanter the plains that open between them, which one might well call Mesopotamia, since they are enclosed on both sides by rivers."

units.la: Quod ad specialiora: haud procul Tanari, Pado semiscentis, ostio Bassiniana cernitur, Bassignana vulgo: Plinio, Augusta Vagiennorum; Ptolemaeo.
units.tr: As for more particular places: not far from the Tanaro, near its mouth into the Po, is Bassignana, which is Bassiniana in the vernacular. Pliny calls it Augusta Vagiennorum, Ptolemy...

units.la: Circa haec loca Bondicomagum olim ad Padum fuit, cuius in Padi descriptione meminit Plinius libro II natur. hist. cap. XV, & in Ligurum Cis-Apenninorum commemoratione lib. III. cap. V. Unde dictum, alias notavi. Putat Leander fuisse, ubi nunc Odolengo: probans id ex antiqua inscriptione. Censet idem finitimam illi, in Mediterraneo tamen, Industriam fuisse, Plinio item nominatam.
units.tr: Around these places Bondicomagus once stood by the Po. Pliny mentions it in his description of the Po in Book 2, chapter 15 of the Natural History, and in his account of the Ligurians on this side of the Apennines in Book 3, chapter 5. I have noted elsewhere why it was so called. Leander thinks it was where Odolengo is now, proving this from an ancient inscription. The same writer holds that Industria, also named by Pliny, was a neighbour of it, though inland.

units.la: Antiquum hunc Opidum Valentia sequitur; Plinio Valentinum, quod & Forum Fulvij.
units.tr: This ancient town is followed by Valenza; Pliny calls it Valentinum, which is also Forum Fulvii.

units.la: Colli dein Pomarium insidet cum Arce. Haud procul inde Fraxinetum & Casale D. Evasij, Civitatis jus adeptum ab Sixto IV anno cIↄ CCCC LXXIV: Episcopatus fulgens dignitate: Sedes Marchionum Montis-ferrati. Duplex ibi Arx; Vetus, Marchionum quondam domicilium, & Nova, quam exstruxit Vincentius Gonzaga, Mantuae Montis-que Ferrati Dux, anno cIↄ Iↄ XC, quae vulgo La Citadella. Ortu superbit Othonis, ex nobilissima Alerami progenie, & Theodori Palaeologi, Cardinalium; Bernardi Romani, Primi Urbis Episcopi; Georgii Caratopici, Theologi & Philosophi; aliorumque. Consulendi Platina, Blondus, Leander, alij.
units.tr: Then Pomaro sits on a hill with its castle. Not far from there are Fraxinetum and the Casale of St Evasius, which obtained civic rights from Sixtus IV in 1474. It is a bishopric glorious in dignity, and the seat of the marquises of Monferrato. It has a double citadel: the old one, once the residence of the marquises, and the new one, which Vincenzo Gonzaga, Duke of Mantua and Monferrato, built in 1590, commonly called La Citadella. It takes pride in the birth of Otto, from the most noble line of Aleramo; of Theodore Palaeologus, Cardinal; of Bernardo Romano, first Bishop of the City; of Giorgio Caratopico, theologian and philosopher; and of others. See Platina, Blondus, Leander, and others.

units.la: In Tanari dextra Burgetum est.
units.tr: On the right bank of the Tanaro is Borgo.

units.la: Post Bassinianam mediterranei Colles undique nitent Opidis, inter quae, vernacule dicta, Monte Castello, Pavon, S. Salvatore, ubi Arx munitissima, Gerella, Suizan, Castelletto, Lugo, Monte Magno.
units.tr: After Bassignana the inland hills shine on every side with towns, among which are those called in the vernacular Monte Castello, Pavone, San Salvatore, where there is a very strong citadel, Gerella, Suizan, Castelletto, Lugo, and Monte Magno.

units.la: A Casali per Padi ripam pergenti multa occurrunt Opida Ponte di Stura, cum Arce valice valida: in colle dein, Camino, mox Galbiano, ab Gabieni Liguribus, quorum meminit Plinius libro iii, cap. xv conditum; intus supra Casale Fanum est D. Georgy; item Occimiano, antiqua Marchionum Montis-ferrati Sedes.
units.tr: Going from Casale along the bank of the Po, many towns meet you: Ponte di Stura, with a strong castle; then on a hill Camino, and soon Galbiano, founded by the Ligurian Gabieni, whom Pliny mentions in Book 3, chapter 15. Inland, above Casale, is the shrine of St George; likewise Occimiano, the ancient seat of the marquises of Monferrato.

units.la: Situs finitimo Borgo di S. Martino, Mon-Calvo, Galliano, aliaque sunt plura.
units.tr: Near these lie Borgo di San Martino, Moncalvo, Galliano, and many others.

units.la: Ad confluentes Bormiam Tanarumque Alexandria viitur, cui nomen ab Alexandro iii, P. M. cognomen a Palea: quod, quae nonnullis mens est, stramineam hic coronam Imperatores designati quondam accipere consuerint. Fabulae. Conditam anno clo c lxxviii mense Maio, notante unanimi consensu Blondus libro xv Histor. Merula lib. iii, Volaterranus libro iv Commentar. Urban. Platina in Vita Alexandri iii, Corius in Histor. Vernacula, Annalium Mediolani & Laudae Auctores; a Mediolanensibus, Placentinis, & Cremonensibus. Sita est inter duos Amnes, Tanaro suburbia divellente, amoenissimo loco, ubi quondam Roveredo. Incolae animi ingeniique excelli. Diu in Vicecomitum fuit potestate, post in Sforziarum; inde in Franciae Regum, quamdiu quidem illi Mediolanensibus imperarunt; nunc Regis Hispaniae subest ditioni. Calamitatem magnam passa est, quod Gallis favet, ab Francisci Sfortiae Mediolanensium Ducis cohortibus, anno cio io xxxii. Episcopatus gaudet dignitate. Ortu floret Georgii Merulae. Trans Tanarum medio ponte est Borgolium, ipsa Alexandriae suburbia, sic ab vico Borgolio dicta, qui ibi ante urbem conditam.
units.tr: At the confluence of the Bormida and the Tanaro lies Alessandria, named after Pope Alexander III, and given its surname from Palea (straw). Some hold that the emperors-elect were once accustomed to receive a crown of straw here; but these are fables. It was founded in May 1178, as Blondus in Book 15 of his Histories, Merula in Book 3, Volaterranus in Book 4 of his Commentaries on Urbanus, Platina in the Life of Alexander III, Corio in his Vernacular History, and the authors of the Annals of Milan and Lodi all agree unanimously; it was founded by the Milanese, the Piacentines, and the Cremonese. It lies between two rivers, the Tanaro separating its suburbs, in a very pleasant place where Roveredo once was. Its inhabitants are excellent in spirit and talent. For a long time it was under the power of the Visconti, afterwards of the Sforza, then of the Kings of France, as long as they ruled the Milanese; now it is under the dominion of the King of Spain. It suffered a great calamity, because it favoured the French, at the hands of the troops of Francesco Sforza, Duke of the Milanese, in 1532. The bishopric enjoys dignity. Georgius Merula was born there. Across the Tanaro, by a middle bridge, is Borgoglio, the suburb of Alessandria itself, so called from the village of Borgoglio, which was there before the city was founded.

units.la: Bormia transmisso, sursum, laeva ripa, Boscum est, Al Bosco vernacule, Marchionatus quondam titulo nobile. Monasterium ibi est Ordinis Praedicatorum, a Pio v. P. M. erectum, positis Inscriptionibus.
units.tr: Crossing the Bormida, upward on the left bank, is Bosco, called Al Bosco in the vernacular, once notable for the title of marquisate. There is a monastery of the Order of Preachers there, founded by Pope Pius V, and inscriptions have been placed.

units.la: Altius inter Bormiam & Burdam Incisa est: olim Ἀλσάνα Ptolemaei, Liburna Plinii.
units.tr: Higher up, between the Bormida and the Burdo, is Incisa: formerly Ptolemy's Alsana, and Pliny's Liburna.

units.la: Altero ab Alexandri milliari Marticorum visitur Opidulum.
units.tr: At the second mile from Alessandria there is visited the small town of the Marticori.

units.la: Supra Alexandriam est Nicea, Palea cognominata, cum Felicino honesto Opido; deinde Morum.
units.tr: Above Alessandria is Nizza, surnamed Paglia, together with the respectable town of Felizzano; then Moro.

units.la: Visuntur ulterius Castella Soierium, Quadringentum, Arx Annonis, vulgo Novi, & Arx Araffi.
units.tr: Further on are seen the castles of Soiero, Quadrengento, the Arx Annonis, commonly called Novi, and the Arx Araffi.

units.la: Moro Amne superato, Asta Civitas antiqua se pandit. Asta Plinio, Claudiano, & Cassiodoro libro ii Variar. Ἀσία Ptolemaeo; Vulgo Asti. Urbs nobilis, dives, frequens, splendida; sita ad Morum. Colonia est Plinio & Ptolemaeo. Patronum habet D. Secundum. Ortu nobilis est Conradi, Sodalitatis Praedicatorum Magistri, Theologi, Scriptis clari, quae in Bibliotheca ibi Praedicatorum. Primum in Vicecomitum fuit potestate; post dotis nomine ad Gallos pervenit; hodie conditionibus Pacis Cameracensis in Sabaudiae Ducis est ditione. Calamitates passa graves, ex contentionibus odiisque civilibus. Ager ipsi fecundus.
units.tr: Having crossed the river Moro, the ancient city of Asti opens up. Asta in Pliny, Claudian and Cassiodorus, Book 2 of the Variae; Ἀσία in Ptolemy; commonly Asti. A noble, rich, populous and splendid city, situated on the Moro. It is a colony in Pliny and Ptolemy. It has St Secundus as its patron. By birth it is that of Conrad, master of the Order of Preachers, a theologian famous for his writings, which are in the library of the Preachers there. At first it was under the power of the Visconti; afterwards, as a dowry, it came to the French; today, by the terms of the Peace of Cambrai, it is under the dominion of the Duke of Savoy. It has suffered grave calamities from civil strife and hatreds. Its land is fertile.

units.la: Haud procul Arvernus Francorum est, sic ab ejus gentis strage dictus. Consulendus Paullus Diaconus libro v. Histor. Langbard.
units.tr: Not far off is Arvernus of the Franks, so named from the slaughter of that people. To be consulted: Paul the Deacon, Book 5 of the History. Langbard.

units.la: Succedunt mox Guarnacum, Monticellus, ad D. Victoriam; & altius Pollentia. Sic Livio, Plinio, Silio, Prudentio, Claudiano, aliisque dicitur, quae πολλὰ Ptolemaeo, unico λ. Hodie Palanza. Dictam quidam volunt vel a praestantia nativi coloris vel a potentia: quoad laevam Tanarum haberet; stadiis lxxx ab Asta fluentem: ut scribit Corius libro iiii Histor. Liguriae adiacent Ptolemaeus: in Alpibus Cottii locat Iornandes. Colonia Romanorum est apud Livium, cum Pisauro, Mutina, Placentia, Parmaque deducta: M. Antonii conflictu nobilis, quo Cn. Planctus Cos. fusus & occisus; infausto item Stilichonis proelio, quod cum Alarico Gothorum Rege commisit, celebris. Legendi praeter alios Blondus & Sabellicus. Ager oves nutrit lectissimae lanae: Pollentinae Nigrae maximum pretium tributi.
units.tr: Next come Guarene and Monticello, at St Victoria; and further on Pollenza. It is so called by Livy, Pliny, Silius, Prudentius, Claudian and others, while Ptolemy has the many-lettered form with a single λ. Today it is Pollenzo. Some hold that it was so named either from the excellence of the natural colour or from its power: it lies on the left of the Tanaro, flowing eighty stadia from Asti, as Corio writes in Book 4 of the History. Ptolemy assigns it to Liguria; Jordanes places it among the Cottian Alps. It is a Roman colony in Livy, founded together with Pisaurum, Mutina, Placentia and Parma. It is famous for the battle of Mark Antony, in which Gnaeus Planco, consul, was routed and killed; likewise celebrated for the unlucky battle of Stilicho, which he fought with Alaric, king of the Goths. Among others, Biondo and Sabellico are to be read. Its land pastures very choice sheep: the black Pollentian wool fetches the highest tribute price.

units.la: Plinius. Laudat & Martialis: Non est lana mihi mendax, nec mutor aheno: Sic placeant Tyriae, me mea tinxit ovis.
units.tr: Pliny. Martial also praises it: "My wool is not false, nor do I change for bronze: thus may the Tyrian women be pleased, my sheep has dyed me."

units.la: Sic Silius libro viii de bello Poenico: Fuscique ferax Pollentia Villi.
units.tr: So Silius in Book 8 of the Punic War: "And Pollentia, fertile of dark fleece, of Villus."

units.la: Altius dein Ceva, Opidum honestum; Marchionatus quondam.
units.tr: Further up is Ceva, an honourable town; formerly a marquisate.

units.la: Itinere hinc Albam versus, mille quingentis ab ea passibus Rodum se prodit, Picorum Mirandulae Castellum. Sequitur ad lævam Tanari Alba. Sic simpliciter veteribus quibusdam dicitur, hodieque: quæ Alba Pompeia (forte an, quod a Pompeio restaurata) Plinio, cui inde Albenses Pompeiani nominantur. Sic Inscriptio apud Onuphrium Panvinium, qui Coloniam Romanam factam credit.
units.tr: From here, on the journey towards Alba, at fifteen hundred paces from it, Roddi presents itself, a castle of the Picards of Mirandola. On the left of the Tanaro follows Alba. It is simply so called by some of the ancients, and still today: Alba Pompeia (perhaps because it was restored by Pompey), in Pliny, from whom the Pompeian Albans are named. So also the inscription in Onofrio Panvinio, who believes it was made a Roman colony.

units.la: Q. MANLIVS. Q. F. CAM SEVERVS ALBA. POMPEIA
units.tr: Q. MANLIVS. Q. F. CAM SEVERVS ALBA. POMPEIA

units.la: Amplitudine superat Casalem D. Evasij; clementia cœli inferior. Marchionum Montis-ferrati prius, nunc Ducum Mantuæ subjacet Imperio. Episcopatus floret dignitate. Ager omnium fœcundissimus, qui Langvilla vulgo. Videndus Procopius libro 1. Goth.
units.tr: It surpasses Casale of St Evasius in size, but is inferior in the mildness of its climate. It was formerly under the rule of the Marquises of Monferrato, now under that of the Dukes of Mantua. Its bishopric flourishes in dignity. Its land is the most fertile of all, which is commonly called Langhe. Procopius, Book 1 of the Gothic War, is to be seen.

units.la: Haud procul Alba Opidum est, quod Acqui vulgo. Aquæ Statyellorum Plinio libro III cap. v, in Liguribus ponenti: Ἀκουαι Στατιέλλαι Straboni libro v: In vulgatis est, ἡ Ἀλβα ... ἐ Γενύα; legendum, Ἀκουαι Σταιέλλαι: Aquæ simpliciter Antonino ab Aquis proculdubio & Fontibus, qui hic sunt, calidis & medicatis: Sunt enim in hoc Opido Thermæ publicæ, cum Mensis lapideis & gradibus. Incolæ Statellates Livio, Ligurum populus facienti; Statiellenses M. Tullio libro 11 Epistolar. Hinc Statellas Ager Livio lib. xLII. Conditam ab Statiellis, Alpina gente, colligitur ex Plinio. Antiquitatem testantur vetusta mœnia. Olim frequens: hodie Civium dissidijs ad summam devenit calamitatem. Episcopatus gaudet dignitate.
units.tr: Not far from Alba is a town called Acqui in the vernacular. The Waters of the Statyelli, in Pliny Book 3 chapter 5, placing it among the Ligurians: Ἀκουαι Στατιέλλαι in Strabo Book 5. In the printed texts it reads, ἡ Ἀλβα ... ἐ Γενύα; it should be read Ἀκουαι Σταιέλλαι. Simply "Aquae" in Antoninus, undoubtedly from the waters and springs which are here, hot and medicinal; for in this town there are public baths, with stone tables and steps. The inhabitants are the Statellates in Livy, a people of the Ligurians making ... ; Statiellenses in Cicero, Book 11 of the Letters. Hence the Statellan land in Livy Book 42. That it was founded by the Statiellians, an Alpine people, is gathered from Pliny. Ancient walls bear witness to its antiquity. It was once populous; today, through the discords of its citizens, it has fallen to the utmost calamity. Its bishopric enjoys dignity.

units.la: Supra Aquas Opida sunt, quæ vernacule Bestagnano, Crutimilio, Carnilio, & Monteví, Latine scribentibus Mons Regalis, ab situ, qui in monte, dictus. Civitas mediocris, natura loci murorumque crassitudine tuta.
units.tr: Above the Waters there are towns which in the vernacular are called Bistagno, Cortemiglia, Carcare and Monteu, in Latin writings Mons Regalis, named from its situation, being on a mountain. A middling city, safe by the nature of its site and the thickness of its walls.

units.la: In Borbi læva Diano vicitur: & ad fontem, quo profuit, Canacchio.
units.tr: On the left of the Borbo, Diano is seen; and at the spring, which benefits, Cannero.

units.la: Sequitur inde Monte Calerio, Opidum cum Italiæ multis committendum.
units.tr: From there follows Monte Calerio, a town to be counted among the many of Italy.

units.la: Occurrit mox Cherium, frequens olim, sed bello inter Karolum v & Franciscum 1 misere afflictum.
units.tr: Soon Chieri comes into view, once populous, but grievously afflicted by the war between Charles V and Francis I.

units.la: Succedunt inde Villa Nyova, Puerino, Rovigliasco, Carmagnuola, Opidum ortu Francisci Buxonij, viri militaris, clarum.
units.tr: Next come Villanova, Pinerolo, Roccaforte, Carmagnola, a town, the birthplace of Francesco Buxonio, a famous military man.

units.la: Convicina sunt Carmagna, Foffano, S. Moro, Casalgrasso, Polonciara, Reconigi, Moretta, Rana, Savigliano, Lagnasco, Centale, Carade, ubi Pons Padi ripas jungit.
units.tr: Neighbouring are Carmagna, Fossano, San Mauro, Casalgrasso, Polonghera, Racconigi, Moretta, Ranna, Savigliano, Lagnasco, Centallo, Caraglio, where a bridge joins the banks of the Po.

units.la: Hinc sursum versus Salutium: Σαλύαι Ptolemæo, ut quidam centent. Civitatis jus largitus est Julius II. P. M. qui Episcopum Primus dedit Bartholemæi Roborei filium: ab eo tempore Episcopatus dignitate cœpit florere. Genitrix cum aliorum, tum Francisci Cavaciæ & Francisci Varcæ ICC. Calamitatem ingentem accepit ab Francisco 1. Galliarum Rege, anno MDXIII. De Principibus ejus Leander.
units.tr: Thence upwards towards Saluzzo: Σαλύαι in Ptolemy, as some think. Julius II, Pontifex Maximus, granted it the rights of a city, and he gave as its first bishop the son of Bartolomeo Roboreo; from that time its bishopric began to flourish in dignity. It has produced both others and Francesco Cavacia and Francesco Varca, jurists. It suffered a huge calamity from Francis I, King of the French, in the year 1513. Concerning its princes, see Leandro.

units.la: Haud procul Salutio sunt, quæ vulgo Verculo, Costilgole, Busche, S. Pietro, Castel Dolfino.
units.tr: Not far from Saluzzo are the places commonly called Verzuolo, Costigliole, Busca, San Pietro, Castel Delfino.

units.la: CAPUT XXXV. Langbardia Trans-Padana.
units.tr: CAPUT XXXV. Lombardy Trans-Padana.

units.la: Sic se habet Æmilia vel Langbardia Cis-Padana: offert se jam-nunc Italiæ Novæ, ejusque Planioris pars illa, quæ trans Padum Langbardia cognominari solet ab situ Trans-padana. Appellationis Langbardiæ causam hoc loco non repetam. Regionis Trans-Padana, universaliter sumtæ, mentio in Basi Statuæ, quæ in horto Ducis Vrbini: C. LVXILLIO. C. F. POMPT SABINO. EGNATIO PROCVLO. CN. CVR. RER PVBLICAR. PISAVR, ET. FANEST LEG. LEG. X. GEM. GORDIAN IVR. REG. TRANSPAD. CVR VIAR. ET. PRAEF. ALIMENT CLODIAE. ET. COHERENT LEG. PROV. ACHAIAE. PRAET AEDIL. CAERIALI. QVAEST PR. PR. PROV. CRETAE. CVR TRIB. LATICL. LEG. IIII FLAV PATRONO. COLONIARVM PISAVR. ET. FANEST
units.tr: Such is Æmilia, or Cisalpine Lombardy. Here now begins New Italy, and the part of its plain that lies beyond the Po is commonly called Lombardy Trans-Padana, from its position across the river. I shall not repeat here the reason for the name Lombardy. Mention of the Trans-Padane region in general occurs on the base of a statue in the garden of the Duke of Urbino: To Gaius Luxilius Sabinus Egnatius Proculus, son of Gaius, of the Pomptine tribe; curator of the public works of Pisaurum and Fanum; of the tenth legion Gemina; Gordian, judge of the Trans-Padane region; curator of the roads; prefect of the Clodian food supply; of the Coherent legion; propraetor of the province of Achaia; aedile; praetor; quaestor with propraetorial power in the province of Crete; curator of the Laticlavian tribune; of the fourth Flavian legion; patron of the colonies of Pisaurum and Fanum.

units.la: Regio hic ex distributione Octaviani Augusti, x 1, cui, ut ait Plinius, Maria cuncta fructuoso alveo important.
units.tr: This region belongs to the eleventh division made by Octavian Augustus, into which, as Pliny says, all the seas pour through their fruitful channel.

units.la: Fines Langhardia Trans-Padana ab Ortu Mincius & Sarca fluvij, cum dextra Benaci Lacus ripa; ab Septemtrione Alpes Italiam ab Helvetia separantes: qua Ocatus est, eadem Alpes Italiam ab Gallia dirimentes, ductu usque ad Varum linea: qua denique Meridies, magna Padi portio.
units.tr: The boundaries of Lombardy Trans-Padana are: on the east, the rivers Mincio and Sarca, together with the right shore of Lake Benaco; on the north, the Alps, which separate Italy from Helvetia; along the same line, the Alps separate Italy from Gaul, the boundary running as far as the Var; and finally, on the south, a large portion of the Po.

units.la: Totam Regionem his coloribus delineat Leander: Naturae luculentissimis dotibus varie locupletatam esse: Campos enim latissimos, & tritici, aliarumque frugum, item vini nobilis abundantia beatos habere: Lacus insuper immensos & altos, insignia Flumina, tam Piscium capturae, quam navigationi opportuna: felicem denique ibi esse ingenuorum excellentiam, quae cum ad litteras & arma, tum ad mercaturam promptissima.
units.tr: Leander sketches the whole region in these colours: it is richly endowed with the most brilliant gifts of nature, blessed with broad plains and an abundance of wheat and other grains, as well as of fine wine; it has, besides, vast and deep lakes and famous rivers, suited both to catching fish and to navigation; and finally its people are happily distinguished by their talents, being most ready both for letters and arms and for trade.

units.la: Habitarunt quondam hanc Italiae partem plurimae gentes, docentibus Livio, Strabone, Plinio, Ptolemaeo, Tusci, Cenomani, Insubres, Mesauci, Bechuni. Singulis certae quondam fuerunt Sedes; de quibus hodie nihil exploráti, nisi ex mera coniectura, tradi potest. Antiquissimi fuerunt Tusci, de quibus plene supra. His profligatis plerique, qui sequuntur, cum Venetis, Anamibus, Boiis, Egonibus, & Senonibus, qui suis locis explicantur, successerunt. Cenomani, Κενομανοὶ Ptolemaeo; Cenomanni duplici NN Plinio. Hos in migrasse in haec loca ex Gallijs, Thuscis ejectis, scribunt Polybius, Trogus, Livius. Facessant quae de iplorum origine fabulatur fabulosissimus Annius Viterbiensis Berosus. Eorum memoriam servari vult Chrysostomus Zanchus in suo de Orobijs libello, in oppidulo Bergomatis Agri, quod Cenum vocant in Valle Seriana. Insubres Livio lib. xxi & multis aliis locis, Tacito, Plinio, Fastisque Consularibus qui Ἰνσοῦβροι Straboni & Ptolemaeo: Ἰνσούβαρες Stephano: Padi adcolas esse & Ἰνσοῦβραι etiam dici, addenti Ἰνσούβαρες Polybio: sunt & Ἰνσούμβροι apud eundem. Leguntur quoque Ἰνσοῦβροι apud Stephanum ex Polybij x v. Scudus aliquę Mediolanenses interpretantur. Venerunt & hi ex Gallis, teste Livio libro v. Insubres Leander his quasi finibus circumscribit: ut ipsis ad Orientem sit Addua cum Lario: ad Meridiem Padus: ad Occasum Ticinus, ab Septemtrione Rheti Vennonetes. P. Iovius Insubriam Ticino amne claudi tradit, uberrimisque diffusam campis ad Abduam usque sese extendere, ita ut Urbs Mediolanum quondam Umbilici speciem praebeat. Mesauci Plinio noti lib. iii, cap. xix. Sedes ipsis proculdubio fuit in Valle, quae & nunc Mesauca, inter altissimos, asperrimosque montes. Bechuni, Βεχουνοὶ Ptolemaeo, qui Focunates Plinio: ut censet Hermolaus, in Valle Sulsia, cui ab Divo Bartholomaeo nomen, eos collocans. Leander Vallem Serianam colere notat. Fuerunt procul dubio & alij multi. Rhati Vennonetes, Cantiani, Camuni, Breuni, Taurisci, quos nonnulli superioribus addunt, pertinent proprie ad Germaniam.
units.tr: Many peoples once inhabited this part of Italy, as Livy, Strabo, Pliny and Ptolemy teach: Tusci, Cenomani, Insubres, Mesauci, Bechuni. Each once had fixed seats, and about these today nothing can be stated with certainty, only by mere conjecture. The most ancient were the Tusci, about whom I have written fully above. After these were overthrown, most of those who follow succeeded them: the Venetis, Anamibus, Boiis, Egonibus and Senonibus, who will be explained in their places. The Cenomani (Κενομανοὶ in Ptolemy; Cenomanni with a double N in Pliny): Polybius, Trogus and Livy write that they migrated into these places from Gaul, after the Tuscans were driven out. As for the tales about their origin invented by that most fabulous Annius of Viterbo, Berosus, let them go. Chrysostomus Zanchus wishes their memory to be preserved in his little book on the Orobii, in the small town of the Bergamo territory which they call Cenum, in the Seriana valley. The Insubres are mentioned by Livy in book 21 and in many other places, by Tacitus, Pliny and the Consular Fasti. Strabo and Ptolemy call them Ἰνσοῦβροι, Stephanus Ἰνσούβαρες; they were neighbours of the Po and were also called Ἰνσοῦβραι, as Polybius adds in his Ἰνσούβαρες; the same author also has Ἰνσούμβροι. Ἰνσοῦβροι is also read in Stephanus, from Polybius book 15. Scudus interprets them as some Milanese. They too came from the Gauls, according to Livy in book 5. Leander circumscribes the Insubres within boundaries such as these: on the east the Adda with the Lake of Como; on the south the Po; on the west the Ticino; on the north the Vennonetes of Rhaetia. P. Jovius writes that Insubria is enclosed by the river Ticino, and that, spreading out over fertile fields, it extends as far as the Adda, so that the city of Milan once presented the appearance of a navel. The Mesauci are known to Pliny, book 3, chapter 19. Their seat was undoubtedly in the valley which is now called Mesauca, between very high and very rugged mountains. The Bechuni (Βεχουνοὶ in Ptolemy; Focunates in Pliny): Hermolaus thinks they lived in the Valsassina, which is named after St Bartholomew, placing them there. Leander notes that they inhabited the Seriana valley. Doubtless there were many others too. The Rhati Vennonetes, Cantiani, Camuni, Breuni and Taurisci, whom some add to the above, properly belong to Germany.

units.la: Principium descriptionis sit Mantua. Sic Ovidio, Silio, Martiali, Statio, Plinio dicitur: Μαντουα Straboni & Ptolemaeo: Μαντουα Stephano: quae Mantoa hodie. Meminit eius Cippulus marmoreus apud Gentilem Delphinium:
units.tr: Let the description begin with Mantua. It is so called by Ovid, Silius, Martial, Statius and Pliny; Strabo and Ptolemy write Μαντουα, Stephanus likewise Μαντουα; it is today Mantoa. A marble tombstone, reported by Gentilis Delphinus, mentions it:

units.la: PPPP C. RVTIC . RVTILIO . C . F SAB . HOMVNCIONI . MANTVA MIL . COH . VII . PR 7 . VALLI . MIL ANN . XIIII . VIX ANN . XXXII A . B . M . F . C
units.tr: P P P P. To Gaius Rutilius Rutilius Homuncio, son of Gaius, of the Sabine tribe, of Mantua, soldier of the seventh cohort, of the first century... of the Valerian (?) ... served fourteen years, lived thirty-two years. His heirs erected this monument; A.B.M.F.C.

units.la: Galatheam vocat Allegorice Virgilius in Eclogis, ut notat Servius. Vide Petri Nanni Miscellanea libro vi. Conditam ferunt quidam ab Manto, Tiresiæ Vatis filia: non nulli ab Ocno Bianore, Tuscorum Rege, & Mantus ipsius Matris nomine nuncupatam. Virgilius libro x. Æneidos: Ille etiam patriis agmen ciet Ocnus ab oris, Fatidicæ Mantus & Tusci ficius amnis, Qui muros Matrisque dedit tibi Mantua nomen: Mantua dives avis: sed non genus omnibus unum. Gens illi triplex: populi sub gente quaterni: Ipsa caput: populis Tusco de sanguine vires.
units.tr: Virgil, in the Eclogues, allegorically calls it Galatheam, as Servius notes; see Petrus Nannius, Miscellanea, book 6. Some say it was founded by Manto, daughter of the seer Tiresias; others that it was named after Ocno Bianore, king of the Tuscans, and after the name of his own mother Manto. Virgil, Aeneid book 10: Ocnus also leads a host from his native shores, son of the prophetess Manto and of the Tuscan river, who gave you your walls and his mother's name, Mantua: rich in ancestry, but not all of one stock. She has three peoples, each with four communities beneath them. She herself is the head, and her strength comes from Tuscan blood.

units.la: Cui loco inlustrando videndi, præter Servium, Æquicola, Patriæ Præco, & apud eum Leonardus Aretinus, Epistola ad Ioannem Franciscum Gonzagam, Virgilium non infeliciter explicans. Catohi Semproniloque Annianis parum apud me fidei. Initium Urbis ponunt varij varie. Aretinus, quem dixi, ccc circiter ante Romam conditam annis: ante Mediolanum, cccc. ante Cremonam & Placentiam, 1ccc. sed infirmo fundamento: Leander anno ante bellum Trojanum lx. non firmiore. Quidquid sit, antiquissima ipsi est origo. Posita est in medio Paludum, quas Mincius, ex Lacu Benaco egressus, creat, nec nisi Pontibus, qui eximij admodum, aditur: hinc ob naturam loci munitissimis Italiæ concensenda. Ampla est, & magnifice publicis privatisque ædificijs ornata, rectisque plateis decora. Templum Cathedrale pulcerrimum. Forum satis amplum, in quo Horologium summi artificij. Arcem habet munitam. In Curia, quæ splendidissima, Locus est, qui La Grotta vulgo, rebus preciosissimis, multisque Antiquitatum monimentis ab Isabella, Francisci Marchionis ultimi Conjuge, refertus. Videre ibi est duos Cupidines excellentis operis, Cornu insigne Monocerotis, precij magni Gemmas, Vasaque aurea & argentea innumera. Vngari Locus vocatur, ad perpetuam rei memoriam, quod Vngari aliquando Urbem everterint. Episcopatus floret dignitate. Incolæ ad Litteras, Arma, Mercaturam apti promtique. Concilium hic habuerunt Nicolaus II. & Pius II. pp. MM Ortu superbit Virgilij, Poëtarum apud Latinos Principis, cuius ingenium, inquit Munsterus, tantum omnes efferre debent, quam imitari nulli possint. Natus tamen in Vico Andes, hodie Petola, altero ab urbe lapide. Hinc Silius lib. viii: Mantua mittenda certavit pube Cremona: Mantua Musarum Domus, atque ad sidera cantu Evectla Andino, & Smyrnaï æmula plectris.
units.tr: For illustrating this passage one may consult, besides Servius, Equicola, the Herald of the Fatherland, and in him Leonardo Aretino, in his letter to Gianfrancesco Gonzaga, who explains Virgil not unhappily. I put little trust in Cato, Sempronius or the Annian forgeries. Various writers give various dates for the city's beginning. Aretino, whom I mentioned, puts it about 300 years before the founding of Rome; before Milan, 400 years; before Cremona and Piacenza, 1300 years; but on a weak foundation. Leander puts it sixty years before the Trojan War, no firmer. Whatever the truth, it has a very ancient origin. It is set in the middle of marshes, which the Mincio creates on leaving Lake Benaco, and it can be reached only by bridges, which are exceptionally fine. Because of the nature of the site, it is for this reason counted among the best fortified cities of Italy. It is large and magnificently adorned with public and private buildings, and handsome with straight streets. The cathedral is very beautiful. The forum is quite spacious, and in it stands a clock of the highest craftsmanship. It has a fortified citadel. In the Curia, which is most splendid, there is a room which is commonly called La Grotta, filled with very precious things and many monuments of antiquity, gathered by Isabella, wife of Francis, the last Marquis. There one may see two Cupids of excellent workmanship, the remarkable horn of a unicorn, gems of great value, and countless vessels of gold and silver. A place is called Hungary, in perpetual memory of the fact that the Hungarians once overthrew the city. The bishopric flourishes in dignity. The inhabitants are apt and ready for letters, arms and trade. Nicholas II and Pius II, popes, held a council here. The city takes pride in the birth of Virgil, the prince of Latin poets, whose genius, says Münster, all ought to extol as much as none can imitate. He was born, however, in the village of Andes, today Petola, one mile from the city. Hence Silius, book 8: Mantua, which vied with Cremona in sending forth its youth, the home of the Muses, raised to the stars by the song of Andes, a rival to the lyres of Smyrna.

units.la: Produxit quoque Mantua Franciscum, Sigismundum Francisci ultimi Marchionis Fratrem, Pyrrhum Fratrem Ludovici, Herculem Friderici Primi Ducis Fratrem, Gonzagas omnes, Cardinalium ordini adscriptos: Georgium Andriasium, Regij Lepidi Episcopum: Baptistam, Carmelitatum Sodalitatis Antistitem, Theologum & Poëtam: Marcum Guacium, Historiographum: Matthæum Silvaticum, summum Philosophum. Militares Duces cum alios, tum ex nobilissima Gonzagarum gente, morant alij. Sanctos numerat Mantua Ioannem Bonum, Eremitam: Ofannam Andriassam, Dominicanam: Matthæum Carrarum, Prædicatorij Ordinis Monachum. Imperium primum fuit penes Tuscos, Urbis auctores: hinc penes Gallos Cenomanos: post quos Romani rerum ibi sunt potiti. Maximam sub Triumviratu cladem tulit. Quum enim Cremona victoribus eripienda esset concessa, propter vicinitatem magnam Agri sui partem amisit. Hinc Virgilius:
units.tr: Mantua also produced Francesco, Sigismondo, brother of Francis, the last Marquis; Pyrrhus, brother of Ludovico; Hercules, brother of Frederick I, Duke: all of them Gonzagas, enrolled in the order of cardinals; Giorgio Andriasio, Bishop of Reggio Lepido; Baptista, head of the Carmelite fraternity, theologian and poet; Marco Guacio, historiographer; Matteo Silvatico, a leading philosopher. Others, besides those from the most noble Gonzaga family, have won fame as military commanders. Mantua counts among its saints Giovanni Buono, a hermit; Osanna Andreasi, a Dominican nun; and Matteo Carra, a monk of the Order of Preachers. Power there was first in the hands of the Tusci, the founders of the city; then in those of the Gauls, the Cenomani; after whom the Romans took control of affairs there. The city suffered its greatest disaster under the Triumvirate. For when Cremona had been granted to the victors to be seized, it lost a large part of its territory because of its close proximity. Hence Virgil:

units.la: Mantua veh misera nimium vicina Cremona, Respublica Mantuana nominatur in Inscriptione, quæ apud Onuphrium Panuinium ius verbis concepta: C. VALERIO. C. F PAP. MARIANO HONORES . OMNES . ADEPTO . TRIDENT FLAMINI. ROM. ET. AVG PRAEF. QVINQV. AVGVR ADLECTO . ANNON. LEG. III ITALIC . SODALI. SACROR TVSCVLANOR . IVDICI SELECTO : DECVR . TRID DECVRIONI . BRIXIÆ CVRATORI . REIP. MANT EQVO. PVBL . PRAEF . PABR PATRONO . COLON PVBLICE
units.tr: Mantua, alas, too near to unhappy Cremona! The Mantuan Republic is named in an inscription, given by Onofrio Panvinio, which is worded thus: To Gaius Valerius Mariānus, son of Gaius, of the Papirian tribe, who obtained all the honours, flamen of Trent and of Rome and of Augustus, prefect of the fifth division, chosen augur, adlected to the ... of the third Italic legion, companion of the sacred Tusculan judges, decurion of Brescia, curator of the Mantuan republic, public prefect of the equestrians, patron of the colony, by public decree.

units.la: Successerunt Romanis Gothi, & Langhardi; quibus profligatis, Vrbs ad Imperatorum potestatem est retracta: ea rursus labante, in libertatem se cum multis aliis vindicavit, quam optinuit. donec ab Othone II. Imperatore Theodobaldo Comiti Canaliano donaretur. Subrogatus illi Bonifacius Filius, eique sine mascula prole defuncto Beatrix coniunx, cum Mathilde Filia, quæ Mantuam summopere amplíavit. Libertatem iterum nacta post aliquot annos ditioni subiecta est Sordelli Vicecomitis, qui primus omnium post Mathildem Comitem Mantuæ principatum gessit: quo circa annum c1o cc lxxiv mortuo, Duces habuit suos, primo Bonacolsios, annos fere LV. deinde ab anno c1o ccc xxviii. Gonzagas, qui adhuc summæ rerum præsunt. Plene Leander, qui accurate Principes commemorat ad sua usque tempora. Videndi & Blondus, Sabellicus, Corius, Æquicola, Francisci Vigilij ac Bandelli Funebres Orationes. Venenohic perijt Karolus Calvus, Magni Filius; Hebræo Medico pecuniacorrupto. De Mantua sic Facius lib. III. Danticorum: Noi summo alla citta, che fe tu ispy Manto n'ha il pregio, e Virgilio corona Chiusa dal Po, da Menzo, & da piu Rij. Qnivi il Corpo di Longin dimora In santo Andrea, & con gran riverenza Si fa la Festa sua, & vi s'adora. L'honore, la grandezza, & la potenza Della citta tien quello di Conzaga! Tre Fratei sono, & son d'una conscienza. Molto e la Terrabella, e grand', e vaga, E' l bel suo porto intempo di pace, L'entrata e buona di quel che si paga.
units.tr: The Romans were succeeded by the Goths and Lombards. When these were overthrown, the city was brought back under the power of the Emperors. When that power weakened again, it claimed its liberty, along with many other cities, and kept it until Emperor Otto II granted it to Count Theodobaldo of Canossa. He was succeeded by his son Bonifacius. When Bonifacius died without a male heir, his wife Beatrix ruled, together with her daughter Mathilde, who greatly enlarged Mantuam. After some years the city regained its liberty, but it later came under the rule of Sordelli Vicecomitis, who was the first after Matilda to hold the principate of Mantua. Around the year 1274, after his death, the city had its own Duces: first the Bonacolsios for nearly 55 years, and then, from the year 1328, the Gonzagas, who still hold supreme power. Leander relates the princes accurately down to his own time, and see also Blondus, Sabellicus, Corio, Equicola, and the funeral orations of Francesco Vigilio and Bandello. Here Charles the Bald, son of Charlemagne, died of poison, a Jewish physician having been bribed. On Mantua, Facio writes thus in book III of the Danticorum: No city is higher than the one that Mantua holds in honour, and Virgil crowns it, enclosed by the Po, the Mincio and more rivers. There the body of Longinus dwells in the church of St Andrew, and his feast is kept with great reverence, and he is adored there. The honour, the greatness and the power of the city are held by the Gonzaga. There are three brothers, and they are of one mind. The land is very fair, large and charming; its fine harbour, in time of peace, and its entrance are good for whoever pays the toll.

units.la: Extra Vrbem videre est Team, Villam suburbanam, nobilem & ornatam: ab Friderico I. Mantuanorum Duce exstructam.
units.tr: Outside the city one may see Te, a suburban villa, noble and adorned, built by Frederick I, Duke of the Mantuans.

units.la: Transito Lacu, quinque milliaribus ab Mantua Villa visitur Marmirolum ab Friderico I. quem dixi, magno artificio, magnoque sumtu ædificata.
