units.tr: Crossing the lake, five miles from Mantua, one sees the village of Marmirolo, built by Frederick I, whom I mentioned, with great skill and at great expense.

units.la: Secundum Mincium adverso itinere Vallecium Oppidum se offert, ubi Pons amnis ripas jungit.
units.tr: Following the Mincio in the opposite direction, the town of Valeggio presents itself, where a bridge joins the banks of the river.

units.la: Altius deinde ad erumpentem ex lacu fluvium munitissimum est oppidum Pisceria cum Ponte: ab Scaligeris, Veronæ quondam Principibus, conditum.
units.tr: Further on, higher up, where the river flows out of the lake, is the very well-fortified town of Peschiera, with a bridge. It was founded by the Scaligers, once the lords of Verona.

units.la: Post eam ad dextram Lacus ripam tertio lapide Parencum: hinc altero Lagisum, inde mille quingentis passibus Cisanum, parique mox intervallo Bardolinum sequitur.
units.tr: After it, on the right bank of the lake, three miles away, is Parenzo. From there two miles to Lazise, then 1500 paces to Cisano, and after almost the same distance comes Bardolino.

units.la: Ulterius secundo milliari in sinu Lacus Oppidum Garda, unde Lacui, qui Benacus olim, nomen.
units.tr: Further on, two miles away, in a bay of the lake, is the town of Garda, from which the lake, once called Benacus, takes its name.

units.la: Ab Garda huis mille quingentis passibus ad D. Vigilium pervenitur.
units.tr: From Garda, 1500 paces brings one to San Vigilio.

units.la: Altero hinc lapide Turris est: hinc item duobus P. M. Paium: inde pari spacio Castellum: paulloque deinceps majori Brenzonium: mox Portus; post quem Fons frigidus & Casinum cum Valle Soni. Fuit hic olim Vicus Soni, cuius hodieque adparent rudera.
units.tr: One mile from here is Torri. From there, likewise two miles, is Pai; from there the same distance to Castelletto; and a little further, a larger place, Brenzone; then Porto; after which come Fonte Freddo and Cassone, with the Valle di Sogno. There was once a village here, Sono, whose ruins still appear today.

units.la: Ab Casono ad Masesinum millia sunt quatuor; inde totidem ad Navenum; idemque hinc spatium ad Cornu bonum; nec majus deinde ad Turbulum: à quo mille passibus Amnis Sacra defluit in Lacum ex montibus Tridentinis.
units.tr: From Cassone to Malcesine is four miles; from there as many to Navene; and from there the same distance to Cornu Bonum; and no greater distance then to Torbole, from which, a thousand paces away, the river Sarca flows down into the lake from the Trentine mountains.

units.la: Dextra Sarcæ ripa multa sunt Castella, multi Pagi; nominatim Arcus, Drenna, Madrucium.
units.tr: On the right bank of the Sarca there are many castles and many villages, namely Arco, Drena and Madruzzo.

units.la: Post, ad exigui Lacus inter montes dextram Vocianum; & altius in Valle Poncionum: & circa fontem amnis Ad D. Mariam.
units.tr: Afterwards, on the right, is Vezzano, by a small lake among the mountains; higher up in the valley is Ponzone; and near the source of the river is Santa Maria.

units.la: Iam ab Urbe Mantua per lævam Mincij ripam decimo lapide Goitum Opidum occurrit: inde quinto Volta Caprianaque.
units.tr: Now, from the city of Mantua along the left bank of the Mincio, ten miles away, the town of Goito comes into view; from there, five miles on, are Volta and Cavriana.

units.la: Dehinc per lævam Benaci à Pischeria P. M. VIII. ripa Lacus adeo prominet, ut peninsulam fere efficit, ubi Sirmio Opidum, Catulli ortu versibusque celebratum: Peninsularum Sirmio, Insularumque Ocelle, quascumque in liquentibus stagnis, Marique vasto fert uterque Neptunus, Quam te libenter, quamque laetus inviso, Vix mihi ipse credens Thyniam, atque Bithynos Liquisse campos: & videre te in tuto. O quid solutis est beatius curis, Quum mens onus reponit, ac peregrino Labore fessi venimus Larem ad nostrum, Desideratoque acquiescimus lecto. Hoc est, quod unum est, pro laboribus tantis. Salve o venusta Sirmio, atque hero gaude; Gaudete vosque ludia Lacus undæ; Ridete quidquid est domi cachinnorum.
units.tr: Then, along the left bank of Benacus from Peschiera, eight Roman miles, the shore juts out so far that it nearly forms a peninsula, where the town of Sirmio stands, celebrated for the birth and verses of Catullus: Peninsula and jewel of islands, Sirmio, whatever Neptune bears in the clear pools and the vast sea, how gladly and how happily I revisit you, scarcely believing that I have left Thynia and the Bithynian fields and see you safe. O what is happier than to lay down our cares, when the mind sets its burden down, and we come weary from foreign labour to our own hearth, and rest on the longed-for bed. This alone is worth all those toils. Hail, lovely Sirmio, and rejoice in your master! Rejoice too, you waters of the lake of Lydia! Laugh with all the laughter that is in my home.

units.la: Ad quem locum Iosephus Scaliger: Scaligerorum Principum amœnissimus secessus Sirmio a Theodorico usque Scaligero Gotho, quem Dietrich von Berna vocant Germani, ad Avum usque meum Benedictum Scaligerum, qui profugit ad Gentilem suum Matthiam Regem Vngariæ, cognomine Corvinum. Scribit apud eumdem Parthenius de Sirmione hoc modo: Nunc quidem est angustum cum Theatri lateritij reliquis Opidum. Olim autem Vrbs neque exigua, neque obscura, à Pannonicis sive Vngaris aliquando instaurata, ut ego in quodam eleganti atque antique Grammatici cujusdam Epigrammate comperi. Meminit & Antoninus. Hodie Sermione.
units.tr: On this place Joseph Scaliger writes: Sirmio was the most pleasant retreat of the Scaliger princes, from Theodoric the Scaliger Goth, whom the Germans call Dietrich von Bern, down to my grandfather Benedetto Scaligero, who fled to his kinsman Matthias, King of Hungary, surnamed Corvinus. Parthenius writes about Sirmione in this way: Now indeed the town is cramped, with the remains of a brick theatre. But formerly it was a town neither small nor obscure, restored at some time by the Pannonians or Hungarians, as I found in a certain elegant and ancient epigram of a grammarian. Antoninus also mentions it. Today it is Sermione.

units.la: Sequitur quarto fere lapide per ripam Ripaltella: mox primo Defencianum: & ulterius Cornu Spinæ: dehinc altero Padengaum: paulloque supra mille pass. Monica: mox Dusanum, Arx Minerbæa, Pons Dusanus & ulterius nobile Opidum Salodium, vel, ut alij vocant, Longa Salona.
units.tr: About four miles further along the shore comes Ripalta; then, at one mile, Desenzano; and further, Cornu Spinae; then at two miles Padenghe; and a little above it, 1000 paces, Moniga; then Dusano, the fortress of Minerbe, the bridge of Dusano, and further on the noble town of Salò, or, as others call it, Longa Salona.

units.la: Haud procul hinc Barbaranus amnis sequitur & ab eo milliari quarto alius, Bornicus: paulloque altius Madernum: postea Fluvius Tusculanus, quo transito Vicus cognominis invenitur, ubi vestigia Benaci Opidi, aquo priscum Lacui nomen. Inundatione jacet subversum. Meminit fortean Vopiscus in Probi Principis vita: Posteri Probi vel odio invidia, vel timore Romanam Rem fugerunt, & in Italia circa Veronam ac Benacum ac Larium, atque in his regionibus Larem locaverunt: nisi quis velit Lacum ibi designari. Hinc Benacenses, Opidi Incolæ, vel Lacus Adcolæ (prius malim) in Inscriptione, quæ apud Onuphrium Panuinium: IMP . CAESARI DIVI. ANTONINI. AVG PII. FIL. DIVI. HADRIANI. NEP. DIVI. TRAIANI. PARTHICI. PRO NEP. DIVI . NERVAE ABNEP . M . AVRELIO ANTONINO. AVG : ARMENIACO. PONT. MAX TRIB. POT. XVIIII. IMP. II COS . III. BENACENSES
units.tr: Not far from here the stream Barbarano follows, and four miles further another, the Bornico; a little higher up is Maderno. Afterwards comes the river Tusculanus, across which is a village of the same name, where the remains of the town of Benacus lie, overthrown by a flood; from it the lake had its old name. Perhaps Vopiscus mentions it in the life of the Emperor Probus: The Posteri of Probus, out of hatred, envy or fear, fled from the Roman state, and settled in Italy around Verona and Benacus and Larius, and in these regions they set up Larius; unless someone wishes the lake to be meant there. Hence the Benacenses, inhabitants of the town, or (I would prefer) the Adcolae of the lake, in the inscription that Onuphrius Panvinius gives: To the Emperor Caesar, son of the divine Antoninus Augustus Pius, grandson of the divine Hadrian, great-grandson of the divine Trajan Parthicus, pro-grandson of the divine Nerva, great-great-grandson, Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus Armeniacus, Pontifex Maximus, holding tribunician power for the 19th time, imperator for the 2nd time, consul for the 3rd time: the Benacenses.

units.la: In alia, quam idem Onuphrius profitetur se Tusculani super Lacum Benacum vidis-se, & accurate descripsisse: IMP . CAES . M . AN TONINI . PII . GERM . SARMATICI . FIL . DIVI . FII . NEP . DIVI HADRIANI . PRONEP . DIVI . TRAIANI . PARTH . ABNEP . DIVI NERVAE . ADNEP . M. AVR . COM MODO : ANTONINO . PIO . FEL AVG . SAR . GER . MAX. BRIT P . M . TR . POT . XIIII . IMP VIII . COS . V . P .P. NOBILISSIMO . PRINCIPI
units.tr: In another inscription, which the same Onuphrius says he saw at Tusculanum above Lake Benacus and described accurately: To the Emperor Caesar Marcus Antoninus Pius Germanicus Sarmaticus, son of the divine Pius, grandson of the divine Hadrian, great-grandson of the divine Trajan Parthicus, great-great-grandson of the divine Nerva, adnepos of Marcus Aurelius Commodus Antoninus Pius Felix Augustus, Sarmaticus, Germanicus, Maximus, Britannicus, Pontifex Maximus, holding tribunician power for the 14th time, imperator for the 8th time, consul for the 5th time, father of his country, to the most noble prince.

units.la: BENACENSES
units.tr: The Benacenses

units.la: Succedunt inde Viavetrum, Boiacum, Villa, Carnianum ; unde quinque millium iti-nere ad Pratum famis devenitur.
units.tr: Next come Viavetrum, Boiacum, Villa, Carnianum; from there one reaches Pratum famis after a journey of five thousand paces.

units.la: Visuntur mox Flumina Campio, Brosa, Linion & Ponalis: hinc nobile Castrum Riva; altera in ripa Turbulum est.
units.tr: Soon the rivers Campio, Brosa, Linion & Ponalis come into view. Here is the noble castle of Riva; on the other bank is Turbulum.

units.la: Lacu relicto, Padum persequar. Iuxta eum, post Ostium Mincij, Burgum est si-tum, ab Mantuanis aedificatum, anno cIↄ cxı, ut Æquicola notat libro 1. Histor. Mantuan.
units.tr: Leaving the lake, I will follow the Po. Beside it, after the mouth of the Mincio, lies Burgum, built by the Mantuans in the year 1111, as Equicola notes in book 1 of his Mantuan History.

units.la: Sequitur introitus in Padum Olly, de quo supra. Itinere secundum eum adverso, dextra, se pandunt Opida Macheria & Aqua Nigra.
units.tr: Next is the entrance of the Olly into the Po, mentioned above. Going upstream against the current, on the right, open the towns Macheria & Aqua Nigra.

units.la: Supra Macheriam sunt Ad S. Martinum, Rodondescum, Casaletium (Gazzoleto) Ca-stellum Vgonis, Casalmorum, Rodecum, Castellum Ziphraum: inde Nugularia, Ceresaria, Publica, Medole, Volta, Sulphurinum.
units.tr: Above Macheria lie Ad S. Martinum, Rodondescum, Casaletium (Gazzoleto), Castellum Vgonis, Casalmorum, Rodecum, Castellum Ziphraum; then Nugularia, Ceresaria, Publica, Medole, Volta, Sulphurinum.

units.la: Rursus ab Ostio Clisij, per dextram eius sursum post Aquam Nigram Martana est; & altius Asola, castellum a Brixianis eversum anno cIↄ cxxv.
units.tr: Again from the mouth of the Clisius, up along its right bank beyond Aqua Nigra, is Martana; and further up is Asola, a castle destroyed by the Brescians in the year 1125.

units.la: Dehinc Aqua Frigida, Carpenodulum, Ad D. Georgium, Mons Clarus ab Imperatore Friderico II subrutus: mox Castilio Stiverorum (Castion dalle Stivere) cum Arce; item Calcina & Lonatum Opidum.
units.tr: Then come Aqua Frigida, Carpenodulum, Ad D. Georgium, Mons Clarus, undermined by the Emperor Frederick II; soon after, Castilio Stiverorum (Castion dalle Stivere) with its citadel; likewise Calcina & Lonatum, a town.

units.la: Interius in mediterraneis Poponacium est, altiusque Pozeum, Calvalcazesium, Calvalcesium, Musculon, & Ripa ad ostium Lacus Idrini; in cuius dextra Idrum, unde Stagno nomen. Alij Hydrum vocant, ab Hydra, quam Hercules hic obtruncasse fallo à qui-busdam perhibetur.
units.tr: Further inland, among the hills, lies Poponacium, and higher up Pozeum, Calvalcazesium, Calvalcesium, Musculon, & Ripa, at the mouth of Lake Idro. On its right is Idrum, from which the lake takes its name Stagno. Others call it Hydrum, from the Hydra, which some falsely say Hercules slew here.

units.la: Post confluentem Ollio Clisium Canedum cernitur ; unde Canedolorum nobilis Bononiæ gens.
units.tr: Beyond the confluence with the Oglio, Clisium Canedum comes into view; whence the noble Bolognese family of Canedolorum.

units.la: Sequuntur altius Castellum Gofredi & Volonium.
units.tr: Further up follow Castellum Gofredi & Volonium.

units.la: Læva Clisij sursum post Navilium flumen varia visuntur Opida, quæ vernacule Monastero ; Romadello, cognomine di sotto, inferum ; Casal-Moro ; Romadello di sopra, superum; Calvisano, Latinis Forum Calcisij, à Q. Calvisio, ut quidam augurantur con-ditum ; cuius mentio apud Cæsarem in Ephemeridibus.
units.tr: On the left of the Clisius, upstream beyond the Navilio river, various towns are seen, which in the vernacular are called Monastero; Romadello, surnamed di sotto, the lower one; Casal-Moro; Romadello di sopra, the upper one; Calvisano, in Latin Forum Calcisij, founded, some guess, by Q. Calvisio, whose mention is found in Caesar's Ephemerides.

units.la: Altius deinde inter Clitium & Navilium amnem Malpaga, Montron, Castagnedulo, Borgo Saiolo, Pavon, Guidazuola, Gavardo.
units.tr: Higher up, between the Clisius and the Navilio river, lie Malpaga, Montron, Castagnedulo, Borgo Saiolo, Pavon, Guidazuola, Gavardo.

units.la: Iuxta fontem Navilij Sabium etiam inde Muntia & Vasium.
units.tr: Beside the spring of the Navilio lies Sabium; from there also Muntia and Vasium.

units.la: Ludronum in editissimis montium jugis sett situm.
units.tr: Ludronum is situated on the highest ridges of the mountains.

units.la: Ab Ollio Melaque, qui ipsi commiscetur, Opidate pandunt Gambara, Prato Albuino, S. Cervaso, Civole, Pauno, Ottolengo, Bede, Leno, Isolella, Mazzanello, Ponsano, Bagnuolo, Panzarata, Le Chiavigne, Latine scribentibus Clavinia; Eclur, Verzian, La Torre, S. Gegnesio.
units.tr: From the Oglio, and the Mella (Melaque), which joins it, the towns open out: Gambara, Prato Albuino, S. Cervaso, Civole, Pauno, Ottolengo, Bede, Leno, Isolella, Mazzanello, Ponsano, Bagnuolo, Panzarata, Le Chiavigne, which Latin writers call Clavinia; Eclur, Verzian, La Torre, S. Gegnesio.

units.la: Tum ad Montis radices nobilis est Civitas Brixia.
units.tr: Then, at the foot of the mountain, lies the noble city Brixia.

units.la: Sic Livio multis locis, Plinio lib. iii. natur histor. cap. xviii. & Iuniori in Epistolis, Nazario in Panegyrico, aliis; Βρεξία Straboni & Ptolemaeo dicitur: quae hodie Brescia. Meminerunt & Antiquae Inscriptiones: quarum I. Romae juxta S. Blasij ad Viam latam: | II. Noviomagi in Gelriae Ducatu, in Aedibus, quae quondam fuerunt V. CL. Gerarti Falcoburgij; a me ibi descripta: D. M | Q. BISIVS. SECVND C. NIGIDIO. C. F | Q. F. DOMO. BRIXSAE FAB. MARCELLI | MIL. LEG X. G. 7. COMINI NO. BRIX. MIL | CELSI. AN. XIX. S. VII COH. I. PR. 7. LEPIDI | HERED. EX. T. C. MIL. AN. V. VIX. ANN | XXIIII. D. RESTIANVS | IVSTVS. B. M. F |
units.tr: So Livy in many places; Pliny in Natural History, book 3, chapter 18; the younger Pliny in his Letters; Nazarius in his Panegyric; and others. Strabo and Ptolemy call it Brexia [Βρεξία]; today it is Brescia. Ancient inscriptions also mention it. Of these, I: at Rome, near S. Blasius on the Via Lata. II: at Nijmegen in the Duchy of Guelders, in the house that once belonged to the most distinguished Gerard Falkenburg, which I copied there myself: "To the spirits of the departed. Quintus Bisius Secundus, son of Gaius Nigidius, of the Quirina tribe, from Brixia, a craftsman of Marcellus, soldier of the tenth legion, Gemina, century of Cominius, from Brixia, soldier; Celsus, aged 19 years, of the seventh cohort, century of Lepidus, heir by will; soldier, aged 5 years, lived 24 years. Restianus Justus set this up." (B.M.F.)

units.la: De Origine varia traduntur, sed parum explorata. Aliis certiora forte apud Livium, quem multi sequuntur. Notat is ab Cenomanis (incmendatiores Codices Germanos praeferunt) conditam; cum Elitovio & Belovelo Ducibus ex Gallis, per Taurinos & Alpes Iulias in Italiam transgressis. Hinc Cenomanorum genti tribuitur etiam a Plinio & Ptolemaeo, quin & Livius libro xxxii. Brixiam Cenomanorum signat caput. Civitas est pervetusta, dives, populosa, ampla, validis munita muris, Arce superbiens inexpugnabili: pulcra aedificiis cum publicis, tum privatis. Eam Amnis perlabitur Garcia, quem aliqui Melam vocant: de quo alibi. Ad Situm pertinent haec Catulli Poëtae: Flavus quam molli percurrit flumine Mela Brixia, Verona Mater amata mea:
units.tr: Its origin is reported in various ways, but poorly established. Perhaps more certain accounts are found in Livy, whom many follow. He records that it was founded by the Cenomanis (the less faulty manuscripts prefer Germanos), when the Gallic leaders Elitovius and Belovelus crossed into Italy through the Taurini and the Julian Alps. Hence the people of the Cenomani is also credited to it by Pliny and Ptolemy; and Livy in book 32 calls Brixiam Cenomanorum their caput. It is a very ancient city, rich, populous and spacious, strongly fortified with walls, proud of an impregnable citadel, and handsome with both public and private buildings. The river Garcia flows through it, which some call the Mela, about which more elsewhere. To its site pertain these lines of the poet Catullus: Flavus quam molli percurrit flumine Mela Brixia, Verona Mater amata mea:

units.la: O dulci iucunda viro, iucunda parenti
units.tr: O Brixia, pleasing to your husband, pleasing to your parent,

units.la: Salve, teque bona Iupiter auxiet ope.
units.tr: Hail, and may good Jupiter aid you with his help.

units.la: Castrum habet munitissimum e vertice Vrbem despicients, & egregio firmatum ab Venetis Praesidio: Templa magnifica Monasterio stupenda; Hospitale pulcrum. In Palatio Capitanei haec leguntur:
units.tr: It has a very strong castle overlooking the city from its summit, and a splendid garrison established by the Venetians. Its temples are magnificent, its monastery astonishing, and its hospital fine. On the Captain's palace these lines are read:

units.la: Hic locus edit, amat, punit, conservat, honorat;
units.tr: Here the place proclaims, loves, punishes, preserves, honours;

units.la: Requiritem, pacem, crimina, jura, probos.
units.tr: It seeks out crimes, keeps peace, upholds laws, and protects the upright.

units.la: Templum & Episcopi Palatium, quin tota Civitas, eiusque Territorium, omnia ingnam, passim lectissimis Marmorum Inscriptionibus, Statuis, Statuarum titulis & elogiis, variorumque Epitaphis sunt plena. Incolae locupletes, lauti, nobiles, ingenui. Juvenum Brixiana nominatur in Inscriptione, quae in Hispania legitur Cazagi in Saccilo D. Mariae: M. PVBLICIO. M. P SAB. SEXTIO CALPVRNIANO EQVO . PVBLICO FLAM. DIVI V. IVLI PRAEF. ADIL. IOT QVAESTOR . ARAR SACERD. IVVEN. BRIX COLLEGIA CENTON. IT. FABROR
units.tr: The cathedral and the bishop's palace, indeed the whole city and its territory, are everywhere full of choice marble inscriptions, statues, statue-titles and eulogies, and the epitaphs of various people. The inhabitants are wealthy, elegant, noble and free-born. A youth of Brixia is named in an inscription, which is read in Spain at Cazagi in Saccilo, at the church of St Mary: "To Marcus Publicius, son of Marcus, of the Sabine tribe, and Sextus Calpurnianus, public horseman, flamen of the deified Julius, prefect, aedile, quaestor, sacrificial priest of the altar, youth of Brixia; of the colleges of the Centonarii and the Fabri."

units.la: Sic Synagoga Brixianorum mentionem facit Lapis, qui apud Onuphrium Panuinium: COELIAE . PATERNAE MATRI.SYNAGOGAE BRIXIANORVM
units.tr: Thus a stone, which Onuphrius Panvinius records, mentions the synagogue of the Brixians: "To Caelia Paterna, mother of the synagogue of the Brixians."

units.la: Familiae Nobiles ibi non paucae; in quis principem habent locum Gambarae, Martinengi, Madi, Advocati, Averoldi, Luzagi & Almilii, qui ab Romanis orti. Idem colonia legitur perpetuo Populo Romani; praefectum Bello Punico post cladem ad Trebiam Amnem ab Hannibale inlatam. Colonia deducta est cum reliquis Transpadanis ab Cn. Pompeio Strabone, anno 10 CLXV; & postea cum aliis ab C. Caesare Dictatore Civitatis jure donata. Vide Paedianum in Pisonianam, Plinium lib. III, cap. XIX, Suetonium in Iulij Caesaris Vita. Eo pertinent Inscriptiones: quarum ibi I. in Aedibus Episcopi | II. ad Turrim Palatij: COLL. FABR. ET. CENT | COLLEGIA. FABR. ET. CENT SEX. SEXTIO. ONES.GENI | L. CORNELIO. PROSODICO ORNAMENTIS | VI. VIR AVG. BRIXIAE ET DECVRIONALIBVS | VERON. SACERD. COLLEG BRIXIAE. VI. VIR. AVGVSTAL | IVVENVM. BRIXIAN PATRONO. COLLEGIORVM | PRIMVM. INSTITVTI FABROR. ET. CENTENARIOR. ET | OB MERITA. LIVS DENDROPHOROR VM | HONORL. CONTENTVS. IMPENDIVM REMISIT. IS. IN. TVT. HS::1 N . D
units.tr: There are not a few noble families there; the chief place among them is held by the Gambara, Martinengo, Madi, Advocati, Averoldi, Luzzago and Almici families, who are descended from the Romans. The same city is read to have been a colony of the Roman people in perpetuity, and it supplied a prefect in the Punic War after the defeat inflicted by Hannibal at the river Trebia. It was made a colony, together with the other Transpadane towns, by Gnaeus Pompeius Strabo in the year 665, and afterwards, with others, was granted the rights of a city by Gaius Caesar the Dictator. See Asconius Pedianus on Piso's oration, Pliny book 3, chapter 19, and Suetonius in the Life of Julius Caesar. To this belong the inscriptions found there: I, in the house of the bishop; II, at the tower of the palace: "To Lucius Cornelius Prosodicus, sextumvir Augustal of Brixia and decurion of Verona, priest of the college of Brixia, sextumvir of the Augustales, patron of the youth of Brixia and of the colleges, first founder of the Fabri and Centenarii; and because of his merits the Dendrophori honoured him with the decoration of the office; he remitted the expense, HS 1000. Set up according to his will."

units.la: Deinceps in Imperatorum fuit potestate, quamdiu salva stetit sua Romano Nomini maiestas. Post ab Radagaiso Gothorum Rege incendio vastata, anno CCCCXIII hinc ab Attila Hunnorum principe subversa, sed refecta anno CCCCLII, imperante Martiano: mox ab Langobardis possessa usque ad captum ab Karolo Magno Desiderium: quo extincto, successit Francorum Imperium. Inde ab Othone Saxone Cæsare libera Imperij Romani Civitas est facta, anno cIↄ cxxxvi: mox ab Henrico vi directa, muris nudata, suisque spoliata Privilegijs: ab Scaligeris, Veronæ Ducibus, opera Guelforum est capta. His successerunt Vice-comites, Mediolani Principes; à quibus sæpe vexata ad Venetos, defecit; quibus ab Gallis rursum adempta, paulo post ijs est restituta. Opibus hodie floret, Urbis veneta Sponsa cognominati solita. Fidem Christianam suscepisse traditur ab D. Apollinari, Ravennatium Præsule. Episcopatus habet titulum. Viros genuit Brixia præstantissimos: Martinum Colocerum, Martyrem; Corradum Donatum & Sebastianum Madinum, Sanctorum numero adscriptos: Vbertum Gambaram, Cordinalem: Gaulam, ex Ordine Prædicatorum & Cerardum Madinum, Patriæ Episcopos; Altobellum Averoldum, Antistitem Polanum: Item Theologos, Albertum Mandugasinum, qui floruit circa annum ab Christo nato cIↄ cccxl; Bernardinum Gadolium, Abbatem Camaldulensem, Lucam Bernardum, Iacobum Brixianum, Gratianum & Franciscum Samsones, Theophilum Bonum; Antonium denique Locatellum: Iurisconsultos: Laurentium Calcaneum, Bartholemaum, Brixianum cognomine: Lanfrancum Orianum: Stephanum Federicum: Andream Brixianum: Medicos, Franciscum Caballum, & alios: Historicos, Antonium Brixianum: & Corradum VVengerum: Philosophos & Litteratores: Carolum Valgulium, Calpurnium, Bonifacium Bembum, Petrum Lazarinum, Ioannem Britannicum. Dedit & præclaros Militiæ Duces: in quis Gerardus, Ioannes Franciscus, Bruno Ioannis filius, Gambaræ: Matthæus Madius: Casper, Antonius, Marcus Antonius Baptista, Martinengi: Thaddæus & M. Antonius, Metellani: Aloysius Advocatus: Pictores celebriores: Octavianum Pandricium, Bartholemaum Textorinum, Vincentium Brixianum cognomine. Historiam Vrbis, simulque dignitatem & splendorem multis prosequitur Capreolus. De ea sic Baptista Mantuanus: Brixia, magnorum genitrix animosa virorum, Gallia seu genuit, seu te Germania mater: (Nam genus abscundit tenebris adoperta vetustas) Tu Cenomanorum quondam Regina fuisti: Vive diu Veneti sub maiestate Senatus: Atque age sub Divo placidissima tempora Marco.
units.tr: Afterwards it was under the power of the emperors, as long as the majesty of the Roman name stood firm. Later it was laid waste by fire under Radagaisus, king of the Goths, and in the year 413 was overthrown by Attila, prince of the Huns, but was restored in the year 452, in the reign of Marcian. Soon it was held by the Lombards, until Charlemagne captured Desiderius; with his death the empire of the Franks succeeded. From then on, by Otto the Saxon Caesar, the city was made free of the Roman Empire, in the year 936. Soon Henry VI brought it under direct rule, stripped it of its walls and despoiled it of its privileges; it was taken by the Scaligeris, dukes of Verona, through the efforts of the Guelfs. These were succeeded by the Vice-comites, princes of Milan. Often harassed by them, it turned to the Venetos; but it was taken from them by the Gallis and shortly afterwards restored to them. Today it flourishes in wealth, and is accustomed to be called Urbis veneta Sponsa, the bride of the Venetian city. It is said to have received the Christian faith from D. Apollinari, bishop of Ravenna. It has the title of a bishopric. Brixia has produced very distinguished men: Martinum Colocerum, a martyr; Corradum Donatum and Sebastianum Madinum, enrolled among the saints; Vbertum Gambaram, cardinal; Gaulam, of the Order of Preachers, and Cerardum Madinum, bishops of their homeland; Altobellum Averoldum, prelate of Pola; likewise theologians: Albertum Mandugasinum, who flourished around the year of Christ's birth 1340; Bernardinum Gadolium, abbot of Camaldoli; Lucam Bernardum, Iacobum Brixianum, Gratianum and Franciscum Samsones, Theophilum Bonum; and finally Antonium Locatellum. Jurists: Laurentium Calcaneum, Bartholemaum surnamed Brixianum, Lanfrancum Orianum, Stephanum Federicum, Andream Brixianum. Physicians: Franciscum Caballum, and others. Historians: Antonium Brixianum and Corradum VVengerum. Philosophers and men of letters: Carolum Valgulium, Calpurnium, Bonifacium Bembum, Petrum Lazarinum, Ioannem Britannicum. It has also given distinguished military leaders, among whom are Gerardus, Ioannes Franciscus, Bruno, son of Giovanni, of Gambaræ; Matthæus Madius; Casper, Antonius, Marcus Antonius Baptista, of Martinengi; Thaddæus and M. Antonius, of Metellani; Aloysius Advocatus. Celebrated painters: Octavianum Pandricium, Bartholemaum Textorinum, Vincentium Brixianum surnamed so. Capreolus pursues the history of the city, and at the same time its dignity and splendour, in many ways. Of it Baptista Mantuanus says thus: Brixia, spirited mother of great men, whether Gaul bore you or Germany is your mother (for ancient time, veiled in darkness, hides your birth), you were once the queen of the Cenomani. Live long under the majesty of the Venetian Senate, and then pass the most peaceful times under divine Mark.

units.la: Territorium late patet: opidis, vicis, pagis stipatum, aquis irriguum salubérrimis: uberrimum tritici, riliquorumque frumenti generum, item vini oleique fertile, neque carens ferri ærisque fœcunditate.
units.tr: The territory extends widely, crowded with towns, villages and hamlets, watered by very healthy streams, very rich in wheat and other kinds of grain, fertile also in wine and oil, and not lacking in iron and copper.

units.la: Occurrunt extra Brixiam versus montes Reggiate. Bottesino, Virle, Novolara.
units.tr: Outside Brescia, towards the mountains, lie Reggiate, Bottesino, Virle and Novolara.

units.la: Altius inde ad Melæ dextram Castella jacent Mon-piano, Concisio, Serezzo: ad lævam Choriò, Villa, Vncino.
units.tr: Higher up from there, on the right of the Mella, lie the castles Mon-piano, Concisio and Serezzo; on the left lie Choriò, Villa and Vncino.

units.la: Haud procul inde Brozzo & Lodrio.
units.tr: Not far from there are Brozzo and Lodrio.

units.la: Ad Mormæ fontem Pessazza: postq. nonnullum intervallum Borato & Coio: succedentibus inde post Melæ Ostium in Ollij læva Regna, Balci, S. Bassam, S. Cervaso, Verola Vecchia, Scarlarolo, Cadignano, Minerbe, Favenzano, Cignano, Quinzenello, Cortesfelle, Boldenizzo, Ponte del Castello, Logrado, Torbolo, Travata, Cocaglio, Carabo, Rozzadello, Spedaletto (Hospitaleto) Manduola, Monastero, Roato, Castegnaro, Caladugo, Paseram, Gusago, Lata: in eiusdem Ollij dextra Senega, Fianello, Ponte-Vico, Montesfello, Quinzano (quod patria Ioannis Francisci Stoa, Poetæ nobilis & Dominici Phœnicis, Fratrum) Codalunga, La Pieve, Verola Vecchia, Motella, Villa Grana, Gabiano, Ogica, Barche, Orzi Nuovi: Orcos Novos vocant Latinè scribentes, & nonnulli Vrceanum, ante D. Georgy dictum, egregiè munitum ab Venetis, Arce structa: Episcopatus titulo insignitum.
units.tr: At the source of the Mormia lies Pessazza; after some distance come Borato and Coio. Then, after the mouth of the Mella, on the left of the Oglio, come Regna, Balci, S. Bassam, S. Cervaso, Verola Vecchia, Scarlarolo, Cadignano, Minerbe, Favenzano, Cignano, Quinzenello, Cortesfelle, Boldenizzo, Ponte del Castello, Logrado, Torbolo, Travata, Cocaglio, Carabo, Rozzadello, Spedaletto (Hospitaleto), Manduola, Monastero, Roato, Castegnaro, Caladugo, Paseram, Gusago and Lata. On the right of the same Oglio lie Senega, Fianello, Ponte-Vico, Montesfello, Quinzano (the homeland of Giovanni Francesco Stoa, a noble poet, and of the brothers Domenico Fenice), Codalunga, La Pieve, Verola Vecchia, Motella, Villa Grana, Gabiano, Ogica, Barche and Orzi Nuovi. Writers in Latin call it Orcos Novos, and some call it Vrceanum; it was formerly called San Giorgio, and it is a town well fortified by the Venetians with a built citadel, and is adorned with the title of a bishopric.

units.la: Obserunt inde se Fodiano, Campizzo, Padernello, Farfengo, Barbarica, Cauriolo, Geriola, Favanzano, Rudiano, Vrago, Ludriano, Castrozago, Chiario, Latinis Clarium, ab Aquis claris denominatum, frequens & amœnum, Præsulatu clarum; Palazzuolo, ubi pons Ollij ripas nectit.
units.tr: From there the following present themselves: Fodiano, Campizzo, Padernello, Farfengo, Barbarica, Cauriolo, Geriola, Favanzano, Rudiano, Vrago, Ludriano, Castrozago and Chiario. Chiari, called Clarium in Latin and named from the bright waters, is populous and pleasant, and famous for its bishopric; then Palazzuolo, where a bridge joins the banks of the Oglio.

units.la: Succedunt mox Capreolo, Sarnego, Isco, quod Lacui antiquitus Sebino, nomen hodie largitur.
units.tr: Soon come Capreolo, Sarnego and Isco, which today gives its name to the lake that was called Sebino in antiquity.

units.la: Ad Ollij Lacui concurrentis finem Castellum est Pisogno; & ad concurrentem cum Ollio Griniam, Bueno: mox Cividale & Breno.
units.tr: At the end of the lake where the Oglio flows in is the castle of Pisogno; and at the place where it meets the Oglio are Griniam and Bueno; then Cividale and Breno.

units.la: Iuxta Padum ab Ollij ostijs, ut eo redeat locorum commemoratio, primo Dosiolo est: per est: per laevam eiusdem amnis sursum incedenti Bozzolo occurrit: supra confluentem Clisij Platina, opidum ortu Baptiste Platina, qui Vitas scripsit Romanorum Pontificum celebre, de quo ipse in Canone. Platinam sequuntur ad eamdem ripam Ostian & Labina, Bebriacum Tranquillo in Vitis Othonis & Vitellij Imperatorum, Tacitoque libro 11. Historiar. cui Vicus inter Cremonam & Veronam. Lipsius legit apud Tacitum Bedriacum, ex Vaticano Codice. Testatur Pulmannus in quibusdam membranis extare Betriacum: sic apud Plutarchum Βητριάκον: Φρυγιάκον est apud Iosephum corrupte. Audiamus & antiquas Glossas in Iuvenalis Sat. 11. ad illud Poëtae.
units.tr: Next to the Po, from the mouths of the Oglio, so that the description of places may return there, first is Dosiolo. Going upstream along the left bank of the same river, one meets Bozzolo; above the confluence of the Clisio is Piadena, the town of birth of Bartolomeo Platina, who wrote the Lives of the Roman Pontiffs, famous, about whom he himself speaks in the Canon. Following Platina on the same bank are Ostiano and Labina, and Bebriacum, mentioned by Suetonius in the Lives of the Emperors Otho and Vitellius, and by Tacitus in book 2 of the Histories, a village between Cremona and Verona. Lipsius reads Bedriacum in Tacitus, according to the Vatican manuscript. Pulmannus testifies that some parchments have Betriacum; so in Plutarch it is Betriacon [Βητριάκον]; in Josephus it is corruptly Phrygiacon [Φρυγιάκον]. Let us also hear the ancient glosses on Juvenal, Satire 11, on that line of the poet:

units.la: Ille tenet speculum
units.tr: He holds a mirror

units.la: Occiso, inquit, Galba Imperatore, Otho invasit Imperium: qui tam probrosa cura in pulchenda forma fuit, ut humecto pane faciem linires ad sollicitandum candorem: utebatur & speculo. Hunc incomparabilis vita bello Civili Vitellius vicit apud Bebryacum Campaniae. Horum bellum scripsit Cornelius, scripsit & Pompeius Planta, qui ait Bebryacum vicum esse, a Cremona vicensimo lapide. alias Bebriaci, dicit Pontici, unde Pelles Bebrinae. Galba enim Ponticus fuit. Expendant haec locorum gnari.
units.tr: "When the Emperor Galba was killed," it says, "Otho seized the empire. He was so shamefully concerned with his beauty that he smoothed his face with moistened bread to make his complexion shine, and he also used a mirror. Vitellius, an incomparable man in his life, defeated him in the civil war at Bebryacum in Campania." Cornelius wrote their war, and Pompeius Planta wrote it too, who says that Bebryacum is a village twenty miles from Cremona. Others say Bebriaci; Ponticus says it, whence the Bebrinian skins. For Galba was a Pontic. Let those who know the places weigh these things.

units.la: Vtrerius Sabioneda, cui originem suam debent Familia nobilis Comitum Persicorum, Cremonensium: & Vitalianus Vitalani, Ducis militaris.
units.tr: Vtrerius Sabioneda, to whom the noble family of the Counts Persico of Cremona owes its origin; and Vitaliano Vitaliani, a military commander.

units.la: Altius dein conspiciuntur Sozzanello, Robecco, Scandolera, Boedolla, Castell Visconte, Cadibalbi, Romenengo, Zanello, Trigolo, Casaletto, Soncino, quod Incolis stipatum, varias passum cum ab Friderico Ahenobarbo, tum ab aliis calamitates, varios habuit Dynastas, Mediolanenses, Francos, Venetos, postremo Karolum v. Imperatorem; qui illud defuncto Francisco Sforzia 11. Mediolanensium Duce, donavit Maximiliano Stampe, Patritio Mediolanensi, cum titulo Marchionatus. Nati ibi Paulus Barbus, Praedicatorum Ordinis, Scriptis clarus, Bernardinus Corvus, Guido Zappa, Orator & Poëta.
units.tr: Higher up then are seen Sozzanello, Robecco, Scandolera, Boedolla, Castell Visconte, Cadibalbi, Romenengo, Zanello, Trigolo, Casaletto and Soncino. Soncino, crowded with inhabitants, has suffered various calamities, both from Frederick Barbarossa and from others; it has had various lords: the Milanese, the French, the Venetians, and finally the Emperor Charles V, who, when Francesco Sforza II, Duke of Milan, had died, gave it to Massimiliano Stampa, a Milanese patrician, with the title of marquisate. Born there were Paolo Barbo of the Order of Preachers, famous for his writings; Bernardino Corvo; and Guido Zappa, orator and poet.

units.la: Visuntur inde Galignan, Villa Nuova, Pumenengo, & altius Calze.
units.tr: From there are seen Calignano, Villa Nuova, Pumenengo and, further up, Calvisano.

units.la: Ad laevam Padi ripam ab Ollij ostio post Doriolum, de quo ante, Viadana se pandit, Latine scribentibus Vitelliana, ab Vitellio Imperatore, quae Blondo Platinaque mens est, nominatum.
units.tr: On the left bank of the Po, after the mouth of the Oglio and after Dosolo, of which we spoke before, lies Viadana, called Vitelliana in Latin writing, after the Emperor Vitellius, as Biondo and Platina think.

units.la: Succeduntinde Casal Maggior, Torrigella, Castel de i Ponzoni, & Cortese.
units.tr: Next come Casalmaggiore, Torricella, Castel de' Ponzoni and Cortese.

units.la: Superato Navilio, Padi incola, ad Cremonam devenitur.
units.tr: Having crossed the Naviglio, a stream of the Po, one comes to Cremona.

units.la: Antiquum Opidum: nomen retinens, motum Livio multis locis, Straboni libro v. Tacito, Plinio lib. 111. cap.xviii. Ptolemaeo, aliis. Troiam ante dictam, & ab Hercule Iasonis comite in memoriam victi ab ipso ad Padum Gigantis conditam, matrisque triusque nomine Climenam, lapsuque temporis Cremonam nuncupatam pervetusta tradunt Chronica. Pado tam vicina, ut ab exundatione eius detrimentum subinde patiatur. Plinius in Decima locat Regione: Ptolemæus in Cenomanis. Plateas habet latas: Ædificia splendida, cum privata, tum publica: cum primis Arcem validam, hostibusque formidabilem: & Turrim, stupendæ altitudinis, anno cIↄ ccLXXXIV. conditam, Europæ mirabilibus consensu solitam. Colonia Romanorum facta, T. Sempronio & P. Cornelio coss. anno 15 xxxvii. ingruente in Italiam Hannibale, uti propugnaculum esset, memoriæ proditur ab Livio & Tacito. Sequentibus annis ab externis bellis intacta mansit, Civilibus infelix, ut Tacitus loquitur: multas magnasque perpessa calamitates Antonianis præsertim temporibus, quum Victor Octavianus Veteranis suis Agrum Cremonensem adjudicaret. Hinc Virgilius in Eclogis:
units.tr: It is an ancient town, retaining its name, mentioned by Livy in many places, by Strabo in book 5, by Tacitus, by Pliny in book 3, chapter 18, by Ptolemy and by others. Ancient chronicles relate that it was formerly called Troy, and was founded by Hercules, the companion of Jason, in memory of the Giant he defeated at the Po, and was named Climena after his mother, and in the course of time was called Cremona. It is so close to the Po that it suffers damage from its flooding from time to time. Pliny places it in the Tenth Region, Ptolemy among the Cenomani. It has wide streets and splendid buildings, both private and public, above all a strong citadel, formidable to enemies, and a tower of astonishing height, built in the year 1284, which by common consent is counted among the wonders of Europe. That it became a Roman colony in the consulship of T. Sempronius and P. Cornelius, in the year 537, when Hannibal was advancing into Italy, so that it might be a bulwark, is recorded by Livy and Tacitus. In the following years it remained untouched by foreign wars, but unlucky in civil ones, as Tacitus puts it; it suffered many great calamities, especially in the time of Antony, when Octavian the victor assigned the territory of Cremona to his veterans. Hence Virgil in the Eclogues:

units.la: Mantua væ miseræ nimium vicina Cremonæ.
units.tr: "Mantua, alas, too near wretched Cremona!"

units.la: Sic M. Valerius Martialis: Ingera perdiderat miseræ vicina Cremonæ, Flebat & abductas Tityrus ager oves: Risit Tuscus eques, pauperemque malignam Reppullit, &c.
units.tr: So too Marcus Valerius Martialis: "Mantua had lost its fields, being near wretched Cremona, and Tityrus wept for his sheep carried off; the Tuscan horseman laughed and drove off the poor and spiteful man, etc."

units.la: Post ab Gothis misere vastata, item ab Langobardis toto propemodum eversa, anno 15 cxxx. Mox quum Italiæ Regibus aliquamdiu paruisset, sui juris, aliatum Urbium exemplo, sub Imperij Romani nomine esse cœpit. Bello implicata civili, quod inter Guelfos & Gibellinos gestum, splendorem amisit cum libertate; aliis atque aliis imperium rapientibus Palavicinis, Doverianis, Cavalcabis. Tandem in Galeatiorum, hinc in Sfortiarum ditionem redacta, ab Ludovico xii. Galliarum Rege occupata, ex pacis legibus Venetis cessit; à quibus decennium possessa ad Gallos redijt: quibus Italia profligatis, Sfortiæ, Mediolani Duces, successerunt. His deficientibus cum tota Insubria ad Karolum v. eiusque Heredes, Hispaniæ Reges, est devoluta. Consulendi Sabellicus, Paullus Diaconus, Blondus, Corius, Merula, alij. Ob Fidem, quam suis Principibus servare consuevit, Fidei meruit cognomen. Episcopatus floret titulo. Magnorum Virorum genitrix: in quis primi loci Franciscus Sfondratus, Cardinalis: Eusebius, D. Hieronymi discipulus: Micolaus, Episcopus Placentinus: Gulielmus, Sodalitatis Eremitarum Magister, & Episcopus Navarræ: Franciscus Regatius, Minorita, Episcopus Bergomi: Moneta, Prædicatorij Ordinis, Professor Iuris Bononiensis, Auctor Summæ Casuum Conscientiæ: Orlandus, eiusdem Ordinis: Apollinaris, Cremonensis cognomine: Ioannes & Martinus Bosiani: item Richardus Malumbra & Hieronymus Ponzonius, Iurisconsulti: Gerardus Sabuloneta, Medicus & Philosophus: Ioannes Balistarius, Blondi Præceptor: Petrus Somentius & Daniel Cajetanus, Linguarum doctissimi. His adcensendi M. Furius Bibaculus & Quintilius antiqui ævi Poëtæ. Ante mœnia fuit Mephitis Templum, quod vel loco vel numine defensum, notat Tacitus: quum Vitellianis temporibus tota Civitas diriperetur, omniaque sacra profanaque in igne considerent. Agerilli planus & campestris: tritici, milij & aliarum frugum fructuumque, Vini item linique ferax.
units.tr: Afterwards it was laid waste by the Goths and almost entirely overthrown by the Lombards, in the year 1130. Then, having obeyed the kings of Italy for some time, following the example of other cities it began to be its own master, and under the name of the Roman Empire it began to exist. Caught up in the civil war waged between the Guelphs and the Ghibellines, it lost its splendour together with its liberty, as one after another the Palavicini, the Dovara and the Cavalcabò seized power. At last it was brought under the rule of the Galeazzi, then of the Sforza, was occupied by Louis XII, King of the French, and by the terms of a peace passed to the Venetians; held by them for ten years, it returned to the French; when the French were routed, the Sforza, Dukes of Milan, succeeded. When they failed, the whole of Lombardy fell to Charles V and his heirs, the Kings of Spain. Consult Sabellico, Paulus Diaconus, Biondo, Corio, Merula and others. Because of the loyalty which it was accustomed to keep to its princes, it earned the surname "Faithful". Its bishopric flourishes in title. It is the mother of great men, of whom the first rank belongs to Francesco Sfondrati, Cardinal; Eusebius, a disciple of St Jerome; Nicolò, Bishop of Piacenza; Guglielmo, Master of the Congregation of Hermits and Bishop of Navarre; Francesco Regazzi, a Franciscan, Bishop of Bergamo; Moneta, of the Order of Preachers, Professor of Law at Bologna, author of the Summa of Cases of Conscience; Orlando, of the same Order; Apollinare, called "of Cremona"; Giovanni and Martino Bosiani; likewise Riccardo Malumbra and Girolamo Ponzoni, jurists; Gerardo Sabuloneta, physician and philosopher; Giovanni Balestrieri, teacher of Biondo; Pietro Somenzio and Daniele Caetano, most learned in languages. To these may be added the ancient poets Marcus Furius Bibaculus and Quintilius. Before the walls there was a temple of Mephitis, which Tacitus notes was protected either by its place or by its divinity, when in the time of the Vitellians the whole city was plundered and all sacred and profane things were consumed by fire. The fields of Cremona are level and open country, fertile in wheat, millet and other grains and fruits, and also in wine and flax.

units.la: Ab Cremona secundum Navilij, moxque Ollij ripam superiora petenti se offerunt Braganegra, Grugno Torto, Paduno, Farferico, Casal Botroam, Casal Moran, Fiese, Corte de i Cavalcabo: Salverola, Sorresina, Trivoli, Rivolta, Fontanella, Issa, Antignan, Barbar.
units.tr: Beside Cremona, along the Naviglio, and soon as one heads upstream along the bank of the Oglio, there present themselves Braganegra, Grugno Torto, Paduno, Farfengo, Casal Bottrino, Casal Morano, Fiesco, Corte de' Cavalcabò, Salverola, Sorresina, Trivoli, Rivolta, Fontanella, Issa, Antignano and Barbata.

units.la: Succedunt deinde Torre dalle Pasere, Palosco, Telgato, Calepio, Livere, Ciolo, Gurlago, Calcina, Laminella, Grumello, Spino.
units.tr: Next come Torre dalle Pasere, Palosco, Telgate, Calepio, Livere, Ciolo, Gorlago, Calcinate, Laminella, Grumello and Spino.

units.la: Ab Adduæ, Pado se miscentis, ostio sursum incedenti Crypta occurrit: inde ultra Lecium Orcum Piceleo cum arce munitissima, cuius, atque adeo Opidi auctor Philippus Maria Vicecomes, Dux Mediolanensis.
units.tr: From the mouth of the Adda, where it flows into the Po, going upstream one meets Crypta; beyond it, past Lecco, Orco, and Piceleo with its very strongly fortified citadel, whose founder, and indeed the founder of the town, was Philip Maria Visconti, Duke of Milan.

units.la: In Serij amnis dextra sursum Vizzaga & Rivoltella visuntur: item Castiglione, Opidum ab Cremonensibus conditum contra Cremenses, teste Corio parte i.
units.tr: On the right bank of the river Serio, further up, Vizzaga and Rivoltella are to be seen; also Castiglione, a town founded by the Cremonese against the Cremonesi, according to Corio, part 1.

units.la: Sequuntur Marghera, Issa, Ottonengo, Camisan, Torre Cosso, Romano, Monasterio, Martinengo, Chisalba, Malpaga, Gavermago, Padreno, Basilia, Scanzo, Costa, Gandino.
units.tr: Marghera, Issa, Ottonengo, Camisan, Torre Cosso, Romano, Monasterio, Martinengo, Chisalba, Malpaga, Gavermago, Padreno, Basilia, Scanzo, Costa, Gandino follow.

units.la: Ad Adduæ ripam lævam sursum ad ostium Secij amnis est Monte Dodon: inde de Abbadia di Cerete, & Rivolta: mox Opidum nobile Crema. Fuit hic olim, ut locorum periti adferunt, Φόρος ᾿Αγροιῶν, Oppidum Ptolemæo notum, Ceno-manis adcensenti. Latini Interpretes vertunt Forum Diuguntorum. Condita fertur Crema ab Catholicis Civibus Urbis Parrhasy, post deletam Cremasamque (unde loco nomen) ab Archiepiscopo Mediolanensi: vel, uti alii placet, ab Henrico 1111. Imperatore, patriam, anno 1occcc1. Sita est in perpulcra planicie, mœnibus fir-missima. Amplitudine, elegantia, divitiis, ædificiorum splendore, Civium frequen-tia, rerum omnium copia multas Italiæ Urbes superat. Censetur inter nobilissima
units.tr: On the left bank of the Adda, upstream at the mouth of the river Serio, is Monte Dodon. From there come Abbadia di Cerete, & Rivolta, and soon the noble town Crema. As local scholars report, this was once the Forum of the Agroeans [Φόρος ᾿Αγροιῶν], a town known to Ptolemy, counted among the Cenomani. The Latin translators render it the Forum of the Diuguntes. Crema is said to have been founded by Catholic citizens of the city of Parrhasy, after Cremasa (from which the place takes its name) was destroyed by the Archbishop of Milan; or, as others prefer, by the Emperor Henry IV in the year 1100. It lies on a very beautiful plain and is very strongly walled. In size, elegance, wealth, splendour of its buildings, the number of its citizens and its abundance of everything, it surpasses many Italian cities. It is reckoned among the most noble castles of Italy.

units.la: Italiæ Castella: unde vulgo, ut alias notavi: Barlettain Puglia, Prato in Toscano, Crema in Lombardia. Prima Crema mentio incidit in ævum Friderici Ahenobarbi Imperatoris: ab cuius milite, auxilio Cremonensium, Laudensiumque, matere legitur habita, anno c1ɔclx. Corio scribente, parte 1. Instauratam mox ab eodem Imperatore, ut Blondus memorat libro xiv. Historiæ Cremonensibus adtribuit Henricus ipsius filius c1ɔcxcı. eodem Corio notante parte 11. Occuparunt inde imperium eius Palavicini, Benzoni, Turriani, Dovetiani, Vicecomites Mediolanensium Reguli, Veneti, Francorum Reges, tursumque Veneti. Præsulatum retinet Urbis, quam antea dixi, subvertiæ, sed vehementer imminutum & truncatum. Genuit claros Viros, in quis agmen ducunt Benzoni. Ager illi optimus, supraque modum fœcundus: non pauci ibi aquarum rivuli, in quis optimi provenient Pisces, præsertim Mustelæ, & qui voce patria Marsoh.
units.tr: Hence the common saying, as I have noted elsewhere: Barletta in Puglia, Prato in Tuscany, Crema in Lombardy. Crema is first mentioned in the age of the Emperor Frederick Barbarossa. Its capture by his soldiers, with the help of the Cremonese and the Lodigiani, is recorded in the year 1159, according to Corio, part 1. Soon afterwards it was restored by the same Emperor, as Blondus relates in book 14 of his History. His son Henry assigned it to the Cremonese in 1191, as Corio notes in part 2. Then its rule was seized by the Palavicini, Benzoni, Turriani, Dovetiani, the Visconti, lords of Milan, the Venetians, the kings of France, and finally the Venetians again. It keeps the bishopric of the city I mentioned before, which was overthrown, but it is greatly diminished and cut down. It has produced famous men, led by the Benzoni. Its land is excellent and beyond measure fertile. There are not a few streams of water, in which excellent fish are found, especially lampreys, and what are called marsoh in the native tongue.

units.la: Haud procul Crema in Mediterraneis pandunt se quæ vulgo Vaite, Mazzanega, & Barian, quod Barra Plinio, Orobiorum esse Urbem, interiisse, indeque Bergoma-tes originem duxisse ex Catonis sententia notanti. Decuno ab Urbe Bergamo distat lapide, apud Zanchum.
units.tr: Not far from Crema, inland, lie the places commonly called Vaite, Mazzanega and Barian. Pliny says that Barra, a city of the Orobii, perished there, and that the Bergamasks derived their origin from it, following the opinion of Cato, as noted. Bergamo is ten miles from the city, according to Zanchus.

units.la: Sequuntur Morengo, Cologno, Orguano, S. Maria della Basella: cui unde nomen, aperit Leander.
units.tr: Morengo, Cologno, Orguano and S. Maria della Basella follow. Leander explains where the name of the last comes from.

units.la: Visuntur hinc sursum versum Campagnuola & Seriato.
units.tr: From here, upward, Campagnuola and Seriato are visible.

units.la: Occurrunt dextra Abduæ ripa adverso itinere Spino, Pandino, Rivolte, quod Ripa-Alta Historiographis, Cladem Venetis ibi anno c1ɔ 1ɔ ix. prid. Eidus Maii illatam delineantibus.
units.tr: On the right bank of the Adda, on the opposite road, come Spino, Pandino and Rivolte, which historians call Ripa-Alta, describing the defeat inflicted there on the Venetians in the year 1509, the day before the Ides of May.

units.la: Offerunt se inde Acquadello, Galvazzano, Cesaren, Tricilio, Caravaggio, quod Victoria Francisci Stortiæ, Mediolanensium exercitus Præfecti contra Venetos, nobilitavit. Consulendi Blondus, Simoneta, Platina, Corius, Sabellicus.
units.tr: Then Acquadello, Galvazzano, Cesaren, Tricilio and Caravaggio present themselves. Caravaggio was made famous by the victory of Francesco Sforza, commander of the Milanese army, against the Venetians. For this matter consult Blondus, Simoneta, Platina, Corio and Sabellicus.

units.la: Dextra Brembi, Abduæ concurrentis, ripa superiora petenti adparent Arceno, Bolcetto, Cesarino, Verdel Maggiore, Spira, Verdel Minore, Como Nuovo, Stezza, Seiato, Offio, Offio di sopra, Cologno, Dalmo, Albigna, Trevolo.
units.tr: On the right bank of the Brembo, which joins the Adda, appear to those making their way upstream: Arceno, Bolcetto, Cesarino, Verdel Maggiore, Spira, Verdel Minore, Como Nuovo, Stezza, Seiato, Offio, Offio di sopra, Cologno, Dalmo, Albigna and Trevolo.

units.la: Spectatur hinc Bergomum. Sic Trogo, Plinio, Orobiorum stirpis ex Catone aicnti, Paullo ti, Paullo Diacono, aliisque; item Inscriptioni, quam in Mediolani historia ponam: Βέργαμον Ptolemaeo: quod iamnunc, antiquum retinens nomen, Bergamo. Conditum ab Gallis Cenomanis nomen indicat; quorum prisca lingua, ut hodie nostrae, Berg, Mons; quod in iugo montis situm. Insulios esse, qui Pergamum scribunt, & nescio quos Graecos fingunt conditores, notarunt alii. Loco situm est amoenissimo. Ambitus cum quatuor Suburbiis, quae cohaerent, non minor quam Mediolani. Facius lib. 11, Cantico 111. Passati al Serr, la Lama, e'l Brenno, Trovamo il Bergamo in su la costa Chi è parlar grosso, & è sottil di senno. La lor Citta pero, che è si ben posta, In fronte pregio porta, pregio, è fama, Ch'alcuna volta da Milan s'accosta.
units.tr: Bergamo can be seen from here. So say Trogus, Pliny (who says the stock of the Orobii came from Cato), Paulus, Paulus Diaconus and others; likewise the inscription which I shall set out in the history of Milan. Ptolemy calls it Βέργαμον [Bergamon], which, keeping its ancient name, is now Bergamo. The name shows it was founded by the Gauls Cenomani, whose ancient language, as in ours today, had Berg meaning mountain, because it is situated on the ridge of a mountain. Others have noted that those who write Pergamum are mistaken, and that they invent some Greek founders, I know not who. It lies in a most pleasant place. Its circuit, with four adjoining suburbs, is not less than that of Milan. Facio, book 2, canto 3: "Having passed the Serio, the Lama and the Brembo, we find Bergamo on the hillside. He who speaks plainly, and is subtle in wit. Their city, then, which is so well placed, bears a prize in front: a prize, it is said, which from time to time comes close to Milan."

units.la: Aedificiis superbit splendidis, tum publicis, tum privatis. In D. Mariae Sepulcrum est magnificum, ex Marmore, Bartholomaei Colconij, strenui militiae Ducis, cum equestri eius statua. Episcopatus floret dignitate. Incolae sermonis quidem rusticani; sed ingenii magni, cunctarumque artium capaces. Doctum est & elegans Carmen de Bergomatum Indole Moribusque Viri nobilissimi Iulii Caesaris Scaligeri: Ingenium, corpus, mores, obtutus, amictus, Tecta, cibus, gressus, guttura, sermo, sonus: Omnia crassa modis insignibus; omnia dura, Su valeant silices ut superare suos. Ista domi: sed vicinus si aspergat acetum; Artibus atque dolis vincitur ipsa suis.
units.tr: It is proud of its splendid buildings, both public and private. In the church of St Mary there is a magnificent marble tomb of Bartholomew Colleoni, a valiant military leader, with his equestrian statue. The bishopric flourishes in dignity. The inhabitants speak a rustic dialect, but they have great talent and are capable of all the arts. There is a learned and elegant poem on the character and customs of the Bergamasks by the most noble Julius Caesar Scaliger: "Their talent, body, manners, looks, dress, houses, food, gait, throat, speech and sound: all are coarse in their remarkable ways, all hard, so that flints might surpass their own hardness. This is at home; but if a neighbour sprinkles vinegar on them, they are overcome by their own arts and tricks."

units.la: Splendore suo Bergomum illustrarunt: Gulielmus Longa, Familia, Cardinalis: Gerardus, Savonensis Episcopus; Thomas Cataneus, Cerviae Praesul; Cosparinus Bargizza, Petrus Almaduranus, Ioannes Cerefolas; Theologi: Albericus Rosates, Matthaeus Foresti, Ioannes Suardus, Gabriel Alexander; Iurisconsulti: Bonifacius Clusonius, Guido Carrarianus, Filiusque eius Michael, Joannes Augustinus Turrius; Medici: Bartholomaeus Ossanus & Iacobus Philippus; Historiographi: Ambrosius denique Calepinus primus Dictionarii Auctor; qui eam suo coepto consecutus est felicitatem, ut Opus, quod rude & impolitum edidit, licet ab Viris doctissimis saepe supra modum sit auctum & illustratum, variis etiam adpositis linguis, semper tamen ipsius nomino fulgens prodeat, quod paucis contigit. Tanti est, felicia rebus aeternum duraturis ponere fundamenta. Est item Bergomas Damianus, Praedicatorij Ordinis Monachus, stupendus componendorum ex ligno segmentorum & vermiculatorum Emblematum artifex. His adienseri digna Bergomensis illa Lucretia, singulare pudicitiae exemplum, Antonia, Virgo (Elogij, quod ab Civibus in Palatio positum, versbis dicam) non minus animi, quam corporis pulchritudine pollens: quae quum a Friderico Imperatore violentum in se stuprum parari videret, mortem pro conservanda pudicitia vilipendens, gladiaque violatori erepto intrepidum sibi pectus transfodiens, singulari Castitatis exemplo Urbem hanc perpetuo illustravit, cIↄ c lxiix. In Praedicatorum Coenobio Bibliotheca est insignis, quam Alexander Martinengus, Malpagae Dinasta, instituit. Sub Conditorum, quos Gallos dixi, primo constituta potestate, inde ab Romanis inditionem est redacta. Respublica Bergomatis iub Trajano Imperatore mentionem facit Lapis Brixianus ad S. Faustum:
units.tr: The following have illustrated Bergamo by their distinction: Gulielmus Longa, Familia, Cardinal; Gerardus, Bishop of Savona; Thomas Cataneus, Bishop of Cervia; Cosparinus Bargizza, Petrus Almaduranus, Ioannes Cerefolas; theologians: Albericus Rosates, Matthaeus Foresti, Ioannes Suardus, Gabriel Alexander; jurists: Bonifacius Clusonius, Guido Carrarianus, and his son Michael, Joannes Augustinus Turrius; physicians: Bartholomaeus Ossanus & Iacobus Philippus; historians: Ambrosius; and finally Calepinus, the first author of the Dictionary. He was so fortunate in his undertaking that the work, which he published rough and unpolished, though often greatly enlarged and illustrated beyond measure by most learned men, with various languages added, still appears always shining with his name alone, which has been granted to few. Such is the value of laying foundations for things destined to last forever. Also from Bergamo is Damianus, a monk of the Order of Preachers, a remarkable craftsman of wooden inlay and of emblems made of small pieces of wood. To these may be added that Bergamasque Lucretia, a singular example of chastity, Antonia, a virgin (I shall give the inscription, which the citizens placed in the Palace, in words): no less powerful in the beauty of her mind than of her body; who, when she saw that Frederick the Emperor was preparing violent defilement against her, despising death for the sake of preserving her chastity, snatched a sword from her violator and fearlessly thrust it through her own breast, and by a singular example of purity has made this city famous for ever, 1169. In the convent of the Preachers there is a notable library, which Alexander Martinengo, lord of Malpaga, founded. Under the founders whom I called Gauls, power was first established here; afterwards it was brought under subjection by the Romans. The Republic of the Bergamasks is mentioned under the Emperor Trajan by the Brescian stone at S. Faustus:

units.la: P. CLODIO. P. F. FAB. SVRÆ Q. FLAMINI. DIVI TRAIANI. PONTIF. IIII VIR. QVINQ. TRIB. LEG II ADIVTRIC. PIÆ. FID CVRAT. REIP. BERGOM DAT. AB. IMP. TRAIANO CVRAT. REIP. COMENS DAT. AB. IMP.HADRIANO
units.tr: To Publius Clodius Surus, son of Publius, of the Fabian tribe, quaestor, flamen of the deified Trajan, pontiff, quattuorvir, quinquennial, tribune of the Second Legion Adiutrix Pia Fidelis, curator of the commonwealth of Bergomum, appointed by the Emperor Trajan; curator of the commonwealth of Comum, appointed by the Emperor Hadrian

units.la: COLLEGIA FABROR. ET. CENT
units.tr: COLLEGIA FABROR. ET. CENT Colleges of the Smiths and Centonarii

units.la: Successu temporis ab Attila Hunnorum Duce vastatam, uti Paullus Diaconus scribit libro xv ad Eutropium, possederunt diu Langobardi sub Pra fidibus, qui Duces Bergomates audiebant. Post hos Italiae Reges habere coepit Dominos; inde sui facta juris exemplo reliquarum Civitatum sub Imperatoribus horuit Romanis. Duravit status ille usque ad Philippum Turrianum, a quo per vim anno MCCCLXIV occupata, variisque inde experta Regulos, Galeatios, Scaligeros, Suardos, Visconitos, Malatestas, aliosque, & multis concussa calamitatibus ad Venetos defecit; inde ab Gallis Sfortiis que subjugata, tandem ab Venetis est recuperata. Diaconum vide, quem dixi item Merulam, Blondum, Corium, Simonetam, Æquicolam, Capreolum, aliosque. Ager surburbicarius supra modum fertilis, praeterquam qua Septemtrio, ubi totus asper, montosus, sterilis. Ferrum habet & Cotarias, lapidemque Cadmiam, ex quo aes conficitur. Consule Plinium lib. xxxiv natur. hist. cap. 1. Vellera suppeditat magni precii.
units.tr: Over time, after being laid waste by Attila, leader of the Huns, as Paulus Diaconus writes in book xv, addressed to Eutropius, the Lombards held it for a long time under prefects, who were called Dukes of Bergamo. After them the Kings of Italy became its lords; then, made subject to its own law as an example for the other cities, it flourished under the Roman Emperors. That condition lasted until Philip Torriani, by whom it was seized by force in 1264. After experiencing various petty lords, the Galeazzi, Scaligeri, Suardi, Visconti, Malatesta and others, and being shaken by many calamities, it fell to the Venetians; then it was subjugated by the French and the Sforzas, and at last recovered by the Venetians. See Diaconus, whom I mentioned, and likewise Merula, Blondus, Corius, Simonetta, Aequicola, Capreolus and others. The surrounding land is exceedingly fertile, except to the north, where it is entirely rough, mountainous and barren. It has iron and whetstones, and the stone cadmia, from which brass is made. Consult Pliny, Natural History, book xxxiv, chapter 1. It supplies wool of great value.

units.la: Valles circa Bergomum, Vini Oleique suavissimi feraces, sunt passim multae, in quis primas facile tenet Seriana. Sunt in ea, quae vulgato Idiomate Sertago, Gorle, Aizano, Nembri, Albe, Defenza, Gazaniga & Barlo.
units.tr: The valleys around Bergamo, rich in very sweet wine and oil, are numerous everywhere, and among them the Seriana easily holds first place. In it are those places which in the vernacular are called Sertago, Gorle, Aizano, Nembri, Albe, Defenza, Gazaniga and Barlo.

units.la: Post Brembanam Vallem pandunt se inter montes, cum aliis. Vici Castellaque S. Pietro & Menio.
units.tr: Beyond the Brembana valley, they open out among the mountains, along with others. Villages and castles: S. Pietro and Menio.

units.la: In Valle D. Martini visuntur Pontida, Cesano, Caurino, Callozzo, Refino & Lorentino.
units.tr: In the valley of D. Martini are seen Pontida, Cesano, Caurino, Callozzo, Refino and Lorentino.

units.la: In Mancana Valle sunt Villa di S. Pellegrino, S. Giovanni, Platia, & Roncola.
units.tr: In the Mancana valley are Villa di S. Pellegrino, S. Giovanni, Platia and Roncola.

units.la: Inter Brembum & Adduam Caveriato invenitur.
units.tr: Between the Brembo and the Adda, Caveriato is found.

units.la: Lava Brembi ripa superiora versum incedenti occurrunt Frama, S. Cervasio, Ranzo, Caurio, Filago, Bonare di sotto, Bonare di sopra, Temo, Castelletto: dextra vero, S. Cervase, Cereto, Putanengo, Medolago, Cerignano, Colza, Torre di Cesare, Calepio & ulterius validissimum Opidum Leucum, Mediolanensium subditum potestati. Ab eo proximo Lacui nomen: secundum quem incedenti usque ad Larium offerunt se Abbatia, Mandello, Lierna, Vicbatia, Varrena, Bellano, Correno, Prona, & alia.
units.tr: Going upstream along the upper bank of the Brembo, there come into view Frama, S. Cervasio, Ranzo, Caurio, Filago, Bonare di sotto, Bonare di sopra, Temo, Castelletto; on the right, however, S. Cervase, Cereto, Putanengo, Medolago, Cerignano, Colza, Torre di Cesare, Calepio, and further on the very strong town Leucum, subject to the power of the Milanese. From the nearby lake it takes its name. Going along it up to the Lario, there present themselves Abbatia, Mandello, Lierna, Vicbatia, Varrena, Bellano, Correno, Prona, and others.

units.la: Vbi Abdua Lario miscetur Vogro visitur, octoque ab eodem lacu milliaribus Morbigno; quod Latine scribentibus Morbinium: Iovio autem Morbonium, ob coeli gravitatem. Sequuntur inde Sacco, Rasura, Podesan, Abbare, Gerola: item ad Abduae dextram Telamona, Colorina, Toro, Fusine, Cedrarco, Castolo, Boffaglia, doctioribus Albosagia, Pisatedo, Boffetto, Ponte di S. Giacomo, Stazzona, Tirano, Lovere, Tovo, Mazzo: spatio inde xv M. P. inter asperrimas rupes Grosio, Lopie, Cipina, Bormio, Civibus frequens. Secundo hinc lapide, Bagni di S. Martino.
units.tr: Where the Adda mingles with the Lario, Vogro is seen, and eight miles from that lake Morbigno, which writers in Latin call Morbinium, but Jovius Morbonium, on account of the heaviness of the air. Then follow Sacco, Rasura, Podesan, Abbare, Gerola; likewise on the right bank of the Adda Telamona, Colorina, Toro, Fusine, Cedrarco, Castolo, Boffaglia, and, for the more learned, Albosagia, Pisatedo, Boffetto, Ponte di S. Giacomo, Stazzona, Tirano, Lovere, Tovo, Mazzo. Then, within a space of fifteen Roman miles, among very rough cliffs, Grosio, Lopie, Cipina, Bormio, crowded with citizens. Two miles from here, Bagni di S. Martino.

units.la: Ab Abduae capite in Lario, laeva ripa sursum versus Martello & Troana reperiuntur: haud procul inde in monte Caspano, dives nobileque Opidum: succedunt hinc Ardeno, Baio, Barbeno, Castiono.
units.tr: From the head of the Adda on the Lario, on the left bank going upward, Martello and Troana are found. Not far from there, on the mountain Caspano, a rich and noble town. From here follow Ardeno, Baio, Barbeno, Castiono.

units.la: Ad finem amnis Malengi, qui cognominem percurrit Vallem, Sondrium jacet, lautum frequensque Castrum.
units.tr: At the end of the river Mallero, which runs through the valley of the same name, lies Sondrium, a well-built and populous castle.

units.la: Ulterius deinde Pendulasco, Tresivo, Ponte, Chiavre, Giero, Teglio, Boale, Rianzono, Villa, La Madonna da Tirano, Versio, Grossuto, Grosso, Sandolo, & alia.
units.tr: Further on: Pendulasco, Tresivo, Ponte, Chiavre, Giero, Teglio, Boale, Rianzono, Villa, La Madonna da Tirano, Versio, Grossuto, Grosso, Sandolo, and others.

units.la: Iuxta caput in Lario Meirae fluminis, Turris Volonij fuit, vulgo Torre di Falegno, quam superioribus annis exiderunt Grisones.
units.tr: Near the mouth of the river Mera, on the Lario, there was the Tower of Volonius, commonly called Torre di Falegno, which the Grisons destroyed in recent years.

units.la: Vallis ibi incipit Clavennae, cui nomen ab Opido nobili Clavenna. Sic Paullo Diacono dicitur lib. vi Langbard.cap.xxi, Clavena Antonino; quod Chiavenna Italis, Cleven Incolis.
units.tr: The valley of Chiavenna begins there, named after the noble town Clavenna. Thus it is called Clavena by Paulus Diaconus, in book vi of the History of the Lombards, chapter 21, and by Antoninus; Chiavenna to the Italians, Cleven to its inhabitants.

units.la: Inter Volonium & Clavennam Nova visitur. Dextra Clavennæ Meræque fluminis sursum Cosisfana & Stampa; sinistra, Piur, Latinis Plurium: ulterius Vesperanum est, vernacule Vespram. Ab Clavenna Liræ læva sursum Taurelium jacet, vulgo Taure.
units.tr: Between Volonius and Clavenna, Nova is seen. On the right of Clavenna, up along the river Mera, Cosisfana and Stampa; on the left, Piur, in Latin Plurium; further on is Vesperanum, in the vernacular Vespram. From Clavenna, on the left of the Liro going upward, lies Taurelium, commonly Taure.

units.la: Vbi Addua Pado confluit, in ripa læva, Castellum conspicitur Novum, ab Ostio fluminis cognominatum, Castel Nuovo di Bocca di Adda. Subversum ab Mediolanensibus Placentinisque anno cIↄ clxxxix, testauratumque à Parmensibus in gratiam Cremonensium, memorat Corius.
units.tr: Where the Adda joins the Po, on the left bank, a castle is seen, Novum, named after the mouth of the river, Castel Nuovo di Bocca di Adda. Corius records that it was destroyed from the ground up by the Milanese and Piacentines in 1189, and rebuilt by the Parmesans in favour of the Cremonese.

units.la: Visuntur inde Camarago, Codogno, & Castellono.
units.tr: From there are seen Camarago, Codogno and Castellono.

units.la: Mox in Abduæ ripa Lauda Civitas se pandit; vulgo Lodi. Laus simpliciter Antonino, Laus Pompeia Plinio lib. iii. cap. xvi, Insubrum notanti urbem, & Itinerariæ Tabulæ: Laus Nova fortean Ciceroni. Meminit Laudis Pompeia Cippus ad Viam Flaminiam erectus in Villa Iulia, haud procul Roma: DIIS. MANIBVS L. TITI, L.F. PVPINIA MACRI. VI. VIRO DECVRIO LAVDE. POMPEIA VIXIT. ANNIS XXX TITIA. RHOPE MATER. ET SALVIVS. VICTOR CONLAC. F
units.tr: Soon the city of Lauda opens out on the bank of the Adda; in the vernacular Lodi. Antoninus simply calls it Laus; Pliny, book iii, chapter 16, calling it Laus Pompeia, notes it as a city of the Insubres, and so do the Itinerary Tables; Laus Nova perhaps to Cicero. The Laus Pompeia is mentioned by a cippus erected on the Via Flaminia, in the Villa Iulia, not far from Rome: "To the spirits of the dead: Lucius Titius, son of Lucius, of the Pupinian tribe, a sexvir and decurion of Laus Pompeia, lived thirty years. Titia Rhope, his mother, and Salvius Victor, his fellow freedman, [set this up]."

units.la: Nomen Vrbi impositum memorant Mediolanensium Chronica ab Laudo Mediolanensi, Civitate ob seditionem profligato, & cum suis in hæc loca profecto. Eadem mens Merulæ, lib. iii Histor. Viceconomitum. Blondo aliisque fabulosa hæc censentur. Plinius Bojos Gallos facit Conditores. Polybius tamen, Strabo, Trogus, alii, Vrbes ab Gallis condita recensentes, hujus, quod mirum, nullam faciunt mentionem. Quidquid sit, sive Laus solum initio fuerit dicta, sive Laus Pompeia simul; cognomen putat Leander inditum à Cn. Pompeio Strabone, Cn. Pompei Magni Patre; qui vel Colonos huc deduxisse, vel Vrbem restauraße existimatur. Civitas est perhonesta, dives, rebus, quæ ad vitam necessariæ, abundans. Incolæ armis tractandis, exercendæque mercaturæ apti. Episcopatus floret titulo. Clarosgenuit Viros, non paucos: inquis D. Bassanus, Vrbis Præsul, Divorum adscriptus classi, Raimundus Summa-ripensis, Civitatis item Antistes; Iacobus Arrigineus, Prædicatorij Ordinis Monachus; Ambrosius Vineatus, Matthæus Vegius, & alij. Co'oniam Romanorum facit Onuphrius Panuinius. Antiqua Vrbs eversa funditus legitur ab Mediolanensibus, anno ab Christo nato cIↄclviii, ob Civiles dissensiones: anno vero xlix post ab Friderico Ahenobarbo Imperatore, hostiliter in Mediolanenses animato, nova, tertio à priscæ Vrbis ruinis lapide, ædificata: quæ sensim civibus, ædificijs, opibus crescens, libera diu suique juris fuit, sub auctoritate tamen Imperij Romani: post quum Gibellinorum & Guelforum in Italia Factiones essent exortæ, communi totius populi consensu Respublica decennali magistratu anno cIↄ ccl Vestarino est commissa: ab Philippo Turriano, Mediolani Tyranno, anno cIↄcclxiv, occupata, rursus anno cIↄ cccxxi ad Vestarinos una cum Principis titulo communibus suffragijs est translata: quibus amotis, in potestatem Mediolanensium Ducum anno cIↄ cccxxxv est redacta, frustra aliquoties ad Venetorum adspirans clientelam. Legendi, præter Merulam, Corium, aliosque, ipsius Vrbis & Mediolani Annales. Regi nunc paret Hispaniarum, ut Mediolanensium Principi. Ager urbicus valde uber, & rei pecuariæ peridoneus: Tritici, Silignis, Milij, Lactis, Butyri, Caseï supra fidem, Vini, Lini, eliarumque rerum ferax.
units.tr: The Milanese chronicles report that the city received its name from Laudus, a Milanese, who, after being defeated in a sedition, departed with his followers to these places. Merula holds the same view, in book iii of his History of the Viscounts. Blondus and others consider this fabulous. Pliny makes the Boii, Gauls, its founders. Polybius, however, Strabo, Trogus and others, who list cities founded by the Gauls, strangely make no mention of it. Whatever the case, whether Laus alone was first called so, or Laus Pompeia at the same time, Leander thinks the surname was given by Gnaeus Pompeius Strabo, father of Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus, who is thought either to have led colonists here or to have restored the city. The city is very honourable and rich, abounding in things necessary for life. Its inhabitants are fit for handling arms and for carrying on trade. The bishopric flourishes in title. It has produced not a few famous men: D. Bassanus, bishop of the city, enrolled among the saints; Raimundus Summaripensis, likewise bishop of the city; Jacobus Arrigineus, a monk of the Dominican Order; Ambrosius Vineatus, Matthaeus Vegius and others. Onuphrius Panvinius calls it Colonia Romanorum. The old city is read to have been utterly destroyed by the Milanese in the year of Christ's birth 1158, because of civil dissensions; but forty-nine years later, by the Emperor Frederick Barbarossa, hostile to the Milanese, a new city was built, using stone from the ruins of the old city as a third source. Growing gradually in citizens, buildings and wealth, it was free and self-governing for a long time, yet under the authority of the Roman Empire. Afterwards, when the factions of the Ghibellines and Guelphs had arisen in Italy, by the common consent of the whole people the republic was entrusted in 1250 to Vestarinus with a magistracy for ten years. It was seized in 1264 by Philip Torriani, tyrant of Milan; again in 1321 it was transferred by common votes to the Vestarini, together with the title of Prince; and when these were removed, it was reduced in 1335 under the power of the Dukes of Milan, having several times aspired in vain to the protection of the Venetians. For reading, besides Merula, Corius and others, there are the Annals of the city itself and of Milan. It now obeys the King of Spain as Prince of Milan. The land of the city is very rich and well suited to cattle-raising: it produces wheat, rye, millet, milk, butter and cheese beyond belief, wine, flax, and other things in abundance.

units.la: Ab Lauda sursum procedenti occurrunt quę vernaculo Idiomate Torretta, Comora, Calgagno, Villa, Algne, Busna, Muzzano, Zoloben, Perfico, Pau, Merlino, Corrazo, Cornillano.
units.tr: Going upward from Lauda, there come into view what in the vernacular are called Torretta, Comora, Calgagno, Villa, Algne, Busna, Muzzano, Zoloben, Perfico, Pau, Merlino, Corrazo, Cornillano.

units.la: Succedunt, Mutia amne superato, Irocazzano, & Cavaton: dein ad dextram Melgolae ripam Septana: ad laevam Mutiae Albignano; medioque horum fluminum Meizi, Melpum, ut nonnulli putant, Primo opulentia praecipuum, abdenti, sed deletum ab Vicinis, eo die, quo Camillus Vejos cepit.
units.tr: Then, after crossing the river Muzia, come Irocazzano and Cavaton; then on the right bank of the Melgola, Septana; on the left of the Muzia, Albignano; and between these rivers lie Meizi and Melpum, which some think was the most prominent in wealth among the Insubrians, but was destroyed by its neighbours on the day Camillus took Veii.

units.la: Occurrunt hinc Biunzago, & Pezzono; & ad sinistram Adduae Cassano: altius Crotello, mox, Navilio transito, Vetena, Gorgonzola, Tormace, Inzago: sequuntur inde Massa, Vaccaro. Merulae lib. vi Vicecomitum Vaprium, Poetaque Ligurino Vaccae. Intus sunt Baffano, Cicsa, Castellazzo, Cambiago, Homa, Cavernago; & altius Gurnago, Micerato, Ornago, Romello & Monzero.
units.tr: From here come Biunzago and Pezzono; and on the left of the Adda, Cassano; higher up, Crotello; then, after crossing the Naviglio, Vetena, Gorgonzola, Tormace, Inzago; next follow Massa and Vaccaro. Merula, in book vi of the Viscounts, mentions Vaprium, and the poet Ligurinus mentions Vacca. Within are Baffano, Cicsa, Castellazzo, Cambiago, Homa, Cavernago; and higher up Gurnago, Micerato, Ornago, Romello and Monzero.

units.la: Viterius ad Abduam validissimum est Oppidum Trecium à Barnaba Vicecomite conditum anno MCCCLX.
units.tr: Further up the Adda is the very strong town of Trecium, founded by Barnabas Visconti in 1360.

units.la: Altius adhuc Rocca di Cusano, Busnagna, Beinsio, Oldenigo, Mizzago, Cantone, Rusnello, & Coinago.
units.tr: Higher still lie Rocca di Cusano, Busnagna, Beinsio, Oldenigo, Mizzago, Cantone, Rusnello, and Coinago.

units.la: Dein propter Abduam, sursum, Portesino: intusque Osnago, Idro di sotto & di sopra, Inferiorum & Superiorum; Caurzi, Fatecano, Novato, Cerusiolo, Rebia, Imberfago; & secundum Abduae ripam Brezzo, quod Latinus Brepia: dein Rocca d'Anono, Og na, Rovega; & altius Galea.
units.tr: Then, further up the Adda, lie Portesino; inland, Osnago, Idro di sotto and di sopra (Inferiorum and Superiorum), Caurzi, Fatecano, Novato, Cerusiolo, Rebia, and Imberfago; and along the bank of the Adda, Brezzo, which the Latin writers call Brepia; then Rocca d'Anono, Ogna, and Rovega; and higher up, Galea.

units.la: Rursum in Padi ripa, post Abduae confluentia, Guardamei, Somasia, Hospitaletto, Ori.
units.tr: Again on the bank of the Po, past the confluence with the Adda, lie Guardamei, Somasia, Hospitaletto, and Ori.

units.la: Ad dextram Lambri, iterum, Landa Vetus conspicitur, cujus antea memini: mox Bulfone, Mota, Tavazzano, Casal Pusterlengo, Mulazzano, Gorzignano, Medi, Celofora Magno, Latinis Agnus Fori Magni: Linato, Pescara, Gonzaga, Panachia, Lucino, Rodeno, Lunardi, Rugnesa, S. Petrino, Lambrato, Segrato, Vogna, Lesiato, Vimodrone, Proseello, Casina Bianca, Casina di Paoli.
units.tr: On the right of the Lambro, again, Landa Vetus comes into view, which I mentioned earlier. Soon after come Bulfone, Mota, Tavazzano, Casal Pusterlengo, Mulazzano, Gorzignano, Medi, and Celofora Magno, which the Latins called Agnus Fori Magni; then Linato, Pescara, Gonzaga, Panachia, Lucino, Rodeno, Lunardi, Rugnesa, S. Petrino, Lambrato, Segrato, Vogna, Lesiato, Vimodrone, Proseello, Casina Bianca, and Casina di Paoli.

units.la: Iterum trans Navilium, offerunt se Cologno, Cermusello, Bufere, Membrugie, Caponago; & in Brigantinis Montibus, Teffono, Bannugato, Monteze, Casa di Basion, Imbrazzia, Pescaroia, Comorreggio, Vil Mercato, Latinis Vicus Mercatus, nonnullis Vicus Martius ex Inscriptione, quae ibi in aede D. Stephani: MERC. IN VIC. VOT. MARTIVS. IVSOR. ALLVCIVS. L. D. D. D.
units.tr: Again across the Naviglio appear Cologno, Cermusello, Bufere, Membrugie, and Caponago; and in the Brigantine hills, Teffono, Bannugato, Monteze, Casa di Basion, Imbrazzia, Pescaroia, Comorreggio, and Vil Mercato, which the Latins called Vicus Mercatus, though some call it Vicus Martius from the inscription that is there in the church of St Stephen: MERC. IN VIC. VOT. MARTIVS. IVSOR. ALLVCIVS. L. D. D. D.

units.la: Adparent dein Oren, Pasica, Arcon, S. Martino, Lesino, Vella, Vfina, Bernaregio: juxtaque Lambrum Canonica.
units.tr: Next appear Oren, Pasica, Arcon, S. Martino, Lesino, Vella, Vfina, and Bernaregio; and beside the Lambro, Canonica.

units.la: Intus Campo Florentino, Triasio, Monte, Aia, Cazzeno, Beffoza, Casale, Misericordia, Lomagna, Monte Seggio, Torrefolla, Cassago, Cremella, Rovagnato, Hoes & alius Anono, Ogione, Ciisui, Illo, Sara.
units.tr: Inland are Campo Florentino, Triasio, Monte, Aia, Cazzeno, Beffoza, Casale, Misericordia, Lomagna, Monte Seggio, Torrefolla, Cassago, Cremella, Rovagnato, Hoes, and another Anono, Ogione, Ciisui, Illo, and Sara.

units.la: Visitur ultra Lacum Puscianum, de quo alibi, Vallis Affina, in qua Cantium, vulgo Canzo: & altius Ossio, S. Agatha, Casalino & Sarena.
