units.tr: Beyond Lake Pusiano, which I discuss elsewhere, is seen the Vallis Affina, in which lies Cantium, commonly called Canzo; and higher up, Ossio, S. Agatha, Casalino, and Sarena.

units.la: Rursum in Padi ripa post Lambri ostium Cagnola S. Giacomo, Vena, Belgiojoso, castrum opulentum, ditionis Comitum Barbianorum.
units.tr: Again on the bank of the Po, past the mouth of the Lambro, are Cagnola, S. Giacomo, Vena, and Belgiojoso, a rich castle in the lordship of the Counts Barbiano.

units.la: Sequuntur hinc Mettona, Saggiarella, S. Columbano, quod ab Friderico Ahenobarbo Imperatore anno MCCLXIV conditum, pessime superioribus bellis, inter Karolum & Franciscum Galliarum Regem gestis habitum.
units.tr: From here follow Mettona, Saggiarella, and S. Columbano, which was founded by the Emperor Frederick Barbarossa in 1164, and was badly treated in the recent wars waged between Charles and Francis, King of the French.

units.la: Per ripam Lambri sursum incedenti Villantum se pandit, cum S. Angelo, quod ab Regina Scaligera, Barnabae Vicecomitis Coniuge, anno ab Christo nato MCCCLXXI aedificatum.
units.tr: As you go up along the bank of the Lambro, Villanto opens before you, with S. Angelo, which was built by Regina della Scala, wife of Barnabas Visconti, in the year of Christ 1371.

units.la: Secundum Ticinellum Turris spectatur Tertia, quae vulgo Torre del Terzo: eo transito, Landriano & Gregnane: hinc ultra D. Angeli rivum Cuselle, Andreae Alciati Villas; moxque Arcegnano, Cignano, Pizza Gragia, verti sque Lambrum, Rozzo, Balgape, Carpiono, Cernare: & ad Lambrum, Melignano, quod ab Mediolanensibus anno MCCCXLIII muris cinctum, Marchionatus titulo nobilitatum.
units.tr: Along the Ticinello is seen the Third Tower, which is commonly called Torre del Terzo. Past it lie Landriano and Gregnano; beyond the stream of S. Angelo, hence, Cuselle, the villas of Andrea Alciati; and soon Arcegnano, Cignano, Pizza Gragia, and on both sides of the Lambro, Rozzo, Balgape, Carpiono, and Cernare; and at the Lambro, Melignano, which the Milanese walled in 1343, and which was ennobled with the title of a marquisate.

units.la: Succedunt dein de, rivulo transito, La Rocca, Vilo dono, Locato, Opera, Ponte Sesto (Pons Sextus) S. Giuliano juxtaque Lambrum, Cotrono, Zerida, S. Donato, Chiaravalle, Ronchetto, S. Maria in Asso, Caffinazzo, Viglino, altiusque, S. Martino, Bisighera, Trivultio, Monfenita, Monico: dein haud procul Mediolano, Casinello, Bianchetta, Casoneto, Cimiano, Casengo, Turate: transque Navilium, Martesana, Broco, Precentana: circa dextram alvei ripam Suse & Brego rum in meditullio Buccea, quam Gallorum cladesanno cıo ıɔ xxıı coepit nobilitare: mox Prechetto, Torretta, Sefto, Peluca, S. Rocco & in mediterranis Ballamo, Cinofello, juxtaque Suelas Cusano.
units.tr: Next, after crossing a small stream, come La Rocca, Vilo dono, Locato, Opera, and Ponte Sesto (Pons Sextus); S. Giuliano beside the Lambro, Cotrono, Zerida, S. Donato, Chiaravalle, Ronchetto, S. Maria in Asso, Caffinazzo, Viglino, and higher up S. Martino, Bisighera, Trivultio, Monfenita, and Monico; then not far from Milan, Casinello, Bianchetta, Casoneto, Cimiano, Casengo, and Turate; and across the Naviglio, Martesana, Broco, and Precentana. Along the right bank of the channel lie Suse and Bregorum, and in the middle of the plain Buccea, which the defeat of the Gauls began to make famous in the year 1522. Soon after come Prechetto, Torretta, Sefto, Peluca, S. Rocco, and inland Ballamo, Cinofello, and, beside the Suelas, Cusano.

units.la: Lambro adsidet nobile opidum Moncia, vulgo Monza : Paullo Diacono libro ıııı Rerum Langbardic. Modoetia, Insubrum scribenti Vrbem, xıı r. m. ab Mediolano. Moguntiacum dicitur, nonnullis censentibus, Lapidi, qui Mediolani ad D. Victorem:
units.tr: Beside the Lambro sits the noble town Moncia, commonly Monza. Paul the Deacon, in book 4 of his History of the Lombards, calls it Modoetia, writing of the city of the Insubres, twelve miles from Milan. It is called Moguntiacum, as some think, from a stone that is at Milan by the church of S. Victor:

units.la: C. SERTORIVS. L. F
units.tr: C. SERTORIVS, SON OF L.

units.la: OVP: TERTVILIANVS VETERANVS.LEG.XVI CVRATOR. CIVIVM. ROMAN MOGVNTIACI
units.tr: OVP: TERTVILIANVS, VETERAN OF THE SIXTEENTH LEGION, CURATOR OF THE ROMAN CITIZENS AT MOGUNTIACVM

units.la: Medium opidum perfluit Lamber. Auxit supra modum, structa etiam splendida Basilica, nobilitavitque Theodoricus i. Gothorum in Italia Rex; teste, ante Blondum lib.viii Histor. Paullo Diacono, qui addit, Theodolinam Reginam condidisse hic magnificum D. Ioannis Fanum, & sumtuosam Regiam, Sedem diu Langbardiæ Regum. Lapsu temporis muris nudatum refecit Azo Vice-comes anno cıç ccxxxv, scribente Corio. Imperium diu fuit penes Mediolani Principes. Donavit superioribus annis Imperator Karolus v Antonio Leva, Hispano, virtutis ergo.
units.tr: The river Lambro flows through the middle of the town. It has grown beyond measure, and King Theodoric I of the Goths in Italy, who built a splendid basilica there, also raised its standing. This is attested by Blondus, book 8 of his Histories, before whom Paul the Deacon, who adds that Queen Theodelinda founded here the magnificent church of St John and a sumptuous palace, long the seat of the Lombard kings. Time had stripped its walls, and Azzo Visconti restored them in 1235, according to Corio. For a long time power in the town lay with the princes of Milan. In recent years the Emperor Charles V gave it to Antonio de Leyva, a Spaniard, for his valour.

units.la: Visuntur ulterius Nova, Massago, Defio, Vedono, Biasin, Lisono, Macchi, Seregna, Sevese: in ripa Lambri: Suigo, Albi, Cararo, Chanca, Meda, Mocarello, Marliano, alijs Martanum seu Manliianum.
units.tr: Further along are Nova, Massago, Defio, Vedano, Biassono, Lisone, Macchi, Seregno, Seveso, on the bank of the Lambro; and Suigo, Albiate, Carate, Canzo, Meda, Mocchirolo, Marliano, and by others Martanum or Manliianum.

units.la: Mox Verano & Incino, ubi Parochialis ædes, Plebem vocant Incini, La Pieve di Incino. Censet hic fuisse Licini Forum Leander, cujus meminit Plinius apud quem & Laccini, Octavæ Regionis in Italia populis tribus, teste Ortelio, exemplaribus Licinos præferentibus, Fori Licini procul dubio Incolas.
units.tr: Soon come Veranno and Incino, where there is a parish church, which the locals call Incini Plebs, La Pieve di Incino. Leander thinks that Licini Forum was here, which Pliny mentions, and in whose neighbourhood, according to Ortelius, the Laccini dwelt, one of the three peoples of the Eighth Region of Italy. Some copies give Licinos, but the inhabitants of Forum Licinum are without doubt meant.

units.la: Sequuntur Canago, Carrenna, Monsular, Figino, Arosio: & in collibus Inverigo: juxtaque Scvesam Cantu, recentioribus Cantuarium; item Brena, Cernagio, Clorago, Noble, Fabrica, Alzato, Alfiatum Latinis, Alciatum V. CL. Andreæ Alciato, qui ab Alciato, Parthaonis Ætoliæ Regis filio, dictum indicat. Patria Virginij Rufi, teste Plinio, Alsiam nominante locum.
units.tr: Next come Canago, Carenna, Monsolaro, Figino, Arosio; and on the hills Inverigo; and near the Seveso Cantù, called Cantuarium by more recent writers; likewise Brenna, Cernaggio, Clorago, Nobile, Fabrica, Alzate, Alfiatum in Latin, and Alciatum, which the most learned Andreas Alciatus shows to be named after Alciatus, son of Parthaon, king of Aetolia. It was the home of Virginius Rufus, according to Pliny, who calls the place Alsia.

units.la: Spectantur mox Infimano, Matteorfin, Latine scribentibus Mons Orfanus; Paravisin, Monguzzo, verius fortean Moguntiacum, de quo supra. Sic sane volunt Merula & Corius. Andreas autem Alciatus Moguntium sibi videri scribit Montem Acutum potius appellandum. Haud procul inde est Cnisamo.
units.tr: Next are seen Inverigo, Mariano, which Latin writers call Mons Orfanus; Paravisio, Monguzzo, perhaps more truly Moguntiacum, of which I have spoken above. Merula and Corius indeed think so. Andreas Alciatus, however, writes that Moguntium seems to him to be better called Montem Acutum. Not far from there is Cnisamum.

units.la: Supra Serium Lacum visuntur Erba & Creveña.
units.tr: Above Lake Como are seen Erba and Creva.

units.la: Circa Britiæ amnis principia Morbio, Canosso, & Vacallo.
units.tr: Around the sources of the river Breggia are Morbio, Canosso and Vacallo.

units.la: Per lævam Leuci lacus incedenti offerunt se Mulgratone, altiusque circa Larium tamquam in Peninsula Belasio: hinc Comum versus pergenti Nessio, Caren; Pluniana, fons à Plinio nominatus: qui de eo libro ii, cap. cvi. In eius ripa surfuni Torno est, frequens olim Vicus; sed ab Comensibus male habitus jamnunc ad pristinam fortunam redire incepit.
units.tr: On the left as one goes past Lake Lugano, Mulgrato presents itself, and higher up, around Lake Lario, as if on a peninsula, Bellagio. Going from here towards Como, Nesso and Careno; and Pluniana, a spring named by Pliny in book 2, chapter 106. On its bank, further up, is Torno, once a busy village, but since it was ill treated by the Comensians, it has now begun to recover its former prosperity.

units.la: Sequitur Parlasca Vicus; Hironymi Parlasci, olim apud Bononienses Hæreticorum Inquisitoris, ortu nobilis.
units.tr: Next comes the village of Parlasca, the birthplace of Girolamo Parlasca, formerly Inquisitor of heretics at Bologna.

units.la: Conspiciendum se juxta præbet Comum.
units.tr: Here, next to it, Como shows itself to be looked at.

units.la: Comum Trogo lib. xx, Livio libro xxxvii, Plinio lib.iii natur. histor. Ammiano lib.xv, & aliis; Κώμου, Straboni libro iv & v, atque Ptolemæo: Como Tabulæ Itinerariæ & Cassiodoro, apud quem accurata ejus descriptio: Hodie Como. Apud Ottonem Frisingensem & Chunradum Lichtenavium ubique depravate Cuma, Incolæque Cumani vocantur. Trogus ab Gallis conditum memorat, cum Mediolano, Bergomo, Brixia, Tridento, Verona, Vicentia: Plinius ab Orobijs, Alpium incolis, horum tradit. Condiderunt procul dubio, ut alia hoc tractu, Tusci: quibus pullis, occupatum fuit ab Gallis. Vetus excisum perhibetur ab Anselmo Pusterula, Mediolanensium Archiepiscopo, aliudque hoc loco conditum, Cancri specie; quod ego, in medio relinquo. Vrbs parva, sed nobilis & opulenta, rebus omnibus affluens,
units.tr: Comum in Trogus book 20, Livy book 37, Pliny book 3 of the Natural History, Ammianus book 15 and others; [Κώμου] in Strabo books 4 and 5 and in Ptolemy; Como in the Itinerary tables and in Cassiodorus, in whose work there is an accurate description of it. Today it is Como. In Otto of Freising and Conrad of Lichtenau it is everywhere corruptly called Cuma, and its inhabitants Cumani. Trogus records that it was founded by the Gauls, together with Milan, Bergamo, Brescia, Trent, Verona and Vicenza; Pliny says that these were founded by the Orobii, the people of the Alps. Without doubt, as with other places in this region, the Etruscans founded it, and when they were driven out, the Gauls occupied it. It is said that the old town was destroyed by Anselm da Pusterla, Archbishop of Milan, and another town was built on this spot in the shape of a crab; I leave this question open. It is a small town, but noble and wealthy, abounding in all good things,

units.la: adsluens, Incolasque habens industrios & diligentes. Muros, qua Mediolanum spectat, constructus ab Ioanne Viceconite, Archiepiscopo & Principe Mediolanensi, anno cIↄ cccLIV, à quo & Castellum Turris Rotundæ excitatum. Ab Marcello deditione quondam captum, tradit Livius libro iam laudato. Coloniam fuisse mediocrem, sed Pompeium Strabonem, Magni Patrem, Colonos restituisse; Rhætos eam vastasse, C. Scipionem tria millia hominum addidisse, Cæsaremque quinque millia, in quis quingenti erant Græci Civitate donati; hos Novum Comum vocasse, memoriæ prodit Strabo libro v. Scribit & Appianus lib. ii bellorum Civilium Cæsarem (legendus item Suetonius incius Vita) Novum Comum condidisse in Alpibus, & qui illic magistratum gessissent, Cives Romanos esse voluisse. Hinc frequens Magistratuum Coloniæ mentio in Inscriptionibus. Vnam dabo, quæ ibi in æde D. Andreæ.
units.tr: and well watered, with industrious and diligent inhabitants. Its walls, on the side facing Milan, were built by John Visconti, Archbishop and Prince of Milan, in the year 1354, and by him too the castle of the Round Tower was raised. Livy in the book already cited tells that it was once taken by surrender to Marcellus. It was a modest colony, but Pompey Strabo, father of Pompey the Great, restored its colonists; the Raetians had laid it waste; Gaius Scipio added three thousand men, and Caesar five thousand, among whom were five hundred Greeks granted citizenship; Strabo in book 5 records that these called it New Como. Appian too, in book 2 of the Civil Wars, writes that Caesar founded New Como in the Alps, and wanted those who held office there to be Roman citizens. Hence the frequent mention of the magistrates of the colony in the inscriptions. I will give one, which is there in the church of St Andrew.

units.la: D. M C. VIRI TERENTIANI VI. VIRI COMI
units.tr: TO THE GODS OF THE DEAD. C. VIRIUS TERENTIANUS, SIXVIR OF COMO

units.la: Nominantur Municipes Comenses in Lapidea Tabula, quæ in templo Vici Intemeani, in Agro Comensi:
units.tr: The citizens of Como are named on a stone tablet which is in the temple of the village of Vico Intemelio, in the territory of Como:

units.la: L. CÆCILIVS. L. F. CILO IUL. VIR. A. P
units.tr: L. Caecilius, son of Lucius, Cilo, duumvir of the Iulian tribe, A. P.

units.la: QVI. TESTAMENTO. SVO. HS. N. XXX. MVNICIPIBVS. COMENSIBVS LEGAVIT. QVORVM. REDITV. QVOTANNIS. PER. NEPTVNALIA. OLEVM IN.CAMPO.ET.IN.THERMIS.ET.BALINEIS. OMNIBVS. QVÆ. SVNT COMI. POPVLO. PRÆBERETVR. T. F. I
units.tr: Who, by his will, left 30,000 sesterces [HS N XXX] to the citizens of Como, from whose yearly income oil was to be provided to the people at the Neptunalia, in the Campus, in the thermae, and in all the bathhouses that are in Como. T. F. I.

units.la: & quæ sequuntur. Sic Reipublicæ nomine decoratur in Inscriptione Brixiana, quæ paullo ante posita, ubi de Bergomo. Ab Gothis Langobardisque diu possessum, Karolí Magni manu & auspiciis in Cæsarum Romanorum venit potestatem: sub quibus libera aliquamdiu Romani Imperij fuit Civitas: Ruscorum Vitanorumque factionibus multos annos vexatum ad extremum in Mediolanensium ditionem est redactum, similemque cum Mediolanensibus expertum fortunam, nunc Francia, nunc Hispa-nia nia Regum paruit Imperio. Consulendi Merula, Corius alij. Ingentem Parrum ævo calamitatem accepit ab Cæsaris Legionibus, quod fusos acie Gallos intra mœnia recepisset Episcopatus floret dignitate. Patria cum Idviorum, Benedicti, Paulliqué, Episcopi Nuceriní Scriptis nobilissimi; tum Plinij Avunculi, Naturalis Historiæ conditoris, & Poëtæ Cæcilij, de quo Martialis: Poeta tenero meo sodali Velim Cæcilio Papyre dicas: Veronam veniat, Novi relinquens Comi mœnia, Lariumque littus.
units.tr: and what follows. Thus the Republic is named as an honour in the Brixian inscription, which was set up shortly before, where it speaks of Bergamo. Held for a long time by the Goths and Lombards, it came into the power of the Roman emperors through the hand and auspices of Charlemagne. Under them it was for some time a free city of the Roman Empire. Long harassed by the factions of the Ruscs and Vitani, it was at last brought under the rule of the Milanese. Sharing the same fortune as the Milanese, it obeyed now France, now the kings of Spain, in turn. See Merula, Corio and others. In ancient times Parra suffered a huge calamity at the hands of Caesar's legions, because it had received within its walls the Gauls who had been routed in battle. The episcopate flourishes in dignity. The homeland of Idvius, Benedict and Paulus, bishop of Nocera, most noted for their writings; also of Pliny the uncle, author of the Natural History, and of the poet Caecilius, of whom Martial says: Poet, tell my tender comrade Caecilius Papyrus to come to Verona, leaving behind the walls of New Como and the shore of Lake Larius. Comi mœnia, Lariumque littus.

units.la: Ager illi ab meridie peramœnus & fertilis: adversa parte Lacui adsidet, qui ab eo Comacenus apud Antoninum, antiquis Larius, de quo alibi.
units.tr: The land to the south of it is very pleasant and fertile. On the opposite side it sits by the lake, which from it is called Comacenus by Antoninus; anciently it was Larius, about which more elsewhere.

units.la: Ab Como lævam Lacus ripam sursum ambulanti exhibent se, post Presam amnem, Cernobio, Multravasio, Vrio, Cartalagio, Breno, Arzenio, Galbiano; superatoque Perlana fluvio, Lava, Turre, Promontorio, Torre, Leno: & in monte paullo altius, Abbatia di Acqua Fredda, Grianto, Menasio, Nobiale. Vlterius, Acqua Serta, Arzenica, Cremia, Pianello. Visitur hinc in celso difficilique monte Mesio, quod rebus ab Ioanne Iacobo Medicco gestis nobilitatum, Marchionatus induit sub Karolo v dignitatem. Sequitur in ripa Dungo; hinc torrente, non magni nominis, transitio, Gravidona, Domaso, Gera, Songo.
units.tr: Going up the left bank of the lake from Como, after the river Presa there appear Cernobbio, Moltrasio, Urio, Cartabbio, Brenta, Arzeno, Galbiate; and after crossing the river Perlana, Lava, Torre, Promontorio, Torno, Lenno; and a little higher on the mountain, the Abbey of Acquafredda, Griante, Menaggio, Nobiallo. Further on, Acquasarta, Argegno, Cremia, Pianello. From here is seen on a high and steep mountain Musso, which, made famous by the deeds of Gian Giacomo Medici, received the dignity of a marquisate under Charles V. Next on the bank is Dongo; then a crossing of a stream of no great name, and Gravedona, Domaso, Gera, Sorico.

units.la: Relicto Lacu, Padum repetam: ubi post Lambrum Ticini sequitur Ostium; supra quod quarto lapide Vrbs est Papia. Sic (quasi Pietatis aut Piorum virorum. Papia ut Sacco videtur: aliis alia placent Etyma) Latinis hodie, quin & Paulo Diacono lib. 11 Langb. Hist. cap. xv; vulgo autem Pavia nuncupatur: quæ Ticinum Tacito lib. iii alibi, Plinio, aliisque; Ticinus Straboni lib. v & Ptolemæo; Ticinus apud eundem Diaconum, loco indicato. Flaviam Papiam nominari scribit in Numino Argenteo Angelus Breventanus in Regum Langbardorum Tabula: Secundam Romam appellari in vetere saxo, notat Henricus Farnesius. Conditam adserit Plinius lib. v. cap. ab Levis & Marius Ligurius; alij ab Gallis Boijs & Cenomanis, Ticini amnis adcolis, à quo illi nomen. Sunt qui Auctorem ejus ferunt Ticinum quemdam Gallum. Fabulis, quas hic Burlellius adponit, referendis Lectori non ero molestus. Admiranda Vrbi est cœli temperies: ipsa tamen parum amœna & populosa. Castellum ibi ab Ioanne Galcario Viceconite factum, hodie semirutum, in quo nobilissima est Bibliotheca. Fora ibidem duo, cum Platea, quæ in Arcem ducit, amplissima. Templum D. Petri aureum habet cœlum, & monumentum D. Augustini marmoreum. Visitur ante Ecclesiam Cathedralem Statua ex ære equestris: Antonini Pii Imperatoris, an Theoderici Gothi, an Odovacris Herului; an alterius, incertum. Sua nobilis est Academia, quam Karolus iiii Imperator fundavit anno cio ccclxi: petentibus id Galcario 11 Earrabaque Vicecomitibus, Mediolani Principibus. De ea multi scribunt Doctores. Docuit ibi provectioris jam ætatis Baldus, moriuus ibidem anno cio cccc xx, Aprilis iv, & sepultus in Minorum Cœnobio. Duo ibi Collegia Litterarorum: unum à Pio 11 P. M. erectum; alterum ab Karolo Borromæo Cardinale. Episcopum habet Papia, exemtum. Claros viros tulit plurimos: in quis Ioannes xiix P. M; Thesaurus Beccaria, Vallis Umbrosæ Abbas, Martyr, teste Volaterrano libro xxi Commentar. Vrbanorum; Cato Sacius, Syllanus Niger, Lanfrancus, Iacobus Gualla, iurisconsulti: Antoninus Gaynerus Medicus; Lusprandus Levita, Historicus; Ennodius, Poëta. Romano succumbente Imperio, cladibus adfectam magnis ab Attila Hunnorum Rege & Odovacro Herulorum Principe, Gothi Lanbardiqué armis subegerunt, sedemque Regni lectam multis præclari operis ornarunt ædificijs. Iis ab Karolo Magno profligatis, Italia Regibus paruit utque ad Ottonem 1 Augustum, à quo fracta Berengariorum potentia, suæ restituta legitur libertas: cui tuendæ, anno cio cclix Præsuli Ravennæ se commisit: nacta inde: Principes an Tyrannos?) Turriaros, Langusios, Beccarias, tandem in potestatem est redacta Vicecomitum & Sforziarum, Mediolani Ducum: post cum universa Insubria Karolo v Imperatori cessit, qui de eius principatu armis decertavit anno cio io xxv cum Francisco Galliarum Rege; defendente tunc fortissime Ticinum, ab Rege obsessum, Antonio Leva Hispano. Paret hodie Hispaniarum Regibus, sub Mediolanensi comprehensa sta-tu, Vitu. Videndi Paullus Diaconus variis Historiae Langbardicae locis, Luitprandus Levita lib.III Histor. Platina in Vita Leonis I P.M. Blondus II & XVIII Histor. Corius Partei & III, Iacobus Wimphelingus in Histor. Merula libris V, VI, VIII & IX Histor. Vicecomitum; & alij. Scripsit Antiquitates Ticinenses Iacobus Gualla, IC. de quo antea dixi; Encomiumque Urbis Henricus Farnesius Eburo. Via, qua Mediolanum itur, Vivarium est, quadrata forma, circuitu XX milliar. Italicorum, vulgo dictum Il Barro; desinens ad nobile sumtuosumque Carthusianorum Monasterium, vulgo La Certosa. Ager optimus, supraque modum fertilis tritici, vini, reliquorumque fructuum; tantae passim ubertatis, amoenitatisque, ut vulgo Il Giardino di Milano, Mediolani Hortulus, audiat.
units.tr: Leaving the lake, I shall return to the Po: where, after the river Lambro, comes its mouth on the Ticino; and four miles up from it is the city of Pavia. It is called Papia (as if from Pietas or pious men; Sacco thinks it so, others prefer other etymologies) by Latin writers today, and also by Paul the Deacon in book 2 of the Lombard History, chapter 15; but commonly it is called Pavia. It is Ticinum in Tacitus book 3 and elsewhere, in Pliny and others; Ticinus in Strabo book 5 and in Ptolemy; Ticinus in the same Deacon, in the place indicated. Angelo Breventano, in the table of the Lombard kings, writes that it is named Flavia Papia on a silver coin; Henricus Farnesius notes that it is called Secunda Roma on an ancient stone. Pliny in book 5, chapter ... says that it was founded by the Levi and Marius Ligurius; others say by the Gallic Boii and Cenomani, neighbours of the river Ticino, from which it took its name. Some say that its founder was a certain Gaul named Ticinus. I will not trouble the reader with the fables that Burlellius adds here. The climate of the city is admirable, though the city itself is not very pleasant or populous. There is a castle built there by Galeazzo Visconti, now half-ruined, in which there is a very noble library. There are two forums there, and a very spacious square leading to the citadel. The church of St Peter has a golden ceiling, and the monument of St Augustine is of marble. In front of the cathedral stands an equestrian bronze statue: of the Emperor Antoninus Pius, or of Theodoric the Goth, or of Odoacer the Herulian, or of someone else, it is uncertain. It has its own noble university, which the Emperor Charles IV founded in 1361, at the request of Galeazzo and Barnabò Visconti, rulers of Milan. Many doctors have written about it. There taught the aged Baldus, who died there on 4 April 1420 and was buried in the monastery of the Minorites. There are two colleges of letters there: one founded by Pius II, the Supreme Pontiff; the other by Cardinal Charles Borromeo. Pavia has its own bishop, who is exempt. It has produced very many famous men, among whom are Pope John XIX; Tommaso Beccaria, Abbot of Vallombrosa and a martyr, according to Volterrano in book 21 of his Urban Commentaries; the jurists Catone Sacco, Sillano Nigro, Lanfranco, Giacomo Gualla; the physician Antonio Gaynerus; Liutprand the Deacon, historian; and Ennodius, poet. When the Roman Empire fell, the city, badly damaged by the great disasters inflicted by Attila, king of the Huns, and Odoacer, prince of the Heruli, was subdued by the arms of the Goths and Lombards, who made it the chosen seat of their kingdom and adorned it with many fine buildings. When these were overthrown by Charlemagne, it obeyed the kings of Italy, until under Otto I Augustus, by whom the power of the Berengars was broken, its ancient liberty is recorded to have been restored; in 1259 (?) it entrusted itself to defend that liberty to the Archbishop of Ravenna. Then, having got into the hands of the Torriani, Langosco and Beccaria (princes or tyrants?), it was at last brought under the power of the Visconti and Sforza, Dukes of Milan; afterwards, together with all Lombardy, it passed to the Emperor Charles V, who fought for its principality by arms in 1525 against Francis, King of the French; at that time Antonio de Leyva, a Spaniard, defended Ticino very bravely while it was besieged by the King. It now obeys the kings of Spain, and is included in the state of Milan. For Paul the Deacon see various places in the Lombard History; Liutprand the Deacon, book 3 of the History; Platina in the Life of Leo I, Supreme Pontiff; Blondus, books 2 and 18 of the History; Corio, part 1 and 3; Jakob Wimpfeling in his History; Merula, books 5, 6, 8 and 9 of the History of the Visconti; and others. Jakob Gualla, doctor of law, of whom I spoke before, wrote the Antiquities of Ticino; Henricus Farnesius wrote a eulogy of the city in Eburo. The road by which one goes to Milan is a paved road of square shape, with a circumference of twenty Italian miles, commonly called Il Barco, ending at the noble and sumptuous Carthusian monastery, commonly called La Certosa. The land is excellent and beyond measure fertile in wheat, wine and other crops; everywhere there is such abundance and charm that it is commonly called Il Giardino di Milano, the Garden of Milan.

units.la: Post Vivarium, cuius memini, occurrunt Mandrina, Vidigulfi, & Ticinello fluvius; laxaque eius ripa Metnno. Ultra Ticinellum, Cavagnera, Sucan, Campo Morto, Basiá, Figenaschu, Ferrabo, Bisdon, Moirago, Cassin, Bazzaello, Ajagon Barriana. Ad Ticinellum rursus incedenti offerunt se dextra ripa, Charella, Binasco, (Ad Bacinas Alciato, alijs Binx) S. Nuevo, Cazzan, Sportan, S. Giacomo, Intercisio, & Rovido. Rursus ad Ticinellum Rosa, Benda, Vignan, Vermizzo. Haud procul inde Zelo, Cado, Gazzano, Bonhola, Terzano, Corsico.
units.tr: After Vivarium, which I mentioned, come Mandrina, Vidigulfi, and the river Ticinello; on its broad bank lies Metnno. Beyond the Ticinello are Cavagnera, Sucan, Campo Morto, Basiá, Figenaschu, Ferrabo, Bisdon, Moirago, Cassin, Bazzaello, Ajagon Barriana. Coming back to the Ticinello, on the right bank present themselves Charella, Binasco (Ad Bacinas in Alciato, Binx in others), S. Nuevo, Cazzan, Sportan, S. Giacomo, Intercisio, and Rovido. Again at the Ticinello: Rosa, Benda, Vignan, Vermizzo. Not far from there lie Zelo, Cado, Gazzano, Bonhola, Terzano, and Corsico.

units.la: In conspectum mox venit Mediolanum.
units.tr: Soon Mediolanum comes into view.

units.la: Sic Latinis omnibus Scriptoribus, Livio, Trogo, Tacito, Ammiano Marcellino, Paullo Diacono, Antonino, Itinerariae Tabulae, aliisque Μεδιολάνιον Polybio, Straboni Plutarcho in Vita Marcelli, Procopio lib.II Histor.Goth. Ptolemaeo, cui & Μεδιολάνα: quod Italis hodie Milano; Germanis Mey-landt. Urbs Melana patens, inquit Gotfridus Viterbiensis, pro Mediolano. Olanum ab Conditore dictum, notat suppositicius Cato. Sunt qui prius Insubriam; alij, qui Albam: quidam, qui Peutheciam vocatam volunt, ut scribit Castilioneus. Insubria meminit apud Abrahamum Ortelium Nummus antiquus M. Valerij Messalae. Mediolanum ab Gallis Insubribus conditum: auctores sunt Livius, Trogus, alij; qui, Bellovefo Duce, in Italiam profecti, pulsis Tuscis, fundamenta illic Urbis locarunt: anno, ut quidam computant, ante Christum natum CCCXXXIXXXVI aut alij, CCCI.XXX. Quidquid sit, antiquissima est. Nomen illi natum, judicio V. CL. Isaaci Cataneboni ad lib. IV Strabonis, ab Santonum in Galliis Urbe, Mediolanio: quod, magni viri sententiae subscribens, libro III indicavi, cap. XXXIV, Guiennam explicante. Vocem quidam ajunt esse Germanicae originis, quali Mey-land ab Agro vernante, qualis Maiomensc solet esse; vel Mid-land, quod medium esset & velut umbilicus, uti etiam Jovius indicat, Insubriae, Ticino amne clausae; vel denique Maegdeland sive
units.tr: Thus all the Latin writers (Livy, Trogus, Tacitus, Ammianus Marcellinus, Paul the Deacon, Antoninus, the Itinerary tables, and others) call it Mediolanum; Polybius, Strabo, Plutarch in the Life of Marcellus, Procopius in the second book of the Gothic History, and Ptolemy call it Μεδιολάνιον, and Ptolemy also Μεδιολάνα [Mediolanion, Mediolana]. Today Italians call it Milano and Germans Mey-landt. "The city Melana, spreading wide," says Gottfried of Viterbo, for Mediolanum. That it was called Olanum by its founder is noted by the spurious Cato. Some say it was first called Insubria, others Alba, and some, as Castiglione writes, want it called Peuthecia. Insubria is mentioned by Abraham Ortelius on an ancient coin of M. Valerius Messala. Mediolanum was founded by the Gallic Insubres: the authorities are Livy, Trogus, and others, who, under their leader Bellovesus, set out for Italy, drove out the Tuscans, and laid the foundations of the city there, in the year (as some reckon) 339 or, by others, 301 before the birth of Christ. Whatever the truth, it is very ancient. The name, in the judgment of the most distinguished Isaac Casaubon on the fourth book of Strabo, comes from Mediolanium, a city of the Santones in Gaul. I indicated in the third book, chapter 34, that I agree with this great man's opinion, when I explained Guienne. Some say the word is of German origin, such as Mey-land from a meadow in spring, as Maiomense usually is; or Mid-land, because it lay in the middle and was like the navel of Insubria, enclosed by the Ticino river, as Jovius also indicates; or finally Maegdeland or

units.la: Qqqq 4
units.tr: Qqqq 4

units.la: Mediolanum Virginis Regio vel Terra, ab Minerva, cujus ibi templum fuit, quod olim S. Salvatori, post D Virgini, hodie D. Teclæ. Elegantes adponam ea de re versus doctissimi viri Andreæ Alciati: Bituricus Vervex, Heduis dat Sucula signum: His populis patria debita origo mea: Quam Mediolanum sacram dixere Puellæ Terram: nam vetus hoc Gallica lingua sonat. Culta Minerva fuit, nunc est ubi numine Tecla Mutato, Matris Virginis ante domum. Lanigerae hunc signum Suis est, animalque biforme Acribus hinc setis, lanitie inde levi,
units.tr: Milan is the Virgin's region or land, named from Minerva, whose temple once stood there. It was formerly dedicated to St Salvator and later to the Blessed Virgin, and is today dedicated to St Thecla. I will add some elegant verses on this matter by the learned Andreas Alciatus: "The Biturigan ram and the Aeduan sow give the sign. To these peoples my native origin is owed. The maidens called me the sacred land Mediolanum, for in the old Gallic tongue this is what it means. Minerva was worshipped here; now, with the godhead changed, Thecla stands where she was, before the house of the Virgin Mother. The sign is of the woolly sow, and a two-formed animal, bristling with sharp bristles on one side and with smooth wool on the other."

units.la: Vbi notandum etiam illam opinionem, qua nomen Vrbi impositum contenditur ab Heduis & Biturigibus, cujus Conditoribus; quorum illi Porci, hi Arietis sive Vervecis signo usi, suae memores originis, unum Lanata Suis ex duobus factum civitati huic dederunt, & ex eo nomen Mediolani fecerunt. Respicit eo Claudianus in nuptijs Honorij & Mariæ: Iam Ligurum terris spumantia pectora Triton Adpulerat, lassoque fretis extenderat orbes Continuo sublime volans, ad mœnia Gallis Condita, lanigeri suis ostentantia pellem Pervenit.
units.tr: We should also note that opinion which claims the name was given to the city by the Aedui and the Bituriges, whose founders used, respectively, the sign of a pig and that of a ram or wether. Mindful of their origin, they made one woolly sow out of the two and gave it to this city, and from it made the name Mediolanum. Claudian alludes to this in his poem on the wedding of Honorius and Maria: "Now Triton had brought his foaming breast to the lands of the Ligurians, and, flying high over the tired seas, had spread his circles; and he came to the walls founded by the Gauls, displaying the hide of the woolly sow."

units.la: Male vulgo legitur lanigeris ovis. Sic Sidonius Apollinaris libro VII Epistolarum: Rura paludicola temnis populosa Ravenna, Et quae lanigero de suae nomen habet.
units.tr: It is commonly and wrongly read lanigeris ovis ("woolly sheep"). So Sidonius Apollinaris in the seventh book of his Letters: "The fen-dwelling, sea-surrounded, populous Ravenna, and the one that takes its name from her woolly sow."

units.la: D. Ambrosius aliique nomen derivant ab Apro, qui media parte lanatus in Vrbis fundamentis fertur repertus. Situs illi inter Ticinum Abduamque, haud procul Alpibus, peropportunus; natura cœli soliqúe temperatus. De ea sic Strabo lib. v: Ἰνσούβροι δὲ καὶ γὰρ νῦν εἰσί. Μεδιολάνιον δ᾽ ἔχον μητρόπολιν, πύλας μὲν καὶ μῆλον ... ἐπὶ πόλιν ... Πάδα συναφθεῖσα ... Λ ... Sane inter maximas Europæ censetur Vrbes, mercatura opibusque florens: splendore superbit Ædificiorum, Templorum magnitudine, Prætoriorum amplitudine, pulchritudine Vicorum; mœnibus, propugnaculis, armamentarijs supra modum instructa: spacium complectens immensum, Suburbia habet longa, lataque, quorum nonnulla cum maguis Civitatibus committi possent, altis fossis, non secus ac Vrbs ipsa, undique cincta. Post Ædem Sacram, quam Domum vocant, magnifice speciosèque ad Forum exstructam, D. Laurentij Fanum est ingens in ruinis Templi Herculis excitatum, quod Maximianus Herculeus Imperator in Patria, ut tradunt quidam, sua sumtuosissimum exstruxerat cum Thermis, quae ab ipso Herculeae. Exstant etiamnum sedecim striatae Columnae peraltae, magnificentissimi operis vestigia. Arcem ibi videre est, omnium fere, quae in hoc terrarum orbe munitissimam, cui Porta Iovia nomen; inexpugnabilem, quaque in Europa nihil celebrius. Describit accurate Fr. Schottus Itinerar. Italici lib. 1. Xenodochium ibi vel Nosocomium suburbanum, via Bergomati, jugerum aliquot spatio amplissimum; ab Sforzijs inchoatum, nondum absolutum. Est & Curia Vetus, ubi exiguum D. Gothardi Fanum, nobilibus aliquot Vicecomitum sepulcris decoratum. Multae sunt in hac Vrbe prisci aevi Inscriptiones, aliaque veterum monumenta. Academiam habet antiquissimam, ubi etiam Virgilius litteris operam dedisse creditur. Meminit ejus saepe Aurelius Augustinus, quem volunt ibi Eloquentiae fuisse Professorem. Florucrunt ibi Iason IC, Hermolaus Barbarus, Franciscus Philelphus, Georgius Merula, Celius Rhodiginus, Hieronymus Cardanus, Guasparinus Bergomas, ab Philippo Vicecomite accersitus, & alij. Ad Prædicatores tam insignem esse Bibliothecam scribit Leander, ut celeberrimis Italiae non cedat. Magna semper Civium, qui mire navi & industrij, hic fuit frequentia: uti & olim; ut non immerito πολυάνθρωπον vocent Plutarchus in Vita Marcelli & Suidas. Artificum diversa ibidem genera, tanta frequentia, ut vulgato Proverbio dicatur, Che chi volesse raffettare Italia, si ruina Milano; Mediolanum scilicet destruendo, Italiam instruere posse, nimirum quorumvis artificum copia. Mediolanum Patriam agnoscunt; Imperatores Didius Iulianus & Maximianus Herculeus: Pontifices Alexander II, Urbanus Celestinus V, Gregorius XIII Cardinales, Simon Borsenus, Ioannes Antonius Sangeorgius Bragdus Castiglioneus, S. Aramucia & Augustinus Triuulsiy, Iacobus Simoneta, Ioannes Morenus, Ioannes Angelus Medices: Archiepiscopi plurimi, quorum hi occurrunt; Barnabas, Anastasius, Caius, Calocerus, Datius, Castritianus, Calimerus, Monas, Mirocles, Protasius, Maternus, Eulogius, Dionysius, Auxentius, Arrianus, Ambrosius, Simplicianus: Iurisconsultos dedit, Salvium Iulianum, Didij Iuliani Imperatoris Avum paternum, Obertum Ortinum Feudorum Scriptorem, Gerardum Catapultum, Vincentium Grossatorem, Paullum Ficazarum, Ioannem Lignanum, Pileam Modicensem, Sigismundum Homodeum Christeplorum & Guernerum Castiglionceos, Iasonem Maynum, Philippum Decium, Andream Aliciatum, & alios: Produxit item Caelium, Comicum Poetam, & M. Valerium Maximum, Astrologum, de quo Lapis ibi ad S. Simplicianum:
units.tr: Ambrose and others derive the name from a boar, which is said to have been found half-woolly in the foundations of the city. Its site, between the Ticino and the Adda and not far from the Alps, is very well placed, and its climate and soil are temperate. Strabo on it, in book V: "The Insubres, for they still exist, have Mediolanum as their metropolis, ... [Ἰνσούβροι δὲ καὶ γὰρ νῦν εἰσί. Μεδιολάνιον δ᾽ ἔχον μητρόπολιν, πύλας μὲν καὶ μῆλον ... ἐπὶ πόλιν ... Πάδα συναφθεῖσα ... Λ ...]". Certainly it is counted among the greatest cities of Europe, flourishing in trade and wealth. It takes pride in the splendour of its buildings, the size of its churches, the spaciousness of its public palaces, and the beauty of its streets, and it is supplied beyond measure with walls, bulwarks, and arsenals. It covers an immense area and has long, wide suburbs, some of which could be compared with great cities; like the city itself, they are surrounded on all sides by deep ditches. Beyond the Sacred Church, which they call the Domus, magnificently and handsomely built near the Forum, stands the great church of St. Lawrence, raised among the ruins of a temple of Hercules, which the Emperor Maximian Herculeus, as some relate, had built most sumptuously in his homeland, together with baths named after himself, the Herculean baths. Sixteen fluted columns of great height still stand there, traces of magnificent work. There one sees the citadel, almost the most strongly fortified of any in this world, called the Porta Iovia: impregnable, and as famous as anything in Europe. Francis Schott describes it accurately in the first book of his Italian Itinerary. There is also a suburban hospice or infirmary on the road to Bergamo, very spacious, covering several acres, begun by the Sforzas and not yet finished. There is also the Old Court, where a small church of St. Gotthard, adorned with several noble tombs of the Visconti, stands. This city has many inscriptions and other monuments from ancient times. It has a very ancient university, where Virgil is believed to have studied literature. Aurelius Augustine often mentions it, and they think he was professor of rhetoric there. Jason the jurist, Hermolaus Barbarus, Francesco Filelfo, Giorgio Merula, Caelius Rhodiginus, Girolamo Cardano, Gasparino of Bergamo, summoned by Filippo Visconti, and others flourished there. Leander writes that the library at the Dominicans' house is so remarkable that it is not inferior to the most famous in Italy. There has always been a great crowd of citizens here, who are wonderfully clever and industrious, as there was of old; so that Plutarch in the Life of Marcellus and Suidas rightly call it "populous" (πολυάνθρωπον). There are many different kinds of craftsmen here, in such numbers that a common proverb says: "If anyone wanted to ruin Italy, he would ruin Milan," meaning that by destroying Milan one could equip Italy, given the abundance of every kind of craftsman. Milan acknowledges as her native sons the emperors Didius Julianus and Maximian Herculeus; the popes Alexander II, Urban, Celestine V, and Gregory XIII; the cardinals Simon Borsenus, Giovanni Antonio Sangiorgio, Bragdus Castiglioneus, S. Aramucia, Agostino Trivulzio, Giacomo Simonetta, Giovanni Morone, and Giovanni Angelo Medici; and very many archbishops, of whom these occur: Barnabas, Anastasius, Caius, Calocerus, Datius, Castritianus, Calimerus, Monas, Mirocles, Protasius, Maternus, Eulogius, Dionysius, Auxentius, Arrianus, Ambrose, and Simplicianus. It has also produced jurists: Salvius Julianus, paternal grandfather of the Emperor Didius Julianus; Oberto dell'Orto, writer on fiefs; Gerardo Catapulto, Vincenzo Grossatore, Paolo Ficazario, Giovanni Lignano, Pileo of Modena, Sigismondo Omodei of the Christophori, and Guerniero and Castiglioni; also Jason Mayno, Filippo Decio, and Andrea Alciato, and others. It has likewise produced Caelius, the comic poet, and M. Valerius Maximus, the astrologer, to whom the stone there near St. Simplicianus refers:

units.la: M. VALERIVS MAXIMVS SACERDOS D. S. I. M. STVD ASTROLOGIÆ SIBI ET SEVERIÆ. APR VXORI H. M. N. N. S
units.tr: M. VALERIUS MAXIMUS, PRIEST. TO THE GOOD AND GREAT GOD (D. S. I. M.). HE STUDIED ASTROLOGY. FOR HIMSELF AND SEVERIA APRA, HIS WIFE. THIS MONUMENT SHALL NOT PASS TO HEIRS.

units.la: Genitrix etiam Sabæ & Bonaventura Castiglioni, qui de antiquis Gallorum Insubrum Sedibus scripsit: item Ioannis Iacobi & Camillis Glaiorum Triuiani Calis, Galeatij Cappellæ, Ioannis Stephani Cottæ, Platini Platonis, Lancini Curtij & Andreæ Bilij. Oriu quoque superbit multorum, qui militari gloria clari, cum aliorum, quos longum esset commemorare, tum Virginij Rufi, de quo non solum Tacitus, Dio, Plutarchus, Quintilianus, & Plinius in Epistolis, verum etiam, quod sequitur. Epitaphium: Hic situs est Rufus, qui pro Vindice quondam Imperium asseruit, non sibi, sed patriæ,
units.tr: The mother also of Sabas and Bonaventura Castiglioni, who wrote on the ancient seats of the Gallic Insubres; likewise of Giovanni Giacomo and Camillo Glaiori, Trivulzio Calco, Galeazzo Cappella, Giovanni Stefano Cotta, Platina Platone, Lancino Curzio and Andrea Bilio. Oreo also takes pride in many men distinguished by military glory, among others, to list whom would take too long, and above all in Virginius Rufus, of whom not only Tacitus, Dio, Plutarch, Quintilian and Pliny in his Letters speak, but also the following epitaph: Here lies Rufus, who once asserted the empire against Vindex, not for himself but for his country.

units.la: Archiepiscopatus floret dignitate. Primus Ecclesiæ Antistes fuisse perhibetur Barnabas Pauli Apostoli in sacrolancto Munere Collega. Vrbs primo multos annos sub imperio fuit Gallorum, donec auspicijs M. Marcelli Cos. Virdumaro Iulsubrium Rege Clastadium debellato, in ditione coepit esse Romanorum. quorum Imperatores sepe sedem hic suam Regni e habuisse ob loci opportunitatem commoditatemque belandi contra Gallos Germanosque, notum est exemplis C. Iulij Cæsaris, Nerva, Traiani (quem ferunt Regiam hic ædificasse, qui locus adhuc Palatij nomen servat) Hadriani, Maximiani Herculei, & aliorum, quos, senescente jam Roma, plurimum hac urbe defecerant fuisse constat; quorumque præsentiaque ita crevit, ut Procopius eam post Romam ceteras facile superare Vrbes scribat, magnitudine, Civium copia, reliquisque fortunæ bonis. Ab ijs tanta ibi publicorum operum, qualia Romæ, quorumque plerraque temporis longinquitate perierunt, copia: de quibus paucis agit Ausonius. Et Mediolani mira omnia, copia rerum, Innumera culuaque domus, facunda virorum, Ingenta, antiqui mores, tum duplice muro Amplificata loci species, Populique voluptas Circus & inclyti moles cuneata Theatri: Templa, Palatinæque Arces, opulentsque Moneta, Et Regio Herculei celebris sub honore Lavacri, Cunctaque marmoreis ornata perisfy'a signis, Mœniaque in valli formam circumdata limbo. Omnia quæ magnis Operum velut æmula formis Excellunt: nec junctis premit vicinia Roma.
units.tr: The archbishopric flourishes in dignity. The first bishop of the Church is said to have been Barnabas, colleague of the Apostle Paul in the most sacred office. The city was for many years first under the rule of the Gauls, until, under the auspices of M. Marcellus the consul, Virdumarus, king of the Insubres, was defeated at Clastidium and it came under the dominion of the Romans. It is well known that their emperors often had their royal seat here, because of the convenience and advantage of the place for waging war against the Gauls and Germans, as the examples of C. Julius Caesar, Nerva, Trajan (who they say built a royal palace here, and the place still keeps the name of Palace), Hadrian, Maximian Herculius, and others show; and it is established that, when Rome was already growing old, they had largely deserted that city for this one. Through their presence it grew so much that Procopius writes that, after Rome, it easily surpassed all other cities in size, number of citizens and other good things of fortune. From them there was such abundance of public works there, like those at Rome, most of which have perished through the length of time; Ausonius treats some of these briefly: And Milan, wonderful in all things: the abundance of goods, countless and cultivated houses, a fertile people of men, great ancient manners; then the appearance of the place enlarged by a double wall, the people's delight, the Circus, and the wedge-shaped mass of the famous Theatre; temples, Palatine citadels, and the rich Mint; and the royal bath celebrated under the name of Hercules, and all things adorned with marble statues, and walls surrounded in the form of a rampart with a border. All these things excel, like rivals in the great forms of their works, and neighbouring Rome does not overshadow them when joined with them.

units.la: Sub Imperatoribus Medio'anum Reipublicæ gloriatum est nomine, quod expressum non solum in Tabula confracta, quam posui in mea Hispania libro II cap.XVII; verum rum etiam in Inscriptione, quam ipsa servat Vrbs in Ianua S. Ambrosij, Porta Vercellensi:
units.tr: Under the emperors Milan gloried in the name of the Republic of the Mediolanenses, which is expressed not only in the broken tablet that I set down in my book on Spain, Book II, chapter XVII, but also in the inscription which the city itself preserves at the Gate of St Ambrose, the Vercellese Gate:

units.la: D. S. I. M. P. ACIL. PISONIANVS PATER.PATRATVS QVI. HOC. SPELEVM. VIOL. IGNIS.ABSVMPTVM COMPARATA. AREA.A. REIPVBL. MEDIOL.PECVNIA.SVA RESTITVIT
units.tr: TO THE GODS ABOVE AND BELOW, PUBLIUS ACILIUS PISONIANUS, FATHER PATRATUS, WHO, WHEN THIS CAVE HAD BEEN DESTROYED BY FIRE, RESTORED IT AT HIS OWN EXPENSE, THE AREA HAVING BEEN BOUGHT WITH MONEY FROM THE REPUBLIC OF MILAN.

units.la: Sub Imperatoribus Patronis interalios Reip. Mediolanensis fuit L. Fabius Cilo. Vir maximis functus honoribus, uti de eo testatur Lapis, qui Romæ apud Carpenses: L. FABIO. M. F. GAL. CILONI SEPTIMIO. COS. PRAEF. VRB LEG. AVGG. PROPR. PANNON SVPER. DUCI. VEXILL. LEG. PRO PR. PROVINCIAR. MOESIAR. SVPER PONTHI. ET. BITHYNIAE COMITI. AVGG. LEG. AVGG. PRO PR. PROV. GALATIAE. PRAEF AER. MILITARIS, PRO COS. ITEMQVE. LEG. PROV. NARBONENS. LEG. LEG. XVI. ET. SAMOSATE SODAL. HADRIANAL IR. VRB. TRIB. PLEB. Q. PROV CRETAE. TRIB. LEG. XI. CL. X. VIR. STLITIB. IVDICANDIS MEDIOLANENSES PATRONO
units.tr: Under the emperors, among the other patrons of the Republic of Milan was Lucius Fabius Cilo, a man who held the highest offices, as the stone at Rome in the Carpenses church attests: To Lucius Fabius Cilo, son of Marcus, of the Galerian tribe, Septimius, consul, prefect of the city, legate of the Augusti with propraetorian power, commander of the Pannonian army, standard-bearer of the legion, propraetor of the provinces of Moesia, Pontus and Bithynia, companion of the Augusti, legate of the Augusti with propraetorian power of the province of Galatia, prefect of the military treasury, proconsul, and likewise legate of the province of Narbonensis, legate of the Sixteenth Legion and of Samosata, sodal of the Hadrianic order, tribune of the plebs, quaestor of the province of Crete, tribune of the Eleventh Legion, decemvir for judging lawsuits: the Milanese (dedicated this to) their patron.

units.la: Adhunc sub Imperatoribus statum pertinet Elogium Q. Audacij VIviri Augustalis quod Madoctiæ in æde S. Ioannis Baptistæ.
units.tr: Still under the emperors belongs the epitaph of Q. Audacius, an Augustal sevir, which is at Madoctia in the church of St John the Baptist.

units.la: D. M. AVDASIÆ Q. F. CALES Q. AVDASIVS ACMAZON VI VIR.AVG.MEDIOL. ET.FORO.POL.PATER. QVÆ. VIXIT. AN. V M. IIII. DIES III
units.tr: TO THE SPIRITS OF THE DEAD. AUDASIA, DAUGHTER OF QUINTUS, OF THE CALES TRIBE. QUINTUS AUDASIUS ACMAZON, SEVIR AUGUSTAL OF MILAN AND OF THE POLISH FORUM, HER FATHER, TO HIS DAUGHTER, WHO LIVED FIVE YEARS, FOUR MONTHS AND THREE DAYS.

units.la: Et ne sacros quidem Magistratus defuisse, docet Inscriptio Bergomensis, quæ in Sacello D. Petri apud æde m D. Alexandri, mentionem faciens Flaminis Divi Traiani Vrbe Mediolanensi.
units.tr: And that sacred magistracies were not lacking either is shown by the Bergamo inscription, which, in the chapel of St Peter in the church of St Alexander, mentions a Flamen of the Divine Trajan in the city of Milan.

units.la: C. CORNELIO C. F. VOT MINICIANO
units.tr: Gaius Cornelius, son of Gaius, Vot Minicianus

units.la: Et post paucos versus: BERGOMI. PATRONO FLAMINI. DIVI. TRAJANI MEDIOLANI PLEBS. VRBANA
units.tr: And a few verses later: AT BERGAMO, TO THE PATRON, PRIEST OF THE DEIFIED TRAJAN; THE URBAN COMMONS OF MILAN.

units.la: Privatorum Elogia praetereo. Debilitata Caesarum, ut eo redeam, potentia, variorum haec Vrbs Barbarorum impetu convulsa est & labefactata; Gothorum, Hunnorum. Langbardorum: quibus, Karoli Magni auspiciis, Italia exactis, fidei se commisit Francorum Regum; inde Germanorum Caesarum, quorum plerique Ferream Coronam, Imperij solemnia, accipere ibi, in vetusta celebrique D. Ambrosij aede, consuerunt; uti singulorum exemplis probat Leander Albertus. Tandem sub Friderici s I & II Caesaribus, quibus perpetuo rebellavit, novos fortita est Dominos, Galeatos Vicecomites, qui deinde, anno c10 ccc xcv Duces a Wenceslao Imperatore nominati. Vicecomitum Stemma legitur apud Merulam libro v Historiae Vicecomitum Volaterranum libro iv Commentarior. Vrbanorum, & Onuphrium Panuinium libro iv Romanorum Principum, corumque, quorum maxima in Italia fuerunt Imperia. His deficientibus Sforzia Ducum Insignia sunt adepti, consentientibus Civium suffragijs, & accedente Romani Imperij auctoritate; quod Galeatij numquam obtinere potuerant. Horum stirpe Majorum nostrorum aevo extincta, successit Karolus v Imperator, qui Principatum ad Reges Hispaniae, Successores, transtulit. Vide Procopium libro ii: Paullum Diaconum lib. xv. & xvi Histor. Rom. ad Eutropium continuatae, item libro iii. Hist. Langbard. Sebastianum Munsterum Cosmogr. libro ii: Merulam lib. i, ii, iii & seqq. Vicecomitum: Volaterranum in libris Commentar. Vrbanor. variis locis: Platinam in Vitis Leonis i, Hilarii, & aliorum; Blondum libr. Histor. iii, iv, v, viii, xi, xv: Corium Part. i & seq. Leandrum Albertum in Langbardia Trans-Padana: Annales Mediolanensium & Laudensium: aliosque. Memoratu dignum est, quod de Attila, Vrbem hanc cum Victoria ingressio, scribit Sudas: cum, quum Vrbem cepisset, ibique reperisset Pi‐ctruram, in quo ante Pedes Romanorum Principum, in aureis soliis sedentium, occisi Scythae jacebant, accivisse statim Pictorem, & se quidem in solio sedentem; Romanos vero Principes sacculos humeris gestantes, & ante suos pedes aurum spargentes, pingere jussisse. Complectitur Ducatus Mediolanensis suo ambitu ccc milliaria. Dicitur Hispaniae Rex ex hoc statu proventum habere octoginta aurecorum millia. Administratio Causarum Civilium & Criminalium pendet ab Senatu Mediolanensi: in quo xvi sunt Doctores, & nonnulli Praelati Patritiique Mediolanenses. Ab Urbe Roma distare mill. io xxviii, notatur in Itinerario Antonini. Incredibilis agro est fertilitas, copiaque rerum omnium stupenda.
units.tr: I pass over the praises of private persons. As the power of the Caesars weakened (to return to my point), this city was shaken and overthrown by the assaults of various barbarians: the Goths, the Huns, and the Lombards. Under the auspices of Charlemagne, after the Lombards were driven out, Italy committed itself to the trust of the Kings of the Franks, and then to the Emperors of the Germans, most of whom customarily received the Iron Crown, the solemn mark of empire, here in the ancient and famous church of St Ambrose; Leander Albertus proves this with examples of each one. At last, under the Emperors Frederick I and II, against whom it rebelled constantly, it obtained new lords, the Galeazzo Visconti, who were afterwards named Dukes by the Emperor Wenceslaus in the year 1395. The family tree of the Visconti is found in Merula, book 5 of his History of the Visconti; in Volaterranus, book 4 of his Commentaries on Urban Matters; and in Onofrio Panvinio, book 4 of Roman Princes, and of those whose greatest empires were in Italy. When these failed, the Sforza obtained the insignia of Dukes, with the consent of the citizens' votes and the authority of the Roman Empire joining in; the Galeazzi had never been able to obtain this. When the line of our ancestors was extinguished in our own age, the Emperor Charles V succeeded, and he transferred the principality to the Kings of Spain, his successors. See Procopius, book 2; Paulus Diaconus, books 15 and 16 of the Roman History continued from Eutropius, and likewise book 3 of the History of the Lombards; Sebastian Münster, Cosmography, book 2; Merula, book 1, 2, 3 and following, on the Visconti; Volaterranus in the books of his Commentaries on Urban Matters, in various places; Platina in the Lives of Leo I, Hilarius and others; Biondo, books 3, 4, 5, 8, 11 and 15 of his Histories; Corio, part 1 and following; Leander Albertus on Trans-Padane Lombardy; the Annals of the Milanese and the Lodigians; and others. It is worth recording what Suidas writes about Attila, who entered this city in triumph: when he had taken the city and found there a painting in which Scythians lay slain before the feet of Roman princes seated on golden thrones, he at once summoned a painter and ordered him to paint himself seated on a throne, and the Roman princes carrying sacks on their shoulders and scattering gold before his feet. The Duchy of Milan encompasses, within its circuit, 300 miles. It is said that the King of Spain derives from this state an income of 80,000 gold pieces. The administration of civil and criminal causes depends on the Senate of Milan, in which there are 16 teachers (doctors), and some prelates and Milanese patricians. It is noted in the Itinerary of Antoninus that it is 1,028 miles from the city of Rome. The fertility of the land is incredible, and its abundance of all things is astonishing.

units.la: Dextra Mediolani parte, quae laeva Sevesiae fluminis, adparent, quae lingua vulgari Mirabello, Vergano, Quarto, Frisiana, Bruzzano, Vialba, Bola, Nova, Noia, Corma, Cassina Matta, Carbagna, Sinago, Castelletto, Cesata, Solera, Limia, Boisio, Cervato: & ad amnis Lurae dextram Cadfatti, S. Dalmasio, Mombello, Cesa, Mesnite, Barlassina, Canago, Lazarte, Rovellasca, Birago, Lenta, Crivello, Bricola: altiusque Chiasse & Mandrusio.
units.tr: On the right of Milan, on the left bank of the river Seveso, appear these places, which in the vernacular are called Mirabello, Vergano, Quarto, Frisiana, Bruzzano, Vialba, Bola, Nova, Noia, Corma, Cassina Matta, Carbagna, Sinago, Castelletto, Cesata, Solera, Limia, Boisio, Cervato; and on the right bank of the river Lura Cadfatti, S. Dalmasio, Mombello, Cesa, Mesnite, Barlassina, Canago, Lazarte, Rovellasca, Birago, Lenta, Crivello, Bricola; and farther up Chiasse and Mandrusio.

units.la: Laeva Mediolani, ad Oronae dextram, conspiciuntur Cagnola, la Certosa, Misoco, Rose, Cassina dei Pero, Hospitale, Paltanello, Reozo, Mazzo, Torreta, S. Maria, Rossa, Caronno, Leina, Poltano, Zacona, Orugio, S. Lorenzo, S. Vettore, Legnano, ubi Pons in Orona, Cerro, S. Maria, Serona, ad sinistram Lurae: ulterius, Germano, Rovello, Aip, Orona, Marcia, Casielago, Mezza, Prospiano, Carbona, Gorla, Loro, Rovelasca, Venian, Senegra, Abiagnazzo, Lunicipino, Trada, Somalle: & in montibus Castiglione, Venegono Inferiore & Superiora, Canofio, Bellegazzo, Apiano, Guenzo, Lomazzo, Borgoro, Solerona; altiusque, Sulbia, Rocca, Cagno, Monello, Pianasca. Visuntur eodem tractu Ponte Vidon, Vedano, Rovera, Binago, Mocagna, Malno, Lagurno, Lignanetto, Cazzan, Rodere, Bisuchio, Imbrusa, Viglavi, Salno, Monte, Arso.
units.tr: On the left of Milan, by the right bank of the Olona, are seen Cagnola, la Certosa, Misoco, Rose, Cassina dei Pero, Hospitale, Paltanello, Reozo, Mazzo, Torreta, S. Maria, Rossa, Caronno, Leina, Poltano, Zacona, Orugio, S. Lorenzo, S. Vettore, Legnano, where there is a bridge over the Olona; Cerro, S. Maria, Serona on the left of the Lura; and further on, Germano, Rovello, Aip, Orona, Marcia, Casielago, Mezza, Prospiano, Carbona, Gorla, Loro, Rovelasca, Venian, Senegra, Abiagnazzo, Lunicipino, Trada, Somalle; and in the hills Castiglione, Venegono Inferiore and Superiore, Canofio, Bellegazzo, Apiano, Guenzo, Lomazzo, Borgoro, Solerona; and farther up, Sulbia, Rocca, Cagno, Monello, Pianasca. In the same tract are seen Ponte Vidon, Vedano, Rovera, Binago, Mocagna, Malno, Lagurno, Lignanetto, Cazzan, Rodere, Bisuchio, Imbrusa, Viglavi, Salno, Monte, Arso.

units.la: Deorsum Papiam versus inter Vivarium, cujus ante memini, & Fossam Belriguardi Fistura & Caporate cernuntur: inferius trans fossam, Belriguardo, Zelata, la Motta: altiusque Bessi, Farangia, Ozeno; superiusque Abia Crassa, quod Albiate apud Merulam lib. v, Opidum, quum situs non incommodi, dives quondam & frequens Supra Albate Kolecco spectatur, altiusque Brena.
units.tr: Downstream towards Pavia, between the Vivarium, which I mentioned before, and the Ditch of Belriguardo, are seen Fistura and Caporate; lower, across the ditch, Belriguardo, Zelata, la Motta; and higher, Bessi, Farangia, Ozeno; and further up Abia Crassa, which is Albiate in Merula, book 5, a town of no unpleasant situation, once rich and populous. Above Albiate is seen Kolecco, and higher still Brena.

units.la: Ab Albiate laeva fossae, quae ex Ticino Mediolanum trahitur, videre est, quae vernacule, Binsa, Rosa, Terzago, Cefano, S. Christoforo: hinc supra Mediolanum, Oronae simultra, Maddalena, Lampognano, Fagnan, Polieto, Treno: intus Baggio, Morano, Cusago, Barreggio, S. Pietro, l'Olmo, Cassina, Quinto, Casadella Quarta, Luferna, Arsano, Vernazzago, Pregnano, S. Stephano, Nerviano, Parabiago, Cosorrezzo, Busto piccolo, Canegra (Latine loquentibus Casa Nigra) S. Giorgio, Villa Cortese, Busto grande, Selva Longa, Castellazzo, Olina, Sulbia, Fagnano, Arna, Cassano. Porro in Oronae laeva Castellazzo, Borgoro, Bolarello, Cara, Peverazza, Sultano, Carnago, Travaino, Carenghi, Mortezon, Schiano, Gorra, Cavon, Lizza, Piozeto, Bosii, Varesia, quod Latinis Varisium, Vallesium, & quibusdam Vicus Varonus: sequuntur mox Induino, & S. Ambrogio: ab Albiate per dextram ejusdem Fossae Mediolanum versus pergenti occurrunt Castelletto, Fagnano, Belfagno, Albate, Corbetta (Latine apud Alciatum Curia Ptetia) Ceriano, Cisiano, Sidrano, Desiderio, Desiderio nominant Latine loquentes, tamquam ab Desiderio, Langbardorum Rege, conditum) Vittone (Vicus Tadonis Alciato) Mazzenta vel Masitia (cui nomen a Maximiano creditur natum, vel Maxentio tyranno) Offiona, Bufalora, Misero, Bugiono, Terbigno, Mala, Tata, Castano, Magnago, Bieno; & prope fossae caput in Ticino, Tincella, Lona, Pezzoldo, Ferna, Samara, Casa Vergara, Arna, Carlano, Galerato, (quibusdam Galliorum Area) altiusque Bettolino, Albiza longa, Arna, Albiza, Abiegazzo, Carda, Villa, Fort: mox in edito monte Fanum D. Mariae Montana. Tum rursus ab Ticino sursum versum Golla Secca, Gallam Siccam vocant Latini, & altius Sesto, Latinis Sextium, & quibusdam Sextum Kalendas, quod hic eo die singulis mensibus Conventus celebrari consuerint ab rusticis: intus offeruntur Soma, Cesora, Mezzana, Arsago (nonnullis Ara Caesarus) Besna, altiusque Vergia.
units.tr: From Albiate, on the left of the ditch which is drawn from the Ticino to Milan, one can see those places which in the vernacular are called Binsa, Rosa, Terzago, Cefano, S. Christoforo; from here, above Milan on the Olona side, Maddalena, Lampognano, Fagnan, Polieto, Treno; inland Baggio, Morano, Cusago, Barreggio, S. Pietro, l'Olmo, Cassina, Quinto, Casadella Quarta, Luferna, Arsano, Vernazzago, Pregnano, S. Stephano, Nerviano, Parabiago, Cosorrezzo, Busto piccolo, Canegra (in Latin Casa Nigra), S. Giorgio, Villa Cortese, Busto grande, Selva Longa, Castellazzo, Olina, Sulbia, Fagnano, Arna, Cassano. Moreover, on the left of the Olona: Castellazzo, Borgoro, Bolarello, Cara, Peverazza, Sultano, Carnago, Travaino, Carenghi, Mortezon, Schiano, Gorra, Cavon, Lizza, Piozeto, Bosii, Varesia, which in Latin is Varisium or Vallesium, and by some Vicus Varonus; soon follow Induino and S. Ambrogio. Going from Albiate along the right bank of the same ditch towards Milan, one meets Castelletto, Fagnano, Belfagno, Albate, Corbetta (in Latin in Alciatus Curia Ptetia), Ceriano, Cisiano, Sidrano, Desiderio, Desiderio (those who speak Latin name it so, as if founded by Desiderius, King of the Lombards), Vittone (Vicus Tadonis in Alciatus), Mazzenta or Masitia (whose name is believed to derive from Maximian or from the tyrant Maxentius), Offiona, Bufalora, Misero, Bugiono, Terbigno, Mala, Tata, Castano, Magnago, Bieno; and near the head of the ditch on the Ticino, Tincella, Lona, Pezzoldo, Ferna, Samara, Casa Vergara, Arna, Carlano, Galerato (by some called Galliorum Area), and higher Bettolino, Albiza longa, Arna, Albiza, Abiegazzo, Carda, Villa, Fort; soon on a high hill the Shrine of Our Lady of the Mountain. Then again, going up from the Ticino, they call Golla Secca "Galla Sicca" in Latin, and higher Sesto (in Latin Sextium, and by some Sextum Kalendas, because on this day of each month the country people were accustomed to hold assemblies here); inland are met Soma, Cesora, Mezzana, Arsago (by some Ara Caesaris), Besna, and higher Vergia.

units.la: Visitur ulterius amoenum Praedium Sfortiaca, sic ab Ludovico Sfortia, Mediolani Duce nominatum: juxta est in mediterraneis Gambolate, ubi duas Columnas, quarum Ammianus meminit libro xv, fuisse quidam opinantur. Pagus est lautus; uti & Gropetum, qui non procul inde.
units.tr: Further on is seen the pleasant estate Sforziaca, so named after Ludovico Sforza, Duke of Milan. Near it, inland, is Gambolate, where some think there were the two Columns which Ammianus mentions in book 15. It is a prosperous village; so too is Gropetum, which is not far from there.

units.la: Sequitur ad Ticinum amnem Vigievano, Civitatis jus adeptum anno MDXXX ad Clemente VII P.M, in gratiam Francisci Sfortiae, Mediolanensium Ducis. Vicus Veneris Corio, Carinum laudanti, dicitur: Merulae lib. v. Histor. Vicecomitum & Simonetae in Sfortiadibus Vigevanum; Volaterrano lib. iv Comment, Vrban. Vegevanum; Dominico Machanco in Verbani Lacus descriptione Viglivenum, Incolaeque Viglivenses, aliis Vergeminum: Mediolanensium Ducum opus, quibus frequens hic habitatio. Captum Ludovicus xii Francorum Rex Ioanni Iacobo Trivultio donavit, cum Marchionis titulo: ejectis Gallis, Maximilianus Sfortia Cardinali tradidit Sedunensi: receptoque ab Francisco Rege Mediolani Ducatu, in ejusque quoque potestatem redijt; ab eo in Francisci Sfortiae ditionem; cui Carolus v in universum Mediolani imperium successit. Civitas est lauta, rerum omnium copia abundans. Patria Petri Candidi, qui Plutarchi Parallela & Appianum Alexandrinum, aliaque fecit Latina. Genuit & Hieronymum Fantonum Theologum, Scriptis clarum. Agrum habet uberem frumenti, vini, reliquarum frugum foecundum.
units.tr: Next, on the Ticino river, is Vigevano, which obtained the rights of a city in 1530 from Clement VII, Pope and Supreme Pontiff, to please Francis Sforza, Duke of the Milanese. Corio, praising Carinum, calls it Vicus Veneris; in Merula, book 5 of the History of the Visconti, and in Simonetta's Sforziadi, it is Vigevanum; in Volaterranus, book 4 of the Commentaries on Urban Matters, Vegevanum; in Domenico Macanco's description of Lake Maggiore, Viglivenum, and its inhabitants Viglivenses; by others Vergeminum. It is a work of the Dukes of Milan, to whom this was a frequent residence. Louis XII, King of the French, when he had captured it, gave it to Gian Giacomo Trivulzio, with the title of Marquis. When the French were expelled, Maximilian Sforza handed it over to the Cardinal of Sion; and when Duke Francis I had recovered the Duchy of Milan, it returned to his power, and from him to the authority of Francis Sforza, to whom Charles V succeeded in the whole rule of Milan. The town is prosperous, abounding in every kind of goods. It was the birthplace of Pietro Candido, who made the Parallel Lives of Plutarch, an Alexandrian Appian, and other Latin works. It also produced Girolamo Fantoni, a theologian famous for his writings. Its territory has rich land, fertile in grain, wine and other crops.

units.la: Succedunt in laeva Ticini ripa Valle di Piomba, Borgo del Tesino, & ulterius Castelletto.
units.tr: On the left bank of the Ticino follow Valle di Piomba, Borgo del Tesino, and further on Castelletto.

units.la: Inter Amnes Ticinum & Goniam Opidum est Mortaria. Sic, quum antea Silva bella, dici coepit tempore Karoli Magni, victoriam hoc loco desiderio Rege, cum multa Langbardorum strage mortequie, adepti; teste, praeter alios, Corio parte i. De eo Facius Vbertus lib. iii, Cantico v: Gjunti à Mortara quivi vedemo à pienos Che per i molti morti il nome prese, Quando gli due compagni venner meno.
units.tr: Between the rivers Ticino and Gogna is the town of Mortara. Thus, since it was previously called Silva bella, it began to be called so in the time of Charlemagne, when King Desiderius won a victory here, with a great slaughter and death of the Lombards; this is attested by Corio, part 1, among others. Concerning this, Fazio degli Uberti, book 3, Canto 5, says: "Coming down from Mortara, here we see the many dead by whom it took its name, when the two companions came to an end."

units.la: Sequitur inde Burgum Lavetium, Borgo Lavezza; Latine loquentibus Forum Libetorum, vel Lebuorum. Lebui Livio Galliae Cis-Alpinae Populi; Aebirei, vel, ut alij legunt Aτάξιοι apud Polybium, Sigonio indicante, libro singulari de Iure Italiæ: Incmendatius Libici Plinio; Αἰβυκοι, Ptolemæo: uti censet Gaudentius Merula.
units.tr: Next comes Burgum Lavetium, Borgo Lavezza, which in Latin is called Forum Libetorum or Lebuorum. The Lebui were a people of Cisalpine Gaul according to Livy. Polybius has the Aebirei, or, as others read it, Ἀτάξιοι, as Sigonius points out in his single book on the Law of Italy. Pliny more correctly has Libici, and Ptolemy Αἰβυκοι. So Gaudentius Merula thinks.

units.la: Dextra est Barbariga; medioque hoc spatio Lumello. Sic vulgo audit, quod Laumellum Paulo Diacono lib. iii. Hist. Langbard. Antonino in Itinerario, & Ammiano Marcellino libro xv, apud quem tamen Lacmellium legi notat Gaudentius Merula, scripturam illam magis adprobans. Ῥαυμέλλον vitiose Ptolemæo. Censet Xylander Ἰχτεμμλον, Vercellensis agri, forte dici apud Strabonem & Plinium, quorum judicio Auri ibi sunt fodinæ. Eversum scribit Corius Parte ii ab Mediolanensibus anno cIↄ ccxv. Ab Laumello Laumellina nuncupatur totus inter Ticinum & Gomam Trafius.
units.tr: On the right is Barbariga, and midway between them lies Lumello. This is the common name, since Paulus Diaconus (Histories of the Lombards, book III), Antoninus in his Itinerary, and Ammianus Marcellinus (book XV) call it Laumellum. Gaudentius Merula notes, however, that Ammianus is read as Lacmellium, and he approves that spelling more. Ptolemy's Ῥαυμέλλον is a mistake. Xylander thinks that Ἰχτεμμλον, of the territory of Vercelli, may be the name in Strabo and Pliny, and in their judgment there are gold mines there. Corio, in part II, writes that it was overthrown by the Milanese in the year 1215. The whole district between the Ticino and the Gogna is called Laumellina after Laumellum.

units.la: In Agro Laumellino Civitas est Novara. Sic vulgo dicitur; quæ Novaria Tacito, Plinioque: Novaeia Ptolemæo & Procopio. Cippus oblongus Romæ ad domum Matthæi Porcarij: C. LIVIVS. C. F. IVSTVS NOVARIA. MIL. CHO. IIII. FR D. LICINI. MILIT ANN. XVIII VIX. ANN. XXVII H. S. E. T. F. I
units.tr: In the Laumellian territory is the city of Novara. This is what it is commonly called. Tacitus and Pliny call it Novaria, and Ptolemy and Procopius Novaeia. In Rome, at the house of Matthaeus Porcarius, there is an oblong cippus inscribed: Gaius Livius Justus, son of Gaius, of Novara, soldier of the fourth cohort, [century] of Decimus Licinius, soldier, lived eighteen years, died aged twenty-seven; this monument is his heir's, by decree of the council, and the ground is given to him.

units.la: An Aria, Lybia, Leonina quondam; disputent ex supposititio Catone alij. Ab Elito Trojano, Veneris filio, fertur condita cum Vercellis, Novariaque dicta, quasi Nova Ara, eidem Veneri consecrata. Plinius ex Vertamaeoris Vocontiorum scribit ortam. In modico sita colle, diu sub Mediolanensium Ducum fuit ditione; inde ab Turrianis, Vicecomitibus, Sfortiis, Franciaque Regibus possessa, cum Ducatus capite Mediolano in potestatem venit Karoli v, Regumque Hispaniæ. Fruitur ea certis legibus Parmensium Princeps. Episcopatus gaudet dignitate. Pernobiles habet Familias Tornicellorum, Caballatiorum, Brusatorumque, quorum intestinis bellis misere est labefactata. Traditus est venditusque in Urbis Castro ab Helvetijs Gallo Mediolani Dux Ludovicus Sforzia, anno cIↄ 15. Claros genuit Viros Albutium Silonem, magnum Augusti principiarum Oratorem; Petrum Lombardum, Episcopum Lugdunensem, Sententiarum Auctorem; Joannem Mariam Catanensem, Poetam. Novariensem quoque nonnulli faciunt Petrum Comestorem, Ecclesiasticæ Historiæ Scriptorem. Viros Militares prætereo. Habuit circa annum cIↄ cccviii Dulcinum, haereliarcham, in quem ejusque Conjugem animadvertendum censuit Clemens v P.M. Auger ipsi partim planus & fertilis, partim sterilis & montosus.
units.tr: Some dispute whether it was once called Aria, Lybia or Leonina, relying on the spurious Cato. It is said to have been founded by Elitus the Trojan, son of Venus, together with Vercelli, and named Novaria, as if "New Altar," consecrated to the same Venus. Pliny writes that it arose from the Vocontii of Vertamaeor. Set on a modest hill, it was long under the rule of the Dukes of Milan. Then it was held by the Torriani, the Visconti, the Sforzas and the kings of France. When the capital, Milan, came into the power of Charles V and the kings of Spain, Novara came under the Prince of Parma on certain conditions. Its bishopric enjoys dignity. It has very noble families, the Tornielli, Caballatii and Brusati, whose internal wars have miserably weakened it. In the year 1515 it was handed over and sold to the French by the Swiss, in the castle of the city, by Ludovico Sforza, Duke of Milan. It has produced famous men: Albutius Silo, a great orator of the Augustan age; Peter Lombard, bishop of Lyons, author of the Sentences; and Giovanni Maria of Catania, a poet. Some also make Peter Comestor of Novara, writer of Ecclesiastical History. I pass over its military men. Around the year 1308 it had Dolcino, a heresiarch, against whom and his wife Clement V, the supreme pontiff, decreed punishment. Its territory is partly flat and fertile, partly barren and mountainous.

units.la: Haud procul inde Monti Gaciarono adjident Triverio, Cazzola, Crepacore.
units.tr: Not far from there, at Monte Gaciarono, lie Triverio, Cazzola and Crepacore.

units.la: Ad Senciæ fluminis in Pado ostium Bremidum jacet: Ad dextram ripam sursum Palestri & Romagnano, victoria Populi Romani duce C. Marij & Q. Catuli de Cimbris relata nobilitatum. Iuxta est Camarianum, sic dictum quasi Castra Mariana, ut vult Alciatus: vel, ut alij, quasi Arcus Marianus, cujus etiam nunc exstant vestigia.
units.tr: At the mouth of the river Sesia where it enters the Po lies Bremidum. Upstream on the right bank are Palestro and Romagnano, made famous by the victory of the Roman people over the Cimbri, won under the leadership of Gaius Marius and Quintus Catulus. Next to them is Camarianum, so called as if "Marian Camp," as Alciatus maintains; or, as others say, as if "Marian Arch," whose remains still survive.

units.la: Visuntur eo tractu nonnulla Opida, quæ Lacubus conjacentibus nomen indiderunt, Mona, Trina, Comabio, Corzino, Varrano. Interius sunt Le Ci oci & S. Pancratio. Haud procul inde Biendrono spectatur; statim Barbia; mox Gavira a quo Gavirathius Lacus cognominatus: dein Cellano & Co Lago, Caput Lagus: alia latere Azza, Latinis Altarium: & ulterius S. Francesco.
units.tr: In that district there are several towns which gave their names to the lakes lying beside them: Mona, Trina, Comabio, Corzino, Varrano. Inland are Le Ci oci and S. Pancrazio. Not far from there Biendrono is seen; then Barbia; soon Gavira, from which Lake Gavirathius takes its name; then Cellano and Co Lago, "Head of the Lake"; on the other side Azza, in Latin Altarium; and further on S. Francesco.

units.la: Confident utrimque Lugano Lacui Brusino piano, duobus hinc milliaribus Marco: parique intervallo Porto: mox Brusino Cisso, & Rina. Offerunt se paullo post Marozzo, Biffono, Campiono, Hoiten, Cima vel Cacumen Lacus, Corlezza, Lichime, Valsoldo. Est etiam hoc situ Gandrie: & intus Sonvigo, Lugano, à quo Lacui nomen. Arcem habuit. olim munitissimam: tribus hinc millibus Mili: utraque pari spatio Murco. Tribus ab Murcotio millibus Caforo, totidemque hinc Caslano. Ad Verbanum, de quo suo loco, venio. Post Sextium, ubi stagnum se pandere incipit, Lisanza se offert: mox, tamquam in peninsula, verus Opidum Angleria, sic dictum, quod ad Glaream Verbani situm. Conditum volunt alij ab Anglo Troiano, alij ab Anglo Ascanij filio: fabulis nixi: nonnulli ab Anglis & Saxonibus, qui cum Langbardis huc profecti creduntur. Deletum legitur ab Gothis, instauratum inde non eodem loco, neque prisca amplitudine. Situm est in amœna planitie. Ortu superbit primo & incunabilis Vicecomitum, de quibus alij. Possidetur nunc ab Bonromeis, Patritijs Mediolanensibus. Sequitur inde Ranco: mox medio curvantis se ripæ sinu Incusa; summoque in cornu Ispra. Succedent inde Arole, S. Catharina, Cerro, Laverno; post amnem Tresiam Luino & Degmeza; mox Machanenum, vernacule Maccagno, patria Domini Machanei, Scriptis noti. Occurrunt dein Monte Scipazzo, Poggio, Saffo del Pino, Zeno, Martignoni, Vira, Magadino. Dextra Ticini ripa sursum Vicus invenitur, qui vulgo Cra; dein Offogna, & Biasca: utrumque Beinzena: Paullo Diacono & Gregorio Turonensi Castrum Bilinctonii. Bonaventura Catilinoneus Berinzonam, Bellizonam, aut Bellinzonam quoque nominari notat, id est Breuzonum Castrum; vel Brennizonam, tamquam Brenni Agri Zonam. In faucibus jacet Opidum inter montes, non una Arce validum. Muctij ripam sursum legenti conspiciendum se præbet Rogoretum, quod vulgo Roveredo, Arcem habens nunitissimam. Offerunt se haud procul inde Pouffen, Capeno & Fam
units.tr: On both sides of Lake Lugano, facing Brusino piano, two miles away from here lies Marco, and at the same distance Porto; soon after, Brusino Cisso and Rina. A little later Marozzo, Biffono, Campiono, Hoiten, Cima, or "Summit of the Lake," Corlezza, Lichime and Valsoldo present themselves. Gandrie is also in this place, and inland Sonvigo and Lugano, from which the lake takes its name. It once had a very strongly fortified citadel. Three miles from here is Mili, and each of them is the same distance from Murco. Three miles from Murcotio is Caforo, and as many from here Caslano. I come to Lake Maggiore, of which I will speak in its place. After Sesto, where the lake begins to spread out, Lisanza appears. Soon, as if on a peninsula, is the true town Angleria, so called because it is situated on the shingle of Lake Maggiore. Some hold that it was founded by Anglus the Trojan, others by Anglus the son of Ascanius, relying on fables; some say by the Angles and Saxons, who are believed to have come here with the Lombards. It is read that it was destroyed by the Goths, and restored afterwards in another place and without its former size. It lies on a pleasant plain. It takes pride first in being the birthplace and cradle of the Visconti, about whom others write. It is now possessed by the Borromei, patricians of Milan. Next comes Ranco; soon, in the middle bend of the curving shore, Incusa; and on the highest horn, Ispra. Then follow Arole, S. Caterina, Cerro and Laverno; after the river Tresa, Luino and Degmezza; soon Machanenum, in the vernacular Maccagno, the homeland of Domenico Macanei, known for his writings. Then Monte Scipazzo, Poggio, Sasso del Pino, Zeno, Martignoni, Vira and Magadino come into view. On the right bank of the Ticino, going upstream, a village is found which is commonly called Cra; then Offogna and Biasca. Both are Bellinzona: Paulus Diaconus and Gregory of Tours call it the castle of Bilinctonius. Bonaventura Castiglioneus notes that it is also called Berinzona, Bellizona or Bellinzona, that is, "the castle of Breuzo," or Brennizona, as if "the belt of the Brenni territory." It lies in the pass, a town among the mountains, strong in more than one citadel. For one going up the bank of the Maggia, Rogoretum, which in the vernacular is Roveredo, appears to view, with a very strong citadel. Not far from there Pouffen, Capeno and Fam present themselves.

units.la: Sic fere se habent, quæ ad ripam Lacus Verbani dextram: perlustranda sequuntur, quæ ad sinistram. Supra Ciconiolam, ubi crescere Lacus incipit, lapide quarto, nobile Castrum est Arona, cum Portu commodo. Arceque, si necessarijs instructa, inexpugnabili. Succedunt inde Lessa, Bugira, Stressa, Palanza, Vicus valde frequens, Intra, Bighinzolo, Visi, Eugiabio, aliisque Diœcesis Novariensis Pagi. Mox Cannero Opidum, fertilis agri; hinc Carmino, edito in loco; Fanum D. Eusebij, in colle; postque caput saxosæ rupis Borgo di Canobbio: quod ita portibus, turribus, ædificijs instructum, ut Civitatis potius formam referat, quam Pagi. Quatuor à Canobio p. m. Brisacum jacet; nec procul inde pagus Afiona, cujus priscam opulentiam frequentiamque magna veterum ædificiorum vestigia testantur, vastæque murorum ruinæ: Hinc secundo lapide Locarno vituir, Pagus frequens, Diœcesis Novocomensis. Circa postremum Lacus angulum in planitie Gordula monstratur, prope Verciaseæ fluminis ostium: quo superato per campos opimos Contasium aditur. Sequitur eodem itinere Belinzona, moxque Lepontina Vallis. Suggerit inde Vallis Dolia, quæ vernacule loquentibus Vegnoto, Cordanco, Cono, Zumano, Sunco, Mogeno, Laveleza, Brontal, Marzono, Broilo, Sornico, Fusio, Maggia, & Verizzino: Rovana autem, quæ Cerenzino, Rusio, Caurino, Campo, Lugnasio. Ad Athisonem descendenti Castrum adparet Domodossella. ὁ σιχιΐα Ptolemæo, quod volunt Blondus, Dominicus Machanceus, Ægidius Tschudus, Castilioneus, Leander Albertus, Iosias Simlerus, alij: Thum dicitur Germanis. Ab Ossa originem fabulatur suppositicius. Cato. Honestum est Opidum, Arcem habens munitissimam: uti & Voconia prope fauces Vallis Anciasæ, ab Ofcella millib. vii. Adsident hinc Lacui Ortano, qui & D. Iulij, Orta, Buffono, Omegna; Pagique Meno & Armeno, cum alijs, non magni nominis.
units.tr: Those places which lie on the right bank of Lake Maggiore are roughly as described. Now follow the places to be surveyed on the left. Four miles beyond Ciconiola, where the lake begins to widen, is the noble castle of Arona, with a convenient harbour, and, if equipped with necessities, impregnable. Then come Lesa, Bugira, Stresa, Palanza, a very crowded village, Intra, Bighinzolo, Visi, Eugiabio, and other villages of the diocese of Novara. Soon the town Cannero, of fertile territory; from here Carmino, set on high ground; the shrine of S.
