Eusebius on a hill; and after the head of a rocky cliff Borgo di Cannobio, which is so equipped with harbours, towers and buildings that it resembles a city rather than a village. Four miles from Cannobio lies Brissago; and not far from there the village of Afiona, whose former wealth and crowds are attested by large remains of ancient buildings and vast ruins of walls. Two miles from here Locarno rises, a crowded village in the diocese of Como. Near the far corner of the lake, in the plain, Gordola is shown, near the mouth of the river Verzasca. Having passed it, Contone is reached through rich fields. Next on the same road comes Bellinzona, and soon the Lepontine Valley. From there the valley of Dolia offers Vegnoto, Cordanco, Cono, Zumano, Sunco, Mogeno, Laveleza, Brontal, Marzono, Broilo, Sornico, Fusio, Maggia and Verzasca to those speaking the vernacular; and the Rovana valley offers Cerenzino, Rusio, Caurino, Campo and Lugnasio. Descending to the Toce, a castle, Domodossola, comes into view. It is Ptolemy's ὁ σιχιΐα, which Blondus, Domenico Maccanei, Giles Tschudi, Castiglione, Leandro Alberti, Josias Simler and others think is right; the Germans call it Thum. The impostor Cato invents its origin from Ossa. It is a respectable town with a very strong citadel, and so is Vogogna near the narrows of the Anzasca valley, seven miles from Ossola. Opposite, on the shore of Lake Orta, also called Lake of St Julius, lie Orta, Buffono and Omegna, and the villages of Meno and Armeno, together with others of no great name.

units.la: Descriptis quæ Lacui Verbano utrimque conjacent, locis, ad Langbardiæ recurrendum censeo planiciem, cis Padum. Ibi ab Amnis Sceniæ ostio sursum, sinistra ripa, Balzola jacet; mox Villa Nuova; hinc Civitas antiqua Vercella. Sic Latinis scribitur, Tacito lib. i. Histor. Plinio lib. iii cap. xvi, Silio lib. viii belli Punici; ὀὐτρκέλλαι Straboni lib. v, & Ptolemæo, cui Lybicorum Civitas; ἐρκέλλαι Scholastico lib. iii, cap. vii: quæ hodie Vercelli. De ea Martialis Epigramm. ad Domitium: Aemilia gentes, & Apollineas Vercellas, Et Phaethontei qui petiit arva Padi. Ne vivam, nisi te, Domiti, permitto libenter: Grata licet sine te sit mihi nulla dies.
units.tr: Having described the places lying on either side of Lake Maggiore, I think we should return to the plain of Lombardy, on this side of the Po. There, going upstream from the mouth of the river Sesia, on the left bank lies Balzola; then Villanova; and from here the ancient city Vercelli. This is how it is written in Latin: Tacitus (Histories book I), Pliny (book III, chapter 16), Silius (book VIII of the Punica) write Vercellae; Strabo (book V) and Ptolemy, to whom it belongs as a city of the Libici, write Ὀὐτρκέλλαι; the Scholiast (book III, chapter 7) writes Ἐρκέλλαι. It is today Vercelli. Martial, in an epigram to Domitius: "The Aemilian peoples and Vercellae sacred to Apollo, and the fields of the Po that received Phaethon's fall. May I not live, Domitius, unless I gladly grant you alone; though without you no day may be pleasing to me." Those who are credulous in fables say it was founded before the fall of Troy by Venus, a noble Trojan woman, who came to these parts with her son Eltius; and from her Vercellae was named as if "Venus' Cell." The Paradise testifies that it was earlier called Maropolis: on what authority? Indeed the Annals of Milan, which...

units.la: Conditam volunt, qui fabulis credulì, ante Trojæ excidium, ab Venera, Trojana nobili, cum Eltio filio huc locorum profecta: & ab ea Vercellam, tamquam Veneris Cellam fuisse nominatam. Maropolam etiam ante dictam testatur Paradisus: qua fide? fde? Nam Mediolanensium Annales, quos laudat Leander, non magnæ hic rei. Plinius Vercellæ Lybicorum ex Sallyis (de quibus in Gallia) ortas tradit. Annij Viterbiensis nugas insuper habeo. Quamvis Hieronymus scribat eam raro habitatore suo tempore jacuisse semidirutam: hodie tamen Vrbs est honesta, nobilis, & Episcopalis. Concilium hic celebravit Leo ix. P. M. adversus Berengarium, Archidiaconum Turriensem, uti in Decretis legitur. Claros genuit Viros, non paucos inter alios, Eusebium, Episcopum, Divorum adscriptum numero; de quo Elogium ibi legitur in Ædibus Episcopi. L. Valerij Crescentis Vercellensis mentionem facit Inscriptio, quæ Budæ in Hungaria, in pavimento Ecclesiæ S. Mariæ Magdalenæ.
units.tr: Those who credit fables hold that it was founded before the fall of Troy by Venus, the Trojan noblewoman, who came to these parts with her son Eltius, and that it was named Vercella from her, as if it were "Venus's Cell." Paradisus also testifies that it was formerly called Maropola, but on what authority? The Annals of Milan, which Leander cites, are of no great weight here. Pliny reports that the Vercellae were descended from the Libyan Sallyes (of whom I shall speak in the account of Gaul). I dismiss the nonsense of Annius of Viterbo. Although Jerome writes that in his time it lay for the most part uninhabited and half-ruined, today it is an honourable, noble city and a bishop's see. Pope Leo IX held a council here against Berengar, archdeacon of Tours, as is read in the Decretals. It produced many famous men, among them Eusebius, bishop, who is numbered among the saints, and whose eulogy is read in the bishop's palace. An inscription at Buda in Hungary, on the pavement of the church of St Mary Magdalene, mentions Lucius Valerius Crescens of Vercelli.

units.la: D . M L. Ø VALERIVS. L. F ANI Ø CRESCENS VERC Ø MIL. LEG. II. ADL. P. F 7. COMINI . PAVLINI ANN. XXXX STIPENDIORVM. XVIII T. F. I. H. F. O H. S. E.
units.tr: To the spirits of the dead. Lucius Valerius Crescens, son of Lucius, of the Ani tribe, of Vercelli, soldier of the Second Legion Adiutrix, faithful, of the century of Cominius Paulinus, aged forty years, with eighteen years of service. His heir set this up under the will. Here he lies. May the earth lie lightly on him.

units.la: Lalij item l. r. Ani. Paulini Vercellensis, cum aliis, Fragmentum Tabellæ marmoreæ, quod Romæ in Hortis Euryali Rufni, ad Busta Gallica, Civilibus olim dissensionibus miscere jactata legitur, maxime Tittionum & Advocatorum; quorum hi victoriam adepti, tandem anno ab Christo nato cıɔ cccx dominatum ejus rapuerunt; post successu temporis in Marchionum Montis ferrati; hinc Ducum Mediolanensium, tandem in Allobrogum Principum potestatem redacta. Legendi Merula, Corius, alij. Quotannis Nundinarum conventibus bis frequentatur, præcipuaque Negociatio est pecuaria & lanaria. Agrum Vercellesem, qui uberrimus, frumentique, vini, aliarumque frugum fertilis, etiam Aurifodinis fuisse divitem, paret ex Plinij naturali historia, lib. xxxiii, cap. iv.
units.tr: Likewise a fragment of a marble tablet, which is read to have been thrown together with others, from the Gallic tombs in the gardens of Euryalus Rufnus in Rome, mentions Lalius and L. R. Ani Paulinus of Vercelli. Vercelli is also to be read about in Merula, Corius and others. The town was ruled by the Tizzoni and the Avvocati factions in the civil disputes of former times. Those who won the victory at last seized its rule in the year of Christ 1310, and afterwards it passed by succession to the Marquises of Monferrato, then to the Dukes of Milan, and finally into the power of the princes of Savoy. Twice a year it is crowded with the gatherings of its fairs, and its chief trade is in livestock and wool. That the Vercelli territory is very fertile, rich in grain, wine and other crops, and was even wealthy in gold mines, is clear from Pliny's Natural History, book 33, chapter 4.

units.la: Ab Vercellis læva Senciæ ripa procedenti Castellum occurrit D. Germani, ortu nobilitatum Antonij, ex Prædicatorum sodalitate, Divis conscriptum. Succedit Burgum; dextraque prope Sarvum amnem Andurnum, & altius inter montes Biella, Latinis Buggiela. Læva dein Betullum est, vernacule Bedulo. Nomen natum credit Alciatus ab Arbore Betulla, quæ ad Vasorum circulos expetitur.
units.tr: Going up from Vercelli along the left bank of the Sesia, one meets the castle of St Germanus, made noble by the birth of Antonius, of the Dominican order, who has been numbered among the saints. Next comes Borgo, and on the right, near the river Sarvus, Andorno, and higher up among the mountains Biella, called Bugella in Latin. On the left is Bettolo, which in the vernacular is Bedulo. Alciatus believes the name derives from the birch tree (betulla), which is sought for making the hoops of barrels.

units.la: Rursus in Padi ripa, quingentis ab ora passibus Tridinium est Opidum, Italis Trino, magnum beneque munitum: patria non solum Brolia, strenui militiæ Ducis, verum etiam Nicolaī Faletti, excellentis Poetæ. Ducis est Mantuani. Haud procul inde in Padi dextera Castella visuntur Morano & Fontanella; item Palazzuolo; altiusque Crescentino, patria Vbertini Crescentinatis, qui suis Commentarijs Valerium Maximum & Epistolas M. Ciceronis illustravit. Intus est S. Maria di Locedo, nobile olim Cænobium, ab Montis-ferrati Marchionibus ædificatum. Vlterius inter paludes est Livurno; prope Duriam S. Giorgio & Salugia, Opida non magni momenti.
units.tr: Again on the bank of the Po, five hundred paces from the shore, is the town of Tridinium, in Italian Trino, large and well fortified. It was the native place not only of Brolia, a vigorous military commander, but also of Nicolò Falletti, an excellent poet. It belongs to the Duke of Mantua. Not far from there, on the right of the Po, the castles of Morano and Fontanella can be seen, also Palazzuolo; and further up Crescentino, the birthplace of Ubertino of Crescentino, who illustrated Valerius Maximus and the letters of Cicero with his commentaries. Inside is S. Maria di Lucedio, a noble monastery once built by the Marquises of Monferrato. Further on, among the marshes, is Livorno; near the Dora are S. Giorgio and Saluggia, towns of no great importance.

units.la: A Pado læva Duriæ ripa sursum pergenti Verolengo se offert; altiusque Rivarolia inque mediterraneis inter Montes Iulia Civitas. Sic hodie dicitur, quæ Eporedia Tacito lib. vii, Plinio lib. iii, cap. xvi, aliisque Latinis; Ἐπορηδία Ptolemæo, Salaforum in Insubria Vrbem facienti, in cujus quibusdam Codicibus Ἐπορηδία vitiose scribitur; Ἐπορηδία Straboni; Eporedia Ciceroni in Epistolis, multitudinis numero; Eporizium denique Libro Notitiarum. Appellatur in docto Latinorum vulgo Lamporegium & Hipporegia. Scribit Plinius Eporediam Sibyllinis libris à Populo Romano condi jussam: Eporedicas enim Gallos vocare bonos equorum domitores: unde & Romanorum Colonia apud Strabonem & Velleium Paterculum. Situs illus editus inter duos montes; secaturque ab amne Duria. Arcem habet; & Templum antiquæ notæ, Divæ Virgini sacrum, in quo D. Besis reliquias servare se ajunt Cives.
units.tr: On the left bank of the Dora, as one goes up from the Po, Verolengo presents itself; higher up is Rivarolo, and among the mountains inland the city of Ivrea. This is what is called today Ivrea, which Tacitus (book 7), Pliny (book 3, chapter 16) and other Latin writers call Eporedia; Ptolemy calls it Eporedia, making it a city of the Salassi in Insubria, though in some manuscripts of his it is wrongly written with another spelling; Strabo calls it Eporedia; Cicero in his letters uses the plural Eporediae; and finally the Notitia lists it as Eporizium. In the learned Latin usage it is called Lamporegium and Hipporegia. Pliny writes that Eporedia was ordered by the Roman people, from the Sibylline books, to be founded, since the Gauls called these people Eporedicae, "good tamers of horses"; hence it was also a Roman colony, as Strabo and Velleius Paterculus record. Its site is raised between two mountains, and it is cut by the river Dora. It has a citadel, and a temple of well-known antiquity, sacred to the Blessed Virgin, in which the citizens say they keep the relics of St Besas.

units.la: Ortum ipsi debent cum alij, tum Ioannes Stephanus, & Bonifacius Fratres, ipsorumque nepos Philibertus ex nobili Ferrariorum omnes familia, Cardinalium Collegio adscripti; primus ab Alexandro vi, secundus ab Leone x, tertius a Paullo iii, PP. MM. Ager varius: ad Austrum non infertilis; qua Septemtrio est, perasper & horridus, pascendis tamen gregibus non idoneus.
units.tr: Several men owe their birth to it, among them Giovanni Stefano and Bonifacio, brothers, and their nephew Filiberto, all from the noble Ferrero family, who were enrolled in the College of Cardinals: the first by Alexander VI, the second by Leo X, the third by Paul III, Supreme Pontiffs. The countryside is varied: toward the south it is not unfruitful, but toward the north it is rather rough and bleak, and not suitable for pasturing flocks.

units.la: Eporediam excipit Vallis Augusta Praetoria, de qua suo loco. Nomen illi ab Vrbe Cognomine Sic Plinio dicitur, Salassiorum Coloniam noranti; αὐγέστα Πεφιπεία Strabonis & Ptolemæo: quæ Italis Osta Germanis Augst. Situm est Opidum in aditu Vallis, juxta geminas Alpium fauces, inquit Plinius libro iii, cap. xvi, Grajas atque Poeninas, de quibus alibi. Cæsarem Augustum (unde dicta) tria Romanorum millia ibi collocasse, quum prius eo loci castra habuisset Varro, à quo reliquiæ Salassorum erant deletæ, scribit Strabo. Meminit Coloniæ Augustæ Praetoriæ Ti. Imperatoris Numismus. Videre ibi est Arcum Triumphalem: sed Imaginibus suis nudatum, & Inscriptione. Eam nonnulli fuisse augurantur, quæ apud Plinium libro iii natur. Hist. cap. xix, corrupta admodum, sic restituenda:
units.tr: Beyond Ivrea lies the valley of Aosta, of which I shall speak in its place. It takes its name from the city of the same name, which Pliny calls Augusta Praetoria, a colony of the Salassi; the Greeks Strabo and Ptolemy call it Augusta Prætoria. In Italian it is Aosta, in German Augst. The town lies at the entrance to the valley, near the twin gates of the Alps, which Pliny, book 3, chapter 16, calls the Graian and Pennine passes, about which I shall speak elsewhere. Strabo writes that Caesar Augustus, after whom it is named, settled three thousand Roman soldiers there, after Varro, who had previously had his camp at that place, had destroyed the remnants of the Salassi. A coin of the Emperor Tiberius mentions the Colony of Augusta Praetoria. There a triumphal arch can be seen, but it is stripped of its statues and its inscription. Some suppose that the inscription which, in Pliny's Natural History book 3, chapter 19, is greatly corrupted, was once on it, and that it should be restored as follows:

units.la: IMP. CÆSARI. DIVI. F. AVGVSTO PONT. MAX. IMP. XIIII. TRIB. POT. XVII. S. P. Q. R.
units.tr: TO THE EMPEROR CAESAR AUGUSTUS, SON OF THE DIVINE, HIGH PRIEST, IMPERATOR FOR THE FOURTEENTH TIME, HOLDING TRIBUNICIAN POWER FOR THE SEVENTEENTH TIME: THE SENATE AND PEOPLE OF ROME
