BRVNI. NAVNES. FOCVNATES VINDELICORVM. GENTES. III. CONSVANETES. VIRVCINATES. LICATES CATTENATES ABISONTES. RVGVSCI. SVANETES COLLVCONES. BRIXENTES LEPONTII. VIPERI. NANTVATES. SEDVNI VERAGRI. SALASSI. ACITAVONES. MEDVLLI VCENNI. CATVRIGES. BRIGIANI SONTIONTII. EBRODVNTII. NEMALONI EDENNATES. EBVSANI. VEAMINI GALLICÆ TRIVLATTI. ECTINI. VERCVNNI EGVITVRI. NEMENTVRI. ORATELLI VERVS I. VELNANI. SVETRI
units.tr: Because under his leadership and auspices all the Alpine peoples from the Upper Sea to the Lower were brought under the rule of the Roman people: the Triumpilini, Camunni, Vennones, Venostes, Vennonetes, Isarci, Breuni, Naunes, Focunates, the three tribes of the Vindelici, Consuanetes, Virucinates, Licates, Catenates, Abisontes, Rugusci, Suanetes, Calucones, Brixenates, Leponti, Viberi, Nantuates, Sedunni, Veragri, Salassi, Acitavones, Medulli, Ucenni, Caturiges, Brigiani, Sogiontii, Ebrodunti, Nemaloni, Edenates, Esubiani, Veamini, the Gallic Trullatti, Ectini, Vercunni, Egituri, Nementuri, Oratelli, Vennonetes, Velauni, Suetri.

units.la: Quorum omnium explicatio cum apud alios, tum apud Iosiam Simlerum de Alpibus.
units.tr: All of these are explained both by others and by Josias Simler in his work on the Alps.

units.la: Haud procul Augusta ad ripam Duriæ lævam Mazzadium conspicitur: inde relictis cum Valle montibus rursum in Padi ripa fluminis Orci est Ostium, cujus dextræ nobile Opidum adsidet Danasum, altiusque D. Martini, unde Comitibus San-Martinis nomen Orci læva Clavasium: jacet, cum Vulpiano: & in montibus Marcinasciun: interiusque Strambinum. Sunt item eodem tractu, quæ vulgo S. Benedetto di Fruttera; utraque & citra Sturam, cum aliis, Caselera, Grangia, Lanzo, & Belengerio.
units.tr: Not far from Augusta, on the left bank of the Dora, Mazzadium is seen. From there, leaving the mountains behind with the Valley, on the bank of the Po again is the mouth of the river Orco. On its right side sits the noble town of Danasum, and higher up St Martin, from which the Counts of San Martino take their name. On the left of the Orco lies Clavasium, with Vulpiano, and in the mountains Marcinasciun, and further inland Strambinum. In the same tract are also the places commonly called San Benedetto di Fruttera. Both of these, on this side of the Stura, together with others: Caselera, Grangia, Lanzo and Belengerio.

units.la: CAPUT
units.tr: CHAPTER

units.la: CAPVT XXXVI.
units.tr: Chapter XXXVI.

units.la: Venetia vel Marca Tarvisina.
units.tr: Venetia or the March of Treviso.

units.la: DIXI de Langobardia Transpadana: occurrit trans Padum, in occidentalioribus Novae planiorisque Italiae Partibus Venetia, vel Marca Tarvisina. Habitarunt hic olim Euganei, quibus nomen, si Etymon ex Graecia petendum, ab genere nobili clarisque Natalibus. Quae de Euganeorum origine apud Catonem & Sempronium Annianos, quia parum solida, omitto. Eorum multifaciunt mentionem; cum primis Livius lib. I. ab V.C. & Plinius libro III natural. Histor. cap. XVIII, eorum Opidum Veronam scribens; item cap. seq. ubi Catonem Latini juris Euganearum gentium opida XXXIV enumerasse memorat. Ab Euganeis Euganei Colles Lucanus de bello Pharsalico libro VII:
units.tr: I have spoken of Transpadane Lombardy. Beyond the Po, in the western parts of the newer and flatter Italy, lies Venetia, or Marca Tarvisina. The Euganei once lived here, and their name, if its etymology is to be sought in Greek, comes from a noble stock and illustrious birth. I omit what is said of the origin of the Euganei by Cato and Sempronius Annius, since it is of little solidity. Many writers mention them, above all Livy in book 1, from the foundation of the City, and Pliny in book 3 of his Natural History, chapter 18, where he writes of their town Verona; likewise in the following chapter, where he records that Cato listed thirty-four towns of the Euganean peoples under Latin law. From the Euganei the Euganean Hills take their name, as Lucan says in book 7 of the Pharsalia:

units.la: Euganeo, si vera fides memorantibus, AugurColle sedens, Aponue terris ubi fumifer exit, Atque Antenorei dispergitur unda Timavi.
units.tr: "Euganean, if we trust those who report it, sitting on the Augur hill, where the smoky Aponus rises from the earth, and where the wave of the Antenorean Timavus is scattered."

units.la: Oves mollissimae Lanae apud Euganeos, notat Iuvenalis:
units.tr: Juvenal notes that the Euganean sheep have the softest wool:

units.la: Euganea quantumvis mollior agna.
units.tr: "Softer than a Euganean lamb, however soft."

units.la: Euganeos his sedibus profligarunt, ut Livius notat libro I, Veneti, à quibus tota Regio Venetia dicta. Legitur apud Strabonem libro V duplex de Venetorum origine sententia; eos vel ab Enetis, Galliae Populis, Oceano adcolis, descendisse; vel ab Enetis, qui post bellum Trojanum, auspiciis ductuque Antenoris, ex Paphlagoniae finibus huc commearunt. Quod ad priorem opinionem, Venetos celerrimos olim Galliae ad Oceanum fuisse populos, docui lib. III, cap. XXXI, quod Brittanniae delineationi datum: Quod ad posteriorem, in eam, quum illustrior (nam quae non gens ab deviis Trojanis originem mentitur?) plerique inclinat Scriptores; uti Sophocles apud Strabonem lib. XV, Polybius, Cornelius Nepos, Pompeius Trogus lib. XX, Cato apud Plinium libro III, cap. XVIII, Livius libro I ab V.C. aliique; maxime vero Poetae. Sic Virgilius lib. I:
units.tr: The Euganei were driven from these seats by the Veneti, as Livy notes in book I, and from them the whole region is called Venetia. In Strabo book V there is a twofold opinion on the origin of the Veneti: that they descended either from the Eneti, a people of Gaul dwelling by the Ocean, or from the Eneti who, after the Trojan War, under the auspices and leadership of Antenor, came here from the borders of Paphlagonia. As to the former opinion, that the Veneti were once a very swift people of Gaul by the Ocean, I showed in book III, chapter XXXI, which was given to the description of Britain. As to the latter, most writers incline to it, since it is the more illustrious (for what people does not falsely claim descent from the Trojan exiles?). So Sophocles in Strabo book XV, Polybius, Cornelius Nepos, Pompeius Trogus book XX, Cato in Pliny book III, chapter XVIII, Livy book I from the founding of the city, and others; but especially the poets. Thus Virgil, book I:

units.la: Antenor potuit, mediis elapsus Achivis,Illyricos penetrare sinus, atque intima tutusRegna Liburnorum, & fontem superare Timavi: Unde per ora novem vasto cum murmure montisIt mare proruptum, & pelago premit arva sonanti: Hic tamen ille Urbem Patavi, sedemque locavitTeucrorum; & genti nomen dedit: armaque fixitTroia: nunc placida compostus pace quievit.
units.tr: Antenor was able, escaping from the midst of the Achaeans, to penetrate the Illyrian gulfs and reach safely the inner realms of the Liburnians, and to pass beyond the source of the Timavus, where through nine mouths it rushes forth from the mountain with a vast roar and presses its fields with the sounding sea. Yet there he founded the city of Padua and the seat of the Teucrians, and gave his name to the people, and fixed up the arms of Troy. Now he rests, settled in peaceful quiet.

units.la: Sic Silius Italicus libro VIII de bello Poenico:
units.tr: Thus Silius Italicus in book VIII of the Punic War:

units.la: Tum Troiana manus tellure antiquitus ortiEuganea, profugique sacris Antenoris oris,Nec non cum Venetis Aquileia superfuit armis.
units.tr: Then the Trojan band, the Euganeans sprung long ago from that land, and the fugitives from the sacred shores of Antenor, and Aquileia too survived together with the arms of the Veneti.

units.la: Tertia de Venetorum origine sententia, quae apud Catonem & Sempronium, ab Viterbiensi suppositos, frivola omnino est, meraque sapit fabulas. Memoriam Venetorum celebrat etiam, cum aliis, Tacitus lib. XI. Licet hos Populos quidam scribant vel Enetos, vel Henetos; plerique tamen Venetos appellant.
units.tr: The third opinion on the origin of the Veneti, which Cato and Sempronius, as imposed by Viterbo, is utterly frivolous and savours of pure fable. Tacitus also commemorates the Veneti in book XI, along with others. Although some write these people as Enetos or Henetos, most call them Venetos.

units.la: Postrema Regionis denominatio Marca Tarvisina fuit. Quia Marca, dictum supra cap. XXIII, ubi de Marca Anconitana. Cognomen dedit Urbs Tarvisium, sedes olim & domicilium Marchionum Langobardici nominis, qui huic Tractui cum imperio praerant. Consulendi Blondus, Volaterranus, Rafanus, alii. Tarvisinum appellant Cassiodorus libro X Variar. Procopius, Paullus Diaconus, & Regino. Tarvisinos Montes indicat apud Plinium libro III, cap. XVIII Pintianus; ubi alii Codices habent Taurisanos. Hodie vernacule Marka Trevigiana.
units.tr: The last name of the region was the Marca Tarvisina. The word Marca was explained above, in chapter XXIII, where I dealt with the March of Ancona. The name Tarvisium was given by the city of that name, once the seat and home of the Marquises of Lombard name, who held command over this tract. Consult Blondus, Volaterranus, Rafanus and others. Cassiodorus, book X of the Variae, calls it Tarvisinum, as do Procopius, Paul the Deacon and Regino. Pintianus indicates the Tarvisinos Montes in Pliny, book III, chapter XVIII, where other codices have Taurisanos. Today in the vernacular it is Marka Trevigiana.

units.la: Quod ad Fines, scribit Leander ab Occidente Venetiam claudere Mintium, Benacum, & Sarcam flumen; à Septemtrione, Montes Taurisanos, Italiae Germaniaeque discrimen; ab Oriente Timavi Ostium, partemque Hadriatici maris; ab Meridie ridie, Ostium Athesis, Paludesque Melarianas ac Brigantinas: hos autem Venetia Veteris terminos esse, non Marka Tarvisina, quæ multo erat angustior, suamque habebat longitudinem inter Mincium Alsamque fluvios: trans Alsam enim Forojuliensem Agium adnecti: præterea Marcam Tarvisinam, quæ nunc vocatur, nonnulla continere loca Cenomanorum, &c. Videndus etiam Paullus Diaconus lib. II. Histor. Langbardicæ cap. XIIII.
units.tr: As to its boundaries, Leander writes that Venetia is enclosed on the west by the Mincius, the Benacus and the river Sarca; on the north by the Tauriscan mountains, the boundary between Italy and Germany; on the east by the mouth of the Timavus and part of the Adriatic Sea; and on the south by the mouth of the Athesis and the marshes of Melaria and Brigantia. These, however, are the limits of old Venetia, not of the Marka Tarvisina, which was much narrower and had its length between the rivers Mincius and Alsa, for beyond the Alsa the Forojulian territory was joined. Moreover, the Marca Tarvisina as now called contains some places of the Cenomani, and so on. See also Paul the Deacon, book II of the History of the Lombards, chapter XIV.

units.la: Regio est, uti videre est apud eumdem Leandrum, pernobilis & lauta, ditissimis Opidis, urbibusque splendidissimis nitens, Colunius & ingenio tum ad litteras omnemque disciplinam, tum ad rerum publicarum administrationem aptissimis, & manu armisque, quum tempus exigit, promtis, nec minus in re faciendæ cumulandisque divitiis solertibus. Campos habet amœnos, ac frumenti ceterarumque frugum, item omnigeni fructus ac vini maxima fertiles. Non desunt calidi frigidique fontes, ad medicinam mortalium utiles. Adest Metallorum ubertas: multi nobiles amnes & lacus; cœlum salubre, jucundum & temperatum: tantis denique & tam multis munificæ naturæ dotibus adsatim ornata est & locupletata, ut inter principes Italiæ Regiones optimo jure censeri possit;
units.tr: It is a region, as may be seen in the same Leander, very noble and rich, shining with most splendid cities and wealthy towns. It is fertile in men, most fit both for letters and all learning and for the administration of public affairs, ready with hand and arms when the time demands, and no less clever in making and piling up riches. It has pleasant fields, and is most fertile of grain and other crops, and of every kind of fruit and wine. Warm and cold springs are not lacking, useful for human medicine. There is abundance of metals, many noble rivers and lakes, and a healthy, pleasant and temperate air. In short, it is so richly and abundantly endowed with the gifts of bountiful nature that it may rightly be counted among the foremost regions of Italy.

units.la: Specialiora delineaturus, initium statuam haud procul ostio Mincij Padoque, in Sacchetta; quæ Caprianorum patrimonium: secundum Padi ripam deorsum Serrazallis est Arx munita, ab Mantuanis anno MCCC XX condita, teste Æquicola libro I Comit. Mantuanorum. Celebris est armorum militarium officina, Haud procul inde montratur Hostia, Opidum frequens, opulentum; arce, fossis, mœnibus, paludibus bene munitum. Hostia Tacito lib. II. & I I Histor item Antonino, & aliis. Padum adluere scribit Plinius. Hostiensis loci meminit Cassiodorus Variar. lib. II ad Dromanarios. Instauratum ab Veronensibus, notat Blondus. Imperium ejus penes Mantuanorum Principem.
units.tr: Intending to describe the particulars, I shall begin not far from the mouth of the Mincius and the Po, at Sacchetta, which is the patrimony of the Caprians. Down along the bank of the Po is the fortified citadel Serrazallis, founded by the Mantuans in 1320, as Equicola witnesses in book I of the Mantuan Commentaries. It is a famous workshop of military arms. Not far from there is Hostia, a populous and wealthy town, well fortified with citadel, ditches, walls and marshes. Tacitus mentions Hostia in book II of the Histories, and Antoninus and others likewise. Pliny writes that it washes the Po. Cassiodorus, Variae book II, mentions the Hostiensis locus in the letter to the dromedaries. Blondus notes that it was restored by the Veronese. Its rule lies with the Prince of Mantua.

units.la: Inter Tartarum Minciumque multa sunt loca, cum aliis, ad Ostium amnis, læva Bastiona, & la Torre dalle Zinzale, Latinis Turris Culicum: dividitque se infra, post XII fere stadium in duo Cornua, quorum unum tendit ad Pontem Molinum, alterum ad Turrim Mediam. Supra Paludem, ultra Turrim Culicum hæc se offerunt Castella, quæ vernacule, Monte Vzatico, Castellaro, Ponte Polero, Erba, Ferrazzolo, Poscia, Grezano, Sifagna, Nugarolo, Castion Mantcano, Monte Zancano, Tornezzo, Villa Franca, Sancto Zeno, Gersa, Borgetto, Vallezzo: sequuntur altius Salvozze, Castel Nuovo, & Cazaca Selle. Inferiora versum inter dextram Tartari ripam, Menaciqueœvam Fons Molinus est, & Castilio D. Michaelis. Haud procul inde Sanguinedo, Norage, Alpreto, Solazuolo, Isola della Scala, Vicus Opidum referens, amœnissimus olim Scaligerorum, qui condiderunt, secessus: sequuntur Vigazze, S. Maria, Pingiano, & Butta Preda: dein, Ostio Menaci transito, Castagnaro & Carpo: ultra quem Villa Bartholemea, mox Athesis, de quo supra: Ejus læva Lignago occurrit frequens & amplum Opidum, Veronensis quondam ditionis, nunc Venetis subjectum, qui præsidium in eo habent firmissimum: Succedunt Ango, Rovecchiara di Sotto, Gollozo, Manrega, Rovecchiara, Ronco Torre di Magnan, Pezzo, Gegno, altiusque Verona.
units.tr: Between the Tartarus and the Mincius there are many places, among them, at the mouth of the river on the left, Bastiona, and La Torre dalle Zinzale, in Latin Turris Culicum. Below, about twelve stadia further on, it divides into two horns, one stretching to Pons Molinus, the other to Turris Media. Above the marsh, beyond Turris Culicum, these castles present themselves, which in the vernacular are called Monte Vzatico, Castellaro, Ponte Polero, Erba, Ferrazzolo, Poscia, Grezano, Sifagna, Nugarolo, Castion Mantcano, Monte Zancano, Tornezzo, Villa Franca, Sancto Zeno, Gersa, Borgetto, Vallezzo. Higher up follow Salvozze, Castel Nuovo and Cazaca Selle. Lower down, between the right bank of the Tartarus and the left of the Menacius, lie Fons Molinus and Castilio D. Michaelis. Not far from there are Sanguinedo, Norage, Alpreto, Solazuolo, Isola della Scala, a village resembling a town, once the most pleasant retreat of the Scaligers, who founded it. Then come Vigazze, S. Maria, Pingiano and Butta Preda. Then, passing the mouth of the Menacius, Castagnaro and Carpo; beyond which Villa Bartholemea, and soon the Athesis, of which I spoke above. On its left occurs Lignago, a populous and large town, once under the rule of Verona and now subject to the Venetians, who keep a very strong garrison there. Then follow Ango, Rovecchiara di Sotto, Gollozo, Manrega, Rovecchiara, Ronco, Torre di Magnan, Pezzo, Gegno, and higher up Verona.

units.la: Verona vocatur Livio, Tacito, Silio, Plinio, Paullo Diacono, Antonino, Itineraria Tabulæ, aliisque; Οὐρπία Ptolemæo: quæ οὔπεων Suaboni; Βίρωνα Stephano. Nomen hodie retinet. Germanis Dietriche Bern vocatur. Meminit Verona Cippus, qui Romæ repertus è regione Templum Teutonicum, ad Agonem.
units.tr: Verona is so called by Livy, Tacitus, Silius, Pliny, Paul the Deacon, Antoninus, the Itinerary Tables and others. Ptolemy calls it Urpia [Οὐρπία]; Strabo calls it Oupeon [οὔπεων]; Stephanus calls it Biron [Βίρωνα]. It retains the name today. By the Germans it is called Dietriche Bern. Verona is mentioned by the cippus which was found at Rome, opposite the Teutonic Temple, near the Agon.

units.la: Ab Vero, nobili Etrusca familia, dictam fabulantur apud Annium Viterbiensem Cato & Sempronius. Alij nomen natum volunt à Brenno, Gallorum Duce, priusque Brennonam nuncupatam, post autem lapsu temporis Veronam. Ptolemæus Cenomanus tribuit; Libuis Livius; Euganeis Plinius: hodie Marke Tarvisine concentetur. Aerem habet tenuem. Non absimilis Helvetiorum Basileæ, natura, situ, pulcritudine ædificiorum est nobilis; æquo solo recumbens, ad Meridiem, Ortum. Occasumque conversa brumalem, tellure ad Septemtrionem leniter adsurgente, jugisque Theatralem pene formam exprimentibus. Athesi amne non tam dividitur, quam munitur & circumquaque cingitur. Silius lib. VIII:
units.tr: Cato and Sempronius, in Annius of Viterbo, tell the fable that it was named from Vero, a noble Etruscan family. Others want the name to derive from Brenno, leader of the Gauls, and say that it was first called Brennonam, and afterwards, with the passage of time, Veronam. Ptolemy assigns it to the Cenomani, Livy to the Libui, Pliny to the Euganei; today it is reckoned in the Marke Tarvisine. It has a thin air. Not unlike Basel of the Helvetians in its nature, situation and beauty of buildings, it is noble. It lies on level ground, facing south, east and west, turned toward the winter sun, with the land rising gently to the north, and its hills forming almost the shape of a theatre. The Athesis river does not so much divide it as fortify it and surround it on every side. Silius, book VIII:

units.la: Tum Verona Athesi circumflua & undique solers.
units.tr: Then Verona, encircled by the Adige and clever on every side.

units.la: Mille Antiquitatum vestigia veterem testantur Urbis magnificentiam & divitias. Vias habet rectas & amplas, coctili stratas lapide; Templa circiter xxxv, quorum præcipua pervetusta Ædes Cathedralis, & D. Anastasij; Monasteria Monachorum & Monialium x; Pontes quatuor insignes, fluvio impositos. In summo clivo duæ sunt Arces nobilissimæ, D. Petri, & S. Felicis, quarum illa Athesi pene incubat, ab Cane Scaligero excitata; hæc eminentiore loco & quasi Vallis supercilio sedens Urbis mœnia despectat, & longe latèque in circum-Padanos Agros, totamque fere Cis-Alpinam Galliam pandit prospectum. Sunt item aliæ Arces; Castellum Vetus, & quæ vulgo Citadella. Amphitheatrum ibi visitur, omnium maximum, & quo nullum fere integrius; media Urbe adsurgens: de quo plene & accurate Taurellus Sarayna, Iustus Lipsius, Franciscus Schottus, & alij. Civitas hæc Episcopatus gaudet dignitate. Ortu gloriatur Antistitum xxxvii, qui Sanctorum numero adscripti: in quis D. Zeno, Scriptis etiam clarus; & Petrus, Martyr, cujus Vitam ad posteros transmisit Ioannes Antonius Flaminius. Incolæ magnifici, splendidi, jucundo adspectu, ingenij summi, maximeque ad litteras idonei. Genuit Verona Catullum & Aemilium Macrum Poetas, Plinios, Cornelium Nepotem. De Catullo Martialis: Tantum parva suo debet Verona Catullo; Quantum magna suo Mantua Virgilio.
units.tr: Countless traces of antiquity bear witness to the city's old magnificence and wealth. It has straight, broad streets paved with baked stone. There are about thirty-five churches, the most notable being the very ancient Cathedral and the church of St Anastasius. There are ten monasteries of monks and nuns, and four notable bridges spanning the river. On the highest slope stand two most noble citadels, that of St Peter and that of St Felix. The first almost overhangs the Adige; it was built by Cangrande della Scala. The second, set on higher ground, as it were on the brow of the valley, looks down on the city walls and commands a wide view over the surrounding Po plain and almost the whole of Cisalpine Gaul. There are also other citadels: the Castello Vecchio, and what is commonly called the Citadella. There is an amphitheatre there, the largest of all and one of the best preserved, rising in the middle of the city. It has been described fully and accurately by Taurellus Sarayna, Justus Lipsius, Franciscus Schottus and others. The city enjoys the dignity of an episcopal see. It boasts thirty-seven bishops born there who have been counted among the saints, among them St Zeno, also famous for his writings, and Peter the Martyr, whose life was handed down to posterity by Giovanni Antonio Flaminio. The inhabitants are magnificent, splendid, pleasant in appearance, of the highest talent, and especially fitted for literature. Verona produced the poets Catullus and Aemilius Macer, the Plinies, and Cornelius Nepos. Of Catullus, Martial says: Verona owes as little to her Catullus as great Mantua owes to her Virgil.

units.la: De eodem Plinio que Eobanus Hessus: Magna tuo salve maior Verona Catullo Plinius hic cunas unus & alter habet.
units.tr: Of the same Pliny, Eobanus Hessus says: Hail, Verona, greater than great through your Catullus; here Pliny, one and another, has his cradle.

units.la: Maiorem tamen Plinium Novocomenses sibi vindicant. Macram laudat Ovidius: Saepe suas volucres legit mihi grandior ævo Quaeque nocet serpens, quaeque iuvat herba Macer, &c. Veronensis etiam fuit M. Vitruvius, nobilis Architecturæ Scriptor. Natalem quoque locum Veronam agnoscunt, Theologi: Petrus Scaliger, Episcopus, cujus præter alia leguntur Euangelistam Matthæum commentaria: Rachelius, item Vibis Antistes: Leonardus, ex Novarula familia, multis functus honoribus, variarumque doctus linguarum: Ludovicus, Franciscus, Alexander, fratres, ejusdem familiæ: Celsus Maphæus, qui difficilem illam & elegantem Quæstionem typis editam disputavit, Vllane Resp. sine peccato Iudæos recipere queat gratia sa noris exercendi, & an Pontifex Maximus Permittere, ut id sat, sine peccato possit: Iurisconsulti: Joannes Madius, Iacobi 1 & 11 Lazarioli: Bartholomæus Cepolla, qui Cautelas concinnavit: Christophorus Lanfranchinus: Taurellus Sarayna, qui Veronam patriam descripsit, ejusque origines, amplitudinem, imperium, antiqua monimenta, aliaque, quatuor peculiaribus libris: Medici: Hieronymus Franciscus: Ioannes Baptista Montanus: Hieronymus ex Familia Turria. His omnibus adcenscendi, Guarinus, inter primos Latinæ linguæ Instauratores locandus: Matthæus Bossius, Domitius Calderinus, Antonius Pantheus, Hieronymus Veritatius, Adamus Fumanus, Marcus Medices, Rechus Cataneus: plerique editis ab se monimentis celebres. Nec defuerunt omni memoria præstantes, bello Duces: inter quos Petrus Vernius, ejusque Filii Lodovicus & Iacobus: Ludovicus II ex eadem gente, cujus crebram historia facium mentionem: Antonius, ex nobili Amilioni Familia: Georgius Catallus: Bartholomæus San-Sebastianus: Paullus Luciasius: & alij. Nobilibus superbit Familijs Marchionum Malaspinarum: Ccmitum San-Lonsfaiorum, Sarezorum, Pompeiorum, Iusiorum, Berriaquarum, Novarulerum: item gentibus, quæ vernaculo idiomate Pellegrini, Medici, Marcobruni, Monti, Mafei, Negani, Redofi, Turchi, Dionysii, Minisihalibi, Curi, Guagnini, Spolverini, Saibanti, Alberti, Guarienti, Cartolari, Cioni, Ciulani; alijque. Conuidisse feruntur Tusci, apud alios (in quis principis loci Livius lib. v & Tregus, Galli Ceromani, in Italiam Brenno Duce transgressi: quibus ejectis, in t de diu fuit & potestate Romanorum: quorum auspicijs Coloniam eo duxit Cn. Pompeius Strabo, Magni Pater, uti probat cum alijs argumentis, tum sequentibus Panegyrico ad Constantem Imperatorem verbis Onuphrius Panninius: Pugnacissimo praefecto ut quam Coloniam Cn. Pompeius aliquando deduxerat, Pompeianus everteret, omiserabilem Veronensium calamitatem: item Taciti in Historijs: Quæsitum inde, quæ sedes bello legeretur; Verona potior visa patentibus circum campus ad pugnam equestrem, qua præ aliebant: simul Coloniam copijs validam auferre Vitellio in rem famamque videbatur. Fo pertinet Inscriptio, quæ in Arcu antiquo, pro Vrbis porta aliquando usurpata, hodieque Porta Burfarea vulgodicta: quæque docet Veronam ab Aurelio Licinio Gallieno Imperatore restitutam, & ab eo nomen accepisse Colonia Augusta Nova Gallieniana:
units.tr: Yet the Novocomenses claim the elder Pliny for themselves. Ovid praises Macer: Often the older Macer read me his birds, and which serpent harms and which herb helps, etc. Marcus Vitruvius, the famous writer on architecture, was also a native of Verona. Theologians too acknowledge Verona as their birthplace: Pietro Scaligero, bishop, whose commentaries on the Gospel of Matthew, among other works, are read; Rachelius, likewise bishop of Vibo; Leonardo, of the Novarola family, who held many offices and was learned in several languages; Ludovico, Francesco and Alessandro, brothers of the same family; Celso Mafeo, who disputed in print that difficult and elegant question, whether the civil government may admit Jews to the freedom of practising their religion without sin, and whether the Supreme Pontiff can permit this without sin. Jurists: Giovanni Madio, Giacomo Lazarioli (I and II), Bartolomeo Cepolla, who compiled the Cautelae, Cristoforo Lanfranchini, and Taurellus Sarayna, who described his native Verona, its origins, extent, government, ancient monuments and other matters in four separate books. Physicians: Girolamo Francesco, Giovanni Battista Montano, and Girolamo of the Torre family. To all these must be added Guarino, to be placed among the first restorers of the Latin language; Matteo Bossi, Domizio Calderini, Antonio Panteo, Girolamo Verità, Adamo Fumani, Marco Medici, Recco Catanei, most of them famous for the monuments they published. Nor were there lacking military leaders who excelled in every age: among them Pietro Verni and his sons Lodovico and Giacomo; Lodovico II of the same family, whose frequent mention is made in the histories; Antonio, of the noble Emilioni family; Giorgio Catallo; Bartolomeo San-Sebastiano; Paolo Luciasio; and others. Verona takes pride in the noble families of the Marquises Malaspina, and the Counts San-Lonsfaiorum, Sarezzo, Pompei, Iusii, Berriaqua and Novarola; also in the families which in the vernacular are called Pellegrini, Medici, Marcobruni, Monti, Mafei, Negani, Redofi, Turchi, Dionisi, Minisinalchi, Curi, Guagnini, Spolverini, Saibanti, Alberti, Guarienti, Cartolari, Cioni, Ciulani, and others. The Tuscans are said to have founded it, and among other authorities, Livy in book v and Trogus, have it that the Gauls of Cenomani, under their leader Brennus, crossed into Italy; after they were driven out, the place was for a long time under the power and authority of the Romans, under whose auspices Gnaeus Pompeius Strabo, father of the Great Pompey, led a colony there. This he proves by other arguments and by the following words of Onofrio Panvinio in his panegyric to the Emperor Constans: so that the most warlike prefect, Pompeianus, might overthrow the colony which Gnaeus Pompeius had once founded, the pitiable calamity of the Veronese. Likewise Tacitus in the Histories: It was then asked which seat should be chosen for the war; Verona seemed the better, with its open plains around for cavalry battle, where they were pressing; at the same time it seemed to Vitellius a matter of advantage and reputation to seize the colony, strong in troops. To the same point belongs the inscription on the ancient arch, once used as a gate of the city and still commonly called the Porta Borsari, which teaches that Verona was restored by the Emperor Aurelius Licinius Gallienus and took from him the name Colonia Augusta Nova Gallieniana:

units.la: COLONIA. AVGVSTA. VERONA. NOVA. GALLIENIANA. VALERIANO. II. ET. LICINIO. CONS. MVRI. VERONINSIVM. FABRICATI. EX. DIE. III. NON. APRILIVM DEDICATI. FR. NON. DECEMBRIS. IVBENTE. SANCTISSIMO. GALLIENO. AVG. N. INSISTENTE. AVR. MARCELLINO. V. P. DVC. DVC. CVRANTE. LIV. MARCELLINO
units.tr: COLONY. AUGUSTA. VERONA. NEW. GALLIENIAN. IN THE CONSULSHIP OF VALERIAN II AND LICINIUS. THE WALLS OF THE VERONESE WERE BUILT AND DEDICATED ON THE THIRD DAY BEFORE THE NONES OF APRIL. COMPLETED ON THE FOURTH DAY BEFORE THE NONES OF DECEMBER, BY ORDER OF THE MOST HOLY EMPEROR GALLIENUS AUGUSTUS, WITH AURELIUS MARCELLINUS, MOST EXCELLENT, PRESSING ON, AND LIVIUS MARCELLINUS, DUKE, DUKE, OVERSEEING.

units.la: Ab Attila, Hunnorum Rege, post vastata, varijs inde subdita fuit Tyrannis, quotum agmen duxerunt facile Gothorum Reges: hos expulerunt Langbardi Langbardos, Karolo Magno Duce, Franci: post quos, Berengarys ab Othone I Imperatore Italia ejectis, sui juris facta quietem aliquandiu habuit sub auctoritate fideque Romani Imperij. Per vim adeptus Aćtiolinus Romaninus Præfecturam in Dominatum convertit, exacto Azone Atestino, quem S. P. Q. Verone Prætorem designarat. Eo defuncto circa annum cio cc lix communibus Civium suffragijs Scaligeri magistratum gesserunt cum titulo Vicariorum & Principum, annos propemodum cxxviii: quibus exturbatis partim, partim veneno necatis, suæ ditionis fecerunt Galeatij, inde Carrarienses. Hos exterminarunt Veneti, in quorum etiamnum potestate constanter & tranquille perseverat. Videndi Paullus Diaconus lib. xv Histor. ad Eutropium, & 11. Hist. Langbard. Blondus, Sabellicus, Merula, Taurellus Sarayna, Corius, Leander Albertus, & alij. Addam Elogium, quod in Vrbis Porta munitissima. VERONA. NON. MINUS. NOBILIS. QVAM. ANTIQVA. CIVITAS. AC. PRISCÆ. VIRTVTIS. MEMOR. VENETÆ. REIP. BENEFICIO. NON. SOLVM MVROS. TEMPORIS. CORRVPTOS. INIVRIA. IN. MELIVS RESTITVIT.SED EA.QVOQVE SIBI. TEMPLORVM. VIARVM. PONTIVM. AC. PORTARVM. ORNAMENTA ADIECIT. VT. PVBLICORVM. ÆDIFICIORVM. MAGNIFICENTIA. NVLLI. VRBIVM. POSTPONENDA VIDEATVR.TANTVM. ILLI PROFVIT. BONORVM.PRINCIPVM. TVTELA. AC. FAVOR.
units.tr: After being laid waste by Attila, King of the Huns, it was then subjected to various tyrannies, of which the Kings of the Goths easily led the line. The Lombards expelled these, and then the Franks, under Charlemagne as leader, drove out the Lombards. After them, when Berengar had been expelled from Italy by the Emperor Otto I, the city, made subject to its own right, enjoyed quiet for some time under the authority and faith of the Roman Empire. Acciolino Romanino, having obtained the prefecture by force, turned it into a lordship, Azzo d'Este, whom the Senate and People of Verona had appointed praetor, having been expelled. After his death, about the year 1259, the Scaligers held office by the common votes of the citizens with the title of Vicars and Princes, for almost 128 years. When they were partly driven out and partly poisoned, the Galeazzi made it their own domain, and after them the Carraresi. These were driven out by the Venetians, under whose power it still remains, constantly and peacefully. See Paul the Deacon, book xv of the History, to Eutropius, and book ii of the History of the Lombards; Biondo, Sabellico, Merula, Taurellus Sarayna, Corio, Leandro Alberti, and others. I will add the inscription which is on the most fortified gate of the city: VERONA, NOT LESS NOBLE THAN AN ANCIENT CITY, AND MINDFUL OF ITS EARLY VIRTUE, BY THE BENEFIT OF THE VENETIAN REPUBLIC, HAS NOT ONLY RESTORED ITS WALLS, CORRUPTED BY TIME AND INJURY, FOR THE BETTER, BUT HAS ALSO ADDED TO THEM THE ORNAMENTS OF TEMPLES, STREETS, BRIDGES AND GATES, SO THAT IT MAY SEEM NOT TO BE INFERIOR TO ANY CITY IN THE MAGNIFICENCE OF ITS PUBLIC BUILDINGS. IT GAINED ONLY THIS PROTECTION AND FAVOUR OF GOOD PRINCES.

units.la: Ager Vrbi circumiectus optimus est: tritico, oleo, vino, pecoribus, vellerum item preciosorum, ceterarumque frugum copia abundans; nobilissimas etiam habens lapidicinas, item flumina, flagna, lacus, in quis Benacus omnium amoenissimus: praeterea insignes salubrium aquarum scaturigines, lectissimos medicinalium herbarum thesauros praecipue in monte Baldo, quibus legendis undique eo confluit Æsculapii proles. Territorium Veronense longitudo, quae à Bruchelio Opido sumitur Rivam usque in ultimo Benaci recessu positam, lxv est milliarium: latitudo ab Turre Confinium Rivoltellam usque xl. Inter Veronam Hostiliamque Campi sunt Veronenses spatio xx milliar. multorum victoriis nobilitati: de quibus Franciscus Schottus Itinerarij libro i circa Vrbem ad quartumque lapidem Tractus visitur, qui vulgo Campagna di Verona, incultus & saxis horrens. Veronensium Agris anteaquam excedam, coronidis loco Scaligerorum Patris Filijque hic adponam de sua Verona versus:
units.tr: The land surrounding the city is excellent: it abounds in wheat, oil, wine, sheep, a supply of valuable wool, and other crops; it also has most noble quarries of stone, and rivers, pools and lakes, among which Benaco is the most pleasant of all. Besides these, it has notable springs of healthful waters, and very choice storehouses of medicinal herbs, especially on Mount Baldo, to which the offspring of Aesculapius flock from every side to gather them. The length of the Veronese territory, measured from the town of Bruchelio to Riva, which lies at the far end of Lake Benaco, is sixty-five miles; its breadth, from the tower of Confini to Rivoltella, is forty. Between Verona and Ostiglia are the Veronese fields, twenty miles in extent, made famous by many victories; of these Franciscus Schottus, in book i of his Itinerary, speaks. Near the city, at the fourth milestone, lies the tract commonly called the Campagna di Verona, uncultivated and bristling with rocks. Before I leave the Veronese fields, I will set here, by way of a crown, verses on his own Verona by Julius Caesar Scaliger, father and son:

units.la: Iulij Cæsaris Scaligeri:
units.tr: Julius Caesar Scaliger:

units.la: Italia canimus semper-florentis ocellum. Calliope neque ai grandius ulla loqui. Auctá deis, auctura pòs Verona Quirites: Quot cives, tot habens sidera digna Iove. Non animi, non ingeny vigor acrior usquam: Nulla creat plures Martia terra Duces. Trans ferre in cælum voluit sibi Iupiter: atqui Clarior in nostris maluit esse locis.
units.tr: We sing of Italy's ever-flowering jewel; Calliope herself could sing nothing greater. Verona, increased by the gods, will be greater still for the Romans of the future. She has as many citizens as there are stars worthy of Jove. Nowhere is there a keener vigour of mind or genius; the Martian land produces more leaders than any other. Jupiter wished to carry her up to heaven for himself, but she preferred to shine more brightly in our own land.

units.la: Iosephi Scaligeri, Iul. Cæs. F.
units.tr: Joseph Scaliger, son of Julius Caesar:

units.la: Ocelle Mundi, sidus Itali cæli, Flos urbium, flos, corculumque amœnarum: Quot sunt, erunt ve, quot fuere, Verona: Brenni smaragde, Transpadane beryllæ, Gallorum ispis, margarita Benaci, Apex supremus elegantia rerum, Et meta summa, Dædalaque natura. Quam fronte prona fatibus iuc sumissis Vrbes adorent: & libenter agnoscant Sublime maiestatis ardua lumen: Nisi orba lucis viveres, salutisque, Iniuriosa servitute prædonum. O Diva, nam quæ vorticosa tempestas Quis turbo? quæ effluantis aura fortuna Te mutat alium, quive casus affligit? Quæ tristis, exspes, sessa lucis, atrata, Squallentis obsoleta sordibus luctus Mæres, ut orba, quaeflet unicum mater? Reginatot rerum, & tot urbium princeps, Vbi tuorum est lux vetusta sceptorum? Et aureo splendore fulta maiestas? Totoque maior orbe, par polo fastus? Illiqué magni gloria tua fasces? Vbi Quirites heu tui, sus cives, Delecta pubes, flosculus iuventutis? Vbi divi alumni principes, Iovis semen? Proceres beati: debitum genus cælo? Fulmen duelli: terror Adriæ magni: Opum hostilium Martiale tormentum: Tutelo patriæ, spes labantium rerum; Pacis sequestri: civibusque devoti, Scaligera soboles: qui Feretrium tantis Tot olim opimis, teque, Diva, mactarunt: Quis tot triumphos, tot trophæa, tot laurus? Quis sceptri honores, atque nomen Augusta Accepta debes: queque mole sublimi Educta Mausolæa provocant cælum? Proh fortem acerbam, proh volubilem casum; Quanta è supremo culmine è statu rerum Quanta excidisti? non tibi obfuit tantum (Nec posse credam) nauta lapidis ripæ: Quantum una, sudos quæ tibi dies, quaeque Fortuna præter propter invidet lucem. Ast o venusta mater o parens salve, O mea creatrix: vosque rite maiorum Salvete manes. Ille ego nepos vester, Pila, atque lusus, ludicrumque fortunæ Currens parentis exulis cursum: Pro farre salso, proque adoreo libo, Vt, quam ruina me superstitem vestra Pro ture, proque februo parentali, Par est dolere, tam ne later, ut resto Hic vos saluto latus. Este felices, E messe tanta semen: e procellisque, Pioque, manes o, nepote gaudete. Tanta domus tabella, naufragi tanti.
units.tr: O jewel of the world, star of the Italian sky, flower of cities, little heart of pleasant places! As many as there are, or will be, or have been, Verona: emerald of Brennus, beryl of Transpadana, pearl of the Gauls, pearl of Benacus, highest peak of elegance and utmost limit of things, a work of Daedalian nature. With bowed brow and lowered rods, let the cities worship you, and gladly acknowledge the lofty light of your sublime majesty, unless you, bereft of light and safety, lived under the injurious slavery of plunderers. O goddess, what whirlwind, what storm of fortune, what blast has changed you into another, or what fall has struck you? Why do you mourn, sad, hopeless, sitting in the dark, clad in black, grieving in squalid and faded filth, as a mother weeps for her only child, bereft? Queen of so many things and princess of so many cities, where is the ancient light of your sceptres, and the majesty supported by golden splendour? Greater than the whole world, and proud as the equal of the sky, where is your glory, your fasces of great power? Where, alas, are your citizens, your chosen youth, the flower of your young men? Where are your divine sons, the princes, seed of Jove? Your noble nobles, a race owed to heaven? The thunderbolt of war, the terror of the great Adriatic, the martial engine against hostile wealth, the guardian of the homeland, the hope of falling affairs, the mediator of peace, and the devoted Scaligeran offspring, who once sacrificed to Feretrius, and to you, goddess, with such rich offerings? Who gave you so many triumphs, trophies and laurels, the honours of the sceptre, and the august name you received? And who raised the Mausoleums with lofty mass that challenge heaven? Alas, bitter fate, fickle fall! From what supreme height and state of affairs have you fallen! Not as much harm came to you from the sailor's stone on the shore (I would not believe it could) as from the one day that envied you the light, and the fortune that, near enough, grudges you the light. But O lovely mother, O parent, hail, O my creator; and hail, you spirits of my ancestors, rightly honoured. I am your grandson, the ball and toy and plaything of fortune, running the course of an exiled parent. Instead of salted spelt, and instead of the sacrificial cake, and instead of the incense and the February parental offering, it is right that I grieve, lest I be hidden, so that I greet you here from the side. Be happy, you who are the seed of so great a harvest; and rejoice, O spirits, in your grandson, out of storms and so great a shipwreck, a tablet of so great a house.

units.la: Supra Veronam, secundum Athesin procedenti, læva Pontanum se offert Opidum, altiusque Barcum & Catenum: nec procul inde Motium, & Ignatium, Formicarium: & ad Athesis fontem, Lanium.
units.tr: Upward from Verona, proceeding along the Adige, on the left Pontano presents itself as a town, and higher up Barco and Cateno; not far from there Motio, Ignatio and Formicario; and at the source of the Adige, Lanio.

units.la: Locis, quæ ripæ Athesis sinistræ adsident, obiter perlustratis, veniendum ad ea, quæ dextræ. Initium sit ab Ostio, quo Hadriatico se miscet Pelago fluvius: ubi Turris Nova, contra vectigalium fraudatores ædificata: hinc sursum cunti occurrunt quæ vernacule Capo di Basttono, Rocca di Campo Nuovo, La Torre Marchesana: altius Athesis dextra, Castel Baldo; succedente mox Opido non ignobili Portu, cum Vico pulcerrimo Cereta (læva inde Avella, Castroque D. Bonifacy: ulterius Villa Nova, Porcitia, Verona, quam paulo ante delineavi.
units.tr: Having briefly surveyed the places that lie along the left bank of the Adige, we must come to those on the right. Let us begin at the mouth, where the river joins the Adriatic Sea: there stands Torre Nuova, built against those who defraud the customs. From here, going upward, one meets places commonly called Capo di Bastone, Rocca di Campo Nuovo and La Torre Marchesana; higher up on the right bank of the Adige, Castel Baldo; and soon after, the not undistinguished town of Porto, with the most beautiful village of Cereta (on the left from there, Avella and the castle of St Boniface); further on, Villanova, Porcile and Verona, which I have already described.

units.la: Supra Veronam dextra Pelusium est; mox Licena, Poveredo, Latinis Roboretum, Petra, Bisino.
units.tr: Above Verona on the right is Peluso; soon Lisena, Povedero, called Roboretum in Latin, Petra, and Bisino.

units.la: Sequitur ulterius Tridentum; Italiæ ab Septemtrionalioribus Ianua. Tridentum Trogo lib. xx, Antonino, alijsque dicitur, quo Τρίδεντα Phlegonti & Ptolemæo, in Cenomanis locanti, uti & in Inscriptione, quam supra posui. cap. xxiv, quo Umbria explicatur, nisi quis velit in Auferendi casu ibi usurpatum, ab Recto Tridens. Vernacule Trento; Germanis Trient. Hinc Tridentini Plinio, in Mediterraneo Regionis x eos numeranti; Τριδεντινοί, Straboni. Tridentina Regionis meminit Cassiodorus lib. v Variar. ad Feltrinos. Dictum quidam volunt ab Tridente Neptuni, cui quondam Urbs sacra: vel à Tribus Torrentibus, Ferfina, Salero, & Persio (qui mihi anno cIↄ Iↄ LXXX, mense Septembri, quum hæc loca peragrarem, fere fuit fatalis) ad Urbem hanc in Athesin confluentibus; vel denique à tribus Alpium cacuminibus, quæ altissima, trium dentium instar, Urbi imminent. Inter editos situm est montes, in planicie fertili & peramœna; in extrema Italiæ ora Germaniam versus: Athesi ab Occidente, torrentibusque, quos dixi, qua Oriens, circumflua. Urbs est parva quidem; sed nobilis, opulenta, populo frequens, muris vallata lapideis, vias habens latas: ædes supra magnitudinem magnificas, Arcem conspicuam, beneque munitam, cum Palatio Itupendo & Viridario perpulcro. Incolæ Itali partim, partim Germani, sermone moribusque sunt diversi, plerique tamen bilingues: homani, placidisque moribus. Ab Tuscis primum condita, vel, ut Trogus adscrit, ab Gallis Cenomanis, diu sub ditione fuit Populi Romani; inde ab Gothis vexata multoque annos possessa, quibus Italia emotis, in Langbardorum, hisque victis, in Cæsarum fuit potestata. Anno denique cIↄ cccLxxvii ab Wencaslao Pontifici Romano donata, Præsulum suorum hactenus habita fuit imperio. Videndi Platina in Gelasio, Blondus lib.ix, Corius, alij. De gestis Ducum Tridentinorum scripsit Pyrrhus Mantuanus. Concilio celebris est Oecumenico, quod cæptum anno cIↄ Iↄ xlvi, finem hic habuit decimo septimo post anno. Illustrarunt Urbem præter alios Cardinales duo, Hugo Candidus, & Bernardus Clesius. Laceratus hic avorum memoria anno cIↄ ccc lxxv ab Iudæis Simon, Christianus Puer, duos natus annos, coriarij cujusdam filius. Describunt Urbem præter Leandrum Albertum aliosque, Ioannes Poncio, Andreas Vegas, & Paullus Gerardinus. Ager vini generosi feracissimus. Antoninus ab Opitergio iter ducit Tridentum usque per M. P. CX.
units.tr: Next further on is Trident, the gateway of Italy from the more northerly regions. Tridentum is so called by Trogus (book 20), by Antoninus and others; Phlegon and Ptolemy, who place it among the Cenomani, call it Τρίδεντα, as also in the inscription I set out above in chapter 24, where Umbria is explained, unless one prefers to think that the word used there is in the ablative case, from the nominative Tridens. In the vernacular it is Trento; in German, Trient. Hence Pliny calls its people Tridentini, when he counts them among the inland peoples of the tenth region; Strabo calls them Τριδεντινοί. Cassiodorus, in book 5 of the Variae, to the Feltrini, mentions the Tridentine region. Some hold that the name derives from the trident of Neptune, to whom the city was once sacred; or from the three torrents, the Fersina, the Salère and the Pèrsen (which, when I was travelling through these places in September 1580, was nearly fatal to me), flowing together into the Adige near this city; or finally from the three peaks of the Alps, the highest, which overhang the city like three teeth. The city lies among hills, on a fertile and very pleasant plain, at the extreme edge of Italy towards Germany: it is surrounded by the Adige on the west and by the torrents I have mentioned on the east. The city is indeed small, but noble, wealthy, full of people, surrounded by stone walls, with wide streets; its buildings are magnificent beyond their size, and it has a conspicuous and well-fortified citadel, together with a stupendous palace and a most beautiful garden. Its inhabitants are partly Italian and partly German, differing in speech and customs, though most are bilingual; they are humane and of gentle manners. Founded first by the Etruscans, or, as Trogus records, by the Gallic Cenomani, it was long under the rule of the Roman People; then it was harassed and long held by the Goths, and when the Goths were driven out of Italy, it came under the power of the Lombards, and when they were defeated, under that of the Caesars. Finally, in the year 1377, it was given to the Roman Pontiff by Wenceslaus, and until now has been governed by its own bishops. On it see Platina in the life of Gelasius, Blondus book 9, Corio and others. The deeds of the Dukes of Trent were written by Pyrrhus Mantuanus. The city is famous for the Ecumenical Council, which began in 1546 and ended here seventeen years later. Besides others, two cardinals have adorned the city, Hugo Candidus and Bernard Clesius. Here, in the year 1475, within living memory, a Christian boy named Simon, two years old and the son of a certain tanner, was torn to pieces by the Jews. Besides Leandro Alberti and others, Giovanni Poncio, Andrea Vega and Paolo Gerardini have described the city. The surrounding land is extremely fertile in fine wine. Antoninus gives the road from Opitergium to Trent as 110 Roman miles.

units.la: Extra Tridentum versus Septemtrionem fluvius est paullo ante memoratus Ferfena; ad quem quæ vernacule Secozzano, Parchiafo, Vefo, Canazzo. Est & aliud juxta flumen, in cujus dextra Valese, Fespergo, & Guidono; lœva vero Chiusa, Septum Latinis; & haud procul inde nobile Opidum Colzano, quod Banzanum Blondo libro xi Histor. & Haliæ Capreolo Histor, Brix. libro iv. Opidum frequens, mercatu nobile annuo; ad Sarcam, Athesis incolam, situm. Ulterius Casa Nova est, & altius Maranum Italiæ quidem, sed Germanis habitatum.
units.tr: Beyond Trent to the north is the river Fersina, mentioned a little earlier; near it lie places commonly called Secozzano, Parchiafo, Vefo and Canazzo. There is also another place beside the river: on its right Valsugana, Fèsperga and Guidono; on its left, Chiusa, called Septum in Latin; and not far from there the noble town of Colzano, which Blondus in book 11 of his histories calls Banzanum, and Capreolus in book 4 of his History of Brescia calls Italian. It is a populous town, noted for its annual fair, situated on the Sarca, a tributary of the Adige. Further on is Casa Nuova, and higher up Marano, which is indeed Italian but inhabited by Germans.

units.la: Hactenus quæ utrique Athesis ripæ consident, indicavi, regressus per eumdem amnem Volturnum versus, reliqua dabo. In Leneri, qui ad Castellum Baldi petit Athetit Athesin, læva, sursum, non temnendum est Opidum Colonia; inde Alons Bellus, frequens Castrum; Guidonis, Episcopi Ferrariensis natalibus clarum: ad fontem Amnis Brendulum jacet: nec procul inde ad fluminis dextram Leonicum adparet, multis Italiæ non ædens; Nicolas & Omniboni patria, qui monumentis suis posteritati inclaruerunt.
units.tr: So far I have described the places lying on both banks of the Adige. Returning along the same river towards the Po, I shall now give the rest. On the left, on the Lenro, which runs towards the Adige at Castel Baldo, upward, stands the town of Colonia, not to be despised; from there Alone Bello, a populous castle, famous as the birthplace of Guido, bishop of Ferrara; near the source of the river Brenta lies Brendulum; and not far from there, on the right bank of the river, Leonico appears, not unknown to many in Italy; it was the homeland of Nicolò and Omnibono, who made themselves famous to posterity by their writings.

units.la: Succedit Atefte. Sic Tacito in Historiis, Plinio lib. iii nat. Hist. cap. xix, Coloniam facienti Romanorum, Antonino, apud quem Miliar. numerus inemendatior, dicitur. Atrès Ptolemæo: quæ Atefta Inscriptioni Romanæ, in Vinea Cardinalis Carpentis in Monte Quirinali: L. CASSIVS. L. F ROM. NIGER DOMO. ATESTE MILES. COH. I. PR MILITAVIT. ANN. XVII VIXIT. ANN. XXXVII
units.tr: Next comes Ateste. So it is called by Tacitus in the Histories, by Pliny in book 3 of the Natural History, chapter 19, where it is said to be a Roman colony, and by Antoninus, in whose text the milestone figure is less accurate. Ptolemy calls it Atrès. The name Ateste also appears in a Roman inscription in the vineyard of Cardinal Carpentis on the Quirinal Hill: Lucius Cassius Niger, son of Lucius, of the Romilian tribe, of Ateste, served as a soldier in the first praetorian cohort for seventeen years; he lived thirty-seven years.

units.la: Hodie vulgo Este vocatur. Incolæ Atefini, quos controversum aliquando de Finibus cum Vicentinis habuisse, indicat Lapis in Agro Veronensi, apud Villam, quæ Latiis nominatur, Leonicum, cujus supra meminì, versus: SEX. ATILIVS. M. F. SERRANVS PRO. COS. EX. S. C INTER ATESTINOS ET VICENTINOS FINIS, TERMINOSQVE STATVI IVSSIT.
units.tr: Today it is commonly called Este. That the people of Ateste once had a dispute over boundaries with the Vicentines is shown by a stone in the Veronese territory, near the villa called Latiis by Leonicus, whom I mentioned above. Its inscription reads: "Sextus Atilius Serranus, son of Marcus, proconsul, by decree of the Senate, ordered the boundary and limits between the Atestines and the Vicentines to be fixed."

units.la: Subversum anno MCCCXLVII ab Actiolino Romanino, pulso Actio, loci Marchione scribunt Corius parten & Leander Albertus in Marka Tarvilina. Origo hinc Atestina familia.
units.tr: It was destroyed in 1347 by Actiolinus Romaninus, who drove out Actius, the lord of the place, write Corius and Leander Albertus in his Marca Tarvisina. From this came the Atestine family.

units.la: Non procul Atefte Opidum visitur, quod vernacule Monselice, Latinis Mons Silicis: Acelum Plinio; Aslum Paullo Diacono; Αχαδον Ptolemæo; cui reponendum Αχαλον, nonnulli arbitrantur. Excisum ab Langbardis cum Patavio, scribunt Paullus Diaconus libro iiii. Histor. Langbard. & Blondus libro viii. Histor Azonem Atestinum anno CIO.CLVI Aethelano Romanino creptum Pontificis Legato tradidisse; annoque CIO CCCXVIII Canem Magnum Scaligerum occupasse, priusque Montem Divisiarum fuisse nuncupatum, memoriæ produnt idem Blondus lib. xviii Histor. & Corius Parte ii & iii. Inde anno CIO CCC XXXVI in Venetorum venit potestatem quibus paruit usque ad annum CIO CIX. Eo cum aliis in Maximiliani Imp. ditionem reductum, tandem anno CIO CXVII ad Venetos redijt.
units.tr: Not far from Ateste stands a town which in the vernacular is called Monselice and in Latin Mons Silicis. Plinius calls it Acelum; Paulus Diaconus, Aslum; Ptolemy, Αχαδον [Achadon], which some think should be corrected to Αχαλον [Achalon]. It was razed by the Lombards along with Padua, as Paulus Diaconus writes in book 4 of his History of the Lombards, and Blondus in book 8 of his History. Blondus also records in book 18 of his History, and Corius in parts 2 and 3, that in 1156 Azo of Ateste took it from Aethelanus the Roman and handed it over to the papal legate, and that in 1318 Can Grande della Scala seized it; before this it had been called Mons Divisiarum. From there in 1336 it came under the power of the Venetians, whom it obeyed until 1409. Then, along with others, it was brought under the rule of the Emperor Maximilian, and at last in 1517 it returned to the Venetians.

units.la: Occurrunt inde Roborētes, vulgo Rovere; moxque Montaniana; tantæ frequentiæ, ut Civitas potius sit, quam Opidum, ortu superbiens Bartholomæi Montaniana, præstantissimi Philosophi & Medici, quod libri ab ipso editi, cum primis, qui de Infirmitatibus & Balneis abunde testantur.
units.tr: From there one comes to Roborētes, commonly Rovere, and soon after to Montagnana, a place of such crowds that it is more a city than a town. It takes pride in its birth of Bartolomeo Montagnana, a most distinguished philosopher and physician, as the books he published, especially those on diseases and baths, abundantly attest.

units.la: Sequitur inde Bacchilio fluvius, de quo alibi. Mille ab eo passibus, sexto supra Vicentiam lapide, Austrum versus, Castellum est Custodia: dictum, quod ibi quondam noxij homines custodiri consueverint in vastis Latumijs ad cædendos ædificijs faciundis lapides. Qua de re legenda apud Leandrum Epistola Ioannis Georgij Trissini, loci adcolæ, harum que rerum curiosi Cosozza vulgo audit.
units.tr: From there the river Bacchiglione follows, about which I shall speak elsewhere. A thousand paces beyond it, six miles above Vicenza toward the south, lies the village of Custodia. It is so called because guilty men were once accustomed to be kept there in the vast stone quarries, to cut stones for building. Concerning this matter one should read Leandro's letter of Giovanni Giorgio Trissino, a native of the place and a curious investigator of such things; the village is called Cosozza in the vernacular.

units.la: Conspiciendam se præbet altius Vicenza. Sic Trogo Pompeio, Tacito libro iv Annalium, aliisque Vicetia Plinio & Antonino: Βιέντια & Βιτητια (variat enim lectio) Æliano; Οικιυζα, Ptolemæo: quæ vulgo Vicenza. Dicta, ut Baptista Palatinus auguratur, vel ob gentis incolæ victoriam, vel ab Villis centum, ex quibus junctis facta fertur Civitas. Sita juxta radices collis, duobus amnibus, qui navigabiles, Rerone & Bachilione inæqualiter divisa. Non usquequaque elegans & magna: sed populosa, rerumque omnium copia abundans. Quatuor ibi notatu digna, Palatium Prætoris magnificum: Pons unius Arcus; Saxum solidum Arae majoris in Eg-
units.tr: Vicenza, which is called Vicetia by Trogus Pompeius, by Tacitus in book 4 of the Annals, and by others, and Vicetia by Pliny and Antoninus, appears more prominently as one approaches it. The Greek forms are Biéntia [Βιέντια] and Bitētia [Βιτητια] (the reading varies) in Aelian, and Oikiyza [Οικιυζα] in Ptolemy. As Baptista Palatinus conjectures, it was named either from the victory of the people who inhabited it or from a hundred villages, which, when joined together, are said to have formed the city. It lies near the foot of a hill, divided unequally by two rivers, the Retrone and the Bacchiglione, both navigable. It is not everywhere elegant or large, but it is populous and abounds in every kind of goods. Four things there are worth noting: the magnificent Praetor's palace; a bridge of a single arch; a solid stone altar of the greater ... in the church of St Lawrence, of astonishing length; and finally the theatre, commonly called L'Accademia. In the same place is the monastery of St Corona, where there is a most beautiful library.

units.la: Incolae. in Ecclesia D. Laurentij, stupendæ longitudinis; Theatrum denique, vulgo L'Accademia. Canobium ibidem D. Coronæ, ubi pulcerrima Bibliotheca. Incolæ, qui Vicentini in memorato paullo ante lapide, ingenijs sunt vividi; ad litteras, militiam, mercaturam promtissimi, sed faciendæ rei perpetuo sudantes: splendide vivunt, honeste vestiuntur. Nobiles habet & antiquas Familias, uti videre est apud eundem Paliarinum libro v & vi. Episcopatus gaudet dignitate. Inlustrarunt hanc Vrbem suo ortu DD. Fortunatus & Felix Martyres; A. Caecina, Consul Romanus, & Vitellij Imper. Legatus, apud Tacitum lib. iii Historiar. Palemon, cuius Eusebius meminit: Ioannes, Ifuardus, Bartholomæus, Vrbis Præsul, Vincentius Colceus, Hieronymus Plegafeta, omnes Prædicatorij Ordinis Monachi; Antonius Lusius, Matheus Bassarius, Georgius Trisinus, Oratores & Poetæ. Ab Tusciis, vel, ut scribit Trogus, ab Gallis condita, sequenti ævo in fide diu stetit Populi Romani, usque ad Attilæ tempora; à quo vastata, post in Gothorum; inde in Langbardorum, postremo in Italiæ Regum fuit potestate. Ijs pulsis, libertate sua sub auctoritate Imperij Romani est usque ad Friderici II Imper. principatum, à quo directa cremataque varios habuit Dominos, Carrarienses Patavinos, Scaligeros Veronenses, Galeatos Mediolanenses, Venetos. Tandem Maximiliani I Imperatoris armis infestata, ejusque fidei subjecta, Venetiis ad extremum est reddita. Consulendi Blondus lib. xvii & seqq. Histor. Corius Parte II, Merula libro iiii Vicecomit. Taurellus Sarayna libro II, Helias Capreolus libro viii. Histor. Brix. Describunt Vrbem Baptista Paliarinus lib. vi, & Zacharias Lilius. Fecit M. Antonius Sabellicus Carmen, quod Vicentinus Crater inscribitur. Ager ipsi ut amoenissimus; ita vini, frugum, aliarumque rerum fertilissimus; præcipue Mororum, quorum frondibus Bombyces alluntur. Haud procul urbe duæ nobiles Lapidicinæ, in Monte, qui Cornelius Larinis, vulgo Covelo.
units.tr: The inhabitants, who are Vicentini in the village of Custodia mentioned a little above, are lively of wit, very ready for letters, soldiering and trade, but always toiling hard at making their fortune; they live splendidly and dress honourably. The city has noble and ancient families, as may be seen in Paliarinus, books 5 and 6. Its bishopric enjoys dignity. This city has been made famous by its natives: Saints Fortunatus and Felix, martyrs; A. Caecina, Roman consul and legate of the Emperor Vitellius, in Tacitus, Histories book 3; Palemon, whom Eusebius mentions; Giovanni, Ifuardus, Bartholomew, bishop of the city; Vincenzo Colceo, Girolamo Plegafeta, all monks of the Order of Preachers; Antonio Lusio, Matteo Bassarus, Giorgio Trissino, orators and poets. Founded by the Tuscans, or, as Trogus writes, by the Gauls, it remained for a long time in the loyalty of the Roman People into the age that followed, until the time of Attila, by whom it was laid waste; afterwards it was under the power of the Goths, then of the Lombards, and lastly of the Kings of Italy. When these were driven out, it remained under the authority of the Roman Empire and kept its freedom until the reign of the Emperor Frederick II, after which, razed and burned, it had various lords: the Carraresi of Padua, the Scaligeri of Verona, the Galeazzi of Milan, and the Venetians. At last, harassed by the arms of the Emperor Maximilian I, and subjected to his allegiance, it was finally surrendered to Venice. On this one should consult Blondus, book 17 ff. of the Histories; Corio, Part II; Merula, book 4 on the Visconti; Taurellus Sarayna, book 2; Elias Capreolus, book 8 of the Brescian Histories. Baptista Paliarinus, book 6, and Zacharias Lilius describe the city. Marcus Antonius Sabellicus wrote a poem, which is entitled Vicentinus Crater. Its territory is most pleasant and very fertile in wine, grain and other produce, especially of mulberry trees, whose leaves feed the silkworms. Not far from the city are two noble stone quarries, on the mountain which is called Cornelius by the Larinates and Covelo in the vernacular.

units.la: Supra Vicentiam Opidum est, quod vernacule Caldoggio, altiusque ad Bachilionis scaturiginem, Portelletto, & Villa Genne, Sabellico libro III Villa Genua.
units.tr: Above Vicenza is a town which in the vernacular is called Caldogno, and higher up, near the source of the Bacchiglione, Portelletto and Villa Genne; Sabellicus, book 3, calls it Villa Genua.

units.la: Succedit tandem explicanda Civitas antiquissima Patavium, flos & decus Vrbium, quascumque tellus Itala continet. Sic autem Livio multis locis, Tacito lib. II & III Histor. Plinio libro III, cap. xviii, Pomponio Melæ lib. II, Solino in Polyhist. Antonino, Itinerariæ Tabulæ, ubi vitiose Patavis, pro Patavio, alijque Παταυίον Straboni lib. V; Παταυιον Ptolemæo & Æliano dicitur: quæ hodie Padua.
units.tr: Next at last comes the most ancient city of Padua, the flower and glory of all the cities that the Italian land contains, which is to be explained. It is thus named by Livy in many places, by Tacitus in books 2 and 3 of the Histories, by Pliny in book 3, chapter 18, by Pomponius Mela in book 2, by Solinus in the Polyhistor, by Antoninus, and in the Itinerary Tables, where Patavis is wrongly given for Patavium; and by others; by Strabo in book 5 it is called Patauion [Παταυίον]; by Ptolemy and Aelian Patauion [Παταυιον]. Today it is Padua.

units.la: Ptolemæo etiam alio loco Βαταδιον nominatur. Nomen natum quidam putant à Padi vel Paludum vicinitate, sicque dictum quasi Padavium. Facius Vbertus lib. III Cant. iiii:
units.tr: Ptolemy also calls it Bataidion [Βαταδιον] in another place. Some think the name arose from the nearness of the Po or of the marshes, and so was called as it were Padavium. Fazio degli Uberti, book 3, canto 4:

units.la: Da Pado, o da Palude prese il nome,Che prasso ne assai questa Cittade:Brenta la cerchia, chiude come un pome.
units.tr: From the Po, or from the marsh, it took its name, for it is near both this city; the Brenta encircles it and closes it like a pomegranate.

units.la: Alij ἀπὸ τῆς νίκης, ab volando, dirivant, quod captato augurio fuerit condita: nonnulli à petendo, quod avem Antenor, Vrbis, ut dicam, conditor, telo petiverit: Incertis omnes conjecturis. Condidisse memoratur Antenor, Troja profugus, apud Virgilium lib. 1 Æneid. cujus versus initio hujus capitis laudavi, Livium libro 1 ab V. C. Pomponium Melam, Solinum in Polyhistore, alios. Legitur de Antenore, quod sequitur, Epitaphium, non magni ævi, in D. Laurentij æde:
units.tr: Others derive the name from flying, from the Greek apo tēs nikēs [ἀπὸ τῆς νίκης], meaning from victory, because it was founded after an augury taken from the flight of birds; some from seeking, because Antenor, the founder of the city, as I shall say, aimed at a bird with a missile. All these are uncertain conjectures. It is recorded that Antenor, a fugitive from Troy, founded it, as in Virgil, Aeneid book 1, whose verse I cited at the beginning of this chapter; also in Livy, book 1, from the foundation of the city, in Pomponius Mela, in Solinus's Polyhistor, and in others. Concerning Antenor, the following epitaph, not of great age, is read in the church of St Lawrence:

units.la: Conditor.
units.tr: The founder.

units.la: Inclitus Antenor, post dirutamœnia Troja,Transtulit huc Henetum Dardaniumque fugas: Expulit Euganeos, Patavinam condidit Vrbem,Quem tegit hic humili marmore casa domus.
units.tr: Illustrious Antenor, after the walls of Troy were razed, brought hither the Heneti and the Dardanian exiles; he drove out the Euganei and founded the city of Padua, which this humble house of marble covers.

units.la: In Porta etiam Portelij hæc leguntur: Hanc antiquissimam Vrbem, literarum omnium t Asylum, cujus agrum fertilitatis sumen natura esse voluit, Antenor condidit, anno ante Christum natum cIↄ cXVIII. Senatus autem Venetus his bello propugnaculis ornavit, anno à Christi adventu cIↄ IↄXVIII. Sita est Vrbs loco fertili & plano; placidissima cœli fruens temperie, summa soli bonitate; Euganeorum Montium amœnitate, Alpium Marisque vicinitate, beatissima. Perfluit eam Brenta amnis, de quo alibi. Ambitus duplex hodie, olim triplex: Exterior sex millia, ducentosque passus continet, cum sex Portis magnificis: Interior tria millia passuum, altissimus, supernè deambulacrum habens perpetuum. Magnifica porro, splendida, rebus omnibus, quæ ad vitam necessariæ, affluens, Silice strata ab Vberto Carrariensi, Duce III, anno cIↄ ccc xl: Fossis, Vallisque, & Propugnaculis undique bene tuta.
units.tr: On the Portello gate these also are read: Antenor founded this most ancient city, the refuge of all letters, whose fertile land nature willed to be most fruitful, in the year 1118 before the birth of Christ. The Venetian Senate adorned it with these bulwarks in war, in the year 1518 after the coming of Christ. The city lies in a fertile and level place, enjoying a most mild climate and the highest goodness of soil; it is most blessed in the pleasantness of the Euganean Hills and in the nearness of the Alps and the sea. The river Brenta flows through it, about which I shall speak elsewhere. Its circuit is now double, formerly triple: the outer circuit contains six thousand two hundred paces, with six magnificent gates; the inner circuit is three thousand paces, very high, with a continuous walkway along the top. Moreover, it is magnificent and splendid, abounding in all things necessary for life, paved with stone by Ubertino da Carrara, Lord III, in the year 1340; it is well protected on all sides by ditches, walls and bulwarks.

units.la: Situs.
units.tr: Situation.

units.la: Ambitus.
units.tr: Circuit.

units.la: Qualitas.
units.tr: Quality.

units.la: Audiamus hic Fr. Guicciardinum lib. Histor. vIII: Patavium, inquit, nobilissima, & antiquissima Vrbs & Gymnasiu præstantia celebris, triplici muro circumdata, & quam Brenta atque Bacchilio amnes alluunt: ambitu fortasse tanto, quanto alia vel è maximis Italiæ Vrbibus: in fertilissimo solo, salubri ac temperato cælo sita: quæ quamvis jam supra centum annos Venetorum, Carrariensibus exactis, imperio premeretur; tamen superba atque ampla Ædificia, multaque Antiquitatis vestigia memoranda retinet, ex quibus priscina Vrbs amplitudo, splendorque cognoscitur: & quæ sequuntur. Rectè monet magnus Scriptor de Ædificiorum superbia atque amplitudine. Habet sane ea Patavium Sacra, Profana, Publica, Privataque: magnifica & sumptuosa. Templum Cathedrale, ab Henrico Imperatore structum, xIII tub se habet Basilicas intra Vrbem, ob splendorem tali matre dignas, plurimas etiam superiores. Monasteria Virorum sunt xxiii: D. Iustinæ, Benedictorum: olim Concordiæ, vel, ut alij censent, Martiu ut item nonnullis videtur, Junoni sacratum caput Episcopij; hodie plane novum, xxii m. aureorum reditus superare fertur: Pratalea, ejusdem Ordinis, in Collibus Euganeis, sexto ab Vrbe milliari: S. Ioannis in Viridario, Canonicorum Regularium S. Augustini, pulcerrimum: S. Mariæ Angelorum, Eremitarum tertij Ordinis S. Francisci: D. Hieronymi de Fesulis, Mendicantium: Cruciferorum, Prioratus: S. Mariæ Magdalenæ, Eremitarum D. Onofrij: D. Antonij Viennensis, Camalduensium: D. Benedicti Novelli, Benedictinorum, qui ab D. Iustinæ differunt, vestium candore, morumque severitate: D. Augustini, angustissimum, Prædicatorum, xii columnis sustultum, sex Arcubus maximis: ubi sepulcra Carrariensium: S. Maria in Vantio Vico; Sacerdotum Secularium: S. Mariæ Gratiarum, ad Pratum vallis: Prædicatorum: Capucinorum, prope Portam S. Crucis, observantium primi Ordinis Franciscanorum: D. Antonij Thippiponensis, Franciscanorum; Junonis olim, inde B. Mariæ, tandem Antonij tectum habens plumbeum, duas turres, pavimentum marmoreum: D. Francisci, Minoritarum: Eremitarum, D. Augustini: Carmelitarum, ad Portam Candæ longæ: Servorum S. Mariæ; olim ædes Iacobi Carrariensis ob crimen perduellionis publicatæ: Iesuitarum, extra pontem S. Sophiæ: Sacerdotum Iesu, olim Fratrum Equitum Alemannorum: S. Salvatoris, novum, cum amœnissimis Hortis, Clericorum Regularium. D. Pauli: & S. Francisci Parvuli. Virginum Sacrarum intra mœnia numerantur collegia xxix: inter quæ excellunt D. Stephani, & D. Magdalenæ Conversarum, seu Illuminatorum, ad ædem S. Sophiæ. Palatium ibi, Henrici Imp. opus, in quo Ius dicitur; tota Italia nominatissimum, nullis sulcum columnis, plumbo rectum. Curia in
units.tr: Let us hear here Francesco Guicciardini, book 8 of the Histories: Padua, he says, the most noble and most ancient city, famous for the excellence of its university, surrounded by a triple wall, and washed by the rivers Brenta and Bacchiglione, is perhaps as large in circuit as any of the greatest cities of Italy, set in very fertile soil and a healthy and temperate sky; although for more than a hundred years it has been held under the rule of the Venetians, since the Carraresi were driven out, it still keeps proud and spacious buildings and many notable remains of antiquity, from which the ancient greatness and splendour of the city are known: and what follows. The great writer rightly remarks on the pride and magnificence of its buildings. Padua certainly has sacred, profane, public and private buildings, magnificent and costly. The cathedral church, built by the Emperor Henry, has within it thirteen basilicas in the city, worthy of such a mother for their splendour, and many more besides. There are twenty-three monasteries of men: St Justina, of the Benedictines, formerly dedicated to Concordia, or, as others think, to Mars, or, as seems to some, to Juno, the seat of the bishopric, now entirely new, is said to have an income of more than 22,000 gold pieces; Praglia, of the same Order, on the Euganean Hills, six miles from the city; St John in the Garden, of the Regular Canons of St Augustine, most beautiful; St Mary of the Angels, of the Hermits of the third Order of St Francis; St Jerome of Fiesole, of the Mendicants; of the Crosiers, a priory; St Mary Magdalene, of the Hermits of St Onofrio; St Anthony of Vienne, of the Camaldolese; St Benedict Novello, of the Benedictines, who differ from those of St Justina in the whiteness of their robes and the severity of their manners; St Augustine, very narrow, of the Preachers, supported by twelve columns and six very large arches, where the tombs of the Carraresi are; St Mary in Vanzo Vico, of the secular priests; St Mary of the Graces, at the meadow of the valley, of the Preachers; of the Capuchins, near the Gate of the Holy Cross, of the first Order of the observant Franciscans; St Anthony of Tibiponense, of the Franciscans, once Juno's, then St Mary's, and at last Anthony's, having a leaden roof, two towers and a marble pavement; St Francis, of the Minorites; of the Hermits, of St Augustine; of the Carmelites, at the Gate of the Long Canal; of the Servants of St Mary, formerly the house of Jacopo Carrara, confiscated for the crime of treason; of the Jesuits, beyond the bridge of St Sophia; of the Priests of Jesus, formerly of the German Knights; St Saviour, new, with most pleasant gardens, of the Regular Clerks; St Paul; and St Francis the Little. Within the walls are counted twenty-nine colleges of sacred virgins, among which those of St Stephen and St Magdalene of the Converts, or the Illuminati, near the church of St Sophia, excel. There is there a palace, a work of the Emperor Henry, in which justice is administered, most famous throughout all Italy, supported by no columns, roofed with lead. The court in
