units.la: Curia. ria insuper publici consilij, cum Porticu, columnis marmoreis suffulta, saxo constructa, plumbeis item laminis intecta: Fora maxima sunt v: primum congressibus & deambulationi Nobilium civiumque dicatum est; alterum, olitorium; tertium, frumentarium; quartum lignarium; postremum palearium. Pontes xxxix, ex lapide, fornicati, supra Brentam: Porticus amplissimae: Areae spatiosissimae: Nosocomia iii, Lazarettum, peste infectis attributum; S. Lazari, Leprosis; S. Francisci, reliquis aegrorum morbis: Xenodochia totidem, S. Antonij de Vienna; S. Leonini, ad Pratum Vallis, juxta Portam S. Crucis: & S. Jacobi: omnia pauperum peregrinorum: Est & Orphanotrophium in Vico Omnium Sanctorum: & Domus Dei, Exposititijs Infantibus dicata: Mons Pietatis institutus est anno cIↄ cccc xci, exterminandae Iudaeorum Foeneratoriae qui pro centenario xx exigere consueverant: Aerarij sors xxxiix Aureorum millia ex Civium liberalitate superat. Præficiuntur septem Dominus, quæ opportuno Urbis loco sitæ, Viri Nobiles: datis Fidei jussoribus annuatim, qui pro pignoribus mutuo dant; infra xxx solidos, gratis supra, quinque tantum fœnoris nomine pro Centenario exigentes, ad ministrorum impensas, quæ tria millia aureorum quotannis superant, sustinendas: quod superest, in pauperes annuatim dividitur, forte semper manente, & ex piis eleemosynis, præsertim quæ festo Paschatis colliguntur, quotannis crescente: res nulli non instituta laudabiliter Reipublicæ imitanda. Domorum quatuor millia hodie suo ambitu complectitur: Ante bellum Maximiliani Imp. 1, quod gestum anno cIↄ IↄXIX, extra Murorum ambitum 20 in Suburbiis tria millia Domorum connumerabantur: Monasteria Virorum quatuor: Virginum tex: Templa quinque: Xenodochia septem: quæ postea ab Venetis solo sunt æquata, ne hostibus deinceps, ab Urbis detrimentum, receptacula essent. Inter Domos eminent Regia Carrarensium, urbe media; Doctorum, ad D. Firmi, cum Colosso lapideo; Capitularum, ad D. Danielis cum Equo Trajano. Episcopatus superbit Patavium dignitate. Primus Præsul memoratur D. Prosdocimus, Græcus, D. Petri Discipulus: Reditus ad xi aureorum millia adsurgit. Incolæ summis præditi sunt ingenijs, ad arma, litteras, omniumque virtutum studia promti. Familiæ Patavinæ primum disperse anno cccc xxi in Rivum Altum migrarunt, Alarici West-Gothi, qui Romam everterat, metu magis adhuc, Attila inundante, 30 anno cccc lvi: Et hæc Venetæ Urbis nobilitatisque fuerunt seminaria. Sub Henrico iv firmata Rep. Patavina, quatuor Familiæ Principes exstiterunt, Ateitina, Honoria, Carrarensis, (cujus propago stirps Comitum Anguillaria, itemque Papafavorum & Campsampertæ. Florent etiamnum hodie, Transalgarda, Sforzatae, Capilista, Tada, Comitum Baonorum, Comitum S. Bonifacij, Lioncellorum, Daulorum, Dottarum, Maltraversorum, Nontanorum, Vici Aggeris, Rusticæ, Trapolina, Malfattorum, Zacchorum, Cortusiorum, Capivacciorum, De S. Cruce, Sanguinaciorum, Perachinorum, Leoniorum, Buzzicharinorum, Disalciorum, Lionamineorum, Trivisanorum, Cumanorum, Zakarellarum, Vigentiorum, Musatorum. Cavtentorum, Scardeoncorum, Dalesmaninorum, Screvinierum, S. Andreæ, Liminercorum, Consilviorum, Caldenactorum, Solimanorum, Bolpariorum, Ridiorum, Beraldorum, Bigolinorum, Soncinorum, Rubeorum, Obicorum. Quid de Literatis dicam? Urbs magnis celebrata Viris: hac Livius ille Historia Pater est genitus: servantur eodem Illius ossa loco, statuis tutiloque superbo; Hic, ubi juncta fora, nullis fulcrita columnis Plumbea marmorea pulcre stant tecta Palatij. Hic etiam Paullus Iuris Legumque peritus, Et statuas aly meruerunt Urbis Alumni. Hac quoque Valerio Patria est, qui Iasona laudat: Hac Patria Asconio & Stellæ: Prætoris in Arce Effigies quorum & titulos spectare licebit: Atria Romanum referunt ubi picta Senatum.
units.tr: The Curia, the hall of the public council, with a portico supported by marble columns, built of stone and likewise roofed with lead plates. There are five very large fora: the first is given over to the meetings and promenades of the nobles and citizens; the second is the vegetable market; the third the grain market; the fourth the timber market; and the last the straw market. There are 39 bridges of stone, arched, over the Brenta; spacious porticoes and very large squares. There are three hospitals: the Lazaretto, assigned to those infected with plague; that of St Lazarus, for lepers; and that of St Francis, for the other sicknesses of the sick. There are as many hostels for travellers: that of St Anthony of Vienna; that of St Leonine, at Pratum Vallis, near the Porta S. Crucis; and that of St James. All are for poor pilgrims. There is also an orphanage in the Vicus Omnium Sanctorum, and a House of God dedicated to foundlings. The Mount of Piety was established in 1491, to rid the city of Jewish moneylenders, who had customarily charged twenty per cent for a hundred. The treasury of the institution exceeds 39,000 gold pieces from the generosity of the citizens. Seven lords, noblemen, are set over it; it is situated in a convenient place in the city. Each year they give sureties of faith, who lend money against pledges: for sums under thirty shillings, free of charge; above that, they charge only five per cent interest per hundred, to meet the expenses of the officials, which come to more than 3,000 gold pieces a year. What remains is divided each year among the poor, the capital always remaining, and growing each year from pious almsgiving, especially that collected at the feast of Easter. It is an institution worthy of praise and of imitation by every commonwealth. Today it embraces four thousand houses within its circuit. Before the war of Emperor Maximilian, waged in 1509, there were counted three thousand houses in the suburbs outside the city walls, twenty of them... Monasteries of men: four; of women: ten; churches: five; hostels: seven. These were afterwards levelled to the ground by the Venetians, so that they should not later serve as refuges for the enemy to the detriment of the city. Among the houses the Carrarese palace stands out, in the middle of the city; the Doctors' house, at St Firmus, with its stone colossus; and the Chapter house, at St Daniel, with the Trajan horse. The bishopric takes pride in the dignity of Padua. The first bishop on record is St Prosdocimus, a Greek, a disciple of St Peter. The revenues rise to about 11,000 gold pieces. The inhabitants are endowed with the highest talents, and ready for arms, letters and the pursuit of every virtue. The families of Padua were first dispersed in the year 421, when they migrated to Rivus Altus, fleeing the West Goth Alaric, who had overthrown Rome, and even more the fear of Attila's invasion in the year 456. These were the seedbeds of the nobility of the city of Venice. Under Henry IV the Paduan commonwealth was established, and four princely families arose: the Ateitine, the Honorian, the Carrarese (whose offshoot was the stock of the Counts of Anguillara), and likewise the Papafava and Campsampiero families. There flourish to this day the Transalgardi, Sforzate, Capilista, Tada, Counts of Baono, Counts of St Boniface, Lioncelli, Daulo, Dotta, Maltravers, Nontani, Vicus Agger, Rustica, Trapolina, Malfatti, Zacchi, Cortusii, Capivacci, De S. Cruce, Sanguinacci, Perachini, Leoni, Buzzicarini, Disalci, Lionamineri, Trevisani, Cumani, Zakarelli, Vigenti, Musati, Cavtenti, Scardeoni, Dalesmanini, Screvini, S. Andreae, Liminerci, Consilvi, Caldenacti, Soliman, Bolpari, Ridi, Beraldi, Bigolini, Soncini, Rubei and Obici. What shall I say of the learned? The city is celebrated for its great men: from here came that Livy, the Father of History; his bones are kept in the same place, with statues and a proud tomb. Here, where the fora are joined, the lead-roofed marble palace stands finely, propped on no columns. Here also Paulus, skilled in law and the laws, and other sons of the city have earned statues. To this place Valerius, who praises Jason, also owes his birth; from here came Asconius and Stella; their statues and inscriptions may be seen in the citadel of the praetor. The painted halls there recall the Roman senate.

units.la: De Livio canit etiam libro i Epigrammatum Martialis: Censetur Apona Livio suo Tellus.
units.tr: Martial also sings of Livy in the first book of his Epigrams: "Aponus, the land that is counted Livy's own."

units.tr: Forums, bridges, porticoes, squares, hospitals, orphanages, the House of God, the Mount of Piety, houses, bishoprics, inhabitants, noble families and illustrious men flourish under the Roman Empire.

units.la: Forum Iudiciorum ad occidentalem partem repositA cum effigie ejusdem anea & Inscriptione:
units.tr: The Forum of Judgment, placed on the western side, with a bronze statue of the same and an inscription:

units.la: V . F T . LIVIVS LIVIÆ . T . F QVARTÆ. L CONCORDIALIS PATAVI SIBI. ET. SVIS OMNIBVS
units.tr: While living, Titus Livius (made this) for Livia Quarta, daughter of Titus, and for Lucius Concordialis of Padua, for himself and all his family.

units.la: T. Livius quarto Imp. Caesaris anno Vita excessit, aetatis suae LXXVI. Item, quae sequuntur, sub Veneri statua in antiqua Lapide: Ossa tuumque Caput Cives tibi maxime Livi, Promto animo hic omnes componere tui. Tu famam aeternam Romae Patriaque dedisti, Hinc oriens, illi fortia facta canens. At tibi dat Patria haec; &, si majora liceret, Haec flares totus aureus ipse loco.
units.tr: Titus Livy died in the fourth year of the Emperor Caesar, in the seventy-sixth year of his age. Likewise, what follows, under a statue of Venus on an ancient stone: Your bones and your head, citizens, most of all, Livy, with ready spirit all here lay to rest. You gave eternal fame to Rome and to your homeland, singing from the beginning of her brave deeds. Yet this your homeland gives you; and if it were permitted to give greater things, you would be a golden statue yourself in this place.

units.la: Alia, quae ibi ad Tumulum, in quo ipsa ossa, praetereo. Nobilitarunt & prisco saeculo Patavium ortu suo C. Valerius Flaccus, Argonauticorum Scriptor, de quo idem Martialis: O mihi curarum pretium non vile mearum, Flacce, Antenoreae spes & alumne Laris:
units.tr: I pass over the other things there at the tomb in which the bones themselves lie. In ancient times Patavium also gained fame from the birth of C. Valerius Flaccus, the writer of the Argonautica, of whom Martial says the same: O Flaccus, no small reward of my cares, hope of Antenor's land and nursling of its hearth.

units.la: L. Arruntius Stella Poeta, & Volusius Annalium Scriptor; hic aemuli Catulli, ille Martialis carminibus noti: Q. Asconius Pedianus, Grammaticus insignis, Orationum aliquot Ciceronis illustrator: Julius Paulus, IC. qui Alexandro Imperatori in corrigendo Reip. Romanae statu adfuit. His adcensendus C. Cornelius, Augur Patavinus, qui in collibus Euganeis prope templum Geryonis sedens, Pharsalicae Pugnae faciem inter Caesarem & Pompeium lymphatus vidit: reciprocas belli vices narravit; Caesarem vicisse, exclamavit: uti testantur Julius Obsequens, Agellius lib.xv, cap. xviii, Lucanus de bello Pharsalico, libro vii, Plutarchus in Caesare. Idem Tiberio Imperium praesagit, jactis in Aponi fontem talis aureis, summum numerum ostendentibus, scribente Suetonio. Addendus & Maximus Olibius, qui Plutoni sacram illam & ingeniosam dedicavit lucernam, quae per multos annos sub terra arsit juxta Atestem, municipium Patavinum, anno CIO 15 inventa in urna fictili, inter duas ampullas, aureo alteram, alteram argenteo liquore plenas, cum versibus elegantissimis urnae majori inculptis. Edidit quoque Patavium, post Imperii Romani cladem, plurimos magnae celebritatis viros: in quis famam sibi suis scriptis conciliarunt Marsilius Mainardinus, Minorita, Theologus, qui Ludovici Bavari partes contra Ioannem XXII P.M. tutatus est, edito libro acutissimo de Potestate Papae & Imperatoris, anno ab Christo nato CIO CCC XXIV, sub titulo, Defensor Pacis, quem Albertus Pighius in Ecclesiastica Hierarchia oppugnavit: Iacobus Alvarottus, qui in Usus Feudorum scripsit; Franciscus Zabarella, Episcopus primum Florentinus, inde Cardinalis; Ludovicus Cortusius, qui Repertorium Iuris concinnavit; Antonius de Roselle, Iudiciorum, Torturae, Indulgentiarum, Legitimationis, Successionum ab intestato, & Usurarum enarrator; & alii, Iurisconsulti: Petrus Aponensis, Conciliator dictus, haereseos & magiae nomine ab aemulis accusatus; Marsilius, Iacobus Dondus, qui de fluxu & refluxu maris, deque tale conficiendo ex aquis Aponi candidissimo absque coctione, scripsit; Michael Savonarola, & alii, Medici: Albertinus denique Musatus, Kalandinus, Lupatus, Zuccho Polentonus, Typhus Odaxius, Petrus Montagnana, Io. Antonius Maginus & alii, Historici, Poetae, litterarumque humaniorum doctissimi. Genuit & claros militia Duces, L. Cassium, Centurionem, ab Augusto, cui mortem minabatur, in exilium pultum: Borjeum, Tribunum militum, qui Sertorium sequutus,
units.tr: L. Arruntius Stella, a poet, and Volusius, a writer of Annals; the one known for the songs of his rival Catullus, the other for those of Martial. Q. Asconius Pedianus, a distinguished grammarian, illustrator of several orations of Cicero. Julius Paulus, a jurist, who assisted Emperor Alexander in correcting the state of the Roman commonwealth. To these should be added C. Cornelius, augur of Padua, who, sitting on the Euganean hills near the temple of Geryon, saw in a frenzy the course of the battle of Pharsalus between Caesar and Pompey; he related the alternating fortunes of the war, and cried out that Caesar had conquered, as Julius Obsequens, Aulus Gellius book 15 chapter 18, Lucan in his book 7 on the Pharsalian war, and Plutarch in his Life of Caesar bear witness. The same man foretold the empire to Tiberius, when dice of gold were thrown into the spring of Aponus, showing the highest number, as Suetonius writes. Maximus Olibius should also be added, who dedicated that sacred and ingenious lamp to Pluto, which burned for many years underground near Ateste, a town of Padua, found in the year 1500 in a clay urn, between two flasks, one full of golden liquid, the other of silvery, with most elegant verses engraved on the larger urn. Padua also produced, after the fall of the Roman Empire, many men of great renown, among whom the following won fame for themselves by their writings: Marsilius Mainardinus, a Franciscan theologian, who defended the cause of Louis of Bavaria against John XXII, the supreme pontiff, publishing in the year of Christ 1324 the most acute book on the power of the pope and the emperor, under the title Defender of the Peace, which Albert Pighius attacked in his Ecclesiastical Hierarchy; Jacobus Alvarottus, who wrote on the Usus Feudorum; Franciscus Zabarella, first bishop of Florence, then cardinal; Ludovicus Cortusius, who compiled a Repertory of Law; Antonius de Roselle, expounder of the law on judgments, torture, indulgences, legitimation, succession without a will, and usury; and other jurists. Petrus Aponensis, called the Conciliator, accused by his rivals of heresy and magic; Jacobus Dondus, who wrote on the ebb and flow of the sea, and on making salt from the waters of Aponus, very white, without boiling; Michael Savonarola, and other physicians. Lastly Albertinus Musatus, Kalandinus, Lupatus, Zucco Polentonus, Typhus Odaxius, Petrus Montagnana, Io. Antonius Maginus, and others, historians, poets and most learned in the humanities. It has also produced famous military leaders: L. Cassius, a centurion, who was thrown into exile by Augustus, who threatened him with death; Borjeus, a military tribune, who followed Sertorius,

units.la: ipso tus, ab Catilina caesus: Caecinnam Petum, qui Scriboniani, Illyrici Legati, partes contra Claudium secutus, eo militum proditione obtruncato, Romam est pertrahus, Arria uxore semper comitante: Ibi dilecto mortis dato, Arria, ne super viveret, gladio, quem sinu abditum gerebat, pectus suum confodit, eundemque marito porrigens,
units.tr: ... struck down by Catiline. Caecina Paetus, who followed the side of Scribonianus, legate of Illyricum, against Claudius; when he was cut down by the treachery of his soldiers, he was dragged to Rome, his wife Arria always accompanying him. There, when death was granted to her beloved, Arria, so as not to survive him, stabbed her own breast with a sword which she carried hidden in her bosom, and, offering it to her husband, said:

units.la: {10} Si qua fides, vulnus quod feci, non dolet, inquit: Sed quod tu facis, hoc mihi, Pete, dolet.
units.tr: {10} "If there is any faith in it," he said, "the wound I made does not hurt. But what you do, Paetus, hurts me."

units.la: Meminit praeter Martialem Plinius iunior libro III, Epist. ad Nepotem. Genere ejus fuit Thrasea Petus, Patavio quoque oriundus. Vir Consularis & Sacerdos, Philosophus, Poëta, Orator summus, Senecae aequalis, virtutis existimatione ipsimet Neroni invisus: morique jussus, dato mortis arbitrio, praecisis utriusque brachii venis exspiravit: Legendus Tacitus. Cives inter praecipuas artes Lanificium exercent hodie, uti & olim, quemadmodum constat ex Strabone libro V, qui scribit Patavium, Urbium eius regionis esse praestantissimam; addens, non multo ante suum aevum censos ibi fuisse 500 Viros equestres, & antiquitus ad bellum Patavinus militare CXX militum millia; item multitudinem Mercium, quas Romam ad mercatum mittere solití, cum aliarum rerum, tum Vestimentorum, ostendere, quantum & viris & opibus praestarent. De Tunicis Patavinis Martialis: Vellera quum sumant Patavinae multa tribuces, Et pingues tunicas serra secare potest.
units.tr: Besides Martial, Pliny the Younger mentions him in book III of his Letters, to Nepos. He was of the family of Thrasea Paetus, also born at Padua: a consular man and priest, a philosopher, a poet and a supreme orator, a contemporary of Seneca, and hated by Nero himself for his reputation for virtue. Ordered to die, he was allowed to choose his manner of death, and he expired after both his arms' veins had been cut. Read Tacitus. Among the principal arts the citizens practise wool-working today, as they did of old, as is clear from Strabo, book V, who writes that Padua is the most outstanding of the cities of that region. He adds that not long before his own time 500 equestrian men were registered there, and that in antiquity Padua sent 120,000 soldiers to war. He also notes the great quantity of goods they used to send to Rome for sale, both other things and clothing, and shows how greatly they excelled in men and wealth. On the Paduan tunics, Martial: When the Paduan women take up and spin many fleeces, and a saw can cut through the thick tunics.

units.la: Academiam habet Patavium nobilem, quae Natales suos debet Karolo Magno Imperatori, vel, ut alii placet, Friderico II; Adolescentiam Urbano IV, P. M; maturitatem illustrissimae Venetorum Reipublicae. Clarissimum est omnium Disciplinarum Artiumque Emporium: Iuris Legumque corona, Et sacra Themidis, Iustitiaeque Domus.
units.tr: Padua has a famous Academy, which owes its birth to the Emperor Charlemagne, or, as others prefer, to Frederick II; its youth to Pope Urban IV; and its maturity to the most illustrious Venetian Republic. It is the most famous emporium of all disciplines and arts: the crown of laws and rights, and the sacred house of Themis and Justice.

units.la: Scribit de ea in hunc modum Iason IC: Si quem neque Urbis Patavinae vetustas movet, quam constat a Trojano Antenore conditam esse, neque amplitudo, sive triplicem murorum ambitum, interfluente Timavo, consideres, sive Praetorium, omnium, quae in orbe memorantur, dignissimum; moveat saltem Patavina Academia gloria. Est enim totius Italiae celeberrima, & veluti Atheniensis Areopagus, quae semper Viros in omni ingenuarum artium genere claros & celebres fovit, auditique, ac nobilium Auditorum frequentia semper abundavit, non modo illorum, qui Venetae ditionis subsunt, sed etiam exterarum gentium ac remotissimarum nationum. Ornata est longa consuetudine ipsdem, quibus Bononienses, Privilegiis, uti testantur Bartolus §. haec autem tria, Proem. D. Baldus Auth. Habita, C. Ne filius pro patre, Fr. Zabarella Cardinalis Clement. Dudum, de sepult. Anchoranus, reliquique Iuris Canonici Doctores in c. quum de diversis, De Privilegiis in Sexto: & utrum ea Privilegia, si Bononiensi Academiae adimantur, etiam huic ademta censeri debeant, pulcre disputat Castrensis. Professus ibi jus Civile quatuor integros annos Bartholemaeus Saluzius: edidit ibi ad gloriam Academiae Commentaria Paullus Castrensis in universum fere Ius; quae Praelectiones Patavinae ab Iurisconsultis nuncupantur: dedicavit ibi Commentaria in Clementinas; itemque Observationes in Panormitanum & Alexandrum de Imola Zabarella Cardinalis clarissimo Iuris utriusque Collegio Patavino. Sunt & Patavy Collegia literaria, gratuita, ix, sustentandae Studiosorum inopiae institituta; Foro-Iulien-sium ad D. Antonii; Feltrensium, ibidem; Spinellium & Riadium, apud Pontem Corvum: Campionis, in Vico Vignalium; Neapolitanorum, apud S. Katharinam, vetustissimum; Thomae, Philologi, Ravennatis Medici, juxta Pontem Molitorum; Brixianorum, apud S. Lucam: Cyprlorum denique, ab Archiepiscopo Graeco non ita pridem conditum. Habent suum ibi Hortum Medici, Simplicium, forma sphaerica, amplum & irriguum; Sebastiani Foscari & Nicolai Teupuli auspiciis coeptum. Videre ibidem est Bibliothecas varias, Graecis Latinisque libris abunde instructas: unam, apud S. Ioannem in Viridario; alteram, apud S. Iustinam: tertiam, apud S. Antonium. Amica perpetuo sociaque Populi Romani, uti paret ex Livi lib. XLI & M. Tullii Philippicis, Colonia deducta multo meliore fuit conditione, quam aliae Coloniae, nam Patavinus jus etiam Suffragiorum datum legitur, tamquam Civibus Romanis. Videndus Asconius Paedianus. Capta direptaque cum aliis ab Attila Hunnorum Rege, annisque centum post ab Langbardis, qui & igne cremarunt, cum Karoli Magni principatu partim sub Regibus coepit esse Italia, Franciaque Caesaribus, partim sub Berengario: sui tandem juris quodam-modo facta imperante Othone I, Praetorem ex suis creavit & Populi Praefectum. Duravit haec Reipubl. forma usque ad Fridericum II, cujus jussu auspiciisque Urbem occupavit Actiolinus Romaninus: post quem Dominos habuit Carrarienses, Scaligeros, Galeatios, & circa annum ab Christo nato MCCCCIV Venetos: quibus adhuc paret, tamquam pia Mater, prae senio virium non satis compos, piae Filiae (nam Patavinorum Colonia, Venetia) non tam imperio, quam ministerio regenda. Consulendi lib. xv. ad Eutropium, & iv. Langbard. Histor. Blondus lib. II, VIII, XVI & XVIIII, Sabellicus, Merula lib. I Histor. Vicecomit. Corius part. II & III, Aequicola, Leander Albertus, & alij. De laudibus, situ, antiquitate, & statu totius Urbis: nec non Viris praeclaris ex ea ortis, inibique sepultis, ceteris item omnibus, quae ad eam pertinent, justum scriptie volumen Bernardinus Scardeonius, Canonicus Patavinus. Ager Patavinus frumenti, variorum fructuum, vini etiam generosissimi fetax: unde Martialis: Pictaque pampineis Euganea arva jugis:
units.tr: Jason the jurist writes of it in this manner: If the antiquity of the city of Padua does not move you, which is agreed to have been founded by the Trojan Antenor, nor its size, whether you consider its triple circuit of walls, with the Timavus flowing between them, or its Praetorium, the most worthy of all those recorded in the world, let at least the glory of the Paduan Academy move you. For it is the most celebrated in all Italy, and like the Areopagus of Athens, it has always fostered men famous and renowned in every kind of liberal art, and its lecture halls have always been full of noble students, not only from those who are subject to the Venetian dominion but also from foreign and most remote nations. By long custom it has been adorned with the same privileges as the Bolognese, as Bartolus testifies (in §. haec autem tria, Proem.), as do Baldus (Auth. Habita, C. Ne filius pro patre), Francis Zabarella the Cardinal (Clement. Dudum, de sepult.), Anchoranus, and the other doctors of canon law (in c. quum de diversis, De Privilegiis in Sexto). Castrensis discusses well whether those privileges, if they were taken away from the Bolognese academy, ought to be considered taken away from this one too. Bartholomew Saluzzo taught civil law there for four full years. Paul of Castro published there, to the glory of the Academy, commentaries on almost the whole of law; these are called by jurists the Paduan Lectures. Zabarella the Cardinal dedicated there his commentaries on the Clementines, and likewise his observations on Panormitanus and Alexander of Imola, to the most distinguished college of both laws at Padua. There are also at Padua nine literary colleges, free of charge, founded to support the poverty of students: the Forum Iulii college at St Anthony's, the Feltre college in the same place, the Spinelli and Riari colleges near Corvo Bridge, the Campion college in Vignali Street, the Neapolitan college at St Catherine's, the most ancient; the Thomas college, for the philologist and Ravennese physician, near the Molino Bridge; the Brescian college at St Luke's; and finally the Cypriot college, founded not long ago by the Greek Archbishop. There the physician Medici has his garden of simples, spherical in shape, large and well watered, begun under the auspices of Sebastiano Foscari and Niccolò Teupolo. There can be seen various libraries there, well stocked with Greek and Latin books: one at St John in Viridario, another at St Justina, and a third at St Anthony. Friendly and a constant ally of the Roman People, as is clear from Livy book XLI and Cicero's Philippics, Padua was founded as a colony on much better terms than other colonies, for it is read that the Paduans were granted the right of voting, like Roman citizens. Asconius Pedianus should be consulted. Padua was captured and plundered, along with other cities, by Attila, King of the Huns; a hundred years later the Lombards, who also burned it with fire, took it. With the rule of Charlemagne, Italy and France began partly under kings and partly under emperors, and partly under Berengar. Finally, under the Emperor Otto I, it became in a way its own master, and it elected from its own citizens a Praetor and a Prefect of the People. This form of republic lasted until Frederick II, at whose command and under whose auspices Actiolinus Romaninus seized the city; after him it had as lords the Carraresi, the Scaligeri and the Galeazzi, and around the year of Christ 1404 the Venetians. Padua still obeys them, like a pious mother who, because of old age, is not quite in control of her strength, and whose pious daughter (for the colony of Padua is Venice) governs it more by service than by rule. Consult book XV of Eutropius, and book IV of the Lombard history; Blondus, books II, VIII, XVI and XVIIII; Sabellicus; Merula, book I of the History of the Visconti; Corio, parts II and III; Aequicola; Leander Albertus, and others. On the praises, situation, antiquity and condition of the whole city, and likewise on the illustrious men born there and buried there, and on everything else that pertains to it, Bernardino Scardeone, canon of Padua, has written a full volume. The Paduan territory is fertile of grain and of various fruits, and even of very fine wine; whence Martial: The Euganean fields painted with vine-clad ridges.

units.la: Venationibus insuper, Aucupijs & Piscationibus frequens. Mirabilem rerum omnium copiam Incolae trivialí celebrant Proverbio: Bologna la grassa, Padoua la passa. De Agricolis vulgo circumfertur: Vildanos generat tellus Paduana Diablos.
units.tr: It is also much given to hunting, fowling and fishing. The inhabitants celebrate the wonderful abundance of all things in a common proverb: Bologna the fat, Padua the dried. Among the farmers this saying is passed about commonly: The Paduan soil breeds Vildani and Diablos.

units.la: Describitur Ager Patavinus apud Bernardinum Scardeonitum his terminis: A Meridie Athesis fluvius procurrit: a Septemtrione Musone amnis parvus delabitur, ab Oriente aestuaria Venetiarum, ac Occidente vero Colles sunt Euganei & Ager Vicentinus. Patet omnis hic circuitus c LXXX r. M; in quo sexcenta & quadraginta septem Villa seu Pagi, & quae sequuntur. Dicere solitus scribitur ab Caelio Rhodigino Constantinus Palaeologus; nisi sciret a sanctissimo viro affirmari, in Oriente Paradisum esse, arbitrari se non alibi eum reperiri posse, quam in perfuavi Patavina amoenitate.
units.tr: The Paduan territory is described by Bernardino Scardeone in these terms: From the south the river Adige runs down; from the north the small stream Musone flows down; on the east are the lagoons of Venice, and on the west the Euganean hills and the Vicentine territory. The whole circuit extends 180 miles, in which there are six hundred and forty-seven villages or districts, and so on. It is written that Constantine Palaeologus used to say, as Celio Rodigino reports, that unless he knew that a most holy man had affirmed that Paradise is in the East, he would think that it could be found nowhere else than in the delightful Paduan countryside.

units.la: Iter Patavio Venetias secundo amne una nocte peragitur. Venetia (vulgo Venegia) multitudinis numero nominatae, quod Conditores vel non unius Urbis fuerint Cives, ut quidam volunt: vel quod varii Venetiae Regionis populi, relicta ob summam Attilae omnia vastantis crudelitatem & saevitiam continente, in modicas has Stagnorum Insulas, tamquam in Arces quasdam, migrarint: Patavinis quidem in Rivo Alto fundamenta circa annum cccc LVI (alij alium edunt) feliciter orsis; aliis autem, quae convicinae, gentibus opus coeptum paullatim in summum splendorem emolientibus. Videndi Blondus in libris de Rebus Venetorum; itemque libr. I. & II. Histor. Italiaque illustrata: Volaterranus lib. III. Comment. Urbanorum; Sabellicus lib. I. Dec. I. de Reb. Venet. Io. Iovianus Pontanus libr. Histor. sui temporis I: Candidus in Comment. Aquileiensium. Ludit de Venetiarum nomine elegantet his versibus Nicodemus Frischlinus: Aut Venus à Venetis sibi fecit amabile nomen; Aut Veneti Veneris nomen & omen habent. Orta maris spuma fertur Venus; & Venetorum Si Videas Urbem, creditur orta mari. Iuppiter est illi genitor: sed Mars pater huic est Mulciberi conjunx illa, sed ista Maris: Complet amore sui Venus omnia, qui Venetam Urbem Non amat, hanc numquam debet amare Venus.
units.tr: The journey from Padua to Venice is made in one night by the second river. Venice (in common speech Venegia) is named from its multitude, either because its founders were citizens of not one city, as some hold, or because various peoples of the Venetian region, having left everything because of the extreme cruelty and savagery of Attila, who laid waste everything, migrated to these small islands of the lagoons as to certain citadels. The Paduans, indeed, happily began the foundations on the Rialto around the year 456 (others give a different date), while others from the neighbouring peoples began the work, which gradually grew to the highest splendour. On this, consult Blondus in his books on the affairs of the Venetians, and likewise books I and II of his Italia illustrata; Volaterranus, book III of his Commentaries on Urban matters; Sabellicus, book I, decade I, on the affairs of Venice; Giovanni Gioviano Pontano, book I of his history of his own time; and Candidus, in his Commentaries on the Aquileians. Nicodemus Frischlin elegantly plays on the name of Venice in these verses: Either Venus made for herself a lovable name from the Venetians, or the Venetians have the name and omen of Venus. It is said that Venus arose from the foam of the sea; and if you see the city of the Venetians, it is believed to have arisen from the sea. Jupiter is her begetter, but Mars is the father of this one; she is the wife of Vulcan, but this city is the wife of the sea. Venus fills all things with her love; whoever does not love the Venetian city ought never to love Venus.

units.la: Urbs, modicas complexa insulas circiter LX, sita est in intimo Sinus Hadriatici recessu, mediis in stagnis, quae in aestu singulis senis horis irrigua: adfuso, qua Oriens est. Pelago, quod tamen, ne sua violentia vel ira sit noxium, praejectis aliis quibusdam Insulis, tamquam aggeribus cohibetur. Georgius Sabinus: Ambit aquis Nereus pro muro spumeus Urbem, Finitibus est omni tutus ab hoste locus.
units.tr: The city, embracing about sixty small islands, lies in the innermost recess of the Adriatic Gulf, in the middle of lagoons, which are watered at each tide every six hours. On the east it is struck by the open sea, which, however, lest it be harmful by its violence or anger, is held back by certain other islands placed before it, as by dykes. Georgius Sabinus: The foaming Nereus surrounds the city with waters as a wall; the place is safe from every enemy within its boundaries.

units.la: Sic Georgius Fabricius Chemnicius: Pro portu illi Nereus, pro maenibus aequor.
units.tr: Thus Georgius Fabricius Chemnicius: For a harbour, Nereus; for walls, the sea.

units.la: Licet non muris, non propugnaculis, non turribus ullis sit munita; loci tamen natura est tutissima. Quamplurimis dividitur Canalibus. Vicis pene omnibus sunt Rivi, conjungentibus ipsos Pontibus ex lapide lignove circiter ccccl. Inter Canales principis loci, qui vulgo Canal grande, longitudinis trium milliarium, qui Urbem totam in duas quasi dirimit partes; circa medium Pontem gestans visendum. Ita commoditas passim Urbem vel pedibus percurrendi, vel Cymbis, quarum numerus octo dicitur millium. Vulgus Gondolas appellat. Ambitus Urbis viii circiter milliarium. Imperij magnitudine, populi frequentia, opum splendore, mercium varietate, inlustris: Ingenijs excellentibus virtuteque eruditissimis beata: bonis Legibus laudabilibusque Institutis ornata. Bene Poëta:
units.tr: Although it is fortified with no walls, no bulwarks and no towers, the nature of the site is itself very secure. It is divided by very many canals. Almost every street has a watercourse, joined by bridges of stone or wood, about 450 in number. Among the canals, the principal one, commonly called the Canal grande, is three miles long and divides the whole city into two parts; a bridge spanning its middle is worth seeing. Thus there is convenience for getting about the city everywhere, either on foot or by boat, of which there are said to be eight thousand. The people call them gondolas. The circuit of the city is about eight miles. It is distinguished by the greatness of its empire, the crowds of its people, the splendour of its wealth and the variety of its merchandise; it is blessed with excellent talents and very learned men, and adorned with good laws and praiseworthy institutions. As the poet well says:

units.la: Urbs Venetum fœcunda viris, z emerauda Senatu
units.tr: The city of the Venetians, fruitful in men, an emerald in its Senate,

units.la: Purpureo, & magnæ virtutibus æmula Romæ.
units.tr: purple, and a rival in the virtues of great Rome.

units.la: Frumenta, quod ex diversis orbis partibus advehitur, vinis multiplicis generis, inter quæ generosum illud, quod vulgo Malvaticum vocant; aliisque rebus humanæ vitæ necessariis, ita adhuc, ut recte Paradisus Deliciarum ab latone appelletur, ad l. 45. D. de verbor. obligation. Regiones ibi seu Parochiæ lxiv. Ædificia cum publica, tum privata ibidem magnifica, splendida, sumptuose ornata. Inter Templa preciosissimum illud, quod D. Marco Evangelistæ dicatum, auro multis locis ornatum; cuius pavimentum tessellatum, & marmore variorum generis in frustula contuto compositum. In Choro Columnæ iiii marmoreæ, quæ adhibito lumine sunt pellucidæ. Supra Portas Statuæ æneæ Equorum quatuor; Constantinopoli, quum Veneti eam occupassent, advectæ. Inteueri mihi datum hic, præter alia singularia, Thesaurum D. Marci immensum & admirandum: in quo Mitra Ducalis gemmis plurimis interrexta; in apice Carbunculus est præcij inæstimabilis: sunt ibidem Coronæ Regiæ aureæ xi; Thoraces aurei totidem; Rubini, inter quos duo extremæ magnitudinis, Adamantes, Smaragdi, Chrysolithi, Hyacinthi, Uniones, aliæque gemmæ numero incredibili: duo, præter illa, Monocerotis Cornua, terriumque minus; Vasa, omnis generis ex Agate, Chalcedonio, Auro, Argento: indicata omnia cum ab alijs, tum ab Leandro Alberto, qui totum Templū universis suis partibus accurate describit. Habet insuper Urbs Monasteria Monachorum xxxix; Cœnobia Monacharum xxviii, Oratoria xviii; Hospitalia, ut vocant, xvii; Turres c xv, in quis eminentissima, quæ in foro D. Marci contra Basilicam, intervallo predum lxxx, lata quaquaversum xl pedes: alta cc xxx, fastigio aureis veltito tegulis, quod Sole fulgente quam longissime ab Istria Liburniaque navigantibus conspicitur. Fora numerantur ibi liiii, in quis primarium D. Marci, ubi præter Templum, Turrim, Palatium, aliaque, duæ visuntur Columnæ cum Statuis DD. Marci alati, & Theodori Martyris, intenta hasta Draconi incubantis. In ipso Intercolumnio supplicia sumuntur de Condemnatis. Stant & in Foro Mali tres cum Velis nauticis. Numerantur item Venetijs Fontes publici c xlviii: Statuæ marmoreæ c lxiv, æneæ xxiii; Equi ænei ix; Portæ æneæ x. Ab his omnibus excipiuntur circumvicinæ Insulæ, in quibus adhuc Monasteria Virorum xi, Vestalium i, Turres xiiii, Statuæ v. Armamentarium (vulgo Arsenale, tamquam Ars Navalis) cujus circuitus duorum circiter milliarium, describit Daniel Barbarus in Commentario ad Vitruvij libros, laudans illud ab insigni Triremium & Navium adparatu, Instrumentorum omnium copia, Tormentorum & Machinarum multitudine, Munitionum & Armorum omnis generis thesauro, infinitorum Artificum serie, rerum ordine, facili usu, promtaq; ad omnes necessitates expeditione. Quid dicam de Navi Reip. pulcerrima, quæ vulgo Bucentaurum? Ea vectus quotannis ad Maris introitum, ubi Castella Æstuarij. Princeps, Senatu Primoribusque Urbis comitatus, ceremonijs ab Episcopo peractis, Mare sibi despondet; injecto ad perpetuandum Dominium aureo Annulo. Iuxta Armamentarium locus est, Tuna vulgo dictus; funium rudentumque ad naves intorquendorum officina. Scholæ monstrantur vij, Caritatis, Joannis Evangelistæ, Misericordiæ, S. Marci, S. Rocchi, S. Theodori, & Passionis. Bibliothecam, à Bessarione Cardinale Nicæno legatam, auxit supra modum Senatus. Sunt & aliæ, S. Joannis & Pauli, S. Francisci, S. Stephani, Servorum Mariæ, S. Georgij Majoris, S. Dominici, S. Antonij, quæ fuit Pici Mirandulani. Visuntur & privatorum, Jacobi Contareni, Danielis Barbari, Joannis Delphini, Rochi Contareni, Sebastiani Erici, Ludovici & Marci Antonij Mocenigorum, rum, Hieronymi de Mula, Ludovici Balbi, Aldi Manutii, Pauli Paruta, Ludovici Gradenici, Francisci de Ponte, Ludovici Michaelis, Iacobi Marcelli, Ludovici Lolini, Francisci Sorantij, Ludovici Malapetrae, Iosephi Zarlini, Augustini Amadei. Antiquitatum maximus est numerus apud Ioannem Grimanum, Patriarcham Aquileiensem, Andream Lauredanum, Gabrielem Vendramium, Leonardum Mocenigum, & alios. Inter Aedificia, post Ducis Palatium, maxime conspicua sunt Monetaria, vulgo Zeccha, Rivus altus, Ri-alto; Domus Germanorum, Il Fontego de Todeschi; Iudaeorum Habitatio, Ghete; Palatium Procuratorum D. Marci: item Marci Michaelis apud S. Antonium, de Forlani, de Gruti, de Trivisani, Malpetri, Patriarcha Aquileiensis, Georgiorum de Priuli, de Capelli, de Pisani, de Lauredani, Nicolai de Ponte, de Leni, de Contarini, Iuliniani, de Gonella, de Grimani, de Cornari, de Michaeli, de Soranzi, de Foscarini, de Emi, de Mocenigi, de Bragadini, de Molini, de Barbarigi, de Nani, de Negroni, de Tefolis, de Mori, Vendramini, de Donati, de Delphini, de Fodeni, de Gusfoni, de Troni, de Capelli, de Pisani, de Bonaldi, de Dandulo, de Coccina; item Ducis Urbinatis, Ducis Ferrariensis, Ducis Mediolanensis, Regus Cypri, & aliorum. Scribit Donatus Ianotius vicies mille propemodum Lares seu Familias in hac Urbe esse, quarum singulae si binos homines praestent, qui ferendis armis sint idonei, numerus efficietur XL millium: Patriciios ad tria millia repertu addens. Horti sunt CLVII, in quis praecipui Caesaris Erici, Andreae Michaelis, Francisci Bonu, Caesaris Zilioli, Petri Rosselli, Francisci Tedde, Monasterij B. Mariae Virginis, Thomae Contarenii, Andreae Pasqualigi. Leonardi Mori, Grimanorum, Iacobi Contarenii, Maffei Medicis, Augustini Amadi, Alexandri Victoris, Andreae Dandulo, Gritti Mocenigi, Vendramini, & Cornari. Adiciebam huc, qui ad D. Marcum legitur, Dialogilimum inter Advenam & Senem.
units.tr: There is grain, which is brought from various parts of the world; wines of many kinds, among which is the noble wine that they commonly call Malvaticum; and other things necessary for human life, so abundantly that the Paradise of Delights is rightly called by Latona's ... (see law 45, D. de verborum obligationibus). There are sixty-four districts or parishes. The buildings, both public and private, are magnificent, splendid and richly decorated. Among the temples the most precious is the one dedicated to the Evangelist St Mark, adorned with gold in many places; its pavement is of tesserae, composed of pieces of marble of various kinds. In the choir are four marble columns, which are translucent when a light is placed behind them. Above the doors are four bronze statues of horses, brought from Constantinople when the Venetians captured it. Here I was allowed to view, besides other rarities, the immense and admirable treasury of St Mark: in it is a ducal mitre inlaid with very many gems, and at its top a carbuncle of inestimable value; there are also eleven golden royal crowns and as many golden breastplates; rubies, among them two of the largest size; diamonds, emeralds, chrysolites, hyacinths, pearls, and other gems in incredible number; besides these, two horns of the unicorn and a third, smaller one; vessels of every kind made of agate, chalcedony, gold and silver. All these things are described both by others and by Leandro Alberti, who describes the whole church accurately in all its parts. The city moreover has thirty-nine monasteries of monks, twenty-eight convents of nuns, eighteen oratories, and seventeen hospitals, as they are called; one hundred and fifteen towers, among which the most conspicuous is the one in the Piazza of St Mark, opposite the basilica, eighty paces from the base, forty feet wide on every side and two hundred and thirty feet high, with a roof of gilded tiles, which can be seen from far off by those sailing from Istria and Liburnia when the sun shines. There are fifty-four squares in the city, of which the chief is that of St Mark, where, besides the church, the tower, the palace and other buildings, two columns with statues of St Mark, winged, and of the martyr Theodore, who holds a spear pointed at a dragon crouching beneath him, are to be seen. In the very space between the columns, punishments are inflicted on condemned persons. In the Piazza of the Mint there are also three [columns] with nautical sails. In Venice there are also one hundred and forty-eight public fountains, one hundred and sixty-four marble statues, twenty-three bronze statues, nine bronze horses and ten bronze doors. Beyond all these lie the neighbouring islands, in which there are also eleven monasteries of men, one of vestals, fourteen towers and five statues. The arsenal (commonly Arsenale, as if Ars Navalis), whose circuit is about two miles, is described by Daniel Barbaro in his commentary on the books of Vitruvius, who praises it for its remarkable equipment of triremes and ships, its abundance of all instruments, its multitude of artillery and machines, its store of defences and arms of every kind, its endless series of craftsmen, its orderly arrangement of things, its ease of use, and its readiness for dispatch in every need. What shall I say of the most beautiful state ship, commonly called the Bucentaur? Carried in it each year to the mouth of the sea, where the forts of the estuary stand, the Doge, accompanied by the Senate and the leading men of the city, betroths himself to the sea with ceremonies performed by the bishop, casting in a golden ring to perpetuate the dominion. Next to the arsenal is a place commonly called the Tuna, a workshop for twisting ropes and cables for ships. Seven schools are shown: of Charity, of John the Evangelist, of Mercy, of St Mark, of St Rocco, of St Theodore, and of the Passion. The Senate has greatly enlarged the library bequeathed by Cardinal Bessarion of Nicaea. There are also others: of St John and Paul, of St Francis, of St Stephen, of the Servants of Mary, of St George the Greater, of St Dominic, of St Anthony, which was once that of Pico of Mirandola. There are also private libraries: of Jacopo Contarini, Daniele Barbaro, Giovanni Delfino, Rocco Contarini, Sebastiano Erizzo, Lodovico and Marcantonio Mocenigo, Girolamo da Mula, Lodovico Balbi, Aldo Manuzio, Paolo Paruta, Lodovico Gradenigo, Francesco da Ponte, Lodovico Michiel, Giacomo Marcello, Lodovico Lollino, Francesco Soranzo, Lodovico Malipiero, Giuseppe Zarlino, Agostino Amadi. The largest collection of antiquities is with Giovanni Grimani, Patriarch of Aquileia, Andrea Loredan, Gabriele Vendramin, Leonardo Mocenigo and others. Among the buildings, after the Doge's palace, the most conspicuous are the Mint (commonly Zecca), the Rialto, the high bank; the house of the Germans, the Fondaco dei Tedeschi; the dwelling of the Jews, the Ghetto; the palace of the Procurators of St Mark; also the houses of Marco Michiel near St Anthony, of Forlani, Gritti, Trevisan, Malipiero, of the Patriarch of Aquileia, of the Giorgi, of Priuli, Cappello, Pisani, Loredan, of Nicolò da Ponte, Lion, Contarini, Giuliani, Gonella, Grimani, Cornaro, Michiel, Soranzo, Foscarini, Emo, Mocenigo, Bragadin, Molin, Barbarigo, Nani, Negroni, Tiepolo, Morosini, Vendramin, Donà, Delfino, Foscari, Gussoni, Trono, Cappello, Pisani, Bonaldi, Dandolo, Cocina; also the houses of the Duke of Urbino, the Duke of Ferrara, the Duke of Milan, the King of Cyprus, and of others. Donato Giannotti writes that there are nearly twenty thousand households or families in this city, and if each of these furnishes two men fit to bear arms, the number will amount to forty thousand, adding about three thousand patricians found there. There are one hundred and fifty-seven gardens, among which the chief are those of Cesare Erizzo, Andrea Michiel, Francesco Buon, Cesare Zilioli, Pietro Rosselli, Francesco Tedde, the monastery of the Blessed Virgin Mary, Tommaso Contarini, Andrea Pasqualigo, Leonardo Moro, the Grimani, Giacomo Contarini, Matteo de' Medici, Agostino Amadi, Alessandro Vittori, Andrea Dandolo, Gritti Mocenigo, Vendramin and Cornaro. I would add here the dialogue, read at St Mark's, between a stranger and an old man:

units.la: A. Dic, antique Senex, Venetae qui conditor Urbis? S. Iuppiter: A. Vade Arcesi? S. Attica: A. Scorta? S. Venus: A. Moenia? S. Neptunus: A. Nummi? S. Dido: A. Bellica? S. Martis: A. Artesi? S. Mercurius: A. Iura? S. Minerva dedit. Non mirum est, si alias inter caput extulit Urbes, Cum tot coelestes composuere Deae.
units.tr: A. Tell me, ancient old man, who was the founder of the city of Venice? S. Jupiter. A. Who gave it its wine? S. Bacchus. A. Its harlots? S. Venus. A. Its walls? S. Neptune. A. Its money? S. Dido. A. Its warfare? S. Mars. A. Its arts? S. Mercury. A. Its laws? S. Minerva gave them. It is no wonder if she raised it above other cities, since so many heavenly goddesses built it.

units.la: Datus Urbi Primus Episcopus, Obealtus Maximus, anno 10 CCIXXIV. cui deinde alij successerunt, usque ad annum CIO CCCCL, quo Episcopatus ab Eugenio IV P. M. in Patriarchalem dignitatem est conversus. Primas enim Dalmatiae vocatur, alios habens Suffraganeos Praelatos. Catalogus Episcoporum & Patriarchatum est apud Leandrum, & utitur in Palatio ipsius Patriarchae. Genuit haec Urbs multos insignes, clarosque eruditione Viros: inter quos Pontifices recensentur, Gregorius XII, Eugenius IV, Paulus II: Cardinales fuisse legimus; Petrum Maurocenum, Marcum Landum, Antonium, Gregorii XII Nepotem, Ioannem Amedeum, Ioannem Baptistam Zenonem, Dominicum Grimanum, Marcum Cornarium, Marinum Grimanum, Dominici Nepotem, Gasparum Contarenum, Petrum Bembum, Franciscum Cornarium, Marci Fratrem, Franciscum Pisanum, Ioannem Grimanum, Marini Fratrem: Item Pantaleonem Iustinianum, Primum ex Latinis Patriarcham Byzantinum; Hermolaum Barbarum, virum doctissimum, Aquileiae Patriarcham; Laurentium Iustinianum, Episcopum Castelli, inde Primum Patriarcham Venetiarum & Dalmatiae Primatem; quem in Patriarchatu sequuti sunt Mapheus Contarenus, Andreas Bondimerius, Gregorius Corarius, Ioannes Baroti, Mapheus Gerardus, postea Cardinalis, Thomas Donatus, Antonius Surianus, Ludovicus Contarenus, Antonius Contarenus, Hieronymus Quirinus. units.tr: The first bishop given to the city was Obealtus Maximus, in the year 10 CCIXXIV; after him other bishops succeeded, down to the year CIO CCCCL, when the bishopric was raised by Pope Eugene IV to the dignity of a patriarchate. For it is called the primate of Dalmatia, having other prelates as suffragans. A catalogue of the bishops and patriarchs is in Leandro, and it is kept in the palace of the Patriarch himself. This city has produced many distinguished men, famous for learning: among them are numbered popes, Gregory XII, Eugene IV, Paul II; we read that there were cardinals: Pietro Morosini, Marco Lando, Antonio, nephew of Gregory XII, Giovanni Amedeo, Giovanni Battista Zeno, Domenico Grimani, Marco Cornaro, Marino Grimani, nephew of Domenico, Gasparo Contarini, Pietro Bembo, Francesco Cornaro, brother of Marco, Francesco Pisani, Giovanni Grimani, brother of Marino; also Pantaleone Giustiniani, the first Latin Patriarch of Constantinople; Ermolao Barbaro, a most learned man, Patriarch of Aquileia; Lorenzo Giustiniani, Bishop of Castello, then the first Patriarch of Venice and Primate of Dalmatia; after him in the patriarchate followed Matteo Contarini, Andrea Bondimerio, Gregorio Corario, Giovanni Barozzi, Matteo Gerardo, afterwards cardinal, Tommaso Donà, Antonio Suriano, Lodovico Contarini, Antonio Contarini, Girolamo Quirini. Venetians were the prelates of their own homeland: Orso Partecipazio, the fourth in order; Giovanni Sanudo, the fifth; Mauro Vincenzo, the sixth; Domenico Partecipazio, the seventh; Crasso Faccio, the eighth; Giovanni Sanudo, the ninth; Lorenzo Tiepolo, the eleventh; Domenico Mauro, the twelfth; Domenico David, the thirteenth; Orso Magadis, the fifteenth; Domenico Partecipazio, the sixteenth; Pietro Quinavalle, the seventeenth; Gregorio Gregorio, the eighteenth; Marino Cassiano, the nineteenth; Domenico Gradenigo, the twentieth; Domenico Gradenigo, the twenty-first; Domenico Contarini, the twenty-second; Enrico Contarini, the twenty-third; Vitale Michiel, the twenty-fourth; Bonifacio Faletro, the twenty-fifth; Giovanni Polani, the twenty-sixth; Vitale Michiel, the twenty-seventh; Filippo Casolo, the twenty-eighth; Marco Nicolò, the twenty-ninth; Vitale Michiel, the thirtieth; Marco Morosini, the thirty-first; Pietro Pino, the thirty-second; Gualtiero Agnus Dei, the thirty-third; Tommaso Arimondo, the thirty-fourth; Tommaso Franco, the thirty-fifth; Bartolomeo Quirini, the thirty-sixth; Simeone Mauro, the thirty-seventh; Giacomo Contarini, the thirty-ninth; Bartolomeo Quirini, the fortieth; Michele Calergi, the forty-first; Angelo Delfino, the forty-second; Niccolò Morosini

Ex iis, qui maximis potiti victoriis nomen Venetum terra marique plurimum auxerunt, memorantur cum primis Ioannes & Raynus Polani, Marinus Grandonicus, Dominicus Maurocenus, Ioannes Basilius, Thomas Falerius, Reinherus Dandulus, Rugerius Permarinus, Ioannes Trevisanus, Petrus Thomas Ioannes Grittus, Nicolaus Balestrerius, Marcus Bonus, Andreas Tocanus, Leonardus Quirinus, Marcus Onisforus, Rainerus Zeno, Laurentius Theupolus; Andreas Zeno, Marcus Gradonicus, Marcus Michael, Gilbertus Dandalus, Iacobus Dandalus, Ruggerius Maurocenus, Ioannes Superantius, Benedictus Iustinianus, Petrus Zeno, qui primus omnium Dux in Turcas ab Venetis ivit: Successores nactus Marinum Falerium, Andream Co[ntarenum], Petrum & Marcum Canales, & Marcum Iustinianum. Civium frequentia Venetijs plane stupenda. Numerus trecentorum circiter millium censetur. Præter hos, Mercatores ibi innumeri & advenæ, qui vario cultu ex omnibus mundi partibus negociationis gratia confluere soliti: Turcæ, Æthiopes, Slavi, Arabes, Syri, Cretenses, Cyprij, Macedones, Germani, Vngari, Hispani, Galli, alij. units.tr: Distinguished men: Nus XLIII, John Barbus XLIV, Paul Fuscarus XLV, John Amadeus XLVI, Angelo Cavarius XLVII, John Loredan XLVIII, Francis Faletrus XLIX, Leonard Delphinus L, Francis Bembus LI, Mark Landus LII, Francis Mariopetrus LIII, Lawrence Justinian LIV, and the last, the first, as I said above, created Patriarch in the year 1451. Elsewhere the bishops were Henry Contarenus of Castello; Dominic Dominicus and Peter Aemilianus of Vicenza; Fantinus of Padua; Peter Montens of Brescia; James Zeno of Feltre and Belluno; Dominic of Torcello. Among the leaders who won fame for learning were Andrew Dandalus, who wrote a notable history; Charles Zeno, and others. Venice produced jurists: Mark Lippomano, Barbone Mocenigo, Lewis Foscari, Vitale Landi, Candiano Polani, Nicholas Canal, Laurus Quirinus; as historian, Andrew Navagero; as orators, Zaccaria Trevisan, Leonard Giustinian, Francis Barbaro, Hieronymus Donatus, Hieronymus Giorgio, a gilded knight; as polymaths, the Manutii and John Baptist Egnatius; as poets, Andrew Mocenigo, Hermolaus Donatus, and others. Nowhere, however, have more men won immortal glory in the art of war. Among those who, having gained the greatest victories, greatly extended the name of Venice by land and sea, the following are especially recorded: John and Rainer Polani, Marino Gradenigo, Dominic Mocenigo, John Basilio, Thomas Falier, Reinher Dandolo, Ruggiero Permarini, John Trevisan, Peter, Thomas, John Gritti, Nicholas Balestrerio, Mark Buono, Andrew Tocani, Leonard Quirini, Mark Onisforo, Rainerio Zeno, Lawrence Theupolo; Andrew Zeno, Mark Gradenigo, Mark Michiel, Gilbert Dandolo, James Dandolo, Ruggiero Mocenigo, John Superanzio, Benedetto Giustinian, Peter Zeno, who was the first of all the Doges to go against the Turks for the Venetians. Their successors were Marino Falier, Andrew Contarini, Peter and Mark Canal, and Mark Giustinian. To be added are Andrew Mocenigo, Simon Dandolo, Nicholas Gradenigo, Pancrazio Giustinian. The highest praise as commanders of the fleet was earned by Nicholas Pisani, John Delfino, Paul Loredan, Mark Michiel, John Sanudo, Mark Cornaro, Bernardo Giustinian, Dominic Michiel, Crespo Molin, Michael Delfino, James Moro, Mark Giustinian, Charles Zeno, Michael Giustinian, Peter Emo, Fantino Giorgio, Mark Grimani, John Barbo, Victor Fabio, Francis Bembo, Peter Loredan, Andrew Mocenigo, Stephen Contarini, Aloysius Loredan, Victor Capello, Orsato Giustinian, James Loredan, Nicholas Canal, Peter Mocenigo, Hieronymus Canal, Vincent Capello, Andrew Trevisan, a gilded knight, Lawrence Amulio, and others. The crowd of citizens at Venice is truly astonishing; it is reckoned at about three hundred thousand. They are of three kinds: patricians, to whom the administration of the Empire and the Republic belongs; citizens, who hold the offices of secretaries and other posts of honour; craftsmen, who practise the mechanical arts. Besides these there are countless merchants and foreigners there, who are accustomed to flock together from every part of the world for the sake of trade, in varied dress: Turks, Ethiopians, Slavs, Arabs, Syrians, Cretans, Cypriots, Macedonians, Germans, Hungarians, Spaniards, French, and others.
