units.la: Quae Munera totamque Venetorum Rempublicam plenius explicant cum P. Bembus, C. Contarenus, M. Sabellicus, Baptista Egnatius, aliique, tum M. Franciscus Sansovinus, docto libro, cui Titulus, Del Governo & Administratione di diversi Regni & Republiche. De Opibus hujus Civitatis judicare quis potest, quod ex solo Venetiis annuatim vicies centena millia Ducatorum capiat; eiusque Duci, ut maiore fulgeat pompa, singulis annis xxxv millia aureorum numerentur, quos in adparatus regios & magnificentiam expendat. Coepit Rerum, quas summa laude felicitateque gesserunt Veneti, gloria ab iis, qui mare infestum habebant: quibus classe sæpe superatis & in potestatem redactis, Insulas coeperunt & Nationes externas subigere. Crescente imperandi cupiditate, observatis diligenter Vicinorum, vel dissidentium inter se, vel ab suis Principibus oppressorum occasionibus, in finitimam itum est Continentem; ubi lapsu temporis mirum in modum fines ipsorum sunt propagati. Nervose Paullus Iovius: Paruere eis ab initio, inquit, quo tempore classibus maxime valebant, Istri, Liburni, Dalmatæ, atque Illyriciora: multæ item nobiles Graeciæ Urbes, cum Eubœa, Cretaque Insulis. Mox transgressi in proximam Continentem, Patavium, Verona, Tarvisium, atque Vicentia, quæ ab infimis minimisque Regulis tenebantur, accesserunt. His quoque Ravenna addita est, Regia quondam Gothorum, atque alterum totius Italiæ Navale pulcherrimum. Quo rerum successu et actis, & terrestribus ac Ethiopis non multo post Ithippo Vicecomiti pluribus bellis defatigato, Brixiam & Bergomum ademere. Cessit & eis Crema, Francisco Sfortiæ concedente, exinde Venetorum potentia cunctis in Italia maximo terrori esse coepit, & quæ sequuntur.
units.tr: Paul Bembo, C. Contarini, M. Sabellico, Baptist Egnatius and others explain these offices and the whole Venetian Republic more fully, and M. Francis Sansovino in a learned book entitled Del Governo & Administratione di diversi Regni & Republiche. Who can judge the wealth of this city, which takes in from Venice alone two thousand million ducats a year; and to its Doge, so that he may shine with greater pomp, thirty-five thousand gold pieces are paid each year, which he spends on royal equipment and magnificence. The glory of the deeds which the Venetians performed with the greatest praise and good fortune began with those who held the sea hostile: when they had often defeated them with a fleet and brought them under their power, they took islands and began to subdue foreign nations. As their desire to rule grew, having carefully watched for opportunities among their neighbours, either quarrelling among themselves or oppressed by their own princes, they went to the neighbouring mainland; there, with the passage of time, their borders were extended in a remarkable way. Paulus Iovius vigorously says: "At first they obeyed them," he says, "at the time when they were most powerful at sea, the Istrians, Liburnians, Dalmatians, and those of Illyria; likewise many noble cities of Greece, together with the islands of Euboea and Crete. Afterwards, having crossed to the nearest mainland, Padua, Verona, Treviso, and Vicenza, which were held by the lowest and smallest petty rulers, came over to them." To these was also added Ravenna, once the royal seat of the Goths, and the most splendid naval base in the rest of Italy. "With this success in their affairs and deeds, both on land and at sea, and not long after, having worn out Filippo Visconti with many wars, they took Brescia and Bergamo from him. Crema also passed to them, Francesco Sforza yielding it; from then on the power of the Venetians began to be the greatest terror to all in Italy, and what follows."

units.la: Quæ omnia, plurasque, quæ addi possent, adeo sunt vera, ut Venetiarum Urbs hodie omnium Urbium clarissima censeatur & florentissima, Mundi Theatrum, commune totius Orbis Emporium, Victrix domitrixque tot tantorumque Hostium, Hadriatici Regina Maris, Italici nominis gloria decusque. Quamvis multa bella gesserit, variamque fortunam mille annorum spatio sit experta, in externi tamen Hostis potestatem numquam devenit. Divini plane sunt Versus Actij Synceri Sannazarij: Viderat Hadriacis Venetam Neptunus in undis Stare Urbem, & toto ponere Iura Mari: Nunc mihi Tarpeias quamtumvis Iuppiter Arces Objice, & illa tui Moenia Martis, ait: Si Pelago Tibrim præfers, urbem adspice utramque: Illam Homines dices, hanc posuisse Deos.
units.tr: All these things, and many more that could be added, are so true that the city of Venice today is considered the most famous and flourishing of all cities: the theatre of the world, the common market of the whole globe, victor over and conqueror of so many great enemies, queen of the Adriatic Sea, and the glory and ornament of the Italian name. Although it has waged many wars and experienced changing fortunes over a thousand years, it has never fallen under the power of a foreign enemy. Sannazaro's verses from the Actius Sincerus are truly divine: "Neptune had seen Venice standing on the Adriatic waves and laying down laws over the whole sea. Now, says Jupiter, though you set before me the citadels of the Tarpeian hill and those walls of your Mars, if you prefer the Tiber to the sea, look at both cities: you would say that men founded the one and the gods the other."

units.la: De Hexasticho illo Epigrammate refert in Sannazarij Vita Ioannes Baptista Crispus, auditum à se ex Aldo Manutio Paulli F. Poetam ab S. P. Q. Veneto pro singulis versibus singulos centenos aureos, honoris gratia, dono accepisse.
units.tr: Giovanni Battista Crispo, in his Life of Sannazaro, reports that he heard from Aldus Manutius that the poet, son of Paulus, received from the Venetian Senate, as a mark of honour, a hundred gold pieces for each single line of that six-line epigram.

units.la: Concludam cum Vaticinio, quod de Venetorum Vrbis fato scripsit Gauricus, insignis Astrologus: Virginei partus facLis bis octo peractis, E pelago emergens tellus fœcunda colonis, Pæbebit miseris alimenta è frugibus altis: Nec Nauta pisces capient in littore sicco, Sed varios pueri flores, & gramina pingues Læta boves, bellia non remis pulchra Iuventus Certatim ludent, mæsto spectante Senatu.
units.tr: I will conclude with the prophecy that Gauricus, the notable astrologer, wrote about the fate of the city of Venice: "When sixteen years of the virgin birth have passed, the land, fertile for its settlers, will rise from the sea and provide wretched people with food from the rich harvests. Sailors will not catch fish on the dry shore, but boys will play, and the joyful oxen and the lovely, warlike youth will vie with one another in games, while the Senate looks on in sorrow."

units.la: Quibus versibus Venetis Dominium Poeta pollicetur usque ad annum MDCCCXXX; Urbem prædicens ex Insula in Terram Continentem commutatum iri. Tempus docebit. Ego quidquid rerum humanarum est optima Dei Omnipotentis providentia gubernari scio, cujus solius est mutare Imperia, alioque transferre: quem penes arbitrium, Civitates ut floreant, ut pereant. Cingit Urbem magnus Insularum numerus: in quis præcipuæ Iudaica, distans dimidio fere milliari, longitudine mille passuum: Templis sinis, Cœnobiis, splendidis nitens ædificiis; culcissimisque hortis plena. Dicitur & Ossoduro. Maranum, mille diremtum ab Urbe passibus, ambitu tria colligit milliaria: Incolis frequens; sicu jucundo & amœno, XIV habet Templa. Domus singulæ Hortis mire conditis ornantur. Celebre vitreis Vasis, quæ ibi XXIV Officinis excellenti artificio maxima copia elaborantur, in diversas orbis partes exportari solita. Methamaucum, vulgo Malamocco, Ducis Veneti sede quondam nobile portum habet profundissimum, quem Meduacus fluvius efficit. Alii minorum gentium sunt D. Georgii Monasterio Hortoque celebris; S. Iacobi, S. Nicolai, S. Bernardi, S. Helenæ, Majorlanum, Torcellum, S. Francisci de Deserto, Lazaretum Novum & Vetus, S. Clementis, S. Angeli, Concordia, S. Clara, S. Iuliani, S. Secundi, S. Chrisophori, S. Michaelis, &c.
units.tr: With these verses the poet promises dominion to the Venetians until the year 1530, foretelling that the city will be changed from an island to a mainland. Time will tell. As for me, I know that whatever happens in human affairs is governed by the best providence of Almighty God, to whom alone it belongs to change empires and transfer them elsewhere, and in whose power it lies that cities should flourish or perish. The city is surrounded by a great number of islands, among which the chief are Iudaica, about half a mile away and a thousand paces long, shining with splendid churches, monasteries and buildings, and full of very pleasant gardens; it is also said to be Ossoduro. Murano, a thousand paces from the city and with a circuit of three miles, is crowded with inhabitants and pleasant and charming; it has fourteen churches. Each house is adorned with wonderfully laid-out gardens. It is famous for its glass vessels, which are made in great quantity by skilled craftsmen in its twenty-four workshops and are customarily exported to different parts of the world. Malamocco, commonly so called, once the seat of the Venetian Doge, has a very deep harbour formed by the river Meduacus. Among the smaller islands are the monastery and garden of St George, well known; and those of St James, St Nicholas, St Bernard, St Helen, Majorlanum, Torcellum, St Francis of the Desert, the New and Old Lazaretto, St Clement, St Angelo, Concordia, St Clara, St Julian, St Secundus, St Christopher, St Michael, etc.

units.la: Viginti quinque ab Urbe Venetorum Pass. millibus Portus est Clodianus; juxtaque Chioggia: quæ Fossa Clodia Plinio & aliis: ab Clodio, Albanorum Duce, conditæ uti censet Volaterranus libro III. Commentar. Urbanorum. Quidam tamen apud Sabellicum libro III. De Situ Vrb. Venet. produnt ædificatam ab Atestinis{n1} & Silicensibus. In longum protenta stagnis marinis undique circumfunditur. Civitatis ius adeptum est hoc Opidum anno cIↄ cv, translato huc Methamaucensi Episcopatu. Natus ibi Petrus Calaetus, Monachus, cuius de Vitis Divorum volumina Bononiæ servantur in Dominicana Bibliotheca. Adsident Vibi passim Salinæ.
units.tr: Twenty-five Roman miles from the city of Venice is the port of Clodianus, and next to it Chioggia, which Pliny and others call the Clodian Ditch. According to Volaterranus, in book III of his Commentaries on Urban Matters, it was founded by Clodius, leader of the Albans. Some, however, according to Sabellicus in book III of On the Situation of the City of Venice, report that it was built by the Atestines and the Silicenses. Stretched out lengthwise, it is surrounded on all sides by sea-lagoons. This town gained the rights of a city in the year 1105, when the bishopric of Malamocco was transferred here. Peter Calaetus, a monk, was born here; the volumes of his Lives of the Saints are kept at Bologna in the Dominican library. Salt-pans lie scattered about the islands here.

units.la: Relictis cum Venetorum Urbe Insulis, in Continentem revectus ad Brentam redeo, in cuius dextra supra vicum Liminam, Opidum visitur Cittadella; a Patavinis conditum anno ab Christo nato cIↄ cI, nobile, lautum, frequens. Excipit hoc{ 10} aliud, quod vulgo Marestica; supraque Bassanum, Carrariensium, qui quondam Patavij principatu potiti, ortu clarum. Succedunt inde Cisinum Castrum, ad Huvium cognominem, cuius fonti Pemecum adiidet Opidulum, supra Cisinum, haud procul amne, Grumum sequitur, cui nomen praeterlabente Havio. Inde Castrum est Bavanum; altiusque Tusupum & Caldonatium.
units.tr: Leaving the islands of the city of Venice and returning to the mainland, I come back to the Brenta. On its right bank, above the village of Limina, is seen the town of Cittadella, founded by the Paduans in the year of Christ's birth 101; it is noble, handsome and populous. Next to it is another place, commonly called Marostica; and above Bassano, which is famous as the birthplace of the Carraresi, who once held the principality of Padua. Then come the castle of Cisinum, on the river of the same name, at whose source lies the little town of Pemecum; above Cisinum, not far from the river, follows Grumum, which takes its name from the Havius flowing past it. From there is the castle of Bavanum, and farther up Tusupum and Caldonatium.

units.la: Stagna repeto, ubi ad Mutonum amnem Opidum sese pandit Mestrium, Mestre vulgo, Menstra, Sabellico lib. VIII, Ennead. IX. Opidum olim, quam nunc opulentius: occurrunt inde adverso Metono, Villa Nova, Campus D. Petri, & juxta fontem Opidulum Collis Musoni. Ad dextram ripam interius Castellum Francum, supraque nobilius Asolum, quod ex nonnullorum judicio Ἀσόλο Ptolemæi.
units.tr: I return to the lagoons, where, at the river Mutonus, the town of Mestrium opens out, commonly called Mestre, Menstra, as in Sabellicus, book VIII, Ennead IX. It was once a town, now richer than it was. From there, facing the Metonus, appear Villanova, Campus St Peter, and near the spring the little town of Collis Musonis. On the right bank further inland is the castle of Francum, and above it the more noble Asolum, which in the judgement of some is the Asolo of Ptolemy.

units.la: {10} Lines of marginal reference numerals are printed.
units.tr: {10} Lines of marginal reference numerals are printed.

units.la: Fluvius inde Silis in conspectum venit. Ad ejus ostium modica visuntur vestigia Altini, urbis antiquæ; Tacito, Plinio, Pomponio, Antonino, Itinerariæ Tabulæ, aliisque memoratæ: Ἀλτῖνον item non solum Ptolemæo & Herodiano, sed & Straboni, cui situm, uti Ravenna, in Paludibus: quod verum, Stagna enim ibi, finitique Septum Marium, quibus Silis immergitur. Ad Situm pertinent Martialis Sila lib. I. Æmula Baianis Altini litora villis; Et Phaethontei consciaque silva roris: Quaeque Antenorio Dryadum pulcerrima Fauno Nuntit ad Enganeos sola puella lucus.
units.tr: From there the river Silis comes into view. At its mouth there are small remains of the ancient city of Altinum, mentioned by Tacitus, Pliny, Pomponius, Antoninus, the Itinerary Tables and others. Ptolemy and Herodian, and also Strabo, likewise mention Altinum (Ἀλτῖνον), which, like Ravenna, lay among marshes; this is true, for there are lagoons there, and the marshy inlets into which the Silis is swallowed. To this place Martial's lines refer, in book I, "The shores of Altinum, rival of the villas of Baiae, and the grove that knows the dew of Phaethon, and that beautiful grove of the Dryads which, for the Antenorian Faun, announces only one girl to the Euganean groves."

units.la: Sola? Nondum enim erant Venetiæ, quibus solis jam lusibi & Imperium. Altinatium meminit Lapis, qui Feltriæ ad lævam, quum Cathedrale Templum ingrederis: C. FIRMIO . C . F MENEN. RVFINO EQ. PVB. LAVREN. LAV DEC. FLAMIN. PATRONO COLLEGIORVM . FABR CENT. DENDR. FELTRIÆ ITEM. QVE. BERYENS COLLEG FABR . ALTINATIVM PATRONO
units.tr: "Only"? For Venice did not yet exist, to which alone the sea-lagoons already belonged as their rule. A stone that mentions the people of Altinum is seen at Feltre on the left as you enter the cathedral church: "To Gaius Firmius Rufinus, son of Gaius, of the Menenian tribe, equestrian, of the Lavrentine tribe, decurion, flamen, patron of the colleges of craftsmen, the Feltrians likewise, and the Beryensian college of craftsmen of Altinum, to their patron."

units.la: Deletum ab Attila, & ob ejus interitum ædificatum fuisse in proxima Insula Torcellum, notant Ioannes Candidus libro III, Gregorius Amalcus Aquileiensi Hist. & alij.
units.tr: That Torcellum was destroyed by Attila, and that after his death it was built on the nearby island, is noted by Giovanni Candido in book III, by Gregorio Amalcus in his History of Aquileia, and by others.

units.la: Inter Silin & Musonum Castellum jacet, quod vulgo di Novale, frequens & nobile.
units.tr: Between the Silis and the Musonus lies a castle, commonly called di Novale, populous and noble.

units.la: Silin ascendenti Tarvisium occurrit, vulgo Trevise. Urbs ædificijs splendida opibusque potens, editiore jacet loco, in Campo spatiosissimo, amne Sili divisa: Fontium amœnitate salubritateque stupenda: antiqui sæculi Scriptoribus non nominata; ideoque non magni ævi. Primam ejus memoriam habent Gothorum Historiæ. Cives humanitate sunt singulari, ingenijs igneis, quæque percipiendis litteris, mercaturæ, aliisque honestis studijs promptissima. Episcopatus floret dignitate. Nobilitavit hanc Vrbem ortu suo Totilas Gothorum rex, cujus pater ejus situ supra modum capiebatur. Genuit item, praeter alios, Benedictum xi P. M. & Ponticum Virunium, Virum Latinis Graecisque litteris doctissimum, uti scripta probant. Post Gothos sedem hic suam posuerunt Langbardorum Marchiones, unde toti Regioni Marka Trevisina nomen inditum, ut initio capitis dictum. Pressa deinceps Actiolini tyrannide, Imperatorum Italiaque Regum, inde Carrarienfium, hinc Scaligerorum, postremo Venetorum subdita est imperio & potestati. Videndi Paullus Diaconus lib. v Hist. Langbard. Merula lib. vi & viii Histor. Vicecomit. Candidus lib. vi & vii Com. Aquileiens. Corius parte iii, Taurellus Sarayna lib. ii; Andreas Mocenicus, Leander Albertus, & alij. Magna hic Agrorum est ubertas, ingons rei pecuariae studium, copia tritici optimi, unde panis confit candidissimus) Vini nobilissimi, aliarumque rerum admiranda. Facius Vbertus libro iii, Cantico ii: Nei trovamo Trevíso nel camino, Che da chiare Fontane tutta ride; Et dal piacer d'Amor, che quivi è sino. Il suo contado la Piava recide, E' l Silio: è ciascun d'essi alcuna volta A chi li passa per gran piova uccide. Questa per se il Venetiano l'ha tolta.
units.tr: On the way up the Silis one meets Treviso, commonly called Trevise. The city, splendid in its buildings and powerful in its wealth, lies on higher ground, in a very spacious plain, divided by the river Silis. It is remarkable for the pleasantness and healthiness of its springs. It is not named by writers of ancient times, and so it is not of great antiquity. The first mention of it is found in the histories of the Goths. The citizens are of singular courtesy, of fiery talent, and most ready for learning, commerce and other honourable pursuits. The bishopric flourishes in dignity. This city was made famous by the birth of Totila, king of the Goths, whose father was held in extraordinary esteem for his position. It also produced, among others, Benedict XI, supreme pontiff, and Pontico Virunio, a man most learned in Latin and Greek letters, as his writings prove. After the Goths, the Lombard margraves established their seat here, whence the whole region received the name March of Treviso, as was said at the beginning of the chapter. Then, oppressed by the tyranny of Ezzelino, it was subject to the rule and power of the emperors and kings of Italy, then of the Carraresi, then of the Scaligers, and finally of the Venetians. See Paul the Deacon, book V of the Lombard History; Merula, books VI and VIII of the Histories of the Visconti; Candido, books VI and VII of the Commentaries on Aquileia; Corio, part III; Taurellus Sarayna, book II; Andreas Mocenicus, Leander Albertus, and others. Here there is great fertility of the fields, a remarkable zeal for cattle-breeding, an abundance of the best wheat, from which the whitest bread is made, and of the most noble wine, and other things of admirable quality. Fazio degli Uberti, book III, canto II: "We find Treviso on the way, which laughs with clear fountains all round, and with the delight of love, which is there without limit. The Piave cuts through its countryside, and the Sile; and each of them at times kills those who cross them in heavy rain. This the Venetian has taken for himself."

units.la: Supra Tarvisium haud procul Silis fonte Castellum jacet Casa Corba.
units.tr: Just above Treviso, not far from the source of the Sile, lies the castle of Casa Corba.

units.la: Piavis inde sequitur fluvius, qui Priscis Anaxus, ut supra docui. Objecta visitur faucibus ejus Insula Aequilis, in qua quondam Aequilium fuit Opidum, ab Heraclianis conditum, ubi hodie Citta Nova, teste Leandro; vel, uti censent M. Niger & Iulius Faroldus, Iesolo. Fuit eodem situ quomdam & Heraclia, cujus auctores Concordienses & Altinates, post suarum urbium cladem. Desertum fuit utrumque Opidum tempore Pipini, Italiae Regis, à Patre Karolo Magno cum validis copijs in Venetos missi. Tunc enim illi, ut belli calamitates declinarent; adsumtis suis omnibus, Venetias migrarunt. Consulendi Blondus & Sabellicus. Aequilium inde & Heraclia à Pipino occupata, post autem ab Hunnis cremata, hodie paucis vix vestigijs se produnt. Ab unam Anaxi vel Plavis ripam Opida se offerunt, quae vernacule Venetto, Limina, Aquorio; & in excelsis montibus Feltro, quod Latine scribentibus Feltrium, Antonino (qui Venetiae tribuit) Feltria: Episcopatus gaudet dignitate; Victorini, qui cum alijs eximius Latinae linguae restaurator, patria. Feltrinos habet Cassiodorus lib v. Var. qui Fertrini Plinio lib. iii cap. xviii, inemendatius. Altius inter montes juxta Plavem parvum quidem, sed nitidum conspicitur Opitū, quod vulgo Cividad di Belluno. Ulterius sunt Perarolo, Fieve, Valle, Bastagne, Cadore, Zolte, Lorentaga (Laurentiacum Latinis) Tre Ponti, Aurono, Comeri. Ad ripam Plavis alteram Opida sunt Madino & Vettoro: supraque ad Calori, qui Plinio Varamus, in Anaxo ostium, Tefeca; dein Belluno, quod Plinio lib. iii, cap. xviii Belunum; Ptolemaeoi Civitas Episcopatus jure nobilis.
units.tr: The river next to follow is the Piave, which the ancients called Anaxus, as I showed above. Opposite its mouth lies the island of Aequilis, where there was once a town, Aequilium, founded by the Heraclians. Today it is Citta Nova, according to Leandro, or, as M. Niger and Iulius Faroldus think, Iesolo. Heraclia was once in the same place, and its founders were the people of Concordia and Altinum, after the ruin of their own cities. Both towns were deserted in the time of Pepin, King of Italy, whom his father Charlemagne sent against the Venetians with strong forces. The inhabitants, to escape the miseries of war, took all their belongings and migrated to Venice. Blondus and Sabellicus should be consulted. Aequilium and Heraclia, occupied by Pepin and later burned by the Huns, now show scarcely a few traces. On the one bank of the Anaxus or Plave there appear towns, which in the vernacular are called Venetto, Limina, Aquorio; and high in the mountains Feltro, which writers in Latin call Feltrium, and which Antoninus (who assigns it to Venetia) calls Feltria. The bishopric enjoys distinction there; it was the homeland of Victorinus, who, with others, was an outstanding restorer of the Latin language. Cassiodorus in book v of the Variae has Feltrinos, while Pliny in book iii, chapter xviii, has the less correct Fertrini. Higher up among the mountains, beside the Plave, a small but neat town is seen, which commonly goes by the name Cividad di Belluno. Further on are Perarolo, Fieve, Valle, Bastagne, Cadore, Zolte, Lorentaga (Laurentiacum to Latin writers), Tre Ponti, Aurono, Comeri. On the other bank of the Plave are the towns Madino and Vettoro; and higher up, at Calori, which Pliny calls Varamus, at the mouth of the Anaxus, is Tefeca; then Belunum, which Pliny in book iii, chapter xviii, calls Belunum, a city of Ptolemy, noble by the right of a bishopric.

units.la: Ad Liquentiam venio flumen, cujus ripis adsident hinc Turritium; inde, ubi Muteca ipsi miscetur, Opitergium. Sic Tacito, Plinioque; o' Ὀπίτεργον Ptolemaeo dicitur, quod appellatione corruptiore Oderfo. Ἐπίτεργον legitur emendatius apud Strabonem libro v, quum Ὀπίτεργον sit scribendum, monente etiam Cl. V. Isaaco Casaubono. Meminit antiquus Lapis: L. ARRIVS. T. F SEX. VIR OPITERGI SIBI. ET. SVIS T. F. I
units.tr: I come to the river Liquentia, on whose banks lie Turritium on one side and, on the other, where the Muteca joins it, Opitergium. So Tacitus and Pliny call it; Ptolemy calls it Opitergon [Ὀπίτεργον], which by a more corrupt name is Oderfo. Epiterghon [Ἐπίτεργον] is read more correctly in Strabo, book v, though Opiterghon [Ὀπίτεργον] should be written, as the distinguished Isaac Casaubon also advises. An ancient inscription mentions it: L. ARRIVS. T. F. SEX. VIR. OPITERGI. SIBI. ET. SVIS. T. F. I.

units.la: Opitergini Coloni memorantur apud Lucanum in Pharsalicis libro iii: Hic Opiterginis moles onerata Colonis Constitit. Refert Cæsar Opitergines sibi necem in suis navibus adferre maluisse, quam in Pompei venire potestatem. Opitergium ab Attila subversum tradit Blondus libr. 11 Histor. instauratum deinde Rotarem Langbardorum Regem cremasse, norant Paullus Diaconus lib. 1111 Histor. Langbard. & Sabellicus lib. 111 de situ Vrb. Venet. quorum etiam ille lib. v, Rerum Langbardic. hic autem lib. v, de Antiq. Aquil. indicant ab Grimoaldo excisum. Vestigia superfuni veteris fortunæ, à me visa, quum hæc loca peragrarem. Opitergini Montes Portusque sunt apud Plinium.
units.tr: The colonists of Opitergium are mentioned by Lucan in book iii of the Pharsalia: "Here, weighed down by the mass of the Opitergian colonists, it came to a halt." Caesar reports that the Opitergines preferred to bring death upon themselves in their own ships rather than fall into Pompey's power. Blondus, in book ii of his Histories, says that Opitergium was overthrown by Attila; Paul the Deacon, in book iv of his History of the Lombards, and Sabellicus, in book iii of his work on the situation of the city of Venice, record that it was afterwards restored and then burned by Rothari, King of the Lombards; Paul in book v of his Lombard Affairs, and Sabellicus in book v of his work on the antiquities of Aquileia, state that it was destroyed by Grimoald. I myself saw remains of its former fortune when I travelled through these places. The Opitergini Montes and Portus are mentioned by Pliny.

units.la: Iuxta Moreci scaturiginem Conegianum jacet; Opidum frequens, rebusque ad vitam necessariis abundans.
units.tr: Near the spring of the Moreco lies Conegianum, a busy town, abounding in the necessities of life.

units.la: Succedit ad Orientalem Liquentiæ ripam Ostium Meduni, ad quem una quidem ripa, quæ vulgo audiunt Colveri, Pordonone (Latinis Portus Naonis) altiusque Prata, & intus Porcighe, quod cum Brognara, haud procul inde, Comitum Porcilianorum patrimonium, Sacile, Opidum ditissimum, splendidisque ornatum ædificiis: altera vero Portus Eufakesus, Civitonium, & ulterius inter montes Castrum non ignobile Sera-Vallis, celebris armorum bellicorum officina; Opidum opibus populique frequentia cum multis Italiæ Civitatibus committendum. Dextrorsum incedenti inter Colles mille ab Seravalle passibus Ceneda occurrit, quam Ἀξιδες Ptolemæi censet Cynthius, cujus alumnus; Acedensem inde se nominans.
units.tr: On the eastern bank of the Liquentia comes the mouth of the Meduno. On one bank are the places commonly called Colveri, Pordonone (Portus Naonis to Latin writers) and, further up, Prata; and inland Porcighe, which, together with Brognara not far from there, was the patrimony of the Counts of Porcia; and Sacile, a very wealthy town, splendidly adorned with buildings. On the other bank is Portus Eufakesus, Civitonium, and further on, among the mountains, the not unimportant fortress Sera-Vallis, a famous workshop of weapons of war, a town to be compared in resources and population with many cities of Italy. Going to the right, between hills, a thousand paces from Seravalle, Ceneda comes into view, which Cynthius thinks is the Axides [Ἀξιδες] of Ptolemy, and of which he was a native; hence he calls himself Acedensem.

units.la: Memoria ejus apud Agathiam libro 11 & Paullum Diaconum in Langbardicis non semel. Cenita est apud Fortunatum in Vita D. Martini. Episcopum habet, penes quem Civile etiam loci Imperium. Cenetensis Episcopi in Istria (quæ vicina Venetiæ) meminit Synodis vi Constantinopolitana. Itinere ab Sera-Valle Sacilem versus Cordiniarum adparet, monti inlocatum, insigne Propugnaculum.
units.tr: It is mentioned by Agathias in book ii, and by Paul the Deacon in his Lombard history more than once. Cenita is mentioned by Fortunatus in the Life of St Martin. It has a bishop, in whose hands is also the civil government of the place. A Cenetensis bishop in Istria (which is near Venetia) is mentioned at the sixth Synod of Constantinople. On the road from Seravalle towards Sacile, Cordiniarum appears, placed on a hill, a conspicuous stronghold.

units.la: Sequitur in ripa Liquentiæ Motta, Castellum non magnum, sed frequens, quæ Motta Sabellico libro viii, Ennead. xi, notum natalibus Hieronymi Leandri, Cardinalis. Intus ad eundem fluvium, supra Mottam, Pratina, Penegaia, Lamiduna, Prodolo, Cusani, Zopola.
units.tr: On the bank of the Liquentia follows Motta, a small but populous castle, which Motta Sabellicus, in book viii of the eleventh Ennead, notes as the birthplace of Hieronymus Leander, Cardinal. Inland, along the same river, above Motta, are Pratina, Penegaia, Lamiduna, Prodolo, Cusani, Zopola.

units.la: Ad Amnem Limenem, qui Limes, ut alibi à me dictum, inter Markam Tarvisinam & Forum Iulium, Concordia rudera monstrantur in æde S. Stephani paucissimisque tugurijs. Nota est Plinio, Pomponio Melæ, Antonino; Kornophia Ptolemæo. Apud Strabonem libro v pro ἀχὴ ἰφδία, vel saltem ἰφδία, reponendum Κερνοφδία. Legendus de ejus excidio Blondus libro 11 & 111. Supra Concordiam ad eundem fluvium Castellum est Sextium, vernacule Seito.
units.tr: At the river Limene, which is the Limes, as I have said elsewhere, between the March of Treviso and the Forum Iulii, the ruins of Concordia are shown in the church of St Stephen and in a few hovels. It is known to Pliny, Pomponius Mela and Antoninus; Ptolemy calls it Kornophia. In Strabo, book v, instead of akhē iphdia [ἀχὴ ἰφδία], or at least iphdia [ἰφδία], Kernophdia [Κερνοφδία] should be read. Blondus, in books ii and iii, should be read about its destruction. Above Concordia, on the same river, is the castle Sextium, in the vernacular Seito.

units.la: CAPVT XXXVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXVII.

units.la: Forum Iulij.
units.tr: Forum Iulii.

units.la: QVÆ in Nova, eaque planiore & ab montibus liberiore Italia, Meridionaliora versus sunt Provinciæ, percurri: pandunt se jamnunc ad Borealiorem plagam cis Tergestinum quidem Sinum Forum Iulii; ultra vero, Istria. Tete
units.tr: The provinces I have described lie further south in New Italy, which is flatter and freer of mountains. Now they open toward the northern region: on this side of the Gulf of Trieste lies Forum Iulii, and beyond it, Istria.

units.la: Nomen huic Regioni vel ab Foro-Iulio, urbe primaria, uti Blondus censet lib.vııı Histor. vel, ut alij volunt, ab Iulio Cæsare, qui aliquot Legiones hac adversus Germanos duxerit, cujus rei monimentum ferunt ostendi in marmore antiquo, quod in monte Crucio. Italis hodie Friuli; Germanis, Friaul: Venetis alijsque Patria nuncupatur. Caussam indicant Candidus lib.ı & Amalæus in Aquil. Commentar. Aquileiensem etiam appellatam fuisse ab Aquileia Metropoli, paret ex Historijs.
units.tr: The region takes its name either from Forum Iulium, its chief city, as Blondus thinks in book 8 of his Histories, or, as others hold, from Julius Caesar, who led several legions here against the Germans. A memorial of this is said to be shown on an ancient marble in Monte Crucio. Today the Italians call it Friuli, the Germans <bl>Friaul</bl>, and the Venetians and others call it Patria. Candidus in book 1 and Amaseo in his Aquileian Commentaries give the reasons. That it was also called Aquileiensis after its metropolis, Aquileia, appears from the histories.

units.la: Regio est ex distributione Augusti xviii. Fines illi apud Leandrum & Candidum ab Ortu Istria; ab Aquilone, Montes Iapidij: qua Occasus, Alpes Vindelicæ Noricæque; qua Auster, Sinus Hadriaticus.
units.tr: By Augustus' division it is the eighteenth region. According to Leander and Candidus its boundaries are: on the east, Istria; on the north, the Iapydian mountains; on the west, the Vindelician and Noric Alps; on the south, the Adriatic gulf.

units.la: Tradit idem Leander, incipere à planicie,quæ mari adpolita,moxque paullatim crescere in Colles, tandem in montes altissimos evchi; qui propemodum undique fines adeo claudunt, ut eadem planities, montium jugis vallata, tamquam muro, Theatrum videatur, faucibus autem unis pateat, per quas, uti Porta Sontij flumi-nis trajectu,ab Tarvisio aditur.
units.tr: The same Leander relates that it begins as a plain lying close to the sea, which soon gradually rises into hills and finally climbs into very high mountains. These enclose its borders almost on every side, so that the plain, walled in by the mountain ridges as if by a wall, looks like a theatre. It opens only through a few narrow passes, one of which is the Porta Sontii, crossing the river, and from Tarvisium it is entered through this.

units.la: Beant Regionem Cœlum temperatum; Aer salubris; Campi lati, irrigui, fructuumque omnigenorum fertiles: Prata nitidissima; Pascua pecoribus gratissima; item Vites vina generantes generosissima,etiam Plinio celebrata laudataque libro xiiii, cap.vi; Silvæ quoque tam materia cædenda, quam Venationibus munificæ; Montes Metallorum, Marmorumque variorum,nec non preciosorum lapidum feraces: & præter hæc omnia Portus quamplurimi.
units.tr: The region enjoys a temperate sky and healthy air. Its fields are wide and well watered, fertile in every kind of fruit. Its meadows are very bright, its pastures most pleasing to livestock. It also has vines that yield very fine wines, celebrated and praised by Pliny in book 14, chapter 6. Its forests are generous both for timber to be cut and for hunting. Its mountains are rich in metals, various marbles and precious stones. And besides all these, it has very many harbours.

units.la: Indigenæ ad humanitatis artes, Mercaturam, aliaque honesta studia aptissimi. Foro-Iulienses Transpadani leguntur apud Plinium lib. iii natur. Histor. cap. xviii. Inhabitarunt primum Euganei, inde successu temporis Veneti, mox Galli; uti in Marka Trevisina demonstravi: postea sub Populi Romani fuit imperio, cujus majestate inclinante in Langobardorum venit potestatem. Ijs successerunt Imperatores, his Berengarij; quibus excisis in ditionem redijt Imperij Romani. Donavit bonam ejus portionem Aquileiensi Ecclesiæ Otho Imperator; reliquamque cum Istria Conradus. Fecerunt tandem sui juris Veneti, circa annum cıɔ ccccxx; qui hodieque ibi dominantur; licet pleraque Comitibus, Dominisque subtiç peculiaribus. Consulendi Paulus Diaconus lib. v Hist. Langobard. Candidus lib. iii, v, vii, viii Comment. Aquil. Amalæus, Sabellicus lib. ix Ennead. ix, & alij.
units.tr: The natives are very well suited to the liberal arts, to trade and to other honourable pursuits. The Forum Iulienses Transpadani are mentioned in Pliny, Natural History book 3, chapter 18. The Euganei first inhabited it, then in the course of time the Veneti, and soon the Gauls, as I have shown in the Marca Trevisana. Afterwards it was under the rule of the Roman people, and when their majesty declined it came into the power of the Lombards. The Emperors succeeded them, and the Berengars succeeded the Emperors; when these were destroyed it returned to the dominion of the Roman Empire. Emperor Otto gave a good part of it to the Church of Aquileia, and Conrad gave the rest together with Istria. Finally the Venetians made it their own, about the year 1420, and they still rule there today, though most places are subject to counts and lords with their own peculiar rights. On this see Paulus Diaconus, Lombard History book 5; Candidus, Aquileian Commentaries books 3, 5, 7 and 8; Amaseo; Sabellicus, Ennead 9, book 9; and others.

units.la: Ut specialioribus explicandis me accingam; Ad Orientalem Limenis, quem limitem antea dixi inter Markam Tarvisinam & Forum Iulium, ripam Portus Grauariae inveniтur; Plinio libro natur. Hist. iii, cap. xvii Portus Romatinus. Romatianæ Civitatis Episcopum Niceam nominant Vsuardus in Martyrologio ad ix Kalendas Iulij, & Honorius Augustodunensis. Romatinum Plinio Carnorum fluvius est, qui hodie omnium doctorum judicio Timavus appellatione notus. Ulterius deinde Sumaga: & in adversa amnis ripa Cordeva: utrinque in mediterraneis Prodolo.
units.tr: To explain the more specific places, I will now set about it. On the eastern bank of the Limes, which I said earlier is the boundary between the Marca Trevisana and Forum Iulii, lies the Port of Grauaria. Pliny, Natural History book 3, chapter 17, mentions the Portus Romatinus. The bishop of the city of Romatia they call Nicea: Usuard in his Martyrology on the ninth day before the Kalends of July, and Honorius of Autun. The Romatinus of Pliny is the river of the Carni, which today, by the judgment of all learned men, is known by the name Timavus. Further on is Sumaga, and on the opposite bank of the river Cordeva; inland on both sides is Prodolo.

units.la: Tiliaventa sequuntur inde flumina duo, quorum Major, vernacule nunc Taiamenta; Minus, Stella; ut tuo loco dixi. Ripam Majoris Occidentalem legenti occurrunt S. Vitus supraque in mediterraneis Cafani, Zopola, Falcajure: & in montibus Splimbergum, natura loci opereque munitissimum altius Castel Nuovo: Orientalem autem, Tfina, Opidum dives, frequensque, remotius, Matabie, Farmo, Farcoda sotto, supra, Belgrado; ulteriusque Codroipo, & Cucagna; inde in arduo difficilique monte nobilissimum Opidum S. Danielis: juxta fontem denique turris Castellum Dugnano.
units.tr: After the Tiliaventum come two rivers. The larger is now called vernacularly Taiamenta, the smaller Stella, as I said in its place. On the western bank of the larger, as you travel, you meet St. Vitus, and further inland above it Cafani, Zopola and Falcajure. In the mountains lies Spilimbergum, most strongly fortified by nature and by works, and higher up Castel Nuovo. On the eastern bank lies Tfina, a rich and populous town, and further off Matabie, Farmo and Farcoda sotto, and above it Belgrado. Further on are Codroipo and Cucagna. Then on a steep and difficult mountain is the very noble town of S. Daniele; and near the spring, finally, the castle of Dugnano with its tower.

units.la: Stellae, de quo monui, margini adpositum est Palatiolum. Opidum non inhonestum; supraque juxta Stagnum Cornarum, alivd vernacule Marano, quod frequentia divitiisque clarum. Varanum Sabellicus, Marianum Candidus putant antiquis dictum. Ego, quod ingenue fateor, neutrum apud probatos Scriptores legi: Marauvi quidem apud Ptolemaeum est, sed Promontorium & Urbs Corticae. Marianum diu ab Venetis possessum, post cladem Abduanam dolo probitam est Maximiliano Caesari. Quum rursus fraude ceperint Venetii quidam exules, accedente iis Petre Strozza, tandem Senatus Veneto, magna pecunia celerunt. Secus flagnum ad amnem, qui huc defluit. Caorle est; in ipsis autem aestuariis insula Gradus, cui quondam Urbem cognominem fuisse aedificatam ab Aquileiensibus, post vastatam ab Attila patriam, indeque Nova Aquileia appellatione insignitam. & ibidem Aquileiensem Ecclesiam auctoritatem prius & jus Primatus habuisse, feribunt, praeter Blondum, Volterranus libro 1111 Comment. Vrbanor. & Candidus lib. iii & iv Comment. Aquil. Gradus Vrbs, maximis saepe calamitatibus adfecta, infrequentius hoc tempore habitatur.
units.tr: Next to the Stella, of which I warned, is placed Palatiolum, a town of no little repute. Above it, near the Lake of the Cornari, is another town, called Marano in the vernacular, famous for its population and riches. Sabellicus thinks it was called Varanum in ancient times, and Candidus Marianum. I freely confess that I read neither name in approved writers. Marauvi does occur in Ptolemy, but as a promontory and city of Corticae. Marianum was held for a long time by the Venetians; after the defeat at Adda it was won by trickery by Emperor Maximilian. When some Venetian exiles took it again by fraud, with Pietro Strozzi joining them, the Venetian Senate finally recovered it at great expense. Along the lake, toward the river that flows down here, is Caorle. In the estuaries themselves is the island of Grado. A city of the same name is said to have been built there by the Aquileians, after their homeland was laid waste by Attila, and it was marked with the name New Aquileia. Besides Blondus, Volaterranus in book 4 of his Commentaries on Urban Matters and Candidus in books 3 and 4 of his Aquileian Commentaries write that the Church of Aquileia first held authority and the right of primacy there. Grado, a city often struck by very great calamities, is now inhabited less frequently.

units.la: Ad Tiliaventum magni sternuntur Campi, quibus insidet Vrbs nobilis Vtinum, vulgo Udene. Germanis Weyden. Conditum hoc Opidum volunt apud Leandrum Albertum quidam ab Austrasiis, quod Austriae Duces diu hunc tractum possiderint: alii Attilam, Hunnorum Regem, ejus auctorem tradunt; addentes Hunnorum potius appellandum: quidam ab Vdinus, Scythiae apud Plinium populis, in haec loca profecti factum nocant, eamque ob causam Vdinum nuncupandum: nonnulli denique prisca adferunt originis, argumento cum Arcis ab Iulio Caesare refectae, nomenque ejusdem latis; tum multarum, quae hic indies inveniuntur, Antiquitatum. Aliorum opiniones praetereo. Arbitratur tandem ipse Leander, post indicatas variorum sententias, antiquum esse Opidum, ejusque mentionem fieri apud Plinium duobus locis, lib. iii natur. Histor. cap.xix, & lib. xxxv, cap.xiii sed priore Utina legitur; posteriore, Mutina: priore, mihi facile persuaderim vitiose scriptum Utinum, pro Vtina, praecipue quum ex Venetis haec Urbs interijse tradatur: loco posteriore, quod Mutina litteris omnibus exprimatur, nobilia vasa clarissimae Vrbi administranda non censeo. Niger credit Ptolemaei alioquin Forum Iulium esse: non bene, ut ex sequentibus parebit. Vtinum Montem dicit se vidisse Otto Frisingensis libro 1111 ab Attilae militibus in modum aggeris comportatum in obsidione Aquileiae: quem alii ab Iulio Caesare factum perhibent. Quidquid itaque faciendum sit de prima origine, Vrbs est ampla & magnifica; rebus omnibus necessariis affluens. Ambitus ejus milliarium est quinque. Claros viros genuit non paucos. Vtinense fuerunt Leonardus, Petrus Cavalcantius, Benedictus, Parisius, Franciscinus, Thomas & Leonardus 11, omnes ex Praedicatorum familia, Theologi: Iacobus Turrianus, & Antonius Bredus, Iurisconsulti: Paullus ex Eremitanorum Ordine, Logicis & Philosophicis scriptis clarus: Iacobus Candidus, Scriptor Aquileiensium Commentariorum, quae ab Gregorio Amasaeo magna parte sunt aucta. Gregorii filius fuit Romanus, Bononiae Professor Artium Humanitatis, qui multa edidit. Subverta Aquileia circa Friderici 11 Imperat. tempora migrasse scribunt huc Candidus & Amatus Patriarchae: sub quibus crevit supra modum ex nobilissimis Italiae Familiis, quae domestica seditione pulsae, fortunis adsumtis, sedes ibi quietas legerunt, semperque habuerunt. Potentia Patriarcharum labante in Venetorum venit potestatem anno cio cccxx; quibus magna clade anno cio io ix adfectis, in Maximiliani hunc i lapsum est ditionem: dein mutato sæpius imperio, tandem ad Venetos redijt: in quorum tutela nunc tranquille quiescit.
units.tr: Over the Tiliaventum stretch great plains, on which sits the noble city of Udine, commonly called Udene. The Germans call it Weyden. Some, as Leander Albertus relates, hold that this town was founded by the Austrasians, because the Dukes of Austria held this tract for a long time. Others say that Attila, king of the Huns, was its founder, adding that it ought rather to be called Hunnorum. Some say that it was founded by people from Udinus, a Scythian people mentioned by Pliny, who had come to these parts, and that it should therefore be called Udinum. Some finally bring an ancient origin, citing the citadel rebuilt by Julius Caesar and the name derived from the same man, together with the many antiquities found here every day. I pass over the other opinions. Leander himself, after setting out the various views, judges that the town is ancient, and that it is mentioned by Pliny in two places: book 3, chapter 19, and book 35, chapter 13. In the former it reads Utina, in the latter Mutina. I could easily persuade myself that Utinum in the former is a corrupt writing for Utina, especially since this city is said to have perished at the hands of the Venetians. In the latter place, since Mutina is written out in full, I do not think the noble vessels should be assigned to this most famous city. Niger believes that it is otherwise Ptolemy's Forum Iulium, but not rightly, as will appear from what follows. Otto of Freising, in book 4, says that he saw Mount Utinum, heaped up like a mound by Attila's soldiers during the siege of Aquileia; others say Julius Caesar made it. Whatever must be thought about its first origin, the city is large and magnificent, abounding in all necessary things. Its circuit is five miles. It has produced not a few famous men. Natives of Udine include Leonardo, Pietro Cavalcanti, Benedetto, Parisio, Franceschino, Tommaso and Leonardo II, all of the Dominican order and theologians; Giacomo Turriano and Antonio Bredo, jurists; Paolo of the Order of Hermits, famous for his writings on logic and philosophy; and Giacomo Candido, writer of the Aquileian Commentaries, which were greatly enlarged by Gregorio Amaseo. Gregory's son was Romano, professor of the humanities at Bologna, who published many works. Writers say that when Aquileia was overthrown, around the time of Emperor Frederick II, the Patriarchs moved here, Candido and Amatus among them. Under them the town grew beyond measure with the most noble families of Italy, which, driven out by domestic strife, took their fortunes with them, chose peaceful seats here and always kept them. When the power of the Patriarchs declined, the town came under Venetian power in the year 1320. Struck by a great slaughter in 1509, it fell under the rule of Maximilian; then, after its government changed often, it returned at last to the Venetians, under whose protection it now rests in peace.

units.la: Supra Vtinum ad primos colles pergenti hæc se offerunt Opida, Fagnana, Villi Aira, Murgo, Mel, Brucas altitudque Pens, Colorede, Trigesimo, Taro. Paullo Diacono in Langbardicis ulterius inter montes Pranper & Cemona, quæ Glemona eidem Diacono, Blondoque & Sabellico.
units.tr: Going above Udine toward the first hills, these towns present themselves: Fagnana, Villi Aira, Murgo, Mel, Brucas, and the high Pens, Colorede, Trigesimo and Taro. Further among the mountains, in Paulus Diaconus's Lombard history, are Pranper and Cemona, which is Glemona to the same Diaconus, to Blondus and to Sabellicus.

units.la: Ad Tiliaventum dein est Osopum, quod eidem Diacono Osopium; & ulterius Venetionis Fines, vulgo Venzone, qui hoc tempore Venetorum, Ducumque Austriæ, Stitiæ & Carinthiæ terminus.
units.tr: From the Tilaventum onward lies Osopum, which the same Deacon calls Osopium. Further on are the Boundaries of Venetia, commonly called Venzone, which at this time marks the limit of the Venetians and of the Dukes of Austria, Styria and Carinthia.

units.la: Sequitur inde Aquileia. Sic Livio, Tacito, Plinio, Pomponio Melæ, Antonino, Itinerarii Tabulæ, aliis vocatur. Ἀκυλήια Straboni lib. iv & v, itemque Stephano, Ἀκυλήια, Ptolemæo; Ἀκυλεια, Eustathio: quæ Aquilegia volgo; Aglar Germanis. Hinc Aquileiense Sinus, Ptolemæo Eustathio & Stephano; qui Tergestinus Plinio; hodie Golfo di Trieste, ut alibi dictum. Romatiana Civitatem, cujus Episcopum Niceam nominat Vuardus, eandem esse cum Aquileia, censet Vir eruditionis summæ, infinitæque lectionis Baronius. Ortelius V. Cl. cum hic adsentio, Romatianam Civitatem eandem facit cum Romatino Plinij Portu, qui nunc Grauris, de quo supra. Dicta, ut quidam volunt, ab fontibus aquarum perennibus, quibus abundat; vel, ut alijs visum, ab Aquila, militari Romanorum Legionum Signo; vel, quæ nonnullis mens, ab Aquilone flienti, quem ferunt in Italiam venisse cum Antenore. Conditam ab Romanis memorat Strabo libro v, munitionis loco contra Barbaros. Livius libris xxxix & xi. Coloniam scribit Latinam in Agro Gallorum, deductam ab iii. Viris P. Scipione Nasica, C. Flaminio & L. Manlio Acidino: inde Fundis extra Vibem non paucis nomina adhuc Romana manere, sed corruptiora, docent Amasæus & Candidus. Sita ad Natisonem fluvium, Plinio in Decima est Italiæ Regione; Ptolemæo, in Carnorum Mediterraneis, in Agro Gallorum, Livio lib. xi; in Venetia, eidem lib. xxxix; ἐξω, quod mirum, τῶν Ἐτεικῶν ὀρῶν, Straboni lib. v: quibusdam vitium subesse putantibus. Distare ab Mari lx Stadia, indicat idem Strabo. Ab Urbe Roma Mediolanum numerantur apud Antoninum M.P. lxxxviii; inde vero Aquileiam cclx. Varia ducuntur apud Antoninum ab Aquileia huc illuc Itinera: propter celebritatem. Urbs enim olim fuit ampla, copiosa, mœnibus firmissima; Templis, magnifico Theatro, aliisque operibus publicis & privatis supra modum ornata. De ea Ausonius: Non erat ipse locus: merito tamen aucta recenti Nama inter claras Aquileia celeberis Urbes: Italis ad Illyricos objecta Colonia Montes; Mari Imbri, & Portus celeberrima.
units.tr: Next comes Aquileia. Livy, Tacitus, Pliny, Pomponius Mela, Antoninus and the Itinerary Tables call it by this name, among others. Strabo in books 4 and 5 gives it as Akyleia [Ἀκυλήια], as do Stephanus [Ἀκυλήια] and Ptolemy; Eustathius gives Akyleia [Ἀκυλεια]. In common usage it is Aquilegia, and among the Germans Aglar. Hence the Gulf of Aquileia, as Ptolemy, Eustathius and Stephanus call it, and the Tergestine gulf in Pliny; today it is the Golfo di Trieste, as I have said elsewhere. Baronius, a man of very great learning and wide reading, thinks that the Romatian City, whose bishop Vuardus names as Nicea, is the same as Aquileia. I agree with this, but the most learned Ortelius takes the Romatian City to be the same as Romatinum, the harbour of Pliny, which is now Grauris, as I said above. It is named, as some hold, from the perennial springs of aquarum with which it abounds; or, as others thought, from the Aquila, the military standard of the Roman legions; or, as some suppose, from the Aquilone (north wind) that blows there, which they say came into Italy with Antenor. Strabo in book 5 records that it was founded by the Romans as a stronghold against the barbarians. Livy in books 39 and 41 writes that a Latin Colony was led into the Land of the Gauls by the three commissioners, P. Scipio Nasica, C. Flaminius and L. Manlius Acidinus. Amasaeus and Candidus show that from this, many place names outside the city of Rome, still Roman but more corrupted, survive in the Friuli. It lies on the river Natiso; in Pliny it belongs to the tenth region of Italy, in Ptolemy to the inland parts of the Carni, and in the Land of the Gauls according to Livy book 41, and in Venetia according to the same Livy book 39. Strabo in book 5 says it lies outside the Etican mountains, which is surprising, and some think there is a fault in the text. Strabo also states that it is sixty stadia from the sea. Antoninus counts 88 miles from the City of Rome to Milan, and from there to Aquileia 260. Many roads run from Aquileia hither and thither, according to Antoninus, because of its fame. The city was once large, populous and very strongly walled, and it was adorned beyond measure with temples, a magnificent theatre and other public and private buildings. Ausonius writes of it: The place itself was nothing; yet Aquileia, rightly raised by recent renown, is numbered among the famous, celebrated cities: a colony set against the Illyrian mountains of Italy, a most famous port by the Imbrian sea.

units.la: Augustum amœnitate loci captum mensibus octo apud Aquileiam cum Conjuge habitasse, auctor est Suetonius; cumdemque hic controversias Herodis & Filiorum audisse, deque ejus judicasse, retert Iosephus. Quin & Tiberij aliorumque Imperatorum sæpe fuit domicilium: unde sensim tantum incrementi cum opibus, tum ædificiis est adepta, ut altera diceretur Roma. Hodie intrequens est Colonis, & ad solitudinem propemodum perducta, quæ quondam summo fuit splendore, summaque amplitudine. Fidem sequuta legitur constantissime (quod multis doceri potest exemplis) Imperij Romani usque ad Attila, Hunnorum Regis, tempora: à quo totum obsessa triennium magna Annonæ inopia laborans, tandem capta est & vastata, obtruncatis triginta fere septem hominum, qui in ea degebant, millibus: reliquis Gradus insulam fuga claplis. Post ab Narsete restituta, in Langbardorum aliquamdiu fuit potestate, usque ad Karoli Magni in Italiam adventum; ex quo Italiæ Regibus, deinde Imperatoribus parujt. Post sub ditione Patriarcharum, quos diligenter enumerat Leander Albertus, esse cœpit: ab ijs ad Venetos venit, sub quibus jam nunc pace alta & tranquillitate fruitur. Addam huc insignem Karoli Sigoni; locum libro i Historiæ de Regno Italiæ: Ecclesia, ait, Aquileiensis, cujus Patriarcha secundum a Pontifice locum obtinet, à Marco Evangelista, Petri Apostoli, & Hermæ a, Marci Discipulo, instituta, quum innocentissimos plerosque Antistites obtinuit semper; tum præsulos multos sanctitate homines tulit. Urbs ipsa, quum olim opibus gratia Populi Romani ac Principum, caeterea nobilitate aedificiorum ac Civium magnificentia floruisset: nihil tamen ex antiqua fortuna nisi nomen atque ipsam Patriarchale decus retinuit. Neque enim ab Attila, Hunnorum Rege, ex eo, licet Narsetis opera restituta, retinere Iacobarum celebritate frequentata a monachis fuit. Aquileia permultos genuit Viros illustres: in quis D. Syrus, quem D. Hermogoras Tiemensibus dedit Episcopum, attributis ipsi Collegis, Iuventio & Pompeio Diaconis, Chrysantio & Fortunato Presbyteris: Epiphanius, Tiemensis item Episcopus: Erasmus & Tecla Valentiniano nati, Martyres; Cromatius, ad quem multas scripsit Epistolas D. Hieronymus; Rufinus Sacerdos & Paulus Diaconus, Scriptis clari: Pius: P. M. Patriarchas, qui Sedem non solum pia cura, verum etiam ortu suo nobilitarunt, indicat, ut jam monui, cum aliis Leander Albertus. Scripsit de vetustate Aquileiae libros VI M. Antonius Sabellicus. Aquileiensia etiam Commentaria composuit Iacobus Candidus, quae Gregorius Amatacus multis additis insigniter auxit.
units.tr: Suetonius records that Augustus, captivated by the charm of the place, lived with his wife at Aquileia for eight months; and Josephus relates that he also heard the disputes between Herod and his sons there and gave judgment on them. Indeed Tiberius and other emperors often made it their home; and so it gradually gained as much growth in wealth as in buildings, until it was called a second Rome. Today it is thinly inhabited by colonists and has been reduced almost to a desert, though it was once of the greatest splendour and greatest size. It is read that it remained most faithful to the Roman Empire (as can be shown by many examples) until the time of Attila, King of the Huns. Besieged by him for three years and suffering a great shortage of food, it was at last taken and laid waste, and about 37,000 of the people who lived in it were slaughtered; the rest fled to the island of Grado. Afterwards it was restored by Narses, and for some time it was under the power of the Lombards, until the coming of Charlemagne into Italy; from then on it obeyed the Kings of Italy and later the Emperors. Afterwards it came under the rule of the Patriarchs, whom Leander Albertus lists carefully; from them it came to the Venetians, under whom it now enjoys deep peace and tranquillity. I shall add here the notable passage of Carlo Sigonio in book 1 of his History of the Kingdom of Italy: "The Church of Aquileia," he says, "whose Patriarch holds the second place after the Pope, was founded by Mark the Evangelist, and by Hermas, a disciple of Mark, with Peter the Apostle. Since it has always had most of its bishops of the most blameless life, so it has also produced many prelates of holiness. The city itself, once flourishing in wealth, in the favour of the Roman people and the princes, and in the nobility of its buildings and the magnificence of its citizens, has retained nothing of its former fortune but its name and the dignity of the Patriarchate. For it was not, after its destruction by Attila, King of the Huns, and although restored by the labour of Narses, kept in its former state..." and it was frequented by monks for the fame of the Holy Places. Aquileia produced many famous men: among them St Syrus, whom St Hermagoras gave to the Tiemensians as bishop, with the deacons Juventius and Pompeius, and the elders Chrysantius and Fortunatus, assigned to him as colleagues; Epiphanius, also bishop of the Tiemensians; Erasmus and Tecla, sons of Valentinian, martyrs; Chromatius, to whom St Jerome wrote many letters; Rufinus, a priest, and Paulus the Deacon, famous for their writings; Pius; and Patriarchs of the Pope, who ennobled the see not only by their pious care but also by their birth, as I have already said, Leander Albertus shows along with others. Marcus Antonius Sabellicus wrote six books on the antiquity of Aquileia. Jacobus Candidus also composed the Aquileian Commentaries, which Gregorius Amatacus greatly enlarged by many additions.

units.la: Supra Aquileiam Septemtrionem versus, inter montes ad Natisonem Civitas jacet, quae Forum Iulium Tacito non uno loco; Ptolemaeo; Castrum Iulense, Paullo Diacono: hodie vulgo Cividal d'Austria. Causam mutatae appellationis notat apud Leandrum Candidus libro II Comment. Aquileiens. Quum enim Vetus Forum Iulium primum a Theodorico Gothorum Rege, dein ab Cancano Pannonum Tyranno eversum esset, ut memoriae produnt Paullus Diaconus & Blondus: instauratum iterum ab Ilsemunda Austria, Luitprandi Langbardorum Regis Vidua, Cives in memoriam tanti beneficii Civitatem Austriae ab ea dixerunt. Iacet in faucibus Italiae loco natura munitissimo: Pontem habens in flumine percurrente lapideum. Ab ea universa Regioni nomen.
units.tr: North of Aquileia, among the mountains by the Natiso, lies a city which Tacitus in more than one place calls Forum Iulium, Ptolemy calls the Julian Camp, and Paulus the Deacon calls Castrum Iulense; today it is commonly called Cividal d'Austria. Candidus, in book 2 of his Commentaries on Aquileia, gives the reason for the change of name. For when the old Forum Iulium was first overthrown by Theodoric, King of the Goths, and then by Cancanus, tyrant of the Pannonians, as Paulus the Deacon and Blondus report, it was restored again by Ilsemunda of Austria, widow of Liutprand, King of the Lombards. In memory of so great a benefit the citizens named the city after her, Austria. It lies in the throat of Italy, in a place strongly fortified by nature, having a stone bridge over the river that runs through it. The whole region takes its name from it.

units.la: Sequuntur in Montibus Cuca, Pretesta, Attin, Cerigne, & Cucogne: haud procul inde ad Turrim Amnem Saffimbergo: secundum eumdem Turrim ad Alpes pergenti Saxognano occurrit; & prope fontem, Tapoco: descensu inde per Amnem offert se Dorso; Civitatisque vel Foro Iulij dextra Rosaccio & Cormona; mox S. Martino de Cirna.
units.tr: In the mountains follow Cuca, Pretesta, Attin, Cerigne and Cucogne. Not far from there, at the river Torre, is Saffimberg; following the Torre towards the Alps, one meets Saxognano; and near its source, Tapoco. Then, descending along the river, Dorso presents itself; and on the right of the city or the Forum Iulium, Rosaccio and Cormona; soon after, San Martino di Cirna.

units.la: Occidentaliore Sontij ripa sursum Propugnacula visuntur duo contra Turcarum excursiones ab Venetis exstructa Gradisca & Folsana; sic ab finitimis pagis terminata: posterius deleri coepit, metu Turearum cessante; prius etiamnunc colitur.
units.tr: On the western bank of the Isonzo, higher up, two fortresses built by the Venetians against the incursions of the Turks can be seen, Gradisca and Folsana; they are bounded in this way by the neighbouring villages. The latter began to be destroyed when the fear of the Turks ceased; the former is still inhabited.

units.la: Amne transito pandit se in ora maris nobile diversque Opidum praecelso in monte, quod vulgo Monte Falcone, ab Theodorico Gothorum Rege conditum, priusque Perruca notum appellatione: scribentibus Blondo libro III Hist. Sabellico lib. I. Ennead. VIII Candidoque & Amasaeo lib. III Comment. Aquilejens.
units.tr: When the river is crossed, a noble and famous town opens out on the seashore, on a very high mountain, which is commonly called Monte Falcone. It was founded by Theodoric, King of the Goths, and was earlier known by the name Perruca; this is recorded by Blondus in book 3 of his History, Sabellicus in book 1 of the Enneads 8, and Candidus and Amasaeus in book 3 of the Aquileian Commentaries.

units.la: A Monte Falconis juxta littus excelso in jugo munitum conspicitur Castellum Duinum: moxque in minore colle Molaunum; deinde Pucinum; Vino nobile, quod Plinius lib. XIII natur. histor. cap. VI in centura Vinorum summopere commendat.
units.tr: From Monte Falcone, along the shore, on a high ridge is seen the fortified castle of Duino; soon after, on a lower hill, Molaunum; then Pucinum, famous for its wine, which Pliny in book 14, chapter 6, of his Natural History highly commends among the rankings of wines.

units.la: Succedit ad littus Tergeste. Sic Caesari in Commentariis & Plinio vocatur: Tergestum, Tergeston Straboni lib. VII; Tergeston Ptolemaeo; Tergesta Lapidi, quem post dabo: Tergesta Stephano; Tergestaeorum urbs Diodoro & Dionysio: quod hodie Triefte. Sic dictum volunt, quod ter regiberit radicem, id est, ter fuerit subversum. Facius Vbertus lib. III, Cantico II. Vedi Triefte con le sue pendice, E al nome udio, che cosi era detto, Perche tre volte ha tratto la radice.
units.tr: Next on the shore is Tergeste. Thus it is called by Caesar in his Commentaries and by Pliny; Strabo in book 7 gives it as Tergeston [Τέργεστον], Ptolemy also as Tergeston; Stephanus gives it as Tergesta, as does an inscription I shall give later; Diodorus and Dionysius call it the city of the Tergestaeans [Τεργεσταίων]; today it is Trieste. They say it was so named because it had uprooted its root three times, that is, been overthrown three times. Fazio degli Uberti in book 3, Canto 2, of his Dittamondo: "You see Trieste with its slopes, and hear the name it bears, because three times it has torn up its root."

units.la: Plinius in decima locat Italiae Regione, ex distributione Augusti, Ptolemaeus in Istris, secus Maris Hadriatici flexum Strabo distare scribit Aquileia stadijs CLXXX; Plinius M. P. XXXIII. Columnam faciunt Romanorum Plinius & Ptolemaeus. Pertinent eo Inscriptiones duae, quarum
units.tr: Pliny places it in the tenth region of Italy, according to Augustus's division; Ptolemy places it among the Istrians, along the bend of the Adriatic Sea. Strabo writes that it is 180 stadia from Aquileia; Pliny says 33 miles. Pliny and Ptolemy make it a Roman colony. Two inscriptions relate to it, of which

units.la: 1. In ipso Opido in basi Turris Ecclesiæ S. Martyris:
units.tr: 1. In the town itself, on the base of the tower of the Church of S. Martyr:

units.tr: To the spirits of the dead. Quintus Caedius, son of Publius, sevir of Tergeste, of the Vinissa tribe; his wife Apusidia Q. P. Maxima, ... ; his daughter Secunda, Gaius's daughter; Gaius Caedius, son of Publius, his brother.

units.la: Tributariam Venetis fecit Henricus Dandalus ipsorum Dux; teste Blondo libro XVI Histor. Post in Austriæ Ducum fuit imperio usque ad annum MDVII, quo Venetis iterum subjecit Bartholomæus Alvianus: biennio post ad Austriacos est retracta. Episcopatus gaudet dignitate.
units.tr: Henry Dandolo, Doge of the Venetians, made it tributary to Venice, according to Blondus in Book XVI of his Histories. Afterwards it remained under the rule of the Dukes of Austria until 1507, when Bartholomew d'Alviano again subjected it to Venice; two years later it was taken back by the Austrians. It enjoys the dignity of a bishopric.

units.la: Senis ultra Tergestam millibus, etiam Plinij indicio, amnis est Formio, antiquus auctæ Italiæ terminus; de quo alibi. Risanus nunc audit; Mugilamque interfluit Opidum.
units.tr: Six miles beyond Trieste, as Pliny also indicates, is the river Formio, the ancient boundary of enlarged Italy; I shall treat of it elsewhere. It is now called the Risano, and the town of Muggia stands on it, washed by its waters.

units.la: In mediterraneis contra Duinum inter montes, haud procul Natisone, Goritia jacet. Sic hodie vocatur Opidum, quod judicio Leandri Alberti Iulium Carnicum Antonino & Ptolemæo. Alij de Iulio Carnico aliter statuunt. Faciunt inde Villacum Carinthiæ Opidum, in Alpibus situm, Aventinus & Pyramius; Zuglium, Simlerus; Velam vel Felam, ut Germani pronunciant, Lazius lib. XII Reip. Rom. Certe quum Plinius lib. V Nat. Hist. cap. XIX, Iulienses Carnorum in decima videatur collocare Italiæ Regione, atque adeo sub Istria complecti: Iulium Carnicum nulli loco magis convenit, quam Goritia. Amasæus libro de Venet. finib. Gorttiam notat, ubi quondam Noreia, quod Straboni Plinioque Taurisco rum Opidum. Noritiam notat Candidus lib. III Comment. Aquil. Goritia suos habet Principes, qui Ducibus Austriæ parent. Opidum est opibus & nobilitate clarum.
units.tr: Inland, opposite Duino, among the mountains not far from the Natisone, lies Gorizia. This town is so called today; but in the judgement of Leandro Alberti it is Iulium Carnicum of Antoninus and Ptolemy. Others hold different views about Iulium Carnicum. Aventinus and Pyramus make it Villach, a town of Carinthia situated in the Alps; Simler makes it Zuglio; Lazius, in Book XII of his Roman Commonwealth, makes it Vela or Fela, as the Germans pronounce it. Certainly, since Pliny in Book V of his Natural History, chapter 19, seems to place the Iulienses of the Carni in the tenth region of Italy, and so to include them under Istria, Iulium Carnicum agrees with no place better than Gorizia. Amasaeus, in his book on the boundaries of Venice, marks Gorizia as the place where Noreia once stood, which Strabo and Pliny call the town of the Taurisci. Candidus, in Book III of his Commentaries on Aquileia, marks it as Noritia. Gorizia has its own princes, who obey the Dukes of Austria. It is a town famous for its wealth and nobility.

units.la: Succedunt inde Grisfor, Rincan, Dorus, Cernice, Focewo; indeque supra Tergestam sub Alpibus Castel Nuovo, ultraque magnus Pagorum numerus.
units.tr: Next come Grisfor, Rincan, Dorus, Cernice and Focewo; and from there, above Trieste under the Alps, Castel Nuovo, and beyond it a great number of villages.

units.la: Adscribam hic iter, quod Antoninus ducit ab Arimino Aquileiam usque, ut ex eo cognoscamus quorundam locorum distantias, quæ non solum ad Flaminiam pertinent, Langbardiasque tam Cis-Padanam, quam Trans-Padanam, sed etiam ad Markam Tarvisinam & Forum Iulij, nobilissimas Italiæ Regiones; proximis capitibus à me explicatas. units.tr: I shall add here the route which Antoninus traces from Ariminum as far as Aquileia, so that from it we may learn the distances between certain places, which pertain not only to the Flaminian Way and to the Lombard lands on both sides of the Po, but also to the March of Treviso and Friuli, the most famous regions of Italy; I have explained them in the nearest chapters. Antoninus, Itinerary Table, common version: from Ariminum (Rimini) to Cesena, 20 miles; to Confluentes, 8; Cesena to Faenza, 24 miles; Carvia to Forlimpopoli, 7; Forum Cornelii to Forlì, 10; Forum Populi to Bologna, 24 miles; Forum Livii to Faenza, 10; Faventia to Seno river, 3; Sinnum river to Imola, 6; Forum Cornelii to Sillaro river, 7; Silarum river to Idice river, 7; Claterna to Bologna, 6; Isex river to Modena, 8; Bologna to Forum Gallorum, 17; Forum Gallorum to Modena, 8, a Roman city of 25 miles; Regium 18 miles; Parma 19 miles; Fidentiola, a village, 20 miles; Placentia 24 miles. Modena to Lepidus Regius, 17; Tannetum, 11; Parna (wrongly), 2; Fidentia, 15; Florentia, 10; Placentia, 15; Mediolanum, 20; Laus Pompeia, 36; Como ...; Bergamo, 33 miles. Bergamo, 20 (Modena, Regio, Tanedo, Parma, Fiorenzola, Piacenza, Lodi, Milan, Como, Bergamo). Near Cauriolum, Brescia; Lonato, or thereabouts; Sirmione; Verona; Vicenza; Padua. It makes for the mouth of the Sile, where traces lie; collapsed, it lies in the church of S. Stephen, with very few huts. Aquileia. Brescia to Sirmione, 18 miles, a stopping place; Verona, 27 miles; Vicenza, 34 miles; Padua, 27 miles; Altinum, 33 miles; Liquentia, 35. Brescia, 35; Ariolica, 13; Verona, 33; Vicenza, 23; Padua, 30; Altinum, 30; Concordia, 31 miles; Aquileia, 31 miles. Concordia, 30; Aquileia ...
