units.tr: CHAPTER XXXIIX.

units.la: Istria.
units.tr: Istria.

units.la: RESTAT in Nova, eaque pleniore Italia, versus ortum, ultra Tergestinum Sinum, Istria: Latinis Graecisque Scriptoribus satis nota; nomen hodie servans: Germanis Histerreich, quasi Istria Regnum, dicta. Iapydiam quondam fuisse nuncupatum, indicat non obscure Plinius lib. xxxii. Istria nominarunt, eodem notante, Colchi, Asiae populi; qui ad Argonautas persequendos missi feruntur ab Acera Rege. Perhibentur enim hi a Ponto Istrum ingressi, & Savi amnis alveo penitus invecti, navibus per iuga montium usque ad litus Maris Hadriatici comportatis, quum Argonautas nullibi reperissent, sive metu Regis, sive taedio longae navigationis, iuxta Aquileiam consedisse, Istriqué ex amnis nomine, quo ab mari concesserant, fuisse appellati. Ego huiusmodi coniecturas in medio relinquo; non minus, quam quae apud supposititium Catonem, aliosque cum sequutos, qui Istriam volunt appellatam ab Istro principe, quem Ianus, Italiae olim Imperator, in haec loca misisse fertur.
units.tr: Istria remains to be described, in the New and fuller Italy, towards the east beyond the Gulf of Trieste. It is well known to Latin and Greek writers and keeps its name today; the Germans call it Histerreich, as if it were "Istria Kingdom." That it was once called Iapydia Plinius clearly indicates, in Book 32. The Colchians, a people of Asia, named it Istria, as the same writer notes. They are said to have been sent out by King Aeetes to pursue the Argonauts. For they are reported to have entered the Ister from the Pontus and, carried far up the channel of the river Save, to have carried their ships over mountain ridges down to the shore of the Adriatic Sea. When they found the Argonauts nowhere, whether from fear of the king or weariness of the long voyage, they settled near Aquileia, and were called Istriqué after the name of the river by which they had come from the sea. I leave such conjectures aside, no less doubtful than those of the spurious Cato and others who followed him, who want Istria named after Istro, a prince whom Janus, once emperor of Italy, is said to have sent to these parts.

units.la: Peninsulae formam refert; pleraque, inter duos sinus Tergestinum & Carnarium, mari cincta Hadriatico: ab Septemtrione Alpibus munita Carnicis & Noricis; ab Occasu antequam in mare excurrere incipiat, Formionem habens amnem; Arsiam vero flumen, ab Ortu. Latitudo XL P. M; Ambitus, cxxii, ab Formione, quem dixi, ad Fanaticum usque Promontorium, vel initium Carnarij sinus angulum extensa.
units.tr: It has the shape of a peninsula. For the most part it is surrounded by the Adriatic Sea between the two gulfs, Trieste and Carnaro. On the north it is protected by the Carnic and Noric Alps; on the west, before it begins to jut out into the sea, it has the river Formione, and the river Arsia lies to the east. Its breadth is 40 Roman miles. Its circuit is 122 miles, stretching from the Formione, which I mentioned, to the Fanatic promontory, or the beginning of the corner of the Carnaro gulf.

units.la: Tota Regio asperior est; Collibus tamen potius, quam Montibus ornata: qui vini, olei, aliorumque fructuum feraces; Frumenti cæterorumq; Leguminum infœcundiores; exceptis Agris Piscino & Humago. Mons ibi est, qui Major vulgo benignus Herbarum Simplicium, quas avide extranei quæsitum huc properant Medici genitor. Salem Istria abunde præbet: Piscibus etiam dives, ob sinuum & Insularum, quæ conjacent, copiam. Ad D. Vincentium vastissimæ sunt Silvæ, Materia navibus fabricandis munificæ. Saxifodinæ ibi non inutiles. In Rovinienti Agro Marmor cæditur, quod Istricum dicitur, maximi per Italiam precij.
units.tr: The whole region is rather rugged, adorned with hills rather than mountains, which are fertile in wine, oil and other fruits, but less productive in grain and other pulses, except for the fields of Piscino and Humago. There is a mountain there which the natives call Major, the father of medicinal herbs, which foreign physicians eagerly seek and hasten here to gather. Istria supplies salt in abundance and is rich in fish because of the number of bays and islands lying off the coast. Near S. Vincenzo are very vast forests, generous in timber for building ships. The quarries there are not unimportant. In the territory of Rovigno marble is cut, called Istrian, of the highest value throughout Italy.

units.la: Incolæ rc sunt tenuiore; Venetis omnem negociationem ad se trahentibus. Istro-rum sæpe meminerunt Antiqui, Ennius, Livius, Florus, aliique, qui Istricum bellum describere.
units.tr: Its inhabitants are rather poor, since the Venetians draw all trade to themselves. The ancients often mention the Istrians: Ennius, Livy, Florus and others, who describe the Istrian war.

units.la: Luculentam Istriæ delineationem habet Cassiodorus lib. iv Variarum. Ejusdem Chorographiam scripsit Petrus Coppus.
units.tr: Cassiodorus, in Book 4 of the Variae, gives a splendid description of Istria. Petrus Coppus wrote a chorography of it.

units.la: Specialiora videamus. Per oram incedenti occurrit statim Iustinopolis, Vrbs Chersonesi primaria. Sic doctis vocatur, quæ vulgo Cabo d'Istria. Nomen prius ab Iustino Imperatore. Legendus Sabellicus lib. II. Ennead. VIII. Habent confirmandis ijs Incolæ Inscriptionem, non magni meo judicio ævi, quæ cum apud Leandrum & alios legitur; tum in Auctario V.C.L. Iusti Lipsij, qui ab Nic. Florentio profitetur se accepisse. D. N. CÆSAR. IVSTINVS. P. SAL. PIVS FELIX VICTOR AC TRIVMPHATOR SEMPER. AVGVST. PONT. MAX. FRANC. MAX. GOTTH. MAX. VANDALIC. MAX. COS. III. TRIB. VIII. IMP. V. CONSPICVAM HANC ÆGIDIS INSVLAM INTIMA ADRIATICI MARIS COMMODISS. INTERIECTAM VENERANDÆ PALLADIS SACRARIVM QVONDAM ET COLCHIDVM ARGONAVTARVM PERSECVTORVM QVIETEM OB GLORIAM PROPAGANDAM IMP. S. C. IN VRBEM SVI NOMINIS EXCEL LENTISS. NVNCVPANDAM HONESTISS P. P. P. DESIGNAVIT. FVNDAVIT, C. R. F. Q. ET GENTE HONES TISS. [illegible, ~6 letters] Posteriore deinceps nomine coepit dici, quod Foro Iulio egressis in capite adituque Regionis occurrat. Parvam occupat Insulam, quae pallibus longa mille, latitudine modica: trino telii actu divisa ab Continenti, cui iungitur Pontibus, qui variatiles. Arcem habet in medio, quatuor munitam turribus. Castellum vocant Leontium. Blondus libro vii Histor. a Bucchino Gallo quondam crematam tradit quo auctore, mihi non constat. In Venetorum hodie est ditione. Ornamentum attulit Urbi non exiguum Petrus Paullus Tergestus, Vir doctissimus.
units.tr: Let us look at the more particular places. Going along the coast, the first town one meets is Iustinopolis, the chief city of the Chersonese. Learned writers so call it, but commonly it is Cabo d'Istria. The name was first given after the emperor Justin. Sabellicus, Book 2 of Ennead 8, should be read. The inhabitants support this with an inscription, not of great antiquity in my judgment, which is read both in Leander and others, and in the Auctarium of the most learned Justus Lipsius, who professes to have received it from Nicolaus Florentius: "Our lord Caesar Justinus, pious, fortunate, victor and triumphator, ever Augustus, pontifex maximus, conqueror of the Franks, Goths and Vandals, consul for the third time, tribune for the eighth time, imperator for the fifth time, having set apart this conspicuous island of Aegis, most conveniently placed in the innermost part of the Adriatic Sea, once a sanctuary of venerable Pallas and a refuge of the Colchian pursuers of the Argonauts, for the propagation of glory, by decree of the Senate, has designated that it be called by the name of our city, most excellent... founded it (C. R. F. Q.) and [the most honourable people] [illegible, about six letters]." Afterwards it began to be called by a second name, because it lies at the head and entrance of the region for those coming out of Forum Iulii. It occupies a small island, a thousand paces long and of moderate breadth, separated from the mainland by a triple channel and joined to it by bridges which can be moved. It has a citadel in the middle, fortified with four towers. They call the castle Leontium. Blondus, in Book 7 of his Histories, reports that it was once burned by the Gaul Bucchinus, though on what authority I do not know. Today it is under the rule of the Venetians. Petrus Paullus Tergestus, a most learned man, brought no small ornament to the city.

units.la: Succedit in ora quinto fere lapide Castellum Insula; Continenti Ponte lapideo nexum. Sequitur mox Tanum: Sic Graeci vocabant, notante Leandro, quod Itali ei Castellatum, & postea Castellerium: vulgo Castelier. Quingentis hinc passibus ad D. Simonem devenitur: inde milia quinque Tranum abest, ad collem montis: totidem hinc, Salvorium; parti propemodum intervallo Vinaceum in scopulo, qui marinis undis circumfusus. Ab Vinaco milliario duo numerantur ad D. Peregrinum; hinc ad D. Ioannem de la Corne passibus mille: totidemque dein, ad D. Laurentium vulgo di Dada: mox ad alterum lapidem ipsa Dada & ad terrium Civitas Nova, olim Almonta, uti censent Volaterranus Leander, & Dominicus Niger, sine Auctore.
units.tr: Next on the coast, about five miles on, comes the island of Castello, joined to the mainland by a stone bridge. Soon follows Tanum. The Greeks called it so, as Leander notes; the Italians called it Castellatum and later Castellerium, commonly Castelier. From here five hundred paces brings one to S. Simone. From there Tranum is five thousand paces away, at the foot of the hill; as far again from here is Salvore; at nearly the same distance is Vinaceum, on a rock surrounded by the waves of the sea. Two miles are counted from Vinace to S. Pellegrino; from here a thousand paces to S. Giovanni della Corna; and as many again to S. Lorenzo, commonly called di Dada. Soon, at the second milestone, comes Dada itself, and at the third the New City, formerly Almonta, as Volaterranus, Leander and Dominicus Niger think, though without citing any authority.

units.la: Post Quietum fluvium tria milia sunt ad Portum Cervium. Visitur quarto inde lapide Parentium Civitas. Sic Plinio dicitur, Antonino & Itinerariis Tabulae; Ravennae, Ptolemaeo & Stephano: quod hodie Parenzo. Iacet in Peninsula, moenibus turribusque egregie munitum: Portu maximis excipiendis navibus opportuno. Direptum flammisque exustum ab Genuensibus, Venetorum hostibus, anno cIↄcccc LIV, produt Corius parte III.
units.tr: Past the river Quieto, three thousand paces bring one to Porto Cervio. Four miles on is seen the city of Parentium. So it is called by Pliny, by Antoninus in the Itinerary Tables, and by Ravenna; by Ptolemy and Stephanus it is also named; today it is Parenzo. It lies on a peninsula, excellently fortified with walls and towers, with a harbour suited to receiving the largest ships. It was plundered and burned by the Genoese, enemies of the Venetians, in the year 1354, as Corius reports in part 3.

units.la: Sequitur mox Opidum Oser, Latinis Piserium, Dioecesis Parentinae.
units.tr: Next comes the town of Oser, Piserium in Latin, in the diocese of Parenzo.

units.la: Superato Lemo, Raventum occurrit Opidum in Insula, cujus ambitus mille passuum: Portus habet duos.
units.tr: Past Lemo, Raventum appears, a town on an island whose circuit is a thousand paces. It has two harbours.

units.la: Offerunt le mox quae vulgo Le Colonne, Portesuai, Murazzer indeque Promontorium Cesanum. Putat Leander hic olim fuisse Nesactum Plinii: Ptolemaeus Nesaxon vocat; Nesactium legitur apud Livium. Niger tamen ex Nesactio Castellum Novum fabricat ad Arsiam flumen.
units.tr: Then come the places commonly called Le Colonne, Portesuai and Murazzer, and then the Cesanum promontory. Leander thinks that Nesactum of Pliny was once here; Ptolemy calls it Nesaxon, and Nesactium is read in Livy. Niger, however, builds a New Castle from Nesactium on the river Arsia.

units.la: Muratio Phalasium tria sunt milia, hinc ad Vallem Bandoniam, duo; totidemque, ad Marcodasinum; tria inde, ad Portum Polae.
units.tr: From Muratio to Phalasium is three thousand paces; from there to the Valley of Bandone, two; and as many again to Marcodasino; three from there to the harbour of Pola.

units.la: Comprehendam dein te te praebet in alto emincliqué Monte Urbs Episcopalis Pola, priscum nomen retinens. Strabonis, Plinio, Ptolemaeo, Antonino, aliisque nota. Plinius Colonia vocat: conditam olim ab Colchis exsulibus. Polam enim Exsulum Civitatum Colchorum lingua volunt dictam. Addit Plinius suo seculo Iuliam Pietatem appellatam, quum, quod augurot, ab Iulio Caesare Octaviano Augusto esset renovata. In tolo plano sita, Terqete multibus circiter e abest; Ancona, trajectu maris Hadriatici, mil. cc. x. Dirpectam & crematam ab Andrea Theophilo Venetorum Duce, memorat Blondus & Sabellicus. Genuit Maximianum, Ravennatum Archiepiscopum, qui eius Ecclesiae Praesulum Annales concinnavit ad suaviusque tempora. Amphitheatrum videre est in suburbanis locis ex quadrato lapide; aliudque amplissimum Aedificium, vulgo Zadro dictum; cum multis aliis Antiquitatum variarum monimentis.
units.tr: Next, the episcopal city of Pola, lifted up on a high hill, keeps its ancient name, known to Strabo, Pliny, Ptolemy, Antoninus and others. Pliny calls it a colony, founded long ago by Colchian exiles, for they say Pola was named in the Colchian language after the exiled cities. Pliny adds that in his own age it was called Julia Pietas, having been renewed, as he reports, by Julius Caesar Octavian Augustus. Set on a completely flat site, it is about sixty miles from Trieste and, by crossing the Adriatic, 210 miles from Ancona. Blondus and Sabellicus relate that it was plundered and burned by Andrea Theophilo, Doge of the Venetians. It produced Maximianus, Archbishop of Ravenna, who compiled the annals of that church's prelates for later times. In the suburbs one may see an amphitheatre built of square stone, and another very large building, commonly called Zadro, along with many other monuments of ancient times.

units.la: Succedunt ad litus quarto Pola milliari Brancefo; inde totidem, Insula di S. Maria di Gratia; decimoquinto, Veruda: uno, Oimo; duobus, Omesso: quinto hinc, Medolin; sexto, Mo lette: duodecimo, Arsia flumen, de quo alibi.
units.tr: Along the shore, four miles after Pola, comes Brancefo; then as many more, the island of S. Maria di Grazia; at fifteen miles, Veruda; at one, Oimo; at two, Omesso; five from here, Medolin; at six, Molette; at twelve, the river Arsia, of which I shall speak elsewhere.

units.la: In Mediterraneis porro litriae supra Iustinopolin, in Montibus, Iustinopolitanae Dioecesi subjecta sunt, quae vernacule Salso, Roggio, Bule, Almian, Nigram Antonionem cujus nonnullis exemplaribus Mungam expressum est, quod ad hodiernam appellationem magis accedit; S. Lorenzo, Portole, Grisignana, Pinguento (Nαχευτ Ptolemaeo) & Pietra Pelosa.
units.tr: Further inland, above Iustinopolis, in the mountains, are towns subject to the diocese of Iustinopolis. In the vernacular they are Salso, Roggio, Bule, Almiano, Nigra Antonio (which in some copies is written Mungam, a form closer to the present name), S. Lorenzo, Portole, Grisignana, Pinguente (Ptolemy's [Ναχευτ]) and Pietra Pelosa.

units.la: Reperiuntur ibidem, quae minoris momenti, Piemonte, Castel Nuovo, Cervical, S. Servo, Mocco, Meterna, Sacrtenic Stapa, Sannofez, Povera; Sdrigna, quam Blondus in sua Italia Stridonem appellans, multis modis probare conatur. D. Hieronymi esse Patriam; ab Leandro refutatus. Hinc inter Quietem & Arsiam fluvios in montibus apparent Valle, Duo Castro, Montagna, Pysino. Occurrunt inde Landa, Trevisio, Galignana, Pedena (Opidum Episcopali fulgens dignitate) Sombra, Costiae, Lupoglan, Dragù, Chirizzo, Termo, Castel Nuovo, S. Vicenzo.
units.tr: Found in the same area, of lesser importance, are Piemonte, Castel Nuovo, Cervical, S. Servo, Mocco, Meterna, Sacrtenic, Stapa, Sannofez and Povera. Sdrigna, which Blondus in his Italia calls Stridon, he tries to prove in many ways was the birthplace of St Jerome; Leander refutes him. Hence, between the rivers Quieto and Arsia, appear in the mountains Valle, Duo Castro, Montagna and Pysino. Then there are Landa, Trevisio, Galignana, Pedena (a town shining with episcopal dignity), Sombra, Costiae, Lupoglan, Dragù, Chirizzo, Termo, Castel Nuovo, S. Vicenzo.

units.la: A Promontorio Fanatico Arsiam versus incedenti supra Carnarium sinum editò in loco Algona jacet; & haud procul inde Terra Nova: Opida Istriæ, simulque Oræ hic Italiæ extrema.
units.tr: Proceeding from the Promontory Fanatico towards Arsia, above the Gulf of Carnaro, lies the town of Algona, and not far from it Terra Nova. These are towns of Istria, and at this point they mark the far end of the Italian coast.

units.la: Iter adscribam, quod Antoninus ducit ab Aquileia Polam usque, commissum cum Itineraria Tabula, vulgataque Nomenclatura: Antoninus: | Itineraria Tabula: | Vulgata Nomencl. 10 Ab Aquileia Fontem Timavi, M. P. xii. | Fonte Tumavi. XIIII. | Tiveno. Tergeste, M.P. xii. | Tergeste, XLVIII. | Trieste. Ningum, M. P. XXVIII. | . . . | Mimian. Parentium, M.P. XVII I. | Parentio, XXX. | Parenzo. Polim, M.P.XXXI. | Pola. | Pola.
units.tr: I will set down the route that Antoninus traces from Aquileia as far as Pola, compared with the Itinerary Table and the common nomenclature. Antoninus | Itinerary Table | Common nomenclature. 10 From Aquileia to the source of the Timavus, M.P. xii. | To the source of the Tumavus, XIIII. | Tiveno. Tergeste, M.P. xii. | Tergeste, XLVIII. | Trieste. Ningum, M.P. XXVIII. | . . . | Mimian. Parentium, M.P. XVIII. | Parentio, XXX. | Parenzo. Polim, M.P. XXXI. | Pola. | Pola.

units.la: CAPUT XXXIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXIX.

units.la: Liguria.
units.tr: Liguria.

units.la: HACTENVS Planiorem & ab Montibus liberiorem Italiam, qua debui fide, quaque potui diligentia delineavi: sequitur Montosior, cui duas tribui in mea Distributione Regiones, Ligüriam & Pedemontium.
units.tr: Having delineated the flatter Italy, which is freer of mountains, with the fidelity I owed and the care I could, I now come to the more mountainous part, to which I have assigned two regions in my Distribution: Liguria and Piedmont.

units.la: Ligvriæ unde nomen varie disceptatur. Quidam inter quos Paullus Diaconus lib. ii Langbardic. cap. xv) ab legendis Legumimbus trahunt; alij ab Ligone, uno ex fabulosis lapeti ducibus; suppositum ab Annio Viterbiensi Berosus, Cato, Fabius Pictor, & Sempronibus ab Ligure, Phaethontis Ægyptij Filio. Λιγυεία & Λιγυστική Græcis scribitur: Hodie Riviera di Genoa vocatur, ab Genua, clarissimi nominis Urbe.
units.tr: Opinions differ on the origin of the name Liguria. Some, among them Paulus Diaconus (Langobardic History, book 2, ch. 15), derive it from legendis Legumimbus (gathering pulses). Others derive it from Ligo, one of the mythical leaders descended from Iapetus. The spurious Berosus of Annius of Viterbo, along with Cato, Fabius Pictor and Sempronius, derive it from Ligur, son of the Egyptian Phaethon. The Greeks write it Λιγυεία and Λιγυστική [Ligyeia, Ligystike]. Today it is called the Riviera di Genova, after Genoa, a city of the highest renown.

units.la: Ampliores illi quondam fuerunt, quam hodie, limites. Iustinus ex Trogi lib. xx versus Orientem ultra Arnum producit; Pisas illi tribuens: ad Occidentem ea protenta legitur, ut & Narbonensem Galliam ad Oranum usque fluvium comprehenderit, multo trans Alpes: unde Ligures Transalpini in Epitome Liviana lib. xlvii. Videndi & Ptolemæus, Strabo lib. iv, Livius lib. xii, & xliv, alique. Hodie fines ipsi ab Occasu Alpes, Galliam Narbonensem ab Italia dividentes; ab Ortu; Etruria, Macra intersluente: quæ Meridies est, cognomine pullatur Mari: qua Septemtrio, Apennino claudiitur. Plinius auctor est, inter Macræ ac Vari ostia millibus p. cc xi, etiam patere. Ptolemæus hoc spatium quatuor graduum esse tradit: gradus singuli m. p. xliii continent: hinc mensura redit milliariorum c i xxviii, a qua nec multum abscedit Blondus, binis millibus superans. A Monœco ad Etruriæ confinia, ut Strabo notat lib. iv, totu littus continuum, & importuosum; imminent undique rupes immanes & præcipites. Intus omnia fere montosa, silvosisque saltibus horrida: frequentissimam ædificandis navibus materiam vastasque arbores producentia. Λιγγύριον, Lingurium, quod Electrum alijs, hic proveniebat.
units.tr: Its limits were once wider than they are today. Justin, from Trogus book 20, extends them eastward beyond the Arno, assigning Pisa to the Ligurians. To the west the territory is said to have reached so far that it included Narbonese Gaul as far as the river Orange, well beyond the Alps, which is why Livy's Epitome, book 47, speaks of the Transalpine Ligurians. Ptolemy, Strabo book 4, Livy books 12 and 44, and others may also be consulted. Today the boundaries are: to the west, the Alps, which divide Narbonese Gaul from Italy; to the east, Etruria, with the Macra flowing between them; to the south, the sea, which gives the region its name; to the north, the Apennines enclose it. Pliny states that the distance between the mouths of the Macra and the Var is 211 miles. Ptolemy says this stretch covers four degrees, and each degree contains 43 miles, so the measure comes to 128 miles, from which Blondus does not differ much, exceeding it by two miles. From Monaco to the borders of Etruria, as Strabo notes in book 4, the whole coast is one unbroken stretch with no harbours; huge, steep cliffs overhang it on every side. Inland almost everything is mountainous and bristling with wooded glades, producing huge trees and timber most abundant for shipbuilding. Lingurium, which others call amber (Electrum), was found here; the Greek is Λιγγύριον [Lingyrion].

units.la: Genti equo militare usus infrequens: pedestribus maximeque tumultuarijs prælijs summe valebat; æreis, Græcorum more, Parmis armensunde Græcæ esse originis ratiocinabantur. Hinc etiam Sagulû Ligustici nomen fuit. De iis Florus lib. ii; cap. iii: Ligures imis Alpium jugis adhærentes, inter Varum & Macrum flumen, implicitos dumis silvestribus, major aliquanto labor erat invenire, quam vincere. Tutum locis & fuga, durum atque velox genus, ex occasione magis latrociniis quam belli faciebat. Livius lib. xxxix singulatim arduum hujus Regionis situm, ritusque populorum memorat, quum Ligures hostem velocem, levem, ac repentinum dicit: in quo vincendo difficultatis laboriisque plurimum, prædæ haud multum esset, ob aspera montanaque loca. Virgilius lib. ii Georg. duram eorum atque laboriosam vitam haud obscure notat, quum ait: Adspectumque malo Ligurem.
units.tr: The people made little use of cavalry. They excelled in infantry, and especially in skirmishing. They carried bronze shields in the Greek manner, and for this reason they reckoned themselves of Greek origin. Hence also the name Ligurian cloaks (Sagula Ligustica). Florus, book 2, ch. 3, describes them: "The Ligurians, clinging to the lowest slopes of the Alps, between the rivers Var and Macra, entangled in wild thickets, were a far greater labour to find than to conquer. Safe in their terrain and in flight, a hardy and swift race, they waged war by chance raids rather than by battle." Livy, book 39, recounts the steep site of this region and the customs of its peoples one by one, calling the Ligurians a swift, light and sudden enemy. To conquer them took much difficulty and toil, and yielded little booty, because of their rough mountain places. Virgil, Georgics book 2, clearly marks their hard and laborious life when he says: "and I have seen, to my cost, the Ligurian."

units.la: Huc pertinet quod de hac gente Lucanus lib. i belli Pharsal. Et nunc tonsæ Ligur, quondam per colla decoraCrinibus effusis toti præfulgeat Comatæ.
units.tr: To this people belongs what Lucan says of them in book 1 of the Pharsalia: "And now the shorn Ligurian, who once shone with hair flowing down his neck, the whole of Gaul long-haired..."

units.la: Ligures comatos vocat Dion, qui Alpes Maritimas colebant.
units.tr: Dio calls the Ligurians who inhabited the Maritime Alps long-haired Ligurians (Ligures comati).

units.la: Ligures Strabo bifariam secat libro 1111; Τῶν Λιγύων, inquit, τ̄ μὲν ὄντων Ιγγαύων, τ̄ δ᾽ Ιντημελίων; addens duas eorum Colonias mari adpositas, unam Ἀλβιγγαύνων, alteram, Ἀλβιον Ιντημέλιον. Albingaunos novit Vopiscus in Proculo; Ingaunos Ligures, Livius lib. xxviii, xxx & xl, ubi multa de rebus, quæ ab ipsis gestæ. Intemelios Populos habet idem Livius lib. xl. Periérunt illi apud Tacitum in Vita Agricolæ: Sequens annus gravi vulnere animum domumque ejus afflixit. Nam Classis Othoniana licenter vagabatur, dum in templo, Liguria pars erat, hostiliter populatur, matrem Agricolæ in prædys suis interfecit: pro in templo repone Intemelios. Plinius lib. iiii natur. hist. cap. xix Ligurum celeberrimos Colonos ultra Alpes nominat Sallyos, Deceatos, Oxubios; Ὀξυβίων Ἐκ Δεκιατῶν habet etiam Polybius apud Strabonem: sunt & Ὀξυβιοι Stephano noti: citra autem Venenos, & Caturigibus ortos Vagiennos, Statyellos, Vibellos, Magellos, Euburiates, Casmonates, Vellates. De Sallyis, Deceatibus, & Oxubys ego in Provincia mea libro iii, cap. xxxix: Venenorum, Vibellorum, Magellorum, Casmonatum & Vellatum nescio an quis præter Plinium alius meminerit. Euburiates etiam apud Florum memorantur libro ii Hist. Rom. cap. iii. De Vagiennis & Statyellis alibi a me dictum. Vesturiorum, Ligurię populorum, hic mentio in Antiquissima ex ære Tabula, qua sculptum Decretum Arbitrum Finium regundorum inter Genuates & eosdem Vesturios. Augustinus Iustinianus putat hos habitasse cum locum, quem hodie Voltaggio appellant, in Genuatium territorio. Ἰ Ὀιχμροι apud Stephanum Ligurię Populi, quos quoque Ἀ ρ̄εαξανος dici tradit: Ἀρεαξανοι legantur alio in loco.
units.tr: Strabo divides the Ligurians into two groups in book 4: "Of the Ligurians, some are the Ingauni, others the Intemelii," adding two colonies on the sea, one of the Albingaunes, the other Album Intemelium. Vopiscus knows the Albingauni in his Life of Proculus; Livy, books 28, 30 and 40, mentions the Ingauni Ligurians and the many deeds done by them. The Intemelii are also named by Livy, book 40. They appear in Tacitus, Life of Agricola: "The following year struck his spirit and his house with a grievous wound. For the Othonian fleet roamed without restraint, and while in the temple, which was part of Liguria, it plundered as an enemy and among its booty killed Agricola's mother." For "in templo" read "Intemelios." Pliny, Natural History book 4, ch. 19, names the most celebrated colonists of the Ligurians beyond the Alps: the Sallyes, Deceates and Oxubii. Polybius, quoted by Strabo, also has the Oxybii from the Deciates, and the Oxybii are known to Stephanus. On this side of the Venenes, and descended from the Caturiges, are the Vagienni, Statyelli, Vibelli, Magelli, Euburiates, Casmonates and Vellates. I have treated the Sallyes, Deceates and Oxubii in my Province, book 3, ch. 39. I do not know whether anyone other than Pliny mentions the Venenes, Vibelli, Magelli, Casmonates and Vellates. The Euburiates are also mentioned by Florus, book 2 of his Roman History, ch. 3. I have spoken of the Vagienni and Statyelli elsewhere. Here is mention of the Vesturii, a people of Liguria, in the most ancient bronze tablet, on which is engraved the decree of arbitrators settling the boundaries between the Genuates and these same Vesturii. Augustinus Iustinianus thinks they lived in the place now called Voltaggio, in the territory of the Genoese. Stephanus names the Oichmroi [Ὀιχμροι], a Ligurian people, which he also says are called Areaxanoi [Ἀρεαξανοι]; Areaxanoi is read in another place.

units.la: De Rebus vel contra Ligures ab variis Romanis præcipue, vel ab ijs contra varios bene felicitérque gestis legendi præter Dionysium Halic. Livius lib. xx, xxix, xxxix, xli, xlii, xlix, Diodorus Siculus lib. xi, L. Florus lib. ii, cap. iii, Eutropius lib. iii, Auctor de VV. Inlustr. cap. xiiii, Orosius lib. iiii, cap. xi & xii, Strabo libro iv, Augustinus lib. iii de Civit. Dei cap. ix, & alij.
units.tr: Concerning the Ligurians, and the wars waged well and successfully against them by various Romans, or by them against various peoples, one may read, besides Dionysius of Halicarnassus: Livy, books 20, 29, 39, 41, 42 and 49; Diodorus Siculus, book 11; L. Florus, book 2, ch. 3; Eutropius, book 3; the author of De Viris Illustribus, ch. 14; Orosius, book 4, chs. 11 and 12; Strabo, book 4; Augustine, City of God, book 3, ch. 9; and others.

units.la: Ad Specialiora venio. Ora Genuensis hodie duplex, Occidentalis & Orientalis; quæ vulgo ab Metropoli, quæ in medio utriusque, Riviera di Genova, Di Ponente, & di Levante. Occidentalem prius explicabo.
units.tr: I now come to more particular matters. The Genoese coast today is twofold, western and eastern, commonly named after the metropolis which lies between them: the Riviera di Genova, di Ponente and di Levante. I shall explain the western part first.

units.la: Haud procul Varo, qui inter Italiam & Galliam limes, Nicea est. Sic Plinio dicta, quæ Νίκαια Ptolemæo: Nicia Antonino, variis locis: Νίκαια hodie. Urbs maritima, quondam ab Massiliensibus condita, ut Plinius & Ptolemæus notant, dorso Alpibus inmitens, partim in juga, partim in planiciem porrecta. Nomen Græcum ab vi- ctu. Niceum hic tabulatur Annius ad Berolium, Etruriæ Larthem. Urbs jamnunc munitissima, firmam habens Arcem in colle, ditionis Sabaudiæ Principis.
units.tr: Not far from the Var, which forms the boundary between Italy and Gaul, lies Nice. Pliny calls it Nicea, Ptolemy Νίκαια, and Antoninus Nicia in various places; today it is Nice. It is a maritime city, once founded by the Massilians, as Pliny and Ptolemy note. It rests against the Alps, stretching partly along the heights and partly across the plain. Its Greek name comes from victory. Annius sets "Niceum" here, in place of Berolium, the Larthes of Etruria. The city is now very strongly fortified, with a firm citadel on a hill, under the rule of the Prince of Savoy.

units.la: Non procul in montibus agro Cemeno, editiore loco vestigia sunt urbis, quæ Κεμελίων Vestantiorum Ptolemæo: Cemelion Vesdiantiorum, Plinio; Cemenelum Antonino, Gemenelium Itinerariæ Tabulæ. Inde Populi Cemelenses, de quibus ego lib. iii, cap. xxxix. Sunt tamen, qui Rudera illa Veteris putant Niceæ.
units.tr: Not far off, in the mountains of the Cemenus territory, on a higher site, there are the remains of a city. Ptolemy calls it Κεμελίων of the Vestantii, Pliny Cemelion of the Vesdiantii, Antoninus Cemenelum, and the Itinerary Table Gemenelium. Hence come the Cemenelenses, of whom I speak in book 3, ch. 39. Yet some think those ruins belong to old Nice.

units.la: Inter Niceam & Portum Herculis, qui sequitur, ponit alios etiam Antoninus in Itinerario Maritimo ab urbe Arelatum usque, Olivulam, Anaonem, & Avisionem. Pro prima statione legit Surita ad Olbiam; inter quam & Antipolim Strabo Navale Cæsaris Augusti, Forum Iulii nuncupatum, statuit; sed remotius abit, versus Gallias, quam itinerum ratio patitur.
units.tr: Between Nice and the Port of Hercules, which follows, Antoninus in his Maritime Itinerary, from the city of Arles onward, also names some other stations: Olivula, Anaon and Avision. For the first station Surita reads at Olbia. Between it and Antipolis, Strabo places a naval station of Caesar Augustus, called Forum Iulii; but this lies further off, toward Gaul, than the route allows.

units.la: Portus autem Herculis Monæci, quem Nicæ statuo hic succedentem, Tacito in Historiis, Plinio & Antonino nominatur, qui simpliciter nunc Portus Herculis Valerio Maximo & Ptolemæo, nunc Μονοικος Λιμὴν Straboni & eidem Ptolemæo (nam utrumque unum illi est, ejusdemque loci) simplicius Μόνοικος Stephano; Arx Monæci Virgilio libro vi, ubi Servius; Arx & Portus Monæci Ammiano lib. xv: Arces Monæci Herculis Panegyrico, qui Maximiano Imp. ductus: Herclemannicus, & alijs modis, mendose, pro Hercules. Monæcus vel Herclemonæcus Antonino in Itinerario, quod dixi. Hodie Monaco apud Blondum & Leandrum, qui Portum Herculis disjungere non debuerat à Portu Monæci; illum Villam Francam faciens; hunc Monacum. Strabonis ævo statio fuit, ut ipse auctor est, nec multarum, nec magnarum navium capax. Stationis huius meminit Lucanus lib. 1, qui in eam venisse Iulium Cæsarem, quum in Italiam tenderet, memorat: Quaque sub Herculeo sacratus nomine Portus, Vrget rupe cava pelagus; non Corus in illum Ius habet aut Zephyrus: solus sua litora turbat Circius, & tuta prohibet Statione Monoeci.
units.tr: The Port of Hercules of Monaco, which I place here as following Nice, is named by Tacitus in his Histories, by Pliny and by Antoninus. Valerius Maximus and Ptolemy sometimes call it simply Portus Herculis; Strabo and the same Ptolemy call it Μονοικος Λιμήν (for both names belong to one and the same place), and Stephanus more simply Μόνοικος. Virgil, book 6, speaks of the Citadel of Monaecus, on which Servius comments; Ammianus, book 15, has Citadel and Port of Monaecus; the Panegyric addressed to the Emperor Maximian has Citadels of Monaecus Hercules; other forms, such as Herclemannicus, are wrongly written for Hercules. Monaecus or Herclemonaecus is in Antoninus' Itinerary, as I have said. Today it is Monaco, in Blondus and Leander. Leander ought not to have separated the Port of Hercules from the Port of Monaco, making the former Villa Franca and the latter Monacum. In Strabo's time it was a station, as he himself says, capable of neither many nor large ships. Lucan, book 1, mentions this station, recording that Julius Caesar came to it when he was heading into Italy: "And where the port, consecrated under the name of Hercules, presses on the sea with its hollow rock; neither Corus nor Zephyrus has power over it; only the Circius disturbs its shores, and it forbids the safe anchorage of Monoecus."

units.la: Supra Portum Herculis Monoeci ad alterum lapidem editis in montibus Torbia jacet, vel Turbia: Τρόπαια Σιβάστ Ptolemaeo, uti censent Blondus, Bracellius, Leander.
units.tr: Above the Port of Hercules Monoecus, at the second milestone, in the mountains, lies Torbia, or Turbia. Ptolemy calls it [Τρόπαια Σιβάστ], and Blondus, Bracellius and Leander agree.

units.la: Hinc propter littus, post Arcem Brunam, quae Rocca Bruna vulgo, & Mentonium, locis sterilibus, offert ie Vintimeglia, olim, ut vult Leander Albium Intemelium: sic dictum Strabonis, ut antea monui, Plinio & Tacito lib. xvii, apud quem, ante ccl.v. Iusti Libij castigationem, erat Albintimilium ut & Ausonio: quod Ἀλβιντιμίλιον Ptolemaeo, corrupte; Albentimillum Itinerariae Tabulae: Intimelium simpliciter Ciceroni lib. viii Epist. An Intimelium hodie Vintimiglia dicatur, dubitat doctissimus Ortelius: quod videat Vintimilij hoc tractu etiam mentionem facere Varronem lib. iii, de re Rust.
units.tr: Next along the shore, after Arcem Brunam, commonly called Rocca Bruna, and Mentonium, in barren country, comes Vintimeglia, which was formerly, as Leander holds, Albium Intemelium. It was so named by Strabo, as I said earlier, and by Pliny and Tacitus in book 17, where, before Justus Lipsius corrected the text, it appears as Albintimilium, as also in Ausonius. Ptolemy has [Ἀλβιντιμίλιον], which is a corruption; the Itinerary Table has Albentimillum; Cicero in book 8 of his Letters simply has Intimelium. Whether Intimelium is today called Vintimiglia the most learned Ortelius doubts, since he sees that Varro, in book 3 of De re rustica, also mentions the Vintimilii in this district.

units.la: Tertia ab Vintimilia lapide D. Remi est Opidum, S. Remo; peramoenò & fertili agro; qui citris, palmis, medicis, limonibus, aliisque fructiferis arboribus mirum in modum ornatus.
units.tr: Three miles from Ventimiglia is the town of S. Remo, the D. Remi Opidum; it lies in a very pleasant and fertile countryside, wonderfully adorned with citrons, palms, medlars, lemons and other fruit trees.

units.la: Occurrit mox Castellum Tabia: ambitu exiguo, sed nomine celeberrimum, ob generositatem vinorum Apianorum, de quibus alibi. Patria Ioannis Tabiani, qui Summam Casuum Conscientiae scripsit.
units.tr: Soon comes the little castle of Tabia. It is small in circuit but very famous for the excellence of its Apian wines, of which more elsewhere. It was the birthplace of Ioannis Tabiani, who wrote the Summa Casuum Conscientiae.

units.la: Ponunt hoc fere loco Coitam Balena Antoninus & Itineraria Tabula.
units.tr: Antoninus and the Itinerary Table place Coita Balena at about this spot.

units.la: Succedit x milliari Portus Mauri, ut Antonino dicitur: hodie Porto Marisio nomine magis, quam re Portus.
units.tr: Ten miles further is Portus Mauri, as Antoninus calls it; today it is Porto Marisio, a port more in name than in fact.

units.la: Altero dehinc Villis Onelia; pagis vicisque multis nitens: Ulterius quarto Dianium, Dian: Diana procul dubio memoriam servans.
units.tr: Then, at the second milestone, comes Villis Onelia, shining with many villages and hamlets. Further on, at the fourth, is Dianium, now Dian, which without doubt preserves the memory of Diana.

units.la: Relictis inde Opidis Cerio & Andoria, per oram Albingaunum devenitur. Sic Plinio dicitur lib. iii, cap. v, & Antonino: quod Ἀλβιγγαῦον Strabonis; Ἀλβίγγουον Ptolemaeo, ut & Tacito lib. xviii: Hodie Albenga. Vrbs antiqua, situ plano, quingentis a mari passibus, gravioris coeli, praesertim quum in flumine vicino Centa maceratur Cannabis. Hinc vulgus Albengana piana, se fosse fana, si dimandarebbe Diana. De Diana antea dixi. Aliquai opulenta est, rebusque necessariis adfluens. Captam direptamque anno cIↄ c Lxxv a Pisanis, restaurarunt Genuenses. Civitatis jus illi tribuite, Episcopumque primus dedisse legitur Alexander iii, P.M. Alii ad Innocentium iii referunt. Incluta est ortu Proculi Imp. Spartiano & Eutropio scribentibus.
units.tr: Leaving behind the towns of Cerio and Andoria, one comes along the coast to Albingaunum. Pliny in book 3, chapter 5, and Antoninus call it so; Strabo has [Ἀλβιγγαῦον], Ptolemy [Ἀλβίγγουον], and Tacitus in book 18 likewise. Today it is Albenga: an ancient city on level ground, five hundred paces from the sea, with rather heavy air, especially when hemp is steeped in the nearby river Centa. Hence the local saying, that Albenga the flat, if it were a temple, would be called Diana; of Diana I have spoken before. The city is somewhat wealthy and abounds in necessities. It was captured and plundered by the Pisans in the year 1175, and restored by the Genoese. It was granted the rights of a city, and it is read that Alexander III first gave it a bishop; others attribute this to Innocent III. It is famous as the birthplace of the emperor Proculus, according to Spartianus and Eutropius.

units.la: Mox percurus Ceriali, Burgetto, Ovo, & Petra, aperit se Finarium, Opidum nobile, haud procul mari; in faucibus Vallis, ubi valida arx colli impositta tutelam ejus tenet. Finarium, della Finezza dell' Aria dictum censet Blondus. Marchionatus, qui penes familiam Carettorum, titulo & dignitate est celebris.
units.tr: Soon, passing Ceriale, Burgetto, Ovo and Petra, one reaches Finarium, a noble town not far from the sea, at the mouth of a valley, where a strong citadel set upon a hill guards it. Blondus thinks Finarium was so named della Finezza dell'Aria, from the fineness of its air. The marquisate, held by the family of the Carretti, is famous for its title and dignity.

units.la: Septimo hinc lapide Naulum, Noli vulgo, est; ab Genuensibus Sabatijsque conditum, infrequentius nunc habitatum. Civitati factae Episcopum praefecisse perhibetur, ab his Innocentius iiii, ab illis Alexander iii P. M. Portus hic eximius; ubi Promontorium, quod vulgo Capo de Noli.
units.tr: Seven miles from here is Naulum, commonly Noli. It was founded by the Genoese and the Savonese and is now less populated. It is said that a bishop was set over the city once it was made a city: Innocent IV, according to some, and Alexander III, according to others. This harbour is excellent, and near it is the promontory commonly called Capo de Noli.

units.la: Quinque inde milliaribus Vada sic simpliciter Bruto dicitur lib. xi. Epist. ad Ciceronem, & Σάβατα Ptolemaeo; Sabbatia, Pomponio: quae junctis vocibus Σαββάτων ὡάδα Strabonis, cui hinc Alpes incipiunt: Vadum Sabbatinum Plinio: in antiquis ejus libris Vadorum Sabbatur; Vada Snada, Antonino, ut meliioribus codicibus, Vada Sabbata, & Vada Sabatis: Vada Sabates scriptum est in Itineraria Tabula pro Sabatis: Vadi hodie Leandro, confusius hic scribenti; Vai (diverse enim pronunciatur, Paradino) Vnada & Vae Nigro, ex Sabbatiis & Vada duas urbes facientes. Quoquo modo sit scribenda, intelligendus de ijs Brutus ad Ciceronem scribens: Constitit nusquam priusquam ad Vada venire, quem locum volo tibi esse notum. Iacet inter Apenninum & Alpes, impeditissimus ad iter faciendum.
units.tr: Five miles on is Vada, simply so called by Brutus in book 11 of his letters to Cicero; Ptolemy has [Σάβατα], Pomponius Sabbatia. Joined together these words make Strabo's [Σαββάτων ὥαδα], and Strabo says the Alps begin here. Pliny has Vadum Sabbatinum; in his older books it is Vadorum Sabbatur; Antoninus has Vada Snada, but better manuscripts have Vada Sabbata and Vada Sabatis; the Itinerary Table writes Vada Sabates for Sabatis. Leander, who writes rather confusedly here, calls it Vadi today; Paradinus says it is pronounced differently, Vai; Nigro, making two towns out of Sabbatia and Vada, gives Vnada and Vae. However it is written, Brutus must be understood to mean this place when he writes to Cicero: "He stopped nowhere before coming to Vada, a place I want you to know. It lies between the Apennines and the Alps and is most difficult for travel."

units.la: Millia hinc v Savona est Civitas, Livio nota lib. xxxviii, cui & Savo dicitur libro xxviii. Priusnomen retinet. Vrbs antiquissima, aedificiis ornata magnificis, praecipueque pueque nobilissima Iulij 11. Pont. R. Domo. Variorum Principum ditionis superio- ribus saeculis fuit; Genuensium, Piacecomitum, Sfortiarum, Mediolanensiû, Gallorum; quan-doque etiam libera suique juris: nunc cum pleraque Liguria sub Cenuensium est imperio, qui anno cıɔ ıɔ xxvı ıı. multas ob causas ipsorum Portum corruperunt. Patria est Gregorij vıı. Sixti ıııı. & Iulij ıı. PP. MM. item Petri & Raphaelis Riariorum Sixti Neporum; Marci Vgery. Augustini Spinolae, Cardinalium: Caesaris, Patriarchae Constantinopolitani: Octaviani, Episcopi Viterbini: Sforziae, Lucensium Praesulis; & aliorum.
units.tr: Five miles from here is the city of Savona, known to Livy in book 38, and called Savo in book 28. It keeps its former name. It is a very ancient city, adorned with magnificent buildings, and especially famous as the noble home of Pope Julius II. In earlier centuries it was under the rule of various princes: the Genoese, the counts of Piacenza, the Sforzas, the Milanese, the French; at times it was also free and under its own law. Now, since most of Liguria is under the rule of the Genoese, who for many reasons ruined its harbour in 1527. It was the native place of Popes Gregory VII, Sixtus IV and Julius II; also of Peter and Raphael Riario, nephews of Sixtus; of the cardinals Marco Vigerio and Augustine Spinola; of Caesar, Patriarch of Constantinople; of Octavian, Bishop of Viterbo; of Sforza, Bishop of Lucca; and of others.

units.la: Virgium mox est, Opidum, quod & Virago & Voragium quibusdam dictum: sunt & qui Viam Virginis vocatum dici tradunt. Vicum Virginis lego in itiner. Tabula Celebre est satis: Patria Iacobi, Genuensium Archiepiscopi, scriptis nobilis, defuncti anno cıɔ cc xciiii.
units.tr: Next is Virgium, a town which some have called both Virago and Voragium; some also say it is called Via Virginis, and I read Vicus Virginis in the Itinerary Table. It is quite famous: it was the native place of Jacopo, Archbishop of Genoa, noted for his writings, who died in 1294.

units.la: Succedunt inde quae vernacule Vutro, Sestro di ponente, & Cornegliano; vicus insignis, gentis ex Genua nobilis Spinolae.
units.tr: Then come the places called in the vernacular Voltri, Sestri di Ponente and Cornigliano, a notable village belonging to the Spinola family, who are noble of Genoa.

units.la: Hinc salutato S. Petro Arenoso, qui vulgo S. Pier d'Arena, subit Genua. Insignis primum Urbis Portus offertur, ad Africum & Austrum patens, ingenti mole ad securam stationem praemunitus. Impositia illi potens ipsa superbaque Civitas. Genua, Livio, Plinio, Antonino, Tabulae Itin. Vrbs, Straboni, Ptolemaeo, aliis. Tnéu, inquit Stephanus, πόλις ... Ianua dicitur Luitprando Ticinensi, & eius aetatis Scriptoribus: Hodie Genoa & Genova. Incolae Genuenses plerisque: aliis etiam Gennates, ait Stephanus; Gennates etiam appellat elegantissimum illud decretum Finium regundorum inter Gennates & Veiturios, quod Genua visitur in aenea tabella, ab rustico terram fodiente reperta anno cıɔ ıɔ vıı. mense Februario, & in summo templo collocata: incisa est literis Romanis antiquissimis minutulis: longa palmas duas & paullo amplius, lata sesquipalmam. Quod ad situm: Fronte Meridiem Cirnumque spectat insulam; amplissime circa litus consurgens, dorso Septemtrioni obverso, leniter in planitiem; veluti ad quiescendum descendens, montium innixa radicibus, quorum a tergo contra saevorum Septemtrionum afflatum vallo munitur: non tota montosa, nec vicissim tota plana, sed mixta specie. Circuitu palmos colligere tricena quina millia, supra nongentos quinquaginta quinque, Nebianus Episcopus tradit. Palmus haud multo minor antiquorum est pede. Hinc mensura totius urbis si palmos septenos passui demus, milliariorum erit quinque: sin senos, sex, demptis quadraginta quinque palmis: nec moles, nec portus in hanc dimensionem venit. De Nominis ratione & etymo multi multa frigide. Somniantur varij: Ianus Genius Priscus, primus Italiae Rex: Ianus, Rex Trojanorum: Ianus Bifrons: cuius insigni Civitas utitur; Ianus Geminus ex Phaetontis Comitibus Aegyptius: Genus, Saturni filius, Genua, Prometheï Filia: additur & Ianua, quod quasi sit porta & ostium Italiae: quin nec Genu omittitur, quod ea quasi genu habeat recurvum ab littore maris. Ego nihil adfirmare possum. Antiquissimae sane censenda est originis. Portui olim castellum ab Lodovico xii. Galliarum Rege, anno cıɔ ıɔ vıı. quo loco nunc est Lupanar, fuit impositum. Briglia dicebatur, nota notione: cuius praesidio civitas in officio continetur; sed quum frenum hoc infestum equus ferox non ferret, Antoniottus Adurnius dux, libertatis conservandae gratia, ad fundamenta dejecit: opus alioquin stupendum ingentique sumtu factum. Vrbs Parochias habet xxxii. Palatium Serhatus pulcrum est; & ab quingentis militibus Germanis custoditum. In medio areae Statua marmorea Andra Auria, forma gigantis, tempora circum laurea coronana redimiti, triaque Turcarum capita pedibus calcantis. Ladarfina locus navibus saciendis consecratus. Portui marino adjacet Domus, quae Arsinale vulgo, fabricandis triremibus dicatus: ibi Fons incredibilis pulcritudinis ob materiam, quae tota marina. Poggio vicus est in maris littore, in quo Palatium Centurionis Adami: Civis Genuensis, latissimusque hortus cum admirabili fonte: Praedium denique cuius situ nihil pulcrius. Laterna turris est excelsa, lumen praebens noctumum navigantibus, cuius limini inscriptum: Anno à Christo nato cıɔ ıɔxliii restituta libertatis anno xvi instaurata Turris hac, olim structa à maioribus nostris, & cıɔ ıɔxii. in oppugnatione arcis Laternae diruta, Genua de se, ad S. Andream:
units.tr: After greeting S. Pier d'Arena, commonly so called, one comes to Genua. First appears the city's notable harbour, open to the southwest and south, fortified by a huge mole to provide a safe anchorage. Upon it sits the powerful and proud city itself. It is Genua in Livy, Pliny, Antoninus and the Itinerary Tables, and Urbs in Strabo, Ptolemy and others. Stephanus says [Γένουα], a city. It is called Ianua by Liutprand of Cremona and the writers of his age. Today it is Genoa and Genova. Its inhabitants are commonly Genuenses, though Stephanus says others call them Gennates. The elegant decree settling the boundaries between the Gennates and the Veiturii also calls them Gennates; it is seen in a bronze tablet which a farmer found while digging in the year 1506, in February, and which was placed in the main church. It is inscribed in very old Roman letters, small, two and a little more than two palms long and one and a half palms wide. As to its site: it faces south and the sea, and looks towards the island; it rises very broadly along the shore, with its back to the north, sloping gently down to the plain as if to rest, leaning against the foot of the mountains, which at the back shelter it with a wall against the harsh blasts of the north wind. It is neither wholly mountainous nor wholly flat, but of mixed character. Bishop Nebianus reports that its circuit measures 35,955 palms, not counting 955. A palm is not much smaller than the ancient foot. So if we give seven palms to a pace, the measure of the whole city is five miles; if six, six miles, less forty-five palms; neither the walls nor the harbour fit into this measurement. Many have written much, and frigidly, about the reason and etymology of the name. Various fancies are proposed: Janus Genius Priscus, the first king of Italy; Janus, king of the Trojans; Janus Bifrons, whose image the city uses; Janus Geminus, an Egyptian among the companions of Phaethon; Genus, son of Saturn; Genua, daughter of Prometheus. Also added is Ianua, because it is as it were the gate and door of Italy. Nor is Genu omitted, because the city has as it were a bent knee along the shore of the sea. I can affirm nothing myself. It must certainly be considered of very ancient origin. A castle was once set on the harbour by Louis XII, King of France, in the year 1507, on the spot where the brothel now stands. It was called Briglia in its ordinary meaning, and by its garrison the city was kept in obedience; but since the fierce horse could not bear this bridle, Antoniotto Adorno, the doge, to preserve liberty, pulled it down to its foundations. The work, otherwise amazing, had been made at enormous cost. The city has thirty-two parishes. The palace of the Signory is handsome, and it is guarded by five hundred German soldiers. In the middle of the square is a marble statue of Andrea Doria, in the form of a giant, its temples wreathed with laurel, and treading underfoot three heads of Turks. The Ladarfina is a place consecrated to building ships. Next to the sea harbour is a building commonly called the Arsenale, devoted to building triremes; there is a fountain of incredible beauty there because of its material, which is entirely of marble. Poggio is a village on the seashore, where is the palace of the citizen of Genoa, Adamo Centurione, with a very wide garden and a wonderful fountain; in short, an estate whose situation could not be finer. The Laterna is a tall tower, giving night light to sailors, and on its threshold is inscribed: "In the year of Christ 1543, in the sixteenth year of restored liberty, this tower, built long ago by our ancestors, was restored; and in 1512, when the citadel of the Lanterna was attacked, it was destroyed," and, from Genoa about herself, at St Andrew's:

units.la: Sum munita viris, muris circumdata miris: Et virtute mea pello procul hostica tela, Si pacem portas, licet has tibi tangere portas: Si bellum quares, tristis victusque recedes. Auster & Occasus, Septemtrio novit & Ortus, Quantas bellorum superavi Ianua motus.
units.tr: I am defended by men and walled about with marvellous walls, and by my valour I drive far off the enemy's weapons. If you bring peace, you may touch these gates; if you seek war, you will go away sad and defeated. South wind and West, North and East know how many storms of war this Gate has overcome.

units.la: Incolæ magna valent in Negotiando industria, nullas non mundi plagas adire quæstus gratia soliti. Ipsam urbem elegantissime depingunt Franciscus Petracha, M. Antonius Sabellicus, Natalis Comes lib. Histor. sui temporis 111. & xxx. Munsterus lib. 11. Cosmog. Laurentius Schraderus in Monumentis Italiæ. Captam dirutamque ab Magone, Amilcaris filio, refert Livius libro xxviii. restauratam ab Lucretio S.P.Q.R. iussu, narrat idem lib. xxx. Direpta iterum ab Rhotare, Langbardorum Rege, capto Desiderio, Pipino, Karoli filio, Italiæ Regi se subjecit; mox Imperatorum, qui Carolo Magno successerunt, arbitriis devota: à quibus potestatem accepit Præfectos sibi legendi, qui Remp. regerent. Quo pacto ab Consulibus, Prætoribus, Populi Præfectis, Abbatibus, Antianis, ut vocant, & Ducibus, mirum quanta varietate multos annos fuerit gubernata: & qualis Reip. forma, institutis Concilio Nobili, Duce uno, Gubernatoribus octo, totidem Procuratoribus, Syndicisque quinque, cœperit anno cIↄ IↄXXVIII. plene exponunt Leander Albertus in Liguria & alij.
units.tr: The inhabitants are very industrious in trade, and they are accustomed to go to every quarter of the world for gain. Francesco Petrarca, Marcantonio Sabellico, Natale Conti in the third and thirtieth books of his history of his own times, and Münster in the second book of his Cosmography describe the city itself most elegantly, as does Lorenz Schrader in his Monumenta Italiae. Livy, in book 28, reports that it was captured and destroyed by Mago, son of Hamilcar. The same author, in book 30, relates that it was restored by Lucretius at the command of the Senate and People of Rome. Plundered again by Rothari, King of the Lombards, and then, after Desiderius was taken, it submitted to Pepin, son of Charles, King of Italy. Afterwards it was devoted to the will of the Emperors who succeeded Charlemagne, and from them it received the power to choose its own prefects to govern the commonwealth. The authors Leander Alberti in Liguria and others fully set out how, under consuls, praetors, prefects of the people, abbots, the so-called Antiani, and dukes, the city was governed for many years with remarkable variety, and what form of commonwealth began in the year 1528, with a Noble Council, one Doge, eight Governors, as many Procurators, and five Syndics.

units.la: Viros illustres Genua plurimos edidit: inter ceteros Innocentium v. & Hadrianum v. Romanos Pontifices, ex nobili familia Flisca: quæ eadem plus xxx. Cardinales genuit, multosque Præsules alios, uti Archiepiscopos, Episcoposque. Cibonum è gente magnifica fuit Innocentius viii. P.M. è Fregosia Paullus, cum Frederico: è Flisca, Nicolaus: ex Saulia Bendinellus: omnes Cardinales. Alios huius classis prætereo. Genuenses etiam fuerunt Viri eruditione scriptisq. clari: Augustinus Iustinianus, Nebiæ Episcopus, qui ingens volumen de rebus Genuensium vernacula lingua edidit; Ioannes Balus, Vocabularij, quod Catholicon dicitur, auctor: Andalotius Niger, Iacobus Cepa, Iacobus Bracellius, qui situm locaque huius Regionis diligenter est persequutus: Gothardus Stella, Baptista Fregosus, Stephanus Bracellius, Antonius Gallus, Iacobus Furnius, Hieronymus Palmarius, Bartholemæus Iustinianus, Nicolaus Brignalius, Bartholemæus Facius, qui præter alia de rebus ab Alfonso i. Neapolis Rege, gestis libros scripsit xii. Franciscus Marchio, L.C. Sperindeus Palmarius, Aloysius Spinosa, qui de Reip. est commentatus: Dominicus Saulius, & alij. Quid dicam de præstantissimis re militari Ducibus, Lamba, Philippo, Pagano, Luciano, Oberto, Petro, Andrea Magno, Philippino, & aliis, quos vel una domus dedit Auria? Christophorus etiam Columbus Genuensis fuit: qui. Occidentalibus Insulis repertis, Admirantu nomen obtinuit ab Hispaniæ Principibus.
units.tr: Genoa has produced many illustrious men. Among the others were the Roman Pontiffs Innocent V and Hadrian V, from the noble family of the Fieschi, which also gave more than thirty Cardinals and many other prelates, such as archbishops and bishops. From the magnificent Cibo family came Innocent VIII, Supreme Pontiff; from the Fregosi came Paul, together with Frederick; from the Fieschi came Nicholas; from the Sauli family came Bendinelli. All of these were Cardinals. I pass over others of this rank. There were also Genoese men distinguished for learning and writings: Agostino Giustiniani, Bishop of Nebbio, who published a huge volume on the affairs of the Genoese in the vernacular; Giovanni Balbi, author of the vocabulary called the Catholicon; Andalò Nigro; Giacomo Cepa; Giacomo Bracelli, who diligently traced the site and places of this region; Gotardo Stella; Battista Fregoso; Stefano Bracelli; Antonio Gallo; Giacomo Fornari; Girolamo Palmieri; Bartolomeo Giustiniani; Nicolò Brignole; Bartolomeo Facio, who, besides other works on the deeds of Alfonso I, King of Naples, wrote twelve books; Francesco Marchese, a Doctor of Canon Law; Sperindio Palmieri; Luigi Spinola, who wrote a commentary on the commonwealth; Domenico Sauli; and others. What shall I say of the most outstanding military commanders: Lamba, Filippo, Pagano, Luciano, Oberto, Pietro, Andrea the Great, Filippino, and others, whom the single house of the Doria alone produced? Christopher Columbus, too, was a Genoese, who, having discovered the Western Islands, obtained the title of Admiral from the princes of Spain.

units.la: Archiepiscopatus floret dignitate, sub quo sunt Episcopatus Lunensis, Bobiensis, Aprumacensis, vel Brumacensis: Metenensis, vel Maranensis: & alij. Præter Augustinum Iustinianum, & Iacobum Bracellium etiam S.P.Q. Genuensis rerum domi forisque gestarum Historias atque Annales libris xxiii. composuit Petrus Bizarus Sentinas. Vrbis ager, quamvis saxis asper: lætus nihilominus, Vinetis præsertim.
units.tr: The archbishopric flourishes in dignity, and under it are the bishoprics of Luni, Bobbio, Brugnato (or Aprumacensis), Mariana (or Metenensis) and others. Besides Agostino Giustiniani and Giacomo Bracelli, Pietro Bizari Sentinas also composed histories and annals of the deeds of the Genoese Senate and People, both at home and abroad, in twenty-three books. The land around the city, though rough with rocks, is nevertheless fertile, especially for vineyards.

units.la: Hactenus Occidentalis fuit Ora Genuensis: sequitur Orientalis. Egressis Genua occurrunt Nervium, Buliascum, Saulum: Modici vici: moxque Recca (in Itineraria Tabula hoc loco est Recina) & Camolium. Tractus autem littoris ab Genua Camolium usque universus tanta ædificiorum, quæ cum in collibus, tum vallibus exstructa sunt, copia nitet: ut oram navigio legentibus una perpetuaque videatur Civitas.
units.tr: So far has been the western shore of Genoa; the eastern shore follows. Those who leave Genoa come upon Nervi, Bogliasco and Sori, small villages; then soon Recco (in the Itinerary Table it is called Recina in this place) and Camogli. The stretch of coast from Genoa all the way to Camogli shines with such a multitude of buildings, built both on the hills and in the valleys, that to those sailing along the coast the whole thing seems one continuous city.

units.la: Haud procul Sumario Promontorio, cuius antea memini, Portus est Delphini, quem nominant Plinius & Antoninus: hodie Porto Fino.
units.tr: Not far from the Sumario Promontory, which I mentioned earlier, is the Port of Delphinus, which Pliny and Antoninus name; today it is Portofino.

units.la: Sex inde milliaribus paullo ultra Fanum D. Margareta Sinus se pandit Rapallinus, ab Repallo, Vico nobili, dictus. In initimo eius recessu Claverium vel Claverum est, Chiaveri vulgo: Opidum, quod annis ante se natum cl muro cinctum non fuisse, scribit Blondus: Nebiæ Antistes, conditu perhibet ab Genuatibus anno cIↄclxv. Nundinario mercatorum conventu certis anni temporibus ob summam loci opportunitatem frequentatur.
units.tr: Then, about six miles further on, the Gulf of Rapallo opens out past the Church of Santa Margherita, named after Rapallo, a noble village. In its inmost recess is Chiavari, or Chiaveri as it is commonly called, a town which, according to Blondus, had not been surrounded by a wall in the years before it was founded; the Bishop of Nebbio says it was founded by the Genoese in the year 1165. Because of the great convenience of its position it is frequented at certain times of the year by a fair-like gathering of merchants.

units.la: Lavania, Lavagno, vicus est ad fluvium cognominem: cuius in Ripa etiam sunt Ripa Rubra Mulinum que: & juxta fontem Arx casa. Lavania originem attribuunt illustris Familiæ, Genuensis Comitum Flisicorum, qui & Lavania comites. Lavania quibusdam putatur Ἀιζάρια Ptolemæi: male, quum Ἀιζάρια Ptolemæo trans Apenninum
units.tr: Lavagna, or Lavagno, is a village on the river of the same name. On its banks are also Ripa Rossa and Mulino, and near the spring is Arx Casa. Some attribute the origin of Lavagna to the illustrious Family of the Genoese Counts Fieschi, who are also called Counts of Lavagna. Lavagna is thought by some to be the Ptolemaic Aizaria [Ἀιζάρια], wrongly, since Aizaria is placed by Ptolemy beyond the Apennines
